text: Many years ago, the Civil War came to an end. It was a big war in the U.S. between the North and the South. People wanted to remember their fallen soldiers. In May, they decorated the graves with flowers. This was known as Decoration Day.

title: Origins of Memorial Day Part 2
text: In 1968, Congress made a law. They made Memorial Day a holiday. It was a day where people would remember our fallen soldiers.

title: Honoring Our Soldiers
text: On Memorial Day, we honor our soldiers. Some people put flowers on soldiers' graves. Others go to parades. You will see many American flags on Memorial Day.

title: What is Memorial Day?
text: Memorial Day is on the last Monday of May. It is a Day to remember the men and women who died for our country.

title: The Fourth of July
text: Independence Day is also called the Fourth of July. This is because the Declaration of Independence was signed on July 4, 1776. That was more than 200 years ago!

title: Independence Day

title: The Declaration of Independence
text: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence. The Declaration of Independence told Great Britain that America was a free country. It's a document that lists all the rules of America. What do you think Jefferson wrote on this special paper?

title: Columbus' Ships
text: Columbus had three ships. He sailed on them with his crew. They were called the Niña, the Pinta and the Santa María.

title: Columbus Day
text: Americans honor Christopher Columbus on Columbus Day. It is the second Monday of October. Columbus came to America on October 12, 1492.

title: Indigenous Peoples' Day
text: Some people don't want to honor Columbus. Columbus wanted lands and gold. His crew hurt people. Many American Indians died. Some were made slaves. Today, some cities have Indigenous Peoples' Day instead of Columbus Day. It honors American Indians.

title: Who Was Christopher Columbus?
text: Christopher Columbus lived over 500 years ago. He was a famous explorer. He wanted to sail the world with his crew. They sailed to the New World.

text:
The people who are part of the armed forces help us in many ways. They help us on land when there is a fire or a terrible storm. Others help us in the ocean waters. They guard our waters and ship supplies to people in need.

Some people of the armed forces fly airplanes. They provide aid around the world.

title: Armed Forces
text: The armed forces protect our country. They help keep us safe. When a person is in the armed forces, it is their job to protect our country.

title: Veterans Day
text: Veterans are brave people who have served in the armed forces. They are patriots. Patriots are people who love their country.

title: Veterans Day
text: We remember and honor the brave men and women who have served in the armed forces. This holiday is called Veterans Day. It is celebrated on November 11.

text: The Pilgrims and the American Indians had a big feast. They were celebrating the fall harvest. This feast became known as Thanksgiving.

title: Thanksgiving Day

title: The Pilgrims
text: The Pilgrims came to America in 1620. They sailed from England in the Mayflower. They wanted to start a new community. They wanted to be free to worship in their own way.

title: Laws Are Rules for the Community
text:
Laws stay the same everywhere in your community. Speed limits are laws everyone in town must follow. Laws against hurting others are for your whole town. You can't hit other people at home, at school or at your friend's house.

There are city laws, state laws and country laws. City laws must be followed by everyone in town. State laws must be followed by everyone in the state. Country laws must be followed by every citizen.

text:
Rules help keep us safe. Laws also keep us safe.

What is the difference between rules and laws?

title: Rules
text: Rules tell us what we can and can't do. They help to keep us safe. They also help people work together. Think about school rules. They keep kids safe and also make it easier to learn. When you break a school rule, you get in trouble with your teacher.

title: Rules Change from Place to Place
text: Rules often change from place to place. Your parents make rules for you at home. Your teachers make rules for you at school. There may be different rules when you go to a friend's house.

title: Follow the Rules
text: You have a bedtime at home. At school, you have other rules. You must be quiet when the teacher is speaking. It is important to follow the rules to stay safe and respect others.

title: How Can You Be a Good Citizen?
text: How can you be a good citizen? Follow the rules. Obey the laws. Treat others with respect. Be kind and help others. Vote for what is fair in your classroom.

title: Voting
text: What does a good citizen do? A good citizen votes. Voting is how citizens elect (choose) their leaders. The person that gets the most votes wins. This way, the country makes a choice that makes most people happy.

title: Ways to Decide
text: What if your teacher says your class can have 15 minutes of outside recess or 15 minutes of free play inside? How would you decide? You could vote. Voting is a fair way to decide.

title: The Mayor

title: The President

title: Showing Respect
text:
We show respect to our country when we sing the national anthem. We stand up and put our right hand over our heart.

We show love for America when we say the Pledge of Allegiance. We also stand up and put our right hand over our heart. The word "pledge" means "to promise."

title: The Pledge of Allegiance
text: I pledge allegiance to the flag of the United States of America, and to the republic for which it stands, one nation under God, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all."

title: Honor and Respect
text:
Revere is at a baseball game at school. Before the game, they start to sing a song: "Oh, say can you see..."

It's the national anthem, America's very own song. Revere loves America so much, and he loves to show it! When we sing the national anthem, we show that we love America.

title: Showing Allegiance to Our Country
text:
Every country has a national anthem. This is a song for the country. The national anthem in America is called "The Star-Spangled Banner."

Francis Scott Key wrote the song in 1814. He saw the American flag over a fort after the U.S. had won a battle against England. He went home and wrote a poem. Today, this is our national anthem. It shows how thankful he was for his country.

title: What Is a Patriot?
text: The national anthem and The Pledge of Allegiance are two ways to show that we are patriots. What is a patriot? A patriot wants the best for their country. Patriots respect and honor their country. If you love America, then you are a patriot too!

title: The Tennessee State Flag
text: The Tennessee state flag was adopted in 1905. The flag is red, white, and blue. It has three stars in the middle. Some people say the stars stand for the three Presidents from Tennessee. Some people think they show the three parts of Tennessee.

title: Why Is Tennessee Called the Volunteer State?
text: Tennessee has a cool nickname. It's called the Volunteer State. The nickname is over 150 years old. That's a long time! Tennessee got its nickname when many of its people joined the military. They fought in the War of 1812. They fought in the Mexican-American War. A famous man was a Tennessee volunteer. His name was Davy Crockett!

title: More Tennessee Symbols
text:
The state tree of Tennessee is the tulip poplar. The mockingbird is Tennessee’s state bird. It is grey and white. The mockingbird makes sounds like other birds. It can even sound like music!

Did you know Tennessee has an official animal? The state animal is the raccoon.

title: Symbols of Tennessee
text:
Symbols stand for something. Every state has symbols. They have state birds and flowers. Some have state animals!

What is the state flower of Tennessee? It is called the iris. It became the state flower in 1933.

text: Memphis is on the southwest edge of Tennessee. In Memphis you will find a culture that loves blues and rock music.

title: One Big Family
text: Each culture makes the state better. American Indians keep ancient traditions alive. African Americans help create blues music, which is unique to America. The cultures make one big family.

title: Tennessee Cultures
text: Culture is the language, customs, art and ideas of a group of people. Tennessee is a state with many cultures. Each culture brings its own special things. It is the combination of these cultures that makes Tennessee so special.

title: Nashville
text: Nashville sits in the middle of Tennessee. The culture in Nashville loves Southern food and country music. Here you can listen to the oldest radio show in the country, The Grand Ole Opry.

title: A Variety of Cultures
text: Tennessee has many cultures. We have American Indian culture. We also have African American culture. And there are different European American cultures.

The Scotch-Irish are part of our culture. They came to our state many years ago. Their cooks made holes in small cakes. This was to keep bad spirits away. This is where the idea for doughnuts comes from.

title: Chickasaw Culture
text:
The Chickasaw have many ancient traditions. One of them is called the stomp dance. They use turtle shell rattles when they dance.

Another Chickasaw tradition is storytelling. This is when a story is told by someone. They share stories from their people. These are passed down from one generation to the next.

title: African American Culture
text: African Americans are an important part of our culture. They made the blues popular. Bessie Smith was a blues singer. She was born in Tennessee. They called her the Empress of the Blues.

title: Cherokee Culture
text:
The Cherokee still make clothing such as tear dresses and ribbon shirts. They also make beautiful baskets.

The American Indians are part of Tennessee culture.

text: Tennessee has many different cultures. Each of these cultures has its own traditions. Jazz music is an African American tradition. African Americans made this music. People love jazz all over the world. Tennessee has jazz festivals. You can go to a festival and listen to jazz.

title: Family Traditions

title: What Is a Tradition Anyways?
text:
The world has many cultures. Each culture has its own traditions. Traditions help people remember their history. Traditions also remind people what is important in their culture.

American culture has traditions like Thanksgiving. Each culture in America also has its own traditions.

title: Cultural Traditions
text:

St. Patrick's Day is an Irish American tradition. On St. Patrick's Day you wear green and eat corned beef and cabbage.

A tradition of American Indians is to tell stories. The stories help them remember their history. The stories teach important lessons.

title: American Traditions
text:
Americans have many traditions. We celebrate Independence Day on July 4. It reminds us of when the U.S. became a free country.

Thanksgiving is another American tradition. We have a meal with our family and give thanks. It reminds us of the help American Indians gave the first European settlers.

title: Tennessee Cultures Part I
text:
Rev goes to his Grandma. He asks, "Grandma, where did our traditions come from?"

His Grandma asks, "Such as what?"

"Well, we always have oatcakes and shortbread for dessert. Where did that come from?"

"Those recipes are from your Scotch-Irish great-great grandma."

"And you always bring out the deerskin boots."

"Those are from your Chickasaw great-great-great grandpa."

title: Tennessee Cultures Part II
text:
"And now we are going to play mancala. We always play mancala after dinner."

"Mancala is a game that your many-times great grandpa brought from Africa."

"And when I start school next year, you will give me a paper cone full of treats."

"That is a tradition from my German mother."

"Are all of these traditions important?"

"They are all important to me. They are part of who I am."

title: Holiday Traditions
text:
Many families celebrate winter holidays. The Cherokee hold a Winter Festival. They dance and wave tree branches. They eat a big feast.

Many African Americans celebrate Kwanzaa in the winter. Families light a candle each day for seven days. It is a time to remember their African culture. Does your family have a holiday tradition?

title: Families in Tennessee

title: Producers Seeking Consumers
text:
Today, we will talk about goods, services, producers and consumers.

Goods and services are very important. They make up our economy.

Most people are consumers. Some people are also producers. You can even be both!

title: What are Goods and Services?
text:
Goods are things that you can buy. Food, books and video games are all goods. Cars and houses are goods, too! Goods are made by producers. Can you think of other kinds of goods?

Services are things people do for others. The person who fixes cars is doing a service. Barbers, doctors and babysitters provide services. Teachers do a very important service!

title: Are You a Producer or a Consumer?
text:
Consumers are people who pay for goods or services. They can buy many goods and services in their own communities. Some things they need and want come from other communities.

Producers are people who make goods or provide services for consumers. Some producers market (try to get people to buy) and sell their goods and services in their own communities. Producers can send goods to other places, too.

title: Producers Can Be Consumers, Too!
text:
Some people are producers and consumers at the same time. Think about a car wash service. The owners need to pay for water. They also need soap. They provide a service by washing cars. They are consumers of water and soap. They are producers of clean cars.

The baker does a service. He is also a consumer. He needs to buy flour for his cakes. He can bake special cakes that people order.

title: Producer or Consumer?
text: Producers can provide goods or services. Goods are things people buy. Services are things you do for other people. What do you want to be when you grow up? Will you provide goods or services?

title: Let's Go On A Trip!
text: Let’s go around Tennessee to see where some of goods and services come from.

title: A Field Trip Filled With Goods
text:
Ms. Johnson has a box of stuff. "Look at each item and tell me if it is a service or a good."

She takes out a small tractor. "Is this a good or a service?"

Rev says, "It's a service because you use it to farm."

"Right! What about these?" she pulls out a candle and a toy.

Rev's friend says, "Those are goods! You can make and sell them!"

"How about this wheat?"

"I think that's a good," another friend says.

"And this?" Mrs. Johnson takes out a guitar.

"That's a service! You play guitar for people!"

"It could also be a good, because you can make your own guitars!"

"Very good, class!"

title: Let's Draw!
text: Draw a picture of where you would like to go in Tennessee.

title: Music
text: Nashville is the capital of Tennessee. A lot of music is made there.

title: Searching for Needs, Looking for Wants
text: A need is a thing you must have. A want is something that you would like to have.

title: Do You Really Need It?
text:
Revere Wants a New Book

Revere: "Grandma, I need this new book."

Grandma: "Do you need it? A need and a want are different."

Revere: "I think I need it ... "

Grandma: "You want the book."

Revere: "How do I know if it is a want or a need?"

Grandma: "A need is something you must have. You need food. You need water. You do not need the book."

Revere: "I get it! I still want the book."

title: Things You Need
text:
There are many kinds of needs. You need food and water to live. You need clothes to stay warm. You need books and pencils for school.

The things you need are more important than the things you want.

title: Mark the Picture
text: Mark the pictures of things people need.

title: Things You Want
text:
What are your favorite games? What are your favorite toys? Do you have a favorite book?

It is great to get what you want. But if you don't get what you want, you will still be okay.

title: Fill in the Blanks
text:
Word bank: want, food, ice

1. I need ____ when I am hungry.

2. I want ____ cream for lunch.

3. If I don't get what I ____, I will still be okay.

title: What Makes People Save?
text:
You know what Rev would like to get? Rev likes oatmeal and peanut butter. What do you like to buy?

Last year, he saw a candy bar for sale. He really wanted the candy bar. Then he counted his money. He had enough for oatmeal and peanut butter, or candy. He would have no oatmeal for breakfast if he bought the candy. He bought the oatmeal and peanut butter. He made a good choice.

title: Pennies, Dimes and Dollars
text: Revere the Rat is putting money in his piggy bank. Rev has a lot of money from all his work. He likes to think about what he will get with his money. It helps him decide what he will save his money for.

title: Why Save?
text:
What if a good or service costs more money than you have? You can save your money until you have enough.

What would you save your money for? When have you saved money by not buying something?

title: Let's Write
text: Write about a time you saved your money. What did you get with it? What did you have to pass up?

title: Saving Is Important
text: Saving money is very important. People save money to buy things in the future. Many families save money to buy a car or a house. The more something costs, the more you have to work to save enough money to buy it.

title: Math and Money, Part I
text:
Use the pictures to solve the problem.

Carlos wants to buy a teddy bear for his sister’s birthday. The teddy bear costs $3. Carlos has $2. How many more dollars does Carlos need?

Write your answer on a separate piece of paper.

text:
Use the pictures to solve the problems.

yes no

buy the ball now save money to buy the ball

title: Types of Maps
text:
There are many kinds of maps. Road maps like Rev's have drawings of roads to help people with directions.

Political maps show a whole state or country. Cities are usually marked by a star or dot on a political map.

Physical maps show physical features like lakes, rivers, mountains and oceans.

There are even maps of the world. World maps can be flat or can be on a round globe.

title: Take Me to the Beach!
text: People need maps to help them get places. Without maps, people would get lost. Can you help Revere the Rat use a map to find the beach?

title: Directions
text: A compass rose can be found on most maps. This symbol shows the directions north, south, east and west. Complete the compass rose by writing the directions where they belong.

title: Review and Learn
text: What kind of map would you use for directions to another town?

title: Let's Write
text: How could you use a globe to plan a trip? Write a sentence.

title: Map Activity
text: Can you help Rev get back home from the beach? Make a roadmap to help him. Write a sentence to explain your map.

title: Globes
text: Globes can show the continents, countries and bodies of water on Earth. Look at the globe. It shows the continent of North America. A continent is a large area of land. Do you remember that the United States, Canada and Mexico are countries in North America? Find the Caribbean Islands on the globe. They are part of North America, too.

title: Globe Shape
text:
Did you know that a globe helps to accurately see what the Earth is shaped like? Unlike a map, a globe is a 3-D model of the Earth.

The shape of a globe is a sphere. That's the same shape as our planet!

Even though a globe is much smaller than the Earth, the distance and direction on a globe are still accurate when sized down. A globe is just a smaller representation of our amazing planet!

title: Continents and Hemispheres
text:
When you know how the world is split into parts it is easier to learn about new places and new people.

Look at the globes. Identify and locate the four hemispheres (Northern, Southern, Eastern, Western).

Identify and locate the equator and prime meridian.

Identify and locate the North and South Poles.

Identify and locate the seven continents (North America, South America, Africa, Europe, Asia, Austrailia, Antartica).

title: Our World
text:
Did you know our world can be divided into parts? Earth is round like a ball. We call a ball shape a sphere.

Half of a sphere is called a "hemisphere."

If we were to divide Earth in half from top to bottom it would make two halves. We call these halves the Eastern Hemisphere and the Western Hemisphere on a globe.

If we were to divide Earth in half side to side, that would also make two halves. We call these halves the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere on a globe.

title: The Equator and Prime Meridian
text:
The equator goes around the middle of Earth and separates the Northern Hemisphere from the Southern Hemisphere.

The prime meridian separates the Eastern Hemisphere from the Western Hemisphere.

Which hemispheres do you live in?

title: Continents
text:
Our world has seven big land masses known as continents. Can you name any of them? Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America are all continents.

Have you heard of the North Pole? There are two poles on Earth: the North Pole and the South Pole. What do you think the weather would be like there?

title: Dividing Lines
text: Did you know there are two invisible lines that go around Earth? We can't see them but they help us split the world into hemispheres. Can you find these on a globe?

title: Let's Write

title: Where Are We?
text:
Rev is "It"! Ms. Johnson asks him to look at the spot his left hand is touching. She asks what hemisphere and continent he is touching. We can play, too!

If your left hand is on the U.S.A., you are touching the Northern Hemisphere. You are also touching the Western Hemisphere. You are touching the continent of North America.

title: North America
text:
What else is in North America?

The U.S.A., Canada and Mexico are on our continent.

We share a border with Canada to the north and Mexico to the south. What is a border? A border is a line at the edge of a country, state or city.

title: Hot Potato!
text: Rev loves playing hot potato! Ms. Johnson passes a big globe around the class while playing music. When the music stops whoever has the globe is "It." Let's play!

title: Eastern and Western Borders
text:
What is on our eastern and western borders?

To the east, there is the Atlantic Ocean.

To the west, there is the Pacific Ocean.

text:
Our southeastern states are bordered by another body of water. It is the Gulf of Mexico.

text: What is a border? Give an example.

title: Niagara Falls
text: This is the Niagara Falls. It borders the U.S. and Canada. How would you get there? Which way would you go?

title: Physical Maps
text: A physical map has features such as mountains, valleys, lakes and streams. It shows rivers and oceans. It does not show cities and roads. A physical map is full of landforms.

title: Different Maps do Different Things
text: Rev isn't sure if he should use the political map or the physical map to get to his vacation spot. Which map should he use to find the town he is going to?

title: Physical and Political Maps
text: Revere is going on a trip for the weekend outside the state of Tennessee. He has two maps and he is not sure which map is the best to use. Can you help?

title: Which Map?
text: Rev made it to the town. Now he has to cross a lake and hike in the mountains to get to the cabin. Which map will show him where the lake and the mountains are? Lakes and mountains are geographical features, or landforms.

title: Political Maps
text:
A political map has lines that divide countries, states and counties. These are the borders.

There are also roads and cities listed.

A political map is flat and has no features like mountains. It does show large bodies of water such as oceans, large lakes and big rivers.

title: Political Map Activity
text:
Political Map: Draw a red line around Tennessee.

This is a border.

title: Color the Physical Map
text:
Physical Map: To show geography:

Color the state green.

Color the Tennessee and Cumberland rivers blue. You may need to get help from a classroom map.

title: Let's Find Another Place!
text: Sam Houston lived in Tennessee long ago. He was once governor here. He was a teacher, pioneer, soldier and statesman. Since we're traveling, let's visit Sam Houston's schoolhouse. It is the oldest one-room schoolhouse in Tennessee. The schoolhouse is in Maryville. We need to use a political map to find Maryville. Let's look at the map!

title: Let's Use a Physical Map
text:
To find the zoo and Sam Houston's schoolhouse, we use a political map.

Now it's time to use the physical map. Let's find the highest and lowest points in Tennessee.

Clingmans Dome is the highest point. The lowest point is at the Mississippi River.

Can you find these places on the physical map?

title: How close are you to a zoo?
text:
There are zoos in Nashville, Memphis, Knoxville and Chattanooga.

Which of the zoo cities is closest to your town? Maybe you live in one of them!

Make sure to look at the compass rose on the map so you know which direction to go.

Which zoo should you visit? Which direction should you go to get there? Should you go north, south, east or west?

title: How close are you to a zoo?
text:
Here are two maps of Tennessee. There is a political map and a physical map.

You can use them to find places to go in your favorite state.

Let's go to a zoo. Can you help find one?

title: Review and Learn
text:
Answer the questions:

1. What kind of map would you use to find mountains?

2. If you went to the zoo, what direction would you go to get there from your town? Should you go north, south, east or west?

3. What if you went to Clingmans Dome? Which way would you go?

title: Map Legends
text:
Map legends are on political and physical maps. Sometimes legends are called "keys."

Map legends tell you what the symbols on a map mean. These symbols are small pictures that represent something in the real world.

title: Create a Map Legend
text: Create a map legend for your town or city. What symbols should be used for the fire station, parks and ice cream shops? What other kinds of symbols would you like to add to the legend?

title: Lookout Mountain
text: Did you know there is a mountain called Lookout Mountain? You can see seven other states from there. WOW! Would you like to climb to the top of Lookout Mountain? Talk to a friend about how Lookout Mountain got its name.

title: Label the Landforms
text:
Label the types of landforms and water.

Word Bank

mountain, hill, lake, river, plateau, plain

title: Bodies of Water in Tennessee
text:
There are lakes, rivers, streams and creeks in Tennessee. There is Center Hill Lake, Norris Lake, Douglas Lake and Kentucky Lake.

The major rivers are the Tennessee River, Cumberland River, Mississippi River and Duck River. You can swim, boat and fish on the water. Have you explored any of these bodies of water?

title: What makes a mountain a mountain?
text: Tennessee is full of all kinds of landforms and bodies of water. A mountain is the tallest landform. Mountains have sloping sides and ridges. The ridges can be rounded or sharp. Mountains have a high point that is called the summit or peak. A landform is usually called a mountain if it is 1,000 feet tall or higher.

title: Exploring Our State
text: When you are exploring, you may come across these four kinds of landforms. They are mountains, hills, plains and plateaus. Plateaus are flat, high landforms that rise up higher than the land around them. But not always on all four sides. Hills are smaller than mountains. Plains are flat, grassy land with hardly any trees. Tennessee has all of these. Which do you think you would like to explore?

title: Let's Draw
text: Draw a picture of what you think Tennessee looks like from a rocket ship.

title: Water Features
text:
An ocean is a large body of water that takes up most of our planet! There are four oceans in the world. The closest one to us here is the Atlantic Ocean.

An island is a landform surrounded by water from all directions. Have you ever heard of Hawaii? What about Puerto Rico? These are examples of islands!

A peninsula is a piece of land that is part of a mainland and is mostly surrounded by water. You may know Florida as a state but did you know that it is also a peninsula?

title: Reporting Live from the Classroom
text:
It's time for Ms. Johnson's class to teach her what they know about maps and land. She puts the class into groups, one for each part of the U.S.

"I'm Rev and I'll be your news man for today," Rev says. "We live in Tennessee. Let's take a look at the map behind me. Which part of the U.S. is our state in?"

Look at the map and give Rev the right answer.

title: More Regions
text:
The Great Plains is mostly flat. The Great Lakes are here. This region can have really bad snow storms too. The only beaches are on the shores of the lakes.

Columbus, Ohio in the Great Plains has over 800 thousand people living in it. That's almost a million people living in one place!

The Southwest can be dry and hot. It has mountains, deserts, highlands and deep places called basins. One of the most well-known landforms here is the Grand Canyon. It is very deep!

Los Angeles, California is in the Southwest. It has more than four times as many people than Columbus! This region also has Phoenix, Arizona, which houses one and a half million people on its land.

title: Review and Learn
text:
Answer the questions about the U.S. regions.

1. Which region has the highest mountains?

a. Rocky Mountain

b. Great Plains

2. Which region has the biggest lakes?

a. Southwest

b. Great Plains

3. Which region shows lower lands?

a. Southeast

b. Pacific Northwest

4. Which region has a very dry climate?

a. Northeast

b. Southwest

title: U.S. Regions
text:
How are U.S. regions alike and different?

The Southeast is the southern states on the eastern side of the country. They have warm summers and winters that aren't too cold. You can go to the beach or the mountains.

The Northeast is the northern states that are on the east side of the country. They don't have as much good soil for growing things. Their winters are cold.

New York City is the most populated city in the Northeast. There are over 8 million people that live there!

Memphis and Nashville have two of the largest populations in the Southeast Region. The population is small compared to New York City, but 600 thousand people is still a lot!

title: Regional News
text: The U.S. is a big country. Because it's so big, the land is not all the same. Some land is flat as far as the eye can see. Some land has rocks and mountains. Some land has lots of people and some has just a few. Let's learn more about the different parts of our country!

title: Even More Regions
text:
The Rocky Mountain Region is in the West. There are many high mountains and lots of outdoor recreation here.

The Pacific Northwest can be very rainy! There are a few mountains and some big rivers here.

Denver for the Rocky Mountain Region and Seattle for the Pacific Northwest Region have similar population numbers. Though their environment is different, the number of people living here is almost the same.

title: Let's Write
text: You get to visit any region in the country. Where will you go? Why do you want to go there? What will you do when you get there?

title: Tennessee is in the Southeast
text:
The Southeast Region is close to many bodies of water. A lot of people work in the fishing industry. The soil is also very fertile. Farmers grow soybeans, cotton and rice. Did you know that Tennessee is in the Southeast Region? Well, now you know!

In this region, people use the rivers and oceans for transportation. The port of Miami in Florida has a lot of cruise ships that come and go. People call this city the "Cruise Capital of the World."

title: The Ways People Live
text: Did you know the U.S. is divided into regions? Revere is going on a road trip to see them all. He is going to learn how the location of regions affects the way people live. For his road trip, he packed shorts for the warmer regions. He also packed long pants for the cooler regions. He is bringing a coat to the mountains where there might be snow. Sometimes, there's even snow up there in the summer!

title: Let's Write
text:
What regions of the U.S. have you visited?

What time of year did you go?

What clothes did you wear?

title: Track Rev's Trip
text:
Track Rev's trip: Start at Tennessee and draw a line to the states Rev stopped in for each region.

(Florida, New York, Colorado, Utah, Washington, Arizona)

title: Living in the Northeast
text: In the Northeast, the winters are long and cold. The summers are hot and humid. The region is home to many businesses. There are also big cities such as New York City. Because space in New York is hard to find, people live and work in very tall buildings. This allows more people to live there.

title: The Great Plains and the Southwest
text:
The Great Plains Region is known for its extreme weather. People there have really cold and harsh winters. They also have hot and dry summers. What kind of clothes do you think they wear in the winter? And in the summer?

The Southwest Region is home to the vast Grand Canyon. More than 5 million people visit the Grand Canyon in Arizona every year. Have you ever been to the Grand Canyon?

title: Outdoor Adventures! Delicious Seafood!
text:
The Rocky Mountains are a major mountain range. This means that a series of mountains are side by side. People who live there enjoy the outdoor adventures. Some people like to hike in the summer. Others like to ski in the winter. These are popular activites in states like Colorado and Utah.

The states of Washington and Oregon are in the Pacific Northwest. They are near the Pacific Ocean. What kind of food do you think they enjoy there? What jobs do you think the people have there?

Also, due to their rich soil, fruits such as apples and many other crops are grown in Washington.

title: Fun and Games
text: Rev receives a poster from his teacher Ms. Johnson with these Americans' pictures on it. Ms. Johnson asks them to match the people on the left with the items on the right. Can you help Rev? Draw a line from each person on the left to the matching item on the right. One is done for you.

title: Courageous Americans
text:
Neil Armstrong was the first man to walk on the moon. He said, "One small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." He was brave. He opened the door to space exploration!

David Crockett was a great congressman from Tennessee. He explored new lands. He made friends with American Indians. He was the “King of the Wild Frontier.” He helped others have a better life.

Benjamin Franklin learned about electricity by experimenting with lightning. He also helped write and signed the Declaration of Independence.

Martin Luther King, Jr. was a minister who fought for equal rights in the 1960s. He led peaceful protests and gave the famous speech, "I Have a Dream." He said that someday all men and women will be equal.

Rosa Parks was an African American woman who refused to give up her seat on a bus to a white man. After her arrest, many people all over the country protested and asked equal rights for all people.

title: Courageous Americans (Cont'd)
text:
Wilma Rudolph was the first American woman to win three gold medals in a single Olympics. She was very sick as a child and worked hard just to walk again.

Jackie Robinson was the first African American to play in the modern Major League Baseball league. He also fought for equality. He wanted other African Americans to have the right to play in the league.

Sequoyah was a half Cherokee Tennessean silversmith. He created a writing system for the Cherokees so they could read and write.

George Washington was once a farmer. He was also a brave army commander. He became the first President of the United States. He helped create the United States of America!

Courage is doing something difficult, even when you're afraid. When are you courageous?

title: Do you know who I am?
text: Rev is learning about famous people in American history. These people did great things for science, government, sports, human rights and education. Let's learn about these courageous Americans.

title: Showing Courage
text:
Which American did you enjoy learning about the most? _____________

How did this person show great courage? ______________

Finish this sentence: I show courage when I ______________________________.

title: Happy Birthday!
text:
Since we celebrate birthdays every year, ages vary. Some people are really young and some people are really old. You're probably eight or nine years old. There are people who can live up to 100 years old! That's a century! When babies are born, they're aged by weeks or months.

At an animal shelter, which puppy is bigger: the one a few weeks old or the one a few months old?

title: Time Flies
text:
Have you ever heard the saying, "time flies when you're having fun"? Sometimes, time may seem to be going so fast that you can't keep up! Minutes turn to hours and hours to days!

You fill up your days with so many different activities. Homework could take you a couple of hours. Going to camp can take a few days or even a week. The seasons change every three months. Every year, you celebrate your birthday.

title: Plan for the Future
text: You can start planning for the future now. You will continue to get older every year. How old will you be in 10 more years? Where do you think you can be in 10 years?

title: Days and Weeks and Months, Oh My!
text:
There are 7 days in a week.

There are 4 weeks in a month.

There are 12 months in a year.

There are 10 years in a decade.

There are 100 years in a century.

title: Short and Long-Term Goals
text: Oh no! It's been an exciting year so far, but Rev still has so much to do! He needs to do all of his homework, visit the elderly, pet the animals and get ready for his big soccer game before school ends. With Grandma's help, Rev is sure he can do it!

title: Fun & Games
text: A tree in Georgia called Lover's Oak is 900 years old. That is nine centuries old! You will know a tree's age by counting it's dark rings. Count the dark rings of the trees below to know their age.

title: Let's Draw
text: In a decade (10 years), Rev wants to play soccer in college. Draw a picture of what you want to do in 10 years.

title: My Timeline
text:
On the timeline, fill in the blanks with your own answers.

What year were born?

How old are you now?

How old will you be in 10 years?

title: Timelines Measure
text:
A timeline shows many events across a period of time. Some can be measured in days. Others can be measured in months or even years! Some teach us about history. Others can help us reach our goals.

This is what a timeline should look like. The left side is the start of the timeline. Across the line, there are different dates that point to an event. All the way to the right is the final date meaning the end of a timeline. Do you see if the timeline is measured in days, months or years?

title: Timelines
text: We all have goals. What are some of yours? Do you have a way to keep them organized? Timelines can help us keep track of our goals and other things that happen in our lives. Revere knows what his goals are, but needs help organizing them. Let's show him how it's done!

title: Make a Timeline
text: A timeline shows things in the order they happened. Make a timeline of your life. You will need a blank piece of paper and some markers. Ask your parents for three pictures to put on your timeline. Write a sentence about each picture. The timeline below shows you how you could start your timeline.

title: Historic Events
text:
Timelines help us learn about history too! They help us learn about events that happened in the past. These are usually measured in years, decades or centuries. Use the timeline to help you answer the questions.

When did Davy Crockett die?

Which happened first: the first public library opens in Nashville or the state constitution being amended?

How many years after the state constitution was amended was Vanderbilt University founded?

title: Draw a Weekly Timeline
text: Draw a timeline of things you want to accomplish this week. Have an event for at least three different days in the week.

title: Secondary Sources
text: A secondary source is a report of an event by someone who was not there when it happened. These sources take information from primary sources and then tells about the event in their own words. Some examples include textbooks, internet sites and magazine articles.

title: Doing Research
text: Writers and students use primary and secondary resources to learn more about a specific event. Let's say you were doing a report on the flood of 2010 in Tennessee. What would you use? How would you find sources? You can start by searching for articles that were written about the flood. You can go to your local library and search for books. You can try and contact any witnesses of the 2010 flood in Tennessee. You just have to go out and search for it!

title: Questions and Answers
text: List some good primary sources.

title: Primary and Secondary Sources
text:
Rev's friend can't find his soccer ball. He last saw the ball in the gym. Has the ball been stolen or is it just lost? Rev will find out. He is off to the gym where the other kids are practicing.

Rev talks to them about the missing soccer ball. He also remembers that there's video footage of the game. The security team lets Rev know that the ball was kicked over to the other side of the gym and rolled under some bleachers. After hearing that from the security team, Rev runs over and finds the ball there. Rev was able to solve the mystery!

title: Primary Sources
text: A primary source is someone who actually saw or heard what happened. Some examples of primary sources include diaries, news reports from reporters who were there and documents written by witnesses.

title: Library Sources
text: Primary sources can be found in many different places. If you want to find out about an event that happened long ago, the library is your best friend. Ask your librarian to help you find books, diaries and interviews by people who were actually part of the event.

title: Let's Draw
text: Draw a picture of Rev the Detective solving the case.

title: Let's Write
text: Write your own detective story. You can include primary sources and/or secondary sources in your story.

title: How was it written?
text: "The Star-Spangled Banner" was a poem at first, but later put to a famous tune. Key wrote it during a battle in 1814. This battle was part of the War of 1812.

title: The Star-Spangled Banner
text: Our national anthem is the "The Star-Spangled Banner." A national anthem is a song that represents a country. Francis Scott Key wrote "The Star-Spangled Banner" in 1814. In 1931, a law was made to make the song into the national anthem.

title: The Rocket's Red Glare
text: Have you wondered what the words of the song mean? Key saw the sky flashing, "the rocket's red glare, the bombs bursting in air." Since the sky was lit up by the bombs, he could still see the flag. The American flag was there in the morning "by the dawn's early light." This meant that the Americans had not lost the battle.

title: Oh, Say, Can You See...?
text: Revere went to a baseball game last night and heard a song at the beginning of the game. He can't stop thinking about "The Star-Spangled Banner." The song has been stuck in his head. He decides he needs to learn more about it. He will do so during this exciting week!

title: Let's Write
text: Have you ever been to an event where someone sings "The Star-Spangled Banner?" If you have, write about when you heard it. What were you doing? Where were you? How did you feel?

title: The Star-Spangled Banner
text:
O say can you see by the dawn's early light
What so proudly we hailed at the twilight's last gleaming?
Whose broad stripes and bright stars through the perilous fight
O'er the ramparts we watched, were so gallantly streaming?
And the rocket's red glare, the bombs bursting in air
Gave proof through the night that our flag was still there
O say does that star-spangled banner yet wave
O'er the land of the free and the home of the brave?

title: The White House
text:
Did you know that the White House did not always have that name? The White House was not called by that name until President Theodore Roosevelt gave it in 1901!

The White House is a national symbol. George Washington began building it in 1792. John Adams was the first president to live there in 1800. The White House has 135 rooms, 35 bathrooms, and the residence has six levels. U.S. presidents live in the White House.

title: Symbol Treasure Hunt
text: Revere learned about "The Star- Spangled Banner." Now he wants to know more about national symbols. Ms. Johnson is hanging photos of U.S. symbols for the class. Rev finds a map that has a mountain, a house, a lady and a bird on it. Can you help him find the items from the photos in the classroom?

title: American Symbols
text: Every country has national symbols. The U.S. has many symbols. They represent something of value and meaning to our people. Some of our symbols include Mount Rushmore and the Statue of Liberty. Mount Rushmore has four U.S. presidents carved into the side of a mountain. They are George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Abraham Lincoln. The Statue of Liberty was a gift from France to the U.S.

title: Monuments
text: Mount Rushmore is located in Keystone, South Dakota. It took 14 years to carve it and was completed in 1941. The Statue of Liberty has been standing proudly in New York Harbor since 1886.

title: The Bald Eagle
text: Another symbol is the bald eagle. The bald eagle has been an American symbol for more than 200 years. On June 20, 1782, the bald eagle was placed on the Great Seal of the United States. The bald eagle was chosen due to the freedom it represents when it is flying through the skies, its impressive beauty and long life.

title: True or False
text:

True False

2. The Statue of Liberty was a gift from Italy to the U.S.

True False

3. There are five U.S. presidents carved into Mount Rushmore.

True False

4. John Adams was the first president to live in the White House.

True False

5. Our national symbols represent something of value and meaning to our people.

True False

text: Which national symbol have you seen or would like to see?

title: Favorite National Symbol
text:
You helped Rev find and learn about every item on his national treasure hunt. Good job!

Which is your favorite national symbol? Why?

title: The Framers
text: The Constitution was written in 1787. The Framers decided to help the country by creating the Constitution. Your rights are protected by this. This means that our government needs to make sure everyone's rights are respected. We need to respect the rights of all Americans.

title: Fill in the Blanks
text:
Fill in the Blanks

The men who wrote the Constitution were called the ___________.

The Amendments to the Constitution protect the ______________ and _____________ of all Americans.

title: Laws
text: Every country needs laws. Laws help us live peacefully with our neighbors. The U.S. Constitution is the law of our country. It says how our government works. Our government is made up of three powers. Each power is important for our country to do well. The executive power is run by the president. The legislative power is run by Congress. The judiciary power is run by the Supreme Court.

title: Constitutions are Critical
text:
Rev just woke up from a terrible nightmare! In his dream, everyone in the United States did what they wanted without respecting each other's rights! Rev rushes to his computer to make sure the U.S. Constitution is still there.

"Yes!" says Rev. "It starts with 'We the People.'"

text:

title: The Constitution
text: The Constitution lists all American rights. Your rights provide you with freedom. Freedom is a gift for you to pursue your own happiness. The U.S. Constitution belongs to all of us!

title: The Bill of Rights
text: After passing the Constitution, the Framers added the Bill of Rights. This document has the first ten changes to the Constitution. These changes are also called amendments. These amendments protect the rights and freedoms of all Americans.

title: Tennessee Has a Constitution, Too!
text: Rev loves the monkey bars. He can climb all the way across by himself. While crossing the monkey bars, he hears his teacher tell one of his friends that Tennessee has its own constitution. "These are rules that everyone who lives in this state has to follow," Ms. Johnson says. Rev races over to her. He's ready to learn more about this!

title: Share What You've Learned!
text: Did you have fun learning from the playground example? Making rules for your own state is fun. You learned why every state needs it's own constitution. The state laws rule over each state to make sure everything goes well. No one got hurt on the monkey bars, and everyone took turns. Now you can share what you've learned with your family and friends.

title: How does it work?
text: All 50 states have a state constitution. This document tells people what they can and cannot do in the state. It is long with many rules. These rules cannot go against what the U.S. Constitution says. It works hand in hand with it.

title: State Constitutions
text: States have their own constitution. This means that each state makes its own rules. Let's use a playground as an example. Pretend that each part of the playground is a state. The states are Swings, Slides, Monkey Bars, Sand Box, Ball and Jump Rope. Each one of you can represent one state. You will get to make rules for the people who come to your state. But remember, your rules must be fair.

title: Word Search
text:
Word Search

Find these 5 words in the puzzle below:

• Rules

• Law

• State

• Free

• Rights

title: We Are Protected
text: Every state can have its own rules. The rules are made by the state's legislative power. However, these rules cannot go against the U.S. Constitution. The U.S. Constitution is the highest law of our country. As citizens, we are protected by both. It's our duty to respect and follow the rules of both.

title: Let's Draw
text: Rev was over Monkey Bar State. If you were in his class, draw the playground state you wish Ms. Johnson would put you over. What is one rule for your playground state?

title: Government Branches
text: Rev built a clubhouse for him and his friends. He invites his friends to come over, but they just can't seem to get along. They decide they need to have their own government. They think they can solve their own problems. Let's learn how you can help them create a government for their clubhouse.

title: The Constitution, Part I
text:
The Constitution lists the basic laws of our country. The Constitution says that a government needs to be formed. The U.S. government has three branches. You can think of these branches as being essential parts of a strong tree. Each branch has its own functions.

The three branches are the executive, the legislative and the judiciary. Their mission is to provide security and to protect the rights and freedoms of all Americans.

title: Fill in the Blanks
text:
Fill in the Blanks

1. The President is part of the ____________ branch.

2. The Supreme Court is part of the ___________ branch.

3. Congress is part of the _________ branch.

4. The ______ and the ______ are the two parts of Congress.

title: The Judicial Branch
text: Another branch of our government is the judicial branch. This branch includes the Supreme Court and other federal courts. The Supreme Court has nine judges called justices. Their motto is “Equal Justice Under Law.” All courts must obey the decisions made by them. They also make sure the president is following the Constitution. They set laws that are fair to everyone.

title: Checks and Balances
text:
What is the system of checks and balances?

Each of the three branches of our government keeps track of the other branches. Each branch makes sure that things are running as the Constitution says they should. Each branch has certain powers. They must operate from a fair and legal stand. The power of government is balanced with each other as the branches check on each other.

title: The Leaders of Our Country
text:
The executive branch is formed by the president, the vice president and the Cabinet. The Cabinet is a group of people who help the president do their job. They are the leaders of our country. The executive branch's job is to carry out the laws of the country.

Next, there is the legislative branch. This branch includes senators and representatives. Its job is to make laws that meet the needs of the people.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you and your friends have your own clubhouse and need a government. What branch would you want to represent? Why?

title: The Constitution, Part II
text: This is the U.S. Constitution. Why do you think this document is important to our country?

title: Don't Run with Scissors!
text:
You may have heard the phrase, "Don't run with scissors!"

What do you think this means?

Let's take a look at the meaning of laws in our society. Laws are made by the leaders of our country. Some are nationwide and some are local. The purpose of these laws is to protect us. Laws are also made to keep things in order. When we know the law and decide not to follow it, there are consequences.

So don't run with scissors in your hand!

title: The Laws Protect Us
text: Congress is responsible for making and passing laws in our nation. As citizens, it's our duty to live by the laws of our country. What do you think could happen if someone runs through the red light? They might cause an accident and get hurt. They also might get a ticket. That's why it's important to always think before you act. Remember, the laws are made for your own protection and safety.

title: Decisions and Consequences!
text:
Consequences are the results of our decisions. There are good and bad consequences.

Let's say someone is late for work. Because they are late, they decide to speed up when driving. The cop nearby catches up and pulls them over. Now, they have to pay for a speeding ticket. This was a bad consequence because of a bad decision.

Rules protect us. Does your teacher have rules for your classroom? If so, what are they? How do they help you?

title: Need for Speed!
text: Rev likes to drive his car whenever he can, and he likes to go really fast! One day when he was driving his car to see his friend, a police officer pulled him over. "Sir," they said, "Did you know you were going 10 miles over the speed limit?" Rev had seen the signs that said to go 55 mph but he just felt like going faster. Now he will have to pay the consequences.

title: Fun and Games
text:
Play a game with your friends. Think about how the game would go if there were no rules to follow.

Pretend you are the mayor of your city. What laws would you make to keep the people safe?

title: Discrimination
text: There are laws against discrimination. Discrimination is when you are not being treated fairly by others because people think you're different. In our country, the law protects us from this at work. Suppose someone has applied for a job. Then, they are denied the job because of their skin color, religion or gender. This is wrong and should not happen. It is punishable by law. Everyone in our country should enjoy fair treatment and equality.

title: ABC Order
text:
Put these words in ABC order.

Laws

Rules

Consequences

Obey

Safety

title: Making Laws
text: Congress meets together to make laws. Why is it important to have laws in our country?

title: Rights are Freedoms in America!
text:
Every citizen of our country has rights. These rights are protected by our laws.

The Bill of Rights contain 10 rights or freedoms from the Constitution. Some of these freedoms are: freedom of speech, religion, press, assembly and petition.

title: Responsible U.S. Citizens
text: Revere will pay close attention to today's lesson. Ms. Johnson will teach about rights and responsibilities. Rev knows that it's important to learn about them to do well in life and in school. He has heard great stories of our armed forces who protect our country. Rev is excited to learn what he can do to be a better citizen.

title: Fun and Games
text: List two responsibilities at school and the good consequences that come from them.

title: Being Responsible
text: We have responsibilities at home and at school. Being responsible means doing your homework on time. It also means doing your chores at home.

title: Let's Draw
text: Draw Rev casting a vote in a state election in Tennessee.

title: Let's Write
text: What right is the most important to you?

title: Voting is a Right
text:
In the United States, voting is a right. When you turn 18 years old, you can vote.

Every child in our country has the right to go to school. If you attend school, you are preparing yourself for a great future.

title: Other Ways to be Responsible
text:
You are a responsible citizen when you throw your trash away in a trash can. This helps keep your community clean. Another way to be responsible is to recycle. These items can be made into other things.

What are some other ways of being responsible?

title: You Have the Right to Vote!
text:
Voting is citizens choosing their government leaders. In the U.S. we can vote for our local, state and national leaders.

Not all Americans could vote in the past. After a long wait, both African American and women were given the right to vote.

Today, all U.S. citizens of age have the right to vote!

title: Voting is a Right in America!
text:
In order to vote, one must be a U.S. citizen. One must be at least 18 years old. Voting is private. This means that nobody can see who or what someone is voting for.

There are countries where people have to vote or they would get in trouble. In the United States, a person is not required to vote.

title: Voting Rights
text: Rev has his great-grandma's diary. Rev wishes he could have met her, but she comes alive through her words. He puts on a song and reads an entry from August 19th, 1920: the day women got the right to vote!

title: Let's Write
text:
Answer the following question.

Why do we vote in the United States?

title: Women's Right to Vote!
text: At first, women were not allowed to vote in our country. Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton believed they can help change the law. They worked together going around the country to get more help. After years of trying, the law was changed. Women were finally given the right to vote in 1920.

title: Where do people go to vote?
text: On election day, people can go to public buildings to vote. These are schools, recreation centers and other public facilities. Although the vote is private, the locations are not. This makes it easy for people to find where they can vote so that they can do their civic duty.

title: Let's Draw
text: Draw Rev's Grandma casting a vote.

title: True or False
text:
Write T for a true sentence and F for a false sentence.

1. All U.S. citizens were allowed to vote since 1776. __________

2. In our country, you don't have to be a U.S. citizen to vote. __________

3. In the United States, voting is voluntary. __________

title: Naturalization
text: Immigrants can become U.S. citizens by naturalization. It is a list of the things they must do to become citizens. They need to be at least 18 years old. They need to know English. They need to pass a test about U.S. history. They must also promise to obey the laws and be loyal to the country. Once these things are done, they can enjoy all the rights and freedoms of being a U.S. citizen!

title: Fill in the Blanks
text:

title: How to Become an American
text: Rev is reading his great-grandmother's diary. He learns that her parents came from Scotland on a ship. When they arrived, his great-grandmother was born. That made her a citizen of the United States. Her parents worked hard to become citizens. Rev is curious. What do people have to do to become U.S. citizens?

title: U.S. Citizenship
text: Most people who live in our country are U.S. citizens. Some people who live in our country are immigrants. They hope to become U.S. citizens someday.

title: Let's Write
text:
Answer the following question.

What are some ways you can become a citizen of the United States?

title: How do people become citizens?
text: If you are born in the United States, you are a U.S. citizen. If your parents are citizens, you are a citizen no matter where you were born.

title: Fairness for All
text:
Have you been treated unfairly? Do you remember how it felt?

Everyone wants to be treated fairly. We all deserve to be treated with respect. In our country, democracy means we all have the same rights. We get a fair chance to tell our side of a story.

If you are being treated unfairly, what should you do? You can talk to an adult you trust and ask for help.

title: Fun and Games
text: Look at the picture and write the first letter of each picture on the line. Write the secret word you found on the bottom.

title: What is democracy?
text:
Democracy means a government run by the people.

We can vote for our leaders in our country. Our leaders can help us have equal rights. They can make sure we are treated fairly. We can follow the golden rule by respecting each other's rights.

In a democracy, we care for other people. We let them take care of their own things. We respect their property.

title: Practicing Democracy
text: When Rev has friends over, his friends have to follow the rules of the house. When they follow the rules, it shows respect for the home.

title: Equality for All
text: Equality means that everyone is equal. It does not mean that everyone is the same. We should all have the same opportunities. No matter what we look like, where we live or what background we come from.

title: The Golden Rule
text:
Have you heard of the golden rule? It means that you should treat others the way you want to be treated.

Before you do or say anything that you are not sure is right, stop and think. Ask yourself, "Would I want to be treated that way?" If the answer is "no," don't do it.

title: Unscramble the Words
text:

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend a new boy comes to your class. He is from a different country, and he is still learning to speak English. At recess, some kids make fun of the way he talks. What would you do? How could you show respect?

title: Do you know where you’re from?
text: Rev has a lot of friends in his classroom and in his community. Most of his friends are American, but they are from different cultural backgrounds. Do you know where your family came from before they moved to America?

title: The American Dream!
text: The United States is home to people from different countries. They left their home to become Americans. They brought their culture, customs and traditions with them. Do you know where your parents and grandparents came from?

title: African Americans in Tennessee
text: There is a large number of African Americans in our state. Tennessee is an important state in the Civil Rights Movement. You could go visit the National Civil Rights Museum in Memphis with your family!

title: What is culture?
text:
Culture is all the beliefs, traditions and features of a group of people. This includes its food, clothing, music, beliefs, language and much, much more.

There are different cultures that helped shape the U.S. over time. This includes the American Indian and Latin American cultures, just to name a few. Feel free to learn more about the many other cultures in our country.

title: Diversity in Tennessee
text:
Diversity can be found in Nashville, Tennessee. The Filipinos and the Kurds now live there. Filipinos come from Southeast Asia. Kurds come from the Middle East in countries like Iraq and Iran. Kurds love to play soccer. Filipinos are big fans of basketball!

The Filipinos take a whole day to celebrate flowers! They have a parade with people dressing up in colorful costumes to show gratitude for the growing season.

The Persian New Year (or Nowruz) is a major holiday in the Kurdish culture. It starts on the first day of Spring. This holiday lasts for 13 days! They prepare by cleaning the house and planting new flowers. Once the day arrives, the real party begins! They take the time to reflect on the old year and start something new for the next year.

title: Activity Page
text:
Circle the items that are part of the Filipino culture.

Box the items that are part of the Kurdish culture.

title: Cultures in Our Backyard
text: A culture means a way of life. Your language, food, beliefs and customs make up your culture. You probably have had food that was from another culture. Have you ever had a taco or a pizza? It is fun to learn about other cultures. It is fun to share our culture, too!

title: India
text:
In India, many religions are practiced. Many people from this country practice Hinduism. Hindus believe in many gods. They also believe in karma. Karma is the idea that your actions cause what happens to you in the future.

If you're Christian, Muslim or Jewish, you believe in one God.

title: China
text: Have you ever burped out loud after a good dinner? Did someone tell you to mind your manners? In China, burping out loud after eating is considered good manners. It is a compliment to the cook.

title: Mexico
text: Have you ever heard of a "Sweet 16" birthday party? In Latin America, your 15th birthday is the special day. In Mexico, it is the day of your quinceañera. This is a celebration of you becoming an adult. During this day, there are many ceremonies. During what they call the Change of Shoes ceremony, a family member gives you your first pair of high heels!

title: Ireland
text: Have you worn green or a shamrock (a plant with three leaves) on St. Patrick’s Day? Then you are following an Irish tradition. The color green is for Ireland’s nickname, the Emerald Isle. The shamrock is for good luck.

title: Draw a Picture
text: When you greet someone in India, you put your hands together, bow and say “namaste.” Draw a picture of how you greet someone in your culture.

title: Fill in the Blanks
text:
Word Bank: karma, culture, China, shamrock

Language, food, beliefs and customs make up your _______________.

__________ is the idea that your actions cause what happens to you in the future.

A _____________ is a plant with three leaves.

Burping after a meal is considered good manners in ____________.

title: Cultures and Traditions
text:
Long ago, only American Indians lived in America. Then settlers came from Spain, France and England. Next, slaves were brought from Africa. Today, many people from different places live here. Our country is like a "melting pot" of many cultures.

Culture is all the traditions, principles and goals of a group of people. It is food, clothing, celebrations, beliefs, music and much more.

title: Halloween
text: Do you like to dress up for Halloween? This spooky holiday comes from Ireland and Scotland. In the 1800s, many Irish and Scottish people came to America. Every year on October 31st, they wore costumes, played games and held festivals. Today, we celebrate Halloween in similar ways.

title: Independence Day
text: In America, we celebrate Independence Day every July 4th. This day marked when America became a free nation from England in 1776. Other countries celebrate their own day of freedom, too! Ghana (a country in Africa) observes their day on March 6th. They light fireworks and watch parades.

title: Principles and Goals
text: Just like traditions, countries also share principles and goals. A principle is a guiding set of beliefs. A goal is an overall result that a person or a group of people wants to achieve.

title: American Principles
text: In America, we believe in the right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness for all. This is a principle we share in our country. The U.S. Constitution states principles and goals we have as a nation. Other countries share similar principles and goals, too.

title: South Korea
text: Freedom of religion is a right in South Korea. This means all people can believe in any faith they choose.

title: Germany
text: In Germany, all genders and races are treated equally. They also believe in the freedom of expression. This means all people can have their own opinions and ideas.

title: Chile
text: The right to an education is a right and also a goal. In Chile, a country in Latin America, the freedom to learn is important. Chile provides free education to children between six and 21 years old.

title: Draw a Picture
text: Do you set goals for yourself? Draw a picture of a goal you would like to reach one day.

title: Matching Game
text:
Match the country to one of its traditions or principles.

Ireland Ghana South Korea Chile

title: Write a Sentence
text: Is there a principle you share with others at your school? Write a sentence about one principle.

title: Think and Review
text:
Answer the following questions.

1. As a consumer, what things does your family normally purchase?

2. As a producer, what things could you make for other people to buy?

3. Why do producers need consumers? Why do consumers need producers?

title: Lemonade Stand
text: Let's say you set up a lemonade stand. You do this on the weekends. You start making lemonade to sell to your neighbors. People start buying lots of lemonade from you. Over time, your lemonade stand is a success! Now, can you tell who's a producer and who's a consumer?

title: We Need Each Other!
text: Producers create goods and provide services to make money. American farmers grow food like corn. They sell these things to consumers. Consumers need these things to live. Stores buy the corn from the farmer. Your family buys the corn at the store. They pay money for them. Producers need money to keep making products. Consumers need goods and services. We need each other to exist!

title: Business Shoppers
text: Ms. Johnson tells her class of two important groups of people. These are producers and consumers. She has the class pretend they have a business that sells things to other classmates. Rev listens and is ready to play the game!

title: Producer and Consumer
text:
A consumer is someone who buys goods and services. You, your parents or anyone who buys things is a consumer. In America, we consume movies, popcorn and soda all of the time! Some American stores buy things made in China. Companies can buy things from all over the world. This makes our country a consumer, too!

A producer is someone who creates or makes goods. For example, goods can be food, clothes and cars. Did you know Crayola Crayons are produced right here in the U.S.? Walmart and McDonald’s are American producers as well.

Are you a consumer or a producer? Can you be both?

title: Let's Draw
text: When you buy pizza, you're a consumer. Draw your favorite pizza to eat!

title: Goods Producers
text: The food we eat comes from crops. Farm workers prepare the soil and plant the seeds. They harvest the crops and pack them for shipping. This is called agriculture.

title: Service Providers
text: An airport provides transportation. Airport workers have many jobs. Some sell tickets. Some move luggage to the planes. Pilots and flight attendants make sure people have a safe flight. Other workers serve food in the airport.

title: Touring U.S. Industries
text: Rev is so excited! He will tour different industries this week. They provide many kinds of goods and services. We will learn about the agriculture, manufacturing, tourism and transportation industries.

title: Let's Write
text: This week you have learned what goods and services are. In a paragraph, explain the difference between goods and services. Check your sentences for correct spelling, capitalization and punctuation.

title: Car Factory
text: A car factory is an example of manufacturing. Each person does a small part of the job. Some workers design the car. Others put together its parts. They paint it or give it a test drive.

title: The Construction Industry
text: The construction industry builds things. Workers build bridges. Bridges help us cross over things like rivers, railroad tracks and other roads. Workers who design bridges are engineers.

title: The Tourism Industry
text: The Dollywood theme park in Tennessee is in the tourism industry. Some workers sell tickets or work as cashiers. Some work the hotel front desk or clean guest rooms. Others work in the gift shop. Workers make sure guests have a great vacation.

title: People Depend on Each Other
text: People around the world depend on each other. The United States does not produce everything our citizens need and want. We get goods from other countries. We send goods to other countries too.

title: Going, Going, Gone!
text: Rev can't wait to see the solar eclipse. This is when the sun and moon cross each other in the sky at the same time. It is only a few days away. You have to wear special glasses to watch this. The glasses keep your eyes safe, and they only cost $1. But the next day when Rev looks at the price, the glasses have gone up to $2. And on the third day, the glasses go up to $3. Why does the cost of the glasses keep going up? Let's find out!

title: Want some apples?
text: Do you like apples and apple juice? Imagine that the weather this year is great for growing apples. The people who grow apples will have lots and lots of apples to sell. The supply of apples will be high, so the price will go down.

title: Right Clothes, Wrong Weather!
text: Have you ever seen a swim suit in a store at winter time? No! Who wears swim suits when it's cold outside? If you do find one of these in a store, it will be on sale. The cost will be low because nobody wants it. It's too cold for it. The cost will be higher in the summer. It's hot and everybody wants it!

title: Supply and Demand
text: The price of a resource (something people can use) depends on two things. It depends on how much of it there is for people to buy. That's called "supply." It also depends on how many people want or need that resource. That's called "demand." When the supply is low and the demand is high, the price goes up. When the supply is high and the demand is low, the price goes down. That's why the price of Rev's glasses kept going up! The supply was low but the demand was getting higher.

title: Fun and Games
text:
It's wintertime. Look at the swimsuits below. Why are the prices so low?

It's summertime. Look at the swimsuits below. Why are the prices so high?

title: Think and Review
text:
Answer the following questions.

1. What is supply?

2. What is demand?

title: Buying Fruits and Vegetables in the Winter?
text: Why is it difficult to buy certain fruits and vegetables during the winter time?

title: The Fruits and Vegetables Highway
text: Revere loves going grocery shopping with his Grandma. He knows that fruits and vegetables come from his state. Some goods come from other places. Tennessee sends their goods to other places too. Let's find out more about where some goods come from and where they go!

title: Tennessee Exports
text: Exporting is a good thing in our state. We send goods to countries like China and Japan. Some of these items are vehicle parts and computers. When we send goods to other places, our state grows. When we export more goods than we import, our economy does better. We make more money than we spend. Do you see how this is good for us?

title: Exporting and Importing
text:
People all over the United States and around the world depend on each other for many things. The U.S. sends airplanes, cotton and other things to other countries. This is called exporting.

In the same way, people in the U.S. buy things like cars, clothes and coffee. These items come from other countries. This is called importing.

title: Fun and Games
text:
Name an item the U.S. imports. Name an item the U.S. exports.

1.

2.

title: The U.S. Imports and Exports
text: Imports are things our country buys and brings in from other countries. Exports are things our country sells and sends out to other countries. Major U.S. imports include oil, machines and electronics. The U.S. exports these same products to other countries as well.

title: Let's Draw
text: Draw two items that Tennessee exports to other countries.

title: Define the Terms
text:
Define the following terms in your own words.

Importing

Exporting

text:

title: Trading
text: How does trade work? Trade helps countries get the things they need. People can exchange money or goods for the things they need. For example, a country grows more vegetables than they need. They can sell them to other countries in exchange for money. It's that easy!

title: Imports and Exports
text: Ms. Johnson's class is baking today. Rev is part of Team Cookie Bakers. There is Team Muffin Bakers too. The Sugar Cookie team is busy getting all of their ingredients out and making their cookies. But Rev's team has a problem! They have no chocolate chips to make their cookies. They have to make them today. They must use what is in the classroom. Oh, wait! Team Muffin Bakers has chocolate chips but they have no sugar. Can the teams work this out? Can a trade be made so everything is done on time?

title: Meeting the Needs of People!
text:
The U.S.A. can meet the needs of its people through imports and exports. Imports and exports create new jobs. Some things can be made more easily here than in other countries. This helps the people here.

If we need something we don't have, we can always import it from a place that does have it. That way we get what we need.

title: It Benefits Everyone!
text: What if a country needed cookies we make in the United States? Maybe they don't have everything they need to make the cookies. The U.S. could sell them the finished cookies and export them to that country. The country can also say that they will trade them muffins for their cookies. The U.S. could import the muffins. When countries trade like this it benefits everyone. Each place gets what it needs.
