title: Language Arts Connection
text: As you read this week’s cover story, circle or highlight all of the adjectives in yellow and all of the adverbs in green. (CC ELA L.3.1)

title: Bellefonte: The “Beautiful Fountain”
text: During the late 1700s, the French Prince Talleyrand made a visit to Pennsylvania. When the settlers in this area showed the famous Frenchman Big Spring, a huge natural spring, he exclaimed, "La belle font!" In French, this means, "The beautiful fountain." The townspeople decided that "Bellefonte" was the perfect name for their village. About 6,000 people live in the town of Bellefonte today. Bellefonte is a beautiful town in the mountains in about the middle of our state. William Lamb first settled the spot in 1785. He built a flour mill just downstream from Big Spring, using the water from the spring to turn the millstones to grind wheat into flour. In 1794, William sold the mill, the spring, and 800 acres of land to James Dunlop. James and his son-in-law, James Harris, planned out the village that is now Bellefonte, and settlers soon began moving to the pretty little town. Today, Bellefonte has some of the best examples of restored Victorian-style homes in the United States. On a visit to Bellefonte, you will see former governors' mansions, a restored 19th-century train station (where you can hop on the train and take a ride through the countryside), Big Spring (that pumps as much as 13 million gallons of water a day) and beautiful Talleyrand Park.

title: Ancient Stone Tools Help Archaeologists Learn About the Earliest People in North America
text:
How do we learn about ancient peoples in the Americas? There is no time machine we can use to go back and see how they lived. Instead, we learn about how people lived in the past through clues left in the present. Sometimes ancient peoples left clues about how they saw the world in stories passed down to their descendants. They also left behind creations we still use. For example, corn only exists because of ancient American people who bred grasses into a new crop. We can also learn about ancient people through objects they made. Scientists called archeologists search for ancient objects, buildings, or even garbage heaps to learn about how people lived in the past.

Unfortunately, many of the clues disappear over time. Weather often wears away wood tools and buildings. Food decomposes. Clothing usually falls apart. Because stone wears away more slowly, stone clues are easier to find.

Studying stone tools has helped archeologists create theories about ancient Americans. Stone tools over 15,000 years old have been found in North and South America. These tools show people have lived on both continents since before the first cities in the world began. While there are still many questions about how they lived, the careful craftsmanship on their tools shows that ancient Americans used their ingenuity to survive. These early peoples prepared the way for hundreds of nations that developed later all across the Americas.

title: Studying History
text:
When it's time to study social studies each day, do you wonder why you have to spend so much time learning about things that happened many years ago? Studying history helps us to understand the things that are happening in our world every day. Studying history can also keep us from making some of the same mistakes that others before us have made.

Why is It Important to Study History?

History is the study of our past. It is important to study history to understand things that happened long ago. If we know what happened before, and why it happened, we can see how these events brought us to where we are today. As we study history, we learn what people and places were like before we were born. We see how these people and places changed from what they were once like into what we know today.

If we learn about the mistakes that others have made in the past, we can avoid making bad decisions in the future. For example, when we see the way the American Indians were treated by the early settlers, we are able to see the mistakes that were made, and we can learn to treat others fairly. As poet and author George Santayana once said, "Those who do not remember the past are condemned to repeat it."

Eras of History

To make it easier for us to keep track of when different things happened, history has been divided into eras, or periods of time. If we know when different events took place, we can understand how all these events fit together.

When we know that Columbus began the exploration of America during the Era of Exploration, for example, we understand that others were also exploring the earth at the same time.

Once people came to live in America, a new era called the Era of Colonization and Settlement began. To colonize an area means to settle it, or to build towns and cities. If we talk about things that happened during the Era of Colonization, we can see that these events will probably have a lot to do with building houses, getting along with the American Indians, planting crops and making new governments.

By dividing history into eras, it makes it easier for us to understand why things happened as they did and what made people act in certain ways.

Besides dividing history into eras, we also use special words to help us understand when things happened. These special words tell us if something happened millions, thousands, hundreds or even 10 years ago. These words can even help us talk about things that are happening right now!

Prehistoric

When we say that something is "prehistoric," we mean that it was around before people started writing history down. Dinosaurs lived in prehistoric times, which means either that no people were here to write about them or that those who were here didn’t know how to write. "Pre" means "before," so "prehistoric" means "before history."

Ancient

"Ancient" means "very old," so when we say that something happened during ancient times, we know that it happened long ago. Many people use the word "ancient" to talk about history before the year A.D. 500.

Modern

The word "modern" is used to talk about things that have happened in the more recent past. Modern history talks about things that happened and people that lived several hundred years ago up to the present.

Contemporary

"Contemporary" means "living or happening at about the same time." You and your friends are contemporaries, which means that you live at the same time. Explorer Henry Hudson and Pocahontas were contemporaries, too, even if they didn't know each other, because they lived at the same time.

Circa

We use the word "circa" when we don’t know exactly when something happened. "Circa" means "on or about a certain date." If we know that Betsy Ross made one of the first American flags, but we don’t know exactly when she sewed it, we can say that Betsy Ross made the flag circa (or about) 1776.

title: Liverpool, England
text:
Liverpool is found on the River Mersey in western England, near the Irish Sea. During the 1700s, the shipping port at Liverpool was very busy. Ships from Liverpool also carried goods all over the world. Ships from Liverpool even carried slaves from Africa to the West Indies and North America.

When factories first started using machines to create things that people used to make by hand, Liverpool was at the heart of this new way of doing things. People came from all over England to get jobs in the new factories. They also found jobs working in the shipyards, helping to send the products made here to places all over the world.

During the 1800s, business was booming in Liverpool, and the city grew quickly. When World War II started, however, many German airplanes bombed the docks at Liverpool, damaging or destroying them. Many of the docks were rebuilt, but because of changes in the way shipping is done, Liverpool never became the great shipping city that it once was. Many people have lost their jobs, and unemployment is a big problem here. The way business is done has changed and so has the city of Liverpool. By studying the history of Liverpool, we can see how things that happened in the past made the city what it is today.

title: Henry Heinz
text:
Henry Heinz grew up in Sharpsburg, Pennsylvania, where his family had a nice garden spot next to the house. Henry loved to grow vegetables in the family garden. He also liked to make money. By the time he was 12 years old, Henry was selling fresh vegetables to the neighbors. He learned that if he had good, fresh vegetables to sell, people would buy them. If the vegetables were old or tasted bad, no one bought them. He tried hard to give his customers, or people who bought his products, the best vegetables possible. When he got older, Henry started a business making and selling horseradish. Horseradish is a spicy, hot sauce made from the horseradish root.

Many other companies at the time used poor ingredients in their sauces and put them in colored bottles so that people couldn't see how bad the sauces were. Henry put his horseradish in clear bottles to show everyone the good quality of his sauce. People liked the idea, and Henry soon started selling pickles, vinegar and sauerkraut as well. Soon the H. J. Heinz Company began making tomato ketchup, pepper sauces, olives, pickled cauliflower, pickled onions, mustard, baked beans and even soup. Even though Henry died in 1919, the H. J. Heinz Company is still known for making some of the best-tasting foods around!

title: The Ballpoint Pen
text:
When the Pilgrims wrote about their lives in America, they didn't have pens like those that we use today. They used pens made from feathers dipped in ink.

Later, people used fountain pens. These pens were messy and ran out of ink often, and their scratchy points made holes in the paper. Many people tried to make a pen that had its own ink stored inside, but the ink in these pens either clogged or leaked out all over.

In 1938, Ladislo and Georg Biro, two brothers from Hungary, came up with an idea to make the ink in a ballpoint pen flow more smoothly. They created a special rough ball at the end of the pen that worked like a sponge, sucking the ink into the point when someone wrote with it.

Other companies, like Papermate and Bic, improved the ballpoint pen and sold it for a price that everyone could afford. Today, most of us write with ballpoint pens, which are cheap, clean and easy to carry.

title: Pocahontas Saves Jamestown
text: Pocahontas, whose American Indian name was Matoaka, was the favorite daughter of Powhatan, a powerful chief of the Virginia Confederacy of Tribes. Captain John Smith, the leader of America's first English colony, wrote in his journal that Pocahontas saved his life. He had been captured by her father's warriors and was to be killed. Pocahontas also brought food to the people of Jamestown at times when they were starving. Pocahontas converted to Christianity and married John Rolfe, an English tobacco planter, who took her to England. "To convert" means "to join another religion." This marriage was the first alliance, or friendship, between the American Indians and the English settlers. Powhatan was happy about his daughter marrying an Englishman, and the king of England breathed much easier knowing he had a powerful ally (friend) such as Powhatan. Many English settlers moved to America because this marriage helped the English and the American Indians get along better. Pocahontas later moved to England and had a son, who moved back to America to raise his family. Pocahontas died in England in 1617.

title: Milk Carton Log Cabin
text:
Build your own log cabin out of a milk carton!

Materials

Half-gallon waxed-paper milk or juice carton, emptied

Grease pencil

Scissors

Cardboard

Glue

Waxed-paper scraps

Pretzel sticks

Cheerios or pasta

Acrylic paint

Water

Water container

Paper towels

Ruler

Instructions

1. Measure three inches down the side of the carton. At three inches, draw a line around the entire carton with a grease pencil.

2. Cut along the line and separate the top from the bottom. Discard the bottom. You will use the top.

3. Draw the outline of the door and windows with a grease pencil.

4. Cut out the windows and door. If they are too small for scissors, ask your teacher to use an X-acto knife and help you. You can leave one side of the door attached and fold it out so that it opens and closes.

5. Glue a piece of waxed paper over the inside of each window.

6. Glue the cabin to a cardboard base that is slightly bigger than the cabin. Let the pieces dry before proceeding.

7. Glue pretzel sticks along the base of the carton walls and build up. If necessary, cut the pretzels to fit around the door and windows.

8. Glue a stack of Cheerios or pasta together as a chimney. Glue this on the roof of the cabin.

9. Cover the roof with pretzels or acrylic paint. Note: Watercolor and tempera paint will not stay on the waxed carton.

Note: Watercolor and tempera paint will not stay on the waxed carton.

title: People and Events in History
text: On the chart, there are different people and events from history listed down the side. Some of the special words we use to describe history are listed across the top. Find the word that describes the person or event and make an X in the correct box. The first one has been done for you. Good luck!

title: The Canal of Lehighton
text:
Lehighton is located about 30 miles north of the Allentown-Bethlehem area and about 100 miles north of Philadelphia. Nearly 6,000 people live in this town, but Lehighton actually began as a small American Indian settlement.

In 1754, a group of Moravian Brethren (a religious group) built a small village on the east side of the Lehigh River. They called the spot New Gnaden Huetten, which means, "The New Huts of Grace." They started a mission there, with plans to teach the American Indians about their religion. Many Delaware Indians living in the area were baptized and lived with the Moravians in peace. In 1755, many of the American Indians living around New Gnaden Huetten became angry with the white settlers and joined together to attack them. The American Indians invaded the village, and 10 people were killed. The rest of the settlers ran away to Bethlehem, and the American Indians burned all of the buildings in New Gnaden Huetten to the ground.

In 1756, Benjamin Franklin brought 200 men to the empty village and built Fort Allen. Many years later, Jacob Weiss and William Henry began planning a city near the fort. They called the spot Lehighton, after the Lehigh River. Lehighton was a popular resting place for people traveling from Berwick to Easton. The people of Lehighton built many taverns (places to buy dinner and drinks) and inns to give these travelers some place to eat, sleep and rest.

When the Lehigh Canal was built in 1829, many people used the canal to travel from place to place. Many of these travelers stopped in Lehighton as well. When the Lehigh Valley Railroad was finished, even more people settled here. Today, Lehighton continues to be a beautiful, quiet place to live. What was once home to peaceful American Indians and settlers is now a great place to live, work and play.

title: Can Facebook Save Dying Languages?
text:
Can you say a few words in Siletz Dee-ni? No? How about saying "hello" in Aka? If you can't, you're not alone! These two languages and 3,500 more could become extinct by the end of this century. Almost 80 percent of the world's population now speaks only one percent of the world's 7,000 languages. This has happened because of globalization. Globalization means that countries are more connected through trade, money and workers. When countries work together, people must be able to communicate with each other. That means many people have to learn another language. English is the main language used throughout the world for business and the Internet.

Why is this a problem? When the last person who is able to speak a particular language dies, some of the knowledge that is found within that language dies with them. A language contains the history of its people, how they used their environment and their beliefs and ideas. Technology may just save many of these languages from extinction! With YouTube, Facebook and other forms of social media, languages that are spoken by even 5 or ten people can be taught to others around the world.

National Geographic has been working on the Enduring Voices Project. Its goals are to record native speakers of endangered languages into talking dictionaries and help communities learn ways to save their languages from extinction. What language do you want to help save?

title: American Indians in Pennsylvania
text:
The American Indians who lived in Pennsylvania and across America in the early days of this country lived together in tribes, or communities, much the same way we do today. Although each community was different from other communities in some ways, American Indian communities also shared many beliefs, values and ways of living in common. This week, we will look at how the tribes of Pennsylvania were the same in some ways and different in others. In the early days of Pennsylvania, there were two main groups of American Indians living here. These two groups were the Algonquian tribes and the Iroquois tribes. There were many other smaller tribes that were part of these larger ones. The Delaware and the Shawnee were important Algonquian tribes, while the Susquehannocks were the most important Iroquois tribe.

Shared Ways of Life of the Pennsylvania American Indian Tribes

Both the Algonquian and the Iroquois tribes lived together in communities. Both groups believed in a Great Spirit who watched over the Earth. They also believed that animals, birds and even the Earth itself had their own spirits.

Algonquian Shamans

The Algonquian villages each had a shaman, or a special priest who talked to the Great Spirit. He also made trips to the underworld to visit the ancestors (family members who lived long ago) of the tribe. The Algonquians believed that the shaman had magical powers and that he could heal sickness.

Iroquois Evil Spirits

The Iroquois also believed that there were many gods and spirits in the world. Each spring and fall, the Iroquois would hold a special ceremony to get rid of any evil spirits who may be within the tribe. They would wear scary masks and travel around the village, frightening away the evil spirits.

Algonquian and Iroquois houses

Wigwams

Both the Algonquian and the Iroquois built houses to protect themselves from the weather. The Algonquian tribes usually built wigwams for shelter. The women of the tribe built the wigwams by cutting down thin, young trees and bending them so that both ends could be pounded into the ground, making a semi-circle. The bent trees were then covered with birch bark, animal skins, cornhusks and grasses. Each family lived in its own wigwam.

Long Houses

The Iroquois also built houses to protect themselves, but the Iroquois built long houses instead of wigwams. A long house was a large house where many families of one clan, or group of relatives, lived together. The houses had no windows and were between 50 and 150 feet long. Each family had a small space of its own with beds on the bottom and a "bunk" above the beds where the family could keep its things.

Differences Between Tribes

Family Relationships

The Algonkian tribes lived in a patriarchal society, which means that the men were in charge of each tribe. The chiefs of each tribe were men, and men were in charge of fighting battles, making decisions and guiding their families. When young people were old enough to marry, the man was in charge of asking the young woman to be his wife, and it was his job to take care of his bride once they were married.

The Iroquois tribes were different from most of the other American Indians because they lived in a matriarchal society. This means that the women of the tribe were the leaders and made decisions for the group. The women owned the houses and all the other possessions of the tribe. The children became members of the mother's clan, or family, and the men had to obey the women. The chief of each tribe was a man, but the mothers of the tribe chose him. In the matriarchal society of the Iroquois, mothers were still very tender with their babies and carried them on their backs in cradle boards. Mothers provided most of their infants' care.

American Indian tribes were different in many ways, but they all lived in communities, built houses for their families, hunted animals to survive and believed in a Great Spirit that watched over them.

title: Tokyo, Japan
text:
When a Japanese husband and wife have a child, they stop calling each other by their first names. Instead, they call each other "otousan" (father) or "okaasan" (mother). They do this to show that being a parent is more important than being a husband or a wife.

Japanese parents teach their children that the group they belong to is much more important than each separate person is. The children must always do what is best for the group. Parents and teachers tell the children that they must behave well or it will make their families and their friends look bad.

Japanese children study hard and doing well in school is very important. Children go to school all day and into the evening. They eat lunch together in their classroom and spend part of their school day cleaning the rooms, halls, toilets and yards of the school.

Japanese children are taught to show great respect for their parents and grandparents. Many Japanese families have their grandparents living with them and the family takes care of them in their old age.

Japan is a great place to learn how to work, study and show respect for others.

title: Kenora, Ontario, Canada
text:
Kenora, a beautiful city in Ontario, Canada, was once the home of the Ojibwe Indian Tribe. The Ojibwe people settled here to be near Lake of the Woods, a good source of water and animals that came to drink there.

The first European to come to Kenora was a Frenchman named Jacques de Noyon. In 1688, de Noyon visited Lake of the Woods on a trip into the wilds of what was then an unknown area. He found the Ojibwe people and saw the large amounts of furs and skins they had gathered.

In 1836, the world-famous Hudson's Bay Company built a fur-trading post on the Winnipeg River. This post was later moved to the site of the present city of Kenora in 1860. When the railroad came through Kenora, the town began to grow. Businesses in the area used the railroad to send timber, fur and fish to people in the East.

Today, lumber and fish are still important to the city of Kenora. A large paper company uses the trees in Kenora to make all kinds of paper products. Fishing is also a popular sport in Kenora. People come from all over Canada and the United States to fish in Lake of the Woods. Tourists also come here to hunt, swim, water ski and boat.

The Ojibwe people came to Kenora because of the many furs, skins, fish and trees near Lake of the Woods. Many of the people who live in Kenora today came here for the very same reasons.

title: Chief Cornplanter
text:
Chief Cornplanter was the son of a white father and an American Indian mother. He was raised as a member of the Seneca Indian Tribe in Pennsylvania. When the French were in control of the area, Cornplanter was friendly with them and fought against the British, but when the British took control, Cornplanter made friends with them. During the Revolutionary War, Cornplanter joined with the British in fighting against the Americans. When the British leaders asked, Cornplanter would often lead his warriors into battle against the Americans. During the war, Cornplanter and his men attacked many white settlements in New York and the valley of Wyoming.

When the Americans won the Revolutionary War, Cornplanter decided that life would be better if he became friendly with the Americans. He spoke out against other American Indians who hated the white settlers and tried to get his tribe to stop drinking alcohol.

The United States gave Cornplanter a section of land along the Allegheny River for his own. He lived here and farmed the land until he died at the age of nearly 96.

title: The Atlatl
text:
"Atlatl" is an Aztec Indian word that means "spear thrower." Before the bow and arrow were invented, early American Indians used the atlatl to help them hunt animals for food. The atlatl was a special spear thrower that let the American Indians throw their spears farther and with more power than they could by using their arms alone. Historians believe that people have been using the atlatl for more than 40,000 years. The American Indians even used the atlatl as a weapon against the Spanish when they came to the New World in the late 1400s. A spear thrown with an atlatl could pierce the metal armor worn by the Spanish soldiers.

Today, many people have rediscovered the atlatl. They hold competitions to see who can use the atlatl to throw a spear the farthest and who can come closest to hitting the center of a target.

title: Squanto
text:
Kidnapped by Spanish explorers as a young man and sold into slavery in Spain, Squanto managed to escape from slavery and return to his people. When he got back to America, he found that all of his tribe had died from smallpox, so he went to live in a nearby Wampanoag Indian village.

Squanto made friends with the settlers at the Plymouth settlement in Massachusetts and taught them to plant corn and to find and prepare seafood. Without his help, the Pilgrims might easily have starved to death.

Squanto also arranged a treaty, or an agreement, between the settlers and the local American Indians that helped the two groups get along with each other. This treaty remained unbroken for 50 years. Squanto performed many other acts of friendship for the English colonists before he died in 1622.

The Pennsylvania American Indian tribes were the same in some ways and different in others. title: Trip to an American Indian Village
text: Imagine that you traveled back in time to an American Indian village in our state. What did you find there? Were the people friendly? Draw the people and things you saw on your trip back to the American Indian village.

title: Let's Visit Germantown
text:
The city of Krefeld, Germany, was built as a refuge, or safe place, for all religions. Many people had come to Krefeld to be able to practice their religions any way they chose. When the government of Krefeld changed and freedom of religion began to be less free, many members of the Mennonite and Quaker religions decided to come to America. They had heard of a man named William Penn and of his promise to build a place where people could practice their religions in peace.

On Oct. 6, 1683, 13 families from Krefeld arrived in Philadelphia. William Penn met the group of new settlers and showed them to a spot about six miles north of Philadelphia. The settlers quickly dug cellars, or underground rooms, and covered them with roofs to keep out the weather. These cellars became their homes during their first winter in America. Because the setters didn't have much at first, they called their little town "Armentown," which means, "town of the poor." The town didn't stay poor for long, though. The settlers from Germany were hardworking weavers, tailors (people who make clothes), carpenters and shoemakers. They planted flax, a plant that can be made into cloth, and set up their spinning wheels. They also planted grapes, peach trees, vegetables and flowers. Soon, the little town was a beautiful and pleasant place to live. Germantown built a school and a church and made rules about how the town should be run.

One of the first rules of Germantown was that there could be no slaves held in the town. The Mennonites and Quakers believed that slavery was wrong and would not let anyone practice slavery in their town. Today, many of Germantown's historic buildings have been restored. Visitors can tour Rittenhouse Mill, the first paper mill in America. There are also 49 houses along Germantown Avenue that are being restored to look as they did when the first settlers built them. Germantown was built by hardworking Germans who came here to find the freedom to worship as they pleased.

title: Celebrating An American Hero's Trip Around the Earth
text:
It was 1957 when the Soviet Union launched the first spacecraft into orbit. Americans were shocked! The space race had just begun and we were already behind! In 1961 President John F. Kennedy announced that the U.S. planned to land a man on the moon by the end of the decade. The Russians responded by first launching a dog into orbit, and later two men. The race was on!

On Feb. 20, 1962, a Marine Corps fighter pilot from Ohio stepped up to put his life on the line. John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth. The success of his Mercury mission was one of the first steps to landing a man on the moon in July 1969.

John Glenn served as the U.S. senator from Ohio for 24 years, but he longed to go back into space. In 1998 at the age of 77 he was able to see that dream come true. He traveled on the space shuttle Discovery and became the oldest person to ever go into space! On Feb. 20th, 2012, America celebrated the 50th anniversary of John Glenn's first orbit. Mr. Glenn and the remaining members of the Mercury mission space team were given a hero's welcome at Cape Canaveral in Florida. Because of Mr. Glenn's service to our country as an astronaut and a senator, he has been called an American hero.

title: Explorers in Pennsylvania
text:
The first people who explored and settled in America and Pennsylvania came here for many different reasons. Some came here looking for gold and other ways to get rich. Others, like the Pilgrims, came here searching for a place to worship God in their own way. Some came to America hoping to find freedom from unfair governments. A few even came here hoping to find good health and a long life. This week, we will look at several different explorers and settlers to discover what they hoped to find when they came to America and Pennsylvania.

Christopher Columbus

When Columbus set out on his journey across the ocean, he hoped to find a new way to get to the Far East. If his plan worked, Spain would have a new way to get to China. Sailors could sail west and bring back all kinds of gold, spices and silks to sell in Europe. Columbus didn't realize that North and South America were blocking the way!

Juan Ponce de Leon

Ponce de Leon, a Spanish sailor, was an unusual explorer. He didn't sail west looking for gold, freedom or honor. He came looking for a way to stay young forever. Ponce de Leon had heard legends (stories that may or may not be true) about the Fountain of Youth. The Fountain of Youth was a spring that was supposed to make anyone who drank from it stay young and healthy forever. He explored the Bahamas, searching for this famous spring. Instead of finding the Fountain of Youth, Ponce de Leon became the first European to explore Florida.

Jacques Cartier

Jacques Cartier sailed northwest from France hoping to find a new trade route to Asia. A trade route is a pathway that can be used for traders to bring their goods back and forth. Like Columbus, Cartier wanted to find a new way to get to all the wealth and riches that could be found in China and other Asian countries. Cartier landed near the mouth of the St. Lawrence River. He thought that if he sailed up the river, he would reach the open sea. He hoped to reach Asia by using this waterway. In 1534, Cartier sailed up the St. Lawrence River and found that it never reached the ocean. His plans to sail to China were blocked by the American continent. He never found his trade route, but Cartier claimed Quebec for France.

Early Pennsylvania Explorers and Settlers

Samuel de Champlain first saw Pennsylvania on his journey to Quebec, Canada. He was so impressed with the beautiful woods in the area that he sent a French soldier and explorer named Etienne Brule (Broo-LAY) to explore the area. As the years went by, the Dutch, English and Swedes fought over the land that we now call Pennsylvania. Finally, it was the English who got to keep the land for their own. The first settlers to come to Pennsylvania to stay came here searching for freedom to practice their religions in their own way. When William Penn started his new settlement, promising religious freedom for all, people came from Germany, England, France and Ireland hoping to find a place where they could practice their religions without being bothered by the government. People also came to Pennsylvania to find freedom from unfair governments. Many of those who came here from Europe were used to having kings who told them what to do. In America, they would have the freedom to govern themselves.

title: The Zipper
text:
Most of the world's greatest inventions happened because someone had a problem that needed to be solved. The zipper is one invention created for this very reason.

Whitcomb L. Judson loved machines and gadgets. He spent much time tinkering with new ideas for making life easier.

Whitcomb had a friend with a problem. His friend had a stiff back that made it impossible for him to bend over and use both hands to hook up the hooks on his shoes. Whitcomb set out to solve this problem for his friend.

After working for a few weeks, Whitcomb came up with a special slide fastener that could be opened and closed with just one hand. By 1893, Whitcomb had received a patent, or license from the government giving him and only him the right to make and sell his new invention.

After a few years, other inventors came up with even better "hookless fasteners." Because they were so easy to "zip" up, the fasteners soon became known as zippers. By the 1920s, zippers were used in galoshes (rubber boots), clothing, luggage and bags. Today, the zipper is found on almost everything, from pants to dresses to tents. Whitcomb Judson's invention helped his friend and people everywhere who needed an easy way to open and close almost anything.

title: William Penn
text:
A young man named William Penn was one of the best-known Quakers in England. A Quaker is a member of a religious group who believes in living a peaceful life. By 1680, William had decided that the Quakers needed a new home where they could live their beliefs in peace. He asked King Charles II to repay some money he owed to the Penn family by giving him land in America. King Charles agreed to the deal in 1681. The king named the colony "Pennsylvania" (which means "Penn's Woods") after the Penn family.

William passed out pamphlets, or handouts, about Pennsylvania to both Quakers and non-Quakers in England, Ireland, Wales, Scotland, Germany, the Netherlands and Switzerland. Hundreds of people wrote letters to William and bought land in Pennsylvania. William could not go to his colony until 1682. In the spring of 1681, he sent his cousin William Markham to Pennsylvania as his deputy governor. Markham brought a letter from William to the Swedes, Finns, Dutch and English who had lived in Pennsylvania before it became Penn's colony. Calling them "My Friends," Penn promised the old colonists that "you shall be governed by laws of your own making and live a free people."

title: Timbuktu, Mali, Africa
text:
Timbuktu is a city in the Western African nation of Mali. You may have heard someone say something like, "Trash is scattered from here to Timbuktu," and wondered exactly what that meant. Timbuktu is in a very out-of-the-way place, far from other large cities. People often use the word "Timbuktu" to describe something that is far away, or out in the middle of nowhere.

Timbuktu wasn't always such an out-of-the-way place. The city of Timbuktu was once the center of learning, wealth and religion in Africa.

The city started in the 1100s as a camp for African nomads, or people who traveled from place to place. Later, as Mali became a rich African kingdom, Timbuktu became an important city for trading gold and salt. People came from all over northern Africa to trade in the wealthy city.

Besides the many traders who came to Timbuktu to do business, many wise men, artists and Muslims came here as well. Timbuktu was a beautiful city with large buildings, interesting people and wonderful places to eat and sleep.

Today, Timbuktu really is near the middle of nowhere. The famous city has crumbled, and its wealth is gone. Small traders still bring their camels, loaded down with salt, to the city to trade, but there is no longer any gold here to trade for. A few brave visitors still make the trip to Timbuktu, hoping to find out more about this city in the middle of nowhere.

title: Cesar Chavez
text:
At the age of 10 years old, Cesar Chavez became a migrant worker when his father lost his farm in Yuma, Arizona. A migrant worker moves from place to place, working in the fields when the crops are ready. Cesar moved to California, working in the fields, orchards and vineyards to earn money for himself and his family. He joined many different groups that tried to help the migrant workers get more money, better houses and shorter working hours.

After years of work, Cesar Chavez started the United Farm Workers of America, the first successful farm workers' union in United States history. A union is a group that works for fair pay, safe places to work and good working hours for men and women working at the same type of job. The union started by Cesar Chavez is still around today and works to make sure that farm workers are treated fairly.

Cesar and his union started strikes against fruit and vegetable growers who refused to give farm workers fair pay, reasonable working hours, and safe places to live. A strike happens when workers refuse to come to work until the owners of the company promise to give them what they are asking for. These strikes made people across the nation aware of the needs of the farm workers and helped to bring important changes to the farm industry.

title: Sharing Public Space: Vitus Bering and Russian Colonies in Alaska
text:
Imagine traveling 6,000 miles over land with supplies for an expedition, and THEN sailing through frigid seas to look for a new world. This was the job given to Vitus Bering, a Danish navigator who sailed for the Russian navy. Peter the Great, czar (ruler) of Russia, asked Bering to explore the eastern coast of Russia. He was wondering if land connected Asia and North America.

Bering's first trip began in 1725. After spending three years getting his supplies to eastern Russia, Bering sailed along the coastline. He didn't see any land to the east, and he didn't realize he was sailing in the narrow passage between Russia and Alaska. This waterway is now called the Bering Strait.

Bering led another expedition in 1741. This time his ship landed on Kayak Island, off the coast of Alaska. They explored some of the Aleutian Islands and met the native people there, the Aleut. He was the first European to arrive in present-day Alaska.

Bering died before returning to Russia, but his voyages paved the way for Russian settlements in North America. Many fur traders came to the area. In 1799 the Russian government established a fur-trading operation in Alaska. Furs from foxes, sea otters and seals were very valuable.

Unfortunately, the Russians took advantage of the native people just as some Europeans had done in settling New England. The Russians took over their lands and forced them to hunt for furs. They also brought new diseases, which killed many natives.

Today, the Aleut people continue to live along the western coast of North America, and their population has grown. What might have been different if the Russians and the Aleut had shared public space fairly? Where in your community is there a debate over public land? How should such debates be handled?

title: Let's Visit the Busy City of Reading
text:
The community of Reading (pronounced "Reding") was first planned in 1730 by Richard and Thomas Penn, two of William Penn's sons. The Penn brothers called the new town Reading after the city of Reading, Berkshire, England, where their family was from. The two brothers planned the town with straight streets and neat squares of land for houses, farms, businesses, and parks. Reading grew when new kinds of transportation came to the area. There were ferries (boats used to take people and goods across the water) that brought people across the Schuylkill River until bridges were built at Penn Street and Bingaman Street. Reading was also joined to other cities by several turnpikes, or toll roads. These turnpikes had toll booths where the people traveling on the roads paid money before they were allowed to use them. In the late 1820s, a system of canals, or large ditches, was built that joined the Susquehanna River with the Delaware River. These ferries, bridges, and canals made Reading a popular place for shipping goods from place to place. By 1837, the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad had come to Reading. This brought even more business to the community of Reading.

One of the largest new businesses to come to the city was a coalburning engine factory. The first coal burning railroad engine was designed and built in Reading. Other businesses that made their homes here were iron and nail companies, steel mills, knitting and sock companies, and factories that made beer, cigars, shoes, and boots. Many people came to Reading to find jobs during the late 1800s. People came from other cities in America, but they also came from countries like Ireland, Poland, Italy, and the Ukraine. These new citizens found jobs working in the many factories in Reading.

By the mid-1900s, cars, bricks, hardware, and socks were the most important items made in Reading factories. Reading was once one of Pennsylvania's largest business and transportation centers. Today, many old historic buildings in Reading are being rebuilt to make sure its great history is preserved.

title: Early Pennsylvania Communities
text:
Pennsylvania had to fight the American Indians and the British, as well as help form a new country during the time that it was building its first communities. In the early 1800s, Pennsylvania began to grow like never before. New canals and railroads made it easier for people to get to and from Pennsylvania. When Robert Fulton launched a steamboat from Pittsburgh, people became more excited than ever about making their homes in our great Pennsylvania. Let's look at some of Pennsylvania's early communities and how they were settled.

Philadelphia

On the banks of the Delaware River, William Penn started a city called Philadelphia. "Philadelphia" is Greek for "The City of Brotherly Love." In England, where William was from, the roads wandered and curved around like the cow paths that they once were. When William started his new city, he wanted it to be organized and easy to get around in. He planned the city of Philadelphia with straight streets that ran both north and south and east and west. He wanted no curving cow paths for the streets in his city! William also laid out plots of land for houses, farms, businesses, parks and public squares. Because it was so well organized, Philadelphia quickly became the center of business, government and art in the 13 colonies.

Pittsburgh

When George Washington surveyed the Pennsylvania area in 1753, he wrote that the spot now called Pittsburgh was "extremely well situated for a fort, as it has the command of both rivers." Fort Pitt was later built at the place where the Allegheny and Monongahela Rivers meet to form the Ohio River.

After the Revolutionary War ended, people came to Pittsburgh by the hundreds. The city had jobs for coal miners, glass and iron makers and shipbuilders.

In 1811, a steamboat named the New Orleans was built in Pittsburgh. This steamboat made its first trip by chugging down the Ohio River to Louisiana. Not long after this, Pittsburgh became a major shipping city. When the railroad came to Pittsburgh in the late 1800s, the city grew even larger as it shipped glass, iron, steel and cloth both by ship and by train.

Lancaster

Lancaster was first settled by German farmers around 1709. This makes Lancaster one of the oldest inland (not near the coast or ocean) cities in the United States. The German farmers who came here were hardworking settlers who helped Lancaster grow into a beautiful community.

Pennsylvania Rifle

Lancaster is famous for being the home of the Pennsylvania Rifle, sometimes called the Kentucky Rifle. A Swiss gunsmith (someone who makes and fixes guns) named Martin Meylin put long, spiral grooves in the barrel of a rifle he built. The grooves made the gun easy to aim and helped it hit its target up to 300 yards away. These improvements helped the early settlers feed and defend their families. The Pennsylvania Rifle was used during both the Revolutionary War and the War of 1812.

Conestoga Wagon

The Conestoga Wagon, the most popular wagon during the late 1700s and early 1800s, was also built in Lancaster. This type of wagon was built by hand and was strong enough to travel well on the bumpy, muddy roads of early Pennsylvania.

The Conestoga wagon had four wide wheels that helped keep it from getting stuck in the mud. The body of the wagon was shaped in a way that kept the load inside the wagon from sliding around as the wagon traveled along. The Conestoga wagon also came with a canvas cover to protect the goods inside from bad weather.

title: Athens, Greece
text:
Athens is a large city in the country of Greece. In Athens, the men are the leaders, both at home and in the government. The most important job of the women is still to take care of the home and raise the children. The men go to work and make money to take care of the family.

After work, Greek men usually meet at their favorite coffee houses to have some refreshments and visit with their friends. The women often get together with their friends as well. They go to church activities, let their children play together, join together to cook a meal or just visit.

Men are in charge of the money in the family. The women are in charge of the home and the children. Many women now have jobs and work outside their homes, but it is still the woman's job to run the household and raise the children. Women also have the right to own land, vote, hold jobs and speak out in public, just like women in the United States.

title: Montreal, Quebec, Canada
text:
The famous French explorer Jacques Cartier arrived in what is now Montreal in 1535. About 100 years later, in May of 1642, the first French settlers came to Montreal. They shot guns to scare away any evil spirits that might already be living here and dedicated the island to the Virgin Mary. They named the spot "Ville-Marie," or the City of Mary. Over the years, Montreal was controlled by France, England and even the United States. Today, Montreal is part of the country of Canada.

Montreal has some neighborhoods in which most people speak French, and some neighborhoods in which most people speak English. There are strict laws about which languages can be used in business, in government and in schools. Many people have very strong feelings about which language should be used.

Today, Montreal is a famous meeting place for people from countries all over the world. Many conventions, or meetings of large groups of people, are held in Montreal each year. The city makes money from its airport, hotels, restaurants, convention centers and shopping malls.

title: Daniel Boone
text:
"I have never been lost, but I will admit to being confused for several weeks." -Daniel Boone

Born near Reading, Pennsylvania, Daniel was one of the greatest American trailblazers of all time. A trailblazer is someone who goes first and makes a path for others to follow. In 1769, a friend of Daniel's named John Findley asked him to help him blaze a trail to Kentucky. Boone, Findley, and five other men set out along the small trails and pathways leading through the Cumberland Gap in the Appalachian Mountains into Kentucky. They found a "hunter's paradise" filled with buffalo, deer, wild turkey, and meadows thatwere perfect for farming. Daniel was so excited about this new land that he promised to bring his family back here to live. A few years later, Daniel and 30 other woodsmen were hired to build what became known as the "Wilderness Road" into the heart of Kentucky. By 1775, Daniel had built a fort and a small town called Boonesborough. He soon moved his family here to live.

When Kentucky became part of the United States, Daniel lost all his land. His son, Daniel Morgan Boone, had moved to St. Charles, Missouri, and he invited his parents to come and live there. Daniel and Rebecca went to Missouri, where Daniel became a judge. Daniel died in Missouri, but his body was later buried in Kentucky, the "hunter's paradise" that he loved so much.

title: The Steamboat
text:
In 1787, John Fitch showed the first working steamboat to a crowd gathered near the Delaware River in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The first steamboat was 45 feet long and was pushed along by a steam engine that turned 12 paddles. When these paddles turned, the boat moved along the river.

In 1807, Robert Fulton created the first steamboat that could carry passengers and freight (a load of goods). His first steamboat, called the Clermont, traveled from New York Harbor, up the Hudson River, to Albany and back. Many people thought that the steamboat would fail, and they were surprised when it was a success.

The steamboat made life much easier for people living near the rivers. It could bring people and goods up and down the rivers much more quickly than a wagon could bring them on land. It was also cheaper to travel by steamboat than by wagon. The invention of the steamboat helped Americans settle in new towns all over the country.

title: George Washington
text:
"First in war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen." - Henry Lee

George Washington was born in Westmoreland, Virginia, in 1732. His father died in 1743, and George went to live with his half brother, Lawrence, at Mount Vernon.

George wanted to be a sailor, but became a surveyor (someone who measures and marks the land) instead. After surveying for a short time, George joined the army and became a lieutenant colonel. He was only 22 years old, but he learned quickly and did very well. By 1755, George became a colonel and then the commander-in-chief of the Virginia militia (small army). George decided to quit the army for a while and began serving in the Virginia House of Burgesses.

When the Revolutionary War started, George was chosen as the commander-in-chief of the Continental Army. He was a great leader and helped the United States win its independence from England. His men loved him and respected him for his honesty and his leadership skills.

After the war ended, George served as president of the convention that wrote the U.S. Constitution, the paper that tells how our country should be run. He was later elected as the first president of the United States. Because he was our first president, he is often called "The Father of Our Country."

title: The Job of a Museum Director: 'A Little Bit of Everything'
text:
The Campbell House Museum is a beautiful Civil War-era home in St. Louis, Missouri. The wealthy Campbell family lived there from 1854 to 1938. Studies Weekly asked Andrew Hahn, the director of the museum, about his job.

SW: How is a house museum different from other types of museums?

AH: A house museum is different because it gives you an opportunity to get the full experience of the past. If you go to an art museum, you can see paintings from the past that may tell a story about history or a particular event. But when you come to a house museum, you get the full picture of what it was like to live in the past. When people come here, they get to experience what it was like to be welcomed into the house or to work in the house. The house was so well preserved, and the Campbells’ collection is still here. This is their house and how they lived in it.

SW: What does a museum director do?

AH: I do a little bit of everything. We have to raise money so that we can keep the doors open and pay the utility bills. I write the checks for all the bills, and I organize our volunteers who do most of the work at the house. We do research, so I look into the Campbell story and read old documents and newspapers that tell stories about the past. I even take out the trash!

title: Let's Visit Lancaster
text:
Lancaster is known as one of the oldest inland (not near the coast or ocean) cities in the United States. It is about 70 miles west of Philadelphia and borders the Susquehanna River.

Lancaster was settled by people who came here from Germany to find religious freedom. The first settlers came here in 1709, and by 1729, the city had been mapped out with streets, building lots and farmland. John Wright, one of the city's most respected citizens, named the city Lancaster after the English city of Lancaster where he once lived. The city was the capital of the 13 colonies for one day in September of 1777.

British soldiers were on their way to the original capital in Philadelphia, so the government leaders left in a hurry. They met in Lancaster before moving on to York. Lancaster was the capital of Pennsylvania from 1799 to 1812, when it was moved to Harrisburg.

The city of Lancaster works very hard to rebuild and preserve its old buildings. When you make a visit to Lancaster, you will see many places where exciting things happened long ago. One of these great old buildings is the Trinity Lutheran Church, built in 1766. Until 1800, the church's steeple was taller than any building west of Philadelphia. The Fulton Opera House is another beautiful old Lancaster building. Built in 1852, the opera house was named after Robert Fulton, the inventor of the steamboat. The Fulton Theatre is the oldest theater in continuous use in America. This means that the theater has been used since it was built and has never been closed down.

The Benjamin Mishler House is another interesting site to see. Someone once bet Benjamin that he couldn't build a house in one day, so to prove him wrong, he did it! The house he built in only 10 hours' time still stands today. Lancaster is one of Pennsylvania's most beautiful and historic cities with plenty to see and learn.

title: Joplin Works to Rebuild After a Deadly Tornado
text:
Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/ for more Connections and Current Events articles.

On May 22, 2011, a tornado hit the city of Joplin, Missouri. It wasn't just any tornado. It was a monstrous EF-5, with winds over 200 miles an hour. This huge tornado was almost a mile wide and cut a path over 22 miles long. It crushed almost 1/3 of the city, killed 162 people and destroyed almost 8,000 buildings. It is considered one of the deadliest tornadoes in over 50 years.

Joplin is working hard to rebuild. Think about all of the parts that make a city work. In addition to houses and businesses, cities need electricity, sewers, roads, hospitals, parks and government buildings. In January 2012 federal and civic organizations in Joplin got together to give the "ok" to a plan called Joplin Area - Next Steps Plan. The plan outlined how to replace what was destroyed in the tornado. 4,000 building permits have been given to homeowners so they can begin construction on new homes. After the tornado hit, 530 businesses were either destroyed or badly damaged. The good news is that 420 of those businesses have reopened. Work has begun on a new hospital. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) is helping to clean up waste and keep the area safe for residents.

The people of Joplin will never forget that terrible day. Recovering from something this devastating is difficult, but Joplin is showing how it's done!

title: Studying History
text:
As we study the history of Pennsylvania, America, and the world, we find that there are many things to think about. Have you ever wondered how we know what happened long ago? Or why things happened in the order they did? Or why people see the same event in different ways? This week, we will be learning how to find out what happened in the past, how to organize these events and why different people see the same event in different ways.

Thinking "Chronologically"

When we study history, it is important for us to be able to ask, "What happened first?" "What happened next?" and "What happened last?" Putting events in order of when they happened is called organizing them chronologically. Chronological order is a lot like ABC order. Only instead of organizing a list of words by which letter they start with, you organize a list of events in order from which happened first to which happened last.

Using a timeline makes it easy to see which things happened first and happened later. A timeline is a list of events, starting with the first and ending with the last. Look at the timeline below. It shows the main events that happened during the Civil War. You will see that the timeline is in chronological order, with the events that caused the war at the beginning and the assassination of Lincoln at the end.

Primary or Secondary

When we try to find out what happened in the past, we need to look in many different places. We can read journals, letters and reports. We can also look at pictures, read books, watch movies and listen to people tell about their experiences. All these different places to get information are called sources. Each of these sources can be put into one of two groups: primary sources and secondary sources. Primary sources are actual records that have survived from the past, such as letters, journals, photographs and articles of clothing. Primary sources come from people who actually lived through an event. "Primary" means "first," or "main," so primary sources are usually the first places we should research when trying to find out what happened.

Secondary sources are created sometime after an event has happened by people who weren't actually there. "Secondary" means "less important," or "coming later," so we usually look at secondary sources after we have already looked at the primary sources first. Some secondary sources are textbooks, history books, research papers and movies. Both primary and secondary sources are good places to look for information when we are studying the past.

Point of View

When we study history, we also notice that our sources don't always agree on what happened, why it happened or why it is important. If two people were part of the same event in history, how could they tell different stories about this event?

Each person who tells a story has a different point of view about what happened. Point of view is the way that a person sees things. When we study the Civil War, we notice that those in the North had a different point of view from those in the South. We also see that those who owned slaves had a different point of view from those who were held as slaves.

If this seems strange to you at first, think about your life today. Do you have a different point of view about some things than your parents? Do you think you have a different point of view about what happened on September 11 than someone who lives in Africa, Afghanistan or France? Do you think that you see the Civil War differently than a child who actually lived through it?

When we read what different people have written about things that happened in the past, we need to look at what their point of view was. Then we can understand the things they say.

title: Chihuahua, Mexico
text:
Chihuahua is the capital of the state of Chihuahua, Mexico. Chihuahua is in the northern part of Mexico, in a little valley surrounded by hills.

Chihuahua is known for playing a part in many of the changes that have happened in Mexico's government over the years. During the Revolution of 1810, Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla, a famous priest who fought against the government, was put in prison in Chihuahua. The brave priest was held for 98 days and was fed only bread and water. He was later executed, or killed, for trying to get rid of the Mexican government. The night before he was executed, he wrote a poem on his cell wall thanking his guard for being so kind to him. Today, a flame is kept burning on the patio of the Government Palace to remind those who visit of the price Hidalgo y Costilla paid for their liberty.

Chihuahua was also part of another Mexican revolution, fought more than 100 years later. The famous bandit Pancho Villa fought to get rid of a government that he felt treated the people unfairly. He had a home in Chihuahua where he often hid from the Mexican army. The mansion still stands, and many visitors tour here. The car that Pancho Villa was in when he was shot to death is also on display.

Chihuahua is a city where visitors can see the past and the present, all at the same time!

title: Molly Pitcher
text:
Many women helped the Continental Army during the American Revolution. They cooked, made clothing and cared for the wounded, and some even fought in battle. One famous woman was named Mary Ludwig Hays. Her nickname was "Molly." Her husband, John, from Carlisle, Pennsylvania, was camping at Valley Forge. Molly missed him very much. In spite of the bitter cold, she rode many days on horseback to reach him. He was very happy to see her. In the spring, when the Army went to battle at Monmouth, Molly was there. One terribly hot day in June, the men were dying, not only in battle, but of sunstroke. Seeing men faint from the hot sun, Mary took a pitcher and brought cool drinks of water to the soldiers. "Molly! Pitcher!" a soldier cried. "Molly! Here! Pitcher!" cried another. From that day on Molly Hays was called Molly Pitcher. Her husband fell back wounded, and Molly quickly bound the wound with a piece of her petticoat. Then she took John's place at the cannon. She kept firing the cannon until the battle ended at dusk.

Molly Pitcher is remembered for her bravery and compassion. There are two monuments in honor of Molly. One is in Carlisle, and the other is at the Monmouth Battlefield in New Jersey.

title: The Sewing Machine
text:
Can you imagine having to sew all of your own clothes with just a needle and thread? Before the invention of the sewing machine, that is exactly what clothing makers had to do.

In 1755, an American inventor named Charles T. Wiesenthal designed a double-pointed needle, with a sharp point on each end, to make sewing faster. In 1830, a Frenchman named Barthelemy Thimonnier used this double-pointed needle to make the first sewing machine. He attached the needle to a rod connected to a wheel. When the wheel turned, the needle went up and down, sewing stitches.

By 1846, Elias Howe, an American inventor, had figured out how to make the first lock-stitch sewing machine. This machine pulled the stitches tight so they didn't come loose later. It was used in clothing factories to make sewing faster and easier.

In 1851, Isaac Merritt Singer, a Boston machine maker, built the first small sewing machine that could be used at home. He made it easy for people to have their very own sewing machines for making their own clothes at home. The Singer Sewing Machine Company went on to become the world's largest maker of home sewing machines.

Just think of all the time, money and energy saved by the invention of the sewing machine!

title: Jonas Salk
text:
Jonas Salk was born in New York City in 1914. After graduating from medical school, he became a professor of epidemiology (the study of diseases and how to control them) at the University of Michigan. He later began teaching at the University of Pittsburgh, where he made the first polio vaccine. Polio is a disease that attacks the nervous system, often leaving its victims paralyzed. A vaccine is a special medicine that keeps people from getting certain diseases. The polio vaccine was first given to children in 1953, and it turned out to be a great success. Today, babies and children regularly get the polio vaccine to protect them from this terrible disease.

In 1963 Dr. Salk built the Institute for Biological Studies in La Jolla, California, to study diseases and ways to stop them. He left his home in Pittsburgh and spent the next 30 years in the San Diego area trying to find ways to protect people from contagious illnesses, or sicknesses that can be passed from person to person. He died in 1995.

Dr. Jonas Salk made the world a better place by fighting the germs that make us sick.

title: Weaving
text:
Materials

9-inch by 12-inch rectangle of thick cardboard

strips of cloth (quarter inch to half thick)

scissors

safety pin

Directions

1. Cut notches one-quarter inch apart into the nine-inch sides of the cardboard. Tie a strip of cloth to one corner of the cardboard, and then wrap it back and forth between the notches. Tie the other end of the strip at the corner of the rectangle diagonally across from the one you began with. You have now made your loom.

2. Attach another strip of cloth to the safety pin and close the pin. Begin weaving by threading the pin under the first strip at the top of your loom. Push the pin over the next strip, then under the one after it. Continue in this way, over and under, all the way across the loom.

3. When you reach the end of your loom, weave back the way you came, looping the cloth strips, as shown. This time, however, go under each strip you went over the first time, and go over each strip you went under.

4. Continue this for each row you want to weave, pulling the cloth strip over and under the loom. Make sure not to pull the strip too tight, or the edges of your final product will not be even.

5. Once you have woven a few rows, push the rows snugly together. If you come to the end of a strip of your weaving material and want to keep weaving, tie on a new strip with a strong double knot.

6. When you have finished weaving, be sure you are at the end of a row. Tie off each end of your cloth to the loom strip next to it, and lift both strip ends off the loom. To remove your work from the loom, bend down the tabs between the notches and slide the loom out. You can also break the loom by cutting it in half and removing the pieces.

title: Pittsburgh, Town of Steel
text:
Pittsburgh has been nicknamed the "Steel City" because of the many steel mills and factories built here. Because Pittsburgh was close to many good sources of coal and ores, many companies brought their businesses here to use these natural resources.

During the late 1800s, Pittsburgh was one of the largest steel and machinery centers in the United States. Because of the many steel mills and factories, there was much pollution (harmful poisons) in the air. The city was often called the "Smoky City" until the steel mills and factories found ways to get rid of most of this pollution.

Today, Pittsburgh makes products from metal, wood, plastic, paper and glass. It is also a center for printing all kinds of books and magazines. Pittsburgh makes clothes and computers and refines oil and chemicals. The city of Pittsburgh is a busy place because of the many businesses that are found here.

Pittsburgh was built on the spot where an American Indian town called Shannopin once stood. The English claimed the land and called their settlement Fort Pitt. When the town was settled in 1760, it was called Pittsburgh, after the fort.

The busy city of Pittsburgh is home to Carnegie Mellon University, the University of Pittsburgh, Chatham University, Duquesne University and Carlow University. Visitors enjoy exploring the Andy Warhol Museum, the Carnegie Library, Old Fort Pitt and the Pittsburgh Zoo.

title: Be a Citizen Scientist!
text:
Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/ for more Connections and Current Events articles.

Did you know that you could help scientists study how climate change affects plants and animals? You can become a citizen scientist with the National Phenology Network no matter how old you are!

The word "phenology" means the study of how timing affects plants and animals. Scientists observe things like when birds migrate, when flowers bloom or when insects swarm. There just aren't enough scientists to study all of the plants and animals in the country. That's where all of us come in!

By going to the National Phenology Network at www.usanpn.org you can sign up to follow a particular animal or plant in your own backyard. For example, you might sign up to monitor goldfinches in your yard. You would record what they are eating, how many you see at your bird feeder and where they build a nest. The site will show you how to register to be a citizen scientist, observe your chosen species and report what you have seen. All you need is Internet access. Anyone under the age of 13 needs an adult to register on the site for them. By contributing to the network you will be joining government agencies, universities and other professionals that use the data to monitor invasive species, manage wildlife and study the effects of climate change. All you have to do is be curious and observant!

title: Our Resources
text:
This week, we will be learning about the economy of our state. The economy of a community is its ability to earn money by using its resources. Resources are things that are found in a community that can be used to make money, or capital. We will learn about natural, human and capital resources and how people use them to get the things they need and want.

Natural Resources

Natural resources are the riches that are found naturally in an area. These riches include land, forests, mineral deposits, water and wildlife.

Human Resources

Human resources are the people who live in an area. The people who live in a community may be the most important resource of all. Without human resources, natural resources would be of no use. It takes people to plant and harvest crops, dig ditches and move water, break rocks to mine minerals and sail the oceans and rivers to catch fish. Human resources, or people, choose what to do with the natural resources found in a community.

Capital Resources

Capital resources are the riches and wealth that people own. This capital can be money, land, jewelry, factories or anything that is valuable and could be sold. People use their capital resources to buy the things they need and to make changes that will help them to earn even more capital. The more capital a person, business or community has, the more they can do with their natural and human resources.

Using Our Resources

Most of Pennsylvania's early settlers were farmers. They came to Pennsylvania and used its great natural resources of good soil, plenty of rain and pleasant sunshine to help them grow good crops. Pennsylvania's early farmers also used their own capital resources, or money, to buy seeds, tools and farm equipment. They also put in plenty of their own human resources, or strength, clearing and plowing the land, planting their seeds and harvesting their crops. By using all these resources, Pennsylvania's first farmers could raise enough food to keep themselves alive and to make some money as well.

Today, Pennsylvania farmers still use these same resources to raise crops and make money to support their families. Pennsylvania raises and sells dairy products, cattle, hay, corn, wheat, oats, mushrooms, poultry, potatoes and fruit.

Pennsylvania also used its natural resources to make money in other ways. Our state had a great supply of both iron ores and timber. The ore could be turned into steel when it was heated in a certain way. The timber in our state was burned to make the ore hot enough to make the steel.

Businesses came to Pennsylvania and used these natural resources to make steel. They used their capital resources, or money, to build large factories and buy expensive equipment. They also used their human resources to mine the ore and make the steel.

People who live in Pennsylvania also make and sell metal products, transportation equipment, machinery, chemicals and many kinds of plastic, rubber, stone, clay and glass products.

Others use their human resources to provide a service that people will pay for. They work in restaurants, banks and hospitals doing things for people that they can't or don't want to do for themselves.

People chose to settle in Pennsylvania because it had the natural resources they needed to survive. They built communities in places that had good soil, plenty of water and a mild climate. Communities that had what people needed to live well continued to grow and succeed. Today, our Pennsylvania communities use their natural, human and capital resources to make money and get the things they need and want.

title: Chandigarh, India
text:
Families who live in Chandigarh, India, enjoy spending time together, just like we do here in the United States. There are some differences between Indian and American families, though. Many parents in the United States pitch in and do the housework together, but not in India.

In India, the mother is almost completely in charge of everything around the house. She takes care of cooking, cleaning, shopping and anything else that must be done to keep the household running. The father doesn't get involved in these chores.

The job of the father in India is to support the family by earning money. Most dads in India believe that their work on the job is the most important thing in their lives. When they come home at night, however, they leave their work at work and enjoy spending quiet time with their families. They don't bring their work home with them like many American fathers do.

They also spend a lot of time talking to their children and learning how their children feel about things. Indian fathers see themselves as the head of the family, and they try to stay connected to their children.

title: Santiago, Chile
text:
Santiago is the capital of the South American country of Chile. The city is the center of the country's economy, or money-making activities.

Chile has one of the best economies in South America. The country has a great climate for growing many types of fruits and vegetables, especially grapes. Some of the grapes grown in Chile are made into wine, but most of them are shipped to North America as table grapes, or grapes to be eaten fresh. Chile's grapes get ripe just in time for Christmas, so most of the grapes we eat over the holidays come from here.

Chile also makes money by selling fish, wheat, potatoes, corn, sugar, beets, onions, beans, copper, wood and clothes to countries all over the world. The country uses its natural resources, like a good climate and rich soil, to help produce things that it can sell to make money. Santiago, Chile, is a good example of a city that uses what it has to get what it needs.

title: Christopher Sholes
text:
Christopher Sholes was born in Danville, Pennsylvania, in 1819. When he was a young teenager, he got a job working for a printer. After he had learned more about the printing business, he moved to Wisconsin where he worked as a printer, editor and reporter.

Because of his work in the printing business, Christopher started trying to build a machine that would let people print words using their hands. He experimented until he came up with the first typewriter in 1867.

Christopher tried to sell his amazing new invention, but he wasn't a very good salesman, and no one would buy it. He finally sold the rights to make the typewriter to the Remington Arms Company, and the company started making the Remington typewriter. Christopher kept working on his invention until he found a way to put a Shift key on his new machine. The Shift key made it possible to type in either lower case or upper case letters.

Because Christopher sold the rights to the typewriter to the Remington Company, he never got rich from his invention. He died in 1890 without a penny to his name.

title: The Typewriter
text: Christopher Sholes invented the typewriter in 1867. He was a printer who believed that it would make life much easier for people who did a lot of writing if they had a machine to help them. Christopher built the first typewriter using keys attached to metal letters. When someone struck the keys with their fingers, the typewriter printed the letters on a piece of paper. The keys were arranged in alphabetical order, but this arrangement didn't work out very well. When the keys were struck, they often jammed together because many of the keys used most often were too close together. James Densmore, a friend of Christopher's, suggested splitting the keys so that the keys used most often were mixed in with the keys that weren't used as much. The two men built a new typewriter with the keyboard arranged as it is today, and the problem of jammed keys was solved. After the invention of the computer, most people stopped using the typewriter, but we still use the same "QWERTY" letter arrangement on our computer keyboards today.

title: Sam Walton
text:
Sam Walton, the founder of Wal-Mart, believed that "individuals don't win, teams do." Born in Oklahoma in 1918, Walton went on to build a team that made him the second richest man in the world.

After graduating from college in 1940, Sam Walton began running a variety store, and in 1962, he opened the very first Wal-Mart in Rogers, Arkansas.

Sam Walton believed in offering his customers name-brand products at low prices and found that customers loved the idea. He didn't keep all the profits (money leftover when all the store's bills were paid) for himself when the company did well. Instead, he passed the savings along to the customer by cutting the prices of his products. He also gave his employees stock (shares, or part ownership) in the company so that they could make money when the store did well.

Wal-Mart is now the largest retail store in the world. Sam Walton's desire to share the money his stores made with his customers, as well as his employees, helped make him one of the most successful businessmen in the world.
