title: Welcome, Scientists
text:
There are billions of things to discover and wonder about in this world. What is everything made of? How does electricity work? And, what is this stuff stuck to the bottom of my shoe? With science, we can find answers to these fascinating questions and more!

Over the years, people have come up with some pretty smart ways of getting answers to questions. Scientific discoveries usually come over time, by trial and error. Science is a set of tools, knowledge, and methods. We use it to figure out the way the world and the universe work. Using scientific methods, or tools, we have learned to cure diseases, fly to the moon, understand ancient life, and create new ways of communicating, traveling, and getting information!

As you read Science Studies Weekly - Challenger this year, you will learn about three main areas of science: physical science, life science, and geo- and astro-science. The first few weeks will be about physical science. In this section, you'll learn what things are made of. Next, in geoscience and astro-science, we will look at the Earth, planets, stars, and the universe. Finally, in the life sciences section, we will learn about animals and living things.

Each week, you will read about famous scientists. You'll learn about current discoveries. You'll learn about the science behind our modern technologies and what makes them work. And you'll even learn how to be a scientist as you work in the lab. There are so many fun things to discover in Science Studies Weekly that we better get started right now, so put on your lab coats and turn the page!

title: Welcome to Another Year of Discovery!
text: Studies Weekly reporters are always on the job, looking for exciting developments in the world of science. And if you love science as much as we do, you'll want to keep an eye on something we've seen cropping up in neighborhoods all over the United States. School districts and community business leaders are teaming up to build STEM schools. STEM centers are dynamic institutions of learning that provide students with opportunities to specialize in Science, Technology, Engineering and Math. So ... are you eager to conduct another controlled investigation after tweaking the variables? Do you love to perform operations with different types of numbers? Are you ready to design and engineer the next generation of spacecraft? Or have you always dreamed of becoming a doctor? Well, chances are there's a STEM center-based school in your community that is looking for hard-working students. Meanwhile, be sure to check back here in the coming weeks to see what's up. We'll bring you the news!

title: Introduction to Science
text:
Here are a few brief descriptions of some branches of science. We will discuss more in the upcoming issues. . .

Life Science

Life science is the study of life, what living things are made of, and how they behave. The life sciences include biology, which is the study of living things such as plants and animals. Branches of biology include botany (the study of plant life, flora), zoology (the study of animal life, fauna), and physiology (the study of the human body). Have you ever wanted to enter an ancient tomb and find a mummy or dig up dinosaur bones? An archaeologist is a life scientist who investigates remnants of past human life by studying bones, artifacts, relics, monuments, etc. A paleontologist is a scientist who specializes in finding prehistoric fossils of dinosaurs and plants. Some of the tools used by life scientists are the microscope, greenhouse, underwater marine equipment, specialized digging equipment, and electronic dating equipment.

Geoscience & Astro-science

Geoscience is the study of the Earth and the things on it, such as icebergs, rocks, and ocean currents. Have you ever wanted to climb into a volcano or ride in a submarine to study the ocean floor? Geoscientists do these things. Some of the branches of geoscience are geology (the study of the Earth), geography (the study of the land, oceans, atmosphere, and where things are on maps), meteorology (the study of weather and atmospheric conditions), and oceanography (the study of ocean chemistry and life).

Astro-science includes astronomy, the study of objects in outer space, and astrophysics, the study of matter and chemistry in space. We rely on the information gathered by these scientists to help us know about our planet, to take better care of it, and to understand things like earthquakes and hurricanes! Some of the tools used by geoscientists and astro-scientists are the geologist's pick, seismograph, microscope, barometer, Doppler radar, telescope, weather balloon, space probe and space station.

Physical Science

Physical science is the study of how our physical world works. It is the science of all the things around us: what they are made of and how they interact and work with others. Two main branches of physical science are chemistry and physics. Chemists study what things are made of and make new materials that we can use every day, like new lighter materials for shoes or less expensive materials for clothing and food products. Chemists use many fancy words, such as element, compound, molecule, atom, electron, proton, neutron, acid, base, and many more to describe things. Physicists study the laws of matter and motion. The discoveries from physicists and chemists help people invent better technology, such as new means of transportation and communication.

Social Science

Social science is the study of how and why people do things. Social scientists are very important in helping us solve problems in a complex world. Social scientists come up with programs to help people avoid taking drugs, stop violence, communicate better, and help families become more healthy. Some of the branches of social science are psychology (the study of human behavior, thinking, and learning), sociology (the study of social groups and society) and anthropology (the study of human cultures).

The Scientific Method

Throughout history, people have always had questions. What is lightning? What makes rivers flow? Why do the seasons change? What causes the waves of the oceans? Why do people get sick and then recover or die? What causes a shooting star? People have used many different methods for finding answers to their questions.

Scientists are usually pretty bright, and they have a method of their own that's worked very well for answering questions. But, when it came to naming their method, they could have been a little more creative. What do you think it is? Hope you're ready for this. . . Drum roll, please. . . . The name of the method that scientists use to answer questions is . . . tah dah . . . the scientific method!

It may not sound flashy, but it seems to work very well, and it has three basic parts:

You must start with a good educated guess for the correct answer to your question. There's a $50 word for this type of guess. It's called a hypothesis.

You must design and carry out experiments and gather data (information) to test your hypothesis. Some experiments are done in a carefully controlled environment called a laboratory. Others are done in a natural setting such as the ocean, Earth, or outer space!

Based on the results collected in your experiments, you come up with a conclusion or a judgement about what it all means.

What's Your Theory?

When scientists gather more and more information from experiments, observations and mathematical calculations, they develop an idea about how it works. This is known as a theory.

Remember to Share...

Scientist like to share theories and ideas with other scientists (peers). This is called a peer review. Many scientific peers will carry out the same experiments to see if they get similar results.

title: So Many Questions
text:
How does a refrigerator work? What makes a pendulum keep swinging? Why does the moon look bigger when it first comes up? Is it possible to make the words on a page change without an eraser, pen, or pencil?

Surely, you have tons of questions about technology and how it works. That's what this column is all about. Each week, we'll take a quick and simple look at some pretty amazing technologies and briefly describe the science behind them. So watch carefully, and don't miss a single week. Then, when someone asks questions like one of those above, you'll be the smart kid with all the answers.

By the way, the moon looks larger when it first comes up because your eyes compare it to the horizon and not the larger open sky, which makes it appear smaller by comparison. It's an optical illusion.

title: Introducing Book Science
text:
Hey, science adventurers! We bet many of you love science-fiction books. There's nothing like settling in on a rainy Saturday afternoon to read about our favorite sci-fi characters zipping across space to battle evil aliens, traveling across time to prevent the end of the world or stalking strange creatures like dragons and shapeshifters.

But how much of that science fiction is pure fiction and how much is science? Have you ever asked that question? Check out this spot each week as we explore what we know about the scientific theories that give authors their ideas. We'll also try to point out technology we use today that was science fiction not long ago! Someday, in real life, will our technology be capable of doing the things we read about in books? And how long do scientists think it will be until our technology catches up with the amazing stuff in authors' imaginations?

We'll try to answer these questions and many more as we venture through some of the latest science fiction books, as well as some all-time classics. Next week we'll look at how one of the world's favorite wizards and his friends change matter. Is it real or are we being bamboozled by those bewitching books? Tune in next week to find out!

title: What does it mean to be objective?
text:
By testing their hypotheses (educated guesses - plural form of "hypothesis") with experiments to see if they are true, scientists are being objective. Being objective means that we don't just rely on our own imagination to explain something. Instead, we carefully examine the evidence to come up with accurate answers based on observations.

Some early ocean explorers saw strange animals such as manatees and thought they were magical creatures like mermaids, sea serpents or monsters. Too bad they didn't have a marine biologist to study the ocean animal life.

When scientists finally looked closely at the Florida manatee, they found not a mermaid or a monster, but a gentle animal who gracefully swims and nurtures its young.

Maybe those explorers were just at sea too long, because the Florida manatee can weigh up to 1,500 pounds and resembles a swimming baked potato, not a mermaid! They weren't very objective - that's for sure.

title: Sir Isaac Newton 1643-1727
text:
Sir Isaac Newton lived in an era when people didn't know too much about how the world worked. People still searched for answers about light, sound, the heavens above and the vast oceans that surrounded our shores - to say nothing of the living world around them.

Young Isaac grew up in a poor family in England. He was sent away at an early age to become a minister, but he really wanted to study mathematics. During his studies, Newton came up with many brilliant ideas. Legend has it that he once saw an apple fall from a tree in his orchard. Newton wondered what force pulled the apple to the Earth. He also wondered if that same force kept the moon from flying off into space. Eventually, Newton came up with the idea that is known today as the law of gravity. This law has explained why the apple fell, how the Earth keeps the moon from spinning out of its orbit and why planets and objects hold each other in place. Newton wrote about the laws of nature as he observed them. Newton also created a system of mathematics called calculus. Today, scientists, engineers and economists use calculus to calculate change.

Scientists have used Newton's ideas and theories to study everything around us. Today, all branches of science use his methods of study. Newton was one of the most influential scientists of all time.

title: Let's Investigate
text:
Scientists are like detectives. They investigate things to find out what's true. As you read Science Studies Weekly this year, you will be investigating things, too. We've included lots of activities that will help you find out what's true. You'll find at least one investigation in each weekly newspaper. We even gave your teacher some extra ideas for things you can investigate.

It's important for you to know how to do an investigation correctly. And it's just as important for you to come up with your own ideas about what to investigate. Read this column each week and before you know it, you'll be a top-notch science detective!

title: All About Matter
text:
Has anyone ever asked you, "What's the matter?" The next time someone asks that, try answering, "Well, actually, everything is matter!" You see, the universe is made up of lots of different things! Stars, planets, toothpaste, your toenails, gum, trees and . . . well, everything that takes up space - like a bacon, lettuce and tomato sandwich or pocket lint - is matter. But you wouldn't want a BLT with lint on it, so yep, it all matters how it's put together.

Can you think of how some things are similar or different - like a rock and a feather, for example? Some things are hard, others soft. Some things are smooth like glass, and others are rough like tree bark. Other things are colorful like flowers. Some things are cold like ice while others are hot like molten lava. When we talk about shape, size, color or texture (how it feels), we are describing properties of matter. What properties can you use to describe matter around you? What about this newspaper? Is it smooth or rough? What shape is it?

More than 2,000 years ago, a Greek thinker first guessed that everything must be made of tiny particles that could not be cut or divided into smaller particles. He called them atomos, which means "indivisible."

Nowadays, we call these tiny particles atoms. There are a limited number of different kinds of atoms that make up all matter! When the atoms in a chunk of matter are all the same, we call it an element. There are more than 100 basic materials called elements that make up everything we know of in the universe. Some of these elements you can see in their pure form, like gold or iron metals. But they can be combined to make anything. It is how atoms are put together that makes everything the way it is. So what's the matter? Turn the page to learn more.

title: Dr. Patricia Bath
text: Patricia Era Bath was born in Harlem, New York, in 1942. As an African American girl, she faced a childhood of stereotypes. To overcome these challenges, Patricia carved her own path and was quickly inspired to study science. The National Science Foundation scholarship that she was awarded in high school was the first of many honors to come. During her career as an ophthalmologist (a physician who treats eyes), Dr. Bath broke barriers in the field, both as a woman and as an African American. After attending Howard University College of Medicine, Bath worked to provide eye care for those in poor neighborhoods. Together with three other physicians, Dr. Bath founded the American Institute for the Prevention of Blindness; she was the institute's first president. She also patented a device to help remove cataracts from the clouded lenses of an eye. This device uses a fiber optic laser called a Laserphaco Probe. The laser tube is inserted in the eye through a tiny cut. It then vaporizes the cataract within moments. It was a revolution in eye care, especially for patients faced with possible blindness from cataracts. Dr. Bath's procedure and invention made eye surgeries easier, safer and faster. It also made her the first African American female doctor to patent a medical device. Since then she has continued to develop and refine her eye-saving techniques, and she educates people about eye health. Dr. Bath believes that eyesight is a basic right!

title: Understanding Matter
text:
Everything's Made of Atoms

As we were saying - all matter in the known universe is made of only about 100 different kinds of atoms or elements. Everything else is just a combination of those different atoms. Water, as you probably know, is a combination of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom - called H2O. Carbon dioxide, the stuff we exhale from our lungs, is a combination of carbon and oxygen atoms. In carbon dioxide, there are two oxygen atoms and one carbon atom. It's also known as CO2.

In this lesson, let's take a look at the basic structure of atoms and how they combine with each other to form all kinds of different matter.

Elements

Elements are made of molecules that have all the same atoms. Elements cannot be broken down into simpler substances. For example, gold is an element. It is made of only gold atoms. There are about 100 elements. Ninety-two occur in nature without our help. The number of protons in the nucleus determines what element it is. This is called the atomic number.

Molecules

When two or more atoms link together, they make a molecule. A molecule can be made up of atoms from the same element or a combination of different atom types.

Mass, Volume, Density and Weight

Mass is the amount of matter in an object. Volume is a measure of how much space matter takes up, like a gallon of milk or a two-liter bottle of soda pop. Density is a measure of how much mass is in a specific volume. You can measure things by their volume or their mass.

Gravity pulls on objects here on Earth because they have mass. Because of gravity, objects have weight. The mass of an object stays the same, but weight depends on gravitational force. The same object in outer space has the same mass as it does here, but the weight changes due to changes in gravity. An object that weighs 100 pounds on the Earth will weigh about 17 pounds on the moon because the moon's gravity doesn't pull as hard. There is one more thing you should know about the weight of matter: The weight of an object or substance is always equal to the sum of the weight of its parts.

Democritus

Ancient Greek thinkers such as Democritus noticed that things could be broken down into smaller pieces. He thought that everything could be built out of atoms, or the tiniest particles of matter that cannot be cut. He thought that these atoms moved around and flowed.

Actually, atoms can be split. Scientists discovered how to split atoms and release massive amounts of energy. This is known as nuclear fission and is what makes an atomic bomb.

Three Main Parts of an Atom

Atoms are made of three main parts: protons, neutrons and electrons.

Nucleus

The nucleus, or center of an atom, is where the neutrons and protons exist.

Check It Out!

Look very closely at this tiny atom. Actually, you can't! It is too small to see. Atoms are millions of times smaller than a speck of dust.

Electrons

Spinning around the nucleus of an atom are the electrons. Different types of matter have different numbers of electrons. Hydrogen only has one electron. Some atoms have many electrons like the uranium atom, which has 92!

Chemical Bonding

Shells

Can you see the rings around the nucleus in these illustrations? Each ring is called a shell. The first ring nearest the nucleus needs two electrons to fill the shell. Different atoms have various layers of shells.

Bonds

A bond happens when atoms come together and share electrons. If an atom has only one electron instead of two, like hydrogen, then it is attracted to other atoms like oxygen, which lacks two electrons in its outer shell. Two hydrogen atoms bond with the oxygen atom forming H2O, or water.

Mixtures

The next time you drink lemonade, think of it as a mixture. Mixtures are different materials that are mixed together but do not bond, or change into a new molecule. For instance, if you mix some salt in water, you can boil the water out, and the salt will still be there because it did not bond.

Compounds

Compounds are molecules that are made up of different types of atoms. For instance, when oxygen combines with hydrogen, water molecules are formed.

title: High-Tech Ink!
text:
You probably know a lot of people who would rather read a newspaper or a book than a computer screen. Papers and books are easier to read and carry around than most laptops. People continue to buy millions of newspapers and books every day. But now people have a choice. Have you heard about Electronic Paper Displays? EPDs can be read from any angle just like paper, and you can read them even in bright sunlight. They also have a long battery life, because they only use power when the image changes.

A company called E Ink developed the EPDs. They use technology called an "active matrix ink display." The technology uses black-and-white ink in tiny micro-capsules that can be controlled by electric fields. The electric fields determine which part (top or bottom) of the capsule the white and black inks move to. If they want black letters, they "zap" the black ink to the top, and they have readable print! This process can be used to form letters and pictures on a "page" that looks like the ones you're reading right now! The ink capsules are imbedded inside plastic film, which has a layer of electronic circuits attached to it.

E Ink makes electronic-ink books and screens for computers, cellular phones, digital cameras-even wearable images. Imagine wearing a T-shirt that flashes the current time and temperature throughout the day. The screens really do look a lot like a newspaper. Hey, maybe someday soon you'll be reading Science Studies Weekly on an EPD. Now that is smart technology! Check out www.eink.com to learn more.

title: Transfiguration: ‘Harry Potter’ series by J. K. Rowling
text:
If you've read the "Harry Potter" books you know Harry, Ron and Hermione take a class called transfiguration. In transfiguration, they change one item into another, like a matchstick into a needle, or a rat into a goblet. Professor McGonagall can even change herself into a cat! Is that really possible?

Well, matter is constantly changing, but not in the magical ways you read about in Harry Potter. Physical changes to matter happen all the time. For example, ice melts into water, and water can be heated into a gas. But it's all still good old H2O.

Chemical changes happen a lot, too. Chemical changes turn one substance into another. When you burn your toast in the morning, that's a chemical change. When the milk in the refrigerator goes sour, that's a chemical change. You can't reverse chemical changes.

But what they do in the "Harry Potter" books isn't a physical or chemical change. They're taking elements and molecules and changing them into different elements and molecules. They're changing the metal in the needle into wood, and the flesh and bone of the rat into glass! We know changes like that aren't possible because these things are made of different elements. Some people used to believe that it was possible to change one element into another, like turning lead into gold. But scientists haven't found a reliable way to do that. So for now, the magic in the "Harry Potter" books is just that - magic!

title: How do scientists know atoms exist if atoms are so small?
text:
Scientists have many ways to detect atoms. In the early days, Greek thinkers believed atoms existed just because it seemed to be the most obvious theory. But because of amazing scientific inventions, we can now actually see individual atoms! Scientists use the new Scanning Tunneling Microscope (STM) and scanning probe microscopes to see single atoms. They take "pictures" of atoms using a tiny needle that sends electrons over atoms on a surface. The device detects when there is an atom, and the needle moves up and down. The movement of the needle lets scientists use computers to make a picture of the shape of the surface of the atom.

How do they keep atoms from flying away? Well, they have to cool them to freezing temperatures so that they don't move on their own. Recently, they also discovered how to control atom movement at higher temperatures.

Even more amazing, scientists at Oxford University used the tip of the STM to move 37 atoms to spell the letters IBM, thanking the IBM company for their help with the project. You may have heard the saying, "Always read the fine print," but that's ridiculous!

title: Marie Curie 1867-1934
text:
Marie Curie was a great scientist! Like many scientists of her day, she wondered about X-rays. She wanted to know why an element called uranium fogged up photographic film when it was nearby. She thought there must be some sort of energy coming from it. So, she got permission to use a university storage room to do experiments. Marie and her husband, Pierre, studied radioactivity, the energy that fogged up the film. Radioactivity is a form of energy that comes from very special elements. They were the first to discover two radioactive elements called radium and polonium.

The Curies won the Nobel Prize in 1903 for their discovery. The Nobel Prize is considered by many to be the highest award for people who make a big contribution to the world. Marie Curie became the first person to win two Nobel Prizes! In 1911, she won another Nobel Prize for her continued research in radioactivity.

Back then, people did not know that too much exposure to radiation energy increases the risk of some cancers. Sadly, Marie Curie died of cancer at age 67. Her research was very important in helping us understand radioactivity, and many scientists used her findings to make even more discoveries and uses for radioactive elements.

title: Let's Investigate
text:
Welcome back to Let's Investigate, science detectives. This week we're going to talk about the steps in doing a science investigation correctly. Did someone say, "Where do I start?" You just did! Asking questions is the first step in an investigation. Here's a step-by-step list of what to do:

Ask a question.

Think of a possible answer. Scientists call this a hypothesis.

Make a plan to test your hypothesis.

Test your hypothesis.

Record the results of the test.

Share your results with others.

It's a good idea to write these steps in your science journal or cut out this article and save it. You'll need to know these steps many times this year. Next week we'll work together to plan an investigation!

title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
text:
It took more than 2,000 years to find out if Greek thinkers were right about the existence of atoms. Since those days, we have learned much about matter and how matter works. Matter can exist in three main states or "phases." What are they? They are solids, liquids and gases.

Solids are things like rocks, metals and stuff that keeps its shape. Solids have shape and volume.

Liquids are things that you can pour, like water or maple syrup. Liquids have volume, but no shape.

Gases don't have shape, and they flow. Oxygen is a gas; you breathe it. It has matter, but you can't see it. Most gases cannot be seen.

As matter changes states, it still keeps the same chemical structure. For instance, when water freezes into a solid (ice), it's still two parts hydrogen and one part oxygen, or H2O.

Solids, liquids and gases are found all over the place! The family car has all three-metal, gasoline, and exhaust gases. A bottle of soda pop has all three-bottle, drink, and bubbles. Even your body has them. Your bones and teeth are solid, your blood and bile are liquids, and the oxygen carried in your blood is gas, needed for life. That unwelcome burp at the lunch table - well, those are gases making their escape from the surrounding liquids and solids in your stomach. Excuuuuuuse me!

Now we're going to ask you the same question Greek thinkers asked themselves more than 2,000 years ago: Why are some things solid, liquid or gas? But, instead of waiting 2,000 years to learn the answer, all you have to do is turn the page.

title: Philanthropy and Values
text:
Maybe you have heard the word "philanthropy" before. What does it mean? It describes actions that people make for the good of other people. What is a value? It's a way of behaving that people believe is good - like believing it's good to be honest. Is honesty one of your values?

One way you can practice philanthropy today is to help yourself and others learn good values. How do you learn good values? You can learn them from your parents and grandparents, your teachers at school or church and other people you trust.

You can also learn them from people that have been recognized for doing good things for society. An easy way to learn about people that have done good things is to visit values.com. Values.com has lots of stories and short videos that highlight the traits that make each of us better people. They even have billboards on the highway to remind you about good values.

For example, you may have seen a billboard that looks like the one shown here.

This billboard is about Oral Lee Brown, who saved money from her job to send 19 kids to college...all by herself! Wow! Isn't that cool? You can learn about lots of other people who practice philanthropy at values.com. Be sure to look for more of their "billboards" on Page 4 of Studies Weekly this year. We think they're so cool we want to remind you to check them out!

title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
text:
Why is a solid a solid?

Matter can exist as a solid, a liquid, or a gas. Solids keep the same shape because their atoms move very slowly around each other. Some solids are made of atoms that are almost completely still and just slightly vibrating. When an object's atoms are packed closer together, then that object tends to have a higher density. Very dense solids, like lead, are also very heavy. If you have a piece of styrofoam and a piece of lead the same shape and size, the lead is more dense and packed more tightly with atoms. It also weighs more!

When molecules lose enough heat energy, they freeze, or become solid, like an iceberg.

Why is liquid a liquid?

If solids are solid because their molecules are close together and hardly move, can you guess why liquids are liquid? Well, for the most part, because the atoms move around more. When a solid becomes a liquid, the atoms speed up, usually because of heat. The molecules break away from each other and start to slide all over. Because it does not keep its shape like a solid, a liquid may be poured and will take the shape of any container it is poured into.

When liquids are exposed to air, they evaporate, especially if the air is warm. Some of the molecules break away and mix into the air.

What makes gas a gas?

When a liquid is heated enough, it will turn into a gas. Gas molecules are always on the go. They vibrate and move around so much that they can't stay together like a solid or liquid. They just float away! Gases come in handy. Neon gas, when heated by electricity, glows. We trap it inside those multi-colored lights that can be seen at night. Gases usually try to escape through the atmosphere. The air we breathe has different kinds of gases in it, mostly nitrogen, oxygen, and carbon dioxide.

Sometimes, water drops form on objects when the air cools. That is called condensation.

Changing States

Matter changes state when it's heated or cooled. So, water changes from solid (ice) to liquid at about 32 degrees Fahrenheit (which is its melting point) and transforms from liquid to gas (steam) at 212 degrees Fahrenheit (boiling point).

Different molecules melt at different temperatures: Gold stays solid (or frozen) until melted at 1,948 degrees Fahrenheit. It boils at a whopping 5,085 degrees!

title: The Power of Changing States
text:
Some pretty smart people realized that if you put water in a closed container and use heat to change its state from liquid to steam (gas), it will take up more space as the molecules move farther apart. As a result, great pressure is created that can push a piston and make an engine turn.

In the 1800s, trains and steam ships were powered by steam engines. Today, nuclear power plants use steam turbines, and the Navy uses steam-powered catapults to launch jet fighters from aircraft carriers. Steam power is still very much in use today. For many jobs that need lots of power, steam is simply the best!

All this technology is made possible because of a scientific understanding of the changing states of matter.

title: There’s No Place Like Somewhere Else!
text:
Do you ever wish you could just disappear from one place and appear in another? During a spelling test you might have thought, "Why can't I be out on the playground?" When your parents tell you to clean your room, you'd probably rather be just about anywhere else on the planet. You might have even tried closing your eyes, clicking your heels and saying, "There's no place like Disney World," kind of like Dorothy in the Wizard of Oz!

Will that ever be possible? Well, the idea of instant (quantum) teleportation of matter from one location to another has been a popular idea in books for hundreds of years. The djinns in "The Arabian Nights" stories could travel instantly between different countries. In the X-Men comic books, Nightcrawler teleports in a puff of red smoke. Harry Potter and his friends use Floo Powder to teleport through fireplaces. But in real life? Well, that's a different story. Atomic particles are tricky because they can move incredibly fast, and that makes recording them at any point in time a big problem. Some scientists argue that anyone who steps into the teleporter would disintegrate (be destroyed) as his or her information is sent to the other side! If it worked, would that be you, or a copy of you, on the other side?

Scientists at the University of Innsbruck, Austria, have shown how to take a photon (particle of light energy) and in an instant make a replica of it in a different place. The researchers don't believe this will lead to teleporting people. Instead it will be used for making super "quantum" fast computers and communications. For now, we'll just have to settle for "teleporting" ideas.

title: How do hot air balloons work?
text:
Have you ever heard the expression "you are just full of hot air!"? Well, if you were, you might be a bit lighter. When you heat a gas, it expands. If you trap hot, expanding air in a ballon, it becomes lighter than the cooler air outside and goes up! People control balloons by heating them up with a flame. When heated, the balloon goes up, and when it's cool, it comes back down. Balloons are steered by going up or down to find air currents to blow them in the right direction.

Hot air balloons were first used centuries ago. Did you know that the first recorded passengers in a hot air balloon were a sheep, a rooster, and a duck in 1793? The first manned flight was a few months later. Since then, balloons have been made for many uses.

Airships, such as blimps, have been around for about 100 years and were once used to fly people across the Atlantic. At first, they were filled with hydrogen, which is flammable, but now they are filled with helium.

People still fly in hot air balloons. In 1999, Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones were the first to fly a balloon around the world nonstop. They did it in 19 days, 1 hour, and 49 minutes.

Nowadays, scientists and students send up equipment such as cameras or measuring devices in helium-filled balloons and blimps. This lets them study the Earth's weather and atmosphere.

title: George Washington Carver c.1864-1943
text:
If you want to read an inspiring story, read about George Washington Carver! He was a teacher, scientist, businessman, farmer, writer, artist and performer. George invented things using chemistry and food. Food?

George lived in the South after the Civil War. Things were hard for people in the South. It was hard for them to sell their crops. Carver thought of ways they could make new products out of the vegetables and fruits they grew. You have probably used or eaten something Carver invented. He invented an early form of peanut butter! He developed grease for cars, bleach, chili sauce, dyes, ink, conditioning shampoo, shoe polish, shaving cream, Worcestershire sauce, dried milk, face creams, paints, paper, and many other useful things.

In his day, Carver was considered one of the world's greatest chemists. It didn't come easy for him. He was on his own at age 13 and had to work to pay for his schooling. He did not make money from his products. He gave them away to help people. Mr. Carver was honored with a national monument dedicated by President Franklin Delano Roosevelt on July 14, 1943. Before his death in 1943, Carver was given many prestigious awards. The scientific field that now continues to make useful things out of agriculture by using chemistry is called biochemical engineering.

title: Let's Investigate
text:
This week we're going to help you plan an investigation about how matter changes. We'll start by asking a question: Which melts faster-an ice cube on a sunny windowsill or an ice cube under a lamp? Now, you need to think of a possible answer (hypothesis) and write it down. Next, you need a plan. Make a list of things you'll need to test your hypothesis and the steps you will follow in the test.

Here's the fun part. Do the test. Record your results by writing down how long it took each ice cube to melt. Finally, share your results. What's the best way to do that? You can write a paragraph, draw a picture, use a computer or give a report to your class. And those are just a few ideas. Different ideas work for different investigations.

title: Turn On the Heat!
text:
Every living thing needs energy to grow and work. Energy is inside us and all around us. One form of energy is heat. Rub your hands together. What happens? They heat up. There are many sources of heat. Rubbing sticks together can make heat from friction. Electricity produces heat in machinery, stoves and furnaces. Mixing certain chemicals together can produce heat. Don't forget that the sun warms our whole solar system. Heat energy is all around us and is very important for life. This week in Science Studies Weekly, let's take a close look at the nature of heat energy.

Here's a trick question: Which has the most heat: a red-hot horseshoe or a big chunk of ice the size of a school bus? If the question had been a little different - like "Which has a higher temperature?" - "red-hot horseshoe" would be the right answer. But the big chunk of ice actually has more heat in it because of its size. Now go ask your mom or dad the same question. It's easy to forget that temperature and amount of heat are two different things.

Here's another question: Do things just "cool down," or does heat "move away"? That's a trick question because things do cool down, but it's important to realize that they don't cool down because more "coldness" gets into them, but because the heat energy inside them moves away, or is transferred.

Here's one more question: Have you ever noticed the "chi-chunk, chi-chunk, chi-chunk" sound that your family's car makes as it goes over a bridge or a highway? Now that's a weird question. What does the sound of tires driving over a bridge have to do with heat? Well, turn the page, and you'll learn the answers to that question and all the others we've brought up: What's the difference between amount of heat and temperature? How does heat energy move from one object to another? And why do tires make the "chi-chunk, chi-chunk, chi-chunk" sound while crossing a bridge?

title: Temperature and Heat
text:
What's the difference between temperature and heat?

Temperature gives a report, or measurement, about how hot an object is. This is the same as saying how fast its molecules are moving, but not how many molecules there are. The faster the molecules of an object are moving, or vibrating, the higher the temperature of that object rises.

Heat is the name of the energy that's inside an object because its molecules are moving. The red-hot horseshoe has a high temperature because its molecules are moving very quickly. However, the huge ice chunk has more heat energy because of its great size. It's kind of like the molecules inside the bus are saying to the molecules inside the horseshoe, "We may be co- co- co-colder, but there are more of us than there are of you."

Heat Transfer

If you stepped out of a helicopter onto the ice of the Arctic, it would be very cold. Why would you feel cold? Well, the heat in your body escapes, or transfers into the cold environment. That is why people wear insulating clothes. What would happen if you flew to a hot place, like the equator? Would you want to wear insulating clothes? Why not? Well, in hot weather, you want to stay cool and comfortable. So you tend to do things to cool off, like take a swim. You want to transfer heat away from you.

Heat tends to move around from hotter objects to colder ones. This evens out differences in temperature. It does this in three different ways: conduction, convection and radiation.

Conduction

Have you ever been totally bored? Just sittin' there with nothin' to do? Then all of a sudden, your friends come by. They're so excited because they're going to the park. Pretty soon, you get excited because they're so excited. Their excitement "rubs off" onto you. Conduction is kind of like that. If the molecules of an object are "bored," and they're hardly moving, then that object is cold. But when it touches another object that has faster-moving molecules, its molecules start moving faster.

Some materials conduct heat better than others. Metals are very good conductors. Wood is a very poor conductor. That's why a metal pan has a wooden handle. The metal conducts heat to your food, but the wooden handle keeps the heat from conducting to your hand. Materials that are poor conductors, like wood, plastic, and cloth, are called insulators.

Convection

Heat makes air rise. When heat moves with air flow, it's known as convection. Eventually, the air cools and comes back down again, causing circulation. Heat is a major source of weather changes as we will discuss later in geoscience! The heater in your home or school works from convection as warm air is circulated around the room with blowers or fans.

Radiation

Almost everything radiates heat - even people. Have you ever been in a crowded room with no air circulation? Why does it get so hot? It gets hot because everyone in the room is warm blooded, and all that body heat is radiating into the room. Have you ever held your hand a few inches from a bulb? Light bulbs radiate heat. Of course, the best heat radiator of all is the sun.

Expansion and Contraction

What does heat have to do with the "chi-chunk, chi-chunk, chi-chunk" sound as you drive over a bridge? We thought you'd never ask. As the molecules inside an object move around and vibrate, they heat up. So, the hotter something gets, the more its molecules are moving. As the molecules move more quickly, they also tend to take up more room, and the object stretches or expands. As the object cools down, it will contract, or get smaller. This is because the molecules aren't moving as much and require less space. Water is one exception. When water freezes, it actually expands. So, does that mean you're taller in the summer and shorter in the winter? Of course not. But a piece of bridge that's one mile long can expand more than 18 inches. Yikes! Concrete and steel are not that stretchy! So engineers, knowing about expansion and contraction, design bridges with expansion slots. These slots are usually no wider than a half inch, and they're spaced about 10 to 20 feet apart. That gives the bridge plenty of room to expand and contract without breaking and falling apart. As you drive over these expansion slots, your tires make a "chi-chunk, chi-chunk, chi-chunk" sound.

title: Refrigeration
text:
Refrigeration was one of the "coolest" inventions to come along in modern times. This is how it works: When we transfer the heat energy away from an object, the atoms in the object slow down, and the temperature of that object drops. You see, if you take two objects that are different temperatures and put them together, they will eventually equalize, or become the same temperature. Refrigerators use liquids, known as refrigerant, which are very cold, to absorb the heat. The heat is expelled from inside the refrigerator. That is why you feel heat coming from the back of the refrigerator.

Your body has its own refrigeration - sweating! When you sweat, heat from your body is removed, absorbed in the sweat on your skin, and then transferred to the air as the sweat evaporates. Computers use gadgets called heat sinks. Heat sinks are materials that are put into computers or machines to absorb heat and expel it, helping the machine stay cool. Fans are also handy for blowing away the heat! That's right - fans help transfer heat as well!

title: Heat Transfer: ‘Granny Torrelli Makes Soup’ by Sharon Creech
text:
This week's book isn't a science fiction book, but it's a great book and there is science in it. How? Through cooking, of course. "Granny Torrelli Makes Soup" is about Rosie, who lives near her best friend, Bailey. Granny Torrelli, Rosie's Italian grandmother, is a great cook. When you cook, heat is transferred from the stove to the pot. The heat cooks whatever is in the pot, leaving you with a delicious meal.

When the two friends have a falling out, Granny Torrelli gets them into the kitchen to help her make soup and pasta. Both the soup and the pasta are cooked by conduction. The fast-moving molecules of the stove were heated. The stove was touching the pot, and the fast-moving molecules were touching the slow-moving molecules. What happened next? That's right. The slow moving molecules started moving faster, and the pot and the soup heated up.

Heat transfer happens throughout "Granny Torrelli Makes Soup." Anytime Granny, Rosie and Bailey are cooking anything, they are transferring heat from the stove or oven to the pots, pans and food.

Heat transfer is a big deal in the real world, and it's a big deal in some books, too. Rosie and Bailey don't just learn about heat transfer in this book. They learn about how to make and keep friends, and that's a recipe we all can use!

title: How are fossil fuels formed?
text:
Fossil fuels are substances like oil, coal and natural gas that are buried inside our Earth. They are used by humans today to produce fuel for transportation, to provide power to homes and businesses, and to create many other products.

Fossil fuels are here on our planet because of our sun. Millions of years ago, plants used energy from the sun to make food. Ancient animals ate those plants and other animals that had eaten the plants. The animals stored all of that energy in their bodies. When the plants and animals died, their remains were buried by mud in swamps, lakes, rivers and other bodies of water. The force of the water moved the mud around and covered the remains under many layers of muck.

As time passed, the plants and animals were buried deeper. Pressure and heat began to change their form. Over millions of years, these remains were changed into fossil fuels. Can you understand why we need to conserve these non-renewable resources and keep looking for renewable sources of energy? Will we be around for a million years while new fossil fuel is being formed?

title: The Temperature Team
text:
Daniel Fahrenheit, 1686-1736

Daniel Fahrenheit invented the mercury and alcohol thermometers. Because a thermometer would make more sense if it had numbers on it, he developed the Fahrenheit scale. This scale uses 32 degrees as the freezing point and 212 as the boiling point of water. Fahrenheit discovered that different liquids boiled at different temperatures.

Anders Celsius, 1701-1744

Anders Celsius was a Swedish astronomer, but is most famous for his temperature scale. He made one point of the scale zero degrees where water boils and 100 degrees where ice melts. Later, the scale was reversed so that zero was freezing and 100 was boiling.

Lord Kelvin, William Thompson, 1824-1907

Lord Kelvin studied mathematics and found that math could be used to measure and calculate heat and other forms of energy. He proposed using what is called an absolute scale of measurement. With the Kelvin scale, absolute zero is the temperature at which an atom is totally at "rest" and has zero heat or thermal energy. This point is the same as -460 degrees Fahrenheit.

title: Let's Investigate
text:
How did your ice cube investigation go last week? Did it make you think of more questions about ice cubes? If so, then good work! When scientists do an investigation, they almost always come up with more questions to answer. Make a list of some questions you thought of after the ice cube investigation. (Would a stronger or weaker light bulb change the results? Would it make a difference if the ice cubes were in a container made of different material-glass, plastic, metal? What would happen if you took the shade off the lamp?)

Was your hypothesis true? If not, then good work! What? It's good to be wrong? Scientists often learn more from their mistakes than from their successes. If your first guess seems to be right, you probably won't try again. But scientists know that it's important to do an investigation many times. That's how you find out what's really true.

title: Measuring Energy
text:
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, but it can be transformed (changed) into other forms of energy. For example, the sun's energy is used by plants to create food energy. Energy can also be measured, so that scientists know how much energy is being transformed.

How do scientists measure energy? One basic measurement is the British thermal unit (Btu). A Btu is the amount of energy it takes to raise the temperature of a pound of water one degree Fahrenheit at sea level. A peanut butter and jelly sandwich has more than 1,000 Btus of energy! A joule is another measurement of energy. A joule is the amount of energy it takes to lift a one-pound object to a height of nine inches. One thousand joules is equal to 1 Btu. We measure the flow of electrical energy in watts. One watt is equal to one joule per second flowing through an electrical system.

Use the information above to help you solve the following problems:

If you lift a one-pound object 36 inches, how many joules of energy did you use? _______________________

If you lift a five-pound object 18 inches, how many joules of energy did you use? _______________________

If you lift a seven-pound object 54 inches, how many joules of energy did you use? _______________________

title: Light and Sound
text:
Hey, you science adventurers! This week, we're talking about two very exciting things: light and sound. Why? Because when you think about it, we'd be in pretty sad shape without them - especially light. Did you know that without light your car wouldn't work? In fact, just about everything in this world is "solar" powered in a roundabout way. You see, all the fossil fuels that we use for energy come from . . . well, fossils (traces of organisms that were once alive). You see, plants use energy from the sun to make their own food in a process known as photosynthesis. Eventually, plant material is fossilized and turned into coal, oil, and other materials we burn for energy. We need light so much that if the sun took a vacation, in a few days we'd all freeze solid, break into tiny pieces, and basically become a lifeless planet for future aliens to study.

Most people think about light and sound together because seeing and hearing things are the primary ways we communicate. But actually, light and sound are very different things. Light is an electromagnetic energy that travels through space at 186,000 miles per second, and sound is made from air that has been pushed by something moving.

Light and sound can be tricky sometimes. For example, when you look at the stars at night, you might wonder, "Are they really there?" It takes light billions of years to travel from some stars before it reaches your eye. By the time we see the light of the stars, how do we know they're still there? We don't.

Sound can be tricky, too. When an explosion goes off some distance away, the explosion is seen before it is heard. You may see a supersonic fighter jet flying toward you before you hear it. It takes awhile for the sound traveling at 1,115 feet per second to reach your ears. Light can travel through outer space, but sound can't. There is no air in outer space. So when you see a movie that has sounds of rockets and explosions in outer space, that's just for effect.

Turn the page, and let’s talk about light and sound, two very different forms of energy.

title: The Viral Numbers of YouTube™
text:
Ever wonder how many people watched the video on YouTube™ that made you laugh uncontrollably? How many videos are posted on the website each day? How often do they change? YouTube™ has become a viral form of entertainment and communication. A virus is something that is contagious and spreads quickly. A viral video is one that spreads like wildfire across the Internet, and YouTube™ knows all about them. In fact, judging by the statistics, you could say that it has become a viral website. It spread so quickly that it has exploded into a multi-million dollar enterprise. Let's look at some numbers.

According to the numbers on the company's website, there are over 2 billion views each week. Over 24 hours of new video are uploaded every minute. The average user spends at least 15 minutes on YouTube™ each day. Keeping track of statistics like these can be a big part of a company's success. Collecting, organizing and interpreting data helps a company like YouTube™ sell ads. If you want to advertise your product, would you rather have 2 billion viewers a day or a few million (the average number of TV viewers)? YouTube™ is counting on advertisers to pick them over its competitors.

title: Light and Sound
text:
What is a spectrum?

Light is part of the electromagnetic (EM) energy spectrum. A spectrum is a range of something. Take, for instance, height: How tall are you compared to all the other students in your school? If you line every student up in order of height from the shortest to the tallest, there would be a wide range, or spectrum, of student heights.

What is the electromagnetic (EM) spectrum?

The EM spectrum is a wide range of energy waves that radiate from the sun and other sources. If there is a whole spectrum of waves, then there must be waves of many different sizes, right? Gee, you're a fast learner.

Let's talk about some different kinds of waves you already know. Even if you've never been to the ocean, you know that for surfing you want big waves, but for water skiing you want little waves or no waves. Electromagnetic waves work the same way. Different sizes of waves work for different purposes. Some waves are just the right size to make them visible to our eyes. This part of the EM spectrum is called visible light.

Light is just a small part of the EM spectrum. You are already familiar with many different types, or sizes, of waves on the EM spectrum. You've listened to the radio, cooked food in microwaves and flipped channels on the television. You may have gotten an X-ray at the doctor's office, or maybe you've seen police officers hand out speeding tickets. The police use radar waves to help catch speeders.

Light Particles?

A particle of light is called a photon. Photons can result from atoms that get excited and more energetic. If an atom becomes excited, as it does with electricity, electrons give off photons, or light energy. That is why you can see electricity (sparks).

So, light can be looked at as waves or as particles. Light waves are very short. They are only a few atoms long. Sound frequencies we can hear range from about 20 to 20,000 hertz (vibrations per second).

Light frequencies are several hundred trillion times faster.

Refraction

Light can bend when it passes through something like a glass of water. That is called refraction. It is why a straw looks bent when you put it in a glass of water. When light bounces off of something, it is called reflection. This is what happens when you look in the mirror.

About Sound

Both sound and light travel in waves. However, sound travels more slowly. Sound is energy caused by objects moving or vibrating. For instance, when you clap your hands, it makes vibrations in the air, which travel a certain distance. The sound waves bounce off other objects as well. Sound cannot travel in outer space (a vacuum), but can travel through air, metal and other materials. Sound travels through water at about 4,600 feet per second. It travels more slowly through air at 1,115 feet per second.

There are a lot of aircraft that can travel faster than sound. The fastest jet we have is the SR 71 Blackbird. It's an American spy plane that can go more than 2,200 miles per hour. That's almost three times the speed that sound travels (about 740 mph). If a jet flies at the speed of sound, its speed is referred to as Mach 1. The Blackbird flies at almost Mach 3. You would see the jet coming on the horizon before you heard it.

Dynamics of Sound

The loudness of a sound depends on the wave height or amplitude. Sound amplitude is measured in decibels, or how loud something is. A rock concert can be more than 100 decibels. Check out the chart on the right to see how loud things are. The pitch of the sound depends on the frequency of the waves, or how fast they vibrate the air. For instance, 256 vibrations per second (256 Hz) makes musical note middle C. The faster the vibration, the higher the pitch. Sound frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), or vibrations per second - just as light is.

title: The Sound of Silence!
text:
Noise pollution is a problem for people who want peace and quiet. If you live near a busy freeway, or a railroad track, you probably know this. Some cities put up sound walls to help bounce the sound waves away from neighborhoods.

In the future, neighborhoods may hear less annoying noise as researchers design ways of blocking sound. For instance, in Florida, neighbors complained about the loud circus. So experts developed a way of using sound to "fight" sound. Engineers created a "wall" of sound that deflected the noises of the circus.

Sound travels from an object in waves. If we know the frequency and amplitude (height and shape of the wave), we can actually cancel out the waves by creating a wave with the exact opposite wave shape or pattern. Using this principle, Sony has made noise-canceling headphones that reduce outside noise by up to 70 percent!

title: Seeing in Darkness: ‘Fablehaven’ by Brandon Mull
text:
From Greek mythology to the Harry Potter series, readers love stories about heroes with super powers. The fantasy series "Fablehaven" introduces readers to 13-year-old Kendra and her younger brother Seth. They discover an exciting hidden world of fairies, witches and other mythological creatures. Kendra drinks magical milk that gives her the power to see in total darkness. Is this really possible? Let's look at how the eye works.

The front part of the eye is called the cornea. It's like a clear window where light enters the eye. The colored part you see is the iris. Its muscles make the opening in the center of the eye (the pupil) larger or smaller. You can see the iris change by looking in a mirror as you move from a dark room to a light room. The lens focuses the images we look at. Then rods and cones inside the retina (the membrane that line the inside of the eye) add color. Finally the image travels through the optic nerve to the brain. Voila! We can "see" it.

In other words, no light, no sight. Thanks to technology, goggles and binoculars that have something called "night vision" allow us to see an object two blocks away on a moonless night. They amplify the tiny bit of light present. Many nocturnal animals have eyes which can pick up very small amounts of light. They can see much better than humans can, but none can see in total darkness.

Kendra's super vision helps save the day in Fablehaven. For us regular folks, milk can be a source of calcium and Vitamin D, but it won't let you see in the dark.

title: Why do we see color?
text:
Light energy is just part of the electromagnetic (EM) spectrum. There are many different sizes of waves, or wavelengths, in the EM spectrum. Humans have the ability to detect differences in the wavelengths of visible light. How is that, you ask? Simple. Our eyes and brains detect differences in wavelengths as differences in color. Violet is the shortest wavelength we can see. Red is the longest. White light is what we see when all the colors are mixed together in equal amounts.

The tricky part is light absorption. The sun, light bulbs, fire and lightning have one thing in common: They produce light. But most things either reflect light or absorb light - they don't produce it. Different materials absorb different parts of the light spectrum. The parts they don't absorb are reflected. A banana looks yellow because it absorbs all of the light hitting it except for the yellow part of the spectrum - which it reflects. If you have black hair, your hair absorbs all of the wavelengths of light. White hair reflects all of the spectrum of light.

Think of your cordless phone. If it gave off shorter energy waves, they would be part of the visible spectrum. You'd be able to use your phone as a flashlight while you're talking on it. Wow, it's a good thing we can only see part of the EM spectrum. With all of the millions of radios, televisions and microwaves that are beaming around, it'd be really confusing to go anywhere at night!

title: Alexander Graham Bell 1847-1922
text:
Pick up any phone book, and chances are you will see the word "Bell" on it. Alexander Graham Bell, a Scottish inventor, was not very good with his hands, so he hired young Thomas Watson, a mechanic and model maker, to help him make a new telegraph machine. In 1875, he invented a machine that could send more than one signal across electrical wires.

Sound was important to Alexander. His father was a speech expert, and his mother was deaf. Alexander taught deaf people to speak by feeling the vibrations of sound.

He believed that he could send human speech over electrical wires. He invented a device that was sensitive to the vibrations made from speech. It changed the vibrations of speech into electrical signals that were conducted over electrical wires. On the other end, the electrical impulses were then fed into an instrument that converted them into vibrations that reproduced the sound of speech.

Now, almost everyone has a telephone! Alexander didn't stop there, though. He invented a device that used beams of light to send sound as well. It was sort of an early model for today's fiber optics.

title: Let's Investigate
text:
Let's talk a little bit more about your ice cube investigation. Did you remember to list everything you needed? Or did you start your test and find out you forgot something? Here's our list:

2 ice cubes (the same size)

a sunny windowsill

a lamp

a clock

2 clear plastic cups

Your list doesn't have to look exactly like ours. But some things in an investigation need to be the same. Would this investigation work if one ice cube was big and one was small? What if you put one ice cube in a plastic cup and one in a metal pie pan? How would you know what was really true if the ice cubes were different sizes or in different containers? When you do an investigation, be sure to eliminate (get rid of) anything that might make it hard to find out what's true.

title: Electricity and Magnetism
text:
It is amazing to think about how electricity and magnets have changed our world! Most appliances in your home wouldn't run without the use of magnets and electricity. Computers need both. Your refrigerator, family car and electric guitar wouldn't work without them, either!

Do you know who invented electricity? Was it Benjamin Franklin? Actually, that is a trick question. Electricity has been around as long as there have been atoms. We just learned how to use it as a powerful friend over the last couple of centuries.

People have known about electricity for ages. The ancient Greek thinker Thales found that if you rub cloth with a piece of amber, the cloth attracts objects such as feathers. So rubbing things together made them electrically charged. Amber, or fossilized tree sap, was called "elektron" in ancient Greek, hence the name electricity. That sounds better than "ambericity."

The ancient Greek thinker Aristotle knew about magnetic stones known as lodestones that attracted metal. So, people have known about magnetism for a long time as well.

In 1794, Alessandro Volta, the Italian inventor, discovered that if two metals were put together in a salt solution they produced electricity. Batteries today use the same basic idea.

In 1820, a Danish scientist named Hans Christian Oersted discovered that magnets and electricity are very closely related. He found that electricity can be used to make magnets and that magnets can be used to generate electricity. What a discovery! People could make gobs of electricity with magnets! This discovery led to the invention of the generator and the electric motor. It didn't take very long until the world started changing like crazy! Tons of devices and gadgets have been invented to use and produce electricity and magnetic force.

So plug yourself into Science Studies Weekly and learn all about the stuff that makes the world go 'round!

title: Who Invented the World Wide Web?
text:
What do you like to do in your spare time? Some of you probably like to play on the computer or even search the Internet. Thanks to British scientist, Timothy Berners-Lee, we have that option. In 1989, he invented a software program that allows us to easily send and receive information from the Internet. He named this new program the World Wide Web (www or Web).

Are you wondering what the difference is between the Web and the Internet? The Web is only one of the ways that information can be shared over the Internet. For example, e-mail and instant messaging do not use the Web. They are completely separate programs that don't need the Web to work.

Timothy Berners-Lee was born in England in 1955. Both of his parents were computer scientists and loved technology. As Timothy grew up, they passed their love of computers on to him. Timothy's favorite subject in school was math and he was also interested in electronics. He used these two interests to start a future in computers. Today, he is the director of the World Wide Web Consortium and has also published a book called "Weaving the Web." In his book he describes how he developed the Web and why it is so important.

title: Electricity and Magnetism
text:
Where Electricity Comes From

Electricity comes from atoms. Remember that each atom has tiny electrons that orbit around a nucleus, which has protons and neutrons in it. Both protons and electrons have something called an electric charge. Each proton has a positive charge (+), and each orbiting electron has a negative charge (-). Neutrons have no charge at all. They are neutral. Positive and negative charges balance each other out in an atom. So when you have equal numbers of electrons and protons in a single atom, you have a neutral atom, or one with no charge.

Positively charged atoms are atoms that have more protons than electrons. Negatively charged atoms are atoms that have more electrons than protons. If they're connected to a material that conducts electricity, the extra negative electrons will flow to atoms that have a positive charge. Then - ZAP! - you have an electrical current. Remember, the electrons move from atom to atom in search of positive atoms or matter. The atoms themselves don't travel.

Electrical Flow

A battery has two terminals. One is positive (+), and the other is negative (-). The electrons flow toward the positive terminal when the circuit is turned on. Positive and negative electric wires in your home also carry electricity in this way.

Electrical Currents

When electricity flows, we call the flow a current. When electricity flows in only one direction, we call it Direct Current or DC power (battery). When it regularly changes direction of flow, then we call it Alternating Current or AC power (wall plug).

Using Circuits

When you turn on something that uses electricity, you are activating an electrical circuit. A circuit is a pathway for the flow of electricity. When you switch off the device, you are breaking the circuit.

Fuses and Breakers

A fuse heats up and melts faster than wire. When fuses melt, the circuit is broken, and by breaking the circuit, a fire is prevented.

Breakers are more common now and do the same job better. When they "blow," an adult just switches them back on instead of buying another fuse. When you "trip" the circuit breaker, that means too much power is being used on that circuit.

Conductors and Insulators

Electrons, just like heat energy, pass through some materials easily. These materials are called conductors. Copper and silver are excellent conductors.

Materials that do not conduct electrons are called insulators. Cloth, plastic and rubber are good insulators. Insulators protect us from being shocked!

Measuring Electricity

An ampere, or amp, measures the strength of an electric current. For instance, a typical light bulb uses about one amp.

Heating Up with Resistors

Electrons get caught in substances called resistors, causing energy to build up. Heat is produced as the energy makes the atoms vibrate faster. That is how electric stoves, toasters, hair dryers, waffle makers and curling irons work - they have resistors that build up heat.

Magnetism and Electricity

Magnets and electricity are closely related. You can make magnets with electricity, AND you can do the reverse - make electricity with magnets. You'll always find them together in the motors and generators of many appliances and tools.

Magnets also have opposite forces, but we don't call a magnetic force a charge. Every magnet has two poles: north and south. Opposite poles attract each other (north and south), but like poles (north and north or south and south) repel or push away from each other. You can try this out with two magnets. This principle is what causes some modern trains to hover, float or levitate.

Static Electricity

When Thales rubbed cloth and amber together, the result was static electricity. Static electricity stays in one place, charged up and waiting for something to provide a flow for current. Static electricity can happen when insulators are rubbed against each other. The electrons break loose and build up charges. For example, when you rub a balloon on your hair, electrons break free from their atoms. One object gains more electrons, making it negative, and the other object loses electrons, making it positive. Hold the balloon away, and it will cause your hair to stick up. This is evidence that opposite charges attract each other. Static electricity in the air also causes lightning. So if you're outside, and your hair starts standing up like that, go inside!

title: Superconductors
text:
Have you ever plugged in too many electrical devices at your house? When that happens, it usually causes the power in part of your house to go off. That's because your house has circuit breakers, or fuses, that make the circuit shut down when the wires are overloaded. The wires, or conductors, used in homes and businesses overload easily.

Superconductors are wires or special materials that can carry gigantic amounts of electricity without getting too hot. Electricity doesn't create friction as it moves through a superconductor. Superconductors do all this without losing or slowing down any electrons!

So if these things are so "super," why don't we use them everywhere? The challenge is that superconductors need to be kept at extremely low temperatures (hundreds of degrees below zero) to work. Scientists would love to discover one that worked at room temperature.

Superconductors are used in computers, medical-imaging devices, scientific experiments and new forms of transportation. Superconductors of the future will enable scientists and engineers to develop smaller, more efficient and amazingly powerful electrical devices.

title: Magnetic Fields: ’X-Men’ comic books by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby
text:
In the "X-Men" comic books, mutant leader Magneto uses magnetic and electromagnetic fields to control metal objects. A magnetic field is the magnetic force around a magnet or electrical field. Magneto uses his power to bend metal bars, destroy satellites and short-circuit all of Earth's electric devices. In an X-Men movie, he even moved the Golden Gate Bridge!

Magnetic fields are powerful forces. Magnets are used in many motors and generators to create electricity and power. The Earth has a magnetic field - that's why a compass points north. Earth's magnetic field, or magnetosphere, also protects it from dangerous solar storms. Solar storms can cause a lot of damage to satellites in space and can interrupt communication on Earth. Research has found that Earth's magnetic field can even protect parts of the moon from solar storms!

An electromagnet isn't like a regular iron magnet. It's a magnet created by an electric current. An electromagnet can be used to power trains. A train powered by an electromagnetic force in Japan has reached speeds of up to 361 miles per hour! Can you imagine traveling on something that fast? While scientists and engineers can do a lot with magnets, don't expect the Golden Gate Bridge to go anywhere anytime soon.

title: How is electricity produced?
text:
What a great question. Thank goodness there's a simple answer, and here it is:

magnets + copper wire + movement = electricity

Generators and electric motors are basically the same thing. Whether you use water power, steam power from burning coal, or wind power to turn the shaft, you get electricity from the negative and positive terminals. You have a generator - a water, steam or wind generator. If you hook up the positive and negative terminals to an existing source of electricity, then the shaft starts spinning, and you have a motor.

Power plants use basically the same methods except everything is gigantic in comparison.

title: Count Alessandro Volta (1745-1827)
text:
How do you become a count and a senator of the kingdom of Lombardy, France? Discover how to create and store electricity, invent the battery, and show it to the Emperor Napoleon! That is what Alessandro Volta did, and much more.

Volta was an Italian scientist and a pioneer in the study of electricity. He discovered that electricity could be produced and conducted with metals and chemicals. In 1775, Volta, a professor of physics, invented a device that stored static electricity, known as the electrophorus. In 1794, he invented the Voltaic pile, the first battery. He also discovered a gas called methane. He used electric sparks to ignite gases inside of glass containers. Because of Volta's inventions and discoveries, the study of electricity was easier for other scientists. We can thank him when we work, play on computers, or talk on the phone. Volta's work was the beginning of the field of electrochemistry.

title: Respecting Electricity
text: Electricity can be dangerous, so be careful! Don't ever touch anything electrical while you are wet. Remember, water is a conductor. Don't touch broken wires or play around power stations or power lines! Never attach electrodes from a car battery to your tongue! If there is lightning outside, stay indoors! Never place anything other than a plug into an electrical outlet! If something starts to smoke when you plug it in, unplug it fast! Ask adults and experts about electrical safety.

title: Let's Investigate
text:
What were the steps in your plan for the ice cube investigation? Here's our plan:

Place one ice cube in each cup.

Put one cup on the windowsill.

Put the other cup under the lamp.

Write down the exact time you put the ice cubes in place.

Check each ice cube every few minutes. When one is almost completely melted, keep an eye on it.

Write down the time when each ice cube melted completely.

Figure out how long it took each one to melt.

Your plan may have been different. Maybe you timed one ice cube, then the other instead of timing both of them at once. Scientists often repeat investigations many times to find the truth. When you repeat an investigation in exactly the same way, you should expect to get the same results.

title: A Universe in Motion!
text:
Scientists are good observers. When it comes to motion and force, there is a lot to observe and learn. At this very moment, you are either standing, sitting or lying down somewhere, on a very big chunk of rock called Earth, which is spinning very fast and moving around the sun. The sun is moving around a great galactic core, which is moving around the universe. A giant rock called the moon spins around us every day. It has scars all over it from millions of years of rocks smashing into it. Things are falling left and right; others are sailing through the air.

But wait a minute. It doesn’t seem like we are moving at all. Well, that is because we are moving with the Earth. Movement, or motion, is relative. Things move in relation to each other. When you’re moving with them, it doesn’t seem like you’re moving at all.

But what are we doing just sitting here on Page 1? Move your hand, move this paper into the Page-2 position, and put your brain in motion. We hope you had plenty of Wheaties for breakfast this morning because we need some Science Studies Weekly champions to keep up with the velocity of this week’s lesson. So move it!

title: Are you ‘Feeling the Pull’?
text:
Would you like to go to college in outer space? Sounds like a crazy idea, doesn't it? NASA, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, runs a highly selective school called Microgravity University (MGU). The forces of gravity at MGU are very, very small - or micro. It is as close to zero gravity as we can get here in our atmosphere. NASA uses this small force as a way to train astronauts for work in space.

When you are a college student and are "feeling the pull" toward space study, then MGU might be the place for you! First, you design an experiment at your college and apply to test it on a special NASA plane. The reduced gravity aircraft flies in a cone-shaped pattern (like one half of the McDonald's® arches). After the aircraft climbs to the top, it then dives toward Earth. As it travels downward the plane simulates (imitates) the weightlessness of outer space. Weightlessness only occurs for about 25 seconds before the plane has to pull out of the nosedive. Pretty cool, huh? Many of the students who are accepted to MGU offer outreach programs for younger STEM students. Here are a couple of websites to check out:

www.yale.edu

microgravity.caltech.edu

title: Motion Energy
text:
Isaac Newton observed things. He paid careful attention to the way things behaved when they were at rest and when they moved. He summarized the things he learned in three statements known as Newton's Laws.

Law No. 1: Everything either stays at rest or keeps moving at the same rate in a straight line unless it is acted upon by another force.
