Law No. 2: When a force hits an object, the object will move in the direction of the force. The change in motion, or acceleration of the object, depends on the power of the force (how strong it is).

Law No. 3: To every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

About Law No. 1

It's easy to understand the first part of Newton's First Law. Rocks and things don't just start moving around by themselves. They stay at rest until some kind of force moves them. But have you ever seen anything keep moving in a straight line without ever slowing down? The reason is that here on Earth opposing forces ALWAYS cause things to slow down. Take a baseball, for instance. What forces keep it from going on forever in the direction you hit it?

Gravity stops objects in motion from going on forever. However, what if you hit a baseball off the wing of the space shuttle? Without gravity pulling on it, the ball would keep going until it bumped into something else.

Friction is another big one. Everywhere you turn, it's there. Think of how much faster you slide down a water slide than a dry slide. Because of the water, there is less friction. When you drop a feather, you can see how thick the air must be as it slows the feather down. There's even friction slowing aircraft down. NASA's X-43A is the fastest jet craft in the world. When it set a world record of almost 7,000 miles per hour, there was so much friction that its nose heated up to about 3,600 degrees Fahrenheit!

Potential Energy

Potential energy is stored energy. Stand on a stool, and you are potential energy. When you jump off the stool, that is kinetic energy.

Motion

Motion is relative. You, the chair, and Science Studies Weekly may not appear to be moving thousands of miles per hour. But if you measure the speed the Earth is moving around the sun (relative to the sun), you'd find you're moving extremely fast! If the Earth were to suddenly hit a giant marshmallow in space, you would know. So keep watching!

Riding in an airplane is another example of how motion is relative. Say you're traveling several hundred miles per hour. But look out the window, and it seems as if you're sitting still. There are no objects nearby to which you can relate your speed. When you land, you'll see how fast you are really moving!

Kinetic Energy

If a moving object bumps into you, the force you feel is kinetic energy. The amount of kinetic energy depends on the mass of the object and how fast it is moving. A bicycle and a train moving at the same rate have different amounts of kinetic energy. You can easily imagine the difference in force (kinetic energy) between a freight train and a bicycle running into something at equal speeds.

About Law No. 2

A bat hits a baseball. According to Newton's Second Law, the baseball will change direction to match the direction the bat is swinging. How fast the ball will travel in the new direction (acceleration) depends on the bat's force. There are three factors that determine the direction and distance a baseball will go: mass, velocity and Newton's First Law.

1. Mass is the amount of matter that is in the bat and the ball. Size is not the same as mass. You could hit a ball with a hollow plastic bat, and it would not travel as far as when you hit it with a solid wood bat. The bats may be the same size, but the wood bat has more mass. The same is true about the ball. A plastic ball would have far less kinetic energy, or momentum, than a baseball. Friction would slow it down more quickly.

2. Velocity is the other factor. Velocity is similar to how fast something is traveling, but it's not exactly the same thing. Velocity is the rate something is traveling in a certain direction. Speed is the rate something travels in a certain time. You may be traveling 15 miles per hour on a Ferris wheel, but your velocity is constantly changing. When a bat hits a baseball, the ball will travel in the exact direction of the bat's velocity at that moment. The rate of velocity is important, too. A bullet that's shot at a tree with a slingshot will bounce off. But if that bullet is fired from a gun, it can blow a hole in the tree!

3. Mass and velocity determine how fast the object will change direction and where it will go. When it will stop moving is determined by gravity and friction. (See Newton's First Law.) Since there's no friction in space, the ball keeps going forever, as long as it's outside the gravitational pull of planets, stars and everything else.

About Law No. 3

To every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. When you jump on a trampoline, the force of gravity pulls you toward the ground. The force of the springs attached to the mat is equal to the force of gravity when you reach the bottom of your bounce. The equal reaction comes next as the force of the trampoline throws your body upward.

title: Storming the Castle
text:
Technological advances don't have to be complicated, use electricity or have lots of parts to change the world.

In the Middle Ages, they hurled massive rocks and iron balls at high speeds to break large stone castle walls into pieces. Early engineers designed the rock-throwing trebuchet (pronounced "treh-boo-shay").

Recently, American and French engineers built two working trebuchets. They thought, "Instead of just reading about things, it'd be fun to build the real thing!" Here's how it works. The counterweight on the long arm of the trebuchet would be released, forcing the heavy stone high into the air. The force (momentum) of the stone would smash the wall! The wall, at rest, was acted upon by another force.

title: Gravity: ‘Galileo’s Leaning Tower Experiment’ by Wendy Macdonald
text:
You had your first experiences with gravity at an early age. Every time you threw a ball up in the air, it fell back down to you, right? That's what science experiments are. We repeat an action many times and observe what happens.

But new experiments can change the way everyone understands a science principle. Galileo's Leaning Tower Experiment is a fictional account of a turning point in science history.

In this book, a young Italian boy named Massimo lives in the same city as the famous professor and scientist Galileo. One day Galileo saw Massimo dropping his uncle's lunch of bread and cheese off a bridge. It landed in his uncle's boat. Galileo knew that Aristotle, an ancient Greek thinker, taught that objects of different weights fall at different speeds. That sounds logical, doesn't it? But Galileo noticed that the loaf of bread, which was lighter, landed at the same time as the heavier wheel of cheese. Could the great Aristotle be wrong?

Galileo and Massimo test many different objects by dropping them from a high tower. Their experiments proved that any objects dropped together will accelerate (speed up) at the same rate and land together. Aristotle was indeed wrong.

Massimo and his uncle's lunch are inventions of the author. Galileo's experiments with gravity really happened. His findings led to Isaac Newton's laws of motion and gravity. Albert Einstein later added improvements with his theory of relativity. Perhaps you will be the next scientist whose experiments change the world's thinking.

title: What are centrifugal and centripetal forces?
text:
What is centripetal force? No, it's not an army of multi-legged creatures! Centripetal force happens when you spin something around. It is the force needed to keep something you're spinning from flying away. Tie something to a string and spin it around your head. The string is the force that keeps the object from flying away. This is centripetal force.

But wait a minute! It feels as if the object is pulling outward. Yep! That's happening, too. Centrifugal force is the outward force of the object trying to get away. Centrifugal force is inertia at work. If you let go of the string, the object will obey Newton's Law and fly off in a straight line (until the force of gravity pulls it down). You will feel centrifugal force on a roller coaster ride or when a car takes a corner and you slide toward the side of the car.

title: Stephen Hawking (1942- )
text:
One of the most brilliant geniuses ever, Stephen Hawking, has built a career by forming scientific theories about gravity. He holds the very prestigious position that Sir Isaac Newton held at Cambridge University in England. Despite having a crippling disease since the 1960s, Stephen Hawking has discovered much about gravity and the universe.

One of his greatest works is his theory of black holes and gravity. Some stars and objects are so dense, so packed with matter, that they collapse. The gravity from this collapse is so strong that nothing can escape it, not even light! So it looks to us like a big black spot or hole in space. There are probably black holes all over our galaxy.

The center of a neutron star is made of neutrons. The protons and electrons are forced to become neutrons as well, so it is just a solid ball of neutrons. It's so dense that a neutron star 10 miles wide would weigh as much as our sun! A piece of a neutron star the size of your pencil eraser would weigh about 10,000-20,000 tons. Stephen Hawking has been on "Star Trek" and "The Simpsons" and has written several theory books on how the universe was made. He is considered by many to be the greatest scientific mind since Albert Einstein.

title: Let's Investigate
text:
This week you're on your own, science detectives. You are going to design your very own investigation about what you learned in Science Studies Weekly this week. Remember to follow the steps you learned in Week 2.

First, you need a question. Did you think of any questions as you read the articles about motion and force? Would you like to know more about friction or gravity or the way things move? You may want to look back at some of the articles and write down as many questions as you can think of. Then choose one you think will make a good investigation. Follow the rest of the steps for doing an investigation: hypothesis, plan, test, record and share. If you want to, you could work with a friend or two to make things easier.

title: Technology of the Past and Present
text:
Imagine you live 200 years in the future. Galactic Alliance gives you the job of helping a primitive alien race on a faraway planet. You get to the planet and see that they have almost no basic technologies. They don't even use the wheel! What would you do? Would you show them how to make a wheel or other simple machines? Would you teach them about combustion engines so that they can drive cars instead of riding 10-legged beasts? Would you give them all cell phones to hold up to their pointy ears? Would it be good for them to get all that new technology at once?

Well, that's almost what has happened here in the past 150 years. Just 150 years ago, everyone traveled by animal, cooked with fire, used few medicines to treat diseases, thought flying was for the birds, and, on average, lived to the ripe old age of 35. All this technology on our planet has made a big difference. Today, the average person in the United States lives to be about 78.

You may have a hard time teaching those aliens about complex technologies. First, they'll have to get used to some of the basic tools that have been around on our planet for thousands of years. Before you teach them about computer chips, you should start with a basic counting device like an abacus. Before you teach them about engines, you may want to start with simple machines. What kind of machines? Turn the page and you'll find the Science Studies Weekly list of simple machines no planet can live without. It's required reading for anyone working with primitive aliens on faraway planets.

title: Floating Stop Signs?
text:
Have you ever heard your parents use the term “gas mileage”? If so, do you know how many miles per gallon (mpg) your family car gets? Ten? Thirty? Most cars these days get between 25 and 50 mpg on the highway. As Earth’s fossil fuels decrease, scientists are working around the clock to find cleaner and more efficient ways to travel. Chances are you’ve heard of hybrid cars and electric cars. Now make room for flying cars. Also known as a Roadable aircraft, flying cars may hit the road—and air—at some point in the future.

Who are these scientists making a dream coming true? Lots of scientists have devoted time and money to developing a flying car, but the first to offer one for sale may be Terrafugia. This U.S. company was founded by aeronautical (air and space) engineers. The model with folding wings may only get about 35 mpg on the road, but over 400 mpg in the air! Do you think your high school might have Flyer’s Ed someday? In order to fly one of these Roadable aircrafts, you must have a special license with a minimum of 20 hours of flight time. And the price tag? Well, it’s more than most of us can afford, but much less than you might imagine. According to the latest estimates, the Terrafugia Transition could sell for just under $200,000. Keep putting your spare change in your piggy bank.

title: Technology Past and Present
text:
Science and technology have been best friends for a long time. They depend on each other.

Science depends on technology for tools to measure (how hot, how big, how heavy, how dense, etc.), observe, calculate, analyze, collect and store information, and much, much more.

Technology depends on science, too. For thousands of years, ancient people like the Egyptians used scientific knowledge to come up with new technologies that make our work easier. Science helps us design new technologies by helping us predict what will happen before we build something. For example, engineers wouldn't try to build an engine that runs on ice cream. An experiment like that would be a total waste of time. Engineers depend on scientific knowledge when they design new technology to solve problems.

Much of our modern technology came from simple ideas about machines we've known for a long time. Let's look at some basic technologies, or simple machines, that are just as useful now as they were 3,000 years ago.

Simple Machines

Some of the most useful changes in technology are very simple. Simple things that are used the right way can make work a lot easier and allow us to do things we couldn't do before. All simple machines work on the rules of motion and force.

Simple Winch: A winch is a handy, simple machine. It is actually like a circular lever. It has an axle that acts as a fulcrum and a wheel that is turned by a handle that acts as a lever.

Pulley: The invention of the pulley made lifting things much easier. A pulley increases the amount of force used. A pulley doubles the amount of load you can lift with the same amount of force

Ramp or Incline: A simple incline can make work much easier. It is harder to climb or push something without an incline.

Lever: A lever is a simple device that increases force and movement to lift a load. A bar or beam is placed on a pivot point called the fulcrum.

Wedge: A wedge forces things to separate.

Complex Machines

Over the years, people have discovered how to use science to make very complex machines. Above is a complex modern crane. The person who invented it knew a lot about science and engineering. If you look closely, you'll see that many parts are simple machines that have been used for thousands of years. It uses pulleys, levers, winches, and counterbalances. It also uses complex electronics, like an on-board computer to control the machinery. The inside of the crane has gears and a powerful engine with more than 2,000 parts to control the crane's movements. This crane can lift more than 50 tons of materials 250 feet in the air. The ancient Egyptians probably wished they had a crane like this. Imagine what the pyramids would look like if they did!

The Internal-Combustion Engine

Air is sucked in through a valve and mixed with fuel.

The piston moves up and compresses the mixture.

The spark plug ignites fuel, forcing piston down.

Exhaust is pushed out through a valve, and the cycle starts over.

Information Technology

Over many centuries, small improvements were made in computing tools until the late 20th century. Then modern computers were invented and they're changing almost every day!

title: Edison’s First Dud
text:
Just because we have the science to invent something doesn't mean people will like it. Many inventors have learned this the hard way. Take Thomas Edison, for example. One of his very first inventions was a machine that electronically counted and tallied votes of lawmakers making decisions. Instantly, lawmakers could see who had voted, what their vote was, and who had not voted. This made lawmakers uncomfortable. They didn't want everyone "looking over their shoulder" while they were making up their minds. Young Mr. Edison decided then and there that inventors (especially himself) should only spend their time inventing things that people actually wanted.

How about the horse-powered minibus? This invention actually holds a British patent. It's powered by a horse that walks on a conveyor belt inside the vehicle. Uh, why don't we see those driving around? Could it have been an exhaust problem or too many flies?

title: Computer Bugs: ‘Zuto: The Adventures of a Computer Virus’ by Udi Aharoni
text:
Would you like to see what happens inside your computer? Then you will love the book "Zuto: The Adventures of a Computer Virus." This fun story will help you understand how computers work.

Zuto, a clever green computer virus, lives in the Recycle Bin of a computer. Zuto's friend Super Media 2.0 is a movie player who was sent to the Recycle Bin when a newer version was installed. Silver Shield, a robot anti-virus, has been trying to eliminate Zuto. But a computer worm invades them, and that is a much more dangerous threat. Now the characters must work together to save their city.

Real computer viruses are programs that interfere with computer operations. They can copy themselves and spread just like a human virus. Some will delete data or even erase a computer's hard drive. Computer worms are programs that infect real computers, too. They sometimes spread to everyone in an email address book and keep spreading to all the addresses in every email they reach.

Early computers contained lighted tubes. These attracted moths which crawled inside and caused malfunctions. That's how people started calling computer problems "bugs." Just like Silver Shield, there are many real antivirus programs which destroy bugs, viruses, and worms trying to invade computers.

Zuto has his own website, zutopedia.com. You can watch a video about the book, learn about the author and download free sample chapters.

title: What does it take to make an invention?
text:
Most people have had ideas about things that should be invented. It's too bad, but these ideas are forgotten almost as fast as they come. Sometimes, someone will have an idea for an invention and keep it a secret for many years - thinking one day he'll produce it. Then he sees a TV commercial advertising the product made by someone else! Here's the process inventors go through to get credit for their ideas:

Think of a product many people would want that's not available in stores, and keep it a secret.

Establish your invention date by registering your idea with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office.

Keep a detailed journal of your invention as you build models, make sketches, and write descriptions of the product. Write the date on every entry.

Produce detailed drawings and plans of your gizmo.

Get a patent attorney to help you file for a patent. It's not required, but some inventors choose to do this.

After your patent is approved, you're free to make your idea and sell it to everyone who wants one. It can cost a lot of money, but some businesses will help produce the gadget for a share of the money you make. Some people buy patents from inventors.

title: Albert Einstein 1879-1955
text:
Little Albert Einstein was very special. Not only did he learn to play the violin before age 5, but he became the most famous scientist of modern time. Chances are that you have seen a picture of Einstein - you know, the happy-looking gentleman with frizzy hair. Perhaps you have even seen his great equation, E=MC2, and wondered what it meant. (Don't worry. Most adults don't understand it, either.)

Einstein was not afraid to ask questions. He wondered if Newton was right about space and time. His Theory of Relativity showed that Newton was not completely right about time and space. Basically, the Theory of Relativity showed that time and distance in the universe were different depending on where you stood.

That was just one of his revolutionary ideas that changed modern science. He came up with the idea that photons (particles of light) existed. He created the idea of energy and matter being related (his E=MC2 formula). He developed a system of counting and measuring atoms, a theory that light is both a particle and a wave, and many other great theories. Einstein even answered the question, "Why is the sky blue?"

When did he do all of this? Well, most of his great ideas came while he was working at a patent office in 1905. Einstein's quest for knowledge about the universe inspired many more scientists to keep trying to answer those questions.

title: Let's Investigate
text:
We have a different challenge for you this week, science detectives. It's part science and part writing. Your challenge is to come up with a way to remember the steps in doing a science investigation. To make it easier, we shortened each step to just one word that will remind you what to do: Question, Hypothesis, Plan, Test, Record and Share.

Now, take the first letter of each of those words and make up a sentence to help you remember the steps. It can be a funny sentence or a serious one. It's up to you. You can use a dictionary or a thesaurus to help you think of words if you need to. Be creative and have fun!

title: Our Technological World
text:
Beeeeeeeeeeeeeeep!" goes the digital alarm. It's 6:30 in the morning and time to get ready. A flip of a switch, and lights come on. You take a quick hot shower, thanks to an efficient water heater. Of course, your clothes are clean and smell like lilacs, thanks to chemical laundry detergents and fabric softener. Your hair is perfect because of the electric hair dryer and the "mega hold" hair gel. Breakfast is ready in two minutes in the microwave. A press of the key chain transmits a signal to start the car, and another button opens the garage door. You fasten your seatbelt and zoom!

Traffic lights, MP3 players, anti-lock brakes and radial tires make your trip safer and more entertaining. Once at work, you swipe your ID tag through the security system and smile at the camera on the elevator, and off you go to the 32nd floor. You plop down in your automated, comfort-controlled chair. Using your personal digital assistant, you check your email and voice mail. Later, the PDA reminds you that the videoconference with a government official in Tokyo will start in 30 minutes. You check the local time in Tokyo and listen as your PDA tells you how to say "good day" and a few other phrases in Japanese. You quickly download a podcast of the TV show you missed last night-just in time. With a click of the mouse, the videoconference begins.

"Konnichiwa!"

Imagine what a person from long ago would think of this modern electronic world. Would they think you were performing magic? Why are things so different now? Well, one answer is technology.

Technology affects almost every part of our lives. Turn the page and take a closer look at what technology has done to change our world.

title: What’s That You’re e-Reading?
text: Have you been to the library lately? In case you haven't, your school or local library may be offering newer technology. Only a few decades ago, students learned how to use a card catalogue to locate books on the shelves. Librarians also collected cards from pockets inside the covers of books, and they filed the cards as a way of keeping track of borrowed books. By the late 1990s, most libraries had computerized databases, and librarians scanned bar codes into the system. Card catalogues became antiques - almost as hard to find as LP's and record players. LP's you say? What on Earth are those? Setting that history lesson aside for the moment, ask your friendly librarian if there is an electronic book on hand. An e-book may be exactly what the teacher ordered. The e-Ink in these readers impersonates ink and paper, making these e-books unique. Unlike a computer or smart phone, an e-reader works without a backlight. Instead, millions of microcapsules carry positive or negative charges. These microcapsules are suspended in a clear fluid and respond to electric fields. The black and white capsules rearrange themselves into words! The original research for e-book technology was conducted at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Media Lab in Boston. Now, about LP's ...

title: Technology in Society
text:
"Technology, like art, is a soaring exercise of the human imagination." - Daniel Bell, 2005

Ways Technology Changes Our World

Technology is the science of problem solving. Using technology to solve a problem usually ends up with an invention. Right now, many engineers and scientists are trying to solve problems all over the world. A little bit at a time, here a little, there a little, new technologies evolve. When someone solves one problem, usually someone else will use that new invention as part of the solution to a different problem.

What kind of problems? You name it. Anything that people think is inconvenient can be a problem. For instance, some people think it takes too long to wash dishes by hand, wash clothes, cook food, walk to town, or send a message. These are "problems" that technology has solved or has helped make them easier to deal with.

We live in a time when inventions have changed the world faster and more completely than at any other time we know of in history. Let's take a look at how technology has changed our world in the areas of (1) communication (how we send, receive, and process information), (2) transportation and exploration (how we move around and discover new worlds), (3) production (how we get our work done and how much work we get done), and (4) lifestyle (how technology helps us live longer and healthier).

Communication

Many little advances in science and technology made it possible for information to be relayed to larger groups of people. For example, in 1450, Johannes Gutenburg invented movable type. Before that, people had to write copies of books by hand. Only powerful leaders and very rich people could afford books. The printing press made it so that people could get books much more easily. As books became less expensive, people became more educated. That made a huge impact on society.

Newspapers were first published in the 1600s. In the late 1800s, information was first carried over electrical wires by the telegraph (Samuel Morse, 1837) and later by telephone (Alexander Bell, 1876). Wireless broadcasts with radio waves began in 1895. The first computer was built in 1945 and filled three rooms.

Today, computers and the Internet are major parts of how we send, receive, and understand information.

Lifestyle

Medical technology has saved countless lives. In the Middle Ages, people would use blood worms (leeches) to suck blood out of sick people. Doctors often made deep wounds in their patients to "let all the bad blood out." This practice was called bloodletting. Historians believe that this may have been one of the causes of George Washington's death at age 67 as he suffered from a strep infection.

A microscope that made it possible to see the germs that cause sickness was invented in 1674. Using microscopes, in 1928, Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin. It has killed infections and wiped out many diseases. Other terrible diseases like smallpox, rabies and polio were prevented with the development of vaccines. Louis Pasteur invented a process called pasteurization to keep food safe and clean. In the 1900s, mass water-purification machines and chemicals made the world's water supplies cleaner. Nowadays, hospitals use all kinds of technologies such as X-ray machines, imaging scanners, and laser surgery to care for our health. We've come a long way since the days of leeching and bloodletting!

Transportation and Exploration

From the first wheel to horse-drawn carriages to automobiles and race cars, inventions have improved transportation and our ability to explore the universe. Over time, people have developed technologies that helped them get around more easily and go places that they couldn't go before. Believe it or not, the horseshoe is an ancient example of one such simple invention. With shoes on, horses could go much farther and could be used longer for transportation.

Some gadgets help us know where we are going. The Chinese invented the compass in A.D. 100, making it possible to navigate ships without looking at the stars. Starting with Marco Polo and Christopher Columbus in the 1400s, many sea-going explorers navigated the oceans of the world. With a modern Global Positioning System in your car, you'll never get lost again!

The steam engine, a more complex invention, changed our modern world. With steam engines, inventors improved transportation on land and on water. Suddenly, in the mid-1800s, steam-powered trains carried people and things over great distances very quickly, especially when compared with wagon trains pulled by oxen or mules. On the water, steam-powered ships carried people and goods upstream and against the wind more quickly. The automobile was invented in 1895. The first airplane flight was in 1903, which led to the jet engine in 1937 and the space shuttle in 1981. Think of how our culture and world have changed from advances like these. How do you travel from place to place? Wagon, sail, steam, gasoline engine, or jet?

Production

Improvements in transportation and communication technologies have made huge changes in how much work we get done. How much work we do is called productivity. For example, with modern equipment, one farmer can do the work that used to take dozens of people.

With powerful computers, one person can keep track of information that would have kept 30 filing clerks busy 30 years ago.

title: Traditions vs. Technology?
text:
Are traditions worth keeping even when technology could do a better job? It all depends. . . .

There's nothing more traditional than a good old American baseball game. But umpires are getting a little worried. Nowadays, there are radar gadgets to measure the speed of the baseball as it flies over home plate. They've even got a gizmo called Pitch Trax that can accurately measure and track the exact course of a fast ball. It can tell if the ball is in or out of the strike zone. But some fans are calling foul! They like the sound of the ump screaming, "Yeeerrrrr oooouuuut!"

Others think that these new technologies should replace umpires in baseball games. But for now, this device is only used to help umpires be more accurate, not to replace them.

Gee, what's next - an electronic version of apple pie?

title: ‘Robotics: Discover the Science and Technology of the Future’ by Kathy Ceceri
text:
Think you might like to be a roboticist some day? That's a scientist who creates, builds and operates robots. If you are picturing C3PO and R2D2 from Star Wars, you'll be surprised by the robots in today's world.

Robots are everywhere. NASA uses robotic arms for space repairs and rovers to explore the surface of Mars. An underwater robot named ABE explored ocean depths up to 14,000 feet. Doctors guide robotic hands to do surgery. Police use robots to defuse bombs. Hybrid cars use robotics to switch from gas to electric power. Some cars can even park themselves.

In Kathy Ceceri's book "Robotics" you'll learn that robots (machines used to do jobs) can be shaped in a large disk like the Roomba vacuum cleaner or toy insects like Hexbugs. Her book also has 20 real robotics projects you can do at home. Most projects use supplies you have around the house. For example, you can make a working model of a robotic hand using card stock, scissors, clear tape, drinking straws, marker and string. Have fun with the great "Try This" experiments, like using a digital camera to see infrared light beams. The "Words to Know" boxes and funny cartoon drawings help make robotics easy to understand.

Look for a robotics club you can join in your school or community. There are robotics competitions for all ages. It's a popular hobby that might lead to a scholarship or a career.

title: What technology has helped society the most?
text: That is a hard question to answer. Purifying water supplies with chlorination or filtering water stamped out many diseases, and medicines have ended plagues. Electrical systems power our cars, homes, and television sets. In 1809, Nicolas Appert invented canning, which made preserving and delivering food much easier. Millions are fed thanks to his discoveries every day. Maybe the greatest technology was plumbing that sends waste safely down the drain. Before indoor plumbing, getting rid of waste and hauling clean water was a chore. Could the automobile be the most important invention for society? Well, judging by how many people drive cars, you may think so. What about the telephone? We can call someone across the world or get emergency help when someone is hurt. And television - we get our news and plenty of entertainment from television. Movable type made it possible for people to be educated. It is hard to say which is the most important; all of them help society in their own ways. What do you think?

title: Thomas Edison 1847-1931
text:
Have you ever thought about inventing something that would improve the lives of your friends and family? You're not too young! One of the world's most famous inventors started at the age of 10. As a boy, Thomas Edison read as much as he could, and he managed to put together his first chemistry and engineering labs. He read, experimented and tinkered with things. He figured out how things worked, and then he tried to improve them.

While young, Edison worked as a candy butcher, which is an old-fashioned name for someone who sold things like candy, gum, newspapers and sandwiches on trains. However, no one was surprised when he quit his various jobs to build a laboratory. From that new workshop came the electric light bulb, moving pictures (movies!) and alkaline batteries - just to name a few. Thomas was hooked! He just couldn't stop inventing. His favorite invention was the phonograph, which was an early type of recording machine. Perhaps one of the most impressive things he did was originally for the city of New York. He created the world's first power station in 1882.

On the day of Thomas Edison's funeral in 1931, people all over the world dimmed their light bulbs for one minute. It was a fitting honor for this great inventor. Edison had 1,093 U.S. patents, which has been more than any other person!

title: Structure of the Earth
text:
You know, a candy bar and the Earth we live on have a lot in common. How so, you ask? Have you ever taken a bite out of a big ol' candy bar and then stood back to have a look? From the outside, a candy bar looks like it's all made of rich brown chocolate. But inside? Well, that's a different story. Notice that the chocolate makes up just one thin layer around the outside. Below that, you might notice a layer of gooey caramel and below that, a layer of peanuts. Well, the Earth is that way, too. We don't mean it's all caramel and peanuts inside. We mean that it has layers. For example, the layer that you're standing on is called the continental crust, and it's only a few miles thick (5 to 20 miles). The entire outer layer, or crust, of the Earth, plus the upper mantle, is also called the lithosphere.

Beneath the crust, farther toward the Earth's center, there's a super-thick layer called the mantle. Scientists think the "upper mantle" is mostly made of iron and magnesium. It's about 430 miles thick. There is a transition layer between the upper and lower mantles where materials are blended. The thickest layer is called the lower mantle. It's about 1,800 miles thick. Scientists can only guess from seismic readings what makes up the lower mantle. (See This Week's Question.) They think it's made of materials like silicon, magnesium, oxygen, iron, calcium and aluminum.

At the center of the Earth is an ultra-hot, mostly molten place called the core (a little like the gooey center in some candy). The core of the Earth is made of iron and possibly nickel. It is under a lot of pressure from all the weight above, and it's as hot as the surface of the sun (about 10,000 degrees F). Scientists recently detected areas on the outer rim of the core using seismic data, which suggest areas of solid iron floating over the molten core. These areas of solid metal on one side may explain why the Earth has a tiny wobble in its spin.

If you like what's on the outside of our planet, you ought to see what's shakin' on the inside. Go ahead. Put down that candy bar, turn the page, and let's head underground!

title: Music: Not Just for People!
text:
Do whales sing? Well, actually they do. Thanks to Dr. Roger Payne, Founder and President of Ocean Alliance, we now know that some whales do sing. In 1967 Dr. Payne, along with Scott McVay, discovered that male humpback whales sing songs during breeding season. Dr. Payne has studied whales since the late 1960s and has a new theory that fin whales and blue whales can communicate across entire oceans.

Dr. Payne was born in 1935 in New York. He works as a biologist and an environmentalist. In addition to studying whales, he has also become an important leader in the campaign to end commercial whaling. Commercial whaling occurs when people hunt and kill whales for their meat and oil that comes from their blubber (fat). Commercial whaling was banned in 1986.

According to Dr. Payne, the whale songs have "themes." The songs change slightly depending on the season. Dr. Payne is continuing to research the songs of humpback whales as well as other types of whales. Check out these cool websites to hear whale songs and to test your knowledge with a whale song quiz.

www.whalesounds.com

www.lawrencehallofscience.org

title: Plate Tectonics
text:
The Mighty Earth Changers

Earthquakes are another amazing force that can make big changes to the Earth's surface in just a few moments. Earthquakes generally happen right on the borders of the Earth's plates, along large cracks called faults. The plate edges, moving against each other, don't always slide smoothly. They bend and stretch until, all of a sudden - Pop! One side suddenly gives, sending out shock waves, sometimes hundreds and hundreds of miles from where the slipping happened. The exact place where the movement begins is called the epicenter of the earthquake. People who live along these faults run the risk of having things shaken up by Mother Nature from time to time. Scientists are always looking for ways to predict earthquakes and to keep people and property safe from the damage that can result from these mighty Earth changers.

What Is Plate Tectonics?

Have you ever looked at a pond covered with lily pads? Those lily pads, sometimes floating near each other, sometimes pushing away, have a lot in common with the Earth. Right now you're standing on a continent that's slowly, slowly floating around on the surface of the Earth, like a lily pad on a pond. See, each continent on the Earth's surface is part of its own gigantic "plate." The Earth's plates fit together like a puzzle, but it's a puzzle that's always changing.

Look at a world map. If you look carefully and use a little imagination, can you see how the part of Africa sticking out into the Atlantic Ocean looks like it fits in the space between North America and South America? Scientists believe that long, long, loooong ago, those continents did fit together. Look for other places where the shapes seem to fit and you'll find them.

The theory of the Earth's plates is called plate tectonics. That's a term worth remembering! Where one plate bumps another, we call it a convergent boundary. When this happens, the plate that's heavier (the ocean plate) slides under the lighter plate (the continent). As a result, the land near the convergent boundary often crumples and forms great mountains, hills and valleys. That's how we got the Himalayan Mountains (the world's tallest). Where two plates are moving away from each other, we call it a divergent boundary. This is where seafloor spreading takes place.

Catch the Wave

Sometimes big changes happen so fast that humans and animals are lucky to get out of the way in time. For example, a huge ocean wave called a tsunami can reshape a shoreline in a hurry. Waves like that are created by mighty undersea earthquakes and rush toward an unsuspecting shoreline at incredible speeds - sometimes more than 500 miles per hour! The big ones can be 150 feet high.

It's Gonna Blow!

Volcanoes can make big changes quickly to the Earth's features. A volcano is an opening in the ground that leads all the way down to the molten rock far beneath the surface of the planet. Every once in a while molten rock can rush up to the surface, bringing millions of tons of brand-new rock to the landscape. A volcano can bring so much rock to the surface, that it could form an island in the middle of an ocean. The Hawaiian Islands were formed that way. The entire nation of Japan was also formed that way. Volcanoes often give warning signs when they're about to blow, giving people time to clear out of the way. A river of molten lava could rearrange your living room in a hurry.

Under the Sea

Would you like to see where new rock is made? If you head to the middle of the ocean and dive down, down, down to where the Earth's plates meet, you might find an undersea mountain split by a deep trench. It's called a mid-ocean ridge. Up through such trenches, brand-new molten rock is bubbling. That's the newest rock on Earth! How does the ocean floor make room for all that new rock? Simply by pushing the old rock aside. In fact, the ocean floor is actually spreading right at this minute, out away from the deep trenches where new rock is being formed. The oldest rock can be found farthest away from the trenches, right up near the continents. It's all part of a process called seafloor spreading. It's been going on for millions of years (at the rate of a few centimeters per year), but scientists are just now getting to know more about it. In fact, because evidence of seafloor spreading was first discovered in the 1940s and 50s, your great-grandparents may have never heard of it!

title: Measuring Earthquakes
text:
What's the earliest technology used to record information about earthquakes? The answer may surprise you. A Chinese scientist named Chang Heng invented a machine called the Dragon Jar, which dropped a small, metal ball from the mouth of a carved dragon every time an earthquake happened. That was in A.D. 132.

These days, the instrument scientists use to measure the intensity of earthquakes is called a seismograph. A seismograph measures the strength of the energy waves sent out by an earthquake. A seismograph can tell a scientist just how far away a quake occurred and how big it was. An English scientist (working in Japan) named John Milne invented the horizontal pendulum seismograph in 1880.

title: The Power of Boron: ‘The Hunter Chronicles’ by E. J. Patten
text:
Next time you face down a botanical monster as Sky Weathers does in "The Hunter Chronicles," remember boron! Boron is a compound that can be found in the Earth's crust. Volcanoes, weathering and other events introduce boron into the environment.

Plants need boron, but finding the right balance can be hard. Too much boron, and the plant dies; too little, and the plant dies. Too much or too little boron would kill botanical monsters, too! (Scientists are still studying how boron affects us humans.)

You can find boron in fiberglass, fire extinguishers, fertilizers and bleach. In nuclear reactors, boron is used as a shield against radiation. Finally, no more mutated humans running amuck! As a semi-metal, boron can conduct heat, work as an insulator and lubricate like a graphite pencil. Best of all, boron gives fireworks that pretty green color.

So, if you ever come across a hungry plant monster, douse it with bleach and thank boron! It just might save your life.

title: How do we know the Earth’s structure?
text:
If you pick up a rock and throw it into a pond, ripples spread out. If the ripples hit a log in the pond, they'll bounce off, sending ripples in the opposite direction. If you could see the ripples but not the log, you could still guess that there was something hard and log-shaped in the water because of how the ripples behaved. That's the genius of seismology!

Seismology is the study of earthquakes. Geologists use seismic waves to see what is inside the Earth. When an earthquake hits part of the Earth's crust, it sends shock waves in all directions. This is like the ripples that you see in a pond. Because the Earth is a sphere, we can measure the waves from all over the Earth's crust. By studying how shock waves are deflected (bounced off) deep in the Earth, we can imagine what kinds of materials are down there.

Seismology can measure two types of waves. Compression waves (P waves) travel through solids and liquids. Shear waves (S waves) can only travel through solid things like hard rock. Scientists knew there was a liquid core when S waves did not go through the core. Seismic waves also tell us how hot it is inside the Earth. That's because waves slow down or speed up depending on the temperature of the material.

Studying how those waves behave gives scientists an idea of what is underground, even if they can't see it. Sometimes the best helper in the study of what makes up the Earth is Mother Nature and her seismic waves.

title: Alfred Wegener (1880-1930)
text: Have you ever wondered about who the pioneers of geology and astronomy were? The Earth and the space surrounding us are enormous, almost beyond measure. But it wasn't too much for scientists who could visualize the big picture. One such scientist was Alfred Wegener. Born in 1880, Wegener earned his doctorate degree (Ph.D.) in astronomy by the time he was 24 years old. He also studied the Earth's structure. Wegener formed the theory that Earth's continents actually float on our planet's surface like giant plates. His idea is the foundation of current theories that support plate tectonics. Wegener constantly studied, observed, drew conclusions and learned from his colleagues. He formed new understandings in the fields of geology and astronomy. Wegener wrote a textbook on climatology, and he worked his entire life on making sense of our universe. Many scientists may have rejected Alfred Wegener's ideas about the Earth when he first presented them, but most now accept them as fact.

title: Let's Investigate
text:
Safety is an important part of every investigation. Science can be lots of fun but not if you get hurt. Safety is all about tools and rules.

Many science tools help keep you safe. Gloves or potholders protect your hands when your investigation involves heat. Use them any time you're working with a stove, oven, an unshaded lamp or any other heat source. Aprons or smocks help keep your clothes clean, so your mom doesn't have such a hard time getting out the stains! Wear them any time you work with something messy. Goggles protect your eyes, and they're always in style in the science lab.

Rules help keep you safe, too. Before you begin an investigation, make sure you know the rules. Read all the steps in the investigation before you start, and always listen to your teacher. That way you'll have fun and be safe in every investigation.

title: Let’s Talk Rocks!
text:
Deep in the outback of Australia is Uluru, the world's largest rock monolith. (Monolith means all one stone.) It is about one mile thick and rises about 1,000 feet in the air. That's as tall as a 100-story skyscraper. For ages, the Anangu (native people, or aborigines) of Australia have considered the rock sacred and full of mystical power. Where did this giant rock sitting in the middle of Australia's flatlands come from? Did it just drop there from outer space? It may be hard to believe this, but about half a billion years ago, this rock was just part of a sandy ocean floor.

How do giant rocks like this one wind up in the middle of the outback? How were they made? Where did they come from?

Actually, it's not uncommon to find rocks, even great big ones, that look like they should be sitting somewhere else. In fact, it's common to find rocks that started out as different kinds of rocks entirely. You see, the material inside the Earth that rocks are made of changes, moves and recycles over time. Because it usually takes millions of years, we just don't have the time to sit around and watch. A brand-new rock, fresh from the molten underground, is called an igneous rock. After millions of years, that same rock might settle down and become a sedimentary rock. But, later, that same rock, under tremendous heat and pressure, might make another change into a metamorphic rock. The process of rocks forming from other materials and changing from one kind of rock to another kind is called the rock cycle. And if you always thought that the rock cycle was a motorbike driven by Fred Flintstone, this is the issue for you. So, turn the page, and rock on!

title: Man and Nature Battle for Pacifica Beach
text:
"Tonight on Erosion TV: Man vs. Pacific Ocean - who will win this epic battle for the Pacifica Cliffs? Will it be man, who built an apartment building too close to the cliffs' edge, or the Pacific Ocean, pounding away at the coast day and night for millions of years? Tune in and see!"

Sometimes the Earth changes so slowly we don't realize it is happening. We have a hard time seeing the Earth constantly changing with the slow and steady attacks of the elements. We might plant a small tree next to our house, only to discover years and years later that the tree is breaking the house's foundation with roots and breaking the roof with branches. Is that the tree's fault?

In Pacifica, California, residents of a cliff-side apartment building were recently evacuated from their homes. The cliff they built on top of is slowly breaking apart and falling into the ocean. Residents probably noticed their backyards slowly getting smaller over the years, but some residents had only hours to get out of their apartments before pieces of their porches tumbled 80 feet down to the surf.

Engineers have placed tons of boulders at the bottom of the cliff to slow the surf and put 50-foot nails into the cliff itself to try to hold it together. Nevertheless, the engineers appear to be losing the battle.

The city doesn't have enough money to build a giant sea wall, and banks won't loan money to individual residents for what seems like such a hopeless cause. Things sure get interesting when man and nature argue over the same piece of land.

title: Shaping the Earth
text:
Igneous Rock

Magma starts it all. Sometimes magma (hot, molten liquid rock) pushes up to the surface through volcanoes or cracks in the Earth's crust. That super-hot, flowing magma will become rock when it cools. Magma that has cooled into rock is igneous rock. Granite is one good example of igneous rock. And while some igneous rock is old, it's still generally the youngest rock out there. What happens to igneous rock as time flies by? Read on!

Sedimentary Rock

Igneous rock sure takes a beating on this planet! Water might slowly wear it away, wind might blow it here and there bit by bit, or it may be broken up partly by big dramatic forces like earthquakes. Whatever causes it, as igneous rocks break down, the particles they were once made of tend to settle in layers on the Earth's surface, like sand in the bottom of a jar. In fact, in some places (like where a hill has been cut away to make room for a road), you can see the layers made by millions and millions of years of breaking down igneous rock. By this time, the rocks that make up these layers aren't called igneous rocks anymore. They're called sedimentary rocks. Flint, sandstone and conglomerate rocks are good examples of sedimentary rocks. But even then, the rocky journey's not over!

Metamorphic Rock

Often, tremendous pressure and heat can build up inside the Earth. If an igneous or sedimentary rock is caught in the middle of that heat and pressure, changes occur. Sometimes the changes are so great that a rock becomes an entirely new rock, with a new name: metamorphic rock. Here are some examples. Under heat and pressure, granite (an igneous rock) turns into a metamorphic rock called gneiss (how gneiss!). Limestone, a sedimentary rock, might turn to beautiful marble under that same pressure.

Back to the Beginning

Finally, we're almost back where we began. What happens to rock at the end of the rock cycle? It goes back where it came from. That's why they call it a cycle. Sooner or later (usually much, much later, like millions and millions of years later), igneous rock, sedimentary rock and metamorphic rock make it back underground to be melted into magma again. How does it get down there? Well, sometimes magma will come to the surface and melt even the most solid rock. Of course, after a loooong time and after a lot of sloooow movement, most rock that sits on oceanic plates will finally make its way to the edge to be pushed under the continental plate next to it, deep underground, to be super-heated and melted again. Eventually, it comes to the surface again and is eroded back into the ocean as sediments. And this happens over and over. . . .

Mother Nature's Dirt Mover

When it comes to shaping the land, Mother Nature has all kinds of tools. One tool she's used a lot is the glacier. Glaciers are her version of a bulldozer and a plow mixed together.

When more snow falls in the winter than melts in the summer, year after year, it builds up and packs down. It becomes a huge, solid "ice cube" called a glacier.

Glaciers made many famous landforms. Ever heard of the Great Lakes? How about Glacier National Park?

Here's some trivia for you: Two percent of the Earth's water, or twice the amount of all the water in all the lakes, rivers, and streams on Earth, is frozen in glaciers!

Ice Cubes in the Ocean

After a glacier moves through a narrow valley, you can bet that valley will be much wider. But glaciers move very slowly over thousands of years. What happens to them when they run out of land? They break off and become icebergs floating around near the north and south poles.

Look Out Below!

You would not want to build your home downhill from a glacier because they start moving downhill after they get about 300 feet thick. Anything that's not heavier than a glacier is pushed along in front of it or pushed out of the way (just as a bulldozer would do to anything in the way). Sometimes big rocks that are frozen into the bottom of a glacier scrape huge trenches in the ground as the glacier passes (like a great big plow being pulled by a tractor).

title: Geologists and Mining Technology
text:
Geologists are scientists who study the many kinds of rocks, metals and minerals that can be dug up from the Earth. They work hand in hand with mining companies, underground construction projects (like subway tunnels), and anyone else who needs to get a good look at what's beneath the surface before they dig it up.

How do they look down there without lifting a shovel? One way is to measure seismic waves. Last week you learned that scientists use these waves to study what is inside the Earth. Geologists use the same machines to help mining companies know whether there is coal or gold or just bedrock underground. By using high-tech imaging computers (sort of like an x-ray for Mother Nature) to analyze how those waves behave, a geologist can get a pretty good idea of what's down there without getting his or her hands too dirty.

title: ‘Pandas’ Earthquake Escape’ by Phyllis J. Perry
text:
When a giant earthquake hit China in 2008, Wolong Panda Reserve was only seven miles from the earthquake's center. As its walls crumbled, workers gathered up the protected animals as best they could. One panda ran away in panic but was later rescued. What might have happened to that terrified panda during those days?

Author Phyllis J. Perry has written a book based on that event called "Pandas' Earthquake Escape." In her fictional story, a mother panda Liling and her cub Tengfei live in a nature preserve. Humans protect and feed them. One day they are sleeping high in a tree when an earthquake shakes the ground. Liling's instinct to protect her cub causes her to run, and soon they are lost. Their adventures show how they struggle to find food and shelter. We are reminded that natural disasters affect animals as well as people.

What causes earthquakes? The earth's surface is made from plates of rock that are constantly sliding around like a cracked eggshell. When these plates move, an earthquake occurs. The earth shakes for many miles around and aftershocks can last for months.

Scientists say that there can be as many as 500,000 earthquakes a year, but most can't be felt, and only about 100 cause damage. An informative section at the end of "Panda's Earthquake Escape" has lots more facts to help you learn all about earthquakes and that loveable endangered animal, the panda.

title: How are diamonds formed?
text:
Diamonds are formed from carbon (the same stuff that turns a match black when you burn it). That carbon, deep in the Earth, under tremendous pressure and heat, over hundreds of millions of years, forms the beautiful, clear stones that we call diamonds. Of course, when a diamond is first found, it doesn't look very pretty at all. It's covered with a dull film. But when cut by a diamond expert, it begins to shine like the diamonds you've seen people wear in jewelry.

Some scientists also believe that some diamonds are truly out of this world. They may have been formed elsewhere in space and have come to Earth. Exploding stars may form some, and meteors slamming into the Earth's atmosphere may form others. Diamonds have been found inside of meteorites and in meteorite craters. And there are other diamond mysteries, as well. For example, a strange black diamond was first discovered in Brazil. It has scientists wondering where on Earth (or off Earth) it came from.

title: Georgius Agricola (1494-1555)
text: For today's spotlight, we're headed all the way back to the good ol' 1500s, around 500 years ago. In those days, in the land that would someday become Germany, you might find a doctor named Georgius Agricola hanging around the local mines and staring for hours on end at rocks. People might have thought him a little strange, but Agricola's patient study paid off. Most folks nowadays consider him the father of geology. (Geology is the study of rocks and the Earth.) Here's just one reason why: By studying the mines in his town, Agricola observed that underground rock seemed to be stacked in layers, or strata. His studies made the foundation for modern knowledge of how our layered Earth is put together.

title: Let's Investigate
text:
This week your challenge as a science detective is to come up with an investigation that involves rocks. Of course you start with a question. Maybe you want to know which rocks are hardest or which rocks are the most colorful. Once you've got your question, go on to the other steps you learned in Week 2. Use the sentence you made up in Week 8 to help you remember the rest of the steps or look back at Week 2, if you need to. Working with a friend or two can make the investigation easier and more fun!

Here's a hint: A book about rocks can be a very valuable tool in your investigation. Head for the library!

title: What’s in Dirt?
text:
Dirt, soil, mud - just a few names for the stuff that is the foundation of our world. It took thousands of years to make it. Kids use it for mud pies, and miners sift through it looking for treasure. We grow veggies and flowers in it, and we harvest corn from it. It's also what your mom tells you to "wipe off your feet." Scientists call it soil!

Along with water, soil is one of the most important parts of the Earth. Without soil, we wouldn't be here. About 10 percent of the Earth is covered with useful soil, and it takes quite some time and a lot of effort to create it. Soil that we use to farm and garden starts out as rock. Over thousands of years (yes, thousands), the weather breaks down rock. First, the water from rain and snow soaks into the cracks of large rocks. As the water freezes it expands, forcing the rock to break apart into smaller pieces ... and smaller pieces ... and smaller pieces. You get the idea. Plant roots help, too. They reach down into the cracks and help to break rock apart. After more time - millions of years, that is - those broken pieces of rock look less like boulders and rocks and more like dirt or soil ... but not quite. There's still more work to do.

So far, we have battered, crumbled-up rocks called parent material. Next, the lifeless remains of animals and plants are digested by microorganisms and added to the mixture of broken-down rock. Throw in some animal waste, such as horse and cow manure, and you have some much needed minerals and nutrients. Now we have a material called humus, which is a mixture rich in minerals and organic matter. Parent material continues to break down and mix with humus, air and water as the soil develops.

Farmers throw in fertilizers to help the materials become even richer, and we are all growing more and more careful about adding only natural fertilizers. Chemicals added to soil may help some crops grow faster and bigger. They may also help prevent insects from invading and destroying the plants, but there is a cost. Chemicals added to the soil may also wash into the water table and seep into rivers or streams. As a result, farmers look for different ways to improve the yield, or harvest, safely. They like to rotate crops into different locations each year, which is a process that prevents nutrients from getting used up too quickly. It's also important to keep the soil from eroding, or washing away with wind and rain. Planting trees, grass and other plants can keep soil from eroding. Crop rotation and erosion prevention are two great examples of soil conservation.

In places like a school playground, soccer field or local park, people usually try to keep the soil in good shape. Want to know more? Read the lesson to get the rest of the scoop on soil!

title: All About Soil
text:
Sand, Silt and Clay

Soils are made of different materials in different places. Of course, there are a million different mixtures of minerals and organic material, and probably no two places have the exact same mixture. But there are three main types, or grades, of soil. The grade of soil has to do with texture (how it feels) and not what the soil is made of.

Sand, for example, is soil with a very coarse texture. But sand can be made of all sorts of different minerals, or ingredients.

Soil with a medium texture is called silt. Silt varies, just like sand, and can be made of all sorts of different minerals.

Finally, soil that is very fine is called clay. Are there different ingredients in different kinds of clay? Yep!

It's Raining . . . It's Pouring . . . Acid?

Sometimes pollution can harm soil and even kill the plants growing in it. When factories and machines like cars pollute the air, rain sometimes mixes with the pollution and becomes an acid. Then the acid rain carries the pollution into the soil. That acid in the soil kills plants and has been shown to make some forests sick. It also pollutes groundwater so that animals cannot drink from (or survive in) rivers, ponds, and lakes. Recent advances in technology have helped reduce such pollutants. In places where soil has become full of acids, lime and other chemicals are sprayed. This helps neutralize the acid and make the plants healthy again.

Keep That Soil Where It Belongs!

Because rain and weather can wash away precious soil, people have learned to shape the land by using landscaping techniques such as terracing to save soil. Terracing is making large, flat steps in hilly areas so that rain and wind don't erode the soil away as quickly. The ancient Inca in the Andes Mountains in South America used terracing for growing crops along steep mountains, where soils often are whisked away in a storm or mud slide.

Soil Horizons

Driving down the highway, you might see different layers of dirt and soil, rocks, clay, and other materials where the road was cut through a hillside or along a cliff face. When you drive by cut-away hillsides and roadways, you are passing by a snapshot of thousands of years of Earth history. Those layers of dirt, clay, and rock make up soil. You can even see how the lower layers are often harder materials, with more rock than the top layers, which are often sand, clay, or silt. Another word for a soil layer is horizon. Topsoil, the first horizon, is that dark, rich, humus-filled soil. It is usually looser and ideal for growing things. Subsoil, the next horizon down, is just below topsoil. It is a layer that has a lot of clay and tiny particles of material that have filtered down. It's often reddish or brown in color. Below the subsoil is typically a layer of rocks of all sizes mixed with some soil from above. Below that are large, solid rocks called bedrock.

title: Making Compost
text:
What do rotting vegetables and grass clippings have to do with soil? Well, that gooey, bug-infested, decomposing gook is called compost, and it contains nutrients that can help gardens grow like wildfire.

Ancient Chinese, Mesopotamians, Romans and other people used compost to grow better foods. And guess what? Modern people still use it today. Composting is simple. Gardeners all over the world use it to enrich their gardens.

Plants, banana peels, leaves and other organic materials can be used to make compost. Composting can be a useful way to control garbage. Most people use an old barrel or a big bin to hold the compost. Food scraps and clippings of vegetation are added to the bin. Then tiny bacteria, fungi and other tiny organisms break it down into a humus-like material. Chemical reactions occur as the different organisms do their jobs. Compost must be stirred every so often to let oxygen in. Water may be added to help the process.

On some occasions, compost can catch fire because of the chemical reactions. So, people need to make sure their compost is getting plenty of ventilation and is not placed in a structure that could burn.

title: ‘There’s a Hair in my Dirt! A Worm’s Story’ by Gary Larson
text:
It's not likely that earthworms would make anyone's Top 10 Favorite Animals list. They are not cute and cuddly, and they don't seem very important. But author and The Far Side cartoon creator Gary Larson 's book "There's a Hair in my Dirt! A Worm's Story" will give readers new respect for the lowly worm.

"I hate being a worm!" says the son as the earthworm family sits down to dinner one night. "Bird food. Fish bait. We never even go to the surface unless the rains flood us out of our burrows! Oh, and how can I forget? We eat dirt!"

So Father Worm tells his son a story. The youngster learns the value of his species because they "till, aerate and enrich the earth's soil, making it suitable for plants." As Father Worm explains, "No worms, no plants, and no plants, no so-called higher animals running around with their oh-so-precious backbones."

Father Worm (a.k.a. Gary Larson) knows his science facts. Earthworms are indeed invertebrates, animals without an inside skeleton. They must live in moist places to survive, so they spend most of their lives underground. They are also one of nature's greatest recyclers. They eat decaying leaves and roots. Then they swallow dirt as they burrow and their waste leaves behind mountains of rich soil full of nutrients for plants. They are powerful earth movers. Their tunnels leave air spaces for plant roots to grow more easily.

Enjoy this book. It's a fantasy tale, a fable and a science lesson all rolled into one.

title: Do earthworms make soil?
text:
Earthworms are like little soil factories. They range in size from microscopic to (believe it or not) several feet long! Worms have no eyes, no head, and no teeth, and they like to eat dirt. (Wouldn't they have to be missing their heads to like dirt?) When worms eat soil, they release waste in the form of "castings." Earthworm castings are the finest forms of humus on the planet. They're rich in nitrogen, potassium, and phosphorus.

Worms can multiply very quickly, and they love to dig tunnels in soil. Worms especially like soils with lots of organic material. As they consume that stuff, they make additional humus that's even more mineral rich.

Some people compost with worms. It's called vermi-composting, and it's becoming very popular with gardeners. In fact, so many gardeners want to use worms in their gardens that millions of worms are being grown in farms for sale to farmers and to the public.

But watch out. Not all worms are good for soil. Some flatworms have invaded English soils, killing helpful earthworms. It is amazing how even something like a simple worm can do big things for the stuff that winds up on your table.

title: James Hutton (1726-1797)
text:
James Hutton was one of the first geologists to view the layers of the Earth as part of a cycle that spanned millions of years. He developed an idea that the Earth had undergone the erosion of rock, the creation of sediments, the deposit of materials on the Earth being pressed down in layers, and volcanic rock being pushed up to the surface. Sounds familiar, doesn't it? Remember the rock cycle?

He also saw that some layers of the Earth were pushed up at odd angles. He believed that forces deep in the Earth pushed the rocks up over many years.

Hutton's ideas were brand new in the 1700s, and many people considered them foolish. He explained all his observations in a paper that he published in 1798 called "Theory of the Earth." Hutton's teachings are said to be the first ideas of modern geology and became the "bedrock" for what we know about Earth science today.

title: Our Living Oceans
text:
We recently learned about the layers that make up the structure of the Earth, from the crust on the outside, all the way down to the core on the inside. Well, this week we'll be looking at another very important layer, so to speak. It rests on top of the Earth's crust and gets everything it touches wet. It's called the hydrosphere and is made up entirely of water. In fact, the hydrosphere is made up of all the water on Earth, including every drop in every nook and cranny. Rivers, lakes, oceans - they're all part of it.

When you look into the deep blue ocean, you may get dizzy imagining just how deep the water goes: down, down, thousands and thousands of feet. But the truth is, compared with the size of the rest of the Earth, the thickness of the water is many, many times thinner than an eggshell compared to an egg. Still, even such a thin layer, barely covering most of the Earth's surface, does a whole lot for our planet. For example, did you know that the hydrosphere helps keep the Earth's temperature steady? It's true. Water retains (or holds onto) heat much better than dirt or rocks do. Water takes longer to cool down when the Earth gets cold and longer to heat up when it gets warm. And, because most of the Earth is covered with it, it makes good insulation.

All this is just a "drop in the bucket" compared to all there is to know about the hydrosphere. Want to know more? Turn the page, and let's dive in!

title: Bottom of the Ocean, Top of the Sanctuary Charts!
text:
We live in a gorgeous country that has it all - towering mountains, waving grasslands, sandy deserts and even beautiful oceans. Much of our land is privately owned, but the government tries hard to protect as much as it can. It is important to protect the land and water for us to enjoy, but we also need to protect the wildlife sanctuaries (places set aside for wildlife). One small slice of this national treasure, about 16 miles off the coast of Georgia, is Gray's Reef National Marine Sanctuary.

A reef is a long rock or sandbar that lies beneath the surface of the water. Gray's Reef is a sanctuary because it is rich in marine (ocean) wildlife that scientists are eager to protect and learn more about. Marine biologists refer to a seafloor that can support lots of invertebrates (animals without spines) as a "live bottom." Gray's Reef has a rich and diverse population of wildlife that lives on a rocky shelf 60 feet below the surface. With the large amount of wildlife living there, it is almost impossible to see the rocky bottom in places. Divers and scientists sometimes call it a carpet of living creatures! Do you want to learn more about the ocean sanctuaries in American waters, including Gray's Reef? Visit any of the National Ocean Service (NOS) websites, beginning with: sanctuaries.noaa.gov.

title: The Mighty Ocean
text:
Thanks for the Air!

About half of the world's oxygen comes from the oceans. Tiny, one-celled algae called phytoplankton are hard at work all the time, making air for us land creatures. There are so many of them in the ocean that without them, it would be a different color. And those little guys produce as much oxygen as all the plants and forests in the world combined.

Thanks for the Food!

Do you like to eat fish? Without the hydrosphere, there would not be any fish for you to eat. But there are more than just fish in the sea. Anyone who has enjoyed a tender, buttered lobster tail knows that. And it doesn't even stop there. Between all the regular fish, all the shellfish, all the tasty crustaceans, all the kelp, all the seaweed, and all the other scrumptious eats available in the hydrosphere, it's really nature's buffet table.

Thanks for the Water!

Now this may seem a bit obvious, but we wanted to thank the hydrosphere for what it's made of - wet, wet water. Everyone knows we need it to survive, and it's a good thing the hydrosphere's full of it. You may not know that almost all of the water in a tall, cool glass, cooling you down on a hot day, was once part of Earth's mighty oceans and then evaporated and found itself in rivers and streams near your home.

Thanks for the Currents!

Powerful forces are at work all the time on the hydrosphere, and it's always moving. In fact, compared to how slowly the land moves, the world's rivers and oceans are lightning fast. In the oceans, currents form and flow slowly in circles between the continents. They carry with them warm or cool water, depending on where they are. That warm or cool water warms or cools the continents nearby, like a massive heating/air-conditioning system. For example, there's a current called the California Current that pushes cool water all down the West Coast of the United States, keeping people cool on hot summer days. Another current called the Gulf Stream moves warm water past the East Coast, warming them up even in the very north. The rotation of the Earth also affects how water moves around in the ocean. It spins clockwise in the northern hemisphere and counterclockwise in the southern hemisphere. Constant winds influence the currents of the ocean as well.

Thanks for the Science Laboratory!

The ocean is also a big chemistry lab. One average bucket of seawater contains most of the elements known to mankind. But, of course, most of those elements are found in very small amounts. In ocean water, you will find hydrogen and oxygen of course, sodium (salt), chlorine, sulfate, magnesium, gold and silver, just to name a few. There are carbon dioxide, oxygen, and other gases such as nitrogen as well. Some chemicals and elements come from the mantle by way of molten rock pushing up through the ridges. Others come from sediments washed from eroding mountains to the ocean by rivers and streams.

Thanks for the Petroleum!

Petroleum is the fuel that powers the machines of our world. Cars, factories, planes and boats all run on it, and the need for it has formed alliances, built governments and even caused wars. At first, all the oil we knew of came from deep wells on land. Since 1897, we've been getting oil from deep wells under the ocean, too. Think about it for a moment: If petroleum is hidden under the surface of the Earth, and most of the Earth's surface is covered with water, it makes sense that the hydrosphere is a good place to drill.

Of course, petroleum at sea causes problems, too. When oil spills on the ocean's surface, it harms birds and animals, sometimes in huge numbers. Someday we hope to have cleaner, safer fuels to burn in our engines, but we still owe the ocean a big thank-you for all the oil it's given us.

Ocean Features and Boundaries

Gravity pulls water toward the center of the Earth, so it runs downhill to the oceans, where it has collected for billions of years. The oceans cover the lowest areas of the Earth's crust. The Earth's crust under the oceans is made of different parts. The shallowest part of the ocean is the continental shelf. That's where the oceans meet the dry land. The shelves go down about 200 feet and are the favorite places for scuba divers to explore.

Where the continental shelf ends, the oceans drop almost straight down in some places to more than 10,000 feet (about two miles). This is called the continental slope.

At the bottom of the ocean are large, flat areas called the ocean floor. In some regions, called the abyssal plains, the ocean floor is especially flat over great distances.

title: Robots Under the Sea
text:
It's tough sometimes to figure out just how to explore the deepest parts of the oceans. For one thing, no diver could make it down there. The deeper he or she went, the greater the pressure of the water would be, until it squashed that diver like a grape. And although better, stronger diving suits are being made all the time, some people think there's an even better solution. In an undersea adventure film called "The Abyss," a special undersea robot goes where humans can't. And that's not science fiction! Robots are at work right now, going where no human undersea explorer could survive.

Special scientific robots that "swim" thousands of feet underwater in the Pacific Ocean are right now helping scientists study weather patterns and ocean currents. The U.S. Navy's AUSS (Advanced Unmanned Search System) and other "search robots" help spot sunken vessels such as the Titanic or other wrecks. The AUSS gets commands in the form of sound waves from a ship on the surface. No wires are needed!

title: ‘Out of the Deep’ by Gloria Skurzynski and Alane Ferguson
text:
Jack and Ashley Landon often get to travel with their mom, a wildlife veterinarian, when she investigates mysterious animal problems. In this book they go to Acadia National Park. Whales, seals, and other ocean animals are washing ashore and dying along the coast of Maine. The family's 14-year-old foster child, Bindy, stumbles on to the secret causing the strange animal behavior.
