The three children help rescue a stranded baby humpback whale, but soon find that Bindy's discovery puts their own lives in danger.

"Out of the Deep" is one of a series of wildlife mystery novels set in America's national parks. All the stories involve animals and adventure, giving readers excitement and wildlife education at the same time.

If you love the ocean and its animals, you might like a career in oceanography. Marine biologists specialize in the ocean's plants, animals and ecosystems. They study everything from tiny plankton to mighty whales. They do research and experiments with plant and animal life. Many are certified scuba divers.

There are lots of other oceanography careers. Marine geologists study the ocean floor with its mountains, canyons and underwater volcanoes. Physical oceanographers examine the movement of the ocean's waves, currents and tides. All of these things have important effects on our environment.

Oceanographers are dedicated to preserving and protecting the world's oceans. They often join together to study pollution, endangered coral reefs and other problems in ocean environments. Since our Earth has more oceans than land, that's a really good thing!

title: What is desalination?
text: Desalination is a fancy name for a special process. Before we describe it, we'll remind you first that neither people nor some animals and plants could live very long drinking seawater. Most living things need fresh water to grow. But what about places where seawater is the only water around? Can fresh water be made from salt water? You bet it can! That's what desalination is. It's actually simple. Seawater is full of salt and other minerals. But when the water gets hot and evaporates, the minerals are left behind, leaving clean, salt-free water vapor floating around. If that vapor can be gathered somewhere and cooled down into water again, voila - a drink fit for any human, animal, or plant is produced. It's a process that's catching on. Some island nations have huge desalination plants generating fresh water all the time. Many modern ships can do it, too! On a smaller scale, there are personal desalination kits for sailors who might find themselves in the middle of the ocean without a drink.

title: Jacques Cousteau (1910-1997)
text:
When is a scientist also an Oscar-winning filmmaker? When he's Jacques Cousteau, the world-famous oceanographer, that's when! Captain Cousteau, aboard his famous ship Calypso, brought the ocean right into the living rooms of millions of amazed viewers with his movies, TV shows, and books about ocean life. His documentary film called "The Silent World" earned him an Oscar in 1957, and it wasn't his last. Over his long career, he would win three more.

Your parents and grandparents may remember gathering around the TV set for the latest episode of "The Undersea World of Jacques Cousteau" or "Those Amazing Animals." And though Captain Cousteau is no longer with us, his legacy lives on among millions of ocean lovers who got their first undersea glimpse through the lens of Jacques Cousteau's camera.

And here's one more thing: Jacques Cousteau also helped invent the aqua-lung. Nowadays, we call it SCUBA equipment.

title: Let's Investigate
text: Water - every living thing on Earth needs it to survive. What would a good science detective want to know about water? Are you wondering how long certain plants can survive without water or what would happen if you watered them with root beer instead? Maybe you'd like to invent a way to water your plants while you're on vacation. It's always fun to work with some friends. If you're ready to try an investigation on your own, then go for it!

title: Save Our Planet!
text:
Earth is an amazing planet. Its water, atmosphere and soil give life to hundreds of thousands of species of flowering plants and more than a million species of animals. Humans are just one species, but it turns out that not all of us are good at sharing our planet. Many of the problems facing Earth's species are caused by people. And many of the people causing the problems are right here in the good old U.S.A. American cars, factories, machines and chemicals are polluting the air, water and soil.

Although air pollution has decreased in the past 30 years, many areas in the United States still exceed the national standards set by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). The EPA also tests America's rivers, lakes and estuaries (coastal areas where freshwater and saltwater mix). Many of them are polluted by chemicals. The pesticides (chemicals that kill bugs) and herbicides (chemicals that kill weeds) that help farmers grow food can get into the soil and eventually into food.

People are also responsible for the destruction of the habitats of many plants and animals. As Earth's population increases, people are sprawling out across the Earth and sometimes destroying places other species used to call home. What about natural disasters? Floods, storms, droughts and earthquakes also cause problems for Earth's species. Natural disasters can destroy the habitats of plants and animals, and that includes human habitats. Hurricane Katrina left more than one million people homeless after it hit the Gulf Coast in 2005.

Have you heard the phrase "between a rock and a hard place?" In many ways people are between a rock and a hard place as they look for solutions to these problems. For example, people need cars to get around, but cars pollute the air. Another thing that makes finding answers a real challenge is that experts don't always agree about how to fix things. And many solutions would be very expensive.

That's the bad news. The good news is many thousands of people do know how to share our planet. They are working to find solutions to the problems we all face. Not only scientists, but also ordinary people like us can help. Turn the page and read about what is being done now and what can be done in the future.

title: Students Get Serious about Solar-Powered Cars
text:
Students at Stanford University are getting hands-on experience with solar-powered technology.

Students involved in the Stanford Solar Car Project build solar cars for a race across Australia.

Nathan Hall-Snyder, a Stanford student and the team lead of the Solar Car Project, said the purpose of the project is first educational and secondly competitive.

"Building a solar car is an incredible exercise in all aspects of an engineering project," Hall-Snyder said.

Students are responsible for raising funds for the project, along with building the car. That gives students a chance to develop real skills, Hall-Snyder said.

The students also try to build the fastest car possible for the race.

The trans-continental solar car race is called the World Solar Challenge. Since 1987 there have been 10 World Solar Challenge races, which are open to race cars from university students and private companies.

The objective of the challenge, besides going fast and winning the race, is to raise awareness of solar-powered possibilities while finding ways to make better machines. The Stanford Solar Car Project has built 10 cars, each faster and more efficient than the last.

"As newer technologies become available to us, we try to incorporate them in order to produce the fastest solar vehicle possible," Hall-Snyder said.

The project at Stanford is also having an effect on technology used outside of the college campus. The battery pack for the Tesla Roadster, an electric sports car, was developed in the Stanford shop as a battery pack for a solar car.

"The students who designed and built that battery system went on to join the founding team at Tesla (Motors), which is now selling electric vehicles," Hall-Snyder said. "Many team members go on to make a splash at other companies, especially in the founding of startups."

title: Finding Solutions
text:
What Are We Doing Now?

One of the most important things scientists and others can do to save our planet is to make people aware of the problems. Articles in magazines and newspapers like Science Studies Weekly, television programs and news reports, and even movies can help spread the word. Once people know about the problems, they can start helping to find solutions. What can you do? Write reports, make posters, or do science fair projects that inform people about pollution, global climate change, endangered species and other issues.

Probably the most popular campaign to get people involved has been "Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle." The three Rs stand for reducing the amount of packaging, reusing containers instead of throwing them away and recycling things like cans, bottles and papers. The goal is to decrease the amount of trash that is going into landfills, because we are running out of space. Each year, Americans generate more than hundreds of millions of tons of trash. And most of us don't recycle as much as we should. What can you do? Recycle everything you can, and remind your family and friends to recycle, too. Reuse bags, boxes and plastic containers over and over. Buying things with less packaging and things that are made from recycled materials will help, too.

How are governments around the world helping to save the planet? Many governments have laws and regulations that help make things better. (Regulations are special rules that control the way things are done.) Some laws regulate how much pollution factories can put into the air or water. Some rules protect endangered species of plants and animals. Other rules protect wilderness areas. Some laws control how people and business use and dispose of (get rid of) chemicals. In many countries, there are laws that say companies that cut down trees must replace some or all of them with new trees. Governments have also made rules that required automobile manufacturers to build cars that get better gas mileage and produce less pollution.

How Do Scientists Work Together?

Scientists from around the world need to work as a team to continue to look for ways to protect the environment. Everyone on the team should feel free to reach their own conclusions and develop their own hypotheses. Some ideas may not work because they create new problems. Before trying a new method, creating a new chemical, or building a new machine, scientists have to do their best to find out how their idea might affect other people. New ideas must be safe and should not create a different problem.

As they search for answers, researchers must communicate with each other. Sharing ideas, observations and the results of experiments is very important. Experiments need to be repeated many times to verify results and make sure the data is correct. Scientists have to make careful observations and record the results clearly and accurately. They need to compare and contrast their results with the results of other researchers. By working together, scientists will accomplish much more than they could on their own.

Celebrate Earth!

One person who has worked hard to make Earth a better place to live is Senator Gaylord Nelson of Wisconsin. Senator Nelson is the man who came up with the idea to have Earth Day every year in April. During the 1960s, he became really worried about pollution and its effect on the Earth. Earth Day actually started as a protest against what was happening to the environment. Senator Nelson started talking about his idea, and soon people all over the country were organizing protests and other activities. April 22, 1970, was the first Earth Day. More than 20 million people and thousands of schools and communities took part. Over time, Earth Day became a celebration of Earth and a way to get information to people. Find out if your community is planning some Earth Day activities next April. If so, don't miss it. You'll have fun, you'll learn something, and you'll be helping to save our planet!

Arbor Day is another special day to celebrate Earth. But this day is dedicated just to trees. More than 100 years ago, Julius Sterling Morton, a journalist and politician from Nebraska, started thinking about how trees could help both the environment and the economy of his state. He started planting orchards and wind breaks on his own farm and talked many of his neighbors into doing the same thing. In 1872, he persuaded the state to set aside April 10 as Arbor Day. It was a huge success, and more than one million trees were planted in Nebraska on that day. Today, every state has an Arbor Day. Other countries, including Japan, Israel, India and Korea have their own versions of Arbor Day, although they don't use that name for it. Plant a tree (or several trees) on Arbor Day, and say thanks to Mr. Morton!

title: Conserving Natural Resources
text:
Natural resources are very valuable, but they won't last forever unless we conserve them (use them carefully and responsibly). For centuries, people have found ways to conserve natural resources. When American Indians killed a deer or buffalo, they used every part. Nothing went to waste. They ate the meat, sewed clothing from the hides, and made tools from the antlers and bones.

Water has always been one of our most important natural resources. You can conserve water by turning off the faucet while you brush your teeth and taking short showers. Ask your parents to run the dishwasher or washing machine only when there is a full load. When you boil water to cook pasta, don't pour the water down the drain. Let it cool off, then use it to water your house plants.

The world is running out of nonrenewable energy (energy that cannot be replaced). Walking, riding bicycles or taking public transportation instead of driving saves lots of gas. Using biofuels (fuels made from plants) and geothermal energy (energy from inside the Earth) cuts down on the amount of fossil fuels we need.

As the population of the world increases (6.5 billion people and counting), it is even more important to use resources wisely. If we all do our part, the Earth will provide us with natural resources for generations to come.

title: Models
text:
Think about a model car. How is it different from a real car? Size is one difference, of course. Since it's smaller, the model car doesn't have as many details as the real car. It's not made of the same materials, and it doesn't have a working engine. Some other parts of the model car might not work, either.

But some models are very useful. Models can be handy science tools. They help us learn about real things that are too big, too small, too expensive, or too dangerous to use in school.

You've probably made models before. Maybe you created a model of our solar system or a volcano for a science project. Making a model instead of using an already-made model helps you learn even more about the real thing you are studying.

In This Week's Lab, you will make a model of a woodland or wetland. The plants and animals in your model habitat depend on each other (and on you) to survive. You will set up the habitat and will need to add water and appropriate food occasionally so that the plants and animals will live and grow.

Look around your classroom. Do you see any models? A globe is a model of the earth. Some science classrooms have a model of a skeleton or the inside of a human body. What other models do you know about that help us learn about science?

title: What is ozone?
text:
Ozone is an oxygen molecule with three atoms. It is the main ingredient in smog, and it is released into the air by some factories and machines. Ozone in the Earth's lower atmosphere is unhealthy, especially for people who have respiratory problems like asthma. But ozone is not always a bad thing.

There is a thin layer of ozone surrounding the Earth that helps protect us from the harmful ultraviolet rays of the sun. The ozone layer is about three millimeters (one-eighth inch) thick. That's only about as thick as the cover of a hardback book. Scientists have found evidence that there is a hole in the ozone layer above the continent of Antarctica. They believe the hole was caused by chemicals used in refrigerators and air conditioners, as well as in the manufacturing of things like styrofoam. They are worried that the hole may become larger or that holes may develop in other places. If that happens, the number of people who develop diseases like skin cancer will probably go up.

title: Ellen Swallow Richards
text:
Pollution has been a big problem throughout the world for centuries. Over the years scientists have tried to make people aware of the problem. They have researched ways to reduce pollution in our air, water and soil.

During the 19th century, very few women were chemists, because most universities did not admit women. In 1873, Ellen Swallow Richards became the first woman to graduate from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). She got a degree in chemistry and became interested in protecting the environment.

Richards and a team of researchers tested 20,000 samples of water in Massachusetts. They found that there was way too much chlorine in the water. Some of it came from natural sources. But a lot of it came from things people were doing, like factories dumping chemical waste into waterways.

Chlorine is an element, a substance made of only one kind of matter. It is used in bleach to whiten clothing and in very small amounts to kill harmful bacteria in drinking water. A little chlorine helps make drinking water safer, but too much makes it unhealthy.

Richards talked the state into regulating what factories dumped into rivers and streams. Thanks to her, Massachusetts was the first state in our country to have rules and regulations that helped make water cleaner.

title: Let's Investigate
text:
Everyone’s talking about “going green” these days. People all over the world are looking for ways to protect the environment and save natural resources. Check out this website for ways kids can help: sfenvironmentkids.org

Your investigation assignment for this week is all about saving the Earth. You could test how much water that leaky faucet in your kitchen is wasting or compare rechargeable batteries to disposable batteries. Whatever you do, be sure to follow the steps for doing a science investigation. The Earth may depend on it!

title: The Greenhouse Effect
text:
This investigation will help you understand the greenhouse effect, the term scientists use for the way the sun's energy is absorbed by the Earth's surface (both water and land) and warms the Earth. Many scientists are afraid that carbon dioxide is increasing the greenhouse effect. Carbon dioxide is produced by industries that use fuels like coal and oil. Many scientists believe that the Earth is slowly getting warmer. Climatologists who keep track of Earth's surface temperature have found that the average surface temperature has gone up about one degree over the past century. They worry that global warming may get worse, melting the ice at the poles and making sea levels rise. Floods caused by rising sea levels could change Earth's climate completely.

At first, some scientists thought the change in Earth's average temperature might be part of the natural pattern in the world's climate. A few still think that's possible. But most scientists agree that global climate change is real. And it could be a real problem.

title: Water All Around You
text:
Have you ever traveled anywhere far away? Where's the farthest place you've been? Canada? Alaska? Hawaii? Australia? Mexico? Maybe, if you've traveled a lot, you might have something in common with another world traveler we know. In fact, of all the big travelers in the world, this one might just win the prize. Who is it? Well, it's not exactly a "who" at all. It's the Earth's water, all around you.

Although it may be hard to imagine when you look at the surface of a peaceful lake, the water on this planet is always on the move. Sometimes, if you're water, the best way to travel is simply to roll along a riverbed toward a lake or the ocean. But there are other ways of getting around, too. Sometimes, water might head underground for a subterranean trip through the layers of rock under your feet. Other times, water might just steam up and take to the air.

Where's the water always going? Oh, around in circles mostly, the same trip, over and over again. It's called the water cycle, and it's the process by which water evaporates from the Earth's surface into the air and then falls back to Earth again as water. Will it ever get tired of all that traveling? Not as long as the sun keeps shining! In fact, you might say that the sun drives the water cycle. After all, the sun's warmth evaporates the water in the first place. Do you want to find out more about the amazing trip that water takes, over and over? Turn the page, and let's go!

title: The Water Cycle
text:
Evaporation

Have you ever watched water boil? Have you ever seen the steam rise from a whistling kettle? If you leave water on a heat source too long, the liquid will eventually disappear altogether! That's because as water heats, it evaporates. Evaporation is the process in which a liquid turns into a gas, and any source of heat will start evaporation. Take the sun, for example. It shines down on the Earth's surface, and ocean and river water evaporates into the atmosphere and enters the water cycle!

Condensation

Moving through the cycle, warm, evaporated water (moist air) rises higher into the air. The higher the evaporated water rises in the atmosphere, the cooler the air is - and guess what happens to moist air as it cools. That's right! It begins to turn into liquid again. This part of the cycle is called condensation. On a cloudy day, you can see it in the sky when you look up. Those clouds floating by are really nothing but huge gatherings of tiny water droplets. When they are cool enough and big enough, they'll fall to back to the Earth's surface as precipitation.

Precipitation

After water condenses and forms clouds of water droplets, it may fall back to Earth in many forms. It might fall as rain. If the air is cold enough, the condensed water may freeze and fall as snow. Or picture this - a tiny, frozen water droplet is part of a stormy atmosphere and gets blown high up through a tall cloud. It will pick up other water particles as it goes, just like rolling a snowball will make it bigger! By the time it strikes the ground, it's a ball of ice called hail. No matter what the form, water falling from the sky is called precipitation. It comes from the word precipitate, which means to fall.

Transpiration

Trees and other plants are big water drinkers, and much of the moisture they consume is stored in their leaves. Through a process called transpiration, moisture is released directly from the leaves of trees and plants into the air. Transpiration is the second largest source of water vapor in Earth's atmosphere!

Wind

Remember: Everything is made of matter, and air is no different. It takes up space because it is made of tiny particles, or molecules. Cool air is dense, which means the molecules are packed closely together. Warm air is less dense because there are fewer particles, and they have more room to move. Air particles always seem to want to hang around in the least crowded space they can find. That means that dense, cool air is always trying to move into the space where warmer air is. That air, moving around and looking for space, is called wind.

Runoff

Water that falls from the sky, as precipitation, always finds its way into rivers, lakes and oceans. In mountain regions where rivers have their headwaters, snow typically stays on peaks until spring when it melts to create cold, fast and rushing streams. Most of the time, however, precipitation falls as rain and runs into the nearest river immediately. Either way, water that runs across the surface of the Earth and into lakes and rivers is called runoff. Runoff might flow for hundreds or even thousands of miles, all the way to the ocean. That is, if it doesn't evaporate first!

Groundwater

Not all water that falls from the sky collects on the surface to become runoff. Some precipitation soaks into the ground, collecting in pores, or tiny holes, in the ground, just like water in a giant sponge. Some soils and even rocks can have pores in them, such as sand and sandstone. Surfaces that have pores are called permeable, while those that do not - like clay and bedrock - are called impermeable. Water that is absorbed into permeable surfaces drains down until it reaches an impermeable layer. The water then fills up, or saturates, the porous layers of rock above. Layers of rock that hold a lot of water and allow it to circulate are called aquifers. Groundwater is part of the water cycle, too. It eventually makes it way out into the open through fresh water springs or wells, ready to be evaporated and to start all over again!

title: Getting Water From the Ground Into Your Glass
text: People have been digging wells to find shallow groundwater for many thousands of years. You may have seen someone lower a bucket deep down into a well and pull it up again, full of cool water. But what if you want to get the water to come up to you without a bucket? One way is to install a pump that will pump the water up from underground. But there's a simpler way. You can dig a well deep enough that it passes through impermeable layers of rock into an aquifer. The pressure of the rock layers pressing on the aquifer from above and below will squeeze that water right up to where you're standing, just like squeezing a giant tube of toothpaste. Wells like these are called artesian wells, and farmers have found them to be very useful over the years, because most freshwater is found underground.

title: ‘The Waterhole’ by Graeme Base
text:
You probably started studying the water cycle in kindergarten. Maybe you did simple experiments, placing a cup of water in a window for several days to observe evaporation. Perhaps you watched condensation form on the outside of a glass of ice.

Now that you're older, you understand that water moves in repeated patterns in the hydrologic (water) cycle. You're learning about things like precipitation, erosion and runoff. You can draw diagrams and label the parts. You might do more challenging investigations with terrariums and stream tables.

But what's the point? Open Graeme Base's beautiful picture book "The Waterhole" and you'll never look at the water cycle in the same way. The book opens with a watering hole set in Africa, where one rhino comes for a drink. You turn the page and see two tigers drinking from another water hole, this time in India. Then three toucans are drinking - it's the Amazon.

At first glance it's a simple counting book, with each page set in a different habitat of the world. But wait - the die-cut waterhole gets smaller on each page. A serious message, as ten kangaroos in Australia face a dusty, dry watering hole. And then the next page features a single, giant raindrop...

This book puts the reader inside the water cycle. For puzzle lovers, more animals from each continent are cleverly hidden in the amazing illustrations. The page borders show animal silhouettes, with descriptions in the back of the book. You won't believe studying the water cycle could be so educational, and so much fun!

title: How do meteorologists predict the temperature?
text:
Almost everyone has asked that question. While meteorologists have lots of fancy training and equipment, here's one simple way to predict the weather:

For decades, weather people have carefully kept records of the temperature on every day of the year. They simply add up all the high temperature readings, divide the answer by the number of days, and there you have it - tomorrow's high temperature.

Here's one example from sunny Florida. In the last 48 years, there have been only 23 August days below 85 degrees in Ft. Lauderdale, Florida. Only 72 days have been above 95 degrees. There were 1,123 August days total. That means that on any given August day, there's a good chance that the temperature will be between 85 degrees and 95 degrees.

Temperature averages can be a great way to predict the high and low temperature for any given day. Adding current information on cloud cover, air pressure, and wind can make the prediction even more accurate.

title: Lewis Fry Richardson (1881-1953)
text:
Imagine that you were a member of the French army in World War I and you had been wounded. How would you have felt if you had to wait a while for an ambulance because your ambulance driver was finishing his math project? Lewis Fry Richardson, a young British meteorologist, really was an ambulance driver with the French army in World War I. While other people fired at the enemy, Richardson wrote furiously on pieces of paper, trying to come up with a logical way to predict the weather. He finally did it, too. He came up with a way to predict the weather in pretty much any corner of the world. All it required was a way to divide the world up into thousands of squares on a grid, and thousands of people to gather weather information from each square, and thousands of mathematicians to do thousands of calculations each. Needless to say, the idea didn't get him very far. Most people figured that by the time the math was finished and predicted rain, it would already be raining.

Of course, these days, computers can easily do thousands, or even millions, of math equations in only a moment. And that's just what we do! In fact, meteorologists all over the world predict the weather by using Richardson's ideas, combined with lots of high-tech equipment. And, while the people of his own time might have thought his ideas weren't practical, these days, most folks who know about him think that Richardson was a smart guy who was way ahead of his time.

title: Watching the Sky!
text: Some warm night, head outside and gaze up into the sky. Seems quiet, doesn't it? If the moon's out, look at it, too. It looks peaceful up there. It might be hard to believe that the peaceful, still-looking objects that you see in the sky are actually hurtling through space at incredible speeds, sometimes at thousands and thousands of miles per hour. In fact, even the solid Earth that you're standing on is really rocketing through space many times faster than the fastest airplane. Where's it all going in such a hurry? Around in circles, mostly, or almost circles. (Almost circles? Don't worry; we'll explain more inside.) The Earth, for example, travels in a huge path around and around the sun. It takes a year to make the complete journey. While that's happening, the moon is whizzing around and around the Earth, once every month. Those huge, outer-space companions (the sun and moon) have a lot to say about life here on Earth. The sun, for example, keeps us warm and gives us light. It grows crops and forests and even keeps Earth from spinning off wildly into space, never to be heard from again. The moon, even though it's smaller than the Earth, still determines how high the oceans are during certain times of the day. It's a crazy relationship that suns, planets and moons have, and, this week, it's all right here in Science Studies Weekly!

title: Space Junk: High-Speed Litter in Orbit
text:
Have you seen the movie WALL-E? Maybe you remember that movie's depiction of the planet Earth in the not-too-distant future: covered with garbage. Do you remember the junk floating in space around the earth? WALL-E has to fly through all the broken satellites, pieces of rockets and other trash to get into space and later back home.

The WALL-E story may be made-up, but the trash floating in circles around the earth is real, and it's causing problems right now. There are more than 21,000 pieces of debris (junk) being tracked in space, and those are only the ones bigger than softballs. That may not sound big, but at the speeds they travel (15,000 miles per hour!), if one hit your spaceship, you'd be in trouble.

Where did this junk come from? Well, we put it there. Most if it is made up of old satellites and rocket parts. Those pieces start out big, but eventually they crash into each other as they orbit the earth, and make thousands of smaller pieces. China once blew up an old satellite while testing a missile and created 3,300 pieces of junk where before there was only one.

Maybe your first thought is "When will this stuff come crashing down, and what if I get hit?" Well, don't worry. Most of the junk, if it ever does drift low enough to be dragged down to Earth by gravity, will get burned up in Earth's atmosphere. Only one person, Lottie Williams from Tulsa Oklahoma, has ever been hit by a piece of space junk as it fell from the sky. She was struck in the shoulder by a six-inch chunk of rocket. In case you were wondering, the odds of that happening were one in a trillion.

How should we clean up the space garbage? Working in space is tricky. WALL-E was good at cleaning up junk on the ground, but what do you think we should do about space?

title: Watching the Sky
text:
Why Do We Have Seasons?

Why are there seasons on the Earth? Well, when the Earth orbits around the sun, its position changes throughout the year. The Earth is at an angle to the sun, tilted about 23 degrees. As the Earth revolves around the sun, sunlight hits us at different angles during different parts of the year. When it's summer in North America, the sun is sending light that is more direct to the northern hemisphere because the northern hemisphere is tilted toward the sun. More direct sunlight means more energy, and that means it gets warmer. When it's winter in the northern hemisphere, the southern hemisphere is getting more direct sunlight and more warmth. During that time, it's summer in the southern hemisphere. Wow, summer in January! Do you wonder what that would be like? Head south!

Our Earth

The Earth moves around the sun in an elliptical orbit. That means that it is not perfectly circular. It's more like an oval. What it also means is that, in some parts of the year, we are actually closer to the sun by a few million miles. We're closer enough, in fact, to have some big climate changes during those parts of the year.

The Peculiar Poles

As a basic rule, the farther north or south you live, the cooler the temperatures are going to be all year long. That much you could probably figure out. But here's something that might surprise you. Right at the North and South Poles, because they are at the top and bottom of the curve of the Earth, they almost never get direct sunlight. They're also the places that are most dramatically tilted toward (or away from) the sun, which makes something weird happen. While the sun never seems to travel very high in the sky in those places, it also hardly ever goes down during spring and summer at all. No kidding! During the summer at either of the poles, the daylight could last pretty much the entire season. On the other hand, in the winter, it would usually seem like night.

Earth's Northern Hemisphere in Summer

The sun's rays shine directly on the northern hemisphere.

Earth's Northern Hemisphere in Winter

The sun's rays are indirect in the northern hemisphere.

Phases of the Moon

If you and a friend take an orange and a small flashlight outside on a dark, dark night and then shine the flashlight at the orange, what will you see? An orange, of course. But what if your friend held the flashlight and aimed it at the side of the orange that you couldn't see? Now you see just an orange-shaped shadow. (Your friend's side is lit up.) If your friend aimed the light so that you could see part of the lit-up orange, you might see a shape that was part orange and part shadow. What you see depends on where you stand and where the light is. Now, imagine that the light isn't a flashlight, but the sun. And imagine that the orange isn't an orange, but the moon. And, finally, imagine that you are standing on Earth, looking at the moon. Look at the chart below this article. It will show you what the moon looks like at certain times of the month. There are even names for the different ways the moon can look from Earth (or the phase of the moon). You'll see those in the chart, too. And don't worry about the crazy names. Just check out the box where you'll find their meanings!

Moon Phases

New Moon - Just shadow. Looks like no moon at all

Full Moon - Big white circle, like a silver dollar

Gibbous - More than a half circle, but less than a full one

Crescent - More than no moon at all, but less than a half circle.

Waxing - Getting bigger every night

Waning - Getting smaller every night

Check Out the Backside!

Those of us who have never been to outer space have never, ever seen the backside of the moon. It's true. The moon always faces us exactly the same way, and only a few astronauts have seen the other side. Want to try something? Take an orange and draw a smiley face on one side of it. Now take a basketball. You can leave it on the table and move the orange slowly around the basketball. Make sure the smiley face is always facing it. See how you have to turn the orange as it moves around the ball? The moon is turning, just like that, at exactly the speed that makes it face the Earth the same way all the time.

title: Foucault’s Pendulum
text:
Sometimes a simple invention can teach you a lot. Take, for example, the big pendulum made by a French scientist named Jean Bernard Leon Foucault in 1851. Foucault's pendulum demonstrated that the Earth is constantly rotating. It's true! He hung a heavy steel ball from the ceiling by a long cable and stood a bunch of small pegs on the floor in a circle around where the ball hung. Then he gave the ball a push. It swung away from him, knocked down a peg, and then swung back toward him, where it knocked down another peg. According to Newton's laws of motion, it should have continued like that all day, passing over the same two fallen pegs, as long as the ball kept swinging. But, at the end of the day, Foucault was amazed to see that the pendulum had knocked down other pegs in different parts of the circle.

Remember Newton's laws of motion? "An object set in motion stays in motion unless acted upon by another force." Foucault figured that other pegs were knocked down because the pendulum still swung in its same path according to Newton's laws, and the Earth rotated beneath it. He was right!

title: ‘A Child’s Introduction to the Night Sky’ by Michael Driscoll
text:
What can you see in the night sky? "In addition to constellations you might see...a planet...a satellite...the moon...a ghost (doubt it)." This is one of the first pages in the book "A Child's Introduction to the Night Sky," so you know right away that it's going to be fun. It's written by a science author with a sense of humor and illustrated by an artist who combines amazing photographs with imaginative drawings of things like the Hubble Telescope and the Mars Rover.

The table of contents shows that this book is different from most astronomy guides. After an introduction about the universe, the next two sections are "What We Can See" (stars, the Sun, some planets, hunks, chunks and flying objects) and "What We Can't See" (black holes, dark matter, gravity). Next comes "What Astronauts and Astronomers Do" and "What You Can Do." The fun text is geared to students ages 8 and up.

The stars have fascinated night sky watchers since ancient times. At first people named the star patterns for animals like the lion, scorpion and bull. Then the Greeks and Romans invented myths about their gods and goddesses to match the constellation patterns. The author explains these stories and adds a star-finder wheel so you can locate the constellations on your own. There are glow-in-the-dark star stickers, too!

This book is a great homework resource. "A Child's Introduction to the Night Sky" belongs on the bookshelves of children of all ages.

title: What are tides?
text: If you've ever spent an entire day at the beach, you may have noticed that the waves came farther and farther up the sand as the day went on. You may even have had to move your stuff a couple of times. You were seeing what's called a tide. At certain times of the day (high tide), the ocean water washes farther up the shore than at low tide. And, though it may seem like magic, gravity from the sun and moon actually cause the tides. (The moon has a bigger effect because it's closer to the Earth.) The gravity of our outer-space neighbors isn't strong enough to pull houses and trees off the Earth, but it is strong enough to pull on the oceans just enough to cause them to rise higher during the day. Once every month, the moon and the sun are on the same side of the Earth. When that happens, it's like they're teaming up on us, and the waves are even higher than they are during the rest of the month.

title: Johannes Kepler (1571–1630)
text:
Not all scientists have an easy life. Take the young Johannes Kepler. Now, he had a tough childhood. His home was the location of a 30-year war in Europe; he was sick most of his childhood; he caught small pox and other diseases and had poor vision. He was denied a position at a university because of his crazy theory that the sun was the center of the solar system (he was right, of course), and, to top it off, his mother was accused of being a witch!

Though Kepler's life in the 1500s was rough, it didn't keep him from making some great contributions to science. Kepler first studied philosophy and religion and later studied astronomy and mathematics. He believed that the universe was founded on mathematical perfection. He thought that mathematics could help answer our questions about the solar system and stars. Kepler demonstrated that planets orbit the sun, not in circles, but in ellipses. (Take a circle and squash it a little, like an oval.) This is true for planets, moons, comets, satellites and other objects that orbit bigger objects. Kepler was famous for other interesting things as well. He predicted that the Turks would invade his country, and they did! He also predicted that there would be a cold wave that would hit the region, and that happened, too! NASA's Kepler mission is named after him. The goal of the mission is to look for Earth-sized planets by putting a special telescope in orbit. The telescope is designed to discover other planets that orbit distant stars.

title: Where’d It Go?
text:
If the Earth is in the middle of the lineup, it keeps sunlight from reaching the moon. (It's called a lunar eclipse.) On a night like that, the moon would look dark, like a deep shadow. If the moon is in the middle of the lineup and gets between the Earth and the sun, it keeps sunlight from reaching the Earth. This one's called a solar eclipse.

From Earth it might look like a dark shadow over part of the sun, even during broad daylight! If you ever have a chance to see a solar eclipse, never look directly at the sun. You could hurt your eyes. Always use special "eclipse" glasses, or poke a small, round hole in a piece of paper and hold it above the sidewalk. You'll see the eclipse projected there on the ground.

title: Explore Our Vast Solar System
text:
Welcome to another week of Science Studies Weekly. This week, we will study our solar system. The word solar means sun - the star of the show. Everything in the solar system revolves around the sun. Planets, big chunks of rock and metal, ice, and other materials swirl around it. And hey, don't forget about us! We live on one of those giant chunks of rock. When you think about it, the Earth is a lot like a spaceship flying around the sun carrying us billions of miles through outer space. That makes us space travelers!

Imagine what it would be like if you traveled to another planet. Would you want to step out of your spacecraft to explore the red surface of Mars? Or would you want to go much farther into space to skate on the ice-cold surface of Pluto? Imagine flying through the rings of Saturn or even being in a race with a comet!

Is that kind of space travel possible? For many years, people thought it would be impossible to go to the moon. But in 1969, American astronaut Neil Armstrong became the first human being to set foot on the moon's dusty surface. So never say "never."

In this issue, you will learn about all the major objects in our solar system. So put on your spacesuits and blast off with us!

title: Hubble: A Look Back in Time
text:
Looking through the Hubble telescope is like looking back in time.

The Hubble Space Telescope is a telescope taken into space by the Space Shuttle back in 1990. For more than 20 years it has been taking pictures of distant stars and galaxies. Because the light from distant objects travels so far, and for so long, to get to the Hubble, the telescope is actually seeing what those objects looked like hundreds, thousands or even millions of years ago. The Hubble has sent back amazing pictures of galaxies that are just being born! With the Hubble's help, we have a better idea about how the Milky Way came to be.

Recently, the Hubble needed some repairs. Astronauts changed out the old camera for a new one that could take pictures of things so far away, they can only be viewed in special areas of the light spectrum, like ultraviolet and infrared.

The Hubble Space Telescope is getting old and will be replaced soon, but in the mean time it is the closest thing to time travel we have. Visit hubblesite.org to see some of the amazing pictures the Hubble has given us. Look closely at them - you're looking millions of years into the past!

title: Our Solar System
text:
One System Is Part of Another

The Earth is a pretty big place compared to you and me, but it's really just a very small part of a system of planets, moons, and asteroids that orbit the sun. This "system" of planets, moons, and asteroids revolving around the sun is called the solar system. Our solar system is pretty big, but did you know it's just a small part of a much larger system? This system is the Milky Way Galaxy. And although our galaxy has billions of stars that are similar to ours, there are probably more than 100 billion galaxies in the universe.

Sun - Did you know that you can fit about 1 million Earths inside the sun? Inside the sun is the core. Energy shoots out from the core to the surface, or photosphere, where most of the energy escapes. Surrounding the sun is the chromosphere. Above that is the corona. The sun is very hot, millions of degrees. It is also very active. Sometimes, huge explosions can be seen. These are called solar flares. They can shoot thousands of miles into space.

Mercury is the planet closest to the sun. It is small and rocky and has craters like our moon. There is no atmosphere on Mercury.

Venus is the second planet from the sun. We call it our sister planet because it's about the same size as Earth. Venus is a very dangerous place. Swirling clouds, high temperatures, and a crushing atmosphere would make it a very poor choice for a summer home. Next time you drink soda pop, think of Venus. The gas in fizzy drinks is called carbon dioxide, and Venus is loaded with it!

Earth - We live on the third planet from the sun. Earth is the only place that we know has life on it. It is the fifth largest planet in the solar system. Earth has a nickel-iron core. It spins on a 24-hour cycle.

Mars, the fourth planet, is often called the Red Planet. It has polar ice caps like Earth. Scientists now believe Mars once had liquid water on the surface. Mars has two moons, Deimos and Phobos. Dust storms can sometimes be seen on Mars.

Jupiter - You can fit about 1,000 Earths into Jupiter, the largest planet. Some believe Jupiter has a liquid core. Jupiter produces large amounts of electricity and has storms bigger than the Earth, which have been raging for hundreds of years. Jupiter has several rings and 62 satellites (moons).

Saturn, sixth from the sun, is most famous for its giant rings. Saturn's rings are made of ice chunks, dust, and rock. When sunlight hits them, they show as colorful rings. Saturn is a gaseous planet, like Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune. We call them Gas Giants. Saturn has at least 60 moons. In 2004, space probe Cassini/Huygens arrived at Saturn. It is helping scientists learn more about the giant Titan, one of Saturn's moons.

Uranus, seventh from the sun, is a blue-green planet with 27 known satellites. Uranus lies on its side, and it has at least 11 rings. Uranus may have more moons and rings that are yet to be discovered.

Neptune was discovered by mathematicians who noticed that something was pulling on Uranus. Neptune is the farthest planet from the sun for about 20 out of every 248 years, when Pluto drifts inside Neptune's orbit. The wind on Neptune is very powerful. It's about 15 times more powerful than an average hurricane here on Earth. Neptune has four rings and 13 moons.

Pluto - In 2006, scientists voted to classify Pluto as a dwarf planet. Pluto has three satellites. There are two other dwarf planets in our solar system. Ceres orbits the sun between Mars and Jupiter. Eris is farther from the sun than Pluto.

The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite. It is about 1/4 the size of Earth. Some believe the moon is a piece of Earth that split off when a larger object hit us. The moon used to have volcanoes. It has been struck by many large objects over billions of years. You can see the impacts of those objects when you look at the moon's craters through a telescope. The moon is actually not round; it is slightly egg-shaped.

Comets are big chunks of dirt and ice. In the center is a nucleus. As a comet flies closer to the sun, ice vapors are heated, creating a large shining tail. In 1992, scientists discovered a large belt of comets, called the Kuiper Belt, at the edge of the solar system, just outside Pluto's orbit.

Asteroids - About 4.5 billion years ago, the solar system was formed. Asteroids are believed to be leftover rocky chunks from this formation. A belt of asteroids lies between Mars and Jupiter.

Meteors are pieces of space stuff that hit the Earth's atmosphere. They usually burn up before they hit the Earth. Meteorites are large pieces of meteors that land on the Earth's surface. You can find them lying around the planet. Most meteors are from our own solar system, but some may be from deep in outer space.

Orbits - Each object in our solar system follows a circular path around another larger object. Moons circle around planets, and planets and asteroids circle around the sun. These circular paths are called orbits. The list below tells you how many Earth days or years it takes for each planet to orbit, or circle, the sun:

Mercury = 88 days

Venus = 243 days

Earth = 365 days

Mars = 687 days

Jupiter = 12 years

Saturn = 29 1/2 years

Uranus = 84 years

Neptune = 165 years

Pluto = 249 years

title: Telescopes
text: In Galileo's time, telescopes were very simple compared to today's telescopes. Galileo's telescope was a long tube with two glass lenses. The lenses are shaped so that when you look through them, you can see things that are far away. Telescopes have gotten much bigger since then. Large telescopes, housed inside mountain observatories like the Mauna Kea Observatory on the island of Hawaii, see much farther into space. The famous Hubble Space Telescope takes pictures of outer space from high above us as it orbits the Earth. The Hubble pictures have helped us see many stars much farther away in space. Radio telescopes are large dishes that detect radio waves from space. With radio telescopes, scientists can better understand what stars and other objects in space are made of and how they were formed. For many people, telescope viewing is a fun hobby because the discoveries are endless.

title: ‘13 Planets: The Latest View of the Solar System’ by David A. Aguilar
text:
My very excellent mother just served us nine pizzas. Have you ever heard that sentence? Students used to learn it to help remember the order of the planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune and Pluto. But it doesn't work anymore. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union (IAU) revised the definition of a planet, and Pluto was demoted to a dwarf planet.

What makes a planet a dwarf? Dwarf planets orbit the sun, but their mass is so small that their gravity is not strong enough to keep other objects out of their orbit. The IAU now recognizes five dwarf planets: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and MakeMake. So there are eight official planets and five dwarf planets, making 13 in all.

The book "13 Planets: The Latest View of the Solar System" does a great job of explaining the changes. The author combines interesting text with some amazing, computer-designed artwork. He describes each planet (official and dwarf) and discusses comets, the Oort Cloud and Saturn's "dark ring."

NASA's space probe New Horizons should reach Pluto in 2015. It will send us photos of the dwarf planets. Who knows what exciting discoveries it will make?

title: What are satellites and space probes?
text: Good question! A satellite is an object that revolves, or orbits, around something bigger. The planets are satellites to the sun. It takes 365.24 days for the Earth to go all the way around the sun. The moon, our own satellite, revolves around the Earth approximately every 28 days. The first man-made satellite sent into orbit was a Russian satellite named Sputnik. It was launched into orbit on Oct. 4, 1957. Satellites are much fancier now. Man-made (artificial) satellites are machines that do important things, like send radio and TV signals, look at weather and take pictures of the Earth and outer space. Space probes differ from satellites in that they fly throughout the solar system and send back pictures and information about planets, asteroids, comets and other objects in our solar system. Most space probes are designed not to come back to Earth. Much of what we know about the solar system we have learned from satellites and probes.

title: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642)
text:
For years, people have looked up at the sky and wondered what was out there. Galileo Galilei, an Italian mathematician, wanted to know, too. In the fall of 1609, he pointed his homemade telescope at the sky and looked out into the universe. What he discovered forever changed the way we look at things. He found mountains and valleys on the moon, similar to the ones on Earth. He discovered that the universe was much bigger than we thought, and he identified stars that no one had seen before. Galileo looked at the planets and actually proved that Jupiter had moons. He also discovered sunspots.

Galileo loved math. He used it to prove that the Earth and other planets revolved around the sun. For thousands of years, people had believed the Earth was the center of the universe. Some people were upset with Galileo for disproving this. They arrested him for writing about his discoveries. Before he died in 1642, Galileo did many other experiments. His discoveries were the start of modern science. There are many more science discoveries to be made out there, so follow Galileo's example - look out at the universe and see what you find!

title: The Universe
text:
This is the Andromeda Galaxy, the closest major galaxy to our own - it's 2.2 million light years away!

The universe is a giant laboratory, according to scientists. Our planet is flying through a large cosmos of marvelous things we are just beginning to learn about.

Scientists have many ways of looking out into the universe. Sometimes, we see large amounts of energy from stars in the form of light and radiation.

X-rays, radio waves, gamma rays, cosmic rays, and other energies constantly shower us from deep in space. Scientists measure this energy using telescopes, radio receivers, X-ray devices and all kinds of other scientific instruments. There's even some talk about someday making the Earth into a giant telescope by placing sensors all over the planet that detect cosmic and other forms of radiation. How's that for science?

It's mind-boggling just how much space is out there that is filled with strange things for us to discover. For example, light travels about 186,000 miles per second in outer space. That's pretty fast (like 7.5 times around the Earth in one second), but, still, the light from distant stars has to travel so far in space that we may not see it until millions of years after it began shining.

Think about it: That faraway star you think you see in the sky is actually just the light that shot out of it a long, long time ago (in a galaxy far, far away, no less). That star may be much different today than you see it. It may be a bit cooler now, it may have begun to burn out, or it may have even exploded, centuries ago.

Yes, sir, it's a big one, our universe. Who knows what else is out there yet to be discovered. Maybe a Science Studies Weekly reader will be the one to discover something new and exciting. Let's hope so!

In the meantime, let's explore the cosmos and learn just a few of the interesting things in the universe that scientists know something about.

title: Space Taxi: Regular Folks in Outer Space
text:
Have you ever been in a taxi? It's fun. First, you wave your arms, whistle and stand in the road until one stops for you. Then, you jump in the back seat. The driver starts his meter, which will calculate how much your ride will cost. He'll say "Where to?" and you'll reply "Outer space, please!"

Sound crazy? Don't tell Space Adventures, the only private company to have sent ordinary citizens like you and me into space. That's right, with a little training (six months) and a little cash ($20 million) you can buy a ride into space to the International Space Station. Got extra money? How about a trip around the moon, or a 90-minute space-walk in a spacesuit?

Space isn't just for NASA anymore. As NASA winds down its Shuttle program, private businesses are racing to be the company hired to get not only people, but also important satellites into space. The company at the front of that race, SpaceX, recently launched its Falcon9 rocket successfully. That success is the start of what will probably be a long space-taxi service for anyone who wants to put something into space and has the funds.

Like any new business, the competition is fierce. Companies from the United States, Russia and Europe are all hoping to be the No. 1 choice for space-travelers, and that should keep the prices relatively low. Once transportation is not a problem, plans to build space hotels are already in the works.

One day, going to the moon will be easy. Maybe we will all stop to get a space-burger on the way home, as long as when we're done, we can still catch a cab.

title: All About Stars
text:
Scientists are continuing to make spectacular discoveries. We have telescopes that can see more stars at greater distances than ever. Here is some of what scientists currently know about things like distant stars, nebulae and galaxies.

How Hot Is Your Star?

Stars are really nothing more than giant spheres of burning gases. Scientists know that different kinds of gases burn at different temperatures. They also know that the color of a flame depends on how hot it is. Stars, especially when looked at through a powerful telescope, have colors of their own. By observing the color of a certain star, scientists can learn a lot about it. Red stars are the coolest, about 5,400º Fahrenheit. Orange stars are a bit hotter, about 7,600º Fahrenheit, and yellow stars like our sun are close to 10,000º. White stars are about 19,000º Fahrenheit, and blue stars are the hottest at more than 35,000º Fahrenheit. Blue and white stars are young stars. They're generally pretty small, as stars go. As they get older, they cool and expand to become yellow, orange, and red. Some old stars become huge, swollen fireballs called red giants, growing to more than 10 times the size of our sun. When our star, the Sun, grows as old as some of those, it will possibly become so large that it will fill much of our solar system.

This is probably the most popular star in our galaxy, even though we don't think of it as a star. This is a very close-up picture of our sun. You can see the solar flares coming off of the surface. Imagine what kind of sunburn you'd get that close to the sun!

How Bright Is Your Star?

If someone asks about the magnitude of a star, he or she is asking how bright it looks from Earth. There are three things that determine a star's magnitude: 1) the heat of the star, 2) how far it is from the Earth, and 3) its size. For example, close, old stars might look brighter than faraway, younger ones, even though they are cooler. Big, faraway stars might look brighter than close, small ones. Which of all these would have the greatest magnitude? Care to guess?

Twin Stars

Some stars, just like on Luke Skywalker's home planet of Tatooine in the movie "Star Wars," are found in pairs. These are called binary stars. In one scene, Luke is looking at a sunset with two suns. There really are star systems like that (minus the humans, monsters and robots, of course - no evidence of that yet)! Scientists can tell if a star is binary from studying the way its light reaches Earth. If the light from a star "wobbles" in a certain way as it reaches Earth's telescopes, it means that something big is pulling on the star. That "something big" is probably another star or maybe a large planet.

Nebulae and Interstellar Medium

Most of space is a vacuum. That means it's just empty space, with nothing there. But there are also many gasses, dust, and particles floating around called interstellar medium. Among this floating-around stuff are huge clouds of gas and dust called nebulae. And, though they may not look like it, those clouds contain the basic ingredients for building stars. The Horsehead Nebula and Crab Nebula are examples of nebulae that we know about and have pictures of. Some nebulae glow because of matter that is ionized or charged. Sometimes, stars and nebulae sort of decorate each other. For example, the Lagoon Nebula has clouds of glowing gas and shimmers beautiful colors in the light from nearby stars. Solar wind (energy) from stars whips through the nebula and makes it glow even brighter. When a nebula shrinks because of gravity that builds up, it becomes a proto-star. Eventually, when there's enough gravity, the materials in the nebula combine, and what do you know? A star is born!

Galaxies

Galaxies are large clusters made up of billions of stars and other celestial objects that float around the universe together. The gravity from so many stars holds them all together.

In the center of the galaxy is a core. Some galaxies, including our own Milky Way Galaxy, are called spiral galaxies because the stars near the outside spiral gracefully around the core. There are about 100 billion stars in our galaxy. If you look up at the sky on a clear night, you can see a large strip of many, many stars, right down the middle of the sky. (This works especially well in the country away from city lights.) When you see that strip, you're looking toward the center of the Milky Way Galaxy. This center has billions of stars and is about 30,000 light years away. The galaxy stretches about 100,000 light years across. We are on the rim of our galaxy, and our solar system is orbiting around the Milky Way center (galactic core) at about 600,000 miles per hour. (It takes light about three seconds to travel 600,000 miles.)

Want to hear something amazing? Scientist think there are at least 100 billion galaxies in the universe and that each one is made up of billions of stars.

The Whirlpool Galaxy is shaped a lot like our own Milky Way Galaxy. Can you see the spiral arms coming out of the center?

Invisible Stars

When a star becomes very old, it can run out of nuclear energy and stop radiating light altogether. Without the radiating force of energy, the star's core collapses. This results in a giant explosion called a supernova. Kapow! They're very rare, but occasionally scientists see one. A neutron star might result from a supernova. Some neutron stars become black holes. Others might become what we call pulsars. Pulsars send energy out into space, but they do it in pulses. You may have felt your own pulse. The energy that pumps your blood through your veins comes in a steady rhythm, your heartbeat. Pulsars send out energy in much the same way. They sort of "blink" with energy, instead of shining steadily like young stars.

When a supernova explodes, it releases a huge amount of energy and the star collapses. Then it throws off an expanding shell of gas, known as a supernova remnant, in all directions at very high speeds.

title: Edwin Hubble
text:
Equipped with his five senses, man explores the universe around him and calls the adventure Science. - Edwin Powell Hubble (1889-1953)

You may have heard of the Hubble Space Telescope that orbits the Earth. The Hubble has given us massive and spectacular photos of stars and galaxies from extragalactic space, which is beyond the Milky Way! The Hubble was named for Edwin Powell Hubble, one of the most important astronomers of the 20th century. Hubble was born in Marshfield, Missouri, and he was a well-rounded student athlete at the University of Chicago. He boxed and ran track, and he played basketball, football and baseball. He studied mathematics, read constantly and worked hard to become a lawyer before giving in to his love of science and space. He went back to school and earned a doctorate (PhD) in Astronomy. He never looked back - he looked up!

Hubble's first work after serving in World War I was at Mount Wilson Observatory near Pasadena, California. At Mount Wilson, Hubble studied distant space objects, including nebulae, those giant clouds of gas and dust. Eventually he determined that many of the objects he focused on were actually distant galaxies. He developed a system of classification that was based on their shapes. He showed us that the universe is ever expanding and that galaxies are moving away from our own. A dedicated scientist, Hubble received medals from both the British and U.S. governments in acknowledgment of his work. Edwin Powell Hubble has given us so much knowledge about the universe around us!

title: What is a black hole?
text:
A black hole is an object that has collapsed under its own gravity, like a huge, old star. Scientists used to call them frozen stars (maybe because they no longer give off the fiery light that stars do). A scientist named John Archibald Wheeler first named them black holes. We still use the name today. A black hole is so dense that the gravity it creates pulls in everything that comes near it. If you could magically take a flashlight into a black hole, the light from the flashlight would not be able to shine out. Even light itself is pulled into the core of a black hole. (That may be why they're called black!) Sometimes, black holes are near other stars, and the gasses from those stars are sucked into the black hole, like something going down a drain. These swirling, superheated gasses send out X-rays as they spiral into a black hole. Scientists can look for the X-rays and guess that maybe a black hole is nearby.

So, what happens to everything that is sucked into the center of a black hole? The center of a black hole is called a singularity, and here's the sum total of what we know about what goes on there: nothing! No one knows what happens to the things that get pulled into a singularity.

title: Making New Matter on Earth to Figure Out the Universe
text: How do you find out how something as big as the universe is put together? Simple: start small. See, scientists can figure out how the huge stuff is put together by studying the smallest elements we know about, kind of like taking apart a car made of Lego bricks to see how it was put together. And what are the smallest elements we can study? Why, atoms and subatomic particles, of course! (Subatomic means smaller than atoms.) Of course, to study those small particles takes some big equipment. Scientists use giant particle accelerators and super-colliders to smash subatomic particles together like derby cars, sometimes breaking off smaller atom pieces for us to study and sometimes recombining them to make new kinds of matter. Scientists hope that getting to understand the smallest stuff will lead to an understanding of the biggest stuff as well.

title: ‘SPHDZ’ (Spaceheadz) series by John Scieszka
text:
Is there life on other planets? Could aliens visit Earth? Writers have been exploring this mystery for a long time. The Star Trek series, begun in 1966, continues to thrill fans. Then there's Superman, a "strange visitor from another planet." Now author John Scieszka has a fascinating and funny series of novels in which aliens live among us, maybe in the desk next door!

Michael K. is a new fifth grader at P.S. 858 in Brooklyn, New York. He meets Jennifer and Bob who say they are Spaceheadz from a distant planet. They need Michael to help them recruit 3.14 million Earth kids to save Earth from being "turned off" because of radio and TV waves. But Agent Umber of the AAA (Anti-Alien Agency) is on their trail. Naturally, zany adventures follow.

Do you think there could be life on other planets? The scientists at SETI (Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence) are trying to answer that question. The Allen Telescope Array (ATA) is a series of 42 giant radio dishes in the mountains of northern California. These dishes work together to pick up signals being sent by any other life forms in the universe. The ATA hasn't picked up any alien signals yet, but they are "listening" 24/7!

title: In the Lab
text:
Constellations are very vivid parts of our universe. A constellation is a group of stars that form a picture in the sky. In this week's lab, we're going to learn about some of the constellations in our skies at different parts of the year. Look at the chart here and talk about which constellations are visible at what time of the year.

Why do you think we see different constellations at different seasons? Do the constellations move in the sky? If so, why? Go outside tonight and see if you can pick out any of these constellations in the sky at your house. Look for the Big and Little Dippers. See if you can find Polaris, or the North Star, at the end of the Little Dipper's handle.

title: Welcome, Life Scientists!
text:
Hey, science adventurers! Welcome to a super-duper special issue of Science Studies Weekly. This is the first week we start learning about something we all have in common - life! We are now entering the "living zone," and this is the first issue of life science.

Ever notice how many living things there are crawling, flying and buzzing around? Whether you live in the city, in the country, or on an island, life is all around you. Some living things hang out in the tiniest places, like in your blood and in dust. Scientists have identified about 2 million types (species) of living things on Earth.

Life science is the science of observing and gaining knowledge about living things. As we learned way back in Week 1, there are lots of different kinds of life scientists. But all life scientists were once kids interested in learning more about living things.

Perhaps the best way you can learn about life science is to find a living thing you are interested in, like a pet, and learn about it. Some people like to have furry pets, or they are interested in creepy-crawly things. Other people grow flowers and plants as a hobby. You may want to start a cactus garden or grow your own beans as a way of studying life.

It is very important for us to know as much as we can about life science. It helps us survive. So we observe living things very closely. Scientists often hide in bushes, look into microscopes, or swim in the ocean to watch living things in action. They do some pretty amazing things, and watching them is sometimes like watching a great show.

In the past 200 years, we've discovered lots of different forms of life. The problem is, we've found so many types of living things that it is hard to remember them all. So we had to come up with a way of classifying, or keeping track of, living things. You might call it a filing system. So get ready because this week, we're going to learn about the basic "groups" of living things and how we keep track of them.

title: Curiosity Solves a Mystery!
text:
Do you remember reading about Alfred Wegener and his idea that there was once a super-continent called Pangaea? Many people disagreed with Alfred's idea of "continental drift." They didn't understand what could cause the continents to move. Thanks to Frederick J. Vine we now have evidence that this really did happen.

Frederick Vine was born in England in 1939. He became interested in geology (study of rocks) when he was 15. In school, he read about how scientists believed that South America and Africa were once connected but they couldn't prove it. (Have you noticed how those two continents look like puzzle pieces?) Frederick decided to learn more about continental drift.

After many years of hard work Vine and a scientist named Drum Matthews were able to provide evidence of continental drift. They did this by showing how the bottom of the ocean spreads apart, causing ridges to form. When these ridges form, the minerals in the rocks are magnetized in the direction of Earth's magnetic field. The magnetic force pushed the continents apart.

Vine is still studying the history of Earth. His successful career all began with reading and curiosity. Next time you are reading and you ask why, it just may lead to an amazing discovery!

title: Diversity of Life
text:
Biology comes from the Greek word meaning "knowledge of life."

The Father of Taxonomy

The famous Greek thinker Aristotle traveled along as the tutor and teacher of Alexander the Great. During their travels, Aristotle created a system of labeling things, called taxonomy.

What is taxonomy? A taxon is a group of similar things with similar traits. One group is part of another group, and so on. For instance, put all the fifth graders in your school who are wearing blue in one group. Keep going until you have a taxon of fifth-graders for each color. Put all the ones who are wearing blue and have long hair in a smaller group, and so on.

Since the days of Aristotle, we've discovered millions of different kinds of living things. But scientists still use Aristotle's basic approach of labeling different life forms or putting them into different taxons. That is what taxonomy is all about.

Important Traits

There are three traits scientists consider important when they place living creatures in different kingdoms:

The structure of an organism's cells - Scientists look at an organism's cells to help them decide where it belongs in the taxonomy. The cells of living things are structured differently. For example, some cells have a well-defined nucleus surrounded by a membrane and specialized parts outside the nucleus called organelles. Organisms with cells like that are called eukaryotes. Animals, plants, fungi, chromista and protozoa are all eukaryotes. Other cells don't really have a nucleus at all, just a clump of genetic material that isn't surrounded by a membrane. Those organisms are called prokaryotes. Most prokaryotes have just one cell. Bacteria and Archaea are prokaryotes.

How creatures get their food, or the energy and nutrients they need to stay alive - For instance, some animals eat plants, and some animals eat other animals. Some creatures (plants) absorb sunlight, and some absorb chemicals from the surface they are attached to.

How creatures reproduce, or have offspring - Do they hatch from eggs, give live birth, grow from seeds, or just split in two?

Scientists also consider how an organism developed over time when they put it into a certain kingdom. Then they keep putting the creatures into smaller and smaller groups based on their traits. Scientists are still studying how to classify all the species on Earth, and not all scientists agree. Here are eight groups that scientists are researching. The more they learn, the more things may change!

The Plant Kingdom

You can't be a member of the plant kingdom unless you can make your own food with the help of sunlight. Plants produce a substance called chlorophyll that lets them use sunlight to convert water and carbon dioxide into plant food.

Plants have complex cells with rigid cell walls. You'll learn about plant cells later on. As you'll learn later, there are many different groups of plants. But the two largest groups of plants are vascular plants and non-vascular plants.

Vascular plants are plants that have tubes inside themselves to move water and other fluids around from the roots to the leaves. We get most of our food from vascular plants.

Non-vascular plants never have flowers, and they don't have any tubes inside themselves to move fluids around; they only grow where it is wet. Algae and moss are non-vascular plants.

Animal Kingdom

Almost all members of the animal kingdom can move around without the help of wind or water currents. Humans, fish, bugs, birds, snakes and snails are all members of this kingdom. In fact, there are more than 1 million species, or "citizens," of this kingdom.

We'll learn a bunch more about all the different groups, but the two largest groups are vertebrates (animals with backbones) and invertebrates (those without backbones). Vertebrates are outnumbered 24 to 1.

The Fungi Kingdom

Fungi absorb nutrients from the surface they are attached to. You can find fungus on old food that has been left in the fridge too long. Mushrooms are also fungi. Some look like plants, but they do not make food with sunlight.

Fungi do some great services. They help bacteria decompose dead organisms (garbage).

Chromista

These organisms can have one cell (unicellular) or many cells (multicellular), but most have just one. They are usually found in watery habitats. Chromista are eukaryotes because their cells have organelles and a nucleus surrounded by a membrane. Diatoms and kelp are examples of chromista. Kelp grows in forests in the clear water of shallow oceans.

Protozoa

These water-loving critters are all unicellular, but they come in many different shapes and sizes. They are also eukaryotes. The name protozoa means "first animals." Two common members of this kingdom are the amoeba and the paramecium. Some scientists group chromista and protozoa together in a kingdom called Protista.

Bacteria

All bacteria have just one cell. Inside the cell is a cluster of genetic material called a nucleoid. Since they do not have a well-defined nucleus, they are prokaryotes. Many bacteria are helpful, like the kind that make cheese out of milk. Many others cause diseases. Bacteria live everywhere-including inside your body! The oldest fossils on Earth are bacteria fossils that scientists believe are 3.5 billion years old.

Archaea

These microscopic organisms have only one cell. Most of these prokaryotes are less than 1 micron in length. That's less than one-millionth of a meter. No wonder you need a microscope to see them! Some archaea (and some bacteria, too) live in the most extreme environments you can imagine - the hottest, coldest, saltiest and deepest places on Earth.

Viruses

Viruses have no cells at all. They're parasitic pieces of genetic material covered with protein. (Say that three times fast!) Viruses cause diseases like colds, influenza, chickenpox and rabies by infecting a host - like a fifth-grader, for example. As a matter of fact, viruses can't grow or reproduce outside a host.
