We talk about studying dinosaur bones all the time, but what about the remains of actual HUMANS? The first ancient human skeleton was found in Neander Valley, Germany. The skeleton was hunched over and practically dragged his knuckles on the ground. Scientists wondered if everyone used to walk that way until they discovered that the skeleton they had found had a disease called osteoarthritis, which made his bones all twisted and deformed, making him hunch over like that. Sometimes, when all you have is one skeleton, it's tough to know what everyone was like. Hundreds of ancient skeletons and many years later, we're still learning!

Triassic Period

250-205 Million Years Ago

Lots of reptiles in crazy styles, shapes, and sizes and the beginning of dinosaurs!

Jurassic Period

205-135 Million Years Ago

Dinosaurs were the most popular kids in school. They RULED! Everywhere from the water to the land was dino country. Even the sky was filled with them.

Cretaceous Period

135-65 Million Years Ago

This is the period in which bad boys like T-Rex started to appear. But on a gentler note, it was also the time that angiosperms (flowering plants) grew. Of course, by the end of this period, dinos were altogether extinct.

Tertiary Period

65-1.5 Million Years Ago

Out with scales, and in with fur! Mammals took the stage and set the fashion in the Tertiary Period! T-Who?

Quaternary Period

1.6 Million Years Ago to Today

Many new mammals emerged. The earliest written record of humans goes back to about 6,000 years ago, though many fossils have been found that suggest humans may have been on the Earth for 100,000 years or even much, much longer. Many large mammals, such as mammoths and saber-tooth tigers, died out in the last 10,000 years, since the most recent Ice Age. In addition to all that, remember that the Quaternary Period includes the present: the age of skateboards, Wii and bungee jumping.

title: How old is it?
text:
By looking at the elements inside fossils and other rocks, scientists believe they can tell how old some objects are. Here's how it works: Plants and animals take in carbon dioxide, and some of those molecules contain a substance called carbon 14 (or C-14). Over time, C-14 decays, and (lucky us) we happen to know exactly how fast it decays. Knowing the rate of decay, scientists count the number of C-14 molecules in a stone or a fossil and can figure out about how long ago it formed.

Scientists know how certain other chemical elements (such as potassium and argon gas) behave and change over long periods of time as well. When they find rocks, fossils, or artifacts that contain certain chemicals, they can guess pretty closely how old they are.

title: ‘Feathered Dinosaurs’ by Christopher Sloan
text:
Dinosaurs with feathers? The stereotype that all dinosaurs look like colossal lizards is quickly disappearing. Evidence of feathers has been discovered in well-preserved dinosaur fossils. Some have been found in China, Germany and Canada. Many paleontologists (scientists who study the Earth's history using fossils) now agree that certain dinosaurs did have feathers.

Christopher Sloan's fascinating book "Feathered Dinosaurs" is chock-full of color photos, illustrations and diagrams of these dinosaurs. It's easy for the reader to imagine what these feathered dinosaurs might have looked like. The book also traces the fossil records of some of these species. It explains how research from dinosaurs' nesting habits and parenting behavior might show links between dinosaurs and modern-day birds. This book makes some complicated science theories easy to understand for kids and grownups alike.

The Jurassic Park movies came out in the 1990s.They gave audiences the first glimpse of how real dinosaurs might have looked and acted. The movies used animatronics, or technology that allowed the dinosaur models to actually move using computer programming or remote control. The dinosaurs seem animated, almost life-like.

Today, animatronic dinosaurs may be coming to a museum near you. There are several traveling exhibits that feature full-size models of moving (and roaring!) dinosaurs. Some displays include carefully researched models of dinosaur skeletons and fossils. One exhibit features dinosaurs ranging from the familiar Apatosaurus and Stegosaurus to the feathered Sinosauropteryx recreated from the Chinese fossils. One thing is certain - new discoveries about prehistoric life are only a dig away.

title: What is a fossil?
text:
When an ancient living thing dies, sometimes it's covered up by sediments, like sand in the ocean. Over millions of years, more and more layers of sediment are laid over the remains of the creature, burying it deep in the ground. The soft parts of the animal decompose quickly, but shells and bones dissolve over time, leaving a mold, or a space in the rock where the creature used to be. Minerals often drip into that mold and harden. Over millions of years, the pressure from sediment above turns those minerals into stone. Those new stones - shaped exactly like the creatures that died there - are called fossils.

Often, scientists have to dig deep to find fossils. Other times, the Earth layers where fossils lie are pushed back up to the surface by earthquakes or erosion, and fossils can be found just by walking around. Once a fossilized bone or shell is discovered, it is studied, numbered, and photographed. Then it's carefully unearthed, packed in a plaster cast, and taken to a lab, where it just might become part of a dino skeleton, reconstructed over a metal and plastic framework.

title: John William (Sir William) Dawson
text:
In 1817, when a young Canadian named John William Dawson went to school, his parents and teachers might not have known that he'd grow up to be one of the world's leading geologists and paleontologists. They still might not have known it when, at age 16, he presented a speech to the local scientific society about a paper he'd written. But, by the time he decided to travel 5,000 miles to study science at a college in Edinburgh, Scotland, one thing seemed certain: This young man was serious about science!

Mr. Dawson went on to discover some of the most important fossils in North America (like the oldest snail fossil and the oldest millipede ever found), and his studies of ancient plants set the stage for work that scientists would do for 100 years after him. His work even earned him a knighthood. So when you think of ancient plants and animals, think of William Dawson, and remember, that's Sir William Dawson to you!

title: Ecosystems and Biomes
text:
Ninety-nine percent of all the species of life that have ever lived on the Earth are now extinct. Many animals like dinosaurs lived for millions of years and eventually died out. Even with all of those disappearing animals, there's still quite a variety on this old planet. Millions of species of plants and animals are all parts of the many communities of living things working together to make life bearable for each other.

We call communities of living things ecosystems or biomes, depending on the size. In the United States, these systems range from the wetlands of Florida to the mountain wilderness of Alaska, and even the tiniest creatures on Earth are important to them. The study of those systems is called ecology.

Ecologists look at how living things exist together in a system. For example, a rainforest is an ecosystem that has lots of plant and animal life crawling around in it. Even nonliving things, such as sunlight, soil, water and temperature, are part of the delicate balance in a rain forest. A rain forest is also a good example of a biome. Remember, biomes are kind of like large ecosystems, and temperature and precipitation are two factors that we can use to define them. Some forests, such as the Sarawak Rain Forest on the island of Borneo, can have as many as 8,000 species of plants and 20,000 species of animals. Talk about a vibrant, noisy community of life!

Every ecosystem or biome really is kind of like its own little world, and they are really easy to mess up. Something as simple as destroying the trees in a rain forest, or introducing a new species of animal or plant, could throw things out of whack for good. That's why, in many parts of the world, inspectors at airports and seaports ensure that no new animals or plants have hitched a ride into their ecosystem. It's also the reason that many people work hard to prevent too many trees from being cut down in rain forests and other places. It's also why lumber companies invest millions of dollars replanting trees after they harvest lumber. We may be different people living in different environments with different plants, animals and climates, but one thing is for sure - we're all part of an ecosystem or biome that supports our fragile balance.

Biomes

There are two categories of biomes: Biomes that are primarily on land are called terrestrial. Biomes in water are called aquatic. Check out the brief descriptions of each:

Terrestrial Biomes

Grasslands are large, open spaces where mostly grass grows. Trees only grow near rivers or streams. The soil is very rich.

Deserts are very, very dry. During the day, it can get above 100 degrees Fahrenheit (F), but at night the temperature can drop into the 40s and 50s F.

Tropical rain forests are found near the equator. They are very warm and very wet. Some of them can get as much as 400 inches of rain every year.

Temperate rain forests are found along the coasts in places like the northwestern United States. They can be very wet but are much cooler than tropical rain forests.

Temperate deciduous forests are forests where the seasons change. The leaves change color in the autumn and fall off in the winter. Summers are warm and winters are cold in temperate deciduous forests.

The tundra is located near the North Pole. A thin layer of soil covers something called permafrost, a layer of ground that is permanently frozen, so it never thaws. Most of the year the temperature is below freezing, and very little rain falls there.

Aquatic Biomes

Oceans are the largest biomes on Earth. They can be warm or cold. They are home to plants like seaweed and animals like fish, whales, turtles and sponges.

Freshwater biomes are rivers, lakes, streams and ponds. They are home to animals like fish, frogs and birds. Many plants grow in or near fresh water.

Now look at the two different terrestrial biome graphics on this page. One is a 3-D chart and the other is a line graph. Both use the same variables for the horizontal and vertical axes - temperature and precipitation. Both are tools that we use to help us understand the biomes on our planet. Which graphic is easier to read? How are colors used to represent the biomes?

title: Ecosystems
text:
A food chain like this one takes the sun's energy through a community from producers such as grass and other plants to consumers such as animals.

The Food Chain

All living things need energy from food, and in an ecosystem everyone helps everyone else to get it. Every plant or animal first finds a way to get food and then winds up being food for some other living thing. That's what you and I call a food chain, and every food chain, whether on land or at sea, has some important links. At the bottom of the chain are producers, or things that make their own food. Plants are the world-champion producers. Farther up the food chain are consumers, living things that can't make their own food but are great at eating things. Animals that eat plants (or even other animals) are the consumers in an ecosystem. But the chain doesn't stop there. Every ecosystem is also full of organisms called decomposers. (Bacteria are good examples of decomposers.) Decomposers break down dead animals and plants. Once they're broken down, they get made into food again. Who makes it? New producers, of course.

A food chain is a pretty simple way to describe what happens to pass energy around in an ecosystem. But the truth is that an ecosystem is more complicated than a chain because creatures and plants from one chain are also part of another. Parts of food chains overlap in almost every ecosystem. In fact, it's really less like a food chain and more like a food web.

One Depends Upon the Other

It's no use wondering which living things in an ecosystem are most important. Every living thing in an ecosystem depends on the others for the system to stay balanced. Here's an example: On a small island in Lake Superior, a huge group of moose used to eat like crazy and grow in population until the food was all gone. Then, many would die of starvation. With the moose gone, the plants would grow back, and the whole thing would start over again - lots of moose but no plants, followed by lots of plants but no moose. Is that any way to run an ecosystem? Well, one day some predators (animals that hunt and eat other animals) came to the island - timber wolves. And they ate a bunch of the moose. With the numbers of moose kept under control by hungry wolves, the ecosystem on the island balanced itself out. Soon there were always plenty of moose, plenty of plants, and, of course, plenty of satisfied timber wolves.

Something Small Can Change It All!

In cold ecosystems like the Tundra, mosses and lichens are pretty much the only living things that can hang around all year. When it warms up in the summer, birds migrate, and reindeer, caribou and foxes show up. What would happen if the Tundra suddenly got warm all year round instead of just in the summer? The summer animals might stick around longer, making for big changes in that ecosystem. The truth is, even small changes in the environment (like temperature, for example) can change a whole ecosystem in big ways.

Home Sweet Home

Ecosystems are usually well-suited to the handful of living things that call them home. Desert systems, for example, are full of plants like cacti and animals like lizards, living things that can get by without much water. River and lake systems are full of things like fish, turtles, and mosses, living things that can live well in fresh water. Oceans are the biggest ecosystems in the world and are home to living things that love salt water, some of the biggest living things (like whales), and some of the smallest (like plankton).

Looks Can Be Deceiving!

Deep in the ocean, a big, hungry fish swims through a coral reef looking for a snack. Suddenly, he spots a couple of clown fish playing happily in the wavy branches of an anemone. He gets closer, and suddenly one of those branches sweeps across his face. Yikes! That stings! The stinging arms of the anemone are harmful to some animals but not to clown fish. In fact, among the anemones is where they feel most safe. Sometimes what's helpful for one organism might be harmful to another. What if there were somehow a whole lot more anemones in a certain part of the reef? How would the clown fish feel about that? How about their predators? It just goes to show, when it comes to ecosystems, you can't please everyone.

title: Studying the Forests From Space
text: The Boreal Forest of northern Canada is huge! It is about 30 times larger than Texas and is very important to our Earth's ecosystems. But it is so cold and big up there that people have a hard time studying it. Now, using satellites, we can study it from space. In fact, we can study all kinds of ecosystems from up in space. We can see what kinds of chemicals are in the air, tell if the forests are getting warmer, and examine the damage caused by population growth and deforestation. Ground instruments can also be placed in forests to help scientists gather data.

title: ‘EcoMazes: 12 Earth Adventure’ by Roxie Sloan
text:
Fans of hidden picture books and puzzle books will be doubly delighted with Roxie Sloan's book about the Earth's ecosystems, "EcoMazes: 12 Earth Adventures." Readers get a birds-eye view of 12 different biomes with the animals that live there camouflaged and hidden in their habitat. Each colorful illustration also comes with a maze and a challenge. In one, you need to guide a baby elephant lost in a savanna back to its herd. In another, you're a scientist trying to spot a rare snow leopard in the alpine high mountains.

These entertaining Earth adventures provide a wealth of information about the environments they visit. There's also a summary of each in the back of the book with more super-cool facts. For example, you'll learn about the four different kinds of deserts in the world, and why few large mammals can live there.

Can you see a tree outside your window? It's an ecosystem by itself. There's one community of animals, birds, and insects living among the branches. Down among the roots, there's a completely different population, maybe burrowing animals like worms and mice. Above ground, plants like lichen and mosses can grow on tree bark. Underground, special fungi help the roots absorb nutrients from the soil. All these plants and animals work together and depend on each other.

Draw an aerial view of an ecosystem that interests you. Find out which animals live there. Then hide them in your drawing by using their habitat and camouflage like the author did. Don't forget to add a maze!

title: Why is ecology important?
text:
Introducing an animal or plant from one ecosystem to another can create all sorts of problems. In 1935, people introduced the cane toad from Central and South America into sugar cane fields of Australia. They hoped that the toads would eat all the cane beetles that ate the sugar cane. Well, the cane toads ate the beetles all right, but they also ate all the mice, smaller frogs, lizards, geckos and more. Suddenly, they had a whole bunch of toads causing all kinds of trouble in a completely messed up ecosystem.

Another example? Rabbits. This fast-breeding animal was introduced to Australia in 1859 for people to hunt and eat. Today they have been declared pests throughout the country because they cost farmers and the Australian government millions and millions of dollars.

Ecologists are important because they help us understand what can happen if we fiddle around with ecosystems. Sometimes we think that we are making something better, and we end up in rabbits and toads up to our ears!

title: Rachel Carson (1907-1964)
text:
Rachel Carson studied marine biology as a scientist and became a world-famous conservationist. The vast oceans covering the Earth provided a lifetime of fascinating subjects for her to discover, observe and finally write about. Published in 1951, Carson's highly praised work "The Sea Around Us" was awarded the National Book Award, one of the highest honors awarded to authors in the United States. It was the first of a trilogy of books about sea life, all three of which were bestsellers at the time.

Writing about Earth's oceans was not the only passion that Rachel Carson had. She is also famous in the fields of conservation and ecology. She studied how pesticides and other man-made chemicals kill wildlife and disrupt the natural order of fragile ecosystems. Carson observed, for example, that bugs would consume pesticides, and birds or other animals would then eat the bugs, poisoning several links in the food chain. Writing, researching and speaking to large audiences, such as the United States Congress, Carson inspired concerned citizens all over the world. One of her greatest and lasting achievements was the grassroots movement that eventually led to the creation of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). She was posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Jimmy Carter in 1980.

title: The Human Body
text:
Where's the most fantastic, complex system in the universe? Just look in the mirror! Some scientists believe that, as far as systems go, nothing gets more amazing than the human body. In your body, there are actually many different systems working in harmony with one another. Just take a look: The skeletal system is made of bones and is the framework that supports muscles. Inside the bones is marrow, which makes blood cells. The muscular system connects to bones and helps a person move, jump, run and play. The nervous system is the body's control center. It includes the brain and spinal cord. Your heart is part of a system that pumps blood throughout your body called the cardiovascular system, a combination of the circulatory and respiratory systems. Blood carries oxygen, which helps cells work. The digestive system breaks down food into tiny pieces so that it can be used for energy by the body. The respiratory system helps us get oxygen from the air into our blood. There's even an immune system that contains little cells that kill whatever microbes might be attacking the body.

So, the next time you look up at the sky, go ahead and be amazed by the organized orbits of planetary systems or the spinning arms of flaming stars that make up galaxies or the massive systems of cosmic gasses or deep black holes. But when you're done, remember that there's some mighty cool action going on right here, too. And to find it, you don't have to look anywhere but in a mirror - at the wild and amazing systems of the good ol' human body.

Your body is an amazing piece of work. It helps you run and jump and kick that soccer ball into the goal.

title: Want Some Help With That?
text:
Do you stop and make a plan before you pick up a pencil or step down from the car? Probably not, but your brain and limbs do! They plan so quickly and efficiently that you don't even realize it's happening. Motor planning, or planning and organizing movement, is something that we typically take for granted - until we can no longer do it effortlessly. If we become injured and lose a limb, if we're sick and can't move, or if we are born with a small "glitch" in our motor planning system called apraxia, then we will probably need some assistance from an engineer or a therapist who specializes in movement.

If we lose a limb, chances are we would have to use an artificial limb, or prosthesis. Inventors and engineers have been designing artificial limbs since the 1500s, but fast-forward to the year 2014 for just a second. Brilliant mechanical and bioengineers are hard at work, creating lightweight, durable and sometimes even bionic, or super-strong, prostheses. Some even have working fingers. Take an even wilder ride into 21st-century technology and you'll find a 3-D printer that produces a prosthetic right there before your eyes! Recipients of artificial limbs still have a lot of work to do before they can recapture a full and active lifestyle. But with the help of engineers, physicians, occupational therapists and physical therapists, they stand an excellent chance!

title: Body Systems
text:
Skeletal System

Your skeletal system is the frame inside your body, around which the rest of you is built. Your skeleton is made up of lots of bones, large and small - 206 in all, and you have every one of them from the moment you're born. Bones are attached at joints by bands of strong tissue called ligaments. Ligaments are bendable and stretchable. That's how your knees can bend without your leg bones breaking away from each other. Covering the ends of some bones to absorb the energy from hard bumps is a flexible tissue called cartilage. You can feel the cartilage in certain parts of your body. Go ahead - reach up and grab your bendy ol' ear. That's cartilage. Now push on the end of your nose. That's cartilage, too. And, it's all part of your skeleton.

Muscular System

Your skeleton may be holding you up, but it couldn't get anywhere on its own. In order to move around, your skeleton needs the help of the muscular system. There are more than 600 muscles in the human body, and each one can only do two things: contract (or shrink) and relax. Some muscles, the ones attached to bones, are called skeletal muscles. When a muscle attached to a bone in your arm contracts, it pulls the bone (and your arm) toward it. When it relaxes (and other muscles contract), your arm moves away. Suddenly, you're moving around! The strongest muscle in your body is your heart. It contracts and relaxes in less than a second and does it about 100,000 times a day. Unlike most of your other muscles, it never gets tired.

Immune System

Another system in your body is the immune system. Cells in the immune system, like macrophages, hunt down harmful bacteria and destroy them. The immune system is always on the alert, looking out for anything that might be waiting to make you sick. Some people have immune systems that don't work well. For a person like that, even an itty-bitty cold might become a very serious thing.

Respiratory System

It may sound crazy, but your respiratory system (the system that brings oxygen into your body and sends carbon dioxide out) is partially controlled by a member of the muscular system. Your diaphragm, a sheet of muscle stretched out beneath your lungs, moves up and down when you breath. When it's down, air rushes in through your mouth and nose and into your lungs. When it's up, air rushes up from your lungs and out of your mouth and nose. But getting air in and out of your lungs is only half the story. The lungs are full of tiny air vessels whose ends are surrounded by tiny blood vessels. The air vessels drop off fresh oxygen to be picked up by the blood vessels and taken to the rest of your body (where oxygen does the most good). The blood vessels trade the new oxygen for old carbon dioxide, good for nothing in your body but to be breathed out.

Nervous System

We won't talk much about the nervous system in this issue of Science Studies Weekly. But here's a little preview: There are more nerve connections in your nervous system than there are stars in the universe that we know about. At the center of it all is the brain, the subject of next week's entire issue. The brain is the central part of the nervous system, and the heart is the central part of the circulatory system. Without these two vital organs, your body wouldn't run. In fact, your brain tells all the rest of the systems in your body how to run properly and efficiently.

Circulatory System

Your heart is at the center of one super-important body system. It's called the circulatory system, and without it, the cells in your body would die of starvation and lack of oxygen. Pumped by your heart, blood travels through your blood vessels, whose job it is to get nutrients (from food) and oxygen (from air) to your cells. This is called the circulatory system because the blood moves in a sort of circle: out from the heart and full of nutrients and oxygen and then, once it's been emptied of all those goodies by the cells, back to the heart again for a refill.

Digestive System

How does your body get energy from food? This looks like a job for the digestive system. First, food (hopefully yummy, nutritious food) heads on into your mouth. Your teeth and your saliva break down food into pieces small enough to pass down a tube called the esophagus and into your stomach. There, acids break the food down even more, and stomach muscles mix it around. Finally, the useful part of food heads for your small intestine, where it passes into the blood stream. The non-useful part of food passes into your large intestine (or else from your blood, through your kidneys, and into your bladder) and winds up outside your body again as waste.

title: Tracking Bodies with Technology
text:
For years, law enforcement agencies around the world have used fingerprints to catch criminals. Every human being has unique fingerprints. That means that no one else's body has fingerprints exactly like yours.

Forensic scientists (people who use science to answer legal questions) can use DNA to catch criminals. They compare DNA samples from a crime scene with samples from a suspect. DNA samples can come from tissues like bone, skin or hair, or from body fluids like blood or saliva. Many people think a DNA match is absolute proof that a suspect is guilty, but that's not true. DNA matches are much more accurate than some other evidence, but they are not 100 percent accurate. In court, a jury makes the final decision about whether a person is guilty based on the evidence they heard in the trial.

title: ‘The Case of the Infected Tick: Annie Biotica Solves Circulatory System Disease Crimes’ by Michelle Faulk, Ph.D.
text:
"Heart of gold." "I love you with all my heart." Ancient Egyptians thought the heart was the center of wisdom, emotions, memory and movement. Today we know that the human heart is the major organ in the circulatory system that pumps blood throughout our body in less than a minute. It has nothing to do with love or the Valentine-shaped hearts we draw.

Annie Biotica is the fictional narrator in a series of books called the "Body System Disease Investigations." Each book introduces five "crimes" (diseases that attack a body system). Annie uses CSI-style crime-solving methods leading readers through clues and suspects to find what is making people sick.

In "The Case of the Infected Tick," Annie discovers that a camper named Eric got Lyme disease from the B. burgdorferi bacteria in a tick bite. Thanks to Annie's detective work, he was treated with antibiotics and made a full recovery. Annie then solves more crimes against the circulatory system like "The Case of the Broken Heart."

In each book, Annie's investigations are followed by three "You Solve the Case" challenges. Readers use Annie's crime-solving tools with the scientific method to solve new medical mysteries with information from the book.

This entertaining series also covers the digestive, respiratory and nervous systems along with diseases of the skin. Each book contains colorful photos and illustrations. Microscopic views show Annie's "arch germ enemies" like the Varicella zoster virus that causes chicken pox in children and shingles in adults. Guaranteed fun for all biology super sleuths and future doctors.

title: What is physical fitness?
text:
The human body is a complex system. And a system as complex as you are needs some pretty complex fuel to run it. In order to keep your body in tip-top shape, eating healthy is very important. Fruits, vegetables and foods that are not high in fat or sugar help our bodies perform better. Certain fruits and vegetables have been found to contain chemicals that help oxygen get to your cells and nutrients that help you grow.

But the right fuel is just part of what makes you healthy. Exercise is important as well. It helps make healthy muscles, keeps your brain younger, and gets you growing. When you exercise, remember to warm up and to exercise correctly so that you are not injured. Pay attention to your body. If you are in pain, slow down or stop. When you are fit, you are less likely to be injured when exercising or doing sports, so stay active! People who are sedentary (inactive) and seldom exercise are at higher risk for health problems as they get older. So keep your body revved up with plenty of exercise and good food.

title: Galen A.D. 129–216
text:
Galen was born in a town far across the world called Pergamum back when the Romans were in charge of most of the known world. (Pergamum is now part of the country Turkey.) There they worshiped Asclepias, whom they believed to be the god of helping. Galen wanted to study medicine. He traveled to Alexandria, in Egypt, to learn all he could about health and sickness.

Galen became famous for his study of the body, but it wasn't easy. For one thing, it was forbidden to study human bodies at the time, so he mostly studied animal bodies. Before Galen's work, people thought that blood vessels carried nothing but air. He proved that they carry blood. He wrote books and illustrated body systems. He taught people about how the heart has chambers, about how the nervous system controls the body, and about other body systems like the kidneys and circulatory system.

Galen became an advisor to the emperors of Rome. He even served as a doctor to gladiators. He wrote hundreds of works that became medical textbooks on anatomy. And, while we've learned a lot more about the human body since then, some of Galen's works are still used today. Medical scientists still follow Galen's scientific and precise techniques of studying the human body.

title: The Magnificent Mind
text:
At this very moment, reading the front page of Science Studies Weekly, your eyes are detecting information: light and dark spaces on the surface of the page in front of you. Starting from your eyes, the information you see, in the form of chemical and electrical impulses gets sent lightning-fast to your brain. And, in your magnificent, high-tech brain, the light and dark spaces that you saw on the page get turned into words that you can understand. You may think you read with your eyes, but what you mainly read with is your brain.

The human brain is the most complicated of all the body organs we know about. It makes you able to do everything you know how to do. And your brain is always active, even when you are asleep. Billions of cells called neurons make up trillions of tiny connections, firing information in and out and up and down and around and around, controlling everything your body does, from breathing to dreaming to moving blood around your body in order to keep it alive. It's like a super-duper computer network inside your head.

All a person sees, feels and hears is done in the brain. Your eyes, ears, mouth, nose and skin are just sensors that send information to your brain.

Inside of our brains, many chemicals are formed (called neurotransmitters). These chemicals, racing back and forth, carry information from one nerve cell (neuron) to another. It all happens so naturally that you don't even know it's happening. But, the truth is, more little nerve connections than you can possibly count are going on right this second as you read.

So let's keep those connections going. Activate some neurons by turning the page of Science Studies Weekly for a close look at your body's headquarters, the amazing brain.

title: Music and the Brain
text:
Do you have trouble waking up in the morning? Try listening to music. Do you have trouble falling asleep at night? Try listening to music. Do you have trouble staying excited about a project? Try listening to music. Do you have trouble concentrating? Try listening to music!

Music can do all these different things because of what your brain does when it hears music.

Your brain loves music. You might think, "I don't like country" or "I don't like rap," but guess what? Your brain loves it all. When you hear music, even music you don't think you like, your brain gets excited. It can't help but try to analyze, understand and predict what's going to happen next.

Have you ever thought something had a catchy beat? That's your brain predicting what will happen next, and then being happy because it was right.

In his book, "This is Your Brain on Music," author Daniel Levitin explains how the brain reacts to music. He describes how the brain predicts what will happen, and how it is stimulated when something slightly different happens instead. Songs that are too "perfect" and predictable aren't as cool for the brain as songs with a more "human element."

Studying music is good for you, too. Studying and learning music can make your brain grow - especially in the auditory (listening) and motor skills (moving) parts.

So what are you waiting for? Fire up some good tunes, go practice an instrument or go see a concert - your brain can't wait.

title: Science Lesson
text:
The brain interprets everything that your eye sees, that your ears hear and that your hands touch. It's a pretty amazing piece of equipment!

The Amazing Brain

If you've ever seen a picture of a brain (or an actual brain!), you may have thought that it just looked like a big, mysterious-looking lump. But if you looked closer, you might have noticed that the brain is made up of separate parts, all connected but with different jobs to do. Right at the bottom of the brain is the brainstem. It connects the brain to the rest of the body, but that's not all. It controls your heartbeat and your breathing - stuff you usually don't think much about. Just above the brainstem is the mid-brain. It helps relay messages to other parts of the brain and controls how your body reacts to sudden movements and sounds. Wrapped around the mid-brain is a bunch of stuff called the limbic system, which handles emotions and the instinct for survival. But the biggest part of the brain is the cortex. (The cortex is so big that it's divided up into four parts, or lobes.) The cortex is the center for most of the things you think about. It's where scientists believe that you make decisions, learn math, read books, have memories and much more.

Is It Jell-O in There?

So what's the brain made out of anyway? You might be surprised. The truth is, the brain is made up of water, fat and protein. It's about the size of a big grapefruit, and when yours is fully grown, it will weigh about three pounds. Compare that to a gorilla's brain at about one pound or a dog's brain at about 2 1⁄2 ounces.

Why Do I Feel Pain?

Each nerve cell (neuron) in the brain contains special chemicals called neurotransmitters. They act as the messengers of the brain, sending information from neuron to neuron, helping the brain tell the body what to do.

There are many kinds of neurotransmitters in the brain, sending messages to billions of neurons through trillions of synapses connections (the tiny space between cells). Messages carried by neurotransmitters travel through tube-like parts of neurons called axons. So if you step on a tack, your foot sends messages right up those axons to the brain, which interprets the information: "Yeeeeeeeeeeoowww!" The brain then sends instructions back down the axons to your foot: "Get off that tack!"

Nerves send messages as fast as 200 mph. It's much slower than the electricity moving through the wires of your house, but it is fast enough because it only has to go a few feet at the most.

The World Through Your Brain's Eyes

Your body senses the world through tiny chemical machines called receptors. Receptors are amazing things. They tell your brain when they sense something (just like a grocery store door sensor tells a computer to open the door when someone comes close to the sensor). For example, tiny little receptors in the human eye, called rods and cones, send messages to the brain, which makes sense out of color and light. Receptors for sounds in your ears, receptors for touch, heat, and pain in your skin and body, and receptors for smell and taste in your nose and tongue all send information to the brain as well. But remember, it is in the brain where we make "sense" of all those things. So, really, it's your brain that does the tasting, touching, smelling, seeing and hearing. Your eyes, ears, mouth, nose and skin are just sensors.

The 'Electric Wires' of the Brain

In humans, axons (the "wires" that carry information inside your body) are coated with fatty sheaths made of something called myelin. Myelin actually makes impulses move down the axon more quickly and insulates the neuron much like a rubber or plastic coating insulates a wire. When something happens to the myelin sheath around an axon, messages (like the message for your legs to walk or for your mouth to talk) sent to and from the brain slow down. Scientists are very interested in myelin so that diseases that affect myelin like multiple sclerosis can be treated.

title: Legos and Brains
text: A brain is just a bunch of tissue and some electrical impulses, right? It shouldn't be too tough for a really smart scientist to construct one, right? Boy, nothing could be further from the truth! The brain is so complicated that we're hardly able to understand it, let alone make something like it. The closest we've come to making something that works like a brain is building ultra-simple robots, like the Lego robot in the picture, that can react to simple problems in the same way that a brain would. For example, such a robot might have sensors that tell it to avoid bright light or to roll toward a certain noise when it sounds. Some of the machines are pretty fancy, but the smartest of them is really only about as smart as a common cricket. It just goes to show how amazing the human brain really is. For more information on the Lego robots we talked about, as well as other inventions, check out www.lego.com.

title: ‘Mudshark’ by Gary Paulsen
text:
Mudshark, aka Lyle Williams, is a 12-year-old phenomenon (a person or thing that's extraordinary and marvelous). He reads all the time and remembers everything he observes. His friends turn to him for everything from finding lost homework to curing a stomachache from a school lunch of Anchovy-Grape-Turnover Surprise.

Mudshark's school is full of zany characters, too. There's Kyle the amateur magician, a custodian who loves classical music, and a librarian with an armadillo purse and a psychic parrot.

If you think "Mudshark" sounds like a lot of fun, you're right. Gary Paulsen, author of "Hatchet" and other award-winning books, has a grand time exploring Mudshark's "almost" photographic memory. But when you read between the lines, you discover that the way Mudshark uses his brain is what makes him remarkable. He has learned to pay attention to details and move quickly (thanks to his triplet baby sisters). That's how he solves problems like the disappearing classroom erasers and the escaping gerbil.

But is there really such a thing as photographic memory? Scientists call this phenomenon "eidetic memory." They tell us it is very rare, if it exists at all. They have found people with exceptional memory skills in special areas, but there is very little proof of long-term total recall. It seems to occur more often in young children, but most lose the ability after about age six. After all, remembering every single event and image could be a huge burden. The human brain was designed to use knowledge to solve problems, not just to store information.

title: How much of our brains do we use?
text:
That depends. For a long time, people have believed that we only use about 10 percent of our brains. Brain scientists know that this is a myth (or made-up story that lots of people have come to believe). The myth started in 1908 when a famous psychologist wrote that we only use a small bit of our abilities. But many people thought that by "abilities" he meant to say "brains," and the myth was born. It's a myth that is still believed by many people. Some people have made a lot of money convincing people that they can help them use the other 90 percent of their brains.

The funny thing is, you already are. We use 100 percent of our brains. Besides, there is no really practical way to measure how much of our brains we use. Studies of blood circulation in the brain and EEGs (electrical recordings of the brain) show us that the whole brain is active, even when you are asleep. Now, in all fairness to the myth, it is true that as you grow older, there's less brain to use. That's because as we grow older, our brains lose brain cells at a rate of 10,000 per day. It's usually not a problem, though. We still have billions and billions of cells to work with when we are older. Scientists say that learning about things like science helps us not lose so many brain cells when we get older. So keep reading Science Studies Weekly. It's good for your brain.

title: Dr. Alois Alzheimer (1864–1915)
text:
This scientist has a name that you may recognize. He was a professor of psychology, a neurologist and a brain scientist. Dr. Alzheimer studied people with unknown diseases or brain problems. He helped educate people about things that can go wrong with the brain.

In 1907, he described a woman with a severe form of dementia. Dementia occurs when the brain loses brain cells at a rapid pace and people forget things and have problems thinking. It can also make it hard for them to control their emotions. The woman's case was very important for learning about one brain disease in particular.

Doctors later named the disease Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's research and findings were very important to the search for a cure for Alzheimer's disease. But we're still searching. Alzheimer's disease is the most common kind of dementia, and more than 4 million people in North America suffer from it. Today, medical scientists are working hard to find a cure for what we now call dementia of the Alzheimer's type. Without Dr. Alzheimer's good thinking and smart work, we may not have known much about the disease until years later. Thanks, Dr. Alzheimer!

title: American Stories
text: Hi! This year Studies Weekly will tell you the story of our amazing country—the United States of America. You will learn about some American heroes and how they helped America become a great country. We hope you enjoy reading our "American Stories!"

title: Democracy in Action
text:
Natalia was waiting for Steven at an after-school event to clean up a neighborhood park, organized by their teacher, Ms. Johnson. “Hey, Steven!” Natalia exclaimed. “Where have you been?”

“Sorry I’m late, Natalia. You’ll never believe what happened. We had to stop at a police checkpoint,” said Steven.

“What for?” she asked.

“My dad says it was to check to see if all the people in the car were wearing their seat belts,” Steven said.

“I remember Ms. Johnson talking about seat belt laws in class last month. Did everyone have their seat belts on?” Natalia asked.

“Yep. My dad always makes us wear them. Even riding in the back seat,” he said.

“I wonder why you have to wear a seat belt in a car, but you don't need a helmet to ride a motorcycle,” she said as she handed him a trash bag.

“I’d definitely wear one if I rode a motorcycle. I can’t imagine not wearing a seat belt. It just feels normal to have one on,” he said.

They started walking toward a play area. “Ms. Johnson said our representatives in the state legislature made those laws. I’ll bet more people wanted a seat belt law than wanted a law to require helmets for motorcycles,” said Natalia.

“Yeah, that would be an example of representative government. Our parents elected those people to make the laws they wanted,” Steven said.

“That definitely makes passing a law easier,” said Natalia. “Imagine if all the adults in Ohio all had to make and approve laws. Nothing would ever get done.”

“I remember Ms. Johnson said there were lots of legislators in Ohio to represent all citizens,” added Steven. “Citizens who live in Ohio vote for them. That still seems like a lot of people. I bet they get into arguments sometimes. Guess they know how to compromise.”

Natalia bent down to pick up an aluminum can. “I wish people would show more respect for nature,” she said as she put it into the recycling bag she carried.

“Wonder if we could get our state representative to make a recycling law?”

“Sounds like a neat idea,” Natalia responded.

“Here’s another one,” said Steven as he also picked up a can and put it into her bag. “Your bag is as full as my garbage bag. Seems like a lot of people still need to think about recycling.”

“Let’s do some research and then talk to Ms. Johnson,” she said excitedly. “Maybe we can start something that will help save the world!”

title: Let's Learn About Colorado This Year!
text:
Our weekly paper is prepared to help in your study this year of COLORADO (the state whose name comes from the Spanish language, meaning "colored red"). You'll find pictures, puzzles, crafts and games as you discover fun and exciting facts about our state. From its oldest rock formations to the most current environmental concerns, we'll explore what makes the "highest state in the nation" one of the most popular western states in which to live.

When Katherine Lee Bates, a writer and educator from Massachusetts, first visited Colorado's Pikes Peak and looked out over the beauty of the surrounding mountains and sky, she was inspired to write the lyrics of the now famous patriotic song, "America the Beautiful."

Colorado's "spacious skies" stretch over majestic "purple mountains." These mountains produce major rivers, flowing "from sea to shining sea," because of the famous continental divide. (Did you know that Colorado is the source of more major rivers than any other state?) Fruited plains provide abundant harvests. The Rocky Mountains are rich with mineral resources. Towering plateaus produce "amber waves of grain," vegetables and grazing lands for sheep and cattle. The state is crowned with hundreds of her own natural lakes.

Millions of years ago, glaciers, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and major upheavals in the Earth's crust all combined to give the state its unique form. Colorado's journal of geology is packed with exciting stories.

Some of this hemisphere's first known people left their own records carved in canyon walls right here in Colorado! Many American Indian tribes came after that, followed by fur trappers, mountain men, explorers, miners and merchants, all adding to the bustling activity of the western frontier. Soon statehood was celebrated, and Colorado became the 38th state to unite herself with the 100-year-old nation, thus earning the nickname "Centennial State."

Fascinating events unfolded throughout the state's exciting history. Politics, precious metal prices, and progress in transportation and communication brought challenges as well as opportunities to the new state. Urban growth, industry, agriculture and production of natural resources created employment and convinced others to come to Colorado, "the land where the columbines grow." Today, over 5 million people cooperate within her communities, creating a unique culture and contributing to her prosperity - all of them call Colorado their home.

title: Philanthropy and Values
text:
Maybe you have heard the word "philanthropy" before. What does it mean? It describes actions that people make for the good of other people. What is a value? It's a way of behaving that people believe is good - like believing it's good to be honest. Is honesty one of your values?

One way you can practice philanthropy today is to help yourself and others learn good values. How do you learn good values? You can learn them from your parents and grandparents, your teachers at school or church and other people you trust.

You can also learn them from people that have been recognized for doing good things for society. An easy way to learn about people that have done good things is to visit values.com. Values.com has lots of stories and short videos that highlight the traits that make each of us better people. They even have billboards on the highway to remind you about good values.

For example, you may have seen a billboard that looks like the one shown here.

This billboard is about Oral Lee Brown, who saved money from her job to send 19 kids to college... all by herself! Wow! Isn't that cool? You can learn about lots of other people who practice philanthropy at values.com. Be sure to look for more of their "billboards" on Page 4 of Studies Weekly this year. We think they're so cool we want to remind you to check them out!

title: Physical Colorado
text:
How old is Colorado? A thousand years old? No. A million? Guess again. Some rocks from the northwestern mountains actually date back to 2.3 billion years ago! Scientists determine age by measuring radioactivity from these ancient pieces of our planet.

The Changing Earth

What do people believe about geologic events in this part of the world? Some of the story has to do with plate tectonics, or the shifting of landmasses due to movement beneath the Earth's crust. This shifting caused continents and islands to bump up against each other. When that happened, the land buckled - like the body of a car crunched in a fender bender.

The history of Colorado's land is different from any other region in this hemisphere (half of the globe). There is some educated guesswork involved, since we can't go back that many years or dig down 60 miles to see what's there.

While all the shifting and bumping was going on, magma or molten rock from deep beneath the surface erupted as lava through volcanoes, forming cone-shaped mountain peaks. Although no active volcanoes remain within the Colorado Rockies, the San Juan Mountains are examples of real "hot spots" historically.

In other places, the liquid rock never made it through the surface, but bulged up in an underground pool like a blister. Erosion from wind, rain, snow and sand eventually wore away the land to expose the cooled formation of arched, layered rock. Pikes Peak's pink, granite dome is a more recent example of this.

As the land was changing and mountains and valleys were being formed, the flat expanse of the Colorado plateau remained solid. It was thrust upward also, but rose in one great mass. With the Colorado River carving the stone, the transformation of the plateau created one of nature's most spectacular displays - the Grand Canyon.

Meanwhile, icy glaciers shaped other valleys, canyons and basins. Fast-moving water began cutting into the mountainside. Ice and snow then formed at the heads of "stream valleys." As the glaciers flowed downhill, they carved more deeply. Finally, when a glacier melted, the valleys they had gouged were exposed. A mountain lake or tarn may have been left behind from the melted glacier. Several small glaciers exist today in the northern ranges.

Colorado as we see it today settled into its current form only about 20,000 years ago: basins and plateaus in the west, plains in the east, and mountains in the middle. These mountains display the most amazing variety of landscapes! Sometimes gentle, rolling folds resulted, such as those we see in the Sangre de Cristos. Often, steep, jagged, knife-edge peaks emerged, known as faults. The Front Range, Park Range and Wet Mountains show this dramatic effect. The Great Plains of eastern Colorado are geologically more similar to Kansas than to the Rockies. The Western Slope (a name given to the west side of the Rockies) is made up mostly of the Colorado Plateau.

Many forces that combined to create Colorado's breathtaking scenery are in effect even today. Some evidence suggests that the Rockies are still rising! Erosion continues to shape the land. Imagine what the land would look like in another 100 million years.

Scientists have evidence that, at one point 500 million years ago, water flooded the Colorado region and formed a shallow sea. Sand and mud from higher elevations washed down and covered shells, coral reefs, plants and animals in sediment as thick as 1,000 feet.

Similar flooding occurred hundreds of millions of years later. As water crept in and covered low-lying areas, it created white, sandy beaches, and a new era began. The white rocks at Dinosaur Ridge in Morrison are remains of these ancient white beaches. Much of the rest of this period's history is buried beneath part of Colorado's Great Plains, known as the High Plains.

title: Florissant Fossil Beds
text:
Florissant Fossil Beds National Monument in Teller County is world renowned for its treasures. Here, you can see everything from petrified giant sequoia tree stumps to fossilized insects (bees, butterflies, ants and dragonflies) trapped by volcanic ash.

Located approximately 35 miles west of Colorado Springs, this national park was formed in 1969 when the area was threatened by tourist companies who took money from visitors and allowed them to take whatever fossils they could find.

Nearly 10 square miles in size, the park is also a near-perfect example of the "montane" ecosystem (a community of plants and animals that live at a certain elevation and function as an interconnecting unit). Present-day specimens of ponderosa pine, Douglas fir, aspen and bristle cone pine trees stretch above mountain meadows carpeted by many types of grasses and wildflowers. The name "Florissant" (FLOH-ri-s'nt) actually means "blooming" or "flowering" in French.

Many coyotes, porcupines, some mule deer and a large herd of elk have made the monument their home. The elk are especially interesting to watch in the early morning as they move out from the trees to feed in the meadows. You may be lucky enough to hear the bugle or mating call of a male elk near dusk on a late August or September evening. A few black bears and even fewer mountain lions are also in the area.

Visitors can enjoy self-guided tours and trails, interpretive programs, picnicking and indoor displays at the visitor's center from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. through the summer months. (The park closes at 4:30 p.m. after Labor Day weekend.)

title: What is an Aquamarine?
text:
You probably already know that it was gold and silver that brought many prospectors to Colorado over the years, but how much do you know about the valuable mineral chosen as our state's official gemstone?

Aquamarine was first discovered in 1881 on Mount Antero by Nelson Wanamaker. He built a small, stone cabin there, 13,500 feet up the mountain, right under the main summit. It was in this cabin, parts of which still stand today, that he stayed during the summers. He climbed up another 5,000 feet (just less than one mile) every morning and down again every night for the four-month summer. That was the only time when collecting was possible, because of snow and extreme weather conditions that were hazardous to such work during the rest of the year.

Mount Antero is the highest known gemstone-collecting site in North America, and it still yields gem-quality aquamarine 100 years after that amazing first discovery. The gemstones range from pale blue to deep green and can be up to 2.5 inches long. Aquamarine is also the birthstone March.

title: Stegosaurus
text:
More than 150 million years ago, it would have been common to see a stegosaurus in Colorado. Scientists believe that this type of dinosaur grew to be around 11 feet tall and approximately 30 feet long. It could weigh up to two tons (4,000 pounds). Considered a herbivore (plant eater), it may have also soaked up the sun's energy through plates on the outside of its body. It used spikes on its tail to defend itself against carnivore (meat-eating) predators like tyrannosaurus rex.

In 1877, a fossilized stegosaurus was first uncovered near Morrison by a minister and school teacher named Arthur Lakes. Today, the Denver Museum of Nature and Science has one of only six stegosaurus skeletons on public display. Other museums with excellent dinosaur exhibits include the Museum of Western Colorado in Grand Junction and the Henderson Museum at the University of Colorado in Boulder. Dinosaur Ridge, north of Morrison, contains many footprints and some bones as well. The Dinosaur Quarry at Dinosaur National Monument exhibits bones as they are found in situ (in place) along a massive wall. Amateur fossil hunters can search for traces of ancient reptiles and observe the footprints and bones of 14 species found in the area.

title: Direct Context Clues
text:
Direct context clues are words that say, “Look here!”

Learning how to guess words you don’t know is an important skill. If you learn how to guess what a word means, then you won’t have to read with your dictionary open all the time. There are different strategies to guess word meaning. One way is to find other words or phrases nearby that point to the definition. We call those words or phrases direct context clues. Below is a list of words that are often used to point to direct definitions. In items 1-5, circle the words from the list below. Underline the direct definition in each item.

is/are was/were
is/are called, means, or, such as
is/are known as, different from
is/are like is/are similar to
unlike is/are considered

1. Mammoths lived during the ice age. A mammoth was something like a very large elephant. It sported very long tusks that curled on the ends.

2. The Spanish explorers used a very fast, three-masted ship. This ship is called a caravel. Because it was smaller, the caravel could be used to explore shallow coastal waters.

3. Do you want the thrill of your life? Then try the Texas Tornado out for size. The Texas Tornado is a looping roller coaster found in the Six Flags amusement park.

4. Jason’s bedroom is chaotic, unlike Harry’s room, which is tidy.

5. Check the BBC Web site for a list of monarchs, or rulers, of England.

title: Picture the Earth!
text:
"Hi! I'm Jackson, the historian." "And I'm Alana, the photographer. We're going to take you on a tour of our history from ancient times to the westward expansion of our nation. Starting now, you are a history tourist just like us. Welcome to the club!"

"Along the journey, you'll read about things that are happening right now in our 'Current Events' section. In 'American Character,' we'll introduce you to people who demonstrate great character traits (qualities). This week we talk about perseverance. In the 'Trades and Technology' section, you'll discover some cool tools and technology that have affected our lives in some amazing ways. In the 'Biography' section, you'll read fascinating life stories of people who have had an important impact on our world. Inside, you'll find the section that shows off my writing talent and Alana's photography genius. Be sure to check out the back page. That's our favorite part! We've included crossword puzzles, comics and other fun things to do. There's a lot to learn, so test yourself in the 'Think and Review' section to see if you remember everything." "Right, Jackson. This is going to be so much fun! But before we get started, we have to start with the big picture - the big picture of Earth, that is!As you might know, the Earth is mostly made up of water.

About 70 percent of Earth is covered with water. There are seven large landmasses, or continents. They are Asia, Australia, Africa, Antarctica, North America, South America and Europe. The world's five major oceans are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. Did you know that until recently only four oceans were recognized by most geographers?" "I sure did, Alana. And I know that geographers are people who study the Earth and its features. They use globes and maps to represent the Earth. Globes are three-dimensional scale models of the Earth. Maps are flat, detailed representations of places on Earth. Each half of the world is known as a hemisphere. The imaginary line that runs west to east, or horizontally, around our Earth is the equator. It divides the Earth into northern and southern hemispheres.

title: Title of the Article
text:
The Spanish Armada was a fleet, or group, of ships that was sent to invade England. This fleet of about 128 ships was sent by King Philip II of Spain to invade England and remove Queen Elizabeth I from her throne. The commander of these ships was the Duke of Medina Sidonia.

Philip II met with his military leaders to plan the invasion. However, even before ships could be hired or supplies and troops could be gathered, rumors of Philip’s plan to build the Spanish Armada had already spread across Europe. At this time the queen hired Sir Francis Drake as a privateer and he began raiding many of the Spanish ports.

England was anticipating Spain’s plans to invade. Sir Francis Drake organized strikes against the Spanish Armada to weaken their forces. He specifically targeted ships to undermine Spain’s ability to supply its armada with food, water, and gunpowder.

Back in Spain, launching the invasion was not going according to plan. Again and again, plans had to be delayed. The biggest and most difficult reason for this was a lack of financial backing. Spain simply did not have enough money to pay for everything. Another difficulty was that heavy storms made it too dangerous to sail. This delayed the fleet from setting out for weeks at a time. Drake’s raids on supply ships also meant the Spanish fleet was still not adequately prepared.

Finally, in 1588, the Spanish ships under the command of the Duke of Medina Sidonia began their voyage from Spain. However, things began to fall apart even on the first leg of the journey. Just off the coast of Plymouth, England, the Spanish Armada was spotted. English ships captained by Sir Francis Drake and Lord Charles Howard met them in the English Channel on July 31, 1588, and a naval battle ensued. That first battle ended with no clear victor. A second battle was fought days later, also without a clear victor.

The Spanish Armada docked their ships in the port city of Calais on the coast of France.. However, after dark, Drake sent eight “fire ships” into the harbor. These boats, made to burn easily, were set on fire and sailed by very small crews to crash into enemy ships. Sidonia, seeing the burning ships approaching on a collision course, ordered a fast retreat. Many Spanish crews, in their hurry, cut the cables to their anchors in order to get away. The smoke, fire, and confusion led to the loss of three Spanish ships, and the remaining ships were scattered.

Another battle took place the next day, which came to be called the Battle of Gravelines, many Spanish ships were badly damaged in this battle. The Spanish Armada began sailing north toward Scotland with the English fleet following behind. With the Spanish Armada damaged and in retreat, the English forces ceased their pursuit. England, for the time being, was safe once more.

After the loss of several ships and thousands of men, dwindling supplies, and low morale, the Spanish decided to retreat back to Spain. With many ships still missing their main anchors, the Armada lost dozens more ships to storms and wrecks on their way back to Spain.

Of the roughly 128 ships that originally set out to invade England, only an estimated 65 survived and returned to Spain.

title: I Am a Member of a Community
text: A community is a group of people who live in the same place. People from many places come together in a community. You are a member of a community. One community you are a part of is your family. This includes the people who live together in your house. You are a part of a third grade classroom community. Your school community includes the other students and the teachers in your school. You are also a member of a local community that includes your neighborhood, city, or town.

title: Why Do People Form Communities?
text:
The Spinning Wheel

Many types of cloth are made from threads that are woven together. Traditionally, those threads are made using the wool of a sheep and a spinning wheel. People in Europe started using the spinning wheel in the 13th century, during the Middle Ages.

Compass

A compass often looks like a pocket watch, but instead of showing the time, it helps find direction. They were invented in China around 200 B.C.E., but they came to Europe in the 12th century. A compass uses the magnetic field of the Earth to help travelers find magnetic north.

Astrolabe

Not many people use an astrolabe today, but in the Middle Ages, the Astrolabe was an important tool for navigation on a journey. an astrolabe can help you measure your location and the position of the stars. This can keep you on course. Astrolabes were invented in the Middle East, but they came to Europe in the Middle Ages.

Tide Mills

Using energy from nature is not new. People have been using the power of sun, wind, and water for thousands of years. In Europe, the tide mill became widespread during the Middle Ages. It used the power of water. As the ocean tide came in, water pushed past a water wheel and filled a pool. As the tide went out, the water from the pool would turn the wheel on its way back out to sea. The wheel turned and could be used to grind grain to make flour.

title: Rules and Laws in Classroom, School, and Community COMPLETE TEST
text:
When people live in communities, they create rules and laws. These rules and laws protect our rights, keep us safe, and help us solve problems. What are some rules in your classroom community? What about your school community? School leaders, teachers, and students help make rules for our school.

Laws are formal rules that apply to everyone in the community. Our government leaders help make laws to benefit our communities. In many communities, people vote on rules and laws. testing update

title: Communities Work Together to Improve
text: It is important that all members actively participate in making our communities better. It takes everyone working together to make a community successful. We can do this by volunteering and serving in the community. Some people serve the community as leaders. It is important to have good leaders who serve the people. How could you work together to improve your third grade classroom community?

title: Being a Good Community Member
text: As a member of a community, you have responsibilities. We show we are good members of a community by respecting others. It is also our responsibility to follow the rules and laws of the community. Good community members actively participate in the community. They serve in the community to make it grow. Think of the different communities you belong to. What responsibilities do you have in each community?

title: Communities Change Over Time
text: Communities often change and adapt. Sometimes, change happens because people grow. Last year, you were part of a second grade community. This year, you will be part of the third grade community. As communities grow, their needs change. Responsible community leaders and members work hard to meet needs and improve their communities.

title: Demo Page 4 Actvities
text:
One of the most important things to have on a trip is a map. So, we definitely need to talk about the maps we use. Each map has its own special purpose. In fact, mapmakers develop each map specifically with its own theme or purpose.

Political Maps

Some maps show the boundaries between countries, states or provinces. These maps often show the major cities found within those areas. They also mark the separation between the governments of the world. Since these maps focus on the political parts of the world, they are called political maps. For example, the political map of North America shows the boundaries between countries like Canada, the United States and Mexico. Each country is usually indicated by a different color to make it easy to see where one country ends and another begins, just like on this map.

Physical Maps

Mapmakers create other maps to show the physical features (characteristics of a place) of an area like landforms or major bodies of water. We call these physical maps. For instance, the physical map of the United States shows the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, the islands of Hawaii, the Rocky Mountains, the five Great Lakes and the Mississippi River. Many times physical maps will also include varying colors to indicate elevations of the land and landforms. Notice on the map above that the highest points in the Rocky Mountains are a darker green than the lower lying area of the Great Plains. This allows us to easily see the changes in elevation. People use maps for a variety of reasons. Most often, people use maps to plan a route, find their way or locate something like a specific place, landmark or landform.

Once, for fun, Alana’s parents made a “treasure map” for her and Jackson. The two friends followed the map to the “treasure”— tickets to a hometown baseball game! What a fun way to use a map!

Map Features

Although different types of maps have different purposes, all maps include a title and a theme. Maps have other similar parts as well. One such part is a legend. It is a very important component, or part, of a map. A legend shows symbols that represent man-made or natural features on a map. For example, a red line on a road map might represent a highway, or a tent on a park map might show where a campsite is located.

Another important part of a map is a compass rose. A compass rose shows directions on a map like north, south, east and west. One reason it is important is that you can use a compass rose to figure out which direction you need to go to get where you are going. An additional important feature on a map is the map scale. Because maps are not the same size as the areas they represent, a map scale is necessary to provide actual distances. These distances are usually in either miles or kilometers. It is another key part of a map because people can use the map scale to calculate distances. This can be very important, especially to travelers who need to figure out the actual length and time of their trips.

There is one last feature on a map that we need to talk about. Some maps have lines numbered in degrees that run both vertically and horizontally. Lines that run vertically (up and down) are called lines of longitude, or meridians. Lines that run horizontally (across) are called lines of latitude, or parallels. Lines of latitude and longitude are important because they create a grid that can be used to find the exact location of any place in the world. You can see a map with lines of latitude and longitude on Page 4.

Geography in Review

Use what you read in “Geography and Maps” to help you match the words and definitions on the right:

____ 1. shows symbols used on a map

____ 2. type of map that shows boundaries and cities

____ 3. helps travelers figure out distance

____ 4. horizontal lines or parallels

____ 5. type of map that shows landforms, bodies of water, etc.

____ 6. shows directions

____ 7. vertical lines or meridians

A. lines of latitude

B. political map

C. physical map

D. map scale

E. lines of longitude

F. legend

G. compass rose

To wrap things up let’s think about our location on a map. We live in North America, the third largest continent behind Asia and Africa. The largest countries in North America are Mexico, the United States and Canada. The country we live in is the United States, and within our country there are 50 states. We live in the state of Florida, and this is where our trip begins. Now hang on for the ride of your life because things are just getting started!

See you next week!
