title: Are Tar Pits Hiding Beneath U.S. Roads?
text:
If you live in Los Angeles, California, the answer may be yes. And those tar pits may contain the best-preserved fossils ever found! Near busy Wilshire Boulevard you can see the La Brea Tar Pits. The area is still bubbling with the sticky tar that trapped animals up to 50,000 years ago. Scientists have found the bones of bears larger than any on Earth today, lions bigger than today's African lions and camels larger than the elephants you can see at a zoo. Over one million bones have been found in the pits so far. (No dinosaur bones have been found because they were already extinct.) And in 2006, 16 new tar deposits were found where a parking garage was being built at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. Some scientists think they will find a million bones there too.

The tar pits show that many large animals went extinct at about the same time. Why? Many scientists say evidence points to the climate change that took place at the end of the ice age. The large animals couldn't adjust fast enough to the warmer temperatures. At about that same time, man first migrated over the land bridge that used to exist between Asia and North America. Another theory is that man may have hunted many of these giants to extinction. What's underneath that road you were on when you came to school today? Maybe more than you think!

title: Prehistoric Pennsylvania
text:
Giant creatures once roamed what is now Pennsylvania. Let's get to know a few of our prehistoric (before recorded history) friends this week.

Which Dinosaurs Called Pennsylvania "Home"?

Most of North America's dinosaur (ancient reptile) fossils have been discovered in the Utah/Colorado/Wyoming area. Many bones and entire skeletons have been found. We know that dinosaurs roamed the Pennsylvania area millions of years ago as well. A fossil is a "picture" of a plant or animal that is formed in rocks. The fossil was formed when animals or plants died in the swamps. Mud, rain and rocks packed the remains hard against the Earth. They turned into rocks through the fossilization process. Today, we can dig those fossils up and see just what kinds of animals and plants lived here millions of years ago.

1. Stegomus

This guy was an herbivore (ate plants). He looked a bit like a crocodile, but had a pig-like snout. We know he lived in central New Jersey, and his skeletons have been found in Europe and South America, too.

2. Coelophysis

You wouldn't want to meet this guy on a trail through the forest. He was 10 feet long and very vicious. He was a carnivore (meat eater), and his tiny teeth would tear you to shreds. Some Coelophysis skeletons discovered in New Mexico gave evidence that this dinosaur was a cannibal. They actually ate their young! Montgomery County was home to this predator in Pennsylvania.

3. Phytosaur

Here's another dino that resembled a crocodile. His nostrils were mounted just above the eyes, however. Crocodiles' nostrils are at the tip of the snout. Phytosaur was a nasty fellow who ate lots of fish. These aggressive amphibians' fossils were discovered in Chester County.

4. Placerias

This is a dinosaur you wouldn't mind meeting in the park. He was a gentle, lumbering herbivore. He was quick to use his tusks to defend himself, however. He loved company. He and his buddies lived in herds. One of his Pennsylvania homes was near York Springs.

5. Icarosaurus

This was one of the earliest lizards. He loved acrobaticflying, and his fossils have been found in Chester County.

6. Metoposaur

This guy looked like a large salamander with a broad, slab-like head. He was an amphibian (lives in both water and on land) who lived on the bottom of ponds. He couldn't crawl very far over land. The Metoposaur hung out in York County among other places in our state.

The Bone Cave

"Help! Help! I'm falling!" Those were the cries of several prehistoric mammals as they fell to their deaths near what is now Valley Forge. Quarry diggers in the area blasted into a deep cave. Inside this cave were found the fossilized remains of several hundred prehistoric mammals - giant sloths, saber-toothed cats and mastodons. They lived in Pennsylvania about 3 million years ago. Mammals are hair- or fur-covered animals that give live birth to their young. Paleontologists (scientists who study fossils) dug out fossils from that blasted cave at Port Kennedy. By the way that their bones were all tangled in the cave, it looked as if these creatures fell into a giant blender. From this, scientists figured that a great flood panicked them, and while stampeding to higher ground they fell into this deep chasm. Water poured through the cavern, and over the centuries, sediments covered the opening of the cave.

Chickens?

This is a trick paragraph....Or is it? Most people think that the animals named in the Bone Cave article are dinosaurs, but they're not! And some would say our delicate, little chicken is in no way a dinosaur! But it's actually a very close relative. According to scientists, that chicken you had for dinner last night has more similarities to the dinosaurs than any of the ancient critters we've mentioned above. If you go for a picnic in the park next weekend, you better be sure that bucket of fried chicken that you're carrying doesn't jump out and attack you!

title: William Penn and the Pennsylvania Quakers
text:
William Penn spent less than five years in America, but he had a big impact on American history. His ethics (standards, values and principles) - especially his beliefs about freedom - had lasting effects on American democracy.

Penn was born in London in 1644. He was well educated and became interested in a religious group called the Society of Friends, or Quakers. They believed in equal rights for all and would not bow, remove their hats or take an oath to royalty.

Although Penn was raised in the Church of England, he agreed with the Quaker beliefs. He insisted on going to jail with his Quaker friends saying, "My prison shall be my grave before I will budge a jot; for I owe my conscience to no mortal man."

Some Quakers moved to America, but the Puritans in Massachusetts did not want them in their colony. King Charles II gave William Penn a land grant for territory in America to repay a debt owed to Penn's father. The colony was named Pennsylvania (Penn's Woods) in honor of William's father. Penn designed a city there named Philadelphia, meaning "city of brotherly love."

Penn wrote a constitution called "The Frame of Government." It guaranteed freedom of religion, trial by jury, fair taxes and many other liberties we take for granted today. Penn also established peaceful relations with the American Indians, buying land from them and writing successful peace treaties.

William Penn spent a lot of time in England, and he died there in 1718. He only lived in his colony for four years, but his ethics influenced Americans for generations to come. How might your life have been different without William Penn's constitution and the liberties he stood for?

title: Oil and Lake Countries
text:
No, Texas wasn't the first place where oil was discovered! No sir-ee. Any school child in this commonwealth can tell you about Drake Well - 30 miles east of Meadville. It's where the world's first successful oil well was drilled. Another way to get the feel for Oil Country is to visit the ghost town of Pithole. It was an oil-boom town in the late 1860s and was abandoned when the oil business lost momentum. If you really want to see this part of the state, take a train. Check in at the Oil Creek and Titusville Railroad. Take a two-hour trip to Rynd Farm, four miles north of Oil City. Pittsburgh has the most kid-friendly attractions in this part of Pennsylvania. You'll never forget your first visit to the Pittsburgh Children's Museum - a "must visit" while in town. Check out Kids Kingdom at the Pittsburgh Zoo (as well as the cool elephants)!

Take a ride on a Gateway Clipper (riverboat) - The Goodship Lollypop Ride is a fun cruise! Get a great view of the area on the Duquesne or the Monongahela Inclines. Children have a great time at the Hall of Sculpture in the Carnegie Museum of Art. There are also ARTventures, or fun family activities, where you and the folks can create your own art while visiting the museum. Now it's time to go on over to West Mifflin for a great thrill - Phantom's Revenge - that great ride at Kennywood Park. Kennywood's sister park in West Homestead is the Sandcastle Action Park. It's a major riverside water park with a boardwalk and 14 water slides! Yep, this part of Pennsylvania is just waiting for you and your family to come on over and explore. Have fun!

title: What happened to the dinosaurs?
text:
The disappearance of the dinosaurs 65 million years ago is one of science's greatest mysteries. Changing climate, starvation, cosmic radiation, parasites, diseases, erupting volcanoes and competition from new animals are just a few of the causes scientists guess at.

Some say the dinos starved because, when butterflies and moths first appeared, they ate all the vegetation, and there was none left for the "big boys." Others say that when small mammals came, they ate all the dinosaur eggs, and no more babies were hatched. One important theory (scientific belief) says that the dinosaurs' disappearance started in Mexico. A comet or meteorite struck the area, causing huge forest fires. The clouds of dust and ashes choked all living plants and animals.

title: Fox Squirrel
text:
These little mammals are found in many parts of this region and elsewhere. They are about 2 feet long, including their long, very bushy tails, and weigh about 2 pounds. They are mostly grayish with rusty-yellow overtones. They have orange bellies and tail hairs tipped with yellow.

This animal is very aggressive and chatters constantly. The young females give birth once a year, while the older females have two litters per year. A litter usually has two to four young.

Unlike the gray squirrel, the fox squirrel isn't usually found in urban areas. They hang out in pine and hardwood forests. They like to eat nuts, fruits, seeds, flowers, bird eggs, acorns and insects. When they do go into civilized areas, they can cause big problems if they get into the attic or crawl into spaces of your home. They may chew your mom's potted plants or vegetable crops, dig in the yard, raid your bird feeder and eat your kitty's or dog's food. Watch out for them at home, but enjoy them while you explore the wilds of northwestern Pennsylvania.

title: Law and Order
text:
When you ride in your mom’s car, do you notice she stops at red lights and stop signs? Which side of the street does she drive on? Would things work as well if she drove on the left side of the street and ignored all the red lights? Think about the mess that would cause! Every day people in your community follow lots of rules and laws that help make life easier and safer. Without these rules, life just wouldn’t be as safe. Below are some general Pennsylvania laws. Next to each one, describe the impact you could have on others if you didn’t obey the law. An example is given for you.

1. “All drivers of any kind of motor vehicle must be wearing the provided seat belt. Even if you are over 18, you must wear your seatbelt:”

By not wearing your seatbelt, you could get seriously injured in a car accident and your parents could receive a fine of up to $100 per child.

2. “Every pedestrian crossing a roadway at any point other than within a crosswalk at an intersection or any marked crosswalk shall yield the right-of-way to all vehicles upon the roadway.”

3. “All motorcycle riders must have on eye protection.”

4. “Shoplifting (including concealing items or switching price tags) from a store or business is a crime.”

title: The Ice Age and Pennsylvania
text:
Did you know the Appalachian Mountains were once islands in the Atlantic Ocean? This was millions of years ago, of course. The land of Pennsylvania was buried in water, and many plants and animals lived in this watery world. Then the seas began to back away as the Earth started to rise. Great mountains rose out of the sea. The land left behind was an oozing swamp! Then the land was covered by water again. How many times this happened over hundreds of millions of years is unknown.

But then, much later, it turned cold - very cold. Great glaciers grew in the north and pushed down into what is now the United States. These glaciers came and melted four separate times. Only the last two came into what is now Pennsylvania.

The first of these was the Illinoian Glacier. It covered the northeastern and northwestern corners of the commonwealth. Later, the Wisconsin Glacier moved into the same areas, but did not reach quite as far. Big Pocono Mountain was the only land left standing.

These glaciers filled in some valleys and carved others more deeply. The land creased and buckled into a series of mountain ridges running from northeast to southwest. The great glaciers ground their way south from the Arctic, shearing off the peaks of the mountains and strewing rocks and boulders over the land. A few remains of ancient animals have been found in Pennsylvania. The oldest of these are worms. Dinosaurs and, much later, birds and mammals, including the woolly mammoth and the giant sloth, all left their traces on this land. This week in Pennsylvania Studies Weekly, we'll look at the regions those glaciers left behind.

title: Scientists Believe Volcanoes Caused a ‘Little Ice Age’
text:
An ice age usually lasts thousands of years. But between A.D. 1300 and A.D. 1900 the northern hemisphere experienced a cooling called the "Little Ice Age." The cooling was so intense that glaciers moved south, causing northern European towns to be destroyed. It was so cold that the Thames River in London and canals in the Netherlands froze! A scientist at the University of Colorado, using plant fossils from this period, may have discovered why this happened.

The plants died suddenly between 1275 and 1300. That's exactly when many volcanoes erupted. Fifty years later, volcanoes erupted again. Billions of tiny particles from the eruptions were in the atmosphere, reflecting the sun's heat away from the Earth. This caused the land to cool, the plants to die and the ice cap to grow. But there's more.

The growing ice cap sparked a feedback loop. A feedback loop causes something to happen over and over. First, the tiny particles stopped a lot of the sun's heat from reaching land. This cooling caused the ice cap to grow. The ice reflected more of the sun's heat back into the atmosphere. This caused more cooling. Finally, the glaciers became so large that they stopped the warmer ocean currents from melting the ice cap. Over centuries the glaciers grew to cover northern Europe.

Volcanic eruptions started the cooling, but it took the feedback loop to keep the "Little Ice Age" going for centuries!

title: Regions of Pennsylvania
text:
Pennsylvania is made up of six beautiful natural regions. This week, let's look at how these regions are divided.

The World is a Giant Grid

To make it easy to locate any spot in the world, map makers have drawn imaginary lines around the globe called longitude and latitude. Each line has a different number. To find any location in the world, all you need are the numbers from the two lines that cross each other on this giant grid. This crossing is called an intersection. It's much like two streets crossing each other. Pilots can find their way through the skies by using the two-number coordinate system.

Natural Regions of Pennsylvania

The Lake Erie Plain

This plain is a flat strip of land about 4 miles wide that borders Lake Erie.

The Allegheny Plateau

This plateau covers more than half of Pennsylvania. A plateau can be flat or hilly, as long as it's higher than all the land around it. This region is part of the Appalachian Mountain Range.

The Ridge and Valley Appalachians

This region is made up of long, narrow mountains called ridges. Between these ridges are stretches of flat land or valleys. (On some maps you may see this region combined with the Great Valley Region.)

The Great Valley

This valley is a big, sweeping arc across Pennsylvania. Many rivers and roads follow this large valley, which is home to many of Pennsylvania's cities, including our capital.

The Piedmont

This area is made up of many low, rolling hills and valleys. This region is some of the best farmland in the world.

The Coastal Plain

This is a narrow strip of flat land along the Delaware River. Philadelphia, our largest city, is located in this region.

title: That’s One Big Place!
text:
What's the biggest place you've ever been? Disney World? The Grand Canyon? Some scientists believe that there was once a place on Earth bigger than any place you've ever been. We're talking bigger than Philadelphia, bigger than Pennsylvania, even bigger than all of North America! This huge place was called Pangaea, which means "worldwide land." Pangaea was one huge continent, they say. Imagine being able to travel over all of the world's land without getting in a boat or a jet! What happened to this giant continent? Over millions of years, the land broke up into huge sections and moved over the face of the planet to become the continents we know today. You may have visited some pretty big places, but you'll never visit a place as totally huge as Pangaea. Don't feel bad though, because nobody ever visited Pangaea. This "worldwide land" broke up into continents millions of years before people ever lived on Earth.

States on Plates

What would the world look like with no water? If you had a machine that could suck up all of the world's oceans, you would see that the continents are resting on top of huge landmasses called tectonic plates. These plates are all touching each other under the oceans. The world is changing every day, little by little, as these huge plates rub against each other. When two plates start rubbing, earthquakes suddenly happen. We always think "California" when we hear "earthquake." Well, did you know that Pennsylvania has had earthquakes, too? Ask your grandparents if they remember the Sinking Spring quake of 1954, the Wilkes-Barre quake of 1954, the Lehigh Valley quake of 1961, the Philadelphia quake of 1961, the Cornwall quake of 1964, or the Darby quake of 1968. Hey, California, we're "all shook up," too!

title: Friendliness
text:
You know, just being friendly can make the difference between a bad day and a good day. The United States is home to some of the friendliest people around. Maybe that's why America has so many good days! Friendliness can turn driving in a car, riding on a bus or taking a walk in your neighborhood into a pleasant memory all its own. Friendliness can make someone glad you were the one who answered the phone. Of course, some people choose to be unfriendly most of the time, but why would you want to do that? After all, you hardly ever hear anyone say, "I just love coming over for a visit. You're all so nice and grumpy!"

Make friendliness one of your character traits, and anyone who ever visits you will go away feeling as warm as the sun!

title: Mountain Lions in Pennsylvania
text:
Is the mountain lion the Big Foot of Pennsylvania forests? Many people who live in Pennsylvania would love to believe that mountain lions- also known as cougars, pumas and panthers- would be able to survive in the forests of Pennsylvania. So far, there has been no evidence showing that it is possible. In 2001, there was a rumor a vehicle on Interstate 80 killed a cougar. This attracted some attention from Penn State University. But the body of the cougar that was supposed to show up at the university never made it.

This is not the only rumor of cougars that has been floating around. For years, people have been saying that they have heard big cats scream in the night, seen paw prints that were never proven to be cougars' prints, and heard of photos and videos that never materialized. But so far, no proof has been found.

The hopes were this body could prove that there really are wild eastern cougars in Pennsylvania. It has been a decades-old controversy. State wildlife authorities, however, say the accident never happened and nothing was reported.

So the search goes on. And people like Gary San Julian, a hunter and angler - a person who likes to fish - continue to track down every report of a sighting, every footprint, every source possible to prove whether these creatures exist in Pennsylvania. Penn State University's mascot is the Nittany Lion, and they have a cougar that was killed in Susquehanna County in 1856 mounted near the library. So the university would especially like to know if cougars live in Pennsylvania. Someday, they could be proven right.

title: Is the ice age over?
text: Winters never ended in North America 18,000 years ago as they do now. Thick ice sheets sprawled across most of Canada and down into Manhattan Island, most of Pennsylvania, central Illinois and Washington state. Mammoths, mastodons, short-faced bears and other mammals lived here. Eventually, the climate began to warm up. The glaciers melted, slowly at first, then with a rush. They're not gone yet, however. We are now in the Interglacial Age. Sheets of ice are still found on Greenland and Antarctica. Scientists believe the ice may return if global warming doesn't take place.

title: Black Bear
text: Would you like to run into a black bear in the wilderness? No? Then don't go to the Allegheny National Forest! That's where bears hide in the marshy thickets to play and raise their cubs. (Did you know that all cubs are born in January?) Are black bears mean, and do they attack campers in their sleep? No, you must be thinking of the grizzly bear. The black bear is the most common bear in this country and usually backs away from people, even when their cubs are threatened. However, any wild animal can be unpredictable, so beware! Bears have better hearing than we do, and their big, soft feet allow them to move quietly downwind when humans approach. If need be, they can run faster than 25 miles per hour or climb trees as fast as squirrels. They usually like to forage for wild foods away from people. They will seek food in campsites only when nuts and berries are scarce. Just keep your distance if you should encounter one, and don't feed them! Are all black bears black? No, body fur can also be brown, blonde or the rare albino white. The muzzle is brown. The eyes are blue at birth, then turn brown.

title: My Name is Susquehanna
text:
I am 10 years old and very excited. My father, the chief of our small tribe, has finally given me permission to take the trip I have longed to take for several years. I learned as a small child that I was named for a great river east of here that I've never seen. It's located in this big country that the white man calls "Pennsylvania."

There are not many people in this small tribe of ours. We are the only ones left of a once very great and proud nation. We are American Indians, and our people were here many, many years before the Europeans came. I love to hear the stories my grandmother tells about our people. Most white men don't even know we still live in these woods. But that's a story for another time.

Today, I just want to grab my dog, Towanda, jump into our family canoes, and paddle down "my" river - the Susquehanna. I will remember every moment of this exciting trip.

We put our canoes in near the city of Athens, in northeastern Pennsylvania. It is very beautiful here. Turning southeast, the river flows by tall Rummerfield Mountain. My father calls out, "Susquehanna, there's Standing Stone!" What a huge rock, right on the bank of the river. My brother tells me it is at least 13 feet wide and 25 feet high! Also on the banks, I see some of my favorite trees - black walnuts, spotted sycamores and umbrella shaped elms.

Now the river breaks out of mountain ridges in Wyoming Valley. This is coal country. We spy Wilkes-Barre, a settlement built on the richest coal deposits in Pennsylvania. The waterflows southwest now and wanders past Nanticoke and Shickshinny. My father points to the high bluffs of Berwick. Many trees again crowd the banks. Trained in the ways of the woods, I am proud that I can name them all to my little cousins.

As we get near the town of Northumberland, we see off to our right the great waters of the West Branch. This is called the "wild brother" of the Susquehanna. I chuckle because I, who was named for the river we're traveling, also have a wild brother. The meeting of these two great rivers brings the threat of flooding. Many times in the past, floods have swept big trees and heavy stones upon the quieter lands downstream. Now the river turns again and runs south and east through the big settlement of Harrisburg. Here, beside the water, stand stately houses surrounded by green lawns and shade trees. Towanda barks at other dogs along the shore.

Now, near the end, we see the river's most splendid stretch. The waters speed down a long staircase. Here swim fish that love the swift water. Above the banks fly orioles and goldfinches. Midstream stands an island called Mount Johnson. It looks like the rounded peak of an underwater mountain. Above, I see an eagle's nest. I wonder if an eagle lives there.

Now it's time to leave this beautiful river and make one last camp before we head back to our woods. How happy I am to at last see and travel the beautiful, great river for which I was named!

title: Pennsylvania’s Waterways
text:
Pennsylvania has five major rivers and 250 lakes. Let's learn about them this week.

Pennsylvania's Amazing Rivers

Imagine yourself standing with a bucket of water at the top of "Headwaters Mountain" in Potter County. Pour the water out and watch where it goes from the headwaters (where rivers begin). Part of that bucket of water would run northwest into Lake Erie and pass through the St. Lawrence Seaway to the Atlantic Ocean. Some would tumble to the Allegheny River, which would carry it to the Ohio River and, from there, down the Mississippi to the Gulf of Mexico. The rest of it would roll to the Susquehanna River, then on to the Chesapeake Bay. Isn't it amazing that Pennsylvania rivers end up in three major water systems of the world - the Great Lakes, the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico?

Did you know that there are more than 45,000 miles of rivers and streams winding across our commonwealth? Pennsylvania's waterways have been a major force in shaping the history of the state. Why do you suppose the major cities in Pennsylvania were built along rivers and other good water supplies?

How Did We Get the Great Lakes?

Would you believe that during the ice age, the area that is now the Great Lakes was just a plain? There's a giant rock formation north of here called the Canadian Shield. During the ice age, glaciers hammered away at the shield and piled up rocks to the south of it. These deposits of rocks dammed the runoff of the melting glaciers. Where was the water to go? Well, as it turned out, the melted glaciers went nowhere! That's why today we have the beautiful, freshwater Great Lakes; they're the "puddles" left behind by the giant glaciers.

From west to east, they are Lake Superior, Lake Michigan, Lake Huron, Lake Erie and Lake Ontario. Have you learned the easy way to remember their names? Just think of the word HOMES. Now, match the first letter of each lake to its respective letter. (This is an example of a mnemonic, a memory device for learning specific items.) With which of the five Great Lakes are Pennsylvanians most familiar?

What is a Man-Made Lake?

Pennsylvanians need water in their homes, schools and places of business. Where does this water come from? Some of it comes from wells sunk deep into the Earth. Some of it is brought by pipes from reservoirs. Reservoirs are places where water is stored before it is needed. The stored water can then be pumped to cities and into people's homes as needed.

When a dam is built across a river, it causes water to back up. The valley behind the dam becomes flooded and turns into a lake. A lake made by people in this way is a reservoir. The lakes behind them provide not just drinking water, but also wildlife habitats, water sports, fishing and many other water activities.

What Good is Water?

No one would ever deny that water has some important uses; just ask any farmer, sailor or thirsty person. Or ask a fish! And let's not forget another thing that water is great for: pure, clean fun! Pennsylvania is just full of ways to use water.

Rivers were highways for many years. Rivers provide hydro-electric power. Rivers are wildlife habitats. Rivers provide for beavers and raccoons. People used these animals' pelts for clothing in early Pennsylvania. Rivers provide recreation - boating, swimming and skiing. Rivers provide drinking water. Rivers provide food and sport.

What other ways can Pennsylvania's rivers and water be useful?

title: Adam Smith
text:
Consumers and producers have been a big part of markets since the early civilizations. Markets are actually a way that people can trade with one another. Markets bring consumers to producers and producers to consumers. Through these markets, exchange economies came to be. No one ever really invented an economy. It just happened as people traded with each other. As markets grew larger, many people began asking questions. Then they studied people as they traded for goods and services. That study is what we now know as economics.

One of these early economists was named Adam Smith. He was born in Scotland in 1723. He went to the University of Glasgow at the age of 14! That seems very young to be going to college now, but it was very common back then. He graduated and then went on to Oxford University in England. He became a professor and began looking at exchange markets. Smith didn't know it, but he was really starting the study of economics. In 1776, he put out his book, "The Wealth of Nations." The book is about what he had found through 30 years of research.

Smith suggested that there was an "invisible hand" that guided trade in an economy. Think about sitting down to enjoy a nice bowl of tomato soup. Most people give little thought to all the steps and processes that go into putting that soup on your table. There are the tomato farmers and the soup makers. There are the marketing team who advertises the soup and the people who design the label. Don't forget the truckers who transport the soup. How about the grocery store that places it on the shelf? Who controls all of this? Is there someone leading each company? How does it all work?

According to the "invisible hand" theory, no one directly oversees companies trading with each other. Instead, markets bring people together. From that, producers find other producers to assist them. Then consumers are guided naturally to buy those products that they need. This process of trading in an economy is known as voluntary exchange. When this is the main way of organizing production of goods and services, economists call it a market economy. These early ideas from Adam Smith still affect economists today, more than 200 years later. It is because of his work and study that Adam Smith is known as the father of economics.

title: Oil and Lake Countries
text: In French, Presque Isle means "almost an island." This is one of the most remarkable places in Pennsylvania. There's enough here to keep you busy for weeks. Presque Isle State Park is a 3,200-acre peninsula extending from the city of Erie into Lake Erie. Over 4 million people visit Presque Isle a year. Yet, if you avoid the peak summer swimming season, it's possible to walk for hours along the beaches and in the woods without seeing another human being. Go online to presqueisle.org to find short descriptions of 20 different walks you can enjoy in the park. You'll want to rent rowboats, canoes or motorboats. And be sure to tour the great lighthouse! In the city of Erie, visit the reconstructed Flagship Niagara, an American warship that helped win the Battle of Lake Erie during the War of 1812. It's the official flagship of Pennsylvania. Are you a stargazer? Have an awesome experience watching the movements of the sun, moon, planets and stars at the Erie Planetarium owned by the Erie County Historical Society. Then take a tour of the Land Lighthouse, originally built in 1818. It is one of the first lighthouses built on Lake Erie. Ask the folks to take you to the ExpERIEnce Children's Museum while you're in the area, too. But you'll probably have the most fun at the Waldameer Park and Water World. Boating, swimming, water sports - the lake Country just about has it all!

title: Is quicksand really dangerous?
text: It looks so solid. But that's not true. Also not true is the idea that if you put one foot in quicksand, you'll be sucked under, never to be seen again. It happens that way only in the movies. In North America quicksand is rare, but where it does occur, it's the result of an underground spring that has bubbled up into sand. Most quicksand is anywhere from just a few inches deep to less than waist deep. You're not likely to drown in it unless you fall in head first. Even if quicksand is more than waist deep, you really can't go under all the way. That's because quicksand is more dense than saltwater, so you'll actually float in it! The only real problem with quicksand is that the solid ground you might need to help pull yourself out may be out of reach. If you do happen to step in some, don't panic. Just roll onto your back and try to float to the edge.

title: Osprey
text:
While you're visiting this beautiful area of our state, you'll see lots of wildlife. Your fun days at Presque Isle State Park will be even more fun if you know what animals and plants to watch for. You'll even see dragons and elk! Those are two types of rare plants - dragon's mouth and elk sedge.

You'll want to watch for sandpipers, swans, geese, ducks and, if you're lucky, you'll spot the uncommon snowy owl. Would you know the endangered osprey if you saw one, or a black tern or a redheaded woodpecker?

The osprey ("fish hawk") soars over Lake Erie and searches for fish by hovering over the water, watching the surface below. When prey is sighted, the osprey dives steeply into the water with its talons open. It quickly comes to the surface, adjusting the fish in its claws so the head is pointed forward.

Ospreys began dying drastically because of pesticides during the 1950s and 1960s, but since then they are nesting here again.

title: A Flood to Remember
text:
Mark finally climbed down from the roof of his house. He walked through the front door, his feet softly sinking into the drenched floor. He stared around the now-empty room where his television, couch, many pictures and personal items of remembrance had once been. But they were all gone now, lost in a matter of seconds. He called up to his wife, who came down with their children. At least they were safe. If it had not been for the warnings, they may not have been so lucky.

This scenario describes what could happen in a flood. Floods and flash floods are natural disasters that happen in a matter of seconds and can impact a life forever. There are warning signs, but often people are not warned soon enough to do anything about it.

In June 1972, Hurricane Agnes hit Florida as a category 1 hurricane and diminished to a tropical storm as it moved northeast up the coast. Category 1 is the smallest hurricane possible, normally not causing much damage except to plants, but this happened to be the worst natural disaster to occur in Pennsylvania. It was more than 1,000 miles in diameter and almost hovered over Pennsylvania.

Prior to June, there had been only 2-3 inches of precipitation, so the runoff (the lack of water soaking in, causing it to run along the ground) was extreme. The water caused the Susquehanna River to flood at a rate of 7.5 million gallons per second!

Total damage to the Middle-Atlantic states reached more than $3.1 billion. Damages in Pennsylvania alone totaled more than $2.12 billion, which made it the most costly U.S. hurricane at the time. The death total was more than 117 in these states, 48 in Pennsylvania.

If a flood occurs and you are ordered to evacuate, you should pack your car with your disaster kit—which should include a battery-powered radio, flashlight, water, food, blankets and a first-aid kit. Listen to the radio to get directions so you know where to go to evacuate. If you are not told to evacuate, you should always be prepared to leave.

Often, floods do not give warnings before they occur, like in the situation with Mark and his family. He only learned about it on the news just moments before it happened with just enough time to get to higher ground. At times, that is the only thing to do to protect yourself.

Talk to your parents. Find out if you live in an area that could have floods occur. If you do, discuss what actions you should take and make sure they have a kit ready for you if it ever happens. Weather can be very dangerous, and you don’t want to give it a chance to prove it to you.

title: What is Weather?
text:
Weather is made up of three parts: Temperature - how hot or cold the air is; Precipitation - moisture that falls to Earth. It can fall as rain, snow, sleet or hail; Wind - movement of air from high- to low-pressure areas

As Pennsylvanians, you should be prepared for possible extreme weather over the horizon. Do you know the facts about lightning, those electrical sparks in the sky? Here's your chance to test your weather knowledge in Pennsylvania Studies Weekly this week!

Is It Climate or Weather?

You're lying on your back on your lawn, watching the clouds above. The clouds form a horse, then a clown, then a clown on a horse! What a great way to spend a lazy summer day. . . .

Suddenly, a brisk wind comes up. The sky turns dark and you feel big, warm drops of water on your face! Help! The lazy summer day has been taken over by a cloudburst. What you've just experienced is a sudden change in the weather. The term weather refers to rain, snow, heat, cold, ice, etc. It changes from hour to hour, day to day and month to month.

The term climate, on the other hand, describes the kind of weather a particular area has year after year. Alaska, for instance, has a much different climate than Hawaii. We think of Alaska's climate in the winter as freezing, snowy and very cold. We think of Hawaii's winters as balmy, sunny and pleasant.

Pennsylvania's climate is altogether different. Climatologists call our state "temperate." This means that our climate is not terribly hot (like Nevada) or terribly cold (like North Dakota.) We live somewhere in the middle of these two extremes.

I Want to Be a Weather Person!

The man or woman who stands by the weather map on television, pointing to different areas of the country and telling you about thunderstorms and heat waves, isn't just a person off the street with a pretty face. Generally speaking, the woman or man is a person with a degree in meteorology. Here are a couple of good words for you:

Meteorologist - a scientist who studies atmosphere, weather and weather forecasting

Climatologist - a scientist who studies climate and its many changes. How much education is required and how difficult is it to become one of these scientists? That's for you to research and report to your class!

Punxsutawney Phil

He's been predicting the weather for more than 120 years!

On Groundhog Day each year, the world turns its attention to the little town of Punxsutawney and a groundhog named Phil. If he climbs out of his burrow on Gobbler's Knob and sees his shadow, so the story goes, winter will be sticking around for another six weeks. Phil's an old hand at this prediction stuff - he or his ancestors (great-grandparents) have been doing it every year since 1887!

How did this funny tradition get started? The story is much older than you might think. The Romans knew Feb. 2-3 was the halfway point between the start of winter (Dec. 21) and the start of spring (March 21). The Romans noticed that, when it was stormy in early February, spring usually came early. If an animal could see its shadow, it was sunny out and spring was at least six weeks off!

Following this old Roman tradition, on Feb. 2, 1887, some German settlers took a groundhog to the top of Gobbler's Knob in Punxsutawney. They showed off the animal so all could see for themselves if there was a shadow cast. This was the start of Groundhog Day in Punxsutawney.

But you don't have to wait until February to get a glimpse of Phil. He can be found living with his family at Groundhog Zoo. Each summer, the town celebrates its favorite son with a week-long Groundhog Festival in July. But how accurate are Phil's predictions? He's right only 39 percent of the time! Sh-h-h, don't tell anyone - You'll spoil the fun!

Hey, Now That's Enlight(e)ning!

Question: Is lightning always produced by a thunderstorm?

Answer: Yes, lightning is always produced by a thunderstorm. Lightning causes thunder, and you can’t have a thunderstorm without thunder!

Question: What are the odds of getting struck by lightning in a given year?

Answer: About a million to one—but you still need to go inside when a storm comes along!

Question: How many people die each year as a result of being struck by lightning?

Answer: An average of about 60 in the U.S. That makes lightning the second most deadly weather phenomenon. Flash floods are the worst. Lightning kills even more people than hurricanes or tornadoes!

Question: Are people always killed when they’re struck by lightning?

Answer: No. About 300 survive with injuries each year in the U.S. from lightning strikes. People can learn how to do CPR to help others who are struck by lightning!

Question: How can I protect myself from being struck by lightning?

Answer: Don’t stand around wondering if the storm is going to pass. Take cover immediately. When thunder roars, go indoors!

Question: How can I tell how far away a storm is?

Answer: Count the seconds (thousand one, thousand two, etc.) between the time you see the flash and the time you hear the thunder. For every second you count, add 1,000 feet. So if the time between a flash of lightning and a crack of thunder is five seconds, that storm is about a mile away.

title: Weather Watch
text:
By scanning the sky for colors and other clues, people have tried to predict the weather since time began. Test these bits of ancient meteorology to see if they are really true.

1. A rose red sunset means fair skies are coming ("Red sky at night, sailor's delight, red sky at morning, sailors take warning!")

2. A pale yellow sunset means rain is on the way.

3. An evening rainbow predicts fair weather.

4. A morning rainbow in the West means rain.

5. A pre-dawn, copper-colored sky in the East means rain.

6. When the moon hangs in halo, there will be rain, especially if the halo is far from the moon.

title: Preparedness
text:
Have you ever heard the motto of the Boy Scouts of America? It is, "Be prepared," a very good motto. But have you ever thought about what it means to be prepared?

Preparedness is being ready beforehand in order to keep from being surprised. Many people use preparedness. The military is always prepared. They are prepared so they are not surprised if they are ever attacked. The military is not the only group that is prepared. Teachers prepare every day to give you a better education. Police officers prepare to make sure that we are all safe. You should prepare for natural disasters. Hurricanes, tornadoes, blizzards and many other forms of weather disasters occur all over the world, including Pennsylvania. Many organizations prepare in case there is a disaster. You can prepare at home by helping your parents create plans for when there's a fire or blizzard.

When you get up in the morning, you get prepared to face your day. You get dressed, brush your teeth and get your homework. You also prepare for things you may have to confront. If you have a test, you prepare for it by studying and by putting it in your head that you are going to try your best. You also prepare for growing up by being taught things by your parents and your teachers. Life is not easy, but if you prepare for it, you can take on anything that comes your way.

title: Jakob the Fiddler
text: There's a hill just outside Adamstown in Lancaster County where a horrible crime took place nearly 100 years ago. The victim was Jakob, a sweet, little man - a German immigrant who lived on that wooded hill in a humble cabin. Jakob would often come into town, to churches, grange halls and fire companies, to entertain with his fiddle. He was well known at weddings and carnivals. The locals donated what they could to Jakob's cash box at his feet. He was saving to bring his mother over from "the old country." Jakob also had a job as a farm hand, but the wages earned there went to the church and for little bags of candy he gave to the village's children. Tradition has it that it was Oct. 24 of that year when Jakob was attacked in his cabin. It was just before midnight. Jakob was returning from a local fiddling gig. He was horrified to find a pair of thugs waiting for him inside his front door. The two intruders demanded his money. The fiddler stood his ground, refusing to lead them to his secret stash. The robbers killed Jakob. And then they tore the cabin apart, looking for the cash box. They didn't find it and in frustration they torched the log walls and burned the place to the ground.

title: Is the Earth getting hotter?
text:
It's getting hot out there, and scientists are worried. Some call it global warming. Others call it global climate change. The average temperature on Earth has gone up 1.4 degrees Fahrenheit since 1880. That may not seem like much, but it's causing other things to change, too. Arctic ice is melting fast. Polar bears and other animals could lose their habitat. Glaciers are disappearing, and coral reefs are dying. Some scientists blame global warming for the increase in extreme weather, too. They believe the changes are causing more storms, floods, wildfires and heat waves.

Most scientists say it's our fault the Earth is getting hotter. Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide are trapping heat near the Earth. And those gases came from our cars and factories. People have cut down too many trees and caused too much pollution.

title: Ruffed Grouse
text:
What could be more appropriate in an issue of Pennsylvania Studies Weekly than to introduce you to our state bird? This beautiful bird became the official game bird of Pennsylvania on June 22, 1931, by an act of the General Assembly.

The Pennsylvania ruffed grouse, sometimes called the partridge, is known for its plump body, feathered legs and mottled, reddish-brown color. This protective coloring makes it possible for the ruffed grouse to conceal itself in the wilds. The bird is known for its great, beating wings when it is moving through the brush. The grouse's mating call, a low, rolling thunder, is a familiar sound, especially in spring.

The young are hatched on the forest floor, raised solely by the female and are out on their own very quickly.

title: Help a Rat and Learn to Run the Country This Year!
text:
Hey, kids! I’m Revere the Rat, but you can call me Rev. I’m your online Studies Weekly friend and I need your help. You can help me get great stuff by earning points while you learn. Just scan the code or go to www.studiesweekly.com and click on my picture.

Has your family ever bought something that came with an owner’s manual? Cars, TVs and other things have an owner’s manual, a book on how to use them. Your social studies class is the “owner’s manual” for the United States of America. You’ll learn about history, geography, government by the people, and much more, so you can do a good job of running our country someday.

In America rats can’t vote, so “you the people” govern (run) the country. Someday you will be in charge of this country, and you’ll choose leaders and representatives by voting. Then you can tell the representatives you help elect how you think the country should be run. In fact, Studies Weekly kids are so smart, that many of you will someday be mayors, senators, governors—maybe even the president!

For now you have two jobs: Learn about the country and how it works and earn points for me so I can get that great stuff I told you about. It’s easy. Just scan or click and you’re on your way!

title: Big Canoes With Sails!
text:
The year is A.D. 1000 and it's a wondrous, terrible day for Siutut, the American Indian sitting on an island rock jutting out into the North Atlantic ocean. He stared with disbelief at a magnificent "canoe" unlike any other he had ever seen. But even more than that, the strange vessel was bringing men - men of light skin with fair hair and blue eyes. He stared for a moment longer, then fled in terror.

The white man had reached the continent of North America, and American Indians would never again be the only inhabitants of this land.

The captain of this ship was the Viking Leif Erikson. He sailed from Greenland in his long ship with its striped, square sail and fancy prow. Other ships had prows with carved dragons or serpents on them. He had crossed the stormy North Atlantic to settle in Iceland, then later in Greenland. From there, Erikson sailed to the island of Newfoundland, where he struck terror in the hearts of members of the Beothuk (Eskimo) Tribe.

"Leif the Lucky" did not stay long on this continent, however. It was nearly 500 years later and far, far to the south, when the next light-skinned explorer reached our shores. This was the famous Christopher Columbus, who landed in San Salvador in 1492. He thought he'd landed in India and called the darker-skinned inhabitants here "Indians." The name has persisted all these centuries.

Many adventurers sailed to our shores following Columbus. These included Cabot, Corte-Real, Verranzano, Cartier, Frobisher, Davis, Baffin and Hudson. Amazing stories of their exploits were very exciting to the Europeans. An irresistible urge to settle this new land took over.

So to the homelands of the Algonquians and Iroquois came the English, the Dutch, the French and the Swedes with their traders, soldiers, adventurers, colonists and pilgrims. To the newcomers, arriving in their "big canoes with sails," the American Indians graciously shared their ancient knowledge of how to survive in the woodlands of the great Northeast. What the American Indians received in return cost them their homes, their liberty and their very lives.

title: Pennsylvania’s First People
text:
For the next three issues, we'll be learning about the native inhabitants of Pennsylvania. This week, let's take an overall look at some of the earliest Pennsylvanians. Many American Indian tribes lived in Pennsylvania before Europeans came, but historians haven't been able to identify them all.

The "Three Sisters"

The most important foods to all American Indians were the "Three Sisters": maize (corn), beans and squash. The picture shows the American Indian Shuffle Dance. A woman carrying a basket containing the seeds of these vegetables leads a parade of the "Givers of Life" - women holding bread. They shuffle as they move around a cooking pot, rubbing Mother Earth with their feet to feel a closeness to her. This was a dance of deep gratitude.

Pick a Name - Any Name!

Almost all ancient Pennsylvania natives belonged to two language families: Iroquois or Algonkian. Here's a grammar usage question for you:

Algonquian?

Algonkian?

Algonquin?

Algonkin?

Even most books and teachers can't agree! The following should be helpful (from the Handbook of North American Indians):

Algonquian: The tribes or communities of the Algonquian nation

Algonkian: The name of the language family

Algonquin: An out-of-date form of the word Algonquian

Algonkin: An out-of-date form of the word Algonkian

Writers of books and articles use them all. Ask your teacher. Which form of the word does she or he prefer to use in your classroom? Fill in the blank: Algon________

Let's Make Moccasins!

There were two basic kinds of moccasins worn by all American Indians: hard soled and soft soled. It was quite common for children your age to make moccasins for their elders. Almost all of them were made from soft, tanned skins and many were decorated with beads and porcupine quills.

title: William Bradford and the Mayflower Compact
text:
Imagine that someday you join a group that is going to start the first colony on the moon. What is one of the first things you might need? If you said a set of rules or laws to live by, you'd be thinking clearly. That's exactly what William Bradford helped write for the Pilgrims in 1620.

William Bradford decided early in his life that he did not agree with the Church of England, and this was the only church the English laws allowed in those days. He joined a separatist church, one that had separated from the Church of England. Bradford wanted to avoid being arrested and put in prison, so he led a group of church members and moved to the Netherlands. But they faced persecution for their religion there too.

In 1620, the separatists returned to England to meet others with their beliefs and sail for the New World on a ship called the Mayflower. The group received a patent (land grant) from the king of England to establish the first permanent colony in Virginia. The Mayflower was blown off course and landed near Cape Cod instead of Virginia. William Bradford and the other leaders of the colony decided that they needed to write an agreement for all people to have protection and to keep the peace. This unique document, signed by 41 men, is called The Mayflower Compact.

William Bradford was later elected governor of the colony over 30 times, so his clarity of thought must have been well respected. The Mayflower Compact has been called the inspiration for the U.S. Constitution. Look it up. Rewrite it in your own words to see how it reads in today's language. Would you have signed it? Why or why not?

title: Allegheny Forest Region
text: For an outdoors person, the next best thing to paradise is the North Central Region of Pennsylvania. This is the land some call God's country. In fact, every June, runners participate in a race called God's Country Marathon. Driving along Route 6, you won't be surprised to learn that the highway is one of America's most scenic drives according to National Geographic. As you drive east, you'll encounter the magnificent Grand Canyon of Pennsylvania near Wellsboro. But be careful! There's a 1,000-foot drop into the rugged Pine Creek Gorge. For a real treat, head to the bottom of the gorge and take a covered-wagon ride along the stream. Spend some time among the white pine in an area called Hearts Content. You'll have fun at the Autumn Leaf Festival in Clarion in October. Last week, we told you about the Groundhog Day celebrations in Punxsutawney. You should visit the Cross Fork Snake Hunt in Potter County if you like adventure. And don't forget the Bark Peeler's Convention and the Red Suspenders Weekend, both around the Fourth of July weekend in Galeton. There's something going on all year. In the winter, it's a wonderland. In the spring, the air is sweet with mountain laurel blossoms. In the summer, it's refreshing and cool. And in the fall, you'll find hundreds of thousands of acres of red, yellow and gold. Come visit this magical land of never-ending things to see and do!

title: Do we say “Native American” or “American Indian”?
text: Some individuals and some entire tribes of Native Americans prefer to be called American Indians. Some are offended by the name Indian because the name was a mistake that Christopher Columbus made when he sailed to America and thought he had reached India. It is considered correct to use the terms Native American, American Indian, Indian or indigenous people, according to the tribes' websites. Everyone agrees that we are all proud to be called Americans!

title: Rattlesnake
text:
Hi there! My name is Drake. You know, "Drake the Snake." I am a timber rattlesnake. I hesitated to give you a real picture of myself because some people, especially kids, always shy away from the real me. I feel bad because snakes are always given such a bad rap. For one thing, people think we're cold and slimy. That's not true. We're rather cool, yes, but very dry. Did you know that timber rattlesnakes in the commonwealth are found only in central Pennsylvania? I grow to be 36 to 54 inches long, and I'm black and yellow. My tail is black. Rattlesnakes are found only in North and South America and we're the only snakes that give birth to our young. The other snakes lay eggs. And we're a lot smarter than other snakes! Rattlers get through mazes faster than others and we can even tell the difference between various people!

There are 21 varieties of snakes in Pennsylvania. Three of us are poisonous: the northern copperhead, the eastern massasauga and yours truly. But I'm not aggressive. I'll only strike if you chase me or handle me carelessly. Those folks who take us to the Cross Fork Snake Hunt in Potter County every June pretty much know what they're doing. We're measured and prizes are given. Then we're returned to our natural habitat. I've been captured six or seven times, and I've never bitten anyone!

title: Absolutely Powerful?
text:
The government of the United States is becoming a model for new governments all over the world. Why is this? This is because the government of the United States has succeeded in giving its people many freedoms. What is it about the United States that preserves the freedom of the people? A big part of it is the structure of its government. Before looking at the government of the United States, it is important to understand the history and evolution of other governments in world communities.

The first European people in the Americas came seeking many different things. One thing was similar among all of them. They came from countries ruled by kings and queens. A king is the leader of a monarchy. What is a monarchy? A monarchy is a kind of government where the executive power (the same power the president of the United States holds) is held by one person for life. When that person dies, the power goes to someone else. There were generally two different ways a new king or queen came into power when an old one died. The first was through the family lines. Often one of the king's children would be the next to rule. The second was through the choice of the people. Sometimes the people would choose who their next king was. Sometimes people fought and forced a king out of office, replacing the king with another political figure. In most cases it didn't matter how the king got his power, because he had absolute power. Absolute power meant that he didn't have to explain himself or check with anyone else before doing anything. Many people believed that the king only had to explain his actions to the god that he believed in, and no one else. This belief is called the divine right of kings. Often opponents of the king objected to the amount of power held by the king. They would form other groups to limit the power of the king. When this happened it created a new governmental structure called a constitutional monarchy.

After some time in the New World people from England that were living in America began to feel that the English government wasn't treating them fairly and that they needed to have their own government. The people felt that the government should only have the power that they gave to it and that they should always have a hand in how the government worked. This kind of government is called democracy. It wasn't a new idea. Democracy began in Greece over 2,000 years earlier. Abraham Lincoln described democracy as, "government of the people, by the people, for the people." Every citizen in a democracy can take part in the government. People can be directly involved (by holding a governmental office) or indirectly involved (by having representatives that work for a group of people). Elections are the process through which representatives are chosen. While no government is a perfect democracy, the ideas of democracy help to ensure the freedoms of the people. This is because it is really the people who make the rules and vote for them. It is by the people and for the people, just as Lincoln stated.

title: How Do I Use a Dictionary?
text:
What does “native” mean? How do you pronounce “shaman”? To find the answers to these and many other questions, grab a dictionary. The dictionary just might be a student’s best friend. A dictionary lists and defines words.

Know Your ABCs

The words in a dictionary appear in alphabetical order. At the top of each page, two guidewords show the first and last words on that page. Guidewords help you find the word you need more quickly. For example, the word “tepee” might appear on a page with the guidewords “tension” and “territory” at the top of that page.

Is your word followed by numbers? That means it has more than one definition. Look up the word “native” and see all the definitions for it. Write some of them here:

After each word, you will find a letter that stands for a part of speech. For example, n. means “noun,” v. means “verb,” and adj. means “adjective.” Sometimes, one word can have two or more parts of speech. It depends on how it’s used in a sentence. title: What is a powwow?
text:
If you want to get a taste of real American Indian culture, you should plan to attend a powwow in your area. The word “powwow” is a Narragansett word used by mountain men and frontiersmen to describe a large meeting, or ceremony, held by the American Indian tribes in the area. Once friendships had been made, these white men were often invited to join the powwows and celebrate with their American Indian friends.

Today, powwows are held all over the state of Pennsylvania at different times of the year. The American Indians sing songs of the seasons and perform special ceremonies. Many people dress in colorful costumes, often representing birds, bear, fox and deer. Some even dress in costumes that honor flowers, grasses and other plants. Each costume is made to show respect and love for nature.

Dancers join together and make a "grand entry" into the arena where the powwow is being held. A single line of costumed American Indians dances into the middle and forms a circle around the drum. Once everyone is ready, a medicine man (spiritual leader) performs a special pipe ceremony. During this ceremony, no photographs may be taken and everyone listens quietly. The pipe ceremony is very sacred and the medicine man's actions represent a prayer for everyone at the powwow.

Most powwows welcome visitors. Besides watching the dancers and singers perform, you will also be able to meet and visit with American Indians from right here in your own state. You will find food, crafts and fun for everyone.

Powwows are held throughout the state, with most of them being held during the summer months. Visiting a powwow is a great way to find out more about the earliest Pennsylvanians.

title: Tree Rings Tell an Ancient Story
text:
Could a city the size of New York City be destroyed by a drought? Many scientists believe that's what happened to a city called Angkor in what is now Cambodia. Angkor was the capital city of an empire that stretched from Myanmar (Burma) to Vietnam. This city of about 750,000 people lasted 600 years, from the ninth to the fifteenth century.

The Angkor area doesn't have the kind of summers and winters that many U.S. cities do. It has drought for about six months, and a rainy season for six months. Angkor had a complicated network of canals, reservoirs and dams to catch water during the rainy season so it could be used during droughts. The system worked well for almost 600 years.

Recently, scientists studied tree rings from 900-year-old trees near Angkor. The rings showed that year after year the droughts and the rains got more severe. Here's what scientists think may have happened: The reservoirs went completely dry during the drought seasons and the canals were badly damaged. The people of Angkor could no longer control one of their most important resources, water. Without water their civilization collapsed.

Isn't it amazing what you can learn from a tree?

title: Industrial Revolution—Good or Bad?
text:
Today, we think of the Industrial Revolution as a marvelous period of invention and progression. Many items that make life easier today had their beginnings during the Industrial Revolution. The Industrial Revolution really began in Europe in the early 1700s. It did not reach the United States until after the Revolutionary War. New machines were developed in Europe and America. They changed the way people lived, worked and thought. The machines began to make manufacturing easier. More jobs became available in the cities. New changes in transportation also helped life for the farmers. The speed and distance of goods being shipped improved.

Before this, goods were usually not shipped more than 150 miles. It cost too much to do so. This meant communities were self-supporting. With the newer machines and better transportation, the way of life in America began to expand and change.

For Pennsylvania, the period between the Civil War and the turn of the century was a time of fast industrial growth. Pennsylvania was a leader as industry surged forward. Here, new developments helped industry quickly grow.

Before the Industrial Revolution, skilled craftsmen learned every step involved in making an item. For instance it might take a cobbler several days to make a pair of boots, or a gun smith may take an entire week to make a gun. With the growth of industry, mass production became more practical. This idea was to divide the jobs between many people to make one item. If each person did only one step of the production, they would become faster and better. Less skilled workers could also be used, making more workers available. This idea was called division of labor. It did a lot to speed up production. Many former craftsmen were unhappy about this new method. It often meant they might lose their job. At best they would be required to repeat the same small task over and over.

title: Algonquians of Pennsylvania
text:
Let's look at the Algonquian nation this week. What was daily life like for them?

1. Family History

In the Algonquian tribes of the Northeast, the lineage was matrilineal. This means it came through the mother. This mother teaches her daughter about her clan heritage.

2. Marriage

This young man is explaining to this girl what he will do for her if she agrees to become his wife. In this culture, there wasn't much courtship or ceremony. Marriage was often just an agreement between two people to become man and wife. A man gave a woman an animal bone to show that he would provide for the family. She gave him an ear of corn as a vow that she would grow the crops. Some tribes allowed a man to have two wives as long as the women came from two different clans.

3. Wigwam

The Algonquian women were in charge of building their shelters. The wigwams were constructed with thin young trees. They were bent into semicircles and set into the ground by the men. The bent trees were then covered with available materials. This included birch bark, animal skins, cornhusks and reeds or grasses. They were woven into mats. The cooking was done indoors in the winter time. A hole was left in the roof to allow the smoke to escape.

4. Learning for Survival

This young girl is watching her mother prepare an animal. It is being prepared for its many uses. Everyone helped in the Algonquian way of life. "Woman's work" and "men's work" were well defined. There were times for play, but survival was the most important thing in the minds of all tribe members.

5. Deer, Elk and Moose

Wild game of any size was very useful to American Indians. They were used in every part of the country. They believed Great Spirits had blessed them with these creatures for their survival. They never killed more than they could eat. The spirit of each animal had special meaning to them. They used all the parts of each animal for many things.The animal was used for food, shelter and clothing. It was also used for tools, toys and decorations.

6. Corn

This food was a staple of all tribes everywhere. When it was ground, as this woman is doing, it was used in bread, soup, ash cakes cooked in the campfire and foods for the trail. A favorite way to eat corn was right off the cob or as popcorn, as we do today.

7. Pottery and Baskets

The Algonquian people made pottery from clay. This clay was powdered and mixed with shells, gravel or sand. They used the coil method. This was common to many American Indian cultures. Baskets were constructed mainly of reeds found near streams. They were often very beautiful in addition to being functional.

8. Canoes

Around Pennsylvania, the Algonquian people built their canoes of the prized birch bark. What if there were no big birch trees? They constructed their canoes of the heavier elm, sycamore or hickory bark. Sometimes they made dugout canoes from logs. The canoes were so well designed that today the design is still used.

9. Home of the Shaman or Powwow

A spiritual leader is called a "shaman" or "powwow." One lived in every village. This man's magic helped him make journeys to the underworld. He went to visit the "old people" or spirits of those who had died. By going into a trance a shaman could visit the land of the spirits. He must not accept food from them. If he did, his spirit would be captured and his entranced body on Earth would die. It was the reports of these shaman that convinced the American Indians there was life after death. The name given to the Great Spirit by the Algonquians was "Manitou."

10. Visitor

This is a visitor from the Nanticoke tribe to a Shawnee village. The Algonquian people were peaceful and made all visitors, even white men, feel welcome. Are they speaking of past battles and brave deeds?

11. Maple Sugar

This man is carrying back to camp the final batch of maple sugar. The tribe made this great treat in the maple groves. It was well loved by all Algonquians. A feast will be held soon to celebrate the end of winter. The same methods of sap gathering are used today. It is used to make fine maple syrup and candies.

12. Bow and Arrow

A wood craft learned from boyhood was bow and arrow making. Bows were made by eastern woodlands tribes from springy wood such as shagbark hickory, white ash, cedar or white oak. Even young boys became expert shots and were able to kill a bird in flight at a young age. Their lives depended on how well they could hunt.

13. Moccasins

This footwear is a true American Indian invention. Styles varied with the tribes, yet many were soft soled and came up to the ankles. Depending on the tribe, the tops could be puckered. They may have long side flaps reaching to the ground instead. Many were decorated with flattened porcupine quills. "Moccasin" is an Algonquian word we borrowed into English.

14. Dogs

These animals were common among American Indian tribes. They were just as common as they are today. They were used as pets and beasts of burden. Under some extreme starvation circumstances, they were used as food.

title: The Gift of Corn
text:
One spring, a long, long time ago, a chief's son came of age. The chief told the boy that he must leave the village to find the spirit that would guide him through life. He could not eat or drink, and the guiding spirit would come to him in a dream.

The boy went into the forest. By evening, he was very hungry, and his mouth was dry from thirst. His thoughts wandered, and he began to dream. He felt the sun on his skin as though it were midday. He opened his eyes and saw a tall stranger standing beside him. It was Corn Spirit. He was wearing a green robe. The spirit spoke. "I bring you a gift from the sun - a gift that you must worship above all others."

Corn Spirit told the boy that he must wrestle with him and take from him his green robe. The boy must throw the spirit to the ground, and only then would he receive the gift. If the spirit lost, the boy must place the spirit in the rich soil on the spot where he falls. At the end of the third full moon, his gift would be ready to harvest. The boy was weak from hunger, but he swiftly took hold of Corn Spirit's arms and held tight. They wrestled with each other for three, long days. At the end of the third day, the boy felt great strength fill his body. With one big tug, the boy was able to pull the robe from Corn Spirit. The boy followed the directions that the spirit had requested and buried him in the ground.

After the third full moon, the boy returned to the spot where he had buried Corn Spirit. Waiting for him was a huge cornstalk with ears of corn. The spirit's gift was indeed great - food from a plant that the American Indians could grow to feed their tribes for many generations to come.

title: Where did corn come from?
text:
Way back in 1,500 B.C., there was a wild grass called teosinte among the natives of Mexico. As this wild grass was cultivated and cross-pollinated, it developed into the sweet corn they later called maize.

Squash and beans also found a place in ancient Pennsylvania as these foods were brought from migrating tribes. Eventually, these vegetables (corn, squash, and beans) were nicknamed "The Three Sisters" because they became the basic foods of the majority of the American Indian nations.

title: Bluebird
text: The bluebird was rarely seen in northern Pennsylvania as late as the 1980s due to land-use changes and pesticides. Its nesting spots had become very hard to find as well. Old, dead trees are often removed, leaving the birds no place to build their nests. Other birds, such as the English Sparrow and the starling, enjoy similar spots for nesting. These birds are very competitive and will fight and even kill bluebirds in order to take their nesting spots. In recent years, many people - individuals as well as organizations - have become interested in helping the bluebird by building nesting boxes. These boxes provide the bluebird with safe, comfortable places in which to lay and hatch their eggs. An organization called Bluebirds Across Susquehanna County is actively encouraging bluebirds to return. Wouldn't it be fun to have a bluebird house of your own? This beautiful bird's song is being heard throughout Pennsylvania more and more these days. Let's do all we can to help that song be sung!

title: Economics Competition
text:
Have you ever played on a sports team? Maybe you played soccer, basketball or baseball. If so, then you know the best way to become a winning team. Each player must play the best he or she can. Everyone must work together.

This same kind of competition is in a marketplace. Producers compete against each other. They try to give customers the best prices and products for their money. Monopolistic competition is when businesses offer similar products. The products are not identical, though. Each business can raise or lower its price. Each tries to reach a price where it can sell the most products. This is why economists call these businesses "price searchers."

An oligopoly is a market where a few (usually three to five) companies control the competition. They provide the most products. For example, airplane manufacturing is very hard and so only a few large companies compete against each other. When there is only one seller of a product, it is called a monopoly. No companies are making a product to use instead of this product, either. So there is no competition for the company.

The company can charge whatever price it wants, because customers have to buy their product. A monopsony is a market that has only one buyer. Sellers will compete with one another to make the best quality product. They try to offer this product at the best price. An example would be the U.S. government. They are the only buyers for aircraft carriers in this country. Businesses compete to make the best aircraft carriers. But there is only one buyer.

Now that you know about the different kinds of markets, can you decide which one you would prefer for a business you owned?

title: How Do I Use an Encyclopedia?
text:
Sometimes you can find a wide range of information about a certain subject using an encyclopedia. An encyclopedia is a set of reference books ranging from A to Z. (It can also be a CD-ROM or a subscription to a website.) Each volume has a number and a guide letter that shows the first letter of the article titles in that volume.

1. To find out what topics the encyclopedia includes, look through the index volume.

2. Scan the entries until you see the topic listed. You can look up someone’s name, a place or a general subject such as “reservations.”

3. Go to the appropriate volume listed in the index.

4. Scan the guidewords printed in dark type at the top of each page until you find your entry word.

5. You may need to skim through some entries until you find the information you need. This is because there may be more than one entry word for a given topic.

6. If you find a cross-reference after an entry word, then that means you will find information about the topic under another entry word. The cross-reference will tell you which volume of the encyclopedia to look in.

Using an encyclopedia, look up a tribe from your state that is discussed in this paper and summarize what you learned here. You may be able to find out what their name means, where they came from, what language they speak, what they ate, how they acquired food, how they dressed, if there are any members of this tribe living today, where they live today, how many are living today, etc.

title: From Boys to Men
text:
In the Shawnee tribe, when a boy was about 12 years old, he was considered old enough to join the men for their first trip away from the women and children of the tribe.

The men of the clan would leave the women and children at home and travel to a summer campsite to set up fish weirs, or traps. One kind of trap was a fence of sticks and brush placed across the mouth of the river. In the spring, salmon and other fish swim from the sea up the river to spawn, or lay their eggs. A hole in the fish weir with a net behind it would catch the fish as they swam through.

The young men would learn how to build wigwam homes from tree bark, bulrushes and other plants. They would also build a special wigwam - a sweat house. Shawnee men would paint their skin for both protection and decoration. Every day, they would use grease and oil to protect themselves from weather and insects. They would place hot stones in the sweat house, then pour water over the stones to produce steam. Every evening, the men would go in for a sweat bath to clean the grease and paint from their bodies.

The boys would also learn to make weapons. The Shawnee men used many different weapons for hunting. They made bows, arrows, clubs, traps and nets. Arrowheads were made from sharp stone, wood, bone, copper and deer antlers.

After the camp was set up, the women and children of the tribe would travel to join the men. They would plant crops and dry the meat and fish that the men caught.

title: People of the Long House
text:
All families of each clan lived together
