There were two main groups of American Indians in the Northeast: the Algonkian-speaking tribes and the Iroquois tribes. Just like the Algonquians, the Iroquois were composed of several tribes that shared a language and similar culture. They called themselves the Haudenosaunee, (ho day no SHOW ne aye ), which means "people of the long house." The French traders adopted the name Iroquois for them.

After many years of fighting among themselves, the Iroquois achieved peace. Well-organized villages with councils and elected leaders gave the Iroquois a stable life. Hunting and farming provided plenty of food.

The Iroquois villages were made of groups of long houses. A long house had no windows. Each long house was 50 to 150 feet long. Many families of one clan lived in one long house. Each family had only a very small space that was like a large bunk bed. The family slept on the bottom bunk and kept belongings on the top. Fires burned in the hallway going down the center.

Iroquois villages were usually found on a high riverbank. A palisade was put around the village for protection. This was a tall fence made of sharpened tree trunks that were driven into the ground. During the 1600s, the Europeans came to the Iroquois lands. Sometimes, the Iroquois made peace with them and other times they fought. After the American Revolution, the U.S. government wanted the Iroquois lands for their own development. The government moved the Iroquois onto reservations in New York and Canada.

The Unusual Matriarchy

The word matriarchy means "ruled by women." A patriarchy would be a culture ruled by men. Male rule was the common way of life throughout most of history of the world, including the history of American Indians.

The matriarchal society is what makes the Iroquois culture so unusual. Women owned the long houses and all the contents. They also ruled the tribes. The adult males were members by marriage only. Their family lines were traced back through the mother's family and all children born became members of their mother's clan. The sachem (chief) was always a man, but he was chosen by the clan mothers. Children were treated well and they, in turn, were taught great respect for their elders.

This system worked very well, as the Iroquois League of Nations was and is one of the strongest of all American Indian powers.

title: Death of Kim Jong-il Means New Leader for North Korea
text:
The sixty-nine-year-old leader of North Korea, Kim Jong-il, died of a heart attack on December 17, 2011. Kim Jong-il held the title of Supreme Leader of North Korea for 17 years. He took over when his father, who was the first dictator of the country, died in 1994.

North Korea is a very secretive and poor communist country. People in North Korea have very little freedom. Some people say it is the world's most repressive state. That means its leaders force people to do only what the leaders want them to do. No one is allowed to disagree.

Before he died, Kim Jong-il chose his youngest son, Kim Jong-un, to follow him as Supreme Leader. Kim Jong-un went to school in Switzerland and can speak four languages. The world isn't sure how old Kim Jong-un really is. He is thought to be in his late 20s. Because he is so young, he has little experience in leading a country. Many people believe that North Korea will actually be led by top members of Kim Jong-un's political party, at least for a while.

Since North Korea has nuclear weapons, many people around the world have been worried about what North Korea will do with those weapons. With a new leader, many are even more worried. If there is a coup (a takeover) by another member of the family or by the military, it could make the country very unstable and dangerous. The eyes of the world are on Kim Jong-un!

title: The Iroquois Confederacy
text:
Let's look at the wisdom of the Iroquois this week. Keep in mind that Pennsylvania was inhabited mostly by Algonquian tribes. However, several Iroquois subtribes lived in north-central Pennsylvania.

The Iroquois Confederacy

Long before the French and other white men came to this continent, the Iroquois were fighting with their neighbors and among themselves. Their skills as warriors made them a strong force to the people of the Northeast, but the constant wars and killing between their own tribes nearly destroyed them. After centuries of fighting, five of the Iroquois tribes were united in peace. Deganawida, a prophet, had a vision of peace. "The Peacemaker" enlisted the help of the medicine man, Onandogan, Hiawatha. Together, they convinced the Mohawk ("Men of Steel"), Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca to establish peace by replacing fighting and bloodshed with peaceful decision making. The result was the Great Peace. The structure of government established for the tribes to accomplish this great peace is one of the oldest forms of democracy in the world.

These five tribes called themselves the Haudenosaunee. The French called them the Iroquois Confederacy and the English called them the League of Five Nations. Later, they became six nations when they were joined by the Tuscarora, who migrated from North Carolina.

Strength in Numbers

What's Benjamin Franklin doing here in the Pennsylvania Studies Weekly American Indian issue? The League of the Iroquois is called an oligarchy. That means that it's ruled by a small group of people. The Iroquois League was ruled by 50 council members. Pennsylvania's own Benjamin Franklin was so impressed by the league that he used it as a model when helping to form certain ideas for the newly created United States of America.

Having a Ball the Iroquois Way!

Lacrosse was named by the French but originally played by the Iroquois. Each player had a long stick with a curved end that had a net woven through it. The ball, which they could catch and throw with the netted end, was made of deerskin and stuffed with moss or hair. Two teams of six to eight tried to hit the ball into the opponents' goal. Tribes would play against other tribes on special occasions. Teams planned how they would play. Today, lacrosse is a fun sport to play, but for the Iroquois, it was serious battle training!

First Money Made in America

The first money in America wasn't paper or coins. It was made from seashells! It was called wampum. The Algonquian tribes made beautiful wampum belts from a very hard and thick clamshell. Wampum was usually purple or white. The beads were very hard to shape and took a long time to make. At first, the Algonquians used the beads as a way to send messages to other tribes or to record history. The Iroquois tribes did not make their own wampum, but traded with the Algonquian tribes to obtain it. Sometimes, they stole it! The white traders also wanted wampum because they could use it to buy furs from the Iroquois. As the wampum became more valuable, it began to be used as money is today.

Mother and Child

It's true that women ruled in the matriarchal society of the Iroquois. Mothers were very tender with their babies and carried them on their backs in cradle boards. Mothers provided most of their infants' care.

title: North and South American Governments
text:
The citizens of the United States enjoy many freedoms that are not enjoyed by people in other parts of the world. This is because of something that happened many years ago. When the Constitution was first written many states refused to ratify it without a Bill of Rights. The Bill of Rights is a section in the Constitution that lists the rights that all the citizens of the United States have. What is a right? It is the ability of a person to do something without being prevented from or punished for doing it. The rights given to citizens of the United States in the Bill of Rights are some of the most important parts of their lives. Rights, such as the right to say anything (freedom of speech) without being punished by the government for doing so, are exercised every day.

Many other countries in the Western Hemisphere have also adopted laws like our Bill of Rights to ensure good lives for the people that live there. In Canada there is a part of the constitution called the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The charter lists the rights of the citizens of Canada. The rights that are listed include: Fundamental Freedoms, Democratic Rights, Mobility Rights, Legal Rights, Equality Rights and Language Rights.

Like the United States and Canada, Latin American countries have constitutions. They help state the laws of the land. The difference is the types of governments built by each constitution. There are many kinds of governments. They range from federal republics to representative democracies.

America was the first independent democracy in the Western Hemisphere. Other countries didn't set up democracies until later. For example, Mexico was the first country in Latin America to set forth a democracy. It began with a man named Francisco Madero. Madero gathered people who opposed the dictator of Mexico, Porfirio Diaz. Madero became the first president of Mexico on Nov. 6, 1911. He established the first real attempt at a democratic government. Madero's democracy was short-lived. The people that helped him start the democracy soon turned against him. Within two years a military revolt had assassinated Madero. Another ruler was placed in his stead. This was the first try at democracy in a Latin American country, although it failed. This attempt paved the way for other Latin America federations and democracies today.

Prime Minister Dean Barrow leads the country of Belize. Belize is a small country in Central America. It is a parliamentary democracy. In this kind of political system the parliament picks the prime minister and the cabinet ministers according to the party strength.

The prime minister and cabinet are responsible to both parliament and the people in this system.

President Luis Guillermo Solis Rivera leads the country of Costa Rica in Central America. Costa Rica is a democratic republic. In this type of government, the citizens that are allowed to vote elect representatives responsible to them. Governors are not elected officials, but are chosen by the president.

President Raul Castro leads the communist state of Cuba. Communism is a system of government in which the state party plans and controls the economy. The communist party is the only party permitted to function in Cuba.

Raul took over from his brother Fidel Castro, who had been in power since 1959, when he transformed Cuba into the first communist state in the Western Hemisphere.

President Enrique Peña Nieto is the political head of Mexico. Mexico is a federal republic. The powers of the federal government are limited. The states hold a degree of self-government. Voters choose their government representatives. While America is also a constitution-based federal republic, there are some differences. For example, in Mexico, the president selects the candidate to succeed him in the elections.

title: Allegheny Forest Region
text:
McKean County was formed in 1804 and named for Thomas McKean, who was our very-well-known, second governor at the time. The county is a leading producer of natural gas and crude oil. After oil was discovered in the town of Bradford and the fields around it, the area yielded 100,000 barrels a day. By 1881, Bradford was producing 83 percent of all the crude oil in the United States and 77 percent of the world's supply.

Until 2003, the most outstanding landmark of this area was the Kinzua Bridge. Built in 1882, it towered 301 feet high and was 2,058 feet long - the highest and longest bridge in the state. A tornado destroyed much of the bridge in the summer of 2003, but in 2011 workers repaired its remains to be used as a walkway called the Kinzua Viaduct. Visitors to Kinzua Bridge State Park can walk 600 feet out on the old bridge's support towers and catch a great view. There's an interesting story about the bridge. In 1890, a man robbed a bank in the town of Emporium, then fled north with $40,000 in coins and bills. As he wandered through the rugged forest, he became disoriented and exhausted and he eventually collapsed. He died a short time later, after confessing that he buried the money within sight of the Kinzua Bridge. Many people have searched, but no one has turned up the treasure.

Do you have family members who like to hunt? It's very popular in McKean County and throughout the state, such as in the Kinzua Quality Area. Many people hunt for deer, duck and turkey. With permission, go online here to learn more about Pennsylvania wildlife and hunting regulations.

title: Where are Pennsylvania Tribes Today?
text: Today, approximately 80,000 Iroquois live in the United States and Canada, although the total number is hard to prove. There are nine Iroquois reservations in New York state and one in Wisconsin. There are five reserves in Ontario and Quebec. Some Iroquois live in Oklahoma. Many have left the reservations and live in cities in the Unites States and Canada. Most Algonquians live and work in cities from Maine to Virginia. The children attend public schools and often go to college. The Lenni Lenape (Delaware) culture is being preserved by the Lenni Lenape Museum and tribespeople of Allentown. Other Algonquians live on reservations, but the reservations are different from the ones run by the U.S. government. One of the largest New England reservations is located in Maine, where about 550 Penobscots occupy one island on the Penobscot River. One of the smallest reservations is in Trumbull, Conn. It's the size of a city block.

title: Wild Turkey
text: The Pennsylvania Game Commission saved the wild turkey from extinction in the 1800s. The bird is classified as big game. With a wingspan of 4 to 5 feet, this bird can fly for short distances, but it mostly wanders about on foot, with other turkeys, looking for food. They eat fruits, buds, seeds, insects, nuts and acorns. Turkeys nest on the ground, but roost at night in large trees. During the spring mating dance, males fan out their beautiful tails to attract females to a clearing. Usually, three to five females drop by to see what's going on. When the chicks are hatched, the males pay no attention to them. It's a good thing for the females that the young turkeys learn to forage for food almost as soon as they're hatched. They can fly to tree roosts a month after being born! The turkey is mostly black with a red gullet, a white head and red markings down the breast.

title: Why Should I Follow Directions?
text:
Here’s a really good story about why it’s important to always follow directions. Once you read it, you’ll never have trouble following directions again!

One time a teacher handed out a test to her students. It was a long 10-page test. At the end of class, some students thought they did very well. They got most of the questions correct. But nobody passed! After the teacher had graded the tests, she pointed out the directions at the top: “Write your name on the top of page one and hand the test in. Do not complete any of the questions.” You can bet those students wished they had read the directions rather than do the whole 10-page test!

Reading directions carefully can mean the difference between an A and an F in school. It can mean the difference between a delicious pan of muffins and a mess of burnt, yucky dough.

1. Read the directions from beginning to end before you do anything else.

2. Make a list of any material you will need. Gather it up!

3. After you have everything you need, read the directions again carefully. Do you understand every step?

4. Do you still have questions? Ask your teacher, parent or a friend for input.

5. Follow the directions carefully, step by step.

If you follow all these steps, you will do all your assignments correctly. Practice following directions by making the Pemmican recipe below.

How to Make Pemmican

2 cups buffalo jerky or beef jerky, shredded

1 cup dried chokeberries or tart red cherries, chopped

6 Tablespoon tallow (beef fat) or butter, melted

Combine all ingredients and form into six patties. Refrigerate until serving.

title: French Scout Discovers Our Woods!
text:
First European to Explore Pennsylvania

Samuel de Champlain was the Frenchman who founded Quebec, Canada. He was impressed with the beautiful woods of our area and sent a young French soldier/scout, Etienne Brulé, (Broo-LAY) to explore the river valley next to the Iroquois lands. Brulé took a canoe and some Carantouan guides with him. They started at the headwaters of the Susquehanna River, near present-day New York, and floated down through Pennsylvania and into the Chesapeake Bay. The trip took place during the fall, winter and spring of 1615-1616. Brulé made many observations regarding the climate, the animals and the natives he met along the way. The various tribes loved the French, but disliked the Dutch because they were mistreated by them. At the end of his trip, Brulé's party was attacked and scattered by an Iroquois war party. Alone and lost, Brulé wandered into an Iroquois village. The Iroquois captured him and started to torture him. One story says that just then, a terrific thunderstorm came up. Brulé thought quickly. He told his tormentors that the storm was the wrath of God coming down on them and that they should let him go. The frightened Iroquois then released Brulé.

In the 1620s, Brulé deserted the French and joined the English. This made the Hurons angry because they were friends with the French. They captured Brulé later in Canada and murdered him.

title: Celebrating An American Hero’s Trip Around the Earth
text:
It was 1957 when the Soviet Union launched the first spacecraft into orbit. Americans were shocked! The space race had just begun and we were already behind! In 1961 President John F. Kennedy announced that the U.S. planned to land a man on the moon by the end of the decade. The Russians responded by first launching a dog into orbit, and later two men. The race was on!

On Feb. 20, 1962, a Marine Corps fighter pilot from Ohio stepped up to put his life on the line. John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth. The success of his Mercury mission was one of the first steps to landing a man on the moon in July 1969.

John Glenn served as the U.S. senator from Ohio for 24 years, but he longed to go back into space. In 1998 at the age of 77 he was able to see that dream come true. He traveled on the space shuttle Discovery and became the oldest person to ever go into space! On Feb. 20th, 2012, America celebrated the 50th anniversary of John Glenn's first orbit. Mr. Glenn and the remaining members of the Mercury mission space team were given a hero's welcome at Cape Canaveral in Florida. Because of Mr. Glenn's service to our country as an astronaut and a senator, he has been called an American hero.

title: Early European Explorers
text:
Native Pennsylvanians never "owned" land - they believed you can't own something you can't take with you beyond death. They simply lived here and blended well with nature. They were puzzled, therefore, by the activities of the next 65 years, between 1615 and 1680. New Americans thought differently than American Indians.

A 65-Year Saga!

It's hard to remember specific dates while studying history. Fix the number "65" in your head. That's the number of years between the time Brulé sailed down the Susquehanna (1615) and William Penn petitioned the king of England for land in New England (1680). This week, we'll look at the events that took place in those 65 years between the Dutch, the English and the Swedes. Those were the three countries that fought for possession of this beautiful land of ours.

Swedes, English and Dutch Race to Own Pennsylvania

1615 - Etienne Brulé starts exploring the Susquehanna River and takes information to the French explorer Champlain.

1623 - The Dutch construct Fort Nassau on the New Jersey side of the Delaware River, the first settlement.

1638 - The Swedes arrive. The Swedes are led by Dutchman Peter Minuit. He is the first governor and builds Fort Christina. "New Sweden" is born.

1643 - Johan Printz becomes our third governor (after a short term by Peter Hollandare) and moves the capital of New Sweden to New Gothenburg on Tinicum Island.

1644 - Swedes found Upland. The colony of Upland is called Chester, which has become famous for its shipyards.

1644 - William Penn is born in London.

1654 - John Claesson Rysingh becomes the fourth governor. Rysingh makes the mistake of attacking the Dutch forts along the Delaware River. He makes Peter Stuyvesant of New Netherland angry.

1654 - Stuyvesant seizes New Sweden. Stuyvesant sends an army to get the Dutch fort back with five armed ships and 600 men. The Swedes lose their colony. Pennsylvania is known as New Netherland and includes New York and New Jersey. Stuyvesant was governor for nine years.

1664 - England claims New Netherland. King Charles II sends four warships and 400 men to New Netherland. He demands Stuyvesant's surrender, who does so without a shot. New Netherland is renamed New York after the Duke of York, King James' brother.

1673 - The Dutch retake the Delaware settlements. For a brief period, the Dutch are in control of the Delaware settlements.

1674 - English regain the Delaware settlements under the Treaty of Westminster. Sir Edmund Andros is appointed governor.

1680 - William Penn petitions King Charles for a land grant. In future issues of Pennsylvania Studies Weekly, you'll see the exciting story of Pennsylvania unfold!

title: Perseverance
text:
Has anyone ever told you that you have "staying power"? Do you find it hard to start something and not finish it? If these things are true about you, then you might have what is called perseverance. Perseverance is where you stay strong in a course of action, a belief or a purpose. It means that you do not change what you decided to do after you started. When you start a project with a friend for science, you finish it with him or her. If you join the basketball team, you keep on trying and don't give up.

Many explorers and travelers during the 1600s had perseverance. They knew what they wanted to do, and they stuck to it. They did not turn back because the waters got rough or because it seemed they did not have any way of succeeding. If they had not had perseverance, many of our states - and maybe even all of America - may have gone undiscovered for a very long time. It is because these brave explorers did not give up that Pennsylvania is what it is today. If Etienne Brulé had not persevered and kept searching, who knows when Pennsylvania would have been discovered? If it had not been discovered for many years, who knows where we would be right now?

title: Where Did Thunder Come From?
text:
HenQ was one of seven brothers of an Iroquois tribe who lived together long ago. HenQ was happy and wild by nature. He was very big and swift, too, and just joyful about life. He was rowdy and loved to play all kinds of pranks on his six brothers. But HenQ was too innocent to realize just how much he bothered his brothers with his pranks. And he had no idea how his strength often caused so many disasters. He would often smash things to pieces when just reaching out to touch them. For instance, he once laid his hand on a pole of the lodge, and the lodge fell to the ground!

At last, HenQ's six brothers had had enough. They still loved him, but they just had to get rid of him and his wild ways! They told him one day that they were all going hunting on a large island in the middle of the river. They paddled their canoes to the island. One brother took HenQ to the dense forest in the middle of the island. He told HenQ to sit very still and watch for deer. Then the brother sneaked away and joined the others on the shore, and they quickly paddled away back to their village.

HenQ waited and waited. When it grew dark without a sign of his six brothers, he found his way through the forest to the shore. When he found the canoes gone, he realized he'd been abandoned. He cried and roared out his sorrow all summer long. When winter came, he slept, and when spring and summer came again, he continued to roar now and then. He came to realize why he'd been abandoned, but it didn't make him any less lonely or sorrowful.

That is why, to this day, we still hear his mourning in the form of thunder from time to time in the spring and summer, and less so in the winter, when HenQ mostly sleeps.

title: Why do leaves change color?
text: Look out your classroom window. Soon our Pennsylvania world will be filled with glorious colors. Not all people in this country are as lucky as we are to witness the beautiful changes we enjoy each autumn. The secret is a substance called chlorophyll. Each year, as the temperature falls and days shorten, a corky layer of cells forms at the joint between each leaf stem and twig. These cells cut off the flow of sap to the leaf. The leaves' chlorophyll, the substance that makes them green, dies. Pigments, the colors we couldn't see while the chlorophyll was there, remain in the leaves. The amounts of these pigments and their combinations in the leaves determine which stunning colors will paint our landscape.

title: Elk
text:
Once so numerous in Pennsylvania that a county was named for it in 1843, the elk was wiped out by hunters in the 1870s. It was reintroduced by the Pennsylvania Game Commission in 1913. Several herds of elk now roam the Allegheny Forest region. They are closely monitored by the commission. You can watch for elk roaming the Pennsylvania Wilds Elk Country Visitor Center near Winslow Hill.

The elk is a member of the deer family. It weighs from 400 to 1,100 pounds and can be as long as nine feet. The animal is dark reddish brown in summer and gray in winter, with a dark mane and a white rump patch. Males have large, wide branching antlers that sweep upward and back. A 5-foot antler spread is not unusual.

Small herds are made up of cows, calves and young bulls. Mature bulls live alone or in small bachelor groups until late August. Every August, the bulls find the cows, and the competition begins with other bulls to organize their harems. Visitors to the area at the right time of year are often rewarded with more than sightings. They may also hear the mating calls of the bulls, which sound like a distant chorus of bugles.

title: Let's Write
text: Exploring is really just investigating—kind of like detective work. All of you have explored some place or some thing. Tell us about something you explored. Did you take a walk through the woods? Look up at the sky at night? Surf the Internet? Why did you choose to explore that particular thing? What did you learn? Did you learn something useful? Was it fun? Evaluate your experience.

title: Our Dutch and Swedish Heritage
text:
Read the two paragraphs below. Listed below the paragraphs are several customs/foods that have added to our way of life. Place a “D” beside the word or phrase that describes a Dutch custom or an “S” if the custom is Swedish or from some other Scandinavian country.

Dutch settlers had customs that have added to our way of life today. They brought ice skates and sleighs to the New World. Certain styles of houses are called “Dutch Colonial.” A half door is called a “Dutch door.” We use the words “cookie” and “waffle,” from the Dutch language. Tulips were brought here by the Dutch, of course! Sinterclaus from the Netherlands has become Santa Claus in this country. Cole slaw, doughnuts and crullers (a kind of Dutch doughnut) are Dutch foods as well.

The Swedes built the first log cabins and brought the first cows to America. They are also known for their beautiful wood carvings and sculptures. Swedes introduced us to the smorgasbord, the first buffet style of restaurant. You’ll find Swedish thin pancakes with lingonberry (a Swedish fruit) butter and Swedish meatballs (kottbullar) at a smorgasbord. And don’t forget soccer — the national sport of Sweden!

title: Language Arts Connection
text: As you read this week’s lesson, circle or highlight five verbs in any color. On a piece of paper, write a sentence for each verb using the progressive form (-ing). (CC ELA L.4.1)

title: Penn’s “Holy Experiment”
text:
The First Settlers in Pennsylvania

"This day, my country was confirmed to me... by the name of Pennsylvania, a name the king would give it in honor of my father. My God that has given it to me... will, I believe, bless and make it the seed of a nation."

- William Penn, writing on the spring day in 1681 when he was granted Pennsylvania

A young man named William Penn, who was jailed several times for his beliefs, was one of the best-known Quakers in England. By 1680, Penn had decided that the Quakers needed a new home where they could pursue their beliefs in peace. He asked King Charles II to repay a debt owed to the Penn family by granting him land in America. Charles agreed to the deal in 1681. The king named the colony "Pennsylvania" (Penn's Woods) for the Penn family.

Pennsylvania was a carefully planned colony. Penn wrote to a friend that his colony would be a "holy experiment," meaning that he was going to give people the chance to live in love and harmony according to Quaker beliefs. With that in mind, Penn decided his colony should be a haven for non-Quakers, too. He distributed pamphlets about Pennsylvania to both Quakers and non-Quakers in England, Ireland, Wales, Scotland, Germany, the Netherlands and Switzerland. Hundreds of people responded and purchased land from Penn.

Penn could not go to his colony until 1682. But, in the spring of 1681, he sent his cousin William Markham to Pennsylvania as his deputy governor. Markham brought a letter from Penn to the Swedes, Finns, Dutch and English who had lived in Pennsylvania before it became Penn's colony. Calling them "My Friends," Penn assured the old colonists that "you shall be governed by laws of your own making and live a free people."

Calling All Colonists!

Before leaving England for America in 1692, Penn convinced 750 Quakers to invest in his province (a district or region). Each investor paid 100 pounds for 5,000 acres that had not even been located or surveyed yet! (A pound in those days was a lot of money. Today, it is worth less than $2.)

Penn made his colony sound so great that 23 shiploads of immigrants came to the commonwealth in the year 1682 alone. But of all the land Penn sold, only half of the new owners ever came to Pennsylvania to settle their new property.

title: Pennsbury Manor
text:
Have you ever thought of your home being used as a museum someday? What would you think if you knew that there would be thousands of people every year exploring your house and looking at your furniture? Would it make you nervous? Would you want to make sure your house is always clean? We'll bet that William Penn, the founder of Pennsylvania, never even thought about this happening to him. But his house is a museum today.

William had a country home that was located in Bucks County, Pennsylvania. It was known as Pennsbury Manor. More than 250 years after the construction of Pennsbury Manor was completed, some people decided to re-create his home and use it to educate people about the life of William Penn.

Pennsbury Manor is open for much of the year so that people can take tours of the place. There are also various workshops, demonstrations, celebrations and a living history theater, among other things. People can even relive life from more than 300 years ago with "Just for Families" events, such as "Waking Up in the 17th Century," where you spend the night in the manor, wake up to families wearing clothing from the 17th century and then spend the day doing various work around the estate. They also learn how to enjoy a cup of tea with the same proper manners that families used 300 years ago.

The manor also offers various educational workshops for children in school. These meet the national and state history standards for education. Students can see a 15-minute orientation video, have a tour of the manor house and other buildings and participate in a 30-minute hands-on-history activity. No matter the weather, it happens throughout the year.

Not only is there the tour, but there are also special event days for schools. Some of these include Pennsylvania Day, when children learn to do chores from the 17th century, write with a quill pen and visit William's garden for the beginning of spring. There are also Sheep Shearing Day and William Penn Day, among others. For those young children who are not yet in school, there are even preschool programs.

It is because of people like William Penn that we have the great state of Pennsylvania today. Had he not arrived and founded this area, we may never have been here. It is great that we can honor him by exploring his house, his land and his lifestyle.

title: William Penn Forges His Colony
text:
The gift of Pennsylvania to William Penn from the British king made Penn the owner of the largest piece of land ever owned by any private citizen in the world at the time.

1. The City of Brotherly Love

Work was already under way on the new capital that William Penn carefully planned while still in England. Penn named this town "Philadelphia," which means "brotherly love" in Greek. Penn's dream was that Philadelphia would be an almost heavenly place where everyone would live in peace and understanding. He wanted Philadelphia to be not only spiritually good, but physically beautiful. Many Colonial towns were dirty, crowded, disease-ridden firetraps. Penn planned Philadelphia as a "green-country town" that would have broad streets and houses on large lots. When he arrived, Philadelphia had only about 10 houses. Soon the newcomers were putting up more houses and laying out streets in a grid pattern. Several Philadelphia streets that are important today were named by Penn. Among them are Chestnut, Walnut, Spruce and Pine streets.

William Penn Divided His Land into Three Categories

common land

private estates

huge manors (very large homes) or baronies

Penn's home was planned and built on a barony (large grant of land) he called Pennsbury Manor. Many early settlers had so much trust and respect for William Penn that they were willing to pay 100 pounds (almost $200) for 5,000 acres of land they had never seen.

2. Penn Pays American Indians for Land

Although King Charles' land grant gave Penn legal ownership of the commonwealth, Penn insisted that no land be occupied until the American Indian inhabitants were paid. Pennsylvania took shape as the result of purchases from the American Indians by William Penn and his family over a period of 100 years.

The first purchase was done at the famous Goodwill Conference on Oct. 24, 1682, beneath the Treaty Tree, a majestic elm on the banks of the Delaware at Shackamaxon, now Kensington.

3. Penn's Amazing Letter

The letter William Penn wrote to the American Indians living in Pennsylvania in 1682 is one of the most remarkable documents of Colonial times. Although the American Indians had taught the colonists to plant corn and survive in the new land, most colonists hated, disliked or barely tolerated their new neighbors. These colonists were full of prejudice (an unfair opinion formed without knowing all the facts).

Penn was different. He was a fair man. He insisted that the American Indians and colonists were equals, despite differences in lifestyle. Ninety-four years before Thomas Jefferson wrote that "all men are created equal" in the Declaration of Independence, Penn took steps toward putting that noble thought into action in Pennsylvania. Penn's letter said:

My Friends:

There is one great God and power that hath made the world and all things therein, to whom you and I and all people owe their being and well being and to whom you and I must one day give an account for all that we have done in the world ...

May we always live together as friends ... I have great love and regard for the Indians ... I hope to win your love and friendship. Any colonists who harm you will be punished ... I look forward to meeting you.

Your loving friend,

William Penn

title: King Philip’s War
text:
Metacomet was an American Indian who lived in New England. His father, Massasoit, was the great Wampanoag chief who had welcomed the Pilgrims in 1620. Metacomet became sachem (chief) in 1662 and continued friendly relations with the colonists. He became known as "King Philip."

The American Indians and colonists had their differences, but overall things were peaceful. They depended on each other as trading partners. However, some Colonial leaders began making unfair demands on the Indian tribes. The colonists ignored previous agreements and expanded into Indian territories. They forced natives to sell their land. They even demanded that Metacomet's people surrender all their weapons.

Metacomet organized an army. He formed an alliance with other American Indian tribes. His goal was to force the Puritan colonists out of Indian territory. Puritans and some American Indians united to fight Metacomet's warriors. Colonel Benjamin Church formed the first American Ranger unit in Plymouth Colony.

Many bloody conflicts followed. Both sides attacked and burned towns. They killed and enslaved hundreds of people. They destroyed land, crops and livestock. Every Colony and tribe in New England suffered huge losses. One of Church's soldiers killed Metacomet in 1676, and the battles stopped shortly after. Historians call this period King Philip's War.

Both sides of this conflict chose to abandon ethical behavior instead of solving their problems peacefully. The war forever changed the way of life for colonists and American Indians in New England.

Was there any chance this war might have been avoided? Have you experienced people ignoring ethical behavior in order to get what they want?

title: Susquehanna Valley
text: Welcome to our valleys! Do you like to fish? You'll want to drop your line in Penn's Creek - one of the best trout streams in the country. Or visit Bucktail, Susquehanna, Hyner View, Milton and Shikellamy state parks on the river itself, where the smallmouth-bass fishing is the best. On the back trails of this area, you can hike those lands traveled by American Indians - the Susquehanna, Tuscarora and Golden Eagle trails. Or discover the Black Forest Trail through Clinton County's lush, unspoiled Big Woods. If bicycling is your love, pedal quiet country roads and peaceful hills and valleys through lush farmland that many Amish and Mennonites call their home. At Mifflinburg, visit the Buggy Museum, where awesome buggies were built at the turn of the 20th century. This busy town was at that time home to at least 50 buggy works. Ask the folks to take the family to Boalsburg to see the Pennsylvania Military Museum and tour a chapel that belonged to Christopher Columbus' family in Spain. Our valleys are proud of our celebrations. There are at least 13 fairs and festivals held here each year. The one with the most unusual name is the McClure Bean Soup in Snyder County every September. That's the actual name of the festival as well as the main dish served there. The first Bean Soup was held in 1865, after the Civil War ended. The Army held reunions for the vets in the area. They served bean soup and hardtack because that's what the soldiers ate in the Army. The festival has now expanded to include rides, booths, lots of other foods, storytelling and fun for all. Enjoy your visit to the Susquehanna Valley!

title: What is a Quaker
text:
A Quaker is a member of the Society of Friends, which was formed in England in the mid 1600s by George Fox. Members of this society would not call themselves Quakers, however.

Restrictions about religion had the Quakers moving in 1675 to New Jersey, where around 230 English Quakers founded Burlington, New Jersey, in 1678. In 1681, William Penn was granted the territory which became known as Pennsylvania. Within two years, there were about 3,000 Quakers living there.

The Society of Friends is an alternative Christianity that emphasizes the personal experience of God in one's life. They believe in equality regardless of race, social status or gender. They also believe that violence is intolerable.

title: Bald Eagle
text:
The bald eagle can be found in many areas of the United States, from Alaska to the Gulf Coast. It is a national symbol of the United States. It is not really bald but has snowy white feathers on its head. Bald eagles mate for life and live near water in high places where they build large nests of sticks. The female generally lays two eggs each year, and the parents both raise their young. These are birds of prey and prefer to eat fish, but they will take what other animals kill as well!

Eagles are making a slow comeback following near extinction (being completely wiped out) because of hunting and pesticides. The birds are once again able to nest in natural habitats that were unsafe during the 1960s. The U.S. government took the bald eagle off the endangered and threatened species list in 2007.

In Pennsylvania, you can find these majestic birds throughout the almost 200,000 acres of the Bald Eagle State Forest.

title: Did You Know?
text: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, is the home of the Liberty Bell and Independence Hall. It was also the capital of the United States until 1800. Can you find your way through to the current state capital of Harrisburg?

title: Let's Write
text: Talk about your nationality. What countries did your ancestors come from? When? Do you have relatives living there today? Are there family traditions, beliefs, languages or menus that your ancestors gave you? Ask your parents for help to write about one or many of the influences in your life that come from your ancestral homeland.

title: International Organizations Help Promote Peace Around the World
text:
There are many different beliefs and viewpoints in the world today. Most people want peace despite their differences. How can countries work together to achieve peace? Many international groups have been created in the last hundred years. Their purpose is to promote peace, economic development and cooperation. These organizations are sometimes composed of representatives from governments of many countries. Sometimes these people are just citizens working toward a common goal.

Perhaps the most active and well-known international organization is the United Nations. The name United Nations was created by Franklin D. Roosevelt. It was used in the Declaration by the United Nations on Jan. 1, 1942. This declaration stated the intent of 26 countries to work together. These countries would fight against the Axis powers. People felt it would be good for countries to cooperate after World War II. The United Nations held the Conference on International Organization. They met in San Francisco from April 25 to June 26, 1945. They created a charter that was signed by 51 countries. The United Nations then officially came into existence on Oct. 24, 1945. Since then the number of members has grown to 193. The most recent admission to the United Nations was South Sudan on July 14, 2011.

The United Nations has four main purposes. They are: (1) maintain international peace and security, (2) develop friendly relations among nations, (3) cooperate in solving international problems and in promoting respect for human rights and (4) be a center for harmonizing the actions of nations.

The United Nations is not a world government. It does not make laws. It does provide the means to help resolve international conflict. It also creates policies on matters affecting all people. All member states have an equal voice in decision making.

There are six main divisions of the United Nations. There is the General Assembly, the Security Council, the Economic and Social Council, the Trusteeship Council, the Secretariat and the International Court of Justice. The General Assembly is composed of representatives from all the member states. It is like a parliament or congress for the nations of the world. They meet to discuss the world’s most pressing problems. The assembly cannot force action by any state, but its recommendations are very important.

The Security Council is responsible for maintaining peace and security. There are 15 council members. Five of them, China, France, the Russian Federation, the United Kingdom and the United States, are permanent members. The other 10 members are elected for two-year terms. Decisions require nine “yes” votes, but cannot be made if one of the permanent members votes no. The council can enforce its decisions through various means, but reserves force for the last resort.

The Economic and Social Council coordinates the economic and social work of the United Nations. The council plays a key role in fostering international cooperation for development.

The International Court of Justice is the judicial part of the United Nations. There are 15 judges elected for three-year terms. They help settle disputes between countries. Countries are not forced to face the court. If they choose to, they must obey its orders.

The secretariat carries out the administrative work of the United Nations. It works under the direction of the General Assembly, Security Council and other divisions.

title: Quakers Move to America
text:
Pennsylvania Takes Shape

The Society of Friends had many enemies in England, where the religion originated. Most English people were members of the Church of England. In a country that was almost always at war, the Friends' stand against warfare was very unpopular. And in an age when important people expected special treatment, the Friends annoyed the rich and famous by treating them the same as the poor and unknown. For example, the Friends would not take off their hats for anyone - not even the king and queen.

George Fox, the founder of the Society of Friends, once told a judge "to tremble at the word of the Lord." Because of Fox's reference to trembling, the judge called him a "Quaker," and soon all the members of Fox's sect were being called Quakers. England persecuted the Quakers, who by 1682 numbered 60,000. It was time to make a change. William Penn's offer of freedom of religion in a place that was reported to be beautiful and lush was very appealing.

Many people make the mistake of lumping all of Pennsylvania's early immigrants together. Try to remember that the Quakers came from England, and the Amish from Germany and Switzerland. The Mennonites, who had similar beliefs to the Quakers, were from Germany and chose to settle in Germantown. The Moravians came from Germany as well. Other groups seeking religious freedom were Roman Catholics from Ireland and Germany, Protestants from France and Jews from Portugal.

Pennsylvania was founded on religious freedom, and there were many different faiths represented, just as there are today. As we work to protect each others' religious freedoms, we're all members of a big society of friends!

title: Move Over, Brothers Grimm—Make Room for New German Fairy Tales
text:
There's a magical world out there full of elves, evil queens and beautiful princesses! If you enjoy "Cinderella," "Little Red Riding Hood" and "Rapunzel," you have already discovered the work of the Brothers Grimm. These German fairy tales and legends were collected by the Grimm brothers and put into popular books about 200 years ago.

A new world of fairy-tale magic has just been revealed. Researchers found a collection of 500 stories gathered by Franz von Schonwerth, a German historian who did his work at the same time as the Grimm brothers. Because Schonwerth was a historian, he wrote the stories exactly as the German people told them to him. The Grimm brothers changed some of the stories to make them less frightening for children. The Grimm brothers admired Schonwerth's work. Jacob Grimm said, "Nowhere in the whole of Germany is anyone collecting (fairy tales) so accurately, thoroughly and with such a sensitive ear." Schonwerth's collection was never as popular as the Grimm brothers' books. His three volumes of stories collected dust for 150 years until they were rediscovered.

Schonwerth's collection includes a story of a beautiful girl who gets away from a witch by turning herself into a pond and another tale about a turnip princess. As soon as the stories are translated into English, you will have a whole new collection of fairy tales to read!

title: Life in “Penn’s Woods”
text:
Pennsylvania grew with the arrival of more colonists. A famous woodsman and a famous wagon came on the scene at that time, too. Penn's widow, Hannah, had ruled the colony until her death in 1726. Then their three sons, John, Thomas, and Richard, were in charge.

"Father of the Westward Expansion" - Daniel Boone

Daniel was the sixth of 11 children, born Nov. 2, 1734, near Baumstown, Berks County. He was fascinated by American Indians, and he tracked the local tribes and learned their customs and ways of thinking. This knowledge made Boone a highly regarded scout, tracker and folk hero. When Daniel was 16 years old, his father sold the homestead and moved his large family to North Carolina. He knew a little about how to read and do figures, because Daniel preferred surviving in the wilderness around the Oley Valley. His boyhood home is now a state museum.

If you're as fascinated by this folk hero as many people are, do an Internet search for "Daniel Boone." You'll find lots of cool stuff, including stories written about Boone's many adventures. Have fun!

Covered-Wagon Days: Bad Roads, Tough Vehicles

She'll be comin' 'round the mountain when she comes, as the song goes. The horses and mules made their way over Pennsylvania's very rough trails. They pulled the Conestoga Valley wagons built by the German people of Lancaster County in the early 1700s. The wagons hauled Army supplies during wartime, and farmers used them to carry their crops across the mountains to market. Pioneers also moved west in Conestoga wagons.

One very nasty habit was also established during that time. Shoestring tobacco grown in south-central Pennsylvania was rolled into big sweetened cigars that commercial drivers (those who were paid to transport goods) of covered wagons loved to smoke and chew. These foot-long cigars, made popular by the teamsters, became known as "stogies" - after the well-known wagons they drove.

When you get a chance to visit the Smithsonian Institute in Washington, D.C., be sure to check out one of the original Conestoga wagons on display there.

Penn's Son Betrays the American Indians: The Walking Purchase

Thomas Penn claimed to have a treaty supposedly signed by his father and a few Lenape chiefs. This treaty gave William Penn land west of the Delaware River as far "as a man can go in one day and a half." However, no one had ever made the walk for the land. The Lenape agreed to let a walk take place.

The American Indians found out later that the area had already been surveyed, a trail blazed on trees, and the swiftest-footed woodsman prepared to make the "walk." Not only this, but he was paced by men on horseback. Some American Indians started out with him, to see that their interests were protected, but soon dropped out in disgust, saying that he was running - not walking! They thought the Lehigh River would be about the limit of the walk, but the runner reached the river before the end of the first day. And what further disgusted them, the lines of the survey had been slanted upward for a long distance to take in the whole of the valuable Minisink country, which the American Indians had been unwilling to sell all along!

These American Indians never forgot a kindness. And they never forgot a trick. They remembered William Penn and thought highly of him. But, years afterward, they remembered what Penn's son had done to them during the Walking Purchase. When the French and Indian War broke out, the Penn family regretted the trick they'd pulled on the Lenape.

title: Father Junípero Serra and the California Missions
text:
Do you like to give speeches? Can you convince others to see things your way? Then maybe you have a gift for expressing yourself clearly.

Father Junípero Serra was a Franciscan monk who some might call one of the "founding fathers" of California. He was born in Spain in 1713 and became a priest in his mid 20s. Many people noticed how well he spoke, or how clearly he expressed himself, during his powerful sermons, and he soon became a university professor.

Father Serra wanted to work as a Spanish missionary, so he first traveled to Mexico City in 1749. He started missionary work with the Sierra Gorda Indians. Soon he was made head of the Spanish missions in Baja (lower) California. Next, the Spanish governor asked him to start missions in Alta (upper) California. Father Serra personally built eight missions there and supervised the start of many more from San Diego to San Francisco.

Father Serra helped convert thousands of American Indians to Christianity. They lived and worked in the missions, but life was harsh. Many Indians died from overwork and diseases. But the missions kept going because of Father Serra's preaching and care. His sermons were so dramatic that he would sometimes pound his chest with a stone or touch a lit torch to his chest.

Father Serra used his clarity of expression for what he thought was good. He argued with the Spanish army to get control of the missions. He even convinced Mexican officials to send more money and soldiers for his missions. Spanish colonists settled the area around the missions, which is all now the state of California.

Do you think you have a good ability to express yourself clearly as Father Serra did? What topic do you feel strongly about?

title: Respect
text:
Have you ever run into someone whom you really did not like or maybe did not get along with? What did you feel like doing or saying to that person? Maybe you felt like telling him or her exactly how you felt. But what do you think you should do? Should you be rude to people just because you may not get along with them, or should you be respectful and be courteous to them because they are human beings also?

Respect is where you are willing to show courteousness and appreciation for something or someone. That means that it could be someone you like, such as your friend, or it could be someone you do not like, such as a bully at school.

People who moved to Pennsylvania known as Quakers dealt with this. Many people did not like them because of their beliefs and their religion. These people had to choose if they were going to respect the Quakers and their beliefs or if they were going to hold it against them because they did not believe the same thing.

Respect is very important if we hope to live among each other in the world. Not everyone has to believe the same thing, but everyone should be respectful of everyone else. It would make the world a much better place.

title: Phantom Panther of Snyder County
text:
It happened more than 50 years ago, and the farmer's name was Sam Jackson. Old Sam caught a male panther entering his chicken house and shot it dead. Now, a fellow can let a panther pass by in the woods; after all, panthers eat all the sickly, weak animals and birds. But a man's chicken coop? No sir-ee. No one in the county quite understood why, but Sam took a notion to stuff that panther's hide. Yep. He stuffed it with straw and leaves and left the eye sockets empty. It measured 9 feet from nose to the tip of its tail. The old man then attached his "prize" to the roof of his shed, which was right along the public road leading to Middleburg. It became the wonder of the neighborhood. With the jaws propped open to show the enormous teeth and with the tail high in the air, it looked just like a live panther. Horses shied at it, and dogs barked at it and tried to climb up on the shed. Children on their way to school were frightened by the carcass. One unknown and unfortunate feature of this tragedy was that the dead panther had a mate. These animals are very devoted to each other, and if one is killed, the survivor hardly ever mates again. Well, sure enough, the female kept prowling the edge of old Sam's yard on moonlit nights. She howled pitifully at her mate's carcass. The neighbors kept begging Sam to take the panther down. "It keeps the mate in the neighborhood, and our families can't have any peace - day or night."

But Sam refused to take it down. Night after night, the female came to mourn. One memorable night, a pack of angry, howling hound dogs clawed their way to the roof of the shed. As they began tearing at the stuffed animal, suddenly something that seemed like a shadow swept across the yard from the edge of the woods. It was no shadow, of course. It was the sleek form of the stuffed panther's mate. Up she flew like black lightning to the roof of the shed. First she flung off the attacking dogs. Then she slowly began licking the open sockets where her mate's eyes had once blinked at her. She moaned softly as she rolled the carcass from side to side. Suddenly, she gave an awful yell, and, fixing her fangs tightly in the nape of its neck, she leaped from the roof and dragged the carcass across the yard and into the forest.

Sam immediately took off with his two sons and three hounds after the scent of the she-panther. After trailing the female and her stuffed mate all night long, they finally came to a clearing with a stream running through it. And what made their eyes open wide in astonishment? Why, two panthers, drinking leisurely from the stream. One was the female, who turned and growled at Sam's family as they approached. The other was her mate, drinking from the stream alongside her. Her mate?! Yes! The Jackson men stared in amazement as both the female and the male drank from the stream. When they'd both had their fill, they slowly padded away. The female looked back once, gave a parting snarl through bared teeth, crossed the clearing, and entered the forest, never to be seen again in Snyder County.

Young readers, don't you ever underestimate the power of love!

title: Why are the Germans of Pennsylvania called “Dutch” when they came from Germany, not Holland?
text: German immigrants spoke Deutch, which is the official language of Germany. When the word Deutch came to America, it got twisted and became Dutch. Therefore, we now say, "Pennsylvania Dutch" when referring to the Germans who moved to Pennsylvania.

title: Pennsylvania Panther
text: Also called a lion, this animal was the most magnificent that ever lived here. Averaging 8 feet long, the animal was a scavenger (ate sick and dying animals), but never killed more than it could eat and never attacked people. When William Penn arrived here, the panther was found only within Philadelphia's city limits. Hunters chased them north and west, and by 1830 great numbers lived in the large area of Susquehanna, Lycoming, Centre, Fulton and surrounding counties. Uncontrolled hunting nearly wiped out this beautiful animal by 1900. Bounties, such as Luzerne County's for $1,800, were placed on a single hide because of their commercial value. Hides became rugs and bed covers. The meat tasted like chicken or pork. Its oil was used as a remedy for gallstones and rheumatism. The Pennsylvania panther/lion did not die out completely, however. The animal is nearly extinct, but rare sightings have taken place in the Susquehanna Valley Region, such as Snyder County. Do you think you'll be lucky enough some day to see one?

title: Let's Write
text: Do you know of people in your family or church or among your friends who had to fight or move to other states or countries for what they believed in? What did they do? Did people make fun of them? You may share those stories in this space.

title: How Do I Use a Graph?
text:
Graphs present numerical amounts of something and show the relationship between sets of numbers.

Figure out what the graph is trying to show. The type of graph used to present the information will depend on what is intended by showing the graph. Here is an explanation for some possible graphs.

Types of Graphs

Bar Graph — Bar graphs use bars of different lengths to give information. The bars can run from left to right across the graph or from the bottom up. You can use a bar graph to show how the numbers compare.

Look at the bar graph about the U.S. population growth.

Pictograph — Pictographs are like bar graphs except they use pictures or symbols instead of bars.

This pictograph shows how much ice cream people from different countries eat.

Pie Graph — Pie graphs use a circle to show 100 percent of something. The circle is divided into sections, or slices, of the pie. Each slice gives different information.

Of the population in 2003, what percentage lived in China?

Line Graph — Line graphs show how information changes over time. One line shows units of time. Another line shows the information being measured. Inside the graph you’ll see points that meet. You can use a line graph to see if the information is going up or down.

This line graph shows the number of hurricanes since 1970. Have hurricanes increased or decreased?

Try It!

Create a graph using the data below. First, decide which type of graph would be the best way to present the information. Then create it, using the examples above for help.

Number of New Settlers in the United States

title: Pennsylvania Goes to War!
text:
The French came here as trappers and liked it so much, they wanted to own Pennsylvania. But they weren't going to get it without a fight! Great Britain wasn't about to let this beautiful area go to those French trappers and traders inching their way onto the land west of the Allegheny Mountains. They came from Canada and claimed the land for France. The French began building forts from Lake Erie to the Ohio River.

Pennsylvania, Virginia and other British colonies claimed the land as theirs. In 1753, the governor of Virginia sent George Washington to Fort Le Boeuf to tell the French to leave. They refused.

The Frenchmen had a lot of helpers, too. The American Indians were angry because the white people were moving onto their lands. Even though William Penn had paid the American Indians for much of the land, they were still feeling pushed westward much too quickly. They were also still angry over the trickery involved in the Walking Purchase.

The British had convinced the French that they meant business. The French got tough and built the largest of their forts, Fort Duquesne. It was located where the Allegheny and Monongahela Rivers meet and form the Ohio River.

Washington was sent a second time by the Virginia governor. His plan was to attack the big French fort. But first he needed instant protection. They quickly built a structure they called "Fort Necessity."

The French soldiers weren't about to wait for Washington to come to them. There were many French soldiers and angry natives, who outnumbered the young George Washington's band from Virginia. Colonel Washington and his small troop of brave soldiers fought hard for 10 hours in pouring rain. Finally, Washington was forced to surrender.

In George Washington's long military career, this was the first time - and the last time - he ever surrendered.

title: Merci to the French
text:
The French may have lost the French and Indian War, but their influence lives on in America today. While you may not notice it as you go about your daily activities, a closer look will show you just how much the French have really influenced our American way of life.

Since the early days of the United States, the French have had an impact on what we wear. At the beginning of the 19th century, French gloves and lace were important American fashion accessories. Later, men began wearing beards because that is what the fashionable Frenchmen were doing. Today, France is considered the fashion capital of the world and most of the latest styles come from Paris.

Many of the foods we enjoy each day have their roots in French cooking. The French brought the first yeast breads to America, along with their rice-growing and wine-making skills. Most of you have probably eaten French foods without even knowing it. Rolls, buns, breads, pastries, omelettes, and soups all come from France, along with mayonnaise, casseroles and hors d'oeuvres.

Finally, many of the words we use each day come from the French language. Early French explorers used words like portage, rapids, bayou, butte, peak, gopher, prairie and pass to describe some of the things they saw as they journeyed through America. These same explorers gave French names to many of our cities, including Baton Rouge, Detroit, Couer d'Alene, Marquette, Joliet, Des Moines and Terre Haute. Other French words you may be familiar with are croquet, poker, roulette, automobile, garage, restaurant, crayon, bouquet and boutique.

Merci (thank you) to the French for all they have given to our American way of life!

title: Taxes
text:
You are standing in line at the grocery store. You have counted all of your change, and you have $1.03. It's just enough to buy the biggest pack of bubblegum you've ever seen in your life. The bubblegum costs $1.00. You get to the front of the line and the cashier rings it up. Your total comes to $1.06. What? That can't be right. You are three cents short. How did that happen? Then you remember about sales tax. Lucky for you, you find an extra nickel in your pocket and pay for your gum. Taxes are sums of money that the government collects from people and businesses. They use this money to provide services for the citizens. There are many different kinds of taxes, like the sales tax you pay at the grocery store. Sales tax is a tax that is usually added to the price of your purchase for goods or a service.

There are three main types of taxes: progressive tax, regressive tax and proportional tax. A progressive tax can change. The tax depends on how much money a person makes. People that make more money pay more in taxes. People that make less money pay less in taxes. A proportional tax is the same tax for everyone. Regressive taxes are opposite of progressive taxes. This means that people with more income pay less in taxes and people with less income pay more in taxes. Which tax do you think is the most fair?

title: The French & Indian War
text:
The French, the American Indians and the British fight over Pennsylvania

A Difficult Journey to Fort Le Boeuf - 1753

Major George Washington was not having a good time. In the last two days, he had been shot at by an American Indian and fallen off a raft into icy water, and now he and his guide were trapped on an island. It was December and very cold. Washington had been sent to deliver a letter to the French at Fort Le Boeuf to tell the French to leave the area. The French had written an official reply that Washington was carrying back to the governor. In the letter, the French wrote that they refused to leave. But how would the governor know if Washington couldn't deliver the letter? Then the freezing weather did them a favor. It was so cold over night that the river froze. Washington and his guide walked to the shore. Washington completed his journey and delivered the letter. He had traveled 900 miles, in the winter, about half of it through wilderness, and had accomplished his mission.

Rain, Mud and a Battle - 1754

Again, George Washington was in a bad spot. He thought a large number of French and their American Indian partners might attack him, but he was prepared. His troops had built a circular fort in only five days. He had been satisfied with the stockade. There were very few open areas in the wilderness. The forest seemed to go on forever. The Great Meadows was a perfect spot for a fort. However, things were not going well the day of the battle. The French found one spot where the woods were too close to the fort. They did not come out in the open to fight, but hid in the woods. All day, they had been firing on Washington's troops. To make it worse, it rained and rained. The water and mud clogged the guns. Washington did not have enough cleaning tools. Finally, Washington surrendered.

General Braddock Makes Mistakes - 1755

Redcoats (British soldiers) had arrived in America to help defeat the French. Their fighting skills were well known. They were under the command of General Edward Braddock. But Braddock was stubborn and didn't listen to advice. Benjamin Franklin warned him that the American Indians who fought with the French were very good warriors. Braddock smiled and said that they may be good against untrained colonists, but they wouldn't be anything for his professional soldiers. Americans told Braddock he needed American Indians on his side, but he insulted the American Indians, and they didn't join him. On the day of the battle, Braddock found out he was wrong. They had almost reached the French Fort Duquesne when the battle began. The American Indians with the French were very good fighters. More British soldiers were killed. Finally, Braddock was wounded, and the army retreated. It was a terrible defeat. Braddock died four days later.

Shingas, King of the Delaware

Shingas was an important leader of his people. He wanted to make sure they had the things they needed to live - forest for hunting, rivers for fishing and land for crops. He also wanted to trade with the British and the French for items that made their lives easier, such as guns, knives, cooking pots and clothing. Although the Delaware wanted to trade, they did not want settlers taking their land. Many were still angry over being tricked out of land in the Walking Purchase. Shingas wanted to help Braddock and his British army. He had only one question for him: "Would the Delaware be allowed to live on the land with the British?" Braddock said "no." Shingas was so mad that he went and joined the French. He was an excellent warrior. He raided the Pennsylvania frontier and was feared by settlers.

A Victory for General Forbes - 1758

General Forbes was determined not to make the same mistakes Braddock did. He built a road with forts along the way to supply his army. He worked with the American Indians. Progress was slow. The last fort they built was Fort Ligonier. It was 50 miles from the French at Fort Duquesne. Although Forbes wanted to capture Fort Duquesne, it was November, and he needed to get ready for the winter. Then Washington captured an enemy soldier. He said that the French were weak. Forbes marched immediately. The French retreated and burned the fort. Forbes captured the ruins of Fort Duquesne. The next year, the British built Fort Pitt.

The Battle of Bushy Run - 1763

The American Indians were upset with the British. The British had made many promises in the Treaty of Easton. They promised not to allow settlers on American Indian land and to do away with forts after the French were defeated. The fighting with the French had ended three years before, but the British were not keeping their promises. The British were not selling them enough gunpowder and supplies to hunt for their families. All over the region, American Indians followed Ottawa Chief Pontiac's example and attacked British forts. Colonel Bouquet was sent to help Fort Pitt. A group of American Indians ambushed him, and things were going poorly. But Bouquet had a clever plan. He tricked the American Indians and forced them to retreat. When the British changed their harsh trading rules, Chief Pontiac and the other chiefs surrendered.

title: How can I be an active reader?
text:
To get the most out of what you read, you should be an active reader.

Be Involved

When you are an active reader, you are involved because you think about and respond to what you read. Here are some strategies to use for becoming an active reader.

Ask Questions

Ask yourself questions as you read. What kinds of questions should you ask? Well, any question that comes to mind as you are reading is a good question. But some questions you could ask follow:

How do I feel about what I am reading?

Do the characters' actions make sense to me?

Do the characters remind me of any people I know?

Do I understand the events that are happening?

Could similar things happen to me?

What do I hope will happen next?

What would I most like to ask this author?

Read As a Group

Sometimes, you can get a better idea of what to think about a book after talking to someone else about it. Discussion about books can make your reading more interesting because different people have different ideas about the same text. Follow these steps and try forming some discussion groups in your class.

Assemble a small group of interested readers. Include enough people to make the discussion interesting, but not so many that the group is hard to manage.

Pick a book that you all want to read.

Allow time for everyone to read it.

Write down a list of questions and ideas before the meeting.

Meet to discuss your reactions to the book. Before beginning, pick someone to lead the discussion.

Connect With the Words

Make a connection with what you read, even if you are reading about someone very different from you. Try putting yourself in different characters' shoes so that you will understand why they act the way they do. You can also make a connection with what you read by forming opinions about it.

Respond to Your Text

Keep a response journal where you can write your feelings, ideas, questions, reactions and thoughts about what you read. You can also note facts, copy quotations you liked or talk about passages that you thought were well written.

Try these active reading strategies, and you will get the most out of what you read.

title: Susquehanna Valley
text: Kids love caves. Penn's Cave has been attracting visitors for centuries, since the Seneca Indians discovered it. Another word for caving is spelunking. The cave we're talking about here doesn't take much spelunking, however. All you have to do is climb aboard a motorboat and go deep into this water-filled cave. For an hour, you'll see amazing stalactites and stalagmites. No matter what the temperature is outside, it's always 52 degrees inside the cave, so bring a jacket. Outside the cave, you'll have fun touring 1,000 acres of an operating farm (Feed the animals!) and a wildlife sanctuary (Don't feed the animals!). You'll see elk, mountain lions, deer, wolves and mustangs. Professional guides take you through the park in four-wheel-drive vehicles, pointing out animals and telling about their habits. East of Penn's Cave, you'll find Woodward Cave and Campground, one of the largest caverns in Pennsylvania. Keep going east, and you'll drive right up to Knoebels Amusement Park and Campground. You'll find more than 50 rides (including five giant water slides), a giant swimming pool and a roller coaster that has been rated in the "top 10" of the world! Ask the folks if you can spend the night in campsites, log cabins or tepees. What fun!

title: Why does Pennsylvania have so many caves?
text: Hundreds of millions of years ago, shallow seas existed where Pennsylvania is now. Millions of tiny marine animals lived their lives and shed their shells underwater. The shells formed limestone. As the landmasses moved and mashed together - ever so slowly - the limestone washed away as the water covering the land rolled out to sea. As the limestone washed away, many nooks and crannies were formed. And those underground rooms and hallways are what we call caves.

title: Muskrat
text:
Take a trip to Rose Valley Lake in the central portion of Lycoming County. The best way to encounter wildlife is by row boat or canoe. Another way is to quietly walk the shoreline. You'll see great blue herons, snapping turtles, red-winged blackbirds and many ... muskrats!

This rat-like rodent has a long tail, short ears and thick body. In other words, it's not very attractive. Its front feet are small, the hind feet are long, and the toes are partly webbed. These furry critters average 24 inches in length. The muskrat is similar to the beaver in habits. It builds stick houses in marshes and swamps. Breeding months are March and April, and only a month later, litters of up to 6 to 7 kits are born. As many as five litters are born each year. The muskrat eats a lot of corn in farming areas. Here at the lake, they'll eat roots, freshwater mussels, leaves and cattail. The mink and the hawk are the worst enemies of the muskrat. Ask your teacher, your parents or your grandparents to sing you a few bars of "Muskrat Love" - a very popular song from the 1970s by Captain and Tennille.

title: Let's Write
text: Can you remember your first day of school? If you can’t, ask your mom or dad if either of them remember that first time they sent you off. Were you scared? Excited? Nervous? What was your favorite thing about school? The library? Snack time? Your teacher?

title: Colonial Agriculture
text:
People grew crops in the Colonies to sustain their families and to sell to other New England Colonies. They also grew crops to sell to England. Study the map and then answer the following questions. Color the map when you are done.

1. What is the only crop that Connecticut and Rhode Island produced?

2. In which region was fishing a major industry?

3. What did New Jersey contribute?

4. Which three Colonies were the only ones that produced rice and indigo?

5. Which product did Virginia produce?

6. Tobacco was grown in which three Colonies?

7. What two things were produced in Maine? What is the third thing to come from Maine?

8. If you were a colonist, in which area would you choose to live? What job would you most likely find there?

title: From Printer to “Mr. America”
text:
A Man for All Seasons and Reasons

Little Ben lived in the town of Boston. When he was 5 years old, he could read; at 7, he could write. When Ben was 10 years old, he helped his father, who was a candle maker. He didn't like candle making, so he went to work for his brother James in a printing shop. He liked the work, but he and James didn't get along very well. When he was 17 years old, he decided to run away to Philadelphia.

When Ben reached the city, he was very tired and hungry. At a bakery, he asked for three pennies' worth of bread. To Ben's surprise, the baker gave him three big, puffy rolls!

Ben walked up the street with one roll under each arm and eating the third. Ben's clothes were untidy from his long journey. His pockets were stuffed with shirts and stockings. He was a funny sight. A girl standing in a doorway laughed at him, but Ben didn't care.

Ben found a printer who needed a helper. Some years later, Ben became the owner of the little printing shop. When he was 24 years old, he married Deborah Read, the girl who'd laughed at him seven years earlier in the street. Ben printed a newspaper and some books, and before long he had a fine business.

So began the long and very unusual career of the now-famous Benjamin Franklin. He is known as a printer, musician, inventor, statesman (involved in politics), philosopher (person who studies philosophy or wisdom), writer, scientist (someone who studies science) and economist. Who else have you ever read about in the history of this country who could wear the title "Mr. America" as well as Pennsylvania's own Benjamin Franklin?

title: The Heart of the Matter
text:
Samuel Vaughan Merrick and William H. Keating founded the Franklin Institute in Philadelphia in 1824. In January 1934, the Franklin Institute Science Museum was opened to the public.
