In 1933, Samuel S. Fels donated the money to build the Fels Planetarium. It has become a wonderful place for visitors to experience hand-on science. Through the years, the institute gained many different and exciting things, including the Mandell Center, the Tuttleman Omniverse Theater and the Musser Theater, which opened in May 1990. The theaters show great interactive videos that help you learn about science in a way different from watching a regular television or movie screen. New exhibits, films and interactive presentations have helped keep the institute going by making science and technology fun.

One of the most popular exhibits at the Franklin Institute is called "The Giant Heart." It is a huge model of a human heart. In fact, it is so large that visitors can walk through it, learning exactly how a real human heart works. This display was originally opened in 1954 as a temporary exhibit, but it was so popular that it became a permanent part of the Franklin Institute. It was recently remodeled with the latest technology, making the heart even more life-like than before. It is still one of the favorite exhibits at the museum.

For more than 175 years, the museum has been a very popular place and is continuing to offer fun and exciting ways to look at science and technology. If Benjamin Franklin were alive today, he would probably be very proud of what the Institute is and where it is headed.

title: How Can I Be a Critical Reader?
text:
Critical readers carefully examine what they read so that they can make informed decisions about it. They might decide if they should believe what they read or if they like what they read.

Examine What You Read

There are many ways to be a critical reader, but they all involve looking at the text and thinking about what you read. Here are some strategies for being a critical reader.

Learn to Separate Fact from Opinion

Writers sometimes present their opinions as facts, so it is important to be able to tell the difference between facts and opinions. How do you tell a fact from an opinion? A fact is a statement that can be proven true. An opinion cannot be proven true in a way that everyone will agree on because it is a belief or judgment. Here are some questions you can ask to help you figure out if something is fact or opinion:

- Can this be proven?

- Is it generally agreed upon?

- Could someone disagree with this?

- Is this supported by facts or opinions?

Watch for Faulty Logic

Make sure the writer's logic makes sense. Do the writer's arguments make sense? Are they supported by evidence? Here is some faulty logic to watch out for:

- Either/Or Thinking - When a writer says that there are only two ways to think about a situation, he or she may be engaging in faulty logic. You need to think, "Are there more ways to think about this?" What is faulty about this statement: "No one should drive, or we will have too much pollution."

- Faulty Cause and Effect - When a writer claims that one event leads to another, but doesn't show any clear connection between the two, then you are reading faulty cause and effect. What is faulty about this statement: "He passed the test because he ate beans."

- Overgeneralization - When the writer makes a statement that goes beyond what the evidence supports, he or she may be engaging in overgeneralization. Use of too many generalizing words such as "all," "always," "must," "never" and "none" could be a sign of overgeneralization. What is faulty about this statement: "My cat likes water, so all cats like water."

Identify the Writer's Point of View

The point of view is the set of personal opinions that influence the way the author writes about a subject. You need to be able to recognize the writer's point of view to figure out how it might have affected the writing.

- Take note of sources. Are all the sources from one side of the issue or are they balanced over many sides of the issue?

- Ask what the writer is trying to say. How is this point of view supported? Do you agree with it? Why or why not?

Critical reading can be tough, but if you practice these strategies, you'll be on your way!

title: Philadelphia’s Ben Franklin
text:
Benjamin Franklin loved Philadelphia, and Philadelphia loved Ben. It was the finest city in the Colonies. Ben thought of ways to make it an even better place to live. This week, we'll take a look at some of the amazing talents of this remarkable man.

Ben Franklin - Family Man

In 1730, Benjamin Franklin married Deborah Read. Ben already had a young son named William, and Deborah had been divorced from her first husband, so they were happy to find each other to start a family. Ben and Deborah settled in Philadelphia where Ben ran his print shop and Deborah opened up a general store out front. She stayed busy helping with the family's income. Ben was also busy and took frequent trips to England where he stayed for months at a time. He wanted Deborah to join him on these long journeys, but she hated ocean travel and chose to stay home. So, Ben took William with him, and the two grew very close. In the years that followed, Ben and Deborah welcomed two new children into the family, a son named Francis (they liked to call him "Franky") and a daughter named Sarah (nicknamed "Sally").

Sadness struck the family when little Francis caught smallpox and died at age 4 in 1736. The family struggled through that tragedy and continued on. And then tragedy struck again several decades later. Ben was in England in 1774 when Deborah suffered a stroke and died.

William was a full-grown man by then. He had been schooled in England and liked it there. When the Revolutionary War started, William was in England and chose to support the British. This hurt his father deeply and it ruined their relationship. When Ben died, he willed most of his estate to his surviving daughter, Sarah.

Benjamin Franklin's Accomplishments

Franklin Stove

A practical invention, manufactured in 1742, was his Franklin Stove. It was a cast-iron fireplace that gave much more heat for the same amount of fuel. They're still used today as great energy savers.

Electricity

By the time Franklin was 40 years old, in 1746, he was a rich and successful printer and businessman in Philadelphia. At that time, he came to fame the world over for his discoveries in electricity. He invented the lightning rod.

Bifocals

At the age of 70, Ben became annoyed at having to carry two sets of eye glasses, so he invented bifocals. These glasses had lenses with separate areas to correct near and far vision. Unfortunately, they cost $100, which was about 15 months' pay for a soldier in Washington's army.

Printing, Writing and Language Talents

Franklin was a great publisher and writer. He published the Pennsylvania Gazette, the Saturday Evening Post and the very popular "Poor Richard's Almanack." He also taught himself French, Spanish and Italian!

Fire Company

Franklin organized the first volunteer fire company in America. His interests in this area led him to organize the first fire-insurance company as well.

Medical Talents

Ben was one of the first people to realize that a cold can be passed from one person to another. He believed in fresh air and proper ventilation. Along with Dr. Thomas Bond, he started the first hospital in the province of Pennsylvania. It still stands at Eighth and Spruce streets in Philadelphia and is now more than 200 years old!

Armonica

No, there's no "H" missing from this word! Among Franklin's many talents was the invention of this unusual instrument. It was made from 24 glass bowls mounted on a rod.

title: Sarah Josepha Hale: “Mother of Thanksgiving”
text:
Did you know that it was a Pennsylvanian who started the tradition of Thanksgiving Day? It would not be the great American holiday it is if not for a determined editor in Philadelphia who believed that our nation was in desperate need of a special day set aside to give thanks.

Mrs. Sarah Josepha Hale was the publisher of a women's magazine called Godey's Lady's Book. In this magazine, she featured advice on how to stuff turkeys and bake mince pies with pictures of family reunions. She wrote letters to the governors of every state and territory urging them to set aside a special day as Thanksgiving Day.

Finally, in the months of the Civil War, President Lincoln responded to personal letters from Mrs. Hale by proclaiming a national day of thanks. The fourth Thursday in November was eventually proclaimed as a National Day of Thanksgiving.

Now you know of another blessing to give thanks for this month - our own Pennsylvanian Sarah Josepha Hale!

Have a happy holiday!

title: ‘Poor Richard’s Almanack’
text:
"Early to bed, early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy and wise." How many times have you heard this saying? You have probably heard it many times when you have wanted to stay up late and your parents would not let you. Well, these famous words came from a man who called himself Richard Saunders. What? You have never heard of him? Maybe it is because you know him better as Benjamin Franklin.

This book is full of good advice including, "There are no gains without pains" (sacrifice and work hard), "Have you something to do tomorrow? Do it today" (don't procrastinate) and "'Tis hard but glorious to be poor and honest" (humility, honesty).

Benjamin Franklin first wrote "Poor Richard's Almanack" in 1732. He wrote about many things that he believed could help people. These ideas still apply today, and if we follow them, we can be better people and lead happier lives.

title: Rose Lady of Alden House
text:
When Gloria Adams moved into the Alden House on Main Street in Lititz, north of Lancaster, in 1989, she became aware of a very peculiar problem. A very heavy scent of roses was present in one particular room. "When I cleaned the room, the rose scent left, but when I came back, there it was again. This went on for several months, so I felt that whoever or whatever the scent was coming from was quite comfortable, and it certainly brought warmth to the room!"

The aroma faded in and out and returned in full strength, Gloria said, when she felt most stressed, angered or ill. "It seemed to be concerned for me. There was never any ghost to actually see, but always some sort of presence." The owner decided to name this unseen force the "Rose Lady."

Eventually, in the early 1990s, what had begun as the innocent scent of roses and the invention of the name “Rose Lady” had become a more worrisome power that, Gloria felt, must be dealt with. "There were times when lights would go on unexpectedly, showers would run, and curtains would draw back for no reason," she explained.

Gloria finally decided to ask the minister next door to come over and pray for the house. He came and, starting upstairs, anointed surfaces and cast out whatever mischievous spirits were there. He repeated his blessings in every room all the way to the basement.

Is the Rose Lady still in residence at Alden House? Gloria says that things have been pretty quiet since she combined her own faith with the blessings bestowed by the minister. Still, she keeps her ears open for any unexplained sounds and her nose ready should the Rose Lady make another fragrant visit.

title: How did George Washington meet Benjamin Franklin?
text:
It was March 1755. Benjamin Franklin was very involved with the training of General Braddock's redcoats at their camp in Virginia. One day as Franklin was coming out of Braddock's headquarters, he came face to face with a tall, broad-shouldered young Virginian dressed like a Colonial officer. The two men stopped and looked at each other. One was 49, short and stocky; the other was 24, tall and slender. Smiles lit up the faces of both:

"Mr. Benjamin Franklin, I believe. I am honored, sir!"

"Colonel George Washington. I am delighted, sir!"

It was the first, but not the last, meeting of these two men who did so much, only a few years later, to turn our scattered Colonies into a free and united nation.

title: Passenger Pigeon
text: At one time, passenger pigeons darkened the skies across central North America like a living tide, in numbers that stagger the imagination. There were more of this species of bird than all other birds combined! One flock of about 4 billion traveled over Ontario, Canada, in 1866. Measuring 1 mile wide and 300 miles long, the flock passed overhead for 14 hours. And the birds flew 60 miles per hour! Each flock ate 8.7 million bushels of acorns and beechnuts in just one day! Slaughter of the birds took place daily, and over time the great forests of beech, oak and hickory that fed these flocks were replaced with farmland and towns. Pigeon populations were sent into a fatal tailspin. They ran out of food! Their biggest enemy was mankind, however. Thousands of passenger pigeons were hunted for their excellent meat. Most, however, were shot for sport. The last known passenger pigeon in Pennsylvania was shot in 1902. The very last of the species, Martha, died in the Cincinnati Zoo on Sept. 1, 1914 at 1 p.m. This is possibly the only instance in history when we know the exact moment a species became extinct. It took only 50 years for humans to exterminate the passenger pigeon.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you have a paper route. (Maybe you do.) Every January, your boss gives you a statement of your earnings. You have to pay taxes on the money you earned from the newspaper company. The money you send to the government pays for the same things your parents pay taxes for, too. But your parents are old enough to vote, and you aren’t! Do you think that this is an example of taxation without representation? Talk to your parents and teacher about it. Tell us what you think.

title: Let’s Have a Tea Party!
text:
The citizens of the Colonies were angry. King George of England and his Parliament were trying to pass a new tax, which the colonists had been resisting for months. Parliament refused to allow our representatives to be present when it made laws that governed us. The tax on tea hurt the most—tea was the colonists' favorite beverage. The time was ripe to do something drastic!

Britain's East India Tea Company was almost bankrupt (completely out of money). The owners had lots of tea they couldn't sell. England wanted to help this tea company and at the same time tax the American Colonies. Parliament passed the Tea Act, which allowed the tea company to sell its product directly to the Colonies. Colonists were not allowed to purchase any tea that didn't have the British Parliament seal on the package. The colonists loved their tea, but they didn't like being forced to buy only British tea!

Samuel Adams and his Sons of Liberty proclaimed the tea importers to be "enemies of America" and vowed to stop them. Colonial women organized and refused to buy English tea. They drank coffee instead.

When tea ships arrived in Boston Harbor, the colonists demanded that they turn around and go right back to England! The captains refused. It was time for the Sons of Liberty to take action!

On Dec. 16, 1773, that loyal group of patriots disguised themselves as a local tribe of Mohawks. They stealthily boarded the three tea ships. Very quietly, they dumped hundreds of chests of tea into the Boston Harbor!

But Boston wasn't the only place to react against the tax (money citizens pay to their government) on tea. Pennsylvanians were angry, too. On Christmas Day, nine days after the Boston Tea Party, the British ship Polly sailed into the harbor at Chester, Pennsylvania. Eight thousand people went to the state house in Philadelphia to protest. The ship had to sail back to England with its cargo still intact. As the news spread through the Colonies, similar incidents took place in New York and Charleston.

This was the first big act against "Mother England" that would lead to the American Revolution. (A revolution is when people forcefully throw off an existing government.) The Colonies were about to become their own country!

title: Jefferson Smiles on New Nickel
text:
Since 1938, the image of Thomas Jefferson has appeared on the U.S. nickel. Until 2004, Jefferson's profile, or a side-view of his face, appeared on one side of the nickel and a picture of Monticello, Jefferson's home, appeared on the other. In 2004, to celebrate the Louisiana Purchase and the Lewis and Clark expedition, the United States Mint issued two new nickels, each with pictures of Thomas Jefferson on the fronts and a keel boat a buffalo or a view of the Pacific Ocean on the backs. On Jan. 12, 2006, the mint issued the last of the new Jefferson nickels, this one with an unusual twist. Jefferson is facing forward, with a smile on his face. This is the first time that a forward-facing image of a president has ever been used on a U.S. coin, and also the first time that a president has been shown smiling. The back of the new nickel once again shows the president's home, Monticello.

The designers of the coin chose to have President Jefferson looking forward to show that he was a president who looked toward the future of this great nation. He knew that our country would need room to grow, so he made the Louisiana Purchase and sent Lewis and Clark to explore this new region for those who were brave enough to help settle it. Jamie Franki, the artist who drew the smiling picture of Jefferson, says, "It isn't a silly smile or a smirk, but a sense of optimism that I was trying to convey with the expression." His drawing was chosen out of 147 entries.

The new nickel also shows the phrase, "In God We Trust," in the upper right-hand region of the nickel and the word, "Liberty," written in Jefferson's own handwriting, above the date in the lower right-hand region. The image of Monticello on the back of the nickel has also been made clearer and more detailed.

The 2006 design is expected to be around for a long time, as there are no plans for any future changes in the nickel.

title: What is a Tax?
text:
The colonists were really angry about the British taxes. All this talk about taxes might make you wonder … what IS a tax? Are all taxes bad or unfair? Why were the colonists so upset about them?

A tax is money paid to the government. Sometimes it is an extra amount of money that is added to the cost of something you buy. Most workers are taxed on the money they earn. The government collects the extra money and uses it to pay for things that everyone uses. For example, today Pennsylvania's government collects taxes and then uses the money to pay for roads, parks and schools. These are things that everyone in the state uses, so it is fair that everyone pays a tax to the government to build them. As you can see, not all taxes are unfair or bad. In fact, they are useful.

In Colonial times, the British believed it was fair to tax the colonists because Great Britain was spending money to protect all of the colonies. The king could not understand why the colonists were so angry about the taxes. He would not listen to their complaints about them.

In America today, if people think a tax is too high or unfair, they can vote against the taxes. Voters have a say in how much tax they pay. They also have a say in how the tax money is spent.

But the colonists did not get a say in the British taxes, or how those taxes were spent. It was taxation without representation. That means colonists were being taxed without having any say in the matter. That is what made those taxes unfair.

title: The Shot Heard ‘Round the World!
text:
It is September 1774. The French and Indian War has ended. The 13 American colonies are at peace again. Some of the "redcoats" have gone back to England. Some are still stationed in Philadelphia. Pennsylvania has been a Colony for around 93 years.

March 1775

The French and Indian War cost the British government a lot of money! After all, the government bought uniforms and food, paid salaries and transported all those soldiers from England to our Colonies.

Who is the king, and what does he want us to do about his big bills?

His name is King George III, and he wants to start a tax system here. Naturally, we have to pay for the goods we use and the food we eat. But the king has bills to pay for the war he started, and he wants to tax us to pay his bills!

So, let's pay taxes. Taxes are used to keep our cities, counties, states and the U.S. governments going, aren't they?

Not the way King George wants to do it! Parliament (Great Britain's ruling body) is refusing to let our colonists have representatives sit with them who could vote fairly for the colonists in these tax matters.

What does the king want to tax?

He's taxing sugar, printed materials, tea, lead, paint and other things we can't produce ourselves. And, hey, we're still housing and feeding the redcoats who still live in Philadelphia!

What are we going to do about it?

We're pretty upset. The people of Philadelphia have agreed not to buy any more goods from England until Parliament ends this taxation without representation! You should see us! We're wearing our old clothes, and we've even stopped drinking tea!

Do you think this will lead to war?

We're sure of it! The tea parties caused Parliament to pass a series of laws we're calling the Intolerable Acts to punish us. These acts have closed the Boston Harbor. King George sent a military commander to rule in place of our Colonial governor! More troops are on the way. The people of Boston had to close down their shops and businesses and are literally starving. Pennsylvania and other Colonies are sending food to them. The Intolerable Acts have really united us.

Have you heard any rumors about organizing an army?

Yep! We're gathering guns and ammunition. We've stored them in the towns of Lexington and Concord. Sam Adams has organized the minutemen (Colonial citizen soldiers). These are groups of men and boys who are drilling to become soldiers. They're trained to leave their farms or shops and, in a "minute," take up arms against England. We'll have to wait and see what happens …

John Dickinson—Man of Peace

John Dickinson of Pennsylvania was a gifted writer. His nickname was "Penman of the Revolution." He wrote many letters to the English king to try to settle the question of independence peacefully. This was prior to the Boston Tea Party. His essays were called "Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania to the Inhabitants of the British Colonies." They were printed and read by thousands of colonists and sent to King George III. Dickinson's pleas to the king were rejected.

Pennsylvania didn't want war. Remember, this Colony was founded on religious freedom by people who didn't believe in killing. Dickinson himself was a Quaker. Later, Dickinson was assigned by Congress to write the "Articles of Confederation and Perpetual Union."

April 1775

We're at war again! What happened?

When British General Thomas Gage got the news of the guns and ammunition being stored in Concord, he sent a detachment of soldiers to seize them and capture the American leaders Sam Adams and John Hancock, who were in Lexington. When we learned that the British were marching toward Lexington, our famous silversmith, Paul Revere, rode through the night and warned Sam Adams and John Hancock that the British were coming! Our two leaders fled Lexington just in time!

Thank goodness! Then what?

As the church bells tolled, the town's minutemen gathered on Lexington's village green. About 75 minutemen were waiting for the British when they arrived at Lexington Green at dawn on April 19, 1775. British Major John Pitcairn ordered them to put down their guns. We were terribly outnumbered. Our men and boys began to run for home. Then someone fired a shot. No one knows from which side the shot came. The British began firing on the minutemen, killing eight and wounding 10. Wow!

Because this first shot of the American Revolution changed so many lives and so many boundaries over the next few years, it's often referred to as "the shot heard 'round the world."

First Continental Congress Meets in Philadelphia

Sam Adams of Massachusetts and Ben Franklin of Pennsylvania suggested that representatives (people who voice the concerns of a larger group) from all the Colonies meet to discuss the troubles with Britain. It was decided that this Congress of Colonial leaders (group representing the colonies) would meet in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The First Continental Congress opened in Philadelphia's Carpenters' Hall on Sept. 5, 1774. From that day on, Pennsylvania played a leading role in the creation of the United States.

title: Our Flag
text:
Respect for the American Flag

Showing respect for our flag is one way to show our loyalty to the United States, and there are laws about how we should display and honor the American flag. The laws are called the Flag Code.

When you say the Pledge of Allegiance, stand up straight, place your right hand over your heart and face the flag. If you are wearing a hat, take it off before you say the pledge. The flag should never touch the ground or anything else that is under it, and it should not be used in any way that would damage the flag or get it dirty. No company or business may use the flag as an advertisement in any way. Flying the flag upside down is a signal of extreme distress and should only be flown that way in an emergency. When a flag becomes old and worn, it should be burned. Many veterans' organizations will burn old flags as a service to citizens in their community.

The law says that schools should display the American flag on all school days. Flags can only be flown after dark if the flag is lighted in a way that allows it to be seen clearly. Otherwise, it should be put up and taken down each day. No other flag may be placed above the American flag. The union (the blue field with the 50 stars) should be at the top, nearest the flagpole. Anyone who is present when a flag is being raised or lowered should remove his or her hat and stand up straight with hand on heart. After you take down the flag, there is a special way to fold it into a triangle, with only the stars showing.

That may seem like a lot of rules, but it's only part of the Flag Code.

What Does the Pledge of Allegiance Mean?

You've probably said the Pledge of Allegiance hundreds of times. Have you ever stopped to think about what it means? Sometimes, it's easy to take for granted things like the Pledge that are so familiar to us. We forget how important they really are.

Let's start at the beginning. "I pledge allegiance to the flag of the United States of America …" A pledge is a promise. Allegiance is another word for loyalty. So, when you recite the Pledge of Allegiance, you are promising to be loyal to the flag of the United States of America.

You are also promising to be loyal to the United States, when you say, "… and to the republic for which it stands …" A president elected by the citizens leads our country. That makes it a republic. "… one nation under God, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all." These words tell us that America is one country united under God and that we cannot be divided. We are indivisible. We also believe in freedom and fairness for everyone. That's one thing that makes America such a great place to live.

Next time you recite the Pledge of Allegiance, think about the words as you say them. Say those words as if you really mean them. They're very powerful and important words.

title: Philadelphia/Lehigh Valley
text:
Welcome to the region of Pennsylvania that is the most historical part of the state! Philadelphia is the town of William Penn and the city of Ben Franklin. Independence National Historical Park is one of the most historical places in the United States and the home of the famous Liberty Bell. You'll have a great time at the Mummer's Museum, too. See how costumes are made and practice your "Mummer's Strut." Kids especially love the Betsy Ross House and the dinosaurs at the Academy of Natural Sciences. Out in the Lehigh Valley, be sure to visit the Childventure Museum in Fort Washington, where you can dress up in costumes in the Storybook Room. Visit Dorney Park & Wildwater Kingdom near Allentown. Ride one of the world's longest water slides. And Crystal Cave between Allentown and Reading will give you a thrill. A real kid-friendly zoo, Elmwood Park Zoo in Norristown, has a duck pond, a petting zoo, cougars, deer and bison, and it's free!

Whew! These are only a few of the things to do and see in this region. Maybe your folks will give you a whole summer to take it all in!

title: What happened to the Liberty Bell during the Revolutionary War?
text: During the American Revolution, while British soldiers were occupying the town of Philadelphia, people took the incredibly heavy Liberty Bell to Allentown, Pennsylvania. Once there, they hid the bell under the floorboards of a church. What were the American people worried about enough to hide the bell? They did not want the British soldiers to take the bell and melt it down for ammunition.

title: Great Dane
text:
This week's wildlife is not all that "wild." The next time you visit the governor's reception room in Harrisburg, look for a portrait of William Penn with his Great Dane. The Great Dane is now a popular pet here. It was a hunting and working dog in frontier Pennsylvania. This dog was developed in Germany to hunt wild boars. It didn't originate from Denmark, but its name did. The name is a translation of an old French name, grand Danois, which means "big Danish." Great Danes make good family dogs, but require a lot of companionship and attention.

The choice of the Pennsylvania Official State Dog is unusual for the way it was approved in the commonwealth's House of Representatives. On Aug. 15, 1965, the speaker of the House called for a voice vote to approve the Great Dane. His request was met with yips, growls and barks from every part of the chamber! The speaker rapped his gavel and, with a smile, confirmed that "the 'arfs' have it." The "barking dog vote" then became a nice little note in the official history of Pennsylvania legislature.

title: How do I use a Thesaurus?
text:
Do you use many of the same words over and over when writing? Are you getting bored with those same words? It’s time you learned to use a thesaurus!

Search for Synonyms

The word “thesaurus” almost looks like a name for a dinosaur, doesn’t it? It’s actually a book (it can be found online as well). This book or website provides synonyms (words similar in meaning) for common words. Using a thesaurus is a great way to broaden your vocabulary with more interesting words.

A thesaurus is usually alphabetical. Some are similar to dictionaries because they give you the part of speech, definition and sample sentences for words. Sometimes a thesaurus will give you directions to look up other entries. Here’s what you’ll find in a typical thesaurus.

Entry Word...........................................The word you look up to find synonyms
Part-of-Speech Label.........................Tells you if the word is a noun, verb, adjective, etc.
Definition...............................................Tells you what the entry word means
Example Sentence...............................Shows you how the entry word might be used in a sentence.
Synonyms...............................................Words whose meanings are the same as or similar to the entry word
Antonyms...............................................Words whose meanings are the opposite of the entry word

Try It!

Look up the word “grow” in a thesaurus. Write all the synonyms here.

Look up each synonym for “grow” in the dictionary. Are the definitions for these words exactly the same as the definition for “grow”? How are they different? Use the lines below to write some of the definitions and discuss how they are different.

title: Let's Write
text: You are the boss of all schools, and you’re going to write a “Schools Ordinance” for all kids to follow. Write an essay explaining some freedoms you’d like to have and why.

title: We Declare Our Independence!
text:
"Baby" Uncle Sam is about to be born.

You may wonder why we read and write so much about the history of the United States during this time, when the rest of the year we talk about the history of Pennsylvania. There are two reasons. First, if the 13 colonies had not won independence (freedom from outside rule), there would be no commonwealth of Pennsylvania.

The second reason we study U.S. history at this time is that the most important events in the history of our nation took place right here in Philadelphia! Wow! That gives more meaning to Pennsylvania's nickname: The Keystone State. We were key (very important) in breaking away from England and then forming a whole new country.

The birth of our nation was full of labor pains, however. Thomas Jefferson was a good young man. He knew he was writing an important document. There are many who believe that the Declaration of Independence was inspired by God.

In the original declaration (strong statement), Jefferson stated that England made slaves of black people from Africa. This was not right, he wrote. All the Colonies except South Carolina and Georgia were against slavery. The declaration stated, "all men are equal." Weren't slaves equal? There were many debates. Sadly, Jefferson was forced to cross out words that offended the slave-owning colonies. On the independence issue, all the Colonies but New York voted for freedom from England. New York agreed at a later date.

This famous document was signed on July 4, 1776, by the first two people. (The rest of the Founding Fathers signed the Declaration of Independence in August.) It was read to Pennsylvanians and many others from the steps of the state house in Philadelphia at noon on July 8. The Liberty Bell and many church bells rang their big and little clappers in jubilation!

A new country was about to be born.

title: Signing Your “John Hancock”
text:
Have you ever heard the expression, Sign your John Hancock"? It means sign your name, nice and big! That saying comes from the signing of the Declaration of Independence. You see, there really was a man named John Hancock! Here is how a "John Hancock" became the nickname for a signature.

At the Second Continental Congress in 1776, Thomas Jefferson presented the Declaration of Independence for all of the representatives to read and approve. After it was approved, all of the representatives signed it at the bottom.

Signing the Declaration of Independence was serious. It meant you were declaring yourself to be an enemy of Great Britain. There was a reward offered for arresting someone signing the Declaration of Independence. The British troops could arrest you and might even kill you for signing it! Obviously, the signers were very brave.

The first person to sign the Declaration of Independence was John Hancock. Did he sign it in tiny letters or over in a corner somewhere? No! He signed his name with bold, strong writing and even wrote a flourish, or decoration, under his name. In fact, his name is bigger than all the others. As he signed, he said, "The British ministry can read that name without spectacles; let them double their reward." By his words and actions, John Hancock was telling the world that he was not afraid to stand up for America's freedom.

And ever since then, a signature has been nicknamed a "John Hancock."

title: Pennsylvania Enters War for Independence
text:
The first shots of the American Revolution were fired in April 1775. The first real battle in this war fought on Pennsylvania soil, however, was at Brandywine in September 1777—more than two years after the killing of the minutemen in Lexington. The colonists here were peace-loving, religious people. It was hard for many of them to fight, kill and die for any reason. But they believed in freedom, and many died defending it.

Victories At Trenton and Princeton

On Christmas Day, Washington Crossed the Delaware River and Captured Hessian Troops.

Washington's Continental army camped on the Pennsylvania side of the Delaware River. They did not plan to stay long. On Christmas night, Dec. 25, 1776, Washington ordered his half-frozen men into boats. Blood appeared on the snow where the shoeless men stepped. The boats crossed the ice-packed Delaware River in the dead of night. Not a sound was heard as the American forces disembarked on the New Jersey side of the river. The Hessian troops had celebrated Christmas and were sleeping in their beds when they heard the sound of musket fire. The American army had them surrounded.

Later in the day, Washington's small army took 900 prisoners. Many of the Hessians joined the American army rather than spend their days in jail. A few days later Washington's men marched quietly into Princeton, a neighboring city. After a short fight against General Cornwallis, Princeton was also under American control.

Victory at Saratoga

French Join Continental Army

The British had a plan to quickly defeat the colonists. They planned to drive a wedge from Canada down through New York and cut off New England from the Southern colonies. General Burgoyne said, "We will divide and conquer." But the British plan did not work out. Burgoyne's troops were weak from dragging supply wagons and cannons through the rough forested country. They ran out of food.

Washington's army moved north and met them at Saratoga, New York. Daniel Morgan's riflemen made a signal like a turkey gobble each time they attacked with their rifles. They stayed hidden behind the cover of trees. The American forces surrounded the British and Burgoyne surrendered. Saratoga was an important victory. Americans took about 4,000 to 5,000 British prisoners and lots of guns and ammunition. The most important outcome was that the American victory helped persuade the French to join the American cause.

Washington's Ragged Army Suffers at Valley Forge

While the British soldiers enjoyed warm houses and good food in Philadelphia, the small American army made camp at Valley Forge, only 20 miles away. It was bitter cold that winter and the snow was deep. Washington's army was in rags. His men were sick and hungry. Food and shoes were scarce. Many soldiers lost hope and deserted Washington. Martha Washington visited the camp and wore thorns in her clothing to symbolize her feelings of sorrow for the suffering troops. General Washington never gave up. He made the men drill harder than ever. Colonel Friedrich von Steuben, a veteran soldier of the German army, helped teach the men how to be good, efficient soldiers. He taught Washington's men how to use bayonets properly. He was a stern taskmaster who made the soldiers drill for hours. Nevertheless, the Americans came to love him. He worked himself as hard as the men he drilled. When the terrible winter was over, a better and more determined army marched forth to fight the British.

Clark Captures Vincennes

Assures Northwest Territory for America

George Rogers Clark, a young Virginian with a force of less than 200 men, made a long and cruel wilderness march through flooded prairies and forests to capture the fortified British post at Vincennes, in the future state of Indiana. The surprised British surrendered without firing a shot. This victory gave the Americans the oldest settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains.

Clark hoped to capture other British forts in the West, but they were many miles apart, so it was necessary to make careful plans and suffer great hardships on their march from one fort to another. They tramped across the snowy plains during bitterly cold weather. Their clothes became thin and ragged, and often there was not enough food. Some men became sick and died. But those who could, moved on. In time, Clark's brave band captured many British forts. This gave the Americans the Northwest.

Cornwallis Surrenders at Yorktown

British Lay Down Their Arms

The British gave up trying to win the New England colonies and concentrated their efforts on the Southern colonies. They began having success. They took over Georgia and South Carolina. It seemed nothing could stop the British until a force of frontiersmen stopped them at King's Mountain. Cornwallis then made a mistake by taking his troops to Yorktown, which is on a peninsula near Jamestown, Virginia. There, Cornwallis hoped to get supplies and reinforcements that were coming from England by sea.

Washington saw this as the opportunity he had been waiting for. A fleet of French warships had just arrived, and they blocked the Chesapeake Bay escape route to sea. The American and French armies moved down the peninsula to cut off Cornwallis' escape by land. The British were caught in a trap. On Oct. 19, 1781, General Cornwallis surrendered. With this defeat, England was finally ready to stop fighting. After many years of suffering, the 13 colonies had finally won their independence!

title: Loyalty
text:
What would you do if a new person who was popular came to school and wanted to be your friend, but in order for this person to do that, he or she wanted you to stop being friends with your best friend? Would you dump your best friend, whom you have known for years, to be with the popular kid, or would you be loyal to your friend? If you were loyal, you would stick with the friend you knew best, even if it meant you would not be as popular.

Loyalty means being faithful to your homeland, government, a person or your duty. Loyalty is something that the colonists had to think about during the American Revolution. Would they side with the Americans, or would they help the British? Many people had to choose depending on which side they wanted to be loyal to. If people who used to be loyal to one side changed their minds and became loyal to the other side, they were called traitors.

Thankfully, many people who were involved in the American Revolution chose to be loyal to the American side, and we won our freedom. Who knows what could have happened if more people had sided with the British. The war would have been tougher and longer, and things may even be different than they are today.

title: A Famous Painting
text:
Below is a sketch of a famous painting by Arnold Friberg. Mr. Friberg painted "The Prayer at Valley Forge" for our country's 1976 bicentennial (200 years) celebration.

Mr. Friberg says that he has always admired George Washington. "At age 12, I drew what I thought was a fine picture of George Washington sitting on his white horse. . . . I then learned the American legend of his praying at Valley Forge. . . . I waited many years to picture him again, in prayer now, in the snow, dismounted from his strong horse. To prepare for this painting, I made a pilgrimage to Valley Forge in the dead of winter. In the summer, the place is filled with visitors. But now, in the snows of February, it was deserted, the wind moaning through the great trees—silent, lonely, cold. It was a cold that chilled to the bone, a cold that froze my fingers until I could no longer sketch nor even snap my camera. . . . I sought to pay tribute to the tall and heavy-burdened man who alone held our struggling nation together. For while the British grew fat and warm and well fed in Philadelphia, it was Washington who stayed with his starving and freezing Army through that dreadful winter at Valley Forge."

Thank you, Mr. Friberg, for your beautiful painting.

title: What was the Pine Creek Declaration of Independence?
text: The Scots-Irish settlers here had a deep-rooted dislike for the English government that went back to 1763 when they were forbidden to settle the back country of Pennsylvania. Some of these colonists along Pine Creek, a branch of the Susquehanna in today's Clinton County, drew up their own Declaration of Independence. By coincidence, they signed it on July 4, 1776. They had no way of knowing that Jefferson's document was being signed and approved in Philadelphia the exact same day, many miles away.

title: Eastern Box Turtle
text:
This interesting creature has a high dome and a flat shell. The shell is brown, black and yellow. The male box turtle has red eyes, and the female has yellow or brown eyes. Its legs are short, and it has webbed feet. The turtle's head is covered with scales. It doesn't have any teeth. It has a hard beak, which is used to cut through food. Box turtles are creatures of cool forest floors. You'll see them most active after a rainstorm. They spend their mornings searching for earthworms and insects. Its body temperature is 75-80 degrees.

Sometimes, box turtles can become pets. They are "loners" and don't need companions of any sort. They're not cuddly and furry like cats and dogs! If you DO keep one at home, make sure it gets plenty of light during the winter. They like to eat three times a day, and you'll make them happiest with a diet of earthworms, bananas, chicken-flavored dog food, and—ready?—cockroaches!

title: Let's Write
text: The process of building our country was a long, difficult process. Many people had to make compromises for the good of the group. As a member of a family, what kinds of compromises do you have to make for the general good of your family group? Write an essay explaining about compromises made in your family. Give examples and be specific.

title: The British are Coming
text:
Put the information in the chart onto the timeline, showing the historic events surrounding the Revolutionary War. Include the date the event occurred by the line. Study the timeline and then answer the questions below.

Paul Revere’s ride — April 18, 1775
British surrender at Battle of Yorktown — Oct. 19, 1781
British move to Concord — April 18, 1775
Declaration of Independence issued — July 4, 1776
Boston Tea Party — Dec. 16, 1773
12,000 British troops arrive — March 1775
Stamp Act passed — Oct. 1765
Clash at Lexington — April 19, 1775
Britain recognizes American independence — 1783
Townshend Acts — Nov. 1767
American cannons cause British evacuation of Boston — March 17, 1776
Boston Massacre — March 5, 1770
Battle of Bunker Hill — June 17, 1775
Patriot victory at King’s Mountain — 1780

1. How many years are there between the first event and the final event on the timeline?

2. How many years are there from when Britain surrendered to when American independence was granted?

3. When did the Boston Massacre take place?

4. How long after the Boston Massacre did the Boston Tea Party take place?

5. When did the British evacuate Boston?

title: A Capital on the Move
text:
Let's find a permanent home!

Philadelphia remained the capital of the new United States, as well as the capital of Pennsylvania, until 1800. (The previous U.S. capital for eight months was York.) In 1800, the United States built a new capital along the Potomac River that we named Washington, D.C.

By the end of the 18th century, it was time for Pennsylvanians to choose a capital for the commonwealth. In the East, cities continued to grow and prosper. Philadelphia was the largest city in the United States in 1790 with 28,522 people.

The summer of 1793 brought a terrible epidemic (serious, widespread sickness) of yellow fever. It hit Philadelphia with such force that 5,000 people died. At that time, no one knew the cause of or cure for the disease. People were naturally scared, and thousands left the city.

In 1799, the legislature moved the capital of the commonwealth to Lancaster. Rural people didn't trust the idea of a big-city capital. But the people of Pennsylvania wanted a more centrally located capital. By 1810, the capital was again moved to the small mid-state town of Harrisburg. Our commonwealth finally had a capital!

Harrisburg is on the beautiful Susquehanna River. The town was named after John Harris. Harris owned a trading post and a flat boat to ferry people across the wide river. There was no bridge at the time. The trading post became a village, and the village became the beautiful city it is today.

The capitol building is magnificent. (The capitol is the building that houses the government.) The dome of this building is copied after St. Peter's Church in Rome, Italy. There are many exhibits to visit. When your family tours the Capitol Park, be sure to take peanuts to feed the friendly squirrels!

title: Visit the Pennsylvania State Capitol
text:
Pennsylvania's state capitol building is located in Harrisburg, the state capital. Harrisburg was chosen as the capital of our great state because of its location along the Susquehanna River. Harrisburg was easy to get to, which made it a logical choice for the center of state government.

The state capitol building was dedicated by President Theodore Roosevelt in 1906. At the dedication ceremony, President Roosevelt said the Capitol was "the handsomest building I ever saw." The outside of the building is very impressive, with its towering columns and its curved dome rising 272 feet in the air. You have probably seen the outside of the Capitol, at least in pictures, but did you know that the inside is just as beautiful? The grand staircase, modeled after the one in the Paris Opera, is sure to catch your eye. Be sure to look down as you walk, or you might miss part of the tour. On the floor of the main hallway are tiles showing Pennsylvania's state symbols. There are also huge murals on the walls and life-like sculptures throughout the building.

If you have never visited the Capitol, you have missed a great adventure in history. Free tours of the amazing building are offered nearly every day of the year. If you visit during January and February, the Capitol even offers a skit for children 8-12 years old. The skit is called "Pass the Bill," and it teaches students how ideas are written into bills and passed into state laws.

One of the most interesting stops on the Capitol Tour is the Welcome Center at the Capitol. The Welcome Center is located in the East Wing of the Capitol and is full of hands-on exhibits and activities that teach about Pennsylvania government and how it works. Be sure to make the Welcome Center part of your visit.

A trip to the Pennsylvania State Capitol will take you back in time, teach you about the history of our state, and show you how our state government works. It is well worth the effort to take a tour of this great building.

title: Heroes of the Revolution
text:
There were many important Pennsylvanians who helped in the fight for independence from Great Britain. This week, let's take a look at just a few of the people whose names made history in our commonwealth.

1. Molly Pitcher

Many women helped the Continental Army during the American Revolution. They cooked, made clothing and cared for the wounded, and some even fought in battle. One famous woman was named Mary Ludwig Hays. Her nickname was "Molly." Her husband, John, from Carlisle, was camped at Valley Forge. Molly missed him very much. In spite of the bitter cold, she rode many days on horseback to reach him. He was very happy to see her.

In the spring, when the army went to battle at Monmouth, Molly was there. One terribly hot day in June, the men were dying, not only in battle, but of sun stroke. Seeing men faint from the hot sun, Mary took a pitcher and took cool drinks of water to the soldiers.

"Molly! Pitcher!" a soldier cried.

"Molly! Here! Pitcher!" cried another.

From that day on, Molly Hays was called Molly Pitcher. Her husband fell back wounded, and Molly quickly bound the wound with a piece of her petticoat. Then she took John's place at the cannon. She kept firing the cannon until the battle ended at dusk.

Molly Pitcher went down in history with a reputation as a great fighter and as a woman of compassion. There are two monuments in honor of Molly. One is in Carlisle. The other is at the Monmouth Battlefield in New Jersey.

2. 'Mad Anthony' Wayne

This colorful character did it all during the revolution: recruiting, training, fighting, finding supplies and settling a mutiny (uprising by troops against their officers). A drunken soldier, made unhappy by his commander's quick temper, is said to have given him the nickname "Mad Anthony." He was born on New Year's Day 1745 in Chester County.

Wayne rose quickly in the ranks of the Army. He fought in every battle and in all dangerous situations. He was a careful planner of his military moves, but his men claimed he fought like a madman - totally fearless. He was perhaps Pennsylvania's greatest general.

3. Haym Salomon

In time, the religious requirement for holding public office was changed from having to be a Christian, to "having a belief in one God." This meant that, for the first time, Jewish residents of Pennsylvania could hold office.

One well-known Jew in early Pennsylvania did not hold office, but he is highly thought of in our history for his financial help during the revolution and for spying for the Americans. His name was Haym Salomon (1740-1785).

Salomon was born in Poland. He came to Philadelphia on the run from the British. He was very skilled at buying and selling goods. Haym also spoke German. When he was captured by the redcoats, he was put to work as a translator between the British and the Hessian soldiers. He encouraged them to desert the British and come over to the American side. He also made huge sums of money in his business and donated it to pay government and soldiers' salaries. Because he spoke other languages, he also helped get loans from France. He died penniless, but he helped his adopted country gain its liberty.

title: The Adventures of ‘Miss Liberty’
text:
The diary of the 'belle' of Philadelphia

Oh, I've had an exciting life! And I expect to be around for thousands of years to come. I want to tell my story so that all you young students of Pennsylvania history will know how I came into being. I plan to give you entries from my diary from time to time. And please, come on down and visit me sometime!

1732 - The colonists of Pennsylvania build a fine big state house in Philadelphia. One man said, "We need a good-sized bell for our steeple."

1751 - I am ordered from England because no one in the colonies knows how to make a bell. The chairman of the assembly writes a letter to London asking for a fine bell weighing about 2,000 pounds. He wants one of his favorite Bible quotations engraved on me:

"Proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof."

- (Leviticus 25:10)

Sept. 1, 1752 - The people waited and waited for the ship carrying me - their beautiful new bell. Finally, the Hibernia arrives.

Sept. 2 - Workmen bring me up the hill today. I am very heavy. They build a wooden frame for me.

Sept. 8 - The VIPs bring their wives in silk and satin gowns. The Quakers are there in quiet gray cotton. The wives of the tradesmen come in homespun dresses with big aprons. The bell ringer raises the clapper. I ring out in full deep-throated tones. There are many smiles and cheers. Once, twice, I ring, and then . . . thud! I sound like a dented kettle! Their beautiful big bell had cracked! I'm so sad and hurting. . . .

Two men who own an iron foundry said that they would try to recast me, although they had never done such a thing before. Iron casting and bell casting are two different things, for bells have no iron in them. We are made of tin and copper. The amount of each metal determines the tone of the bell. (To cast is to form something by pouring liquid metal into a mold.)

Jan. 1753 - The two men make a mold and then break me into pieces to remelt me. Once again, I am hot and uncomfortable. The assembly men decided to add a little more copper. They thought it would strengthen me so that I would not crack again. They did not think they were adding enough to change the tone.

March 1753 - I, the great liberty bell, am finished. I am hung in the steeple, and the assembly men order a big feast on the state lawn to celebrate. But when they ring me, my voice is high and tinny and unpleasant! The iron makers will have to recast me again!

May 1754 - This time, I am hung quietly in the tower with no celebration. For 82 years, my new voice calls loudly and clearly to the good people of Philadelphia and the neighboring towns. During the early years of my life, I ring often!

Feb. 1761 - I toll in honor of King George III ascending the throne in our mother country, England. I represent freedom to America.

(Why is there still a crack in "Miss Liberty"? Watch for the answer in a future issue of Pennsylvania Studies Weekly!)

title: International Trade
text:
You have learned so much about money. You have learned how it is used. You know how it is made. It would seem that using one form of money around the world would be a good way to trade. However, many countries have their own form of currency, or money. In fact, today there are about 140 different types of currency in the world! So how do countries trade with one another if their money is so different?

To solve this problem, countries have what is called the foreign exchange market. Here, dealers in different major cities like New York, Tokyo or London trade money between countries. They decide what the exchange rate should be. In other words - how many pesos, euros, francs or baht will it take to buy one U.S. dollar? The exchange rate is based on the ideas of supply and demand. For example, if people in the United States wanted to buy goods from Mexico, they would need Mexican pesos. This would create a demand for pesos. What happens when there is a greater demand for something? That's right, the value goes up. The value of the peso would then increase.

As the value of the currency goes up, so does the price of the goods. If the price goes too high, then the demand for that product goes down. When the demand is down, the value of the currency falls. It's a real economic roller coaster!

Have you ever thought of money as being weak or strong? Well, when the U.S. dollar has a high value, it is strong. It is usually strong when there is a great demand for American-made goods. The opposite can be true, too. If the value of the dollar is low, then the American dollar is weak.

title: Honesty
text:
Do you have a hero? When you think about your hero, what things do you think about? Maybe they are brave and strong. Maybe they stood up to someone or something that tried to push them down. Maybe they risked their lives for something they believed in. But one thing that is not normally associated with a hero - even though it makes a great hero - is honesty.

One of the most important character traits for a person to have is honesty. If someone tells lies, it is hard to believe that person. If it is hard to believe people, it is hard to trust them. Would Americans have had a chance against Great Britain if the people were not able to believe in and trust their leaders? If General Washington lied to his troops or if "Mad Anthony" Wayne had been a dishonest man, the soldiers would have had a hard time deciding if they wanted to fight for these people. Today, these men are great heroes, not only for their courage and for believing in what they did, but also for their honesty, which helped them become great leaders. So the next time you think of your hero, remember that in order for that person to be such a strong influence, honesty is very important.

title: Healing with Herbs
text:
We speak of healing with herbs in the "Legends" column, because herbal medicine was legendary to nearly all former cultures. But many people use herbs for healing in today's culture. Scientists are making more discoveries every day about their healing powers. Watch the news and ask your teacher or parents if some of these ancient remedies (treatments that cure diseases) are based in truth:

1. Sassafras (root of a tree from the laurel family) tea was given to children who had measles. It made the spots come out and speeded recovery.

2. Each spring, children received a dose of sulfur and molasses "to get the blood moving."

3. For colds, a tea was made from powdered ginger, sugar and hot water. Drink, go to bed and sweat out the cold. If it's a bad cold, add red pepper.

4. For sore muscles, a poultice (a medicated paste spread on cloth) of baked onions was placed on the body to draw the soreness out.

5. Rhubarb tea was given to children regularly to keep them cleaned out and free from disease.

6. For coughs, onions were used. They were cooked with sugar, and the sticky syrup was taken as an aid to cough up the congestion.

7. To cure warts, put a dry bean on the wart, and then plant the bean. When the plant sprouts, then dies, the wart will disappear.

title: What’s the difference between a state and a commonwealth?
text: "Commonwealth" is a British word that William Penn brought with him from England. The terms "commonwealth" and "state" mean the same thing in this country. A commonwealth is a community formed for the common weal, or common good and welfare of all, in which the citizens choose their government and make their laws by majority vote. Although Pennsylvania is actually one of the 50 states, its official title is "The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania." There are four commonwealths in this country. Can you name them? Look on page 4 for the answer.

title: Copperhead Snake
text:
The copperhead snake has a copper-colored head. Its body colorings make it difficult to see among leaves as it lies ready to strike such passing prey as mice, birds or frogs. Although its bite is poisonous and very painful, it's seldom fatal to humans. Small children are the most likely to suffer from a copperhead bite. Copperheads are like many snakes - diurnal (active during the day) in the spring and fall, but nocturnal (active at night) in the summer. The copperhead is native to the eastern states. Baby snakes are born in late summer in litters of 10-15.

During the Civil War, people living in the Northern states who sided with the Southern states were called "Copperheads" because it was believed their ideas poisoned others.

title: How do I read Nonfiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring. But it really isn’t. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you will find it easier to understand—and maybe even fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will talk about the problem and solution pattern.

Problem/Solution

With this information pattern, the writer begins by stating a problem. Then the writer presents various solutions or ideas for solving the problem. This pattern is common in newspaper articles, as well as science and social studies texts. One strategy for finding the problem and solution of a nonfiction passage is to create a cluster map. A cluster map will help you remember what you have read. Begin by writing the subject of the passage in the middle of a blank sheet of paper. On one side of the subject, write “problems.” On the other side, write “solutions.” Then write details you want to remember that illustrate the problems and solutions around these bubbles. Remember to draw lines connecting the problems to the word “problems” and connecting solutions to the word “solutions.” This way, you show how the information connects.

Try It!

To the right is a passage about transportation. Read the passage. Then create a cluster map showing the problems and solutions discussed in the passage. The cluster map has been started for you.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend that your state has just decided to move the capital to a new city. Do you think your city would be a good capital? Use your imagination and come up with some great ideas as to why _____ would be the next great capital.

title: Pennsylvania Becomes a State!
text:
Founding a commonwealth (state)

The American Revolution had ended. A new baby nation had been born. Each of the original 13 colonies had the huge task of forming their own states - politically independent units of a nation having their own governments. Many eyes were turned toward Pennsylvania. Our nickname, "The Keystone State," meant we were at the heart of, or "key" to the development of this new country. But just like every newborn, this state took falls, picked itself up, dusted itself off, took baby steps and finally grew into the proud commonwealth (state) it is today.

Pennsylvania had its share of both conservatives and liberals (see below) in its early government. This state has been ruled by several state constitutions. The first one was drawn up in September 1776 by a group of liberals. Many conservative patriot leaders were bitterly against the new state constitution. There was a long four-year fight with the liberal Constitutional Party. The liberals accomplished two important tasks: They passed the act for the gradual abolition of slavery (one person owning another). (Abolition means to put an end to something officially.) They also paid the Penn family, then took control of their lands.

The conservatives were determined to rewrite the state constitution. By 1789, the two parties began to compromise (each side gave in a little). In 1790, the second state constitution was adopted, and Thomas Mifflin became our first governor. We were an official state of the United States of America!

title: Political Parties
text:
Democratic Party

Thomas Jefferson founded the Democratic Party in 1792. The Populist Party was the popular party of that time. The new party was called the "party of the common man," and its official name was the Democratic- Republicans. In 1800, Thomas Jefferson was elected as the first Democratic president. The name was shortened to Democratic Party. Democrats tend to be liberal (favor reform, government programs and social progress).

Republican Party

This party is nicknamed the GOP for "grand old party." It was founded in 1854 when the issue of slavery forced a division between the existing Whig and Democratic-Republican parties. The new party was founded on the idea of keeping government out of the people's social and economic lives. Abraham Lincoln was the party's first president. Republicans tend to be conservative (oppose change).

(These descriptions are only generalizations.)

title: David Bushnell and the Turtle
text:
A submarine was used in the American Revolution? Absolutely. David Bushnell, American patriot and inventor, used reason and logic to build the first military submarine.

David Bushnell was born on a farm in Connecticut in 1740. He experimented with underwater explosives during college and built a submarine that would carry them. Bushnell's vessel was nicknamed "the Turtle" because it was shaped like two wooden turtle shells joined together, standing on end. Its hull filled with water to submerge and was pumped out by the operator to rise. Two propellers and a rudder were used to guide it. Benjamin Franklin and others were impressed with Bushnell's invention. When British warships blockaded New York Harbor in 1776, the Turtle was called into action. The submarine operator was supposed to use a giant screw to attach the powder keg (called a mine) to the bottom of the British flagship, the HMS Eagle.

The plan seemed like a failure when the mine could not be fastened to the ship. However, the gunpowder made a frightening explosion underwater. The British quickly moved their warships from the area. Although it didn't work as planned, Bushnell's invention did have an effect on the British navy.

Bushnell then turned his skills to improving underwater mines. These were placed in harbors to protect American rivers and forts. General George Washington was pleased with Bushnell's work and gave him a commission (job) in the Army.

Today David Bushnell is given credit for inventing the first military submarine and for making valuable contributions to the American Revolution. You can visit a replica (an accurate model) of the Turtle in the Connecticut River Museum in Essex, Connecticut. By yourself or with a partner, think of a person who has used reason and logic to develop something that helped America.

title: Our New State Grows with New Cultures!
text:
The American Revolution has ended, and there's been a "meeting of the minds" among our leaders. Pennsylvania is a state. Now that we have powers of our own, we begin to make new laws. Also, many other cultures join us.

Slavery Abolished in Pennsylvania!

Slaves had been tolerated in Pennsylvania since the beginning of the colony. Most people opposed the use of African American slaves, and in February 1780, former Pennsylvania President George Bryan introduced a bill to abolish (do away with) slavery gradually. All children born of slave mothers were to be free when born. Those children who were already slaves were to be set free when they reached the age of 28. All slaves were to be registered by Nov. 1, 1780, or be set free. Pennsylvania was the first state to pass any sort of abolition law. This did not completely outlaw slavery, but the number of slaves in the state became smaller.

Culture Explosion!

Our rich heritage of many nationalities and languages began in the early 1800s. People started arriving in Pennsylvania from all over the world! Culture is the food, art and traditions of a group of people.

Immigrants came to America and some were very poor and had to travel without a bed to sleep in. Thousands of immigrants came to America for many reasons. Here are several that helped make Pennsylvania the state it is today.

1. Our Scot-Irish Heritage

So many people were dying because of the potato famine in Ireland during the 1840s that thousands escaped to America. One of the largest groups of European settlers was the Scot-Irish. They were a hardy population who often pushed our western boundaries beyond their limits, making the American Indians angry. There were so many Irish soldiers in the Revolutionary War in Pennsylvania that the continental line was often called the "Line of Ireland." (Heritage is the cultural values held by ancestors.)

Our Lithuanian Heritage

Russia and Poland began fighting over Lithuanian lands in the 1820s, forcing several hundred refugees out of the country. Many came to America. Lithuanian Independence Day in Pennsylvania is celebrated on February 16 each year. It began in 1989 as a day to recognize the contributions "from art to sports and everything in between" that Lithuanians have made to our state and the country.

2. Our Polish Heritage

One of the most professional soldiers in the American Revolution was Count Casimir Pulaski from Poland. He commanded all the cavalry in the American forces. Pulaski brought cheer and high hopes to Washington's soldiers at Valley Forge. His skill in the battles of Germantown and Brandywine earned him the title "Father of America's Cavalry." Casimir is honored every October on "Pulaski Day" in Philadelphia.

3. Our French Heritage

In the late 1700s, the behavior of Queen Marie Antionette and other upper-class Frenchmen was the cause of the French Revolution. In 1793, about 200 French aristocrats escaped to America and settled in Azilum ("refuge" in French) in present-day Bradford County. About 50 log houses were built around a marketplace. There were taverns, shops, a bakery, gristmill, chapel, theater and wharf for ferry boats. By 1803, French Azilum faltered, and the settlers left for what is now New Orleans, Louisiana.

4. Our Italian Heritage

The first public concert on record in the city of Philadelphia was given by an Italian conductor. It was in 1757 and the conductor was John Palma. Also, in Northampton County, there's a small town made up of the descendants of immigrants from the province of Roseto, Italy. Naturally, this Pennsylvania borough is named Roseto, too!

5. Our Hungarian Heritage

Some of the first Hungarian settlements in Pennsylvania were in the state's anthracite coal region. Many lived in the Scranton/Mount Carmel area. Most people worked in the deep hard-coal mines. Lajos Kossuth led the 1849 revolt against the feudal Habsburg Dynasty of Austria-Hungary. He became a hero of Hungarian nationalism. A town in Clarion County is named for him.

6. Our Russian Heritage

One of the first known Russian immigrants to eastern North America was Charles Thiel, from St. Petersburg, Russia. He came here in 1769 and changed his name to Charles Cist, and then moved to Philadelphia in 1773. He was trained as a scientist and was among the first to discover that anthracite coal could be used as a fuel. Most Russians who immigrated here later found jobs in factories and coal mines.

7. Our Slovakian Heritage

Immigrants from the eastern European area of Slovakia were anxious to come here when agents of the coal and steel companies traveled there seeking workers. The people were happy to escape starvation in their country and settle in the coal regions of Pennsylvania. They suffered a lot of prejudice from English-speaking Americans and have preserved their strong Slovakian heritage and Roman Catholic and Lutheran religions.

title: Philadelphia/Lehigh Valley
text:
This is a great region for fairs and festivals (events celebrating specific themes). If you love the sport of horse jumping, visit Devon, Chester County, in September for the American Gold Cup and Country Fair. It's an exciting event with delicious food and fun shopping thrown in.

Each July, Chester County also hosts the Kimberton Community Fair. The specialties are doughnuts, pierogies and cabbage rolls. And after the great rides, you must eat some oatmeal surprise cookies!

The Middletown Grange Fair is actually held in Wrightstown, Bucks County. Head there in August for good, old-fashioned fun. These folks are best known for their barbeque chicken dinners. Ask the cooks about the surprise barbeque sauce ingredients.

Ever been to a fish fair? Try the Shad Festival in Bethlehem, Lehigh County, in May. Moravians settled this area long ago. They still celebrate the abundance of shad in 1772 (5,300 caught that year!) that kept them from starving. You'll love eating the roasted shad while listening to live folk music. Children like the catch-and-release photo contest and the casting contest.

And don't forget the Goschenhoppen (Gush'n hup'n) Folk Festival in Montgomery County. A thousand volunteer workers arrive every August to preserve the folk culture of the area with food, dress and activities. It's a huge event with sheep shearing, blacksmithing, concerts, sausage making and wonderful German food everywhere! (Culture is the pattern of social behavior of a group of people.)

Have a fun time at the many festivals (exciting events celebrating a specific theme) in this great region!

title: Is it ‘Scot’ or ‘Scotch’?
text: You see the word "Scotch" everywhere. Most often, the word is used to describe someone who was born in Scotland. Actually, "Scotch" is a type of whiskey. Also, it is the brand name of cellophane tape made by the 3M Company. "Scot" or "Scotsman," on the other hand, is the correct way to describe a person who comes from Scotland. Old textbooks use "Scotch," and the newer ones use "Scot" or "Scottish." Most Scotsmen prefer "Scot" rather than "Scotch."

title: Horehound Mint
text: Horehound candies are hard to find in your local supermarket. Maybe it's because their bittersweet taste is not a popular flavor. Yet for a long time, this confection served as more than just candy. The horehound mint plant has a jellylike substance that can soothe mucous membranes in the throat and respiratory passages. Horehound has been a remedy for colds and chest infections since ancient times and is a member of the mint family. The leaves can be used as a tummy-soothing mint tea that can help relax you before bedtime. It's native to Europe and is grown in many gardens there. It grows well in sunny locations in dry, sandy fields. The horehound mint also grows wild in many parts of Pennsylvania. It can be identified by its woolly, whitish-gray square stems and characteristic round or oval toothed leaves, which are downy and wrinkled.

title: Fun Facts
text: The movie "Titanic" cost about $200 million to make, while it would cost about $123 million to build the ship in today's dollars.

title: Here Comes the Turnpike!
text:
First road of its kind

How many times have you traveled with your family on the Pennsylvania Turnpike? Did you know the road is famous in the history of transportation in the United States? Kids as far away as California and Alaska grow up learning about the Pennsylvania Turnpike, but most of them never have a chance to ride or drive on it. Lucky you! Why is it so famous?

The early Philadelphia to Lancaster Turnpike Road was the first major toll road in America. A toll road is one where travelers pay at stops along the way. It was 62 miles long and a hard-stone road, topped with macadam. This is a special mix of crushed limestone named for its inventor, John L. McAdam, a Scottish immigrant. In 1818, the Cumberland (or National) Road opened. It ran through southwestern Pennsylvania and was used mainly for settlers moving west. By 1840, turnpikes had been built all over the state and provided 3,000 miles of road.

At first, the roads followed rivers. Ferries carried travelers across for a toll charge. Bridges gradually replaced ferries. One of our state's first bridges was built over the Schuylkill at Philadelphia in 1817.

The "Dream Highway," the super-highway across the state as we know it today, actually began in January 1935. It was the brain child of State Representative Cliff Patterson from Monongahela. Because this was such an expensive project, and because no lengthy highway had ever been built before, it took Representative Patterson a long time to convince politicians to approve the funds for the project. Finally, President Franklin D. Roosevelt granted the tax dollars needed, and the highway was begun. The first portion, from Carlisle to Irwin, was opened in October 1940.

This new idea for superhighways (turnpikes, toll roads, parkways, freeways and expressways) that would eventually crisscross all over the country began right here in Pennsylvania.

title: Transporting People and Goods
text:
Pennsylvania was growing by leaps and bounds. New settlers were arriving from other colonies and from foreign shores. Farms were thriving. Thousands of people passed through, and many stayed here to settle. The problem soon became, "How do we transport all those goods and people to where they need to be?"

Boats of Pennsylvania

Waterways (rivers, lakes, canals and oceans) were considered the best means of transportation whenever possible. Rafts, flatboats and keel boats were used on the rivers that were deep enough to float their cargoes. But they had a hard time going upstream.

John Fitch of Bucks County built a paddle boat driven by steam engine, and three years later, he was operating a steamboat on the Delaware River between Philadelphia and Burlington, New Jersey. Robert Fulton of Lancaster County developed the first commercially successful steamboat, which he operated on the Hudson River in New York in 1807. By 1811, Nicholas Roosevelt had gone to Pittsburgh to build the New Orleans, the first steamboat on western waters.

The rivers were shallow, rocky or had too many rapids for boats - steam powered or otherwise - to keep up with the increasing demand for transportation across Pennsylvania. The canal system looked like the best bet for the future.

Let's Build Those Canals!
