Before turnpikes and railroads, there were always rivers to transport goods from town to town. But some rivers, like the Susquehanna, were too rocky and shallow for big boats to travel. So a system of canals - water-filled ditches connecting rivers, lakes and oceans - was begun. There were many canals in the old countries of England, France, Holland and others. Settlers from Europe were accustomed to them.

Mules or horses towed a canal boat by a long rope. The horses walked on the towpath beside the canal to the lock. A canal boat crawled along at three or four miles an hour. The Schuylkill Canal was one of the first to be built in Pennsylvania. It was opened in May 1825. This canal was 108 miles long, and barges could carry coal from the mining area of Pottsville to Philadelphia. Settlers by the thousands moved into our state by way of canals. Passenger boats were called packets.

Who Dug the Canals?

Boys your age and many men were needed to dig them. It was hard work. Boys ran to get water, cleared away trees and bushes and removed mounds of dirt, tossing them into the woods. It was long, tiring, backbreaking work. There was no modern equipment to dig holes. Workers lived in huts that were no more than a few boards nailed together with a flat roof. The men and boys were crowded inside at night. The huts kept out the rain, but not the cold and dampness of the night. Many people became very ill while building Pennsylvania's canals. Some people even died.

Were the Canals Worthwhile?

Many officials thought the canals may not have been worthwhile, because they were so expensive and dangerous to build. But, the purpose of the canal system was to provide transportation by water. The digging and the operating of the canals provided employment for thousands of Pennsylvanians. Numerous immigrants traveled westward over the canals. Many tons of materials moved through the waterways that would have mired wagons in the mud. Yes, there were injuries and death, but accidents occur in the building of any kind of transportation system. Canals served a purpose when no other means of transportation could have done as well.

Today, you may enjoy a canal boat ride on the Delaware Canal in Roosevelt State Park. Riders board the boat at New Hope. The boat is drawn by mules. It is a pleasant ride, passing old inns and going under bridges. Take the family and have a picnic!

Railroad Replaces Canals

The first locomotive in Pennsylvania was called the Stourbridge Lion. It ran on wooden rails. The locomotive soon proved to be far too heavy for the wooden rails.

Matthias Baldwin, a Philadelphia watchmaker, built a steam locomotive called "Old Ironsides" made of iron and wood. The train ran between Philadelphia and Norristown for 20 years. The engine burned wood, and smoke and cinders poured from the engine all over the passengers. In 1833, however, it was wonderful to go 16 miles per hour. The Baldwin Locomotive Works eventually became the largest manufacturer of locomotives in the country.

In 1846, the Pennsylvania Railroad Company was born. It became the largest carrier of passengers and freight in the world. Because rails could be built anywhere they were needed, railroads quickly replaced canals as the main means of transportation. By 1860, coal was used for fuel instead of wood. When the Civil War started, railroads proved to be of great value.

title: Mark Twain
text:
Samuel Langhorne Clemens was born in 1835 in a little town in Missouri called Florida. When he was 4, his family moved to Hannibal, a city on the Mississippi River where young Samuel met all sorts of interesting riverboat travelers. Riverboat travel sparked Samuel's imagination. When he was 18, he set out to travel around the country. He stayed in many American cities, working cheaply for printers in the places he stayed.

In 1857, he planned to go to South America and set out down the Mississippi on a riverboat. But the river got the best of him, and instead of going to South America, he convinced the boat's captain to teach him to be a riverboat pilot! He spent the next few years piloting boats up and down the Mississippi. That's when he gave himself the name "Mark Twain," a river term that means "two fathoms deep." His career as a riverboat traveler ended when the Civil War began, and Mark Twain headed for California.

In the West, Twain began to realize that he wanted to write for a living. He took a long trip to Jerusalem and Europe and wrote about his adventures. When he came back to the United States, he bought a grand house in Hartford, Connecticut. Mark Twain was an interesting man in Hartford, who liked to wear funny white suits and smoke a big cigar. He wrote some of America's most beloved books during that time, like "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer" and "The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn." People all over the world loved his writings, which were often very funny.

But in the 1880s, Twain's luck began to turn bad. Two of his three daughters died, as well as his wife. He lost a lot of money in a failed business. His writing became sad and even angry. Mark Twain died in 1910 at age 74. He remains one of the greatest American authors ever, and his books are still read by millions of people.

title: Poconos/Endless Mountains
text:
The first permanent railroad in America was built in 1810 in Pennsylvania by Thomas Leiper. The rails were strips of oak planks on which a horse pulled a cart down the rails. The cart was the first railroad "car."

Nineteen years later, right here in our region, the Stourbridge Lion was born - the first locomotive! The locomotive, with a lion's head painted on the front of the engine, went three miles from Honesdale through Wayne County on wooden rails. Steel rails were later added. Eventually, more powerful locomotives replaced the Stourbridge Lion, which was put under a shed to rust in peace. Many years later, it was moved to the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., where it's on display in all its shining glory. It is also on display at other museums throughout the country from time to time. An exact replica is permanently exhibited in a special building in Honesdale.

This area is also famous for the town of Jim Thorpe (formerly the town of Mauch Chunk). Jim was an American Indian Olympic athlete and football player from Oklahoma. He is buried in the town named for him, even though he'd never been anywhere near it in life! In 1912, he had won two gold medals and broken many pentathlon and decathlon records to become a hero at the games in Stockholm. He was later stripped of his medals, only to be reinstated 70 years later, in 1982. Visit his mausoleum and learn the whole story.

Be sure to visit the Lackawanna Coal Mine in this region. Descend more than 300 feet into the Earth to explore abandoned tunnels of rock and coal. See for yourself how miners worked on their hands and knees to mine "black diamonds." Get firsthand accounts of stories and legends from tour guides - some of whom mined the coal themselves. This is a very interesting region to visit. Have a great time!

title: Where did the word “turnpike” originate?
text:
To pay for early Pennsylvania roads, the users were charged tolls. Every 10 miles, a tollhouse was erected with a gate in the form of a long shaft, known as a pike, across the road. To open the "pike" cost a wagoner 25 cents. A horse and rider was charged four cents. This turning of the pike gave the road the name "turnpike." Up to 100 Conestoga wagons a day traveled to Philadelphia from Lancaster. Stagecoaches carried passengers over the route in 12 hours for $3.50. The road soon paid for itself.

An original tollhouse can be seen at Addison in Somerset County. It still stands along the modern concrete Route 40 that follows the same route as the old National Road of 1806.

title: Striped Skunk
text: Mount Pisgah State Park in the northern Endless Mountain area is a good place to find this frisky animal. The scientific name for the skunk is "mephitis mephitis," which means, "noxious gas, noxious gas." (The gas is so noxious that it has to be said twice!) You'll find this critter (we hope not too often!) in the woods of northeastern Pennsylvania and lots of other places. If you get in its way, it will spray you, but it will give you some warning: It'll lift its tail high and stamp its feet. Then it'll hiss. And it can spray as far away as 12 feet with great accuracy! Skunks have poor vision, but their senses of smell and hearing are good. They're resistant to snake venom - they can survive 10 times the venom needed to kill other animals of the same size. There's a popular notion that skunks cannot spray their musk if they are lifted off the ground by the tail. This is untrue. Don't try it! This creature is mostly black with the big white warning stripe down its back. Have fun hiking in Pennsylvania's forests, but watch your step!

title: How do I read Nonfiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring. But it really isn’t. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you will find it easier to understand—and maybe even fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will talk about cause and effect.

Cause/Effect

With this information pattern, writers organize their material to show how one thing leads to another. Cause is the reason why something happens. Effect is what happens as a result of the cause. Effects often turn into causes for different effects. Writers often use this pattern when they want to explain a chain of events. One way to find the cause and effect of a passage is to make a Cause/Effect diagram that allows you to show the cause and effect relationship graphically. You start by writing the cause of the events. Draw an arrow from the cause bubble pointing right, and then next to the arrow, write the effect of that cause. Draw a new arrow from the effect bubble pointing left and down and write the next effect. Draw the next arrow pointing right and continue in that manner until you have reached the final effect. See the sample diagram below.

Try It!

To the right is a passage about immigration to the United States. Read the passage. Then create a Cause/Effect diagram that shows the causes and effects of immigration.

title: Let's Write
text: You are a resident of our state in the 1800s. You are moving yourself and all your belongings from the country to the city. Of the various means of transportation, would you rather travel by stagecoach, horseback, steamboat, keel boat, canal boat, wood-burning train or foot? Tell us how you’re traveling and why you chose your method of transportation.

title: Fake or Real News?
text:
Have you ever read something online, like on social media sites, that sounded fishy? Maybe it was real, but it could be fake news! The big danger, though, is news that sounds real but isn’t. Fake news is becoming common because anyone can post things online. Fake news can be in the form of a story. Fake news can be a photo or video that has been changed. The problem is that these fake items look real. Fake news can cause problems and it spreads misinformation.

Sam Wineburg, a professor, did some research. He found that 80 percent of students cannot tell the difference between real and fake news. Do you want to become a media-savvy person? You have to be able to find out if news is real or fake. How do you do that? You have to become a detective and search for the truth. You can learn about the author or company that posted the news. You have to think about the purpose of the news. Is there a hidden plan to get you to buy something or to make you think a certain way? Your teacher or a trusted adult can help you learn how to spot fake news. It takes a little time, but democracy depends on real information! Do your part and discover what is real and what is fake!

title: Brother Against Brother
text:
A Great Tragedy of the Civil War

There were hundreds of families during the Civil War (War Between the States) that had relatives on both sides fighting each other - father against son, cousin against cousin, and brother against brother. Only a few, however, were known to participate in the very same battles. One such battle involved the Drayton brothers.

The Drayton family members were citizens of South Carolina. William Drayton, the father, became an outstanding lawyer in Charleston. When leaders of that state began to talk about leaving the Union (Northern states), William spoke out against the idea in a stirring speech at an Independence Day celebration. He lost many clients - so many, in fact, that he was forced to give up his practice and move to Philadelphia. He became president of the Bank of the United States.

His youngest son, Percival, a Navy commander, agreed with William. Percival later asked state officials to have his name registered as an official citizen of Pennsylvania.

William's older son, Thomas, a general in the Army, disagreed. He loved the South and remained there until the end.

Percival was ordered to take his ship, the USS Pocahontas, to Port Royal, South Carolina, and attack Fort Walker. Within two hours, Fort Walker was abandoned, and its commander fled on horseback. Only later did Percival learn that the commander was Confederate Brigadier General Thomas Drayton - his very own brother! The official record states that had Commander Percival Drayton known he was firing upon Commander Thomas Drayton, he would have followed orders and done it anyway. Such are the bitter decisions that come in times of terrible war.

title: Pennsylvania Enters the War Between the States
text:
What caused the Civil War? Why would brother fight brother, father fight son, and people of the same nation rise up against their neighbors? This question is harder to answer than the usual, "They were fighting over slavery." The North thought slavery was wrong, and it was an issue, but it didn't cause the war.

States' Rights or Federal Rule?

The issue of states' rights asks the question, "How much power does each state have to govern itself?" The South claimed that states had the right to decide for themselves how to carry on their business. They said, "If we need slaves to help us earn a living, then we have a right to own slaves. If we want to leave the United States and form our own country, we have the right to do it." The North claimed that the central government had the right to federal rule - forcing states to stay together in one country. The South said, "We'll leave the Union and form our own country and army." President Lincoln said, "Don't leave - we must preserve the Union."

Finally, South Carolina voted to withdraw, or secede. The new leaders demanded that Fort Sumter, which was in Confederate territory, be turned over to its new government. President Lincoln would not agree to it. The South took the fort by force. Shots were fired. The war had begun. It became a contest to see who was right. Will it be states' rights for the South or federal rule from the North? The story is about to unfold.

The Battle of Gettysburg

The War Between the States had been raging on Confederate soil since April 1861. Pennsylvania had 30,000 volunteers anxiously waiting to go to battle. Those reserves set up camp north of Harrisburg. In September 1862, President Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation declaring freedom for all slaves in the rebellious Southern states. The South was really angry!

The Battle of Gettysburg was not really supposed to take place. The whole thing was an accident. General Robert E. Lee only wanted to capture supplies. He'd heard there was a supply of shoes stored there. Footwear was badly needed. But when he marched into Gettysburg to take the shoes, he met Pennsylvania's General George G. Meade and his Union army instead!

What has been called the biggest and bloodiest battle ever fought on American soil took place on July 1-3, 1863, in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. The people of this small town used their homes, churches, schools, barns, halls and stables to care for the wounded. There was no Red Cross organization, so townspeople became nurses, cooks, waiters and grave diggers. Local doctors cared for the wounded until aid was sent in from other towns. A tent hospital, set up east of town, was used for four months. In just three days of fighting, thousands of people died. More than 34,500 Union soldiers were Pennsylvanians, including 15 generals. Prior to the battle at Gettysburg, the Confederate army was winning the war, but the Union army won this key battle, and Gettysburg became the turning point of the Civil War. (A civil war is a war that takes place within the boundaries of a single nation.)

Underground Railroad

So many black slaves were mistreated prior to the War Between the States that they often escaped to the North. Many of them dropped out of sight in slave-free Pennsylvania. A slave owner once remarked, "There must be an underground railroad out of here." Thus a name was given to the dangerous practice of helping slaves escape to freedom. Slave owners hired bounty hunters to chase runaways. These bounty hunters collected several hundred dollars for each slave they brought back alive. They carefully spied on "stations" (homes of citizens who sheltered slaves.) Most of the "conductors" were free blacks who hid slaves in secret rooms during the day then moved them at night to the next station. This process was repeated over and over until the runaways arrived in Canada and elsewhere. Quakers and other whites also participated in the Underground Railroad.

Henry "Box" Brown

Henry Brown, a Virginia slave, decided that because he was considered a "white man's property," he would, in his escape attempt, travel as a piece of property. He persuaded a carpenter to build him a box lined with fabric, just long enough for Brown to sit in. Then, with a supply of biscuits, water and a small hand drill, he got into the box and had himself sealed and shipped to Philadelphia. It was a long, uncomfortable trip, but the crate was eventually delivered to the Anti-Slave Society 26 hours later. When the lid was pried off the box, Henry Brown stiffly rose to his feet, saying, "How do you do, gentlemen?" From that day on, he was known as Henry "Box" Brown, a hero to the anti-slavery cause.

title: Conviction
text:
Most people gain their beliefs from their family, religion, or community. A deeply-held belief is called a conviction. To do something with conviction is to do it because of the deeply-held belief a person holds. Often, people who do things with conviction are described as "having conviction," meaning they live by their beliefs.

At the time of the Civil War, many people in Pennsylvania followed their convictions. Abolitionists strongly believed that slavery was wrong. They worked to persuade their fellow citizens to this belief. Conductors on the Underground Railroad held conviction that enslaved people deserved freedom. They were willing to risk their own lives based on this conviction.

Soldiers from Pennsylvania who fought for the Union Army fought with conviction. President Lincoln made this observation in his Gettysburg Address in 1863. He was dedicating the battlefield to be a cemetery for the fallen soldiers. However, he remarked that it was actually the soldiers who had consecrated that land. They had been so dedicated to their cause and fought so bravely.

People throughout history have made remarkable impacts because they lived with conviction. Some are famous, while some are not. Each held to their deeply-held beliefs in how they lived and treated others.

title: ‘Black Moses’ of the Underground Railroad
text:
Why are we telling the story of Harriet Tubman in the "Legends" column? Because this woman was indeed a legend in her own time.

Harriet Tubman was a woman of great faith. She was around 28 years old in 1849 (historians list her birth year as around 1820) when she escaped from her master in Maryland and traveled on the Underground Railroad to Pennsylvania. She lived in Philadelphia for two years and worked hard to earn enough money to rent a tiny apartment and furnish it. Then she bought a set of men's clothes and returned to Maryland with the intention of helping her husband escape and go back with her to Philadelphia. Upon her return, she was shocked to learn he'd married another woman. Harriet was heartbroken. Her faith and simple prayers saw her through, however, and that's when she became determined to help fellow slaves escape as she herself had. She made about 15 trips from Maryland to Pennsylvania and other places in the North to help others. She gained the nickname "Black Moses - the Deliverer" because of her deeds. People in the South put a $40,000 reward on Harriet's head. She was a very brave woman who helped more than 300 people to freedom. Thankfully, Harriet Tubman was never captured.

title: What was the famous Gettysburg Address all about?
text: "Fourscore and seven years ago our fathers brought forth, upon this continent, ..." You will hear those words quoted many times throughout your lives. President Abraham Lincoln's 273-word speech in the cemetery at Gettysburg took place four months after the battle. Lincoln himself said, "My speech fell like a wet blanket." A Harrisburg paper dismissed the address as "silly remarks." An Illinois paper called it "a perfect gem, deep in feeling." Most everyone in this country has agreed that this is one of the finest speeches ever given by a U.S. president.

title: Barred Owl
text:
Beltzville State Park is a large park that lies along a dammed section of Pohopoco Creek, a tributary of the Lehigh River. At this park and all over this region, you'll find the barred owl. There are many, many varieties of owls in the world. This one is distinctive by its call. It sounds like it's saying, "Who, who, who cooks for you? Who, who, who cooks for you all?" (Kind of makes you hungry, huh?)

This bird is round headed, with brown eyes and a yellow bill. The face is whitish-brown with dark-brown trim. The body is mottled brown and white. It loves wet areas and deep woods and likes to nest in hollow tree cavities. These very gentle birds can often be seen and heard during the day, and you'll find them dining on rodents, small mammals, birds, frogs and insects. Did you know that if you wanted to see as well as an owl, your eyes would have to be the size of softballs?

title: Chambersburg is Burning!
text:
The town of Chambersburg, Pennsylvania, west of Gettysburg, is often overlooked in general Civil War history. Yet this town suffered great losses both before and after the famous Battle of Gettysburg, the northern-most battle of the Civil War.

In the autumn of 1862, nine months before Gettysburg, the town was raided by the Confederacy (South). General J. E. B. Stuart marched in and stole shoes, 1,000 horses and ammunition. They set the railroad station on fire on their way out of town and burned stores of Union army clothing and weapons. One year after Gettysburg, the same citizens were again hit — 3,000 Confederate soldiers surrounded Chambersburg and demanded $100,000 in gold or $500,000 in cash. When the citizens refused, they set the whole town on fire this time and left thousands of people homeless. Chambersburg was the only northern town completely destroyed in the Civil War. Citizens from all over the state sent money to help. People in other towns had trouble with Confederate soldiers, too. These boxes tell what happened in Hanover, York and Carlisle.

title: The Civil War Today!
text:
The Civil War began when Confederate troops attacked Union soldiers at Fort Sumter on April 12, 1861. The war lasted four years. The two sides fought over 50 major battles and hundreds of smaller clashes. The war ended after General Robert E. Lee surrendered to General Ulysses S. Grant on April 9, 1865.

2011 to 2015 marked the 150th anniversary of the Civil War. Many towns and communities took time to celebrate and remember this important part of our history. During those years, anyone who owned an iPad could “watch” the war happen using “The Civil War Today” app. The app showed users what had happened on that day 150 years ago. The app used pictures, maps and newspaper stories to show the events of the war one day at a time.

The anniversary has passed, but the app is still available. People with the app can look up any date during the war and read newspaper articles, letters soldiers wrote to their families and detailed descriptions of battles. If you or someone you know owns an iPad, ask for permission to look at “The Civil War Today” app. It can help you relive the drama of the Civil War with just the push of a button!

title: How do I read nonfiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring. But it really isn’t. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you will find it easier to understand—and maybe even fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will discuss classification.

Classification

With this pattern, the nonfiction piece is organized into categories or groups that share certain characteristics. In other words, the content is classified.

One idea for finding out how the content of a nonfiction piece is classified is to chart the information into categories. Charting information can help you see the categories graphically. You will also better remember the characteristics of each category.

Try It!

Here is a passage about the war between the states. Read the passage. Then chart the important information into categories.

title: Let's Write
text: You are a nurse or doctor during the Civil War. Men from both the Confederate side and the Union side are coming to you for help. Do you turn away the soldiers that others consider your enemies? Or do you help them regardless of the color of their uniforms? What do you say to other doctors or nurses who disagree with your actions? Write a short essay about your feelings.

title: ‘Black Diamonds’ Discovered in Pennsylvania!
text:
Coal is not the only good thing about Pennsylvania, but it sure is at the top of the list! Some would say that coal is the most valuable mineral deposit on Earth. Where would we be if early explorers hadn't discovered the substance that has brought so much good to mankind - and so many trillions of dollars into our state pocketbook? No wonder coal has been nicknamed "black diamonds"!

The whole thing started with the early swamps and dinosaurs of millions of years ago, of course, but coal as we know it today began . . . well, there are several versions of this story, actually.

An early claim came from a blacksmith named Obadiah Gore, who used anthracite (hard, slowburning, home-heating) coal to heat his forge, or workshop. Several attempts were made to sell anthracite in Philadelphia, but few people believed it would burn. Later, there was Necho Allen, a hunter, who claimed to have discovered it when the campfire he'd built for the night caught the rocks around it on fire. The "rocks" were coal, of course. Or have you read about Keystoners Isaac Tomlinson's and Phillip Ginther's claims of finding anthracite while in the wilds?

Actually, American Indians were the first people in America to use anthracite. They're the ones who gave blacksmith Obadiah Gore his anthracite in the first place! They gave it to him to repair their rifles when the smith ran out of charcoal. Whichever story is true, both anthracite and bituminous (soft, fast burning, industrial-use) coal have done wonders for the country and the world and brought fame to Pennsylvania.

Where Does Coal Come From?

Millions of years ago, most of Pennsylvania was a heavily vegetated coastal swamp, as we discussed in the first issues of Pennsylvania Studies Weekly. As plants and animals died, they sank into the marshes, and the shifting coastal tides poured even more dead plants and animals on top of them. Through the ages, erosion and landslides added very high heat and pressure.

The gas and moisture were gradually squeezed out of the decayed yuck, turning it into coal.

title: What is Hydraulic Fracturing?
text:
People in the states of Colorado, Texas and Ohio have been feeling small earthquakes over the past few years. Some people are saying those quakes are the result of hydraulic fracturing.

Hydraulic fracturing is a way to get natural gas from underground rock formations up to the surface. We use natural gas for energy in homes and businesses. Water and chemicals are pumped underground through long, deep wells. The liquid causes fractures, or cracks, in the rock. Natural gas escapes through the cracks and gets piped up to the surface. Over 200,000 new wells have been drilled in the U.S. during the last 10 years.

The National Research Council released a report in 2012 that said hydraulic fracturing does not seem to be the culprit, but other human activity might be the problem. Some groups believe that it's the wastewater (leftover water and chemicals), not the fracturing itself that is causing the earthquakes. The wastewater from the process is either treated at a facility or sent deep underground. When the liquid is injected back into the ground, it can make the tectonic plates slip and rub against each other, causing earthquakes.

The companies doing the drilling say that they are following safety regulations and protecting their workers, the residents and the environment. Companies have been injecting waste liquids into the ground since the 1930s, and only recently has there been an increase in earthquakes. We will certainly be hearing more about hydraulic fracturing in the years to come.

Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/ for more Connections and Current Events articles.

title: Pennsylvania’s Industries
text:
New industries were coming to Pennsylvania - glass, iron and the most dangerous occupation of all: underground mining.

Glass in Pennsylvania

It's hard to imagine that something so clear and pure could come from a substance like sand! And yet that's how glass is made. And it's been around for a long, long time - at least 5,000 years that we know of!

America's first glass factory west of the Allegheny Mountains was established by Albert Gallatin at present-day New Geneva in 1797. The main ingredient for making glass is silica, a chemical in fine, white sand, which is mixed with lime and melted at a very high temperature. Silica is dredged from the bottom of Lake Erie and the Allegheny River for Pennsylvania's glass. Pittsburgh Plate Glass Company (PPG) is one of the largest makers of plate glass. It's very heavy and shatter resistant.

A German immigrant, William Henry Stiegel, started out as an iron worker near present-day Manheim. He added "Baron" to his name and invented some beautiful glass called "Stiegel Glass," which is highly prized today. You may see one of the world's largest collections of it in the Hershey Museum.

There is still a touching tradition in Manheim. Baron Stiegel will not be forgotten by the people of Manheim, the town he founded, nor by the members of the Zion Lutheran Church there. The second Sunday in June each year, the church pays a single red rose to Stiegel's descendants as rent for the property. There is a great ceremony attached to the paying of the rent as part of the morning church service. It has become a tourist attraction. Many members of the Stiegel family gather each June for what has become today's modern Red Rose Festival and family reunion.

Industrialization - a New Personality for Pennsylvania

Pennsylvania was one of the last colonies to get into the iron-making business, but by 1790 the commonwealth was producing half the country's supply of iron. Thomas Rutter established the state's first successful ironworks in 1716 near Pottstown.

Miners Lived a Hard Life

Anthracite-coal mining has certainly had its downside. The new industry attracted many immigrant workers. They were new to the state, often had language difficulties, and were willing to work for very little money. The "coal barons" knew this and exploited, or took advantage of, the unskilled workers.

A typical mine worker earned $20-35 per month and lived with his wife and five to 10 children in a tiny company row house a block from the mine. The rent was $5 per month. Mine operators forced their employees to shop in the company store for food and merchandise that was overpriced. Miners who refused to shop there were treated badly.

Time to Rebel!

The poverty-stricken Irish miners in the anthracite-coal region of Pennsylvania were in pretty bad shape. They decided to rebel against the mine operators. The miners held secret meetings and formed a secret society called the "Molly Maguires." They plotted against the mine owners and foremen by attacking them, sometimes killing them. Then the men used illegal means to get away with the crimes. They even had a secret greeting among themselves so that they could tell when they were meeting a real "Molly." One Molly would encounter another member on the street and put his right hand on his hip. The other man, if he were really another Molly, would respond by putting his left thumb on his left ear.

Who was Molly Maguire?

The original Molly Maguire was a woman in Ireland who was also very poor. She rebelled against the cruel and brutal agents who collected her high rent. She killed one of them. The Irish coal miners named their new rebel society in her honor. The secret society finally came to an end when an agent hired by the railroad was able to work his way into the organization and later gave evidence that sent 20 Mollies to their deaths by 1877. Many more were sent to prison before conditions finally improved.

title: Resources
text:
Productive Resources

Productive resources are found in every good or service. Resources are the basic things used to make products in our community. Economists study resources a great deal and have put them into three groups. They help answer these three economic questions: How is a product made? What product is made? Who makes a product?

Natural Resources

Natural resources are unaltered or undisturbed gifts of nature. Fresh air, minerals, water and trees used for timber are all natural resources. They are things taken from the Earth that cannot be made any other way.

Human Resources

A secretary, a doctor, a mechanic and a teacher are all kinds of human resources. Human resources, or labor, require people to be creative. People must have skills and knowledge to help them put physical and mental effort into their work.

Capital Resources

The last type of resource can be found everywhere. Buildings, tools or machines people use to produce other goods and services are known as capital resources.

These productive resources are all around you every day. Let's say that you wanted to make cookies. Each of these resources would be very important. Most of what you put into the cookies—eggs, milk, sugar, salt and flour - would be natural resources. The human resource would be you making the effort to make the cookies. Lastly, your mixing bowl, measuring cups, spoon, baking sheet, mixer and oven would all be types of capital resources. All these things come together to make your product—yummy cookies! Can you think of other examples of natural, human and capital resources?

title: Poconos/Endless Mountains
text:
Are you ready to go to some great festivals right here in this great region? Well, hang on! In February, enjoy the Horse-Drawn Sleigh Rally in Forksville, Sullivan County. Take a sleigh or bobsled ride and enjoy the food. The county also boasts the Eagles Mere Toboggan Slide. It's a man-made toboggan run that starts right in the middle of town.

In April, go to Troy in Bradford County for the Endless Mountains Maple Festival, marking the end of winter. Learn that it takes 40 gallons of sap to make 1 gallon of syrup. Smell maple everywhere and taste it in all the food offered!

In June, attend Hay Days in Monroeton, Bradford County. You'll get a living history lesson in how hay was cut and baled the old-fashioned way - with horses!

August brings the Blueberry Festival in Montrose, Susquehanna County. A great auction is held along with anything blueberry you'd possibly want - pies, syrups, muffins, breads and "blue" desserts of all kinds! It's the Wayne County Fair in Honesdale next, with its concerts, tractor pulls, livestock roundups and stunt shows. Visit the Moscow County Fair in Moscow. It's huge - with a hot-air balloon rally, top music artists in concert, a classic car show, over 75 craft shows and several vendors serving delicious food. Schuylkill County Fair is next. There's a huge turnout every year. You'll also love the carnival and church-bazaar atmosphere at the Harford Fair in Susquehanna County. It's very New England-ish, with clam chowder as its main food attraction.

September should find you at the Wyoming County Fair in Tunkhannock with its scarecrow contest and scrumptious buffalo shrimp to eat. October means the Apple-Cheese Festival in Canton, Bradford County. Enjoy a cheese-tasting table, many crafts and anything you can think of made with apples or cheese. Have fun in this "festival happy" region!

title: Who was Clara Barton?
text: One of the outstanding figures in the rescue efforts following the Johnstown Flood was a little 67-year-old woman named Clara Barton. She came quickly from her headquarters near Washington, D.C. Her new organization, the American Red Cross, was to go to work at its first real test. Clara and her 50 doctors and nurses worked around the clock to distribute nearly half a million dollars worth of clothing, food, blankets and cash. Upon her return to Washington, President and Mrs. Benjamin Harrison honored her at a formal dinner with many guests.

title: Scarlet Tanager
text:
Visitors to this region should look for the beautiful scarlet tanager. The brilliantly colored adult male is red with black wings and tail and can gleam in the sunlight. The younger male has a lighter red or orange body, and a female scarlet tanager is olive green to yellow with brownish wings. They are sometimes hard to see in the thick forest.

This bird lays her three or four brown-spotted, greenish eggs in a shallow nest. They like to hang around mostly oak and pine trees. You'll hear them make a call similar to a robin. It comes out sounding like a nasal "chik-burr."

Would you be surprised to learn that the most popular sport in America is not football or baseball? It's bird watching! You'll find an amazing number of books and websites on the subject. It gets people of all ages out in open fields and walking through beautiful forests. You'll learn more than the sport of watching for birds. You'll learn a lot about trees and small animals, too. And don't forget all that fresh air and exercise that bird watchers get! What better place than beautiful, forested Pennsylvania to learn a new sport? Try it!

title: How do I read nonfiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring. But it really isn’t. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you will find it easier to understand—and maybe even fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will discuss the main idea and supporting details.

Main Idea/Supporting Details

With this pattern, the writer presents a main idea and then backs it up with factual supporting details as evidence. You should be able to find this pattern when reading nonfiction because you probably already use it in your own writing. One strategy for finding the main ideas and supporting details is to create an outline of what you are reading. With the outline, you will be able to see the main ideas at a glance. Use the main ideas as headings and the supporting details as subheadings in your outline.

Try It!

To the right is a passage about the Great Depression. Read the passage. Then outline the information in the passage so that the main ideas are the headings, and the supporting details are the subheadings.

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine that you go to school one day and are told that you are the new principal. You are now in charge of making all of the school rules. What would the new rules be? Tell us about your ideal school.

title: Andrew Carnegie
text:
How did such a small man come to have such great power? After all, he only stood somewhere between 5 feet, 2 inches and 5 feet, 6 inches. He was born a poor immigrant from Scotland. How did he become the richest man in the world? Read closely, and you will learn just how it happened.

Andrew Carnegie was born in Dunfermline, Scotland, in 1835. His parents were weavers. Back then, weaving machines were invented, and the people who wove by hand lost their jobs. The Carnegie family sailed off to America and ended up in Pittsburgh when Andrew was 13 years old. The teenager found a job in a fabric mill as a bobbin boy for $1.20 per week. When he turned 14, he worked in a telegraph office for $20 per month.

Andrew had a great desire to learn and study. The more he studied, the more he figured out ways to improve every job he ever had. He learned how to make the new business of sending telegraphs better. He learned and studied the railroad industry when he worked there. Andrew became a superintendent. Carnegie then invested in an oil company. He studied and learned how steel was made while on a trip to England and came back here and built a steel company. The company became very successful, and he sold it for $480 million. He was the richest man in the world.

But that wasn't enough for this man of great character. He practiced philanthropy. That means he spent the rest of his life giving his money away to worthy causes.

Because Carnegie had earned great wealth by reading, studying and then applying what he learned, he decided to provide the same opportunities to millions of people just like us. He built many libraries full of wonderful books. He established research institutes and universities. And he could have given his money directly to poor people, but he strongly believed that money, by itself, would not make people rich. It was studying and working hard that would help people earn their wealth.

Andrew Carnegie was a very rich and a very wise man. He counted his wealth by how much he'd used his brain during his life, not by how many dollars he had in the bank. He died in 1919 at the age of 83, but not before he'd given away 90 percent of his fortune. Andrew was a man short in height, but tall in character.

title: Hungry? Ask a Robot!
text:
Have you ever watched a movie on the couch and wished that a robot could bring you a snack from the kitchen? Japanese and German scientists are working on that very thing!

The PR2 is programmed with a computerized version of common sense. It "knows" to look for food in the refrigerator. And it knows that if there is no food in the refrigerator, the place to look for food is a restaurant. The robot has maps of the building in its "brain," and is able to find its way through the building.

The robot is programmed with a semantic search program. That means the robot uses old information to help it understand new messages. You do something similar when you're in a new place. Think about the first time you walked into your classroom. What did you do the first time you had to throw something away? You looked for a trashcan by the front door. Needed to sharpen your pencil? You probably looked around at the walls to find a pencil sharpener. The robot operates in the same way.

Watch the amazing video of the robot and its search for a sandwich: tinyurl.com/3tkq2cr. Maybe in the future we'll have robots in school that can bring us lunch. I'd like turkey and cheese, please!

title: Inventions and Discoveries
text:
Coal, oil and other industries were becoming well established in Pennsylvania. This week, we'll take a look at some of the fun inventions and discoveries of the final few decades of the 1800s.

Inventors and Their Inventions

1. Story with a Twist

In the 1850s, a homeless man was passing through Lititz, a little town north of Lancaster. He stopped at a local bakery and talked the owner into giving him breakfast. In return, he gave the man a recipe for something he called "pretzels." The owner wasn't interested, and he tossed the recipe aside. Julius Sturgis, an apprentice in the bakery, picked it up and baked a few. They were a big hit with his family and townspeople. He opened his own bakery in 1861. Today, his place is a national historic landmark as the First Pretzel Bakery in America. You may go to Lititz and take a tour of that historic bakery. They'll even show you how to make your own pretzel!

2. Root Beer

In 1870, Charles Hires, age 19, was a successful pharmacist in Philadelphia and newly married. While on his honeymoon, the landlady of his boardinghouse served a homemade brew of herbs, roots, spices and sassafras (a tree from the Laurel family.) Hires was a non-drinking Quaker and decided to develop a soft drink similar to what he'd tasted at the boardinghouse. It was his way of fighting the alcoholism he saw around him everywhere. He called it "root tea." A friend advised him that hard-drinking coal miners would be more likely to buy something with a more "macho" name. So he changed it to "root beer."

3. Please Pass the Ketchup!

Little Henry John Heinz from Sharpsburg sold vegetables door to door when he was 8 years old. He grew lots of horseradish and began to bottle it. Ketchup itself was invented in China in 1690. Henry Heinz, who'd moved to Pittsburgh, figured out how to mass produce it. Heinz became very wealthy! Ketchup is now found in nearly every household in the country.

4. The Peanut King

Amedeo Obici came to America from Italy in 1889. He moved to Wilkes-Barre and set up a fruit and nut stand in the street. There he met Mario Peruzzi, who was also an Italian immigrant. They went into business together and formed the Planters Peanut Company. (It's unsure how the two Italians arrived at that name.) It became one of America's greatest corporations. In 1916, a contest was held to find a company logo, and the winner was a 13-year-old boy from Virginia. He designed "Mr. Peanut." For his crayon drawing, he won $5! That was several days' pay back in 1916!

5. Typewriter Born in Pennsylvania

Christopher Sholes, from Mooresburg, Montour County, began his career as a printer's apprentice at the local newspaper. In 1868, he invented the first typewriter, which was called a writing machine. He arranged the keys by figuring out the most commonly used letters in the English language. This keyboard layout also helped prevent the keys from becoming jammed. But, Sholes decided to sell his idea after improving his design. He asked for and received a single payment of $12,000 for his invention. Sholes later added a shift key to the keyboard so that both uppercase and lowercase letters could be used.

6. Pennsylvania Clockmakers

America's first known clock was made in 1685 by Abel Cottey from Philadelphia. Pennsylvania's early clockmakers were treated with great respect. David Rittenhouse of Norristown was a well-known scientist, mathematician and paper manufacturer. He was also the first director of the U.S. Mint. He built a 9-foot clock with 16 chimes. Songwriter Henry Clay Work gave this new tall case clock its popular name, "My Grandfather's Clock." He wrote a song by that name probably around 1876 while he was living in Philadelphia.

title: The Adventures of ‘Miss Liberty’
text:
The Diary of the 'Belle"'of Philadelphia

I told you I'd be back! Let me tell you about some more of my adventures in Pennsylvania:

October 1765 - They muffle me to make me sound sad as ships carrying tax stamps sail up the Delaware River.

February 1770 - I toll to gather the people to petition the king for a repeal of those stamp taxes.

December 1773 - Shortly after the Boston Tea Party, they ring me to announce the arrival of another tea ship in Philadelphia.

April 1775 - I peal loudly to announce the Battle of Lexington and Concord.

Fourth of July 1776 - No, I do NOT ring for the Declaration of Independence! I didn't know about it until the . . .

Eighth of July 1776 - I ring all day, loud and clear, along with every bell in the city, announcing the birth of our brand new nation!

July 4, 1777 - I ring for our very first birthday.

September 1777 - What's happening? They're cutting me down! Our country is at war, and the patriots are afraid English troops are going to melt me down to make bullets! How rude! I'm hiding in a damp, dark basement of the Zion Reformed Church in Allentown. Humph!

June 1778 - They bring me back to Philadelphia, but don't rehang me. My old steeple is too rotten. I hear them say that they're going to put me in storage for seven years! Help!

1785 - I'm finally brought out and am hanging in my new steeple. Whew! What a musty, lonely seven years that was!

1790 - I toll at the death of Benjamin Franklin.

December 1799 - I toll at the death of George Washington.

September 1824 - I toll at the return of Lafayette to Philadelphia. (No one realized until nearly 100 years later that I had cracked that day . . . again!)

title: Trustworthy
text:
What would you do if your friend told you a secret? It was very important to your friend, and she wanted to share it with you, but she did not want others to know. Would you go and tell other people? Or what would you do if your mother gave you some money and asked you to get some things from the store but to bring back her change? Would you keep some of it or maybe buy yourself something with it and give her the rest? If you said no to these, then you are trustworthy.

Being trustworthy means that people can trust you to do what you say you will do. If they give you a job to do, they know that you will do it without them having to check on you all of the time.

When people invent things, sometimes they have people who help them. Sometimes, they even tell their friend or other people about it because they are excited and want to share the news. They hope that these people are all trustworthy. If they aren't, they may go and tell others or they may claim that they invented it instead. Sometimes, people might even try to buy the information from these other people in order to learn what the secret is. If they were trustworthy, even the thought of money would not make them tell others.

Being a trustworthy person is very important. It shows that people can trust you and believe you, and they won't be worried about being hurt or lied to. So always be a good, trustworthy person.

title: The Legend of Monopoly
text:
Most people know the story of Monopoly being invented. Legend says that a man named Charles Darrow, who was an unemployed engineer in Germantown, Pennsylvania, made the game on an oil cloth in his home. In 1934, he showed the game to Parker Brothers but was turned down because they felt that it was too complicated and would take too long to play. The next year, however, Darrow had success selling the game on his own, and Parker Brothers decided to buy it from him.

This legend does not say, however, that Monopoly is closely related to a game called The Landlord's Game, which was created in 1904 by Elizabeth Magie. Elizabeth's game had the same amount of spaces, railroads and utilities as well as jail, go to jail, luxury tax and parking spaces. She made this to show her belief in the single-tax theory, which many people believed in at the time.

Elizabeth's friends helped her make pieces and began to make rules that sometimes changed as they went along. In 1924, she presented the game to George Parker but was turned down because the game was too political.

No one knows for sure if Darrow came up with the idea on his own or if he got the idea from Elizabeth Magie's prototype. The legend never says. But we do know that Monopoly is widely popular and is one of the best-selling games in the world.

title: Why is there a Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C.?
text: Pennsylvania Avenue would be about 100 miles long if it started way up here! Back in 1800, the capital of the United States was moved from Philadelphia to Washington, D.C. Independence Hall was sold to the city of Philadelphia, and the leadership of the nation moved south. There were many bitter feelings over these changes. In order to keep some peace in Pennsylvania over the decision, the nation's leaders agreed to name the main street in the new capital after the home of the old capital.

title: Snowshoe Hare
text: The Promised Land State Park and Bruce Lake Natural Area are a must-visit part of this region. They include about 6,000 acres of woodland and lakes that are full of wildlife year round. Snowshoe hares, which are rarely seen elsewhere in the state, are one of the many mammals to inhabit this area. This beautiful animal is shy and sweet. And it blends in perfectly with its surroundings. It's brown in the summer and pure white in the winter. Snowshoes have about four litters per year, numbering one to nine. They are born fully furred, open eyed and able to hop around almost immediately. Rabbits are born blind and naked. Hares love to eat strawberry plants and the bark of trees. According to Algonquian mythology, spirits are white, and the Great Spirit was often referred to as the White Hare. These animals have natural enemies, including fox, coyote and mink. Even the great horned owl often attacks them. The lynx is its greatest enemy. They're so closely connected that when the hare population declines, about every 11 years, so does that of the lynx! But the hare's biggest killer of all is disease. They suffer from many kinds. Our hare-y friend has large, furry hind feet - where do you think he got his name?

title: Why should I keep a writer's journal?
text:
Have you ever had to write something, but you did not know what to write about? Have you ever had a good story idea, but when you started to write the story, you realized that you could not remember the idea anymore? A writer’s journal can help solve this problem.

Keep a Record

You can record your memories, observations and thoughts in a writer’s journal. You can even write colorful words and phrases or the events of the day in your journal. One very good use of your journal is free writing. Free writing is a kind of practice writing that allows you to sketch your thoughts and feelings without limits. Free writing can include single sentences or long strings of words that might not make sense to anyone else but you. You can even put drawings and diagrams in your journal. Just remember that no one else has to see your writer’s journal—unless it is a class assignment, and then your teacher will want to see it.

Here are some tips for starting your writer’s journal:

1. Find a special notebook to use as your writer’s journal. You should use a notebook that appeals to you because it is your very own journal. Color and draw on them so that they reflect your personality. You can also use a computer or index cards in a box for your journal.

2. You should write in your journal when you want to. You might want to write in it every day or just once a week. You might like to write at the same time every day so you have a routine. Just remember that the more you write in your journal, the more useful it will be to you.

3. Find a special, quiet place to do your journal writing. Make sure you have all the supplies you need to keep your journal: pencils, pens, markers, scissors and glue.

4. Write whatever comes to your head, almost as if you are having a conversation with yourself. Do not worry about editing, rewriting or spelling until later when you transfer something from your journal into a writing project.

Try It!

Start a writer’s journal using the suggestions and tips we have provided. You will be amazed what you might discover about yourself.

Ideas for Your Writer’s Journal

1. Collect cartoons and articles to give you ideas for future writing projects.

2. Compose imaginary letters to people you wish you knew.

3. Record quotations, song lyrics, jokes, poems or riddles.

4. Describe interesting people and places.

5. Keep learning notes—Take notes about your learning process. Record new facts and ideas you’ve learned in school, write about the progress you’ve made in class and list questions you have about confusing content.

6. Record reading reactions—Explore ideas and feelings about what you have read. Write about your favorite character, predict what might happen next in the story, tell your opinion of the writer’s style or summarize the story. You can even tell how the story relates to events in your own life. What is interesting about the story? What angers, amuses or puzzles you?

title: Let's Write
text: You have read of some fun discoveries and inventions this week. Have you ever invented anything? Is it a secret? Are you afraid others will laugh at you? Well, so were all the people who have ever invented anything! Don’t be afraid. Write a short essay about your idea and send it to us.

title: Women Win Right to Vote!
text:
Many exciting things were happening in America as we entered a new century. Airplanes and automobiles were being invented, and the radio had arrived. One last big change was needed: Women in the United States of America did not have the right to vote. By 1912, women's fight to win the right to vote (called "suffrage") had become a very heated issue. In Pennsylvania, women enjoyed a certain amount more of freedom than their sisters in other states. A lot of the credit for this goes to the Quaker religion that William Penn brought to his new commonwealth. The Deutch Friends Society had always elevated the status of their women - long before they sought religious freedom in "Penn's Woods." It set a great example for other women to fight for. And fight they did!

In 1850, the Female Medical College opened in Philadelphia. By the early 1900s, there were many professional women - 1,000 lawyers, 3,000 ministers and 7,500 physicians in the United States. This city was like a war zone as women rebelled against the suppression they'd known for centuries. In 1868, they formed the Pennsylvania Women's Suffrage Association with Susan B. Anthony as its leader. Miss Anthony read her famous "Declaration of Rights for Women" in front of Independence Hall in Philadelphia in 1876.

Other well-known Pennsylvania women such as Lucretia Mott, Ann Davies, Florence Kelley, Ann Preston, Josepha Hale and Emma Guffey Miller were all active in the long battle that finally ended when, after many tries, Congress approved the 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution in 1920. Finally, women could vote.

title: Has Amelia Earhart’s Plane Been Found?
text:
A research group that looks for historical aircraft has been trying to solve one of the greatest mysteries of the 20th century. What really happened to Amelia Earhart? Earhart was the first woman to try to fly around the world. She disappeared without a trace while flying over the Pacific Ocean in 1937.

Earhart and Fred Noonan, her navigator, could have landed somewhere near Gardner Island, now called Nikumaroro. Others believe they crashed into deep water. By using technology to study a 1937 photo of the island's shore, researchers may have new evidence in the case. The photo shows what may be the landing gear of her Lockheed Electra airplane sticking out of the water. This could mean Earhart and Noonan lived on the island for some time after the crash. Artifacts have also been found on the island that could have belonged to Earhart and Noonan.

The oceanographer who found the undersea wreckage of the Titanic says the photograph might be the clue that helps us find out what really happened. Underwater robotic submarines and mapping equipment will help the International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery look for the plane's remains. Perhaps an old photograph and new technology will help solve a 75-year-old mystery!

Reference: History News Network (hnn.us)

title: Many Changes in the 1900s
text:
The turn of a new century was an exciting time in Pennsylvania history. The inventions of the automobile, airplane, radio and many other things were taking place. No one could guess that two world wars and a great depression lay just ahead. This week, let's take a peek at those carefree days before our country began to suffer.

Who Really Invented the Radio

The history books give credit to Italian inventor Guglielmo Marconi for the invention of the radio. But the citizens of Wilkes-Barre would tell you a different story.

In 1905, the Reverend Joseph Murgas was a Slovak priest at the Sacred Heart Church in Wilkes-Barre. He was a curious man with many hobbies and talents. He built a laboratory in the rectory and invented the forerunner of radio.

A group of wealthy men from Philadelphia was amazed at the invention and planned to market Murgas' product. At the same time, Marconi was working on the same invention in Italy.

Marconi heard about the minister's invention and came to America to visit him in Wilkes-Barre. He asked him many questions about radio transmission. Soon after, Murgas had several financial setbacks. Meanwhile, Marconi went on to claim all the aspects of the great invention and was eventually accepted as the official inventor of the radio.

Father Murgas died in 1929 and was forgotten by the radio industry. Today, a monument in front of the Sacred Heart Church, Wilkes-Barre, honors the inventor/priest Rev. Joseph Murgas.

Trolley Comes to Pennsylvania

These trolleys weren't like other streetcars running through the streets of major cities across the country. These trolleys went outside the cities and took passengers all over Pennsylvania! They were called interurban trolleys, and between 1890 and the 1950s, there were 80 trolley companies operating. They were powered by electricity along regular rails. The interurbans brought farm folks to the cities - that's how suburbs started in Pennsylvania!

Philly Songwriter

Jack Norworth from Philadelphia loved show business. His father didn't want him to be associated with that "riffraff" world, however, so he sent his son off to sea. Young Jack had different ideas. He went ashore and pursued his stage career. One day, in 1908, Jack sat on a New York subway. He noticed a baseball poster. He grabbed a pencil and, within a half hour, composed a song titled, "Take Me out to the Ball Game." If you don't know it, ask your teacher to sing it to you! In later years, Norworth also wrote "Meet Me in Apple Blossom Time" and "Shine on, Harvest Moon." You'll have to ask your grandparents to sing those songs to you! It wasn't until 1942, 34 years after he wrote his baseball song, that Norworth finally attended his first baseball game!

Coal Miners Strike!

Trouble was brewing in the hard-coal-mining areas. By the turn of the century, the miners had formed a union called the United Mine Workers. There was already a union formed in the soft-coal mines. Unions are formed to protect workers from too much overtime, bad working conditions and being taken advantage of.

In May 1902, the union went to the mine owners and demanded a 20-percent raise in pay and a reduction of the work day from 10 to nine hours. They also demanded that the United Mine Workers be recognized as a union. The owners said, "No way!" The miners simply stopped going to work. That's what a strike is. They stayed home for five months! Members of the union in the soft-coal areas sent $2 million to aid the men on strike.

October came, and cold weather approached. People all over the country started shivering, and the demand for coal increased. The National Guard was called because violence was expected. President Theodore Roosevelt stepped in and studied the issue. The strike was finally settled without violence. The mine workers got only a 10-percent increase in pay, but they got the nine-hour workday. Many more changes were to take place in the mining industry in the years to come.

title: The Adventures of ‘Miss Liberty’
text:
The Diary of the 'Belle' of Philadelphia

As you recall, last time, I left you "hanging" when I told you I cracked again in September 1824. Unfortunately, no one knows for sure if that's when I began my famous zigzag crack!

1828 - Philadelphia decided to build another state house steeple in which to hang me. It's about time I got out of that rotten tower! Little did I know that the city fathers were planning to push me aside for a brand-new, shinier, bigger bell! They paid a foundry owner named Wilbank to cast a new bell and haul me away and dump me somewhere! Humph! Then this Wilbank man insults me further by telling the city fathers it would cost more to haul me away than I'm worth! Double humph!

Late 1828 - I'm hung in the new steeple anyway. I toll to celebrate Catholic emancipation. My small crack is getting bigger, but only I can feel it.

July 4, 1831 - I tolled for our nation's birthday.

February 1832 - I tolled for George Washington's birthday. The crack is getting bigger. I wish someone would find it and fix it. It hurts.

April 1841 - I am muffled and toll upon the death of President William Henry Harrison.

February 1846 - The churches in the area are arguing over me. The city wants to pay my church $30 every time I'm rung. The other churches are jealous. I toll for Washington's birthday. This time, there is no question: My small fracture becomes a huge crack and a painful wound up my side. (They say that I cracked and quit from sadness because the churches were arguing over me. They're right.)

1852 - I am brought down from the steeple and placed in "Declaration Chamber" of Independence Hall.

title: How many capitols have we had?
text: There have been two buildings. The first one was built in 1819 and burned down in 1897. The new century brought a beautiful, huge new building, completed in 1906. President Teddy Roosevelt loved it and even came here and dedicated it. Unfortunately, scandal and fraud were involved in building the capitol. The people who put paneling in one office, for instance, charged the state $15,500 for it. In reality, it should have been only $1,800! The architect, the contractor, the former state treasurer, the state auditor general and 10 others were found guilty of fraud in 1908. Few of them served time in jail, however. It was one of the biggest political scandals in Pennsylvania history.

title: ‘Raptor Watch
text: You're in for an exciting event! Ask your folks to take you to Landisburg anytime between mid-August and mid-November. Go to a place called "Waggoner's Gap" on the Cumberland-Perry County border. You're about to witness a phenomenal event. Thousands of raptors (birds of prey), including hawks, falcons and eagles, will soar past as they journey south. The last week of September brings Cooper's hawks through the area. Late September through October, visitors may see merlins and peregrines. Red-shouldered hawks are common through October, and if you like red-tailed hawks, go in November. From late October to mid-November, Waggoner's Gap is one of the best places in Pennsylvania to see golden eagles. The "Raptor Watch" on Waggoner's Gap is a breath-taking experience. Pack a picnic lunch, take some good "bins" (binoculars), and go with people you like to be with!

title: Hershey/Dutch Country
text:
Welcome to this fun region of our state! This is one of the most "tourist-y" areas of Pennsylvania, and there are many good reasons for that. You'll see the Amish and Mennonites clinging comfortably to their old ways. They travel in horse-drawn buggies and still farm with horses. People of all ages will appreciate their crafts, especially the beautiful German-style quilts in the shops. Drive carefully, have great respect for our Deutch neighbors in their buggies, and most of all, don't hang out your car window taking pictures of them. They hate that! Please respect their privacy.

You will really love to hang out in Hershey. Have you been there yet? Have fun on the thrilling rides of Hershey park and visit the world-famous gardens. And those mounds of rich, milk chocolate you've heard about really are there! In Lancaster, look for America's oldest farmers market. In this area alone, you may travel across 28 of our famous covered bridges. Part of the Appalachian Trail crosses this region, and camping here is so fun! Be sure to visit the Landis Valley Museum for a shot of early German culture. Travel westward, and you'll find the famous Gettysburg Battlefield. Have a wonderful time in the Hershey/Dutch Country region!

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you’re on a mission to Earth from another planet. Part of your mission is to check out the planet Earth and report back to your home world if you find places where your friends can live. While exploring in your spaceship, you find a city in our state that you know everyone back home will just love. Tell us the name of the city you like best, and write a description that will make your friends and relatives back home want to go there to live.

title: Margaret “Molly” Corbin
text:
There are only two Revolutionary War soldiers buried near the Old Cadet Chapel in West Point Cemetery, and one of them is Margaret "Molly" Corbin. Who was this woman and why would she receive such a remarkable military honor?

Margaret was born in Pennsylvania in 1751. She married John Corbin when she was 21. John enlisted in the Continental Army when the Revolutionary War began. Wives sometimes went with their husbands to war. They helped with cooking and cared for wounded soldiers. Women often carried pitchers of water to pour on overheated cannons during battle. They were nicknamed "Molly Pitchers."

But Margaret did much more than that. When John was given the job of loading and firing a cannon, Margaret worked as his assistant right on the battlefield. In November 1776, the British army attacked Fort Washington where the Corbins were stationed. During the battle John was killed. Margaret immediately began loading and firing John's cannon by herself. What courage and quick thinking that must have taken! Margaret continued firing until she was wounded too.

Margaret was disabled for the rest of her life. Congress awarded her a lifelong pension (retirement pay) just as if she had been a soldier, something no woman had ever received.

In 1926 the Daughters of the American Revolution had Margaret's remains reburied in West Point Cemetery with full military honors. A memorial plaque also stands near the battle site in New York City. It reads "Capt. Molly Corbin ... the first American woman to take a soldier's part in the War for Liberty." Think of a woman you know who demonstrates agility of mind. Who is she?

title: The Roaring ’20s
text:
My name is Lois Thompson, and I was born in 1913 in McKean County. I am 91 years old. My great-grandson, Thayne, is in fourth grade this year, and he's studying the early 20th century in social studies. He asked me if I know anything about the Great Depression and the two world wars. Do I know anything? Thayne, honey, I lived those events!

I remember my father coming home from World War I in 1918. I was 5 years old, and my mother sure was happy! The war was awful, but this country was really united.

Then came the "Roaring '20s." There was plenty of money and food, and I became a flapper. We danced the Charleston and wore dresses with fringe and long beads that "flapped" around. It was really fun!

Then suddenly, it was Oct. 29, 1929.

The Great Depression

The date Oct. 29, 1929, lives in the memories of all us "ancient ones." I was only 16, but I remember the stock market crash. We were plunged immediately into the Great Depression. Our world caved in. Thousands of Americans lost their jobs. My father lost our home and the bakery he owned. Those were awful times. My family laughs at me now because I can't bear to throw anything away—leftover memories of my youth when I hardly owned anything, I guess. Governor Pinchot was elected for the second time in 1930. He took action to provide food and jobs for Pennsylvanians. My father found work on the Pennsylvania Turnpike.

I was 28 when the United States entered World War II in 1941. By then, I was married and so sad to see my husband join the Navy. I didn't sit around and mope, though. I took a job in the Eldred Munitions Factory here in town. We women were proud of the work we did in the war effort. Many jobs were available then, though rationing (see Page 2) was in force. My younger sister Jewel and I planted a victory garden. (See Page 3.) The war that killed so many of our young men also put an end to the Great Depression. We were so happy to see our husbands return in 1945.

Times are better, but I often think back to the events of my youth. Those days were both sad and happy. America was very united, and our moral values were firmly in place. Lois Thompson passed away in 1996 when she was 83 years old.

title: Pennsylvania Veterans Tell Their Stories
text:
As veterans (those who have served in the military) of foreign wars grow older, our country risks losing the stories of these brave soldiers forever.

Thousands of war veterans die each week, and along with them go their stories. The Library of Congress'Veterans History Project hopes to record these amazing historical stories before the war veterans are no longer around to tell them.

Project participants have gathered thousands of war stories from veterans of foreign wars. For many years, these veterans have kept their stories to themselves, not wanting to burden their families with their pain. As they age, however, many veterans feel the need to finally talk about their experiences and let someone know what war was really like.

Guy Stephens, a 78-year-old former school principal, told his interviewer about being rescued from a German prison camp where he was held as a prisoner of war, or POW.

He says, "It's hard for POWs to talk to your family about combat or what you've experienced as a POW. There's something about POWs, we never talk about things. I told him things I've never told my family ... I don't know why."

Pennsylvania youth have even gotten involved in the project. History classes, Boy and Girl Scouts, and members of other service clubs have spent time interviewing our brave Pennsylvania veterans for the project. A group of students recently interviewed Harold Williams, an 86-year-old veteran from Huntingdon. He told the students about meeting actor James Stewart while serving in World War II. Stewart was a very popular movie star during the '40s who starred in movies such as "It's a Wonderful Life" and "Harvey." Stewart served as a fighter pilot during World War II. In describing the movie star, Williams says, "He was a nice fella, but he was strictly business."

If you know any veterans, consider interviewing them for the Veterans History Project to keep their stories alive forever.

title: Made in the U.S.A.
text:
Have you ever been surprised to see a sticker on something that says it was made in another country? Every country makes different kinds of goods. Countries trade with one another to get those goods. These goods are called imports. Imports are brought into one country, but they are for sale by another country.

Exports are just the opposite. A country sends products to other countries for sale. Let's say a car is made in Japan and then sold in the United States. In this case, Japan exported the car. The United States imported the car. It is a simple idea of in and out. Imports are brought in. Exports are sent out.

International trade can improve the standard of living for people around the world. A country can meet many needs through importing and exporting. Importing and exporting create new jobs. Yet, there are challenges too! Sometimes importing and exporting create competition at home.

Many times, things can be made for cheaper wages in other countries. Also, these countries are not subject to the same taxes that U.S. businesses pay. What is the effect? The prices of those products made in other countries may be much less than those same products made in the United States. Which products do you think people will want to buy?

Importing and exporting can be both helpful and harmful. We will learn about strategies used to control international trade in later issues. For now, can you name a product that is imported to the United States? Can you name one that is exported from the United States?

title: Wars and Depression
text:
World War I, the Great Depression, and World War II were trying times for the United States of America. Many men and women died in the line of duty for their country. This week, let's take a look at how Pennsylvania fared through these trying times.

World War I

In 1914, war broke out in Europe among many fighting nations. The United States tried to stay neutral. Neutral means that you do not take one side or the other. But Germany would not stop blowing up our ships!

Finally, we got angry and joined the Allied Powers in 1917. It was the U.S., England, France, Italy and Russia fighting the Central Powers. These countries were Germany, Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire. About 325,000 Pennsylvania sailors, soldiers and Marines fought in the war. Most fought in France.

Hundreds of women served as nurses. Here in Pennsylvania, our steel industry played a big part in the war effort. Our factories were used to make guns, ships and tanks. Women worked in the factories. We became the top shipbuilding state. The Allied Powers finally defeated the Central Powers in 1918, ending World War I.

Prohibition: 13-Year Failure

Many religious leaders in the United States were convinced that drinking alcohol was the root of all crime in this country. In 1920, an amendment (the 18th) was added to the U.S. Constitution to make the buying and selling of liquor illegal. But it didn't work—people just bought it outside the law and drank even more! Illegal bars called "speakeasies" opened. Sometimes, drinkers made their own liquor at home and many people died of alcohol poisoning. Also, mobsters took over the illegal liquor industry and crime actually increased!

Finally, in 1933, Prohibition was repealed (officially taken back) and many people were happy.

The Great Depression

You've read that the stock market crashed on Oct. 29, 1929. But just what is the stock market? Stocks are shares, or parts of ownership, in various companies. The "Roaring '20s" were good times for this country. Many people bought stock in many companies. They hoped to get even richer as the prices of these shares rose. In October 1929, for several reasons, the prices of stock began to fall. People grew worried. They began to sell their stocks that month.

Finally, the prices fell to the very bottom because so many people sold their stock. The stock market had crashed, or broken down.
