This was the beginning of many years of hard times for the people of this country. Many banks failed. Most people could not afford to buy things. Companies laid off workers. Eight out of 10 Pennsylvania miners and steelworkers were out of work. The Great Depression had begun. A depression is a time when people are out of work and business is slow.

World War II

Dec. 7, 1941—Pearl Harbor Day

By 1939, the Second World War had already begun in Europe. Germany and Japan were trying to conquer the whole world! Again, the United States tried to stay neutral. But again, the enemy would not let us. The Japanese bombed our ships stationed in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on Dec. 7, 1941. We were plunged into another world war.

This time, the Allied Forces were the United States, England, France and, later, the Soviet Union. The Axis Powers were Germany, Italy and Japan. Adolf Hitler of Germany was truly the worst of the "bad guys." You'll read in years to come of the Holocaust, when millions of Jews and others were murdered by Hitler.

More than 1 million Pennsylvania men and women served in this war, second in number only to New York. Our state provided more than 100 generals. Thirty-two Pennsylvanians, more than in any other state, won the Medal of Honor, our nation's highest military honor.

Miners and steelworkers were no longer unemployed. They worked long and hard. They produced coal, steel, cement, ships, food, clothing and weapons. Our state was the largest producer of rifles and ammunition. More steel was produced in Pennsylvania than in Germany and Japan combined!

The Great Depression had ended, but nearly 100,000 Pennsylvanians were killed or wounded in World War II.

What is Rationing?

Rationing was done during WWII to establish a fair way to give out meat, sugar, shoes, gasoline, tires and automobiles. The plants that manufactured these items were focused on producing food for soldiers and sailors. The plants also manufactured ships, weapons, tanks and other items to fight the war.

Coupon books full of ration tickets were issued to every family according to its size. You not only had to have the money to purchase an item, but you also had to have the correct number of ration coupons. Farmers were allowed extra coupons to purchase gasoline and vehicles because they had to grow the food to feed those who were fighting as well as those at home. Pennsylvania farmers played an important role during WWII. The motto for the folks back home was, "Use it up, wear it out, make it do, or do without!"

title: Clarity of Expression: FDR and the Four Freedoms
text:
For most people around the world, the years of economic depression and war between 1929 and 1945 were dark and dangerous. Resources such as food, clothing and fuel were in short supply. Families were often torn apart as parents looked for work, served in the armed forces, or as children were sent to safe, sheltered areas. It was a time of stress and hardship, when people desperately looked to leaders for safety and hope. In the United States, that leader was Franklin D. Roosevelt, our 32nd president who served from 1933 to 1945.

During that time of chaos, on Jan. 6, 1941, President Roosevelt delivered to Congress a historic speech, which we now call the Four Freedoms Speech. After years of economic depression, his words were not angry. When world war was happening, his tone was not fierce or mean. But knowing that there were still darker days of war to come for many, he spoke with passion about peace, good fortune, safety, and about the freedoms that humans everywhere deserve. "In the future days," Roosevelt said, "we look forward to a world founded upon four essential human freedoms." Even today those four freedoms are essential (important). Can you list them? They are: the freedom of speech and expression, the freedom of worship for every person, the freedom from wants such as hunger and lack of shelter and the freedom from fear.

How are we doing? Have we achieved those freedoms for everyone? Everywhere?

To read or listen to the entire speech, with the permission of a parent or teacher go to www.americanhetoric.com. To see the paintings by Norman Rockwell inspired by the Four Freedoms go to www.archives.gov

title: Keeping Records
text:
Back in the old days, they were called "diaries." Now the most common term is "journal." Whatever you call it, keeping a record of your life is a good idea. You can keep your journal in a bound book with blank pages, or a loose-leaf notebook (so later you can throw those pages away you wish you hadn't written!), or on a computer so you can keep your thoughts "pass protected."

A journal is a good place to sort out your feelings and remember friendships and experiences. It's also a good place to state your resolutions and goals — the short-term goals and the long-term goals.

You've lived a lot of years. Have you written down your funniest, scariest and saddest experiences? Write things like what your mother's eyes looked like when she found out about that fib you told. Describe the sunset you saw on March 12, 2012. Write about that lump in your throat when you took a plate of homemade cookies to that neighbor down the street. Those are the things you will love to go back and read when you become an adult.

Years from now when you go back and read what you've written, you'll discover a whole new friend — yourself! Not only that, someday your great-great grandchildren will enjoy reading what you did as a kid.

title: WWII Homefront Heroines
text:
The men who went off to fight the Nazis (Hitler's Germans) were not the only heroes of World War II. Back home, thousands of American women were called upon to join the war effort, too. They were defense workers, building ships, aircraft and weapons. The women who worked in factories during the war were called "Homefront Heroines." One such home front operation was the Eldred National Munitions Company in Eldred, McKean County. During the war, about 1,500 people worked there, 95 percent of them women. They made thousands of bombs, grenades and mortar shells.

You know how sparks fly between you and another person when you rub your foot on the carpet then touch his arm? That's called "static electricity." The workers at this plant had to wear white cotton uniforms with rubber buttons and special shoes, all designed to reduce the risk of making static electricity, because those sparks would make the plant blow up. What a dangerous job! Later, they were given Army Ordnance uniforms, which they proudly wore to places like church and parades.

The women earned between 35 and 50 cents an hour; the men earned 75 cents an hour. They were all proud to be part of the Allied Powers' defeat of the Central Powers in World War II.

title: What is a Victory Garden?
text: Hundreds of thousands of Pennsylvanians planted gardens during WWII to grow needed food. As more people grew their own food, commercial farms could send more food to those fighting overseas. They were called "victory gardens" because the war had united all citizens in a spirit of positive thinking. Throughout the country, approximately 40 percent of all the produce we ate during the war years was grown in victory gardens. Some of those same gardens remain today. They're devoted mostly to flowering plants and are kept as WWII memorials. Tourists visit victory gardens all over the country.

title: Do You Have a Nose for Wildlife?
text:
No, we don't mean, "Can you smell skunks?" It's easy to get excited about spotting various forms of wildlife in the woods of Pennsylvania. There's so much to see and hear in our state. But developing the ability to identify wildlife by smell is a whole experience in itself.

Here are some common forms of plant life for you to look for. They all have pleasant aromas:

wild cherry (bark)

sassafras (bark)

spice bush (bark)

wild mint (leaves)

sweet fern (leaves)

sweet cicely (roots)

hemlock (needles)

wild garlic (roots)

If you're in an area where picking small sprigs of plants is permitted, try an experiment. Pick some sprigs and take them home. Crush them slightly while they're fresh and put each in a small paper bag. Make a game of testing your friends and family members to see how close they can come to identifying at least eight plants by smell alone. Have additional sprigs in small plastic bags and learn to identify them by sight as well. Have fun!

title: Design Your Poster
text: In the space provided here, draw a poster or advertisement to gain U.S. military support in 1917. Make your advertisement an attention-getting, eye-catching way to convince young men to fight in Europe.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you’re a kid in 2100 and you’re looking back 100 years. Your cyber teacher has given you an assignment to write about a technology that is no longer used, why it was replaced, and what new technology replaced it. For instance, you could write about how wheels were replaced by anti-gravity thrusters. Pick anything we use now and tell us how it will be replaced in the future. Use your imagination!

title: Best Farmland in America!
text:
We have milk! We have ice cream! We have lumber! Get a load of our cattle, hogs and sheep! Pennsylvania is the third-largest producer of eggs in the nation and No. 1 in mushrooms! And have you ever eaten better apples, grapes, pears, peaches or cherries? We're first in pretzels, potato chips and yummy chocolate! But it wasn't always so.

Agricultural societies and activities had been founded in Pennsylvania prior to World War II. People here have always known what rich, valuable farmland we live on. The Grange (a society for farmers) was organized, and country fairs were popular. The Agricultural College of Pennsylvania, (later renamed Pennsylvania State or Penn State) was founded. The State Farm Show was a popular event in early Pennsylvania.

But following World War II, farming wasn't all that popular. Equipment became expensive. Ranchers from Texas moved in and bought 9,000 acres as a place to bring their cattle and fatten them up for market. Thousands of small farms were abandoned. Many housing sites were built on them. We had used all our energy making materials for the war. Then in the 1950 and '60s, methods of farming began to improve. Transportation also improved because of better roads. Many small farms joined together to make big farms. There were fewer actual farmers, but production increased in giant leaps and bounds!

Today, we can boast about being "the largest producer of . . ." because of our rich farmland and the agricultural men and women who take such pride in what they do. The beautiful, rolling hills of Pennsylvania farmland are a reality. Go to any store where picture postcards are sold, and you'll find our commonwealth—famous for its covered bridges and its lovely farmland. In this issue of Pennsylvania Studies Weekly, we hope you'll learn a little bit more about both.

title: Boom to Bust, and Back Again
text:
You may have heard people compare the recent economic recession (2007-2009) to the Great Depression of the 1930s. But what some people call the "Great Recession" actually had more in common with a depression in the 1890s and something called "boom and bust."

In the early 1890s, the U.S. economy grew quickly ("boomed") but couldn't keep growing at that rate. When many companies and the housing market failed, there was an economic "bust." The railroad industry had been booming since the end of the Civil War, but in the 1890s more than 150 railroad companies closed. Other industries that depended on the railroads closed, and many people lost their jobs. Over 500 banks closed. Thousands of unemployed men marched to Washington, D.C., in 1894 to demand that the government take action to help families. Unemployment was over 10 percent for most of the 1890s. About one of every ten people had no job.

In the recent recession, the housing market slumped after several "boom" years. Some automakers went out of business and others filed for bankruptcy. The economy went "bust," just as it did in the 1890s. Hundreds of banks and thousands of businesses closed. The unemployment rate was about 8 percent — about one of every twelve people had no job.

Make a chart or Venn diagram that compares these two events in history.

title: Nature’s Bounty
text:
No longer viewed only as "that coal state," Pennsylvania is now known for its beautiful and productive farmland. Tourists are pouring into our state every year to see firsthand the unusual farming methods of the Pennsylvania Dutch.

M-m-m-mushrooms!

This delicious treat has been growing in America for only 100 years. But it's been enjoyed for centuries all over the world. In ancient times, Egyptian pharaohs and Roman emperors forbade the commoner from eating mushrooms. They were reserved for kings and noblemen only. Later on, they decided the mushroom had strengthening powers and fed this "food of the gods" to soldiers going into battle. The Chinese called the mushroom "the divine fruit of mortality." Did you know that over 800 million pounds of mushrooms are produced in the United States every year? And more than half of them come from a five-square-mile area in Pennsylvania known as Kennett Square near West Chester. Kennett Square is called the "Mushroom Capital of America."

Mushrooms are very nutritious. So if you must eat pepperoni pizza, at least say, "Double mushrooms, please!"

Is What We Eat Important?

Have you ever seen a Doritos® tree? A Ding Dong® plant? How about a pepperoni pizza bush? Silly, huh? Here in Pennsylvania, our farmers produce wonderful, nutritious food. The "junk food" we eat is made from many things farmed here. It goes through many changes and becomes processed (canned, packaged or frozen). And the more a food is processed, the less nutritious it is and the less good it is for you.

Let's take a look at the food guide produced by the USDA (United States Department of Agriculture). It's an easy way to show the groups of foods that make up a good diet.

Bread, Cereal, Rice and Pasta Group

This group gives you plenty of carbohydrates, B vitamins and iron. This is where you get your energy. Try to eat whole grains as often as you can.

Fruit and Vegetable Group

You get tons of vitamins and minerals from carrots, tomatoes, broccoli and spinach. Fruit is easy to find in Pennsylvania, because we grow so much of it! Vitamins A and C, carbs and fiber are the big pluses in this group. Half of the items on your plate should be fruits and veggies.

Milk, Yogurt and Cheese Group

Dairy foods are important because of calcium, but try choose lower-fat items. Kids your age need about three cups a day from this group.

Meat, Poultry, Fish, Beans, Eggs and Nuts Group

Talk about choices! These foods are produced all over Pennsylvania, and you'll need them for a super-important nutrient: proteins. Be sure to get two to three servings a day.

Fats, Oils and Sweets Group

This may be sad news, but your body only needs a small amount of foods from this group. Cut way down on those Twinkies® and Snickers®.

title: Take a Covered Bridge Tour!
text:
Most visitors to Pennsylvania can hardly wait to take a driving tour of our wooden bridges. The most popular area is Lancaster County. See if you can coax your family to jump in the car and take off this weekend for a tour of our wonderful covered bridges.

1. Pinetown Bridge Lancaster County, 133 feet long, built in 1867

2. Sporting Hill Bridge Lancaster County, 96 feet long, built in 1874

3. Landis Mill Bridge Lancaster County, 53 feet long, built in 1873

4. Kurtz's Mill Bridge Lancaster County, 94 feet long, built in 1876

Plus, there are many more!

title: Specialization and Interdependence
text:
Imagine a day in the life of a bread baker. First, the baker buys the wheat seeds. Then he plants the seeds and takes care of the farm until the wheat is ready to be harvested. After harvesting the wheat, the baker grinds it into flour. He uses the flour to make the dough and then bakes the bread. But he is not done yet! After the bread is baked, he has to package it, write the advertisements and manage the store that sells the bread. How could one person possibly do all those tasks? That poor bread baker would not have a very successful business because he would be exhausted and too busy focusing on things besides baking the bread. That is exactly why businesses specialize to produce one type of product or provide one certain service.

Thanks to specialization, today's bread baker is only responsible for making the dough and baking his delicious bread. So, who does the rest of the work? Many other people including farmers, mill workers, people in the packaging factory, advertisers and store employees all play an important role in getting the bread to the consumers. They each specialize, or do one specific job, to make the product—bread. Specializing allows companies to make more product in less time and improve the quality of the product. Because one specific worker (or a small group of workers) focuses on each step of production, the baker has more time to focus on his special talent—bread baking.

So what would happen if one of the people along the way didn't do his or her job well or didn't do it at all? What if the packaging factory didn't make any bags for the bread? The bread would get stale before it made it to the store. Then no one would buy the bread, and the farmer, baker, mill workers, advertisers and store employees would all lose income. All the workers in the process are interdependent. That means each worker relies or depends on the others for help or resources to make the final product.

When you think of specialization and interdependence, you might picture an assembly line. Each worker on the line has a job to do before the product moves on to the next worker. This increases the amount of product made because each person is responsible for only one part or phase of production. Therefore the work gets done more quickly. The worker gets faster and more efficient at his or her job by only focusing on that one duty. In an assembly line it is very important that each worker does his or her part. Everyone else is counting on the other people to help get to the finish. Now that takes cooperation!

title: Hershey/Dutch Country
text:
January brings the Pennsylvania Farm Show in Harrisburg. This week-long event offers something for everyone. It's the biggest farm show of its kind. If it's beautiful handmade quilts you want, take in the Gordonville Auction in Lancaster County in March and the Mennonite Relief Sale in Dauphin County in April. Chow down on great oyster stew and strawberry pie while you're there!

Enjoy a fireworks show at the Festival of the Candles in Lititz, Lancaster County in July. The Mifflin Fair (small) and the Shippensburg Fair (large) in Cumberland County, during the same month, both have a real "down home" feeling. August brings the Lebanon Area Fair. The Buchanan Valley Picnic in Adams County is special. It celebrates the life of Mary Jemison, a "white Indian squaw" of 1758. If you love yummy things made from corn, head for the Corn Festival in Shippensburg in August. (A festival is a celebration like a fair, auction or picnic.) The week-long York Fair in September is huge and fun-filled. It's the oldest fair around!

Later that month, take in the Harvest Festival in Lebanon County. Watch the oxen perform while you enjoy a Pennsylvania Dutch dinner. If chicken ("hinkel" in German) is your choice, better go to the Hinkelfest in Fredericksburg. Yum! Doesn't something like the Falmouth Goat Races sound fun? It's in Lancaster in October. So is the National Apple Harvest Festival in Adams County. Catch the Heidlersburg Beef and Oyster Dinner in Adams County in November. You have to see the "Pickle Drop" on New Year's Eve in Dillsburg to believe it! Have a great time celebrating in this region!

title: Why were Pennsylvania’s bridges covered?
text: In the 1800s, there was a great need for bridges because of Pennsylvania's many rivers and creeks. Farmers needed to move their produce, and travelers needed to move west. They could transport by ferry, or they could build bridges. There was certainly enough timber here to build them of wood! But wood rots. So the logical thing for Lewis Wernwag, Theodore Burr, Menander Wood and the other bridge designers to do was to cover their bridges to slow down the rotting process.

title: Mushrooms
text:
What exactly is a mushroom? Is it a plant? Is it an animal? Actually, it's neither one. It's a fungus. It has elements of both animals and plants. It can't get up and walk around like an animal, but it eats organic matter, just like we do! The mushroom has no chlorophyll like a plant, but it grows in the ground. It reproduces with spores.

Did you ever wonder what would happen if there were no fungi? Well, we'd be knee-deep in corpses and dead stuff! The Earth could not function without fungi (along with bacteria) with their digestive systems, dissolving dead and decaying matter. Most trees and many plants couldn't grow without their fungi partnerships. Antibiotics, that medicine your mom gives you for sore throats, wouldn't exist. Yeast is a one-celled fungus. No yeast means no bread.

Pretend you are lost in the woods of the Hershey-Dutch Region. It's getting late, you're starving, and you spot some mushrooms growing along the trail. Should you stop, pick some, wash off the dirt in a stream and eat them? Never! There are many poisonous varieties. If you eat one of those, you could die or be so sick that you wish you could die. Eat only the mushrooms from your refrigerator or at restaurants. This is very important.

We want this fungi to remain a "fun guy" in your lives!

title: Fun Facts
text: The male platypus is born with spurs on its ankles that contain venom. They rarely attack humans, but it’s a painful sting!

text:

title: Taking a Closer Look at the U.S. Constitution
text:
Do you know where the U.S. Constitution was signed? At the bottom, of course! Seriously, the Constitution was signed right here in Pennsylvania (Philadelphia, to be exact). Just how much do you know about the U.S. Constitution? Let's take a closer look at this grand old document.

A constitution is a written list describing the duties of government and the rights of people. The U.S. Constitution is the supreme law of our country and the blueprint for our government. It defines the basic responsibilities of the federal (national) government, organizes the three branches of government (legislative, executive and judicial), and guarantees our basic rights. Whew! That's a great deal of work!

The Constitution also performs a tricky juggling act, balancing government powers in order to protect both the demands of the many and the rights of the few. It binds the 50 states together with a central government, while still allowing individual states to govern themselves. You could think of the Constitution as a police officer who lays down the law, or as your own personal bodyguard who daily defends your freedoms.

The U.S. Constitution was born during the hot summer of 1787, when 55 representatives from the original states met at Independence Hall in Philadelphia to create a new government for our young nation. Hammering out a constitution was no easy task. These representatives came from different backgrounds—there were lawyers, farmers, merchants and teachers, to name a few—and they each brought very different ideas with them. A great deal of arguing and grumbling occurred. There were conflicts between big and small states and Northern and Southern states, and there were disagreements about the size and power of the federal government. But the representatives' common goal was to build a stronger country, and their conflicts cooled into compromises (an agreement in which each side gives up a little). The Constitution of the United States was the result of their efforts. It was approved by a majority of the states in 1788 and took effect in 1789.

Our country has been governed by the Constitution for more than 200 years, making it the world's oldest written constitution still in effect. But that doesn't mean it has always remained the same. Over the years, the Constitution has occasionally been amended (added to or adjusted) to further explain government's responsibilities and to increase protection of our freedoms.

Shortly after the Constitution took effect, a group of 10 amendments was added. These first 10 amendments are known as the Bill of Rights. They list several basic freedoms that cannot be taken away from any U.S. citizen, such as freedom of speech, freedom of the press, freedom of religion, freedom of peaceful assembly and many other rights that allow each of us to live our lives the way we want. The Constitution is only amended to correct very rare and critical issues. For example, the 13th Amendment (adopted in 1865) outlawed slavery in the United States. And the 19th Amendment (added in 1920) guaranteed the right to vote to women across the country. So far, the Constitution has been amended 27 times.

The Constitution of the United States is not just some dusty old document penned on crumbling parchment paper. It is a respected, powerful guardian that provides the government organization and the freedoms that make the United States of America one of the greatest countries in the world.

title: "Power Packs" Fight Hunger
text:
Most kids can't wait for school to get out on Friday afternoon. They love heading home for the weekend and dread coming back to school on Monday morning. But for some Pennsylvania kids, the weekend means only one thing: hunger. For these children, the free school breakfasts and lunches they receive are the only regular meals they can count on, so when school ends on Friday, so does their chance to get a good meal.

Some great Pennsylvania heroes have stepped in to help these children get through what could be some very hungry weekends. The Central Pennsylvania Food Bank sponsors something called the Power Packs Program. The program gives out special backpacks filled with kid-friendly foods that children can take home over the weekend to help them get enough to eat. Breakfast cereals, granola bars, raisins, crackers, refried beans, canned tuna, soup and instant mashed potatoes are just a few of the items included in the backpacks.

Most of those who take backpacks home over the weekend are children who already receive free school breakfast and lunch, but who may not have anything to eat at home over the weekend. Children get the backpacks from special Kids Café locations where they can go during the week to get a free meal. The children use the backpacks for school during the week and then stop at the Kids Café on Friday afternoon to pick up enough food to last through the weekend.

Food for the backpacks is donated by Pennsylvania businesses and by people who want to help those in need. About 2,500 children take Power Packs home with them each Friday afternoon.

If you or someone you know is going hungry, don't be afraid to let your teacher or principal know. If you want to help, ask your parents if you can make a donation to the food bank in your area. Together, we can make a difference in the fight against hunger.

title: Pennsylvania Government
text:
We are fortunate to live in wonderful Pennsylvania. We're governed by men and women of integrity and character. This week's history lesson helps us understand how the law-making process works in our commonwealth.

A Government by the People, for the People

Like all of the 50 states, Pennsylvania has its own government. It is located in Harrisburg. The head of Pennsylvania's state government is the governor. Every four years, citizens of Pennsylvania elect a governor. The governor administers (manages or runs) more than 20 different agencies or departments. Like the president, the governor can be elected for a second term, but not for more.

The governor makes decisions about how the state should be run. He or she decides on such things as new laws and how to spend state money. The governor also appoints people to certain positions in the government. Pennsylvania also has a lieutenant (loo-TEN-ant) governor who is elected to office. The lieutenant governor helps the governor run the state and leads the meetings of the state Senate (which has 50 members). Memorize these three branches of the government. You will be hearing about them many times throughout your lives.

Legislative Branch

The members of the legislative branch write the laws for Pennsylvania. Citizens of Pennsylvania elect these men and women to represent them in the state government. At the beginning of each year, these Senators (elected for four-year terms) and Representatives (elected for two-year terms) all meet in Harrisburg in the capitol building. They work together to make laws for the people of Pennsylvania.

Executive Branch

The people in this branch work to administer (carry out) the laws of the state. They make sure, for instance, that the roads are kept up, that schools are run properly and that the state has enough money.

The Three-Legged Stool

Pretend you won a contest for "Pennsylvania Governor for a Day." You start the day by sending your whole school to Disney World for spring break. Then you order the state police to arrest that bully down the street from you. Next you order the school cafeteria to supply ice cream sundaes for afternoon break every day. Wow! Sounds like fun!

Have you ever tried to sit on a two-legged stool? You can't. You'd tip over. Your stool needs at least three legs. The founders of our U.S. government had the same idea. They created a three-legged government - executive, legislative and judicial. The three legs form a system called "checks and balances." If you, as governor, sent your school to Disney World, the people in Congress would gang up on you. They would go to the state supreme court and complain, "That's the craziest, dumbest idea we ever heard!" The court would agree. This is how all three branches work together to balance and keep each other in "check."

Judicial Branch

The men and women of this branch make up the Pennsylvania Supreme Court and all the other courts of our state. They decide if the laws made by the legislature are constitutional.

They also decide what punishment a person should receive for breaking the law. Judges do this in court cases.

Two-Party System

Both parties have good qualities. While the two belief systems often seem to oppose each other, the ideal government operates best when Republicans and Democrats work together for the common good while still keeping their individual personalities - much like the ideal marriage. Look again at the eagle. Can you imagine this bird with only one wing? It takes both the left wing and the right wing for this mighty bird to take flight!

Republican Party

This party is nicknamed the GOP for "grand old party." It was founded in 1854 when the issue of slavery forced a division between the existing Whig and Democratic-Republican parties. The new party was founded on the idea of limiting government's role in the people's lives. Abraham Lincoln was the party's first president.

Democratic Party

Thomas Jefferson founded the Democratic Party in 1792. The Populist Party was the popular party of that time. The new party was called the "party of the common man," and its official name was the Democratic-Republicans. In 1800, Jefferson was elected as the first Democratic president. The name was shortened to Democratic Party.

title: From an Idea to a Law
text:
Here's an example of how a future voter just like you was responsible for an idea becoming a law in Ohio, our neighbor state to the west.

In 1991, Jacob Mercer, a fourth-grader in Fairborn, near Dayton, discovered that Ohio did not have a state reptile. The Buckeye State had a state flower (red carnation), a state animal (white-tailed deer — same as ours!), and even a state drink (tomato juice) — but no reptile.

Jacob suggested that the black racer be made Ohio's state reptile. He shared his idea with his state senator, Merle Grace Kearns. Senator Kearns agreed to introduce a bill in the Senate. The bill became known as Senate Bill 250. Jacob even gave a speech before the Senate. The Senate approved Bill 250. Then they sent the bill to the House of Representatives. The members of the House listened to discussions about the bill and approved it. Then the bill was approved by (then) Governor Voinovich.

On Aug. 25, 1995, the bill became a law, and Ohio has a state reptile — the black racer! (Can you think of an idea you'd like to see become a law in Pennsylvania?)

title: Conscience
text:
Have you ever used a compass? A compass is a handheld instrument with an arrow that always points north. A compass helps people figure out which direction they should go. If a hiker wandered deep into the woods without a compass, he might soon find himself lost and in danger. Compasses help people stay on course and avoid getting lost.

Did you know you have your own built-in "compass" that guides you and helps you stay on course? This compass is called your conscience. Your conscience is a sense, instinct or feeling you get inside that helps you judge between right and wrong. Your conscience prompts you to do things that are right. Just as a compass always points north, your conscience will always point out good and steer you away from bad.

When you follow your conscience, it will lead you to be honest, kind, helpful and responsible. It will help you make good decisions. A person relies on his conscience to help him make all kinds of decisions — even decisions about how to vote during elections. Your conscience may prompt you to vote for candidates and issues you believe are right and good.

Following your conscience can help you make good choices and can help keep you out of trouble.

title: A Constitution for Pennsylvania
text:
Did you know Pennsylvania has its very own constitution? In fact, each of the 50 states has its own constitution. In the same way the U.S. Constitution outlines how our country will be run, the Pennsylvania Constitution outlines how our state will be run. Pennsylvania's Constitution guarantees citizens' rights, defines the structure of government and outlines how elections, taxes and other government duties will be managed.

Pennsylvania has actually had five constitutions that have governed the state through its long history. The first constitution was written in 1776, and the most recent was drafted in 1968. Each new constitution has simply updated and modernized the constitution before it. Some of the changes made by these updates include creating the State Senate, developing a public education system, creating the office of Lieutenant Governor and allowing the governor to seek reelection to a second term of office.

Our state constitution has been updated several times, but we don't need to change the whole constitution every time we want to adjust or add something. Lawmakers and voters can work together to amend (change or add to) our existing state constitution.

The first Pennsylvania State Constitution worked so well that the Founding Fathers actually borrowed ideas from it when they wrote the U.S. Constitution! Our state constitution helps our state run smoothly, defends our liberties, and helps make Pennsylvania a great place to live.

title: CapiTAL vs. CapiTOL
text:
We don't know why they made it so confusing for us, but the actual building is the capiTOL. The city in which the capiTOL is found is called the capiTAL. To help you remember, close your eyes and think of taking a trip to a capiTAL on the l-o-n-g roads from your house to Harrisburg or Washington, D.C. Those roads are long like the sides of the letter "A."

Think of the building itself. Your dad is looking for a parking spot so that you can all get out and go inside to tour the capitol building. He's getting madder and madder as he keeps driving around the capitol in circles to find a place to park. The circles he keeps driving in remind you of the letter "O." Does that help?

title: George Clymer: Pennsylvania Patriot
text:
George Clymer was a famous Founding Father who lived right here in Pennsylvania. George was born in Philadelphia on March 16, 1739. His parents died when he was very young, leaving him to be raised by a generous uncle. George was kind and smart. He enjoyed reading, science and art.

George grew up to become a businessman, politician and great patriot. He was one of the first to recommend the United States fight for independence from England, and he signed the Declaration of Independence. George also served faithfully at the Constitutional Convention, where he signed the newly-written U.S. Constitution.

The British army disliked George and his patriotism. Once while George was away from home, British soldiers marched to his house. They destroyed all of his furniture and many other belongings. His frightened children and wife, Elizabeth, hid in the nearby woods.

George served in the Pennsylvania legislature, was one of the first continental treasurers, helped negotiate a treaty with the Cherokee and Creek Indians, was the first president of the Philadelphia Bank and was a leader of the Philadelphia Academy of Fine Arts and the Philadelphia Agricultural Society. George died in 1813 at age 73.

text: In a few decades, Studies Weekly might be looking back to the early years of the new millennium. What kinds of articles do you think you might see? What will your children find interesting about the time you live in now? Think of new technologies, important events, changes in traditions, advances in the sciences or influential people. Be creative—you can’t go wrong!

title: Bushkill Falls
text:
One of Pennsylvania's Most Beautiful Wonders

His neighbors laughed at young Charlie Peters when he decided in 1904 to open a tourist attraction. He wanted people to come and see the beautiful waterfalls on his family's property in the Poconos. "Who would pay money to see waterfalls?" they asked. Even Charlie's family thought that it was a silly idea.

But Charlie was convinced that people would come once he built trails and bridges over which to hike. Charlie pounded a sign in the ground that read "The Niagara of Pennsylvania—admission 10 cents."

Pretty soon, his family and neighbors stopped laughing. Charlie worked all his life at improving the grounds. His business was nearly wiped out in 1925 when all the forest around the falls was ruined by a devastating fire. Charlie worked hard to build the area back up and continued on until his death in 1949. Bushkill Falls is still in the Peters family.

Bushkill Falls is among the state's most famous attractions. When you visit, try to see all eight waterfalls. Bushkill Falls is about 1,200 feet above sea level, and the drop from the top of the highest waterfall to the bottom of the Lower Gorge is nearly 300 feet. Hiking to the falls is as much fun as the falls themselves. There are dozens of trails and bridges. You will stand staring in silence at your first sight of the 100-foot Main Falls.

Also, check out the Pennsylvania Wildlife Exhibit and the Native American Exhibit on the grounds. You may even fish in Twin Lakes or take a paddle-boat ride. How about some miniature golf? There are also some fun shops, including the Fudge Kitchen for a sweet treat.

Bushkill Falls is truly one of Pennsylvania's—and the country's—most beautiful natural wonders.

title: Play it Safe
text:
Do you enjoy playing sports? Sports and other physical activities are great ways to stay in shape and have fun with your friends. While playing sports is good for your body, it is important to learn to play in a safe way to keep from being injured. Sports injuries are very common, but there are things you can do to keep yourself from getting hurt:

Wear the right gear. This means that you should wear proper pads, helmets, mouth guards, and face guards needed for the sport you are playing.

Get flexible. Stretch out your muscles both before and after you play to keep your muscles and ligaments flexible.

Strengthen your muscles. Do conditioning exercises, such as running, jumping rope, or biking, to make your muscles stronger before you play your sport.

Take breaks. It is important to rest during a game or practice to let your body recover.

Stop if you feel pain. If you feel that you have injured yourself, tell your coach and take a break. Don't keep playing through the pain or you could make the injury worse.

Play it safe in hot weather. Drink plenty of water, wear light clothing, and don't exercise during the hottest part of the day.

See your doctor. It is important to have a doctor's exam before you begin playing a new sport or if you are injured while playing a sport.

Playing sports is a great way to keep your body healthy. Be sure to play it safe so that you can enjoy your favorite sports for many years to come.

title: Pennsylvania's Wonders
text:
Which is best: a man-made or a natural wonder? Pennsylvania has so many of both types, it's easy to find many wonders of Pennsylvania. This week, we'll take a look at just a few.

Wonder of Roller Coasters

Hold onto your hot dogs and snow cones! You're about to turn upside down on one of Pennsylvania's many roller coasters. Throughout the years, Pennsylvania has been home to over 190 roller coasters. Today, Pennsylvania's theme parks still bring a lot of visitors to our state.

This roller coaster is the oldest operating roller coaster in the United States. It's called "Leap the Dips," and you may ride it at Lakemont Park, Altoona.

Wonder of Carousels

It doesn't matter how old we get. We all love the merry-go-round. Just ask your parents and grandparents. Did you ever wonder who carved those beautiful horses? Only a small handful of Pennsylvania and New York craftsmen were responsible for all the wooden horses you see on the carousel. These master carvers came from Germany, Russia and Austria. The "Philadelphia-style" horses were made by Gustav Dentzel and John Zalar. The original horses are worth many thousands of dollars today—a true man-made wonder for Pennsylvania!

Fallingwater

What is so special about this building? It was designed by the famous architect Frank Lloyd Wright. It was built as a residence in 1935 in Mill Run. It's open to the public and is so famous that thousands of people go there every year to take tours. It's a special design that blends its natural surroundings right into the building itself. The building is both a natural and a man-made Pennsylvania wonder!

Famous Gardens

Want to visit another place that combines both natural and man-made wonders? Ask your folks to take the family to Longwood Gardens in Kennett Square. There, you'll find 20 outdoor gardens, 20 indoor gardens, 11,000 different types of plants, spectacular fountains, musical theater, fireworks displays and many things for kids. You'll like the Indoor Children's Garden. There are programs called Children's Storytimes, Children's Garden Adventures and the Summer Ice Cream Concert series. Grab a special kids' map and find all the awesome things to do!

Cathedral of Learning

What are schools like in other countries? The tour guides in this beautiful 42-story building in Pittsburgh are waiting to tell you all about them! Each classroom will take you to an exciting foreign place like Ireland, Austria or Lebanon. You will find at least 23 classrooms with people who love to take kids on tours. Besides being an exciting place to visit, the building itself is one of Pennsylvania's beautiful man-made wonders.

title: The Adventures of Miss Liberty
text:
Man-Made Wonder of Philadelphia

1885 – It's time for my first trip out of Pennsylvania! I traveled by train to New Orleans for the World Industrial and Cotton Exposition and to help promote national unity.

1893–1915 — I traveled to Chicago for the World's Fair, to Atlanta, and then back south again to Charleston for more expositions (public shows to display items of interest — me, in this case!). I went to Boston to celebrate the Battle of Bunker Hill, then to St. Louis for another exposition. Then I went back home to Philadelphia to parade the streets of my hometown. After that, I went all the way across the country to San Francisco for another exposition. Everybody loved me, but, whew, was I worn out by 1915!

1926 — I helped celebrate the 150th birthday (sesquicentennial) of our nation. Microphones were placed around me, and the mayor's wife tapped me with a specially designed mallet.

June 1944 — It was D-Day. World War II had ended. I was tapped in a special ceremony by the mayor 12 times (the number of letters in "independence"), then seven times (the number of letters in "liberty").

1976 — I celebrated our nation's 200th birthday (bicentennial) by being moved to an outdoor pavilion across the street from Independence Hall.

I'm old and tired now, but I'm still beautiful and the "belle" of Philadelphia. I moved in 2003 to my own house, the Liberty Bell Center. I want to just hang around here and be admired by visitors from all over the world. Come on over and see me sometime. You know where to find me.

title: How Do I Read a Map?
text:
Maps can tell you a whole lot about the world. They show you which direction to travel and how to find an unknown place. But wouldn't you like to know how high the mountains are around you? And just where are those lakes and railroads? If you want to know all that and more, maps are for YOU!

These map functions will help you read a map:

Scale — On a map you'll often see: 1 inch = 1 mile. That means one inch on the map represents one mile of the land around you. Easy, huh?

Legend — What do those little pictures or symbols on a map mean? The legend is a box, usually in a corner of the map. It lists the symbols, then tells what they mean.

Grid — Many maps are arranged on a grid. See the lines going up and down the sides of the map? There are more lines at the top and bottom. Those grid lines help you locate places on the map. Grids have letters along the sides and numbers across the top and bottom.

Index — To use the grid to find a location, go to the map's index. The index lists locations with a letter and a number for each location. Find the spot on the map where that letter and number cross. For example: House — D, 9

title: Laurel Highlands
text:
Welcome to this, our last region to visit for the school year. Did we save the best region for last? People who live in the Laurel Highlands/ Southern Alleghenies Region would sure tell you that!

The best way to visit this region is by train. So hop aboard the Pennsylvanian from Altoona to Johnstown as it winds over the Alleghenies. Visit Horseshoe Curve and the Gallitzin Tunnels. See how boats (yes, boats!) crossed these mountains on the Allegheny/Portage Railroad. We've talked in the past about our "Rails-to-Trails" program in Pennsylvania. You'll see some of the greatest trails in the country in this region, so bring your bike!

If you'd rather drive, take Route 40, the trail that took the pioneers westward. Washington traveled in this area to put down the Whiskey Rebellion. On the way, he stopped in Bedford—you should, too. It's the home of 14 covered "kissing bridges." Old Bedford Village preserves the way of life of our early settlers.

Remember the French and Indian War? This is a great time of year to visit Fort Ligonier, the Bushy Run Battlefield and Fort Necessity. The tragedy of the Johnstown Flood is shown in an exhibit at the Johnstown Flood Museum. Come in the summertime and ride the raging rapids of the Youghiogheny River, swim in the lakes of our humongous state parks and plan a few days of perfect fishing. The state's largest man-made lake, Raystown, is here.

Yep! You're going to have a great time in the Laurel Highlands!

title: What four holidays originated in Pennsylvania?
text:
We've already written about two holidays in the paper: Groundhog Day and Thanksgiving. The two others are:

Memorial Day—On July 4, 1864, two Boalsburg women visited the graves of family who had died in the Civil War. They placed flowers on the graves of all soldiers in the cemetery. The custom spread and is now an annual national holiday, celebrated the fourth Monday of May.

Mother's Day—This holiday was initiated by Anna Jarvis of Philadelphia. Her mother died the second Sunday of May 1905. She fought hard for years to have that day set aside to honor all mothers. Miss Jarvis finally succeeded in 1914. The Jarvis garden was full of carnations. That's why many people wear that flower on Mother's Day: red if your mother is living, white if she's not.

title: Firefly
text:
The firefly is our state insect. Why do fireflies light up? In the first place, they're not "flies" at all. They're soft-bodied beetles. The sparkling they do may look random to us, but to other fireflies, they have special meaning. There are more than 130 species in North America alone. Each one has its own color of "lantern" and pattern of flashes. Some blink only at twilight, while others go on and on through the night. The colors of lights range from clear yellow in some species, to greenish-white or orange in others. The brightest-colored fireflies give off enough light by which to read a newspaper. It's the male that flies around and flashes to the females on the ground. The female spots a "flying suitor" she thinks is cute and sends a flashing signal to him.

He answers the call and flies in to mate with her. While most females flash in courtship, other species flash to eat. A clever female firefly of one species flashes a fake message to an unsuspecting male from another species. When he lands on the ground for what he thinks is a mating session, he is in for a surprise. The female "enemy firefly" eats him instead! Try not to think about those tricky female fireflies, and have a fun summer watching them make your summer twilights sparkle.

title: How do I give an Oral Presentation?
text:
Standing in front of a crowd and telling them what you think is not easy, but it can be done if you prepare well!

Preparing for an Oral Presentation

1. Know your audience. What you say should be directed toward them. Is it to be given in your classroom? This will make it easier!

2. How long should it be? If your teacher says 15 minutes, stick to the time.

3. What’s the topic? Did your teacher assign it? Make sure you can cover it in within the time limit.

4. Make notes. Use index cards and put them in the order you want to use them. Index cards are not so large that they cover your face. You may write your presentation on numbered pieces of paper, but do not staple the pages.

5. Practice, practice and practice some more!

Making the Oral Presentation

1. Introduction—Get the audience’s attention with the introduction. You can do this by asking a question, telling a story, using a quotation or making a statement. Once you have their attention, state your topic.

2. Body—State your main points and give information that support your main points. You may ask rhetorical questions, (questions that don’t need answers) use emotional words or repeat important information.

3. Conclusion—Repeat your main point. Conclude with something that leaves a lasting impression by asking a rhetorical question, making an emotional plea or using a quotation, story or statement.

Try It!

When you’re asked to give an oral presentation, make sure you prepare well. Organize logically. Practice, practice, practice. Good luck!

title: Pennsylvania’s Great Women
text:
Welcome to another issue of Pennsylvania Studies Weekly, the magazine that brings right to your desk the exploits of the heroic he-men who have made Pennsylvania the mega-state that it is today! This commonwealth was founded by men with brave hearts, rippling muscles and bushy beards—hey! Hold on a second! Men aren't the only people in the world, you know! What about women? Aren't there any females in the story of Pennsylvania?

Women have been working, thinking, fighting, writing and exploring right from the beginning to make this a great state in a great country. And they're still doing it! We've discussed several great Pennsylvania women in prior issues. We presented the great Iroquois matriarchy as well as Deborah Read Franklin and Sara Josepha Hale in the fall issues. Then there were Molly Pitcher, Harriet Tubman and Clara Barton, the legendary nurse who helped the Johnstown Flood victims in the winter issues. Susan B. Anthony, her suffrage sisters, and the "home front heroines" of WWII were celebrated in these spring issues. And don't forget "Miss Liberty!"

Women all over Pennsylvania today are flying planes, fighting fires, writing books, taking care of families, running companies, making laws, arresting bad guys and selling cars as well as any man. This week in Pennsylvania Studies Weekly you'll meet some women who have helped put the commonwealth on the map. Some of them are Pennsylvania natives. Other women proudly say: "I wasn't born in Pennsylvania, but I got here as fast as I could!"

title: Research Shows Madagascar Was Founded by Women
text:
Picture an ancient ship full of explorers, searching for a new land. Many people would imagine that such a ship was filled with male passengers and crew. Though many explorers were men, scientists have discovered that the founders of Madagascar were a group of 30 women who traveled a long way from their home!

Madagascar is an island off the east coast of Africa in the Indian Ocean. The women's ship traveled 5,000 miles from Indonesia to Madagascar, stranding them there. How do scientists know this? DNA researchers have studied 3,000 blood samples of people from Indonesian islands and compared them to samples from 300 people from Madagascar (called the Malagasy).

They discovered that many Malagasy have an Indonesian gene in their DNA. This gene was passed down from generation to generation of Malagasy. Computer simulations have calculated that only 30 Indonesian women were responsible for beginning the Madagascar population about 1,200 years ago. Most people from Madagascar today have a mix of Indonesian and African DNA, and are descended from these 30 women.

Researchers have also been able to trace a special chromosome that is only found in men in the Malagasy people. Can you guess where it came from? If you guessed Indonesia, you are right! It looks like a few men as well as women sailed on that ship to Madagascar so long ago.

Reference: History News Network (hnn.us)

title: “Keep My Red Couch!”
text:
This story takes place in Lebanon in the old home of a family that has lived in it for several generations. Jenny, the present generation's mom, noticed the strange happenings first. She could feel a "presence" when she went to the basement to do the laundry. The presence was so strong that it sent Jenny screaming up the stairs on several occasions. Another time, as she was bathing her daughters in the upstairs bathroom, she felt something brush against her head. Shortly after that, Jenny was locked out of her bedroom—by a lock that could only be worked from the inside. Quite frequently, all family members saw a shadow going up and down the stairs. One day, while talking to friends about the strange happenings in the house, the family realized they'd been going on only during the prior three month period. What could be causing these strange hauntings?

Then the family remembered: Grandma Mabel. Yes, that had to be it! Grandma Mabel loved her possessions. She was a devout Catholic with a large collection of Madonnas, pictures of Christ, rosaries, statuettes and other symbols of her Catholicism. She kept them all in her bedroom. Grandma Mabel sat on her favorite red couch in that room, day after day, praying for hours. "She would talk to God and to our deceased relatives. It was a regular ritual," Jenny recalled.

She wouldn't allow anyone to sit on that red couch, Jenny explained. Before she died, Grandma Mabel warned the family they were never to dispose of her sacred items or her beloved red couch. Grandma threatened she would come back to haunt the whole family if those items were ever removed.

But it had been many years since her death, and the time had come to clean out the bedroom and throw everything away . . . including the red couch. And that had been about three months earlier! Suddenly, the family had the answer to the mysterious happenings taking place in the old family home in Lebanon: Grandma Mabel had indeed kept her threat to return and haunt the family if they ever dishonored her demands!

title: Hemlock
text:
The eastern Hemlock is our official state tree. It's plain to see why. This tree can be found in every county of the state. It is most plentiful in the mountainous regions. The eastern Hemlock is large and lives for a long time. The Hemlock is one of the most graceful trees in the forest. In winter, deer love the Hemlock. They eat the tender green shoots. Often, the Hemlock is the only thing that keeps the deer alive. Many birds nest in the Hemlock's branches.

The Pennsylvania legislature adopted this tree as its own with the following words: "The Hemlock yielded to our pioneers the wood from which they built cabins . . . . It lends kindly shelter . . . . Lighted Hemlock at Christmas time dazzles the bright eyes of the child . . . a sign and symbol of faith and mortality."

title: Sharing Public Space: Susan B. Anthony and Equal Rights for All
text:
From the time she was a young girl, Susan B. Anthony believed that what was open to one person should be open to all people. As a teacher, she felt that having separate schools for girls, boys and free African Americans was not fair. She believed that the minds of all genders and races were equal and that education should be equal, too.

As Susan grew older, she joined other fights as well. She hated slavery and thought working women should be paid more money. She began fighting for women's suffrage, or the right for women to vote. She once was arrested for voting illegally and was fined $100. She wouldn't pay the fine. She said, "Trust me that as I ignore all law to help the slave, so will I ignore it all to protect an enslaved woman." Until women were allowed to vote, just like men, Susan felt they were no better off than slaves. She fought for this right until her death in 1906, but at that time, women still couldn't vote.

Susan's efforts finally paid off when the 19th Amendment to the Constitution was passed in 1920. It gave all American women the right to vote. In her honor, the amendment is also called the Susan B. Anthony Amendment.

title: Fairness and Justice
text:
Have you ever seen someone cheat on schoolwork or in a game? Or have you ever been in trouble for something you didn’t do? How did it make you feel? Have you ever yelled in frustration, “Hey, that’s not fair! I want justice?”

Fairness and justice are two related character traits that help people get along well. Fairness means treating everyone equally. Justice means supporting fair treatment for all.

Are you a good example of fairness and justice? Do you treat your friends and family fairly, or do you play favorites? Do you follow the rules, or do you cheat? Do you share things equally, or do you always take the best part?

To make the world a fair and just place, we must start by being fair and just ourselves. We can demonstrate fairness by sharing, taking turns, following rules and treating others with equal respect. We can demonstrate justice by refusing to listen to jokes that make fun of another’s race or religion, by standing up for someone who is bullied, and by making sure others aren’t excluded from activities.

Some of the famous Pennsylvania women spotlighted in this issue of Studies Weekly are great examples of justice and fairness. They overcame many of the unfair obstacles women have experienced throughout much of history and achieved many great accomplishments. As we practice being fair and just, we can bring trust, friendship and peace to our classroom and our community.

title: Great Women of Pennsylvania
text:
Here are a few past and present great Pennsylvania women. Which of you will be the great women of the future?

1. Rachel Carson

Rachel Carson from Springdale was a gifted scientist who influenced forever the use of poisonous chemicals found in our food. Rachel studied DDT, the chemical that had been routinely sprayed on American crops for many years to kill bugs. In 1962, she published a book titled "Silent Spring." In it, she told of the dangers of the deadly DDT. She took dull, scientific facts and made it easy enough for all to read and understand—even children! The federal government sat up and took notice, and eventually the laws were changed. We grow much healthier food now because of Pennsylvania's own Rachel Carson.

2. Ethel Waters

Ethel Waters was born in Pennsylvania and raised by her grandmother. She had a very tough childhood. She quit school when she was 13 to earn money cleaning houses and found time to sing at church or on "amateur nights" in local restaurants. After slowly gaining an audience and the title "Sweet Mama Stringbean," she began recording songs. She sang the blues, danced and performed in movies and vaudeville shows. She performed with other well-known musicians such as Bessie Smith, Fletcher Henderson and Duke Ellington. Eventually she became one of the highest paid performers on Broadway! In her old age she returned to gospel music and passed away in 1977.

3. Grace Kelly

Grace Kelly was born in Philadelphia in 1929 to a very wealthy family. She became a very famous movie actress in the 1950s. Grace married Prince Rainier III of Monaco and retired from acting in 1956. Princess Grace was asked many times to go back to Hollywood and act in more movies. She always refused. Grace Kelly Rainier had a stroke and died while driving her car in 1982.

4. Louisa May Alcott

Miss Alcott was born in 1832 in Germantown. She didn't spend much time in Pennsylvania, however. She moved with her family at the age of 2 to Massachusetts. Louisa is best known for her novel "Little Women." The story is mostly autobiographical (a story someone writes about his or her own life). She had many things in common with Jo in the story. She also wrote many other stories, poems and plays. Louisa died at the age of 55.

5. Nellie Bly

Miss Bly was a great investigative newspaper reporter. She once pretended to be insane in order to find out about treatment of the mentally ill. Her articles about cruelty to patients brought reforms. Her real name was Elizabeth Cochrane, and she was born near Pittsburgh in 1864. She made a trip around the world in 72 days, six hours and 11 minutes. She was looking to emulate the trip around the world taken in Jules Verne's “Around the World in 80 Days” all for the sake of an article she was researching for her newspaper.

6. Mary Cassatt

Miss Cassatt was born in 1844 in the Pittsburgh area. Mary loved art. She fell in love with painting on a visit to Paris with her parents when she was only 7. She returned to Paris as a young woman and lived there the rest of her life. Mary became friends with several struggling French male artists of that time. They were called Impressionists. Some of their names may be familiar to you, like Degas, Monet and Manet. Mary created brilliant paintings that show women attending the opera, drinking tea, reading, writing letters and playing with and caring for children.

Mary Cassatt is remembered for her ability to capture on canvas the tenderness between child and mother. Today, her paintings are sold for thousands of dollars.

7. Stephanie Kwolek

Stephanie Kwolek looks like your typical grandma, but this "little old lady" has saved the lives of hundreds of police officers and soldiers. As a child, she explored the woods of Pennsylvania with her father. After he died, she majored in chemistry at Margaret Morrison Carnegie College. She got a job at DuPont just to pay for medical school, but, while working there, she became very interested in the projects that took place. As she did her research, she discovered a kind of polymer (a long chain of molecules). It looked like buttermilk, but it grouped together to form a fiber that is stronger than steel! The material has been used in sports equipment, vehicles, oven mitts and, most importantly, bulletproof vests.

title: Express Your Creativity at the Erie Art Museum
text:
Besides being a great place to go to see paintings, crafts, folk art and ceramics, the Erie Art Museum is also a terrific place to learn to express your creativity. The museum offers a whole list of art classes just for kids. The classes are fun, exciting and much more educational than any video game.

One of the museum's most popular classes is called Clay for Kids. The class lasts for 10 weeks and parents and children learn how to throw pots on a potter's wheel, how to paint and glaze and how to handle pottery. Students make cups, pots and even small sculptures. The class is so popular because it gives parents and children a chance to be creative and get to know each other better, all at the same time.

Another popular class for kids is called Cartooning and Comic Book Drawing. In this class students learn the basics of creating their own characters. In the class students have the opportunity to create their own comic strips with their new character.

The Drawing, Painting and Printing class, for kids 7-11 years old, teaches kids about color, line and texture. Once kids learn the basics, they are able to express themselves in amazing ways. The class offers all kinds of projects, so kids are able to find out which type of art they enjoy the most.

The Erie Art Museum isn't the only place that offers fun art classes and activities for children. Many other Pennsylvania museums, libraries and university campuses also offer workshops and art classes for kids of all ages. The next time you are feeling creative, ask a parent to look into signing you up for a few hours at an art class. You just may discover a hidden artistic talent that you never knew you had!

title: Great Men of Pennsylvania
text:
1. Chocolate King of the World: Milton Hershey

This famous Pennsylvanian was born of Mennonite parents in a farmhouse in Hockersville, Dauphin County, in 1857. As a teenager, he learned how to make candy in an ice cream parlor in Lancaster. He traveled to several cities in the East, starting many businesses. Many sad things happened to him in these enterprises, including accidents and bad partners. He was broke many times, but he never gave up. Milton made many kinds of candy before he learned the chocolatemaking business. In his day, chocolate didn’t taste very good. It was Milton Hershey who went to Germany and discovered that milk was the secret ingredient of good chocolate. He returned to Dauphin County and established what became an awesome career in chocolate. How many men do you know who have whole cities named for them? Milton Hershey never forgot the lean years, however. He and his wife, Kitty, never had children of their own, so they founded the Milton Hershey School. The school offers free housing, clothing, meals, medical/dental care and recreational activities. They gave millions of dollars to this and to many other worthy causes over the years. Those are the qualities that make good men great. Milton Hershey died in 1945 at the age of 88.

2. Fred Rogers

Most people know this famous Pennsylvanian as Mr. Rogers. Fred Rogers was well known for his educational television program, “Mr. Rogers’ Neighborhood.” The show ran on PBS from 1968 until 2001. He was a puppeteer, composer and organist. Rogers’ success earned him many awards over the years. In 2002, he was presented the Presidential Medal of Freedom, our nation’s highest civilian honor. This honor was for his career in television that showed kids the importance of learning and caring for others. Fred Rogers passed away in 2003, but his non-profit company is following in his footsteps. It makes shows, like “Daniel Tiger’s Neighborhood,” that follow in Mr. Rogers’ impact on educational television.”

3. Guy Bluford

Astronaut Guy Bluford from Philadelphia has flown many missions into outer space, including the Space Shuttle and the Challenger.

4. Andrew Wyeth

This man is known all over the world as one of America’s best artists. Andrew Wyeth was born in Chadds Ford in 1917, where he spent his childhood alone in the woods surrounding his family’s home, wandering and exploring. His studio is still there, but he spends his summers in Maine, painting beautiful pictures worth many thousands of dollars. There are several other famous artists in his family. They like to keep their lives very private. Wyeth’s most famous painting, “Christina’s World,” hangs in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Thousands of people visit the painting every day.

5. Jimmy Stewart

You probably know this famous actor best from the movie “It’s a Wonderful Life.” Do you watch it every Christmas with your family? (Remember the last line of the movie? “Every time a bell rings, an angel gets his wings.”) Jimmy Stewart was born in Indiana, Pennsylvania, in 1908. He acted for more than 60 years, so your parents and grandparents loved him, too! He was a student at Princeton University when he was discovered by a famous director. We know Jimmy as one of the most famous actors of all time. Jimmy Stewart died of a heart attack in his Hollywood home in 1997. If you go to Indiana, Pennsylvania, today, visit the Jimmy Stewart Museum, as well as see a big statue of him in town.

6. W. C. Fields

William Claude Dukenfield was born in Philadelphia in 1879 and led a colorful life that lasted 67 years. He left home at age 11 and spent the remainder of his youth sleeping in alleys, caves and gutters. He became good at shoplifting and card cheating. William changed his name to W. C. Fields, and over the years, he became a well-loved radio comedian, a movie star and one of the world’s best jugglers. His hard-drinking habits finally took his life in 1946. W. C. Fields was loved and quoted by many. His legend lives on today. His humor was sarcastic—we’ve included two samples below.

7. Wilt Chamberlain

This very tall man (7 feet, 2 inches) was born in Philadelphia in 1936. He was one of 11 children—the only tall one! He had many health problems as a child and nearly died when he was in the fourth grade. His saddest problem as a child was that he felt bad because he was always teased about his height. “Wilt the Stilt” went on to become a big star center for the Philadelphia ’76ers and the Los Angeles Lakers. He was the first player ever to score 100 points in a single game.

title: Laurel Highlands
text:
You're going to want to visit all six festivals in this beautiful region this year! Start in January with the Ligonier Ice Fest in Westmoreland County. Professional ice carvers from all over the country fill the streets with carvings of birds, musical instruments and people in funny poses. But if the sun heats up, your fun will soon melt away! The Meyersdale Maple Festival in Somerset County is really fun in March/April. Visit the sugaring building and taste some spotza (hot maple syrup drizzled over snow.) There are many shops to visit, and you may chow down on yummy sausage and pancakes covered with—guess what?—maple syrup! The Fayette County Fair in Dunbar in July/August is more like a small city in action than a country fair. It's huge! You'll love the rides, the displays and the big-name entertainment.

This county is famous for its pepperoni rolls—you'll want to eat a dozen! The Jacktown Fair in Greene County every July dates clear back to the Civil War. It features a fair queen, professional wrestling, pony pulls and country music on stage. Doesn't something called a "Flax Scutching Festival" sound intriguing? To scutch means to "beat," and that's what was done to flax in early Pennsylvania days when it was our biggest crop. Have fun at this festival in Westmoreland County every September. And if you don't attend Bedford's Fall Foliage Festival in October, you've missed a really great time! It's a high-class event in a town that looks like a movie set. Your family will like the antique-cars parade. Have a great time "festival-ing" in the Laurel Highlands!

title: Brook Trout
text:
This beautiful fish is the only trout native to Pennsylvania, and it is our state fish. Native means that it has always been here. All other trout were brought here by mankind. The brook trout has a brilliant orange belly, and its olive-green back has dark markings.

Wild brook trout are most likely to be found in smaller, high mountain streams flowing off mountain ridges. Common nicknames for this fish are "brookies" and "speckled trout." They like to eat shrimp, insects and worms. If they're lucky, they'll find some delicious minnows or frogs now and then. Trout are one of the favorite freshwater catches of anglers (fishermen.) A great deal of money has been spent, worldwide, on making sure there are enough trout for everyone who wants to fish for them. You'll often find them on menus in restaurants, as well. They average about 10-12 inches in length. Other trout found in Pennsylvania are the brown trout and the rainbow trout. Pick out those bones and happy eating!

title: Governor Tom Wolf
text:
How much do you know about our governor? His name is Tom Wolf, and it’s time to learn about the man who leads our state.

Tom Wolf grew up in York, which is about 20 miles south of Harrisburg. After he finished high school, Wolf went to Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. Wolf spent part of his college years working for the Peace Corps in India. He would go on to earn more degrees from the University of London and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Wolf’s first job was in his family’s company. The company helped people move lumber and building materials to work sites. He later bought the business from his family and was able to help it more than double in size. He sold the company before taking a job as Pennsylvania’s secretary of revenue.

Wolf was thinking about running for governor, but heard that his former company was about to close down. He decided to go back and help the business. He bought it and helped the company grow even bigger than before. Wolf did this by giving employees more money and benefits. He also changed what the company did. The business started making their own products and selling them across the country.

With the company doing well again, Wolf decided to go back to helping the people in Pennsylvania. He talked with groups that wanted to help schools, doctors and artists. Wolf decided that he’d like to make a difference in the state. He ran for governor of Pennsylvania. He won the election with almost 55 percent of the vote and became our state’s 47th governor.

Even though our state has a house just for the governor, Wolf wanted to keep living at his home in York. He lives there with his wife, Frances. He and his wife have two grown daughters, Sarah and Katie. Do you have a question or concern for Governor Wolf? Ask an adult to help you send him a message. Visit this website: https://www.governor.pa.gov/contact/

title: How do I create an outline?
text:
You can use an outline to help you organize your nonfiction writing, especially when writing reports and research papers. An outline will help you effectively plan your writing.

Start with I, Then II and III…

This list will help you create an outline:

1. Formal outlines have the main topics in Roman numerals (I, II, III…).

2. Subtopics are indented and listed with capital letters (A, B, C…).

3. Supporting details are indented more than subtopics and listed with Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3…).

4. More details that support those supporting details are indented more and listed with lowercase letters (a, b, c…).

5. You must have at least two items at each level.

Below is a sample outline that someone might put together for a report on World War II.

The Two Wars Fought During World War II

I. Background Information (Main Topic)

A. Germany’s defeat in World War I

B. Japan’s need for more land

II. The War with Germany

A. Adolf Hitler

1. The Nazis

2. The supreme race

3. The Holocaust

a. Jews

b. Other races targeted by the Nazis

B. Germany’s pride

III. The War with Japan

A. The attack on Pearl Harbor

B. The atomic bomb

1. Hiroshima

2. Nagasaki

IV. The End of World War II

A. Germany’s defeat

B. Japan’s surrender

Try It!

The next time you have to write a nonfiction piece, such as a report, write an outline first. You’ll be amazed how it will help you organize your information and be sure to include all the important details.
