title: Johnny Appleseed
text:
Rome Beauties? Pippin? Delicious? Granny Smith? McIntosh? Jonathan? Pick your favorite, thanks to Johnny Appleseed.

For 49 years, John Chapman roamed the American wilderness, devotedly planting apple trees. He created apple orchards in the wilderness areas of Pennsylvania, Ohio, Kentucky, Illinois and Indiana. He wandered over 100,000 square miles. Some of the trees Johnny planted are still bearing fruit after 150 years!

We don't know why "Johnny Appleseed" did what he did. Some say that he dreamed of a land covered with blossoming apple trees, of a land where no one went hungry because apples were plentiful.

John's gentleness and courage were a legend even in his own time. He walked alone in the wilderness, without a gun or knife. He never chopped down trees or killed animals. John was respected and appreciated by the American Indians, as well as the new settlers.

John lived very simply. He slept outdoors, often walked barefoot, and ate berries and tender stems from trees. He made his clothes from bags and wore a tin pot for a hat. He also cooked food in that "hat." In the wintertime, he melted snow with his bare feet to get drinking water. Even the people of his time were amazed at his ability to survive.

After his death, it was discovered that John was not poor at all. He owned many acres of land — on which he planted apple trees, of course. John died of pneumonia at the age of 70, in the home of a friend near Fort Wayne, Indiana. He lies buried there under a marker that says, "He lived for others." Arbor Day is coming in April. Why don't you consider planting a tree in Johnny's memory? (Circle one or more: Legend/Lore/Folklore/Myth/ Fact/ Factoid.)

title: The ‘Irish’ Saint Who Wasn’t Really Irish
text:
People parade in New York City and turn the rivers green in Chicago every year on St. Patrick's Day. This saint (holy person) lived 1,500 years ago. But did you know St. Patrick wasn't even Irish?

Patrick was born in Britain to wealthy parents. When he was 16, Irish pirates attacked his home and took him prisoner. They took him to Ireland and held him captive. He worked as a shepherd and became a Christian. After six years he escaped and went back to Britain. But he had a dream in which an angel told him to go back to Ireland as a missionary (person who does religious work in other countries). After Patrick became a priest, he did just that. Many Irish at that time practiced a nature-based religion, so Patrick used some of their symbols to teach them about Christianity. For example, they worshiped the sun. So he put the sun on a cross. This is where the Celtic cross comes from. Historians think he died on March 17 about A.D. 460. Irish villagers mourned his death every year on that day.

The Irish people have always been great storytellers. These stories often became more exaggerated over the years. The story of St. Patrick chasing the snakes out of Ireland is one of these exaggerated stories. St Patrick's Day started out as a religious holiday, but today he is remembered all over our nation with parties and parades. Does your community celebrate St. Patrick's Day?

Reference: History News Network (hnn.us)

title: Good Judgement
text:
You may have heard advertisements that sound something like this: "Hurry and order Gullible Gloves today! By simply placing Gullible Gloves on your hands, you will grow a foot taller by tomorrow, pass spelling tests without studying and instantly become the most popular kid in school!"

Every day, we are bombarded with information, and we must use good judgment to sort out the good, the bad, the true, and the false. Do you think the claims made in that silly advertisement are true? Good judgment says, "No way!"

Good judgment means using common sense and clear thinking in order to make good decisions. We can develop good judgment by investigating facts, examining evidence, thinking logically and thinking through the consequences of our actions.

Good judgment can help you make good decisions every day. For example, is it a good idea to pull a cat's fluffy tail? Good judgment says, "Not unless you want to get scratched!" Or is it a good idea to eat three pieces of pie right before bedtime? Good judgment says, "Not unless you want to wake up with a stomachache!"

The next time someone tells you a myth, legend or tall tale, exercise your good judgment. Stories about curious characters such as Pennsylvania unicorns and men who mold steel with their bare hands are entertaining, but are they true?

title: Gravity Hill
text:
Have you ever wanted to defy gravity? How about fly like a bird or "leap tall buildings in a single bound" like Superman? Well, here's your chance! Drive on over to Schellsburg in Bedford County. While on a covered bridge tour, ask your parents to take you to Route 96. The local folks will point you to Bethel Hollow Road. You'll soon see a spray-painted sign on the road with the letters, "GH" ("Gravity Hill" of course). Stay calm — keep cool. Drive down the hill and stop. Then take your foot off the brake. Viola! Ever so slowly, your car will roll backwards, uphill! Some folks like to test the site with a tennis ball or maybe a jug of water, poured out, only to flow mysteriously up the hill.

Some say that it's an optical illusion. Kids think it's some kind of weird, cool psychic classified thing. Just try it — it works!

title: Who is Uncle Sam?
text: Many people call the U.S. government "Uncle Sam." It all started a long time ago when a man named Sam Wilson opened a meat-packing plant in Troy, New York. During the War of 1812, meat shipped by Wilson's company to the Army was stamped "U.S.," meaning "United States." But workers at the plant jokingly said that the letters "U.S." stood for "Uncle Sam." The name stuck, and by 1815, the U.S. government was called Uncle Sam by many, including cartoonists who like to have ways to show things in political cartoon form.

title: How Do I Read Historical Fiction?
text:
Treat It As Art Full of Historical Facts

While nonfiction is about information, fiction is all about creativity. Reading fiction can be exciting and moving. When you read fiction, you are trying to understand a character deeply, imagining the story as you read the words, reflecting on the events in the story and exploring the ideas and feelings created by the story.

Historical Fiction

Fictional pieces are imaginary stories, but they can be based on historical facts. Fictional stories based on historical facts are called "historical fiction." When reading historical fiction, it is important that you understand which details are factual and which are fictional. Sometimes, you need to do background research on your story before you can understand the difference between fact and fiction in a story that is historical fiction. Fiction is the most popular genre of literature and ranges from short stories (a page or two) to novels (up to thousands of pages). Fiction has three basic elements: characters, plot and setting.

Characters

The characters are the people (or animals) in the story. In well-written fiction, the writer will describe what the characters look like, how they act, what they think and feel, what others say about them, what they talk about and many other details. Because of this, you will finish reading it and feel like you know some of the characters very well, like friends or family. Sometimes, they will seem like real-life people. Characters in historical fiction can help you understand what it felt like to live through that event or period. Most stories have a main character, or protagonist.

Plot

The plot is what happens in a novel or story. It is the sequence of events. Generally, fictional writing begins with a conflict, or a problem that needs to be resolved. The events that happen after the conflict is introduced are called the rising action. The rising action draws out the character's problem. The story's turning point is called the climax. This is when there is a dramatic shift in the story, especially regarding the conflict. In the end, the conflict is resolved or changed into a different conflict. This is called the falling action. You can illustrate how a story's plot goes with a graph like this:

The plot in historical fiction will often follow a timeline of actual historical events, adding fictional details along the way.

Setting

The setting is the time and place in which the story happens. Stories can take place in the past, present or future and can last anywhere from one day to several years. Stories can also take place in a single room or city, or the action might happen in one big country or a planet. In historical fiction, the setting is, of course, in the past. If you imagine yourself in the setting of historical fiction, you will understand what conditions were like back then.

Theme

The theme of a fictional work is the idea that the author is examining in the work. The theme is a general topic, which allows the author to do a great deal of exploration.

Try It!

The next time you read a story or novel that is historical fiction, identify the main characters, the plot, the setting and the theme. You can even plot the theme as shown above. Think about the details in the story. Ask yourself which details are probably historical fact and which ones are fiction created by the author. Doing this will help you more fully understand the historical context being represented.

Below is a list of historical fiction you can read over the summer:

title: Legends and Lore
text:
It's the end of the school year and time for a little fun with a few legends from Pennsylvania! Circle whether the stories below are a legend (story from the past with fact and fiction), lore (a lesson that is taught with a story), folklore (story told about traditions among people), myth (story about historical events that contain a person's beliefs), fact (real and true information) or factoid (an invented fact believed to be true, because it was printed).

1. King of the Keel-Boat Men

I'm the original iron-jawed, brass-mounted, copper-bellied corpse-maker from the wilds of Pennsylvania! Look at me! I'm the man they call "Sudden Death" and "General Desolation." My father was a hurricane; my mother was an earthquake. Cast your eye on me, gentlemen! Lay low and hold your breath, for I'm about to turn myself loose! His name was Mike Fink, and he was born in the 1700s of Scot-Irish parents near Pittsburgh. By the age of 12, his nickname was "Bang-All." He was ready to bang away with a musket at anything or anybody. He killed deer with one shot, but mostly missed humans because he just wanted to show them how close he could come without hitting them. Roads were terrible in early Pennsylvania, so keel boats on the rivers were a practical way to travel. "Captain" Mike Fink and his crew of three were the best—and the wildest. When his boat was tied up to dock, Mike was as wild and reckless as they came. He headed for the nearest saloon—he could find it by its smell. Wild fights always ended the evenings.

Legend/Lore/Folklore/Myth/Fact/Factoid

2. Hex Signs

Hex signs were brought to Pennsylvania by German and Swiss immigrants in the early 1700s. They believed that witches existed in America as well as in Europe. They put these "charms" on the sides of barns as protection. A witch trying to go into the barn to do damage would get entangled in the complicated hex design with no way to escape. Today, hex signs are used solely for decoration ... or so they say. You'll find them on barns mainly in Berks, Lehigh and Montgomery counties. The Mennonites don't use them. They consider them sinful.

Legend/Lore/Folklore/Myth/Fact/Factoid

3. Joe Magarac

Joe was a big, big man. He was built of solid steel and could make 2,000 tons of steel a day. He could stir boiling steel with his bare hands and mold railroad rails between his fingers. Joe was born in an iron-ore mine and lived on a pile of ore near the blast furnace. One day, Joe Magarac heard that the local village was in desperate need of steel to build a new mill. They couldn't afford to buy the steel to build it, so Joe sat in a giant tub of boiling steel and melted himself down so that the townspeople could have their new mill. Joe was a man of steel, but he had a heart of pure velvet.

Legend/Lore/Folklore/Myth/Fact/Factoid

4. Bigfoot

Here's a good one for you! Numerous sightings were made of a creature resembling Bigfoot in Westmoreland County in 1973. There were 123 reports from 250 witnesses who gave the same general description: 8 to 9 feet tall, walking upright, large red eyes, body covered with dark hair and smelling like rotten eggs. Scientists say that there may have been (or still are) five types of Bigfoot roaming around western Pennsylvania. One theory is that because Pennsylvania has such a large network of caves and abandoned mine tunnels, it's easy for Bigfoot to "pop up" and disappear so easily.

Legend/Lore/Folklore/Myth/Fact/Factoid

title: Washington Irving
text: Washington Irving was a famous writer who was named after the real life legendary figure (you guessed it) George Washington. Irving wrote several books and stories. Have you heard of "Rip Van Winkle"? How about "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow"? Those are some of his most famous stories. They are treasured as American folktales. Check one out the next time you're at the library! Washington Irving, curious to see what the American West was like, went on a camping trip to Oklahoma and in 1835 he wrote a book about it. It’s called "A Tour On the Prairies." He helped many others learn about the beautiful land out West. Irving also helped other writers. He wanted to make sure that authors followed rules, so that no one could copy someone else's writing. You don't like it when someone copies your work, do you? Washington Irving is a true American character!

title: Let’s Learn About Oregon This Year!
text:
Welcome to Oregon Studies Weekly! Hang on tight for the ride of a lifetime as we explore our state from top to bottom, start to finish, inside, outside, upside and downside. We'll climb the highest mountain, drop into the deepest hole, roam with the buffalo, hunt with the mountain men, build a boat, fly an airplane, discover gold and walk with the pioneers! This is Oregon Studies Weekly, your weekly time capsule of historical events.

Each issue of the paper will include a current event on the front cover that discusses a real news item. Our cover story will help you get a head start on this week's history lesson. We will take you on a journey into the experiences of great people and great events with our cover stories.

And there's more: We will tell you about Oregon animals, birds, trees and plants. We will give you games, crafts and activities to enjoy and help you learn new words. Would you like to write a creative story or article? Then check out the Let's Write section and flex your creative muscles!

So, let's get started! Turn the page and jump right in. The water is fine - and so is the land. What land? Why, the land you're standing on. How did it get here?

Let's find out. (Hint - click on the Oregon History article)

title: Philanthropy and Values
text:
Maybe you have heard the word "philanthropy" before. What does it mean? It describes actions that people make for the good of other people. What is a value? It's a way of behaving that people believe is good - like believing it's good to be honest. Is honesty one of your values?

One way you can practice philanthropy today is to help yourself and others learn good values. How do you learn good values? You can learn them from your parents and grandparents, your teachers at school or church and other people you trust.

You can also learn them from people that have been recognized for doing good things for society. An easy way to learn about people that have done good things is to visit values.com. Values.com has lots of stories and short videos that highlight the traits that make each of us better people. They even have billboards on the highway to remind you about good values.

For example, you may have seen a billboard that looks like the one shown here.

This billboard is about Oral Lee Brown, who saved money from her job to send 19 kids to college... all by herself! Wow! Isn't that cool? You can learn about lots of other people who practice philanthropy at values.com. Be sure to look for more of their "billboards" on Page 4 of Studies Weekly this year. We think they're so cool we want to remind you to check them out!

title: Entrepreneurship (AWN tre pruh ner ship)
text:
Benjamin Franklin was one of the greatest entrepreneurs in history. An entrepreneur takes risks to create something or find a better way to do something. Ben Franklin was imaginative, creative and very smart. He was able to try many things. He was respected for the things he did. When he died in 1790, Franklin was known around the world as a businessman, politician, printer and inventor.

Franklin was born in 1706. Even as a little boy, he loved to read, write and collect books. He left school at the age of 10. By the time he was 12, he was helping as a printer for his older brother, James. When Franklin was 22, he owned his own printing press and started his own newspaper, The Pennsylvania Gazette. He also printed "Poor Richard's Almanack." That book became one of the most popular books in the colonies!

Franklin soon became one of the colonies' busiest printers. He was named the official printer for Delaware, New Jersey and Maryland. He printed money and legal documents. Franklin made so much money that he retired when he was 42. He then became a full-time inventor. Franklin invented many things, including the lightning rod!

Franklin was very important in the colonies. He started one of the first libraries in the United States with some of his friends. He signed the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. Franklin served as an ambassador from the colonies to France. He was the oldest member of the Constitutional Convention!

Ben Franklin did many things to be considered an entrepreneur. Like Franklin, there are many entrepreneurs today. Do the names Bill Gates, George Lucas, Henry Ford and Oprah Winfrey mean anything to you? All of these people are entrepreneurs. They brought great ideas and business to our economy. Can you think of any entrepreneurs where you live?

title: Physical Features of Oregon
text:
We are starting our study of Oregon this year by looking at how Oregon's physical features were formed, such as the rock far below our feet, the mountains, lakes, rivers and the basic land forms of Oregon. It all began with the "Lost World" of ancient oceans and exploding volcanoes.

What's That Under Your Feet?

Have you ever wondered what lies deep beneath you and how it got there? The Pacific Northwest has a history filled with some of the most powerful and destructive forces on Earth. No one knows how many changes our state has seen over the ages. There have been times when we were buried under hundreds of feet of ancient oceans. Other times, the Earth's crust buckled, sending great, granite slabs into the sky to form mighty mountains. We probably had a great view of our neighbors from up there! Let's learn how our state was formed - a process we will follow from the very beginning!

3 Billion Years Ago: Our earliest mountains were worn down by wind and rain and then washed into the sea. At least 10 more sets of mountains rose during the next three billion years. Our state was covered by ocean water during most of this time, but our various mountain ranges may have stood above the water to form islands. Those mountains didn't last long.

600 Million Years Ago: About 600 million years ago, our first permanent layer of rock was formed. We call this rock igneous because it was formed by heat and fire. "Igneous" is a great word that comes from a Latin word meaning fire. (Ever heard of "ignite"? Same kind of word.) The igneous layer is two miles beneath us. (Don't go digging; you'll never find it!)

200 Million Years Ago: The Earth began to quiet down during this period. Around our state, there was a lot of volcanic activity, but plants were growing and some ancient birds and mammals were roaming around the places that stood above the ancient oceans. Most of our state was still underwater.

60 Million Years Ago: Suddenly, there occurred a great uprising of mountains to the east of Oregon and Washington. This became our new coastline and oceans washed over our state for millions of years. Zillions of small sea creatures died and formed a chalky layer of rock thousands of feet thick. We call this the sedimentary layer. Sediment is another great word. It means to sink or settle (like cookie crumbs in a glass of milk).

15 Million Years Ago: Our third layer of rock was formed by molten granite, or lava, that oozed from cracks in the Earth's crust. This torrential lava flow covered more than 200,000 square miles of the western United States with a layer one mile thick.

13 Million Years Ago: The backbone for our Cascades to the west and northern Rocky Mountains popped up from the grinding, cracking action of the Earth's crust.

3 Million Years Ago: Volcanic action began enlarging the Cascades to something close to what we see today.

13,000 Years Ago: For millions of years, great sheets of ice would collect on the northern parts of the Earth. These sheets of ice are called glaciers. The long periods of time when the glaciers stayed around are called ice ages. The last ice age came to an end as the glaciers began melting away. Some animals had become frozen in the ice. The mighty mammoth (similar to an elephant) has been found in many places where the glaciers once stood. The mammoths must have fallen into cracks in the ice while looking for water or food and were frozen solid. Scientists learn a lot by studying these beasts.

Today: Today, our state continues to change. The 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens is a good reminder of the power of the Earth's buckling and heaving crust far below us. Thanks to the millions of years of collisions of natural forces inside and all around the Earth, we have this beautiful and peaceful place today. It is so green and exciting to explore, spreading out in all directions - a place we love to call home, sweet home.

title: Mountain Building in Oregon
text:
Teacher: Class, thousands of years ago, Oregon might have been as flat as Kansas.

Student: If the land was spread out flat, where did all of the mountains come from?

Teacher: The mountains came in several different ways. Down deep in the Earth, the rocks were squeezed into lava, which is hot, melted rock. Sometimes, this lava would find a crack and squirt out to form a volcano.

Student: Are there any active volcanoes in Oregon now?

Teacher: Since the eruption of Mount St. Helens in 1980, new volcanoes have been discovered on the sea bed off our coast. There are also other kinds of volcanic mountains that are common in Oregon. These were formed by lava pushing up through a crack. Instead of breaking through the crust, the lava would run between layers of rock and sand beneath the surface of the ground and form a sort of blister or huge hump in the ground.

Student: Are all mountains volcanoes?

Teacher: No, some mountains are made by the slipping of the Earth way down below the surface. When the Earth slips, we feel an earthquake. The cracks between huge blocks of Earth and rock are called faults. Fault-block mountains are made when one block is pushed up and another sinks down. There are many such faults in Oregon.

Student: Are there any more kinds of mountains in Oregon?

Teacher: Yes, there are mountains we call folded mountains. Sometimes, the Earth was not only pushed up, but it was shoved sideways. It is a lot like putting your finger on the back of your hand and pushing the skin along. Notice how the skin piles up to form tiny mountains?

title: The Cascades
text: Volcanoes are as much a part of Oregon as are the Pacific coastline and the Columbia River. Nowhere else in the Northwest are volcanoes more awesome than in the high Cascades. Many volcanic cones, or their remains, dot the landscape from northern California to the Canadian border. Lassen, Shasta, Three Sisters, Jefferson, Hood, St. Helens, Adams, Rainier and Baker are some of the larger volcanoes. Many are icebound, and two rise higher than 14,000 feet. Although geologists are uncertain as to their real ages, the cones formed long after the rise of the surrounding Cascade Range, sometime in the last several million years. The High Cascades are part of a great "Ring of Fire" encircling the Pacific, which includes such volcanoes as Krakatoa (Indonesia), Fuji (Japan), Cotopaxi (Ecuador), Popocatepetl (Mexico) and others.

title: Is the Ice Age over?
text: Winter never ended in North America 18,000 years ago. Thick ice sheets and snowpack sprawled across most of Canada and down into Pennsylvania, central Illinois and Oregon state. Mammoths, mastodons, short-faced bears and other mammals lived here. Eventually, the climate began to thaw. The glaciers melted, slowly at first, then with a rush. However, they're not completely gone yet. Interglacial Age sheets of ice are still found on Greenland and Antarctica. We all need to work together to keep the Earth cool!

title: Petrified Wood
text: If you go shopping for some lumber, the salesperson might ask if you're looking for hardwood or softwood. Tell them you want genuine Oregon rock wood and see what they say. Thousands of years ago, acres of cypress, oak, elm and ginkgo trees growing in swampy areas became covered over by massive lava flows and were otherwise trapped underwater. Over time, water seeped into the wood and deposited silica as the wood fiber rotted away. After many years, a perfect duplication of the tree's shape and detail was created by the silica deposits - and it was as hard as rock. This is called petrifying. People like to take small pieces, polish them and make jewelry. But don't try making a doghouse out of this Oregon rock wood - you're guaranteed to break your saw and bend all your nails!

title: Head Flops
text:
Have you ever wanted to create 27 pictures by drawing three? Watch as one person gradually turns into another and another.

Materials

paper

pencils

scissors

crayons

Instructions

1. Fold a piece of 12-inch by 18-inch drawing paper in half lengthwise. Open it up. Fold the long sides of the paper into the middle crease you just created. (You will now have four long sections.) Unfold the paper and cut off one of the long sides. (See picture.)

2. Orient the paper so the fold lines are horizontal. Fold the paper into thirds.

3. Cut the two fold lines on the two outside thirds of the page. Do not cut into the middle third. (See picture.)

4. In the middle third of the paper, draw ears, eyes and a nose in the center panel. Draw the mouth and chin in the lower panel and draw the forehead and hair in the top panel. You can draw a self-portrait or a picture of a hero or a historical figure.

5. Fold the left-hand panels in and add different features, creating another complete face. Repeat this step with the right-hand panels. You now have three complete faces.

6. Flip flop the sections and see how many different faces appear.

Extra Activity: You can turn your paper over and create 27 more faces.

title: Did Oregon Have Dinosaurs?
text:
Chances of finding dinosaur bones in Oregon are pretty remote. The problem is that our state is just too young - in fact, younger than the dinosaurs.

While dinosaurs were enjoying dinner-time snacks elsewhere in the United States during their reign 225 million years ago to about 65 million years ago (when they died out), most of the Northwest was either buried by the ocean or bubbling over with volcanoes and lava flows. Even so, there are still a lot of fossils (remains of prehistoric animals) in our state. A good question to ask is, "Are these dinosaur fossils or fossils of something else?"

Most people would be surprised to learn that there are a lot of ancient animals that were not dinosaurs. The word dinosaur is a combination of two Greek words meaning "terrible lizard" (deinos = terrible + sauros = lizard). Scientists use the term to describe extinct gigantic reptiles. If the ancient animal you're thinking of doesn't fall into this category of being extinct, gigantic and reptilian, it is technically not a dinosaur - it is a "non-dinosaur."

Here are some examples of non-dinosaurs that you might have heard about:

Trilobites: This group of animals lived around Oregon 250 million years ago and belonged to a group that included horseshoe crabs, spiders, insects, shrimp and lobsters. If you go fossil hunting in the right part of the state, you might find a fossilized trilobite. Trilobites are old, but they are not dinosaurs.

Dimetrodeon: If you have some toy dinosaurs at home, chances are pretty good that you have a dimetrodeon in the collection. This mammal-like creature had a fin along its back and has large, sharp fangs. It lived long before dinosaurs - about 250 million years ago.

Mammoth: A mammoth looks like a super-sized elephant. Although you might see a mammoth pictured in your dinosaur book or in the cartoons helping Fred Flintstone get a car wash, the mammoth is a prehistoric mammal and not a dinosaur. Mammoths arrived about 55 million years ago and were seen in the Northwest as recently as 9,500 B.C.

Phobosuchus: How about meeting up with a crocodile that is as long as your classroom (50 feet)? The skull of this meat eater was 6 feet long and it probably ate any lingering dinosaurs that had not died out by 60 million years ago. Phobosuchus was not a dinosaur, just the biggest crocodile that ever walked the Earth!

Birds? This is a trick question. While most people think the animals listed above are dinosaurs, those same people would probably also say that our delicate, little birds could not be at all similar to dinosaurs. But, according to scientists, that chicken you had for dinner has more similarities to the dinosaurs than any of the animals listed above. Scientists have found fossils of the archaeopteryx. It had sharp teeth, claws, a tail, wings and feathers, and it lived about 150 million years ago. Of course, not all paleontologists agree on the bird-dinosaur connection, but they will continue to work on figuring out the pieces to the puzzle. So, if you go to the park for the day, make sure your bucket of chicken isn't the petrified type - that would be one heavy bucket of extra-crispy!

title: Are Tar Pits Hiding Beneath U.S. Roads?
text:
If you live in Los Angeles, California, the answer may be yes. And those tar pits may contain the best-preserved fossils ever found! Near busy Wilshire Boulevard you can see the Le Brea Tar Pits. The area is still bubbling with the sticky tar that trapped animals up to 50,000 years ago. Scientists have found the bones of bears larger than any on Earth today, lions bigger than today's African lions and camels larger than the elephants you can see at a zoo. Over one million bones have been found in the pits so far. (No dinosaur bones have been found because they were already extinct.) And in 2006, 16 new tar deposits were found where a parking garage was being built at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. Some scientists think they will find a million bones there too.

The tar pits show that many large animals went extinct at about the same time. Why? Many scientists say evidence points to the climate change that took place at the end of the ice age. The large animals couldn't adjust fast enough to the warmer temperatures. At about that same time, man first migrated over the land bridge that used to exist between Asia and North America. Another theory is that man may have hunted many of these giants to extinction. What's underneath that road you were on when you came to school today? Maybe more than you think!

title: Money
text:
When the English colonists first came to America, they brought some of the money they used back in England. They called their money shillings, pence and pounds. They soon found out it was of no use to them in the New World. The American Indians didn't care for their money. It didn't mean anything to them. The American Indians bartered with the colonists. As you can imagine, that became very hard. Therefore, the early colonists of Massachusetts started using wampum. Wampum consisted of purple and white shells. The purple ones were worth twice as much as the white ones. They used it the same way as money. American Indians had traded wampum with seacoast tribes since the 1640s. Both the colonists and the American Indians soon used it in addition to bartering. This made for less trouble in the colonies.

Economists like to say, "Money is what money does." This was as true for the American Indians and English colonists as it is for us today. Money has three main functions. First, it must be a way of exchange that people accept. This means that people have to agree on what they will use for money. Second, money must be a measure of value. This means that the people using the money must know how much the money is worth in their community. Last, money must be a store of value.

People should be able to save their money and use it later. Storing value is very hard when bartering. Often the goods or products people are trying to trade go bad before they can find someone in the market for them. For example, milk is hard to keep in hot weather. Bartering milk without a way to keep it cold for a long time would be very tricky.

Money must also be easy to carry. It must be sturdy, easy to recognize and able to be broken down into smaller parts. Our U.S. money is small. It's easy to carry and uniform, or all the same. People in the country accept it all over. You can divide it easily. This is nice for everyone because it is so easy. What if you lived in a country that used bowling balls for money? That wouldn't work very well at all!

title: The Five Regions of Oregon
text:
It's important to know the shape of the land. Oregon divides itself into five natural regions. Which do you live in?

Where in the world are we?

Before we can study Oregon history, we need to know a little about the place where we live.

Do you "half" any idea where Oregon is?

The world is a big place! To better understand and describe where we live, we can think of the world as divided into parts. These parts are called hemispheres because imaginary lines divide our sphere (or globe) into halves (hemi means "half"). If you imagine a piece of string wrapped around our world from left to right, you would have a top half and a bottom half. An imaginary line called the equator does just that - the top half is called the Northern Hemisphere and the bottom half is called the Southern Hemisphere. Now, imagine a string wrapped around the world from top to bottom. That line is called the prime meridian and it divides the world into halves called the Eastern Hemisphere and Western Hemisphere. Can you figure out where Oregon is? Here's a clue: it is North of the equator and West of the prime meridian.

Natural Regions of Oregon

A natural region is a part of the Earth that has one major kind of natural feature, such as mountains or plains.

1. Coastal Region

Oregon's Coastal Region is a mixture of wide beaches, sand dunes, 1,000-foot cliffs and mountains covered with spruce and lodge pole pine. The Coast Range running parallel to the coastline is a belt of low and even-crested mountains, the highest of which is about 4,000 feet. The Klamath Mountains are a continuation of the Coast Range to the south, but they are a little higher - 4,500-5,000 feet with some peaks more than 8,000 feet. There were many coastal lakes formed here when streams were dammed up by sandbars. Along the beaches, huge masses of basalt are present, constantly doing battle with the ocean waves and erosion. Narrow, deep and steep-walled valleys lie among the mountains and the famous Rogue River cuts through the Klamath Mountains from east to west. The rivers emptying into the ocean, especially the Columbia, abound with salmon and other fish.

2. Western Lowlands

The fertile Willamette Valley is sheltered by two mountain walls - the Coast Range on the west and the Cascades on the east. This fairly flat region is watered by the Willamette River and has the greatest area of good farmland - greater than any other natural area in Oregon. The valley is 15-30 miles wide and extends 125 miles south of the Columbia River.

3. Cascade Mountains

The Cascade Range has a crest line of 6,000-7,000 feet, overshadowed by volcanic peaks such as Mount Hood, Mount Jefferson and Three Sisters. This is the highest part of the state. The western side has heavier rainfall and most of the commercially valuable timber grows in this region. Farmlands are scarce, but the area is good for sheep and cattle.

4. Basin Region

Even though the basin region is an average of 4,000 feet above sea level, it is surrounded by even higher lands, giving it the form of a basin. The Cascades prevent moisture from reaching the basin region and most streams sink into the ground or flow into lakes. Much of the area is a desert and many of the small lakes are alkaline or salty. They only appear for part of the year before drying up.

5. Columbia Plateau

(A plateau flatland pushed up from below.) This region once was a very old mountain range. The valleys between the peaks were filled to the top by great flows of lava from ancient volcanoes. Through the ages, the lava layer has crumbled and eroded, creating some of the richest soil in America. The Blue-Wallowa Mountains are the peaks that were not covered by the lava flows. The mountain slopes are heavily forested and the famous John Day fossil beds are here. The Snake River region lies at the southern end, where the Snake River feeds irrigation systems made possible by the Owyhee Dam.

title: What happened to the dinosaurs?
text:
The disappearance of dinosaurs 65 million years ago is one of science's greatest mysteries. There are no eye witnesses; there is no smoking gun.

Changing climate, starvation, cosmic radiation, parasites, disease, erupting volcanoes and competition from new animals are just a few of the causes scientists guess at for the dinosaurs' sudden disappearance from the Earth.

Was it mammals? Others say small mammals ate all the dinosaur eggs and no more babies were hatched.

One important theory (scientific belief) says that the disappearance of the giant beasts started in Mexico, near the Yucatan Peninsula. A comet or meteorite struck the area, causing huge forest fires 65 million years ago. The clouds of dust and ashes choked all living plants and animals.

Do you have a favorite theory as to why the dinos of the world are no longer with us?

title: Whales
text: Ever since the dinosaurs died out, the largest visitors ever to set fin on Oregon's coast are the whales, in all of their varieties. Whales can be spotted during their spring and fall migrations. They like to spend their summers in the cool Arctic and then move south to the tropics for the winter months. Oregon is right in the middle of their migration route. These giants can swim against the current and need not fear any enemy. Among their numbers are the gray, blue, piked, humpback, finback and sei whales. Others joining the migration include the killer whale, Baird's beaked, Indo-Pacific beaked and goose-beaked whales. As the whales lumber along, their great movement in the water is marked by frequent geysers and spouts of water as the friendly creatures blow off air when they breathe. If you visit the coast during these migrations, you won't be the only curious onlooker as the whales go by. Families of dolphins also like to join the parade. And who knows? Maybe the whales and dolphins are looking at the funny-looking creatures, with strange scales and hairy heads standing on the beach - you!

title: Critical Analysis: The Salem Witch Trials
text:
Can you imagine a group of children who did something terrible and then told an enormous lie about it? That is what began a shameful period in American history called the Salem Witch Trials.

In 1692, Salem Village, Massachusetts, was a strict Puritan community where children were expected to devote every minute to church, chores and studies. Toys and games were frowned upon. The minister Samuel Parris had an enslaved girl named Tituba. She entertained his daughter Betty and her friends with fortune-telling games and stories of magic. When Betty and some of the girls began to have strange symptoms like babbling and convulsions that doctors could not explain, they were declared victims of witchcraft. Tituba was beaten and jailed. Salem had laws against witchcraft. When the girls accused others in the community of being witches, terror gripped Salem and the girls became the center of attention.

Accused people did not get lawyers, but they were not put to death if they confessed and named other witches. Soon hundreds were thrown in jail. Prisoners were left there for months, and many got sick and died.

John Proctor was a wealthy farmer who spoke out against the witch hunt. But he was accused of witchcraft himself and hanged. Twenty people were executed before clear thinking ended these unfair trials in 1693.

The Salem witch trials were based on hysteria and fear rather than on critical analysis. Ann Putnam was one of the girls who accused people. She wrote an apology in 1706 saying, "... now I have ... good reason to believe they were innocent persons...." Think of a time in school when someone you know used critical analysis to solve a problem or make a decision and discuss it with your class.

title: Oregon's Lakes and Rivers
text:
"There is no force on this planet more powerful than water flowing over time." Rod Nash, scientist

Oregon's rivers and lakes help water some of the richest soils on Earth. They also provide lush, safe homes for wildlife and scenic recreation for visitors. These water resources, along with the wondrous mountain ranges and vast desert plateaus, make Oregon one of the most beautiful places to live. Let's read a little about some of Oregon's great rivers!

Columbia River

The Columbia River system is the largest in the west, draining 258,000 square miles. The Columbia River is 1,240 miles long, with 740 miles in the United States. A total of 14 hydroelectric dams help produce the region's power as the Columbia stairsteps gradually from 2,690 feet to sea level.

Snake River

The Snake River is the largest tributary of the Columbia. It flows into the Columbia at an average of 50,000 cubic feet (or 375,000 gallons) of water every second - about 1/5 of the Columbia's total flow. The 1,038-mile-long river begins at Yellowstone National Park and flows through North America's deepest gorge. The Snake River also provides power for western states through its hydroelectric dams.

Willamette

The Willamette River is a major tributary of the Columbia and is 190 miles long. The river helps farmers. It waters the Willamette Valley, where 70 percent of Oregon's population lives, and much of the state's economy is generated. At Oregon City, it tumbles over the Willamette Falls and passes through Portland before joining the Columbia.

Deschutes

The Deschutes River drains 1/8 of Oregon and carries the water for 210 miles to the Columbia River. It has cut a canyon through the lava flows of the Columbia Basin. The Deschutes was also used by early fur traders seeking a water route to the Columbia.

title: Turn Off the Water!
text:
Did you know that each person in American uses between 80 and 100 gallons of water each day? That adds up to about 400 million gallons per day! You may be surprised to learn just where all this water goes. Most of the water you used each day goes to flush the toilet. Large amounts of water are also used for taking baths and showers, for washing dishes, and for doing the laundry. Many people believe that it is time for us to try to use less water. These people have even convinced the government to pass laws for conserving, or saving, water.

You may have heard that more than 70 percent of the Earth is covered with water. If this is true, then you may be wondering why we need to worry about saving water. The fact is that only 1 percent of the water on Earth can be used by people for drinking, bathing, and cooking. Most of the water is ocean water, which is full of salt. Salt water cannot be used by humans, so we must rely on fresh water to meet our needs.

Fresh water comes from rain and snow that melts and ends up in rivers, streams, and lakes. With millions of people living in the United States using the same sources of fresh water, we sometimes run low, especially during years when the rain and snowfall amounts are less than normal. If we don't start conserving water, some people may go without.

So, what can we do to conserve water?

Businesses and cities have been working to solve this problem for years. Some companies recycle wastewater and use it to water farms, golf courses and parks. The government has also passed laws that require new showers, faucets and toilets to use less water than in the past. Check the labels on these items in your home. They should tell you how many gallons per minute each item will use.

What are some ways that you can save water?

Turn off the water while brushing your teeth and washing your face.

Take showers instead of baths. Showers use less water!

Only run your dishwasher for full loads. The dishwasher uses the same amount of water to do each load, no matter how many dishes are in it.

Only run the washing machine with full loads of laundry. Running the washer for just a few items wastes water.

When washing the car, use a spray nozzle that can be turned on and off as needed. Don't just let the hose run.

Fix leaky faucets as soon as you notice them Leaky faucets and toilets waste millions of gallons of water each year.

These tips can save millions of gallons of water from being wasted, right down the drain. Lean to conserve water today. By learning to conserve today, you can make sure that there will be enough water for everyone tomorrow!

title: Lakes, Bays, Mountains & Rivers
text:
Oregon's Lakes

Upper Klamath Lake is surrounded by the Cascade Mountain Range. The Klamath River and Klamath Falls are on the lake's southern end.

Crater Lake lies in a huge pit created when prehistoric Mount Mazama exploded in a violent eruption 7,000 years ago. The lake has no inlets or outlets and is formed by rain and snowfall. It is the second-deepest lake in North America at 1,932 feet. Wizard Island and The Phantom Ship Island were both created by volcanic activity.

Malheur Lake and Harney Lake are neighbors, but they're pretty different. Malheur Lake has freshwater and drains into Harney Lake. Most of the water evaporates from Harney Lake, so it's shallow and has a lot of mineral deposits.

Goose Lake is about 25 miles long and is one of several shallow alkali lakes in the Great Basin. It is on the Oregon-California border. Migratory birds like to stop here.

Oregon's Mountains

The Pacific Coast Range runs 5,500 miles along the western coast of the United States and Canada. These mountains are not very high compared with the Cascade Mountains. But the mountains keep some rain from reaching the Western Lowlands. So that region gets less rain than the Coastal region. The highest point in the Coast Range is Marys Peak at 4,097 feet. Saddle Mountain is a wellknown landmark south of Astoria.

The Cascades form the mountainous backbone running north-south across the entire state of Oregon. It divides the state into the "dry" eastern and "wet" western sides. The major mountain peaks in the Cascades include Mount Hood and Mount Bachelor. Crater Lake was formed by the empty cone of an ancient Cascades volcano that erupted thousands of years ago.

The Blue Mountains make up one of the largest uplifts in Oregon. The highest point in the Blue Mountains is Rock Creek Butte, a peak on Elkhorn Ridge a few miles west of Baker City with an elevation of 9,097 feet. Strawberry Mountain near Prairie City is almost as high, with an elevation of 9,052 feet.

The Klamath Mountains are also a segment of the Pacific mountain system. Peaks exceed 8,000 feet with numerous subranges. A popular stop for cave explorers is the Oregon Caves National Monument.

The Wallowa Mountains are in northeast Oregon, containing the Eagle Cap Wilderness. The Wallowa River and Lostine River both originate in these mountains. This wilderness has plenty of high alpine lakes and meadows, bare granite peaks and ridges, glaciated valleys, heavily-timbered lower valleys and scattered alpine trees in the higher elevations. Elevations range from 5,000 to 10,000 feet.

title: Coastal Region
text:
Astoria sits right at the mouth of the Columbia River on the Pacific Coast. The Chinook and Clatsop Indians lived in the area for thousands of years. Robert Gray sighted the Columbia River in 1792, and Lewis and Clark paddled by in 1805. It is the oldest American settlement west of the Rockies. Thousands of explorers and pioneers passed on their way inland to settle in Oregon or out to the Pacific to other adventures. Astoria is the settlement that strengthened America's claim to the Northwest. Today, visitors can see several old forts, museums, the 4.1-mile-long Astoria bridge and the Astoria Column built in 1926.

It rains an average of 63 inches a year in Astoria, but the weather is otherwise mild. There are an average of 300 frostfree days. However, in some years severe storms happen, causing terrible floods that destroy property. If you visit Astoria, charter a boat and go deep-sea fishing. You might have the exciting thrill of landing your own salmon or crab.

title: Where is the highest mountain in the world?
text: It is in Asia, on the border of two countries, Nepal and Tibet. This mountain is 29,028 feet high - that's like stacking up two Mount Hoods. A long time ago, it was named Chomolungma, which means "Mountain-So-High-No-Bird-Can-Fly-Over-It." It now has the name of Mount Everest. Sure is a lot easier to say "Everest," isn't it? This mountain is so high, it has snow and ice all year round, and blizzards bring high winds. It is very dangerous to climb.

title: Beaver
text: The American Beaver loves Oregon's lush forests and streams. It is North America's largest rodent, weighing as much as some fourth graders (35-65 pounds) and is sometimes taller (3-4 feet, including its 16-inch, flat tail). The beaver is like a miniature boat. Its large webbed feet help propel it through the water while its broad, flat tail acts as the rudder. A beaver mates for life and can live up to 20 years. Beavers build dams with logs and sticks they cut with their teeth. The dams create lakes where beavers may safely raise their families. Beavers usually build at night and can repair dam breaks quickly. The largest beaver dam is in Canada; it is 2,790 feet long and can be seen from space!

title: Make a Rain Gauge
text:
Materials

1 plastic bottle

scissors

bricks

a ruler

Directions

1. Ask an adult to help you cut the top half off the bottle

2. Put it back on upside down.

3. Stand your rain guage outside. Put bricks around it to hold it steady.

4. Each time it rains measure how much rain has fallen, with your ruler.

title: What is Profit?
text:
Pretend you and your friends decide to be entrepreneurs for the day. You find a table in Jack's garage. Mary's mom helps you make some lemonade. Together, all three of you make a big sign that says, "Lemonade, 10 cents." You put all of your items on the sidewalk in front of your house and wait for your customers to come.

Soon people are lined up around the block for a taste of your delicious lemonade. You work quickly to serve your customers. Then you realize you are almost out of cups. Mary and her mom run to the store to buy some more. When they get back, you take the extra cups and keep on selling lemonade until there is no more. Together, everyone cleans up the lemonade stand. You start to count the money you've made.

You count it all up, and you have $5.80. Then you think about the extra cups that you had to buy. They cost $1.25. You give Mary's mom that amount from the money you made. Now you have $4.55. This new amount is your profit. Profit is the money a business makes after all of the expenses are paid. In this example, the extra cups that cost $1.25 are your only expense.

You and your friends have learned about profit motive today. Profit motive is the desire to benefit from the time and money people put into a business. In other words, you wanted to sell lemonade because you thought you could earn some money. In the same way, a business sells goods in hopes of earning a profit. Now the question is, what will you do with your profit?

title: Oregon State’s Climate
text:
The daily weather (temperature, moisture, and wind) is important to all of us. The normal weather over a long period of time is even more important. This is our climate.

Oregon's climate has an interesting story. The story begins far out over the Pacific Ocean, and it moves from west to east. Most of the winds that blow over our region come from the west. As air passes over the ocean, it picks up moisture. This wet air blows over the coast and continues east. Soon these ocean winds reach the coastal hills and mountains. The air must rise to get over them. As the air rises, it cools. Cool air cannot hold so much moisture, so it falls to the Earth as rain or snow. As a result, the coastal lands receive a lot of precipitation. Precipitation includes rain, snow or other falling moisture.

The story continues. The winds keep blowing from west to east, toward the Cascade Mountains. Again, the air must rise and cool. The west side of the Cascades is very rainy. Some parts of western Oregon receive more than 100 inches of rain each year.

The Cascade Mountains divide the state's climate in another way. Eastern Oregon has hotter summers and colder winters. Western Oregon's climate is more mild. This means it is not too hot or too cold.

These differences in climate are caused by the Pacific Ocean. The ocean stays at about the same temperature all year. Ocean breezes help keep the coastal lands cool in summer and warm in winter. The wet and mild climate of western Oregon is called a marine climate. "Marine" means "having to do with the ocean."

The Cascades keep the mild ocean temperatures from reaching the eastern side of the state. Instead, eastern Oregon has a semiarid climate. It is hotter in the summer and colder in the winter than marine-climate areas. This is common in lands on the inside of the continent, away from the oceans.

title: Energy of the Future
text:
Here's a question for you. What energy source is always invisible, sometimes warm and gentle, but other times, cold and harsh? If you guessed wind, then you are right!

Did you know that wind is a great source of natural, renewable energy? Renewable energy is energy that isn't used up. It can be renewed, or made useful, again and again. Much of the energy we use today is non-renewable, which means that once we use it up, it cannot be used again. Our country uses a lot of oil and coal to create non-renewable energy to run everything from cars to the furnaces in our homes. These sources of energy will eventually run out, so we need to find renewable sources that will give us the energy we need for centuries to come.

Many Oregon farmers use the wind to make energy for themselves, as well as for their neighbors. One of Oregon's largest and most successful wind farms is The Klondike Wind Farm located in Sherman County. Wind farmers build huge windmills that turn in the breeze, storing energy in large turbines, or machines that make electricity. Since wind is a renewable resource, these windmills will continue to make electricity as long as the wind blows.

What are some other renewable resources? Have you heard of cars that run on fuel made from French fry oil? It's true! Cars can run on fuel made from vegetable oil, corn, mustard seeds, and many other plants.

Many lawmakers would like to make laws that encourage new forms of energy use. The goal is to have companies that produce energy get at least 15 percent of their energy supply from renewable sources, such as wind, plant, or solar (sun) power.

Who knows? Maybe in the future, computers will run on grass clippings and cars will run on wind. Perhaps you will discover a new form of renewable energy!

title: The Role of Prices
text:
"And your total comes to $2.40."

You've shopped in many stores either with your parents or by yourself. Most products contain bar codes that tell the scanner what the price is for the item. The prices let you, the consumer, know how much money the store is willing to sell the item for. However, that's not the only purpose.

Prices have three main functions. First, prices help ration scarce goods. Things cost money, and money is a limited resource. We can't buy everything we want all of the time. Therefore, items need to be rationed, or spread out to many people.

Second, prices provide a reason for buyers to buy goods and sellers to sell them. Prices make the process of buying goods organized. They motivate sellers to provide more goods based on the idea of profit motive.

Finally, prices send signals about how a market is doing. Let's say that prices are too high, and no one is buying those goods. Then economists can study this and ask questions. They can find out what prices are in other markets. Then they decide what in this market made the price rise so high.

Economists can then figure out the price for the product. It should balance the amount of buyers who want to buy with the amount of sellers who want to sell. This price is called the market-clearing price, or the equilibrium price. By figuring out this price, both the buyers and sellers are happy, and goods continue to be sold.

Can you think of any other reasons prices are important to our economy?

title: Oregon's Wacky Weather
text:
Do you like to experience different types of weather? Then you're living in the right place! From hot, to mild, to rainy, we have it all!

The climate of a place affects where people settle and what crops they can grow. The eastern part of Oregon has a cold semiarid climate. Arid means dry, so there is not much rainfall. The summers are hot and the winters are cold. The low amounts of rainfall mean that different types of trees and plants naturally grow in this area. Farmers in this climate zone often need to use irrigation systems for their crops. Canals bring in water from rivers and other water sources so that crops can grow.

The marine climate of the western coast of Oregon provides a lot of rainfall. Many different kinds of crops benefit from this climate. Lots of rain means that you'd better keep your umbrella handy! Some spots in western Oregon receive more rainfall in a month than places in eastern Oregon receive in a whole year. The marine climate is mild, which means that temperatures remain about the same all year. Of course, it's not always raining here!

The highland or alpine climate runs down the central part of the state, following the Cascade Mountains. Large trees grow here and supply our state with timber. The highlands don't get quite as much rain as the west coast, but the precipitation that falls in this area helps irrigate the crops in the semiarid region. Which of these areas has the lowest population? Why?

If you're tired of the weather in your area, grab your suitcase and take a trip to another region in our state!

title: Climate and the Cascades
text: The Cascades are a range of mountains that were once very active volcanoes. Two of the tallest are Mount Rainier in Washington at 14,410 feet high and Mount Hood in Oregon, at 11,245 feet high. This mighty range of mountains affects the climate in the Pacific Northwest. On the seaward side of the Cascades, wet air from the ocean gets trapped against the mountains and drops some 100- 130 inches of annual precipitation. Farther west, the Puget-Willamette lowlands receive an average of 45-50 inches yearly. But on the east side of the Cascades, where much of the moisture is blocked by the mountains, parts of the state have a desert climate. Only 10-12 inches of rain falls on average each year. Through this land of contrasts, the Columbia River flows 1,200 miles from its source in Canada to the Pacific.

title: "Woodchuck" Punxsutawney Phil
text:
On Groundhog Day each year, the world turns its attention to the little town of Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania, and to a groundhog named Phil. (Here in Oregon, we call groundhogs woodchucks.) If he climbs out of his burrow on Gobbler's Knob and sees his shadow, the story goes, winter will be sticking around for another six weeks. Phil's an old hand at this prediction stuff. He or his ancestors (great-grandparents) have been doing it every year since Feb. 2, 1887!

Punxsutawney Phil is a legend in his home state. There are groundhogs (woodchucks) in Oregon, too. They are rodents of the squirrel family. They are found in the woodlands and brush lands, are brown, and have darker feet. These guys are found in most of the United States except for the deep South.

title: Weather Watch
text:
Since time began, people have tried to predict the weather by scanning the sky for colors and other clues. Test these bits of ancient meteorology to see if they are really true.

1. A rose-red sunset means fair skies are coming. A red sunrise means there will be a storm. ("Red sky at night, sailors delight; red sky at morning, sailors take warning.")

2. A pale yellow sunset means rain is on the way.

3. An evening rainbow predicts fair weather.

4. A morning rainbow in the west means rain.

5. A pre-dawn copper-colored sky in the east means rain.

6. When the moon has a halo, there will be rain, especially if the halo is far from the moon.

title: What's the difference between a meteorologist and a climatologist?
text:
They both study weather, but they use the information in different ways! Meteorologists study current weather patterns and give forecasts of what might happen in the future. If you watch the local news to see what the weather will be like over the weekend, you're probably seeing a meteorologist.

A climatologist is a scientist who studies weather and climate. They look at an area's climate over a long period of time. Climatologists also make predictions. You may hear climatologists talking about global warming (a rise in temperatures on Earth's surface) and other changes. Both types of scientists help keep people safe and prepared for the weather ahead!

title: Let's Write
text: Write about an experience you have had in our state’s weather. Have you been in an ice shower, snowstorm, hail storm, thunderstorm or drought?

text: As you read this week’s magazine, circle or highlight five words that are new to you. Write the words on a piece of paper. Try to figure out the meaning of the words by reading the other words and sentences around them. Write what you think the words mean and compare your definition to a dictionary definition. title: Oregon's First Inhabitants
text:
The first people to live in Oregon arrived about 12,000 years ago. These early people may have migrated from the mountain-desert regions of Utah and Nevada in search of a better life. Here in the Pacific Northwest, they found more than enough.

The American Indians of Oregon found this land to be a special garden of life-giving forests and waters. They built homes and raised their families in gratitude to the unseen forces that they believed guided and influenced all living things.

The first American Indians lived in caves. Scientists have discovered that these cave dwellers were creative artists. They knew how to weave sagebrush bark to make sandals, baskets and mats. They used stone awls, polishers, flakers, smoothers and punchers. They even used the atlatl, a throwing stick used to propel a spear through the air. Later, they became skilled with bows and arrows. They also decorated their bodies with fur, beads and feathers and enjoyed the berries, nuts and roots that were easily available.

With the passage of time, the early American Indians began to differ one from another. Weather changes, new migrations, failing food supplies and contact with other people forced the various tribes to move around and sometimes combine. The geography of the region kept the groups divided into three main categories. Over the next three weeks, we will study each of these groups: Coastal People, Inland or River People and Plateau People.

title: Scientists Believe Volcanoes Caused a 'Little Ice Age'
text:
An ice age usually lasts thousands of years. But between A.D. 1300 and A.D. 1900 the northern hemisphere experienced a cooling called the "Little Ice Age." The cooling was so intense that glaciers moved south, causing northern European towns to be destroyed. It was so cold that the Thames River in London and canals in the Netherlands froze! A scientist at the University of Colorado, using plant fossils from this period, may have discovered why this happened.

The plants died suddenly between 1275 and 1300. That's exactly when many volcanoes erupted. Fifty years later, volcanoes erupted again. Billions of tiny particles from the eruptions were in the atmosphere, reflecting the sun's heat away from the Earth. This caused the land to cool, the plants to die and the ice cap to grow. But there's more.

The growing ice cap sparked a feedback loop. A feedback loop causes something to happen over and over. First, the tiny particles stopped a lot of the sun's heat from reaching land. This cooling caused the ice cap to grow. The ice reflected more of the sun's heat back into the atmosphere. This caused more cooling. Finally, the glaciers became so large that they stopped the warmer ocean currents from melting the ice cap. Over centuries the glaciers grew to cover northern Europe.

Volcanic eruptions started the cooling, but it took the feedback loop to keep the "Little Ice Age" going for centuries!

title: Oregon's First Inhabitants
text:
Oregon's first people lived in all parts of our state. By separating them into three groups, we can study what the tribes had in common and what made them unique.

The Coastal People

Oregon Coastal People lived off the sea. They harvested the oceans for kelp, sea slugs, salmon, herring, tasty halibut, dog salmon, whales and sea otters. From these, they obtained food, clothing, fishing line, ropes and tools. Their villages were usually near the sea and their culture was built around sturdy cedar canoes, fishing and enduring the endless rains. They built nice villages, but also kept homes in the valleys, away from the winter ocean storms. Some of Oregon's Coastal Tribes include Clatsop, Tillamook, Siletz, Alsea and Coos.

The Plateau & Plains People

Oregon Plateau and Plains People had a harder time living in areas where food was scarce. Because of this constant search, these groups didn't settle and were always on the move, chasing the food. In early spring, the people had very little to eat - usually snails and slow rabbits. By May or June, they moved to the rivers to catch the spawning salmon. By fall, they left the rivers and stalked deer, elk, antelopes and mountain goats. In preparation for winter, the women harvested nuts, berries and roots. Animal and fish flesh was dried and preserved. Some of Oregon's Plateau and Plains Tribes include Cayuse, Northern Molalla, Southern Molala, Klamath, Modoc and Northern Paiute.

The Interior People

Oregon Interior People didn't need the kind of strong, ocean-going canoes the Coastal People used. Their canoes were shallower and designed for the more gentle currents of rivers. They became expert at catching salmon as it migrated from the ocean to spawn in the rivers. These American Indians didn't cultivate the land because so much food grew freely around them. An occasional deer that wandered into camp was surrounded and killed for a feast. Their villages usually stayed in about the same place as long as the food was there. Some of Oregon's Interior Tribes include Skilloot, Multnomah, Yamhill, Clackamas, Umatilla, Wallowa and Coquille.

title: Eastern Oregon
text: Early settlers in Oregon had their first look at the state by entering eastern Oregon. It is mostly dry flatland where the average rainfall is about 10 inches a year. Many people now live in eastern Oregon. Some are involved in mining, others in the raising of cattle that graze on the vast grasslands of eastern Oregon. Baker City is the 17th oldest city in Oregon and grew out of the early gold rush days of the 1890s. At Flagstaff Hill, visitors may see the original 150-year-old wagon-wheel ruts on the Oregon Trail. At the eastern side, you can see the deepest canyon in North America. Hells Canyon was carved by the Snake River and is 8,000 feet deep in some places. Hells Canyon National Recreation Area is 652,488 acres of some of America's most unique geology, scenery, plants and wildlife.

title: What is the heaviest animal on Earth?
text: The blue whale is longer and heavier than any other animal. A female blue whale averages 86 feet long (longer than most houses) and weighs up to 120 tons. And don't get too close to a blue whale if you don't want to get wet. When a whale breathes, it blows water out a hole in its head. The blue whale holds the record for the highest blast of water: 40 feet high!

title: Is that a salmon or a trout?
text: Oregon's juvenile Chinook salmon and rainbow trout look a lot alike. They can be found in many freshwater rivers, but only the salmon spends much of its adult life in the salty ocean. Can you tell the difference between a Chinook salmon and a rainbow trout?

title: Budgeting
text:
Making sure more money comes in than goes out

Have you ever asked your mom or dad for something, only to be told that it wasn't in the budget? A budget is a plan of how to manage your money. It has two main ideas.

First, you must think about how much money is coming in. Maybe you earn an allowance. Maybe you mow a neighbor's lawn to make money, also called income. If you earn money every week or month, like an allowance, then it is called a steady income.

Next, we look at how much is going out, or how much it costs you to live. Maybe you subscribe to a magazine or go to a movie every Friday night. These are types of expenses. Adults also have expenses. They pay bills every month to buy things we all need, like food, clothes and cars. These expenses come out of their income every month.

To make a budget, you must first look at your income (money coming in). Then add up all of your expenses (money going out). Now subtract the total amount of your expenses from your total income. This new number lets you know how much money you have for other things that you want. This helps you plan and make wise choices when spending your money.

The goal of a budget is to try to balance your income with your expenses. It is best if your income is more than your expenses. That way, more money is coming in than going out. Now it is your turn to make a budget. Good luck!

title: The Moon in Myth
text:
To the people living long ago, the moon was a god or goddess of special mystery and power. Not only did the moon outshine the other nighttime lights, but it also changed its shape and had its own strange motion in the sky. The moon had visible markings on its face that fascinated people on every land for thousands upon thousands of years.

Some said the markings were a rabbit on the moon; some said it resembled a frog. Other people said the markings were a human face - a Man in the Moon. In Scandinavia, however, there was no Man in the Moon, but instead two children, and they were carrying between them a pail of water. Little of the myth remains except an old nursery rhyme:

Jack and Jill Went up the hill To fetch a pail of water...

Once, long before this myth became a nursery rhyme, this story may have helped people remember how, throughout the month, the moon waxes (gets larger) to the full moon, then wanes (gets smaller) to the new moon and increases to full again. You see, Jack gets his name from the Scandinavian word "jakka" - to increase, and Jill's name comes from "joila" - to dissolve.

Take this article with you on the next full moon and see if you can find the above markings.
