text: Compare your life to that of an early American Indian. What do you think would be different? What would be the same?

title: Fun Facts
text: The cell phone company Motorola was originally focused on making record players for cars. Victrola record players were very popular back then, so they named themselves Motorola.

title: Americans Discover Columbia River
text:
It was during the quiet, early-morning hour of 4 a.m. on May 12, 1792, that American trader and explorer Robert Gray spotted something strange along the coast. He and his men had been searching for the entrance to a great river that earlier explorers had spoken of and that the American Indians said existed.

Capt. Gray peered at the distant, muddied, brown water. A dark line contrasted against the blue of the ocean, breaking against the shore so far away. Surely, this must be it, he thought. He had seen it before, on an earlier voyage, and this time he was determined to find out what it was. He ordered his men to sail toward the muddy water eddies, but they had a problem. Heavy waves were crashing up against a sand bar that blocked the way. Capt. Gray sailed back and forth, hunting for an opening where the water was smoother, but like explorers before him had discovered, there was no opening. After some delays Capt. Gray finally ordered his men to sail through the breakers anyway and head for the muddy water. It took some hard effort to get beyond the sand bar, but ultimately they did, and they sailed into the mouth of the mighty Columbia.

The next thing the crew knew, numerous American Indians from all around poured into canoes and paddled out to greet Capt. Gray and his men. The American Indians wanted to trade. The captain stayed a full nine days, trading with them before pulling anchor and sailing farther inland. Unfortunately, he made a wrong turn in these unchartered waters, and his ship ran aground. After the men jumped out to free the vessel, Capt. Gray ordered the ship turned back downstream, where they would do more trading. He then put back to sea for Nootka, a protected harbor on the west side of Vancouver Island. The river's name, Capt. Gray declared, would be that of his trustworthy ship, the Columbia.

This discovery was an important beginning because explorers in the region were trying to claim new lands and rivers for their own countries.

Spain claimed several areas along the coast and sent some ships and men to Nootka in 1789 to build a permanent settlement. When they arrived, they found both British and American ships already docked there. Not fearing the Americans, the Spanish captain captured three British ships and claimed that the British were violating Spain's claim as sole trader in the area. The resulting uproar almost led to war between England and Spain, but was settled with a treaty called the Nootka Agreement. The British sent representatives to Nootka to work out the details of the agreement and placed Capt. George Vancouver in charge of the expedition. During the same trip, Vancouver was also ordered to hunt for the Northwest Passage and chart the Pacific Northwest coast.

In April of 1792, Vancouver's ships passed the entrance to the Columbia River, but in his haste, he didn't take time to try and cross the sandbars and examine the muddy waters along the shore. When word came that the American Capt. Gray had succeeded, the embarrassed Vancouver pointed out that Gray had only discovered the mouth of the river, and that wasn't much of an accomplishment, he said.

But it was too late. By the time word of the Columbia River's existence spread, American fur traders traveled to the area in large numbers and began establishing trading camps. The British couldn't keep up because their ships had to travel so much farther than the American ships. The United States now had a solid claim to the land.

title: “Let ’Er Buck”
text:
Horses, bulls, leather, ropes, dirt, sweat, and guts--all of these words conjure up a picture of the rodeo. Oregon has dozens of rodeos each year. They range from junior rodeos to professional events. Fans of all ages attend to see their favorite cowboys buck, rope, and race.

Pendleton Round-Up is the largest rodeo in Oregon and one of the most celebrated round-ups in the country. The round-up began following a Fourth of July celebration in 1909. It consisted of bronco riding and horse races by American Indians and non-Indians. There were American Indian feasts and native war dances. Some of the community leaders put their heads together and decided to make it an annual event. The next year, the round-up was moved to September. This allowed the local farmers to finish their harvest before the celebrations began. The slogan "Let 'Er Buck" was also inspired at that time. It was a common rodeo phrase. Today, just hang around Pendleton during the round-up, and you'll hear "Let 'er buck" more often than "Good morning."

Pendleton Round-Up is unique because it celebrates the cowboy and American Indian cultures equally. Each year, an American Indian village of about 150 tepees is set up next to the rodeo. The village consists mostly of the Umatilla, Walla Walla, and Cayuse Tribes. Part of the village is American Indian arts and crafts. Visitors can purchase many gifts, from belt buckles to handcrafted beaded clothing. It's more than just tepees and beads. Tribal members also participate in the rodeo. They wear traditional dress while they parade horses. They dance traditional dances. One of the favorite events of the round-up is the Indian Bareback Relay Horse Race. It is thrilling to watch the riders as they race around the track. They trade horses and riders after each round.

Perhaps the most notable event is the Happy Canyon Pageant. This show tells the story of the development of the region. Both American Indians and non-Indians take part in this pageant. The Happy Canyon Pageant has been a family tradition for many generations

The round-up is fast, furious, and exciting What a great multicultural tradition, right here in our great state of Oregon!

title: People of the Coast
text:
Tillamook and Kalapuyan

The peoples of the Northwest Coast were weavers. Among the Tillamook and Kalapuyan tribes, this art produced robes of exceptional beauty. The women combined plant fibers with the wool of mountain goats and other furs and drew them out on a unique form of spindle to create their yarns. Blankets were highly prized and traded widely through the Northwest. The older woman wears the traditional clothing of their tribe, while the younger woman with the partially completed basket wears a new style made from trade cloth. Both have their arms and legs tattooed.

As with all the people of the Northwest Coast, most of their food came from fish taken in a wide variety of ways. Salmon, the most favored fish, were caught on their spawning runs up the rivers.

Chinook

A large group of Chinook Indians lived in an exciting place where the mighty Columbia River poured into the Pacific Ocean. They witnessed the early American and European explorers trying to find the great Northwest Passage, a mythical river that people believed ran from the Pacific to the Atlantic. Nobody knows when the Chinook settled at their homes on the river. Some anthropologists believe the Chinook might have once lived farther upstream. They share some similarities with the American Indians of the Columbia Plateau.

The Chinook built houses made from cedar planks. The planks were split off the trunks of large red cedars and used to build rectangular-shaped houses in which many families could live. The Chinook did not farm the land because all the food they needed grew naturally in the forests around them. The women collected crab apples, nuts, various roots, ferns, lupine, cow parsnips, thistle, blackberries, and more. They made bread from camas roots, which they served with fish oil, much as we eat bread with butter. The men caught salmon and trout by stretching nets in the water. The women cooked the salmon by suspending salmon steaks over a fire on sticks poked into the ground. Sometimes, they would steam the salmon in small fire pits lined with rocks on which they poured water. For supper, they sat on woven mats, washed their hands and mouths, and served the food with wooden ladles or clam shells.

The Chinook say that the first white man they ever saw was American trader Captain Robert Gray, who first sailed into the Columbia River in the ship Columbia, from which the river received its name. The Chinook traded with the whites, offering native items such as elk hide in exchange for manufactured items.

The Chinook received their name from the Chehalis Indians, their neighbors to the north. The Chinook name has been applied to a variety of things including a wind, a salmon, a trade jargon word, a canoe, vehicles and business establishments.

Products From Nature

The best-known symbol of the Northwest Coast is the totem pole. In fact, "totem pole" is not a proper name for these objects, since they did more than symbolize a family crest, or totem. They were ornamental house posts, entryways for dwellings, memorials, and grave markers for the dead. Increased wealth through trade with the white man, as well as the introduction of metal tools, led to their great elaboration and growth in popularity.

Many of the Coast Indians made their whaling canoes out of large trees. They would paint the tips of pegs with a red dye and pound them into the bottom of a large log split in half. They would turn the log over and use hot rocks and coals to burn the wood down and hollow out the log until they could see the tips of the red pegs. This showed them to burn and carve no farther. In this way, they prepared the canoe with boards and outside carvings before going to sea. The canoes could be small enough for two people or large enough to seat 60.

The working dress of most men along the coast was similar. It was often a front apron of hide that could be tucked through the legs and into the back of the belt during work. For warmth, a cloak or vest of fur was added. The influence of the Coastal People can still be felt and seen in Oregon today.

title: The Oregon Coast
text: From the Columbia River sand bar to the Gold Beach, Oregon's coast and 325 miles of shoreline are a mixture of fog, rain, sunshine, fishing, flowers and trees. The mouth of the Columbia has been a graveyard for ships. Dozens of vessels from the earliest times have wrecked upon the sandy and rocky shoals. The first lighthouse to help boats make it to shore was called "Terrible Tilly." It was built atop 120-foot-high Tillamook Rock in 1881. Several times, high waves crashed boulders, fish and seaweed through the windows of the lighthouse, putting out the light and leaving traveling ships at risk in the darkness until repairs could be made. Farther down the coast in the Tillamook region, logging became big business. The ancient forests had trees more than 1,000 years old, many more than 12-15 feet across and taller than 250 feet. In 1933, a fire destroyed 331,000 acres of timber. Ships 500 miles from shore were rained on with hot ashes and glowing bits of charcoal. Farther south toward Newport, sea otters play along the shore where the mountains crowd against the ocean. Oregon's wonderful coast nears California with a harvest of cranberries, coal beds, and numerous game fowl and animals.

title: Do We Say "Native American" or "American Indian"?
text: Some individuals and some entire tribes of Native Americans prefer to be called American Indians. Some are offended by the name Indian because the name was a mistake that Christopher Columbus made when he sailed to America and thought he had reached India. It is considered correct to use the terms Native American, American Indian, Indian, or indigenous people, according to the tribes' websites. Everyone agrees that we are all proud to be called Americans!

title: Marmot
text: It barks like a French poodle. It whistles like a parrot and sleeps most of the year. What is this strange creature? It's the marmot, cousin to woodchucks and squirrels. The marmot is a stout-bodied, short-legged, plant-eating rodent with coarse hair, a bushy tail, and very small ears. Marmots grow to 30 inches from nose to tail and weigh on average 20 pounds. Newborn marmots are naked and blind. After a month, their eyes open, and they grow enough fur to leave the nest. By August, the new marmots venture away from their parents to burrow homes of their own. During hibernation, marmots' breathing and heart rate slow down, and they sleep for six to nine months. They hibernate best when there is heavy snowfall. In the spring, they wake up and search for food. Marmots post a guard while they find berries and plants. If you go hiking in the high forest and hear a sound like a French poodle bark, or maybe a chirping whistle, that might be a marmot alerting his friends that an intruding biped is coming--you. (biped: bi=two, ped=foot or leg)

title: How do I use an encyclopedia?
text:
If you need to get some basic information on a topic before you begin in-depth research, use an encyclopedia. Sometimes you can find a wide range of information about a certain subject using an encyclopedia. An encyclopedia is a set of reference books ranging from A to Z. (It can also be a CD-ROM or a subscription to a website. Each volume has a number and a guide letter that shows the first letter of the article titles in that volume.

1. To find out what topics the encyclopedia includes, look through the index volume.

2. Scan the entries until you see the topic listed. You can look up someone's name, a place, or a general subject such as "reservations."

3. Go to the appropriate volume listed in the index.

4. Scan the guide words printed in dark type at the top of each page until you find your entry word.

5. You may need to skim through some entries until you find the information you need. This is because there may be more than one entry word for a given topic.

6. If you find a cross-reference after an entry word, then that means you will find information about the topic under another entry word. The cross-reference will tell you which volume of the encyclopedia to look in.

Using an encyclopedia, look up a tribe from your state that is discussed in this paper and summarize what you learned here. You may be able to find out what their name means, where they came from, what language they speak, what they ate, how they acquired food, how they dressed, if there are any members of this tribe living today, where they live today, how many are living today, etc.

title: Potlatch
text:
Directions:

After reading the description below, start on your way to the Potlatch to gain a great reward. Begin in the center of the circle and find your way to the treasure. One of the most important ceremonies practiced by the Northwest and other Coast Indians was the potlatch. A potlatch was a tremendous feast given by a wealthy man. At the conclusion, he would give away all kinds of expensive gifts—canoes, the enslaved, mats, blankets, jewelry, baskets, carved wooden boxes, dishes and food. It took years to prepare for a potlatch, and it would last days at a time. The most important guests received the most expensive gifts. The host knew that each gift he gave away would have to be matched by the man who received it when he held his potlatch. The host knew he would receive something of equal or greater value. Over the years, this is how a wealthy man would increase his wealth. A person who couldn’t give back something of equal or more value at his own potlatch was shunned and in disgrace.

title: On the Trail with Jedediah Smith
text:
Jedediah Smith didn't like having his head stuck in a bear's mouth. It wasn't his idea of having a good day. But that old grizzly was after some dinner, and this tall, tasty-looking human was making a whole lot of noise for just one man. When Jedediah finally escaped, he had an ear chewed off, but that didn't stop him from high-tailing it off into the woods.

Jedediah ran quite awhile until he found safety. He was known as a religious man, and after finding a resting spot, he nursed his injuries and opened his Bible to read the 23rd Psalm. When his men found him safe and sound, they bandaged him, sewed his ear back on, and continued on their way.

Jedediah was born in 1799 and was reared as a devout Methodist. At age 23, he joined a beaver-hunting group made up of Jim Bridger, David Jackson, Thomas Fitzpatrick, and William Sublette. They named their group the Rocky Mountain Fur Company.

Jedediah's travels, good heartedness and endurance made him one of America's greatest mountain men ever. He was an excellent shot with a rifle, always remained a gentleman, was cool under pressure, and was faithful to his religious upbringing. These qualities won him respect and friends - among both American Indians and trappers alike - all over the western United States.

In 1826, Jedediah led an expedition to California in search of beaver. The travelers had little more than their horses, rifles or pistols, knives, hatchets and maybe a bag full of food, tobacco, tools and bullets. When their food ran out, they decided to shoot a cougar for dinner - its shiny, white meat tasted a lot like pork. When the men's horses died of exhaustion and starvation, the explorers had to cross the Mojave Desert on foot. This incredible journey made Jedediah famous as the first white man to enter California on a land route from the east.

The following year, Jedediah left California for Fort Vancouver, becoming the first white man to reach the Columbia River by traveling up the coast.

Jedediah carved his place in the Pacific Northwest territory as one of the bravest men to explore the land. His extraordinarily wide travels opened up the rich fur-trapping and trading country and established trails and territory that were used by American pioneers coming west.

In 1831, he set out with a company to Santa Fe, New Mexico. When they neared a place called Wagon Bed, Kansas, Jedediah was out in front looking for a place to water the horses. A group of Comanches were watching a watering hole, waiting for deer or elk to wander by. When they saw this lone white man, Jedediah Smith, they became afraid and killed him. Jedediah was 32 years old.

title: American Indian Tribes Saving Salmon
text:
What do you think of when you hear the word "fry," "fingerling," and "eggs"? Maybe a McDonald's Happy Meal? Actually, these words describe salmon.

Did you know that salmon make an incredible journey during their lifetime? They travel hundreds of miles to the ocean and later swim upstream against the current all the way back to spawn (lay eggs).

For centuries, American Indians in the Oregon area would come to the Columbia River during the salmons' migration to catch them by using long-handled dipping nets. The American Indians were careful to respect the fish and only catch as many as they needed to survive.

In the 1860s, when settlers began commercial fishing, so many fish were caught that they used draft horses to pull the nets out of the water. Later, fish wheels were used to scoop up tens of thousands of fish. Dams were also built on the river, which confused the migrating salmon and stopped them from completing their journey.

Today, several species of Pacific salmon are endangered. But the descendants of American Indians are working to help them survive. Members of the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs are working with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the state of Oregon to protect the wild spring Chinook salmon and steel-head trout. They run a hatchery that produces eggs, inch-long fry and two-inch-long fingerlings. They let these fish grow as big as possible. When they are about 16 months old (called "smolts") they release them into the Warm Springs River to join wild salmon on their journey to the ocean. After one to four years, they return to the river to spawn.

Thanks to the hard work of many people, more salmon are finishing the journey.

title: Credit and Debt
text:
Trying not to spend more money than you have

You've made your budget, and you are trying to stick to it. You take care to plan what you will buy. You try to make sure that your income is greater than your expenses.

Then you see it - the bike you've always wanted! It is on sale for $55. You rush home and count all of the money in your piggy bank. You find you only have $30.

Discouraged, you decide to go talk to your dad about the situation. He agrees to loan you the remaining $25. He says he will take it out of your allowance for the next few weeks. You think this is a great idea! Together, you go down to the store and purchase your brand new bike.

Even though you most likely didn't know it, you just bought something on credit. Credit is money that is loaned and must be paid back. Usually, credit lenders require a fee, known as interest. The person who borrows money must pay back the money he or she owes. He or she also must pay some extra money for being able to borrow from the lender.

You are also now in debt. Debt is money you owe when you buy something by borrowing money. Although credit can help people in tight spots, it should be used carefully.

Sometimes, people just buy things on credit, usually with a credit card. They forget that they have to pay the money back with interest. This can add up to huge amounts of debt that people have a hard time paying back. You should always remember that having things today and paying for them tomorrow is tricky business. Try to avoid it!

title: American Indians of the Interior
text:
This week, let's learn about the American Indians who lived inland from the coast of Oregon.

Oregon Interior People didn't need the kind of strong, ocean-going canoes the Coastal Indians used. Their canoes were shallower and designed for the more gentle currents of rivers. They became expert at catching salmon as it migrated from the ocean to spawn in the rivers. River people didn't cultivate the land because so much food grew freely around them. An occasional deer that wandered into camp was surrounded and killed for a feast. Their villages usually stayed in about the same place as long as the food was there. Some of Oregon's Interior Indians include: Skilloot, Multnomah, Yamhill, Clackamas, Umatilla, Wallowa, Coquille and Molalla.

Umatilla

Umatilla comes from a word that means "many rocks." The Umatilla people lived in the north-eastern corner of Oregon. Their numbers were estimated at 1,500 in 1790, but had dwindled to between 10 and 100 in 1962. Before the arrival of the horse, the Umatillas depended on salmon and other fish for their food. They used very creative nets, baskets, traps and spears to catch the fish. They even had an important ceremony they performed in hopes of increasing their catch during the first salmon run of the year. They also gathered mussels from the river. Inland, they sought out berries, camas, pine nuts, seeds, bark, and sap. They cooked their food in roasting ovens made of dirt or boiled and steamed their food in water heated by hot rocks.

The Umatilla homes were made out of poles and mats. Their houses were sometimes as large as 16 feet wide and 60 feet long and could accommodate several families. As part of their religion, they used sweat lodges to condition both their bodies and their spirits. When horses arrived in the early 1800s, their hunt for game and other forms of food expanded over a larger territory.

Clackamas

The Clackamas people once occupied 12 villages located on the banks of the Columbia River near the town of Troutdale, Oregon. The Clackamas lived in wooden houses that sometimes were large enough for three to four families. Even though they migrated during the summer to obtain salmon, roots and berries, their homes were permanent, and they always returned there. An important root that they relied on was the wappato root. They used it in their own diet and traded it with other tribes.

The Clackamas were very skilled with their canoes, which they carved from logs. They were also very adept at using nets and baskets to catch leaping salmon at Willamette Falls. In 1790, their numbers were estimated at 2,500. When Lewis and Clark counted them, they estimated about 1,800. Some think the Clackamas are an extinct tribe, although many others don't believe that to be true. The Europeans were very happy to get the bulk of the Clackamas's land because it bordered the south side of the Columbia, the perfect loading place for crops that were raised in the fertile lands of Willamette Valley. The Interior People appreciated the gifts that the land provided.

title: Hood River County
text: Hood River County is home to some of the world's greatest wind surfing on the Columbia River. Visitors discover a world of outdoor recreation, historic landmarks and lots of friendly people. The county is not very large. It was established in 1908 with only 533 square miles. Its county seat is Hood River. The people who live and visit here enjoy the spectacular view of the eastern slope of Mount Hood on one side and the mighty Columbia River on the other. You'll notice lots of apple trees here. Hood River is one of Oregon's major apple growing regions. Don't forget to try out the Barlow Road. In 1845, Samuel Barlow blazed his own trail around Mount Hood to the Willamette Valley. He charged $5 per wagon. People paid because the only other route was on a log raft going down the Columbia. You can still travel his road or take a train ride up the slopes of Mount Hood. Built in 1906, the Mount Hood Railroad is one of the last switchback railroads in the country.

title: What do you call a group of geese?
text:
Animal groups have some unusual names— for example a gaggle of geese, a tittering of magpies, a herd of cows, an exaltation of larks, a pride of lions, a chatter of parakeets, a murmuration of starlings, a troop of monkeys, and a swarm of bees.

There are hundreds of others! Have you ever heard of a pizza pie of fourth graders? Neither have we!

title: Camas Root
text:
We hear a lot about American Indians and pioneers in Oregon living off camas. What makes camas so important? Camas is a lily that grows from British Columbia to California, from Alberta to Montana, Wyoming and Utah.

It has beautiful purple and blue blossoms. Its round bulb resembles an onion, but tastes sweet. It is rich in protein and is a good source of fiber, calcium, phosphorus and iron. The young bulbs are harvested in mid-July through September.

They are cooked for three days in a fire pit beneath layers of grass and dirt. When ready, they may be eaten or pounded, dried and used to make bread. The camas lily grows wild, but early American Indians cultivated it and would go to war to protect their camas fields.

Chief Joseph waged the Nez Perce War in part to protest against the destruction of camas fields under his tribe's control.

title: Let's Write
text: You have joined the Rocky Mountain Fur Company with Jedediah Smith. Write about your travels through the Mojave Desert or up the coast to Fort Vancouver. What do you see? What adventures do you have?

title: Language Arts Connection
text: Use any color to highlight three relative adverbs (where, when, why) in this week’s magazine. Underline the clause that contains the relative adverb and circle the noun that the clause modifies. (CC ELA L.4.1)

title: American Indian Sovereignty and Intergovernmental Cooperation
text:
Every nation in this world has a government. They make laws and have their own governing body. A nation is a group of people that lives in a certain area or territory. Nations often have the same history, culture, religion and language. The United States is a nation. American Indian tribes are nations, too! These tribes are nations that live within the U.S. and while part of it are also separate from it, having their own governing bodies and citizens.

Have you ever heard of the term sovereignty? This term applies to American Indian nations across the United States. A nation has its own government and rules. Sovereignty means that the American Indian nations have the power to govern themselves and that this right is inherent. That means they have the ability to make their own laws and govern themselves and that power existed far before the U.S. government was formed. The American Indian nations do not get their power from the U.S. government. They have the right to live their lives in the way they want to continue their lifestyle and culture.

Since the Nations have their own government, they and the U.S. government — local, state and national — have to work together to find solutions to many issues. This is known as intergovernmental cooperation. This is a big term for something unique in our country because the American Indian governments existed from “time immemorial,” which means something has existed since before the beginning of recorded time. American Indian governments exist today alongside the U.S. government. American Indians are both U.S. citizens and members of their respective Nations.

title: The Mystery of Whale Cove
text:
It was Sept. 26, 1580, and the famous British captain Sir Francis Drake pulled his ship, "The Golden Hinde," into Plymouth Harbor, England. It had been three long years, and people had feared Drake was lost at sea. But he returned safely back home. As Drake's crew hurried off the ship, the wharf rats tried to sneak on.

But there was something strange about Drake's vessel. Those standing nearby noticed it almost immediately. The ship, they saw, was sitting heavy in the water - much lower, in fact, than a ship should be that had just crossed the ocean. Little did the cheering crowds know that the ship's hull was weighed down with tons of gold - gold stolen from the Spanish, half a world away.

Drake's mission started three years earlier, in 1577. He led five small ships and 200 men on a trip financed by Queen Elizabeth to explore the Americas, set up fur-trading agreements, and help fight the settlement of Spain in the New World.

When Drake arrived in South America in 1578, he discarded two of his smaller ships and set sail for the tip of South America, where he ran into a great wind. By the time he emerged around the other side into the Pacific Ocean, Drake was alone - the other ships had lost him and returned to England, fearing he had drowned in the storm.

The Spanish didn't expect enemy ships in their waters and couldn't catch Drake as he zipped northward. Along the way, he robbed Spanish galleons out on the high seas. It wasn't long before the hull of the Golden Hinde was overflowing with Spanish gold, silver, precious stones, and pearls. In 1579, Drake turned for home and returned to England, arriving in 1580.

This is where the mystery begins. Queen Elizabeth spread the word that Drake was the first Englishman to circle the globe and that he traveled only a little way up the western coast of America. The queen's report said that Drake stopped near the San Francisco area for ship repairs, a place Drake named "New Albion." "Albion" is a Celtic word meaning "Great Britain."

But some historians believe Drake went much farther north - in fact, all the way to Vancouver Island. New research shows that Drake might even have landed at Whale Cove, halfway up Oregon's coast, to make his repairs. Drake described seeing muskrats, an animal native to Oregon, not California. His maps published after 1603 show a land drawing matching Whale Cove, not San Francisco Bay. Drake described an American Indian house similar to one found in Whale Cove - none exist in California.

Why the secrecy? Some historians believe that Queen Elizabeth wanted to keep details of the trip secret. Drake might have mistaken the Strait of Juan de Fuca as the mouth to the Northwest Passage, the important shortcut Queen Elizabeth wanted Drake to find. Keeping this secret would give England a great advantage over the Spanish. After Queen Elizabeth died in 1603, details of Drake's voyage began to leak out. Maps he had drawn showed he had indeed traveled farther up the coast than earlier believed. And that's the mystery of Whale Cove.

title: Plateau and Plains People
text:
This week, let's look at Oregon's first people who lived on the plateau and plains of Oregon.

Oregon's Plateau and Plains Indians had a harder time living in areas where food was more scarce. They were always searching for food and could never settle down. In early spring, they had very little to eat - usually snails and slow rabbits. By May or June, they moved to the rivers to catch the spawning salmon that were in abundance at that time. (When something is in abundance, there is plenty of it.) By fall, they left the rivers and hunted deer, elk, antelope and mountain goat. In preparation for winter, the women harvested nuts, berries and roots. Animal and fish flesh was dried and preserved. Some of Oregon's Plateau and Plains Indians include Cayuse, Klamath, Modoc, Northern Molala, Southern Molala, and Northern Piute.

Klamath

Klamath means "people," or "community." Because the Klamaths lived so far into Oregon, away from the coast, they were able to avoid contact with the whites for a long time. When Peter Skene Ogden visited them in 1826, they numbered about 1,000, and in Ogden's words, they were "a happy race." The Klamath were good with their bows and arrows and could shoot waterfowl with an arrow. They harpooned fish and hunted game. They traded enslaved people (usually captured in California), beads, the seeds of wocas (used for soups and breads) and other items in exchange for horses, blankets, buffalo skins and dried salmon. Both men and women wore fiber skirts and basket caps. In the winter, they wore tule leggings and sandals, coats or aprons of skin and fiber and fur mittens. Tule is a reed similar to cattails or papyrus. Their winter homes were earthen lodges dug 2 to 4 feet deep into the Earth. The Klamath didn't begin using buckskin clothing and footwear until the early 1800s. They also tattooed their bodies. Today, there are more than 2,300 Klamath, most of whom still live in the Klamath Lake and Klamath Marsh areas.

Cayuse

Early French-Canadian fur trappers called the Cayuse the "cailloux," which is a French word meaning "stones" or "rocks." We don't know if this referred to the land in which the Cayuse lived or to the kind of stubborn people they were. The Cayuse called themselves an American Indian word that meant "superior people." They rode a sturdy horse called the Cayuse horse. The Cayuse would ride around to intimidate their neighbors who did not yet have horses. They were so proud of their horses that some were buried with their favorite horse. Their horses grazed in green Cayuse pasture lands. When tensions with whites became bad, the Cayuse started a war by murdering Dr. Marcus Whitman, his wife, and 12 others. In 1850, five Cayuse were hanged for the murders, and things quieted down. After years of suffering and wars, they finally gave in and moved to a reservation. As a final upset to these proud people, white men rounded up and sold the Cayuse horses and turned their grazing land into farms.

title: Baker County
text: Baker County borders with Idaho on Oregon's east-central side. It was the first part of Oregon viewed by the 250,000 pioneers who crossed the 2,000-mile Oregon Trail. One such group stopped near a stream to rest. A little girl took her blue bucket to fetch water, but instead, wasted away her time collecting pretty rocks. Later on, when it was discovered that the pretty rocks were pure gold, an anxious search began to find the legendary Blue Bucket Gold Mine, but no one has. In 1861, gold was discovered near Powder River, and Baker City suddenly became one of the most popular gold rush boom towns of the West. By 1900, Baker City was larger than Spokane and Boise. To the east, Hells Canyon, carved out by the Snake River, is the deepest canyon in North America. It is almost 8,000 feet deep. The next time you're in Baker County, try shouting into America's deepest canyon. You may be waiting a long time for an echo to return!

title: Why do animals get scared and howl before earthquakes?
text: Our best guess is that they may have senses we still don't understand. A man in California is studying strange animal behavior before earthquakes. He reports that a lot of critters seem to abandon their homes just prior to an earthquake. Here are some examples of this: snakes have deserted their dens, homing pigeons have become lost, the number of runaway pets suddenly skyrockets, and confused swarms of bees have flown past their hives and right into dark buildings.

title: Spotted Owl
text: There's a quiet, little owl called the northern spotted owl that lives in our old forests and tries to mind it's own business. It depends on old-growth forests for hunting and mating because the giant trees provide a protective covering overhead. During the night, the spotted owls quietly go about hunting their food. Their hoot sounds like a soft, dog-like bark, and their feathers are spotted, helping them to blend in with the trees. Each owl needs at least 300 acres of forest to survive. When loggers began cutting old-growth forests, the number of owls began to shrink. Today, there is a big argument between loggers, who need the old-growth lumber, and people worried that the owls will die out. Logging operations in old-growth forests are stopped while people work out a compromise. Meanwhile, the owls happily go about their business. If you go camping in the forest, watch carefully - you might spot a spotted owl taking a nap.

title: The Next Frontier: Mars?
text:
Humans have explored and made maps of almost every part of the Earth. What should be the next place we visit? Some people think it should be the Red Planet: Mars. Satellites have taken pictures and mapped parts of the surface. NASA has landed equipment on Mars to search for signs of life. While NASA is planning for future unmanned machine landings on Mars, another company wants to send people there.

Mars One is a company that is organizing a human mission to Mars. Their goal is to launch a spacecraft in 2026 that will send four astronauts to live on Mars. It is a seven- or eight-month journey to Mars, and it is a one-way trip. There will be no way for the astronauts to return to Earth. Even with this knowledge, over 200,000 people applied for the positions!

Once the astronauts have landed, they will settle in housing units and get used to life in a new place. That sounds a lot like what other explorers and pioneers did long ago! The Mars astronauts will study the environment and get their habitat ready for more people to arrive. Keep an eye out for Mars news from NASA and Mars One. Would you like to be one of the first humans on the Red Planet?

title: Make a Totem Pole
text:
American Indians of the Northwest such as the Kwakiutl, the Haida and the Tlingit are well known for their totem poles, which are hand carved from large logs. They are usually painted red, black, blue and green and often have important animal or spirit designs on them, or may tell a family’s history.

Directions:

1. The full-sized patterns are on Page 4. Trace each of them with a pencil and cut them out.

2. Make a circle onto a scrap of poster board, cut out, and glue to the bottom of a paper-towel tube. It should be larger than the tube size.

3. With markers or crayons, color the bear, wolf and bird. Draw feathers on the wings with red, black, blue, green and yellow markers or crayons.

4. Starting at the bottom, wrap the bear around the tube. Overlap and glue in the back as shown.

5. Wrap the wolf above the bear (tuck the feet behind the bear’s ears); overlap and glue in the back. Wrap the bird above the wolf (tuck the feet behind the wolf’s ears); overlap and glue.

6. Glue two halves of a Popsicle stick to the back of the bird’s wings to keep them from curling up.
