title: The Vitamin That Changed the World
text:
Did you know that the secret to Oregon's discovery is in your own kitchen? It all got started because of a little thing called vitamin C.

After Columbus discovered America in 1492, the Spanish sent hundreds of settlers to Central America and Latin America. Their settlements grew large. After 70 years, the Spanish began sending ships across the Pacific Ocean to trade with Asia. (Find Asia on your map).

In the 1560s, the Spanish conquered the Philippines and used the islands as a giant Asian marketplace. They would trade gold and furs for goods from Asian merchants such as spices porcelains, oriental silks and other luxuries. The Spanish shipped the goods to Acapulco, Mexico, and then on to Europe, where they were sold for a huge profit.

This is where vitamin C became important. A serious danger for ocean-traveling ships was lack of nutrition for the sailors. Sailing west from Mexico to the Philippines was fast because the westerly trade winds blew the ships straight there. But coming back toward America took seven long months at sea because the wind was blowing against them. Sailors had to steer their ships in a zig-zag fashion, something they called "tacking." By the time Spanish ships reached Mexico, many sailors had died or were suffering from a disease called scurvy because they didn't have vitamin C.

How do you fix this problem? For a long time, no one knew exactly what caused scurvy. The Spanish decided their health problems resulted from poor diets and being at sea too long. They hoped a resting place along the coast of Oregon and Washington would be the solution. They began looking for a place where a captain could land his ship, replenish supplies, and nurse his crew back to health before continuing on to Mexico. While the Spanish looked for a safe harbor, the scurvy problem was solved by English Captain James Cook. He discovered that by slightly pickling vegetables in vinegar, the vegetables would not go bad on long sea voyages. Sailors who ate these vegetables did not get scurvy. Little did they know that it was the vitamin C in the vegetables that helped the sailors.

With a cure for scurvy helping sailors all over the world, the word got out that the Spanish were trying to claim the Pacific Northwest. Other nations wanted part of the discovery and began sending explorers.

Some people believe that if the cure for scurvy had been found sooner, our territory might have been ignored for a long time while nations concentrated on trade with Asia.

In the next few weeks, we will look at the many explorers who came here and try to understand why our territory was so valuable to people all around the world.

title: Attention All Space Tourists
text:
Grab your camera, reach for your passport, and put on your spacesuit. Your vacation flight into outer space is about to blast off! If you have ever dreamed of exploring the unknown and seeing places that others have only imagined, you may have found the perfect vacation spot: space.

The good news is that the space tourism program is officially open for business. beginning in 2001, space tourists have made the trip of a lifetime aboard Russian rockets flying to the International Space Station, or ISS. These "space tourists" loved their vacations and returned to Earth with a great respect for the outer limits of the place we call home.

The bad news is that if you are interested in becoming the next space tourist, you may want to find an extra summer job. Becoming a space tourists costs more money than most people could carry, let alone afford to spend. A week-long vacation aboard a rocket headed for space will cost you between $20 and $40 million per person. So much for making this a family vacation!

If the price of traveling to space seems a bit out of your reach, there are other options for enjoying a space vacation. You could spend about $10,000 per person and travel to Moscow, Russia, for the Zero-Gravity flight program, the MiG-25 Edge of Space Program, or the MiG-21 High-G Flight Program. If this still sounds like too much money, you could wait and hope that former-astronaut Buzz Aldrin's idea to let people enter a lottery and allow the winners to fly into space becomes a reality.

On the bright side, it is expected that in the future the price of vacationing in space will come down. It is also expected that within the next 20 years, space planes could be taking off for the Moon as often as airplanes flying between New York and Los Angeles. Start saving your money now and maybe you could reserve a seat on one of these super vacation flights!

title: Early Exploration of the Northwest
text:
Let's choose an explorer for the Greatest Sea Explorers Hall of Fame. This year's candidates all came to the Pacific Northwest by ship. Who do you think deserves to be in our hall of fame?

Greatest Sea Explorers Hall of Fame

Our election works like this:

1. Read the list of explorers below.

2. Discuss the importance of each explorer's discovery as a class or with a partner.

3. Decide in your own mind the discovery that did the most to open up Oregon and the Northwest to settlers and for development. List your reasons on a piece of paper.

4. If your teacher wants to, hold elections. Vote for the explorer of your choice. In your newspaper, write beside each explorer the number of votes he receives in your class. Circle the winner. If there is a tie, talk about what each man did and then hold a tie-breaking election.

1. Bartolomé Ferrelo-Spanish, 1542. Ferrelo was the first European to see our coast.

2. Sir Francis Drake-English, 1578. Drake was the first to land on Oregon's coast and the first Englishman to sail around the world.

3. Juan de Fuca-Greek, 1592. We're not sure that his story is true, but de Fuca is credited with discovering the Strait of Juan de Fuca.

4. Sebastian Vizcaino-Spanish, 1603. Vizcaino and Martin D'Aguilar looked for a resting place along our coast for Spanish ships coming from the Philippines trading route. (See Cover Story.)

5. Vitus Bering-Russian. Bering never visited our coast, but starting in 1728, he helped Russia gain control of the Alaskan coast fur trade. This worried other countries into laying claim to the Pacific Northwest as quickly as possible. The Bering Strait and Sea were named after Vitus Bering.

6. Juan Perez-Spanish, 1774. He was the first to land on Vancouver Island.

7. Bruno de Heceta-Spanish, 1775. Heceta was the first to land on Washington's coast. He also saw the mouth of the Columbia River, but didn't try to enter.

8. Captain James Cook-English, 1778. Cook discovered the Society Islands, New Zealand and the Hawaiian Islands. He sailed up our coast, but didn't find the Columbia River. He discovered a cure for scurvy.

9. William Barclay-English, 1787. Barclay rediscovered the Strait of Juan de Fuca.

10. John Meares-English, 1788. Meares also rediscovered the Strait of Juan de Fuca and named it after Juan de Fuca; Meares built the first ship on the Northwest coast.

11. Captain George Vancouver-English, 1792. He was a great explorer whose maps of our coast remain some of the best ever. More than 50 place names in use today were chosen by Vancouver. His name is on Vancouver Island; Vancouver, British Columbia; and Vancouver, Washington.

12. Captain Robert Gray-American, 1792. Gray made two trips to our region and discovered the Columbia River. He was the first American to sail around the world. Gray's Harbor was named after him.

title: Coastal Region
text: Oregon's coast has miles of beach and is dotted with dozens of towns. If you took a boat trip down our coast, you would start at the mouth of the Columbia River. You're not too far from Astoria, the first permanent U.S. settlement west of the Rockies. The movies "Free Willy" and "Kindergarten Cop" were filmed here. Continue your trip down the coast and see Haystack Rock at Cannon Beach. Stop for some cheese at Tillamook, then continue past Lincoln to Newport and see Devil's Punch Bowl, a beautiful, powerful place where ocean meets the coast. About 400 gray whales stop here for summer snacks of plankton. Continuing south, you'll stop at Heceta Head Lighthouse, the most photographed of Oregon's nine lighthouses. Oregon has sand dunes on its coast. The Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area stretches from Florence to North Bend and Coos Bay, the coast's largest urban areas. Have your camera ready for a sunset photo-stop at Bandon. Sea stacks, tidal pools and clam diggers add mystery to this beautiful place. Boardman State Park stretches for 10 miles along the last section of coast, and then you reach Brookings. This is a good place to rest your feet in the ocean - you'll be really tired!

title: How big is the biggest seashell?
text: The biggest seashell is the marine giant clam (Tridacna gigas), which can grow more than 4 feet across and weigh more than 700 pounds. The smallest seashell is the coin shell (Neolepton sykesi). It is a very rare shell that measures only .047 inches across. If you had a Tridacna gigas clam, you probably could make enough clam chowder for your whole school!

title: Northern Sea Lion
text: Sea lions love to sun themselves by the hundreds along our rocky shores. They are probably the biggest marine mammal you'll ever see in such numbers. The bulls grow up to 12 feet long and weigh up to a ton (equal to 2,000 pounds). The females are much smaller - 8 feet long and 800 pounds. They give birth to their pups on land because the young cannot swim at birth. Sea lions love to eat fish and squid. If you see some sea lions on shore, keep your distance. The bulls will roar and bark and chase intruders away. The females howl and bleat. Together, these finned and whiskered animals make their beach sunning places awfully noisy and crowded places to be. Don't confuse the Northern sea lion with the California sea lion. These smaller animals like it here, too. You'll recognize the California version as the kind of seal usually trained for the circus or water park.

title: Make Your Own Coat of Arms
text:
Many years ago, people would use a coat of arms to show which group or family they belonged to. They put their coat of arms up on flags in the territories they explored. A coat of arms was used as a symbol of one's great achievements, goals and beliefs.

Believe it or not, we still use the concept of a coat of arms today. Each state has a state seal, and we have a national seal. They are used to show achievements, goals and beliefs of the country or region they represent.

Now draw your own symbols in your coat of arms. You may wish to put decorations around your coat of arms. Ask your parents or grandparents if you have a family coat of arms. If you do, ask them to sit down with you and explain what the symbols mean.

Symbols are very important to us. In fact, we cannot do without them. We go to school to learn about symbols. The words on a page are symbols of meanings or things. Pictures and icons are symbols, too. Although some words are used on a coat of arms or seal, we mostly use pictures because everyone, even those who do not know how to read words, can understand them at a glance. Another reason not to use words on symbols is the language barrier. Can you read the Latin inscription on our country's seal? Sometimes, animals are used to stand for things. Colors can mean different things, too. What do the red, white and blue of our flag stand for? On a state seal, what might an eagle, olive branch, arrows, stars, eye or pyramid mean?

title: How Do I Read Tables?
text:
By learning to read tables, you can quickly compare and contrast data.

Use Categories

Tables are lists or boxes of information, organized into categories. Categories of information appear across the top and down the lefthand side. And the information in each column shows the hard data for these categories. Tables have labels and numbers. When reading a table, carefully read the title and labels so that you interpret the information correctly.

Try It!

Study the table below and then answer the questions that follow.

1. What does this table show?

2. Who traveled the shortest distance?

3. How far did John Cabot travel?

4. How far is it from France to Michigan?

5. How far did Jacques Cartier travel?

6. Who traveled 4,693 miles?

7. How far is it from England to Hawaii?

8. How far is it from Spain to Tampa Bay, Florida?

9. How far did Bernal Diaz del Castillo travel?

10. How far did Francis Drake travel?

11. Which trip is the longest, Spain to Peru or Spain to Mexico?

12. How far is it from Africa to Florida to Spain? (Hint: See Panfi lo de Narvaez and Estevanico?

title: Let's Write
text: It’s the year 1730, and you’ve just arrived in our state after a long journey across the ocean. People are asking, “What will you be in this new state of ours? A farmer? A fisher? Will you run a business?” Describe your new job and how you will get started.

title: A Furry Story
text:
Imagine getting up every day before the sun came up, crawling onto a rocky, dirty ground for a bed, using only your clothes as a pillow, and having to hunt and trap a small, furry animal for a living. That is exactly what many men did in Oregon in the 1800s.

After Lewis and Clark brought a group of explorers from Wood River, Illinois, to the Pacific Ocean in 1804, many people were excited about traveling to the unexplored west to find water filled with beaver, mink, otter, and other animals.

One man, John Jacob Astor, listened very closely to the reports from the Lewis and Clark expedition and decided, as one of America's first millionaires, to build a post on the shore of the Pacific Ocean. He knew if he did this, he would have many trappers and traders bringing fur in to help make him richer. He would send fur to the Russian American Company in Alaska and his Columbian River post with his fleet of ships. Besides the Pacific Fur Company that he built in Oregon at the Columbia River watershed (where the river drains into the Pacific Ocean) in 1810, he also founded the American Fur Company in the Rocky Mountain region in 1808 and the South West Company in 1811.

He sent people on boats and by foot toward the Columbia watershed. He began a colony called Astoria that is still part of Oregon today. The Pacific Fur Company post proved to be difficult to maintain, however. Supplies did not come very often. Many men were starving, so they built Willamette Post to relieve pressure that was put on the stores at the mouth of the river.

When Astor's partners in Astoria heard about the War of 1812, they feared that British ships would enter the river and take over the post. So in 1813, they sold the post to the North West Company, ending Astor's dreams. The Pacific Fur Company may not have worked for Astor but the investment he made helped pave the way for other companies and many fur traders, which was a large part of the economy in early America.

During the 1810s, the North West Company and the Hudson's Bay Company, the oldest fur trading company, which was founded in 1670, actually got into a fight in the Red River Valley in Canada! The British Parliament wanted to end the conflict and forced the two companies to merge, or combine. Only the Hudson's Bay Company survived this merging, and so they took over the work in the Oregon area.

title: Eager Beavers Causing Problems
text:
While fur trappers once flocked to Oregon because of all the beaver found here, these busy little animals are now giving many Oregon residents huge headaches. As more people build homes and businesses in the beavers' natural habitat (the place where they live and grow), the beaver have become eager about claiming their territory. Beaver cause problems for business and home owners by cutting down trees, chewing on bushes and shrubs, and coming inside attics and crawl spaces to have their babies. Beaver also dam up rivers and streams, causing floods that damage property.

Beaver have very long teeth that continue to grow throughout their lives. This is one reason why they are so eager to chew. If they don't keep chewing, their teeth will grow too long. With all of this chewing, beaver can cause a lot of damage in a short amount of time. When they chew on trees, they either cause them to fall over, or they damage them so badly that they die. They will even chew on telephone poles and fence posts, causing even more damage.

So what can be done to stop the beaver problem? Many new companies are taking on the beaver problem, offering their services to Oregon residents who need to get rid of these persistent animals. These companies specialize in trapping and removing the beaver from ponds, rivers and pools. They also "beaverproof" the property, using special fences and pipes to drain ponds in the area so the beaver won't come back.

While beaver were once a very important Oregon resource, there are few people who wear beaver fur anymore. Today, the beaver that were once such big money-makers for the early settlers are sometimes thought of as giant, unwanted pests.

title: Fur Traders and Trappers Come to the Northwest
text:
The popularity of beaver-skin hats in Europe was the main reason the fur trade grew. Fur trading became the first big business in the Northwest.

Fur Trade Changes the Northwest

The fur trade changed our region in four ways: (1) It made people interested in exploring our territory, and furs paid for the trips, so people could come back again and again. (2) It helped spread European culture into North America, where settlers could trade furs for tools, furniture and books, which they were accustomed to having back in their homelands. (3) It helped bring Europeans into friendly contact with American Indians (to trade instead of conquer) and introduced modern goods such as knives, axes, firearms, kettles and blankets to the American Indians. (4) It started international competition (contest, race, rivalry) between nations. This led to wars, treaties and, finally, the settling of America's boundaries. The following timeline shows the course of the fur trade in the Northwest.

1540-1774

Spain explores Pacific Northwest, but doesn't settle it. The Spanish were discouraged when they couldn't find gold, so they ignored the Northwest for a long time.

1700s

Fur hats become the latest fashion in Europe. People loved hats and caps made of fur, and the demand kept the ships coming to America.

1741

Russia discovers Alaska's abundance of furs. Vitus Bering (a Dane by birth) landed in Alaska and found a fortune in sea-otter and beaver furs. Hundreds of Russian trappers followed in Bering's footsteps.

1750s

Russians strip the north of sea otters. American Indians normally did all the hunting in Alaska, but when the Russians began making unfair demands, the American Indians refused to hunt for them. The Russians responded by kidnaping the American Indian women and children and holding them for a ransom (demand of something valuable in exchange for a captive) of more furs. This soon led to the killing and pillaging (plundering, looting, stealing) of American Indian villages until the Russian leader, Catherine the Great, put a stop to the terrible crimes.

1774

Spain tries to stop Russian expansion. Perez sailed here to stake a claim in the region for Spain.

1786

Britain tries to license the fur trade by requiring traders to purchase a license before they could trade furs in the Pacific Northwest. British traders Charles Barkley (1787) and John Meares (1786, 1788) got around the licensing requirement by registering their ships with another country.

1788-1792

American trader Robert Gray trades for furs. Gray sailed here to stake a claim for America. More than 85 American ships followed over the next 15 years to trade for furs. Spanish and British traders couldn't compete.

1812

Demand for coastal fur shrinks. An Italian hat designer invented the silk top hat in the 1780s. With demand for silk hats replacing fur hats, plus the near extinction (dying out of a species) of sea otters and the beginning of the War of 1812, the fur business nearly died out completely. Everyone's attention turned to the inland fur trade and the valuable beaver skin.

title: Coastal Region - Overview
text: Did you know that the biggest ocean in the world crashes up against our coast? The Pacific Ocean covers 71 million square miles — that's more than one-third of the entire surface of the Earth. The ocean is loaded with life, from giant whales to their major food source, the microscopic plankton, and to all kinds of plants and animals in between. The warm ocean currents that move from Asia to Alaska keep our coast pretty comfortable. Lots of moisture carried by southwesterly winds bring rain and snow to our mountains. Walk along the beach and look between the rocks when the tide pulls back to see an overflowing abundance of marine life. Our coast has slowly risen over time. In some places, shell deposits and old beach terraces can be found 1,500 feet above sea level. There are beautiful water-worn caves, eroded arches and cliffs all along our coast. The water is usually too cold and dangerous for swimming, but walking barefoot is a lot of fun. On your way, watch out for slippery seaweed, and don't step on any of the 25,000 assorted crustaceans (free-moving critters with jointed legs, like crabs) or any of the 100,000 different mollusks (clams, snails, etc.) that live on our coast. They may see your toe as a surprise afternoon snack!

title: How big is your skin?
text: If you take your skin off and lay it out on the ground, it will measure 10-12 square feet and weigh about 4 pounds, depending on your size. By the time you're an adult, your skin covers more than 18 square feet and weighs about 6 pounds. Some adults wish that their skin could get smaller, especially after eating too much pumpkin pie during a big Thanksgiving dinner.

title: Wild Turkeys
text: Oregon has a lot of wild turkeys gobbling around. Our state has three types of turkeys, the Rio Grande, Merriam and hybrid. They love to strut their stuff, even in November. Our wild turkeys have excellent vision and hearing. Their field of view is 270-degrees. This is the main reason most hunters have a hard time catching them. If you spook a turkey, it will sprint away at a top speed of 20 miles per hour or burst into flight at 50-55 miles per hour. Turkeys can adopt just about any place as home, but they love grassy areas in hardwood forests the most. Turkeys spend the night in trees and fly to their roosts (resting and sleeping places) at sunset. At sunup, they fly to the ground to find fruit, nuts, bugs and salamanders for breakfast and continue eating until midday. They love to gobble and begin before sunrise, continuing past lunchtime. During mating season, the males (gobblers) like to strut around to attract females. Do you know how to recognize the youngsters from the adult turkeys? A young turkey's middle tail feather is taller than the adults', while the adults' feathers are all the same. Tracks in the mud are just the opposite. If a track has a middle toe that is 4 inches long, it is made by a full-grown adult gobbler.

title: Sharing Public Space: Vitus Bering and Russian Colonies in Alaska
text:
Imagine traveling 6,000 miles over land with supplies for an expedition, and THEN sailing through frigid seas to look for a new world. This was the job given to Vitus Bering, a Danish navigator who sailed for the Russian navy. Peter the Great, czar (ruler) of Russia, asked Bering to explore the eastern coast of Russia. He was wondering if land connected Asia and North America.

Bering's first trip began in 1725. After spending three years getting his supplies to eastern Russia, Bering sailed along the coastline. He didn't see any land to the east, and he didn't realize he was sailing in the narrow passage between Russia and Alaska. This waterway is now called the Bering Strait.

Bering led another expedition in 1741. This time his ship landed on Kayak Island, off the coast of Alaska. They explored some of the Aleutian Islands and met the native people there, the Aleut. He was the first European to arrive in present-day Alaska.

Bering died before returning to Russia, but his voyages paved the way for Russian settlements in North America. Many fur traders came to the area. In 1799 the Russian government established a fur-trading operation in Alaska. Furs from foxes, sea otters and seals were very valuable.

Unfortunately, the Russians took advantage of the native people just as some Europeans had done in settling New England. The Russians took over their lands and forced them to hunt for furs. They also brought new diseases, which killed many natives.

Today, the Aleut people continue to live along the western coast of North America, and their population has grown. What might have been different if the Russians and the Aleut had shared public space fairly? Where in your community is there a debate over public land? How should such debates be handled?

title: Early American Trades
text:
This week is a good time to learn about early American trades.

The colonists could not easily buy everything they needed as they had in England. Many became tradesmen. They learned to make their own goods locally. Everything, from furniture, metal tools, glassware, cloth, and food, was produced locally. It would be fun to make a display of these skilled tradesmen and women to show in your classroom.

A good way to do this is to follow the directions on page 3 for the quadrarama. First, make a “quad” as shown. Then draw or cut out the tradesmen’s pictures that are on this page. Next, color them and mount them with glue onto your quadrarama.

You will want to write about each of the trades so that those viewing them will learn something about early colonial America!

title: Lewis and Clark Embark on a Pioneering Trip
text:
One of the most exciting adventure stories in early America is the heroic trek of Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to the Pacific Northwest. Their group was called "The Corps of Discovery." President Thomas Jefferson wanted them to explore the recently purchased Louisiana Territory. He wondered if dinosaurs might still be living there. He also wanted to strengthen America's involvement in the unexplored western United States.

Their goal was simple: follow the Missouri River to its source and, from there, try to get to the Pacific Ocean. They accomplished their goal, but not without near starvation, sickness, one death, and dangerous encounters from start to finish.

Sacagawea Joins the Expedition

The party of 33 departed in May 1804 from St. Louis. By late fall, they reached North Dakota, where they wintered. Their French guide had brought with him his wife, an American Indian woman named Sacagawea. She was a Shoshone and knew much about the country. She also helped negotiate with American Indians as an interpreter. Her first baby, Jean-Baptiste, was born in camp, and Clark nicknamed him Pompey. During a difficult journey over the Bitterroot Mountains, the group stumbled onto Sacagawea's home tribe and family. There was dancing, crying and embracing when she found her brother, friends and relatives, which she had not seen since she was a little girl.

CONTINUED IN OREGON LESSON

title: Lewis & Clark Explore the Northwest
text:
The United States purchased the vast Louisiana Territory from France. President Jefferson was anxious to find out what the unexplored territory looked like. He sent his personal secretary, Meriwether Lewis, and his friend William Clark to explore it.

The Journey Becomes Difficult

As the group traveled further into the new territory, the journey became very hard. The party only had berries to eat. Another time, they only had bear grease and candles. Their moccasins were too thin and they feared freezing their feet off, but they pressed onward. The Nez Percé Indians in Idaho were very curious about Clark's enslaved man, York. The American Indians would wet their fingers to rub off the color, thinking York was painted to ward off some spirit. The American Indians were also amazed the white men would eat dogs. This was done because the constant diet of salmon was so tiring. Here's where our otherwise close and agreeable Lewis and Clark differed. Lewis enjoyed dog meat, while Clark couldn't stand it.

As they journeyed down the Columbia, they found European goods among the various tribes. Europeans had not traveled this far inland, but the American Indians had traded the goods upriver from the coast. By the time the party reached the ocean, everyone was very tired. They constructed Fort Clapstop for the winter of 1805-1806 and ate a native diet of berries and fish. The group rested here for 106 days. Christmas was just another cold, rainy day as they forced themselves to eat spoiled elk and fish with a few roots.

Great Success

The Lewis and Clark expedition (a group with a special mission to perform) was a great success. They were welcomed back home the following year. They were called men "returned from the dead," as they were feared lost. Accounts of their stories, maps and friendly contacts with the American Indians were printed in newspapers back East. This paved the way for future travelers and strengthened America's claim on the western U.S. territory.

Captain Clark is taking a position sight with a brass compass. This compass is now in the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C.

Trace the trail that Lewis and Clark's expedition took across the vast Louisiana Territory.

The explorers met Chinooks near the mouth of the Columbia River.

Captain Clark meets the Shoshone Chief Cameahwait, and the guide Sacagawea is reunited with her family and tribe after many years of separation.

Sacagawea served the expedition as a guide, and she and her husband Toussaint Charbonneau were interpreters among the American Indians.

On November 7, 1805, after about 18 months of tiresome travel, the explorers had their first view of the Pacific Ocean.

title: Coastal Region
text:
All along our coast are hundreds of hotels, restaurants, and boating, fishing and tourism services that help visitors to the Oregon coast enjoy the beauty of our long beaches and foggy ocean horizons. These places also provide thousands of jobs to people living on the coast and help our state economy grow. Fisheries and the seafood industry are very active here, adding hundreds of millions of dollars to the local economies. Tillamook is home to one of the world's largest cheese factories. Bandon is famous for its huge cranberry harvest. Coos Bay is the coast's largest urban community and a major wood-product shipping center. A lot of lumber and wood pulp is shipped from Coos Bay, so ships are coming and going all the time. Between tourism, lumber and seafood, the coast has a job for just about anyone who wants one.

Visitors to the Oregon coast enjoy the beauty of long beaches and foggy ocean horizons. Try visiting some fisheries or the tourism sites in Tillamook, Bandon or Coos Bay.

title: Can crickets tell temperatures?
text: Yes! If you can count cricket chirps, you can tell the temperature. Count the number of cricket chirps from one cricket or a group chirping in unison for exactly 15 seconds and then add 37. That will be the temperature in Fahrenheit. Celsius is a little harder. Count the chirps in 25 seconds, divide by three, add four, and that will be the temperature in Celsius.

title: Elk
text:
The original name for elk is wapiti. It is pronounced to rhyme with "hoppity." Hippity hoppity goes the wapiti.

During the 106-day stay of Lewis and Clark at the mouth of the Columbia River, elk was their primary food source. The men killed 131 elk for meat, clothing, moccasins and tents. This very large member of the deer family grows 7 to 10 feet long. Bull elk have more mates than any deer in America and will assemble one to 15 females—sometimes up to 60 females—in their family. The bulls weigh more than 1,000 pounds and sport huge racks of antlers, which they shed each spring. Females weigh about 600 pounds. Elk are grazers. They enjoy grasses, sedges (coarse, grass-like plants that live in wet land) and non-woody plants. In the winter, they will eat what is available, usually oak brush, aspen, serviceberry, sagebrush and willow. Lewis wrote in his journal that he watched elk enjoy the leaves of an evergreen shrub he called "shallon" ("salal" in modern terms). Regulated elk hunting continues each fall, primarily in the western United States.

title: Making the World a Kinder Place
text: We sometimes wonder why bad things happen to innocent people. Although we may never understand it, we can do our best to keep things like this from happening in the future. When we do this, we are doing our part to make the world a kinder place, without anger and violence. One way to do this is by making a plan to replace bullying and violence with kindness. The Cool to Be Kind (C2BK) program was developed to help students create programs in their classes and schools that are based on pro-kindness – doing nice things for others. Students look for ways to “pay it forward” each day. Paying it forward means that when someone thanks you for doing something nice, you ask that person to pay it forward by doing something nice for someone else. By paying it forward, kindness continues to spread across the world and people start thinking kinder thoughts and ways that they can help other people. What are some ways you could practice paying it forward? How about doing yard work for an elderly neighbor for free? Or inviting a new student to eat lunch with you and your friends? What about giving up your seat on the bus to someone who looks tired, or helping someone pick up something they have dropped? Thinking kind thoughts and acting on them with acts of kindness is a simple change that you can do to change the world.

title: How can I be an active reader?
text:
To get the most out of what you read, you should be an active reader.

Be Involved

When you are an active reader, you are involved because you think about and respond to what you read. Here are some strategies to use for becoming an active reader.

Ask Questions

Ask yourself questions as you read. What kinds of questions should you ask? Well, any question that comes to mind as you are reading is a good question. But some questions you could ask include:

• How do I feel about what I am reading?

• Do the characters’ actions make sense to me?

• Do the characters remind me of any people I know?

• Do I understand the events that are happening?

• Could similar things happen to me?

• What do I hope will happen next?

• What would I most like to ask this author?

Read As a Group

Sometimes, you can get a better idea of what to think about a book after talking to someone else about it. Discussion about books can make your reading more interesting because different people have different ideas about the same text. Follow these steps and try forming some discussion groups in your class.

• Assemble a small group of interested readers. Include enough people to make the discussion interesting, but not so many that the group is hard to manage.

• Pick a book that you all want to read.

• Allow time for everyone to read it.

• Write down a list of questions and ideas before the meeting.

• Meet to discuss your reactions to the book. Before beginning, pick someone to lead the discussion.

Connect with the Words

Make a connection with what you read, even if you are reading about someone very different from you. Try putting yourself in different characters’ shoes so that you will understand why they act the way they do. You
can also make a connection with what you read by forming opinions about it.

Respond to Your Text

Keep a response journal where you can write your feelings, ideas, questions, reactions and thoughts about what you read. You can also note facts, copy quotations you liked, or talk about passages that you thought were well written.

Try these active reading strategies, and you will get the most out of what you read.

title: Let's Write
text: You were a member of the Lewis and Clark expedition. Describe what your typical day was like. What things would you record in your journal?

title: Make an Astrolabe
text:
During his historic voyage, Christopher Columbus used simple instruments and his knowledge of the sun and stars to guide him. Follow these steps, and you will be able to determine your latitude in the same way. Materials

• Protractor

• Rectangular piece of cardboard or index card big enough for the protractor to be traced on

• String (about 10 inches)

• Drinking straw

• Metal washer or paper clip

• Tape or glue, scissors

• Fine-point marker

• Atlas or globe

Directions

1. Lay the straight edge of the protractor against one edge of the cardboard. Trace the semi-circle edge, and cut out the cardboard along this curved line.

2. With the protractor as a guide, mark and number the degrees shown. Also, mark the vertex.

3. Tie one end of the string to the middle of the drinking straw. Use the tape or glue to hold it.

4. Tie the other end around the washer or paper clip.

5. Glue the straw just above the 90-degree marks with the string over the vertex.

6. On a clear night, take your astrolabe outside. Face north. (The sun sets on your left if you are facing north.) Find the Big Dipper and use the two stars farthest from the handle. They point to the last star in the Little Dipper’s handle. This is Polaris.

7. Look at Polaris through the straw. Try not to move anything and put your thumb over the weight (paper clip or washer) as it hangs. Go inside where it is light and read the number. Look on the globe or map to find your latitude. What do you notice about your astrolabe reading and your latitude?

title: Westward Ho!
text:
The Oregon Trail was the long, hard path used by early pioneers to walk from the eastern United States to the Pacific Northwest. It was 2,000 miles long, and a wagon needed five or six months to make the journey. To make the trip easier, pioneers used a lightweight wagon called a "prairie schooner." These shorter, lighter wagons needed fewer animals to pull them.

The Oregon Trail began at Independence, Missouri, and ended in Oregon City. The trail was not a single road like today's freeways. In some places, the wagons spread out over large areas, coming together again to cross rivers or pass through canyons. This changed in 1843 with the "Great Migration," when a permanent cut was made in the prairie sod (grass and roots that cover dirt) by the 900 people and 1,000 head of cattle which passed over that year. Other pioneers followed those ruts, which can still be seen today.

In 1805-06, Lewis and Clark were the first to map out a land route from east to west. This route was hard for people to follow until 1813, when Robert Stuart made a discovery. He was traveling the route backwards, from Oregon to the eastern United States, when he found a pass through the Rocky Mountains farther south than Lewis and Clark's. He named it "South Pass." In 1832, Capt. Benjamin de Bonneville took the first wagons over South Pass.

Two years later, 1834, the missionaries came. They built forts and taught Christianity to fur traders and American Indians. A Protestant missionary named Marcus Whitman settled near Walla Walla with his wife, Narcissa. They built a fort where pioneers could stop for food, medicine and rest. In 1847, the Whitmans and 12 others were killed by angry American Indians. This tragedy led to war between the U.S. and the American Indians, bringing more supplies, settlers and forts to the West. There were 15 other missions built, and these became stopping places for early pioneers.

Dr. John McLoughlin helped hundreds of these early pioneers with food, water and protection. He stood 6 feet 4 inches tall and had a full head of white hair. The American Indians called him "The Great White-Headed Eagle." His kindness and hard work encouraged early pioneers to make the journey on the Oregon Trail. It is estimated (judged, guessed) that 200,000 pioneers came west on the Oregon Trail. Grateful pioneers named him the "Father of Oregon." He was British, but became a U.S. citizen in 1849.

Pioneer journals and diaries tell of a hard life on the trail. Pioneers broke camp at 4:00 a.m. and then walked all day until the sun went down. About one in 10 people died, mostly from accidents or disease. Boredom was a real problem, too. And if a group couldn't make the trip in six months, they risked getting caught in the snow as did the Donner Party in 1846. Out of 87 Donner pioneers, 40 of them froze to death in the snow.

Our pioneers didn't let death and hardship scare them. All along the trail, there were marriages, births, holidays and celebrations. It was a great time in our state's history, one to be very proud of. Do you have an ancestor who came here over the Oregon Trail?

title: Oldest Home in America?
text:
Researchers found an exciting clue about the lives of early Americans in the Pacific Northwest. About 50 miles from Crater Lake, Oregon, a home site was discovered that is about 9,500 years old. Scientists say that the home site was preserved because it was buried beneath 2 feet of volcanic ash when Mount Mazama blew up about 7500 B.C. This is the same volcano that formed Crater Lake.

Researchers say that the home was in a shallow pit that measured about 14 feet by 16 feet. The stumps of five lodge-pole pine support posts are there, indicating that a tepee structure was erected above the pit. In the middle of the floor is the fireplace, or hearth. The researchers sifted through the ashes and found the remains of hazelnuts, blackberries, choke cherries, and other fruits and nuts. They also found obsidian tools that had blood on them. Obsidian is a dark natural glass formed from cooled molten lava. When the blood was analyzed, it turned out to be nothing more than part of dinner—rabbit blood.

Using DNA analysis, scientists learned that other blood stains on the rocks around the house are those of bear, bison (commonly called buffalo), sheep, and deer or elk that were butchered. The researchers also found the remains of ponderosa pine and sagebrush wood. The early dwellers used the bark to make rope, matting, clothing, and coverings for their tepee and floor.

The next oldest American Indian homes discovered in the area are about 7,500 years old. Researchers are calling this latest find the best discovery yet, showing how early Americans lived on a day-to-day basis in the Pacific Northwest. They knew that people first arrived here about 11,000-13,000 years ago, but had little knowledge about their living arrangements and eating habits.

As strange as it may seem, the newly-discovered home site shows that the region around Crater Lake was once a great place to live. Forests, game and food were there before the volcano exploded. After the volcano, there was nothing but a bare, lifeless pumice desert. The eruption of the powerful volcano must have destroyed the lives of many American Indians.

title: The Oregon Trail
text:
The Oregon Trail brought the first permanent settlers to the Pacific Northwest. Pioneers settled in Idaho, Oregon and Washington. The trip took six months and cost $800-$1000 per wagon. Pioneers had to buy supplies before and during their journey and sometimes had to pay fees to cross rivers. That was a lot for people earning only $1.50 a day. Was the trip worth the risk? Some people lost all their belongings, their wagons and sometimes their lives.

This game will help you understand some of the dangers in crossing the Oregon Trail. Follow the instructions and play it with a partner.

How to Play

1. Two to four people may play the game at one time.

2. Make a spinner as shown to the right. It should have the numbers 1-6 on it. If you have dice, use one die.

3. Have each person find a token such as a coin, ring, plastic figure or other small item different from the others.

4. Take turns flipping the spinner or rolling the die to see who is first. The highest number wins. Move clockwise around the group.

5. On your turn, spin the spinner or roll the die and move your token the number of spaces you spin or roll. Follow the instructions, if any, in the space. The first one to Oregon City is the winner.

You may want to decorate the game board by coloring with felt markers or crayons. It will last a long time if you have it laminated and mounted on cardboard.

Play the Oregon Trail game found in this week's newspaper.

title: Bartering in the Colonies
text:
Bartering is trading goods, but without the use of money. In early cultures, people were able to get many things they needed and wanted through bartering. Merchants would often travel with ships laden with goods. These goods were bartered for items that could be taken back. Then they would be either bartered for other goods or traded for money. People, towns and even countries bartered for items they did not produce or grow.

Bartering was easy as long as there was a simple trade between two people. However, sometimes bartering had to span several persons to get the goods wanted. Then it wasn't so easy. Suppose one merchant had a barrel of allspice. He wanted to trade with another merchant for some cloth. However, the merchant who had the cloth did not want or need a barrel of allspice. What do you think a good solution might have been? The people would barter for something they didn't need. They hoped they could later trade it for something they did need!

Bartering can be done with anything people value and assign a worth to. In Jamestown, tobacco was used. Colonists could pay with tobacco for items they needed but could not make or grow themselves. In New England, English fishermen worked on the coast years before the Pilgrims settled Plymouth. Fishing camps established along the coast eventually became the New Hampshire colony. First, the fishing camps began trading with the local American Indians. They traded their knives and supplies for furs. The camps became larger and larger until they turned into small towns. These small towns grew to be large trading centers. Eventually the New Hampshire area became a colony.

Another form of bartering was trade-offs. The same company that financed Jamestown also financed the Pilgrims' journey to the New World. However, the company asked the pilgrims for seven years' worth of crops to pay back the money for the journey. This arrangement was required of anyone who wanted to come to America but couldn't afford it. People settled in areas where the natural resources would allow them to repay the company in crops. This was what is known as a trade-off. Although people didn't really want to give up seven years worth of crops, it was often the only way they could come to America. They were willing to trade something they didn't want to do (give crops) for something they wanted more (to be in America). This happens all the time, even to you. You may give up a few movies, so that you can buy a video game. Countries and all levels of governments do it as well. It's all a matter of deciding what is most important.

Bartering is still going on today. People, companies and even countries barter for things they need or want. Countries that raise great amounts of beef may barter with countries that grow large amounts of grain. Companies may trade services to support one another. Even children barter! When was the last time you tried talking someone out of a big chocolate chip cookie in exchange for your apple?

In Jamestown, Captain John Smith wrote about trading blue beads with the native tribes for food. The American Indians valued the glass beads, and the colonists needed food. Copper ornaments and beads were also highly prized by the chiefs of local tribes. At first, the Powhatan traded with other tribes to obtain copper. Over time, the Europeans gave copper beads and ornaments for barter. The Powhatan turned to the colonists for the copper items.

title: Keep Track of Information
text:
How will you keep track of all the good information you find while researching? Take notes! Here are some tips for taking research notes:

1. You will probably find that index cards are the best way to take notes. You can write one fact or quotation on each card and then organize and rearrange them based on how you want to write your report, give your presentation or study for your test.

2. Label your notes with subject headings.

3. Paraphrase and summarize information in your own words. Summarize information by writing the main ideas and most important supporting details. This will help you prevent plagiarism, which is copying writers' words without giving them credit.

4. If you like how a writer has said something, use a direct quotation. Be sure to record the quote exactly. Include punctuation and spelling just as written by the writer. Put quotation marks around the quote so that you know it is a quotation and not your summary.

5. Write down the title, author, publisher, city of publication, date and page numbers of each source after you have recorded the fact or quotation. This way, you can include this information in a bibliography, and you can go back and double check a quotation if you have questions.

6. Abbreviate the information you have researched to save time. Write in groups of words and phrases instead of complete sentences. Use abbreviations and symbols as long as you will remember what they mean. You can transfer the information into complete sentences later when you use it in your report or presentation. This will save you time when you start writing your report.

7. Organize your notes into the most useful order for you, your report or presentation. For example, you can organize them by subject or theme.

Try It!

Do some research on the subject you are currently studying in social studies. Use research notes to record the information you find. Use the research notes to write a report or make a presentation, depending on what your teacher assigns. Once you've organized your notes, write the report. Explain your ideas clearly and support them with details from your research. Be sure to follow all of the steps above!

title: Make a Compass
text:
Materials

• magnet

• large sewing needle

• a cork

• glue

• a cup filled with water

Directions

1. Stroke the needle with the magnet at least 30 times. Rub only in the direction of the sharp end.

2. Put a dab of glue on the center of the cork and put the needle in the glue as shown. Let the glue dry.

3. Place the cork in the water and wait. Shortly, the sharp end of the needle will point
to the north.

Compass Rose

Color and cut out the compass pattern below. After you have determined where north is by using your compass, tape the compass rose to a table or your desk with north in the correct position. Now you can learn the other directions as well.

title: Pushing the Rails West
text:
Building train tracks in America began in the East in 1825 and followed the frontier. The trains were often only 10 years behind the settlement of new areas. By 1850, there were tracks all over the eastern United States and a few scattered in the West, but there were no main lines to connect the East coast with the West coast.

Americans wanted the tracks to run near their favorite cities, something that would be impossible. This made it hard to decide what part of America an east-west line should run. When the Civil War started and the southern states left the Union, Congress decided to build tracks in the middle part and the north part of the country. Thus, the Union Pacific and Central Pacific Railroad companies were born in 1862. In 1864, President Abraham Lincoln signed the act of Congress that permitted the Northern Pacific Railroad to be built. Our line began at Lake Superior (see your classroom map) and ended at Puget Sound.

While our railroad was being built, the first track to run the whole length of America was finished by Union Pacific. The year was 1869. This track was built from two directions, one company starting in California, the other company starting in Omaha, Nebraska. For six years, construction moved these tracks toward each other until they met at Promontory Point, Utah, where the famous "Golden Spike" was driven to connect the two. Settlers began coming to the Pacific Coast by rail instead of the Oregon Trail. Why take six months by wagon when you could get here in only six days by train?!

Building these large railroads took a lot of money and property. Congress helped the railroad companies by giving them millions of acres of land. Our Northern Pacific Railway company received 44 million acres. The actual area reserved for track construction was 200 feet wide and more than 1,000 miles long. Our tracks ran over vast plains, rivers and mountains. The rest of the free land was used to obtain lumber, mine coal, sell or lease, or house construction workers while also providing them with goods and services. Many of these railway settlements later developed into towns and cities.

Our railroad took almost 20 years to complete because the Northern Pacific Railroad faced many problems, such as the difficulty of the route and financial issues. At one time, 10,000 workers labored on the project. The last spike was finally driven in a place about 60 miles west of Helena, Montana. The day was Sept. 8, 1883.

At the west end, the track officially ended in Tacoma, Washington, but everyone wanted the track extended. People in Oregon built a line going south (Portland to San Francisco, California) so they could hook up with the other east-west mainline. Another track was built north, from Portland to Puget Sound. A dozen other railroad companies were started in Oregon and Washington, but over time, most of these joined together to form single large companies.

The railroad is very important to our state. It has been used to move billions of dollars of lumber, fish, produce, cars, and just about everything else including you. Have you ever ridden a train?

title: Move Over, Brothers Grimm - New Fairy Tales Found
text:
There's a magical world out there full of elves, evil queens and beautiful princesses! If you enjoy "Cinderella," "Little Red Riding Hood" and "Rapunzel," you have already discovered the work of the Brothers Grimm. These German fairy tales and legends were collected by the Grimm brothers and put into popular books about 200 years ago.

A new world of fairy-tale magic has just been revealed. Researchers found a collection of 500 stories gathered by Franz von Schonwerth, a German historian who did his work at the same time as the Grimm brothers. Because Schonwerth was a historian, he wrote the stories exactly as the German people told them to him. The Grimm brothers changed some of the stories to make them less frightening for children. The Grimm brothers admired Schonwerth's work. Jacob Grimm said, "Nowhere in the whole of Germany is anyone collecting (fairy tales) so accurately, thoroughly and with such a sensitive ear." Schonwerth's collection was never as popular as the Grimm brothers' books. His three volumes of stories collected dust for 150 years until they were rediscovered.

Schonwerth's collection includes a story of a beautiful girl who gets away from a witch by turning herself into a pond and another tale about a turnip princess. As soon as the stories are translated into English, you will have a whole new collection of fairy tales to read!

title: Trappers and Traders Explore and Open New Territory
text:
This week, let's discuss some important people who helped open up our land so that the trains could come.

Fur Trappers & Traders Pave the Way for Progress

Hundreds of early American and Canadian settlers came to trap furs. Companies were formed, groups were combined, and all kinds of money was spent because the fur business was making many people rich.

Traders coming by ship hunted sea otters. Traders coming by land wanted beaver. The fur-trading posts they built later became towns; fur-loading docks grew into major coastal cities; and the paths, trails, and roads used 200 years ago are today's railroads and highways. Here are some of the key players who opened our region for the trains:

Hudson's Bay Company

In 1669, Britain gave the Hudson's Bay Company total control over the American fur trade. About 115 years later, the company expanded its operations to the western part of the continent. The company hired American Indians to do all the hunting and traded trinkets and cheap goods for the furs. It was hard for smaller fur companies to compete. Everywhere a man turned, he heard that famous name, "Hudson's Bay Company."

Voyageurs were French-Canadians who trapped fur in Canada and transported furs for other trappers. They were very hard-working men who would paddle their birch bark canoes 12-16 hours a day, travel over mountains, wade across lakes, hike for days with one or more 90-pound packs on their backs, live off the land, and keep going in a blizzard. They dressed in colorful clothing and sang loudly as they worked. Everyone knew about the voyageurs.

The North West Company

In 1784, a group of Scotsmen formed a trapping company and hired the voyageurs to work for them. The Scotsmen had a clever way of getting their furs. They would intercept the American Indians and buy their furs before they could sell them to the Hudson's Bay Company. Several explorers were sent to find river routes to the Pacific Ocean. These men included Simon Fraser, who tried to survey the Columbia River and instead discovered the Fraser River in 1808; David Thompson, who founded four important trading posts and whose maps were so exact, they remained in use for 100 years; Alexander Mackenzie, the first European to travel across the continent by land and river in 1793; and Dr. John McLoughlin, who was Britain's chief agent and the most powerful man in the region for 22 years.

Mountain Men

The Americans also sent trappers into the interior of the United States to find fur. These hearty men lived off the land, endured many hardships and often gathered together for a rendezvous to exchange information, goods, weapons, maps and ideas. Jedediah Smith and Jim Bridger are two famous mountain men.

The Pacific Fur Company

American businessman John Jacob Astor had a good idea. In 1811, he decided to find a place near the coast where his fur trappers could bring their furs. His ships would pick up the furs and leave supplies to maintain a fort. He established Fort Astoria, the first American trading post on the coast and site of today’s Astoria, Oregon.

title: Portland
text: For years, settlers in Portland tried to interest the Northern Pacific Railroad in building a railroad track along the bank of the Columbia River into Portland. By 1870, it became apparent that some city on Puget Sound was going to be the terminal for the train — It turned out to be Tacoma, Washington. People in Portland were afraid the train would take away a lot of business from Oregon. Rich business people worked long and hard to get tracks into Portland, and eventually they did. Portland sits at the meeting point of the Willamette and Columbia rivers. It was founded in 1845, and its name was decided by toss of a coin. Portland won, and Boston lost. During World War II, Portland was an important shipbuilding center. Today, its chief products include lumber, flour, furniture, knitted goods, woolen textiles, canned fruits and vegetables, iron and steel, and the list goes on and on. It is known as the city of roses because of its many beautiful rose gardens. Every June, tens of thousands of people enjoy the Rose Festival. Portland is the largest city in Oregon and one of the largest lumber-shipping ports in the world. If you don't live in Portland, it's time to go pay a visit!

title: Where is the world's longest railway?
text: You will have to travel to Russia to see the world's longest railroad. The Trans-Siberian Railway from Moscow to Vladivostok is 5,777 miles long. In the United States, our longest single track is 1,780 miles long. This track was completed in 1869 when the Central Pacific Railroad built east from Sacramento, California, and the Union Pacific Railroad built west, meeting up at Promontory Summit, Utah.

title: Wood for Ties
text: Building the railroads required a lot of wooden ties. We're not talking the kind of ties men wear to work; we're talking about a wooden board 8 feet long and about 8 inches by 7 inches square. In England, they call them "sleepers" because the timber lays at rest under the rails. These ties were laid on gravel about 21 inches apart. In the Pacific Northwest, ties were cut from the center sections of Douglas fir trees. Ties had to be strong enough to hang onto the spikes that were driven into them to hold the rails. They had to endure the hot, blistering sun all summer long and the freezing blizzards and deep snows in the winter, year after year. To keep the insects and weather from destroying the ties, they were soaked in three gallons of an oil made from tar. (Ever hear of creosote?) Each timber weighed more than 60 pounds. It took a lot of trees to make the ties for our Northern Pacific Railroad. Our first track from Puget Sound to the Great Lakes required about 3 million ties. That's a lot of trees!

title: Clarity of Expression: Father Junípero Serra and the California Missions
text:
Do you like to give speeches? Can you convince others to see things your way? Then maybe you have a gift for expressing yourself clearly.

Father Junípero Serra was a Franciscan monk who some might call one of the "founding fathers" of California. He was born in Spain in 1713 and became a priest in his mid 20s. Many people noticed how well he spoke, or how clearly he expressed himself, during his powerful sermons, and he soon became a university professor.

Father Serra wanted to work as a Spanish missionary, so he first traveled to Mexico City in 1749. He started missionary work with the Sierra Gorda Indians. Soon he was made head of the Spanish missions in Baja (lower) California. Next, the Spanish governor asked him to start missions in Alta (upper) California. Father Serra personally built eight missions there and supervised the start of many more from San Diego to San Francisco.

Father Serra helped convert thousands of American Indians to Christianity. They lived and worked in the missions, but life was harsh. Many Indians died from overwork and diseases. But the missions kept going because of Father Serra's preaching and care. His sermons were so dramatic that he would sometimes pound his chest with a stone or touch a lit torch to his chest.

Father Serra used his clarity of expression for what he thought was good. He argued with the Spanish army to get control of the missions. He even convinced Mexican officials to send more money and soldiers for his missions. Spanish colonists settled the area around the missions, which is all now the state of California.

Do you think you have a good ability to express yourself clearly as Father Serra did? What topic do you feel strongly about?

title: Paper - Bag Puppets
text:
Materials

Palm-paper bag

Glue

Eraser

Pencil

Colored pencils

Tempera paints or crayons

Scrap materials felt, yarn, fabric, cloth, cotton, twigs, buttons, construction paper, etc.)

Instructions

1. Fold the bottom of the bag flat. On the bottom of the bag, draw the face of your puppet down to its mouth.

2. Draw the mouth on the fold so that the puppet can talk when you move the fold up and down. (See picture.)

3. Draw the rest of the body of your puppet on the remaining part of the bag. Try to express a personality with your puppet: grouchy, silly, prim, etc.

4. Use colored pencils, crayons or tempera paint to add color to your puppet.

5. Glue various bits of scrap material to the puppet.

6. When your puppet is finished, you can read a story with it or make up your own dialog for your puppet. Have fun!

Extra Activity: Have everyone in the class make a different puppet. Write a script and put on a puppet show. You can use a historical setting that you read in Studies Weekly to write your script and make puppets of historical figures.
