title: How Do You Start a State?
text:
Have you ever wondered how our ancestors started Oregon? It all began with a funeral.

In 1841, a very rich settler died. His name was Ewing Young. He had a lot of cattle and money, but no wife or children to inherit it. The biggest problem was Young's cattle. The people couldn't just leave the cattle wandering around without an owner.

In those early days, the missions were the center of community activity. The Methodist mission was asked to solve the problem of Young's cattle. The mission formed a committee that gave away Young's cattle to other settlers. But there were other problems, too. The settlers needed a sheriff, a judge and jury, and somebody who could record their land claims. Could this committee help them do that? For a couple of years, nothing happened.

Wolf Meetings

In 1843, the committee was again called to action. Wild animals were killing cattle and scaring the settlers. What could be done? The committee decided to ask everyone to donate money to a fund. This money was used to pay hunters a reward for killing a wolf, bear or mountain lion. The people met often to talk about animals, and their meetings became known as the "Wolf Meetings."

Later that spring (1843), the people at the Wolf Meetings decided to form a government. Twelve men were chosen to come up with a plan and report back. On May 2, 1843, a meeting was held to vote on the new government. American settlers and former employees of the Hudson's Bay Company met to vote in Champoeg (15 miles southwest of Portland, Oregon). The settlers approved the very first American government on the Pacific Coast. On July 5, 1843, the new government was written down in a document called the "Organic Act of the Provisional Government of Oregon." Washington and Oregon were still a single territory at this time.

How did the Organic Act work? It allowed 640 acres of land for every family. However, as a minimum commitment you had to live on your land for one year and make improvements (build a barn, cut a road, etc.). The Organic Act did other things: It set the borders of the new territory; declared the territory an anti-slavery region; and established three branches of government. In 1845, the people chose George Abernathy as the first governor. There remained one last problem to solve: Would the U.S. Congress make the Oregon Territory a part of the United States?

Congress took a long time deciding. The southern states hated the idea because they didn't want another anti-slavery region to join. Plus, the Mexican War had everyone very worried, and a lot of Congress' attention was focused on it. Finally, on Aug. 13, 1848, President Polk signed the bill making our region a part of the United States. He sent General Joseph Lane to be the first territorial governor. What about George Abernathy, the temporary governor? Abernathy stepped down so Lane could take over.

Are we a state yet? Not at this point in our story. Before statehood, there needed to be a lot more growth and organization. Read more on statehood in the next issue!

title: Apparently We Have a State Fruit
text:
Oregon has many state symbols, or items that represent our state. For example, the state animal is the beaver, the state tree is the Douglas fir, and the state flower is the Oregon grape, but did you know that our state also has a state fruit?

The pear is Oregon's state fruit and has been since 2005. Pears are the #1 tree fruit crop grown in Oregon with about 800 million pears being produced in our state each year.

Pear trees were first brought to Oregon by Westward pioneers in the 1800s. The trees loved the climate of the Pacific Northwest and it wasn't long before pear orchards began springing up all over the state, particularly in Hood River, Jackson, Wasco, Josephine and Marion counties.

Pears are different from most other fruits because they are picked before they are ripe and allowed to ripen in a cool, dark place. To check if a pear is ripe, you should gently push the stem end of the pear with your thumb. If you can leave a mark, the pear is ready to eat.

Pears are very healthy. They are a good source of Vitamin C, potassium and fiber, with only 100 calories per serving. There are many great recipes using Oregon pears, including poached pears, pear salads, broiled pear sandwiches and pear tarts. There is no excuse not to make Oregon's state fruit part of your daily diet.

title: The Making of a Territory
text:
The boundaries of the Oregon territory were set by Congress in 1848. The Oregon territory was very large. It ranged from the Pacific Ocean along the 49th parallel to the crest of the Rocky Mountains. It included all of Washington, Oregon and Idaho, and parts of Wyoming and Montana. Over the years, the territory was broken up into individual states, as shown below.

Map 1

(Oregon Territory in 1848)

In 1848, Congress carved out a piece of the Northwest that was bigger than Texas—almost 290,000 square miles.

Map 2

(Oregon and Washington Territories in 1853)

In 1853, settlers in Washington became discouraged because they had to travel so far to participate in politics in Oregon. The Washington settlers thought the Oregon settlers south of the Columbia River didn't pay enough attention to the Washington area. Congress voted that Washington should be a separate and new territory. Only 4,000 settlers lived there at the time.

Map 3

(Washington Territory in 1859)

In 1859, Oregon was made a state. Congress didn't want the state of Oregon to be so large, so they chopped off a big piece of land along the Snake River. This river became Oregon's eastern border.

Map 4

(Pacific Northwest in 1868)

In 1868, Congress divided up the rest of the Pacific Northwest to make new states. Four new states took large pieces of the original Oregon territory. Washington and Montana became states in 1889, and Idaho and Wyoming became states in 1890.

title: Willamette River
text: A lot has been said about Willamette Valley. But this 125-mile-long valley wouldn't be much without its river. The Willamette River was to its valley what the Mississippi and Ohio rivers were to mid-America - very important transportation routes. From the time the first French trappers were there in 1811 until the railroad arrived in 1871, the river was the only way to move furs, crops and timber. Towns grew up all along the river. The river could be used by deep-sea vessels, so shipping things was easy for farmers and manufacturers. Ships would steam 14 miles up the river from Portland to Willamette Falls, where goods were carried around the falls. The powerful Willamette Falls roared down 45-foot-high cliffs that are 450 feet across. The falling water meant power. A lumber mill was built there in 1842, then a flour mill in 1844 and a woolen mill in 1846. The first paper mill was built there in 1867, and the first hydroelectric plant in 1889. These mighty river waters and the rich soils of Willamette Valley created a center of production that helped early settlers prosper. And what did prosperity finally bring? Statehood!

title: Mother Joseph
text:
Born with the name Esther Pariseau, Mother Joseph became one of the most important people in Oregon Territory. She is one of two Oregon citizens with a statue in the nation's capitol. For years, she worked with other nuns in Canada, near her family's home. She mastered many skills including nursing, gardening, candle and soap making, weaving, sewing and carpentry. She also learned how to run a business.

Mother Joseph started seven hospitals, 12 schools, and two orphanages. She helped build many of the buildings herself. She kept working until she was almost 80 years old.

title: Why do ponds and lakes freeze from the top down?
text: When the air temperature over lakes drops below freezing, the top of the lake will freeze. Ice expands when it freezes, making it lighter than water. The floating ice acts like a big blanket and helps prevent more of the lake from freezing. This is important because fish are living in the water and don't want to become frozen leftovers during the winter. We are lucky that ice floats. If ice were heavier than water, it would sink during winter, and by spring, our lakes and oceans would be solid blocks of ice, and every creature in them would die.

title: The Black Bear
text: One of the animals that caused the early settlers to come together and form a new government was the black bear. The black bear, a predatory animal, was destroying livestock and scaring the settlers. (See cover story.) This bear weighs about 300 pounds. Black bears can run very rapidly when they need to and are skilled tree-climbers for their size and weight. Most black bears are timid, though they would make dangerous enemies. They seldom attack humans unless they have been hurt or are defending their young. Black bears spend much of the winter sleeping in snug shelters (caves, hollow trees, or holes dug in the earth). Cubs are born in midwinter weighing half a pound and measuring 7 to 9 inches long. They have very little hair, and their eyes are closed for about a month. They stay inside the den with mom for about two months. Black bears live 15-25 years. If you venture into the forest, be kind to all animals, and they will be kind to you — but always keep your distance, especially when the animal is bigger than you! Here's a new word: What do you call a group of bears? A sleuth of bears!

title: Talking Pictures
text:
You can create the illusion that pictures are talking! How? Draw, fold and move your picture just right, and it will look like it speaks.

Materials

• Paper • Pencils

• Scissors • Crayons

Instructions

1. Fold your paper in half. Then fold it in half again so that you have four equal parts. Open the paper and refold it lengthwise.

2. Draw a line in the center of the lower half you created when you folded the paper into fourths. This line should be as long as you want your mouth to be. Draw dotted lines in a diamond shape around this line. (See picture.)

3. Cut a mouth along the heavy line you drew. Fold the mouth halves down along the dotted lines as shown.

4. Fold the top half of the paper back.

5. Draw and color a face around the mouth you have created. You can draw your hero, someone famous, or a historic figure. You can also try making the face of an animal!

6. Poke the mouth out from the back so that the folds pop out as the paper is closed and pull back together as the paper is opened.

Extra Activity: Write a script and put on a skit that reenacts a historical scene you have read about in Studies weekly.

title: What Are Some Tricks to Spell Correctly?
text:
Are there some words that you just have a hard time spelling, maybe every time you try to write them? Perhaps some guidelines will help you spell these words in the future.

Understanding the Code

Spelling is kind of like a code—it’s a combination of letters that join to form a word. And that code can sometimes be hard to crack. It is difficult to provide “rules” for spelling in the English language because not all words follow the rules. You can probably find an exception to every “rule” we provide here. But we wanted to give you these guidelines so that you could have a basic understanding of how spelling usually works.

“ie” and “ei” Words

You probably already know this one: I before E except after C or when sounded like A, as in “neighbor” and “weigh.” If you follow this guideline, you will spell most of those “ei” and “ie” words correctly. Basically, a word is spelled with “ie” for the long “e” sound, except when the “e” follows the letter “c.” When the vowel sound is a long “a,” the word is usually spelled with “ei.” Some exceptions to this rule are “either,” “seize,” and “weird.” See if you can explain how each of these words follows the rule:

Piece

Receive

Neighbor

Plural Words

Generally, you make a word plural by adding “s” to the end. But, as you know, that is not the case with all words. Remember that there are exceptions to these guidelines.

•If the word ends with “ch,” “s,” “sh,” “ss,” “x,” “z,” or “es,” then you should add “es” rather than just “s” to make it plural. (buzzes, mosses)

•For most nouns that end with a single “f,” you change the “f” to “v” and add “es.” (“leaf” becomes “leaves”)

•For most words that end with a consonant followed by “o,” add “es.” (heroes, potatoes)

Adding Endings to Words

Sometimes when you add an ending to a word, it’s not as simple as adding “ed,” “ing,” “s,” “est,” or “er.” You have to change the word before you can add the ending. Here are some guidelines for doing this successfully.

•Before adding an ending to a word that ends with “y,” check to see if a consonant comes before the “y.” If the word ends with a consonant and “y,” then change the “y” to “ie” before adding the ending. (“hurry” becomes “hurried”)

•If a word ends with “y” and has more than one syllable, change the “y” to “i” before adding “ness” or “ly.” (“happy” becomes “happily”)

•For most one-syllable words that end with one vowel and one consonant, double the consonant before adding an ending that begins with a vowel. (thinnest, bigger)

•For most two-syllable words that end with one vowel and one consonant, you double the consonant only if the accent falls on the second syllable. (referred, beginning)•

For words that end with a silent “e,” drop the “e”

when adding an ending that begins with a vowel.

(riding, largest)

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend somebody just discovered a big piece of land south of where you live, and Congress wants you to make a state out of it. What will you call your state? Who will be the leader? What will you do if other states try to take your land away from you?

title: Big Land Squabbles
text:
The Americans came west to rule the land. They came to conquer all that lay in their path. And if the American Indians were in their path, they would help them become modern people. First came the missionaries. They hoped to convert the American Indians and show them how to raise their own crops and run their own farms. The American Indians didn't see it that way. To them, the white settlers were intruders (not invited, not welcome) on their sacred lands.

Outbreaks of violence began to occur. In 1847, some Cayuse murdered an American missionary, Marcus Whitman, his wife and 12 others. Hundreds of American troops chased the Cayuse Indians to capture the murderers. They finally found five, and they were hanged for the murders. The fighting made some peaceful tribes join others who were at war. The Rogues, Klamaths and Modocs fought for a long time, but they were beaten back by the whites.

By 1853, several tribes rose in anger and attacked more white settlements. The U.S. Army fought the American Indians until, finally, a peace treaty (agreement between parties) was signed, and things were quiet for two years.

One of the biggest wars took place just north of us and was talked about all over the Pacific Northwest. The new governor of the Washington Territory, Isaac Stevens, was sent to move the American Indians onto their reservations. In 1854, Stevens talked tribes into leaving the Washington counties of Thurston and Pierce as well as parts of Mason and King counties. At another meeting, Stevens convinced more than 5,000 American Indians to sign away 45,000 square miles of special tribal land. The American Indians knew they were being cheated and began fighting again. One battle involved the Yakama and a U.S. Army of 84 men. The Yakama killed five soldiers, wounded 17, and scattered the rest.

The last tragic fight was with the Nez Perces, the tribes that had first welcomed Lewis and Clark half a century before. The Nez Perces' reservation was agreed upon in a treaty, but later it was cut in half and half again. Chief Joseph was angry at the lies and cheating. He led 300 men, 400 women and children, 1,500 horses, and cattle on an escape journey. They traveled 2,000 miles in four months, traveling through Montana, almost into Canada, and ending up at Yellowstone. Here, they were finally overcome.

At his surrender, Joseph spoke these beautiful words of peace: "All men were made by the same Great Spirit Chief. They are all brothers. Whenever the white men treat the Indian as they treat each other, then we shall have no more wars. We shall all be alike— brothers of one father and mother, with one sky above us, and one country around us, and one government for all. Then the Great Spirit Chief who rules above will smile upon this land and send rain to wash out the bloody spots made by brothers' hands upon the face of the Earth." For better or worse, the Pacific Northwest was open for white settlers.

title: Lumber, Mining and Agricultural Industries Grow
text:
Until sawmills came along, all lumber was cut by hand. The gold fever spread, and so did the treasure hunters. In the early 1860s, rough boomtowns sprang up everywhere

Pioneers loved moving to Oregon Territory. They found so many ways to make a living. Lumber was needed for homes and ship building. Mining was needed for ores and coal. Agriculture was blossoming in ways nobody could have imagined.

Lumber

Nowhere in America was the lumber industry so rich as it was in the Pacific Northwest. Until sawmills came along, all lumber was cut by hand. By the 1880s, sawmills were producing more than 1 million board feet per day. (A board foot is one foot of finished lumber.) By the 1890s, the annual total topped 1 billion board feet. Major cities grew up around the sawmills. Logs were floated down rivers to the mills, and ships took the lumber to distant customers. In Oregon, the trains moved the lumber to the interior where rapid (fast, quick) building was taking place. Logging camps and mills were producing $15 million in lumber a year. If Paul Bunyan, hero of the logging camps, were a real man, he'd be having a very hard time keeping up with the new steam- and water-powered logging machines. Timber was king!

The areas perfect for crops were quickly planted, such as the good land in western Washington and in the Willamette and Tualatin valleys in Oregon. Apples have become one of the greatest crops from the Northwest.

Mining

The gold rush in California in 1847-1848 caused a lot of excitement in the Pacific Northwest. People came back from California with pockets full of gold! Their riches helped create a demand for other products from Oregon and Washington —wheat, produce, timber and boats. The gold fever spread, and so did the treasure hunters. In the early 1860s, gold was discovered in several places in Idaho and Montana. But gold wasn't the only important metal to be found. Big strikes of copper, silver, lead and zinc made many people rich. In Washington, coal became its major mining product. In Oregon, small pockets of low-grade coal were found. Both states tried to make steel, but couldn't compete with the giant steel mills back East. Hundreds of small mining towns grew up around the richest mining sites. When Alaska's gold rush started in the late 1890s, Seattle swelled. It became the launching place for people to sail to Alaska. What was the price for a ticket? $1,000 one way!

Agriculture

Farmers had a lot of things to learn. In the western parts of the state, there was plenty of moisture, but crops wouldn't grow well where old forests had been cleared. And in the east, things were just too dry. But the areas perfect for crops were quickly planted, such as the Willamette and Tualatin valleys in Oregon and along the same belt of good land in western Washington. The farmers' biggest problem was lack of helpers. In the beginning, American Indians were hired to work the farms. As more settlers arrived, agriculture began to grow. By the 1840s, settlers were doing pretty well. One year, they sold 15,000 bushels of wheat, 2 million pounds of tallow, 1,000 barrels of wine and brandy, 200 ounces of gold, some soap and thousands of hides and furs—all homegrown, caught or mined. Things were looking up!

In our next issue, we'll study Oregon statehood!

title: Snake River
text: Before Congress would let Oregon become a state, they had to decide on its borders. When the Oregon Territory was first established, the eastern part included Idaho and parts of Montana and Wyoming. Congress took away a lot of land, but the leftovers still make Oregon a pretty big state. Its eastern border was set far enough away from population centers so that the settlers wouldn't fight over who was in charge. The perfect dividing line, Congress decided, was along the Snake River. The Snake River makes up about 216 miles of Oregon's eastern border—about half of the border. Part of this river border is a very deep gorge worn into the Earth over a period of thousands of years by the Snake River. There is a section of the Snake River gorge that is more than a mile deep for about 40 miles. Part of that is called Hells Canyon, because it is the deepest in the United States at 7,900 feet deep. The Snake River is also the largest tributary of the Columbia. It starts at the Continental Divide (See your classroom map) near Yellowstone Park and snakes its way clear across the continent. From Yellowstone Park, you could travel the Snake River to the Columbia and out to the ocean, if you wanted to. But don't think that it would be easy. There are several very high waterfalls, dangerous rapids and dams that stand in your way!

title: What is dust and where does it come from?
text: Look around your classroom or at home for a flat surface that has not been touched for a week or two. It will be covered with a fine layer of dust. Believe it or not, most dust in a house or school is dead skin fragments from human bodies. (Yuck, that's YOU lying all over the place!) Other dust particles come from particles of pollen and plants, factory smoke, soil and tobacco smoke. In 1980, Mount St. Helens launched thousands of tons of dust into the air when it erupted. Dust can come from outer space, too. Could that thin layer of dust actually be millions of miniature UFOs all over the top of the piano? Who knows!

title: Coast Rhododendron
text: Perhaps you have seen them growing all around you. This strange word, "rhododendron," comes from Greek and means "red tree." This evergreen plant has large, beautiful blooms that appear in the spring in many colors, including lilac purple, white, red, light rose, apple-blossom pink, deep rose and rosy lilac. Rhododendrons can grow along the ground or climb up trees and houses to more than 40 feet high. There are a lot of different types of rhododendrons. They are part of a family of 10,000 different types! Rhododendrons love our state and are the state flower for our neighbor, Washington. Do you have any growing where you live? Do you know what Oregon's state flower is? (The answer can be found below the picture of rhododendrons.)

title: Panning for Gold
text:
Where do you find gold? Gold can be found in some rivers and their tributaries.

Materials

A 12-inch gold pan (even a pie tin will work) and a desire to find gold.

Instructions

1. Fill your pan about 3/4 full of sand from the riverbank. (It's okay to have grass and clay in it.) Submerge the pan just under the river, keeping it level with the top of the water. Stir with your fingers to break apart the clay and root particles until everything is separated and moving about freely. If you've done this thoroughly, your gold will already be at the bottom of your pan.

2. Hold the pan with one hand on each side, dividing the weight equally (still level and under water). Shake it with quick clockwise and counter-clockwise motions to be sure your material is loose all the way to the bottom. Using a rotating motion in a somewhat oval pattern, start moving the material and water about.

3. This motion washes the lighter material over the lip of your pan and will look as though the rocks are floating as they move over the edge. Continue this pattern three or four times until about half of the overburden (rocks, sand and roots) is washed away. Next, hold your pan filled with water just out of the river, and give it sharp clockwise then counter-clockwise motions to resettle the black sand and gold.

4. As the residue of pebbles and light sand washes away, less and less material will be left in your pan. Gradually, raise the edge of the pan nearest to you. This action will allow the particles to float off the front of the pan. Continue to wash the lighter material over the lip of your pan, shaking and dipping until only black sand is left. Do not wash out the black sand, because that's where the gold is. All that is left to do is separate the gold from the black sand. This is done by adding just a little water and rotating the level pan as you coax the black sand to separate from the gold. Those shiny particles are gold!

title: How do I read nonfiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring, but it really isn’t. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you find it easier to understand—and maybe more fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will talk about the problem and solution.

Problem/Solution

With this information pattern, the writer begins by stating a problem. Then the writer presents various solutions or ideas for solving the problem. This pattern is common in newspaper articles, as well as science and social studies texts.

One strategy for finding the problem and solution of a nonfiction passage is to create a cluster map. A cluster map will help you remember what you have read. Begin by writing the subject of the passage in the middle of a blank sheet of paper. On one side of the subject, write “problems.” On the other side, write “solutions.” Then write details you want to remember that illustrate the problems and solutions around these bubbles. Remember to draw lines connecting the problems to the word “problems” and connecting solutions to the word “solutions.” This way, you show the connections between the information.

Try It!

To the right is a passage about transportation. Read the passage. Then create a cluster map showing the problems and solutions discussed in the passage.

title: Let's Write
text: Tell about your huge tree house that you and your friends have built. What furniture does it have? Who is allowed inside?

title: Fake or Real News?
text:
Have you ever read something online, like on social media sites, that sounded fishy? Maybe it was real, but it could be fake news! The big danger, though, is news that sounds real but isn’t. Fake news is becoming common because anyone can post things online. Fake news can be in the form of a story. Fake news can be a photo or video that has been changed. The problem is that these fake items look real. Fake news can cause problems and it spreads misinformation.

Sam Wineburg, a professor, did some research. He found that 80 percent of students cannot tell the difference between real and fake news. Do you want to become a media-savvy person? You have to be able to find out if news is real or fake. How do you do that? You have to become a detective and search for the truth. You can learn about the author or company that posted the news. You have to think about the purpose of the news. Is there a hidden plan to get you to buy something or to make you think a certain way? Your teacher or a trusted adult can help you learn how to spot fake news. It takes a little time, but democracy depends on real information! Do your part and discover what is real and what is fake!

title: The Long Road to Statehood is Finished!
text:
Our early ancestors were a rugged bunch who wanted the Oregon territory to become a state as soon as possible. They didn't like the non-Oregon "foreigners" (people not from our state) sent here from Washington, D.C. (where the federal government is) to be in charge. Our ancestors wanted their local neighbors to serve as leaders. But which local neighbors should lead? That's where a lot of bad feelings started between settlers.

Some settlers worried that the people in Salem would always be in charge. And the miners in southern Oregon hated taking orders from Salem. The miners threatened to change the land boundary so that they could become part of California. They were mostly immigrants from the southern states where slavery was practiced. (An enslaved person is owned by someone else.) The people in Salem and Portland were worried that the pro-slavery miners would force Oregon to allow slavery. Could anything be done to stop the arguing?

The slavery issue was very important in the 1850s. In the eastern United States, the Civil War was about to be fought over slavery. The southern states only wanted pro-slavery states (states that wanted the right to own enslaved people) to join the Union. They tried to block anti-slavery states (states against having the enslaved), such as Oregon, from joining.

This put a lot of pressure on the anti-slavery people in Oregon. They knew that once a territory became a state, a lot of federal money was sent to help the state get started. Many in Oregon wanted that money to build roads, buildings, schools, dams and other things. Should they allow slavery so that they could get money? It was a hard decision.

Our ancestors decided to reject slavery and move forward on their own to organize themselves into a state. In 1857, Oregon settlers elected 60 delegates to hold a meeting to write up our new state laws. It was called a constitutional convention. The delegates did not include a word about slavery in the new constitution. On Nov. 9, 1857, everyone in Oregon voted on our new constitution by answering these three questions: "Do you vote for the constitution?" "Do you vote for slavery in Oregon?" "Do you vote for free [Blacks] in Oregon?" The results were surprising. The constitution was accepted with 7,200 in favor, 3,100 against. Slavery was rejected with 7,700 against, 2,600 in favor. And what about free African Americans? The people voted to make African Americans stay out of Oregon by a vote of 8,600 to 1,100! These were strange times. This last decision was eventually overturned (thrown out).

Just before the Civil War, Oregon was finally allowed to become a state. The president signed the Act of Congress on Feb. 14, 1859. And on that day, our state constitution went into effect. Without the telegraph, it took nearly a month for our ancestors to learn they were admitted as a state. When word reached Oregon, celebrations broke out everywhere. There were still a lot of laws to pass, work to do, and local leaders to elect, but they were a state and could start to grow. After 200 years of struggle, the people of Oregon State were in charge!

("Federal" refers to the central government of the United States.)

title: Kid Power - Creating Helmet Laws
text:
Did you know that you have the power to create new laws? Because we live in a free country, anyone who wants to make a positive change can turn his or her idea into a new law! It is not a quick process, but it may be worth your effort!

Here's a story about kids and parents that banded together to pass the Oregon helmet law:

In 1994, statistics were released about the dangers of people riding bikes without helmets. The news wasn't good. About 800 cyclists die in the United States each year. One in eight injured cyclists ends up with brain damage. Half of all bicycle-related deaths happen to children under the age of 15 years old. With these statistics in mind, Oregon parents and kids decided our state needed a law to protect bike riders.

A large group of students and their parents headed for Salem, our state capital. There, the idea was introduced in the House of Representatives. Then it was put on the next bill. A committee reviewed it to see if it was a good bill. They decided is was! Then the House of Representatives voted, and the helmet bill passed.

Next, the helmet bill went to the Senate. They set up a committee and reviewed it. The Senate liked it too. They voted and passed it! Finally, it went to the governor's office.

The governor decided to sign it into law. The whole process took months, but now the law says every Oregon cyclist must wear a helmet.

title: Symbols of Oregon
text:
What are Oregon's state symbols? This week, learn what they are and why they were chosen.

Oregon State Facts and Trivia

State Flag

The Oregon state flag, adopted in 1925, is navy blue with gold lettering and symbols. Blue and gold are the state colors. On the flag's face, the legend "STATE OF OREGON" is written above a shield, which is surrounded by 33 stars. Below the shield, which is part of the state seal, is written "1859," the year of Oregon's admission to the Union as the 33rd state. The flag's reverse side depicts a beaver. Oregon has the distinction of being the only state in the Union whose flag has a different pattern on the reverse side.

State Motto

"She Flies with Her Own Wings" was adopted by the 1987 legislature. The new motto replaces "The Union," which was adopted in 1957.

Father of Oregon

The 1957 legislature bestowed upon Dr. John McLoughlin the honorary title of "Father of Oregon" in recognition of his great contributions to the early development of the Oregon Country. Dr. McLoughlin originally came to the Northwest Region in 1824 as a representative of the Hudson's Bay Company.

Mother of Oregon

Honored by the 1987 legislature as the Mother of Oregon, Tabitha Moffatt Brown "represents the distinctive pioneer heritage and the charitable and compassionate nature of Oregon's people." At 66 years of age, she financed her own wagon for the trip from Missouri to Oregon. The boarding school for orphans that she established later became known as Tualatin Academy and eventually was chartered as Pacific University.

State Animal

American beaver

State Nut

With Oregon providing the U.S. with 99 percent of its supply of hazelnuts, it seems only natural to choose it as our state nut! It was chosen by Oregon legislature in 1989.

State Dance

In 1977, the legislature declared the square dance to be the official state dance.

State Flower

Oregon grape

State Gemstone

The 1987 legislature designated the Oregon sun stone as the official state gemstone.

State Fish

The Chinook salmon, also known as spring or king salmon, was declared the state fish by the 1961 Oregon legislature.

State Song

J. A. Buchanan of Astoria and Henry B. Murtagh of Portland wrote "Oregon, My Oregon" in 1920. With this song, Buchanan and Murtagh won a statewide competition sponsored by the Society of Oregon Composers, gaining statewide recognition. The song became the official state song in 1927.

State Insect

Oregon swallowtail butterfly

State Tree

The Douglas fir

State Rock

The thunder egg was named our state rock in 1965 when rock enthusiasts throughout Oregon voted for it. Thunder eggs are geodes, meaning their plain outsides are hiding hollow insides filled with colorful patterns and crystals. These rocks can range in sizes as small as less than one inch and as big as four feet in diameter. Thunder eggs are mostly found in Crook, Jefferson, Malheur, Wasco and Wheeler Counties.

State Seashell

John Howard Redfield, a conchologist, or shell expert, named the Fusitriton oregonesis after the Oregon Territory in 1848. Also known as the Oregon hairy triton, this unique shell is one of the largest in the state and can reach up to five inches in length.

State Bird

The Oregon Audubon Society polled schoolchildren in 1927 to decide the state bird. They chose the western meadowlark.

Capital

Salem, established in 1854

Size

Oregon is 395 miles wide (east to west at widest point), is 295 miles in length (north to south at longest distance), and has an area of 97,073 square miles.

Highest Point

Mount Hood is 11,235 feet high. Its lowest point is sea level at the Pacific Coast.

Deepest Lake in the United States

Crater Lake, located in Klamath County, is 1,932 feet deep.

Second Highest Waterfall

Multnomah Falls, at 620 feet high, is located in Multnomah County.

title: Salem, Oregon
text:
Salem became the capital of the new Oregon Territory in 1851 and was later voted to become the capital of Oregon state in 1864.

Salem lies along the Willamette River about 43 miles from Portland. Jason Lee, an early Methodist missionary, settled the area in 1840. The American Indians already had a name for the site and called it Chemeketa, meaning "place of rest." This was translated into the biblical name of Salem (from Hebrew "shalom" for "peace").

The missionaries sold home sites in their new settlement to finance the creation of the Oregon Institute. This grew up into today's Willamette University. Salem was an early river port. When the train came in the 1870s, Salem became a center for dairy, fruit, vegetable and wood processing and some manufacturing.

The state capitol building in Salem was completed in 1938. The state fair is held here each year.

title: What is Oregon's most recognized state symbol?
text: It's a toss-up between the Oregon Coast and Mt. Hood. Pictures of the Oregon Coast have been used in calendars and magazines for many years. People see the Oregon Coast and exclaim– "Oh, that's Oregon. I'd know it anywhere!" Mt. Hood is also associated with Oregon. Its distinctive shape and the thousands of beautiful color photos appearing in magazines and calendars make it a symbol of Oregon.

title: State Bird: Western Meadowlark
text: The meadowlark's song is one of the most beautiful heard in the spring. They are commonly found perching on a fence post or telephone pole. The male sings to let the others know he is in charge of that territory. In spring, they are found in pairs. In late summer, flocks of 12-15 are seen. They roost in tall grass. They can sing a number of different tunes. Their enemies are birds of prey and ground animals (like cats). They eat large amounts of grasshoppers, alfalfa weevil, crickets, worms, cutworms and ants, which makes them valuable for ridding us of pests. The meadowlark is the state bird for six different states.

title: Oregon State Symbols
text:
By now, you probably know about state symbols. And you probably know that every state has unique symbols that are special to them. Each state has a state bird, state tree, state flower, state song and many others.

Oregon is no different from any other state. As you'll find out in this week's paper, the Oregon grape is the state flower, the western meadowlark is the state bird and the Douglas Fir is the state tree. But have you ever heard of a state having an official seashell or beverage? How about an official microbe? Recently, Oregon added these icons when they were officially voted in as symbols of our great state.

In 1991, the legislature named the Oregon hairy triton–or the Fusitriton oregonesis in Latin–the official state seashell. This shell was named after the Oregon Territory in 1848. This special shell is one of three in the world named for a location, and it is the only shell named after a U.S. state. You can read more about the Oregon hairy triton in this week's lesson.

A strange, but official, symbol for Oregon is the state beverage. In 1997, the state legislature realized how important milk was to the economy of Oregon, so the lawmakers decided to make it the official beverage.

A recently named, and perhaps the strangest state symbol, is the offical state microbe. The state legislature decided to name a type of yeast as the official microbe. This yeast is used in making bread, cheese and beer. Just as with milk, the legislature realized how important the yeast is to the economy of Oregon. So in 2013, it became Oregon's official state microbe.

As you can see, many of Oregon's state symbols have to do with the economy. The economy of a state is very important in helping the state grow and succeed. So whenever you see a cheese sandwich or Oregon hairy triton, or drink a glass of milk, just remember that these are Oregon's official state symbols, and they are for a good reason.

title: Color the Oregon State Bird and Flower
text: The meadowlark's song is one of the most beautiful heard in the spring. They are commonly found perching on a fence post or telephone pole. The male sings to let the others know he is in charge of that territory. In spring, they are found in pairs. In late summer, flocks of 12-15 are seen. They roost in tall grass. They can sing a number of different tunes. Their enemies are birds of prey and ground animals (like cats). They eat large amounts of grasshoppers, alfalfa weevil, crickets, worms, cutworms and ants, which makes them valuable for ridding us of pests. The meadowlark is the state bird for six different states.

title: Counting on the Counties
text:
Is it ok to set up cities and counties before you become a state? Yes! Organizing our land into sections was needed long before we could become a state.

How would you divide Oregon? Early pioneers had little to work with. There were no large cities, only towns, small settlements, or single-family farms, all separated by miles of thick, green forest. It was dangerous to spread out in those days because the American Indians were still fighting the new settlers. So, the early pioneers built their communities outward from a strong central fort or mission. When the first county lines were drawn, the land was divided up to include as many of these towns as possible.

The 1843 Organic Act divided the Pacific Northwest into four sections or districts. The two districts below the Columbia River were Yawhill County (along the coast) and Champoeg County, a massive chunk of land that extended from the Willamette River eastward to the Continental Divide (near Yellowstone Park area and extending north). The top section of Champoeg County became Clackamas County.

By 1846, England decided that it did not want to fight a war with America over who owned the Pacific Northwest. England agreed to set the boundary between America and Canada at the 49th parallel. However our ancestors wanted the boundary to be 54 degrees 40'. Most people thought the Pacific Northwest would automatically become a territory of the United States. But this didn't happen for many more years.

During the 1840s, two big things happened. First, pioneers came here by the thousands. They felt that it was a safe place to settle because its borders were finally established. The second big thing was war with the American Indians. The American Indians didn't like all these strangers taking their land, and many American-Indian wars broke out.

These were hard years on the early families that moved here. The men went around on snowshoes in the winter to gather wood and food. The women shivered in log cabins that were wet and leaked from the rain and snow, and some moved back to the ships that brought them here because the weather was so bad. When the weather warmed, the settlers could finish their homes and clear the land to plant farms. When new pioneers arrived, they, too, had to cut out their portion of the forest to build a home.

Thanks to the new county governments, pioneers began to find strength in numbers. They could combine their talents and resources to make towns, roads and buildings that helped everyone. Every household could vote on things that were important for keeping the peace and helping everyone prosper.

This first decade of organization helped lay a foundation that to this day remains very important and very helpful to our growth as a state. Do you know what county you live in? Do you know what city is the county seat (governing city of a county)?

title: Clackamas County
text:
One of the four original districts created by Oregon's provisional legislature was Clackamas County. It was named after the Clackamas Indians and was so large, it covered portions of four states and one province in Canada. At the time, the Columbia River was its northern border. Since then, Clackamas County has been chopped down in size, and instead of more than 100,000 square miles in size, it is only 1,879 square miles. Oregon City is the county seat, the very first city incorporated or recognized by the federal government, west of the Rocky Mountains. In the early years, Oregon City was the most important city in the whole territory, welcoming pioneers and providing a meeting place for hunters, American Indians, trappers, or traders. The county is mostly thick forest. Many rivers flow through the area, including the Willamette, Clackamas, Sandy, Pudding, Molla and Salmon. Have you seen any of these? Also, Mt. Hood towers over it all. The county's main activities include growing crops, cutting timber, manufacturing goods, and all the related business that goes along.

title: How much does it snow in the Antarctic?
text: Would you believe the Antarctic is drier than the Sahara Desert! How can this be? The answer is simple: The Antarctic receives only one or two inches of snow a year, but it is so cold there, the snow never melts. The snow has been piling up for thousands of years. Today, the snowpack is compressed into a layer that is more than two miles thick. It gets thicker every year, but only by an inch or so.

title: Pileated Woodpeckers
text: Hey, who's that knocking on the door? If you're in the forest, that knocking sound is probably a pileated woodpecker. These big birds are very shy, and you won't see them too often, but you'll hear them a lot. Besides making noise to knock huge holes in both live and dead trees, this woodpecker has a loud call: "wuck a wuck a wuck a wuck a." This bird is black with a red crest and a white face. What are they looking for when they go pecking around? They want the ants, termites and beetles that are living inside the trees. The pileated woodpeckers are 16-19 inches long and love to live in mature forests. In fact, a healthy population of this bird means a forest's ecosystem is also healthy. Each bird needs about 1,000 acres. All this hunting and pecking helps break up decaying trees, speeding up the return of nutrients to the forest floor.

title: President John Adams and the XYZ Affair
text:
Can you imagine following in the footsteps of George Washington? John Adams did. America's first president was greatly admired and respected for leading the troops in the Revolutionary War and helping to build our new country. When Adams became our second president in 1797, America was at peace. We had begun rebuilding our friendship with Great Britain. The former enemies were now buying and selling products from each other. Their ships crisscrossed the Atlantic with goods to trade.

Unfortunately, France was in the middle of its own revolution and was at war with Britain. France began capturing American trading ships to cut off supplies to their enemy. Some Americans were angry and wanted to declare war on France.

President Adams firmly believed in peaceful solutions. He sent a committee to France to work out the problem. The discussions did not go well. The Americans brought home a disturbing report. The three French delegates were angry at America for trading with Britain. They demanded that a large amount of money be paid to the French foreign minister as a bribe, along with a big loan.

When Adams sent the report to Congress, he disguised the names of the Frenchmen with the letters X, Y and Z. News of the "XYZ Affair" traveled across the nation. Many people were furious with France. Merchant ships from the United States and France were battling at sea in an undeclared war.

But Adams had confidence in his critical analysis of the situation. First, he called for Congress to build up America's armed forces. Then he sent new ambassadors to France who were able to work out a treaty that ended the fighting. The XYZ Affair was peacefully put to rest. When have you used critical analysis to help end an argument?

title: Self-Driving Car
text:
Think of how exciting it was for people to take their first train ride. After years of traveling on foot, on horseback or in wagons, riding a train must have seemed like a transportation miracle.

Are you ready to see your own transportation breakthrough? It might be here sooner than you think. People who work for Google have been working on a self-driving car. When you think about driving a car, one of the first things to come to mind is probably the steering wheel. You won’t see any of those in one of Google’s cars! They want to build a car that doesn’t need a person to drive. All you would need to do is push the start button, type in where you want to go and enjoy the ride!

So how does it work? The car uses a system called “LIDAR.” LIDAR stands for “Light Detection and Ranging” and uses lasers to “see” the road and anything else nearby. A computer uses that information to control the wheels and steer the car.

Test versions of the car have driven thousands of miles to make sure they are safe. Do you think that self-driving cars will be for sale by the time you’re ready to drive? The cars are big enough for two people. Talk with a partner about how you think self-driving cars might change how we get around.

title: How do I read nonfiction?
text:
How do I read nonfiction?

Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring, but it really isn’t. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you find it easier to understand— and maybe more fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/ solution, (2) compare/ contrast, (3) cause/ effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/ supporting details. This week, we will talk about cause and effect.

Cause/ Effect

With this information pattern, writers organize their material to show how one thing leads to another. Cause is the reason why something happens. Effect is what happens as a result of the cause. Effects often turn into causes for different effects. Writers often use this pattern when they want to explain a chain of events.

One way to find the cause and effect of a passage is to make a diagram

that allows you to show the cause and effect relationship graphically. You start by writing the cause of the events. Draw an arrow from the cause bubble pointing right, and then next to the arrow, write the effect of that cause. Draw a new arrow from the effect bubble pointing left and down, and write the next effect. Draw the next arrow pointing right, and continue in that manner until you have reached the final effect. See the sample diagram below.

Try It!

To the right is a passage about immigration to the United States. Read the passage. Then create a Cause/Effect Diagram that shows the causes and effects of immigration.

title: Polly Lane, Oregon's First Lady
text:
The early morning slumber of 1814 was suddenly shattered by bloody screams as 12-year-old Polly woke to find American Indians killing her family. The attackers killed her stepfather, then her mother, and then two of her siblings. Polly grabbed her quilt, jumped out a window, and headed for the river. She found the family canoe, pushed it into the water, jumped in, and wrapped up to stay warm. She watched as her cabin home erupted in flames.

Polly didn't know what to do. It all happened so fast. The family home on the banks of the Ohio River in Kentucky was quickly turning to ashes, and all her family was dead. She fell back into the canoe in a state of shock. She passed out in a dazed slumber. Polly drifted on the river for two days when her canoe ran aground near the homestead of the Hart family. This kind family found her barely alive. They took her in, nursed her to health, and made her part of the family.

Three years later, Polly married one of the sons of the Hart family. He died shortly after their first baby was born. Polly was only 16 at the time. Being a young widow with no means for support, she gave up her infant, Nathaniel Joseph Hart, to one of her foster sisters. It was an act of love and kindness that she later said was the hardest thing she ever did. When she turned 18, she married another member of the Hart family, a man named Joseph Lane. This was the beginning of a long, hard life that eventually brought her to Oregon.

Polly was a strong woman. For many years while her husband was fighting in the Mexican-American War or serving as a delegate in Washington, D.C., she raised the family. They were very poor. Joseph sent money, but she didn't spend it. She sewed it into his shirts or buried it in a jar in the shed. Polly labored hard with her own hands. She cooked, sewed, tended, nursed, plowed, sowed, and harvested just to keep her family going.

Polly never did learn how to read and write. Letters from Joseph were read to her, and her letters back were written by one of her children. When the Mexican War ended, President Polk assigned Joseph to be the new territorial governor of Oregon in 1848. Joseph took the Oregon Trail route, but he didn't want Polly and the children to take that dangerous way. He sent them by boat around South America and up the California and Oregon coast. The family united in Roseburg, Oregon, with 640 acres. By this time, they had 10 children.

And then came a big surprise. In 1858, a wagon pulled up in front of their home. Out stepped a man who looked a lot like Polly's dead husband. The man announced he was Nathaniel Joseph Hart - the baby she had surrendered 40 years ago had finally returned!

About this time, Joseph Lane's career in politics took a bad turn. He finished his term as governor, but just before the Civil War, he announced that he was in favor of the South, slavery and the Confederates. He even ran for vice president. People tried to kill him, and he was shot twice. He lost the election to Abraham Lincoln and Hannibal Hamlin.

After this defeat, Joseph retired from politics and returned to Oregon. He and Polly settled down at their farm in Roseburg, Oregon. Polly died in August of 1870, and Joseph died 11 years later in 1881. Polly leaves a legacy as one of Oregon's finest first ladies and pioneer women.

title: Wildfire and Dinosaurs
text:
For a tyrannosaurus rex during the Cretaceous period, (the time period between 145 and 65 million years ago) life was pretty good. These fierce predators ate whichever creatures they chose. Almost every other dinosaur feared them. However, researchers have discovered that many very strong wildfires happened a lot during the Cretaceous period that even the great tyrannosauruses were afraid of.

Scientists have found many charcoal beds from the Cretaceous period. Charcoal is what is left after plants are burnt, and scientists find it preserved with fossils. Many of these large charcoal beds were filled with dinosaur fossils. That means dinosaurs like the tyrannosaurus rex were killed in a fire.

Several things caused the extremely hot wildfires during the Cretaceous period. Lightning strikes started most of the fires. Also, the global temperature was higher than it is today, but like today, hot weather often means more forest fires. There were higher levels of oxygen in the atmosphere during the time, too, and oxygen fuels fires. The fires caused great changes in the environment. They destroyed vegetation and made the soil unstable, which caused runoff and erosion. Erosion increased flooding after storms.

In the past, researchers did not think about the impact of wildfires on the dinosaur population and their environment, but now that has changed. More interesting information about dinosaurs and the life they lived is sure to come!

Reference: History News Network (hnn.us)

title: Lane County
text:
Lane County is in west-central Oregon. It was established on Jan. 29, 1851, and was named after Joseph Lane, the first territorial governor. In 1853, different cities competed to become the county seat. The "Mulligan donation" and the "Skinner claim" were joined to form "Eugene," named after Eugene Skinner. In 1860, there were only 4,780 people living there. Most people had jobs in the timber and agricultural businesses. Timber is important because the county is on the edge of Oregon's largest stand of timber. The fertile soil in Willamette Valley makes this one of the richest farming areas in America. It is also home to the University of Oregon. Visitors love to come to Lane County to see the beautiful crops, orchards, farms and coastal area that this county has to offer. And plan to have lots of fun. Go sailing, hiking, fishing, dune buggy riding, kite flying, eating, museum visiting, park visiting, mountain climbing and a whole lot more. You can get a great taste of Oregon in Lane County!

title: How do cats purr, by exhaling or inhaling?
text: Do you have a cat staying warm indoors this winter? Have you ever listened to it purr? A cat does its purring the same way a lion roars or humans hum. It draws breath to make its vocal cords vibrate. Cats normally purr when they are happy or content. But this isn't always the case. Cats also purr when they are injured or in pain as a way of coping with the hurt. Some researchers believe that this kind of purring may be a form of self-hypnosis. This helps a cat comfort itself and show a good mood.

title: Mountain Lion
text: What animal has more names and nicknames than any other animal in the world? What animal can live almost anywhere, from deserts to the humid coast, from sea level to 10,000-foot-high mountains? And what animal eats deer, elk, mice and grasshoppers and, if it isn't finished eating, buries its food and comes back for it later? If you guessed a mountain lion, or cougar, you are right! This graceful member of the cat family can be found in many parts of the North American and South American continents. It is the champion jumper among cats, able to leap 30 feet from a standing position and 18 feet straight up. They weigh 100-200 pounds with a 28-inch tail, grow to almost seven feet from head to tip of the tail, and can live up to 18 years. They prefer their own territory (25-100 square miles) and only meet up with other mountain lions to have kittens. Because they kill livestock when there is a shortage of food, Oregon and Washington allow mountain lions to be hunted.

title: How do I read nonfiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring, but it really isn’t. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you find it easier to understand— and maybe more fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will discuss classification.

Classification

With this pattern, the nonfiction piece is organized into categories or groups that share certain characteristics. In other words, the content is classified.

One idea for finding out how the content of a nonfiction piece is classified is to chart the information into categories. Charting information can help you see the categories graphically. You will also better remember the characteristics of each category.

title: Before the Civil War Came the Pig
text:
One summer day in 1859, an American farmer named Lyman Cutler was tending his garden on San Juan Island. Suddenly, a big old pig from the British settlement wandered over for the THIRD time that summer and started eating all the new potato plants. Cutler was so angry, he grabbed his gun and shot the pig. This nearly caused war! The British called for Cutler's arrest, but local Americans protected him and asked for U.S. military protection. The British responded by sending a warship with soldiers, and more American troops were sent. Finally, the whole thing grew until more than 2,000 British and U.S. troops faced off to battle over the incident. The so-called "Pig War" ended after four months when troops were withdrawn and peace was restored. No shots were ever fired, and the only casualty was the pig.

About a year after the Pig War, the Civil War started in 1861. This was a terrible fight between the southern states and the northern states over issues of economy, states rights and slavery. With everyone's attention focused on the fighting, life changed for the Oregon-Washington region.

There was no Red Cross during the Civil War, so women all over America were asked to prepare clothing and hospital supplies to help the wounded. It is said that women from the Pacific Northwest provided more supplies than women from any other state or territory in America.

In the middle of the war, when things were going badly on all sides, President Abraham Lincoln gave permission for railroads to be built to the West Coast. Even though there were no supplies, money, materials or workers to build the rails, Congress passed the bills so that people could begin making plans.

Most of the men teaching school had to leave their jobs to fight in the war. They were replaced by female teachers. During the Civil War, about 80 percent of teachers (up to 12th grade) were women. It has remained about the same ever since.

Many of the leading figures in the Civil War had ties to the Pacific Northwest. General Grant, for example, had been stationed as an Army officer at Fort Vancouver in 1853. Governor Stevens, who had been Washington Territory's governor and delegate to Congress, was a famous general for the Union troops.

Washington and Oregon residents were very angry when Captain Waddell brought his Confederate ship, Shenandoah, into Washington waters and captured 38 merchant ships. Waddell burned 30 of the ships. At the war's end, Waddell fled to England to surrender his ship to the British. The British promptly returned the ship to the Americans.

Oregon voted against slavery, even though pro-slavery pioneers had settled in southern Oregon. Loyal Oregonians kept the pro-slavery people from being very vocal. They also volunteered to protect the frontier from American Indian attacks and to guard the forts until regular troops returned.

For all the sadness, fighting and uncomfortable feelings the Civil War caused, our nation eventually healed. Both Oregon and Washington voted to accept the 13th Amendment to the Constitution, an amendment that banned slavery forever.

title: Grant County
text:
Grant County was formed in the thick of the Civil War, in 1864. At the time, it was the largest county in the state. It was named after a local hero, General Ulysses S. Grant. Grant was commander of the Union Army during the Civil War and earlier had been stationed at Fort Vancouver. He helped protect immigrants traveling the Oregon Trail. Oregon decided to set up a government and form Grant County when gold was discovered on Whiskey Flat in 1862. They say that within 10 days after gold was discovered, more than 1,000 miners were camped along the Canyon Creek! At least $20 million in gold was mined from Canyon Creek and Susanville. When the gold declined, people raised stock, and agriculture became the main work in most of the county. Parts of four national forests are in Grant County. The headwaters of John Day River are here. This river has more miles of wild and scenic land than any other river in the United States. The main industries in this county are forestry, agriculture, livestock and recreation. If you visit Grant County, don't forget your gold-panning pan. Who knows– there might be some gold in those hills!

title: What is a "Blue Moon"?
text: The expression "blue moon" means a second full moon in the same month. If there's a full moon on the first or second day of a month, there will be another, a so-called "blue moon," at the end of that month. This happens only once every two years, on average. The term "blue moon" is probably 400 years old and means "once in a long while," or "very infrequently." "Say, does he ever get to school on time?" "No, only once in a blue moon."

title: Bald Eagle
text: A wonderful pastime during visits in the country or forest is watching bald eagles. These beautiful birds with their snowy white heads and dark bodies soar through the blue sky with grace and majesty. Eagles depend on rabbits as a main source of food, as well as on salmon in nearby rivers. When rabbits are hard to find, eagles usually move to other places where food is easier to find. Eagles hatch in the late spring and are flying when they are about 12 weeks old. A young eagle doesn't mature for about five or six years – that's when its brown head feathers are replaced with white. The female is the larger of the pair and weighs eight to nine pounds. She has a wingspan of six or seven feet. Eagles mate for life and typically have two or three eggs each year. They build two nests. When the first nest gets grungy and is infested with bugs, the eagle family moves to the other nest while the first airs out. Wouldn't Mom and Dad like that idea for some of THEIR kids?!

title: The Civil War Today!
text:
The Civil War began when Confederate troops attacked Union soldiers at Fort Sumter on April 12, 1861. The war lasted four years. The two sides fought over 50 major battles and hundreds of smaller clashes. The war ended after General Robert E. Lee surrendered to General Ulysses S. Grant on April 9, 1865.

2011 to 2015 marked the 150th anniversary of the Civil War. Many towns and communities took time to celebrate and remember this important part of our history. During those years, anyone who owned an iPad could “watch” the war happen using “The Civil War Today” app. The app showed users what had happened on that day 150 years ago. The app used pictures, maps and newspaper stories to show the events of the war one day at a time.

The anniversary has passed, but the app is still available. People with the app can look up any date during the war and read newspaper articles, letters soldiers wrote to their families and detailed descriptions of battles. If you or someone you know owns an iPad, ask for permission to look at “The Civil War Today” app. It can help you relive the drama of the Civil War with just the push of a button!

title: Pounded Plant Prints
text:
Materials

several sheets of plain, ink-free newsprint

just-picked leaves and flowers

hammer

100-percent cotton fabric

washing soda

hard surface for hammering (such as a sidewalk or sturdy table)

water

soap

paint brush

bowl

pan

clothes line or dryer

Directions

1. Gather plants. Choose thin, flat leaves; juicy leaves do not work well. If you want to print flowers, choose small, bright flowers like pansies, violas and baby carnations. Remember, you never know how the dye is going to transfer to the fabric. The surprise is part of the fun.

2. Cover a hard surface with eight to 10 newsprint pages. Place a piece of fabric on the newsprint. We strongly recommend testing several plant parts on scrap pieces of fabric.

3. Place a leaf or flower on the fabric. Cover the plant with a double layer of newsprint.

4. Hammer the newsprint covering the plant. The tannin coloring in the plant will transfer to the fabric. Carefully lift your paper cover to see if your plant design is transferring to the cloth.

5. Dip cloth in a solution of 1/2 cup washing soda to 2 cups water. The green tannin of the leaves “fixes” successfully with the washing soda solution. After “fixing” the colors, wash your cotton in soapy water, rinse and dry. All flower petals “fix” differently. Many pinks and purples “fix” aqua and bright blue.

title: How do I read nonfiction?
text:
How do I read nonfiction?

Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring, but it really isn’t. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you find it easier to understand—and maybe more fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will discuss the main idea and supporting details.

Main Idea/Supporting Details

With this pattern, the writer presents a main idea and then backs it up with factual supporting details as evidence. You should be able to find this pattern when reading nonfiction because you probably already use it in your own writing.

One strategy for finding the main ideas and supporting details is to create an outline of what you are reading. With the outline, you will be able to see the main ideas at a glance. Use the main ideas as headings and the supporting details as subheadings in your outline.

Try It!

Above is a passage about the Great Depression. Read the passage, then outline on your own piece of paper the information in the passage so that the main ideas are the headings, and the supporting details are the subheadings.

title: Oregon Sprints to the Next Century
text:
What a race! After more than 200 years of exciting history, the people of Oregon could hardly wait for the Civil War, or War Between the States, to end (1861-1865), so they could get this state of ours on the fast track to growth.

When this family first came to the Pacific Northwest, they lived in the small cabin in the left picture. They built it themselves with rough boards. When their city grew up, the family was able to buy the materials to build a big fine house. Their way of life had changed.

Look at how fast people began moving here. In 1860, only 52,500 people lived here. In 10 years, that number almost doubled to 91,000. Ten years later, it almost doubled again to 175,000. By 1890, we had 318,000 people. At the turn of the century, 414,000 called Oregon their home. In the same year, we crossed the half-million mark with 673,000. In only 50 years, we grew more than tenfold!

Before the railroad in 1883, the Oregon Trail remained the main route to Oregon. From the late 1840s and on, people began pouring into our state. Naturally, there came problems with all the newcomers. In fact, several wars with the American Indians broke out. The Modoc War was fought in 1864-1873, and the Shoshone War was fought in 1866-1868. Things eventually quieted down, and treaties were signed.

There were plenty of jobs in our state for the newcomers. Coal (a kind of fossil fuel), for example, had been discovered in 1855 in Coos Bay and later along the foothills of the Coast Range and Cascades. By 1908, we were mining about 86,000 tons of coal a year.

People found other minerals, too. Gold was discovered in 1852 in the Rogue and Klamath Rivers and later in greater quantities in the streams and rivers of Baker and Grant Counties. In 1894, our total gold output was $2.1 million, but this output dwindled to $865,000 by 1908. Silver, copper, lead, platinum, iron ore, zinc, quicksilver, and other minerals were found, but no strong mining effort was underway by the turn of the century to get these minerals out. Lumber made up for the difference. In 1870, we sold only $1,014,000 worth of lumber. However, by 1905, we were selling lumber across the nation with nearly $12.5 million in sales per year.

Many people raised animals for a living. By 1910, we had more sheep than we had people, with 2,581,000 sheep! By 1910, we had a steer for every person in Oregon (698,000 cattle) and more than enough milk from our 174,000 dairy cows.

Oregon has some of the best soils in the world for agriculture. In 1900, we had more than 35,000 farms in our state. By 1910, our farmers had 810,000 acres planted in wheat and produced a huge crop of 16,377,000 bushels. Other field crops grew well, too. In 1850, somebody tried to grow hops. Hops are used in various beverages drinks and other foods. The hops grew so well, Oregon became the country's biggest producer. In 1905, we sold 20,500,000 pounds of hops!

How do you water the land to do all this work? Western Oregon had all the rain it needed. Elsewhere, we built reservoirs. In 1909, the Umatilla Project helped us irrigate 20,400 acres, and the Klamath Project let us irrigate 181,000 acres in Klamath County and a couple of counties in California.

Oh, and lest we forget, the fish! Salmon provided many jobs, especially after people invented a way to safely can salmon meat. By 1908, we were selling almost 25 million pounds of salmon a year.

At last, we could welcome the new century of 1900. There was such a great feeling in our state–so much to do, so much growth, and so many places to visit, live, and enjoy. The sprint to the new century was worth every pioneer, every dollar, and every fish, tree, or gold nugget carved out of our land. But not too far away was a great challenge that nobody wanted, even though they knew it was coming. As we will discuss in our next issue, headlines around the world cried out the news: WORLD WAR!

title: What is Hydraulic Fracturing?
text:
People in the states of Colorado, Texas and Ohio have been feeling small earthquakes over the past few years. Some people are saying those quakes are the result of hydraulic fracturing.

Hydraulic fracturing is a way to get natural gas from underground rock formations up to the surface. We use natural gas for energy in homes and businesses. Water and chemicals are pumped underground through long, deep wells. The liquid causes fractures, or cracks, in the rock. Natural gas escapes through the cracks and gets piped up to the surface. Over 200,000 new wells have been drilled in the U.S. during the last 10 years.

The National Research Council released a report in 2012 that said hydraulic fracturing does not seem to be the culprit, but other human activity might be the problem. Some groups believe that it's the wastewater (leftover water and chemicals), not the fracturing itself that is causing the earthquakes. The wastewater from the process is either treated at a facility or sent deep underground. When the liquid is injected back into the ground, it can make the tectonic plates slip and rub against each other, causing earthquakes.

The companies doing the drilling say that they are following safety regulations and protecting their workers, the residents and the environment. Companies have been injecting waste liquids into the ground since the 1930s, and only recently has there been an increase in earthquakes. We will certainly be hearing more about hydraulic fracturing in the years to come

Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/ for more Connections and Current Events articles.
