title: Deschutes County
text:
The last county formed in Oregon was Deschutes County. It was named after the Deschutes River, which flows through the area, and was formed in 1916. The Deschutes National Forest is a very popular camping and visiting stop. It attracts more than 7 million people every year. The county seat is Bend, a fast-growing city that was settled in 1904 on the Deschutes River. It was the place at which early pioneers crossed the river, a place they used to call "farewell bend." People love living there for its mild climate, year-round outdoor activities, and easy access to the eastern slopes of the Cascades and many other recreational areas. Other major cities are Sisters and Redmond. Lumber and wood products are the county's main income producers, with tourism as second. If you visit Bend, plan to see the five wilderness areas in the Deschutes National Forest, or the six wild and scenic rivers, or the Metolius Conservation Area, or visit the Oregon Cascades Recreation Area and the Newberry National Volcanic Monument. There you can almost get lost in the numerous alpine forests, volcanic attractions, dense evergreen forests, mountain lakes, caves, desert areas, and alpine meadows.

Using the provided map, find the agricultural products that are produced in the counties above. Write one on the second line under the county descriptions in this week’s lesson (above).

title: Why do we say 'It's raining cats and dogs?'
text: Old superstitions (strange beliefs) about weather, which go back for thousands of years, always included cats. A long time ago, people believed cats had a great influence on weather. Some people even believed witches changed their shape to cats and would ride through storms. Others believed in a king of storms, a god called Odin, who was helped by a dog to produce wind. The cats came to represent down-pouring rain, and dogs represented strong gusts of wind.

title: Spotted Skunk
text: Here's a puzzle: What do these three things have in common: a skunk, your breath, and the natural gas that runs your furnace? If you guessed the smell, you are absolutely right! A chemical called mercaptan is produced by skunks in their spray. Bad breath includes mercaptan, and your local gas company adds mercaptan to natural gas so that you can tell if there's a gas leak. Everybody knows what skunk smells like. The spotted skunk is the most common variety in our plateau and desert areas. They grow to about 22 inches long; the female is smaller. They are most active at night when they go snooping for insects, seeds and small animals. Spotted skunks like to build their dens under brush, homes, barns and sometimes fallen trees or rocks. Like raccoons, skunks will invade your campsite for food if you're not careful when you go camping. Make sure you lock things up before going to bed. Close the cooler, put food away and pick up your litter.

title: Why Should I Keep the Writer’s Journal?
text:
Have you ever had to write something, but you did not know what to write about? Have you ever had a good story idea, but when you started to write the story, you realized that you could not remember the idea anymore? A writer’s journal can help solve this problem.

Keep a Record

You can record your memories, observations and thoughts in a writer’s journal. You can even write colorful words and phrases or the events of a day in your journal. One very good use of your journal is free writing. Free writing is a kind of practice writing that allows you to sketch your thoughts and feelings without limits. Free writing can include single sentences or long strings of words that might not make sense to anyone else but you. You can even put drawings and diagrams in your journal. Just remember that no one else has to see your writer’s journal—unless it is a class assignment, and then your teacher will want to see it.

Here are some tips for starting your writer’s journal:

Find a special notebook to use as your writer’s journal. You should use a notebook that appeals to you because it is your very own journal. Color and draw on them so that they reflect your personality. You can also use a computer or index cards in a box for your journal.

You should write in your journal when you want to. You might want to write in it every day or just once a week. You might like to write at the same time every day so that you can have a routine. Just remember that the more you write in your journal, the more useful it will be to you.

Find a special, quiet place to do your journal writing. Make sure you have all the supplies you need to keep your journal: pencils, pens, markers, scissors and glue.

Write whatever comes to your head, almost as if you are having a conversation with yourself. Do not worry about editing, rewriting or spelling until later when you transfer something from your journal into a writing project.

Try It!

Start a writer’s journal using the suggestions and tips we have provided. You will be amazed what you might discover about yourself.

Ideas for Your Writer’s Journal

Collect cartoons and articles to give you ideas for future writing projects.

Compose imaginary letters to people you wish you knew.

Record quotations, song lyrics, jokes, poems or riddles.

Describe interesting people and places.

Keep learning notes—Take notes about your learning process. Record new facts and ideas you’ve learned in school, write about the progress you’ve made in class, and list questions you have about confusing content.

Record reading reactions—Explore ideas and feelings about what you have read. Write about your favorite character, predict what might happen next in the story, tell your opinion of the writer’s style, or summarize the story. You can even tell how the story relates to events in your own life. What is interesting about the story? What angers, amuses or puzzles you?

title: Let's Write
text: Suppose you lived in 1915, and you get hit by lightning and travel into the future to 2015. After a few days, you suddenly fizzle, pop, wheeze, go blurry, and reappear in your own bed, back in 1915. Knowing what the future holds, what will you do differently? Who will you tell about computers, airplanes, space travel, medicine and digital watches? If you could bring one thing back from the future, what would it be? Why?

title: Frog Jumper
text:
Materials

• One square piece of paper, about 6 inches on each side

Directions

1. Fold the paper square in half horizontally, crease firmly and then unfold.

2. Fold the square in half vertically, crease firmly, unfold.

3. Fold each of the corners diagonally to the center.

4. Fold the top edges down to the middle line, creating a kite-shaped figure.

5. Fold the end of the kite, as shown.

6. Fold the bottom corners so that they meet on the middle line.

7. Fold the straight bottom up and then fold half of it down again.

8. Fold the top triangle down to make his head and turn over your frog.

title: Oregon's Early World Records
text:
Welcome to another terrific issue of Oregon Studies Weekly! We finally made it to the 1900s. This century brought more fantastic change than anyone ever dreamed. Let's jump back 100 years and take a closer look at our own Oregon world records of the first 20 years of the 1900s.

If somebody wanted to write a book of Oregon World Records, the first 20 years of the 1900s would have been a good time to do it. In 1900, Frederick Weyerhaeuser started one of the largest timber empires in the world when he bought 900,000 acres of prime forestland in Oregon. In 1901, the very first automobile ever to drive in Oregon proudly coughed and wheezed its way down Portland streets. And then Mr. J. Willis Sayre decided to set a new world record traveling around the Earth the fastest. He left the Pacific Northwest using trains, boats, cars, carriages, and just about anything that moved to complete a trip around the globe and returned 54 days, 9 hours, and 42 minutes later—a new world record!

Want to buy a farm? Want to buy one for cheap?! Land was selling for $5 an acre at the turn of the century. Ten years later, farmland around Portland was up to $228 an acre. By 1914, some Oregon orchards sold for $4,000 an acre!

In 1904, we became the first state to elect senators by popular vote, instead of having them appointed by our legislature.

In 1905, we held a big 100-year celebration of the Lewis and Clark Centennial Exposition. It was a huge fair that attracted 2 million people from all over the country. This prompted us to start the first of our annual June Rose Festivals in 1907. Shortly afterwards, the first underwater cable from the Pacific Northwest to Alaska was laid so that people could communicate by telegraph. In 1905, we could grow 20,500,000 pounds of hops, the most of any other place in America.

Got milk? We do! Our dairy farmers were learning how to do a better job. Simply by watching the cows' diets, our farmers doubled milk output at the turn of the century. Word spread across the country! One local cow set a world's record for the most milk given: 3,555 pounds of milk in one month! We were major cheese producers, too—a record 124,586 pounds in 1909. We exported the most grain shipments in the Northwest, 13 million bushels in 1909, the same year President Taft proclaimed Oregon Caves a national monument, our first.

Oregon's harbors and shipyards were busy, too. As a show of strength as tensions in Europe increased, America's fleet of battleships took its first round-the-world tour in 1908, parading up Oregon's coast on its way to Puget Sound. In 1915, as war erupted in Europe, Norway and France ordered 20 wooden ships from Portland. By June 1919, we were helping to build 141 wooden sailing ships and 156 steel freighters to fight the war in Europe.

In 1912, women were finally given the right to vote in Oregon. Portland organized its first symphony orchestra, and in 1920 Jacques Gerskovitz organized and conducted the first Junior Symphony in the country.

In August 1914, word came that Germany had declared war on Russia. The First World War was not fought in America, but we were involved. Our whole country was involved. And Oregon did its part helping us win!

title: Giant Trees
text:
The Douglas fir is one of the Pacific Northwest’s most popular trees. Oregon adopted this giant tree as the official state tree in 1939.

Douglas firs produce a hard wood that is moderate in its weight. Builders love to use it in construction because they say that it is stronger than concrete! To build the average house, it takes 11 trees. Most Oregon homes are built from wood. It may surprise you to find out that the average person uses at least one tree a year just in paper goods!

Generally, Douglas fir trees reach a height between 180 and 200 feet and measure between 4 and 6 feet wide at their base.

Many giant fir trees have been discovered to be more than 300 feet tall! When a tree gets to be that tall, it usually means that it is more than 1,000 years old. Some Douglas fir and California redwood trees are taller than the Statue of Liberty!

At Christmas time, Douglas firs are the trees of choice. Christmas tree farms report that they sell more Douglas fir trees than any other. The White House has even requested a Douglas fir Christmas tree on several occasions.

There are many good reasons that the Douglas fir was chosen as our state tree. Its beauty, strength and usefulness help make it one of Oregon’s greatest resources.

title: Oregon During the First World War 1900s-1920s
text:
When a war involves many countries, we call it a world war. The First World War involved 23 of the biggest countries in the world, including America. It started when Germany attacked Russia, and other nations quickly joined sides. The cost of the war was terrible. Almost 8 million soldiers died, and the cost in money was $200 billion. The First World War began in 1914 and ended in 1918. The state of Oregon sent a total of 44,166 people to fight.

Victory Gardens

In most cities, people turned vacant lots and backyards into gardens. Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts watered and tended, as did families and communities. "Victory Gardens" sprang up everywhere with peas, beans and potatoes.

Labor

During the First World War, workers were frustrated. They had to work long days at dangerous jobs for pay that was different from place to place. Workers organized themselves into labor unions, and in 1919, they went on strike. This means they refused to go back to work until pay and the long working hours were made more fair. Companies and factories were forced to change because nobody would come work for them. The strike lasted five days and brought Portland to a standstill. Another group of workers in the region was the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW). They were viewed as unpatriotic by American Legion workers, who were celebrating the end of World War I. A fight broke out between the groups, and in a 10-minute shootout, seven people were killed and 50 were wounded. This focused national attention on the labor movement in America.

Agriculture

The first change the war brought in Oregon was on the farm. Most farm workers had gone to war. Others took higher-paying jobs in factories or in Canada where pay was better. The farm problems were solved by our communities—women drove the tractors, high-school students donated after-school hours, and college professors worked holidays and weekends. We built more meat-packing plants and dairy and poultry farms. Twenty new grain mills were built to make more flour.

The Spruce Squadrons

When America entered World War I, we quickly learned we had no way to build airplanes. Even though the United States invented it, the Europeans were the ones interested in planes to fight wars. But Europe couldn't build planes fast enough because they didn't have the right kind of wood. That's where we helped! Our spruce wood was the very best for airplane wings—strong, long, flexible and lighter than other woods. In 1918, about 50,000 soldiers came here to work with another 100,000 lumberjacks in cutting the spruce and trimming and shipping it overseas for airplane manufacturers. These groups of soldiers and lumberjacks became known as "Spruce Squadrons."

title: Coastal Timberlands
text:
In 1900, about 56 percent of our state was covered by thick stands of Douglas fir, spruce, yellow pine, cedar, hemlock and other trees. From the base of the Cascades to the ocean, we were covered in trees except in small prairies and clearings in the Willamette and other valleys. The most important tree has been the Douglas fir, sometimes called the Oregon pine. These grow up to 300 feet tall and were used in ship masts and bridge timbers. In World War I, the Sitka spruce on Oregon's coast became very important because it was perfect in airplane construction as wing beams. During the war, we produced 120 million feet of "wing beam spruce," and our loggers were nicknamed "The Spruce Squadron." Our coastal counties of Clatsop, Tillamook, Lincoln, Lane, Douglas, Coos and Curry had many busy lumber towns. But the war was causing us to use up our trees four times as fast as they were growing. Laws were passed to slow this down. We replanted areas that had been logged out and set aside large blocks of forest that would not be cut down. Today, logging and wood manufacturing is closely watched. It has always been an important part of our state's economy and is now a permanent piece of our growth and our future!

Beautiful forests give Oregon a strong lumber industry that continues today. New trees are planted to take the place of the ones cut for lumber.

title: Was there ever a year without a summer?
text: Did you know there was a year when there was no summer? It started in 1815 when the huge Tambora volcano in Indonesia exploded, sending mountains of heavy ash, dust and gases into the upper atmosphere. Winds quickly spread the dust around the Earth. The hazy sky made the sun appear dull and reddish for several years after. In 1816, the dusty shroud changed the weather. During June, July and August, it snowed and froze in the northeastern United States. In Europe, widespread famine resulted from the summer of no crops. Maybe we can do without a winter, but never a summer!

title: White Pelican
text: You'll never forget your first pelican! This huge bird has a wingspan of up to 10 feet and can be as tall as five or six feet. They are among the largest of the living birds. Pelicans have a really neat way of eating. They fly in formation, driving fish to shallow water, and then swoop down and scoop them up. They catch fish using a sort of dipping-net, a pouch under their beak. Other pelicans use the dive-bomber approach and plunge into the water to get their fish. But the white pelican is happy to work in teams. Pelicans lay one to four bluish-white eggs in a nest they make of sticks. The babies are born after about a month, and it takes three or four years for them to mature. The young birds eat by thrusting their beaks down Mom's throat for food already eaten by her. That's not our favorite way of feeding, but for pelican babies, it works just fine! On land, pelicans look pretty wobbly as they walk around, but in flight they are just beautiful. They fly in small groups and enjoy flapping their wings in unison. The male and female look about the same, but the male is slightly larger. If you ever see pelicans on an inland lake or near the ocean, don't disturb them, but do enjoy watching. They are large and beautiful birds that lend a lot to our scenic landscape.

title: Woodrow Wilson and the Fourteen Points
text:
All presidents have important responsibilities, but few are more critical than those faced by presidents during times of war. While the United States was fighting in World War I, President Woodrow Wilson addressed Congress on Jan. 8, 1918. He presented a plan for peace called the Fourteen Points.

Woodrow Wilson was elected in 1912. World War I began in 1914 between Great Britain and Germany and other European nations. It was called The Great War. Everyone thought there would never be another war like it. President Wilson wanted to keep the United States out of the war. He tried to help Great Britain and Germany end the conflict. But when German submarines began sinking American ships, he asked Congress to declare war.

Wilson's Fourteen Points plan described his ideals for achieving world peace and democracy. He had consulted with a team of about 150 foreign policy advisors. He assured Americans that the war was being fought for good causes and would lead to peace in Europe. The Fourteen Points included free trade, freedom of the seas and returning territories taken in the war. Wilson also wanted to establish a League of Nations to protect the independence of "great and small states (nations) alike."

Wilson's Fourteen Points faced opposition from some people, but it was used as the basis for the German surrender at the end of the war. The Armistice took effect on "the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month" in 1918. America and other nations remember those who died by celebrating Armistice Day (now called Veterans Day) every November 11. Woodrow Wilson was awarded the 1919 Nobel Peace Prize, thanks to his clarity of expression. Why is it important for our leaders to be clear during times of war?

title: How Do I Take Notes While Researching?
text:
If you haven’t already, soon you will need to do some research to write a report, study for a test, or give a presentation.

Keep Track of Information

How will you keep track of all the good information you find while researching? Take notes! Here are some tips for taking research notes:

1. You will probably find that index cards are the best way to take notes. You can write one fact or quotation on each card and then organize and rearrange them based on how you want to write your report, give your presentation, or study for your test.

2. Label your notes with subject headings.

3. Paraphrase and summarize information in your own words. Summarize information by writing the main ideas and most important supporting details. This will help you prevent plagiarism, which is copying writers’ words without giving them credit.

4. If you like how a writer has said something, use a direct quotation. Be sure to record the quote exactly. Include punctuation and spelling just as written by the writer. Put quotation marks around the quote so that you know it is a quotation and not your summary.

5.Write down the title, author, publisher, city of publication, date and page numbers of each source after you have recorded the fact or quotation. This way, you can include this information in a bibliography, and you can go back and double check a quotation if you have questions.

6. Abbreviate the information you have researched to save time. Write in groups of words and phrases instead of complete sentences. Use abbreviations and symbols as long as you will remember what they mean. You can transfer the information into complete sentences later when you use it in your report or presentation.

7. Organize your notes into the most useful order for you, your report or presentation. For example, you can organize them by subject or theme.

Try It!

Do some research on the subject you are currently studying in social studies. Use research notes to record the information you find. Use the research notes to write a report or make a presentation, depending on what your teacher assigns.

Be sure to always take organized research notes when doing any research. It will save you time in the future when you start writing a report.

title: Let's Write
text: Have you been downtown in our biggest city? Do you live near there? Write and tell us about your favorite things to visit in our state’s biggest city! Or, if you haven’t visited yet, write about another city you’ve visited.

title: The Great Tillamook Burn of 1933
text:
On a hot August afternoon, tired loggers had just returned from lunch to finish their tree-cutting work. Engines started up, hoists and tractors roared to life, and everyone began their work. The machines hooked into fallen logs, cut off branches and made the heavy timber ready to move. Loggers scurried over the ground like ants beneath the giant Douglas firs. High above, a length of steel rope was stretched across the trees, winching a log away from its stump. A man on the ground glanced up just in time to see something terrible. The steel rope rubbed against a dead wind-felled tree, and suddenly, there appeared a tiny puff of smoke. "Fire!" he yelled, and everyone came running.

Despite their best efforts, they could not scale the tree or cut it down quickly enough. In seconds, the top of the tree popped into long, lapping flames of fire and instantly ignited the trees nearby. As the flames spread, loggers jumped into their trucks and began to race for safety.

Miles away, the lookout atop a tower on Saddle Mountain suddenly spotted a great cloud of smoke billowing out of Gales Creek Canyon. He grabbed the phone: "Fire!" The date was Aug. 14, 1933.

In minutes, the fire had spread to dozens of trees and then hundreds. A giant cloud of smoke and ash mushroomed over the forest. Within hours, sailors at sea and people in towns all around could see the terrible cloud taking shape.

The beautiful Tillamook Forest was filled with ancient firs—many more than 500 years old, 300 feet high, and spread out across thousands of acres. This was Tillamook County's pride and joy—a lush, thick forest that had stood before Columbus arrived. And now, a wicked fire was killing it at 1,000 acres an hour.

The terrific heat from the fire caused a giant wind to form, pushing and feeding the fire at the same time. The winds grew to hurricane force, ripping trees out by their roots. The column of smoke rose to 40,000 feet, and ash began falling on houses 50 miles away. On the beach, the tide deposited mounds of ash two feet thick.

More than 2,000 men fought the blaze along a 15-mile front, but the fire rushed forward. Camps, houses and fire trucks all fell prey to the flames. At one point, the fire exploded in intensity and burned 10,000 acres an hour, for 20 hours straight. Gradually, the fire burned itself out.

On Aug. 24, a fog blanket drifted in from the coast and finally smothered it. In all, 240,000 acres were burned, twice the destruction from the Mount St. Helens volcano explosion in 1980. Twelve and one-half billion feet of logs were destroyed, enough to meet the timber needs of the entire country for a year. While many of Tillamook's trees still stood, they had been killed. Insects would soon invade to finish the job. Untold numbers of wildlife were killed. Bloated fish floated belly up, and charred birds, grouse, pheasants, squirrels, deer and more lay about.

But that was then. Today, a new forest is growing, thanks to hard work by forest workers and volunteers. But those who saw it will never forget the great Tillamook Burn of 1933.

title: Welcome Home
text:
During the 20s, 30s and 40s, people were thrilled to have such incredible luxuries as indoor plumbing, electric lights, radio and washing machines. Today, our homes have become filled with gadgets that our great-grandparents could never have imagined. Technology has taken over, especially when it comes to our homes.

Many of today's new houses are filled with gadgets that make life more comfortable than ever before. There are showers that come on automatically and adjust to the proper temperature while the homeowner is still getting out of bed. Tubs can be programmed to fill themselves with warm, bubbly water just in time for the lady of the house to arrive home from work. Air conditioners and furnaces can be set to come on half an hour before you get home from school, making the house comfortable to welcome you home.

If you hate the annoying beep of your alarm clock, there is a gadget that will automatically open your blinds to wake you in the morning. Meghan Henning, a spokeswoman for the Consumer Electronics Association, says, "In the morning, instead of setting your alarm, you set the drapes to open so you wake up to natural light and the sound of music playing." What a pleasant way to greet the day!

A lot of the new technology used in today's houses can also be operated by remote control. "You carry this panel about the size of a credit card and you can turn on anything in your kitchen with it," says Henning. Some of the appliances can even be turned on while you are at work or school.

Other popular uses of technology in today's homes include wireless Internet access, sound systems that deliver music of your choice anywhere in the house and home theater rooms that include programmable popcorn makers.

Things have really changed since the 20s, 30s and 40s. Technology is a way of life for families of the 21st century, making today's homes more comfortable than ever before.

title: Oregon During the '20s and '30s
text:
First came the Roaring ‘20s, and then the Great Depression hit.

In our last newspaper, we talked about the first 20 years of the 19th century and the First World War. During the next 20 years, we had two important events occur in our state that you will want to remember. The first we call the Roaring '20s. Afterwards, came the Tillamook fire and then the Great Depression. Ask your grandparents and great-grandparents about these—perhaps they are old enough to remember.

Roaring '20s

The war was over, and Oregon wanted to grow! We had 783,000 people in our state in 1920. Most of these had settled west of the Cascades. Our number of farms stood at 50,200. Lumber was still our No. 1 industry. In 1923, we produced 13 percent of the nation's softwood timber. We had 14 new national forests, and we ranked first in the nation for timber land and second in lumber production. But without a war, the country didn't need ships. In a short time, our shipyards nearly collapsed. We had fewer than 1,000 workers in the shipyards by 1921, and about 150 vessels that were on order were suddenly canceled. Employment in Oregon dropped 31 percent — a third of our workers lost their jobs. The price for lumber was cut in half, and 7,000 Oregon lumberjacks were laid off. And wheat prices were slashed. These were hard times for everyone. In fact, right when these hard times hit, 50,000 native Oregonians moved out to find better jobs elsewhere. Ten years later, our birth rate was the lowest in the country. And just when things looked bad, disaster struck!

The Great Depression

In 1929, a panic spread across America. People who gave money to companies to help them grow wanted their money back. Most companies couldn't give the money back, and thousands of companies began to die and go out of business. They had to lay off workers, close their doors and sell off their land and equipment to pay back the loans. It was a terrible time. In Oregon, thousands lost their jobs. It was common to see long lines of people waiting just to get food so that they wouldn't starve. Wheat that sold for $2.04 a bushel during the war was selling for 34 cents a bushel. Lumber prices were slashed by two-thirds. Farmers couldn't afford to keep up with their orchards and pulled up their apple and prune trees and burned them for fuel.

For 10 long years, people suffered. Everything became cheap, but no one had money or jobs to buy things. Many poor people wore rags and ate very little. Some labor unions (organized workers) tried to go on strike, but that only made things worse. By 1933, one-fifth of our state was getting welfare help just to stay alive.

The federal government finally stepped in to help. It gave enough money to give thousands of Oregon workers a job. In 1935, approval was given to start the Grand Coulee Dam. The Bonneville Dam would be finished in 1937. By the end of the 1930s, people began to make a little money, and recovery seemed just around the corner. But the world wouldn't settle for recovery. The world was about to break out in war, again. And for us, that meant more jobs.

title: Tillamook County
text:
Tillamook County is in northwestern Oregon and enjoys a 75-mile stretch of coastline. It was established Dec. 15, 1853. About 88 inches of rain keep the forests watered each year, and it never gets too hot or too cold during the year. Even though they had the terrible forest fire of 1933, and another big fire in the 1940s, residents still have plenty of forest and land to work. Agriculture and forestry are major employers in the county. The timber industry is coming back, thanks to so many years of effort to replant all the timber lost in the Tillamook fire.

Other people are employed in recreation and fishing. One great thing to do when you visit the city of Tillamook (the county seat) is to see the creamery. Tillamook is famous for its Tillamook cheese and cottage cheese. Other events include the Tillamook County Fair and the June Dairy Festival and Rodeo. Four bays and nine rivers offer plenty for the outdoors adventurer.

title: How Does a Plane Fly?
text: This puzzle is answered in the shape of the wing. Notice that bird and plane wings are curved on top and flat on the underside. When a wing moves through the air, the air passing over the top is thinned out, but the bottom air isn't. What happens? The more dense (thicker) bottom air wants to push up, and that's exactly what happens! Prove it yourself by holding a thin strip of paper close to your lips and blow across the TOP (not underneath) of the paper. Does the paper rise up? Yes! That's how wings work. The propeller or engine gets the wings moving through the air fast enough until this bottom air is pushing strong enough to lift the aircraft, and off you go!

title: Peregrine Falcon
text: One of the fastest birds in the sky is the peregrine falcon. The peregrine has mastered the use of wings and speed better than most other birds. It will dive and strike in mid-air, killing its prey with a blow at speeds of more than 200 miles an hour. These medium-sized hawks have long pointed wings that are dark blue-gray, with pale undersides. The word peregrine means "foreigner" or "traveler." It probably has this name because it migrates to warmer climates in winter and feeds throughout its journey on other birds. They are about the size of crows, with wingspans of 40 inches. The females are larger than the males. Peregrines love to live along coastlines, mountain ranges and river valleys. They don't like stick nests and make their nests in gravel or in the side of a cliff. That's why sometimes they'll make a nest on a ledge of a skyscraper, tall tower or bridge. Peregrines are endangered because they ate so many other birds that had consumed pesticides (mostly DDT). The DDT made peregrine egg shells too soft, and babies couldn't develop. If someone points out a nesting peregrine, stay far away! We must help peregrines regain their place in the world.

title: Agility of Mind: Teddy Roosevelt Wins Nobel Peace Prize
text:
agile (adjective) :able to move quickly and easily; ex.: as agile as a monkey, an agile mind.

Teddy Roosevelt was president of the United States from 1901 to 1909. He was also a great hunter, explorer, author, outdoorsman and soldier.

As a child Teddy was often sick and could not play sports. But he became a good problem solver. He wasn't afraid to put his thoughts into action or think of different solutions. If his first idea didn't work, he had the mental agility to change his mind quickly.

When Roosevelt was president, Japan and Russia were at war. He invited diplomats (official representatives) from Russia and Japan to Portsmouth, New Hampshire to talk about peace. At first, he didn't know how their problems could be solved but he acted quickly to get the diplomats together. He helped them compromise. After a lot of discussion, they worked out their differences and signed the Portsmouth Peace Treaty, an agreement that ended the war and saved many lives. President Roosevelt won the Nobel Peace Prize for helping end the war. His way of helping others solve problems is still used today.

Teddy Roosevelt had an important power skill—an agile mind. You can use this power skill when you act on your good ideas. Remember that an idea can be good without being perfect. People with agile minds often fail before they succeed. The ability to think on your feet, or think while doing, can help you find solutions that will benefit others.

title: What are Homophones and Homographs?
text:
Homophones and homographs are the same but different! To find out the meaning of a word, carefully read the words and sentences surrounding it.

Homophones

Homophones are words that sound the same but have different spellings and different meanings. You can remember what a homophone is by remembering that a phone makes a sound, so a homophone sounds the same as another word.

It is important to know a homophone when you write it. If you need help with a homophone when you read or write, look it up in a dictionary. This will help you keep from making mistakes. For instance, would you write you have “bear hands” or “bare hands”?

Here are some common homophones:

Beat, beet

Earn, urn

Eye, I

Heal, heel, he’ll

Made, maid

Plain, plane

Rain, reign, rein

To, too, two

Homographs

These are words that are spelled the same but have different meanings. Sometimes they are pronounced differently even though they are spelled the same. You can remember what a homograph is by remembering that a graph is something you look at, so a homograph looks the same.

Here are some common homographs that are pronounced differently and have different meanings:

Bass: a low voice or Bass: a fish

Content: things found inside or Content: satisfied

Minute: 60 seconds or Minute: tiny

Try It!

The next time you are not sure which homophone or homograph to use, be sure you know the meaning of the word you are trying to use. This will help you spell it correctly. A dictionary will help you a lot!

title: Let's Write
text: Some of our biggest trees are hundreds of years old, and more. Pretend you are an old Douglas-fir that has been standing a thousand years. Describe some of the history you have seen. What things did you watch? Was there a fire you survived? How many groups of people camped beneath your branches? Did you endure some very hard winters? Was there a solar eclipse? Were you the home for some little animals or birds? Did children climb your branches? What have you seen in a thousand years?

title: Language Arts Connection
text: As you read this week’s lesson, use any color to circle or highlight all of the conjunctions.

title: That Terrible Day in December!
text:
December 7, 1941, was another sleepy Sunday morning in Oregon. The newspaper delivery trucks were completing their rounds, dropping off bundles to young delivery boys and girls who were waiting with their bicycles. The milk trucks were finishing their rounds, leaving ice-cold milk in boxes on front porches. A few early risers might have stepped into the early darkness to enjoy the crisp, damp air of the coming winter.

Far away to the west, a completely different morning was breaking over Hawaii. From far at sea, low to the horizon, a strange formation had gathered in the morning sky. As it approached, people watched from a distance. What were so many planes doing in the air at this time of day? Was it some exercise? Suddenly, it became very clear what the planes were doing. It was an attack!

Pearl Harbor in Hawaii was the home of America's largest naval base on the Pacific. The 100 planes that attacked that morning were all from Japan. The Japanese had declared war on America and came to destroy all of our biggest ships that were parked in the harbor.

Immediately, the alarms sounded all over Hawaii, and the cry went out, "Pearl Harbor is under attack!"

Japanese fighting planes, torpedo bombers and dive bombers took only 1 hour and 55 minutes to empty their bombs and bullets. When it was over, five of our eight battleships were sunk and the other three damaged. (Three were later repaired and went to war.) Five other ships were sunk and several damaged. About 325 of our planes on the ground were destroyed. Among the dead were 2,343 American sailors, soldiers and Marines; 1,272 were wounded, and 960 were missing. Many of the docks, repair facilities, hangars and runways were damaged or destroyed.

When word of the attack reached Oregon, people began to panic, especially in our western cities. Instead of a day of rest, Sunday became a dark day of worry. Would the Japanese continue their attack along the Pacific Coast? Would they bomb naval and aircraft facilities in our area? No one knew what to expect.

In that spirit of panic, people turned against their Japanese neighbors. There were 14,000 Japanese in Oregon, most of them living west of the Cascades. People suddenly viewed their Japanese neighbors and friends as enemies and called for these American citizens to be moved away simply because they were of Japanese descent. By March of the following year, more than 13,000 had been moved out of the state to Idaho or California. Their homes and lands were all sold. Other states did the same thing. After the war, two-thirds of the Japanese returned to Oregon, and some received money for the homes and land that were taken from them.

After this first blow to the United States in Hawaii, our whole country began preparing for all-out combat. And here in Oregon, we were right in the middle of it all.

title: Sally Ride Leaves a Legacy
text:
America lost a hero in 2012 when astronaut Sally Ride died. She was born in 1951 in California. She played tennis and loved science and English literature classes. Ride studied physics, which is the science of matter and energy. Her journey to space began when she applied to a NASA program for astronauts. She was one of the 35 people chosen from over 8,000 applications! Ride worked hard in the training program and helped design the robotic arm on the space shuttle. Her 1983 mission on the space shuttle Challenger launched her into space and into the history books. Sally Ride was the first American woman to fly in space!

Ride flew into space again on a mission in 1984. She worked on the investigations into the space shuttle tragedies of 1986 and 2003. Sally Ride was also an educator. Ride saw that as girls got older, they lost interest in science and math classes. She wrote children's books and started a company that provides exciting science materials to schools. Ride was proud to be a role model for girls who wanted to be astronauts and scientists.

When Ride began her space career, most of the other astronauts and engineers were men. When asked about being one of the few women in this profession, she said, "I never ran into a teacher or a counselor who told me that science was for boys." Thanks to Sally Ride, both boys and girls know that they can reach for the stars!

title: Oregon Helps Win the War
text:
As America prepared to fight World War II, Oregon was called upon to provide a great deal of help— mostly food.

The soldiers fighting in the war left Oregon's farms empty; our vast, rich resources for food production needed workers. About 900,000 people were put to work on Oregon farms, fisheries and orchards. These workers were of all ages, including youth and women, soldiers, white-collar professionals, displaced Japanese Americans, returning war veterans, workers from other states, migrant workers from Mexico and Jamaica, and even German prisoners of war.

Women

Most women were put on daytime schedules so that they could be at home during the evening hours to tend their families. So-called "Housewife Specials" (buses) picked up women and delivered them to farms where help was desperately needed. They weeded, hoed, thinned and harvested all kinds of crops. Some women worked all year on dairy and poultry farms. The women dairy workers began their morning with a 4:00 a.m. milking of cows and ended the day the same way, 14 hours later. Other women tried to interest more women to help, or they supervised youth groups. Nearly 135,000 Oregon ladies went to work during 1943-1947.

Prisoners of War

When U.S. troops captured enemy soldiers, we put them to work instead of locking them up in prisons. From 1944 to 1946, we had 3,500 captured prisoners from Germany working on Oregon farms. In Malheur County, they planted and harvested 7,500 acres of potatoes, 3,500 acres of onions and 3,000 acres of lettuce. In Jackson County, they harvested almost a half million bushels of pears and 3.8 million pounds of hops in the Willamette Valley. They also harvested 1.5 million pounds of pole snap beans in Marion, Polk and Yamhill Counties. When the war ended, everyone was released and sent home.

Japanese Americans

Many Japanese Americans were forced from their homes and jobs at the beginning of the war and moved inland away from the coast. Even though most farmers didn't want their help, about 1,000 were put to work in Malheur County's beet and onion fields.

Youth

Youth 11 to 17 years of age became one of the largest single group of workers in the state. The 270,000 youth were extremely valuable in harvesting fields that otherwise would have gone to waste. Sometimes, schools would close during harvest time so that students could help. They were allowed to put in six-hour days.

Mexican Nationals

About 15,000 Mexican nationals were used as "shock troops"– that is, they were moved from place to place where emergency help was needed. They were very efficient (organized) workers, could be called on anytime, including Sundays, and could be quickly transferred to any place in the state. Even though they were good workers, they had problems with poor living conditions, too few interpreters who spoke Spanish, and unfair payment problems. And when Oregon citizens were released from their war-industry work, a Mexican worker would be fired so that the Oregon person could have a job. This unfair practice caused some unrest.

Others

Just about everyone was helping raise food during the war. When harvest time came, businesses would shut down and all the employees would head for the fields. Teachers spent their summers at the farms, businessmen and women worked after dinner, soldiers passing through or on leave stopped by to help. Even inmates from our state prison in Salem were sent to the farms. People who refused to fight in the war were even sent to farm in Tillamook and Coos Counties to help out.

Oregonians

The largest of all the groups were Oregon citizens. Our parents, grandparents and great-grandparents left their regular jobs during the summer months and worked hard to make the farms productive. When the harvest ended, they returned to the regular jobs– many went back to the forests to continue cutting trees.

While the farm work continued, our factories helped in other ways, producing flax, sand, steel castings, engines, landing gear for large B-29s (airplanes), crystals for radiophones, steam locomotives and more.

title: Malheur County
text:
Malheur County was an important farming area during World War II. Many fields were planted with potatoes, onions, beets, lettuce and other vegetables to support the war effort. The county first became popular in 1863 when someone discovered gold. Many hopeful miners settled in the area, and farms and ranches were started. Sheep raising became another large project in the county. The name "Malheur" comes from explorer Peter Skeen Ogden's journal entry. He named the main river "Riviere au Malheur," meaning "unfortunate river," because he lost many goods that were stolen nearby. Malheur County is Oregon's second largest county with 9,874 square miles of great farm and pasture land. It was established as a county in February 1887. Vale is the county seat, and two other major cities are Ontario and Nyssa. The main industries are agriculture, livestock, food processing and tourism. If you become a tourist in Malheur County, bring your hiking shoes and a keen eye– there is a great deal of beauty to explore here.

During the war, many women filled the men’s places in the factories and on the farms in Malheur county. A common term, “Rosie the Riveter,” was used to describe the women workers.

title: Who is Uncle Sam?
text: Ever since the War of 1812, Americans have looked to Uncle Sam as a symbol for the United States. Uncle Sam is a real person from Massachusetts named Samuel Wilson. He fought in the Revolutionary War. People who liked him, both family and businesspeople, called him "Uncle Sam." In the War of 1812, his meat-packing business provided troops with pork and beef. He marked his boxes with a "U.S.," meaning "United States," but some thought that it meant "Uncle Sam." People soon applied this term to ANYTHING supplied by the federal government. The image we identify as Uncle Sam evolved over the next 150 years.

title: Honeybees
text: It's hard to believe, but spring is just around the corner. With each warming day, you might notice a few bees flying around. Where do they come from, and why are they out while it's still cold? A beehive is usually only two or three miles away from a bee you might see, and as soon as it gets in the 40s, thousands of bees leave the hive to look for nectar. Honeybees are amazing insects. They are organized, hardworking and very efficient. In the winter, they huddle in their beehives in a great big ball of 20,000-30,000 bees. In the middle of this mass is the queen, staying nice and warm. During winter, they eat honey, and on the coldest nights, some of the bees on the outside of this ball will freeze. As the weather warms up, the hive becomes active. Worker bees clean out the dead bees and scrub the honeycomb clean, and the queen starts laying eggs. Workers go out looking for early blossoms. Nearly all the bees are female. They keep five to 10 drones (males) around just in case the queen is killed. If so, they feed a special royal jelly to a newly laid egg and grow a new queen. As bees gather nectar, they also spread plants' pollen. This keeps all vegetation healthy and producing fruits. If you see a bee, don't be scared. Be respectful. This is one hardworking insect!

title: Dimensional Graphics
text:
To make dimensional graphic designs, begin by making a square, any size. The basic idea is not as difficult as it looks. It is simply a matter of drawing each line so it misses the oncoming corner. The closer together the lines, the better the results.

Materials

paper

pen or pencil

ruler

tape or glue

crayons or markers

Directions

1. Start in a corner and use your ruler to draw the line to the next corner but miss it by a little bit.

2.Next, ricochet, or bounce, off that corner and go to the next and miss it by a little bit.

3.Continue doing the ricochet thing to the next corner, and after a great deal of going in a circle, you'll begin to see a pattern develop.

Extra Activity

After you do one design in a clockwise manner, try doing one with a counterclockwise pattern. Then put the two together. These patterns can be arranged and rearranged to make a number of fascinating designs. When color is added - wow!

title: What are Idioms?
text:
Have you ever heard an adult say, “I’m sorry, but we’re up a creek on this one”? What did he mean? He was standing on dry ground when he said it! Well, you’ve just heard an idiom.

Idioms are Not Meant to Be Taken Literally

Idioms are sayings that mean something different from the literal meaning of their words. “Literal” means “following the exact wording.” But idioms are not literal, so the words do not mean exactly what they say. Listen carefully for clues to figure out an idiom.

Try It!

The best way to learn what an idiom means is to learn it and use it in your own speech or writing. Ask someone what it means. Then use it in your own writing. Here are some idioms in sentences. See if you can figure out what they mean. Once you know what the idiom means, use it in your own sentence.

They were both so shy they had a hard time breaking the ice. Use “breaking the ice” in your own sentence.

When it comes to modesty in dress, I have to draw the line somewhere. Use “draw the line” in your own sentence.

By halftime, the game was in the bag. Use “in the bag” in your own sentence.

Chris and I are in the same boat because neither of us have extra cash to spend on the field trip. Use “in the same boat” in your own sentence.

Would someone lend me a hand with the dishes? Use “lend me a hand” in your own sentence.

title: Let's Write
text: We have learned about all the men and women who have fought for our country. Many died or came home wounded. Every day, you probably meet a war veteran, but you just don’t realize it. Write a letter to a World War II veteran thanking him or her for the great contribution to our country. Ask questions, and perhaps you’ll even receive an answer. Work with your local VFW organization to connect with veterans.

title: Welcome to the Future!
text:
The years since WWII make up our state’s Modern Period. During the Modern Period, Oregon has stretched, grown, enlarged and shrunk in ways our forefathers could never have imagined.

Most of our citizens live in Portland, Eugene and Salem. Salem is our state capital and a leading food processing city for the entire country. Here is something really strange: Nearly all of our cities and towns east of the Cascades are built in places where the land is irrigated (thanks to the dams). Does that mean if there were no dams, there would be no cities? Let’s hope not!

It didn’t take long for the world to notice all of our trees! Since 1938, Oregon has been the leading softwood producer in America, and we have shipped a great deal around the world. About half our state is covered in forests. After World War II, we had more than 1,300 lumber mills. During the Modern Period, that number has continued to shrink. But travel anywhere in America, and at the local building supply store you will see plenty of Oregon wood!

Many of our small towns provide jobs in the timber, farming and fishing industries. Their horizons don’t include tall buildings but hundreds of grain elevators, something we jokingly call prairie skyscrapers! And an abundance of food processing plants are nearby to handle the harvests. How do all these people stay connected? With 96,000 miles of roads with 2,700 bridges.

So, how does the rest of America see Oregon? We think everyone might be a little jealous of all that we have here! Oregon is the top grower of Christmas trees, and we’re in the top five states in producing many types of berries, onions, grass seed and mint. Do some research and find out what else we grow that’s number one! We’ve made our mark on the world. Don’t you think Lewis and Clark would be surprised?

It’s no wonder people love coming here. In fact, tourism is now a major part of our economy. Some people even visit, and then decide they want to stay! Do you know someone who is new to our state? Ask them why they moved to Oregon.

We can fly you, drive you, boat you and ski you to all kinds of destinations. We will educate you, train you, give you culture, give you religion and give you a taste of the entire world without leaving your own city borders. If you get sick, we can give you the world’s best treatment. We’ll employ you, entertain you and give you all kinds of things on which you can spend your money. If you’re out of money, we’ll help you find a job, or if hard times remain, we will help you until you get back on your feet. Is there anything we don’t have or can’t do in our state? We doubt it!

title: Wasco County
text: Wasco County was established in 1854 and was at the time the largest county in the entire United States! It included 130,000 square miles and was named after a tribe of Chinook Indians who lived near The Dalles. This big piece of land stretched from the Cascades to the Rocky Mountains, including parts of Idaho, Montana and Wyoming. It has been trimmed down to 2,396 square miles, and The Dalles is the county seat. Much of the county’s development came thanks to the Oregon Trail. This county was a crossroad for much transportation in Oregon. Those who wanted to go around Mount Hood would turn south, and those who wanted to continue along the Columbia River kept on straight ahead. Today, this great crescent bend in the Columbia along the northern border of Wasco County is popular for whitewater rafting, fishing and windsurfing. People who live in Wasco County have many orchards, wheat farms and livestock. They also enjoy a nice tourism trade. If you travel through Wasco, bring your swim trunks, a windsurf board and sunblock–you'll need it!

title: Trash to Treasure
text:
Cateura, Paraguay, is a city built on top of a landfill. This means that the people of the community actually live on garbage. The daily dumping of trash is swarmed over and picked through for objects to salvage and sell. The people who live here may be some of the poorest of the poor, but hope still remains.

A visionary music teacher teamed up with locals to create instruments from the trash. He wanted to provide the instruments for children that lived in the slum. They used oil drums to create violins, water pipes and spoons to build flutes and even packing crates to make guitars.

Soon, the Recycled Orchestra project was formed. Today, children from the area have an alternative to the drugs and gangs that are in their environment. These instruments have given them the chance to learn, perform and even travel the world. It is an inspirational story that reminds us that one person’s trash really can be another’s treasure.

For more information about the Recycled Orchestra, and to see a performance, please visit www.mim.org

title: The Modern Period
text:
After World War II, our state started growing, and growing, and growing! Here are some of the big changes.

Laws

For a long time, some people were not allowed to enter public buildings because of their race or national origin. In 1953, we passed a new civil rights law that made access fair to everyone. For some kinds of work, women were not being paid the same as men doing the same job. In 1955, we passed a law so that everyone received the same pay for the same work.

Landscape

Our landscape keeps changing. If it isn’t a new building, road or community, it’s a volcano! Our active volcanoes lie on the ocean floor. Some of them are rumbling and grumbling about 200 miles off the Oregon coast. Mount St. Helens has also affected our landscape.

Agriculture

We have around 40,000 farms and 16 million acres of farmland. Our hens lay over 700 million eggs in a year. We grow around 2 billion pounds of potatoes a year, making us one of the top states for this crop. Our wheat harvest is usually strong as well. Winter wheat grows well in Oregon, producing millions of bushels a year. What about the flowers and trees we plant to make our yards beautiful? Yes, many of those are grown here too!

Electricity

Since 1920, more than 40 power dams have been constructed on the Columbia. Have you visited one? It’s worth doing—they are fantastic structures to see. With all of this inexpensive electricity, we do many great things. But don’t forget to turn off the lights when you leave the room!

Population

Oregon’s population is around 4 million people. In recent years, our state has been growing by about one percent each year. When babies are born, our population grows. When people die, our population shrinks. Lately, there have been more births than deaths. In addition, more people have been moving into our state than have been moving out of our state. So, we’ve been growing! Check out the U.S. Census Bureau’s website. See how Oregon compares to other states in population and growth.

Shipping

We can’t say enough about our good harbors. Oregon has 23 ports, and we ship millions of tons of goods out each year. Portland is one of the busiest ports in the whole world! A port is where ships dock. Have you visited a port this year?

title: Opportunity Cost
text:
Let’s say you’re at the store with some birthday money. You have enough money to buy either a video game or sports equipment, but not both. Every time you have a choice to make, you have an opportunity cost too. You can think of it as an opportunity that you decide to give up. The cost of making the decision is to give up an opportunity. If you go to an ice cream store, you must decide what ice cream flavor you want on your cone. Every flavor you don’t choose becomes the opportunity cost. You had the chance to get strawberry, but you chose chocolate instead.

Many times, you have to think about needs and wants when you’re deciding what to buy. Needs like food, clothing and shelter have to be met first! If a family’s monthly budget only has enough left for a house or rent payment, then the opportunity cost is the items they couldn’t buy (like tickets to an amusement park). Think about the end of summer, when it’s time to buy new clothes for school. What might be an opportunity cost in that situation?

Now think about some recent choices you’ve made (at home, school or a store). In the first column, write the two things you had to choose between. Circle the item you chose. In the second column, write whether your choice was a need or a want.

title: How many loaves of bread are in a bushel of wheat?
text: There are about 1 million kernels of wheat in a bushel! This wheat will make 42 pounds of white flour or 60 pounds of whole wheat flour. With the flour, bakers can make about 70 loaves of white bread or 90 loaves of whole wheat bread (one-pound loaves).

title: Wheat
text: Wheat is a grass-type plant. It belongs to the group of grains called cereals and is probably the most important food. Other important cereals are rice, oats, corn, barley and rye. Wheat is better for bread because the kernel has more gluten than other grains. Gluten is a stretchy material that, along with yeast, makes dough rise and become fluffy and edible. Farmers plant about 20 pounds of wheat per acre and harvest more than 4,000 pounds of wheat! The new wheat plants grow best in mild, dry climates. They look like green grass and grow two to five feet tall. They turn golden brown when they are ripe. The leaves are long and slender, and the wheat heads hold 50-150 or more kernels. They also have course prickly hairs called beards. The kernels can be white, red, yellow or purple and are almost 1/4 inch long. Wheat is grown in the winter or spring. In Oregon, our winter crop is mostly common white winter wheat—good for bread, rolls, tortillas and Asian noodles. Our spring crop is mostly soft white wheat—good for flat breads, cakes, pastries, crackers, muffins and snack foods.

title: What is Etymology?
text:
It is History

It might sound like some scientific field or medical study, but etymology is the history of a word. Did you know that words can have histories, too? Where did words come from? Did someone just wake up one day and decide to name things randomly? Most words came about for a reason, and knowing the history of a word can help you understand its meaning.

Word histories can be fascinating. Some root words came from the ancient Greek and Latin languages. Others were borrowed from other languages, such as Spanish, French and German. And new words are added all the time.

For example, the word “kindergarten” means “children’s garden” in German. The term was coined in 1840 by Friedrich Frobel to refer to his method of teaching young children.

Try It!

Below are some words and where they came from. Do some research and find out what each word originally meant, why it was invented and how its meaning has changed. Your community library should have an etymology dictionary, often called an Oxford English Dictionary. And you can find information on the Internet as well. One good site is http://www.etymonline.com/.

Here is an example of what a passage might look like in an etymology resource:

Algebra— From Arabia

Route— From France

Zero— From Arabia

Bronco— From Mexico

Gorilla— From Africa

title: The Constitution - Mightier Than the Sword!
text:
Have you heard someone say, "The pen is mightier than the sword"? This means that things written down on a piece of paper can be more powerful than a person swinging a sharp sword. How can this be? Written words are easily more powerful than a sword. For example, a treaty can stop armies from fighting; a law can stop us from hurting others; and a newspaper can help people find ways to solve problems without fighting.

A perfect example of this is a document called a constitution. A constitution is a body of laws that everyone agrees we should obey. Our country has a Constitution, and our state has a constitution, and both protect our rights. What rights might those be? Here are some examples from our U.S. Constitution:

Right to Privacy (Fourth Amendment)– Can people walk into your house and start snooping through your closets and drawers, taking things, just because they feel like it? Our Constitution says "No!" because we all enjoy the right to privacy. Students in some states are forced to take drug tests to see if they are using drugs. Do you think this is a violation of the right to privacy? Do you think it is helpful in fighting the drug problems?

Freedom of Speech (First Amendment)– Can you say anything you want? Matt Fraser, a student in Washington, gave a talk at a school assembly using indecent language, causing the audience to hoot and holler. Angry teachers suspended him from school. Matt went to court saying the teachers violated his right to free speech. Was Matt right or wrong? The Supreme Court said that Matt was wrong because free speech is protected only when the words don't hurt other people. A school, the court said, is a protected place where students, teachers and parents can expect protection from disruptive language.

Freedom of Religion (First Amendment)– Do you go to church or participate in a religious belief? If you do, you are free to practice any part of your religion as long as it doesn't hurt other people. If you don't practice a religion, no one can force you to join a church or practice a religious observance.

Innocent Until Proven Guilty (Sixth Amendment)– In our country, a person can't be put in prison unless someone can prove the person is guilty of a crime. In other countries, people are sometimes thrown in jail and kept there until they can prove they are innocent. What do you think about this right?

Right to Bear Arms (Second Amendment)– In early America, England tried to take the guns from colonists as a way of keeping control over the people. (Such things continue in other countries even today!) When our Constitution was written, the right to keep a weapon by individuals was protected. Today, some people think that this right refers only to a local militia or National Guard. Others want to ban guns, hoping that will reduce crime. What do you think?

Our U.S. and state constitutions protect many rights. They also provide a way to make new laws as we need them. Turn to pages 2-3 and learn more about it!

title: Our Constitution
text:
Our state constitution is a document that describes the basic laws, organization, and character of our government. It lays out a government where "we, the people," rule and "we, the people," have certain basic rights.

Our Three-Headed Eagle

Our state constitution is patterned after the national Constitution, which uses three branches of government. We are depicting this unique and dynamic form of government using a three-headed eagle. Each of these three branches of government has a special job to do as you can see here. Each branch also checks on each other to ensure that we have a balanced government that lives by the laws of the Constitution.

The Executive Branch

This branch consists of the governor, attorney general, and Secretary of State. These men and women have the power to enforce the laws made by the legislature. Judges, the police, and National Guard help them do this.

The Legislative Branch

This branch is called the state legislature. It makes up the laws or rules for us to follow. There are two parts to the legislature: the House of Representatives and the Senate. These men and women are chosen by the people of our state to represent them in making the laws.

The Judicial Branch

These men and women make up the Supreme Court of our state. They decide if the laws made by the legislature are constitutional. They also decide what punishment a person should receive for breaking the law.

These three branches of government work together as we govern ourselves.

The American Way of Life! Here are some of the rights we enjoy because of our state and federal constitutions. How many of these are important to you?

Right to worship God in your own way

Right to free speech and free press (newspapers)

Right to gather in groups (assemble)

Right to ask for problems to be solved (The government must remain willing to fix problems.)

Right to privacy in your home

Right to no excessive bail (That means if you are jailed, the money paid to get out must match the crime.)

Right to trial by jury

Right to always be innocent until proven guilty

Right to freely move about the country and world (You are not trapped here!)

Right to own private property

Right to free elections and secret ballots

Right to work at any job, committee or group you choose

Right to go on strike and bargain with employers and employees

Right to go into business and make some money

Right to bargain for goods and services in a free market

Right to make contracts with people (The government can't undo contracts, if legally made.)

Right to ask the government to serve and protect us and referee our problems (military, police and agencies)

Right to one law for all (The government can't make a law just for you - laws must apply fairly to everyone.)

Something to Celebrate!

After reading the rights that are guaranteed to all U.S. citizens by both the U.S. Constitution and our own state constitution, list below some of the responsibilities you have as a citizen to maintain those rights.

title: Oregon's State Capitol Building
text: Did you know that our state capitol building has changed four times? In 1855, the brand new Statehouse was destroyed by fire. Local government moved to a nearby building in Salem and stayed there for 17 years until a new building was finished. The new Statehouse was patterned after the U.S. Capitol Building in Washington, D.C. But guess what happened in 1935? Another fire burned it down. Not to be discouraged, another was built and dedicated in 1938. The current four-story building is faced with beautiful marble on the outside and polished rose travertine (a beautiful marble-like stone) on the inside. The floors and staircases are also marble. In 1977, we expanded our capitol with wings to include more office space. This is where the governor, secretary of state and the state treasurer work. Walk into the rotunda and see the capitol dome 106 feet above. There are 33 stars painted on the ceiling to symbolize Oregon becoming the 33rd state in the Union. Beautiful murals depict major events in our history: Captain Grey discovering the Columbia River, Lewis and Clark, the first woman to cross the continent by wagon (greeted by Dr. John McLoughlin), and the first wagon train migration in 1843. Would you like to visit? The capitol is open Mon.-Fri., 7:30-5:00 and is closed Saturdays and Sundays. Admission is free. There are regular tours of the capitol and the tower. You can get more information and schedule your own tour by calling (503) 986-1388.

title: Where is Our U.S. Constitution?
text: In a bomb shelter? That's right! Our actual U.S. Constitution is behind bulletproof glass in the rotunda of the U.S. Archives in Washington, D.C. Along with the Declaration of Independence and other important documents, our Constitution shares space in a climate controlled container. Each evening, after visitors leave, the container is lowered into a bomb-proof vault for protection. These precious documents are copied and spoken of all over the world, but the originals live part time in a bomb shelter!

title: Chokecherry or Wild Cherry
text:
Early settlers probably first learned that chokecherries can be used as medicine from the Americans Indians. These people used a bark tea for diarrhea and lung ailments. The settlers added the bark in cough medicines. The fruit can be used to make a delicious wild cherry-flavored jam or jelly. The fruit is sour by itself, which is why the cherries are called chokecherries.

Caution: The leaves and cherry pits are poisonous and can cause difficult breathing, loss of balance and convulsions.

title: Governor Kate Brown
text:
Kate Brown has spent over 25 years serving the people who live in Oregon. She was a state representative for five years and was in the state senate for 12 more years. Brown was the first woman to serve as Oregon’s Senate Majority Leader. She also served as Oregon’s Secretary of State. Before she ran for office, Brown worked as a lawyer and helped families and young people. She has spent a lot of time working to help the people in our state.

Brown grew up in Minnesota before going to college at the University of Colorado in Boulder. She decided to study law and chose Oregon’s Lewis and Clark Law School. As a lawyer, Brown worked with the Juvenile Rights Project and helped form the Oregon Women’s Health and Wellness Alliance.

Kate Brown’s work as a lawyer and state politician helped her to become Oregon’s Secretary of State. She made a lot of changes to how Oregon operates. She helped make it easier for active military members and people with disabilities to vote.

As governor, Brown is known for being very active and involved. She can be seen going to a lot of meetings and chatting with everyone she meets on the way. Brown lives in Salem with her husband, Dan Little. When she has spare time, she enjoys horseback riding and hiking.
