title: Famous Oregon Landmarks and Parklands
text:
The school year is about to end. We've had a great deal of fun studying things about our state and the people who have lived here. Now it's time to think about places to go and things to do when summer vacation arrives. Do you have any plans?

In this issue of Oregon Studies Weekly, let's look at places to visit in our beautiful state. You don't have to travel far to have fun. Sometimes, the greatest adventure can be in your own backyard.

What are your goals (tasks you wish to accomplish)? While you are trying to decide, here are some ideas for places to visit and things to do. Jump in and let's have fun!

Mount Hood and Columbia River Gorge

This part of our state can give you breathtaking scenery and a nice change of pace. Start your trip at either end of Highway 84, and get your camera ready! At Crown Point or Rowena Crest, you will see a spectacular view of the Columbia Gorge. Did you pack your windsurfing gear? If not, enjoy watching those who did as they catch wind on the mighty Columbia River.

Beautiful Multnomah Falls and several other waterfalls line the highway. With some, you'll need to stop to get a closer view, but don't get wet.

As you get closer to the famous Mt. Hood, you should stop in at Timberline Lodge, a National Historic Landmark built right on the slopes of the 11,235-foot Mt. Hood, which overlooks Portland. From a high vantage point (lookout point), search out Hood River Valley.

title: Boom to Bust and Back Again
text:
You may have heard people compare the recent economic recession (2007-2009) to the Great Depression of the 1930s. But what some people call the "Great Recession" actually had more in common with a depression in the 1890s and something called "boom and bust."

In the early 1890s, the U.S. economy grew quickly ("boomed") but couldn't keep growing at that rate. When many companies and the housing market failed, there was an economic "bust." The railroad industry had been booming since the end of the Civil War, but in the 1890s more than 150 railroad companies closed. Other industries that depended on the railroads closed, and many people lost their jobs. Over 500 banks closed. Thousands of unemployed men marched to Washington, D.C., in 1894 to demand that the government take action to help families. Unemployment was over 10 percent for most of the 1890s. About one of every ten people had no job.

In the recent recession, the housing market slumped after several "boom" years. Some automakers went out of business and others filed for bankruptcy. The economy went "bust," just as it did in the 1890s. Hundreds of banks and thousands of businesses closed. The unemployment rate was about 8 percent - about one of every twelve people had no job.

Make a chart or Venn diagram that compares these two events in history. (Teachers: You can find background information and activities that relate to this article at hnn.us)

title: Regions With the Most!
text:
How would you like to visit the parts of our state that are the most (highest, hottest, southern, etc.)? If you would, here's a checklist of places to visit. How many have you already visited?

Highest place–Mount Hood at 11,235 feet (Climb to the top of Mt. Hood with a stool, stand atop the stool, and YOU would be the highest place in Oregon!)

Lowest place–The Pacific Coast

Coldest place–Seneca (western part of Grant County), -54 degrees on Feb. 10, 1933

Hottest place–Prineville (western part of Crook County), 119 degrees on July 29, 1898, and 119 degrees in Pendleton (central Umatilla County) on Aug. 10, 1898

Northernmost place–Hammond sits right at the mouth of the Columbia River, even farther north than Astoria!

Southernmost place–Our southern border is a straight line, so nothing is more southern than that - unless you sat in a boat on Goose Lake and drifted into California–and then YOU would be the southernmost part of Oregon!

Easternmost place–The Snake River makes up part of our eastern border. In the northeastern corner, in Wallowa County, our border snakes over toward Idaho just north of Seven Devils Mountains.

Westernmost place–Cape Blanco is a little pointy bump along our southern coast about 50 miles south of Coos Bay. This is our farthest western outpost in the state.

Most intelligent class–Yours, because you read Oregon Studies Weekly!

title: Where Does the Word
text:
Have you noticed in the news lately a great deal of talk about the meeting of our state legislature? These people pass laws for our state.

What does "legislate" mean? Our English language uses a great deal of Latin. For example, the Latin word "legis" means "law." The Latin word "latio" means "to bring." Put them together, and what do you get? "Law to bring," or "bring about laws." What do you think is Latin for "cheesie pizza"? How about "cheezio pancake"? Ok, we're just joking. But who cares as long as the pizza comes steamy, drippy and in great quantity!

title: Oregon's Strangest Creature!
text:
Try to guess this most strange of all creatures.

It walks about on two legs but sometimes all fours. It doesn't hibernate but does prefer to stay in a shelter or den during winter and will feed at any given time. It has a thick, heavy winter coat during the cold seasons that it sheds when spring returns. It doesn't like temperature extremes and is happiest in the warm spring or summer sun. It bears its young in litters of one, sometimes two, and rarely more. It eats both meats and vegetables. It is very crafty and sneaky and is one of the few creatures in Oregon that uses tools. It is not typically nocturnal, although the older species tend to forage for food and seek mates well after darkness has set in. It has assorted skin colors, and the lighter-colored skins tend to darken when exposed to prolonged summer sun. It enjoys water, but doesn't feed from it as much as some carnivores. It lives in communities made up of families and is perhaps the smartest living thing in all of Oregon.

So, just what is this strange creature? It is the mysterious and amazing homo sapien, also known as rug rat, or sugar-slurping, computer-savvy future terror behind the wheel of a suped-up sports car– YOU! ...the most sophisticated wildlife our state has known and hopefully its greatest friend, too.

title: Places to Go and See in Oregon
text:
Treasures on Our Coast

From Astoria to the redwoods near Brookings, our coast is a great place to vacation.

Along the ocean, stand near massive sea stacks, rocks that jut out of the beach like giant shark teeth. Stop by Astoria and visit a replica of Lewis and Clark’s winter outpost back in 1805-1806. Drive a little farther and enjoy a two-mile beachfront at Seaside. Haystack Rock and the Needles are more giant rocks along the coast at Cannon Beach. If you’re ready for lunch, Tillamook is ready for you. Stop by the largest cheese factory in the West.

Lincoln City greets you with beautiful kites. Try one out. The breeze is perfect. At Depoe Bay, you can see the world’s smallest navigable harbor, and at nearby Spouting Horns, you can wait for geysers that shoot streams of water above the sea wall at high tide.

Don’t miss the Oregon Coast Aquarium and the Hatfield Marine Science Center at Yaquina Head near Newport. There is so much to do here–sandy beaches, charter boats for fishing, shops, restaurants and galleries, lighthouses, fresh seafood for lunch, fishing villages, nature trails, ancient forests and beautiful sea life at the water’s edge! It’s way too much for one day!

By the time you reach Florence, things change fast. Now you’re in sand dune (large pile of sand) country, a 47-mile stretch of dunes where you can watch all kinds of birds and go dune riding. Camp, hike and visit quiet lakes, forest trails and mysterious places.

Coos Bay has Oregon’s deepest natural harbor and has always been a major shipping port and fishing spot.

As you continue south, you will stop at more towns with lighthouses, quiet beaches, sea stacks and plenty of things to do. As you approach the California border, get ready for the most amazing trees you’ll ever see. The mighty redwoods remind us just how young and little we really are!

Big-City Life

So, why do they call Portland the "City of Roses"? Stop by the International Rose Test Garden in Washington Park and find out for yourself. There are more than 500 varieties to smell and admire. But beware of thorns!

Portland is a wonderful place to visit and explore. For a city split by a river, it isn’t that hard to get around. There are fantastic parks in Portland, such as the 5,000-acre Forest Park, America’s largest forested park. There’s Mt. Tabor Park, home of an extinct volcano. Find within the city several refuges and rookeries where beavers, bald eagles and herons live. You can take a wildlife tour or go hiking yourself.

Climb aboard the MAX light-rail train and travel just about anywhere–museums, old mansions, fairs, markets, fresh fish, fruit, foods and crafts, from as near as the streams and rivers or from around the world. Or stop at the zoo where animals are so close that you won’t know who is watching whom!

Wildlife Safari!

This is as close as most people will ever come to the wild animals of the jungle or of an African veldt (a wild, open African plain).

The 600-acre Wildlife Safari reserve in Winston is home to hundreds of wild animals that roam free and uncaged. This is Oregon’s only drive-thru park. Here, the animals live much as they would in their natural habitat.

You don’t have to sit in the car the whole time you’re visiting–visit the petting zoo, the restaurant, gift shop and theater, ride a train; or take a trek on a real camel! Animal shows, exhibits, films and so much more make this a great vacation spot this summer.

Other Popular Stops in Oregon

Our state has so many wonderful places to visit and explore that we just can’t list them all. But don’t forget to visit our amazing Crater Lake (which was formed when a volcano blew its top), or the deepest gorge in North America at 8,000 feet called Hells Canyon, or Willamette Valley with dozens of covered bridges, waterfalls, rivers, rich farmlands and orchards, holly and Christmas trees, and all kinds of nuts and fruits. All over our state, you’ll find water recreation and sites, forests, beaches, animals, hiking and swimming.

Is there anything we don’t have in our state? Probably not. You just need to go traveling and find it. And above all, don’t forget your camera!

title: How Do I Listen to an Oral Presentation?
text:
Listen closely to your classmates when they give presentations. Pay attention. You can learn a lot from them. Your teacher may tell you to take notes. You may also be asked to make written comments. Also, it’s just plain polite to be a good listener!

1. Be an active listener. Don’t daydream. Focus on the speaker’s main idea.

Listen for the way he or she ties details to that main idea. Take notes, either in your mind or on paper.

2. Your teacher may help you to evaluate (to examine and judge carefully) your classmates’ presentations.

Keep in mind that being honest can help your classmates learn how to give better presentations.

3. You may not agree with everything the speaker says, but you should listen to his or her ideas.

4. Don’t interrupt your classmate unless he or she has asked for you to join in.

5. Think about the speaker’s conclusion. Is it logical?

Try It!

When your classmates give presentations, be a good listener. It will help them feel more comfortable. Make eye contact. Your evaluation will help them improve their future presentations. And you might learn something. Besides, you will want them to listen to you when it is your turn to give an oral presentation.

title: Who were the first Americans to establish a permanent settlement in Oregon?
text: The first Americans to establish a permanent settlement in Oregon were Methodist missionaries. In 1834, they– including Jason Lee– established Willamette Valley along with Methodist missions (churches or congregations that depend on support from larger religious organizations) in western Oregon. In nearly 10 years, by 1843, thousands of American pioneers were migrating west on the Oregon Trail. It began in Independence, Missouri, and ended in Oregon City. Through the very long journey, the pioneers traveled more than 2,000 miles of prairie, desert and mountains. The Methodists were quickly trying to expand their missions to keep up with the amount of pioneers coming to Oregon.

title: Alligator Lizard
text:
When you think of a lizard, you probably think of a little four- or five-inch lizard that zips around between rocks. But did you know that Oregon has a lizard that would dwarf those others?

The Oregon alligator lizards can grow up to 12 inches in length if they keep their first tails. They easily lose their tails when predators or people grab them. The tails will grow back, but they will not be as long as before. They are usually a light- or medium-brown color with spots or bars on the back.

All of these lizards have a fold of skin along the lower sides, where the scales of the belly meet the scales of the back. When the lizard breathes in, or eats a big meal, the folds expand.

The alligator lizard got its name because it looks like a small alligator, it can swim well, and it has a very bad bite. Sometimes, they even bite and twist their bodies at the same time, much as alligators do. They eat small invertebrates (lacking a backbone or spinal column), including spiders.

title: Critical Analysis and Rumination: President Truman and The Atomic Bomb Decision
text:
rumination (noun): the act of giving serious thought and consideration to something

Adolf Hitler was defeated in May 1945 after years of war in Europe, and American troops would be coming home–wouldn't they? Victory in Europe meant that some U.S. soldiers would be returning home. Others would go to the Pacific to face Japanese armies. Scientists in the U.S. had made a weapon that could certainly end the war with Japan, but it was so powerful that tens of thousands of people would be killed, including civilians (citizens not in the military). President Harry Truman had a decision to make that would greatly affect the world. What would the commander in chief do?

In the years leading up to President Truman's decision, the Japanese had been a brutal enemy. They had killed thousands of Americans at sea and on Pacific islands, including the surprise attack on Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The president wondered how many more lives would be lost if we tried to end the war without the atomic bomb. What would happen if another country improved the weapon and used the bomb before we did? Would they use it on us?

President Truman tried several times without success to work out surrender with Japan. He then ordered atomic bombs to be dropped on the cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945. Within a week of the second attack, Japan did surrender, which put an end to World War II. Historians estimate that between 150,000 and 240,000 Japanese were killed from effects of the two bombings. They also estimate that thousands of American lives were saved. Do you think President Truman made the right decision?

title: History Continues to Happen
text:
History goes back to way before any of us were born. From the very beginning of time, history has been happening, and it continues today. Many different events have happened in the past, and many more will happen in the future, all of which are very important to the creation and well-being of Oregon and America.

History is something that is looked back upon and remembered. It can be very helpful to us, but it can also bring back painful memories. But no matter what it makes people remember, it is important to us as a whole, especially those people who have helped make history.

If you think about it, authors can be historical figures too! Authors write books that inspire, encourage and entertain the people who read them. One modern-day author is Molly Gloss. She lives in Portland. She writes historical fiction set in Oregon, as well as science fiction. One of her novels for young readers is “Outside the Gates.” Readers say that Gloss is a great author. She has the awards to prove it! See if her books are in your school library.

Francis Pettygrove and Asa Lovejoy were a couple of men who made a very important decision about Oregon, although they did not agree on it.

Francis came from Portland, Maine, in 1842 with his sister, Mary, and her husband. Mary brought a lilac start that survived the trip and is still growing today in Eagle Creek. Before Francis came, William Johnson had already settled in Portland. He had no intent of starting a city when he moved to Johnson Creek to start a sawmill. In 1843, Asa pulled his canoe out of the Willamette along with William Overton, who claimed land in the name of Lovejoy. Overton took half of his claim on the land and sold it to Francis, who had been running a country store.

In 1845, Francis and Ava both were in the new city, but both men wanted to name it after their hometowns. They decided to do it the easy way and flipped a coin. Francis won the flip and named the city Portland instead of New Boston, which Ava wanted to name it.

People like Molly, Francis, and Ava are why the state of Oregon is very great. They also helped make America the great country that it is today. If you would like to read about more people who have helped make Oregon what it is today, turn the page!

title: Smithsonian Dinosaurs Take a Break
text:
How do you move 10,000 dinosaur bones? Very carefully. The world-famous National Fossil Hall at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History is undergoing a huge renovation. In order to make the exhibition even better, workers took apart the collection piece by piece. The hall will be closed during renovation, but some dinosaur artifacts will be moved to other locations in the museum.

While the exhibition hall is being updated (it opened in 1910), paleontologists will be studying the dinosaur bones. They will take apart the dinosaur skeletons, clean them up and examine them. Paleontologists hope to learn more about the dinosaurs during this process and maybe even determine how old some of the fossils are. Recent research about dinosaurs will help the paleontologists put the skeletons back together accurately.

The new and improved hall will have a very large resident: an almost-complete skeleton of a T. rex, discovered in Montana. The museum has about 46 million fossils, so there will be plenty of other items to look at!

While you’re waiting for the exhibit to reopen (hopefully in 2019), do some research about your own dinosaurs. What dinosaurs lived near your area? Is there a natural history museum near you? If not, ask an adult to help you search for information on the Internet, so you can get your dinosaur fix.

title: Famous People of Oregon
text:
Charles Edwin Anson Markham

Charles Edwin Anson Markham was born in Oregon City, Oregon Territory, in 1852. His parents had come by wagon to settle in the West. Markham studied, taught and became a school administrator (manager) in California.

Markham is best remembered as a poet. He was very interested in the lives of poor working people. After looking at a painting of a worker in a field, he wrote his most famous poem. Here are a few lines from his poem, “The Man with the Hoe”:

“Bowed by the weight of centuries he leans
Upon his hoe and gazes on the ground,
The emptiness of ages in his face,
And on his back the burden of the world.”

The poem became popular in many countries. What do you think those lines mean? At the dedication of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., Markham read a poem he wrote about our fallen president. Oregon honored Markham by naming him our first poet laureate. A laureate is someone who is honored for great achievements in the arts or other areas. It’s like being named the official state poet for Oregon! Markham was our poet laureate from 1923 to 1931.

Beverly Cleary

Beverly Cleary was born in McMinnville, Oregon, and grew up on a farm in Yamhill, where there was no library. Her mother worked with the state library to send books to the small town. This is where Cleary learned to love books.

Cleary’s family moved to Portland where she attended grammar school and high school. She was in the low reading group at first but worked through her problems by the time she was in third grade. She spent much of her childhood reading or waiting for more books to arrive from the state library.

Cleary graduated from college in Ontario, California, and then from the University of California at Berkeley. She then went on to the School of Librarianship at the University of Washington, Seattle, where she specialized in library work with children.

Cleary was the children’s librarian in Yakima, Washington, until she married and moved to California.

Her books have earned her many awards, including the John Newberry Medal, the Newberry Honor Award, the American Library Association’s 1975 Laura Ingalls Wilder Award, the Catholic Library Association’s 1980 Regina Medal, and the University of Southern Mississippi’s 1982 Silver Medallion. She was also nominated in 1984 for the Hans Christian Andersen Award, a very prestigious award.

John McLoughlin

John McLoughlin was born on Oct. 19, 1784, in Quebec. He began to study medicine at the age of 15. After studying for only four and a half years, he applied for his license and received it on April 30, 1803.

He was very important in the negotiation (to come to an agreement) between the Northwest Fur Company and the Hudson’s Bay Company, two very large and powerful fur trading companies at the time.

McLoughlin was known for his fair treatment of all people, whether they were British citizens, Americans or American Indians. The Columbia District, the place he was appointed Chief Factor of and built a fort on, became very profitable. This was due to the way McLoughlin treated people and the popularity of hats made from beaver.

He later retired from the Hudson’s Bay Company and moved his family to Oregon City. His store, where he sold food and farming tools, became the last stop on the famous Oregon Trail. In 1847, Pope Gregory gave him the Knighthood of St. Gregory. Two years later, he became a United States citizen. He served until 1851 as the mayor of Oregon City where he later died of natural causes on Sept. 3, 1857.

In 1957, Oregon’s legislature passed a resolution naming him the “Father of Oregon.”

title: Jackson County
text:
Jackson County was established in January 1852. It is in southern Oregon and borders California. The county covers 2,800 square miles. The county seat of Jackson County is Medford.

The Modoc, Shasta, Rogue River and Umpqua Indian Tribes lived within the present-day Jackson County. In the early 1850s, both the Klickitats and the Deschutes raided and settled in the area. The discovery of gold and the completion of the wagon road that connected to California led to many non-native settlers coming to Jackson County.

The main industries in Jackson County are lumber, agriculture, manufacturing and recreation. Attractions include a Shakespearean Festival, Historic Jacksonville, Southern Oregon University, the Britt Music and Arts Festival, the Rogue River, Lithia Park, and the Crater Lake Highway, all in the great county of Jackson.

title: How Do I Create an Outline?
text:
You can use an outline to help you organize your nonfiction writing, especially when writing reports and research papers. An outline will help you effectively plan your writing.

Start with I, then II, and III…This list will help you create an outline:

Formal outlines have the main topics in Roman numerals (I, II, III…).

Subtopics are indented and listed with capital letters (A, B, C…).

Supporting details are indented more than subtopics and listed with Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3…).

More details that support those supporting details are indented more and listed with lowercase letters (a, b, c…).

You must have at least two items at each level.

To the right is a sample outline that someone might put together for a report on World War II.

Try It!

The next time you have to write a nonfiction piece, such as a report, write an outline first. You’ll be amazed how it will help you organize your information and be sure to include all the important details.

title: Let's Write
text: Write about a legendary person who you feel has made a big impact on your life or our state. The person may be real or make believe. Explain why this person is so important and the things he or she has accomplished. How has your life been helped by this person?

title: What are Legends?
text:
Legends (unverified stories handed down from time) are a major part of life no matter where you go. Some places have monsters or mythical beasts that grace the pages of their legends, while others have people, heroes and evil people who are their legends. Some places celebrate their legends, while others keep them quiet. No matter what, though, there is probably a legend where you are right now.

One very well-known legend is that of the unicorn. The legend says that a very long time ago, when the world was very young, wild and wonderful creatures roamed free. The most beautiful of all of these creatures was the unicorn. They were constantly sought after because they had magic in their horns, but they were very hard to capture. The unicorn was a very gentle and kind creature, but it was also quick and graceful. The one way hunters could capture a unicorn was to use an innocent maiden, because they were attracted to pure things. The hunters would capture the unicorn and remove the horn. Eventually, they became extinct.

Another very well known legend is that of the Loch Ness Monster. Some believe that “Nessie” lives in Scotland’s Loch Ness, or Lake Ness. Nessie is one of the most famous and worldly known legends.

The earliest recorded sighting of Nessie was in the biography of St. Columba by Adamnan in A.D. 565. It supposedly attacked and killed a man who was swimming in the River Ness.

It did not make a disturbance again until August 27, 1930, when three fishermen reported seeing a disturbance in the water. The men watched and saw a 20-foot-long creature approach their boat and throw water in the air. The men were convinced that it was a living creature. After this story came out, several people claimed to have seen the strange creature from the Loch.

In 1962, the Loch Ness Investigation Bureau was formed. At first, they would only conduct research for a few weeks out of a year, but in 1964, they had set up permanently around the Loch. They used vans with cameras, set up camera stations and used hot-air balloons, infrared night cameras, sonar and underwater listening devices. They have come up with a great deal of information about the Loch, but there has been no photographic proof of the monster.

These are only a couple of the many legends and lore (facts, traditions or beliefs of a subject) throughout the world. If you want to learn about some legends from Oregon, keep on reading!

title: Does Bigfoot Live in Oregon?
text:
You have probably heard stories of Bigfoot, but did you know that there are people right here in Oregon who claim to have seen the huge monster? A team of researchers even spent some time here recently, hoping to find the hairy beast, but no one has ever been able to prove that Bigfoot really exists.

About 35 researchers from the Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization recently visited the forests around Bend, hoping to see the mysterious monster. The researchers didn't find any evidence of Bigfoot, but they aren't giving up. Matt Moneymaker, head of the group, says, "We're looking for a needle in a haystack, but we're using a magnet..." Moneymaker claims to have seen Bigfoot dozens of times and he uses his special skills to try to attract the monster. He calls the beast in a sad, mournful voice and shakes the trees as he walks through the forest. Still, the group had no success in its search for Bigfoot in Bend.

People who have seen Bigfoot say that it is a tall, hairy, very smelly creature that lives in the woods and only comes out at night. Legends of similar creatures are told all over the world. You may have heard stories about Sasquatch, Bigfoot or even MoMo, the Missouri Monster. If you have seen Rudolph, the Red-Nosed Reindeer, you've heard of the Abominable Snowman, or Yeti, as it is called in Tibet.

No one knows for certain if these huge monsters are real, or if they live only in legends. Most researchers believe that Bigfoot is an imaginary monster based on legends, hoaxes and practical jokes. There are some, however, who believe that Bigfoot is real, so they continue to search for proof. Until someone proves for certain that Bigfoot doesn't really exist, there will be those who continue to search for this legendary beast–even right here in Oregon.

title: Legends and Lore
text:
Bridge of the Gods

According to American Indian legend, two mountain brothers Wy’est (Mt. Hood) and Pah-toe (Mt. Adams) lived in harmony until a woman mountain fell in love with Wy’est, because he was more handsome. The woman started flirting with Pah-toe to make Wy’est jealous, and this soon started a feud (a bitter fight between two or more people, states or families) between the brothers. They threw fire and debris (scattered remains of something broken or destroyed) at each other until the land bridge—located in Cascade Locks—over the Columbia was smashed and fell into the river.

D. B. Cooper

Dan Cooper, who was mistakenly called D. B. Cooper, hijacked a 727 airplane from Portland International Airport in 1971. He had a briefcase with wires and red sticks that he said was a bomb. The plane landed at the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, and he released the passengers for $200,000 and four parachutes. He jumped from the airplane over the Columbia River with the $200,000! Almost 10 years later, in 1980, $5,800 was found along the banks of the Columbia. Years later, a diver found a parachute close to the location where he supposedly jumped, but no further trace of D. B. Cooper has ever been found.

Woody Guthrie

Woody Guthrie was born in Oklahoma in 1912. He is recognized as an important figure—even a legend—in American folk singing, having more than 2,000 songs and ballads. Woody Guthrie was commissioned by the federal government for $266.60 to write a song that would help sell the idea of the Bonneville Power Administration harnessing the river for power. He wrote songs about the Columbia River and the dams that were being built on it. He came to Oregon in the spring of 1941, and in only one month, he wrote 26 songs from the inspiration of the river valley. The songs he wrote are among the best he ever created. Some of his more famous songs are, “This Land is Your Land,” “It’s Been Good to Know You,” and “Roll on Columbia.”

Bigfoot

Legends of Bigfoot—also known as the abominable (thoroughly unpleasant or disagreeable) snowman or Sasquatch—have existed for ages. American Indians have rich history of this half-man, half-ape creature. They celebrated him in both ritual and art. But in more modern times, in 1958, a bulldozer driver from Humboldt County, California, reported that he had seen huge footprints on the ground around his bulldozer. The son of the bulldozer driver said that, before his father died, he confessed that he and his friends used a wooden “foot” to make the footprints as a joke. Bigfoot is thought to roam the Blue Mountains of Oregon. There are photos, videos and even audio recordings of strange creatures, which some people believe prove that Bigfoot exists. What do you think?

title: How Do I Read Historical Fiction?
text:
Treat It As Art Full of Historical Facts

While nonfiction is about information, fiction is all about creativity. Reading fiction can be exciting and moving. When you read fiction, you are trying to understand a character deeply, imagining the story as you read the words, reflecting on the events in the story and exploring the ideas and feelings created by the story.

Historical Fiction

Fictional pieces are imaginary stories, but they can be based on historical facts. Fictional stories based on historical facts are called "historical fiction." When reading historical fiction, it is important that you understand which details are factual and which are fictional. Sometimes, you need to do background research on your story before you can understand the difference between fact and fiction in a story that is historical fiction. Fiction is the most popular genre of literature and ranges from short stories (a page or two) to novels (up to thousands of pages). Fiction has three basic elements: characters, plot and setting.

Characters

The characters are the people (or animals) in the story. In well-written fiction, the writer will describe what the characters look like, how they act, what they think and feel, what others say about them, what they talk about and many other details. Because of this, you will finish reading it and feel like you know some of the characters very well, like friends or family. Sometimes, they will seem like real-life people. Characters in historical fiction can help you understand what it felt like to live through that event or period. Most stories have a main character, or protagonist.

Plot

The plot is what happens in a novel or story. It is the sequence of events. Generally, fictional writing begins
with a conflict, or a problem that needs to be resolved. The events that happen after the conflict is introduced are called the rising action. The rising action draws out the character's problem. The story's turning point is called the climax. This is when there is a dramatic shift in the story, especially regarding the conflict. In the end, the conflict is resolved or changed into a different conflict. This is called the falling action. You can illustrate how a story's plot goes with a graph like this:

The plot in historical fiction will often follow a timeline of actual historical events, adding fictional details along the way.

Setting

The setting is the time and place in which the story happens. Stories can take place in the past, present or future and can last anywhere from one day to several years. Stories can also take place in a single room or city, or the action might happen in one big country or a planet. In historical fiction, the setting is, of course, in the past. If you imagine yourself in the setting of historical fiction, you will understand what conditions were like back then.

Theme

The theme of a fictional work is the idea that the author is examining in the work. The theme is a general topic, which allows the author to do a great deal of exploration.

Try It!

The next time you read a story or novel that is historical fiction, identify the main characters, the plot, the setting and the theme. You can even plot the theme as shown above. Think about the details in the story. Ask yourself which details are probably historical fact and which ones are fiction created by the author. Doing this will help you more fully understand the historical context being represented.

Below is a list of historical fiction you can read over the summer:

title: Crook County
text:
Crook County, Oregon, which was established in October 1882, has almost 3,000 square miles of land. It was named after United States Army Major-General George Crook, a hero of the Snake Indian War. This part of Oregon does not have much rain, with only an annual rainfall of 10.5 inches. The county seat is Prineville. There are other communities in the county, but Prineville is the only incorporated, or official, city.

White settlers first arrived in the 1860s. The Cascade Mountains made travel to the area pretty tough! Visit the Bowman Museum at the Crook County History Center in Prineville to learn about the pioneers.

Mint and hay are grown on many farms here, and the land is good for cattle ranching. The cattle graze, or feed on growing grass. Lumber used to be a major industry, but now tourism brings in money to the economy. Visit the Ochoco National Forest to see some beautiful, old trees, including the ponderosa pine.

title: Where did the Ponderosa Pine get its name?
text: The great ponderosa pine received its name from the ‘ponderous’ (having great weight) size. Not only do they average around 30 meters (98 feet) in height, but they can be as big as 50 meters (164 feet) tall and two meters (seven feet) around. That is quite a tree! They also have very long and deep root systems to catch the water that is deep in the Earth. The roots also keep them from being blown over because the trees are so tall. The tree also has a thick bark to protect it from forest fires. Not much about the tree isn’t ponderous. Even the pine cones can be up to six inches long.

title: Pygmy Rabbit
text: The pygmy (dwarf, very small) rabbit is found in Oregon, as well as many other states in the area. Being the smallest rabbit species in North America, it faces a real danger. The rabbits are losing much of their habitat (the area where it lives), as well as being introduced to many diseases. When we say smallest, we mean it in two ways. The pygmy rabbit is on the list as a species of concern in Oregon. But we also mean that they are small animals. They generally range from nine to 12 inches in length and weigh less than a pound. They dig their own burrows, unlike most rabbits, and feed off the sagebrush. The rabbits’ predators include the weasel, coyote, badger, bobcat, raptor and humans, because rabbit hunters often cannot tell the difference between these rabbits and other rabbit species. The Oregon Zoo has been involved in a project to keep them from facing extinction (to no longer exist).

title: Let's Write
text: What makes a hero? When you think of a hero, what do you think of? Do they have superhuman powers? Do they invent amazing things? Or are they just regular people who have touched your heart in a special way? Explain what a hero is to you.

title: Expedition, Ho!
text:
You are going to plan your trip to the North Pole! Have a parent or teacher help you plan your trip to the North Pole. You must stay within a $40,000 budget for your expedition.

On the map, draw the route for your trip. Include stops, layovers, travel by plane, ship or other transportation. Then, on the blank space provided, write a list of things like equipment and clothing for camping and staying warm, food, things like ice picks and a satellite phone, rope, a guide you might want to hire, people you might bring along who would be helpful and any other things you think you might need for your trip. Be sure to label all the places you visit. Include a legend on the map.

title: Streaming Morning News!
text:
Natalia: Hi everyone, I'm Natalia.

Steven: And I'm Steven.

Natalia and Steven: We're best friends!

Steven: Natalia, these students haven't met us before. Why don't we introduce ourselves?

Natalia: Great idea, Steven! I am part Cherokee, one of the American Indian peoples. My ancestors escaped the Trail of Tears by hiding in the Smoky Mountains. My family and I are active in the Cherokee community.

Steven: I am part African American and part Hispanic. My mom and grandma are musicians. Their family took part in one of Tennessee's famous sit-ins during the Civil Rights Era in the 1960s. My dad is a Mexican immigrant. Years ago he came to Tennessee for work. After that he put himself through college where he and my mom met.

Natalia: We love history and we love Tennessee. We have a great teacher named Ms. Johnson. She has a lot of fun activities planned for the year.

Steven: And you get to come, too!

Natalia: But only if you promise to keep our awesome kids-only secret ...

Steven: We can travel through time!

Natalia: That's right! When we touch primary sources, we travel to that era of history. Primary sources are like historic documents, photos or artifacts. They can be audio recordings, diary entries, antiques or personal items.

Steven: It is so cool! But it only works on primary sources, not secondary sources. Secondary sources are created after an event, by people who were not at the event. These include books or articles.

Natalia: There is also a third level of sources. These are called tertiary sources. They give a broad overview of a topic, and include encyclopedias and dictionaries.

Steven: Primary sources are vital. This is because accounts from someone who lived through an event tend to have better information. They are not filtered through the lens of someone who never experienced the event.

Natalia: Let's pretend we are going to make a movie about early settlers. I would first try to find accounts by colonists from that time. These would include diary entries, journals or other sources. I would also visit the sites where the settlements were first located. Then I would look at the tools and other objects they used in daily life.

Steven: After that, we would look at secondary sources such as books or biographies. These help us learn more about the historic context of the period.

Natalia: Both primary and secondary sources help us learn about a time period.

Steven: But we can only time travel using primary sources.

Natalia: Time traveling lets us see historic events. It also helps us learn about the great things in our state and nation. We can talk to people we meet and follow them as they go about their daily lives.

Steven: We can always get back to our own time. We just touch the same primary source, then we appear right back where we were. There is no visible lapse in time, so nobody ever misses us!

Natalia: We have had some amazing adventures.

Steven: We are going to have even more this year. We hope you come along with us!

Ms. Johnson: Natalia? Steven? Are you in there? We need to wrap up the webcast for today. Let's get back to the classroom. I've got some exciting activities planned!

Steven: Looks like we're almost out of time.

Steven and Natalia: See you in class!

title: North Pole Bound
text:
Traveling to the North Pole is difficult even in modern times. A hundred years ago, it was especially perilous. The North Pole is a fixed point, but it is located on drifting sea ice. Pinpointing its location can be tricky. The South Pole is different because it is on the landmass of Antarctica. Early explorers took two months or longer to reach the North Pole. They had to deal with extreme cold. They also had to travel by foot, sled, skis and boat. There was no air support or rescue. The ice shifted and moved. There were few animals to hunt, and starvation was a real concern.

What is it like to travel to the North Pole today? The cold is still a problem, but it is slightly warmer than it was a hundred years ago. Climate change has been thinning the arctic ice, and it breaks erratically. Wind blows the now broken and floating ice miles in many directions. Explorers now have to travel long distances in freezing water instead of over icy land. Thinner ice also makes it hard for planes and helicopters to land and rescue stranded explorers. A hundred years ago, explorers could safely camp on thick ice. Modern-day explorers must be much more cautious about where they pitch their tent. Thinner ice could crack in the night under an explorer's tent, dumping them in the frigid water. Would you like to explore the North Pole region?

title: Think and Review
text:
How do we know whether Dr. Frederick A. Cook or Robert E. Peary made it to the North Pole first or if either man made it at all?

What difficulties do modern explorers face traveling to the North Pole today?

What are the differences between the North and South poles, and why is one more difficult to get to than the other?

What are the differences between time zone lines and lines of longitude?

What is the main idea of the article "North Pole Bound"?

Give one detail from "North Pole Bound" that supports your answer.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you are a reporter for a newspaper. Your editor wants you to write about the first explorers to reach the North Pole. Gather ideas from this week's issue. Then, write an original news article. Don't forget to include the 5 Ws: Who, What, When, Where and Why.

title: Making Their Mark on the Map
text:
When Natalia and Steven got back to the classroom, they took a seat at their worktable. Ms. Johnson had already laid out several maps on the table. There was also a box filled with metal pieces. Natalia immediately reached for it.

"What is it?" she asked in wonder.

"It looks like a puzzle," Steven replied.

"What's that, Ms. Johnson? You said you found this at an antique market?" Natalia said.

"I wonder who it belonged to," Steven mused as they began to assemble the globe. As the friends put the globe together, they discovered that the countries in the Northern Hemisphere and Southern Hemisphere were divided by the equator.

"You see this line?" Natalia asked as she pointed to the thin line that went all the way around the middle of the globe. "This is the equator, and it divides Earth into the Northern and Southern hemispheres. These lines that are parallel to the equator are the lines of latitude."

"Look! This line here is the prime meridian!" Steven said as he pointed to a line that ran from the top to the bottom of the globe and crossed through Greenwich, England. "It divides Earth into eastern and western hemispheres. These lines parallel to it are lines of longitude. "

Natalia traced the jagged lines that also ran from north to south. "These aren't lines of longitude though. These are time zones. They follow political boundaries, not longitude lines."

She traced the lines of longitude up and down the globe. "They end here on the North and South poles."

"I wonder what it's like being on the bottom of the Earth on the South Pole," Steven wondered aloud as he finished putting the last piece of Antarctica in place.

"Well, they don't feel like they are upside down or in a different direction than we are because of gravity," said Natalia.

"I'm sure they are much colder though!" Steven remarked. He handed Natalia the last two pieces. "You should put the North Pole together."

"That's strange," she said slowly.

"What is it?" Steven asked.

"It almost looks like the ice is moving."

"You're right, it sort of does, doesn't it?" Steven said, entranced.

"Does it feel cold in here to you?" Natalia asked as she put the final piece of the puzzle in place.

"I—whoa!" Steven yelled and Natalia shrieked as they were transported to the ice sheets near the North Pole.

"What happened? Where are we?"

"When are we, you mean." Natalia inspected the globe that was in her hand. "Made in 1908."

"Is that when we are?" Steven asked. He jumped up and down trying to keep warm. "I need a coat."

"What about a fire?" Natalia asked.

"Sure, if you have one."

"I don't but they do," she pointed to a glowing light in the distance. She and Steven trudged through the ice and snow in that direction. They came to a large cave and went inside. The wind died down but it was still cold. They moved closer to the fire that was burning in a portable stove, but still stayed out of sight.

There was a group of men sitting around the fire.

"We have made it to the North Pole, but I fear we will not return home, Dr. Cook," remarked one man.

"Wait! I thought Robert E. Peary was the first to officially make it to the North Pole in April of 1909?" Steven asked softly. "So who is this?"

Natalia shook her head and whispered, "Some people believe that Dr. Frederick A. Cook was the first to reach the North Pole in 1908. His descriptions of the polar sea, ice islands and the western drift of the polar ice match what we know today about the area."

"We must have faith," Dr. Cook replied. "We will wait here in this cave for conditions to improve."

"That could be months!" exclaimed another man.

"At least I left a brass tube with a note at the North Pole," Dr. Cook sighed and sagged back onto the greasy furs. "If anyone finds it, they will know for certain we were the first to reach the North Pole."

"No one has found it," Natalia whispered to Steven. "Experts had only a few primary sources from which to draw their conclusions. There were just the diaries and journals of Peary and Dr. Cook, and the eyewitness accounts of the indigenous people that accompanied them."

"We were there!" Dr. Cook said loudly, then coughed. "We saw the North Pole! I took measurements with a sextant."

"That's an instrument that establishes geographic position. You remember that video we watched about it, right?" Steven said to Natalia, who nodded.

"Peary did not have anyone with him who was able to read a sextant," she mused. "So he could have made a false declaration. According to his travel records, he also claims to have moved faster than what was believable. But people also argue that Dr. Cook was bad at taking sextant readings and that the data he submitted was fabricated."

"I guess that's the problem with primary sources," Steven remarked as they watched Dr. Cook add more fuel to the little stove. "People can always lie."

"Yes," agreed Natalia, "that's why you should always verify from multiple sources. Even then, we sometimes just can't know for sure."

They grabbed the globe and looked at each other and then disappeared in a gust of icy snow back to their warm classroom.

title: North and South Poles
text:
As you probably know, the North and South poles are at the top and bottom of the globe. At the poles, the sun never rises during part of the winter, and never sets during part of the summer. The South Pole region is called Antarctica, and it is a continent. There is actually land under all that ice and snow! It is the colder of the two poles. In fact, it is so cold that it can't snow very often, but it is very windy. It usually doesn't get above freezing even in the summertime. Penguins live there, but not polar bears. In fact, people don't even live there. The only people you would find at the South Pole are scientists.

The North Pole region is called the Arctic. It is not a continent because there is no land under it, only the frozen water of the Arctic Ocean. The ice is about six to 10 feet thick and floats on top of the ocean. In the winter the Arctic region is about the size of the United States, but in the summer, half of it melts into the ocean. There are many more animals living in the Arctic than in the Antarctic. Here you will find killer whales, seals, walruses and polar bears, just to name a few. Brrrr! The poles are a beautiful, exciting and very chilly part of our Earth.

title: Where is Memphis?
text:
Ms. Johnson strolled into class holding several maps of Tennessee and the United States.

"Some of those maps look really old," said Natalia. She helped Ms. Johnson lay them all out on the desk.

"Today, class," said Ms. Johnson, "we're going to learn where Memphis is." The children chuckled. "Yes, I know Memphis is in Tennessee, but where is Tennessee located? Are we in the central part of the United States? Are we in the western section or the eastern section?"

"My family went on vacation last year to Atlanta, Georgia," said Steven. "It took about six hours to get there."

"Why is it important to know how long it will take to drive from one place to another?" asked Ms. Johnson.

"My dad said we needed to know so we could decide the best time to leave that morning so we would arrive in Atlanta before the rush hour traffic."

“That’s one reason, and there are many others,” replied Ms. Johnson. "Do you know how your dad found the mileage between the two cities?"

"He checked his GPS," said Steven.

"Today, class, we want to learn how to find directions and mileage without using computers or GPS. What if you were stranded in a place with no phone or computer service? It's important to learn how map scales and legends work."

Ms. Johnson held up a large map of the United States and pointed to the symbols at the bottom. "Does anyone know what a map scale is?"

Natalia raised her hand. "It's the connection between the distance on the map and the distance in real life."

"Thanks, Natalia. That is correct. One inch might equal 100 miles. So if it's four inches between Atlanta and Memphis, then it's 400 miles. But how will we find a good restaurant to eat or a hotel to spend the night?"

Steven spoke. "My dad showed us this. Map keys or legends tell you where and what things are."

"Right again, Steven. Thanks. The map legend tells you what each thing is. A park is represented by trees. A gas station might be shown as a big red gas pump. A hotel might be shown using a bed. Roads are usually shown as blue lines. Railroad tracks are shown as black lines with cross marks. Campgrounds have wooden logs with fire." Ms. Johnson passed around some maps so the kids could see what she was talking about.

"It shows the number of miles between cities on this map," said Natalia.

"Yes it does," replied Ms. Johnson. "That means we could use math to find out the distance between cities. So let's get out our paper and pencils."

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you are an early settler. You just bought a plot of land in Tennessee and now you want to build your home right in the middle of it. How will you find the middle of your property? What other structures will you need to build?

title: What is Cartography?
text:
For many years, people made maps of the areas where they lived by hand using carefully made measurements. Why did they have to do that? How are maps made today?

Before science and computers changed how we make maps, cartographers had to rely on observation, measurements and experience to make accurate maps. Now, we can view far-away places of the world with satellite imaging and airplanes. We have better tools for recording distances more accurately than ever before. The internet and computers make it easy to record your findings. You can even trade information with other mapmakers around the world.

Old maps may look different than today's maps, but they are basically the same. Maps show the location of cities, forests, parks and hotels. There are places to eat and cool things of interest. The main difference in today's maps is accuracy. A hundred years ago, a map might show the general town borders. You could look at a coastline and see where places jutted out. But the map wasn't very accurate.

Maps today are more exact. You can see where a county line is located. You can get true distances from one place to the next. This helps out people in many ways. Let's say you buy an acre of land. How will you know where the borders are? In what ways does modern technology help answer this question?

title: Tennessee Perspective
text:
Carefully study the map of Knoxville. This type of map is called a perspective map. It's similar to a regular map that shows a bird's-eye view. What are some things that are the same on both types of maps? Are there differences?

On a separate sheet of paper, make a list of things that are the same and which things are different from a regular map (buildings, streets, parks, etc.). Which do you think is a more useful map? Why?

title: The Historic City of Memphis
text:
All week, Ms. Johnson taught her class about maps. On Thursday, the teacher surprised everyone. "Today, class, we're going to take a trip across America. We want to learn something fun or important about each city we visit. Since we are leaving from Memphis, who can tell me something fun about this town?"

Natalia raised her hand. "Memphis is known as Elvis Presley's home. It is an important city in the music world."

Steven spoke. "My dad says Memphis has the best barbecue."

Ms. Johnson nodded. "Both of you are correct. But do you know what Memphis was famous for 100 ago?" No one raised their hand. "In the early 1900s, farmers grew thousands of acres of cotton on the land. The cotton was reaped, then sent to other places that needed it."

"We read that Memphis was once also known for its trees," said Natalia.

"Yes, we read that a few weeks ago," said Steven. "People needed lumber to build houses and furniture. They got their lumber by cutting down trees that grew nearby."

"Yes, Steven," said Ms. Johnson, "even today, there are still forests near Memphis. People will always need wood to build things. The land here is so fertile. It is still a good place to grow trees, vegetables and fruits."

"Maybe we could start a class garden and grow tomatoes," said Natalia.

The whole class was excited about this idea. Ms. Johnson was sure she'd never get them talking about the history of Memphis again.

Memphis has been home to over 30 lumber mills during the height of the lumber industry boom in the early 1900s. What are some impacts on the environment the lumber industry caused? What are some impacts this industry had on the people of Tennessee?

title: All on the Grid
text:
Some maps use a grid system, or a system of numbered and lettered lines, to help you find places more easily. On a map that uses a grid system, there will be letters such as A, B, C, etc., running across the top of the map and numbers such as 1, 2, 3, etc., running down the side of the map. These are called coordinates. If you know that a certain city is located at point 2A on the map, you can find it easily using the grid system of the map. In our study of history, geography and social studies this year, we will be using maps to help us find out where things are and how they relate to each other.

Memphis, Tennessee

Washington, D.C.

Los Angeles, California

Phoenix, Arizona

title: How to Figure Distances from One City to the Next
text:
All week, Ms. Johnson's class talked about how to read a map and why maps were important. On Friday, Ms. Johnson brought several new maps of Tennessee and the United States.

"Today, class," Ms. Johnson began, "we are going to take a virtual road trip from Memphis to New York City. We must figure out how many miles it is. Then we can use math to decide how many miles per day we can travel in our bus. That will tell us how long we will be gone."

"It will take several days," said Natalia. "Will we stay in hotels and eat at restaurants?"

"Yes, of course. But these will be virtual hotels and restaurants. We will also learn to use cardinal directions and intermediate directions. We already know how to use a map scale and legend to find good places to stop."

The whole class seemed excited about taking a virtual road trip. Everyone talked about staying at hotels along the way. Then they debated about where they would eat. Some wanted hamburgers and some wanted tacos. Ms. Johnson was glad to see the kids getting so involved.

Natalia raised her hand and asked, "Ms. Johnson, what are cardinal directions?"

"Good question, Natalia. Cardinal directions are the four directions of north, south, east and west."

"What about intermediate directions?" asked Steven.

"Intermediate directions are the directions between each of the cardinal directions. These are called northeast, southeast, northwest and southwest." Ms. Johnson laid her map out on her desk. "Now, how will we decide which highways to take?"

"I think we should take major highways," said Steven. "My dad always takes them. He says you can make the best time on an interstate highway."

"But what if we want to go sightseeing along the way?" Natalia asked.

"That's a good point, Natalia. We could take the highway if we made a travel plan about where to stop along the way," said the teacher. She took her red marker to draw their route on the map. "If we take Highway 40, the first big town is Nashville. Let’s use the map scale to see how long it will take to get there.”

Steven used a ruler to measure the distance. "It looks like about 200 miles."

"If we are traveling at 50 miles per hour, how long will the trip take?" asked Ms. Johnson.

Natalia and Steven worked together to do the math. Together, they found the answer. "Four hours, Ms. Johnson!" Steven and Natalia shouted excitedly.

"You kids are very good at math," said Ms. Johnson.

"Will we stop in Nashville?" asked Steven.

"If we want to," Ms. Johnson answered. "That's the fun part of a road trip. You can stop wherever you like. After four hours of traveling, we will need to stretch our legs. We might be hungry. We could go sightseeing, too."

Everyone agreed that they would like to visit the state capitol building. Steven was tracing their route with his finger. "Ms. Johnson, when we leave Nashville, we need to head northeast, but there is no straight highway that goes that way."

"Can you look at the map and tell why, Steven?" Ms. Johnson replied.

"Now I see! Because Daniel Boone Forest is there. We have to go north to find a highway that goes around the forest," he said.

"Very good, Steven," said Ms. Johnson. "We will go north to Highway 64. Then we can begin to travel northeast again."

All the while, Natalia was adding up distances. "It looks like about 200 miles from Nashville to Lexington, Kentucky. That's another four hours of traveling."

"The Mary Todd Lincoln House is in Lexington. We could stop there and take photos," said Ms. Johnson.

"We could find a nice hotel and spend the night there, too," added Steven.

"That's a good idea, Steven," said Ms. Johnson. "I know the whole class would enjoy that."

By now, everyone was talking about what cities they wanted to visit. Some were sharing about past family vacations. The class seemed to be enjoying their virtual road trip.

Finally, Steven spoke. "My family and I have taken many vacations in the car. I never knew how my dad decided which way to go or where to stop. But now I understand. You simply decide what places you want to see."

"And you do have to keep in mind your budget," said Ms. Johnson. "What other things do you need to think about when planning a trip?"

"How long it will take," answered Natalia. "It looks like it would take our class about 20 hours of driving to get to New York City. If we traveled eight hours per day, then that would be almost three days just to get there."

"And three days to get back," added Steven. "So if we spend three days sightseeing in New York, we would be gone a total of nine days."

"That's exactly right, Steven," said Ms. Johnson. "And most of you would really miss your family if you were gone that long. So I guess it's a good thing this is only a virtual trip. Not a real one."

The class all laughed and agreed. Then they went back to tracing their route on the map. Everyone had ideas about where to stop and what to see on this trip and ideas for future trips. Steven wanted to go to Nutbush, Tennessee to view the home of the singer Tina Turner.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you are a travel writer. Your next job is to write a short article about one of Tennessee's six physical regions. Choose a region that you find interesting. Describe the unique features of the region that tourists might want to visit. In a one-paragraph essay, persuade your readers to visit your chosen region.

title: Let's Visit the Great Smoky Mountains National Park!
text:
One of the most beautiful places to visit in Tennessee is the Great Smoky Mountains National Park. A national park is an area of land that is protected by the National Park Service, or NPS. These are special places where people can go to enjoy nature. The United States has 59 areas that are protected as national parks.

The Great Smoky Mountains National Park is located in the Unaka Mountains region. The park covers just over 800 square miles! This makes it the largest national park in our country. The park has many amazing sights. Did you know that there are over 10,000 different types of plants and animals that live there? Some of the animals that are found there are white-tailed deer and black bears.

In 2015 and 2016, more than 10 million people visited this park to enjoy its beauty. No other national park in our country had more visitors than the Great Smoky Mountains!

One special place to visit at the park is Clingmans Dome. It is the highest point in the state of Tennessee and stands at 6,643 feet! There is an observation tower at the top of the mountain. It offers an amazing view. If you visit on a clear day, you can see for 100 miles in every direction. You can even sometimes see out to several different states!

title: What is a Topographic Map?
text:
You have learned that there are many types of maps. When choosing a map, think about how you will use it. If you go on a vacation, you may use a roadmap to help find your way. If you want to see the borders between states or countries, you should use a political map. If you are curious about the physical features of an area, you may use a topographic map.

A topographic map shows the physical features of land. You can use them to look for features such as mountains, rivers or plains. You could also use them to look at the land’s elevation. Elevation is how high the land is above sea level. Mountains are one type of area with high elevation. Valleys are a type of land with low elevation. The height of the land is shown on a map by using special lines called contour lines. If you want to find the highest or lowest lands in Tennessee, a topographic map would be a great tool!

Topographic maps have many other uses. They can be used by farmers to figure out how water will flow over their land. They can also be used by meteorologists. They may use the maps to study the landforms that help them predict weather patterns. Finally, everyday people can use these maps. If you wanted to go on a hike, you could use the map to find hills and mountains.

title: Raccoons: More than Just a Pesky Mammal
text:
What do you think of when you hear the word raccoon? Some people might think of a pesky mammal that sneaks into garbage cans at night. Others might just think of the great state of Tennessee!

The raccoon is an official symbol of Tennessee. A symbol is something that represents, or stands for, something else. Every state in America has state symbols. These symbols represent the state's culture, history and geography. So, why is the raccoon a state symbol?

Raccoons are important game animals in Tennessee. They have a high population in the wild. They are nocturnal animals. This means they are awake at night. Raccoons are furry with bushy tails. They are hard to find, but easy to identify because of the black hair around their eyes that look like masks. Raccoons here usually weigh between 12 and 25 pounds. They are good swimmers and like to eat fish and frogs. Did you know that the word raccoon actually comes from the American Indian word "aroughcoune?" It means "he who scratches with his hands".

Raccoons were adopted as Tennessee's state wild animal in 1971.

title: Tennessee's State Wild Animal
text: Do some research and find out how the raccoon came to be Tennessee’s state wild animal. Were there any other wild animals being considered? Is the raccoon a state symbol of any other states? Do you agree with this choice? Explain your position.
