title: Journey with Geography
text:
This week we will learn all about the geography of Tennessee. Geography is the study of the earth's surface. It is also the study of how people use the earth and its resources. The people that study it are called geographers. They study what makes one place on earth different from another.

Physical features like mountains, valleys, rivers and oceans differ from place to place. This is something geographers take note of. Geographers also study natural resources. These are things that are found in nature. The air we breathe and the water we drink are natural resources. Other examples are minerals, plants and animals. We use these resources to help us live. Geographers learn where each of these resources can be found.

Another thing that geographers study is regions. A region can be made up of many things. Each region has something that is different from the regions around it. Can you think of any regions in your school or town? What makes them different from the regions around them?

The United States is often divided into five regions. The regions were created because the areas share things in common. They may share a similar location, climate or geography. The five main regions are the West, the Southwest, the Midwest, the Northeast and the Southeast. Tennessee is in the Southeast.

Sometimes, regions are made up of areas that share the same physical features. All of the areas in a region might have flatlands or mountains. Regions can also be made up of areas that grow the same crops. Sometimes they are made up of areas where people speak the same language. Some regions share the same weather patterns. All areas in one region must share something in common.

This week, we will study the physical regions of Tennessee. A physical region is an area of land divided by natural borders. We will see the many natural features that are found in our state. Join Natalia and Steven as they go on an adventure to discover what makes each region of Tennessee special!

title: Amazing Race: A Geographical Journey through Tennessee!
text:
Natalia and Steven can hardly wait for class to begin. Ms. Johnson said they'd be going on an adventure today. Sitting still in their seats is a chore as they wait to find out what type of journey she had in mind.

Ms. Johnson: Class, are you ready for an adventure?

Natalia: Yes! I'm so excited!

Steven: Where are we going, Ms. Johnson?

Ms. Johnson: Today, we will be going on an amazing race to locate some of Earth's fascinating geographic features!

Steven: Ms. Johnson, what is a geographic feature?

Ms. Johnson: Great question! They are the different types of landforms that we find on Earth, such as mountains, rivers and plateaus.

Natalia and Steven: Awesome!

Ms. Johnson: We're going to be using these maps and globes for our adventure. Your job is to locate all of the features on your list to finish your race.

Ms. Johnson hands out the materials. Some groups have maps of the U.S., others have globes, some are given maps of Tennessee.

Steven: We have a map of Tennessee!

Ms. Johnson: Let the race begin!

Natalia: Okay, so we've got a physical map! It's divided up into the six regions of Tennessee.

Steven: You're right! I see the Gulf Coastal Plains, the Highland Rim and Central Basin, the Cumberland Plateau, the Valley and Ridge and the Unaka Mountains.

Natalia: Let's start with the Gulf Coastal Plains.

Natalia and Steven give each other a sly smile before both grabbing the map at the same time. Suddenly, they find themselves in the Gulf Coastal Plain.

Steven: Wow! The land here is so flat and seems to stretch on for miles without any trees.

Natalia: You're right! We've located an item on our list. This is definitely a plain. The land in this region is very flat.

Steven: There's the Tennessee River!

Natalia: Wow! Look at the boats passing through the canal! Those canals sure do make it much easier to transport things.

Steven: We better keep moving! Did you remember to bring the map and list?

Natalia: Of course! They're right here in my pocket. It says that we need to find a basin.

Steven: Let's visit the Highland Rim and Basin regions. I'm sure we'll find one there.

Steven and Natalia touch the region on the map ... WHOOSH!

Steven: We're here! Check out this land! It's so high and flat.

Natalia: Look over there, I see a basin! It's so much lower than the rest of the land. Let's try standing in the middle of the basin to check out the view.

Steven: What an amazing sight! We're completely surrounded by the Highland Rim.

Natalia: We better hurry along. Let's explore the Cumberland Plateau next.

The children each place their hands on the map. In the blink of an eye ...

Natalia: We're here! This view is incredible. I think I can see all of Tennessee from up here!

Steven: That's because we're on top of the Cumberland Plateau. It looks like we're about 500-900 feet above the land surrounding us.

Natalia: Ms. Johnson said that this plateau is home to a huge canyon called the Tennessee River Gorge.

Steven: I remember! She said it is 26 miles long. It's so cool how the river flows right through the land.

Natalia: In science, we learned that canyons take many years to form. The water carves away at the rock. I wonder what this area will look like in the future?

Steven: Me too. It's amazing how land is always changing.

Natalia: Let's check out the Appalachian Ridge and Valley region next.

Steven and Natalia once again touch their map.

Steven: We're here! The land sure looks different here. I bet those long ridge areas on the top of the mountains would have a great view of the valleys below.

Natalia: Definitely. Look, there's Clinch Mountain. Our textbook says that it's a 4,000-foot ridge. It offers an amazing view into the valleys below.

Steven: Well, just a few more features left to find! Let's finish this race!

The children touch the map and are transported to the Unaka Mountains region.

Natalia: Look! We're in the Great Smoky Mountains! I visited here last summer. The view from Clingmans Dome is incredible!

Steven: These mountains are huge! It sure is cold up here.

Natalia: That's because the elevation is so high. We're thousands of feet up in the sky!

Steven: Brr! Let's look for a desert, it's the last thing on our list. Maybe we can warm up there.

Natalia: I don't think we're going to find one of those in Tennessee! We better ask Ms. Johnson about that. Let's head back to the classroom.

The students touch the location of their school on the map. Before they know it, they're back in their classroom. Steven raises his hand.

Ms. Johnson: Yes, Steven?

Steven: We've only got one item left on our list, but we don't think we can find it on our map. We know that deserts are hot, dry land, but we don't think there are any deserts in Tennessee.

Ms. Johnson: You're absolutely right! Tennessee does not have any desert land. I was hoping you'd realize that when you studied the map. Can you name the regions of the U.S. where deserts can be found?

Steven: The West and Southwest regions.

Ms. Johnson: Yes! Congrats on finishing your race! Was it as amazing as you'd hoped?

Steven and Natalia look at each other and remember to keep their secret.

Natalia: It was amazing, Ms. Johnson! I can't wait to see what adventure we'll have next ...

title: Making Islands! (Did You Know)
text:
An island is a piece of land that is surrounded by water on all sides. Some islands are created by volcanic activity and some islands are even man-made.

The Grand Strand has barrier islands. Barrier islands are formed by wind and ocean tides. These islands are built by layers of sand, silt and sediment that build up off the coast. These barrier islands help protect the mainland from erosion. Barrier islands that are big enough have also become home to resort towns and tourist spots.

Sometimes people don't want to wait for nature to create islands for them, so they make their own. The U.S. has a couple of man-made islands. The Venetian Islands off the coast of Florida are one such example. These islands are home to incredible beachfront properties and houses. This has helped the economy. People come to visit Miami to see these artificial islands.

Another example of man-made islands can be found in the city of Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates. The Palm Islands were built to look like palm trees from a bird's-eye view. They were built for much of the same reasons as the Venetian Islands. To help develop the area and boost the local economy.

These islands are made by dredging up sand and soil from the ocean floor. This has been found to have a negative impact on the ocean environment. It damages coral. It also destroys natural habitats and seagrass. The loss of these resources harms the local marine life of these areas. Even though these artificial islands are amazing examples of human ingenuity, there are negative side-effects we must consider before continuing to develop man-made islands such as these.

title: What Is the Grand Strand?
text:
The Grand Strand is a series of beaches on the southeast coast of the U.S. It stretches from Little River to Georgetown, South Carolina. Myrtle Beach, a now popular destination spot on the Grand Strand, got its name when a woman named Mrs. F. E. Burroughs suggested naming the area after the myrtle shrub that grew there. Mrs. Burrough's husband's company, Burroughs and Collins, helped grow the area into a resort spot starting in 1900. Before this, it was unchanged and considered unlivable by settlers and explorers. They found it too remote and too swampy.

Long ago, the Grand Strand area was inhabited by the Waccamaw and Winyah American Indians. No one really knows what happened to these tribes. They may have disappeared from the area due to sickness, or tribal and colonial warfare could have driven them out. They were among the tribes who made a trail from Boston, Massachusetts to Charleston, South Carolina, which became the King's Highway. People today still travel this Highway. It is the oldest continuously traveled road in the U.S.

Today, the Grand Strand economy relies heavily on tourism to the area. Myrtle Beach became a town in 1938 and then a city in 1957.

In October of 1954, Hurricane Hazel ripped through the resort town and destroyed nearly all of the Grand Strand. According to the National Weather Service, Hurricane Hazel caused $136 million in property damage. Hundreds of deaths and injuries were recorded. Rebuilding after all this damage led to a golfing boom in the area, however. Now, there are over 110 golf courses around Myrtle Beach. Hurricane damage, as terrible as it can be, sometimes leads to improvements in an area.

title: Amazing Race: The Race Continues!
text:
It's the start of a brand new school day. For Steven and Natalia, that means a new opportunity for an amazing adventure! This week, Ms. Johnson is having them continue their amazing race.

Ms. Johnson: Are you ready for another amazing race, class? This week, you will all have an opportunity to find new and exciting geographical features around the world. Let the race begin!

Steven and Natalia: Yes!

Steven: Last week we had a map of Tennessee. What's our map this week, Natalia?

Natalia: We have a physical world map, Steven. Do you have this week's list of physical features we should look for?

Steven: Right here! Let's see, last week we found a plain. We saw a canal on the Tennessee River.

Natalia: We saw a basin, and a plateau, too! Those were all physical features of Tennessee. Let's look for new places. How about a peninsula?

Steven: Well, I was thinking of finding a gulf. Maybe we could find somewhere that has both? They are similar. Peninsulas are land surrounded by water on three sides, and a gulf is sea or ocean water that is surrounded by land.

Steven and Natalia look down at the map together. Their eyes darting furiously over the map looking for somewhere in the world with both geographical features.

Steven: I got it! The Scandinavian Peninsula.

Natalia: Let's go!

Steven and Natalia, excited by their find, reach forward and touch their map ... WHOOSHH!

Natalia: Here we are, I think. Are we on an island?

Steven: We must be! Let's see, if we look at the map ... this must be the Gulf of Bothnia we are looking at. It's where the Baltic Sea stretches up between Sweden and Finland. We're on the islands located where the sea meets the gulf.

Natalia: Sea! we have a sea on our list, too!

Steven: Awesome. This place really hit three birds with one stone. What should we look for next? A bay?

Natalia: Let's go someplace closer to home. What about here?

Steven and Natalia, touch the map and are whisked away once more ...

Steven: The Mississippi River Delta! This place is part of Louisiana's coastal plain.

Natalia: A river delta is a physical land formation that is created when a river drains into a slow-moving body of water. In this case, the sand and silt deposits carried downstream by the Mississippi River created this area. The sand and silt settle and build up since the waters in the gulf are relatively calm.

Steven: The Mississippi River is the second-longest river in the U.S. On the map, you can see the Mississippi originates all the way up in Minnesota.

Natalia: River, delta, peninsula and gulf!

Steven: Don't forget, we need to find a stream.

Natalia: There are probably hundreds around the Mississippi River. A stream is just a small, narrow river after all.

Steven: Good point. Maybe we should focus on tackling the bigger physical features.

Natalia: What's the next feature we should go find an example of?

Steven: Oh, I've got one! Quick, let's go!

Touching their world map again, Steven and Natalia are zipped away!

Steven: Ta-Da! The Matterhorn! This is my favorite mountain in the whole world. It is a nearly perfect naturally occurring pyramid. And each of its four sides faces a cardinal direction. It's almost like a big compass rose.

Natalia: It'd be hard to get lost when your compass rose is as big as a mountain! We have one more physical feature on our list. We need to find a strait.

Steven: Alright, let's get going.

They reach out and touch the map one more time ...

Steven: Where are we now? It's so c-c-cold, here. Brrrrrrrr!

Natalia: That's because we're way up in north Alaska! The map took us to the Bering Land Bridge National Preserve. We are far enough north that the weather stays cold most of the year. title: As the World Turns!
text:
How are people in the world different? How are they alike?

Just now, all over Tennessee, the U.S. and elsewhere in the world, children are waking up and starting their day. You have probably wondered what children in other cultures are like. What do they eat for breakfast? Do they have chores before they go to school? Do they go to school? In some ways, they are very different from you. In other ways, they are not so different.

There are people around the world today who may live much as their ancestors did thousands of years ago. Other people live in huge cities with modern apartments. They are able to stay connected with people all around the world. They use telephones, televisions or computers. What makes the difference in the way people around the world live? There are several things that separate different cultures in our world.

Wealth

Wealth (money or resources) is not evenly spread out among the countries of the world. Some countries like Canada, the United States or Japan have a greater amount of wealth. We call these nations "developed" nations. Other countries, mainly in Africa, Asia and Latin America, are less wealthy. They are called "developing" nations. Wealth can affect something as basic as the water we drink. Did you know that one in five people in the world today do not have safe drinking water? Each day, more than 25,000 people die from illnesses they catch from drinking unclean water. Most unsafe water is in the developing nations.

Geography

The geography of an area may also be a reason that cultures are separated. There are some Amazon tribes that have remained hidden for centuries in the dense rainforest. They live as they always have. Because they live in such a remote location, they are undisturbed by popular cultures of today.

Multicultural

Many parts of the world are multicultural. This means many people with different cultures live in the same place. A society is multicultural when people from one country migrate to another. As they do, they take with them their customs, fashions, religions and food.

They take with them their culture. Children everywhere live different sorts of lives. Though many things are different, many things are also the same. Children all over the world have many of the same joys and fears that you have. Children everywhere love to play games and go to school. They love holidays and celebrations. They like spending time with family and friends. They worry about wars and wish for peace. In some ways they are different, but in some ways, they are just like you!

About 70 miles west of Panama City, there is a valley known as Anton Valley, known to locals as simply “El Valle” (the Valley). A valley is a low-lying area between two mountains or hills. El Valle is situated in one of the worlds largest extinct volcanoes.

text:
When you look at a map, it should look like it's been peppered with black dots. These black dots stand for major cities. Cities are one of the most important features on a map. Highways and railroads connect major cities. We might even drive with our families from one city to another.

title: Are Map Features Real?
text:
Even though maps have black dots to represent cities and lines to represent roads, you won't see any black dots or lines on the ground when you pass through counties into other towns and cities. What we see on a map doesn’t match up to the actual ground!

Boundaries like county lines are decided by people. People draw them on the map, but the lines don’t really exist on the ground. There is no dot to find on the road when you are coming up to a city either. Usually, the only way to know when you've reached a city is when you drive past a welcome sign, such as "Welcome to Nashville." But maps help us find our way around when we travel. Even though they're just lines and dots, they really help us find our way!

title: Political Features on a Map
text:
Different types of maps show us different information. Topographical maps help us determine elevation. Physical maps show us where to find mountains, rivers and other physical features. Political maps show where countries, cities and counties are. They also show major roads and sometimes other features like railroads or important bodies of water. Map keys use symbols to help us find what we need on the map.

City: A city is a large town. A city found on a map that has a star by its name is a capital city. Most times, cities are listed on a map beside a dot.

Highway: A highway is a major road that connects places like towns and cities. Interstate 24 is a major highway in Tennessee. What symbols are used to identify highways on a political map?

Rivers: Cumberland River and Tennessee River are two important rivers in our state. Rivers are usually identified with the color blue on a political map.

National Parks: Some political maps will also show you where state or national parks can be found. Take a look at this map of Tennessee. If you lived in Chattanooga and wanted to visit the Great Smoky Mountains National Park, which direction would you have to drive to get there?

Boundary: A boundary is a dividing line. On a political map, boundary lines are used to separate countries and states. They can even be used to separate counties. They show where one place ends and another begins.

text:
Ms. Johnson: Now that all of you have learned about maps, I would like you to put your knowledge into practice. The students all work hard on their virtual road trips. They each want to make the best trip possible with the time they have!

Steven: I planned a road trip through the whole state of Tennessee. I love to go camping in the Blue Ridge Mountains, so I made that my ending point. I’m starting my journey all the way in the western part of the state in the city of Memphis. You can see it here on the wall map. It’s this black dot in the southwestern corner of the state. This long blue line here is the Mississippi River.

Since we don’t have a lot of time to spend in Memphis, I’m just going to take you to one place: Graceland. That’s where the Elvis Presley lived. He was the King of Rock and Roll. Now we are going to head north because I really want to visit the Country Music Hall of Fame in Nashville. See these red lines? These are different highways. I need to take Interstate 40. It's the one that leads to Nashville. If you look closely at the route, you’ll see that the highway passes through gray lines that surround plots of land. Those are county lines. We have to pass through many counties to get to Nashville. I learned that the drive takes about four hours to get from Memphis to Nashville.

After I visit Nashville, I will have to find a route that takes us east toward the Blue Ridge Mountains. I could stay on I-40, but if we take I-24, we can travel down south to Chattanooga. In Chattanooga, I can visit the Tennessee Aquarium. It has a cool alligator exhibit I want to see. After that, we can finally head to the Blue Mountains.

It looks like we will have to take I-75 starting in Chattanooga and switch here to I-81 to reach the Blue Ridge Parkway. The Blue Ridge Parkway leads us through the mountains. This bumpy looking area on the map is the mountains of eastern Tennessee. If we were really going there, we’d all have fishing poles and would be wearing our best hiking shoes to go exploring.

I also learned that railroads aren't solid lines like roads. They are lines made up of dashes. That’s how you can tell a highway from a railroad when you are looking at a map. I wanted to take the same trip Steven took by train, but that’s not possible. There are not many passenger trains that travel around the state. I learned that there are more roads in Tennessee than railroads.

I decided to find a railroad that was for people only. So I am climbing aboard the Three Rivers Rambler. It starts at the depot in Knoxville. A depot is another word for a train station. Can you guess why this train is called the Three Rivers Rambler?

Steven: I know. Because it crosses three rivers?

Natalia: If you look at the map, you’ll see that the dotted line that leads from Knoxville ends here at the start of the Tennessee River. There are also two other rivers that the railroad passes: the French Broad River and the Holston River.

Ms. Johnson: What kinds of things will you see on your railroad journey?

Natalia: This journey isn’t very long, but it passes by many places that are on some maps like the Knoxville Airport. It also passes over many railroad bridges that go over the water. If you look at this rail map, you can see just where the bridges are.

Before there were cars, people had to use trains to get from one place to another. Now the railroads in our state are used mostly for products instead of people.

Ms. Johnson: That’s right Natalia. Railroads are still important, but many of us travel by car or even plane to reach other cities in our state. title: Mapping Your World
text:
Steven: Good morning, everyone! I'm Steven.

Natalia: And I'm Natalia! Welcome to the news!

Steven: We're talking about maps today. The first thing we learned is that they can be both primary and secondary sources. Natalia has a report on that. Natalia?

Natalia: Thank you, Steven! We talk about primary sources a lot on our show. A map can be both a primary and a secondary source. When a map is made, it is a primary source for that time period. Maps are made using eyewitness accounts, which is firsthand experience with an area and scientific data.

A long time ago, people could only draw a map from what they could see. They could make a map from a lookout point, either from a high mountain or the deck of a ship. They could record how long it took to travel between two places. Today, we use pictures taken from airplanes or even spaceships to make a map. A map made today has old information, like natural landmarks. These can be forests or mountains. It also has new information. It shows all of the roads, bridges and highways. Steven has our report about modern development. Over to you, Steven!

When you check the bus schedule, that's a kind of map. We use that information to make other city maps. A map that shows population and topography has the information you need to build a new road.

Natalia: Check the School Library in the reference section to see for yourself. Tune in tomorrow morning for another exciting news report!

title: Maps: Primary or Secondary Sources?
text:
Maps can be either a primary or secondary source. Primary sources are documents or records of an event or place made by someone who was there and experienced it firsthand. Secondary sources are documents made by someone who did not experience something firsthand. Maps made long ago by mapmakers who had to rely on physical measurements and personal experience of an area are primary sources. The maps explorers drew on their expeditions are good examples of primary source maps. They made these maps through careful observations of the stars and the land as they traveled.

Mapmakers and scientists today use historic and modern data to make today's maps more accurate. Physical maps made from pictures taken by airplanes or satellites are examples of maps made using modern data.

Let's take a look at this map. It was made in the 1800s. That means it is a primary source for the decade it was made in. The mapmaker didn't have modern technology and collected data to make it. But through carefully made surveys of the land and personal and compiled knowledge of the state to make it. A modern mapmaker may need to reference this map when making a new one. It shows many if not all of the same physical features, like rivers and mountains, a modern map would.

Take a look at the map and see if you can find familiar landmarks, physical features, cities and counties that may appear on maps today.

title: Stories and Maps
text:
Natalia: Wow, look at all these maps! I didn't know our school had so many. I never used the reference section much. I thought there were only dictionaries back here.

Steven: Wow, there are all kinds of maps. There are new maps that show different things, like population and geography. See, this one shows where the mountains are. The valleys, too. And this one is about voting districts, so it shows how many people live here.

Natalia: Ms. Johnson told us that voting districts are determined by population. Voting maps and population maps must use similar kinds of data ...

Natalia: Cartographers use satellites and aerial photos now to make these kinds of maps. A bird's-eye view of the area!

Steven: Right, just knowing the geography isn't enough anymore.

Natalia: What do you mean, Steven?

Steven: Back in the day, maps were made by a person who had experience traveling in an area. Someone like a fur-trapper would follow a river through the forest enough times until they knew it well enough to make a map. They would just draw it by hand, relying on their experience to make it as accurate as possible. Old maps like this are great primary sources of areas, but they aren't as accurate as maps that can be made today. There are some really old maps in this collection.

Natalia: Just because they're old doesn't mean the information isn't useful. Comparing old and new population maps can help you understand how quickly an area has grown. Comparing old and new street maps can show you how the population of an area has changed that landscape over time, too.

Steven: We can use that in our news report. We can talk about the changes in our own state, using both an old and new map of Tennessee!

Natalia: Great idea!

title: Looking Through Maps
text:
One of the most important things to have on a trip is a map. So, we definitely need to talk about the maps we use. Each map has its own special purpose. In fact, mapmakers develop each map specifically with its own theme or purpose.

Political Maps

Some maps show the boundaries between countries, states or provinces. These maps often show the major cities found within those areas. They also mark the separation between the governments of the world. Since these maps focus on the political parts of the world, they are called political maps. For example, this political map of North America shows the boundaries between countries like Canada, the United States and Mexico. Each country is usually indicated by a different color to make it easy to see where one country ends and another begins, just like on this map.

Physical Maps

Mapmakers create other maps to show the physical features (traits of a place) of an area like landforms or major bodies of water. We call these physical maps. For instance, a physical map of the United States shows the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, the islands of Hawaii, the Rocky Mountains, the five Great Lakes and the Mississippi River. Many times physical maps will also include varying colors to show mountains and valleys of the land and landforms. Notice on the map that the highest points in the Rocky Mountains are a darker green than the lower areas of the Great Plains.

People use maps for a lot of reasons. Most often, people use maps to plan a route, find their way or locate something like a specific place, landmark or landform.

Once, for fun, Steven's parents made a "treasure map" for him and Natalia. The two friends followed the map to the "treasure"—tickets to a hometown baseball game! What a fun way to use a map!

Population Maps

Sometimes city planners, lawmakers and historians need population density maps to do their jobs. City planners look at these maps to see where people are living. They can also see which areas are growing in population. This helps them decide where to build. Growing populations need more houses, parks and schools.

Lawmakers use population density maps to help draw district lines for voting. This helps them know in which areas their voters live.

Historians can look at population density maps to find patterns in population growth around an area, state or country. This can show when an area booms due to an increase in trade or discovery of a natural resource like gold. It can also show when an area experiences hard enough times that the population shrinks.

Climate Maps

For a school project, Natalia needs to find out how much rainfall different areas of our state have over the course of a year. To do this, she must look at a climate map. There are different kinds of climate maps you can look at. Some climate maps focus on temperature. The kind Natalia needs is one that shows average yearly rainfall.

Scientists can use maps like these to find patterns in weather. These patterns are used to determine the effects of climate change on an area. It can also help farmers plan ahead for growing things.

Map Features

An important part of a map is a compass rose. A compass rose shows directions on a map like north, south, east and west. You can use a compass rose to figure out which direction you need to get where you are going.

An additional important thing on a map is the map scale. Because maps are not the same size as the places they represent, a map scale is used to show actual distances. These distances are usually in either miles or kilometers. It is another key part of a map because people can use the map scale to figure out distances. This can be very important, especially for travelers who need to figure out the actual length and time of their trips.

There is one last feature on a map that we need to talk about. Some maps have lines numbered in degrees that run both vertically (up and down) and horizontally (side to side). Lines that run vertically are called lines of longitude, or meridians. Lines that run horizontally are called lines of latitude, or parallels. These lines are important because they create a grid that can be used to find the exact location of any place in the world.

Geography in Review

To wrap things up, let's think about our location on a map. We live in North America, the third-largest continent behind Asia and Africa. There are many countries here in North America. Some of the largest and most populated countries are the United States, Canada and Mexico. The country we live in is the United States. Within our country, there are 50 states. Which state is your home state? Now, hang on for the ride of your life. Things are just getting started

title: The Power of Water
text:
People first came to Tennessee and saw the mountains and rivers as obstacles. They had to climb over them, travel between them or go long distances to avoid them. They were a nuisance and a bother! Modern engineers, however, see mountains and rivers as a way to generate power. Hydroelectric power.

Look at a map of the state. Tennessee has many rivers, mountains and valleys. That means that the geography is ideal for two things. The first is for electric power. The second is for controlling water for floods or irrigation.

Do you want to build a hydroelectric plant? You need to build a dam. And that dam needs a river. A river that is big enough and strong enough to move a turbine. This is a machine that creates electric power. You can find a location like this by using a map that shows elevation. That's how high something is. If a big river flows from a high elevation, it's strong enough to move a turbine. There are 29 dams in the Tennessee Valley area that generate power. These dams started to be built as early as the 1930s.

Some dams are used for recreation, water storage or as part of a natural preserve. They can store drinking water that can be used later. Nearby areas are safer if there is flooding. They can make a dangerous river safer for fishing or swimming. Recreational areas and green spaces are important to modern development, too!

title: Meet the Continents
text:
The surface of the Earth is divided into continents and oceans. These are bodies of land and large bodies of water. There are seven continents in total. They are Asia, North America, Antarctica, Australia, Africa, South America and Europe. Europe and Asia are different from the others as they are not separated by water. However, the people of Europe and Asia live differently, so they are considered separate continents. Some geographers (experts on Earth's land) and scientists feel Europe and Asia should be one continent, and they call it Eurasia. If you think Europe and Asia should be one continent, then you can call it Eurasia. This would also lower the continent count from seven to six.

North America is where you will find our own United States. It also includes Canada, Mexico, Central America, Greenland and the islands of the Caribbean. North America boasts the most varied climate of all the continents. Everything from desert to the ice-covered polar regions can be found in North America. The narrowest part of North America, Panama, is only 30 miles wide.

South America is the fourth-largest continent. There are 12 countries in South America. The world's largest tropical rainforest covers one-third of the continent. South America is also the home to one of the driest deserts in the world. The Atacama Desert has areas where it has not rained for hundreds of years.

Antarctica is the fifth-largest continent. Antarctica's center is the South Pole. It is so cold in Antarctica that most of it is uninhabitable. A handful of scientists will live there anywhere from three months to a year at a time to study the environment. They also study the animals that can live there. The land of Antarctica is covered by a huge ice cap. It is the only continent without a country. It is probably the quietest continent, too!

Europe is the sixth-largest continent. It is the home of 35 countries. Vatican City, the world's smallest country, is in Europe. Vatican City is where the Pope (head of the Catholic Church) lives. Although Europe is the second-smallest continent, it has more people than any other continent except Asia.

Asia is the largest continent in size. It is bigger than North America, Europe and Australia all put together. More people live in Asia than anywhere else in the world. It includes thousands of islands including Cyprus, Sri Lanka, Indonesia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Japan.

Australia is the smallest and flattest continent. It is home to more than 45 different species of kangaroo. Australia has 10 different deserts. These deserts have many giant sand dunes. Some dunes are more than 200 meters high.

You may have heard people refer to the continent of Africa as a country. But actually, Africa is home to over 50 independent countries. Just like every other continent in the world, all of these countries have their own unique culture, customs, languages and traditions. Africa is the second-largest continent. Six hundred and seventy million people live in Africa, and more than half are younger than the age of 15. The largest desert (the Sahara), the second-longest river (the Nile) and a large tropical forest (the Congo) are all found in Africa.

title: All Around the World
text:
Ms. Johnson has planned a scavenger hunt for her class today, but it looks like we're all in for a globetrotting adventure. Let's see what happens after she gives Natalia and Steven a world map from the East India Trading company.

Natalia: Steven, look at this map. It looks ancient. Do you think it might be authentic?

Steven: Not likely. It's really cool though. Look at all that water! I want to explore the oceans one day. How cool would that be? I mean, there's so much to learn. For example, what's underneath the waves? Or, how do the oceans affect the people living near them?

Natalia: The oceans are really interesting, Steven, but I would like to visit every single continent. I bet people live so differently on each continent. Judging from this map, it looks like this sailor visited almost every continent. This map reminds me of the video that we saw on the Studies Weekly website about all of the different continents.

Steven: Yeah, let me see the map again, Natalia.

They both take hold of the map and are zapped through time and space, but this time they end up in different locations! Natalia finds herself in Chennai, India. Steven finds himself on the Okeanos Explorer, a National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA vessel. Let's see what happens.

Natalia: I can't believe it! I'm in India, by the Indian Ocean! Steven isn't here. He must have ended up someplace else. I hope he's okay! I'll just take a quick look around and hopefully, Steven and I will find each other. Oh, here's someone. Hi, I'm Natalia. I'm...new here. Could you tell me what's happening?

Samrit: Hello, Natalia, I'm Samrit. My cousin Jesminder is getting married today.

Natalia: Her wedding gown is so colorful. Where I come from, most brides wear white.

Samrit: Well, our family is Tamil, and Tamil weddings are very colorful and usually last for three days. The bride wears a colorful silk sari and many pieces of gold jewelry. On the last day of the ceremony, the bride and groom get ready for the wedding during the Mangala Snanam. At the end of the wedding, they hold hands and walk around the sacred fire seven times to show the strength of their union.

Natalia: Samrit, thank you for explaining the wedding to me. I'd love to stay and learn more, but I should probably go now. Bye!

Natalia runs off in hopes of finding her friend. Steven, on the other hand, finds himself aboard a ship.

Steven: Wow, look at this ship! The sign says it's the Okeanos Explorer. I don't see Natalia. I'll take a look around. I'm sure we'll find each other. Oh, here comes someone now.

Meme Lobecker: Hi there, young man.

Steven: Hi, I'm Steven. I'm a bit lost, but could you tell me about your ship?

Meme: I'm Elizabeth Lobecker, but everyone calls me Meme. I'm one of the physical scientists aboard the Okeanos Explorer. Our team explores the geology, marine life and habitats of the ocean. Part of my job is to map the ocean floor.

Steven: That's great! I have this map here, and I think it belonged to a sailor that actually sailed this ocean. Wait, which ocean is this?

Meme: We're currently off the coast of South Africa, where the Indian Ocean meets the Southern Ocean. You can be my junior scientist today. We'll gather data to help us understand how the ocean floor affects the currents at the beach.

Steven: OK!

As Steven is collecting samples on the beach, he touches the map again.

Whoosh! Steven and Natalia are reunited at school.

Natalia: Steven!

Steven: Natalia! I've been exploring the ocean with a scientist. I've learned so much about how the ocean structure affects the life around it.

Natalia: I visited India and saw a Tamil wedding. I learned so much about some of the customs of the people in India.

Steven: We've got so much information to share with our class.

Natalia: Let's get started!

title: Our Five Oceans
text:
An ocean is a large body of salt water. Most of our continents are separated from one another by these five large bodies of water. These oceans cover about 70 percent of the Earth's surface!

Using the descriptions of our oceans, label the globes!

The Atlantic Ocean - The Atlantic is the second-largest ocean on Earth. It is located on the eastern side of the Americas. This ocean separates the American continents from Europe and Africa. Many early European explorers traveled across this ocean while searching for new lands.

The Pacific Ocean - The Pacific is the largest ocean on Earth. The explorer Ferdinand Magellan is credited with giving this ocean its name, Pacific, which means peaceful in Spanish. This ocean separates the North American continent on the west from Asia and Australia. A few island countries can be found in the Pacific Ocean and one U.S. state. Can you name it? If you said Hawaii, then you are correct!

The Arctic Ocean - This ocean is north of Canada, Europe and Asia. It is also known as the North Pole Region. Even though you can travel across the North Pole Region on foot, it's not a continent because there is no land under it, only the frozen water of the Arctic Ocean. The ice is about 6 to 10-feet thick and floats on top of the ocean. In the winter, the North Pole region is about the size of the U.S., but in the summer, half of it melts into the ocean.

The Southern Ocean - This ocean is found on the southern Polar Region of our Earth - the South Pole! It connects to the southern ends of the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans. Like the Arctic, it is a cold ocean. Unlike the Arctic, however, it surrounds a landmass - the continent of Antarctica!

The Indian Ocean - The Indian Ocean is south of the continent of Asia, west of Australia and east of Africa. This ocean is rich in natural resources like oil, fish and minerals. This ocean is the third-largest ocean on Earth.

title: Look Down! Ocean Cartographer Marie Tharp (1920-2006)
text:
“Don’t look down!” is a line you may have heard in movies, usually while the heroes are walking on a narrow bridge over a dangerous pit. For Marie Tharp, however, “looking down” was just part of the job.

Tharp was a very smart woman, and she spent most of her life learning new things. She earned several college degrees, including degrees in English, music, math and geology. During World War II when many men were off fighting, Marie’s college invited young women to join the geology department, and Marie accepted. She became interested in studying the bottom of the ocean. Unfortunately, this was during a time when women were not allowed to work “in the field.” Marie thought about quitting until her father encouraged her to find a way to do what she loved. Thanks to this, she continued to follow her dream of exploring the ocean.

Her hard work and determination paid off. In 1965, she was able to join a cartographer named Bruce Heezen on an ocean expedition. Together, Marie and Bruce completed several maps of the ocean floor, made discoveries about how the Earth’s tectonic plates and ridges fit together and sparked a new wave of interest in ocean exploration. Her discoveries also helped to prove the theory of continental drift, which was under debate at that time. Tharp was named one of the greatest cartographers of the 20th century and received many awards and honors for her work. Although she died in 2006, Marie Tharp remains an inspiration to many people to this day.

title: A Trip to the Louvre
text:
Dear Diary,

It was an exciting day at school. Our class celebrated World Tourism Day. Ms. Johnson made food and set up exhibits from other countries. The entire classroom felt like a world market. Steven and I could not believe all of the cool things we saw!

We watched a short video about the Great Wall of China. Steven and I ate crème de papaya— a Brazilian ice cream. Want to know the best part of all? Steven and I were transported to the Louvre Museum in Paris, France. I have never been so excited in my life! Stepping into the museum was like a dream come true. The first thing Steven wanted to see was the "Mona Lisa." Can you believe that painting has been in the Louvre since 1797? The "Mona Lisa" is so popular, it has its own wing at the Louvre!

Did you know over 7 million people visit the Louvre each year? In fact, it is the most popular museum in the world. It contains large collections of art and jewelry. Steven and I saw earrings that were once owned by Emperor Napoleon's wife. It must have been over 150 years old!

I guess that's all for now. Steven and I can't wait for our next trip! I wonder where it will be.

Until next time,

Natalia

title: Around the World in a Day
text:
Steven and Natalia, excited to see what Ms. Johnson had planned for them today, headed to their classroom. They opened the door and could hardly believe their eyes. Ms. Johnson had transformed the room into different countries!

"Wow! Look at the room, Steven. It's beautiful!" The room was filled with artifacts from places like Brazil, France, China, Egypt and Japan. On Ms. Johnson's desk, Steven and Natalia found some travel pamphlets with images of more artifacts and places for each country on display.

"School starts in 15 minutes. Let's explore a country, Natalia," Steven suggested, grabbing a pamphlet.

"Great idea. Where do you want to go first?"

"How about Brazil?"

Natalia and Steven walked to the display of Brazil. They saw pictures of the Amazon Rainforest and exotic animals. The two touched the picture of an exotic bird in the display and suddenly, they were transported to a boat on the Amazon River.

"This is incredible, Steven! The trees are tall and green. There are colorful birds everywhere!"

"I can't believe we're in a jungle, Natalia!"

"Did you know there are 40,000 types of plants in the Amazon, Steven?"

"Sure did. I also know this jungle has over 2.5 million insects."

"Yikes! That's a lot of bugs. It's getting dark, Steven. Open the pamphlet and take us to another country."

"Close your eyes, Natalia. This next country is a surprise."

Steven pointed to France and placed Natalia's hand on the page. Before they knew it, they were standing in front of the Louvre Museum, in France. Steven and Natalia ran as quickly as they could to see the "Mona Lisa."

"What a beautiful painting!" Natalia exclaimed. "Leonardo Da Vinci painted her over 500 years ago."

"Wow! That's a pretty old painting," Steven said in surprise. "Hey, Natalia, let's go see a few more places! Where should we go next?"

"I've always wanted to see Mount Fuji in Japan, let's go there next!" Natalia and Steven touched the island country of Japan on their pamphlet and were transported to the city of Tokyo.

"Wow! I didn't know you could see Mount Fuji from Tokyo. We're lucky it's a clear day outside," Natalia said looking at the volcano.

"In Japan, they call Mount Fuji 'Fujisan,'" Steven said. "It is one of three holy mountains in Japanese tradition."

"Where to next, Steven?" Natalia asked.

"If we're in Japan now, we're not too far away from China. They are both in Asia. Let's go there next. We can take a look at the Great Wall."

The children touched the pamphlet and found themselves standing on the Great Wall of China.

"Ms. Johnson's pamphlet says the wall was first built during the Qin dynasty," said Steven. "The Chinese built it to isolate themselves from outside threats."

"That's right, Steven. It's also made up of many different structures, too. They wind across the country, but the wall doesn't cross the entire country."

"This is incredible, Natalia! But we can't stay here forever. Where should we go to now?"

"Oh! Let's go see the Taj Mahal!"

Natalia and Steven zipped to the city of Agra in India, where the 240-foot tall Taj Mahal can be seen.

"This is amazing, Steven! It took about 20 years to build. The name Taj Mahal name means 'Crown Palace' and was built to be the resting place for the Emporer Shah Jahan's late wife, Mumtaz Mahal."

"It has been made a World Heritage Site and is considered one of the Seven Wonders of the World," Steven said, whistling in appreciation at the incredible structure before them.

"We sure saw a lot, and look at the time! It's almost time for class to start. Let's get going, Steven."

Steven and Natalia touched the pamphlet once more and were whisked back to their classroom, and just in the nick of time. Ms. Johnson walked in moments later and smiled to see Steven and Natalia were early for class. "Hello, Steven and Natalia! Are you ready to learn about some new countries today?"

"We sure are!"

title: Let's Write
text: You and your family have been invited to spend two weeks with an Egyptian family during your summer vacation. This family has never traveled to the United States. They asked you to bring three items that represent your life in the United States. What three items would you bring? In one or two paragraphs, describe the items you would bring and discuss their importance in your daily life.

title: Globe Trotting
text:
Egypt

Take a moment to think about Egypt. What pictures come to your mind? If you are like most people, you probably immediately think of pharaohs, mummies and pyramids. Egypt, however, has a rich history. Located on the continent of Africa, this country has given many gifts to the world.

As a student, you use paper to write notes and record your work. Paper is an important part of your life. At first, Egyptians wrote messages in stone. In 3000 B.C.E. they created sheets of paper using papyrus. This is a plant that grew in Egypt. Egyptians recorded their messages on this paper. They shared their messages with each other. This inspired other countries to create their own forms of paper.

Italy

Italy is a boot-shaped peninsula surrounded on all three sides by the Mediterranean sea. The capital of Italy is the city of Rome. Here, you can see the Leaning Tower of Pisa, the Colosseum and many other structures dating back to the Roman Empire.

Italy is part of the European continent and is another country that has given us many gifts that we still use today. One such example that we use every day is Roman letters. In fact, we're using them right now! The letters used today for writing in English and many other languages come to us from the Roman Empire. The Romans themselves adapted it from older alphabets of the Semitic and Etruscan writing systems before 600 B.C.E.

Spain

"¡Hola!" is how you say, "hello!" in Spanish. Many countries on the American continents speak Spanish as their primary language. This is because, during the Age of Exploration, sailors and explorers from Spain traveled to the American continent from Europe and brought their language with them when they landed.

Madrid is the capital of Spain, but one of the more famous cities in this country is Pamplona. Every year, thousands of Spanish natives and visitors from all over the world come to this city to participate in fiestas celebrated to honor San Fermín. San Fermín is the patron saint of Pamplona.

The most famous of these celebrations is probably the Running of the Bulls, or the Encierro. The tradition arose from the need to move bulls from their corrals to the bullring.

Great Britain

England, Wales and Scotland make up Great Britain. These countries are also part of the greater United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. All of these countries (England, Wales, Scotland and Ireland) make up the British Isles.

Great Britain is ruled over by the British monarchy. The current head of the British monarchy is King Charles III. The British monarchy does most of its governing from the capital city, London.

You may know that at one point during the early history of the United States, we were ruled over by the British government. It didn't last for very long, however. During the 1700s, we fought a war against Great Britain known as the American Revolution. After this war, we separated and formed our own country with our own government.

Great Britain is part of the European continent. Roughly 5,000 years ago, this land was mostly covered in thick forests and woodland. As settlers and migrants from different parts of Europe moved to the British Isles, they cleared these forests for farmland.

Russia

The country of Russia has experienced many changes over the course of its history. It is the northern-most country on the Asian continent and is currently the largest country in the world. It takes up one-tenth of all the land on Earth. That is a lot of land! But can you believe it was once even bigger than it is now?

During the early 1900s, Russia was part of the USSR, or the Soviet Union. The USSR was comprised of Russia and 11 other countries. By the 1980s, however, many countries wanted to separate from the Soviet Union and form their own governments. The capital of Russia is the city of Moscow.

title: Meet Author Paulo Coelho
text:
Childhood Dreams

Paulo Coelho was born in Brazil on August 24, 1947. Paulo was shy. He spent much of his time alone. As a young child, Paulo loved writing stories. He dreamed of becoming a writer. That is all he ever wanted to do. His parents had other ideas. They didn't think writing would be a good job for him. They wanted him to go to law school. Paulo did not want to study law. He went to law school to make his parents happy, but he quit school after the first year.

A Life-Changing Event

Paulo left Brazil to explore South America, North Africa, Mexico and Europe. In 1986 Paulo walked 500 miles. He traveled throughout Spain. This journey changed his life. Paulo never forgot his dream of becoming a writer. He wrote a book about his journey. It's called, "The Pilgrimage." The book was published in 1987.

A Best-Selling Author

Paulo quit his other jobs as a songwriter and actor to become a full-time writer. He was happy about his new career. In 1988 he wrote "The Alchemist." This book made him famous. It has sold over 65 million copies. Paulo has written over 20 books. He currently lives in Switzerland with his wife. He loves to encourage children to follow their dreams.

title: An Amazing Archipelago
text:
Japan is actually a chain of islands known as an "archipelago." Most of the 125 million Japanese citizens live on the four large islands of Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu, and Shikoku. If you add in all the smaller islands, you’ll see that Japan is actually comprised of more than 6,000 islands. That may sound like it’s a large country, but it’s not. Compared to the United States, Japan is relatively small. The state of California is nearly the same size as the entire country.

Obviously, being so close to the Sea of Japan and the Pacific Ocean, water plays a significant role in the lives of the Japanese people. Fishing is a major industry, and seafood plays a large part in their diet. Bluefin tuna, salmon, pollock, sea cucumbers and crabs are some of the valuable fishing species pulled from these waters. The Sea of Japan lies between Japan and the Asian mainland countries of South Korea, North Korea and Russia.

Mountains dominate the landscape of Japan. Nearly 70 percent of the land is mountainous. Alongside these mountains lie millions of acres of forest. Of the mountainous land, two-thirds of it is covered by forests of spruce, fir, oak and beech trees.

Many of the world’s active volcanoes lie in Japan. In fact, snow-capped and cone-shaped Mount Fuji, which rises more than 12,000 feet above sea level, can be seen from Japan’s capital city of Tokyo nearly 60 miles away. Volcanoes, however, are not the most widely feared natural disaster. The island nation’s location in the Pacific Ring of Fire means that earthquakes, and the tsunamis (long sea waves caused by earthquakes) they create, have caused more trouble. In 2011, a massive undersea earthquake off the eastern coast of Japan triggered a tsunami with 30-foot waves. More than 20,000 people died in the disaster.

title: Traveling the World!
text:
There are so many neat physical features around the world, but one you may not know much about is the Gobi Desert.

The Gobi is approximately 500,000 square miles of desert, covering parts of Mongolia and China. When most people think of deserts, they think of a hot, sandy region. However, the Gobi Desert can reach minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit and is mostly rocky. So, why is it considered a desert? The defining characteristic of a desert is lack of water, not heat. Average rainfall in this region is only about 7 inches per year. The name 'Gobi' in Mongolian roughly translates to "the waterless place." The high winds this area receives, combined with the lack of rain, means that the desert grows bigger every year.

Very few people live there (only about three people per square mile). The two major groups of inhabitants are Han Chinese and Mongols. The Chinese live in clay brick homes and earn a living through limited farming. The Mongols are largely nomadic. They travel across the desert, moving with their herds of cattle such as sheep and goats.

title: The Sahara Desert
text:
A desert is an ecosystem that does not see very much rain during the year. Some parts of the Sahara desert only see 3 inches of rain in a year. The Sahara Desert stretches across several northern African countries. It is one of the largest, hottest deserts in the world. The Sahara covers about a third of the entire continent.

Even though the Sahara is extremely dry, some experts think this wasn't always the case. Historians have found old rock paintings in the western part of the desert. The paintings show animals like elephants and rhinos. Experts think that these animals lived in the area about 3,000 to 8,000 years ago and left the area, moving south, when the dry times began.

The Sahara Desert is a hard place to live. Strong winds create sand dunes. Some dunes grow up to 600 feet tall. Temperatures can reach a sweltering 136 degrees Fahrenheit. Even with these challenges, people have found ways to travel across the Sahara Desert safely. Nomads travel across the desert with sheep, goats and camels. They walk from oasis to oasis. An oasis is a small area in a desert with water, trees and fertile land. These oases can be several days of travel apart from each other.

The harsh desert is home to resourceful animals like foxes, hyenas, jackals and antelopes. Many of these animals are nocturnal. This means they sleep during the day and come out at night. It helps them avoid the hottest parts of the day.

title: Let's Write
text: Congratulations, reporter! You have been asked to write a news article about what it's like to travel to the Himalayan Mountains. You've been given the opportunity to take a luxury trip to visit this incredible mountain range. Write an article from the perspective of a first-time traveler to this area of the world.

title: A World of Natural Wonders
text:
Rivers

Amazon

Located in South America, as of 2007, the Amazon is now considered the longest river in the world. Some Brazilian scientists traced the source of the Amazon to a tall mountain in the country of Peru. The Amazon winds its way along the northern part of South America from Peru and drains into the Atlantic at a point found in northern Brazil.

Nile

Have you ever wanted to visit the Nile River? It is found along the northeastern side of the African continent. It flows northward for just over 4,000 miles from Uganda and Ethiopia and empties into the Mediterranean Sea. For a long time, it held the title of the longest river in the world.

Mountains and Ranges

Alps

The Alps are the tallest mountain range in Europe. They are one of the most popular sites for skiing in the world. Two of the more famous peaks are Mont Blanc and the Matterhorn.

Andes

This mountain range is the longest in the world. The Andes Mountains run for 5,000 miles along the entire western length of the South American continent beginning in Venezuela and ending at the southern tips of Chile and Argentina. These mountains were once home to the ancient Inca civilization. Over 50 volcanoes can be found along this mountain range and many of them are still active!

Himalayas

The Himalayas are a mountain range found in Asia. The world’s tallest mountain, Mount Everest, is part of this range. Over the years, many people have attempted to scale Mount Everest to reach its summit. The geography of the Himalayas means that the peaks are covered in ice and snow year-round, which makes it very difficult and dangerous to climb. The first people to successfully reach the summit were Sir Edmund Hilary and Sherpa Tenzing Norgay in 1953.

Deserts

Gobi

The Gobi Desert is located in the northern part of Asia. Several cities along the Silk Road were once found through the Gobi Desert. Every year the Gobi devours grassland in China. Scientists are so alarmed that they intend to plant a line of new forest on the border of the desert to slow down the expansion. It has been called "The Green Wall of China."

Sahara

The Sahara Desert, which covers most of North Africa, is the largest hot desert on Earth. Despite the extreme heat and lack of water, people and animals have still been able to live in the Sahara thanks to a few oases and the northern highlands.

Bodies of Water

Mediterranean Sea

The Mediterranean Sea is a sea almost entirely encompassed by continental land. To its north is Europe, south is Africa and to its east is Asia. Some of the earliest human civilizations formed around the Mediterranean. The Phoenicians, ancient Egyptians, Greeks and Romans frequently used this sea for trade and travel. Many of these old civilizations also used this sea to help them conquer or colonize other countries on the surrounding continents.

Straits of Magellan

A strait is a narrow waterway that is both wide and deep enough to let a ship sail through the land or islands that encompass it. The Straits of Magellan are a series of navigable sea routes found along the islands of the southern tip of South America. They were named after the famous colonial explorer Ferdinand Magellan of Portugal.

Landforms

Great Barrier Reef

Found along the northeast coast of Australia, the Great Barrier Reef is the largest coral reef system on our planet. A coral reef is made up of living organisms that have symbiotic (mutually beneficial) relationships with the algae found in the ocean water around it. This relationship has allowed the Great Barrier Reef to grow into the expansive system it is today. In fact, it is large enough that it can be seen with the naked-eye by the astronauts in orbit around the Earth. Many fish and other marine life call the Great Barrier Reef home.

Niagara Falls

These falls can be found along the border between the U.S. and Canada. Niagara Falls is actually a series of three waterfalls, which are called Horseshoe Falls, American Falls and Bridal Veil Falls.

title: Oral Traditions and the Great Barrier Reef
text:
The Great Barrier Reef is a massive underwater feature off the western coast of Australia. It is home to all kinds of marine life. Did you know that there may have been a time when this reef was not underwater? Experts have found clues that tell us that this area was possibly dry land during the last Ice Age.

Aboriginal tribes in Australia have tribal memories told through stories dating back over 10,000 years ago. These oral traditions have been passed down through the years. One tribe has a story about several unique places, that are now all under water.

These stories could be true for many reasons. The tribes in the region are divided by many hundreds of miles. But, they all have stories that describe the now wet coral reefs as massive floodplains. They also all have stories that describe the sea water rising and drowning this dry land. Since the Australian Aboriginals value truth, their oral traditions help them preserve facts. This helps give credibility to the claim that the Great Barrier Reef may have once been livable land.

title: Excitement at Niagara Falls
text:
Niagara Falls. Today on October 24, 1901, Annie Edson Taylor became the first person to survive a trip over Niagara Falls! Mrs. Taylor chose the date of her birthday to complete this brave act of derring-do. The destitute widow and former schoolteacher designed and built a custom barrel to survive the plunge. The side of the barrel reads, "Queen of The Mist."

Originally from Auburn, New York, Mrs. Taylor lost her husband in the Civil War. Since then, she has traveled from place to place working as a schoolteacher. Citing financial hardship, she decided to complete this incredible stunt. She chose Horseshoe Falls on the Canadian side of the river. It is over a 150-foot fall down to the depths below.

Annie's barrel is 5 feet high and 3 feet wide. It is made out of Kentucky oak. The barrel is supported with iron hoops and has several cushions inside for padding. Mrs. Taylor has even strapped a 100-pound anvil to the bottom for ballast. Before taking the trip herself, Mrs. Taylor and her manager needed to first test the barrel for safety. So, they decided to send a cat over the falls first. The cat was shaken and had a small gash on its head, but it survived! Mrs. Taylor then posed for a photo with the cat and decided to continue with the stunt.

Many people crowded the falls to witness the spectacle. Mrs. Taylor, with some help, climbed inside the barrel. Making sure she had her lucky heart-shaped pillow with her, the barrel was then towed out into the middle of the Niagara River. This was when the barrel was cut loose! Mrs. Taylor was tossed around violently by the rough waters before she was carried over the falls. 20 heartpounding minutes after her journey began, Mrs. Taylor arrived on the shore. Miraculously, she was alive!

Several people have already stated that they, too, will try and brave the falls. When asked for comments, Mrs. Taylor had this to say, "Nobody ought ever do that again."

The Heroine of Horseshoe Falls already has a number of speaking engagements lined up, so be sure to hear her recount her tale.

title: From Territories to States
text:
The U.S. has seen a lot of change since the colony of Jamestown was founded in 1607. Several European nations fought in wars for the right to claim America for their own. The 13 Colonies began under British rule, but Americans grew unhappy with their treatment by the British. They eventually decided to break away from Britain and become their own nation. As an independent nation, the American people could self-govern.

Before everything west of the original 13 Colonies became states, the land was sorted into territories or areas of land that hadn't been organized into the U.S. As the country grew, more and more people began to move west. As people successfully colonized areas, they would often want to officially become a U.S. state. At this time, the 13 Colonies began to see changes. Massachusetts Colony used to include the state of Maine, which later became its own state in 1820. Some areas that petitioned for statehood were accepted, and some were not.

For example, Texas proposed cutting the state in half and petitioned the federal government to make the southwest half into the State of Lincoln. Tennessee also submitted such a petition shortly after American Independence. Before being made into a state, the northeast part of Tennessee was called the State of Franklin. People wanted it to become the 14th state, but it was never accepted into the Union.

The U.S. has a lot of states now. We added new states to our great country all the way up until 1959! Alaska and Hawaii were the last two states to be added that year. If you ever watch an old black-and-white movie and someone says they're going out of the country to Alaska, you'll know why now!

title: The Impact of Manifest Destiny
text:
By the mid-1800s, many Americans believed that the United States should spread all the way to the Pacific Ocean, “from sea to shining sea.” The United States, they felt, had the right to take over other countries’ lands in North America. These lands would provide wealth and opportunity to Americans. The belief that the United States had the right to claim new lands was called Manifest Destiny. These words mean “obvious fate.”

There were many consequences that this belief caused. Manifest Destiny and the spread of settlers westward is one of the reasons why we have our 50 states. However, European settlers, through treaties and violence, drove many American Indians off their lands in order to settle them. This lead to things like the Indian Removal Act and the Trail of Tears. The Trail of Tears was the forced march of thousands of Cherokee from their native lands in the Southeast to the state of Oklahoma in 1830.

This journey on foot took these displaced (without a home) Cherokee through many states and territories. The trail was long and difficult and many Cherokee died along the way. Use the scale and compass rose provided to find out how long the journey was on each trail.

title: The Treaty of Paris
text:
It was the start of a new day at school and Ms. Johnson was leading her class in a song that would help them learn the names of each of the 50 states. They sang the lyrics several times, naming each state.

As the singing subsided, Steven asked, "Ms. Johnson, this song helps us learn the names of each state, but how can we learn where each state is located?"

"Good question, Steven. There are a couple of tricks you can do. You can imagine that the shape of each state stands for a letter or familiar object," Ms. Johnson said. "Louisiana is shaped like a giant 'L' and the bottom of Nevada is shaped like a 'V.'"

Ms. Johnson dug through her chest of maps and artifacts. "Of course, the locations and sizes of each state changed over time as our country grew older. Look at these, class," she called holding up an ancient-looking map. "This map was drawn by John Mitchell in 1755. He was a physician and botanist, but also drew several early maps of America. This one shows the boundaries of the North American Colonies owned by Great Britain before they became states!"

As Ms. Johnson laid the map out on her desk, Natalia and Steven placed their hands on the map at the same time and they appeared on the sidewalk out in front of the Hotel D'York, in Paris. They had been transported to 1783!

"This is where they signed the Treaty of Paris. Let's go inside this hotel and see if we can spot Ben Franklin," Steven suggested.

Inside the old hotel, in a large room, sat a massive desk. On one side stood Benjamin Franklin, John Jay, Henry Laurens and John Adams. On the other side stood two Englishmen: Richard Oswald and David Hartley.

"Those two are here to represent King George III. They are his aides," Natalia whispered.

The men seemed to be discussing important matters, such as boundary lines and how the 13 Colonies would change. They also talked about releasing the prisoners of war. On the desk, the children could see a map of the 13 Colonies that looked just like the one that transported them here! They must've used Mitchell's map during the signing of the Treaty of Paris and that's why they were transported here.

“We’d better go,” Steven whispered. He took Natalia's hand and they tiptoed out of the room. After quietly closing the door behind themselves, Steven held up the map and Natalia reached out to touch it. In a flash, they were transported back to their classroom.

"Can anyone tell me which states the original 13 Colonies would become?" Ms. Johnson asked.

Steven and Natalia both shot their hands up. After their adventure, they felt prepared to answer this question.

"Go ahead, students."

"Well, there was Pennsylvania, Delaware, New Jersey, Georgia ..."

"Connecticut, Massachusetts, Maryland, South Carolina, North Carolina, New Hampshire, New York and..."

"Rhode Island!"

"That's correct. Now, does anyone remember what the signing of the Treaty of Paris meant?" Ms. Johnson asked.

"The end of the Revolutionary War!" several voices cried.

"Very good!" Ms. Johnson beamed.

title: Hustle & Bustle: Big City Life
text:
What are cities?

A city is an urban area where lots of people live, work and spend their time. They have large populations and can be very exciting! Population is the number of people who live in an area. Cities have higher populations than suburban and other living areas do.

Cities are full of diversity! This means they have people from many different places, cultures and religions. Because of all this diversity, there are many exciting things to do, see and even eat in cities. Cities are a great place to learn about how other people live.

Why do people live in cities?

People choose to live in cities for many reasons. Some people migrate to cities for job opportunities. Migration is when someone moves from one place to live in another. Cities provide many places where people can work. There are jobs at businesses, schools, shops and almost anywhere else imaginable.

Another reason people choose to live in cities is for education. Cities are often home to many colleges and universities. There are special schools for younger children as well. You can study almost any topic imaginable in a big city.

Finally, people love to live in cities for entertainment. There is always something to do! Cities are full of life. There are restaurants everywhere. You can find food from almost any country. There are also many places to see music or plays. You can choose from hundreds of places to shop. You might spend a day relaxing in a park or exploring a museum.

How can so many people live so closely?

title: The Island of Hope
text:
Did you know that about 40 percent of United States citizens can trace their family history all the way back to Ellis Island? Over 12 million people passed through Ellis Island between 1892 and 1954. As they sailed into the port, their ships would pass the Statue of Liberty. In fact, the tall statue would often be the first landmark they could see from afar. A symbol they would associate with their hopes and ambitions. They called Ellis Island “The Island of Hope.” They came here, after all, hoping to find a better life for themselves and their families.

When they traveled here by ship, first and second class passengers were processed on the ship. When people were processed, this meant they had to be healthy, answer a lot of questions and have the right paperwork to enter the country. The U.S. government wanted to be careful and make sure no new diseases were brought into the country.

Third class passengers were processed on Ellis Island. As Many as 5,000 people went through Ellis Island on busy days. They often waited for hours or days before it was their turn. Doctors checked them for illnesses and disease. If they seemed sick, they were sent for more tests. Some sick people were sent to a hospital on the island. They were allowed to stay in the U.S. if they got better. They were sent home if they did not.

Every immigrant (a person who moves to another country) was asked roughly 30 questions. They were asked about where they were born and how much money they had. They were also asked about where they were going.

Today, Ellis Island is a museum. Many people visit to learn more about their family history.

title: Chicago Citizen Wins Pulitzer Prize
text:
Did you know that a woman from Chicago was the first African American to win a Pulitzer Prize? Her name was Gwendolyn Brooks. She won the Pulitzer Prize for a book of poems that she wrote in 1950 titled, "Annie Allen."

The Pulitzer Prize is an award given to writers and photographers whose work is the best of the year. The prize was started by an American newspaper owner named Joseph Pulitzer.

Gwendolyn Brooks was born in Kansas but grew up in Chicago. Her love for words began when she was young. Her mother would take her to the library when she was about four or five. She loved reading poetry. She even tried rhyming her own words when she was just seven years old.

Brooks was writing her own poems by age 11. She even mailed some of them to a Chicago newspaper. Her first poem was published in a children’s magazine when she was 13. She wrote hundreds of poems during her lifetime.

Brooks often wrote about what everyday life was like for black people. She wrote about racism and being poor. She also wrote about the struggles of black women in the 1940s and 1950s.
