title: Visiting the Big Apple and Other Major Cities
text:
New York City is a major city located in the northeastern part of the U.S. and the southeastern part of the state of New York. It is situated where the Atlantic Ocean and Hudson River meet. It has a population of about 8.6 million people. New York City is the largest city in the state. It is also the largest city in the U.S. and covers 302.6 square miles of land. While it is not the largest city geographically, it is the largest city from a population standpoint with the largest population density. New York City is made up of five boroughs and three islands. The boroughs are called Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island. The islands of New York are Manhattan, Long Island and Staten Island. New York City is known for being the cultural, financial and media capital of the world. One of New York City’s most famous nicknames is “The Big Apple.” What is another nickname for New York City?

Chicago is a major city located in northeastern Illinois. It is situated on Lake Michigan, one of the Great Lakes. It has a population of almost 3 million people. Chicago is the largest city in Illinois. It is also the third-largest city in the U.S. and covers 237 square miles of land. Chicago is known for its diverse neighborhoods, food and culture. In fact, on St. Patrick’s Day, it is the city’s tradition to dye the Chicago River green. Chicago's location next to the Great Lakes makes Chicago quite windy. In fact, one of Chicago’s nicknames is “The Windy City.” Can you discover another one of Chicago’s nicknames?

Los Angeles is a major city located in southern California. It is situated on the Pacific Ocean. It has a population of about 4 million people. Los Angeles is the largest city in the state. It is also the second largest city in the U.S. and covers 472 square miles of land. Los Angeles is known for its rich cultural diversity, its great weather and its entertainment industry. In fact, Los Angeles is considered the entertainment capital of the world. It is also nicknamed the “City of Angels” because of the Spanish meaning of its name. Los Angeles means “the angels.” What is another nickname for Los Angeles?

Seattle is a large city located in the northwest part of Washington. Seattle has a population of about 700,000 people, making it the largest city in the state. In fact, it is the largest northernmost city in the Continental United States and is only about 100 miles from the Canadian border. It is situated on the eastern shore of Puget Sound in the northern Pacific Ocean and covers 83.9 square miles. Seattle is known for its coffee, rainy days, glassblowing and beautiful mountains. One of Seattle’s nicknames is the “Emerald City.” Can you discover another nickname for Seattle?

Miami is a large city located in the southeastern part of Florida. It is situated on the Miami River between the Florida Everglades and the Atlantic Ocean and covers 56 square miles. It has a population of about 460,000 people. Miami is known for its rich Latin American culture, its Cuban American cuisine, its Art Deco and many neighborhoods, including Overtown — popular during the Harlem Renaissance. Miami has been nicknamed the “Magic City.” Can you find out why?

Washington, D.C., or the District of Columbia, is the capital of the United States of America. It has a population of almost 700,000 people. It is a territory and not a state. It has a mayor and a city council. It is considered a federal city because it is the seat of our nation’s government. It is situated on the northern shore of the Potomac River. It is bordered by Maryland on the north, east and west and Virginia on the southern shore of the Potomac River. Washington, D.C. is home to the White House, Capitol Hill, the Supreme Court, many memorials, monuments and museums. Can you discover one of the nicknames for our nation’s capital?

title: Symbols of Freedom
text:
In the U.S., we use symbols (something that stands for something else) to represent ideas that are important to us, such as freedom, courage, liberty and patriotism. Let's look at some of our country’s most famous symbols, where they can be seen and what they represent.

The Statue of Liberty

One of our most famous symbols is the Statue of Liberty. She can be found in the state of New York. At 150 feet tall, Lady Liberty proudly welcomes citizens, visitors and immigrants alike to New York Harbor. Her raised torch lights the way for all who want the peace, freedom and human rights the U.S. offers. The statue was a gift to the U.S. from France in 1886. They sent it to us to celebrate our alliance during the American Revolution. The statue has since become a symbol of our country's commitment to democracy and freedom to all.

The Flag of the United States of America

Our country’s first flag was made more than 200 years ago in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. There have been many changes to the flag over the years. Today, the American flag is made up of 13 red and white stripes which represent the original 13 colonies. The flag also has a square of blue in the upper-left corner with 50 white stars. These represent the 50 states that currently make up the United States.

The Liberty Bell

In July of 1776, the Declaration of Independence was completed. The Liberty Bell was hung in the tower of Independence Hall in Philadelphia. It rang out, calling people to listen to the public reading of the new document and to celebrate! This meant the U.S. had decided to separate itself from Great Britain. The Liberty Bell is a symbol of the courage of our forefathers in declaring themselves free to create their own government.

The Bald Eagle

The bald eagle became the national emblem of the United States in 1782 in Pennsylvania. The eagle represents freedom, as it is free to fly wherever it wishes. The bald eagle can be found on the backs of the silver dollar, the half dollar, the quarter and our gold coins.

title: What’s in a Name?
text:
Dear Natalia,

Thank you for your last letter. I am so excited that you are learning about cities with American Indian names.

The first people to live in the Miami area were the Calusa. They were a group of American Indians. The name Miami comes from the Calusa word “Myami.” It means “big water.” Their village was located on the north bank of the Miami River. Eventually, it became the city of Miami.

Seattle, in Washington, is named after an American Indian leader. His name was Chief Seattle. He was friendly to the settlers that came to the Pacific Northwest area. They named their village after Chief Seattle because they were so thankful to him.

The city of Chicago has its American Indian origins, too. There are a few different theories about the name. One is that it comes from the word "shikaakwa." This was the Algonquin name of an onion-like plant that grew in the area.

There are many other cities with American Indian names. Can you think of any?

I hope to see you soon!

Love,

Grandma

title: Human Geography
text:
Geography is the study of Earth's natural features. Physical geography focuses on landforms like mountains, plains, rivers, lakes, plateaus, hills and valleys. North America has a lot of different features. What you see changes based on where you are. Some people live near oceans and rivers, while others live on mountains or near forests.

Another way to study the Earth is to look at human geography. Human geography is the study of how people interact with their environment. People have to adapt to what is around them. Everything from plants and animals to the weather can change the way people live.

Human beings interact with the land in several ways in order to meet their needs. The actions of human beings can have a negative impact on the environment.

Rivers have been polluted by chemicals that are released into the water by persons who use pesticides and insecticides. Trees get cut down and land is cleared to make way for farming and building houses and buildings. There's also air pollution from factories and cars. Excessive hunting and fishing have affected or changed the ecosystem.

Not all human interactions with the environment are negative, though. For example, a lot of people do what they can to take care of their physical environment. Some people practice recycling, which is less harmful to the environment and makes use of existing resources. There are wildlife preserves and national parks that protect land from pollution and development (building of houses and buildings). There are also clean energy resources, such as solar and wind energy, which don't create harmful pollutants.

Taking care of our environment takes work, but the first step starts with you! Turn off the faucet when you brush your teeth. Use the recycling bin instead of the garbage. Just remember, a little bit goes a long way!

title: Lewis & Clark's Exploration
text:
Meriwether Lewis and William Clark explored the vast wilderness of the West. While journeying, they wrote down their experiences with the land and the American Indians they encountered on their way.

Lewis and Clark were looking for a water route that would lead to the Pacific Ocean. Read the excerpts from their journals below and find clues that tell us about their experience. Look for familiar things that tell you which features they are writing about. As you read, also take note of the differences in spelling and punctuation from how we write today.

Captain William Clark
June 18th Tuesday 1805

we Set out early and arrived at the second great Cataract [waterfall] ... this is one of the grandest views in nature and by far exceeds any thing I ever Saw, the Missouri falling over a Shelveing rock for 47 feet 8 Inches ...

...we proceeded on up the river a little more than a mile to the largest fountain or Spring I ever Saw, and doubt if it is not the largest in America Known ...

Meriwether Lewis
Saturday June 29th 1805

...a most violent torrent of rain ... appeared to decend in a body and instantly collected in the rivene and came down in a roling torrent with irrisistable force driving rocks mud and everything before it ... Capt. C. fortunately discovered it a moment before it reached them and seizing his gun and shot pouch with his left hand with the right he assisted himself up the steep bluff shoving occasionaly the Indian woman before him who had her child in her arms ... and but for Capt. C. both himself and this [wo]man and child must have perished ...

Captain William Clark
August 17th Satturday 1805

We Set out at 7 oClock and proceeded on to the forks ... I saw at a distance Several Indians on horsback Comeing towards me, The Intertrepeter & Squar [Sacagawea] who were before me at Some distance danced for the joyful Sight, and She made signs to me that they were her nation ...

...The Great Chief of this nation proved to be the brother of the Woman[Sacagawea] with us and is a man of Influence ... & reserved manners, appears to possess a great deel of Cincerity ...

...This nation Call themselves Cho-shon-nê [Shoshone].

title: The Grand Canyon
text:
The Grand Canyon is considered one of the seven natural wonders of the world because of its huge size and amazing beauty. The canyon, located in northwestern Arizona, is 277 miles long, up to 18 miles wide and more than 5,000 feet deep. The canyon is one of the greatest examples of water erosion in the world. Visitors to the canyon can see the path cut through the soft sandstone by the Colorado River over a period of about 6 million years. More than 5 million people visit the canyon each year.

One of the most interesting ways to explore the canyon is by walking the breathtaking new Grand Canyon Skywalk. The skywalk is a U-shaped glass bridge that extends out 70 feet away from the canyon wall and seems to float 2,000 feet in the air. Visitors can take a walk on the bridge and get a bird's-eye view of the gorge.

title: Storytime on the Mississippi
text:
When they touched Ms. Johnson’s first edition copy of The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, Natalia and Steven arrived on the muddy banks of a vast and rolling river. They stood near a small dock toward the back of a small crowd facing a man standing on the dock. He had a thick head of white hair, a white handlebar mustache, a light-weight suit and a cane. He looked out toward the river and smiled.

"I remember the first time I saw the Mississippi. I had never been so impressed. I was impressed by the water and eventually by the men who piloted the steamboats traveling it," the man said. "I knew that one day I would be one of them. They were truly free men who lived by their skill and their wits," he added. "As with most things in my life, it took me a while to get around to the business of being a steamboat pilot, but I did it," he said with a wink.

"Hey," Steven said. "Isn't that Mark Twain?"

"I think so. He looks just like the author's picture from the video about his life that Ms. Johnson showed us," Natalia replied.

The man continued speaking, "When my family moved here to Hannibal, Missouri, this river began to shape my life. I played along the river with my friends. I met new and interesting people who stopped in our town going up and down the Mississippi. I also enjoyed many experiences which I later used as inspiration for my writing.

"It wasn't all fun. There were sad times, too. I helped my brother, Henry, get a post on a steamboat. He died in a boiler explosion. Bad business, that. It was the beginning of me leaving my life as a steamboat pilot.

"I returned to writing for newspapers. Many of my pieces shared stories from my time on the Mississippi. My novel about Huckleberry Finn is based on a dear childhood friend of mine. He was poor and not much on schooling. However, he also proved to be one of the smartest and most loyal people I would ever meet."

"Wow, I never knew that he based a lot of his writing on his own experiences," Steven said.

"Did you know that Mark Twain's real name was Samuel L. Clemens?" Natalia asked as they turned away from the small crowd gathered at the docks. "He changed his name to Mark Twain because he liked riverboats so much. It's a measuring term. If something was measured as "mark twain" that meant the water was deep enough for a boat to pass safely."

"That's so interesting!" Steven said. "Come on, let's get back to class."

title: Physical Features of the U.S.
text:
These images show the physical features of the continental United States (states that are in direct contact with each other). These are the states of our nation that span (spread across) the whole North American continent. These continental states share many physical features. Some examples are lakes, rivers, oceans, mountains, deserts and plains. Natural landmarks are well-known geographic features that mark a certain place, like the Grand Canyon.

Alaska Range

The mountains of Alaska extend from the Alaska Peninsula to the border of the Yukon Territory in Canada. It was originally named the Alaskan Range, but over time, popular use changed the name to “Alaska Range.” The Alaska Range has the highest mountain in North America, called Denali, which rises to an elevation of 20,343 feet. It is also part of the Pacific Ring of Fire, which is a horseshoe-shaped line around the Pacific Ocean where frequent earthquakes and volcanoes happen.

Rocky Mountains

The Rocky Mountains are about 3,000 miles long. They stretch from New Mexico up through the western United States and into Canada. The Rockies, as they are nicknamed, are a popular tourist destination, thanks to the abundance of ideal places for hunting, fishing, camping, hiking, skiing, snowboarding and other outdoor activities. There are several national parks along the Rocky Mountains including popular ones like Glacier National Park and Yellowstone National Park.

Appalachian Mountains

The Appalachian Mountain range is about 1,500 miles long. It spreads from central Alabama through the New England states and Canada. The Appalachians used to be as tall as the Rocky Mountains, but natural erosion has worn them down over time. Now, the tallest mountain in the Appalachians reaches an elevation of 6,684 feet. One of the things the Appalachian Mountains are most famous for is the Appalachian Trail. It stretches from Springer Mountain in Georgia all the way up to Mount Katahdin in Maine. The entire trail runs for 2,175 miles. That’s one heck of a hike!

Great Plains

The Great Plains are in the middle of North America and stretch as far north as Canada. In Canada, the plains are more commonly called the prairie. The land is mostly flat with large, treeless areas and shallow river valleys. The Great Plains are commonly used for farming and cattle ranching.

Great Basin

The Great Basin is an arid area of land between the Wasatch Range and the Sierra Nevada Range. It covers most of Nevada and parts of Utah, Wyoming, Idaho, Oregon and California. The Great Basin has the largest amount of natural basins in the country. Rains fall in the winter months, and in the summer months, the heat evaporates the water from the basins. This results in places like the Bonneville Salt Flats. The Great Basin is home to Great Basin National Park, where you can find some of the oldest trees in the world!

Grand Canyon

The Grand Canyon is a 277 mile-long canyon located in northern Arizona. It is over a mile deep at its deepest point and was formed by the Colorado River, which runs along its floor. People from all over the world come to Arizona to visit this natural wonder. Rafting, sightseeing, hiking, and helicopter tours are among the most popular activities at the Grand Canyon.

Great Lakes

The Great Lakes include Lake Huron, Lake Ontario, Lake Michigan, Lake Erie and Lake Superior. They are in the northeastern part of our country and form a border between the U.S. and Canada. These lakes are the largest freshwater lakes on Earth. For as long as they’ve been around, the Great Lakes have played a significant role in trade and transportation in the Great Lakes Region.

Gulf of Mexico

The Gulf of Mexico is located along the curve of the southern coast of America and the eastern coast of Mexico. It is believed to have been formed by plate tectonics over 300 million years ago. Due to the small opening that connects it to the Atlantic Ocean, the Gulf of Mexico experiences little variance in the rise and fall of the tide.

title: Major Rivers of the U.S.
text:
In the U.S., rivers connect us to the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. Let’s take a look at a few of some of these amazing natural features.

The Mississippi River

“Mississippi” means “great water” in Chippewa. This river flows from Minnesota to the Gulf of Mexico. Along with its tributaries (streams or rivers flowing into a larger body of water), it is the fourth-largest river in the world. The Mississippi was an important river in the old days. Now, even though the land has changed and there are more roads and trains, the river's importance hasn't died. The Mississippi River is still used by barges and towboats to carry crops, industrial products and other things from state to state. In fact, of all the freight that travel America's waterways, about 60 percent of it travels the Mississippi.

The Rio Grande

The Rio Grande begins in Colorado of the United States and flows 1,896 miles down to the Gulf of Mexico. It forms part of the border between Mexico and the U.S. where it runs along the southwestern side of Texas. Despite past disputes, today, the U.S. and Mexico share the water from the Rio Grande thanks to a series of agreements.

The Ohio River

The mouth of the Ohio River is located near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. The Ohio River is the largest tributary of the Mississippi River. It was once a major transportation and trade route. Together, the valleys created by the Mississippi and Ohio River systems provide water to farmlands in over half of the U.S.!

The Colorado River

Water is a powerful force of nature. It passes over stones and rocks, eroding them away over many millions of years. In fact, it took the Colorado River over 6 million years to carve out the Grand Canyon! However, the Grand Canyon is not the Colorado River's only major feat. Like the Arkansas River, its source can be found in the Rocky Mountains of Colorado. From there, the river runs almost 1,500 miles, all the way to California. Along the way, it provides water to 30 million people. Talk about a resource!

title: Tennessee's Beauty ... Underground?!
text:
Ms. Johnson: Welcome class! Today we continue to learn about Tennessee. We will use maps to find cities, rivers and mountains in our state. As we work together using these maps and our books, we will learn interesting things about each city. Each city is different as you will see, but many cities we find will share something in common. Let's look at the map. The first city I want to find is Nashville. Can anyone tell me where it is?

Steven: It's in the middle of the state, Ms. Johnson. It's listed right next to that star.

Ms. Johnson: Can you tell me why there is a star next to Nashville on the map?

Natalia: It's the capital city of our state. Capital cities are shown by a star on the map.

Ms. Johnson: Very good. Yes, Nashville is our state capital. Let's look at what else we see on the map near Nashville. Can you see any physical features we should know about?

Steven: I can see the Cumberland River. It flows through Nashville.

Ms. Johnson: Nashville is also the largest city in Tennessee. Can you think of any other reasons why Nashville is important to our state?

Steven: One reason it is famous is for its music. The Country Music Hall of Fame is there.

Natalia: Nashville is also important because it has lots of schools and universities.

Ms. Johnson: Great job, students. Let's move on to a different place on the map. I want to find another city famous for its music. Can anyone name it?

Natalia: I think you must mean Memphis. This city is called the Birthplace of Blues.

Ms. Johnson: Yes! Also the Birthplace of Rock and Roll. Memphis is in the southwestern part of the state. As you can see, it is located on the Mississippi River. There is another river flowing into the city too. Can you find it?

Steven: I see it. It's the Wolf River. It flows into the Mississippi River.

Ms. Johnson: That's right. Memphis grew to be a large city because of these two rivers. Many boats on the rivers stopped at Memphis to trade goods. Memphis is one of the largest cities on the Mississippi today. So far, the cities we've found have been on flat ground. But Tennessee has many mountains. Can anyone look at the map and find where the mountains are located in our state?

Natalia: The map on the wall looks different on the eastern part of the state. The lighter area stands for mountains on some maps.

Ms. Johnson: Precisely! A physical map shows with symbols or colors where features like mountains are located. There are many mountains in the eastern part of Tennessee. The Great Smoky Mountains are part of the Appalachian Mountain Range. They are some of the oldest mountains in North America. These mountains form part of the border with our neighbor, North Carolina.

Steven: I went camping there before. There are a lot of rivers and creeks. I went fishing with my grandpa in the Little Tennessee River in the Great Smoky Mountains. And my dad and I went for a swim in Abrams Creek.

Natalia: I once drove through the Great Smoky Mountains with my grandparents. We saw a lot of forests and meadows filled with flowers like hardy orchids. Those are my grandma's favorites.

Ms. Johnson: Do you see the green area near the mountains on the map? These are the forests of the Great Smoky Mountains. They are home to fir, beech and maple trees. Now that we've seen some mountains, let's look for two famous cities in our state on the Tennessee River. First, find the river. Then you can look for the cities.

Steven: I see Knoxville. Oh, and there's Chattanooga!

Ms. Johnson: Yes, those are the two cities I was hoping you'd find! There are about 100 miles between these two cities. You can drive in your car from one to the other. You can also take a boat. Knoxville was the first capital of the state. Chattanooga is a popular place to visit. Many people come to see the natural attractions there like the river and mountains. Here, kids. Take this map. Spend the rest of your class time trying to find other important physical features in our state.

Steven and Natalia reach out to the map Ms. Johnson put in front of them. They touch it and ... WHOOSH ...

Steven: Natalia, we've been sent to Ruby Falls in Chattanooga! Looks like we've joined some cave explorers trying to reach the famous underground waterfall.

Natalia: Wow. I can't believe that we're actually being held up in a cave by ropes. Do you see the waterfall, Steven?

Steven: Yes! There's Ruby Falls straight ahead. I just heard the lead explorer say that the waterfall is 145 feet tall. The water comes from rain and natural springs.

Natalia: I see it too. You can't tell on a map how spectacular this place is. It's a good thing that I wore my sweater. It's chilly here! I heard it never gets warmer than 59 degrees. Let's climb down from the ropes now. I want to explore part of the cave.

Steven: Did you know this cave is made of limestone? And that it's connected to Lookout Mountain Cave? Boy, I thought Tennessee was interesting above ground. It's even more interesting underneath it!

Natalia: Hey, look. There's a gift shop. Let's go inside. Maybe we can find a fun souvenir to bring back with us.

Steven: Let's get these postcards of Ruby Falls. We can bring some along to present to the class!

Natalia: Great, idea Steven!

They touch the map and return safely to their classroom, having had another exciting adventure!

title: All About the Mississippi
text:
The Mississippi River is one of the longest rivers in North America. It begins in the state of Minnesota and flows south for over 2,000 miles. The mouth of the river can be found in the state of Louisiana. It empties into a body of water called the Gulf of Mexico.

The Mississippi River winds its way through 10 states on its way to the Gulf of Mexico. There are many cities and towns on the shores of this great river. The Tennessee city of Memphis is right on the water's edge! Throughout history, the river has been used for boats trading goods between river towns, or even shipping supplies to soldiers during wars. The river is still used to move goods today.

The name Mississippi means "Great River." It was named by the Chippewa Indians. At its deepest point near New Orleans, the river is 200 feet deep. At its widest point, in Minnesota, the river is 11 miles across. There are many bridges across the river today. The first one was a railroad bridge. It was built back in 1856. Unfortunately, just 15 days after its completion, a steamboat collided with it. This accident burned and destroyed sections of the bridge, making it unusable.

The great river is home to many kinds of animals, like birds and fish. Humans need the river, too. It supplies water for more than 18 million people who live near it.

title: Down by the Riverside
text:
Steven and Natalia are packing their things up for a picnic on the Mississippi waterfront. They are excited to spend time playing outside next to such an amazing physical feature.

Natalia: What kind of sandwich are you making, Steven? I'm going to bring peanut butter and jelly for the trip.

Steven: I made a turkey sandwich, and I'm bringing apples and crackers for all of us. We better hurry. Our parents are getting anxious to leave.

Natalia: We're all set. I already packed a few things that Ms. Johnson suggested we bring like a road map and a journal so we can write down all the cities and towns we pass through. We can also write down any rivers or creeks we pass, too.

Steven: I've got my camera. I want to take photos of interesting places we pass on the trip like cool bridges, mountains or lakes.

Natalia: When we get to the Mississippi River, I bet we'll be able to take lots of good pictures to show all our classmates and Ms. Johnson!

After a few hours of playing games, writing in their travel journals and taking pictures of passing towns, Steven, Natalia and their families arrive at the Mississippi River in Southwestern Tennessee.

Steven: We're finally here!

Natalia: Memphis sure is busy today. I've never seen so much traffic. There must be lots of families who want to visit the river today, too. Hey, do you see that ferry boat, Steven? Ms. Johnson said ferry boats used to be common sights on the Mississippi River.

Steven: I see it! I got a postcard from my grandmother once with a picture of a ferry boat on it. I wish we had a boat to go sailing. Imagine all the towns we could pass on the Mississippi.

Natalia: I know, let's make one! We can make a boat out of this piece of bark and some paper. Look, all I need is a small stick to prop the paper up as a sail.

Steven: This looks like a safe spot to launch our boat, let's set it into the water right here!

Natalia: There it goes. I guess it will flow south with the river. What do you think our boat will pass on its journey?

Steven: I wonder if it will make it to the city of Little Rock in Arkansas.

Natalia: I wonder if it will make it down all the way to the Gulf of Mexico where the Mississippi River ends.

Steven: Someday, I'm going to take a ferry boat trip down the Mississippi River, Natalia. Will you go with me?

Natalia: I sure will! Only, no peanut butter and jelly sandwiches for that journey. Mine was soggy. bleeggh! I think we'll have lunch on the ferry.

Steven: That's a deal!

title: Three Rivers, One State
text:
Tennessee's three major rivers are the Mississippi, Cumberland and Tennessee Rivers. The Mississippi is the longest of these rivers. It is over 2,000 miles long. The Cumberland River is roughly 688 miles long. It's just a bit longer than the Tennessee River, which flows for about 651 miles.

Each of these rivers is important to Tennessee. People use them for farming, drinking water and recreation. Many people like to live by rivers. They are often used to ship goods on boats from one place to another. Sometimes people just visit these rivers because it's fun! We can fish, sail and sit by these rivers to enjoy the views. These are just a few reasons why some river cities grow large, like Memphis!

title: Music of Memphis
text:
With WWII and the Great Depression finally over, people were starting to feel upbeat about the future for the first time in a long time. New music reflecting this upbeat attitude began to develop right here in Tennessee! A new and exciting style of music was being made when musicians started adding electric guitars, drums and saxophones to slower blues songs. This upbeat sound was called rhythm and blues, or R&B. Memphis became known for its R&B music.

Many whites were going to blues clubs and listening to music performed by African Americans. This exposure helped people to reconsider segregation. Attitudes about race were starting to change. In the years to come, music would be an important part of the civil rights movement!

If R&B wasn't enough, another new sound was being made by Memphis musicians! It mixed blues, pop, country and gospel music. Sam Phillips thought this new sound would be very popular. He opened Sun Studio where anyone, African American or white, could record a song for $4. One day a young artist recorded the song "That's All Right," and it was the sound Sam Phillips wanted to make popular! Who was that singer? It was Elvis Presley, and that unique sound became known as rock 'n' roll! Soon Elvis was the biggest music star in the world, selling over 1 billion records. Is it any wonder why he's nicknamed the "King of Rock 'n' Roll"?

Yet another form of music has its roots in Memphis, too: soul music. Stax Records helped popularize this mixture of blues, R&B and gospel. Stax produced many hits and artists as well. So, as you can see, Tennessee was a hotbed for music innovation worldwide in post WWII America. New forms of music were created along with the ever-popular country and blues music already established in Nashville and Memphis. The mixing of new sounds and new forms of music brought many African Americans and whites together. I think music is always good for bringing people together ... don't you agree?

title: The Frisco Bridge
text:
The Frisco Bridge, or the Memphis Bridge, crosses the Mississippi River. It connects Tennessee to Arkansas. It was built in 1892 as a railroad bridge. In 1892, it was the third-longest bridge in the world and the highest bridge in the United States. It was the first bridge to cross the Lower Mississippi River. Today there are other nearby bridges, like the De Soto Bridge and the Memphis Arkansas Bridge.

The Chief Engineer of the project was George S. Morison. Older, shorter railway bridges used wood. Morison knew that wood was not strong enough for a long bridge. He needed to think of something different. His team of workers used a new material, open-hearth steel, to build the bridge. They used a truss design. That means they used steel triangles to make the bridge. It had to carry a heavy train engine a long distance. Six different steel companies worked with Morison on the project. Construction began in 1888 and was finished in 1892.

Today, the longest span of the bridge is more than 790 feet. The entire bridge is almost 5,000 feet long! The bridge is still in use by a local railway company. It is being improved for future use. The bridge is designated as a Historic Civil Engineering Landmark in our state.

title: Local Industries
text: Water is an important natural resource. What local industries rely on water, and how do they use water every day? Write your answer on the lines provided or on a separate sheet of paper.

title: Water for the Future
text:
It's 1541, the Age of Exploration, and some Spanish explorers have landed in North America. Hernando de Soto and his men began their journey inland from Florida and traveled all the way to our state. De Soto kept a record of this progress so other explorers could follow the same path he took. Some cartographers used his record to help them make maps. Future travelers used the same information when they moved west. 200 years later, another European explorer, the Marquis de Montcalm, made note of the river.

In 1756 the Seven Years' War began. During this time, France had claimed the central part of America and they were eager to expand their hold from the coasts to further inland. However, in order to survive, people had to take supplies with them. Moving goods and animals by land back then was often a very slow, risky business. Animals were sometimes stolen or they would get sick and die. Goods could be stolen or spoil before they could reach their destination. That's why water transport was favored. It was a faster, cheaper, easier way to transport goods quickly and safely from the coasts to settlements further inland. However, there wasn't a very good waterway to connect the southern coast with the northern end of the country.

It was the French explorer, Montcalm, who noticed how useful the rivers were. He even wrote to the King of France about it. He told him that joining the Tombigbee and Tennessee rivers could make it easier to move goods and people. He also said that if the King wanted to conquer the New World, he should consider the idea seriously. The idea was considered, but nothing was done about it for over 200 years. Today, the Tennessee-Tombigbee Waterway, or Tenn-Tom as it is called, connects the middle of America to the Gulf of Mexico. It is used very effectively to transport goods up and down the rivers.

title: Tennessee Train Tunnels
text:
Sometimes when builders and city planners plan out a route for a road or a railway, they encounter literal roadblocks. In some cases, it’s much easier to just build the roads around such obstacles. However, sometimes the most direct route is to carve right through those blocks. One instance of this can be found in our very own state: the Cowan Tunnel, or Cumberland Mountain Tunnel.

Construction on Cowan Tunnel began in 1849. It was completed three years later in 1852. Workers of all different cultures and colors worked on digging the tunnel through the rock. This railroad tunnel later served an important role during the Civil War. Trains delivered soldiers, supplies and information to and from various places where they were needed. Because of its significance in the Civil War, Cowan Tunnel is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Today, the railroad itself is owned by the CSX Railroad and is still using Cowan Tunnel on its trips.

title: The Tennessee-Tombigbee Waterway
text:
The Tennessee-Tombigbee Waterway is an important part of our state. It connects the Tennessee River with the Black Warrior-Tombigbee River in Alabama. The waterway combines the two names. Many people throughout early U.S. history had ideas of joining them when they saw the two rivers. However, It wasn't until the 20th century that it happened.

The steamboat arrived on the river and everything changed. Engineers came to survey the area in 1875. They wanted to make the river deeper so more ships could travel on it. A canal would require locks and other features to control the water, so they decided the project was too expensive at the time.

50 years passed and the rivers stayed the same. In 1933, President Franklin D. Roosevelt created the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA). In the next 10 years, the TVA built several dams and canals. However, these were not the same as the "Tenn-Tom" that we see today.

President Nixon ordered that construction begin of the Tennessee-Tombigbee Waterway in 1961. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers began their work on the project in 1972. It was completed in 1984. That seems like a long time, but, actually, they finished it early. Two years ahead of schedule! But it was not an easy path. Not everyone agreed that a big public project was a good idea.

Some people were against the construction of the waterway. Many citizens and politicians said not to build it. They thought building the waterway was dangerous. Workers might get hurt. It would damage the environment. Members of Congress opposed the plan. President Carter stopped funding the project in 1977. The public outcry in favor of the project made him change his mind. In the future, this would be looked at as an example of a government project that helped rural America.

Many people were also concerned about the waterway's impact on the economy. People were worried the waterway would cost more money than it would be able to make. Tennessee and Alabama citizens feared the construction would leave them in a lot of debt. Other people asked about the law. Did the federal government have the right to build things in a state? What if the state refused? Was the government breaking a law?

There were other problems, as well. The dam's location meant that some cities in the area could become flooded. People would have to move since their homes would become fully submerged by the rising water level. You can see the remains of some of these lost cities. There are memorials along the waterway that mark their old location. In fact, maps dating from before the 1960s still have these cities listed on them, but if you look at a new map, those cities are nowhere to be found.

Railroad companies complained that the waterway would hurt their businesses. These companies filed lawsuits to try and stop the project. Many politicians agreed with them. But the courts still ruled in favor of the Tenn-Tom. Work slowly proceeded.

In 1988, a drought lowered the waters of the Mississippi by a significant amount. The water became too low for people and goods to travel like they did before when the river was higher. The Tenn-Tom was available as an alternative route. This improved the economy and allowed goods to keep moving. Today the Tenn-Tom is still used to transport natural resources. Most of these are coal and timber, which are used for power, heating and building houses.

title: A World of Water
text:
Steven and Natalia: Good morning, fellow students!

Steven: I'm Steven, and this is my co-anchor, Natalia.

Natalia: Good morning, everyone! Today we're talking about something important. Something that nobody can live without, water!

Steven: Water is important for life for many reasons. In Tennessee, we have a lot of water! Humans can't survive without a supply of fresh water. Natalia has a report about the waterways in our state. Natalia?

Natalia: Thanks, Steven! The history of our lakes and rivers begins a long time ago. More than 300 million years! Look on a special map that shows lakes, rivers and other waterways. You can see how many we have. They connect with each other like a highway. There are pathways of water all over Tennessee.

Natalia: One specific river is a famous example. The Tennessee River has a second name, the Cherokee River. The Cherokee people used its fresh water for drinking, traveling and for food. You could follow the main river and smaller rivers for hundreds of miles. You could use the river as a guide as you walked. Earlier explorers used the waterways to go further west. When the settlers arrived, they began to use the rivers in different ways. I believe Steven has something to say about that.

Steven: Yes, I do, Natalia, thank you! The early settlers used the waterways as a natural resource. They used them for irrigation. That means they changed the waterways to help water their crops. They built gristmills to grind wheat to make bread. They used the river to transport people and goods further inland.

People come to Tennessee for the water today. People enjoy fishing in streams or swimming in lakes. In the present day, water is critical to our economy. We have a special government group that manages all the water in the state. They're called the Tennessee Valley Authority, or TVA for short.

Natalia: President Franklin D. Roosevelt formed the TVA in 1933. The TVA was created to help combat the Great Depression by creating projects that would improve the economy. The projects would offer construction jobs. The TVA would also improve farming and health by managing water. We have to care for our freshwater supply and keep it going for everyone. The TVA helped do that. They modernized the state water system, and the new dams provided electrical power to more people.

Steven: But that can lead to other problems. Too much development can damage the environment. Modern cities create a lot of trash. A lot of people means a lot of items to throw out. That trash gets into our freshwater supply and that's not good. What happens if the water gets polluted?

Natalia: It kills the animals and plants. And it makes us sick, or worse! Part of the TVA's job is to make sure our drinking water is safe. Drinking water can't be near a factory or a dump. Have you seen that dump outside of town, Steven?

Steven: I sure have smelled it! And, it's actually a landfill, not a dump.

Natalia: Oh? What's the difference?

Steven: A landfill is part of a city. The city government makes sure the landfill follows certain rules. The city makes sure it doesn't make contact with drinking water or damage the soil. We need a clean freshwater supply.

Natalia: And a dump is outside of a city? Is it regulated at all?

Steven: Not by the same rules as a landfill. Because of this, dumps are more dangerous to the environment than landfills. Dumps might be located in a place away from water and people, but a flood or heavy rainfall can wash garbage or chemicals into our waterways.

Natalia: There are several dams and locks in our state. They help manage water when there's a flood. Flooding was a serious problem in the Tennessee Valley.

Steven: Too little water is also bad, like when there's a drought. Today we can store freshwater when there is too much. We can use it later when there's too little. We have a complex system to carry water all over the state. I bet our viewers didn't know that!

Natalia: If they didn't before, they sure do now, Steven. Stay tuned for more about water and Tennessee!

title: Almost a Family Reunion
text:
After Natalia touches her grandmother's necklace she and Steven are whisked away to someplace that feels very familiar ...

Steven: Look at this place, Natalia. I think I've been here before ... These are the Great Smoky Mountains!

Natalia: My grandmother was raised here. As a matter of fact, entire generations of my Cherokee family lived right here in these mountains.

Steven: Look, there are some people over there. Some might be your relatives! What are they doing?

Natalia: It looks like they're celebrating ... a festival or ceremony, maybe.

Steven: There are some people over there exchanging animal skins.

Natalia: This must be a Friends Made Ceremony! This is one of our seven sacred ceremonies. I recognize this custom. They're exchanging their clothes to symbolize the mending or building of a friendship.

Steven: Their clothing is different than ours. They mostly used the skins of animals to make their clothing. I remember seeing traditional Cherokee clothing in a video during class. I know there are other groups of American Indians besides the Cherokee that wear similar outfits.

Natalia: The clothing, housing and tools of the people depended on where they lived. That home over there, is made of cane and woven branches. They were plastered with mud from the nearby river and tall grass was used for roof thatching.

Steven: They used the materials that are nearby. That's so smart!

Natalia: Yes. For instance, the people of the plains followed the bison. So their homes were more portable and made of bison hide. Their clothes were too.

Steven: What about the native tribes in the Northeast like the Mohawk?

Natalia: Often they would try to build their homes very close to a nearby river. They are very different than what we see here. Their homes were built using long wooden logs.

Steven: Great! I learned a lot, thanks, Natalia! We'll have so much to tell the rest of our classmates.

title: Tsali Cherokee Hero
text:
American history has many well-known heroes. They are men and women that were brave and did the right thing even during very hard times. Some even died for what they knew to be right. You may have learned about some of the more well-known American heroes, already. There are other American heroes that are less famous. One of these heroes is Tsali.

There are some facts that we know about Tsali. We know that he was born and lived near the shores of the "Little Tennessee" in Bryson, North Carolina. He was a farmer, hunter and member of the Cherokee nation. At the age of 60, he was living there in a small cabin with his wife and three sons. He farmed a small piece of land and also hunted to provide food for his family. His life was not unusual in any way until the year of 1838. This was when he became the leader of a resistance against the forced removal of the Cherokee people from their homelands.

Tsali's story gets a little fuzzy after that. Oral traditions of the Cherokee tell us that Tsali didn't plan to be a resistance fighter, but he became one when he had to. These stories also tell us that Tsali was willing to make the ultimate sacrifice of his own life to try to save the Cherokee people. In fact, the story of his surrender and death are still a symbol of strength and courage for the Cherokee.

Tsali's story, as told by the Cherokee goes like this ...

Tsali's brother-in-law came to his home and warned him that 7,000 soldiers were gathering all of the Cherokee people and forcing them to leave their homes. He told him that all Cherokee must leave their homes and begin a long march to the west. He said they must leave before the next new moon.

Tsali listened to the words of his brother-in-law but did not prepare to leave. He and the other Cherokee living in the hills of North Carolina had not agreed to leave their lands. They were called traditionalists. They believed that being forced to move was against their rights and they did not intend to go. They thought that if they continued to work and live their lives as they always had that the soldiers would leave them in peace. Tsali believed this, but he was wrong.

As Tsali continued to work, the soldiers steadily moved closer. They removed Cherokee men, women and children as they went, by force if necessary. Finally, the soldiers arrived at Tsali's door. It was his family's turn to be removed. Even though he knew the soldiers were wrong, he and his family obeyed. They left their home and began the march with other families toward the new land. Tsali's wife couldn't walk as quickly as the soldiers wanted her to and so they began to push her along with the end of a bayonet (a pointed blade attached to the end of a rifle). This was too much for Tsali.

He told the other Cherokee there to prepare to take the soldier's weapons when he pretended to fall down. He spoke in the Cherokee language so the soldiers did not know what they were saying. During the struggle, one of the soldiers was killed. It wasn't planned, yet the revolt had begun. Tsali and his family ran into the woods near Clingmans Dome in Tennessee to escape. They hid in a cave. They had no idea what would happen next or what it would mean for the Cherokee people.

Orders were given to hunt Tsali and all those with him. They told the other Cherokee people that Tsali's capture would mean that they could stay in their homeland. Tsali then willingly surrendered so that his family and people would be left alone to live in their ancestral homeland.

Historical documentation of this event tells us different stories about Tsali's end. Instead of surrendering willingly, some written accounts of the event indicate that Tsali was actually captured. What we do know is that sometime on or after November 1, 1838, Tsali was put to death. Though some of the Cherokee people were allowed to remain in the North Carolina hills it did not save the thousands of other Cherokee. The forced march of the Cherokee people is now known as The Trail of Tears.

Even though the accounts of the end of his life are different, Tsali is still a symbol of strength and fairness to the Cherokee people. The legend of his life is often shared among the Cherokee. There is even an outdoor drama written by Kermit Hunter called "Unto These Hills," which retells the dramatic tale of Tsali's sacrifice.

title: Mapping the People
text:
Natalia and Steven had quite an adventure. They learned about some of the customs of the Cherokee and later read about some of the customs of other American Indian tribes. Now they want to share what they learned with their classmates.

Natalia: I'm really excited! There's so much to tell. Let's use this map to organize our information.

Steven: That's a great idea! We can identify the areas where each group lived.

Natalia: And then tell about the customs and shelters of those groups.

Steven: So, let's start with the Cherokee since we spent time with them today.

Natalia: The Cherokee lived about ... here on the map. They were a part of what we call the Southeastern tribes. So Tennessee, of course, and Georgia, Alabama, North Carolina and South Carolina ...

Steven: Kentucky, Virginia and West Virginia. Let's color that part of the map in blue. What about the Plains Indians?

Natalia: They were here. Kind of in the middle of America. East of the Rocky Mountains and west of the Mississippi River. We'll color this area green. The Cheyenne, Arapaho and Comanche are a few of the more well-known Plains Indian tribes.

Steven: The Comanche are sometimes known as the Horsemen of the Great Plains. The Spaniards left horses in the New World when they came exploring. Many American Indian tribes picked up riding horses. This allowed them to be faster hunters and travelers. The Comanche, however, took to the horses very well.

Natalia: They became famous for being the best bison hunters on the plains.

Steven: I remember you said the Southeastern tribes had more stable shelters built of cane and mud. And the Great Plains tribes had portable shelters made from bison skins.

Natalia: Teepees! The differences in where they lived and what resources they depended on shaped how they lived, what they wore and how they ate. The Plains Indians were largely nomadic. This meant they needed to be able to travel easily. Teepees were lightweight and easy to setup and take down.

Steven: We've got so many native tribes to explain, but this map really is helping. Let's get back to it! The Northeast Indians are next.

Steven: Those were made up of the Algonquin, Iroquois and Chippewa, to name a few. They lived in a large woodland area between the Great Lakes and the northern Atlantic border in New York.

Natalia: The Northeastern American Indian tribes are also sometimes called the Woodland Indians. They lived in a climate that was humid and had cold winters and hot summers. So how they dressed changed from season to season.

Steven: In the summers they would dress cooler and wear things like breechcloths. In the winter they would have to bundle up. Near the Great Lakes area, it gets icy and frigid. They would wear warmer things like fringed tunics and high moccasins with leggings made of animal skin. Let's color this area orange.

Steven and Natalia have a lot of information to compile before sharing with their classmates. Each group of native peoples had different clothing, shelter and customs. The geography of where they lived had a lot to do with how they lived. They used the resources in their areas to provide food and shelter and the best way of life.

title: Let's Write
text: Natalia and Steven had an amazing adventure in the Cherokee village. Wouldn't it be fun if you could join them? Imagine that you were with Steven and Natalia and you joined in the Friends Made Ceremony. Write about your experience. Do some additional research about this sacred ceremony. title: Friends Made Ceremony
text:
The Friends Made Ceremony or "Atohuna" was a time to renew friendships. It was a symbol of the lasting bonds between friends and family. It was also a time to end quarrels and start anew. It was the fifth festival in a series of seven sacred events held each year in the Cherokee community.

The ceremony took place in the fall about 10 days after the Great Moon Festival. It lasted for four days. Each person participating in the festival was given a duty. Some of the duties included leading the songs or playing music. Others might have been responsible for hunting or cooking. Others were put in charge of cleaning the council house. One of the most important jobs during Atohuna was Fire Keeper. The Fire Keeper was responsible for the sacred fire. They had to build it and ensure it didn't go out. The Keeper would stop eating or "fast" for seven days before the festival. This fasting time was to make sure that the Fire Keeper was purified before caring for the sacred fire.

The Fire Keepers were not the only ones to fast for the ceremony. Atohuna was also a time for cleansing. Fasting and cleaning showed a willingness to put away the old and start fresh. So, on certain days, other festival participants would fast to cleanse and prepare. There was also a final "ritual" of cleansing in the running water of a river. The cleansing rituals, renewing the sacred fire and strengthening friendships were viewed as a new start for the Cherokee people.

What significance might this ceremony have to a person who is not a member of the Cherokee tribe?

title: Let's Write
text: The European settlers and American Indians had conflicts over land, nature and religion. How would you settle a conflict? Pretend you are a judge in the 1800s. You have to settle the conflict between the European settlers and American Indians in a fair way. Write one or two paragraphs that provide three solutions to the conflict between these two groups.

title: Exploring the Cherokee Trail of Tears
text:
Imagine the government just passed a law that says your family must move to another state. What would you do?

This happened to American Indians in 1830. Congress passed the Indian Removal Act. The law forced American Indians living east of the Mississippi to leave their land and move to Oklahoma.

In 1791, the U.S. Government gave Georgia to the Cherokee Indians. In 1829, gold was discovered in Georgia. Because of this, President Andrew Jackson wanted to take that land back.

The Cherokee people knew the land belonged to them. They asked the Supreme Court to look at their case. The court ruled in favor of the Cherokee people. President Jackson and Congress ignored the ruling. They continued to force the Cherokee Indians out of Georgia.

Some Cherokee left peacefully. Others stayed to fight for the land. In 1838, U.S. troops forced them to leave.

The Cherokee packed up what belongings they could carry and then walked from Georgia to Oklahoma. The trip took four months, and they traveled over 1,000 miles.

Life was hard for the Cherokee Indians on the trail. The conditions were harsh. They walked in the snow without shoes. They had to sleep on the cold ground. At least 4,000 people died from starvation and disease. The path they took is now called "The Trail of Tears." This was and still is a very sad time in U.S. history.

Trail of Tears Historic Trail

Congress made this trail a national landmark in 1987. The trail goes through nine states. Sites along the trail include:

Rome, GA (Home of Major Ridge)

Cherokee, NC (Cherokee Indian Museum)

Grantsville, IL (Crabb-Abbot Farm)

Fort Payne, AL (Fort Payne Cabin Site)

Steelville, MO (Snelson - House)

Joy, KY (Mantle Rock)

Parkhill, OK (Cherokee National Museum)

North Little Rock, AK (North Little Rock Riverfront Park)

title: A Tale of Two Sides
text:
Conflicts can happen at any moment. Some last for a short time. Others last months or years. It can be hard for people to settle a conflict.

Beginning in the 1500s, European settlers came to the Americas. At first, American Indians and the settlers worked together. The American Indians helped the settlers to grow crops and provided support during the winters. Europeans would trade with them, too. The American Indians were interested in the fabrics, tools and weapons that the settlers brought with them.

Over time, both groups began to fight over land. Settlers wanted to live in the resource-rich areas inhabited by the American Indians. Through treaties, the settlers slowly pushed the American Indians off their lands. European settlers also brought with them an invisible and deadly enemy: disease. Never having been exposed to smallpox and measles, American Indians had no immunity to these diseases like the Europeans did. This caused whole villages and tribes to become sick and even die.

Do you think it was possible for the settlers and American Indians to resolve their problems without fighting?

title: Warring Tribes: Sacagawea's Abduction
text:
There were many different tribes and villages competing with one another for land and resources long before Europeans began to colonize America. Sometimes one tribe would attack another to steal food and supplies. Other times, tribes would attack one another out of revenge for loved ones who had been killed in other battles. Sometimes warriors would take people captive to take back to their own tribes. These people would either join the tribes or be servants.

Have you ever heard of a woman named Sacagawea? She is the American Indian guide who helped Lewis and Clark on their journey. She was a Shoshone woman born in 1788 near present-day Salmon, Idaho. When she was just 12 years old, her people fought with another tribe called the Hidatsa. During the battle, she and several other young girls were taken captive. From there, she was taken away from her home and family to live with the Hidatsa. A year later, she was sold and married to a man named Toussaint Charbonneau.

It was terrible for her to be taken from her family and all she'd known. But Sacagawea made history with Lewis and Clark and she was fortunate enough to be reunited with her family. On their travels, the group unexpectedly met a group of Shoshone. These people turned out to be Sacagawea's own tribe! In Lewis and Clark's journals, they wrote that she danced with joy at the sight of her people.

title: American Indian Conflicts
text:
Usually, when we think about conflicts or wars that American Indians fought in, we think about the conflicts they had with European settlers. However, American Indians also fought with each other. One such conflict is known as the Beaver Wars.

The Beaver Wars took place north of Tennessee in the Great Lakes Region. French fur trappers and Algonquin tribes had control of that area. These fur trappers and American Indian tribes made their living catching beaver and selling their pelts. These pelts were used to make hats that were quite fashionable back in England, France and other European countries. The Iroquois were eager to take over control of the fur trade and expand their territory. This caused problems between the Iroquois and the Algonquin tribes in that area.

These conflicts lasted more than a couple of years. They are considered to be some of the bloodiest battles ever fought in the history of North America. The Iroquois were friendly trade allies with the Dutch and English that came through their territory. These Europeans stood to gain a lot if the Iroquois were successful in these conflicts so the Dutch and English gave the Iroquois weapons.

Over the course of these conflicts, the Iroquois appeared to succeed in taking control of most of the area. They destroyed many tribes like the Shawnee, Huron and Erie. They pushed many tribes that lived west of the Mississippi eastward. They also pushed tribes as far south as the Carolinas. By about 1670, the Iroquois controlled most of the land in the Ohio River valley.

This conflict goes back many years before 1670. Other tribes often fought with the Iroquois over land. One such example is when Samuel de Champlain, a famous fur trapper and explorer, traveled to the St. Lawrence River area in 1603. While there he sided with the Algonquin tribes in a fight with the Iroquois. Champlain and other French exploreres decided they would not trade with the Iroquis. This kept the Iroquois from gaining European-made weapons.

These conflicts between the tribes are an example of wars for economic reasons. Fighting between American Indian tribes happened all over the United States.

The Cherokee knew the power of teamwork. Crops had to be picked. Meals needed to be prepared. Food needed to be hunted and grown. Clothing needed to be made. By sharing the work, the Cherokee grew into a strong nation.

Cherokee villages were large. They held around 500 people. Each village had about 40-50 houses. A town square was located in the village. They held meetings in a council house. It was large enough to hold every person in the village.

Each village had two chiefs. The White Chief was an elder. He led the village in peaceful times. The Red Chief was a young man. He led the village when they were in a war. The Village Council helped the chiefs make good choices. The men hunted and were the ones who fought in wars with settlers and other tribes. The women led their homes and sometimes took part in tribal affairs, too. Some women also fought in wars.

They made weapons from flint and constructed bows and arrows. The Cherokee also traded with settlers for weapons, too. Eventually, they also used guns and axes just like the European settlers. Weapons were important. They were used for hunting and to protect their village from settlers and other tribes.

The Cherokee had often had conflicts with the Shawnee Indians. The Shawnee lived in the Cumberland area during the Beaver Wars. They fled southward, away from the Iroquois. The Shawnee were closely allied with the French. The Cherokee were mainly allied with England. When the Shawnee had overstayed their welcome in the Cumberland Gap area, the Cherokee worked with the Chickasaw to force them to move back north. The main conflict took place between the years of 1710-1715. But the fighting would continue for 50 years after 1717. This rivalry wouldn't officially end until a peace treaty was made in 1768.

Looking to expand their hunting grounds, a group of Cherokee tried to take control of Chickasaw hunting grounds in what is now the state of Alabama. They fought with the Chickasaw for 11 years before losing in 1769.

It wasn't just the Shawnee and Chickasaw that the Cherokee had conflicts with, either. They have a long military history with many other tribes. And at one point in history, the Cherokee tribes fought amongst themselves, too.

During the American Civil War, the Cherokee found themselves split. The war was famously known for pitting brother against brother. Some Cherokee sided and fought with the North (the Union), but many allied with the South (the Confederacy). The South, seeing benefits of allying with the Cherokee, sent many letters, offers and promises to Cherokee chiefs. In exchange for access to their lands during the war, the Cherokee could maintain control of their territory afterward and have representation in the Confederate Congress.

Many Cherokee were still grieving the loss of their ancestral homelands at the hands of the federal government. They found reasons to side with the South and fight against their Cherokee brothers who fought with the North.

title: Hearing the Other Side
text:
"I just don't understand it, Steven. Why couldn't they just get along?" Natalia asked.

"I don't get it either, Natalia," Steven responded with a shrug. "Maybe there is another side to the story we aren't thinking about."

"I guess you're right, Steven."

Steven and Natalia continued looking through their box of Cherokee pictures and artifacts.

"An arrowhead!" Natalia exclaimed.

"Oh, cool! These were used as weapons. Did you know that the Cherokee sharpened arrowheads with deer antlers?" Steven asked.

"Really?"

Steven nodded as they looked at the arrowhead carefully.

Ms. Johnson's voice interrupted their thoughts, "Class, you have 15 more minutes to complete your assignment!"

"Let's hurry, Natalia. We don't have much time. We still need to add five more facts to our list," said Steven

"Oh! I have an idea," replied Natalia.

"You always have an idea, Natalia."

"I'm serious, Steven. We have no time to play around. Follow me!"

Steven and Natalia quickly walk to the other side of the room. Natalia picks up a tablet.

"Before class, Ms. Johnson uploaded maps of Cherokee territory onto our tablets. Let's explore the Smoky Mountains in Tennessee."

"Great idea, Natalia! The Cherokee lived there. We can use the map to get more information."

Steven touched the map. Instantly, they were transported to the Smoky Mountains. Steven and Natalia walked around the village. They noticed there weren't any people walking around or doing chores.

"Where are all the people? The village looks empty, Natalia."

"I don't know, Steven. It's getting close to dark. We should keep walking. Look, there's the council house! Looks like there's a meeting in the village. Let's go inside."

They quietly tiptoed inside and stood in the back of the room.

"They all look so worried, Steven."

"I know. We have a few minutes. Let's stay and listen."

The chief presided over the meeting. "I am concerned about the settlers. When they arrived, they were friendly. They showed us their way of life and we showed them ours. Now it seems like they want to take over our land."

The Cherokee nodded in agreement. The chief continued to speak, "They want to change what we believe. The settlers have expanded their territory. Our people are getting sick. We may have to ..."

Before he finished, they heard a loud noise. Steven and Natalia raced to the door. Together, they touched the map on their tablet and were transported to their classroom. Looking at each other, they both realized that their adventure had been a close call.

title: Discovering the other 'Yellow Metal' in Tennessee
text:
We've heard a lot about early explorers. Did you know that some of them even made their way into Tennessee? Hernando de Soto started his journey into inland North America in Florida in 1539. They traveled through several states including Tennessee!

He and his men had a negative effect on the native peoples in the area. They devastated the American Indian population. Disease spread out of control. De Soto and his men attacked many tribes and enslaved a number of the American Indians.

For a while, historians did not believe Hernando de Soto made it very far inland. However, there are many Cherokee stories and survivor accounts from members of the expedition that support his journey. There's also archeological evidence. De Soto was looking for gold but did not find it. However, he may have found Zinc, another yellow metal. Zinc is found in present-day Knoxville.

De Soto met with several Cherokee tribes as he and his men marched along the Smoky Mountains into the Little Tennessee Valley. They heard stories of yellow metal in a place called Chisca. Scouts went to look at the mines. However, they reported that some of the metal was copper. While the other metal wasn't gold, they did not know what it was. De Soto decided not to visit the mines himself. He and his men were tired, injured and sick. Instead, he and his men camped in present-day Memphis to build boats and barges. De Soto would not make it home, however. He died from a fever. It's believed that he was buried in the Mississippi River. Luis de Moscoso led the last of the journey down the river. They reached a Spanish settlement in Mexico in 1543.

title: Let's Write

title: Onward to the Spice Islands!
text:
Below is a fictitious account from a sailor on Magellan's attempt to find a western passage to Asia. What can you learn about the journey? What were daily conditions like for these explorers? What were they looking for?

Ship's Log: October 1, 1520

We set sail over a year ago. No one thought the journey would be this long. Yet here we are. Our crew braved storms, mutinies and aggressive natives. Now we will soon round the horn of a continent and sail onward to the Spice Islands! It shouldn't be long now; maybe a week. Though I am from North Africa, I know the languages of the Spice Islands. I was supposed to be an interpreter but we have not encountered anyone I can speak to.

This journey is important for Spain. We are trying to locate our own route to Asia. In 1498, a Portuguese explorer, Vasco da Gama, discovered a path to sail around the horn of Africa to reach India. This made it so European merchants no longer had to rely on the Ottoman Turks for spices. However, the Portuguese have control of the route. Christopher Columbus's journey west inspired Ferdinand Magellan to attempt to find a western passage to Asia. 13 years after Columbus' death, we set out.

Exploration is a dangerous business. I have heard whispers of the exploits of Hernán Cortés and his battles in the New World. He is attempting to conquer and convert the natives. I believe he will be successful. Perhaps I should have cast my lot with his ...

Our journey started out well enough. We set off from Spain on August 10, 1519. We had five ships total with a crew of 270 men and enough food and water for a long journey. Magellan expected to find a crossing through the Americas closer to the equator. However, we found no such passage. Desperate, we sailed south, then sailed some more. The food stores ran low and harsh rationing commenced. We still did not find a passage. Many of the men were angry. I, too, was frustrated, but I kept my feelings to myself. We spent the winter in a temporary settlement named Puerto San Julián. While we were there, mutiny broke out. Our leader, Magellan, took quick action and the mutineers were killed.

This was not our only hardship. We lost another ship in a storm. It was sent to scout ahead but wrecked. All souls are alive, thankfully.

Now we wait and regroup. The men found briny water deep inland, and Magellan believes this must be the passage to the Spice Islands. Only God knows.

-Aban

title: Hard Times At Sea
text: Last time we saw Ferdinand Magellan, he was on his ship, the Victoria. He and his crew sailed across the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, looking for an easier route to the Spice Islands. Today, we know them as the Maluku Islands. Back then, ships making long journeys often lacked a variety of foods. Magellan originally made sure his ships were stocked with many different kinds of food and plenty of fresh water. However, he did not realize how long the journey across the Pacific Ocean would be. His crew was forced to ration the food. The water also went bad. Crew members got scurvy. This is caused by a lack of Vitamin C, found in citrus. While crossing the Pacific, the crew ate spoiled biscuits and were reported to have also eaten sawdust. They also ate leather from the ship's rigging to survive. During the crossing, rat meat was a luxury! Yikes!

title: A Challenging Decision
text: Imagine you had been faced with the challenges early explorers encountered. Would you have kept going or would you have gone home? Why did you make your decision?

title: Mar Pacifico
text:
This week in Ms. Johnson's class, Natalia and Steven are learning about early explorers.

"You see these lines here," Natalia unrolled a map in front of Steven. She traced a dotted line with her finger. "This is the route Christopher Columbus took on his first journey to the Americas. He had three ships: the Niña, the Pinta and the Santa María. He originally thought he landed in India. He was actually bouncing around the Caribbean islands looking for gold, pearls and spices. He didn't find much, however. He did start a settlement on present-day Haiti and the Dominican Republic. The settlement kept failing from bad leadership. He never did bring back much material wealth to Europe. He did provide a lot of knowledge, however. On one journey, he passed the mouth of the Orinoco River. He decided that such a large amount of fresh water must be coming from a land 'of continental proportions'"

"Yeah I remember," Steven said. "We learned about it in class!"

"These lines here show Amerigo Vespucci's trips to South America. He landed in present-day Brazil on his third and most successful voyage. Christopher Columbus's belief that North America was a continent gave Vespucci the idea that South America was also its own continent. That's why he called it the New World."

"It's funny they named both North and South America after him when he only went to South America!" Steven said.

Natalia laughed. "Yeah, I know. His discoveries about South America were vital in helping Ferdinand Magellan find a route west to Asia."

"While all of this was going on, Hernán Cortés was conquering the Aztec people in Mexico," Steven added.

"Hernando De Soto explored Florida and eastern parts of North America as well," Natalia reminded Steven. "He even explored parts of Tennessee and crossed the Mississippi!"

"I think I would rather be exploring inland than stuck on a boat like Magellan," Steven decided.

Natalia rifled through the stack of maps and paper.

"Speaking of Magellan," she said and pulled out a piece of paper triumphantly, "look! This is a picture of the actual sextant he used."

"Wow!" said Steven, "that's so cool! I can almost smell the ocean."

The two friends closed their eyes and took a deep breath. Then coughed and sputtered as a wave washed over them. They tumbled onto a hard wooden deck. Thunk! Thump!

"Where are we?" Steven murmured, rubbing his head.

"Shh!" Natalia hissed. "Look!"

Around them, several grim-faced men stood looking out into a cold and treacherous landscape. Large rocks jutted out from the water forming a narrow passage. The ship rocked and jerked as it squeezed through the last perilous part of the pass.

"We're in the Straits of Magellan!" Natalia whispered. "This is Magellan's ship!"

"Look!" Steven whispered back. "That's him!"

They watched as a short man with a full beard slowly made his way to the front of the ship. The two friends looked on in awe as the narrow passage opened up to reveal the vast expanse of the Pacific Ocean.

Magellan and his crew were silent as they regarded the striking vista. Giving his head a slight shake, Magellan said softly, "Mar Pacifico!"

"Peaceful ocean," Steven said with a smile. "It's how the Pacific Ocean got its name!"

title: Amerigo Vespucci
text:
Have you ever wondered just where America got its name? You might be surprised to learn that America was named after an Italian merchant and explorer named Amerigo Vespucci.

The Latin name for Amerigo was "Americus." A German mapmaker named Martin Waldseemüller gave the New World the name of America on his world map in 1507. The word "America" was the feminine version of the Latin name Americus. He chose the feminine version because Europe and Asia got their names from women, too. He also felt that the New World should be named after Amerigo, since he was the one who discovered South America and figured out that the Americas were a whole new continent.

Waldseemüller's map was the first map to show the New World as a separate continent, which was labeled as "America." When 1,000 copies of Waldseemüller's map were printed and sold, you can imagine how the new name started to stick!

title: The Long Way Around
text:
Early European explorers to the Americas faced risky conditions. They were also hindered by a lack of exact information. So why did so many people sail west? Kings and Queens of Europe were looking for gold. More importantly, they wanted a new route to Asia. India and other Asian territories supplied exotic spices. Merchants had to sail all the way around the southern tip of Africa to reach these goods.

Even though they were looking for a shorter route, Magellan's path turned out to take much longer than sailing east around Africa. At the time, no one knew this would be the case. When an explorer named Amerigo Vespucci sailed to South America, he thought it was a different continent from Asia. He was right! No one at that time knew how big South America was or how close it was to Asia. Everyone wanted a faster route to Asia, though. Explorers did not have the internet or even accurate maps. They had to travel and use the stars to guide them and hope they would reach their goal. They faced many challenges, which were talked about in the ship's log. These included mutinies, lack of food and delays. Many, including an entire ship in Magellan's own party, quit and went home. In the end, he and his crew reached the Spice Islands. However, he died there. It took the crew much longer than they had planned to complete the trip.
