title: Around the World and Back Home Again
text:
We know that it took much longer to cross the Pacific Ocean than Magellan and his crew had thought. Once they finally landed in the Philippines, he and his men made friendly relations with the local people. But how did they get back home again? Magellan never made it back home. He was killed while helping fight in a tribal dispute. The crew had to make their way back to Europe, but it was difficult. After their long journey, they were left with just one ship.

Officially, Magellan, a Portuguese-born explorer, was sailing for Spain, not Portugal. Therefore, his remaining crew was forbidden to stop at any Portuguese ports. This meant the men had another long and hungry journey ahead of them. They had to sail all the way around the southern tip of Africa. Their ship was filled with expensive spices, which they could not eat. Three years after starting the journey, the ship, Victoria, limped back to Spain. Only 18 of the original 270 crew members returned with it.

title: Joseph Brant Negotiates for the Indian Tribes
text:
The Age of Exploration (period of time between the 1400s and 1600s) was an amazing time for people from Europe. They sent explorers to the "New World" to learn more about the land. They came here searching for new trade routes. America was a land of great new ideas. It was also home to many American Indian tribes.

The American Indians lived in America for a long time before the Europeans came. While they got along with these new settlers in some instances, there were territorial disputes that would happen as well. The more Europeans came over, the more frequently these disputes would happen. The American Indians were not willing to give up their rights to the land. They got mad when they saw people from England living on their land. They fought the soldiers for years. They knew the land better than the new settlers and were very good hunters and fighters.

Joseph Brant was a Mohawk Indian War Chief. He worked with the new American settlers. He went to schools run by Christians. He spoke English as well as many other tribal languages. He helped the English understand what the American Indians were saying. He could see how the war was hurting everyone. He wanted the people to stop fighting. He tried to get them to live in peace.

Brant went to England several times. He met with King George III. He spoke to many English leaders. He tried to get everyone to sign a peace treaty. A treaty is a written agreement that when signed is a promise to stop fighting. He also met with tribal leaders. He tried to make them see that their world was changing. They would now have to share their land. But many of these tribal leaders would not listen.

Instead, they kept fighting with the U.S. Army. As the conflicts continued, and it became apparent that the new European settlers weren't going to be leaving, Brant tried to broker peace agreements between the new U.S. government and the American Indians. But there were many Indian tribes led by people who wanted war. He could not get all of them to agree. Eventually, most American Indian territory had been taken over by the U.S. government, and they had to leave their ancestral homelands. Lots of American Indians died from hunger and sickness.

title: American Indians Fight for their Land
text:
After school one day, Natalia and Steven walked home still talking about seeing Mohawk Indian, Joseph Brant.

"He looked Indian but spoke like the British captains," Steven said.

"Yes, he was well-educated," Natalia said. "I wish we'd had more time to hear more about his life."

"Yeah," said Steven. "But it just so happens that Ms. Johnson let me borrow the powder horn that she brought to class a few days ago. Maybe if we both touch it, we can go back to the forest and find Brant again."

As soon as they got to Natalia's house, they sat down on the porch. "I asked Ms. Johnson if I could bring this home to show my father," said Steven, pulling the powder horn from his jacket.

Natalia reached to touch it and suddenly, a mist surrounded the two of them. When they opened their eyes, they expected to be in the forest again. Instead, they were standing on the dirt road of a city.

"Where are we?" asked Natalia.

Steven pointed to a sign at the end of the street. "I ... think we're in New York City."

The children walked along the dirt road looking around at the strange buildings and stores. They walked past a dry goods store and on the next corner there stood Joseph Brant.

"Look! There he is!" Natalia said excitedly.

"Shh! Keep your voice down!" Steven pulled Natalia into a doorway out of sight.

"Sorry," Natalia said sheepishly.

"That's okay. Come on, let's follow him before we lose him."

The two checked to make sure the coast was clear and then darted across the road to the next corner.

They saw Brant talking to two other men in front of a restaurant. Brant gestured to the two men and then all three of them went into the restaurant.

"Come on, I bet we can sneak in and find a place to sit and listen in," Steven said, pulling Natalia's arm. The kids followed closely behind the three men and sat down at a table nearby.

"Thank you for agreeing to meet with us for an interview, Mr. Brant," the first man said.

"Of course," the Indian said.

The three of them sat down at a small table to talk.

"So, first off, there were a lot more Indians than white people back in 1770," one of the men said. "Why didn't the Indians win the war?"

"Good question," Brant replied. "It was sad, really. There were many Indian tribes all over America. They were fine warriors and hunters. But when the europeans came, they could not band together. Instead of coming together to fight them, the Indian tribes fought each other."

"I wonder why," Natalia murmured.

"Why do you think that was?" the second man asked.

Brant scratched his head, "I think it's because they had always fought among themselves. They just didn't realize that the white men were a much bigger threat to their survival."

"Is it true that you went to England in 1777 to meet with the king?" the first man asked.

"Yes, that is true. I went to England several times, actually. I met with King George III and spoke to other leaders. I tried to get everyone to sign a peace treaty. I also met with Indian tribal leaders."

"What did you talk to them about?"

"I tried to make them see that their world was changing. They would now have to share their land. But they would not listen."

"That's very noble of you. How very sad they wouldn't heed your counsel," the second man said.

The three men got up. "I really enjoyed talking to you gentlemen," Brant said. "Let's get together again sometime."

Natalia and Steven took this as their cue to leave. They quietly snuck out of the restaurant and disappeared down a side alley. In the alley, they joined hands and were sent back to Natalia's front porch.

title: Bison or Buffalo
text:
You may know this animal as a buffalo, but it's not really a true buffalo at all! The first explorers and settlers mistakenly called these animals buffalo, and the name stuck. The American buffalo is actually a bison. It belongs to the Bovidae family of mammals just like the common cow.

Once, about 20 million of these shaggy beasts roamed around the Great Plains. The bison was sacred to many American Indian tribes. They depended on it for food and many other things such as clothing, shoes, tools, soap, glue and even snow toboggans.

In the late 1800s, hunters began killing millions of bison for their hides and for sport. It is believed that more than 10 million bison were killed between 1870 and 1885. These hunters took only the animals' hides and left the carcass to rot where it fell. This was not how the American Indians hunted the bison. They believed that one must use every part of the bison to honor its sacrifice. Leaving the carcasses to rot was considered sacrilegious to the American Indians.

By 1889, only about 540 bison were left in the entire United States. Laws were made to prevent the bison from being killed, and luckily, they did not become extinct.

Today, there are more than 500,000 bison in the northern United States and Canada. Bison feed mainly on grass and can live to be 20-years old. The mother bison has one calf each year in May or June. Their populations have bounced back since being hunted to near extinction. However, you won't find many bison roaming the plains anymore. They can still be seen on land preserves and on some farms and ranches.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you are a Mohawk Indian. You have a family and winter is coming. How will you feed your family? The new European settlers have killed many of the bison and the land is not growing crops anymore. Should you fight for the right to hunt on new lands? Should you stay put and see if you can trade or work for supplies? Or should you move to a new area? Explain what you think would be the best course of action and support your reasons.

title: The Trail of Tears
text:
American Indians lived on millions of acres of land in North America. A lot of this land was in Georgia and Tennessee. Some of the land was also in Alabama, North Carolina, and Florida. They had lived there for thousands of years. Then the Age of Exploration brought European explorers and settlers to America.

At first, the American Indians were friendly to the colonists. They welcomed them. But over time, things changed. The colonists brought diseases like smallpox to America. They began moving west and building farms on Indian land.

The American Indians fought hard against these changes for many years. But they couldn't win against the Europeans. The white armies had guns and other weapons. The American Indians only had bows and arrows. The war went on. The new leaders of the United States got stronger.

Many American Indians died due to hunger and sickness. In 1830, Congress approved the Removal Act of 1830. This act forced the American Indians to live on new property under the protection of the United States government. It also said that the army had to help the American Indians travel to their new locations.

Eventually, all of the American Indians were forced to leave. They had to walk all the way from their homelands to Oklahoma. It was a long trip. Many American Indians died on the way. As they were walking, they would cry. They were sad to leave their homes, and sad for their loved ones. This is why the trip was called the Trail of Tears.

title: Think and Review
text:
Describe the part that European settlers played in the American Indians losing their land.

Why didn't the Indian tribes win the wars with early settlers?

How did Joseph Brant help the American Indians?

Why did so many American Indians die when the settlers first came?

title: American Indians and How Their Lives Changed
text:
It was early one morning. The class was waiting for Ms. Johnson to arrive. Everyone was excited to learn more about the first European explorers. Many came to North America in the 1700s.

Just then, the door opened. Ms. Johnson was carrying a box of old items.

"Let us help with that," said Natalia, and she rushed over to help Ms. Johnson.

Natalia helped their teacher place the box on the front desk as the class gathered around.

"Good morning, students," Ms. Johnson said. "As you can see, I have with me a box of items today. These are all examples of things traded between the settlers and American Indians."

"But why did the American Indians trade with colonists?" asked Steven.

"Well," the teacher began, "in those days, there were no stores. You could not go buy food and clothes. People often traded what they had with others who had something they needed. For instance, if a colonist mother needed a blanket for her new baby, and there was an American Indian woman who spent many hours making beautiful blankets, she could trade something like beans to the American Indian for a blanket. These types of trades were fairly common."

Natalia spoke, "My grandfather told me stories of how diseases like smallpox spread. Many American Indian communities vanished as a result. How did that happen?"

"Well," said Ms. Johnson, "when the white settlers came, they brought illnesses with them from Europe. The American Indians had never had diseases like smallpox. Since it was a new disease to them, they had no immunity. Smallpox would spread throughout the tribe. Many died before anyone knew what was going on. This is one of the sad ways that the American Indian culture changed."

The kids went back to looking through the box. "What are these engravings?" asked Steven. "Are these American Indian writings?"

Just then, Natalia noticed a powder horn."Oh, look! I know what this is."

She and Steven touched the powder horn at the same time. Suddenly, a mist surrounded them, and their class faded away. They looked at their new surroundings attempting to find their bearings. They saw that they stood in the middle of a big forest.

"Wow!" Steven said. "I wonder where we are."

Before Natalia could answer, a man rode up on horseback. He was dressed like an American Indian but seemed different to her. He reigned his horse to a stop and then slid down from the saddle, leading the horse into a grove of trees.

"Who's that?" Natalia whispered a little too loudly to Steven.

"I don't know," Steven whispered back a little more quietly, "Let's see if we can find out."

The two children tiptoed over to the grove of trees to follow the man as quietly as they could. When they caught up to him, there was another man in the trees. Steven and Natalia crouched behind a large rock and watched the two men shake hands.

"My name is Joseph Brant. My Mohawk name is Thayendanegea," the man dressed as an Indian said. "I work for the British army."

"How did that happen?" asked the other man.

"A Christian missionary taught me to speak English. Now I help the army understand what the Indians are saying. I also help them to make peace with the Indians."

"His work sounds very important," Steven whispered. Natalia shushed him to try and hear better.

"I understand you've gone all the way to the top to try and make peace between whites and Indians?"

"Yes, I have," Brant replied. "I've traveled to England to speak to King George III. I told him that the Indians could help the white men."

Just then, the four of them could hear the sounds of soldiers coming on horseback. The two men tensed.

Natalia pulled on Steven's sleeve, "We should get back to our classroom," she whispered. Steven nodded and pulled the powder horn back out. The two kids touched the horn together and disappeared. In a flash, they were back in class with Ms. Johnson.

Natalia and Steven decided to do more research on Joseph Brant. They learned that he tried to make peace between the American Indians and settlers. Brant wanted to make sure that the American Indians could stay on their land. He knew that many more colonists might come. Colonists were now building houses and planting crops on Indian land.

U.S. Army soldiers came, too. They fought to make the Indian tribes leave. The colonists were afraid of the Indians.

title: Lost Colony of Roanoke Chart
text:
In the chart below, draw a picture and write your description of each term.

Term Picture Description

John White

Croatan Indians

Archeologists

title: Think and Review
text:
In 1584, the first English expedition arrived in Roanoke. Why did the English want to establish colonies in the new world?

Archaeologists often set up dig sites to search for artifacts. Make a list of artifacts that you might expect to find at the site of the Roanoke colony.

When John White returned to the empty colony of Roanoke, he saw the word "Croatoan" carved onto a post. What conclusions could he draw about the disappearance of the colonists?

The colonists at Roanoke had a close relationship with the Croatan Indians. What caused the colonists to become friendly with them? What effect did the relationship have on the colonists?

title: England Seeks Riches
text:
In the late 1500s, England began to notice that the Spanish colonies (settlements far away from the country that rules it) in America were turning out to be successful. These colonies' successes were making Spain very rich. The English, wanting a share in the riches, decided to start their own colonies. England claimed land north of the Spanish colonies in Florida and named the land "Virginia." This is where The Queen of England decided that their first colony would be. She sent explorers to the land in 1585. The explorers discovered an area called Roanoke. They became friendly with the American Indians living in the area. It was decided that this would be the best place to start their first colony.

The First Colony at Roanoke

The first group of settlers was sent to the colony. It was a group of 107 men led by Sir Richard Grenville. They built a fort at Roanoke. They quickly learned that they were in trouble. They had hostile relations with a local group of American Indians and much of their food supply was ruined on their voyage. Captain Grenville returned to England to get more supplies for his colony.

Another English explorer, Sir Francis Drake, visited the colony while Grenville was away. He saw that the colony was failing and offered to help by taking them back to England. When Grenville finally returned to the settlement, he found it was abandoned. The first colony at Roanoke was no more. So, leaving a few of his men behind, Grenville returned to England.

The Second Colony at Roanoke

England was not ready to quit. They decided to try again. They sent more colonists to Roanoke in 1587. This time the group was led by John White. A group of 115 colonists was sent to Roanoke. The colonists expected to find the men that Grenville had left behind. All they found was a human skeleton.

The colonists worked hard to build their settlement. It was very difficult. They continued to have strained relations with the group of American Indians the first colony had conflicts with. Some of the men were killed because of disagreements with them. The colonists soon realized they once again did not have enough supplies. John White returned to England to gather more. A war between England and Spain made it impossible for White to return for several years. When he finally made it back to the colony, he was met with a mystery. Everyone had disappeared without a trace. The only thing left behind was the word CROATOAN carved into a wooden post and the letters C-R-O carved into a tree outside the settlement.

title: The Mystery of the Lost Colony of Roanoke
text:
Natalia and Steven walked excitedly towards their classroom. They couldn't wait for class to begin. They knew Ms. Johnson always had something fun up her sleeve for history class. As they entered the classroom, they noticed that Ms. Johnson was nowhere to be found. A group of their classmates was huddled together in the back of the room. Natalia and Steven hurried towards their friends to see what was going on.

When the children reached the back of the room, they noticed that their classmates were examining a box full of items. There was an old-fashioned detective hat, magnifying glass, flashlight, camera and a small notebook. "I wonder what we're going to do with these," Natalia said excitedly to Steven. Just as Steven was about to reply, Ms. Johnson walked into the room and greeted the class.

"Good morning class! It's time to put your detective skills to work. This week, we're going to be exploring one of America's biggest mysteries, the lost colony of Roanoke!" The class cheered in excitement. Ms. Johnson had been teaching them all about the English colonies and John White's journeys to the New World. They couldn't wait to learn more.

"Today," Ms. Johnson said dramatically, "We're going to do some research to figure out what may have caused the colony's disappearance." She pointed to a table set up with supplies. "I have textbooks, maps and photographs for you. You are also welcome to use the class computers for your research. Use your detective skills to determine what caused the colony to disappear. I can't wait to hear your theories!"

Steven and Natalia gathered around the table with supplies. They decided to take an old map and a book about the history of Roanoke. As they started to work, Ms. Johnson stood over them. "Great choices," she said. "That book has some interesting photographs that might help you."

Natalia opened the book and flipped carefully through the pages. "What's that?" Steven asked. He was pointing to an old photograph. It looked sort of like an old painting.

"That's the tree!" Natalia said excitedly. "When Ms. Johnson taught us about the Roanoke Colony, she said that all John White could find was a post and a tree with only one word and some letters carved into them." The two children grinned at each other and touched the photograph.

When Natalia and Steven opened their eyes, they found that they were transported back to the Roanoke Colony. The children walked around the colony but saw no signs of life. The colonists were nowhere to be found. The settlement appeared to have been long forgotten. Just as Natalia was about to speak, they spotted a few men walking towards them.

Natalia and Steven quickly hid behind a thick group of trees, careful not to be seen. The men looked around the colony as if searching for something.

"That's John White," whispered Steven, "I remember him from the pictures Ms. Johnson showed us."

The children watched closely as the men approached a tree. John White looked closely at the tree and discovered the letters C-R-O carved into it. Steven and Natalia listened as the men talked about what they had found. According to the men, there were no signs that the colonists had been in any danger. Before John White returned to England for supplies, he had instructed the colonists on what to do if they had to leave the colony before he returned. White had instructed the colonists to carve their destination into a tree. He also told them to carve a cross next to the destination if they had left due to serious danger. There was no such cross.

The men seemed confused. If they weren't in any serious danger, what could have caused the colonists to leave? It had been three long years since John White had left the colony. The men wondered aloud about the fate of the colonists. It was clear that the colonists had been gone for a long time. There was no sign that the colonists had been in trouble. They knew that the Croatan was a friendly American Indian tribe that lived in the area. They wondered if the colonists had turned to them for help.

As the men started to turn away from the tree, the children knew it was time to leave. "Let's head back before any of the men see us," whispered Steven, "I bet we'd give those men quite a fright if they saw us." They both touched the photograph in their book.

Before they knew it, they were back in Ms. Johnson's classroom. Natalia turned to Steven and said, "I think I've got some ideas about what may have happened to the colonists. Let's start writing them down!"

"Great idea," Steven replied. "But let's watch the video about the Roanoke Colony, first."

title: Dig This!
text:
Did you know that people are still trying to find the lost colony? These people are called archaeologists. They learn about history by studying items that were left behind. These objects from the past are called artifacts. Studying them helps us learn about how people used to live.

Archaeologists look for items by using special tools to dig up the land. They must be careful not to cause damage while they dig. These researchers have been digging up places where they think the colonists may have gone. The places they look at are called dig sites.

At one site, they found pieces of an item that they believe may have once been a pot. They believe it belonged to the colonists. Unfortunately, they can't be certain. More digging and testing must happen before we can ever truly solve the mystery of the lost colony.

title: Let's Write
text: The fate of the Roanoke colonists remains a mystery today. This week, you learned that curious historians are still looking for clues to find out what happened to the colonists. In a short essay, explain what you think happened to the colonists. Why did the colony fail? Where do you think the colonists went? Use the stories and theories in this week's issue to help you.

title: The Lumbee and Chesapeake
text:
On August 18, 1590, when John White finally returned to the settlement at Roanoke Island, he found that everyone was gone and that it looked as though it had been deserted for a while. Where they went and what happened to them is still one of the greatest unsolved mysteries in history.

There are many theories and explanations for their apparent disappearance. One explanation is that they were all killed by a nearby American Indian tribe that was hostile to them. Another theorizes that they could have been taken or killed by Spanish explorers or raiders. One theory, however, offers that the Roanoke colonists left the Island to live with a local American Indian tribe that was friendly to them; the Croatans.

Today there is a tribe of Lumbee Indians in North Carolina that believe their ancestors migrated there from the local Croatoan region where the Croatan lived. Many historians believe the Lumbee to be the descendants of the Lost Colony and the Croatan tribe. Proof, they say, can be seen in their surprisingly long held English traditions and in the way they looked. They had been known to speak English, even amongst themselves. Many of them also practiced Christianity. Many Lumbee have also been said to have fair skin and gray eyes. This would have indicated that the Lost Colony had made families with the Croatan tribe.

Another theory suggests that the Lost Colony joined the Chesapeake Indians. The chief of the Powhatan Indians, in 1608, had apparently confessed to killing the Lost Colonists to English explorer, John Smith. Never having written down the confession, he only spoke about it 14 years later to a friend. If this theory is true, that means that there would be no surviving members of the Lost Colony and that joining the Chesapeake to the north, spelled doom.

title: Planning a Colony
text: This week you learned about the Lost Colony of Roanoke. Imagine that you were one of the early English colonists at Roanoke. Work with a partner to come up with a plan of what you must do in order to help your colony be successful. Be sure to answer the following questions: Where will you live? What will you eat? How will you decide what jobs everyone will do? Who will lead your colony? When you finish, share your plan with your classmates. Did any other groups come up with similar ideas? Did any groups come up with ideas that are different from yours?

title: John White's Journeys
text:
John White was born in London in 1540. He was a talented painter and mapmaker. In 1585, he joined an expedition to the Americas.

John spent time taking notes about his experiences in America. He also painted what he saw. His notes and paintings have helped us learn about the American Indian people that lived there. Because of White, we have learned a lot about the Algonquin tribes.

In 1585, White returned to England. While there, he was offered the job of returning to start an English colony. He agreed to take the job and gathered 113 people to join him in the colony. His daughter and her husband made the journey with him.

The colonists set sail for the Americas in 1587. White was named the governor of the colony. When they landed, the colonists quickly realized they were not prepared. They did not have enough food and supplies. Their fights with the American Indians were dangerous.

White returned to England at the end of the year to gather supplies for the colony. A war broke out between England and Spain. This kept White from returning to his colony for three years. When he finally returned, the settlers had vanished. John searched but never found them. He returned to England, defeated.

title: Jamestown Beats the Odds
text:
The settlement of Jamestown was not a democracy. Leadership was not chosen through elections. The Virginia Company, which funded the settlement, appointed governors who set the rules for the colony. These rules were based on what would make the settlement profitable. The appointed governors would often arrive with supply ships, but wouldn't stay in the settlement for long.

It was hard living in Jamestown. They did not have a great deal of food on hand. The settlers also didn't know how to farm in their new home. They also suffered from illness. They were often on the brink of giving up because they couldn't find a profitable crop.

Then came a new governor, Sir Thomas Gates and another settler, John Rolfe. These individuals helped Jamestown change its course.

Sir Thomas Gates and John Rolfe arrived in 1610. They were part of a ship carrying supplies and settlers that became shipwrecked in Bermuda during the previous fall. They built two boats and finished traveling the remainder of the way to Jamestown. What they found was starvation, disease and conflict with the local tribes. Sir Thomas Gates took charge and decided to abandon Jamestown. Everyone boarded the two ships to depart. But before they got far down the river, they crossed paths with the relief ships of Governor Thomas West coming up the river. The colonists decided to return to Jamestown.

In the coming years, John Rolfe discovered a profitable crop for the settlement. He began to grow a new type of tobacco. The crop thrived and finally allowed the settlement to begin to pay for itself. The Virginia Company finally began to receive a return on its investment.

When Jamestown began to send tobacco for sale, the Virginia Company was able to reinvest the profit in supplies for the colony. They also sent more settlers to help cultivate the crop and contribute to the growth of the settlement.

title: Jamestown's Uncertain Beginning
text:
Ms. Johnson set up a video about Jamestown to display on the class whiteboard. She explained that the video would help them understand the artifacts she planned to share with them. Ms. Johnson shared with the class that she spent time doing research of her own in Virginia before the discovery of Jamestown's true location in 1996. During her research, she found a collection of arrowheads, pottery scraps, small coins and small blue beads.

"After the video, you and your study partner will be given an artifact from my collection to consider." Ms. Johnson said. "I'd like for you to imagine how the items would have been used."

Steven and Natalia sat patiently, excited to learn more from their teacher's presentation. Afterward, Ms. Johnson passed out her artifacts. She gave them a beautiful glass bead. Steven and Natalia held the blue bead between them and traveled to Jamestown in 1608.

"Hey, look over there!" Steven pointed. He and Natalia could see the gates of the Jamestown Fort from the treeline where they now stood.

"Those are the Powhatan Indians Ms. Johnson told us lived in the area," replied Natalia. "What do they have in those baskets?"

As they watched, both groups set things between them. When the Powhatan opened their baskets, Natalia and Steven saw food items like corn and dried fish in the baskets. The settler's boxes contained copper and blue glass beads like the ones Ms. Johnson shared with the class.

As Steven and Natalia observed the interaction, they noticed there seemed to be a great deal of tension between the settlers and the Powhatan. The leaders of the two groups seemed to negotiate for a bit. The settlers offered several cases of their items and the Powhatan presented what they believed to be a fair trade.

"Hey, they're bartering!" Natalia exclaimed softly. "Remember what Ms. Johnson said about people discussing a fair value of one thing for another when there wasn't money?"

They turned back and saw as the two groups picked up the items they'd gotten in the exchange. Both groups then backed away from the other, neither turning their backs.

"They're heading this way," Steven said. "We'd better get back to class."

title: American Indian Craft
text: The totem pole is an American Indian sculpture carved from trees. Totem poles were found in the Pacific Northwest. There is no evidence of totem poles being carved by Powhatan Indians. What do you think a totem pole carved by the Powhatan might look like? Animals, nature and other designs were most often carved and painted on totem poles. Decorate the totem pole provided using your own drawings. Be creative!

title: Forced Labor in an Emerging Democracy
text:
When Africans arrived in Jamestown, they were not all enslaved. Some were indentured servants with a term of service to complete for a person or a company. They became free men when they completed the term.

My name is Elizabeth Key Grinstead. My father was a white Englishman named Thomas Key. He was a planter who also belonged to the Virginia House of Burgesses. My mother was an enslaved black woman.

When my father moved back to England in 1636, he gave me to my godfather, Humphrey Higgonson, making him my guardian and owner for nine years. He insisted that I be treated as a member of the family and that I be freed at the age of 15.

My father died in 1636. That same year, my godfather sold me to Colonel John Mottram as an indentured servant for an additional term of nine years. He moved to Coan Hall in Northumberland County and took me with him. I served in the Colonel's household until 1650.

He paid passage for more indentured servants from England to add to his household. Many of those who came to the colonies entered into indentured servitude for six years to pay for their passage to America. One of the new servants was my future lawyer and husband, William Grinstead. He came to seek his fortune. As a younger son, he could not inherit any of his father's estate.

We fell in love and began a family. The law kept us from getting married. Indentured servants could not marry during their term of service.

After the Colonel died in 1655, my son and I were described as an enslaved servant and son while affairs of the estate and property were being settled. I was not. I was indentured. I sued for my freedom. William acted as my lawyer.

We won our suit in 1656. According to law, as the daughter of a free man, I was free as well. My status passed on to my son. William and I married and had another son.

title: Think and Review
text:
What does "Pocahontas" mean, and what were her other names?

What were the issues encountered by the colonists?

Do you think indentured servitude was a good option for people to travel to America? Do you think it was a fitting punishment for people who broke the law?

How did the arrival of the new type of tobacco introduced by John Rolfe affect the Jamestown colony?

title: Popham: Jamestown's Twin Colony in Maine
text:
Popham and Jamestown colonies were both established in 1607. King James wanted the English presence in the New World to grow quickly. He also wanted to trade with the native people and profit from local resources. Even though it would be harder for England to send supplies to two colonies, the king established a northern colony, Popham, and a southern colony, Jamestown, to increase the odds of success.

Popham was set in Maine. Jamestown was set in Virginia. Two different groups from the Virginia Company gave support to the towns. One group worked from London. The other worked from Plymouth. The London Company took charge of Jamestown. The Plymouth Company took charge of Popham. Whichever town proved successful would receive an additional land grant.

The Popham colony seemed to have a promising start. Just like Jamestown, they began to build a fort and houses. They also built the first English ship to be constructed in North America.

However, they had very little success making contact with the local Indian tribes to begin a trading relationship. They came into conflict during a meeting and could not reach an agreement. The settlers also suffered from food shortages and disease. However, they still managed to do better than the settlers in Jamestown.

The failure of the Popham colony came when they lost their leadership. Their original leader, George Popham, died shortly after food shortages caused half of the colonists to return to England. The other leader of the group, Raleigh Gilbert, guided the colony through the rest of that winter. Unfortunately, supply ships brought the news that one of the colony's main financiers, Sir John Popham, had died.

Despite recent success trading furs with the Indians, the colony completely fell apart a few months later. Gilbert learned that his brother had died. He inherited his family's estate and decided to return to England. After many hardships and mishaps, the remaining colonists did not wish to stay and returned to England as well.

title: Let's Write
text: Talk about how you think the Powhatan people felt when the colonists arrived. What do you think about the way they treated the settlers?

title: My Name is Not Pocahontas
text:
Natalia and Steven continued to explore the artifacts Ms. Johnson had on hand. Natalia noticed a scrap of cloth and pointed to it.

"What do you think this was?" She asked. They both reached out to it and were transported to an English sitting room.

They found themselves seated looking at a large gathering of people chatting and sipping tea. All of these people were gathered around a young American Indian woman. A few of them passed her tea and cookies while others asked her questions about her home and her tribe.

"I will tell you my story," the woman said looking at those gathered around her. "I am the daughter of Chief Powhatan, and I am the youngest of his children. My tribe and my father treasured me. They called me Pocahontas, but that was merely a nickname. It meant 'playful one.' My people have a tradition of giving each other many names. In addition to Pocahontas, some called me Matoaka and others called me Amonute. When I was 11 years old, strangers arrived in our lands, and their presence changed our world ... my world."

The young woman told them about the early struggles of the settlers and the aid her tribe offered to them.

"When we saw that they did not know how to grow food or hunt, we brought food. Then, we showed them how to grow their own food and hunt. We thought we had an agreement, an understanding. They did not understand because they began to wander farther and farther into our territory. There was one of the people who traveled beyond the borders given to the settlers one winter. He trespassed and entered our village ..."

"Steven, I think she's referring to John Smith," Natalia said. "Didn't she save him from being killed by her father for trespassing?"

"There isn't much evidence, besides John Smith's version of the story, to know what actually happened. She may not be talking about John Smith at all." Steven replied. "It could have been a different settler who trespassed."

" ... we treated him as an honored guest. I was young and curious and used his time with us to ask him as many questions as I could about him and his people. I thought him a friend.

"Over the years, they kept trespassing on our territory. This created much conflict between my people and his. Each of us began to raid the other. After one such raid, I was taken as a prisoner of war. Needless to say, this was a good way to keep my father from attacking Jamestown.

"The rest, you know. We made a peace agreement, the Powhatan and the people of Jamestown. I married John Rolfe and now we have a son, Thomas. I traveled here to England to share my story. I count the days until I can visit home." She ended with a smile.

"What about when you saved his life, Rebecca? What about when you saved John Smith?" one of the guests asked.

"Rebecca?" Natalia repeated, perplexed.

"When she married John Rolfe, she became a Christian," Steven explained. "Back then, when American Indians were baptized they were given new names."

They missed what Pocahontas said in response to the question, but they caught the next part of what she said.

"My father is a skilled diplomat. He kept the peace between his people in the Confederacy and with the people of Jamestown. We offered a hungry stranger shelter during the long winter and returned him fit and well to his people."

Natalia and Steven returned to the classroom and looked up her story. They learned that she held many salons like the one they'd witnessed. However, her life ended the next year in 1617.

"How sad ... no one really knows how she died," Natalia said. "She was traveling back to North America. She was in good health when she and John Rolfe boarded a ship to leave for America, but she got very sick by the time they had sailed to a town called Gravesend in England. It looks like she was taken ashore and died shortly after and is now buried there."

title: Colonists Establish Jamestown for Economic Gain
text:
England's King James gave permission for a group of 100 men, the Virginia Company, to settle in North America. In 1607, they chose land near a river and built Jamestown, in honor of King James. They hoped to get rich by finding gold.

Life in the colony was hard and dangerous. The water in Jamestown was brackish and not good for drinking. The marshland was not good for farming. The men focused on getting rich instead of hunting or growing food. Disease and hunger killed most of them, and only 38 men survived eight months after arriving.

One who survived was Captain John Smith. Late in 1607, he found himself at the mercy of the Powhatan Indians. Historians disagree about what took place. Some say he was to be executed and was saved by the chief's daughter, Pocahontas. Others say he was cared for as an honored guest. Whatever happened, Smith was allowed to leave. He stayed friends with the Powhatan. They taught the colonists about hunting, fishing and planting crops.

Smith was a good leader and the settlers elected him council president. Smith made sure everyone worked hard to keep the town from failing. He said, "Work or starve!" to get people through the "Starving Time."

The settlers never became rich by finding gold or silver. They got rich with tobacco. An Englishman named John Rolfe began planting tobacco, which grew well in Jamestown's soil and climate. This became the "gold" of Jamestown. People in England bought as much tobacco as possible. Jamestown traded it for food and supplies.

Jamestown grew quickly, and in 1619, the House of Burgesses was formed to make laws. The people now had some say in how their colony operated. They did not have this privilege in England.

Unfortunately, Jamestown's success did not continue. Settlers began to fight with the Powhatan, and the price of tobacco dropped. Government leaders were not always honest, and people died of disease. In 1624, King James took back the land and made Virginia a royal colony.

title: Mayflower Compact
text:
Natalia: Are you ready for our journey, Steven? Here's the passenger list for the Mayflower ship. All we have to do is touch it and we'll be able to jump back in time to the ship.

Steven: I can’t wait! I’ve never been on a ship on the Atlantic Ocean before. I’m looking forward to this!

Natalia: Remember, we need to pay extra special attention to the Pilgrims when they talk about their agreement. The rules they decided on following and how they will live became important examples for our Founding Fathers when they wrote the Constitution.

Steven: Oh, yeah, the Mayflower Compact. Well, I’m ready. Are you?

Natalia: Absolutely! Here we go …

Steven and Natalia touch the list and are transported away.

Steven: It’s really cold on the Mayflower! I’m sure glad we dressed warmly. The ship set sail in July, but here we are in November and it sure is damp and chilly on the Atlantic Ocean today.

Natalia: I’m freezing, but at least we aren’t far from land. We're in Provincetown Harbor. It’s not very far from Plymouth or Massachusetts Bay. This is where the Pilgrims, aboard the Mayflower, signed their Mayflower Compact. This compact was the first form of government in the colonies.

Steven: Come on, let’s go into the cabin where the discussions are being held. Then we can learn about this historic agreement.

Natalia and Steven sneak into the cabin where a group of Pilgrims is gathered.

Natalia: That’s better. There are no sea winds in the cabin! That's funny ... Steven, there aren't any other women in this room! There were some women on deck, but there aren't any in here.

Steven: That’s true. Pilgrim women didn’t take part in the discussion about the colony or the rules for it. In fact, only Pilgrim men signed the Mayflower Compact. Forty-one men signed the agreement. These men made the laws for their colony that everyone there would have to follow.

Natalia: I’m sure glad that women get to help make laws today. Let’s see if we can read what rules the Pilgrims are writing there while they're talking. I see that one rule says that the Pilgrims will follow their Christian faith.

Steven: Another one says that the Pilgrims will create one community. Everyone will work together to support the community.

Natalia: This rule is surprising. It says that the Pilgrims would stay loyal to King James of England. I thought the reason that the Pilgrims left England is that they didn’t have religious freedom under his reign?

Steven: Ms. Johnson said that the Pilgrims wanted to govern themselves in a new colony but they did not want to break with England completely. In fact, they had plans to trade with England once they set up their colony.

Natalia: Why did the Pilgrims want to leave England then? I'm confused.

Steven: The Pilgrims were angry that the King of England said that everyone had to be part of the Church of England. The Pilgrims didn’t think the Church of England was true to the Christian faith. They wanted to set up their own church but were not allowed to in England. That's why they crossed the ocean to live in a place where they could. The Puritans were another group of people that sailed to the New World for religious freedom. They believed in the teachings of the Church of England, but they came here wanting to “purify” these teachings. They wanted to return the religion to its roots.

Natalia: I see. They must have had very strong beliefs. This ship is so small on this large and dangerous sea. They risked their lives to travel to America! I think they are very brave.

title: American Indians Help Out
text:
Thanksgiving is a popular holiday in our country. We trace the first Thanksgiving to the Pilgrims and American Indians who lived in the area of Plymouth and Massachusetts Bay Colony. We love to eat delicious foods with our families on Thanksgiving. We talk about what happened during the year that we are thankful for.

The Algonquin helped the Pilgrims learn about the new land they came to. They taught the Pilgrims about maple syrup. But there were other friendly American Indians around too, like the Wampanoag. They also taught the Pilgrims about new foods and about the animals they could hunt. The Wampanoag were there with the Pilgrims on this first Thanksgiving.

Some of the foods the Wampanoag shared with the Pilgrims were corn, squash and beans. During the growing season, the Pilgrims tended their gardens. They grew herbs, vegetables and wheat. Other foods served at the first Thanksgiving were venison, wild turkey, pumpkins and freshly baked bread.

All in all, about 60 Pilgrims gathered for the feast after they had harvested their crops. As they were celebrating, Chief Massasoit, a great king of the native people, and 90 of his tribesmen arrived on the scene. Massasoit and his people had been a great help to the Pilgrims in teaching them the ways of farming and hunting in the New World. The Pilgrims and Indians feasted and celebrated peacefully together. The natives went out and killed five deer and brought them back to the feast. People played games and talked and rejoiced together. After so much hardship, they finally saw an end to all the loss and sadness they experienced. Even though they didn't call their celebration Thanksgiving at the time, they were grateful all the same to have so much.

title: Anne Hutchinson: A Different Opinion
text:
On board the Mayflower, women didn’t have much say about the rules for life in Massachusetts Bay Colony, even though there were many women on the ship. One such woman, Anne Hutchinson, had her own ideas about how to practice her Christian faith.

In 1638 in Portsmouth Colony, Anne Hutchinson lived with her 14 children. The Puritans in Massachusetts Bay had put her on trial. She didn’t share all the same beliefs as the Puritans. She believed that the Puritans were too strict. They put her in prison; then they exiled her. That means they kicked her out of the colony. She went to live in Portsmouth. She signed an agreement known as the Portsmouth Compact.

The Portsmouth Compact helped Anne and her followers set up a colony that was Christian, but not as strict about its rules for worship. This compact isn’t as famous as the Mayflower Compact, but it was still very important.

Anne was truly brave. The Puritans who imprisoned her tried to make her change her beliefs, but she refused. She and her husband, their children and other followers who agreed with her lived in a colony in Rhode Island for many years.

After her husband died, Anne moved to Long Island in New York. She and her family, except for one, were killed by American Indians who were involved in a territorial dispute. All those who came out to the New World had to be brave. They faced many dangers as they tried to make a new life in this land.

title: Pilgrims, Puritans: What’s the Difference?
text:
A lot of people think that Pilgrims and Puritans are the same group of people. In some ways, Pilgrims and Puritans were similar. They both wanted religious freedom. They both settled in the area of Massachusetts Bay and Plymouth. They both dressed in a similar manner, too. Even though they looked the same and shared similar religious beliefs, there are differences.

The Puritans believed in the teachings of the Church of England but believed it had gone astray. They came here to purify it. That's how they got their name, Puritans. They had very strict rules. They believed women were subordinate (lesser than) men. Even though they came here for religious freedom, they did not tolerate the religious views of others.

The Pilgrims came here in order to break away from the Church of England. They came to the New World in order to practice their faith without fear of being arrested. In England, you could not be a member of any other church. The Pilgrims came over in the Mayflower.

title: Massachusetts Bay and Plymouth Colonies
text:
Ms. Johnson: Welcome to the city of Boston, students! As I told you during our trip, Boston is the capital city of Massachusetts. As you look around, you may notice this city looks very modern. Over there is the John Hancock Tower. It is the tallest skyscraper in Boston. Down this street is the New England Aquarium. But I want you to try to imagine what this land would look like without all of its tall buildings, roads and streets. Can you imagine what the Puritans and Pilgrims saw when they explored this area?

Steven: I bet they saw lots of forests.

Natalia: I think they saw some American Indians, too.

Ms. Johnson: In my hand, I am holding the diary of Anne Bradstreet. She was a Puritan who became the first writer in the colonies to be published. Her work hints at what it was like to live in those times. I’ll pass it around. Here, Steven and Natalia. You look first while the rest of us have a seat on this building’s step to view my Boston Map.

Steven and Natalia touch the diary and zip back in time.

Steven: Wow! I can’t believe it! Where did all the cars and buildings go?

Natalia: There weren’t any cars in Massachusetts Bay Colony in the year 1628. Not far from here is Plymouth Colony. It was founded by Pilgrims in 1620. Can you imagine what it must have been like to get off the boat and step onto this land? What would the Pilgrims have done for food? What would they do for shelter? I guess they still had food on their ship. Maybe they cut down some trees to make cabins for shelter.

Steven: They did bring some supplies with them to the New World. I read about that in a book Ms. Johnson gave me. They also used the land for wood. They brought tools along to chop down trees and to plow the ground to grow crops. Why do you think these early people to the New World settled here at Massachusetts Bay and Plymouth Rock?

Natalia: Because that’s where they landed first?

Steven: Not quite, Natalia. The Pilgrims actually sailed along the shore in search of a good place to settle in this area. This spot has a good bay as you can see. There are also streams and creeks nearby where fresh water can be found.

Natalia: What happened when their supplies of food ran out?

Steven: Both the Puritans and Pilgrims had to learn about the land quickly. It was difficult for them. They had to hunt, fish and build farms in order to survive here. Learning to survive in a new land was hard, but these groups were determined to make their lives here work. It’s that drive that helped build the city of Boston.

title: Let's Write
text: As the Puritans settled in America, they listed many strict rules that colonists had to follow or they could be jailed or kicked out of the colony like Anne Hutchinson. People who missed church were fined. A husband could not kiss his wife in public and a woman was not allowed to wear lace. If you were starting your own colony, what types of rules would you set?

title: Importance of Trade
text:
Syrup was important for trade in the early days of Massachusetts Bay Colony. The colonists, Puritans and Pilgrims, liked to put it on their hot cakes as much as you and I do. But they couldn't just run down to the store to buy it.

Making syrup was a long process. The Europeans learned how to collect sap from the natives and then put their own twist on collecting it. They would drill holes into maple trees where they would insert a wooden spout, kind of like what you'd see on a tea kettle. They would then hang a bucket from the spout to collect the sap when it came out. The sap then had to be boiled to the right thickness. This usually took a long time.

Maple syrup was something the colonists didn’t know about at first. The Algonquin knew how to harvest syrup. They traded it to the colonists for metal items like tin pans and tools. The colonists kept some syrup but also traded some. They even traded things like animal furs and timber from the forests of Massachusetts. This made Massachusetts Bay a busy place for trade. Massachusetts is still busy with trade today.

title: Colonists Settle Plymouth for Religious Freedom
text:
People looking for religious freedom started the Plymouth Colony. Back in England, there was a law that said everyone must be a member of the Church of England. A group called the Separatists wanted to worship in their own way and refused to join. They moved out of England to Holland, now known as the Netherlands. They suffered persecution there, too. To be persecuted means that people treat you poorly because of your religion, race or beliefs.

In 1620, these Separatists, now known as Pilgrims, decided to sail to North America on a ship called the Mayflower. The ship landed at Plymouth Bay in what is now Massachusetts. The Pilgrim leaders came up with a government plan to help people live together peacefully. All the men signed the agreement called the Mayflower Compact. The Mayflower Compact is an early example of self-government.

Like the Jamestown settlers, the Plymouth colonists had hard times at first. The winter was very cold. Food ran out quickly. Half the settlers died the first winter. Some English-speaking American Indians taught the Pilgrims to plant corn, catch fish and gather maple syrup. One of them was named Squanto. He also helped arrange a peace treaty between Chief Massasoit and the Pilgrims. The Wampanoag and the Pilgrims promised to help each other.

Plymouth colonists elected William Bradford as their governor in 1621. Under his leadership Plymouth grew and became successful. Europeans learned of the chance for freedom in America, and more people came to seek a new life. Although groups came for freedom of religious expression, they did not all agree with each other in their beliefs and faced challenges getting along.

title: Geography and History
text:
Natalia: Good morning, fellow students! Welcome to your school news! I'm your host, Natalia.

Steven: And I'm your host, Steven! Our show today focuses on the 13 original colonies. You know what that means from your history class.

Natalia: What were the colonies first like? Our report today has all the information. We discuss geography, too!

Steven: That's right, Natalia! The history of the 13 colonies gives us information on natural geography. And it discusses our neighbors to the north and south.

Natalia: What do you mean, Steven?

Steven: The 18th century was a busy time. Three different European countries were in North America. They built settlements all along the coast. They settled in places that were nearby the Atlantic Ocean first. France built colonies further north and in parts of Canada. The Spanish colonized further south and into the Caribbean. Today, we call this region Latin America. The original 13 colonies were between these two French and Spanish locations. The English colonists divided this area into three different parts. Each region had a different landscape and climate. Natalia, you have a report on the New England colonies. Natalia?

Natalia: Thank you, Steven! Welcome to New England, everyone! This is the oldest and coldest of the original 13 colonies. Glaciers covered this area a long time ago. It left some sandy dirt behind and pushed all the good soil to the south. That was bad if you were a farmer. The cold climate made farming even worse! The growing season in New England was short. Farmers could grow crops for only five months. That isn't a long time at all.

Steven: Wow, Natalia, it sounds like life was hard in New England. How did the colonists survive?

Natalia: They used the natural resources. Today the region is famous for its wood products. The colonists cut this timber from the forests. Whaling was a popular industry in New England, too. Today people visit the state to go fishing in rivers and on the coastline.

Steven: I'm glad the whale-hunting stopped.

Natalia: Me too! We have lights powered with electricity instead of lanterns that burned whale oil. Modern discoveries changed the economy. You discuss that in your Middle Colonies report, don't you, Steven?

Steven: Yes, I do, Natalia! While the melting glaciers took the good soil from New England, they left that soil in the Middle Colonies. The Middle Colonies were sunnier and rainier. They had a longer growing season. The farmers could grow different plants.

Natalia: Climate and growing season improved further south. The Southern Colonies had the best farmland. And they had the longest growing season.

Steven: That's right, Natalia. The area has lots of water, too. The Tidewater is to the south. The interior has the mountain rivers and streams. Most of the colonists settled in that area. They were farmers and hunters. Most of the farms were small so they could fit on narrow, steep hillsides.

Natalia: The Tidewater is important. The region's economy depends on it. It's the same in the present day. Think of all the seafood!

Steven: That's true! Modern development is important. We need it for the economy, too. People like to build houses by the seashore. A company that builds a petroleum rig in the water built it to access the natural resource. However, modern developments like this can be dangerous. It can leak chemicals or toxins that spill into water. Sometimes these leaks are even catastrophic. Seafood comes from the water. Can the two exist at the same time? Or should they?

Natalia: I can see the problem. That's one example. A lot of things have changed since the historic days of the 13 colonies.

Steven: Some things haven't, though! Tune in again tomorrow morning for another exciting episode!

title: The Appalachian Trail
text:
A long time ago, hunters and settlers used the Appalachian Trail for traveling, hunting, fishing and trading. The trail was a vital part of the original 13 colonies. Today, it is a scenic trail that follows the mountains. The trail starts in central Maine and ends in northern Georgia.

This national park preserves history and nature. Some regions of the park are famous for the variety of plants and animals you can find growing and living there. People like this trail because of the natural scenery. You can see almost every geographic feature imaginable. The trail has views of mountains, forests, canyons and valleys. You can walk along rivers, next to lakes and along the shoreline. It's popular with naturalists and tourists.

The trail starts in Maine. This was the most northern part of the original 13 colonies. It was wild and rocky then. It is wild and rocky now! You can see moose, loons and lakes. Be careful, as parts of the trail can be dangerous. The trail isn't modern. You have to travel carefully like the settlers did.

The states of New York and Vermont are close to one another, but when you hike through those states on the trail, the differences between these regions couldn't be more obvious! Vermont has lush, green forests. It has a mud season too, and hikers are told to stay home as hiking through the mud can be very dangerous. New York has big trees and impressive hills and valleys. It is also possible to encounter black bears on the New York trail. We must always be respectful and cautious of these animals, as the forests and hills the Appalachian Trail winds through are these animals homes.

The Laurel Highlands, a famous section of the trail, is located in Pennsylvania. This is one of the Middle Colonies. The area has a diverse environment. It's so diverse that scientists break it into seven different parts. That's a lot! The Laurel Highlands has a lot of rivers and lakes. Modern tourists like to go there. It's a nice place for kayaks and canoes. People like to fish there, too.

Follow the trail to the south, and you'll start to feel the weather become warmer. The settlers in this region had more farmland. They had a longer growing season. In Virginia, the trail looks over a mix of forests and farmland. Finally, the trail reaches its endpoint, Georgia. You might think of peach trees or peanut farms. But the mountains in Georgia will surprise you. It's cold! Snowfall can be heavier here than more northern parts of the trail. Compare this landscape to the geography in Maine, or even in Pennsylvania. You can see how different the regions are.

The trail is quite popular today. You can hike the trail for a day, or take a tent and stay for a night. "Thru-hiking" is a popular trend. It's an interesting challenge. It means that you complete the whole trail in one visit. That's more than 2,000 miles. This hiking project can take a few months. Many people do it today. Walking the whole trail on foot is like what the colonists did. While some things continue to change, some things stay the same.

title: Diverse Economies: A Timeline
text:
1600 to 1650: Several countries have built colonies in North America. French to the north, near the St. Lawrence Seaway. The Dutch and Swedish have fur trade posts on the shores of the Hudson River. These colonies hunt for natural resources. They need wood and metal for building ships. They want to trade furs for spices.

England builds a colony in Virginia. The London Virginia Company hoped to find gold. Many people search for gold at this time. The Spanish found a lot of gold down south. The money from the gold made Spain a powerful country.

1650 to 1700: Nobody finds gold. But the colonists in Virginia discover a new plant. Tobacco becomes the British colony's cash crop. Between 1607 and 1662, the New England, Middle and Southern Colonies form. The economy of New England depends on whaling, fishing and timber. Shipbuilding becomes a major local industry. Colonists export the resources to England. They trade with the Middle and Southern Colonies, too. The Southern Colonies have plenty of water and a long growing season. They grow rice and cotton. A lot of cotton goes to England. The cheap cotton is in high demand. The cotton is cheap because slaves are the workforce. Slaves don't get paid any wages.

1700 to 1750: Britain has a global trading network. It includes colonies all over the world. The trade between the colonies continues. Other goods come from British colonies all over the world. Tea, glass, textiles, rum and sugar are a few examples.

1750 to 1800: The British Empire controls most of the world. The colonies make England rich. They produce raw materials, like timber. The colonies also produce luxury goods, like tobacco. The goods are in demand all over the world. The Middle and Southern Colonies produce tobacco and cotton. Both items have a high value on the global market.

The British colonies expand. The French colonies in the north get bigger, too. The French and British fight the Seven Years' War. The war decides which country will control North America. The British win the war with help from colonial forces.

The colonies continue to make money. The population grows. Settlers and colonists come. They build towns, farms and mines. A group of colonists decided they didn't agree with the British King. They feel it is unfair to be taxed and not have representation in British Parliament. They try and have this changed, but end up in a revolt against British rule in the following decades. In 1776, the colonies become the United States of America. Trade continues based on laws made locally. The King of England no longer controls the economy. The American government makes their own laws.

The 1800s: An inventor creates a machine that turns cotton into cloth. Other mechanical inventions follow, and machines soon replace horses on the farm. Train tracks and power lines start to appear. The electric light bulb replaces candles and whale oil.

title: Great Hopes Plantation
text:
Hey everyone! Welcome to the Great Hopes Plantation. Check out these cool pictures I took! And I didn't even have to go back in time. The plantation is part of Colonial Williamsburg, a massive living history site in Virginia. A living history site has historic reenactors or interpreters. These people dress in old clothes and pretend to be people from that era. A reenactor's job is to help us imagine life in the past.

In the 18th century, Williamsburg was a colonial city of about 2,000 people. Many people lived outside of the city on farms. The Great Hopes Plantation did not originally exist in Williamsburg. It was constructed for people to come and learn what life was like for early Williamsburg colonists. The farmland, buildings, clothing and tools that you see are all authentic to the time period.

Many Williamsburg colonists did not live on plantation estates like the famous ones in the south, rather, they lived on modest farms. These farms consisted of a kitchen, corn house, smokehouse, tobacco house and a log house. The property would often have a well, too. Tobacco was the first cash crop that many of these farmers relied on. This tradition has survived into the present. Tobacco is still a profitable industry, even though it has slowed down. Corn was also an important food crop in the region at the time. It was used to make meal or grits. Today, farms in Virginia don't grow as much corn. When you go to The Great Hopes Plantation, you'll see most or all of these features of farm life, as well as crops being grown. The climate allowed for some fruit trees, so there's also an orchard. It has a fence to keep out wild animals.

We can't forget the farm animals! Great Hopes has some livestock, too. Several of the animals kept there are the same rare breeds of the past. The geography of the region means more forests than fields, so cattle and pigs often roam instead of staying in a pasture. Even the animals are historic! It's brilliant!

text:
In this week’s issue, you learned about how the geography of the New World impacted the original 13 colonies. You also learned about colonies that were owned by different countries.

title: Life of Lydia Broadnax
text:
Sometimes beginnings are not the best. However, a bad start does not mean there will be a bad end. Lydia Broadnax is an example of this. She had an unfortunate start in life, but by the end of her life, she had overcome many hardships.

Lydia Broadnax was born into slavery around 1742. We don't know the exact location of her birth and many details of her early life are also unknown. The history of enslaved people can be hard to track because they were seen as property and could be bought, sold or traded. With no way to keep track of these events, what life was like for an enslaved person is often a mystery to historians and genealogists. What we do know about Lydia Broadnax is that at some point prior to 1783, she became a member of George Wythe's enslaved "staff."

We know much more about George Wythe's life then we do about Lydia's. He was a respected lawyer and the first Virginian to sign the Declaration of Independence. He was also America's very first law professor. His love of the law might have been a partial reason for his hatred of slavery. After his appointment as a judge, he issued a ruling against slavery. He stated that Virginia's Declaration of Rights included African men. Sadly, his bold ruling was denied. Although Wythe was a critic of slavery, he was also a slave owner. The reason for this disagreement between his words and deeds is not clear. However, in 1787 after the death of his wife, George Wythe freed Lydia Broadnax.

Lydia stayed on as the cook in the Wythe household. But with a huge change. She was no longer a slave. She was now an employee of George Wythe. She was her own woman. From then on, Lydia was able to make decisions about her life and future.

One of her major decisions was to own some property. The records don't show if Lydia purchased it herself, or if Wythe gave it to her, but she found herself the owner of a modest wooden home that sat on a half-acre of land. Owning property was a symbol of freedom. When she was a slave she could not own property. In fact, the laws of America at that time said that she herself was property. This was a huge achievement for Lydia. She saved her money and bought a plot of land and a large house. The house was not just a home for Lydia, but also a wise business investment. She used the home as a boarding house.

Richmond had a growing free African American community. All of these people would have needed places to live. Lydia's boarding house was perfectly located to bring her steady tenants. In a short period of time, Lydia had gone from a slave to a free and successful businesswoman. It was quite a remarkable change.

Sadly, not all of the changes in Lydia's life were so positive. For example, the death of her former master and long-time employer George Wythe brought her considerable hardship. George had three main heirs: Lydia Broadnax, Ben (another former slave) and George Wythe Sweeney (a grandnephew). George Wythe Sweeney was not a good person. He was greedy and dishonest. He wanted George Wythe's wealth, and he decided to get it. In 1806, Sweeney poisoned Wythe, Ben and Lydia in the hopes of claiming George Wythe's estate. He was nearly successful. Ben died first. Then George Wythe, but not before he removed Sweeney from his will. Lydia survived but was never the same after the poisoning. She was left physically weak and nearly blind. Lydia might have been a witness to Sweeney's crime, but she was never allowed to tell this in court. The law of the time made it so African people could not testify in court against white people. So, Sweeney was set free.

In spite of the new misfortune, Lydia Broadnax showed a final act of quiet strength. She wrote a letter to President Thomas Jefferson to request a pair of glasses. She hoped this would remedy her ever failing sight.

When Lydia Broadnax died, she was a free woman, a business owner, a literate citizen and a survivor. She remains a great example of finishing well.

In spite of unfair laws of the times, Lydia Broadnax was able to overcome many disadvantages and obstacles in her life. Can you think of one or more challenges you have been able to overcome in your life?

title: Letter to Father and Mother
text:
Life for settlers in the 13 colonies could be very difficult. This was especially true for enslaved people and indentured servants. In the case of indentured servants, they might have come from distant lands alone to build a better future. Often they would leave behind loved ones. The only means of contact back then would have been in the form of written letters. Below is a letter from Richard Frethorne, an indentured servant. As you read the letter, ask yourself what it would have been like to be an indentured servant. How would it have been to leave your family and travel all the way to the New World? As you read, also take note of the differences in spelling, grammar and punctuation from how we write today.

March 20, 1623

Loveing and kind father and mother my most humble duty remembred to you hopeing in God of yo[u]r good health…I yor Child am in a most heavie Case by reason of the nature of the Country is such that it Causeth much sicknes, as the scurvie and the bloody flix [dysentery], and divers other diseases, wch maketh the bodie very poore, and Weake, and when wee are sicke there is nothing to Comfort us; for since I came out of the ship, I never ate anie thin but pease [porridge], and loblollie [that is water gruell] as for deer or venison I never saw anie since I came into this land, there is indeed some foule, but Wee are not allowed to goe, and get it, but must Worke hard both earelie, and late for a messe of water gruell, and a mouthful of breead, and beife, a mouthful of bread for a pennie loafe must serve for 4 men wch is most pitifull if you did know as much as I, when people crie out day, and night ...

... wee live in feare of the Enimy evrie hour, yet wee have had a Combate with them and wee tooke two alive, and make slaves of them, for our Plantacion is very weake, by reason of the dearth, and sicknes, of our Companie, for wee are faine to get other men to plant with us ...

... and I have nothing to Comfort me, nor ther is nothing to be gotten here but sicknes, and death, except that one had money to lay out in some things for profit; But I have nothing at all, no not a shirt to my backe, but two Ragges nor no Clothes, but one poore suite ... I have not a penny, nor a penny Worth to helpe me to either spice, or sugar ...

... I am not halfe a quarter so strong as I was in England, and all is for want of victuals, for I doe protest unto you, that I have eaten more in a day at home than I have allowed me here for a Weeke. I should be in a poore Case, but he like a father and she like a loving mother doth still helpe me, for when wee goe up to James Towne that is 10 myles of us, and when wee went up to Towne as it may bee on Moonedaye [Monday] … that Goodman Jackson pityed me & made me a Cabbin to lye in always when I come up, and he would give me some poor Jacks [fish] home with me ... Oh they bee verie godlie folks, and love me verie well, and will doe anie thing for me, and he much marvailed that you would send me a servaunt to the [Virginia] Companie, he saith I had been better knockd on the head ...

... Indeede so I fynd it now to my greate greife and miserie, and saith, that if you love me you will redeeme me suddenlie, for wch I doe Intreate and beg, and if you cannot get the marchaunts to redeeme me for some little money then for Gods sake get a gathering or intreat some good folks to lay out some little Sum of moneye, in meale, and but for Gods sake send beife and Cheese and butter ...

... Good father doe not forget me, but have mercie and pittye my miserable Case. I know if you did but see me you would weepe to see me ... for Gods sake pittie me, I pray you to remember my love my love to all my freinds, and kindred, I hope all my Brothers and Sisters are in good health, and as for my part I have set downe my resolucion that certainelie Wilbe, that is, that the Answeare of this letter wilbee life or death to me, therefore good ffather send as soone as you can, and if you send me anie thing let this be the marke. ROT

Richard Ffrethorne

Martyn’s Hundred.
