title: Settling the Colonies
text:
The American colonies each had different founders, settlers, economies and governments. Let’s take a look.

Massachusetts Bay

John Winthrop led the Puritans to Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1630. Around 20,000 people came in what was called “The Great Migration.”

Puritans wanted freedom of religion, but they did not tolerate others’ religions. They had strict laws about how to behave, and heavy punishments for rule-breaking. Their government was based on religion. The only people allowed to vote were members of the church. If you weren’t a Puritan, you had to live somewhere else.

Rhode Island

One person banished from Massachusetts Bay was Roger Williams. He was a minister, but he wanted to worship differently from the Puritans. They wanted him to go back to England, but instead, Williams started a new colony in 1636, Rhode Island. Rhode Island had a government where not all laws were based on religion.

A woman named Anne Hutchinson joined Roger Williams. She had 15 children. She also wanted to be different from the Puritans. Both Williams and Hutchinson believed people should have the freedom to worship as they chose. Soon others looking for religious freedom came to Rhode Island.

Connecticut

Thomas Hooker was a Puritan who didn’t agree with what people did in Massachusetts Bay. Hooker wanted rules based on the “free consent of the people,” so he wrote the Fundamental Orders. This was one of the first constitutions in the New England Colonies. One of his rules was that only men could vote.

New York

The New York Colony was known for tolerance. Every religion and ethnic group was welcome. New York gave citizenship to any Christian. In 1683, New York made laws for freedom to worship in any religion, the right to a trial by jury and freedom to elect lawmakers. That made many people want to settle there.

New Jersey

New Jersey had the Concession and Agreement of 1665. This set of rules included religious freedom, no taxes without approval by the assembly and a governor appointed by the people. By 1765, New Jersey had so many different religious groups, that some of them met in homes or barns.

Pennsylvania

King Charles II owed William Penn's father money, so he gave an American colony to William Penn. The king also wanted to get Penn out of England because he was a Quaker. Quakers refused to pay taxes and wanted everyone treated equally. You might see why a king wouldn't like that! So, William Penn began a Quaker colony, Pennsylvania. The Puritans influenced the New England Colonies, while Pennsylvania and the other Middle Colonies allowed freedom of religion. The New England Colonies had freedom of religion from the Church of England, but only if you were a Puritan. In the Middle Colonies, anyone could practice any religion, including Quakers.

Delaware

The Dutch settled the Delaware Colony because it was a good place for whaling. Later, Swedish settlers took it over. Soon after that, American Indians killed many of the European settlers. Then, English colonists took control. Delaware was diverse. In addition to the English, Dutch and Swedish, some Finnish and French settlers made Delaware their home.

Georgia

James Edward Oglethorpe settled the Georgia Colony, named after King George II. It began as a colony to help poor people stay out of prison in England. Back then, people who owed money and couldn't pay it back were put in debtors' prisons. Georgia's settlers were mostly farmers of different religions. Oglethorpe made a rule against slavery, so the farms in Georgia stayed on the small side. The farmers grew rice, tobacco, indigo and cotton.

The Carolinas

North and South Carolina were good places to raise cash crops, like tobacco, rice and indigo.

People knew South Carolina for religious tolerance. One group there was French Protestants called Huguenots. There were also wealthy settlers from the Caribbean island, Barbados. They brought hundreds of slaves to the Carolinas. Their relatives, the Gullahs, have lived in the coastal areas of the Carolinas ever since.

In North Carolina, there were people who wanted to get away from the religious rules in Virginia. They were also trying to get around the English taxes. They were supposed to pay taxes on anything they shipped in the colonies. That led to a lot of smuggling (bringing items into the country illegally). North Carolina quickly became a favorite place for pirates.

Maryland

Sir Calvert, Lord of Baltimore, was a wealthy Englishman. He was Catholic and wanted to escape the rules of the Church of England. So he began planning the colony of Maryland. Maryland accepted Catholics, Protestants and others. As long as you were a Christian, you were accepted. Maryland didn't welcome Jews or anyone who didn't believe in God. The religious groups fought over power in the colony.

The colonies had many challenges!

title: Elias Legarde
text:
Many of the settlers of the original 13 colonies had things in common, but some of the settlers also included people from different backgrounds. There were varied cultures and religions. One of those settlers was Elias Legarde. Elias Legarde was born in 1593 in Languedoc, France.

Legarde came to Jamestown in 1621 as an indentured servant. An indentured servant agreed to work without pay for a certain number of years in exchange for passage to America and housing, then they would be granted freedom at the end of the term. An indentured servant was different from a slave. An enslaved person was usually never freed and was made to work without pay for their whole life. It was common for people to arrive in Jamestown as indentured servants. However, there were two things that made Elias Legarde unique. They were his profession and his faith. Elias was a vintner. A vintner is a person who makes wine. It is because of this skill that he came to the New World. Elias was to teach others how to grow grapes and make wine.

Elias was also a Sephardic Jew. This means that he was a Jew whose ancestors came from a region called the Iberian Peninsula. This region is made up of Spain and Portugal. Many years ago the Jews were forced out of that region. It was that exile which would have sent many like Elias out into other parts of the world. They were seeking religious freedom.

Some of the first colonists arriving in the 13 colonies sought religious freedom, too. In most cases, that meant freedom for the Christians. For this reason, Elias Legarde was very unusual. In fact, he may have been the first Jew to arrive in the 13 colonies.

We don't know everything about Elias' life in the colonies. We don't know if he was able to practice his faith. We do know that he eventually leased 100 acres of land in Virginia. He might have planted a vineyard there. We know that he had a son named Thomas. We know that at some point Elias changed his last name from Legarde to Allgood. It is a common name today. So if you know any Allgoods, they could be descendants of Elias Legarde. Elias died in Buckroe, Virginia around 1670.

title: Let's Take a Trip to Historic Jamestown, Virginia
text:
Jamestown is important to U.S. History. It's where the first settlers lived in 1607. It was the first capital of Virginia.

Early Years

The first years were hard for settlers. They had conflicts with American Indian tribes. Some settlers got sick and died. They were often busy looking for gold and could not find food or grow crops.

In 1610, they had to make a choice. Should they leave? Or should they work to improve their land?

England sent help and supplies. A new strain of tobacco was planted that thrived in the climate, this helped them greatly in achieving prosperity. The settlers stayed. In a few years, their land began to grow.

Today

Jamestown is near Williamsburg. Many things have changed since 1607. It is a historic site. It has become a fun place for people to visit.

There are many things to do in this town. You can tour ships on the James River or explore the land.

Events in the History of Jamestown

1607 - The first settlers arrive.

1611 - Settlers start new cities. They are Henrico and Elizabeth City.

1614 - Settlers grow tobacco.

1619 - The first legislative assembly meets.

1624 - Virginia becomes a royal colony.

1699 - Jamestown is no longer the capital.

title: U.S. Democracy Timeline
text:
July 30, 1619

Colonists hold their first meeting. It takes place in Jamestown. This is when they form their government. They talk about laws and taxes.

November 11, 1620

Pilgrims set up a government in Plymouth. They sign a pact on the Mayflower. It gives them rights. They can choose leaders. They can make laws.

January 14, 1639

Leaders make the first laws in Connecticut. Common people can vote. They took power from Britain. They gave it to their courts.

April 21, 1649

Maryland passes a new law. Christians get religious freedoms.

September 19, 1676

The first rebellion takes place. Some people do not like the laws. They set Jamestown on fire. It burns to the ground.

September 5, 1774

Colonies hold a meeting. It takes place in Philadelphia. They boycott British goods.

April 19, 1775

A war starts against the British. Colonists fight for freedom. It lasts eight years.

July 4, 1776

Leaders meet in Philadelphia. They declare their freedom from British rule.

September 17, 1787

The war is over. The colonies win. Leaders make new laws for the land in the form of a Constitution.

December 15, 1791

The Bill of Rights is approved. People have the rights to free speech, bear arms, and the right to worship as they choose. The Bill of Rights gives powers to the states.

February 3, 1870

Congress approves a new law. African American men can vote.

August 18, 1920

A new law passes for women. They get the right to vote.

title: Town Hall Meetings and Direct Democracy
text:
It's obviously the most democratic form of government one can imagine. It's the closest to the people, it involves the largest number of people and it's the most open. New Englanders should be tremendously proud of it and cherish it and participate in it. -Christopher Collier, American Historian and Author

What Are They?

Town hall meetings in the United States are a form of direct democracy (a type of government where citizens make decisions by vote, in person and without the need for representation). These meetings take place in town halls and are sometimes just called town meetings. The idea behind them is very simple. Gather townspeople, allow them to speak freely about decisions that affect the group, and vote! These meetings are some of the simplest, most direct forms of our government. We have the chance to speak, to listen to our neighbors, discuss concerns and ideas, make informed decisions and in many ways be the best American citizens that we can be. Town hall meetings allowed early New England settlers to practice their First Amendment right to free speech—150 years before the Bill of Rights was even written and ratified (approved)! No wonder these meetings have such an important role in our history.

Town Hall Meetings, Historically Speaking

Small New England towns and villages have been using town hall meetings for almost 400 years. Dorchester is now a booming neighborhood in the city of Boston, Massachusetts. But in 1633, it was a Puritan settlement that became the first New England village to establish the town meeting form of local government. Every Monday, the townspeople would gather at the meetinghouse. There they would make decisions about important issues in the town. For example, they might discuss water rights for livestock farmers. They might also share ideas on how, when and where to educate local children and how to protect the settlement. Following in Dorchester's footsteps, other settlements quickly established their own guidelines for local government. And so the town hall meeting, New England-style, was born.

Today, the idea of town meetings remains strong in many communities. All citizens in the United States have the right to take part in general elections and in a representative government. Some also continue to use the town meeting format to carry out their local business. In Vermont, the first Tuesday in March is Town Meeting Day. Citizens in towns across the state join with their neighbors to talk about and vote on important issues. Look for information about your own community's local government processes by checking your town's website. Maybe you can go to a town hall meeting!

Town Hall Meetings in Other Times and Places

Direct democracies, such as town hall meetings, aren't unique to New England. Hundreds of years before Puritans, Pilgrims or European explorers set foot on the New England coastline, Ancient Greek citizens gathered in Athens. They ate, talked and shared ideas in an environment where everyone's ideas were welcome. In other words, they were given equal opportunities to speak, regardless of their background, how much money they had or what their status was in the community. And just as those early colonists in New England followed Dorchester's example, other European countries followed the lead of the Ancient Greeks. In Italy and France, men and women began to meet on a regular basis to share ideas, artistic opinions and eventually their political views in a safe environment. In Switzerland, there is a popular, 700-year-old tradition of having meetings in at least two different towns. These meetings take place outdoors, and sometimes several thousand citizens might go and vote!

We didn't get the idea of town hall meetings purely from European examples, either. The government structure of the Seven Iroquois Nations set an important example to our founding fathers as well. Have you ever heard the word caucus? We get it from the Algonquin speaking tribes that European settlers interacted with. It means, to advise. They would hold town meetings or caucuses for important decisions that would impact the member tribes of the Iroquois Confederacy. These Iroquois Nations valued direct democracy and helped teach these values to the early settlers. Without their example, we might not have the type of government we do today.

The New England Confederation

A few short years after the first town meetings took place, colonists formed the New England Confederation. Established in 1643, the New England Confederation allowed for "the mutual safety and welfare" of its members. The league also represented the Colonies of Massachusetts Bay, Connecticut, New Haven and Plymouth. They were confident they would be stronger standing together in the face of rivals for their territory. They even wrote and adopted a constitution that outlined the benefits and responsibilities of membership. However, the Confederation only lasted a short time and split up in 1684 after only 41 years. Can you think of reasons or disagreements in a league of nations or communities that might cause them to break apart?

title: Democracy in Action
text:
Natalia: The class election is next week, Steven. Can you believe it?

Steven: I know! I am happy that you want to be class president, Natalia.

Natalia: With you as Vice President, we will be a great team.

Steven: My name is Steven. I approve that message. Haha.

Natalia and Steven are in the library. They are brainstorming ideas for their speech.

Natalia: It's hard to find the right words to say, Steven. I want to be president because I can help our class. But I have so many ideas, I don't know where to start.

Natalia takes a break from writing. She opens a history book to get ideas.

Natalia: I wonder how colonial leaders got people to vote for them, Steven.

Steven: I'm not sure. Voting was probably different 400 years ago.

Natalia: I know ... wouldn't it be nice to see the first democracy in action?

Natalia flips through the pages of her book. She sees an interesting picture.

Natalia: Look, Steven! This is the first legislative meeting in the colonies. It took place in 1619.

Steven: The people look serious. I bet they had a lot of things to discuss.

Steven moves the book to get a closer look. He puts his finger on the picture. In the blink of an eye, they are in colonial Jamestown.

Natalia: Where are we, Steven? This is not our library.

Steven: Looks like we are in a church, Natalia. Men are wearing waistcoats, stockings and breeches.

Natalia: Hey, this looks like the video we saw in class, Steven! We are at the first House of Burgesses meeting.

The meeting begins. The room gets quiet.

Steven: It must be 100 degrees in this place, Natalia.

Natalia: It's the end of July here, Steven! Let's listen. Maybe we can get some ideas.

The governor of colonial Virginia stands and begins to speak.

Governor: Gentlemen, welcome to our meeting. There are many things to do. We must set a price for tobacco. We will work together to make fair laws for our colonies ...

Natalia: I think it's time to go. Watching this meeting has given me a few ideas, Steven.

Natalia opens her history book. Within seconds, they are back in the library writing their speech.

title: Virginia's General Assembly
text:
There were many ups and downs during the early years of Jamestown. Despite any early signs of success, things started going downhill for the Jamestown colonists quickly. By January 1608, only 38 colonists were still alive. Many died from disease or hunger. Some were killed during attacks by hostile American Indians that lived nearby. In addition, in January 1608, the fort caught fire. Most of their supplies burned in the fire. More colonists arrived from England, but many of them died during the years of 1609 and 1610.

When tobacco became a successful crop, Jamestown was on its way to becoming a permanent colony. As more people came to live in Virginia, the colonists needed rules to live by to keep the colony running smoothly. Two groups made the rules. One group was the governor and his assistants. The second group was made up of 22 men. They were known as the House of Burgesses and they represented each town or plantation in Virginia. Together these two groups made up Virginia's General Assembly.

Learning about the General Assembly is important. It was the first time the settlers were in control of their own government. The colonists of Jamestown made their own laws. They set prices for tobacco. They made laws for the treatment of American Indians and decided the consequences for those that broke their laws. Today, Americans believe it is important to be able to elect representatives who help make our laws. We have the colonists of Jamestown to thank for starting this representative type of government for us.

Unfortunately, not everyone was allowed to take part in the House of Burgesses. Women, indentured servants, slaves and men who didn't own land were left out. It took many years, but that eventually changed. All U.S. citizens today can vote and even run for office if they want.

In the 1640s, the House of Burgesses became its own legislative body and made laws for all of Virginia. Today, the representative system of government continues in all 50 states of our nation.

title: Two Row Wampum—A Historic Treaty
text:
"Wow." Steven leaned back in his chair, "The relations between colonists and American Indians sure were complicated."

Natalia nodded, "Yes. American Indians weren't all one group. There were hundreds of different tribes. Each had their own language and culture. They all dealt with and thought of the colonists differently."

"The colonists also weren't all one group. There were Dutch, English, French and Spanish colonies in early America. The French and Dutch seemed to be more respectful of the American Indians compared to the Spanish and English." Steven flipped through a stack of pictures on their workstation as he talked.

"Well," said Natalia, "that might be a misconception. It is true that the Spanish enslaved many American Indians. Especially during their expeditions to Central and South America. The English did some of this as well. But, also some of the English settlers weren't as cruel. In fact, many of the first interactions between American Indian tribes and English colonists were friendly. They would trade for furs, supplies and other goods. You remember that video we watched in class, The Pilgrims Intro?"

Steven interjected, "But then something would happen and the relationship would sour."

"Exactly," said Natalia. "In the beginning, there were more American Indians than settlers. They did not fear them. They didn't mind teaching them how to farm and hunt. Relationships became tense when more settlers arrived. English companies and the crown also promised cheap land to whoever would come to the new world. Many poor people jumped at the chance to finally build wealth."

Steven pulled out another picture of the Jamestown settlement, "Many American Indian tribes did not believe you could own land, right? But the colonists came from a culture that believed they could put a fence around land and claim it."

Natalia nodded, "The settlers also brought smallpox and other deadly diseases. These wiped out entire villages of American Indians. As their numbers dwindled, the colonists' numbers grew every year. American Indian tribes had different ways of dealing with the European settlers. A few tribes chose to fight. Some tried to form alliances. Some made treaties. Some simply traded. Some even married European settlers. Some tribes did not survive at all."

She pointed to a picture of fur traders in American Indian villages, "Dealings with the French were somewhat better. The French were more interested in furs. They were more willing to learn the languages and customs of the tribes with whom they traded. Many French traders even married and had families with American Indian women."

"Fascinating," Steven said. "But if I recall, the Dutch and the Haudenosaunee did have one of the more successful treaties with the Two Row Wampum." Steven grabbed a photograph of a white and purple wampum belt from the pile. "Is this it?"

"I—woah!"

The two friends were suddenly transported to a misty low-lying area. They saw a large boat sail up and the two friends hid behind a tree to watch. Several Europeans got off the boat.

"Those are the Dutch," Steven whispered. They watched as the Dutch greeted several American Indians on the banks.

"This is where they agreed to the treaty!" Natalia said excitedly. They watched as the two groups tried to converse with a lot of pointing, hand gestures, and halting translations.

Natalia said, "They agreed on three principals to make the treaty work: friendship, peace and forever, because the agreement is to last forever. Each nation is to respect the other's ways. The Haudenosaunee don't write things down, so they made wampum to mark the treaty. The purple lines signify the two boats of the Dutch and the Haudenosaunee people traveling down the river of life."

"Amazing!" said Steven.

title: Squanto, Friend to the Pilgrims
text:
Tisquantum, or Squanto, as we more commonly know him, was born into the Pawtuxet tribe of the Wampanoag Indians in New England. In 1605, he was kidnapped and taken to England, where he learned the English he would later use to help the Mayflower Pilgrims.

Ten years later around 1615, he was able to return home with John Smith. He was then captured again and made a slave in Spain. However, he was able to escape back to his village in 1619. Sadly, it had been wiped out by disease. He joined another Wampanoag village near Plymouth.

When the Pilgrims arrived, he helped them learn how to fish, grow crops and survive the harsh winter. He was later made an envoy (messenger) between the colony and the American Indians. He died in 1622 while on an expedition around Cape Cod. Despite all the bad things that had happened to him, Squanto only wanted to help others and to live peacefully.

title: How Did Fur Trade Impact Native American Cultures?
text:
In the 1600s and 1700s, furs, especially beaver, were in high demand in Europe. These furs were used to make hats. Traditionally in tribes, women tended crops and men hunted for food. After the demand for furs increased, American Indian men hunted not just for food but for furs to trade. This gained them more status in the community. This changed the social structure of many tribes. Men were in charge of trapping animals, and the women were in charge of the animal furs. This gave women an important role in the fur trade.

Many different tribes competed for hunting grounds for beavers. This led to more violence. American Indians traded the furs for European goods. Guns and metal tools replaced wood and bone tools and weapons. The beaver trade collapsed in the mid-1800s. Many tribes were plunged into poverty. They had become too dependent on the fur trade for their way of life.

title: Attitudes Towards European Colonists (TWQ)
text: Imagine if you were a member of an American Indian tribe. The first English settlers arrive in North America. How would you treat the colonists? Would you help them? Write your answer below.

title: Peace Treaty
text:
Sometime after the Pilgrims came to Plymouth. Squanto, Massasoit and the Pilgrim leaders met and agreed to a treaty. There was entertainment and gifts were given, and then William Bradford wrote in his journal:

... after friendly entertainment and some gifts given him, they made a peace with him (which hath now continued this 24 years) in these terms:

I. That neither he nor any of his, should injure or do hurt to any of their people.

II. That if any of his did any hurt to any of theirs, he should send the offender that they might punish him.

III. That if any thing were taken away from any of theirs, he should cause it to be restored; and they should do the like to his.

IV. If any did unjustly war against him, they would aid him; and if any did war against them, he should aid them.

V. That he should send to his neighbours confederates to certify them of this, that they might not wrong them, but might be likewise comprised in the conditions of peace.

VI. That when their men came to them, they should leave their bows and arrows behind them.

title: American Indians' Mixed Feelings on Colonists
text:
American Indian tribes had differing opinions on how to interact with colonists. A lot of these differing opinions came from how the colonists treated the American Indian tribes.

French settlers early on treated them a bit better. They were more willing to join into American Indian ways of life. It helped them get better furs to sell. American Indians that were in contact with Spanish explorers, however, were often forced to suffer disease and slavery. English settlers arrived later on. At first, American Indians were willing to help the small groups. The story of John Smith and his time spent with the Powhatan is a good example of this.

In the mid to late 1600s, more colonists arrived. They began to quickly claim land and cut down all of the trees. Good relations turned sour. In the mid-1700s, things got so bad that the King of England even ordered that only the Crown could buy land from the tribes. Colonists fought this order. It changed boundary lines that put some of the lands they were already living on outside of the boundary. They were angry about having land they developed taken from them. Some colonists felt they had a right to the land. Some even believed that the American Indians were less than human and did not deserve the land.

Some tribes were able to resist settlers expansion at first. The Iroquois in the New England region were one such tribe. They formed the League of the Iroquois in 1570. The League treated the Europeans with caution. However, they still chose to trade with them. They even allied with the British in a war against the French. However, they could not agree on a side to take during the American Revolution. After the war, the League was no more.

Many American Indians got tired of being treated poorly by Europeans. Throughout the mid to late 1600s, there were a series of violent battles between Europeans and American Indians. This included the first important Indian uprising in 1622 in Virginia. There was also the Pequot War in 1637. These skirmishes did not just happen on the East Coast. Pueblos in New Mexico rose up against the Spanish in 1626. In a few cases, some small battles were won. In most cases, these battles meant defeat for Amerian Indians. They also lost more and more of their homeland.

title: Hope For Better Days
text:
Below is a fictional diary entry from Ahanu, a young Algonquin girl, October 10, 1615

I was just a little girl when the colonists first arrived from across the sea. At first, I thought it was exciting. We had heard stories from other tribes about the Spanish explorers who had come up from the South. Now we had our own explorers. I remember them visiting our village for a few days. My uncles showed them how to hunt for mussels. One of the men gave me a shiny trinket of thanks. I thought this was the beginning of a beautiful friendship.

When they arrived, they were ill-equipped to deal with our way of life. We helped them survive the first few years. We brought them deer, corn and other foods. We showed them how to smoke and dry meat and fish. We showed them how to plant corn, beans and squash. They were grateful for the help. When I was younger I used to enjoy going to the settlement with my father and uncle.

When the land entered a drought period, the colonists demanded food. We did help them, because it was the right thing to do. However, instead of being humbled, they kept expanding their settlements. They brought more and more people to our land. It seemed that all they wanted to do was take, take, take. They cut down all the trees and fenced the land, saying it was all theirs. Their diseases are still wreaking havoc on our communities. Now they say we cannot follow the traditional paths to the sacred sites. They do not understand our culture. Violence has already broken out among our people. I fear there is more to come. I remember when the colonists would be glad to see me and my family, but now the settlers look upon us with fear and anger.

I mourn the friendship that could have been. There is room enough for everyone to live peacefully. However, I fear the settlers do not believe this. I fear they want everything for themselves and we will be pushed out of our home.

Diary entry from Patience, a young colonist, June 05, 1615

I remember when I first caught sight of Virginia, my new home. I was so excited, but a little scared to be an indentured servant. I saw one of the native people right when we landed. I was so excited! I had only seen drawings of them in England.

The settlement had already been established for several years before I arrived. It was still difficult to survive during the months of winter starvation and summer droughts. Other settlers told me that the native people used to bring food and offer aid, but that they had stopped. We are able to survive without their help now. The timber the men cut down fetches a good price back in England. I work out in the fields. The first year I came we planted a foul-smelling plant called tobacco. My master lost money in this endeavor. Our countrymen back home found the plant to be too harsh and of bad flavor. I thought for sure he would sell my contract. I was so scared! I think everything will be fine, though. John Rolfe has brought back a new type of tobacco from the West Indies. It is supposedly more mild on the tongue. I have been tending the plants today. They still make me ill, but it is worth it for a chance to see the colony thrive! I do believe there are better days ahead for Virginia!

title: What will you do?
text: Imagine you want to travel to a new place where there are no houses. There are no cars, businesses or people, but there are plenty of trees, animals and rivers. What will you take with you? title: Who was William (Billy) Bean?
text:
William Bean was born on December 9, 1721. He was a long hunter and early settler in the area that would become Northeast, Tennessee. He and his friend, Daniel Boone, rode on horseback looking for places to hunt. The valley near the Watauga River was pretty and the area had lots of promise. They wanted to live there. The land was fertile, too. People could grow corn, beans and potatoes to feed their family. There were lots of small animals that they could kill for food. There were many tall trees. They used the trees to build their homes.

William Bean fought in the Revolutionary War from 1776-1780. He was Captain of the Watauga Riflemen. Before the war began in 1768, he cleared some land near Boone's Creek on the Watauga River. On this land, he built a home and brought his family to live there. His wife gave birth to his fifth child, a son, Russell, soon after moving. This was the first white child born to settlers west of the mountains.

After living in that area for a while, Billy Bean and his family moved farther into the wilderness. On a previous long hunt with his friend, Daniel Boone, they had spotted an area of rich, fertile land on the banks of the lower Watauga River. There they built a log cabin that would be used as an inn for settlers and other long hunters heading further west. Eventually, a blacksmith shop and tavern were built near this cabin. These modest buildings would grow over time into a small village and then become a town known as Bean Station.

When people saw what Billy Bean was doing, it inspired them to build a new life, too. Within a few years, there were many pioneers in northeast Tennessee. They built homes, stores, roads and towns. Life was hard for these early settlers. Bean Station became an important place where travelers could rest and get food. It provided safety from conflicts with American Indians and cold winter weather.

This area that Billy Bean made his home was part of the Cherokee Indian territory in Northeast Tennessee. These Cherokee did not want the white settlers on their land. They tried to make them leave. Billy Bean, along with many other settlers at Bean Station, refused to leave. This created hostilities between them and the Cherokee. The two groups fought often.

The winters were cold in Northeast Tennessee. It was hard to find enough food to feed a family. The living conditions were bad in those days. But people had the dream of starting a new life. Each time a family would move to Tennessee, it caused others to come. Soon there were many new people in the area.

Billy Bean and Daniel Boone would go hunting for weeks. They were called long hunters because they were gone for so long on their expeditions. They would hunt animals to feed their families. They would bring back animal skins that would be used to make clothing and shoes. Daniel Boone built his cabin on the banks of Boone Creek, close to Billy Bean's cabin.

Men like Billy Bean and Daniel Boone are still remembered today. They faced many dangers but stayed and built on the land. They made it easier for other settlers to move to Tennessee and start a new life. Both men risked their lives to settle the land of Tennessee.

title: Heading West with William Bean and Daniel Boone
text:
Ms. Johnson and her class were on the bus heading for Watauga River in Gray, Tennessee to visit the site of William Bean's cabin.

"Who can tell me what a long hunter is?" asked Ms. Johnson.

Natalia spoke, "Long hunters were men who would go on expeditions for longer periods of time. They were sometimes gone for six or more months. They traveled long distances into the wilderness on these expeditions."

"Right," said Ms. Johnson. "Steven, why don't you tell the class what William Bean is most famous for?"

"Well, he was the first permanent settler of European descent in the area that became our state. Also, his wife gave birth to a boy named Russell. Records show that Russell was the first white child born to settlers west of the Appalachians," said Steven.

"Why is that significant?" Ms. Johnson asked.

"Because it showed that people were moving further west to live," answered Natalia.

"That's right!" Ms. Johnson said. Just then, the bus arrived at their destination. The class got off and followed their teacher to the stone marker where Bean's cabin was built in 1769.

Steven and Natalia reached out and touched the marker. All of a sudden, a mist surrounded them. The rest of the class faded from sight. They were replaced by two men dressed strangely.

"Who are those men?" Steven whispered.

“Looks like William Bean and Daniel Boone. We just saw a video of them in class. Let's hide in the bushes so we can hear what they're saying." The two kids found a big bush and hid.

Daniel Boone spoke, "I think this is a good place to set up camp tonight. We could do some fishing in that creek over there."

Bean nodded, "I agree. Later, let's go hunting. There's small game 'round about this area ... bound to find something we can eat."

The two men unloaded their packs from the horses. They started making a fire. Boone found an old coffee pot while William Bean pulled out some biscuits and dried meat for their dinner.

Natalia and Steven were surprised at how well the two men worked together. They watched as Boone went to get his gun so he and Bean could go hunting.

"We'd better get out of here," whispered Steven. "Those long hunters might think we're small game."

Natalia took his hand, and once Boone and Bean were out of sight and then crept forward and touched the rock in front of the campsight. They closed their eyes and in a moment were back with the class.

text: Pretend you are a writer in Tennessee in 1772 and you've just heard about long hunters like Daniel Boone and William Bean. You track one of them down and interview them for your newspaper story. Write out a fake interview with Daniel Boone, William Bean or Thomas Spencer.

title: The Life of Daniel Boone
text:
Daniel Boone was a well-known American frontiersman, woodsman and long hunter. He explored and settled land in Kentucky and Tennessee. He would go out for weeks at a time hunting for food. Boone became famous for exploring and settling the area now known as Kentucky. He founded the town of Boonesborough, Kentucky. It was one of the first English-speaking settlements west of the Appalachian Mountains.

As a young man, Boone went hunting for small game. He killed the animals so his family could eat. But he kept the animal pelts. These he sold to traders. When he got older, he was fighting in the French and Indian War when he met a fur trader named John Findley on the trail. Findley told him about the wild game to be found in Kentucky. Twelve years later, Boone went on his first hunting trip to Kentucky.

After a few years, Boone knew the backwoods of Kentucky very well. He drew maps for others wanting to go. He would show other men the best routes to take. Boone also knew where the rivers and valleys were. He became familiar with the area. Others would seek him out for advice.

In the 1700s, much of Tennessee and Kentucky was treacherous land. Cherokee and a few other American Indian tribes lived in the dense forests, tall trees and brush. Small game animals were plentiful. There were also large, dangerous animals living in the forests, too. It was important for new settlers to learn all they could from Daniel Boone. He became very famous for being a brave and daring explorer. People knew him as a mighty hunter who traveled into dangerous areas.

Boone was an officer in the U.S. Army in 1775. He fought in the American Revolution. After the war, he worked as a merchant and as a surveyor. He never finished school so he did not have much book learning. But there were very few who knew the woods of Kentucky and Tennessee better than Boone. He became a legend among the people. He was brave, strong, worked hard and wasn't afraid of anything.

He married a neighbor woman named Rebecca. They lived in a cabin on his father's land. They had 10 children.

title: Tennessee Statehood
text:
Tennessee became the 16th state of the Union on June 1, 1796. It is about 115 miles wide and stretches westward for nearly 440 miles from the Appalachian Mountains. North Carolina borders the eastern section. Missouri and Arkansas border the western part. Tennessee's two largest cities, Memphis and Nashville, are known as cultural centers of blues and country music. But this wasn't always true.

In the 1700s, Tennessee was beautiful, wild and unsettled. The only people there were American Indians. There were rivers full of good fish to eat. The forests were populated with plenty of small game to hunt. Settlers could grow crops like potatoes, corn, beans, melons and tomatoes in the fertile soil. This is how families survived in those days. They cut down trees to build cabins. They planted crops. They fished and hunted. Soon, people built stores. It took settlers and long hunters like Daniel Boone, Thomas Spencer and Billy Bean up to 10 years to build a small town. However, these people worked hard each day. This hard work is how Tennessee became such a great state.

title: Bean Station Store
text:
Include information the bubble next to each item in William Bean’s store to explain why that item was important to early settlers in Tennessee.

Consider the items that would be available to you on the frontier and think about the things you would have to live without. Would you follow the examples of Daniel Boone and William Bean and become a pioneer? Why or why not?

title: Thomas Sharp Bigfoot Spencer
text:
The deeds and exploits of many of the early long hunters and fur trappers that settled and explored the wilderness west of the Appalachians have become a thing of legend. Some of these men we know much about. For example, Daniel Boone's life and history have been explored and written about by historians in great detail. Other long hunters, however, not so much.

One of these men is Thomas Sharp "Bigfoot" Spencer. His adventures out west and tales of his size and physical strength have become the stuff of Tennessee legend.

Spencer was one of the first, if not the very first settler of European descent in Middle Tennessee in 1776. He came to the area while on a long hunt. Some historians who have studied the time period believe that Spencer made history by becoming the first white settler to plant a crop in Middle Tennessee.

If stories are true, one winter, he lived alone inside a hollowed out sycamore tree. The tree must have been big since it had to fit his hulking frame in it for a whole winter! They didn't call him "Bigfoot" for nothing. Spencer was said to have been so large he weighed nearly 400 pounds. All of it solid muscle. His feet were so big that an Illinois hunter, stumbling across Spencer's footprints, confused them with that of a giant animal too big to be taken down by just one man. The hunter chose to turn around and go home.

Another story often told as a testament to his strength places him at a campsite around the year 1786. The story goes that two men were fighting over the ownership of a hunting knife. Spencer stepped in to end the dispute and while doing so, a swinging punch landed square on his jaw. Spencer, instead of hitting the man back in retaliation, picked the man up as if he weighed nothing and tossed him over a fence over 8 feet high.

Thomas Sharp "Bigfoot" Spencer was nothing if not a larger-than-life explorer. Tales of his resilience and strength have helped set a historical precedence that these long hunters and explorers were a group of brave men.

title: Long Hunters: Why Were They So Important to Settling the West?
text:
Imagine having only a horse to go places, or even just your feet! Could you live in a place with no grocery stores, hotels or restaurants? Where would you sleep each night? What would you eat?

Long hunters had to spend months out in the wilderness. If they wanted food, they had to hunt for it. If they wanted to stay out of the weather or sleep somewhere safe, they made or found their own shelter. Some of the local American Indians were not friendly. The term "long hunter" means that these men often stayed out on their expeditions for a long time. Also, they often carried guns that were called "long rifles".

Early settlers in Tennessee were brave men like William Bean and Daniel Boone. They knew how to build a fire and set up a camp. They could hunt and fish. With no restaurants or grocery stores around, this was important. These settlers had to protect themselves from bears, wolves, insects, bad weather and other dangers.

Because of their hard work, other people moved west and came to Tennessee. People built log cabins. They began to get married and have children. They built stores, houses and dug wells for fresh drinking water. Over time, all those people's efforts would create small towns and villages where there was once wild forest.

title: Life on the Tennessee Frontier
text:
Natalia and Steven were squirming in their seats. Today was going to be an exciting day. The class was going on a field trip! Ms. Johnson had been teaching the class all about pioneers and it seemed like an adventurous life! Today the class was going on a trip to the William Blount Mansion. Neither Steven nor Natalia had ever been there before. They couldn't wait to see what it would be like.

Ms. Johnson walked to the front of the room with a clipboard in her hand. "Good morning class! Today we're going to take a trip back in time to the Tennessee frontier. Well, not back in time exactly, but it sure will feel like it!"

Natalia and Steven gave each other an excited look. Taking a trip back in time sounded like a great idea to them.

"Okay, class," Ms. Johnson said, "Today we will be visiting the William Blount Mansion." She pointed to a large poster of the mansion, "It was one of the first homes of its type to be built on the frontier. It was a wood-frame home and had wood siding. At the time, all of the other homes on the frontier were log cabins. While we visit, learn as much as you can about the early frontier life in Tennessee. When we get back, everyone will be giving a report about what they've learned. Now, grab a map and let's get on those buses!"

It seemed like almost no time had passed when the class reached their destination. The class quickly got off the bus and started walking towards the mansion. As Natalia and Steven approached the mansion, they both reached out to touch the side of the building.

The next thing they knew, the children found themselves in a much different time and place.

"We must have gone back to the Tennessee frontier," Natalia said excitedly. "Let's take a look around to see what it was like to be a pioneer!"

As they looked around, they saw many people at work. To their right was a group of men working in a field. Natalia and Steven heard giggling off in the distance. When they looked over, they saw several pioneer children collecting eggs from chickens. The children look very young, much younger than Natalia and Steven. They also noticed that several other children seemed to be working. Some older children were milking cows and chopping wood for fires.

"It looks like everyone in the family had to work hard on the frontier. They must have had a very difficult life," Steven said. "It seems like there's no time to rest."

Natalia noticed that several American Indians were talking with some of the pioneer men. "I think those people are Cherokee!" she whispered excitedly. "They may even be some of my ancestors. Let's get closer so we can see what they're doing."

As Natalia and Steven got closer to the group of men, they noticed that they appeared to be trying to come to an agreement. The Cherokee men were holding up animal skins and furs. The pioneers were inspecting the skins closely. One of the pioneer men held up a few small tools. The men exchanged items and parted ways.

"Wow!" Steven said. I can't believe we actually got to witness the pioneers trading with the Cherokee. Ms. Johnson said that the two groups were friendly at first. She also said that eventually, things didn't go as well."

Natalia and Steven continued on their way through the small frontier settlement. They noticed a Conestoga Wagon off the distance and hurried toward it. The children remained hidden among some trees as they approached the wagon. Several pioneers were walking alongside it. They looked dirty and tired. One man was directing the equally tired looking horses to some water.

"Wow," Natalia whispered. "They sure do look exhausted. They must have been traveling for hundreds of miles. I can't imagine being brave enough to make such a huge journey to an unknown place.

"Me neither," Steven replied. "But, I'm sure glad they did. Their bravery and determination to move westward helped the United States grow. Without them, our country would not be what it is today."

"We've been here a while," Natalia said. "We'd better head back."

Natalia and Steven made their way back to the William Blount Mansion and touched the outer wall again. Before they knew it, they were standing alongside their classmates in front of the William Blount Mansion.

"I bet we'll have plenty to talk about when we share our report with the class," Steven said. Too bad we can't tell them everything, he thought to himself.

title: Chief John Ross Speaks for The Cherokee
text:
The Cherokee were living in Tennessee when the pioneers began to move west. Everyone got along alright at first. The Cherokee agreed to let the settlers stay if they gave them some of their tools, weapons and other items. After a while, some people grew tired of the agreement. Attacks broke out. The settlers wanted more and more of the Cherokee land. The Cherokee did not want to give it to them.

Then a Cherokee man named John Ross came into the picture. Ross had a Cherokee mother and a Scottish father. He was raised bilingual and bicultural. This means he knew both cultures and languages of the pioneers and the Cherokee. This helped him to become a great leader to the Cherokee. The Cherokee people eventually elected him to be their new Chief. Ross went to Washington DC many times to fight for Cherokee rights. Since he was the only one fluent in English, he played a large part in speaking for his people.

Unfortunately, in spite of all his efforts, the Cherokee still lost all of their lands.

title: Davy Crockett
text:
Early settlers often entertained each other with stories. Some of these stories were true and others were not. These made-up stories are called folktales or tall tales.

There are many stories about Davy Crockett. He is known as the "King of the Wild Frontier." Crockett was a real man who grew up in a pioneer family. Many stories, both true and false, have been told about him.

Crockett was born in Tennessee to John and Rebecca Crockett. At age 13, he ran away from home and learned how to survive by himself. Crockett grew up to be a tough and rugged man. During his life, he traveled farther and farther west. He is perhaps known best for having died during the Texas Revolution at the Battle of the Alamo in 1836.

Crockett, while he lived, was perhaps the primary contributor to his own legend. He served in the state of Tennessee as a Congressman. During his time on the campaign trails, he would tell stories of his adventures on the frontier. He hoped that having a reputation larger than life would help him get elected. There are stories about him hunting bears at the age of three, and one tall tale says that Crockett, having seen the sun frozen on the horizon after a cold night, thawed the sun with the blood of a bear and kicked down its rays.

While we may not know the full truth about Davy's adventures, we do know that Crockett will always hold a special place in frontier history. His stories tell us much about how folktales were made on the Tennessee frontier and what feats pioneers most liked to imagine were possible.

title: Experience History in Tennessee!
text:
Do you love learning about history? You can learn all about history without leaving Tennessee. James White's Fort and the Marble Springs Historic Site are two great places to visit.

James White was the founder of Knoxville. His fort is the first permanent building in the city. Visitors can learn all about John White and the history of Knoxville there. If you visit during Knoxville Homecoming, you can see a real blacksmith working! You can also see open fire cooking and basket weaving.

Marble Springs Historic Site is another fun place to visit. There you can learn about John Sevier. He was the first governor of our state. You can tour what is left of his cabin. You can also see a loom house and smokehouse.

The next time you want to experience history, look no further than Tennessee's own famous places!

title: Travel Like a Pioneer: Conestoga Wagons
text:
Many pioneers used Conestoga wagons on their long journeys to their new homes. These wagons were first built in the Conestoga Valley of Pennsylvania in 1770.

Conestoga wagons had a large wagon box. The box was curved and raised at both ends. This helped when it went up and down hills. It helped keep the load from moving around. It also helped prevent the tailgate from breaking open.

The wagons had a hood made of canvas. The hood helped to protect the items in the wagon from bad weather or extreme heat. The hoods were waterproof. This was done by soaking them in linseed oil.

Conestoga wagons could carry up to 6 tons. The wagons were usually pulled by 6 horses or oxen. The driver walked alongside the wagon to direct the horses. No one rode in the wagon. Everyone walked during long journeys to put less stress on the horses.

The wagons were expensive because it took many special craftsmen to build them. The wagons were very sturdy. This allowed them to travel over all types of land.

title: Living Like a Pioneer
text:
Imagine that you and your family are getting ready to move hundreds of miles across the country. You are moving to a place where no one has ever lived before. You are a family of pioneers.

A pioneer is someone who is the first to move and live in a new area. It was a difficult way of life. People chose to be pioneers for many reasons. They wanted to own their own land. They were looking for a fresh start. They wanted to raise their families however they chose.

Pioneers traveled a long way over difficult land. Sometimes they encountered dangerous people. They could only bring their most important belongings with them. Many pioneers only brought a couple changes of clothes with them. They had to take along all the food they would need for their journey. Packing months worth of food left little room for other items. Pioneers packed their belongings onto handcarts or in covered wagons. Since all of the items were packed onto the carts, they had to walk the entire way.

When the pioneers finally made it to their destination, there was much work to do. They had to build their own homes. They put up their own fences. They cleared the land to grow important crops for food. Pioneers also had to hunt wild animals for food. They chopped down wood for their fires. The fires were important to keep warm and cook food.

Pioneer life was not easy. Pioneers had to learn how to survive in a new place. The pioneers worked from sunup until sundown. They worked each day no matter the weather. They had to grow or make everything they needed. There was no time for rest.

The United States would likely not be where it is today if these pioneers had not had the courage to move west.

title: Three Grand Divisions of Tennessee
text:
Tennessee is a unique state! That means our state is one of a kind! Why? Maybe it's our great music or our fun festivals. Maybe it's all the famous people to learn about and all the historical places to see. Maybe it's our amazing geography. From the Mississippi River to the Great Smoky Mountains and everything in between. All of those things—and much more—make Tennessee unique!

How much do you know about the geography of our state? Have you heard of the Grand Divisions? They are East Tennessee, Middle Tennessee and West Tennessee.

East Tennessee

For thousands of years, American Indians were the only people who lived in what we now call Tennessee. In the 1700s, the Cherokee and the Chickasaw were the two major tribes here. The Cherokee lived in villages in East and Middle Tennessee. This changed when explorers and settlers from Europe began to arrive. More and more people came. Their settlements grew and they expanded westward to other parts of the territory. Soon the settlers decided they wanted Tennessee to become a state. In 1796, Tennessee became the 16th state in the United States.

East Tennessee has many natural resources. It is covered in thick forests that run all along the eastern part of the state. The cities of Knoxville and Chattanooga are found here. Much of the state's logging industry relies on East Tennessee's forests. Until recently, this part of the state relied on subsistence farming. Now, this area's natural resources help our state through tourism. Thousands of people every year come to see the Cumberland Plateau, hike the Appalachian Trail or scale to the top of Clingmans Dome on the Great Smoky Mountains.

About 33 percent of Tennessee's total population lives in East Tennessee.

Middle Tennessee

This division is the largest of the three. It takes up the middle section of the state from the Cumberland Plateau in the west to the Tennessee River in the east. Middle Tennessee's geography is made up of the Nashville Basin and Highland Rim. The basin has land that is excellent for farming and raising livestock.

This division is home to our state capital: Nashville. Nashville has been made famous for being considered the birthplace of American country music. This city employs many people in local business, government, tourism and entertainment.

The Highland Rim Region contains many natural minerals, like iron. During the 19th and 20th centuries, this region yielded enough iron ore to sustain a thriving steel and iron economy that provided jobs to a diverse community of workers of different ages, race and gender.

West Tennessee

The third division of Tennessee is located between the Tennessee and Mississippi rivers. This Grand Division consists of the Gulf Coastal Plain and the Mississippi Flood Plain. Plains are lands that are mostly flat and level. The Gulf Coastal Plain is rich farmland. Farmers in this area grow cotton and corn. The Mississippi Flood Plain regularly floods when the river overflows.

We don't often think about earthquakes taking place in this area of the United States, but the risk for earthquakes is actually somewhat high in this Tennessee area. Here you can find the New Madrid Fault Line. Three of the largest earthquakes in the history of the United States hit this area during the years of 1811 and 1812. One such earthquake knocked down trees and collapsed riverbanks. It was reported that windows and furniture shook as far away as Washington, D.C. and that the shaking caused church bells to ring in parts of Virginia. It also briefly reversed the flow of the Mississippi River.

Memphis is located in West Tennessee. More people live in Memphis than any other city in the state of Tennessee. With an estimated population of over 670,000, thousands more come each year to Memphis as tourists. They come to see historical sites, museums and parks. They also come for the music! Memphis is known as the Birthplace of Blues. Music has always been an important part of our state's history and culture.

title: Invading Species Threaten Local Trees
text:
Tennessee's forests are under invasion. Tennessee's booming lumber industry is in jeopardy due to a foreign invader, the Emerald Ash Borer beetle.

The Emerald Ash Borer is believed to have entered the U.S. in the 1990s. The pest is native to China, Mongolia, North Korea, South Korea, Japan, Taiwan and the Russian Far East. The beetles' larvae prefer Ash trees and feed on the trees' inner bark. Their feeding disrupts the trees' ability to take in nutrients and water. This damages the trees. When they go through their growing period, they lay under the tree bark. As adults, they exit the trees and leave behind D-shaped pockmarks in the wood. Damaged trees can't be used to build houses or furniture. Currently, 47 Tennessee counties are under quarantine. No ash wood may be moved into or out of them. Most of the areas that have been quarantined are in the East Tennessee division. Scientists have predicted that the infestation could cost the lumber industry billions of dollars. This could really hurt the economy of the East Tennessee division.

The Emerald Ash Borer beetle is an aggressive and rapidly spreading species. Since their official discovery in Michigan in 2002, the bugs have spread to 31 states according to the United States Department of Agriculture. You can help contain their spread with three actions: Buy your wood locally and don't transport wood within the state for camping or other activities; Don't bring in wood from outside of the state; If you have ash trees, check them periodically for signs of infestation.

title: Tennessee State Flag
text:
Tennesseeans were known to have fought in the Revolutionary War for freedom back in 1776. Many people from Tennessee volunteered to go fight, which contributed to the state's nickname of The Volunteer State. However, after the Revolution, Tennessee didn't get a state flag for another 85 years.

The first flag that came into play was proposed in 1861. The design had two red stripes and one white stripe. The upper left corner had a blue square with the state seal in the middle of it. This flag was not adopted, but it did stir interest in the idea of a state flag. In 1879 the first state flag was officially adopted. This flag had three slanting stripes of red, white and blue. In the lower right corner was the number 16 to represent the state being the 16th state to join the Union. In the middle, the state's nickname "The Volunteer State" is written diagonally across the blue stripe.

This flag served as the state flag all the way until 1905. In that year, a new design was submitted by an American Colonel named LeRoy Reeves. This is the flag we know and use today. If you don't know what it looks like, it has a red field with a blue circle in the middle with three white stars in the middle of that. There's also a blue stripe down the right side of the flag. The flag has the blue stripe along its edge so that it can be easily recognized even when there's not a breeze to make the flag fly. The three stars on the flag represent the three divisions of Tennessee: West Tennessee, Middle Tennessee and East Tennessee.

Do you think Tennessee's state flag is a good representation of our state?

title: From Forests to Floorboards
text:
Natalia and Steven listened to Ms. Johnson as she described Tennessee's natural resources. Tennessee has many mines, farmland and forests. She passed out maps for the students to study. They noticed sawmills dotting the forests of the Tennessee landscape.

"Hey, my Dad said the wood for our new floors came from Tennessee," Steven exclaimed, "I wonder if it came from one of these sawmills."

"I remember seeing a video about lumber on the Studies Weekly website. Wood is called lumber before it is made into other things." Natalia replied.

"Wow!" Steven exclaimed. "That's pretty amazing."

Natalia nodded in agreement. "Let's visit one of these sawmills to get the whole story," she said.

They both placed a fingertip on one of the sawmill locations on their map. The classroom began to fade away. They arrived in a dense forest near the sawmill's main building. The sounds of tree harvesting, buzzing saws, cracking wood, falling trees and distant cries of "Heads up!" surrounded them.

Steven and Natalia saw someone who looked like they worked at the mill leading a group of people around. The children scurried over and joined the group as quietly as they could. They were interested in finding out what was going on and what the people were there for. The mill employee was just starting to explain the work they did there.

"Sawmills process different types of wood depending on what grows best in the surrounding forest or what they ship-in. We maintain tree farms and this sawmill. We process mostly Tennessee hardwoods, oak, hickory, maple, ash and tulip poplar. The wood comes from the surrounding forests and tree farms to promote sustainable tree harvesting."

Natalia noticed that the wood in the main yard created a semicircle of lumber in various stages of production. Fresh cut logs rested at one end, followed by rough-hewn two-by-fours of matching lengths and stacks of smooth finished planks in bundles sat at the opposite side of the semi-circle. Natalia touched Steven's arm to get his attention and pointed to the different stacks.

The guide handed out hard hats to everyone and led them to a viewing walkway. "To turn timber, raw cut trees, into usable lumber, we send it through a de-barker. It removes the tree bark. Next, each log is laser scanned, and a computer lets us know how best to cut the wood to minimize waste. Let's go up into the viewing tower."

From the viewing tower, he pointed to a second tower. "The worker in that tower uses the computer data to sort the logs. After sorting, each log gets trimmed into a four-sided plank. Each plank receives another cutting into various sizes based on the computer's recommendations. Let's head to another part of the floor."

They stopped near workers marking the wooden planks with different colored pencils. "Here we grade the lumber. Different grades of wood go to customers depending on how they will be used. For example to build furniture, to create floorboards or for external construction," said their guide. "We have one more stop."

They headed back outside to a large building which sat to the back of the semicircle Natalia had pointed out to Steven. The guide paused in front of the building. One of the huge doors opened. Another worker rolled a towering stack of finished and bundled lumber into the building. "That's hot!" Steven exclaimed feeling a blast of heat as the door opened.

The guide smiled. "We need it to be. Our drying kiln removes moisture from our lumber before we ship it to customers. This is important to prevent rot, mold or insects from damaging the wood. Those stacks of lumber are cured and ready to go," he said pointing to the stacks at the far end of the semicircle.

The guide escorted the group to the main yard and gave them each a miniature plank of lumber engraved with the sawmill's logo and name on a keychain. "Have a safe trip home," he said.

Natalia and Steven walked into the treeline and touched their map again. They arrived back in Ms. Johnson's classroom, souvenirs of their trip to the sawmill in hand.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend for a moment that you are one of Ms. Johnson's students. She has just told the class that they are going to create a Mock Trade Show like the one Steven and Natalia visited. title: Reading Import and Export Charts
text:
Ms. Johnson: Good morning, students. Today, we will be learning about different kinds of charts and graphs. Over the weekend, Steven and Natalia attended a fun student Trade Fair. They were able to see many types of graphs and charts. I hope you two can share some of the information you learned with the rest of the class.

Natalia: We saw lots of charts. Nearly every student group used a chart or graph.

Ms. Johnson: I'm not surprised. Charts and graphs are an important way to share information. Sometimes words aren't the best way to share information. For example, here is a bar graph. It shows how many millions of dollars of items that were sent to our state over the last four years. As you can see, the bar easily shows us how many millions we received in products just last year. It was more than we received the year before.

Steven: I saw a chart like that at the fair.

Ms. Johnson: Bar graphs let us see information at a glance. Bar graphs are good for helping information scientists recognize patterns or trends. We could expand this graph if we wanted to include the last 10 years or even 20 years. Now, I want you all to take a look at this chart. It's called a flowchart. This chart shows one of Tennessee's main exports, cotton. At the beginning of the chart, we see cotton being harvested from a field. This product begins in the fields where it grows.

Steven: I see, this flowchart is showing us the order that cotton takes from field to store!

Ms. Johnson: So, after the cotton is harvested, it is sent to a factory where it is turned from a raw material into a piece of cloth. The cloth is then designed into clothing. Finally, our flowchart ends with the cotton being turned into a shirt! From here, it is sent to a store where we can purchase it.

Natalia: We saw a flowchart like this at the fair. A group of students that represented China showed how a toy starts and ends up at a store. But the beginning of the chart had many pictures of wood, rubber, plastic and metal.

Ms. Johnson: Very good, Natalia. That's because toys can be made from many different materials. So a factory in China will need many materials to make a toy. You can use flowcharts in many different ways. They help us learn important information about our state's economy and history!

Natalia: Speaking of China. At the fair we saw a lot of information about who we trade with. If you look at the chart, you'll see the goods our state exports. These are items we want to sell to other parts of the world that need them. One graph shows that our state sends out lots of different items. Factories in Tennessee make many medical tools. The factories sell the tools to hospitals and dental offices in places like Canada, Mexico, China and France. Other Tennessee exports that are listed on the graph are cotton, airplane parts, car parts and cell phones.

Steven: These charts and graphs you see show the products that we want to bring to our state. One of the most popular items, as you can see, is medicine. When you get sick and the doctor gives you medicine, it might come from a place like Canada. Our state also imports things like shoes, wire for electronics and rubber. The wire and rubber are used by Tennessee factories to make other things like cell phones and car tires. The cell phones and tires can be sold in our state or anywhere else around the world.

Ms. Johnson: Just like you learned at the fair, Tennessee items like these come from countries such as China, Japan, Canada, Mexico and Ireland. Our state trades with nations all over the world. If we didn't trade, how could we get items like rubber to make tires?

Natalia: Trade is important for our everyday life. We need things from other countries. Other countries need things from us, too.

title: Trade Fair Fun
text:
Natalia: Hello, students. I'm here with Steven at Mock World Trade Fair! Mock in this situation, means to pretend. This trade fair is being held by students. None of the students are doing any official trade business, so it's all pretend! Trade fairs like this help students learn the principles and practices of both international and national trade for our state.

Steven: Tennessee has lots of things to trade. Our state also needs many things. We trade with states in our country as well as with other nations.

Natalia: Ms. Johnson asked us to keep an eye out for graphs and charts about trade. We are going to be studying different kinds of charts in class. Many businesses use charts at trade fairs to explain about their products.

Steven: We are excited to see the students here pretend to be businesses from countries all over the world. Some of the students represent businesses in Tennessee. Other groups of students represent countries that our state trades with like Mexico, China and Canada.

Natalia: Look, Steven. There are some groups of students with Tennessee exports. Let's see what they want to trade.

Steven: What is an export, again, Natalia? I always confuse export with import.

Natalia: An export is an item that we send out of the state. I remember what this word means because the word "exit" is like export. Exit means to leave. So, exports mean to leave the state or the country. An import is the opposite of export. Imports are items that come into the state or country.

Steven: Good trick. Now I think I'll remember what those words mean.

Natalia: I see the students who represent Tennessee. There's a group that's selling timber. I know our state sure has lots of trees. I wonder who they want to sell wood to?

Steven: Look, Natalia. They have a chart that shows what kinds of businesses can buy their wood. This chart shows that they sell most of their wood to builders. I guess it takes a lot of wood to build houses and buildings.

Natalia: The next highest buyers of wood are furniture makers. It's funny to think that our desks at school could be made from the wood of a Tennessee tree. If the students sell their wood to a furniture maker from Japan or Mexico, they might make desks for school students in those countries.

Steven: Let's see what other students are trying to sell Tennessee businesses. I see the flag of China over there. Ms. Johnson said that we get many items from China.

Natalia: Wow. Look at their charts and graphs. They have a long chart of all the types of products that China exports to Tennessee. Electronics are at the top of the list. It looks like we get many parts for our machines from China, too.

Steven: The chart shows that China sends lots of clothing to Tennessee. Here's another graph. It shows how many billions of dollars in products China sends around the world.

Natalia: China has lots of things to trade. I see that Japan sends many products to our country and state, too. Japan also has lots of electronics to export.

Steven: I just listened in to the students making a mock trade deal. The students representing the United Kingdom want to buy lots of timber. But they want to buy it cheaply. The Tennessee students don't want to sell it too cheap or it won't be a good deal for them.

Natalia: What did they do to make a good deal so both groups would be happy?

Steven: Tennessee said it would not sell the wood more cheaply. But they said they would lower the cost to ship all the timber to the United Kingdom. That's a very good deal for the buyer because it's very expensive to ship items across the Atlantic Ocean. Both groups are happy about the deal.

Natalia: I can't wait to tell Ms. Johnson about everything we learned here and all the graphs and charts we were able to see.

title: Exporting That Tennessee Sound
text:
We've been talking about many items that Tennessee trades with the world. One thing that wasn't on the list that the world loves is our music. Tennessee musicians sell millions of records to fans all over the world.

Lots of people love country music, blues and R&B. The state of Tennessee is known as the birthplace of these genres. Dolly Parton has sold more than 100 million albums. Johnny Cash has sold over 90 million (Cash was born in Arkansas but lived the majority of his life in Tennessee). Chet Atkins has sold 35 million. Martina McBride has sold 14 million. Using this data of top-selling musicians from our state, create a bar graph or pie chart!

These records bring the sound of Tennessee music to cities and homes all over the world. If you have a Dolly Parton record, you have something special from Tennessee.

title: Made in China
text:
Tennessee imports more products from China than any other country. China's primary port for shipping products and other goods to their trade partners around the globe is the port of Shanghai.

One reason why China's products are imported often to our country is that it costs less to make those items in China. This ties into something called cost of living. The amount of money needed to buy wants and needs in the U.S. is higher than in China. This means that China can pay its workers much less than U.S. companies must pay their workers. Here is a graph comparing the cost of items in the U.S. and China. With lower cost of living, manufacturers in China can sell lots and lots of products around the world. People will buy them because they don't cost as much as many other products. Pricing is an important part of trade.

The cost of living in China is actually increasing over the years. Soon it may cost the same to live in China as it does in the U.S.

title: Tennessee Crops Feed the World
text:
In the state of Tennessee, Marshall County has produced more corn than any other county in recent years. This chart shows that 25 percent of the state's crops and livestock are sold to other places outside of Tennessee. This county, specifically, has many farms, but you will also find farms all across our great state.

A Marshall County farm might produce corn and also livestock. The farmer might also keep pigs and chickens. Many of the items from farms stay in Tennessee. Many farmers produce more items than our state needs. So they sell the extra things to nearby states like Alabama and Mississippi. Some crops might be sold to far-away states like Alaska, which doesn't have a good farming climate like Tennessee. Our state grows many types of crops. Some, such as corn, we eat. Others, like cotton, are used to make products like clothing. Sometimes we use our own farm crops, like milk, and products we import, like cocoa beans, to make delicious foods like chocolate.

This chart shows many of our state's farm exports like cotton, soybeans, wheat, corn, tobacco and more. Farming has been important to Tennessee long before it was a state. People who lived here needed things like corn and wheat. They also needed milk, fresh eggs, poultry, lamb and beef. This farm in Marshall County and other farms in our state make sure that Tennessee has plenty to eat. Today, our farms ship crops and livestock to many places in the world.
