title: Not Enough!
text:
Steven: Good Afternoon, students! And welcome to your School Newsroom. I'm one of your hosts, Steven.

Natalia: And I'm your other host, Natalia. Today, we're going to talk about money!

Steven: And everyone's favorite activity, shopping!

Natalia: Shopping and money are part of economics. Other important parts of economics are supply and demand. Low supply and high demand lead to scarcity. That means higher prices. High supply and low demand mean the price is cheaper. Sometimes, if we're lucky, equilibrium happens! That means the supply is equal to the demand.

Steven: We see examples of supply and demand every day. At home, at school, and many other places. Sometimes there's only one bag of chips left, but both you and your brother want a bag. And sometimes, when there aren't enough chairs for the assembly, some kids have to sit on the floor. These are small examples of scarcity.

Natalia: If you have to share the brushes in art class because there isn't enough to go around, that's another example of scarcity. We can see how supply and demand affect the economy. We can start with everyday examples. What about another resource? What happens if a natural resource is scarce?

Steven: Good questions, Natalia. There are three different types of resources. Natural resources are things like wood, water or minerals. We need them to build houses, grow crops or run factories. Capital resources are things used to produce goods and services. Human resources refer to the jobs the people do.

Natalia: People need natural resources like fuel and water in order to live. When water or fuel is scarce the economy changes. It can impact how we use capital resources. It can also impact human resources.

Steven: Natural resources and capital resources are related. Wheat is a capital resource. We use it to make flour. Think of the things we eat or use that have flour. It's a lot more than only bread. If the supply is really low or non-existent, no more donuts or pasta! You won't be able to make those holiday decorations with the salt, flour and water clay mix this year.

Natalia: It's a domino effect. Anything you make with that scarce capital resource is scarce, too. Therefore, donuts would be more expensive.

Steven: This has another effect. Innovation! People will seek out other ways of making something. For instance, did you know you can make flour out of other products instead of wheat? People have found ways to make flour out of rice, corn and other grains!

Natalia: Rice and corn are also important capital resources. If wheat was scarce, people could use rice or corn to make flour instead. Then the demand for those products would rise.

Steven: And so would the price! Which is what happened to the Mesh Sport backpack over the weekend.

Natalia: That's right, Steven! Except that nobody needs a Mesh Sport backpack to live.

Steven: But you will die without food or water. That's the difference between luxuries and necessities. We also call these needs and wants. Speaking of necessities, it's time for class!

Steven: Tune in again for another report from your school newsroom. You don't want to miss it!

title: Let's Write

title: What is Inflation?
text:
Inflation is an economic term. It describes what happens when the prices of goods and services increase over time.

Do your grandparents ever tell you how much they used to pay for something? A car or new pair of pants probably cost them less than what we pay now. On average, things increase in price about 3 percent each year. For example, if a toy costs $10 this year, it will cost around $10.30 next year. This is a natural rate of inflation. Because it is a slow rise in cost over time, people are able to figure out how to meet it. However, sometimes inflation can happen too quickly. What causes this kind of inflation?

Inflation that happens quickly is caused by too much money being added to a country's economy. However, just because there is more money, that doesn't mean the number of goods you can buy increases as well. With more people being able to purchase these goods, the goods will then disappear much faster. The businesses will find themselves in a situation where the demand is high and the supply is low. So they will increase the price of the items knowing people are willing to pay a lot to have it.

This means people who work for less money are often unable to afford these goods. If their income does not increase, they won't be able to afford the goods and services that people with more money can. The purchasing power of their money decreases.

A low inflation rate allows more consumers to better plan, or budget, how much money they need to live and survive.

title: The Law of Supply and Demand
text:
Steven: Natalia, check this out!

Natalia: Oh, wow, the new Mesh Sport backpack! Where did you get it?

Steven: The really big mall out by the airport. My parents took me all the way out there just to get one.

Natalia: I thought there weren't any left. Everyone said they were sold out in the mall downtown. I saw it listed online but it was really expensive.

Steven: Yes, there were hardly any left when we got there. A lot of people were still waiting to buy them. My dad said there wasn't going to be enough for everyone. What was that word again, Ms. Johnson? The one that means there isn't enough?

Ms. Johnson: Oh, you mean when something is scarce. In economics, we call this scarcity. It's related to supply. Do you remember what else it's related to, Natalia?

Natalia: What do you mean?

Ms. Johnson: You said that you saw the bag listed online. Now you know why the price was so high.

Natalia: Oh, yeah! Prices go up when demand increases. Especially if the thing in demand is scarce. If there is a lot but demand is low, the opposite happens.

Steven: That's why the ugly bags that nobody wants are always cheaper. Did you see that orange thing? Yuck!

Ms. Johnson: Prices rise and fall depending on demand, supply and scarcity. So, Steven, your bag is a great example of the economic theory in action. You're lucky you got one.

Steven: Yeah, it's so cool! It even has a secret pocket inside with a lock!

Natalia: Well, it's not a secret anymore. Is that a special pocket for your phone?

Steven: Yup! It even has a special place for the plug-in.

Natalia: What goes in this part?

Steven: Other kids use it for a pencil case. I put my water bottle in there. See the special stripe?

Natalia: Oh wow, does that glow in the dark?

Steven: Yeah, it has reflectors if you're walking or biking at night. And you can move them around, see?

Natalia: Nice! I wonder if they'll make more backpacks to meet the demand for them?

Ms. Johnson: As long as people are willing to buy them, you can be sure they will. With any luck, the producers will make enough of them to help lower the price on them.

Natalia: If they do, then maybe I can get a backpack to match yours, Steven!

Steven: That would be cool!

title: Tulipmania
text:
What is an "economic bubble"? This is when people invest a lot of money but are wrong about how valuable or popular what they invested in is. In the 1600s, this happened in Holland. And what was the commodity everyone wanted? Tulips.

This simple and beautiful little flower is an icon of Holland, but it is not native to Holland. It's actually an exotic import. Explorers brought the flowers to Holland from Turkey during the 16th century. This era is known as the Dutch Golden Age. Holland was one of the richest countries in the world. People had a lot of money to spend on luxuries, or wants. They invested in successful companies, too.

Tulips became very popular flowers. They were so popular that everyone had to have them. That's a simple question of supply and demand. When the flowers were first brought over, the supply was low. So, the prices for tulip bulbs were initially high. The increase in demand caused more people to import the bulbs to Holland. For a while, this created an equilibrium where demand and supply were equal. The equilibrium did not last for long, however.

The tulips began to adapt to the new land. Some of them began to develop patterns and different colors. This made them rare and valuable. The demand for these rare bulbs skyrocketed. People traded acres of land for single bulbs. At the height of the tulip craze, one person would have to work for ten years to buy one.

But there was another detail to consider. Tulips only grow at a certain time of the year. When tulips were not available, people could buy them in advance. This is called speculation. People predicted how much tulip prices would rise or fall which drove the prices of tulip bulbs even higher.

In February of 1637, the price of tulip bulbs returned to normal. This was like a stock market crash. Investors lost all of their money. Rich people became poor people. Fortunately, the Dutch economy was strong and survived the crisis. Today, we look back on Tulipmania to study the economy and the effects of popular trends.

title: I Want That!
text:
In a perfect world, there would be enough of the item, toy or video game system for everybody that wants one. In economics, this is called equilibrium. However, this can often be too hard to achieve.

What happens when lots of kids want a special toy at Christmas time, but the company can't make enough of the toy in time for Christmas Eve? The TV news sometimes shows adults going crazy over the ones in the stores because there aren't enough of them for everyone to get one. The supply is low for something in high demand! You might see adults pushing and shoving each other over the toys. Other people are willing to pay hundreds of dollars in an online auction for a toy that only cost $15 at the store. Is that toy really something to fight over? Why do people do it?

Have you ever asked your parents for a gift that was in great demand? How about the latest video game system? That's something lots of kids want. What effect does the fact that lots of people want something have on the price? What if nobody wants the product? What does that do to the price?

If you're interested in finding out the answers to these questions, step into the rest of the articles of this week's edition of Studies Weekly.

title: The Story of Anna Schwartz
text:
Anna Schwartz was a Jewish American economist. That is to say, she studied finances and money. She was born in 1915 in New York City to Pauline (Shainmark) Jacobson and Hillel Jacobson, both of whom had immigrated to the United States from Eastern Europe during the first decade of the century. In 1963, she wrote a book with another Jewish American economist, Milton Friedman. The book's title is "A Monetary History of the United States." It's a book about how the supply of money affects the economy.

The book is important. It explains the economy and its connection to U.S. history. The book begins at the end of the American Civil War. It ends with the Great Depression. The Great Depression was an economic disaster. Economists like Anna Schwartz wanted to study this problem. They were looking for trends and patterns. If we can identify a trend, it helps us figure out how something like the Great Depression happened. They wanted to make sure it would not happen again.

In the book, Schwartz talks about inflation. This was one of the major problems the economy had in the 1930s. Inflation can be complicated. Schwartz and Friedman's studies lead them to believe that certain policies of the Federal Reserve's lead to the inflation that caused the Great Depression. Their criticisms of these policies helped the Federal Reserve to change how they did things.

In 1976 the Nobel Society decided to give the book an award. They honored Milton Friedman but Anna Schwartz didn't get an award. Milton himself said that Anna did most of the work.

Anna Schwartz continued her work. For most of her life, she worked in New York. She wrote other books. She wrote two books about the British economy. She also wrote about the financial crisis in 2008. She warned that many of the things she saw cause the Great Depression had returned. She was old enough to remember. She passed away in 2012 at her house in Manhattan.

title: Confederate Money
text:
During the Civil War, when the 11 slave states left the Union, they decided to print their own money. As their own nation, they were going to need to have money to exchange in their own economy. The money was first printed in Columbia, South Carolina. The printing headquarters were destroyed during the Civil War. Before this, nearly $2 billion in Confederate money had been printed.

At first, the money was worth a lot. In 1860, before the Civil War began, the economy of the southern states did very well. Cotton and tobacco trade between states and other countries was very lucrative. However, as the South continued to lose more battles during the war, the value of the Confederate dollar went down. Additionally, the Union had made it very difficult for the Confederate states to transport their cotton and tobacco to other countries. This helped to reduce the Confederate dollar even more and cripple the economy. Near the end of the war, Confederate soldiers had to pay 500 Confederate dollars for a pair of shoes!

The money was printed using large metal plates that were heated and pressed onto paper. Unlike our money we use today, Confederate money was all different colors. Some bills were red, tan, or tinted blue or green. Often, pictures of Southern scenery or politicians appeared on the front of the bills.

Confederate money wasn't worth much in 1865, but today, such a bill is worth a lot as a collector's item. If you happen to have any Confederate money, you may even find a collector willing to barter with you for it!

title: Tennessee Longboard
text:
The visit to the World Fair inspired Natalia and Steven. They have decided they are ready to be a part of the supply chain. They will create their own product and sell it to their fellow Tennessee citizens. Let’s listen to their plan.

Natalia: I’m excited about our new skateboard business!

Steven: So am I. The Tennessee Longboard will be the biggest product on the market since cotton candy.

Natalia:We have to find sources for all of the materials that we’ll need to build our skateboards.

Natalia: But we should make sure to find the lowest cost for our supplies.

Steven: Yes, that way we can increase our profits.

Natalia: Should we make our boards out of wood?

Steven: I think that’s a great idea. There are a lot of lumber producers in Tennessee. We would be helping the local industry.

Natalia: And using local resources will help us reduce shipping costs. This would lower our production costs.

Steven: Which will help us to have a higher profit margin. What about the wheels for our skateboards?

Natalia: The wheels will have plastic and metal parts. Tennessee has several rubber and plastic factories. This means we’ll be able to purchase the plastic parts at competitive rates.

Steven: Same with the metal parts of the board. I think this will be the easiest part of the supply chain for us. Some companies focus on making one product very well. It’s called specialization.

Natalia: That’s right, Steven. Putting the parts together into a whole might be harder for us. If we assemble the boards ourselves, we could save a lot of in labor costs.

Steven: But would we lose the savings in wasted time and slow production? We won't get our boards into the market fast enough to earn money back from our investment.

Natalia: That’s a good point, Steven. This is why many companies produce their goods overseas. They take advantage of cheaper labor costs.

Steven: … And increased production speed. It’s an option, but there are some problems with producing products overseas. We also might lose potential customers if we don’t use local labor. Can we call them Tennessee Longboards if they’re not made in Tennessee?

Natalia: Good question. Still, we need to compare our options.

Steven: You’re right. We’ve learned a lot about the supply chain, but we need to know more so that our Tennessee Longboards will be a success.

Natalia: Let’s keep working on our plan, Steven. We can do it!

title: St. Louis World Fair of 1904
text:
Natalia and Steven are at a school carnival waiting in line to get cotton candy.

Steven: Hey, Natalia, did you know that cotton candy was invented by a dentist?

Natalia: Really a dentist? That's pretty ironic if you ask me.

Steven: Yeah, but it sure is a good treat! We have William James Morrison to thank for it.

Natalia: I'll say! A dentist AND inventor? He must've been a person of many talents.

Steven: Well, he was actually also a lawyer and an author.

Natalia: That is incredible, Steven! Oh, I do love cotton candy. I can’t believe that a machine like this one made some of the first batches of cotton candy.

Steven: Right? I would really like to have seen that. The first time cotton candy was produced commercially was at the 1904 St. Louis World’s Fair by William Morrison and his partner John C. Wharton.

Natalia: What was the World's Fair?

Steven: It was an exposition where people from all over the world came to display all kinds of things like new foods, scientific inventions and even people from places of the world no one had seen before. In fact, people from over 60 countries came, and people from most of the United States went, too. It was so big that it lasted for 184 days!

Natalia: Wow! That's a long time for a fair to be open. Can you imagine our school carnival lasting that long?

Steven: I don't think ours is big enough to last that long. The World's Fair had over 1,500 buildings and had 75 miles of roads and walkways connecting everything together. It was one heck of a fair! I sure wish I could have seen it.

Natalia: Well, maybe we could still see it.

Steven: Hey, that's a great idea! Let’s go.

They both reach the front of the line and touch the cotton candy machine. They are suddenly transported back to the St. Louis World’s Fair of 1904.

Steven: This place is amazing! There is so much to see. I never imagined that it would be so huge. Just look at all these vendors and people buying and selling things!

Natalia: All of the buying and selling reminds me of the video from Studies Weekly about goods and services.

Steven: Look! I think that might be William Morrison.

Natalia: It looks like he's got a customer.

Steven and Natalia hide and listen to William’s sales pitch.

William Morrison: Madam! Try our sweet confection, fairy floss!

Natalia: Fairy floss?

Steven: That's what William Morrison called it. Actually, the name "cotton candy" came from a copycat, but the new name stuck.

Woman: What is fairy floss, sir?

William: It is a delectable new sweet as light as a cloud! The world has never seen the likes of it before!

Woman: This is certainly a very interesting candy. I’ve never seen anything like it.

William: You're quite right, madam. It is brand new. It’s going to be a worldwide success. Try a sample and see for yourself.

Woman: Why, this is delicious! I've never tasted anything like it! I’m sold. I’d like to buy some.

William: Wonderful! I’ll whip up a batch for you.

Natalia: Steven, I think we just witnessed the birth of cotton candy!!!

Steven: I think we did, too! And you know something, it really was a huge success. William Morrison actually sold 68,655 boxes of fairy floss at the fair for 25 cents per box. Morrison and Wharton ended up earning a total of $17,163.75!

Natalia: Holy crow! That was a lot of money back then!

Steven: It sure was!

Natalia: We've seen some pretty amazing things here at the fair. I guess this fair was a great opportunity for people all over the world to make money and get their products out there.

Steven: Yup. Just like William Morrison. I really liked seeing the transportation exhibit. That was cool to see how we went from carriges to cars!

Steven: I can't wait to share what we've learned with our class.

Natalia: Me neither! Let’s go now!

title: Tennessee's Early Economy
text:
It takes a lot of people to create a functioning economy. During the Civil War, people in the Northern states had to come up with a substitute for the sugar that they used to purchase from the South. They learned to make a syrup out of sorghum cane. Sorghum cane looks like a corn plant without the husks. Growing sorghum was a booming business during the Civil War, because the crop had a short growing season, and everyone needed something to use in place of sugar.

After the war, a new group of people came to the U.S. that had an impact on the Southern economy: Chinese immigrants. The Chinese settled in the South, hoping to find fair work on the plantations. They found out that the plantation owners didn’t want employees. They wanted replacement slaves. The Chinese immigrants realized this and left the plantations.

At the same time, newly freed African Americans were sharecropping. Sharecropping was when part of a farmer's crops was used to pay rent. They worked to build a life for their families. Times were hard. They found added trouble when they tried to buy goods. It was difficult to find any shops or stores that would sell to them. Plantation owners, who ran plantation stores, would either sell goods at overpriced rates or not at all. They did this to punish the former slaves and keep them in debt. This unfair system unwittingly created economic opportunities for Chinese and Jewish immigrants in Tennessee. Both groups sold dry goods to former slaves at lower prices, helping to grow the Tennessee economy. Around 1880, many of the Chinese immigrants became grocers. They sold products such as milk, bread and sugar to the sharecroppers at fair prices. These new suppliers filled a crucial demand in the market. They provided a new way for African American sharecroppers to get what they needed at a cheaper price. This greatly impacted the plantation owner's store income. Without the former African American slaves buying their goods, the plantation stores went out of business.

By the 1900s, 95 percent of Chinese men in the area were grocers. Many of these Chinese-owned stores stayed in business until the 1970s. They closed when large chain stores became popular. Even so, they played a crucial role in the local and regional economies during a time when it was most needed.

title: Local or Regional?
text:
Long ago, before money was invented, people bartered for goods and services. Bartering is trading goods and services without the use of money. If you were a farmer, you might trade a chicken for sugar, bread or a pot. You could trade for goods and services, but could only get what was in the local area. Another problem with bartering was that sometimes you had an item that no one would trade for. If you had animals or food to trade, those animals could die or the food could rot. Plus, you couldn’t exactly carry a chicken around in a wallet!

At first, people decided to use objects to exchange, like shells, salt, feathers or elephant-tail bristles. Most of these objects didn’t work out. Feathers can blow away and salt can get eaten! Traders wanted something that everyone would accept. That’s when they began to use metals as money. Precious metals, like gold or silver, were hard to find. This made them valuable. People made money from them because others wanted these metals and would accept them.

Nobody knows exactly who first made and used money. The ancient Egyptians melted and shaped metal into bars and stamped them with symbols that showed their weight. The Egyptians used the bars as currency. Later, Greeks and Romans created coins. Coins became so popular that people all over the world started using them! People make coins out of metals like gold, silver, bronze, copper and iron. Countries stamp coins with symbols like flowers, animals and pictures of their leaders.

If you wanted goods or services that weren’t from your area, you had to go farther away to buy them. There were problems with that, though. Sometimes the coins used in one country or town were different from the coins used in another. This made it hard to trade with money because not everyone used the same type. The good part was that you could get goods and services you might not be able to get at home.

So, let's compare. If you stayed close to home, you could only get the goods and services that were available from people in your town. But, if you were able to go a little farther away, the kinds of goods and services available might be better. Or at least different. You would have the additional items from the people out in the entire region. Staying local meant that the resources available to you for producing goods and services were limited. Broadening the region would give you the choice of more resources, so you could produce more goods and services. Also, if you get local goods, you know where they are and you can get them quickly. If you need to get goods and services from farther away, you'll need more time to get them, and maybe add the cost of travel or shipping. If you stayed local, you'd get few goods and services but you knew you could pay because you'd trade with the local money. On the other hand, you could go out farther into the region, get a better choice of goods and services, but risk not having the right kind of money. Using money hasn’t been perfect, but it’s much easier than bartering!

title: Let’s Learn About Budgets
text:
Have you ever asked your mom or dad for something, only to be told that it wasn't in the budget? A budget is a written plan for managing your money. A budget follows two main ideas.

First, you must think about how much money is coming into your household, or in your case, piggy bank. Maybe you earn an allowance. Maybe you mow a neighbor's lawn to make money, called income. If you earn money every week or month, like an allowance, then it is called a steady income.

Next, we look at how much is going out, or how much it costs your family to live. Maybe you subscribe to an educational magazine or go to a movie every Friday night. These are types of expenses. Adults also have expenses. They pay bills every month to buy things we all need like food, clothes and cars. These expenses come out of their income every month.

To make a budget, you must first look at your income (money coming in). Then, add up all of your expenses (money going out). Now, subtract the total amount of your expenses from your total income. This new number lets you know how much money you have for other things that you want. This helps you plan and make wise choices when spending your money.

The goal of a budget is to try to balance your income with your expenses. It is best if your income is more than your expenses. That way, more money is coming in than going out.

title: People Interact With the Environment
text:
What is interaction? It means that people change the environment and the environment changes people. Since the beginning of time, people have used their environments to get what they need and what they want. But sometimes, the environment has a say in all that. Long ago, people relied on their environment for water, food, shelter and even clothing. Today, we don't have to rely only on natural resources. We can add to what's in our natural environment by making things like plastics, fabrics and food out of things created in labs.

One important part of the environment has always been fresh water. Of course, we all need water to drink. But, we have also used bodies of water as a source of food, for washing, for fun things like boating and fishing, and for transportation. We ship goods on big rivers in boats. Today, we use flowing water in factories to make electricity. And, we use water on our crops to help keep the soil fertile so we can grow food like corn and soybeans, and cash crops like cotton. One way humans affect water is that we pollute it. Our fertilizers run off into it. Our trash sometimes ends up in it. We can use way too much of it if we are wasteful. Water is a renewable resource, but we have to be careful not to harm our water supply.

The climate is another part of our environment that affects us. We build houses to withstand stormy weather and to keep us warm in the winter and cool in the summer. If you lived in the middle of a desert, you wouldn't need a house that held up in a snowstorm! Our weather dictates what kinds of houses we have, and what we wear. We wear shorts in the summer and coats in the winter! Sometimes, when it's very cold or hot, the environment makes us uncomfortable. Luckily, we don't have to rely on tree bark or moss for clothing like they did long ago. And, we can go indoors to a temperature-controlled environment. Our environment changes us and we change it.

People used to live in trees or caves, or whatever they could find in their environment. But when they figured out that they could live where they wanted to if they built houses out of other materials, that's what they did. You'll notice that people are smart, though, and they built settlements near - you guessed it - water! That way they could use the water for all their needs and build more and more houses. When settlements began to spread around the water, people built bridges to cross over it. Then, they built roads so they could go all the way to other settlements. Since their towns stayed in one place, they could use the land better, too. They made farms to plant food and they stayed around all year to watch it grow and harvest it. Soon, bigger houses and more houses were built and some places got very crowded and overpopulated. When there are too many people in one area, the resources are stretched thin. Pollution is common. Also, when there are lots of people around, there is a greater need for goods and services of many types. Industries pop up to help people meet their needs and wants. Factories, stores and businesses are built. The natural environment is replaced with human-made buildings and parking lots. We build homes and other buildings using materials we want and in places we like, while avoiding things like drastic climates, dangerous water, steep mountains or rocky ground. Sometimes we cut down a lot of trees. That's called deforestation. That can affect everyone on Earth, since it changes the oxygen supply. We need to be careful with our trees and our planet!

With more people in an area, there is more need for transportation. Long ago, most people walked everywhere. Then, they started using small boats to travel on rivers. Later, they began to ride horses from place to place. Imagine what life was like when the first car was invented! The roads we build go just about anywhere today. Curvy roads go around mountains. Flat, long roads go across prairies. We even blast holes in mountains to build roads in tunnels! Today, we all use the same types of transportation: cars, boats, trains and airplanes. When a lot of people are using transportation at the same time, the environment can become clogged with traffic, smog and noise. Riding a bike is a good way to avoid going by car!

Our communication has changed a lot, too. When settlements were very small and distant from each other, the only people you could communicate with were the ones you lived with. You would never know what people in other settlements were doing. Talking was just about the only way to express your thoughts. As time passed, people began to live closer together. They got more curious about what other people were like, so they began to travel. That meant people started to cross the ocean in ships to see what was out there. They communicated across continents. There's still a lot to explore in the oceans! Information was communicated, but so were ideas, culture, foods, behaviors and even diseases. Through the years, people have created ways to communicate faster and easier. And, we have become physically closer together. Think about all the communication devices. There was the telegraph, then the telephone, then the TV, then the computer and mobile phone. First, we built poles with wires everywhere. Now, we are using wireless technology. Today we know what people across the whole world are doing. Our electronic environment has taken over!

So, the environment changes us in many ways, but we change it, too. People and the environment will always interact!

title: Welcome to Fourth Grade!
text:
"Hey fourth grade friends! Welcome to U.S. History Studies Weekly! My name is Natalia, and I'm in fourth grade, just like you. Each week, I'll meet you here in the pages of U.S. History Studies Weekly -- your very own newspaper! U.S. History Studies Weekly will tell you everything a social studies textbook can, but it'll be a lot more fun! Each issue of U.S. History Studies Weekly is filled with cool articles and activities. It’s available in paper and online! You can write in it, color in it, highlight it, underline stuff in it, and you can take it home! Unlike a textbook, it's yours to keep! I'll be happy to see you here each week. And I won't be alone! Joining me in every issue will be my best friend, Steven. In fact, here he is now! Steven, you wanna say hello?"

"You bet I do! We're excited to join you this year on a trip through American history! We'll learn about more than a hundred years of history together, from George Washington to Abraham Lincoln, and beyond. But first, a little bit about Natalia and me. You wanna start, Natalia?"

"Sure! For starters, Steven and I have a television show. It broadcasts to our whole school! All year, you'll get to sit in on our broadcasts, right here in the pages of U.S. History Studies Weekly. Our broadcast is all about stuff from American history. We talk about all sorts of things, and sometimes we show videos. You can see the videos we show! As you read, we'll tell you how to find them."

"So, yeah. We have a TV show, and that's cool. But it's not the coolest thing we want you to know about us. There's something even cooler! We don't tell this to everyone, but we think we can trust you. Natalia and I have a sort of … kind of a … well, it's a little hard to explain, but we've got … powers."

"What Steven is trying to say is that he and I can travel back in time! We don't know how we got these powers, but we use them all the time. It's crazy cool! We've met Lewis and Clark and Paul Revere! We watched the Boston Tea Party! Having this power is really incredible."

"All we have to do in order to travel back in time is to touch a primary source. Do you know what that is? A primary source is a document or object that actually came from the time we are studying. For example, if we were to touch the Declaration of Independence, we might go back to 1776! If we were to touch Abraham Lincoln's hat, we might go back to the Civil War! We've gone back in time by touching old letters, vintage newspaper articles, family heirlooms and more."

"We never know when or where we'll find a primary source. Sometimes we're surprised! Each week, you'll learn about our time travel adventures.

"And, as you read U.S. History Studies Weekly, we'll tell you where you can see some media related to where we go. So keep an eye out!"

"We'll spend this issue getting acquainted. After that, we're off on our adventures!"

title: It's Not Just a Story. It's Our Story!
text:
Steven and Natalia sat at a table in the school cafeteria. They were eating lunch. Steven munched on a celery stick.

"It's easy sometimes to think that when you're studying history, you're studying faraway people and places that don't have anything to do with you," he said. "But the truth is, the history of a country tells the story of people who are part of us."

"What do you mean?" asked Natalia. She slurped milk through a straw.

"Well, I've been thinking about my family. My mom is African American. Her great-great-great-great grandma was an enslaved person before the Civil War. We're going to study the Civil War this year. We'll be studying a lot of famous people, but in some ways we'll be studying the story of my family, won't we?"

"Wow," said Natalia. "I never though of it in quite that way. But it's true. Studying American history will be like studying family history for you."

"And for you, too," said Steven.

"Yeah!" said Natalia. "My grandmother is Cherokee. One of our ancestors fought in a battle at Fort Loudoun during the French and Indian War. I've heard my grandmother tell that story."

"We're studying Fort Loudoun next week!" said Steven. "And when we do, it'll be like learning the history of your family!"

"I guess that's true!" said Natalia. "I suddenly feel more excited than ever to study American history this year."

"No kidding," said Steven. "And I bet that every kid in our class has a story just like we do. No matter who they are, and no matter where they came from, just being here makes them part of the story of our country."

title: Got Maps? by Steven
text:
Hi! This is Steven. I love tech stuff. Cell phones, tablets, computers and GPS devices. That's my thing! But sometimes, there's nothing like a good ol' map to get you where you're going. Since we're going to be using lots of maps this year, let's brush up on some map skills. Most maps have basic features that help us use them. Here are just a few of them:

-A title. This tells us what part of the world we're looking at.

-A compass rose. This is a cool name for the part of a map that shows “cardinal directions.” Cardinal directions are the main directions: north, south, east and west. The compass rose shows directions but it is not a flower.

Maps also have symbols such as the following:

-A legend. This is another cool name for that part of the map that tells you how to understand all the lines and symbols used on the map. The legend might tell you that a capital city is marked with a star, or that a hospital is marked with a large blue H. Often, the legend will also teach you how the map measures distances, by using a "scale." This helps you figure out how far it is from one place to another on the map. For example, the scale could show that one inch on the map is actually equal to 100 miles in real life.

Maps can show continents, oceans, mountains, rivers, lakes and other landforms. Maps help us understand the shape, size and location of the areas that we will be studying. As we use maps this year, be sure to pay attention to all of the important labels and symbols on the maps.

Label the legend and compass rose below to test your map skills. And look for another map activity on the back page of today's issue of U.S. History Studies Weekly!

title: Today's News: Primary Sources
text:
Steven and Natalia sat in their seats, shuffling papers. It was almost time for their first broadcast of the year. In just a few moments, they'd be on!

"Will someone shout, “Action!” or something?" asked Steven.

"I think we just start to talk when the camera's red light comes on," said Natalia.

"When will the light come on?" asked Steven.

"Well, one of us will have to turn it on," said Natalia.

"I'll do it! I love that stuff!" said Steven. He pushed the button on the camera that said 'record.' A red light came on. "Here we go!" he said.

Natalia and Steven looked at the camera and smiled.

"It's the very first news show of the year!" said Natalia.

"We're excited to be here!" said Steven.

"In today's issue of U.S. History Studies Weekly, you might have heard us talk about a thing called a primary source," said Natalia.

"Like, I might have talked about being able to … oh, I don't know … travel back in time or something, just by touching a primary source," fumbled Steven.

"Um … yeah," said Natalia. "Not everyone can travel back in time when they touch a primary source, but primary sources are great ways for people to learn about the past. We thought we'd spend this show telling you just what we mean when we call something a primary source."

"A primary source is an artifact or document created or used during the time period you're studying, by the people you're studying," announced Steven.

"Let me see if I can give you an example," said Natalia. "Make believe that you're working on a class project about the Declaration of Independence. As part of your project, you've gathered three things to help you study:

a brand-new history book about the Declaration of Independence

a newspaper article, printed just last week, about a museum in town with a copy of the Declaration of Independence on display

the Declaration of Independence itself

Of those three things - the book, the article, and the Declaration itself - can you guess which one is the primary source?" asked Natalia.

"Here's a hint," said Steven. "Only one of those three things was created or used during the time period you're studying by the people you're studying."

"Not the history book," said Natalia. "Someone wrote that many years after the Declaration of Independence."

"And not the article," said Steven. "That was also written much later."

"So it must be the Declaration itself. That's the primary source!" said Natalia.

"You got it!" said Steven. "The Declaration of Independence is a primary source. It was created or used in the time period you're studying, by the people you're studying."

"Do you have another example?" said Natalia.

"I sure do," said Steven. "Make believe that I'm doing a report on the life of my great-great-great-great-great-grandmother. She was an enslaved person in the time of the Civil War. I wish like anything I could go back in time to change that for her! To help me learn what it was like, I've come up with three things:

a book about slavery

a website that gives a timeline of the Civil War

a photograph of my great-great-great-great-great grandmother

One of those things is a primary source. Can you guess which one it is?"

"Easy," said Natalia. "It's the photo, right?"

"Right!" said Steven. Unlike the website and the book, the photo was created or used during the time period I'm studying, by the people I'm studying."

"Is that what you guessed, too?" said Natalia to the camera.

"There's the lesson in all of this," said Steven. "When you're working to understand the story of our great land, it's good to read books,"

"And look at websites," said Natalia.

"And read articles," said Steven.

"But it's also important to look at primary sources," said Steven.

"In other words," said Natalia, "If you're studying the Declaration of Independence, make sure that part of your study is to read the Declaration itself. If you're studying the Constitution, make sure that you read the Constitution. Get it?"

"Got it," said Steven.

"Well, that's everything for today's show," said Natalia.

"We'll see you next time!" said Steven.

title: Introducing Ms. Johnson
text:
Hello everyone! I'm so glad you're getting to know Steven and Natalia. They're very good students, and they'll be very good guides as you learn about the history of our great country this year. Allow me to introduce myself. My name is Ms. Johnson. I'm a 4th grade teacher, and Steven and Natalia are in my class. I spend time with them every day at school, and I'll be spending a lot of time with you too! I hope you enjoy your visits to my classroom, and that you feel as comfortable there as you feel in your own 4th grade class.

You'll learn all sorts of things about American history in each issue of U.S. History Studies Weekly. You're sure to enjoy the articles and activities in each weekly newspaper that arrives at your desk. But that's just the beginning! There's much more to see, hear and do by visiting Studies Weekly online. Your teacher can show you how to get there.

As you learn about history, you'll almost certainly want to know more. You'll find yourself visiting the world of the Internet for more information about the things we study together. Searching the Internet can be a great way to learn, as long as you remember a few things:

-When you visit the Internet, make sure you're supervised by an adult whenever possible. At school, you can ask for the help of a teacher or librarian. At home, you can ask for the help of a parent or guardian.

-Not all information you find on the Internet is reliable. You will find things that simply aren't true. As you look for facts on the Internet, it's a good idea to make sure you can find a fact in at least three different places before you try to use it in a report or project. If you have questions about whether a website contains reliable facts, you can ask your teacher for help. Teachers are great for things like that!

I'm very glad to meet you. I hope you have a wonderful year, and I'll see you soon!

title: Learn to Run the Country, and Help the Studies Weekly Explorers While You're at it!
text:
Hey, kids! We're Studies Weekly Explorers, your Studies Weekly online pals! We need your help. You can help us get great stuff by earning points while you learn. Just go to www.studiesweekly.com and click on our picture!

Has your family ever bought something that came with an owner's manual? An owner's manual is a book that comes along with a product, teaching you how to use the product. Cars, TVs and other things have owner's manuals. Your social studies class is kind of like an "owner's manual" for the United States of America. You'll learn about history, geography, government and much more. After all, you'll run the country someday, and you'll need a good start on knowing how!

Does it surprise you to think that you'll run the country when you grow up? It's true! Every one of you will play a part in running the country by voting. Voting is the way we choose the leaders who make and enforce our laws. Voting is how the people tell their leaders how they think the country should be run.

Some Studies Weekly readers might someday be mayors, senators, governors or presidents. Most of you will have a job or own a business. The way the government runs the country affects our jobs and businesses, so it's important to pay attention to how well you think they're doing. If you think someone else can do it better you can help fix that by voting. Every Studies Weekly reader can someday be a voter.

To prepare for the kind of voter you'll be, you've got a job to do right here: Learn about the country and how it works. U.S. History Studies Weekly will help you do that job! As you learn, you can earn points for us so we can get that great stuff we told you about. You learn; we get stuff. Got it? It's easy. Just click and you're on your way!

title: Four War Facts
text:
Fact 1 - From Flub to Favor: Washington had to surrender at Fort Necessity. But his men bragged about how brave Washington was in the war. Though he made mistakes, his work during this war helped his career.

Fact 2 - A War by Any Other Name: It's tough to come up with a good name for this war. Some people call it the French and Indian War, even though it wasn't a war between the French and the Indians. Some people call it the Seven Years’ War, even though it didn't last for seven years. What would you call it?

Fact 3 - Forever Florida: Florida is one of the 50 United States of America. If not for the French and Indian War, there's a chance that this would not have been the case. Before the French and Indian War, Spain ruled Florida.

Fact 4 - Yankee Doodle is Born: The song "Yankee Doodle" might have been made up by the British during this war. They sang it to tease the colonists. The colonists were poorly dressed as they fought alongside the fancy British redcoats. Later the tables were turned, and it became a song for the colonists to tease the British.

title: An Adventure at Fort Loudon
text:
Steven was doing homework at Natalia's house. He saw an old gun and an old belt buckle hanging over the fireplace.

"Those belonged to one of my Cherokee ancestors," Natalia told him. "They were used in the French and Indian War." They were primary sources to be sure! Natalia reached up and brushed some dust off of the belt buckle. As she did, Steven and Natalia felt a rush of wind. Touching the buckle -- an actual thing that had been around since the French and Indian War -- was sending them back in time!

Before they knew it they were standing outside a fort.

"I think this is Fort Loudoun!" said Natalia.

"Hey! That’s here in Tennessee," said Steven. "It's in Monroe County.” He looked at the warriors around the fort. “This looks bad. It looks like a siege. But aren’t these Cherokee people? Weren’t they allies of the colonists? Did they change sides?”

"It’s a mess,” Natalia said. “Colonists killed some of their friends. Then the Cherokee didn't trust the English anymore. Look!” She pointed at one of the warriors. “That's Attakullakulla. He's a peacemaker."

She pointed to another warrior. "That's Oconostota. They’re cousins. He was with the English until they killed 24 Cherokee. He was so angry he asked the French for weapons and bullets to attack the colonists."

“It doesn’t look good for them,” Steven said. “And it might not be too good for us in a minute!”

“Let’s go!” Natalia said. She picked up the belt buckle. They felt the familiar rush of wind. They were headed forward in time again. In a moment, they were back at Natalia’s house. In front of them, they saw their homework.

“Whew!” Steven said. “I’ve never been so glad to see homework.”

Steven and Natalia tried to settle down to their books. Natalia's father looked in. “How are you doing?” he asked.

“We’re writing reports,” said Natalia. “What happened to the Cherokee after the French were driven out of the Ohio and Mississippi valleys?”

Her dad pulled up a chair. He told them that during the war the English and the French kept trying to get American Indian allies to fight along with them. The French made treaties with some tribes. The English made treaties with others. The Cherokee and Iroquois often allied with the English.

"England and France wanted more territory," Natalia's dad explained. "England had 13 colonies. Spain had Florida. France had a large area of land called New France. Their borders were not well defined. It made trouble in the Ohio River Valley."

“France and Spain teamed up to defeat England. England declared war on Spain. Spain was badly defeated.

“At first the French were winning because they had more troops and supplies. Then English Secretary of State William Pitt took control. Pitt came up with money for better gear and more soldiers. Things turned in England's favor! England kept driving France farther and farther back. Soon everyone just wanted peace."

"So they signed the Treaty of Paris in 1763.” said Natalia. “England got all the land France had claimed in America. England also got Spanish Florida. But England had to give Cuba back to Spain."

"And the English made the Proclamation of 1763,” her father said. “It said colonists could not live west of the Appalachian Mountains. That land was saved for American Indians."

"So things worked out great for Britain and the American Indians," Steven said.

"Sort of," Natalia's father said. "But the colonists moved west anyway. And the war cost England a lot. They paid for it by making the colonists pay new taxes. That made the colonists mad and they began to rebel. Do you see? The events caused by the French and Indian War led to the American Revolution. Make sure you put that in your report."

"We sure will!" Steven and Natalia said together.

title: Getting Ready for a Big Report!
text:
Steven and Natalia were glad that Ms. Johnson had assigned them to work on a report together. Ms. Johnson had asked them to study the French and Indian War. It was pretty complicated. They had already done a lot of research, and they were trying to decide what to include in their report.

“OK," Natalia said, "we need to say what caused the war. France and England both wanted more land. Land is filled with raw materials like lumber, fish, furs, and more. They hoped those things would make them rich!"

"I get that," said Steven. "More trade makes more money. More money makes more power. The trouble is they all wanted the same land."

"Right!” said Natalia. “England, France and Spain were all fighting for control of land, and the American Indians were caught in the middle of it all. The two biggest rivals were England and France."

"They were also at war in Europe. In Europe, this war is called The Seven Years War. We could show the 'French and Indian War Intro' video. That’ll show how the French and English were headed for a collision!"

"That's right! A big land crash!" Natalia said. "The English and the French both tried to grab the Ohio River Valley and Mississippi River Valley."

"Yep," Steven added. "The first battle in the French and Indian War happened where Pittsburgh is now. It was between the French and 21-year-old George Washington. That was kind of a crazy battle. It only lasted about 15 minutes!"

“That fight was called Jumonville Glen," said Natalia. It’s a good example of what a mess things were. The Virginia militia was part of the English army then. That means Washington was a British officer. It's weird to think of him like that, right? He and his men were ordered to build a fort. The French came to tell them to stop building. Washington was ordered to go tell the French to mind their own business. He found a group of French soldiers hiding. He thought they were going to attack so he attacked them first. A lot of those French soldiers were killed."

"Right." said Steven. "Washington went back to building the fort. Then more French soldiers came. The English were outnumbered. Washington surrendered to the French. It was his only surrender." Steven thought for a minute. “Washington had Indians fighting along with him. We need to talk about the Indians. Both countries used Indians as soldiers."

"Right," said Natalia. "Jumonville Glen was only the beginning. Things would get a lot worse. There were more casualties in the French and Indian war than there would be in the Revolutionary war a few years later. And all because everyone wanted the same land."

Hey readers! You can watch the video Steven and Natalia used in their report. Just visit Studies Weekly online. And stay tuned! There's a closer look at Steven and Natalia's time travel adventures coming up in U.S. History Studies Weekly!

title: Attakullakulla, The Peacemaker
text:
Attakullakulla was a famous Cherokee leader. You say his name like this: At-tah-cuhl-la-cuhl-la. He lived in what is now Tennessee. He became the right hand man of the high priest of the Cherokee Nation.

In 1730 he was one of six Cherokee chosen to go to England. He met the English king and English statesmen. They became allies. They signed a trade treaty.

In 1739 he was captured by the Iroquois. They took him to Canada. The French were in Canada. He got to know French traders and soldiers and the French governor.

He saw the Iroquois working to get the French and the English to fight each other. That helped the Iroquois feel secure. The Iroquois traded with both sides. Attakullakulla went back home. He tried to make the kind of deals he had seen in Canada.

The Cherokee and the English were allies. They were both worried about French soldiers in the Mississippi Valley. The English built Fort Loudoun to protect them. But some of the settlers and the Cherokee fought. There were deaths on both sides. This caused the Cherokee to turn against the English.

The Cherokee surrounded the fort. They kept food from reaching the fort. Then, they waited till the soldiers got hungry enough to come out. That’s called a siege. Attakullakulla helped an English captain named John Stuart escape. They were friends. But the Cherokee killed many soldiers and took the fort.

In some ways, the siege of Fort Loudoun looked like a victory for the Cherokee. But half the Cherokee towns were destroyed. The Cherokee hoped for peace. They signed a treaty with John Stuart. They gave the English a large piece of land. They hoped it would bring peace.

Attakullakulla worked to avoid war. But his people’s lands grew smaller and smaller. Some of his people rejected him. His own son turned from him. Still, Attakullakulla worked for twenty years on peace treaties.

title: Big Changes and New Ways
text:
When Europeans began to realize that there was money to be made in America, a lot of things happened. Some of those things caused the troubles that led to the French and Indian War. Here's a look:

-French explorer Jacques Cartier came to Canada in the 1500’s. He began trading goods to American Indians for beaver pelts. Those pelts would one day be used to make shiny top hats in Europe. Thousands of beaver pelts left America and went to Europe. That’s a lot of money for the people doing the trading! White men began to trap their own furs as well as trade for them. They spread out into the country looking for beavers.

-Cod fishing in New England became profitable at about the same time. Cod fish could be dried. When they were dried they could be shipped back to England and to Europe. There was money to be made in the cod fish trade.

-As business grew, European settlers cut down trees for their timber. They cleared land for farming. They hunted wild animals for food. They brought diseases with them. The native peoples of North America were not immune to these diseases. Thousands of them died.

Some tribes pushed back. Wars sprang up. But there were always more European settlers. The tribes were moved farther and farther west.

These things changed life forever for native people. Tribes were pushed off their land. The animals they depended upon for food became overhunted by the settlers. The American Indians were forced to change their ways. Some old ways of life were lost and new ways of life came.

Then the French and English began fighting over the land. They wanted Indian tribes to do some of the fighting for them. That fighting became the French and Indian War!

title: Join or Die!
text:
I'm Benjamin Franklin. This is my printing press. I own and run one of the most important newspapers in the colonies, "The Pennsylvania Gazette." I have been working in printing since I was a boy.

We are all worried about this war. There are many deaths. Indian tribes fight on both sides. The French have strong native allies. The Iroquois are our allies. Our government in England is concerned that treaties with the Iroquois Nation have broken down. We must settle our relations with the Indians to keep ourselves safe.

For the May 9, 1754 issue of my paper I drew a picture called a cartoon. I named it "Join, or Die." It showed a snake cut into eight pieces. Each piece stands for a colony. I put the four New England colonies in one piece to show unity. People could see the snake must stay together. Otherwise it’s just a dead snake. I wanted the public to see the strength in unity.

I’m just back from the 1754 Albany Congress in New York. A "congress" is a group chosen to discuss the matters of government. Those people are called delegates. Some members of the Northern colonies and Six Iroquois Nations met. In the congress, I presented my "Albany Plan of Union." I thought the colonies should unite. A central council would handle Indian policy. It would settle disputes between colonies. It could charge taxes to support itself. They discussed my ideas. I suggested each colony elect delegates for an American Continental Assembly. This would be presided over by a royal governor.

The plan was rejected by the British. Our colonial assemblies did not like the idea of a central council taxing them. England did not want strong colonial unity. They thought the colonies would get too much power. Perhaps one day people will see things differently. We do not wish to pay now for our own protection. I fear we will one day pay for it in taxes to England. We shall see.

You’ll find a video at Studies Weekly online called “Join or Die!” Franklin’s plan was important. It was the first attempt to unify the colonies. They were not ready to give up individual independence to become one country. This did not happen until after the American Revolution. Many of Franklin's ideas for the Albany Congress would later be adopted in the Constitution. These are just a few of the contributions of Benjamin Franklin during this era. He was a big deal!

title: Political Cartoon
text:
Benjamin Franklin was always thinking about making life better. He got things going. He made the first newspaper chain. He started the first fire brigade in his city. He helped build the first library building in America. He was also one of the first people working to unify the colonies. He was worried during the French and Indian War. He thought unified colonies could defend themselves better. He was worried other people might not listen. He made the “Join, or Die” cartoon in his paper telling the colonists they had to come together or they might die.

Is there something in your own school or town that you think could be changed to make things better for everyone? Think about the change you would like to see. Make a list of things you can do to make it happen. Now draw a “political cartoon” to show your thoughts!

title: George Washington Fights!
text:
George Washington fought the first battle of the French and Indian War before the war even started. You can learn about this part of Washington's life by visiting Studies Weekly online. Search for a video called "George Washington Military Career Intro."

Washington was very brave. He led his men in the thick of the fighting. In one battle of the French and Indian War two horses were shot out from under him, one after the other! He also ended up with four bullet holes in his coat!

The French and Indian War was between England, France and Spain. Because the colonies were English, Washington fought for the English army!

Washington mostly educated himself. He couldn’t read French. When he was made to surrender at Fort Necessity, he had to sign a statement. It was written in French so he could not read it. It laid a lot of blame on Washington that he might have felt he didn't deserve. He must have wished he had taught himself French!

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine that you are a colonist living in 1754. Would you be for or against uniting with the other colonies to form your own laws and government? Why or why not? What would uniting mean for the colonies? Write using ideas from the articles in this issue to support your point of view.

title: Point of View: Religion in the Revolution
text:
Read the religious points of view of the following people and groups, about the Revolutionary War. Then, write at least one sentence reacting to each point of view. How did religion play a part in the Revolution?

1. Joseph Galloway: speaker of the Pennsylvania Assembly, friend to Benjamin Franklin. Galloway believed that the Revolution was a religious fight. He thought the colonial people had “principles of religion ... (that were against) … those of the established Church (of England) and Government.” He went back to England in 1778.

2. Jonathan Mayhew, a Boston preacher, thought the Church of England was a dangerous enemy of the colonists. He said that resisting the tyrant (King George) was the “glorious” duty of the Christians.

3. Abraham Keteltas, a preacher in New Jersey and New York, gave a sermon and said that, "the cause of truth, against error and falsehood … against bigotry, superstition, and human invention ... is (like) the kind Parent of the Universe against the prince of darkness, and the destroyer of the human race."

4. The Quakers are a religious sect whose members believe in pacifism, or peacefulness. They believe any type of violence is wrong and refuse to engage in it or participate in wars. William Penn of Pennsylvania was a Quaker. A group of Quakers during the Revolution started calling themselves, “Free Quakers.” They decided it was okay to take up arms against the British, causing a rift in the Quaker population.

title: Paving the Road to Independence
text:
"Hey, Steven. See that little red light on the camera?"

"Um ... yeah," said Steven.

"That little red light means we're on the air!" said Natalia.

"Oh, right! Well ... er ... here we go then," stammered Steven. "Hello classmates! On today's edition of our show we're talking about some of the things that led to the American Revolution."

"And there were a lot of them," said Natalia, "so we'll get right to it!"

"In the early 1700s the French and English wanted more territory in the New World," said Steven. "They fought over it. That war was called the French and Indian War."

"England won the war," said Natalia. "They got the land France had claimed, without regard to lands of the American Indians. But they also got a big problem!"

"What's that, Natalia?" said Steven.

Natalia kept going. "A war costs lots and lots of money," she said. "England borrowed money to fight the war. They won the war. Now they had to pay the debt."

"Parliament decided to raise money by taxing their people," said Steven. "Parliament is the British congress. They make laws for England. They taxed all British citizens, and that included people living in the American colonies."

"British armies protected American colonies during the war," said Natalia. "America was all the way across the Atlantic Ocean from England. It was expensive to have an army so far from home. The English government thought colonists should help pay for the armies in America. They put taxes on lots of things the colonists used every day."

"The colonists didn’t want to pay for the English army," said Steven. "People in England couldn’t understand that."

"After all," said Natalia. "Colonists were English citizens!" All English men had to pay for their country’s wars. They made laws stricter so the colonists would have to pay taxes. They passed laws in Parliament called acts. Most of the acts had to do with colonists paying taxes to England.

Parliament passed the Sugar Act. It changed the tariff on sugar. Tariffs are taxes on goods coming into or out of a country. The Sugar Act made English sugar cheaper than sugar from other countries. It also cracked down on smugglers who brought in sugar illegally. This hurt colonial trade with other countries that sold sugar."

"I get it!" said Steven, "Those countries didn’t want to buy American goods if the colonists didn’t buy their sugar."

"That's right!" said Natalia. "And there's more. Parliament taxed all official papers. That was called the Stamp Act. Colonists had to buy a stamp for any legal document. Even newspapers and playing cards had to have stamps. The price of the stamp went to the English government. It was supposed to help pay the war debt."

"These acts made the colonists mad," said Steven. "They thought they should be ruled according to what the people living in the colony wanted. They felt like they should have a say in the government. But there were no leaders from the colonies in Parliament."

"Colonists thought it was wrong for Parliament to tax people they didn’t even know," said Natalia. "Benjamin Franklin went to England and told them that the colonies needed representatives in Parliament if colonists were going to be taxed to pay England’s debts."

"But the English didn't get it," said Steven. "They thought of Parliament as a group of wise, great men. Those men made laws they thought were good. They thought that regular people should just do as they were told."

"Both sides were sure they were right," said Natalia. "Both sides dug in and got stubborn."

"The stage was set for a terrible struggle!" said Steven. "And how did it turn out?"

"Read today's U.S. History Studies Weekly for more, and tune in next time as things in the colonies get even hotter!"

The red light on the camera turned off. Steven and Natalia looked at each other.

"Were you nervous?" said Natalia. "There was some important stuff in that broadcast."

"Nervous? Nah," said Steven. "Let's do that again as soon as we can!"

"Alright," said Natalia. "But in the meantime, we've got some studying to do."

"I guess so," said Steven. "I suppose life isn't easy, even when you're a TV star."

title: Taxation Without Representation is Tyranny
text:
In today's issue of U.S. History Studies Weekly, we're talking a lot about taxes. You’ve heard of taxes. We pay taxes today. Taxes are how government pays for itself. Usually, people who pay taxes today voted to pick the people making the tax laws.

But that's not how it worked in the American Colonies. Back then, no one from the colonies got to help make laws in England. They didn't have a say in how the money should be used. The colonists wanted a voice. In America they got to vote on issues in their local governments, but they still were not allowed to help with laws made by England. The English thought the colonists should be okay with that.

Colonists started saying, “Taxation without representation is tyranny.” Tyranny means a person or group in power is cruel or unfair. These taxes were one thing that brought about the Revolution.

title: Resistance to Imperial Policies
text:
It seemed like every British law made the colonists angrier. And they showed it.

The Proclamation of 1763 tried to save land for American Indians. Because the colonists were angry, they ignored it. They moved into those lands anyway.

They refused to buy British goods during the Sugar Act and the Currency Act. They met in groups to complain.

The colonists hated the Stamp Act, and they got organized to fight it. British workers called Stamp Agents collected the tax. The colonists terrorized the Stamp Agents. Many of the Agents were so scared that they quit their jobs.

The colonies got together and wrote a letter. They sent it to England. It described all the reasons they were mad about the stamps and other acts. It said England shouldn’t tax them unless it gave them a voice in Parliament. They stopped buying things from Britain again.

That worked. The Stamp Act was repealed. But the fight wasn't over. England passed a law that said it could make any laws in America it wanted to.

title: Religion and Revolution
text:
Religion was a big part of colonial life. A wide range of religious ideas helped bring about the American Revolution. Many clergy said that rebelling against Britain was good. They taught that God was on the colonists’ side.

Preachers took many jobs as the colonies began to rebel. They wrote letters for committees of correspondence. They served in state assemblies. Some preachers were army chaplains. Some led troops in battle.

Jonathan Mayhew was the preacher in the Old West Church in Boston. He gave fiery sermons. He wrote letters and pamphlets. He preached that taxation without representation was tyranny. He told his church that to fight against a tyrant was a Christian duty.

Peter Muhlenberg was a preacher who went to war. He lived in Virginia. One day he ended his sermon and threw off his preacher’s robe. Under it he was wearing an army uniform!

John Witherspoon was a preacher who signed the Declaration of Independence. He served on more than a hundred committees.

Not all preachers were on the Patriots’ side. The King is the head of the Church of England. The clergy from that church swear to be loyal to the King. Their prayer book asked God to take care of the King and help him win all his wars. It was hard for them when the colonies began to rebel.

In Maryland the church decided to take prayers for the King out of the book of prayers. They put strips of paper over any place that talked about the King.

More than half of the preachers in the Church of England left the country. Joseph Galloway was one of them. He was Benjamin Franklin’s good friend. But he was against the rebellion. He fled to England in 1778.

Many Church of England preachers who stayed in the colonies stopped preaching. Some worked to help the British. One of these was Jonathan Odell. He wrote strong articles making fun of the Patriots. He tried to hurt their cause. He was loyal to the King.

title: Think & Review Questions
text:
1. Why did colonists hate the Quartering Act?

2. List at least two events that led people to want independence for the colonies.

3. In your own words, explain what "taxation without representation" means and why this phrase was important to the colonists.

4. In your opinion, why did Parliament heavily tax the colonists?

title: The Quartering Act and the Townshend Acts
text:
Most of the English tax acts were to get the colonists to pay the debt from the French and Indian War. But some of them were to pay British workers in America. These were the Quartering and Townshend Acts.

The Quartering Act was passed in 1764. It required colonial governments to pay for the housing and feeding of British soldiers. The colonists were angry about it for two reasons: First, this was another tax no one had asked them about. Secondly, they didn’t think British soldiers should be in America. It was a time of peace. They were afraid the English wanted an army in America to make them obey the tax laws. They didn’t believe the army was to protect them. It seemed to them like an army should be on the inland border. That way it could protect them from French soldiers or Indian tribes if they attacked. These soldiers were on the coast. That’s where goods came into the country. That’s where taxes were paid.

Most of the colonies just didn’t pay for the troops. They ignored the law. Then, one day, 1,500 British troops got off boats in New York harbor. Because New York refused to take care of them, Britain closed New York’s Assembly. That was the colony’s government. So New York agreed to pay some of the cost of the soldiers.

The Townshend Acts passed in 1767. Those were supposed to pay British officials working in the colonies. They taxed glass, paint, lead, paper and tea. The colonists didn’t make those things themselves. They had to import those goods.

John Dickinson in New York and Samuel Adams in Boston published letters condemning these acts. So did most of the other colonies. The colonists stopped buying English goods again. It got so bad for English merchants that most of the Townshend Acts were repealed. But England left some in place to show they were in charge. Also, England moved their troops into Boston where most of the protests were.

title: Rising Tensions in the Colonies
text:
"What's up in here?" Steven asked as they walked into their classroom.

"Don't you remember? A traveling history exhibit is visiting today. It's a mobile museum," explained Natalia.

"Boys and girls, look around," Ms. Johnson said. "You’ll see artifacts from before the American Revolution. There are even newspaper articles you can read. Be careful! Some are over 250 years old."

"This is cool, Natalia. I'm so excited!" said Steven. "There were so many political, religious and economic ideas that led to the American Revolution. Look! This article is from 1765. It's from the Virginia Gazette."

Steven carefully handed Natalia the folder with the article in it. As she took it, they felt the rush of wind. The classroom disappeared. They were headed back in time!

Before they knew it, they were standing in a grassy place in front of a large building. Two men were walking slowly across the grass, talking.

"I think that's George Wythe," Steven said. "He was Thomas Jefferson's teacher. He taught law."

"Let's listen to what they're talking about." They listened to the men.

"I've met Patrick Henry. Is he a man of the law?" Thomas Jefferson asked with concern.

"I would not give him the bar exam," replied George Wythe. "However, I have heard that he is well studied in law. He will serve well in the Virginia House of Burgesses. He might be just the man to represent us in Virginia."

"I hope you are right," said Jefferson. "After the Parson's Cause, Henry has earned much respect. His is the strongest voice opposing the Stamp Act. So many of us agree. England should not tax us for every printed piece of paper!"

"I am grateful he fights for the colonies,” replied Wythe. “He may be just the spokesman we require at a time like this."

Steven looked at Natalia. "Wow! I didn't know all of this about Patrick Henry."

"Neither did I! We better get back to school! See that kid with the Virginia Gazette? It’s the same paper that brought us here."

Natalia and Steven walked up to the boy. “Can I see that paper for a moment?” asked Steven. “I’ll give it right back.”

The boy held out the paper. Steven and Natalia reached out. The moment their hands touched the paper, they felt the rush of wind. Before they knew it, they were sitting in Ms. Johnson's classroom.

They looked at each other, remembering the conversation they’d heard.

“Boy!” said Steven. “The Stamp Act sounds pretty unfair. I’d be angry if I lived in the colonies back then. I bet the pressure was building. With all that pressure, something was going to blow up!

“Yeah,” said Natalia. “That was one of the economic interests that brought about the American Revolution. I’m glad they put their faith in guys like Patrick Henry. They may have doubted his outspoken ways, but he and others like him sure got down to business.”

“They sure did,” said Steven. “And we got a front row seat!”

Visit Studies Weekly online and look for a video called, "Mounting Tensions in the Colonies." Check it out!

title: Redcoats
text:
British soldiers wore bright red coats. That's how they got the name "Redcoats." To be a Redcoat was a pretty good job. In addition to money, they got food and a place to live. In the days of the American Revolution, it was one of the only jobs that paid men after they retired.

Rich men often paid money to be officers, but poor men were normally just regular soldiers. Officers rode horses. Everyone else marched on their feet.

If soldiers broke the rules, punishment was harsh. Redcoats could be whipped. If they stole things or ran away they could be hanged.

Some Redcoats brought their families with them to war. Their wives worked for the army, too. They nursed the men, washed, sewed or cooked.

Redcoats were very well trained. They were one of the best armies in the world. The colonists knew it would be hard to stand up to them.

title: An Adventure With the Sons of Liberty
text:
Natalia was in the library reading about Boston at the time of the Stamp Act. She thought about ships and cargoes. She could almost smell the sea and hear the gulls. Someone suddenly ran up behind her. "Look at this note I found! It’s written to the Sons of Liberty!" Steven yelped.

"What? Who?" Natalia was lost.

Steven pulled an old paper out of a book. "Check this out. 'The true born Sons of Liberty are desired to meet under the Liberty Tree at 12 o'clock, this day.'"

"Wow! That paper looks incredibly old. Can I see it?" Natalia reached out. She touched the parchment and felt a rush of wind. She and Steven were on their way to the past.

Steven and Natalia found themselves in a town square. They could hear the clip-clopping of horses' hooves pulling wagons and carriages. Across the square men were meeting under a large tree.

"That's got to be the Liberty Tree!" Steven exclaimed. "Let's get closer so we can hear."

The friends ducked behind a carriage near the men.

" ... I am Benedict Arnold," a man was saying. "My business lies in ruins. But I will continue to trade and sell as if no Stamp Act existed. I shall smuggle tea and sell it on the black market if I must. I shall not bow to England!”

"Samuel Adams!" another man was saying. "Must you always be so angry? Is violence to be the only way forward?”

"What then, John Hancock?” Samuel Adams replied. “How do you propose to fight the British?"
