Hancock looked thoughtful. "If we can achieve change on a political or diplomatic level that would be best. I am hoping for the best."

"Mr. Edes ... " a man began.

Steven choked when he saw who was speaking. “That’s John Adams!” he said.

Natalia craned her neck to see around the carriage. “He’ll be our country’s second president!”

Steven frowned. “Are John and Samuel Adams brothers? I can’t remember.”

“Cousins,” Natalia said. “Shhh!”

“I wonder,” John Adams said, “if your Boston Gazette would publish a piece from James Otis’ recent pamphlet. I tell you, the man is the father of our cause. He is a flame of fire. He boldly says taxation without representation is tyranny!”

"I shall do it!" Benjamin Edes replied. "My paper is at the service of our cause. I hope to spread anti-British views far and wide across the colonies. And I'll tell you who else is a flame of fire! Your cousin Sam!"

“I know it,” John Adams frowned. “I hope all shall be well. Some of us worry.”

Samuel Adams came striding over. “Otis, you say? Otis is a good man! A great man, when he speaks truth right out and is not so careful. 'Taxation without representation is tyranny!' The Sons of Liberty have taken his words as our motto!”

Suddenly, the carriage Natalia and Steven were hiding behind pulled away and they were left standing in the open.

"Time to go!" Steven said.

The two touched the paper that had brought them there. They felt the rushing of wind. Before they knew it they were back in the school library.

Steven grinned back. "Hey, I'm pretty sure I saw a video called, 'Sons of Liberty Intro.' I bet that will have some awesome info about the different forms of protests colonists used to promote change in British policies."

Do you want to watch the video Steven and Natalia talked about? Visit Studies Weekly online!

title: Give Me Liberty or Give Me Death!
text:
Not all the Sons of Liberty lived in Boston. They were scattered through the colonies. Thomas Jefferson, George Washington and Patrick Henry came from the colony of Virginia.

Patrick Henry was a talented lawyer and speaker. He was very brave. He became famous when he was a lawyer in the Parson’s Cause. In that court case he called the king a tyrant, and speaking against the king was treason. People who commit treason are called traitors. Cries of treason rang through the room during that case, but it wouldn’t be the last time.

Henry was voted into the House of Burgesses. That was Virginia's local government. Many lawmakers wanted to keep the peace. They feared King George. Patrick Henry did not. He thought it was important to resist unfair taxes. He feared giving more control to Britain. Henry spoke out against the Stamp Act. He challenged anyone listening to charge him with treason! Traitors could be hung.

Henry gave another famous speech at St. John's Church in Virginia. He argued that it was time for war. He convinced his fellow Virginians to send soldiers. That speech is famous for the statement, “I know not what course others may take; but as for me, give me liberty or give me death!”

Henry commanded Virginia's troops during the war. After the war he continued a life of public service. He served as Virginia's first governor and helped draft the Bill of Rights.

For more about Patrick Henry's famous speech, you can visit Studies Weekly online to see a video called "Give Me Liberty or Give Me Death!"

title: Committees of Correspondence
text:
Patriots didn’t have phones or email. How could everyone hear their ideas?

Samuel Adams got people at a Boston Town meeting to form a "Committee of Correspondence." Their job was to write letters. Both men and women wrote letters.

The Committees wrote to every town in Massachusetts Colony. They shared news. They told about meetings. The towns made groups of their own, and wrote back to Boston. Soon all the Patriots were talking to each other.

The other colonies did the same thing. They could talk to their own towns, and to other colonies too.

To write letters like this was a big risk. If letter writers were caught they could be hung. This kind of thing was treason!

Letters were passed in secret from person to person, and only Patriots got to see them. They hid them in saddles on horses. They even hid them in the British mail!

Through these letters, leaders in the colonies got to know each other. After a while they met to discuss their plans. These big meetings of leaders from every colony eventually formed the Congress of the United States.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend that you heard Patrick Henry make his famous speech. Write a letter to the editor explaining the impact it had on you. Did he convince you that the time for revolution had arrived? Why or why not? Would you have supported going to war against the British, or would you have continued to try to find a peaceful solution?

title: Parson’s Cause
text:
England made lots of decisions in the colonies. In Virginia there was an official church. It was the Anglican church. That is part of the Church Of England. The ministers of the church were paid with tobacco, and later, currency. England approved how much ministers should be paid.

After a poor tobacco crop forced changes, there was a dispute over wages. The king got involved and vetoed a law Virginia had made. One minister sued Hanover County in Virginia for more money. The judge in the case was named John Henry. The lawyer defending Hanover County was the judge’s son. You might recognize his name: Patrick Henry.

Patrick was young. He was not well known but he was very smart. He was a great speaker. In court he gave a strong speech. He said if a king vetoed a good local law, he wasn’t “the father to his people.” Patrick said that kind of king was a tyrant.

Some people in the courtroom shouted, “Treason!” when Henry said that. Treason is when someone works against their own country. Henry was an English citizen. He was speaking against the English king.

Patrick Henry won the case. The minister who brought the case to court was awarded one penny in damages, and the king’s veto was made null. It was the start of Americans questioning English law in court. The Parson’s Cause case was the first case where colonists acted so directly against the king.

People found out Patrick Henry was a great speaker. For him this was just the beginning of a fight for liberty. After the court case Henry led in many fights against British rule. He always worked for the colonies’ rights. The colonies were starting to get ready for a revolution.

title: Primary Sources: The Boston Massacre
text:
Are historic pictures always perfectly accurate? Some historians claim the Boston Massacre was really the first gunfire of the American Revolution. But was it truly a massacre, or just a terrible mistake? We know five people were killed. When the Redcoats opened fire, did they simply kill innocent people, or were they defending themselves against an aggressive mob?

Well, Paul Revere would say the British soldiers were murderers. His famous engraving shows soldiers in a line, firing at a group of people. It shows wounded men bleeding on the ground while a British commander gives a signal to keep shooting. However, some eyewitness accounts say the colonists started the whole thing, throwing insults first and hard objects later. The soldiers were forced to protect themselves.

At the time, Loyalists said Revere’s engraving was exaggerated and the Patriots were to blame. Some people today believe the engraving was propaganda. Propaganda is the spreading of information (often false) to convince others of an idea.

Directions: Compare the two images of the massacre. Which one do you think tells the true story? Do you think Paul spread propaganda or patriotism? Was this a massacre or a mistake? You be the judge. On a separate sheet of paper, write a paragraph about your thoughts.

title: The Boston Massacre
text:
Boston had a busy harbor with many ships. Tariffs and taxes had to be paid there. Britain filled Boston with troops to help collect taxes and keep the peace. People in Boston rebelled. They called the soldiers names. They fought with the Redcoats and spat at them.

On March 5th, 1770, a group of angry people started yelling at a British guard. Someone ran to tell the British captain what was happening. The captain came with seven of his men.

The crowd started throwing snowballs and rocks and sticks. One of the Redcoats fired his gun. The other soldiers thought they had been ordered to fire. They shot into the crowd. They ended up killing five people and wounding six others. Crispus Attucks was the first killed. He was a sailor of African and American Indian descent. He is often remembered as the first death in the American Revolution.

Newspapers on both sides started telling the story before it could even come to court. Samuel Adams got Benjamin Edes to write an article for the Boston Gazette. They called it a “horrid massacre.” British officers and Loyalists wrote their side. They said it was a sad event but not the Redcoats’ fault.

The soldiers stood trial for murder. A team of lawyers defended them. One of the lawyers was John Adams. John was a Patriot but he didn’t like violence. He believed in the rule of law on both sides.

Some Patriots worried that Britain would punish them if the Redcoats didn’t get a fair trial. John Adams did a good job in the trial. All but two of the Redcoats were found innocent. Those two were not convicted of murder.

The British troops were removed from Boston because of the massacre. But that didn’t stop the trouble that was brewing. The pressure was building.

title: The Sons of Liberty
text:
"Hello all," said Natalia. The camera was on. People all over the school could see Steven and Natalia.

"It's time for an exciting chapter on the road to the American Revolution!" added Natalia.

"But first, a quick review," said Steven.

"On last week's show," said Natalia, we talked about the Stamp Act."

"The Sugar Act, too!" said Steven.

"Yeah," said Natalia. "And we talked about Benjamin Franklin. He went to England to tell the British why they were mad. He warned that America would stop buying things from England."

"But no one listened," said Steven. "He finally sailed for home."

"That's the review," said Natalia.

"And now, for the new stuff," said Steven.

"The colonists were mad," said Natalia. "Groups of men met to talk about how they felt. They were mad that they had no voice in making laws. A secret group began. They were called The Sons of Liberty. Their motto was, 'No Taxation Without Representation.'"

"The Sons of Liberty started in Boston and New York," said Steven. He was excited. He loved this stuff. "Many famous men were part of the group. Samuel Adams was a leader in Boston who joined. He was very good at getting folks angry. John Hancock and Paul Revere joined when the Stamp Act hurt their businesses. Benjamin Edes was the editor of the Boston Gazette. He used his paper to fight the British."

"Groups spread all through the colonies," said Natalia. "Thomas Jefferson and Patrick Henry joined in Virginia."

"Ben Franklin joined in Pennsylvania," said Steven.

"They fought the taxes in many ways," said Natalia.

"Tell 'em what kinds of ways!" said Steven.

Natalia went on. "They got people to boycott, or stop buying, British goods," she said. "That cost the British a lot of money. The Sons of Liberty wrote to Parliament. They wrote to the King, too. They sent letters all through the colonies. They wrote news articles. They made posters."

"They did other things too," said Steven. "Some of the Sons used violence. They threatened the Stamp Agents and most of them quit their jobs!"

"But things got worse," said Natalia. "Some people were beaten up. Someone hung an effigy of Andrew Oliver in a tree."

"An effigy is a dummy made to look like a person," said Steven.

"Oliver was a Stamp Agent," Natalia went on. "A mob burned Oliver's property. They burned the effigy to show how mad they were. Some of them broke into Oliver's home and stole his things."

"And it worked," said Steven. "Britain repealed the Stamp Act. It was a win for the Sons of Liberty!"

"Not so fast, though," said Natalia. "Britain was just warming up. They passed the Townshend Acts, remember?"

"The battle had just begun," said Steven."

"Today's issue of U.S. History Studies Weekly will tell you all about the Sons of Liberty!" said Natalia. "Thanks for tuning in!"

title: Think & Review Questions
text:
1. Why did the colonists object to the taxes placed on them by the British government?

2. How did the Patriots get their ideas out to the colonies?

3. Why were there so many Redcoats in Boston?

4. Patrick Henry and John Edes resisted unfair tax laws the same way. How did they do it?

title: A Tea Party to Remember
text:
Steven and Natalia met in the library.

“I have questions," said Natalia. "In the Boston Tea Party, who dumped the tea? Whose idea was it? What happened after they were done with their tea-dumping?”

Steven brought over a book. “This says everyone knew about the Boston Tea Party. But almost no one knew who dumped the tea. The men wore disguises. Not many people admitted they were part of it even after the war. We only know a few names.”

Natalia was reading too. “Hey! Look at this!” She held up a small painting of a woman. “This painting was stuck between the pages of this book. Sarah Bradlee Fulton,” she read. “Mother of the Boston Tea Party.”

“Wait! What?” Steven leaned over.

“People think she had the idea of dressing the men as Mohawk Indians. They met at her house. She helped them with their costumes and painted their faces.”

“What? They disguised themselves as American Indians? That doesn't seem right. Let me see that,” Steven said. As he touched the little painting, they felt a rush of wind. They were headed into the past.

Steven and Natalia stood outside a small house. It was very dark. Soft light came from house windows around them. They could smell the sea.

They stepped up to a window and listened. People were speaking quietly inside.

“The ships will never unload that tea!”

“But the governor refuses to let the ships return to England! He says we must allow them to unload.”

“Let them! The tea can rot on the docks as it has in other colonies.”

“My friends,” said a deep voice. Steven and Natalia jumped.

“That’s Paul Revere!” they said together.

Revere said, “We must take another course. We must end this tyranny.”

Now the voices were too low to hear. Steven and Natalia leaned closer.

“Done!” a voice said suddenly. “Mistress Fulton advises us to dress as Mohawks and paint our faces. No one must know who we are.”

“I shall heat water for your return,” Sarah’s voice said. “You must wash off the paint.”

“Clean the tea from your shoes before you leave the ships,” another woman said. “You must not be caught.”

The door opened. Steven and Natalia hid in the shadows. A crowd of men silently moved toward the harbor. People peeked at them from around houses and through windows and doors. No one spoke.

The two children could barely see the three tea ships. “The Dartmouth, the Eleanor and the Beaver,” Natalia whispered. The men boarded the ships. They told the crew they would only harm the tea. They would not hurt the American-owned ships or the men.

The men began their work. They pushed and pulled huge chests of tea onto the deck. They broke the chests open with axes and hatchets. The men heaved the tea over the side. “342 chests of tea,” Steven breathed.

They heard footsteps.

“It’s Sarah Fulton!” Natalia said. “Quick!” She held out the little painting. Both children touched it. They felt wind rush over them. They found themselves back at their library table.

“Oh man!” Steven said. “I can’t believe that! What happened next?”

Natalia shook her head. “The British were livid. They closed Boston harbor. They planned to keep it closed until colonists paid the damages. They closed down Massachusetts’ government. They put more soldiers in Boston. They changed the Quartering Act. People had to keep soldiers in their houses. People thought it was intolerable. That means they couldn’t stand it. They called it the Intolerable Acts. War was one step closer.”

title: The Daughters of Liberty
text:
The Boston Tea Party is one of the most famous acts of rebellion in our country’s history. Men threw the tea overboard. But women helped with the protest!

Women at the time did not have much political power. They could not vote or run for office. But they were passionate about independence. Many women used the power they held at home to support the cause. Some women formed a group. These women were called the Daughters of Liberty.

The Daughters refused to buy British products. That kind of protest is called a “boycott.” It must have been hard on business to boycott British goods. Some women owned shops. They would make more money if they sold British products. Still, the Daughters of Liberty refused.

All over the colonies, women boycotted English tea. Instead, they drank smuggled Dutch tea. They also brewed raspberry leaves, mint and basil. They had a name for any tea that wasn't British tea. They called it "liberty tea."

Women also signed agreements pledging they would not drink any British tea offered to them. Susan Boudinot was one very young Daughter of Liberty. Her father would one day be president of the Continental Congress. Susan was only nine years old when she pledged not to drink British tea.

One day Susan was at New Jersey’s governor home. He and his family were Loyalists. When Susan was served a cup of British Tea she said thank you, but she wouldn't drink it. She took it politely, walked to the window and threw the tea out!

Women made their own cloth so they wouldn't have to buy British clothing. They got together and spun wool into yarn and thread. Those parties were called “spinning bees.” The cloth they made was called “homespun.” It was rougher than the cloth from England but it became very fashionable!

Protests even got in the way of romance. During the Stamp Act, some girls put an ad in a New York City paper. They said they would not marry their fiancées because they would not marry any man who got a stamped marriage license.

Women did not have the power of public office. But they were clever and strong. They led the way in the fight against tyranny!

title: The First Continental Congress
text:
The Intolerable Acts changed things in America. These hardships caused the people in the colonies to become strong friends. They knew what happened in Boston could happen anywhere. They were united. Leaders in all the colonies kept in touch with each other by writing letters. Finally, leaders decided that they should all meet in person to be more united. It was far away for some, and not everyone could come to the meeting. But twelve of the colonies sent people to represent them. The meeting was called the First Continental Congress. Only Georgia was absent from that first meeting.

Leaders at the Congress tried to figure out what to do. Some hoped to leave England and start their own country. Some hoped to remain British citizens if England would start to treat them fairly again. Each colony got one vote. In the end, they voted to stay with Britain and try to work things out.

The Congress wrote letters to the King. They wrote to Parliament, too. They tried to explain that they had rights. They asked to be repaid for harms done under the tax acts and they asked that the Intolerable Acts be repealed.

Then they wondered how to force Britain to go along with them. People said they should try a complete ban on all British goods. They wouldn't even sell their products to Britain.

Colonies in the South didn’t like that idea. England bought a lot of their rice and other goods. A complete ban would cost them too much. So the Congress compromised. They chose not to start the ban until the next year. That would give the colonies time to get ready.

The Congress agreed to meet again in a year. They also told all the colonies to get their militias ready. They hoped for peace. But they needed to be ready for war.

When the king and Parliament received their letters they answered with force. They seized ammunition in Massachusetts and they made Boston a military base. War was on its way.

title: Let's Write
text: Try to imagine something like the Tea Act in today's world. For instance, every time you logged onto the internet, you had to pay $1. However, if you owned a special laptop from the government, you only had to pay 10 cents. Do you think that would be fair? Why or why not? How do you think people might react?

title: Think & Review Questions
text:
1. The British are often portrayed as the villain in the story of the Tea Act and the Boston Tea Party. Do you think that they were trying to make things unfair for the colonists? Or, do you think they had good intentions? Support your ideas with evidence from the Student Edition.

2. Think about the concept of "taxation without representation." Why would it be unfair to pay taxes in a government where you weren't allowed to vote? Support your ideas with evidence from the Student Edition.

3. Why do you think that the colonists chose to dress up as American Indians in order to board the ships bringing the tea?

4. Even though women were involved in planning the Boston Tea Party, they didn't actually participate. Why do you think that is?

5. What were ways that colonists worked to promote change in British policies? Explain at least two using evidence from the text.

title: Strong Women Revolt!
text:
“With ladies on our side, we can make every Tory tremble.” People say Samuel Adams said that. It was true that the women of the time were tough. Abigail Adams wrote about women in a letter to her husband John Adams.

In her letter, Abigail told her husband about a wealthy, stingy merchant that had lots of coffee in his store. Coffee was scarce because of the boycotts, so this man charged very high prices.

She wrote that a hundred or more women got together. They brought wheelbarrows and wagons. They marched down to the warehouse and demanded the keys. The merchant wouldn’t give them up. Mrs. Adams wrote in her letter that a woman grabbed the merchant by his neck and tossed him into a wagon!

The man gave up his keys to her, and she tipped him out onto the ground! The women then opened the warehouse, loaded up the coffee, and took it away.

Abigail said a large crowd of men stood amazed, watching the whole thing. Way to go, women!

title: Timeline: Tension in the Colonies
text:
This week you read about many events that created tension in the Colonies and eventually led to the Revolutionary War. Complete the timeline by following these steps:

1. Put the 10 events below in order by finding the date each one happened and writing the years on the lines.

2. Draw a long horizontal line on a blank piece of paper turned sideways (landscape).

3. For each event draw two diagonal lines. (See the example.)

4. Write the year with its event(s) on one line.

5. Write a short description of the event on the other line. If you have room on your timeline, you can draw extra diagonal lines to write more.

title: The Sons of Liberty Defy British Tyranny
text:
"If the colonists threw five chests of tea per minute into the harbor, how much tea would be in the harbor after an hour?" Ms. Johnson looked around the classroom. Students were writing and counting on their fingers.

Suddenly a girl raised her hand.

"Ms. Johnson? Didn’t that tea belong to someone? Weren’t they stealing it?" The girl frowned.

“Good question!” Ms. Johnson said. “Yes! The tea belonged to the British East India Company. It cost the company about a million dollars in today’s money. Does anyone know how much tea was dumped in the harbor?”

Steven raised his hand. “About 92,000 pounds of tea. That’s 18.5 million teabags!”

A student asked, “Did everyone in America think that was okay?”

“No.” Ms. Johnson said. “Loyalists thought it was a crime. Some Patriots were against it. George Washington thought private property should be left alone. Lots of people agreed. Many saw the Boston Tea Party as vandalism.”

A boy raised his hand. “Vandalism?” he asked.

“Vandalism is when you harm someone else’s property,” Ms. Johnson said. “Still, in other cities, colonists boarded British ships and dumped the tea, just like in Boston. It happened in New York, Maryland and in South Carolina, and it happened again in Boston. Tea parties began to catch on.”

Natalia raised her hand. “Tea parties?” she asked.

Ms. Johnson laughed. “That’s a nickname for the dumping of the tea into the harbor. It wasn’t called a party until later. ”

“Why were they so angry?” a girl asked.

“You remember that the Townshend Acts included a tax on tea.“ Ms. Johnson said. The class nodded. “Many of those taxes were removed, but the British left the tax on tea to show they had the right to tax the colonies. The colonists stopped drinking British tea. They smuggled in Dutch tea.

“The East India Company couldn’t sell its tea. It owed a huge debt to the British government. So in May of 1773 Parliament passed the Tea Act. It lowered the tariff on British tea. It made British tea very cheap even with the tax. It was cheaper than the smuggled tea.

“The colonists were furious! They had never been so angry at England.”

Ms. Johnson smiled. "I’m thrilled you’re all so interested in the Boston Tea Party! I have a video about it we can watch after lunch! Now. If the colonists threw ten chests of tea per minute into the harbor, how much tea would be in the harbor after an hour?" The class groaned and Ms. Johnson grinned.

Do you want to watch the video on the Boston Tea Party that Steven and Natalia saw in Ms. Johnson's class? You can! Just visit Studies Weekly online.

title: Britain Strikes Back and the Colonies Unite
text:
Colonists had fought taxes for ten years. But the Boston Tea Party was a big deal. It made King George mad.

Parliament passed the Coercive Acts. The Acts closed Boston Harbor until the cost of the tea was repaid. They put a British General named Gage in charge of Boston.

The Quartering Act had changed. It required that British soldiers could stay in people’s homes and eat their food. The laws England made after to the Boston Tea Party were called the "Intolerable Acts."

Since most of the trouble in America started in Boston, the English thought the rest of the colonies would blame Boston for these horrible new laws. They hoped the colonies would turn against Boston. But that didn't happen. The laws were so unfair that the colonies united. They stood by their friends in Boston.

All the colonial leaders wrote to each other in their committees to share the news. They decided to meet in person. That meeting would be the first Continental Congress.

title: Unfair!
text:
Colonists fought unfair British rule in many ways. They started boycotts. Boycotts are when people refuse to buy something on principle. They wrote letters. They did violent things. They threatened Loyalists. They put signs on doors of Loyalists’ businesses. The signs told people not to shop there. They even tarred and feathered people.

Tarring and feathering is a very old punishment. It used things that many people had on hand. Lots of people had tar. Tar was used to stop leaks in ships. Lots ot people had feathers, too. People had feathers in their pillows and mattresses.

Colonists heated the tar until it was a liquid. They poured or brushed it onto a person. The tar stuck. They dumped feathers onto the tar. That way everyone would see what happened. If that sounds awful, that's because it was. No one died of it, as far as we know, but it was super-painful and embarrassing.

Colonists also used their pens as weapons. They did this by writing. They wrote all kinds of articles about the British. Newspapers helped spread the word. They hoped to unite the colonies.

Many colonists wrote letters of protest. They wrote to other colonists. They wrote to their state governments. They wrote to Parliament. They wrote to the king.

The colonists were very angry about unfair laws. They did everything in their power to change things. They were not going to allow it any longer.

title: Touring the Capitol
text:
Natalia and Steven were on a school field trip. The class was visiting the United States Capitol. Their guide took them into Statuary Hall. The students were amazed at how beautiful it was. The room was full of statues of people important to the history of the United States. The guide told them each of the 50 states chose two statues to be displayed there.

"Which two did Tennessee send?" Steven asked.

"Tennessee sent Andrew Jackson. He was our seventh president,” the guide answered. “And they sent John Sevier. Sevier was the first governor of Tennessee. He and Jackson were lifelong rivals. They almost fought a duel! Sevier was governor of North Carolina for a time. He was also the only governor of the State of Franklin. That was territory split from North Carolina in 1785. It ended up part of Tennessee. Sevier later served as a Senator."

The class walked through the Rotunda of the Capitol. They were right under the great dome of the building. “I can’t believe this place!” Steven said. They all looked up at the inside of the dome.

The class stopped in front of the famous painting, "Declaration of Independence." The kids began to talk excitedly.

“Look! Is that Ben Franklin?”

“Are they signing the Declaration?”

Their tour guide smiled. "This painting is by John Trumbull. The men in the painting are presenting the first draft of the Declaration of Independence to the Second Continental Congress. The painting shows the signers and even the room where it was signed.”

Someone asked if the class would get to see that room. “The Declaration wasn’t signed here,” the guide told the class. “It was signed in Independence Hall in Pennsylvania.”

“Why is the painting here?” a boy asked.

“This building is where our country’s government meets,” the guide said. “You might say the Second Continental Congress is where that began. That was where we became a country.”

“Did they declare war?” a girl asked.

“No,” the guide answered. “Fighting had already begun. They did put George Washington in command of their army. They started a postal service. They created a navy. These men were the government through the war. They cut ties with Britain.”

"This painting looks so real," Natalia whispered. She was looking at all the faces.

"I know," Steven whispered back. "It’s like we could step right into the picture."

"Are you thinking what I'm thinking?" Natalia asked.

Steven nodded. "Let's do it!"

Steven and Natalia reached out to the painting. The tour guide called, "No! Young people! You can't touch the picture!"

But it was too late. Natalia and Steven are already headed to the late 1700s.

title: All Men are Created Equal ... but Many are Still Missing Some Rights!
text:
Jefferson wrote, “... all men are created equal.” Today, that phrase means all people. But when those words were written, certain groups weren’t given full rights. Women, African Americans, and American Indians are examples of groups that had fewer rights than white men.

The words say all people have the right to liberty. But in those days, African Americans were seen as property. Enslaved people couldn’t vote. Brave men and women fought for a long time to end slavery.

In 1870 all men were given the right to vote under certain conditions. But women couldn’t vote until 1920. Americans Indians could not vote until 1924. Many African Americans couldn’t vote until 1965. And even after that, African Americans were kept from voting in some places.

People in these groups did great things, even though they did not have full rights. They are a part of the story of our nation. Here are some examples:

Phillis Wheatley was the first African American to publish a book. She was also the first enslaved person to publish a book. In fact, she was the first person of any kind in the country to publish a book of poems.

Sacajawea was a Shoshone woman. She was the guide for Lewis and Clark, the explorers. She could speak to Indian tribes they met. Their journey was very hard, and they might not have made it without her help. She made part of the trip while she was pregnant, and part of the trip with her infant child.

Lucretia Mott helped start the Women's Rights Convention. Her home was one of the stations on the Underground Railroad. She put her life at risk every day to fight slavery.

Elizabeth Cady Stanton helped start the Seneca Falls Convention. That was start of the women's voting rights movement. She never stopped in her fight for the vote. Like so many other brave people, she also worked to end slavery. She didn't live to see women get the vote. She died in 1902.

You can watch a video about rights for all on Studies Weekly online. Just click on the "Declaring Freedom For All" video.

title: Our Lives, Our Fortunes and Our Sacred Honor
text:
Everyone who signed the Declaration of Independence volunteered to sign it. No one forced them to do it. They took a big personal risk by doing that. From the king's view all the people who signed the Declaration were traitors. By British law, traitors can be hung.

Even though signing the Declaration was an enormous risk, all but eight of the 50 delegates signed it.

They signed so they could “mutually pledge” to each other. They said they were bound to support the Declaration with “our Lives, our Fortunes and our sacred Honor.”

John Hancock signed first. He didn't try to hide his signature. He used big fearless letters. He is thought to have said King George would be able to read it without his glasses.

They were brave. They were also careful. The names of the signers weren’t published until after George Washington won some big battles -- when it looked like the war was going well!

Want to learn more about the signers and the dangers they faced? Visit Studies Weekly online and watch the "Signers of the Declaration of Independence Intro."

title: A Visit to the Second Continental Congress
text:
"Quiet in the room," John Hancock ordered. He rapped his gavel just as Steven and Natalia appeared in the room.

One man stood. "Are we truly ready to declare independence from Great Britain?" he asked. "Who will protect us then?"

"Wow!" Steven exclaimed. "That’s John Hancock! He’s the president of Congress. We must be at the Second Continental Congress. It's like being in the 'Declaration of Independence Intro' video!”

“We're in Independence Hall in Philadelphia!" Natalia whispered. "Let's hide and listen."

They dove under a desk.

The men spoke in loud voices. They had strong feelings. Some were faithful to the Crown. They hoped to work things out with England. But the Patriots wanted independence. The Second Continental Congress tried to figure out what to do. But they couldn't seem to agree.

"We've tried many times to talk with Parliament," one Patriot said. "The last Congress asked them to hear our concerns. We asked them to repay our losses. And what have they done?”

“Filled Boston with soldiers!” a man shouted. “Stolen our powder and shot!”

“That would be gunpowder and bullets?” Steven guessed.

"Yeah. I think so," said Natalia.

Another man stood up. He pounded his fist on the table. “Declaring our independence is the next step. It is the only way."

Steven gulped. “Wow. That’s John Adams!”

"What of loyalty to our King?” John Dickinson asked. "What of our duties as British citizens?"

"What of your Olive Branch?" a man scoffed. “What of the war the king makes on us?”

“We cannot fight Britain! We will not survive,” the delegate from South Carolina said.

“Where’s Thomas Jefferson?” Natalia whispered.

“Over there with the Virginians,” Steven said. “He doesn’t like debate. He’s writing down what they say.”

"Have you not read Thomas Paine's 'Common Sense'?" Ben Franklin was speaking. “Paine wrote that things seem right to us because we have the habit of thinking they are right. To see if we are right, we need to unite and let the people have their voice."

“Yes!” Dickinson said. “Let them speak. Ask the colonies if they want independence. Let us be ruled by them.”

“Virginia has so declared!” Richard Henry Lee stood to speak. “The resolution has lain on the table this past week!”

"Quiet in the room, please," John Hancock said as he hammered his gavel loudly. The men were too busy talking to pay attention.

They did not come to a final agreement that day. But they did agree on two things. They agreed to ask each colony if it wanted independence from Britain.

They also created a committee to draft a Declaration of Independence in case they needed it. They selected young Thomas Jefferson to write it. He was a good writer.

They ended the meeting. Steven and Natalia were alone in the room.

They climbed from under the desk. Steven could not believe he had been in the same room with so many great leaders.

"We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal," Steven quoted a line of the Declaration. "Jefferson did write it well!" he said. "56 of 60 delegates voted in favor of independence. It was made official on July 4, 1776."

"That's right," Natalia said. "They finally got their unity."

Go to this article online to watch the “Declaration of Independence Intro” video.

title: Thomas Jefferson ... and I Quote
text:
Thomas Jefferson was the third President of the United States. He served two terms.

When Thomas was 33, Virginia sent him to the Second Continental Congress. There, they chose him to write the Declaration of Independence. He finished it in two weeks.

Jefferson was a lawyer. He had defended enslaved persons in their fight for freedom. He was a little on the quiet side. He didn't enjoy being in loud debates. Instead, he took good notes during Congress. That’s how we know what took place there.

Jefferson also served as governor of Virginia. We remember him every time we've got a handful of change. His face is on one side of our nickel. He planned and built his home and named it Monticello. You can see his home on the other side of the nickel.

He was interested in lots of different things like math, gardens and design. He loved books and bought thousands of them. When the Library of Congress burned in 1814, Jefferson sold his books to Congress.

He also wrote thousands of letters in his life. Those letters are full of wisdom. Here are some quotes from those letters:

He wrote, "Honesty is the first chapter in the book of wisdom," to Nathaniel Macon.

"I like the dreams of the future better than the history of the past," is from a letter to John Adams.

"The tree of liberty must be refreshed from time to time with the blood of patriots and tyrants." That’s from a letter to William S. Smith.

This is from a letter to his wife, Martha. "Determine never to be idle. No person will have occasion to complain of the want of time, who never loses any. It is wonderful how much may be done, if we are always doing."

In a love letter, he wrote, “Every moment was filled with something agreeable... what a mass of happiness had we travelled over!”

You can watch the video, "Thomas Jefferson Intro" online. You’ll learn even more about this Founding Father.

title: Drawn-ology: Artistic Chronolgy
text: Create your own road to revolution! You’ve heard of chronological order, right? Well, this is drawn-ological order! Using the articles this week, find the most important events in the passage. Recreate them on the “road” provided, in the correct order. In the boxes, you can either draw scenes or cut out small magazine pictures to glue in the boxes. (You probably won’t be able to find exact pictures of colonial events in today’s magazines, so look for main ideas. For example, instead of a picture of Minutemen hiding gunpowder, look for a picture of someone hiding something. Then, label it with correct colonial information.) On the “road” write brief captions for your scenes. Decorate the background when you finish!

title: An Olive Branch
text:
The First Continental Congress had set a date for a second congress to meet. On May 10, 1775, the group met again. All the colonies but Georgia sent representatives. They had to decide what to do next. Britain had not repealed the Intolerable Acts. Fighting had begun.

Some of the leaders still hoped to remain British subjects. They were loyal to the King. They blamed Parliament for their troubles. They hoped laws could be changed. They hoped to avoid war.

Other delegates wanted to form their own government. They wanted to break ties with Britain. They did not like the idea of a war. They were not sure the colonies were ready, but they feared they had no choice.

Congress compromised. Both sides gave a little. They decided to send one last appeal to the king. It was called The Olive Branch Petition. An olive branch is a symbol for peace.

The Olive Branch Petition said that if King George would help fix the laws that hurt the colonies, the colonies would remain loyal to England. John Dickinson from New York wrote it. He was a famous writer.

William Penn and Arthur Lee took copies of the Olive Branch Petition to England. They tried to give a copy to the King. King George wouldn’t read it. The week before, he had declared the colonies were at war with England. The King urged Parliament “to put a speedy end to these disorders.”

The Congress had tried to make peace. The king had set the stage for war.

title: Think & Review Questions
text:
1. What was the main reason the colonists wanted to break away from Britain?

2. Compare the treatment of women and minorities to the rights promised in the Declaration. Focus mainly on "life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness."

3. Why was Thomas Jefferson chosen to write the Declaration of Independence?

4. Why was it dangerous for people to sign the Declaration of Independence?

5. What was John Hancock's role and significance in the signing of the Declaration of Independence?

6. Even after the Declaration was written, three main groups of people were still treated unfairly. Consider the video "Declaring Freedom for All." Why do you think the Founding Fathers did not give rights and freedoms to women, slaves, and American Indians?

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine your family was alive during the Second Continental Congress. Write a short letter to Thomas Jefferson. Tell him two things you want him to include in the Declaration. Think about your family and the freedoms or limits that you would have. Would your family have the right to vote? Would your mother be able to work any job she wanted? Would your friends have the same rights as you?

title: Would France Help?
text:
The Second Continental Congress met in 1775. No one knew yet if it would decide to separate from Great Britain. For that to happen, someone needed to state clearly why we needed to be independent.

If leaving England caused a war, the Patriots knew they might need to get help from other nations. Benjamin Franklin and others hoped France would be their ally. They hoped the French would help them in a fight. But they knew the French would not help British colonies. To ask for help from France, we had to be independent. It was time to write! It was time to create a document that would show the world that we weren't part of England anymore. The document was the Declaration of Independence. Ever heard of it?

The Declaration meant friendly foreign governments would see the colonies as a new country. It meant other countries might give help in the war to come.

title: Outwitting Them All: Agent 355, Revolutionary Female Spy - Cipher Code Activity
text:
George Washington had a reputation for honesty, but as a general in the Revolutionary War, he used spies, hidden messages and trickery to fight the British. As you know, as part of this strategy, Washington formed the Culper Ring. Spies in this group worked hard to protect their identities, and they only used numbers when communicating with each other and with Washington. Washington’s own code name was 711! One of the best spies in this group was the woman who went by the code name Agent 355.

Very little is known about Agent 355, although historians agree she was most likely from a wealthy British family. She lived in the New York area, and she was the one who would leave coded messages in the pockets of laundry hanging on a clothesline. One day, however, the messages simply stopped. Historians believe she was caught and executed by the British. Today, there are still people guessing the identity of Agent 355. Some believe she was Anna Strong, a known spy and Patriot of the time. Others have guessed she was Betty Floyd, a cousin of one of the leaders of the Culper Ring. Although we will probably never know for sure who Agent 355 was, her actions and bravery helped the colonies win the Revolutionary War.

Directions: Create a coded message about something you read in Studies Weekly. Trade with a friend and see if you can break each others’ codes! (HINT: Make a code by having one letter stand for a different letter, or a number stand for a letter, or use common symbols. Keep your secret code on separate paper.) Write your message:

title: Let's Write
text: The heroes of the American Revolution were real people with real courage and talents, just like you. Based on your own talents and personality, which person or group of people that we studied this week did you identify with the most? How are you similar? If you had lived back then, would you have acted the way they did? Why or why not?

title: Some Stayed Loyal to Britain
text:
Loyalists felt they were British citizens. They thought colonists should pay the taxes and obey the laws of Britain. About one fifth of the colonists were loyal to the king.

Some of these people kept quiet about their feelings. They never spoke out for Britain. Some of them stayed in the colonies after the war, and kept their land and their businesses.

Some Loyalists went to England when the fighting began. Many went to Canada. But some stayed in America, and fought for the king with the Redcoats.

Joseph Brant was an Iroquois warrior. He was a captain in the British army. He led four of the six Iroquois nations against the colonies. He went to Canada after the war. The British gave him land there. He was a good ruler.

John Murray was a Scottish lord. He was governor of Virginia. He said he would free every enslaved person who ran away and became a British soldier. Hundreds of slaves made it to him. They were good troops. But Murray’s troops got smallpox. They were dying or too sick to fight. Murray went back to England. He worked all his life to help Loyalists.

Colonel Tye was an enslaved person who escaped and came to John Murray. He was a good fighter. He was given command of a small group of very good fighters. They were called the Black Brigade. They performed many daring secret raids. Tye almost never lost a man. He died of battle wounds.

title: Steven and Natalia Discover Heroes
text:
Natalia and Steven were in the school library. Ms. Johnson assigned the class to write reports about Revolutionary War heroes. But this report had a twist. These heroes had to be people the students had never heard of before their research.

Natalia was getting grumpy. “I don’t get this. How do we look up someone we have never heard of?” she asked Steven.

Steven didn’t answer.

Natalia looked around the corner. Steven was kneeling on the floor. An open book lay beside him. He seemed to be trying to read a piece of paper.

“Hey!” Natalia said. “I’ve been talking to you! What are you doing?”

Steven looked up. “I found this paper folded up in that book. The book is about spies during the Revolution.” Steven sounded excited. “Natalia, I think this is a cipher code!”

Natalia picked up the book. “Washington the Spymaster and the Cupler Ring,” she read. “Wait! General Washington had spies?”

“Lots!” Steven said. He spread out the folded paper. It had long rows of numbers. Across from the numbers were words. "Look how cool this writing is!"

“See?” Steven said. “Each number stands for a word. The spies could write a message with numbers. It’s called a cipher. No one could read it unless they had the key to the code!”

“No way!” Natalia said. “Can I see it?” As her fingers brushed the paper both children felt wind rush over them. They were headed back in time.

Natalia and Steven found themselves in a crowded colonial coffee house. People were coming and going. “Yikes!” Steven said. “Redcoats!”

British officers sat at a table. They talked and laughed. A man wearing an apron stood by them. He laughed along with the Redcoats.

“That’s Robert Townsend!” Steven whispered excitedly. “I was reading about him when I found the code. He’s part of the Culper spy ring. His code name is "Culper Jr.”

Townsend stepped to the back of the room. He wrote on some paper with a quill pen. He dipped the pen in a bottle hidden behind a stack of books. Steven and Natalia tried to see what he was writing. There was nothing on the paper!

Townsend walked to a table. A lady was sitting alone, wearing a heavy cloak. Her hood was pulled over her face. Townsend filled her coffee mug. “355?” he asked softly.

“Culper Jr.?” she answered.

Townsend walked back to the officers’ table. “He left the paper under that woman’s mug!” Natalia said.

The children watched the lady roll the paper up tightly. She took out a quill pen. Carefully she slipped the paper inside the pen! Then she stood up and walked quietly out the door.

Her cloak brushed the cipher code Steven held. Both children grabbed at it. All at once they were blown back to the present.

Steven and Natalia dived for the spy book. They started reading it out loud to each other.

“George Washington had lots of spy rings.”

“The spies wrote with invisible ink. That must have been what Townsend was using!”

“Female spies sent coded messages when they hung up their laundry.”

“Some African American enslaved people were double agents. They pretended to be Loyalists so they could spy on the British!”

“Steven!” Natalia was so excited she could hardly talk. “355 was a secret agent! Even today no one is sure who she was! The spies said she 'shall be able to outwit them all!'"

Steven laughed. “I guess we know who your report will be about.”

“Yes!” Natalia said. “Agent 355 is perfect for this assignment. I had never heard of her, and no one knows for sure who she was!”

title: Training the Army
text:
General Washington didn’t like working with the militias. He said it was like walking with “a broken staff.” He kept trying to get Congress to give him regular troops. Militia men kept leaving the war to take care of things at home. And they used rifles. Rifles were good for hunting. They shot straight. But it took a long time to reload them. Redcoats used muskets. Muskets didn’t shoot quite so straight. But they were very fast to reload. Washington had to fight the best trained army in the world, and sometimes colonial militias were a poor fit for the job.

Finally, Congress decided they had to create the Continental Army.

Most of the new army soldiers were 15 to 19 years old. They didn’t get paid much or very often. There wasn’t much food. But being a soldier was better than no job at all.

Washington had to work quickly. His new army had to be trained. Some of the most important training came from Baron Friedrich von Steuben. He was a German who came to help the Americans.

Steuben taught the Continental Army how to be soldiers. First he trained 100 men. Then those men helped him train more soldiers. He put the soldiers in groups. The newest soldiers learned basic skills. They worked up to harder skills.

Steuben taught the men to load their muskets very quickly. The Americans had to learn to fire faster than the Redcoats. Steuben has been called the “first teacher” of the American army.

Steuben also made rules to keep the camps clean. He made the men dig holes for bathrooms. He made them move dead animals out of the camps. He made them keep their tents tidy.

Being clean helped the soldiers stay healthy. Learning to shoot and reload quickly helped them win battles. Washington and Steuben turned the young colonials into a trained army.

title: Militias in the Colonies
text:
Colonial law said men aged 16 to 60 had to have a working firearm. They had to be in a part-time army. The part-time armies were called 'militias.'

Militias only trained a couple of times a year. They voted on who the officers should be, and most of them were not paid. Unlike full-time soldiers, militiamen only signed up to protect their own towns. They left battles to take care of their families. They left the army to farm and do their jobs.

Part of each militia was made up of trained Minutemen. Those men drilled and trained more than most militia soldiers. They had to be ready with their weapons just a minute or so after being called. Unlike other militia soldiers, they were paid by the colonies.

Colonial militias hadn't done much since the French and Indian War. They hadn't trained much, or practiced fighting. The First Continental Congress feared that war was coming. They told the colonies to get their militias ready. A lot of people began to train very quickly.

Of course, getting ready for war meant more than training. Militias had to make sure that their men would be loyal to the new country. Any Tories had to leave the militias. Any officers who were loyal to England had to resign. Everyone in the militia had to swear to be loyal to the revolution.

When it came to who could fight and who could not, dealings between Patriots and Tories were sometimes tricky. Here's an example:

Major Robert Rogers was a hero in the French and Indian War. But during the revolution, George Washington feared Rogers was a Tory. He wouldn’t let Rogers serve in the army. That was alright with Rogers. He started his own fighting group called The Queen’s Rangers. They were very well trained. They fought for the British.

title: Think & Review Questions
text:
1. What is the difference between a militia and a full time army?

2. How did spies hide information?

3. The war was hard for the soldiers. How was it hard on the home front?

4. How did Baron Von Steuben help the Continental Army?

title: Loyalists, Tories, Minutemen and Patriots
text:
Here's one of Steven and Natalia's broadcasts that you can perform right in your own classroom. You can do this with any Studies Weekly lesson but this one makes it easy. It's written like a script. Ask your teacher to help you assign people to take turns reading the parts of Steven and Natalia. Have fun!

Steven: Red light's glowing on the camera! Rolling! Hello, students, teachers and friends! Today we’re looking at important groups of people in the American Revolution.

Natalia: The first people we'll talk about are called the "Loyalists." They were colonists who were true to the king and to Britain during the war.

Steven: They were also called Tories or King’s Men. Many of them worked for Britain. Some of them owned large farms or businesses. They stood to lose a lot of money in a war.

Natalia: The next group we'll talk about are the "Patriots." They wanted to break away from Britain. They wanted to form their own government.

Steven: Many Patriots thought war was the only way. Some even looked forward to it! But many wished and hoped for peaceful outcomes.

Natalia: We'll talk about the "Minutemen" next.

Steven: Right! Laws in the colonies required adult men to keep a working firearm.

Natalia: You know ... a gun.

Steven: Yes ... and to be ready to defend the area around their town. That was called the militia. Some of the men agreed they would always be ready to grab their guns and go. They might only have a few minutes' warning!

Natalia: That's why they were called Minutemen. We’ll see what a big part they play as the fighting began.

Steven: We’ll also look at a skilled soldier who came from another country. He helped George Washington train his army. Our country owes a great debt to him.

Natalia: We might not have won the war without him.

Steven: But I’m super excited about another group of people. We’ll be looking at spies! Some enslaved people spied for the Patriots. And, some people living in England and spied for the colonies. Rich people and poor people were spies. Lots of women were spies!

Natalia: We’ll also see how women at home helped during the war. And we’ll talk about regular people who didn’t fight at all.

Steven: All these people were part of the war effort on both sides. So hang on. It’s going to be a wild ride!

title: Life on the Homefront
text:
Most colonists did not fight in the revolution. They were farmers or blacksmiths or merchants. They tried to get along and do their best. But times were hard.

The boycotts put lots of people out of work. Some men joined the army just to get paid.

Sometimes a battle destroyed crops. Sometimes cannons knocked houses down. People sometimes had to run for their lives. These were just a few of the damages that came along with the war and affected everyone -- even the people who weren't fighting.

The people on the home front tried to support their loved ones who fought in the war. Here's an example:

Lucy Knox was Henry Knox’s wife. Henry was an important American officer. She wrote to him about troubles on the home front. Their children were sick, and it was hard to get medicine. Food prices were high. People who wouldn’t take a side in the war were arrested by one side or the other. Lucy wrote to Henry about how hard things were. But Lucy also told Henry she loved him. And she sent him a box of pickles!

title: Women and the War
text:
Women were often left behind when the fighting began. When that happened, they had to do all the work their husbands and sons used to do, in addition to their own work. They ran businesses and farms.

The women spun wool and wove cloth for soldiers' clothing and blankets. Women raised money to pay soldiers.

Soldiers ate food the women grew. Eggs, meat, fruit, vegetables and grain for bread came from farms. Many women and their small children grew the food.

Women worked in the military camps. They made bandages. They nursed wounded or sick soldiers. They cooked. They washed clothing.

The women of the revolution were very brave. Here's just one example:

Sarah Fulton is known as the Mother of the Boston Tea Party. Once, she saw the British taking a load of firewood. The wood had been intended for the American army. Sarah went right out, turned the wagons around, and took the wood back. She told the British soldiers to shoot her if they wanted to! They just watched her go. They were amazed!

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you are one of the midnight riders. Write a letter to a parent or friend about your ride. Describe what it's like to ride alone in the dark. Tell about British scouts searching for you. How did you feel when you heard the alarm bells ring? What were your feelings after the battles at Lexington and Concord? Were you proud? Close with an affectionate greeting.

title: Research and Chart: Where There’s a Will, There’s a Way
text: There were terrible battles during the Revolutionary War. In some, Americans suffered greatly by losing soldiers, land and control. Some call the American victory against the British in the Revolutionary War a miracle. Have you heard that where there’s a will, there’s a way? Here’s a chart of some important battles. Do some research to find out who won each battle and write the answers in the “Winner” column.

title: A Midnight Visit
text:
Steven set a heavy leather history book on the library table in front of Natalia. “Check it out!” he said. “Firsthand accounts from the start of the American Revolution! We can examine major battles in the words of people who were there!"

"Perfect! We need to put together our news show," Natalia began scanning the book. A piece of parchment fell out of its pages.

"Hey!" Steven pulled it toward him. "This is odd. No, it's awesome! It's a letter written by Paul Revere!"

"No way!" Natalia reached for the page. As she touched the it, the pair felt a rush of wind. They were going back in time!

“Where are we?" Steven asked, looking around. They were standing among trees at the edge of a river. “It’s the middle of the night!”

They could hear splashing in the water. They looked down the river saw a rowboat with three figures bent low.

"Quick!" Natalia pulled Steven behind a tree.

The people came ashore. Now the kids could hear them talking.

"We slipped past that British warship with them never the wiser!” a man said. “Thank you, my friends. I know the risk you have taken this night. I must get Joseph Warren’s message through."

"That must be Paul Revere!" Natalia whispered excitedly.

"Our risk is well worth it!” one of the men replied. “You must at all cost warn John Hancock and Samuel Adams. The British must not take them!”

"Dr. Warren tasked me also to wake the countryside around Lexington and on to Concord," Revere continued. “William Dawes has already ridden out. He goes another way.”

"Take care here in Charlestown! British officers are abroad. And you must avoid Loyalists. Many live hereabout," the other man added.

“I shall!” Revere replied. “I have ridden these roads carrying messages for the Sons of Liberty this past year. I do not intend to be taken tonight!”

“Look!” the first man said suddenly. ”Two lights in Boston’s North Church tower!”

“My signal!” Revere said. “A friend has set lanterns there to show the countryside the Redcoats are coming by sea! I must find a trusty steed to make the rest of my journey."

“Go to John Larkin,” the other man said. “He is a Patriot and keeps a very good horse.”

"This is amazing!" Natalia said. "Let's get back to the library. I gotta know more about this midnight ride!"

"Agreed!" Steven said.

Together, the two headed back to the present.

title: Think & Review Questions
text:
1. Why did General Burgoyne attack at Saratoga even though he was outnumbered?

2. How did the Patriots get out the word the British were coming to Concord?

3. Why was taking Bunker Hill important?

4. What were some of the ways women helped the men on the battlefield?

5. How did the Americans surprise the British at the Battle of Bunker Hill?

title: Help From France at the War's Turning Point
text:
The Battle of Saratoga is called the turning point of the war. The colonists won the battle, and it was a major event in the story of the American Revolution.

Losing the battle changed the way Britain saw the American army. The Redcoats were amazed at the rebels’ skill and their courage.

Success filled the Patriot soldiers with good cheer. It showed the country that they could really fight. More people joined the cause. The British lost the support of Loyalists in the colonies.

The battle made the French think the rebels might win the war. France joined with America and entered the war. The French sent soldiers, money, weapons and supplies.

The French attacked Britain in the West Indies and Europe. The British army had to fight the colonists and the French, too. Without French aid the colonists might not have won the war.

Other countries also noticed. Spain entered the war. Then the Dutch sent help. They were all happy to weaken their British rival.

title: A Report on Prince Estabrook
text:
"Steven, you're next!" Ms. Johnson called out.

Ms. Johnson’s class was giving reports on Revolutionary War heroes. The catch? Students had to pick someone they'd never heard of.

Steven walked to the front of the room. "As I examined the major events of the Revolution, I found a man named Prince Estabrook. His name was Prince but he wasn't royalty. He was an enslaved person. Estabrook was the first African American to enlist in the American army. He fought at both Lexington and Concord. Those were the first battles of the war.

“The British wanted to disarm the rebels. General Gage ordered his troops to seize the colonists’ weapons supply at Concord.

The Redcoats marched all night. But so did the Minutemen. They had been warned by Paul Revere and others. The British ran into 77 Minutemen at Lexington just as the sun came up. No one knows who fired the first shot. The Americans fought bravely.

“At Concord the Redcoats destroyed the supplies they could find. The Minutemen fought them back at a bridge. The rebels shot at the retreating British.

“Estabrook was wounded during the fight at Concord. Reports say he was shot in the left shoulder.

“He survived the wound and went back to fight. He fought in the entire war. Because of his loyalty and determination, Estabrook was set free.

“I've brought a video to share. It's called, 'African Americans during the Revolution.'"

You can watch Steven’s video, too! Just go to the online version of this article!

title: Midnight Riders!
text:
On April 18, 1775, Dr. Joseph Warren sent two brave men to rouse the militias. Their names were Paul Revere and William Dawes. British troops were marching to Concord. They had orders to take the colonists' weapon stores.

Many people have heard of Paul Revere and his midnight ride. William Dawes was also a Patriot. He stole cannons through the back window of a British gun house! Americans used those cannons throughout the entire war.

As Revere rode he woke the countryside. Riders went out from the towns. They warned other towns. Men began to gather.

At Lexington Dawes and Revere met again. A man named Samuel Prescott rode with them. They ran into British scouts. Revere was captured. Dawes escaped but his horse threw him. Prescott kept riding into the night.

Revere was released and had to walk back to Lexington. Dawes limped through the dark. He heard the bells at Concord ringing. He knew Prescott had made it. When the sun rose, Minutemen were ready at Lexington and Concord.

title: Molly Pitcher, an American Hero
text:
Maybe you’ve heard the name “Molly Pitcher.” She’s legendary! But “Molly Pitcher” is just a nickname. People agree the stories of Molly Pitcher come from the lives of several different women.

It was common for wives to go with their husbands to war. They helped in many ways on the battlefield. One thing they did was bring water to the thirsty soldiers. They used pitchers or small buckets to carry water. The men may have called all these women “Molly Pitcher.” Imagine how brave they’d have to be, with bullets flying around!

At least two famous women inspired legends of Molly Pitcher. Their names are Mary Hays and Margaret Corbin. Their stories are much alike. They both had the nickname Molly. They both went to battle with their husbands.

Mary Hays' husband was manning a cannon during the Battle of Monmouth. Mary was carrying water on the battlefield when he was hurt. She knew how to load the cannons. She took her husband's place for the rest of the day. A witness said a cannonball tore through her skirt. She kept on working behind the cannon. What a brave woman!

Margaret Corbin's husband was killed during the Battle of Washington. After he died, Margaret fired the cannon for him. She was terribly wounded. She stayed in the military. She became the first woman to receive a military pension. She was a leader before her time!

These "Molly Pitchers" were heroes. They were very brave during battle. We can't be sure exactly who the real Molly Pitcher was. The contributions made by women in the American Revolution are inspiring.

Find out more about Molly Pitcher by visiting the online version of this article. You’ll find a video there you won’t want to miss!

title: The Battle of Saratoga, 1777
text:
British General Burgoyne had orders to invade New England. His Redcoats marched through thick woods. They dragged heavy cannons and wagons. They had to build roads as they went. Americans shot at them. They took all the food from the farmlands before the British got there.

The British were low on supplies. Burgoyne sent soldiers into a town called Bennington to take horses and food. General John Stark and the militias were waiting. They attacked the Redcoats. The British lost nearly 1,000 men at the Battle of Bennington. Burgoyne’s men marched on without supplies.

Burgoyne lost his Native American scouts at that battle. He didn’t know where the rebels were. He didn’t know how many men they had. But he wasn’t worried. The British still didn’t think rebel soldiers could fight.

The Americans knew Burgoyne was coming. General Gates’ army built defenses near Saratoga. They blocked the British.

George Washington sent some of his best officers to help Gates. Benedict Arnold arrived with troops. Daniel Morgan came with his Riflemen. Rifles were slow to reload but they shot straight and far. Morgan’s men were deadly shots.

Burgoyne couldn’t advance. On Sept. 19 he tried to break through Gates’ line. Benedict Arnold and Daniel Morgan met the attack. Morgan hid his sharpshooters behind trees. They shot almost every officer as the British advanced.

Arnold and the troops fought fiercely. Gates called the Americans back when it got dark. Burgoyne gained some ground but he lost nearly 600 men. Gates lost about 300. That was the first battle.

General Gates and Benedict Arnold argued that night. They didn’t like each other. They both wanted to lead. Gates confined Arnold to his tent.

Burgoyne thought more soldiers and supplies would arrive. Nothing came. Burgoyne’s soldiers grew weaker. They were running out of food. More soldiers arrived to help Gates. They had food and ammunition.

Burgoyne couldn’t wait any longer. His officers advised a retreat. But on Oct. 7 Burgoyne decided to attack.

Morgan’s shooters hid in the woods again. They shot at the Redcoats and killed more officers. But riflemen need to fall back and reload. The American troops faltered.

Just then Arnold rode up. He ignored Gates’ orders. He led fresh soldiers in a wild charge at the British troops. Arnold was shot in the leg. His horse was killed. The British fought hard but the Americans swarmed over them. That was the second Battle of Saratoga.

Burgoyne had few men and little food. He lost six of his ten cannons. Most of his officers were gone. He had bullet holes through his hat and waistcoat.

On Oct. 8 Burgoyne’s troops fell back. On Oct. 12 John Stark and his troops arrived. Stark had beaten Burgoyne at Bennington. Stark blocked the other road out of Saratoga. By Oct. 13 the Redcoats were surrounded. On Oct. 17 Burgoyne surrendered.

Gates lost 515 dead or wounded. The British lost 1,200 dead or wounded, and 5,800 were captured.

The British learned Americans could fight. One officer wrote about how surprised the British were. The Redcoats realized they faced a brave and skillful enemy.

Would you like to learn more about the major events and battles of the Revolutionary War? Ms. Johnson has a great video called, "The Road to Independence.”

title: The Battle of Bunker Hill
text:
The Battle of Bunker Hill was actually fought at a place called Breed’s Hill. It was a major event in the American Revolution.

After Lexington and Concord, the Americans blocked the British inside Boston. The Redcoats couldn’t get out by land.

But Britain had a strong navy. The British came and went on their ships. The colonists couldn’t stop them.

There were hills outside Boston. Whoever had cannons on the hills could control the harbor. Colonel William Prescott was ordered to take Bunker Hill. Prescott took Breed’s Hill instead.

Prescott’s rebels used dirt and rocks and trees to build walls. They dug quietly all night without food or water. Riflemen could shoot from behind the walls they made.

The British heard them doing something in the dark. General Gage thought they were just noisy. He thought the Americans were very silly soldiers.

When daylight came, Gage couldn’t believe the Americans had built a strong place on top of the hill. The Redcoats marched in tight groups uphill to attack. The terrified riflemen had not seen much battle. But they shot very well. When the rebels opened fire, the British fell in piles. The colonists aimed at officers. The Redcoats withdrew. “The dead lay as thick as sheep in a fold,” wrote an American officer.

The British advanced again. The Americans shot as they came. But now the Americans were out of powder. They couldn’t shoot anymore. The British marched up the hill a third time. The rebels threw rocks at them. They hit the Redcoats with their rifles. Then they ran.

The Battle of Bunker Hill lasted about two hours. It was the bloodiest battle of the war. 268 British soldiers were killed. 828 were wounded. The Americans lost 115, and 305 were wounded, mostly as they retreated.

Dr. Joseph Warren was killed at Bunker Hill. The doctor was an honored rebel leader. He had sent Paul Revere and William Dawes on their midnight rides.

The British took Breed’s Hill but at great cost. The Redcoats learned the colonists could fight. The Americans learned that, too.

title: New Boots and a Lesson about Valley Forge
text:
Steven and Natalia trudged through Steven’s backyard. The snow was deep and it was hard to walk.

"Check out my boots!" Steven said. His mom had bought him new blue snow boots. They were perfect for snow days like this.

"Awesome!" Natalia smiled.

They cleared snow off Steven’s swings and climbed on. They wanted to swing through the falling flakes. The friends worked their legs, swinging higher and higher.

Steven felt his boots slipping. His mom had bought him a larger size than he needed so he could grow into them. He tried to hold on with his toes. Suddenly, his boots soared off his feet and flew away. They disappeared into the snow.

"Your boots!" Natalia shouted.

"I’ve got them," Steven said. He jumped off his swing and his feet sank into the snow. It was really cold. It hurt.

His boots had flown clear across the lawn to the fence. Slowly, Steven walked through the deep snow in his socks. His feet were numb. Both boots were full of snow. He tried to empty one and lost a mitten. His hands were wet and cold. By the time he got his boots on he was shaking.

"Let's go back inside." Natalia was worried.

Steven felt better sitting at the kitchen table drinking hot cocoa.

"You know," Natalia said, "you reminded me of that video Ms. Johnson showed us called 'Valley Forge Intro’."

"Oh, yeah!" Steven looked sober. "Some of those soldiers walked all the way to Valley Forge with no shoes! They trudged 25 miles! I can't imagine how hard that must've been. I barely made it to the fence!"

"I know what you mean. They wrapped their feet in rags that winter! And they were starving.”

"Yeah. And hardly any coats or blankets. Some didn’t even have shirts."

They were quiet and thoughtful as they finished their cocoa.

Valley Forge was a major event in the American Revolution. Catch the video Steven and Natalia saw in class by visiting the online version of this article. Click on “Valley Forge Intro.”

title: Snow Day at Valley Forge
text:
Steven and Natalia were playing checkers at Steven’s house. Snow was falling outside. All the snow meant that school had been cancelled!

Steven's mother was knitting on the couch. "Aren’t you two working on a Valley Forge project?" she asked.

The kids groaned. “It's a snow day! NO SCHOOL!” they said together.

Steven’s mom raised her eyebrows. “Martha Washington might have used these knitting needles at Valley Forge. I thought you’d be interested.” She smiled to herself. "But if you're looking for a break from your homework, never mind.”

The kids forgot their game and rushed to the couch.

“No way! That’s so cool!”

“Can I see them? Is that even true, Mom?”

“Well, we can’t be sure. They've been passed from person to person for years."

“Why knit at Valley Forge?” Natalia asked. “Things were bad there! Wouldn’t Martha rather be home at Mount Vernon?"

“I’m sure she preferred Mount Vernon. George said he’d rather be home than anywhere. But he stayed with his army all through the war. For over six years he never went home.”

"I didn’t know women were at Valley Forge," Steven said.

“Martha and other women were an important part of life there,” his mom said. “She ran the headquarters and hosted visitors. She oversaw the women’s work. They nursed the men, cooked, sewed and cleaned. And knitted, of course."

“Martha gave a birthday party for George. There was a concert and good food. The men shared it all. It cheered them up."

“Martha was George’s closest friend. He needed her to be there when she could. She lived at every winter camp. It was dangerous because the British might want to capture the commander’s wife! She had guards for most of the war.”

"That's awesome!" Natalia was impressed by Martha's bravery.

The doorbell rang. "Back in a minute." Steven's mom left her knitting and went to answer it.

"Are you thinking what I'm thinking?" Natalia asked, grinning.

"Yeah! Let’s try out those needles!" Steven was excited.

They touched the knitting needles and were pulled into a whirlwind. It was freezing when they stopped. Snow covered the ground. They were in Valley Forge!

"Oh, man," Steven said. "I left my jacket!"

"Let's get inside," Natalia pointed to a small wooden cabin. They slipped in and ran right into Martha Washington.

"Excuse me, little ones," Martha smiled but she seemed to be in the middle of something.

Natalia and Steven backed out of the way.

"This is so cool!" Natalia whispered.

The room bustled with activity. Women came and went. They wrote or knitted or sewed. They seemed to be managing all the daily tasks of the camp.

Martha was planning a performance with two ladies. "Lucy, I love your idea of Joseph Addison’s Cato. Kitty, have you thought about costumes?"

"She’s so comfortable," Natalia said. "I mean, she’s rich. Isn’t it weird she'd be happy in a grim place like this?"

"She's an impressive lady," Steven agreed. "They're busy. Let's get out of the way."

Together, they touched the knitting needles. The warmth of Steven’s home soaked into them. They were grateful after the harsh cold of Valley Forge.

“Remember the 'Map of the Valley Forge Encampment'?” Steven asked. “It had Washington’s quarters on it. That must have been near the women’s workplace."

Steven’s mother came back and picked up her knitting. "Where were we?” she asked. “Oh, yes. Martha Washington."

Natalia and Steven grinned. They had examined a major event of the American Revolution up close!

Find the map Steven mentioned at Studies Weekly online. Look for “Map of the Valley Forge Encampment” under images.

title: Meat, Veggies, Milk and a Baking Hero
text:
At Valley Forge General Washington promised he would “share in the hardship” with his men. Officers and soldiers ate the same food. Each man was supposed to get a pound of meat, a pound of flour, three pints of vegetables, a pint of milk and a little rice, corn and molasses every day.

Depending on what was around, the meat could be beef, pork, or salted fish. Vegetables might be dried peas or beans. If there was no milk they went without.

Soldiers mixed their flour with water and a little salt, if they had it. They baked it in iron kettles. Sometimes the flour was full of bugs. It was flat and hard and tasteless. Washington’s heart ached for his men because of the lack of good food. He wrote angry letters to Congress.

The quartermaster Congress assigned to Valley Forge hated his job. He didn’t get food for the men. He used the excuse that the roads were bad. In January and February there was almost no food. Some men starved to death.
