title: The Battle of New Orleans: A Turning Point for America
text:
The treaty to end the War of 1812 was signed far away in Europe. It was signed in a city called Ghent, in Belgium. But news traveled slowly in 1814. And before they got the news the war was over, American troops fought one more battle. Their leader was a man named Andrew Jackson. He was such a tough commander that his men called him "Old Hickory."

In late 1814, Jackson had to find a way to keep British troops from conquering the city of New Orleans. He knew that if the British held New Orleans, they could control the Mississippi River. That meant they could control nearly all the land in the Louisiana territory. Jackson had to keep that from happening.

The first thing to do was to build an army. He called on all able-bodied men who could get to New Orleans to come and fight. Jackson's army was quite a sight. Some of his men were experienced soldiers. But many of his men were volunteer farmers, frontiersmen, African Americans, Choctaw Tribesmen, and even a band of pirates. People came from all around to join Jackson's army -- about 4,500 of them.

But the British army was almost twice as big as Jackson's -- 8,000 well-trained soldiers. A lot of them had fought in the wars that defeated Napoleon. Any chance of beating them seemed like a long shot. The British believed they would easily win a battle against Jackson's odd collection of fighters. They called Jackson's soldiers "dirty shirts."

But Jackson's forces gave the British more than they bargained for. They made daring midnight raids on British camps. In an old canal, they dug trenches and built high walls out of dirt. From here, they fired on British troops. The main conflict in the Battle of New Orleans happened on January 8, 1815. In that fight, some say that more than 2,000 British soldiers were dead or wounded in just 30 minutes. Less than 100 of Jackson's troops had fallen.

After the battle, Jackson and his army rode into New Orleans to the sound of people singing "Yankee Doodle." Later, when news of the treaty of Ghent finally reached New Orleans, there was even more celebration.

Jackson's win at New Orleans made him a national hero. It told the world that America was a first-class country!

title: The Indian Removal Act and The Trail of Tears
text:
"Attention class!" Ms. Johnson's voice rang through the school bus. Slowly, the kids quieted down. "We've come to Birchwood to see some of the ways the Cherokee Removal Memorial Park has honored the memory of the Trail of Tears."

"The Trail of Tears? What's that?" asked Steven. Natalia shot him a look.

"What's the Trail of Tears?" asked Ms. Johnson. "Good heavens. I'll explain a bit, and you'll learn more in the Park. In 1830, Congress passed a law called the Indian Removal Act. It gave President Jackson permission to negotiate with American Indian Nations, with the idea of moving them to lands west of the Mississippi River."

"'Negotiate' is a pretty polite word for what the government did," muttered Natalia.

"What's that, Natalia?" said Ms. Johnson. "Feel free to speak up so we can all hear."

"My family is part Cherokee," said Natalia, "so I know a little something about this. The bottom line is that the government forced tens of thousands of American Indians to leave land they'd lived on for generations.They did it because the government wanted their land. Those who wouldn't move on their own were marched by soldiers at gunpoint. In 1838, more than 15,000 Cherokee were marched nearly a thousand miles to live on land in Oklahoma. More than 4,000 of them died."

The bus was quiet. Ms. Johnson spoke. "You're right, Natalia," she said. "And it wasn't just the Cherokee Nation that was affected. The removal affected five main tribes: the Choctaw, the Creek, the Seminole, the Chickasaw, and the Cherokee."

Steven raised his hand. "Ms. Johnson," he said, "Did the Indian Removal Act really say that the government could force people from their land?"

"No," said Ms. Johnson, "it didn't. It said that the government could try to make treaties with American Indian tribes, offering them land in the West in exchange for the land they were already living on. The government tried to make the American Indian nations believe it was a good deal for the tribes. They told them that on their new land, they'd be protected from white settlers. They said that they'd be able to govern themselves peacefully, without being bothered. Only a few American Indians were interested. But men in the government wanted all American Indians moved. So they forced them to move, which was, in many cases, against their own rules."

"I can see why they called it 'the Trail of Tears,'" said Steven. "It's just about the saddest thing I've ever heard in your class, Ms. Johnson."

"Yes. There are a few things in the history of our country that must never be forgotten, and never repeated," said Ms. Johnson. "This is one of them." She paused, and then added, "One can also be inspired by the way American Indian tribes have continued to be important to America's story. Many of our important statesmen, business people, artists, and thinkers have been American Indians. Now, class. It's time to get off the bus. Go and see the Park."

To learn more, visit Studies Weekly online for a video called "Cherokee Intro."

title: A Chat with Stan
text:
Natalia and Steven stood at the edge of an enormous map. It was printed on the floor of the amphitheater at the Cherokee Removal Memorial Park. The map showed that there were many routes by which American Indians were removed to the west. Some of the routes were over land. Some were water routes.

"It's quite a map," said a voice behind them. Steven and Natalia jumped.

"I didn't mean to startle you," said the guy. "My name is Stan. I'm happy to answer questions about the park if you've got them."

"How could anyone just kick so many people off their land?" asked Natalia.

"That's a toughie," said Stan. "We don't have a very good track record when it comes to dealing with people who seem different."

"Different?" asked Natalia.

"Well, yeah," said Stan. In the 1600s when the first colonists started coming to America, they thought the native people were 'savages'. Over the next two centuries, the Cherokee proved them wrong. They formed a government. They fought alongside the colonists in wars. In 1821, a man named Sequoyah created a written version of their language. They used this writing system to transcribe several books and adopt a written constitution. They even started a newspaper called the Cherokee Phoenix, in 1828. Many people spoke and wrote both Cherokee and English."

"It sounds like a pretty advanced society," said Steven.

"Of course! They were smart, hard-working, and talented; as much as anyone else," said Stan. And the other tribes were the same way. A lot of people remember the Cherokee forced march in 1838 because it was so huge and so severe. A lot of people died on that march. But the entire Indian removal, among all five nations, went on for about 20 years. From 1830 to 1850. And there's no state east of the Mississippi that wasn't affected. This park is just one place you can go to learn and remember. The truth is, there are places like this all over."

"It's good to know that," said Natalia. "Because we've got friends all over!"

title: Steven and the Cherokee Removal
text:
When the rushing of wind stopped, Steven found himself standing in snow. He had been so wrapped up in the stories of Natalia's grandmother, it hadn't occurred to him that touching the doll made of corn husks would send him back in time. But there he was. Before him, he saw a village. Among the houses of the village, he saw uniformed men with guns. Out of the houses came Cherokee families. They carried some of their belongings in their hands. Among the families, Steven saw a little girl. She came out of the house and stood on the frozen ground. She didn't have any shoes on. In her hands, Steven saw a doll made of corn husks. The girl shivered.

This must be 1838, Steven thought. I'm watching the forced Cherokee removal. Into his mind came thoughts of the upcoming thousand-mile march. He thought of the soldiers, driving these people along at gunpoint.

Something in Steven snapped. He looked at one of the soldiers on horseback, and shouted.

"Hey, you!" he said. "These people at the end of your guns are moms, dads, farmers, mechanics, weavers, spinners, business men and...well, all kinds of stuff! They've organized governments and speak multiple languages and they've got more of a right to this land than you do!"

Steven felt a hand on his arm. It startled him. He turned to see a young soldier.

"Do you want to get yourself in trouble?" said the soldier. "The Removal Act was a narrow vote, but President Jackson signed it eight years ago. That's history. We're taking the land these folks live on in the East, and sending them to live on land west of the Mississippi. It's a trade. Besides, leaders from all five Indian Nations have tried to fight this removal and failed. What do you think you can do? All this hollering is just going to get you in trouble."

As the soldier spoke, Steven saw that the people had begun to march. He saw the little girl with no shoes. She had dropped her corn husk doll. Steven broke away from the soldier's grip and ran to where the doll had dropped. "You dropped your doll," he shouted to the girl. As soon as his fingers touched the doll, the village disappeared. The girl disappeared. The soldier disappeared. Steven felt himself headed away from the cold winter, and back toward the warm kitchen of Natalia's grandmother.

title: Preserving the Union
text:
When people think about Andrew Jackson's presidency, they usually think of the tragic things that the government did to American Indians during his time in office. In fact, that's often all they can think about. Like Ms. Johnson said on the bus, there are a few things in the history of our country that must never be forgotten, and never repeated. But there's another way in which Jackson impacted the country. He worked to preserve the Union.

In 1828, right at the beginning of Jackson's time in office, a fight was brewing. It was a fight over taxes. The federal government had issued taxes that some states didn't want to pay. These states thought that they should have the right to ignore an order from the federal government if they wanted to. They thought that the states should have more power than the federal government when it came to making decisions for their people.

On a famous night in 1830, many officials had gathered for an annual dinner. Many of them stood and made toasts to the rights of states to ignore federal taxes or laws that they didn't agree with. Andrew Jackson was at the dinner, and most people thought he would agree with them, and make a toast himself about states' rights. But when Jackson rose to give a toast, he said, "Our Federal Union! It must be preserved!" The people in the room were surprised. In the words of his toast, they heard a strong commitment to preserving the strength of the federal union, even if it meant that the states had to obey laws they didn't want to obey.

Jackson's toast has become a famous example of his will to keep the Union strong.

title: The Trail of Tears
text:
"That was pretty heavy stuff, huh," Steven said as he and Natalia walked. Today, Natalia was going to her grandmother's house. Steven walked with her.

"Yeah," Natalia said. Ms. Johnson had started a new unit. They were learning about Andrew Jackson's presidency. "I was okay when we talked about Jackson's desire to keep the Union strong. But when Ms. Johnson began to talk about the American Indian Removal Act..." Natalia's voice trailed off. Then she turned to Steven, "Did you notice how quiet the classroom got?"

"I sure did," said Steven. "I think that was rough on all of us. It's hard to believe that some of the people who did such great things in our country were also responsible for forcing American Indians from their homes."

They arrived at Natalia's grandmother's house. Natalia turned to Steven. "Are you coming in? We could work on our reports." Steven smiled at his friend.

"I can stick around for awhile," Steven said. They walked into the house, and headed for the kitchen.

"Hello Grandma," Natalia called out. "I'm here. I brought Steven."

Natalia's grandmother came into the room. "What are you two studying?" she said.

"We're studying the Trail of Tears, Grandma," said Natalia.

"Hmm. This must be hard on you, Natalia," said her grandmother. She turned to Steven. "We're a Cherokee family, you know," she said.

"Yes, I know," said Steven.

"Here, I made cookies," she said. She smiled at the two friends. "Would you each like one cookie, or two? Oh, bother," said Natalia's grandmother. "I'll bring the whole jar." She brought a big jar to the table. The jar was filled with cookies.

They munched on cookies for awhile. There was a question Steven wanted to ask, but he wasn't sure he had the courage. Finally, he spoke. "Your family still lives in Tennessee. Weren't your ancestors removed West?"

"No," said Natalia's grandmother. "People who lived on Cherokee land were forced to go, but my grandma was allowed to stay. Her family lived on land that wasn't owned by the tribe. It was purchased by Chief William Holland Thomas in the Smoky Mountains. It wasn't really Cherokee land, so the people living on it weren't subject to the Indian Removal Act. But my grandmother had a good friend who was removed, along with her parents, and even grandparents. Grandma didn't see her friend for years until decades later she was able to make it out west to Oklahoma. It had been many years, but grandma's friend still cried bitter tears as she told my grandma about the long, brutal march. It was in the wintertime, and many were sick. They lacked good clothes or shoes. A lot of people collapsed and were left to die alone in the woods. Their families were forced to keep marching. I only heard my grandma tell this story one time. It made her too sad to talk about very often. She said she felt guilty that her friends had to leave, while she was able to stay in Tennessee."

"That's hard to think about," said Steven.

"Yes," said Natalia's grandmother. "I've got something to show you," she said. She got up from the table.

The phone rang. Natalia got it. "Oh, hi Dad," she said. She turned to Steven. "It's my dad. He's just checking on me. I'm going to take it in the living room. I'll be just a minute, okay?" Steven nodded. A moment later, Natalia's grandmother came back. She put something down on the table. It was a doll made of corn husks. It looked very old.

"This doll was given to my grandmother by the friend I told you about," said Natalia's grandmother. "Grandma's friend had carried it on the trip. That means this doll traveled more than a thousand miles, in the dead of winter."

Steven looked at the doll for a moment. "Can I touch it?" he said.

"Sure," said Natalia's grandmother. "But be careful. It's very old."

Steven reached out carefully. His hands touched the dry corn husks that made up the doll. Suddenly, he felt the rushing of wind. Natalia's grandmother disappeared. So did the kitchen. Steven was headed back in time.

title: John Ross: an Opposing Voice
text:
The people who wanted to take land from American Indian tribes were strong. In the end, they succeeded. But there were many people who fought against them. John Ross was one of those people.

Part Cherokee and part Scottish, John Ross was born in 1790. He fought in the Creek War under Andrew Jackson in 1813. He was involved in the Cherokee tribe his entire life. For awhile, he served as leader of the Cherokee Nations Council. He revealed attempts by government officials to bribe him into approving the sale of native land. Later, he was the Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation. In this position, too, he fought to protect the land owned by his people. He paid a high price for his work. He was put in jail, and his home was taken. Finally, he lost the fight. It was then part of his sad job to oversee the removal of the Cherokee from their land. When they arrived and settled in Oklahoma, Ross helped write a constitution for the United Cherokee Nation in 1839. They made him chief of the new government. He held this position until his death.

title: Seminoles Choose to Fight!
text: Though it was unjust to make them do it, most American Indians walked the Trail of Tears toward the West. But some chose to fight instead of leaving their land. The Seminoles were a tribe that lived in Florida. They were ordered to move west like everyone else. But led by Chief Osceola, they chose instead to fight. Osceola's fighters were far outnumbered. But they used ambushes, hit-and-run attacks, raids, and more to fight against their enemies. They were able to survive for a long time. For years, the U.S. Army didn't know how to beat Osceola's warriors. So they began to burn Seminole farms and villages. This turned the tide of the fight. When it was over, only a few hundred fighters and their families were left. They retreated deep into the Florida Everglades. The Second Seminole War lasted from 1835-1842. It claimed the lives of 2,000 U.S. soldiers and countless numbers of Seminoles. It cost the U.S. government close to half a billion dollars in today's money.

title: The Erie Canal: How Was it Done?
text:
In 1825 the Erie Canal opened. This new waterway went from Albany to Buffalo, New York and allowed boats to travel from the Atlantic Ocean to the Great Lakes. Barges were pulled along the canal by teams of horses or mules. The canal was a great success and became important to all of America. The Erie Canal actually helped settle the West. Settlers began streaming into western New York, Ohio, Illinois, Wisconsin and Michigan. The Erie Canal made it possible to transport goods in less than half the time it used to take, and at a much lower cost.

title: Riding on a Railroad
text:
Just as machines and factories made it easy and inexpensive to make products of all kinds, railroads made it easy to get those products from place to place. In the South, people used boats on waterways to ship goods from place to place. But in the North, the railroad was king! By 1860, every major city in the North was connected by railroads. In the Midwest, where lots of food crops grew, 80 percent of farms were within 5 miles of a railroad. This means that goods could be easily moved from wherever they were made to wherever people wanted them. Trains carried passengers, too!

In the North, railroads began to replace rivers and waterways as the main way to get things from place to place. In many ways, railroads were better and more reliable than rivers. Rivers would freeze in the winter, and boats couldn't travel on them. Also, boats sank much more often than trains crashed.

Even today, goods and passengers move across the country on railroads.

title: A Store Filled with Wonders
text:
"I'm glad we came here," said Steven. "I think it was a great idea. And all this stuff is so cool!"

Steven and Natalia wandered through the antique store, looking at all sorts of interesting things. They all looked old.

"Can I help you?" said a voice. Steven and Natalia turned to see a nice-looking woman. She had white, kinky hair. She wore glasses with red frames. "I'm Ida, and this is my store."

"Hello, Ida," said Natalia politely. "We came here to see if we could see anything that might help us understand what it was like in the early 1800s, during the Industrial Revolution. Our teacher showed us a video called 'Industrial Revolution Intro.' Then she assigned us to do some research."

"Ah!" said Ida, "The Industrial Revolution. That's the period from about 1760 to about 1840, when machines began to make all sorts of products cheaply and quickly. It changed everything!"

"We know," said Steven. "We thought some of the old stuff here in your shop might help us get a feel for the time when the Industrial Revolution was happening," said Steven.

"What a good idea!" said Ida. "Is there anything special you're looking for?"

Natalia shook her head. "I don't really know," she said. "Do you have anything in the shop from the early 1800s?"

"Hmm, let me see," said Ida. "I'm sure I can find something." Suddenly her eyes lit up. "I've got just the thing!" she said. "I'll be right back!" Ida disappeared behind stacks of old records and shelves filled with china dolls.

"'I'm kind of excited to see what she comes back with," said Steven. "Do you think it will be a silver coin? Or an old Bible?"

"I wonder if it will be a beautiful antique coat," said Natalia, "or a musical instrument."

"Any of those things would be amazing," said Steven. They heard Ida coming back toward them. When she reappeared from behind the stacks of records, she was holding something. She held it out for them to look at.

"It looks like a giant spool of thread," said Steven.

"That's exactly what it is!" said Ida.

"It's a lot bigger than the spool of thread that my mom uses when I need a button sewn on my jacket," said Natalia. "It's gotta be a foot long!"

"I know! It's huge, isn't it!" said Ida. "This spool of thread is almost two hundred years old."

"Wow," said Steven and Natalia together.

Ida continued. "It fit into a spinning machine from a mill owned by Samuel Slater himself!"

"Um...wow," said Steven and Natalia again. They weren't quite sure who Samuel Slater was.

"Trust me," said Ida. "This is really impressive. Would you like to touch it?"

Natalia and Steven shrugged. "Sure," they said. They reached out together, and touched the thread on the enormous spool. Suddenly, they felt the rush of wind. The antique shop began to disappear. Steven and Natalia were headed back in time!

You can watch the video "Industrial Revolution Intro." Just visit the online version of this article!

title: Samuel Slater
text:
In this issue, Steven and Natalia met Samuel Slater. Here's a little more about him. Slater was from England. There, they had machines that could make cloth many times faster than it could be made by hand. People in America had heard of these machines, but didn't know how to make them.

Samuel Slater knew how to make them. He hoped to build them in America. But England had strict rules against sharing the plans for these machines. Because he couldn't bring plans on paper to America, Slater memorized how to make them, and brought the plans in his brain!

The English were mad that Slater helped Americans with these machines. They gave him a nickname. They called him "Slater the traitor."

If Slater minded, he didn't show it. He built mills to make cloth. Before he died, he had thirteen mills. He had become a millionaire. Because of the machines and ideas he brought to America, Slater got another nickname. People called him "The Father of the American Industrial Revolution"!

title: A Visit to the Industrial Revolution!
text:
Steven and Natalia hadn't thought of Ida's enormous spool of thread as a primary source. But as soon as they touched it, they knew they were headed back in time. Before they could catch their breath, they were standing in an enormous room. Around the room, there were windows looking out on the night sky. The room was filled with machinery that Natalia and Steven didn't recognize. Next to them was an enormous machine. One side of it showed places to put many spools of thread, just like the one Ida had shown them in the antique shop.

"This is amazing!" said Steven.

"I wonder where we are?" said Natalia.

Just then, from behind the machine, they heard a clanking sound. It startled them. A man's head peered from around the side of the machine. He had a high forehead and light hair.

"You startled me," said the man. "Shouldn't you be home with the other workers?"

"Other workers?" said Steven. "We don't even know where we are."

"Ah," said the man. He came from behind the machine, wiping his hands on a rag. "Forgive me. I thought you must work here. Everyone in town does. In fact, I built the town around the mill so that people could live close to where they work," he said. "I'm Samuel Slater. Welcome to Rhode Island."

"Rhode Island!" said Natalia and Steven together.

"Yes. Slatersville, to be exact. You like the name?"

"It suits you," said Steven.

"Would either of you like a job?" said Mr. Slater.

"We're both pretty young," said Natalia. "Only nine."

"Nine? That's old to start working for me," said Mr. Slater. "I've got folks working in this very mill who are younger than that. They, and their brothers and sisters, and their parents. Sunup to sundown."

"Wow. No thanks. I don't like the sound of that," said Steven.

"Ah. Well. What can I do for you then?" said Mr. Slater. "I was just checking the machines so they'll be ready in the morning."

"We're just here to find out what it's like to be living when you lived...er...I mean...when you live," said Natalia.

"Ah. It's quite a time," said Mr. Slater. "You know, I came from England to build these spinning machines. People didn't think I knew what I was talking about. Finally, I had to tell them that if I failed to make better yarn with my machines than the yarn available in England, they could not only refuse to pay me, but they could throw whatever I had made into the river! That got 'em."

"I bet," said Steven.

Mr. Slater continued, "The northern cities of the United States are remarkable. I can see a day when factories will dot the landscape, making all sorts of products for all sorts of people. I see a day when those products can travel from place to place on trains and on rivers! In fact, I heard they're even talking about digging a canal from the Hudson River to Lake Erie."

"Yeah," said Steven. "They're going to call it the Erie Canal."

"Really? What an appropriate name," said Mr. Slater. "Well, whatever they call it, when they finish it, that river will fill up with boats carrying goods like the goods we make on these machines. It's quite a thing to think about."

"It sure is," said Natalia.

"Did you know that seven out of every eight people coming to this country settle here in the Northern States?" asked Mr. Slater. "That's an awful lot of workers. Think of the factories we could keep running!"

Steven leaned over and whispered to Natalia. "Wow," he said. "I can really see how new machines changed things in America."

Natalia whispered back to Steven. "Yeah, she said. It's kind of a lot to take in. Let's head back to the Antique shop, yeah?"

Steven and Natalia reached out to touch one of the spools of thread on Mr. Slater's machine. As soon as they did, they felt the rush of wind. The Industrial Revolution had been quite a place to visit, but they were glad to be headed home!

title: The Mill Women
text:
Hey everyone! Natalia here. Ms. Johnson gave me an assignment. She wants me to write a letter as if I were a girl working in a mill in the 1800s. It sounds like a hard life, but I gave it a try. Before I wrote, I did a little research. Here are some of the things I learned:

Traditionally, women sewed their families' clothing from "homespun," which they made with spinning wheels and hand looms. When the new textile factories opened for business, they offered an alternative to homespun clothing. But these factories needed workers to run the machinery. They discovered that local women were excellent at such work.

By the early 1800s, stay-at-home women were seen as extra mouths to feed. When small commercial spinning mills began to appear in New England, many women welcomed the chance for paid work. They wanted to make money to help take care of their families, and they knew that they could do the work being offered by the textile mills. The word textile means cloth or fabric.

Working in a mill was no picnic. Sometimes workers were treated cruelly or unfairly.

Anyway, there's some of what I learned. Do you want to read the letter I wrote? It might help you imagine what it was like to work in textile mill. It doesn't sound like much fun!

Dear Jenny,

I am starting to feel very frustrated with the mill owner, as are all the other girls and women here. He has said he is going to cut our wages and raise the cost of our rent. He knows we just barely make enough to help our families. It is not fair that he wants to pay us less. I have talked with the other mill girls, and we are going to go on strike. We will show him how important we are to his factory.

I admit I am worried how the owner will react. He is not known for being a nice man. He may fight back by firing some of us. But I don't know what else to do. We cannot work for such low pay.

If I still have my job after the strike, I hope to graduate to a better position in the mill.

Sincerely,

Natalia

title: Mass Production! It's the New Thing!
text:
Before the Industrial Revolution, people couldn't just run to the store if they needed something. Instead, they knew how to make and repair most of the things they used at home. If they couldn't make a thing themselves, they took it to someone in town to make it for them. If someone in the family needed clothes, the mother of the family might go to a store to buy fabric. Then, she took the fabric home and made the clothes herself. If the family was rich, they might hire a seamstress or tailor to make the clothes. That's how it had been for generations.

But the Industrial Revolution changed it all! The sewing machine came along in 1846. Soon, factories could make clothes faster and more cheaply than it could be made at home. Families bought clothing from stores or through catalogs. It saved them time and money, and gave them more styles of clothes to choose from.

Clothes weren't the only thing that changed during the Industrial Revolution. Machines were able to make all kinds of things. They made tools, farm equipment, chairs, tables, beds, vehicles, and more! Stuff that had always been made slowly by hand could be made quickly by machines. It was called "mass production."

As mass production became more popular, fewer and fewer people worked on farms, and more and more people worked in factories. People who had lived in the country moved to the city. That way, they could be close to where the factories were. The way people lived and worked had changed forever.

title: Steam Power
text:
Hello all,

Steven here. In this week's adventure, we had all sorts of fun in Ida's antique shop. We traveled back in time to meet Samuel Slater, too. We've read about machines that make all sorts of goods easy to create in large numbers. And as we've studied these machines, one question keeps popping into my head: What sort of power made all these machines go? I mean, come on, we're talking about the early 1800's here! This was before wind power was being used to make electricity. It was long before nuclear power, or natural gas. It was long before solar power, or batteries. So what gives? What sort of power could make all these machines run?

Well, I found the answer. And here it is: steam power.

Have you ever boiled water in a tea kettle? When the water is hot enough, evaporating water, or steam, shoots out the kettle whistle and lets you know. When you see that happen, you're getting just a glimpse of how steam can be used to do mechanical work. As it turns out, steam can be pretty powerful stuff. If you heat water hot enough, and keep the steam under pressure, it can be used to run the pistons or turbines in powerful engines.

The idea for using steam to do work is many centuries old. The oldest record of anything like a steam engine is from the first century C.E. That's 2,000 years ago! In the years since, more and more improvements have been made to the steam engine. By the time of the Industrial Revolution, men like Thomas Newcomen, James Watt, and George Corliss had helped steam engines advance far enough that they could so some real work!

How powerful can steam engines be?

They can make trains move forward pulling tons of freight. They can paddle enormous steamboats upriver. They can spin the blades on the big saws in lumber mills. They can run the machines in a textile factory. No doubt about it: steam power was the power that ran the Industrial Revolution.

title: A Factory Economy: The North
text:
The North and South are really different from each other. The North had a factory economy. There were many reasons. Here are just a few of them:

• soil and climate made small farms common

• more natural resources were located in the North

• there were many more large cities

• seven out of every eight immigrants settled in the North

The North began to build factories while the South was focused on farming. While the South enslaved Africans and African Americans for their labor, the North used labor from immigrants who needed jobs. The immigrants were not generally well-paid. All those workers helped factories grow. It was easy to transport goods in the North. At least 65 percent of the train tracks were in the North.

title: Population Charting
text:
In the 1800s the North and South were very different places to live. A manufacturing economy along with a large population of immigrants caused a growth in urban (city) development in the North. Because most people in the South lived and worked on farms and plantations, it was known as a rural (country) population. The table shows the largest U.S. cities in 1860. title: Think & Review Questions
text:
1. This week we learned about several inventions that made life easier during the Industrial Revolution. Name one invention and describe how it made life easier.

2. Think of a modern invention that has made your life easier. What is the invention? Describe how it has made your life more efficient or better.

3. Why was this time period called the Industrial Revolution?

4. What is the most basic difference between the economies of the North and the South?

title: Different Lives
text:
In the 1800s, many people in the South were enslaved. Enslaved people were considered property and were not free to make any choices or decisions about their lives. What was their life like? Many enslaved people lived on plantations, but they also lived on small farms and in cities.

Plantations were large farms that grew cotton, tobacco, rice or sugar. These were cash crops that were sold for a profit. To make a better profit, plantation owners used enslaved labor to do the field work. Enslavers did not invest much into caring for enslaved people, who received no pay at all.

Enslaved people usually lived in small cabins with dirt floors. Plantation owners often did not provide enslaved workers with food that was fit to eat. Some enslaved people were allowed to grow vegetable gardens.

Whether exhausted or hungry, enslaved people had to complete their difficult work. Men, women, and children raised and tended to crops. If they stopped to rest, supervisors would often beat them. They often returned home very late.

Some enslaved people worked in the plantation owner's home. Their jobs were cooking, cleaning and watching children. These were still difficult jobs if the owner was unfair or cruel. In the mid-1800s, almost 400,000 enslaved people lived and worked on plantations.

Enslaved people also worked on smaller farms, alongside the farmer. Enslaved people sometimes became close to the farmer and his family. But life could also be difficult on a small farm. If a farmer did not do well, there might not be enough food. Enslaved people often had to sleep in the kitchen or a small building near the home, such as a barn.

Plantations and small farms were not the only places that enslaved people worked. Enslaved people could also be found living and working in cities, becoming skilled laborers. After harvests, some enslaved people on plantations would be hired out to blacksmiths, carpenters and other industries. Enslaved people who lived in cities could sometimes earn a little money from a trade. Sometimes this money could buy their freedom after a very long period of time. Even if they couldn't buy their freedom, enslaved people in cities sometimes lived in small communities on the outer edge of town. Some worked in homes as domestic workers who would cook, clean, serve food and help with other chores. While enslaved plantation workers rarely left the plantation and were isolated, enslaved people in cities were exposed to more of the world and were able to travel around town if they had a pass to do so. Even though the lives of enslaved people who lived in cities were different from those who worked on large or small farms, all enslaved people were under the control of their owners.

All enslaved people were subject to Slave Codes. These laws varied from state to state, but some of them were common. It was illegal for an enslaved person to learn to read or write. Fines and jail time were given to anyone caught educating African Americans. Enslaved people could not hold a meeting unless there was a white person present. Families could be separated and sold by their white owners. Enslaved people on plantations, farms, and in cities lived differently, but they were all seen as property and not as people.

title: Let's Write
text: Cotton is used in clothing, like T-shirts and jeans, but did you know it is also a fiber to help bind things? Cotton is in book bindings, coffee filters and paper. You can't eat cotton balls, because they are impossible to digest. You can eat cottonseed oil, though! And cows eat cotton seeds. So how does a cotton boll become a shirt? Tell a story about what steps cotton must go through to become clothing. Then, do some research to find out the real process.

title: The Cotton Industry Was a Huge Success ... but Not for All
text:
How did the cotton industry make people rich? Here's how the process worked: First, the southern growers bought slaves. Where did the slaves come from? They came from Africa. Some of them were kidnapped, while others were bought from their village leaders. They were parents and children just like us, suddenly forced to go to America on a crowded slave ship, only to be sold to the farm owners to work for the rest of their lives without any kind of compensation. From then on, they were treated as property, not people. Many times their families were split up, never to see each other again. The enslaved people were helpless to do anything about this, because they were harshly punished for even the slightest protests.

On the plantations, the slaves produced the cotton by planting, growing and picking it. The enslaved people did all the field work and harvesting and received no pay at all. They were treated very poorly even though they worked as hard as they could. The southern plantation owners who owned the cotton farms got rich when they sold their cotton to northerners. The northerners bought the cotton and shipped it to England. The English bought the cotton and made materials out of it, which they then sold. Each time the cotton changed hands, more money was made. Everyone made money and improved their lives, except the enslaved people.

title: The Industrial Revolution: Eli Whitney
text:
"Hello, fellow students!" said Steven. He and Natalia were in front of the camera. It was time for their news show.

"It's great to be with you!" said Natalia. "On our show today, we want to talk about an invention that changed the South. We started to learn about it in a video called, "Cotton Gin Intro," and then we did some of our own research."

"Also, we want to tell you about the man who invented it." said Steven.

"The inventor's name was Eli Whitney," said Natalia, "and his invention is called the cotton gin."

"Though it may not sound like it," said Steven, "the word 'gin' is short for the word 'engine.'"

"Eli Whitney was born in 1765, in Massachusetts," Steven continued. "His dad was a farmer, so young Eli had plenty of chances to learn about farming, and about the machines that helped farmers. As he grew older, Eli would make things on his family's farm. He built his own nail forge. He built a violin. When it was time to go away to study, Eli went to Yale College - the school that would one day be called Yale University."

"Eli Whitney graduated from Yale College in 1792," said Natalia. "He thought he would leave school and go work as a tutor. Instead, he went to stay with a woman named Catherine Greene. She owned a plantation in Georgia. The plantation grew cotton, so Eli had the chance to learn about growing cotton."

"Cotton was a common crop," said Steven. "Farmers could grow it without too much difficulty. And once the plant was grown, the farmers could store the fibers of the plant without having to worry about them rotting. There were a few problems, though."

"There were a couple of kinds of cotton in the South: short-staple cotton and long-staple cotton," said Natalia. "Short-staple cotton could be grown just about anywhere in the South. This made it very popular. But short-staple cotton had seeds that took a lot of effort to separate from the cotton. The seeds had to be separated before the cotton could be sold. Another type of cotton, long-staple cotton, was easier to remove the seeds from. But long-staple cotton could only be grown easily on the coast."

"This means that most of the cotton in the South was short-staple cotton," said Steven.

"The difficult kind," said Natalia.

"To clean short-staple cotton, a person had to go through the cotton and pull out each seed by hand. It took hours to do the work. Sadly, the people who did this job were slaves, forced to work day in and day out, carefully picking seeds from the raw cotton fiber. In fact, a slave could only remove the seeds from about a single pound of cotton per day," said Steven.

"Eli Whitney learned just how hard it was to process cotton," said Natalia. "He thought and he thought, and built a machine designed to make the job easier. His intent was to make things better."

"The cotton gin worked by pushing the cotton through a wooden barrel that had hooks sticking out to grab the cotton threads," said Natalia. The hooks pulled the threads through a mesh. The holes in the mesh were big enough for the cotton threads to pass through but too small for the cotton seeds to pass through. Eli's machine could process 50 pounds of cotton in a day."

"That's fifty times more cotton than a slave could process by hand," said Steven. "With a machine that could do part of their jobs, you might think that some plantations would let some of the people they kept enslaved go free. But unfortunately, that's not the case. Plantations simply grew even more cotton, and used even more slaves to do the planting."

"The cotton gin greatly increased cotton production in the South," said Natalia. "And it greatly increased the number of enslaved people as well. The slaves were working as hard as ever, and there were way more of them."

"Also, Eli Whitney never got rich from his invention," said Steven. "Farmers made copies of it, and did not pay him for them. But his invention did make it possible for cotton to grow into a bigger industry than ever before."

Visit the online version of this article and look for the video, "Cotton Gin Intro."

title: A Cotton Economy: The South
text:
Even before cotton was king, the South focused mostly on agriculture. They also grew tobacco and sugar cane. New Orleans was the only large city, and almost everyone worked on farms. It was hard to travel around the South quickly. Of all the train tracks in the United States, just 35 percent of them were in the South. The advent of the steamboat improved transportation issues in the South. There were big differences between the ways that the Industrial Revolution changed the North, and the ways it changed the South. Here's a list of some of the things about the South that made it able to successfully grow crops and become "Cotton Kingdom":

• fertile, rich soil

• a warm climate

• large areas of land to grow crops

• a large and free labor force, comprised of enslaved Africans and African Americans

title: Inventions of the Industrial Revolution
text:
The Industrial Revolution was a time of developing technology. Let's look at just a few of the inventions of that time:

Steamboats - Robert Fulton built the first steamboat that could carry passengers and cargo. Before that, travel was much, much slower. He built his steamboat in the North, but steamboats were used all over the South as well.

Watermills - Watermills were used in the production of flour, lumber, cloth, and paper. The mills used a water wheel and flowing water as their source of power. All mills were located near flowing water.

Cotton Gin - Eli Whitney made the first cotton gin. His invention made it easy to process cotton much more quickly than before. This led to major growth in the cotton industry. Unfortunately, it also increased the need for slave labor. It turned the South into a Cotton Kingdom.

Interchangeable Musket Parts - Eli Whitney continued to be an important figure in manufacturing when he created pieces for guns that would later be used in the Civil War. Whitney's interchangeable parts made it possible to fix muskets quickly instead of building a whole new musket. Ironically, Whitney's cotton gin turned out to be detrimental to slavery, but his interchangeable musket parts would help the North win the Civil War, leading to the abolishment of slavery.

Flying Shuttle - Before this was invented, a weaver could only make a piece of cloth as wide as his or her arms. But the flying shuttle made it possible for one person to make a much wider piece of cloth. The flying shuttle changed the textile industry.

Spinning Jenny - The spinning jenny made it easy for a single person to make more fabric than ever before. It was first made by a man in England named James Hargreaves in 1764. But it had a big impact in America, too. The spinning jenny allowed people to work eight spools of thread at once. By the time the spinning jenny was fully developed, it let one person work 120 spools.

Factory System - Samuel Slater was an English-American who brought the textile technology of Britain to the U.S. He was the first person to design textile mills in America. His focus on factory techniques and efficiency makes him an important figure in the Industrial Revolution.

title: Watermills and Steamboats
text:
Water has been used throughout history to transport people and goods and as a source of power. The watermill was used in the ancient world as well as in early U.S. history. It was used in the production of flour, lumber, cloth and paper. The mills used a water wheel and flowing water as their source of power. The vertical water wheels were often used in watermills and were most popular in areas where hills and waterfalls could be found.

A type of water wheel, called a paddle wheel, was used in ships too. On March 28, 1803, onlookers gathered to see a test of a brand new ship. The ship had been built by William Symington, It was called the Charlotte Dundas. There was something special about this ship. Unlike any other ship in history, it didn't run by rowing, or by the power of the wind. The Charlotte Dundas ran on a new kind of engine. It was powered by steam.

An American named Robert Fulton was in Scotland to watch the tests of the Charlotte Dundas. He came back home with many ideas. With his partners, he built a ship powered by steam that had two side paddle wheels. That ship was called the Clermont. Before it sailed, people called it "Fulton's Folly." They didn't think it would be much of a success. But they were wrong! The Clermont chugged up and down the Hudson River, carrying people and cargo. It began a new era for river travel in the United States.

The Clermont wasn't the first steam-powered boat in America, but it was the first one to be successful at hauling cargo and passengers. And though it operated in northern rivers, it made a huge impact on the South. When people saw that steamboats could be successful at moving people and goods from place to place, they started popping up everywhere! What trains were to the North, steamboats were to the South.

title: Keeping it Simple: Dressing like a Pioneer!
text:
It was time for Natalia and Steven to present their news story to the school. They were excited to tell everyone about the clothes that the pioneers wore on the trail.

Natalia and Steven head into the newsroom to tell their story. Steven turned the camera on, and they were on TV!

"Hello, everyone," said Natalia. "We are here to tell you all about the clothes worn by the pioneers on the trail. First, we want to show you a short video called, "Living Like a Pioneer Intro." It will give you an idea of what pioneer life was like. Then, Steven will tell you about pioneer clothing," said Natalia.

After the video, Steven picked up his notes and looked at the camera. He smiled. "Pioneers tried to keep their clothes simple," he said. "Families carried two or three changes of clothes with them as they traveled. Men wore loose pants and shirts. They held their pants up with a leather belt or suspenders. Women wore long dresses, usually made out of wool or cotton. Under the dresses, they wore linen petticoats. Kids over six wore clothes like their parents. Boys and girls six and under wore linen dresses. Everyone who could afford a pair wore heavy boots to protect their feet," he said.

Natalia grinned at Steven, then turned to the camera. "It is kind of hard to imagine what pioneers looked like without seeing it for yourselves. That's why Steven and I are going to dress up like pioneers one of these days," she said. "Just wait! You're in for a treat!"

Would you like to see the video that Steven and Natalia showed in their broadcast? Visit Studies Weekly online, and look for a video called, "Living Like a Pioneer Intro."

title: Luzena Wilson Makes a Mistake on the Trail
text:
Hey all! Natalia here. Ms. Johnson gave me an assignment. She wanted me to write a letter as if I were Luzena Stanley Wilson. Luzena was a real pioneer who traveled to California by wagon with her family. Here's what I came up with.

Dear Mother,

My husband asked me to lighten the load for the oxen. I found a few things I thought we could do without - three lumps of bacon and a dirty apron. I threw them out of the wagon and we went on our way.

Unfortunately, when we set up camp I discovered that I had no lard to cook with. My only choice was to run back to find the bacon. I was lucky enough to find it. I brought all three pieces back, along with the apron. And guess what? With the oxen rested overnight, the bacon and apron I threw out didn't make any difference at all!

When I told my husband what I did, he just laughed. How silly to think a little bacon and an apron would make any difference.

I miss you and hope to see you again one day.

With Love,

Luzena

Watch the video, "Three Lumps of Bacon and a Dirty Apron" to learn more about Luzena Wilson.

title: At the Speed of an Ox
text:
Often, when you see an image of a pioneer wagon, you see oxen pulling it. Oxen allowed pioneers to take their belongings and their families across thousands of miles of rough terrain. But traveling with oxen was not easy. They only walked about two miles per hour. They also needed to be given water, fed and kept healthy for months of hard work.

Many people think that oxen were a special breed of animal. But they were really just regular cattle that had been trained to pull wagons. The oxen that pulled a pioneer's wagon might be the same milk cow that had been used at home (though steers were preferred as oxen).

Unlike most cows you see today, oxen always had horns. The horns were important for keeping the yoke on the ox. Without the horns, the yoke might slip off. Many cattle you see today do not have horns because they have been cut off for safety. But to pull a wagon takes an ox with horns!

One of the main reasons why oxen were used by pioneers was that they were easy to get. Many pioneers already had cows for milk or for meat. All they had to do was train the cow to pull a wagon and they would have all the energy they needed to go west. Cattle were also much less expensive than horses or mules. During the time of the pioneers, a horse might cost five times as much as a cow.

People driving oxen across the plains got used to delivering certain commands. They would say "Get up!" when they wanted the oxen to move forward. They would say "Gee!" when they wanted the oxen to turn right. They would say "Haw!" when they wanted the oxen to turn left. They would say "Whoa!" when they wanted the oxen to stop.

Oxen were valuable to pioneers headed west. And using oxen to pull heavy loads is nothing new. Oxen were first harnessed and put to work more than 6,000 years ago!

title: This Week's Question
text: You've learned this week about some of the different overland trails that pioneers took when they went west. On a separate sheet of paper, list the trails you read about in this issue. Write down the answers to these questions: Where did each trail end? Why might pioneers have chosen each trail? Which trail do you think you would have taken and why? Who you would have taken with you? What clothes would you need for yourself and your group?

title: James K. Polk and Manifest Destiny
text:
In the 1800s, our country wasn't nearly as large as it is today. Other countries controlled much of the land that is now the Western United States. But many people thought that America would grow and grow until it stretched all the way to the Pacific Ocean. That idea was called "Manifest Destiny." That phrase was first used by a reporter named John O'Sullivan. In his paper, he talked about "...our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions." O'Sullivan knew that more people came to our country each day. Like many others, he thought that democracy was the best way to govern a country. Our country was a democracy. The countries that controlled the West were not. Many Americans thought that because of this, our country would get control of the land in the West, and would spread all the way to the west coast.

James K. Polk was the eleventh President of the United States. He gave a speech that talked about the destiny of the country. In his speech, he said that if people went west, it would make the country stronger.

Manifest Destiny was a term that stuck in the minds of many people. For many, it was a vision of how the nation ought to be. It helped pioneers make a hard and dangerous trip west. They went thousands of miles to start a new life. By going west, they felt they would make things better for all.

However, we know that the lives and homelands of many American Indians were not considered in the concept of Manifest Destiny. It would impact their cultures forever.

Today, our country stretches from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean. Many lives were changed in the process.

title: Mapping the Westward Trails
text:
How did the early pioneers know how to get to where they were going? Were there roads or highways leading to the new frontier? Well, there weren’t really roads, but there were the trails. At first, the early settlers followed American Indian trails hoping these would lead them to where they wanted to go. Eventually, the trails became easier to follow because of all the wagons traveling along them. They were still very rough, though, and nothing like real roads or highways.

The four main westward trails are marked on the map provided. Use the map to answer the following questions:

title: Let's Write!
text: Many pioneers thought about Manifest Destiny when they went west. Imagine you are a pioneer about to leave on the trail. Write a letter to the people you are leaving behind. Explain how your journey will help your family.

title: Heading West on the Overland Trails
text:
"Natalia, wouldn't it be cool if we could make costumes that showed exactly what the pioneers wore on the Oregon Trail?" said Steven.

"That's a great idea, Steven. I guess we could go to the library to do some research on what the pioneers wore," said Natalia.

"I've got a better idea," said Steven. "Let's go check it out in person!" Steven smiled and opened his backpack. He pulled out a letter, old and yellowed. "Check this out," he said. "It's a letter from a pioneer headed west from Independence, Missouri, in 1863. Let's go back and see what we can find out."

Natalia reached out and grabbed the letter. They felt a familiar rush of wind. They closed their eyes. When they opened them again, they found themselves standing in the dirt next to a big, wooden wagon. The wagon was parked outside of a store. Adults were piling things into the wagon. They were trying to make all their supplies fit. It didn't look easy. A young girl and a young boy were running around the wagon while the adults packed. A pioneer woman was sitting on a broken wheel writing a letter. The pioneer girl wore a long dress with many petticoats. The boy wore long pants with a loose shirt and suspenders.

Natalia said, "How can she wear so many layers? She must be so hot!"

The pioneer girl said, "Come on, little brother. Time to go. This Oregon Trail isn't gettin' any shorter."

Steven said, "Look at the brother. He's wearing long pants and boots. He's probably hot, too, but I bet he's glad when he has to walk through prickly bushes! I wonder why they're taking that trail. How did they choose?"

"Look," the pioneer girl said. She gestured to another family trying to organize their wagon. "They're friends of ours. I don't want to be separated from our friends, and I know you don't either. But Mama says we have to go our own way. Other families are taking the Mormon Trail because they are Mormons looking for religious freedom. That family over there is going to Montana by the Bozeman Trail, too, looking for gold. Some are going on the California Trail. Everyone starts here, but then they take different trails depending on where they want to go. We go where Mama and Papa say we go. We're going on the Oregon Trail. Now, hurry up!"

The two pioneer kids jumped onto the wagon without tripping over their clunky boots.

"Good-bye, pioneers," whispered Natalia and Steven. "Good luck on your journey!"

Would you like to watch the video that gave Steven and Natalia the idea for their costumes? Visit Studies Weekly online, and look for a video called, "Oregon Trail Intro."

title: The Oregon, Mormon, California and Bozeman Trails
text:
Which way to the West? Some people might have thought there was a single road to the West, or perhaps no road at all, but they were wrong. Pioneers headed west took one of any number of roads, based on where they wanted to go. Let's take a look at just a few of the westward trails, and why pioneers took them. In this article, we'll learn a little about the Oregon Trail, the Mormon Trail, the California Trail and the Bozeman Trail.

In spite of the stories in many movies, American Indians didn't just randomly attack the pioneers on the trails. The trails did pass through American Indian homelands that had been there since time immemorial, and that caused problems. While there were occasional confrontations and even some outright battles, remember that the American Indians helped the pioneers with stuck wagons, or traded food or horses, in exchange for clothing or rifles. The pioneer trails had many challenges, both in terms of nature and the behavior of people.

Oregon Trail

The Oregon Trail covered 2,170 miles. It began in Independence, Missouri. It ended in the Willamette Valley of Oregon. The trail went through land that would be the states of Kansas, Nebraska and Wyoming. Fur trappers on foot or on horseback started the trail. Over time, they cleared the trail so that wagons could roll over it. People tried to make the Oregon Trail better each year. Pioneers built bridges and ferries to make travel easier.

Many pioneers took the trail to go to Oregon. But the eastern part of the trail was also used by people traveling to California, Utah and Montana. The Oregon Trail went through the homelands of the Cheyenne and Pawnee nations. Around 400,000 pioneers used the Oregon Trail.

The California Trail

This trail started off with the Oregon and Mormon Trails. It mostly followed the Platte, North Platte and Sweetwater rivers. It branched off and headed toward San Francisco, California. By the mid-1800s, thousands used this trail to make their way to California, seeking gold.

Mormon Trail

The Mormon Trail began in Nauvoo, Illinois. This was the central city for a religious group called Mormons. The Mormons stayed in Nauvoo from 1839 to 1846. But Mormons had many difficulties with their neighbors, and in the spring of 1846 they chose to head west to find a new home. Around 70,000 Mormons took the Mormon Trail from 1846 to 1869. Most of them went to Utah, with all their belongings in wagons. Some of them carried their things in small wooden carts that they pushed or pulled by hand. Pioneers on the Mormon Trail ended their trip in the Salt Lake Valley, in Utah. East of Wyoming, the Mormon Trail and the Oregon Trail were nearly the same. In Bridger, Wyoming, the Mormon Trail changed direction to head toward Utah. In 1869, the transcontinental railroad was completed. After that, people didn't take the Mormon Trail to get to Utah. Instead, they took the train.

Bozeman Trail

When people found out that there might be gold in Montana, they worked to get there as fast as they could. The Bozeman Trail followed parts of ancient American Indian paths. It was named for a man named John Bozeman, who created it in 1863. He helped build a route from the Oregon Trail straight to Montana. The trail went along with the Oregon Trail for awhile. Then, in Wyoming, it branched off of the Oregon Trail and took pioneers to Virginia City, Montana. Once in Virginia City, they could look for gold. The Bozeman Trail went across Crow Indian territory, and also some of the lands of the Arapaho, Cheyenne and Lakota nations.

It took several months to go from one end of these trails to the other. Pioneers had to prepare before making the trip. They began traveling in the spring. They walked all summer and through part of the fall before they got where they were going. People who left too late in the spring risked getting caught in winter snow before they reached their destination. A few pioneers died because of wild animals, drowning in rivers, severe injuries, or attacks on the trail. Many more died from illness or cold.

title: There's Gold in Them Thar Hills!
text:
When James Marshall agreed to work on a new water-powered sawmill at the fort of John Sutter, he had no idea what was in store. Like a lot of people out west, James had come to California from his home in the East to help build cities, not to find gold. But on January 24, 1848, there it was! Golden metal nuggets were shining up through the water in the mill's tailrace. James showed the shining metal to Mr. Sutter. Together, they read an article in an encyclopedia about gold. Soon they were convinced. They had found gold at Sutter's Fort!

At first, Mr. Marshall and Mr. Sutter tried to keep the discovery secret. But it didn't stay secret for long. There was a guy name Sam Brannan who owned a store at Sutter's Fort. As more gold was found, Sutter's employees began to pay for Brannan's store goods with gold nuggets. Brannan took them to San Francisco and showed them off. Soon, California was filled with prospectors! The gold rush made Sam Brannan rich. He stocked his store with the picks, shovels and pans that people used to hunt for gold. He'd buy a pan for $2, and sell it to a prospector for $15. In 1849, Brannan's store sold about $150,000 worth of goods each month. He was rich!

When the Gold Rush in California began, only a small number of Californians migrated to the goldfields to make their fortune at first. But word spread, drawing in prospectors first from nearby states. In 1849, a massive migration to California began. Around 90,000 people went to California in that year. About half came by sea, and about half came by land.

The dream of every 49er was to make it rich by collecting gold. But like Sam Brannan, many who made money didn't mine for gold at all. They served the needs of miners instead. Run by both men and women, businesses sprang up in every mining town. They sold goods that the miners needed, washed their clothes, cooked their meals and more.

Before the Gold Rush, California was sparsely populated and relatively unknown to the rest of the world. But the new immigrants brought great change. They built towns and cities. They created a state constitution. They held elections. They even convinced the U.S. to make California a state in 1850.

The Gold Rush brought a major increase in population. It also led to a huge increase in wealth. San Francisco grew from 500 residents in 1847 to 150,000 residents in 1870. The railroad from the east coast to the west coast was completed in 1870. People and goods could now travel much faster across the country.

Westward expansion increased quickly due to the California Gold Rush. In the time before the Gold Rush, only around 2,700 settlers had made their way to California. By the end of the Gold Rush, there were at least 300,000 settlers in the state. Gold laid the foundation for the state of California!

The Gold Rush had a big impact on people of all kinds. Some of those people were newcomers to California. Others had been there for generations.

For a look at how the Gold Rush changed life for California's American Indians, visit the online version of this article and look for a video called, "The Gold Rush and California's Indians."

title: Hastings Cutoff: A Wrong Turn for the Donner Party
text:
Not everyone who set out for a new life in the West found it. The journey was long and hard enough that some westward-bound groups met with disaster.

The Donner Party was a group of American pioneers led by George Donner and James F. Reed. Their journey is one of the most tragic of all the stories about people moving west.

The Donner party left Illinois in May of 1846. This was late in the season. Still, the party set out for California, carrying their belongings in wagons pulled by oxen. The group turned off the main trail to try a new route called the Hastings Cutoff. They were told the new path would be easier. There was no way they could have known it, but taking the shortcut was a big mistake.

On the new trail, the travelers encountered rugged, dry terrain. The ground damaged their wagons. There was little grass or water for their animals. Day after day the pioneers were forced to repair broken wagons and search for animals that ran away. These things slowed them down.

By the beginning of November 1846, the settlers had reached the mountains of Sierra Nevada. They were trapped by an early snowfall. The storm caused icy conditions and 10-foot snowdrifts. The party was low on supplies, and the weather forced them to set up camp for the winter. During the winter, many people died. For food, many people ate the bark of trees or boiled the residue from old animal hides. Several people starved to death.

There were 87 members of the party at the beginning of the trip. Only 48 survived to reach California. One of the survivors was Virginia Reed. She was the daughter of James F. Reed, one of the original captains of the group. She was just thirteen years old during the hard trip to the West. She wrote a book about the trip, called "Across the Plains in the Donner Party." Perhaps you can find it in your library. Her writings make a great primary source in the study of this sad story.

title: Let's Write
text:
A gold prospector is a person who searches for gold. Pretend that you are a gold prospector in
1849. Write a paragraph about your journey to the West. What is life like in your mining camp?
Be sure to include facts about what happened in 1848 to cause the Gold Rush.

title: Dame Shirley Talks About the Mining Life
text:
Louise Clappe was born in New Jersey, grew up in Massachusetts, and went west with her husband, Fayette, during the Gold Rush. During their gold rush adventures, Louise wrote 23 long letters. All of the letters are written to Louise's sister, Molly. Louise calls herself Dame Shirley in the letters. Those letters are famous now. They're great primary sources for studying the Gold Rush. Below, you'll find parts of two of the letters Louise wrote. In the letters, she calls her husband "F."

In this letter, Louise writes about how hard it was to travel by mule, with little food:

"Although we had eaten nothing since noon the day before, I bore up bravely until we arrived within two miles of the rancho, when courage and strength both gave way, and I implored F. to let me lie down under a tree and rest for a few hours. He very wisely refused, knowing that if I dismounted it would be impossible to get me onto my mule again, and we should be obliged to spend another night under the stars, which, in this enchanting climate, would have been delightful, had we possessed any food; but, knowing that I needed refreshment even more than I did rest, he was compelled to insist upon my proceeding."

In this letter, Louise writes about how dangerous it was to risk money on a gold mining project, called a "claim":

"It is impossible to tell whether a claim will prove valuable or not. F. has invariably sunk money in every one that he has bought. Of course a man who works a claim himself is more likely, even should it turn out poor, to get his money back, as they say, than one who, like F., hires it done. A few weeks since, F. paid a thousand dollars for a claim which has proved utterly worthless. He might better have thrown his money into the river than to have bought it, and yet some of the most experienced miners on the Bar thought that it would pay."

Letters like these are great ways to learn about what people from history thought and felt about the places they lived and the things that happened to them.

title: Then and Now: How Do We Mine for Gold?
text:
Mining for gold is hard work, but there are tools and methods that can make it easier. Here's a look at just a few of the ways that people looked for gold:

Panning

Gold panning was the first method used by miners in the Gold Rush. Panning uses a large, shallow pan to collect sand in the river. The pan is dipped under water and shaken to separate the gold from the sand and other materials. The sand floats away. But gold is heavier than sand. It sinks to the bottom of the pan.

Sluicing

Miners also used sluice boxes to find gold. Sluice boxes were long, wooden boxes with ridges along the bottom. They would place sand at the top of the box. Then they would let the current carry the sand over the ridges. The ridges would catch gold as the sand passed over them.

Dredging

Some people looked for gold by using a process called dredging. In this process, boats collected sediment from the river bottom. Then the sediment passed through screens to separate the gold from the rest of the minerals in the water.

Hydraulic Mining

Hydraulic mining used water jets to spray away large sections of riverbanks. The material that washed away from the riverbank passed through large sluice boxes. Hydraulic mining could sift through a lot of dirt in a hurry, but it was pretty damaging to the environment. It destroyed large sections of the riverbanks.

Underground Hard Rock Mining

Larger mining operations in the Gold Rush hired miners to build tunnels underground. They looked for veins of gold in the hard rock below. Miners collect ore, which is then crushed and processed to separate the gold. Hard rock mining is still done all over the world today. But machinery makes it possible to go much deeper into the ground.

Lots of people try their hand at panning for gold, even today. If you'd like to know how it's done, visit the online version of this article and check out the video!

title: Tennessee 49ers - Life on the Overland Trail
text:
"That video Ms. Johnson showed us about the Gold Rush was so interesting!' said Natalia. "Imagine how exciting it must have been to travel to California hoping to strike it rich! When people heard about the discovery of gold in 1848 and 1849 it only makes sense that they wanted to try it for themselves. People from all over the United States, and all over the world, wanted to get in on the action! I think I might have been tempted to go west myself!"

"Yeah, Natalia," said Steven. "I can definitely see why people would want to head west to look for gold. Some said that in one day, a prospector could make 10 or 15 times as much money as a laborer could back in the East. But look at this journal I found in the library. It was written by a Tennessee 49er as she traveled across the country to California."

"Wow," said Natalia, looking at the journal. "She describes how hard life was for prospectors headed west."

"Yeah," said Steven, "Day after day, she and the other 49ers with her had to fight to survive and keep going. They had to deal with heat, cold, rain, snow and more. People got sick and rarely had the help of a doctor. And they had to worry about hunger and thirst. It seems like getting to California was really tough."

"That's true," said Natalia. "And even if you made it to California in one piece, there was still no guarantee that you would find gold." She noticed something about the journal. "Steven, look!" she said. She was excited. "The woman who wrote this journal was from Tennessee. Like other 49ers from Tennessee, she was too far from the California Trail and the Mormon Trail to use either of those trails to get to California. Instead, she and her group used the Butterfield Overland Trail. They left from Memphis and met up with other pioneers who had left St. Louis, in Fort Smith, Arkansas. I bet we could travel back in time to meet her using her journal."

"Let's do it!" said Steven. They touched the journal together. They felt the rush of wind, and before they knew it, they were siting on a pile of sacks and other baggage, bouncing along a rutted trail.

"We're here, Natalia!" said Steven. "Right in the back of a real wagon!"

"Oh my, it's so dusty. And hot," said Natalia. "Steven, you can definitely tell there's a lot of livestock around."

"How can you tell?" asked Steven.

"By the smell," said Natalia. Steven laughed.

"Yeah, I also smell coffee. I remember reading that everyone on the trail drank coffee, even the children! They said it made the bitter water they found on the trail taste better."

"Man, Natalia, this wagon ride is so bumpy. I feel like my teeth are going to rattle out of my head!"

"Let's get down and walk," said Natalia. It looks like most everyone else is walking. The wagons appear to be completely full of supplies, so there is not much room for riding. Fortunately, the wagon train is going pretty slow. An average day on the trail only covered about 15 miles."

"Natalia, if you think about it, going slow and steady was necessary if you wanted keep it up, day after day, for five months," said Steven. "That's how long the journey took. Some of the 49ers traveled over 2,000 miles to get to San Francisco."

"Whoa, Steven, I think I hear the sound of a river in the distance. If they are about to cross a river, we better head back home. River crossings were some of the most dangerous events on the trail. Wagons overturned, people drowned and many others were injured."

"You're right, Natalia. Let's head back and prepare our report for our classmates!"

You can see the video that got Steven and Natalia excited about the Gold Rush! Just visit the online version of this article!
