title: Back to Ida's Shop
text:
When Steven and Natalia entered the antique store, they heard the bell on the door jingle. The shop was so full of wonderful things, there was hardly any room to walk. Almost immediately, they heard the voice of Ida, the owner of the shop.

"I'm coming!" sang out Ida cheerfully. In a moment, they saw her. Her white, kinky hair stood out on all sides of her head. Her red-framed glasses hung on a chain around her neck. "Ah! I remember you two!" she said.

Natalia smiled. "It's nice to see you again, Ida," she said. "In school, we're studying about life in the northern states in the 1800s."

"Yeah," said Steven. "We each have to do a report. We thought there might be a thing or two in your shop that we might learn from."

"What are the topics of your reports?" asked Ida.

"I think I'll do mine on how the railroad changed the way people and goods were transported from one place to another. We studied the railroads a little bit when we were learning about the Industrial Revolution. I'd love to learn more. Do you have anything railroad-y around here?"

Ida laughed. "I bet we can find something," she said. "And how about you, young lady?"

"Trains are so cool," said Natalia. "But I think I'm going to do a report on how people lived in the North. I'm interested in how they lived, thought and felt."

"That sounds interesting," said Ida. "What do you know already?"

"Well, I know that the industries of the North and South really had a big impact on what they thought. The economy in the North was based on machines and factories. The economy in the South was all about growing stuff on farms and plantations."

"Sounds like you already know quite a lot," said Ida.

"Yeah," said Steven. "It's crazy how much Natalia knows."

Ida smiled. "You asked about something to do with trains. Something ... um ... railroad-y, I think you called it. I've got something you may be interested in."

Steven and Natalia followed Ida to a wooden box. It was filled with what looked like enormous, rusty nails.

"Railroad spikes!" said Steven.

"Yes," said Ida. "These were gathered from the grounds of the New York Central Railroad in the 1800s. The truth is, you never know what you're going to find in my antique shop."

"Wow!" said Steven. He took a step toward the box of railroad spikes.

"Hang on!" said Natalia. "What's this on the floor?" She pointed to a small, black-and-white photo that looked like it had fallen to the floor. The children bent down to get a closer look.

"It looks like an old postcard," said Steven. It says, "1853 Exhibition of the Industry of All Nations at New York's Crystal Palace."

"That's in New York City! We watched a video about that in Ms. Johnson's class!" said Natalia.

The two friends reached down to touch the postcard. Suddenly, they felt the rush of wind. The box of railroad spikes disappeared. Ida disappeared. The antique shop disappeared. Steven and Natalia found themselves standing in an enormous building. They heard the noise of thousands of voices. They were in the Crystal Palace!

"Wow!" breathed Natalia, looking around. "It's beautiful!" They looked around the huge space. It seemed to be made entirely of glass and cast iron.

"Look!" said Steven, grabbing a pamphlet off of the floor. "It says this is the Crystal Palace. It's the largest building in the country. See that dome," he said, pointing up to the clear, sparkling dome high above them. "It is one hundred feet in diameter and 148 feet high. This is where Elisha Otis first showed off his elevator with safety breaks. That elevator made modern skyscrapers possible."

"It says this place is called The Temple of Industry and Art," remarked Natalia. "Seems fitting for New York City."

"I see a lot of art and neat inventions. But I wish we could learn more about how working class people lived in the city," Natalia said.

Steven looked around. "These people don't really look like the working class," he said. "Maybe people in the working class don't come here much."

"Why not?" said Natalia.

"Probably because it's ten dollars for a season ticket," replied Steven pointing to the pamphlet.

"That's not bad."

"Well in today's dollars it's about $250."

"Oh," said Natalia, "That's a lot."

"Let's go out into the city," said Steven, "and see how people who couldn't afford these prices lived."

"Sounds good!" said Natalia.

Steven and Natalia saw a video about the Crystal Palace in Ms. Johnson's class. Would you like to see it too? Visit Studies Weekly online, and look for a video called, "What is a Crystal Palace?"

title: The Irish Influx
text:
Potatoes originated in the Americas but soon traveled to Europe and became popular food staples. Ireland's poor relied on potatoes for their main source of food. From 1845 to 1849, the potato crops in Ireland were almost completely wrecked by a type of mold. When the crop failed, people starved. The potato famine led many to leave their homes and come to the United States. In the 1840s and 1850s, about a million people came from Ireland. Many lived in poverty and faced bigotry from those who were already here. Some didn't like the Irish immigrants. They thought the Irish would take jobs from other people who needed them. Many of the Irish who could afford it went west, where they had heard there was lots of land. But the majority of Irish immigrants stayed in New York City or Boston. They shaped the history of these cities, and others, too. The large influx of Irish immigrants had a big impact on American culture. Many Irish people went on to do great things.

Since the first explorers, this has always been a place filled with people who came here from other lands. In the 1800s, the U.S.A. became, more than ever, a nation of people from all over the world. You may have heard some call our country a "melting pot." To understand this term, think of making a soup. Into a pot of water go all sorts of things: meat, veggies, spices, noodles and more. The things you put into the pot join together to make a single, great-tasting soup. Some looked at America that way: lots of different folks came to our land. And as long as they followed the laws of their new home, each new immigrant added to the great flavor of the whole "soup." Get it?

Irish immigrants were just a small part of the story of how folks from other lands have shaped this country. To look at another immigrant group, visit the online version of this article. You'll find a video called, "Asian American Cultural Contributions Intro."

title: The New York Central Railroad
text: Hello all! Steven here. Remember how we were about to travel back in time by touching a box of railroad spikes in Ida's shop. Then Natalia found that postcard. It turned out okay, because we got a real look at life in the cities of the North by visiting New York. That was incredible, wasn't it? When we got home, though, I was still thinking about railroads. So I hit the library. I learned about the New York Central Railroad company. It was founded in 1853, and lasted for more than a hundred years. The area around New York was the center of economy for a huge region of the country. It had a busy harbor connecting it to the rest of the world. It had canals leading all over the state and beyond. The New York Central Railroad company took people and cargo to places all over the North. Rails led to Pennsylvania, Ohio, Michigan, Illinois, Massachusetts and West Virginia. It even had tracks that went to parts of Canada. I'll tell you, when you can't go back in time, thank goodness for libraries!

title: Let's Write
text: It is New York in 1853. You are a recent immigrant from Ireland. Write a letter home to tell your parents about America. Describe your hopes and fears for the future. Use the articles you've read to help you imagine what your life might have been like. What details would you want to share with your family?

title: A Visit to New York in the 1800s
text:
Natalia and Steven exited the Crystal Palace and started walking.

"It sure doesn't look like New York City," said Natalia. They expected to see enormous buildings. Instead, they saw single family homes with yards.

"I think we're going the wrong direction," Steven said as the houses got more spread out and the area looked more and more rural. "We need to go the other direction, down to where all the big buildings are."

"Alright," said Natalia, "In a second. Since we're here, we should look around."

They wandered around until they saw a sign. The sign said Seneca Village.

"What is this place?" Steven asked.

"Oh!" exclaimed Natalia. "I know what this is. It was founded in the 1820s. African Americans purchased enough land to enable them to vote. The village population mostly consisted of African Americans with some Irish immigrants. It was a thriving community until the city government came in and took all their land to build Central Park in 1858."

"Wow, so they just lost their homes?" Steven asked.

"Yep," said Natalia. "They were paid for them, but yeah, they had to leave."

"Where did they all go?"

"I guess some of them went downtown. That's where all the factories and docks are." After a very long walk, the two friends entered an industrial district.

"Phew," said Steven. "I can smell the docks. It smells like fish."

"Let go see," said Natalia.

The docks were a buzz of activity. There were new immigrants disembarking from passenger ships. There were cheers and laughter as families and friends were reunited. It was punctuated by the shouts of grimy dock workers unloading and loading ships and freight cars. The men scurried around, stacking barrels and crates, tying stacks of goods so they wouldn't fall into the water. One man slipped from a tall stack of crates. He hit the ground with a thud.

"Oh no!" exclaimed Natalia. They watched as the man was helped up. He was shaken but alive.

"He was lucky," said Steven. "This is dangerous work."

"So is that," Natalia said pointing to a factory spewing thick black smoke a few blocks over.

"Let's go see," said Steven. They pushed their way through the crushes of people.

"Let's go through here," Steven said pointing down a street.

"I think this is an immigrant neighborhood," said Natalia. Everywhere there were kids outside playing with hoops and sticks, selling rags, or just chasing their friends around. Women carried babies and their shopping. A group of women were doing their washing.

"Their clothes can't be getting that clean," said Natalia as they watched one woman lean out of her window and hang up her washing to dry. Natalia brushed soot off of Steven's shoulders. "It's so dirty here."

"That's why there was such a push to build Central Park," said Steven. "To give people a place to get some fresh, clean air and let kids experience nature."

They made their way to the factory and opened the heavy door.

"I'm glad it wasn't locked," said Natalia. "Usually the owners locked the doors to keep workers in and strangers out. It was dangerous if there was ever a fire." The factory floor was loud. The friends plugged their ears at the noise generated by the heavy clanking machines. Young women stood in front of the machines, feeding thread into the machines.

"Oh!" said Steven, shocked. "There are children in here." Small children, smaller than Natalia and Steven, scurried among the machines when something would get stuck inside the intricate sets of parts.

"They used children because their hands were tiny enough to get into the machines and change a part or pull out something stuck in there. Many kids lost limbs or even their lives."

"Let's get out of here," Steven said, "It's sweltering." They went back outside. It was cooler, but it was still hard to breathe.

"Watch out!" Steven yelled as Natalia was about to step into the street. She shrieked as she narrowly missed being run over by a horse.

"It's dangerous here," Steven observed. Then he sneezed, "Ah-ah-ah-choooo!"

"Bless you," said Natalia. "I don't blame you for sneezing. It's all the horse manure," Natalia said. There were piles of it everywhere, covered in flies.

"The people, the wagon wheels, and the horses grind the dried manure up into a powder that blows everywhere. Between the manure, the poor quality of the housing, and the factory smoke, a lot of the poor people who live in the city are sick much of the time. The middle class and the upper class could afford to escape to the country, but the poor had nowhere to go," Natalia explained.

"All of this reminds me of the video we watched in Ms. Johnson's class. You know, the "Moving to North America" video."

A pig ambled down the street. The friends stared for a moment. Then they laughed.

"That would be an unusual sight for our time," said Natalia. "But we've traveled to a time before there were many laws about keeping the city clean. There was such a huge influx of immigrants in the 1840s and 1850s that the city was overwhelmed with the population swell."

"A population of people, and also animals," said Steven.

"Obviously," said Natalia.

"Where were all these people living?" Steven asked.

Natalia pointed to a building across the street. "There. Tenements. It's basically an apartment building. But these tenements were often small, crowded and dirty." They walked into the building.

"So there's one family per floor?" Steven asked.

"Ha!" said Natalia. "Not by a long shot. Tenements were usually five to six stories, with four apartments on each floor. Families back then were large, and they would take in boarders to help pay the rent. You could have twelve people, maybe more, in each apartment. And we've come here before the Tenement House Law of 1867 which dictated some minimum standards. A lot of these tenements didn't have adequate bathrooms. Some apartments didn't even have a window."

"Wow," said Steven. "Things sure have changed from the mid-19th century."

"Yes," said Natalia. "This was quite a visit. Do you still have the postcard?"

"I do," said Steven. "It's right here."

They both touched the postcard, and before they knew what was happening, the sights, sounds and smells of New York in the 1800s disappeared. They were headed back to Ida's antique shop, with quite a story to tell!

You can see the "Moving to North America" video. Just visit the online version of this article.

title: Slavery and New York City
text:
Slavery was a part of the story of New York until it was outlawed in 1827. Even after that, many African Americans faced a lot of bigotry. For instance, white people could vote, but black people had to own at least $250 worth of land before they could vote.

Sometimes, African Americans could only take difficult and low-paying jobs. There were many of them in New York. It was a hub for enslaved people escaping from the South. From New York, some made their way to Canada. The laws in the U.S. still said that slave owners could find people who had escaped and take them back to the South, even if they were living in the North when they were found. So African Americans in New York City would often fight to keep formerly enslaved people safe from capture and harm.

Sometimes free Blacks would be kidnapped in New York City, taken to the South, and sold into slavery. This even happened to children.

Life was difficult for African Americans in both the North and the South. We've made a lot of progress since then. We hope we make even more.

title: Sectionalism
text:
The country was divided into 3 sections: North, South and West. Tensions between North and South resulted in the Civil War. The West stayed mostly out of it, focusing on mining, ranching and agriculture. The Gold Rush sent thousands of people west in search of fortunes only a few would find. The “free” land for farming and “free” animals for ranching were big draws as well.

So what were the issues in the North and South? You may need to also use next week’s issue to get all the answers.

title: Plantation Life
text:
"Belle Meade Plantation!" said Steven. He climbed down from the bus in the warm sunshine. "What a class trip! This'll make a great news report for our next show!"

"You bet it will," said Natalia. "Look how big this mansion is! It makes a perfect museum, but I'm not sure I would want to live in it. There are too many rooms to clean."

"Yeah," said Steven. "It took a lot of people to take care of the mansion and the land around it. Remember the video we watched in class before we left? There were many enslaved people working on a plantation, and the plantation owners were busy too."

"Hey Steven," said Natalia, "the house is beautiful, but if we are going to produce a good news report, we need to see the whole plantation. All this beauty is supported by a terrible practice. Let's go look at the quarters where people lived in slavery."

"You're right, Natalia. We are news reporters, after all," said Steven.

Steven and Natalia walked toward a small wooden cabin with two rooms.

"Wow, Steven," said Natalia. "This cabin is a lot different than the mansion. It's so plain. There are only two rooms, and a few pieces of furniture."

Natalia reached out to touch a wooden chair. At the same time, Steven tripped and grabbed the chair to catch himself. Hardly realizing what was happening, they both felt the rush of wind. They were headed back in time!

When they stopped, Steven and Natalia looked around. They were in the very cabin they'd left only moments ago. Only now it was the Antebellum South!

"I guess we'd better do some exploring for our news report," said Natalia.

"I'm glad we could come explore the South this week, Steven," said Natalia. "We reported on the North last week. Now we can cover the South too."

"What do you say about splitting up?" said Steven. "We can learn more if we each research different areas."

"Sounds good," said Natalia. "Why don't you go learn more about transportation and business? I'll go look into the social life and political beliefs of the people."

"Okay," said Steven. "Let's go!"

Steven and Natalia left the cabin and headed towards the fields of the plantation. They walked past the fields of cotton, tobacco, sugar and rice. Enslaved people were scattered through the fields, working and sweating in the heat. The children stood still for a moment, too saddened to move.

We'll leave Steven and Natalia to do their exploring. But you can catch their news report when you're ready to turn the page! In the meantime, you can check out the video you heard Steven talking about. Just visit Studies Weekly online and look for a video called, "Drayton Hall: Life in a Colonial Plantation."

title: Think & Review Questions
text:
1. List 3 differences between the North and the South during the Antebellum Period.

2. What is the word used to describe a plantation owner?

3. How do you think the differences in climate may have affected the developments of the North and South?

4. What are the parts of the word "Antebellum," and what do they mean?

title: The Antebellum South
text:
It was the day after the trip to the Belle Meade Plantation. Natalia and Steven were in the TV studio. Their show was only minutes away!

"Hi, Steven. Are you ready to report on all the things you learned at the plantation?" said Natalia.

"Of course!" said Steven. "But you'll have to wait until I give my report to hear about it."

Natalia and Steven sat down in front of the camera. The red light came on. Their show had begun.

"Hello, fellow students," said Natalia. "I'm Natalia, and this is Steven. We are here to tell you about the Antebellum South. The South was very different from the North. Many people in the North lived in cities. Most people in the South lived on plantations and farms in the countryside. The nearest town could be miles away. Travel by horse was the fastest way to go over land. But it was still pretty slow. Farmers and planters had to make sure they could grow their own food. Farmers needed to be able to feed everyone living on their land. They also needed to be able to make most of what they needed, like clothes, tools and buildings."

"They had to make their own tools?" asked Steven.

"That's right," said Natalia. "They made and repaired lots of things, right on the farm or plantation."

"Hmm," said Steven. "I'm not sure I'd survive if I needed to make everything I need. For example, I don't know a thing about making smartphones. Do you?"

"Um ... I'm afraid not," said Natalia. "But back to what I was saying: the South was divided into three groups, or 'classes.' The planters were the class at the top. Planters were the ones who owned plantations. They were the wealthiest people in the South. Then came the poor white farmers. The lowest class was made up of enslaved African Americans. There were also others treated as part of the lower class, such as American Indians, in the South. Now Iet's turn it over to Steven. Steven, what other things did you learn about the South?"

"Thanks, Natalia. I discovered that the economy in the South was all about cotton. In fact, the South was known as the 'Cotton Kingdom.'"

"Was there an actual king?" asked Natalia.

"Not a king, just a king crop. They called it 'King Cotton.' Cotton was the most important crop in the South."

Natalia added, "Think of the clothes you wear, and the sheets on your bed, and the linens on the table, and the stuffing for sofas, and everything else we use cotton for, even today. Cotton is all around us."

"Right," said Steven. "And the cotton industry depended on one terrible thing."

"What's that?" said Natalia.

"It's the thing you were talking about before, Natalia," said Steven. "Slavery. The industry was run by the work of enslaved African Americans. Planters did not pay them, and they treated the slaves as their property. They saw them as a necessary part of cotton production. Before machinery was invented to pick cotton, it had to be picked by hand. Picking cotton by hand takes a lot of time. Slave labor made growing cotton much more profitable. It did not matter how much time it took to pick the cotton because the planters were not paying the people who were picking it. People in the South wanted to keep their economy strong. They saw slavery as the best way to do that. As long as they had unpaid labor, they could keep growing cotton like crazy."

"Yeah," said Natalia. "I learned a lot about slavery, too. I didn't enjoy it. I'm glad we got rid of that practice."

"Everybody's glad about that," said Steven.

"Did you learn anything else?" asked Natalia.

"You bet I did," said Steven. "I learned that there were fewer large plantation owners than most people realize. Only a select few were wealthy enough to own a large plantation. Only the wealthy could afford to enslave enough people to work a large piece of land. This meant that there were only a few people in the South making big profits from cotton. Many of the white farmers in the South were poor."

"You've told us a lot about industry in the South," said Natalia. "What about transportation? You were going to talk about that, too, weren't you?" said Natalia.

"Yes I was," said Steven.

"If people wanted to travel long distances, or if they wanted to ship goods from one place to another, steamboats were the way to do it. Steamboats were enormous river vessels moved forward by great big wheels that paddled them through the water. The boats were powered by steam."

"I bet that's why they were called 'steamboats,'" said Natalia. She grinned at Steven.

"Seriously?" asked Steven. "But it's true! Steamboats could transport large amounts of passengers, rice, tobacco and cotton."

"Thanks, Steven. It seems that the South was much different from the North. The economy of the South relied on farming instead of factories. The lifestyle was rural instead of urban."

"The word 'rural' means 'out in the countryside.' And the word 'urban' means 'in the city,'" said Steven, helpfully.

"Thanks, Steven," said Natalia. "And the best way to transport large amounts of goods was steamboat instead of train."

"Well, fellow students, thanks for watching!" said Steven. "I'm Steven."

"And I'm Natalia," said Natalia. "And that's our report on the Antebellum South."

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend that you are a reporter just like Natalia and Steven are. Think about the important things you learned today and write a news report about the Antebellum South. Write about the economy, slavery and transportation.

title: The Life of a Slave
text:
Neither Steven nor Natalia liked learning about slavery. Like you, they both wished that no one in our country had ever been enslaved. But that's just not how it was. As you heard from Natalia, as much as 1/3 of the population of the South was made up of African Americans kept as slaves. Even slaves who were treated kindly by their masters had very difficult lives. Most masters treated enslaved people like property, and not like people. Enslaved African Americans were looked upon as the lowest class, so they were treated worse than others. Let's take a look at what life was like for a slave:

Living quarters: Slaves lived in tiny cabins made of wood. They often had no windows. To save money and space, the slaveholder would squeeze as many as he could into one cabin.

Work life: Slaves worked from dawn to dark. Overseers or drivers would manage the slaves to make sure they completed their work. Some drivers were enslaved people themselves. They were rewarded for making sure the work got done. Domestic slaves worked in the house.

Food and Clothing: Some enslaved people only had rags to wear. Often, they were given shoes during the colder months. They got little food, and the food was often poor. Enslaved people didn't have much spare time, but what they had, they spent making clothes, fishing, or hunting for more food.

Slave Codes: Many states had laws called 'Slave Codes.' The codes stated that enslaved people were the property of the plantation owner. They could be bought, sold, auctioned or given as gifts.

Family: Marriages between slaves were not legally recognized. Most planters saw children as extra profit. Often, husbands, wives and children were separated and sold to other plantations, sometimes in other states.

To learn more about what life as an enslaved person might have been like, visit the online version of this article. There, you'll find a video called, "Slavery Intro."

title: Fanny Kemble
text:
Hello all. Natalia here. Ms. Johnson gave me an assignment. She wanted me to try to write a paragraph as if I were Fanny Kemble. Fanny was a real person. She was born in 1809. Fanny fought against slavery, even though her husband was a slave owner. This was a tough assignment, but here's what I came up with:

"I am an abolitionist. My husband, Pierce Butler, just inherited a plantation. He now keeps people in slavery. He doesn't like it when I speak my mind, but I know slavery is wrong. He tries to convince me that slavery is important to our economy in the South. He can say anything he wants about how important slavery is for our economy, but he is not going to change my mind. Slavery is a sin. It's wrong. And it's every human's duty to make sure slavery ends. I have been on our new plantation for four months and I have recorded the cruel and unjust treatment of enslaved people. I have gathered up all of my diary entries and letters and will publish them in a book. I want all of America to see the truth about slavery."

title: Auntie Bellum? Who's That?
text: In many places in today's issue, you've heard a fancy word. The word is "antebellum." It's a word that we use to describe the South before the Civil War. In fact, that's what the word means. We'll explain: The word antebellum is actually made up of two Latin words. Latin is a very old language, but there are a lot of words in English that come from Latin words. You can see the two words right in the word antebellum. The first word is "ante." That word means before. The other word is "bellum." That word means war. Is it starting to make sense? Put those words together, and you have a word that means before war. To talk about the antebellum South is to talk about the South before the Civil War. The things you learn, eh?

title: Life in the Antebellum Period: North vs. South
text:
The way it was in the North:

• Warm summers/cold winters
• Major cities located in the North
• Location of most factories
• Many people worked in factories
• Had public education
• Railroad was the main form of transportation for goods and people

The way it was in the South:
• Long hot summers/rainfall
• Mostly rural
• Plantation owners were the upper class
• Majority of population were farmers and enslaved African Americans
• Most people lived on self-contained plantations and farms
• Steamboat was the main form of transportation for goods and people

title: Point of View from a Historical Perspective
text:
A person’s point of view is the way he or she looks at and thinks about an event. Different people often experience history in a variety of different ways. Not everyone who experiences a historical event feels or thinks the exact same way about it.

A number of things determine a person’s point of view. Life experiences (positive and negative), future needs and wants, and an emotional connection to the event all influence a person’s point of view.

After reading this week’s Studies Weekly, consider all the different points of view of people living in the United States during the mid-1800s. After reading each of the primary source statements below, add one or two sentences to support the speaker’s point of view.

“I am naturally anti-slavery. If slavery is not wrong, nothing is wrong. I can not remember when I did not so think, and feel. And yet I have never understood that the Presidency conferred upon me an unrestricted right to act officially upon this judgment and feeling.” —Abraham Lincoln

“I know no South, no North, no East, no West, to which I owe any allegiance. I owe allegiance to two sovereignty, and only two: one is the sovereignty of this Union, and the other is the sovereignty of the state of Kentucky.” —Senator Henry Clay

“I shall see, this day … from the slave’s point of view. … What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July? I answer: a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.” —Frederick Douglass

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine that you had a chance to write an article to inspire others to join the fight for emancipation. Imagine that your article would even be published in The Liberator! What would you say? What would your argument be?

title: A Newspaper From the Past
text:
"That was one of the most intense trips we've ever taken!" Steven said as he stepped off the bus. Natalia nodded. "I don't get it, though," he continued, thinking about their adventure. "How could anybody ever think slavery was an acceptable thing? I mean, how could someone look at other humans and think it was okay to treat them that way. I don't understand."

"I know what you mean,” said Natalia. "But not everyone thought slavery was okay. I mean, there were tons of people fighting to end slavery, even before the Civil War."

“I guess so,” said Steven. “I wonder who some of those people were," he said. "Do you think ... ?”

“I’m way ahead of you!” said Natalia.

Ten minutes later, the two were at a table in the corner of the library, their noses in thick history books.

"Check this out!" Steven said. He held out a yellowed piece of paper. “I found something tucked between the pages of this book! It’s from something called The Liberator. It looks like a newspaper. Someone named William Lloyd Garrison published it. He was an abolitionist leader, and this newspaper was his approach to ending slavery. And look at the date: January 1, 1831."

"Oh, wow! What does it say?"

"It's about abolitionists!” said Steven.

"Abolitionists are people who fight against slavery. What are we waiting for?" Natalia asked.

Together the two reached down and touched the top page of the newspaper. They felt the familiar rush of wind as they were swept back in time.

When they finally stopped, Steven and Natalia looked around. They were standing in what looked like a great big office. The walls were lined with shelves packed with books and loose pages. An old typewriter sat on a desk near a window. Behind the desk sat a man with white hair and glasses. He had been staring at the typewriter. But now he was staring at them.

"Can I ... er … help you?" said the man, blinking. Steven and Natalia knew he must be surprised to see them suddenly appear in his study.

"Yes, sir," said Steven, stepping forward. "Sorry for the interruption. We’re in search of a man named William Lloyd Garrison. He publishes a newspaper called The Liberator. Do you know him?”

"I’m Garrison,” said the old man. “The Liberator is my newspaper.”

"Fantastic!” said Natalia. “Tell us all about it!”

"Well,” said Mr. Garrison, “I started in the paper business when I was 13. Working with newspapers feIt … oh, I don’t know … like a calling, I guess. I felt particularly inspired by a fellow named David Walker. He was a black man who spoke and wrote about ending slavery. Some people thought his ideas were a bit extreme, but they caught my imagination. I thought I might be able to help spread some of those ideas," he said.

"What kind of ideas?" Steven asked.

"Well,” said Garrison. He sat up straight in his chair. “I'd like to see the immediate emancipation of all slaves. Set ‘em free! The Liberator publishes articles that call attention to acts of slavery, and about those who work toward emancipation."

"Wow," said Natalia. "I can see why your paper was so popular!”

"Was?” Garrison smiled crookedly. Then he sighed. “Well, it's not that popular yet. However, I'm hoping this story I’m writing now will really put The Liberator on the map! It’s a story about the Pennsylvania Society for Promoting the Abolition of Slavery. They help young African American kids find jobs and get educations. I have high hopes for the article. I was working on it right here when you … um … arrived.”

Steven turned to Natalia. “I remember that group,” he said. There’s a video in Ms. Johnson’s class about them. It’s called, "Declaring Freedom for All." We gotta watch it when we get back!"

“When you get back … where?” asked Mr. Garrison.

“It’s a long story,” said Natalia. “And I bet your article is going to be a hit!”

Natalia wasn’t sure Mr. Garrison heard that last bit. The rush of wind had already begun, and the children were already sweeping forward through time.

You can watch the video Natalia mentioned. Just visit the online version of this article!

title: Women Abolitionists
text:
"Ugh!" Natalia slouched at her laptop. She had been searching the Internet all afternoon for articles about abolition. She had notes about William Lloyd Garrison, Frederick Douglass, David Walker and more. "Hmm," she thought. "All these great men. But what about girl power? Where were all the women in this fight? What was their approach to ending slavery?"

Natalia punched the keys, and words popped up in the search bar: “abolitionist women.” Her screen lit up with search results. She clicked on a name. “Sojourner Truth,” she said under her breath. “That’s quite a name.”

A page sprang to life. Natalia read.

Sojourner Truth was an enslaved person turned abolitionist. She spent her young life being bought and sold, over and over, by harsh slave owners. Back then, her name wasn’t “Sojourner” at all; her name was Isabella. People called her Belle for short. In 1826, when a master went back on a vow to free her, it was the last straw for Belle. She took her child, left her home, and set out for freedom.

As a free woman, Belle began a life of fighting slavery. In 1828, she sued her former owner to have her son given back to her, and became the first black woman to win a court case against a white man. In 1843, she gave herself the name “Sojourner,” and hit the road again, this time to preach about abolition. She spent almost 40 years speaking on slavery and women’s rights. Today, people look on her as an American hero. In fact, watch for her in the year 2020 in a place where she’ll be seen by millions: on the back of a new $10 bill!

"Wow!" thought Natalia. "Sojourner Truth took a white man to court and won? That's amazing!"

Excited about great women in the abolitionist movement, Natalia clicked back to her search results, eager for more. A set of words caught her eye: “Harriet Tubman…Underground Railroad.” Natalia blinked. "A Railroad?" She wondered. "Underground?"

Natalia clicked, and began to read.

Harriet Tubman was a leader before and after the Civil War. When she escaped from slavery her religious beliefs made her want to help others, too. Risking her life, she rescued more than 300 people from slavery by using another approach: the Underground Railroad. It wasn’t really a railroad at all. It was a system of secret roads, safe houses and helpers.

Harriet Tubman kept fighting slavery all during the Civil War. She was an armed scout and a spy for the Union Army. She was also the first woman to lead an armed expedition in the war. It was a raid on the Combahee River that liberated more than 700 slaves!

Knowing all this, it's no wonder that Tubman was chosen to replace Andrew Jackson on the $20 bill.

Natalia stopped reading, and settled back in her chair with a grin on her face. "This is perfect. I didn't find one female abolitionist leader; I found two. With such great examples, it’s exciting to think about what someone like me might do for a cause I believe in! I can't wait to tell Steven about this!"

title: A Song to Fight for Freedom
text:
There’s a famous song that people like to sing on New Year’s Eve. You’ve probably heard it. It’s called “Old Lang Syne.” The name sounds a little strange, but if you heard it, you’d probably recognize it. You'd probably say, “Oh! That song.”

As one approach to end slavery, William Lloyd Garrison wrote a song called “I Am An Abolitionist.” He wrote words to the same tune as that famous old New Year’s Eve song. You’ll remember Mr. Garrison. He’s the abolitionist leader who published The Liberator. He’s the guy that Steven and Natalia visited in today’s issue.

The song had four verses. Below, find the words to just one of them. You may not understand every word here, but you’ll get the idea.

I am an Abolitionist! Then urge me not to pause,
For joyfully do I enlist In Freedom’s sacred cause;
A nobler strife the world ne’er saw, th’enslaved to disenthral;
I am a soldier for the war, Whatever may befall.

title: Think & Review Questions
text:
1. Imagine what it was like to escape along the Underground Railroad. What difficulties do you think the slaves and conductors faced during their journey? Cite your sources from the Student Edition.

2. Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel is fictional. That means the story was completely made up. If everything in the story didn't actually happen, why was it so effective at changing the minds of so many people? Cite your evidence from the Student Edition.

3. Analyze the biography of Frederick Douglass. He was able to accomplish so many things without any real education. What kind of person do you think Douglass was since he was able to do so much with his life?

4. Harriet Tubman was an amazing person. She put herself at risk to help others gain a better life, and she worked hard to create equality in her world. Predict: If Harriet Tubman lived in today's world, what kind of injustices or inequalities do you think she'd fight against today?

title: Frederick Douglass
text:
Frederick Douglass is a famous African American who worked to free slaves during the Civil War. He wrote many books, like an autobiography called Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass. He is thought of as one of the greatest writers in American history.

Douglass was born the son of an African American slave mother and an unknown white father. Sophia Auld, the wife of his owner, broke the law and taught Douglass to read and write. Literacy set the stage for his success. He escaped from slavery and joined the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society in 1841.

Douglass spent time in England and Ireland, trying to keep from being captured as a runaway slave. After friends bought his freedom, he came back to the U.S. He organized two groups of African American soldiers during the Civil War.

After the war, Douglass worked for the government as a minister to Haiti. He believed all people deserved to be treated equally. He spent his life working toward that goal.

title: Map Your Way to Freedom
text:
This is a map of the routes used by Harriet Tubman and others as they traveled the Underground Railroad. Use the map to answer these questions.

To what country to the north were slaves traveling?

List three free states that slaves traveled through on their way to that country.

Some slaves traveled south. To what countries were they traveling?

Was Tennessee a free state or a slave state?

Did the Underground Railroad travel through Tennessee?

title: Nothing Like a Train Ride
text:
The Underground Railroad was one approach abolitionist leaders used to end slavery. But it really wasn’t a railroad at all. There were no trains or tracks. There were no crossings or signal bells. There were no cars. Instead, the Underground Railroad was a system of roads, safe houses and helpers used to get enslaved people safely to freedom in Canada.

The Underground Railroad relied on people called “conductors.” You’ve read a little bit about Harriet Tubman in this issue of Studies Weekly. She was one of the most famous conductors after she escaped from slavery. Some conductors pretended to be enslaved. That way, they could easily get onto plantations and into homes. There, they’d lead people away, and help them get to safety.

It was a long way from slavery to freedom. As people traveled, they spent nights at homes, churches or schools. These places were called “stations.” The helpers who owned those places were called “station masters.” They gave food, clothes and rest to those bound for freedom.

There were stations all over the place. There were some in Topeka, Kansas and Tarrytown, New York. There were others in Reading, Pennsylvania and Worcester, Massachusetts. There were stations in lots of other places, too!

It took a lot of money to run the Underground Railroad! That’s why another group became important. These people were called “shareholders.” They had money, and they used it to keep things moving.

Everything about the Railroad was a secret. The brave men and women who worked as conductors, station masters and shareholders risked big trouble. After all, helping slaves escape was against the law. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 said that slaves must be returned to their masters, even if they were found in free territory. But for many people, the risks were worth it. It’s hard to say just how many people were helped by the Underground Railroad, but some think it’s more than 100,000!

If you'd like to hear more about this part of history, take a look at the video, "The Underground Railroad."

title: Uncle Tom's Cabin
text:
Oh, man. Just breathe. I can do this, thought Steven. He gathered his notecards and slowly walked to the front of the room. This is just another book report. I can get through it.

Looking up at the class, Steven took a deep breath. Then, he began.

"Uncle Tom's Cabin is a novel written by a woman named Harriet Beecher Stowe,” said Steven. “The story follows an enslaved man named Uncle Tom. He suffers a lot in the book. That stuff is kind of hard to read about, but the book made slavery into a national issue in the mid-19th century. People all over the place learned what it was like to live in slavery. They reacted to it with a lot of emotion. In fact, that’s the way I reacted, too.” Steven stopped talking for a moment, thinking about how glad he was that the days of slavery were long gone. Then he continued.

“Some readers were angry,” he said. “They said that the things in the book were a lot worse than the things that happened in real life. Others felt like the book made them want to help in the fight toward emancipation. They wanted to put an end to the kinds of things they read about in the book.” Steven paused. But there was something else he wanted to say.

“There’s just one more thing,” he said. “This book really changed things. Abraham Lincoln knew about it. He even called Harriet Beecher Stowe 'the little lady who started a war.' He was talking about the Civil War, and he was probably kind of joking, but also kind of serious. Sounds like a pretty big deal to me.”

As Steven sat down, he felt like a different person. He felt great for surviving his book report, but there was more. He felt like a book could make a difference. After all, it had made a difference for him.

"Good job, Steven," said Ms. Johnson. "Let's follow that great report with a video about Harriet Beecher Stowe. It's called, "Harriet Beecher Stowe Intro."

You can watch too! Just visit the online version of this article!

title: A Woman Divided
text:
Shortly after Lincoln won the election in 1860, eleven states left the Union. Lincoln’s stance against slavery was too much for them. War was coming.

Many people had reasons to love both the North and the South. For these people, choosing a side to support must have been very difficult. Mary Todd Lincoln was such a person.

Mary Todd was born in Lexington, Kentucky, in December of 1818. Mary’s mom died when she was about six years old. Her father got married again, to a woman who treated Mary pretty badly.

With a difficult life at home, Mary studied hard in school. In the late 1830s, she went to Illinois to be with her sister. There, she met a man who came from a poor family. He had big goals as a politician. This man was Abraham Lincoln. They were married in 1842.

Mary and Abraham both loved politics and books. They were deeply in love with each other.

When war came, Mary was divided. Her family was from the South, and very much pro-slavery. Her husband was president, working to free the slaves. It must have been difficult for Mary. However, she stood by her husband's side and supported the Union. In fact, she even accompanied him to Washington and often gave him advice about what he should do.

Mary had many hardships as the 16th First Lady. She lost two of her sons, due to illness. She was sitting next to her husband at the theater when he was shot and killed on April 14, 1865.

Some say Mary Todd Lincoln never got over the heartbreak and loss in her life. However, she will always be remembered as a woman of strong will and great intelligence.

title: Compromises, Acts and Decisions
text:
Here's one of Steven and Natalia's broadcasts that you can deliver right in your own classroom. It's written like the script of a play. Ask your teacher to help you assign a person to read the part of Steven, and another student to read the part of Natalia. Have fun!

Steven: Testing … testing … is this thing on?

Natalia: Yeah. It’s on. The camera’s rolling too, Steven. It’s time for our show!

Steven: Okay. Hey, viewers. Today, we tackle a difficult subject. We're talking about how slavery became a national issue.

Natalia: We're focusing on the 1800s.

Steven: Yes. You may already know that in the 19th century, things were getting rough. The southern states wanted to keep enslaving people. The northern states wanted slavery to end. Some people called the states in the South “slave states.” They called states in the North states “free states.” Trouble was brewing!

Steven: The states tried to keep the peace by making big compromises. In a compromise, no one gets everything they want, but everyone gets something they want.

Natalia: That’s right. In 1820, there was a deal that allowed Missouri into the Union as a slave state. But Maine, a free state, was added as well. That way neither slave states nor free states had the upper hand in representation or votes.

Steven: That deal was called the Missouri Compromise.

Natalia: Another compromise came in 1850. This one let California into the Union as a free state. It also let Utah and New Mexico become territories, and decide for themselves if they’d like to allow slaves. What’s more, it created the Fugitive Slave Act. That act said that escaped slaves had to be returned to their owners in the South, even if they were found in free states.

Steven: That was called The Compromise of 1850. If you'd like to learn more, there’s a video to watch, right here in Ms. Johnson’s class. It's called, "The Compromise of 1850." Easy to remember, right?

Natalia: In 1854, Congress passed an act that allowed Kansas and Nebraska to decide for themselves whether or not to allow slavery in their borders. The act caused a lot of trouble. Both pro-slavery and anti-slavery people jumped into their wagons, headed to Kansas and Nebraska, and fought it out! Some of this fighting was just done with words. But some was actual violence. In the end, there was so much fighting and confusion about the votes that, Kansas wasn't allowed to become a state until later.

Steven: That act was called the Kansas-Nebraska Act.

Natalia: A few years later, in 1867, an important court case was decided. An enslaved person named Dred Scott tried to sue for his freedom. But the Supreme Court ruled that slaves weren't citizens. This meant they weren't protected by the laws or the court. What’s more, the case ruled that it was unconstitutional for Congress to say slaves were illegal in any state.

Steven: That was the Dred Scott Decision. It declared the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional.

Natalia: That's right, Steven. It was a time of confusion. The North and South were at odds. Slavery had become an issue so important that it was deciding the very shape of the nation.

Steven: The tension was rising. The stage was set for a major conflict. Could war be coming?

Natalia: Until next time, this is Natalia ...

Steven: ... and this is Steven, signing off!

title: Let's Write
text: Many people saw Lincoln's appearance and mannerisms as a flaw. He was not from a wealthy family, and some looked on him as not being high-class enough to be a good president. Do you think this is a flaw for a president to have? Or is it better that the president knows what it's like to be a regular citizen? Explain your ideas.

title: The Little Giant
text:
The election of 1860 was a big one. The whole country was tense about it. The North and the South were at odds over whether or not slavery should be legal. The next president would play a major role in which way the scales would tip.

Abraham Lincoln was up for election. So was Stephen A. Douglas. Douglas was a senator from Illinois. He was also a charmer. He was a great speaker. Plus, he was just over five feet tall. People called him "The Little Giant."

Douglas took politics seriously. As part of his work in the Senate he expanded the country's territory and built the Pacific Railroad. He wasn't for slavery. He wasn’t against it. In fact, historians today still argue over what his true feelings about slavery might have been. One thing’s for sure: he wanted to keep the Union together. He was very patriotic. He loved his country. It was hard for him to see its people fighting so much. He was one of the leaders fighting to pass the Compromise of 1850. He hoped to mend the crack slowly forming between the North and the South.

The public got to hear plenty from Douglas about his ideas. In 1858, he and Lincoln toured seven cities in Illinois. In each city, they held a debate. The debates between Lincoln and Douglas remain famous, even today. They’re the most famous presidential debates in the history of the country.

In the end, Stephen A. Douglas lost the election. People in his party didn't want to vote for someone who wasn't pro-slavery. Douglas chose to side with the North during the Civil War. He died less than a year after the war started.

title: The Elections of 1860 and 2012
text:
Every four years the U.S. voters elect a new president. In 1860, Abraham Lincoln ran. In 2012, Barack Obama, our first African American president, ran for reelection. Let’s take a closer look at these two important elections.

Election of 1860

In 1860, people from both the northern and southern states were worried, since they disagreed about slavery. This election was very unusual because there were four candidates instead of two. The Republicans nominated a lawyer from Illinois named Abraham Lincoln, who was against slavery. Before the election, the Democratic Party split into two groups. One group nominated Vice President John C. Breckinridge. The other Democratic group nominated Senator Stephen Douglas of Illinois. Douglas believed that people in each state had the right to decide about slavery for themselves. A third party, the Constitutional Union Party, nominated John Bell of Tennessee. Bell did not take a stand for or against slavery, but he did not want the South to secede. On November 6, 1860, the voters had to choose among four candidates. Abraham Lincoln won the election, with more votes than any of the other candidates. He also won the most votes from the Electoral College. In early 1861, he was sworn in as president.

Election of 2012

Barack Obama entered the 2012 election as the incumbent, or person who already holds the office. The Republican Party nominated Mitt Romney. On Tuesday, November 6, 2012, the two candidates competed to earn 270 electoral votes, the amount required to become president. Each state has a set number of electoral votes. The population of the state determines the number of electoral votes. For example, California has 55 electoral votes while Tennessee has 11 electoral votes. On election night, the votes started coming in. The race wasn’t as close as many thought it would be. The final results were 332 electoral votes for Barack Obama and 206 electoral votes for Mitt Romney. Obama was reelected President of the United States. Barack Obama was the first president in more than 50 years to win at least 51 percent of the national popular vote in two elections.

Think about what you learned about both elections. How were they alike and different? Compare the maps of 1860 and 2012. How did our country change?

title: Think & Review Questions
text:
1. Compare and Contrast: How was Lincoln's point of view on slavery different from Stephen Douglas' ideas? Use evidence from the Student Edition to support your ideas.

2. Why do you think that despite saying that he'd allow slavery to continue in the South, Douglas didn't get elected as president? Use evidence from the Student Edition to support your ideas.

3. Many of the acts passed during this time period allowed certain states to enter as a slave state or a free state. However, tensions always arose when the split of slave states and free states got too far away from being equal. Why was this?

4. What do you think of the actions of John Brown in his raid near Harper's Ferry?

title: John Brown
text:
"Let's all turn to page 208 in our history books," Ms. Johnson directed the class.

"Okay, page 2 - oh - 8," Steven exclaimed as he pulled out his book and began to flip through the pages.

Next to him, Natalia had already found the page. "It looks like we're talking about a man named John Brown today. I feel like I've heard of him..." she trailed off thoughtfully.

"John Brown was born in a small town in Ohio in 1800," Ms. Johnson began. "He was raised to be very religious, and he had strong anti-slavery beliefs. He was even one of the people who traveled to Kansas during the conflict.

"In 1857, Brown decided to go back east. He had a vision of a massive uprising. He wanted enslaved people to revolt against their masters. Brown thought it would be a simple matter of giving them the confidence to do it. He began to grow an army of sorts, for a raid near Harper’s Ferry in West Virginia. There was a government complex near there where weapons were manufactured for the army. Brown wanted to capture thousands of guns and give them to slaves for the uprising."

The bell rang, interrupting Ms. Johnson's lecture.

"That's all for today. We'll pick up our lesson on Monday. Enjoy your weekend!"

Outside the class, Steven expressed his frustrations to Natalia, "I can't believe we have to wait all weekend to find out about Brown and his raid. This is going to take forever."

"We can always look for answers ourselves," she said with a smile.

"You're right! Let's head to the library!"

A few minutes later, the two entered the library. The familiar scent of dust and books greeted them at the door.

"Where to start?" Steven asked.

"Over here." Natalia headed toward the history section with a spring in her step. Halfway down an aisle, she pulled out a book. "I knew Brown's name sounded familiar. I've heard this story before!" She opened the book and handed it to Steven.

"Wow!" Steven blurted. "He actually went through with the raid!"

"Yep," Natalia replied. "He took over a government building that housed a bunch of weapons and even held some hostages. But it didn’t work out for Brown. He never captured anything and a lot of people died, including two of Brown's sons. The raid was a failure."

"Look here," Steven said, pointing to a spot on the page. "He was found guilty of treason and murder. And his execution only made tensions worse. Yep. This guy definitely added fuel to the flames that led to the Civil War."

“That’s true,” said Natalia. “The fights in Kansas and the raid near Harper’s Ferry helped make slavery a national issue. But it’s also true that by this time, war was probably coming anyway. Not even people like Abraham Lincoln could stop that. In fact, his election in 1860 was the last straw for a lot of people. Wait. What's this?" Natalia pulled a small piece of paper out of the book. It had some scribbling on it, but they couldn't tell what it was. It looked like a scrap torn from the minutes of a meeting. They could make out a date. It said, "June 16, 1858."

"Let me see that!" Steven said, reaching for the small scrap. "That's a primary source! I wonder where it will take us?"

As Steven's fingers touched the page, the two were whisked back in time surrounded by the sound of rushing wind. When the rushing stopped, they found themselves in a crowd of people. Standing before them was a tall man in an even taller hat.

“That’s … that’s Abraham Lincoln!” stammered Natalia.

title: The Election of 1860
text:
Imagine that you're eating cookies with a friend. Your cookies all have red frosting. Your friend’s cookies all have blue frosting. Then a third friend comes along. That friend wants cookies too, but he only wants blue cookies. Your two friends will have to divide the blue cookies, while you keep all the red cookies. You’ll get more cookies than either of your friends.

In the election of 1860, Lincoln, Douglas, Breckinridge and Bell all wanted to be president. But the Democratic Party didn't agree on who to vote for. This divided their votes, just like dividing the blue cookies.

In the end, Douglas only won Missouri. Bell only won 3 states. Breckinridge won ten states. Lincoln didn't win a single southern state. Yet, he still won the election by winning the Northern states – just like winning all the red cookies.

Want to learn more about this election? Watch, "The Election of 1860 Intro" at Studies Weekly online.

title: Not the News We Were Hoping For
text:
In 1846, an enslaved person named Dred Scott had been taken to free states and free territories by his owners. So, Dred Scott tried to sue for his freedom. The case went all the way to the Supreme Court. In 1857, the Supreme Court ruled that slaves weren’t U.S. citizens. Because they weren’t citizens, they weren’t kept safe by federal laws or courts. The Court also said that it was against the law to tell a state that it couldn’t allow slavery.

The outcome became known as the “Dred Scott Decision.” It showed how slavery had become a national issue.

Many people were angry about the case. It is still denounced to this day. One sign from the time of the decision, announcing a local meeting, said:

“A public meeting will be held on Thursday at 7:00 to discuss the atrocious decision of the Dred Scott case, and other outrages to which colored people are subject under the Constitution.”

Discuss the sign with classmates. In 1868, the 14th Amendment guaranteed full citizenship rights to all African Americans.

title: Let's Write
text: What did the Confederate States earn from the battle of Fort Sumter? In two to three paragraphs, explain the importance of the Confederate Army's victory. Think about the effects that this battle had on the Confederate States' enemies. Also, think about the reasons Fort Sumter was an important location to protect.

title: Think & Review Questions
text:
1. What would have happened to the Union soldiers if they hadn't surrendered?

2. Why did the Confederate ships attack the Union vessel?

3. In two to three sentences, describe why the southern states wanted to maintain slavery.

4. The border states did not oppose slavery. Why didn't they leave the Union and join the Confederacy?

title: Border States: a Line Drawn in the Sand
text:
Imagine a line separating the northern states from the southern states. Some states were far north of the line. Some states were far south of the line. Others are right against the line: touching it, even. The states touching the line were known as the "border states." And they were very important during the war.

Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, West Virginia and Missouri all formed the border between the North and the South. All of them were slave states, but they also had firm beliefs in a strong, central government. They didn't want Lincoln to be president, but they also didn't want the country to split.

The border states were really valuable. A lot of crops were farmed and many animals were raised there. That meant they could help give soldiers the supplies they needed to win the war.

Lincoln knew that these states were important. In fact, he hoped that he could sway them to his side, even though they were slave states. He tried to win them over. But it didn't work. Lincoln couldn't convince the border states to side with the Union. He knew that the time for bargaining was over. He had to start making demands. In a lot of ways, this failure led him to write the Emancipation Proclamation.

In some ways, the border states were a bad place to be during the war. Because they were right in the middle of all the fighting, they fought, too. Brothers fought against brothers. Fathers and sons battled. Families fought their neighbors.

Where did each of the border states stand? Here’s a rundown:

Kentucky and Missouri tried to declare that they were neutral. But, with bloody battles all around, they couldn't hold on to that status. Even though the border states were formally pro-Union states, they were still divided. Both Kentucky and Missouri ended up having military camps for both sides within their borders.

Delaware always sided with the Union. They never even considered seceding.

Maryland was very divided on which side to choose. The Union even had troops in place in that state, just in case things went badly.

Virginia was also divided during the war. In fact, that's how we ended up with two states: Virginia and West Virginia. West Virginia wanted to side with the Union, and they split the state in two so they could.

In the end, each of these states played a role in helping the Union win the war.

title: SECEDE Acrostic
text:
Create an acrostic using the letters in the word, secede. For each letter, think of a phrase or topic that is a detail about this week’s learning. How do acrostics work? Like this:

W - war is a terrible conflict, usually over land and power, between two countries or sections of a country

A - armistice is a truce, or an agreement to stop fighting

R - radical times call for radical solutions; no one wants war but sometimes people feel it is the only way to solve a problem

Now, you try it.

title: Countdown to Battle
text:
Hey, everyone. Natalia and Steven here. We’re in the library. We wanted to know how a battle that lasted only 34 hours could start the Civil War. There had to be more to it, right?

Right! In fact, there were a bunch of big issues that pushed the fight over the edge. To help you get it, we've made a timeline for you. Check it out:

1. June 16, 1858: Lincoln is chosen as the Republican candidate for Senate. That means he gets to run in the Senate election. He gives his famous "House Divided" speech. Lincoln's ideas are a lot to take. He ends up losing.

2. May 16, 1860: Lincoln is chosen as a candidate for president. He'll get to run in the election.

3. November, 1860: Lincoln is elected the 16th President. Check out the file in the media tab called, "Tennessee and the Civil War - The Election of 1860 Intro." A lot of people in the South are really mad. Lincoln is against slavery, and they’re worried that they'll lose their rights.

4. December 20, 1860: South Carolina is the first state to secede from the Union. To secede means to leave.

5. January 1861: Lincoln tries to send food and medicine to Fort Sumter. Confederate ships block this attempt. Lincoln knows that the fort can't win against a land attack. In fact, all 60 of the fort’s cannons face the water.

6. February 1861: Six more states secede. They form the Confederate States of America. They send letters saying they have a right to all military forts within their territory.

7. March 1861: Lincoln takes office.

8. February-April, 1861: General Beauregard of the Confederate Army tries to make a deal. Major Anderson of the Union says, “No.” Fort Sumter slowly runs out of supplies.

9. April 12, 1861: The Confederates start shooting. Soldiers in the fort know they won't last long. Amazingly, no one is hurt.

10. April 13, 1861: The fort surrenders.

11. April 14, 1861: Federal troops leave. They march out of the fort carrying an American flag. Fort Sumter is one of the most significant battles in the war. It will be nearly four years until the Union gets the fort back.

There were lots of things that led to the battle of Fort Sumter, which became the start of the Civil War.

title: A 34-Hour Battle
text:
The Battle of Fort Sumter wasn't like a battle scene in a movie. In fact, the fight began long before any guns came out.

After Lincoln became president, people all over the South were mad. They were so mad, they seceded from the Union. We know that to secede means to formally leave a group. These states came together as Confederate states. Fort Sumter was in Charleston, South Carolina. That city was in Confederate control. The fort was held by federal troops, but the Confederates wanted it for themselves. The troops that held the fort served the Union. They didn't want to give up the fort.

With enemies all around them, the federal troops knew they were in trouble. The fort didn't have many supplies. Lincoln tried to send food and medicine to the fort, but the South wouldn't have it.

Pierre Beauregard, the leader of the Confederates, called for the federal troops to give up. But the Union leader, Major Robert Anderson, wouldn't surrender. On April 12, 1861, the Confederates attacked.

Both sides fired on each other, but no one was hurt. The fort's residents knew they didn't have the supplies it would take to win. After 34 hours, the men in the fort gave up.

The fall of Fort Sumter had a big impact on other states in the South. Before the fight, seven states had left the Union. After the fight, four more joined them. Those states were Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina and Tennessee.

title: Attack on Fort Sumter
text:
"Okay, class, let's hit the lights!" Ms. Johnson called as she readied her computer. The kids were in for a treat.

Natalia and Steven felt a rush of excitement. It was time for a video. They sat quietly in their seats as the words, "Attack on Fort Sumter Intro," appeared on the screen. When the video was over, so was class.

"That was quite a movie," Steven exclaimed as he walked with Natalia out of the classroom. They walked slowly, knowing that they had plenty of time to get home.

"Want to know something even better?" Natalia said with a grin. "I got something for us!"

"What is it?"

"It's a telegram. A real primary source from the events at Fort Sumter!" Natalia held out a small piece of paper.

"Let me see." Steven peered over at the paper and read, "As leader of this Confederate Army, we call for a ceasefire and surrender."

"Yep. They sent this to the Union on April 13, 1861. Pretty cool, right?"

"Definitely!" Steven replied. "But, why Fort Sumter? Out of all the places the war could've started, why did the South choose to attack there?"

"That's a great question," Natalia said thoughtfully. "Why don't we evaluate the significance of Fort Sumter by going there in person?"

"Let's! Great idea, Natalia!"

Together, the pair touched the telegram. They felt the rush of wind as they were transported back to 1861. When they felt themselves stop, they looked around and realized that they were on top of a hill, far away from the battle below.

"Oh, wow, they're right on the water! It's like the fort juts out into the harbor on the back side," Steven observed.

"Yes, and they haven't even finished building it yet. Check out those unfinished walls. It looks like it was meant to defend against people coming from the ocean, which is probably why the men there weren't ready to fight against people coming over land."

"That made it an easier place to attack."

"Plus, they didn't have a whole lot of supplies. That made them even weaker when the South started their invasion."

"Man ... the Union didn't even have a chance," Steven said.

"Yeah," Natalia agreed. "I can't watch this anymore. Let's head back."

"Okay."

And together, the two traveled back to the present.

Do you want to learn more about Fort Sumter? You can watch the video that Steven and Natalia saw in Ms. Johnson’s class. Check it out in the Bonus Media sources online.

title: What is Secession?
text:
Imagine that you're part of your favorite basketball team. You love the game. You get along pretty well with the other kids on your team. Then, one day, you get a new coach. The new coach knows you love basketball, but says you’re going to play baseball instead. He doesn’t even ask you about it! How would you feel? Would you be upset?

That's a bit how the South felt when Abraham Lincoln was elected president. They worried that he'd change the game by getting rid of many of their rights. They thought they'd be ignored when it came to government decisions.

As a way to protest the election, the states decided to secede from the Union. Seven states left the Union right away. After the Battle of Fort Sumter, four more states seceded. In all, eleven states left the Union.

Tennessee was the last state to leave, and it almost split the state apart. Tennessee was in favor of slavery, but one half wanted to secede, and the other half didn’t. Those who didn’t want to secede saw another option: an amendment to the Constitution. In fact, the governor of the state, Isham Harris, had an idea for five amendments. They made sure slavery would be allowed in the state. They also made sure that the amendments couldn't be changed without a vote from all the slave states. When the Civil War started, Tennessee knew they had to make a decision: Secede from the Union, or pass amendments. On June 8, 1861, Tennessee seceded.

Want to learn more about Tennessee's troubling decision? Check out the video, "Secession Divides the Union and Almost Tennessee" at the online version of this article!

title: Jefferson Davis
text:
Abraham Lincoln was the President of the Union during the Civil War. You already know that. But who led the Confederate states? They had a president, too. His name was Jefferson Davis. Davis was one of the leaders who played a big role in the war. He was born in 1808, and grew up in Mississippi. He went to West Point along with Robert E. Lee. Before the Civil War, he had already served in the U.S. House of Representatives. He had also been a war hero. He had fought in the Black Hawk War, and in the Mexican-American War. In 1853, he became Secretary of War.

Davis strongly believed states had the right to choose what they wanted to do. Because he believed this, he supported the South. In fact, he was named President of the Confederacy.

When General Lee surrendered, Davis planned to leave the country. Later, when President Lincoln was killed, some thought Davis had something to do with it. He was captured in Georgia in 1865, and spent two years in prison at Fort Monroe in Virginia. But in the end, the charges were dropped.

title: Our 16th President: Abraham Lincoln
text:
Abraham Lincoln was the 16th President of the United States. He served from 1861 to 1865. He played an important role in the Civil War. He is known for freeing the enslaved African Americans and saving the Union.

Abraham Lincoln was born in Kentucky in 1809. He didn’t go to school much. Some say he had only about twelve months of school in his whole life. Still, he learned a lot because he loved to read. All through his life he read and read. He borrowed law books to learn how to be a lawyer. He started to practice law when he was 27 years old. A couple of years later he ran for office, and served in the Illinois House of Representatives for eight years. He was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1846. In 1858, he ran for U.S. Senate. He spoke out against slavery during that campaign. But he lost that race. Still, in 1860, Lincoln was chosen as the man Republicans wanted to be president. Not too many people in the South were glad about that. But because so many people in the North liked him, he won!

Lincoln took office on March 4, 1861. By that time, seven southern states had left the Union. America was still pretty young then, and this was its biggest challenge ever! In April of 1861, Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter, in South Carolina. Lincoln called for volunteers to defend the Union. The Civil War had begun.

In late 1862, Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation. It said that if the South did not stop fighting by January 1, 1863, all enslaved people would go free. But the South did not stop fighting in 1863. The war would drag on for two years more. Lincoln was sad about that. So was everyone else. The country was discouraged, and Lincoln wasn’t very popular.

In July of 1863, soldiers from the North fought against soldiers from the South in a fierce battle. The battle was in Pennsylvania, in a place called Gettysburg. About 8,000 lives were lost. A cemetery was built there to honor the people who died in that battle. In November, 1863, Lincoln visited the cemetery. He gave a short speech. It was only two minutes long. You may have read it. It starts with the words “Four score and seven years ago … ” He talked about a "new birth of freedom" for America. He vowed that government "of the people, by the people, for the people" would not "perish from the earth."

We know this speech today as the Gettysburg Address. It remains one of the greatest speeches ever given by a president. It’s the most quoted speech in American history.

Lincoln ran for president again in 1864. In this election, he did something unusual. Lincoln was a Republican from the North. But he selected a Democrat from the South as his running mate.

Lincoln’s second term began on March 4, 1865. The nation looked forward to a time to heal from the war. But about a month later, President Lincoln was shot and killed in Ford's Theater, on April 14, 1865. The shooter was a famous actor named John Wilkes Booth. The nation mourned Lincoln’s death. Even today, many people think Lincoln was one of the greatest presidents of all time.

Do you want to learn more about the Gettysburg Address? Visit your media tab for a video called “Gettysburg Address Intro.” It’s quite a speech!

title: Think & Review Questions
text:
1. Explain how different parts of the Anaconda Plan were put into practice.

2. Lincoln faced numerous setbacks during the Civil War. However, he showed that he was devoted to saving the Union. Give facts that support this claim.

3.This week we learned about our first African American senator, Hiram Revels. In your opinion, what was Revels' most important success and why?

4. Discuss some of the important people in the Civil War, and what they did.

title: Look! It's a Snake!
text:
Natalia and Steven looked through a pile of old maps in the library.

"Oh! it's a snake!" Steven said. He looked at a map of the United States. A drawing of a huge, black snake wound around the coasts, surrounding the country.

"Scott's Great Snake," Natalia read the title on the map. She reached out and touched the tail of the snake. Steven and Natalia felt the rushing of wind, and found themselves high on a hill. The hill overlooked a wide river. It was so big they could hardly see across it.

“The Mississippi!” said Natalia.

“And what’s that?” said Steven. He pointed at a small ship, chugging toward them.

“It’s a blockade runner!” said Natalia. “Blockade runners are little and fast. The Union ships control the river, but those little blockade runners get right through!”

“What are they carrying?” asked Steven.

Natalia shrugged. “Sometimes mail. Sometimes medicine. Sometimes goods to sell.”

“Wait a second. Lemme see the map!” said Steven. He looked excited. The map that had brought them there was lying on the hill beside them. They crouched down to look at it.

"I get it now! This is a map of the Anaconda Plan,” said Steven. “I know about this! In the early part of the war, Union leaders worked to keep the Confederates from getting supplies. They also wanted to keep the South from being able to get money by selling cotton. General Winfield Scott had a plan. He wanted to block Southern ports and capture at least one port city to supply the coal-powered boats. He also wanted to send soldiers and boats down the Mississippi to cut off inland access to the Confederacy through America's largest waterway. Scott’s plan was called the Anaconda Plan."

"Like the snake?” Natalia asked.

“Yeah, just like the snake,” said Steven. “The plan used geographic features like rivers and coastlines to isolate and defeat regions of the South.”

“Just like a big snake squeezing its kill,” said Natalia. “Did it work?”

"Not all of the plan worked out," Steven said, “But some of it did. Lincoln had already ordered blockades on all Confederate ports. It was one of his roles in the war. So that part of Scott’s plan was sure to happen. The blockades kept big boats from docking and doing business. This made it tough for the Confederacy. They had a hard time selling their goods."

“But they had a hard time stopping these little blockade runners!” said Natalia. She pointed at the ship, which had docked on the river below them. Men ran back and forth on the deck, unloading cargo.

“Yeah,” said Steven. “These blockade runners are the reason that most folks think the Anaconda Plan was only a partial success. Scott thought the plan would end the war without much bloodshed. He was wrong about that.”

“Yeah,” said Natalia. “Still. Scott’s Great Snake. It sounds like quite a plan,” said Natalia. She reached out to the map between them, and touched the yellowed paper. They felt the rush of wind, and before they knew it, the river was gone, along with the blockade runner. They were back in the library. Far away, they smelled lunch cooking in the cafeteria.
