Plus, they wanted to make sure their party, the Republicans, had all the power of the government, even in the southern states. Plus, they wanted the South to pay them back for the war. That’s a whole lot of punishment.”

“Wow. You found different stuff than I found. Maybe that's because different people had different ideas about how to recover from the war."

Ms. Johnson looked up. She wasn't surprised that Steven and Natalia wanted to spend most of their lunch hour studying in her classroom. She knew them pretty well. "What are you two talking about?" she asked.

"We're comparing the things we learned about Reconstruction," said Natalia.

"Yeah," said Steven. "Lincoln's ideas about bringing the country back together after the war were really different from the ideas Congress had."

"That's right," said Ms. Johnson. "And it's important to remember that before any of these ideas could be put into practice, Lincoln was killed. It was Andrew Johnson, the next president, who would lead the country in its first steps toward getting back together."

"Oh, man," said Steven. "A new president! And with him, yet another set of ideas about Reconstruction!"

"I can see how the Reconstruction period was going to be a long, difficult time," said Natalia. "When so much pain has been caused for so many, it's tough to agree on how best to get through it."

"We're talking about Johnson's plan today, as soon as the rest of the class gets back," said Ms. Johnson.

"We can't wait!" said Steven. "We're excited to hear how this complicated story turns out!"

Are you excited too? Visit Studies Weekly online and take a look at a video called, "Reconstruction Intro." It'll give you a better understanding about some of the conflicts Natalia, Steven and Ms. Johnson are talking about!

title: Think & Review Questions
text:
1. Compare and contrast: In what ways were Lincoln's and Congress's plans for Reconstruction the same? In what ways were they different? Cite your evidence from the Student Edition.
2. Compare and contrast: In what ways were Lincoln's and Johnson's plans for Reconstruction the same? In what ways were they different? Cite your evidence from the Student Edition.
3. Analyze the situation. Sampson W. Keeble had some great ideas, especially in terms of making things equal for the newly freed African Americans. Why do you think that his bills didn't end up passing and becoming laws?
4. Abraham Lincoln was very much a person who fought for what he believed in. Even more, he'd already used his presidential veto to block the Wade-Davis Bill. He had no problem battling Congress and their extreme ideas for getting revenge on the South after the Civil War.

title: Let's Write
text: There were many ideas about how to put the country back together after the Civil War. Some wanted to punish the South. Some wanted to be more forgiving. Some wanted to restrict the rights of newly freed slaves. Others wanted to give them the same rights as other citizens. Write a letter to explain why this is. Be sure to discuss both perspectives.

title: Think & Review Questions
text:
1. Summarize the effects of the Compromise of 1877. Cite evidence from the Student Edition.

2. Belva Lockwood was actually the first woman to run for president. Why was this significant during this time period?

3. Why was it so important to southern Democrats to keep the newly freed African Americans from voting?

title: Reconstruction Review
text:
Natalia: Hi, everyone! Welcome to our broadcast! It's great to bring you history like it's happening today.

Steven: And have we got a treat for you! Over the last two weeks, we've all been studying Reconstruction.

Natalia: You know, the period when we tried to rebuild the country after the Civil War.

Steven: And after studying so hard, we thought we'd give you a little review.

Natalia: There's nothing like a good review.

Steven: Let's start at the end of the Civil War. You might think that the country could just go back to being friends, with the North and the South on good terms, as if the war never happened. However, that definitely wasn't the case.

Natalia: That's right, Steven. Many in the South still wanted to govern themselves. And they wanted to continue to get free or cheap labor to work their farms and plantations, even though all enslaved people had been freed.

Steven: In fact, you'll see that even the branches of the government couldn't get along. President Lincoln debated heavily with Congress. They both knew that they needed to find a way to reunite the North and the South. They just couldn't find a middle ground on how to do it.

Natalia: Lincoln wanted to bring the country back together as quickly and as easily as possible. He said that just 10 percent of registered voters had to sign an Oath of Loyalty for the state to rejoin the Union. He didn't want to be too harsh toward the Confederates. Even more, he wanted to create laws that would give the freedpeople many rights. That way, they'd be able to join society more easily.

Steven: Congress wasn't so nice. They wanted to punish the South by taking away their land and making them pay for all the war debt. Plus, they wanted more than half of the state to take an Oath of Loyalty before the state could rejoin in the Union.

Natalia: It's easy to see why these ideas led to so much conflict. And we'll never know who won that fight because Lincoln was assassinated before they could make a decision.

Natalia: After that, Vice President Andrew Johnson had to step into those presidential shoes. He managed to find a bit of a middle ground. He didn't punish the Confederates as much as Congress wanted. Plus, he didn't make sure the freedpeople got the rights they needed. That led to a lot of problems later.

Steven: Andrew Johnson wasn't popular as a president. Congress tried to kick him out of office! And when it came time for a new election, his party didn't nominate him for the job.

Steven: I think that about catches us up. Nice review, Natalia.

Natalia: Thanks. What are we learning today, Steven?

Steven: Today, we'll talk about the end of the Reconstruction years, and the election of Rutherford B. Hayes.

Natalia: I can hardly wait!

title: Separate but Equal
text:
In many ways, The Compromise of 1877 reached its goal. Reconstruction came to an end. But there was still plenty of work to be done, and not everyone was happy.

Reconstruction was over, but African Americans didn't have many more rights than they had before. In fact, one of the conditions of the Compromise of 1877 was that the South could deal with African Americans in the way it saw best, without the North telling them what to do. States and cities in the South began passing "separate but equal" laws. These laws would become known as the "Jim Crow" laws. "Jim Crow" was a made up black character made famous by a white actor named Thomas Rice years before the Civil War, in the 1830s. The words "Jim Crow" were used by some white people to mock their black neighbors. When laws were made that kept black people and white people separate, people called them "Jim Crow" laws.

What did "separate but equal" mean to the black population? It meant that they would be kept apart from their white neighbors. It began in 1896, when black people were made to ride in "separate but equal" train cars. But it went on from there. They were made to use separate drinking fountains. They were made to use separate public bathrooms. They were even made to use separate restaurants. They weren't allowed in certain buildings, and they had to stay separated from whites at every turn. Separate libraries and schools were created. Each of these services was clearly labeled with "Colored" and "White" signs.

These laws lasted a long time. If your grandparents or great-grandparents are in their sixties or seventies, they may remember when many of these laws were still in effect. Only many years of legal action and protests would finally get rid of these unfair laws.

You can watch a video about how some of these laws came to be. Visit the online version of this article, and look for the video!

title: An End to Reconstruction
text:
"Okay, class. Calm down," Ms. Johnson called over the noise of the classroom.

It was presentation day for the students, and everyone was excited to give their reports. They'd all chosen someone they thought was important during the end of Reconstruction.

"I know we're all anxious to present, so let's get started. That way, everyone will get a chance to show what they've learned. Let's see ... Steven?"

Steven perked up at the sound of his name. He'd been hoping to get chosen first! He gathered his notecards and the poster he'd made and walked toward the front of the room.

Clearing his throat, Steven began to speak. "Hello. Today, I want to tell you about President Rutherford B. Hayes."

He paused for a moment, making eye contact with Natalia. She gave him a smile of encouragement, and he continued.

"President Hayes was born in Delaware, Ohio, in 1822. He never knew his father, who'd died a few months before he was born. But he had a mother and sister, and they lived with his Uncle Sardis, who was very successful in business.

"He went to school in Ohio. He graduated at the top of his class from Kenyon College. Then, he earned a law degree from Harvard University. After that, he began to practice law. In the 1850s, he joined the Republican Party to help fight the spread of slavery. This was before the war.

"When the Civil War broke out, Hayes was quick to join up and become a soldier. He was a major in the 23rd Ohio Regiment, and he got promoted to brevet major general by the end of the war. He was injured pretty badly during the Battle of South Mountain in Maryland.

"After the war, he became a politician. He held a seat in the House of Representatives, but he left that seat to become the governor of Ohio. Then, during the nominating convention in 1876, the party was split over who to nominate. Some wanted to re-nominate President Grant for a third term, and others wanted James G. Blaine, who was Speaker of the House at the time. They compromised and nominated Hayes. He was an easy choice because he had a reputation for being honest.

"Hayes managed to end Reconstruction within his first year in office. This was a result of the debated election results, and also because he pulled the rest of the troops from the South. This eventually became known as the Compromise of 1877."

"Could you say more about that?" said Ms. Johnson.

"Um ... sure," said Steven. "The election of 1876 was between Hayes and a man named Samuel Tilden. When the votes were in, it looked like a tie. The Republicans thought they'd won. The Democrats thought they'd won. It was hard to figure out who really had the most votes. In the end, Tilden's side said they'd give up the final few votes though that would lose them the election. But they'd only do it on certain conditions. They wanted Hayes to pull the last Union troops from Louisiana and South Carolina, and they wanted a guarantee that he would appoint at least one southerner to his cabinet."

"That was David M. Key, from right here in Tennessee," said Ms. Johnson. "He served as Hayes' Postmaster General."

"That's right," said Steven. "Hayes also had to promise to build southern industries, and to let the southern states solve some of their problems without interference from the North."

"Very good, Steven. That's right," said Ms. Johnson.

"Hayes never ran for a second presidential term," said Steven. "However, he will always be remembered as the man who ended Reconstruction."

The class erupted in applause, and Steven gave a little bow before returning to his seat.

"Thank you for that wonderful report, Steven," Ms. Johnson said with a smile. She peered down at her clipboard. "Natalia? You're up next!"

"Okay!" Natalia called from her desk. She gathered her notes and walked to the front of the room. She could feel the butterflies in her stomach. But, she was determined to give an excellent report.

Taking a deep breath, Natalia began. "Some women are trailblazers. They set their mind on a goal, and they make a path that allows other women to follow.

"Belva Lockwood was one of these trailblazers. She knew what she wanted, and she wasn't afraid to go after it. And what did she want? Well ... she wanted to practice law. And she became the first woman to do so. But, that's not saying she wasn't met with a few challenges.

"Back then, some people believed that women's brains were too sensitive for the strain of mental exercise. So if a woman tried to do something that took brains, she was sometimes met with hostility.

"Lockwood didn't back down, though. She was poor and didn't have a high social standing. But she worked hard and got a college degree. She started as a teacher, but when her husband's health began to fail, she realized she needed to do more. And she wanted other women to be able to do the same. She wanted women to be free of having to depend on others.

"Because her college peers didn't want to graduate with a woman, she went to President Ulysses S. Grant himself. He gave her the degree.

"Once she had her law degree, she continued to fight. The Supreme Court refused to admit her to the bar, simply because she was a woman. Again, she persisted. She lobbied Congress and got them to pass a bill to say women could practice law. Lockwood became the first woman to be admitted to the Supreme Court bar."

Natalia smiled to herself. Here comes the best part! she thought.

"You might think that Lockwood stopped there. But, no. She pushed forward. In 1884, she became the first woman to run for President of the United States. She even outlined many plans, like federalizing family law and protecting public land. She got less than 5,000 votes but was never discouraged.

"Lockwood definitely serves as an excellent role model. Her story tells us that even in the face of adversity, we should always continue to fight."

Again, the class applauded. Natalia felt herself blush, and she walked confidently back to her desk. As she passed Steven, she gave him a high five.

"That was lovely," Ms. Johnson exclaimed! "And it was such a wonderful moral for all of us. Great work, Natalia!"

Natalia smiled at Ms. Johnson from her seat.

Pulling out her clipboard, Ms. Johnson continued, "Okay ... let's see who's next ... "

title: Lemonade Lucy
text:
Lucille "Lucy" Hayes was the wife of President Rutherford B. Hayes. She became First Lady after the Compromise of 1877. Lucy was one of the most popular First Ladies to ever live in the White House.

Lucy Hayes had a good education. In fact, she was the very first First Lady to get a college degree. She also banned all alcohol from the White House. Anyone in White House would simply have to drink something else. Can you guess what they drank? Here's a hint: Lucy Hayes' nickname was "Lemonade Lucy."

During Lucy's time in office, she worked hard. She made sure there was funding for mental health and education. She visited veterans and sent flowers to children's hospitals. She also led the way in helping the poor. Lucy and her husband donated over $1,000 of their own money to poor people of Washington.

What's more, President Hayes listened to the things his wife had to say. She swayed her husband on many topics, like women's rights.

Clearly, Lemonade Lucy set a high standard for the future.

title: Let's Write
text: Suppose you are running for president. What is your platform? What are the issues that you will focus on in order for people to listen to you? Explain how you will get elected.

title: An Election with Two Winners
text:
As Johnson's term came to an end, Ulysses S. Grant was elected president. Remember him? He was the Union general who accepted Lee's surrender at the end of the Civil War. Grant served as president for eight years, or two terms. Then, in 1876, one hundred years after the Declaration of Independence, Republican Rutherford B. Hayes battled Democrat Samuel J. Tilden for the presidency. The two fought hard. And, when the final ballots came in, there were ... two winners?

Wait. That couldn't be right, could it? But it looked like the election of 1876 might just be a tie!

In most states, it was pretty clear which candidate had the most votes. But both parties claimed that they had won the votes for Florida, Louisiana and South Carolina.

It was a tricky problem! To solve it, Congress created a group of 15 people to figure out who was the real winner in each state. The group was made up of five members of the House of Representatives, five members of the Senate, and five members of the Supreme Court. They studied and thought, and argued and thought some more. The election had taken place in November, and it took them until January to make a final decision. In the end, they decided that Hayes was the winner in each of these states. He won the election by a single vote: 185 electoral votes to 184 electoral votes.

Talk about a close match!

You'll learn more about the famous election of 1876 in this issue. Steven is about to give his report. But before you do, you may have just enough time to see a video about President Hayes. Just visit the online version of this article.

title: A Freed Man
text:
Hey, all! Steven here. Ms. Johnson gave me an assignment. She asked me to make up a journal entry as if I lived at the time Reconstruction was ending. Here's what I came up with.

Dear Journal,

I saw it in the paper today they finally picked a winner for the election. They're calling it the Compromise of 1877. People are cheering and screaming about it everywhere.

I'll tell you what, though, not everyone agreed to that Compromise. I know I sure didn't. It's been more than ten years since the war ended, and we're still not getting the rights that every normal citizen deserves. I just know that means hard times are coming.

In a lot of ways, it seems like we're almost in the same way as before the war. Sure, we're not enslaved anymore, but we don't get much say in how people treat us, and it seems we don't get much say in how the country is run, either.

It doesn't seem like such a fair deal. Maybe it'll be better for my children. I sure hope so.

title: Facts in Four
text: This week we read about lots of different ideas on how to manage Reconstruction. Work in groups to fill out the main ideas in each box. Get into a group of four students. One student in your group takes one box. On a separate piece of paper, list at least three details about the person or their plans. Get back together and share your answers.

title: It's Tough to Vote Around Here!
text:
The 15th Amendment was supposed to give every man the right to vote, regardless of the color of his skin. But that's not exactly how things went.

Many were upset at the idea of formerly enslaved people being allowed to vote. To keep them from voting, some cities and states made special rules. For instance, many freedpeople never got much education. For years, in many places it was against the law to educate a slave. After the 15th Amendment passed, some voting places would require all voters to pass a reading test. Understandably, many freedpeople were unable to pass.

Other places might charge a fee in order to vote. That meant the poor couldn't vote. Since many freedpeople didn't have jobs that paid well, they'd often be turned away from the voting booths.

In some places, people would simply threaten black voters, scaring them away from voting.

The 15th Amendment was a big step, but it wasn't enough to guarantee that African Americans could vote. There was more work to be done.

title: Women in the Reconstruction Period
text:
The 15th Amendment was a great improvement in our country. For the first time ever, African American men were allowed to vote. They could vote for laws, and their votes could help decide who'd be in charge of the government. But one little word was still a huge problem for half of the population. That word was "men."

That three-letter word was in the text of the 15th Amendment. That meant it only guaranteed the right to vote to men. Women weren't guaranteed the same right.

If you were a woman in that time period, would you be happy? Think about it. You'd probably see the 15th Amendment as an important step. After all, white men wouldn't be the only ones making choices for the country anymore. But you'd also see that women were still left out. And you probably wouldn't like that!

Some women felt like the 15th Amendment was an important step, and supported it. Others chose to fight it. They said that both men and women needed the right to vote. Women like Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton chose to fight. Together, they formed the National Woman Suffrage Association in 1869. Remember the word suffrage? That means "the right to vote."

Women in favor of the 15th Amendment formed a group, too. They thought that the 15th Amendment would soon lead to women getting the right to vote. Lucy Stone was a leader among these women. So was Harriet Beecher Stowe. Their group was called the American Woman Suffrage Association.

See how similar the names of those two groups are? It's easy to confuse them.

The two groups battled over the topic of the 15th Amendment. By 1890, the two women's groups would come back together in a group called the National American Woman Suffrage Association. They knew that it was more important to work together. And they both wanted the same thing.

It would be another 50 years before women would gain the right to vote.

title: Change Can be Difficult
text:
Steven and Natalia sat at lunch in the cafeteria. Steven was quiet. Finally, he spoke. "I just can't understand why anyone would have opposed giving African Americans the same rights as everyone else," he said.

Natalia thought. Then she said, "It was wrong to try to keep African Americans enslaved, that's for sure. But there are reasons why the South was upset about things like the 13th Amendment. Here's how I see it," she said. "Imagine that your school would like to make a new rule. They want to ban all sports that use any kind of ball."

"That's a silly rule," said Steven."

"Sure it is. But bear with me," said Natalia. "Now, if you're on the swim team you might not care about the new rule."

"I suppose I get that," said Steven.

"But what if you're a basketball player?" said Natalia. "How would you feel about the new rule?"

"I hate it already," said Steven. "I love baskeball!"

"Well," said Natalia, "maybe that example makes it easy to see how a rule can have almost no effect on some people, but can affect others in huge ways. During Reconstruction, there were lots of rules like that."

"I think I see where you're going," said Steven.

"In the North," said Natalia, "the economy depended on factories and shops. They ran their factories and shops without slave labor. When the 13th Amendment outlawed slavery, it didn't affect the North much. It was easy for them to accept the 13th Amendment. They felt fine about it."

"I get that," said Steven.

"But it was different in the South," said Natalia. "The economy of the South depended on farms and plantations. Those places had depended on slave labor for many, many years. When the 13th Amendment outlawed slavery, it changed their whole way of life."

"But equal rights for everyone is obviously the right thing," said Steven.

"You're right. It is," said Natalia. "But many people thought it was difficult, and fought against it."

"I hope we can be the kind of people who are always willing to do the right thing, even when it's hard," said Steven.

Natalia smiled at her friend. "I think you're on the right track, pal," she said.

title: Due Process? What's That?
text:
The 5th and the 14th Amendment both use some of the same words. They say that the government can't deny someone the rights of life, liberty or property "without due process of law."

What does "due process of law" mean? It means that your rights can't be taken away without a legal process to determine whether you're guilty of a crime. Here's an example: let's say your neighbor is having a bad night. He calls the police on the phone. Your neighbor tells them that you should be locked up for the rest of your life. Do you think the police would do what your neighbor asks?

With due process, they wouldn't lock you up -- or punish you in any way at all -- based on a simple phone call. They'd have to go through the steps established by law. The process would include gathering evidence and going to trial to determine whether or not you had actually committed a crime. If due process determined that you had done something wrong, you might be punished; but if you were innocent, nothing would happen.

title: Let's Write
text: How did the Reconstruction Amendments change African American people's everyday lives? Explain the ways an African American's life was different in the post-Civil War society. Be sure to mention examples of things that an African American could not do before the Civil War.

title: Three-Fifths No More!
text:
To learn about one important part of the 14th Amendment, it helps to go back a little further than the Civil War. In fact, let's go back all the way to 1787, when the Constitution was written. We'll talk about something called the "Three-Fifths Compromise."

In 1787, enslaved people made up one-fifth of the total population of our nation. Most of them lived in the South. They worked in fields, on farms and on plantations. Governors in the South hoped to include them in their population count. Because the number of Representatives each state sent to Congress was based on how many people it had living in it, a larger count would give the South more members in the House of Representatives. That would mean more power for states in the South when it came to taxes and law-making matters. States in the North feared that if states in the South were allowed to include enslaved people in their population count, northern states might lose power in Congress. They hoped to find a way to keep those people from being counted. It may sound strange to you, but in the end, states in the North and states in the South agreed to count each enslaved person as only three-fifths of a person. This was the Three-Fifths Compromise.

That decision created a big problem. Before the Civil War, enslaved people were thought of as nothing but property. But what about after slavery ended? Would each African American still be counted only as three-fifths of a person? That's where the 14th Amendment came in. It declared that African Americans were citizens. And it said that each citizen counted as one whole person. It was a big step.

title: Three Amendments - Topic Webs
text: On a separate piece of paper, fill in the Amendments topic webs using details from this week’s reading.

title: Three Important Amendments
text:
"Okay, you ready?" Natalia asked Steven.

They were sitting at the desk of their news show. The camera was ready. They were about to go live.

"Yep," Steven replied. He set his notes in front of him. He hoped he wouldn't need them, but it was good to have them just in case. "Let's do this!"

Natalia pushed the record button on their camera. The red light went on. The whole school was watching.

"Welcome to today's show!" said Natalia. "I'm your host, Natalia."

"And I'm your host Steven," added Steven.

"Over the last few weeks, we've been talking about the time after the Civil War," said Natalia. "It was an important time, when people on both sides of the War worked to put the country back together."

"That's right," said Steven. "And during that time, three important changes were made to the Constitution. They were efforts to help former slaves begin a new life."

"We want to talk about those changes today," said Natalia.

"They're called the Reconstruction Amendments to the Constitution," Steven continued. "They're the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments."

"Remind us, Steven. What's in those amendments?" Natalia questioned.

"Well, let's start with the 13th Amendment. It's very short: just a couple of sentences. It banned slavery. We can quote some of it right here. Here's what part of the first sentence says: 'neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States.' See that? No more slavery, except as punishment for a crime. That's the 13th Amendment. It was the only one of the Reconstruction Amendments passed while Lincoln was still alive.

"How about the 14th Amendment?" asked Natalia.

"The 14th Amendment said that all citizens of the United States had rights."

"Including African American citizens," said Natalia.

"That's right," said Steven. "It said that no state could take away the rights of any of its citizens. It also said that states had to use their laws to protect all citizens equally. It laid out consequences for states that didn't give the right to vote to every man over 21 years of age. The 14th Amendment was passed in 1868, about three years after the War ended."

"Okay," said Natalia. "We've talked about the 13th and 14th Amendments. Now, how about the 15th?"

"The 15th Amendment was very simple, and very important," said Steven. It said that no state could keep people from voting based on the color of their skin, or based on whether or not they had been enslaved in the past."

"These three amendments were big changes to the Constitution," said Natalia. "But even after the changes were passed, true freedom was still pretty far off."

"Last week, we studied things like 'Jim Crow' laws, and 'Separate but Equal' laws. Remember those?" said Steven.

"It was hard for African Americans during Reconstruction. But through many years of hard work, things slowly got better. Did you know that Congress funded over a thousand schools just for African Americans?"

Natalia paused. Then she said, "The Reconstruction Amendments definitely meant well. But, in the real world, they were only steps in a process that's going on even today. People of different races are still working to get over their differences. The good news is that with the hard work of may people, we're getting closer all the time."

"Every one of us can work to make things better in a country that's already pretty great," said Steven.

"Thanks for joining us," said Natalia. "We've really enjoyed bringing you the news!"

"We sure have," said Steven. "And we hope you've enjoyed it, too."

Steven and Natalia looked at each other and smiled. Then they looked back at the camera. "Until next time!" they said, together.

Would you like to hear more about Reconstruction? We've got a video for you. It's called, "Growing Pains After the Civil War Intro." You can find it in the media tab on the Studies Weekly website.

title: The Reconstruction Amendments
text:
Welcome to the very last issue of U.S. History Studies Weekly! After a few weeks of studying the people, places and ideas of the Reconstruction period, today's issue is all about some important amendments to the Constitution that came about because of what was happening at the time.

Steven: We've already done a lot of studying about the Reconstruction. Why do we have to do this report?

Natalia: No study of the Reconstruction is complete without a look at the Amendments to the Constitution that came out of that time. Those Amendments affect us even today.

Steven: Yeah, you're right. Let's get down to it. What do we already know?

Natalia: Well, we know an amendment is a change to the country's Constitution. For our report, let's look at the three amendments that came right after the Civil War. We call them the "Reconstruction Amendments."

Steven: Which ones were they again?

Natalia: The 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments. They helped restore and create more rights for the freedpeople.

Steven: By "freedpeople," you surely mean American citizens.

Natalia: Yes, that's what I mean. Let's look at the Amendments one by one. The 13th said slavery shouldn't exist in any form in the nation. Congress voted on this Amendment on January 31, 1865. But not everyone was in favor of it. Delaware, Kentucky and Mississippi rejected it.

Steven: I'm glad it passed anyway.

Natalia: Me, too!

Steven: Oh, look. The 14th talks about the rights of people, including the rights of former slaves. It says that no one can pass a law that would deny those rights. That one was signed July 28, 1868.

Natalia: Perfect. Now, how about that last one?

Steven: The 15th Amendment gave all adult men the right to vote, no matter what color their skin might be. That one passed February 26, 1869. Is that it?

Natalia: I don't know. Everyone in class will have all this same stuff. We need something to help our project stand out.

Steven: Oh, I know! How about this? It's a photo of my great-great-great-great uncle Lewis. His father was white, but his mother was African American. He was born a slave, but when the Civil War ended, he was free. He learned to work with wood. He even started his own shop. His shop was really successful, too. We could use his story to show how the lives of former slaves changed because of these changes to the Constitution.

Natalia: Great idea! Let's put all this stuff together.

title: Starting Over After the War
text:
"Where are you going in such a hurry, Alana?" Jackson asks, running to catch up with Alana at the end of the school day.

"I'm helping my neighbor clean out her attic. She told me I could bring a friend. Want to help?"

"Sure," says Jackson, "you never know what we may find."

Alana's neighbor was waiting for her on the front porch. "Alana, glad you could come. I see you brought Jackson. Jackson, do you still write interesting historical facts in your notebook? When we get to the attic, I have something to show you."

She leads them into her house, up the stairs, into an attic full of stacked boxes, covered furniture and lamps.

"I wanted to show you this ring. It belonged to Mattie Jane Jackson. She was a slave before the Civil War. Here Jackson, take a look," She offers Jackson the ring. "When you're able, please bring the boxes downstairs."

"I'll be back to check on you two in about twenty minutes," she calls, heading down the stairs.

Alana smiles, "I'd really like to meet Mattie Jane Jackson."

Jackson smiles as he and Alana both touch the ring. They have a secret. They can touch historical objects and travel back in time! Not just any old thing laying around, though. It has to have witnessed historical events that made the U.S. what it is today.

Whoosh! They arrive in a rural town, just outside of Nashville, in 1863. A group of former slaves has gathered, some holding luggage, appearing ready to travel. A nearby plantation is in ruins; several buildings on the plantation have broken windows. One building appears to have recent fire damage.

Among the group, Alana notices a young woman wearing the same ring that was shown to them in the attic.

"That must be Mattie Jane!" Alana exclaims. They get close enough to hear what Mattie Jane is saying to an older woman.

"I'm getting ready to leave for Massachusetts," Mattie Jane says. "The Union soldiers destroyed this plantation and my home is gone. Even this money I saved is worthless," she continues, holding up a small stack of strange looking bills.

"This is a difficult time," the other woman says. "But if the North wins, I think we'll come out okay. I hear there are plans to build schools for everybody. And I heard they're going to have a special bureau that helps former slaves get good jobs, find places to live, and get food. I think I'll stay."

"What ended up happening, Jackson?" inquires Alana.

"The North did win ... about two years later," Jackson says, reading his notebook. "The government created the Freedmen's Bureau to help former slaves. And there was a lot of rebuilding after the Civil War. Many of the big plantations broke up. Some former slaves became sharecroppers, people who rented farmland, then paid the owner with crops. Northern companies created jobs for Tennesseans, mostly in the mining and logging industries. And a lot of people moved to the cities."

"I wonder if Mattie Jane made it all the way to Massachusetts?" Alana asks. "But we need to hurry back." Whoosh!

The two arrive in the attic to see Alana's neighbor coming up the staircase. "Did you get a chance to look at the ring, Jackson?"

"Yes, I did. What happened to Mattie Jane?" Jackson asks.

"Some African Americans moved West to settlements that were almost all African American; the most famous of these settlements was in Nicodemus, Kansas. Mattie ended up moving to Lawrence, Massachusetts with her stepfamily. She ended up writing an autobiography in 1866; it's called The Life of Mattie J. Jackson."

"That's only three years after we saw her!" Alana whispers to Jackson.

title: New Industries and Inventions
text:
Several inventions helped industries grow during the Industrial Revolution. Many new machines made work easier. Four of the most important were the cotton gin, the railroad, the telephone and the gas-engine car. Three of these are still in use today.

Eli Whitney invented the cotton gin well before the Civil War. It changed cotton farming. Before its invention, it took a worker about one day to pick and remove the seeds from a pound of cotton. With the cotton gin, invented in 1794, workers could remove the seeds from 50 pounds of cotton each day. This meant that plantation owners could sell much more cotton. Cotton became much more profitable. More slaves were brought to the South to work the plantations. By the mid-1800s, cotton was a leading export of the South. Cotton was used to make clothes in factories.

The development of the railroad changed transportation. The first trains were used in the 1830s. They were powered by steam. During the Civil War, trains moved troops and supplies. Two rail companies, Central Pacific and Union Pacific worked to build tracks across the country. In 1869, tracks joined Sacramento to Western Iowa.

Samuel Morse invented the telegraph, which let users send messages using a special code. This telegraph was invented in the 1830s and '40s. Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone in the 1870s. This allowed people talk to each other over long distances.

The development of the gas-engine car also changed transportation. In the 1880s, Karl Benz and Gottlieb Daimler developed the gas-powered engine. Karl Benz produced the first car that ran on gas. Henry Ford used assembly line production to build cars at his Ford plant, including the first mass-produced car. It was called the Model T.
