title: Create a Timeline
text:
Use information from the paragraph to construct a timeline of Reconstruction events of 1865.

The First Year of Reconstruction

Before the Civil War had officially ended, the U.S. Congress had already approved the 13th Amendment to the Constitution in January 1865. Ratified in December of that same year, the amendment abolished slavery forever in the United States. By March, Congress had started the Freedmen’s Bureau to provide newly emancipated slaves with assistance in finding food, shelter, education and jobs. Unfortunately, President Lincoln, who was responsible for the Emancipation Proclamation, did not live to see its results. On April 14, 1865, just five days after the end of the Civil War, a Confederate supporter named John Wilkes Booth assassinated him. Lincoln’s successor, Andrew Johnson, took charge of Reconstruction plans. He made them public in May. Reconstruction was not an easy process. Some states actually tried to find ways to bring slavery back to the South. In November of 1865, Mississippi enacted (passed) the Black Codes to limit the civil rights of freed slaves.

title: Industrial Age in the New South
text:
Between about 1760 and 1840, the North and Great Britain were experiencing the Industrial Revolution, while the South remained a farming economy. Factories drove the Northern economy. In 1870, the South experienced the second Industrial Revolution, which lasted 50 years. During this time, companies began using more and more machines. Companies grew bigger; some had thousands of employees. Companies divided jobs among workers, which sped up production.

Cities grew, too. In 1900, Memphis had over 100,000 people. Nashville had about 80,000. Knoxville and Chattanooga had around 30,000 each. About 25 million immigrants came to the U.S. between 1870 and 1916. Immigrants were a source of labor in plants and factories. The total U.S. population grew from 40 million to about 100 million.

The growth of the railroad sped the growth of other industries. Trains could take raw materials across the country more quickly than ever before. By 1900, there were over 200,000 miles of railroad. These also supplied grocery stores in towns with coffee, flour, cornmeal, sugar and other goods. People went to towns to buy these items. Trains also allowed Tennessee to begin exporting lumber from its forests. Iron ore and coal were also important exports.

Banks grew, too. Banks gave loans to businesses. Successful companies sold stocks and bonds, which allowed others to make money from their successes. The sales of stocks and bonds gave companies more money to use to invest in newer machines and more workers.

Farming changed during the Industrial Revolution, too. Plantations and large farms no longer had slaves. For the first time, Southerners had to pay for workers. With the end of slavery, many slaves became sharecroppers. They rented farmland from owners. They got to live on the farm and paid the owner with the crops they grew.

During this time, more people came to believe that everyone should be treated equally. The Reconstruction Amendments were passed after the Civil War. These amendments outlawed slavery, allowed all men to vote, and protected everyone equally under the law.

title: This Week's Question
text: As you've seen, Tennessee changed greatly before and after the Civil War. What were some of the new industries you've read about? Can you think of any that weren't discussed in the article? Why was it so important to develop new industries in Tennessee after the Civil War?

title: Let's Write
text: Based on what you have learned this week, write one paragraph explaining the reasons the South had to embrace industrialization after the Civil War. Be sure to check for correct grammar, spelling and punctuation.

title: The Birth of the Blues
text: In the early 1800s, African Americans developed a new musical form, the blues. At first, the music was played on homemade banjos. Banjos and banjo players got better over time. Some players developed new types of music. The early blues used bits of folk music, spirituals, hymns and field songs. Some songs were even made up on the spot. After the Civil War, songs became more personal. Music became a way to discuss the oppression and lack of jobs for African Americans. Around 1900, musicians began using the guitar to play the blues. They often replaced the nylon strings with cheap steel strings or bailing wire. The most famous early blues musician was Robert Johnson. According to legend, he sold his soul for his ability to create, play and sing. After his death, he became known as King of the Delta Blues. His music survives to this day. Many think of him as one of the best blues musicians of all time.

title: The End of the Confederacy
text:
At the time of the Civil War, Tennessee's economy was based largely on farming. Large plantations used slave labor to plant, pick and sell cotton. Tobacco was another important crop. Most Tennesseans lived on subsistence farming, meaning that they grew their own food to survive. When these farmers had more than they needed, they often traded or sold it. Trade routes on land were limited to short distances. Trade also grew along port towns on major rivers. There were port cities along the Tennessee, Ohio and Mississippi Rivers.

When Abraham Lincoln was elected president, the Southern states declared themselves a separate country. They called it the Confederate States of America. They formed a new government, electing Jefferson Davis as president. They even had their own money. They hoped leaving the Union would be peaceful. It was not. President Abraham Lincoln used the military to keep the country together.

The Confederacy had early success in the Civil War. The South had many trained soldiers and generals. The South, though, was poor. Producing food and supplies for an army was expensive. The Union was able to limit the South's trade with other countries. As a result, the South quickly ran low on money. The South tried selling bonds, or loans to the government and printing more money. When this failed, the new government raised taxes. One policy was hard for farmers and planters who didn't have much money. They had to give one-tenth of their crops to the government! Sometimes, the Confederate army took crops, livestock, wagons and machines from poorer farmers. There were no taxes on cotton, land or slaves, which would have affected rich plantation owners. This angered many poorer Southerners. The Civil War became unpopular.

On September 22, 1862, Lincoln threatened to end slavery if the South did not stop fighting against the Union. The South ignored the warning and continued to fight against the North. On January 1, 1863, Lincoln gave the Emancipation Proclamation, stating that slaves in the Southern states were free.

The South continued to struggle to supply its army. Even though Memphis was taken by Union soldiers in 1862, supporters sent some food and supplies to Confederate troops. The South built and used railroads to move troops and supplies. The Confederacy took over the Southern railroads. During the war, industries that supported the war effort began to grow. The Confederacy supported foundries and companies that built ships, ammunition and other war-time supplies.

But it wasn't enough. The pressure to end the war grew. At the long-fought Battle of Petersburg, General Ulysses Grant's Northern troops surrounded much of the Confederate Army in Petersburg, Virginia. Over the next nine months, the Northern troops cut off supply lines into the town. Southern soldiers went without food and supplies. Eventually, Confederate General Robert E. Lee retreated, surrendering shortly thereafter.

After the Civil War, the South had to repair the damage from the battles. Tennessee suffered less damage than other states, however, and recovered quickly. In the following years, the people used more machines. Companies grew larger. People moved to the cities. All three factors were traits of the Industrial Revolution. The Industrial Revolution began around 1870 and continued until about 1920.

title: Buffalo Soldiers Keep the Peace
text:
One of the least known and honored groups of United States soldiers ever to go into battle was a group of African American soldiers called Buffalo Soldiers. These soldiers played a huge role in keeping the peace between the American Indians and early western settlers during the late 1800s.

Large numbers of African American soldiers fought during the Civil War, and after the war ended, many of these soldiers chose to remain in the military. In 1866, the 10th Cavalry was formed at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. This unit was made up of African American soldiers who had fought in the Civil War, and Civil War hero Benjamin Grierson led the group. The standards set for joining this military unit were very strict, and the group was made up of highly qualified soldiers.

The commander of Fort Leavenworth felt that African American soldiers had no place in the regular Army, and he made life as difficult as he could for the 10th Cavalry. Eventually, Benjamin Grierson asked that his unit be transferred, and by the summer of 1867, the group had been moved to Fort Riley. For the next eight years, the 10th Cavalry made its home at forts throughout Kansas and Oklahoma. This group of African American soldiers was treated very poorly. They often received the worst horses, the poorest food and the toughest assignments. Despite the ill treatment they received, the 10th Cavalry provided protection to settlers traveling the westward trails, kept the workers on the railroads safe from American Indian attacks and even strung miles of new telegraph lines throughout the West.

Because of their bravery and willingness to take on difficult assignments, the African American soldiers impressed their leaders, as well as their enemies. The Cheyenne tribe was particularly impressed by these soldiers and gave them the name Buffalo Soldiers, after the symbol of bravery, the buffalo. The soldiers were proud of the nickname and used it like a badge of honor.

The Buffalo Soldiers fought against the American Indians to keep the peace throughout Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas. They fought against Mexican rebels and famous outlaws as well. The Buffalo Soldiers spent more than 20 years serving in some of the most unpleasant and harsh assignments available throughout the West and Southwest. Their bravery and loyalty to the United States can never be questioned.

More than 100 years later, General Colin Powell fought to bring the Buffalo Soldiers the honor they deserved and never received. General Powell urged the U.S. government to honor the great accomplishments of the Buffalo Soldiers with a monument of their own. The Buffalo Soldier National Monument was dedicated in Leavenworth in 1992. General Powell then made the statement that "the terrible overlooking of black heroism in the military finally has ended."

title: Western Trails Mapping Activity
text:
Several Western trails are marked on the map. Using the descriptions and color key, label each trail and trace it with the appropriate color. Draw a compass rose. (Present-day state boundaries are on this map.)

Mormon Trail (yellow - This one has been done for you.)

Mormon pioneers followed this route from Illinois to Utah. The trail began in Nauvoo, IL, and extended through Council Bluffs, IA, Ft. Bridger, WY, and on to Salt Lake City, UT.

Lewis and Clark Expedition (blue)

Lewis and Clark left from St. Louis, MO, and traveled westward, across the Rocky Mountains and on to the Pacific Coast, ending up at Fort Clatsop, OR.

Oregon Trail (green)

This trail began at Independence, MO, and wound its way through what is now Kansas, Nebraska, Wyoming, Idaho and Oregon, ending up at Oregon City, OR.

Pony Express Trail (red)

The Pony Express began in St. Joseph, MO, and crossed the Great Plains, the Rocky Mountains and the Sierra Nevada into Sacramento, CA.

Transcontinental Railroad (orange)

The route stretched from Omaha, NE (where the existing railway lines had ended), to Sacramento, CA. The Union Pacific and Central Pacific railroads worked their way across the country toward each other, finally joining up at Promontory Point, UT.

California Trail (brown)

The California Trail traveled along much of the same route as the Oregon Trail. In Idaho, the California Trail split from the Oregon Trail, as settlers headed southwest to find gold.

title: Westward Expansion
text:
"Hey, Alana, are you ready to learn more about westward expansion?"

"Sure, I'm ready, Jackson, but what exactly do you mean by 'westward expansion'?"

"'Westward expansion' describes the way Americans spread out across the western half of this country once the U.S. began taking control of the area. We will look back at some events that shaped the West."

"Yes, Jackson, sometimes we have to look back to understand what happened next!"

Louisiana Purchase

In 1803, U.S. President Thomas Jefferson approved the purchase of 828,000 square miles of land from the French for $15 million. The Louisiana Purchase doubled the size of the U.S. and extended our western border all the way to the Rocky Mountains.

Expedition of Lewis and Clark

In May 1804, explorers Meriwether Lewis and William Clark set out on their historic journey to explore the Louisiana Purchase. President Jefferson had three specific goals for the Corps of Discovery, as this group of explorers was called.

Search for a water route to the Pacific Ocean.

Start building relationships with some American Indians in the area.

Record their findings about the soil, plants and animals in the area.

The expedition lasted 28 months and covered nearly 8,000 miles, from St. Louis to the Oregon coast and back. Lewis and Clark didn't find a water route to the Pacific Ocean, but they did accomplish the other goals. Part of their success was due to the help of the Shoshone Indian guide and interpreter, Sacagawea. She made the trip much easier for all. Finally, the Corps of Discovery succeeded in mapping a huge amount of land, making life much easier for those who traveled after them.

Indian Removal Act

During the 1820s and 1830s, many settlers moved to land that was home to the Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Chickasaw, Choctaw and Seminole tribes. In 1830, Congress passed the Indian Removal Act. This gave President Andrew Jackson the power to move American Indians to land west of the Mississippi River, now part of the state of Oklahoma. This was devastating for the tribal populations.

California Gold Rush

In 1848, James Marshall discovered gold near California's American River. Word spread quickly, and more than 80,000 people came to California in 1849 alone. The work was hard, prices for supplies were high and very few actually struck it rich. But because of the Gold Rush, the population of California grew quickly.

The Homestead Act of 1862

In 1862, Congress passed the Homestead Act. This gave any head of a household, widowed women or any man over 21 the right to claim one 160-acre portion of land. The homesteader had five years to build a house, live in it and farm the land. Under this act, 270 million acres were claimed and settled. Some of this land was taken from the American Indians. Their homelands were shrinking more and more.

The Transcontinental Railroad

Traveling west by wagon, stagecoach or horseback was difficult. In 1862 President Abraham Lincoln signed the Pacific Railway Act. Two companies began building a transcontinental (across the continent) railroad, linking the East with the West. Chinese and Irish immigrant workers were hired to do dangerous work on the railroad, including blasting through mountains and building steep bridges. The westbound track and the eastbound track finally joined at Promontory Summit, Utah on May 10, 1869. People could now travel from one coast to the other in under 10 days!

"Wow, Jackson, it certainly took a lot to settle this great country of ours."

"You're right, Alana. The early pioneers were brave, hardworking men, women and children who moved west for many different reasons."

"We can't forget about the American Indians, Jackson! It wasn't easy for them to change their way of life.They didn't seem to have much choice in the matter."

"That's true, Alana. By 1890, most American Indians lived on reservations. As the year 1900 approached, many U.S. citizens considered the West to be settled."

"Jackson, do you think our friends can help us fill in the missing dates and events on the timeline?"

"Sure they can!"

title: Let's Write
text: Write two paragraphs about westward expansion, using details and information from this week's text. Write from the point of view of two different parties, such as the white settlers and the American Indians. What is happening in your life? How are things changing? What does the future hold?

title: Think and Review
text:
1. How did the bison play a part in westward expansion? Give two different perspectives.

2. List the three main goals of the Lewis and Clark expedition. How did the expedition affect American Indians?

3. What was the main reason for building the transcontinental railroad? Why do you think immigrants chose to do dangerous jobs?

4. How did the Pony Express improve communication in America?

5. How were the Buffalo Soldiers treated unfairly?

title: The Pony Express
text:
Sometimes stories about historic events get exaggerated or even made up. Read this story and do some research to decide whether you think Charlie Miller's tale is true.

Howdy, students! I'm "Bronco" Charlie Miller. People have told many stories about the Pony Express, the mail service that ran from April 1860 to October 1861. Not everyone believes that I was the youngest rider ever to join the Pony Express. Let me tell you, it was a wild ride!

When I was only 11 years old, I saw a Pony Express poster that said: "Wanted: young, skinny, wiry fellows, not over 18. Must be expert riders, willing to risk death daily. Orphans preferred. Wages: $25 per week." It was just the job for me!

We Pony Express riders rode between 75 and 100 miles from station to station along the 1,800-mile route from St. Joseph, Missouri to Sacramento, California. We got the mail delivered in only 10 days! (That's a lot faster than the near 25 days it would take to deliver mail by stagecoach.) Besides sore backsides, we also dealt with numbing snowstorms, brain-frying heat and drenching rains. Oh, and how could I forget sometimes being attacked by American Indians or outlaws? I'd do it all again, though, if I had half a chance!

title: The Wonders of the West
text:
Throughout the 1840s, the idea that the United States had the right to spread across the continent became very popular. More and more people started to move west. This idea was called "manifest destiny."

Life was hard for the settlers who came to the Dakota Territory hoping to live on the land and buy a homestead. Laura Ingalls Wilder and her husband, Almanzo, tried their hand at homesteading in the Dakotas during the late 1800s. Read this short paragraph about their experiences written by their daughter, Rose Wilder Lane.

“Conditions had changed when I was born; there was no more free land. Of course, there never had been free land. It was a saying in the Dakotas that the Government bet a quarter section against fifteen dollars and five years’ hard work that the land would starve a man out in less than five years. My father won the bet. It took seven successive years of complete crop failure, with work, weather and sickness that wrecked his health permanently, and interest rates of 36 percent on money borrowed to buy food, to dislodge us from that land. I was then seven years old.”

title: Where the 'Buffalo' Roam?
text:
Actually, buffalo roam in Africa and Asia, not in America. Settlers mistakenly called the American bison "buffalo," and the name stuck, even though it's wrong. Great herds of American bison were once a common sight throughout the Midwest and West. In the mid-1800s, an estimated 30 to 75 million bison roamed the prairies of the Great Plains region. By 1884, the estimate of free-roaming bison in the entire United States was 325! What caused these great beasts to become nearly extinct? The settling of the West, that's what!

From 1872 to 1874, hunters using horses and guns killed an average of 5,000 bison per day. They sold the hides and meat for money. Others killed only for the thrill of the hunt, leaving the carcasses behind to rot. American Indians relied on bison for everything from food, to clothing and tools. This hunting left them without an important natural resource. Life as they knew it was gone forever.

When government officials realized what was happening to the bison, they passed laws to protect them. In 1894 Congress passed a law making it illegal to hunt bison in Yellowstone National Park. Later, officials passed laws to protect other species of plants and animals as well. The Endangered Species Act was passed in 1973 to protect endangered species and keep them from becoming extinct. The act helps endangered species to recover and grow strong.

title: Chief Black Kettle: Powerful Peacemaker
text:
In 1861, Southern Cheyenne Chief Black Kettle moved his people to Sand Creek, Colorado, as part of a treaty. Even though Black Kettle cooperated with the government, soldiers attacked his camp and killed more than 200 Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho people.

In 1867, Black Kettle moved his people to Indian Territory in Oklahoma as part of another treaty. The tribe never received the food and supplies the government promised them. Some of Black Kettle's warriors raided settlements in the area for the things they needed to survive. Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer led an attack on the tribe at Washita River. Black Kettle and his wife were both killed. The man who tried to help the settlers and American Indians live together in peace lost his life in a violent battle. Chief Black Kettle is still remembered as a man who only wanted peace.

title: The American Federation of Labor
text:
The American Federation of Labor (AFL) was the most influential early labor union. The AFL formed when the Knights of Labor were unable to get better pay for cigar-making employees.

The AFL began in 1886 and was led by a man named Samuel Gompers. Gompers' leadership was instrumental in the early days of the AFL. He knew how important it was to get the public on his side. He convinced many important writers to write pro-union pieces in their publications. Gompers died in 1924.

The AFL first represented small trade organizations instead of individuals. However, the early AFL fought fiercely for the workers.

Today, the American Federation of Labor lives on. It merged with the Congress of Industrial Organizations to become the AFL-CIO.

title: The First Labor Day
text: Historians are not certain who actually came up with the idea for Labor Day. Some believe that Peter McGuire (below) founded it. He was the first secretary of the American Federation of Labor. Others say the idea belonged to Matthew Maguire. He was the secretary of the Central Labor Union. New York's Central Labor Union chose to make the idea a reality by organizing the first Labor Day on Sept. 5, 1882, in New York City. The holiday was created to honor American workers who used their strength and skills to make life better for the entire country. The first Labor Day was celebrated with a parade, speeches and a picnic for workers and their families. In 1894, Labor Day became an annual national holiday. People now celebrate it on the first Monday in September. What do you do on Labor Day?

title: Let's Write
text: Describe at least one way that John D. Rockefeller helped shape America as you know it.

title: Who Was John Rockefeller?
text:
One of the most influential figures of the Gilded Age was John Rockefeller. He became the richest man of all time in modern America.

His early money came from oil refining. He was one of the first to make money on refining oil instead of simply drilling for it.

This turned out to be a case of "right time, right place" for Rockefeller. America grew more and more dependent on kerosene and gasoline. This drove his profits through the roof. His control of gas and oil allowed for the cost of oil for lighting and heat to come way down. This opened up a new world in homes everywhere. People could read, do things at night and be more productive and comfortable. It was truly a new age.

Rockefeller owned around 90 percent of the oil refineries and pipelines. In 1911, the Supreme Court said this was a violation of anti-trust laws and created a monopoly. The government broke Rockefeller’s corporation into several smaller companies. This was to encourage competition and capitalism.

These companies eventually became more and more valuable. This made Rockefeller into a billionaire. He chose to give back to the nation and became a leader in philanthropy, donating over $500 million. He helped fund corporations that focused on science, medicine, education and more. He tried to live to 100 to continue his good work, and moved to an ideal spot, Ormond Beach, Florida, to do so. He made it to age 97.

title: Gilded Age Timeline
text:
The Gilded Age was a time of conflict between workers and employers. Look at the timeline to see how major events developed during the Gilded Age.

1868: Ulysses S. Grant elected president

1869: Knights of Labor (KOL) formed

This union was formed to unite skilled and unskilled workers alike. The KOL wanted an eight-hour workday, the end of child labor and equal pay for equal work.

1870: John D. Rockefeller incorporates Standard Oil

1872: Crédit Mobilier Scandal

Some members of Congress received free stock in return for protecting this railroad construction company

1873: Mark Twain publishes "The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today," a satire of the times.

1876: Alexander Graham Bell invents the telephone.

1877: The Great Railroad Strike

Railroad workers in West Virginia went on strike to protest wage cuts and poor working conditions. The strike spread to other states. It ended 45 days later, with over 100 men dead. Workers did not gain much from the strike. The railroad companies were determined never to let the workers unite against them again.

1886: The Haymarket Square Riot

When labor union members and supporters joined together for a rally in Chicago's Haymarket Square, police officers arrived to break it up. A pipe bomb killed eight officers. Four men were convicted in connection with the bombing and executed. Many people turned against labor unions because of this event.

1886: The American Federation of Labor formed

Samuel Gompers organized the American Federation of Labor to work for better wages, an eight-hour workday, safer working conditions and the end of child labor.

1892: The Homestead Strike

When the manager of Andrew Carnegie's Homestead steel plant cut wages, union workers fought back by striking. Violence erupted and several people died. Eventually, the strike ended in failure for the union workers.

1894: The Pullman Strike

Workers went on strike to protest low wages and layoffs. The strike shut down railroad traffic throughout the Midwest. Unions gained some popularity after the Pullman Strike, although Pullman workers did not gain much from it.

1905: Industrial Workers of the World Founded

This union was called "One Big Union" and was formed with the idea that all workers should be united in one group.

1913: First Secretary of Labor, William Bauchop Wilson, appointed by President Woodrow Wilson

This position was created to protect American workers. The Department of Labor makes sure workers have reasonable wages, fair taxes, safe working conditions and retirement benefits.

Why do you think there were so many labor issues? What does that tell you about the Gilded Age?

title: Think and Review Questions
text:
What does "gilded" mean? Explain why this time period is often called the Gilded Age.

Compare and contrast the terms "robber barons" and "captains of industry." Why do you think that wealthy business leaders of the Gilded Age could go by either nickname?

Analyze why so many labor unions were formed during the Gilded Age. What was their purpose? What method did they use to try to improve conditions for their workers?

What was the Progressive Movement? What did Progressives hope to accomplish?

title: A Tale of Today
text:
"Has anyone ever heard of the Gilded Age?"

Ms. Johnson's question to the class sounded hopeful, but no one raised their hands. Jackson looked over at Alana, and she shrugged, indicating she had not heard of it.

"It comes from a book written by Mark Twain," Ms. Johnson continued. "In The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today, Twain discussed how we don't notice what is wrong with society because we are busy focusing on superficial things."

"I know about Mark Twain," Alana said. "He's one of the best-known American authors of the 19th century."

Ms. Johnson went on with the lesson, and then she put the old book in a center for kids to look at.

"Hey, Jackson. Let's go 'read' the Mark Twain book at the reading center, okaaaayyyy?"

"'Sure, Alana. Hmmm. The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today, by Mark Twain. I know he wrote The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. It looks like this particular book was published in 1873 - perfect! Let's go visit Mark Twain. Maybe he can tell us more about the Gilded Age and how this time period got its name."

"Great idea, Alana. One, two, three ... let's go!"

(Jackson and Alana each grab the book and are transported back to the late 1800s, where they find themselves joining the famous author Mark Twain on his porch.)

"Mr. Twain? I'm Alana and this is my friend, Jackson. We've come a long way to ask you about your book, The Gilded Age."

"So, you've read my book, have you? What did you think of it, my young friends?"

"Well, we haven't exactly read it, but we're curious about the title. What exactly is the Gilded Age, anyway?"

"Well, Jackson, the times in which I live are full of wealth and success, but not everything is as golden as it seems. There are many factory owners, land developers and oil and steel tycoons. Tycoons are powerful business owners who make a lot of money and live a life of wealth. But there are also many poor factory workers and farmers who barely get by. 'Gilded' means covered with a thin layer of gold, and that's what American society is like during this period. Most of society is living with very little money while some make up the thin layer of wealth. Gilding makes it pretty on the outside, but the gold doesn't go all the way through."

"You mean the Gilded Age was great for those who owned businesses and factories, but it was hard for those who worked for them?"

"That's exactly right, Alana. Now you know why I chose that title for my book."

"Thanks for your time, Mr. Twain. We promise to read your book when we get home."

"You do that. Nothing like a book to pour a little knowledge into you!"

title: How Do Unions Work?
text:
A labor union is a group of workers who try to get better working conditions. Their leaders meet with leaders of the company to try to reach an agreement. This is called collective bargaining. Hopefully, they can all reach a compromise that both sides are happy with.

Sometimes, if an agreement can't be met, members of a union go on strike. This means they refuse to work. This is a form of protest against things like low pay and poor benefits for workers. A strike is a last resort, since most workers need to work to earn a living.

An early example of unions in America was the Knights of Labor. This union started in the late 19th century. It soon ended due to poor organization and poor leadership.

The American Federation of Labor began in 1886 and was longer-lasting. This organization is still around today.

Today, unions are a controversial issue. Some see them as getting in the way of a free market.

Others continue to see them as the best hope for workers to get fair pay and fair treatment.

title: World's First Skyscraper
text:
Did you know that the world's first skyscraper was built in Chicago in 1884? When you think of skyscrapers, you probably imagine today's giant buildings that climb as high as 163 floors (2,722 feet) in the air. This building was only 10 stories high and measured 138 feet from bottom to top. That may not seem like much compared to today's skyscrapers, but in 1884, it was an amazing accomplishment!

The Home Insurance Building was the first skyscraper to use a steel frame skeleton to support not only the walls, but also the weight of the whole building, inside and out. William LeBaron Jenney designed the building, and its success led to the construction of many future skyscrapers. New York City's Empire State Building and One World Trade Center are some of today's examples.

title: Political Cartoons
text:
This picture is a political cartoon, or a comic with a message. The cartoon is called “Monopoly Millionaires Dividing the Country,” and it appeared in “Puck” magazine in 1885. The picture shows the powerful railroad owners and investors William Henry Vanderbilt, Jay Gould, Cyrus West Field and Russell Sage. After looking at the cartoon, answer the following questions.

1. What do you think these men are doing?

2. How are the knives being used?

3. Why is one of the men rolling dice?

4. How do you think the cartoonist felt about these “robber barons?” Why?

Now on a separate sheet of paper, draw your own political cartoon using information from this week’s magazine. You may look back at the lesson if you need help. Make your drawing colorful by using colored pencils or crayons. Be creative and have fun!

title: The Gilded Age
text:
The period in history from about 1877 to 1893 was called the Gilded Age because of the fancy lifestyles of those who got rich for the first time. The wealthy were few in number, but they liked to show off their money with nice clothes, expensive jewelry and parties. "Gilded" means covered with a thin layer of gold, and that's what American society was like during this period. Most of society was living in poverty while some became wealthy. These wealthy people made up the thin layer of wealth on top. Life was good for the wealthy, but for those who worked in factories, mines and mills, it was very hard.

The rich were actually few in number during this time period, but they were very good at spending their money and showing off their wealth. There were 12 million families living in the United States during the Gilded Age. The wealthiest 10 percent of Americans controlled about 75 percent of all the country's wealth.

Barons or Business Leaders?

Where did the wealthy earn their money? Many of them earned it by using natural resources, as well as poor workers. Some people called the leaders of industry during the Gilded Age "robber barons" because of the way they made their money. They felt that these people robbed from the land and the poor to become barons, or powerful business leaders.

Andrew Carnegie, John C. Osgood and John D. Rockefeller are sometimes called robber barons. Andrew Carnegie used iron ore to create the largest steel company in the world. John C. Osgood bought acres of land in Colorado where he mined coal and created the Colorado Fuel and Iron Company. John D. Rockefeller founded Standard Oil Company by buying up oil reserves and forcing other oil companies out of business. He used this natural resource to become the richest man in the world. He once said, "Do you know the only thing that gives me pleasure? It's to see my dividends [profits] coming in."

Fortunately, these men did many good things for the country as well. Their companies created jobs and produced useful products. They also gave millions of dollars to help the poor and built libraries, universities, hospitals and museums. Some people like to call them "captains of industry" rather than robber barons. This was because of the jobs they created and the contributions they made to the world of business and industry. They developed new technology for the Industrial Revolution. They took risks that resulted in inventions that improved peoples’ lives. They built new industries and made a significant contribution to the economy of the United States by adding a great deal of wealth to the nation. J.P. Morgan actually bailed out the U.S. Treasury by loaning it $65 million! What would you consider these men to be: robber barons or captains of industry?

The Progressive Movement

The Progressive Movement was an effort to reform (improve) the problems that had come about after the Industrial Revolution. Progressives, as they were called, joined together to help the poor in many ways. They influenced government welfare services, the building of affordable, safe housing and the passing of laws. This was to keep business owners from taking advantage of their workers and the environment. Progressives also worked to keep large companies from becoming too powerful. They wanted to make taxes more affordable for the poor, give the common people more power to vote on laws and hold the rich accountable for their actions. Presidents Woodrow Wilson and Theodore Roosevelt were both considered Progressives. Eventually, the government passed laws that improved some of these situations. By the 1920s, women could vote, and businesses had to follow certain rules.

title: Hello, Alexander Graham Bell
text:
Pick up any phone book, and chances are you will see the word "Bell" on it. Alexander Graham Bell, a Scottish inventor, invented a machine that could send more than one signal across electrical wires.

Sound was important to Bell. His father was a speech expert, and his mother was deaf. Alexander taught deaf people to speak by feeling the vibrations of sound.

He believed that he could send human speech over electrical wires. He invented a device that was sensitive to the vibrations made from speech. It changed the vibrations of speech into electrical signals that were conducted over electrical wires. On the other end, the electrical impulses were then fed into an instrument that converted them into vibrations that reproduced the sound of speech.

After some years, telephones were found in nearly every household in the country! Modern life without telephones is hard to imagine. Next time you use a modern smartphone, remember its beginnings with Bell's first wired telephone.

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you could have dinner with any inventor or entrepreneur and ask them questions. What would you ask them? What would you have for dinner?

title: Inventors and Entrepreneurs: What's the Difference?
text:
Alana and Jackson are working together on a class project about inventions we use today. They come up with three important inventors. Alexander Graham Bell was the inventor of the telephone. They also chose George Washington Carver and what he did for agriculture, and Thomas Edison and his development of the light bulb.

Alana points to a passage in a book they are reading, "George Washington Carver was born into slavery and after he was freed, he worked hard to get an education."

Jackson held up a very old photograph in a frame and said, "My grandmother said if I was extra careful, I could show this photograph of George Washington Carver she bought at an estate sale. She said it's important to recognize his contributions to the world."

"Jackson, it says here in this book that George Washington Carver created over 300 uses for peanuts," said Alana.

"What's so special about peanuts?" said Jackson quizzically.

"I know how we can find out," said Alana with a smile.

"Let's go!" said Jackson.

They both put their hands on the photograph and were transported to the year 1897 in Tuskegee, Alabama. George Washington Carver was speaking at a gathering of farmers. He was explaining the need to rotate their crops with peanuts for bigger harvests of corn, wheat, and other crops.

This doesn't seem like a happy meeting. The farmers are happy the harvests are bigger but now there is another problem. The farmers are complaining now that they have been rotating their crops, there are too many peanuts and no one wants that much peanut butter.

Carver explains there are many things to make from peanuts to make money. He listed peanut oil, recipes with peanuts, animal feed and paper. They could also make dyes for cloth, leather and wood. The farmers agree that when their animals are fed a mixture of corn and peanuts, the result was high-quality bacon and hams from their pigs. They begin to name many things they can do with peanuts.

"Wow," said Alana. "I understand why the peanut was so important to George Washington Carver now."

"Me too," said Jackson. "Let's get back to class."

title: George Washington Carver: Scientist, Inventor and Teacher
text:
George Washington Carver was born in 1864 into slavery in Missouri. When he was an infant, raiders kidnapped George, his mother and his sister. The kidnappers sold the three of them, and only George was found.

The end of the Civil War in 1865 brought an end to slavery in Missouri. The man who had once owned George and his brother let them live with him after they were freed. Moses Carver and his wife taught the boys to read as the local school would not accept black students.

George drove himself to learn as much as he could. He attended a school for black children ten miles away. His grades were good and he graduated from high school. He was accepted at a college in Kansas until the school learned his race and turned him away. George did not give up and kept learning. He conducted experiments with plants and studied geology. He was later accepted into a college in Iowa where his skills and interest in plant biology led to him being the first African American student at Iowa State University.

Later in life, he taught at Tuskegee University in Alabama. During that time he developed a method of crop rotation for farmers. Farmers were able to grow more food and made more money. Although he didn't invent peanut butter, Carver did invent nearly 300 uses for peanuts from paper to oil and paint which launched an industry around peanut growing.

George Washington Carver died in January 1943 at the age of 78 after falling down the stairs of his home. His contributions to biology benefit the world today and he is remembered as a pioneer among inventors.

title: Who had the greatest impact?
text:

Who had the greatest impact? Be sure to defend your reasoning. Persuade the reader to agree with you.

title: Entrepreneurs and Inventors Work Together
text:
Entrepreneurs bring an idea into the marketplace. Inventors create ways to achieve tasks with new ideas.

Sometimes they team up. Henry Ford, owner of the Ford Motor Company, worked with George Washington Carver. They developed a type of rubber to compensate for the rubber shortages in 1942.

Not every inventor is a success in business. Thomas Edison, credited with inventing the light bulb, worked with inventor Nikola Tesla. He laid out ideas about sending information through the air. This later became a technology called wireless local area networking. You probably call it Wi-Fi. Tesla received money from J.P. Morgan to build a tower that would send information by way of light waves. He wasn't able to complete the tower, though. An Italian inventor eventually received credit for this technology, which we now call radio.

Edison was a success, but Tesla did not get as much fame for his inventions. Tesla died in poverty. Perhaps he was more interested in invention itself rather than making money from it. Edison, on the other hand, was a businessman. He formed a successful company and made a lot of money.

title: Think and Review Questions
text:
1. How did George Washington Carver become successful even though he was born into poverty and slavery?

2. Thomas Edison is credited with many inventions including the light bulb and the phonograph for playing records. How would your life be different without electricity?

3. How did Madam C.J. Walker become a self-made millionaire? Why was this so significant?

4. Which of the inventors or entrepreneurs do you consider the most important?

title: Madam C.J. Walker
text:
Sarah Breedlove McWilliams Walker was orphaned at age seven. She was the daughter of former slaves.

As a teen, Sarah began having problems with thinning hair. She tried mixing different ingredients to find something that might help. She used them on herself. She found something that worked!

Walker then moved to Denver, changed her name to Madam C.J. Walker and began selling her hair products to other black women. When she started, Walker walked door-to-door to make sales. Walker went across the U.S. and even to the Caribbean Islands, teaching women about hair care. Walker also taught women how to sell her products and make a living. Later she opened a beauticians’ college in Pittsburgh.

Walker came to employ thousands of “Walker Agents.” Her products and training took off, and Madam C.J. Walker became the first self-made African American female millionaire. Madam Walker will be remembered for creating not only her own success through hard work, but also for helping many other women succeed in sales and industry.

title: How Entrepreneurs and Inventors Change the World
text:
The world needs both entrepreneurs and inventors. Business owners create not only products and services for people to own or use, they create jobs. For example, Henry Ford needed people to work in his factories to produce cars. Those workers spent the money they earned buying homes, food and other items. This helps the economy of an area to grow. Henry Ford and Thomas Edison are both examples of inventors who were also successful entrepreneurs.

George Washington Carver created jobs and products to help farmers make use of their surplus of peanuts. Farmers were able to make more money because their crops had bigger yields using Carver's methods of farming.

Cornelius Vanderbilt did not invent anything but he was a shrewd businessman. He first started with steamships transporting people from New York to San Francisco. Then he began buying into the new method of transportation across the United States: the railroad. Because he owned so much of the railroad business, he could coordinate schedules. Travel became more convenient when traveling long distances. It was more efficient, but Vanderbilt was aggressive in keeping control. In doing so, he became one of the richest Americans in the 19th century. He had enormous control over the railroads in the U.S.

Alexander Graham Bell is best known for inventing the telephone. The first telephones do not look much like the phones of today as they had dials instead of buttons. Early on, having a phone was expensive and several neighbors shared a single line.

Andrew Carnegie had a steel company. Think of everything that steel might be used to produce. It's the base metal for many things from buildings, to roads, railroads and more. He took control of most other steel companies and put others out of business. Andrew Carnegie sold his company to another famous businessman named J.P. Morgan. Upon leaving the business world, Carnegie worked in charitable causes for the rest of his life.

Imagine life without the inventions of the telephone, the lightbulb, or modern farming methods. What if Vanderbilt never developed the railroads or Ford never built a car? Our lives would be very different in the present without both the inventions and the men who created successful businesses to expand industries such as transportation.

title: Beulah Louise Henry
text:
Beulah Louise Henry was one of history's most important inventors. In her long career, she created more than 100 inventions! Her ideas ranged from toys and fashion to machines and office supplies. People of the time called her "Lady Edison." This name came from famous inventor Thomas Edison. People in her time thought she couldn't be successful because she was a woman. She proved them wrong time and time again.

In 1912, she invented a new kind of ice cream freezer. In the 1920s, she moved to New York and got into the fashion business. In the 1930s, she turned her attention to household products. Her ideas were truly diverse!

Inventing came easily to Beulah. To her, problems were nothing but ideas. When she saw a problem, she found a way to fix it. She was a smart business person. She turned her ideas into a career. We remember her as one of our greatest inventors of all time. Thank you, Lady Edison.

title: Will It Work?
text:
Two great minds are better than one.

Henry Ford heard about the advances George Washington Carver had made in biology and wanted to meet him. Ford and Carver wrote letters and visited each other starting in 1934. Ford made a car body made from soybean plastic. The two also talked about the invention of other fuels to use in cars.

During World War II, there was a shortage of rubber. Ford contacted Carver to work with him on making a new type of rubber. They experimented with potatoes and dandelions. Within a year they were able to create a good substitute rubber from goldenrod plants.

Carver died in 1943 and Ford died in 1947. Even so, their organizations worked together for many years. Ford has given money to support Tuskegee University, where Carver taught.

title: Think and Review Questions
text:
Identify three or four factors that led the U.S. to become involved in the Spanish-American War. Cite your source.

Predict the outcome of the Spanish-American War if General Weyler had never been Governor of Cuba.

Design a headline about recent events at school or in the news that uses the principles of yellow journalism.

What are similarities and differences between the Rough Riders and the 9th and 10th Cavalry?

title: Who Fought the War?
text:
At the time of the Spanish-American War, African Americans weren't treated fairly. Some people felt that African Americans shouldn't be allowed in the Army. Some African Americans even refused to fight for the United States. They said they wouldn't join until everyone was treated equally.

The 9th and 10th Cavalry, known as the Buffalo Soldiers, were African American. They moved to Florida to prepare for the Spanish-American War. While in Florida, they were poorly treated by some locals. Even so, the 9th and 10th Cavalries went to Cuba. There, they fought with the Rough Riders at Las Guasimas and San Juan Hill.

The 9th and 10th Cavalry were respected for their courage in battles. Edward L. Baker, of the 10th Cavalry, was awarded the Medal of Honor for bravery during the Battle of San Juan Hill. After landing at Tayabacao, Dennis Bell, Fitz Lee, George Wanton and William Thompkins volunteered to rescue wounded soldiers. All four also received the Medal of Honor.

The United States sent many other troops to fight in Cuba. One of the most famous group was the 1st Volunteer Cavalry. Under Lt. Colonel Teddy Roosevelt, they became "Roosevelt's Rough Riders." Newspapers celebrated the Rough Riders after defeating the Spanish. Roosevelt became a war hero. He went on to become President.

Teddy Roosevelt praised members of the 9th and 10th Cavalry. He famously said, "... no one can tell whether it was the Rough Riders or the men of the 9th who came forward with the greater courage to offer their lives in the service of their country."

title: The USS Maine
text:
In 1911, the Navy was able to bring the Maine to the surface. They were then able to see the damage. They decided that a mine had caused an explosion in the magazine, where they stored the ammunition. Other experts disagreed. They thought that the explosion was a result of spontaneous combustion of coal stored nearby. Whatever happened in the harbor that day may always be a mystery, but we know a lot about the ship.

The USS Maine was a second-class battleship, built in Brooklyn, New York. It cost $2 million and took almost nine years to complete. It was commissioned, or launched, in 1895. The Maine was 324 feet long, as long as a football field. It was 6,682 tons, but with three engines, it could go as fast as 15 knots, or about 17 miles per hour.

Three hundred fifty-five crew members lived on the ship. Ninety-four survived the accident. Some of the sailors that died were first buried in Cuba but moved to the United States. Many were buried in Arlington National Cemetery near Washington, D.C. The ship's main mast serves as a memorial to those sailors.

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you live in Cuba in the 1890s and write for a local newspaper. Write a newspaper editorial addressed to the United States. Explain whether or not you believe the U.S. should get involved. Why or why not? How would the U.S. benefit from becoming involved?

title: The Spanish-American War
text:
The Spanish-American War had a number of causes. Below is a timeline of events that contributed to the war, events during the war and war's aftermath.

1492: Christopher Columbus lands in Cuba. He claims it for Spain.

1511: Spain sends three ships and an army to create a settlement in Cuba and colonize the island. After three years of fighting, the Spanish take control of Cuba.

1823: The Monroe Doctrine. President James Monroe makes the United States' position on European expansion formal. He issues the Monroe Doctrine. The doctrine states the United States would oppose future European settlements in Latin America. In reality, the United States does not have the forces necessary to enforce the doctrine. Great Britain, however, supports the doctrine. It uses its large navy to protect British trade interests.

1868–1878: The Ten Years' War. Cuba fights for independence from Spain. Spain defeats Cuban rebels.

1879–1880: The Little War. Cuba's second failed attempt at liberation.

1890s: Yellow journalists tell exaggerated stories about how poorly the Spanish treat Cubans. General Valeriano Weyler becomes the Spanish Governor of Cuba. Weyler is a frequent target of yellow journalists.

1895–1898: Cuba begins its War of Independence against Spain. This is Cuba's third attempt at revolting against the Spanish. Partly because of yellow journalism, many people in the United States feel that Cubans are mistreated. The fighting costs the U.S. trade opportunities with Cuba. At the time, the value of trade between the U.S. and Cuba is about $100 million per year.

Early 1898: President William McKinley sends the USS Maine to Cuba to protect American business, people and property.

February 15, 1898: The USS Maine mysteriously sinks in Cuba's Havana Harbor. There are several theories on what caused the explosion that sank it. Right afterward, yellow journalists blame the Spanish. After a short investigation, the official U.S. position is that the Maine hit a mine.

April 20–25, 1898: Under growing pressure to act, McKinley signs a joint resolution. With congressional approval, the United States declares war on Spain. The United States Congress adds the Teller Amendment. The amendment states that the U.S. will not take control of Cuba.

May 1, 1898: The first battle of the Spanish-American War. Commodore George Dewey sails from Hong Kong. Dewey encounters and attacks the Spanish fleet in the Philippines. Most of the fighting is in Manila Bay. The battle is over in about six hours. The United States is victorious.

June 22, 1898: United States troops arrive in Cuba. Among the soldiers are the Rough Riders and the African American 9th and 10th Cavalries. Cuban rebels also join U.S. troops.

July 1, 1898: The United States wins the battle of San Juan Hill. By taking San Juan Hill, U.S. forces are in a position to attack the Spanish fleet. The fleet sails from the harbor. The U.S. attacks and defeats the fleet over the next few days.

July 17, 1898: Spanish forces in Cuba surrender.

December 10, 1898: The Treaty of Paris. The treaty gives the U.S. control of Guam, the Philippines and Puerto Rico. Spain removes its army from Cuba.

title: Imperialism
text:
Imperialists were those who believed that the U.S. should take control of areas of the world that would give them a military, political or economic advantage. William McKinley was an imperialist who served as president during the Spanish-American War. He fought the war with Spain to both free Cuba from Spanish rule and spread America’s influence throughout the Pacific. During McKinley's presidency, he worked to gain control of the Hawaiian islands and in 1900, Hawaii became a U.S. territory.

John Hay was another imperialist who introduced the famous “Open Door” policy after the end of the Spanish-American War. The policy stated that there should be an “open door” for nations wanting to trade with China. European nations had special trade agreements with China already. Hay encouraged equal access to Chinese ports and for taxes to be paid to the Chinese. Most countries did not object to the policy, but it made an impact on U.S. trade with China.

The U.S. began to take control.

title: The Sinking of the USS Maine: Eyewitness Report vs. Yellow Journalism
text:
When tensions between Spain and Cuba began heating up, publisher William Randolph Hearst sent an artist named Frederic Remington to Cuba to report on the situation. When Remington told Hearst that things were quiet and there would be no war, Hearst reportedly responded, “You furnish the pictures, and I’ll furnish the war.”

Here are two accounts of the sinking of the USS Maine on Feb. 15, 1898. Read both accounts and answer the questions that follow.

Account #1

Telegram from Charles D. Sigsbee, Captain of the USS Maine, February 15, 1898

Maine blown up in Havana Harbor at 9:40 tonight and destroyed. Many wounded and doubtless more killed or drowned. Wounded and others aboard Spanish Man of War Ward Line Streamer. Send Light House Tenders from Key West for crew and the few pieces of equipment above water. No one has clothing other than that upon him. Public opinion should be suspended until further report. All officers believed to be saved. Jenkins and Merritt not yet accounted for. Many Spanish officers including representative of General Blane now with me to express sympathy.

Account #2

The New York Journal, February 17, 1898

NAVAL OFFICERS THINK THE MAINE WAS DESTROYED BY A SPANISH MINE.

George Eugene Bryson, the Journal’s special correspondent at Havana, cables that it is the secret opinion of many Spaniards in the Cuban capital, that the Maine was destroyed and 258 men killed by means of marine mine or fixed torpeda. This is the opinion of several American naval authorities. The Spaniards, it is believed, arranged to have the Maine anchored over one of the harbor mines. Wires connected the mines with a … magazine, and it is thought the explosion was caused by sending an electric current through the wire. If this can be proven, the brutal nature of the Spaniards will be shown by the fact that they waited to spring the mine after all the men had retired for the night.

Compare and contrast the two accounts of the sinking of the USS Maine. Write your answers on the lines below. Use a separate piece of paper if needed.

How are the accounts alike?

How are they different?

Which one is based on fact? Which is an example of “yellow journalism”?

Why do you think Cpt. Sigsbee asked that, “Public opinion should be suspended until further report”?

title: A Visit to Havana Harbor
text:
"As you can see, class, there were a lot of reasons for the Spanish-American War," Ms. Johnson tells her class. "Tomorrow, I can't wait to see what you've all learned."

Jackson and Alana have learned a lot so far. Their class has almost finished a unit on the Spanish-American War. Tomorrow, Jackson and Alana, and the rest of the class will present on the roles of major players in the war. Jackson and Alana are going to play the role of sailors on the USS Maine. The class will hear from two other groups: yellow journalists and Rough Riders.

After school, Alana joins Jackson in the library.

"You ready for tomorrow, Jackson?" Alana asks.

Jackson checks his notebook. "I've read a bunch of different things about what happened to the USS Maine. But I think," says Jackson, "we should check for ourselves."

Alana smiles. "I hoped you would say that."

An old photograph of the USS Maine is hanging on the board at the front of the class and the pair don't hesitate to touch it. Jackson and Alana arrive in Havana Harbor about an hour after the USS Maine sinks. Debris floats in the water. Rescue boats bring survivors to shore. Doctors are tending to injured sailors as they arrive. Local authorities are talking to witnesses.

Alana notices a family of onlookers on the docks. "Come on, Jackson." Alana runs over to speak with them.

"What happened?" Alana asks the family.

"Everyone is saying the USS Maine was attacked," says the youngest girl, about 14. "They think it was the Spanish."

"No, no, no. They probably hit a mine," argues her older brother.

"We were a couple of blocks away," says their mother. "To me, it just looked like the boat was on fire. I don't know what happened," she adds.

Jackson writes "no one seems to agree" in his notebook. Jackson and Alana talk to others. They hear three different explanations of what happened. These include a mine, an explosion on the boat and a Spanish attack.

"It's getting late, Alana," Jackson says, "let's head back home."

****
The next day, the class buzzes with excitement. The first group presents a report on the Rough Riders. They are wearing faded blue uniforms. The Rough Riders were volunteers in the 1st United States Cavalry. They served under Colonel Leonard Wood. They didn't have enough supplies. Since they didn't have horses, people called them "Wood's Weary Walkers." Fighting under Lieutenant Colonel Roosevelt, they became "Roosevelt's Rough Riders." They were sent to fight Spanish forces shortly after the Spanish-American War began. They landed in Cuba on June 23, 1898. They easily defeated the Spanish.

The group reporting as yellow journalists, dressed in tweed coats and fake mustaches, present next. First, they explain that the term yellow journalism came from a war William Randolph Hearst and Joseph Pulitzer had over a cartoon. The term evolved into meaning writing sensational headlines and stories to sell newspapers. Next, they describe how they wrote stories about the "evil" Cuban governor, General Valeriano Weyler. The yellow journalists, working for either Hearst or Pulitzer, said the Spanish sank the USS Maine. They think these stories convinced President McKinley to declare war on the Spanish, beginning the Spanish-American war.

Jackson and Alana, dressed as sailors from the USS Maine group, disagree with the yellow journalists about how the ship sank. President William McKinley sent the USS Maine into Havana Harbor in early 1898. On February 15, sailors heard an explosion moments before the ship began to sink. To this day, no one is certain of the cause. An early investigation found the explosion was the result of a mine. Yellow journalists blamed the Spanish.

"Great job, class!" Ms. Johnson says. "This is a good example of how there might be different views about the same story."

title: I'll Give You the War!
text:
In the late 1890s, New York had two popular newspapers. The first was the New York Journal. William Randolph Hearst was the publisher. The second was the New York World, published by Joseph Pulitzer. To sell papers, both wrote sensational, shocking headlines. This was called yellow journalism. Hearst and Pulitzer were critical of the Spanish being in Cuba. They ran stories about General Weyler mistreating Cubans. When the USS Maine sank, yellow journalists blamed Spain.

In a famous story, a reporter told Hearst there was nothing in Cuba to write about. Hearst replied, "You furnish the picture, I'll furnish the war." Though this story may not be true, it speaks to the power of journalists. For many years, historians believed yellow journalism influenced many Americans to support the Cubans. Not only that, it has been claimed that Hearst's and Pulitzer's papers inspired the president and Congress to start the war. In recent years, historians have begun to question the influence of yellow journalism.

title: General Weyler and the Press
text:
General Valeriano Weyler was in charge of troops in the Philippines when he became Governor of Cuba. Spanish troops did not know how to fight rebels that blended in on the island and fought by hit-and-run tactics. To protect the Cubans, Weyler thought he needed to try something different.

Weyler ordered Cubans to leave their homes. Nearly two million Cubans moved into camps guarded by Spanish troops. The move wasn't planned well. The camps didn't have enough food or medicine. As a result, many Cubans got sick, went hungry or died.

Yellow journalists wrote stories about these living conditions. The stories about Weyler shaped popular American opinion. Americans felt bad for the Cubans. Many thought the U.S. should send troops to help. Spain removed Weyler as Governor in 1897 before the Spanish-American War began.

title: Welcome to the Land of Opportunity
text:
“Good afternoon, Jackson,” Alana called. “What'cha doing?”

“My mom gave me this,” he answered. “It's my great-grandfather's diary. His name was Lyle Small; he immigrated here from Barbados.”

“Cool,” Alana said. “May I read a bit?”

He handed her the handwritten book, peering over her shoulder as she read.

“Oh, look,” Alana said. “He came through Ellis Island. I've always wanted to see what it was like there when immigrants were coming through.”

“Well,” Jackson smiled, “what are we waiting for?” They joined hands, touched the journal, and found themselves standing in line in a large building filled with people speaking many different languages. They found a translator and explained who they were. The language assistant helped them talk to a group of immigrants about their experiences.

“It was hard even before the ship,” one girl said. “I had to walk two days to the train to get to the harbor. Then, I stayed in a boardinghouse, called an 'emigrant hotel,' for almost a month awaiting the arrival of the ship.”

“And, when we boarded the ship, officials interrogated us,” said another. “The ship official wrote the 31 answers on the manifest, or passenger and cargo list; I heard interviewers will ask the same questions here. They queried whether or not we could read and write, are in good physical and mental health, and have at least $25, and more.”

“Why are you immigrating?” Jackson asked.

“My family is very poor,” one young man said. “I came to America to earn money to send to them. When I'm settled, I'll send a ticket for my brother; he'll do the same, and, one day, our whole family will be here.”

“I'm from Ireland,” the translator said. “The potatoes were rotting from late blight, and there was no food. My da, my father, came here in 1850, so he wouldn't starve.”

“My name is Lyle,” said one man. “Where I lived, discrimination kept black people from getting good jobs. The same is true here, but I hear there are opportunities in the black neighborhoods in New York City.”

“What was the voyage like?” Alana said.

“It was horrendous,” Lyle told them. “We traveled in steerage, the cheapest at $30 a ticket. It was very crowded and dark. The hold was lined with bunks, one right above each other. We only had saltwater in the toilets and washrooms; there was little ventilation, so the filthy, unsanitary area smelled disgusting, with no fresh air.”

“That's awful,” Jackson said. “You must be discouraged, after that experience.”

“No,” Lyle smiled. “We are still very optimistic about our futures here in the land of opportunity.”

title: Let's Write
text: You've learned a lot about the immigrant experience. Pretend that you are an immigrant. Write a letter to your family in your home country, describing your experience on the ship or Ellis Island.

title: Immigration in the United States (1880s–1950s)
text:
Between 1880 and 1950, about 29 million immigrants arrived in the United States. Why did they come? How did they survive in this new land? What challenges did they face, and what impact did they have on the United States?

Where Did They Come From, and Why Did They Come?

Until the 1880s, most immigrants came to the United States from Ireland, Great Britain, Germany and Sweden. Most of them came here searching for a better way of life. In their home countries, many of these people were poor, hungry and persecuted, without basic freedoms of speech and religion. For example, over 1 million people left Ireland and came to America in the late 1840s. A horrible disease destroyed the potato crop there, which caused a terrible food shortage in the country.

From 1880 to 1920, most immigrants to the U.S. came from Southern and Eastern European countries, such as Italy, Austria-Hungary, Poland and Russia. Many of these immigrants came here searching for freedom and to escape persecution or poverty. During this time period, many Jews in Eastern Europe were being persecuted (treated unfairly because of race or religion). In Russia, Jews lost the right to worship, hold jobs and even attend school. Many immigrants came to America hoping to escape from poverty. They wanted to find good jobs and better homes. America was the “land of opportunity,” and they hoped their new country would make them rich. Everyone who immigrated to America hoped to find a better life.

Different groups tended to settle in different places. For example, Irish immigrants generally settled in large cities. About half of German immigrants settled in cities, half took up farming, mostly in the Midwest. Today, North and South Dakota and Wisconsin have the most people of German descent. Most Jewish immigrants moved to cities, with the majority first moving to the Lower East Side in New York.

Settling In

Most immigrants during this time period settled in large cities such as New York, Chicago, Boston, Philadelphia and San Francisco. American cities were growing places with factories that offered jobs to the newly arrived immigrants.

Cities were good places for immigrants to find others who had come from their home countries. These people spoke the same language, shared the same culture and helped new arrivals live in a strange, new land. Immigrants from the same country often lived together in certain sections of large cities. These people worked hard to make new lives for themselves in America. Unfortunately, life wasn’t as easy as many had hoped. Jobs were sometimes hard to find, and cities were crowded and dirty.

Because of the difficulties they faced, Italian immigrants came up with a saying that described the life they found here in America:

"I came to America because I heard the streets were paved with gold. When I got here, I found out three things: first, the streets weren’t paved with gold; second, they weren’t paved at all; and third, I was expected to pave them."

Italian immigrants in this time period usually remained in cities, particularly New York City.

Life on the farms of rural America wasn’t always better. Many immigrants from Northern Europe moved west from the big cities. Swedish immigrants settled most often in the Midwest. Minnesota and Wisconsin received the highest numbers of Swedish newcomers. They found land, but they also struggled. One Swedish farmer reported:

"None who are not accustomed to hard, agricultural labor ought to become farmers in this country. No one who is any other way well off in his native land ought to come hither."

What can you learn about the immigrants’ lives by reading these quotes?

In addition, people already living in the U.S treated some immigrant groups poorly. Some anti-immigrant feelings eventually became laws. The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 limited the number of Chinese workers allowed to come to the United States. The Immigration Act of 1924 limited the number of immigrants allowed entry into the United States through a national origins quota that severely limited immigration from Southern and Eastern Europe. Would you still want to move to the U.S.?

Immigrants’ Impact on the United States

What impact did these immigrants have on the United States? They filled jobs in factories, spread out across America and helped the American economy grow by leaps and bounds. They also brought their diverse array of languages, foods and music, contributing to the mix of different cultures that we know as the United States of America.

title: Angel Island
text:
During 1910 and 1940, hundreds of thousands of immigrants landed at Angel Island, California. These immigrants were from all over, including Mexico, Australia, Russia and Asia. Once the immigrants had arrived, they were taken to the Angel Island Immigration Station. The station was used as a detention and interrogation center. This was a process that had to be followed before immigrants were allowed to stay in America.

Unfortunately, Asian immigrants were not treated the same, especially Chinese immigrants. There were restrictive laws against the entry of Chinese immigrants. They were required to show that they had relatives who were U.S. citizens or they’d be sent back.

Li Ken Wong is an Asian American who came to California from China. She wrote a book called "Good Fortune: My Journey to Gold Mountain," in which she tells her amazing story. Her family was forced to live on Angel Island in San Francisco Bay for about a week. It wasn't easy for them. They faced many challenges and were often discriminated against.

title: Charting American Immigrants
text:
