title: Ellis and Angel Island Inspections
text:
Alana and Jackson heard about the inspections immigrants faced when they arrived in the United States. What was the process like? Was it hard?

The cabin passengers, those in first or second class, were checked on the ship and released. Steerage passengers were given a name tag with their manifest number (record of their ship and arrival date) on it, and arranged into groups of 30, according to those numbers. They were loaded onto barges and brought to the island.

Translators met them there. They went up the stairs to the registry room. A doctor awaited passengers at the top. He watched them for lameness and shortness of breath. Then he looked over their faces, hair, neck and hands. If he saw anything suspicious, he marked their right shoulders with chalk. Those who were marked were sent to a detention for further inspection.

If they passed that fast medical check, the eye doctors checked for trachoma (infections in the eye). Finally, they passed through the "primary line" inspection, which took about two minutes to verify the manifest information.

And if they didn't pass everything, they were sent back home. Children under 12 had to be accompanied by a parent; there was often weeping over having to split the family.

title: Think and Review Questions
text:
1. What were three important reasons that people immigrated to the United States?

2. The years between 1930 and 1965 saw a dramatic decrease in immigration. What accounted for the lower numbers?

3. What happened in Angel Island between 1910 and 1940? Why is it significant?

4. How were the conditions in steerage different from second or first class when they arrived in America?

title: Sadie Frowne: Her Own Story
text:
The following is the story of Sadie Frowne, a Jewish Immigrant from Poland who came to New York City as a girl during the early 1900s after her father died. She and her mother struggled to pay rent, and they had heard that it was easier to make money in America. Read her story, in her own words, and answer the questions that follow.

We came by steerage on a steamship in a very dark place that smelt dreadfully. There were hundreds of other people packed in with us, men, women and children, and almost all of them were sick. It took us twelve days to cross the sea, and we thought we should die, but at last the voyage was over, and we came up and saw the beautiful bay and the big woman with the spikes on her head and the lamp that is lighted at night in her hand.

Aunt Fanny and her husband met us at the gate of this country and were very good to us, and soon I had a place to live out [Sadie is referring to becoming a live-in domestic servant] while my mother got work in a factory making white goods. I was only a little over thirteen years of age and a greenhorn, so I received $9 a month and board and lodging, which I thought was doing well. Mother, who, as I have said, was very clever, made $9 a week on white goods, which means all sorts of underclothing, and is high-class work.

But mother … liked to go around and see everything, and friends took her about New York at night and she caught a bad cold and coughed and coughed. She really had hasty consumption [tuberculosis], but she didn’t know it, and I didn’t know it, and she tried to keep on working, but it was no use. She had not the strength. Two doctors attended her, but they could do nothing, and at last she died and I was left alone. I had saved money while out at service, but mother’s sickness and funeral swept it all away and now I had to begin all over again.

title: Guess Who Passed Through Ellis Island
text:
A number of important people came to the U.S. through Ellis Island. See if you recognize any of these names or their accomplishments. Immigrants like this, and many more, have changed America for the better.

1897– Mosel Teichman, Austria-Hungary

Mosel Teichman came to the U.S. when he was two years old. Later, he changed his name to Arthur Murray. He opened dance studios around the country to teach people like J.D. Rockefeller and Eleanor Roosevelt about ballroom dancing.

1905– Johnny Weissmuller

Johnny Weissmuller is best known for playing Tarzan in 12 movies. He was also an Olympic swimmer. He set 67 world records and won five gold and one bronze medals.

1905– John and Mabel Ringling

Along with four of John Ringling's seven brothers, this couple merged their Ringling Brothers Circus with the Barnum and Bailey Circus. The circus continued to entertain the country until May 2017.

1914– Ettore Boiardi

Ettore Boiardi came through Ellis Island as a 16-year-old boy. In 1928, Chef Boyardee, as he was then called, opened a factory for Italian food. Chef Boyardee foods are still available in grocery stores.

1938– Maria von Trapp

Maria von Trapp and her family fled Austria when the Nazis took over. They toured as the Trapp Family Choir. The 1965 film The Sound of Music shared Maria's story with the world.

title: The Work Was Hard and the Pay Was Low
text:
Hi! This is Jackson. Did you know that most immigrants who came to the United States in the early 1900s found work in factories? They had few job skills and often didn’t speak English. Most of the time, these were the best jobs they could find.

Most men worked 10-12 hours a day, six days a week. Long hours and unsafe conditions caused industrial accidents that killed thousands of workers each year. Workers brought home between $400 and $500 per year, but most families spent more than that just to live!

Look at this picture of factory workers. How old do you think some of these people are? Teenagers and young children often had to work to help support their families. How would you feel if you had to work long hours in a dirty, dangerous factory and then come home to a crowded apartment? For many immigrants, this was life.

title: Tennessee Influences the Vote
text:
Harry Burn was a 24-year-old representative that cast a vote to break the tie. Burn did not want to vote for women's suffrage. He changed his mind after he received a letter from his mother pleading for him to act in favor of her right to vote. His vote helped to ratify the 19th Amendment!

If you visit the State Capitol in Nashville, you may see a painting, Pride of Tennessee. Eleven citizens are recognized for their efforts. Or perhaps you might drive on Anne Dallas Dudley Boulevard in Nashville. These recognitions of Anne Dallas Dudley are due to her contributions to Tennessee, the country and women.

Anne grew up in a well-known Nashville family. She lived in an age when women were not allowed to vote. But Anne did not think that was right. She helped women stand up for their rights by leading suffrage efforts. She led the first suffragette parade in Nashville.

She organized marches and campaigned around Tennessee. She began to speak across the United States. Most of Anne’s social circle did not think women should be able to vote, but Anne kept working toward it. Some said that it would ruin American family life. Anne often appeared at suffrage rallies with her children and encouraged photographers to record her with the children. She showed that motherhood and women’s rights go hand in hand. She continued to fight for women’s rights for the rest of her life.

Sue Shelton White, from Henderson, was the state chairman of the Women's Party. She was a national leader for the suffrage movement, even being arrested for protesting at the White House in Washington, D.C.

Lizzie Crozier French was the organizer of the Knoxville Equal Suffrage Association and involved in other women's groups. She spoke in public meetings to help the state to realize the need for educating women, improving their working conditions and rights of women. She was the first woman to speak at a City Council meeting. She demanded the city hire a female matron to look after the female prisoners in the city jail.

Efforts from these residents all had a crucial role in the story of women’s rights.

title: The Life of Secrecy: The Progressive Era
text:
"This week we will be studying the Progressive Era," Ms. Johnson announced to the class. "I think you will like it. If it were not for the changes that happened during that era, we might not be in class today!"

Curious about what she meant, the class wanted to know more.

"There were changes to how the country felt about alcohol, women and children. Many children were forced to work during the day. Once child labor laws changed, it allowed children to go to school," said Ms. Johnson. She then made assignments for the class projects. Jackson and Alana received different assignments. Jackson was assigned to research prohibition while Alana was going to work on women's suffrage.

After school, Alana and Jackson ran up the stairs to Alana's attic. Jackson made his way to the boxes near the window, while Alana looked through the photographs near the doorway.

A few minutes later, Alana called out, "Jackson! Look at this! I found it in a box belonging to my grandparents."

In her hand, she held a photo of a woman and two children.

"It says 'Anne Dallas Dudley, suffragette, and her two children,'" Jackson read aloud.

"See Jackson, a real suffragette! And my grandparents must have known them."

"It's possible," Jackson agreed. Looking back in the box, Jackson picks up another photo of an old car. Next to the car is a young man leaning against it with his hands in his suspenders, smiling.

"Hey, I know who that is!" Alana yelled excited.

"Who?" Jackson asked.

"That's my uncle Tim. Grandpa told me he was a bootlegger during the Prohibition era."

"What's a bootlegger?"

"A bootlegger," Alana continued, "was someone who worked to move alcohol and other outlawed items in secret."

"Oh right," Jackson says, "The 18th amendment was part of the 'temperance' movement where people believed that outlawing the sale of alcohol would make society better."

"Right!" Alana replied, "They believed that alcohol was a cause of many of society's problems, that being drunk makes people do bad things."

"Yeah," said Jackson. "I read that the temperance movement was a big part of the Progressive Era. Banning alcohol overlapped with other ideas, like making safe working environments for all workers, and allowing women the right to vote. Ms. Johnson told us that Tennessee was key to getting the right to vote for women through Anne Dallas Dudley."

"Wasn't there another person involved with the suffrage movement in Tennessee, that Ms. Johnson brought up?"

"Hmm, I think the last name started with Burn, or something or another?"

"We can ask Ms. Johnson tomorrow, let's go eat!"

title: Bootleggers and Moonshine
text:
For years, prohibitionists had tried to pass laws against making, selling or drinking alcohol. Reformers thought an alcohol ban would reduce poverty. Women’s leaders said that liquor added to unemployment and violence in the home. Business leaders thought alcohol made workers less efficient.

In 1919, the 18th Amendment, which banned alcohol, was ratified. The nation was divided between the “wets” (who opposed Prohibition) and the “drys” (who favored it).

People who wanted alcohol found endless ways to get it. Bootleggers made their living by smuggling (moving and selling) liquor illegally. Many people simply brewed their own bathtub gin or moonshine. It was called moonshine because it was said that it was made at night, by the light of the moon.More than a few people died from drinking homemade liquor.

By the late 1920s, it had become clear that Prohibition could not be enforced. In 1933, the 21st Amendment repealed Prohibition.

title: Successful Outcomes of the Progressive Era
text:
Not only did the Progressive Era have different ideas and challenges, but the era was filled with faith and hope. Reform (when something is made better by change), inventions and changes to society started to transform the face of the nation.

Thomas Edison's light bulb was being used in more and more homes, offices, hospitals, libraries, schools and other public buildings.

Henry Ford used the moving assembly line to produce affordable motor vehicles. Travel would never be the same!

Wright Brothers invented the first successful airplane. They also inspired society to show humans can achieve when they put their mind to it.

Kodak developed the Brownie, a portable camera that allowed people to record their adventures.

Bootleggers led the creation of what would become NASCAR. Since the bootleggers were keeping what they carried a secret, they needed to transport everything quickly, so they did not get in trouble! Eventually, they became so good at it, they created a game from it. So NASCAR was born.

At the same time, society was starting to change.

The suffrage movement created the 19th Amendment. Women finally had the right to vote.

W.E.B. Du Bois and others changed the future of civil rights and founded the NAACP.

Booker T. Washington worked on improving African American education.

Better health and living conditions helped prevent outbreaks of deadly diseases.

Working conditions improved, especially for children. Children were required to attend school.

Presidents Theodore Roosevelt, William Howard Taft and Woodrow Wilson worked to rid the government of corrupt leaders and practices.

Suffragettes and W.E.B. Du Bois had a lot in common. They both worked for equal rights. The key people during this time worked toward making society a better place.

title: The African American Influence on Progressive Change
text:
Even before the Progressive Era, African Americans faced painful struggles. Jim Crow laws (those that kept the races separate) meant they didn't have the same rights as others. Women were getting equal rights, but not African Americans.

Booker T. Washington worked to make it easier to get into schools and business. He helped improve schools. He taught others how to discover the best business practices. African Americans came a little closer to having the same chances as everyone else. In 1881, he founded the Tuskegee Institute. This school for African Americans worked to train new teachers. These new teachers would add more voices to the community.

Another important African American in the Civil Rights Movement is W.E.B. Du Bois. He was the co-founder of the NAACP. He also fought for equal rights in all aspects of African Americans' lives. He spoke for them until other leaders made it onto the scene in the 1950s.

Both men helped make African Americans lives happier. They opened many doors that were not available before.

title: Challenges of the Progressive Era
text:
Business and industry grew fast in the first 20 years of the 20th century in the United States. Before the turn of the century, the government tried hard not to get too involved in private businesses. By 1900, many people felt businesses were getting too big and too greedy. They wanted the government to help control large industries and keep the free enterprise system fair.

These people were called progressives. They asked the government to pass laws that would make sure businesses could compete with each other. Laws were passed that would prevent one large company from controlling a whole industry.

The people that lived during the Progressive Era faced several challenges. Employees had poor working conditions, often having to work long hours. Children worked in jobs that were dangerous. Segregation, the act of setting someone apart from others, meant African Americans and people of other races were not treated fairly.

Several people helped fix those problems.

Theodore Roosevelt's colorful character helped him push for programs to expand the power of the presidency. He believed the government had the right to regulate businesses. He worked with employers and employees to pass laws to make sure both sides were being handled right.

Woodrow Wilson set up the Federal Trade Commission in 1914. It was to regulate and advise companies that did business in many states and foreign lands. The FTC could enforce rules that made the companies act in a fair and honest manner and to allow free competition. Labels on products had to be honest, and false claims were declared illegal.

Progressives were asking the government to pass rules which banned child labor. Wilson helped created child labor laws which eliminated some of the dangerous jobs for children. These changes led children to be able to attend school. He also signed laws that limited railroad employees to work an 8-hour day.

Booker T. Washington, a former slave, founded the Tuskegee Institute, a school to train teachers. He believed African Americans should have chances for college, jobs and justice in the courts. He said that through education and hard work, African Americans would be accepted into all parts of society.

Grace Abbott became director of the Child Labor Division in 1917. She enforced the laws that banned child labor. When the Supreme Court overturned the law, she tried to get a constitutional change to ban child labor. While the amendment never became law, progressives helped pressure businesses to ban child labor.

She was also the first director of the Immigrants' Protective League which created legal protections for immigrants against mistreatment from others.

W.E.B. Du Bois was the first African American to earn a Ph.D. from Harvard University. Du Bois was a poet, historian, writer and teacher. In 1909, he co-founded the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). He wanted equal treatment for African Americans during a time when the country was dominated by whites.

title: The First Modern War
text:
During World War I, both sides used many new and dangerous weapons. Soldiers were faced with machine guns, capable of shooting many bullets in a short time and killing dozens. Much of the fighting took place from trenches dug into the ground. These were meant to keep soldiers out of sight of machine guns. Modern weapons could kill so quickly that the best strategy was to hide in trenches, sometimes for months.

To hit enemies in trenches, artillery weapons were developed. These shot explosive rounds high over the ground to fall directly into the trenches and explode. Sometimes the trenches were under artillery fire 24 hours a day. Soldiers couldn't do much but hope they didn't get hit. Most of the time, leaving the trenches meant certain death.

The British first used tanks in WWI to cross trenches, crush barbed wire and shoot at the enemy, all from the safety of an armored vehicle.

Both sides also used poison gas. These gases caused temporary blindness, skin blisters and lung damage. Injuries caused by gas were known to be cruel and painful. Soldiers carried gas masks to protect themselves from the awful effects of the chemicals. Today, using poison gases in war is illegal under international law.

Airplanes were also turned into weapons during this war. These newer inventions were used to drop bombs on the enemy and fire machine guns at enemy planes. Submarines were important during WWI as well. German U-boats could stay underwater for two hours at a time. Torpedoes fired from submarines sank many ships.

The awful destruction of World War I was unlike any previous war. The Civil War had taken place only about 50 years before, but the technology in the 1860s was vastly different. No airplanes, no poison gas, no tanks were seen in the fight between the Union and the Confederacy. Perhaps this is one reason why the U.S. didn't want to get involved in the war.

title: WWI Military Bases
text:
A military base is a place where military service members live and work. These bases store weapons, supplies and equipment. They also provide housing, stores and hospitals for service members and their families. Bases are important to service members and the communities where they are located.

During WWI, the U.S. government built military bases and camps across the nation. Service members were trained at the bases and then sent overseas. Bases and camps also provided jobs for civilian workers, or people not in the military. In addition, local businesses loved the money the service members spent when they headed off base!

Camp McClellan in Anniston, Alabama, was once one of the largest training sites in the nation. More than 27,000 service members were trained there as part of the 29th Infantry Division during WWI. Camp McClellan (later named Fort McClellan) was a permanent military base from 1929 until 1999, when it was officially closed.

title: Telegraphing the News
text:
"Alana," her mom called. "Jackson is here. Would the two of you like to work at the kitchen table?"

"Thanks, Mom," she replied. "That would be great. Come on, Jackson; let's get started on our map for social studies class."

"We're supposed to code it some way, aren't we?" Jackson asked. "Something about the countries that fought together during World War I?"

"Yes, the Allied Powers and the Central Powers," Alana nodded. "Why don't you look up the Allied Powers, and I'll research the Central Powers? Then we can figure out how to show them on the map."

"Sounds like a plan," Jackson replied, reaching for his laptop. A few minutes later, he said, "I think I've found out which countries were part of the Allied Powers, but I haven't found out why yet."

"Well," Alana said, "we're going to need to know both parts before the project is over. Write down the countries, and then keep looking to see what you can find out about the reasons. I'll do the same thing."

"Okay," Jackson said. "It looks like Great Britain, France, Russia and Italy were the Allied Powers."

"According to this book," Alana shared, "the Central powers were Germany, Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire. I think that last country became Turkey after the war."

The friends read quietly for a few more minutes before Alana spoke again. "From what I can see, there was some kind of alliance, or agreement, between the four Central Powers countries before the war started. They were also called the Quadruple Alliance. I think they each had different reasons for wanting to defeat each of the countries in the other group, but I'm still reading about that."

"The Allied Powers had another name, too," Jackson said. "They were called the Triple Entente. It looks like Italy already had a treaty with Germany, but they secretly joined with the Allies. This says that Serbia and Belgium were part of the group, too."

Alana looked at her book for a moment longer, then she said, "Hmm, it seems that some members of the Quadruple Alliance came together because of national pride and because they had lost land to some of the Allied countries; the Ottoman Empire thought it was a good economic strategy for them to join with Germany. They mobilized more than 25 million soldiers for World War I, and more than 3 million were killed during the fighting. Germany had the biggest army, so they were the main leader during the war."

Jackson nodded. "Yeah, I found out that by the end of the war, there were 25 different nations in the Triple Entente group. They had 42 million soldiers, with 5 1/2 million men lost. And this site says that there were some neutral countries, too, like Norway, Denmark, Switzerland, the Netherlands and Spain."

A minute later, he continued, "We're supposed to be studying American history, but there's nothing about the United States in this so far. So why are we doing this project, anyway?"

"The U.S. did enter the war," Alana told him, "but I think it wasn't until, like, 1917. I don't get why we decided to join in."

Alana's dad had come into the kitchen a few minutes earlier, and he joined their conversation. "Have you heard about the German U-boats and RMS Lusitania?"

"I've heard about the submarines," Jackson said, "but what's that Lusi thing?"

Mom interrupted. "That sounds like something you'll want to research for your unit project. Do you know about the Zimmermann Telegram? It had a pretty important role in our country deciding to ally with Great Britain and the others."

Jackson and Alana looked at each other. "Wow," Alana said. "It sounds like we have a lot to learn about for this project. I'm starting to get a little more excited about it!"

"Me, too," Jackson said. "But it's going to have to wait. If I'm late to dinner again this week, my mom's going to be mad at me. I'll see you at school tomorrow, Alana!"

title: President Woodrow Wilson
text:
As president of the United States from 1913 to 1921, Woodrow Wilson led the country through the turbulent years of World War I.

As a Progressive candidate, he won the election of 1912 in a landslide. To start his first term, he introduced economic reforms. President Wilson believed that large corporations had too much power in the country. He pushed for laws that stopped companies from creating monopolies. He also created the Federal Trade Commission, which makes sure that companies obey the law. He also created laws that protected workers unions, which fight for better working conditions.

When World War I broke out in Europe, Wilson insisted that the U.S. remain neutral. He wanted to help negotiate peace instead. His resolve was tested when the Lusitania was sunk, but at that time, he still believed in neutrality. In 1916, he won a second term under the slogans "He kept America out of the war" and "America First." When the Zimmermann Telegram came out, many Americans demanded war. When attacks on American ships started again in February 1917, Wilson changed his mind. Come April, Congress declared war on Germany.

Apart from the war, President Wilson made critical decisions on human rights. Here, his track record was mixed. Wilson came to support women's right to vote. He spoke with many members of Congress, convincing them to support suffrage for women. In 1920, the 19th Amendment was approved and women could now vote. We can thank Wilson for his work in this area.

On the other hand, his actions on race were a major step backward. He made federal jobs segregated, wiping out progress for equality. Some government buildings were declared "white only." The president even defended some of these policies to civil rights leaders.

title: War Half a World Away
text:
Tensions between European countries had been building for years before World War I began. Many nations had alliances, or agreements, with other nations. They agreed to support each other if a war started. There were so many alliances that, if a conflict began, numerous countries would get involved.

The large empire of Austria-Hungary controlled an area with many different peoples, languages and cultures. The rulers were Austrian and spoke German. Other ethnicities were sometimes treated as second-class citizens in Austria-Hungary. Groups formed that wanted to separate from the empire and become independent nations. A group called the Black Hand believed that the South Slavic people should form an independent country. On June 28, 1914, this group killed Archduke Franz Ferdinand. He was heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne. The Austrians blamed Serbia and later declared war. This led most of Europe to join the conflict, and the Great War had begun.

Have you ever seen a big argument on the playground? Maybe you thought you should stay away because you didn't want to get involved in the mess or get hurt. If you've been there, you can see how many Americans felt when the war broke out. President Woodrow Wilson didn't want to send Americans to die in a European war. To make things trickier, people in the U.S. disagreed about whom to support, if anyone. German Americans supported the Central Powers. Many others felt that we should help Great Britain and the Allies; we speak English too, after all. At the start, the U.S. didn't fight but did send money and weapons to the Allies. Even so, some Americans got hurt by the war.

Germany had a large navy, but its ships were kept close to port due an English blockade. In retaliation, U-boats (submarines) had fanned out across the Atlantic and started sinking merchant ships in the waters off England and France. They almost brought merchant shipping to a standstill. Germany declared waters that were off the coasts of its enemies as war zones. On May 7, 1915, the British passenger ship RMS Lusitania was sunk by a U-boat. Nearly 1,200 aboard died, including 128 Americans. Germany claimed that the ship was carrying ammunition from the U.S. to England, so attacking it was justified. It was, in fact, carrying ammunition, but the public didn't know for sure until years after the war.

Americans were angry with Germany. Germany agreed not to attack passenger ships. Even so, many believed that the U.S. should prepare for possible war after the Lusitania sank.

Things continued this way for a while. The straw that broke the camel's back came in January 1917. British agents got hold of a telegram sent from Germany to Mexico. This message is called the Zimmermann Telegram. The message is short, but its consequences were enormous. The first two sentences read:

"We intend to begin on the first of February unrestricted submarine warfare. We shall endeavor in spite of this to keep the United States of America neutral."

This was enough to cause trouble. Germany was going back on its promise not to attack non-military ships. This meant more Americans could die in U-boat attacks. And as the letter continued, the U.S. government became even more troubled. Germany made an offer to Mexico:

"[W]e make Mexico a proposal of alliance on the following basis: make war together, make peace together, generous financial support and an understanding on our part that Mexico is to reconquer the lost territory in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona."

This meant that Germany and Mexico would fight together. In return, Germany would help Mexico fight the U.S. and take over states that were once Mexican territory: Texas, New Mexico and Arizona. This clearly meant that Germany intended to go to war with the U.S. True to their word, German U-boats sunk two American ships in February.

The following April, President Wilson spoke to Congress and said, "The world must be made safe for democracy." He asked Congress to declare war. The House of Representatives and the Senate voted strongly in favor of this proposal, and the U.S. was at war.

title: Timeline of WWI
text:
June 28, 1914: Archduke Ferdinand of the Austro-Hungarian empire is shot, which is one of the key causes of WWI. The war begins as Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia.

August 1– August 29, 1914: Much of the world goes to war apart from the U.S. Britain declares war on Germany and France declares war on Austria-Hungary.

June 17, 1915: In Britain, women fight for the right to work in factories.

April 1, 1916: Marie Curie develops X-ray equipment to help with the wounded in the war.

January 19, 1917: The Zimmerman Telegram is intercepted by British agents.

April 6, 1917: The U.S. joins the war.

November 11, 1918: Germany signs an armistice (surrender) with the Allies. The war ends.

February 14, 1919: The constitution for the League of Nations is announced.

July 10, 1919: The Treaty of Versailles is submitted to Germany.

August 1920: Women win the right to vote in the U.S.

title: Let's Write
text: Why did the U.S. Senate reject the League of Nations? What were some of the things the League of Nations was able to do?

title: This Week's Question
text: What are some key transitions that the U.S. went through during World War I?

title: Woodrow Wilson and the League of Nations
text:
The Treaty of Versailles was meant to establish peace between the Allied European countries and that of Germany. Germany, however, was not allowed to have nearly any part in the demands of the treaty. Many aspects of the treaty prevented Germany from taking part in anything that meant potential war. Limits were made on things, such as having certain weapons and changing the boundaries of the country itself. Germany was also forced to pay severe fines to the Allied nations due to the effects of the war.

The French prime minister, Georges Clemenceau, wanted revenge against Germany and the French and British both thought Germany should pay war costs. Prime Minister David Lloyd George of Great Britain was willing to compromise. President Wilson wanted world peace and disarmament. He wanted a way to have nations talk over their differences without fighting.

President Woodrow Wilson attempted to develop the League of Nations to spread peace after the war. After the war, all of the major Allied forces wanted to make sure that something like this would never happen again. This was started with the Treaty of Versailles, but Wilson was also interested in an alternative idea. He proposed the creation of a League of Nations. It would develop goals for countries to have peaceful solutions to their conflicts, as opposed to resorting to war. It was good in theory. But, U.S. senators rejected Wilson’s idea. They didn’t like Article X, a section that said that member nations would send troops to any other member to help in a war. Senators didn’t want to lose that much control over U.S. foreign policy and get us involved in wars we had no interest in.

Despite the lack of U.S. membership, the league helped some nations solve problems. The league also created the World Court of Justice, where international legal matters could be brought before judges. Out of this effort grew the United Nations, which still works for peace today.

title: Alvin C. York, Pacifist War Hero
text:
Jackson and Alana learned a lot from their field trip.

Alvin York, a Tennessee native, was honored for his bravery in battle during World War I.

Alvin was born in a two-room cabin and was the third of 11 children. His family was very poor, and he was forced to drop out of school to help on the family farm. Alvin became an expert hunter so that he could feed his family.

When Alvin registered for the draft, he wrote on his form, “don’t want to fight.” Oddly, when he was drafted at age 30, Alvin refused to ask for a waiver (statement of belief) so that he could take care of his family or honor his religious beliefs. As a pacifist, Alvin believed that killing was wrong. He was drafted into the U.S. Army, assigned to the Infantry Division. He still did not want to fight. He was allowed to return home and think about what he should do. He returned, convinced that he should fight for his country and that God would keep him safe.

In October 1918, Alvin York and 16 other soldiers were ordered to sneak behind German lines in France. His unit peacefully took 132 German prisoners when the Germans launched a counterattack, killing six of the American soldiers. Taking only a rifle and a revolver, he went alone to attack the German gunners. He killed about 20 gunners with his sniper rifle before they realized Alvin was alone. The remaining six Germans charged him and he killed them all with his pistol. Alvin was awarded the Medal of Honor, the highest military award, for his bravery.

title: Did It Make a Difference?
text:
When the United States entered the war, it was after two years of fighting between the Allied Powers and the Central Powers. The entry of the U.S. provided fresh troops and essential supplies to Allied Powers. Just as important that was, it boosted the spirits of the war-weary Europeans.

Food, Clothing and War Equipment Shortages

With millions of farm workers taken from the farms and factories in Europe, there was a huge demand for food, clothing, machines, munitions, guns and supplies. This was a big boon to American business. Our nation prospered by supplying both sides in the war. When blockades began to prevent the United States from selling to Germany’s supporters, the United States sold only to Britain and its allies. This made Germany mad. It sent agents to America to get workers at munitions plants to strike. Agents and spies derailed trains in the United States that carried war supplies. And there were mysterious explosions at munitions plants and other acts of terrorism by German agents or spies.

The Western Front

America's greatest contribution to ending the war was made along the Western Front, a 350-mile line from the Swiss Alps to the North Sea. Opposing forces dug miles and miles of trenches in which they took shelter from machine guns. Each side protected the trenches with barbed wire and landmines. The land between the two sides was called "no man's land," where thousands died. Fearing death in no man's land, the soldiers on both sides spent months in the stinking, rotten trenches, enduring lice, mud, rats, stench and death.

America Breaks Through the German Lines

In 1918, the Germans launched five massive offensives (attacks) against Allied troops. They tore a huge hole in Allied lines and tried to reach the English Channel and Paris. American troops helped stall both drives. For two months afterward, the Allied nations began a counterattack all along the Western Front. The fighting was bitter, and U.S. casualties (wounded and killed) grew quickly to 100,000. Finally, the Americans broke through the German lines and began advancing on them. All across the Western Front, Allied troops pushed the Germans and their supporting troops back. It was too much for the Central Powers. Bulgaria begged for peace on September 29, and the Ottoman Empire signed an armistice on October 30. Austria-Hungary surrendered to Italy on November 3. The Allied troops finally pushed Germany into surrendering and demanded that the German Kaiser step down before a peace treaty (agreement between nations) could be signed.

The War Is Over

At 11 a.m. on Nov. 11, 1918, the war ended. Poetically, it was the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month. Troops climbed out of the trenches and couldn’t believe that it was over. England and France drafted the Treaty of Versailles. It laid out conditions that had to be agreed on before there would be peace. Germany would give up its colonies around the world, surrender most of its fleet, all of its artillery and heavy military equipment and pay for the damages they caused during the war. WWI led to the fall of four great dynasties: Germany, Russia, Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire. It spawned the Bolshevik Revolution in Russia in 1917 that led to the overthrow of the czar (Russian ruler) and gave rise to communism. It also destabilized Europe and laid the groundwork for the next great war, World War II.

title: Tennessee Helps Win the War
text:
Life in the early 20th century was an exciting time for the state and nation. Farms and factories were spreading. New inventions were springing up everywhere.

The war changed the lives of the people of Tennessee. As a result, 43,730 whites and 17,339 African Americans were among the 100,000 Tennessee residents that served.

The government has a policy of not letting large groups of men from one state serve in the same division overseas. But the 30th Infantry Division (nicknamed the Old Hickory Division in honor of Andrew Jackson) included men from Tennessee, North Carolina and South Carolina. The division helped break the Hindenburg Line. It also fought in battles in La Selle, St. Mihiel and Meuse-Argonne.

At home, women, both African American and white, worked together in factories. There were many factory jobs available for two reasons: 1. The men who once worked there were gone overseas fighting the war, and 2. Factories converted their production to materials needed for war. This boosted the economy. For example, the Firestone tire company stopped making car tires and started making life rafts and tires for the military. Ford stopped making cars and started making airplane parts. Other factories made medicine or ammunition.

They joined groups such as the American Red Cross and the Davidson County Liberty Loan organizations. During the worldwide influenza epidemic of 1918–1919, women helped nurse the afflicted back to health. Even with their efforts, many died. Chattanooga alone lost 5,848 people.

Farmers grew more crops. Property owners of vacant lots used their land to help grow more food. School students were asked to plant "Victory Gardens." Home guards kept a watch over railroad bridges and trestles to make sure they were safe. A gunpowder plant was built in the Nashville area. It cost $80 million and employed over 20,000 people. The state created the Tennessee State Council of Defense. Every county created a council as well. Tennesseans helped win the war in many ways.

title: Field Trip: World War I Here We Go
text:
Alana and Jackson have started learning about the U.S. involvement in World War I in Ms. Johnson's class and were excited about their field trip to Pall Mall. They prepared for the adventure by learning basic facts about World War I.

Ms. Johnson wanted to show the class how Tennessee played a big role in both world wars, so they traveled to the Alvin C. York General Store and Visitor Center to begin their study. They are here to answer the following question:

Whose World War was it really?

Ms. Johnson told them it's very informative to use the exhibits in the different places they visit to research U.S. involvement in World War I.

"Alana, look at this cool tractor!" Jackson pointed to a rusted yellow tractor in the field.

"Cool Jackson. What does the sign say?" Alana asked.

"It says this belonged to Alvin C. York himself."

"Oh, Alvin C. York. Wasn't he a famous sergeant?" Alana tapped her head trying to remember what Ms. Johnson had said in class.

"Yes, Alana. He went from being a really troubled kid in his youth, but once he was married and received his draft notice, he turned himself around."

"That's right. Alvin was a real war hero. He led men to defeat the German army and received the Medal of Honor. Well, that is one positive thing that happened in this war, I suppose. But it just seems weird that the United States would join a war that was across the world in Europe. It technically didn't affect us," Alana said.

"That wasn't the only positive, Alana. Remember, because we entered the war, we began having more women in the workforce. They became a huge part of making sure we were victorious. Also, this is when women won the right to vote!"

"Oh, I almost forgot that!" Alana recalled.

"Since the war was so big, it might have been hard for the U.S. to stay out forever. Remember how American ships were sunk by German U-boats? And the Zimmermann Telegram?" Jackson inquired.

"That's right, I remember now! President Wilson said that we needed to keep democracy safe, so we joined the Allied Powers," Alana agreed.

"Well, there's definitely more to learn! We could do some research," Jackson stated.

"That's what museums like this one are for!" Alana pointed out.

title: Primary Sources: A Poem by Langston Hughes
text:
The following poem was written by Langston Hughes during the Harlem Renaissance. A literary work is considered a primary source. Read the poem and answer the questions that follow.

I, Too, Sing America

By Langston Hughes

I, too, sing America.
I am the darker brother.
They send me to eat in the kitchen
When company comes,
But I laugh,
And eat well,
And grow strong.

Tomorrow,
I'll be at the table
When company comes.
Nobody'll dare
Say to me,
"Eat in the kitchen,"
Then.

Besides,
They'll see how beautiful I am
And be ashamed—
I, too, am America.

1. What is the main idea of this poem?

2. Go back and read about the push and pull factors of the Great African American Migration and the Harlem Renaissance. With this in mind, what do you think the speaker of the poem is trying to say?

3. Do you think this poem is still relevant today? Why?

title: Automobiles and Appliances
text:
Many of the cultural changes of the 1920s went hand in hand with changes in technology. Do you ever wish you could drive a car? Do you want to be able to go where you want, when you want? You might be looking forward to turning 16 when you can get a driver's license. Imagine all the places you can go!

The dream of driving became a reality for many Americans in the 1920s. Henry Ford's moving assembly line made the car cheaper to buy for a large portion of people. Owning a vehicle gave many people a sense of freedom, and for many, nothing could be more American. The freedom to travel became a part of the "American Dream."

Changes in society were felt strongly, especially by women. For much of history, household chores like cooking and cleaning were thought to be women's responsibility. Men, on the other hand, went out in the world and got careers and engaged in politics. In the early 20th century, many homes gained access to electricity. Electricity allowed machines to do a lot of the work that women usually did by hand. Washing machines, vacuum cleaners and refrigerators freed up hours every day for women at home. In fact, some historians believe that the washing machine has given women more freedom than anything else.

With more free time, the right to vote, electrical appliances and cars, many women found new ways to live. Perhaps they would go out and have a good time flapping. Or start a career. Or get involved in politics. The future was brighter for women and held endless opportunities!

title: Give the '20s Some Credit
text:
At the end of WWI, the American economy slowed down. Weapons and military equipment were no longer bought and sold. A few years later in the early 1920s, things changed and the economy grew quickly. One major reason for this was new technology: affordable cars and electronics like radios, vacuum cleaners and washing machines.

Earlier, people usually saved money and only bought what they needed. In the 1920s, however, people wanted nice things. They were willing to spend money on those radios. Many people also started buying things on credit. That means that a bank or company lends someone money to buy something, and the buyer pays the lender back over time. More than half of cars in the 1920s were bought on credit. This practice still exists today. Many people have credit cards to buy things, and most people need a loan to buy a house.

The average pay of workers increased in the '20s. More women started working and became financially independent. People were making more and spending more, and the economy grew.

The good times didn't last, though. The Great Depression hit in 1929.

title: Charles Lindbergh
text:
Born in Detroit, Michigan in 1902, Charles Lindbergh was always interested in finding out how things worked. By the time he was 11, Charles' parents had put him in charge of both driving and fixing their car. Soon, Charles started dreaming of working with something even more exciting than cars—he wanted to work with airplanes. To become a pilot, Charles had to work and study hard. He wanted to be the best pilot there was, so he studied during every spare moment. His hard work paid off, and he earned the highest grades in his class.

After becoming a pilot, Lindbergh started flying an airmail route from St. Louis to Chicago. Before long, Lindbergh heard about a contest offering a prize of $25,000 for the first nonstop flight from Paris to New York. He decided to enter. Lindbergh called his plane the Spirit of St. Louis. In 1927 Charles Lindbergh became the first person to cross the Atlantic Ocean alone in an airplane. Millions of people got together to celebrate this event.

title: Pop Culture of the 1920s
text:
"Hey, Alana! I found this amazing old phonograph at my grandparents' place, and I’ve been listening to some cool jazz and blues albums from the 1920s. These cats were the bee’s knees!”

“What did you say, Jackson?”

“Sorry, Alana, just a little 1920s slang there. It means that these jazz musicians were excellent! People listened to the music of blues composer W.C. Handy, jazz and blues singer Bessie Smith and famous jazz singer and trumpet player Louis Armstrong during the ‘20s. Jazz music was part of the Harlem Renaissance, which was in full swing during this period. Many famous African American writers and artists were also part of this movement, including authors Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston.”

“That’s right, Jackson, but I’m also interested in the popular products of the ‘Roaring ‘20s,’ like automobiles, airplanes, radios and household appliances. Speaking of airplanes, I’d like to see Charles Lindbergh make his famous flight across the Atlantic! I would also love to ride in a Model T Ford and maybe even join the suffragettes, or women who fought for the right to vote. They marched to win the vote for women!”

“Hold on a minute, Alana! I doubt we’ll have time to do all that on our trip back to the 1920s. Find a picture from this period, and we’ll see where we end up.”

“Here’s one of a woman. On the back it says, ‘Zelda Fitzgerald, flapper. Later married author F. Scott Fitzgerald.’ That sounds like the perfect picture to me. Grab on and we’ll see where it takes us!”

“OK, Alana, as long as you promise that we get to visit a few jazz clubs while we’re there. I want to hear some real finger zingers and listen to some balloon lungs play.”

“Enough of the 1920s slang, Jackson. We’ll be sure to hear some hot jazz. Or is it cool jazz? Oh well, let’s grab the picture and go!”

title: Let's Write
text: Zora Neale Hurston wrote about being encouraged to "jump at de sun." Explain what that means. Then, tell how you "jump at de sun" or how you wish you could.

title: The Roaring '20s
text:
The Serious Side

“Learning about the Roaring ‘20s surprised me, Alana. I thought the ‘20s were all about hot jazz music, amazing art and literature, and new freedoms. I found out they also had a serious side.”

“That’s right, Jackson. Some people grew rich, and many people enjoyed a better way of life. However, our nation made decisions during the 1920s that soon brought the U.S. into the Great Depression. Let’s share what we learned on our trip. …”

Economy

People called this period the “Roaring ‘20s” because times were good, and life improved for most people. The American economy experienced a boom. Factories produced more goods, prices were reasonable and many people worked shorter hours while enjoying higher wages.

Presidents Warren G. Harding and Calvin Coolidge both worked to cut taxes for the rich. Coolidge also encouraged Americans to spend and save wisely. By 1927, over half of American families owned cars. Consumers purchased groceries and other items at chain stores, or companies with stores in many locations. President Herbert Hoover continued to push Americans to take advantage of the country’s good times. He said, “We shall soon, with the help of God, be in sight of the day when poverty will be banished from this nation.”

Unfortunately, life wasn’t good for everyone. World War I had ended. Many farmers had borrowed money to buy land and plant more crops to feed the Allied troops, but they were left with large debts. They had more crops than they could sell. Food prices dropped, and farmers struggled to pay off their loans.

Factories also produced more goods than they could sell, forcing them to lay off workers. People who were out of work couldn’t afford to buy goods made by factories, so the problem got worse. Factories lowered the wages they paid to workers.

Many Americans invested in the stock market, which is an organized system for buying and selling units of company ownership. Stock prices rose throughout the 1920s. Investors, or people who bought the stocks, hoped to get rich. In October 1929, however, the stock market crashed. This meant that stock prices fell to record low levels. Many people lost their savings, their homes and their businesses. Banks closed, and about one in every four people lost their jobs. The U.S. was about to enter the Great Depression, a time of extreme economic hardship.

Immigration

After WWI, many Americans were nervous about the number of immigrants that had entered our country. They thought American jobs would be lost to foreigners. They also wanted to keep possible enemies from entering the country. The U.S. started to set limits on how many immigrants could come here, as well as from which nations they could come. President Calvin Coolidge signed the Immigration Act of 1924. It limited the number of southern and eastern European immigrants coming to the United States. Only two percent of the total U.S. population of residents from those countries would be allowed to move here. The act also stated that no immigrants would be accepted from many parts of Asia. This system of limiting immigrants into the country remained essentially the same until 1952, when immigration laws were changed again.

The Sunny Side

“Well, we’ve learned about the serious side of the Roaring ‘20s. Now let’s learn about the sunny side of this era!”

Great African American Migration

With the beginning of WWI, several “push and pull” factors drew millions of African Americans from the South to busy Northern cities. The military needed engines, ships and weapons to fight the war, and Northern factory workers produced most of these items. The hope of stable, paying jobs in Northern factories pulled many African Americans north.

Harsh discrimination that African Americans faced in the South pushed many of them away from the Southern area. They went north, hoping for a better life. The huge number of African Americans who settled in America’s largest cities led to a great cultural movement called the Harlem Renaissance. This movement was a wonderful, “sunny” outcome of the push-pull factors in the Great Migration.

Harlem Renaissance

Harlem was a section of New York City where many African Americans settled. The Harlem Renaissance, named after this area, was a rebirth and blossoming of African American literature, art and music. Langston Hughes was a famous poet from this movement. He wrote using the language of average folks and included jazz-inspired rhythms. Zora Neale Hurston, called the “Queen of the Renaissance,” wrote stories and plays that celebrated everyday African Americans. She wrote, “Mama exhorted her children at every opportunity to ‘jump at de sun.’ We might not land on the sun, but at least we would get off the ground.”

The Jazz Age

The African Americans who gathered in America’s big cities also introduced the world to a new style of music—jazz. Many jazz bands created the music as they played, which was a style called improvisation. Trumpet player and singer Louis Armstrong was one of the most famous jazz musicians. Nicknamed “Satchmo,” he created a new style of trumpet playing that brought people out of their seats and onto the dance floor. Whites as well as African Americans soon had a taste for jazz, and young women called “flappers” flocked to nightclubs to dance to the beat. Flappers shocked society by cutting their hair short, wearing make-up and shortening their skirts.

This period of growth and new activity in the arts has been a bright part of our American history.

title: Be a Cultural Critic!
text:
The Harlem Renaissance and the Jazz Age produced some amazing songs, poems and works of art. With the help of your teacher, find a song, poem or work of art created during this time. Answer the following questions. Share your ideas with the class!

What is the title of your artwork, and who is the creator?

Describe what is happening in your piece. Use plenty of adjectives!

What is the message of this work of art?

What emotions do you feel while listening to, looking at or reading this piece?

How might this artwork relate to the events of the Roaring ‘20s?

title: Think and Review Questions
text:
Look at the list of people below. Choose 3 of them. For each person you picked, give three descriptive words, give one major accomplishment and tell at least one way the person contributed to society in the Roaring '20s.

Langston Hughes

Bessie Smith

Charles Lindbergh

Zora Neale Hurston

Louis Armstrong

Calvin Coolidge

W.E.B. Du Bois

Zelda Fitzgerald

John T. Scopes

Amelia Earhart

Helen Keller

title: They broke the mold!
text:
1. W.E.B. Du Bois

“The problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color line.”

W.E.B. Du Bois was the first African American to earn a doctorate degree from Harvard University. He founded the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) with the goal of ending discrimination against African Americans.

2. John T. Scopes

“I was hired to teach science, and I went ahead and taught it.”

John T. Scopes was a young high school science teacher who was put on trial for teaching the theory of evolution in a public high school. The theory of evolution states that all life, including humans, changed and evolved from earlier organisms. Natural selection, mutations and other forces lead to new species over millions of years. Scopes was found guilty and fined $100. The guilty verdict was later overturned.

3. Amelia Earhart

“The most effective way to do it, is to do it.”

Amelia Earhart was the first female pilot to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean. In 1928, she was the first female passenger to fly across the Atlantic. She crossed it alone in 1932. In 1937, Amelia attempted to become the first woman to circumnavigate (fly around) the world, but her plane disappeared somewhere near Howland Island in the Pacific Ocean. Amelia was never heard from again.

4. Helen Keller

“I will not just live my life. I will not just spend my life. I will invest my life.”

At just 19 months old, Helen Keller suffered a serious fever and became unable to hear or see. Helen’s mother hired teacher Anne Sullivan to work with Helen, who eventually learned to speak. Helen went to college, wrote books and worked to help others who were deaf or blind.

5. Zelda Fitzgerald

“I did not have a single feeling of inferiority, or shyness, or doubts …”

The ultimate “flapper,” Zelda Fitzgerald grew up as a Southern belle and went on to marry author F. Scott Fitzgerald. She was the inspiration for some heroines of his popular novels. Zelda was also a writer, dancer and painter.

title: Sometimes Even Icky Vegetable Soup Tastes Good
text:
"I like helping out in the cafeteria, don't you?" said Alana to Jackson.

"Yes, it's fun to help and we get to see our friends," said Jackson, scooping out steamed broccoli.

"At least you get to serve broccoli, Jackson," said Alana, "I have to serve this icky vegetable soup. At least I don't have to eat it."

The lunch lady was listening and said, "Alana, there was a time in the 1930s when that icky soup would have been the only meal some people got all day."

Alana felt a little embarrassed for what she said about the soup. She asked the lunch lady what she meant.

"In the 1930s, times were hard and some people didn't have enough food. It was called the Great Depression. It started in 1929 with the crash of the stock market. A stock is basically part ownership of a company. Sixteen million shares were lost in one day. The investors, people who owned shares, included banks. Those banks lost a lot of money. Banks even closed because they didn't have enough money. Businesses and people that had their money in those banks lost it and they were now suddenly poor."

"So poor they couldn't eat?" asked Alana.

The Lunch lady explained. "Since businesses were closed and people didn't have money, they couldn't even afford food. Churches and charities started serving soup and bread. They didn't always serve soup, but most often that was the meal served."

The lunch lady continued, "Alana, what's something people need to exist besides food?"

"Water?" said Alana.

"You're right. People banded together and moved to be close by rivers or creeks for fresh water for drinking, cooking and bathing. They lived in tents or improvised shelters called shanty towns. These settlements became known as Hoovervilles, named after President Hoover. Many people blamed the Depression directly on the president. However, many things happened that caused the Depression."

The lunch lady went on to talk about how her grandmother was a teenager and remembered a lot of the things that happened during the depression. "People were buying more and more things on credit and were in debt. When the stock market crashed, those people lost their jobs and couldn't pay their bills and lost their homes. About 30 percent of the workforce was without a job. Soup kitchens allowed people to eat, even if they had to eat icky vegetable soup," the lunch lady concluded with a grin.

title: This Week's Question
text: You wake up in a Hooverville Shanty Town, what is your day like?

title: Think and Review Questions
text:
After people lost their life savings in the stock market and banks in the crash in 1929, why do you think they put money back into banks so quickly a few years later?

President Hoover did not act on the signs that a crash was coming. Could he have stopped it from happening?

Can you think of other jobs people might do to earn money during the Depression?

If you could write a letter to President Hoover right before the stock market crash happened, what would you tell him?

title: Was President Hoover alone responsible for the Great Depression?
text:
How did things get so bad that the Depression happened? President Herbert Hoover took office in 1929, the same year the stock market crashed and many banks and companies failed and people went broke. There was no deposit insurance at the time and people lost their life savings in a single afternoon on October 24, 1929.

This happened early in Hoover's term as president. He didn't create all the circumstances that caused the crash resulting in the Depression, but he had a hand in it. He ignored signs that a crash was coming or couldn't recognize them.

After the crash, Hoover vetoed several bills that would have given direct relief to struggling Americans. He felt that help given to people should come from their local cities and states. He believed the federal government didn't need to be involved directly. This made Hoover look like he didn't care about struggling families.

As people lost their jobs and homes, shanty towns sprang up all over the country and were nicknamed "Hoovervilles" to blame the president for the plight of people who lived there. Hoovervilles didn't have running water so they would locate by rivers, creeks or lakes. People cooked sparse meals in the same waters they bathed in. Conditions were poor and people got sick.

Hoover was blamed for the shortage of food in communities. He wasn't funding federal programs, so there was no money for states and cities to help their citizens. His reason was that he felt that the United States could not be saved by continuing to spend money from the treasury. People who were in Hoovervilles and eating one meal a day felt like Hoover wasn't interested in helping them.

People were in debt and because the banks were closed, no one could get a loan to get by. It would take years to rebuild consumer trust in credit again. The Depression grew worse throughout Hoover's presidency. He wasn't making significant changes that created jobs, he was seen as not caring about the citizens of the United States.

By the time the 1932 presidential election rolled around, Hoover's opponent beat him easily. Franklin D. Roosevelt, often called FDR, became the president. Soon-to-be President Roosevelt promised a "New Deal," a range of programs that would create jobs, stabilize the economy, and help those left penniless by the stock market crash.

Hoover spoke out against many of the New Deal programs that FDR introduced. However, the social programs that FDR created helped many people, businesses and banks get back on their feet. Jobs were created and Hoovervilles became a thing of the past. Even after several years under the New Deal, it was World War II that turned the Great Depression around. The need for everyone to work for the war effort brought good health back to the economy. President Hoover still bore the label as the man that was responsible for the Depression.

title: Help for Americans in Tennessee
text:
Tennessee was among the hardest hit states during the depression. Bank failures created a loss of $7 million. People with good jobs had to leave and could get only poor jobs. People with poorer jobs ended up with none. Farmers who owned large tracts of land had to reduce their crops to grow just what they needed to survive. People in urban areas lost factory jobs and homes, and moved back out into the countryside. Charities were overwhelmed with the needy. With the election of President Roosevelt, help was on the way. A Tennessee man wrote him a letter and said, “The hope that had almost ceased to glow, now burns anew.” Roosevelt’s New Deal policies would pull Tennessee out of the depths and improve life for all Americans.

In 1933, President Roosevelt signed the Tennessee Valley Authority Act, also called the TVA. This created a way to control flooding from the Tennessee River, opened up more farmland, and helped bring in more jobs. The TVA built 16 dams and a steam plant. This brought power to thousands of people at a price that was affordable.

Another valuable part of the Tennessee Valley Authority Act helped farmers change old ways of farming. They improved crop yields by rotating crops with alfalfa and clover. That put nitrogen in the soil and kept it healthy for yearly planting. The TVA helped to replant trees and gave funds to the National Forest Service to protect and maintain federal lands.

The Civilian Conservation Corps provided jobs, mostly for young men. They created five state parks. They had 77 work camps throughout the state, segregated between white men and African American men. Many residents did not want CCC camps for African Americans located near them. By law, African Americans were to receive the same jobs and benefits as white workers, but this often did not happen.

Other programs helped put people to work. The Civil Works Administration employed over 50,000 to work on roads and other community projects. The Public Works Administration provided jobs building roads and building public buildings. The PWA was used to build the Tennessee Supreme Court Building. High school and college students constructed a new high school in Van Buren County while serving in the PWA program for youth.

title: Mortgage Crisis
text:
In 1933, about 1,000 home loans were foreclosed every week. This means the bank took over the house because the owner couldn't make their payments. People were not making as much money as they used to. Homes were also falling in value.

Savings & loan firms offered long-term mortgages (a loan used to buy a house), allowing homeowners several years to pay for their home. Normally, people pay back a little of the mortgage every month. Banks and insurance companies offered short-term loans. Once people started losing their jobs, they were no longer able to make payments on their loans. Banks lost money because people couldn't pay them. As banks began to fail, getting a loan was almost impossible.

HOLC, or The Home Owners Loan Corporation, was a government program meant to help people struggling to pay their mortgages. They were one of the federal agencies created to help homeowners from losing their home. They helped people refinance their homes.

title: Out of Work, Out of Food
text:
In the fall of 1929, the stock market crashed. People and businesses that had invested their money lost it. Banks that had invested also lost money, losing the life savings of their customers. Banks and businesses started closing.

People became alarmed that they might not have enough money for their expenses. They stopped buying items, only purchasing those things they really needed. Goods began to pile up in warehouses. Factories started to slow down their production. Workers were fired. People lucky enough to have jobs had their wages cut time and time again. One in three people was out of work. Men out of work "bummed" rides on the trains and wandered about the country in search of work. People moved from place to place looking for work, often unsuccessfully.

Farms were struggling due to falling food prices and drought. Farmers could not afford to harvest their crops. They were forced to let their crops rot in the field, yet people were starving. In the coastal communities, people could catch fish for food, but they couldn't sell any for lack of buyers. Canadians poured across the border to the United States in search of work until the United States sealed the border to protect the few jobs that were still available.

In the fall of 1930, people started losing confidence in their banks. They started demanding cash for their deposits. Banks were forced to dip into their reserve funds. Banks ran out of money and were forced to close. By early 1933, thousands of banks across the country had closed.

title: Making Ends Meet
text: During the Great Depression, families struggled to make ends meet. They had to get creative to earn money to provide for each other. Take on the role of an American during this time. How will you earn money? Decide on a good or service you will provide and create an advertisement to help sell or trade your product. Remember that others may be selling or trading the same goods or services. What sets yours apart?

title: Let's Write
text: Do you think President Hoover was responsible for the Great Depression? Why or why not? Write an essay to convince someone of your point of view.

title: How did people earn money during the Depression?
text:
During the Depression, there were no jobs. People lost their money in banks. How do you suppose they got money for food, clothes, and other things? People found ways to earn money to buy food and other necessities.

Ms. Johnson showed the class a 1930s photograph of a man wading in a river fishing. Remember the shanty towns called Hoovervilles? People living by water caught and sold fish, crabs and clams to provide food for their families with their catches. Others grew food at home and sold it door-to-door. Going door-to-door became a common way to sell items and some families would travel from town to town selling things such as baked goods, quilts, baskets and shoes.

Men who worked in offices took any job that came along, no matter how menial. African Americans were hit especially hard. White men were now doing jobs they traditionally performed. African American men had a tough time finding work.

People became creative at finding anything that could earn them money. Kids would sell newspapers on the streets. Kids that brought other kids in to sell were called "corner captains" and would earn money from the others they brought in. Yard and road work were places where jobs could sometimes be found. People who were selling food products often went to job sites to sell their seafood, sandwiches or other items. Some families rented out rooms in their home to make ends meet.

To save money, families would make clothing out of feed sacks. When soles of shoes wore out, cardboard would be placed inside.

title: National Parks Too?
text:
People in the State of Tennessee went through hard times during the Depression. The Tennessee Valley Authority was one way many people were helped in the state with jobs created that are still done today.

There was a great need to create jobs. Jobs were necessary for helping the economy recover. When people receive paychecks from jobs, they spend the money in their communities on food, rent and other items. This helps the economy. As more cities created jobs under the New Deal's programs, cities and towns around both Tennessee and the rest of the country began to recover.

The Works Progress Administration (WPA) was another agency that provided jobs for about 8 million Americans. These workers built schools, hospitals and other important public buildings.

Another important part of the New Deal was the Civilian Conservation Corps, also called the CCC. When he was governor of New York, FDR had expanded the forestry service in his state. He was ready to do it on a national scale as president. This job creation program ran for nine years and gave the unemployed jobs in the environmental industry. The CCC created trails and shelters in over 800 national parks. This laid the foundation for the national parks we enjoy today in the U.S.

As the CCC created jobs, there was more work available in the Western areas of the United States. Most of the unemployed men were located in the Eastern part of the country. President Roosevelt called on the U.S. Army to help move workers to the West coast. This method moved more than 300,000 men into jobs.

Along with planting trees, workers had jobs from building safe habitats for wildlife to fighting forest fires. To encourage the public to make use of these public lands, FDR had the CCC build bridges and create campgrounds. Men from all walks of life and backgrounds were encouraged to be a part of the CCC. World War I veterans, American Indians living on reservations, and African Americans worked in CCC camps.

By 1942, when the Civilian Conservation Corps ended its service, it had planted more than 3.5 billion trees and created over 700 new parks across America.

Reform

Roosevelt's New Deal also worked to reform, or change, the conditions that had led the nation into the Great Depression. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) was created to make sure that people ran the stock market fairly and that everyone followed the same rules of the system. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) was set up to insure, or protect, the money people deposited in U.S. banks. This meant that depositors could not lose their money to bank failures in the future.

Recovery

Another of Roosevelt's goals was to start the nation's economy on the road to recovery. The CCC and the WPA could be considered recovery programs as well as relief agencies. These programs provided paychecks to those who could spend their earnings, helping businesses recover from hard times. The Home Owners' Loan Corporation (HOLC) was a program that gave loans to people who needed help to pay their mortgages. Many families were then able to keep their homes.

title: Think and Review Questions
text:
Do you think America would have come out of the Depression without The New Deal?

Visiting National Parks is still very much a recreational activity for many Americans. Do you feel the government should continue funding their upkeep or should people who use the parks pay for the upkeep?

The Tennessee Valley Authority brought power to rural communities in seven states for the first time. How do you feel this helped communities grow?

title: Let's Write
text: Solar and wind energy are becoming more available and less expensive. Should Tennessee make electricity in other ways? Write a letter with a few paragraphs to convince someone in one way or the other.

title: Tennessee and The New Deal
text:
Alana and Jackson are in class. Ms. Johnson has a photo of President Roosevelt.

"Last week we covered how the Depression changed the lives of millions of Americans from 1929 through the 1930s," said Ms. Johnson to the class. "Today we're going to look at the New Deal programs enacted by President Roosevelt. They helped people in Tennessee and all over America."

"We learned about the Tennessee Valley Authority," said Alana, "What else did the New Deal do?"

"Roosevelt attacked the problem from many sides," said Ms. Johnson. "First he set up the Emergency Banking Act. The Act helped reopen banks and created confidence from consumers. The federal government insured their deposits. People felt safe putting their money into banks once again," Ms. Johnson continued, "then he changed how veterans received pensions and legalized and taxed wine and beer."

"Hoover did not believe in the federal government helping states. Did Roosevelt?" asked Jackson.

"Yes, under the Federal Emergency Relief Act (FERA), over $3 billion in aid went to states to help their citizens recover," answered Ms. Johnson. "Look at this campaign button. It’s a picture of Franklin Delano Roosevelt, or FDR for short. It has the words ‘For a New Deal’ along the top."

"People were more than ready to give Roosevelt and his New Deal a chance when he ran against Herbert Hoover for president in 1932," continued Ms. Johnson. "Roosevelt won the election by a landslide."

"Under FERA," explained Ms. Johnson, "the federal government gave aid to 20,000,000 people, about one out of every six Americans. That money was used to give work to unemployed people. One program was intended to help jobless teachers! Also, help was given to farmers."

"Ms. Johnson, weren't the '30s really tough on farmers?" asked Alana. "I read that a lot of crops were destroyed by dust storms."

"Yes, Alana, that was called the Dust Bowl. It was an awful drought that ruined many farmers' livelihoods. They had no crops to sell and needed assistance. FERA and other programs helped soften the blow. Even so, some left their homes and looked for work elsewhere. They soon found out that jobs were hard to find everywhere!"

Ms. Johnson then showed the class some images of railroads, homes, farmers and schools. "All of these sectors of the public were helped through New Deal programs designed to stimulate business."

"Because more business means more jobs, which means more money to spend for people," said Jackson.

"Exactly," said Ms. Johnson. "The state of Tennessee couldn't just get money and then be told to fix the problems of the people. It had to be the entire country working together to make positive changes happen for all."

"And later," concluded Ms. Johnson, "FERA was replaced by other programs over a few years, starting with the Works Progress Administration in 1935. There was a lot of need and a lot of laws passed to give relief!"

title: This Week's Question
text: Roosevelt's New Deal started many programs to help people and businesses recover from the Great Depression. Which do you feel was the most important of FDR's New Deal programs?

title: A Timeline of New Deal Programs
text: Find five New Deal programs that were created under President Roosevelt's administration. On top of the timeline, write the year the act was created and what the act was called. Underneath each act, briefly explained how it helped people get through the Great Depression. You may have to use the internet as a way to research New Deal programs.

title: How did the New Deal help Tennessee?
text:
Ms. Johnson asked the class to name the ways that FDR's New Deal helped the people of Tennessee. Hands go up and there are many answers.

Ms. Johnson calls on Jackson. He shows a photograph his grandmother gave him of a man in her family working on the TVA project in 1934. He tells how they helped work on one of the first hydroelectric plants to bring power to the area.

Another student talks about collecting the flood waters. Doing so made more farming available in Tennessee. Areas that had difficulty watering their crops in the past now had the ability to irrigate.

Alana brings up the fact Social Security helped people who were out of work and still helps people today.

Ms. Johnson said she was going to be enjoying another benefit of The New Deal this coming weekend, with a visit to the Great Smoky Mountains National Park.

title: What is Social Security?
text:
In August 1935, President Franklin Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act, creating a system that would pay money to retired workers to help them meet their needs. Most of the money to fund Social Security is taken out of each American worker's paycheck as a payroll tax.
