At the beginning of the program, the Social Security tax was about 2 percent of each employee's paycheck. The Social Security tax withheld from each paycheck more recently is about 6.2 percent.

The Social Security system pays money to those who have retired, those whose spouse has died or those who have become disabled (unable to work because of illness or injury). About 65 percent of people receiving payments are retired workers. Spouses and children of retired and disabled workers also receive payments. Adults age 61 and older can apply for these benefits in person or online. Payments are made to Social Security recipients each month.

Many people worry that the Social Security system will run out of money before today's workers retire. People are living longer, so they receive payments for a longer period. There are fewer workers paying taxes to replace the large number of retiring workers. Congress is working on finding ways to fix the system so that tomorrow's retirees will have the money they need.

title: How Does Water Make Electricity?
text:
Electricity made from water is called hydroelectricity. To create this type of power, you need to first build a dam. The dam holds millions of gallons of water and allows the water to enter the power station through an intake. The water held by the dam is called a reservoir.

The intake looks like a long tunnel underground. The water flows to a turbine that is attached to a generator. As the water passes through, it forces the turbine to spin. The faster the water flows, the faster the turbine spins. The force of gravity causes the water to "fall" through the power plant.

The spinning action powers up the generator. There are power lines connected to the generator and that electricity is brought to homes and businesses all over the area.

In some hydroelectric power plants, the water simply flows through the turbine and out to a river. In other plants, the water is pulled up through a pump and returned to the dam to be reused the following day. This method is called pumped storage. This is often done in areas where there is a lack of rain or drought.

title: The Creation of the Tennessee Valley Authority
text:
The Tennessee Valley Authority solved some major problems in the area. Seven states are served under the TVA, including Tennessee. The result of the TVA is that many rural communities were able to have electricity for the first time. This lead to the creation of jobs and better living conditions.

Every year during the rainy season, an average of six feet of water would flood the area. This forced people to deal with problems. The flood was a plague for people living in the area. The flooding drowned out any hope of having animals, crops, or other uses for the land. One of the projects of the TVA took on was creating dams. The dams would trap the runoff water and then that water was used on the crops. Dams also created electricity for the region. Did you know the TVA is still America's largest public power provider?

There are not only 30 hydroelectric plants providing power. There are also coal, natural gas and nuclear power plants in the Tennessee Valley region. In addition, there are 14 solar energy sites and a wind energy plant. These have been created as the world starts looking forward to different types of power for communities.

title: The Decision to Bomb Hiroshima
text:
On July 29, 1945, Japan refused to surrender following the demand to do so by the Allies at the Potsdam Conference. The next day, President Truman decided to authorize the atom bomb to be dropped on Hiroshima. It was dropped on Aug. 6, 1945.

The bomb blast killed 86 percent of the people within a half-mile of ground zero. It wounded another 10 percent in that circle. Between 1/2 and 1 1/2 miles from ground zero, 27 percent of the people were killed instantly and another 37 percent were wounded. When there is an atomic blast, it creates radioactive dust called fallout. This fallout comes back down to the ground as radiation-contaminated rain. The fallout from the Hiroshima blast affected an area 12-15 miles from ground zero. Much more was carried by winds around the area. Fallout causes radiation sickness and death. The sickness can last from a few hours to several decades. It killed and sickened many more people. Some people got terrible burns and others got different kinds of cancer.

When the Japanese still did not surrender after that bombing, the president authorized another bombing on Nagasaki. After that, Japan surrendered.

Was President Truman justified in using the nuclear bomb? Why do you think no nuclear bombs have ever been used since the two in Japan in 1945? What do you think the president discussed with his advisers before authorizing the use of the bombs?

title: Internment Camps
text:
After the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor on Dec. 7, 1941, U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt issued Executive Order 9066. Because Japan attacked America, some people became openly distrustful of and hostile toward Japanese Americans. Thousands of Japanese immigrants and their families had settled along the West coast of the United States. These Japanese Americans, half of whom were children, were jailed for up to four years. Any citizen who was of Japanese ancestry had to leave their homes and report to prison-like internment camps located in seven states. More than 120,000 Americans were moved to these camps.

People feared people with Japanese backgrounds, thinking they were spies or enemies of the U.S. Some Japanese Americans died in the camps because they were not given good medical care. They were also very scared, hungry and tired every day. They never knew when they would be set free. Even after the U.S. government freed the Japanese Americans, many people still felt the trauma of the internment camps. It takes time for the body and mind to heal from such experiences.

title: Think and Review Questions
text:
List four outcomes resulting in the aftermath of World War II. Rank them, in order, of what you believe to be the most effective sanctions for preventing another World War. Explain why.

Identify the cause and effect of Japan bombing Pearl Harbor.

Predict what might have happened if Japan had not bombed Pearl Harbor.

List the major countries involved in World War II. Categorize as either Axis or Allied Power.

title: The Manhattan Project
text:
World War II was a time of great destruction. It was also a time of dramatic scientific progress. Before the United States entered World War II, scientists worried that Adolf Hitler was building a powerful bomb. With that kind of weapon, people feared that Germany would be unstoppable.

The United States asked famous scientists to make a special bomb. This bomb was called an atom bomb. They used uranium to make it. Albert Einstein, J. Robert Oppenheimer and Enrico Fermi helped. They were part of the Manhattan Project.

In 1945, the scientists tested the first atom bomb in New Mexico. On August 6, the United States dropped an atom bomb on Hiroshima, Japan. Three days later, the United States dropped another atom bomb on Nagasaki, Japan. This ended the war with Japan.

Research from the Manhattan Project also led to the development of nuclear power, which is used to make electricity.

title: Isolationism
text:
This is Jackson. I have to say that I was upset when I learned that the U.S. didn't immediately help when Germany attacked France, Great Britain and the Soviet Union. Why didn't the president send weapons, troops and money right away?

I did a little research and learned more about the Neutrality Acts. After WWI, the American people were tired of war and wanted to deal with their own issues, rather than try to solve the world's problems. Here's what I learned:

First Neutrality Act

In 1935, Congress proclaimed that the U.S. could not export any weapons, ammunition or "implements of war" to belligerent (warring) nations. Americans were also warned that if they sailed on a belligerent's ship, they did so at their own risk.

Neutrality Act of 1936

This law renewed the First Neutrality Act for another 14 months and said that no loans or credit could be offered to belligerent nations.

Neutrality Act of 1937

This act renewed the previous neutrality acts and made it illegal for any U.S. ships to carry military equipment to belligerent nations. Citizens could no longer sail on belligerents' ships. It also gave the president the power to sell supplies (but not weapons and ammunition) to belligerent nations, as long as they paid for these items at the time of purchase.

Neutrality Act of 1939

By this time, Germany was at war with Great Britain and France. Congress passed a law stating that the U.S. could sell weapons, ammunition and other military supplies to belligerent nations. Again, nations had to pay for supplies at the time of purchase.

Lend-Lease Act of 1941

This law marked the end of U.S. Neutrality Acts. It allowed the U.S. to lend, sell or give war supplies to its allies. President Roosevelt could now offer our foreign friends more than just a few kind words. He could, and did, send them money, weapons, vehicles and, after Pearl Harbor, U.S. troops.

title: Letter from Churchill to Roosevelt: What does it mean?
text:
The prime minister of Great Britain, Winston Churchill, and U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt sent letters and telegrams back and forth, even before the United States entered WWII. What do you think they talked about? Here is a copy of a letter that Churchill sent to Roosevelt before the U.S. officially entered the war. Read the letter carefully and answer the questions. (You may use a dictionary to look up unfamiliar words, if necessary.) Answer the questions on a separate sheet of paper.

BRITISH EMBASSY,

WASHINGTON, D. C.

December 7th, 1940

My dear Mr. President,

As we reach the end of this year I feel that you will expect me to lay before you the prospects for 1941. I do so strongly and confidently because it seems to me that the vast majority of American citizens have recorded their conviction that the safety of the United States as well as the future of our two democracies and the kind of civilization for which they stand are bound up with the survival and independence of the British Commonwealth of Nations. Only thus can those bastions of sea-power, upon which the control of the Atlantic and the Indian Oceans depends, be preserved in faithful and friendly hands. The control of the Pacific by the United States Navy and of the Atlantic by the British Navy is indispensable to the security of the trade routes of both our countries and the surest means to preventing the war from reaching the shores of the United States.

Questions

1. When was this letter written?

2. In the letter, Churchill says he is confident that most Americans believe that the future of the two democracies, the United States and Great Britain, are “bound up with the survival and independence of the British Commonwealth.” What do you think he meant by this?

3. What does Churchill believe is the “surest means to preventing the war from reaching the shores of the United States”?

4. What do you think Churchill hoped Roosevelt would do to help Great Britain?

title: Dr. Seuss vs. Isolationism
text:
You are probably familiar with the characters created by Dr. Seuss (real name: Theodor Seuss Geisel). Did you know that in addition to writing children’s books, he spent several years drawing political cartoons? Political cartoons are drawings that use characters and words to make a comment about a current event.

Ted, as Dr. Seuss was known in those days, was opposed to isolationism. He believed that the U.S. should help its friends defeat Germany and Japan. One of his cartoons shows a drawing of Mount Rushmore, but instead of the faces of U.S. presidents, the famous landmark displays the faces of the German and Japanese leaders. The drawing has a caption that reads: “Don’t let them carve THOSE faces on our mountains.” His cartoons leave no question about his stand on the war. Dr. Seuss wanted the U.S. to join the fight against the people trying to conquer the world. If you want to see the cartoons, see what you can find at the library or on the internet (with parent permission).

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you are President Roosevelt. The Allies have just won World War II. What do you think the United States and Axis powers should do? What do you do with Germany, Italy and Japan? How can you prevent another World War in the future?

title: Reconstruction and Recovery
text:
On September 2, 1945, the Japanese formally surrendered to the United States on board the USS Missouri. This formally ended World War II. Years of fighting between the Allied and Axis Powers, destroyed much of Europe. Cities lay in ruin. Armies and Navies had lost ships, tanks, planes and, many, many soldiers. Millions of civilians also lost their lives due to the fighting.

On top of the ruin was a great fear that there would be another World War. The Allied Powers did what they could to prevent another great war. In the weeks following the surrender of the Japanese, the victors created and signed a number of treaties. The treaties divided Germany into four zones. The United States, France, Great Britain, and Russia each occupied one zone.

The US army occupied Japan. The United States took away Japan's army. The US Army helped rebuild Japan. It changed Japan's government, taking away most of the emperor's power. It created a parliament, instead.

In 1948, George C. Marshall proposed a plan to help rebuild Europe. The Marshall Plan directed $13 billion, including food, supplies, and equipment to the effort.

The Paris Peace Conference involved treaties with "minor" Axis powers. The United Nations was created on October 24, 1945. The U.S., British, French and Soviets tried Nazi leaders and organizations for war crimes.

title: The U.S. Joins the Fight
text:
The day after the Pearl Harbor attack, the U.S. declared war on Japan. On December 11, Germany and Italy declared war on the United States. The U.S. then joined the Allies in the fight against the Axis Powers. Let's take a look at some of the major battles and events of WWII. Use your classroom map to pinpoint each location.

Until this point, the U.S. was hesitant to join the war. Americans wanted to avoid repeating the bloodshed of World War I. The government followed a policy of isolationism. This was the idea that the U.S. should avoid any involvement in foreign conflicts. Laws were passed to prevent the U.S. from getting involved in outside conflicts. Even weapons or money couldn't be sent to other countries. With an unexpected attack on American soil in Hawaii, the country was forced into the war.

1. Japanese Forces Sweep Through the Pacific

For six months after Pearl Harbor's attack, the Japanese pushed forward with little resistance. Allied troops already stationed in the Pacific fought bravely, but were no match against the large and efficient Japanese war machine. The Japanese swept over nearly the entire southwestern Pacific and were ready to invade Australia and India.

2. The United States and Its Allies Push Back

One thing the Japanese felt confident about was the remote distance of their homeland. When U.S. Colonel James Doolittle led 16 B-25s to bomb Tokyo, Kobe, and Osaka on April 18, 1942, the Japanese were terrified. Suddenly, they realized the war was coming home to them.

Terrible sea battles were waged to hedge in the Japanese. The Battle of Coral Sea forced the main Japanese fleet back toward safer waters. When they tried to take the American-held Midway Island, they were engaged by the Americans in the Battle of Midway. In the end, four Japanese aircraft carriers and many Japanese aircraft and ships were destroyed. It was the turning point of the war. A similar Japanese attack on the Aleutians near Alaska took place, but the Japanese couldn't hold the islands very long until the United States attacked and got them back.

The fighting at Coral Sea, Midway and the Aleutians signaled the end of Japanese expansion.

3. Stalingrad, Beginning of the End

In the summer of 1942, the German army headed for the important Soviet city of Stalingrad. Hitler believed that capturing the city and its supplies would break the will of the Soviets. Germans dropped 1,000 tons of bombs on the city, and soldiers battled in the streets. Things looked grim for the Soviet Union. However, the battle took a turn as winter approached. Around 500,000 Soviet soldiers surrounded the German army. The Soviets cut off German supply routes, and soldiers starved in the freezing temperatures. In February 1943, the Germans were forced to surrender. The losses on both sides were almost unbelievable. Estimates of military and civilian casualties (wounded, killed or missing) are as high as 2 million people. Many historians point to this battle as the beginning of the end for Hitler's forces. The German army never recovered from the great loss of soldiers.

Invasion of Normandy

Allied soldiers were about to begin the invasion of Normandy, a region in northern France, on June 6, 1944. General Dwight D. Eisenhower told them, "The eyes of the world are upon you. The hopes and prayers of liberty-loving people everywhere march with you."

The invasion of Normandy began with almost 160,000 Allied troops crossing the English Channel from Great Britain to France, which the Germans occupied. The Allies supplied over 5,000 ships and 11,000 planes. The invasion, now known as D-Day, gave the Allies a base for shipping and storing military supplies. By the end of June, over 1 million Allied troops had crossed into France. Hitler's troops were slowly pushed back toward Germany.

title: That Terrible Day in December
text:
What were so many planes doing in the air at this time of day? Was it some kind of exercise? Suddenly, it became very clear what the planes were doing. It was an attack!

Dec. 7, 1941, was another sleepy Sunday across America. Families were coming home from morning church services, others were settling down after brunch with the Sunday paper, and others were simply enjoying Sunday listening to music on the radio.

However, far away to the west, a completely different kind of morning was breaking over Hawaii. Out across the sea, low to the horizon, a strange formation had gathered in the morning sky. As it approached, people watched from a distance. What were so many planes doing in the air at this time of day? Was it some kind of exercise? Suddenly, it became very clear what the planes were doing. It was an attack!

Pearl Harbor (Hawaii) was the home of America's largest naval base in the Pacific region. At 7:55 a.m. Hawaii time, more than 400 Japanese airplanes attacked American ships and people. Japan was officially at war with the United States.

Immediately, the alarms sounded all over Hawaii, and the cry went out, "Pearl Harbor is under attack!"

Japanese fighter planes, torpedo bombers and dive bombers took only one hour and 55 minutes to empty their bombs and bullets. When it was over, five of our eight battleships were sunk, the other three damaged. (Six were later repaired and went to war.) Five other ships were sunk and several damaged. About 325 Navy and Army planes on the ground were destroyed. Among the dead were 2,343 American sailors, soldier and marines; 1,272 were wounded, and 960 were missing. Many of the docks, repair facilities, hangars, and runways were damaged or destroyed.

When word of the attack reached the mainland United States, panic and anger spread from coast to coast, especially along the western coastal cities, where people feared a direct attack from the sea. Instead of a day of rest, Sunday became a dark day of worry. Would the Japanese continue their attack along the Pacific Coast? Would they bomb farther inland? No one knew what to expect.

And just like that, America was at war again. Some historians believe that there never were 20 years of peace between the end of World War I and the start of World War II. It was more like an armed truce. In 1939, Germany again attacked its neighbors and began a costly attempt to take over Europe. America helped its Allies for the first couple of years before jumping in with both feet to end Germany's threats and power in Europe. By 1942, the United States was heavily involved in two war zones in the Pacific against Japan and in Europe against Germany and its allies.

title: The Allies and the Axis Across the Globe
text:
Soviet Union: Axis Power allied with Germany at the start of the war. Germany betrayed the Soviet Union by invading in 1941. The Soviet Union became an Allied Power. Leader: Joseph Stalin

Great Britain: Allied Power, one of the last countries to hold out against Hitler. Leader: Winston Churchill

United States: Allied Power, last to join. Leader: Franklin D. Roosevelt

France: Allied Power, but overtaken by Hitler in 1940. The French Resistance keeps fighting. Leader: Charles De Gaulle

Germany: Axis Power, goal was to take over all of Europe. Leader: Adolf Hitler

Italy: Axis Power, fascist country. Hitler was inspired by the leadership here. Leader: Benito Mussolini

Japan: Axis Power, bombed Pearl Harbor. Leader: Emperor Hirohito

title: Trouble in the World
text:
"Jackson, it was really cool to meet Winston Churchill and learn about how Britain was fighting World War II. But how did the war begin?"

"Good question, Alana. We know that there was a lot of political trouble in the countries that were involved in World War II."

"Let's take a look at some of the Axis countries to see what happened!"

Note: Use the map to locate the following countries. Keep track of those doing the invading and those being invaded!

Italy

After World War I, Italian leaders had to deal with unhappy citizens. Benito Mussolini stepped in. He created many programs to help the people. But he also set himself up as dictator, or a government leader with absolute power. He called himself “Il Duce,” or “The Leader.” In 1935, Mussolini sent the Italian military to Africa. He invaded Ethiopia, then known as Abyssinia, and added this country to his empire. Mussolini later sent help to fascists in Spain during the Spanish Civil War, hoping to show his power. Fascists are people who believe a nation or race is more important than an individual. In 1939, Mussolini officially joined with Adolf Hitler, creating the “Pact of Steel.” This alliance joined the two countries together throughout World War II.

Germany

Adolf Hitler became chancellor of Germany in 1933. He led Germany’s Nazi Party. In 1934, Hitler stepped in as dictator and took control of the government. It was a time of economic struggle. Hitler promised the millions of poor and unemployed that with his help, Germany would rise again.

Hitler believed that people of what he called an "Aryan" or Germanic race, or those from certain European backgrounds, were racially superior to others. Superior means better than. He said that those who were inferior, specifically Jews, must be eliminated. Ultimately, the Nazis decided that the best way to do this was to murder all Jews. In March 1938, Hitler took control of the country of Austria, his birthplace. Nazi troops marched into Austria and no one fought back. Many Austrians felt that all German-speaking people should belong to a united country. Some celebrated the arrival of Nazi rule. Some who were against it were put in prison. Austrian Jews were immediately stripped of their rights and faced persecution, or ill treatment.

Soon after, Hitler moved to take control of German-speaking areas in Czechoslovakia. Hitler claimed ethnic Germans in the area were mistreated. The Nazis came in ready to invade. Czechoslovakia's allies would have also gone to war against Germany if this happened, starting another war like World War I.

In October 1938, Hitler, Mussolini, the prime minister of France and British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain met in Munich. They talked about Hitler's demands to take control of the area. They agreed that the Sudetenland would come under German control. Neville Chamberlain hoped to make Hitler happy. He thought that would prevent another war. After that, Chamberlain said, "I believe it is peace for our time." At the time, it sounded hopeful. But, those words have become famous for how wrong they were. A year later, Germany invaded Poland to start World War II.

Soviet Union

Like Germany, a dictator led the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) during this period. Joseph Stalin was the Communist leader of the USSR, or Soviet Union, from the mid-1920s until his death in 1953. In a communist government, there is no private property. Stalin wanted the Soviet Union to rise from its problems and become a world power. He took farmland from the poor and put it under government control. He also set and reached many goals for mining and manufacturing. These goals were part of his “Five Year Plans.” The Plans made the Soviet Union an impressive industrial nation. Still, millions of Soviets and people from other countries died under Stalin’s command.

Stalin and Hitler disagreed on most matters, but they signed an agreement in 1939. It said that their nations would never attack each other. Just two years later, Hitler broke the agreement. Stalin joined the Allies in the fight against Germany during World War II.

Japan

In the late 1860s, Japan began a period of imperialism, slowly expanding control in Asia. Other nations came to think of Japan as the leader of the region.

During the Great Depression, many countries blocked Japan’s exports. They did that to preserve the value of their own goods. The Japanese economy was hurt by this. Japan had to do something to stay wealthy. So, Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931. Manchuria is a region in northern China that is rich in resources.

War broke out between China and Japan in 1937. In December of that year, Japan invaded the city of Nanking and murdered thousands of people. Brutal crimes were committed against survivors. Historians do not know the exact number of people killed. Most think it is between 200,000 and 300,000. The war between China and Japan continued until 1945. When the U.S. declared war on Japan in 1941, China joined the U.S. and its allies in the fight against Japan.

Military leader Hideki Tojo wanted Japan to join with Germany and Italy in the Axis Powers. Historians do not agree about who really controlled Japan; the military or Emperor Hirohito. Some say Hirohito is responsible for Japanese crimes in Asia and for Japan's role in the war. Others say that he was only a figurehead, or symbol, used by the military. Why did the military use him for a symbol? Because the people were loyal to the emperor. Historians do agree that the emperor was adored by his subjects, almost like a god.

As you can see, trouble was brewing all over the world.

title: World War II Begins
text:
In the years leading up to World War II, Germany under the Nazi party took control of several territories without combat. The British prime minister before Churchill, Neville Chamberlain, used a policy called appeasement. This meant that by letting Germany take land it wanted, he thought Hitler would be satisfied and not resort to starting a war. Chamberlain thought he had secured "peace for our time." Those words of his have become famous because of how wrong they proved to be.

Hitler signed a non-aggression pact with Russia and then stormed Poland on Sept. 1, 1939. Immediately, Great Britain, France, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa declared war on Germany. World War II was officially started.

Hitler's plan was to conquer and control all of Europe. After Hitler and the Soviet Union split up Poland, Hitler swept into Norway and Denmark. Some Norwegians tried to fight back with British help, but they failed.

On May 10, 1940, Hitler's troops invaded the lowlands. In just a few days, the Germans marched over the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxemburg and then pushed into northern France. By this time, Allied troops were trying to strengthen the battle lines with other European nations. One such effort was broken in two by the German troops. Some 300,000 British and Allied troops were left stranded on the northern coast of France at Dunkirk. Horrific artillery bombardment pushed the 300,000 into the sea, where British rescue-vessels and hundreds of civilian boats picked them up and sailed them to safety. Six weeks later, France fell to the German invasion.

title: Think and Review Questions
text:
What type of government leaders took control of the European and Asian nations during the Great Depression? Analyze and explain why you think these leaders were able to come into power.

Compare and contrast Italian fascism with German Nazism. How were they alike? How were they different?

How did Stalin help the Soviet Union recover from the Depression?

Describe the actions that Japan took during the 1930s.

title: Let's Write
text: Write a radio broadcast as Charles De Gaulle. Your goal is to get people to join Free France and the French Resistance.

title: De Gaulle and the French Resistance
text:
At the beginning of the war, France was an Allied nation that fought alongside Great Britain against Germany. However, France's military power was short-lived. Tensions between Germany and France were high after World War I, since France blamed Germany for the Great War and forced the Germans to pay France back for damages.

Charles De Gaulle was a great soldier who loved France. He fought in WWI where he was wounded three times. His experience made him think about how France was fighting battles. He thought they could do better and began to write books on the subject. When WWII came along and the French began to give into the Germans, De Gaulle did not agree with the French government at all.

When France began to surrender, De Gaulle decided he would do what he could to fight the Nazis. He fled to Great Britain and from there he began to establish his own government: Free France. The French leaders who had surrendered called him a traitor. He made pleas to the French people to fight! To resist!

De Gaulle created the French Resistance. Many of these were soldiers who had fled when France surrendered but a lot of them were ordinary people. The Resistance did much to help the Allied Powers during the war. When it came close to victory, and the Allied Forces invaded France, the French Resistance was a key factor in its liberation. De Gaulle worked closely with General Eisenhower to assure a victory on D-Day.

De Gaulle went on to become President of France. He worked with the people through the rest of the war and helped with the recovery of France when the war was over. He helped France create a new and stronger government.

title: Alliances: Where Do They Belong?
text:
Below, you will see the names of countries and individuals that are associated with World War II after the bombing of Pearl Harbor. Each one of these countries or individuals was part of the Axis Powers or part of the Allied Powers. Place the country or individual in the correct box.

Britain

Charles de Gaulle

Germany

Franklin D. Roosevelt

United States

Emperor Hirohito

Japan

Adolf Hitler

Italy

Winston Churchill

Soviet Union

Benito Mussolini

France

Joseph Stalin

title: Meeting Mr. Churchill
text:
"WWII was a war that shook the world," says Ms. Johnson. "There were key players on both sides. One was known as the Allied Powers and the other the Axis Powers. Britain, France, the Soviet Union, and the United States made up the Allied Powers. The Axis Powers consisted of Germany, Italy, and Japan."

"The Axis nations had to be defeated. There were evil things taking place, and Hitler was planning to take over as many countries as he could. Much of the planning for the defeat of Hitler fell upon this man," said Ms. Johnson as she held up a picture of Winston Churchill.

Jackson and Alana looked at each other and smiled. Later, they touched the picture and were whisked away to find themselves standing in the office of Mr. Churchill. It's 1941 and England is desperately planning to defeat Germany and the Nazis.

"Mr. Churchill, do you have a plan for going up against the Axis Powers?" asked Jackson. "It seems like an overwhelming job."

"One of the main things I have done is to help to pull together the Allied Powers. We need a strong front to combat the evil Hitler is spreading. This war is not going to be easy to win, and the people need encouragement," said Mr. Churchill. "I truly believe we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills; we shall never surrender as I told the people in a speech."

"One of the main strategies I am planning on using is aerial bombing. I think it will take several years of that in order to invade Germany," he told Alana and Jackson. "The invasion of Germany is the goal and the protection of England. It will be a long, hard road but we will persevere, especially now that the United States has agreed to help."

"Thank you for talking with us, Sir," said the children. As soon as they shook his hand, they were immediately back in the classroom. Their friends couldn't wait to hear more about Prime Minister Churchill and how America helped win the war.

title: Cordell Hull and Cornelia Fort
text:
One of the most influential people from Tennessee is Cordell Hull. He holds the title of longest-serving secretary of state. During his time in office, Hull finished tasks that promote peace and safety for Americans and other countries.

With President Roosevelt, Hull tried to keep global alliances peaceful and prosperous. They created the "Good Neighbor" policy. The policy prevented the U.S. from meddling with Latin America and their issues or dealings. It also helped improve each country's economy and trade abilities.

This successful agreement with Latin America was just the beginning. Hull was interested in linking more countries with worldwide trade agreements. In 1934, the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act (RTAA) ensured that trading between countries would be cheaper for all involved.

Another step he took toward making peace for all countries was the formation of the United Nations. Woodrow Wilson wanted to start a worldwide peace group called the League of Nations after the end of World War I. Due to many issues, the League was not successful. But Cordell Hull was able to achieve what President Wilson had planned. He created a unifying force to help promote peace and security throughout the world. During the time of its creation, World War II was raging on. The free world hoped to stop the Axis powers from creating more devastation and destruction. If nations could unite together against threatening forces, then they would not have to face issues alone.

With the help of many world leaders, this group became a reality on October 24, 1945, with the United States and 50 other countries. Since then, the United Nations has been an influential force in keeping the peace and security in the world.

For his efforts, Cordell Hull received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1945. He indeed has been one of the most influential government officials in U.S. history.

-----

Cornelia Fort is another influential Tennessean. She became the very face of the war effort during World War II. She is best known for being the first female pilot in the Civil Air Patrol. At an early age, Cornelia always wanted to fly. Inspired by the famous pilot Amelia Earhart, Fort went to flying school to learn how to be a pilot.

Once she received her pilot license, she got a job in Fort Collins, Colorado. When the war started, she wanted to contribute. At first, she taught at Andrews Flying Service to teach men in the military to fly. But she wanted to do more. And so, when she received word to join a female pilot expedition to help the war effort, she couldn't resist. She became one of the original members of the Women's Auxiliary Ferry Service (or WAFS). She spent her time delivering needed supplies to those in the war.

Unfortunately, Fort didn't fly for her country for very long. On March 21, 1943, her plane was clipped by the landing gear of another craft. Cornelia Fort's life ended in the crash. Sadly, she didn't receive the same military honors that a man might have. However, a historical marker was built in 1945 at her family's home in Davidson County, Tennessee. On the marker, one can read Fort's own words: "I am grateful that my one talent, flying, was useful to my country."

title: Victory Gardens
text:
During WWII, American farmers were now fighting in the war. Food production in the United States was down due to the Great Depression. Millions of people in Europe were starving. To support the troops and the Allies, Americans planted victory gardens. The more food they grew on their own, the more farm food could be used by soldiers and sailors. They were called victory gardens because the war had united them all in a spirit of positive thinking.

In cities, people turned empty lots, backyards and even rooftops into gardens. The government encouraged neighbors to cooperate and plant different types of foods. Because steel was limited, many people shared garden tools, taking turns tending the gardens. Magazines printed stories about victory gardens. Stories gave instructions on how to grow and preserve garden crops. Posters told citizens to "Sow the seeds of victory" by planting gardens. People responded by growing, canning and bottling their own food. Troops were then able to receive canned foods.

With men off to war, women took on the burdens of the family farm. Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts watered and tended them, as did families and communities. Victory gardens sprang up everywhere. Some schools turned their playgrounds into gardens. Cities turned their parks into gardens. Items planted included beans, beets, cabbage, carrots, kale, lettuce, peas, tomatoes, turnips, squash and potatoes. Even First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt planted a victory garden, right on the White House lawn!

More than 20 million victory gardens were planted. Fruits and vegetables harvested totaled up to 10 million pounds of food. That's the same amount of fruits and vegetables grown on farms. People at home could feel proud they were doing their part in the war effort. Some of those same gardens remain today.

title: Rationing for the War Effort
text:
During World War II, people couldn’t just go to the store and get whatever they wanted. The military needed a lot of supplies to keep fighting, and that meant people at home needed to ration, or limit their amount of, supplies. Many factories in Tennessee were converted to produce military goods. Families were only allowed to use small amounts of foods like sugar, bread and butter. Rationing also limited things like paper, cloth and gasoline.

The government handed out ration cards to keep track of what everyone had bought and used. The ration books contained removable stamps for certain items like meat, cooking oils and canned goods. People could not buy that item without providing the grocery with the right stamp. Once the stamp was used, people would have to wait until the next month to receive another stamp. That meant everyone had to plan their meals carefully and not waste food. More than 8,000 rationing boards across the country managed the program.

Leaders also encouraged people to collect things like food, metal and rubber. Ration books reminded people to save their tin cans and waste fats. They were needed to make munitions for soldiers and sailors.

During the war, almost everyone came together to help give our troops what they needed. What are some other things you think might have been rationed? How do you think you would have felt if your family had to limit how much food and gas you used? Share your thoughts with a classmate.

title: Rosie the Riveter
text:
This picture is a propaganda poster that shows a female worker named Rosie the Riveter. Answer the questions about the picture.

Describe the picture.

What do you think Rosie the Riveter represented?

Do you think women entering the workforce would help them move toward equal rights in the future? Why or why not?

title: Let's Write
text: How did women prove they were one of the essential components to America's success in World War II?

title: Oak Ridge
text:
During World War II, the United States was competing with some of the advancements the Axis powers (like Germany and Italy) had made developing weapons. To keep up, the U.S. developed a secret project called the Manhattan Project to develop the atomic bomb. The bomb was dropped on Hiroshima and then Nagasaki during World War II.

To keep other countries from determining how it was being built, the United States created a "fake" city. It could not be identified on any map. It was called Oak Ridge, Tennessee. Based on maps and other official records, the city didn't exist. The men and women that were asked to live and work there had no idea what they were helping build. All of their work was kept a secret. Residents were told not to talk about their life or jobs in Oak Ridge for fear of enemy spies catching wind of the Manhattan Project. By 1945, Oak Ridge had a population of about 75,000; not bad for a city that technically wasn't real!

title: Symbols and Slogans
text:
Who was Rosie the Riveter? Was she a relative of Uncle Sam? In a way, yes, because both became symbols of our American values.

More and more American men went off to fight WWII, so women entered the workforce, replacing these "lost" employees. During the war years, about 6 million women found jobs outside of the home. By 1944, 3.5 million women worked in factories, making weapons and other goods. Women also worked in the aviation industry building planes.

Posters of Rosie the Riveter entered popular culture. A riveter is a worker who joins metal plates together with rivets. On one magazine cover, "Rosie" sat on her machinery and ate a sandwich. Another poster showed a woman dressed in blue with a bandana covering her hair. It included the caption, "We Can Do It!" Rosie the Riveter became a symbol of the women who helped America win the war. She showed other women they could help by keeping things running here at home.

America was not the only country using symbols and slogans.

During WWII, the British government printed posters to encourage its citizens to stand strong during difficult times. One of these carried the message "Keep Calm and Carry On." The copyright for this poster expired 50 years after it was printed, so now anyone can use the design and slogan. The design has become very popular and appears on all types of products throughout Great Britain and around the world.

A British woman, Moragh Turnbull, found a batch of original "Keep Calm and Carry On" posters in her father's home. Her father was once a member of the Royal Observer Corps. The corps was a group of civilians who watched for enemy attacks during WWII. He had been asked to put up the posters around town during the war. Moragh took the posters to a filming of a popular TV show where antiques are appraised (examined to see how much they are worth). She discovered that they are very rare posters worth about $1,000 each! The "forgotten" posters are in great shape and are valuable primary sources!

At the beginning of WWII, Great Britain expected that the Germans would begin massive airstrikes on British cities. The government printed posters that were meant to lift people's spirits and help them face the future with courage. These posters were messages designed to persuade people to think or behave in a certain way. Just as in WWI, the government used posters to build morale. Themes included cheerfulness, confidence, courage and commitment to the war effort.

These were some of the other slogans used on the British posters: "Your Courage, Your Cheerfulness, Your Resolution Will Bring Us Victory," "Freedom is in Peril. Defend It With All Your Might." Discuss with a partner the meaning behind these slogans.

Both Allied and Axis powers encouraged their citizens to keep sensitive information to themselves. Slogans were used such as "Loose Lips Sink Ships." Documents, songs, cartoons, movies and radio were all used. Positive aspects of the war were portrayed, such as supporting troops, rationing food and buying war bonds. Some efforts told people to save resources, such as their food fats, tin or paper. Recycling efforts paid off. Forty-six billion pounds of paper, 538 million pounds of waste fat and 800 million pounds of tin were recycled. Saving butter, coffee and rubber was patriotic. The troops could then use those products.

Post offices, railroad stations, schools, restaurants and retail stores all displayed the posters. Over 200,000 poster designs were created and printed during the war.

text:
