title: An Overview of Early American Time Periods
text:
American Indian history began around 14,000 years ago. Scientists have named four time major periods in American Indian history. In general, these periods include where and how tribes lived. They also include progress in their daily life.

Paleo Period: 12,000–8,000 B.C.E.

This is the first period of American Indian history. At this time, the first tribes began moving to North America. People moved from place to place, following game animals. Most groups were 20-60 people. These groups probably did not have leaders. They used basic tools for hunting. People gathered much of their food. The Coats-Hines site was built during this period. The site is near I-65 in Williamson County. In addition to mastodon skeletons, several ancient stone tools have been found there.

Archaic Period: 8,000–3,000 B.C.E.

During this period, tool use became more common. Hunters began to use the atlatl to throw spears. This allowed for more success in hunting animals, like deer and small game. American Indians also began to create and use hand tools. During this period, they started making pottery. They often used pots to hold food and water. American Indians built the Pinson mounds during this period. The mounds, in Madison County, are now part of a state archaeological park. There are at least 15 American Indian mounds.

Woodland Period: 3,000 B.C.E.–1,000 C.E.

During this period, there were advances in farming. The people got better at growing food. The found it was easier to grow food than to hunt it. People could stay in one place more. They started building structures, such as mounds. People began making several different types of pots. Pots were used for storing and cooking food. Some traded pots with settlers. Old Stone Fort, another state archaeological park location, is located in Manchester. The Woodland peoples used this beautiful site as a ceremonial meeting place.

Mississippian Period: 1,000–1,500 C.E.

Farming became even more important. Corn was often the primary crop. American Indians began forming villages and towns. Towns had leaders, such as chiefs. Some people had jobs hunting or farming. Trade became more and more important. Several more earthen mounds were built during this period. Chucalissa Indian Village was built during this period. Chucalissa is Choctaw for “abandoned house.” It’s in Memphis, overlooking the Mississippi River. The well-preserved village is on the National Registration of Historic Places.

title: Name That State!
text:
Do you ever wonder where states get their names? What do you think the name "Tennessee" means? The name was proposed by Daniel Smith, a secretary of the Southwest Territory, in 1796. Primary source documents, such as maps and letters have various spellings of Tennessee, including “the land of the Tannassy,” Tinnace, Tanisee and Tennecy, Why do you think there were so many spellings?

No one quite knows from where the name came. There are a few stories to explain the origins of the name, "Tennessee." What all the stories agree on is that the name has its roots in American Indian language. In one story, Captain Juan Pardo led an 16th-century expedition through a Cherokee town called "Tanasqui."

Another explanation is that the name comes from the Yuchi, a tribe that lived in the eastern Tennessee River valley. They called their "meeting place" or "joining of two rivers," Tana-tsee. One interesting fact is that the Yuchi have a language unrelated to any other native language. That’s unusual!

No matter how you spell it, Tennessee is a great state with an unforgettable name!"

title: The Early Peoples of Tennessee
text:
From finds like the Coats-Hines site, we learn a lot about the earliest people on this continent. Who were they? What did they eat? How did they spend their time? What did they do for fun?

As with any people in the world, their culture changed over time. The Paleo People were different from the tribes that European settlers encountered much later. We'll talk about four tribes of American Indians that lived in Tennessee before colonial times. They were the Cherokee, the Chickasaw, the Shawnee and the Creek.

American Indians from Tennessee ended up relocating a few times. As American settlements grew, settlers wanted more land. There were lots of arguments and sometimes fighting over what land belonged to whom. Once in a while, American Indians sold land, like in the Treaty of Fort Wayne. In 1838, though, most of the tribes were forced to move out west to Oklahoma.

The Cherokee

The Cherokee were very socially and culturally advanced. Their culture thrived many hundreds of years before European contact. The Cherokee lived in Georgia, the Carolinas and the eastern part of Tennessee. In the 1600s, there were around 20,000 Cherokee! They mostly lived in towns. Cherokee towns had between 30 and 60 log cabins. There were two types of towns. The first type was the "red" town, meaning it was a warring town. The second type of town was the "white" town; it was peaceful.

They grew corn, beans and squash. These were staples of the diet and were called the "Three Sisters." They also wove baskets and made pottery. Some of the early Cherokee made stone knives, axes and chisels.

The numbers four and seven were important in their ceremonies. The four represented the cardinal directions of east, west, north and south. Adding the upper world, the lower world and the center made seven. The number seven also represented the seven clans of the people. The Cherokee had a particular regard for the owl and cougar. Pine, cedar, spruce and holly played an essential role in ceremonies. Cedar was considered the most sacred. In ancient days, it was used to carry the honored dead.

The Creek

There were two groups of Creek, the Upper and Lower Creek. They mostly lived in Georgia and Alabama. There was about as many Creek as there were Cherokee, about 20,000. And just like the Cherokee, the Creek towns were either red towns, the ones that went to war, or white peaceful towns. They held peace ceremonies in the white towns, and the red towns held war ceremonies.

They built their cabins to surround a central meeting area. The women were mostly farmers. They grew corn, squash and beans. Corn was an essential staple of their diet. They made sofkey from it, a soup of soured cornmeal, lye and water. Visitors to Creek homes could expect a bowlful waiting for them. Sweet potatoes, pumpkins, peaches and apples were also part of their diet.

In the summers, the Creek held a thanksgiving harvest. The Green Corn Festival celebrated coming harvests. And, at this ceremony, the Creek forgave wrongdoings committed by members of the tribe. Creek men had tattoos all over their bodies. They had animals, abstract scrollwork, natural objects and even hunting and battle scenes. Both men and women wore body paint, earrings and jewelry.

After Europeans settled in the area, the Creek adapted to many European customs. They used their hunting skills to trade for metal tools. They traded deerskins for brightly colored cloth. They used guns to help with hunting and protecting their villages.

The Chickasaw

The Chickasaw were a smaller tribe. There might have been 3,000 tribal members. They made villages on high bluffs or high hills. From here they could see enemies or invaders. Some of their towns had forts to help keep them safe. Stickball grounds were also in the village. A council house was a place where they made important decisions.

The clan was the most important group to which they could belong. A Chickasaw belonged to their mother's clan. Clans names came from animals, such as raccoon, panther, fox or wolf. The Three Sisters were planted together to help each other grow. As with the other tribes, these were the basics of their diet. They also had a harvest ceremony each year.

The Shawnee

The Shawnee mostly lived in the Midwest. They were one of the larger tribes. There are now three smaller Shawnee tribes. Like the Creek, the women grew crops. Men hunted for food, at least for most of the year. The Shawnee spent most of the year in their houses. In the winter, the Shawnee moved to hunting cabins. During this time, they focused their efforts on hunting deer and small game.

The Shawnee had a special dance in spring, called the Bread Dance. This was usually right after planting crops. The Shawnee held a Green Corn Ceremony to celebrate their growing crops in summer.

text: Picture the life of a member of the Shawnee tribe. It is summer, so the member is living in a village. What do you predict daily life would look like? What do you think life would be like in winter when the tribe moves to a hunting cabin?

title: Coats-Hines, A Mammoth Discovery!
text:
"I can't wait for the trip today!" says Jackson as he eagerly joins Alana at the door of their fifth-grade classroom at the beginning of the school day.

"I could barely sleep last night, Jackson! I kept thinking about what we might see," Alana responds.

Jackson and Alana step into their classroom. Excitement hangs in the air. The two quickly put their belongings away and take their seats. The rest of the class is already waiting.

Ms. Johnson calls the class to attention. "Class, today we're going to visit the Coats-Hines site. As we talked about yesterday, Coats-Hines was the site of a mammoth discovery!"

The class laughs as Ms. Johnson directs students out of the room, then out the doors of the school to the waiting buses. Jackson and Alana are the last to board the bus. "Mammoth discovery," Alana giggles. "Get it, Jackson? Mammoth discovery?"

"The discovery of the Coats-Hines site in eastern Tennessee was a complete accident," continues Ms. Johnson. "Back in 1977, workers were clearing an area in eastern Tennessee to build a golf course. As a bulldozer operator worked, he noticed something strange sticking out of the ground. Bones. Impossibly large bones. The discovery intrigued scientists. They determined the bones belonged to a mastodon. The mastodon lived all the way back during the Paleo Period, about 12,000 to 14,000 years ago! That wasn't the only discovery. Scientists also found early tools nearby and what looked like tool marks on some of the bones. Scientists concluded early mastodon hunters used the tools."

Jackson peers out the bus window. "You know Ms. Johnson's joke about a 'mammoth discovery?' Mammoths and mastodons are different animals. Mammoths lived in colder places and had humps on their backs. They also had special teeth for crushing food."

"It was a joke, Jackson. Still pretty funny."

"Yeah, sounds like one my dad would tell."

Jackson checks his notebook. "There are lots of great historical places in Tennessee for us to visit. I've got notes about one place called Chucalissa Village."

"I visited Chucalissa Village with my family last year," Alana says. "There were a bunch of mounds there. Our tour guide told us that American Indians used the site during the Mississippian Period. They used the area for three thousand years. It was discovered by people working in the area, kind of like Coats-Hines. People working for the Civilian Conservation Corps found bones, bricks and pottery.

"The mounds were used for ceremonies and also burials. And there were houses there, too. They were grouped around a meeting area. Our tour guide told us that the leaders of the village had the largest houses. The people there got their food by hunting, fishing and farming."

"Wow!" exclaims Jackson. "It sounds a lot like the Pinson Mounds. The 15 mounds were built during the Middle Woodland Period, around 2,000 years ago. American Indians lived there in houses; they got most of their food through farming. Two-thousand years ago was during the Woodland Period of American history."

"Have you been there?" Alana asked.

"Nope. I read about it. One of the coolest things I read was that second tallest mound in the U.S. is located at the Pinson Mounds. It's 70 feet tall!"

"Wow!" cries Alana. "Now that's a mammoth discovery! Are there any mastodons there?"

title: Pottery
text: Over the years, pottery became an important part of American Indian culture. The oldest pieces of pottery were found in Georgia. The pieces were about 4,000 years old! Some tribes, those that hunted or moved frequently, did not make as many pots as those that farmed. Rituals surrounded the gathering of clay. Early pottery was made by hand, using a process called coiling. Coiling involved rolling clay into long strands. The coiled strands formed the shape of the pot. The coils were later pinched down or scraped smooth. The pot was then heated to harden the clay. Pottery served a number of uses, such as holding water and food. American Indians used some pots to cook; they traded some pots, too. They also decorated their pots. Pottery has been an enduring tradition. Some tribal members still sell traditional pots, beautifully decorated.

title: A Hope for Peace Brings War Instead
text:
This is a story about two leaders of the Cherokee people: Little Carpenter and Dragging Canoe.

Little Carpenter's Cherokee name was Attakullakulla. The Cherokee adopted him when he was a baby. When he grew up, he became the Cherokee's first Beloved Man. That means he was a tribal chief.

When Little Carpenter was a chief, white settlers wanted to buy or lease land from our people. A man named Richard Henderson asked for a meeting with the Cherokee. More than 1,200 Cherokee gathered at Sycamore Shoals. Little Carpenter and other chiefs were there as well. Beloved Woman Nancy Ward was there too. Henderson offered several wagonloads of goods in exchange for the land. Little Carpenter and other chiefs agreed to the deal.

Not everyone thought selling the land was a good idea. Many Cherokee did not like signing a treaty with white settlers. It was hard for them to trust the settlers. One Cherokee who disagreed with Little Carpenter was his son, Dragging Canoe. Dragging Canoe got his name by trying to prove that he was ready for war by carrying a canoe. The canoe was too big, so he could only drag it.

Dragging Canoe begged his father not to make the treaty. He reminded him that other tribes had given away land, and it turned out badly. Little Carpenter did not listen to his son or the other Cherokee who opposed the treaty. He wanted to be at peace with the settlers. This made Dragging Canoe very angry with his father. Dragging Canoe spoke to the settlers about the land saying, "It is a dark and bloody ground." He warned them not to take it. I guess Henderson wasn't scared, but I think I would have been! For many years Dragging Canoe led the Cherokee in attacks against the settlers in hopes of taking back the land.

A Cherokee Beloved Woman Saves Settlers

One influential person in the conflict between the Cherokee and settlers was Nancy Ward. Nancy's Cherokee name was Nanye-hi, which means "one who goes about." She was part of the Wolf Clan. Nanye-hi married Tsu-la, known as Kingfisher, of the Deer Clan. Stories say that while he was fighting the Creek in battle, Nancy stood by his side and chewed bullets. That gave them sharper edges and made them more deadly. When Kingfisher died in battle, she picked up his rifle and kept fighting.

The Cherokee believe the Great Spirit spoke through Beloved Women. She attended council meetings and helped the tribe make decisions about going to war. Nanye-hi is most famous for helping save the lives of some Watauga settlers. In July 1776, the Cherokee were planning an attack on the Watauga settlement. Nanye-hi secretly warned one of their leaders, John Sevier. The settlers fled. Her actions prevented a lot of fighting. One of the people she saved was Lydia Bean. She took Lydia back to her home and nursed her back to health. She taught Nanye-hi a new way to sew that changed the way the Cherokee made clothing. She also gave the Beloved Woman two dairy cows and taught the Cherokee people how to raise them for milk. Stories say this helped the Cherokee during bad hunting seasons. Later in her life, Nancy became known as Granny Ward because she cared for so many children.

For years, Nanye-hi worked to keep the peace between settlers and the Cherokee.

title: The Watauga Association
text:
Once the Watauga settlement had grown to 70 families, the residents decided it was time to organize. Each family attended a planning meeting to discuss what the future held for them in this land. The Cherokee had agreed to a ten-year lease of "all the country on the waters of the Watauga." This area was outside of any of the 13 Colonies at the time. The settlers needed a government of their own.

This government was called the Watauga Compact. The settlers elected five magistrates to govern the area. These magistrates also served as judges in the settlement's court. They also chose a sheriff. The compact used the Virginia code of laws as the outline for their own system. They probably didn't need to write too many laws, because they adopted laws that Virginia wrote.

The Watauga Compact was blazing a trail of its own, much like Daniel Boone did. Only this trail wasn't through mountains and over lands. Instead, it was through the development of self-governing communities. It would provide an example for many when the time came to separate from England. In fact, the Watauga Compact and settlements joined the Revolutionary War. They took part in the stand for freedom for the British colonies.

In 1777, the region became part of North Carolina. This meant that the settlement was under the government of North Carolina. The Watauga Compact was dissolved as North Carolina took over the affairs of the colony.

title: The Washington District
text:
The British had not granted any colonists permission to settle at Watauga. This was one more thing that caused tension. Then the settlers heard about the people in Boston. They were being forced to quarter, or provide shelter and food to, British soldiers. By this time, the settlers were not happy with the British at all. They formed committees to protect themselves from the British. In honor of George Washington, they called themselves the Washington District. William Bean, John Sevier, James Robertson and several others were elected to be leaders of the District.

The British started working with the Cherokee, who were now led by Dragging Canoe. He and other warriors wanted to fight to get their land back, so they agreed to help the British. The British gave the Watauga settlers 20 days to leave the Washington District. The settlers refused. The Cherokee planned an attack. But Nancy Ward had sent word to warn the settlers. Once again, the Beloved Woman saved lives.

The leaders in the Washington District realized the Revolutionary War would soon spread to their territory. They feared for their safety. They sent letters to Virginia and North Carolina asking for protection. These letters became known as the Watauga Petitions. Virginia turned them down, but North Carolina agreed. The District was allowed to send delegates to a state constitutional convention. They sent four delegates to sign North Carolina's first state constitution. One of the signers was John Sevier.

title: Beyond the Appalachian Mountains
text:
The Cumberland Gap is a pass that goes through the Appalachian Mountains. It cuts through Tennessee, Kentucky and Virginia. American Indians used the pass for a long time before European settlers discovered it.

In 1750, Dr. Thomas Walker put together the first expedition to explore what he called the Cumberland Gap. What an exciting time this was! They were seeing and exploring where no white people had ever been. These men would open up a whole new world to settlers seeking new lands.

In 1763, something happened that had a serious effect on many people in the area. The British put the Proclamation of 1763 in effect. The tribes in Tennessee and nearby areas worried about the new settlers taking over their lands. This proclamation was designed to protect the rights of those tribes and the lands they claimed as their own. There had been much bloodshed and fighting between American Indians and the settlers. The proclamation was supposed to stop it. But the colonists didn't all see it that way. They thought that their rights were being threatened too, so the proclamation was often ignored as exploration took place. This was just a few years before the Revolutionary War. Many people were unhappy with British laws. For that reason, the settlers may not have taken the Proclamation very seriously.

In 1769, Daniel Boone explored the Cumberland Gap area. This opened up the gap as a means for settlers to come into Tennessee and the surrounding areas.

In 1772, the Watauga Association created the Watauga Compact. The settlers had agreed with the Cherokee to lease the land. Now it was the time to establish a government for the new settlement. They appointed five men, one of whom was John Sevier, to oversee the settlement. This small settlement did not claim to be out from under British rule. Yet they had their own set of laws and leaders that had nothing to do with the British Government. This was the first government west of the Appalachian mountains not created by American Indians.

In 1775, a land spectator, Richard Henderson, sent Daniel Boone to explore parts of the Appalachian Mountains. Mr. Henderson wanted to buy some of the Cherokee lands. Little Carpenter, the Cherokee chief, agreed to sell him land. The treaty they drew up became known as the Transylvania Treaty. When the Watauga group heard about this, they decide to petition to buy their land, too. This led to fighting. Some tribal members disagreed with selling their land to white settlers. One of them was Dragging Canoe, the son of Little Carpenter. During the Revolutionary War, the Cherokee decided to help the British in hopes of getting their land back.

Daniel Boone blazed a trail through portions of the Cumberland Gap which became known as the Wilderness Trail. Once the purchase of the land became final, Boone and a group of axemen cut their way through a portion of Cumberland Gap. The land was rough and narrow. Boone's team made the trail easier to travel on, although still not something that was traveled easily. In time, the trail would be widened to allow wagons to move through. Thousands of settlers would use the Wilderness Trail as a gateway to the west and new lands. It brought many people into Tennessee and the Appalachian Mountains.

title: Daniel Boone, Famous Frontiersman
text:
Daniel Boone was born in Pennsylvania.

He became friends with the Delaware tribe at a young age.

He was a great hunter and was the main provider of meat for his family as a teen.

His family moved to North Carolina in 1751.

He was such a good hunter that he was able to sell enough skins to buy 1,300 acres of land for his family.

During the French and Indian War, he was a blacksmith and supply wagon driver for the British.

He married a woman named Rebecca, and they had ten children.

He founded Boonesborough, Kentucky.

He loved to read and would take books with him when exploring.

He was 14 years old when he killed his first bear.

He was famous as a sharpshooter.

You might think that Daniel Boone was born to live in the wild. His work in exploring the Cumberland Gap and eastern Tennessee was critical to our state's history.

title: John Donelson and James Robertson
text:
John Donelson was selected to lead a group of settlers to the Cumberland River region. Several families and their supplies boarded the Adventure on December 22, 1779. More people joined them when they reached the mouth of the Cinch River. The group took four months to reach their new home.

The group suffered from hunger, cold weather and smallpox outbreaks. Once Donelson arrived at Big Salt Lick (now Nashville), he was the fifth signer of the Cumberland Compact. This created a basic constitution for the settlers. Donelson's family and slaves planted corn and cotton along the Stones River. Then the river flooded. Reports of attacks started to come in. He was able to harvest his corn, though the cotton was ruined. But some of the party were attacked on their journey home. Donelson moved his family away to a home that was safer and had more food.

Meanwhile, James Robertson was leading a group on land. When he arrived at a site along the Cumberland River known as French Lick, he created a settlement. They built cabins to help them survive the cold winter. They later built Fort Nashborough, on top of the bluff along the river. The settlers survived several attacks from the Chickamauga. Many of the settlers were killed, including James' two brothers and two sons.

George Washington appointed Robertson a brigadier general. He helped lead the settlement, which resulted in fewer attacks and the arrival of more settlers.

title: The Battle of the Bluffs
text:
Hey all, Jackson here! I am currently working on my part of the research report that Ms. Johnson has the class doing. My topic is the settlers who came over to Tennessee from England to form the Cumberland Settlements. Ms. Johnson spent some time with us going over life as a pioneer. Many of the settlers faced problems adjusting to a new life, even in Tennessee. Below is my report, I hope you enjoy it!

Jackson's Report:

Many colonists moved from England to settle in the northern part of America. While many went north to Virginia and Pennsylvania, some went south to Tennessee. They were pioneers by being first to settle in the new area.

There were a lot of challenges trying to live in the colonies. The land was still wilderness. They did not know how to hunt or live off the land. Many became sick or went hungry. Many of them did not even make it during the voyage from England. Diseases were the primary cause of death.

Colonists relied on help from the American Indians, who taught them how to hunt. They learned how to create clothing and supplies from the materials that were in nature around them. Sadly, many American Indians caught deadly European diseases. It caused a loss of huge numbers in the tribes. The settlers and the Cherokee enjoyed many years of friendship. They worked together, but there was tension between the two groups, as well. The new friends often paid the American Indians to help them survive. Tensions were also building between the colonists and Britain. Eventually, they would fight over control of the land. In England, many of the settlers could not own land because you had to be extremely wealthy. By moving to the colonies, there seemed to be a wealth of land to be had.

Many of the settlers that moved to Tennessee were in violation of the Proclamation of 1763. Issued by King George III, it forbade colonists from settling in American Indian territories. Even so, settlement leaders went to present a peace treaty to the Overhill Cherokee living in this region. They had earlier formed the Transylvania Company. They met with Cherokee leaders such as Dragging Canoe and exchanged goods for land. For many years, the settlers of Cumberland needed to be on high alert at all times.

The founders of the Cumberland settlements were James Robertson and John Donelson. They brought in 200 men, women and children. They faced many challenges along the way such as smallpox, frostbite and possible attacks from the Cherokee and other tribes.

In 1781, Dragging Canoe, a chief, led American Indians to attack Fort Nashborough when the men were away from the fort. Two Cherokee approached the fort and fired. Twenty men left the fort in pursuit. But it was a trap. Five of the settlers were killed, two were injured. They were cut off from the fort when they tried to return. The horses were able to return to the fort. As the attackers tried to capture them, they were distracted. This attack became known as Battle of the Bluffs.

Many histories of this battle say that Charlotte, James Robertson's wife, quickly released all the hunting dogs. The dogs chased the attackers, giving the men time to get back to safety inside the fort. The settlers lost 19 horses and five men. However, many primary source accounts of the battle have been discovered recently. Only one of them mentions dogs and none of them say that Charlotte let them loose. This makes historians wonder whether it actually happened like many books have written. Even though this event happened long ago, there can always be new things to learn!

Hey all! Alana here. I hope you learned a lot of information from Jackson's report. Life as a colonist was rough.

I am doing Part 2 of the report, as Ms. Johnson encourages us to look at things from as many perspectives on an issue or topic as possible. My section will focus on the American Indians lives affected by the colonial settlements.

Alana's Report

A large number of Cherokee lived in what is now known as Tennessee. They were a peaceful tribe and were led by Dragging Canoe. When white settlers came to the area, the Cherokee helped their new friends. They taught settlers how to hunt, fish and grow crops. But the settlers kept coming, needing more space for their settlements.

In 1775, Dragging Canoe met with several leaders of the settlers in a treaty council. The settlers wanted to take over the land that the Cherokee held in Tennessee and parts of Kentucky. The treaty asked for the Cherokee to give up their land. In exchange, the settlers gave goods and weapons, about $50,000 worth.

Dragging Canoe refused. He feared that agreeing would mean the end of the Cherokee, that the settlers would always want more. The other members of neighboring tribes were not able to resist some of the offers the settlers gave. Then the Revolutionary War began in 1775. Many of the tribes had mixed feelings on who to help during the struggle: the colonists or the British.

Dragging Canoe decided that this was their chance to keep the settlers from taking over their land. He and other tribes decided to fight back. This led to the Battle of the Bluffs in 1781. Dragging Canoe tried to take over a fort led by James Robertson. After that battle, there were more attacks on the people living in the Cumberland Settlements.

All the Cherokee wanted was to keep the land that they rightfully owned. Fights continued until the "Indian Removal Policy" was enacted in 1838. That is when the Cherokee Nation was forced to leave and move to lands past the Mississippi River.

title: Battle of Kings Mountain
text:
Jackson had been looking forward to visiting Kings Mountain National Military Park since Ms. Johnson told them about it. He knew that on some weekends, there were people who came to the park to reenact aspects of battles and answered historical questions. The last thing he wanted was to be transported into the middle of a war.

Currently, they were at the Kings Mountain National Military Park. Ms. Johnson wanted to give them an idea of what they would have experienced had they lived during that time. The park itself has many different artifacts and Ms. Johnson gave them a researcher scavenger hunt to find out as much history as possible while they were there.

Walking around the battlegrounds, Alana and Jackson came upon a man playing the role of a colonial soldier. Rather than wearing a military uniform, he had clothing a colonist might have been wearing. This was their chance to get some answers for their research.

"Uh, hello, sir," Jackson said.

"Good day. What brings you to these parts?"

"We are looking for some answers about the of the Battle of Kings Mountain. Were you there?" Alana asked.

"Oh yes, I was, miss. And what a terrible, dark day it was."

"Who are you supposed to be?" Jackson asked the soldier.

"I represent the colonists." Seeing the quizzical look on their faces, he went on to explain. "You see, Kings Mountain was not a battle between the British and the colonists, it was a battle between colonists. Those that were loyal to the British, or Loyalists, and those that wanted independence, the Patriots."

Alana then said, "We learned that the South was a stronghold for Loyalists."

"Yes, that is very true," the soldier explained. "Most of those living in the South were Loyalists. Many people were afraid they might lose their land if they fought against England. This kept them from joining the Patriots, those opposed to the unfair British taxes and laws. As the Patriots started to win battles, the loyalties to the British began to turn."

Alana and Jackson thanked the soldier for his time and went to find another soldier. This time they found a man dressed in historical clothing from 1780. The approached the soldier to ask him some questions.

"May we ask you who you represent?" asked Jackson.

"I am an Overmountain Man. We were not soldiers; we tried to stay out of the war. We are just Patriot settlers who farmed and hunted. We are frontiersmen from west of the Appalachian Mountains. We used knives and rifles for hunting and protecting ourselves. In fact, we were pretty handy with them. When one of the British commanders threatened to lay our country to waste, we decided to defend our land and families in the Battle of Kings Mountain. There was hardly a regular soldier around; it was just Patriots and Loyalists having it out. Militia against militia. We weren’t about to let the Loyalists win! This battle was a big turning point in the Revolutionary War. We demoralized the British, who never thought a bunch of people like the Overmountain Men could beat them. It was a huge victory for the Patriots! We fought the Battle of Kings Mountain using our rifles, unlike the battles fought elsewhere that used muskets.”

"What's the difference between muskets and rifles?" Alana wanted to know.

"That's a good question, commonly asked," answered the soldier. "Muskets, used by the Loyalists, were fast to load. But they were not very accurate. In fact, they could be fired up to three times a minute. Rifles were slower but more accurate. Rifles could hit a target 200 to 300 yards off. Muskets were usually only accurate to about 100 yards."

Alana and Jackson thanked him for his time. He tipped his hat to them and wandered off.

title: Cumberland Settlements
text:
Life on the frontier was not easy. People came to the area because they wanted land for their families. While most of the land belonged to the Cherokee, Creek and Chickasaw, white settlers believed they had rights to the land as well. Many settlers traveled over the Cumberland Gap, which is a rough and steep pathway through the lower section of the Appalachian Mountains where Tennessee, Kentucky and Virginia meet. There were no roads, so new paths had to be cleared. Most traveled by horseback or on foot. Wagons were used to carry supplies. When possible, men would lead women and children by boat because it was a faster, safer and easier way to travel.

As more people settled on the frontier, trading businesses began to boom. Trade goods were moved down the Cumberland, Tennessee and Ohio rivers. After selling their products, merchants returned home on the Natchez Trace, a path that linked the Cumberland, Tennessee and Mississippi rivers. Merchants would sell things like corn, whiskey, tobacco and furs.

When families found a location they liked, they would clear the land of trees to make room for cabins and crops. The trees were then used to build log cabins. Spaces between the logs were filled in with mud or clay, called chinking. During the summer months, settlers would knock out the mud to allow for more airflow into the cabin.

Men and women lived very different lives. Men spent their time farming and hunting for food, while women took care of the home. Women spent many hours preparing food, sewing clothing and making soap. Music was an important form of entertainment for those living on the frontier. They sang hymns, played the fiddle and danced. Settlers also enjoyed telling tall tales. Education was important on the frontier as well, but it took time to build schools. Most children were taught to read and write at home before formal schools were opened.

title: This Week's Question
text: You've heard about the early leaders of the lost state of Franklin and the Territory South of the River Ohio. Pick one person and write three to five phrases that could have been placed on the person's gravestone to explain why the person was important.

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine that you are a settler in the Southwest Territory. Write a letter to a cousin in Massachusetts. Describe living in the territory when it became the 16th state. Describe the territory and tell how you and your neighbors feel about now living in the new state of Tennessee.

title: Taking It One Step at a Time
text:
Jackson and Alana discovered that there are several steps for a territory to become a state:

Congress passes an enabling act, or a law, stating what the area has to do before writing a constitution. The act usually includes having a certain number of people as well. The Territory South of the River Ohio had to have 60,000 residents. The act also usually requires proof that most of the people want to become a state.

The territory writes a constitution. Then they send it to Congress for approval.

Congress debates the constitution and either approves it or sends it back for changes. Importantly, it has to abide by the U.S. Constitution's laws.

If it is approved, Congress tells the president to issue a proclamation approving the new state's entry into the United States.

title: It Took Some Time to Get There
text:
1750: Dr. Thomas Walker led Virginians to the Cumberland River.

1754: The French and Indian War began between British and French settlers.

1763: The French and Indian War ended. The French gave lands east of the Mississippi River to Britain.

1768: The Iroquois gave lands of modern Tennessee to the British.

1769: William Bean became the first permanent white settler in the area.

1772: The Watauga Association formed to organize the area.

1775: The American Revolutionary War began.

1779: Jonesboro became the first chartered town in the area.

1784: The state of Franklin was formed from North Carolina lands.

1789: North Carolina gave land back to the U.S.

1796: Tennessee becomes the 16th state.

title: Working Around the Obstacles
text:
After Franklin failed to become a new state, the U.S. Constitution laid down the process for a new state to join the Union. Even so, the path to statehood is often long and tough. Most territories have to overcome obstacles to become a state. Let’s learn about the challenges that the Southwest Territory faced to become the state of Tennessee.

William Blount was a delegate to the Constitutional Convention in 1787. At this historic event, he met George Washington. Washington, of course, would go on to become president in 1789. He knew Blount and appointed him as governor of the Southwest Territory. Blount also took on another role: Superintendent of Indian Affairs. This was fitting in a way since conflicts between local tribes and settlers had not stopped. Treaties had not ended the fighting.

Blount’s first concern regarding the native people was to protect the settlers from their attacks. Should the federal government send the Army to repel these attacks? Many in the Southwest Territory believed so. Blount himself owned large areas of land in the territory and wanted them protected. (He probably wasn't too interested in tribes’ claims to the land.) Decision-makers in Washington weren’t interested in sending the Army to help those distant settlements.

Blount decided that they needed help. The territory would have to become a state to be treated fairly back east. In 1795, the population climbed above 60,000, making the Southwest Territory able to become a state. Blount wanted statehood right away, but Congress was in no hurry. The Federalist Party controlled Congress, and they didn’t think western settlers would vote for them.

Blount wouldn’t wait. He brought officials together to draft a state constitution quickly. Once done, Blount declared that the Southwest Territory was gone. The state government of Tennessee was open for business. Since things had come so far, Congress saw fit to admit Tennessee to the Union on June 1, 1796. The Federalists didn’t manage to stop this.

Tennessee became a state in part because William Blount was stubborn and determined. By doing so, he made history in our state and our nation.

title: Where Did It Go?
text:
“Fifty nifty United States, from 13 original colonies,” warbled Jackson, Alana and their class.

“Excellent job,” Ms. Johnson said. “You'll soon be able to recite all 50 states! Okay, we have a few minutes until lunchtime; keep practicing in your study groups until then. Jackson, Alana, I could definitely hear you. You sounded fantastic.”

“Thank you,” Alana answered. “I think it's interesting to know about all the states.”

“Did you know that there were almost 51 states?” Ms. Johnson asked.

“Fifty-one? I've never heard of that,” Jackson said. “What happened to the extra one?”

“Well,” Ms. Johnson said, “it was quite a while before the U.S. admitted all 50, but the area that is Tennessee now was once part of the lost state of Franklin.”

“Franklin?” Alana asked. “Where was it?”

“In the 1780’s, we had just ended the American Revolution and there was a lot of land that had the potential to become part of the new United States. North Carolina ceded, or gave, some land between the Allegheny Mountains and the Mississippi River to the U.S. settlers there. They worried that Congress might sell the land to Spain or France to pay war debts. Then, North Carolina retracted, or took back, the land. But Washington, Sullivan and Green counties petitioned the U.S. for admission as a new state called Frankland. When rejection looked likely, the settlers even changed the name to Franklin. They hoped it would get Benjamin Franklin's attention.”

“What happened after that?” Jackson asked.

“At the time, we didn't have the U.S. Constitution yet. We had the Articles of Confederation. States had quite a bit of individual power under the Articles, and that resulted in lots of differences across the nation. More than half of the states approved of Franklin becoming a state. But the Articles said that it took two-thirds to approve a new state, and not that many voted yes. Seven voted yes, but nine were needed. So, on Aug. 23, 1784, those counties declared their independence. They wrote their own constitution and spent four years going it alone. They chose John Sevier, a Revolutionary War hero, as the governor. They also negotiated treaties with the tribes in the area.”

“But we don't have a Franklin state,” Alana said. “What happened to it?”

Ms. Johnson smiled. “Franklin didn't have a strong enough economy to pay for everything they needed. The Cherokee, Chickamauga and Chickasaw in the area resisted settlement in their homeland. The federal government was trying to make treaties with the Muskogee and Cherokee, but there were so many agreements and separate deals that Franklin couldn’t keep up with everything. Franklin decided to join North Carolina again.”

“Wow! That's cool,” Jackson said. “I wonder how things would be different if Franklin did become a state.”

“Who can say?” Ms. Johnson replied. “But the circumstances did cause the addition of a clause in the new Constitution about how states could join the Union. Now, to create a new state from an existing one, the first state and Congress have to agree.”
“And Franklin later became part of Tennessee, right?” Alana asked. “So things worked out, after all.”

title: The Southwest Territory
text:
In 1789, North Carolina became the 12th state to approve the Constitution. The western lands were once again offered to Congress. Congress accepted the land. It became known as Territory South of the Ohio River, or the Southwest Territory. The Northwest Ordinance was a law made to give territories a way to become states. A territory could apply for statehood once they had 60,000 people.

Look at the map. Find the Southwest Territory. Do you recognize any of the states? Name as many states as you can.

Treaty of Holston

On July 2, 1791, the Cherokee Nation and the U.S. government signed the Treaty of Holston. It was negotiated and signed by William Blount, the Southwest Territory governor. The treaty said that the U.S. government would protect the Cherokee. The Cherokee were also promised $1,000 a year. In return, they would allow white settlers to stay in the Territory. All prisoners of war were returned, and they agreed to land boundaries.

From Territory to Statehood

In 1795, the population was counted. It showed that there were enough people in the Southwest Territory to apply for statehood. The Southwest Territory was the first territory to ask the government to become a state. On June 1, 1796, the Southwest Territory was admitted to the Union. Tennessee became the 16th state!

William Blount

William Blount fought during the American Revolution. He was a member of the Continental Congress. He signed the Constitution. After all this, Blount decided he wanted to move west. In 1790, George Washington appointed William Blount as governor of the Southwest Territory. When Tennessee became part of the Union in 1796, Blount helped to write the Tennessee Constitution. John Sevier became the state's first governor, and Blount served as a senator. He served two more years in the Tennessee state government after being dismissed from the U.S. Senate. Blount County is named after him. Blount's wife, Mary Grainger Blount, became the only woman to have a county named after her: Grainger County.

Territorial Capitols

Rocky Mount, built in 1770, was the home of William Cobb. It served as the first capitol of the Southwest Territory. William Blount, governor of the Southwest Territory, wrote "... I arrived in this country and was received with every mark of intention and gladness as I could have wished. I am well accommodated with a room with glass windows and a fireplace ..." Other famous people who stayed at Rocky Mount were Daniel Boone, John Sevier and Andrew Jackson. Blount Mansion, built between 1792 and 1796, replaced Rocky Mount as the territorial capitol of Tennessee.

The Jackson Purchase

If it had not been for Andrew Jackson, Tennessee's western border would not be where it is today! In 1818, Jackson and Isaac Shelby, the first governor of Kentucky, were sent west to buy some land from the Chickasaw tribe. How much land? Oh, only all of the land between the Tennessee and Mississippi rivers! This land deal increased the size of Tennessee by about one-third. They convinced the tribe to give them the land by threatening and bribing them! The official name of the deal was the Chickasaw Cession. For years after, most folks called it Jackson's Purchase. Look at a map and guess which grand division of Tennessee would not exist if not for the Jackson Purchase.

title: Country, Territory or State?
text:
You may have heard of the Northwest Ordinance. This law created the Northwest Territory. It’s talked about more often than the Southwest Territory. It included land in six current states, rather than just one, so it gets more attention.

Most of the laws of the Northwest Ordinance also applied to the Southwest Territory. A territory could elect the lower house of their assembly (legislative branch) when it had at least 5,000 residents. The upper house was chosen by the president; members were suggested by the territory. A territory could apply for statehood when the population reached 60,000.

The capital of the Southwest Territory was Knoxville. Here, Governor Blount and Judges John McNairy, David Campbell and Joseph Anderson were in charge. The first election for the assembly took place in 1793. The territorial government was replaced with the state government in 1796. John Sevier was the first governor of Tennessee. Knoxville was still the capital. Nashville became our state capital later in 1843.

title: Commonwealths and Territories and States, Oh My!
text:
“Hey, Jackson,” Alana said. “I thought what Ms. Johnson told us about Franklin was pretty interesting, didn't you?”

“Yeah,” he said. “But I'd still like to know more about how we get new states and stuff like that.”

“So, the United States has two commonwealths that aren't states: Puerto Rico and Northern Mariana Islands,” Jackson said.

“And American Samoa, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands are territories,” Alana added.

“Yes,” the librarian said. “And there are several U.S. possessions, as well. People who live in the commonwealths are citizens, but they don't pay federal taxes, and they only have a nonvoting representative in Congress. Those in territories are U.S. nationals. They can live and work anywhere in the U.S., but they aren't citizens, and they cannot vote in elections.”

“Whew!” Alana said. “That's a lot of information to remember!”

“We'd better get back to class,” Jackson said. “I can't wait to tell Ms. Johnson what we learned!”

title: The History of Tennessee Government
text:
The first constitution of Tenessee was not approved by the people of the state but by the U.S. Congress. This was in 1796.

In 1835, the second constitution was approved by voters. At the time, there were efforts to abolish slavery, but those efforts were not successful. It said only white men could vote; not even free black men could vote. It also created the state's Supreme Court.

The third constitution came after the Civil War. A requirement to rejoin the Union was that it had to ban slavery. Many parts of it were copied from previous versions. It is the same that we use today, with some minor changes made in 1953. Unlike other states, Tennessee's constitution requires four constitutional officers. They are the governor, secretary of state, state treasurer and comptroller. These officers, other than the governor, are elected by the General Assembly, not by the voters. They all serve four-year terms. The governor can only serve two terms.

The governor is the chief executive of the state. They make decisions about running the state and enforce the laws. The lieutenant governor assists and becomes governor if something happens to the governor.

The secretary of state is in charge of elections. They help businesses start. The secretary is also responsible for keeping a register of official acts. The Tennessee Blue Book is one of the publications for which they are responsible. The Blue Book is a detailed book that describes how the state government runs.

The state treasurer manages all the state investments, where the tax money is kept. They receive funds and pay bills for the state. They also make sure all the state employees receive benefits for their work.

The state comptroller makes sure all the funds of the state are correctly spent and kept track of. They make sure tax dollars are not wasted.

title: Fifth Grade Branches Out
text:
Alana rushes into the classroom, taking her seat next to Jackson mere seconds before the bell rings.

"You know," Alana whispers to Jackson, "I'm still trying to imagine having the State of Franklin; 51 states just seems strange."

"Fifty is a nice even number," Jackson says. "It's pretty amazing that the United States can have 50 states that all work together, isn't it? Imagine what a disaster it would be if we didn't have a government."

Before Alana can respond, Ms. Johnson steps to the front of the room, calling for the class's attention.

"Class, first some unfortunate but important news. Mr. Martinez isn't coming in today. His daughter was sick this morning. The school has been unable to find a substitute, so today's music class has been canceled."

The students, almost collectively, let out a disappointed groan.

"I apologize for the trouble; I know how you all love music," Ms. Johnson continues. "Fortunately, I have two bits of good news. First, Mrs. Green, our principal, has agreed to take you out for an extra recess during your music block, and—"

This time, the class interrupts Ms. Johnson with a cheer.

"This got me thinking about the jobs at our school. I think it will help me explain the various roles of our state's government. To begin, let's construct a list of the essential jobs at our school."

Students begin to call out jobs, while Ms. Johnson writes them on the board.

"Principal, Mrs. Green!"

"Vice Principal!"

"Classroom teacher!"

"Cook!"

"Our custodian, Mr. Williams! ... Librarian! ... Aide! ... Music teacher! ... Art teacher! ... Gym teacher ..."

"And don't forget Mrs. Romero, our secretary!"

"Thanks, class. That's a great list! Our school also has a parent-teacher organization, a student council and an activities club. There are a lot of different jobs in our school. Now, imagine what our school would be like without these jobs."

"Maybe we'd get another 'extra' recess," jokes Alana, giggling.

Jackson raises his hand, addressing the question, "Seriously, I can't imagine coming to school without a teacher. Who would teach us?"

Alana adds, "Without Mr. Williams, the custodian, our school would be dirty."

Elise continues, "Without Mr. Davis, the cook, there would be nothing for us to eat at lunch."

"That's right, class. All the people in our school work together to do different jobs. When they do their jobs, the school runs as it is supposed to. If they can't do their jobs, things don't go smoothly. Luckily for us, Mrs. Green was available this afternoon, but if she wasn't, what would we do?

"Tennessee's state government is like that. Three separate branches of government cooperate to make sure Tennessee is a happy, productive place. The first branch is the legislative branch, which makes the laws. The second group is the executive branch, which enforces the laws. The third branch is the judicial branch, which interprets laws. Next week, we'll have group reports on the three branches of government. I'd also like someone to research the governor. And, as always, make sure to dress the part!"

"Ms. Johnson, why are there are three branches of government?" asks Alana.

"Excellent question, Alana. Remember the idea of checks and balances? It makes it so that one branch is no more powerful than the other."

title: Tennessee's Three Branches of Government
text:
"Chief Justice Alana, I'm ready," jokes Jackson, adjusting his tie. "I'm glad I got this suit for my cousin's wedding."

"Me too, Senator Jackson," says Alana. "But I feel silly in these robes."

After a week of research, Ms. Johnson's class is ready to present its findings on the governor and three branches of Tennessee government. Jackson wears the sharp blue suit of a senator, while Alana wears the robes of a Tennessee judge.

Ms. Johnson walks to the front of the room.

"Wow! Class, you really look the part," Ms. Johnson says, admiring her students dressed in suits, robes and other costumes. "I'd like the executive branch to go first."

Unlike the legislative and judicial branches, however, not all are dressed in suits or robes. A few students are wearing casual attire; one is wearing a lab coat. Jackson spots a police and firefighter uniform. Alana notes one student is dressed as a corrections officer!

"I didn't know the executive branch had so many different jobs," Jackson whispers to Alana.

Marcus, the student in the lab coat, explains, "The executive branch is responsible for day-to-day operation of the state. It carries out new laws when they are passed. It does this through departments. I work for the Department of Mental Health; I'm a psychiatrist. There are also departments for education, tourism, transportation and a bunch of others. We counted 22 departments in all! Each makes sure that people follow the rules and regulations. The Department of Education, for example, helps teachers and makes sure that they do a good job. It also makes decisions about what is taught in schools. The Department of Health tries to help keep people from getting sick and makes sure doctors take care of patients.

"Tennessee's executive branch is run by the governor. The lieutenant governor is second-in-command of the executive branch.

"We think the executive branch is like the teachers in our school. Each classroom is like a department. We also have a department for custodial services, run by our custodian, Mr. Williams. The department of transportation would be for the bus drivers. Our cook, Mr. Davis, would run the department of food services."

Elise, wearing a navy suit, is up next to discuss the role of governor. Elise explains, "The governor is in charge of the executive branch. The governor's job is to come up with a budget for the state. They sign bills from the General Assembly and appoint people to fill positions. I have a lieutenant governor who helps me. The governor has to have lived in Tennessee for at least seven years and be at least 30 years old. Governors are elected to four-year terms. They can be re-elected once, then have to step down for at least one term.

"The governor is a lot like our principal, Mrs. Green. She makes decisions about the school and has to manage a lot of different people and projects."

Alana speaks on behalf of the judicial branch. She is dressed in a long, black robe. "I'm Chief Justice Alana. The judicial branch is made up of courts. They make decisions about laws passed by the General Assembly. The Supreme Court can judge whether state laws agree with the state or U.S. Constitutions. It also decides if people have broken the law. If they have, it decides the penalty. Sometimes, people have lawyers argue cases for them in court. Through appeals, cases can be tried in higher courts. The highest court in Tennessee is the state Supreme Court, which has five justices.

"Schools aren't exactly the same as a government, with separate branches. In our case, the judicial branch is our school's principal, Mrs. Green. Mrs. Green helps decide what to do if someone breaks the school rules. Or last week, since we were supposed to have music, she thought it was fair we have an extra recess."

The legislative branch is the final group. Senator Jackson speaks on their behalf, "The legislative branch is made up of the Tennessee General Assembly. There are two houses in the General Assembly: the Senate, with 33 members, and the House of Representatives, with 99. State senators serve four-year terms. Members of the house serve for two years."

"Our job is to make bills. Bills are like ideas for laws. We talk about bills, make committees to look at them, and sometimes change them. Then we vote on them. If a bill passes the Senate and the House, it goes to the governor to sign. He can also veto it, which is his way of saying that he doesn't agree with it. Even if he vetoes it, the General Assembly can vote on it again to override his veto.

"The legislative branch is like student council, which tries to make changes to the school. But the principal needs to approve the changes."

"Excellent work, class!" Ms. Johnson exclaims. "As a member of our school's executive branch, I need to remind you of the rules. It's time to get ready for lunch!"

title: African Americans in Government
text:
After the Civil War, African Americans made quick political progress. During the 1870s and '80s, 14 African Americans won state elections. They became members of the Tennessee General Assembly. They had been slaves, teachers and farmers. Others won local and national elections. Sadly, Jim Crow laws erased this progress. Meanwhile, many former slaves had no options but to work in poverty as sharecroppers. Until the 1960s, these laws that took rights from African Americans stayed in place. This was especially true in the South. Many people thought this was unfair. From 1888 to 1964, no African Americans served in the General Assembly.

In the 1950s and '60s, Archie Walter Willis Jr. was a respected lawyer. He worked for the NAACP. He tried to make sure everyone could go to good schools. In 1964, he was elected to the state legislature. Keeble, Willis and others helped lead the way to a fairer life in Tennessee. Today, about 13 percent of the General Assembly is African American.

title: Winfield Scott: Friend or Foe to the Tribes?
text:
Winfield Scott was a general in the U.S. Army who wrote the first bylaws of the military and set standards for professionalism in the armed forces. He served during the War of 1812, the Mexican-American War and the Civil War. He hoped to become president, but never succeeded.

In 1832, Scott was called to become Commander of the Federal Troops at the Cherokee Nation. He would replace his good friend, John Wool, who did not support the removal of the Cherokee from their land. Scott quickly got to work, dividing the Cherokee Nation into three sections and setting up forts where the people would live until they could be moved to the Indian Territory west of the Mississippi. Many people died in these forts due to sickness.

That summer, Scott prepared the first group to leave Georgia for the trip. The people asked him as their “warden,” or jailer, to please let them leave later in the year after the worst heat had passed. He agreed and stood up to backlash from President Jackson and many of the military forces. He pleaded with the Cherokee, in "the address of a warrior to warriors," to comply with the removal. Otherwise, he would have no choice but to shed blood.

Scott gave an order to his men to treat the Cherokee with care and if any were sick to let a relative stay with them and give them food and supplies for recovery. He even allowed the very sick and elderly to ride horses for part of the way. Scott also wrote a letter to the Cherokee saying that if they did not fight, he would ensure they were treated well along the travel to their “new homes.”

When they left on October 1, he planned to go with them the entire route, but he was called to return to Washington, DC.

What do you think? Was Scott a friend to the Cherokee? Or was what he did wrong? Did he have a choice, or was there no alternative? Discuss both sides in a small group.

title: Tennessee and the War of 1812
text:
Jackson and Alana are busy reading for their test ...

After selling the Louisiana Territory to the United States, France was at war with Great Britain. The U.S. did business with both countries but stayed out of their war. At first, Great Britain and France were OK with that plan. But soon they began to question whose side we were on. Great Britain and France sometimes stopped U.S. cargo ships on the Atlantic Ocean, searching the cargo areas to make sure we weren’t supplying anyone with weapons. Staying out of the war was getting harder.

President Jefferson decided to do something to end the bullying of our ships. He believed the United States should stop sending supplies to Europe. That would teach them a lesson! So Congress passed the Embargo Act of 1807. The law said that no goods could be shipped to any foreign port. The United States hoped that France and Great Britain would be devastated without our supplies. Unfortunately the Embargo Act backfired. The two nations got along just fine without U.S. goods. When the deliveries stopped, ships full of rotting food sat in American harbors. Americans were unhappy, and President Jefferson repealed (cancelled) the Embargo Act. U.S. ships began sailing again, but soon they were again being treated badly. British ships captured U.S. sailors and forced them to fight for the British Navy. This practice was called impressment.

Our nation was in poor shape. The Embargo Act had caused people to lose a lot of money. People thought that problems with American Indians were caused by the British. Many Americans wanted another war against Great Britain.

James Madison was the Secretary of State. A group of Congressmen called the War Hawks convinced Madison to declare war. Congress agreed, and in June 1812 the United States was again at war with Great Britain.

Jackson stopped reading. "Wow. What a mess. Now, for this test. We're supposed to know about Tennessee's involvement in the war. But if it was mostly about bad behavior on boats, what did Tennessee have to do with it?"

"I know!" said Alana. "Tennesseans wanted to help their countrymen in the war. When the war started, Governor Willie Blount called for volunteers. He got more than 3,500! Tennessee has been called the 'Volunteer State' ever since."

Jackson said, "I know that Andrew Jackson was major general of the Tennessee militia. His early actions didn't make much of a difference. But Jackson wanted glory. He was about to get his chance."

The Creek War

"Even before the War of 1812 started, tribes like the Creek and the Shawnee weren't happy about problems with white settlers."

"Like Tecumseh!" cried Alana. "He was an amazing Shawnee chief. He fought to take back land from settlers. In 1811, he told the Creek they should fight to protect their way of life. The Creek had different opinions. Some wanted to join Tecumseh. Others wanted to be more 'civilized'. They thought that if you can't beat 'em, join 'em. They thought that a war with settlers was hopeless."

"So they couldn't agree?"

"No. The conflict turned into civil war, known as the Creek War," continued Alana. "Some of the Creek started fighting with the British against Americans. In this way, the Creek War became part of the War of 1812."

Jackson went on, "And some white settlements got caught in the war. That's where the Tennessee volunteers made a real difference. General Jackson was called to fight the Creek and defend the settlements. After that, he marched to Pensacola, Florida, to push the British out."

Jackson and the Tennessee Volunteers

Alana said, "Now, General Jackson had about 2,500 volunteer soldiers behind him. This outnumbered just about any Creek group he encountered on his way south. Since the Creek had been fighting, they didn't have the strength to beat back Jackson's force."

"Eventually, Jackson and his men met the Creek at Horseshoe Bend. Over 800 Creek warriors died, the last of the tribe's strength. Later, Jackson and Creek chiefs signed the treaty of Fort Jackson in August 1814. The Creek gave up a great deal of land in Alabama."

Jackson asked, "Did Jackson and the volunteers make it to Pensacola?"

"Yes, and they won against the British," replied Alana. "The War of 1812 ended on Christmas Eve, 1814. Communication was slow in those days, and word of the end of the war didn't reach Jackson in New Orleans. There, in early January 1815, he led an army of over 4,000 men. Some were regular U.S. soldiers, but others were frontiersmen from southern states, former slaves from Haiti and even pirates. They fought against a British army of almost 8,000. When the Battle of New Orleans was over, 2,000 British soldiers had been killed, while the United States lost only 13 men.

"After that string of victories, Jackson was a national hero. The country was encouraged."

"So that explains how he found the popularity to be elected U.S. president," concluded Jackson.

“And,” continued Alana, “the Treaty of Ghent was signed in February 1815, officially ending the war. What did Americans gain from the War of 1812? Something very important: a reputation as a world power.

title: Principal Chief John Ross (1790–1866)
text:
When times get tough, people often look to courageous leaders to make life better. For many years, the Cherokee Nation could count on Principal Chief John Ross to stand up for their rights.

John was only one-eighth Cherokee, but he was raised living in both Cherokee and American cultures. At home, he was taught English and the Cherokee language, and he also had a Cherokee name, Guwisguwi. Because of his mixed heritage and fluency in two languages, he was able to represent the Cherokee Nation before the United States government. His people prepared him to be a leader.

Starting in 1816, John fought for the rights of the Cherokee in Washington. He resisted those who wanted to take Cherokee lands. Some wanted the Cherokee to move west of the Mississippi River, or give up their own government and become U.S. citizens. John refused these plans to take advantage of his people.

In 1828, John Ross was elected as Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation. In this position, he took the affairs of the nation to the Supreme Court. Never before had American Indian rights been brought to this court, and the Cherokee won two cases. This was meant to preserve the Cherokees’ right to their own government and land. President Jackson and Congress ignored these rulings and forced the Cherokee to move. As the nation was to be removed, John wrote, “We are deprived of membership in the human family!”

John Ross suffered with his people on the Trail of Tears and lost his wife, Quatie, on the brutal journey. John led his people as they rebuilt their lives in Oklahoma, through the Civil War, until his death in 1866.

title: Dangers on the Trail
text:
By the 1830s, the United States had grown to twenty-four states. The population was twelve million people. Land was in demand to grow cotton. There were more than 125,000 American Indians living in the Southeastern United States. The European settlers felt they had rights to all the land. From the early days of the colonies, white settlers and American Indians had conflicts that often ended in violence or death. White Americans felt that the American Indians needed to be more civilized (or more European). The tribes of the Southeast became known as the “Five Civilized Tribes.” They tried hard to do all that the white Americans expected. Many learned to speak, read and write English, became Christians and adopted European ideas.

Conflicts continued and the government went ahead with the Indian Removal Act. This law forced the tribes to move to Indian Territory in present-day Oklahoma. They had to leave almost everything behind.

The Choctaw people saw that if they stayed on their land, they would continue to be attacked and harassed. Their homes were set on fire, their animals were set free. The Choctaw tribe chose to go to the new land without a fight. Over three winters from 1831–1833, 15,000 people had to walk across states to their new land. They suffered terribly from the Great Blizzard of 1831. They had little shelter and few supplies to deal with the cold and snow. Then, there was a cholera outbreak in 1833. This is an infection people can get from dirty water. If you don't have clean water to drink, it can make you very sick. Cholera spreads quickly and many American Indians got it. Over 2,500 Choctaw people died.

The Cherokee people decided to stand up to the government. Senators Harry Clay and Daniel Webster agreed that the Indians shouldn’t be forced to move. Missionary Samuel Worcester took their case to court. Two court cases in 1831 and 1832 were heard by the Supreme Court. The first case was won by Georgia. But in the second case, the court ruled that the Cherokee Nation was its own nation. They couldn’t be forced to move by the United States government. President Andrew Jackson went against the decision and ordered the U.S. Army to force the removal of the tribe from the land.

In 1835, a small group of Cherokee called the Old Settlers signed the Treaty of Echota. This treaty stated that the Cherokee gave up all lands east of the Mississippi River. In exchange they would receive money, animals, land and tools. Most of the Cherokee people didn’t agree with the Echota Treaty. President Jackson still used it as a reason to make all the remaining Cherokee move to Oklahoma.

The Cherokee called this long, forced march the Nunahi-Duna-Dlo-Hilu-I, which means the Trail of Crying (or Tears). Nearly 16,000 people were forced into camps to wait for travel. When the time came to head west, some people went on boats through a long series of rivers. Others walked nearly 1,000 miles from Tennessee to Oklahoma. The trip took much longer than they hoped and many people died. Some died of diseases like cholera, which were hard to avoid under the terrible conditions. Some died of hunger. They did not have much time to hunt and gather food like they usually did. They were forced to keep moving along and so many starved to death. There were also deaths from exposure. This means the weather affected them in awful ways. Some froze in the cold winters and others became overheated and dehydrated in the summer. There were even wild animal attacks. The American Indians had few ways to protect themselves. As many as 4,000 Cherokee people died during the march.

The National Park Service has created a Trail of Tears National Historic Trail with sites in nine states. This helps people remember the journey faced by the Cherokee, Choctaw and other tribes in the 1830s. Today, people walk on parts of this trail to honor the people on the Trail of Tears, but they cannot come close to experiencing the terrible hardships faced by the American Indians.

title: The Cherokee Phoenix
text:
This photo shows an excerpt from an 1828 copy of the Cherokee newspaper, the "Cherokee Phoenix." Notice that there are two languages printed in this newspaper: English and Cherokee. This issue has the results of a census taken in the Cherokee Nation.

Why take a census of the tribe? The threat of being removed from their homes loomed large. The tribe hoped that a census would convince U.S. officials that they were "civilized." Then, they might allowed to stay and live peacefully with settlers.

1. In addition to counting the members of the tribe, the census lists other things: "There are in this District, 211 spinning wheels, one grist mill, one blacksmith shop, 308 ploughs, fifty-three looms, 323 sheep ..." How might this information convince others that the tribe was "civilized"?

2. Why do you think the Phoenix was printed in two languages?

3. Another article has a message from the U.S. government to the Cherokee Nation. Read this excerpt:

"Other Governments would have triumphed in your downfall, and held you down by cruelty and oppression. Such has not been the conduct of the United States. She has set an example which the whole civilized world ought to feel proud to follow. It has been the constant study and exertion of the Government to relieve you from your unfortunate condition."

Does this claim agree with what you've read and learned this week? Explain why or why not.

Use a separate piece of paper for your answers.

title: Davy Crockett
text:
David Crockett was a real American hero. Born in eastern Tennessee, Crockett learned to hunt at a young age. At 13, he lived alone in the wilderness for three years! David did not learn how to read until he was 18 years old. He spent his adult life in armed service and politics. Crockett won election to the Tennessee General Assembly in 1821. Three years later, he was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives. Crockett served three terms. After a political defeat, he moved to Texas. He fought for Texas' independence. Crockett lost his life at the Alamo.

Over the years, stories of Davy Crockett caught the American imagination. One account of Davy said he jumped across the Ohio River. Another story told how he hunted wildcats with his bare hands. Ultimately, David Crockett was an impressive historical figure. Davy Crockett was a folk superhero, an exaggerated version of David.

title: James Polk's Manifest Destiny
text:
The United States grew in size during the 1800s. President James Polk, who served from 1845 until 1849, believed in Manifest Destiny. Manifest Destiny was the belief the United States was destined to grow until it reached the west coast. They thought the high cost of growth in dollars and lives lost in fights was worth it. They argued it would be spreading culture, freedom and prosperity.

Polk helped the U.S. grow. He worked with the British to create the Territory of Oregon in 1848. This would become the northwestern states.

After defeating Mexico in the Mexican-American War, the U.S. grew yet again. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo was signed in 1848. This gave the U.S. much of the West, including Texas and California. The U.S. also gained several western states. The U.S. gave Mexico $15 million in return.

The addition of California in 1850 achieved the goals of those who believed in Manifest Destiny. With California and Oregon, the U.S. spanned both coasts.

title: Their Words Live On!
text:
Below, you will find quotes from Sam Houston and David Crockett. Read each quote and write the meaning of the quote in your own words. On a separate piece of paper, draw a picture to illustrate the quote. Next, compare the quotes and answer question 3.
