title: The Jackson Purchase
text:
For thousands of years, American Indians were the only people who lived in what we call Tennessee. In the 1700s, the Cherokee and the Chickasaw were the two major tribes here. The Cherokee lived in villages in East and Middle Tennessee. The Chickasaw lived along the rivers of West Tennessee. They did not stay in one place long enough to build homes or plant their own food. They set up temporary camps and then packed up and moved to wherever the hunting was best.

Things changed when explorers and settlers from Europe got here. By the late 1700s, settlers began moving into Tennessee. More and more people came, taking over land that once was home to the American Indians. The settlements kept growing. Soon the settlers decided they wanted their own state.

The Chickasaw still claimed a large amount of land in West Tennessee. This was hunting grounds for the tribe. They had no villages in the area. The Cherokee were coming closer and closer to Chickasaw land all the time. By this time, Levi Colbert and his brothers had taken over leadership of the tribe. They were bribed by Andrew Jackson and John Selby to sell their 10,700 square miles. In return, they would receive $300,000, with payments each year for 20 years. The Chickasaw people saw that they no longer had to protect their land.

Now that the land was available, white settlers rushed in. Within six years, the area had 16 counties. Memphis was one of the cities that was settled.

title: Let's Write
text: Do you think the Chickasaw should have sold the land commonly called "The Jackson Purchase" to the U.S.? Why or why not? If not, what would have been a fair exchange?

title: Tennessee's Growing Pains
text:
Shortly before the bell rings, students file into the classroom, looking forward to another adventure. Ms. Johnson bounds to the front of the room. She has a blue map of something that sort of looks like Tennessee, only smaller. She hangs it on the board. Jackson guesses that it's about 25-percent smaller than the Tennessee map the class is used to seeing.

"Class, can anyone tell me what this is?"

Alana raises her hand, "That's a map of Tennessee, but the western quarter of the state is missing!" she exclaims.

"That's correct, Alana." says Ms. Johnson, adding the missing quarter of the map, colored red. She asks her students if they know what this quarter represents.

"Yes, Jackson?" says Ms. Johnson, trying to stifle a laugh.

"That's the Jackson Purchase!" he responds. The class laughs.

"Yes, Jackson, it is the Jackson Purchase. The Jackson Purchase had nothing to do with our very own Jackson. It was Andrew Jackson who lived in the 1800s -- and in spite of what you may think, I never had him as a student."

Ms. Johnson explains that the United States grew through a series of treaties with American Indians. In 1816, Andrew Jackson and Isaac Shelby began negotiating with the Chickasaw people to acquire land. In 1818, the Chickasaw agreed to give about 8,000 square miles to the United States. Some sources put the number at 10,000 square miles. Part of the area is in what is now Tennessee. Jackson Purchase is also the name given to a specific land area. About 2,400 square miles purchased fall in Kentucky.

"This is one way Tennessee changed in its early years; it grew bigger. During this time, there were a lot of historical figures who lived Tennessee.

"A bit after the Jackson Purchase, James K. Polk from Tennessee was elected President. David Crockett and Sam Houston both lived in Tennessee, too. Both were involved in the Texas War for Independence. Around the same time, a Cherokee named Sequoyah made a written language.

"Have you heard of these people?"

The class falls silent.

Ms. Johnson smiles knowingly.

"Then it's time for you to do some research," she says. She divided the class into three groups. They will report on Tennessee's famous historical figures from the early to mid-1800s.

Jackson and his group will research Sam Houston, the Alamo and the Texas War for Independence. Alana and her group will study Sequoyah and the Cherokee alphabet. The third group will have President James K. Polk.

title: Tennessee to Texas
text:
The time surrounding the Treaty of Tuscaloosa was one of expansion. American settlements continued to push westward. During this time, many people from Tennessee shined in the national spotlight.

First Group Report: James K. Polk

James K. Polk was born in North Carolina shortly after the Revolutionary War, in 1795. His family settled in Tennessee when Polk was about eight.

Polk was a Democrat. His long political career began in 1819 when he became clerk of the Tennessee Senate. He was studying to be a lawyer. He ended up leaving law to become a member of Tennessee's General Assembly. Polk campaigned for, and won, a seat in the U.S. House of Representatives in 1825. He was elected seven times and served as the Speaker of the House. After two terms as Tennessee governor, Polk lost his bid for a third term in 1841.

In his whole career, Polk believed that the U.S. should continue expanding west. He called this Manifest Destiny. A few years after losing the governorship, he was selected as the Democratic nominee for president. Despite the fact that he was an underdog, he won. He became the 11th president in 1845. He was the first Speaker of the House to be elected president. Many of his plans involved expanding the United States. He was successful. Under Polk, the U.S. grew in size by a third.

Our country was a busy place in the 1800s. Around the time Polk rose to the presidency, many American settlers moved to Texas. The people living in Texas didn't agree with many policies of the Mexican government. Some wanted to become an independent nation. Polk tried to make peace with Mexico. When he found that they were going to move troops into Texas, he ordered U.S. troops to Texas. Mexico ended up sending an army of 1,600 and captured 60 American dragoons (cavalry).

At the same time, Britain was disputing the border of Oregon. It was possible the U.S. might have to go to war with them. The U.S. could not fight the British and the Mexicans. Polk was successful in solving the border dispute, freeing up troops to help defend Texas.

He declined to serve a second term. He died in 1849 becoming a victim of cholera.

Jackson's Group Report: Sam Houston

Sam Houston was a critical figure in the Texas War for Independence. Although he was born in Virginia, Houston moved to Tennessee. He lived among the Cherokee for a few years before fighting in the War of 1812. He served two terms as a congressman from Tennessee, in 1823 and 1825. He became governor of Tennessee in 1827. After one term, he moved to Arkansas, then Texas in 1832.

Houston quickly took up the call for Texas to become an independent nation. He ended up becoming the commander of the small Texan army. After the fall of the Alamo, Houston's forces defeated part of the Mexican army at San Jacinto. They captured General Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna. Houston became the President of Texas in 1836 and again in 1841, avoiding further fighting with the Mexican army.

Texas became a country in 1836. Almost ten years later, when Texas became a state, the U.S. and Mexico fought the Mexican-American War. The war lasted two years. Mexico was not prepared for the war and was defeated rather easily.

title: Remember the Alamo!
text: The most well-known battle of the Texas Revolution was the Battle of the Alamo. Texas declared its independence from Mexico in 1836. It forced Mexican government officials out of San Antonio. The Mexican general, Santa Anna, led several thousand Mexican troops to lay siege on the fort. Some of the Texan armies occupied the Alamo. David Crockett was among them. Although greatly outnumbered, the 150-200 Texans fought bravely. They were able to hold out for 13 days against the much larger Mexican forces. Only a few from the fort survived. The wife and daughter of one of the captains were sent to the camp of Sam Houston. They were to deliver a warning. The same fate lay in store for any others that continued to revolt. Though the Texans lost the battle, they became heroes for their bravery. Ten years later, "Remember the Alamo!" became a battle cry for Americans in the Mexican-American War. The phrase endures as a symbol of freedom ever since.

title: Sequoyah
text:
Alana's Report: Sequoyah

Sequoyah was a fascinating character from the early 1800s. He fought against the British in the War of 1812, under Andrew Jackson. While at war, he saw the written language of the settlers. It was something no Cherokee had ever seen. Some American Indians called newspapers and books 'talking leaves.'

Sequoyah became fascinated with written language. In 1809 Sequoyah began to develop a written form of the Cherokee language. It took a long time. He finished his work in 1821. What he finally decided was that his language should represent the 85 syllables of the Cherokee language. Each symbol represented a sound. It was very easy to learn. People just had to memorize the symbol and the sound it represented. He said most people could learn the written language in about a week.

But not everyone was pleased. Sequoyah and his daughter, A-Yo-Ka, were accused of witchcraft. They were placed on trial. During the trial, he and his daughter showed tribal warriors how they could use the language to communicate. The warriors were so pleased with the display that they asked Sequoyah to teach them. Within a week the warriors were able to read and write their own language.

The Cherokee nation officially adopted the language in 1825. The language spread so quickly that within five years high numbers of Cherokee were literate; even more than their white neighbors.

In 1828 the Cherokee Phoenix was published in Georgia. It became the first newspaper in American Indian history.

There are many honors of Sequoyah's feat. Scientists named sequoias, or giant redwood trees, after him. More than four million pages of books, articles and newspapers had been printed in Cherokee when he died in 1843. Because of Sequoyah's gift, the history, culture and spiritual practices of the Cherokee have been preserved.

title: Tennessee's Path to Secession
text:
Before Abraham Lincoln took office as our 16th president in February 1861, seven Southern states had already seceded from the United States. Those states formed a government and wrote a constitution. This constitution said each state was independent and would govern itself. Slavery was legal in all Confederate states.

Tennessee Governor Isham Harris wanted the state to secede. He was from West Tennessee. Gov. Harris asked the General Assembly to vote on leaving the Union. However, the General Assembly said the voters should decide if the state should discuss secession. Most people in Middle and East Tennessee voted against the convention. West Tennessee was outvoted. In other words, the people of Tennessee didn't vote against secession; they voted against having a meeting to discuss, debate or vote on seceding!

On April 12, 1861, everything changed. Union troops fired on Fort Sumter and the Civil War began. President Lincoln called 75,000 men to put down the rebellion. Gov. Harris sent a message to Lincoln saying, "Tennessee will not furnish a single man for purposes of [force] but 50,000 if necessary for the defense of our rights and those of our southern brothers." Three more Southern states seceded and joined the CSA.

Once again, the people of Tennessee had to make a choice. Gov. Harris called for a vote in the General Assembly. A Bill of Secession was passed. Now it was up to the citizens again. The vote in East and West Tennessee turned out the same. West was for secession and East was against it. But in Middle Tennessee, many voters had changed their minds. On June 8, 1861, Tennessee became the 11th and last state to secede from the Union.

The people in East Tennessee asked the General Assembly to let them form their own state. They hoped the new state would be allowed to join the Union. Instead, Gov. Harris sent Confederate troops to make sure Tennessee kept all three Grand Divisions. As you can see, the state was not united on the issue of secession.

title: Slavery and the Grand Divisions
text:
Ms. Johnson's class is learning about the Grand Divisions in Tennessee and how each was affected by slavery in the Civil War era. Alana and Jackson remembered that the Grand Divisions are West Tennessee, Middle Tennessee and East Tennessee.

To understand how the Divisions were affected by slavery, it is important to know what type of land there is in each one.

"West Tennessee has a lot of farmland and not many hills or mountains at all. It's very flat. Memphis is the biggest city in that area," said Ms. Johnson. "During the Civil War, there were a lot of plantations and lots of farming going on. Wherever there were big farms, a great deal of labor was needed to plant, tend to and harvest the crops. So, West Tennessee depended on slaves to do the work. Pro-slavery feelings were very strong here, since the economy depended on it. As a result, when it came time to vote on secession, West Tennessee was in favor of leaving the Union.

"Let's put that into the perspective of the people who lived in West Tennessee in the 19th century," said Ms. Johnson. "In their eyes, using enslaved people to work their fields was about survival. And even if they agreed slavery was wrong, they didn't see a way of living without it. Even so, some people were beginning to see that making someone a slave was cruel and unfair. These people began freeing their slaves gradually, when the Civil War broke out. Change comes slowly and often only after great struggle."

Next, the class reviewed East Tennessee. This Division is full of mountains, deep valleys and is home to Clingmans Dome. That's the highest point in the state. This part of Tennessee didn't have the large pieces of flat land that were useful for farming. So, East Tennessee was not really dependent on slave labor for its economy. When it came time to decide whether to leave the Union, its residents didn't feel any need to secede.

Now, what about Middle Tennessee? Ms. Johnson reminded the students that Middle Tennessee has some hills and some flatlands. This Division had some dependence on slavery but nothing like in West Tennessee. Some people living in Middle Tennessee wanted secession and some didn't. It all depended on where their incomes came from, and if their livelihoods involved slaves.

So, geography made a big difference in whether people wanted to secede. If their livelihoods depended on slavery in the flat farmlands, they wanted to secede, and if they weren’t dependent on farming, they didn’t want to secede. Can you imagine how torn the people of Tennessee must have been? Families were pulled apart. The entire state had to think about how divided it was. People had to consider the views of the Unionists, the Confederate authority, the rights of states and the deeper issue of slavery itself. Did Tennessee’s unique geography temporarily result in the “Three States of Tennessee”?

"Wow, I knew the Civil War split our country but I didn't know it split Tennessee as well," said Jackson, eyes downcast.

Jackson looked up at her, his eyes turning red. "Ms. Johnson, was anyone really 'free' of slavery? It seems like it affected everyone, no matter where they lived or what they did. It's all so sad."

"I admire your compassion," said Ms. Johnson. "You're concerned about people's feelings. Your kindness is a great strength. I know this can be difficult to talk about. It's hard to understand how people could treat others like property. I'm proud of you for asking difficult questions."

"But ..." Jackson searched for words. "But what can we ... what can I do?"

Ms. Johnson replied, "You are already doing something. You are learning and asking questions. Today, we can learn from the past. We can do our part to make sure that the tragedies of yesterday aren't repeated."

Jackson looked up at her. "That's why we learn history, isn't it?"

"It is. The more you learn, the more you realize that we can make our world better all the time."

Ms. Johnson continued. "Here's something else, Jackson. You can stand up for people who are treated unfairly today. You can do it at school, at home or anywhere. You may not think you're making a difference in the grand scheme of things, but for those individuals you care about, your actions will mean more than you know."

"I think I understand, Ms. Johnson," said Jackson. "I know some things I can do. There's a lot to learn. I know there are kids who are mistreated here at school."

"That's a good place to start," said Ms. Johnson. "And one day, you'll be able to vote, run for office, help your community - so many things! You're capable of quite a lot, Jackson. All of you are!"

title: The Siege of Fort Donelson
text:
The siege at Fort Donelson took place in February 1862. It was a major victory for the North after a string of defeats. This battle was a morale booster for Union troops everywhere. Having lost many major battles so far, this victory at Fort Donelson was a key factor in the Union moving forward. Brigadier General Ulysses S. Grant was in charge of the Union forces. His goal was to create transportation routes through the South.

General Grant attacked the fort from many sides, one being with ironclad gunboats from the water of the Cumberland River. Reports say the ships were bombarded by Confederate artillery. The Confederates were quite happy at this point. General Grant quickly surrounded the fort and called for the surrender of the fort. In time, the officer in charge asked Grant for his terms of surrender.

His answer was, "No terms except an unconditional and immediate surrender can be accepted."

Due to this major victory for the North, which included access to the Cumberland River, General Grant was able to move forward. Nashville was quickly captured. The tide began to turn in favor of the North.

title: Grand Divisions of Tennessee Riddles
text:

title: Major Battles of Tennessee
text:
The Civil War affected the whole country. The battles were fierce and long. More soldiers died in the Civil War than all other wars combined that involved the United States. Several battles were fought within the state of Tennessee. Let's take a look at the major battles.

Battle of Stones River

It's winter in December 1862. The Civil War is raging across the country. Tennessee has recently lost control of Nashville. They will never regain control during the war. General Rosecrans of the Union Army has 41,000 soldiers. He is on the move! His goal: push the Confederates out of Tennessee. Once he has done that he plans on moving to Chattanooga and taking over a crucial railroad station. In the meantime, General Bragg and the Army of Tennessee are on the move. His goal: drive back the Union Army and keep them from taking control of Tennessee and possibly Kentucky. The stage is set.

General Rosecrans camps his troops only one mile from the Confederate Army. The conditions are cold and harsh. Suddenly, the Tennessee Army surprises the Union with an attack out of nowhere. The fighting is brutal. Not only are guns used but bayonets too. General Rosecrans sends in more men. The Union Army is forced across McFadden's Creek. But all is not as it seems because the boys in gray are caught in a trap! The Union side has the high ground. Plenty of artillery is aimed at the Tennessee Army. In minutes, almost 2,000 Tennessee soldiers are killed. Over 1,000 Union soldiers die as well. General Rosecrans beats General Bragg and claims the victory for the Union.

The Battle of Franklin

It's November 1864 and General John Bell Hood is in charge of the Tennessee Army. General Hood has been defeated in Atlanta. General William T. Sherman has won the city. General Hood has a goal to get General Sherman to come out of the Deep South. But now General Sherman has large numbers of soldiers. He splits his troops into two groups. One group goes to fight against General Hood with General George Thomas leading the way. General Hood was trying to defeat General Sherman's "March to the Sea." But General Hood had made many mistakes. He has already lost thousands of men in other battles. This battle was to be a disaster for Tennessee.

One of General Hood's big mistakes was not putting out picket lines at one point. These were the men who watched the lines all night long for changes in troop movements. Because of this, the Union Army slipped right out from under him. Under the command of General Hood, the Tennessee Army is almost completely wiped out. It is a crushing blow for the Confederacy. Six Southern generals are lost in this battle. More generals were wounded.

General Hood could not accept defeat. Even though his army was almost wiped out that day, he still decided to keep attacking. It was a sad day in Tennessee history.

Battle of Nashville

Two weeks after the battle of Franklin, the Tennessee Army is in a terrible position. General Hood has decided to head into Nashville. He only has about 25,000 soldiers but thinks he can retake the city. Everyone was tired and hungry.

A Confederate soldier says, "Our shoes were worn out and our feet were torn and bleeding ... the snow was on the ground and there was no food."

But they march on. General Hood is not making wise decisions and it ends up costing his men a lot, including their lives. He is not well either. He has a missing leg and has been wounded several times. Then the Battle of Franklin occurs and thousands of the Tennessee army are either killed or wounded. This makes his force even smaller. But he is determined to keep attacking.

Now he has less than 20,000 men, while the Union has over 50,000 soldiers. This is a big difference! The fighting goes back and forth and the South actually holds its own for a while. But the Union plunges into the battle with renewed strength and the Tennessee soldiers flee. There are not many of them left now and Hood's troops fall completely apart. The soldiers are tired, they are hungry and they have lost their will to fight. General Hood finally resigns. It's a bitter moment in Tennessee History.

These battles were very hard, disastrous battles for the South. Many soldiers died and many families were affected by these battles.

COOL FACT: Colonel Arthur MacArthur, Jr, known as the "Boy General", was a first lieutenant at 18. He was awarded the Medal of Honor for his bravery in the Battle of Missionary Ridge. At the Battle of Franklin, he led a charge of Wisconsin troops against the Confederates at an important point in the battle. He was shot in the shoulder, then shot in the chest and again in the leg all while fighting. His men saved him before he was trampled to death and he actually survived his wounds. He became the father of Douglas MacArthur, who was a famous general in World War II and in the Korean War. He earned the Medal of Honor, just like his father. Only one other father-and-son team both won these medals: Theodore Roosevelt and his son, Theodore Roosevelt Jr.

title: Jim Crow Erases Two Decades of Progress
text:
In his second inaugural address, Lincoln talked about his plans for Reconstruction. He said it should be "with malice for none, with charity for all." Early on, the Reconstruction included giving freed slaves land and helping them find jobs. Provisions included equal protection and the right to vote for all men. There were other ideas, too. Public schools and transportation are ideas from the Reconstruction.

Reconstruction ran into a few problems. It was hard to agree on what to do with the southern states after the war. Another problem was that there wasn't a single leader during this period. Presidents Abraham Lincoln and Andrew Johnson had different ideas about what Reconstruction should involve. Johnson, and later, President Grant, didn't want to be involved in the South.

Because of this, several laws, later called "Jim Crow Laws," passed in Tennessee around 1889. These laws limited the rights of African Americans. One law was called the Dortch Law. It said anyone unable to read couldn't get help to vote unless they had voted in 1857. Most African Americans could not read, nor were they able to vote in the 1857 election. Because of that, they could not vote now. Another law was the poll tax. The poll tax required payment to vote. Many poor people were unable to afford it.

Jim Crow laws made it so African Americans couldn't vote. Later laws further segregated the South.

text: You've seen how the Tennessee Constitution was rewritten and updated several times. Write a brief constitution for your classroom. Who might want it amended? Why?

text:
1. Summarize the era of Reconstruction in two or three sentences.

2. What were some ways that African Americans were able to learn to read and write during Reconstruction?

3. Identify a political pioneer from a different era. Compare them to a political pioneer of the Reconstruction.

4. Predict at least one future change or amendment to the Tennessee Constitution.

title: African American Political Pioneers
text:
Sampson W. Keeble was the first African American elected to the Tennessee General Assembly.

He was only 11 years old when went to work at a newspaper as a "roller boy." He later became a press operator and studied law before becoming a barber. While in business, he became involved in political causes.

He, along with other African American men, lobbied for the right to vote after passage of the 14th Amendment. Their efforts paid off. The state granted them the right to vote, three years before the 15th Amendment passed. That same year, Nashville elected two African American men to the city council. In 1868, they voted in their first election for U.S. president. Nearly all voted for Ulysses S. Grant.

Keeble won election to the Tennessee General Assembly in 1872. He served in the House of Representatives until 1875. Because of his legal background, he was elected as a magistrate and served from 1877 to 1882. When he ran for the General Assembly in 1878, he was defeated.

David Foote Rivers was only 23 years old when he was elected. People tried to prevent him from serving, but they were not successful. He served in the General Assembly from 1883-1885. He was elected again for a term of 1885-1887. He fled the county before completing his second term, fearing for his safety.

Between 1880 and 1893, there were 14 African Americans elected to the General Assembly. Nationally, around 2,000 were elected in state, local and national government roles. But it was not long until laws changed, preventing the election of African Americans. There were fewer people protecting their rights in government.

Soon, Tennessee didn't have any African Americans in elected positions. There wasn't another African American elected in Tennessee until Archie Walter Willis Jr. That was in 1964.

title: The Tennessee Constitutional Convention of 1870
text:
In 1866, Tennessee was the first Confederate state to regain seats in Congress. To do this, the state had to do two things: outlaw slavery and ratify the 14th Amendment. Tennessee Governor William Brownlow worked to make this happen. The amendment gave citizenship to former enslaved males. They were now allowed to vote.

However, Governor Brownlow passed a law stripping Confederates of the right to vote. These were people who supported the Confederacy during the war. As a result, voters who favored the Union elected Republicans to public office. In 1869, DeWitt Senter was elected governor. He was more lenient with former Confederates. He allowed some of them to vote. As a result, more Democrats were elected to the General Assembly. Former Confederates set out to regain their political power, but could not. African Americans were now voting. This enraged white people who were accustomed to ruling.

With more influence in the state, Democrats called for a constitutional convention in 1870. They wanted to restore voting rights of former Confederates. They succeeded in the new 1870 Constitution of Tennessee. They also wanted to strip former slaves of the right to vote. The new constitution did not do this—it would have angered the federal government. However, the Ku Klux Klan used violence to stop black people from voting. Sadly, they were very effective.

The constitution clearly banned slavery. Even so, it allowed discrimination in other ways. Schools were segregated. Interracial marriage was banned. It also allowed a poll tax, which one had to pay to vote. This kept African Americans from voting. They made no money as slaves, so they could not afford to vote. Although this targeted former slaves, many poor whites were kept out of the polls.

The constitution stated that poll taxes would be used to fund education. Since schools were segregated, racist policies gave good funding to white schools. Schools for African American and other nonwhite students received little money. They had buildings, books and other supplies that were in poor condition.

title: Opportunities for Schools
text:
The South gradually rebuilt during Reconstruction. It was a long, hard process, made more difficult by those that opposed civil rights.

The courts in the South were reorganized, and procedures for court cases were improved. Public schools were built and funded. A fairer tax system was set up to support roads, schools and public projects. And many of the new ideas put into the state constitutions during that period continue even today. In 1867, the Tennessee General Assembly opened all public schools to African Americans. It required that students of different races attend segregated schools. In 1870, the third constitution also required racial segregation.

Before 1865, the government did very little to provide education for freedmen. African Americans found creative ways to teach each other. Charities and churches made efforts to provide access to schools. Children would teach parents, and workers would teach each other on their breaks. By the spring of 1865, more than 4,000 children were being taught. People turned to northern charities for help to set up schools.

The Freedmen's Bureau was established by Congress during the Reconstruction period. Its purpose was to give aid to the newly freed 4 million African Americans. The bureau built hospitals and more than 1,000 schools, including colleges. It gave medical help to more than 1 million and gave out more than 21 million food rations to the poverty-stricken. Schools were set up to teach the former slaves to read and write. It was disbanded in 1872, having done a lot of good. But it was unable to continue due to lack of government and popular support.

In 1896, the Supreme Court ruled that segregation was lawful. At least it was as long as people of different races had access to equal facilities. One member of the Supreme Court, Justice John Marshall Harlan, disagreed with the decision. He wrote, "Our Constitution is colorblind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens."

Segregation was now legal. "Separate but equal" facilities appeared all over the South. In most cases, "equal" usually meant inferior for nonwhite people. The practice was extended to parks, theaters and restaurants. Even cemeteries made the effort to prevent contact between the races. It was not until 1954 that the Supreme Court outlawed the concept.

title: Plessy v. Ferguson
text:
Coming back into the Union meant the former Confederate States had to ratify the Reconstruction Amendments. This was the name for the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments. The 13th Amendment ended slavery. The 14th Amendment said laws protected everyone equally. The 15th Amendment stated that all men had the right to vote.

Even though the South adopted these amendments, some people were unhappy. When Reconstruction ended in 1876, Democrats controlled the states. At the time, Democrats were against the idea of equal rights for former slaves. Leaders began to look for ways around the amendments.

In 1890 Louisiana instituted the Separate Car Act. This law required whites and African Americans to ride in separate railway cars. A group of people thought this was unfair. They called themselves the Committee of Citizens. They also felt that, because of the new amendments, the law might be illegal.

The Committee of Citizens encouraged Homer Plessy to test the law. Plessy, who was part African American, bought a ticket to ride in a "whites only" car. After taking his seat, he told the conductor he was part African American. The conductor told him to leave his seat. When he refused, he was arrested.

He argued his case in court and lost. Through the appeals process, his case made it all the way to the Supreme Court. In 1896, the final ruling was that "separate but equal" was legal. This created a major obstacle to the Civil Rights Movement. The Movement continued, however, for the next 75 years and beyond.

Homer Plessy is now considered a hero of the Civil Rights Movement. New Orleans celebrates "Homer Plessy Day."

title: A Visit with Gramps
text:
"Class, I know we're running out of time," Ms. Johnson says, "But I wanted to squeeze this in before you go home."

Jackson, squirms at his desk, and eyes the clock. There are eight minutes left in the school day.

"We've been talking about the Civil War," Ms. Johnson continues, "which ended when Robert E. Lee surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant at..."

"Appomattox Court House," the class responds, in unison.

"Right! In Virginia. The year was 1865. The country was in shambles. Think for a minute about how people could rebuild the country after such devastation."

The class falls silent, reflecting upon Ms. Johnson's question. The Civil War had, as the saying goes, pitted brother against brother. Much of the country was in ruins. The issue of slavery still divided the nation.

"That question, class, leads us to this," says Ms. Johnson cueing a video about the period following the Civil War.

Jackson eagerly raises his hand. "Gramps, my great-grandfather, told me about how some people in my family fought in the Civil War."

Before Ms. Johnson can respond, the bell rings, ending the school day.

*****

"People in your family fought in the Civil War?" Alana asks Jackson, joining him on the walk home.

"Yes, Alana. I think it was my great-great-great grandfather who fought in the war. He was an African American who later went to Howard. He and his family lived in Tennessee. I've heard most of the stories from Gramps."

Jackson and Alana arrive at Jackson's house. They are surprised to see someone sitting on the porch drinking lemonade. There is a pitcher on a table in front of him next to two empty glasses. "Gramps!" Jackson exclaims.

Jackson tells Gramps how he and Alana have been learning about the Civil War and the end of slavery. He mentioned how his class was getting ready to watch a video on the Reconstruction after the Civil War but ran out of time.

"There's a long story there, Jackson," Gramps says, taking a drink of lemonade. "I grew up in Tennessee long after the Reconstruction, but I sure heard a lot about it. Right after the Civil War, there was the idea of rebuilding the country. The war hurt a lot of people. People lost homes and businesses."

Gramps pours lemonade for Jackson and Alana.

"Right before his assassination, Abraham Lincoln talked about how to rebuild the country. He said he wanted it to be fair to everyone. One of the things he said was that former slaves should be able to vote. After Lincoln, Andrew Johnson became president.

"There were some big ideas for Reconstruction. There were the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments to the Constitution. The 13th Amendment ended slavery, the 14th said that everyone was free, and the 15th said all men could vote ... "

"What about women?" asks Alana.

"That took a while longer," Gramps replies. "There were some other big changes, too. Like building the first public schools. But it didn't last," Gramps adds, sadly.

"What happened?" Jackson and Alana ask.

"Even though the third Tennessee Constitution ended slavery in 1870, it didn't mean everyone was treated fairly. It took a long time until we got there. Some people think we may still have a long way to go. But we live in a much more equal world today. For kids today, kids like you and Alana, the sky's the limit. And part of it is because of the brave people who fought in the Civil War."

title: Questions, Questions ... So Many Questions
text:
Hello, I’m Ella Sheppard, and I have a question for you. What would you do if you had no land, no money, no job and no home of your own? That is exactly what my family, my friends and I were asking after the Civil War. Imagine working your entire life without getting paid, not being allowed to learn to read and write and not having a home of your own. Suddenly, you are free but have no way to make a living or learn a skill! Former slaves like me and my family needed a lot of help. We also needed an education. In 1862, General Clinton Fisk, a Union soldier and chaplain, came to Nashville to capture the city as part of the Union forces. This soldier had an interest in helping former slaves like me.

Gen. Fisk persuaded the Army to let him convert a former hospital barracks located just west of downtown Nashville into a school for recently freed slaves. The school doors opened in January 1866, with 200 former slaves from age seven to 70 enrolled to get a free education. I was one of them! Four months later, the number of students had grown to 900! The school was named in honor of the general and became the Fisk Free Colored School. The students and school were so successful that the next year, the school moved from teaching “primary education” to “higher education” and became Fisk University.

A few years later, those old barracks started to wear out, and the school needed money. The fear was that this successful school would have to close down. “What will we do?” was the question we all asked ourselves. That’s when I was asked to be part of a nine-member student choir organized to perform concerts throughout the country to raise money and save Fisk. We introduced the United States and Europe to spirituals, as a musical art form, a cappella style. Do you know what “a cappella” means? It means that we sang without musical instruments to accompany us. Our name, “Jubilee Singers,” came from the ancient Hebrew practice of requiring all slaves to be set free in the year of Jubilee. The Jubilee Singers were a hit! Our group raised over $50,000 the first year and even more money as we toured year after year. The school was saved! We performed throughout the North, for President Grant at the White House and Queen Victoria in Great Britain. One newspaper reported that the queen was so impressed with our singing that she said, “These young people must surely come from a musical city.” Perhaps this was when Nashville first earned the nickname “Music City”! I think it is a good nickname for the hometown of Fisk University.

Today, the Fisk Jubilee Singers still travel and perform. Our group has won many awards, including the National Medal of Arts, which is the highest recognition of artistic excellence given by our government. The motto of the present day performers is, “We stand on the shoulders of the original Jubilee Singers, continuing their legacy, as we sing Negro spirituals.” In fact, it can be said we all stand on the shoulders of those who came before us. Whose shoulders do you stand on?

title: School to University
text:
One of the schools the Freedmen’s Bureau helped was Fisk University. Fisk began as a school for anyone who wanted to attend in 1866. The school got its name from General Clinton B. Fisk. As leader of Tennessee's Freedmen's Bureau, Fisk converted Union Army living quarters in Nashville into a school. When they opened, they taught students between the ages of seven and 70.

The leaders of Fisk School believed they could do even greater good. They believed that Fisk had the potential to educate people of all races and become one of the best American institutions. Fisk, a school for former slaves, became a university on Aug. 22, 1867. It became an accredited school in 1930, the first African American institution to do so. It has since received many honors and recognitions. In 1978, the campus was designated as a National Historic District due to its buildings, culture and history.

title: Jim Crow Laws
text: After the Civil War, many states throughout both the North and South passed laws enforcing racial segregation, or the separation of people of different races. These laws were called Jim Crow Laws. Jim Crow was a character in traveling minstrel (song and dance) shows that were popular at the time. These laws said that races must be kept separate in places like hotels, restaurants, schools, theaters, parks and trains. African Americans and whites were not allowed to drink from the same drinking fountains, use the same restrooms, be treated in the same hospitals or swim in the same pools. These laws also said that African Americans and whites were not allowed to marry outside their races. Jim Crow laws encouraged fear, hate and mistrust between the races. These unfair laws lasted from the 1870s until the mid 1960s, when the Civil Rights Movement began to get rid of Jim Crow laws for good.

title: A New Start in School
text:
The years after the Civil War were difficult for many Americans. They were tough for former slaves, in particular. This period is called the Reconstruction. This was also when parts of the South were rebuilt. The Reconstruction Amendments (13th, 14th, 15th) freed slaves and gave them more rights. All men could vote. There was greater equality in the eyes of the law. For former slaves, finding work was difficult. Many slaves were unable to read. Few had money or even places to live. Some had lost contact with friends or relatives who moved during the war. To help, Congress created the U.S. Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen and Abandoned Lands in 1865. The Bureau became known as the Freedmen's Bureau. It helped people, like former slaves and the poor, adjust to a new way of life in the South.

The Freedmen's Bureau built hospitals and schools. It helped slaves find jobs that paid good wages. The Bureau also had land. Some of it was claimed by Union troops during the war. Some land had been abandoned. The Bureau gave land to former slaves.

Perhaps the most lasting work done by the Bureau involved schools. It worked with the American Missionary Association or AMA. The AMA was an old anti-slavery group. It had its roots in helping the slaves who mutinied on a slave ship called the Amistad. Later, the AMA fought against slavery. It also tried to provide good schools for African Americans.

The Freedmen's Bureau and AMA worked together to open a number of schools. The AMA alone claimed to have opened over 500 schools. The first schools were created for Southern slaves as they were freed by Union troops. While these schools were created to help freed slaves, they were open to students of all backgrounds and races. Near the end of the Reconstruction, the AMA gave its elementary and secondary schools to state and local governments. These schools became public schools.

The AMA and Freedmen's Bureau also opened several colleges and universities. The AMA founded Atlanta, Dillard, Howard, Hampton and Fisk Universities. It also founded Huston-Tillotson, LeMoyne College, Talladega and Tougaloo Colleges. The AMA was actively involved in helping open the racially integrated Berea College.

The Freedmen's Bureau closed in 1872. The Bureau didn't have enough money to stay open. At the time, it didn't have much popular support and was openly prevented from doing some of its work by groups like the Ku Klux Klan. After it closed, the land given to former slaves was taken away and used by states.

Even though Southern states had to ratify the Reconstruction Amendments, there were many people who didn't support equality. Without the Freedmen's Bureau, African Americans no longer had help voting or negotiating job contracts. Many former slaves became sharecroppers. Sharecropping involved renting plots of farmland. Since they had little money, they paid for land with a share of the crop harvest. As sharecroppers, many formers slaves were doing the same hard work as before and, being so poor, weren't much better off than they were as slaves.

The AMA closed in the mid-1900s. Some of its artifacts and important documents can be found at Tulane University.

title: Continuing Racism
text:
Soon after the Civil War, Congress passed laws to guarantee the rights of all U.S. citizens. These are often called the Reconstruction Amendments. These guaranteed all men the right to vote, ended slavery, and gave citizens equal protection.

Some people in the South, including some lawmakers, were opposed to equal rights for all. The KKK, Jim Crow laws, and "black codes" were ways people opposed equality.

Southern states made "black codes" after the Civil War. These codes differed by state, but placed limits on the freedom of African Americans. The codes forced African Americans into jobs with low pay and made it hard to leave one job for another. African Americans needed to carry proof they had a job. Some states' codes limited the amount or type of property African Americans could own. Punishments for breaking these codes included fines, jail time or forced labor.

The Ku Klux Klan, also known as the KKK, began in the South in 1866. It was founded by former Confederate soldiers in Pulaski, Tennessee. It grew in response to the Reconstruction Amendments. After gaining the right to vote, African Americans in the South won many elections. The KKK opposed African Americans holding office. They tried to scare and sometimes even attacked people they disagreed with. The KKK and other racist people murdered many African Americans. This included anyone that helped African Americans to vote or hold office. Churches and schools were often the targets of KKK attacks. The KKK became very powerful. The U.S. government passed the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871 and began arresting its members. The Klan nearly disappeared for the next forty years.

As Reconstruction ended, "black codes" and the KKK gave way to Jim Crow laws. These laws led to separate Southern facilities: schools, buses, drinking fountains and so on for African Americans. Jim Crow laws prevented interracial relationships and limited voting rights. These laws lasted in the South for nearly 100 years. The Civil Rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s challenged Jim Crow laws.

title: Famous Fisk Graduates
text:
From its beginning, Fisk University prided itself on the quality of its education. Over the years, several famous people attended Fisk. Although you may not have heard of Matthew Knowles, who is on the Board of Trustees, you may know his daughter named Beyoncé, a famous singer. Knowles graduated from Fisk in 1974.

U.S. Representative John Lewis graduated from Fisk. Lewis was born in the 1940s into a sharecropping family. When he was young, Lewis heard Martin Luther King on the radio. He decided he wanted to become a part of the Civil Rights movement. While attending Fisk, he organized protests at segregated restaurants with "sit-ins." The protests were successful. Lewis fast became a recognized leader of the movement. In 1963, at age 23, he spoke at the March on Washington. His activism continues to this day. In 1986, he won an election as a Congressman in Georgia. He has served ever since.

Nikki Giovanni graduated from Fisk in 1968. Born in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1943, Giovanni became a world-renowned poet as a young adult. At Fisk, she organized the Student Non-Violent Coordinating Committee, also called the SNCC. The SNCC was a civil rights group that Representative Lewis had also chaired. Giovanni's first book of poetry was on the tragic losses of political leaders. Her poetry explored the lack of equality faced by African Americans. In 1986, Giovanni began teaching at Virginia Tech.

Diane Nash is another important figure who attended Fisk. Nash was involved in the Civil Rights movement. Nash, much like John Lewis, protested segregated lunch counters in Tennessee by joining in "sit-ins." She helped found the SNCC in 1960. The "sit-ins" were successful. In 1960, Nashville banned segregated lunch counters. After the Civil Rights Act passed, Nash turned her efforts to oppose the Vietnam War.

title: It's a Musical State
text:
One of the most famous musicians from Tennessee was W.C. Handy. He was an African American musician known as the "Father of the Blues." Originally from Florence, Alabama, Handy bought his first guitar without his father's permission. His father was a very religious man who believed musical instruments were sinful. Handy continued to learn how to play many instruments. He even played in a band without telling his parents. Later in his life, Handy ended up playing music on Beale Street in Memphis. Beale Street is famous for blues music. Handy was one of the first African American men to make money by writing and publishing music.

Bessie Smith is another famous African American blues artist from Tennessee. When she was close to 10 years old, she and one of her younger brothers performed on street corners. Her singing career took off in the 1920s when she joined Paramount and Columbia Records. She earned the name, "Empress of the Blues." She also performed on Broadway and in movies.

In 1925 WSM AM radio in Nashville first signed on. They were one of the only AM radio stations in the eastern U.S. to play music. The station broadcast news during the day. On Saturday evenings, "The Grand Ole Opry" was aired. Country music artists performed folk, bluegrass and gospel music. The show made country music famous. It helped The Grand Ole Opry earn its nickname as "the home of American music."

The Carter family members were the first country music stars. Maybelle Carter developed a new style of playing the guitar. She was able to play rhythm on the higher strings of her guitar. At the same time, she played the melody with the fingers of the other hand on the lower strings. The method, called "Carter picking," would be used by artists even until today.

title: Voices of Tennessee
text:
Hey, everyone! Alana here. Jackson and I are here to tell you about some cool things we've learned in class. You learned in our adventure with Elvis that Ms. Johnson has us focusing on famous people that helped create amazing music in Tennessee.

We are also researching how people have impacted the world in more modern times. In this report, I will focus on some famous Tennesseans. These are extremely influential people and experts in their current fields. My portion of the assignment will focus on Al Gore, Alex Haley and Dolly Parton. Here's my report:

Several Tennesseans have changed and influenced the lives of people all over the world. One such person is climate change activist Al Gore. Mr. Gore represented Tennessee in the House of Representatives and Senate. In 1992 he was elected Vice President of the United States. He has also served in many notable companies. He created the Climate Reality Project. They are a non-profit organization focused on taking steps to solve the climate crisis.

He sought to influence others to be more proactive with climate change and the effects of global warming. Mr. Gore has written several books such as Earth in the Balance, An Inconvenient Truth, The Assault on Reason, Our Choice: A Plan to Solve the Climate Crisis, The Future: Six Drivers of Global Change and An Inconvenient Sequel: Truth to Power. His work on climate change led to being awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2007.

Another who has used writing as a means to influence the world is the author, Alex Haley. He is best known for his books such as Roots and The Autobiography of Malcolm X. Alex Haley's historical fiction showed readers the struggle African Americans endured. His book, Roots even became a T.V. show. It was so influential that many people felt it became an important part of the Civil Rights Movement. Since its creation, Roots has won 271 awards. The T.V. show has been nominated for thirty-seven Emmys. Haley is a veteran of the Coast Guard, and they named a cutter after him, the USCGC Alex Haley.

While literature was a way to influence others, some Tennesseans were influential through their music. A modern artist who has done this is Dolly Parton. Ms. Parton grew up in a relatively poor family where music was a big influence in her life. Through the help of her uncle, Bill Owens, she began performing at shows. Her career took off from there. Since then she has been one of the few people to earn a nomination in all four of the major awards. She was nominated for Emmy, Oscar and Tony awards. She also won 8 Grammys. She won several other awards such as the Living Legend Award (2004) from the U.S. Library of Congress, Kennedy Center Honors (2006), and the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award (2011). She holds two Guinness World Records for her music. She has touched the hearts of millions of fans, and she continues to make the world her stage.

Two more Tennesseans that have influenced the world are Oprah Winfrey and Wilma Rudolph. Both have been influential, not only to African Americans but to people all around the world.

Oprah Winfrey had a very hard childhood and adolescence that could have changed the person she was to become. Somehow, she was able to get through these difficulties. She went to college at Tennessee State University in 1971. Then she worked on beginning a career in radio and television broadcasting. She first became a host on the T.V. show, "People Are Talking" and soon became the leading talk show host. In time, she launched her own show, "The Oprah Winfrey Show" on ABC. Once that became a success, she bought the program and started her own production company, Harpo Productions. Despite immediate challenges, Oprah Winfrey strove to keep her show respectable and earned the hearts of millions. Later, she created her own network. She starred in and won different awards for productions and movies. She participates in much charitable work.

Wilma Rudolph is another well-known African American woman. She was the first American to win three gold medals in track and field in a single Olympics. However, she had a challenging path leading up to that achievement. When she was younger, she had pneumonia, scarlet fever and polio at the same time. For the majority of her childhood, she had to wear a brace. She needed to complete sessions of physical therapy to walk. This setback did not stop her, though. She trained hard in high school. She was soon recruited for the Olympics by coach Ed Temple. In her first Olympics, she won a bronze medal for the 400-meter relay. Afterwards, she set her eyes on getting a college degree and training for the next one, where she made history. In the Rome, 1960 Olympics, she broke three world records. After combating several setbacks, she was able to become one of the greatest runners in history.

title: The Start of It All: The Creation of the Music Industry in Tennessee
text:
"This has gotta be one of the coolest trips we've gone on yet, Alana!" Jackson shouted eagerly as they walked through the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in Tennessee. Alana and Jackson could barely contain their excitement. Jackson is Elvis' biggest fan and looked up all the exhibits he could see before heading on the trip. He talked Ms. Johnson's ear off about all the things he learned about Sun Studio in Memphis and all of Elvis' famous songs. Ms. Johnson even played the Studies Weekly video, "Elvis Presley Intro" and the song, "Jailhouse Rock" for the class, which delighted Jackson even more.

Alana, on the other hand, is a big blues fan and can't wait to see some historical exhibits with W.C. Handy and Bessie Smith. There are so many directions that she and Jackson could go in, that they weren't sure which way to go first.

Alana and Jackson wandered down a side hallway labeled, "Costumes and Garb." As they went down the hall, Jackson gasped.

"Alana, look!"

On a mannequin behind glass were several costumes that Elvis wore during his many concerts.

"Alana, you can feel the material on this one!" Jackson said, reaching toward the gold ensemble on the display table.

"That's nice, Jackson," Alana muttered as she read the titles on an assortment of vinyl.

Next thing they knew, they were plunged into a swirling vortex of purple and green.

"Next time, give a girl a little warning, Jackson!" yelled Alana over the loud whirring sound of the time tunnel.

"Sorry, Alana!" He responded.

Suddenly, they landed with a loud thud, coughing and breathing heavy from the journey.

"No matter how many times we do that, I can never get used to it," Jackson coughed as he brushed the dirt off his pants.

"Well, Jackson, where do you think we are? I am going to guess you touched something that sent us here. What did you touch?" Alana asked.

"I touched Elvis' concert clothes back at the museum."

"Okay, then that must mean we are somewhere Elvis visited. Let's think."

They looked around them and saw a brown brick building behind them with the words, "Sun Studio" across the top.

"Oh, Alana! We are where Elvis recorded most of his big hits! I wonder if he is in there right now. Let's go!" Before Alana could give him a response, he was running toward the building's door.

As they walk into the studio, they hear "Hound Dog" being sung and Jackson cheered with excitement.

"Hey, what are you kids doing in here?"

The music stopped as an angry man with his hair slicked back ran up to them.

"Oh it's alright Sam, they're just two kids who probably heard the tunes and came to see what was going on."

And just like that, there he was. The "King" himself. Jackson couldn't close his mouth from the shock.

"Oh thank you, Elvis, uh Mr. Presley, sir." Alana stuttered.

"Oh, did I introduce myself? How do you both know my name?"

"We just heard of this really great singer around town and they had mentioned you, so we assumed it was you when we came in here."

"That's very kind of you both."

"Elvis, do you mind if we ask you a question?"

"Sure."

"What are some of the things that inspire you to make your music? Your songs are just so unique and different." Alana asked.

"Oh, I really like every type of music and try to work with it as best I can. Country, rhythm and blues, you name it. But a lot of the reason I sing is because of my church. I just love gospel music; I did even when I was a kid, and I find myself trying to put that in as many of my songs as possible."

"That's so cool!" Jackson exclaimed.

"Well thank you, thank you very much." Elvis chuckled.

"Okay, well Elvis, I mean Mr. Presley, we really need to get back to where we belong now. We apologize for interrupting your session."

title: Where it All Happened: Famous Tennessee Places
text:
Hey all, Alana here with Jackson. We decided to show you the cool places that were the reason music developed in Tennessee. Here are some of those different musical landmarks:

1. Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum

This museum has over 2 million artifacts of country music (both past and present). In addition, the museum has a small theater, where artists and songwriters come for events throughout the year.

2. Sun Studios

This is where rock and roll was born. Many famous singers like Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Roy Orbison and Jerry Lee Lewis got their big breaks here. Currently the studio showcases different photos, records and other items from the past. It also has new artists come in to record to build up even more musical history.

3. Graceland

This is Elvis Presley's mansion, which pays homage to his life and musical history. Each year, thousands of people come to see where the famous singer lived.

4. Ryman Auditorium

This is the place where bluegrass was born and is best known as the home of the Grand Ole Opry from 1943 to 1974.

6. Stax Museum of American Soul Music

It started as a tiny record store and turned into one of the most famous recording companies in the world. It was one of the birthplaces of the sounds of American soul. It was a real competitor against Motown. The museum has hundreds of vintage records, costumes and instruments.

title: Let's Write
text: You've learned how important agriculture, industry and tourism are to Tennessee's economy. Write the script for a 30-second television or radio commercial, using what you've learned, to convince visitors to come to Tennessee.

title: Taking the Tours, Seeing It All
text:
"Time to travel," Jackson declared at the library. "Let's check out the tourism part of our project!"

Alana laughed at his excitement. "Where should we go first?" she asked.

One place to start is the Beechcraft Heritage Museum in Tullahoma. At this museum in Middle Tennessee, you can learn about Olive Beech, who was called the "First Lady of Aviation.” Olive’s husband, Walter, created the Travel Air company in 1924. At the museum, you can see one famous airplane produced by Travel Air in 1929: The Travel Air Mystery Ship. This plane competed in the National Air Races. The plane was shipped to the race in pieces with great secrecy. The Mystery Ship won the races, beating expected winners from the Army and the Navy.

In 1932, Walter created the Beech Aircraft Company in Kansas. During this time, Olive helped lead the company alongside her husband. As the United States entered World War II, Beech became a top government contractor. It was one of the most efficient producers of military equipment. The company won awards from the Army and Navy.

Olive led the company for many years after Walter died in 1950. Throughout her career, she won more awards and citations than any other woman in aviation history. Other women played a role in the company’s success, too. In 1936 the company entered one of its Staggerwing aircraft into the National Air Races with a woman piloting the craft, Louise Thaden. She won the Bendix Trophy for her success. You can see more about the history of aviation and this influential company at the Beechcraft Heritage Museum.

Next, the friends touched the old vinyl record they'd found at Gramps' house and found themselves on Beale Street, where they met W.C. Handy and Willie Mitchell.

"Mr. Handy," Jackson said, "how did you get famous?"

The man laughed. "Well, my mama and papa were emancipated slaves, so we didn't have a lot. My career sort of started when I wrote "Mr. Crump" as a campaign song. A couple of years later, we recorded it as "Memphis Blues." It's sometimes considered the first blues song published. After that, I performed at the Chicago World's Fair, and wrote a lot more songs. In fact, 25 years after it was published, my song, "St. Louis Blues" is still earning me about $25,000 a year!"

They learned that Willie Mitchell, who wrote "Soul Serenade," played an important role in Memphis's becoming an important place for soul music. Jackson and Alana had to hurry on to their next destination.

"This place is beautiful!" Alana exclaimed. "Where are we?"

Jackson said, "We're in the Cherokee National Forest. My family loves it here. It's the largest public land area in the whole state, with 650,000 acres. There are so many great things to see and do here. My favorite is gold-panning and hiking on the Unicoi Turnpike, which was part of the Trail of Tears."

Alana read a brochure. "This says there are 15 recreational zones, with all kinds of things to do, like camping, fishing, hunting, water activities, bicycling and horse riding. In the Holston Mountain Zone, there's a 30-mile horse trail. And this sounds like fun: you can do geocaching and letterboxing here, too."

Jackson agreed that it did sound interesting, and they decided to talk their parents into coming back for a camping and geocaching weekend soon.

title: Five in One
text:
"Hey, Jackson," Alana said. "Here are two videos we can watch. They are about the regions of the United States, so we can show how they are similar to the Tennessee regions in our project: 'Regions of the U.S.A. Intro' and 'U.S.A.'s Seven Natural Regions'."

Jackson sat next to his friend so he could see the monitor as they watched the movies. After they watched, they compared notes.

Alana said, "It looks like there are five major U.S. regions: Northeast, Southeast, Midwest, Southwest and West. That's simple."

Agreeing, Jackson said, "They're pretty different, just like the divisions in our state. The Northeast has a humid continental climate, with cool summers and snow, while the Southeast, where we live, has a humid subtropical climate, with hot summers."

"That's for sure," Alana laughed. "The Midwest is a lot like the Northeast, except this says snow is really common. The Southwest, it says, has a semiarid steppe climate in the west, but it's more humid in the east. And the West Region has several climate types: semiarid, alpine, Mediterranean, and desert."

"Well," Jackson mused, "we can make two maps for our project. One can show the regions in Tennessee and one can show regions in the whole country."

"And we can use symbols to show the different climates and geographical features," Alana said. "I think we've made a great start!"

title: This Week's Question
text: You've read about the characteristics of the different regions of Tennessee, including their physical features, industries, agriculture and tourism. Create a diagram to compare and contrast the regions.

title: Heading Out Around the World
text:
Early Saturday morning, Jackson and Alana jumped into the car with Jackson's dad and headed to Memphis to visit the FedEx headquarters.

"Welcome to FedEx," their guide greeted them. "What questions can I answer?"

"Thanks," Jackson said. "Where did the idea for FedEx come from?

Laughing, the guide said, "Believe it or not, it came from a term paper the founder wrote in 1965. In 1973 he started an airfreight company with 389 team members and 14 small planes. On the first day, they delivered 186 packages."

"Why did he decide on Memphis for the headquarters?" Alana asked. "Why not someplace like New York?"

The guide answered, "Memphis is a centralized location in the United States, which is good for business. And Memphis International Airport almost never has to shut down for bad weather."

After the tour, they thanked the guide and headed to their next destination.

title: Exciting Innovation
text:
That afternoon, Jackson and Alana visited a Nissan dealership in their town to learn more about the company and their North American headquarters in Franklin, Tennessee.

"Nissan sold their first car in the United States in 1958," the manager told them. "They started manufacturing in the U.S. in 1983."

"Where do they do that?" Alana asked.

"There are plants in Smyrna and Decherd," the manager replied. "In Smyrna, there's a vehicle assembly plant that builds six different models, but Nissan also operates the largest lithium-ion automotive battery plant in the whole country in Smyrna, too."

"And the headquarters?" Jackson asked.

"Nissan North America first announced that they were moving to Franklin in 2005, when they started building a site to open in 2008. They moved from California because the cost of doing business was lower in Tennessee."

title: Moo-ving on the Farms
text:
"Let's go, Jackson," Alana said as her friend came out the school door. "We have a lot of research to do at the library, so move it!"

Laughing, Jackson joined his research partner, and they talked about their day as they walked to the town library. When they arrived, the librarian was waiting for them.

"I remember that you mentioned that you needed information about agriculture in our state, so I picked out some videos and some books for you. I left URLs and texts at your usual table."

They watched the three Studies Weekly videos, "Tobacco," "Harvesting Tobacco" and "Tobacco and Slavery." Then they started reading about modern farming in Tennessee. They shared interesting facts as they found them.

"Hey, listen to this," Jackson said. "Beef cattle are the number one agriculture product in our state, with more than 1 million cows. We also sell hogs, sheep, lambs, honey, wool and meat goats. In fact, we are number two in the whole country for raising goats."

"That's impressive," Alana said. "I was just reading about dairy farms, too. This pamphlet from the Tennessee Department of Agriculture says that about 52,000 milk cows produce 800 million pounds of milk. That's a bunch of milk!"

Jackson said, "According to this graph, broilers are next in production. What's a broiler, anyway?"

"It's a young chicken," Alana replied. "Several crops are pretty strong here, too. My book says West Tennessee grows most of the nearly 44 million bushels of the state. And Tennessee is eighth in the nation for cotton. Farmers here also grow corn, wheat, hay, sorghum, tomatoes, peaches, apples, snap beans and mushrooms."

"Whew!" Jackson said. "And we already learned about tobacco here. This says that it is the number two crop in the state, right after soybeans. More than 45 million pounds were grown in just 2010."

The friends gathered their notes and headed to Jackson's house to turn their new facts into an infographic to add to their project.

title: Going Around in Circles
text:
Saturday evening, Jackson and his parents picked Alana up at her house for another research trip.

Jackson said, "I think this trip is going to be my favorite. I've wanted to visit Bristol Motor Speedway for, like, ever."

"It's pretty cool," Alana said. "When the first NASCAR race ran in 1961, 11 of the competitors were on the 1998 list of the 50 greatest drivers ever. And the course was tough enough that only 19 of the 42 starters completed the race."

"Hey, you've been holding out," Jackson said. "You really know NASCAR, don't you?"

"Sure," Alana said. "And I love BMS. Did you know Kyle Busch broke the track record in 2013, when he qualified for the Food City 500 with a 129.535 mile-per-hour lap?"

Jackson's parents laughed at the look of surprise on their son's face, then led the friends into the Speedway for that night's races.

title: Isn't It Grand?
text:
"This project is going to be great," Jackson said. "All the places to visit! Beale Street for music, the Beechcraft Museum, Cherokee National Park; we'll have a blast!"

"Don't forget that we need to include Tennessee's industry and agriculture, too," Alana reminded him.

"Right!" Jackson replied. "But hey, tourism is a big part of the economy. A lot of businesses are made for tourists. Hotels, for one."

"That's true, Jackson," Alana said, "but we have a lot of other stuff to learn about the Grand Divisions!"

"Okay," he said. "We better figure out exactly what areas we're talking about first. This book says that Tennessee has three Grand Divisions. They are pretty simple: East Tennessee, Middle Tennessee and West Tennessee."

"Okay," Alana said, "the divisions are pretty different. According to the video and this book, East Tennessee has the Southern Appalachians, the Tennessee River Valley and part of the Cumberland Plateau. It's more mountainous than the rest."

"Yep," Jackson said. "And Middle Tennessee has part of the Plateau, the Central Basin and the Highland Rim. It's the largest division, with 41 percent of the state's landmass. Looks like a lot of rolling hills and valleys where the land is fertile."

"And West Tennessee stretches from the Mississippi River to the western Tennessee River Valley," Alana added. "It's part of the Gulf Coast Plain, and the lowest of all three. It has a lot of rich soil, and there was a lot of cotton farming during the antebellum period, which means before the Civil War."

The friends continued their research, sharing bits they found interesting as they worked.

"Hey, did you know that the Grand Divisions have different regions in them?" Jackson said. "In the west are the Gulf Coastal Plain, where they grow cotton, soybeans and corn; there's also the Mississippi Floodplain."

He turned the page and continued. "The middle division has the Highland Rim, which totally surrounds the Central Basin, which is also called the Nashville Basin. Middle Tennessee grows a lot of tobacco. And the east has three regions: the Cumberland Plateau, the Valley and Ridge Region, and the Unaka Mountains. East Tennessee is known for its many dairy cows."

Alana nodded. "I see that the plateau is colder than the rest, and that there was a lot of mining there after the Civil War. And this is cool: the ridges in the Valley and Ridge Region run mostly northeast to southwest, so the major roads run southwest to northeast."

"And the Unaka Mountains have a lot of fast-moving streams, rugged terrain, and the slopes have heavy forests on them," Jackson finished.

"Wow," Alana said. "We're going to have a lot to talk about in our project to compare all the divisions!"

title: Weather

title: Thunderstorms
text: In a thunderstorm there is thunder and lightning. There is heavy rain and lots of wind.

title: Floods
text: Storms often cause floods. Floods happen when bodies of water overflow their banks (the land on the sides). During a storm, floods can happen very fast.

text: The past is everything that happened before now. Yesterday happened in the past.

title: The Present

title: The Future
text: The future is everything that will happen after right now. Tomorrow will happen in the future.

text: A calendar shows us the days, weeks and months of a year. At school, the calendar tells us when we go on a field trip.

title: Community Calendars

title: History in Museums
text: We can learn about history at a museum.

title: Family History
text: We can learn about history from our parents and grandparents. Family traditions are the things your family does and the things your family believes.

title: Family Traditions
text: How does your family celebrate special days? The way you celebrate is a family tradition.

title: Christopher Columbus

title: Past, Present and Future
text: You have probably heard people use these words: past, present, and future. The past is everything that happened before today. The present is happening right now. The future is everything that will happen.

title: The Past

title: The Present

title: The Future

title: Days and Months

title: Calendars

Your teacher will give you a blank weekly calendar. Write in the days of the week and the dates.

title: Tell a Story
text: Tell your friend a story. It can be a story you have read or a story you make up. Try to use words like these: first, next, then and last. You can use the days of the week and the months of the year, too.

title: Changes in Transportation
text: Transportation has changed over time because of technology. Today, we can move people and things from one place to another place faster and more safely.

title: Original Transportation
text: Many of the first people who lived on Earth walked wherever they went. Some people rode animals like camels.

title: Invention of the Wheel
text: The invention of the wheel changed transportation forever. People began to use animals to pull wagons. Bicycles were invented many years later.

title: Boats
text: A long time ago, people had to use poles or oars to move boats through the water. The Egyptians were the first to use sailboats.

title: Engines
text: Engines make things go faster. Cars and trucks have engines. Trains, boats and airplanes have engines, too. This technology has helped people travel farther and faster.

title: Trains
text: Some of the fastest trains in the world are in Japan. They are called bullet trains. Bullet trains can travel 175 miles per hour.

title: What Came First?
text: What kind of transportation came first? Put these pictures in order by writing a number under each picture.

title: Where is Japan?
text: Where is Japan? Use your favorite color to fill in Japan on the map. Draw a fish in the Sea of Japan.

title: Fact or Fiction?
text: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was a real person. He believed everyone should have the same rights and opportunities. He found peaceful ways to change unfair laws. He found peaceful ways to change the way some people treated African American citizens in our country.

title: The Story of Goldilocks
text: Have you ever heard the story of Goldilocks and the Three Bears? Was Goldilocks a real person?

title: The Story of Aladdin
text: Have you ever heard the story of Aladdin? A lamp is real, but it cannot be magic. A carpet is real, but it cannot fly. It is a made-up story.

title: Little Red Riding Hood
text: Have you ever heard the story of Little Red Riding Hood? We know that wolves can’t talk. This is a made-up story, too.

title: Fiction and Folktales
text: We call made-up stories fiction. The stories and the people are not real. Sometimes we call these stories folktales. Can you think of some other stories that are fiction?

title: Abraham Lincoln
text: Abraham Lincoln was our president more than 100 years ago. He led an honest life. Some people called him "Honest Abe."

title: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: A fact is something that is true. The story you read about Martin Luther King Jr. is true. He was a brave American. He helped people get equal rights.

title: Brave and Honest
text: Do you know anyone who is brave like Martin Luther King Jr.? Do you know anyone who is honest like Abraham Lincoln? How were Martin and Abraham similar? How were they different?

title: Fun and Games
