title: Be an Informed Voter
text:
What is important to you? Before even thinking about an election and the candidates and the campaigns, it is important to get a good understanding of your own values. Think long and hard about what you want for your country and community. When elections come around, you will see a lot of television commercials and advertisements. Candidates are trying to get your vote! They may even hold a debate where candidates stand at podiums and answer questions in front of a live audience. They discuss important issues and concerns that people want to know about. If you know what is important to you before listening to the candidates, then you will have a better idea of who you are looking for to fill the position.

After you know more about the candidates, continue to gather even more information. Search the internet, find brochures, and listen to speeches. You can even attend a meet and greet with the candidate you are leaning towards. When it comes to elections, there is no such thing as too much information. The more the better! Remember, you are making an important decision for your community and your country. Elections are meant to put people you trust in a government position. Government positions hold great power. By choosing them, you are saying that you feel they can uphold what is important to you. Never lose sight of what you want for your community and country. You have a voice, and you should use it!

title: Three Branches of Government
text:
The Three Branches of Government

Our government is a constitutional democracy. This means our leaders get their power from the people. Three branches of government keep this power in check. They also make sure that no branch forgets how important our individual liberty is. Each branch has its own job to do and has a way to check, or limit, how much the other two branches can do. This means all the power balances out. The first three articles of the Constitution list the branches and their responsibilities. These branches are the executive branch, the legislative branch, and the judicial branch.

Executive Branch

The executive branch of government makes sure that the laws are carried out. It also is in charge of the military. The head of the executive branch is the President of the United States. The president and vice president are elected together for four years. They may serve two terms, for a total of eight years.

The president doesn't work alone. He or she chooses members of the cabinet, a group of people who advise the president and help run the executive branch. The cabinet is filled with experts in their fields, and they lead their departments. For example, the Department of Education helps schools in the country and enforces laws that have to do with schools. The Department of Defense is in charge of the military.

Other offices carry out laws in different areas. For example, the Environmental Protection Agency carries out laws that help reduce pollution. Including the men and women of the military, more than four million Americans currently work for the executive branch. The Department of Transportation enforces laws that have to do with cars, roads, trains, and airplanes.

Legislative Branch

The legislative branch makes the laws and establishes taxes. Congress, the legislative branch of our national government, is divided into two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate. When someone writes an idea for a new law, it is called a bill. In order for a bill to become a new law, both chambers have to vote for it.

The House of Representatives is the lower chamber of Congress. The number of representatives for each state depends on how many people live there. The states with larger populations send more representatives, and those with smaller populations send fewer. The smallest states send only one. The largest state, California, sends over 50 representatives. In total, there are 435 representatives in the House. They serve two-year terms.

The Senate is the upper chamber of Congress. Every state sends two senators to the Senate, no matter how many people live there. The 100 senators serve six-year terms. Because the Senate is the upper house, it has certain powers that the House of Representatives doesn't. The Senate approves treaties. It also confirms judges and cabinet members chosen by the president.

Judicial Branch

The judicial branch interprets the laws, or decides what they mean. It also decides if the laws follow the Constitution. The judicial branch is headed by the Supreme Court and other federal, or national, courts. The Constitution does not state how many justices should sit on the Supreme Court but allows Congress to decide this number. Since 1869, there have been nine justices serving on the Supreme Court.

And, of course, courts decide whether someone is guilty of a crime. The role of the judicial system is to make sure that the rights of all citizens are protected and that the law is followed. Article III of the Constitution guarantees that anyone who has been accused of a crime has the right to a fair trial before a judge and a jury. It is important to protect the rights of everyone, including those who have been accused of a crime.

Separation of Powers

The people of the United States and the Founding Fathers were concerned about tyranny. Someone like King George or a small group like the British Parliament could get a lot of power and take away the rights of the people. So, to avoid repeating those mistakes, the Constitution was written to stop anyone from getting too much power. This is why the government is split into three branches. This is called separation of powers. The president has a big job, but he or she cannot decide a law is against the Constitution and throw it out. That's the job of the judicial branch. The legislative branch makes the laws, but the executive branch enforces those laws. As long as these powers are kept separate, the three branches protect against unfair government.

Checks and Balances

Each branch of government has the power to check (or control) the other branches in some way. We call it a system of checks and balances, and it keeps all three branches of government playing by the rules! The Founders created a government in which no branch can do its job without help from the others. Each branch has a check (or control) against the other two. This keeps the power balanced. Here are a few examples:

Executive Branch:

The president approves or vetoes bills written by the legislative branch.

The president nominates Supreme Court justices and other judges.

Legislative Branch:

Congress can impeach, or put on trial, members of other branches.

The Senate confirms the president's choices for judges and cabinet members.

Judicial Branch:

The Supreme Court exercises judicial review, meaning it decides whether laws made by Congress follow the Constitution. If they don't, the law is removed.

Judicial review can also make decisions about actions of the executive branch.

title: Learning about Rights and Responsibilities
text:
Personal and Civic Responsibility

In a democracy, citizens have the right and the responsibility to participate in their own government. They do that by voting and being personally and civically responsible. What does that mean? If you are personally responsible, it means you take responsibility for yourself, your family, and your community. That means that as a student, you do your very best at school so you can take advantage of the great educational opportunities we have in this country.

Civic responsibility often starts with voting. It means that you obey the law and respect the rights of others. Civic responsibility also means you work for the common good by doing things that help everyone in your community.

Make Your Voice Heard

People who are elected to an office don't automatically know what you want them to do. They have their own ideas, but they know they have to listen to the ideas of their constituents (people who voted for them) if they want to get elected again. So, tell them what you want. Start by finding out all the facts you can about the issue they will be voting on. Then, send an email or write a letter. Remember that leaders and citizens often have to compromise. Good leaders listen to everyone and decide what is best for their community, state, or nation.

Civic and Service Organizations

We all need to work together to get things done. Civic organizations work for the common good (things that help everyone in the community). A civic organization is made up of people who work on making things better for the community. Some people who work for civic organizations are paid, and some are volunteers (people who agree to work for no pay). Government is a type of civic organization, since its purpose is to make things better in the community. Your local historical association is a civic organization, too.

Service organizations are also very important. Some service organizations may pay many of the people who work there, but they are set up to be non-profit organizations (groups that don't make a profit). The Red Cross, the American Cancer Society, and the YMCA are examples of service organizations. Do you know of any service organizations in your community? When you grow up, you may want to work for or volunteer in a group like these.

Volunteer to Help

When you work for no pay, you are performing a voluntary service. Both civic and service organizations use volunteers. People who volunteer at soup kitchens or help build houses for Habitat for Humanity are providing an important service to the people in need who live in their community.

Leaders Work for Us

It's important to have leaders in order to get things done. That isn't always easy. Sometimes leaders need to do things that are not popular. For example, people don't usually like to have their taxes raised. But an elected official might vote for higher taxes because the extra money may help buy a fire engine or pay more police officers. The job of elected officials is all about public service. They take on the responsibility to do the right thing for the people who elected them. It is important for leaders to be fair, reliable, and honest. And when leaders are doing things that are unfair or dishonest, it's time for citizens to do something and get involved.

title: Declaration of Independence
text:
In the summer of 1776, the Second Continental Congress met in Philadelphia to discuss their independence. The leaders from each of the Colonies wanted the king to know the Colonies wished to govern themselves. Some Colonial leaders did not want to go to war, and they argued for days. Then they sent word home to their Colonies. "Discuss independence, and tell us how we should vote." Answers began coming in, and each time it was the same: "Vote for independence!"

Richard Henry Lee of Virginia told the Congress, "These United Colonies are, and of right ought to be, free and independent states." The Congress decided to declare the American Colonies independent. A document needed to be written. Thomas Jefferson was chosen to do the writing. He worked for two weeks writing and rewriting. After finishing it, he showed it to others, and a few more changes were made.

The first part of the Declaration explains that men have certain rights that can't be taken away. Those who signed declared these truths to be understood by everyone. The second part tells how the king refused to grant these rights. The document was then presented to the Congress. Once again, they argued about it.

The Second Continental Congress made the historic vote late on July 2, 1776. It was officially adopted on July 4, 1776. Though many colonists may have opposed independence, the delegates voted for independence (as did all of the Colonies but New York, who eventually supported it). The Declaration was read to most of the Colonies within a few weeks.

title: Bill of Rights
text:
In 1789, America adopted the United States Constitution. The Constitution made the U.S. a free nation, governed by the people. But the Constitution didn’t say how people’s rights were protected by law. Ten amendments, or laws, were added to the Constitution in 1791. This is known as the Bill of Rights.

The Bill of Rights protects the basic freedoms of U.S. citizens. These include freedom of speech, religion, and assembly. Citizens have the right to protest. They also have the right to bear arms, or to own weapons. No soldiers can enter people’s homes without permission. This is true in peacetime or war. No home or property can be searched or taken away without lawful reason. People cannot be forced to serve as witnesses against themselves if they have been accused of a crime. We all have the right to a speedy and public trial. We also have the right to a trial by jury. We are protected from cruel and unusual punishment. One citizen’s rights cannot get in the way of the rights of someone else. Any power that the federal government doesn’t have, the states can have.

title: The Constitution
text:
Although it seems normal now, the Constitution created a very new type of government. Citizens of the United States were used to living in a monarchy. A monarchy is ruled by a king or queen, and that ruler makes all the decisions. Two philosophers, named John Locke and Baron de Montesquieu, had different ideas. These philosophers believed in a social contract between a government and its people. This means that all people have rights and that the government should protect those rights. Many of the Founding Fathers read Locke and de Montesquieu and agreed with them. The 1776 Declaration of Independence first talked about the rights of people, stating, “We hold these truths to be self-evident: that all men are created equal.” Later, individual rights were guaranteed in the Bill of Rights, which was passed in 1791.

The Founding Fathers wanted to be sure that America did not become a monarchy with one person in charge. This is why the Constitution outlines three branches of government with checks and balances.

American government has these equal branches of government: the executive branch (president), the legislative branch (Congress), and the judicial branch (courts). The legislative branch is the House of Representatives and the Senate. These two groups pass laws. The executive branch is the president, who signs or vetoes laws.

Finally, the judicial branch of courts and judges makes sure the laws follow the Constitution. Think of a tree with three branches that are all the same size. Each of the branches has an equal role and makes sure the other branches do their jobs correctly. That is known as “checks and balances.”

The Constitution created a federal government. Some people worried that this new federal government would be too powerful and take away rights from the states. They wanted states to have more control. The Federalist Papers argued that a strong federal government is necessary. The Federalists said that a strong central government would help protect the United States from other countries. This government would be able to collect taxes. It would also unite the states and make them stronger as they work together. The states also needed a federal government to protect them from other countries.

The Constitution and Bill of Rights set up a government and protected rights. Do you notice that the rights of some groups of people are missing from the original Constitution? While the Bill of Rights guarantees freedoms, it did not always apply to all people living in the United States. Many African Americans were enslaved and did not enjoy those rights. American Indians were also not considered citizens of the United States. Women were denied some of the rights that men had. For example, women had to wait for the right to vote until 1920, when the 19th Amendment was passed. African Americans waited even longer.

The Fifteenth Amendment passed in 1870 and should have let all African American men vote, but in many places, that did not happen. In 1965, the Voting Rights Act was passed, which finally made sure all citizens 21 and older could vote. In 1921, the 26th Amendment was ratified, which lowered the voting age from 21 to 18. Today’s Constitution guarantees the same rights for all.

title: Honoring Celebrate Freedom Week
text:
What do you do to celebrate freedom? For one week in September every year, Texas observes Celebrate Freedom Week. This holiday reminds us to think about the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. Celebrate Freedom Week helps us recognize contributions and sacrifices made by our veterans and Founding Fathers. It also reminds us of our freedoms and rights as guaranteed by the Constitution. They all helped make this country secure, fair, and free. Circle the things you would like to do to celebrate your American freedom, and add some ideas of your own!

visit or talk to a soldier

have a moment of silence on November 11 at 11 a.m.

study the Declaration of Independence

recite part of the Declaration of Independence

study the Constitution

recite part of the Constitution

sing or listen to a patriotic song

discuss our rights as Americans

look at primary source pictures of our freedom documents

watch a video about American freedom

read a story about Thomas Jefferson or another Founding Father

draw a picture or make a poster about celebrating American freedom

wear red, white, and blue clothing

title: The First People in Texas
text:
Paleoamericans were the first people to live in North America. Paleo means ancient. The Paleoamerican way of life ended about 8,500 years ago.

Paleoamerican tools and weapons tell us a lot about these resourceful people. When people are resourceful, they find ways to do jobs using the materials available to them. Paleoamericans made all of their tools from stones, bones, and plants.

Paleoamericans made dart points from flint. Using antlers and stones, Paleoamericans shaped flint into very sharp points. This is called flintknapping. Paleoamericans were very skillful toolmakers. Their sharpest points were five times sharper than the scalpels used by today's surgeons. Since the hide of a mammoth was about six inches thick, they needed very sharp points to inflict a deadly wound.

If you lived during the last Ice Age, your home might have been a rock shelter with other Paleoamericans. A rock shelter is like a cave. It has a wider opening than a cave, but it isn't very deep. Paleoamericans may have also built huts using slender wooden poles and animal hides.

Paleoamericans were skillful fire starters. They knew how to use friction to make a fire by spinning a wooden shaft in a wooden base. This is hard work, and you have to know what kind of wood to use. Your wood has to reach a temperature of about 800 degrees Fahrenheit to start a fire.

title: Coming to North America
text:
Before European colonization, thousands of American Indians lived in the Americas and the Caribbean Islands. However, their ancestors were not originally from these regions. Many theories exist to explain how American Indians first arrived in the Western Hemisphere.

For many years, researchers believed that the ancient ancestors of American Indians came to America from Siberia, a region in northern Asia. They concluded that these people arrived about 12,000 years ago by hiking across a narrow strip of land that once bridged Asia and Alaska. This land bridge is known as the Bering Strait. From there, they settled in other areas of North America.

In recent years, archaeologists have discovered ancient tools, weapons, campsites, and skeletons that are even older than artifacts from the land bridge travelers. The bones, in particular, were very different from those linked to the people who crossed the land bridge. This new research suggests that a large group of migrants crossed the Bering Strait as early as 30,000 years ago. This larger group split into smaller tribes about 15,000 years ago. Some traveled south through the Americas.

Other researchers have proposed that the first people in the Americas traveled here by boat from southern Asia, Australia, India, Japan, or even Europe, arriving long before the land-bridge travelers. These people may have later died out. However, they also could have joined the Siberian tribes who migrated from Asia to Alaska via the Bering Strait. Combined, these groups could represent the American Indians’ earliest ancestors.

title: Albert Redder, Archaeologist
text:
What is an Archaeologist?

Archaeologists are people who study the artifacts of past groups of people. Artifacts are things made by people, then thrown away or left behind. Artifacts tell archaeologists about the culture of these people. When archaeologists study past cultures, they are learning how these people lived, what they made and what they believed. Archaeologists use science to help them learn everything they can from the artifacts they find.

A Childhood Discovery

If you think nothing important happens when you are a child, think again. Children often experience things that change their lives. That's what happened to Albert Redder. As a boy, he found arrowheads in the fields near his home. Al was fascinated with these ancient tools. He wanted to learn more about them and the people who made them. That's when Al ran into a problem. There weren't any books about archaeology in his hometown in northwest Texas.

Interest Grows

Al finally found the archaeology books he wanted to read when he joined the Army in World War II. The Army had some in its library for soldiers. Now he could read about the stone tools that captured his interest as a boy. When the war ended, Al moved to Waco. There, he found more books about archaeology. He continued learning about ancient tools and the people who made them.

An Unexpected Find

On July 4, 1954, Al made another discovery that changed his life. It was a hot summer day, and Al was enjoying a swim in the Brazos River. "I saw a rock shelter across the river," he said. "It was in a cliff overlooking the opposite shore." Al swam across the river to investigate the shelter. It was about 150 feet wide and 22 feet deep. He discovered that someone looking for artifacts had dug a hole in the south end of the shelter. Nearby, he discovered a smaller shelter. This one was hidden from view. He crawled through the brush and into the shelter. On its dirt floor, he found an old stone scraper and some bones. He knew right away that ancient people had lived in these shelters.

Excavating the Shelter

In about 1960, Al put his knowledge of archaeology to work. He decided to look for evidence of early Americans on the Brazos River. "Since someone had already dug in the larger shelter, I decided to excavate the smaller shelter."

When an archaeologist excavates an area, he digs carefully to uncover the artifacts. An archaeologist also uses math skills to measure everything he finds. He uses a grid to record where he finds each artifact.

In the smaller shelter, Al found evidence of early human activity. "That's when I decided there might be more to find in the larger shelter." The larger shelter became known as the Horn Shelter. It was named after the people who owned the property where the shelter was located. The Horn family gave Al permission to work in the shelter.

The Discovery of a Lifetime

Al and three other archaeologists began excavating the Horn Shelter in November 1966. Al Redder, Frank Watts and Tom Francis excavated the south end of the shelter. Bob Forrester excavated the north end. On Aug. 15, 1970, Al made the find of his life. Fifteen feet below the surface he found a skeleton of a girl. "I realized right then that it was a paleoburial," he said.

Keeping their discovery a secret was very important. They knew people would destroy the site to get artifacts to sell or add to their collections. In spite of their efforts, a few people found out. Some even rented a plane and flew up and down the Brazos River looking for the Horn Shelter. Al and Frank knew they had to work quickly.

On Oct. 30, 1970, they began excavating the area around the skeleton. The body had been buried under limestone slabs, so they had to be very careful. Much to their surprise, they found a second skeleton. The second skeleton was a man. The two had been buried together.

Al and Frank completed their work three days later. When their excavating was over, they had found the most complete Paleoamerican burial in North America. It was 11,200 years old! Al and Frank continued excavating the shelter until the early 1990s.

When Al found his first arrowhead as a young boy, he had no idea that it was the beginning of a journey that would lead to one of the greatest discoveries in North American archaeology. When asked what he thought students should learn from his work, Al said, "Collecting artifacts is like burning a book. Each artifact is a page in the book. It tells an important story. The place where you find an artifact is part of that story. When you take one artifact from a site, it is like ripping a page from a book."

You will learn more about some of the artifacts Al found in the Horn Shelter burial. Because these artifacts were left in place for thousands of years, they tell us a lot about the people who lived in Texas during the last Ice Age.

title: Paleoamerican Life
text:
We may not know where the first Texans came from, but we do know something about the way they lived. To understand their way of life, you have to know more about the world in which they lived.

Paleoamerican Food

The Paleoamericans of Texas were not farmers. They gathered the plants they ate. Nuts, berries and wild fruits were part of their diet. Meat was also an important food source. Paleoamerican hunters probably followed the herds of mammoth and bison. They could tell how far they were from a herd by placing their fingers in the dung the animals left behind. If the dung was warm, they knew they were close. If it was cold, they were far behind. If the hunters could not separate a healthy animal from the herd, they looked for injured or sick ones. Old animals near death were also easy prey. They waited for these animals to die or fall behind the herd. When this happened, they would attack. Paleoamericans hunted and ate smaller animals like rabbits, too. They also ate fish.

There is another way the Paleoamericans found the meat they needed. You may want to wait until after you've eaten to read about this one. Paleoamericans also dined on animals that had been dead for days. Remember, these people knew what it was like to starve. They weren't about to turn down a meal, even if it was decomposing, or rotting.

Paleoamerican Clothing

Since the weather in Texas was colder than it is now, Paleoamericans needed to stay warm. Animal hides provided most of their clothing. If they could not find the animals they needed for food, they didn't have the hides they needed for clothes. They may have also used plant materials to make clothes.

Paleoamerican Health

It is difficult for us to imagine how tough life must have been for the Paleoamericans of Texas. They could not always get out of bad weather. They knew what it was like to starve. They lived with serious injuries. Their teeth decayed and often fell out at an early age.

The daily job of finding food was hard work. There were no roads or sidewalks. They had to walk on rocky ground and climb over hills and boulders. They had to push their way through thick brush full of thorns. Crossing rivers and streams could also be dangerous, especially after a hard rain.

And there was another problem facing the Paleoamericans. While they were hunting food, they were also being hunted. Dire wolves, saber-tooth cats and short-face bears may have hunted them for food!

All of these dangers meant these early Texans lived shorter lives. A few may have lived into their 60s, or even older. Most, however, died when they were about half that age. Paleoamericans had to be tough or they could not have lived for more than a week or two.

Paleoamerican Homes

Some Paleoamericans were nomads. Nomads are people who travel throughout the year instead of living in one place. They move from place to place in search of food. Rivers were often their highways. Traveling along a river gave them easy access to water and food. Many times, they followed the animals they hunted, even if the animals left the rivers.

Other Paleoamericans in Texas may have had a base camp. A base camp was their home for most of the year. Instead of following their prey, they left the base camp to hunt for food. When they found it, they brought it back to camp. Archeologists are finding evidence of this at the Gault site. The Gault site is a 13,000-year-old Paleoamerican campsite between Georgetown and Killeen.

title: Horn Shelter Treasures
text:
Two complete skeletons were found in the Horn Shelter. One was a girl about 12 years old. The second was man about 40 years old. Archaeologists wanted to know what the man looked like. Doug Owsley at the Smithsonian Institution worked with an artist named Amanda Danning to re-create the face of the man. They nicknamed him Sam.

Sam's face surprised everyone. He did not look like traditional American Indians or like Europeans. Doug Owsley thinks he may have been related to the Ainu. The Ainu are a tribe of people from Japan. They have light-colored skin and have lived in Japan for a long time.

No one can tell how the two people buried in the Horn Shelter died. The only clue Doug Owsley found was a bad tooth infection in the man. If a tooth infection gets bad enough, it can lead to death. He found no clues about how the girl died.

The only thing buried with the girl was a needle made of bone. Several items were buried with the man. Three turtle shells were stacked under his head. Another turtle shell was in front of his face. A fifth turtle shell was under his hips. It is clear that turtles had special meaning for these ancient people.

Archaeologists found something strange in the man's mouth - six hawk claws and five badger claws. Some of them think this might mean he was a healer or a special person among his people.

Archaeologists also found a tool kit. The stone tools in this kit had not been used. Coyote teeth and parts of two antlers were also found. Many beads were in the burial, including 80 small seashell beads. Some of these beads came from far away. This suggests they met some of their needs by trading with others.

When asked what artifact found in the burial impressed him the most, Albert Redder said, "The bone needle. It was so finely made, and it was the only thing buried with the girl."

The Bosque Museum in Clifton has an excellent exhibit about the Horn Shelter burial. You can also see the bust of Sam on display. Call (254) 675-3845 for more details, or write: Bosque Museum, 301 S. Ave. Q, Clifton, TX 76634.

title: Archaic Indians in Texas
text:
When the last Ice Age ended, the way people lived in North America changed. The large animals they hunted became extinct. The climate grew warmer. The land began to change. This was a slow change that ended about 8,500 years ago. This date marks the end of the Paleoamerican way of life and the beginning of the Archaic way of life.

The Archaic Indians of the Lower Pecos were one of the most interesting ancient cultures in North America. They lived in Texas along the Pecos River, near the present-day towns of Langtry and Comstock. The Lower Pecos region is also part of the eastern edge of the Chihuahuan Desert.

Deep canyons run through the Lower Pecos. Many of these canyons have rock shelters that were once used by the Paleoamericans. When the climate changed, they became the homes and sacred places of the Archaic Indians of the Lower Pecos. Thanks to the dry desert climate, archaeologists are making exciting discoveries in these rock shelters.

Joe Labadie is an archaeologist with the National Park Service in the Lower Pecos. "This is one of the greatest archaeological regions," he said. "Nowhere else in the United States can you find cave paintings and the remains of mammoths and short-faced bears. Other regions just have stones and bones. Because of the dry desert climate in the Lower Pecos, plant and animal matter has been preserved for thousands of years."

The remains Labadie is talking about aren't just plant and animal remains. Many human remains have been found in this area. "The tiny nodes on their molars tell us if they are related to other groups of people,” he said. “The Archaic Indians of the Lower Pecos were a distinct group. They were not related to other groups.”

This week, you will also learn about the cave paintings made by the Archaic Indians of the Lower Pecos. They painted incredible images of humans, animals, and other designs. Some of the scenes show battles. Others show ghostly figures that appear to be half-human and half-animal and are flying through the air.

Do the Archaic Indians of the Lower Pecos sound interesting? They are, but very few people know about them and the archaeological treasures they left behind. You are about to discover them. Get ready to step into the world of these ancient Texans.

title: A Dead Man Tells His Story
text:
Thanks to modern science, the dead can once again tell some of their stories. The science used by police to solve crimes also helps archaeologists learn about the ancient bodies they discover. That's what happened with a mummy found in the Lower Pecos.

A very unusual male mummy was found buried in a rock shelter. The man's body had been wrapped in a woven mat. The mat was secured with 111 feet of rope. That might not seem so unusual, until you hear the rope was made entirely of human hair!

The story of the man gets even more interesting. This poor fellow's insides had been preserved, and his intestines were swollen to an enormous size. Your intestines are part of your digestive system. Archaeologists were interested in this, so they checked the contents of the man's intestines. They found many foods, including a mouse. They also found that he had swallowed an entire ribbon snake. And they found out why his intestines were swollen. The man had Chagas Disease. This is a disease you can get from a conenose bug. The disease blocked the food he ate from leaving his body after it was digested. All of the food kept stacking up inside him, making his intestines swell. Archaeologists estimate that he lived about a year before the disease finally took his life.

title: Becoming a Man in the Archaic Indian World
text:
These stories are historical fiction. The characters are made up, but what they do is probably what real Archaic Indians would have done.

"Lizard Boy, you are not ready to be a man," my father said. His words angered me, because he is wrong. I will go to him again tomorrow with proof that I am ready to stand with our hunters.

"Father, I know the traditions of our people," I will say. Then I will take him to each sacred painting in our rock shelter and tell what they mean. I will show him the painting of the spitting panther that has lost half its blood. He spews blood out of his mouth because our hunters are mightier than the most dangerous animal in the desert.

Then I will take my father to the shaman paintings. "A shaman is a holy man who can turn into animals. He can become a deer, a bird or a rabbit," I will tell him. "A shaman flies to the spirit world and returns with words from the Great Spirit." When my father hears this, he will know I look to the Great Spirit for power.

Next, I will take him to the warriors' handprints in Antler Cave. "Watch as I make sacred paint, Father. When you say that I am a man, I will use this paint to place my print next to those of the other warriors."

Fat is needed to make paint. It is also important to our diet and hard to find. Without fat to eat, we grow sick and die. Then I will show my father the bone marrow I have saved. "I could have eaten this but saved it to make paint," I will say. "This proves I am willing to make sacrifices for my people."

I will tell my father I know about the evil spirits that come out at night and hide in dark places during the day. "I will not fall for their tricks. I know where evil hides, and I will not go near those places, especially Panther Cave. You have my promise that I will die before I enter such a place." Then I will say, "I also know my enemies. The warriors of the Vulture people want to kill us. You must believe that I am brave enough to fight them."

After my father has heard these words, I will give him more proof. I will make a fire drill and start a fire. I will even use plants that are hard to burn to show him that I am ready for challenges.

While my fire burns, I will make stone tools. The points I make are not as sharp as his, but they will kill an animal. I will ask my father if I may use his atlatl and spears to go on a hunt. "Wait for me and keep my fire going," I will tell him. "You will need it to cook the food I bring back. When you see the deer I kill, you will know that I can use weapons to feed and defend our people."

When we have eaten the meat I killed, I will take him to a very sacred place. This place is a deep hole in ground where we send our dead when they have passed from this life. "Great Spirit," I will pray, "teach me to be wise like those who have gone before me."

When my father hears my words and sees my actions, his heart will be changed. He will say to me, "Lizard Boy, you are now a man!"

My People are Starving!

When our hunters did not return, I knew something was wrong. Our camp near Panther Cave was filled with a terrible sadness. Children were hungry and crying. The women were sad. I asked questions, but the old ones did not want me to know about the danger. They think I am too young to know. My father and brother were with the hunters. I had to know. So I hid when the old ones were talking and heard the truth. They believe our hunters are dead. They caught me listening and scolded me. I told them I would help save my people. They laughed and called me Woman Too Young because I am a girl acting like a woman.

I watch as my people do things that will not save us. We only find enough food to hold off death a few more days. We should move to a new camp, but we cannot leave without hunters. The old ones can no longer hunt. The women gather food, but every day they bring back less. They have picked all of the tuna from the prickly pear cactus growing nearby. Roots are easy to find but they must be cooked. It takes many armloads of firewood to heat the rocks to line the hearth, and we have burned up most of the wood in the desert around our camp.

Instead of digging roots, the women now look for holes in the ground. They jab the sharp end of a stick in the hole, hoping to stab rats and snakes, but these tiny creatures are not enough to feed everyone.

Each morning the boys hunt jackrabbits with rabbit sticks. The jackrabbits do not know it, but they are safe around these boys. At least the boys find some grasshoppers to eat while they are hunting.

When my people spend their days looking for snails to eat, I will know we are near death. I fear it will be soon. If our hunters do not return, I will leave our camp and find help. I am Woman Too Young, and I will not let my people starve.

title: Joe Labadie, Archaeologist
text:
"I never got over being four years old." That's how Joe Labadie describes his love for archaeology. "My grandfather sparked my interest when I was a boy. He was a lawyer who worked with the Warm Springs Indians. He sent me letters with an artifact taped to each letter."

Early in life, Joe faced problems that would have stopped many people. He had polio as a child. When he was a young adult, a doctor found a tumor on his spine. Part of his spine had to be removed.

Joe refused to quit. He studied archaeology in college and graduated in half the time it takes most people. After graduating, the best job Joe could find was working as a seasonal archaeologist. Seasonal archaeologists are hired to do a specific job. When the job is over, they have to look for another job.

In 1986, Joe was excavating the earthworks near the Alamo. This is where the Mexican army dug in to fight the Texans. Joe found two cannonballs and three bayonets. "These were surplus goods the British army didn't need, so they sold them to Mexico."

Newspapers around the world reported Joe's finds. National Geographic published an article about him. Joe's accomplishments helped him get a full-time job with the National Parks Service.

Archaeology can be dangerous work. In 1995, Joe slipped off a cliff while doing research. His injuries required four surgeries, but that didn't stop him. He continues to find clues about the past.

When Joe was asked what he hoped fourth-grade students could learn from his work, he said, "Don't make excuses for your failures. Look for reasons why you can do something. Don't look for reasons why you can't."

What great advice for students and teachers! It also describes the Archaic Indians of the Lower Pecos. They were determined to survive. The hard work of Joe Labadie and other archaeologists tells us how they lived.

title: Can I borrow that tool?
text:
Archaeologists use a lot of tools that other people use in their jobs. Trowels, used to put mortar on bricks, are used to help dig through dirt. Shovels, like gardeners use, helps move a lot of dirt. But they are cautious with them so as not to harm artifacts. The handbroom and dustpan you use at home for cleaning are used to move small amounts of soil. Carpenters use tape measures when measuring wood. Archaeologists use tape measures to create maps and help measure the size of the unit and depth of the dig. Transits, like those used by surveyors, are used to help map a site as well. Cameras are used to take pictures of the site. They can study the area, seeing what it looked like during the different stages of the dig. Dental picks and wood tongue depressors, like those in doctors offices, help get soil in tight or small locations. Researchers sometimes even use toothbrushes to clear dirt or clean an object they find.

A lot of the tools are costly and specialized. Computers are used to look down through the soil layers. With these tools, they can see objects without digging or disturbing the area. GPS tools help the workers from getting lost and mapping their finds. Probes and chisels help break away stone from objects. Chemicals can preserve artifacts, keeping them from cracking or breaking up.

Using these tools from other people's jobs helps archaeologists make some fantastic discoveries.

title: Break the Code and Find the Mystery Word
text:
Directions

Each letter of the alphabet below is represented by a number. Use this code to find the missing words or phrases in each sentence below.

title: Making a TimeLine: How Long Ago Did They Live?
text:
Materials

one sheet of legal-size paper

one pen

ruler

Directions

1. Turn your paper so the long side goes from left to right, or across. Draw a line 14 inches long. The left end of the line represents the time when the first people arrived in Texas. The right end represents the current year. Each inch represents 1,000 years.

2. Measure 8½ inches from the right side of your line. Make a mark with your pen.

3. Measure 1½ inches from the right side of your line. Make a mark with your pen.

4. Look at the space between your mark at 8½ inches and the end of the line on the left. This space represents the amount of time the Paleoamericans were in Texas. Write “Paleoamericans” in this space.

5. Look at the space between your mark at 8½ inches and the one at 1½ inches. This space represents the Archaic period in Texas. Write “Archaic” in this space.

6. Save your timeline for next week. That is when you will learn about the next era in Texas history.

title: The End of Prehistoric Texas
text:
We've covered a lot of time - thousands of years! - in Texas Studies Weekly these past few weeks, haven't we? You've learned that during the last Ice Age, Paleoamericans hunted giant beasts like the mammoth. You know that when the Ice Age ended, the climate warmed. The land we call Texas changed. As the giant beasts became extinct, people had to change the way they lived. Last week, you studied the Archaic Indians of the Lower Pecos. You read about many artifacts that were preserved in the desert.

This week's adventure takes place during the Late Prehistoric time in Texas history. We know more about the Late Prehistoric Indians in Texas than we do about the Paleoamericans and Archaic Indians. They were the people who greeted the first European explorers. Some explorers, like Cabeza de Vaca and La Salle, wrote about them in journals.

Big changes were taking place in Texas during the Late Prehistoric time. About 1,500 years ago, an amazing new invention found its way into Texas - the bow and arrow. This new weapon was just as powerful, easier to use and more accurate than the atlatl. Other changes took place when a large group of American Indians known as the Mississippian Culture spread out through much of the eastern part of North America. Some of them came to east Texas and became known as the Caddo. They were farmers and mound builders. Texas gets its name from the Caddo word, Tayshas, which means "allies" or "friends." You'll learn more about them inside.

In South Texas, groups of American Indians known as the Coahuiltecan lived in the toughest conditions of all. Coahuiltecan is really the name of a language, not a tribe. But we use that word when we talk about the American Indians living in south Texas. The Coahuiltecan had fewer resources than any other American Indians in Texas. How they survived is a story you will not want to miss!

Finally, we will learn about the Jornada Mogollon and the Jumano. The Jornada were a Puebloan culture in west Texas. Remember reading about the rock art of the Archaic last week? The Jornada painted amazing rock art, too. The Jumano are more of a mystery. Archaeologists are struggling to learn more about this lost culture. Turn the page - there's more to learn!

title: Who Came to America First?
text:
You have probably learned that some of the first people to come to North America crossed a land bridge between Asia and Alaska around 12,000 years ago. New discoveries on the East Coast support the idea that other people may have arrived earlier.

In sites in Maryland, Virginia and Pennsylvania, archaeologists have found several dozen stone tools and have dated them between 19,000 to 26,000 years old. These tools are similar to ones used by some European groups. This discovery could mean that 10,000 years BEFORE the ancestors of the American Indians crossed the land bridge to Alaska, Europeans had already crossed the Atlantic Ocean and landed in North America.

How did they get here? If these "earliest" people came from western Europe, they would've made the 1,500-mile trip across the Atlantic. The northern Atlantic at this time was covered in almost three million square miles of thick ice for most of the year. One theory is that the people traveled where the ice met the ocean. They could have used boats or walked, hunting for fish and other animals.

With these new discoveries, more archaeologists are looking in other places in Tennessee, Maryland and Texas where they believe even more European Stone Age evidence will be found. Not all archaeologists agree with the Atlantic Ocean theory. There is a lot more work to be done, but someday we might have a clearer picture of who got here first!

title: Late Prehistoric Indians
text:
The Caddo: Mound Builders of East Texas

The Caddo first settled in east Texas in about 700 C.E. They were part of the great Mississippian Culture. By 1050 C.E., the Mississippian culture was the strongest and most powerful culture in the heart of North America. Cahokia (in Illinois) was the center of this culture.

The Mississippian people were mound builders. Their largest mound was in Cahokia. It was 10 stories high. Its base covered 16 acres. This mound was larger than the great pyramids of Egypt. The Mississippian people built temples on some of the mounds, and other mounds were used for burials.

The first Caddo in Texas did not begin building mounds right away. Mound building took place slowly over the next 400 to 500 years. Their mounds were also used as temples and for burials. They only built mounds in the villages where they held ceremonies.

The Caddo had a special kind of government called a confederacy. In this government, many tribes joined together under one leader but kept their own chief as well. It's sort of like the United States being led by the president, but each state has its own governor. This is different from the Comanche who lived in bands, a smaller group than a tribe.

The Caddo were farmers. They planted corn, beans, squash, sunflower seeds, and tobacco. They also grew cotton. Like earlier people, they gathered berries and nuts for food.

Archaeologists think less than half of the Caddo's diet came from farming. They supplied the rest of their food by hunting and gathering. Plenty of game like deer, bear, and wild hogs lived in the woods of East Texas. The Caddo killed bears for their fat. They stored the fat in pots for long periods of time. They hunted birds like turkeys and ducks. Rabbits, snakes, and mice were part of their diet, too.

The Caddo also fished. Modern fishers still use one of their inventions, the trotline. Caddo fishers would stretch a line over the water. They tied smaller lines to the main line. Each smaller line had a hook with bait attached to it. They checked the trotline often.

The Caddo lived in round grass huts shaped like beehives. These huts were very tall. Their diameter ranged from 25 to 45 feet. The diameter of a round hut is found by measuring the distance through the center from one side to the other. About 30 to 40 people lived in each of these homes.

The Caddo were also talented artists. They made beautiful pottery, jewelry, and ceremonial objects. The first Europeans to see the Caddo were surprised by their appearance. Men and women decorated their bodies and faces with tattoos. These tattoos may have told what clan, or family, they belonged to.

During the 19th century, the Caddo were eventually forced to move to a government-assigned reservation on the Brazos River. Later they had to move again, this time to Oklahoma, where many of them live today.

The Karankawa: Natives of the Gulf Coast

Karankawa is a name given to many small bands of people who lived along the Gulf Coast from Galveston Island to Corpus Christi. Each band was a group of 30 to 40 people who tattooed their bodies and pierced their chests and lower lips.

The Karankawa were a tall, muscular people. They bragged about being tough and proved it by doing things like breaking the ice in a pond to take a bath. Karankawa huts were not covered on all sides and were more like windbreaks. They didn't provide much protection from the cold and rain. As tough as they were, the Karankawa couldn't stand mosquitoes. They coated their skin with alligator grease to keep them away.

Karankawa children also lived hard lives. When they were old enough to do small jobs, children were put to work. They had to start taking care of themselves as soon as they were able.

The Karankawa were nomads (people who move from place to place) who seldom stayed in one place for more than a few weeks. During the summer, they lived on the islands where they used their long, powerful bows to hunt fish. In the winter, they moved to the mainland and ate oysters they gathered at the shore. The Karankawa never had an abundance of food.

The Karankawa used the natural resources of the Gulf Coast to make items they needed to survive. They made dugout canoes from trees to travel through marshes and lagoons. They flattened one side of the tree trunk and left the bark on the other. Then they burned or scraped out the inside.

Karankawa pottery was lined with asphaltum. Asphaltum is black sticky stuff that often washes up on Texas beaches. It's sort of like the stuff we use to make roads today. The Karankawa used it to waterproof their pottery and baskets and to attach arrowheads to the shafts.

When Europeans arrived in Texas, the Karankawa fought back. It was a fight they would lose. About 200 years ago, the Karankawa culture died out.

title: Lost and Found Cultures
text:
Jornada Mogollon

In 1975, a pueblo was discovered near El Paso. It didn't appear to be much at first. By 1990, however, archaeologists had uncovered an ancient village of the Jornada Mogollon.

The Jornada Mogollon settled in the El Paso area about 600 C.E. Each family lived in a one-room pithouse. Part of a pithouse was underground. Its only entrance was on the roof. The Jornada were part of the Puebloan Culture that stretched into New Mexico, Mexico and beyond. About 1200 C.E., they stopped building pithouses and built their homes above ground. These new homes had many rooms.

The Jornada raised corn, beans and squash. They also hunted with bows and arrows. Rock art tells us about the religion of the Jornada. Archaeologists believe they were influenced by traders who taught them about a religion from Mexico and Central America. Some of the paintings are of an Aztec god who was a sky and creator god.

Jumano

Very little is known about the Jumano. Archaeologists think there were three groups of these American Indians. The groups lived in an area from New Mexico to Texas and south into Mexico. Some of the Jumano lived around present-day Presidio along the Rio Grande. The Jumano were like the Jornada. They were a Puebloan Culture who built pithouses and grew corn, beans and squash. Other Jumano were nomadic and roamed across Texas hunting buffalo. It is thought that these people spent their winters along the Rio Grande.

Hundreds of rock art paintings along the Concho River at Paint Rock are believed to have been made by the Jumano. Some of the paintings mark the beginning of each of the seasons of the year. A dagger of sunlight marks the beginning of winter. No one knows what became of the Jumano.

title: The Coahuiltecan: Real Survivors
text:
The bands of nomads called the Coahuiltecan often fought against each other. Perhaps that is because the land between San Antonio and Brownsville was a difficult place to live. Food was hard to find. Ground mesquite beans made up most of their diet. One of their favorite foods was made by mixing mesquite flour, dirt, and water in a hole. If the mix didn't taste right, they threw in more dirt. Sometimes they ate pecans, tuna (the fruit of the prickly pear cactus), and the powdered bones of fish and snakes. If these foods weren't available, they ate spiders, grubs, ant eggs, and even deer dung. Wow — they really were tough!

Women did most of the gathering. When a hunter killed a deer, the women had to bring it back to camp. Women also told the men when to go to war. They gathered around a fire to complain about their enemies. If they complained enough, the men would get their weapons and prepare for battle.

The Coahuiltecan lived in huts. Early Europeans said their camps were nasty and smelly, with garbage thrown all around. Maybe they were just too busy surviving to have time for cleaning, especially if they were planning to move soon. Most historians believe that the Coahuiltecan were slowly absorbed into other cultures.

title: Comanche: Lords of the Plains
text:
When people hear the name Comanche, they often think of an exciting and dangerous time in Texas history. The Comanche lived in bands scattered throughout most of Texas. Each band was ruled by a peace chief and a war chief. Their skill in battle made the Comanche the Lords of the Plains.

Before the Comanche came to Texas, they were one of the bands of Shoshone Indians in the northern Rocky Mountains. No one knows exactly why, but they moved to New Mexico in the early 1700s. They found horses the Spanish left behind. It didn't take long for them to become some of the finest horsemen in North America.

School for a Comanche boy was learning how to handle horses. Warriors taught them how to fight on horseback. The warriors knew how to make the horse a moving shield. While the horse was galloping at full speed, a Comanche warrior could hang over the side of his horse and shoot arrows underneath the horse's neck. School for Comanche girls was learning how to put up and take down a teepee. They also learned to tan hides and make them into useful things.

These fearless warriors on horseback pushed into Texas, forcing the tribes who were already there to leave or die. In less than 100 years, the Comanche controlled the southern Plains.

The Comanche were bison hunters. They had dozens of ways of using the bison. Many of the things the Comanche needed to survive came from these animals. All year, they followed the bison. Sometimes this took them out of Texas and far to the north or west.

The first settlers who moved into Texas in the early 1800s made the Comanche angry. The settlers built houses on their hunting grounds. The trickle of settlers coming into Texas turned into a flood after Texas declared its independence from Mexico in 1836. That's when the Comanche declared war on the settlers.

Comanche war parties raided settlers' homes to try to drive them away. They usually killed the men and women. If the women were spared, they might become enslaved. Children were often taken back to their camps and raised as Comanche. Cynthia Ann Parker was the most famous captive. She married a Comanche warrior. Their son became a Comanche chief named Quanah Parker.

Most people think the U.S. Army defeated the Comanche and other Plains Indians. But other things helped end the American Indian way of life, too. Diseases like smallpox and cholera killed many during the 1800s. White buffalo hunters killed bison by the thousands. With fewer and fewer bison, the native people could not survive. Most moved to reservations set up by the U.S. government.

title: A Neanderthal’s Best Friend
text:
Archeologists in both Siberia and Belgium have found dog skulls that show wolves were well on their way to becoming domesticated dogs (pets or helpers for people) about 33,000 years ago. This means the change started about 14,000 years earlier than scientists once thought. How do we know the skulls were 33,000 years old? Scientists use a technique called carbon dating to figure it out. Carbon dating is a way to date things that were once alive by looking at how fast a certain type of carbon in the remains will decay.

This discovery also means that dogs were being domesticated in different areas of the world at the same time. The skulls show that people on two different continents were using dogs as pets or helpers.

Scientists once believed that cows, sheep and goats were domesticated first because they could provide meat and milk for prehistoric people. However, it seems dogs were domesticated first to give companionship and protection and to help during hunts.

Scientists don't think the dogs that were in Siberia or Belgium back then are the ancestors of our modern dog. Instead, they believe that many of these dogs died out during the Ice Age. Through DNA research, scientists have discovered that modern dogs come from the Middle East and East Asia. People and dogs have been best friends for a very long time!

title: Historic American Indians
text:
Comanche Enemies

Lipan Apache

Before the Comanche arrived, the Apache lived throughout the southwest. Apache is the Zuni word for "enemy." The Lipan were an eastern Apache band. In the 1600s, they found horses. They were one of the first tribes to make horses an important part of their way of life. The Lipan hunted bison from the panhandle to central Texas. In the spring, they set up camps where the women planted corn, squash, beans, and pumpkins. After the harvest, they moved on. The Lipan made a journey once a year to trade with pueblo villages in the west.

When the Comanche came to Texas in the 1700s, the Lipan were no match for their warriors. The Lipan retreated to west Texas, where life was more difficult. The women did not know how to grow crops there. The Lipan once captured a boy named Frank Buckelew. The women asked if he knew how to plant crops. Much of what we know about the Lipan comes from Buckelew.

Many Lipan men had a unique hairstyle. The hair on the left side of their heads was cut short enough that it barely touched their ears. They let the hair on the right grow as long as possible, sometimes to the ground. Long hair could get in the way. They usually tied it up so it only reached their shoulders. Like the Comanche, Lipan men did not like facial hair. They even plucked out their eyebrows. Then they painted their faces and other parts of their bodies.

Tonkawa

The Tonkawa lived in central Texas. Tonkawa is a Wichita name, meaning "they all stay together." The Tonkawa called themselves "the most human of people."

The Apache to the north were enemies of the Tonkawa. This kept the Tonkawa from hunting bison on the plains of north Texas. Occasionally, bison would stray south and give the Tonkawa some much-needed food. They got most of their food from fishing, gathering, and hunting animals like deer.

The Tonkawa had a history of helping others fight their battles. When the Comanche came to Texas, the Tonkawa helped them fight the Apache. Later, when the Comanche became a threat to them, they helped the Apache fight the Comanche.

Early white settlers found the Tonkawa to be somewhat friendly. In fact, the Tonkawa took quite an interest in them. Sometimes Tonkawa showed up at church services or weddings without an invitation. They were fascinated by these newcomers and just wanted to watch.

Clint Smith told about the time some Tonkawa men came to their cabin when his father was gone. His mother and sister stopped the band. The men said they were hungry. Clint's mother agreed to prepare a meal if they would stack their guns at the door. When they were full, the men took off their jackets and turned them into pouches. Then they stuffed them with all the extra food before leaving the Smith's cabin.

The Tonkawa helped defend the settlers against the Comanche. Later, they helped the U.S. Army fight other tribes. Sadly, settlers who did not know the Tonkawa attacked and killed many of them in the following years. Very few, if any, remain — a sad ending for those who called themselves "the most human of people."

Comanche Allies

Wichita

The Wichita moved into north Texas during the mid-1700s. The Wichita were dark-skinned people who called themselves the "Kitikiti'sh." This means "raccoon-eyed." Wichita men and women tattooed their faces heavily. The men even tattooed the area around their eyes. This made their eyes look like a raccoon's.

The Wichita had two kinds of houses. They lived in cone-shaped, straw huts during farming season. After the harvest, they hunted bison and lived in tepees.

At first, the Comanche were enemies of the Wichita. Later, French traders succeeded in making the Comanche and Wichita allies. Allies are groups that are on the same side in a conflict or war. This helped the Wichita. They grew stronger while helping the French and Plains Indians trade with one another.

In the 1800s, disease and fighting with the white settlers killed many of the Wichita. While the Comanche continued to fight, the Wichita moved away from the conflicts. Today, the Wichita live in Oklahoma.

Kiowa

The Kiowa were one of the last tribes to come to Texas. Their territory included the eastern part of the Texas panhandle, but most of their land was in Oklahoma. The Kiowa were a small tribe who survived by hunting bison. In about 1790, the Kiowa became allies of the Comanche.

Kiowa warriors were fierce. Their tribe had a number of military societies, or groups, that fought in battle. When boys were ready, they joined a society called the Rabbits. Two warriors trained them to hunt, make war and provide for their people. The Rabbits held feasts where they did a special dance, during which they jumped and hopped like rabbits. The Koitsenko was a society for the bravest Kiowa warriors. Only 10 warriors were chosen for this group. The Kiowa continued to fight on the side of the Comanche. In the 1870s, the Kiowa were finally forced onto a government-assigned reservation in Oklahoma.

title: American Indian Society
text:
American Indian groups like the Wichita and Comanche lived in bands throughout the plains of Texas. Horses were a very important part of life for these native peoples. They were used to hunt game and transport people and goods when they moved their villages. Plains peoples lived in tepees and had to move often to follow the herds they hunted.

Traditionally, men hunted for game, while women gathered foods such as fruits, seeds, roots, nuts, and other things to eat. American Indians used things in nature without hurting or polluting the environment. They used tall wooden poles for their tepees. The poles could also be used to make a travois to transport their belongings. Materials that were light to carry and easy to transport without breaking were favored by the Plains tribes. They wove baskets out of plant fibers and grass mats out of grass for the floors of their tepees. Nothing was wasted, and anything they took from nature was treated with respect. For example, after a hunter killed an animal, they thanked it and honored it for giving up its life to help the tribe. They used every part of the animal and did not waste anything.

The bison in particular was an important animal to tribes of the Plains. Millions of bison once roamed the Great Plains. The bison was a sacred animal to the Plains tribes because it met so many of their basic needs. Dozens of products could come from a single bison. A bison was like a walking department store for native peoples. The bison gave them food, shelter, and much more. The tribes followed the herds of bison to meet their needs.

Bison hides could be made into blankets, tepees, and even shields. Hides were also used to make bags in which warriors carried objects that were sacred to them. Other parts of the bison were used to make items like tools, glue, rattles, fly swatters, bowstrings, and thread for sewing.

One bison could feed several families for many weeks. Because it was such a valuable resource, American Indians and others who hunted for food were careful to not over hunt the bison.

title: Rumination and Contemplation: Bacon’s Rebellion
text:
rumination (n): a thought; a pondering
contemplation (n): a deep thought; reflection

Were you ever in a situation where you reacted quickly without thinking the problem through? What happened? Let's look at Bacon's Rebellion in Jamestown, Virginia, in 1676. As you read, think about whether the leaders used rumination and contemplation during the events.

Most people in the Virginia colony were farmers who had to deal with high taxes, low tobacco prices and problems trading with Europe. Hailstorms, floods and hurricanes destroyed many crops, and some American Indian groups attacked plantations.

Governor William Berkeley ignored the farmers' call for help, and a young Englishman stepped forward. Nathaniel Bacon asked for permission to lead the army to drive all American Indians out of Virginia. Gov. Berkeley refused. He didn't want to upset the friendly American Indians who traded with them. Bacon took a group of volunteer soldiers anyway and led a raid. They attacked American Indians who had not even been part of the earlier attacks.

Gov. Berkeley declared Bacon a rebel guilty of treason, but Bacon gathered almost 500 soldiers and took over Jamestown. They controlled the town from July to September of 1676. When Gov. Berkeley and his army took back control, Bacon was furious. His troops burned Jamestown to the ground.

Suddenly, Bacon got very sick and died. Gov. Berkeley arrested and hanged many of Bacon's men. However, King Charles II of England was not happy with Berkeley and chose a new governor.

Find examples when both leaders acted without rumination and contemplation. What might have been different if they had thought about the situation carefully? Imagine that you were Gov. Berkeley or Nathaniel Bacon. What would you have done differently?
