title: A Comanche Government
text:
As one of the largest tribes in American Indian history, the Comanche were an important part of Texas culture. They began as a hunter-gatherer tribe but soon became extremely skilled horse riders. Riding horses allowed them to travel farther. They migrated to Texas to hunt bison.

The Comanche tribe was made up of 12 smaller tribes. They wanted to continue to expand and sometimes fought other tribes for land. In fact, they became known for their abilities as warriors.

The Comanche were skilled in trade and were known at the surrounding trading posts. They had their own constitution, laws, police, and other services. They also had a tribal council, elected officials, and chiefs who helped to make the laws. Their governmental structure helped the Comanche to make their mark in American history.

The Caddo was another important tribe in Texas. They were farmers. Their descendants were based on a matrilineal system. This means that children would be named based on their mother's side of the family. The caddi was the position that made most of the important political decisions, such as managing relations with other tribes.

The Caddo tribe was similar to the Comanche in their ability to trade and deal with the Europeans. Both tribes had a governmental structure that was unique for this time in history.

title: Looking Back: Texas Geography, Government and First People
text:
Regions of Texas

Texas is a large state. It is located in the Northern and Western hemispheres of the world. It is one of 50 states in America. We can look at Texas in many different ways. We can group it into different regions, or areas, to help us better understand our home.

Our state can be divided into population regions to help us learn more about the number of people who call Texas home. We can also divide Texas into economic regions based on the ways people earn their livings. Perhaps the most common way we divide Texas is into geographic regions. Just like geographic regions of the U.S. and the world, regions in Texas share common plants, animals, landforms and climate features.

There are four geographic regions in Texas: the Mountains and Basins region in far west Texas, the Great Plains region in the Texas panhandle, the North Central Plains region in the middle of the state and the Coastal Plains region in the far eastern area of the state.

The Mountain and Basins region has a desert and the state's only mountains, while the wetter Coastal Plains region has mostly flat land. Winter weather in the Great Plains region can be bitterly cold. However, winters in the southern Coastal Plains region can be pleasantly warm most of the time.

Why Settle Texas?

Early settlers in Texas had to decide where the best places would be to build homes and communities. People settled where the climate was pleasant. They also wanted to live where they could find the natural resources they needed to meet their basic needs of food, clothing and shelter. The most important resource for settlers was fresh water. They built most Texas settlements near a source of water that they could use for drinking. Many Texas communities today are near rivers or along the coast. Plants and animals that settlers used for food, clothing and home building were also found near water. As technology developed, many settlers learned to dig underground wells for water.

Early Texans traveled in boats on waterways to trade goods with other settlements. When railroads came to Texas, people formed communities around the train stations. They could then easily ship and receive goods.

Many Texas communities were small at first. Most people worked as farmers, ranchers, hunters or fishers. Families made almost everything they needed, including their food, clothing, furniture and homes. Over time, many of the small towns grew into larger cities. Some people left farms and ranches and moved to cities to find work and homes. Today, Texas has both large cities and small communities. It is still a good place for people to find jobs and raise families.

Freedom's Gifts

The United States declared its independence from Great Britain in the Declaration of Independence. U.S. leaders wanted the freedom to last, so they wrote a plan for the country's government in the U.S. Constitution. The freedoms of the people were explained in detail in this document. A plan to separate the government into three branches, or divisions, is a part of the Constitution.

Texas also has a special document called the Texas Declaration of Independence. Texas leaders wanted to be free of Mexico's control in the early 1800s. Just like the U.S. Constitution, the Texas Constitution of 1876 guarantees people's rights and freedoms.

The executive branch of the Texas government includes a governor elected by the people of the state. The governor's job is to prepare the state's budget and enforce all state laws. The Texas House of Representatives and the Texas Senate make up the legislative branch of state government. Citizens also elect the legislators in this branch. The legislators make state laws, approve spending and decide how to collect taxes. The third branch of Texas government is the judicial branch. Just like U.S. judges, Texas judges must explain the laws to the people who elected them.

title: American Indians in Texas
text:
Life changed for American Indians in North America when the Ice Age ended and the climate warmed. Mammoths and other animals became extinct, and people had to find other food sources. Before European explorers came to North America, there were many groups of American Indians who lived on the land we now call Texas. A large group of American Indians known as the Mississippian Culture settled throughout much of the eastern part of North America. Scientists who study cultures in history know a great deal about some of the groups and very little about others.

Mound Builders of East Texas - the Caddo

The Caddo lived in the piney woods of the northern Coastal Plains region in east Texas. These American Indians were known for the large mounds they built for temples and burial grounds. The villages had a special kind of government called a confederacy. Many tribes, each with its own chief, joined the confederacy group. The Caddo people were farmers, hunters, gatherers and fishers. They ate what they could find, grow or hunt near the villages. Caddo families of 30-40 people lived in tall, round grass huts shaped like beehives. The Caddo people made and traded beautiful pottery, jewelry and ceremonial objects. Many Caddo ancestors still live in Oklahoma, where the people were forced to move to a reservation.

Gulf Coast Karankawa

Small bands of about 30-40 people lived along the central Gulf Coast of the Coastal Plains region, from Galveston Island to Corpus Christi. These people called themselves Karankawa. Their huts were windbreaks that offered little protection from the cold and rain. They lived as nomads and followed their food to hunt. In summers, they lived on islands, where they hunted and fished. During the winters they lived on the mainland and ate shellfish they could gather at the shore. The coastal land provided all the resources these people needed. They built canoes from trees. They made pottery and baskets lined with tar that had washed up on the beaches. The Karankawa were fierce and often fought with any groups trying to come into their territory. The Karankawa culture died about two centuries ago.

Coahuiltecan Survivors

Bands of nomads called the Coahuiltecan lived in the southern part of Texas in the Coastal Plains region, between San Antonio and Brownsville. Life was difficult for these people, especially since food was scarce (in low supply). Mesquite bean flour was their most important food. They also often ate cactuses, powdered bones of fish and snakes, spiders, grubs, ant eggs and even deer dung!

Women were very important in the Coahuiltecan culture. They did most of the gathering, prepared game after it was killed and even controlled when the men of the tribe would go into battle. The Coahuiltecan lived in huts within very dirty camps. Most people believe the Coahuiltecan slowly became a part of other American Indian cultures.

The Little Known Jumano

Very little is known about the American Indians called the Jumano. Archaeologists learned about this culture through their rock art paintings along the Concho River. Most scientists believe the group was actually three smaller groups that shared similar customs. The groups lived in the Mountains and Basins region from New Mexico to Texas and south into the country of Mexico. Some Jumano lived along the Rio Grande River in south Texas. Families lived in one-room pithouses. Part of the home was underground, and the only entrance was on the rooftop. Some Jumano groups lived in one location. They farmed corn, beans and squash. Other Jumano were nomads. They roamed across Texas, hunting buffalo. There is no information about what became of this group.

The Fierce Comanche

The Comanche lived in bands throughout the Plains of Texas. They were among the first American Indian groups to find and tame wild horses. Comanche warriors were taught at an early age how to ride and fight on horseback. The fearless Comanche warriors forced other tribes off their land and controlled much of the southern Plains. Comanche were nomads who survived by hunting bison throughout the year. They used the bison for food, clothing, tools and shelter. The Comanche often fought with and killed settlers trying to build houses on their hunting grounds. They often got help fighting against the settlers from their allies the Wichita and Kiowa Indians. Diseases like smallpox and cholera killed many Comanche during the 1800s. White settlers hunted the buffalo to near extinction. This made it difficult for the Comanche to survive, too. After many battles with the U.S. Army, most remaining Comanche moved to U.S. government reservations.

The Lipan Apache: Comanche Enemy

Before the Comanche arrived, the Lipan Apache lived throughout the southwest United States in the Plains of Texas. Like the Comanche, the Lipan also depended on horses. They lived a semi-nomadic lifestyle. They hunted bison on horseback, from the panhandle to central Texas. In the spring, however, the Lipan set up camps. The women planted vegetables such as corn, beans, squash and pumpkins. After fall harvest, the Lipan moved on to hunt again. The Lipan also traveled once a year to trade with pueblo villages to the west. The Lipan were fierce enemies of the Comanche. They often battled with one another. However, the powerful Comanche easily defeated the Lipan. Eventually, the Lipan were pushed off their land and onto the west Texas desert in the Mountains and Basins Region. Life there was much more difficult.

title: Rights vs. Duties
text:
If you are 18 years old, a citizen of the United States and you live in Texas, you can vote in all federal and Texas local and state elections. Voting is a freedom that all citizens in our country and state have. It is a right that is guaranteed, or promised, in the Constitution. However, it is also the duty of citizens to learn about the issues and people for whom they will be voting. When a citizen does this, they are called an informed voter.

People elected to public office promise to listen to citizens' ideas about the way the government should work. Even kids can write or email our local, state and national leaders. With permission from an adult, use the internet to identify some of your state and local government leaders.

title: How Did We Get Here?
text: The first people in North America had to get here some way. Scientists who study cultures have developed three theories to explain how humans ended up on the continent. The most widely held belief is that the first people in North America came from Asia during the last Ice Age. Around 14,000 years ago, a land bridge connected Asia with North America. The idea is that hunters followed animals across the bridge. Other people think humans in North America came from Europe even earlier. Perhaps humans walked across an ice bridge connecting the continents almost 20,000 years ago. People have found stone tools from this time period in Texas, which supports this theory. Many American Indian tribes say they have always called North America home.

title: Made in Texas
text: When people discovered oil in Texas in 1901, the world changed forever. Oil made the inventions of the automobile and airplane possible. Today, companies throughout the world sell petroleum products from Texas. Cloth made of oil fiber is used to produce clothes, towels and sheets. Food preservatives made of oil help keep food safe to eat. Oil is even used in toothpaste, dishwashing liquids, contact lenses, shampoo and toys. However, petroleum products are not the only products of Texas that people around the world purchase. Texas sells many agricultural products, such as cotton and pecans. People also buy Texas poultry and timber products. Texas companies produce many different computer and electronic products used around the globe.

title: Early People and Natural Resources
text:
Early groups of people in Texas lived differently throughout history. Paleoamerican life ended and the Archaic way of life began about 8,500 years ago. However, both of these early groups of people had one thing in common. They were both dependent upon their natural resources for survival.

Paleoamericans followed animals and hunted. They made tools from stones, bones and plants. Homes were rock shelters or huts built from wooden poles and animal hides. They cooked food over open fires that they skillfully started.

Archaic American Indians left cave paintings that help us learn about their life. They were hunters, gatherers and fire builders. Their homes were also rock shelters. They made tools from stones and bones and used them to find food and protect themselves.

text:
Oil is an important natural resource. It can be used for many things. What uses come to your mind?

You may know that a lot of oil is used to make fuel for cars, trains, boats, and planes. Did you know oil is also used to make things like paint, tires, ink, and plastic? Texas produces more oil than any other state in the United States.

title: Christopher Columbus was a Failure?
text:
When Christopher Columbus set out on his voyages, he expected to find China, but he never did. He wanted people to respect him, but he was arrested in North America and taken back to Spain in disgrace. (You'll learn why in this week's lesson.) He wanted to establish Spanish colonies and make money in the trade business. Instead, he died a poor man. Many people thought he was a failure. But was he?

Europeans wanted spices, gold and silver from places in East Asia. The only way to trade for those items in 1492 was to travel over land. The journey through Europe and the Middle East took a long time and was very dangerous. Columbus dreamed of finding an ocean route to Asia.

Columbus believed he could sail across the Atlantic Ocean to Asia. He had no idea there were two continents in the way. For seven years, Columbus tried to convince the king and queen of Spain to pay for his journey to find a shorter route to Asia. A long war had left the government in need of money. A shorter trading route to Asia would give them more money. After the war ended, the king and queen decided to pay for Columbus' voyage. In Aug. 1492, Columbus left Spain to find this new route.

On Oct. 11, 1492, Columbus landed on an island off the coast of North America and named it San Salvador. He thought he was near Japan. When he found gold on the island, he was sure he had found Asia, so China and India must not be far away. This explains why he named the islands the Indies and why he called the people he met Indians.

The people Columbus called Indians were actually the Taino. At the time of Columbus’ arrival, the Taino had a large, complex society and a rich culture. They welcomed Columbus and his crew into their home and shared their resources. In time, however, the Taino would suffer greatly at the hands of the Spanish explorers, and many would die.

Columbus may have been wrong about finding Asia, but his voyages to the Americas had a lasting impact on the world, for better and worse. Many stories about Christopher Columbus end here, but not this one. Keep reading to learn about his other journeys.

title: Paddling Across the Atlantic
text:
Do you dream of becoming a big sports star or exploring Mars someday? When Gabor Rakonczay was a kid in Hungary, he dreamed of being alone in a ship on the ocean. By the time he was 30 years old, Gabor made his dream come true.

On Dec. 21, 2011, Gabor set out from Portugal in his 24-foot canoe. His destination was the Caribbean island of Antigua, 3,500 miles away. No one had ever crossed the Atlantic alone in a canoe!

After 26 days at sea, his canoe capsized (turned over). His communications equipment was ruined. For seven weeks he was totally alone, with no way to let his wife know where he was. He didn't use a satellite tracking system because at the last minute the price went up and he couldn't afford it. Three different times he lit signal flares to get the attention of passing ships. But each time the waves were too high and the ships couldn't see his canoe.

His wife, Viktoria, never lost hope. She was sure he was OK and even posted entries on their website. Viktoria kept track of the weather conditions and estimated where Gabor might be.

On March 25, 2012, Gabor landed on the island of Antigua. It took 76 days to cross the Atlantic alone in his canoe. He was even three weeks ahead of schedule! Gabor Rakonczay may never be as famous as Christopher Columbus, but his amazing accomplishment is worth reading about!

Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents for more Connections and Current Events articles.

title: Columbus' Voyages
text:
The Highs and Lows of Columbus' Voyages

Columbus made four voyages. On each trip he had successes and failures. Some of his trouble was caused by bad luck, and some was his own fault. Here's what went right and what went wrong on each trip.

1st Voyage (1492)

What Went Right

1. Columbus' crew wanted to turn around. Columbus said if they didn't find land in three days, they would go back. On the third day they saw land.

2. The Taino welcomed him and he found gold.

3. Columbus proved he was a skilled captain and was named Admiral of the Ocean.

4. Columbus returned to Spain as a hero.

What Went Wrong

1. Columbus' crew was frightened and begged to go back to Spain. They had very little food and they were afraid there were sea monsters in the ocean.

2. The Santa Maria sank and Columbus had to leave behind 39 men when he returned to Spain.

2nd Voyage (1493)

What Went Right

1. The king and queen of Spain were so impressed with Columbus' success, they gave him 17 ships to make another voyage.

2. Between 1,200 and 1,500 people sailed with Columbus. They wanted to be members of Columbus' new colony and believed they would get rich in the New World.

3. Columbus founded a colony on the island of Hispaniola.

What Went Wrong

1. The 39 men he left behind in 1492 had been massacred by American Indians.

2. Columbus enslaved the Taino and forced them to mine gold.

3. The Taino died from diseases brought by the Europeans, and the Europeans died from diseases they caught from the Taino.

4. Many European colonists died from malaria. Malaria is carried by mosquitoes.

5. Living conditions in the colony were poor. Fresh water was hard to find.

6. Columbus searched and searched but never found the emperor of China or India.

7. Columbus ruled his colony harshly. Many angry colonists went back to Spain.

3rd Voyage (1498)

What Went Right

1. Even though they were angry with Columbus, the king and queen of Spain agreed to pay for his third voyage.

2. Columbus was the first European explorer to find South America.

What Went Wrong

1. Because of his reputation for being cruel, few people wanted to sail with Columbus. Most of his crew members were experienced sailors, but a few former prisoners were part of the crew.

2. After arriving in the New World, Columbus was arrested for his cruel treatment of the colonists, put in chains and sent back to Spain.

4th Voyage (1502)

What Went Right

1. The voyage took only 21 days, because Columbus had learned so much about the winds and currents in the Atlantic Ocean.

2. His rotting ships survived a terrible hurricane.

What Went Wrong

1. The king and queen gave him four rotting ships.

2. The ships made it to the New World, but a hurricane was coming. Columbus asked for permission to dock in Hispaniola. The governor wanted nothing to do with Columbus and made him stay at sea during the hurricane.

3. Columbus continued searching for China, never realizing it was 8,000 miles away.

4. Shipworms ate away at the wood on his ships. Finally, the ships sank and Columbus was marooned on an island.

5. Columbus and his men stayed on the island for more than a year. Some of his men turned against him and fought him in a battle.

6. Columbus was terribly ill when they were finally rescued.

title: The Deception
text:
When Columbus and his men were stranded on an island during his fourth voyage, the native people helped them at first. After a while, though, they got tired of the sailors’ behavior and refused to do much for them. Columbus knew the moon was an important symbol to the native people. He used his knowledge of astronomy to deceive them. Columbus knew a lunar eclipse was about to occur. A lunar eclipse happens when Earth passes between the sun and the moon. Earth casts a red shadow on the moon.

Columbus told the people he would cause a red shadow to cover the moon if they didn't feed him. The native people refused. As Earth's shadow crept across the moon and it began to look red, the native people were frightened. They quickly brought food to Columbus and his men. Their help didn't last for long, though. Columbus was stranded for a year before being rescued.

Shortly after Columbus and his men were marooned on the island, he sent one of his men and some of the native people on a canoe trip to Hispaniola. This was a dangerous trip across 100 miles of open sea, and one native person died on the way. Columbus' crew member asked the governor of Hispaniola to rescue Columbus and his men.

The governor of Hispaniola did not like Columbus and refused to send help. Finally, after nearly a year, the governor sent a ship to the island where Columbus and his men were marooned. A representative from the governor came ashore with a gift of pork and wine for Columbus. But that was all. The governor would not allow the ship to save the sailors.

title: The Real Reason Columbus Sailed West
text:
For a long time, school children grew up believing that Columbus sailed west in 1492 because he wanted to prove the world was round. That's a nice story, but it isn't true.

Long before Columbus was born, most people knew the world was round. The idea of a round world was an old one. Thousands of years ago, philosophers in India and Greece suggested the world was round. Where did the false story about Columbus wanting to prove the world was round begin?

We can blame Washington Irving for changing the true story. Irving was an early American author who wrote stories you may have read. Have you heard the story of Rip Van Winkle, the guy who slept for 100 years? Washington Irving wrote it. How about the "Legend of Sleepy Hollow," the spooky story that is a favorite each October? Washington Irving wrote that, too. He also wrote a story about Christopher Columbus. In that story, Irving said Columbus wanted to prove the world was round. It's another interesting story from Washington Irving, but it's just not true.

The real argument for Columbus was not about the shape of the world. It was about its size. Columbus relied on ancient estimates of Earth’s size that said the planet is much smaller than it actually is. He thought that sailing west would reveal a faster trade route to eastern Asia.

title: What was life like on Columbus’ ships?
text:
Sailors mostly ate salted beef, garlic, olives, bread and water. There was a small metal oven on deck for cooking, but most meals were eaten cold. Soon, most of the food began to rot because of the damp sea air. Their biscuits were full of worms, and the water turned sour. Sailors mixed wine with water to cover up its bad taste.

Most sailors slept on the top deck, even in bad weather. In case a wave swept over the deck, they tied themselves to the ship to avoid being washed overboard. There was no toilet, so you can imagine what they did when they had to go the bathroom. Sailors smelled awful while at sea. Except for an occasional swim in the ocean, there was no place to take a bath. They probably didn't have many clothes, and their clothes stayed wet most of the time.

title: Eat Your Fruits and Veggies!
text:
Sailors in Columbus' day started their voyages with fresh food, but it didn't last long. Not having fresh fruits and vegetables caused a nasty disease called scurvy.

People get scurvy when they don't have enough vitamin C. Scurvy causes the little blood vessels in the skin to get weak. This causes blood to seep into the skin. Scurvy also causes bleeding gums. Then it gets worse. Joints ache. Skin and hair dry up. Teeth get loose, and the sailor gets weaker every day. Scurvy was such a serious disease that more than half the crew died from it on some ocean voyages.

It wasn't until 1747 that a doctor gave oranges and lemons to sailors with scurvy. They healed quickly. About 50 years later, the British navy gave lime juice to its sailors. Because of this, they were called limeys.

Next time your parents tell you to eat your fruits and vegetables, follow their advice!

title: Sailing Instruments in the 1400s
text:
Astrolabe

Sailors used an astrolabe to determine the ship's latitude. Latitude is the measurement of a ship's position on Earth from north to south. Sailors could use the astrolabe at night by measuring the angle of the pole star. During the day, they could measure the angle of the sun at noon. Then they compared that measurement to a table of latitudes that told them where they were.

Hourglass and Compass

An hourglass and a compass helped Columbus with dead reckoning. In the 1400s, dead reckoning was the best way sailors had to figure out the ship's longitude. Longitude is the measurement of a ship's position on Earth from east to west. Regular measurements of direction, speed and time were used to determine the ship's position. A skilled sailor kept a record of all his measurements.

title: The New World
text:
Why was the New World Such a Big Deal?

A wave of excitement swept across Europe when people heard about the New World. Imaginations went wild. What kind of people lived there? Was the land rich with gold and silver? These questions drove people to risk their lives and fortunes to find the answers. Coronado, Pineda, Cabeza de Vaca and Oñate were the first explorers to reach Texas. They came for different reasons, but all of them encountered more adventures than they may have expected. What were Spanish explorers looking for in the New World?

Knowledge

Most people are curious, especially about something new. Certainly, the first explorers of the New World were driven by curiosity. Most of the early explorers were sent to the New World by the Spanish government. The Spanish government wasn't just curious; it had other reasons for wanting to know more about this new land.

Wealth

New wealth would make Spain a more powerful nation. Gold was especially important. The explorers may have heard a legend about enormous wealth somewhere across the Atlantic Ocean. The legend said that seven religious leaders left Europe in 711 C.E. According to the story, the religious leaders settled on an island with sand made of gold. It goes on to say that the leaders built seven wealthy cities from this golden sand. When Columbus returned from the New World with gold, some people thought he had found this land of wealth. After Spanish conquistadores defeated the wealthy Aztec and Inca empires, many believed there was more wealth in the New World just waiting to be found.

Land

Another reason Spain sent the early explorers was to claim new land and establish settlements. The more land a country has, the more resources it has to meet the needs of the people. More land can also make a nation more powerful. To protect their claims, Spain brought colonists and priests to start new colonies and missions. That made it harder for other countries to come along later and take away the land.

Spreading Christianity

Spain also wanted to spread Christianity to other parts of the world. The American Indians met by Columbus were not Christians. Spain was a Catholic nation and believed it was their duty to convert the American Indians to the Catholic faith. If the American Indians became Catholics, it would also strengthen the Spanish government's power in the New World. These reasons for exploring the New World seem simple, but the events they set into motion changed the world forever.

Competition

The voyages of Christopher Columbus started a fierce rivalry among European nations to explore and colonize the New World. Portugal, England and France also sent explorers to claim land and settle colonies in what is today called North America. Spain wanted to stay ahead of all the other countries.

title: Making the World a Kinder Place
text:
We sometimes wonder why bad things happen to innocent people. Although we may never understand it, we can do our best to keep things like this from happening in the future. When we do this, we are doing our part to make the world a kinder place, without anger and violence. One way to do this is by making a plan to replace bullying and violence with kindness. The Cool to Be Kind (C2BK) program was developed to help students create programs in their classes and schools that are based on pro-kindness - doing nice things for others. Students look for ways to "pay it forward" each day. Paying it forward means that when someone thanks you for doing something nice, you ask that person to pay it forward by doing something nice for someone else. By paying it forward, kindness continues to spread across the world, and people start thinking kinder thoughts and ways that they can help other people. What are some ways you could practice paying it forward? How about doing yard work for an elderly neighbor for free? Or inviting a new student to eat lunch with you and your friends? What about giving up your seat on the bus to someone who looks tired, or helping someone pick up something they have dropped? Thinking kind thoughts and acting on them with acts of kindness is a simple change that you can do to change the world.

Teachers: Go to www.pifexperience.org to find out more about starting a C2BK program at your school!

title: Modern Europeans Explore Texas
text:
The First in Texas: Alonso Álvarez de Pineda (1519)

Álvarez de Pineda left Jamaica in 1519 to map the Gulf Coast of the New World. He was hoping to find a waterway to China. Europeans still didn't know that Columbus had discovered a new continent.

Álvarez de Pineda began his exploration on the coast of Florida, but he was attacked by American Indians. From there, he moved west to explore the coast of Texas. No one knows much about his expedition. We do know that he was the first person to map the Texas coast and the first known European in Texas.

The First to Travel Across Texas: Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca (1528-1536)

Cabeza de Vaca sailed to Florida in 1528. After reaching Florida, the men lost their ships and were attacked by American Indians. To survive, they killed their horses and ate the meat. They built new boats and used their shirts as sails. They made rope from the horses' manes. They used hide from the horses to make canteens for drinking water. They escaped Florida by sailing west along the gulf coast.

A month later, a storm separated the boats. Cabeza de Vaca and his crew washed ashore near Galveston Island on a cold, wet November day. If it hadn't been for the American Indians who rescued them, they would have died. Many of Cabeza de Vaca's men eventually died from disease and exposure. The American Indians enslaved those who survived, including Cabeza de Vaca. When he finally escaped, he found friendlier American Indians and became known as a healer. He also earned their trust by trading with them. Cabeza de Vaca, along with an enslaved person named Esteban and two other survivors, began to travel across Texas. They were looking for Spanish settlements. Eight years later, they stumbled across a group of Spanish soldiers. After he returned to Spain, Cabeza de Vaca wrote about his journey through Texas.

Across the Texas Panhandle: Francisco Vázques de Coronado (1540-1542)

Coronado had many reasons to look for gold in the New World. The Spanish had already conquered two wealthy nations - the Inca and the Aztec. Cabeza de Vaca wrote about wealthy cities in the New World.

Esteban and Friar Marcos claimed to have seen one of the Seven Cities of Cíbola. You'll read more about Marcos and these golden cities later.

In 1540, Coronado led an expedition to find the cities of gold. For two years, he searched from Arizona to Kansas. He found only American Indian villages. The king of Spain ordered the explorers to treat the American Indians kindly, but Coronado's soldiers fought with them instead.

One of Coronado's men was the first European to see the Grand Canyon. Coronado and his men were the first to travel through the Texas panhandle. When he made his report to the king, Coronado said that Texas land was good for growing crops but not much else. Coronado never found the cities of gold. Angry and frustrated, he blamed the American Indian guides who told him about these cities. He then had them killed.

El Paso: Juan de Oñate (1598-1608)

Juan de Oñate got permission from the king of Spain to establish a settlement in New Mexico. His most important mission was to bring the American Indians to Christianity. Many of the colonists who joined him were hoping to find silver and get rich.

Oñate's path to New Mexico was named El Camino Real, or the Royal Road. In April, he crossed the Rio Grande River from Mexico into Texas. Oñate's people were hungry and exhausted. He claimed the land for Spain. From El Paso, Oñate went north to New Mexico.

title: Escaping Starvation in the Village of Misfortune
text:
"Why are they starving us?" asked the Spaniard, clutching his stomach. Cabeza de Vaca looked helplessly at his friend. "The Indian told me they would not feed us unless I heal their sick."

"You are not a doctor," the Spaniard replied.

"Their medicine man is certainly no doctor. He heals by making a cut where the pain is. Then he sucks on the wound and seals it by burning it with fire. After all of that, he breathes on the wound to blow away the pain."

"Did you explain that you do not believe in that?" asked the Spaniard. "If you cannot make them understand, we will die!"

Cabeza de Vaca sighed. "I explained, but the Indian told me I do not know what I am talking about. He told me about the time he picked up a rock in the field and healed a man by waving it over him." He thought for a moment. "Perhaps I could breathe on the sick man and make the sign of the cross. Maybe that will make them happy."

They heard footsteps swishing in the sand. Down the sand dunes came the Indian they'd been talking about. Behind him were two other Indians carrying a sick man.

"You heal this man or you will starve," said the Indian.

"What will we do?" whispered the Spaniard.

"Do everything I do," de Vaca replied. When the Indians laid the sick man before him, de Vaca knelt before the man and made the sign of the cross over the patient while breathing on him. The Spaniard repeated his actions.

Cabeza de Vaca motioned the Spaniard to lean closer. "Say the Lord's Prayer," he whispered. Together, the two men recited the prayer.

"Hail Mary," Cabeza de Vaca said as he ended the healing ceremony with a prayer that the patient be healed. The Spaniard did the same.

"He is healed," Cabeza de Vaca told the Indian.

Satisfied, the Indian returned shortly with food for the men and gifts of hides and other small things.

title: The Fate of Texas’ First Explorers
text:
Whatever happened to the four men who first explored Texas? Some of their lives ended in ways that were just as interesting as their adventures.

Juan de Oñate

Oñate was a Spanish conquistador in the area of what is now New Mexico and Arizona in the late 1500s. Oñate led Spanish troops against the American Indians he met in his travels. The Acoma were killed and enslaved under his command. When the king of Spain heard about what happened, he ordered Oñate to return to Mexico City to face charges. Oñate was forbidden to return to New Mexico and had to leave Mexico City. He went back to Spain and never returned to the Americas.

Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca

Spain appointed Cabeza de Vaca to serve as governor of Paraguay in the 1540s. He was forced to return to Spain because of the harsh way he ruled the colony. His trial did not go well, and Cabeza de Vaca had to leave Spain and live in Africa. While he was there, the court decided that he was innocent. He returned to Spain and died around 1555.

Francisco Vázques de Coronado

Vázques de Coronado also returned to Mexico City to face charges of treating American Indians and members of his expedition badly. Even though he was found guilty, he later became the governor of a small region in central Europe. He retired in Mexico City and died there in 1554.

Alonso Álvarez de Pineda

In 1519, Álvarez de Pineda led expeditions to map the coastline of the Gulf of Mexico. He verified that Florida was a peninsula of the continent, not an island. Álvarez de Pineda was the first European to map parts of Texas. Álvarez de Pineda was cruel to the American Indians his troops met. He was killed during an encounter with the Huastec people at the Panuco River.

title: How did Cabeza de Vaca get his name?
text:
The name Cabeza de Vaca means Cow's Head. That sounds like a name someone might call his enemy, but it wasn't. It was actually a name of honor in the family of Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca.

The explorer's name has an unusual story. One of his ancestors helped the king's army win an important battle by using a cow's skull to mark a pass that was not guarded. The king rewarded him by giving him the name Cabeza de Vaca. This name was passed down through Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca's mother's family.

Historians aren't certain that this story is true, but we do know that Cabeza de Vaca played an important part in Texas history.

title: The Beginning of the Columbian Exchange
text:
When two people exchange something, both people give and both people receive. The Columbian Exchange describes many exchanges that took place between the Old World and New World. People traded goods like spices and food. Early traders also captured, enslaved and sold men, women and children. Sometimes, people traded things no one wanted. When people from different parts of the world met, they often exchanged deadly diseases.

Traders exchanged animals, too. Explorers brought horses to the New World, and the American Indians became expert horsemen. The horse changed the way of living for people like the Comanche.

No one used the term Columbian Exchange when Columbus and the other explorers were around. It wasn't until 1972 that the exchange of goods, animals, people and diseases got this name.

title: Let's Write
text: When hiking through the mountains in western Texas, you find a stone chest in a cave. When you open it, you discover that it contains stone tablets with writing on them. An interpreter of the Jumano language tells you that it is the diary of a young Jumano child. Who wrote on the tablets? What did they write? title: So Many Explorers!
text:
Here are some famous explorers who contributed during the Age of Exploration.

Portugal

Bartolomeu Días and his crew were the first to make it to the southern tip of Africa, which he named the Cape of Good Hope. The year was 1488.

In 1497 and 1498, Vasco da Gama and his crew were the first to sail around Africa and through the Indian Ocean to the country of India. Only two of the four ships survived the voyage. Many of the crew died from thirst, scurvy, and hunger.

Pedro Alvares Cabral was blown off course on his voyage around Africa, and landed instead in South America in 1500. He discovered the area we know as Brazil.

Spain

Ferdinand Magellan, sailing for Spain (though he was born in Portugal), was the first to try to circumnavigate (travel all the way around the Earth) in 1519 to 1522. Sadly, Magellan and much of his crew died in the Philippines. The remainder of the crew completed the journey. Magellan renamed the South Sea "Mar Pacifico," or the Pacific Ocean. The word "pacific" means "peaceful."

Christopher Columbus: Unable to get Portugal to pay for his expedition, he convinced King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain to do so. He left in 1492 and reached the island of Hispaniola. To his dying day, Columbus was convinced he'd reached Asia, not realizing he'd actually discovered new lands for the people of Europe.

Ponce de León explored Florida in 1513 while searching for the fountain of youth. The settlement St. Augustine became the first European settlement in the Continental U.S.

Hernando Cortés defeated the Aztec Empire of Mexico for Spain between 1519 and 1521.

Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca Empire in South America for Spain. During this time, Francisco Coronado, from 1540 to 1542, explored the southwestern United States. Hernando de Soto also made claims of North America for Spain.

Vasco Nuñez de Balboa was the first European to see the South Sea, or the Pacific Ocean. Balboa claimed the ocean for Spain in 1513. American Indians helped him cut down vegetation in the Panama forest to reach the South Sea.

France

Giovanni Verrazano in 1524 and Jacques Cartier in 1534 made claims of much of the area of Canada for France. Both were unsuccessful in finding a route through North America to Asia. However, they mapped the land from North Carolina to Newfoundland and traveled what we now call the St. Lawrence River. A civil war in France in the mid-1500s ended their involvement in the Age of Exploration.

England

King Henry VII, Queen Elizabeth I and other English leaders hoped to find a northwest passage, a water route through North America to India. Although they were not successful in this effort, explorers did set up colonies in the new world.

John Cabot made his voyage to North America in 1497. He claimed the area of Newfoundland for England.

Holland

Henry Hudson explored the Hudson River in 1609.

title: Motives and Movement
text:
Why did people want to explore the great seas? Why did people want to colonize new lands? The simple answer is they all wanted to find a route for trade between Europe and Asia that was safer.

In addition to finding a safer trade route, many European countries were after more in their many voyages. Each voyage was funded for a specific purpose. Those purposes are often referred to as the three G’s: Gold, God and Glory.

Gold

Many explorers were seeking riches for themselves and their country. They would search for gold and other precious metals. There was even a rumor that Ponce de León was looking for the Fountain of Youth.

God

Religion was very important to many countries. Some explorers wanted to bring their beliefs to people around the world. Many Portuguese and Spanish explorers wanted to spread Christianity, a religion based on belief in Jesus Christ.

Glory

Europe is made of many countries, all of which wanted to claim the most land in the Americas. It was a race for explorers and settlers from each country to start a colony. For example, Jacques Cartier wanted to claim the land for France. Hernán Cortéz claimed land for Spain and John Cabot was the first explorer to claim land for England.

Together, these motivations gave rise to the Age of Exploration.

Settling Texas

The main motivations of Spain to settle the territory we know as Texas was to gain control of the region, gain riches from the land, and spread Christianity. The Spanish colonizers settled by establishing missions and presidios. The missions were mostly managed by friars who hoped to spread Christianity among the indigenous peoples who inhabited the area. The presidios were forts that were inhabited by Spanish soldiers. These soldiers provided protection to the Spanish settlers. Conflict with the indigenous peoples grew as the Spaniards expanded their settlements and sought to convert them to Christianity.

Spain wanted to ensure they kept control of the Texas territory so France wouldn't expand into their claimed lands. After the Louisiana Purchase, Spain strengthened its hold on the Mexican colony to protect it from the United States.

What started as a race for Gold, God, and Glory during the Age of Exploration eventually changed into what we today know as Texas.

title: La Salle: A Strange Man in a Strange World
text:
If you take a close look, you will see that La Salle was not just another explorer who found his way to Texas. His strange behavior was an important part of his colony's failure. It also caused a lot of suffering and death. This week you will read about this unusual explorer and his part in Texas history. Before we do that, let's look at what the New World was like in the 1600s.

Who Controlled the New World?

Less than 200 years after Columbus discovered the New World, Spain controlled what is now called Mexico. In those days, it was called New Spain, and it was growing. Last week you learned that Juan de Oñate was sent to New Mexico to establish new colonies for Spain.

While Spain was growing stronger in the southwest, France was busy establishing colonies in the northeastern part of North America. The vast land in between was still controlled by different American Indian tribes.

Spain had very little interest in Texas until La Salle established the first European colony on the Texas coast. La Salle was French, and France was an enemy of Spain. Next week you will learn what Spain did when they heard there was a French colony in Texas.

La Salle's Plan

La Salle is best known for two famous voyages to the New World. In 1682, he sailed the length of a waterway that cut through the central part of North America - the Mississippi River. He claimed the territory along the Mississippi River for France and named it Louisiana after King Louis XIV of France.

La Salle knew that Spain controlled Mexico. He wanted France to control the central part of North America. The first step in this plan was to establish a colony at the mouth of the Mississippi River where it empties into the Gulf of Mexico. He wanted to use this colony as a base for trading with the American Indians to get furs and other riches to send back to France.

Some plans fail because of bad luck. Other plans fail because of the bad decisions people make. Bad luck and bad decisions worked together to doom La Salle and his expedition.

Before we go on, would you like to know La Salle's full name? It is René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle. Stories about his boyhood say he had a lot of energy. He would have to have a lot of energy just to say his own name.

title: New U.S. National Monuments
text:
Do you know how many national monuments there are in the United States? President Obama approved five new national monuments in March 2013. These and other U.S. monuments preserve national resources so that visitors can honor special people and events of the past.

One is the First State National Monument in Delaware. It's the state's first national park site, and it tells about the early settlement of the Delaware colony and how Delaware was the first state to ratify, or approve, the U.S. Constitution. Another is the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad National Monument in Maryland. It honors Ms. Tubman, who bravely helped enslaved people escape to freedom using the Underground Railroad. It is located on Maryland's Eastern Shore. There is also the Rio Grande del Norte National Monument in New Mexico. It is an important habitat for many birds and wildlife, and it has a collection of petroglyphs (rock drawings or carvings) and other archaeological and cultural resources.

The Charles Young Buffalo Soldiers National Monument is in Wilberforce, Ohio. It preserves the home of Colonel Charles Young, who was an officer in the U.S. Army. He was the first African American to become a Colonel. And last, the San Juan Islands National Monument is in Washington State's Puget Sound. It is a chain of islands, an archipelago, and there are 450 total! People can visit historic lighthouses and view cultural resources and fossils dating back 12,000 years.

President Theodore Roosevelt signed the Antiquities Act into law in 1906. Since then, 16 presidents have used this Act to preserve our national resources. Research the Antiquities Act (https://www.nps.gov/archeology/sites/antiquities/), and find out how many national monuments there are in the United States. (Hint: There are over 100!) Which ones are most interesting to you? Have you ever visited any?

Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents for more Connections and Current Events articles.

title: The Trouble with La Salle
text:
La Salle's 1682 voyage to the Americas was a great success. One of the reasons for his success was his crew. They were tough and willing to endure the hardships that go with exploration.

La Salle's later voyage to the Americas was in trouble before he left France. From the beginning, he had a hard time finding people to join him on this trip. Most of the people who were willing to join him did not have the skills needed to build a colony. He needed carpenters and other craftsmen. He recruited a number of young boys, perhaps thinking they could learn the skills they needed.

La Salle was so desperate to find volunteers that he recruited beggars from the steps of churches. How could La Salle expect to have an excellent crew on his second voyage when his crew was made up of people who had little experience? Nevertheless, the trip began.

Pirates!

In July 1684, four ships left France for the mouth of the Mississippi River. There was trouble almost immediately. Pirate ships from Holland, England, and Spain prowled the waters near the Americas looking for victims. These pirates captured one of La Salle's ships. Now his tiny fleet was cut by one-fourth. La Salle had hoped to get the help of pirates in a plan to take the silver mines in northern Mexico away from the Spaniards. Instead, they were stealing from him.

Are We There Yet?

When La Salle reached the Gulf of Mexico, he was supposed to build a fort at the mouth of the Mississippi River. Instead, he wound up about 400 miles west, in Texas. Some historians think La Salle sailed past the Mississippi River because he was using an inaccurate map. Others think he planned to sail to Texas. A settlement in Texas would increase the size of the land La Salle claimed for France.

What was La Salle like?

It will help you to understand the rest of La Salle's story if you know something about his personality. It is said that La Salle was stubborn. Once he made a decision, it was impossible to get him to change his mind. This was true even when his decision was obviously a mistake. It made him mad when anyone tried to give him advice. La Salle also went into a rage when small things went wrong and would never admit that he was to blame.

La Salle looked down on his crew and made decisions he knew would make them mad. Once, when his ships crossed a special place in the Atlantic Ocean, his crew wanted to have a baptismal service and celebration. This was quite common for sailors in those days, but La Salle would not allow it.

There were other examples of La Salle’s controlling nature. For example, he would not allow anyone to keep a journal. He also told the colonists that they could not sing, dance, or even show a sense of humor. To make things worse, La Salle was physically abusive to his people. Many of them died from this abuse.

Getting Even

La Salle's harsh treatment angered one of his captains, who ran the l'Aimable aground instead of following La Salle's orders. The l'Aimable was a supply ship. When it broke apart, many of the goods they needed to survive were lost.

Fort Saint Louis

La Salle's expedition was in deep trouble. La Salle and the captain of his third ship argued during the entire voyage. When the captain saw where La Salle wanted to settle, he thought it was too wild. He decided to go back to France with 120 other colonists and crew members who were also disgusted with La Salle. The captain also took many of the supplies La Salle had hoped to use to build his new settlement.

Building the Fort

La Salle chose a building site for his new settlement on Garcitas Creek, a creek that emptied into Matagorda Bay, where the La Belle was anchored. Needing materials to build his fort, La Salle ordered his men to haul the wood from the wrecked l'Aimable to the new site. The wood was very heavy and had to be carried six miles. The men were not used to this kind of work. To make matters worse, La Salle refused to give his adult workers any more food than he gave the children. Hard work and small amounts of food caused many of the men to die.

From Friends to Foes

In the beginning, the Karankawa people approached the settlers in friendship. They even joined the colonists on a bison hunt. The friendship took a wrong turn when La Salle discovered that the Karankawa had taken goods from his wrecked ship. He sent some of his soldiers to bring back these goods. The soldiers brought back the goods, but they also stole some canoes from the Karankawa because they knew La Salle wanted them. This ended the friendship and started a war. Attacks by the Karankawa would eventually wipe out the French settlement at Fort Saint Louis.

title: La Salle’s Final Disasters
text:
La Salle believed a waterway near Fort Saint Louis would lead him to the Mississippi River. In January 1686, La Salle and 50 men headed east to find it. After he left, a powerful storm sank the La Belle. His colony was stranded in North America.

La Salle did not find the Mississippi River, but he did find and trade with the Caddo. He had met other members of this large tribe on his earlier voyage down the Mississippi. He had even learned a few words of their language. This small bit of good luck did not help him, however.

When La Salle returned to find that his last ship had sunk, he knew he was in trouble. His only plan was a desperate one. He would leave Fort Saint Louis with some of his men and walk all the way to a fort he'd built earlier in Starved Rock, Illinois. This was more than 1,200 miles away.

With the La Belle wrecked, there was no way back to France. In January 1687, La Salle and 16 men left for the long walk to Illinois. As usual, wherever La Salle went, there was arguing and hurt feelings. Instead of working together to survive, the men took sides in the bickering.

Conflict and competition created living conditions which created desperation. The men lacked trust in one another. A mutiny is when a group of followers turn against the leader. LaSalle’s men mutinied and killed him. Fort Saint Louis was now in great danger and ultimately failed because of conflicts within the community and outside enemies.

title: Questions about La Salle
text:
Q: Did any of La Salle's men make it to the French settlements in the north?

A: Two men made the 1,200-mile trek and then returned to France.

Q: Did anyone survive the Karankawa massacre of Fort Saint Louis?

A: Five children were captured and adopted by the Karankawa.

Q: Is it true that one of La Salle's ship captains died because he ate prickly pear tuna?

A: Daniel Moraud, captain of the La Belle, ate prickly pear tuna without removing the spines. The spines stuck in his throat and caused it to swell. Eventually, he could not breathe and died.

Q: Why were two combs in the wallet found in the wreck of La Belle?

A: One comb was used as we use combs today. The second comb had fine teeth for removing lice from the owner's head.

title: Did La Salle do Anything Right?
text:
Even though La Salle's second voyage was a disaster, it changed North American history. When the Spanish learned that the French were in Texas, they were alarmed. They quickly sent the Spanish army into Texas to look for the French. Before this, Spain had not shown a strong interest in settling Texas. When they thought the French might gain a foothold in Texas, their attitude changed. Because of La Salle, Spain quickly began exploring, settling and building missions in Texas.

La Salle also changed history in the central part of North America. The land he claimed along the Mississippi River brought French traders to the New World to trade for pelts. Beaver hides were especially popular in Europe, where they were used to make hats. Even though France lost the French and Indian War to Britain in the 1700s, French influence in places like Louisiana still remains strong.

Did La Salle do anything right? Not for himself or his colonists. He did, however, change the course of American history.

title: Using Your Wits
text:
What if your teacher told the class that archaeologists found firepots on the LaBelle. She did not, however, tell you what a firepot was used for. Instead, she gave you four choices. Only one of these choices is right. Your teacher then told you to use your common sense to decide which of the following answers is correct. Can you pick the correct answer?

A. A firepot was a metal pot used for cooking while sailors were at sea. Without a firepot to cook in, the wooden ships would catch on fire.

B. Matches had not been invented in the 1600s. A firepot was a metal pot in which sailors kept a fire burning at all times. Whenever they needed fire, they went to the firepot.

C. A firepot was not a pot at all. It was the name of a spicy dish that made a sailor’s tummy burn when he ate it.

D. A firepot was used to fight off pirates. When a pirate ship got too close, they tossed a firepot onto the other ship.

What answer did you pick? Explain why you picked that answer. The correct answer is below.

Answer: D. A firepot was a clay container with a grenade inside. The grenade was covered with a flammable liquid. A wick stuck out of the top of the firepot. When a pirate ship came close, sailors lit the wick and threw the pot onto the enemy ship. The pot broke apart and fiery liquid spread across the deck. The fire also lit the grenade. When it exploded, tiny bits of metal flew through the air.

title: Let's Write
text: Write part of La Salle’s story in your own words. You can choose one of the voyages, the building of the settlement, the decision to walk to Illinois or any other part of his interesting life. If you want, you can take the point of view of someone who was there—maybe even La Salle himself. Be sure your story has a beginning, a high point and an end. Use lots of adjectives to describe what happened and what you think La Salle and his men saw.

title: Spain’s Opinion of Texas
text:
Texas is so famous it's hard to believe there was a time when Spain thought Texas did not amount to much. Why did they think this? The Spanish wanted riches, but no gold or silver had been found in Texas. There were no wealthy empires like that of the Aztec. You may remember that Coronado told the king of Spain that Texas land wasn't good for anything except agriculture.

If Texas wasn't worth much, why did Spain want to keep it? Spain wanted a large empire and there was a lot of land in Texas. Not only that, no other European nation had shown an interest in Texas. Spain thought Texas was safely theirs. After all, Spain was the most powerful military force in the southern part of the New World. Who would dare to challenge them?

That was Spain's attitude toward Texas until 1684. That year a man by the name of La Salle tried to start a little colony near what is now the town of Palacios. The Spanish empire was abuzz. Spies spread the word. France had invaded Texas! Suddenly a territory that didn't matter much became very important. Spain sent 10 expeditions in search of La Salle's colony, but no one could find it. France had to be stopped.

Poor La Salle! He did not accomplish what he set out to do. Instead, he started something even bigger. The man who bungled his attempt to build a colony had succeeded in riling the entire Spanish empire. Thanks to La Salle, Spain had a new interest in Texas. Simply claiming that Texas belonged to Spain was not enough anymore. Spain now had to take action to keep it out of the hands of their enemy - France.

This week you will learn the answers to questions about Spain's first attempts to settle in Texas. What did the Spanish discover when they finally found La Salle's colony? Were the French really the reason Spain built missions in Texas? How successful were the Spanish missions in converting American Indians to Christianity? Why did the Caddo American Indians dislike the Spaniards even though they got along just fine with the French? When you have finished this week's paper, you will have learned that Spanish missions in Texas were much more than Sunday school in the Old West.

title: The ‘Irish’ Saint Who Wasn’t Really Irish
text:
People parade in New York City and turn the rivers green in Chicago every year on St. Patrick's Day. This saint (holy person) lived 1,500 years ago. But did you know St. Patrick wasn't even Irish?

Patrick was born in Britain to wealthy parents. When he was 16, Irish pirates attacked his home and took him prisoner. They took him to Ireland and held him captive. He worked as a shepherd and became a Christian. After six years he escaped and went back to Britain. But he had a dream in which an angel told him to go back to Ireland as a missionary (person who does religious work in other countries). After Patrick became a priest, he did just that. Many Irish at that time practiced a nature-based religion, so Patrick used some of their symbols to teach them about Christianity. For example, they worshiped the sun. So he put the sun on a cross. This is where the Celtic cross comes from. Historians think he died on March 17 about C.E. 460. Irish villagers mourned his death every year on that day.

The Irish people have always been great storytellers. These stories often became more exaggerated over the years. The story of St. Patrick chasing the snakes out of Ireland is one of these exaggerated stories. St Patrick's Day started out as a religious holiday, but today he is remembered all over our nation with parties and parades. Does your community celebrate St. Patrick's Day?

title: The First Mission in Texas
text:
Alonso de León finds Fort Saint Louis

The Spanish were angry when they learned a French colony was in Texas. Ten military expeditions left New Spain to find the colony and destroy it. All of them failed. The 11th expedition finally found it. When Alonso de León reached Fort Saint Louis, no one was alive. All he found were three human skeletons. One was a man, the second was a woman and the third was a child. He immediately had them buried.

France had failed to establish a colony in Texas, but Spain was afraid they would try again. Spain decided to do two things to stop the French. First, they would build a fort where the old French colony stood. Alonso de León built a fort on top of Fort Saint Louis and named it La Bahia. This was the first of three forts named La Bahia. A few years later, La Bahia was moved inland. In 1749, La Bahia was built near the town of Goliad.

France in East Texas?

Rumors about Frenchmen living among the Caddo alarmed Spain. The Caddo also wanted Spain to build a mission in their area. The Caddo showed an interest in Christianity. Rumors about the French and the Caddo's invitation convinced Spain to build a mission in East Texas. If the American Indians became Catholics, Spain believed they would be loyal supporters of the Spanish government. Converting the American Indians was not, however, the most important reason.

Alonso de León led an expedition of soldiers and priests into East Texas to choose a site for a first mission. In 1690, San Francisco de los Tejas became the first mission in Texas. Building this mission so close to Louisiana was a warning to France: Stay out of Texas! That is why the soldiers remained at the mission after it was built. Mission San Francisco de los Tejas was near the Nabedache village. The Nabedache were a band of Caddo in East Texas. The Nabedache also belonged to a group that was made up of other Caddo bands. This group was called the Hasinai.

Trouble at the Mission

At first, the Hasinai welcomed the Spanish, but things soon went wrong. Many of the American Indians did not like the teachings of the priests. In addition, the Spanish soldiers mistreated the Hasinai. The situation got worse when the Hasinai also caught diseases like measles and smallpox from the Spanish. Many of them died. The Hasinai decided the Spanish had brought evil spirits that were killing them. Rather than die, they decided to leave the mission.

When the Hasinai left, it created a real problem for the Spanish priests and soldiers. They depended on the Hasinai for food. The Spaniards believed they were too good to farm. To them, farming was the work of lower class people. When food ran low, the priests wanted the Spanish soldiers to force the Hasinai to bring them food and return to the mission. The soldiers wanted no part of this. They knew the thick forests of East Texas would be a dangerous place to fight.

Destroy the Mission

Because of the problems at San Francisco de los Tejas, the Spanish government decided in 1694 to close the mission and destroy the buildings. The mission failed to convert the Hasinai to Christianity. Since France had not built any more settlements in Texas, Spain felt it was safe to leave the mission. Thinking their problems with France were over, Spain went back to ignoring Texas. This lasted for about 20 years, when another Frenchman showed up in Texas. Once again, the French were about to change Spain's attitude toward Texas.

title: Those Pesky French!
text:
Spain thought its problems with France were over, but they weren't. France was busy building new settlements along the Mississippi River. The French got along better with the American Indians than the Spanish did, because the French weren't trying to chase them off their land. The French traded with the American Indians, but they also needed goods from Spain. There were two problems, however. It was illegal for any Frenchman to set foot on Spanish soil, and it was illegal for Spaniards to trade with foreigners.

France Returns to Texas

In 1713 the French established a trading post in Natchitoches, Louisiana. A year later, the Governor of Louisiana sent Captain Louis St. Denis into Texas to trade with New Spain. He asked the Spanish to build small forts in Texas to trade with the French. The Spaniards were stunned but interested.

While trading with the Spanish, St. Denis fell in love with a young woman, the daughter of a Spanish military leader. After the two married, her grandfather had St. Denis arrested for trespassing on Spanish land. He was taken to Mexico City and put in jail. But St. Denis did not give up. He charmed the Spanish into giving him the job of establishing missions in East Texas. He knew these missions would also be trading posts for the French.

St. Denis helped Spain build a mission in western Louisiana near Natchitoches. Spain claimed western Louisiana as part of its territory. This settlement was called Los Adaes. St. Denis asked Spain to build a mission on the San Antonio River to serve as a trading post between the settlements in East Texas and Mexico.

After the missions were established, a new leader was elected in New Spain. He feared the French were planning to settle Texas again. He arrested St. Denis for trespassing on Spanish land. St. Denis escaped from Mexico City and returned to Louisiana to live with his wife.

In 1719, the French attacked Los Adaes, and the Spaniards left Louisiana. To protect Texas, Spain finally built a mission on the San Antonio River.

title: The Missions in San Antonio
text:
Fray Olivares wanted to build a mission on the San Antonio River in 1709. He wanted to convert the Coahuiltecan people to Christianity, but the Spanish government said no. When the French began trading with American Indians in East Texas, Spain changed its mind. In 1718, Fray Olivares was given permission to build Mission San Antonio de Valero and to convert the Coahuiltecan. The mission was moved three times before it arrived at the site where it stands today. Most people call this mission the Alamo.

Three other missions were built close to San Antonio de Valero. The missions were built because the American Indian tribes in the area did not get along with each other. Each needed its own mission. These missions are also standing today. They are why San Antonio is called the Mission City. Today, Olivares is known as the Father of San Antonio.

title: East Texas Indians
text:
It's easy to get confused when you read about the American Indians who lived in East Texas when the first missions were built. You might think the Caddo, Hasinai and Tejas were three different tribes, but they were all part of the Caddo nation.

Caddo

You have learned the Caddo were a great culture that lived along the Mississippi River in the middle of North America. The Caddo culture was made up of many smaller bands.

Hasinai

Many of the smaller bands, like the Anadarko and Nabedache, in East Texas joined together and called themselves the Hasinai. They were still part of the Caddo nation, but they worked together for trading and protection.

Tejas

Tejas is the Spanish version of taysha, a Caddo word. Taysha means friend. In the 1600s, this was the Spanish name for the Caddo. This was later changed to the word Texas, the name of our great state.

title: Who was José de Escandón?
text: The early Spanish settlements in Texas were either missions or military forts (presidios), and many of these were abandoned over time. To keep the French from moving into Texas, the Spanish government decided that permanent settlements were needed. José de Escandón, an officer in the Spanish army, was chosen to find farmers and ranchers to colonize a new area along the lower Rio Grande Valley, which he named Nuevo Santander. From 1748 to 1755, he helped settle more than 20 towns both north and south of the river. Their ranching methods became the models for future American cattle ranches in the West. Escandón is sometimes called the "father of the lower Rio Grande Valley."

title: Wrapping it Up
text:
This week you learned a lot about the Spanish in Texas, so let's review the important points.

Spain paid little attention to Texas until La Salle tried to establish a French colony in Texas. The colony failed, but it frightened Spain into building a mission to keep the French out of East Texas. The Spanish mission failed because of diseases and Spanish cruelty toward the American Indians.

France began settling in Louisiana and trading with the American Indians. They also wanted to trade with New Spain. St. Denis was a Frenchman who worked to set up trade with the Spaniards in Mexico. Although France and Spain were enemies, he talked Spain into building missions in East Texas and western Louisiana. Later, a new leader in Spain turned against St. Denis and had him arrested. Spain stopped ignoring Texas and built more missions and forts. The missions kept the French out, but they had very little success in converting the American Indians.

text:
This chart shows some of the bands of American Indians in East Texas that were part of the Caddo nation. Use the following terms to complete the chart. Then answer the questions below the chart.
