title: Let's Write
text: Using the information from this week’s articles, explain the reasons for competition between Spain and France concerning the Texas region in the 1680s. Be sure to use correct grammar, spelling, sentence structure, and punctuation.

title: Threats to Spain’s Control
text:
Spanish missions were not very successful at converting Texas Indians to Christianity. They were, however, successful at stopping most French activity in Texas. France no longer had time for Texas because it was heading toward a war with England. Did this mean Spain's worries were over? Not at all. Other groups of people wanted to make Texas their new home.

The First Wave of Newcomers

Most people think white settlers from the United States were the next threat to Spain's hold on Texas. In the early 1700s, a powerful tribe was making its way into Texas. The Comanche were moving in. These fierce warriors attacked tribes like the Lipan Apache. They drove them off land they had lived on for centuries. Before this, the Apache were in control, often raiding and attacking the missions in San Antonio.

The Lipan Apache were no match for the Comanche and began moving south. As the Apache moved south, they did the same thing to other tribes that the Comanche had done to them. They attacked and drove them off their land. The Comanche, however, wanted to control most of Texas. This kept the Apache running. The Comanche followed them everywhere. To make things worse, the Comanche had help from other tribes like the Wichita and the Caddo.

Help from the Spanish?

The Apache knew they were no match for the Comanche. In 1749 they went to San Antonio and asked for help. They wanted to live in the missions, because they knew the Spanish soldiers would help protect them. They were turned down because they did not get along with the American Indians already served by the missions.

The Apache were desperate. If they didn't get help, they knew the Comanche would destroy them. This is when they came up with their best plan. They went back to San Antonio and asked that a special mission be built for them. This didn't mean they were ready to become Christians. The Apache wanted a mission of their own in their old homeland to protect them from the Comanche. They knew that a fort would be built near the mission and soldiers are always in a fort.

Spain's Reply

Spain hesitated. For years, a few priests had wanted to build a mission for the Apache, but the Spanish government said no. It took something else to convince them. Rumors of silver in Central Texas convinced them to build a mission for the Apache. Spain also feared the French might return. In 1757, they built Mission Santa Cruz de San Saba near Menard. Now the Apache had what they wanted. Spanish soldiers would be in their territory to help them fight the Comanche.

title: Have Archaeologists Found James Coryell’s Grave?
text:
In 2010, the Texas Historical Commission found remains that may be those of James Coryell, a famous ranger who defended settlers in the Republic of Texas' early days.

Large stones mark the grave, and the stones cover a shaft in which the skeleton was found. Archeologists say they believe this is Coryell's grave because of the stones' placement near an old African American graveyard.

The graveyard was described in a book written in 1936 by Frank Simmons, a resident of Coryell County (named after the ranger). In the book, Simmons wrote of an account by Tom Broadus, a formerly enslaved person. Broadus said enslaved people from the plantation would bury their dead near Coryell's grave. Later, when the grave collapsed, they covered it with stones to keep the ranger's spirit at rest.

Coryell died in 1837 while fighting American Indians. Tradition says they were from the Caddo tribe. Archeologists say they hope to find answers to this and many more questions.

One of the first Texas rangers, Coryell was a friend of James and Rezin Bowie. James Bowie became fascinated with stories of the "lost" Los Almagres Mine, or Lost San Saba Mine, said to be near the old San Saba Mission west of San Antonio.

Together, Bowie and Coryell set out to find the mine. After a two-and-a-half month search, and a 13-hour fight with 170 American Indians, they still had yet to find the elusive Saba Mine. Maybe someday you will.

title: The Attack at Mission San Sabá
text:
The priests did not want the Mission San Sabá near the fort because they knew soldiers would bother the Apache. The decision to build the mission a few miles from the fort was one they would live to regret.

Where are the Apache?

After the mission was built, the priests were surprised when no Apache showed up. After all, they had asked for the mission. It was two months before any of them arrived. When they did, there were 3,000 of them. The excited priests invited them in, but the Apache told them it was hunting season. They would come another time. They did, however, leave a couple of their sick with the priests. Over and over again, the Apache passed by the mission but would never go in. Three priests sensed that something was wrong and quickly left the mission.

More Hard Times

Both the fort and the mission had been warned to expect trouble from the American Indians. For months, they prepared for an attack, but there wasn't one. By the time winter came, they relaxed, thinking the threat was over. Another problem took its place, however. An unusually cold winter killed most of their livestock. During this time, the Apache rarely visited the mission. Then, they completely disappeared. The Spanish had no idea what was coming.

Surprise Attack

In the spring of 1758, American Indians raided the San Sabá settlement and stole 59 horses. When the soldiers chased after them, they discovered they were greatly outnumbered. They hurried back and told the priests to go to the fort for safety. The priests, however, did not move fast enough. More than 2,000 American Indians from different tribes attacked the mission and burned it to the ground. None of them were Apache. They were the enemies of the Apache, including the Comanche. The mission was set afire. That night, a handful of people hiding in the mission escaped. Although the mission was never rebuilt, the fort lasted another 13 years.

Spain Pushes Back

Spain sent soldiers into Comanche country to punish the American Indians, but their mission failed. They destroyed a Tonkawa village but were defeated in a later battle. The Comanche still ruled a large part of Texas, and the Spanish government could not stop them. In fact, they were barely able to hold on to the handful of forts and missions they had. Spain still claimed Texas as its territory, but the Comanche and other American Indian tribes were in control. About 60 years later, they would try a new strategy. They would let Mexicans and Anglo-Americans build settlements on the Texas frontier. They hoped these settlements would stop the American Indians before they reached the Spanish settlements to the south.

Attack Inspires Art

In 1765, about six years after the attack of the Mission San Sabá, a professional artist in Mexico painted a mural that told the story of the mission. It also told the story of what happened to two of the priests at the mission. Even though the artist had never been to the Mission San Sabá, the painting accurately tells the story. People who were at the mission when it was attacked provided him with a description of the buildings and details of the attack.

Many people think the artist was José de Páez. The painting was paid for by a cousin of one of the priests killed in the attack. The painting still exists. In the 1990s, it was sent to the United States to be sold. The Mexican government protested, so the painting was returned.

title: Moses Austin Gets ‘Settle Texas Fever’
text:
By 1800, Spain had once again lost interest in Texas. Spain was losing power around the world. This allowed a few Anglo-Americans to enter Texas with very little resistance. Some came to live. A few wanted to claim land and establish a new country that wasn't part of Spain or the United States. That idea failed. Only those who came to live were successful. A man with different plans, however, was about to enter Texas.

Moses Austin was a wealthy businessman in the early 1800s. He had moved to Missouri Territory from the United States. At that time, Missouri was part of Spain. When the U.S. economy entered a slump, so did his business. Austin needed another way to make money, and he thought establishing an Anglo-American colony in Texas would be profitable. In the fall of 1820, he left on horseback for San Antonio to present his plan to the Spanish government.

Texas was a dangerous place for a man by himself. Mexico was fighting Spain for independence. The Comanche and the Apache were fighting each other and attacking Spanish settlements. In spite of these dangers, Austin reached San Antonio. The Spanish government turned him down and threatened to arrest him if he didn't leave.

Austin was about to leave when he met an old friend, Baron de Bastrop. Bastrop knew the Spanish officials, and he found Austin's plan exciting. He offered to present Austin to the government. Austin was encouraged as he left for Missouri.

Austin's trip home was miserable. He caught pneumonia in the cold, wet weather. To make matters worse, he was robbed and ran out of food. During the last week of his trip, Austin had to eat roots and berries.

Back in Missouri, Austin learned Spain would let him establish a colony in Texas. Even though he was sick, Moses Austin worked hard on his dream. This hard work made his health worse. On June 10, 1821, Moses Austin died. His last wish was that his son, Stephen F. Austin, continue his work of establishing a settlement in Texas.

title: Fort Saint Louis Survivor Tells his Story
text:
Do you remember reading about La Salle and Alonso de Leon last week? This is the story of someone who traveled with both men. When the Apache were first coming to Texas, Pierre and his brother were guides and interpreters on a French expedition to search for Spanish missions.

My parents brought us to Texas with La Salle. I am Pierre Talon, one of six children. One of my sisters died on the voyage, but the rest of us survived to face more tragedy.

My family worked hard to build Fort Saint Louis, but nothing went right. After La Belle sank, La Salle made me go with him to get help. That scoundrel left me with the Hasinai. He told me to learn their language and ask them to help the people at our settlement. La Salle never came back to get me! The Hasinai took me in and tattooed my face and body.

Alonso de León finally found me. Even though he was Spanish, I was glad to see him. He told me the Karankawa had destroyed Fort Saint Louis, killed my parents and kidnapped my sister and three brothers. Alonso de Leon rescued my siblings. They were also tattooed, and my two youngest brothers had forgotten how to speak French.

We were taken to Mexico City. Later, two of my brothers and I were sent back to Europe. Our ship was captured by the French, but we were not happy because we liked the Spanish. When we got to France, they found out I knew much about the Hasinai. They sent me back to Louisiana to help St. Denis explore the Red River.

My brother Robert and I returned to Louisiana on another voyage and walked with St. Denis all the way to the Rio Grande. Since I knew the Hasinai, I guided him through their country. When St. Denis was taken to Mexico City, my brother and I sneaked back to Louisiana to tell what had happened.

People say my family played an important role in Texas history, especially my brothers and me.

title: Can a fourth-grader be an archaeologist?
text:
If you enjoy history, you might want to be an archaeologist someday. Do you wish you could start now? Believe it or not, you can work with archaeologists on a real excavation. And the news gets even better. They want your help.

Every year, the Texas Archaeological Society holds a field school at an archaeological site in Texas. The field school lasts for one week each June. The archaeologists work with students who are seven years old or older.

Here is what you will do at a field school. You will begin each day working with an archaeologist. Your job will be digging to find artifacts. Of course, you will be taught the right way to dig, but you will also learn how to map what you find. The archaeologist will record and bag your finds. After four hours of digging, the archaeologist will take you and the artifacts you've found to a laboratory where they will be examined. Then the archaeologists in the lab will tell you about the artifacts you discovered.

Each afternoon you learn about the way people used to live at your site. The lessons are taught by an archaeologist who has special skills in earlier technology. For example, you might learn how fires were started before people had matches. You might learn how meals were cooked in the ground. Some of the lessons will include learning about early weapons. You won't be sitting in a chair listening to someone talk all day. You will see how these early skills were performed, and you will try some of these skills yourself.

Does it sound like fun? Your family will have to come with you, and what a great vacation it will be. All of you will work together to learn more about Texas's past. If you are a Boy Scout, you can earn a Merit Badge. Learn more by contacting the Texas Archaeological Society at www.txarch.org.

text:
Before going to Texas, Moses Austin was a successful businessman in two ways. Two of the following are correct. Read each choice carefully, and circle the two you think are correct. Hint: Use this week’s articles to help you find the two answers that cannot be correct.

A. Moses Austin helped the lead industry grow so much that he started what was called the “Moses Austin Period” of this business.

B. Moses Austin established the city of Austin, Texas. It was the first white settlement in Texas.

C. Moses Austin and 300 settlers defeated the Spanish army in Texas.

D. Moses Austin started the Bank of Saint Louis in Missouri.

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine that you went to a field school at the Texas Archeological Society. You liked it so much that when you grew up, you decided to become an archaeologist. Now you’ve been on digs all over Texas. Write about your most exciting experience on a dig. Where did it happen? What did you find? Why was your find important and exciting?

title: The Trouble with Texas
text:
The year was 1820. Spain had made it clear: They would fight to protect their claim on Texas. Now Spain was facing a revolution. New Spain was fighting for independence from Old Spain. New Spain was about to become Mexico.

Raids and Fights

Most of the Spanish missions were a failure. Very few American Indians had converted to Christianity, and very few adopted the Spanish way of life. The soldiers at the nearby forts could do little but protect the missions. The Texas frontier beyond San Antonio was dangerous for European settlement. The American Indians were successfully defending their homelands and way of life.

The Comanche were aggressive in their actions to others. The Commanche and the Apache were mortal enemies in 1820. When the Apache and Comanche weren’t fighting each other, they fought the settlements sponsored by Spain. There was great unrest and strife in Texas.

Filibuster Trouble

Filibusters were trying to take advantage of the confusion in Texas. (A filibuster was a person who entered Spanish territory and fought against Spanish rule.) Just a year earlier, James Long had taken over the settlement at Nacogdoches. He had declared Texas was independent of Spain and had made himself the president. Spain had had to send troops to run him out of Texas, but Long didn't give up. Now, he had sailed back to the Texas coast and was threatening to attack and take over La Bahia.

Spain's Solution

With these conditions in mind, it is easy to understand why Spain decided to let Moses Austin establish a colony in Texas. Baron de Bastrop gave them three good reasons to give Austin permission. Bastrop reminded the Spanish government that Spaniards and Mexicans did not want to settle Texas. He told them that those who tried settling Texas were getting out as fast as they could. He also warned the government that the conflict among American Indian tribes and settlers would never be solved until colonies were allowed in Texas. Finally, he reminded them that Anglo colonies in Louisiana had been very successful. Bastrop believed they would be just as successful in Texas, and they would strengthen Spain's hold on Texas. This was all Spain needed to hear. Spain gave Austin permission to establish a colony of Anglo-Americans. Granting permission was the easy part. Now the dangerous work of settling Texas would begin.

title: Stephen Austin Refuses to Quit!
text:
At first, Stephen F. Austin didn't want to help his father colonize Texas. When his father died, he felt it was his responsibility to continue his work. A weak economy in 1820 helped Austin change his mind. He needed money, and starting a colony in Texas looked like a good way to earn it.

In the summer of 1821, Spain approved Austin's plan to establish a colony, and he began searching for a site. In September, he found the perfect place. He described the area between the Colorado and Brazos rivers as "the most favored region I had ever seen." It was also where he wanted to build a town, San Felipe de Austin.

Old 300

News of Austin's plan for a colony was spreading, and interested settlers began writing him. Austin promised Spain that 300 families would settle his colony, but there were actually 297. When settlers began arriving, Austin went to New Orleans to buy a ship he would use to send supplies to his colony.

A Streak of Bad Luck

Austin's ship left New Orleans for the mouth of the Colorado River in Texas. The captain mistakenly landed at the mouth of the Brazos. When no one was there to meet him, he went back to New Orleans. Austin tried again. This time, his ship ran aground on Galveston Island, and all of his supplies were lost. The lost supplies made life tough for the first settlers in Austin's colony, but the Karankawa made it worse. The colony was on their land, and they attacked the settlement.

The Karankawa weren't Austin's only problem. His settlers couldn't get the papers they needed to prove they owned their land. Austin hurried to San Antonio to fix the problem. When he got there, he learned that his grant to establish a colony was no longer good because Spain no longer controlled Texas. Mexico had just won its independence from Spain in a revolution. Mexico now owned Texas, and agreements with the Spanish government were worthless. This forced Austin to go to Mexico City where he would try to get permission to establish a colony that he'd already started.

Since the road to Mexico City was very dangerous, Austin disguised himself as a beggar to avoid being robbed. When he got there, things were a mess. Two groups were fighting for control of the Mexican government. To make matters worse, Austin did not speak Spanish.

Austin spent more than a year in Mexico. During that time he learned Spanish and convinced Mexican officials that he was an honest man. At first, they gave him permission to establish a colony. Then they changed their minds, but Austin did not give up.

Austin's Hard Work Pays Off

After a year and a half, Austin finally received permission to continue his work, and his settlers were given proof that they owned their land. When he returned with the good news, he found that his colony was in trouble. A drought had killed the crops. Karankawa had killed many settlers, forcing some settlers to give up and go home. Austin formed a militia and forced the Karankawa out of the area. He then made treaties with the Wichita and Tonkawa tribes.

Austin also established new rules that required colonists to be hardworking and dependable. Since all but four of the colonists could read and write, he probably preferred that the settlers have some education. Criminals and lazy people were not allowed. Those who broke Austin's rules were publicly whipped, and families of poor character were forced to leave.

Austin organized trade with the United States to get the goods his people needed. Life at the colony improved so much that some of the colonists who left came back. Finally, a successful colony in Texas was underway.

title: The Mexican War of Independence
text:
As you read in the cover story, New Spain (Mexico) had been fighting with Spain for many years trying to gain its independence, beginning back in 1810.

Many different people lived in Mexico then. There were Spaniards, some born in Spain and some born in the New World, American Indian groups and mixtures of all these peoples. They were strictly divided by class, and only people born in Spain could hold important positions and gain wealth.

Father Miguel Hidalgo was a Roman Catholic priest in the village of Dolores. He urged the people to rise up against the injustices of the Spanish government and claim their independence. He rang the church bells early on the morning of September 16, 1810, and gave a stirring speech now called the "Grito de Dolores" (Cry of Dolores). This event began the movement toward revolution.

A quickly-formed rebel army won some early battles against the Spanish army but was defeated at Mexico City. Father Hidalgo was convicted of treason and executed (put to death). However, another priest, José Maria Morelos, took his place as leader of the revolutionary army, capturing many cities before he was also arrested, tried and executed.

From 1815 to 1820, both Vicente Guerrero and Guadalupe Victoria led the rebels in many brave battles. But in 1821, the revolution was making little progress. Finally, a general in the Spanish army, Augustin de Iturbide, unexpectedly changed sides because he disliked a new constitution in Spain. He formed the Plan of Igala, which made three guarantees: Mexico would gain independence from Spain, the Roman Catholic Church would be the official religion, and all Spanish people would receive equal rights. Iturbide's army joined the rebels, and Spain soon agreed to Iturbide's plan. The Treaty of Cordoba giving Mexico these freedoms was signed September 27, 1821.

The people of Mexico celebrate September 16, Diez y Seis, as Mexico's Independence Day. They remember Father Hidalgo's grito, along with all the heroes of the Mexican War of Independence who died for their freedom, just as we celebrate the 4th of July in the United States.

title: The Meusebach-Comanche Treaty
text:
The Comanche were probably the most feared of all the American Indians during the settling of Texas, but one man brought a group of families to settle in safety right in the heart of Comancheria, or Comanche country. His name was John Meusebach. He negotiated a peace treaty with the Comanche chiefs that was never broken. That was an amazing feat, because unfortunately, history shows that many treaties are later broken.

Just like Stephen F. Austin, John Meusebach led a group of colonists. Mostly German, they were called the Society for Protection of German Immigrants. They received a land grant from the United States to survey and settle an area in Texas between the Llano and Colorado Rivers, prime Comanche hunting grounds. But no surveyors would set foot on this land because of the danger of Comanche attacks.

Meusebach asked U.S. Indian Agent Robert Neighbors, who was on friendly terms with the Comanche, to help. They negotiated a treaty between colonists and Comanche chiefs Buffalo Hump, Santa Anna and others. (This Santa Anna was a Comanche chief, not the president of Mexico.) The Meusebach-Comanche Treaty was signed on Mar. 1 and 2, 1847 and it covered over three million acres of land. Among other things, it promised that the settlers and Comanche could enter each other's territory unharmed.

Most treaties are written between governments of countries. In the article on the Mexican War of Independence, you will read about the Treaty of Cordoba between Mexico and Spain. However, Meusebach negotiated this treaty between the settlers and the Comanche without government input. The U.S. later recognized the treaty. The original document is on display in the Texas State Library.

title: Why go to Texas?
text:
If Texas was so dangerous in the 1820s, why would anyone want to move there? Many people thought it was a foolish idea.

When people left for Texas, they knew they would probably never see family and friends again. The only way to stay in touch with them was by sending letters, but that could be very hard. If they wanted to send a letter back home, they gave it to someone headed in that direction and hoped it would be delivered. The person carrying the letter might be robbed and killed. The letter might wash away during the crossing of a swollen river.

After building a new home in Texas, people discovered that they were living on other people's land. It was all American Indian country. American Indians had lived on this land for centuries. Some of the American Indians were friendly. Others were not. The ways and laws of the settlers had little meaning to the American Indians. The American Indians were protecting their homes, their territory, and their way of life.

There weren’t many doctors in Texas. If people got sick or injured, family and friends would help the best they could. Many medicines were made from herbs and plants found from the local area. There were no antibiotics available, and complications from injuries would cause greater difficulty than the original wound.

The settlers had to make just about everything they needed. Forget about fashionable clothes and a room full of toys. They had one or two pairs of homemade clothes and no shoes most of the time. As for toys, children were too busy helping the family to play.

Why go to Texas? For the opportunity of cheap land, adventure, the chance of a better life, and to be a pioneer.

title: Austin's Colony
text:
To get you to learn more about Texas history, write a poem based on a true event from Texas History.

Read the following poem about Stephen Austin to give you some ideas.

At the end of the poem, choose which answer you think is the correct ending to the story.

Stephen Austin

Stephen Austin had a plan

He colonized Texas’ wild land

Promised Spain 300 families

For San Felipe de Austin Colony

He bought a ship in New Orleans

Which brought supplies to the colony

The ship got lost and all the supplies

Without which the colonists had to get by

Then along came the proud Karankawa tribe

For the land they’d lived on all their lives

On top of that, Spain lost control

Now Texas belonged to Mexico!

To Mexico City Austin traveled to see

The Mexican government about his colony

A long year passed, but Austin, at last

Received proof settlers owned the land

To much turmoil, did Austin return

Karankawa, dead crops and a drought bad luck turned

_________________________________________________

_________________________________________________

Decide what the true last two lines of the poem are and still make sure it is accurate to what really happened to Stephen Austin.

There are three possible endings for the poem, but only one of them is correct. Can you come up with the correct ending?

Once you make your selection, explain why it is the correct one, and also explain why the other selections are wrong.

Ending 1

Austin fought twenty years, till the foes could see

He’d never give up San Felipe de Austin Colony!

Ending 2

Austin fought, made peace, and made a success of the

San Felipe de Austin Colony!

Ending 3

Austin put up a good fight, but it was clear to see,

He couldn’t save San Felipe de Austin Colony.

title: Let's Write
text: Write a description of Texas geography in the area of Stephen Austin’s colony. What resources, rivers, grasslands, and wildlife were there in 1820? Explain why Austin would want a settlement there. Be sure to use correct grammar, spelling, and sentence structure in your writing.

title: Texas and the Mexican War of Independence
text:
During the Mexican War of Independence, from 1810 to 1821, Texas was in constant turmoil. At the time, Texas territory was still a part of Mexico. For this reason, Texas gave Mexico its support in the war for independence. Armies and landowners loyal to Spain fought against those seeking independence. People from the new United States wanted Texas land.

At this time, Texas and other frontiers had few laws or law enforcement. After the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France in 1803, adventurers and scoundrels (mean or wicked people) called free-booters moved into a lawless area between Louisiana and Texas called the Neutral Strip.

Along with free-booters came Americans who truly believed the United States had a right to claim Texas. These Americans thought that if they became landowners, they could force Spain, and later Mexico, to give up Texas.

A group of Americans brought weapons with them into Texas. They joined Bernardo Gutierrez de Lara to aid his quest to win independence from Spain. The group took control of San Antonio in 1813, but Spain later sent troops to retake the area. Spain’s overemphasis on protecting San Antonio meant troops and resources had to be taken from other parts of Texas. This made life in those areas more unstable.

During the independence movement, many settlers died in battle or fled Texas to survive. They lost land and cattle. By 1821, only about 2,000 people remained in three populated areas: San Antonio in south central Texas, Presidio la Bahia in the coastal bend region, and Nacogdoches to the east.

These challenges couldn’t be ignored. A weak government in Mexico City wasn’t able to protect Texas. Americans were eager to buy Texas land. Restless Wichita, Karankawa, and Tonkawa had their own demands.

By 1821, when Mexico achieved independence, the neglect of Texas meant hard choices for Mexico. Strong hands were needed to control that vast province. The problem? The American “empresarios” were ambitious. American settlers poured into Texas and wanted land and cattle. Perhaps more important, they also wanted to be independent of Mexico.

title: Austin Turns Against Mexico!
text:
Stephen F. Austin was a strong supporter of the Mexican government when his colony began in 1822. The government treated the colonists kindly and asked for little in return. There were a few problems. Mexico turned down Austin's request to build roads and public schools in the colony. In Austin's opinion, this disappointment was small when compared to all of the good things Mexico did for the colonists.

In 1825, Mexico passed a law allowing more immigrants into Texas. About two dozen grants for new colonies were issued in the next 10 years. The men who got the grants were called empresarios. Martin de Leon started the only Texas colony made up mostly of Mexican citizens. The Mexican government often favored him in disagreements with other colonies because he was a Mexican citizen.

By 1830, there were more than 20,000 Americans in Texas. They outnumbered Spanish-speaking Texans by five to one. Corn was the biggest crop, but the cotton industry was growing. Austin was happy. In a letter to his sister, he said the Mexican government was the best on Earth. The citizens of Texas were also happy. They paid no taxes. Men were not forced to serve in the Mexican army, and Mexico was not strict about its requirement that every Texan be a Catholic.

Seeds of Trouble

As Texas grew, so did its problems. Courts were needed to try criminals and settle differences between people. The nearest court office was more than 500 miles away.

A new kind of immigrant added to Austin's concerns. He called these immigrants "leather stockings." They were mountain men and frontiersmen who did not like any government, including the Mexican government. While most Texans were happy with Mexico, the leather stockings talked about rebellion.

Mexico paid little attention to Texas because it had other problems. After winning independence, the Mexican government was a mess. Two groups were battling for control. One group wanted a strong central government in Mexico City and strict control of Texas. The other group wanted Texans to have more freedom. During the next eight years, control of the government shifted back and forth between these two groups. Mexico's attitude toward Texas changed often. This irritated the Texans. It also caused many of them to listen seriously to the leather stockings.

Austin continued to defend the Mexican government. If colonists complained, Austin reminded them of the benefits they enjoyed as Mexican citizens. Austin even helped the Mexican military keep control of Texas. When Haden Edwards (a fellow empresario) started a rebellion against Mexico, Austin organized a militia to stop him.

Austin's support for Mexico was about to end. Before long he would join those calling for a revolution.

title: Do You Live Near a Ghost Town?
text:
What is a ghost town? Here's a hint: It's not an imaginary town that is home to cartoon characters like Casper the Friendly Ghost! A ghost town is a town no one (or almost no one) lives in anymore. Sometimes there are a few buildings still standing. In other ghost towns, you could drive right through them without even knowing a town used to be there. Some have historical markers that tell the story of what happened to the town.

Most people use the words "ghost town" when they're talking about towns in the West. Some ghost towns were once very successful because people made good money in mining or another business. When the mines and other businesses closed, the people moved away. Indianola, Texas, became a ghost town after two strong hurricanes struck within 11 years. People who lived in Texas when the railroads were being built hoped the railroad would come through their town. Towns that were bypassed by the railroad often became ghost towns.

How many ghost towns do you think are in Texas today - 20? 50? 100? Actually, most lists say there are more than 800. With that many on the list, you might live near a ghost town!

title: Rebellion in Texas
text:
Worries about the United States

Thousands of settlers poured into Texas after Austin established his first colony. Nearly all of them came from the United States. Mexico allowed the Anglo-Americans into Texas because Mexicans did not want to settle the wild territory. When the United States tried to buy Texas, Mexico changed its mind about immigrants. The Law of 1830 stopped immigration into Texas and forced Texans to pay taxes on trade goods. This law angered the Texans and talk of rebellion grew.

Turmoil in the Mexican Government

A young Mexican military officer wanted control of the government. This man was Santa Anna, and he had the full support of many Texans, including Stephen Austin. This support for Santa Anna shows how little they understood what was happening in Mexico. Stephen Austin was about to find out the hard way.

In 1832, the Texans held a convention and named Stephen Austin as its president. They wrote out what they wanted from the Mexican government. They asked for permission to govern themselves. Texas was part of the Mexican state of Coahuilla, but the convention wanted Texas to be a separate state.

The colonists asked for land to build schools. They also wanted permission to organize a militia to protect themselves from the Indians. When Santa Anna heard about the convention, he was furious. The Texans were told that their convention was against the law. How did the Texans reply? They held another convention to criticize Santa Anna for the way he ruled Mexico with his army. The convention asked that new immigrants be allowed to enter Texas. In April 1833, Austin left to deliver the request to Santa Anna in Mexico City.

Mexico's Reply

Austin had a friendly meeting with Santa Anna. Santa Anna agreed to many of the requests, and Austin left thinking everything was fine. But before he reached Texas, Austin was arrested and sent back to Mexico City. Officials jailed him and would not allow him to read books or write letters. Austin spent the next year and a half in and out of jail.

Santa Anna could have ordered the Mexican president to release Austin, but he didn't. While Austin sat in jail, the Mexican president gave Texans most of what Austin and the other members of the convention asked for. New immigrants were allowed. Three government offices were opened in Texas. English became the official business language of Texas. Yet Austin had to stay in jail because he was part of the convention.

In 1834, Santa Anna forced the Mexican president out of office and took control of the government. Next, he stopped all immigration into Texas and ended other policies Texans liked. He was now a dictator. A dictator is a leader who has all of the power to run a government. Dictators usually jail or kill anyone who opposes them. Santa Anna was no different. He attacked a group of his own people for not supporting him. Even though he was a dictator, Santa Anna did accomplish something Mexico had been unable to do. Many Mexicans were finally rushing to live in Texas - to get away from Santa Anna!

Stephen Austin's Reply

Austin hurried back to Texas after finally being released from prison. A year and a half in prison had changed him. The man who was so loyal to Mexico returned to Texas ready for rebellion. He had learned the hard way that Texans could no longer live under Mexican rule.

title: Sam Houston
text:
Sam Houston's life was filled with adventure long before he arrived in Texas. At the age of 17, he was bored with chores on the family farm and sneaked away to explore an island on the Tennessee River. While exploring, he stumbled into a Cherokee camp. Ready for a different life, Sam joined the Cherokee. He was adopted by the chief and given an Indian name, Raven.

Sam's mother feared her son was dead. Two of his older brothers began searching for him. When they found him, Sam refused to leave and lived with the Cherokee for three years. Houston left the Cherokee to fight in the U.S. Army under Andrew Jackson. Jackson was impressed with Houston's bravery and gave him a promotion. Houston was given the job of working with the Cherokee. When Houston found that the Cherokee weren't getting the supplies the Army promised, he led a group of tribal leaders to see the Secretary of War in Washington, D.C. Instead of wearing his uniform, Houston wore only Indian breechclouts. The secretary was furious, but Houston didn't care.

Houston taught himself law and entered politics. After serving as a congressman, he was elected governor of Tennessee. There was talk that he might become president of the United States.

A failed marriage ended Houston's political career in Tennessee. Houston then decided to move to Arkansas. On the trip he met Jim Bowie and listened to his stories about Texas. Houston wasn't ready for Texas. After reaching Arkansas, he lived with the Cherokee for another three years.

While living with the Cherokee, Houston traveled to Washington, D.C. to represent them. On one of these trips, President Jackson asked him to go to Texas on a mission. No one is sure what the mission was about, but in less than a year, Houston was in Texas working for independence. By Nov. 1835, he was named Major General of the Texas army. Within a few months, he would win Texas' fight for independence at the Battle of San Jacinto.

title: First Shots of the Revolution
text:
In Sept. 1835, Mexican military leaders feared a war with Texas. They took back a cannon they had given the town of Gonzales for protection against the American Indians. They feared it would be used against the Mexican army.

Three hundred Mexican troops were sent to get it. They were also told to avoid a fight. When the citizens of Gonzales learned Mexican soldiers were coming, a call went out to nearby settlements for help. On the morning of Oct. 2, 1835 Texans attacked the Mexican soldiers in the first battle of the revolution. They proudly waved a flag displaying a cannon and the words "Come and take it!"

During a break in the fighting, the commanding officers from both sides met. The Mexican officer explained he wanted more freedom for Texas. He was invited to join the Texans but refused, and the fighting continued. The Mexican army finally withdrew, and the Texans kept their cannon.

title: Houston’s Plan: Blow Up the Alamo
text:
In Jan. 1836, Texans believed things were going their way. The Mexican army lost at Gonzales. Texans controlled the Alamo and La Bahia. Many soldiers went home, thinking the war was over. General Sam Houston knew better.

Spies reported Santa Anna was leading an army of more than 4,000 soldiers into Texas. Houston knew the Texas army was smaller and weaker. He created a bold plan. Part of this plan was to blow up the Alamo and leave. Houston asked the Texas governor to support his plan, but the governor refused. Houston sent Jim Bowie to the Alamo to convince the soldiers to leave. When Bowie got there, he changed his mind and stayed to fight.

Houston was so angry that he thought about quitting his command and going back to live with the Cherokee. In his mind, the battle for independence was lost. In the weeks to come, you will learn how Houston turned a hopeless situation into a victory.

title: Who was the real Santa Anna?
text:
(This article is historical fiction based on quotes from Santa Anna and facts about his life.)

"Welcome home, son," Martin's father said. "We are proud that you are an aide to the great Santa Anna!" Martin frowned.

"Why are you are not happy?" his father asked.

"Santa Anna is not who you think he is. He is mad with power. With my own ears I heard him say, 'Man is nothing; power everything!' "

His father's eyes widened. "That does not sound like Santa Anna."

"It is true. His smiles hide the evil in his heart. I also heard him say, 'Were I made God, I should wish to be something more.' "

Martin's mother gasped. "Why would a brave man say that?"

"Santa Anna is not always brave," Martin scoffed. "He is afraid of water. Sometimes his army waits while he finds the courage to cross a small river. Santa Anna will soon march on Texas. When we get to the Rio Grande, I will cross the river while he worries about getting wet. Then I will join the Texans and fight this monster!"

title: Texas Settlements Become Ghost Towns
text:
Sam Houston and other leaders had just signed the Texas Declaration of Independence, written a constitution and established a government. With Santa Anna moving deeper into Texas, they quickly ended their meeting and fled Washington-on-the-Brazos.

When Houston learned the Alamo had fallen, he ordered citizens to retreat to the Colorado River. Messengers hurried to spread the news that Santa Anna was on the way. Settlements emptied as people raced toward Galveston and Louisiana. Communities throughout Texas became ghost towns.

Known as Runaway Scrape, this retreat began in March 1836. Many people running from Santa Anna died in the cold. Food was in short supply, and diseases claimed many lives. Most Texans did not quit running until Houston defeated and captured Santa Anna at the Battle of San Jacinto. Even then, fear of Santa Anna was so deep that many thought it wasn't safe to return home.

title: Henry Knox and the Cannons
text:
What does it take to be a good problem solver? Why is critical analysis, or careful judgment, so important? A bookseller from Boston named Henry Knox is an excellent example.

Knox was born in Boston in 1750. His father died when he was 12, so he left school to be a clerk in a bookstore. Later, Knox opened his own bookstore. He loved to read and learned a lot about military strategies and weapons from the books he read.

Knox sided with the American patriots and joined the Army in 1775. General George Washington soon noticed him because of his military knowledge.

The British forces were in Boston, and General Washington needed heavy artillery to force them out. Knox suggested bringing cannons from Fort Ticonderoga in northern New York down to Boston. This idea sounded impossible, but Washington trusted Knox's judgment. Using heavy sleds drawn by oxen, Knox and his men traveled 300 miles. They brought over 50 cannons across snow-covered mountains and frozen rivers. They placed them overnight on a hill overlooking the harbor. When British Gen. William Howe saw this, he withdrew his troops. He said, "The rebels have done more in one night than my whole army would have done in a month."

Henry Knox used critical analysis again when he supervised Washington's famous crossing of the icy Delaware River. Knox stood on the shore shouting directions while boats moved troops, horses and weapons across. Washington's soldiers then won the Battle of Trenton. The next day they went back across the river with even more prisoners and supplies.

Washington promoted Henry Knox to brigadier general. When Washington became president, he made Knox the first Secretary of War. Henry Knox used expert knowledge and critical analysis to become a military mastermind. What problem could you use your best judgment to solve?

title: Break the Code and Find the Mystery Word
text:
Directions
