Try to figure out the meaning of the words by reading the other words and sentences around them. Write what you think the words mean and compare your definition to a dictionary definition.

title: Looking Back: European Exploration to Texas Revolution
text:
Exploring a New World

When Christopher Columbus returned to Spain after his 1492 voyage, people all over Europe were excited. News of the "New World" spread quickly. People wondered what kind of land and riches might be waiting for them across the ocean. They were curious about the people who lived there. The European nations of Spain, Portugal, England and France began competing to claim land and settle colonies in what is today known as North America. Spain was first to put its plan into action.

Spain wanted to be the most powerful nation in the world. It needed money and land to do this. Explorers were sent to find gold and other riches in the New World. They had heard legends about entire cities made of gold that were just waiting to be explored and conquered. Spanish conquistadores (conquerors) defeated the wealthy Aztec and Inca empires in North America. These explorers also claimed land and established settlements in the name of Spain. Settlers and priests then went to the New World to form missions and colonies on land Spain had claimed. The American Indians already living in North America were not Christians. Spain was a Catholic nation and believed it was their duty to convert Americans Indians to the Catholic faith. If the American Indians became Catholics, the Spanish believed that it would strengthen Spain's power in the New World. The plan for exploration of North America changed the world forever.

Spanish Explorers in Texas

Spain wanted to lay claim to the New World and its riches as quickly as it could. With the help of many brave explorers, Spain was able to gain knowledge and get a head start on other European nations who also wanted to use North America in a power play.

Alonso Álvarez de Pineda (1519): He left Jamaica in 1519 to map the Gulf Coast of the New World. He hoped to find a waterway to China. He explored and mapped the Texas coastline. His maps made it possible for other explorers to find their way to the New World.

Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca (1528-1536): He washed ashore near Galveston Bay after a terrible trip across the ocean. He and his men were rescued by American Indians who enslaved the Spanish men. For eight years they traveled across Texas with their captors. After escaping, Cabeza de Vaca wrote about his adventures and the land in Texas that could be claimed for Spain.

Francisco Vázquez de Coronado (1540-1542): He led an expedition from Arizona to Kansas looking for the golden Seven Cities of Cibola. In their travels, Coronado and his men saw the Grand Canyon and traveled through the Texas Panhandle. Coronado reported to the King of Spain that Texas land would be good for growing crops. Of course, he never found the legendary golden cities.

France Attempts to Colonize the New World

Less than 200 years after Columbus sailed to the New World, Spain controlled most of the southwest area. France explored the northeastern part of North America. One of the explorers France put faith in was René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle.

La Salle made two famous voyages to the New World. In 1682, he sailed part of the Mississippi River and claimed territory for France. He named it Louisiana, after King Louis XIV. He believed France should establish a colony at the mouth of the Mississippi River, where it empties into the Gulf of Mexico.

LaSalle's journey back to the New World in 1684 did not go well. The explorer had a difficult time finding people to sail with him. Pirates attacked his ships, causing the explorer to become lost. Instead of landing at the Mississippi River, La Salle landed near Matagorda Bay in Texas.

La Salle's crew built Fort Saint Louis near the Matagorda Bay. The fort was doomed because the land was rough and food was scarce. People worked very hard for the demanding leader. However, the tired and angry settlers eventually turned against La Salle and killed him. Karankawa Indians attacked and ended the colony.

After Spain learned that the colony had failed, it stepped in to keep France and other nations from claiming land in the New World. This began the era of Spanish missions in North America.

title: Texas, Our Texas
text:
Spain Tries to Hold on to Texas

Disagreements with other European nations kept Spain busy in the late 18th century. By 1800, Texas was not as interesting to the once powerful nation. Anglo-Americans, however, were interested in settling Texas. Some wanted to live there, while others simply wanted to claim land. Spain began to rethink their position in Texas. By 1820, the Spanish were willing to fight to protect their claim on Texas land. This became very difficult when New Spain (soon to become Mexico) began an effort to free itself from Old Spain's control.

In addition to the ongoing revolution, Spain faced additional troubles. The Spanish missions were mostly unsuccessful. Very few American Indians had converted to Christianity and adopted the Spanish way of life. The Comanche and other American Indian groups roamed the Texas frontier, attacking settlers and other tribes. Filibusters (people who entered Spanish territory and fought against Spanish rule) tried to take over land in Texas as independent nations. Spain had to come up with a plan to help them hang on to Texas.

Stephen F. Austin Takes Over

Moses Austin was a wealthy businessman from Missouri Territory, and he had an idea to make money. He thought establishing an Anglo-American colony in Texas would be a good idea. He traveled to Mexico to meet with Spain's leaders. Austin would get land and Spain would get settlers. It seemed like a good plan. However, Moses Austin died before his dream came true. It was then up to his son Stephen F. Austin to carry on with the plan.

Austin was given permission from Spain to bring 300 Anglo families to settle his colony in Texas. The task was not an easy one. The colony was San Felipe de Austin. It did not have the supplies it needed for quite a while, and attacks by the Karankawa Indians made things worse. Then, Spain lost control of Texas when Mexico won its independence. Suddenly, Austin had to get permission from an entirely new government to establish his colony. He spent more than a year in Mexico trying to convince leaders that the colony was a good idea.

Austin's Colony

Austin finally received permission to continue the work on his colony. But when he returned to Texas, Austin was greeted with bad news. The colony was in trouble. A drought had killed crops, and the Karankawa had killed many people. Some settlers had returned home to the United States. Austin took control. He formed a militia (group trained as soldiers) and forced the Karankawa out of the area. He made peace treaties with other American Indian tribes. He also established rules for the colony. Dependable, hardworking settlers were welcome, but criminals and lazy people were not. To get supplies the colony needed, Austin organized trade with the United States. It appeared Austin's colony would be a great success.

Stephen Austin supported the Mexican government when he began his colony in 1822. There were a few problems, but Austin was happy with the way his colonists were treated at first. Mexico was also pleased with the relationship. They decided to give about two dozen more land grants to men called empresarios. One of these men was Martin de Leon. He started a Texas colony made up of mostly Mexican citizens.

Texas grew larger and so did its problems. Courts were needed, and some immigrants began to talk about a rebellion against Mexico. In addition, the government leaders of Mexico kept changing, so the attitude toward Texas changed often as well. In 1830, Mexico passed a law that stopped immigration into Texas and forced Texans to pay taxes. More and more people, including Austin, became concerned about the future of Texas.

Turmoil in Texas

In Mexico, a man named Santa Anna took control of the government. He ruled Mexico with his army. He expected everyone, including Texans, to obey his every rule. Texans were unhappy about the Law of 1830 and new taxes. They held a convention to discuss their problems. In 1832, they elected Stephen F. Austin as president. They wanted Austin to go to Mexico and talk to Santa Anna. The Texans wanted to ask permission to govern themselves as a separate Mexican state. They wanted land on which to build schools, and they wanted permission to form a militia to protect themselves from American Indians attacks. Santa Anna was furious that Texas had held a convention, and he told them so. The Texans did not give up, though. They held another convention to criticize Santa Anna's government and ask that new immigrants be allowed to enter Texas. In April 1833, Austin returned to Mexico City to discuss their demands with Gen. Santa Anna.

The meeting between the two leaders went well. Santa Anna agreed to many of the Texans' requests. However, before Austin could return to Texas he was arrested and put in prison. He was in and out of prison for the next year and a half. Before long, Santa Anna became a dictator. He expected everyone to do as he wished. He ended all of the policies the Texans liked. Many Mexican citizens fled to Texas to escape Santa Anna's rule. When Stephen Austin was finally released from prison, he hurried back to Texas. He had once been loyal to Mexico, but Austin now knew the Texans could no longer live under Mexican rule.

title: Early Spanish Settlements in Texas
text:
When the Spanish found France's Fort Saint Louis, no one was alive at the failed colony. However, Spain feared France would try again. They decided to build a fort where the old French colony stood. La Bahia Mission was successful, so the Spanish decided to build more missions in east Texas. They could convert the American Indians to Christianity and establish permanent settlements, which would be missions or military forts. They eventually formed many missions throughout Texas.

Over time, people abandoned most missions and forts. To establish permanent settlements, a Spanish army officer named José de Escandón established colonies along the lower Rio Grande Valley. Escandón helped settle more than 20 towns. Today he is called the "father of the Lower Rio Grande Valley."

title: Spain’s Slipping Grip on Texas
text:
Spanish missions were not able to convert many American Indians to Christianity. They did keep the French from colonizing Texas, though. But Spain's problems in Texas were only starting. The fierce Comanche tribe was Spain's next threat.

The Comanche drove other tribes, such as the Lipan Apache, off their land. Rumors of silver in central Texas convinced Spain to build a special mission to help the Apache. Spanish soldiers could protect the Apache, and the mission would keep France out of Texas. Groups of American Indians attacked and burned the mission. These tribes controlled Texas. Spain finally tried another strategy to hold onto Texas. They let Mexican and Anglo-Americans build settlements on the Texas frontier.

title: Why settle Texas?
text: Stephen F. Austin had no trouble convincing nearly 300 Anglo families to leave everything and settle Texas. Pioneers left homes, families and jobs in the United States for the chance at new lives on the frontier. It was almost certain they would never see family and friends again. The trip to Texas was dangerous, and once there, life was hard. Everything the settlers needed had to come from the natural resources around them. American Indians attacked, and even Mexican soldiers threatened life in the colony. Why did anyone agree to follow Austin to Texas? These brave people wanted the chance to own land and make better lives for themselves and their families. Texas was worth the risk.

title: Let the Revolution Begin
text:
In the fall of 1835, Mexican leaders knew the Texans were unhappy with the way they were being treated. The leaders worried the Texans might be planning a war to free themselves from Mexican control. Mexico decided it should take back a cannon it had given the town of Gonzales to use against American Indian attacks. The Mexicans feared the cannon might be used against them.

Three hundred Mexican troops went for the cannon. Citizens of Gonzales fought back. On Oct. 2, 1835, 140 Texans attacked the Mexican soldiers. They proudly waved a flag showing a picture of a cannon and the words "Come and take it!" The Mexicans withdrew, and Texans won the first battle of the Texas Revolution.

title: Main Idea and Details
text: After reading the article “Texas, Our Texas,” identify the main idea of each subsection. List two or three details that support the main idea.

title: Think and Review
text:
What were the key parts of Spain’s plan to become the most powerful nation in the world?

Why were the Seven Cities of Cibola, or cities of gold, important to early exploration of North America?

Predict what might have been the outcome if La Salle had been a better leader.

Do you agree with the Texans’ wish to break free from Mexican rule? Why or why not?

What evidence can you find that shows the Mexicans were concerned about the Texans being more difficult to handle than first expected?

title: Spanish and Mexican Governments in Texas
text:
In 1519, Spain claimed Texas as its own. But running a country that’s more than 5,000 miles away and already filled with independent people is hard. This is true even if you are a king or queen with power in a monarchy. What would you do if an ocean separated you from something you wanted to control?

For almost 200 years, Spain claimed Texas on maps but didn’t create any settlements on the ground! Then, in 1690, Spain sent missionaries.

The goal of missionaries was to teach people about their religion, but Spain also wanted missionaries to control the land. Spain hoped missionaries would keep out the French and convince Texas’s native peoples to obey Spain. Spain also sent soldiers. They built forts called presidios. The army protected the roads, land, and wealth Spain claimed.

But the native peoples in Texas did not want to obey Spain. Neither did most new settlers. Spain also had problems at home and didn’t give Texas much attention and support. There was unrest. Who would control the land?

In 1821, Mexico won independence from Spain. Mexico claimed Texas as its own. But running a country that’s more than 800 miles away is hard. This is true even if you are elected the president of Mexico. What would you do if deserts separated you from something you wanted to control?

Mexico sent businessmen called empresarios. The goal of empresarios was to make money, but Mexico also wanted help controlling the land. The empresarios attracted settlers. The new settlers got land in exchange for developing the property. The empresarios received land as payment for their work. Then they helped govern the land.

In the 1830s, though, Mexico’s government changed and decreased local leaders’ control. The new American settlers and many Mexican Tejanos did not want to obey the faraway government of Mexico. There was unrest in Texas under Mexico’s control, just like there was when Spain controlled Texas. Who would control the land?

title: Travis Holds at the Alamo!
text:
In January 1836, William B. Travis and 30 other soldiers entered the Spanish mission known as the Alamo in San Antonio. Just days later Travis became the commander of all the soldiers at the mission. Although he was only 26 years old, Travis said he was willing to stay strong for Texas — no matter what.

General Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna marched his troops into San Antonio just weeks after Travis and his men arrived. The Mexican dictator and about 1,800 of his soldiers set up camp outside the Alamo. Bugle calls and cannon blasts warned the men in the Alamo that Santa Anna's men were there to crush the uprising.

Inside the mission, Colonel Travis and around 200 other brave men planned ways to hold back the Mexicans. Davy Crockett, James Bonham and Jim Bowie helped make the plan. They decided to move the women and children into safer areas of the mission. The church seemed to be the safest place for them.

Travis ordered one of his men, Albert Martin, to sneak a letter out of the Alamo past the Mexican soldiers. In the letter to Texas leader Sam Houston, Travis explained that he would not surrender even though the Texans were outnumbered and starving. Travis explained that he and his men were waiting for more fellow Texans to come help them fight. Travis signed his letter "Victory or Death."

On the morning of March 6, 1836, the men in the Alamo knew that no help was on the way. For 12 long days the Mexicans had pounded the Alamo with cannon fire. Travis looked out and saw a red flag flying from the steeple of a church. The red flag was Santa Anna's way of saying the Mexicans would "take no prisoners." Travis and his men held strong, just as they had promised. Almost 1,800 Mexicans fought, and about 600 of them were killed or wounded. But there was no way for 189 Texans to win against so many Mexican soldiers.

General Santa Anna and his men killed all of the Texans at the Alamo that day. The bodies were thrown away or burned. Only the women and children who were hiding in the church were not killed.

While the battle at the Alamo was a terrible loss, the courage and honor of the Texans who fought there helped the rest of the Texans stay strong in the fight for independence!

title: Did Davy Crockett Really Go Down Fighting?
text:
Davy Crockett was born in Tennessee. He could survive in any wilderness, and some people say he could kill a bear with no help from anyone. Stories about Crockett's adventures made him an American hero. But just how true are the stories about his death at the Alamo?

In 1834, Crockett was angry when he lost an election to the U.S. House of Representatives. He left Tennessee and headed for Texas. He fought in the battle at the Alamo. General Santa Anna's forces killed Crockett and all the other soldiers at the Alamo. But not everyone agrees about how and when Crockett was killed.

Most stories of the 13-day Battle of the Alamo say that Crockett fought bravely until the very end of the battle. Then he was captured, taken to General Santa Anna and killed.

But a Mexican army officer's diary tells a different story. The diary was found in 1955. It is about 200 pages long. The diary says Crockett was captured and killed early in the battle. If that is true, then Davy Crockett did not live to see the end of the battle.

Historians are studying the diary. (Historians are people who study history.) The diary is at the John Peace Library at the University of Texas at San Antonio. The historians want to find out whether the diary is real and the story is true. Whether Crockett died early in the battle or at the very end, he will always be an American hero.

title: Battle of the Alamo
text:
Who Was Santa Anna?

Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna was born in Jalapa, Mexico, in 1794. When he was a young man, he joined the Spanish army. For several years, he fought against his fellow Mexicans who wanted their independence from Spain. Finally, he left the Spanish army and joined the Mexican army. In 1821, the Mexicans defeated the Spanish army and won their independence.

Santa Anna became a powerful leader. In fact, he served as a president of Mexico 11 times between 1833 and 1855. He was president in 1836, when he led Mexican troops into Texas. He thought the Anglos living there were becoming much too greedy and hard to control.

Santa Anna was a cruel and very powerful dictator. He gave the order to attack the Alamo and take no prisoners. His order led to the deaths of many Texans and Mexicans. Following the terrible attack against the Texans, Santa Anna said, "Much blood has been shed; but the battle is over; it was but a small affair." This "small affair" cost many lives and would later cost Santa Anna his power in Mexico.

Heroes of the Alamo

The men who died at the Alamo on March 6, 1836, had come to the Alamo willing to give up everything - even their lives - for the freedom and independence of Texas. The men came from very different backgrounds, but each one was a true hero.

William Barret Travis

Travis was born and raised in South Carolina. He came to Texas in 1831, bought land from Stephen F. Austin and became a lawyer. Travis was one of the first men to join the Texas army when troubles with Mexico began. In January 1836, Travis and about 30 men went into the Alamo. He and James Bowie shared command of the Alamo. But after Bowie became ill, Travis was in charge. He wrote a letter to the people of Texas from the Alamo asking for help. He signed the letter, "Victory or Death." Although he was only 26 years old, Travis faced the enemy bravely and died as a hero.

James Butler Bonham

Like William Travis, James Bonham was a lawyer from South Carolina. When he got to Texas, he eagerly joined the Texans in their fight for independence. Right away, Bonham was made a lieutenant in the Texas cavalry (soldiers who ride horses). He delivered messages back and forth between leaders. He traveled across enemy lines to carry a message from Travis asking for more men to help defend the Alamo. Bonham got back to the Alamo three days before the final battle.

James Bowie

Jim Bowie was born in Kentucky and grew up in Louisiana. He loved adventure. After he moved to Texas, he spent some time searching for silver and gold with Texas Indians. Later he became a Texas Ranger. He is famous for his use of the Bowie knife. Bowie bravely helped Travis command the volunteers at the Alamo until he became too ill. When the Mexican forces stormed the Alamo, Bowie was shot while lying on his cot.

Gregorio Esparza

Gregorio Esparza was born in Texas. He joined a group of volunteers who came to the Alamo on horseback. Esparza was the last defender to arrive at the Alamo. He brought his wife and four children with him. During the battle, he fired the cannon from the church window and never left his position. Esparza's family survived the attack. They got permission from the Mexican army to bury him. The soldiers burned all of the other bodies of the men who died at the Alamo.

title: What Does the Texas Pledge Mean to You?
text:
You probably start each school day by placing your hand over your heart and saying the pledge to the Texas flag. The pledge is an oath, or promise, that you will be loyal to the flag. The flag stands for Texas. When you promise to be loyal to the flag, you are promising to be loyal to our state.

In 2007, lawmakers added the words "one state under God" to the pledge. It was the second time the pledge changed. In 1965, the start of the pledge was changed from "Honor the Texas Flag of 1836..." to what is found below.

"Honor the Texas flag; I pledge allegiance to thee, Texas, one state under God, one and indivisible."

People sing songs for many different reasons. One song has special meaning to the people of Texas. It's the official state song, "Texas, Our Texas."

In the late 1920s, the state government had a contest to find a song to represent Texas. William J. Marsh and Gladys Yoakum Wright won the contest. Texas lawmakers named "Texas, Our Texas" the state song in 1929. But they didn't pass a law making it official until 1993.

Marsh and Wright used the words "largest and grandest" in one of the verses. When Alaska became a state in 1959, Texas was no longer the largest state, because Alaska has more land than Texas. So the words were changed to "boldest and grandest" instead.

"God bless you Texas! And keep you brave and strong,
That you may grow in power and worth, Throughout the ages long."
- Refrain of the State Song of Texas

You can find the complete words at www.tsl.texas.gov. Sing it with your class!

title: Why does Texas celebrate a state holiday March 2?
text:
Each year on March 2, Texans celebrate the signing of the Texas Declaration of Independence in 1836.

While one group of brave Texans held strong at the Alamo, another group of Texans met to talk about freedom from Mexico. On March 1, the first day of the meeting, they chose five men to start writing a document. The document told everyone that Texans wanted to be free instead of being part of Mexico. The Texas Declaration of Independence was written overnight, and everyone agreed to it the next day. The meeting ended on March 17, when the Texans heard that Santa Anna and his men were getting close to the place where the meeting was being held.

Today, many cities and towns have parades and festivals on March 2. How does your community celebrate Texas Independence Day?

title: Susanna Dickinson: Alamo Survivor
text:
Santa Anna told his men to kill all the Texan men at the Alamo, but he ordered his men to save the lives of women and children. One of these women was Susanna Dickinson, who was only about 22 years old. Her husband was a blacksmith at the Alamo. (A blacksmith is someone who makes things from iron or other metals.) During the battle, she hid in the church with her baby daughter, Angelina. After the battle was over, the women and children were taken to Santa Anna. He gave each of them a blanket and $2. Then he let them go. Susanna lived almost 47 years after surviving the Alamo. She died in Austin in 1883.

No one is exactly sure what happened to Susanna at the Alamo. Some stories say she was shot in the leg by a stray bullet. Some say she hid in the powder magazine (where the gun powder was kept) instead of the church. You may even hear that Santa Anna offered to take Angelina back to Mexico with him. You can do some research on your own to find out more. Check out books from the library, or ask permission to look for information on the internet.

title: Flowcharts
text: Read the story “Travis Holds at the Alamo!” again. Make a flowchart by writing three sentences about what happened at the Alamo. Put one sentence in each of the boxes. Put the sentences in the order the events happened. Ask a friend to check your flow chart. Are the sentences in the right order? Did you put a capital letter at the beginning and a period at the end of each sentence? Are all the words spelled correctly?

title: Let's Write
text: After reading this week’s paper, explain the importance of the Battle of the Alamo to Texas history. Use your own words, and don’t forget to use correct grammar, spelling, and punctuation.

title: Juan Nepomuceno Seguín
text: Juan N. Seguín was born in Bexar (what is now San Antonio, TX) on October 27, 1806. In 1828, he was elected an alderman, a sort of city councilman. By 1833, he was elected alcalde, a very high position that is a combination of mayor, judge, and head of the town council. Within two years, his military career would begin. Like many Tejanos, or Texans of Mexican descent, Seguín’s first goal in fighting against the Mexican government was not for Texan independence. At first, his and others’ aim was to defend the country against the dictator Santa Anna. He led a militia to Monclova in 1835 and fought in the battle of Gonzales. He started to work toward revolution after revolutionary forces overtook the Alamo. Seguín was a defender at the Alamo. He sent out on a courier mission just before the Mexican army arrived, so he did not fight at the Alamo. Seguín accepted Mexico’s surrender of San Antonio in June of 1836. He resigned his military command when he was elected to the Texas Senate in 1837. He was the only Tejano to serve in the early senate. He died in 1890.

title: Jim Bowie
text: James (Jim) Bowie was a frontiersman and is considered a great hero of Texas history. This is because he fiercely defended Texas in the Texas War for Independence. His early life in Missouri and Louisiana helped create the bold and fearless personality that often got him into trouble. After he killed a man in a duel in 1828, he fled to Texas. There, he married the governor's daughter. Bowie acquired a land grant and became a Mexican citizen. He soon got caught up in the Texas Revolutionary Movement and became a colonel in the Texas Army. Under the command of General Sam Houston, Bowie volunteered to go to San Antonio. In San Antonio, he and Colonel Travis both commanded the forces that defended the Alamo against General Santa Anna. He died at the Alamo alongside another hero, Davy Crockett.

title: David Crockett
text: David Crockett joined the Tennessee militia to help protect settlers from attacks by American Indians. David later joined Andrew Jackson’s army in 1814 but was later discharged. Jackson went on to become President and David became a Congressman. David served in Congress from 1826 to 1834. He soon had disagreements with and could no longer support President Jackson. So, David Crockett left and went to Texas where he fought alongside Texans to help them win their independence from the Mexican government. His life ended at the Alamo. David Crockett told great stories, and people hailed him as a hero. Through the years, journalists have shared and embellished his stories, turning him into somewhat of a legend and folk hero.

title: Santa Anna is Coming!
text:
After many Texas soldiers died in the battle of the Alamo, General Santa Anna led his troops towards the Texas coast, raiding and burning every settlement in their path. Susanna Dickinson, an Alamo survivor, quickly told the major general of the Republic of Texas army about the terrible loss. This man, Sam Houston, then ordered all Texans to go towards the Colorado River to keep away from General Santa Anna's coming army. Everyone left their homes as soon as they heard the Mexicans were coming. Ten-year-old Maddie Smith and her family are just one family that left their home near Harrisburg during what was named the Runaway Scrape.

I was setting the table for supper when Papa burst through the door. He was soaking wet from the rain and he looked frightened.

"The Mexican army is coming! We have to leave, now!" He said.

Mama started grabbing supplies from the cupboard. Papa hitched the horses up to our wagon. We carried things out as quickly as we could. Anything we could carry went into the wagon.

The tragedy at the Alamo had happened just a week ago. The Mexican army was heading for us. Sam Houston had sent word that we should run for our lives! Everyone living in Gonzales had already packed up and left. Houston and his men had gathered all the supplies and then burnt the town to the ground to keep it out of Mexican hands!

The last thing I grabbed as we headed out the door was a quilt. Mama had made it years ago, when we'd first moved to Texas. We jumped into the wagon and went off in the rain. I could hear the sound of the Mexican army's drums in the distance. I looked behind at our home as we rode away. The front door was still open. I could see the supper ham on the table and the fire glowing in the fireplace. Tears welled up in my eyes.

On the dirt road east, we met other families from town who were also running away from Santa Anna's men. Many of them walked. A few pulled wagons themselves because they didn't own a horse. We shared what little supplies we had. As the days wore on, the weather became wetter and colder. Everyone was hungry. Some people died and were buried right on the road. We didn't know what was happening with the war, or if we'd ever be able to go home again.

title: Presidio La Bahia: A Texas Landmark
text:
In 1836 near Goliad, Texas, the Presidio La Bahia was the site of a bloody and terrible conflict. Here, 342 Texans died under General Santa Anna's order. La Bahia is about 300 years old and was restored during the 1960s. Thousands of people, including many Texas 4th graders, visit the presidio each year.

Presidio La Bahia ("Fort of the Bay") is a National Historic Landmark on Texas' Independence Trail. It is also the most intact presidio on the northern end of what was once New Spain. In 2010, the presidio got a whole new look that took 3 1/2 years of hard work and cost $500,000.

Within a mile of the San Antonio River, the presidio has 3-foot thick, 8-foot high stone walls with parapets (covered walkways). There is also a bell tower with two bells, cannons (including a restored one made of brass that is more than 250 years old) and a religious statue that's about 300 years old. Inside you can see more than 150 different pieces of historical value (the finest of 54,694 historic items found on the property). That's a lot of history.

The museum features a detailed examination of what life was like for the early Spanish colonial and Mexican people. Up to four adventurous travelers can stay in "The Quarters" overnight, where priests and soldiers used to live. Also, actors in costume reenact events that occurred long ago at the presidio.

Find out more at www.presidiolabahia.org.

title: A Taste of Victory for the Texans
text:
After the massacres at the Alamo and Goliad, a new battle cry urged Texans to action.

After the Texas soldiers lost the battles at the Alamo and Goliad, Texans were scared that no one could stop General Santa Anna. Texas leaders knew they had to rethink their plan if they were ever going to win against the Mexicans.

Only Major General Sam Houston and his army were left to defend Texas and continue the fight for independence. Houston thought he could only win if he had time to better prepare his men. The men camped on the banks of the Brazos River to rest and train. Not everyone agreed with Houston’s decision to take some time off from the battlefield. Temporary President of Texas David G. Burnet wrote a letter asking Houston to get back on the battlefield. “The country expects you to fight,” the letter said.

Houston decided he would have scouts (soldiers sent to gather information about an enemy) help him learn more about Santa Anna’s plans. One of the scouts was a man named Erastus “Deaf” Smith. He lost his hearing after a childhood disease but could speak both English and Spanish. Deaf Smith trained Houston’s troops to look for clues about the enemy. Another scout was Hendrick Arnold, a free African American. Together the men spied on the Mexicans and returned to Houston with valuable information.

Houston learned that Santa Anna and his men were marching towards Harrisburg and hoped to capture the leaders of the new Texas government. But the Texas leaders had already left. Santa Anna and his men burned the city to the ground. Santa Anna then turned back and made plans to attack Houston’s men who had camped on an open plain known as San Jacinto.

Houston prepared his men for the upcoming battle. “Victory is certain!” he cried. The Texas men were ready to take on Santa Anna. They were all prepared to die if necessary.

On the morning of April 21, 1836, more than 1,200 Mexicans had arrived. Santa Anna’s men built a barricade out of sacks of supplies for protection. But the Texans didn’t attack. The Mexicans began to relax. Many of the men, including General Santa Anna, decided to take an afternoon nap.

This was just the chance Houston was waiting for! He had already ordered his men to destroy a nearby bridge, the Mexicans' only way out. Houston led about 900 of his men to the Mexican camp, and the surprise attack began. The Texans went in with cheers of “Remember the Alamo!” and “Remember Goliad!” The Battle of San Jacinto lasted only 18 minutes. About 650 of the Mexicans were killed. Only nine of Houston’s men died.

General Santa Anna escaped on horseback. But the next morning, a search party found the leader hiding in the nearby woods. They brought Santa Anna to Sam Houston. The two leaders struck a deal. Houston agreed he would not execute Santa Anna if the Mexican leader promised to send his forces back to Mexico. With this agreement, the revolution came to an end. The Texans had earned their independence and were free of the Mexicans... for now.

title: Attack at Goliad
text:
During the battle at the Alamo, Texas leaders worked to recruit, or get, more volunteers who could fight against the powerful Mexicans. In Goliad, Colonel James W. Fannin led between 400 and 500 young men who enrolled from about 10 different states to help Texas. The men worked hard to prepare their fort to defend against the Mexican army. They knew the battle would be soon. The Texans readied their rifles, muskets, and cannons.

But these men were in a difficult situation even before they learned that Mexican general José de Urrea was headed right toward them. Just like the volunteers in the Alamo, Colonel Fannin's men had very little fresh water and very few supplies. A number of them were already wounded. They were also not very safe at the fort.

When General Urrea and his 450 soldiers arrived in Goliad, the battle started. Fannin tried to lead his men to safety. But the Mexicans overtook them, and Fannin was forced to surrender.

General Santa Anna gave specific orders to his troops in Texas following the battle of Goliad. Most of the prisoners of war were killed. The actions of the Mexican army against those prisoners of war were tragic. The people of Texas remembered this tragedy as evidence of Santa Anna’s cruel authority.

More than ever, Texans were determined to rid themselves of Santa Anna and the Mexican rulers. Now the Texans cried, "Remember Goliad!" along with "Remember the Alamo!”

title: Who was the Angel of Goliad?
text: A: Only a handful of the Texans at Goliad survived General Santa Anna's ordered execution. Many of those survivors owe their lives to a Mexican woman named Francisca Alvarez. She was the wife of one of General Urrea's commanding officers. Francisca begged the officers to show mercy to the Texas prisoners. She brought food and water and treated the prisoners with kindness. Most importantly, Francisca put her own life in danger when she went against General Santa Anna's orders and helped many men escape. She even convinced other Mexican soldiers to help her get the men to safety. Francisca Alvarez is forever remembered as the Angel of Goliad.

title: A Monumental Battle Remembered
text:
We remember the Battle of San Jacinto today by a monument, or memorial, near the sight of the battle. The San Jacinto Monument is the tallest war memorial in the world. It is 15 feet taller than the Washington Monument in Washington, D.C.

The structure is 570 feet tall and honors everyone who fought for independence during the Texas Revolution. It was built between 1936 and 1939, 100 years after the battle.

Today, visitors to the site can ride an elevator to the top of the monument and look out at the battlegrounds. On the ground, visitors can spend time in a museum with artifacts and documents to better understand the history and culture of Texas. The monument serves as a reminder of the last battle of the Texas Revolution.

title: Treaties of Velasco
text:
On April 21, 1836, General Sam Houston and his volunteer Texas army defeated Mexico at San Jacinto. General Santa Anna had no choice but to make a deal with Houston to give Texas its freedom from Mexico. Houston and Santa Anna made a deal soon after the battle, but the final agreements were made almost a month later.

On May 14, Santa Anna signed two peace treaties with Texas President David G. Burnet. These written agreements were known as the Treaties of Velasco. In the first treaty, Santa Anna promised to send all of his soldiers back to Mexico. He agreed that Mexico would never again fight against Texas, and he promised to return property that had been taken from the Texans. In return, President Burnet agreed that Texas would send Santa Anna back to Mexico and would not attack Mexican troops as they returned home.

This wasn't the only agreement reached in Velasco, however. The Texans also made a secret agreement with Santa Anna. In this second treaty, Santa Anna promised he would do everything in his power to help Texas gain independence from Mexico without any further difficulties. They also agreed that the southern border of Texas would be the Rio Grande River.

Even though both sides agreed and signed the treaties, not everyone was happy. Many men believed Santa Anna should be punished for what had happened at the Alamo and Goliad. When the Mexican troops began their march home, Texas soldiers wouldn't let Santa Anna go free. Mexican officials said the treaties weren't legal because Santa Anna was a prisoner when he signed the agreements. The treaties never worked because both sides violated the agreements. It would still be years before Mexico formally recognized Texas' independence.

title: Reading a Timeline
text:
Directions: Use the information from the timeline below to answer the questions that follow.

1. Which battle(s) came before the Texans’ defeat at the Alamo?

2. About how long after the loss at the Alamo did it take for the Texans to defeat the Mexicans at San Jacinto?

3. Which event on the timeline do you think the Texans were the most proud of? Why?

title: Let's Write
text: The War for Texas Independence involved many Texan men and women. How can these men and women be remembered in Texas today? Be sure to use correct grammar, spelling, sentence structure, and punctuation.

title: Sam Houston — First President of the Republic
text:
Texas won its freedom after winning the battle against General Santa Anna at San Jacinto. Citizens now claimed Texas was a country - the Republic of Texas was born. Texas leaders had signed the Texas Constitution of 1836 even before the Battle of the Alamo. After winning their freedom, the people of Texas now had the right to follow the constitution and choose leaders to represent them.

Texas first had an election for the new president of the Republic of Texas. The people elected Sam Houston, the brave army general. As the new president of a new country, he had a lot of hard work ahead of him.

Sam Houston was born in Virginia on March 2, 1793. As a child he was often in some kind of trouble. He didn't enjoy school. He said it was because he didn't like being told what to do. But Sam did enjoy reading. He read many books and liked to learn new things on his own.

When he was 16 years old, Sam ran away from home. He joined a tribe of Cherokee Indians who lived nearby. He was even adopted by the chief. His Cherokee name was Co-lon-neh, which meant the Raven.

Sam later opened a school on his own so he could repay a loan from his mother. However, he didn't stick to teaching for long. He joined the U.S. Army, fought in battles and became a very respected soldier. He even helped the government solve problems with his Cherokee friends.

Sam decided he liked working in government. He became a lawyer. He was elected to the U.S. Congress in 1823 and became governor of Tennessee in 1828. That same year he was asked to go to Texas to serve as a general in the Texas Army. Texas needed his help fighting against Santa Anna and the Mexicans. The rest of Houston's life story is Texas history.

Everyone did not agree with all of Houston's decisions as the leader of the Texas Republic. But today he is still remembered as a brave man who stood for Texas as its first leader.

title: The Lone Star State on Silver Coin
text:
The Republic of Texas won independence as its own nation when it defeated General Santa Anna's army at the battle of San Jacinto in 1836. Since then, Texans have had their own way of doing things. And in 2010, we even started minting coins. Other states and communities have created their own currency, as well.

The Texas medallion (or coin) has an image of Texas on it, with a large star. The coin is modeled after Texas' original currency from the 1800s.

The Texan coin was created with the help of American Open Currency Standard, an organization that has helped other groups, like the Lakota Nation, mint their own silver coins as well. But why mint new coins at all? Why not just use the quarters, dimes, nickels and pennies that everyone else uses? It has to do with inflation. Inflation happens when the price of goods and services increases with the passage of time. As things become more expensive, units of currency, like our dollar, purchase less.

Some Texans say the economy is hurting the value of American money. And since most coins aren't made from precious metals these days, some people worry that the value of money will keep dropping. By creating money that is actually made of silver (instead of other non-precious metals), they'll keep their value even in the face of rising inflation.

By storing the wealth in the form of silver, trading with other Texans using silver, and making silver money available through this currency, some believe our state can more easily get through a difficult economic time.

You can see more about the new coin here: www.texasrepublic.info

title: New Republic: New Opportunities and Challenges
text:
Texans were very happy about defeating Santa Anna and the Mexicans. They were proud of the new Republic of Texas. But the survivors in Texas had a new battle ahead of them. They now needed to create a modern and successful nation. They soon found that keeping a nation going was almost as difficult as winning their freedom to start with.

Opportunities

Texas did have some positive things going for it. First, there was lots of good land where the people could settle, farm and build communities. Second, there were still plenty of determined people who believed in Texas. They knew only hard work could help make the nation strong.

While Texas was fighting for freedom from Mexico, David G. Burnet served as a temporary president. Burnet was a Texas lawyer and landowner and served for six months. His vice president was Lorenzo de Zavala. De Zavala was a Mexican citizen who believed in democracy. He thought people should have freedom. He spent time in a Mexican prison for his beliefs.

Now that the war was over, the people of the Republic held elections to select new leaders. They elected Sam Houston to be president and Mirabeau B. Lamar to be vice president. Texans then elected a congress, or group of elected representatives, to make laws. They also set up a system of judges and courts to help decide if laws were fair.

Another success for Texas was that immigrants (people from other nations) continued settling in Texas. They were excited to have good land where they could live and farm. The population, or number of people living in the Republic of Texas, increased by about 7,000 people each year.

Challenges

Citizens of the Republic of Texas were excited about their new adventures. However, they were also concerned about some things. They knew their independence, or freedom, would cause great challenges as well.

The new nation's biggest problem was money, or rather, the lack of money. Texas did not have money saved up to help run the country. Texas had also borrowed money from others during the war. Now Texas needed to pay the money back. But how? Leaders decided they would collect taxes from citizens for services they received. They also made money by selling some of the Texas land.

Another concern for the new nation was safety. Many Texans were still afraid of Mexico. They thought the Mexicans might try to attack them again. Government leaders posted troops at the Texas borders. But some people didn't think this was enough to protect them from the Mexicans.

The settlers also wanted to keep peace with American Indian groups. President Houston wanted the American Indians to sign treaties, or agreements, with Texas. He wanted everyone to get along peacefully.

Perhaps the greatest challenge faced by the Texans was the question of statehood. Not all Texans thought Texas should go on as a country. Many people knew being their own country would be difficult, maybe even impossible. Some citizens wanted Texas to become a state in the United States. People began to argue about this point. This argument brought about some of the greatest changes in the history of the Republic.

title: Mirabeau B. Lamar — Father of Texas Education
text:
Mirabeau B. Lamar was born in Georgia to a very successful family. Lamar enjoyed many hobbies and had many talents. He especially enjoyed writing poetry and reading. By the age of 31, he was a state senator.

When his wife suddenly died, he went to Texas to visit with friends. Lamar fell in love with the land and was making plans to move there when he heard about tragedy at the Alamo. He rushed to join the army to help Texas fight for its freedom. Lamar was an excellent soldier and was known for his bravery and quick action. He was even named Secretary of War. During the first elections in 1836, Lamar was elected as vice president of the Republic of Texas. Two years later, he was elected as the second president of the Republic of Texas.

Lamar faced many difficulties and challenges as president. Texas still had very little money. No other countries except the United States even recognized Texas as a nation. The United States did not express a desire for Texas to become a state. There were also threats of war from the Mexicans and frequent attacks by American Indians.

Lamar faced his challenges head on. Perhaps his greatest accomplishment was setting up a school system for Texas children. Today Texas has some of the finest public schools, colleges and universities in the United States. Mirabeau Lamar will be remembered not only as a president of the Republic of Texas but also as the Father of Texas Education.

title: A Capital Decision
text:
Austin, Texas, stands as the capital of Texas today. But this beautiful city right in the middle of the state almost wasn't the state's capital. In 1836, the new leaders of the Republic of Texas set out to find a place for the capital. They first chose Columbia, a town on the Brazos River. Later that very same year, they changed the capital to Houston. This new town had been named to honor President Sam Houston.

But the Texas Congress was still looking for a better place to be the capital. In 1839, President Mirabeau Lamar visited a place he believed would be perfect. He thought the land was beautiful, healthy and would one day be the center of a large community. It was on the banks of the Colorado River, which would supply good drinking and farming water. And there were plenty of trees and stone to use to build a new city. Everyone agreed it would be the perfect capital.

The building process began. The town was named Waterloo. But they later changed the name to honor the man who was known as the Father of Texas - Stephen F. Austin. And that's how Austin became the official capital of the Republic of Texas.

title: What happened to Austin?
text:
Texas may owe its success to Stephen F. Austin more than it does to anyone else. Known as the Father of Texas, Austin worked hard to help Texas become a colony and then a republic.

Austin brought 300 Anglo-Americans (known as the Old 300) with him to live a better life on Texas land. People came to his colony with hope for the future. But Mexican leaders soon took away many of their freedoms. Because of Mexico's tight rules and orders, the people in his colony were unhappy with their new lives. Austin worked with Mexican leaders to solve his colony's problems. In 1830, Mexico made a law that said immigrants could no longer come to the colony. But Austin wanted the colony to keep growing and still let people come live there.

General Santa Anna sent Austin to a Mexican prison for two years. When Austin got out, he supported the fight for Texas independence. After the war ended, Austin ran for president of the Republic of Texas in the elections of 1836. The war hero Sam Houston won the election, but Austin became the secretary of state. He continued to work hard for Texas. He wanted to help Texas become a state.

But Austin's health was getting worse, and he was very weak. Soon he became very sick. He died after serving only a few months in office. He was only 43 years old. Stephen F. Austin did not live long enough to see Texas succeed and become a state. But surely he would be very proud to be the father of such a fine state today.

title: Main Idea and Details
text:
Do you know how to find the main idea of what you are reading? This is an important skill. The main idea is the most important thing the author wants you to know and think about. The author also gives the reader more information with details about the main idea.

Directions: Read the article New Republic: New Opportunities and Challenges. Look at the article’s main ideas shown below. Find three details about each main idea and write them in the correct box.

title: Let's Write
text: Read the article New Republic: New Opportunities and Challenges. Pretend you are a newspaper reporter for a Texas newspaper in 1836. Write an article about the challenges the new country faces. Explain each idea in detail. Remember that reporters usually include only facts. Use complete sentences to write your ideas. Be sure you use correct capitalization, grammar, punctuation and spelling in your final draft.

title: On the Road to Statehood
text:
The story of Texas doesn't end with the victory over Santa Anna's army at San Jacinto. In fact, this marks the beginning of the most amazing time of all of Texas history. The strong people who had first settled the Texas land had to continue to work hard and be brave. There were many obstacles to still overcome.

An Independent Nation

The Republic of Texas stood proudly from the beginning. Men like Sam Houston and Stephen Austin helped get the nation running. The people of Texas began to rebuild after the long war with Mexico. Small settlements became large towns. Farms and plantations grew and did very well. But the people always feared Texas would not be strong enough to stand alone for long.

Many Texans still thought of themselves as Americans. They wanted Texas to join the United States. But some Texans wanted Texas to grow as a nation. People began to argue about whether to become a U.S. state or not. Annexation, or joining a country, was a big question.

Standing as a Lone Star for Nine Years

For nine years, from 1836 to 1845, Texas stood as an independent republic. During this time there were plenty of problems to keep the people of Texas busy. First, the Texas government had very little money. People paid taxes to the government, but it wasn't enough to fund, or pay for, everything the nation needed. Plus, Texas had borrowed money during the war with Mexico, and now Texas needed to pay that money back.

The people of Texas also faced problems with the American Indians living there. President Sam Houston tried to work with the different tribes. He wanted treaties, or agreements, between the nation and the American Indians. He wanted everyone to get along. However the next president, President Lamar, did not understand or get along with the tribes. He did not follow the treaties President Houston had worked hard to make. The American Indians were often treated poorly. President Lamar's actions angered American Indian groups, and they responded with many raids.

Texas also had to deal with the constant threat of Mexican attacks. Mexico was not sticking to the terms of their treaty. In fact, in 1842, Santa Anna again led a group of soldiers into Texas. For a short time the Mexican army held control of San Antonio, Goliad and Refugio. Eventually the Texans drove the Mexicans out of the new nation. But the people of Texas were always watching for attacks.

American Point of View

Most Texans wanted to join the United States. But there were many people in the United States who were not sure if the annexation of Texas would be successful.

Texas had very large debts. The United States would have to take over these debts if Texas became a state. This was a big responsibility. Many people also worried about the Mexican and American Indian attacks. No one wanted to be caught in the middle of disagreements. The biggest concern was slavery. People in Texas, like many southern states in the United States, were allowed to own other people as slaves. These enslaved people were forced to work and did not have the freedoms other Americans had. Many people, especially in the North, did not want another state that allowed slavery.

End to the Journey

In the end, the United States decided Texas would be a good new state. James K. Polk, the U.S. president at the time, convinced citizens that it was a good idea to annex Texas. Most of all, he didn't want another nation, or even one of their enemies, to get Texas first.

On Feb. 28, 1845, the U.S. Congress passed a resolution saying Texas could become a state. But there were certain terms everyone had to agree to. First, Texas had to pay off its own debts. Second, Texas citizens were allowed to continue holding enslaved people. And third, Texas had the right to divide itself into five states if it chose to do so. (Interestingly enough, Texas still has this right today, though there is little chance it would ever be done.) The people of Texas agreed with these terms and voted for the annexation.

The New Flag Flies

On Dec. 29, 1845, Texas became the 28th state of the United States of America. A few weeks later Anson Jones, the last Texas president, lowered the Republic of Texas flag flying in front of the capitol in Austin. He announced, "The Republic of Texas is no more." Many people felt a bit sad that the nation had come to its end. But they were also proud when the new flag, the flag of the United States of America, flew in the breeze that day.

First Leaders of the State of Texas

On its first day as a new state, Texas elected several new leaders. J. Pinckney Henderson became the new governor of Texas. Sam Houston and Thomas J. Rusk became senators representing the new Lone Star State in the U.S. Senate. Texas was off to a strong start.

title: Anson Jones: Final President of the Republic
text:
When Texas lowered the Republic of Texas flag for the last time in 1845, President Anson Jones was the one to do the job. Many people were sad that day, but President Jones knew the annexation had to happen. He knew he had to give up his position as the leader of the republic, even if he was not sure it was what he wanted.

Anson Jones was born in Massachusetts in 1798. He studied medicine as a young man and started a medical practice in Philadelphia in 1826. Jones came to Texas in 1833 and was soon playing a big part in the struggle for independence from Mexico. He was a soldier in the army and worked as an officer and surgeon. Everyone thought he was an intelligent leader. After the war, he was elected as a congressman and later as a senator. He also served as a diplomat in the United States. Jones served as the Texas Secretary of State during Sam Houston's presidency. Then, in 1844, he became the fourth and final president of the Republic of Texas.

Unfortunately, after Texas became a state, Jones’s political life was over. He was not very happy. He retreated from public life and spent the remainder of his life in private. Jones died on Jan. 9, 1858.

title: The Buffalo
text:
Things were changing in Texas by leaps and bounds in the days of the Republic of Texas, but the settlers weren't the only ones affected by all the changes. The next 50 years would completely alter the way of life for the American Indians living in Texas and the Great Plains of the U.S. frontier.

At the heart of this issue was land, where the buffalo roamed. (Sound familiar?) Settlers were moving into territories where the Plains Indians had lived and hunted for generations. The American Indian way of life depended on the buffalo, more correctly called the American bison, which provided food and trade goods as well as material for making clothing, homes, tools, and very strong leather. Therefore, the American Indians fought back when their homes and hunting grounds were invaded.

As you have learned, opinions were divided in Texas about the best way to approach this problem. President Houston made treaties with the Cherokee and the Comanche, which included a fair distribution of land where they could live and hunt buffalo. But the Texas Senate refused to approve the treaties, so the American Indians again protested with raids and warfare. When Lamar took over as president, he was determined to force all American Indians out of Texas or to live on reservations, and many Texans agreed with him.

To make matters worse, the U.S. government encouraged buffalo hunting for profit in the late 1800s. Buffalo hides sold for enormous amounts of money in the United States and Europe. Besides, the large herds of animals took up space that farmers, ranchers, and railroad builders needed. American buffalo hunters killed thousands of animals, stripping the hides off the bodies and leaving the carcasses to rot on the plains.

The population of buffalo, which once numbered millions, was reduced to a few hundred animals. Without the buffalo, the traditional way of life for the American Plains Indians had changed forever.

title: Using Primary and Secondary Sources to Identify Cause-Effect Relationships
text:
Using critical thinking skills can help you understand what you learn from many different sources. As you learn about history, you should be able to identify primary and secondary sources of information.

A primary source is information that comes from a person who was actually at the event. Letters, journals, newspaper articles, interviews and some internet sites can be primary sources. Students can also learn firsthand from a primary source photograph, drawing or artifact from the event. Studying a primary source can be interesting. You can see and feel how it might have been at that point in time!

A secondary source of information comes from someone who was not present at the event. Encyclopedia articles, biographies, textbooks, some computer programs and some internet sites can be secondary sources. These sources are helpful because they help us learn many facts about events in history.

Sometimes it is difficult to find primary sources. If this happens, you might have to find a secondary source that includes parts of primary sources like journals or letters. Both types of sources can help you learn more about the past.

Read the two pieces of information below about the annexation of Texas. One piece is an example of a primary source. One piece is an example of a secondary source. Identify each source.

Use the primary and secondary sources along with information from this issue to complete the cause and effect chart.

title: Statehood or National Independence?
text:
It is 1844. Texas has been an independent nation for nearly nine years now. Most of the leaders in the Republic of Texas believe it would be best for Texas to become part of the United States. Many of the citizens feel the same way. However some people think Texas should remain an independent nation. Read the two letters below written between a Texas citizen and his cousin living in the United States. We see there were definitely two sides to the issue.

June 1844

Cousin Charles,

Our family is doing well here in Texas. We have spent these last years rebuilding our home and farm. The Mexican army and their attacks destroyed many homes in our community. But Santa Anna cannot stop us from reaching our dreams here. We are farming the land and working hard.

There is one thing that is on everyone's minds. Many of us here believe we should continue to push Texas to become a part of the United States. Even Sam Houston thinks annexation, or joining a country, is best for us all. He believes Texas could help the United States. Why, just the other day I heard him say, "The United States cannot... exist without Texas." I must say I agree with him that annexation would be best for us all.

If we become a part of the United States, the people of Texas will be safer. We will have the help of the army. Right now we are afraid of Indian attacks. We are always looking out for Santa Anna's men to sneak back in and attack us. And Texas has very little money. We cannot afford much protection.

If Texas is annexed, there will be better mail service for us. The U.S. Postal Service would deliver letters near and far. The best thing would be that our families could see each other more often. We would be living in the same country again.

Hope to hear from you soon.

Your cousin,

Matthew Adams

September 1844

Cousin Matthew,

It was good to hear that you and your family are doing well. I was worried about your safety when I heard the Mexicans were attacking Texas. All of us here in Boston have heard of the fine land in Texas. No doubt you are building quite a place there.

The question of statehood for Texas has been on everyone's minds here as well. People in the United States also have some concerns. We know Texas owes a lot of money. Most Americans do not want to take on any of this debt.

Perhaps the most important topic is slavery. Texas allows citizens to enslave people. These people are not free. They are forced to work on farms and ranches. Many of our leaders do not want to add another slave state to the Union. But I've heard some of our leaders support the annexation. They believe it will be best to have Texas join us now so we don't risk the two countries becoming enemies one day.

We have heard that Mexico still does not believe Texas is a nation. If this is true, I wonder how much trouble annexation of Texas would cause between Mexico and our country.

I look forward to being able to visit with you and your family soon. I would like to see the wide-open spaces in Texas. I have heard much about your new home. Whatever the outcome of the annexation issue, I look forward to seeing you soon.

Your cousin,

Charles Smith

title: New State—New Set of Rules
text:
Texas became the 28th state of the United States on Dec. 29, 1845. Before that happened, Texas had to write a new set of rules - a new state constitution.

Several men accepted the job to write the new constitution. They knew this was a big responsibility. The constitution would explain how the state would operate and how the people would live. The constitution would let people know what rights they had as citizens of a state within the United States of America. The citizens would also need to know what responsibilities they would have to their new state and nation.

For two months, these men worked very hard writing the document. Only one of the men had been born in Texas. His name was Jose Antonio Navarro. Navarro was known as a very fair-minded man. People often came to him for help settling their conflicts, or disagreements, with one another. People in Texas trusted him to do a good job writing the document.

The writers studied other constitutions very carefully. In the end, the new Texas Constitution was modeled after the ones written for Louisiana and the Republic of Texas. They knew these plans had good ideas that worked well. It made sense to follow them.

The new constitution explained how Texas would elect a state governor every two years. It also told how the Texas legislature would work. A legislature is a group of people who make laws. The Texas legislature would meet every two years to make and review laws for the state.

The constitution also gave details about who could vote in elections in Texas. Only Anglo and Tejano men who were 21 and older could vote. African Americans, American Indians and women did not get this right until many years later.

The U.S. Congress approved the constitution, and a new state with a new set of rules was now part of the United States.

title: What is Hydraulic Fracturing?
text:
People in the states of Colorado, Texas and Ohio have been feeling small earthquakes over the past few years. Some people are saying those quakes are the result of hydraulic fracturing.

Hydraulic fracturing is a way to get natural gas from underground rock formations up to the surface. We use natural gas for energy in homes and businesses. Water and chemicals are pumped underground through long, deep wells. The liquid causes fractures, or cracks, in the rock. Natural gas escapes through the cracks and gets piped up to the surface. Hydraulic fracturing has been used in more than one million wells in the U.S. since the 1940s.

The National Research Council released a report that said hydraulic fracturing does not seem to be the culprit, but other human activity might be the problem. Some groups believe that it's the wastewater (leftover water and chemicals), not the fracturing itself that is causing the earthquakes. The wastewater from the process is either treated at a facility or sent deep underground. When the liquid is injected back into the ground, it can make the tectonic plates slip and rub against each other, causing earthquakes.

The companies doing the drilling say that they are following safety regulations and protecting their workers, the residents and the environment. Companies have been injecting waste liquids into the ground for decades, and only recently has there been an increase in earthquakes. We will certainly be hearing more about hydraulic fracturing in the years to come.

Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents for more Connections and Current Events articles.

title: The United States and Mexico at War
text:
An Act of War

When the United States accepted Texas as a state, Mexico believed it was an act of war. Mexican leaders still thought the Texas land belonged to them, and they refused to give it up. U.S. President James K. Polk offered to buy Mexico's northern land. But Mexican leaders refused to sell. This upset some Americans who thought they had the right to expand, or spread out, to other land.

In addition, Mexico and the United States did not agree on the boundary between the two countries. A boundary is the dividing line between two places. Mexico said the Nueces River in Texas divided the two countries. The United States said the Rio Grande River was the true dividing line. Neither side would change their opinion. They quit talking to one another.

Battle at Palo Alto

President Polk said the Mexicans had invaded U.S. land. He sent troops marching toward the Rio Grande. He wanted to force Mexican soldiers back south towards their home country. General Zachary Taylor led the U.S. soldiers. In April 1846, the Mexicans defeated American troops in a skirmish, or small battle. On May 8, 1846, a major battle began at Palo Alto in southern Texas. The U.S. Congress declared war on Mexico on May 13, 1846. Texas was once again at war with Mexico. But this time, as a part of the United States, Texas was not alone in the fight.

Reactions to War

Mexicans were shocked. They believed they were right to be on the land. The Mexicans believed the United States had invaded their home country. They could not believe they were fighting to keep their own land.

Americans had different views about the war. Many people didn't agree with going to war with Mexico. This was what they had worried about before Texas was annexed. But most Texans were ready to fight. They remembered all of the past trouble with Mexico. They were ready to get rid of the Mexican threat once and for all.

Many Texans began putting up posters to urge, or encourage, men to join in the war against Mexico. Some people offered to give free land to anyone who joined the effort.

Texas Rangers Play a Part

The Texas Rangers were one special group of men who played an important part in the war. These men were volunteers who joined together in Texas in 1835. Their job was to defend Texas from any danger. They were especially on the watch for Mexican and American Indian attacks. They knew the land of Texas and Mexico very well. They were very brave scouts and fighters.

The War Wages On

Both the Mexicans and the Americans were determined to win the war. The United States won many of the battles and also tried several times to reach a peace agreement. An easy end to the war seemed hopeless. In the fall of 1847, Gen. Winfield Scott led the U.S. Army and the Texas Rangers into Mexico. They captured Mexico City. The Mexicans were stunned that the United States had invaded their capital city. Everyone finally agreed to sit down and talk about how to end the war.

The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo

On Feb. 2, 1848, Mexican and American officials met in a small Mexican village near Mexico City. In Guadalupe Hidalgo, both sides decided on a treaty, or written agreement, to end the war. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo named the Rio Grande River as the border between the two countries. The United States received more than half a million square miles of land. This land included present-day California, Utah and Nevada, and parts of Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and Wyoming. The United States agreed to pay Mexico $15 million. At last, the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the Mexican-American War.

title: Jane McManus Cazneau: War Correspondent
text:
Today, very few people would be shocked to see a woman reporting from a war zone. But in the 1840s, this was not common, and Jane McManus Cazneau was a rare type of woman. She worked as a reporter who followed the battles of the Mexican-American War.

As a newspaper reporter, Cazneau was already well-known when the war between the United States and Mexico began. Cazneau wrote many newspaper articles during Texas' annexation process. She was able to convince many people that Texas would be a good addition to the United States.

During the Mexican-American War, President Polk gave Cazneau permission to go on a mission to Mexico. She was the only woman allowed to do so. Her job was to report on the war.

In November 1846, the U.S. government sent her to Mexico City. They wanted her to speak with government leaders there. Everyone thought she might be able to help strike a peace treaty. Unfortunately, she was not able to do so. Even though she was not successful at bringing an end to the war, people still admired Jane McManus Cazneau for her fine reporting and bravery.

title: A Texas Melting Pot
text:
From its beginning, Texas had plenty of land. This land was treasured, protected and even caused many Texas battles. As a state, Texas now wanted to use its land to bring more people and settlements to live there.

Texas leaders decided to give land to people who agreed to settle there. They placed advertisements in many newspapers explaining the deal. These offers brought many people from around the world to live in Texas. Immigrants came from the southern part of the United States, Mexico and Europe.

Many Mexican immigrants settled in the southern and western parts of Texas. Some descendants, or relatives, of these early pioneers still live in places like San Antonio, Laredo and El Paso today.

Europeans who moved to Texas had to make a difficult decision. They would have to make a long journey across the Atlantic Ocean. Once in Texas, many had to walk hundreds of miles to their land. European immigrants left behind family, friends, their culture and even their language. But in return for their efforts, they had a chance to own their own land. Most of these people would never have this opportunity in Europe. Lots of people from Germany, Poland and what are now the Czech and Slovak republics settled in central and southeast Texas.

The immigrants were not the only ones who benefited from the deal with Texas. Texas needed these new settlers on its wide-open land to help stop American Indian and Mexican attacks. Texans knew that the more people living in Texas, the safer they'd be. The risk of attacks decreased with each new community.

Texas was also becoming a very special place to live. Each immigrant group brought their own food, language, clothing, celebrations and religion. The people also brought with them new ideas about farming, building and business. Over time, these new people and ideas helped make Texas successful. Texas quickly became a melting pot of cultures and ideas.

title: Using a Problem-Solving Process
text:
Each day we all face problems we must solve. Some of the problems are simple. Which breakfast cereal should I eat? What outfit will I wear to school? But some problems are more difficult. That’s why it’s important to understand some steps that can help you solve problems.

Think about the following situation President Polk faced in 1846. Complete the problem-solving process.

Texas has just become the 28th state in the United States. Mexico is not happy. The two countries are headed toward a possible war. What would you do if you were Polk?

title: Comparing Data From Map Sources
text:
Directions: Study the two maps of Texas. Use the data from the two maps to answer the questions below.

1. What are the titles of the two maps?

2. Compare the maps. What things do they have in common?

3. What can you tell about size of the state of Texas today?

4. What present-day states were part of Texas in 1848?

5. Why do you suppose some of the borders stayed the same on both maps?

6. Why do you suppose Mexico and the United States were willing to go to war for the land shown on the maps?

title: Let's Write
text: Think about what it would be like to be a citizen of the United States at the beginning of the Mexican-American War in 1846. Pretend you are writing a speech about your opinions to give at your community’s town meeting. What are your concerns about the war? Do you agree or disagree with the government’s decision to fight against Mexico for Texas? Explain your ideas in detail. Present your speech to your class.

title: The Best Day of My Life
text:
The Civil War ended on April 9, 1865. Confederate general Robert E. Lee surrendered to Union general Ulysses S. Grant at the McLean home in Appomattox Court House, Virginia. The Union was saved. At last, the fighting and bloodshed could end. Two years earlier, in 1863, President Abraham Lincoln wrote the Emancipation Proclamation. This legal document emancipated, or freed, the enslaved people in the rebellious states. Lincoln also announced that formerly enslaved people were free to join the Union Army. This news wasn’t published in the Confederate states. Many people didn't hear about the proclamation for years. It wasn't until June 19, 1865 — more than two months after the war ended — that the enslaved people in Texas learned they were free.

There were mixed reactions from emancipated people all over the country about the end of the war. Some people who had just been freed feared retribution from angry southerners and fled. However, in most places, those who had been enslaved were overjoyed about the news of their freedom. Families would no longer be sold and split apart. Married couples who had lived on different plantations could finally live together under the same roof. All children would be born free and belong to no one but their parents. Everyone now had the freedom to come and go whenever and wherever they pleased.

Many formerly enslaved people remembered seeing all of the Federal soldiers passing through on their way back to the North. Others recalled people all around breaking out into joyous cheers and singing at the news of their freedom. Felix Haywood, a formerly enslaved man in Texas, recalled:

"The end of the war, it come jus' like that—like you snap your fingers… Hallelujah broke out… Soldiers, all of a sudden, was everywhere—comin' in bunches, crossin' and walkin' and ridin'. Everyone was a-singin'. We all walkin' on golden clouds. Hallelujah!

"'Union forever,
Hurrah, boys, hurrah!
Although I may be poor,
I'll never be a slave—
Shoutin' in the battle cry of freedom.'
