“Everybody went wild. We all felt like heroes and nobody had made us that way but ourselves. We was free. Just like that, we was free."

title: Enslaved No More!
text:
A letter written after the Civil War has shed light on the relationship between enslaved people and those who owned them. Jourdan Anderson was an enslaved person who gained freedom when he and his family escaped to Ohio from Tennessee. In August 1865, his former master, Colonel Anderson, wrote a letter asking Jourdan to come back to Tennessee to work on his farm.

The formerly enslaved man’s reply gave a clear message about his feelings. He said he hoped that God had opened the colonel’s eyes to the wrongs done to enslaved people for generations. Jourdan wrote that there was one thing that might bring him back to Tennessee. He and his wife wanted to be paid for the 52 years of combined work that they provided while they were enslaved (over $11,000). Without that, he said they had little faith in the colonel’s promises. He ended by asking the colonel to give his best regards to a man named George Carter. Mr. Carter had intervened when the colonel had tried to hurt Jourdan.

Reading letters and newspapers from the past can help us understand the people who lived during that time. Jourdan and his family may have once been enslaved, but their spirits were not broken.

title: An End to War and Slavery
text:
Emancipation Proclamation

The Civil War had been raging for more than a year when President Abraham Lincoln issued a special order called the Emancipation Proclamation. This order helped put an end to most slavery in the United States about 250 years after organized slavery began. It allowed enslaved people in some states to join the army and fight in the Civil War, which helped guarantee freedom for all.

The Emancipation Proclamation didn’t make slavery completely illegal, though. That didn’t happen until 1865, when the 13th Amendment was added to the Constitution. Some of the signers of the Constitution actually owned enslaved people, while others believed slavery was wrong. But, the signers knew the Constitution wasn’t perfect. That’s what amendments like the 13th are for: to fix, or improve, our rules. This amendment officially abolished slavery and indentured servitude in our country.

A Day to Remember

For enslaved people in Texas, June 19, 1865, is a day to remember. This is the day Gordon Granger, a general in the Union Army, announced in Texas that the war was over and the enslaved people were free. This message took almost six weeks to reach all of the enslaved people in Texas and their former owners.

One year later, on June 19, 1866, formerly enslaved Texans gathered to celebrate their new lives. They sang songs, gave speeches and talked about how thankful they were for their freedom. This day is still special to Texans. Each year, people from all cultures gather to celebrate Juneteenth. Families enjoy parades, picnics and speeches. It is especially a time for citizens to discuss progress and difficulties for African Americans.

Life in Texas After Slavery

African Americans were joyful when they heard the news of their freedom. However, they faced many new challenges with their freedom. Life was hard. Most formerly enslaved people in Texas had no education. They had never been allowed to attend school. Most did not read or write. It was difficult for them to find jobs. Formerly enslaved people had to worry about where they would live. Some of these people decided to stay with their former owners. Now they worked for money. Some farmed on their owner’s land and shared the money they made. Others headed north, hoping to find a better way of life in a new place. There were still many people who did not believe African Americans should be free. Many public places were still divided by color. Life would be difficult for many years to come.

Reconstruction in Texas

The period of time after the Civil War is known as Reconstruction. It lasted more than 10 years. During this time, people had to rebuild the South. They also had to rebuild their own lives.

Formerly enslaved people had to find jobs and homes. Former landowners had to find ways to run their farms and plantations without slave labor. Many people had to rebuild homes and farms. People had to deal with the deaths or injuries of fathers, husbands and sons who fought in the war. There was still a lot of anger between the North and the South. Sometimes this anger led to violence against the newly freed African Americans.

The U.S. government decided to set up a special unit to help the newly freed people. In 1865, the Freedmen’s Bureau helped African Americans find jobs and homes. They also established about 150 schools in Texas. These schools were for African American children and adults.

Texas Rejoins the Union

Many of the wounds from the war began to heal. The most difficult things to heal were people’s feelings. The Confederacy had lost the war. But leaders on both sides knew the best thing was to put the United States back together again. On March 30, 1870, Texas once again joined the United States of America. Edmund Davis became the new governor. He was not very popular. People thought he spent too much money. They also thought he gave too much help to African Americans. Eventually, in 1876, the state adopted and signed a new constitution. Now the Texas governor and other state leaders had much less power than they had before.

title: Matthew Gaines — Texas’ First Black Senator
text:
As a young boy, Matthew Gaines learned to read and write. That may not sound very amazing, but Matthew was enslaved on a plantation in Louisiana. Enslaved people weren’t allowed to go to school, and most did not get an education. Matthew made friends with an Anglo boy living on the plantation. They often read together. But they had to hide because it was illegal for enslaved people to learn to read.

In 1850, when he was only 10 years old, Matthew tried to escape from his owner. He hid out on riverboats for six months before he was caught. When he was sold at the age of 23, Matthew tried to escape again. He headed towards Mexico, but the Texas Rangers caught him. Matthew was then sent to live and work in Fredericksburg, Texas.

In Fredericksburg, Matthew worked as a sheepherder and blacksmith. The people liked him. African Americans would come to Matthew with their problems. He always tried to help. He also worked as a church minister. After the Civil War, Matthew Gaines had big plans. He wanted to run for the Texas Senate. He did, and in 1869, he was elected.

Mr. Gaines worked hard to protect the rights of all people, especially African Americans. He wanted African Americans to be able to vote. He wanted people to feel safe. During his time in office, he was responsible for helping pass important laws, including ones that gave people the right to a free education.

Gaines was a Texas senator for four years. Even after he was no longer on the Texas Senate, he still worked hard for people. Every Sunday in church he talked to people about ways they could make their lives better.

title: Sharecropping — A Southern Way of Life
text:
With the Civil War over, many formerly enslaved people had their freedom. But that was about all they had. Most of them did not have any money or even a place to live. Some African Americans decided the best thing to do was to stay right where they were. They became sharecroppers. Sharecroppers were farmers who did not own their own land. Instead, they farmed on someone else’s land. Many landowners had owned enslaved people before and now needed help farming their land.

Sharecroppers worked hard. They gave a portion of their crops to the landowner. This was payment for using their land. Sharecroppers were also able to live in houses provided by the landowner. These homes were usually not much more than a shack. The landowner also provided the tools, animals and seeds that were needed. This was important because formerly enslaved people did not have money to purchase these items.

Sometimes the crops did not grow because of bad weather or droughts. When this happened, sharecroppers could not pay the landowner for using their field. They would get into debt and had to keep working there until they paid back the debt. Many sharecroppers were never able to leave the plantations where they had been enslaved before the war.

Sharecropping continued throughout the South for many years. Eventually Anglo-Americans also used the system to make their living. Because the sharecroppers’ part of the crop was often very small, many sharecroppers and their families were very poor.

title: Six Flags Over Texas — Not Just an Amusement Park!
text:
The U.S. flag proudly flies over the Texas capitol building in Austin, Texas. Directly below this flag flies the Texas state flag, known as the Lone Star Flag.

Today, flags are visible symbols of the state. Texas has a very unique history. Throughout this history, Texas has been home to six different flags.

The first flag belonged to Spain. In the 1500s, early Spanish explorers first set foot on the land that is now Texas. They planted their country's flag and claimed the land. The next flag was for the French. This flag flew over Texas when René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle claimed the land for France in 1685.

By the early 1800s, the Mexican flag was flying over Texas. But when Texas claimed its independence, the Mexican flag came down.

The first official flag of the Republic of Texas went up in 1839. When Texas became a state in 1845, it flew the stars and stripes of the United States' flag.

Texas seceded from the Union in 1861 to join the Confederacy. The fifth flag to fly over Texas was the Confederate States of America's flag. In 1870, the U.S. flag once again flew in the Texas skies. Texas was part of the Union again.

These flags all represent different cultures. In 1961, a man named Angus G. Wynne Jr. had the idea to turn the six flags into something very special. He opened an amusement park named after all of them. This park, Six Flags Over Texas, has areas devoted to Spain, France, Mexico, Texas, the Confederacy, and the United States of America.

title: Salem Poor, a Brave and Gallant Soldier
text:
Do you know people who you admire because of their ethics? What actions show that a person can be counted on to do the right thing? History has very few details about Salem Poor, an African American soldier who fought in the Revolutionary War. However, 14 officers from the Battle of Bunker Hill signed a document presented to the General Court of Massachusetts. It recommended that a soldier named Salem Poor be rewarded for his heroism. He is described as "a Brave & gallant Soldier." That's strong proof of Salem Poor's ethics.

Salem Poor was born enslaved in Massachusetts in the 1740s. He bought his freedom, married and had a son. When the war began, Poor left home to fight with the American colonists. Five times as many African Americans fought with the British because of promises of freedom. African Americans were not allowed to vote and faced many other types of discrimination.

For that reason, Salem Poor's award is even more remarkable. The details of his actions are unknown. The document reads "...to Set forth Particulars of his Conduct would be Tedious." But it does say "...under Our Own observation...we declare that...Salem Poor...behaved like an Experienced Officer, as Well as an Excellent Soldier." From 14 officers present at the battle, that's high praise indeed.

Some sources claim that Salem Poor shot and killed the British Lieutenant Colonel James Abercrombie at Bunker Hill. Records show that Poor continued to fight bravely in other battles. Like many African Americans of that time, exact details of both his birth and death remain a mystery. He was honored with a commemorative postage stamp in 1975.

title: Point of View
text:
Directions: Read the following quotes by Abraham Lincoln and Confederate general Robert E. Lee about slavery. Answer the questions that follow. Write your answers on a seperate piece of paper.

“I am naturally anti-slavery. If slavery is not wrong, nothing is wrong. I cannot remember when I did not so think and feel. And yet I have never understood that the presidency conferred upon me (gave me) an unrestricted (unlimited) right to act officially upon this judgment and feeling.”

—Abraham Lincoln Source: April 4, 1864 — Letter to Albert Hodges

“So far from engaging in a war to perpetuate (continue) slavery, I am rejoiced (glad) that slavery is abolished (done away with). I believe it will be greatly for the interest of the South. So fully am I satisfied of this that I would have cheerfully lost all that I have lost by the war and have suffered all that I have suffered to have this object attained (reached).”

—Robert E. Lee, Confederate General, 1865

1. What is President Lincoln’s point of view on slavery?

2. How do you know?

3. What is General Lee’s point of view on slavery?

4. Why is this interesting?

title: A New Life in a Frontier State
text:
Ten-year-old Jake was born in Alabama. Last year, in 1855, Jake's parents decided the family should move to a new state called Texas. The family loaded all they could fit into a covered wagon and headed west to their new home. Jake kept a journal along the way. Read about Jake's trip and his new home on the Texas frontier.

April 1, 1855

Mama cried as we left our home. I have to say I felt sad too. I said goodbye to our home. The tall trees, the woods and the hills grew smaller as we pulled away. Mama said she will miss her piano the most. She loves to play, but there wasn't room for the piano in the wagon. We packed all the things we need for our new home in Texas. We brought blankets, barrels of food, a cook stove, a box of tin pots and dishes, Pa's tools, trunks of clothes and a rifle.

April 17, 1855

The ride in the wagon sure has been dusty and bumpy. Yesterday one of the wheels broke, but Pa and I were able to fix it right up. We travel all day and camp at night. Mama cooks over a campfire. Pa tells us stories that make us laugh. He also tells us about growing up in Germany. He explains how he came to America for a good life. Now he says he's taking us to Texas for a better life. We'll own our land there. Pa says this is a big dream come true for him. I think maybe it is for me too.

May 23, 1855

We passed another wagon on the road today. The family was from Tennessee. They had been on the road a lot longer than us. Their baby was sick. She was coughing and coughing. Ma gave them some tea for the baby to drink. The man told Pa they had heard of Indian attacks in the area. The American Indians are upset that so many settlers are taking over their land. I guess I wouldn't feel too good about someone taking my land either. Later Pa told me the family decided to go back to Tennessee because the trip was too difficult. I felt bad because Ma cried all night. I think maybe she wants us to go back too.

May 31, 1855

Rain has poured down for days now. The dirt roads are muddy. Yesterday the wagon got stuck in the mud. We had to push and push to get it out. We crossed a river today. It was wide and deep. The water was flowing awfully fast. Pa said the horses could get us across. Sure enough, they did. Water poured into the wagon though. Our clothes got soaked. Ma never let go of my hand. Pa says it won't be long now. We'll be at our new home soon. Ma says she's never seen so many new kinds of wildflowers along the road. She smiled real big today. I think maybe she's happy again. Maybe now Pa's dream is her dream too.

June 12, 1855

Hooray! We're in Texas. Pa says we're heading for a place called Fredericksburg. Our land is near there. There are lots of settlers from Germany living there. Pa has an uncle and friends already living in the town. Pa said he'll be glad to have a good German meal soon. Ma said she would be glad to be off the bumpy wagon. We talked a lot about the home we will soon build together.

June 16, 1855

Our land is beautiful. It is so green. There are trees and a creek nearby. I saw a deer come right up to our wagon. Pa and I started on the house right away. It will take lots of hard work. Ma will have her home soon enough. She already started raking a spot of dirt. She says she will plant a garden. Tomorrow Ma is going to make curtains for the windows of the house. It will be our dream house. We really are home now.

title: Texas in the Civil War
text:
Growth of a Frontier State

Following annexation in 1845, the state of Texas grew rapidly. Texas was a frontier. This means Texas was the farthest part of a settled country. It was next to land that had not been settled yet. Many people continued to settle this frontier state. There were immigrants from Europe and settlers from other states in the United States. They all wanted to buy cheap Texas land. They wanted the chance to be successful.

All the new settlements caused problems for the American Indians who had lived in Texas for centuries. Settlers took over land. Settlers killed bison and other animals the American Indians depended on for food. Settlers built communities on land that was special to the American Indians. Many native tribes became angry and attacked settlers. The groups didn’t live peacefully with each other for many years.

Slavery in Texas

Many people who came to Texas made their money by farming. Some of these farmers had very large farms known as plantations. Here, crops were produced to sell. Many of the workers on these farms and plantations were enslaved African Americans.

Enslaved people had no rights or freedoms. They could not leave their master’s farm without permission. Slaveowners considered the enslaved people their property. They were bought and sold and forced to work very hard. Some of the enslaved people worked in homes or businesses. Most of them worked from sunup to sundown in poor conditions. A few of these enslaved people were able to find freedom. They traveled secretly to places where slavery was illegal in the northern United States.

As farms and plantations grew, landowners made lots of money. They also needed more people to work in the fields. These landowners brought more and more enslaved African Americans to work in Texas. By 1860, about one of every four people in Texas was enslaved.

The United States Divides

Not everyone in the United States agreed slavery was right. Landowners in the South said they needed enslaved people to run their farms. They said they could not make money without these workers. But many people, especially those in northern states, said all humans should be free. They did not think it was right for people to own other people. There were even people in Texas who were against slavery.

The states were divided on other issues as well. Northern states believed all states should follow the nation’s laws. People in the South disagreed. They thought all states should have the right to nullify, or reject, laws they didn’t like.

Abraham Lincoln became the president of the United States in 1860. He did not believe in slavery. Some southerners were afraid he would pass a national law to end slavery. These southern states began to talk about separating from the northern states.

Texas Secedes

The state of South Carolina was the first southern state to secede, or separate, from the United States. Six other states quickly followed. Texas seceded from the United States on March 2, 1861. These seven states formed a new country. They called it the Confederate States of America. Four other states later joined the Confederacy. The group elected a president. His name was Jefferson Davis. People in the Confederacy were upset with the remaining northern states. Those states were now called the Union. People in the Union were very upset that the Confederate states had seceded.

First Shot at Fort Sumter

On April 12, 1861, Confederate troops fired at a Union fort at Fort Sumter in South Carolina. The Civil War had begun. This war between the northern and southern states lasted four long, bloody years. General Robert E. Lee was the main Confederate general. Ulysses S. Grant was the general of the Union troops.

Texans in the War

About 90,000 Texas soldiers fought in the Civil War. Most of them were on the side of the Confederacy, but there were some Union soldiers from Texas. Brave Texans fought in every battle of the war. Texans fought in units called infantries that traveled by foot. Others fought in cavalries, or horseback units. Texans who did not join the military stayed at home to help. Many people kept running farms and businesses. Women made uniforms, tents, blankets, and bandages. Many women also worked in hospitals nursing injured soldiers.

Texas Battles

Texan soldiers were most proud of the fact that Union soldiers were never able to take over their state. But Union ships were able to blockade, or block ships from coming into ports, the Gulf of Mexico. This kept the Confederates from getting fresh supplies. In October 1862, the Union captured the port at Galveston Harbor. Within months, the Confederates took it back.

Several other battles took place in Texas. In September 1863, 4,000 Union soldiers tried to capture the Sabine Pass. Although only 60 Confederate soldiers fought against them, the Union was not successful. The Confederates, led by 25-year-old Lieutenant Dick Dowling, used cannon fire to force back the Union’s incoming ships.

On April 9, 1865, after nearly four years of fighting, the Confederacy surrendered. Unfortunately, the news of the surrender did not reach Texas troops for some time. On May 13, 1865, they fought the last battle of the Civil War at the Battle of Palmito Ranch near Brownsville. Even though the Confederates had lost the war, the Texas troops won this last battle.

title: Mollie Bailey — Circus Queen and Spy
text:
Not all Civil War heroes were men. Mollie Bailey was one Texas woman who put her life on the line. She was born in Alabama in 1844. Little Mollie was not happy with a quiet life at home on her father's plantation. She wanted adventure and excitement. As a teenager, Mollie ran away and married a redheaded cornet player who played in his father's band. The boy's name was Gus Bailey. Together with other family members, Mollie and Gus performed a singing, dancing and acting show across the southern United States.

When the Civil War began, Gus became bandleader (the person who leads the musicians) in a military company in General Hood's Texas Brigade. Mollie traveled with Gus. She helped nurse wounded soldiers. But she wanted to do more. Confederate officers soon had a way to use Mollie's acting skills. She could be a spy!

Mollie dressed up as a poor old woman. She traveled into Union camps and pretended to sell cookies. The Union soldiers did not think she could be working for their enemies. Mollie listened to the soldiers talk. She tried to hear information she could take back to the generals. Mollie also hid packets of medicine in her hair and secretly got it to Confederate soldiers who were sick.

After the war, Mollie spent the rest of her life in the circus business. This was certainly an exciting career. But nothing could ever compare to her days as a Civil War spy!

title: Comparing North and South Economies
text:
Life in the North and the South was very different in the years just before the Civil War. One of the biggest differences was in the way people made their living. In 1860, most people in the United States farmed. Most of these people lived in small towns or rural areas. But things were changing quickly, especially in the North.

Manufacturing companies were popping up all along the East Coast. People in the North quickly changed from farming for a living to working in factories. Many of the factory workers were also immigrants from Europe. There were plenty of skilled people to hold the factory jobs.

These factories made a lot of money. Workers could earn small wages, or amounts of money, for working there. Northern citizens also liked the taxes placed on goods brought in from other countries. They knew these taxes would make people want to buy American-made products because they would be cheaper.

Meanwhile, life in the South went on as usual. There were some factories, but most people still farmed. Cotton and tobacco were popular crops. Southern farmers continued using slave labor to run their businesses. About three million enslaved people worked on farms and plantations in 1860. Southern citizens were against high taxes on goods brought in from other countries. They didn't want other countries to put high taxes on the cotton and tobacco the South exported.

During the Civil War, differences in the economies of the North and the South played an important role. The South used lots of the goods manufactured in Northern factories. They suffered severely when the North stopped shipping these goods to them. The South also stopped shipping crops north, but this didn't have as much of an impact.

title: Summarizing Historical Information
text:
A summary is a short statement, usually only a few sentences, that tells all of the main ideas of an event. A summary should tell only the important ideas. Small details and facts are unnecessary. They should not be included in the summary of an event. When writing a summary, it is sometimes helpful to think about all the big ideas first. Write down notes about these ideas. Then write the summary.

Directions: Read the information from this issue’s lesson under the subtitles “The United States Divided” and “Texas Secedes.” Use this information to fill in the summary chart below. Use your notes to then write a summary with three to five sentences about this period of time in Texas history.

Now use your notes to write a short (three to five sentences) summary of the information.

title: Civil War and Reconstruction in Texas
text:
The Republic of Texas joined the United States in 1845 as a slave-holding state. After the election of Abraham Lincoln in 1860, Texas seceded from the Union and joined the Confederacy.

During the Civil War, 70,000 Texans became soldiers. The most famous fighting unit was the Texas Brigade. The Texas Brigade was led by General John Bell Hood. A West Point graduate from Kentucky, Hood considered Texas his home. Texans fought in many major Civil War battles. The state of Texas also supplied many horses to the Confederacy.

Some Texans did not want to secede from the United States. Sam Houston, the governor, believed in keeping the country together. He refused to declare loyalty to the Confederacy, even when people told him he would have to give up being governor. People like Sam Houston were called Unionists. Two thousand Texans even chose to join the Union Army.

Cotton was the biggest crop in Texas and many other states. Enslaved people planted and picked the crop, but plantation owners earned all the money. Slavery was one of the main reasons Texas joined the Confederate States of America. Plantation owners wanted to keep people enslaved to work the cotton fields.

The Union Navy blocked the southern ports to keep cotton from being sold and exported. This kept the southern cotton plantation owners from getting any money. However, some cotton was shipped from Texas ports on fast ships called blockade runners. These ships evaded the U.S. Navy blockade and took the cotton to English cotton mills. However, many shipments of cotton did not get sold. Texan cotton owners were financially ruined.

After the surrender of the Confederacy, the Union army returned to Texas on June 19, 1865. For the next five years, these troops stayed in Texas. Their most significant assignment was making sure that slavery had really ended. Even though the United States had declared slavery was over in 1863, it wasn’t until the troops reached Texas that many people were freed from slavery. People called the day troops arrived “Juneteenth.” Juneteenth is still a day of celebration.

Texan soldiers returned home after the fighting, but not everyone was happy with the changes happening in the state. The 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments to the Constitution, which promised equal rights to all Americans, were met with violent opposition. People who opposed the new freedoms for African Americans worked to scare others away from voting. They were then able to pass laws that limited African Americans’ rights. These laws lasted until Lyndon Johnson, the first Texan to become the United States’ president, signed the Civil Rights Act in 1965, 100 years after the Civil War.

The time after the Civil War was also a time of violent conflict on the Texas frontier between the American Indians and settlers intruding on their land. The new state police force and the military were all used to try and maintain order.

The land was experiencing strong change from old beliefs to new realities. The cotton market had a long, slow recovery. But cattle and beef took on a new place in the market. Cattle being brought to market on trail drives became a legend still talked about today.

Reconstruction in the United States ended in 1877. The principles of equality in the U.S. Constitution were not yet realities in the lives of many Texans. The struggle for freedom would continue in Texas and throughout the country.

title: Looking Back: Texas Independence to Reconstruction
text:
Santa Anna's Cruel Victory at the Alamo

In January 1836, William B. Travis and 30 other Texans entered the Alamo, a Spanish mission in San Antonio. Along with James Bowie, Travis took command of the Texas soldiers at the Alamo. They were determined to stand up to the Mexican army. When Bowie became ill, Travis was in command by himself.

General Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna, a mexican dictator, had ordered 3,000 of his best soldiers to set up camp outside the Alamo. The Mexicans blasted bugles and cannons for days to threaten the Texans who were inside the mission. The last defender to have arrived at the Alamo was Gregorio Esparza. Travis and 150 brave men planned ways to hold off the threat. Davy Crockett, James Bonham and Jim Bowie helped make a battle plan. In the end, women and children were moved to safer areas of the mission.

Travis vowed the Texans would fight to "Victory or Death" even though they were outnumbered and starving. The Texans waited for help to arrive, but on the morning of March 6, 1836, they knew that help would not come. The Mexican army attacked with cruel force. More than 1,500 Mexicans died in the battle, but every Texan man was killed. Afterward, Santa Anna burned the bodies of the Texas heroes.

Texas Independence Day

While at the Alamo in March 1836, William Travis ordered one of his men to sneak a letter past the Mexican soldiers. He explained the situation at the Alamo to another Texas leader, Sam Houston. He hoped the letter would make it in time for help to be sent.

During this time, another group of Texans was discussing freedom from Mexico. They realized the Texans at the Alamo were most likely doomed. They felt the best thing they could do was declare independence from Mexico. On March 1, the first day of the meeting, five men were chosen to write a document to explain the Texans' decision. They wrote the Texas Declaration of Independence overnight, and everyone agreed to it the next day. The document clearly explained that Texas no longer wanted to be a part of Mexico. Texans wanted to be an independent nation.

They ended their meeting on March 17, 1836, when the Texans learned that Santa Anna and his men were heading their way. The Texans left with the wish to free themselves from Mexico once and for all. Each year on March 2, Texans celebrate Texas Independence Day.

Victory for the Texans

After the Battle of the Alamo, Texans suffered another loss when the Mexican army surrounded Colonel James W. Fannin's troops in Goliad. Fannin was forced to surrender, and he agreed his troops would give up weapons and become prisoners of war. Santa Anna had another plan. He ordered the Texans to be killed. Mexican soldiers executed 332 Texans that day. Texans were furious.

Major General Sam Houston had only 750 men left in his army. Houston felt his men needed time to rest and train. The men camped on the banks of the Buffalo Bayou on an open plain known as San Jacinto. Houston sent scouts to spy on the Mexicans. He learned that Santa Anna and his troops were headed their way for battle.

On the morning of April 21, 1836, 1,200 Mexicans arrived. They settled in and built a barricade, but the Texans didn't attack at first. The Mexicans began to relax. Many of the men took an afternoon nap, including Santa Anna. Houston took this moment to start his surprise attack. The Battle of San Jacinto lasted only 18 minutes. About 650 Mexicans were killed. Only nine of Houston's men died. Santa Anna was captured the next morning, and the revolution came to an end. The Texans had earned their independence and were free of the Mexicans, at least for the time being.

title: Texas: Republic to 28th State
text:
Treaties of Velasco

When Gen. Houston and his volunteer Texas army defeated Mexico at San Jacinto, Gen. Santa Anna had no choice but to make a deal with Houston. Texas would get its freedom from Mexico. On May 14, 1836, Santa Anna signed two peace treaties with Texas President David G. Burnet. The Treaties of Velasco would send all of Santa Anna’s soldiers back to Mexico. Santa Anna also secretly agreed to help Texas gain independence from Mexico without any further problems. Leaders agreed that the southern border of Texas would be the Rio Grande.

Not everyone was happy about the way the war ended or with the treaties. Many people wanted to see Santa Anna punished for all he had done to the Texans. Mexican leaders said the treaties were no good because Santa Anna had been a prisoner when he signed them. It was clear Texas was not completely free from troubles with Mexico.

A New Republic

People claimed that Texas was now a country, the Republic of Texas. Texans had the right to follow the Texas Constitution and choose leaders to represent them. An election was held to find the first president of the Republic of Texas. Stephen F. Austin, Texas founder, ran for the office. However, the people elected war hero General Sam Houston. Mirabeau B. Lamar was elected as vice president. Austin took the job of secretary of state. He continued to work hard for Texas.

Texans were proud of their victory. They wanted to create a modern and successful nation. They found this was almost as difficult as winning their freedom in the first place. However, the people were determined to work hard to make their nation strong. There was a lot of good land on which people could settle, farm and build communities. They had a government in place. The presidency, congress and court system of Texas were modeled after the three-branch system of the United States. Many immigrants from other countries continued to settle in Texas. The population of the Republic grew and grew.

Unfortunately, the Republic of Texas also had problems. The new nation needed money. It had no savings and needed to repay money it had borrowed during the revolution with Mexico. Leaders decided to collect taxes and sell land to earn that money. Citizens continued to be concerned about their safety. They were afraid Mexico might attack again. In addition, settlers wanted to keep peace with American Indians. President Houston wanted to sign treaties with the American Indians.

Nation or State?

The people of Texas rebuilt communities after the long war with Mexico. Towns grew, and farms and plantations did well. However, many people feared Texas would not be strong enough to stand alone for long. Texas still had very little money. The next president, President Lamar, did not get along well with the American Indian tribes. In addition, Mexico was not sticking to the treaty terms. It often attacked Texas. Santa Anna even took control of several Texas towns for a short time again. Many Texans still thought of themselves as Americans. These people wanted Texas to join the United States. Others wanted Texas to grow as a nation.

Americans were not sure if the annexation of Texas was a good idea. The U.S. would have to take over Texas’ debts. Many people also worried about getting involved in disagreements between Texas and Mexico and American Indians. The biggest concern, however, was slavery. Texans, like people in southern U.S. states, were allowed to own other people as slaves. These enslaved people were forced to farm large Texas plantations. People in the U.S. weren’t sure they wanted another slave state. President Polk, however, knew it would be bad if Texas fell back into the hands of an enemy. In the end, the U.S. decided Texas would be a good addition to the country.

On Feb. 28, 1845, the U.S. Congress passed a resolution saying Texas could become a state. Texas would have to pay off its own debts, but people would still be allowed to own enslaved people. Texas would also have the right to divide itself into five states if it chose to do so. The people of Texas agreed to the terms of annexation. On Dec. 29, 1845, Texas President Anson Jones lowered the Republic of Texas flag for the last time. Texas was now the 28th state in the United States of America.

The U.S. at War with Mexico

When the U.S. accepted Texas as a state, Mexico believed it was an act of war. Mexican leaders still believed Texas belonged to them. U.S. President James K. Polk offered to buy land from Mexico. Unfortunately, Mexico would not sell. In addition, U.S. and Mexico disagreed on the boundary between the two countries. On May 13, 1846, the U.S. declared war against Mexico. It was just what many Americans had feared when Texas was annexed. Texas Rangers knew the Texas land well. They were excellent scouts and fighters. Like other Texans, they wanted the Mexican threat to be over at last. The war ended after the U.S. invaded Mexico City in February 1848. Leaders signed the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. The Rio Grande would be the boundary between the countries. The U.S. also gained more than half a million square miles of land. The U.S. paid Mexico $15 million. The Mexican-American War had come to an end.

title: The Runaway Scrape
text:
Gen. Santa Anna was proud of his victory at the Alamo. He had killed nearly every Texan who had been fighting. Some women and children survived. One of these was Susanna Dickinson. Santa Anna freed her and told her to let Texans know he and his troops were coming for the rest of them. Sure enough, Santa Anna led his troops toward the Texas coast. They raided and burned every settlement in their path.

Texas leader Sam Houston ordered all Texans to head toward the Colorado River to keep away from the Mexican army. Families left their homes quickly, sometimes with just the clothes on their backs. The Runaway Scrape proved the Texans knew the advancing Mexicans were angry and dangerous.

title: American Indians Depended on the Buffalo
text: As Texas grew, white settlers claimed more and more land. They invaded territory where the Plains Indians had lived and hunted for generations. American Indians, who relied on the buffalo/bison, found themselves in a terrible situation. Many of them fought with settlers. Some U.S. leaders wanted to work with the American Indians, but others wanted to force them to live on reservations. White settlers began hunting buffalo. Large herds grazed on land the settlers wanted for farming, ranching and railroads. American buffalo hunters killed thousands of animals only for the hides. They left the carcasses to rot on the plains. The buffalo neared extinction, which caused the way of life for the Plains Indians to change forever.

title: Civil War and Reconstruction in Texas
text: When Texas became a state, the practice of slavery continued. People in different states disagreed on many issues, including slavery. Seven states decided to secede from the U.S. and form a new country. Texas was one of these states and helped form the Confederate States of America. In all, 11 states left the U.S. Soon, the U.S. was in the middle of a Civil War. Approximately 90,000 Texans fought in the war. Some Texans helped at home. When the war ended, Texans had to rebuild homes and businesses during the Reconstruction period. People freed from slavery had to find jobs and homes. Texas rejoined the U.S. in 1870 and elected new leaders. A new Texas Constitution gave leaders much less power than before.

title: Making a Living in Texas
text: Before the Civil War, most Texans earned their livings off the land. Many Texans were farmers and ranchers. Cotton and tobacco were popular crops. These farms required large amounts of land, so farmers used slave labor for their businesses. Goods were sold and shipped to other states and countries. Texans, like other Southerners, were charged high taxes. They did not want other countries to put high taxes on the Southern products that were exported. They also did not like taxes put on goods they brought into the state. Manufacturing was not as important in Texas, so Texans purchased many products from Northern states. During the Civil War, Texans suffered greatly because the Northern states stopped shipping products to the South.

title: Cause and Effect
text: Use your knowledge of the annexation of Texas and information from this week’s review issue to complete the cause and effect graphic organizer.

text:
1. Draw conclusions about the kind of man Gen. Santa Anna was. Support your ideas with evidence from this week’s issue.

2. Why do you think no one answered Travis’ call for help at the Alamo?

3. Make inferences about why the Mexicans decided to take an afternoon nap at San Jacinto, even though they knew the Texans were nearby.

4. Predict what might have been the outcome for Texas if the U.S. did not annex the Republic as the 28th state.

5. Based on what you know about Gen. Santa Anna, do you think Houston’s order to run from the Mexicans was the right decision? Why or why not?

6. What evidence can you find that proves the white settlers did not value the buffalo as much as the Plains Indians did?

title: Let's Write
text: Authors often write to inform readers of certain facts. This type of expository writing can be done using several different formats. One of these is the cause-effect format. Use information from this week’s issue, including the Page 4 activity, to help you write. Write three paragraphs explaining the annexation of Texas, its causes and its effects. Write in complete sentences, and support all of your ideas with specific facts and details. Be sure to use correct grammar, spelling and punctuation.

title: Important Texas Historical Documents
text:
The Texas Declaration of Independence and the Texas Constitution gave Texas more freedom and more rights. Originally, Texas was part of Mexico, but the people in Texas didn’t like the way they were governed. In 1835, a war began between Texas and Mexico. In 1836, George Childress wrote the Texas Declaration of Independence. The Declaration said the people had been abused by the Mexican government and that they wanted freedom of speech and equal rights. After it was signed, Texas became a state in the U.S.

The Texas Constitution was signed in 1876. The Constitution describes the basic laws that Texas follows. Many of the laws are unique to Texas because of the Mexican influence on the state. The people writing the Constitution wanted to limit what the local government could do. They wanted the local government to listen more to the people of Texas. The Texas Constitution also covers freedom of speech, equal rights, taxes, how long someone can hold a government office, and education.

title: Scott Joplin and Ragtime
text:
Scott Joplin grew up in a home near the Texas-Arkansas border. He became a popular musician and composer. He was classically trained and studied music at George R. Smith College in Missouri. Joplin was a piano virtuoso.

Known as the "King of Ragtime," Joplin was the son of an enslaved African American. Ragtime is a style of piano music that developed in the African American community. Ragtime has a syncopated rhythm where the accented notes are between the upbeats and the downbeats. Breaking up a melody that way was known as “ragging,” or playing in “ragged time,” or “ragtime” for short. The syncopated rhythms were thought to have originated from African drumbeats. Ragtime was popular not only across the South, but around the world.

Older people disdained this early 1900s music genre. They thought it just wasn’t right to alter long-established musical rhythms.

Joplin earned a living as a piano teacher. He played ragtime and other African American folk music for audiences all over and even used ragtime in his opera, “Treemonisha.” The opera celebrates African American culture and racial pride. Ragtime’s popularity waned after Joplin died in 1917, but ragtime style lived on, evolving into stride music, jazz, and swing.

title: On the Texas Range
text:
After the Civil War, Texas was in trouble. The state had very little money. In fact, it was just about broke. Texas didn't have any cash. But luckily, it did have plenty of something that was almost as valuable.

Texas was home to a lot of cattle. Semi-wild longhorn cows roamed all over the Texas prairies. These animals were large and strong. They could go for a long time with very little water. Their horns sometimes measured up to eight feet across. And what was better than anything else is that these cattle provided beef that people could eat.

Everyone started thinking of ways to round up the cattle. They wanted to sell the cattle to people in other states who wanted to buy beef. In fact, people living east of the Mississippi River wanted to buy lots and lots of beef. From 1865 to 1885, more than five million cattle were sold in the East.

Life in Texas changed almost overnight for many people in the new cattle industry. Many Eastern cities demanded beef, so there were lots of opportunities for big profits. More than 35,000 men worked as cowboys, wranglers and cooks during the two decades after the war. These people worked long, hard hours driving, or guiding, cattle along trails. The cattle were then shipped on railroad cars to meatpacking plants in large cities like Chicago. The cattle industry made some people very rich. Other people worked very hard to make a simple living. Some towns and cities grew and did very well because of the cattle industry. Other communities failed when the cattle industry slowed down.

In this issue, you will learn all about how ranching and the cattle industry grew in Texas. You will learn about how people's lives changed because of it. You will find out how towns along cattle trails grew and changed over time. And you will get to learn about people who lived and worked in Texas during this period. These Texans who made a living ranching and raising cattle were usually independent hard workers. They had to have courage and endurance. The story of the cattle industry in Texas is very fascinating.

title: Beating the Beef Bacteria
text:
There is no doubt about it. Americans like to eat beef. Americans eat about 26 billion pounds of beef per year. This averages out to about 83 pounds of beef per person per year. That's a lot of beef! But beef is one type of food that can make people very sick if it is not processed and cooked properly.

A certain type of bacteria known as E. coli is why people can get sick from beef. This bacteria is naturally found in a cow's digestive system and is needed to help them digest food. But for humans, the bacteria can make you very sick. In rare cases, the bacteria can even cause death. Scientists are working to find ways to keep the beef supply in the United States safe. They have spent millions of dollars experimenting with ways to keep the dangerous bacteria out of the food supply. The answer may be a vaccine for cows.

Researchers at Kansas State University and West Texas A & M University have developed a special medicine for cows. The vaccine prevents the dangerous E. coli bacteria from reproducing and leaving the animal's body. Researchers recently began giving the vaccine to beef cattle, and they hope to see a decrease in the number of E. coli cases soon.

title: Ranching and a Changing Frontier
text:
Cattle Barons

After the Civil War, many people in Texas began ranching, or raising cattle. These people, known as cattle barons, knew they could raise cows on the good Texas land. They also knew they could make a lot of money selling the cows. They built large ranches on the Texas prairies. They hired men to take care of the cattle. These men were known as cowboys and wranglers. They worked on the ranches every day and took the cattle to be sold at a market.

The cattle barons used the money they made to buy more cattle. They also made their ranches larger and better. Some of these ranches are still running in Texas today. Richard King, an Irish-American born in New York City, bought large tracts of land in south Texas between the Nueces and Rio Grande rivers. By using cattle drives to get his animals to northern markets, King revolutionized ranching and made enormous profits. The King Ranch in Kingsville, Texas, has been around since Richard King started it in 1852. Today this is the largest cattle ranch in the United States. The ranch is larger than the state of Rhode Island.

Life on a Ranch

Most ranches in Texas were located on plains and prairies. Usually there were no neighbors for many miles around. Until the 1880s, ranchers kept their cattle on the grassy plains, or the open range.

These ranches had enough food and supplies to last for up to a year at a time. They got water from windmills that pumped water from underground wells.

Most ranches had several buildings. The ranch owner usually lived in the main house. Cowboys, wranglers and ranch cooks usually lived in a nearby bunkhouse. The owner might build different buildings or fences depending on the climate and the ranch's size.

Cowboys

The work done by cowboys on the ranch was very hard. They were responsible for the daily jobs on the ranch. They also were responsible for getting the cattle ready to sell. The cowboys had to brand, or mark, each cow so they knew which ones were theirs. Many ranchers brought their cattle to the markets. And each rancher had his own brand design that they burned into the hide of each of his cows.

The cowboys drove, or guided, the cattle to railroads. From there, the cattle would be taken to a market and sold. These trips were called cattle drives. They were often long, dusty and dangerous journeys. One famous cattle rancher and cowboy, Charles Goodnight, blazed (laid out) a cattle trail with his friend Oliver Loving. The Goodnight-Loving Trail stretched from Belknap, Texas to markets in New Mexico, Colorado and Wyoming. It was used by cowboys for many years to come. Cowboys depended on their horses. These horses had to be hardworking and have great endurance. Cowboys trained their horses to help keep the cattle moving along the trail safely.

Texas Trails

The trails of Texas were often very crowded. Sometimes the cattle even had a difficult time finding enough food on the trail. There were several trails that led from south Texas to the beef markets in Kansas, Missouri, Colorado, Wyoming and Montana. The Chisholm Trail carried two million cattle to Kansas from 1867 to 1871. The Goodnight-Loving Trail was established in 1866. Cattle on this trail were headed to Colorado, Wyoming and Montana.

Trail Drives

In order to make money, ranchers had to drive, or guide, the cattle down trails for hundreds and hundreds of miles. The trip was always hard work. It was sometimes boring. Many times it was dangerous. The cowboys rode near the herd of cows to keep them from wandering off. The men faced wild animals, harsh weather and sometimes even angry American Indians.

But there were two dangers that were always on the cowboys' minds. The first was running out of drinking water on the hot, dusty trail. The second was the chance of a stampede. The wild cattle might be easily scared. They might burst off running for miles. A cowboy caught in the middle of a stampede could easily be hurt or killed.

Barbed Wire

At the beginning of the cattle boom, ranchers let their cattle roam anywhere they wished. But farmers did not like that animals could wander onto their land. Soon these farmers put up barbed wire fences. They wanted to be able to grow crops without wild, roaming animals destroying their fields or eating their crops. Ranchers could no longer let their cattle wander over the open range. The animals had to be kept in pens. Even though the new fencing cost money, it seemed to be a good idea. Ranchers were able to keep wild animals away from their herds. The health of all the animals improved. The farmers' fencing, however, made it impossible to lead the cattle down the trails on drives. Ranchers now had to use nearby railroads to get their animals to market.

The End of the Trail

After only 20 years, the cattle-driving business came to an end. Nobody wanted cowboys to cross their land with thousands of cattle. Many farmers and ranchers put up fences around their land to keep the cowboys away. American Indian tribes wanted to be paid for letting the cattle cross their lands.

At the same time, many cattle on the trails caught a disease called Texas fever. This disease was quickly spreading between the cattle on the trails. Many of them died. To help keep the disease from spreading, many towns did not allow cattle to pass through. Soon the price of beef dropped. Cattle barons were no longer making huge profits.

The cattle-driving business ended, but the trails left their mark on Texas and America. During those two decades, Texans built many new ranches. People also built many new towns along the trails. Many of these communities continued to grow. People began to think about using the railroads more to transport all kinds of goods. Although one period of history was ending, another exciting period was just beginning.

title: Lizzie Johnson Williams: The Texas Cattle Queen
text:
Lizzie Johnson was born in Missouri in 1845. She moved to Austin, Texas, with her parents when she was a very young girl. Lizzie was very well educated. She studied at Chapel Hill College in Georgetown, Texas, and became a teacher and a writer. Everyone always noticed how elegant she looked in her diamond jewelry and fancy clothing.

During the Civil War, Lizzie took over her older brother's job while he fought in the Confederate army. Lizzie worked for cattle barons. Her job was to do the math and keep up with the money for the trail drives. Lizzie was smart and learned a lot during this time. She began buying her own land and cattle and made money for herself. Even after she married and became Lizzie Williams, she always kept track of her own money.

Lizzie earned her nickname, the Texas Cattle Queen, during the last days of the trail drives. Unlike most women of the day, Lizzie went with her cattle on the trail drives to market. Some people used to joke that she wanted to protect her investment all the way to the bank.

After the days of cattle driving ended, Lizzie stayed in the cattle industry. She and her husband even owned a very large ranch in Cuba. After her death in 1924, Lizzie's family found a small fortune in jewels, fabrics and cash in her home. Today, Lizzie Johnson Williams is remembered as one of the most important women in Texas history for helping women blaze the trail in the cattle industry.

title: Joseph Glidden and his Invention that Changed the West
text:
During the long cold winter of 1872 in DeKalb, Illinois, Lucinda Glidden noticed something strange. The large wire hairpins she kept in a glass dish on her dresser were disappearing. Lucinda asked her daughter about the missing pins. Elva Frances did not know anything about the mystery. Day after day, the hairpins continued to disappear.

One evening Lucinda was sitting at the dinner table with her husband, Joseph, when the mystery was suddenly solved. Joseph took two hairpins from his shirt pocket and began bending and twisting them. Lucinda wanted to know what in the world her husband was doing with her pins. Joseph calmly explained that he had an idea to build a new type of fence. Lucinda was excited. She had complained all last spring and summer when the livestock from their farm got into her yard and crushed her plants.

Joseph worked on his idea all winter long. He tried many different designs. Finally Joseph and a blacksmith friend found a way to wrap short pieces of thorny wire around a longer piece of wire. The pointed "barbs" would keep animals in or out of a fenced area. The points would push against the animals and force them away from the fence.

Glidden made the wire himself at first. He used one horse to help him move the equipment he needed for making the wire. He even began using the fencing material at his own home to show people how well it worked.

Within two years, people all over knew about Joseph Glidden's amazing new fencing material. Glidden opened a large manufacturing plant to make the material. Soon he and his family became very wealthy.

Now farmers on the plains and prairies of America had a new type of fencing material - barbed wire - that changed the ways they lived and worked.

title: Solving a Problem of the Open Range
text:
By the mid 1870s, farmers and ranchers in Texas disagreed about whether cattle should be allowed to roam on the open range. Many farmers thought their crops would do better if cattle were kept in pens so they could not eat the plants. Some ranchers believed the cattle should be allowed to graze and eat anywhere they could find food. The two groups had to work together to solve their problem. They had to work as good citizens. Good citizens can use a process to help find solutions, or answers, to problems. Use the process steps below and information from this issue to identify ways that the fencing/roaming problem on the Texas open range could have been solved.

Identify the problem - What was the problem the Texas farmers and ranchers faced?

Gather information - Get all the facts. List three facts about the problem in Texas.

Think about all the options - What were all the possible ways the problem could have been solved? Think about options both ranchers and farmers might have suggested. List them.

Consider each option - What were the good and bad things about every possible solution? Write a sentence about each idea.

Choose a solution - What solution did the farmers and ranchers finally agree upon? Explain that solution below.

Think about the results - Did the plan work? Do you think the farmers and ranchers thought about changing the plan? What could they have done differently? Explain.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you are a farmer in Texas in 1875. Your crops have been eaten and destroyed by cattle that are roaming on the open range. Write a letter to the editor of your local newspaper. Explain why you think ranchers should keep their cattle in pens. Write about the new type of wire fence you will put around your farm. How will the fencing be helpful to both ranchers and farmers? Explain your ideas in detail. Be sure to edit your final work for capitalization, spelling, grammar and punctuation.

title: Railroads Steam Texas into the Future
text:
During the 1850s, railroad companies started building railroads through Texas. In 1860, Texas had only about 400 miles of railroad track. But in 40 years, Texas had more miles of railroad track than any other state. Railroads changed the way people in Texas lived and worked. Read about the first time a young Texas girl took a train ride from Texas to Kansas to visit her grandparents.

Deborah's heart thumped loudly in her chest. The nervous butterflies were dancing in her tummy again. Deborah couldn't help being excited. She was going to get to do something amazing today. She was going to board a train and travel to visit her grandparents.

Deborah had not seen her Grandmother and Grandfather Stewart since her parents moved the family from Kansas to Texas five years ago. Her sister, Angela, had been a baby then. Angela didn't even remember her grandmother's apple pies. They got letters from friends and family back in Kansas pretty often. But it was too long of a trip by wagon to visit. Her daddy couldn't be away from his ranch for very long. It was also too dangerous for her mama to travel to Kansas with the children alone. American Indians were fighting with buffalo hunters, settlers and the U.S. Army over claims for buffalo hunting areas. The railroads and Army forts had taken over even more of the open range that the buffalo needed to survive. But Deborah's family would be protected from these battles riding on a train. The railroad had a train that would take Deborah and her family from their home in Fort Worth straight to her grandparents' hometown in Kansas. The trip would take only a day or so. Traveling would be so much easier now. It would be a grand adventure for Deborah.

Suddenly a shh-shh sound could be heard in the distance. The train was coming around a curve. A long, loud whistle cut through the air. The train started screeching as it came to a halt at the station. The smell of the burning coal from the train's engine hung in the air. Deborah picked up her bag and held tightly to Mama's hand. This was the beginning of a whole new way of life for everyone.

title: Experts Disagree on Railroad’s Effect on Environment
text:
Over time, the cost of gasoline has risen higher and higher. It is very expensive to own and operate a vehicle. Besides, most cars run on non-renewable fossil fuels. This is not very good for the environment. Scientists have been telling people for years that travel by train is cheaper and much better for the environment than other transportation. But recent studies show that travel by train may not be as good for the environment as they thought.

Railroad trains can carry large numbers of people over great distances. Trains can run at high speeds. Trains do not have to stop often during the trip. Train tickets are also very affordable. This means a train ride does not cost a lot of money. Experts say trains use 70 percent less energy than airplanes. Trains also use five times less fuel per passenger than a car. So what is the downside?

The Swedish Research Council recently announced that while trains are ecofriendly, their rails are not. Construction and maintenance of the rails takes a lot of fossil fuel energy. Plus, if the train isn't full of passengers, it really isn't saving energy or decreasing pollution.

Environmentalists say people should carefully consider which form of transportation they use. We all want to keep our environment "on the right track."

title: Railroads Bring 'Boom' to Texas
text:
Why Railroads Were Needed

There weren't very many types of transportation in early Texas. And each type had problems. Many Texas rivers were too shallow for large steamboats to use all year. Horse-drawn coach rides were slow, hot and dusty. The few roads in Texas were not well made and were often too muddy to use.

People didn't have many ways to travel quickly and safely. There were even fewer ways for goods to be shipped in and out of Texas easily. Texas needed new transportation the people could count on.

Railroad companies started laying tracks in the eastern United States in the early 1800s. When people moved and started new communities, the railroads followed them. New tracks helped connect new communities. Texas didn't have many large cities and wanted more people to move to the state. And people wanted an easy way to get from the eastern United States to Texas.

By the 1850s, people in Texas began to see that railroads were important to their future. Bexar County in south Texas was the first to convince railroad companies to lay tracks through their communities. By 1852, the state government was giving away land to railroad companies. In exchange for the land, the companies built new tracks. The railroad companies built so many new tracks that by 1882 Texas ran out of land to give away.

The Boom Begins

During the 1870s and 1880s, a boom began in Texas. A boom is a period of time where something grows very quickly. The state was growing very quickly and railroad companies started building more tracks there. The first railroad tracks were in south Texas by the Gulf Coast. Over time, the boom spread north. Texas started with only about 400 miles of railroad tracks. Soon Texas had more than 8,000 miles of tracks.

The first major change to Texas during this boom period was the number of people who came to the state. People came from many other states and countries. The population of Texas grew from about 800,000 to more than 2 million. Most of these newcomers brought their culture with them. New foods, religions, music, languages and celebrations made Texas more interesting than ever.

Communities Boom

As the railroads grew, so did a lot of new towns across the Texas plains. Some cities had two or more railroads running through them. These cities were known as junctions. The early locomotives, or train engines, used steam for energy. These engines needed water to make the steam. But they could only run for about 30 miles before they needed more water.

To solve this problem, railroad companies hired workers to dig water wells every 30 miles along the tracks. The trains could then stop at the wells for water. Soon businesses opened at the water well sites. People began building homes at these sites. More and more people came and businesses grew. When the town got large enough, the railroad company would build a depot, or train station. This station helped the town grow even more. Today there are many Texas towns that are still about 30 miles apart.

Many of these "railroad" communities are still doing well. For example, Abilene, a city in central west Texas, grew when the Texas Pacific Railroad came to its area. Abilene quickly grew as a cattleshipping center. Abilene is still a growing, successful community.

Businesses Boom

Many businesses in Texas grew because of the railroads. Railroad companies wanted Texas businesses to do well. This would help the railroad companies grow even more. Many businesses worked to help the railroads too. Railroads brought people to their businesses. Railroads shipped products for these businesses. They all worked together so they could all be successful.

Railroad companies helped lumber companies get started. The railroads cut down trees to make way for railroad tracks. Lumber companies processed and sold the wood. Trains then shipped the lumber products out to other parts of the United States. Railroads also helped meatpacking, grain, cotton and sugar businesses. The railroads could make money shipping these products also.

Before the railroad boom, there were many different industries in Texas. Lumber manufacturing and grain milling were the two largest. However these businesses did not grow much. They could only sell their goods to people in a small area. Railroads gave them a huge boost. Industries could now ship goods to many places. This increased trade (buying and selling products) with other states and even other countries. Many people all over the world relied on the products that came from Texas. People in Texas needed foreign goods too, like tea and fruit. People around the world became interdependent. This means they depended on each other. By 1900, the top Texas industries did about $60 million in business each year. People were making money. They were able to build homes and open more businesses.

All over Texas, the railroads were changing the ways people made money and earned a living.

title: Chinese Immigrants — Building the Railroad Legacy
text:
The railroads brought many new people into Texas. Immigrants came to Texas looking for a better life and more opportunities. Among these immigrants were many people from China.

In the 1800s, life in China was very hard. People did not have many chances to own their own land or businesses. Some of these Chinese people heard about the United States. They wanted to come to the new land. Most hoped to make money and return home to China. They sailed across the Pacific Ocean to what is now California. There, most of the immigrants worked mining for gold or building railroads.

In 1869, about 300 Chinese railroad workers came from California to Texas. They began working on railroads in south Texas near Houston. They worked long, hard days. Living conditions were not very good. Most of the Chinese workers lived in tents. They had to agree to work on the railroads for five years.

Over the next 10 years, several thousand Chinese workers came to Texas. Some of them liked Texas and decided to stay. There were several communities of Chinese workers in the state. The largest settlements were near Pecos, in west Texas, and in Calvert, in south Texas. These Chinese workers brought their culture to Texas. They celebrated their traditional holidays. Chinese food and music were a part of their daily lives. They were admired for their hard work. But they were not always treated fairly. By 1883, the number of Chinese citizens allowed to enter the United States was cut back.

Today there are still Chinese families living in Texas who are descendants from, or related to, those first railroad workers.

title: What was the Red River War of 1874?
text:
The railroads cut a path across the buffalo hunting grounds of the American Indians. Their nomadic life following the buffalo on horseback was changing forever. White buffalo hunters were also swarming across the plains, ignoring boundaries promised by treaties. The buffalo population was nearly destroyed in a few short years.

Some American Indians moved to reservations, settlements controlled by the United States, but others fought back. Comanche chief Quanah Parker, joined by Comanche, Kiowa and Cheyenne warriors, led an attack on a buffalo hunters' camp, Adobe Walls, on June 27, 1874. The U.S. Army struck back by surrounding the American Indian camps along the Red River in the Texas Panhandle, and a full-scale war followed. After two years and some 20 battles, the American Indians were defeated by the well-equipped U.S. Army. Their surrender at Fort Sill forced them to move to reservations to live, never to return to their former lifestyle.

title: Agility of Mind: Teddy Roosevelt Wins Nobel Peace Prize
text:
agile (adjective): able to move quickly and easily; ex.: as agile as a monkey, an agile mind.

Teddy Roosevelt was president of the United States from 1901 to 1909. He was also a great hunter, explorer, author, outdoorsman and soldier.

As a child, Teddy was often sick and could not play sports. But he became a good problem solver. He wasn't afraid to put his thoughts into action or think of different solutions. If his first idea didn't work, he had the mental agility to change his mind quickly.

When Roosevelt was president, Japan and Russia were at war. He invited diplomats (official representatives) from Russia and Japan to Portsmouth, New Hampshire, to talk about peace. At first, he didn't know how their problems could be solved but he acted quickly to get the diplomats together. He helped them compromise. After a lot of discussion, they worked out their differences and signed the Portsmouth Peace Treaty, an agreement that ended the war and saved many lives. President Roosevelt won the Nobel Peace Prize for helping end the war. His way of helping others solve problems is still used today.

Teddy Roosevelt had an important power skill - an agile mind. You can use this power skill when you act on your good ideas. Remember that an idea can be good without being perfect. People with agile minds often fail before they succeed. The ability to think on your feet, or think while doing, can help you find solutions that will benefit others.
