title: Qualities of a Leader
text:
Have you ever thought about running for office? How do you know if you’d make a good mayor or president?

Good leaders are smart and have ideas about making life better for their citizens. They like people and know how to talk and listen to them. Effective leaders are brave. They do not give up easily. They are honest. In a republic, people choose leaders to represent them. Good leaders get along well with others, even people they disagree with. Great leaders want to make a difference.

Barbara Jordan was a lawyer and a teacher who ran for the Texas House of Representatives but lost twice. Finally, she won a seat in the Texas Senate. She was the first woman and the first African-American to serve there. Jordan was later elected to the U.S. House of Representatives. Her speeches are considered among the best ever given. Her words inspired people to do hard things that were right and just. She studied the Constitution and helped pass laws to protect it. Jordan was an honest and wise leader who wanted her country to be a safe place for everyone.

When Greg Abbott was a young man, an oak tree fell on him, leaving him unable to move from his waist down. That didn't stop Abbott from becoming a lawyer, a judge, and an attorney general before running for governor in 2014. Abbott won reelection in 2018. Abbott is not afraid to fight for what he believes in, even when others disagree with him.

If you like people and like to solve problems, you might be the leader your state (or school) needs.

title: Looking Back: Reconstruction to the Present
text:
Cattle Ranchers Rule the Frontier

Texas was in trouble after the Civil War. There was little money left for rebuilding communities that had been destroyed by war. Life changed, though, when people began thinking of ways to round-up cattle to sell to people living east of the Mississippi River. Overnight, more than 35,000 cowboys, wranglers and trail cooks began working long days guiding cattle along trails to large eastern cities.

Life on a cattle ranch was very difficult. The cowboys worked to take care of the cattle daily, brand them with the rancher's own design and drive the cattle on trails to markets. These trips were long and dangerous. Charles Goodnight, a famous cowboy and cattle rancher, planned a cattle trail with his friend Oliver Loving. The Goodnight-Loving trail stretched across the state and led to markets in New Mexico, Colorado and Wyoming.

Most cattle ranchers earned small livings, but others found great success in the industry. Cattle barons such as Richard King founded the King Ranch. He made a lot of money ranching and selling Texas cattle. Lizzie Johnson Williams was called the Texas Cattle Queen. She was one of the few women who bought her own land and sold cattle. She is remembered today as one of the most important women in Texas ranching history.

Ranching and cattle drives were changed forever when Joseph Glidden invented barbed wire. Animals no longer roamed wild, and it was nearly impossible to drive cattle across the open land. Ranchers turned to railroads to get their animals to markets. The era of the trail drive was over.

Oil's Well That Ends Well

Railroads brought many new settlers into Texas in the late 1800s. Many of these newcomers thought they might find their fortunes on the fertile Texas land. Two of these men were Anthony F. Lucas and Patillo Higgins. They explored for and struck oil at Spindletop in south Texas in early 1901. Texas was never the same. The oil boom began with a bang!

News of the find quickly spread. Railroads and other industries demanded oil and gas products. Thousands of people headed to Texas hoping to get rich in the oil business. The population grew rapidly. Jobs in the oil field were plentiful, and new communities prospered (did well). Many new towns and cities sprung up wherever oil was found.

By 1928, Texas produced more oil than any other state. Petroleum, or oil, companies opened large offices all over the state and hired many people to work for them. Workers drilled new wells each day for many years after the discovery at Spindletop. Refineries along the Texas coast shipped the oil and gas products all over the world.

The oil industry is an important part of the Texas economy even today. New research and drilling techniques are used to keep Texas a leading producer and supplier of petroleum and natural gas products.

The Boom Goes Bust

The 20th century began with such promise. Railroads shipped goods in and out of Texas quickly. Towns grew quickly. Texans were earning money ranching, farming or working in the oil industry. Texans, like other Americans, believed that hard work and the right opportunities would bring prosperity and success. These good times quickly fell apart, though, in October 1929. This is when the stock market crashed.

Banks and businesses closed their doors. Families lost their homes and farms. The Great Depression fell on Texas and the rest of the nation. In addition, a horrible drought caused great wind and dust storms that ruined crops and made life even more miserable for people everywhere.

The U.S. government did what it could to help people during these hard times. Programs helped people find work and buy homes again. The entire nation was not able to come out of the economic disaster, though, until the U.S. entered World War II in 1941.

Texans provided gasoline and other supplies needed for war. By 1945 when the war ended, the Great Depression was over. People moved back into cities to work and raise their families. It seemed the good times might be back for good.

title: Riding the Rails to the Future
text:
Laying the Foundation

Long before railroad tracks were common, transportation in Texas was difficult. Rivers were not deep enough for large steamboats to cross at all times of the year. Horse and buggy rides were slow, hot, dusty and dangerous. Most roads were poorly made and sometimes flooded because of heavy rain. There seemed to be no easy way to get people from place to place quickly and safely. It was even more difficult for goods to be moved in and out of the state. If Texas was going to grow, there would have to be a solution to the transportation crisis. Railroads were the answer.

In the early years of Texas statehood, railroad companies began laying tracks across the wide-open plains. In 1860, Texas had only about 400 miles of track. However, four decades later, Texas had more miles of railroad track than any other state. Everyone quickly realized that railroads could improve the state's economy. But what could be done to attract railroad companies to Texas? The government began giving away land to railroad companies to build more tracks. Many miles of track were laid, but eventually the state ran out of land to give away.

In the 1870s, building railroad tracks across the frontier was long, hard work. Many railroad workers were people from other countries who had come to America in search of better lives. Immigrants from China often found work laying tracks. The work was hard, and the living conditions for these workers were not very good. Most immigrant railroad workers lived in tents, and they had to sign agreements to work for the railroad companies for five years. After they finished building railroad tracks, some Chinese immigrants stayed in Texas. Many of their descendants live in Texas today and preserve the culture of their ancestors.

Towns and Populations Boom

Railroads contributed to a Texas boom. The state grew quickly during this time. Within years, more than 8,000 miles of railroad track crisscrossed the state. People from many other states and countries traveled on the railroads to farm the fertile Texas land. The population of the state grew from 800,000 to more than 2 million. The newcomers brought their religions, foods, music and languages with them. Texas became a land of many cultures.

New towns sprang up across the state. Railroads came along with them. Some cities, known as junctions, even had two or more railroads running through them. Water wells for steam train engines were located every 30 miles along the tracks. Communities often formed around these stations. When the communities were large enough, railroad companies built depots, or stations, there. These stations helped the towns grow even larger. Businesses began near the stations. Next, people built homes near the businesses. Today there are many successful Texas towns that are 30 miles apart because they began as railroad water stations. Texas cities such as Dallas, Fort Worth, San Antonio, Galveston and Abilene all grew with the help of railroads.

Railroads and Businesses Both Win

Railroads and businesses in Texas worked together to help each other. Railroad companies needed businesses to ship goods in and out of the state. They made a lot of their money by charging businesses for providing shipping services. Businesses needed successful railroads to get their products to other parts of the country. These products could be sold for money too. Meatpacking, grain, cotton, sugar and lumber companies all depended upon the railroads. Trade (buying and selling products) between Texas businesses and other states and countries was made possible because of railroads. Texans also enjoyed foreign goods, like tea and fruits, which were shipped into the state using railroads.

Lumber companies in Texas had an especially good relationship with railroads. Railroad companies cut down trees to make way for tracks to be laid. Lumber companies processed and sold the wood from these trees. Railroad companies then charged the lumber companies to ship the products to other parts of the United States. The products were sold for a profit for the lumber companies. Everyone was a winner.

Railroads' Influence

Railroads dramatically changed life in Texas in the 1800s and into the 20th century. Many new people settled the land. Large cities grew and prospered, and businesses of all sorts opened their doors across the state. Train travel became the most common mode of transportation. Even today, trains are used to ship both goods and people all across the country. People in Texas and other states and countries became interdependent (depended on each other). All over, the railroads changed the ways people made and spent money. Texas would not be as strong and successful had it not been for the influence of the railroad.

title: Life Changes for American Indians
text:
American Indians in Texas faced great changes to their ways of life during the last half of the 19th century. The U.S. government took over large amounts of American Indian hunting land. It used this land to built military forts and lay railroad track. Nomadic buffalo hunting became difficult. To make it worse, white hunters also competed for the buffalo supply. They would often break rules that had been set by treaties with the America Indians. Soon the buffalo population was destroyed. There was no buffalo to eat or trade for other goods.

Some American Indians moved to reservations, but others fought back against the U.S. government. One such fight was near the Red River in the Texas Panhandle in 1874. It led to two years of battles. Eventually the American Indians were defeated and forced to return to their reservations. They never returned to their lifestyle on the Texas frontier.

title: Supply and Demand
text:
There is a free enterprise system in Texas. This is an economic system in which individuals make their own decisions about the goods they will buy and the price at which they can sell them. This gives Texans the power to decide how they can run their businesses.

The system is also based on the concept of supply and demand. Supply is the amount of something that is available. Demand is the amount of something people actually want or need. The price of goods and services depends upon how much the supply and demand are.

Throughout Texas history, supply and demand have played an important role in the success of business and have helped keep the Texas economy healthy. For example, the supply of oil in Texas matched the demand for oil by railroads and other industries.

title: Six Flags Over Texas—More Than an Amusement Park
text:
Texas is the only state to have flown its own flag as an independent republic. However, there are five other flags that have flown over the state through the years.

Spain - 1500s: Explorers claimed Texas land to find gold and introduce Christianity to American Indians living there.

France - 1685: Robert de LaSalle established Fort St. Louis near Matagorda Bay for France. The colony failed, as did LaSalle's adventure in Texas.

Mexico - 1800s: After gaining control of Texas from Spain, Mexico tried to hold onto Texas as Spain had done. They did this by giving out grants of land to white settlers. One large grant was given to Stephen F. Austin.

Republic of Texas - 1836-1845: Texans battled Mexico for control of their own republic.

Confederate States of America - 1861-1865: Texas seceded from the U.S. during the Civil War.

United States of America - 1845-1861 and 1865 to Present: Today, Texans are also proud Americans.

title: Texas: A Multi-cultural Mosaic
text:
Texas is home to people of many cultures. The customs of various cultures make Texas a special state indeed.

Most African Americans in Texas trace their roots back to slavery. Texans celebrate Juneteenth every year to remember African Americans' freedom from slavery. About 36 percent of Texans have a Hispanic ethnic background. They share a strong sense of family and religion. Many celebrate Cinco de Mayo each year as a way to stay connected to their heritage. Texans of German descent came from many different backgrounds, but stay connected today through their food, dances and celebrations. Each fall, Oktoberfest draws people from all over Texas.

Texans from many different cultures come together at many times during the year at other special events, such as different new-year, holiday or religious celebrations. These types of celebrations allow people of all backgrounds to share their heritage with one another.

title: Railroad Era Causes and Effects
text:
Historians understand it is important to know why, or what caused, an event in history to happen. Sometimes it might be important to know what happened as the result of the event. This would be an effect. The words “because,” “so” and “then” can often help you better understand a cause-effect relationship.

Use information in this review issue to complete the cause-and-effect chart. Remember to look for words that signal a cause-effect relationship.

text: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is located in Texas. For decades, the U.S. has led the world in space exploration, but it is no longer planning manned voyages to outer space. Write a letter to your congressman or congresswoman to convince officials that space exploration is still important. title: Think & Review
text:
1. How was life on the Texas range changed forever by Glidden’s invention of barbed wire?

2. Why do you think Higgins and Lucas wanted to drill for oil at Spindletop? Do you think their only goals were to make money and be successful?

3. Why did the Great Depression change life for so many Texans?

title: How Communication Influenced Texas Economic Growth
text:
There was a time when it would take weeks or even months to deliver a message. In the early 1800s, this was the case. When communication is slow, business is slow. The economy slows down, too. When orders only come as fast as the mail can send them, jobs, products, and money end up paused. Then came the telegraph.

The telegraph was invented by Samuel F. Morse. It was a device that transmitted signals over a wire across long distances. By using the telegraph, information could be sent and received the very same day. In 1854, the first telegraph company came to the state of Texas and was held in Marshall, Texas. By 1870, Western Union dominated the telegraphing industry and there were 1,500 miles of telegraph wire throughout the state of Texas. This helped to get business booming. Businesses were now able to easily manage other branches around the country due to the ease of communication. This created more jobs and helped the economy flourish.

The economy also benefited from the relationship between telegraph and railroads. Without the telegraph, the railroads could not run on time, due to a lack of time consistency across the country. By transmitting the correct time over the wire, the nation became in sync.

By the 1900s, the telegraph began to decline. This was because of the new “talking telegraph.” Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone. It was easier and faster to use than the telegraph. Information could now move across long distances and be heard within minutes.

Then in the 1990s, the internet changed the rules about communication. As time has gone on, the internet has gotten faster and easier than ever before. Nearly every part of life can be found and completed on the internet. This includes checking emails and researching, to daily banking and grocery shopping. This made communication worldwide. Now the world has become a whole lot smaller for individuals and businesses alike.

title: Why We Have Pineapples When We Don't Live in Hawaii
text:
Think about all the things you like to eat. Do you know where your food came from before it was in the store or the cafeteria? Maybe you ate an apple today. Are there enough apple trees in your town to grow apples for everybody? Maybe you like cookies; but where did the sugar to make your cookies come from? Where does the corn to make your cereal come from? What about the chocolate to make your candy?

Different crops need different kinds of weather or soil to grow well. No town or state can grow all the kinds of foods we like to eat, so states and countries trade food crops and other goods with each other. This lets us buy the things we need or want when we can’t make everything ourselves.

When one state or country can grow more of something than they need, they can trade with people somewhere else who need that food. For example, farmers in Hawaii can grow more pineapples in their warm, wet climate than they need for themselves. They can sell their extra pineapples to people in Washington, who can’t grow pineapples because it is too cold. But the farmers in Washington can grow lots of red apples or other foods that people in Hawaii want to buy. In the same way, people in Maine can sell their extra fish to people in Kansas, who don’t have oceans with fish but do have lots of corn to trade. The people in Florida can sell oranges to the people in South Dakota, who have lots of wheat to trade.

When people sell their extra products to people in other places, they export those products to the other place. When people buy products from somewhere else and bring those products home, they import those products. So we say that Hawaii exports pineapples and that Washington imports those same pineapples. Maine exports seafood and imports corn. Florida exports oranges and imports wheat.

What is true of states is also true of countries. The United States does not grow cinnamon, so we import cinnamon from countries like Sri Lanka and Indonesia, where they can grow the kind of trees that cinnamon comes from. The United States grows more soybeans than we eat, but China and Mexico need more soybeans than they can grow. Therefore, the United States exports soybeans to China and Mexico.

States and countries import and export many things besides food, too. If you look at the labels in your clothing, you will probably find that your clothes were imported from another country, like India or Bangladesh. Your electronics, like your television, your computer, and your telephone, might have been exported from Japan or Korea and imported into the United States. For example, the plastic parts of your television might have been made from oil that came from Texas. Those plastic parts may have been transported by ships built in China or on train cars built from American steel. The parts may be packed in cardboard boxes made in Germany.

All states, all nations, and all people are interdependent in trade. That means we rely on each other for the goods we want and need. If Mexico did not buy American soybeans, then American soybean farmers would have less money to buy avocados from Mexico. If Japan did not export trucks to the United States, then it might be hard for American farmers to deliver soybeans to Mexico. If Americans did not buy clothing from Bangladesh, then our clothing might be more expensive, and we would have less money to buy other things we need. All countries depend on each other to import what we need and to export what we have to sell.

The next time you eat an apple or put on a shirt or turn on a TV, remember: You are part of an interdependent world, where imports and exports bring you the best the world has to offer.

title: From Lamp Fuel to Lipstick: How the World’s Demand for Oil Has Changed Over Time
text:
Nobody knows who first discovered oil. The Chinese may have known about oil thousands of years ago. Persians knew how to make kerosene from oil over 1,000 years ago. In Texas, American Indians found oil seeping up through the ground. There was very little use for oil until drilling in Pennsylvania in 1859 made oil easier to get.

With so much oil suddenly available, people quickly learned more ways to use it. Kerosene quickly replaced all the old-fashioned fuels for lamps and heaters. People also learned how to use oil to lubricate machinery.

By the end of the 19th century, inventors learned that gasoline made from oil was a good fuel for engines. Using oil to power machines was easier than having animals pull loads. Inventors also learned how to build machines that turned the power of oil into electricity. This happened just as the invention of the light bulb created a demand for electricity.

Soon after 1900, lots of oil was being discovered in Texas. As the oil supply increased, gasoline became cheaper. Cars became more common. Oil used to power ships, trucks, and airplanes helped the United States and its allies win World War I in 1918. With each invention, the world’s demand for oil increased.

In the 1920s, inventors learned how to capture the natural gas that was found along with oil. They could burn natural gas to heat homes. They could use natural gas to power new appliances like refrigerators. Again, the world’s demand for oil and natural gas increased.

Later in the 20th century, inventors learned even more ways to use oil. Oil can be made into jet fuel for modern airplanes. It can be made into plastic of all kinds. It is used for dyes to color everything from clothing to false teeth. It is used to make chewing gum and golf balls and contact lenses. It is used in lipstick and perfume.

As scientists and inventors discover new uses for oil, the world’s need grows larger and larger.

title: From Antique Oil Derricks to Modern Oil Pumps
text:
American Indians in Texas knew about oil hundreds of years ago. Oil seeped from underground pools to the surface of the earth. American Indians taught European sailors about the thick, tarry substance. In 1543, some stranded European sailors used that sticky black oil to plug up the leaks in their boats so they could sail back to Europe.

In 1866, Texans drilled into the ground to find oil for the first time. Lyne T. Barret struck oil near Nacogdoches, Texas. Barret's oil well produced about 10 barrels of oil a day.

Early drilling equipment was primitive. The drills could not go very deep to find big pools of oil. Most of the early Texas oil wells produced very little oil. In those days, the derricks could be made from wood and simple metal parts. The owners of wells stored the oil in barrels. The barrels were transported in wagons pulled by horses.

Things changed in 1901 at Spindletop, Texas. Anthony F. Lucas struck an amazing pool of underground oil. His drill broke through rock into the oil layer. Oil gushed from the drill pipe 150 feet into the air. Many thousands of barrels of oil sprayed out before workers could stop the eruption.

Wells like those at Spindletop needed more complex equipment. Horses and wagons could not transport all the oil produced every day. Oil producers learned how to build pipelines to take the oil to refineries. Refineries turned crude oil into finished products like gasoline, jet fuel, and plastics. Oilmen needed tankers on land and sea to export oil to other places. They needed efficient pumps to pull oil to the surface, day and night. They needed drills to dig into deeper rock looking for oil.

Much of Texas’s crude oil is exported to other places. At the same time, Texas imports materials to help produce oil. Drills are tipped with imported diamonds that stay sharper longer than metal drills can. Sometimes the engines that power modern pumps and the pipes and ships that transport the oil are imported, too.

As the world’s demand for Texas oil increased, Texas exported more oil. At the same time, Texas’s need to import materials to support the oil industry also increased. This shows the interdependence of the world. Imports and exports contribute to the production of goods for everyone.

title: How it All Began in the “New World”
text:
In 1492, an Italian sailor named Christopher Columbus sailed three ships from Spain across the Atlantic Ocean. Spain's King Ferdinand II and Queen Isabella I supported Columbus, who hoped to find a faster trade route between Europe and Asia. Though he never reached Asia, Columbus did sail straight into land that became known as the "New World," at least to the Europeans. It wasn't new to the people who already lived there, of course!

Seven months after Columbus first set sail from Spain, he returned triumphantly to report to the king and queen. He brought back both gold and people his crew captured. The king and queen were very pleased to hear of Columbus' adventures and discoveries. Secretly the two had believed there was little chance the Italian explorer would ever return. Now they hoped to use the information Columbus brought back to make Spain richer and more powerful. Spanish leaders planned further explorations of the New World (the Western hemisphere, including North and South America). They sent Columbus and other explorers (people who travel to gain geographical or scientific information) back across the ocean. The explorers' goals were not only to explore the new lands, but also to set up settlements in the name of Spain and convert the native people to Christianity.

The explorers made their way across the ocean. They found gold and excellent land to settle. Soon, talk of the New World reached other European powers. France and England sent adventurers to explore North America in search of riches. Explorers claimed land for the royalty of their countries. These countries became richer and more powerful with each piece of land the explorers claimed, and they established colonies in the New World. Colonies are areas ruled by another country and not by its own people. European explorers also conquered (took over) the native people of the New World and introduced Christianity to them.

Columbus' explorations marked a turning point in history. People from very different parts of the world began to communicate and trade with each other. Many European countries became rich and powerful after taking over the land and people of North America. The kings and queens of Europe invested great amounts of money in and gathered adventurers to further explore and conquer the New World. The Age of Discovery had begun!

title: Differing Opinions About Christopher Columbus
text:
For more than two hundred years, people in the United States have honored Christopher Columbus in October. In 1937, lawmakers named Columbus Day a federal holiday.

Columbus thought he had landed in the East Indies, but he was wrong. He actually landed on San Salvador Island, part of the Bahamas. Later he explored Cuba and the area we now call Haiti. Historians say that Columbus did not treat the American Indians very well. Historians also say that he and other Europeans brought new diseases that the American Indians had no immunity against.

Some people believe Columbus is a real hero. After all, he sailed back and forth across the ocean four times and helped open up trade routes. But not everyone believes that Columbus is a hero to celebrate because of his actions against the American Indians. Either way, the history is there and cannot be changed.

title: The Age of Discovery
text:
The success of Columbus’ first voyage quickly caught the attention of other explorers. Soon, more Europeans engaged in far-reaching exploration. As they traveled the world, they often conquered the native people they met on their journeys. The explorers mapped the lands and established new trade routes. They traded gold, silver and spices. Most importantly, these early explorers led the way for several European countries to colonize, or settle, the New World. These colonies were the groups of people who settled far from home, but they maintained ties (close bonds) with their home countries.

England vs. France vs. Spain

When the Age of Discovery began, the great powers of Europe included England, Spain and France. All three realized that to be the richest, most powerful nation in the world they would have to explore and conquer as much of the New World as possible.

England’s Chance

England’s King Henry VII gave Italian-born explorer Giovanni Caboto, later called John Cabot, permission to explore unknown land for England in 1497. Cabot sailed north of Columbus’ route across the Atlantic Ocean. He claimed land in present day Canada and explored the United States. However, Cabot believed he was in Asia. His ship sank before he could return home and Cabot never knew what he had really discovered.

Spain Sends More Explorers

Spain also wanted to be the great power in the world. The leaders realized they needed to continue to explore and conquer. People heard tales of New World cities made entirely of gold. Spaniard Hernán Cortés was determined to find gold and silver in the New World. He sailed to present-day Mexico and conquered the Aztec people who lived there in 1521.

There were also stories of magical fountains with water that could turn old people young again. At about the same time Cortés was conquering the Aztec, another Spanish explorer, Juan Ponce de León, set off from Puerto Rico. Some people believe he hoped to find the magic water, the “fountain of youth.” He landed in present day Florida. Of course there was no fountain of youth to be found, but de León claimed the land of Florida for Spain.

France Takes a Turn

By 1521, Spain found a new route to Asia by sailing around the tip of South America. By that time, many knew that North America lay between Asia and Europe. King Francis I of France believed, though, that Asia was still very close to North America’s west coast. He wanted to find a shortcut — a water passage across North America. In 1534, King Francis sent sailor Jacques Cartier to find the shortcut, but there was no such water passage for anyone to find. Cartier instead discovered Newfoundland in Canada. He also claimed land for France around a river he named Saint Lawrence. However, early French settlements there failed. It would be nearly six decades before France would have a permanent settlement in North America.

The Oldest Permanent Settlement in the United States

When Ponce de León landed on the coast of Florida in 1513, its beauty overwhelmed him. There were palm trees, beautiful flowers and exotic birds. The day he landed was the Spanish Feast of Flowers, or Pascua Florida, so Ponce de León named the new land Florida. Both Spain and France made several early attempts to colonize Florida, but these attempts were unsuccessful.

In 1564, word reached Spanish leaders that the French were once again exploring and colonizing the western coastal land. This news angered the Spanish leaders. They wanted a plan to keep France from claiming any more land and riches. They decided to send Pedro Menéndez de Avilés to Florida to establish a base from which to attack the French.

On September 8, 1565, de Avilés and his men organized their territory. He named the new colony St. Augustine. De Avilés and his group had two goals. They were to continue to explore and claim land for their country because Spain wanted to continue to find gold and other riches. The men were there also to protect the land from other countries, especially France, and defend the trade route. They had orders to destroy Fort Caroline, which the French controlled. In addition, the Spanish government wanted control of the American Indians in the area. Within a year, de Avilés and his men had forced the French out of the area. They had also taken over the council house of the Timucua tribe and started using it as a fort.

This makes St. Augustine, Florida, the oldest permanently settled city in the United States. This historic city is a reminder of the importance of European colonization in the New World.

title: Mapping the Age of Discovery
text:
Before Columbus went on his first voyage across the Atlantic Ocean, no one knew much about the world. Mapmakers did not know about the landmasses between Europe and Asia. The explorations that began the Age of Discovery changed world maps for good. European mapmakers got new information about the world from explorers and sailors, and they were able to fill in the blank spaces on their maps.

Maps are plane, or flat, representations of the shapes of landmasses and bodies of water. Today's many different types of maps include features to help people use them. A grid system with lines of longitude and latitude makes locating specific information on a map easier. Each map also has a scale to show distances and a compass rose to show direction.

Even today, maps constantly change. Almost every year cartographers, or mapmakers, change information on world maps because of new information they discover.

title: Worth Their Weight in Gold
text:
Why did early explorers want to find a quicker trade route to Asia? One reason was to bring spices to consumers more quickly. Europeans could not grow most spices in their own countries. Spices we use often like salt, pepper, cinnamon, cloves and ginger were hard to find and very valuable back then. So, why were these spices so important?

Well, in Columbus' time there were no refrigerators. Food often spoiled before people could eat it. Spices came to the rescue! Spices like salt helped dry and preserve meats. Other spices hid the flavor of not so fresh food. People also used spices to make medicines, perfume and incense, which produces a fragrant odor when burned.

Valuable spices were the same as money in some places. People often paid for housing or animals with spices. During the Middle Ages, some said a sack of pepper was worth a man's life. And that's nothing to sneeze at!

title: Clarity of Expression: Henry Hudson
text:
Henry Hudson was an English sea captain and explorer who started off as a failure. He sailed on two voyages for England to find a northeast water route to the rich spice trade in Asia. But both times the icy northern seas blocked his way. He had to return home defeated.

Sounds like the end of his career, right? It wasn't. Hudson next convinced the Dutch East India Company to hire him for exactly the same expedition. In 1609, Hudson and his crew sailed west across the Atlantic. He reached the New World, landing on the island we know today as Manhattan. He sailed inland up a wide river and explored the surrounding valley.

It wasn't a passage to Asia. But Hudson's explorations allowed the Dutch to claim the land and build a fur trading post there in 1614, before the Pilgrims arrived. A Dutch settlement called New Netherland soon followed.

Unfortunately, Hudson's last voyage ended in mutiny. He refused his crew's demands to return home, so the sailors took over the ship, setting Hudson adrift in a small boat. His fate is unknown, but his legacy is Hudson Bay, Hudson River, Hudson Valley and the Dutch settlement that became New York City.

Henry Hudson must have had excellent clarity of expression. He had to be able to explain clearly to the Dutch that his experience and determination made him the best man for the job, even though he was an Englishman and not a Dutchman.

Think about a time that you wanted to convince your parents or teachers to let you try something new. Did you beg and plead? Or did you give them a clear explanation of your reasons? Which way do you think works better?

title: Explorers of the New World
text: Directions: Use the graphic organizer below to organize and compare information about explorers of the New World. Use what you read in USA Studies Weekly to help you complete the graphic organizer. You can write additional notes on a separate piece of paper if you need more room.

title: Tools of Geography
text:
Maps and globes are used to find places, measure distances, and get important information. When you are finished reading, you will be ready to make your own map!

Globes and Maps

You have seen both round globes and flat maps of the world. What is the difference between the two? Both a round globe and a flat map show the same cities, countries, oceans, and landforms, but they are useful to us in different ways.

A globe is a round model of the world. A globe shows Earth just as it is in real life, only smaller. You can see how the Earth rotates, or turns, using a globe. It also shows where each country is in relation to other countries and to the poles of the Earth.

A flat map shows the same information as a globe. However, it allows us to see the entire world all at once. You can only see one side of a globe at a time. When the globe is flattened out into a map, you can see everything all at one time. One type of flat map that is commonly used is called the Mercator map. It is based on a cylindrical projection. This means the map-makers took our round Earth and reshaped it into a cylinder so that all of the lines of latitude and longitude are perfectly parallel with and perpendicular to one another. Flattening the globe this way causes changes to the size and shape of Earth's features. However, flat maps like these are helpful for sailors as navigation charts.

Parts of a Map

Maps include more than just countries, cities, oceans, and landforms. Maps also include many special tools that help you find what you are looking for. Many maps have a title at the top to tell you what information you can find on them. The title of a map can tell you what location the map shows.

Compass Rose

All maps have a compass rose. This is a small drawing showing the directions on the map. The compass rose always shows the cardinal directions. These directions are north, south, east, and west. North is always at the top of the compass rose, east is on the right, south is at the bottom, and west is on the left.

The compass rose can also show the intermediate directions. Intermediate directions are the directions directly between the cardinal directions. The intermediate directions are northeast, southeast, northwest, and southwest. By looking at the compass rose, you can find out exactly where each item on a map is located.

Legend

The legend lists all of the symbols on a map. These symbols stand for things such as streets, rivers, monuments, parks, capital cities, and more. The legend helps you know what each symbol on the map means.

Scale

Another tool used on a map is a scale. A map's scale shows the distances represented on the map. One inch on the map will be equal to an actual distance in miles. For example, an inch on the map may be equal to 100 real miles.

Grid System

Some maps use a grid system. This is a system of numbered and lettered lines. This grid format helps you find places more easily. On a map that uses a grid system, there will be letters, such as A, B, C, etc., running across the top of the map. The numbers, such as 1, 2, 3, etc,. are running down the side of the map. If you know that a certain city is located at point 2A on the map, you can find it easily using the grid system of the map.

title: Places of Community and Worship
text:
As people moved to the United States, they brought their religion with them and formed communities where they could socialize and worship. Religions of all kinds have shaped our country as we know it. Weekends, holidays, and meditation all come from religion. One of the most visible signs of a religious community is their buildings. You might find many religious buildings in your own community.

Cathedrals and Churches

The St. Louis Cathedral, the oldest Catholic church in the U.S., stands in New Orleans. Louisiana has a large Catholic community because of its French heritage. People visit cathedrals to attend Mass, often on Sundays but also on holidays like Christmas and Easter. Christians attend church to study the Bible or participate in services like baptism or communion to become closer to God. People might also get married in a Christian church. Another famous Christian church is Trinity Church, located in New York City. Trinity Church is part of the Episcopal Church, which formed after the Revolutionary War. Many important people from our country’s early days are buried there.

Christians in the United States belong to a wide variety of groups with different traditions. Around one in five Christians are Catholic, while almost half of all other Christians belong to a Protestant group. The largest Christian church that started in the United States is the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Many of these groups have developed their own cultures, such as African American churches. Some of their traditions were influenced by African culture. One example of this is gospel music. This music influenced jazz, soul, and rock and roll.

Although they came to the U.S. looking for religious freedom, early Christians were not always tolerant, or accepting, of other religious groups, including other Christians. But as the country grew, many developed a vision of religious freedom for others. As different Christian groups learned to accept each other, they also began making room for people with other beliefs.

Synagogues/Temples

Mikveh Israel, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, is one of the oldest synagogues in America. A synagogue, or temple, is where Jews gather to pray, study, and worship. Jews in Philadelphia might go to Mikveh Israel to read the Torah and Talmud. They also might go to celebrate a bar or bat mitzvah, when a Jewish boy or girl enters adulthood. These ceremonies are often followed by celebrations.

From as early as 1584, there have been Jews in America. Like other colonists in those times, they farmed and started businesses. However, many colonists discriminated against them because they were not Christians. Some colonies practiced more tolerance. Especially in cities like Charleston, South Carolina, and New York City, people welcomed their Jewish neighbors.

Jews fought in the Revolutionary War. One Jewish man, Haym Salomon, was part of the Sons of Liberty, a secret organization dedicated to revolution. He raised funds and loaned money to finance the colonists’ struggle for independence. He was arrested twice by the British. The second time, he was sentenced to death. Luckily he escaped! When he died, many years after the war, he was buried in the cemetery next to the Mikveh Israel synagogue in Philadelphia.

Throughout the history of the United States, Jews have fought in wars, held major political positions, and supported their communities. Many started important businesses. Levi Strauss was a Jew who founded the first company to make blue jeans! Others fought for important causes, such as civil rights and women’s rights. Unfortunately, Jews are still sometimes discriminated against today. People even vandalize their synagogues.

Mosques

The largest mosque in America is the Islamic Center of America, in Dearborn, Michigan. A mosque is a place where Muslims gather to pray and hold religious ceremonies. Sometimes weddings and funerals are held there. Muslims might also go there to observe religious holidays, such as Ramadan, a holy month of fasting. After Ramadan is Eid al-Fitr, a festival to celebrate the end of the fast. The Islamic Center of America has symmetrical architecture. It’s easy to recognize because of its pointed arches and golden domes.

Muslims have been in America for hundreds of years. Many of the Africans who were enslaved and brought to America were believers in Islam. They tried to practice their religion even when the people who had enslaved them made them work in harsh, inhumane conditions. Often, they were forced to practice Christianity instead.

Records show that Muslims fought in the Revolutionary War. In 1777, the Muslim sultan of Morocco, Mohammed ben Abdallah, was the first ruler to recognize the United States as an independent country. He and George Washington wrote letters to each other.

The Muslim population increased in the late 1800s, when many Muslims from countries like Turkey and Yemen immigrated to the United States. They moved mostly to places like Michigan, in the Midwest.

Hindu Temples, Buddhist Temples, and Gurdwaras

Hindu and Buddhist places of worship are called temples. The first traditional Hindu temple in the U.S. was built in 1957. It is called the Shiva Murugan Temple. Hindu temples serve as links between humans and the gods. Temples can be places of celebration and art for the local community. They can also be used to hold a wedding or a funeral or to celebrate the birth of a baby. The first Buddhist temple was built in 1853 in San Francisco by Chinese immigrants. Buddhist temples use the surrounding environment as well as the building to create a feeling of peace. Sikhs worship in gurdwaras by singing and reciting scripture or by sharing a community meal. Sharing food like this is called “langar” and is a way to demonstrate equality for all.

Many Hindus, Buddhists, and Sikhs have been in the United States much longer than they have had places to worship. Anandibai Joshi was one of the first Hindus to arrive in the United States. She was also the first South Asian woman to get a medical degree in our country, graduating in 1886. Chinese and Japanese immigrants brought Buddhism with them as early as 1820. Sikhs, from places like India and Pakistan, often entered the U.S. through California. In 1912, they built the Gurdwara Sahib Stockton there.

The early days of their migration were hard for many of these worshippers. Asian immigrants in the early 20th century were not considered equal to other Americans. Despite attempts to prevent Asian immigration, Hindus, Buddhists, and Sikhs stayed and worked until 1965. At that point, the Immigration and Nationality Services Act of 1965 gave them the right to become citizens of the United States.

Community Centers

People who don’t practice any religion also come together to find a community. In the U.S., these relationships may be formed through community centers. Established as a way for different groups to learn from one another, community centers first appeared in 1907 in New York. People use community centers for arts, sports, and classes outside of school. Some community centers are even available online. Centers like these can help people become better citizens.

title: Help Wanted: Historical Investigator to Solve Mystery of Roanoke's Lost Colony
text:
Are you looking for an opportunity to learn more about one of the most mysterious events in American history? Are you willing to research historical events and study primary and secondary sources? Can you make inferences (conclusions based on what you know) about causes and effects of historical importance? Well, this job just might be for you!

Job Description:

As a historical investigator you will dig deeper into the case of the lost colony of Roanoke, North Carolina. The year was 1584. As Spain explored the New World, many people saw it as the world's richest and most powerful nation. Spanish ships sailed back and forth between the New World and Europe with shiploads of gold and other treasures.

Sir Walter Raleigh was a British poet, soldier and explorer. He believed that establishing colonies in North America would make England just as wealthy and powerful as Spain. He sent two ships to explore the coast of the continent. The ships landed on an island near present-day North Carolina. The men named the island Roanoke after the native Roanoke Indians who lived there. Word quickly returned to Raleigh of the land's excellent fruits, vegetables, fish and other animals. The men also spoke highly of the friendly Roanoke people. Raleigh believed it would be smart to establish an English colony.

Unfortunately, the first attempt to settle the island just didn't work. English settlers didn't know how to grow food. They also began fighting with the once-friendly Roanoke. Soon the settlers gave up and returned to Europe.

Two years later, Raleigh tried again to establish, or set up, a colony. Although the settlers knew their work would be difficult, 117 people decided to give the colony another chance. Once again the Roanoke did not get along with the Anglo (white, English-speaking) settlers. Captain John White decided to go back to England for more supplies. Sadly, because of England's war with Spain, Capt. White could not return to Roanoke for three years!

When Capt. White finally returned to Roanoke, there was no sign of the settlers. It was as if they had just disappeared! He found a clue - the word "CROATOAN" carved on a tree. Had the colony moved to the island of Croatoan? To this day no one has figured out exactly what happened to the colony of Roanoke.

Job Duties:

In this job you will further research Roanoke's Lost Colony. You will make inferences about what might have happened to the colonists. Did the Roanoke Indians kill them? Could disease have wiped out the colony completely? What was the meaning of "CROATOAN"? Perhaps a skilled detective like you can find the answers to this historical mystery. The case is yours!

title: Philanthropy and Values
text:
Maybe you have heard the word “philanthropy” before. What does it mean? It describes actions that people make for the good of other people. What is a value? It’s a way of behaving that people believe is good- like believing it’s good to be honest. Is honesty one of your values?

One way you can practice philanthropy today is to help yourself and others learn good values. How do you learn good values? You can learn them from your parents and grandparents, your teachers at school or church and other people you trust.

You can also learn them from people that have been recognized for doing good things for society. An easy way to learn about people that have done good things is to visit values.com. Values.com has lots of stories and short videos that highlight the traits that make each of us better people. They even have billboards on the highway to remind you about good values.

For example, you may have seen a billboard that looks like the one shown here.

This billboard is about Oral Lee Brown, who saved money from her job to send 19 kids to college … all by herself! Wow! Isn’t that cool? You can learn about lots of other people who practice philanthropy at values.com. Be sure to look for more of their “billboards” on Page 4 of Studies Weekly this year. We think they’re so cool we want to remind you to check them out!

title: Challenges and Successes of Early American Settlements
text:
The Roanoke colony's failure did not cause England to give up hope. Many people were still committed to establishing settlements, or small communities, in North America. In the early 1600s, England was far behind Spain and France in power. The English could not establish colonies just anywhere they wished. Spain already claimed South America, the West Indies, the Southwest region and Florida. France claimed the areas around many important waterways like the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River. Much of the unclaimed land was harsh, rugged and dangerous. The forests were thick, and natives often made it difficult for Anglo settlers to establish colonies. England began to concentrate on settling land along the eastern coast of North America. They had to plan the colonies very carefully.

Colonists Establish Jamestown for Economic Gain

About 20 years after the failure at Roanoke, England's King James I gave permission for a group of men to form a company and establish a settlement in North America. The Virginia Company sent about 100 settlers - all men - to America in April of 1607. The men hoped to get rich by finding gold and other natural treasures. They chose a piece of land near a river and built their settlement. They named the colony Jamestown, in honor of King James. They chose Virginia as the name of the land around the settlement.

Life in the colony was difficult and hazardous. The water in Jamestown was dirty and not good for drinking. The marshland where Jamestown was built was not good for farming. Plants would not grow in the wet soggy soil. Swarms of mosquitoes carried a serious and often deadly disease called malaria. The men focused most of their efforts on getting rich instead of hunting or growing food. Disease and hunger killed most of the colonists, and only 38 men survived eight months after the start of Jamestown.

One man who survived the first year at Jamestown was Captain John Smith. Late in 1607, a group of American Indians captured Smith. They took him to the chief of their tribe, Powhatan. Many say that Powhatan's daughter, Pocahontas, saved Smith's life. Historians disagree about whether this story is accurate, or true, but Powhatan did allow Smith to return to his colony.

Capt. Smith continued his relationship with Powhatan's tribe. The American Indians taught the colonists about hunting, fishing and planting crops in this unfamiliar land. Smith was a good leader and the settlers soon elected him president of the colony. Smith made sure everyone worked hard to keep the colony from failing. Only 18 died in the second winter.

During 1608 and 1609, more settlers, including some women, arrived. Smith was burned badly in a gunpowder explosion and had to return to England. Soon the colonists were struggling to stay alive again. To keep from starving during the winter of 1609-10, many ate their own horses and dogs! Only 60 people were left at the end of that winter.

The colonists never became rich by finding gold or silver. However, they did find another way to get rich with a plant called tobacco. An Englishman named John Rolfe married Pocahontas and began planting tobacco, which grew very well in Jamestown's soil and climate. This became the real "gold" of Jamestown. People in England bought as much of the crop as possible. Jamestown now had something to trade for food and supplies.

Jamestown began to grow quickly, as each man had land to farm. Two hundred more women came from England to marry the men and start families. In 1619, the colonists elected men to make laws for the colony. They called this group The House of Burgesses, which was made up of mostly wealthy men. It wasn't the best type of government for the colonists, but the people now had some say in how their colony operated. They did not have this privilege (freedom) when they lived in England.

Unfortunately, the colony's successes did not continue. Colonists began to fight with Powhatan's tribe, and the price of tobacco dropped. Government leaders were not always honest, and many people died of disease. In 1624, King James took back the land and made Virginia a royal colony, which meant that King James owned Virginia.

Colonists Settle Plymouth for Religious Freedom

People looking for religious freedom started a third settlement in North America. Back in England, King James had ruled that all people must belong to the Church of England. A group called Separatists wanted to worship in their own way and refused to join. Many decided to move to the Netherlands.

In 1620, the Separatists (now known as Pilgrims) sailed to North America on a ship named the Mayflower. The Mayflower carried Pilgrims from both England and the Netherlands. The ship landed at Plymouth Bay in what is now Massachusetts. They lived on the ship for the first few months. The Pilgrim leaders came up with a government plan that would help all people live together in a peaceful way. All the men signed the agreement, which we know as the Mayflower Compact. Then they elected John Carver as governor. Many people think of the Mayflower Compact as America's first example of true self government.

Like the Jamestown settlers, the Plymouth colonists had difficult times at first. The winter was very cold. Food ran out quickly. Half the settlers died the first winter. Luckily for the surviving colonists, there were English-speaking American Indians from the Wampanoag tribe nearby. One American Indian named Squanto helped teach the Pilgrims to plant corn, catch fish and gather maple syrup. Squanto also helped arrange a peace treaty between Chief Massasoit and the Pilgrims. The Wampanoag and the Pilgrims promised to help, not attack, each other.

Plymouth colonists elected William Bradford governor in 1621. Under his leadership Plymouth grew and became successful. People from England learned of the chance for freedom in the New World, and over time many more people came to settle the region we now call New England.

title: The First Thanksgiving: An American Celebration and Custom
text:
What do you do the fourth Thursday of November each year? Many in America celebrate the day as Thanksgiving. This holiday has its roots in the celebration feast the Pilgrims shared with the Wampanoag.

The Pilgrims had left England and established the colony at Plymouth in order to have religious freedom, but they had barely survived the first winter. Their friendship with Squanto and the Wampanoag tribe was very important. The Wampanoag taught the Pilgrims how to plant corn and use fish as fertilizer for the plants. The Wampanoag also showed Pilgrims how to grow other crops along with the corn. With this knowledge the Pilgrims had a plentiful (overflowing) harvest, or collection of crops, during the fall of 1621. They wanted to celebrate because they had many things to be thankful for! They had warm homes to live in, food to eat and a peaceful relationship with their American Indian neighbors.

Plymouth Governor William Bradford declared a day of thanksgiving, and colonists wanted to share the day with their Wampanoag friends. Chief Massasoit and 90 Wampanoag came with deer to cook and share. The Pilgrims shared goose, turkey, lobster and corn. The celebration lasted three days, and the people ate food and played games.

The tradition of Thanksgiving Day continued each year at Plymouth. During some years the Pilgrims did not have as much food to share, but they still gave thanks for what they had. They might have spent the day praying for better times. Today, the celebration continues in the United States. Americans across the country enjoy the day feasting on food, spending time with family and friends and being thankful for all they have!

title: How did some American Indians already know how to speak English when the Pilgrims arrived?
text: The Pilgrims owed their survival to the help of the Wampanoag people, especially a man named Squanto. An Abenaki man named Samoset introduced Squanto to the Pilgrims. Squanto had learned to speak English from being a captive of European sailors and merchants. Samoset and Squanto communicated with the Pilgrims. The Pilgrims listened and learned of their new home from these men.

title: Slavery Begins
text:
By late summer of 1619, the Jamestown colony had done quite well selling tobacco to merchants in England. It was during this summer that a ship from Holland sailed into the port at Jamestown. Aboard the ship were 20 African men. The captain of a Spanish ship traded the 20 Africans to the Dutch ship, in exchange for food.

Early records from Jamestown list these 20 Africans as indentured servants. An indentured servant is someone who agrees to work for another person for a specific time period in exchange for payment of the fee for passage on a ship. People forced these Africans to work for them in Jamestown. Historians believe they helped the colony harvest tobacco.

History does not list these Africans as enslaved people (people forced to work for another person and considered property). However, this event is probably the beginning of the practice of using enslaved people to operate large farms, known as plantations, in the southern United States.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend it is 1620. Your family wants to leave England and move to North America. You go ahead to investigate both Jamestown and Plymouth to decide which would best suit your family’s needs.
