title: Early Settlements in the Americas
text:
Long before the Pilgrims and explorers came to the American continents, there were people already inhabiting nearly every region of this land.

Arctic

The Arctic and subarctic regions today are known for their extreme climates. The land this far north remains frozen most of the year. The native people who lived in these regions became hunters and gatherers. This means they did not farm for food that they needed to survive. Instead, they hunted or foraged for it nearly every day.

In the Arctic, food was not available in large amounts. That limited the formation of large community groups. This meant that Arctic native groups ended up living in small, nomadic bands. They traveled for food. They would follow the migration patterns of caribou and other game animals. They also used caribou pelts for their clothes to keep warm in the cold climate.

The Inuit, Yuit and Aleut are a few of the Alaska native groups who called the Arctic and subarctic regions home. Many of these groups still inhabit these regions today.

Northeast

The Northeastern region stretches from around the Great Lakes into the state of Maine. Archaeological evidence in this area suggests that before European settlers arrived, there were semi-permanent, or seasonal, settlements of nomadic hunting groups.

European settlers and fur traders started to arrive. Then, these areas became more permanent locations of settlement for both American Indians and European settlers. These two cultures began to work together for economic gain. American Indians in this area were able to farm. They also helped early Europeans to survive by teaching them how to grow corn and other crops.

Southeast

The land found west of the Atlantic Ocean, east of Louisiana, and south of Tennessee is considered the Southeastern region. Some of the first humans began to inhabit the region a little more than 10,000 years ago. They are now commonly referred to as Paleo-Indians.

The Mound Builders also built a successful civilization in the Southeastern region. They are sometimes known as the Mississippi Indians because they built thousands of mounds in the Mississippi Delta area. The Mound Builders didn’t just build mounds. They built a successful culture lasting 700 years. They planted corn, beans, squash, sunflower seeds, and tobacco. They also gathered berries and nuts for food. They farmed, hunted, and fished. They also killed bear for their fat. Rabbits, snakes, and mice were part of their diet too. No other group had ever combined these foods into their diet before. This healthy diet made them less likely to get sick. Their population grew and they had to build more cities. Many of the cities were large urban areas where lots of people lived. Special buildings were built on four mounds around a center plaza. People went to the plaza for special events and ceremonies.

Plains

The Plains area is between the Mississippi River and the Rocky Mountains. The ancestors of the Hidatsa, Cheyenne, Arapaho, and Comanche all inhabited this area. They lived there long before the descendants of the first European settlers began living there.

There were also groups of American Indians in this region who moved around following the migration pattern of bison and other game animals. Other groups also developed permanent settlements on the arable land, or land good for growing.

Northwest and Southwest

The Northwest area has a mild climate with lots of precipitation. There is access to plentiful natural resources. This allowed for early complex cultural developments in the area. Fish was an important food source for most of the native tribes in this region. Salmon fishing and whaling were their main sources of food. These groups also became very good at making canoes and boats from the abundant trees that grow in this region.

The established native cultures in this area were nearly wiped out in the early 1700s. European explorers and settlers brought new diseases with them. Much of the native population did not have any immunity to the diseases.

Many different American Indian cultures lived throughout the west in nomadic bands. They roamed through what are now known as the states of California, Nevada, Utah, Colorado, Wyoming, and parts of Arizona and New Mexico.

The Southwest is arid (dry) and warm. You might think that a dry, desert climate wouldn’t be a great place to settle. You may be surprised to learn that American Indians in the Southwest built some of the largest and most impressive cities of the early American Indian groups. The Spanish explorers called these living quarters “pueblos.” Tribes in this area also built irrigation canals. These canals supplied water to grow corn, beans, and squash.

Permanent villages were the key to a successful culture. Staying put was the way to make your culture grow. More people meant more strength to survive. These people used the nearby natural resources for food, shelter, and clothing. This helped the earliest Americans survive. Many nomadic Indian cultures that lived on the North American continent have descendants that still live today.

title: Olaudah Equiano
text:
How do historians know what it was like to be enslaved? One way is through first-hand accounts. Olaudah Equiano, born in Benin, Africa, published writings that tell the story of his capture, enslavement, and eventual freedom. Read the passage where he tells of his capture when he was eleven years old and home alone with his sister.

“One day, when all our people were gone out to their works as usual, and only I and my dear sister were left to mind the house, two men and a woman got over our walls, and in a moment seized us both; and, without giving us time to cry out, or make resistance, they stopped our mouths, and ran off with us into the nearest wood.”

Equiano and his sister were separated, and he was placed on a ship sailing to Barbados. He traveled through the Middle Passage in miserable conditions on a boat packed with people. In Barbados, many enslaved people from the ship were sold, but Equiano was not. He was then sent to Virginia and was purchased by a sea captain named Michael Henry Pascal. They sailed to England and lived there. Equiano sailed many places with Pascal. Equiano became educated. Eventually, he bought his freedom and began to write about his life.

Olaudah Equiano was an abolitionist, or one who speaks out against slavery. His written stories helped others understand the horrors of slavery. He spoke out against slavery in England, and he helped those who were freed find a place to live. Equiano’s writings and speeches made a difference. Ten years after he died, slavery was outlawed in England. It would take a civil war to finally abolish slavery in the United States.

title: Building a Comfortable Space
text:
As people settle in a land, they often use what is in the natural environment to meet their basic needs. They also adapt natural resources to make the environment suit them. This allows them to build a place that is more comfortable and able to support more people in that one place.

Water

Most early settlements established in the United States by European settlers were developed near large rivers. Rivers provided water for drinking and fish for eating. Rivers also provided a way to travel quickly from one place to another. As people scattered, the demand for water grew beyond the reach of rivers and streams. Settlers built dams, creating reservoirs. Through a system of canals and ditches, farmers could irrigate farms far away from the rivers. There are an estimated 84,000 dams in the United States. Each provides water storage, irrigation, flood control, electricity generation, and other benefits to communities around the country.

Food

Often early European settlers relied on the natural wildlife for food: fish, wild game, and edible plant life native to the area. As they settled, they established farms. People were able to choose what they grew and ate. Sometimes, traditional family farms couldn’t support demands for food. Larger farms developed, growing only a single food. With industrialization of agriculture, farmers became specialized in one crop. They were able to mass produce that food. In the U.S., population centers continued to grow in the east. The expansion westward led to further industrial and agricultural development. Transportation and communication methods improved. Farms in the West were able to support the big cities in the East efficiently. People continued to develop the land in these patterns. Food was grown far away from where most people lived.

Shelter

Just as with water and food, people often start very close to nature when seeking shelter in a new land. Many early European settlers of the U.S. made homes of wattle and daub. This was a method of weaving sticks into a wall and covering it with a mud or clay mixture. As the population grew and settlements became more developed, homes became bigger and used more local wood materials.

Today

During the early days of settlement, newcomers relied heavily on the environment to sustain themselves. Then they worked to shape that environment to suit their interests. In the modern world, people became concerned about how they are shaping the environment. As a result, builders and developers have invested in sustainable building materials. They use things like recycled steel, bamboo, reclaimed and recycled wood, and sheep’s wool. Use of sustainable products let people consider both the environment and their tastes. Similarly, water conservation and protection have become concerns for more people. Our society has begun to recognize the value in shifting the settler-environment balance and renewing resources closer to what the land once was.

title: Settling Pennsylvania: A Peaceful Life in the New World
text:
Imagine a little girl named Mary Alice who was only 11 years old when her family left England to settle in the colony of Pennsylvania. What would life in the New World be like for her family? Maybe something like this fictional diary entry...

November 1681

The snow is falling heavily outside today, but here in our home the fire is warm. It is a perfect day to study God's word and give thanks for our new, peaceful life here in Pennsylvania. It is hard to believe that only a few months ago we were still in England and things were very different for my family.

I remember the day as if it was yesterday. Father had just returned home from a meeting at the Quaker Meeting House. I heard him sharing news with Mother. The talk between the men in the meeting that day had been serious. We Quakers were being mistreated by others in our village. We did not have the same religious beliefs or ceremonies as other churches. Our men will not join the military. Our families dress plainly and we do not believe in paying taxes that will be used for war. These beliefs angered many people in England.

That evening Father said to me, "Thou art to live a peaceable life, Mary. We shall be leaving England for a new home soon. Our friend and fellow Quaker, William Penn, has established a colony in the New World. I spoke with him today. We will move to Pennsylvania. There our family will live safely and in peace. We will be free to worship as we please." Only three weeks later, we sailed across the Atlantic Ocean toward our new home. Many of our Quaker friends sailed with us. Some of the men came alone. Others, like Father, brought their families too. I was scared but excited.

There are many interesting people here in Pennsylvania with us. My friend John is from Ireland. He and his family are also Quakers. Father says we will treat all of our new neighbors with kindness. The American Indians have also become our friends. Father said Mr. Penn made sure to pay them for the land where we now farm the rich soil.

Mother and I are working to make our home tidy and comfortable. Father works long days as he gets ready to plant wheat soon. Each day when I go to the Meeting House, I feel happy to have this new life. I thought I would miss England, but I do not. I feel I am truly home now in Pennsylvania.

title: Where Are Quakers Today?
text:
The Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) began in England several hundred years ago, and there are over 350,000 who live in different parts of the world today. A small slice of the population lives in Europe, with other small slices in Asia and the Western Pacific. But where are the others? Well, a relatively large cluster of Quakers can be found in South America, where 33,000 call Bolivia home. Approximately 87,000 Friends live in the United States. Many of them are in the eastern states, not far from their roots in Pennsylvania, but you can find them in every region of the U.S. You may be surprised to learn that the East African Republic of Kenya has the largest number of Quaker citizens. In 1902, three Friends - Arthur Chilson, Edgar Hole and Willis Hotchkiss - sailed from New York to Kenya on a mission to start meetings there. And today? Thanks to their vision, almost 134,000 live in that Equatorial country!

Look at the pie chart. What percentage of Quakers lives in North America (not including Caribbean countries and Latin America)? ___________

Write that number as a fraction two different ways: ___________ ____________

title: Comparing the New Colonies
text:
The first English colonies in America had both failures and successes. Roanoke disappeared. At Jamestown many things went wrong and many things went right, but it proved that establishing colonies in the New World was possible. Plymouth Colony was a true success story for the people who were determined to find religious freedoms.

Back in England, more and more people wanted a chance at a new life across the Atlantic Ocean. By the middle of the 18th century, there were 13 British colonies along the Atlantic coastline of what would become the United States of America.

There were many similarities and differences in the colonies. Let’s explore three colonial regions. The regions are named for their geographic location. They are the New England Colonies, the Middle Colonies and the Southern Colonies. Read on!

The New England Colonies

The New England colonial region included the Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut and New Hampshire colonies. Most of the people who lived in New England Colonies wanted to create communities where they could practice their own religious beliefs freely.

Some of the colonists in the region, like the Pilgrims of Plymouth, wanted to separate themselves completely from the Church of England. Other people considered themselves Puritans. They wanted to continue some traditions of the English church, but they wanted to have the freedom to change or “purify” others.

It was often difficult to live in the New England Colonies. Winters in the region were cold and snowy. The icy winters, though, discouraged the growth of germs that caused disease. So, many of the New England colonists were healthier than colonists in other regions. Also, in summer there was plenty of rain that helped crops grow well.

The economy in most of the New England Colonies was strong. The Rhode Island soil was very good for farming, and corn, tobacco and beans grew well there. In other parts of the region, the soil was rocky and difficult to farm. In the Massachusetts colony farming was not as successful.

Many colonists in this region made a living by fishing, shipbuilding or raising animals. Because there were many thick forests in the region, people also worked cutting and selling lumber. Colonists earned money by trading goods as well. Ships carried sugar, wool and beef to sell back in England. Some colonists found they could make a good deal of money trading enslaved Africans. Very few New England colonists actually owned enslaved people, though.

The government of each of these colonies was a representative democracy. Men who were church members could vote in colony elections. This was not true in England. Each year, they elected governors and local representatives to help run the colonies. These officials put strict laws into place to protect the people and keep order within the colonies.

The Middle Colonies

News of economic opportunity in the colonies spread quickly to people still living in Europe. Many of these people jumped at the chance to settle where they might make lots of money! The Middle Colonies of New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware filled with people from all over Europe. German, Irish and English citizens hoped to get wealthy and have religious freedoms.

The climate of the Middle Colonies was milder than that of the New England Colonies. Winters were still cold, but they did not last as long. Summers were hot and rainy. This meant there was a longer growing season. Because of this and very fertile (rich) soil, farmers could successfully grow a variety of crops. They farmed wheat, rye, tobacco, corn and other vegetables. It was also common for indentured servants or enslaved people to help harvest crops in the Middle Colonies.

There was a lot to do for work in the Middle Colonies. Merchants often traded crops and furs across the Atlantic. They relied on waterways to help ship their goods. Miners dug up iron from the ground to trade. So, there were plenty of jobs for anyone willing to work in this region.

People in the Middle Colonies did not have much say about how officials ran their governments. In New York, for example, England’s royalty appointed a powerful governor. This governor, and other officials he chose, enforced the laws.

The Southern Colonies

The Southern Colonies of Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia were both alike and different from the other colonies. Founders of these colonies hoped to discover gold and good land. They wanted to get rich. Settlers founded Maryland to give people who practiced the Catholic religion a safe place to live. One reason colonists settled in Georgia was to keep Spain from moving north from Florida. Georgia was also a safe place for debtors (people who owe money) to live. In England, lawmakers sent people who couldn’t pay their bills to prison. In Georgia, the debtors could work and take care of themselves.

The Southern Colonies had mild winters and long hot summers. This was just the right climate for farmers to produce plentiful crops of tobacco, cotton and rice. They sold these cash crops to make lots of money. Farm owners needed many helpers to tend their large farms called plantations. Over time, many enslaved people worked on these farms. Besides farming, people in the Southern Colonies earned money by shipping, fishing, cutting lumber and trading with American Indians.

Colonists had limited input into government in the Southern Colonies. The founders often held great control. After a while, the colonies elected assemblies, but only white men who owned property could vote in the elections. In Georgia, the King of England could revoke, or take back, any law the assembly passed.

title: Colonial Rule Breakers Banished
text:
People wanted to settle the colonial regions for many reasons, one of which was religious freedom. Two colonists learned, though, that true religious freedom was very difficult to find. They broke rules of the church and were punished severely.

Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson both lived in the colony of Massachusetts at one time. Their ideas about religion were different than the ideas of most people, so people forced them to leave their homes and churches and move far away.

Williams was a minister in Salem, Massachusetts. He did not want his church to be like the churches he left in England. He did not think the King of England should be involved in running the church. He wanted the government and the church to be separate. The leaders kicked Williams out of Massachusetts because they didn't agree with him. Before they deported him (sent him away), Williams ran away to live with American Indians. Later, he moved to Rhode Island and founded the city of Providence.

Anne Hutchinson was also a preacher. She spoke out against the Puritan church because she did not agree with the leaders of the church. The leaders in Massachusetts accused her of treason, or being against the government. At that time women were not supposed to speak out against the church or government. Hutchinson also fled to Rhode Island.

Williams and Hutchinson both continued their religious teachings in Rhode Island. Soon, people knew this colony as a place where people with different religious viewpoints were welcome. Williams lived the rest of his life in Providence. Hutchinson lived nearby on a small island. She and five of her children were murdered in an attack by an American Indian tribe. Some people in the church had stayed angry with Hutchinson. They even said her death was a punishment by God for speaking against the church.

title: Slavery in the Colonies
text:
Why might you have settled in the colonies of North America? Some people wanted the chance to get rich. Others wanted religious freedom. Well, one group settled in the colonies for a different reason altogether. These people did not come to the colonies by their own choice. Others forced them to come, and once they arrived they were sold to plantation owners to work on farms. People were captured, put in chains and brought to the colonies by ship.

European traders in West Africa saw that some people there did not have the same freedoms as others. People who were captured during wars or found guilty of crimes were enslaved. Though they were enslaved, these people could still own land and farm the land. Many enslaved West Africans could earn their freedom over time.

The European traders offered to trade cloth, food, guns and tobacco for these people. The traders knew that many plantations in the colonies needed large numbers of workers. The traders wanted to get rich selling enslaved people to plantation owners.

Traders packed West African enslaved people onto ships and took them across the ocean to the colonies. Some did not survive the journey because of disease and malnutrition (not enough food). The ones who did survive were sold to plantation owners at slave auctions. Families were often separated. Fathers would be sold to one plantation, while mothers and children would be sold to others.

Plantation owners did not treat many of the slaves well. Enslaved people often were whipped or even killed for breaking rules or trying to run away. And work on the plantations was very difficult. Very few enslaved people were ever given their freedom.

The system of slavery would continue in America as our nation grew and changed over many decades. It took a Civil War to put an end to slavery.

title: Land Affects Life
text:
The locations where people choose to live also affect the way they live. The geography, natural resources, and climate of a place determine much of the lifestyle of people who live there. If an area is too cold, too wet, or too hot, it would be very difficult to live there. The land affects many aspects of living.

Some areas have rich, nutrient-filled soil where crops will grow well. Many people who reside in these areas make their living by farming. In the central part of the United States, there are many large farms that grow corn, soy beans, wheat, and other food crops. There are also large areas in parts of the Northwest and California that have fertile land and a good climate. These areas are also good places for growing some of the foods we eat.

There are other places, like New England, where the land is more rocky. It is not a good place to farm. People who live in these places have to find another way to make a living. The early settlers in these areas depended on the sea. They fished, hunted whales, and built ships. Today, there are large cities throughout this area where people live and work in many businesses and industries.

Places like Wyoming have high plateaus and mountains. Temperatures are cooler, and growing seasons are shorter. Farming would be difficult, but this land grows grasses that are good for feeding sheep and cattle. There are many large ranches in these areas.

The geography and climate of a given location have much to do with how people live and make a living there. Those who want to live in a specific area have to adapt. Their houses, jobs, and sometimes even the foods they eat and the clothes they wear help so they can successfully survive in their chosen environments.

title: Early European Colonists and the Monarchy
text:
British rulers encouraged building settlements in distant America. Before they settled, however, potential colonists wanted to protect their rights and privileges under English law. To do this, kings granted charters, which were written sets of legal rights to settle in certain areas. All charters guaranteed the rights of Englishmen. They also created legislatures to make laws for a colony. Depending on the terms of the document, colonial settlements could either be overseen by a proprietor (proprietary colony), or be self-governed or governed by a stockholding company (charter colony). They could also be directly ruled by the king (royal colony).

Proprietary Colonies

Maryland, Pennsylvania and Delaware

Under a proprietary colony, the king had the absolute right to award land grants. He made grants to friends, people he owed money, or powerful noblemen. A proprietor governed the colony as he saw fit. He established courts and made laws, with the consent of the colony’s freemen.

Maryland’s proprietary charter was granted to the Calverts. The Calverts were a noble family seeking religious freedom for Catholics. The charter of Pennsylvania was given to William Penn. The king owed Penn’s family a lot of money, so he gave them land in America as payment. William Penn was a wealthy member of the Society of Friends (Quakers). The Quakers sought religious freedom, too. Delaware was originally colonized as part of Pennsylvania.

Charter Colonies

Massachusetts Bay Colony, Rhode Island, Connecticut

Charter colonies either governed themselves or were governed by a stockholding company. Shareholders invested in the colony to get it started. Company officers made the laws for their colony.

In 1620, Plymouth Colony found itself in a unique position. When the Separatists (Pilgrims) came ashore in Plymouth, they created their own government. In their Mayflower Compact, they pledged to enact laws for the common good. Plymouth later merged with the Puritans who came in the 1630s, forming the Massachusetts Bay Colony.

Rhode Island and Connecticut were both created by settlers who left the strict Massachusetts Bay Colony. These two colonies governed themselves, with no direct control from a king, proprietor, or joint stock company. In Connecticut, the government was organized by the Fundamental Orders, a document with a preamble and 11 orders or laws.

Royal Colonies

New York, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Virginia, North and South Carolina, and Georgia

Royal colonies fell under the king’s direct authority. With the exception of Connecticut and Rhode Island, all other colonies eventually became royal colonies.

Under a royal colony, the king appointed governors to rule in his name. Although governors were powerful, colonial legislatures controlled their salaries. This was useful in keeping governors in line. Royal colonies had legislatures elected by landowners or other freemen. The earliest colonial legislature, the Virginia House of Burgesses, formed in 1619 in Jamestown, the first permanent British colony in America.

title: The House of Burgesses
text:
As more people came to live in Virginia, the colonists needed rules and order. They needed to have rules that people could live by. Two groups made the rules. One group consisted of the governor and his council, or assistants. The other group represented each of the largest 11 plantations of Virginia. Each plantation sent two representatives. Each representative was called a burgess. These two groups formed Virginia's General Assembly.

The governor called the first meeting of the General Assembly in the summer of 1619. The burgesses established the first tax law in the colony. They passed laws to punish colonists who did wrong things. They wrote laws about how to treat the native people. They even petitioned for builders to come from England to build a university. Why was this gathering important? The settlers were in control of their own government. This was different from anything they had experienced in England.

Not everyone took part in the House of Burgesses. Only adult men could vote and become burgesses. Fortunately, this practice has changed. Today, all American citizens are allowed to vote and become representatives in the government if they choose to do so.

Democracy in America began that hot summer in Jamestown. In the 1640s, the House of Burgesses became its own legislative body and made laws for all of Virginia. Today, this system of government continues with the General Assembly of Virginia.

title: The Mayflower Compact
text:
The Mayflower Compact was only 166 words long, but it is one of the most famous documents from early American history. A compact is an agreement or contract between individuals or groups of people. Why was the Mayflower Compact so important to the Plymouth Colony?

The Pilgrims' ship was supposed to land in the chartered area of Virginia, but it did not. Most of the ship’s inhabitants were members of a Puritan sect (group) called the Separatists. However, the ship’s passengers were not all Separatists. These people didn’t want to follow religious rules. Pilgrim leaders realized that they needed to set up some temporary rules and laws that everyone could agree on in order to keep peace in the new community. The 41 adult male passengers and crew members came together and created a set of laws that everyone would obey. All of the men signed the document, which was called the Mayflower Compact. Women were not allowed to sign. At that time, only men made the laws and rules in a government.

The Mayflower Compact is an example of self-government. Self-government is the ability of people to work together to pass laws for themselves that benefit all citizens. This is the central ideal behind our government today.

The settlers lived up to the Compact, and the colony survived. One year later, a man named John Pierce expanded the Mayflower Compact so the English government would support it. The Mayflower Compact continued to be used to govern Plymouth Colony for more than 70 years.

title: War in the New World: The French and Indian War
text:
By the 1750s, Great Britain and France were claiming more and more land in the New World. The two countries were bound to clash sooner or later. In 1754, these two powerful countries went to battle over control of an important piece of North American land, the Ohio River Valley.

Why We Fought

Great Britain

We needed the land of the Ohio River Valley. There were many settlers in our colonies who wanted to farm the rich soil there. They had come to the New World for just that reason. If the French wanted the land too, then they'd have a fight on their hands!

France

We had been trapping animals and trading furs for many years in Canada. We had the right to trap beaver in the Ohio River Valley too. We knew we could win this war against the British. No one beats the French - at trapping or at war!

Key Battle Points

Great Britain

Thousands of British soldiers fought side by side with the colonists. At first, things did not look good for our side at all. We lost many battles, but soon everything began going our way. We decided the best way to win the war would be to take control of Canada. In 1759, our troops captured the Canadian city of Quebec. We climbed 300 foot tall cliffs to overcome our foes (enemies). We continued to win battle after battle, ending with the capture of Montreal. We agreed to sign a peace treaty.

France

It was a good thing for us that we were on friendly terms with the American Indians! Because of that, many of the Indians fought on our side. It was easy to surprise the British. They were so easy to spot in their bright red coats! We won several major battles early in the war, but everything changed in 1759. In Quebec, the British defeated us and took over the city. By 1760, it was clear we had lost Canada. The war ended in 1763 when both sides agreed to sign the Treaty of Paris.

Advantages and Disadvantages

Great Britain

We had many more troops than the French. Each of our colonies had its own militia, or volunteer army. Each colony grew its own food, so our soldiers would not go hungry. One problem was that each of our colonies had its own government. Sometimes that caused arguments over small things that weren't all that important.

France

Because we had many settlements near the Ohio River Valley, we knew they would send help quickly if we needed it. They were easy to defend because they were all close together. The settlements were all under the control of one government, so they made decisions quickly. However, we had to have food shipped from France and we sometimes did not have enough for our troops.

After the War

Great Britain

The treaty gave us control of Canada. We also got the land between the Mississippi River and the Appalachian Mountains, the Ohio River Valley. Unfortunately, the war cost a lot of money. Since we spent most of the money on protecting the colonies, we had no choice but to require Americans to pay the debt. We had to raise their taxes, and they weren't happy about that.

France

We lost control of almost all the land we once claimed in North America. One good thing about the war was that we shared our battle techniques with the American Indians. Later, when the American colonists were fighting for their freedom from Great Britain, they used some of our ideas to help them beat the redcoats. That was almost like a victory for us!

title: Tension between the Colonies and Britain
text:
The Proclamation of 1763

After the French and Indian War, many British colonists settled land west of the Appalachian Mountains. The American Indians on these lands were not happy. They did not want European settlers taking the land and hunting the animals. American Indians attacked many colonists' forts and houses. By 1763 almost 2,000 settlers had been killed. Great Britain knew it had to do something to protect the people and stop the fighting. The Proclamation of 1763 was its answer. According to this law, American Indians had a right to all the land west of the Appalachian Mountains. Settlers were not allowed to move there anymore. The law made many of the colonists really mad. Some of them ignored it and moved west anyway. More and more settlers began to talk to each other about not liking Britain's control. This was the first time a British law made the colonists angry, but it wouldn't be the last.

The Quartering Act

After the French and Indian War, Britain was still afraid the colonists would be attacked. Thousands of British soldiers stayed in the colonies to offer protection. Housing, feeding and supplying the soldiers cost a lot of money. Great Britain wanted the colonists to support the soldiers, so Parliament (branch of British government that made laws) passed a new law called the Quartering Act. The law said the colonists had to provide soldiers with places to live, or quarters. The colonists had to supply the soldiers with food, transportation and supplies like candles and fuel for lamps. Once again the colonists got mad about a British law. They did not believe they should have to support the British troops. They thought the British soldiers were rude and loud. They were also angry that the soldiers took part-time jobs away from colonists. Back then the American colonists did not have the right to elect representatives to Parliament. The colonists thought it was unfair that they had no representative to vote in Parliament.

The Stamp Act

Most American colonists had come to North America in search of wealth and freedom. However, it seemed that neither would be possible if Great Britain continued to have control over the settlers' daily lives. The British kept passing laws that the colonists thought were unfair. Britain passed The Stamp Act to help pay off its debts. Colonists would have to pay a tax on all printed papers. Every piece of paper the colonists used had to be marked with a large stamp to prove someone had paid taxes for that paper. Legal papers, newspapers, magazines and even playing cards were all taxed. The colonists were furious and refused to buy the stamps. Some of them protested, or spoke out against, the law while standing in the streets and town squares. A few colonists were so mad they even attacked the men who collected the stamp tax money for Britain.

In October 1765, nine colonies held a special meeting called the Stamp Act Congress. They wanted Parliament to know they didn't think it was fair for the colonists to pay taxes without having representatives to vote. The King of England and Parliament were surprised at how angry the colonists were. They repealed, or cancelled, the Stamp Act in 1766. However, Great Britain let the colonists know it was still Parliament's right to make colonists pay taxes.

Trouble in Boston

In 1770, colonists were still upset by the Quartering Act. Great Britain continued to tax colonists unfairly. Colonist believed the British soldiers were there to help collect taxes and keep peace, not to protect them from American Indians. Soldiers continued to live in colonial towns and cities, and they still did not get along with the colonists. In Boston, Massachusetts, the colonists often made fun of the soldiers. They laughed at the soldiers' red coats and called them "lobsterbacks." The British soldiers didn't always keep their tempers. They often went out of their way to hassle citizens they didn't like. Name-calling and street fights were common in Boston.

On March 5, 1770, the violence between the soldiers and colonists got out of hand. That night a group of Boston colonists began yelling at a British soldier guarding the Custom House, a tax collection building. Soon people were throwing trash, rocks, snowballs and ice at Captain Thomas Preston and seven other soldiers who had come to help him. No one is really sure what happened next. Perhaps the soldiers didn't hear a command correctly, or maybe were tired of having things thrown at them. The soldiers fired their muskets into the crowd. While the smoke from their guns was still in the air, five colonists lay dead. Six more were badly hurt.

The colonists called this awful event the Boston Massacre. A massacre is the murder of people who cannot defend themselves. The soldiers were put on trial for their actions. No lawyer wanted to represent them. John Adams, a local lawyer, finally agreed to take the case. Only two of the men were punished. Some of the people of Boston were very upset because they thought the soldiers did not get what they deserved. John Adams and Paul Revere made sure that news of the massacre spread throughout all 13 colonies. Colonists were more determined than ever to show Great Britain how angry they were. Unfortunately, Great Britain became even more determined to show how much control it had over the colonies. Trouble - and war - was in store for both sides.

title: Benjamin Franklin: Inventor, Scientist, Writer, Patriot
text:
When you think of the title "Founding Father" what comes to mind? We know many men as Founding Fathers. These men worked hard to gain America's freedom from Great Britain. One of them is Benjamin Franklin.

When you hear his name you probably think of him as a very famous inventor or scientist. Of course, he did invent bifocal glasses, medical equipment, a wood burning stove, a lightning rod and the odometer (a tool for measuring distance traveled). His inventions and discoveries made life better for people.

Perhaps you think of Ben Franklin as a writer. After all, he wrote many different books and magazines. People enjoyed reading his advice on money and education. He also wrote many famous sayings people still use today. Franklin was also an excellent printer. This allowed him to make many copies of his books!

Most of all, Benjamin Franklin was highly respected and admired in colonial America. He was a true patriot! A patriot is someone who loves and defends his country. At first, Franklin wanted the colonies to try and work with Great Britain to solve their problems. He went to Great Britain to ask for fair treatment of the colonies. He stayed calm while he tried to persuade (convince) Parliament to repeal, or cancel, unfair laws. And he did help get the Stamp Act repealed. When Franklin finally realized Great Britain still believed they were right to tax the colonists, he came home. He was ready to help America fight for the right to govern themselves.

Another of Franklin's famous sayings was, "All mankind is divided into three classes: those that are immovable, those that are movable and those that move." Franklin wanted the American colonies to move towards independence.

title: Who was John Wise?
text: John Wise was a Colonial American minister who was indeed a very "wise" man. Wise was born and lived in Massachusetts his whole life. He studied at Harvard College and became the minister of a church in Ipswich, Massachusetts. This tall man often spoke forcefully about what he believed. He had strong opinions about how to organize the church. He preached about the democratic rights of people, and how they should have a say in government. One time he spoke out against unfair taxes, and other church leaders punished him by removing him as minister of the church. He had many ideas about how the church and the colonies could be better and stronger. His famous writings expressed ideas that our Founding Fathers later used in the Declaration of Independence.

title: Loyalists, Patriots and Neutralists
text:
As colonists began to argue about whether or not they should declare their independence, they started to take sides.

Some people thought it was better for the colonies to stay under the rule of Great Britain. They wanted to remain loyal, or true, to the King of England. These people became known as Loyalists. Many Loyalists were rich landowners. Some of them had jobs in government or churches.

It was easy to think of a name for the people who did not like the way Great Britain treated the colonies: Patriots. They wanted the colonies to become an independent country that the King of England could not control. The Patriots gave speeches and wrote articles about the unfair treatment of the colonies.

Some colonists did not take sides. They were known as Neutralists. Which would you have been: Loyalist, Patriot or Neutralist? Talk about it with your class.

title: Causes and Effects of the French and Indian War
text:
Historians know it is important to try and understand what caused an event in history to happen. It’s also important to know what happened because of, or after, the event. This is an effect. The words “because,” “so” and “then” often show a cause-and-effect relationship.

Use information in this week’s issue to fill in the cause-and-effect chart below. As you look back at the articles, remember to look for words that show a cause-and-effect relationship.

title: Limited Resources, Economic Growth, and New England
text:
Imagine you are a farmer about 400 years ago. For months, you travel by ship to the Americas, hoping to create economic prosperity. When you settle, however, you discover the uncultivated land is poor for farming. What would you do?

This was the plight of the early New England colonists. The land they found was hilly and densely forested. Because it was shaped by melting glaciers over time, rich soil had been pushed south. It left behind rocky, sandy soil that was bad for crops. New England settlers could farm only enough food for a meager livelihood. They did not have enough food to supply the keys to economic growth and development: sustained increase in production, profit, and standard of living.

If a country wants to grow economically, its total number of goods and services produced must be greater than its population size. And this total must rise steadily over time. Only then can a country’s economy develop. As a result, they see positive changes in their income, education, housing, employment, technology, healthcare, etc.

But what happens when the resources used to create products are limited like farmable soil in New England? Limited resources are those that are in low supply or extremely slow to renew (like coal and oil). This basic economic problem is referred to as “scarcity.”

New England colonists knew what to do. They branched out because the land was rich with raw materials. The region was covered with trees. Rich fishing and whaling grounds were right next door. So colonists collected timber, fished, and hunted whales, which led to a major demand for ships. Shipyards were built. Opportunities for shipbuilders, blacksmiths, various timber-related professions, and traders prospered. Now, New England is known for having built the economic foundations of America. While its lumber and shipbuilding industries continue to thrive, measures are still being explored to ensure sustainability. After all, natural resources are not unlimited.

title: Development of Free Enterprise in Colonial America
text:
When English colonists first came to America, many hoped to become wealthy. Many of the organizations that sponsored the colonists’ journey also hoped that they were going to make a profit on their investment. To accumulate wealth for both themselves and their sponsors, early colonists settling in the Americas looked to the free enterprise system.

The free enterprise system is an economic system in which people are free to do business without government restrictions. The products produced and the prices they are sold for are determined by the market. The market refers to the people buying and selling products and services.

In the early days of American free enterprise, colonists and Europeans exchanged many goods. Europeans were eager to buy furs from America. Spectacular hats, coats, and blankets were being made from beaver, bear, fox, and other fur pelts. In Massachusetts, fishing was a primary source of wealth. However, some basic necessities and nearly all luxuries needed to be imported. Colonists traded cash crops like rice, tobacco, and indigo for these items.

Soon, settlements started to grow. Sawmills and grist mills started to appear. Shipyards were established to support fishing along the coasts. These shipyards later built vessels to be used for trading. Regional patterns of development were occuring. New England was relying on shipbuilding and sailing to generate wealth. Southern plantations grew tobacco, rice, and indigo. Middle colonies shipped general food crops and furs. Colonists were growing and creating products to sell and trade for their own benefit.

As the colonists became more successful, they started to make profits for themselves. The free enterprise system was working for them. This changed when the British imposed trade policies to control the colonists. England only allowed the colonists to trade with the British. The colonists wanted to be free to trade with any country so they could look for the best trade deals. England wanted to control all trade involving their colonies.

Other restrictive policies known as the Navigation Acts were imposed on the colonies. Only British or British colonial ships could carry cargo between imperial posts. Some goods such as rice, cotton, and furs could not be shipped to foreign nations without going through England or Scotland. These restrictions on trade limited the freedom of producers in the colonies. This intrusion into trade policies made the colonists angry. Disputes over free trade and taxation eventually led to war with the British and to independence for the colonies.

title: Early American Economies
text:
The first people living in the original British colonies needed to learn how to adapt to their new homes. People in the three regions of colonies used the distinct geography, natural resources, and climate of their environments to bring forth economic development and prosperity.

New England Colonies

The New England colonies were Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, and Connecticut. The settlers of these colonies experienced cold winters and mild summers. The cold weather helped to lessen the spread of disease in the area. The soil of these colonies was very rocky. This made farming difficult. As a result, much of the economy was based on ocean industries. These industries including fishing, trapping, whaling, and shipbuilding. Codfish were especially plentiful. Later, the New England Colonies became part of the triangular trade. Goods were traded from England to West Africa in exchange for enslaved people. These enslaved people were traded to the Americas for commodities (useful or valuable items) such as cotton, tobacco, and sugar. These products would be shipped back to England to start the cycle again.

Mid-Atlantic Colonies

The Mid-Atlantic Colonies were New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Delaware. They enjoyed a temperate climate, which was not too hot or too cold. The plains along the coast provided excellent farmland. The climate and rich soil combined to make these colonies strong in agriculture, or farming. Barley, wheat, oats, and rye were produced. The Piedmont, an area between the mountains and the coastal plain, included forests that provided wood for logging, shipbuilding, and papermaking. Coastal cities, such as Philadelphia and New York, became major shipping centers. This provided great economic potential. Craftspeople, such as blacksmiths, silversmiths, cobblers, wheelwrights, and wigmakers, also worked in the Middle Colonies.

Southern Colonies

Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia formed the Southern Colonies. People from the Southern Colonies enjoyed a warm climate with hot summers and mild winters. The South had excellent land for farming. They also enjoyed a longer growing season to produce rice, indigo, tobacco, sugarcane, and cotton. These cash crops were often grown on large plantations, which were worked by enslaved people and indentured servants.

title: Samuel Adams and the Sons of Liberty
text:
In 1765, the Parliament of Great Britain passed a tax law called the Stamp Act. Colonists were really angry about having to pay this money. They felt they were being taxed unfairly. They wanted to have representatives in Parliament to help make important decisions. In many colonial cities, groups of men began to meet in secret to discuss the way Great Britain governed (controlled) the colonies. In the summer of 1765, a group of men who called themselves "The Loyal Nine" met in Boston. As the number of members quickly grew, they became known as the "Sons of Liberty." Samuel Adams eventually led the group. They worked day and night to fight against Great Britain's unfair control of the colonies.

Samuel Adams was born in Quincy, Massachusetts, in 1722. His family was wealthy and respected in the community. Samuel and his cousin, John Adams, grew up together and were both very interested in law and politics. Samuel attended Harvard College, but he did not enjoy practicing law. He liked giving speeches and writing articles about Great Britain's unfair treatment of the colonies.

Samuel Adams believed that the British treated the colonies unfairly. He did not like all the taxes Great Britain forced the colonists to pay. He was not happy that the King of England chose the colonies' governors. He argued that the colonies should be able to choose their own leaders. He wanted the colonists to break away from Great Britain and fight for their independence.

In the summer of 1765, Samuel Adams helped organize a secret group of patriots in Boston. The group named themselves the "Sons of Liberty." They were dedicated to fighting against Great Britain's control of the colonies. They met secretly and often encouraged the colonists to disobey British laws like the Stamp Act. In the fall of 1773, the Sons of Liberty became especially upset about a tax on the colonists' favorite beverage - tea. In this issue you will learn about what the Sons of Liberty and other patriots did because of the strict control Great Britain tried to place on the American Colonies.

title: Independence May Be the Only Answer
text:
The tension between Great Britain and the colonies kept growing. The Proclamation of 1763, the Quartering Act and the Stamp Act had all angered the colonists. They believed Great Britain was not treating them fairly. The massacre in Boston brought the colonists closer together in their disagreements with the king and Parliament of Great Britain.

The Boston Tea Party

After the Boston Massacre, British leaders realized that something must be done to calm down the colonists. Parliament agreed to repeal, or cancel, all of the unpopular taxes the colonists had to pay. All except one, that is. They wanted to show the colonists they were still in control, so they put a tax on their favorite drink - tea. When they heard about the tea tax, many colonists refused to buy tea from Britain. This was bad news for the British East India Company, which made most of its money from tea sales. The company lost money quickly.

To save the company, Parliament passed the Tea Act in May 1773. This act made it nearly impossible for colonists to buy tea from any company other than the British East India Company. Of course this act made the colonists angrier than ever. The price of tea went down, but they did not like being forced to buy tea from only one company. They were also worried that Great Britain might soon decide to pass other laws that limited where colonists could buy things.

Colonists protested, or spoke out against, the law. In Boston, the Sons of Liberty decided to take action against the British. On the night of December 16, 1773, Samuel Adams led a group of men dressed as American Indians. They stormed three ships sitting in the Boston Harbor. The men dumped 342 crates of tea into the harbor. The tea was ruined, which caused the British East India Company to lose a large amount of money. The colonists called the event the "Boston Tea Party." People in England were shocked at the colonists' behavior, and King George was very angry. Parliament began to think of a way to punish the colonists for dumping the tea.

The Intolerable Acts

Now the British thought most colonists were just troublemakers. The king passed new laws to punish the colonists and keep them under control. These laws were very harsh. Many colonists said they were so bad they could not stand them. They called these harsh new laws the Intolerable Acts. (Intolerable means unacceptable.) The British closed Boston Harbor in March 1774. Ships could not enter or leave Boston until the colonists agreed to pay for the tea that was destroyed. Many people lost their jobs at the harbor. They had a hard time paying for their homes and food. People in the other colonies agreed to help the people of Boston. Many of them sent money, food and supplies to the city.

First Continental Congress

More and more colonists started thinking it was time to take action against Great Britain. They were tired of taxation without representation and wanted to protect their rights and liberty more than ever. In September 1774, 56 leaders from 12 colonies met in Philadelphia to talk about the problems with Great Britain. (Georgia did not send anyone to the meeting.)

John Adams, Patrick Henry, Samuel Adams and George Washington were there. Most of the delegates wanted to make a peace agreement with Great Britain. But they also wanted Britain to know that an attack on one colony would be considered an attack on them all. The colonies were making the first step to band together against Great Britain.

The First Attacks: Lexington and Concord

After the First Continental Congress, colonists started organizing and training militia. These small armies of ordinary citizens were ready to take on the British if they attacked. Just after midnight on April 19, 1775, British soldiers marched from Boston to Lexington and Concord in Massachusetts. The king had ordered British soldiers to arrest rebel leaders and seize (take away) their weapons. Boston silversmith Paul Revere rode to Lexington with the news that the British Army was on its way. About 60 militiamen faced hundreds of well-trained British soldiers. No one knows for sure who fired the first shot at Lexington, but many have called it "the shot heard 'round the world."

Later that same morning nearly 1,000 colonial militiamen waited in nearby Concord for the British. At the end of the battle, almost 300 British soldiers had been killed or wounded.

The Second Continental Congress

In May 1775, colony leaders met in Philadelphia again at the Second Continental Congress. Sixty-five delegates acted as the government for the colonies. First, they established a Continental Army. Congress chose George Washington to lead the new army because he was an experienced soldier and a strong leader.

The most difficult decision was whether or not to declare independence from Great Britain. Some Patriots, like John and Samuel Adams, were ready for a fight. Most delegates, though, were still loyal to King George. They hoped the colonies could make peace with Great Britain.

Common Sense

Thomas Paine only lived in the colonies a short time before he knew that freedom from Great Britain was best for America. In January 1776, he wrote a booklet called "Common Sense." In it he argued that America should rule itself and show the world a better form of government. He said independence was not only the people's right, but also their only choice. People everywhere were reading it and starting to lean toward declaring independence. In just a few months, Paine convinced many people that independence may be the only answer.

title: Timber: Britain Depended on the Colonies
text: In the 1700s, the British navy was strong and well known, and the country needed timber (wood) to build ships for the sailors. England had already used up most of the timber in their forests. They depended on the American colonies to supply the wood. A special group of the king's men traveled through the colonies to find the biggest and strongest trees. They put the king's special mark on the trees. Later, the trees were cut down and sent to England to build ships. The ships became part of the British navy, and some were used to transport (carry) goods back and forth between the two continents.

title: Minutemen and Militia
text:
The terms minutemen and militia are often both used to describe the volunteer colonial soldiers during the Revolutionary War. But the minutemen and the militia were two different groups.

Almost every town in the colonies had its own militia. The men in these volunteer armies used their own weapons. They came from many different backgrounds. Many of these soldiers were farmers, shopkeepers, craftspeople and blacksmiths. Some of the men had military skills, but many were just ordinary citizens who wanted to protect their families' freedom.

The best soldiers from every militia were chosen to get special training. They were called minutemen because they had to be ready to fight at a minute's notice. The minutemen were usually the first to get to the battlefield. Then the regular militia came to back them up. Soon, the minutemen began to train under George Washington and became part of the Continental Army.

title: George Washington: Gentleman, Soldier, Patriot
text:
Do you know whose face is on a U.S. $1 bill? If you said George Washington, you are right! George Washington was chosen as the first president of the United States in 1789. Many people don't know very much about his early life or his time in the Revolutionary War. They just know him as the Father of our Country.

George Washington was born on the family plantation in Virginia in 1732. He was only 11 years old when his father died. George and his mother worked hard to keep the family's plantation running. George's mother made sure her son behaved well at all times. He was often described as a very smart and polite young man.

When he was 16, George worked as a land surveyor for a British landowner. At 22, he earned a position as an officer in the British military. He fought in battles during the French and Indian War. On several occasions Washington barely missed being shot. His horse was shot out from under him twice!

Later, Washington got married and settled at Mount Vernon, Virginia. He served in the Virginia House of Burgesses. His life on the plantation was busy and successful, but Washington was not happy with the way the British were treating the colonists. Like other Patriots, Washington began to speak up about how unhappy he was with the British. At the Second Continental Congress, other leaders gave Washington the challenge of leading the Continental Army.

General Washington had to work very hard to prepare his soldiers to face the well-trained British army. He led his troops into battles carefully, and he was known for surprising the British army when they least expected it.

During the Revolutionary War, Washington became known as a strong leader. His leadership skills made him a great choice to lead the men who wrote the Constitution in 1787. Two years later he was unanimously (agreed on by everyone) elected as the first president of the United States.

text: Use information from the article “Independence May Be the Only Answer” to put important events leading up to the Declaration of Independence in order on a timeline. Write the date and event in the boxes below. We did the first one for you.

title: First in War, First in Peace - The Founding Fathers
text:
The United States has always been gifted with great leaders. Some of our best leaders were those who turned our original 13 colonies into a nation. Some were brave soldiers. Others fought for equal rights. Some served in the highest courts of law. Others wrote the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution, and the Bill of Rights.

These leaders are known as the Founding Fathers. They played vital parts in the birth of the United States of America. The Founding Fathers were businessmen, lawyers, planters, doctors, politicians, and writers. When they and others felt compelled to separate from England, they became Americans.

Historians differ on how long the list of Founding Fathers should be, but most agree on these men: John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Alexander Hamilton, John Jay, Thomas Jefferson, James Madison, and George Washington. Historians today might add Abigail Adams, Mercy Otis Warren, and Dolley Madison. Other women also played more subtle yet equally important roles.

What made the Founding Fathers so great? They were intelligent, wise, and cared deeply for their homes in the Americas. They did what no other colonial people had done before. They and their followers revolted from a powerful country and won their freedom.

After gaining their independence from Great Britain, the issue of forming a government in a land as large and varied as America seemed impossible. The revolution had thrown people together in battle. However, these people from distant colonies had no other common experiences. Could they join forces as free, united states?

To the new nation’s good fortune, the Founding Fathers had worked together on the battlefield, in the early congresses, and as diplomats in Europe raising money for the revolution. They ate with one another, debated together, and wrote to each other. They knew each other’s strengths and weaknesses. Many were close friends.

Historian Joseph Ellis called the Founding Fathers “the greatest generation of political talent in American history.” Through their creation of the Constitution, courts, and laws, these giants created the United States of America.

title: Sons of Liberty
text:
In 1765, the Parliament of Great Britain passed a tax law called the Stamp Act. The colonists were angry about having to pay this money. They felt that they were being taxed unfairly. They also wanted to have representatives in Parliament who would help make important decisions. In many colonial cities, groups of men began to meet in secret to discuss the way Great Britain governed (controlled) the Colonies. In the summer of 1765, a group of men who called themselves "The Loyal Nine" met in Boston. The number of members quickly grew. They became known as the "Sons of Liberty."

The Boston chapter of the Sons of Liberty met secretly by the "Liberty Tree." Why did they have to meet in secret? They feared the British would arrest them or worse. Even though it was dangerous, they never gave up. They worked day and night to fight against Great Britain's unfair control of the Colonies. Samuel Adams eventually became the leader of this group.

Samuel Adams and his cousin, John Adams, grew up together. Both were very interested in law and politics. Samuel attended Harvard College, but he did not enjoy practicing law. He liked giving speeches and writing articles about Great Britain's unfair treatment of the Colonies.

Samuel Adams and other patriots believed that the British treated the Colonies unfairly. They did not like all the taxes that Great Britain forced the colonists to pay. They were also unhappy that the king of England chose the Colonies' governors. They argued that the Colonies should be able to choose their own leaders. For these and other reasons, they concluded that the colonists should break away from Great Britain and fight for their independence.

John Adams, on the other hand, became a successful and popular lawyer in Boston. He defended the British soldiers who were charged in the Boston Massacre in March 1770. None of the accused soldiers were sent to jail. John also wrote extensively, publishing essays about social, legal, and political issues.

When colonial protests started, following the Stamp Act in 1765, John was reluctant to get involved. He felt that his legal career might be harmed. He did not trust many of the leaders of the protests, including Samuel. He believed that the colonial radicals had a hidden agenda, including gaining independence for America. Over time, however, John became convinced the radicals were correct.

John was one of the four delegates from Massachusetts to attend the First Continental Congress in 1774. He was reelected to the Second Continental Congress, just a few days after the Revolutionary War started. John soon emerged as a leader, advocating for independence. John was one of a small group appointed to draft the Declaration of Independence. John was also elected as the first vice president. He would later become the second president of the United States.

title: Benjamin Franklin
text:
Benjamin Franklin was one of our country’s most well-known Founding Fathers. He was also a writer, printer, inventor, scientist, newspaper publisher, politician, and diplomat. People seem to remember him most for experimenting with electricity.

Benjamin Franklin’s knowledge and experience had a large influence on the events and ideas that led to American independence. In 1775, Franklin returned from a trip to England to find his homeland in conflict. British soldiers filled the streets of cities like Boston. Clashes with the British troops increased. The other colonies watched nervously. By the spring of that year, armed fighting had begun. Patriot leaders decided it was time for the Colonies to demand separation from Great Britain. They wanted to form their own independent nation.

In May 1775, colonial delegates met in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, to decide how to gain independence. As a writer and publisher, Benjamin Franklin had become very well-known for his honesty and originality. He was chosen as a Pennsylvania delegate to attend this Continental Congress. Franklin was asked to be one of five people to help draw up a document to send to King George. They discussed what this declaration should contain, and then the committee assigned Thomas Jefferson to write it. It was called the Declaration of Independence.

Benjamin Franklin was one of the few colonial leaders who signed both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution of the United States. After the Revolutionary War, the new United States needed to create a system of government. Again, delegates came from all but one of the new states. Franklin represented Pennsylvania at this Constitutional Convention too. After weeks of heated debate, the Constitution of the United States of America was adopted on September 17, 1787. It had 39 signatures, one of which said, “Benjamin Franklin.” He died just three years later, in 1790.

title: Celebrate Good Times
text:
Celebrations are an important part of culture. They give people a chance to honor their heritage. People celebrate with festivals, street fairs, and parades. They dance and play music, set off fireworks, and hold contests.

Many local communities host celebrations that are unique to the people who live there. Towns with a large Chinese American population host colorful parades of dragons on Chinese New Year. People in other towns dress in green on St. Patrick’s Day to celebrate Irish culture. Some people celebrate Oktoberfest events in the fall. Oktoberfest is a German tradition. From Swiss Days to a Taste of Thailand, American towns have festivals to celebrate the cultures that people have brought to this country.

Cultures differ. They celebrate different things and in different ways. These celebrations remind us of the wonderful things about our culture. Celebrations give us a chance to enjoy and learn about the cultures around us. They also give us a time to spend with our families and the people we live near. What kinds of celebrations do you have in your community?

title: Physical Features of a Growing Nation
text:
The Atlantic Coastal Plain

The Atlantic Coastal Plain is an area of flat land between New York and Florida. The land slowly slopes to the Atlantic Ocean. The dry, flat area in this region was a gateway to expansion. Here, people built towns and roads. They learned how to successfully grow crops on rocky terrain. In the southern parts of the plain, farmers established plantations on the fertile soil. The middle portion attracted farmers who grew wheat, barley and rye. Longer growing seasons contributed to larger farms. Many farmers also raised cattle and pigs. Access to fur, lumber and fish led to shipbuilding and fishing for settlers along the coast. The many waterways in this region allowed easy transportation of goods. Communities that supported trade grew along these waterways. In addition, expert craftsmen built furniture and made guns and glass. Mining and industrial development also invited many people to settle in the area. Today, this area is the most densely populated area in the United States.

The Great Plains

The Great Plains is a large region that runs from the upper Midwest to the base of the Rocky Mountains. In the southern states of Texas and New Mexico, the Plains are mostly flat. Settlers moving to this area were attracted by the rich soil. These conditions were excellent for farming. Large rivers allowed for transportation of goods. Small communities formed along these routes. The Homestead Act offered free land to settlers willing to improve the land. This resulted in thousands of people pouring into the area. Some of the towns that were settled became major cities that still exist today.

The Great Lakes

The Great Lakes enabled further expansion in the Midwestern states. They served as a sort of highway for traders and explorers. After steamboats began service on the Great Lakes, the lakes became even more important for travel and industry. As a result, several major cities developed along the Great Lakes.

The West

The geography of the West presented unique challenges and opportunities for early American settlers. The steep, rugged terrain of the Rockies made it difficult to travel. The discoveries of silver and gold led to the establishment of towns. Religious persecution was another motivation to move westward. Mormon settlers were driven from their homes in the Great Plains. They trekked west and formed communities throughout Utah and the rest of the region. Mining of valuable minerals, as well as the mild climate of the Pacific Coast attracted people to settle in the region. Farming and orchards attracted even more settlers. Later, the entertainment and technology industries became important to the West.

The Gulf of Mexico

The Gulf of Mexico sits between Florida and Mexico. It has 33 major rivers that flow into it, including the Mississippi River. The rivers were used as travel routes. This encouraged expansion and the establishment of many communities. Fertile soil found in the region was used for cotton and sugar farming. These crops are still important today. Farms in the area today also grow soybeans, rice, corn, sweet potatoes and pecans. Other resources, including petroleum and natural gas, led the way to the growth of big cities.

The Mississippi River

The Mississippi River is one of the longest rivers in the world. The United States gained access to the entire Mississippi River in the Louisiana Purchase. The Mississippi became another opportunity for national expansion. It allowed settlers to travel north and south. It became a starting place for people to travel to the Western U.S.

The Southwest

This area has an arid desert climate. It was difficult land to farm due to sandy soil and little rainfall. American Indians did raise corn, beans, and squash there. People were later attracted to the Southwest, hoping to make their fortunes from the area’s resources. Some of those resources were timber, gold and silver. Other parts of the region were very suitable as grazing land. Today, the area’s warm weather draws many people from colder regions of the United States to this region for the winter.

title: Independence Day
text:
Have you ever wondered why we have picnics and set off fireworks on the Fourth of July?

What are we celebrating, anyway?

In 1777, Congress wanted to celebrate that one year had passed since the Declaration of Independence was adopted. They wanted a huge celebration that included fireworks. They held it in Philadelphia, and it quickly grew into a large party.

A newspaper called the Virginia Gazette wrote that 13 rockets were fired at the start and end of the celebration. Each rocket represented one colony. There were also parades, music, food, and flags. People enjoyed the celebration so much that it became a tradition.

The founders knew that July 4 was an important day. John Adams wrote a letter to his wife on July 3, 1776. In the letter, he said that the day should be celebrated with “…illuminations from one End of this Continent to the other from this Time forward forever more.” As years passed, our country continued to celebrate Independence Day. How do people in your community celebrate Independence Day?

title: The Founding Fathers
text:
Benjamin Franklin. George Washington. Thomas Jefferson. John Adams. Do you recognize these names? These men and others are part of a group we call the Founding Fathers. They risked everything they had, including their lives, to create the country we call the United States of America. Why would they risk so much? As you get to know more about each man, you will begin to understand what drove them all to change the world.

Benjamin Franklin was the oldest of the Founders. He was well-respected by many people.

Franklin was a printer and publisher in Philadelphia for many years. He particularly enjoyed writing articles and poems that poked fun at community leaders and highlighted local issues with humor. As he observed issues in the American colonies, he came to an important conclusion. The colonies needed to unite in order to protect themselves from the French and the American Indians. As a result, he wrote one of the first founding documents called the Albany Plan of Unity.

John Adams and Thomas Jefferson were very good friends. They both had read and studied many people’s ideas about democracy and self-government. As King George and the British Parliament began to increase their efforts to tax and control the American colonies, these two men became leaders in the effort to declare independence from England. Along with Benjamin Franklin, Adams and Jefferson were given the assignment to write a letter to King George.

The letter was meant to explain the reasons the colonies wanted to separate from British rule and form their own country. The letter became the Declaration of Independence.

That declaration was the final step to revolution. The colonies were at war with Great Britain. The Continental Congress chose another Founding Father, George Washington, to lead the new Continental Army. He also strongly believed in the cause of independence and was willing to sacrifice much to form a new nation. Having led the army to victory, Washington was then chosen to be the president of the Constitutional Convention. John Adams and Benjamin Franklin were also part of this convention. They all played important roles in the development of the Constitution which laid out the plan for governing the new United States of America.

title: The Committee of Five Declares Independence
text:
Characters

Narrators 1-10

Robert Livingston

John Adams

Benjamin Franklin

Roger Sherman

Thomas Jefferson

Setting

June 1776, Graff House - Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, in Thomas Jefferson's rented room. All are seated around a table, except the narrators who can be to the side onstage or may read from offstage.

Narrator 1: Thomas Paine's booklet "Common Sense" helped convince the Second Continental Congress that the American colonies should move toward independence from Great Britain.

Narrator 2: On June 7, 1776, Virginia delegates asked Congress to declare that "these United Colonies are, and of right ought to be, free and independent States." Congress decided to think things over for a few weeks before taking a vote.

Narrator 3: Congress chose a group of men to write a document explaining why the colonies wanted independence. The Committee of Five consisted of John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Robert Livingston, Roger Sherman and Thomas Jefferson.

Narrator 4: The five men knew the document had to be well written and thoughtful. Their first job was to decide who would write this "Declaration of Independence."

Benjamin Franklin: Gentlemen, Congress has given us a very important job.

Robert Livingston: We all have ideas, but only one of us should actually do the writing.

Roger Sherman: Which one of us would be the best choice to write this important document?

John Adams: Thomas, you must take on this responsibility.

Thomas Jefferson: But what do I have to give that you have not? You are the well-respected John Adams.

John Adams: (laughing to himself) You are too kind. You know I am somewhat outspoken. Not everyone in the colonies thinks as highly of me as you do.

Thomas Jefferson: You ought to do it, John. What reasons can you have for not writing this declaration?

Benjamin Franklin: Yes, my old friend. What reasons could you possibly have against writing this yourself?
