title: Writing in Sequence
text: Writers must be able to explain historical events in sequence, or order. After reading the article “An Industrial Revolution Begins” on Pages 2 and 3, think about the events in the order they happened. Create an outline of all of the main ideas and put them in correct order. Then write a paragraph explaining the Industrial Revolution using your outline as a guide. Write in complete sentences and support your ideas with facts and details.

title: Human-Environment Interaction
text:
When looking at different time periods, historians often study human-environment interaction. This topic studies how humans change their environment and also how the environment shapes the choices they make. The Northeast in the 1800s is a good example. The Industrial Revolution took hold in the Northeast because of its environment. The new factories were run by water power. The builders chose the Northeast because it had so many rivers. Cities then grew along the coast and rivers, where transportation was easier.

Humans also caused many changes to the natural environment during the Industrial Revolution. The populations of cities increased. This meant more land was needed for houses and factories. Forests were cut down to clear more land. Animals’ natural habitats were disturbed. More people needed more limited natural resources, including water, food, and building materials.

As the Industrial Revolution progressed, more machines were built and the steam engine became popular. Steam engines powered transportation such as railroads and steamships, and also began to power factories. Coal was used to run these steam engines, but it was very dirty to use and caused air pollution. The coal had to be mined, which was a very dirty and dangerous job. When they chose to use coal, humans changed the environment in many ways, from air quality to mining.

title: The Industrial Revolution
text:
A Revolution

The Industrial Revolution changed the way people made their livings. They went from producing goods by hand at home to making them with machines in factories. The invention of machines made it faster and easier than ever to produce goods of all kinds.

The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain. There, factories were built to produce cloth. Samuel Slater was a skilled textile worker in England. He brought his knowledge to the United States. Textiles are fabrics made by spinning threads and weaving them together. Slater built cotton spinning mills in Pawtucket, Rhode Island. They were some of the first in America. This was the beginning of the Industrial Revolution in the United States. American society changed from an agrarian, or farming, society to an industrial, or machine-run, society. Whether people stayed at a farm or moved to the cities to work in factories, the Industrial Revolution changed the lives of everyone in America.

From Homemade to Mass-Produced

Before the Industrial Revolution, people couldn’t just go to the store if they needed something. Instead, they had to find ways to make most of the things they needed at home. If they couldn’t make it themselves, they depended on someone in the community to make it for them. If someone in the family needed new clothing, the women of the household usually made the fabric themselves. The fabric would have been woven from wool or linen. Cotton fabrics imported from England were also available. If the family happened to have a bit more money, they would have a nearby seamstress or tailor do the job. After the invention of the sewing machine in 1846, factories began producing clothing less expensively and faster than it could be made at home. Families began buying their clothing in stores or through mail-order catalogs. This saved time, gave them more styles to choose from, and often saved money as well.

Clothing wasn’t the only item that went from being homemade to factory-produced. Tools, farm equipment, furniture, and just about everything else went from being made individually by skilled craftspeople to being mass-produced in factories by unskilled workers. Specialized farm machinery made it possible for farmers to plant and harvest more crops with far fewer workers than ever before. The number of people working on farms continued to drop as the years went by. Craftspeople of all kinds found themselves unable to make a living the same way they had in the past.

Cities of Promise

Where were the new jobs? You could find most of them in big cities. It was there that large factories produced ready-made goods at low prices. The Industrial Revolution changed American society forever. Immigrants from around the world came to America in search of work. Most of them settled in large cities, like New York, where the factories were. From the 1870s to 1900, most immigrants arriving in the U.S. came from England, Ireland, Italy, and Germany. Many found jobs, but the work was hard, the wages were low, and the living conditions were poor. At the same time, many more products were available for people to buy at much lower prices.

title: George Washington Carver
text: George Washington Carver was born into slavery in Missouri in 1864. Even as a child, Carver loved plants and learned as much as he could about them. After graduating college, Carver became a teacher at what is currently named Tuskegee University in Alabama. He taught agriculture, or farming, at the college. Carver developed hundreds of uses for the peanut. This amazing little plant soon replaced cotton in many areas of the South after the Civil War. Years of growing cotton in the same spots had worn out the soil. Peanuts proved to be a crop that could grow well in the tired ground. Carver encouraged farmers throughout the Southeast to plant peanuts and other crops. They would help make the most of the region's great natural resource, the soil.

title: Specialization and Division of Labor
text:
In every economy, people develop systems for who does which jobs. Some people grow food, some build roads, some make clothing, some teach school, and some work in hospitals. This idea is called division of labor. Not everyone does every job that needs to be done. Instead, people specialize in what they are interested in or good at. Everyone benefits from each other’s specialized skills. They get the goods and services they need by earning and exchanging their own specialized skills.

Early successful companies divided the production process into different tasks on a production line. This allowed for specialization among the workers. Each worker became skilled at one part of the production process. A worker would not make a product start to finish. Instead, a worker focused on making one part of a product over and over. Companies that used this process greatly increased production of their goods. Mass production, or efficient production of a large number of similar products, was made possible by specialization and assembly lines. When workers specialized, they became very efficient at the single thing they were making on the assembly line and were able to make that product in mass.

The idea of division of labor is an important means of economic growth in traditional industries in the United States. One famous example is the automobile industry. Henry Ford, founder of the Ford Motor Company, improved the assembly line technique to produce affordable goods. He used technology to help his workers. He guaranteed exact standards and quality in his products even from untrained workers.

title: The Annexation of Texas
text:
Following the War of 1812, the Industrial Revolution was in full progress in the United States. In many cities, industry changed the way people lived and worked. For some people though, the wilderness still called, and a land named Texas seemed the perfect place to be. In the 1820s, Mexico gained independence from Spain and took control of the Texas territory. Mexican officials realized they needed more Anglo settlers to come to Texas. What might life have been like then? Imagine that in 1845, 11-year-old James Young's family had been living in Mexican-controlled Texas for many years. Read James' journal entry about the day Texas became a part of the United States of America.

Dec. 29, 1845

Today, Pa says that the United States officially annexed (joined with) Texas, and we are now part of the United States. Texas President Anson Jones lowered the Texas flag this morning and the U.S. flag was raised high. Pa says it is what is best for us all, but I know everything has changed since he came to Texas with his parents in 1828.

Before that time, there were very few Anglos in Texas. Most people here were American Indian like the Apaches and Comanche. Pa's family lived in Virginia and wanted to own land. That would not be very easy to do in the United States. So, Pa's family came to Texas and settled on free land the Mexican government had promised them. In return, my grandfather promised to raise crops and animals on the fertile land. He also pledged, or promised, to pay taxes to the Mexican government and practice the Catholic religion. Like all the other settlers to Texas, Pa and his family promised to learn to speak Spanish and follow the Mexican laws.

By 1830, there were many Anglo families living in Texas. Soon the people weren't getting along with the Mexican government. Most of the people never learned to speak Spanish and didn't want to change religions just to please the Mexicans. The Mexicans passed new laws that made life even harder for settlers.

Pa had just married Mama in 1833 when the settlers asked Mexico to let Texas have its own government. The settlers were not happy with Mexico's rules. Pa said when I was just a baby, fighting broke out between the powerful Mexican government and the Texas people. I have heard the stories of the battles in Gonzales and Goliad many times.

Of course, many know the story of the Texans who fought bravely against General Santa Anna at the Alamo. I always enjoy hearing Mama tell me about how she and Pa had to run away from the cruel general when they thought his men were coming to burn down our farm. I was too young to remember it all, but it sure sounds dangerous. I'll bet Pa was very brave. I know the Texans were shouting, "Remember the Alamo!" when General Sam Houston led an attack against the Mexicans at San Jacinto in April 1836.

Since that time, Texas has had its own constitution. We have had our own president and made our own rules. Every time I see the Texas flag, I remember how proud we should all be. The one white star on a red, white and blue background symbolizes that Texas is a "Lone Star Republic." Now that flag will fly below the U.S. flag.

Pa said many people probably cheered when the Texas flag was lowered and the U.S. flag was raised. Texas needs the money and the protection the United States can give. I know Texas might not be able to stand strong on its own right now. Like many other people though, I feel sad that the Republic of Texas is no longer. I just hope the Mexicans can accept that the United States is calling Texas its own.

title: The United States Fights Mexico for Land
text:
The United States Fights Mexico for Land

The idea of Manifest Destiny was not a new one for the United States by the 19th century. After the United States purchased the Louisiana territory and Lewis and Clark explored and mapped the wilderness, many Americans wanted the chance to own land. They excitedly headed into the new territory to build homes, businesses and settlements. The people thought it was their job to spread their way of life as far as they could, even if it meant pushing people aside who were there first.

By the early 1800s, Americans heard about new land that Mexico held in the Southwest. Mexico was eager to have Anglo settlers. Officials were almost giving land in Texas away. Americans began moving into Texas by the thousands and by 1830, more than 20,000 Anglos had settled in the area. Though they had agreed to become Mexican citizens, many of the settlers never let go of the idea of Manifest Destiny. They became very upset that the Mexican government demanded they give up their own ways of living.

Texas as a Republic

The Texans ended up declaring their independence, and they fought a war with Mexico. From 1836-1845, Texas was an independent republic. They had defeated Mexico, but the Mexican culture lived on through the food, the customs, the names of the cities and the architecture of the buildings. Even though it was once a source of discord (disagreement), the Spanish language and Catholic religion are still very much a part of the Texas tradition today.

To Annex or Not?

Without the ability to raise money or form a powerful army, Texas turned to the United States for help. The answer was annexation. There were great debates about whether Texas should become part of the United States. Slavery was allowed in Texas, and many Northerners did not want another slave state. Also, the United States would have to take on the debts (money owed) that Texas had piled up. In the end, the United States decided to annex (join with) Texas, and Texas became the 28th state. The United States now had a very large state with an abundance (large amount) of excellent land with many resources.

Mexico Changes Its Mind

Mexico began to rethink its decision to give up so easily on Texas. The Mexican government suddenly wanted Texas back. The two countries did not agree on the southwestern boundary of Texas. Americans wanted the Rio Grande to be the border, but Mexico wanted it to be about 150 miles further northeast. This would greatly decrease the size of Texas. Tension grew between the neighboring countries.

The War is On!

The argument over the boundary of Texas continued. In 1846, U.S. President Polk sent the Army to protect the Rio Grande. The Mexicans tried to defend the land against U.S. General Zachary Taylor and his men. There was a small battle at Palo Alto, Texas. President Polk then went before the U.S. Congress and asked the members to declare war. The Mexican-American War began two days later on May 13, 1846.

The war continued for nearly two years. Many Americans were against the war. Some people felt the annexation of Texas would lead to war, and now they could say, "We told you so." People felt the United States was being too greedy for land. Others supported President Polk's war. They felt that the land was their Manifest Destiny, and many people joined the army to fight against the Mexicans. They fought to take land that they believed it was their right to have.

The battles were deadly as both sides fought fiercely. General Zachary Taylor led American troops into Mexico City. Even after they captured the capital, Mexico continued to fight. Soldiers also fought battles in Texas and California.

Mexico Surrenders

Mexico finally surrendered. In February 1848, officials signed the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo and ended the war. Mexico ceded (gave up) a great deal of territory. In fact, the country gave up about 55 percent of all its territory at the time. The United States now owned the entire present-day states of California, Nevada and Utah, as well as most of Arizona and New Mexico. They also got small parts of four other states. Mexico finally agreed that the Rio Grande would be the southern border of Texas. The United States agreed to pay Mexico $15 million for the cession.

After the War

Approximately 14,000 Americans lost their lives in the war. Nearly double that number of Mexicans were killed. But the end of the war did not end the bad feelings between the two countries. For many years, the two nations did not get along with one another and often fought in skirmishes (small battles).

The end of the Mexican-American War also brought many changes both to the nation and to people living in the Southwest. Americans poured into the new territories. They wanted to farm, ranch and mine for valuable metals and minerals. People began new settlements. Unfortunately, these newcomers did not always treat the people already living there very well. They treated many American Indians and former Mexican citizens very poorly. Sometimes Americans took over land that other people had already claimed. It's likely that not everyone agreed with the idea of Manifest Destiny. Who might have thought it was a bad idea? Why?

title: The Gadsden Purchase
text:
Five years after the end of the Mexican-American war, the United States set its sights on one additional piece of land. This strip of land was just south of the Gila River in present-day Arizona and New Mexico. It was the perfect pass through the mountains. A railroad system could easily be built to reach the Gulf of California. Mexico needed the money that the sale of the land would provide, so officials from the United States and Mexico began talks.

The U.S. Minister to Mexico, James Gadsden, helped put the deal together. The U.S. Congress agreed to pay Mexico $10 million for an amount of land that was about as big as the state of Pennsylvania. That was a lot of money for such a small area of land. Remember, Mexico got $15 million for about 55 percent of its territory it ceded to the United States after the war.

But the Gadsden Purchase made many Mexicans angry. They did not want to lose all claims to land north of the Rio Grande. The people were so angry that they removed General Santa Anna as dictator and banished him from the country. He was forced to leave Mexico forever. The Mexican people no longer trusted James Gadsden either. The United States had to replace him as minister to Mexico. Unfortunately, Gadsden died before workers completed the railroad route. But the Gadsden Purchase made it possible for railroad systems to begin criss-crossing the continent.

title: Forty-Niners Hit the Gold Mines
text:
In 1848, the Mexican-American War ended. At just about the same time, people discovered gold in the Sierra Nevada Mountains of California. Soon, news of the discovery spread to the United States. Even people in Europe and Asia heard about the possible chance to find a fortune. Suddenly forty-niners (people who rushed to California in 1849 to find gold) were leaving everything behind to head for the hills where they hoped to get rich quickly. The gold rush was on!

Miners found much of their treasure in rivers. They often spent long days panning for gold. First they scooped up dirt and rock from the riverbed in a large pan. Next, the miners swirled the pan around in the river water. Heavy gold would stay at the bottom of the pan while dirt and small rocks floated away.

Life for the miners was hard and lonely. Small communities began to form near large mining areas. However, miners often lived alone in tents or run-down cabins. Sometimes they did not have enough money to buy food or supplies. They often worked many days without finding any gold at all in their claims. A claim was the area of land in which each miner worked. Each miner had the right to all of the gold he found in his claim. Some of the forty-niners became very rich from the gold they found, but most of the miners gave up hope after a while. They returned home just as poor as when they had come to California.

At the end of the gold rush, many of the miners stayed in California. Some went to work for the railroads while others opened businesses or began farming. Many of them found more success after the rush ended.

title: Cause and Effect
text: Complete the cause and effect activity below using what you learned from this week’s Studies Weekly. Write in complete sentences.

title: Writing from First Person Point of View
text: Writers often write in different points of view. They use first person point of view when “I” or “we” act as the narrator. Read “The Annexation of Texas” on Page 1 for an example of first person point of view. Now, pretend you lived in Texas during the time of the revolution and U. S. annexation. Write your own life story using first person point of view. Be sure to support all of your ideas with facts and details.

title: An American Artist: George Catlin
text:
George Catlin was a painter whose artwork is a primary source that helps us learn about history. He painted many pictures of American Indians. Catlin started painting American Indians because he thought the details of their lives should be remembered. He was worried that all the American Indians would die. He traveled west, visiting and painting about 50 American Indian tribes. He was very observant during his many explorations. Catlin sketched the Comanche in Oklahoma often. He did drawings of them playing stickball. He was also fascinated with the way the American Indians hunted in Oklahoma. He made paintings of them hunting buffalo in the Wichita Mountains. Catlin made an "Indian Gallery" of over 600 paintings and more than 700 sketches. His works tell us about the everyday lives of Plains Indians in the 1800s.

George Catlin didn't just paint. He also wrote books and told people about American Indians. He worked for the rights of American Indians. He said they should not be moved from their lands. He tried to get U.S. leaders to listen to him and buy his paintings. The leaders didn't purchase these "Indian Gallery" paintings, but a rich man named Joseph Harrison did. After Harrison died, his wife gave over 500 of Catlin's paintings to the Smithsonian American Art Museum in Washington, D.C. People say Catlin's paintings are important sources of American history. Since he was an explorer recording firsthand observations, his paintings are primary sources.

Look at two paintings of American Indians. List three important things you observe about American Indians from these paintings. What do you think the large group of American Indians is doing? What is the American Indian chief holding? What do the paintings make you think about? What do you wonder when you look at the paintings?

Look at the self-portrait of George Catlin. If you could ask him three questions about each of these paintings, what would you ask?

title: American Progress
text:
You may have heard the saying “a picture is worth a thousand words.” That statement is especially true when you look at a painting called American Progress. It was painted in 1872 by John Gast. He was asked to create it by a man who published travel guides for people going west. This painting was included in many of the travel guides he published. Many people saw it, and the painting became a symbol of westward expansion in the United States. Here are some questions to guide you as you examine this picture and how it reflects what was happening in America at that time.

The angel is bringing the light from the East to the West. How does this relate to the title of the painting?

The angel is carrying a schoolbook in one hand and a telegraph wire in her other hand. What might these two objects represent in this painting? How do they relate to each other?

On the “west” side of the painting, how are people getting places? What is coming from the East that represents progress? How will this change the lives of the different people represented in the painting?

Focus on the group of American Indians in the painting. What clues can you find that might show how the settlers’ movement west is affecting them? Explain your thinking.

The two groups of men in the foreground of the painting represent two different reasons some people moved west. Look at their clothing and tools. Identify who they represent and why they would want to move west.

The word “progress” means movement toward a goal. Analyze how this definition supports the painting’s title and imagery.

Choose one element of the painting and write a paragraph about what it represents and how it was connected to the future of America.

title: Westward Ho!
text:
By the mid-1800s, thousands of Americans had been encouraged to move westward. Western land was cheap and families needed very little money to build homes and start farms or ranches. Word spread through books, magazines and newspapers that the West was full of possibilities. After the discovery of gold in California in 1848, even more people raced west for the chance to earn their fortunes and live out their dreams. Even people from other countries wanted the opportunity for a better life in the American West.

Unfortunately, not everyone found westward expansion to be a positive experience. For many American Indians already living in the West, the expansion brought disruption, great hardship and even tragedy.

At first, the United States tried to maintain good relationships with the American Indian tribes who lived in the West. Both sides often signed treaties, or agreements. However, the settlers who were moving west often broke these agreements. Sometimes they took land from the American Indians. Many tribes lost land that had been their home for hundreds of years.

Settlers also seemed to have little respect for the American Indians' need for the buffalo. Tribes of the Great Plains depended on the buffalo for food, clothing, shelter and tools. White settlers hunted the buffalo herds and often disturbed their migration patterns. The settlers only wanted the hides for trade and didn't use any other part of the animal. It angered American Indians when they would find buffalo carcasses (dead bodies) rotting in the heat.

Some tribes tried to cooperate with the settlers. Other tribes were angered by such poor treatment and often fought back against the settlers. Workers also built railroads through American Indian territory. By the late 1800s, the United States had decided to try and remove all American Indians from their own lands in the West and place them on land in Oklahoma and South Dakota. The idea of living on government reservations made many tribes even angrier. The United States fought battles with the Sioux, the Nez Perce and the Navajo tribes. Many tribe members and U.S. soldiers were killed or injured. The tribes who were forced to live on reservations faced great problems, and many American Indians died of starvation or disease.

So the opportunities in the West held very little promise for American Indians. The anger and bad feelings between the U.S. government and American Indians continued well into the next century.

title: New People Come to a New Country
text:
Imagine packing up everything you own, traveling on a ship for months and beginning a new life in a different country. That is just what 60 million people around the world did from the early 1800s to 1930. About half of those people immigrated into the United States. Why would people choose to leave their home country? Well, there are many reasons. In the early 1800s, most immigrants to the United States came to find economic opportunity. In America, they had the chance to own land, homes and businesses. They could also work to make their family's lives better. People came to the United States from countries all over the world during the 1800s, especially Europe and Asia. There were large groups of immigrants from Ireland, Germany and China and they usually arrived by ship. Let's read and learn about some of their experiences.

Immigrants from Ireland

Life in Ireland during the 19th century was very difficult. There was a great deal of disease and starvation. The people were very poor. Poverty made many Irish citizens long to start a new life in America. But most were sad to leave their beautiful homeland.

The new life in America was not so easy either. Poor Irish were often forced to live in tenement houses. These run-down apartments were dirty, cold and dangerous, but they were affordable. Most Irish immigrants did not have money to move on to other cities, so they often stayed in the city where their ship had first landed. Many of the immigrants had been unsuccessful farmers in Ireland and did not wish to farm again. Instead, they wanted to work in factories in the cities. However, many employers looked down on the poor Irish immigrants. They spoke differently and couldn't read. Sometimes they were thought to be angry and even dangerous. Often signs hung in business windows saying, "No Irish Need Apply."

The Irish immigrants did not give up. They helped each other survive city life. Their strong beliefs in the Catholic Church helped keep them close. Most of the men were actually ready and willing to work at the hard and dangerous jobs America needed. Many Irish men worked to build bridges, canals and railroads. Many also became police officers. Irish women found jobs as housekeepers and hotel cleaners. The signs in the business windows soon disappeared. The Irish immigrants proved they were smart and hard working. Each year when Irish-Americans in the United States celebrate St. Patrick's Day it is a reminder of how important the Irish immigrants have been to this country.

German Immigrants Find New Lives

Germans also faced hardships in their country during the 19th century. The German government was not very stable (secure) and taxes were very high. In addition, there was a lot of violence throughout the country. Germany seemed to be constantly at war with its neighbors. Many Germans immigrated to other countries to find better ways of life. While many Germans were sad to leave their homeland, they were also happy to be able to have a chance to live in peace.

Some Germans stayed in the first large U.S. city they visited. New York City and cities in Pennsylvania had large groups of German settlers as citizens. However, unlike the Irish immigrants, most Germans did not want to live in cities when they arrived in the United States. Many of them had saved money for a new life. They wanted to find land to settle that reminded them of the beautiful land they had left behind. Many German communities began after people migrated to the Midwest in search of good farmland. Those Germans who chose not to farm found work as bakers, butchers, cabinetmakers and tailors. German women who worked outside the home found jobs as bakers, nurses, housecleaners and tailors. Most Germans practiced the Catholic or Lutheran religions. Along with the Irish, their culture and religion helped keep them together.

German immigrants had an easier time fitting into the U.S. culture than the Irish did. Most Germans were skilled craftspeople and farmers. Many of them supported public education and spoke out against slavery. They seemed to have a lot in common with Americans. German difficulties came later in the early 20th century when much of the world feared Germany's leaders during World War I and World War II.

Chinese Immigrants

Tales of California gold reached China in 1851. Within one year, 25,000 Chinese immigrants had sailed to California to look for their own treasure. Most of these were poor people who hoped to get rich and return to China to buy farmland for their families.

When the Chinese arrived, they worked hard to invent new methods and tools for collecting hard-to-find gold. Some of the American miners in the area became jealous of their success. They often threatened the Chinese miners or used violence against them. The government also taxed the foreign miners.

Many of the Chinese immigrants found work building the first transcontinental railroad. They laid tracks across the United States. They were very good workers. Still, life was hard for the Chinese. They often received less pay for longer hours of work in very dangerous conditions. After the railroad was completed, many of the Chinese decided to stay in America. They worked as farmers and fishers. They opened stores and restaurants.

Some Americans didn't welcome the Chinese, partly because they looked different. They did not understand the Chinese culture or language, and they wanted the Chinese to leave America. Many Chinese were treated very badly and some were even murdered. In 1882, the U.S. government passed a law to keep Chinese people from immigrating into the country. For many years, the Chinese Exclusion Act made it much harder for people to come to America from China to live and work.

title: Liberty Enlightening the World
text:
The Statue of Liberty is often the first thing a U.S. immigrant sees of America. The amazing sculpture stands 151 feet and one inch high in the air (top of base to torch). It was given to the United States of America by the country of France in 1884.

A group of Frenchmen wanted to give the U.S. people a gift that would honor the democracy of the country. French sculptor Frederic-Auguste Bartholdi was chosen to design a statue. He imagined a huge sculpture of a woman holding a torch burning with the light of freedom. He created "Liberty Enlightening the World," also known as the Statue of Liberty.

For 21 years, the French people raised money to build the statue. In 1884, "Lady Liberty" was presented to the American people in a French ceremony. The statue was taken apart, placed in crates and shipped across the Atlantic Ocean for people to rebuild on Liberty Island in New York City. Americans paid for and built the pedestal for the statue to stand on. A poem called "The New Colossus" is found on a plaque at the statue's base. Its words have greeted millions of immigrants who have come to the United States to find freedom and a new life. Here are some of those words:

... Give me your tired, your poor,
Your huddled masses yearning
to breathe free, The wretched refuse of your
teeming shore,
Send these, the homeless,
tempest-tossed to me,
I lift my lamp beside the golden door!
- Emma Lazarus, New York City, 1883

title: What is the best way to solve a problem?
text:
A problem is best handled with clear thinking. Here are six steps you can use the next time you have to find a solution to a problem.

Step One: Identify the problem - What issue needs to be solved?

Step Two: Gather information - What are all the facts about the situation?

Step Three: List and consider options - What are all the ways the problem can be solved?

Step Four: Think about the advantages and disadvantages of each option - What are the good and bad things about all the possible solutions?

Step Five: Choose a solution - What is the best way to solve the problem? Put the plan into action!

Step Six: Was the solution successful? - How well did the solution work? Should the same type of problem be solved a different way next time?

title: I Pledge Allegiance…
text:
A pledge is a promise, and allegiance is another word for loyalty. By reciting the Pledge of Allegiance each day, U.S. citizens are promising to remain faithful and true to our nation. The pledge is a reminder that every American, regardless of his or her race, religion or color, should be treated fairly under the laws of the nation.

Francis Bellamy, a Baptist minister from New York, wrote the Pledge of Allegiance. People first spoke the pledge at a special ceremony to honor the 400th anniversary of Columbus Day in 1892. A few changes have been made to the words over the years, but the ideas remain the same.

"I pledge Allegiance to the flag of the United States of America and to the Republic for which it stands, one nation under God, indivisible, with Liberty and Justice for all."

title: Writing Focus: Expository/Comparing and Contrasting
text: Pretend you write for a history magazine. You have just received an assignment to write about people who immigrated to the United States during the 19th century. Write an article comparing and contrasting immigrants from Ireland and Germany in the 1800s. Think of three ways they are similar and three ways they are different. Be sure to support your ideas with details from this week’s Studies Weekly. When you are finished, check your work for correct grammar, punctuation and spelling.

title: The Face of a Migrant Mother
text:
Florence Owens Thompson was a young mother during the Great Depression in the 1930s. Droughts, poor farming practices, and not having enough information about the environment led to the Dust Bowl. Because of this, Thompson’s family had lost nearly everything. She and thousands of other Oklahomans moved to California to look for work. They made it west, but Thompson and her seven children were nearly starving. She moved around California, picking vegetables to earn money for food. However, their car broke down near some pea fields. A freezing rain had damaged the crop. There was no work to be found. They were hungry, sad, and worried. Can you see all of that on this mother's face?

Dorothea Lange was a photographer who worked for the Farm Security Administration. Part of her job was to take pictures of people who were struggling with poverty (being poor). One day, Lange saw a sign that said "Pea-Pickers Camp." She drove there and found Thompson with her children sitting under a tent.

Lange took pictures of Thompson and her family. These were later printed in a San Francisco newspaper. She also sent them to Washington, D.C. No one knew who Thompson was, but the photos helped show officials what people like her were going through. In a few days, the U.S. government sent 20,000 pounds of food to the camp, but by then, Florence and her family had moved on.

The photo of Florence Thompson was called "Migrant Mother" because a migrant is someone who moves around often. No one knew the mystery woman's name until 1978, when Thompson and her family identified themselves. "Migrant Mother" was even used on a U.S. postage stamp in 1998. It is one of the most famous photographs taken in the 1930s.

title: American Indian Contributions to American Culture
text:
Government

Did you know that some American Indians had a form of government very similar to the one we use today? Benjamin Franklin said that the idea of a strong federal government came from the Iroquois League of Nations. The Iroquois League of Nations was made up of six Iroquois groups. They joined together to form a central government. The government had a council that made decisions to keep peace between the nations. The League of Nations also had a written constitution, or a set of rights and agreements that all members of the league agreed to obey. Similarly, the U.S. government today is based on a written constitution and a legislature with representatives from each state.

Arts

Many people enjoy and display American Indian artwork. It is beautiful and usually made from natural materials. Pottery and ceramics are made of clay. Beads are made of bone and seeds, while rugs and baskets are woven from dried plants or strips of wool and hides. Many of today's artists get ideas for their creations from the natural beauty of American Indian artwork.

Foods

Some of our most popular foods come from American Indian culture. Most American Indian diets were based on the "Three Sisters," or corn, beans, and squash. Corn was eaten fresh or dried and used to make tortillas, cornbread, and cornmeal mush. Beans were eaten with most meals. Squash was made into soups and stews. All three "sisters" were often combined to make a dish called succotash. American Indians also grew potatoes, peanuts, pumpkins, tomatoes, peppers, and melons.

Ecology

Ecology is the study of how living things interact with their environment. Today, most people are very concerned about how our lives impact the world around us. Respect for nature was simply a way of life for all American Indians. They tried to respect all forms of life and all parts of nature. They didn't kill animals unless they needed them to survive. They also believed that all things, including the Earth, have a spirit and that we must all try to live in harmony with nature. This idea lives on today in conservation and preservation programs.

Language

Early settlers and trappers interacted with the American Indians. They began using many of their words to describe plants, animals, and places that they had never seen before. Many of the words and place names we use today come from American Indian words used hundreds of years ago. Some of these words are listed here:

• caribou

• woodchuck

• toboggan

• pecan

• skunk

• moccasin

• Wichita

From arts to food to language, American Indian culture is a big part of American culture!

title: A Growing New World
text:
Imagine that you’re moving to a new place to live. Your bags are packed. You’re ready to go. You’re excited to start a new life in your new home. But you’re not moving to another city or even another state. You’re moving to a new country. That’s happening all over the world today. Immigrants everywhere move from one nation to another to start new lives in different places.

Many immigrants move from nations in the east to countries in the Western Hemisphere. Some of the places they move to are the United Kingdom, the United States, Argentina, and Canada. The United States has a larger population of immigrants than any other nation in the world. More than 44 million immigrants live here. They make up 13.5 percent of the population.

People move to the United States from all over the world, including other parts of North America. People also come here from European and Asian nations. They move to the United States for different reasons. Some come here to escape war or harsh leaders. Others come here to find work or go to school.

Immigrants settle in different parts of the country. California has the highest number of immigrants. Almost 11 million people who live there came from another country. Many of them moved there for work. California offers opportunities in many industries, from farming to filmmaking. Other states with a high number of immigrants include New York, New Jersey, Florida, and Nevada.

Those are not the only states with large immigrant populations, however. For example, many immigrants live in Texas. They moved to Texas looking for work in different areas, including in the gas and oil industry. Immigrants also move to Texas because the cost of living can be low. The “cost of living” is the amount of money a person needs to survive. It includes how much you pay for food, a place to live, clothes, and so on.

The immigrants who live and work in the United States help add to our economy. They pay for goods and services. They pay taxes to the government too. As more and more immigrants travel to our shores, our world continues to grow.

title: The Indian Removal Act
text:
By the early 1800s, conflict between European settlers and American Indians was nothing new. As settlers moved westward, violence happened more and more.

Trying to Get Along

The colonists tried to get along with the American Indians, but there were many conflicts. In the late 1700s, colonists signed peace treaties with the Cherokee. One agreement stated that “the hatchet” was “forever buried.” Peace and friendship were restored, but it didn’t last. When Georgia became one of the new 13 states, more people moved in, onto the land that once belonged to American Indians. Georgia was a great place to grow cotton, which was a very popular crop worldwide. However, more land was needed to grow it, so the American Indians were pushed off the land they lived on.

By the early 1800s, the Cherokee felt they were being cheated and treated badly. Their hunting grounds were taken. Roads were built through their land. Their way of life nearly disappeared. In 1827, the Cherokee Nation was formed. They wrote a constitution and elected a president and a council. They created a police force and had a capital city. They hoped this would encourage the settlers to treat them better.

Settlers had heard about gold in the Appalachian Mountains for hundreds of years. They saw American Indians wearing gold, and then they found gold in northern Georgia, along rivers. The first real gold rush started in 1829. A newspaper story told of gold mines in Habersham. This was great news for miners. Unfortunately, the land where the gold was found belonged to the Cherokee Nation. This put more pressure on the Cherokee, who wanted to stay in their homeland.

President Andrew Jackson

In 1829, Andrew Jackson became President of the United States. He was from Tennessee and had become wealthy by growing and selling cotton. During the War of 1812, a major conflict between white settlers and Creek Indians broke out. Jackson led a volunteer militia against the Creek and won. The Creek were no longer able to defend themselves, and they were forced to give up much of their land. Later, Jackson led his soldiers to a major victory, when his men defeated the British at the Battle of New Orleans. Jackson became a war hero. That reputation paved his way into the White House. A few years later, Jackson fought the Seminole tribe in Florida. By the time he was elected president, he already had a long history of forcing tribes out of their homelands.

Digging Up the Hatchet

Even more people came in search of gold. This gold rush was known as the “Great Intrusion,” but it was seen as an invasion. The Cherokee thought the miners were trespassing. They tried to fight the miners in court and on the land, but they didn't succeed. In 1828, Georgians decided to deal with the American Indians on their own. They passed laws that took away the rights of the Cherokee. The Supreme Court said that Georgia couldn’t do this, but they did it anyway.

In 1830, as President of the United States, Jackson encouraged the U.S. Congress to pass the Indian Removal Act. This act allowed President Jackson to force American Indians from their lands. The Supreme Court ruled that the Cherokee Nation was its own nation and could not be removed. The president ignored the Supreme Court's ruling and did it anyway. The Cherokee Nation was promised $5 million if they would move to the Indian Territory. Some agreed to go. Others fought back. The Cherokee were forced to walk to Oklahoma. Many died on this trip, known as the Trail of Tears. Some Cherokee hid in the mountains of northern Georgia instead of leaving.

title: The Story of a Nation
text:
A nation is made up of its people. The people who have come to the United States, the ways they have come, and the histories they bring with them all contribute to our nation’s story.

The First Americans

Some people came to this land thousands of years ago, even before people started writing down histories. These groups, later called American Indians, transformed wild plants into crops we depend on, like corn, potatoes, and tomatoes. They created trade routes many of our highways still follow. American Indians have their own nations, but they also helped build up cities and states throughout the country. They have served in the military in every U.S. war. They perform all sorts of jobs, from school teacher to astronaut.

Exploring and Crossing the Atlantic Ocean

Over 500 years ago, Europe started sending explorers to the Americas. Traders, missionaries, conquistadors, and colonizers followed. These people sailed across the Atlantic. It was a slow, expensive journey. Many came from Spain, France, the Netherlands, the British Isles, and Germany. During the American Revolution, many fought for rights and freedom in their new homes. They made new laws and a new government. Over time, they set up the nation’s banking and school systems.

The Slave Trade

Some early members of our nation did not choose to come. From the 1500s to the 1800s, many people in Africa were kidnapped, chained, packed into crowded ships, brought to America, and forced to work as slaves. Enslaved people built much of the country, including many of the buildings in the U.S. capital.

Some managed to escape. Many spread word about their desire to be free. Some fought in the Civil War to help end slavery in the United States. While most lived in the South at first, many African Americans later moved north or west and affected the history of those places. For example, about one in four cowboys was Black. The invention of jazz music had an impact on American and global culture. Though continued mistreatment made their lives difficult, African Americans built businesses, developed culture, and fought to expand rights for themselves and other Americans.

Crossing the Southern Border and the Caribbean Sea

In 1847, the United States fought a war with Mexico. The United States gained new territory, and the border moved south. Many cities and states between the old and new borders still have names that come from the Spanish language. People kept moving north and south across the new border. Many people have also come to the United States from islands in the Caribbean.

Many people who came north to the United States worked on farms, providing food for the whole country. Others immigrated to big cities. People from Latin America helped build this nation in all kinds of professions, from scientist to Supreme Court justice. Recipes from Mexico in particular have had a huge influence on how Americans eat. Like other groups, Latinos have fought for rights and freedom here.

Crossing the Pacific

The Pacific Ocean is much wider than the Atlantic, but people still crossed it to come to the United States. Many workers from China arrived in the mid-1800s to build the first railroad across the United States. Some of the first immigrants from India came to help build the Panama Canal, then moved to California to farm. Other people from Asia and the Pacific Islands came to find work or escape fighting in their own countries. Many helped with specific needs, like medical care in the United States.

Crossing the Atlantic, Faster

By the late 1800s, transportation across the Atlantic was faster and cheaper. Huge numbers of people from southern and eastern Europe and southwest Asia came to the United States by steamship. Many came from poverty and worked hard to take advantage of new opportunities. They helped build America’s biggest cities into famous places. Many were Catholics and Jews who brought their religious traditions with them.

Crossing the Globe

Each group that has come to the United States and fought for rights has helped prepare the way for others. From all around the world, people continue to come to the United States. They come by boat, airplane, car, and even by foot. Some flee war, poverty, or other dangers. Some search for education, work, or other opportunities. Every new person, tradition, or idea becomes part of our story.

title: Industry vs. Agriculture
text:
The United States had grown a great deal by the beginning of the 1800s. Many people still lived on the eastern coast, but many also settled in the West and South. Settlers developed different ways of living in different areas of the country. People made money in various ways and lived in different types of homes. They also began to differ in their ways of thinking about topics such as slavery and states' rights. By the middle of the 19th century, Northerners and Southerners probably felt as though they were living in two separate countries.

Economic Differences

One difference between the two parts of the country was in the way people made money. The economies of the North and South led to bad feelings between the people who lived in some parts of the country.

For many years, people in the United States had made their livings in agriculture. Most families farmed and raised animals. In fact, about three-fourths of the country's population lived on farms in rural areas before the 1800s. However, the industrial revolution that spread from England to America had changed all of that.

Northern Economy

A growing system of manufacturing plants (factories) was very promising in the Northern states. People could find good jobs and support their families. Work in the factories was usually hard and often dangerous, but employers paid the workers a steady wage for their services. Immigrants from Europe and Asia also came to the North to work in the factories. By 1860, Northern cities were growing quickly. Much of the country's population lived and worked in the North. People also found jobs building new roads and railroads so that goods from factories could be shipped to other places. The Northern economy was strong.

Southern Economy

Life in the South was very different from that in the North. People in this region still made their livings mostly from agriculture, especially cotton. In fact, most Southerners depended on cotton for all of their income. After the invention of the cotton gin, people could harvest large amounts of cotton. But cotton plantations depended heavily on free slave labor. Though a lot of families did not own enslaved people on their small family-run farms, many people in the South accepted the idea of forcing African Americans into slavery. By 1860, there were about 4 million enslaved people in the South. About half of them were forced to work on large cotton plantations. The economy of the South grew rapidly as cotton production increased. Cotton was often shipped to the North, and Northerners sold tools and other manufactured goods to Southern farmers.

To Tax or Not to Tax

The economies of these two areas were not the only differences that became clear in the mid-1800s. The Northern industrial economy depended on reliable transportation systems to ship goods in and out of the region. This meant workers needed good roads and railroads.

Northerners supported tariffs (special taxes on imported goods) to pay for those systems. Tariffs went directly to the government. High tariffs meant that goods produced in the North would be cheaper to buy than heavily taxed goods from Europe or Asia. Northern factories would make lots of money. Southerners generally wanted low tariffs. The South produced very few products on its own. Southerners had to import most manufactured goods from the North or overseas. If tariffs were high, then their cost of purchasing goods would also be high.

Slavery: the Great Difference

When the Founding Fathers wrote the Declaration of Independence in 1776, the phrase "all men are created equal" was an important idea. Yet that idea didn't seem to apply to thousands of enslaved people who were living in the colonies.

Enslaved people were first brought to North America in the 1500s. Over the years, nearly 10 million Africans were brought by ship to the United States. In the South, enslaved people were sold at slave auctions. The enslaved people were considered property that could be bought, sold or traded at any time. Enslaved people had no rights and were not allowed to own property, marry or learn to read or write.

Some enslaved people lived in cities, but most lived and worked on Southern plantations. The work was very hard on the large farms. Often the enslaved people were treated very badly. Most of them had to work from sunup to sundown every day. They were often sold to different plantations, which broke families apart.

By the mid-1800s, slavery was against the law in the Northern United States. Southern states that made their money with cotton continued to allow slavery. Slavery was thought to be one of the most important parts of the Southern economy.

In 1860, people in the North and people in the South did not share the same idea about slavery at all. Southerners wanted new states in the country to allow slavery. Northerners wanted slavery to be against the law all over the United States. The differences between the North and the South became more distinct than ever before, and those differences would soon change the nation forever.

title: John Deere
text:
Much of the success of cotton plantations in the South was because of Eli Whitney's development of the cotton gin in 1793. But Whitney was not the only man whose ideas led to America's agricultural successes in the 1800s. America's farms also owe a great deal of gratitude to a man named John Deere. This blacksmith left his home in Vermont in 1836 to start a new life in Illinois. After making the journey with only $73, he rented land and quickly opened up a new blacksmith shop. He hoped to make enough money to bring his wife and children from Vermont to live with him.

Local farmers in his shop often complained about how hard it was to break up the soil with regular plows. One day in 1837, John saw a broken saw blade at the mill. He asked the owner if he could have it. Within days, John Deere had invented a steel plow with the blade. The tool made it much easier for farmers to cut and turn over the hard prairie ground. Farmers everywhere heard of the new product. Within a few years, John Deere was selling 1,600 steel plows every year. American farmers could more easily plant and harvest crops.

John Deere was an excellent businessperson. He was always trying to find new ways to make better products for farmers. He often loaded plows onto wagons and took them to sell from farm to farm. People were impressed with his dedication and hard work. John Deere's company, Deere & Company, is a successful American tool business, even today.

title: Enslaved Families
text:
Enslaved Families

Enslaved people were considered the property of the man they had to call their master, or owner. This was true of enslaved children, too. For most enslaved children, life was difficult, sad and lonely. A law passed in the late 1600s said that all children would have the same level of freedom as their mother. That meant if an African American woman was enslaved, then all of her children were enslaved as well.

Some enslaved families were separated. Fathers, mothers and children were sometimes sold to different plantation owners. However, some children were allowed to stay with their mother. If the mother of a child worked as an enslaved person in the plantation fields, then the child usually worked in the fields as well. Young children were often expected to work all day in the hot sun. But if the mother worked as a house servant, then the enslaved children might be kept inside also. Enslaved children sometimes played with the white children of the plantation owners. But enslaved children weren't allowed to attend school because most enslaved people were not allowed to learn to read or write.

Life was especially hard for enslaved children. They often lived in small, dirty cabins that were either very cold or very hot. Most enslaved people had very little clothing or food and were often punished very cruelly. Enslaved people had little or no medical care, and diseases such as malaria often took their lives. Many of these children died before even reaching adulthood.

The enslaved people bonded together to help each other deal with their terrible treatment. Children often gathered in the evenings with the adults to tell stories and sing songs. Enslaved adults sometimes taught the children how to survive and avoid punishment from cruel masters. They used religion as a way to help them find the will to survive, which was a true test for enslaved people of all ages.

title: Population Charting
text:
In the 1800s, the North and South were very different places to live. A manufacturing economy along with a large population of immigrants caused a growth in urban (city) development in the North. Because most people in the South lived and work on farms and plantations, it was known as a rural (country) population. The table shows the largest U.S. cities in 1860. Find and circle the 10 largest cities in 1860 on the U.S. map. Then use the information from the table and map to answer the questions on a separate piece of paper.

2. Why do you think these cities were in the top 10 in population?

3. Which city on the table is located in the South?

4. What do you know about this city that would support its place in the top 10 most populated cities?

5. What common geographic features do you notice about the 10 most populated U.S. cities in 1860?
