title: Separate, Yet Interdependent
text:
Separate, Yet Interdependent

During the 19th century, the United States faced many great challenges. The country was separated by many different factors. These differences were strong enough to cause distrust between the Northern states and the Southern states. The United States didn’t seem very united at the time.

Economies

The economy in the North was based mainly on industry while the economy in the South was based mainly on agriculture. However, the North depended on agriculture from the South and the South depended on manufactured goods from the North. Farmers in the South needed tools and machine parts that were manufactured in the North. People who filled the cities in the North depended on the Southern crops for food and clothing.

Since the Southern states were mostly agricultural, they were labor intensive. Many people were needed to plant, grow and harvest agricultural products. The South relied mainly on enslaved people to provide this labor. As a result, the institution of slavery caused a serious division between the North and the South.

Political

Both sides had different ideas on the direction the country should go. Northern states wanted to abolish slavery and keep the country united. Southern states wanted to have the freedom to make their own decisions regarding slavery and considered those decisions states’ rights. There were many disagreements about whether the federal government or the individual states should have more power.

The struggle between the states was growing in intensity. The United States relied on both agriculture and industry, but the states were becoming more divided than ever.

title: Northern Industrialization Stirs Conflict
text:
The Antebellum Era was the time between the end of the War of 1812 and the beginning of the Civil War in 1865. Look at the map showing the connection between the labor of enslaved people and cotton production. Identify the states that are in the South. What do you notice about the economies in this area? How does it differ from those in the North? Think about how these economic differences might have led to conflict between these two sections of the United States.

In 1790, the first American textile mill was built in Rhode Island. Previously, cotton fabric was created in English mills and imported to America. Now cotton grown in the South could be turned into textiles on a large scale in the North.

Eight years later, Eli Whitney introduced the concept of interchangeable parts. Interchangeable parts were separate parts of a product that could be manufactured in mass (large quantities). Previously, each product was made individually. After Eli Whitney’s innovation, the separately manufactured parts could be put together to create identical products. Canals and railroads were constructed across the North to transport the finished goods to markets and ports. This meant that the manufacture of products could be done more quickly and in greater quantities. This is called mass production. These ideas led to rapid growth in the number of mills and factories built in the North. The workers in these mills and factories were often immigrants and young women who came to mill towns from rural farming communities. However, these workers often had to deal with long working hours, low pay, and hazardous working conditions.

What was the South like during this time? While the Northeast was going through major changes during the Industrial Revolution, the South was also changing. Unlike the North, economic development in the South was based on agriculture, which was going through its own transformation.

The South had traditionally been a place of farms, with a population that was spread out. While these farms grew food, they also grew cash crops like tobacco and cotton. During the Antebellum Era, the number of plantations or farms with large fields increased. Many began to focus on cotton since demand for it in the North had increased. While it was labor-intensive to grow and pick, cotton was also very profitable. So, the plantation owners used enslaved African workers to do the hard work. The invention of the cotton gin sped up the process of separating the seeds from the cotton. The amount of cotton that enslaved workers could process increased, which made the plantations even more profitable. As a result, plantations grew in size and increased the demand for enslaved workers.

Not all plantations used enslaved workers. In fact, only about 25 percent (the larger plantations) needed them to help with their farms. Regardless, the population of enslaved people grew during the Antebellum Era. The economy of the South became more and more dependent on this enslaved labor force. The Northern textile mills relied on the cotton grown using enslaved labor. At the same time, the industrialized North was moving to abolish the practice of slavery. The tensions between North and South around these conflicting ideas would drive America to the breaking point.

title: Geographic Regions of the United States
text:
If you drove non-stop from San Francisco to Boston at 60 miles per hour, it would take you 45 hours. Our country is vast. At its widest, it is 2,680 miles from coast to coast.

During this trip, you would travel through very diverse regions of the United States. There are five general regions in America. A region is a group of states that share common characteristics, including climate, land features, natural resources, and geographic location. These regions are commonly organized as the Northeast, Southeast, Midwest, West, and Southwest. As you travel, you will see that each region is unique.

The Northeast

The Northeast Region consists of the states bordering the Atlantic Ocean from Maine to Maryland. This area includes broad valleys, rolling hills, low mountains, and forests. The Appalachian Mountains cross this region. This mountain range stretches from Maine to Georgia. It is an old range, so the hills are not very tall.

New England has rocky soil and a short growing season. Winters are harsh, and summers are mild and semi-humid. There is not a lot of farming in New England. Plants and animals in this area have adapted to the long winter months. The weather becomes milder as you travel south. Winters are shorter, while summers are longer and warmer. This part of the region is better suited to agriculture.

The Southeast

Water defines the geography of this region. The eastern border is the Atlantic Ocean. The Ohio River lies to the north. The southern coastline is the Gulf of Mexico, and the Mississippi River flows through the middle of the region. The Southeast enjoys mild winters. This creates a longer growing season. There is also plenty of rain and good soil.

The Southeastern states are located on the Atlantic Coastal Plain. This plain covers an area over 2,200 miles long. It extends about 62 miles inland. The land is generally flat and sometimes swampy. Florida’s citrus-growing country in this region produces over 70 percent of our country’s citrus fruit. Another fertile area of land is known as the Cotton Belt. This area reaches from North Carolina to the eastern part of Texas. One of the most important resources in the region is the supply of petroleum and natural gas found near the Gulf Coast.

The Midwest

“Waving grasslands as far as the eye can see” is the way early settlers described the Midwest Region. The western part of the region is sometimes called the Great Plains. It is a broad expanse of flat prairie and grassland. Low hills and streams are common. This region borders Canada and the Great Lakes to the north. The western-most part of the region includes North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, and Kansas. The natural vegetation of the region is a variety of tall prairie grasses. Much of the land is covered with large farms. Today, when you drive through these states, you will see virtually endless fields of corn, soybeans, and wheat.

The West

The West is the largest of the five regions. It has a variety of climates. The Rocky Mountains are the backbone of this region. They extend from British Columbia, Canada, to New Mexico. That is a distance of over 3,000 miles through six states. The mountain states have cold, snowy winters and hot, dry summers. They get less rainfall than other regions. As you travel over the Rocky Mountains, you will cross the Continental Divide. The Continental Divide is a high ridge that runs down the center of the Rockies from north to south. It separates the flow of the country’s rivers. Waterways east of the divide travel to the Atlantic Ocean. Those west of the divide empty into the Pacific Ocean.

Two smaller mountain ranges are located between the Rockies and the Pacific Coast. They are the Sierra Nevada and the Cascades. Most of the moisture that moves in from the Pacific Ocean falls west of these mountains. Not much moisture makes it over this barrier. The area between these ranges is in a rain shadow, where rain falls on one side of the mountains only. This results in vast areas of arid desert, like California’s Death Valley. The average rainfall there is only about two and a half inches per year.

Western portions of states along the Pacific Coast have a very different climate than the rest of the region. Parts of California, Oregon, and Washington enjoy a mild climate year-round. These areas normally get plenty of rainfall. There are forested hills and tall volcanic peaks. One of those peaks, Mount St. Helens, is still an active volcano. It erupted in 1980. Food crops, such as tree fruits, berries, vegetables, nuts, and grapes, are grown in the fertile valleys of these states.

The Southwest

The Southwest is the least populated region. The land is covered with immense deserts, mountains, plateaus, and canyons. Plants and animals have to adapt to survive in this region. There is very little water. Temperatures range from very hot to very cold. The deserts provide limited sources of food. Varieties of cactus and other plants that are adapted to store water can thrive in this climate.

title: Effects of Supply and Demand on Agriculture
text:
A young Connecticut entrepreneur began her slime glue business when she was 12. Within two years, she sold thousands of gallons of glue and expanded her business. Like other entrepreneurs, she understands supply and demand in a free enterprise system. She discovered a demand in the market: a need for slime glue. Then she created services that both supplied slime glue and increased demand for it. Producers (like the young entrepreneur) and consumers (like slime glue buyers) drive supply and demand, and thus the market.

Slime glue, however, fills a tiny place in the economy. A huge economic sector in the United States is agriculture. In 2017, Texas alone sold over $26 billion in agricultural goods, such as cattle, sheep, and cotton. Like the slime producer, farmers study supply and demand. This helps them sell goods and increase profit. Today, consumer demand drives this industry more than ever. People want foods and other agricultural products that are healthy, natural, and good for the environment. For many farmers, this guides their business model.

In fact, agriculture in a free market system helped create early America’s wealth. Ironically, it also aided a system that withheld freedom from countless people: slavery.

For centuries, America relied on Southern cash crop plantations. Imagine thousands of acres of tobacco, rice, sugar, and cotton farms, and no modern machines to plow! Plantation owners demanded cheap labor. So, slavery became key. Enslaved people provided labor, but they did not get paid. Thus, when supply and demand for cash crops greatly increased, the demand for enslaved people did too. For example, in the late 1700s, the newly invented cotton gin processed more cotton than ever before. The demand for cotton boomed, and so did the demand for enslaved people. Through dealers and auctions, people of all ages were sold to meet labor demands. Because of these plantations, the Southern states have been called the “economic engine” of the country’s early wealth.

title: Looking Back: Late 18th Century to 19th Century
text:
Government for the People

The Constitution of the United States creates a government for the people. It is the foundation of a strong and lasting government. This document protects the rights and freedoms of the people. It has a system to help make sure the government really does belong to the citizens. This system is called checks and balances. One branch of government cannot have more power than the others. Many people felt the original Constitution could be made even better. They wanted the rights of the people explained and added to the document.

On Dec. 15, 1791, 10 amendments, or changes, were added to the U.S. Constitution. These are known as the Bill of Rights, and they guarantee U.S. citizens certain rights and freedoms. Each of the 10 amendments explains how the government will treat the people.

All 10 amendments of the Bill of Rights are important. However, the First Amendment is often seen as the foundation of the United States of America. This amendment explains that Congress cannot make any law that would take away basic freedoms that people have. This amendment also guarantees that people have freedom of religion, speech and the press. It protects the right of the people to assemble in groups and to petition, or request, that the government change something they believe to be unfair. However, people may not use their First Amendment rights to break the law, hurt others physically, or say or print lies about people or groups.

New Land, New Opportunities

At the end of the Revolutionary War in 1783, the U.S. controlled the land from the Atlantic Ocean to the Mississippi River. Some colonists wanted to own more land in the wilderness. Many decided to head west to the other side of the Appalachian Mountains where resources such as lumber and furs were plentiful. America's leaders knew colonists who settled these lands would help keep foreign countries from trying to claim the land.

Soon, Americans wanted to use the Mississippi River to ship and trade goods. France owned the land through which the river flowed. This land was called the Louisiana Territory. President Thomas Jefferson offered to buy the land from France. The Louisiana Purchase was settled in 1803. The U.S. got a great deal, paying about 3 cents per acre. American Indians living on the land weren't as lucky. Many were pushed off the land and forced to live on reservations. Many died of starvation, harsh weather and disease.

President Jefferson sent Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to explore the Louisiana Territory. They were to learn more about the land, animals and people living there. They spent the harsh winter with a group of American Indians. A Shoshone girl named Sacagawea became their guide and translator. Their maps of the territory gave settlers important information about traveling and settling even further west.

The War of 1812

Just weeks after selling the Louisiana Territory to the U.S., France went to war with Great Britain. The U.S. continued to sell goods to both countries. However, both European powers wanted to know whose side the Americans were on. They began to bully U.S. ships on the Atlantic Ocean. The Americans then decided they would stop sending U.S. supplies to both countries. Congress passed the Embargo Act of 1807.

The plan backfired and soon the act was repealed, or cancelled. Once again, British ships mistreated U.S. ships and sailors. A group of Congressmen called the War Hawks convinced U.S. President James Madison to go to war again with Great Britain in June of 1812.

For over two and a half years, the Americans fought bravely. It was during one battle at Fort McHenry in Maryland that Francis Scott Key watched a violent fight. He wrote a poem called "The Star-Spangled Banner" to remember that night. That poem was set to music and later became the national anthem for the United States of America.

The War of 1812 ended when officials signed the Peace Treat of Ghent in February 1815. The exact outcomes of the war were a bit unclear. There were no major gains or losses for either country involved. Perhaps the only thing the U.S. really gained from the war was the reputation as a true world power.

title: Industry, Economics and Immigrants in a New Country
text:
An Industrial Revolution

Life in the early 19th century wasn’t easy. Most people lived in the country. They farmed and raised animals. They lived the way their ancestors had lived for generations before. There was no electricity or running water. All of the food needed for the family had to be grown or raised. Things began to change rapidly during a time we call the Industrial Revolution. Many people went from living and working on farms in the country to living in cities and working in factories. The Industrial Revolution brought many changes to life in the United States. It continued well into the 20th century.

People developed hundreds of new inventions and products during the Industrial Revolution. The cotton gin, a machine that made harvesting cotton easier and faster, changed the world. Eli Whitney patented this machine, which quickly separated the seeds from the cotton fiber. Farmers could then plant even more cotton than ever. Large cotton plantations covered the South. Enslaved people were used to take care of the large cotton crops. Some historians believe the invention of the cotton gin led to an increase in slavery in the United States. Many other inventions and ideas also led to America’s agricultural successes in the 1800s. Blacksmith John Deere invented a steel plow with a blade. Farmers were able to cut and turn over hard prairie ground much more easily.

The Industrial Revolution changed the United States in many ways. Many families moved from the country to cities. Instead of farming and ranching, people began making their livings using simple machines. Communication, healthcare and transportation improved. However, the Industrial Revolution also marked the beginning of many problems. Cities were often dirty and crowded with people looking for work. These communities had to find ways to provide citizens with food, clean water, healthcare and natural resources, such as coal. Factories caused pollution. For good and bad, the Industrial Revolution changed the nation forever.

Supply and Demand in a Free Trade Economy

During the War of 1812, British ships often blockaded U.S. seaports. This kept goods from being shipped in or out of the country. There was a demand for goods, but the supply was not being met. Supply is the amount of a product that a business has for sale. Demand is the amount of a product that people want to buy. The best thing is when the demand is equal to the supply. During the 19th century, Americans began to realize they needed better systems of manufacturing and transportation. This would help to supply the demands of the people in a free enterprise, or free trade, economy.

People had the right to choose how to spend their money in the free trade economy of the 19th century, as we do today. Many ideas about free trade, or capitalism, had their beginnings during the Industrial Revolution. Americans enjoy the freedom to earn, spend and save money as they choose. We also have the right to own property, including our home and businesses. Profits earned by businesses controlled by an owner belong to the owner.

Immigrants Follow Opportunity

Life in the United States held great promise in the 19th and 20th centuries. So much opportunity convinced 30 million people from around the world to immigrate to the U.S. between the early 1800s and 1930. They came from all over the world, especially from Europe and Asia. Large groups of Irish, German and Chinese immigrants arrived during the 1800s. They usually came by ship. Many of these immigrants arrived at Liberty Island in New York City, where they were greeted by the Statue of Liberty. This gift from France still welcomes people to the United States and reminds us of the freedoms available in this country.

Most immigrants came to the United States to find economic opportunity. They wanted the chance to own land, homes and businesses. They could have the freedom to work hard to make their families’ lives better. Many of these immigrants worked to build bridges, canals and railroads that began to link the cities of the country together.

Industry vs. Agriculture

The United States grew a great deal in the 1800s. Many people lived in large cities along the Eastern Coast, but many people also settled land in the West and South. People in different areas of the country had different ways of living. They earned their money in various ways, and they had different types of homes. By the mid-1800s, many of these people felt as if they lived in different countries. Their ideas about topics such as slavery and states’ rights varied greatly as well.

People once had made their livings entirely in agriculture. Most families farmed and raised animals. The Industrial Revolution changed that. People in the Northern states worked in factories and found homes in cities. Life in the South was very different. People in this region still made their livings mostly from agriculture, especially cotton. Many people in the South accepted the idea that enslaved people were needed to work large plantations. Within a short period of time, these differences in their ways of living would shatter the new nation.

title: Decisions, Decisions
text:
Changes to the U.S. Constitution are called amendments. Congress has power to make these changes. Amending the U.S. Constitution requires a careful decision-making process. Understanding this process helps us understand exactly why amendments to the Constitution are taken so seriously and are rarely made.

First, a situation that requires a decision is identified. Next, lawmakers gather information they need to make a decision about whether an amendment is best for citizens. Then, Congress must consider all options. They will discuss the consequences of an amendment. They often hear arguments from fellow lawmakers or citizens. Finally, Congress must take action. Sometimes the amendment passes. Or, Congress could decide that the amendment is not best for the people of the United States.

title: Manifest Destiny
text:
After the U.S. purchased the Louisiana Territory, more and more American settlers began to head west into new territory. They wanted to establish homes, farms, businesses and towns. Many of these people believed it was their God-given right to spread the American way of life as far west as they could, no matter what the cost. If necessary, they pushed other people, especially American Indians, out of their way. By the mid-1800s, this idea was known as Manifest Destiny.

Not every American believed Manifest Destiny was a good thing. Some people questioned whether it was spreading a good way of life or greed for control of land and people. The idea of Manifest Destiny was a part of the American way of life for many years.

title: Annexation of Texas
text:
In the early 1800s, Americans heard about land that Mexico held in the Southwest. Mexican leaders sold the land cheaply to Americans. By 1830, more than 20,000 white settlers were living in Texas. They held on to the belief of Manifest Destiny and became upset that the Mexican government demanded their full support. Texas became a republic following a bloody revolution. Texans quickly turned to the U.S. for support.

Despite concerns, Texas became part of the United States. Mexico was angry. They wanted to reclaim some of the land that was once theirs. The Mexican-American War lasted nearly two years. At the end of the war, the U.S. took control of about 55 percent of all Mexican territory. The U.S. had grown even larger than ever.

title: The Gadsden Purchase
text:
American leaders knew a railroad system was very important for the country. They made plans to lay tracks across the United States. A strip of land just south of the Gila River in present-day Arizona and New Mexico was the perfect pass through the mountains. If officials could purchase the land from Mexico, a railroad system could easily reach the Gulf of California.

U.S. Minister to Mexico, James Gadsden, helped put the deal together. The U.S. agreed to pay Mexico $10 million for the land. The sale angered Mexicans who did not want to lose claim to all of their land, and Gadsden had to be replaced. However, the Gadsden Purchase made it possible for railroad systems to begin crisscrossing the continent.

title: From Dust Bowl to New Deal
text:
The United States had fallen into terrible economic times when the stock market crashed in 1929. The country was in a Great Depression. Jobs and money were scarce. A long period of little rainfall affected the Midwest during this time too. The drought was made even worse when great wind and dust storms hit the same region. Many families abandoned their farms to look for work elsewhere. Emily Sarah's family owned a farm in the Panhandle of Texas. During the Great Depression they went searching for a better life and a New Deal.

Emily Sarah held Mama's hand tightly as she climbed into the old truck. She could see Papa trying to hold back tears as the truck sputtered away. Through the swirling dust and wind, Emi, as her Mama called her, could see the boarded-up farmhouse getting smaller and smaller as they drove away. To Emi it seemed the road was leading away from her family's dreams.

Papa and Mama had tried as hard as they could to keep the farm. The crops just wouldn't grow in the dry soil. With no crops to sell, they were unable to pay back the money they had borrowed. Now the bank owned the farm. Sadly, Emi wondered if her family would ever be the same again. There was no farm, no home and no money. Some days there wasn't even much to eat. Papa said things would be better in California. He promised he would be able to find work on a farm there.

Mama had also reminded them that the United States had a new leader. President Franklin D. Roosevelt had been elected just months before. President Roosevelt declared that he had a "New Deal" for the country. He had new ideas and programs that would help people. Mama thought that Papa might even be able to find one of President Roosevelt's jobs for building roads or bridges.

Emily Sarah gripped Mama's hand even tighter. Maybe the road ahead would be better for her family. She smiled a thin-lipped smile in Papa's direction, and he nodded at her. Maybe there was hope for them all.

title: Who's Next in Line to be U.S. President?
text:
We know that the vice president is next in line to become U.S. president if anything happens to the president. But who is next in line to be president if something happens to the vice president?

In 1792, Congress passed the Presidential Succession Act, which listed the succession, or sequence, of who would be president if the current U.S. president died, became too sick to work, resigned or was removed from office. After the vice president, it was a leader in the Senate called the president pro tempore. Pro tempore means “for the time being” or “temporary.” Following the Senate president pro tempore was the speaker of the House of Representatives. However, in 1886, this order was changed a bit. Then, in 1947, Congress changed the order again to what we use today. Now, following the vice president is speaker of the House of Representatives, then Senate president pro tempore, then the president’s cabinet members. With permission, you can visit http://www.whitehouse.gov/administration/cabinet/ for the complete list of the order of succession to the U.S. presidency.

So just how many times has the president been replaced? Well, so far in our country’s history, eight U.S. vice presidents have succeeded to the presidency because the president died. One vice president succeeded because the president resigned. How would you feel if our current president needed to be replaced? Remember, there are different reasons why a president could be removed from or leave office. Think about the different reasons and then think about your answer.

title: A New Deal for the United States
text:
Franklin D. Roosevelt was elected president of the United States in 1932 when the nation was suffering and needed immediate help. Roosevelt wanted to put special programs into place to help all Americans quickly. He was especially concerned with “the forgotten man at the bottom of the economic pyramid.” This included the working-class people who had lost everything after the stock market crashed in 1929. Roosevelt wanted to offer jobs to the millions of people who were out of work. He wanted to provide housing to those who had lost their homes when banks closed or foreclosed on farms and homes. He wanted the American people to regain their hope and confidence (feeling of trust or belief) in the nation and its government.

A New Deal is Born

During Roosevelt’s presidential nomination acceptance speech, he promised the American public, “I pledge you, I pledge myself, to a new deal for the American people.” Within days after he was sworn in as president, Roosevelt addressed the nation over the radio to let them know of immediate changes and new programs that would help Americans.

President Roosevelt and Congress first developed a plan to reopen banks, provide money to the states to help citizens and establish programs to help get people back to work.

The government’s new agencies and programs sometimes confused people. Many of them were known by their initials— the CCC, WPA, TVA and many more. So many, in fact, that people often referred to the New Deal programs as Roosevelt’s Alphabet Soup. Despite the confusing names, there was no denying that the programs worked.

New Deal Programs Battle the Great Depression

Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC)

The CCC was one of Roosevelt’s first programs. The purpose of the program was to put workers back on the job! Roosevelt did not want to hand out money to Americans. He wanted them to take pride in themselves by earning money through work. Thousands of young men joined the CCC to work on projects to better the nation. They planted trees, built roads and parks and fought forest fires.

Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA)

The TVA was a program to improve the lives of people who lived along the Tennessee River in the southeastern United States. Many companies hired workers to build dams and provide electrical service.

Federal Housing Administration (FHA)

Many people lost their homes during the Great Depression. The FHA was designed to help make it possible for people to borrow money to buy homes again.

Social Security Act (SSA)

The SSA provided direct help to needy citizens. Under the plan, the SSA made payments to all Americans who lost their jobs and could not find work. The government taxed the payments so workers could receive a pension at the age of 65. This meant when a person was too old to work they would still receive a monthly paycheck from the government.

Roosevelt’s New Deal programs did improve life for many Americans. Not all of the programs were successful, though. The government cancelled some of them after a short time. Others, like the TVA and Social Security, are still in existence. Just as in Roosevelt’s era, government leaders today are still debating and making changes to programs that provide assistance to people.

title: Franklin D. Roosevelt: The Man Behind the New Deal
text:
In 1933 the United States was in the middle of the Great Depression. Businesses had closed. Some banks failed, and others had taken farms and homes away from families. Many workers lost their jobs, and most people had very little hope that things would get better. But in that same year, a man named Franklin Delano Roosevelt was sworn in as the new president of the United States. He brought hope and inspiration with him.

FDR, as he was called throughout his life, was an excellent example of how a man could overcome major life challenges. In the summer of 1921, Franklin developed a serious disease called polio. The disease made it difficult for him to walk or even stand. For the rest of his life, Franklin could not get around without help. He had to use a wheelchair or crutches everywhere he went. However, he did not let his disease slow him down or crush his dreams. Roosevelt was determined to live an active life with a purpose.

As president, Franklin D. Roosevelt faced many more challenges. One was finding a way to bring the country out of the Great Depression. His plan to develop programs that would help the poor and create jobs changed America. People all over the nation started feeling hopeful. They had confidence that President Roosevelt was leading the country in the right direction. They approved of his work so much they elected him president four times! He is the only U.S. president to serve more than two terms. The 22nd Amendment to the Constitution now limits a president to two terms.

In one famous speech, Roosevelt told Americans, "The only thing we have to fearis fear itself." Certainly Roosevelt believed this, and he lived his life as proof the statement was true in his own heart.

title: Famous Faces: The Making of Mount Rushmore
text:
A monument stands in the beautiful Black Hills of southwest South Dakota. It honors four of our nation's great leaders and celebrates American ideals of leadership, courage and strength. Mount Rushmore National Memorial is a giant mountainside carving of Presidents George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Abraham Lincoln's faces. Washington was chosen to represent the founding of America. Jefferson helped the country grow larger. Roosevelt represents the protection of America's great lands, and Lincoln brought the country together.

The U.S. Congress authorized the Mount Rushmore project to begin in August 1927. American sculptor Gutzon Borglum was the leader of the task. The granite carvings were created by hundreds of workers who used special drills and explosives to blast through the mountain rock. The work was difficult. Workers climbed hundreds of steps each day just to get to the site. Men hung dangerously by ropes to do most of the work.

After 14 years, presenters revealed the final creation. It had taken much longer than expected to finish the job. A great deal of time was spent waiting for the government to fund, or pay for, the work. The nation was in the middle of the Great Depression during most of the construction, and the government had difficulty providing the money workers needed to finish the carvings.

More than three million people visit Mount Rushmore each year, and it still represents to many the important values that make America the great nation it is today.

title: Art and the New Deal
text:
The largest of Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal agencies was the WPA, or Works Progress Administration. It was later renamed the Works Projects Administration. The agency was established in 1935 to carry out many different projects. Millions of Americans worked for the WPA and other government programs constructing parks, schools, airports and roads. The WPA also built many public buildings during its existence.

During the Great Depression, over eight million U.S. citizens worked up to 30 hours a week for the agency. Many of the employees were women and young people. A job with the WPA helped many families survive during this terrible time. The agency also sponsored adult education and reading classes. In this way, many more people received the education they needed to be able to find jobs.

One job the Works Progress Administration created was for authors, who wrote tourist guidebooks. The guidebooks provided information on a state's history, agriculture and cities. The WPA also wanted to provide Americans the opportunity to see various works of art. The WPA hired artists to create paintings, sculptures and murals (wall paintings) for public buildings. Many of the nation's post office walls were painted with scenes from American history. Some of those paintings and murals still remain today in public buildings and museums.

The WPA also hired actors and musicians to perform in community cultural programs. At one time, 16,000 musicians were working for the WPA. They performed concerts and gave free music lessons to many people. Over 12,000 actors performed in WPA theaters across the country. They presented live theater performances to people who might have never had the chance to enjoy a play otherwise.

When the U.S. entered World War II, the economy began to grow again. The WPA was no longer needed. All 29 programs were discontinued in 1943, but they provided a great service to many Americans.

title: Clarity of Expression: FDR and the Four Freedoms
text:
For most people around the world, the years of economic depression and war between 1929 and 1945 were dark and dangerous. Resources such as food, clothing and fuel were in short supply. Families were often torn apart as parents looked for work, served in the armed forces, or as children were sent to safe, sheltered areas. It was a time of stress and hardship, when people desperately looked to leaders for safety and hope. In the United States, that leader was Franklin D. Roosevelt, our 32nd president who served from 1933 to 1945.

During that time of chaos, on Jan. 6, 1941, President Roosevelt delivered to Congress a historic speech, which we now call the Four Freedoms Speech. After years of economic depression, his words were not angry. When world war was happening, his tone was not fierce or mean. But knowing that there were still darker days of war to come for many, he spoke with passion about peace, good fortune, safety and the freedoms that humans everywhere deserve. “In the future days,” Roosevelt said, “we look forward to a world founded upon four essential human freedoms.” Even today those four freedoms are essential (important). Can you list them? They are: the freedom of speech and expression, the freedom of worship for every person, the freedom from wants such as hunger and lack of shelter and the freedom from fear.

How are we doing? Have we achieved those freedoms for everyone? Everywhere?

To read or listen to the entire speech, with the permission of a parent or teacher go to: http://www.americanrhetoric.com/speeches/fdrthefourfreedoms.htm. To see the paintings by Norman Rockwell inspired by the Four Freedoms: http://www.archives.gov/exhibits/powers_of_persuasion/four_freedoms/four_freedoms.html

title: Point of View
text:
Read the following quotes by Presidents Herbert Hoover and Franklin D. Roosevelt. They are about the problems of the people before and during the Great Depression. Answer the questions below.

Herbert Hoover

“We in America today are nearer to the final triumph over poverty than ever before in the history of any land. The poorhouse is vanishing from among us.” –1928

“Economic depression cannot be cured by legislative action or executive pronouncement. Economic wounds must be healed by the action of the cells of the economic body — the producers and consumers themselves.” –1930

Franklin D. Roosevelt

“The test of our progress is not whether we add more to the abundance of those who have much; it is whether we provide enough for those who have too little.” –1937

“… true individual freedom cannot exist without economic security and independence. … People who are hungry and out of a job are the stuff of which dictatorships are made.” –1944

1. How did Herbert Hoover feel the United States economy was doing in 1928?

2. Who did Hoover believe was responsible for solving the nation’s economic problems in 1930? How do you know this?

3. What does Roosevelt say that lets readers know he believes a successful nation is one in which all people are taken care of?

4. What is Roosevelt trying to warn the country of in his 1944 quote?

title: The Erie Canal and Capitalism
text:
The country was expanding, and merchants needed a way to move their goods. In New York, this was even more difficult because of the terrain. There were rivers and mountains, making it hard to transport things across a long distance. In 1817, DeWitt Clinton was elected governor of New York. He got a $7 million loan from the state to begin constructing a canal system that went from the Hudson River all the way to Buffalo, which was on Lake Erie. This 360-mile system became known as the Erie Canal.

To build the canal, workers dug trenches and filled them with cement. These trenches were filled with water and would be used to move boats filled with cargo from one place to another. Creating trenches was simple, but the change in elevation was a problem. As the ground got higher or lower, the trenches needed to stay level so that the water would stay even and boats could pass. The solution was a lock system. A lock system is a way to move boats from one canal to another canal that is either higher or lower. The Erie Canal needed 83 locks to move the boats from one elevation to another.

To use the lock system, a boat would first enter a lock. The gates would then be closed so the boat was inside. If a boat had to move to a higher elevation, water was then let into the lock until the boat was level with the next canal. For boats that were moving to a lower elevation, water was drained from the lock until the boat became level with the next canal. Finally, the second set of gates were opened, and the boat continued on its path.

The Erie Canal was a boon to the economy. Now, goods could easily travel from place to place faster and cheaper, meeting the demands of buyers. The canal also increased westward expansion. Settlers used the canal to move to New York, Ohio, Michigan, Illinois, and Indiana. New cities grew along the canal. The face of New York was changing.

title: A Strike in the Pacific
text:
Sixteen million men and women served in U.S. military forces during World War II. There are special stories about each and every one of these brave soldiers. What follows is one true story of courage, hope and honor from Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on Dec. 7, 1941.

William Fomby was born in Hamlin, Texas, in 1919. After high school, Billy, as his family called him, worked several jobs. Unfortunately, times were still hard in Texas. The Great Depression had consumed the nation for years. Good jobs were difficult to find even though FDR's New Deal programs were helping to improve life for Americans.

On Dec. 18, 1940, Billy decided to join the Navy. He would soon turn 21 and knew the U.S. government could draft him. Billy thought he would fit in better with the Navy than the Army, so he volunteered to sign up.

In early 1941, Navy recruit (new member) Bill Fomby reported for three months of basic training in San Diego, California. Afterward, he was assigned to his first job on board a large battleship named the USS Oklahoma. The ship was stationed in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, in the Pacific Ocean.

While on board, Bill cleaned and took care of the large guns. Bill was a hard worker and was liked by many officers on the ship. In fact, they suggested he work as a cook in the ship's kitchen so he could get a promotion.

While Bill was cleaning up after breakfast the morning of Dec. 7, 1941, he suddenly heard one of his fellow sailors shout from the deck, "Boy, they're having a lot of practice drills this morning! Planes are flying all over the place out here." The men watched for a while, thinking the U.S. was just having practice drills.

Suddenly, they heard cries of panic. "Man the anti-aircraft guns! This is a real air raid! No joke!" The Japanese were attacking! Bill ran to his weapons. Suddenly the ship was bombarded with torpedoes. Bill clung to ship ladders while trying to reach his gun. The violent shaking of the ship tossed the men like rag dolls. Within minutes, the USS Oklahoma was sinking.

Bill realized there was nothing more he could do onboard the ship. It was going down quickly. Bill jumped 30 feet into the cold waters of the ocean. For what seemed like hours, he swam through heavy oil and fire. Bombs and torpedoes landed all around. Finally, he was pulled aboard another battleship named the USS Maryland. For hours, U.S. soldiers fought off the attack planes. Bill was exhausted and sick from swallowing oil and salt water, but he continued to fight. For days, the soldiers took care of the wounded and worked to clean and repair the military base.

Back home in Texas, Bill's family heard of the attack. They waited to find out if Billy was safe. On Dec. 12, the family received word that Bill was missing. On Dec. 15, a telegram arrived explaining that Bill was now thought to be dead. With great sadness, the family planned a memorial service for Dec. 22, 1941. That would have been Bill's 22nd birthday. On Christmas Day, the family didn't feel like celebrating. They sat quietly and thought about the dear son they had lost. Suddenly, late on Christmas morning, the family was startled by the telephone ringing. On the other end of the line was their beloved son, Billy, calling to wish them a Merry Christmas. Their courageous son was alive!

Bill Fomby continued to serve in the Navy for six more years. While being stationed all over the world, he worked cleanup and rescue operations in Japan after the atomic bombs were dropped on the cities of Nagasaki and Hiroshima in August 1945. After being discharged in 1947, Bill returned to Texas to marry and start a family. William Fomby never thought of himself as a hero, but what a hero he is!

title: A Changing America in the Second World War
text:
By 1941, the United States was beginning to feel as though it just might pull itself out of the Great Depression. President Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal programs gave millions of Americans job opportunities. Jobs building roads, schools, bridges and parks were popping up all across the country. Rural areas began getting electricity and telephones. Air travel was also becoming common. Planes flew across the oceans of the world, and industry was beginning to grow again. However, in the background of America's climb to recovery was the war in Europe.

In 1939, Nazi Germany had invaded Poland. Because Great Britain and France promised to protect Poland, they immediately declared war. The nightmare of World War II had begun. Americans wanted no part in the war. In fact, President Roosevelt announced that the United States would stay out of the war. The people were so happy with this announcement that they re-elected the president to a third term in office in 1940.

'A Date Which Will Live in Infamy'

The United States tried to stay out of Europe's war, but it proved to be too difficult. Under FDR's leadership, the U.S. began sending aid to Great Britain. This angered Germany. Our country's relationship with Japan was also hanging in the balance when the U.S. put an embargo on shipments of oil and rice to Japan. This meant the U.S. would not allow trade of these products between the two countries.

At dawn on Dec. 7, 1941, over 300 Japanese planes surprised the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor. The attack killed 2,400 people in a matter of minutes. President Roosevelt said it was "a date which will live in infamy." By this, he meant the attack would always be remembered as a dishonor to America. Within days, the U.S. was officially at war with Germany and Japan.

The Sacrifices of War

The United States knew immediately that Americans would have to pull together to win a victory overseas. Millions of men were drafted into, or forced to join, the army while others volunteered to join (offered to serve). Women were also very important to war efforts. Some women joined special units like the Women's Army Corps. Many women took over jobs left open when men went to war. Women often worked in factories building war supplies and equipment. The government encouraged some women with advertising posters. "If you've followed recipes exactly in making cakes, you can learn to load shells," one poster exclaimed. Twelve million women were already working at the beginning of the war. By the time the war had ended, more than 18 million women had joined the workforce. They drove trucks, built heavy equipment and assembled machine guns. For many women, this was the first time they had worked outside of the home.

The government developed new agencies to see that the production of military goods was a priority. To help meet the needs of the military, the U.S. government began rationing supplies the soldiers needed. This meant that items used for war, like rubber and gasoline, were limited for citizens at home. Meat, butter, coffee, sugar and shoes were among the items that had to be purchased with ration stamps. To help meet food needs, the government encouraged all Americans to plant Victory Gardens. The food people grew in these gardens would feed families at home and leave more food available for soldiers overseas.

The Battles Continue

The war dragged on into 1944. Soldiers fought battles in Europe, the Pacific, Asia and Northern Africa. The Allied powers (Great Britain, France and the Soviet Union) fought alongside the U.S. to keep Adolf Hitler and the Axis powers (Germany, Italy and Japan) from taking control of the world.

On June 6, 1944, war was raging in Europe as Allied leader General Dwight D. Eisenhower began a plan to free France from German control. On this day, forever known as D-Day, the U.S. landed in Normandy, France, with more than 5,000 vehicles and 150,000 troops. Over the next few months, thousands of U.S. soldiers were killed. By January 1945, the Germans had been defeated. It seemed the war might be coming to an end. Leaders began to meet and talk about what the world would look like when the war was over.

A Stunning Death, a New Leader and the End of the War

On April 12, 1945, the world was stunned when President Franklin D. Roosevelt died suddenly of a stroke. He was in his fourth term as president of the United States. The American people felt they had lost a hero.

Vice President Harry S. Truman took over the job as 33rd president of the United States. He had many decisions to make. The war was ending in Europe, but there was still a decision to be made about Japan. Either the United States could drop the first atomic bomb on a large Japanese city or thousands of American soldiers could invade Japan. President Truman chose to drop two bombs on Japan in order to save American lives. On Aug. 6, 1945, U.S. forces dropped an atomic bomb on the city of Hiroshima, Japan. After the Japanese still refused to surrender, the U.S. dropped a second bomb on the city of Nagasaki on Aug. 9, 1945. Over 200,000 people were killed in the two bombings. Less than a week later, Japanese troops started to surrender and World War II was over at last.

title: Dedication and Determination
text:
The 442nd Infantry Regiment Goes For Broke

During WWII, one group clearly stood out as a brave group of soldiers. The 442nd Infantry Regiment was a group of Japanese American soldiers who served in the U.S. Army. They were stationed mainly in Europe. People knew the regiment to be an extremely dedicated and determined group of men. Many of them were part of families forced to move to Japanese relocation camps. These camps were virtual prisons for Japanese Americans. For part of World War II, the U.S. government feared that people of Japanese ancestry might side with Japan. As a result, Japanese Americans weren’t always treated fairly. The soldiers of the 442nd Infantry even had to take a loyalty test before joining the military. Nevertheless, the 442nd Infantry became one of the most highly decorated regiments in the history of the U.S. Armed Forces. They certainly lived up to their motto — “Go for Broke!”

The Tuskegee Airmen Fight for the Right to Fly

At a time when many people questioned the skill, courage and bravery of African American men, a group of very intelligent and skilled men emerged. They were the Tuskegee Airmen, the first African American military pilots in America. These men learned to pilot airplanes and trained in other military fields such as intelligence, meteorology and engine mechanics. However, people did not always treat the Tuskegee Airmen fairly. These men were often segregated and disrespected. They did not give up, though. They overcame prejudice to become some of the most highly respected fliers of World War II. In addition, the Tuskegee Airmen led the way for soldiers of all races to serve together for the good of the nation.

title: World War II and Its Unbreakable Code
text:
During World War II, the United States and Japan tried to keep secrets from one another. This was very difficult because both sides were able to break each other's secret codes. Japan kept winning many of the battles because U.S. secrets were lost. The U.S. wanted to develop an unbreakable code, or system of secret communication. A city engineer from Los Angeles, California, Philip Johnston, came up with the idea of using the American Indian Navajo language as a starting point for the code. He knew a code using the language would be difficult to break. Navajo has no alphabet, and most people cannot learn to speak it unless they are taught as children. A group of Navajo men worked to develop the code. They were called Navajo Code Talkers. Soon the U.S. was able to send secret messages back and forth among troops.

In Navajo code, military terms were often replaced with Navajo words for things they resembled, or looked like. For example, the word for "torpedo" was "lo-be-ca," which means fish shell in Navajo. Or, the Navajo word "ne-he-ma" for "our mother" was code for the word "America." Some Navajo words represented letters of the alphabet. For example, the Navajo word "be-la-sana" for the English word "apple" that started with the letter "A" simply represented the letter "A."

The Japanese were unable to crack the code no matter how hard they tried. However, the U.S. was still able to interpret Japan's secret messages. This meant the United States soon had the upper hand in battles. In the end, the Navajo Code Talkers' work saved many lives and ended World War II much faster.
