title: Two Special Fighting Forces
text:
During World War II, American soldiers were fighting the enemies of freedom around the world. Two groups of American fighting men came from populations that did not have all the rights and freedoms others enjoyed. They were the Tuskegee Airmen and the U.S. 442nd Regimental Combat Team. These men risked their lives serving a country that often considered them racially and culturally inferior. Yet these soldiers proved they were among the best and bravest American citizens.

The Tuskegee Airmen were among the first black pilots and crews in the U.S. Army Air Corps. In the 1920s and 30s, many people believed African Americans couldn’t master the complicated challenges of flying an airplane. When World War II broke out in Europe, President Roosevelt saw the need to increase U.S. civilian pilot training. Civil rights groups pressed for African Americans to be included. In 1940, President Roosevelt agreed. The first group of African American pilots began training at the Tuskegee Army Airfield in Alabama. Nearly 15,000 pilots, navigators, and bombardiers were eventually trained. They flew many missions against the Germans in Europe and North Africa. Their successful efforts helped encourage the official integration of the U.S. Armed Forces in 1948.

The war in Europe began in 1939. America tried to stay out of the fight. Then, in December 1941, Japan, an ally of Germany, bombed the U.S. naval station at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. Many Americans feared that people of Japanese ancestry living in the United States would become spies for our enemies. Japanese Americans living on the West Coast were forced to leave their homes and businesses. They were taken to concentration camps. These camps were located in interior desert sites across the West. They became prisoners of the U.S. government in their own country. Despite this treatment of their families, many Japanese American men joined the American combat forces.

In 1943, the 442nd Regimental Combat Team was organized. This team was primarily filled with volunteers from the internment camps along with Japanese American veterans who had served previously. The 442nd team was sent to Europe. They were among the first troops to find and liberate Nazi death camps. This unit received more awards and medals than any other unit of its size in military history.

title: Jane Addams
text:
Jane Addams was born in 1860 in Cedarville, Illinois. She went to college in Rockford. She hoped to become a doctor, but she had to leave medical school due to illness. Nevertheless, Addams was determined to do something that would benefit the urban poor. She and her friend, Ellen Starr, bought a rundown mansion on South Halsted in Chicago's slums. They turned it into a refuge for the needy and named it Hull House. With a great deal of hard work, the women turned it into a center to help people who lived nearby.

Addams then gathered other women who were determined to make the world a better place. Together, the women fed people, found them jobs, taught children, and organized a variety of clubs. Hull House also provided classes to teach immigrants new skills. Social workers were asked to come in and help families in trouble. Addams also worked hard to get laws passed that would improve the lives of women, children, and poor people everywhere. In 1931, Jane Addams became the first American woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. This award recognized all her hard work.

Jane Addams died in 1935. Her settlement home, Hull House, is now on the campus of the University of Illinois at Chicago.

title: America Changes Pace
text:
After World War II, millions of American soldiers returned home. Men and women were ready to pick up where they left off when the nation entered the war on Dec. 8, 1941. The people of America began working to make their lives even better than ever.

The country had changed dramatically in four years. War efforts brought many technological changes as well as advances in medicine and communication. During the war, special medicines called antibiotics were discovered. Medicines like penicillin help the body fight bacterial infections. Millions of lives were saved because of these antibiotics. New medical procedures that were developed in war could be used at home to save lives too.

Changes in communication brought the people of the country closer together. Television became popular in the years following the war. Television made it possible for news to reach people almost as soon as it happened. Many families already had telephones in their homes, and just 10 years after the war ended, most had televisions too. Now people could communicate with each other quickly and easily.

Perhaps the greatest change for many of the returning soldiers was that they returned to a nation that had pulled itself out of the Great Depression. When they got home, the soldiers found jobs and other opportunities. Boys had gone to war, but they returned as men. Now they were ready to settle down. Some soldiers returned to the jobs they had before the war. Others decided to attend college. Many chose to start their families. The marriage and birth rates in the country soared. One of the most important things for these new families was finding a home to live in.

Veterans (people who served in the armed forces) were able to borrow money to buy homes. However, there weren't enough homes available for all the new families. One homebuilder thought he had the answer to the problem. William Levitt's company worked to build housing communities in several cities in the United States. These communities were called Levittowns. The first one was on Long Island in New York. The houses in Levittowns were fast and cheap to build. A family could buy a Levittown ranch-style home for less than $8,000. Americans flocked to housing developments in the suburbs. These suburban areas were located outside big cities. They were smaller communities and offered families a different kind of life. Families who lived in Levittowns reported being extremely happy with their new lives.

Families in Levittowns settled down into their daily routines. The men worked while many women returned home to take care of the children. Some of the women decided to continue working outside of their homes. They liked to work and earn money for their families too. Families wanted to spend their money. Money had been scarce (in small supply) during the Great Depression. Now families had money to spend on extras like store-bought clothing, dinners at restaurants and appliances and furniture for their homes.

Extra money meant most families also owned an automobile. War technology had been used to make military vehicles like the Jeep®. Now this technology was used to make cars sleeker and faster. Some of them even had air conditioning and radios. The automobile industry began to grow quickly in the country.

People describe the time immediately after World War II as a time when life was better for Americans. This was true for many people. However, it was also a time when it became clear that not all Americans were being treated fairly. African Americans and other minorities (smaller groups of people) were not always given equal opportunities. The country still had a long way to go before everyone was guaranteed the life and freedoms that were available here.

title: Two Wars and a Space Race
text:
The Korean War

Happier times in America were shattered five years after the end of World War II, when the United States had to again send Americans to the battlefield. This time, the war was in Asia. Since World War II, Korea was divided into two separate countries, North Korea and South Korea. On June 25, 1950, North Korean troops forced their way into South Korea. Their goal was to force the two countries to unite (join together).

Sixteen countries immediately sprang to help South Korea. The United States provided most of the troops. A few months later, China entered the war and helped North Korea. At first, some U.S. military officials wanted to bomb China and end the war. President Harry Truman was afraid such an attack might start yet another world war, so he did not allow the bombing. Fighting continued and lasted almost three years. When a truce (an agreement to stop fighting) was declared in 1953, the two Korean countries remained divided after all.

The Cold War

Soon after World War II ended, a different war began. This war was not like the previous wars the United States had fought in. This war was known as a Cold War, and it wasn’t really a war at all. The Cold War is the name given to the relationship that developed between the United States and Russia, which was now called the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR).

The two nations had been allies during World War II against Germany and Adolph Hitler. However, the U.S. and the USSR didn’t always agree with each other on how to best fight battles. The Soviet Union, or the USSR, was unaware of how dangerous the U.S. plan to drop atomic bombs on Japan would be. From then on, both sides didn’t trust each other. They never fought against each other on the battlefield, but they often fought with words for their beliefs.

Both super powers began to try and find ways to show the other they were indeed the most superior nation in the world. Both began spending great amounts of money to develop technology such as computers and weapons. Both the U.S. and the Soviet Union continued to involve themselves in world politics. There were several times over the course of the 20th century that the two threatened each other with war. Another war, however, was taking place between the two countries, not on Earth but in space.

The Space Race Begins

After World War II, both the United States and the Soviet Union wanted to show each other how strong they were. They began to produce missiles and rockets that could be used during war times. Soon they began to think about building rockets to take people into outer space to explore the universe. The race to space was on!

At first it wasn’t clear how the space race would be won. Neither the Americans nor the Soviets accomplished exactly what they had hoped to by going into space. Americans soon began focusing on a race to send people to the moon. They wanted to beat the Soviets to Earth’s distant satellite. For many years Soviet officials claimed they wanted nothing to do with a space race. They kept their experiments top secret and did not share any failed attempts. Soviet officials only told people about successful missions.

On Oct. 4, 1957, Americans were shocked to find they had fallen behind in the space race. The Soviets launched an artificial satellite named Sputnik I. Americans feared that Soviets would use this technology to develop weapons that might one day be used to attack the United States. Americans wanted their government to spend more money and time on space technology. They wanted to catch up and then pass the Soviets in the race. Sure enough, in early 1958, America launched its own space satellite called Explorer I. After that, the Soviets knew they weren’t the only ones heading into space.

Space Race Results

The race to space resulted in improved technology for both the U.S. and the USSR. These technological advances improved life for all people on Earth. One invention was the jetliner. Engines that forced out a steady stream of air powered these types of planes. These planes, or airliners, could fly comfortably at nearly 600 miles per hour. People were able to travel all over the world quickly and safely. Weather satellites were also sent to orbit the Earth in outer space. These satellites used space race technology to help meteorologists (scientists who study weather) predict weather patterns and storms. Millions of lives have been saved because of the advanced storm forecasting provided by these satellites.

The First American in Space

It was only a 15-minute trip, but Alan B. Shepard Jr. made history on May 5, 1961, when he became the first American in space. The Navy test pilot was placed in a capsule and launched nearly 120 miles into space by a rocket. He remained weightless in space for five minutes before parachuting safely into the Atlantic Ocean some 300 miles away from the launch site in Florida.

The Soviets had launched the first artificial space satellite and only one month earlier had sent their own cosmonaut to orbit the Earth in a space capsule. The race was tightening now. Americans were certain their country could win the race and be the first to send someone to land on the moon.

title: Dwight David Eisenhower: General and President
text:
One of the most respected and admired military war heroes of World War II was a man named Dwight D. Eisenhower. Born in Texas and raised in Kansas, Eisenhower attended the U.S. Military Academy at West Point. He worked hard to show his intelligence and strategic planning skills as WWII raged across the Atlantic Ocean.

In 1942, Eisenhower was put in command of all U.S. troops in Europe. He was responsible for directing the Allied invasions of North Africa and Italy. Eisenhower became a national hero on D-Day, June 6, 1944, when he led more than 150,000 Allied troops from various countries as they stormed the beaches of Normandy, France. Eisenhower's ability to command the troops was a major factor in the Allied victory over Germany and Adolph Hitler.

After the war, General Eisenhower decided to enter the field of politics. At first, he wasn't quite sure he belonged in the running for president of the United States, but many Americans wouldn't have it any other way. His campaign slogan (saying or motto) was "I like Ike," which was Eisenhower's nickname. People all over the country wore campaign buttons and carried signs to persuade, or convince, others to vote for their hero. In 1952 and again in 1956, Dwight David Eisenhower was elected president of the United States of America.

title: Who is able to vote in local, state and national elections in the United States?
text:
In his State of the Union speech in 1954, President Dwight D. Eisenhower explained his support for allowing suffrage (the right to vote) for all American citizens age 18 and older. However, it took more than 16 years before the right to vote in federal, state and local elections was extended to those age 18 and up.

Some states did not think that 18 year olds should vote in state and local elections. There were many court cases held to decide whether the law was fair. Eventually it was decided that if people aged 18 were old enough to be drafted into the military, then they were old enough to vote in all elections. Today any citizen 18 and older may vote in any election if they meet all other voting requirements for the election.

title: The Population Baby Boom
text:
After World War II, many young men eagerly returned home to the United States. The Great Depression was over, and there were plenty of good jobs for people to find. The young men were also ready to marry and start families. So from 1946 to 1964, the number of children born in the country increased greatly. We call this time in history the baby boom.

In the U.S., almost 76 million babies were born in an 18-year period. For every 1,000 people in the United States, there were almost 24 babies born in 1947. This number had increased from 19 births per 1,000 people in 1932. The greater number of children born in the country increased the need for housing, schools and healthcare facilities.

The first baby boom children have now become grandparents and great-grandparents. The birth rate in 2010 was about 13 children for every 1,000 people. Take a look at the chart to compare numbers.

title: Ten Most Populated States in the U.S.
text:
Use the table provided along with additional online or atlas resources to help you complete the map activity.

Give the map a title.

Draw a map key. Your key should include a different color for each range of numbers. For example, red could stand for populations of 9-10 million people.

On the map, color the states listed in the chart according to your map key.

Label the 10 states‛ capital cities with a star or other symbol of your choice. Be sure to include the symbol and its meaning in the map key.

Add a compass rose.

title: One Giant Leap for Mankind
text:
Over the years, America has been built on technological inventions. Steamboats, railroads and automobiles changed the way people moved from place to place. As the United States rocketed into the 1960s, people were still in awe of the technological changes happening in the world. The U.S. and the Soviet Union were still neck and neck with each other to see who could be the first nation to claim outer space. The two countries sent rockets and explorers into space. The two world powers also continued their Cold War with one another. Together the rivals built up enough weapons to cause more damage than the atomic bombs in Japan. It seemed for a while that their disagreements might lead to yet another world war. During all the political and military drama between the two nations, however, one of the most important goals they still shared was getting the first human to the moon.

In 1961, President John F. Kennedy announced a big goal for the United States. He declared that by the end of the decade, the U.S. would safely land an American on the moon. When Kennedy was assassinated, or killed for political reasons, in 1963, Americans wondered if the president's death would mean the death of the country's space program too. Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson took over as leader of the nation. He quickly announced that the space program would continue as planned.

Millions of dollars and hours of work were put into the Gemini program. When the last Gemini flight ended in 1966, the U.S. was able to take all the information they had gained and build even better rockets and larger spacecrafts. Americans planned the Apollo missions next.

For a while, it seemed the space program might never be a true success. In January 1967, three U.S. astronauts died when their Apollo 1 space capsule caught fire during a preflight test. The deaths of Virgil Grissom, Edward White and Roger Chaffee stunned the nation. NASA (National Aeronautics and Space Administration) was in charge of the country's space program. NASA stopped all space missions for months in order to redesign space capsules and emergency procedures.

Late in 1968, the U.S. launched the Apollo 8 spacecraft. On board, the astronauts prepared to be the first to leave Earth's orbit. The spaceship was able to get close to the moon and orbit it 10 times. However, it did not land. With the success of Apollo 8, President Kennedy's promise to put a man on the moon seemed within reach now.

On July 16, 1969, a giant rocket was launched from Cape Kennedy in Florida. The rocket was as tall as a 28-story building, and right on top was the Apollo 11 spacecraft. Three astronauts, Neil Armstrong, Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin Jr. and Michael Collins, were prepared to do what humans had never done before. They would land on the moon and make America the winner of the space race.

Millions of Americans watched on television as one of the greatest moments in history took place. On July 20, 1969, the Apollo 11 lunar module landed on the moon. Commander Neil Armstrong climbed down the ship's ladder and stepped onto the surface of the moon. "That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind," he said into his radio. The landing and return trip home to Earth went without any problems. Humans had conquered space travel.

The United States was proud to claim they were the first to get a man to the moon. Between 1969 and 1972 the country sent six manned missions to the moon. Twelve men walked on the surface of the moon.

For a moment the nation seemed to stop and celebrate its victory in space. However, turmoil back on Earth soon brought all of the celebrating to an end as the country experienced one of the most troubling of all eras.

title: Civil Rights for All Americans
text:
Lunch Counter Sit-Ins Mark a Milestone

On a cold February day in 1960, four African American college students decided to get a bite to eat. They left their college, North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University, and headed to a restaurant at a local store in the town of Greensboro, North Carolina.

No one paid attention to the young men as they entered the store. It was open to customers of all races. The restaurant in the store, however, was for white customers only. The four students sat down at the lunch counter and asked the server to take their order. The customers in the restaurant were shocked. The server reminded them the lunch counter was segregated and that African Americans were not allowed to eat there. The students were asked to leave.

The Civil War had ended almost 100 years earlier, but in the South, people of different races were kept apart. African Americans were not allowed to sit with white people in theaters, restaurants, buses or in any public place. In 1960, however, civil rights leaders decided something had to be done about the unfair ways people of different races were being treated. They came up with a plan to have “sit-ins” at public places. The four college students sat at the lunch counter and refused to move.

When the store closed for the evening, the Greensboro students left peacefully. The following day, the group of four students brought more people to sit in at the lunch counter. The sit-in lasted for many days. Both African Americans and white people participated. Many people supported the sit-in, while others believed the students were trying to cause trouble. Some people called them bad names. In other cities across the South, thousands of people held the same types of demonstrations (public displays of opinion). Eventually, lunch counters in many cities finally became integrated and allowed people of any race to sit at them.

In 1964, Congress passed the Civil Rights Act, which made discrimination in employment and education illegal. The law protected people of all races from being treated unjustly (unfairly). In our country, the U.S. Constitution and acts of Congress guarantee these rights.

March in Washington, D.C.

Near the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., a crowd of over 200,000 people listened to a message of hope from one of the greatest leaders of the Civil Rights Movement. Millions more watched on television as Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. spoke with passion about civil rights on Aug. 28, 1963.

Dr. King’s speech was the highlight of the march in Washington for civil rights, jobs and freedom. The crowd marched through the city streets carrying signs and demanding equal treatment for all people. They wanted new laws passed that would make sure African Americans were treated equally.

The people gathered in Washington and heard Dr. King describe his vision of America. He spoke of a nation in which people would not be judged by the color of their skin. Throughout his speech, Dr. King said, “I have a dream!” It seemed that Dr. King’s dream just might become reality.

In 1964, Congress passed the Civil Rights Act that ended discrimination in employment and education. People of different races could no longer be treated unjustly (unfairly). The act also made it against the law for hotels and restaurants to segregate based on the color of people’s skin. Life in America did not change overnight for African Americans, but the country was on the right track.

The Assassination of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.

Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. worked for many years to bring racial equality to the people of the United States. His speeches and non-violent protests inspired many to work to improve the nation for all people.

Some people in the country did not agree with Dr. King. Some people still thought the country would be better if schools and businesses remained segregated. Some of these people wanted to hurt Dr. King. They didn’t want him to speak out against discrimination.

Early in the evening of April 4, 1968, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. stepped out onto the balcony of a motel in Memphis, Tennessee. He was shot by a man hiding nearby. The 39-year-old minister was killed instantly.

Americans everywhere were stunned and saddened to learn of Dr. King’s death. He had always spoken against violence and wanted everyone in America to enjoy freedom and equal treatment. People cried and marched in the streets to show their support of Dr. King and his family. Unfortunately, violence also broke out. People were outraged that Dr. King had been murdered. There were large riots in the streets as people showed their anger at the death of their hero.

Even today Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. is remembered as a man whose life symbolized freedom. He is admired and loved by all those who cherish their own freedom. Dr. King’s “I Have a Dream” speech still inspires, or encourages, Americans today to continue to fight for equal rights for all citizens.

Civil Rights Today

Since the 1960s, many laws have been passed to help guarantee civil rights to all Americans. Many changes have helped make our nation a better place to live and work. There is still work to be done, though. Today people continue to try to improve equality for all Americans, including women, ethnic minorities, people with disabilities and the homeless.

title: Rosa Parks — Mother of the Civil Rights Movement
text:
A seamstress in Montgomery, Alabama, named Rosa Parks headed home after a long day of work one December day in 1955. The 42-year-old African American woman climbed aboard a city bus. Mrs. Parks took a seat and settled in for the ride home.

The first four rows of all the buses in Montgomery were reserved for white people. African Americans had to sit in the "colored" section, which was usually in the back of the bus. Mrs. Parks was used to the ways of the bus system. She knew that African Americans could sit in the middle rows until the white section was full. Then they had to move to seats in the back of the bus. If there were no available seats in the back, African Americans had to stand. Sometimes they were even forced to get off the bus to make room for white people.

On that December day, Mrs. Parks refused to obey the bus driver's order to give up her seat to a white passenger. She was arrested, tried and convicted (found guilty of breaking a law).

African Americans were very upset. They boycotted (refused to use) the city bus system. Led by a preacher named Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., people refused to ride the bus for over a year. Through it all, Rosa Parks remained a leader in the civil rights struggle. She continued working for equal rights for all people for over 40 years. Rosa Parks is remembered today as the "mother of the Civil Rights Movement."

title: What was the Vietnam War?
text: In the 1950s, the U.S. began sending support to South Vietnam, a country in Asia. By 1965 the U.S. was in the country fighting to help South Vietnam resist the Viet Cong rebels who were being supported by communist North Vietnam. Many Americans were against the war. There were anti-war demonstrations and rallies back in the U.S. For about nine years, American troops fought a war that seemed hopeless. Almost 60,000 Americans died in the war before America pulled out of the country in 1973. North Vietnam finally overtook the capital of South Vietnam in 1975, and the war was over. Today the Vietnam War is considered one of the nation's worst military disasters.

title: 1969: The End of an Era
text:
In 1961, President Kennedy promised Americans that the United States would land a man on the moon by the end of the decade. The promise was fulfilled on July 20, 1969, when Neil Armstrong stepped onto the moon's surface.

As 1969 ended the decade, it was clear that the nation had come through one of the greatest periods of change ever. World War II was long over. Families were settling into suburbs and working toward the American dream.

African Americans had joined together to fight for rights guaranteed to them by the U.S. Constitution. There was still a way to go, but the nation was on the right track.

The country was speeding into the 1970s, and it would be a bumpy ride!

title: The Value of Debate and Dissent: W.E.B. Du Bois and Booker T. Washington
text:
Disagreements can be unpleasant and cause hard feelings. So what can you do? Have a debate! A debate is a chance for you and your friend to explain your point of view. If you understand why your friend sees things differently, it's easier to respect his or her point of view, even if you don't agree with it.

Booker T. Washington and William Edward Burghardt (W.E.B.) Du Bois were two great American leaders. Both men were African Americans, but Washington was born a slave in 1856 and Du Bois was born free in 1868. Each man spent his life working to improve the lives of African Americans, but they disagreed about the best way to do it.

U.S. laws between 1876 and 1965 said that blacks and whites should be separate but equal. Washington believed that if African Americans worked hard, eventually they would no longer be separate. They would be accepted as citizens with the same rights white people had. Du Bois dissented, or disagreed. He wanted people to protest and fight for the laws to be changed. He worried that Washington's advice would hold African Americans back instead of helping them. The debates and struggle for civil rights went on for years, but both men are remembered as great leaders.

Read the quotes below and have a class discussion about what they mean.

"In all things that are purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress." -Booker T. Washington

"But we do not merely protest; we make renewed demand for freedom in that vast kingdom of the human spirit ..." -W.E.B. Du Bois

title: The Civil Rights Movement in the United States
text: Use information from the article called “Civil Rights for All Americans” in this week’s magazine to complete the Conclusion/Support notes below. Develop at least three conclusions about the Civil Rights Movement. Explain the facts or information you read in this week’s magazine that support each of your ideas.

title: Cesar Chavez
text:
Have you ever heard adults talk about their work environment? Maybe they are unhappy and want better work conditions and higher pay. Many people have fought for these rights. One of them was César Chávez.

Chávez was born in Arizona in 1927. His grandfather came to the United States from Mexico where his parents owned a small grocery store and ranch. Times were hard for his family. They lost their business and moved to California to find work. They became migrant workers. These types of workers travel from farm to farm, working in the fields. Chávez was only 11 years old at the time.

Since his family moved all the time, Chávez went to many different schools. He finally stopped going to school after the eighth grade. However, he never stopped reading and learning about things that interested him. Life as a migrant worker was difficult. Living conditions were poor. Many people lived together in small, dirty shacks without clean water or electricity. Money was limited, and jobs were hard to find.

After returning from serving in the Navy in 1948, Chávez married. He and his wife continued to work as migrant workers. Many of the migrant workers were Mexican Americans. Chávez knew they deserved better. He began working for the rights of migrant workers. In 1962, he helped form the National Farm Workers Association. This group later became United Farm Workers.

United Farm Workers (UFW) was a union (a group formed to protect workers' rights). It worked to get better pay and safer working conditions for migrant workers. His motto was Sí, se puede, which means, "Yes, it can be done." The UFW organized migrant workers and took their demands to the people who owned large farms and ranches. Chávez organized strikes, or "huelgas," against owners if they refused to meet workers' demands. A strike is when workers refuse to work until they receive more money and better working conditions. The UFW also asked Americans to boycott, or refuse to buy, California lettuce and grapes until growers started treating the workers better. Chávez said, "We are not slaves and we are not animals. And we are not alone."

César Chávez practiced civic virtues by working to improve conditions for thousands of migrant workers throughout the United States. While he made great progress, the fight for better treatment of migrant workers continues today.

title: America Becomes a Superpower
text:
As the United States moved into the later part of the 20th century, the country was facing many domestic issues. A domestic issue is anything that concerns a country's internal affairs (operations). Tax rates, road construction and political elections are all examples of domestic issues that most nations face.

In the 1970s, Americans were still concerned with the effects of the U.S. involvement in the Vietnam War. Troops had been withdrawn in 1973, but many people were upset that the U.S. was a part of the Asian conflict. Americans were also still working to protect people's civil rights. In addition to these issues, there was a gas and oil shortage in the country.

In 1974, President Richard Nixon resigned (quit his job) as president after some of his close supporters broke into the headquarters of the Democratic National Committee. They were hoping to find information that might help President Nixon be re-elected. The president did not tell the truth about what had happened. Many people wanted the Senate to impeach President Nixon, or charge him with misconduct while he was in office. Nixon stepped down before he was placed on trial and removed from office if found guilty.

Despite the problems at home at the time, the U.S. continued to grow as an international superpower. As a superpower, the country had the ability to influence many world events during this same time. After World War II, the U.S. and the Soviet Union both became known as superpowers. The two countries had great military, economic, political and cultural power throughout the world. Sometimes the two superpowers agreed with one another, but more often the two countries disagreed on how world governments should run. Both countries supported many other nations around the world. They also kept a close watch on one another. They built up their supplies of nuclear weapons as protection. These weapons could release huge amounts of deadly energy and radiation if ever used.

In the late 20th century the Soviet Union fell apart. Today other nations are growing in power and military strength. However, the United States of America continues to work to help solve both domestic and international problems. We work to strengthen our standing as a great superpower in the world and our relationships with countries around the globe.

title: What Makes a Great President?
text:
Have you ever thought about being president of the United States? Do you think you would be a good president? What about being a great president?

Many people have listed the top five greatest U.S. presidents of all time as being George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, Franklin Roosevelt, Thomas Jefferson and Teddy Roosevelt. But what made them so great?

Some scholars say that to be a great president, a person should have intelligence, political experience, good public communication and team-building skills. It’s also important to have a vision, or a direction in which they want to lead the country. Woodrow Wilson, who was president from 1913 to 1921, said, “We grow great by dreams. All big men are dreamers.”

It’s been said that a great U.S. president does things for the country that sets it on a new course. Some say that a great president is willing to switch strategies to fulfill their vision for the country. A president is first elected for a four-year term. If voters think they have done a good job, then they will elect the person for a second term. When deciding if the president has done a great job, most people think about how our country is doing. One past president, Ronald Reagan, asked, “Are you better off than you were four years ago?”

So, what do you think? Who has been a great president? What about you? Do you think you would someday like to lead our country to greatness?

title: Oil Today … Gone Tomorrow
text:
The 20th century came in with a bang on Jan. 10, 1901. This was when the Lucas No. 1 oil rig blew drilling pipe, mud, gas and oil 100 feet high into the sky at Spindletop near Beaumont, Texas. From that moment on the United States of America was pulled from what was left of a rural agricultural economy and thrown right into a new era of industry.

Seventy years later, the country couldn’t remember a time when it didn’t have all the oil and gas it needed. But that all came to a sudden halt from October 1973 to March 1974, when nearly every gas station in the country often displayed signs that said, “NO GAS TODAY!” Had all the oil and gasoline been drilled?

The gasoline shortage was a result of an oil embargo. An embargo is a ban on the trade of a certain commodity (valuable resource). The United States produced lots of petroleum products, but not enough to supply the entire country’s needs. Millions of barrels of oil were being bought from nations in the Middle East, a region in Asia. These countries controlled more than half of all of the world’s petroleum. Petroleum is the material found in layers of the earth’s rock that can be used to produce fuels such as oil and gasoline.

The Middle Eastern nations became angry at the United States because of its support of the country of Israel. They immediately stopped all shipments of petroleum to the United States and other western nations. Because of the low supply and high demand for petroleum products, the cost of gasoline and heating oil skyrocketed.

Drivers all across the United States had to wait for hours to purchase small amounts of gasoline for their cars. Sometimes the gasoline ran out. Oil used to heat buildings was also in short supply. During the cold winter months, many schools and businesses were forced to cut hours or close altogether. Americans had to find ways to quickly adapt to the serious situation.

The crisis forced Americans to rethink the ways they used fuel. People drove less and shared rides with one another. The highway speed limits were reduced to help save gasoline. At home, people burned wood and lowered their thermostats. Some people even began to try and find other energy sources. Solar energy collectors used energy from sunlight to heat homes and businesses.

The U.S. government introduced a plan to help make the country less dependent upon oil from foreign countries. The plan was called Project Independence. The goal was to find ways to improve energy use in the country. The U.S. wanted to get to a point where it no longer needed to purchase oil from another nation. Americans were asked to conserve energy, or to use it carefully to prevent waste or loss. The U.S. wanted to protect oil and gas from being used unwisely. The government also promised to use the nation’s science, technology and industry to find ways to save oil and gas. Congress also approved the completion of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, which would carry oil from the Arctic region in Alaska to ice-free ports where it could be shipped to other parts of the country.

The demand for oil in the world and in the U.S. is constantly changing. Companies are finding new ways to reach oil supplies too. Do some research to find out how many barrels of oil the U.S. imported last year. Write your answer on the line.

title: Meltdown at Three Mile Island
text:
By the 1970s, the American government knew that the nation’s petroleum reserves (supplies) would one day be used up. Scientists needed to find new ways to produce energy for the nation. One promising energy source was the nuclear energy power plant. From 1968 to 1970, workers built a nuclear power plant near Harrisburg, PA. It was named Three Mile Island Nuclear Power Plant. For years the plant operated without any problems, and it seemed the country might have found a clean and safe source of energy.

That all changed, however, on March 28, 1979, when the nuclear plant malfunctioned. Without warning, a valve in the plant closed and the water supply to the nuclear reactor’s cooling system was cut off. The plant overheated. The radioactive part of the plant began to melt down. Radioactive gases were released into the air. The gases were like those released when the atomic bomb was dropped on Japan during WWII. Scientists were afraid the gases might explode. They worried that thousands of people could be killed or injured.

Thousands of people for many miles around the plant were asked to leave the area. For nearly two weeks, scientists watched the plant and waited for an explosion. Luckily such a traumatic event never happened. The amount was very small, but the damage to one of the nuclear reactors was severe. That reactor remains closed, and all the fuel has been removed from it.

After the accident people all over the United States began to question whether nuclear energy was really worth all of the possible problems. Very few nuclear energy power plants have been built or operated since the Three Mile Island disaster.

title: Super-Computers for the Superpower
text:
Keyboard … monitor … mouse … laptop … PC … tablet ... smartphone ... all of these terms might seem very familiar to you. You probably use a computer of some sort almost every day. You might have a computer you can use in your classroom. Maybe you even have a smartphone with a computer. Can you believe that before the 1970s there was no such thing as a personal computer? The only computers were room-size machines that took enormous amounts of energy to operate. That all changed in 1977 when Apple Computer, Inc. first introduced the Apple II personal computer.

The first personal computer was smaller and cheaper than any of the larger computers that had been available before then. The new machines were perfect for businesses and families. The first computers were used mainly as word processors. They were also popular for game playing. Over time, the personal computer has continued to change.

Today, nearly every person in America has access to a personal computer at home, school or work. They are smaller and cheaper than ever. Many people even have the same computer technology as part of their cell phones and tablets.

Computers today can be used to help people around the world communicate with one another. People can do their shopping and banking on their computers. It is even possible to get a college degree using a computer. Many people also use their computers to work from home. Computers can take us almost any place we need to go!

title: Ronald Reagan: From Hollywood to the White House
text:
Ronald Wilson Reagan grew up in a very poor family in Illinois. After high school he worked his way through Eureka College, where he studied economics and sociology. Reagan also played on the school’s football team and acted in school plays. After graduation he worked as a radio sports announcer. In the middle of the Great Depression, Reagan decided to take a chance on a new career. He went to Hollywood to try his hand at acting. Over the next 20 years, Ronald Reagan became one of the most respected actors of his time.

Reagan became involved with the actors’ union in Hollywood. He even became president of the group. In the 1960s, Reagan’s ideas about what the government could do for the country changed. He switched from the Democratic to the Republican Party.

Reagan was an excellent speaker. He was also very likeable. The people of California elected him governor of the state two times. Soon people all over the nation began to talk about the confident California governor with the great ideas and patriotic outlook. In 1980 voters chose Ronald Reagan to represent his Republican Party in the race for president of the United States.

The country was facing difficult times. Reagan was elected as the 40th president of the United States with the hope he would improve the country. Reagan spent two terms (eight years) in office. He was one of the oldest people ever elected to the job.

During his time in office, many Americans felt confident about the country. They felt the country was strong and peaceful. Many people were certain the best person possible was leading the country. Today, many Americans still remember Ronald Reagan as a strong, patriotic leader who kept America on the path to success.

title: Asking Your Own Questions
text:
Here are explanations of five different types of questions that require different levels of thinking to answer. Read the explanations of the levels, and then use the question starters to help you write 10 questions from this week’s issue. Trade your questions with a partner. Discuss the answers and type of thinking that was needed to answer each question.

RECALL: Recognizing or remembering facts, definitions, rules or principles

What is ______________________________________________________________________________?

Define _______________________________________________________________________________.

ANALYSIS: Dividing a whole into smaller parts

What is the main idea of _________________________________________________________________?

List the main events of __________________________________________________________________.

COMPARISON: Explaining similarities and differences between two or more things

Compare __________________________ to ___________________________. In what ways are they similar?

How does __________________________________ differ from _________________________________?

INFERENCE: Making predictions

EVALUATION: Drawing conclusions and providing support with reasons and evidence

title: Writing Focus: Creative Expository/Informational Writing
text: Share information in a creative way. Pretend you are a nuclear weapon. Write a public notice to the nations of the world. Explain facts about yourself and why it‛s important for the countries to take care of you. Also, describe the technology that was used to create you. Write in complete sentences, and support all of your ideas with facts and details. When you have finished writing, check for correct capitalization, punctuation and spelling.

title: Supply and Demand
text:
Can you name the most popular toy among your friends? It’s not uncommon for kids to go crazy for a new gadget. Whether it’s the latest scooter or a high-tech video game console, two rules usually apply. First, the more popular the toy is, the harder it is to find in stores. This means it will be more expensive to buy.

All products for sale, toys included, follow the rules of supply and demand: if a product is popular and many people want to buy it, then the supply of that product will decrease. It will become scarce. If the product becomes scarce, stores can then charge a higher price. The stores will keep increasing the price as long as people agree to pay more for it.

The second rule, the opposite market reaction, is also true. Have you ever watched a toy lose popularity? Suddenly, people aren’t so interested in buying it anymore. You can see the toy for sale in stores everywhere, and the toy is a lot less expensive.

Here’s what happened. Back when the toy was popular, factories produced more because store owners wanted to sell more at the higher price. The producers were rewarded with a larger profit. Then, when the toy became less popular, fewer people purchased the toy. As the demand decreased, the supply of unsold toys increased. That meant the store owners had an abundance of toys to sell. The easiest way to get rid of their surplus was to lower the price.

Business owners across all industries pay close attention to supply and demand. The last thing a store owner wants is a store full of toys that customers will not buy!

title: Memorial Day
text:
Memorial Day is a national holiday. It is observed each year on the last Monday in May. This day is set aside to honor the nation's armed services personnel who were killed in wartime. It is traditionally a day of parades, ceremonies, and speeches. Originally called Decoration Day, Memorial Day often involves decorating the graves of loved ones with flowers and flags.

Memorial Day was first observed on May 30, 1868. It was ordered by John Alexander Logan for the purpose of decorating the graves of those killed in the Civil War. He was a senator from Illinois and a war veteran.

Today, many people feel Memorial Day has lost its meaning. Some think it has become a camping and picnic holiday. To remind Americans of the true meaning of Memorial Day, the National Moment of Remembrance resolution was passed in December 2000. This resolution asks all Americans to voluntarily and informally observe in their own way a moment of remembrance and respect. They are asked to take time to pause from whatever they are doing for a moment of silence or to listen to “Taps.” This is meant to be done at 3 p.m. local time on Memorial Day.

title: Jobs in the US Today
text:
Approximately 160 million people make up the labor force in America. Many of these people work in similar industries in every state. Examples of employment that exists everywhere include education and health services, transportation, construction, and business and finance. However, there are some jobs and industries that are more common in specific regions of the country. Let’s look at some examples.

Northeastern states border the Atlantic Ocean. This resource provides many jobs to people in parts of Massachusetts and Maine. Here, commercial fishing and shipping are important industries. There are areas of the Pacific Northwest Coast where the fishing industry also provides many jobs. In the past, these two coastal regions contained large areas of forested land. The lumber industry provided many jobs. Today, opportunities in that industry have decreased. However, lumber production still provides about 350,000 jobs in America. Most of these jobs are in Alaska, Oregon, and California.

There are still areas of the country where many people work in agriculture. A significant part of the Midwest is known as the Corn Belt. Large corporate farms and smaller family farms produce commercial crops, such as corn and soybeans. In the South, farmers still grow traditional crops, like cotton and tobacco.

There are many factories in the Midwest that also provide jobs for a large number of people. A majority of U.S. auto manufacturing jobs are in states like Michigan, Indiana, and Ohio. There are also jobs in this region in food processing plants.

Some jobs can only be done in areas where certain natural resources are available. Texas is a good example of this. Parts of the state are rich in oil and natural gas deposits. Many people work to extract and refine these products for people to use to drive their cars and heat their homes.

Tourism, or taking care of people who travel on vacation, is also an industry that depends on specific characteristics of an area. Mountainous places like Colorado, Vermont, and Utah offer great skiing. Many people find jobs at resorts, hotels, and restaurants in these states and others where tourists visit. Areas with mild climates and nearby beaches also offer many opportunities for workers in this industry.

Job opportunities in the technology industry are increasing rapidly. Many technology companies have grown in both the Northeast and Northwest Regions of the country. Areas around Seattle, Washington, for example, are growing very fast. People move there for technology jobs. New technology companies are also employing many people in states like Texas and Utah. This industry is growing so fast that there will be many jobs opening up in the future that are not even thought of today.

title: Presidents From the Past and Present
text:
George Washington (Served 1789-1797)

No political party

George Washington was the first president of the United States. He was voted into office by a unanimous vote (vote agreed by all). Washington has been the only president chosen for office by 100 percent of the electors. Washington didn't known how a president should act. Yet, he did become a role model for all future presidents. Washington's fairness, leadership, gentle nature, and ability to compromise all benefited our country. These traits helped not only during war and peace but also with independence and growth. He helped make the U.S. the respected and successful country it is today.

John Adams (Served 1797-1801)

Federalist

John Adams was an important figure in U.S. history. Adams was elected as George Washington's vice president for two terms in office. He served a term as the second president of the United States. He tried again but lost a second election in 1800. After that, John and his wife, Abigail returned to life in Massachusetts. They focused on their family and friends. John enjoyed working on his autobiography. Abigail died of typhoid fever in 1818. John lived long enough to see his son, John Quincy Adams, elected as the sixth U.S. president. John died in 1826 at the age of 91. It was fitting that he died on July 4.

Franklin D. Roosevelt (Served 1933-1945)

Democrat

As president, Franklin D. Roosevelt faced many challenges. One was finding a way to bring the country out of the Great Depression. He developed programs that would help the poor and create jobs that would change America. People all over the nation started feeling hopeful. They had confidence that President Roosevelt was leading the country in the right direction. They approved of his work so much they elected him president four times! He is the only U.S. president to serve more than two terms. The 22nd Amendment to the Constitution now limits a president to two terms.

In one famous speech, Roosevelt told Americans, "The only thing we have to fear is fear itself." Roosevelt certainly believed this, and he lived in a way that was proof that the statement was true in his own life.

John F. Kennedy (Served 1961-1963)

Democrat

John F. Kennedy became the youngest man ever to be elected president of the United States. He was only 43 years old. He was born in Brookline, Massachusetts, in 1917. John joined the Navy after graduating from Harvard University. He served as a sailor during World War II. Then he returned home to Boston, where he was elected to the U.S. Senate.

John F. Kennedy became president of the United States in 1961. At his inauguration, President Kennedy gave an important speech asking all Americans to join together to serve their country. While he was president, he worked for equal rights for all Americans and had to solve a nuclear weapons crisis in Cuba.

On November 22, 1963, President Kennedy was riding in a convertible through the streets of Dallas, Texas. A gunman shot the president in the head. He was the youngest president ever to die while in office.

Ronald Reagan (Served 1981-1989)

Republican

Ronald Wilson Reagan grew up in a very poor family in Illinois. After high school, he worked his way through Eureka College. There he studied economics and sociology. Reagan also played on the school's football team and acted in school plays. After graduation, he worked as a radio sports announcer. In the middle of the Great Depression, Reagan decided to take a chance on a new career. He went to Hollywood to try his hand at acting. Over the next 20 years, Ronald Reagan became one of the most respected actors of his time.

Reagan became involved with the actors' union in Hollywood. He even became president of the group. In the 1960s, Reagan's ideas about what the government could do for the country changed. He switched from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party.

Reagan was an excellent speaker. He was also very likeable. The people of California elected him governor of the state twice. Soon, people all over the nation began to talk about the confident California governor with the great ideas and patriotic outlook. In 1980, voters chose Ronald Reagan to represent his party in the race for president of the United States. Reagan was elected as the 40th president of the United States with the hope he would improve the country. Reagan spent two terms (eight years) in office. He was the oldest person ever elected to the job.

Barack Obama (Served 2009-2017)

Democrat

On November 4, 2008, the country held its 56th presidential election. Barack Obama was a senator from Illinois. He ran for president against John McCain, a senator from Arizona. On election night, Senator Barack Obama made history when he became the first African American ever to be elected president of the United States.

Many Americans cheered Obama's great victory. In the early decades of the century, African Americans had a difficult time trying to vote. The 15th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution had been ratified in 1870. It gave citizens of all races the legal right to vote. However, African Americans had not always been treated fairly. Nearly 150 years later, an African American man stood proudly as the head of the executive branch of the United States of America.

In 2009, Obama was awarded one of the world's highest honors—the Nobel Peace Prize. The committee chose him because of his efforts to improve relationships between the many different peoples and countries of the world.

Joseph R. Biden Jr. (Served 2021-2025)

Democrat

Joseph Biden represented Delaware in the United States Senate for 36 years. He served as vice president to President Obama from 2009 until 2017. After leaving the White House, he worked with organizations that sought to expand the opportunities for Americans. In 2019, he announced his candidacy for president. He won the election in 2020.

Biden focused his efforts on the environment, infrastructure, and social programs. He also sought to enact measures which would eliminate or at least reduce the COVID-19 pandemic. He announced a withdrawal of U.S. troops from Afghanistan, ending nearly 20 years of military involvement in the country.

Donald J. Trump (Served 2017-2021, 2025-present)

Republican

Before running for president, Donald Trump was known for his experience in business. He won the presidency of the United States in 2016. Trump was a graduate of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School of Finance. He followed his father into the world of real estate development. New York City was home to many of his developments. He also opened and operates developments throughout the world. He was widely known as a reality television star. Trump ran for office on the promise of lowering taxes, an improved regulatory environment, and better trade deals.

Trump became known for communicating many of his policies using social media.

title: Past and Present Congress Members
text:
Have you ever traveled through La Guardia airport in New York City? It was named for Fiorello La Guardia. He was a Republican who served in the House of Representatives and as mayor of New York City. The U.S. House of Representatives and Senate make up the United States Congress, the legislative branch of the government. You may have heard of some other people who also served in Congress.

David Crockett fought and died in the Battle of the Alamo in San Antonio, Texas. David Crockett represented Tennessee in the House of Representatives. He later fought and died in the Battle of the Alamo in San Antonio, Texas.

Sam Rayburn from Texas, served for 25 terms in Congress, including as Speaker of the House of Representatives. George H.W. Bush, also from Texas, served not only as a representative, but later as vice president and president of the United States. He is one of the 35 members of Congress that went on to become presidents. Sixteen senators have been elected president. The latest was Senator Barack Obama of Illinois, the first African American elected as president.

Many African Americans have served in Congress. Hiram Rhodes Revels from Mississippi was the first African American elected to the Senate. Joseph Hayne Rainey, of South Carolina was the first African American elected to the House of Representatives. Representative Shirley Chisholm from New York became the first African American woman elected. However, she was not the first woman elected to Congress. That would be Representative Jeannette Rankin of Montana. Representative Romualdo Pacheco of California became the first Hispanic American to serve. Another representative from California, Dalip Saund, was the first Asian-Pacific American elected.

Other notable members of Congress include James Madison, a Founding Father. He became the first former representative to serve as president. John Marshall was the fourth Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. Before that he was a representative from the Federalist Party representing Virginia. He won the election with the support of George Washington and Patrick Henry.

Senator Fred Thompson from Tennessee and Representative Sonny Bono of California were actors. Senator Bill Bradley of New Jersey was a professional basketball player. Representative Jack Kemp of New York was a professional football player. Senator John Glenn from Ohio, was the first American to orbit the Earth. Later he became the oldest person to fly in space aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery.

Today these Congress members’ names have been in the news. Nancy Pelosi from California is the first woman to serve as Speaker of the House of Representatives. Vice President Mike Pence, a former representative from Indiana, serves as the President of the Senate. He is assisted by Senator Mitch McConnell of Kentucky and Senator Charles E. Schumer from New York.

title: Free Enterprise
text:
Have you ever heard the term free enterprise system? This term refers to a system where individuals and businesses are free to create and sell their products without government interference. The United States has a free enterprise system. Free enterprise markets only work if the laws of a country and the values of its citizens support them.

There are several important factors that keep the free enterprise system in the United States strong. These include the right to private property and an independent pricing system.

Private Property

Do you own a bike, a board game, or a CD player? These things are considered your private property. That's right! No one else has control over what you own.

Private property is the first pillar in the free enterprise system. When a person owns something, like a home or a business, they are responsible for taking care of it. In a free enterprise system, there is motivation to improve your property and use it to make one’s life better.

Price System

Prices provide guidance for producers and consumers. They reflect what the producer thinks their product is worth. They also show the market how much customers value the producer's good if they are willing to pay the price. They also provide clues for economists about whether a market is healthy or not.

Prices also provide incentives, or motivation, for businesses and consumers. For example, when prices are low, consumers usually buy more of a product. In other words, there is a great demand. Producers might have to make more product to keep the supply in line with the demand. Should the price of a product increase, then the consumer's demand for the product might decrease. Producers may end up with more product then they can sell, as the supply exceeds the demand.

You might already know that there is more than one way to divide our resources among all of the consumers. One way is through market competition. It is the third pillar of the free enterprise system.

Market Competition

Scarcity happens when products and resources are rare. Sometimes we want more of something than is available for us to have. Markets have this same kind of competition. Businesses compete every day for resources and products. They also compete for consumers!

Businesses create competition in the economy when they offer money for resources they want. Maybe they are offering money for machines they need. Or maybe they need skilled workers. Did you know that the more skills and education you have, the more companies will compete for you to work for them? As you compete to get a job, companies are competing for the best-trained workers too.

Businesses also compete for products and profit. They mostly do this by keeping their production prices low. They also compete by advertising their products. Businesses often compete with other businesses that have similar products.

Entrepreneurship

The last pillar in the free enterprise system is entrepreneurship. There are many entrepreneurs creating products and competing in our world today.

Entrepreneurs compete by thinking of better products for consumers. If people are unhappy with their breakfast cereal, an entrepreneur somewhere might come up with a way to improve their product. Then the entrepreneur will turn around and use their product to compete with other cereals. Entrepreneurs hope to make a profit competing with other companies. They use creativity to think of ideas that benefit everyone. What are some other ways entrepreneurs affect market competition in the economy?

title: Crude Oil
text:
Just as blood is vital to the human body, petroleum is vital to the United States. Petroleum comes from crude oil that is found underground. Much of it is sitting beneath the Southwestern states.

How did it get there? Millions of years ago, many different plants and animals lived and died in Earth’s oceans. Over time, they were covered in soil and pressure was applied. This process gave us crude oil. Crude oil is used in making gasoline. Some 250 million cars use nearly 400 million gallons of gasoline each day!

To extract crude oil, an underground oil well first needs to be drilled. Oklahoma and Texas have a lot of oil, so it makes sense to continue to drill there. Test wells can tell scientists whether or not there’s oil underground.

Drills from both land and water drilling rigs are used. They drill thousands of feet beneath the Earth's surface to pull out the oil. Technology has made it easier to pull oil from beneath lakes and other areas without harm. Once the oil is extracted, refineries take crude oil and turn it into usable fuels. Jet fuel and kerosene are made from crude oil. Gasoline, diesel, and heating oil are also fuels that refineries make. Did you know all the plastic we have in our schools and homes are made from crude oil too?

The American Petroleum Institute believes we have about 60 to 90 years worth of this nonrenewable resource remaining. Advancements in technology make it easier to get oil from new sources. However, it’s never too early to start conserving and using this resource wisely.

title: Labor Day
text: Historians are not certain who actually came up with the idea for Labor Day. Some believe that it was Peter McGuire. He was the first secretary of the American Federation of Labor. Others say the idea belonged to Matthew Maguire. He was the secretary of the Central Labor Union. New York’s Central Labor Union chose to make the idea a reality by organizing the first Labor Day on September 5, 1882, in New York City. The holiday was created to honor American workers who used their strength and skills to make life better for the entire country. The first Labor Day was celebrated with a parade, speeches, and a picnic for workers and their families. In 1894, Labor Day became an annual national holiday. People now celebrate it on the first Monday in September. What do you do on Labor Day?

title: On an Oil Site
text:
Oil comes from inside Earth. It is made from the remains of plants and animals. Over millions of years, oil forms from these remains due to extreme heat and pressure. To get the oil out of the ground, it needs to be drilled.

Oil is used for fuel in cars, airplanes, and trucks. It is also used to heat homes. Oil is even used to make things like medicine and plastic. Oil and its products can certainly make life a lot easier. However, finding it, making it, and moving it can do very bad things to the environment.

One way oil can hurt the environment is through an oil spill. An oil spill happens when pipelines or ships that move oil have accidents. The oil leaks into the soil or water. At the site of an oil spill, the oil hurts the wildlife. Birds can become covered with oil. The oil makes them too heavy to fly. Sea birds have a special coating on their feathers that makes them waterproof. Getting covered in oil removes this special coating so they cannot swim.

There have been two major oil spills in recent history. The first was the Exxon Valdez. This was an oil ship that hit a reef in Prince Edward Sound, Alaska, in 1989. The second major spill was from the Deep Horizon oil rig in the Gulf of Mexico in 2010. Both of these accidents released millions of gallons of oil into the water.

The federal government has many rules to help keep these accidents from happening again. Making and following strict rules is the only way that moving the oil can be safe. There are also many efforts being made to lower the amount of oil people use. Renewable sources of energy are much better for the planet. Solar and water power are totally clean. They are also much cheaper and do not harm plants and animals. It is hoped that the use of oil will go down as people become more interested in renewable energy sources.

title: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch
text:
The Pacific is the world's largest ocean. Several western states rely on the Pacific for food, resources, jobs, and recreation. Hawaii is completely surrounded by the Pacific Ocean. Thousands of miles of coastline form the borders of California, Oregon, Washington, and Alaska. Sadly, humans sometimes have negative impacts on the ecosystems of the Pacific Ocean.

Have you heard of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch? This floating garbage field sits between California and Hawaii. It is the world's largest deposit of plastic in any ocean on Earth. It measures twice the size of the state of Texas! Countless sea animals are affected by this man-made disaster.

Millions of tons of plastic get dumped into the oceans each year. Plastics and ocean water don't mix very well. Waves, wind, and sunshine break down large plastics but leave behind tiny pieces. There are nearly two trillion pieces of plastic floating in this garbage patch. Since the pieces are so small, ocean creatures, like sea turtles, whales, fish, and birds, eat the plastics while searching for food. These plastics can become stuck inside these animals. The chemicals used in making plastic can hurt them. Humans are at risk because they eat some of these sea creatures. Also, nearly half of the garbage patch is made up of fishing nets. Sea creatures are easily trapped and die in these floating hazards.

There are a total of five garbage patches in oceans around the world. Attempts are being made to clean them up. You can help. Recycle and reuse plastics. Limit your use of plastic straws and bring your own shopping bags when you shop. The oceans will be grateful.

title: Distribution of Cities
text:
Have you ever been to Phoenix, Arizona, in the summer? HOT! Did you ever wonder why people would settle in such a hot place? Or what about Fargo, North Dakota, where the weather can get as cold as -60 °F? Cities start and grow in certain areas for several reasons, like growing food or to start a business.

It’s believed by historians that the first cities were established some 8,000 to 11,000 years ago in Mesopotamia. Today, Mesopotamia is the country of Iraq. They settled because people started to plant and harvest crops and tend animals in one place rather than live a nomadic lifestyle where they were moving from place to place. Agriculture, along with the ease of sharing and growing crops, was the main reason for the growth of many early cities. Trade and commerce was another reason for people establishing businesses and settling in growing cities.

The city of Austin, Texas was settled because the Colorado River helped sustain the crops and livestock and provided the resources needed to survive. The river was a good way to move goods to other areas and import goods that weren’t available to the settlers. As the number of people grew, so did ideas and inventions like factories. Goods were created to provide city dwellers with almost everything they needed and wanted. Governments were formed and medical care became available. It became easier for people to make a living when they weren’t skilled or able to become farmers.

Giant cities on the East Coast like New York City grew because that is where many of the jobs developed. Historical events like food shortages and wars led many people to cities. Large numbers of people came to U.S. cities from Europe. The Great Migration also occurred. This was the movement of 6 million African Americans from the rural South to the cities of the Northeast.

So why would people settle in Phoenix? Phoenix grew because crops could be irrigated by two rivers nearby. People ended up in Fargo because it was along the Northern Pacific Railroad which is known as the “Gateway to the West.”

title: Spread the News
text:
Derek jumped off the school bus and ran as fast as he could toward his house. When he got home, he shoved the front door open and waved an envelope high in the air. “Mom! Mom! My report card is awesome!”

Derek’s mom studied his grades carefully, and soon a smile spread across her face. “Derek, this is a fantastic report card. You should be proud! Why don’t you share it with the rest of the family?”

“That’s a great idea, Mom,” Derek replied happily. He grabbed the report card and headed into the family room. He wanted to call his dad at work first, so Derek picked up his mom’s smartphone and pressed one button. Dad was on a business trip in New York, but he answered right away. He was especially proud of Derek’s improvement in math.

Next, Derek sent his older sister (who was away at college) a text message about his grades. He wanted her to know that he was working hard so he could go to college too one day.

Then, Derek wanted to let Grandma Nancy in Florida know about his report card. He went to the family’s computer and quickly sent her an email. He knew he’d probably hear back from her in just a few minutes.

Grandpa Jim, who lives in Washington, likes to actually see Derek’s report card. Derek headed to the scanner and copied his report card. He then sent his grandfather the digital image attached to an email.

Derek was ready for an after-school snack, so he headed to the kitchen to make microwave popcorn. Mom looked up from behind the counter, where she was working on her laptop. “Did you let everyone know about your big success?” she asked as she gently patted him on the back.

“I sure did, Mom. I called Dad, texted sis, emailed Grandma and sent Grandpa a scanned copy!” Suddenly Derek realized that in just a few minutes he had spread the word all over the country. “I guess good news travels quickly,” he laughed. Then he added, “Really, though, I guess nowadays all news travels quickly!”

Derek ran out of the kitchen before Mom had a chance to respond. “Finish your homework before you watch television, listen to your MP3 player or play video games!” Derek’s mom called out. “And to think ... when I was in school I had to send a letter.”

title: Helping Parents Watch Out For ‘Wired’ Kids
text:
The internet has changed the way people interact with other people all over the world. Today, computers provide tools that allow people to have access to an unbelievable amount of information. According to recent research by the Pew Internet & American Life Project, at least 95 percent of American teenagers use the internet. Parents and teachers often worry that young people are at risk when using the internet. Many of them say it is important for “wired” kids to know about internet dangers and understand there are ways to protect themselves. However, some parents have difficulty knowing how to help protect their children from internet danger because they themselves do not completely understand computers or how the internet works.

Experts say parents should stay well informed on current issues about the internet. They also say parents need to learn to use social networking sites, instant messaging and webcams so they can help their children use them safely too. In addition, children and parents must learn to have open discussions with each other about the internet. Kids should share their favorite things to do online, and parents should show their kids ways to respond if strangers approach them online. If families have open discussions about computers and their dangers, experts believe that children will feel comfortable going to trusted adults when they find themselves in an uncomfortable online situation.

title: The Information Age
text:
Do you ever remember a time when you couldn’t find what you were looking for using a computer and an internet search engine? Probably not. Inventions that make communication easy are common today. Televisions, computers and smartphones are just a few of the devices that people now use to share information. The period after World War II when many of these were first designed is known as the Information Age.

Television Invades American Homes

In the 20th century before World War II, most people read newspapers or listened to the radio to learn about news in the world. At the 1939 World’s Fair in New York City, a new communication invention was introduced. Distant seeing boxes (televisions) had been invented. At first, very few people bought the entertainment boxes. There were no regular programs to watch. Some people called the invention “the idiot box” and predicted that Americans would never want to sit and stare at a box every night. Boy, were they wrong!

After baseball’s World Series in 1947, Americans everywhere rushed to get a television for their homes. The screens were small, and the images were only in black and white. However, people quickly became hooked! All of a sudden, news, sports and entertainment programs were blaring in houses across the country. On early TVs, people had to change the channel by using a dial or button right on the TV. We can thank Dr. Robert Adler for inventing one of the first wireless remote controls for TVs. By 1956, more than half of all American homes had a television, and wireless remotes became popular in the 1980s. According to Nielsen Media Research, half of American homes today have three or more TVs.

Computers

One of the world’s first electronic digital computers was as big as a small house. It weighed 30 tons and amazed scientists with its ability to solve hundreds of multiplication problems in one second. Today, the computer you use in your classroom is even more powerful and certainly a lot more portable than that first computer, which often broke down.

By the 1960s, businesses used computers to do the work of many people. Computers were fast and accurate, but they were still very large. Engineers knew computers needed to be smaller and more powerful. In 1977, Apple Computer, Inc. introduced the personal computer, or PC. Suddenly the computer was small and cheap enough for the average American to own. Information was instantly available at home and at work.
