Today, personal computers are found in around 80% of American households. The demand for personal computers is great, and the cost of producing them has decreased steadily. A consumer can spend anywhere from a few hundred to a couple of thousand dollars on a personal computer. There are also portable microcomputers, or laptops, available so people can easily work from different areas of buildings or their homes. Tablet computers are also becoming very popular. Tiny computers are also found in thousands of other items people use every day. Cell phones, video game systems, watches and DVD players are only a few examples of devices in which computer technology is important.

The Internet and the World Wide Web

In the last decade of the 20th century, the Information Age sped up tremendously. The internet and World Wide Web allow computers all over the world to communicate and share information with each other. Pictures, sounds and movies can be shared using the Web. These two communication revolutions didn’t happen overnight though.

The first internet, or international computer network, was developed in 1969, when computers at two California universities were connected. The computers crashed (quit working) the very first day they were linked. Scientists kept working on the ideas, and by 1971, computers were being used to send the first e-mail messages.

It was only a matter of time before engineers put together the idea of a global computer system. The World Wide Web made it even easier for people to send and receive information. The first web page was developed in 1991. It was a site to explain exactly what the World Wide Web was.

Today the internet and the World Wide Web continue to grow and constantly change our world. Many new jobs have been created because people can use computers to work with information. Advancements in technology have made it possible for people to work from home, in coffee shops, on airplanes and almost anywhere!

A Continually Changing World

Today, the Information Age continues to change the way Americans live, work and play. Social media sites like Facebook and Twitter connect people from their computers, tablets and smart phones. YouTube has brought free video sharing to the public. People all over the world can research information, watch television shows and movies, shop, bank and communicate with other people at any time of the day. It is likely the ways people communicate and share information will continue to grow and change as technology continues to improve and advance. Where is the Information Age headed from here? No one can be sure, but hold on tight because the ride there will certainly be a fast one!

title: U.S. Urban Population
text: Many people in the U.S. today live in urban areas. An urban area is a city with a larger population than the surrounding areas. People often choose to live in these areas because of the jobs and industry available there. Other people enjoy living near shopping, education and entertainment sites usually found in urban areas. Rural areas have smaller populations and use more land for agriculture, or farming. Of course, rural areas also have businesses, shopping, education and entertainment, but the majority of land is used for growing food and producing other things that we need. These products are shipped to urban areas around the nation.

title: America at War: Operation Desert Storm
text:
In August 1990, the United States found itself involved in a war that would forever change the nation and perhaps the world. It was at that time that the dictator of Iraq, Saddam Hussein, ordered his army to attack and capture the neighboring country of Kuwait, even though the two countries had once been allies. (A dictator is a ruler with total power.)

Around the world, people worried Iraq might try to invade and attack the oil-rich country of Saudi Arabia next. The world depended on Saudi oil. They knew the Iraqi dictator would want to control all of the oil if he could. The United Nations agreed something had to be done to get Hussein’s army out of Kuwait. Troops from the United States, France, England, Saudi Arabia and other countries were sent into battle.

In January 1991, the United States began Operation Desert Storm against Hussein’s army. U.S. General H. Norman Schwarzkopf led the troops. The Iraqi army was pounded with bombs and missiles. Air raids went on for a month. Ground forces moved into Kuwait about a month later. The United States demolished almost all of the Iraqi army’s equipment. Almost 200,000 Iraqi soldiers surrendered (gave up) to the U.S. military.

Operation Desert Storm was a great victory for the United States. Kuwait was freed from Iraqi control. In 2003, Saddam Hussein was captured and put in prison. Three years later he was executed (put to death) for crimes against humanity.

title: Create a Bibliography
text:
When you write a research paper, you must keep an alphabetical list of all the sources you used to get your information, or a bibliography. A bibliography is sometimes called a list of works cited (named as a reference or resource).

You have to list different types of sources in different ways in a bibliography. For example, books, magazines and websites are all listed in different ways. Elementary school bibliographies are usually not as detailed as the bibliographies you will do in high school and college.

It is important to be able to create a bibliography each time you research information, but there are also many different online bibliography websites to help you.

Study the different bibliography formats. Next, create a bibliography listing for each piece of information.

Book

Author’s Last Name, Author’s First Name. Name of Book. City of publication: Publisher’s name, Copyright Date.

Magazine Article

Author’s Last Name, Author’s First Name. “Title of Article.” Name of Magazine. MM/DD/YYYY: Pages (numbers only).

World Wide Web

Author’s Last Name, Author’s First Name. “Title of Article.” Title of website. Date created or revised (Abbreviation of month DD, YYYY). Institution or group that maintains the website. Date you visited it. (URL)

title: Changes in Our Economy
text:
New Jobs for a New Age

The jobs your grandparents had are very different from the jobs many of today's students will have when they finish school. Why? Advancements in technology and the widespread use of computers have changed employment. Our desire to develop cleaner energy and stop pollution is also changing the workforce. Of course, we still have farmers and factory workers, but thanks to technology, they do their jobs very differently than they did 100 years ago.

Many of today's jobs involve the use of computers and robotics. Computers are used to record, process, and communicate information. Some computers take the place of human workers. Other computer jobs require more skilled and educated workers to perform them. Many assembly line and manual labor jobs are now being automated. That means that robots are putting products together. They are also performing tasks that human workers used to do. Employment has shifted from manual jobs to careers like engineering, software development, and computer programming. These new careers involve building, using, and maintaining computers for businesses. They also require a great deal of education and training. With the right training and education, you just might become the next big computer animator or video game designer.

Clean and Green

Another change in our economy results from more interest in clean energy. Industries are exploring the uses of alternative energy. Thousands of people work in this field. The number of clean energy jobs has increased. At the same time, employment in other industries has declined. So what is clean energy? Clean energy includes energy from resources like solar and wind power. These forms of energy are environmentally friendly. They do not pollute the air, land, or water. Clean energy resources, such as the sun and the wind, will also never run out.

Production of "green" or environmentally friendly building materials and hybrid vehicle engines also provides jobs. People work to make solar panels, chemical-free insulation, and battery-operated cars. These industries put people to work while making the community a healthier place to live. They also help reduce our dependence on oil and decrease carbon pollution that threatens our natural resources.

Changes in technology and resources have changed jobs throughout the world. In today's economy, employers are looking for critical thinkers and problem solvers. Businesses want employees who are capable of working with new technology. Workers also need to be able to adapt to new situations. Study hard and do your best in school so you can be a worker of the future!

title: Technology of Yesteryear vs Technology Today
text:
What comes to mind when you hear the word technology? High-tech gadgets like smartwatches? Virtual reality? That's only part of it. Technology is the use of scientific knowledge to solve problems or invent tools. It has been making life easier for millions of years. Stone Age tools were the first examples of technology. Some scientists believe primates that predate humans used primitive tools millions of years ago.

It is believed that the wheel was invented in 3500 B.C.E. Thousands of years later, two more transportation advances changed the world again. The first of these inventions was the rudder. That is the part of the steering system of a ship that controls direction. The second major advancement was the compass. Around 1,000 years ago, people began using compasses to navigate. Before that, people relied on the stars to guide them. Four hundred years later, the printing press was invented. The printing press made mass production of books possible. As a result, many more people gained access to information and education. The inventions of the rudder, the compass, and the printing press helped launch the modern era.

As people explored, they exchanged ideas. Knowledge spread. Indigenous people had their own technology long before Europeans arrived in North America. They invented kayaks, canoes, and snowshoes. They also developed farming methods and hybrid seeds. The first people in the Americas cultivated many types of corn, beans, and squash that we still eat today.

The mid-1800s to the mid-1900s was a time of great change in America. It's hard to imagine how different life was in 1844. That is the year that Samuel Morse sent the first telegraph message. At the time, there were only 26 states. In the 1800s, people traveled by horse-drawn carriage. Most Americans had never heard of a flushing toilet. Antibiotics did not exist. Over the next 125 years, the world was transformed. By 1969, Americans had landed on the moon! One hundred and twenty-five years isn't as long as it sounds. Think about the people who lived through these changes. There were people watching the moon landing who were born before the automobile was invented! The technology that developed between 1844 and 1969 changed life in America. Organ transplants and vaccines extended our lives. Cars and planes gave us the freedom to travel. Air conditioning made us more comfortable. Inventions like seatbelts and airbags made us safer. Vacuums and sewing machines made household chores easier. Radio and television entertained and informed us. Technology continues to advance at an incredible rate.

The 50 years since the moon landing have brought us some of the inventions we use the most. The first personal computers were produced in the 1970s. Today, we walk around with little computers in our pockets and on our wrists. Most of us can't imagine life without the internet.

The advances of the last 50 years have changed family and community life in our world. Cell phones, email, and social media have brought us closer in some ways. We can talk to someone on the other side of the state, or even the planet, using a device that fits in our pocket. We can send messages to anyone from just about anywhere. That's pretty incredible!

title: Future Transportation
text:
Think of how exciting it was for people to take their first train ride. After years of traveling on foot, on horseback, or in wagons, riding a train must have seemed like a transportation miracle.

Are you ready to see your own transportation breakthrough? It might be here sooner than you think. Automotive and technology engineers have been working on some pretty creative new designs to help you get where you’re going without negative effects on the environment.

Google has sponsored people to work on a self-driving car. When you think about driving a car, one of the first things to come to mind might be the steering wheel. But you may not see a steering wheel in one of Google’s cars! They want to build a car that doesn’t need a person to drive. All you would need to do is push the “start” button, type in where you want to go, and enjoy the ride!

So, how does it work? The car uses a system called “LIDAR.” LIDAR stands for “Light Detection and Ranging” and uses lasers to “see” the road and anything else nearby. A computer uses that information to control the wheels and steer the car. Test versions of the car have driven thousands of miles to make sure they are safe.

What other ideas are becoming realities that will change your life? In 1962, children in America watched a cartoon show called The Jetsons. It was about a family living in the future. They had lots of cool technology that did not exist in the real world at that time. One of the most unlikely futuristic items was George Jetson’s flying car. No one could ever create a flying car, could they?

The answer is yes, they can. The Samson Motor Company of Redmond, Oregon, has worked on testing a flying car. They estimate that the car will have maximum speeds of 120 mph (miles per hour) on the road and 450 mph in the air. Engineers in China have also conducted successful tests of a drone that can carry a person. A company in Slovakia has created a hybrid-electric road vehicle that can transform into a flying vehicle in three minutes. The future has arrived! Talk with a partner about how these new forms of transportation might affect your future.

title: NASA'S Human Computers
text:
During the 1950s and '60s, before electronic computers, the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) had mathematicians who solved problems and did calculations. Can you guess what they were called? If you said computers, you are correct!

One of these human computers was Katherine Johnson. She was hired to work for the NACA, which came before NASA. At that time, white workers and African American workers were segregated (separated). Katherine worked in a section with other African American women. She was so good at her job that she was asked to help calculate astronaut John Glenn's orbit around the Earth. She also helped astronauts land on the moon. Can you imagine doing all those complex math problems without a calculator?

At NACA, Katherine met Dorothy Vaughan, another African American human computer. She taught herself programming in order to be able to work with the first electronic computers. When NACA later became NASA, segregated units were no longer used. Everyone worked together, and Dorothy became a supervisor.

Mary Jackson was also an African American human computer. Mary worked hard to get permission to take advanced courses in a "whites-only" college. There, she earned her engineering degree. She became NASA's first African American female engineer.

These women never gave up overcoming racial barriers during the Space Race and the Civil Rights era.

title: Medical Technology
text:
We live in an age where we have access to some amazing medical breakthroughs. A combination of scientific inquiry and the development of new technologies have made possible what was once considered impossible. Recently, there have been advancements in medicine: laparoscopic surgery (minimally invasive surgery), robotic surgery, better cancer treatments, and the invention of bionic limbs.

It isn’t just in the U.S. where medical knowledge has grown. Governments around the world are working together to reduce or eliminate diseases. The World Health Organization (WHO) works in 150 countries. It provides leadership, research, and support for disease control. In the U.S., we have an organization called the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The purpose of this organization is to protect Americans from health and safety threats. The CDC works with other nations and WHO to prevent the spread of diseases.

Advancements in communication have helped too. Huge leaps in 20th century technology enable information to be passed much faster than before. Now, in the 21st century, we have the ability to contact one another just about anywhere on Earth using cellular and satellite phones. Information about outbreaks, new diseases, or successful treatments can be broadcast instantly.

The advent of penicillin in 1928 introduced the world to antibiotics. Countless lives around the world were saved from diseases that would have meant a death sentence just a few years earlier. With research in every area of medicine, we will see miracles in the future of healthcare.

title: A Dark Day in American History
text:
On Sept. 11, 2001, America awoke to a new and terrifying threat. It took just minutes for the country to be changed forever, although that dark day in American history seemed to last forever. That was the day America faced one of the worst terrorist attacks it has ever known.

On that bright, clear morning, America was attacked without warning by an enemy we never saw coming, a group of men who were part of a terrorist group that wanted to hurt our country. They didn’t agree with the ideas on which America was built: freedom and equal rights for all people. They planned an attack they hoped would make Americans feel helpless and afraid. The terrorists hoped Americans would panic and blame each other for the attack. They wanted America and its citizens to suffer in a terrible way.

The men belonged to a group led by a man named Osama bin Laden. Men from this group, called al-Qaida, hijacked (took control of illegally) four American airplanes while the jets were in the air. All four planes crashed within one hour.

One of the planes crashed into the Pentagon building, the U.S. Department of Defense headquarters in Washington, D.C. The crash killed 125 people on the ground, along with everyone on the airplane — 59 passengers and crewmembers, plus the five terrorists.

Another plane was heading to crash into the White House or the U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C. Passengers on the plane fought back. They tried unsuccessfully to get control of the jet, and the plane crashed into an empty field in Pennsylvania. All passengers and crewmembers were killed.

The last two airplanes crashed into the World Trade Center towers in New York City. It was not the first time these buildings had been attacked. In 1993, a different terrorist group bombed the towers. The buildings withstood that attack, but many people were injured, and six died. In 2001 the damage destroyed the towers and killed more than 2,700 people. Both towers caught fire after the planes hit them. Soon after being hit, the buildings collapsed, filling the air with smoke, dust and debris. Nearly 500 New York City firefighters, rescue workers and law enforcement officials died trying to rescue victims that day.

Americans were shocked and saddened by the attack. However, they did not react the way the terrorists had hoped. The spirit of America became even stronger, and the people stood together to face the terrible situation. Americans knew they had to stay brave and hold strongly to their belief in freedom. The Pentagon was repaired. The World Trade Center in New York City has been rebuilt as a memorial to those who died. People from all over the nation and the world have donated their money and time to relief efforts.

The United States and the world changed in many ways after the 9/11 attacks. The U.S. wanted to punish the country and the people who had planned the attacks. Military troops were sent to Iraq and Afghanistan to fight terrorists. The leader of the terrorists, Osama bin Laden, was found and killed in May 2011 by U.S. Navy Seals.

Unfortunately, there are still people in the world who want to see the U.S. fail as a free country. This is why the nation continues to fight the war on terrorism. This week you will learn about how the United States of America continues to protect its citizens and works to be strong and successful in the 21st century and beyond.

title: The War on Terror
text:
Since Sept. 11, 2001, the United States has been at war ... with terrorism. Until that day most Americans never thought there could be a large-scale attack on their own country on home soil. Most people never even dreamed other groups would try to gain political power through violent acts against innocent civilians. The attacks on New York City and Washington, D.C. came as a complete surprise. Since that infamous day, U.S. government leaders have worked to find ways to make sure the people of the United States are safe and secure.

Causes of Terrorism

Most people don’t understand why the terrorist attacks on the U.S. happened. After all, it seems hard to believe anyone would want to bring such pain and destruction to any country and its people. Sadly, there are many reasons that individuals and groups throughout the world believe terror attacks can help them achieve their goals. Historians say terrorist acts are most likely to occur in societies where people have little hope of improving their own lives. They also believe many acts of terrorism are fueled by controlling leaders who want their own extreme political or religious plans put into action. For example, it was Osama bin Laden who led the terrorist group called al-Qaida in the plot against the U.S on 9/11.

Changes in Security

Before Sept. 11, 2001, flying on an airplane was fun and easy. There were a lot fewer security rules. All of the hijackers were able to board airplanes carrying small knives they used as weapons. After 9/11, airport security was greatly increased. Today when people fly, they must show identification and pass through detailed security areas. Most airports also use metal detectors and special X-ray machines to check airline passengers, to make sure that no one is carrying weapons.

The Homeland Security Act

Immediately after the attacks of 9/11, President George W. Bush and other national leaders wanted to make sure they did everything they could to help U.S. citizens remain safe. One of the first things they did was pass the Homeland Security Act. The Act created the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and the position of Secretary of Homeland Security. Together these people work to protect the United States from terrorist acts and natural disasters.

United We Stand

In the weeks and months right after the terrorist attacks on the United States, the people of America united to show the rest of the world just how strong and determined our country was. Today the people and government of the country work together to keep everyone safe and secure. Many new programs and regulations (rules) have been enacted (put into place). Both small rural communities and large urban cities have made plans to deal with attempted terror attacks.

There have been other attempted terrorist attacks on the nation since 9/11. However, most of the attacks were uncovered before the most serious damage was done. It is certain that there will always be terrorist groups planning attacks against the United States. However, by working together to fight the war on terrorists, we will continue to keep the United States of America safe, strong and proud.

title: Making Choices When Times Are Tough
text:
September 11, 2001 was a frightening day for the entire country. As Americans watched the news reports, many were scared and upset. Many wondered if more attacks would come and what the future held. All airplanes were grounded shortly after the attacks. When we are afraid, it can be hard to make decisions or figure out the right thing to do. Soon, Americans chose to come together in a spirit of patriotism. We knew that we would remain strong and free during this dark time.

However, fear can motivate negative actions. Because the group responsible for the attacks, Al-qaeda, operates in the Middle East, some Americans believed that anyone from the Middle East was an enemy. Some thought that Muslims were all bad people. This was not true. In reality, many American Muslims and people with Middle Eastern heritage were as patriotic as anyone else. They enjoyed the rights and responsibilities that came with living in America. They have helped to make the United States a great place to live. Middle Eastern Americans and Muslims serve in the U.S. military, making great sacrifices to protect our nation.

The time after September 11 was a difficult period for these Americans. People from the Middle East and Muslims faced hate, suspicion and discrimination. Where people saw friends and neighbors, they now saw enemies. Yet they were as saddened and frightened by the attacks as anyone else. Unfortunately, this hate has not completely disappeared to this day.

As Americans, we should remember that fairness is an important virtue. It is not fair or right to blame innocent people for the actions of a few. All Americans deserve the right to “life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.” We learn this in the Declaration of Independence. When you are angry, sad or afraid, remember that you can make choices. Will you come together with fellow Americans, or will you say or do unkind things?

title: General Colin Powell: American Soldier and Statesman
text:
In the 1990s, the United States was involved in military actions in Asia to push the Iraqi army out of the small, oil-rich country of Kuwait. Operations Desert Shield and Desert Storm were huge successes for the American military. Most people involved agreed that much of the military's success was due to the leadership of General Colin Powell.

Colin Luther Powell was born in Harlem, New York, in 1937. His parents had emigrated from Jamaica to the United States. Powell's parents valued education and were pleased when their son studied geology in college. It was during this time that he became interested in a career in the military.

Powell joined the U.S. Army and served in Vietnam. Lieutenant Powell won 11 awards for his service and bravery, including the Purple Heart, the Bronze Star and the Legion of Merit.

Powell completed his college degree and began working at the White House in Washington, D.C. He also continued to advance in his military career as he advised presidents of the United States. After General Powell retired from the Army in 1993, many people continued to admire and respect him as a great man and leader in the country.

In 2000, Colin Powell was appointed the U.S. Secretary of State under President George W. Bush. At the time, that was the highest rank an African American had ever held in U.S. government. Many Americans were disappointed when General Powell chose not to run for president of the United States.

Today General Powell is devoted to helping America's young people reach the highest goals in their lives, just as he did.

title: A Historic Election
text:
Thousands of people gathered in Grant Park in Chicago, Illinois, on a cold autumn night. Most were not shivering from the cold but shivering with excitement. They were about to hear some news that made history.

On Nov. 4, 2008, the country held its 56th presidential election. Democrat Barack Obama, a senator from Illinois, ran against Republican John McCain, a senator from Arizona. On election night, Senator Barack Obama made history when he became the first African American ever to be elected president of the United States of America.

Many Americans cheered Obama's great victory. Not long before, African Americans were not even guaranteed the right to vote. Even though the 15th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution had been ratified in 1870 and gave all citizens of all races the right to vote, African Americans had not always been treated fairly. Now an African American man stood proudly as the head of the executive branch of the United States of America.

Obama ran for the presidency with the message of change and hope. Many Americans believed he was the right person for the job and elected him to a second term four years later. President Obama faced the same challenges and difficulties many other presidents before him have faced. Economic ups and downs continue, and the country is still fighting the war on terrorism. Still, Americans can feel proud of this historic milestone in racial equality.

title: Main Idea and Details
text: Read the article “The War on Terror” again. Identify the main idea of each section. Then list two details that support the main idea.

title: Looking Back: 1930s to the Present
text:
A New Deal in a New Century

The United States had fallen into a Great Depression by 1932. Millions of people had lost their jobs, homes and hope when the stock market crashed several years earlier. When President Franklin D. Roosevelt (FDR) took office in 1933, he promised to bring hope back to the people with his New Deal plan.

FDR was a dedicated president. The life-long democrat worked hard to develop programs that would help the poor and create jobs for people in all parts of the country. The Works Progress Administration (WPA) and the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) were developed to do just that. Rather than the government offering money to those in need, workers in these programs earned wages. They planted trees, built roads, airports and parks, created art and fought forest fires. Another of Roosevelt’s programs, the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), helped Americans living along the Tennessee River in the southeastern United States. Here, companies hired Americans to build dams and electrical power systems. Homeless Americans had hope that they could borrow money to own property again when the Federal Housing Administration, or FHA, was established. The Social Security Administration also helped needy and elderly citizens.

Roosevelt’s New Deal programs guided the country to better times. His popularity and passion for peace, safety and freedoms that humans deserve helped him get elected as the nation’s president for four terms.

The Fight for the Final Frontier

One of the most defining moments of the 20th century was July 20, 1969. On this day, American Neil Armstrong became the first person to step onto the surface of the moon. This success was a result of many years of technological achievements and failures. Most of them started when World War II ended. The United States and the Soviet Union then began a fierce technological competition with one another.

Americans were thrilled with how technological advances changed the way they worked and traveled. Scientific discoveries led to the invention and improvement of steamboats, railroads and automobiles. But travel into outer space had only been a dream since the Wright brothers flew the first airplane decades earlier.

Presidents Kennedy and Johnson approved the millions of dollars and hours of work that were put into the nation’s space program. Glitches, or failures, along the way did not put the dream of space travel to rest.

The scientific work of the space race era led to the beginning of the Information Age. Today people all over the world have access to and share information through television, cell phones, computers and the internet. The ways people live, work, learn and play are always changing because of improved technology that began as a race between two countries.

Notes on the Notable

Many Americans contributed to our nation’s successes since WWII. While it is impossible to list and detail all of these important people, here are a few notables to remember.

Dwight David Eisenhower was one of our country’s most respected military leaders during WWII. He was smart and used good strategic planning to lead troops against the Axis forces. As president of the United States, Eisenhower was admired and respected for his strong leadership of the entire nation.

Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. helped lead the Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s. Dr. King’s determined but peaceful efforts to help people of all races led to Congress passing the Civil Rights Act. This act established laws against treating people unfairly because of the color of their skin.

Rosa Parks is remembered as the “mother of the Civil Rights Movement.” She earned this title by refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger. Parks remained a peaceful and determined leader in the movement for her entire life.

Ronald Wilson Reagan started out as an actor and ended up as the 40th president of the United States. Reagan’s excellent communication skills and strong leadership style helped make him one of the most admired people ever to hold the office.

title: At War and At Peace in the 20th and 21st Centuries
text:
In 1939, the United States had problems of its own to face. The Great Depression had left millions of Americans without jobs or homes. President Franklin Delano Roosevelt's New Deal programs were bringing promise of better days, however. Slowly but surely, people went back to work, and the nation's industry and economy improved. When word of war in Europe reached the United States, most Americans wanted no part in it. However, World War II was underway, and the United States soon found it was all but impossible to stay out of it. Germany and Japan were angered when the United States aided Great Britain and disrupted the Japanese oil and rice trade. Following Japan's attack on U.S. forces at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii, the United States was in the middle of a war once again.

Millions of Americans worked for the war effort. Many men went into battle while women worked to keep factories open. Families rationed (controlled the amount of) goods they used and planted victory gardens. Several groups of dedicated Americans worked against all odds for the war effort. The 442nd Army Infantry, a group of Japanese American soldiers, took an oath of loyalty before serving the country. The Tuskegee Airmen were the first African American military pilots in America. These flyers were often disrespected and treated unfairly, but they served the nation in the fields of intelligence, meteorology and engine mechanics. American Indian "code talkers" from the Navajo tribe helped the U.S. government send unbreakable code messages back and forth among troops, using the Navajo language. Americans everywhere rallied for the cause. World War II did not end until the United States, led by president Harry S. Truman, dropped atomic bombs on two Japanese cities.

Life After War

Life in America changed dramatically after WWII. Technology established during the war brought changes to communication, transportation and medicine. The nation had pulled itself out of the Great Depression. Returning soldiers were able to find jobs, buy homes and settle into a comfortable life. Families had money again for cars and other "extras." However, a downside to life in America was that African Americans and other minorities did not always get equal opportunities. The fight for these equal rights was quickly overshadowed when war in Korea broke out. The U.S. was once again on the battlefield for almost three more years. During this time, there was another kind of war brewing.

The Cold War, which really wasn't a war at all, was the name given to the relationship between the U.S. and the USSR. Even though the two countries had been friendly toward each other during WWII, they did not always agree. The nations did not trust one another and would often fight with words instead of weapons. As both the U.S. and the USSR grew in power and wealth, they spent great amounts of money and effort to show who had better technology, including computers, weapons and space travel. Both countries wanted to be the first to put a person on the moon.

A Fight for Rights

The 1960s and 1970s were a troubled time in our country. There was an ongoing fight to give equal rights to everyone, regardless of skin color. The Civil Rights Movement grew to a peak when Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. led millions of Americans in demanding that racial segregation be against the law. In 1964, the U.S. Congress passed the Civil Rights Act. This act ended discrimination in employment and education. People of different races could no longer be treated unfairly. The war against discrimination did not end immediately. The assassination of Dr. King was a tragic event that delayed progress. Changes in U.S. laws, though, have helped guarantee that people of many different groups and of all races deserve fair treatment. During this same time, the U.S. became involved in one of the most hopeless wars in South Vietnam. For nearly nine years, the U.S. fought a very unpopular battle. Nearly 60,000 American men and women lost their lives in the war.

By the late 20th century, the United States was known as a world superpower. The Cold War with the USSR ended when the USSR collapsed and reorganized. Other nations around the world gained strength, and several world leaders began to question the role our nation played in world politics. One of these countries was Iraq. Their leader, Saddam Hussein, became very powerful. When Iraq invaded and threatened other Middle Eastern countries, the United States jumped in to try to keep Hussein from becoming a threat to people all over the world. The U.S. found itself involved in Operation Desert Storm and Desert Shield, led by General Colin Powell. By 2003, Hussein had been captured, and the U.S. declared a victory.

Perhaps one of the greatest wars the United States has faced is the war against terrorism. After a surprise attack on American cities on Sept. 11, 2001, by a terrorist group known as al-Qaida, many people felt scared and helpless. New laws aimed at protecting innocent citizens changed the world and the ways people lived, worked and played. Today, the leader of the terrorist group has been killed, but the American government still works to make sure the people of our country are safe from attack. The United States remains a strong superpower of the world.

title: Baby Boomers Enjoy City Life
text:
Early settlers in the United States most often made their livings on farms and ranches. After World War II, many American cities grew rapidly. Soldiers returning from war went to college and found jobs. In many cities there were not enough homes for everyone who wanted to purchase one. Companies began to build homes right outside the cities in suburban areas. New homes were built, and young families moved right into their new lives in these planned communities.

The population rate soared as young families married, bought homes and had children. The women in some families also worked outside of the home, keeping jobs they had taken during the war. In the year before the war, during the Great Depression, most families had very little money for extras. Now families could spend money on automobiles, clothes, furniture, restaurant meals and vacations.

title: Oil’s Well That Ends Well
text:
The U.S. economy changed greatly after people found oil in Texas in 1901. In fact, workers found large amounts of oil and natural gas underground in several areas of the country. People in these places found jobs drilling or processing oil and gas-based products. Suddenly, oil and gas businesses replaced a rural, or agricultural, economy. The nation came to rely heavily on these petroleum products.

Even though the United States produces a large amount of petroleum products, we must buy more from other countries. Many of these countries are located in the Middle East. During the 1970s, some of these nations became angry with the U.S. and refused to ship petroleum products to us. While the crisis came to an end rather quickly, it made Americans realize the importance of conserving, or saving, fossil fuels and finding alternative fuel sources.

title: Do You Compute?
text:
Computers are now a part of everyday life. We use them to operate everything from telephones to automobiles to kitchen appliances. Many people have access to a super-powerful computer right at their fingertips, night and day. Such technology was just a dream before the 1970s. That is when Apple Computer, Inc. first introduced a personal computer that replaced energy-guzzling, room-sized computers.

The newer computers were affordable for businesses and families. They gave people information at the push of a button. They made many tasks quicker and easier. Today, personal computers connect people from all over the world. We can communicate, shop, bank or research topics. Computers have made it possible for people to work and learn from home or on the go. Many people use small hand-held devices such as smartphones or tablets.

title: 2008: Presidential History is Made
text:
On Nov. 4, 2008, a historical event took place in the United States. On this day, a Democratic senator from Illinois, Barack Obama, was elected to lead the United States as president.

Many Americans cheered as the nation’s first African American ever elected as president spoke to the people about change and hope for the future.

Like others who have held the same office, President Obama faced many difficult situations as leader of such a powerful nation. Many people continued to believe in his ability to lead the country. With his re-election to the office in 2012, citizens of the U.S. showed American society continues to progress.

title: Charting U.S. Leaders
text: Use the content frame to organize and compare information about notable American leaders of the 20th and 21st centuries. Use information from this review unit along with information you learned from earlier issues to help you complete the activity.

title: Let's Write
text: Mount Rushmore is an important landmark in our nation. The carvings on the large mountain honor four of America’s great leaders and celebrate courage, leadership and strength. What leader of the 20th and 21st centuries do you think deserves to have their face carved in a new monument? Write a composition in which you identify the leader you feel deserves this honor the most. Support your choice (main idea) with three reasons (details). Be sure to check your work for proper grammar, spelling and punctuation.

title: Think and Review
text:
What was the underlying theme of Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal? What details from his programs support your ideas?

Why do you think the United States wanted to be the first country to place a person on the moon? How was this similar to (or different from) the USSR’s goal?

Which event do you believe was the turning point in America’s fight for civil rights for all citizens?

How do you think life in America has changed for most people since the terrorist attacks of 9/11?

Why might WWII have been helpful in bringing the American economy out of the Great Depression?

What are three questions you would ask a geologist about how technological discoveries in energy conservation might affect society in the U.S.?

title: The Roots of Conflict
text:
People who wanted to live in a constitutional republic founded the United States of America. They wanted a nation in which the people made decisions about who would lead the government and how the leaders would operate it.

At the Constitutional Convention in 1787, delegates spent a great deal of time planning how the government of the United States would work best. Not everyone agreed. The Founding Fathers disagreed about the amount of power the federal government should have. The Constitution cleared matters up a bit. It explained how the rights and responsibilities of the federal government differ from those of state governments.

Members of the Federalist party supported the idea of a strong central government. Members of another political party, the Democratic-Republicans, believed that states had the right to nullify (cancel or declare invalid) federal laws they believed were unconstitutional. They thought this allowed states the right to declare laws unacceptable.

At the beginning of the 19th century, many Southern states believed the federal government was too involved in states' business. They were especially concerned that the federal government might try to control slavery in the South. Southerners also accused the government of favoring the North. Tariffs (import/export taxes) helped the Northern manufacturing economy. Southerners felt the federal government was forgetting them.

As time went on, great differences were seen between the North and South. The economies of the two were different. The North made money in industry, while the South benefited from an agricultural economy. Most of the population in the North lived in large cities. The people in the South mostly lived on farms or in small towns. Many people in the North supported a strong federal government, while most Southerners believed each state should have the right to make certain decisions for itself. The differences became more noticeable as the century went on. Soon it seemed that there could be no peaceful agreement or compromise between the North and the South. Would the disagreements lead to war?

title: Agriculture a Way of Life for Fewer in the U.S.
text:
When the United States began, most of its people were farmers. In 1860, the population of the United States was about 31 million. Almost half of that population listed their occupation (job) as "farmer" that year. Today, less than two percent of people earn their family's money by farming. There are about the same number of farms in the United States today as there were in 1860. This is very unusual because the total population has grown to well over 300 million people. Why do so few people choose agriculture as a way of life today? There are several important reasons.

Farming involves a lot of work. With so many people to feed, farmers must operate their businesses with great care. Farmers say it takes a lot more than planting seeds to own a successful farm. The work is long and hard. Farmers must make many business decisions about the type of crops to plant, the machines to buy, how to pay taxes and how to meet payroll for the workers to run the farm. Crops often fail because of weather and other unpredictable situations. Farmers have to take many risks. Some seasons they make money and some seasons they don't. Many people have tried to make a living by farming but later decided it isn't the life they want. However, the nation has plenty of excellent farm products. The U.S. is lucky to have enough farmers to produce the goods our nation needs to survive.

title: Compromises and Kansas
text:
The Missouri Compromise of 1820

The United States was still a young nation when President Thomas Jefferson approved the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. The land purchased from France nearly doubled the size of the country and included the Missouri Territory. In 1819, the Missouri Territory asked to become a new state. Immediately people became concerned. But why?

Missouri’s state constitution allowed slavery. If it were to be admitted as a state, there would be 12 slave states and 11 free states. A free state was one in which slavery was not allowed. If Missouri became a new state, the balance of the United States’ Congress would lean towards the South and slavery. People in the North were afraid of what might happen to the country if the slave states had more power than free states.

There were many debates in Congress about what to do with Missouri. Many people feared the United States might break apart. Then a senator from Kentucky named Henry Clay suggested a compromise. The situation could be settled if both sides gave up some of their demands.

Missouri was allowed to join the U.S. as a slave state. At the same time, Maine would also be admitted as a free state. The number of free and slave states would remain equal. Clay’s plan also included an imaginary borderline across the western U.S. at 36° 30’ north latitude, Missouri’s southern boundary. Slavery wouldn’t be allowed north of this line except in Missouri.

Clay’s plan became known as the Missouri Compromise. The new plan began to make the people in the U.S. feel better, and it gave them hope that the problems with slavery could be solved for good. However, some Southerners were still concerned that Northerners might one day try to change the way they lived. For the next 30 years, it seemed the compromise had worked.

The Compromise of 1850

At the end of the Mexican-American War, the United States gained a large amount of land from Mexico in the West and Southwest regions. California was part of this land. In 1849, California asked to be admitted to the United States as a free state.

Once again, it was clear that a compromise would have to be reached. By that time, 15 states were free, and 15 were slave states. Adding California would give more power to the North in Congress. In addition, much of California’s land was below the 36° 30’ Missouri Compromise line. Remember that slavery was allowed south of the line. Some Southerners began to think about withdrawing their states from the Union if California joined as a free state.

Senator Clay from Kentucky came up with a way to settle the differences again. Clay offered several plans for new laws to help balance the power. First, California would be admitted as a free state. Second, people would not be allowed to sell enslaved people in Washington, D.C. These laws would make Northerners happy.

At the same time, people in Utah and New Mexico would be allowed to decide for themselves whether or not to allow slavery in their territories. In addition, Congress passed the Fugitive Slave Law. Northern officials would have to help Southerners capture fugitive (runaway) enslaved people. These two laws were aimed at pleasing Southerners.

The Compromise of 1850 was passed into law in September of that year. Even though Senator Clay and the other leaders worked to try and find a way to solve the differences the country had, they weren’t successful. Many people in both parts of the country were more upset than ever. Southerners thought the North was trying to destroy slavery. Northerners thought the South would never be happy until slavery had spread to every state. Soon it became clear that the differences between the two groups were going to be difficult to overcome peacefully.

Kansas: The End of Compromise

The Compromise of 1850 did very little to bring peace to the nation. Instead, the compromise seemed to fuel the fire. This fire began to grow even stronger when the territories of Kansas and Nebraska wanted to become states.

Both territories were north of the 36° 30’ Missouri Compromise line. According to law, both new states would be free from slavery. However, in 1854, a senator from Illinois named Stephen Douglas suggested a troubling plan. He believed the people in Kansas and Nebraska should be allowed to decide for themselves if they wanted to allow slavery. Congress agreed with Douglas, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act became a law.

Suddenly, the southern territory of Kansas became a battleground over states’ rights and slavery. People who supported (approved of) slavery rushed to Kansas. People who opposed (were against) slavery also rushed there to voice their beliefs. Both groups wanted to vote in the election that would make the final decision. The people argued with both words and weapons.

On election day, voters in Kansas approved a constitution that allowed slavery. The anti-slavery leaders believed the election had not been fair. Over 6,000 people had voted, but Kansas had only 3,000 voters. It was clear that some people who did not really live in Kansas had voted. The “free-soilers” (people who did not support slavery) set up their own political party in protest.

People on both sides of the issue became violent. There was fighting throughout the spring and summer of 1856. The issue was finally resolved (settled) when another election was held. In January 1861, Kansas was added as a free state. Neither the North nor the South was satisfied. The nation was now heading toward a war, one side against the other.

title: Abolitionists ‘Build’ an Underground Railroad
text:
Many Southerners felt that slavery was a necessary part of the Southern way of life and economy. Plantation owners used enslaved people to run their large farms. On the other side, many Northerners believed slavery was wrong. Northern abolitionists felt very strongly that all slavery should be abolished (ended) forever.

Some of those against slavery got together and organized the Underground Railroad. The Underground Railroad wasn’t a real railroad, and it wasn’t underneath the ground. Instead, it was a name for a system of people and homes that secretly helped enslaved people escape to free states. Homes were known as stations. At each station, there were people, or “conductors,” to help the enslaved people hide. They gave enslaved people food, clothing and a place to sleep. When it was safe, the conductors helped the enslaved people find their way to the next station.

Many enslaved people traveled from station to station until they felt they were safe. The Fugitive Slave Act allowed formerly enslaved people to be tracked into Northern states. Some of them had to travel all the way to Canada before they felt they were free from slavery forever.

Most Northerners were not part of the Underground Railroad, but many Southerners became distrustful of them. Each group felt the other’s ideas about slavery were wrong.

title: 1860: The Election of Abraham Lincoln
text:
By 1860, the United States was set to elect a new president. Northerners and Southerners both felt uneasy about how the election might affect the nation. Southern congressmen made it clear that unless an "acceptable" man was elected, their states would secede (withdraw from) the U.S.

The Republicans nominated (named as a candidate) a smart and thoughtful lawyer from Illinois named Abraham Lincoln. Lincoln was against slavery. He promised he would leave slavery alone in the South but would not let it spread into new territories. Most Southerners did not vote for Lincoln because of his views on slavery.

The Democratic Party seemed to fall apart in the months before the election. The party split into two separate groups. One group nominated the vice president of the United States, John C. Breckinridge, to be the next president. The other Democratic group wanted Senator Stephen Douglas of Illinois to be the next leader of the nation. Douglas had previously run against Abraham Lincoln in a race for the Illinois Senate. Douglas argued with Lincoln and said that people in each state had the right to decide for themselves if they wanted to allow slavery. While Douglas won that election, Lincoln became well known as someone who would stand up against slavery.

On Nov. 6, 1860, Abraham Lincoln won the presidential election. Interestingly, the other two candidates outnumbered the peoples' vote for Lincoln, but Lincoln won the most votes from the Electoral College. He must have worried that the majority, or most of the nation's people, had not voted for him. He was sworn in as the 16th president of the United States of America. Lincoln's election was the last straw for some states. The end of the country as it had been known was near.

title: Points of View from Primary Sources
text:
A person’s point of view is the way they look at and think about an event. Different people often experience history in a variety of different ways. Not everyone who experiences a historical event feels or thinks the exact same way about it.

A number of things determine a person’s point of view. Life experiences (positive and negative), future needs and wants and an emotional connection to the event all influence a person’s point of view.

After reading this week’s Studies Weekly, consider all the different points of view of people living in the United States during the mid-1800s. After reading each of the primary source statements below, add one or two sentences to support the speaker’s point of view.

title: The Legend of the Woman Who Started the Civil War
text:
President Abraham Lincoln met Harriet Beecher Stowe in 1862. He reportedly said, “So you are the little woman who wrote the book that started this great war.” It is not clear whether Lincoln really said that or not. However, the legend shows how much literature can reflect and impact the time in which it was created.

Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote a book called Uncle Tom’s Cabin in 1852. At the time, slavery was still practiced in the southern United States. At the same time, anti-slavery feelings were growing in the North. Stowe was active in this anti-slavery movement. She had visited areas in the South where slavery existed and had seen firsthand the cruel treatment and severe hardships of enslaved people. She wanted to do something to help people in the North understand what life was like for enslaved people.

In her book, Harriet told the story of two enslaved families and what they had to endure as they tried to find freedom. The book was extremely successful. It outsold every other book in the 19th century except the Bible. Many more people began to acknowledge the reality of the conditions enslaved people lived with. As a result of Harriet’s book, many people became involved in efforts to abolish (get rid of) the practice of slavery.

title: The Union is Dissolved
text:
The presidential election of 1860 was the final push over the edge of discontent (unhappiness) for the Southern states. They were shocked at Abraham Lincoln’s new position as U.S. president. Southern states did not waste any time waiting to see how the newly elected president might do as the nation’s leader. They felt it was time for a big change.

Tension grew after Abraham Lincoln was elected president of the United States. Southern states felt the time was right to make a change. They were afraid that President Lincoln’s election would lead to the end of their right to make their own decisions. They were especially concerned that the U.S. government would abolish, or do away with, their practice of owning enslaved people.

On Dec. 20, 1860, South Carolina’s citizens voted and unanimously agreed “that the union now subsisting between South Carolina and other states under the name of the United States of America is hereby dissolved.” With that declaration (announcement), South Carolina became the first of the Southern states to secede (officially withdraw) from the United States of America. Less than three weeks later, Mississippi became the second state to leave the U.S. By the end of January, Florida, Alabama, Georgia and Louisiana had also left the Union. On Feb. 1, 1861, Texas became the seventh state to leave the Union. Not everyone in the South wanted the states to leave the Union, however. Some people, known as cooperationists, wanted the South to work out its differences with the North. They wanted the South to remain part of the Union.

However, the seven Southern states that had seceded by early 1861 wanted to protect what they thought was their right to own enslaved people. They wanted to have the freedom to make their own decisions. They formed the Confederate States of America. The Confederacy selected its own president — Jefferson Davis of Mississippi.

By April 1861, the lines of conflict were clearly drawn. Northern “Yanks” and Southern “Rebs” were set to fight against one another to protect what they believed to be their property, their rights and values.

title: Quilted Controversy
text:
Is there one Civil War detail that has been kept “under cover” for over 150 years? That’s what some historians think after studying slavery and the Underground Railroad from Civil War times.

Enslaved people in the South often tried to escape to freedom in the North. Many received help from people who lived along the route. This group of people and the secret hideouts in their homes were known as the Underground Railroad. Thousands of enslaved people were able to reach freedom with help from the Underground Railroad. Historians want to learn more about how enslaved people knew where the “railroad” stops were located. Some historians think they sewed secret information about safe houses into quilts. They believe that secret codes were sewn into the designs of the quilts. These special patterns may have given enslaved people the information they needed about where to hide or look for help.

Not everyone believes the colorful bed linens helped the enslaved people. Some historians believe the idea that quilts guided runaways on their path to freedom is just a tall tale. They say there is little evidence that enslaved people had such a patterned code. It is more likely that formerly enslaved people who had already escaped guided the others along the Underground Railroad. White landowners who disagreed with the idea of slavery also guided enslaved people to safety.

Historians are looking for facts and artifacts that prove or disprove this idea. Meanwhile, the story behind the secret-code quilts will surely continue to unfold.

title: The Blue and the Gray
text:
First Shots at Fort Sumter

The first states began to secede from the Union in December 1860. At that time, U.S. soldiers were stationed in South Carolina. Led by Major Robert Anderson, soldiers climbed into boats and took control of Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor. The people in Charleston were angry that the Union soldiers had taken the fort. They considered it a violation of their rights. The next day, Confederate forces took control of three nearby forts. They wanted to remove the Union soldiers from Southern soil.

The Union held control of Fort Sumter for almost four months. President Abraham Lincoln ordered that supplies be sent to the soldiers. The Confederates sent messengers by boat to speak with Major Anderson. They wanted him to surrender, but Anderson would not give up.

At 4:30 a.m. on April 12, 1861, the Confederates began firing upon Fort Sumter. The Civil War had officially begun. The attack lasted 34 hours. The Union soldiers fired back, but they were forced to surrender. Surprisingly, not one soldier on either side was killed in battle.

The Soldiers of War

Like it or not, the United States found itself in the middle of a war that neither side was prepared to fight. Both the North and the South needed to make improvements to their armies. Soldiers needed to be trained. Some men signed up voluntarily (on their own), while the government drafted others to serve in the military. When soldiers were drafted, they were ordered to fight whether they wanted to or not.

Northern men followed President Lincoln’s request that they fight to keep the United States together. Eventually it became clear that the men of the North were also fighting for the freedom of enslaved people being held in the South. The Northern soldiers were mostly from poor farm families, and many were European immigrants. Eventually, African American men were also allowed to serve in the Union army and wore the Union blue uniforms.

Southerners believed they were fighting for their freedom to leave the Union. They wanted states to have the right to make their own decisions, and they were ready to defend the Southern way of life. They were willing to fight for the right to own enslaved people. Many of the Southern soldiers were poor farmers as well. They wore gray uniforms on the battlefield.

The Battle at Bull Run (also known as the Battle of Manassas)

In the summer of 1861, Northerners wanted President Lincoln to hit the Southerners with full force. Most people felt that the North would only need one major win to crush the South and bring the Union back together again. A plan was made for the Union to capture the city of Richmond, Virginia.

In July, troops marched towards the city. The Union soldiers were not well trained. They moved slowly and did not follow orders well. The Confederates built up their defenses along Bull Run stream.

At first, the Union soldiers seemed to be winning the battle easily. A crowd of supporters even gathered to watch the battle. The people were excited to see the Union army defeat the Southern rebels. But the Union plan fell apart quickly. There was great confusion and panic. The Union troops started to retreat (move back). Many soldiers dropped their rifles and ran away.

By the end of the day, over 4,000 soldiers were dead. The Union knew that the Confederate soldiers were serious about fighting back. Everyone soon realized that the war was not going to come to a quick end. Both sides had shown they were in the war to win.

title: The Emancipation Proclamation
text:
The first battles of the Civil War were small compared with battles that followed. By July of 1862, both the North and the South had suffered a heavy loss of soldiers. The Union had won few battles, and the end of the war was nowhere in sight.

President Lincoln was very concerned about how the war was unfolding. People urged the leader to abolish slavery. However, President Lincoln knew the war was about more than getting rid of slavery. He wanted to keep the Union together too. After a year of battles and decisions, Lincoln knew it was time to end slavery altogether.

President Lincoln met with his group of advisors (people who offer ideas and share opinions). They told him to wait until the North had won a major battle before announcing the end of slavery. This chance came in September 1862 after the Battle of Antietam in Maryland (also known as the Battle of Sharpsburg). Over 23,000 men were killed there. The Union Army forced the Confederates back into Virginia. The time was right for Lincoln to announce his plan.

On Sept. 22, 1862, President Lincoln made the Emancipation Proclamation. Lincoln warned the Southern states that most enslaved people would be forever free if the “rebellious states” did not rejoin the Union by January. Lincoln also announced formerly enslaved people were free to join the Union army.

There were mixed reactions to Lincoln’s announcement. Some people thought the war was being fought only to free the enslaved people and not necessarily to bring the nation back together. Others felt the Emancipation Proclamation was the best thing that could have ever happened to bring the country together again. After Lincoln signed the Proclamation into law on Jan. 1, 1863, many enslaved people fled north to join Union forces.

The Emancipation Proclamation helped to free enslaved people, caused Southern plantation owners to lose workers and helped increase the number of soldiers fighting for the Union cause.

title: One War, Two Leaders
text:
Both the North and the South needed strong leaders for their troops. These leaders were Ulysses S. Grant and Robert E. Lee.

Ulysses S. Grant was born in Ohio. His parents were simple, hard-working people. Grant attended the U.S. Military Academy at West Point like Lee, but he did not do well in school. He was, however, an excellent horseman and mathematician. During the Mexican-American War, Grant served as an engineer in the Army alongside General Robert E. Lee. Before President Lincoln chose Grant to lead the Union army, Grant worked as a farmer, a real estate agent and a store clerk. Voters elected Grant president of the United States twice after the Civil War. As president, he supported civil rights for African Americans.

Robert E. Lee was born in Virginia to well-educated parents. His father was the governor of Virginia, and Robert’s mother encouraged him to be religious and responsible. Robert received an education at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point, where he graduated at the top of his class. He served in the Army after graduation and later served as superintendent of the school he had attended. During the Mexican-American War, Lee served as a quartermaster (Army officer). He was a smart man who carefully studied the military leaders he worked with. President Lincoln asked Robert E. Lee to head the Union troops at the beginning of the Civil War, but Lee felt he owed the South, especially his home state of Virginia, his allegiance (loyalty). He became the leader of the Confederate States of America Army. After the Civil War, Lee became the president of Washington College in Virginia.

title: Jefferson Davis: President of the Confederate States of America
text:
Jefferson Davis was shocked to receive a letter on Feb. 10, 1861, informing him that people had chosen him as president of the Confederate States of America. Davis had not asked for such an honor.

Born in Kentucky in 1808, Jefferson Davis came from a long line of soldiers. His father and uncles had been soldiers in the Revolutionary War in 1776. His three older brothers fought in the War of 1812 with Andrew Jackson.

Jefferson Davis attended Transylvania University in Kentucky as a young man and was later appointed to West Point Military Academy. He served in the army for seven years. Davis was an excellent soldier and was admired for his character, leadership and bravery.

After Davis' first wife died, he moved to Mississippi and began growing cotton and studying law. He returned to the military when the United States became involved in the Mexican-American War. After the war, Davis represented Mississippi in the Senate and served a short time as the U.S. Secretary of War.

After Abraham Lincoln was elected, Mr. Davis hoped to be named leader of the Confederate forces. What Davis didn't know was that Confederate leaders had held a meeting. They wanted Jefferson Davis to serve in a more important position.

On Feb. 18, 1861, Jefferson Davis took the oath of office at an inauguration ceremony as the first (and only) president of the Confederate States of America. The job in front of Davis was a huge challenge. It soon proved even more difficult than anyone would have ever imagined.

title: Comparing and Contrasting American Leaders
text:
Think about the North and South during the Civil War. Use information from this issue, along with what you already know, to compare and contrast the leaders of both sides. In each leader’s box, make notes about the man. Consider his background, leadership style, strengths and weaknesses.

On a separate piece of paper, write a paragraph about how the leaders were similar. Next, write a paragraph about how the leaders were different. Complete the assignment by filling in the blanks in the summary sentence below the chart.

Summary Sentence: Leaders of the North and South during the Civil War were alike in that they all ________________ ________________________________________________________________________________________________________, but while Northern leaders _______________________________________________________________________, Southern leaders ________________________________________________________________________________________________.

title: The Boy is a Soldier
text:
Word of the Confederate attack on Fort Sumter in April 1861 spread quickly in the Northern states. President Abraham Lincoln called for men to pick up their arms (weapons) and join the fight against the Rebels. Some volunteers who reported for duty were young boys. Children as young as nine read newspaper headlines or heard adults talk about the fall of Fort Sumter. On both sides, there was a rush to join forces. Men and boys (and even some women) wanted to do their part to help.

The legal age to fight in battle was 18, but many boys were able to slip into an Army unit. There was no easy way to check on a young man's age. Documents to prove how old a person was, such as a driver's license or ID card, simply didn't exist. Some of the boys joined with their parents' permission, while others ran away from home without anyone knowing they joined the fight. Some boys even changed their names to keep their true age hidden.

Most Northern boys signed up because they wanted to be a part of the Yankee forces and not because they wanted to end slavery. Most of them wanted to experience a grand adventure far more interesting than the hard farm work back at home. Southern boys joined Rebel forces for the same sense of excitement. They also felt they needed to defend slavery and their Southern way of life against the large Northern army.

One of the easiest ways for a boy to enlist (join the military) was to be a musician. Drummers, buglers and fife (a type of flute) players were not part of the actual fighting forces. These small bands led the troops into battle by playing marching orders, and they often played to lift the spirits of weary soldiers.

The excitement the boys and young men felt when they signed up for battle quickly disappeared. The marching, training and fighting in battle was grueling (tough). There was little to eat, and many of them became sick from diseases that spread quickly. Many soldiers died from disease while others died from battle wounds. Most soldiers made only about $13 a month for their hard and dangerous work. Unfortunately, many of the boys did not make it back home alive.

title: Robert Smalls: A Brave Father and Civil War Hero
text:
What would you do if you and your family were going to be separated? Would you come up with a plan to stay together? That's exactly the situation in which Robert Smalls, an enslaved man from the 1800s, found himself. He knew that the only way to keep his family together was by escaping slavery. He thought of a plan and took action.

Robert was an enslaved member of the crew of the Planter, a Confederate ship. He decided to take over the ship and sail it to the Union Fleet at Fort Sumter and freedom!

He knew his plan was risky because he would have to get control of the ship, pick up his family and others hoping to escape, and then sail the ship north past Confederate forces to the Union Fleet and convince the Union soldiers he was not an enemy.

Robert managed to get to the Union Fleet without a problem. He sailed right up to the fleet and quickly switched the flag on the ship from a Confederate flag to a white flag of surrender. The Union soldiers let the ship in and were amazed at what Robert had done.

Robert won freedom for his family, crew and others, but he didn't stop there. He went on to fight in the war and became a captain in the Union Army. After the war ended, he became a politician and served in the U.S. House of Representatives. What a brave hero!

title: Behind the Lines and Back at Home
text:
The Battle of Gettysburg

At the beginning of the Civil War, many Southern victories kept the Union Army from capturing the Confederate capital at Richmond, Virginia. The South's leader, Robert E. Lee, decided it was time to make a bold move. He wanted a victory on Northern soil because he was sure this would make the Union want to end the war once and for all.

Lee took his troops into Pennsylvania in June 1863. Union soldiers followed Lee and his Confederate troops and surprised them in the town of Gettysburg. The three-day battle that followed was a turning point in the war. Lee's Confederate Army lost thousands of men and was forced to retreat, or move back, to Virginia. The Confederate Army was never able to invade the North again.

On the Battlefield

Fighting in the Civil War was brutal. Most battles began with a face-to-face attack on an open battlefield. A drummer would beat a drum slowly as a signal for the soldiers to move again into formations. The air was usually thick with black smoke as the soldiers walked in rows toward their enemy's lines.

Most soldiers used rifles when the fighting began. As the soldiers moved closer to one another, they usually switched to hand-to-hand combat. Many were killed or wounded during battle. Other soldiers died months or years later from wounds they got during the war.

On the Home Front

Half of all the men serving in the military during the Civil War were farmers back at home, and most of them could read and write. Letters sent back and forth between soldiers and their families helped keep everyone informed about what was going on.

Northerners wrote about a new income tax passed as part of the Internal Revenue Act of 1862. The government would use money from the tax to pay for the war. It turns out that the federal government spent approximately $2 million each day for war costs. The Northern economy was still strong, though. Workers continued to mine gold and silver in California, Nevada, and Colorado. Factories expanded their businesses to produce war goods including rifles, ammunition, trains, blankets, and shoes.

However, Northern citizens were angry about draft guidelines. The law allowed rich men to pay someone else to take their place on the battlefield. They could also choose to pay the government a fee to avoid serving in the military. Some people thought this was unfair. They felt everyone should be required to serve the country.

The South's economy was based on agriculture, so it could not produce all the war materials its army needed. On top of that, the North had set up blockades at all Southern ports. This kept plantation owners from exporting cotton to sell in Europe. The South did not have the money to pay for a war. To solve the problem, the South simply printed $1 billion in paper money. But the true value of every Confederate dollar was only about five cents.

Most of the fighting took place in the South as well. Southerners lost property when Union troops marched through the territory. Sometimes soldiers stole property or burned homes and farms. Also, food was scarce and hard to find. Food that was available was very expensive. Most Southern families could not afford meat. Poor diets caused many Southerners to become ill.

From Gettysburg to Appomattox

Southern forces never recovered from the defeat at Gettysburg. At almost the same time, General Ulysses S. Grant and his soldiers had captured the Confederate fort at Vicksburg, a Southern city on the Mississippi River. With the North in control of this important waterway, the Confederacy was almost cut in half.

Grant took control of the entire Union Army and decided to attack the South in two states. With orders from Grant, General William Sherman marched through Georgia to the Atlantic Ocean. Grant himself led troops into Virginia to capture the capital of Richmond. Grant was determined to defeat the South at any cost. He believed the North could win if its Army just kept attacking. Sure enough, many Rebels realized they were in big trouble. A large number of them believed the war was lost, and they turned to head home.

The Final Surrender

On April 9, 1865, General Robert E. Lee surrendered to General Ulysses S. Grant in the parlor of a home near Appomattox Court House in Virginia. After four bloody years, the Civil War had ended.

Some describe Grant as a very kind and generous man for the treatment he offered to the defeated Southern soldiers. He allowed Lee’s officers to keep their weapons and all soldiers to return home. Grant also allowed soldiers to keep their own horses to be used at their homes. In addition, he ordered Union troops to share their food with Southern soldiers who were starving.
