When Union soldiers began to cheer at the word of surrender, Grant stopped them and exclaimed, "The war is over. The Rebels are our countrymen again." Later, Grant wrote that at the moment of surrender he felt "sad and depressed" at the downfall of "a foe (enemy) who had fought so long and so valiantly (bravely)."

title: Civil War Secret Agents
text:
If you think spies are only found in good mystery books or in movies, then think again. Believe it or not, spies played an important role for both the North and South during the Civil War. Both sides knew the other was spying on them, but they also knew it was difficult to stop spies from infiltrating, or passing through, enemy lines to access secret information. Civil War spies didn't have all of the special technology that spies have today. They relied on good old-fashioned disguises and tricks to learn their secrets.

Some of the best Civil War spies were not even soldiers. They were women. One particularly clever Union spy was a woman named Sarah Emma Edmonds. Ms. Edmonds was a master of disguise. She first disguised herself as a man so that she could serve in the Union Army. As a spy, she "re-disguised" herself as a woman or an African American man. When her secret was exposed, she spent the remainder of the war as a Union nurse.

The Confederacy had a woman spy named Nancy Hart. She disguised herself to track where Union soldiers were hiding out. She would then lead Confederate Rebels to their positions for an attack. Hart was captured, but she escaped when she tricked a guard into showing her his rifle. She grabbed the gun, shot the guard and headed out.

As long as there are wars, there will certainly be spies. The Civil War was no exception to this rule.

title: Women and the War
text:
Women did not sit and just wait and worry during the Civil War. They played important roles on both sides of the war. Without the help of women, both the North and the South would have had many more problems.

Some women disguised themselves as men and fought in the battles. Many more women worked on the battlefields as nurses. Some women worked as spies, but most women did their part back at home.

Many Northern women entered the workforce to take over jobs that had been held by men who were now off at war. Women worked in weapons factories, on farms, at government offices and in hospitals. Many of the women worked to earn money to help support the troops. Women earned about $50 million total to help the cause. In addition, Northern Women's Aid Societies provided blankets, clothing, medicine and other supplies to troops. Many of these women stayed on the job even after the war was over.

In the South, the women at home worked about as hard as the men on the battlefields. Women worked long and hard to sew uniforms, flags and blankets from fabric they found or made themselves. Women in the South also worked to produce weapons for troops. Some Southern women lost their lives filling rifle cartridges with gunpowder. They also helped tend to the wounded soldiers who returned home. Perhaps most importantly, Southern women kept farms, plantations and homes running as best they could despite the terrible wartime conditions. Many have said the Civil War was a war between brothers. But given the number of women who were affected by the war, people can also say it was a war between sisters.

title: David Bushnell and the Turtle
text:
A submarine was used in the American Revolution? Absolutely. David Bushnell, American patriot and inventor, used reason and logic to build the first military submarine.

David Bushnell was born on a farm in Connecticut in 1740. He experimented with underwater explosives during college and built a submarine that would carry them. Bushnell's vessel was nicknamed "the Turtle" because it was shaped like two wooden turtle shells joined together, standing on end. Its hull filled with water to submerge and was pumped out by the operator to rise. Two propellers and a rudder were used to guide it.

Benjamin Franklin and others were impressed with Bushnell's invention. When British warships blockaded New York Harbor in 1776, the Turtle was called into action. The submarine operator was supposed to use a giant screw to attach the powder keg (called a mine) to the bottom of the British flagship, the HMS Eagle.

The plan seemed like a failure when the mine could not be fastened to the ship. However, the gunpowder made a frightening explosion underwater. The British quickly moved their warships from the area. Although it didn't work as planned, Bushnell's invention did have an effect on the British navy.

Bushnell then turned his skills to improving underwater mines. These were placed in harbors to protect American rivers and forts. General George Washington was pleased with Bushnell's work and gave him a commission (job) in the Army.

Today David Bushnell is given credit for inventing the first military submarine and for making valuable contributions to the American Revolution. You can visit a replica (an accurate model) of the Turtle in the Connecticut River Museum in Essex, Connecticut. By yourself or with a partner, think of a person who has used reason and logic to develop something that helped America.

title: Summarizing Historical Information
text:
A summary is a short statement that tells all of the main ideas of an event. A historical event summary should tell the important ideas about what happened during a time in history. Small details are not included. When writing a summary, it is sometimes helpful to think about all the big ideas first. Write down notes about these ideas. Then write a summary using the main details.

Read the information from the section “On the Home Front” in this week’s lesson. Use this information to fill in the summary chart. Then, use your notes to write a summary of three to five sentences about this time in American history.

Now use your notes to write a short summary of the information.

title: Reconstructing a Nation
text:
After four years, the Civil War had ended. The North had defeated the South, and it was now time to put the country back together. Many disagreed about how to mend, or repair, the nation. Some members of Congress wanted to see the Confederates punished for their part in the war. However, President Lincoln wanted to reunite (bring together) the country quickly during a time called Reconstruction.

Under Lincoln's plan, 10 percent of the Confederate states' populations would need to swear loyalty (faithfulness) to the United States' government. After the people showed they would be faithful to the country, Congress would accept representatives from those states. After a state was represented in Congress, it would then be a part of the United States of America again.

Not everyone agreed with Lincoln's plan. Many Northerners were angry. They thought Lincoln was making it much too easy for Southern states to rejoin the Union. They argued that because of the Confederates, there had been far too much death and destruction. They thought the South needed to change its ways so such a terrible war would not happen again. But Lincoln stuck to his plan. He ignored Congress' Reconstruction advice. Congress wanted to take matters into its own hands, but Lincoln refused to sign a much stricter program into law.

While the president and Congress disagreed, problems only grew in the South. The war had devastated and destroyed most of what was once a successful area. Entire towns were burned to the ground. Farms were overgrown and abandoned. Soldiers returned from the war only to find their homes in ruins. Their families were sick, scattered or even dead. The people of the South were a broken group. Many were angry, and most were exhausted and scared about what the future might hold.

Enslaved people had been freed with the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863. Many freed people who were desperate for help had run away from their owners. They didn’t own land, and very few of them could read or write. They needed food, clothing, shelter and medicine. Congress established the Freedmen’s Bureau in March of 1865 to help the freed people adjust to life away from slavery. By the end of the war, millions of formerly enslaved people were free and excited to begin their lives as American citizens.

The United States had so much healing to do after the Civil War. Unfortunately, it would be a long and bitter process. It was only made worse when the unimaginable happened just days after the South surrendered …

title: Enslaved No More!
text:
A letter written after the Civil War has shed light on the relationship between enslaved people and those who enslaved them. Jourdan Anderson was an enslaved person who gained freedom when he and his family escaped to Ohio from Tennessee. In August 1865, his former owner, Colonel Anderson, wrote a letter asking Jourdan to come back to Tennessee to work on his farm.

Jourdan’s reply gave a clear message about his feelings. He said he hoped that God had opened the colonel’s eyes to the wrongs done to enslaved people for generations. While he was glad his old master was alive, he was surprised that the Yankees hadn’t hanged him yet. Jourdan wrote that there was one thing that might bring him back to Tennessee. He and his wife wanted to be paid for the 52 years of combined work that they provided as enslaved people (over $11,000). Without that, he said they had little faith in the colonel’s promises. He ended by asking the colonel to give his best regards to a man named George Carter. Mr. Carter had apparently taken a pistol away from the colonel when he tried to shoot Jourdan ... twice.

Reading letters and newspapers from the past can help us understand the people who lived during that time. Jourdan and his family may have once been enslaved, but their spirits were not broken.

title: One Nation Again
text:
The Civil War had been four long, bloody years. Neither side had planned on the war lasting as long as it did. When the fighting was finally over, it was time to return to normal life, but that wouldn’t be easy.

Northerners were relieved the fighting had ended. During the Civil War, troops turned many of their cities into defense zones. They were filled with the hustle and bustle of soldiers and medical corps that were taking care of the injured. Now that both the North and South pledged peace, things could get back to normal. Northerners wanted to find a way to bring the nation together again. Most of them also wanted to make sure that all Americans would be guaranteed their civil rights from then on.

Southerners looked at their homes, land and communities with despair. Beautiful plantation mansions were destroyed. Soldiers had burned many to the ground. Fields where farmers grew crops were now overgrown with weeds. Industrial machines lay destroyed among the weeds. Nearly every village was devastated from the effects of a long, brutal war. Confederate soldiers returned home to find their families and communities shattered. White Southerners were tired, frustrated and angry at the whole situation.

Formerly enslaved people felt a mix of joy and fear as they began their new lives as free people. Many of them married, searched for family members and made plans for the future. Some of the freed people wanted to farm the land they knew so well. Others headed north to look for new opportunities.

A President’s Death

During the Civil War, Northerners had looked to President Lincoln as the leader. People hoped he would be able to guide the country through the Reconstruction. However, one devastating event destroyed the nation’s hope. It happened on the evening of April 14, 1865.

President Lincoln and his wife were attending a play at Ford’s Theater in Washington, D.C. During the play, a well-known actor and Confederate supporter, John Wilkes Booth, crept up behind the president and shot him in the back of the head. Soldiers carried Lincoln across the street to a boarding house, where doctors tried to save the president’s life. A crowd gathered to hear if doctors could save their leader.

President Abraham Lincoln died early in the morning on April 15. Federal troops later caught and killed President Lincoln’s assassin (killer). Several other people had helped plan the murder as a way to punish Union leaders. Authorities later executed them for their part in the assassination of President Lincoln.

A New Plan

Vice President Andrew Johnson was immediately sworn in as the new U.S. president. He announced that he would continue with Lincoln’s plan for Reconstruction. At first, Northerners were pleased with President Johnson’s performance. However, they soon realized that while Johnson did not like the rich, white Southern plantation owners, he did not think the formerly enslaved people should have equal rights. Many people became worried and angry. One group in Congress spoke up. The Radical Republicans believed African Americans should have the right to vote and own their own land.

The 13th Amendment

President Johnson’s plan for new state governments to re-enter the Union was simple. The most important thing states had to do was to declare secession illegal and pass the 13th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. This amendment abolished (did away with) slavery forever in the United States. Many of the Southern states did not want to admit secession was wrong. Mississippi even refused to ratify the 13th Amendment for a long time. People in both regions of the country were not getting along with each other the way everyone had hoped they would.

Black Codes

Southern governments passed laws called Black Codes that denied freed African Americans their civil rights. Under the laws, African Americans were not allowed to vote or hold political office. If they wanted to travel, they needed permission from their white employer. Freed African Americans were not even allowed to choose their own careers. If they wanted to work at any job besides farming, they needed permission to do so from a white judge. In addition to these unfair laws, many African Americans were the victims of violence. Many people worried another Civil War was on the way.

The 14th and 15th Amendments

President Johnson and Congress could not agree on how best to carry on the Reconstruction process. Congress was especially upset that Johnson did not support the Civil Rights Act that would give African Americans basic human rights and protect them from unfair treatment. The Radical Republicans led the push to amend the Constitution again. In June 1866, Congress passed the 14th Amendment. Now all citizens, including African Americans, would have their civil rights protected.

Congress soon realized that formerly enslaved people were not truly free without the right to vote. The 15th Amendment to the Constitution passed in 1870. It guaranteed all men the right to vote. Women did not get the right to vote until 1920.

Life in the New South

In the South, life was still far from normal even though the states were making changes. A few free African Americans and formerly enslaved people became members of national and state governments. New state governments established public schools for both African American and white children. Freed people learned to read and write. Agriculture and industry grew again. The South slowly made progress in rebuilding their communities.

Eventually, Ulysses S. Grant replaced President Johnson. Rutherford B. Hayes then followed Grant. All of these men had to fight to continue bringing the U.S. back together again. It was many years before all people in the U.S. would truly have their civil rights protected as promised in the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments. Even today, the U.S. continues to work to provide freedom and equality to all citizens.

title: Sharecropping in the South
text: Eventually, Southern farmland was returned to the wealthy landowners and planters who had owned the land before the war started. Formerly enslaved people and poor whites who wanted the chance to own their own farms found it difficult to raise enough money to buy land. They were forced to become sharecroppers. They rented land to grow crops and would give part of the crop to the landowner as payment for the land. Sharecropping was difficult work. Crops often failed in periods of poor weather or drought. Many sharecroppers found they could not pay their land rents and went into debt. Unfortunately, most Southern sharecroppers never had the chance to call any piece of land their own.

title: Hiram Revels: First African American Senator
text:
At the end of the Civil War, African Americans from the Southern states began to join local governments. Feb. 25, 1870, was an especially important day in U.S. history. On that day, 42-year-old Hiram Revels of Mississippi took the oath of office and became the first African American to serve in the U.S. Senate.

Revels was a teacher and a minister. During the Civil War, he had helped put together troops of African American soldiers, and he established schools for freed African Americans in North Carolina. When he moved to Mississippi, citizens elected him to the state Senate. He was a strong leader whom his co-workers admired. When Mississippi was ready to re-enter the U.S. during Reconstruction, Revels took one of Mississippi’s Senate seats.

Revels only served one year in the senate, but he spent his life working for the equal treatment of African Americans.

title: Carpetbaggers and Scalawags
text:
During the period known as Reconstruction, thousands of Northerners moved to the South. They wanted to take advantage of the opportunities that were available to make money. The South needed to be rebuilt. New industries and businesses were needed. Hired workers built factories that produced farm equipment and machinery. Mines were opened. People replanted cotton and tobacco farms and operated them as big businesses.

Unfortunately, most Southerners did not like the “Yankee invaders.” They called Northerners “carpetbaggers” because Northerners often arrived in the South carrying their belongings in cloth luggage bags. Southerners felt the Northern businesspeople really cared more about making money for themselves rather than improving the lives of Southerners. In fact, most carpetbaggers weren’t rich businesspeople out to make money off the people of the South. Most were former soldiers who had set out to find opportunities that were not available in the North. Most of the anger the Southerners felt was because the carpetbaggers supported the rights of formerly enlsaved people.

“Scalawags” were Southerners who worked with carpetbaggers or supported the formerly enslaved people. Many of these people were white Southerners who joined the Republican Party after the Civil War. Scalawags were often considered traitors. Many of the so-called scalawags held positions in government during Reconstruction. They tried to get state governments to consider equality and rights for all citizens in the plans they made for their states.

Many people still use the terms carpetbagger and scalawag in today’s politics. A carpetbagger is used to describe a person who gets involved in someone else’s business for their own personal gain. The word “scalawag” is still often used to mean a traitor.

title: Creating a Timeline
text:
Use information from the paragraph to construct a timeline of Reconstruction events of 1865.

The First Year of Reconstruction

Before the Civil War had officially ended, the U.S. Congress had already approved the 13th Amendment to the Constitution in January 1865. Ratified in December of that same year, the amendment abolished slavery forever in the United States. By March, Congress had started the Freedmen’s Bureau to provide newly emancipated people with assistance in finding food, shelter, education and jobs. Unfortunately, President Lincoln, who was responsible for the Emancipation Proclamation, did not live to see its results. On April 14, 1865, just five days after the end of the Civil War, a Confederate supporter named John Wilkes Booth assassinated him. Lincoln’s successor, Andrew Johnson, took charge of Reconstruction plans. He made them public in May. Reconstruction was not an easy process. Some states actually tried to find ways to bring slavery back to the South. In November of 1865, Mississippi enacted (passed) the Black Codes to limit the civil rights of formerly enslaved people.

A Timeline of Reconstruction: 1865

title: Let's Write
text: Writers often use cause and effect writing to first explain an event, and then to provide details about what caused it and the effects afterward. These details support the main idea. Think about the period in American history known as Reconstruction. Write three expository paragraphs that explain what Reconstruction is, its causes and its effects. Write in complete sentences, and support all of your ideas with facts and details.

title: A New Era for a Reborn Nation
text:
A presidential election marked the end of the Reconstruction era in the United States. Voters elected (by compromise) Rutherford B. Hayes as president of the United States in 1876. This compromise, or agreement, meant that both the Republicans and Democrats had to give up some of their requests to get something in return. Neither Hayes nor his opponent, Samuel J. Tilden, had enough electoral college votes to win the presidency. A commission (group of people with given authority) came together to make a decision. This group of senators, representatives and Supreme Court justices decided that the Republican Hayes would be the 19th president. Hayes agreed to remove all federal troops from the South. Now the North and the South could finally try to move past the effects from the terrible war that had torn the nation apart for 15 years.

Life for all U.S. citizens did not improve overnight. In the South, white Democrats gained control of most of the political offices after Reconstruction. African Americans had a difficult time entering politics at all. State officials did not always enforce the 14th and 15th Amendments that guaranteed citizenship and civil rights to all people. Unfortunately, a system of segregation, or separation of races, developed throughout much of the South.

Other changes in the U.S. happened as well. The American Industrial Revolution had started after the Revolutionary War and continued throughout the Civil War. This boom picked up after the war between the states ended. During this time, people created inventions and found new ways of manufacturing (making) products. The growth in industry and manufacturing resulted in even more people living and working in cities.

The slow pace of life in America sped up after the Civil War. Steamboats could quickly move goods and people longer distances over water. The West continued to grow with the completion of the transcontinental railroad. A trip across the U.S. that once took months now only took about a week.

In this issue, we'll explore the social, political and economic advances that continued to transform America as it headed into the twentieth century.

title: What is Hydraulic Fracturing?
text:
People in the states of Colorado, Texas and Ohio have been feeling small earthquakes over the past few years. Some people are saying those quakes are the result of hydraulic fracturing.

Hydraulic fracturing is a way to get natural gas from underground rock formations up to the surface. We use natural gas for energy in homes and businesses. Water and chemicals are pumped underground through long, deep wells. The liquid causes fractures, or cracks, in the rock. Natural gas escapes through the cracks and gets piped up to the surface. Hydraulic fracturing has been used in more than one million wells in the U.S. since the 1940s.

The National Research Council released a report that said hydraulic fracturing does not seem to be the culprit, but other human activity might be the problem. Some groups believe that it's the wastewater (leftover water and chemicals), not the fracturing itself that is causing the earthquakes. The wastewater from the process is either treated at a facility or sent deep underground. When the liquid is injected back into the ground, it can make the tectonic plates slip and rub against each other, causing earthquakes.

The companies doing the drilling say that they are following safety regulations and protecting their workers, the residents and the environment. Companies have been injecting waste liquids into the ground for decades, and only recently has there been an increase in earthquakes. We will certainly be hearing more about hydraulic fracturing in the years to come.

Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/ for more Connections and Current Events articles.

title: Industry, Communication and Transportation Take the Nation into a New Century
text:
Industry

The Industrial Revolution started in the United States after the Revolutionary War, and it continued during the Civil War. Shipbuilding and the iron industry were important parts of the economy. As the population of the country moved westward, agriculture, construction and mining industries grew also. By the time Reconstruction was over, the U.S. had become one of the largest and most competitive industrial nations in the world.

Before the Civil War, most people in the U.S. made their living in agricultural businesses. People owned or worked on small farms. Some worked in small family-owned businesses. After the war, industry grew much faster than agriculture. The population of cities increased quickly, especially in the North. Immigrants from all over the world flocked to the U.S. to find work and begin a better life for their families.

The demand, or need, for goods such as machinery and tools also grew quickly. Factories met this demand and supplied goods using power-driven machinery both day and night. Machines now produced what had been hand-made goods. Small, family-owned businesses became large companies with the help of banks and investors. Investors gave money to businesses so companies could expand. Coal mining, steel production and clothing manufacturing were all big businesses.

Managers (people in charge of business) in the factories planned how the companies would operate, while workers took care of the machines. The work was often dangerous and difficult. Hard workers sometimes argued with companies to pay them better wages. They also asked for shorter working days and better conditions in which to do their jobs. The businesses made a lot of money for the owners, bankers and investors. Many of these people became very rich. The workers, though, did not always make a lot of money. Sometimes their families lived in very poor conditions. Problems between rich business owners and poor workers made some people feel unhappy with big business.

Communication

Even before the Civil War, developments in communication changed the way Americans sent and received information. In the 1830s, an American professor named Samuel F. B. Morse improved a way to use electromagnetic signals to send messages along wire that hung between poles. President Lincoln was interested in this communication technology and sent many telegraph messages during the war. Telegraph lines stretched from city to city. Communication was much easier and faster than sending letters by pony express or message carriers.

In the 1870s, as inventors Elisha Gray and Alexander Graham Bell worked on devices to improve telegraph service, they designed devices that could transmit speech electronically. Bell’s design was patented first. The telephone uses electricity to transmit speech along wires. Wires between cities are used for voice communication. Now people in communities that were far apart could communicate easily.

As the nation entered the 20th century, communication technology rapidly improved. Thomas Edison invented the phonograph. High-speed photography, film cameras, the radio, tape recordings, telephone answering machines and motion pictures were all invented before the 20th century was even one-fourth of the way over.

Transportation

After the Civil War, people began to move to different regions of the United States. Freed African Americans could choose to live in the South or move to the North to work in factories. Northerners chose to either stay in their home regions or move south to farm. More and more people wanted to move west. This westward expansion was possible because of the development of the first transcontinental railroad.

The first talk about the possibility of a railroad connecting the West and East regions of the U.S. began in the 1830s. Settlers moved westward to build homes, farms and communities. There had to be a way to transport goods and supplies back and forth between the East and West. Nearly everyone agreed a railroad was needed, but they didn’t all agree on the route the rails should follow.

After much debate, people decided that the railroad route would follow the established Oregon, Mormon and California trails. The line began in Omaha, Nebraska, and followed the Platte River. It crossed over the Rocky Mountains at South Pass in Wyoming, and it then went through northern Utah and Nevada. From there, the train crossed the Sierra Mountains to Sacramento, California. Workers laid more tracks to connect Denver, Colorado, and Salt Lake City, Utah, along with other cities not on the direct route. The Union Pacific Railroad built westward from Omaha, and the Central Pacific Railroad built eastward from Sacramento. After six years, the two lines connected at Promontory Summit, Utah. A total of 1,777 miles of track was laid across the country.

Irish and Chinese immigrants, Mormons and Civil War veterans built the rails. White men working on the rails received higher pay than the immigrant workers did. The railroads also employed blacksmiths, bricklayers, carpenters, engineers, surveyors and cooks during the building process.

Workers officially completed the railroad on May 10, 1869. It changed the United States forever. The population of the western U.S. increased significantly. White settlers and freed African Americans moved to the western region to farm, build homes or start businesses. Railcars carried goods and supplies across the nation easily. Dangerous journeys west using wagons or stagecoaches were no longer necessary. Unfortunately, railroads also meant some American Indians were forced off their lands.

Railroads were responsible for more changes to the country than any other technological advance of the post-Civil War era. Indeed, many historians continue to argue that railroads are the most important invention ever created.

title: The Transcontinental Railroad and American Indians
text:
There is no doubt that the transcontinental railroad changed America forever. The railroad allowed people to travel and settle across the country. It easily shipped goods and supplies. People who had once grown all their own food and made all their own clothes were now able to buy supplies shipped on railroad cars. While the railroad brought the country closer together, it also brought many changes to the lives of American Indians of the West.

Railroad companies built tracks through a number of American Indian territories. One result of building the railroad was the loss of the buffalo herds that roamed freely. The American Indians depended on the buffalo for food, clothing and supplies. The railroads disrupted the everyday lives of the buffalo. In addition, many Americans on trains would often shoot the buffalo for fun as they rode past them. The buffalo then rotted on the ground. This angered many American Indians. By 1880, the buffalo had almost disappeared completely from the Great Plains. This left the American Indians without their most important food source.

Along with the end of the buffalo, American Indians often found themselves in arguments and battles with settlers. The settlers built homes and communities on American Indian territory. These two groups rarely lived together in peace. The U.S. tried to solve problems with the American Indians. Unfortunately, the United States' only solution was forcing American Indians onto reservations.

title: Leaders of Technology
text:
The United States quickly became an important industrial nation after the Civil War. There were many great business people and inventors who created machines and technology to help improve the economy. In 1876, the U.S. celebrated the Centennial Exposition. It was a celebration of the country's 100th anniversary. The main attraction at the exposition was Machinery Hall. This was where inventors from the United States displayed their inventions. Read on to learn more about two men and their important advances in technology.

Andrew Carnegie

Andrew Carnegie was born in Scotland. When he was 13 years old, he came to America and worked hard in a cotton mill. Once Carnegie saved enough money, he bought his own businesses. He soon made millions of dollars in the steel industry. He gave millions of dollars to charities in his later years.

Henry Ford

Henry Ford is best remembered for his work in designing and making the first automobiles in the country. He also perfected the assembly-line, conveyor-belt method of building cars. His ideas led to mass production of cars, and it changed the way people ran factories.

title: Main Idea and Details
text:
Look at the main ideas listed here after reading the article “Industry, Communication and Transportation Take the Nation into a New Century.” Then, find three details about each main idea and write them below the main idea.

The growth of industry following Reconstruction made the United States one of the most powerful industrial nations in the world.

Advances in communication technology brought big improvements to life in the United States.

The building of the first transcontinental railroad brought both positive and negative changes to the United States.

title: Writing Focus: Expository Writing/ ￼￼Informative-Main Idea-Detail
text:
Authors often use the main idea-detail format of writing to inform readers of facts.

Use information from this week‛s lesson and ideas you organized in the activity to help you write. Compose three paragraphs explaining the growth of industry in the United States after Reconstruction. Be sure to write in complete sentences, with each paragraph containing a main idea and at least three facts and details. Be sure to check for correct punctuation, grammar and spelling.

title: The Road Map
text:
1890s: Horseless carriages (what people called early automobiles) were being invented around this time. There was a problem, however. There weren't any good roads to travel on, and the roads that were around had no route numbers. The maps that were used during this time were just as bad as the roads.

1900s: There were many automobile manufacturers, and cars were being purchased by the wealthy people. However, the roads were still terrible, and there were laws restricting the use of motorcars. Maps during this time were usually just used for route descriptions or photo guides. There were still no route numbers, so the guides were not very helpful. Photo route guides were often used to help early drivers navigate. Most maps were difficult to read.

1910s: Roads were very expensive to build even in the early 1900s. Cars were not very popular. No one wanted to pay taxes to have the roads built. In 1911, the American Automobile Association (AAA) began to publish some of their own road maps. They had route descriptions, which were a way of getting around, but you always had to keep an eye on the odometer (an instrument that shows how many miles have been traveled by a vehicle). Colorful signs were being put up all over, identifying major routes such as the Lincoln Highway, National Old Trail, Dixie Highway, and others. The biggest news of the time was when Wisconsin began a program to number its roads.

1920s: Road surfacing began in the '20s, but the roads were still not paved. Maps, which were black and white before, began to use colors to indicate the best roads. The AAA published their first TourBook in 1926. That was the year that many roads received the U.S. Highway designation. The black-and-white shields that you see on highways today began to spring up everywhere. It was possible to travel from coast to coast by following the same route numbers between states.

1930s: The Great Depression occurred during the 1930s. Some people who were out of work were hired to pave roads. Road maps were improved as far as detail, color, readability, and reliability. The AAA was sending out "pathfinders" to travel the roads, measure the distances, and note construction, surface, etc.

1940s: The Pennsylvania Turnpike opened in 1940, but World War II was also around the corner. Tourism almost ended. Gasoline was rationed, maps weren't printed, and road building stopped. After the war, however, many families had a car, and travel was at an all-time high.

1950s: People began to spend more time sitting at traffic lights than actually moving. President Eisenhower saw how the German Autobahns worked and how quickly vehicles and equipment could be moved. The National System of Interstate and Defense Highways was born. Initially, Route 66 was to be used for the military in the early Cold War era, but civilian travel began to take over.

1960s: The big changes of the 1960s were the new interstates. These roads limited entrances and exits to interchanges. There were no more traffic lights, restaurants, attractions, cabins, or other things along the road. Maps showed the interstates as proposed, under construction, and completed. Maps were nearly in full color and showed parks, military bases, and more. Such maps were issued for the World's Fairs and Olympic Games and even to help people visit the Civil War battlefields and historic sites.

1970s: Travel grew quickly until 1973, when the oil supplies became a problem. Prices began to rise, and lines of vehicles could be found where gasoline was available. Things were stable again for a few years, but in 1979, the oil supply problems occurred again. More and more miles were added to the interstate system, and more maps were put out, which were becoming even easier to read.

1980s: Increased use of trucking caused deterioration in the interstate system. By the 1980s, not many oil companies bothered with maps. If motorists wanted maps, they had to buy them, get them through the highway departments, or join AAA.

1990sto present: The digital revolution changed the way travelers looked at maps, starting in the 1990s. There was an ever-increasing accuracy in maps. More detail was added to maps, pointing out hotels, restaurants, and shops. Global Positioning Satellite (GPS) systems allow in-vehicle navigation. Some people still use paper maps, however.

title: The United States Speeds into a New Century
text:
It was the “turn of the century.” The 1800s faded into memory as the 1900s sped into view. America was becoming a world leader in industry. Its abundance (large amount) of natural resources and a manufacturing economy led by giant corporations helped the nation grow stronger and stronger. By 1910, the United States led the world in the production of iron, steel and oil. Miners also mined coal and gold in large amounts. The nation’s agricultural, or farming, economy was also doing well. The transcontinental railroad system made shipping goods across the country easy. Goods and products were also being shipped to and traded with other countries all over the world.

Americans were working harder than ever to earn their living. People in rural, or country, areas were still struggling to get by. Life in overcrowded urban, or city, areas was also difficult at times. However, most Americans were making larger incomes and spending more money than in previous decades. The increase in industry meant there were many more goods for people to buy. People shopped in new department stores and ordered goods from mail-order companies. In cities, people could even order goods using the telephone. Electricity was also reaching more and more people. People used Thomas Edison’s electric light in more and more of their homes and businesses. Communities built hospitals, public schools and colleges, churches, libraries and theaters.

Immigrants continued to pour into the country from all over the world. These people wanted to live the “American dream.” Millions of Europeans crowded into eastern coastal cities while also branching out to farmland in the Midwest region of the country. Many found economic opportunities (new ways to make money) in the United States that they could have only dreamed about in their homelands.

Many Americans felt cheerful as the new century began. After all, the country had been through both the Civil War and Reconstruction. People had reason to believe that only good times were ahead. However, there were still citizens who believed the United States had room to improve.

In this issue, you will learn about people and groups who worked to make the United States of America a strong and fair country as it entered into the 20th century.

title: Manufacturing Medicine Overseas May Put U.S. Citizens at Risk
text:
Remember the last time you had a fever? Your parents most likely went to the local drug store and bought medicine for you. After a couple of doses, you probably felt better. In the United States today, we know our medicine is safe. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) was created in 1906. The FDA makes rules about the safety, quality and effectiveness of medicines.

The FDA works to make sure that companies make medicine that is safe and does its job. For over 100 years, people in the United States have depended on the FDA to protect them from dangerous drugs.

Now, the FDA's job is becoming more difficult. This is because many medicine manufacturing companies are making their drugs in foreign countries. It is difficult to inspect all of the overseas factories and make sure they are following safety rules. FDA officials say that sometimes medicines made outside the United States are made with ingredients that don't work or are even dangerous. In fact, some factories are not as clean as they should be. FDA leaders say that the United States must work with the foreign governments to make sure people who take medicine will remain safe.

title: Turn of the Century Life
text:
The turn of the century brought many new and exciting changes to the country. Many of these changes happened because of the fast growth of industry and cities. Even though the wheels of change were turning quickly, some Americans held on to ideas from the previous century. Therefore, change in other areas didn't happen as quickly.

Technology in Cities

By 1900, four out of every 10 Americans lived in cities. In 1900, New York City had over three million residents. The cities of Chicago, Illinois, and Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, had over one million residents each. Cities had to make advances to keep up with the challenges of an expanding population.

Cities were quickly running out of space to expand outward, so in 1900, cities began to build upward. Builders began constructing very tall buildings called skyscrapers to solve the problem of space in cities.

Cities also found ways to connect neighborhoods together. Networks of electric trolley cars and subway train stations made transporting people easier. More and more people were also brought together with telephones and radios.

Improving Public Education

After the Civil War, the United States made some effort to require children to attend school. Between 1865 and 1895, many states passed laws requiring children between the ages of eight and 14 to attend school for three to four months each year. The schools cost nothing to attend. However, these early schools were not successful. Some of the teachers weren't qualified, and it was difficult to get good books and materials.

As the country entered the 20th century, more and more people realized how important an education was to the future success of the country. By 1918, all American children were required to attend school at least through the elementary years. New schools were built, and high schools began to offer classes in different subjects such as math, science, government and social studies.

Unfortunately, the education children received depended on the color of their skin. White children and African American children did not attend the same schools. Most African American children weren't allowed to attend high school or college. Many of these students were able to continue their education at schools started by African Americans. One such man was Booker T. Washington. After being freed from slavery, Mr. Washington became a teacher. He started Tuskegee University in Alabama, which is still open.

Segregation and Discrimination

The end of the Civil War did not end unfair treatment of African Americans. Discrimination, or unfair treatment, was common. In schools, theaters, restaurants and other public places, segregation was normal. African Americans were set apart from whites. They did not sit together on buses and trains. Most public places had separate restrooms and water fountains for each group.

Many Southern states continued to pass Black Codes. These laws made it difficult for African Americans to vote, own property or work at certain jobs. The legal system and police supported these unfair laws. Decades would pass before all of the unfair laws were repealed, or cancelled.

The Vote for Women

Women did not have the same rights as men at the turn of the century. Many believed that women should only be homemakers. Many believed women were only supposed to take care of their families and not take part in politics or speak out in public. In most places, married women were considered to be under the control of their husbands. Women weren't allowed to own property, sign contracts, attend college or work at high-paying professional jobs. Perhaps most importantly, women did not have the right to vote.

Of course, many people did not think women were being treated fairly. After all, the 14th and 15th Amendments to the U.S. Constitution guaranteed citizenship and the right to vote for all Americans - but not women.

Even before the Civil War, women wanted the chance to vote. They wanted the same opportunities as men. They wanted to go to college, own land and work as doctors and lawyers. By the 20th century, women were fighting for suffrage (the right to vote). Women began forming political groups. The National Women's Party, led by a young woman named Alice Paul, often marched in front of the White House demanding to vote. The suffragettes, as these women were known, were sometimes faced with both verbal and physical violence. Mrs. Paul was even sent to prison for seven months.

Finally, after many years of marching and fighting, the U.S. Congress passed the 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which gave women the right to vote.

title: Susan B. Anthony — Women’s Rights Leader
text:
Many important women worked to improve the quality of life for women in the beginning of the 20th century. One such woman was a Quaker named Susan B. Anthony. Anthony had worked as a schoolteacher before beginning her work for social reform (change). She supported the anti-slavery and women’s rights movements. Anthony proved that women could be leaders in society. She, along with many others, wanted women to have the same rights as men, including the right to vote.

After the Civil War, Anthony and her fellow women’s rights workers wanted both formerly enslaved people and women to have the right to vote. They were disappointed when the 14th and 15th Amendments to the Constitution did not talk about women at all. They didn’t give up, though. Anthony traveled all over the nation to convince people to support her cause. She was once arrested and fined $100 for voting illegally in a presidential election.

Women did not gain the right to vote during Susan B. Anthony’s lifetime. The right came 14 years after her death. She did, however, influence many other Americans to continue with social reform. Thanks to Susan B. Anthony, women today don’t have to worry about being fined or arrested when they cast their votes on election day.

title: The Progressive Era
text:
Business and industry grew fast in the first 20 years of the 20th century in the United States. Before the turn of the century, the government tried hard not to get too involved in private businesses. However, by 1900, many people felt businesses were getting too big and too greedy. They wanted the government to help control large industries and keep the free enterprise system fair.

These people called themselves Progressives. They asked the government to pass laws that would make sure businesses could compete with each other. The government passed laws that would prevent one large company, or corporation, from controlling a single industry. Many agencies were created to make sure businesses made and traded goods according to the laws.

During this time, Congress also passed the 16th Amendment to the Constitution. This amendment allowed the government to collect income taxes from citizens.

title: Henry Ford and Mass Production
text:
In 1913, car designer and manufacturer Henry Ford developed a new system of making cars in his factory. He began using a moving assembly line, where each worker had one job to do in the car's assembly. Using this idea, factories made cars more quickly than if they were assembled one car at a time. Ford believed that this mass production would make his company very successful.

Ford also had new and interesting ideas on how to treat workers in his car factory. He offered them up to $5 a day to work for him. At the time, this was a very large wage to be paid for a day's work. Ford wanted to be sure his own employees could afford to buy one of the cars they were helping to produce.

Today, Henry Ford's ideas about assembly lines and mass production of goods are still used at factories around the world.

title: Using Primary and Secondary Sources
text:
Historians must be able to gather information from many different sources as they study events and people in history.A primary source provides information from a person who was actually at the event. Letters, journals, newspaper articles, photographs or artifacts are all examples of primary sources. A secondary source of information comes from someone who was not at the event. Encyclopedia articles, biographies, textbooks and some internet sites can be secondary sources.

Read the two pieces of information below related to the women‛s rights movement for suffrage in the early 20th century. One is a primary source, and the other is a secondary source. Identify each.

American History— Chapter 13

Women’s suffrage is the right for women to vote and hold political office. In the United States, women did not earn the right to vote until the 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution was ratified in 1920. The road to the Amendment was a long one for the women of America.

In 1848, the Seneca Falls Women’s Convention was held in Seneca Falls, New York. It was there that the idea of women’s suffrage was introduced to the American public. Several important women, including Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott, spoke at the conference. These activists began a 70-year struggle for women to have the right to vote in the United States of America.

Use information from the sources and this week‛s issue to identify three cause-and-effect relationships about women‛s suffrage. Complete the cause-and-effect chart below.

title: It's All About That Jazz: New Orleans and the Creation of American Jazz
text:
Jazz is a style of music that originated in New Orleans in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is a mix of African American musical traditions. It also includes other musical genres, like ragtime and blues. Jazz has a lot of rhythm and can express many different emotions.

Even though jazz is hard to define, it’s a type of music that appeals to many different people. Jazz music uses a lot of brass instruments, like trombones and saxophones. Woodwind instruments, such as the clarinet and drums, and percussion instruments, like the piano, are also used. There is no strict musical form in jazz. It can be slow and sad or fast and joyous. Jazz musicians create their own unique style of playing. Jazz music is very distinctive and interesting to listen to.

Jazz quickly spread across the United States and worldwide after it was first recorded in 1917. Jazz influenced the creation of other styles of music, including swing, hip-hop, and rock and roll. Music lovers enjoyed the songs of jazz musicians like Louis Armstrong, Miles Davis, Duke Ellington, Charlie Parker, and John Wigginton Hyman.

Louisiana is one state that is known for its jazz festivals. One of the biggest is New Orleans’ annual Jazz and Heritage Festival. Every year, hundreds of thousands of visitors flock to the New Orleans’ Fair Grounds. They attend the jazz festival and experience the music, culture, and cuisine of New Orleans. Other states and cities also have jazz festivals. Check your local newspaper or your community’s website to see if there is one coming up near you.

title: Life Before the Panama Canal
text:
It was in the 1800s that American and British business leaders wanted to ship goods cheaper and faster from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean. However, it was the French that first took action to attempt to build a canal to make a shorter route between the Atlantic and Pacific.

At that time, if you wanted to travel by water from the American East Coast to the Indies, you would have to travel around the southern tip of South America. Imagine how many miles early explorers would add to their trips before the 50-mile Panama Canal was there. Sea travel was very dangerous for those early explorers. Sailing around the tip of South America at Cape Horn is still considered very dangerous today. Some early explorers would travel across land rather than navigate through those waters. Even for those who were able to get around Cape Horn, it took months longer to take this route. Early explorers like Vasco Núñez de Balboa talked about making a water route through the area of Panama to shorten the trip around South America.

By 1881, the French decided to start digging the Panama Canal. The work was difficult. There were no ways to prevent or cure malaria and yellow fever. Many people died from these diseases. After working for nine years and losing over 20,000 workers, the French gave up.

The project sat there for a few years until President Theodore Roosevelt took over. Dr. William Gorgas and his team reduced the cases of malaria and yellow fever. They fumigated homes and cleaned pools of water where mosquitoes bred. The Panama Canal was completed in 1914. Ships were able to shave off thousands of miles from their journeys and deliver goods more quickly.

Recent improvements to the Panama Canal allow larger and more efficient supertankers and naval vessels to use the canal. Shorter trips means less fuel used. The money saved by the shipping companies can be passed on to the consumer. The widened canal also allows liquefied gases and oil from the U.S. to be shipped to new markets in Asia.

title: Langston Hughes and The Weary Blues
text:
Some artists and authors use history as the subject or model for their work, such as Henry Wadsworth Longfellow when he wrote his poem, Paul Revere’s Ride, in 1860. Many artists and writers use what is happening around them as inspiration. One creator who did so was Langston Hughes.

Hughes wrote essays, articles, and plays, but he is best known for his poetry. He began writing during what is known as the Harlem Renaissance. New York City saw a huge surge in African American art in the 1920s. An important part of the Harlem Renaissance was jazz. Hughes often visited night clubs and knew many of the most famous jazz musicians at that time. Jazz was an important part of his poetic voice in expressing the experience of African Americans in the early 1900s.

We can see elements of jazz in one of his most famous poems, The Weary Blues. In this poem, Hughes tells of watching a jazz musician:

Down on Lennox Avenue the other night

By the pale dull pallor of a dull gas light

He did a lazy sway . . .

He did a lazy sway . . .

To the tune o’ those Weary Blues.

The repetition of the long A in “sway” reminds readers of the sounds instruments might make in a jazz ensemble. We see musical rhythm with the words, “Thump, thump, thump went his foot on the floor.” We also see repetitive blues-style lyrics when the musician in his poem sings:

“I got the Weary Blues

And I can’t be satisfied.

Got the Weary Blues

And can’t be satisfied—

I ain’t happy no mo’

And I wish that I had died.”

Hughes captured not only what people thought, but how they expressed themselves by using elements of jazz. He didn’t just represent his own ideas, but the values and feelings of the world he lived in.

title: Susan B. Anthony
text:
Many important women worked to improve the quality of life for women. In the beginning of the 20th century, one such woman was a Quaker named Susan B. Anthony. Anthony had worked as a schoolteacher before beginning her work for social reform (change). She supported the anti-slavery and women's rights movements. Anthony proved that women could be leaders in society. She and many others wanted women to have the same rights as men, including the right to vote.

After the Civil War, Anthony and her fellow women's rights workers wanted both former enslaved people and women to have the right to vote. They were disappointed with the 14th and 15th Amendments to the Constitution. The amendments did not talk about women at all. They didn't give up though. Anthony traveled all over the nation to convince people to support her cause. She was even arrested and fined $100 for voting illegally in a presidential election.

Women did not gain the right to vote during Susan B. Anthony's lifetime. Their right to vote came 14 years after her death. She did, however, influence many other Americans to continue with social reform. Thanks to Susan B. Anthony, women today don't have to think twice about casting their votes on election day.

title: Progress and Equality
text:
Throughout human history, people have been stuck in one place in society. Their last name, skin color, gender, and social class dictated how they could live their life. Their skills, abilities, and experience were disregarded. Then, the American Dream began spreading. They heard about the opportunities that were available in America. This meant the lower classes had control of their own destiny. The American Dream meant no matter where they came from, their hard work could earn them a successful life.

America was becoming a world leader in industry. The abundance of natural resources and a manufacturing economy helped the nation grow stronger. By 1910, the United States led the world in production of iron, steel, and oil. Miners extracted gold and coal in large amounts. The nation’s farming economy was doing well. The transcontinental railroad made it easy to ship goods across the country.

Americans were working harder than ever to earn a living. Most Americans were making larger incomes and spending more money than in previous decades. The increase in industry meant there were more goods for people to buy. People shopped in new department stores and ordered goods from mail-order companies. In cities, people could even order goods using the telephone. Electricity was reaching more homes and businesses.

The values of the American Dream and the United States became one and the same. All around the world, the hopeless and oppressed longed to come to America. Immigrants continued to come into the country from all over the world. Millions of Europeans crowded into eastern coastal cities, and branching out to farmland in the Midwest region of the country. Many immigrants found new opportunities to make money. They introduced other Americans to new ideas, foods and products. For many, they went from rags to riches by being able to make money from their new opportunities.

The “American Dream” has been a beacon of hope for many people all over the world. It allows for equal opportunity for all people to reach their potential. The idea of the American Dream has motivated thousands to venture to the U.S. and work hard toward a new life.

title: The United States Rises to a World Power
text:
At the beginning of the 20th century, Americans looked forward to a time of growth and prosperity. There were many new opportunities for people to find wealth and success. Industry was booming, and America took pride in being a world leader.

In 1917 it was time for the United States to use its power and leadership. A war had been waging for control of Europe for over two years. The Allied Powers (France, Britain, Russia and their allies) were at war with the Central Powers (led by Germany and Austria-Hungary). At first America was neutral, or uninvolved, in the war. The country did not support one side or the other. However, the United States was soon sending both money and supplies to help the Allies fight against Germany. It was clear to Americans that they would have to join the fight. On April 2, 1917, the United States declared war against the Central Powers.

American troops poured into Europe by the thousands. Courageous and strong, the U.S. soldiers played an important role in the war. By the fall of 1918, Germany’s chances of a victory had been crushed.

The United States took the lead in the war efforts. U.S. President Woodrow Wilson spent a great deal of time trying to find a way for all of the countries to come to a peaceful agreement and end the war. He wanted to make the world “safe for democracy.” His plan, called Fourteen Points, created the League of Nations. This international organization would settle disagreements between countries. President Wilson believed this was a way to help prevent future wars. Interestingly, the United States would never be a part of this group. Congress never approved the country’s participation.

On Nov. 11, 1918, an armistice (agreement to stop fighting) was declared. The countries at war all agreed to stop fighting for a time. Leaders wanted to discuss peace. For six months, the countries at war discussed the issues during the Paris Peace Conference. World War I finally came to an end when the Treaty of Versailles was signed in France on June 28, 1919. Peace wouldn’t last long, though. Germany was never truly pleased with the way the war ended. They did not think they were being treated fairly. Within years, that country’s anger would lead to the rise of one of the most ruthless world leaders ever, Adolf Hitler.

title: Immunization Week Takes Shot at Saving Lives
text:
The United Nations (U.N.) is a group of 192 countries all working together to achieve peace and development in the world. The group's headquarters is located in New York City, New York. One way the group achieves its goals is through health education for the world's people.

Millions of people all over the world die each year from diseases that can be prevented with vaccines. Many people simply do not have access to the medicines they need to prevent diseases such as flu, measles, polio and tetanus. Others may not understand how the diseases are spread, treated and prevented.

Each year, the U.N. marks Immunization Week throughout 180 countries and territories of the world. During this seven-day period, workers hold vaccination campaigns, training sessions and conferences to educate and treat people in regions of Africa, the Americas, the Eastern Mediterranean, Europe and the Western Pacific.

The United Nations' World Health Organization believes that millions of lives can be saved during the week each year. Now that's a "shot" of good news!

title: Boom to Bust: The Roaring ‘20s to the Great Depression
text:
Flappers and Jazz

The 1920s was a colorful time in U.S. history. It was a time of new ideas and changes in the country. Radios were in almost every home. Charles Lindbergh flew the first solo plane flight across the Atlantic Ocean. Skyscrapers shot up all over the country. The people in the United States were changing too. Many of them wanted lives that were different from their parents' and grandparents' lives.

Some young people became free-spirited. Women, who had gained the right to vote in 1920, could now dress and act differently. Instead of long skirts and stockings, many young women wore short skirts and cut their hair. These women were known as flappers. They learned the latest dances and listened to jazz music. The mood of the country was confident. People bought more and more goods using credit (borrowed money). Soon, however, the happy times came crashing down.

Black Tuesday

Tuesday, October 29, 1929, was the end of a prosperous (successful) and optimistic (hopeful) time in the United States. During the 1920s, millions of people had bought shares of stock, or part ownership of companies. Stock prices continued to rise. People borrowed more and more money to buy more shares. On Black Tuesday, the prices of stocks fell sharply. Suddenly the shares were worth nothing. Many people lost everything they owned that day. The stock market had crashed, and the U.S. economy crashed along with it.

The Great Depression

The stock market crash was only the beginning of tough times for the country. Many banks lost money too. People worried that their money in the bank might not be safe, and they rushed to the banks to withdraw their funds. When banks were out of money, they closed their doors. Some of the banks began to go out of business. People who had deposited money in the banks were out of luck. There was no money left.

Many banks tried to get back some of the money people had borrowed. They asked people to pay back loans (money given with a promise to pay it back) immediately. Sometimes the banks took people's homes and farms back when loans weren't paid. People were left homeless and without a way to make money. Many felt the banks were being cruel to them.

Businesses were hurt by the Depression, too. Some lost a lot of money in the stock market crash. Many of them had to cut back employees' hours and reduce their pay. Many people lost their jobs altogether when businesses closed.

Within a few years, millions of Americans were out of work. Some of these people traveled on railroads from town to town looking for new jobs. Some businesses had more than 1,000 people apply for a single job opening. Farmers who had lost their land traveled all over the country to find work on other people's farms.

The Dust Bowl

To make matters worse, 25,000 square miles in the southwestern Plains suffered terrible drought and severe windstorms. These windstorms were so bad they covered farmland with a blanket of dust. The Dust Bowl affected land in Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico and Colorado.

Farmland in these areas had been overplowed and overgrazed by animals for years before. Because the region was also in a drought and there was almost no rainfall for years, there was very little grass and few trees growing on the land. High winds blew the exposed topsoil away. Huge dust cloud storms blew across the land and destroyed everything in their paths.

Small farms were hardest hit. Many of the farmers were already in debt. They had borrowed money for seeds and tools to operate the farms. When crops didn't grow, the farmers couldn't repay the bank. Unfortunately, banks often had to foreclose on the farms. This meant the farmers no longer owned the land. Suddenly, many farm families were left homeless and without a way to support their families.

Worldwide Effects

Though the Great Depression started in the United States, it quickly became a worldwide problem. After WWI, the United States helped many European countries pay their debts. When the American economy failed, there was no money to send to foreign countries. As a result, the western European countries fell into a period of economic depression too. Great Britain and Germany were the hardest hit.

The Great Depression lasted more than a decade. Unfortunately, it would take another great war to bring prosperity back to the world.

title: Life in a Hooverville
text:
As the Great Depression deepened, so did the troubles of many Americans. Many families who were unable to pay rent or make house payments were forced to leave their homes. Some families who made their living on farms moved to cities, searching for better lives. Some city families even lost their homes. After being evicted (forced to leave), many of these families searched for public bread lines or soup kitchens for food. Cheese sandwiches, watered-down soup and oatmeal were typical free meals.

For shelter, many families shared run-down apartments. But even those were hard to find. Some people resorted to using scraps of lumber and cardboard boxes to build shacks in which to live. Soon, small communities of these shack homes appeared. These new shantytown (shack town) areas were often called Hoovervilles. The name Hooverville was chosen in “honor” of President Herbert Hoover. Many blamed him for causing the Depression. Many workers sent their families to live with relatives while they stayed behind in the slums to look for work.

Hoovervilles had no electricity or running water, but they were often built near rivers. There was no garbage removal system, so trash piled up, and rats ran wild. People living there stayed warm by covering themselves with “Hoover blankets,” or newspapers. They used the restroom in “Hoover villas” or outside public toilets. The communities were dangerous and dirty, but for millions of out-of-work Americans, they were home. Many Hoovervilles were often raided by local law enforcement and sometimes burned to the ground. The people who were living in the shacks were forced to wander to the next town. Life for Americans during the Great Depression was extremely difficult. Hoovervilles are just a small snapshot of the big picture of the United States during this sad time in history.

title: Why is Veterans’ Day celebrated in the United States?
text: World War I, the "war to end all wars," officially came to an end on June 28, 1919. However, the fighting stopped months earlier, on Nov. 11, 1918. Therefore, Nov. 11 became known as Armistice Day. The day was set aside for Americans to show their appreciation to the country's World War I heroes. The national celebrations included parades, speeches and public prayer meetings. After later wars in the 20th century, the name of the holiday was changed to Veterans' Day. Today in the United States, every Nov. 11 is set aside as a day of "celebration to honor America's veterans for their patriotism, love of country and willingness to serve and sacrifice for the common good."

title: Migrant Farm Workers in the Great Depression
text:
During the Great Depression, many found themselves out of work. People living in the Great Plains states lost their farms and businesses because of drought and the economic situation in the country. A great number of these people became migrant farm workers.

Migrant workers moved from place to place looking for work on large farms. Over one million people moved to California in the 1930s. These people hoped to find work easily because of the long growing season and variety of crops produced in the state.

There were so many families seeking work that jobs were still scarce (in limited supply) and wages were very low. Even with the entire family working, many migrant families struggled to pay for housing and food. Most families lived in very poor conditions. Life was difficult, dirty and without much hope. Life for many migrant workers all over the United States did not improve much, even after the Great Depression ended.
