text: Read the article called “Boom to Bust: The Roaring ‘20s to the Great Depression.” Create a flowchart by writing complete sentences about the Great Depression in the United States. Be sure to write the events in the order that they happened during the 1920s and 1930s. Check your work for correct punctuation and spelling.

title: Let's Write
text:
Pretend you are a farmer in Texas during the Great Depression. Write a letter to your banker about your difficulties during the economic downturn.

Persuade the banker to give you and your family more time to solve your problems before the bank forecloses on your home. Using complete sentences, give at least three reasons why your banker should give your family more time. Support all of your main ideas with at least three facts and details.

title: Looking Back: Pre-Civil War to WWI/Great Depression
text:
Differences Between the North and South

People who wanted a democratic country founded the United States of America. They would be able to make decisions about how the government operated. The people would be able to choose their own leaders. However, many of them could never agree on the amount of power the federal government should have. The U.S. Constitution explained how the rights and responsibilities of state governments were different from those of the federal government. Even so, many people were still not happy with the balance of power.

Many Northerners were federalists and supported a strong central government. Democratic-Republicans living in the South believed states should have the right to declare laws unacceptable. In the 19th century, many Southern states believed the federal government was getting too involved in their business. Leaders of these states were especially worried that the federal government might try to interfere with slavery in the South. Southerners also believed the government favored Northern states. Tariffs, taxes on imported and exported goods, helped Northern businesses. Southerners felt they were being treated unfairly.

The differences between Northern and Southern states increased as time went on. Their economies were different. The North made money in industry. Southern states depended on agriculture for money. Many of the agriculture businesses relied heavily on slave labor. Most people in the North lived in large cities while most Southerners lived on farms or in small towns. The differences between the states became more and more noticeable as the century went on, which led to mentions of war.

The 1860 Presidential Election

In 1860, the United States was already in the middle of a great disagreement. How should it decide if new states were declared free or slave states? The Compromises of 1820 and 1850 had only settled the question of slavery in new states for the time being. The trouble in Kansas, as it became a new free state, clearly showed that peace between Northern and Southern states was not going to be easy.

The 1860 presidential election would be a turning point in the relationship between the states. Both Northerners and Southerners alike believed the right person must be elected as the new president. Southern Congress leaders were clear. The Southern states would withdraw from the U.S. if the election choice was unacceptable. Republican lawyer Abraham Lincoln promised to leave slavery alone in the South. However, he also promised he would not allow slavery to spread to new territories.

On Nov. 6, 1860, Lincoln was elected as the 16th president of the United States. Though Lincoln did not receive the majority of the people’s votes, he did win the most votes from the Electoral College. Many Southern states were outraged at Lincoln’s election. People built the U.S. on the ideas of freedom and independence, but it was about to split apart.

Southern States Separate from the Union

After President Lincoln took office, tensions between Northern and Southern states grew. Southern states believed Lincoln’s election was the beginning of the end for them. They believed the federal government would take away their right to make their own decisions. They were especially concerned that the U.S. government would make it illegal to own enslaved people.

South Carolina’s citizens decided to take action almost immediately after Lincoln’s election. On Dec. 20, 1860, they voted to “dissolve” the union between their state and the other states in the U.S. This meant that South Carolina, a Southern state, became the first state to secede from the nation. Other Southern states soon followed its lead and broke away from the Union. Mississippi left three weeks later. By Feb. 1, 1861, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana and Texas had also left the U.S.

Not everyone in the South wanted the states to leave the Union. Some people wanted to work out their differences. However, the majority of people in the South wanted to protect their right to own enslaved people and make their own decisions. They formed the Confederate States of America and named Jefferson Davis its president. By April 1861, the battle lines had been drawn, and a war between the states seemed likely.

title: From a War-torn Nation to a Country Reborn
text:
The First Shots of a Civil War

When South Carolina seceded from the Union in December 1860, Union soldiers took control of Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor. Confederate forces worked hard to remove Union soldiers from Southern soil. For nearly four months, Union soldiers held firm and refused to surrender. On April 12, 1861, at 4:30 a.m., Confederate soldiers fired at Fort Sumter. The Civil War had officially begun. Southerners fought for the right to make their own decisions and for their way of life, including slavery. Northerners followed President Lincoln’s request to fight to keep the U.S. together. Northern soldiers also fought for the freedom of enslaved people in the South.

The Emancipation Proclamation

The war waged on. Both the North and South suffered a heavy loss of soldiers. The end was nowhere in sight, and President Lincoln was discouraged about the war. He knew that getting rid of slavery was important. He also wanted to bring the Union back together. He waited for the right time to announce his plan. On Sept. 22, 1862, President Lincoln made the Emancipation Proclamation. He warned Southern states that enslaved Southerners would be forever free if the “rebellious states” did not rejoin the Union within months. He also announced that formerly enslaved people were free to join the Union Army. Many slaves fled north. The Emancipation Proclamation helped to free enslaved people and caused many Southern plantation owners to lose workers. The number of Union soldiers increased greatly because many formerly enslaved people joined the cause.

On the Battlefield and Back at Home

The Civil War raged on for four years, and soldiers fought many battles. Back home, Northern factories expanded their businesses to produce war goods. The Northern economy was strong throughout the war. After the war, Northerners were faced with a new income tax to pay for the nearly $2 million a day in war costs. Some Northerners were also upset that rich citizens could pay the government a fee to avoid serving in the military. In the South, life was especially difficult. Confederates could not produce all the supplies needed for the army. Neither could they sell their agricultural products for money. Southerners were often left homeless and without food. Southerners could not go on. On April 9, 1865, Confederate General Robert E. Lee surrendered to Union General Ulysses S. Grant. The bloody, four-year war finally ended.

Reconstructing the Nation

Returning to normal life after the four-year war was difficult. Many Northerners wanted to bring the nation together again and guarantee all Americans their civil rights. Southerners were faced with rebuilding families, homes, farms and towns that had been destroyed during the brutal war. Formerly enslaved people experienced their newfound freedom. Many married and searched for family members. They made plans for the future, as well, which was something they had never been able to do before.

Reconstruction plans for the nation took a drastic change on April 14, 1865. Confederate supporter John Wilkes Booth shot and killed President Lincoln at Ford’s theater in Washington, D.C. Andrew Johnson was next in line to lead the nation. Almost immediately, people worried that Lincoln’s plan to bring the nation back together might never happen.

Amendments to the Constitution

President Johnson’s plan for new state governments was simple. Each state had to declare secession illegal and pass the 13th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. This amendment did away with slavery forever in the United States. Some states did not want to admit they had been wrong to secede. Others refused to ratify the 13th Amendment for a long time. Many people still treated formerly enslaved people badly. People in both regions of the country were not getting along with each other as everyone had hoped.

In June 1866, Congress passed the 14th Amendment. Now all citizens, including African Americans, would have their civil rights protected. The 15th Amendment guaranteed that all men would have the right to vote. Women were not able to vote until 1920, when Congress passed the 19th Amendment. The passing of the amendments helped bring the United States back together again, though it took many years to do so.

A Nation Reborn

Life for all U.S. citizens changed after Reconstruction. In the South, white people gained control of most of the political offices. African Americans had a hard time entering politics. In addition, state officials did not always enforce the 14th and 15th Amendments. A system of separating the races, segregation, became common throughout most of the South. Life was still difficult for African Americans.

The U.S. changed in other ways, too. The American Industrial Revolution was booming. People created inventions and developed new manufacturing methods. Industry grew fast, and even more people came to live and work in cities. The slow pace of American life sped up. Transportation methods improved. Steamboats moved goods and people over water. The transcontinental railroad moved goods and people over land at speeds that once seemed impossible. The United States moved beyond the Civil War and made social, political, industrial and economic improvements. These improvements transformed the nation as it headed into the 20th century.

title: Sharecropping in the South
text: After the Civil War, Southern farmland was returned to the wealthy people who had owned the land before the war. Of course, they no longer had free slave labor to work the crops. Freed African Americans and poor whites did not have the money they needed to buy their own land to farm. If they wanted to farm, they were forced to become sharecroppers. They rented land and gave part of the crops as payment to the landowner. Sharecropping was difficult work, and many Southern sharecroppers went into great debt. Most of them never had the chance to own any land at all. It seemed to many that sharecropping was just a new form of slavery.

title: 20th Century Industry, Communication and Transportation
text:
The Industrial Revolution continued after Reconstruction. Shipbuilding, iron, steel, agriculture, construction and mining industries were all important. Industry grew more rapidly than agriculture. Cities grew in population as immigrants came to the U.S. from all over the world seeking better lives.

Developments in communication changed the way people sent and received information. The telegraph, Alexander Graham Bell's telephone, Edison's phonograph, the radio and motion pictures were all developed in the early 20th century.

After the Civil War, people settled all parts of the nation. A transcontinental railroad made this possible. It was built mostly by Irish and Chinese immigrants, Mormons and Civil War veterans. People and goods traveled across the West quickly and safely. Unfortunately, railroads also meant that some American Indians were forced off their lands.

title: The U.S. in WWI
text: In 1917, Americans looked forward to growth and success. Opportunities and industry boomed. America quickly became a world leader. At the same time, there was a war in Europe between the Allied Powers and the Central Powers. America tried not to get involved. Soon, however, the U.S. helped the Allies fight against Germany. The U.S. and thousands of its soldiers took the lead in the war effort. Soon, the Allies defeated Germany. U.S. President Woodrow Wilson's leadership was important in bringing World War I to an end on June 28, 1919. Peace was very short-lived. Germany's anger grew, and one of the most dangerous world leaders ever, Adolf Hitler, rose to power.

title: The Great Depression Begins
text: After WWI, life in America was full of new ideas and changes. People seemed free-spirited and excited about the many opportunities that were available. That happy time came tumbling down suddenly on Tuesday, Oct. 29, 1929. On this "black" day, the U.S. stock market crashed. Many people lost everything they owned when company stocks they had bought became worthless. The U.S. economy quickly crashed, too. Banks ran out of money, and many businesses closed. People lost their homes, farms and jobs. Within a few years, millions of Americans were out of work. Families were separated as grown-ups tried to find work. The Great Depression had settled on the United States, and it would take another war to bring the country out of the terrible situation.

title: Back in Time!
text:
"Alana, are you sure your grandparents don't mind us coming over every day after school? They have so many interesting things to look at."

"Grandpa Frank and Grandma Minnie love having us over. And you're right ... they do have a lot of interesting, old things to look at. I can't wait to see what's up in the attic. Remember, Grandma Minnie promised we could explore it this afternoon."

"How could I forget! As soon as we eat a few of her famous cookies, I vote we head up there and start exploring! She said we might discover a treasure if we look in just the right spot. Do you think there might really be a treasure hidden up in the attic?"

"Well, you never know, Jackson. Did you see Grandpa Frank's face when Grandma talked about the treasure? His eyes crinkled up and his mustache twitched. I think there's some kind of secret hidden up in that attic."

(Jackson and Alana enjoy a few of Grandma Minnie's cookies and then head up to the attic to see what they can discover.)

"Wow, Alana! This place is huge! Ah-choo! And it's dusty. Have you been up here before?"

"Yes, but only with Grandma Minnie or Grandpa Frank. I've never actually looked around up here without them. Where do you think the treasure might be?"

"I don't know, Alana, but there sure is a lot of interesting stuff up here. Look at that old baby buggy. It must be a hundred years old."

"Jackson, let's look through that old trunk by the wall."

(The two friends open the trunk and peer inside.)

"Hey, look at this coonskin cap! I wonder if Daniel Boone wore this when he first settled Kentucky."

"Maybe he did, Jackson. Look at these old shoes with buttons all the way up the sides! I wonder if my great-great-grandmother wore these to march in a women's suffrage (right-to-vote) parade."

"Alana, all of this stuff is really cool, but I don't see any treasures. I mean, we haven't found any gold, silver or diamonds. Where do you think the treasure could be?"

"Maybe there isn't really a treasure here after all. I'm getting kind of tired. Let's sit down for a minute and look at one of these old photo albums. There are lots of them up here! This one looks interesting. It looks like it might be from the Civil War."

"It sure does! That's just what we've been studying in social studies, too. Maybe we'll find a cool picture to show our teacher. He loves it when students bring in primary sources to share, and a photo taken during the Civil War would be a great primary source!"

"You're right, Jackson. Let's take a look. Hey! This Confederate soldier looks a lot like Grandpa Frank!"

"You know something, Alana, with that bushy mustache he really does! Here, let me take a closer look."

Both children touch the photo at the same time and something amazing happens. ... They are transported back in time!)

"Jackson! What just happened? Where are we? Look! There's the soldier in the photo, ... and there's a photographer, taking his picture!"

"Shhh! They'll hear us! Look! He's posing in front of your grandparents' house, but it looks brand new. The soldier looks like he is heading off to war ... the Civil War! Alana, it looks like we've traveled back to the 1860s!"

(The children look again at the photo, and when they both touch the photo, they are quickly transported back to the attic.)

"Jackson, I think we just discovered the treasure! Objects that can take us back and forth in time!"

"Alana, you're absolutely right. It seems that if we both touch the picture together, we will travel through time. Let's try it again!"

"I'm game if you are, Jackson!"

Let's join Jackson and Alana as they travel back to the 1860s to see what happened during the American Civil War.

title: The Blue and the Gray
text:
"Alana, I can't believe we're really back in the 1860s, watching the events of the Civil War!"

"Me either, Jackson. It looks like so many Americans are very angry. Let's find out what's going on. ..."

The Union is Dissolved

"When Abraham Lincoln was elected president, the South worried that he wouldn't let them make their own decisions. People believed that he would abolish, or do away with, slavery.

On Dec. 20, 1860, a committee of South Carolina's citizens voted and everyone agreed "that the union now subsisting between South Carolina and other states under the name of the United States of America is hereby dissolved." With that declaration, or announcement, South Carolina became the ﬁrst of the Southern states to secede (break free) from the United States of America. By Feb. 1, 1861, Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana and Texas had also left the Union. These states wanted to protect what they thought was their right to own slaves. They wanted to have the freedom to make their own decisions. They formed the Confederate States of America, led by President Jefferson Davis.

By April 1861, the lines of conﬂict were clearly drawn. Northern "Yanks" and Southern "Rebs" were set to ﬁght against each other to protect their property, rights and values.

First Shots at Fort Sumter

When the first states seceded, U.S. soldiers were stationed in South Carolina. Led by Major Robert Anderson, these soldiers took control of Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor. The people in Charleston were angry that the Union soldiers had taken the fort. The next day, Confederate forces took control of three nearby forts. They wanted to remove the Union soldiers from Southern soil.

The Union held control of Fort Sumter for almost four months. President Lincoln sent supplies to the fort. Confederate messengers asked Maj. Anderson to surrender, but he would not give up. At 4:30 a.m. on April 12, 1861, the Confederates began ﬁring on Fort Sumter. The Civil War had officially begun. The attack lasted 34 hours. The Union soldiers ﬁred back, but they were forced to surrender. Surprisingly, not one soldier on either side was killed in battle.

The Soldiers of War

Like it or not, the United States found itself in the middle of a war that neither side was prepared to ﬁght. Soldiers needed to be gathered and trained. Some men signed up voluntarily (on their own) while the government drafted, or ordered, others to serve in the military.

Northern soldiers fought to keep the United States together. In time, it became clear that the soldiers of the North were also ﬁghting to free Southern slaves. Eventually, African American men were also allowed to serve in the Union Army and wore the Union blue uniforms.

Southerners believed they were ﬁghting for the right to leave the Union. They wanted states to be able to make their own decisions, and they were ready to defend the Southern way of life. They also fought for the right to own slaves. Many Confederate soldiers wore gray uniforms.

On the Battleﬁeld

Fighting in the Civil War was brutal. Most battles began with face-to-face attack on an open battleﬁeld. A drummer would beat a drum slowly as a signal for the soldiers to move into formation. The air was often thick with black smoke from cannons as the soldiers walked in rows toward enemy lines.

The soldiers shot at one another with riﬂes. Many fell dead within seconds of the start of battle. As the soldiers moved closer together, they usually switched to hand-to-hand combat. They used bayonets (long blades) that were attached to the end of their riﬂes. Thousands of soldiers died from battle wounds during the war.

The Battle of Gettysburg

In the beginning of the Civil War, many Southern victories kept the Union Army from capturing the Confederate capital at Richmond, Virginia. The South's leader, General Robert E. Lee, decided it was time to make a bold move. He wanted a victory on Northern soil because he was sure this would make the Union want to end the war once and for all.

Gen. Lee took his troops into Pennsylvania in June 1863. Union soldiers followed Lee and his Confederate troops and surprised them in the town of Gettysburg. The three-day battle that followed was a turning point in the war. Lee's Confederate Army lost thousands of men and was forced to retreat, or withdraw, to Virginia. The Confederate Army was never able to invade the North again.

The Final Surrender

On April 9, 1865, Gen. Lee surrendered to General Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Court House in Virginia. After four bloody years, the Civil War had ended. Grant allowed Lee's officers to keep their weapons and all soldiers to return home. He also allowed soldiers to keep their own horses. Finally, he ordered Union troops to share their food with Southern soldiers who were starving. When Union soldiers began to cheer at the word of surrender, Grant stopped them and exclaimed, "The war is over. The Rebels are our countrymen again."

"Wow, Alana. I had no idea the Civil War was so brutal. I'm glad I didn't have to choose sides and fight against other Americans."

"I agree, Jackson. It would have been very hard to live during these sad times."

title: The Emancipation Proclamation
text:
After a year of battles and decisions, Lincoln knew it was time to end slavery. President Lincoln met with his group of advisors (people who offer ideas and share opinions). They told him to wait until the North had won a major battle before announcing the end of slavery. This chance came in September 1862 after the Battle of Antietam in Maryland (also known as the Battle of Sharpsburg). The Union Army forced the Confederates back into Virginia.

On Sept. 22, 1862, President Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation. Lincoln warned the Southern states that most southern slaves would be forever free if the "rebellious states" did not rejoin the Union by January. Lincoln also announced that former slaves were free to join the Union Army.

There were mixed reactions to Lincoln's announcement. Some people thought the war was being fought only to free the slaves and not necessarily to bring the nation back together. Others felt the Emancipation Proclamation was the best thing that could have happened to bring the country together again.

After Lincoln signed the Proclamation into law on Jan. 1, 1863, many slaves ﬂed north to join Union forces. The Emancipation Proclamation helped to free many slaves, caused Southern plantation owners to lose workers and helped increase the number of soldiers ﬁghting for the Union cause.

title: 1860: The Election of Abraham Lincoln
text:
In 1860, the United States was set to elect a new president. Northerners and Southerners both felt uneasy about how the election might affect the nation. Jackson and Alana got the chance to interview Abraham Lincoln about this historic election. ...

"Mr. Lincoln, my name is Jackson. Could you tell us about your views on slavery?"

"I'm against slavery, Jackson. When I ran for president, I promised that I would leave slavery alone in the South, but I would not let it spread into new territories. Most Southerners didn't vote for me because of this."

"Mr. Lincoln, I'm Alana. Can you tell us what happened to the Democratic Party right before the election?"

"Absolutely! The party split into two separate groups. One group nominated (named as a candidate) the vice president of the United States, John C. Breckinridge, to be the next president. The other Democratic group chose Senator Stephen Douglas of Illinois. You may remember that Douglas had previously run against me in a race for the Illinois Senate. Douglas believed that people in each state had the right to decide for themselves if they wanted to allow slavery. He won that election, but people came to know me as someone who would stand up against slavery."

"So, what happened in the election of 1860?"

"As amazing as it seems, I won. The other two candidates got more votes from the people than I did, but I won the most votes from the Electoral College. This was the last straw for many Southerners, and the end of the country as we knew it was near."

text:
1.Why did many Southern states secede from the Union after Abraham Lincoln was elected president?

2.What was the Emancipation Proclamation? List three results of this proclamation.

3.Where did Gen. Lee surrender to Gen. Grant? How long did the Civil War last?

4.Explain why many people view General Ulysses S. Grant as a kind and compassionate man.

5.Compare the Civil War with wars fought today. How are they different? How are they the same?

title: Summarizing Historical Information
text:
A summary is a short statement that tells all of the main ideas of an event. A historical event summary should tell the important ideas about what happened during a time in history. Small details and facts are not included. When writing a summary, it is sometimes helpful to think about all the big ideas ﬁrst. Write down notes about these ideas. Then write a summary using the main details.

Read the information from this week’s lesson under the heading “First Shots at Fort Sumter.” Use this information to complete the summary chart. Then, use your notes to write a three- to five-sentence summary about this event in American history.

Now use your notes to write a short summary of the information.

title: Ending the Fighting for Good
text:
"Alana, do you think Grandpa Frank and Grandma Minnie would mind if we went up in the attic again today? I can't wait to explore what happened at the end of the Civil War."

"I already asked them about it, Jackson. Grandma Minnie said that as soon as we're finished with our homework, we can head up!"

(Alana and Jackson eat a snack and finish their homework. Then the two friends climb the stairs to the attic, where they find a battered old journal.)

"Hey, Jackson! I think this journal might help us get back to 1865. It looks like it was written by the wife of a Confederate soldier."

"That's great, Alana. Let's give it a try."

(Both children touch the journal at the same time, and they soon find themselves watching the following events unfold.)

Confederate General Robert E. Lee and Union General Ulysses S. Grant met at Appomattox Court House, Virginia, on April 9, 1865, to discuss the end of the war. The Confederate Army was hungry, tired and ready to go home. The Union Army still had food and supplies to continue the fight. Gen. Lee knew the time had come to surrender. Lee told his soldiers, "There is nothing left for me to do but to go and see Gen. Grant, and I would rather die a thousand deaths."

When the two men met, Grant treated Lee with respect. He accepted Lee's surrender, but then he offered the Southern soldiers the following generous terms: Confederate soldiers could return to their families, taking with them any personal weapons and horses they owned. The hungry soldiers were also given food and supplies.

Over 620,000 soldiers had died during the war, and many towns, farms and homes had been destroyed. When President Lincoln heard that the war was over, he stood before a crowd gathered in Washington, D.C. In honor of the South, Lincoln asked the band to play "Dixie," a Confederate battle song. He hoped to heal the nation, bringing the North and South together again.

"Jackson, I had no idea that so many soldiers died during the war - and I have a feeling that not everyone was as compassionate to the South as Gen. Grant and President Lincoln."

"I think you're right, Alana. Let's see for ourselves."

title: Looking for Lost Soldiers
text:
After the Civil War ended, many people waited and hoped for the return of their family members. If soldiers failed to come home, their families tried desperately to find out what had happened to them. Clara Barton was a nurse who earned the nickname "Angel of the Battlefield" for her work in caring for injured soldiers. Clara opened an office to help these families find their missing loved ones. With the help of 12 clerks, Clara Barton did her best to let these families know what had happened to their soldiers.

Between 1865 and 1868, Clara Barton received over 60,000 letters from families searching for missing soldiers. Clara used these names to put together a list of the missing. Lists were displayed throughout the country for all to see. Those who knew where soldiers had been buried, or where missing soldiers were being cared for, also contacted the office to give information to the soldiers' families. Clara Barton was more than just an angel on the battlefield. She was also an angel to those who lost loved ones during the war.

title: Reconstructing a Nation
text:
"After the Civil War ended, people hoped life would get back to normal quickly. It would take a lot more than wishful thinking to make that happen, though."

"You're right, Jackson. Besides healing the wounds of war, people also needed to fix the damage done to homes, farms, buildings and railroads. It wasn't easy!"

"Alana, when the president and Congress presented plans for Reconstruction, many Southerners were angry."

"That's right. They didn't like being told how to run their states. Let's find out how the country healed and came back together after the war."

Andrew Johnson's Plan

After Abraham Lincoln was assassinated in April 1865, Andrew Johnson became president. He worked to carry out President Lincoln's plan for Reconstruction, or the rebuilding and healing of the United States after the Civil War. Before healing could take place, slavery had to end. The 13th Amendment abolished slavery as of Dec. 18, 1865. Southern states could be readmitted to the Union after declaring secession illegal and passing the 13th Amendment. They had to agree to obey all federal (national) laws and to treat the newly freed slaves fairly.

Sounds simple, right? There was a big problem. The South was free to pass laws called Black Codes. These laws said that African Americans were not allowed to vote, serve on a jury, own guns or work at certain jobs. How do you think this affected African Americans?

Radical Reconstruction

Many members of Congress were upset about the way African Americans were being treated in the South. They believed that the South should be punished for its actions during the war. These men were called Radical Republicans. They passed the Reconstruction Acts, which said that Southern states must write new state constitutions giving African American men the right to vote. These acts also said that some former Confederate leaders and officers could not vote or hold political office.

Reaction of the South

Many Southerners were angry about Reconstruction. They didn't like the new state governments that Congress had forced on them. They were also unhappy that they were being forced to pay high taxes to rebuild roads, railroads and schools. Others were upset that the new state governments had abolished the Black Codes. Some Southerners who felt this way joined together to form the Ku Klux Klan. The KKK was an organization that often did terrible things to African Americans, including burning their homes and schools and attacking them for trying to vote.

Results

"Reconstruction certainly wasn't easy. It wasn't nearly as successful as most people had hoped, especially in making life better for former slaves."

"That's right, Alana. By 1870, all of the former Confederate states had been readmitted to the Union. By 1877, the last federal troops left the South. Reconstruction was successful in reuniting the nation and establishing a public school system. Unfortunately, most of the nation's efforts to help African Americans receive equal treatment in the South had failed."

"Yes, Jackson. Southern states found ways to keep African Americans from voting by moving the voting booths, making them pay a poll tax (a fee to vote) or forcing them to take a reading test before voting. Most former slaves had never learned to read, so this test kept them from voting. Some former slaves returned to the plantations where they once served because they had no place else to go. They became sharecroppers, renting the land from their former owners and paying the rent with money from the sale of the crops they raised. Rents were high, and sharecroppers were nearly always in debt."

"It would be many years before African Americans would be treated fairly in the South."

title: Positive Changes
text:
After the Civil War ended, several new constitutional amendments were passed to guarantee that all Americans would be treated fairly. Most of these laws were passed to protect the rights of the newly freed African American slaves. The 13th Amendment was passed in 1865, abolishing slavery throughout the United States. The 14th Amendment, passed in 1868, gave African American men citizenship. It also says that all states must honor and protect their rights as citizens. In 1870, the 15th Amendment was passed. This gave all male citizens age 21 and over, including African Americans, the right to vote. Notice that this amendment did NOT give women the right to vote. This right wasn't granted until 1920, when the 19th Amendment was passed.

One of the most basic rights of a United States citizen is the right to vote. Other constitutional amendments that deal with this right are listed below, along with a summary of each amendment:

12th: required that the Electoral College hold separate elections for president and vice president

17th: stated that the people would be allowed to elect their own senators

19th: gave women the right to vote

23rd: gave the citizens of Washington, D.C., the right to vote in presidential elections

24th: stated that citizens could not be charged a fee to register to vote

26th: lowered the legal voting age to 18 years

title: The Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen and Abandoned Lands
text:
Congress created the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen and Abandoned Lands (Freedmen's Bureau) to help the 4 million freedmen, or former slaves, after the Civil War ended. The Freedmen's Bureau built hospitals in the South, made legal decisions and helped people find work. It also provided food and supplies to those in need. The bureau had hoped to settle many former slaves on land of their own, but very few freedmen actually received land.

Perhaps the most important contribution of the Freedmen's Bureau was in education. The bureau assisted in building thousands of schools, including several colleges. It also trained former slaves to be teachers. Freedmen's schools hired teachers from the North and the South, both white and African American. The Freedmen's Bureau closed in 1872. Even though the bureau didn't accomplish everything it set out to do, it helped many former slaves start a new life.

title: Jim Crow Laws
text: After the Civil War, many states throughout both the North and South passed laws enforcing racial segregation, or the separation of people of different races. These laws were called Jim Crow laws. Jim Crow was a character in traveling minstrel (song and dance) shows that were popular at the time. These laws said that races must be kept separate in places like hotels, restaurants, schools, theaters, parks and trains. African Americans and whites were not allowed to drink from the same drinking fountains, use the same restrooms, be treated in the same hospitals or swim in the same pools. These laws also said that African Americans and whites were not allowed to marry outside their races. Jim Crow laws encouraged fear, hate and mistrust between the races. These unfair laws lasted from the 1870s until the mid 1960s, when the civil rights movement began to get rid of Jim Crow laws for good.

title: Who were 'carpetbaggers' and 'scalawags'?
text:
During Reconstruction, many Northerners went to the South to start new businesses. Some hoped to make money by taking advantage of the problems in the South after the Civil War. These people were called carpetbaggers because they often came to town carrying all their belongings in small suitcases made of carpet.

Southerners who were in favor of Reconstruction and supported the government's plans were called scalawags. Many scalawags also helped the freed slaves. Other scalawags were elected to positions in new state governments. Carpetbaggers and scalawags were accused of trying to profit from the South's hardships. While some did take advantage of the situation in the South, others were hardworking people trying to find new opportunities. Even today you may hear about politicians being called "carpetbaggers" or "scalawags."

title: A Sharecropper’s Contract
text:
Here is an example of a contract between a Southern landowner and a sharecropper. Read the contract. Then, use the space provided to list the advantages and disadvantages for both the landowner and the sharecropper.

Mr. Smith, the landowner, will provide 40 acres of land and a small house for the sharecropper and his family. Mr. Smith will also provide cotton seed, two mules, one plow and the other tools needed to work the farm. These items will be paid for by the sharecropper at the end of the harvest.

Nathan Jones, the sharecropper, agrees to keep the house and farm in good repair, including all fences and irrigation ditches. He agrees to plant 40 acres of cotton and care for this crop to the best of his ability. This includes harvesting it at the appropriate time. The sharecropper, Nathan Jones, also agrees to buy all food, personal items and farm supplies from the company store. If he is unable to buy these items with cash, he will be given a credit account and this account will be paid out of his portion of the crop harvest at the end of the season.

At harvest time, Nathan Jones, the sharecropper, agrees to give 50 percent of the money received after the crop is sold to Mr. Smith, the landowner. Nathan Jones also agrees to pay Mr. Smith, the landowner, the cost of seed, mules and tools given him at the beginning of the season. Nathan Jones, the sharecropper, will also pay his bill at the company store out of his share of the harvest.

This contract is in effect for one year, from January 14, 1877 – January 14, 1878.

title: Definitely Not Child's Play
text:
"Alana, did you know that children our age, and even younger, once worked in factories and mills instead of going to school?"

"Yes, Jackson. I heard that during the late 1800s and early 1900s, children were often forced to work to earn money for their families. It sounds like a hard life to me."

"Me too, Alana. Hey! Do you think we could go up to Grandpa Frank and Grandma Minnie's attic to see if they have any pictures of children from this era? Maybe we could take a trip back in time to see what life was like for young factory workers."

"It's worth a try, Jackson. Let's go!"

(Jackson and Alana find a picture of children working in a textile [cloth] factory during the late 1800s. They each grab a corner of the photo and soon find themselves in a thread-spinning room at a textile factory.)

"Wow, Jackson, it's noisy in here!"

"I'll say. And look at all those crazy machines. Everything is moving so fast. I wonder how the workers keep from getting their hands and clothes tangled in the machines. Look at all the children working. What are those young girls doing?"

"It looks to me like the girls are keeping the spinning machines running by feeding in yarn and fixing broken threads."

"Look at the boys, Alana. They're taking all the full bobbins (spools of thread) off the machines and replacing them with empty ones for workers to fill up. The littlest boys seem to be sweeping up the floor to keep the factory clean."

"These jobs look dangerous and tiring, Jackson. Did you see the sign that says all children had to work at least 12 hours per day? I can't imagine that."

"And I thought the school day seemed long! So, how was this unfair treatment finally changed?"

"Many states tried to pass laws against child labor, but none of these laws protected children across the entire nation. Finally, in 1938, Congress passed the Fair Labor Standards Act. This law said that children under 16 could not work during school hours. Also, children had to be at least 14 years old to do certain after-school jobs, and no one under 18 years could work certain dangerous jobs."

"It sounds like the Fair Labor Standards Act would keep all of the children we saw today from doing these tiring and unsafe jobs. I'm glad I didn't live 100 years ago!"

"I agree, Jackson. I would not want to work as hard as those children did."

title: A Day in the Life of a Child Factory Worker
text:
Rebecca is a 10-year-old girl living in Greensboro, NC, in 1900. Every morning, she gets up at 5:00 a.m., washes her face and eats a quick breakfast of cold biscuits and milk. Then she and her family hurry to the cotton mill where they all have jobs. They must be there to begin their shift at 6:00 a.m.

As a spinner in the factory, Rebecca walks along the rows of machines. While she walks she looks for broken threads and brushes away lint. She must keep track of as many as eight rows of spindles at one time. Her job is to make sure that each machine runs smoothly. The spinning bobbins make her dizzy, and she must be careful not to get her fingers, dress or hair caught in the machinery.

Rebecca is allowed to take a short break at lunchtime, but she cannot leave the factory. After lunch, she goes back to work until her shift is over at 6:00 p.m. She drags her tired body home to a late dinner of boiled potatoes, bread and cheese. She helps her mother with the dishes and cleaning before falling into bed at 10:00 p.m. Rebecca has no time for games, friends or school. For her work in the factory, she earns 40 cents per day. Each day seems exactly like the last since she and her family work six days a week, with no time off or holidays. The entire family must work to keep food on the table.

title: The Industrial Revolution
text:
By the mid-1800s, the Industrial Revolution was in full swing here in the United States. Thousands of people rushed to the big cities to find jobs in plants and factories.

A Revolution

The Industrial Revolution changed the way people made their livings. They went from producing goods by hand at home to making them with machines in factories. The invention of machines made it faster and easier than ever to produce goods of all kinds.

The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain. There, factories were built to produce cloth. Samuel Slater, a skilled British textile worker, brought his knowledge to the United States. Textiles are fabrics made by spinning threads and weaving them together. Built in the 1790s, Slater's cotton-spinning mills in Pawtucket, RI, were some of the first in America. This was the beginning of the Industrial Revolution in the United States. American society changed from an agrarian, or farming, society to an industrial, or machine-run, society.

From Homemade to Mass-Produced

Before the Industrial Revolution, people didn't just run to the store if they needed something. Instead, they had to find ways to make most of the things they needed at home. If they couldn't make it themselves, they depended on someone in the community to make it for them. If someone in the family needed new clothing, the mom usually made a trip to the general store. There, she would choose material from bolts (rolls) of fabric. Then, she took the fabric home and made the clothing herself. If she wasn't a great seamstress, or if the family happened to have a bit more money, she would choose fabric and have a nearby seamstress or tailor do the job. After the invention of the sewing machine in 1846, factories soon produced clothing cheaply and faster than it could be made at home. Families began buying their clothing in stores or through mail-order catalogs. This saved time, gave them more styles to choose from and often saved money as well.

Clothing wasn't the only item that went from being homemade to factory-produced during the Industrial Revolution. Tools, farm equipment, furniture, vehicles and just about everything else went from being made individually by skilled craftspeople to being mass-produced in factories by unskilled workers. Specialized farm machinery made it possible for farmers to plant and harvest more crops with far fewer workers than ever before. The number of people working on farms continued to drop as the years went by. Farmers, seamstresses, tailors, blacksmiths, furniture makers and craftspeople of all kinds found themselves unable to make a living the same way they had in the past.

Cities of Promise

Where were most of the jobs? You could find most of them in big cities. It was there that large factories produced ready-made goods at low prices. The Industrial Revolution changed American society forever. Immigrants from around the world came to America in search of work. From the 1870s to 1900, most immigrants arriving to the U.S. came from England, Ireland and Germany. Farmers and ranchers across the country also moved to larger cities for work. Many found jobs, but the work was hard, the wages were low and the living conditions were poor.

For many who believed that life in America's big cities would be a dream come true, their troubles were just beginning.

text:

title: Workers, Unite!
text:
Samuel Gompers was a Jewish immigrant who moved with his family from London to New York City as a teenager. He worked as a cigar maker alongside his father. Gompers was unhappy with the low wages and long working hours that workers faced. To help with these problems, he helped organize a labor union. A labor union is a group of workers who join together to fight for better working conditions and higher wages.

Later, Gompers decided that the best way to get the attention of factory owners was to join several small unions together. He led the effort to organize the American Federation of Labor (AFL) and became its first president in 1886. The union united skilled workers from many trades. Together they fought for better wages, an eight-hour workday, safer working conditions and the end of child labor. Samuel Gompers was a smart, patient leader who worked to improve conditions for the American worker.

title: Can You Hear Me Now?
text:
Hello. My name is Alexander Graham Bell, and I invented something you wouldn't want to live without - the telephone!

Other scientists and inventors had worked toward this invention. But I was convinced that I could win the race to make a machine that allowed people to talk to each other across wires. I hired Thomas Watson to help me, and on March 10, 1876, we finally had success. I sent Watson to a separate room with the door closed. Then I said into the phone, "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you." He heard me!

The telephone changed the way people communicated forever, just as I hoped it would. By the time I died in 1922, there were over 13 million telephones in the United States and Canada. To honor me, all telephones were silent for one minute at the start of my funeral. What do you think would surprise me about the telephones of today?

title: What did people do for fun during the Industrial Revolution?
text:
You know that people worked hard during the Industrial Revolution, but what did they do for fun? For one thing, they sometimes visited nickelodeons to see a movie or a show. The first nickelodeon opened in Pittsburgh, PA, in 1905. A nickelodeon was a small theater that charged a nickel for a customer to see a live show or a short film. The word "nickelodeon" comes from the price of the show, a nickel, and the Greek word for theater, odeon.

Other types of entertainment were dance halls, where people went to dance to music played by live bands. During this time period, most large cities also had parks where people could picnic, ride bicycles and enjoy the fresh air. Many of these parks also offered carousels (merry-go-rounds) and vendors selling ice cream, hot dogs and peanuts.
