title: A Tale of Today
text:
"Alana, I'm bored. How about another trip up to Grandpa Frank and Grandma Minnie's attic?"

"I'm sure they won't mind if we do a little more exploring, Jackson. Let's head upstairs."

(Jackson and Alana visit the attic and look around.)

"Hey, Jackson, let's see if we can find anything that might take us back to the time just after the Industrial Revolution."

"Sure thing, Alana, but I'm not sure exactly what to look for. I don't see a mechanical reaper or a cotton gin around here."

"Hmmm, what about a book or picture from that time period? It should be from around 1870, I think."

"Hey, Alana, what about this book? It looks pretty old."

"'The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today,' by Mark Twain: I've heard of him! He wrote 'The Adventures of Tom Sawyer' and 'The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn.' It looks like this book was published in 1873 - perfect! Let's see if we can visit Mark Twain. Maybe he can tell us more about the Gilded Age and how this time period got its name."

"Great idea, Alana. One, two, three ... let's go!"

(Jackson and Alana each grab the book and are transported back to the late 1800s, where they find themselves joining the famous author Mark Twain on his porch.)

"Mr. Twain? I'm Alana and this is my friend, Jackson. We've come a long way to ask you about your book, 'The Gilded Age.'"

"So, you've read my book, have you? What did you think of it, my young friends?"

"Well, we haven't exactly read it, but we're curious about the title. What exactly is the Gilded Age, anyway?"

"Well, Jackson, the times in which I live are full of wealth and prosperity (success), but not everything is as golden as it seems. There are many factory owners, land developers and oil and steel tycoons (powerful business owners) who make a lot of money and live a life of wealth. But, there are also many poor factory workers and farmers who barely get by. 'Gilded' means covered with a thin layer of gold, and that's what American society is like during this period. Most of society is living with very little money while some make up the thin layer of wealth. Gilding makes it pretty on the outside, but the gold doesn't go all the way through."

"You mean the Gilded Age was great for those who owned businesses and factories, but it was hard for those who worked for them?"

"That's exactly right, Alana. Now you know why I chose that title for my book."

"Thanks for your time, Mr. Twain. We promise to read your book when we get home."

"You do that. Nothing like a book to pour a little knowledge into you!"

title: George Washington Vanderbilt's Home
text:
George Washington Vanderbilt II came from a family of "robber barons" who got rich during the Gilded Age. The Vanderbilts made their fortune in the field of transportation, mainly with steamboats and railroads.

In 1889, Vanderbilt began building his new home, Biltmore, near Asheville, NC. The estate covered 125,000 acres! The house took more than six years to build and had 250 rooms. The house included a swimming pool, bowling alley, several kitchens and an elevator, along with telephones and electric lighting. Vanderbilt refused to say how much the mansion cost to build, but it is estimated that the price was as high as $10 million. That's quite a high price, considering that more than half of all Americans made less than $500 per year in 1890!

title: The Gilded Age
text:
The period in history from about 1877 to 1893 was called the Gilded Age because of the fancy lifestyles of those who got rich for the first time. The wealthy were few in number, but they liked to show off their money with nice clothes, expensive jewelry and parties. "Gilded" means covered with a thin layer of gold, and that's what American society was like during this period. Most of society was living in poverty while some became wealthy. These wealthy people made up the thin layer of wealth on top. Life was good for the wealthy, but for those who worked in factories, mines and mills, it was very hard.

The rich were actually few in number during this time period, but they were very good at spending their money and showing off their wealth. Of the 12 million families living in the United States during the Gilded Age, only 1 million were considered wealthy. This means that most people were actually poor.

1. John D. Rockefeller 2. John C. Osgood 3. Andrew Carnegie 4. Woodrow Wilson 5. Theodore Roosevelt

Barons or Business Leaders?

Where did the wealthy earn their money? Many of them earned it by using natural resources, as well as poor workers. Some people called the leaders of industry during the Gilded Age "robber barons" because of the way they made their money. They felt that these people robbed from the land and the poor to become barons, or powerful business leaders.

Andrew Carnegie, John C. Osgood and John D. Rockefeller are sometimes called robber barons. Andrew Carnegie used iron ore to create the largest steel company in the world. John C. Osgood bought acres of land in Colorado where he mined coal and created the Colorado Fuel and Iron Company. John D. Rockefeller founded Standard Oil Company by buying up oil reserves and forcing other oil companies out of business. He used this natural resource to become the richest man in the world. He once said, "Do you know the only thing that gives me pleasure? It's to see my dividends [profits] coming in."

Fortunately, these men did many good things for the country as well. Their companies created jobs and produced useful products. They also gave millions of dollars to help the poor and built libraries, universities, hospitals and museums. Some people like to call them "captains of industry" rather than robber barons. This was because of the jobs they created and the contributions they made to the world of business and industry. What would you consider these men to be: robber barons or captains of industry?

The Progressive Movement

The Progressive Movement was an effort to reform (improve) the problems that had come about after the Industrial Revolution. Progressives, as they were called, joined together to help the poor in many ways. They influenced government welfare services, the building of affordable, safe housing and the passing of laws. This was to keep business owners from taking advantage of their workers and the environment. Progressives also worked to keep large companies from becoming too powerful. They wanted to make taxes more affordable for the poor, give the common people more power to vote on laws and hold the rich accountable for their actions. Presidents Woodrow Wilson and Theodore Roosevelt were both considered Progressives. Eventually, the government passed laws that improved some of these situations. By the 1920s, women could vote, and businesses had to follow certain rules.

Comprehension Check

Highlight one main idea of this article in yellow. Highlight at least three supporting details in pink.

title: Labor Union Timeline
text:
The Gilded Age was a time of conflict between workers and employers. Look at the timeline to see how labor unions developed during the Gilded Age.

1869: Knights of Labor (KOL) Formed

This union was formed to unite skilled and unskilled workers alike. The KOL wanted an eight-hour workday, the end of child labor and equal pay for equal work.

1877: The Great Railroad Strike

Railroad workers in West Virginia went on strike to protest wage cuts and poor working conditions. The strike spread to other states. It ended 45 days later, with over 100 men dead. Workers did not gain much from the strike. The railroad companies were determined never to let the workers unite against them again.

1886: The Haymarket Square Riot

When labor union members and supporters joined together for a rally in Chicago's Haymarket Square, police officers arrived to break it up. A pipe bomb killed eight officers. Four men were convicted in connection with the bombing and executed. Many people turned against labor unions because of this event.

1886: The American Federation of Labor Formed

Samuel Gompers organized the American Federation of Labor to work for better wages, an eight-hour workday, safer working conditions and the end of child labor.

1892: The Homestead Strike

When the manager of Andrew Carnegie's Homestead steel plant cut wages, union workers fought back by striking. Violence erupted and several people died. Eventually, the strike ended in failure for the union workers.

1894: The Pullman Strike

Workers went on strike to protest low wages and layoffs. The strike shut down railroad traffic throughout the Midwest. Unions gained some popularity after the Pullman Strike, although Pullman workers did not gain much from it.

1905: Industrial Workers of the World Founded

This union was called "One Big Union" and was formed with the idea that all workers should be united in one group.

1913: First Secretary of Labor, William Bauchop Wilson, appointed by President Woodrow Wilson

This position was created to protect American workers. The Department of Labor makes sure workers have reasonable wages, fair taxes, safe working conditions and retirement benefits.

title: The First Labor Day
text: Historians are not certain who actually came up with the idea for Labor Day. Some believe that Peter McGuire (below) founded it. He was the first secretary of the American Federation of Labor. Others say the idea belonged to Matthew Maguire. He was the secretary of the Central Labor Union. New York's Central Labor Union chose to make the idea a reality by organizing the first Labor Day on Sept. 5, 1882, in New York City. The holiday was created to honor American workers who used their strength and skills to make life better for the entire country. The first Labor Day was celebrated with a parade, speeches and a picnic for workers and their families. In 1894, Labor Day became an annual national holiday. People now celebrate it on the first Monday in September. What do you do on Labor Day?

title: World's First Skyscraper
text:
Did you know that the world's first skyscraper was built in Chicago in 1884? When you think of skyscrapers, you probably imagine today's giant buildings that climb as high as 163 floors (2,722 feet) in the air. This building was only 10 stories high and measured 138 feet from bottom to top. That may not seem like much compared to today's skyscrapers, but in 1884, it was an amazing accomplishment!

The Home Insurance Building was the first skyscraper to use a steel frame skeleton to support not only the walls, but also the weight of the whole building, inside and out. William LeBaron Jenney designed the building, and its success led to the construction of many future skyscrapers. New York City's Empire State Building and One World Trade Center are some of today's examples.

title: All That Glitters ... is Gilded!
text:
"Jackson, did you know that Mark Twain got the idea for the title of his book from one of Shakespeare's plays? In the play, the character Salisbury says, 'To gild refined gold, to paint the lily ... is wasteful and ridiculous excess.' I think it means that flowers are already beautiful, so they don't need a coating of gold."

"That makes sense, Alana. Many of the rich people who lived during the Gilded Age loved to show off their wealth by building mansions, wearing furs and jewelry and taking vacations to exotic (unusual) places. This quote points out that spending so much money to 'gild the lily' is wasteful and silly."

"I wonder why so many factory owners and business leaders chose to live such extravagant (fancy) lifestyles, Jackson?"

"Maybe it was because most people had been poor for such a long time. When they had money, they wanted to show off."

"That's probably true, but what about all the poor people who worked in factories and mills? They struggled to make ends meet."

"I guess the rich people were so busy 'gilding the lily' that they didn't think much about the poor. There are a lot of people today who still like to gild the lily, when they can."

"That's true, Jackson. If you and I ever get rich, I hope we'll be content to buy what we need to enjoy life, but still share some of our wealth with those who really need it."

"Hey, if I ever get rich, you can count on it!"

title: Think and Review
text:
1. What does "gilded" mean? Explain why this time period is often called the Gilded Age.

2. Compare and contrast the terms "robber barons" and "captains of industry." Why do you think that wealthy business leaders of the Gilded Age could go by either nickname?

3. Analyze why so many labor unions were formed during the Gilded Age. What was their purpose? What method did they use to try to improve conditions for their workers?

4. What was the Progressive Movement? What did Progressives hope to accomplish?

title: Political Cartoons
text:
This picture is a political cartoon, or a comic with a message. The cartoon is called “Monopoly Millionaires Dividing the Country,” and it appeared in “Puck” magazine in 1885. The picture shows the powerful railroad owners and investors William Henry Vanderbilt, Jay Gould, Cyrus West Field and Russell Sage. After looking at the cartoon, answer the following questions.

1. What do you think these men are doing?

2. How are the knives being used?

3. Why is one of the men rolling dice?

4. How do you think the cartoonist felt about these “robber barons?” Why?

Now on a separate sheet of paper, draw your own political cartoon using information from this week’s magazine. You may look back at the lesson if you need help. Make your drawing colorful by using colored pencils or crayons. Be creative and have fun!

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you are a factory worker during the Gilded Age. Would you have voted in favor of going on strike to try to improve your working conditions? What are the possible benefits and risks of striking? Write a paragraph or two explaining your reasons for or against going on strike. Be sure to use correct spelling, grammar and punctuation.

title: Coming to America
text:
"Hey, Jackson, I have a question for you. What would you do if you were poor, your parents couldn't find a job, there was a shortage of food in your country or the government was unfair?"

"Hmmm, that's a good question, Alana. I'd probably leave my home and find another place to live. I'm guessing that we're studying immigration (moving to another country) this week. Am I right?"

"You're pretty smart, Jackson. Did you know that between 1892 and 1954, about 12 million people immigrated to the United States through Ellis Island, near New York City?"

"That's a lot of people, Alana! I think we should see if we can learn more by visiting the attic!"

(The two friends climb the stairs to the attic.)

"Now, what are we looking for this time? A picture? A book? A journal? Hey, what about this coin? It has the year '1892' stamped on it!"

"That's the right time period, Jackson. Let's give it a try!"

(Alana and Jackson touch the coin and are immediately transported to the docks of Ellis Island in New York Harbor.)

"Wow, Alana, look at all these people! A ship must have just arrived. I wonder where it's from."

"Look at that girl with the bright red hair. It looks like she's taking care of her younger brothers. I wonder where their parents are."

"Let's watch and see what's happening."

It is Jan. 1, 1892. Annie Moore and her two younger brothers have just arrived in New York Harbor. They traveled from Ireland on the S.S. Nevada for 12 days. They came to New York to join their parents and older siblings, who had been in America for nearly four years. They came here searching for religious freedom and better jobs.

Crossing the ocean was not fun. Bad food, crowded living conditions and plenty of seasickness made the journey miserable! Annie and her brothers were thrilled to have finally made it to New York. When Annie stepped into the immigration office on Ellis Island, an official handed her a $10 gold piece. She was confused and couldn't imagine why he had given her the money. The coin would be worth about $200 today! The official explained to her that she was the first immigrant to be welcomed to the country through Ellis Island's processing center. The coin was a gift. What a great way to be welcomed to her new home!

"Alana, do you think this is the same coin that Annie Moore had?"

"I don't know, Jackson. Let's go ask Grandma Minnie and Grandpa Frank if they know where this coin came from!"

title: Using Technology for Genealogy
text:
Have you ever wondered about your ancestors? Where did they come from? What brought them to the United States? What were they like? Genealogy, or the study of family history, has become very popular in recent years. Technology has made it much easier to learn more about your family's background!

Genealogy research used to be very difficult. It involved visiting cemeteries, thumbing through dusty record books and trying to read the tiny print in old newspapers. Today, researching family history is as easy as typing on a keyboard or clicking a mouse.

Genealogy websites allow you to research your family tree from the comfort of your own home. To start, you need to find out a few things about your living relatives. For example, start with your parents and grandparents. Collect their birthdates and places, their parents' names and birthdates, marriage and death dates. Then head to your computer! Ask an adult for permission to use one of the genealogy websites. Learn information about your great-grandparents by reading obituaries, birth, marriage and death records. Your new hobby will lead you to all kinds of interesting information about your relatives!

title: Immigration in the United States (1880s - 1950s)
text:
Between 1880 and 1950, about 29 million immigrants arrived in the United States. Why did they come? How did they survive in this new land? What challenges did they face, and what impact did they have on the United States?

Where Did They Come From, and Why Did They Come?

Until the 1880s, most immigrants came to the United States from Ireland, Great Britain, Germany and Sweden. Most of them came here searching for a better way of life. In their home countries, many of these people were poor, hungry, unemployed and without basic freedoms of speech and religion. For example, over 1 million people left Ireland and came to America in the late 1840s. A horrible disease destroyed the potato crop there, which caused a terrible food shortage in the country.

From 1880 to 1920, most immigrants to the U.S. came from Southern and Eastern European countries, such as Italy, Austria-Hungary and Russia. Many of these people came here searching for freedom. During this time period, many Jewish people in Europe were being persecuted (treated unfairly because of race or religion). They lost the right to worship, hold jobs and even attend school. Others came to America hoping to escape from poverty. They wanted to find good jobs and better homes. America was the "land of opportunity," and they hoped their new country would make them rich. Everyone who immigrated to America hoped to find a better life.

Settling In

Most immigrants during this time period settled in large cities such as New York, Chicago, Boston, Philadelphia and San Francisco. American cities were growing places with factories that offered jobs to the newly arrived immigrants.

Cities were good places for immigrants to find others who had come from their home countries. These people spoke the same language, shared the same culture and helped new arrivals live in a strange, new land. Immigrants from the same country often lived together in certain sections of large cities. These people worked hard to make new lives for themselves in America. Unfortunately, life wasn't as easy as many had hoped. Jobs were sometimes hard to find, and cities were crowded and dirty.

Because of the difficulties they faced, Italian immigrants came up with a saying that described the life they found here in America:

I came to America because I heard the streets were paved with gold. When I got here, I found out three things: first, the streets weren't paved with gold; second, they weren't paved at all: and third, I was expected to pave them.

Life on the farms of rural America wasn't always better. Many immigrants from Northern Europe moved west from the big cities. They found land, but they also struggled. One Swedish farmer reported:

None who are not accustomed to hard, agricultural labor ought to become farmers in this country. No one who is any other way well off in his native land ought to come hither.

What can you learn about the immigrants' lives by reading these quotes?

In addition, people already living in the U.S treated some immigrant groups poorly. Some anti-immigrant feelings eventually became laws. The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 limited the number of Chinese workers allowed to come to the United States. Would you still want to move to the U.S.?

Immigrants' Impact on the United States

What impact did these immigrants have on the United States? They filled jobs in factories and helped the American economy grow by leaps and bounds. They also brought their unique languages, foods and music, contributing to the mix of different cultures that we know as the United States of America.

title: Ellis Island - Welcome to America
text:
Ellis Island is a small, 27-acre island in New York Harbor named after Samuel Ellis. It was once an oyster-hunting site for American Indians and a picnic spot for early Dutch settlers. Eventually, the U.S. government bought the island to use as an arsenal, or place to store weapons. The United States formed the Office of Immigration in 1891. Leaders chose Ellis Island for the location for the national immigration station.

Ellis Island opened in 1892 as the main port of entry for immigrants coming to the United States. Ellis Island operated for more than 60 years and processed an average of 4,000 to 5,000 immigrants per day. Its busiest day on record was April 17, 1907, when 11,747 people entered the United States!

Entering the United States through Ellis Island consisted of three basic steps. First, immigrants had to take their belongings to a baggage room. Then, they walked up a long flight of stairs to the second floor. There, they would each receive a medical examination. Those who had trouble making it up the stairs were given more careful medical exams than those who climbed the stairs easily. The simple medical examination lasted about six seconds. The exam was meant to check for any serious illnesses, which would keep the immigrants from entering the country. The last step was to answer a few questions. These questions included the immigrants' names, occupations, how much money they had, where they were planning to go and who would meet them there. If the immigrants passed through these steps successfully, they were allowed to enter the country. The whole process usually took three to five hours.

Immigration began slowing down after the 1920s, and the station at Ellis Island closed in 1954. In 1965, Ellis Island was made a part of the Statue of Liberty National Monument. If you'd like to get an idea of what immigrants experienced, plan to visit these amazing places.

title: Lillian Wald - Heroine of Children's Health
text:
When Lillian Wald was young, she watched a nurse care for her older sister. Lillian decided that this was the career she wanted. After attending nursing school, she worked in the poor neighborhoods of New York City. Seeing the needs of the immigrant families drove Lillian to start the Henry Street Settlement in 1893. This organization provided health care to immigrants who had few resources. Soon, the settlement began offering English classes and other recreational activities. Lillian knew that children needed a place to play, so she raised money to build parks.

Lillian went on to develop a nursing program for public schools. This program allowed poor children to get free health care. Lillian Wald spent her life working so that people could live better, healthier lives.

title: The Work Was Hard and the Pay Was Low
text:
Hi! This is Jackson. Did you know that most immigrants who came to the United States in the early 1900s found work in factories? They had few job skills and often didn't speak English. Most of the time, these were the best jobs they could find.

Most men worked 10-12 hours a day, six days a week. Long hours and unsafe conditions caused industrial accidents that killed thousands of workers each year. Workers brought home between $400 and $500 per year, but most families spent more than that just to live!

Look at this picture of factory workers. How old do you think some of these people are? Teenagers and young children often had to work to help support their families. How would you feel if you had to work long hours in a dirty, dangerous factory and then come home to a crowded apartment? For many immigrants, this was life.

title: Public Schools to the Rescue!
text:
This is Alana, speaking to you from a 1900s schoolroom in New York City. During the late 1800s and early 1900s, American schools were filled with immigrant children trying to adjust to a new and unfamiliar home. Many could not speak English, and they weren't used to the American culture or way of life. School became a place where children could learn to read and write a new language, as well as learn a new culture.

John Dewey, a famous psychologist and educator, believed that education should focus on the needs of the students and not just on memorizing facts. He believed in teaching students through creativity and hands-on experiences. He hoped that schools could help solve society's problems. Dewey's ideas helped some schools reach out to immigrant children in a loving, kind way.

title: Think and Review
text:
1. Before 1880, most immigrants to the United States came from which European countries? Why did they come here?

2. Between 1880 and 1920, most immigrants to the United States came from which countries? Why did they come here?

3. How did John Dewey's ideas help immigrant children?

4. List the three steps that all immigrants had to complete at Ellis Island when entering the U.S. Why do you think they needed to complete these steps?

5. What challenges did immigrants face?

title: Sadie Frowne: Her Own Story
text:
The following is the true story of Sadie Frowne. She was an immigrant girl who came to New York City during the early 1900s. She and her mother came to America from Poland after her father died. Read her story, in her own words, and answer the questions that follow.

We came by steerage on a steamship in a very dark place that smelt dreadfully. There were hundreds of other people packed in with us, men, women and children, and almost all of them were sick. It took us twelve days to cross the sea, and we thought we should die, but at last the voyage was over, and we came up and saw the beautiful bay and the big woman with the spikes on her head and the lamp that is lighted at night in her hand.

Aunt Fanny and her husband met us at the gate of this country and were very good to us, and soon I had a place to live out [Sadie is referring to becoming a live-in domestic servant] while my mother got work in a factory making white goods. I was only a little over thirteen years of age and a greenhorn, so I received $9 a month and board and lodging, which I thought was doing well. Mother, who, as I have said, was very clever, made $9 a week on white goods, which means all sorts of underclothing, and is high class work.

But mother … liked to go around and see everything, and friends took her about New York at night and she caught a bad cold and coughed and coughed. She really had hasty consumption [tuberculosis], but she didn’t know it, and I didn’t know it, and she tried to keep on working, but it was no use. She had not the strength. Two doctors attended her, but they could do nothing, and at last she died and I was left alone. I had saved money while out at service, but mother’s sickness and funeral swept it all away and now I had to begin all over again.

1. Who is the “woman with the spikes on her head” that Sadie mentions in the first paragraph?

2. A live-in domestic servant is a maid, or house servant. Why do you think Sadie took this job away from home instead of staying with her mother?

3. What do you think a “greenhorn” is? (Use a dictionary to check your definition.)

4. Use a dictionary or the Internet (with adult permission) to learn more about tuberculosis. Do you think Sadie’s mother caught the disease from walking around New York City at night? Why or why not?

5. How might it feel to be 13 and on your own? What do you think you might do if you were in Sadie’s place?

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you have just immigrated to the United States from Europe with your family. What will you do now that you find yourself in big, bustling New York City? Write a paragraph explaining your feelings about being in America and what you plan to do now that you’re here.

title: Sodbustin' Settlers
text:
Jackson and Alana pay another visit to Grandpa Frank and Grandma Minnie's attic. ...

"Jackson, look at all this pioneer gear up here. Why do you think the pioneers chose to move west?"

"Well, Alana, there were a lot of reasons people moved west. Fresh air and wide-open spaces were at the top of the list. The offer of free land was nice too."

"Free land? How did that work?"

"In 1862, Congress passed the Homestead Act. This act offered free land to people who were willing to settle the wild frontier. Any man over age 21 could claim 160 acres of land in the West. This also included any head of household and widowed women. For about $10, they could stake a claim to a piece of land if they agreed to live on it for five years and farm the land."

"Oh, you're talking about the homesteaders!"

"That's right, Alana. Hey, look what I found! It looks like the deed to a homestead in Nebraska, and it's dated 1869. Why don't we make a visit and see what it was like?"

"Sounds good to me, Jackson. Let's go!"

(Jackson and Alana touch the document and are transported back in time!)

"Look at that house, Jackson! It looks like it's made of ... dirt?"

"That's right, Alana. It's called a sod house, and it's made from something the early homesteaders had plenty of - sod. Sod is a thick layer of grass, roots and dirt. To clear the land for farming, homesteaders had to dig out the thick, tangled masses of prairie grass. The grass had roots that seemed to go on forever. That's why homesteaders were often called 'sodbusters'! Sod houses were cool in the summer, warm in the winter and safe from prairie fires. They did have a few drawbacks, however."

"Like what, exactly?"

"Well, the sod walls and ceilings were great places for bugs, mice and even snakes. These friendly little critters often came right into the house."

"No thanks, Jackson. I don't think I'd like living in a sod house!"

"Well, if you could stick it out for five years, you could pay another small fee and that land was yours, free and clear. When a farm became more successful, most homesteaders built nicer homes of wood or other materials. Either way, the land was yours to do with what you wanted."

"The life of a homesteader sounds hard, but rewarding. This week, we're exploring the westward expansion of the United States, along with the reasons the settlers moved west and the hardships they faced."

"Let's get started, Alana!"

title: Where the 'Buffalo' Roam?
text:
Actually, buffalo roam in Africa and Asia, not in America. Settlers mistakenly called the American bison "buffalo," and the name stuck, even though it's wrong. Great herds of American bison were once a common sight throughout the Midwest and West. In the mid-1800s, an estimated 30 to 75 million bison roamed the prairies. By 1884, the estimate of free-roaming bison in the entire United States was 325! What caused these great beasts to become nearly extinct? The settling of the West, that's what!

From 1872 to 1874, hunters using horses and guns killed an average of 5,000 bison per day. They sold the hides and meat for money. Others killed only for the thrill of the hunt, leaving the carcasses behind to rot. American Indians relied on bison for everything from food, to clothing and tools. This hunting left them without an important natural resource. Life as they knew it was gone forever.

When government officials realized what was happening to the bison, they passed laws to protect them. In 1894, Congress passed a law making it illegal to hunt bison in Yellowstone National Park. Later, officials passed laws to protect other species of plants and animals as well. The Endangered Species Act was passed in 1973, to protect endangered species and keep them from becoming extinct. The act helps endangered species to recover and grow strong.

title: Westward Expansion
text:
"Hey, Alana, are you ready to learn more about westward expansion?"

"Sure, I'm ready, Jackson, but what exactly do you mean by 'westward expansion'?"

"'Westward expansion' describes the way Americans spread out across the western half of this country once the U.S. began taking control of the area. We will look back at some events that shaped the West."

"Yes, Jackson, sometimes we have to look back to understand what happened next!"

Louisiana Purchase

In 1803, U.S. President Thomas Jefferson approved the purchase of 828,000 square miles of land from the French for $15 million. The Louisiana Purchase doubled the size of the U.S. and extended our western border all the way to the Rocky Mountains.

Expedition of Lewis and Clark

In May 1804, explorers Meriwether Lewis and William Clark set out on their historic journey to explore the Louisiana Purchase. President Jefferson had three specific goals for the Corps of Discovery, as this group of explorers was called.

Search for a water route to the Pacific Ocean.

Start building relationships with some American Indians in the area.

Record their findings about the soil, plants and animals in the area.

The expedition lasted 28 months and covered nearly 8,000 miles, from St. Louis to the Oregon coast and back. Lewis and Clark didn't find a water route to the Pacific Ocean, but they did accomplish the other goals. Finally, the Corps of Discovery succeeded in mapping a huge amount of land, making life much easier for those who traveled after them.

Indian Removal Act

During the 1820s and 1830s, many settlers moved to land that was home to the Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Chickasaw, Choctaw and Seminole tribes. In 1830, Congress passed the Indian Removal Act. This gave President Andrew Jackson the power to move American Indians to land west of the Mississippi River, now part of the state of Oklahoma.

California Gold Rush

In 1848, James Marshall discovered gold near California's American River. Word spread quickly, and more than 80,000 people came to California in 1849 alone. The work was hard, prices for supplies were high and very few actually struck it rich. But because of the Gold Rush, the population of California grew quickly.

The Homestead Act of 1862

In 1862, Congress passed the Homestead Act. This gave any head of a household, widowed women or any man over 21 the right to claim one 160-acre portion of land. The homesteader had five years to build a house, live in it and farm the land. Under this act, 270 million acres were claimed and settled.

The Transcontinental Railroad

Traveling west by wagon, stagecoach or horseback was difficult. In 1862, President Abraham Lincoln signed the Pacific Railway Act. Two companies began building a transcontinental (across the continent) railroad, linking the East with the West. Chinese immigrant workers were hired to do dangerous work on the railroad, including blasting through mountains and building steep bridges. The westbound track and the eastbound track finally joined at Promontory Summit, UT, on May 10, 1869. People could now travel from one coast to the other in under 10 days!

"Wow, Jackson, it certainly took a lot to settle this great country of ours."

"You're right, Alana. The early pioneers were brave, hardworking men, women and children who moved west for many different reasons."

"We can't forget about the American Indians, Jackson! It wasn't easy for them to change their way of life."

"That's true, Alana. By 1890, most American Indians lived on reservations. As the year 1900 approached, many U.S. citizens considered the West to be settled." "Jackson, do you think our friends can help us fill in the missing dates and events on the timeline?"

"Sure they can!"

title: Chief Black Kettle: Powerful Peacemaker
text:
In 1861, Southern Cheyenne Chief Black Kettle moved his people to Sand Creek, CO, as part of a treaty. Even though Black Kettle cooperated with the government, soldiers attacked his camp and killed more than 200 Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho people.

In 1867, Black Kettle moved his people to Indian Territory in Oklahoma as part of another treaty. The tribe never received the food and supplies the government promised them. Some of Black Kettle's warriors raided settlements in the area for the things they needed to survive. Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer led an attack on the tribe at Washita River. Black Kettle and his wife were both killed. The man who tried to help the settlers and American Indians live together in peace lost his life in a violent battle. Chief Black Kettle is still remembered as a man who only wanted peace.

title: The Pony Express
text:
Sometimes stories about historic events get exaggerated or even made up. Read this story and do some research to decide whether you think Charlie Miller's tale is true.

Howdy, students! I'm "Bronco" Charlie Miller. People have told many stories about the Pony Express, the mail service that ran from April 1860 to October 1861. Not everyone believes that I was the youngest rider ever to join the Pony Express. Let me tell you, it was a wild ride!

When I was only 11 years old, I saw a Pony Express poster that said: "Wanted: young, skinny, wiry fellows, not over 18. Must be expert riders, willing to risk death daily. Orphans preferred. Wages: $25 per week." It was just the job for me!

We Pony Express riders rode between 75 and 100 miles from station to station along the 1,800-mile route from St. Joseph, MO, to Sacramento, CA. We got the mail delivered in only 10 days! (That's a lot faster than the near 25 days it would take to deliver mail by stagecoach.) Besides sore backsides, we also dealt with numbing snowstorms, brain-frying heat and drenching rains. Oh, and how could I forget sometimes being attacked by American Indians or outlaws? I'd do it all again, though, if I had half a chance!

title: The Wonders of the West
text:
Grand Canyon

Located in Arizona, the Grand Canyon is 277 miles long, 18 miles wide and one mile deep. It was carved by the Colorado River and is considered one of the Seven Natural Wonders of the World.

Salton Sea

Created when the Colorado River flooded in 1905, the Salton Sea is actually a shallow, 376-square-mile lake in southeastern California. It is more salty than the Pacific Ocean, but less salty than the Great Salt Lake.

Great Salt Lake

Utah's Great Salt Lake measures about 1,700 square miles, and it holds almost 5 billion tons of salt! It is too salty for fish, but brine shrimp do well there.

Mojave Desert

The Mojave Desert covers about 50,000 square miles throughout Southern California, Nevada, Arizona and Utah. It usually receives less than six inches of rain per year and is home to Death Valley, the hottest spot in America. Summer temperatures can reach 120 degrees. That's hot!

text:

2.List the three main goals of the Lewis and Clark expedition. Which goals were achieved and which were not?

3.What was the main reason for building the transcontinental railroad? Why do you think Chinese immigrants chose to do dangerous jobs?

4.How did the Pony Express improve communication in America?

5.What important effect did the gold rush have on California?

6.Explain how the Louisiana Purchase influenced many events of the 1800s.

title: Western Trails
text:
Several Western trails are marked on the map. Using the descriptions and color key, label each trail and trace it with the appropriate color. Draw a compass rose. (Present-day state boundaries are on this map.)

Mormon Trail (yellow - This one has been done for you.)

Mormon pioneers followed this route from Illinois to Utah. The trail began in Nauvoo, IL, and extended through Council Bluffs, IA, Ft. Bridger, WY, and on to Salt Lake City, UT.

Lewis and Clark Expedition (blue)

Lewis and Clark left from St. Louis, MO, and traveled westward, across the Rocky Mountains and on to the Pacific Coast, ending up at Fort Clatsop, OR.

Oregon Trail (green)

This trail began at Independence, MO, and wound its way through what is now Kansas, Nebraska, Wyoming, Idaho and Oregon, ending up at Oregon City, OR.

Pony Express Trail (red)

The Pony Express began in St. Joseph, MO, and crossed the Great Plains, the Rocky Mountains and the Sierra Nevada into Sacramento, CA.

Transcontinental Railroad (orange)

The route stretched from Omaha, NE (where the existing railway lines had ended), to Sacramento, CA. The Union Pacific and Central Pacific railroads worked their way across the country toward each other, finally joining up at Promontory Point, UT.

California Trail (brown)

The California Trail traveled along much of the same route as the Oregon Trail. In Idaho, the California Trail split from the Oregon Trail, as settlers headed southwest to find gold.

title: If You Read it in the Paper, it Must be True
text:
"Wow! Where are we, Alana? One minute, we were sitting in the attic looking at an old newspaper, and the next minute we're standing near an old-fashioned newspaper stand."

"Jackson, it looks like we've been transported back to New York City in the late 1800s. Look at the date on this newspaper - 'Feb. 17, 1898.' The front-page article is about the sinking of the USS Maine. This U.S. battleship was docked in the harbor at Havana, Cuba."

"It says here that the Spanish were responsible for sinking the American ship, Alana. Going to war against Spain is America's only option."

"I've read about this, and there was no clear evidence that the Spanish had anything to do with the sinking of the ship. The newspaper owners knew that war stories would sell more papers. William Randolph Hearst owned the New York Journal. This newspaper and its rival paper, the New York World, printed exaggerated stories. They even made up fake stories in order to sell papers. This type of newspaper writing is called 'yellow journalism.' It makes it nearly impossible for readers to get the real facts about any story."

"Why was it called 'yellow journalism,' Alana?"

"Well, Joseph Pulitzer owned the New York World, which published a comic called 'Hogan's Alley.' This comic featured a character called the Yellow Kid. The comic was printed in color, and the Yellow Kid was dressed all in yellow. Because the comic was so popular, William Randolph Hearst hired the cartoonist away from Pulitzer. He then ran the comic in the New York Journal. Soon, Pulitzer hired another cartoonist to copy the Yellow Kid. Both papers began printing 'Hogan's Alley' in bright yellow ink. The type of writing featured in these two papers became known as 'yellow journalism.'"

"Besides stories about war, what other types of stories did these papers print, Alana?"

"They loved printing stories about politicians, crime, scandals and rumors. They always used eye-catching headlines and outrageous quotes. These stories were often based on facts (with plenty of exaggerations), but sometimes they were completely made up."

"Wouldn't it be nice if 'yellow journalism' was gone for good? Unfortunately, there are still plenty of tabloid newspapers around that use wild headlines and made-up stories to sell papers."

"It looks like 'yellow journalism' is here to stay, Jackson. Just be sure to check your sources to see that the newspapers YOU read aren't filled with yellow journalism!"

title: Caveat Lector
text:
Caveat lector is a Latin phrase that means, "Let the reader beware." Beware of what, you may ask? After reading this week's cover story, you probably realize that everything you read in newspapers or magazines isn't always true. Many of these still exaggerate the truth, or they make up stories just to get people to buy their publications.

You may have seen these types of newspapers and magazines near the checkout lanes at grocery stores. People sometimes call them "tabloids." They usually feature colorful, unattractive photos of movie stars, government leaders or other celebrities. They also include outrageous headlines and unbelievable rumors. There may even be "photos" of strange-looking creatures supposedly discovered at the bottom of the ocean, in the Amazon rainforest or on the surface of Mars!

Here are some actual headlines found in several of these types of magazines:

MAN'S 174-MPH SNEEZE BLOWS WIFE'S HAIR OFF!

WORLD'S SMARTEST APE GOES TO COLLEGE!

OCEANS RISING 150 FT.

DANGERS LURKING IN FRUIT AND VEG

If you find yourself reading a newspaper (or Internet story) with these types of headlines, you may want to spend some time checking the facts. Remember that "caveat lector" is always the best advice!

title: The Spanish-American War
text:
The Spanish-American War lasted less than four months. Cuba won its freedom from Spain, and the United States gained control of Puerto Rico, the Philippines and Guam.

Manifest Destiny and Imperialism

After the U.S. made the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, the idea of Manifest Destiny gained strength. Most Americans believed that the U.S. was meant to extend westward across North America from "sea to shining sea." This belief motivated Americans to settle the wild frontier and claim the land for the U.S.

Spain once had a huge empire in North America. By the late 1800s, Spain held on to just two small colonies, Puerto Rico and Cuba. America's influence had spread to Cuba, and many successful American businesses were located there. Americans heard reports of Spain mistreating Cuban citizens, and many believed that it was time to end Spanish Imperialism. (Imperialism is the practice of gaining power by taking over foreign countries and ruling them.) Other Americans wanted to extend American influence into territories in the Pacific Ocean.

The Beginning of War

In 1898, President William McKinley sent the USS Maine, an American battleship, to Havana Harbor. The ship and sailors were there to protect Americans and their businesses. On Feb. 15, 1898, the Maine exploded, killing 260 Americans and destroying the ship. William Randolph Hearst's New York Journal and Joseph Pulitzer's New York World were quick to blame the Spanish and call for war. On April 25, 1898, Congress declared war on Spain. The Spanish-American War had officially begun.

Attack by Sea

The United States believed that the most effective way to win the war was to conquer the Spanish at sea. Navy Captain Alfred Thayer Mahan was brought in to help plan the U.S. naval strategies. His plans worked! Cpt. Mahan believed that a strong Navy was necessary to protect the U.S. He felt that eventually the U.S. would need to control several islands in the Pacific, including the Hawaiian Islands, to make this happen.

The first goal for the U.S. Navy during the Spanish-American War was to destroy the Spanish fleet in the Philippines. Commodore George Dewey led U.S. battleships to the Philippines and defeated the Spanish fleet. They easily captured Manila Bay. Later on, after soldiers captured San Juan and Kettle Hills, American ships near Cuba had no trouble destroying the Spanish fleet during the Battle of Santiago. The American naval effort was a huge success.

Victory on Land

U.S. soldiers also battled for Cuba's freedom on land. Theodore Roosevelt, who had been the assistant secretary of the Navy, gathered a group of volunteer soldiers that became known as the Rough Riders. They were a cavalry unit, which means that they rode horses into battle. This was a loud, tough group of soldiers made up of cowboys, athletes and American Indians. Theodore Roosevelt's leadership of the Rough Riders drew the attention of government leaders, as well as the American public. The people later elected Roosevelt as president of the United States.

On July 1, 1898, the Rough Riders made their famous charge on Cuba's San Juan Heights. Joining the Rough Riders was First Lieutenant John "Black Jack" Pershing. Pershing led a troop of Buffalo Soldiers. This was the nickname for several units of African American soldiers who bravely served the United States. Pershing impressed his leading officers with his skills, and he later led American forces during World War I. In Cuba, the U.S. soldiers charged up Kettle Hill and then nearby San Juan Hill, attacking the Spanish and defeating them in a matter of days.

War Comes to an End

After only four months of fighting, the United States and Spain agreed to a cease-fire in August 1898. By December of that year, the two nations had signed the Treaty of Paris of 1898. The treaty gave Cuba its independence from Spain. It also gave the United States the Spanish territories of Puerto Rico, the Philippines and Guam. The U.S. paid Spain $20 million for the Philippines. The Philippines remained a U.S. Territory until 1946, when it became an independent nation. Puerto Rico and Guam are still territories of the United States.

The United States gained power in the Pacific. This made it possible for the U.S. to build naval bases there and be a strong naval power. Even though Cuba had its independence and was not under U.S. control, the U.S. was friendly with the nation. American businesses continued to grow rich, particularly sugar and tobacco companies.

title: Walter Reed: Heroism
text:
Walter Reed was a famous Army doctor. Instead of fighting enemy soldiers, Dr. Reed fought yellow fever. This disease killed more American soldiers during the Spanish-American War than the enemy did. Yellow fever causes high fever, vomiting and severe pain in the back, arms and legs.

Carlos Finlay was a Cuban doctor who believed that mosquitoes spread yellow fever, not contact with people who had the disease. In 1900, Dr. Reed went to Cuba as head of the Yellow Fever Commission. The goal of the commission was to find out how yellow fever spread so that it could be stopped. Reed and his assistants tested Dr. Finlay's theory that mosquitoes spread yellow fever. Their experiments proved that Dr. Finlay was correct. By controlling the pesky insects, they were able to stop the deadly yellow fever epidemic (outbreak).

title: Coal - Powered Steam Ships
text:
The first steam ships that the Navy used were powered by burning coal. Ships could hold about 2,000 tons of dusty, black coal. Workers had to refill the coal after it burned to keep the ships running. During the Spanish-American War, Navy leaders made many decisions based on the location of coal supplies. Ships had to plan their voyages so that they could stop at coal stations along the way.

Beginning in 1911, the Navy changed from coal-powered ships to oil-powered ships. In 1914, the Navy launched the first two oil-powered ships, the USS Nevada and the USS Oklahoma. Tankers called "oilers" could fuel these ships while sailing in calm seas. During World War I, one oiler refueled 6 naval ships in a single day.

title: Businessmen Seize Power in Hawaiian Islands
text:
On Jan. 17, 1893, a group of businessmen imprisoned Hawaiian Queen Liliuokalani and forced her to step down as ruler so they could take control of the islands. American and European settlers came to Hawaii in the early 1800s and planted sugarcane and pineapples. Settlers made a lot of money growing these crops. Queen Liliuokalani believed that the planters and businessmen were becoming too powerful, and she wanted to stop them from taking control of the island. She felt that native Hawaiians should be in charge of Hawaii.

In 1893, American planters revolted against the queen, and U.S. soldiers came to help the planters. Queen Liliuokalani realized she couldn't win the fight and gave up her power. The businessmen who imprisoned the queen formed a new government and ran the Republic of Hawaii, which existed until 1898. Hawaii was officially annexed (added) to the United States. What arguments do you think the businessmen made for taking over the Hawaiian Islands?

title: The Sinking of the USS Maine: Eyewitness Report vs. Yellow Journalism
text:
When tensions between Spain and Cuba began heating up, publisher William Randolph Hearst sent an artist named Frederic Remington to Cuba to report on the situation. When Remington told Hearst that things were quiet and there would be no war, Hearst reportedly responded, “You furnish the pictures, and I’ll furnish the war.”

Here are two accounts of the sinking of the USS Maine on Feb. 15, 1898. Read both accounts and answer the questions that follow.

Account #1

Telegram from Charles D. Sigsbee, Captain of the USS Maine, February 15, 1898

Maine blown up in Havana Harbor at 9:40 tonight and destroyed. Many wounded and doubtless more killed or drowned. Wounded and others aboard Spanish Man of War Ward Line Streamer. Send Light House Tenders from Key West for crew and the few pieces of equipment above water. No one has clothing other than that upon him. Public opinion should be suspended until further report. All officers believed to be saved. Jenkins and Merritt not yet accounted for. Many Spanish officers including representative of General Blane now with me to express sympathy.

Account #2

The New York Journal, February 17, 1898 NAVAL OFFICERS THINK THE MAINE WAS DESTROYED BY A SPANISH MINE.

George Eugene Bryson, the Journal’s special correspondent at Havana, cables that it is the secret opinion of many Spaniards in the Cuban capital, that the Maine was destroyed and 258 men killed by means of marine mine or fixed torpeda. This is the opinion of several American naval authorities. The Spaniards, it is believed, arranged to have the Maine anchored over one of the harbor mines. Wires connected the mines with a … magazine, and it is thought the explosion was caused by sending an electric current through the wire. If this can be proven, the brutal nature of the Spaniards will be shown by the fact that they waited to spring the mine after all the men had retired for the night.

Compare and contrast the two accounts of the sinking of the USS Maine. Write your answers on the lines below. Use a separate piece of paper if needed.

1. How are the accounts alike?

2. How are they different?

3. Which one is based on fact? Which is an example of “yellow journalism”?

4. Why do you think Cpt. Sigsbee asked that, “Public opinion should be suspended until further report”?

title: Let's Write
text: Read the article about the Hawaiian Islands (Page 3) again. Rewrite the article in “yellow journalism” style with an eye-catching headline and exaggerated details. Remember to use correct spelling, grammar and punctuation.

title: Win the War, Become a World Power
text:
Jackson and Alana are visiting the attic at Alana's grandparents' house. ...

"Jackson, I loved our trip back to the 1890s. The Spanish-American War was short, but it was certainly fascinating!"

"It sure was, Alana. I loved learning more about yellow journalism and the part that newspapers played in the war. It was also interesting to learn that while pushing the Spanish out of Cuba, the United States took the Spanish territories of Guam, the Philippines and Puerto Rico."

"Don't forget that the U.S. annexed Hawaii in 1898."

"If the real purpose of the Spanish-American War was to free Cuba from Spanish rule, why did the U.S. take control of these other Pacific islands?"

"Well, Alana, the U.S. realized that in order to become a world power, it needed to build naval bases on several islands in the Pacific. These would support the growing Navy and help the U.S. stake its claim in the region."

"Jackson, I heard that some people believed the U.S. had a responsibility to help 'civilize' the rest of the world, making it more like America. By taking over these islands in the Pacific, the U.S. could bring jobs, education and a higher standard of living to these countries."

"And what about Panama, Alana? Did you know that the Panama Canal was built during this time period?"

"That's right, Jackson. President Theodore Roosevelt wanted U.S. ships to be able to travel quickly between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. The U.S. supported Panama in gaining independence from Colombia, the South American nation that controlled it at the time. Panama agreed to let us build a canal through the country. The 50-mile-long Panama Canal officially opened in 1914. It shortened the length of the trip from the East Coast to the West Coast of the U.S. by about 8,000 miles."

"I can see how shortening the trip from coast to coast would be great for the military. It would help travelers and businesspeople too!"

"That's true, Jackson. The U.S. was in charge of the Panama Canal from 1914 until 1999, when Panama took control. This arrangement gave the U.S. plenty of economic, political and military power over the area for a very long time."

"I can't wait to learn more about American Imperialism and the territories that played a role in this particular American idea."

"Hang on to your hat, Jackson. Here we go!"

title: The Panama Canal Today
text:
The Panama Canal was completed in 1914, but you can still see the "Big Ditch." Tourists can visit the canal's balconies and view ships passing through its many locks. These gated sections of the canal make it possible to raise and lower the water level to let ships pass through. More adventurous tourists, and those with a bit more money, can also book a cruise that allows them to experience the canal on the water.

If you aren't able to go to Central America, here are a few facts you should know:

The Panama Canal was started in 1904 and completed in 1914.

More than 5,000 workers lost their lives working on the project.

The United States controlled the canal until 1999, when it gave control to Panama.

The Panama Canal was recently widened. This allows larger ships to pass through.

About 14,000 ships pass through the Panama Canal each year. (That's around 40 per day.)

With the expansion, about 600 million tons of cargo is shipped through the canal each year.

Around 5 percent of the world's shipping cargo passes through the Panama Canal.

Hooray for the Panama Canal! It's still one of the greatest transportation achievements in the history of the world.

title: American Imperialism
text:
The period after the Spanish-American War was marked by imperialism. This is the extending of American influence over other nations of the world. The United States took control over many areas in the Caribbean and the Pacific during this period, which pleased some people and upset others.

Pro-Imperialism

Those who believed that the U.S. should take control of areas of the world that would give them a military, political or economic advantage were called imperialists. William McKinley served as president from 1897 to 1901, during the Spanish-American War. He was an imperialist who fought the war with Spain not only to free Cuba from Spanish rule, but to also spread America's influence throughout the Pacific. Commodore George Dewey won an important naval battle against Spain in the Philippines. The U.S. took control of the Philippines and two other territories in the Pacific. Can you name them? (Look in the cover story for help.)

President McKinley worked to gain control of the Hawaiian Islands once he became president. President Cleveland, who served before him, had opposed the idea. Do you remember the Hawaiian Queen Liliuokalani? The queen was forced to give up her power to U.S. businessmen. What year was Hawaii annexed to the United States? (Look on the cover!) Hawaii became a U.S. territory in 1900.

John Hay, President Roosevelt's secretary of state, was another imperialist who introduced the famous "Open Door" policy after the end of the Spanish-American War. The policy stated that there should be an "open door" for nations wanting to trade with China. European nations controlled areas of China and had special trade agreements. The U.S. wanted to trade as well. Hay encouraged equal access to Chinese ports and for taxes to be paid to the Chinese. Most countries did not object to the policy, but it made a small impact on U.S. trade with China.

Panama Canal

When President McKinley was assassinated in 1901, Vice President Theodore Roosevelt became president. Roosevelt was an imperialist and a Rough Rider who wanted to bring Hawaii under U.S. control. Roosevelt was also the driving force behind the building of the Panama Canal. This was a project he felt was necessary for the U.S. to gain sea power. To take control of the land that he needed to build the canal, he backed the leaders of Panama in declaring their independence from Colombia. Dr. William Gorgas was asked to solve the problems in Panama of yellow fever and malaria, which made the area an unsafe place to work. When the swamps were drained and mosquitoes were controlled, fewer workers suffered from these diseases. The canal was started in 1904 and completed in 1914. President Roosevelt called it the "greatest engineering feat of the ages."

Anti-Imperialism

Anti-imperialists believed that the U.S. should have free trade with the nations of the world, but the nations should be allowed to govern themselves. President Grover Cleveland (in office from 1885-1889 and 1893-1897) was in favor of free trade with Hawaii. However, he did not believe in taking control away from the Hawaiian people. He was also against the Spanish-American War, believing that it was started by "yellow journalists" who only wanted to sell papers. Cleveland was against taking control of the Philippines as well. Others who spoke out against American Imperialism were businessman Andrew Carnegie, union organizer Samuel Gompers and author Mark Twain. Twain wrote: "It should, it seems to me, be our pleasure and duty to make those people free, and let them deal with their own domestic questions in their own way. And so I am an anti-imperialist. I am opposed to having the eagle put its talons on any other land."

title: Meanwhile, Back at the Ranch …
text:
Hi. This is Alana, here to share a report I wrote for my social studies class. During the late 1800s, while imperialists were busy reaching out across the world, there were soldiers, cowboys and cattle ranchers reaching out across the nation.

After the Civil War, troops of only African American soldiers formed, nicknamed the Buffalo Soldiers. The job of the Buffalo Soldiers was to guard settlers as they moved west across the country. One of the most famous Buffalo Soldiers was Tennessee-born George Jordan. He served his country for many years. Jordan earned the Medal of Honor and Certificate of Merit for his courage.

Also after the war, there was a shortage of beef in the East. In Texas, millions of cattle roamed the plains. Ranchers saw an opportunity to get rich by cattle drives. Ranchers hired cowboys to herd, or drive, the cattle north from Texas to Kansas. There the cattle were loaded onto trains and shipped to the East. Ranchers hired many African American and Mexican American cowboys for these famous cattle drives.

People used two main trails to drive the cattle from Texas to Kansas. One famous trail was the Chisholm Trail, which began in southern Texas near San Antonio and ended in Abilene, Kansas. The other was the Great Western Trail. This trail ran from Bandera, just south of San Antonio, to Dodge City, Kansas. Ranchers used these trails for cattle drives from 1867 to around 1890. Cowboys drove more than 10 million cattle north along these trails, and it took two months to make the trip. The cattle sold for about $40 each once they reached Kansas. In Texas, they could only be sold for $4 each. Did the Texas ranchers think the cattle drives were worth the trouble? You bet!

title: Homer Plessy, Equal Rights Hero
text:
The passing of the 13th and 14th Amendments to the Constitution made slavery illegal and gave all U.S. citizens equal protection under the law. Southern states avoided following the 14th Amendment by passing Jim Crow laws. These laws enforced segregation, or the separation of people of different races. They kept African Americans and whites separate in restaurants, schools, theaters, trains and buses.

In 1892, Homer Plessy sat in the "whites only" car of the East Louisiana Railroad. He was part African American. Plessy refused to move and was put in jail. His case went to the Supreme Court, and he lost. The justices ruled that "separate but equal" railroad cars were supported by the Constitution. Plessy's brave act encouraged others to stand up against "separate but equal" treatment. In 1954, the Brown v. the Board of Education of Topeka court case finally struck down this treatment.

title: Hawaiian Harbor
text:
“Jackson, I’ve been thinking about Pearl Harbor.”

“Oh, you mean the Navy shipyard that the Japanese bombed in World War II?”

“That’s what it’s most famous for, Jackson. But did you know that the Navy had been interested in the harbor since 1887?”

“I didn’t know that, Alana. Why did the Navy want a shipyard in the middle of the Pacific Ocean?”

“Do you remember what we learned about huge ships last week?”

“Sure, Alana. Coal-powered ships needed to stop and refuel. Oh! I get it—Pearl Harbor would be a good place for refueling!”

“Right, Jackson. America also wanted to build military bases throughout the Pacific so that it could build a strong Navy and become a world power.”

“If you look at the map, you can see that Hawaii would be a good stopping place on the way to and from Asia. And if a ship needed repairs, it could dock in the harbor.”

“That’s true, Jackson. The U.S. Navy opened the Naval Base at Pearl Harbor in 1908. Today, Pearl Harbor is called Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam. It’s still an important base and is a common ‘pit stop’ in the Pacific for ships, aircraft and submarines.”

title: Amazing Inventions
text:
Hi! This is Jackson. I need to write a report about a famous inventor from the Age of Imperialism, but I'm having a tough time choosing which one. Look at my options, and let me know which one YOU would choose and why. Thanks!

The Wright Brothers

Orville and Wilbur Wright invented, built and flew the first successful airplane. They made their first flight on Dec. 17, 1903.

George Washington Carver

Carver was a scientist who taught farmers to rotate crops to keep the soil healthy. He encouraged farmers to grow peanut plants and developed over 300 uses for the peanut!

Alexander Graham Bell

Bell patented the first telephone in 1876. The first words carried across a telephone wire were, "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you."

Thomas Edison

In 1880, Edison patented the first incandescent light bulb (one that glows from heat). He also invented the phonograph, the kinetoscope (motion picture camera) and the alkaline battery.

title: Uncle Sam Wants YOU!
text:
"Wow! Look at all these cool posters, Alana! Here's one that says, 'Food is Ammunition - Don't waste it!' and another that says, 'Help the Red Cross.' This one has got to be my favorite, though. Check out the serious look on Uncle Sam's face and the way he points his finger right at you when he says, 'I Want YOU for U.S. Army.'"

"These ARE great posters, Jackson. I think our teacher is trying to get us ready for our next social studies unit. Just by looking at these posters, what do you think we'll be studying next?"

"Hmm, I think we'll be learning about soldiers and some type of war. Do you think that first poster really means what it says though? Was food used as ammunition, like in a food fight?"

"I doubt it, Jackson. I think it means that in order to keep the soldiers fighting in the war, the country had to grow plenty of food to send to them. In that way, food was the ammunition used to fight against the enemy."

"That's pretty clever, Alana. The Red Cross poster is pretty easy to understand. The Red Cross needed donations of money and supplies to care for soldiers wounded in battle. Now here's another poster saying, 'Tell that to the Marines!'"

"I think all of these are propaganda posters. That means they were designed to motivate people to fight against the enemy and support the war. Propaganda is information used to promote or support a cause. What do you think Uncle Sam wanted 'YOU' to do, and which war do you think these posters are from?"

"I think these posters were from World War I. Uncle Sam was used as a symbol of the United States during that time. He is calling all young soldiers to action and telling them that their country needs them to fight in the war."

"You're right, Jackson. I just read about this poster online and found out that an artist named James Montgomery Flagg designed it in 1916. Between 1917 and 1918, more than 4 million copies of this poster were printed. They were put up across the country as recruiting posters to persuade young men to join the U.S. Army."

"I really don't know too much about World War I, Alana. I know it was called the 'Great War.' It involved several European nations fighting against each other, and eventually the United States and countries all over the world got involved. Hey, I wonder if your grandma and grandpa have some posters like these up in that attic of theirs!"

"They sure might, Jackson. We can learn more about World War I and how it changed this country of ours. Let's dive right in!"

title: The Military Recruitment Debate
text:
How would you feel about serving in the military? Many young adults choose to join the military soon after graduating from high school. They see military service as a great way to get an education, learn a skill, see the world and serve their country. Other young people choose college or trade school, find jobs that provide career training or even open their own businesses. No matter which path they choose, high school students often have representatives from all sides wanting them to join their "team."

The law requires high schools to allow military recruiters on campus to meet and talk with students about joining the U.S. armed forces. Many parents worry about their children being persuaded to join the military at such a young age. Recruiters often offer free water bottles, pens, computer games, posters and other items. Many items feature military logos in large, bold letters. Parents also worry that recruiters focus on the fun things about serving in the military, such as being able to wear a dressy uniform and travel to exotic places. While many parents are proud of their child's decision to join, other parents wonder if recruiters don't tell students enough about the dangers of military life.

Recruiters point out that the military is a great way for students to get money for college while learning life skills. What's your opinion? Should recruiters be allowed on high school campuses?

title: World War I: The War to End All Wars
text:
"Jackson and I have been studying WWI. We've learned a lot more about the Great War, including its causes and the impact it had on the world."

"That's right, Alana. Let's share some of what we learned with our friends."

WWI and U.S. Involvement

European nations competing with each other for control of land, trade and military power led to World War I. When one nation got angry with another, countries began taking sides and forming alliances (agreements between nations to defend and support each other ). A Serbian terrorist organization assassinated Franz Ferdinand, the archduke of Austria-Hungary, in June 1914. War soon followed. The main alliances that developed were the Allied Powers, made up of Great Britain, France and Russia, and the Central Powers, which included Germany, Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire (part of present-day Turkey).

The United States vowed to stay out of the war, but important events in 1917 made Americans rethink this position. The first was a telegram sent to Mexico from Arthur Zimmermann, the German foreign secretary. The "Zimmermann telegram" asked Mexico to support Germany during the war. In return, Germany would help Mexico get land back from the U.S.

From February to April 1917, German submarines attacked and sank several American trade ships. American sailors lost their lives in these attacks, which angered the United States. Also fresh in Americans' memories was the sinking of the Lusitania, a British passenger and cargo ship. Almost 1,200 people died (including 128 Americans) when the Germans torpedoed the ship in 1915. The Zimmermann telegram and these German submarine attacks convinced U.S. President Woodrow Wilson to ask Congress to declare war on the Central Powers. The U.S. entered the war on April 6, 1917. Italy, Brazil, Japan and other countries also supported the Allies. Bulgaria later joined the Central Powers. It truly was a world at war.

Major Battles of WWI

Much of the fighting in WWI took place on the smooth, rolling lowlands of Belgium and France. Ground troops had nothing to hide behind, so they dug huge networks of trenches. Soldiers lived in those trenches; they ate, slept and died there. Anyone who ventured out of the trenches into "no man's land" ran the risk of being killed. In all, more than 8 million soldiers died during the war.

First Battle of the Marne (1914)

Soldiers fought this battle along the Marne River near Paris, France. The Allies stopped a German push toward Paris and won an important victory. The Germans retreated, and their plans of quickly winning the war were destroyed.

Battle of the Somme (1916)

The Battle of the Somme lasted from July to November 1916 and was fought north of the Somme River in France. The Allies won about six miles of German-occupied territory in this long battle, which resulted in 420,000 British, 200,000 French and 650,000 German casualties. A casualty is a soldier who is captured, wounded or killed.

Battle of Cambrai (1917)

In November 1917, the British launched an attack on the Germans at Cambrai, France. The battle was one of the first to use large numbers of tanks, heavy artillery (large guns or cannons) and airplanes together in battle. The British surprised the Germans by attacking with 476 tanks. This move surprised the Germans, and the British gained some ground. However, the Germans later took back much of what the British had gained.

Battle of the Meuse-Argonne (1918)

Soldiers fought the Battle of the Meuse-Argonne between September and November 1918 in the Argonne Forest of France. General John J. Pershing, commander of the American Expeditionary Forces, led more than 1 million Americans into battle. These American soldiers were nicknamed "doughboys." There are different stories behind this nickname, but one comes from the large buttons on their uniforms. Some people thought the buttons looked like popular pastries.

The Battle of the Meuse-Argonne turned out to be one of the bloodiest of the war for the Americans. More than 26,000 doughboys lost their lives in this battle, and almost 96,000 were wounded. German casualties numbered around 100,000. French forces also fought the Germans alongside the Americans. The battle ended in victory for the Allies and led to the final defeat of the Central Powers. The two sides signed an armistice, an agreement to stop fighting, on Nov. 11, 1918.

Treaty of Versailles

In January 1919, the Allied leaders met in Versailles, France, to write a peace treaty. President Woodrow Wilson represented the United States. He wanted to end the war without punishing the Central Powers, particularly Germany, too harshly. He also wanted to form an international organization called the League of Nations. This group would join together to prevent future wars. When the treaty was completed, it punished the Central Powers harshly, against Wilson's wishes. The treaty stated that Germany must pay huge fines, give up some of its territory and have limits on the size of its military. The treaty did create a League of Nations, but the U.S. Senate refused to approve the Treaty of Versailles or join the league. The Senate feared that the League of Nations would force the U.S. into other wars and keep the U.S. involved in problems overseas. They preferred to take care of America's problems and let the rest of the world take care of its own. This policy became known as isolationism. This way of thinking didn't last long, however, as America's involvement in World War II was just around the corner. What at first was known as the "Great War" soon became known as World War I.

title: Medal of Honor Recipient, Alvin C. York
text:
My name is Alvin C. York, and I was born in Tennessee. I was drafted into the Army during World War I. I really didn't want to go. It wasn't because I was afraid, but it was because I believed the Bible that says, "Thou shalt not kill." My company commander, who was also a Christian, convinced me that we had to protect our country. I headed into battle.

During the Battle of the Meuse-Argonne, I captured a German major. In my journal I wrote, "I told him if he didn't make them [the machine gun operators] stop firing, I would take his head next. And he knowed I meaned it." I forced the men to surrender. My unit captured four officers and 128 German soldiers. I was treated like a hero when I came back home after the war, but I didn't feel like one. I was just doing my duty.

title: Weapons of WWI
text:
Sgt. Alvin York here. During WWI, both sides used many new and dangerous weapons. I had plenty of personal experiences with machine guns that the Germans used to try to kill me! Both sides also used poison gas. These gases caused temporary blindness, skin blisters and lung damage. That's why we carried gas masks. We were trying to protect ourselves from these awful chemicals.

Airplanes were also turned into weapons during this war. These newer inventions were used to drop bombs on the enemy and fire machine guns at enemy planes.

Much of the fighting took place from trenches dug into the ground. The British first used tanks in WWI to cross trenches, crush barbed wire and shoot at the enemy, all from the safety of an armored vehicle. Submarines were important during WWI as well. Torpedoes fired from submarines sank many ships.

title: WWI Military Bases
text:
A military base is a place where military employees and service members live and work. These bases store weapons, supplies and equipment. They also provide housing, stores and hospitals for service members and their families. Military bases are important to service members and the communities where they are located.

During WWI, the U.S. government built military bases and camps across the nation. Service members were trained at the bases and then sent overseas. Bases and camps also provided jobs for civilian workers, or people not in the military. In addition, local businesses loved the money the service members spent when they headed off base!

Camp McClellan in Anniston, Alabama, was once one of the largest training sites in the nation. More than 27,000 service members from New Jersey, Virginia, Maryland and the District of Columbia were trained there as part of the 29th Infantry Division during WWI. Camp McClellan (later named Fort McClellan) was a permanent military base from 1929 until 1999, when it was officially closed.
