title: Pop Culture of the 1920s
text:
"Alana, have I mentioned lately how much I love Grandma Minnie and Grandpa Frank's attic? There's so much great stuff up here!"

"I agree, Jackson. It's even better when we find a picture that takes us back in time. I'm ready for another time-travel experience. How about you?"

"Of course! I found this amazing old phonograph the last time we were up here, and I've been listening to some cool jazz and blues albums from the 1920s. These cats were the bee's knees!"

"What did you say?"

"Sorry, Alana, just a little 1920s slang there. It means that these jazz musicians were excellent! People listened to the music of blues composer W.C. Handy, jazz and blues singer Bessie Smith and famous jazz singer and trumpet player Louis Armstrong during the '20s. Jazz music was part of the Harlem Renaissance, which was in full swing during this period. Many famous African American writers and artists were also part of this movement, including authors Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston."

"That's right, Jackson, but I'm also interested in the popular products of the 'Roaring '20s,' like automobiles, airplanes, radios and household appliances. Speaking of airplanes, I'd like to see Charles Lindbergh make his famous flight across the Atlantic! I would also love to ride in a Model T Ford and maybe even join the suffragettes, or women who fought for the right to vote. They marched to win the vote for women!"

"Hold on a minute, Alana! I doubt we'll have time to do all that on our trip back to the 1920s. Find a picture from this period, and we'll see where we end up."

"Here's one of a woman and two kids. On the back it says, 'Anne Dallas Dudley, suffragette, along with her two children.' That sounds like the perfect picture to me. Grab on and we'll see where it takes us!"

"OK, Alana, as long as you promise that we get to visit a few jazz clubs while we're there. I want to hear some real finger zingers and listen to some balloon lungs play."

"Enough of the 1920s slang, Jackson. We'll be sure to hear some hot jazz. Or is it cool jazz? Oh well, let's grab the picture and go!"

title: Women’s Suffrage Around the World
text:
In 1920, women in the U.S. won the right to vote, but there are still some countries where women don't have full voting rights. Saudi Arabia is only just beginning to allow women to vote in some elections.

Brunei is a monarchy, meaning it is ruled by royalty. This country does not hold elections for national leaders, so neither men nor women vote in national elections. All are allowed to vote in village elections, however.

The United Arab Emirates does not allow its citizens to vote for its leader, but certain people are allowed to vote for members of its national council. Some women have voted in these elections.

Take a look at the timeline to see when each country gave women the right to vote:

title: The Roaring ‘20s
text:
The Serious Side

"Visiting the Roaring '20s surprised me, Alana. I thought the '20s were all about hot jazz music, amazing art and literature, and new freedoms. I found out they also had a serious side."

"That's right, Jackson. Some people grew rich, and many people enjoyed a better way of life. However, our nation made decisions during the 1920s that soon brought the U.S. into the Great Depression. Let's share what we learned on our trip. ..."

Economy

People called this period the "Roaring '20s" because times were good, and life improved for most people. The American economy experienced a boom. Factories produced more goods, prices were reasonable and many people worked shorter hours while enjoying higher wages.

Presidents Warren G. Harding and Calvin Coolidge both worked to cut taxes for the rich. Coolidge also encouraged Americans to spend and save wisely. By 1927, over half of American families owned cars. Consumers purchased groceries and other items at chain stores, or companies with stores in many locations. President Herbert Hoover continued to push Americans to take advantage of the country's good times. He said, "We shall soon, with the help of God, be in sight of the day when poverty will be banished from this nation."

Unfortunately, life wasn't good for everyone. World War I had ended. Many farmers had borrowed money to buy land and plant more crops to feed the Allied troops, but they were left with large debts. They had more crops than they could sell. Food prices dropped, and farmers struggled to pay off their loans.

Factories also produced more goods than they could sell, forcing them to lay off workers. People who were out of work couldn't afford to buy goods made by factories, so the problem got worse. Factories lowered the wages they paid to workers.

Many Americans invested in the stock market, which is an organized system for buying and selling units of company ownership. Stock prices rose throughout the 1920s. Investors, or people who bought the stocks, hoped to get rich. In October 1929, however, the stock market crashed. This meant that stock prices fell to record low levels. Many people lost their savings, their homes and their businesses. Banks closed, and about one in every four people lost their jobs. The U.S. was about to enter the Great Depression, a time of extreme economic hardship.

Immigration

After WWI, many Americans were nervous about the number of immigrants that had entered our country. They thought American jobs would be lost to foreigners. They also wanted to keep possible enemies from entering the country. The U.S. started to set limits on how many immigrants could come here, as well as from which nations they could come. President Calvin Coolidge signed the Immigration Act of 1924. It limited the number of southern and eastern European immigrants coming to the United States. Only two percent of the total U.S. population of residents from those countries would be allowed to move here. The act also stated that no immigrants would be accepted from many parts of Asia. This system of limiting immigrants into the country remained essentially the same until 1952, when immigration laws were changed again.

The Sunny Side

"Well, we've learned about the serious side of the Roaring '20s. Now let's learn about the sunny side of this era!"

Great African American Migration

With the beginning of WWI, several "push and pull" factors drew millions of African Americans from the South to busy Northern cities. The military needed engines, ships and weapons to fight the war, and Northern factory workers produced most of these items. The hope of stable, paying jobs in Northern factories pulled many African Americans north.

Harsh discrimination that African Americans faced in the South pushed many of them away from the Southern area. They went north, hoping for a better life. The huge number of African Americans who settled in America's largest cities led to a great cultural movement called the Harlem Renaissance. This movement was a wonderful, "sunny" outcome of the push-pull factors in the Great Migration.

Harlem Renaissance

Harlem was a section of New York City where many African Americans settled. The Harlem Renaissance, named after this area, was a rebirth and blossoming of African American literature, art and music. Langston Hughes was a famous poet from this movement. He wrote using the language of average folks and included jazz-inspired rhythms. Zora Neale Hurston, called the "Queen of the Renaissance," wrote stories and plays that celebrated everyday African Americans. She wrote, "Mama exhorted her children at every opportunity to 'jump at de sun.' We might not land on the sun, but at least we would get off the ground."

The Jazz Age

The African Americans who gathered in America's big cities also introduced the world to a new style of music - jazz. Many jazz bands created the music as they played, which was a style called improvisation. Trumpet player and singer Louis Armstrong was one of the most famous jazz musicians. Nicknamed "Satchmo," he created a new style of trumpet playing that brought people out of their seats and onto the dance floor. Whites as well as African Americans soon had a taste for jazz, and young women called "flappers" flocked to nightclubs to dance to the beat. Flappers shocked society by cutting their hair short, wearing make-up and shortening their skirts.

This period of growth and new activity in the arts has been a bright part of our American history.

title: The 19th Amendment—A Report by Alana
text:
Since the mid-1800s, many American women had been fighting for the right to vote. Susan B. Anthony was a leader in this movement and argued that women and men should have equal voting rights. Other men and women argued against equal voting rights. Some common reasons were: Most women didn't want to vote; women belonged in the home and women who voted would argue with their husbands.

WWI brought women out of the home and into the job market. In 1918, President Woodrow Wilson said, "We have made partners of the women in this war. Shall we admit them only to a partnership of suffering and sacrifice and toil and not to a partnership of right?"

In 1919, Congress passed the 19th Amendment to the Constitution, giving women the right to vote. In August 1920, enough states had ratified the amendment, and it became a law. The efforts of Susan B. Anthony (above) and other suffragettes had finally paid off, and women could now vote with men in every election. For women who wanted to make their voices heard, this decade was off to a great start!

title: Transportation of the 1920s
text: Two of the most exciting products of the Roaring '20s were the automobile and the airplane. Henry Ford used an assembly line to build reasonably priced cars. In an assembly line, the product moves past workers who each do a unique task for the product. Charles Lindbergh showed off the possibilities of air travel by making the first nonstop airplane flight from New York to Paris. Take a look at the pictures. Write your own captions describing these marvelous new ways to travel!

title: They broke the mold when they made these people!
text:
1. W.E.B. Dubois

"... the problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color line."

W.E.B. Du Bois was the first African American to earn a doctorate degree from Harvard University. He founded the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), with the goal of ending discrimination against African Americans.

2. John T. Scopes

"I was hired to teach science, and I went ahead and taught it."

John T. Scopes was a young high school science teacher who was put on trial for teaching the theory of evolution in a public high school. Evolution is the theory that humans developed from earlier life forms, including monkeys. Scopes was found guilty and fined $100. The guilty verdict was later overturned.

3. Amelia Earhart

"The most effective way to do it, is to do it."

Amelia Earhart was the first female pilot to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean. In 1937, Amelia attempted to become the first woman to circumnavigate (fly around) the world, but her plane disappeared somewhere near Howland Island in the Pacific Ocean. Amelia was never heard from again.

4. Helen Keller

"I will not just live my life. I will not just spend my life. I will invest my life."

At just 19 months old, Helen Keller suffered a serious fever and became unable to hear or see. Helen's mother hired teacher Anne Sullivan to work with Helen, who eventually learned to speak. Helen went to college, wrote books and worked to help others who were deaf or blind.

5. Zelda Fitzgerald

"I did not have a single feeling of inferiority, or shyness, or doubts ..."

The ultimate "flapper," Zelda Fitzgerald grew up as a Southern belle and went on to marry author F. Scott Fitzgerald. She was the inspiration for some heroines of his popular novels. Zelda was also a writer, dancer and painter.

title: The Great Depression Was Pretty Depressing!
text:
"Thanks for making us lunch, Grandma Minnie!"

"You're very welcome, Alana. You and Jackson are actually doing me a favor by helping me use up these vegetables before they spoil. Grandpa Frank and I won't be able to eat all this soup by ourselves, either. Here, Jackson, why don't you chop up these celery stalks? And Alana, you can slice these two carrots."

"Sure, Grandma. I really like soup, but I'm not that excited about using these old vegetables to make it. Look at this carrot. It looks a little wilted to me! Why can't we just use fresh ones?"

"Alana, it might look old, but it will taste just dandy cooked up in my famous 'Clean Out the Fridge' soup. There are still a lot of tasty nutrients in these vegetables, and there's no use letting them go to waste."

"Grandma Minnie, your recipe reminds me of the soup served in soup kitchens during the Great Depression. You've heard of those, haven't you, Alana?"

"Well, I guess so, but I didn't know they used leftovers from the fridge to make their soups."

"They probably didn't, but they did use whatever ingredients they could get their hands on. During the Great Depression, several churches, government agencies and wealthy citizens ran kitchens that served soup to the hungry. The cheapest way to feed lots of people in need was to make huge pots of soup from ingredients that farmers, restaurants and those with extra food had donated. The ingredients donated were different every day - vegetables, rice and occasionally a few tough, fatty chunks of meat. But sometimes the soup was just broth! Many kitchens also served bread to go along with the soup."

"That's right, you two. The cooks got very good at whipping up soups using whatever ingredients were on hand. I'm pretty good at it too, if I say so myself! Why don't you both try a bowl of this soup and see if you agree? Oh, and I want to share this photo with you that I brought down from the attic. It's of a soup kitchen in the 1930s. The people standing in line are waiting for the servers to ladle soup into their bowls."

(With a twinkle in her eye, Grandma Minnie gives Alana and Jackson each a steaming bowl of soup and the photograph. The friends pick up their spoons and both reach for the photo. Suddenly, they find themselves sitting on wooden crates in a small, dirty shack. There is a sign outside the shack that says "Hooverville.")

"Jackson, where are we?"

"I have a sneaking suspicion that we're about to find out firsthand just what the Great Depression was all about. ..."

title: Today's Soup Kitchens
text:
During the Great Depression, many families didn’t know where their next meal would come from. Even today, there are families that struggle with hunger. That’s why religious groups and community organizations still offer soup kitchens and food banks to help solve this very real problem.

Businesses, restaurants, community gardens or even ordinary citizens often donate food to soup kitchens. Volunteers usually prepare and serve the food, and they aren’t paid for their work. They just enjoy helping those in need.

Did you know that kids just like you can volunteer to help at soup kitchens or food banks in your area? Ask an adult for permission to use the Internet to find the location of the nearest soup kitchen. Then you, your friends and family can contact the kitchen to find out when volunteers are needed. Usually, volunteers will help prepare food, serve meals, wipe tables, mop floors and wash dishes. What do you get out of all this service? You’ll get the good feeling of knowing you helped someone in need. What better pay could you ask for? To find a local soup kitchen in your area, visit www.foodpantries.org/

title: The Domino Effect of the Great Depression
text:
Jackson and Alana find themselves transported back in time to a shantytown during the Great Depression. ...

"Jackson, did you notice the sign outside the shack? It says 'Hooverville.' I remember learning that 'Hooverville' was a nickname for the shantytowns, or shack towns, where homeless people gathered during the Great Depression. They built simple shelters from whatever materials were available. These neighborhoods were named after President Herbert Hoover, the person that many people blamed for the Depression. We must be in one of those shantytowns!"

"I think you're right, Alana, and I'd say that the economy during this time period matched the quality of some of Grandma Minnie's soup veggies - wilted, or withering!"

"Good comparison, Jackson. After listening to some of the people who live here, I think I'm starting to figure out why things went downhill for so many people during the Great Depression. It wasn't just the stock market crash but all the other events that went along with it. You could say that there was a domino effect. One bad thing caused several more to happen until the nation found itself in the middle of some very dark times."

"Yes, the stock market crashed in October 1929, and investors eventually lost more than $40 billion! People who had been rich were suddenly penniless. Those who had lost everything had no money to spend. Those who still had money wouldn't spend it because they were afraid that harder times were coming."

"So, when people stopped spending money, factories had to lay off workers because no one wanted to buy their products. Soon, one out of every four American workers was unemployed. Thousands of families were evicted, or forced out, of their homes because they couldn't pay the rent or the mortgage loans on their homes. An estimated 1.5 million people became homeless during the Great Depression. With nowhere else to go, they gathered together in parks and vacant lots. People who lived in 'Hoovervilles' often begged for food and money. They covered themselves at night with newspapers, or 'Hoover blankets.' They also used cardboard, or 'Hoover leather,' to line their worn-out shoes."

"Another problem caused by the stock market crash was that banks lost money, and many of them failed, Alana. Borrowers were unable to pay back the loans they had taken out from the banks. Others tried to take all their money out of the banks because they were scared of losing their savings. When many people tried to withdraw money at the same time, it was called a 'run' on the bank. Banks that couldn't pay their customers failed, and depositors lost all their money. Even those who had worked hard to save just a little suddenly had nothing. More than 4,000 banks closed in 1933 alone! People who lost their money in failed banks couldn't buy things either."

"Things went from bad to worse when a terrible drought hit the Great Plains. The rain stopped, the topsoil blew away and farmers had no way to make a living. So, on top of everything else, farmers couldn't raise crops to earn money or feed their families. Times were definitely hard."

"Yes, they were. The Great Depression really WAS depressing, Alana!"

title: Hooverville Housing and Soup Kitchen Cooking
text:
During the Great Depression, those who lost their jobs, farms and houses were desperate to find someplace to stay and something to eat. In particular, nearly 50 percent of all African Americans were unemployed at this time, which forced many of them out of their homes. The homeless began building shacks, or "shanties," on vacant lots in nearly every large city in America. These shantytowns were called "Hoovervilles" after President Herbert Hoover. He was the leader that many blamed for causing such bad economic times.

People built Hooverville houses out of lumber scraps, cardboard, packing crates, tin, canvas and any other useful materials they could scrounge up. There was no electricity and usually no running water. Most people who lived there were cold, hungry and often sick.

Soup kitchens sprang up near these Hoovervilles to offer food to those in need. Soup and bread lines of hungry people often stretched for blocks. Many believed that hard times would go on forever and that life would never be good again.

title: Herbert Hoover: Did he help or hurt?
text:
President Herbert Hoover had been in office just eight months when the stock market crashed. Some people thought he was a hero for his efforts to end the Depression, but others blamed him for causing it.

When the stock market crashed in late 1929, Hoover asked businesses not to cut wages or lay off workers, but that's exactly what they did. Unemployment and homelessness skyrocketed. Hoover was against giving money directly to the unemployed because he believed it made them less likely to look for jobs. This meant that there were no unemployment checks available during the first part of the Depression.

He also put a tariff, or tax, on goods imported from other countries, and he raised taxes on other items. Hoover acted to keep some banks and businesses open. He also funded construction projects.

In the 1932 presidential election, only six states voted for Hoover. Did he help or hurt things during the Great Depression? You decide!

title: Migrant Mother
text:
Florence Owens Thompson was a 32-year-old mother. She was doing her best to keep the family alive during the Depression. She and her seven children had stopped in a pea pickers' camp in California since her car had stopped running. But the pea crop had frozen, so there was nothing to harvest. Florence was hungry, tired and worried.

Dorothea Lange was a photographer who worked for the Farm Security Administration (FSA). She traveled the country, taking pictures of those who were suffering during the Great Depression.

Dorothea took pictures of Florence and her family. These were later printed in a San Francisco newspaper. She also sent the photos to Washington, D.C., and this prompted the government to ship food to the camp in California. By then, Florence and her family had moved on. The photo was called "Migrant Mother" because a migrant is someone who moves around often. It became a symbol of the suffering of those who lost everything during the Great Depression.

title: Think and Review
text:
1. What was the "domino effect" of the Great Depression? List several events that together brought on such hard times.

2. What was a "Hooverville" and where did it get its name?

3. How did the "Migrant Mother" photo help poor, migrant workers during the Depression? How do you think the woman in the photo, Florence Owens Thompson, felt about having this picture published in newspapers?

4. What were soup kitchens and how did they help those in need during the Great Depression?

title: Relief, Recovery and Reform
text:
"Alana, I'm still feeling a little down after last week's trip back to the Great Depression. Those were pretty gloomy times, that's for sure. I'm really glad I wasn't a kid back then."

"Me too, Jackson. And I agree with you. I'm feeling just a little depressed myself. Do you think that times really got better? I mean, I'm sure they did because our country has come so far since those days. Just think of all our technological advances, for example."

"Hey, why don't we go up to the attic to see if we can find something that will take us to the recovery period of the Great Depression? I wouldn't mind taking another trip back in time, but I don't really want to eat any more of that watered-down soup or keep warm under another Hoover blanket."

"Let's see what we can find, Jackson."

(The kids climb the stairs to Grandpa Frank and Grandma Minnie's attic. They begin looking through different items, trying to find something that will take them back in time to events that led up to the end of the Great Depression.)

"Hey, Alana! Here's an old movie poster advertising the first showing of 'Star Wars'!"

"That's cool, Jackson, but it's not from the right time period. Take a look at this jewelry box, though. I think it was passed down to Grandma Minnie when she was my age."

"Open it! Let's see what's inside."

"Hey! Look at this campaign button. It's a picture of Franklin Delano Roosevelt, or FDR. It has the words 'For a New Deal' along the top. We might have hit the jackpot!"

"What do you mean, Alana?"

"Well, I've heard that the man who brought this country out of the Great Depression was President Franklin Roosevelt. He presented a plan called the New Deal."

"I would have loved a 'new deal' after living in a Hooverville, and I bet most people of the Depression felt the same way."

"Yes, they did, Jackson. People were more than ready to give Roosevelt and his New Deal a chance when he ran against Herbert Hoover for president in 1932. Roosevelt won the election by a landslide, and the country was on its way back from an economic disaster. Grab the button, Jackson, and let's see if we can find out for ourselves what the New Deal was all about."

"Here goes!"

title: Social Security System
text:
In August 1935, President Franklin Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act, creating a system that would pay money to retired workers to help them meet their needs. Most of the money to fund Social Security is taken out of each American worker's paycheck as a payroll tax. At the beginning of the program, the Social Security tax was about 2 percent of each employee's paycheck. The Social Security tax withheld from each paycheck more recently is about 6.2 percent.

The Social Security system pays money to those who have retired, those whose spouse has died or those who have become disabled (unable to work because of illness or injury). About 65 percent of people receiving payments are retired workers. Spouses and children of retired and disabled workers also receive payments. Adults age 61 and older can apply for these benefits in person or online. Payments are made to Social Security recipients each month.

Many people worry that the Social Security system will run out of money before today's workers retire. People are living longer, so they receive payments for a longer period. There are fewer workers paying taxes to replace the large number of retiring workers. Congress is working on finding ways to fix the system so that tomorrow's retirees will have the money they need.

title: Roosevelt’s New Deal
text:
In Roosevelt's first speech as president of the United States, he stated, "... the only thing we have to fear is fear itself." What do you think he meant? Roosevelt was saying that fear of taking action was harming the country more than the Great Depression itself. He then went about putting his New Deal into place, hoping to bring the country out of the depths of the Depression. Roosevelt's New Deal had three goals: relief, recovery and reform.

Relief

Roosevelt's first goal was to help bring relief, or assistance, to the poor and the unemployed. As part of the New Deal, he created the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), which was an agency that gave temporary jobs to young, single men. A total of 3 million young men found jobs planting trees, fighting erosion and building parks. A similar program later gave jobs to over 8,000 young women as well. These workers were paid just $1 per day, but they were also given a place to live and three meals a day. Since many new workers had ridden the rails as hobos, these benefits were often worth more to them than the money itself! Plus, they were taught skills to help them in their future jobs.

The Works Progress Administration (WPA) was another agency that provided jobs for about 8 million Americans. These workers built schools, hospitals and other important public buildings.

These two agencies provided jobs, money and hope to those who were hit hard by the Great Depression.

Recovery

Another of Roosevelt's goals was to start the nation's economy on the road to recovery. The CCC and the WPA could be considered recovery programs as well as relief agencies. These programs provided paychecks to those who could spend their earnings, helping businesses recover from hard times. The Home Owners' Loan Corporation (HOLC) was a program that gave loans to people who needed help paying their mortgages. Many families were then able to keep their homes. The Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) helped parts of several states recover by building dams in the Tennessee River Valley. The electricity generated by the dams helped citizens in this poverty-stricken area. (See Trades and Technology below.)

Reform

Roosevelt's New Deal also worked to reform, or change, the conditions that had led the nation into the Great Depression. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) was created to make sure that people ran the stock market fairly and that everyone followed the same rules of the system. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) was set up to insure, or protect, the money people deposited in U.S. banks. This meant that depositors could not lose their money to bank failures in the future.

The Social Security Act taxed those who worked to provide for the needs of others. Social Security made sure that older Americans would receive income, even after they retired from their jobs.

"Jackson, it sounds like Roosevelt's plan did a lot to get our nation going again after the Great Depression."

"It wasn't perfect, Alana, but it gave our country the boost it needed to get the economy moving in the right direction."

title: A Man With a Plan!
text:
“

Alana, remember how bad things were in the Hooverville we visited last week? Well, the man that many people blamed for causing such hard times was up for re-election as president, and he would have a tough fight!”

When the presidential election of 1932 rolled around, the United States was in bad shape. By the end of that year, nearly one fourth of all Americans were unemployed; 5,000 banks had failed; farmers couldn’t sell their crops; and thousands of families had been evicted, or forced out of their homes. Herbert Hoover had been president the previous four years, and he faced a difficult election ahead.

Many people blamed President Hoover for the Great Depression. They looked for a new leader to deliver the country from hardship and suffering. Franklin Roosevelt began his campaign by saying, “I pledge you, I pledge myself to a new deal for the American people.” Americans listened. After the rotten hand they felt the nation had dealt them the past four years, they were more than ready to accept a “new deal.”

Roosevelt surrounded himself with advisers who helped him make plans for solving the country’s problems. This “Brain Trust” helped him form what became known as the New Deal, a plan to bring the nation out of the Great Depression.

Hoover campaigned hard, but people were critical of the president. Some angry Americans even threw spoiled fruits and vegetables at Hoover. One voter wrote to President Hoover, “Vote for Roosevelt and make it unanimous,” meaning that everyone else in the country planned to vote for Roosevelt, so Hoover should as well. When Election Day rolled around, Roosevelt was victorious. All but six of the existing 48 states voted for Roosevelt.

At a time when the country was desperate for a change, Roosevelt stepped in with a plan. His New Deal soon began pulling the country out of great economic ruin.

title: How to Get an 'A+' in Alphabet Agencies
text:
Roosevelt's New Deal created many new government agencies, or programs. These agencies were given abbreviations. For example, the Civilian Conservation Corps was called the CCC, and the Tennessee Valley Authority was shortened to TVA. The agencies soon became known as the “Alphabet Agencies” or FDR’s “Alphabet Soup.”

Make flashcards for the New Deal programs discussed in this week's issue. Then do some research and find out more about the following agencies:

AAA

NYA

FHA

FERA

Be sure to include the full name of each agency and its purpose. For another challenge, learn about whether the program was successful or not.

title: Three From the 30s!
text:
1. Duke Ellington

Born and raised in Washington, D.C., Edward "Duke" Ellington was a jazz pianist and bandleader. His orchestra played in nightclubs, made records and toured Europe. Some of Ellington's best-known songs from this era are "It Don't Mean a Thing (If It Ain't Got That Swing)" and "Sophisticated Lady."

2. Margaret Mitchell

Margaret Mitchell was a determined, independent young woman who worked as a writer for the Atlanta Journal. In 1926, she began writing her famous Civil War novel, "Gone With the Wind." The novel earned the Pulitzer Prize in 1937. In 1939, it was made into an award-winning movie.

3. Jesse Owens

Jesse Owens was an African American track-and-field star who participated in the 1936 Olympic Games in Berlin, Germany. Owens went on to win four gold medals in Berlin. He later worked in several public relations positions, and he was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1976.

title: Tennessee Valley Authority
text:
Roosevelt and Congress created The Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) in May 1933. It was to help people living in some rural areas of the South. The TVA built dams along rivers in the Tennessee Valley to stop flooding, provide electricity and create jobs.

By building dams, flooding along the rivers was controlled. Farmers learned how to plant crops effectively in the land along the rivers. Reservoirs created by the dams provided places for fishing and recreation. The dams also provided electricity to families in the region. With electricity and healthy farmland, what do think happened next? Businesses flourished! These businesses needed workers, so more citizens found steady jobs.

The TVA was one of the New Deal's most successful programs. Today, it is one of the nation's largest public power companies. Now, reread this article and use colored pens or highlighters to identify the "who, what, where, when and why" of the TVA.

title: Will Santa Deliver?
text:
The following cartoon appeared in the Washington Post in December 1933. It shows President Roosevelt as a little boy with several Christmas stockings lined up along the mantle, ready for Santa to fill. Take a close look at the cartoon and answer the following questions:

1. Look at the “names” on the stockings. What do they represent?

2. Who is the man in the chair? Who does he represent?

3. What do you think FDR is hoping will happen?

4. What is the main message of this political cartoon?

text:

2.List the three main goals of the New Deal and give an example of the programs, or agencies, created to achieve each goal.

3.Analyze the election of 1932. Who were the two candidates? Who won the election? Why do you think the results were so lopsided? What were people hoping would happen after the election?

4.What does TVA stand for? Why was this agency created and what does it do today?

title: Let's Write
text: President Herbert Hoover was a very unpopular person during the campaign of 1932, and many citizens and the media treated him poorly. Should the president be shown a certain amount of respect? In one or two paragraphs, explain your opinion on this issue. Be sure to use correct spelling, grammar and punctuation.

title: Are things getting better?
text:
"Hey, Jackson, how are you doing with memorizing those 'Alphabet Agencies'?"

"Well, Alana, I'm happy to say that these flashcards are really working! I think I have these New Deal agencies down cold. How about you?"

"Same here, Jackson. I think I know them backward and forward. I guess we'll find out for sure when we take the quiz. Learning about all these New Deal programs has made me wonder, though ... did the New Deal really bring the country out of the Great Depression? What would have happened if the government hadn't come up with all these programs?"

"That's a great question. I know the New Deal didn't completely solve the problems of the Great Depression, but it did a lot to bring relief, recovery and reform to our nation during a very difficult time. I've been studying what happened in Europe during the Great Depression, and it seems that life was even worse there than it was here. I wonder if that's because no one like Roosevelt stepped in with a European New Deal to try to make life better for those who were suffering."

"That could be true. I read that in some ways, the Depression hit Europe even harder than it hit America. This was mainly because nations like Great Britain and Germany had a lot of debt from World War I. Germany was even required to pay 'reparations,' or money for damages they caused during the war. When the stock market crashed, these countries couldn't pay back their debts. Their economies struggled."

"That's true, Alana. In Germany, the unemployment rate hit 25 percent, and it was about 22 percent in Great Britain. Governments put huge tariffs on items imported from other countries. The tariffs made it too expensive for nations to trade with each other. Factories couldn't sell their products, so they cut wages and laid off workers. Doesn't that sound familiar?"

"I guess many Americans were grateful that the U.S. government jumped in and worked to get the economy back on its feet. With no New Deal in Europe, things seemed to go from bad to worse."

"This week we'll learn about some of the leaders who did step in to try to solve the problems in Europe, but they were only after complete control of the people in their own countries and in countries around the world. Brace yourself, Alana, because another world war was coming around the corner."

"Oh, no! Here we go again."

title: What kinds of governments exist in the world today?
text:
Did you know that not every country elects a president as its leader? There are many different types of governments in today’s world. Here are a few examples of government types. Do extra research to find examples of countries with these governments

Republic

In a republic, voters elect leaders to run the country according to laws. These leaders are expected to carry out the will of the people when making laws and other government decisions. (A representative democracy is a type of republic.) A country with this type of government is:

Dictatorship

In a dictatorship, a single leader (or small group) that has not been elected by the people rules the country. A dictator usually rules by military force and doesn’t pay attention to the will of the people he or she governs. A country with this type of government is: ____________________________________________

Monarchy

In a monarchy, the head of a family (usually a king or queen) rules the government. Sometimes, the ruler has absolute power passed on from parent to child. In some countries the power of the monarch is limited by a constitution. A country with this type of government is: ____________________________________________

Theocracy

A theocracy is a government in which religious leaders rule. In some places the leader is believed to have divine guidance. A country with this type of government is: ____________________________________________

Under which type of government would you want to live?

title: Trouble in the World
text:
“Jackson, with the Great Depression raging around the world, some government leaders did their best to get their countries back on track. Others had very different ideas.” “That’s true, Alana. There were several leaders who took advantage of the poverty, fear and desperation of their people and forcefully took control of the government. They promised a better life for citizens under their leadership. Many of these leaders attacked neighboring countries, too, setting the stage for another world war.”

Note: Use the map to locate the following countries. Keep track of those doing the invading and those being invaded!

Italy
After World War I, Italian leaders dealt with unhappy citizens. Benito Mussolini stepped in. He created many programs to help the people, but he also set himself up as dictator, a government leader with absolute power. He called himself “Il Duce,” or “The Leader.” In 1935, Mussolini sent the Italian military to invade Ethiopia (then known as Abyssinia), adding this country to his empire. Mussolini later sent support to fascists in Spain during the Spanish Civil War, hoping to show his power. Fascists are people who believe a nation or race is more important than an individual. In 1939, Mussolini officially joined with Adolf Hitler, creating the “Pact of Steel.” This alliance joined the two countries together throughout World War II.

Germany
Adolf Hitler became chancellor of Germany in 1933. He led Germany’s Nazi Party. In 1934, Hitler stepped in as dictator and took control of the government during a time of economic struggle. Hitler promised the millions of poor and unemployed that with his help, Germany would rise again.
Hitler believed that people of a so-called “Aryan” race, or those from certain European backgrounds, were superior to others. He believed that other races were inferior, especially Jews. He said that they must be removed from the Earth. In March 1938, Hitler sent troops to integrate Austria as part of Germany. He easily took control and immediately took away the rights and freedoms of Jewish Austrians.
One year later, Germany invaded Czechoslovakia. This was another part of Hitler’s plan to wipe out “inferior” governments and take over Czechoslovakia’s resources. Hitler’s aggressive actions and deep hatred for non-”Aryans” troubled some Germans and people in other countries.

Soviet Union
Like Germany, a dictator led the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) during this period. Joseph Stalin was the Communist leader of the USSR, or Soviet Union, from the mid-1920s until his death in 1953. In a communist government, there is no private property. Stalin wanted the Soviet Union to rise from its problems and become a world power. He took farmland from the poor and put it under government control. He also set and achieved ambitious goals for mining and manufacturing. These goals were part of his “Five Year Plans” that made the Soviet Union an impressive industrial nation. However, millions of Soviets and people from other countries died under Stalin’s command.

Stalin and Hitler disagreed on most matters, but they signed an agreement in 1939 that their nations would never attack each other. Just two years later, Hitler broke the agreement. Stalin joined the Allies in the fight against Germany during World War II.

Japan
During the Great Depression, the world stopped buying Japan’s exports. The economy suffered. Even though Japan had an emperor and a prime minister, military leaders took control of the government. In 1931, Japan invaded Manchuria, a region in northern China rich in resources. War broke out between China and Japan in 1937. Leader Hideki Tojo encouraged Japan to join with Germany and Italy in what became known as the Axis Powers.

title: Roots of WWII
text:
Word War II didn’t just erupt out of nowhere. The disagreements leading up to this worldwide conflict had been simmering for years. When they finally boiled over, they engulfed the world in a deadly, devastating war. Use the timeline to explore the events leading up to and including this long and painful war.

1921 July: Adolf Hitler becomes leader of the Nazi Party.

1922 October: Benito Mussolini takes over as head of the Italian government.

1925 July: Hitler publishes his book “Mein Kampf” (“My Struggle”).

1926 September: Germany joins the League of Nations.

1929 October: U.S. stock market crashes.

1931 September: Japan invades Manchuria region of China.

1932 November: Franklin D. Roosevelt elected as president of the U.S

1933 January: Hitler becomes chancellor of Germany.

1935 March: Germany builds up its army in violation of the Treaty of Versailles.

1935 October: Italy invades Abyssinia (now Ethiopia).

1936 February: The Gestapo (Nazi secret police) is given absolute power.

1936 December: Chinese Nationalists and Communists combine forces to fight Japan.

1937 July: Conflict erupts between Chinese and Japanese soldiers at Marco Polo Bridge.

1938 January: Roosevelt recommends building up U.S. military defenses.

1938 March: Germany invades Austria.

1939 May: Germany signs “Pact of Steel” with Italy; Japan joins later.

1939 September: Great Britain, France, Australia, New Zealand and Canada declare war on Germany.

1940 April-May: Germany invades Denmark, Norway, France, Luxembourg, Belgium and the Netherlands. May: Winston Churchill becomes prime minister of Great Britain.

1940 June: Italy declares war on Great Britain and France. September: U.S. begins first peacetime military draft.

1941 June: Germany invades Soviet Union. September: German Nazis order Jews to wear yellow stars.

1941 December: Japan attacks Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The U.S. entry into war ends Great Depression.

title: Think and Review
text:
1. Why do you think the Depression hit Europe harder than it hit the United States? What do you think made the difference in helping the United States recover more quickly?

2. What type of government leaders took control of the European and Asian nations during the Great Depression? Analyze and explain why you think these leaders were able to come into power.

3. Compare and contrast Italian fascism with German Nazism. How were they alike? How were they different?

4. How did Stalin help the Soviet Union recover from the Depression?

5. Describe the actions that Japan took during this time period.

title: Extreme Governments
text:
Just before WWII broke out, several countries used extreme forms of government to flex their muscles. Read through the summaries on this page; then use a separate sheet of paper to complete a diagram that shows the relationship between totalitarianism, fascism and Nazism.

Totalitarianism

Totalitarianism is a type of government where the state has complete political, social and cultural control over its citizens. Citizens are often controlled by threats of violence or by persuasive leaders.

Soviet leader Joseph Stalin’s goal was to build a totalitarian Communist government. Even within the Communist Party, those who disagreed with Stalin were often murdered. Stalin renamed cities after himself and had statues built in his honor.

Fascism

Italy embraced fascism when Benito Mussolini came into power. Fascism is a form of totalitarianism in which the nation or state is always more important than the individual. There are no limits on what the state can do, and no one is allowed to disagree with the dictator or the government. Fascists opposed democracy and communism. Mussolini and the fascists took control of the government, army and schools.

Many people considered Japan a fascist country as well. A group of military leaders ruled the country, and citizens feared the actions of the secret police.

Nazism

Nazism is a type of fascism that includes extreme racism. The Nazi government’s goal was to promote an Aryan race and eliminate “inferior” races, especially Jews. It included racist behaviors, extreme national pride and national expansion, or taking over other countries. Hitler was the all-powerful Nazi leader. He used the media, schools and even churches to reach his people. He also used the secret police to spy on German citizens and punish those who went against his wishes.

title: Let's Write
text: German people voted the Nazi Party into power during the 1930s. Why do you think dictators in Germany and leaders in other countries took absolute power during this time period? In one or two paragraphs, give several reasons why you think so many dictators came into power during this period. Be sure to use correct spelling, grammar and punctuation.

title: Sitting on the Sidelines
text:
Jackson and Alana are on the school playground, watching a kickball game between a group of first graders and a group of fifth and sixth graders. ...

"Hey, look at those kids playing kickball. The fifth and sixth graders aren't playing fair. Those younger kids don't have a chance!"

"You're right, Alana. It looks like the older kids are letting all their best players kick every time. The first graders don't stand a chance of catching those high-powered shots!"

"I don't like it, Jackson. Maybe we should go over there and talk to them about starting the game over. We could make the teams even so that everyone can have fun. On the other hand, I'm not sure I want to interrupt them."

"Do you know what this reminds me of, Alana? It's like the beginning of WWII. Germany and the Axis Powers started to beat up our friends across the ocean, and some people in the U.S. wanted to help right away. Many Americans didn't want to get involved, though."

"I guess I can understand that, Jackson. It makes sense that Americans were tired of war after losing so many soldiers in WWI. I think I read somewhere that the United States had decided to remain neutral and not take sides in fights between foreign countries."

"That's right, Alana. The U.S. wanted to be on friendly, cooperative terms with all nations. They wanted to stay out of arguments between other countries."

"Ummm ... I don't think this policy of neutrality, or isolationism, was very successful, Jackson. We know that the United States fought in WWII."

"You're right, Alana. But the U.S. didn't enter the war at the beginning. It was only after years of trying to stay out of the conflict that our nation finally joined forces with the Allies. The United States joined WWII because Japan attacked our soldiers on American soil. President Roosevelt felt like he had no other choice."

"I understand Americans not wanting to send their loved ones into battle again. It just seems that the U.S. might have had a little more sympathy for its friends when the Germans invaded countries like Poland, France and Belgium."

"That's just it, Alana, the U.S. did feel sympathy for its friends! But Congress had passed laws stating that America must remain neutral and that it couldn't take sides in conflicts between foreign nations."

"It sounds like we were between a rock and a hard place, but once the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor, staying neutral seemed impossible."

"That's true, Alana, but Roosevelt found ways to help his friends even before the attack."

"I'm glad to hear that, Jackson. Maybe we should find a way to help our young friends in this kickball game too."

"I'm with you!"

title: Original Posters Discovered!
text:
During WWII, the British government printed posters to encourage its citizens to stand strong during difficult times. One of these posters carried the message "Keep Calm and Carry On." The copyright for this poster expired 50 years after it was printed, so now anyone can use the design and slogan. The "Keep Calm and Carry On" design has become very popular and appears on all types of products throughout Great Britain and around the world.

A British woman named Moragh Turnbull discovered a batch of original "Keep Calm and Carry On" posters rolled up in her father's home. Her father was once a member of the Royal Observer Corps (a group of civilians who watched for enemy attacks during WWII). He had been asked to put up the posters around town during the war. Moragh took the posters to a filming of the popular TV show "Antiques Roadshow" and discovered that they are very rare posters worth about $1,000 each! The "forgotten" posters are in great shape and are very valuable as primary sources!

title: WWII Begins in Europe
text:
"Jackson, after doing some research, I can understand why the U.S. wanted to remain neutral and stay out of the war. But I also see why it was so hard for us to stand around and do nothing while our friends were being attacked."

"President Roosevelt was definitely in a tough situation, Alana, but he never completely deserted our allies. Friends, here's what we learned from our research":

Hitler Invades

In September 1939, Hitler invaded Poland with airstrikes and 1.5 million ground troops. Hitler had promised the German people that he would bring them Lebensraum, or living space, and attacking Poland helped him keep his promise. Hitler had successfully taken over Austria and Czechoslovakia already, so he believed that he could invade Poland as well.

Great Britain and France had joined together to oppose Germany, and they were known as the Allies. When Germany refused to leave Poland, Great Britain and France declared war on Germany. World War II had begun.

It wasn't long before the Germans attacked France and Great Britain as well. Within months, France surrendered to Germany, and Hitler later carried out devastating air raids on Great Britain.

Just days before the war had begun, Hitler and Stalin, the leader of the Soviet Union, signed an agreement that their nations would not attack each other. Two years into the war, in June 1941, Hitler broke the agreement by invading the Soviet Union. Stalin immediately joined the Allies in the fight against Germany.

U.S. Neutrality

After WWI ended in 1918, the U.S. vowed to stay out of all future wars and watch from the sidelines if other nations chose to fight. During the 1930s, the U.S. Congress passed a series of laws called the Neutrality Acts. These laws stated that the United States would not get involved in any conflicts between foreign nations; they would remain neutral.

Once Germany attacked our European friends, Roosevelt wanted to help, but there was little he could do at the time. Americans did not want to send their family members to war, but families in France and Great Britain were losing their loved ones on the battlefield. What could Roosevelt do?

Help for our Friends

When Hitler invaded European countries, President Roosevelt asked Congress to amend, or change, the Neutrality Acts so that the U.S. could send help. Congress passed the Neutrality Act of 1939, which gave the government power to sell weapons and ammunition to these nations. The U.S. could give supplies to its friends, but these nations could only buy weapons if they had the money. In addition, American ships were not allowed to transport the goods.

As the war between Germany and the European nations continued, Roosevelt again asked Congress for help. In March 1941, Congress passed the Lend-Lease Act, which said that the U.S. could lend, sell or give war supplies to Allied nations.

Friend or Foe?

So, who WERE our friends during WWII? The Allied Powers were originally Great Britain, France and the Soviet Union (since Germany had attacked the Soviets). The United States joined the Allies after the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941. A number of less powerful nations, such as Australia and Canada, were part of the Allied Forces as well.

Who were our foes, or enemies? The three main nations that made up the Axis Powers were Germany (including East Prussia), Italy and Japan. Bulgaria, Hungary and Romania later joined the Axis.

title: Isolationism: Trying to Protect Ourselves
text:
This is Jackson. I have to say that I was upset when I learned that the U.S. didn't immediately help when Germany attacked France, Great Britain and the Soviet Union. Why didn't the president send weapons, troops and money right away?

I did a little research and learned more about the Neutrality Acts. After WWI, the American people were tired of war and wanted to deal with their own issues, rather than try to solve the world's problems. Here's what I learned:

First Neutrality Act

In 1935, Congress proclaimed that the U.S. could not export any weapons, ammunition or "implements of war" to belligerent (warring) nations. Americans were also warned that if they sailed on a belligerent's ship, they did so at their own risk.

Neutrality Act of 1936

This law renewed the First Neutrality Act for another 14 months and said that no loans or credit could be offered to belligerent nations.

Neutrality Act of 1937

This act renewed the previous neutrality acts and made it illegal for any U.S. ships to carry military equipment to belligerent nations. Citizens could no longer sail on belligerents' ships. It also gave the president the power to sell supplies (but not weapons and ammunition) to belligerent nations, as long as they paid for these items at the time of purchase.

Neutrality Act of 1939

By this time, Germany was at war with Great Britain and France. Congress passed a law stating that the U.S. could sell weapons, ammunition and other military supplies to belligerent nations. Again, nations had to pay for supplies at the time of purchase.

Lend-Lease Act of 1941

This law marked the end of U.S. Neutrality Acts. It allowed the U.S. to lend, sell or give war supplies to its allies. President Roosevelt could now offer our foreign friends more than just a few kind words. He could, and did, send them money, weapons, vehicles and, after Pearl Harbor, U.S. troops.

title: Dr. Seuss vs. Isolationism
text:
You are probably familiar with the characters created by Dr. Seuss (real name: Theodor Seuss Geisel). Did you know that in addition to writing children’s books, he spent several years drawing political cartoons? Political cartoons are drawings that use characters (and often words) to make a comment about a current event.

Ted, as Dr. Seuss was known in those days, was opposed to isolationism. He believed that the U.S. should help its friends defeat Germany and Japan. One of his cartoons shows a drawing of Mount Rushmore, but instead of the faces of U.S. presidents, the famous landmark displays the faces of the German and Japanese leaders. The drawing has a caption that reads: “Don’t let them carve THOSE faces on our mountains.” His cartoons leave no question about his stand on the war. Dr. Seuss wanted the U.S. to join the fight against the people trying to conquer the world. If you want to see the cartoons, ask permission to go to libraries.ucsd.edu

title: Winston Churchill
text:
Winston Churchill was one of the greatest world leaders of the 20th century. Churchill took a strong stand against Hitler, even before other world powers joined him in the fight.

Churchill attended school at the Royal Military College and joined the British cavalry. He also worked as a newspaper reporter and wrote about war in South Africa. In 1900, he was elected to Parliament and later served as head of Great Britain's navy. Churchill watched events unfold in Europe and warned the government that Hitler must be stopped.

Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain resigned in 1940, and Churchill was chosen to take his place. He led the country through the darkest days of a terrible war, urging the country not to give up. He told the British people, "... we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills; we shall never surrender." Great Britain and the Allies eventually defeated Hitler, and Churchill went on to receive many honors.

title: Poster Propaganda
text:
At the beginning of WWII, Great Britain expected that the Germans would begin massive airstrikes on British cities. The government printed posters that were meant to lift people's spirits and help them face the future with courage. These posters were considered propaganda, or messages designed to persuade people to think or behave in a certain way. Just as in WWI, a government used posters to build morale (cheerfulness and confidence), courage and commitment to the war effort.

These were some of the slogans used on the British posters: "Your Courage, Your Cheerfulness, Your Resolution Will Bring Us Victory," "Freedom is in Peril. Defend It With All Your Might" and "Keep Calm and Carry On." Discuss with a partner the meaning behind these slogans.

title: Letter from Churchill to Roosevelt: What Does it Mean?
text:
The prime minister of Great Britain, Winston Churchill, and U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt sent letters and telegrams back and forth, even before the United States entered WWII. What do you think they talked about? Here is a copy of a letter that Churchill sent to Roosevelt before the U.S. officially entered the war. Read the letter carefully and answer the questions. (You may use a dictionary to look up unfamiliar words, if necessary.) Answer the questions on a separate sheet of paper.

BRITISH EMBASSY,

WASHINGTON, D. C.

December 7th 1940

My dear Mr. President,

As we reach the end of this year I feel that you will expect me to lay before you the prospects for 1941. I do so strongly and confidently because it seems to me that the vast majority of American citizens have recorded their conviction that the safety of the United States as well as the future of our two democracies and the kind of civilization for which they stand are bound up with the survival and independence of the British Commonwealth of Nations. Only thus can those bastions of sea-power, upon which the control of the Atlantic and the Indian Oceans depends, be preserved in faithful and friendly hands. The control of the Pacific by the United States Navy and of the Atlantic by the British Navy is indispensable to the security of the trade routes of both our countries and the surest means to preventing the war from reaching the shores of the United States.

Questions

1.When was this letter written?

2.In the letter, Churchill says he is confident that most Americans believe that the future of the two democracies, the United States and Great Britain, are “bound up with the survival and independence of the British Commonwealth.” What do you think he meant by this?

3.What does Churchill believe is the “surest means to preventing the war from reaching the shores of the United States”?

4.What do you think Churchill hoped Roosevelt would do to help Great Britain?

title: V is for Victory!
text:
Jackson and Alana are in their classroom, reading through some old newspapers that their teacher brought in...

"Wow, Alana! I can't believe these newspapers are really from 1945. I love reading about historic events from primary sources. People who actually lived through these amazing times wrote these newspapers. The stories - and pictures - are incredible!"

"You're right, Jackson, but I'm still a little confused about the headlines in these papers. This one says, 'V-E Day - It's All Over,' and here's one that says, 'Japan Surrenders to Allies, Signs Rigid Terms on Warship; Truman Sets Today as V-J Day.' What do V-E and V-J mean anyway?"

"V-E means 'Victory in Europe' and V-J means 'Victory in Japan.' May 8, 1945, is considered Victory in Europe (V-E) Day because it was the day that Germany surrendered to the Allied Powers. This ended the war in Europe. Japan surrendered to the Allies on Aug. 14, 1945, and this was called Victory in Japan (V-J) Day. It wasn't until Sept. 2, 1945, that leaders signed the final terms of surrender while aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay. But by then, people had been celebrating for weeks."

"That makes sense. Can you imagine what this news meant to the soldiers, their families and other citizens who had suffered so much? The war in Europe had lasted nearly six years, and the war with Japan had lasted nearly four. I'm guessing that people were more than ready to celebrate when they heard that the war was finally over."

"Just look at these photos and you'll know that's the truth, Alana. People had lived with shortages of meat, butter, sugar, coffee, rubber, gasoline, nylon stockings and many other items during WWII. Citizens were hopeful that with the war behind them, they could enjoy life again."

"I hadn't thought much about all the everyday items that people had to live without. They hoped to get these goods back, but I think people were even more excited to have their loved ones come back home."

"The sad part is that many soldiers who went to war never made it back home. People have estimated that more than 60 million soldiers and civilians died in WWII, which was over 2 percent of the world's population. Millions of soldiers who did make it home suffered from war injuries for the rest of their lives."

"I guess it was a sad time in many ways, Jackson, but I'm sure it was also a happy time. After all, the war was finally over and life could be peaceful again."

title: The Mystery of the Kissing Sailor Solved!
text:
When news reached New York City on Aug. 14, 1945, that WWII had finally ended, a celebration erupted. People flooded Times Square, cheering and dancing. Photographer Alfred Eisenstaedt grabbed his camera and began snapping photos. It wasn't long before he had captured the most famous picture of his career - a photo of an enthusiastic sailor kissing an unsuspecting dental assistant. The photo shows what some have called the "kiss heard 'round the world." It's an image that became a symbol of the end of the war.

Who were the people in this photo? Eisenstaedt never got the names of the man and woman, so people have debated this question for decades. A recent book called "The Kissing Sailor" reveals that the man was 22-year-old Navy sailor George Mendonsa. The woman he grabbed at random was a 21-year-old dental assistant named Greta Zimmer Friedman, who had come to America from Austria at the beginning of the war.

The authors of the book interviewed all those who claimed to be the pair in the picture. They identified people in the background of the photo and even asked forensic investigators (people who use science to solve crimes) to prove that Mendonsa and Friedman were actually the couple in the photo. By using modern technology and good detective skills, an old mystery was finally solved!

title: WWII: Drastic Measures
text:
"Jackson, some of the most traumatic events of WWII happened in the Pacific Theater, an area in the Pacific Ocean with several islands."

"That's right, Alana. This week, we'll learn about the most important battles and events in the Pacific Theater. We'll also see how these events led up to the end of the war."

"As we locate each event on the map, we'll see how the Allies made their way closer and closer to Japanese soil as the end of the war approached."

"We'll also see just what it took to finally bring the war to a very decisive end."

1. Battle of Midway

Fill in the blanks with the information you learned from last week's lesson.

The Battle of Midway was fought between the _________________________________________ and the Americans over Midway, a small

____________________ (ring-shaped coral island). American Admiral Chester Nimitz learned about Admiral Yamamoto's plans before the attack on June 4, 19 ________ . The U.S. destroyed ___________________ Japanese aircraft carriers. The ______________________________ won the battle and crippled the Japanese navy for the rest of the war.

Island Hopping

After the Battle of Midway, the Allies started a new strategy called "island hopping." Their plan was to move from island to island, attacking the weakest of the Japanese-held islands while avoiding those with the most military protection. By taking the weak islands, the Allies crept closer and closer to Japan, one island at a time.

2. Battle of Guadalcanal

This battle was fought on the island of Guadalcanal between August 1942 and February 1943. It marked a change in the Allied forces from defenders to attackers. During this battle, the enemies fought on land, in the air and on the sea. The Allies eventually outnumbered the Japanese and took control of the island. Island hopping continued.

3. Battle of the Philippine Sea

This battle took place between the Allies and the Japanese off the Mariana Islands in June 1944. The battle set large aircraft carriers and fighter planes against each other. The Allies lost 130 aircraft. The Japanese lost over 480 aircraft, along with three carriers and two oilers. The losses destroyed the Japanese navy's ability to launch planes from sea.

4. Iwo Jima

The battle for this island and its airstrips, or runways, lasted over a month. The U.S. needed the airstrips to use in air attacks against Japan. In February 1945, U.S. Marines landed on the island and began one of the bloodiest battles of the war. The famous image of Marines raising the American flag became a symbol of the battle for Iwo Jima. More than 6,000 Marines and about 20,000 Japanese soldiers lost their lives during this fight, which ended in a U.S. victory.

5. Battle of Okinawa

Okinawa is a large island about 340 miles from the Japanese mainland. The Allies wanted the island for a base to launch attacks against Japan. Nearly 100,000 Japanese were killed, and many committed suicide during the 82-day battle. Over 12,000 Allied troops lost their lives. In addition, the number of civilians killed likely reached 100,000. The Allies won the battle and took control of the island in June 1945.

Truman's Decision to Drop the Atomic Bomb

When President Franklin D. Roosevelt died in April 1945, Vice President Harry Truman became president. It was a very difficult time. Americans were tired of the war and wanted it to be over - quickly! Allied leaders tried to convince the Japanese to surrender, but they refused. Truman learned that the U.S. had developed an atomic bomb with more destructive power than 20,000 tons of ordinary explosives. He knew the bomb would destroy many Japanese lives, but he also believed that dropping the bomb would force the Japanese to surrender. This could save many more lives in the long run. It was a difficult decision, but he felt it was the only way to end the war quickly.

6. Hiroshima

On Aug. 6, 1945, an American plane called the Enola Gay dropped an atomic bomb on the Japanese city of Hiroshima. Nearly 80,000 people died in a matter of seconds.

7. Nagasaki

When the Japanese still refused to surrender, the United States dropped a second atomic bomb on the city of Nagasaki. This bomb, dropped on August 9, killed another 40,000 Japanese citizens. In both cities, tens of thousands of people died later from effects of the bombs. Finally, on Aug. 14, 1945, Japan surrendered.

8. Japan Surrenders

On Sept. 2, 1945, the Japanese on board the USS Missouri docked in Tokyo Bay signed the written agreement ending WWII. Japanese foreign minister Mamoru Shigemitsu and General Yoshijirō Umezu signed the terms of surrender, along with U.S. Army General Douglas MacArthur.

United Nations Formed

On Jan. 1, 1942, after the U.S. had entered WWII, President Roosevelt named the group of 26 nations that joined together against the Axis Powers the "United Nations." In October 1945, after the war had ended, the United Nations (U.N.) was officially organized in San Francisco. The purpose of the United Nations was to prevent future wars, protect human rights, establish equal rights for all and promote justice and freedom. Almost 200 nations now belong to the United Nations, which has its headquarters in New York City.

title: Navajo Code Talkers
text:
Did you know that America might not have won World War II without the help of a small group of American Indian soldiers? These soldiers didn't win the war with the power of their weapons, but with the strength of their words.

When the United States was in the middle of fighting WWII, leaders realized that the Japanese could break any code the military tried to use. The codes were used to send messages between military leaders and soldiers during battles. When these codes were broken, battles were lost.

In 1942, a man named Philip Johnston had grown up on a Navajo Indian reservation. He came up with the idea of training Navajo soldiers to use their language in writing new military codes. The Navajo language is very complex, and only about 30 non-Navajo people knew how to speak it. At first, 29 Navajo soldiers were trained to make an unbreakable code using their native language. The code was tested and found to work well. Then, 200 more Navajo Code Talkers were trained and sent to the Pacific, where they sent and received messages during battle. These Code Talkers were so successful that not one of their messages was ever deciphered (understood) by the enemy. The codes they wrote were based on the Navajo language and then changed in small ways that made them impossible for the enemy to crack.

By the end of the war, about 420 Navajo soldiers were trained as Code Talkers. During the Battle of Iwo Jima, more than 800 messages were sent and received. These messages helped guide the troops, keeping them safe and allowing them to win the battle and the war. The United States owes much of its success in the war to these skilled American Indian Code Talkers.

title: An Excerpt from ‘The Gaijin Child,’ by Michael Mogilevsky
text:
Michael Mogilevsky was born in Java in 1929. In 1931, the family moved to Japan. Michael's parents were Russian natives, but [they] traveled the world as classical musicians. Michael was considered "gaijin,"... which literally means "outside person" in Japanese. He grew up and lived in Japan until 1950. When World War II began, Michael was just a young boy. ... In this part of his story, Michael is 15 years old.

Note: Napalm is a thick, jelly-like gasoline used in firebombs.

"In 1945, American Air Corps General Curtis E. Le May assumed command of the bomber fleet in the Pacific. Under his orders, the American bombers (airplanes) used a new tactic. The night of March 9, 1945, the planes flew low and seemed to be flying in random directions above the low-lying, densely populated bay area of Tokyo. They dropped napalm bombs that exploded and the city began to burn - it became a giant firestorm! People ran for their lives and many died.

"This scene was repeated two more times, until finally our house was destroyed on the night raid of May 23rd. We were lucky. We lived in the suburbs, with many more open spaces, and although there was a fire storm, we learned about the use of gas masks and were able to breathe through the thick smoke and flying burning cinders. We had some harrowing experiences as we would hurry to un-bombed areas, rest a minute, and then hear the roar of the napalm sticks (which sounded like an approaching freight train) as they descended on the previously untouched areas.

"We had our cart with several valises and suitcase, my father [had] his violin in his hand, the housekeeper had her valise with her, I had my trusted bicycle, and we eventually made it to an open field, where we spent the rest of the night, fully awake and ever watchful until the all-clear sounded. Many homes around us were burning."

title: Cracking the Code
text:
The Navajo Code Talkers often used Navajo words to represent military terms. For example, the Navajo word for “turtle” meant “tank” and the Navajo word for “hummingbird” meant “fighter plane.” Other times, the Code Talkers used Navajo words to represent letters of the alphabet. For example, wol-la-chee, the Navajo word for “ant,” was used to represent the letter “a,” and shush, the Navajo word for “bear,” stood for the letter “b.”

Are you ready to be a Code Talker? Use the Navajo Alphabet Code to decipher the coded message. Then, use a separate sheet of paper to write your own short message. Share your message with other students or family members and see if they can crack the code!
