title: A Fish Story
text:
“Alana, I really enjoyed today’s history lesson, but I have to admit that it made my stomach growl.”

“You mean because we talked about fish? I didn’t even know you liked fish, Jackson!”

“Are you kidding? I love fish! My dad and I go fishing every chance we get. You should taste some of his fresh trout fillets. They’re delicious!”

“Well, if you like to eat fish, then you probably understand the proverb, or popular saying, she used today: ‘Give a man a fish and you feed him for a day. Teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime.’ I like how she compared this saying to what the government did to help veterans after WWII.”

“I do too, Alana. Did you know that after the First World War, soldiers returning home from battle got very little help from the government? They also had a hard time finding jobs. When the Great Depression hit a few years later, many had to eat from soup lines and sleep in Hoovervilles.”

“Soldiers who risked their lives to protect our freedom should have been treated better.”

“That’s what lots of people thought. After WWII, things were different. In 1944, President Roosevelt signed the Servicemen’s Readjustment Act of 1944. This act became known as the GI Bill of Rights because the nickname for American soldiers was ‘GI,’ or ‘Government Issue.’”

“Our teacher said that the GI Bill was important because it didn’t just give veterans money. It gave veterans the opportunity to go to school so that they could get better jobs. It also gave them the chance to get low-cost loans to buy houses and farms or to start businesses. Unemployed veterans were even given weekly unemployment benefits for up to one year if they couldn’t find a job. The amazing part about the unemployment money is that very few soldiers actually used it because most were able to find jobs.”

“So, instead of just giving veterans money, ‘a fish,’ the government gave them the chance to get an education, or taught them how to fish, so that they could find good jobs and support their families. What a great idea!”

“I agree, Jackson. Between 1940 and 1950, the number of college degrees awarded in the United States more than doubled, and almost 2.5 million veterans received home loans by 1952. The economy boomed! It sounds like teaching the veterans to fish was the best idea of all.”

“That’s right, Alana. Maybe it’s time YOU learned to fish. Dad and I are going this weekend. Want to come along?”

“Sounds great to me … as long as I don’t have to eat any!”

title: The Post-9/11 GI Bill
text:
The original GI Bill expired in 1956, but several different versions have helped veterans since then. The Post-9/11 GI Bill was passed in 2008 to help veterans who have served in the military since Sept. 11, 2001. Depending on the amount of time spent serving in the military since 9/11, veterans can get up to 100 percent of their college tuition paid. They may also receive money for books, supplies, living expenses and moving expenses. The bill doesn't just give money for college. It also provides money for testing, flight school and hands-on, on-the-job training. Since the bill was passed in 2008, more than $30 billion has been paid to nearly 1 million veterans and their families.

One difference between the original GI bill of 1944 and today's GI bill is that veterans can pass along their benefits to their spouses and children. If a veteran served at least 10 years in the military, or signs an agreement to serve for 10 years, then his or her spouse and children can also receive money for college books, fees and tuition.

Just like the Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, the Post-9/11 GI Bill makes it possible for veterans and their families to get an education and prepare for a better life.

title: Building a Strong Economy After World War II
text:
A Look Back ...

When WWI ended, veterans headed back to the U.S. looking for jobs and housing. Soon, the job market was flooded. Many veterans were unemployed and roamed the country, desperate for work. The United States had no set plan to deal with the problem of too many workers and not enough jobs. There were also several other economic worries, so the country fell into the Great Depression. Life was difficult for many former soldiers who had served their country with honor. In 1932, WWI veterans marched on Washington, D.C., demanding money and help from the government. There wasn't enough money to go around, and most veterans were disappointed with the treatment they received from the nation's leaders.

Investing in Education

As the U.S. entered WWII, government leaders made a plan to care for returning veterans once the war was over. They didn't want a repeat of what had happened after WWI. What they came up with was the Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, or the original GI Bill. This bill made it possible for returning soldiers to attend college and receive low-cost loans to buy houses for themselves and their families. With a plan in place, veterans who returned from WWII were able to ease back into civilian life without worrying about finding a job immediately. They were able to make the transition from soldier to civilian more smoothly by taking classes and preparing themselves to work at stable, higher-paying jobs.

When government officials first began writing the GI Bill, they didn't expect that nearly 8 million members of the military would take advantage of the education benefits. A college education used to be just for the wealthy. Would the soldiers from different economic backgrounds want to handle this task? The veterans hit the books hard and earned their degrees, taking college by storm, just as they had beaten the enemy on the battlefield. Scientists, engineers, educators, inventors, social workers, medical experts and many other professionals received their training because of the GI Bill. Soon the nation's economy was growing by leaps and bounds. The space program took off, and America worked to send a man to the moon. Computers were developed, making it easier than ever before to process and use information. Scientists made many medical breakthroughs, such as the polio vaccine, as well as new treatments for cancer and heart disease. With so much growth in many industries, there were plenty of good-paying jobs available for skilled workers.

What happened when these new college graduates began earning money? They started spending it! Many of those who used the GI Bill to get an education found good jobs and bought comfortable houses in the suburbs, those communities located just outside larger cities. Car sales went way up, since many new homeowners needed transportation from the suburbs to their jobs in the city. By 1950, one in three women (about 33 percent) were in the workforce as well, enjoying luxuries they could afford when both spouses worked outside the home. America's economy was booming, and life was good for most Americans. The GI Bill had helped prevent another Great Depression by providing training for the troops returning from war. It helped prepare them for a bright future.

title: Four Fabulous Functions
text:
The GI Bill helped the U.S. economy stay healthy and strong after WWII. Our economy is divided into "Functional Four" sectors, or four main areas that work together to produce and distribute goods and services. The Functional Four are the household sector, government sector, business sector and banking sector.

Household Sector

The household sector is the population in general, or all people who produce and consume goods and services. We are all members of this sector. We all buy and use, or consume, goods like cars, clothing, groceries and entertainment. Members of the household sector also produce goods and services at the jobs they work each day.

Government Sector

This sector is made up of local, state and national governments that collect taxes. It uses the money to provide goods and services that private businesses can't or don't provide. The government sector builds schools, roads and bridges. It also provides police and military protection and protects our nation's wildlife and important landmarks. The government sector sometimes buys goods and services from the business sector.

Business Sector

The business sector is made up of companies that use resources to produce goods and services, which they sell to the household and government sectors. This sector works to fill the wants and needs of consumers, or members of the household sector. The business sector also deals with consumers and businesses in foreign countries.

Banking Sector

The banking sector is made up of banks, credit unions and other financial institutions that link those who have money with those who need it. This sector pays interest to those who deposit money into savings accounts. It also offers checking accounts, credit cards and loans to help consumers buy things. The banking sector uses the money that customers deposit to give loans to those who need money to start businesses, get an education and buy things such as homes, cars and other items.

The Functional Four sectors each provide important services and work together to keep our nation's economy running smoothly.

title: Families and Towns Were Booming
text:
World War II officially ended when the Japanese military surrendered on Sept. 2, 1945. With the war over, millions of U.S. soldiers returned to their homes, ready to resume their lives.

Many of these soldiers were in their early and mid-20s, and they were ready to get married and start families. Over the next several years, the United States saw a large increase in the number of babies that were born. It started a period of time known as the baby boom. Between 1946 and 1964, the number of births in the United States was about 76 million. People who were born during this time are known as baby boomers.

These new families needed places to live, and a businessman named William Levitt found a solution. His company worked hard to build large housing communities of affordable homes. Levitt built these communities near many of the country's largest cities. Most of the homes in these new "Levittown" communities were cheap (usually less than $8,000), and they offered a different style of life than people were used to in the cities. Many families who moved into Levittowns reported that they were extremely happy with their new lives.

As families in Levittowns settled into their new daily routines, many found themselves with money to spend. They bought clothes, furniture, household appliances and dinners at the restaurants in town. This economic activity helped the United States emerge from the Great Depression, and it began a period in history that many people agree was a good time to be an American.

title: Post WWII Immigration
text:
After WWII, President Harry Truman worked to change U.S. immigration policy to allow more immigrants into America. Before this time, the United States had put strict limits on the number of immigrants that could come to this country.

Many European people faced suffering and hardships after the war ended. President Truman directed the U.S. government to ensure that displaced persons (DPs), or people left homeless after the war, could enter the United States. Approximately 23,000 DPs entered the U.S. between 1945 and 1947. In 1948, Congress passed a law allowing another 400,000 DPs to enter the United States. Many Jewish people had no homes to return to, and some did not want to go back to a country that had tried to exterminate them. By 1952, almost 100,000 Jewish DPs had immigrated to the United States.

Many immigrants experienced discrimination. Some Jewish immigrants found acceptance in southern states, such as Alabama. They attended universities, started businesses and got involved in the civil rights movement. Asian immigrants hoped to get to the west coast of America. Leaders finally changed laws during 1952 and 1965 to adjust the system, allowing more Asians to enter the United States. In the 20 years that followed WWII, almost 5 million immigrants entered the United States. These new citizens contributed to the economies of their states and the country. But new citizens also meant more government spending for services that immigrants needed.

Today, you may hear adults arguing about our country's policies on immigration. But after the terrible times of WWII, millions of people looked to the U.S. as a land of opportunity. Families came here with the hope of starting over and building a good life. Ask family members or friends if they know of anyone who arrived here after WWII. You'd learn a lot by asking them some questions!

title: ‘Dear Mr. Veteran’
text:
After WWII ended, U.S. soldiers started coming home. The government did its best to help them find work, get an education and adjust to life at home. During the war, the government had to ration many products, or limit how much could be bought or used. People used most of the country’s resources to fight the war. To protect consumers from being charged outrageous prices for the items that were still available, the government set price ceilings. These were price limits that sellers were not allowed to go over. The government also set limits on how much money landlords could charge for houses and apartments. Read the following excerpt from a government pamphlet called “Dear Mr. Veteran,” which the government gave to soldiers returning from WWII. Then answer the questions that follow on a separate sheet of paper.

Dear Mr. Veteran

When there are ten buyers for every sirloin steak (as there have been during these past few years), prices are sure to be bid up. That’s why rationing and price and rent controls were started — to spread out the homefront supply on a fair and square basis, and keep down the cost of living. If the Government had let prices go their dizzy way without controls, many a serviceman’s wife and kids, living on an allotment, would have had to eat less and wear poorer clothing. To avoid that, the ceiling price lid was put on just about everything. Rationing has been lifted now on everything except sugar, but price and rent controls still cover the necessities of living.

You can help avoid high prices, inflation, and depression if you—and everyone else—refuse to pay or charge above ceiling prices and rents. If you think you’ve been over-charged, go to your nearest local OPA [Office of Price Administration] Price Control Board.

(This is from a pamphlet titled “Dear Mr. Veteran,” published by the U.S. Office of Price Administration. http://www.nationalww2museum.org/learn/education/for-students/national-history-day/dear-mr-veteran.pdf.)

Questions

1. Why do you think there were 10 buyers in line to buy every sirloin steak during WWII?

2. What might have happened if businesses had been allowed to set their own prices during this time period?

3. Why do you think the government gave this pamphlet to veterans returning from WWII?

4. Do you agree with the pamphlet that states that price controls kept down the cost of living? Or should businesses have been able to set their own prices without limits from the government? Explain your thinking.

title: Bundle Up!
text:
"Jackson, I see you're wearing a T-shirt and jeans today."

"That's what I wear almost every day, Alana. What's wrong with that?"

"Well, I hope you brought a coat, hat and gloves. I think you might need a warmer wardrobe for today's history lesson."

"Alana, I brought a jacket for recess, but I certainly don't need a coat, hat and gloves. It isn't that cold today. Wait a minute ... did you say something about needing warmer clothes for our HISTORY lesson? Why would I need warm clothes for that?"

"I just talked to our teacher. She said that we're going to be studying the Cold War this week, so you might want to bundle up!"

"Very funny, Alana. But seriously, I thought we were finished studying about war for a while. The world was supposed to be more peaceful, since WWII was over."

"The Cold War was a very different kind of war, Jackson. Instead of being fought by soldiers in trenches, this war was fought with ideas, words, threats and money. There may not have been bloody battles, but the Cold War was still a very scary time."

"That's right, Alana. The Cold War pitted the United States and most nations in Western Europe against the Soviet Union and most nations in Eastern Europe. During WWII, the United States and the Soviet Union fought on the same side, mostly because Germany was their common enemy. Once the war ended, the leader of the Soviet Union, Joseph Stalin, wanted to bring communist governments into power all over the world. The United States, however, wanted to stop the spread of communism and promote freely elected governments. That's when the Cold War started!"

"Yes, the U.S. formed an alliance, or friendly relationship, with the nations of Western Europe. They spent billions of dollars to help these nations recover from WWII. The Soviet Union sent secret police to control the Eastern European areas it had occupied during the war. The Communist Party took control, and people lost many freedoms. Winston Churchill, the former prime minister of Great Britain, said that an 'iron curtain' had fallen across the continent of Europe. 'Iron Curtain' became the popular name for the imaginary line dividing Europe into communist and non-communist countries."

"The Iron Curtain wasn't always imaginary, Alana. In 1961, the communist East German government built the Berlin Wall, which was a barbed wire and concrete barrier between East and West Berlin. They wanted to keep people from escaping East Germany."

"You're right, Jackson. Grab your jacket, and we'll find out how the Cold War impacted American citizens."

title: Auctioning Off the Berlin Wall
text:
The Berlin Wall was built in 1961 and came down in 1989. When East Germans learned that they could freely cross the border between East and West Berlin, they brought hammers and picks and immediately started chipping away at the Berlin Wall. More than two decades later, pieces of this famous symbol of the Cold War are still being sold to those who want to own a bit of history.

After communism's fall, workers used heavy equipment to remove the great wall that once surrounded East Berlin. Much of the concrete from the wall was crushed and used as a building material for roads. Some of the sections were preserved and donated to museums and other public locations throughout the world. Still other pieces were given to artists to use in their work. Many of these valuable works of art were auctioned off. One piece was sold for nearly $100,000!

If that price sounds a little high, you can still buy small pieces of the original Berlin Wall online, without any artistic additions, for around $60. This souvenir is a physical reminder of the suffering of those caught in the middle of the Cold War. If it was once part of the Berlin Wall, even a piece of concrete can be considered a valuable primary source!

title: Key Players and Events in the Cold War
text:
"The Cold War filled the world with fear and distrust for nearly 50 years. What happened during these years to make the Soviets and the Americans so unhappy with each other?"

"Jackson, our teacher has made an outline featuring some key players of the Cold War and the decisions they made as part of this icy conflict. Let's take a look to learn more about this long, unfriendly period of history."

After WWII ended, Truman signed the Marshall Plan. This program was designed by Secretary of State George C. Marshall to help rebuild Europe.

The Soviet Union began the Berlin Blockade in 1948. This blocked the U.S. and its allies from entering West Berlin. The Soviets hoped to take control of the entire city of Berlin.

To break the blockade, the Allies organized the Berlin Airlift. With this system, they dropped food, fuel and supplies by plane to the citizens of West Berlin. The airlift lasted nearly a year. In 1949, Berlin and the German nation were split in two. East Germany (including East Berlin) became communist and West Germany (including West Berlin) became a free republic.

In 1949, Truman led the U.S. in joining the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), a military alliance between Great Britain, Canada and the nations of Western Europe. NATO was created to keep communism from spreading across the continent and the world. The agreement between the nations states that "an armed attack against one ... shall be considered an attack against them all."

Also in 1949, the Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb, and the nuclear arms race between the two countries was on. Both countries spent billions of dollars building up large supplies of nuclear weapons. They wanted to make certain they could compete with each other if war broke out.

Truman believed that the U.S. must keep the Soviet Union from taking control of vulnerable countries and governments. The "Truman Doctrine" committed the United States to supporting the enemies of communism throughout the world.

Eisenhower worked to end the Korean War, which was fought between the communist government of North Korea (supported by the Soviet Union and China) and the free nation of South Korea. United Nations and U.S. forces kept Communists from taking control of South Korea. However, the country remained divided into communist North Korea and free South Korea even after the war ended in 1953.

While Eisenhower was president, Wisconsin Senator Joseph McCarthy headed committees to investigate the spread of communism in America. McCarthy believed that Communists were working in the U.S. government and military. In a speech to a women's group, McCarthy stated, "I have here in my hand a list of 205 [people] that were known to the Secretary of State as being members of the Communist Party and who nevertheless are still working and shaping the policy of the State Department."

The "Red Scare" was the fear that Communists had crept into the government and the arts and entertainment industry. It caused average Americans to look at each other with fear and suspicion.

In 1955, the Soviet Union joined with seven other European nations in signing the Warsaw Pact. These nations agreed to fight together against any nation that attacked one of its members.

Because of the Red Scare, hundreds of Americans had to testify before Congressional committees. Many of those who testified lost their jobs. Reputations were damaged. Some people were even imprisoned. Most of these people were actually loyal Americans with no connection to the Communist Party.

Eisenhower continued Truman's policy of resisting the spread of communism throughout the world. He said, "... forces of good and evil are massed and armed and opposed as rarely before in history. Eisenhower continued the arms race, but he warned against the growing power of the military and related industries.

In April 1961, President Kennedy sent 1,400 Cuban exiles to invade Cuba. These were people who had been forced to leave their country because of their political beliefs. The U.S. hoped they would overthrow communist leader Fidel Castro. Their invasion at the Bay of Pigs was a failure, and the exiles were either captured or killed.

In June 1961, President Kennedy met with Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev in Austria. Khrushchev threatened the U.S. and said that soon, the U.S. might be cut off from entering Berlin. A couple of months later, workers began construction on a wall around East Berlin to keep people from fleeing across the border into free West Berlin.

Khrushchev's threats and actions led Kennedy to increase American guided missiles, air power and military reserves.

In 1962, Soviets began constructing nuclear missile sites in Cuba, just 90 miles from Florida. U.S. spy planes took pictures of these sites. The events that resulted became known as the Cuban Missile Crisis.

Kennedy sent U.S. ships to form a blockade around Cuba. He also demanded that Khrushchev remove the missiles and destroy the sites. Both leaders realized that a nuclear war, which could kill millions of people, was a real possibility. Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles, as long as Kennedy promised not to invade Cuba in the future.

By the end of Kennedy's presidency, the world believed that both the Soviet Union and the United States had enough nuclear weapons to destroy each other many times over. This doctrine was called MAD, or mutually assured destruction. It meant that if one nation attacked the other, both would be destroyed. The nation first attacked would then launch weapons to defeat the attacker. This idea perhaps kept either side from starting another war.

title: How Pingpong Got the Ball Rolling
text:
During the early years of the Cold War, the United States had almost no contact with the communist nation of China, but a game of pingpong changed all that. In 1971, the American pingpong team was in Japan for the World Table Tennis (pingpong) Championships. The Chinese team invited them for a visit to the People's Republic of China.

On April 10, 1971, nine American pingpong players, along with a few journalists and officials, entered mainland China. They were the first Americans to visit since 1949! What did they do? They played pingpong, of course! The group also toured the Great Wall of China and met Chinese citizens.

This "ping" of U.S. athletes visiting China was followed by the "pong" of the Chinese team visiting the United States. Ten months after the American team's trip to China, President Richard Nixon became the first U.S. president to visit this communist country.

title: At Home During the Cold War
text:
While the Cold War raged throughout the world, what was going on here at home? Life was good for most Americans. After all the years of scrimping, saving and doing without during WWII, people now found themselves with jobs and often with some extra money to spend on luxuries. Factories were no longer making planes, tanks and ammunition. Workers built cars, refrigerators and other appliances - and people bought them!

When the troops returned from the war, they needed homes for their families. Banks offered affordable home loans, and housing communities sprang up in suburbs all across the country. Many women who had worked outside the home quit their jobs to be full-time stay-at-home wives and mothers. Others stayed in the workforce, bringing in money to help the family live a more comfortable lifestyle.

Not every family enjoyed this prosperity. Most African Americans experienced life as separate from, but not equal to, white Americans. African Americans were treated differently in jobs, schools, voting practices and many other parts of life. President Truman worked on this issue, and President Kennedy continued to push for social change.

Americans also became more interested in science and technology. When the Soviet Union launched the satellite Sputnik in 1957, it was a wake-up call to Americans. The United States felt pressured to catch up to the Soviets in the race to space. In 1961, the Soviets were the first to send a person to orbit, or circle, the Earth. America sent John Glenn into orbit in 1962. In July 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first people to land on the moon. The United States had finally taken the lead in the space race, beating the Soviets to the moon!

The Cold War was frightening at times, but life here in the United States was also better than ever. A new sense of freedom, opportunity, hope and prosperity made life good for many American families.

title: Point of View: Gail Halvorsen-The Candy Bomber
text:
With the Berlin Airlift, American pilots dropped more than just food and supplies into West Berlin. An American pilot named Gail Halvorsen dropped candy and gum attached to small, white handkerchief parachutes to the children of West Berlin. He started by gathering up candy from fellow pilots, and word of his candy drops spread. American citizens also donated candy and gum to send to the German children. Halvorsen became known as the Candy Bomber. By the time the Berlin Airlift ended, he and his pilot friends had dropped over 20 tons of chocolate, gum and other candies into West Berlin.

Complete the chart by writing the point of view of each person or group of people. How do you think Gail felt about the “bombings”? What do you think the candy deliveries meant to the children of West Berlin? Do you think the American and Soviet leaders approved or disapproved of Gail’s actions? Why? Write your answers on the lines in the boxes. Then on a separate sheet of paper, draw a picture of a child or group of children receiving one of the Candy Bomber’s deliveries.

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you are an American child growing up during the Cold War. Why would it have been important to you to stay ahead of the Soviets in the race to explore outer space? What would you have thought and felt about the Soviets’ ability to launch a satellite into space before Americans? Include lots of examples, and be sure to use correct spelling, grammar and punctuation.

title: Think & Review
text:
1. What was the Cold War? When did it start? How long did it last? Which nations opposed each other in this war?

2. What does NATO stand for? What was the purpose of NATO during the Cold War?

3. Define MAD and explain the MAD doctrine. How did it keep the Soviets and the Americans from attacking each other?

4. What was the Red Scare? Which U.S. senator led this movement? What effect did it have on our nation?

5. Choose a president discussed in the lesson and write about how he dealt with the Cold War. Cite your source(s) in your answer.

title: When Two Superpowers Collide!
text:
Jackson and Alana are visiting Alana's grandparents after school. They spend time exploring the attic, where they discover a collection of old comic books.

"Wow, Alana! I had no idea your grandpa collected comic books. This old Incredible Shadow versus General Scream comic is amazing!"

"Well, my grandpa isn't actually the comic book collector in the family, Jackson. It's my grandma! She loves them, especially the Incredible Shadow comics. They're her favorite."

"You have one cool grandma, Alana. Take a look at this edition. It shows the Incredible Shadow and General Scream, his archenemy, facing off in an epic battle that could destroy millions of innocent people. After all, General Scream doesn't care who gets in his way in his quest to destroy the Incredible Shadow and take over the world."

"Archenemies can mean big trouble, Jackson."

"Yes, an archenemy is the hero's main enemy. Incredible Shadow and General Scream match each other with strengths and weaknesses. It seems that neither one can defeat the other."

"So, what happens when these two archenemies go up against each other?"

"They struggle with each other and cause a lot of destruction, and usually neither one actually wins."

"Do you know what this reminds me of, Jackson? It's today's history lesson."

"Do you mean when our teacher introduced the Korean War?"

"That's right. I mean, think about it. Communist North Korea, supported by the Soviet Union, faces off against free South Korea, supported by the United States. It was a war that pitted two superpowers against each other. Could either country actually win the war, especially when both sides had access to nuclear weapons that could destroy the other?"

"I never would have thought of it that way, Alana. But I can see how the Soviet Union and the United States could be archenemies, just like General Scream and the Incredible Shadow. The Korean War certainly showed how going to battle against an equally powerful enemy leads to a lot of destruction, without any real winners."

"That's just what I was thinking, Jackson. This week, we'll learn more about the Korean War and what happened when two superpowers went to battle against each other."

"Sounds interesting, Alana. Just let me finish this comic book first. ..."

title: Honor Flights for Korean War Vets
text:
Physician assistant and pilot Earl Morse started the Honor Flight Network to bring WWII veterans to Washington, D.C. He wanted them to see the National WWII Memorial. Dr. Morse worked with WWII veterans daily in his medical practice, so he knew how much visiting this important war memorial would mean to these aging veterans. He also knew that most of them had no money or support to take that kind of trip.

In 2005, the first Honor Flight Tour left Springfield, Ohio, bringing 12 WWII veterans to the memorial in Washington, D.C. The trip was completely free for the veterans. Since that time, volunteers and donors from all over the country have stepped up to make the Honor Flight Network a huge success.

Today, many veterans of the Korean War are also invited to fly, free of charge, to visit the Korean War Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C. The Honor Flight website states, "... our veteran heroes aren't asking for recognition. It is our position that they deserve it. Our program is just a small token of our appreciation for those that gave so much."

To learn more about the Honor Flight Network, including how to donate to this organization, visit https://www.honorflight.org/.

title: The Korean War
text:
"Jackson, I know that the Korean War was a major standoff between two world superpowers, the United States and the Soviet Union. But, what was this conflict really about? How did it start? And why is the country still divided into North and South Korea today?"

"Those are good questions, Alana. Let's dig a little deeper and find out some important details about this war. We can use the map to pinpoint the locations where each of these events took place."

The Korean War Begins

After WWII, the Korean peninsula was divided into communist-led North Korea and U.S.-supported South Korea. With the support of the Soviet Union, North Korean forces invaded South Korea on June 25, 1950. About 90,000 soldiers from the North Korean People's Army rushed across the 38th parallel (38 degrees north of the equator). This was the boundary between North and South Korea. North Korea hoped to reunite the country under a communist government. Within a few days, the South Korean capital of Seoul had fallen to the North Korean Army. The United Nations (U.N.) called for its members to help South Korea in its fight against the communist invaders.

America Enters the War

The U.N. passed a resolution calling for its members to send troops to help South Korea. President Truman sent U.S. troops, under the direction of General Douglas MacArthur, to South Korea. North Korea drove the South Koreans and their allies south to an area near the port city of Pusan (also known as Busan). The South Koreans were on the run, and things looked hopeless for the U.N. forces. Gen. MacArthur organized a daring plan to send ships to invade the port of Inchon, near Seoul. The attack was on Sept. 15, 1950, and it surprised the North Koreans. U.S. forces recaptured Seoul, cut the North Korean supply lines and forced the North Koreans back across the 38th parallel. MacArthur believed that the war would be over shortly.

China Joins the War

U.N. forces crossed the 38th parallel and headed toward the Yalu River (the border between North Korea and China). China warned the U.S. to stay away from the border unless it wanted an all-out war with China as well as North Korea. President Truman was afraid that if China entered the war, a third world war could easily start. Such a war would include the danger of both sides using nuclear weapons. Truman warned Gen. MacArthur against approaching the border at the Yalu River with U.S. troops. MacArthur felt that there was "no substitute for victory" and planned to push the communists out of both North and South Korea. MacArthur attacked troops along the Yalu River, but the Chinese had 300,000 troops ready to push them back. The Chinese had entered the war. Truman fired Gen. MacArthur for failing to follow his orders.

U.N. Forces Pushed Back

After China entered the war, the North Koreans and the Chinese began pushing the U.N. forces south again. U.N. forces retreated back across the 38th parallel and out of Seoul once more.

Peace Talks Begin

Leaders met in Panmunjom in July 1951 to work on a peaceful solution. Both sides were willing to sign an agreement that kept the 38th parallel as the dividing line between North and South Korea. But there were other details, including the treatment and release of prisoners of war. This kept the two sides from agreeing to end the war. After more than two years of discussions, officials finally reached an agreement.

Panmunjom Armistice

Dwight D. Eisenhower, the famous WWII general, was elected president in 1952. One of his main goals was to end the Korean War. Officials from both sides finally reached an agreement at Panmunjom on July 27, 1953. The agreement allowed the prisoners of war to choose where they preferred to live, either North or South Korea. It also set a new boundary near the 38th parallel. The boundary included a 2-mile-wide "demilitarized zone" at the border. Neither side was allowed to station military troops or weapons in this zone.

Results of the War

Korea remained divided into North and South Korea, with the communists keeping control of North Korea. Both sides still keep troops stationed outside the demilitarized zone. The U.S. achieved its goal of preventing the spread of communism into South Korea, but this success came at a terrible price. Historians estimate that between 2.5 and 5 million people died in the Korean War. Many of those who lost their lives were Korean civilians, not soldiers. Nearly 40,000 American soldiers died in action, and more than 103,000 were wounded.

title: Redstone Arsenal and Missile Development
text:
Redstone Arsenal was built in Huntsville, Alabama, at the beginning of WWII. An arsenal is a place where weapons are made or stored, and this arsenal was built to make chemical weapons. After WWII, the plant stopped production for a while.

It didn’t take long for the U.S. to realize that its greatest threat came from the Soviet Union and its development of new weapons. Then the Korean War crisis brought an urgent need for the United States to further advance its weapons. The U.S. brought German engineers and scientists to Redstone Arsenal to continue their work. Here, these scientists built the Redstone Rocket. A later model, the Jupiter-C missile, took the first U.S. satellite into space in 1958.

During the Cold War of the 1960s and 1970s, Redstone Arsenal was home to the U.S. Army Missile Command (MICOM) and 19 major missile systems, including missiles used in later conflicts. Today, Redstone Arsenal is home to the Army’s missile testing and development program.

title: General Douglas MacArthur: Determined Soldier
text: Douglas MacArthur graduated from the United States Military Academy at West Point. He went on to lead Army troops into battle in WWI, WWII and finally, the Korean War. Gen. MacArthur retired from the military in 1937, but he was called back into active duty once WWII began. When the Korean War broke out in 1950, Gen. MacArthur was chosen to lead the U.N. forces against North Korea. He and his troops showed great courage and strength when they attacked North Korean troops at Inchon. They eventually drove them north toward China. In his enthusiasm to push the communists out of Korea, MacArthur deliberately disobeyed orders from President Truman. MacArthur was fired for insubordination, or refusing to obey orders. In spite of being fired, he returned home to a hero’s welcome. He stuck by his actions, stating: “In war there is no substitute for victory.” Do you agree with what Gen. MacArthur did?

title: The Korean War Veterans Memorial
text:
"Jackson, I'm so glad we get to visit the Korean War Veterans Memorial on our trip to Washington, D.C.! I had no idea it was this close to the Lincoln Memorial."

"I know, Alana. Many tourists don't know about all of the war memorials here in our nation's capital. The Korean War Veterans Memorial was dedicated in 1995 to honor all Americans who served in the U.S. military during the Korean War. Nearly 40,000 American soldiers lost their lives in battle during this war. I love the simple message engraved on one wall: 'Freedom Is Not Free.'"

"I see that the Korean War Veterans Memorial has three parts, Jackson: a polished granite wall, a group of stainless steel statues and a reflecting pool. The main part of the memorial is made up of a 164-foot wall. I love the look of that polished black granite!"

"I love the 2,500 photographs from the Korean War that are etched into the stone. These images show troops from every branch of the military fighting for freedom in Korea."

"I think my favorite part of the memorial is the 19 stainless steel statues representing the Army, Air Force, Navy and Marines. Look how these 19 soldiers are reflected in the polished stone wall, bringing their number to 38. That represents the 38th parallel, as well as the 38 months that the Korean War lasted."

"I also like the Pool of Remembrance, Alana. It's a shallow pool lined with more polished, black granite. Engravings list the number of soldiers killed, wounded, missing in action and held as prisoners of war. Another engraving reads, 'Our nation honors her sons and daughters who answered the call to defend a country they never knew and a people they never met.'"

"What a perfect field trip. I'm taking plenty of pictures to show our friends and families back home!"

title: MacArthur Versus Truman
text:
As you learned in this week’s lesson, Gen. MacArthur and President Truman disagreed about the goal of the Korean War. MacArthur believed that the goal was to expand the war to rid the world of communism. Truman wanted to limit the spread of communism without attacking China or other communist nations.

Here are brief statements from each of these important leaders. Read the statements and answer the questions that follow.

General MacArthur

“It seems strangely difficult for some to realize that … if we lose the war to communism in Asia the fall of Europe is inevitable, win it and Europe most probably would avoid war and yet preserve freedom. As you [Congressman Joseph Martin] pointed out, we must win. There is no substitute for victory.” —from a letter written by General Douglas MacArthur to Congressman Joseph W. Martin on March 20, 1951

President Truman

“I believe that we must try to limit the war to Korea for these vital reasons: to make sure that the precious lives of our fighting men are not wasted; to see that the security of our country and the free world is not needlessly jeopardized; and to prevent a third world war.

A number of events have made it evident that General MacArthur did not agree with that policy. I have therefore considered it essential to relieve [fire] General MacArthur so that there would be no doubt or confusion as to the real purpose and aim of our policy.” —Speech by President Truman, April 11, 1951

Questions

1. What did Gen. MacArthur believe would happen if no one pushed communism out of Asia?

2. What three reasons did President Truman give for limiting the war to Korea?

3. What did President Truman do when Gen. MacArthur failed to obey his orders?

4. What reason did Truman give for making this choice?

5. Why do you think Truman felt the need to make this information public?

title: Let's Write
text: The border between North and South Korea remained essentially the same at the end of the Korean War, but things were different. Explain how life changed from when the war started in 1950 to the end of the Korean War in 1953. Be sure to use correct grammar, spelling and punctuation.

title: Think and Review
text:
1. What is an “archenemy”? Why were the United States and the Soviet Union considered archenemies?

2. Analyze the goals of the Korean War from North Korea’s point of view. Why did they attack South Korea? Why did China get involved in the war?

3. What is the 38th parallel? Explain its importance to the Korean War. Why is the 38th parallel still important today?

4. What were the final results of the Korean War? Which side won?

title: A Sign Pointing to the Past
text:
Jackson and Alana spend a rainy afternoon in the attic of Alana’s grandparents’ home. …

“I love being up here, Alana. I’m still hoping that one day we’ll find a treasure chest filled with gold coins.”

“I doubt we’ll ever find anything worth quite that much money, Jackson. But we have discovered a lot of valuable primary sources up here.”

“That’s right, Alana. Look, there’s a stack of old yearbooks. I wonder what your grandma and grandpa looked like back in high school.”

“Definitely younger. Let’s have a look!”

“First, I’ll have to move this old road sign out of the way. Wait a minute. Why do your grandparents have a road sign in their attic? It says, ‘Historic Route—Selma to Montgomery: National Historic Trail.’ What does that mean?”

“We should ask Grandpa Frank!”

(The kids take the road sign down to the living room, where Grandpa Frank is reading the newspaper. They ask him about the sign, and he’s happy to explain.)

“This road sign was given to me by a dear friend. It’s a copy, a replica, of the road signs put up to honor protestors in 1965.”

“Oh, it’s a replica, so that’s why we didn’t go anywhere when we touched it.”

“Right, Jackson. The protestors marched from Selma to Montgomery to tell the world that African Americans should be allowed to vote without discrimination. The 15th Amendment was passed after the Civil War, and it gave African Americans the right to vote. Not everyone liked the change. People in many cities throughout the South tried to stop African Americans from voting by making them pass tests and pay money to register.”

“How did marching from Selma to Montgomery change anything, Grandpa Frank?”

“Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC) led a group of protestors on a march from Selma, Alabama, to the state capital of Montgomery. They did this to show support for changing the law. On a previous march, state troopers had beaten demonstrators and sprayed them with tear gas. I joined this larger march, and we didn’t give up. We covered the 54-mile distance in three days and ended up on the grounds of the Alabama State Capitol. Dr. King spoke to the crowd there.”

“Wow, Grandpa, that’s amazing! Did they get the right to vote at this time?”

“Congress passed the Voting Rights Act in August 1965, partly because of the march from Selma to Montgomery. The Act made it illegal to give tests for voter registration. The law also made sure that the federal government had the right to supervise elections.”

“No wonder you hung onto this road sign, Grandpa Frank. It’s a great reminder of an amazing period in our history.”

“That it is, Alana!”

title: The 50th Anniversary of ‘I Have a Dream’
text:
On Aug. 28, 1963, civil rights leader Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his famous "I Have a Dream" speech on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial. Dr. King spoke of his dream that someday people of all races and religions would treat each other as equals and not as enemies. He mentioned the Emancipation Proclamation signed by Abraham Lincoln. Dr. King talked about the day that freedom would ring "from every city." This speech became one of the best known in American history.

Fifty years later, President Barack Obama stood on that same spot to honor Dr. King. He was there to celebrate the years of progress for African Americans and other minorities in their fight for fair and equal treatment. Former presidents Jimmy Carter and Bill Clinton also spoke at the event. They urged Americans to continue to free this country from discrimination and to encourage acceptance and appreciation of people from all backgrounds. Much progress has been made since 1963, but there is still room for improvement!

title: People and Events of the Civil Rights Movement
text:
“Jackson, I can’t wait to learn more about the civil rights movement. I know that civil rights are rights guaranteed to all citizens by the Constitution. What an exciting time in our nation’s history!”

“You said it, Alana! Let’s dive in and explore some of the key people and events of this movement that worked to bring equality to all citizens of the United States.”

1. Desegregation in the Military

Through WWII, the U.S. military was separated, or segregated, by race. African Americans in the military didn’t serve alongside white soldiers. They instead served in their own units.

On July 26, 1948, President Harry Truman issued an executive order. This order made it illegal to discriminate against any member of the military because of race, color, religion or national origin. The desegregation in the military gave hope to civil rights leaders that change was possible.

2. Brown v. Board of Education

In 1951, an African American man named Oliver Brown sued the Board of Education in Topeka, Kansas. He was angry because his child was not allowed to attend Topeka’s all-white public schools. The Supreme Court had previously ruled that as long as conditions were equal, segregation was legal. The 1954 court case, called Brown v. Board of Education, stated that segregated schools had never been, nor would they ever be, equal. All nine Supreme Court justices ruled in favor of Brown. Their decision meant that schools had to begin integrating, or allowing African Americans and whites to attend school together, as quickly as possible.

3. Little Rock Nine

In 1957, nine African American students entered Little Rock Central High School. This was an all-white school in Arkansas. Governor Orval Faubus called in the Arkansas National Guard to stop the African American students from attending. President Dwight D. Eisenhower sent in Army troops to escort the nine students to class. These military guards went with the students to school every day throughout the school year. However, the nine students were still bullied inside and outside the school by people protesting student integration.

4. Woolworth Sit-in

On Feb. 1, 1960, four African American college students sat down at a “whites only” lunch counter inside a Woolworth store in Greensboro, North Carolina. They waited to be served. The students were refused service, and the manager asked them to leave. The young men sat at the lunch counter until the store closed for the day. The next day, over 20 students showed up. By the end of the week, there were over 300 African American students (and some white supporters) waiting to be served. Sit-ins spread across the South over the next five months, and on July 25, the first African American customers were served at Woolworth’s lunch counter. Segregated lunch counters across the South soon followed Woolworth’s example.

5. Freedom Riders

In May 1961, the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) organized a group of protestors to take bus trips throughout the South. Their goal was to encourage the desegregation of bus stations. These passengers were called Freedom Riders. They entered bus stations and tried to use “whites only” rest rooms and waiting rooms. The Freedom Riders were often violently attacked and arrested, but they kept up their protests. In September 1961, rules about segregation in bus stations changed. African Americans would use the same facilities as whites.

6. March from Selma to Montgomery

On March 7, 1965, 600 civil rights protestors began marching from Selma, Alabama, toward Montgomery. They marched to promote equal voting rights for African Americans. The march was stopped six blocks away at the Edmunds Pettus Bridge, where state troopers attacked them. This event became known as “Bloody Sunday.” Under the protection of the federal government, another group of about 3,000 protestors set out a few weeks later. When this group arrived in Montgomery (after walking over 10 miles a day), the number had grown to 25,000 people! Less than five months later, President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

7. Rosa Parks

Rosa Parks was an African American seamstress on her way home from work one day in Montgomery, Alabama. She refused to give up her seat on the bus to a white man, so police arrested her. To protest this unfair treatment, many people boycotted, or refused to use, the Montgomery bus system. This protest lasted nearly 13 months until the Supreme Court finally ruled that bus segregation was illegal.

8. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.

Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was an African American preacher and civil rights leader. He used nonviolent methods to work for fair and equal treatment for all people. Dr. King gave speeches, participated in protests and worked with the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC) to end discrimination. He was assassinated on April 4, 1968.

9. Charles K. Steele

African American preacher and civil rights leader Charles K. Steele worked with Martin Luther King Jr. as vice president of the SCLC. He helped organize the Tallahassee bus boycott. This event helped stop segregation on buses in Florida.

10. Fred L. Shuttlesworth

Civil rights leader Fred L. Shuttlesworth was another member of the SCLC and a minister from Birmingham, Alabama. He was part of the Birmingham Campaign. This project’s goal was to end discrimination in restaurants, stores and public places throughout the city.

11. John Lewis

The work of Martin Luther King Jr. inspired John Lewis. He helped organize sit-in demonstrations at segregated lunch counters throughout Nashville, Tennessee. Lewis was also a Freedom Rider, as well as one of the organizers of the march from Selma to Montgomery. He worked to form voter education programs and was elected to the U.S. Congress in 1986.

title: Thurgood Marshall: A Justice for All
text:
Thurgood Marshall applied to the University of Maryland School of Law, but he was turned down because he was African American. His mother then sold her wedding rings to pay for his tuition at Howard University School of Law in Washington, D.C.

After graduating, Marshall opened a law office in Baltimore, Maryland. He became a lawyer for the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). He worked with this organization for 25 years. Marshall argued the famous Brown v. Board of Education case before the Supreme Court. He won the case and paved the way for African Americans to attend school alongside their white peers.

In 1967, President Lyndon Johnson chose Marshall to serve as the first African American Supreme Court justice. While on the Supreme Court, Thurgood Marshall worked to protect the civil rights of all Americans. He retired in 1991 and died in 1993.

title: Television Contributes to the Civil Rights Movement
text:
Television and the civil rights movement spread throughout the United States at about the same time. In 1950, less than 10 percent of U.S. homes had televisions. Ten years later, when the civil rights movement was expanding, there were about 60 million televisions in American homes. This meant that 90 percent of American families owned a television set!

Television brought the civil rights movement into the homes of American families in a way that newspaper and radio could not. As the civil rights movement continued, people in the North saw footage of the march from Selma to Montgomery, the Woolworth sit-ins in Greensboro and protests in Georgia. Television helped draw support from people who otherwise might not have known much about the battle for equality.

title: Remembering the ‘Not-so-Good Old Days’
text:
Read the following quotes by people who lived during the civil rights movement. Use the lines to explain in your own words what each person might have been thinking and feeling.

Courtland Cox, who registered African American voters, 1964

“We went down to McComb [Mississippi]. The FBI was there. They said to us, ‘Look, don’t make any mistake about it. We’re here to protect the evidence. We’re not here to guard you or protect you.’ … Then the guy said to us, ‘Look, how many guns do you have?’ And we said, ‘We don’t have any guns.’ And he said, ‘Well, I’ve got two and I’m scared to death.’”

Ruby Sales, who registered African American voters, 1965

“What we saw, we would knock on doors [in Alabama], talk with people, and sometimes we saw poverty that was so extreme … we sometimes saw children who were hungry, needed to be in school but had no shoes. We saw men and women out in the fields, picking cotton and picking cucumbers … we saw … a community living under the grind and weight of segregation determined not to be terrorized or intimidated.”

Jewish leader Dr. Joachim Prinz, at the March on Washington, Aug. 28, 1963

“When I was the rabbi of the Jewish community in Berlin under the Hitler regime, I learned many things. The most important thing that I learned under those tragic circumstances was that bigotry [prejudice] and hatred are not the most urgent problem. The most urgent, the most disgraceful, the most shameful and the most tragic problem is silence.”

Dr. Joyce Ann Ladner, speaking about driving with her white roommate, Joan Trumpauer, in the early 1960s

“I used to carry around a black scarf in my pocket, and when were driving back to Tougaloo College at night on this long stretch of road called Hanging Moss Road, there were no lights. And Tougaloo was eight miles from downtown Jackson [Mississippi] … I’d say, ‘Well, you’ve got to put this scarf on you because your long blonde hair is not going to get me killed.’ And because people you know would’ve shot at us even if they’d just known we were movement workers. …”

title: Foods That Fueled the Civil Rights Movement
text:
“Thanks for inviting me to your grandma’s house for lunch, Jackson. I don’t think I’ve ever eaten real soul food before!”

“You’re welcome, Alana. My grandma makes the best food! Right, Gigi?”

“Why thank you, Jackson. My aunt taught me how to cook, and I’ll teach you! Today, I’ve made fried chicken, okra, macaroni and cheese, fried green tomatoes and corn bread.”

“I’ll take an extra helping of fried green tomatoes, Gigi.”

“Not so fast, Jackson. I heard that you learned about the civil rights movement last week. I want to see how much you know.”

“Alright, Gigi. Try me!”

“Who was the famous civil rights leader who led the march from Selma to Montgomery, Alabama, and what was the march all about?”

“That’s easy. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. led the march to help African Americans get the right to vote.”

“That’s right, Jackson! Have an extra helping of tomatoes!”

“How about me, Gigi? I’d love another piece of corn bread!”

“Then answer this question, Alana. Who was Rosa Parks, and how did she contribute to the civil rights movement?”

“She was a seamstress from Montgomery, Alabama, who refused to give up her bus seat to a white man. She was arrested, and this event kick started the Montgomery Bus Boycott. African Americans refused to ride the city buses for more than a year, until the buses were finally desegregated.”

“Good job, Alana! You’ve earned yourself another slab of corn bread. Did you all know that Martin Luther King Jr., John Lewis and other famous leaders of the civil rights movement used to meet at a restaurant named Paschal’s? When they were in Atlanta, Georgia, they often met at the restaurant to discuss their plans for bringing civil rights to the South. Paschal’s gave the leaders free food and a friendly place to plan things.”

“That’s cool! I know I think better when I have a full stomach.”

“That’s right, Jackson. There’s nothing like good food and sharp minds to solve tough problems. Now, if you kids want a piece of sweet potato pie, tell me this. What was a sit-in and where was the first one held?”

“The first sit-in was held at the Woolworth lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina. Four African American college students sat down at the all-white lunch counter and asked to be served. When they were refused, they stayed at the counter in protest. The next day, even more people showed up. Sit-ins spread across the South. Finally, Woolworth’s agreed to serve both whites and African Americans. Other lunch counters soon followed its example.”

“Great answer, Alana. You’ve earned your dessert! Now, let’s talk a little more about the civil rights movement while we eat.”

“We’re ready—for the pie AND the stories!”

title: MyPlate Has Soul!
text:
In 2011, the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) introduced MyPlate, a new set of guidelines for healthy eating. The program uses an illustration of a dinner plate to help kids and adults plan healthy meals. According to MyPlate, half of each meal should be filled with fruits and vegetables, a quarter should be made up of grains and one quarter should be filled with protein. Meals should also include a cup of low-fat milk or yogurt. Your favorite soul foods can fit into these new guidelines if portions are kept small and healthier recipes are used. Try the corn bread recipe here! Be sure to ask an adult for help.

Southern Corn Bread

Ingredients

2 eggs, beaten

1 cup cornmeal (try whole-grain cornmeal)

1 cup milk

1 cup flour (try white whole-wheat flour)

¼ cup vegetable oil

2 teaspoons baking powder

1 teaspoon salt

1 tablespoon sugar

½ cup corn (fresh, canned or frozen—thawed)

Directions

1. Preheat oven to 400° F.

2. Put all the ingredients (except for the corn) into a large bowl.

3. Beat the ingredients together with a large spoon until the mixture is smooth.

4. Stir in the corn.

5. Spray an 8 x 8-inch baking pan with nonstick spray and pour mixture in.

6. Bake in the oven for 25 to 30 minutes or until the cornbread is light brown on top.

7. Remove bread from the oven, let cool for a few minutes and cut into nine pieces.

title: Leaders and Laws of the Civil Rights Movement
text:
“Alana, all that delicious food really made me ‘hungry’ to learn more about the civil rights movement.”

“Same here, Jackson. Let’s see what’s on today’s menu … The Civil Rights Acts of 1964 and 1968, Malcolm X, voter rights and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Sounds like a feast for the brain!”

Civil Rights Act of 1964

President Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 on July 2, 1964. It outlawed discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin. Segregation became illegal in schools, hotels, theaters, restaurants and other public places.

Civil Rights Act of 1968

Four years later, on April 11, 1968, President Johnson signed The Civil Rights Act of 1968. This act, which was also known as the Fair Housing Act, made it illegal to refuse to sell or rent a house or apartment to anyone because of race, religion, national origin or sex.

Malcolm X

Malcolm Little joined a religious group called the Nation of Islam (NOI) while he was in prison as a young man. When he was released, Little decided to change his name. He believed that slaveholders had forced the last name “Little” onto his ancestors. Malcolm replaced his last name with the letter “X,” which represented his unknown past. From then on, he was known as Malcolm X.

Malcolm X later became a minister in the NOI. The NOI preached about evils of the white community and believed that African Americans were a superior race. Malcolm spoke about equal rights for African Americans, but he believed in segregation. He also felt that African Americans needed to practice self-defense, including the use of violence if necessary.

Malcolm X became a powerful leader in the civil rights movement, but he also made many enemies. Three of these enemies assassinated him on Feb. 21, 1965.

title: MLK: One Man, One Dream
text:
Martin Luther King Jr. (MLK) was one of the most famous and influential leaders of the civil rights movement. Use the timeline here to learn more about this important man and his impact on our nation’s history.

Jan. 15, 1929: MLK is born in Atlanta, Georgia, the son of a Baptist minister and a former teacher.

1944: Graduates from Booker T. Washington High School and is admitted to Morehouse College at the age of 15

1948: Graduates from Morehouse College at age 19 and is ordained a Baptist minister

1951: Attends Boston University for graduate school

1953: Marries Coretta Scott; moves to Montgomery, Alabama

1955: Receives doctorate degree of philosophy from Boston University; is elected president of the Montgomery Improvement Association (MIA) and becomes spokesman for the city’s bus boycott

1957: Helps form and becomes president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC)

1960: Moves to Atlanta to work full time with the civil rights movement; joins his father as a pastor at the Ebenezer Baptist Church

1962: Is arrested in Albany, Georgia, and agrees to stop demonstrations there

April 1963: Is arrested for demonstrating without a permit and held in Birmingham Jail for 11 days; Birmingham announces desegregation of stores, restaurants and schools

August 1963: Delivers “I Have a Dream” speech at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C.

1964: Earns the Nobel Peace Prize

1965: Organizes and participates in the march from Selma to Montgomery to draw attention to voter rights

April 4, 1968: MLK is assassinated on the balcony of his hotel room in Memphis, Tennessee.

1986: First national celebration of Martin Luther King Jr. Day

title: Constitutional Amendments and Equal Voting Rights
text:
15th Amendment: The 15th Amendment gave all African American men the right to vote. Many Southern states found ways to keep African Americans from voting by charging a poll tax and requiring literacy (reading and writing) tests.

19th Amendment: The 19th Amendment was ratified, or approved, by each state in 1920. Known as the women’s suffrage amendment, it gave all American women the right to vote. Susan B. Anthony, Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott were just a few of the women’s rights leaders who worked for many years to persuade citizens and Congress to change voting laws.

23rd Amendment: This amendment gave the residents of Washington, D.C., the right to vote in presidential elections. Before this amendment became law in 1961, people who lived in our nation’s capital could not vote for a president!

24th Amendment: The 24th Amendment made it illegal for Congress or individual states to charge citizens a poll tax in order to vote. This change made it easier for African Americans to vote. The amendment was ratified in January 1964.

26th Amendment: During the 1960s, thousands of 18-year-old men were drafted into the Army to fight in the Vietnam War. At the time, the voting age was 21. Many of these soldiers believed that if the government thought they were old enough to fight in a war, they were also old enough to vote. Congress agreed with them, and on July 1, 1971, the 26th Amendment became law. The amendment lowered the voting age from 21 to 18.

title: Songs of the Civil Rights Movement
text:
Hi! Alana here to let you know that the civil rights movement wasn’t just about speeches, marches and food … it was also about music. The movement had its very own “soundtrack”—a mix of songs that helped keep the fire burning in the hearts of reformers across the nation.

Singers and songwriters who believed in the movement used music to tell their stories and to let others know what they could do to help. Famous artists like gospel and soul singer Aretha Franklin, folksinger and songwriter Bob Dylan and even the wildly popular British group the Beatles, sang songs that helped promote civil rights.

“Respect,” by Aretha Franklin, let the world know that African Americans (and women!) expected and deserved to be treated with just that, proper respect. Bob Dylan’s “Oxford Town” tells of a man who was mistreated “because of the color of his skin.” Paul McCartney, a member of the Beatles, wrote and sang “Blackbird,” inspired by the African American women of the movement.

Religious hymns were also an important part of the movement. “We Shall Overcome” became an unofficial anthem at protests and events. The entire crowd would join in and sing the following words:

We shall overcome, we shall overcome,

We shall overcome someday;

Oh, deep in my heart, I do believe,

We shall overcome someday.

Music helped spread the message of the civil rights movement, and it expressed a spirit that words alone just couldn’t convey.

title: Montgomery, Alabama - A Center of the Civil Rights Movement
text:
Montgomery is located along the Alabama River in south central Alabama, and it serves as the state capital. The city was also the original capital of the Confederacy during the Civil War.

During the 1950s and 1960s, Montgomery became an important part of the civil rights movement. Like most cities in the South during this time, Montgomery was a segregated city, meaning that African Americans and whites were separated in public places. African Americans and whites sat apart on public buses, ate in separate restaurants and used separate rest rooms and drinking fountains.

Rosa Parks’ refusal to give up her seat on the bus to a white man led to the famous Montgomery bus boycott, which lasted from early December 1955 to late December 1956 (381 days). During this time, African Americans refused to ride the city buses, causing the city to lose thousands of dollars from lost bus fares. The boycott finally ended when the courts ruled that segregation of buses was unconstitutional.

In 1965, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. led the famous march from Selma to Montgomery in support of voting rights for all African Americans. The march ended at the state capitol building in Montgomery, where Dr. King gave a speech to more than 25,000 people, pleading that the rights of ALL Americans be protected. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 was passed later that year.

If you visit Montgomery, be sure to visit the Rosa Parks Library and Museum, the Dexter Avenue King Memorial Baptist Church and the Selma to Montgomery National Historic Trail.

title: Moving Forward
text:
Jackson and Alana are in the middle of another attic adventure. …

“Hey, Alana, look what I found! I think it’s an old cassette tape recorder.”

“I remember that thing! Grandpa Frank used to let me play with it when I was little. He would give me a blank cassette tape and let me walk around the yard, recording all the sounds.”

“There’s still a cassette tape in here. Let’s hit ‘play’ and find out what’s on it.”

(Jackson pushes the “play” button, and the kids begin to laugh. For some reason, the tape recorder is playing in “fast forward” and the voices sound frantic.)

“Wow, Alana! Is that how this is supposed to sound?”

“No, Jackson, definitely not. I recognize the voices on the tape, though. That’s Grandpa Frank and Grandma Minnie telling me about the day I was born. I used to play ‘news reporter’ sometimes and use this tape recorder to interview them. Listen carefully and you can still understand what they’re saying.”

“Rewind the tape, Alana, and let me hear it again. I can understand the words, but they’re talking so fast that I can’t really put the story together. It sounds like Grandpa Frank and Grandma Minnie had too much coffee!”

“Let’s go show Grandma Minnie and see what she says.”

(The kids bring the tape recorder down to Grandma Minnie in the kitchen. She rewinds the tape, hits “play” and begins to laugh.)

“Oh, I’m sorry but that tape recorder is broken! It sounds like it’s stuck in fast-forward mode. But you know, this actually reminds me of the period in history we’ve talked about lately. The time after WWII, the Cold War, the space race, assassinations and the civil rights movement— we all felt like we were living in fast-forward mode!”

“I never thought of it that way, Grandma Minnie, but I guess you’re right. There really were a lot of things happening all at once!”

“You said it, Alana. Sometimes, I felt like my head was spinning. A person had to pay attention, or you got left behind. Notice that if you listen to the tape very carefully, you can actually understand the information, but if you get distracted, you’re lost!”

“It sounds like we better pay attention during our study of this period or we’ll miss out on the real story.”

“That’s right, Jackson. Are you ready to learn more about one of the most dynamic periods of America’s history?”

“You bet. Let’s get started!”

title: Home, Sweet Hole in the Ground
text:
Would you like to live in a hole in the ground? Well, that’s just what some adventurous Americans have chosen to do. These creative homeowners are turning old Cold War missile silos (deep shafts dug into the ground to house Atlas missiles) into high-class homes.

When the United States and the Soviet Union were gripped by the Cold War, dozens of cavernous cement-lined silos were dug across the United States. They stored deadly missiles that could be fired at the enemy in case of war. By 1965, advances in missile technology made these outdated silos useless, and the government sold them or gave them away.

Now some imaginative silo owners are fixing up these huge holes, turning them into dandy dwellings that can be about nine stories deep. (You can research about how many silo homes are currently in the United States.)

Owners say that silos make great homes because they are strong and secure. (After all, they were built to withstand a nuclear bomb blast.) Tornadoes won’t blow them down, termites won’t chew them up, and these sturdy structures will last for centuries.

Owners have also found other uses for their silos. Some have become factories. One is a museum and warehouse in Weld County, Colorado. Another near Holton, Kansas, has been a high school for more than 30 years. One Texas man even teaches scuba lessons in his flooded silo.

People are discovering that the missile silos of the Cold War make strong, comfortable, creative homes and businesses. About the only thing these underground castles don’t offer is a great view.

title: America's Relationships Abroad and at Home
text:
"The '50s and '60s were a busy couple of decades in our nation's history, Alana. So much growth and change ..."

"They sure were, Jackson! Let's dive into how America's relationships with countries around the world and with its citizens changed during this time."

Working Together on the World Stage

After World War II, many countries realized they needed to do a better job of working together. In the months and years that followed, several groups formed that help leaders from around the world work together to prevent wars and keep economies strong. Some of the more important of these global organizations are the United Nations, NATO and OPEC.

The United Nations

In October 1945, the United Nations, or U.N., was officially organized. The purpose of the group was to create a way for countries around the world to work together to protect human rights, to establish equal rights for all and to promote peace, justice and freedom. Close to 200 countries from around the world have joined the United Nations, which is headquartered in New York City. The United States has been one of the most important countries involved in the U.N. since it was formed.

NATO

The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) was formed in April 1949, when several nations joined together to keep communism from spreading. The organization agreed to mutually defend all its members, stating that an attack on one would be considered an attack on them all. During the Cold War, NATO also worked to prevent a nuclear war by standing against the Soviet Union and its allies, promising to attack the Soviets with nuclear weapons if they ever used theirs. NATO has assisted the United States on several occasions in the last 60 years, including supporting U.S. troops in Iraq and Afghanistan.

OPEC

The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) was founded in September 1960. Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela formed the organization to control the prices and supply of oil to the rest of the world. OPEC tries to keep oil prices stable, in order to protect the economies of oil-producing and oil-purchasing countries. OPEC produces about 80 percent of the crude oil in the world. The United States purchases much of the oil we use for fuel from countries that are members of OPEC.

Affirmative Action in Action!

During the civil rights movement, our country made progress in bringing equal rights to all Americans. President Kennedy signed an executive order in 1961 that created a policy called affirmative action. "Affirmative action" meant that government officials were required to hire people based on their abilities and not on their race, religion or national origin. In 1967, President Lyndon B. Johnson expanded affirmative action by adding gender to the list.

Affirmative action focused on making sure that women, African Americans and other minorities were given the same opportunities at work and in college that white men received. Businesses were directed to change their policies when recruiting and training minorities for job opportunities. Colleges were expected to adjust their methods for awarding college admission or scholarships. Some universities and businesses even created quotas, which meant that a certain number of minorities had to be accepted or hired.

Affirmative action faced some challenges. Some people felt that affirmative action caused reverse discrimination against white males, giving jobs and college admission to less-qualified minority students in order to "look good." As a result, people who still felt they were being treated unfairly filed lawsuits against several businesses and universities. Some of these lawsuits made it to the Supreme Court, which eventually ruled that quotas were unfair.

Today, affirmative action is still a debated topic. Some people feel it has done its job and is no longer needed. Others, however, believe that women and minorities still do not receive fair pay or opportunities and that the government should step in to ensure equal treatment.

title: Where Were You?
text:
People usually remember where they were and what they were doing when a tragedy strikes. People who were alive during the bombing of Pearl Harbor or the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, can probably tell you exactly what they were doing when they heard the news. The same is true for people who remember the assassinations of President John F. Kennedy and his brother, Senator Robert F. Kennedy.

President Kennedy was shot and killed as he rode in an open car through the streets of Dallas, Texas, on Nov. 22, 1963. Nearly five years later on June 5, 1968, Kennedy’s brother Robert, a U.S. senator and presidential candidate, was shot in a Los Angeles hotel after giving a campaign speech. He died from his injuries the next day.

These assassinations shook the nation, and they created feelings of fear, distrust and worry. Both men had become symbols of hope and peace, and people wondered what would happen since they had been killed. In fear and sadness, some people wondered if foreign nations or a government conspiracy had something to do with the assassinations. They feared that they would never know all the answers and that the government was keeping secrets from them. The assassinations made many Americans more fearful, and nearly everyone felt less secure.

Find two people who were alive when the Kennedys were assassinated. Ask where they were when they heard the news. Then ask how they felt and how life changed for them afterward. You may interview teachers, family members, neighbors or people in your community. Use the space here to record the information you collect.
