title: Inventions of the 1950s and 1960s
text:
During the 1950s and 1960s, middle-class families had money to buy luxuries that they hadn’t been able to afford before. With many people in the market for goods that made life easier, businesses produced new inventions and products like never before. Here’s a quick look at some of the popular inventions of the 1950s and 1960s:

1. Barbie Doll

Invented by Ruth Handler in 1959, the Barbie doll wasn’t the usual baby doll toy. It was a doll modeled after a young woman. Barbie became a favorite of young girls across the country, and dressing Barbie in her fashionable outfits became an American pastime. The original Barbie came with either black or blond hair and was dressed in a zebra-striped swimsuit.

2. Cassette Tapes

In 1966, small cassette tapes replaced the large, reel-to-reel tapes of the past. These small cassettes made it easier for people to listen to music. At first, cassette players were only available in cars, but handheld versions soon followed. Cassette tapes are hard to find now since compact discs and MP3 players have replaced them.

3. Artificial Heart

Can you imagine living with an artificial heart? Dr. John H. Gibbon Jr. developed the first successful heart-lung machine in 1953. Four years later, surgeons implanted a plastic artificial heart inside a dog. By 1969, the first complete artificial heart was implanted in a human. This work led Dr. Robert Jarvik to develop the Jarvik-7 artificial heart in 1982. It was implanted into Barney Clark, who lived for 112 days using this device.

4. Calculator

Texas Instruments developed the first handheld calculator in 1967. It didn’t have a display screen, but it printed answers on a paper tape. This calculator was about 6 inches long and weighed less than 3 pounds. The TI Cal-Tech could add, subtract, multiply and divide. Today we use calculators that do so much more!

title: The Space Craze
text:
Jackson and Alana are looking at old TV listings from the 1960s. It seems there were lots of television shows about space!

"Jackson, can you believe there were this many different TV shows about space? Seriously, we could have watched 'The Jetsons,' 'Lost in Space,' 'My Favorite Martian' or 'Star Trek,' just to mention a few. What's the deal?"

"Well, remember how the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the world's first satellite, in 1957? The U.S. was clearly behind in the space race, and they meant to catch up! In 1961, after the Soviets sent an astronaut into orbit, President Kennedy announced that we would send an American safely to the moon before the end of the decade. America reached this goal on July 20, 1969, when Neil Armstrong took 'one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind' on the moon's surface. No wonder everyone wanted to watch TV shows about space!"

"The space race did more than just get people to make these TV shows, Jackson. It also prompted Congress to pass the National Defense Education Act in 1958. The act provided millions of dollars to help American students compete with the Soviets. The government encouraged schools to start foreign language programs and improve math and science courses."

"Guess what else, Alana? I read that parents started buying educational toys like chemistry sets, telescopes and models of the solar system for their kids."

"I guess the whole country was a little obsessed with space, but it turned out to be a good thing in the long run. We won the space race and ended up with better schools as a bonus!"

title: Cheering for the Home Team - USA!
text:
Jackson and Alana are exploring the attic, looking for more treasures. ...

"Alana, are you playing in the community basketball league again this year?"

"I think so, Jackson. It's a lot of fun, and I really like being part of a team. Two years ago, our team took first place. Last year we didn't do so well, but we still had a good time. Are you going to play soccer this year?"

"I'm not sure yet. I might try baseball. I think I want to do something different. But I agree with you, Alana. It's great to be on a team. Hey, what's this? It looks like a pennant from a sports team. It's from Ohio University - check out the bobcat!"

(The kids grab the pennant and find themselves transported to Ohio University in Athens, Ohio. They look around and see that they're in the middle of a large crowd of people who are all listening to someone giving a speech.)

"Jackson, I think we're at Ohio University. Look at the clothes these people are wearing. ... I think we've gone back to the 1960s!"

"Shhh, Alana. I think we're supposed to be listening to the speech. It looks like it might be pretty important."

"Who's speaking? Is it Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.? I've always wanted to meet him. Can you see who it is?"

"It's not Dr. King, but I think I recognize who it is. This is President Lyndon B. Johnson's famous 'Great Society' speech. He gave this speech at Ohio University. In it, he introduced his plans to create a Great Society here in the United States by getting rid of poverty and making life better for everyone."

"Wow! I guess hearing President Johnson speak is pretty amazing, isn't it? Let's listen in and see if we can learn anything about his plans!"

... And with your courage and with your compassion and your desire, we will build the Great Society. It is a Society where no child will go unfed, and no youngster will go unschooled. Where no man who wants work will fail to find it. Where no citizen will be barred from any door because of his birthplace or his color or his church. ... Reach out for it now. Join the fight to finish the unfinished work in your own land and in the rest of the world. ... That is what you can do.

title: The Peace Corps
text:
In October 1960, John F. Kennedy was a senator working hard on the campaign trail to become president. Kennedy gave a speech at the University of Michigan, and he asked the students if any of them would be willing to travel the world after graduation, giving service to struggling nations. Over 1,000 students volunteered. They would have to wait, however, until after Kennedy was elected president and formed the Peace Corps.

President Kennedy wanted the Peace Corps to send trained workers to countries that needed help. He wanted them to teach people in other parts of the world about the United States, and the volunteers themselves could learn about people from other cultures. The first volunteers traveled to Africa in 1961. Since then, the Peace Corps has had more than 7,000 volunteers serving in 65 different countries. Nearly half of Peace Corps volunteers serve in Africa. The rest are assigned to countries in Asia, Latin America, the Middle East and the Caribbean and Pacific Islands.

Peace Corps volunteers must be at least 18 years old and willing to commit to three months of training followed by two years of service in a foreign country. The volunteers aren’t paid, but they do receive a small allowance each month for food, housing and basic supplies. Volunteers live and work alongside the people of the country in which they serve. A majority of volunteers work as educators or health workers, with others becoming involved in the environmental, economic or agricultural issues facing the area.

title: Johnson's Great Society
text:
"When Lyndon B. Johnson became president, he set goals to end poverty, promote equality, improve education and protect the environment."

"It seems like he achieved those goals, Alana. Johnson's ideas for creating a Great Society helped bring real change to the United States."

Johnson Takes Office

Two hours after President Kennedy was assassinated on Nov. 22, 1963, Johnson was sworn in as president of the United States while aboard Air Force One. As the country mourned the loss of their beloved president, Johnson did his best to continue in Kennedy's footsteps. Johnson decided to follow up on some of Kennedy's plans for the nation. This included plans to reduce taxes and protect civil rights.

Johnson led the fight to pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964, first introduced by Kennedy. After Congress passed the law, Johnson continued pushing for a tax cut, and he was successful in this effort as well. In addition, Johnson had to work on his re-election campaign. He was again successful. In the 1964 presidential election, it was clear Johnson had convinced Americans that the country was getting better, and he defeated his opponent, Barry Goldwater, by almost 16 million votes.

Great Society

In the spring of 1964, Johnson began using the term "Great Society" to describe his plan for ending poverty and bringing prosperity, or success and wealth, to all. Johnson was the first president to present such a huge plan to help Americans since Roosevelt introduced his New Deal. Johnson had grown up in a small farmhouse in Texas, and he never forgot the hard times of his youth. During the early 1960s, about 20 percent of American families lived in poverty. Johnson wanted to change this. He announced, "This administration today, here and now, declares unconditional war on poverty in America." Once again, Johnson was successful, and by the end of his presidency the number of people in poverty dropped to 13 percent.

Jobs

The Economic Opportunity Act of 1964 created the Job Corps and other training programs to give people the skills needed to find jobs. The Job Corps is a free education and training program that helps low-income youth 16 years old and older continue their education, prepare for a career and keep a good job. Johnson also said that the act was intended to "help poor farmers stay on their farms" and "help the unemployed heads of families to maintain their skills and learn new skills." The Job Corps has operated out of 125 different centers around the country and continues to offer job training for teenagers in need.

Education

Johnson was once a teacher, and he believed that an important way to end poverty was to make certain that all Americans received a good education. In 1965, Johnson oversaw the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, providing money to teachers and schools in low-income areas. Part of the act called for the formation of a program called Head Start. Johnson wanted a program that provided low-income children and their parents with health, nutrition and education services. Legislation also focused on teacher training. Head Start has helped over 30 million children throughout the country.

Medicare and Medicaid

When Johnson took office, nearly half of older Americans did not have health insurance. High medical bills caused many seniors to face poverty with no hope for relief. As part of the Great Society, Johnson's administration created Medicare, a government program that provides health insurance for Americans 65 years old or older. Medicare helps pay for doctor and hospital visits, medical supplies and prescription drugs. When Medicare first started, nearly one in three Americans over age 65 lived in poverty. Today, this number has been reduced to about one in 10. Medicaid, a program that provides similar health services for the poor, was also created at this time.

Renewal of Cities

Following WWII, many cities suffered a shortage of safe, affordable housing. Businesses and workers began moving to the suburbs, leaving cities that had fewer jobs or safe places to live. African American communities in America's largest cities were hit especially hard by these changes. This led to tension and anger among many who lived there.

On Aug. 11, 1965, white Los Angeles police officers arrested an African American man suspected of drunk driving in the Watts neighborhood. As bystanders watched, a fight broke out that quickly grew into a riot. The riot lasted five days, spreading throughout the Watts neighborhood, and it left 34 dead, 1,032 injured, 4,000 arrested and $40 million worth of property damage. Similar riots later broke out in Detroit, Michigan; Newark, New Jersey; and other American cities.

Johnson knew that something had to be done to improve living conditions and bring new life to America's largest cities. As part of the Great Society, Johnson signed the Housing and Urban Development Act of 1965. This act created the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), which has provided funds to build safe, affordable housing for low-income families.

Conservation

Johnson was also very concerned about the environment. With his support, Congress passed more than 300 conservation acts to protect our country's land, water and natural resources. These acts include the Clean Air Act of 1963 and the Highway Beautification Act.

title: Robert C. Weaver, Advisor to Presidents
text:
Robert C. Weaver devoted his life to helping others. He worked with President Franklin Roosevelt, advising his administration on African American issues. Weaver also advised President Kennedy and was the head of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP).

In 1966, President Johnson appointed Weaver to serve as the first head of the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). He was the first African American to become a Cabinet member. In this position, he worked to provide more housing programs and end housing discrimination. Weaver believed that all families deserve a place to call home, and he spent his career working to make it happen.

title: Johnson and the Vietnam War
text:
The Vietnam War began in 1954 when communist North Vietnam attacked South Vietnam. The North Vietnamese had the goal of uniting the country under communist rule. Presidents Eisenhower and Kennedy both sent money and weapons to help South Vietnam fight back. They also sent American military experts to help teach the South Vietnamese army how to fight.

When Johnson became president, he vowed that he would not let communism spread to South Vietnam. In 1964, Johnson decided it was time to send combat troops into Vietnam. The first troops arrived in February 1965, and in March the president began Operation Rolling Thunder, a series of bombing raids over North Vietnam.

In early 1965, President Johnson proposed a $1 billion development project along Vietnam’s Mekong River if North Vietnam would agree to enter peace discussions. To Johnson’s surprise, this offer was rejected, and the war continued. By the end of 1965, nearly 200,000 American soldiers had arrived in Vietnam as the Air Force continued its bombing campaigns. By the beginning of 1968, more than 500,000 American soldiers were fighting in Vietnam, and almost 20,000 Americans had been killed in action. The war raged on with no end in sight.

Support for Johnson was fading. Many Americans believed that the Vietnam War was a civil war that should be settled by the Vietnamese people without interference from the United States. Money that the U.S. had budgeted to pay for Johnson’s Great Society was now being used to fund the war. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. said, “The promises of the Great Society have been shot down on the battlefields of Vietnam.” Protesters rallied against the war. Meanwhile, the number of soldiers killed rose to 50,000, and few people believed the U.S. military was capable of winning. Trusted news anchor Walter Cronkite declared his belief that the Vietnam War would end in a stalemate, in which neither side would win. In 1968, President Johnson had become so unpopular that he announced he would not run for re-election.

President Johnson died before the Vietnam War ended in 1973. Even though he made progress in many areas, many people remember Johnson for how he handled Vietnam. You will learn more about the Vietnam War in the next issue of Studies Weekly.

title: Let Them Eat Watergate Cake!
text:
Jackson and Alana are with Grandma Minnie in her kitchen. They're discussing plans for a bake sale to raise money for a "Presidential Timeline" school exhibit. ...

"I think your school's idea to make a Presidential Timeline is fabulous, Alana. It will help you and your friends learn about history in a fun way."

"I think so too, Grandma. And thanks for helping us with the bake sale. We need all the help we can get!"

"Yeah, thanks, Grandma Minnie, but I'm not so sure about your choice of recipes. Why did you pick Watergate Cake?"

"Well, your class is in charge of researching President Nixon for the timeline, so Watergate Cake will be perfect, Jackson. It's delicious! It's made with pistachio pudding, lemon-lime soda and chopped walnuts. The best thing about it is the green 'cover-up' frosting!"

"Cover-up frosting? What is that?"

"To understand about the cover-up frosting, you need to know a little bit about the Watergate scandal."

"I've heard of Watergate, but I guess I'm not really sure what it was."

"In June 1972, during President Nixon's re-election campaign, several burglars were arrested for breaking into the Democratic National Committee headquarters in the Watergate building in Washington, D.C. These burglars were caught as they tried to put 'bugs,' or listening devices, on the phones in the office of the Democratic headquarters. These burglars were later connected to President Nixon, and a huge scandal erupted. They were trying to find information to help the president get re-elected."

"Sounds like trouble to me, Grandma. I understand why you want to make a Watergate Cake for the bake sale, but why is this particular cake called Watergate Cake?"

"President Nixon loved pistachios, which is an ingredient in this recipe. During the scandal, pistachio-flavored cakes and treats became very popular. People just started calling them Watergate Cakes!"

"That makes sense, Grandma, but what about the cover-up frosting?"

"That's easy. The frosting covers up the cake, just like President Nixon tried to 'cover up' his involvement in the Watergate scandal. He gave money to the burglars to try to keep them quiet, but the truth came out. Nixon resigned in 1974."

"That's a pretty incredible story, Grandma. Now that we know the history of your Watergate Cake recipe, let's get down to business and start baking. Oh, and let's make two cakes - one for the bake sale and one for us to eat - with plenty of cover-up frosting!"

"Great idea, Jackson!"

title: Presidential Snack Facts
text:
Do you think President Nixon's favorite dessert was Watergate cake? Many U.S. presidents are known for having a favorite food. In fact, some of our recent presidents have so enjoyed their favorite munchies that they have influenced America's snack choices! Here's a peek at some of the go-to snacks of a few of our presidents.

Franklin D. Roosevelt: old-fashioned fruitcake

John F. Kennedy: ice cream with hot fudge sauce

Richard Nixon: pistachios; cottage cheese and ketchup - President Nixon often ate this combination for breakfast, but it was also one of his favorite snacks.

Gerald Ford: butter pecan ice cream

Jimmy Carter: peanuts - President Carter's family was in the peanut business.

Ronald Reagan: jelly beans - His favorite flavor was licorice. President Reagan gave "presidential" jelly beans as gifts to foreign leaders.

George H.W. Bush: pork rinds - These became so popular during his presidency that companies had to increase production to keep up with the demand for these crispy, fried bites.

Bill Clinton: burgers

George W. Bush: pretzels - President Bush choked on a pretzel while watching football and had to receive treatment from a presidential medical team.

Barack Obama: chocolate caramels

title: Problems Abroad
text:
Vietnam War Timeline

1954

Vietnam has been a French colony for many years. Nationalist forces push the French out of the country, and Vietnam divides into communist North Vietnam and U.S.-supported South Vietnam.

1959

Communist leaders in North Vietnam announce the use of force on South Vietnam, to unify the country as a communist nation. (1)

1961

The U.S. increases its involvement by sending money, weapons and military advisors to South Vietnam.

1963

Ngo Dinh Diem, President of South Vietnam, is assassinated. (2)

1964

Congress passes the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution after a skirmish between North Vietnamese and U.S. ships. This resolution gives President Johnson the power to use military force in Vietnam. (3)

1965

Operation Rolling Thunder begins, and the first U.S. combat troops arrive in Vietnam.

1967

U.S. forces engage in many air battles and damage North Vietnamese airfields. (4)

1968

January: North Vietnam begins the Tet Offensive, attacking 100 cities in South Vietnam. (5)

May: Peace talks begin in Paris. The two sides are unable to reach an agreement, and the talks continue for over three years.

November: Richard Nixon wins the 1968 presidential election. (6)

1969

January: President Nixon takes office with a plan for the "Vietnamization" of the war. His plan calls for the slow withdrawal of U.S. troops, while continuing to support the South Vietnamese with money, supplies and weapons. Eventually, the Vietnamese people were to fight their own war.

March: President Nixon approves secret bombings of Cambodia, an ally to North Vietnam.

June: Nixon announces first withdrawal of U.S. troops from Vietnam.

November: War protests increase, but Nixon asks for the "silent majority" of Americans to support his efforts in Vietnam. (7)

1970

An anti-war protest at Kent State University in Ohio ends in disaster when the Ohio National Guard opens fire on a group of unarmed college protesters, killing four students and wounding nine others. (8)

1972

Nixon increases bombings of North Vietnam, hoping to convince the North Vietnamese to negotiate a peaceful end to the war. North Vietnam continues fighting.

1973

The U.S. signs a cease-fire agreement with North Vietnam and withdraws all remaining U.S. combat troops. The agreement establishes a cease-fire and defines a temporary border until the countries are peacefully reunified. Both North and South Vietnam violate the cease-fire, and battles continue.

1974

President Nixon resigns the presidency due to his involvement in the Watergate scandal. Vice President Gerald Ford is sworn in as president. (Read "Problems at Home" for more information!)

1975

Without the support of the U.S., South Vietnam leaders are forced to surrender to North Vietnam forces. The country is reunited under communist rule.

title: Problems at Home
text:
"Alana, what did you think about President Nixon resigning from office in 1974?"

"He had to, Jackson, or he would have been impeached. That's something I learned while researching the Watergate scandal for our Presidential Exhibit."

"Let's share with our friends what we learned about Watergate. ..."

On June 17, 1972, five men were caught breaking into the headquarters of the Democratic National Committee (DNC) in the Watergate building in Washington, D.C. It was an election year, and the men were gathering information they thought would help Richard Nixon win re-election.

President Nixon denied having anything to do with the break in. He claimed that the burglars had acted on their own. Unfortunately, as the investigation continued it became clear that the president was lying. Investigators discovered that the men had broken into the DNC headquarters in order to repair listening devices. These "bugs" had been installed in the office phones a few weeks earlier. The burglars had been paid with money that investigators were able to prove came from President Nixon's re-election fund. Nixon still claimed that these men had acted without his permission, and he went on to win re-election in 1972. In 1973, one of Nixon's staff members told investigators that the president had a tape recording system in his office and that he recorded all his conversations. Congress asked the president to give the tapes to investigators, but Nixon refused.

In July 1974, the Supreme Court ruled that the president must surrender the tapes. He did so, and the tapes proved that he had been involved in the scandal. The investigation also proved that Nixon had used the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) to harass his political enemies. The House of Representatives prepared to impeach the president, or charge him with serious crimes. Rather than face impeachment, Nixon chose to resign as president on Aug. 9, 1974.

title: Vietnam Moratorium Days
text:
On Oct. 15, 1969, two anti-war activists named David Hawk and Sam Brown organized the first Vietnam Moratorium Day. A "moratorium" means a delay, or postponement, of something. Hawk and Brown wanted people to postpone their regular jobs for the day and instead focus on creating peace. Moratorium Days were held all over the country, many on college campuses.

One month later, an even larger Vietnam Moratorium Day was held in Washington, D.C. More than 500,000 protesters gathered and were joined by famous singers and performers. Folk singer and activist Pete Seeger led the crowd in singing John Lennon's song, "Give Peace a Chance." Throughout the song, Seeger would call out, "Are you listening, Nixon?" and "Are you listening in the Pentagon?"

Anti-war demonstrations continued to be held across the country throughout the war.

title: The Helicopter War
text:
Helicopters had been used in World War II and the Korean War, but it was during the Vietnam War that they truly became a valuable part of the military. Helicopters are versatile vehicles, and they were used to transport troops, deliver supplies, evacuate wounded soldiers and perform search-and-rescue operations. Many helicopter pilots received their training at Fort Rucker in southeastern Alabama.

One of the most popular helicopters used in the Vietnam War was the UH-1 Iroquois, nicknamed "Huey." There were not many places in Vietnam where airplanes could land, and the terrain was difficult to travel on foot. Helicopters quickly became the best way to move troops to where they were needed.

Many Hueys were also armed with bombs and machine guns. This meant they could attack enemy soldiers from the air. The U.S. used more than 7,000 of these helicopters in the war, and they greatly supported our troops who fought in the war. The Vietnam War is often called the helicopter war because of the important role the aircraft played in the conflict.

title: On TV Tonight (and Every Night This Week) - Nixon Visits China!
text:
Every evening during the week of Feb. 21-28, 1972, Americans sat down in front of their televisions to watch coverage of President Nixon's historic trip to China. It was the first time any U.S. president had visited the People's Republic of China. Nixon referred to his trip as the "week that changed the world."

The president felt that it was important to build a friendly relationship with the communist nation of China. He hoped that both U.S and Chinese leaders could reach understandings that would allow for trade between the two nations. In addition, Nixon genuinely wanted to see the country and meet the people.

Do you remember reading about the American pingpong team's invitation to visit China? Nixon saw it as an opportunity to make his dream of a visit to China a reality. Soon after the pingpong team's visit, Secretary of State Henry Kissinger traveled to Beijing to arrange a presidential visit.

On Feb. 21, 1972, President Nixon and his wife arrived in China. American TV crews traveled with him and recorded nearly every moment of the visit. Nixon's staff planned carefully to make sure that TV crews always caught the president at his best and that he always looked "presidential." Nixon was about to run for re-election and he knew the trip to China was a great opportunity to persuade the country that another four years of his leadership was just what America needed.

Throughout the weeklong visit, the president attended banquets, met with Chairman Mao Zedong and toured the Great Wall, all with the media nearby. TV coverage of Nixon's trip to China impressed the American public and helped him win re-election, in spite of the looming Watergate scandal.

title: Peace, Love and Flower Power
text:
Alana's grandparents have asked the kids to go up in the attic to find a special box labeled "Flower Power." They need the box before April 22!

"So, we're supposed to find a big box labeled 'Flower Power.' What do you think is inside of it?"

"I don't know, Alana. Maybe some kind of machine that turns flowers into electricity?"

"I doubt that, Jackson, but you never know. What about that box under the window? Look at the huge sunflower glued to the side!"

"Let's see ... yep! It says 'Flower Power' right here on the top. Let's drag it downstairs and open it up."

"I have a better idea! Let's open it right now and see what's inside!"

(The kids open up the large box and find it jam packed with clothes, peace symbols, jewelry and record albums from the 1960s.)

"Look at all this stuff, Alana! It looks like a flower garden exploded in here! We've seen clothes kind of like these before. Look at this wild, fringed vest. Who do you think wore it, Grandpa or Grandma?"

"I think that's a man's vest, Jackson. Try it on! It would look great over this awesome flower-pattern shirt I found."

"You should try these peace necklaces. Oh look! These striped bell-bottom pants are the best. They'll look awesome with this tie-dyed T-shirt!"

"Jackson, I remember what flower power is, and it has nothing to do with electricity. Do you remember how the Vietnam War protesters used peaceful demonstrations to speak out against the war? Look, here's a poetry book by Allen Ginsberg. He told protesters to give flowers to police officers and to those who came to watch their protests."

"Is that why so many hippies wore flowered clothing? Hey! I'll bet it's also why they called themselves flower children. Flowers represented peace, so they planned to stop the war using flower power."

"You've got it now, Jackson. We should take this stuff down to Grandpa and Grandma. I'm sure they have some amazing stories about all these hippie relics."

"They always do! I have one more question, though. Why do you think they need this box before April 22?"

"I just searched for 'April 22' on my tablet. April 22 is Earth Day! Maybe flower power is also connected to saving the Earth somehow. If hippies wanted peace, my guess is that they wanted to save the Earth as well."

"Sounds right to me! Now, let's get this box downstairs. Do you really think that your grandparents used to be hippies?"

"Let's go ask them!"

title: So Long, Hippie Bus!
text:
During the 1960s, the Volkswagen Kombi was one of the favorite vehicles of the hippie movement. The vehicle was inexpensive, roomy and easy to repair. The Kombi was commonly called the "hippie bus." People often repainted hippie busses with bright colors and large flowers. Many hippies used these vehicles as rolling homes.

The Kombi has been a useful vehicle for many different people around the world. They have used Kombis as mail trucks, school busses and even ambulances. Some people have even installed kitchens and used a Kombi to cook and sell food to people on the street. To the hippie generation, however, the bus represented the freedom to hit the open road and travel freely.

Volkswagen officially said "goodbye" to the hippie bus in 2013 after more than 60 years of production. However, thousands of Kombis are still on the road and are expected to last for a while. With a few repairs, a new floral paint job and a little luck, the world can hang on to the hippie bus for years to come.

title: The Hippie Movement
text:
"Where are we, Alana?"

"Look at that street sign, Jackson. We're at the intersection of Haight and Ashbury in San Francisco. It looks like we're in the middle of a huge hippie convention ... good thing we asked Grandma and Grandpa about that box!"

"I know. It's amazing that your grandparents were part of the hippie movement!"

"They sure were. They weren't at Woodstock or in the march on the Pentagon, but they did wear the clothes, promote peace and participate in Earth Day."

"I sure love your grandma and grandpa, Alana. They had all kinds of stories to tell! ..."

Have you ever heard an adult say "My generation didn't have ..." or "This generation just doesn't understand!" Well, these kinds of things were said in the 1960s, too. The hippie movement began during the '60s among our nation's young adults. This generation had not experienced the hardships of the Great Depression or World War II. They had more opportunities and better educations than older generations, and many of these young people wanted to be free to do as they pleased. Many young people felt that the older generation did not understand them.

One goal of the hippie movement was to shock the older generation into changing ideas about "proper behavior and appearance." The "natural" look became popular. Young men allowed their hair, mustaches and beards to grow out. Women also grew their hair long and wore long, flowing skirts. Hippies borrowed clothing styles from other cultures, and tie-dyed shirts and bell-bottom jeans were common. People were often barefoot everywhere they went. As the movement grew, it promoted love, beauty and peaceful solutions to society's problems. Many in the older generation, however, did not like that hippies were rejecting society's traditional ways. People who had lived through the Depression and World War II thought hippies were taking advantage of the hard work their elders had done.

Promoting Peace

During the summer of 1967, an area of San Francisco known as Haight-Ashbury became a center of the hippie movement. Thousands of young people flocked to the neighborhood to join the movement. These months, known as the Summer of Love, marked a time when young people focused on art, music, freedom, drugs and meditation.

The movement made more of a statement in the fall of 1967. Groups of hippies organized gatherings to protest the Vietnam War, the government and society in general. Around 100,000 people gathered in Washington D.C. from October 21 to 23 to join a march on the Pentagon. Writers and war veterans joined the march, and together the crowd spoke out against the Vietnam War. Some protesters brought flowers to place in the gun barrels of police officers. Not everyone remained peaceful, however. A section of protestors became violent, and police fired tear gas into the crowd. Over 600 people were arrested.

President Johnson responded to concerns about the war by telling the people, "We are making progress. We are pleased with the results we're getting." That changed in January 1968 as the North Vietnamese began the Tet Offensive. Americans realized that the war was far from over. Many Americans began to agree with the hippies. Support for the Vietnam War began to drop as more and more people started to ask, "When will there be peace?"

title: Woodstock
text:
Come and make history! An event so huge, it boggles the mind! It's guaranteed to change your life forever!

What: The Woodstock Music & Art Fair - a gathering of music makers and music lovers dedicated to promoting peace, love and flower power.

Who: Some of the greatest musicians of all time! Scheduled performers include Janis Joplin, The Who, Canned Heat, the Grateful Dead, Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young, Country Joe & The Fish, Jimi Hendrix, Joan Baez, Arlo Guthrie, Jefferson Airplane, Blood, Sweat and Tears and Santana.

This event is organized and presented by John Roberts, Joel Rosenman, Artie Kornfeld and Michael Lang.

When: Woodstock is scheduled for Aug. 15-17, 1969.

Where: Thanks to the generosity of dairy farmer Max Yasgur, the Woodstock Music & Art Fair will be held on his 600-acre dairy farm in Bethel, New York, about 50 miles southwest of the city of Woodstock.

(The concert was originally set for an industrial park in Wallkill, New York. However, the city leaders decided that they didn't want a "bunch of hippies" to invade their town.)

Why: Concert organizers hope to raise money to build a recording studio and retreat for rock musicians in Woodstock, New York. They also hope to show the world the strength of the hippie movement and the power of peace.

The organizers of Woodstock originally planned for around 50,000 people to attend the concert, but the number quickly grew to about 500,000! People broke through fences and organizers weren't able to collect tickets, so Woodstock turned into a free concert. This news quickly spread, and even more people tried to attend. Traffic jams clogged the streets and concert-goers abandoned their cars to reach the concert on foot. Heavy rains turned the fields to mud, and there were very few toilets and long waits for food. Concert organizers weren't able to make money on the event. Despite these challenges, Woodstock became known as one of the most influential music gatherings in history.

title: A High-Tech Age Begins
text:
The 1960s were an amazing time for new technologies. Computers had been around, but it wasn't until the '60s that they started showing up in large numbers at businesses and campuses of America. Since then, computers have become an essential part of business and education.

Other technologies were born or made popular during the 1960s. Scientists worked with lasers and launched the first communication satellites. People wore electric watches, wrote with felt-tip pens and used photocopy machines. Advances in machinery allowed for aluminum packaging of food and soda pop. This sudden growth in technology even helped NASA send astronauts to the moon and back!

These new technologies brought new jobs. Americans could now work as computer programmers for technological industries that would have seemed like a dream just a decade earlier. Think about how far we've progressed since the '60s!

title: Earth Day—Not Just for Hippies!
text:
Gaylord Nelson (right) was a U.S. senator from Wisconsin who decided to organize the very first Earth Day. He chose April 22, 1970, as a day of "teach-ins" across the country. The teach-ins were meant to show people how to clean up our world and make it a better place. Around the same time, other groups organized protests to pressure government leaders to start passing laws that protected the environment.

Around 20 million Americans were involved in the first Earth Day. Since then, the movement has spread across the world, with nearly 1 billion people joining together to celebrate every April 22nd.

How can you celebrate Earth Day? Activities can be big or small. Many people your age have spent the day planting trees, making compost bins, recycling, taking walks to pick up trash or sending letters to politicians. The possibilities are endless!

title: Dolores Huerta and Cesar Chavez: Yes It Can Be Done!
text:
The Vietnam War was not the only issue that had people worried. Many of America's farm workers felt they were being treated poorly. Dolores Huerta and Cesar Chavez organized a union in 1962 called the National Farm Workers Association (later called the United Farm Workers). A union is a group that is formed to protect workers' rights. The National Farm Workers Association wanted better pay and safer conditions for migrant workers. The union took their demands to the owners of large farms and ranches. Huerta and Chavez organized strikes, or "huelgas," against owners who refused to meet workers' demands.

In 1965, grape workers in California began a strike, or a refusal to work, in several vineyards. Chavez joined the strike and asked Americans to boycott grapes grown in California until the workers received better treatment. The grape workers' strike lasted until 1970, when growers finally agreed to contracts with workers. The union's phrase "Si se puede!" or, "Yes it can be done!" became the motto for the union and for many workers across the country.

title: Forging Ahead
text:
Let's join Jackson, Alana and their class for a school field trip to Vulcan Park and Museum in Birmingham, Alabama...

"Alana, can you believe the size of that statue of Vulcan? It's a 56-foot-tall, 101,200-pound cast iron statue, and it really blows me away!"

"Vulcan is pretty impressive, Jackson. He's the Roman god of the forge, and I know a forge is a workshop where blacksmiths heat, hammer and shape metal. I'm all for field trips, but I'm not quite sure how visiting Vulcan Park and Museum will help us make connections to WWII."

"Once we finish our tour of the museum, you'll see that steel played a huge role in the war. Take a look at this exhibit, for example. It says here that people settled in this area because of the huge deposits of iron ore. Coal and limestone were also found here. These two ingredients are combined with iron ore to make steel. By 1900, the city of Birmingham was home to blast furnaces and steel mills. The city even took its name from the famous industrial city of Birmingham, Great Britain."

"That's all very interesting, Jackson, but I'm still not sure what steel has to do with WWII."

"Alana, what do you think the Allies needed in order to fight the war?"

"Well, they needed soldiers, uniforms, food, weapons and vehicles. Hmmm ... I think I'm starting to get the picture now. Weapons and military vehicles are made with steel, so the U.S. needed a way to produce these items here at home. That's where Birmingham comes in, right?"

"Bingo, Alana! During the Great Depression, the demand for steel dropped sharply, and many steel businesses closed down. Birmingham was known across the country as a city hit hard by the Great Depression. Once WWII started, however, the demand for steel to make military supplies went way up and Birmingham was back in business."

"Jackson, the exhibit says that some of the steel produced here in Birmingham was used in Mobile, Alabama, shipyards to build more than 200 ships! The Mobile shipyards gave jobs to those who had the most difficult time finding work, including African Americans and women." Factories also used Birmingham steel to build helmets and ammunition for the war. That definitely went a long way to help the Allies fight the Germans and the Japanese!"

"I guess it makes sense that Vulcan, the supercharged blacksmith, stands as a symbol of the city of Birmingham. After all, it took the power of heated metal to help win WWII!"

title: The Power of Oral History
text:
The Holocaust was the mass murder of more than 6 million Jews by the Nazis during WWII. The world was shocked when it found out about the terrible suffering of Jews in concentration camps and the mass murders carried out there. Researchers preserve the stories of those who survived the Holocaust by saving survivors' oral histories (interviews recorded on audio or video). These accounts serve as testimonies to us that these events happened, and they help us to prevent such evils from ever happening again.

Agencies such as the Holocaust Memorial Center in Michigan send interviewers to record the stories of those who lived through this event. They want to visit people who survived being held in concentration camps, those who spent the war in hiding, people who escaped from Germany or those who offered help to Jews during this period. Interviewers are also interested in stories of soldiers who found the horrible results of Hitler's extermination camps at the end of the war.

Many Holocaust survivors have already died. Those who are alive are elderly and often in poor health. It won't be long until the opportunity to record their oral histories disappears, so it is vital that researchers find those with stories to share before time runs out.

title: The U.S. Enters WWII
text:
"Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on Dec. 7, 1941. The next day, the U.S. declared war on Japan. On December 11, Germany and Italy declared war on the United States. The U.S. then joined the Allies in the fight against the Axis Powers."

"That's right, Jackson. Let's take a look at some of the major battles and events of WWII. We'll use our classroom map to pinpoint each location."

1. Pearl Harbor

At 7:55 a.m. on Dec. 7, 1941, Japan attacked the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. In the surprise attack, 21 ships and 328 U.S. airplanes were damaged or destroyed. The attack also killed more than 2,300 Americans and injured over 1,100 others. President Roosevelt spoke to the nation and stated that December 7 would be "a date which will live in infamy." With the declarations of war that followed, the U.S. finally joined the Allies.

2. Midway

The Battle of Midway was fought between the Japanese and Americans over a small atoll (ring-shaped coral island) in the Pacific called Midway. The Americans had a small naval air station there that the Japanese were eager to control. American Admiral Chester Nimitz learned about Admiral Yamamoto's plans before the attack on June 4, 1942, so Adm. Nimitz was prepared. The U.S. was able to defeat the Japanese by sinking four of their aircraft carriers, which were impossible for Japan to replace. The U.S. won the battle and crippled the Japanese navy for the rest of the war.

3. Stalingrad

In the summer of 1942, the German army headed for the important Soviet city of Stalingrad. Hitler believed that capturing the city and its supplies would break the will of the Soviets. Germans dropped 1,000 tons of bombs on the city, and soldiers battled in the streets. Things looked grim for the Soviet Union. However, the battle took a turn as winter approached. Around 500,000 Soviet soldiers surrounded the German army. The Soviets cut off German supply routes, and soldiers starved in the freezing temperatures. In February 1943, the Germans were forced to surrender. The losses on both sides were almost unbelievable. Estimates of military and civilian casualties (wounded, killed or missing) are as high as 2 million people. Many historians point to this battle as the beginning of the end for Hitler's forces. The German army never recovered from the great loss of soldiers.

4. Normandy

Allied soldiers were about to begin the invasion of Normandy, a region in northern France, on June 6, 1944. General Dwight D. Eisenhower told them, "The eyes of the world are upon you. The hopes and prayers of liberty-loving people everywhere march with you."

The invasion of Normandy began with almost 160,000 Allied troops crossing the English Channel from Great Britain to France, which the Germans occupied. The Allies supplied over 5,000 ships and 11,000 planes. The invasion, now known as D-Day, gave the Allies a base for shipping and storing military supplies. By the end of June, over 1 million Allied troops had crossed into France. Hitler's troops were slowly pushed back toward Germany.

5. Battle of the Bulge

Hitler attacked American forces on Dec. 16, 1944, with the goal of splitting up the Allies and taking the supply port of Antwerp in Belgium. The actual name of the battle is the Ardennes Offensive, but it has come to be called the Battle of the Bulge. The Germans created a bulge, or bubble, in the Allied front lines in Belgium and Luxembourg. The Battle of the Bulge was the largest land battle fought by Americans in WWII. Over the next 40 days, the Allies suffered 81,000 casualties and the Germans 100,000. The Allied forces defeated the Germans through fierce fighting and by cutting off the supply of fuel for German tanks. Hitler's plan had failed.

title: Rosie the Riveter
text:
Who was Rosie the Riveter? Was she a relative of Uncle Sam? In a way, yes, because both became symbols of our American values.

More and more American men went off to fight WWII, so women entered the workforce, replacing these "lost" employees. During the war years, about 6 million women found jobs outside of the home. By 1944, 3.5 million women worked in factories, making weapons and other goods. Women also worked in the aviation industry building planes.

Illustrations of Rosie the Riveter entered popular culture. A riveter is a worker who joins metal plates together with rivets. On one magazine cover, "Rosie" sat on her machinery and ate a sandwich. Another poster showed a woman dressed in blue with a bandana covering her hair. It included the caption, "We Can Do It!" Rosie the Riveter became a symbol of the women who helped America win the war by keeping things running here at home.

title: The Tuskegee Airmen
text:
Up until and including WWII, the U.S. military was segregated. This meant that African Americans and whites were not allowed to serve together. During WWII, however, a group of African American servicemen helped break down the barriers between the races by showing what they were capable of.

The Tuskegee Airmen were the first African American aviators, or pilots, to serve in the U.S. military. Most of the men were trained at the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, and they went on to fly in more than 15,000 missions during WWII. The 450 pilots sent overseas earned 96 Distinguished Flying Crosses for their achievements in battle. The Tuskegee Airmen helped bring about the integration of the U.S. military in 1948, while Harry Truman was president. They battled the Germans in Europe and battled prejudice here at home.

title: How could this have happened?
text:
Death and destruction were part of life during WWII. The enemy didn't always cause this suffering, however. In Germany and in the countries it captured, many people were badly hurt and killed by their fellow countrymen. More than 6 million Jews were murdered during the Holocaust. Holocaust means "to sacrifice by fire," and the Nazis wanted to destroy the Jews because they thought Jewish people were an "inferior race."

At the beginning of the war, Hitler required Jews to wear yellow stars to identify themselves. Eventually, Jews were forced from their homes and sent to concentration camps. Here they were beaten, starved, forced to do hard physical labor and often murdered. Other "enemies" of the Germans were imprisoned as well. Most of the world knew very little about these events during the war until Allied soldiers liberated the camps in 1944 and 1945. The most well-known camps were Dachau in Germany (#6 on the map) and Auschwitz-Birkenau in Poland (#7 on the map).

In the United Sates, people were not sent to camps to be tortured, starved or killed. But from 1942 to 1945, more than 120,000 Japanese Americans were held in prison camps known as internment camps. This happened after the attack on Pearl Harbor. Many Americans feared that Japanese Americans were still loyal to Japan and would act as spies (or worse). President Roosevelt signed an order removing Japanese American families from their West Coast homes and placing them in one of 10 internment camps. The camps were located in isolated areas of the Midwest and western United States. (Manzanar, California, is labeled #8 on the map.)

How did these events happen? In both cases, people acted out of fear and hatred, rather than with facts. The Nazis chose to kill Jews because they viewed them as an inferior race. The United States imprisoned innocent Japanese Americans because they viewed them as a threat to our nation's safety. Both of these ideas were false.

title: Strength in Song
text:
Jackson and Alana have been up in the attic again, looking through some old record albums. They have hauled them downstairs to the living room to play them on Grandma Minnie and Grandpa Frank's record player.

"These records are great, Grandma. I'm really glad you saved them instead of tossing them out when technology moved ahead. It's so cool to listen to your music the same way you used to."

"Oh, I could never get rid of these albums, Alana. They're my absolute favorites!"

"Grandma Minnie, it's neat that you know the words to every single song! I noticed that all the singers on these albums are women. What's up with that?"

"You're right, Jackson. These albums are some of my favorites for that very reason. They remind me of the time when women were really finding their voices, so to speak. Women were realizing they had the power to do anything they wanted, even if some of those choices wouldn't have been considered 'appropriate' in the past. This time during the '60s and '70s was sometimes called the women's movement."

"This song by Helen Reddy really says that, Grandma. 'I am woman, hear me roar ... I am strong, I am invincible, I am woman.' What did people think of the song?"

"It reached No. 1 on the music pop chart in 1972! When the United Nations declared 1975 as International Women's Year, 'I Am Woman' was chosen as the theme song. Some people were a little alarmed by the women's movement, but it was time for women to have more options and more opportunities than they ever had before. There are many songs that talk about the different roles that each woman plays and how she can be good at each one. She doesn't have to settle for fulfilling just one role - she can explore all aspects of herself."

"That's a pretty powerful message, Grandma."

"My favorite album in this stack is Carole King's 'Tapestry.' Carole wrote or co-wrote every song on the album. What a tribute to the amazing talents of one woman! What was also amazing was that almost everyone, men and women alike, loved the album. It sold 25 million copies worldwide when it was released in 1971. The album won four Grammy awards and is still one of the best-selling albums of all time. It has my favorite song on it, 'So Far Away.' It always makes me a little sad, but I love it."

"I think these albums give us the perfect soundtrack for our study of the women's movement, Grandma. This may be my favorite topic yet!"

title: Title IX: Overcoming Discrimination in All Areas of Education
text:
Title IX (nine) is part of the Education Amendments of 1972. Title IX says that people cannot be excluded because of their sex from participating in any educational program or activity that receives money from the federal government. The act is called Title IX because it appears in the ninth section of the Education Amendments.

Title IX influences how schools handle career education, financial aid and math and science classes. The most noticeable change was that young women got the same opportunities to participate in high school and college sports. Surveys show that before Title IX passed in 1972, only 300,000 girls were involved in high school sports, compared with over 3.6 million boys. Forty years later, those numbers had increased to 3.2 million girls and 4.5 million boys.

What changes still need to be made? Many schools still need to encourage more girls and young women to take STEM (science, technology, engineering and math) classes, which have traditionally been filled with men and boys. Over time, Title IX supporters hope to overcome discrimination in all areas of education. How do you see Title IX at work in your school?

title: Women Take the Spotlight
text:
"Alana, it looks like the women's movement has really grabbed your attention!"

"It sure has, Jackson! I can't wait to find out how women broke down barriers and opened new pathways for future females...like me!"

Women had been working for equality for centuries, but the women's movement took on new life during the late 1960s and early 1970s. Women wanted to be treated with respect and wanted the same rights as men in all areas, including careers, health care, education and government policies. This was a time of change, and many women fought hard to break down social barriers and exert their power.

NOW is Born

In 1966, a small group of women formed the National Organization for Women (NOW). Founders included: Betty Friedan, author of a controversial book called "The Feminine Mystique"; Pauli Murray, who later became the first female African American Episcopal priest; and Shirley Chisholm, who would go on to be the first African American woman to run for president. The group agreed that NOW's purpose was "to take action to bring women into full participation in the mainstream of American society now, exercising all the privileges and responsibilities thereof in truly equal partnership with men." During the 1970s, the ultimate goal of NOW was the passage of the Equal Rights Amendment. Today, NOW continues to speak out on issues that affect women.

ERA Won't Go Away!

In 1923, women's rights activist Alice Paul wrote the first draft of the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA). She revised the amendment during the 1940s to read, "Equality of rights under the law shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any state on account of sex." In 1972, Congress finally passed the amendment. This was exciting, but the ERA still had to be ratified, or passed, by three-fourths of the states in order to be part of the Constitution. Congress set a seven-year deadline for ratification, which meant that 38 out of the 50 states had to ratify the ERA by 1979 in order for it to go into effect.

NOW went to work holding rallies, giving speeches, recruiting members and sending out letters. Twenty-two states ratified the amendment during the first year, but after that, support for the amendment dropped. By 1979, only 35 states had ratified the ERA. Congress extended the deadline to 1982, but no new states came forward to ratify the amendment. In fact, five of the 35 states that originally ratified the ERA have since rescinded, or taken back, their ratifications.

Many different groups, including some women's groups, oppose the ERA for different reasons. Some believe that it takes away the rights of states to make their own decisions. Others worry that it would deny a woman's right to financial support from her husband and that it would invade the privacy of U.S. citizens. Still others believe that it would force women into military service.

Although the deadline for ratification has passed, NOW and other groups still hope to find a way to pass the ERA and make it part of the Constitution.

Shirley Chisholm Runs for President

In 1972, Shirley Chisholm ran for the Democratic nomination for president of the United States. She was an educator, community organizer, one of the founders of NOW and the first African American woman elected to Congress. While serving her first term as a congresswoman, she hired only women to work on her staff. Chisholm was the first African American woman to run for president, and she knew it would be a tough fight. She lost the Democratic nomination to Senator George McGovern, but she continued to serve in Congress until 1983. Shirley Chisholm was never afraid to let her voice be heard!

Affirmative Action

In 1961, President John F. Kennedy signed an executive order stating that "affirmative action" must be taken to make certain that all government offices and contractors hired people based on their abilities and not on their race, religion or national origin. In 1967, President Lyndon Johnson signed a requirement adding gender to this list. This meant that all government agencies must see that women, as well as minorities, had equal opportunities.

In 1972, President Nixon signed Title IX into law as part of the Education Amendments. Title IX states that no one can be excluded from participating in any educational program or activity because of their sex. This opened the way for women to participate in sports, as well as to join in classes and activities once reserved only for males.

Women In the Workforce - Enter the Latchkey Generation

In the 1960s, nearly 70 percent of families included a stay-at-home mom. The women who did work were usually limited to jobs as nurses, teachers, librarians or secretaries. As the women's movement grew in strength, both of these things began to change. Today, around 70 percent of mothers are fully employed, and women are present in all areas of the workforce, from construction workers and artists to lawyers and physicists.

This change has had an impact on our nation's youth. As more and more mothers work outside of the home, the country has seen a growing number of "latchkey kids" - kids who carry a house key with them and stay at home alone after school. Schools have adapted, and many now offer afterschool programs.

title: Representative Bella Abzug
text:
"It's always shocked me that in this great country we have allowed governing to be done by only one part of the population."

- Bella Abzug

Bella Abzug grew up in New York City. She was the daughter of poor Russian Jewish immigrants. As a young adult, she went to law school and spent her career working to help the overlooked and underpaid members of society. She was known for using sharp words to argue with her critics.

Abzug won a seat in the House of Representatives in 1970. During her first year in office, Abzug persuaded Congress to set aside August 26 as Women's Equality Day. The day celebrated the passage of the 19th Amendment in 1920, giving women the right to vote. After leaving Congress, Bella Abzug wrote books and continued to fight for women's rights around the world.

title: Women in Science and Math - 1970s Edition
text:
There was a time when most scientists and mathematicians were men. Women have gradually gained jobs and respect in these fields. Here are a few of the many women who contributed to science and math during the 1970s.

Dr. Barbara McClintock (below) studied the genes of corn. She discovered that certain genes were responsible for the color of the leaves or kernels of corn. Dr. McClintock won the National Medal of Science in 1970. In 1983, she received the Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine.

Dr. Evelyn Hu worked in a research laboratory in the ‘70s. She also taught electrical and computer engineering and was awarded patents for her inventions.

Have you ever worked on a tough math problem for an hour? Dr. Julia Robinson worked on Hilbert’s 10th Problem, a very complicated math question, for over 20 years. In 1975, Dr. Robinson was the first female mathematician elected to the National Academy of Sciences. She was also the first female president of the American Mathematical Society.

title: Equal Pay for Equal Work
text:
Jackson is at the table while his parents cook dinner. He's reading through a newspaper as part of a homework assignment.

"Hey! This can't be right. It says here that many women make less than men for doing the same job."

"That's true, Jackson."

"I know that you and Dad both work full time, doing the same job. Do YOU bring home the same salary as Dad?"

"Unfortunately, Jackson, I don't. I make a little less than he does, even though we both do about the same thing."

"This article says that on average women earn around 77 cents for every dollar earned by a man. Over a lifetime in the workforce, women take home close to $500,000 less than men. Why doesn't someone change this to make things equal?"

"Well, Jackson, some people are trying, but it seems that change always takes time."

"We should do something to make sure that everyone gets equal pay for equal work. We could sure use that extra money around here!"

title: We're All in This Together!
text:
Jackson and Alana are watching a 24-hour TV news channel with Grandpa Frank and Grandma Minnie. ...

"Is the news almost over, Grandpa Frank? It feels like we've been watching it for hours!"

"I hate to tell you this, Jackson, but this is the 24-hour news channel. News never stops, you know."

"Well, that doesn't sound very interesting to me. Maybe it's time to watch something else, right Grandma?"

"The news might seem a little slow at times, Alana, but it's important to understand what's happening in the world. Did you listen to the story about Michelle Bachelet? She was the first woman to be president of Chile."

"I remember. The story said that 60 percent of Chileans think she's a good leader. What does that have to do with us, Grandma?"

"Well, you never know when the U.S. will elect its first female president. It would be nice if people paid attention to how it's worked in other countries."

"I guess that makes sense, but I still don't think it's very exciting."

"Jackson, you like chocolate, right?"

"Are you kidding, Grandpa Frank? You know it's my favorite!"

"Then did you pay attention to that story about African cocoa beans? It sounds like those are about to get more expensive. Do you think that will affect you?"

"Hmmm ... well, the reporter said that the cost of chocolate will go up. Since I have to buy my own snacks, I guess that DOES affect me."

"Now you're getting it, Jackson! Alana, what about that trip your parents have been planning? There was a story about some trouble overseas that might change gas prices."

"You mean Mom and Dad might change their minds about our trip? I've been looking forward to it for AGES!"

"You'll have to ask them, but knowing how much gas will cost can help them figure out how much money the trip will cost."

"Grandpa is just pointing out that things happen around the world. Sometimes those events change the way we live our lives. Watching the news helps us understand the present and plan for the future."

"I guess that makes sense, right Jackson?"

"Yeah, but can we take a break from the news every once in a while? We don't want too much of a good thing!"

title: What is the G20?
text:
Have you heard of the G20? No, it's not a new video game, energy drink or league of superheroes. The G20, or "Group of 20," is a collection of some of the most powerful business leaders in the world. The group is made up of representatives from 19 different countries plus the European Union (a partnership between several European countries). Member countries include China, Japan, Russia and the United States.

The G20 was formed in 1999. Since 2008, the G20 has held annual meetings to examine global financial problems and make plans to solve them. The G20 discusses ways to strengthen the global economy and to improve financial rules and regulations around the world. Leaders also discuss jobs and global trade. If you were to attend a G20 summit meeting, what would you want to talk about?

title: Global Politics and Wars
text:
"Since the 1970s, parts of North Africa, the Middle East and South Asia have been world 'hot spots' when it comes to conflict."

"Jackson, let's use our classroom's new interactive whiteboard to learn more about how events in these regions have impacted our lives over the last 50 years."

"I'm ready! Let's start with Israel. ..."

Oil Embargo

The Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) was founded in 1960 in Baghdad to control oil supplies and prices to the rest of the world. The original members of OPEC were Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Venezuela and Saudi Arabia.

In 1973, the Arab nations of Egypt and Syria attacked Israel. The U.S. supported Israel, and Arab OPEC members declared an oil embargo against those who opposed their friends. An embargo is a restriction on trade. OPEC cut the amount of oil they would sell to the United States. By the end of the embargo, the price of oil had risen from $3 a barrel to nearly $12! Gasoline prices soared and gas stations were swamped with people who were afraid the country would run out of gas. Most Americans struggled with having to wait in long lines to pay very high prices for small amounts of gas. They demanded that something be done.

Secretary of State Henry Kissinger was given the job of finding a solution. He met with leaders from both sides and negotiated an agreement between the warring countries. As part of the deal, OPEC ended the oil embargo in March 1974.

Camp David Accords

"Let's click on Egypt and see what the Smart Board has to say!"

Israel and Egypt continued to fight over land throughout the 1970s. In September 1978, President Jimmy Carter invited Egyptian President Anwar Sadat and Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin to the presidential retreat at Camp David, Maryland. After 13 days of negotiation, Sadat and Begin signed an agreement that led to a formal peace treaty the following year. The agreements are often called the Camp David Accords because they were negotiated and signed at the famous presidential getaway. Sadat and Begin received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1978 for their efforts. President Carter also received the award in 2002, partly because of his role in bringing these conflicts to an end.

Iran Hostage Crisis

"Now let's click on Iran."

On Nov. 4, 1979, a group of Iranian students stormed the American Embassy in Tehran and took 90 hostages. They were angry that President Carter had allowed their former leader, the Shah of Iran, to come to America for cancer treatments. The shah had been forced out of Iran, and they wanted to send the message that America had no business interfering in their affairs. Over 50 American hostages were held for 444 days. Several failed attempts to rescue the hostages weakened President Carter's image as a strong leader. The Americans were finally released on Jan. 21, 1981, the day after Ronald Reagan was sworn in as president. Many people believed the timing of the release was meant as an insult to President Carter. These events damaged the United States' relationship with Iran, which has remained weak.

The Persian Gulf Wars ('Desert Storm' and 'Iraqi Freedom')

"Click on Iraq, Alana, so that we can learn about the Gulf Wars."

In 1990, the country of Iraq invaded its neighbor, Kuwait. Saddam Hussein, leader of Iraq at the time, hoped to take control of Kuwait's rich oil supply. President George H. W. Bush demanded that Iraqi forces leave Kuwait, but Saddam refused.

In January 1991, the U.S. and over 20 allied nations attacked Iraqi forces in Kuwait. The attack became known as Operation Desert Storm. After six weeks, Iraqi forces were defeated and forced to leave Kuwait. After Desert Storm was successful, Saddam promised to destroy Iraq's weapons of mass destruction. He also agreed to allow experts from the United Nations to inspect his military to make sure these weapons had truly been destroyed.

However, Saddam broke these promises, and in March 2003, American and British forces attacked Iraq's military. This second conflict with Iraq became known as Operation Iraqi Freedom. Just like Desert Storm, the fighting did not last long. In May 2003, President George W. Bush announced, "in the battle of Iraq, the United States and our allies have prevailed." A few months later, U.S. forces found and captured Saddam Hussein. Since then, Iraq has struggled to reform a stable government.

Terrorism and Homeland Security

"OK, Jackson, let's click on the South Asian country of Afghanistan."

1993 World Trade Center Bombing

On Feb. 26, 1993, a huge bomb exploded in the parking garage beneath the World Trade Center. It left a massive crater, killed six people and injured more than 1,000 others. A group of seven terrorists carried out the attack, and six of them were later captured. Investigators uncovered plans for more attacks, and the terrorists were eventually connected to terrorist training camps in Afghanistan.

Sept. 11 Attacks

On Sept. 11, 2001, 19 al-Qaida terrorists (a radical Islamic group) hijacked four planes. The terrorists carried out suicide attacks against targets in the United States. Two planes were flown into the World Trade Center towers in New York City (the same place that was attacked in 1993). A third plane was crashed into the Pentagon, headquarters of the Department of Defense, in Washington, D.C. A fourth plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania. Around 3,000 people were killed in the Sept. 11 attacks.

War on Terrorism

After Sept. 11, President George W. Bush declared a worldwide War on Terrorism. Operation Enduring Freedom was launched to capture al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden and shut down terrorist training camps in Afghanistan and other countries. The Department of Homeland Security was formed to protect the United States from terrorist attacks. U.S. forces found and killed Osama bin Laden on May 2, 2011, and they continue to work to protect the United States from terrorist acts.

title: Alana's Friendship Bracelet Sale
text:

Alana hopes to raise at least $20 to donate to the Carter Center. Her mom donated the materials for the bracelets, so all the money she earns goes directly to the center. How many bracelets will she have to sell to make $20? ___________

Add a splash of color to your new spring wardrobe, and support human rights around the world.

All profits from Alana's bracelet sales will go to the Carter Center, an organization formed in 1982 by former president Jimmy Carter and his wife, Rosalynn. The Carter Center promotes human rights and encourages peace. Human rights are the basic, fundamental rights that everyone deserves. These rights include life, freedom, justice, dignity and equality. Bracelets will be sold in the park every afternoon this week.

title: Remembering Heroes
text:
The Sept. 11 attacks mark a time of grief for many Americans. Nearly everyone who watched the news that day can remember exactly where he or she was when New York was attacked. However, the day is not only remembered for the nearly 3,000 people who were killed. Americans also remember the bravery of the police officers, firefighters, medical rescue workers and ordinary citizens who responded that day.

Hundreds of rescue workers rushed into the burning buildings to help everyone they could, even though they knew it was dangerous. Many of these brave men and women were still inside the World Trade Center buildings as they collapsed.

When a fourth plane was hijacked on Sept. 11, as it headed toward Washington, D.C., several passengers decided to attack the hijackers. No one knows for sure how many were in on the attack, but they kept the plane from possibly crashing into another government building. Americans choose to remember these sacrifices with pride even as they mourn the loss of so many dead.

title: Equal Rights for ALL
text:
Jackson here. Do you remember the Civil Rights Act of 1964? It outlawed discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin. In 1990, Congress passed another law aimed at ending discrimination against people with disabilities. Discrimination isn't only based on race, religion and sex. It can also be based on physical and mental abilities.

The Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 makes it illegal to discriminate against people with disabilities in employment, housing, transportation and access to public places. According to the law, government agencies and businesses must make "reasonable accommodations" for those with disabilities. These accommodations include wheelchair ramps, elevators, Braille signs (for the blind), phone relay services (for the deaf) and special parking spaces for those with special needs. Employers must also make reasonable efforts to help disabled workers perform their jobs. One of the teachers at our school uses a wheelchair. It's nice to know that she can use the ramps and elevator to get where she needs to go!
