title: Another Revolution?
text:
Jackson and Alana are in their classroom after school, packing up before going home for the day.

"Alana, I'm really looking forward to learning about another revolution. After our teacher told us we'll be studying the technological revolution, I got pretty excited!"

"I guess so, Jackson! I know you like technology. After all, it's almost impossible to get you off the computer, and I know you love your MP3 player."

"Sure, I love all that stuff, and I've definitely heard enough about other kinds of revolutions. There's always a lot of violence, with people fighting each other and disagreeing all the time. Life just gets rough. People lose their homes, and everyone has to start over. A technological revolution is different. It's not about robots against humans trying to take over the world ... that actually sounds like a video game! It's about creating and using new technology."

"Robots taking over DOES sound like a video game, Jackson! And you're right; it doesn't describe the technological revolution at all. We're going to study the ways that new technology has made life easier, better and more fun!"

"Have I mentioned how much I think I'm going to like this unit on technology, Alana?"

"Uh, once or twice, Jackson! And remember how the Industrial Revolution changed society by adding machines to make certain jobs faster and easier? Well, the technological revolution has done the same thing, this time using powerful computers. You don't see as many seamstresses, typists or telephone operators anymore because those jobs can be done by automated machines."

"That's true! And new technology is created every day, right? I mean, just look around the classroom, and you can't miss it. We have an interactive white board, a document camera, tests on computers and so much more. It seems like we really are in the middle of a technological revolution!"

"Hey, Jackson. You know how we sometimes transported ourselves back in time by touching different things from the past? I wonder if my grandparents have one of the inventions from the technological revolution up in that attic of theirs. ..."

"Let's go look, Alana!"

title: Cheap Technology
text:
Would you like to have your very own microscope? What if the microscope were small enough to fit in your pocket, strong enough to survive being dropped from a three-story building, could magnify over 2,000 times and weighed less than two nickels? You’re probably thinking that such an amazing gadget would be made of amazing materials and cost thousands of dollars, but you would be wrong. Such a microscope does exist. Surprisingly enough, it’s made of plastic-coated paper and costs less than a dollar!

Stanford University bioengineering professor Manu Prakash and his team of researchers developed the Foldscope, a small microscope that can be folded, origami-style, from a flat sheet of paper. This amazing tool is made of a small lens, a light source and a battery that have been laminated onto a sheet of paper. The microscope is punched out of the paper and folded into a cheap, durable microscope.

The Foldscope was originally designed for use by medical professionals in countries like India, where Prakash grew up. Doctors and health workers need microscopes to identify diseases common in those areas, such as malaria and African sleeping sickness. Traditional microscopes are often bulky and expensive. The affordable Foldscope travels easily, so doctors can diagnose and treat patients quickly, saving many lives. Dr. Prakash also hopes that students like you will use the Foldscope to learn about science and make thier own discoveries.

title: The Technological Revolution: 1970s to the Present
text:
(A few months ago, Jackson and Alana's class entered an essay contest about technology in the classroom. Recently, they heard the good news: They won!)

"Jackson, I can't believe our class actually won the grand prize - a classroom set of tablets!"

"Don't forget the rest of the prize - $1,000 for apps or other school needs. We can make the tablets even better!"

"Our teacher said that our first lesson using the tablets will be to research the history of technology since the 19 70s and explain how it can be used in the classroom."

"Yes, Alana, and we're supposed to use our tablets to create a technological timeline."

"Here goes!"

Technological Timeline

1970s

Video Game

In 1972, Ralph Baer's Magnavox Odyssey becomes the first home video game system to hit the market. It includes games such as pingpong and target shooting.

Cellphone

Motorola engineer Martin Cooper places the first cellphone call in 1973. The phone is nearly one foot long, weighs 2.5 pounds and provides 35 minutes of talk time. It does not have texting capabilities.

Memory Typewriter

IBM introduces a special typewriter in 1974. It stores and recalls information. Later during the 1980s, more word processors based on this design become popular. Advanced versions come with spellcheck, document templates and the ability to print.

Personal Computer

In 1977, Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs begin selling the personal computer, Apple II, to the public. It costs about $1,300 and comes with a keyboard and color graphics.

1980s

Video Camera Recorder

Consumers begin filming important events on hand-held "camcorders." In 1983, these video cameras have color and sound. Some models use tapes that can be played back on machines called VCRs (video cassette recorders).

Doppler Radar

In 1988, weather networks begin replacing traditional radar with Doppler radar. This technology is used to locate precipitation (moisture), predict where it will travel and predict how much it will drop.

1990s

World Wide Web

Tim Berners-Lee leads the development of the World Wide Web (Web). The Web is made up of websites connected to the Internet around the world. In 1993, the Web becomes available for public use.

Digital Video Disc

In 1996, several electronics companies begin selling Digital Video Discs (DVDs) that are used for storing and playing different types of data, including movies and video games. DVDs provide better quality than the tapes used in VCRs.

2000s

Digital Music Player

Apple releases the iPod in 2001, and it becomes the first highly successful personal digital music player. The portable device has enough memory to store and play hundreds of songs while being small enough to fit in a pocket.

Social Networking

In 2004, U.S. college students design Facebook, a way for people to connect with one another using the Internet. Facebook soon opens its site to anyone over the age of 13. Today, over 1 billion people worldwide use Facebook on a regular basis.

2010s

3- D Printer

A 3-D printer manufactures items using a computer program and materials like plastic and metal. A scanner makes a copy of the object, and the printer creates the model layer by layer. In 2014, the body of a car is created with a 3-D printer and assembled.

*Making Connections

In the space provided, choose two of the inventions listed on the timeline and explain how they could be used in the classroom.

title: The Presidential Election of 2008: Two "Firsts"
text:
The 2008 U.S. presidential election was historic for two different reasons:

First, Barack Obama became the first African American to be elected president. Throughout America's history and the civil rights movement, the American people have struggled to provide equal rights and opportunities for people of every race and gender. When Obama won the presidency, it showed that America had finally overcome some of its age-old prejudices. Although we still have a long way to go before our nation truly becomes equal for all, for many Americans, Obama's election symbolized the progress we have made in the struggle to overcome discrimination.

Another "first" that made this election historic was the huge increase in technology used during the campaign. Obama and his staff made heavy use of blogs, Twitter, Facebook pages and Internet videos to share his message with huge numbers of people. His campaign worked right through Election Day, encouraging voters to head to the polls. Citizens who wanted Obama to win (many of them younger voters) forwarded these messages to family members and friends. This use of technology paid off, and Obama won against Senator John McCain.

Our nation elected its first African American president using the latest and most up-to-date technology. These two important "firsts" made the 2008 election one for the history books.

title: How it all Began in the ‘New World’
text:
In 1492, an Italian sailor named Christopher Columbus sailed three ships from Spain across the Atlantic Ocean. Spain's King Ferdinand II and Queen Isabella I supported Columbus, who hoped to find a faster trade route between Europe and Asia. Though he never reached Asia, Columbus did sail straight into land that became known as the "New World," at least to the Europeans. It wasn't new to the people who already lived there, of course!

Seven months after Columbus first set sail from Spain, he returned triumphantly to report to the king and queen. He brought back both gold and captured Indians. The king and queen were very pleased to hear of Columbus' adventures and discoveries. Secretly the two had believed there was little chance the Italian explorer would ever return. Now they hoped to use the information Columbus brought back to make Spain richer and more powerful. Spanish leaders planned further explorations of the New World (the Western hemisphere, including North and South America). They sent Columbus and other explorers (people who travel to gain geographical or scientific information) back across the ocean. The explorers' goals were not only to explore the new lands, but also to set up settlements in the name of Spain and convert the native people to Christianity.

The explorers made their way across the ocean. They found gold and excellent land to settle. Soon, talk of the New World reached other European powers. France and England sent adventurers to explore North America in search of riches. Explorers claimed land for the royalty of their countries. These countries became richer and more powerful with each piece of land the explorers claimed, and they established colonies in the New World. Colonies are areas ruled by another country and not by its own people. European explorers also conquered (took over) the native people of the New World and introduced Christianity to them.

Columbus' explorations marked a turning point in history. People from very different parts of the world began to communicate and trade with each other. Many European countries became rich and powerful after taking over the land and people of North America. The kings and queens of Europe invested great amounts of money in and gathered adventurers to further explore and conquer the New World. The Age of Discovery had begun!

title: Is Christopher Columbus a Hero or a Villain?
text:
“In fourteen hundred and ninety two, Columbus sailed the ocean blue.”

Most children memorize this poem by first grade. For more than two hundred years, people in the United States have honored Christopher Columbus during October. In 1937, lawmakers named Columbus Day a federal holiday. But not everyone believes that Christopher Columbus may be a hero to celebrate.

Columbus thought he landed in the East Indies, but he was wrong. He was in what we know as the Bahamas. Later he explored Cuba and the area we now call Haiti. Historians say that Columbus did not treat the natives there very well, and evidence shows that Columbus forced some of them into slavery. Columbus and his men even killed some native people who opposed his actions. Historians also believe that Europeans brought new diseases that the people of North America had no immunity against.

Other people believe Columbus is a real hero. After all, he helped open up trade routes and begin the Age of Exploration. So the question remains, is Christopher Columbus a hero, a villain or a little of both? What do you think?

title: The Age of Discovery
text:
The success of Columbus’ first voyage quickly caught the attention of other explorers. Soon, more Europeans engaged in far-reaching exploration. As they traveled the world, they often conquered the native people they met on their journeys. The explorers mapped the lands and established new trade routes. They traded gold, silver and spices. Most importantly, these early explorers led the way for several European countries to colonize, or settle, the New World. These colonies were the groups of people who settled far from home, but they maintained ties (close bonds) with their home countries.

England vs. France vs. Spain

When the Age of Discovery began, the great powers of Europe included England, Spain and France. All three realized that to be the richest, most powerful nation in the world they would have to explore and conquer as much of the New World as possible.

England’s Chance

England’s King Henry VII gave Italian-born explorer Giovanni Caboto, later called John Cabot, permission to explore unknown land for England in 1497. Cabot sailed north of Columbus’ route across the Atlantic Ocean. He claimed land in present day Canada and explored the United States. However, Cabot believed he was in Asia. His ship sank before he could return home and Cabot never knew what he had really discovered.

Spain Sends More Explorers

Spain also wanted to be the great power in the world. The leaders realized they needed to continue to explore and conquer. People heard tales of New World cities made entirely of gold. Spaniard Hernan Cortes was determined to find gold and silver in the New World. He sailed to present day Mexico and conquered the Aztec people who lived there in 1521.

There were also stories of magical fountains with water that could turn old people young again. At about the same time Cortes was conquering the Aztec, another Spanish explorer, Juan Ponce de Leon, set off from Puerto Rico. Some people believe he hoped to find the magic water, the “fountain of youth.” He landed in present day Florida. Of course there was no fountain of youth to be found, but de Leon claimed the land of Florida for Spain.

France Takes a Turn

By 1521, Spain found a new route to Asia by sailing around the tip of South America. By that time, many knew that North America lay between Asia and Europe. King Francis I of France believed, though, that Asia was still very close to North America’s west coast. He wanted to find a shortcut—a water passage across North America. In 1534 , King Francis sent sailor Jacques Cartier to find the shortcut, but there was no such water passage for anyone to find. Cartier instead discovered Newfoundland in Canada. He also claimed land for France around a river he named Saint Lawrence. However, early French settlements there failed. It would be nearly six decades before France would have a permanent settlement in North America.

The Oldest Permanent Settlement in the United States

When Ponce de Leon landed on the coast of Florida in 1513, its beauty overwhelmed him. There were palm trees, beautiful flowers and exotic birds. The day he landed was the Spanish Feast of Flowers, or Pascua Florida, so Ponce de Leon named the new land Florida. Both Spain and France made several early attempts to colonize Florida, but these attempts were unsuccessful.

In 1564, word reached Spanish leaders that the French were once again exploring and colonizing the western coastal land. This news angered the Spanish leaders. They wanted a plan to keep France from claiming any more land and riches. They decided to send Pedro Menendez de Aviles to Florida to establish a base from which to attack the French.

On September 8, 1565, de Aviles and his men organized their territory. He named the new colony St. Augustine. De Aviles and his group had two goals. They were to continue to explore and claim land for their country because Spain wanted to continue to find gold and other riches. The men were there also to protect the land from other countries, especially France, and defend the trade route. They had orders to destroy Fort Caroline, which the French controlled. In addition, the Spanish government wanted control of the American Indians in the area. Within a year, de Aviles and his men had forced the French out of the area. They had also taken over the council house of the Timucua tribe and started using it as a fort.

This makes St. Augustine, Florida, the oldest permanently settled city in the United States. This historic city is a reminder of the importance of European colonization in the New World.

title: Mapping the Age of Discovery
text:
Before Columbus went on his first voyage across the Atlantic Ocean, no one knew much about the world. Mapmakers did not know about the landmasses between Europe and Asia. The explorations that began the Age of Discovery changed world maps for good. European mapmakers got new information about the world from explorers and sailors, and they were able to fill in the blank spaces on their maps.

Maps are plane, or flat, representations of the shapes of landmasses and bodies of water. Today’s many different types of maps include features to help people use them. A grid system with lines of longitude and latitude makes locating specific information on a map easier. Each map also has a scale to show distances and a compass rose to show direction.

Even today, maps constantly change. Almost every year cartographers, or mapmakers, change information on world maps because of new information they discover.

title: Worth Their Weight in Gold
text:
Why did early explorers want to find a quicker trade route to Asia? One reason was to bring spices to consumers more quickly. Europeans could not grow most spices in their own countries. Spices we use often like salt, pepper, cinnamon, cloves and ginger were hard to find and very valuable back then. So, why were these spices so important?

Well, in Columbus’ time there were no refrigerators. Food often spoiled before people could eat it. Spices came to the rescue! Spices like salt helped dry and preserve meats. Other spices hid the flavor of not so fresh food. People also used spices to make medicines, perfume and incense, which produces a fragrant odor when burned.

Valuable spices were the same as money in some places. People often paid for housing or animals with spices. During the Middle Ages, some said a sack of pepper was worth a man’s life. And that’s nothing to sneeze at!

title: Clarity of Expression: Henry Hudson
text:
Henry Hudson was an English sea captain and explorer who started off as a failure. He sailed on two voyages for England to find a northeast water route to the rich spice trade in Asia. But both times the icy northern seas blocked his way. He had to return home defeated.

Sounds like the end of his career, right? It wasn't. Hudson next convinced the Dutch East India Company to hire him for exactly the same expedition. In 1609 Hudson and his crew sailed west across the Atlantic. He reached the New World, landing on the island we know today as Manhattan. He sailed inland up a wide river and explored the surrounding valley.

It wasn't a passage to Asia. But Hudson's explorations allowed the Dutch to claim the land and build a fur trading post there in 1614, before the Pilgrims arrived. A Dutch settlement called New Netherland soon followed.

Unfortunately, Hudson's last voyage ended in mutiny. He refused his crew's demands to return home, so the sailors took over the ship, setting Hudson adrift in a small boat. His fate is unknown, but his legacy is Hudson Bay, Hudson River, Hudson Valley and the Dutch settlement that became New York City.

Henry Hudson must have had excellent clarity of expression. He had to be able to explain clearly to the Dutch that his experience and determination made him the best man for the job, even though he was an Englishman and not a Dutchman.

Think about a time that you wanted to convince your parents or teachers to let you try something new. Did you beg and plead? Or did you give them a clear explanation of your reasons? Which way do you think works better?

title: Help Wanted: Historical Investigator to Solve Mystery of Roanoke's Lost Colony
text:
Are you looking for an opportunity to learn more about one of the most mysterious events in American history? Are you willing to research historical events and study primary and secondary sources? Can you make inferences (conclusions based on what you know) about causes and effects of historical importance? Well, this job just might be for you!

Job Description:

As a historical investigator you will dig deeper into the case of the lost colony of Roanoke, North Carolina. The year was 1584 . As Spain explored the New World, many people saw it as the world's richest and most powerful nation. Spanish ships sailed back and forth between the New World and Europe with shiploads of gold and other treasures.

Sir Walter Raleigh was a British poet, soldier and explorer. He believed that establishing colonies in North America would make England just as wealthy and powerful as Spain. He sent two ships to explore the coast of the continent. The ships landed on an island near present-day North Carolina. The men named the island Roanoke after the native Roanoke Indians who lived there. Word quickly returned to Raleigh of the land's excellent fruits, vegetables, fish and other animals. The men also spoke highly of the friendly Roanoke people. Raleigh believed it would be smart to establish an English colony.

Unfortunately, the first attempt to settle the island just didn't work. English settlers didn't know how to grow food. They also began fighting with the once-friendly Roanoke. Soon the settlers gave up and returned to Europe.

Two years later Raleigh tried again to establish, or set up, a colony. Although the settlers knew their work would be difficult, 117 people decided to give the colony another chance. Once again the Roanoke did not get along with the Anglo (white , English speaking) settlers. Captain John White decided to go back to England for more supplies. Sadly, because of England's war with Spain, Capt. White could not return to Roanoke for three years!

When Capt. White finally returned to Roanoke, there was no sign of the settlers. It was as if they had just disappeared! The only clue to their disappearance was the word "CROATOAN" carved on a tree. Had the colony moved to the island of Croatoan? To this day no one has figured out exactly what happened to the colony of Roanoke.

Job Duties:

In this job you will further research Roanoke's Lost Colony. You will make inferences about what might have happened to the colonists. Did the Roanoke Indians kill them? Could disease have wiped out the colony completely? What was the meaning of "CROATOAN"? Perhaps a skilled detective like you can find the answers to this historical mystery. The case is yours!

title: A Slave No More!
text:
A letter written after the Civil War has shed light on the slave-master relationship. Jourdan Anderson was a slave who gained freedom when he and his family escaped to Ohio from Tennessee. In August 1865 his former owner, Colonel Anderson, wrote a letter asking Jourdan to come back to Tennessee to work on his farm.

The former slave's reply gave a clear message about his feelings. He said he hoped that God had opened the colonel's eyes to the wrongs done to slaves for generations. While he was glad his old master was alive, he was surprised that the Yankees hadn't hanged him yet. Jourdan wrote that there was one thing that might bring him back to Tennessee. He and his wife wanted to be paid for the 52 years of combined work that they provided as slaves (over $11,000).

Without that, he said they had little faith in the colonel's promises. He ended by asking the colonel to give his best regards to a man named George Carter. Mr. Carter had apparently taken a pistol away from the colonel when he tried to shoot Jourdan... twice.

Reading letters and newspapers from the past can help us understand the people who lived during that time. Jourdan and his family may have once been slaves, but their spirits were not broken.

title: Challenges and Successes of Early American Settlements
text:
The Roanoke colony's failure did not cause England to give up hope. Many people were still committed to establishing settlements, or small communities, in North America. In the early 1600s, England was far behind Spain and France in power. The English could not establish colonies just anywhere they wished. Spain already claimed South America, the Indies, the Southwest region and Florida. France claimed the areas around many important waterways like the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River. Much of the unclaimed land was harsh, rugged and dangerous. The forests were thick, and natives often made it difficult for Anglo settlers to establish colonies. England began to concentrate on settling land along the eastern coast of North America. They had to plan the colonies very carefully.

Colonists Establish Jamestown for Economic Gain

About 20 years after the failure at Roanoke, England's King James I gave permission for a group of men to form a company and establish a settlement in North America. The Virginia Company sent about 100 settlers - all men - to America in April of 1607. The men hoped to get rich by finding gold and other natural treasures. They chose a piece of land near a river and built their settlement. They named the colony Jamestown, in honor of King James. They chose Virginia as the name of the land around the settlement.

Life in the colony was difficult and hazardous. The water in Jamestown was dirty and not good for drinking. The marshland where Jamestown was built was not good for farming. Plants would not grow in the wet soggy soil. Swarms of mosquitoes carried a serious and often deadly disease called malaria. The men focused most of their efforts on getting rich instead of hunting or growing food. Disease and hunger killed most of the colonists, and only 38 men survived eight months after the start of Jamestown.

One man who survived the first year at Jamestown was Captain John Smith. Late in 1607, a group of American Indians captured Smith. They took him to the chief of their tribe, Powhatan. Many say that Powhatan's daughter, Pocahontas, saved Smith's life. Historians disagree about whether this story is accurate, or true, but Powhatan did allow Smith to return to his colony.

Capt. Smith continued his relationship with Powhatan's tribe. The American Indians taught the colonists about hunting, fishing and planting crops in this unfamiliar land. Smith was a good leader and the settlers soon elected him president of the colony. Smith made sure everyone worked hard to keep the colony from failing. Only 18 died in the second winter.

During 1608 and 1609 more settlers, including some women, arrived. Smith was burned badly in a gunpowder explosion and had to return to England. Soon the colonists were struggling to stay alive again. To keep from starving during the winter of 1609-10, many ate their own horses and dogs! Only 60 people were left at the end of that winter.

The colonists never became rich by finding gold or silver. However, they did find another way to get rich with a plant called tobacco. An Englishman named John Rolfe married Pocahontas and began planting tobacco, which grew very well in Jamestown's soil and climate. This became the real "gold" of Jamestown. People in England bought as much of the crop as possible. Jamestown now had something to trade for food and supplies.

Jamestown began to grow quickly, as each man had land to farm. Two hundred more women came from England to marry the men and start families. In 1619, the colonists elected men to make laws for the colony. They called this group The House of Burgesses, which was made up of mostly wealthy men. It wasn't the best type of government for the colonists, but the people now had some say in how their colony operated. They did not have this privilege (freedom) when they lived in England.

Unfortunately, the colony's successes did not continue. Colonists began to fight with Powhatan's tribe, and the price of tobacco dropped. Government leaders were not always honest, and many people died of disease. In 1624, King James took back the land and made Virginia a royal colony, which meant that King James owned Virginia.

Colonists Settle Plymouth for Religious Freedom

People looking for religious freedom started a third settlement in North America. Back in England, King James had ruled that all people must belong to the Church of England. A group called Separatists wanted to worship in their own way and refused to join. Many decided to move to the Netherlands.

In 1620, the Separatists (now known as Pilgrims) sailed to North America on a ship named the Mayflower. The Mayflower carried Pilgrims from both England and the Netherlands. The ship landed at Plymouth Bay in what is now Massachusetts. They lived on the ship for the first few months. The Pilgrim leaders came up with a government plan that would help all people live together in a peaceful way. All the men signed the agreement, which we know as the Mayflower Compact. Then they elected John Carver as governor. Many people think of the Mayflower Compact as America's first example of true self government.

Like the Jamestown settlers, the Plymouth colonists had difficult times at first. The winter was very cold. Food ran out quickly. Half the settlers died the first winter. Luckily for the surviving colonists, there were English speaking American Indians from the Wampanoag tribe nearby. One American Indian named Squanto helped teach the Pilgrims to plant corn, catch fish and gather maple syrup. Squanto also helped arrange a peace treaty between Chief Massasoit and the Pilgrims. The Wampanoag and the Pilgrims promised to help, not attack, each other.

Plymouth colonists elected William Bradford governor in 1621. Under his leadership Plymouth grew and became successful. People from England learned of the chance for freedom in the New World, and over time many more people came to settle the region we now call New England.

title: Clarity of Thought: William Bradford and the Mayflower Compact
text:
Imagine that someday you join a group that is going to start the first colony on the moon. What is one of the first things you might need? If you said a set of rules or laws to live by, you'd be thinking clearly. That's exactly what William Bradford helped write for the Pilgrims in 1620.

William Bradford decided early in his life that he did not agree with the Church of England , and this was the only church the English laws allowed in those days. He joined a separatist church , one that had separated from the Church of England . Bradford wanted to avoid being arrested and put in prison, so he led a group of church members and moved to the Netherlands . But they faced persecution for their religion there too.

In 1620, the separatists returned to England to meet others with their beliefs and sail for the New World on a ship called the Mayflower. The group received a patent (land grant) from the king of England to establish the first permanent colony in Virginia . The Mayflower was blown off course and landed near Cape Cod instead of Virginia. William Bradford and the other leaders of the colony decided that they needed to write an agreement for all people to have protection and to keep the peace. This unique document, signed by 41 men, is called The Mayflower Compact.

William Bradford was later elected governor of the colony over 30 times, so his clarity of thought must have been well respected. The Mayflower Compact has been called the inspiration for the U.S. Constitution. Look it up. Rewrite it in your own words to see how it reads in today's language. Would you have signed it? Why or why not?

title: How did some American Indians already know how to speak English when the Pilgrims arrived?
text: The Pilgrims probably owed their survival to the help of the Wampanoag people, especially a man named Squanto. An Abenaki Indian named Samoset introduced Squanto to the Pilgrims. Squanto learned to speak English from fishers who sailed off the coast near Plymouth. Many American Indians had relationships with Anglos who hunted or trapped in the area. Squanto spent time aboard English ships. He traveled and even lived for a while in England and Spain. Because both Samoset and Squanto spoke English, the Pilgrims were not frightened of them. Both men communicated with the Pilgrims and taught them better ways to survive in their new home.

title: Slavery Begins
text:
By late summer of 1619, the Jamestown colony had done quite well selling tobacco to merchants in England. It was during this summer that a ship from Holland sailed into the port at Jamestown. Aboard the ship were 20 African men. Sailors from the Dutch ship got the men from a Spanish ship. The captain of the Spanish ship traded the men for food.

Early records from Jamestown list these 20 Africans as indentured servants. An indentured servant is someone who agrees to work for another person for a specific time period in exchange for payment of the fee for passage on a ship. People forced these Africans to work for them in Jamestown. Historians believe they helped the colony harvest (to gather crops when they are ripe) tobacco.

History does not list these Africans as slaves (people forced to work for another person and considered property). However, this event is probably the beginning of the practice of using slaves to operate large farms, known as plantations, in the southern United States.

title: Settling Pennsylvania: A Peaceful Life in the New World
text:
Imagine a little girl named Mary Alice who was only 11 years old when her family left England to settle in the colony of Pennsylvania. What would life in the New World be like for her family? Maybe something like this fictional diary entry...

November 1681

The snow is falling heavily outside today, but here in our home the fire is warm. It is a perfect day to study God's word and give thanks for our new, peaceful life here in Pennsylvania. It is hard to believe that only a few months ago we were still in England and things were very different for my family.

I remember the day as if it was yesterday. Father had just returned home from a meeting at the Quaker Meeting House. I heard him sharing news with Mother. The talk between the men in the meeting that day had been serious. We Quakers were being mistreated by others in our village. We did not have the same religious beliefs or ceremonies as other churches. Our men will not join the military. Our families dress plainly and we do not believe in paying taxes that will be used for war. These beliefs angered many people in England.

That evening Father said to me, "Thou art to live a peaceable life, Mary. We shall be leaving England for a new home soon. Our friend and fellow Quaker, William Penn, has established a colony in the New World. I spoke with him today. We will move to Pennsylvania. There our family will live safely and in peace. We will be free to worship as we please." Only three weeks later, we sailed across the Atlantic Ocean toward our new home. Many of our Quaker friends sailed with us. Some of the men came alone. Others, like Father, brought their families too. I was scared but excited.

There are many interesting people here in Pennsylvania with us. My friend John is from Ireland. He and his family are also Quakers. Father says we will treat all of our new neighbors with kindness. The American Indians have also become our friends. Father said Mr. Penn made sure to pay them for the land where we now farm the rich soil.

Mother and I are working to make our home tidy and comfortable. Father works long days as he gets ready to plant wheat soon. Each day when I go to the Meeting House, I feel happy to have this new life. I thought I would miss England, but I do not. I feel I am truly home now in Pennsylvania.

title: Comparing the New Colonies
text:
The first English colonies in America had both failures and successes. Roanoke disappeared. At Jamestown many things went wrong and many things went right, but it proved that establishing colonies in the New World was possible. Plymouth Colony was a true success story for the people who were determined to find religious freedoms.

Back in England, more and more people wanted a chance at a new life across the Atlantic Ocean. By the middle of the 18th century, there were 13 British colonies along the Atlantic coastline of what would become the United States of America.

There were many similarities and differences in the colonies. Let's explore three colonial regions. The regions are named for their geographic location. They are the New England Colonies, the Middle Colonies and the Southern Colonies. Read on!

The New England Colonies

The New England colonial region included the Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut and New Hampshire colonies. Most of the people who lived in New England Colonies wanted to create communities where they could practice their own religious beliefs freely.

Some of the colonists in the region, like the Pilgrims of Plymouth, wanted to separate themselves completely from the Church of England. Other people considered themselves Puritans. They wanted to continue some traditions of the English church, but they wanted to have the freedom to change or "purify" others.

It was often difficult to live in the New England Colonies. Winters in the region were cold and snowy. The icy winters, though, discouraged the growth of germs that caused disease. So, many of the New England colonists were healthier than colonists in other regions. Also, in summer there was plenty of rain that helped crops grow well.

The economy in most of the New England Colonies was strong. The Rhode Island soil was very good for farming, and corn, tobacco and beans grew well there. In other parts of the region, the soil was rocky and difficult to farm. In the Massachusetts colony farming was not as successful.

Many colonists in this region made a living by fishing, shipbuilding or raising animals. Because there were many thick forests in the region, people also worked cutting and selling lumber. Colonists earned money by trading goods as well. Ships carried sugar, wool and beef to sell back in England. Some colonists found they could make a good deal of money trading African slaves. Very few New England colonists actually owned slaves, though.

The government of each of these colonies was a representative democracy. Men who were church members could vote in colony elections. This was not true in England. Each year, they elected governors and local representatives to help run the colonies. These officials put strict laws into place to protect the people and keep order within the colonies.

The Middle Colonies

News of economic opportunity in the colonies spread quickly to people still living in Europe. Many of these people jumped at the chance to settle where they might make lots of money! The Middle Colonies of New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware filled with people from all over Europe. German, Irish and English citizens hoped to get wealthy and have religious freedoms.

The climate of the Middle Colonies was milder than that of the New England Colonies. Winters were still cold, but they did not last as long. Summers were hot and rainy. This meant there was a longer growing season. Because of this and very fertile (rich) soil, farmers could successfully grow a variety of crops. They farmed wheat, rye, tobacco, corn and other vegetables. It was also common for indentured servants or slaves to help harvest crops in the Middle Colonies.

There was a lot to do for work in the Middle Colonies. Merchants often traded crops and furs across the Atlantic. They relied on waterways to help ship their goods. Miners dug up iron from the ground to trade. So, there were plenty of jobs for anyone willing to work in this region.

People in the Middle Colonies did not have much say about how officials ran their governments. In New York, for example, England's royalty appointed a powerful governor. This governor, and other officials he chose, enforced the laws.

The Southern Colonies

The Southern Colonies of Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia were both alike and different from the other colonies. Founders of these colonies hoped to discover gold and good land. They wanted to get rich. Settlers founded Maryland to give people who practiced the Catholic religion a safe place to live. One reason colonists settled in Georgia was to keep Spain from moving north from Florida. Georgia was also a safe place for debtors (people who owe money) to live. In England, lawmakers sent people who couldn't pay their bills to prison. In Georgia, the debtors could work and take care of themselves.

The Southern Colonies had mild winters and long hot summers. This was just the right climate for farmers to produce plentiful crops of tobacco, cotton and rice. They sold these cash crops to make lots of money. Farm owners needed many helpers to tend their large farms called plantations. Over time, many slaves worked on these farms. Besides farming, people in the Southern Colonies earned money by shipping, fishing, cutting lumber and trading with American Indians.

Colonists had limited input into government in the Southern Colonies. The founders often held great control. After a while, the colonies elected assemblies, but only white men who owned property could vote in the elections. In Georgia, the King of England could revoke, or take back, any law the assembly passed.

title: Colonial Rule Breakers Banished
text:
People wanted to settle the colonial regions for many reasons, one of which was religious freedom. Two colonists learned, though, that true religious freedom was very difficult to find. They broke rules of the church and were punished severely.

Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson both lived in the colony of Massachusetts at one time. Their ideas about religion were different than the ideas of most people, so people forced them to leave their homes and churches and move far away.

Williams was a minister in Salem, Massachusetts. He did not want his church to be like the churches he left in England. He did not think the King of England should be involved in running the church. He wanted the government and the church to be separate. The leaders kicked Williams out of Massachusetts because they didn't agree with him. Before they deported him (sent him away), Williams ran away to live with American Indians. Later, he moved to Rhode Island and founded the city of Providence.

Anne Hutchinson was also a preacher. She spoke out against the Puritan church because she did not agree with the leaders of the church. The leaders in Massachusetts accused her of treason, or being against the government. At that time women were not supposed to speak out against the church or government. Hutchinson also fled to Rhode Island.

Williams and Hutchinson both continued their religious teachings in Rhode Island. Soon, people knew this colony as a place where people with different religious viewpoints were welcome. Williams lived the rest of his life in Providence. Hutchinson lived nearby on a small island. She and five of her children were murdered in an attack by an American Indian tribe. Some people in the church had stayed angry with Hutchinson. They even said her death was a punishment by God for speaking against the church.

title: Slavery in the Colonies
text:
There are many reasons people settled in the colonies of North America. Some people wanted religious freedom. Others wanted the chance to get rich.

In the early 1600s, there were indentured servants in the colonies. Though indentured servitude wasn’t an ideal way of living, it was not slavery. They weren’t indentured servants for their whole lives and there were laws that protected some of their rights.

European traders in West Africa at the time believed that they could get rich by capturing people from Africa and enslaving them. The traders knew that many plantations in the colonies wanted large numbers of workers. The traders wanted to get rich selling enslaved people to plantation owners. Their idea of indentured servitude transformed into slavery. They noticed that some people in Africa did not have the same freedoms as others. People who were captured during wars or found guilty of crimes were already enslaved.

The European traders sometimes traded for enslaved Africans. They offered to trade cloth, food, guns and tobacco for some of the already enslaved people there. Unfortunately, they also simply took and stole Africans from all walks of life. Some tribes were known to force people from their villages regardless of their social status. This included kings, queens, mathematicians and artists. Families were ripped apart for the economic gain of the colonies.

Traders packed enslaved Africans onto ships and took them across the ocean to the colonies. Some did not survive the journey because of disease and malnutrition (not enough food). The ones who did survive were sold to plantation owners. Plantation owners would bid against one another for the right to buy each enslaved person. Enslaved families were often separated. Fathers would be sold to one plantation, while mothers and children would be sold to others.

Though the experiences of enslaved people varied, many were not treated well because of their situations. Enslaved people were often whipped or even killed for breaking rules or trying to run away. Working on the plantations was very difficult. Very few enslaved people were ever given their freedom.

The system of slavery continued in America as our nation grew and changed over many decades. It took a Civil War to put an end to slavery.

title: Slavery Begins in the New World
text:
Imagine that you live in a small village in Africa. You wake up one morning and hear strangers. Before you know it, these strangers capture you and take you to a large boat, even though you fought hard to get away. There are hundreds of Africans on the boat and you barely have room to move. For six weeks, you travel on the boat. You are scared, hungry and sick. Where are you going? What will you do there? When your boat arrives at a port, you are unloaded from the ship. A white man pays money for you and he says you are now his property. For the rest of your life, you will work on his plantation.

More than 11 million people were taken from Africa between 1600 and 1800. Of those who survived crossing the ocean in the ships, about 60 percent went to the West Indies, Central America and the Spanish parts of South America. About 35 percent went to Brazil and 5 percent went to the United States. On Aug. 20, 1619, a Dutch ship anchored in the Jamestown, Virginia, harbor. The captain told the colonists he needed to sell some of his cargo of people for food. The colonists purchased 20 of them. However, they became indentured servants, not slaves. They eventually worked off their obligations and were granted freedom.

As you read in the first paragraph, many slaves were captured against their will and brought to America. They were part of something called the triangular trade. Slaves were bought with a cargo of rum and other trade goods in Africa. They were sold for a cargo of sugar in the West Indies, which was sold for a cargo of rum in the colonies. Then the triangle started once more. Money was made as each cargo was bought and sold. You'll read more about the triangular trade inside.

The new slaves were brought under terrible circumstances - captured by roving gangs of slavers, packed like sardines inside the slave ships without regard for their health or safety, made to endure the terrors at sea in cramped quarters, sold in a strange land to strange people to serve a lifetime as slaves. Families were separated. Work lasted from sunup to sundown in tobacco, indigo, rice, sugar or cotton fields, six days a week. Some slaves worked as servants doing the domestic, or household, chores of the plantation. Many were forbidden to learn to read or write. Plantation owners feared that education would cause a rebellion.

Some plantation owners treated their slaves better than others, but many were cruel. Slavery often meant the loss of health, hopes and dreams, and sometimes even life. It always meant the loss of freedom. There are no former slaves still alive in the United States today because slavery ended in the 1860s. It is important that we learn about the history of slavery in our country so the past is not forgotten.

title: The Amistad
text:
In 1807, there was a law that was passed. The law said that no new enslaved people could be imported, or brought into, the United States. It was a small step in the right direction, but it didn’t completely stop the slave trade or end slavery. If a person was already enslaved, they couldn’t be freed. And the children born to enslaved people were still enslaved.

La Amistad was a ship. Not a big slave ship that carried people across the middle passage, but a smaller ship that traded around Cuba and the Caribbean. In 1839, La Amistad sailed from Havana, Cuba to deliver some general goods and 53 enslaved people to a sugar plantation. However, the enslaved people on the ship had been illegally taken and transported from Africa to Cuba to be sold into slavery. During the voyage, some of the enslaved people rebelled, killed the captain and some of the crew and took over the ship. They wanted to sail back to Africa, but they were caught by a U.S. ship. Because slavery was still legal at the time, the enslaved people on the boat were taken to prison. The slave traders wanted their cargo and the enslaved people returned to them. There was a court case about the situation. Many abolitionists (people who fought against slavery) helped in the case. Former President John Quincy Adams defended the Africans in the trial. They showed the court that the Africans on the ship had been illegally enslaved, and eventually they were freed and returned to Africa.

title: Slavery in the Colonies
text:
Triangular Trade

If you think triangular trade is an exchange of percussion instruments, guess again! Triangular trade is a phrase that describes trade between three continents or ports. This type of trade was common between the 16th and 19th centuries and usually involved Europe, North America and Africa. Many different countries and colonies formed these triangles. Do you remember the Columbian exchange? That's what started it all. People in Europe just couldn't get enough of the goods and resources that came from the Americas. And people in the colonies depended on Europe for goods they couldn't get in America. The African point of the triangle was added when Europeans decided they could use Africans as slaves. In the early 1500s, the Spanish brought slaves to America to help search for gold. A large number of slaves came to Jamestown in the early 1600s. Africans already knew how to work in sugar and indigo fields. The colonists forced them to work without payment - slavery. Slavery here lasted for over 250 years. Let's find out more about each part of triangular trade.

Here's an Example of a Trade Triangle

Leg 1: Great Britain to Africa

Great Britain was a powerful empire in Europe during triangular trade. We know England was competing with France, Spain and the Netherlands for control of the Americas. So you're probably wondering what this has do with Africa? Well, in order to make more money and get more land in America, England needed lots and lots of workers, mostly for the big plantations in their colonies. (Do you remember the three L's - Land, Labor and Loot?) England shipped goods to Africa in exchange for slaves. England traded copper, fine cloth, Asian silk and goods made of glass. Some Africans captured people from other African countries and sent them to England. Perhaps the most valued English goods were guns and ammunition. African town and tribal leaders paid for the goods with healthy people, most of whom would become slaves in America.

Leg 2: Africa to America

Slaves and indigo were Africa's chief exports in colonial times. Hundreds of African families were torn apart when members who could work were shipped to America. Altogether, traders took over 11 million Africans from their homeland. Some were bought and paid for with British goods or goods from America. Others were kidnapped from their towns and put on ships. The Atlantic crossing was known as the Middle Passage, or the middle leg of the triangle. Many Africans were tightly packed below decks where ill treatment, disease and starvation caused many deaths. Of those who survived the Middle Passage, most ended up doing slave work in colonial fields. Some Africans, however, were domestic workers. This exchange of Africans destroyed the populations and family structures of West African villages for hundreds of years. Some free Africans lived in the colonies too. They often farmed or worked at trades.

Leg 3: America to Great Britain

The economy in the Americas developed quickly. The use of slave labor increased profits for cash crops. In the Southern and Middle Colonies, the biggest plantations exported tons of tobacco, cotton and sugar. Other big American crops were rice and coffee. English merchants paid top dollar for Virginia tobacco and rich coffee from the Americas.

Triangular Trade, Then and Now

Countries and colonies in North, Central and South America were all part of triangular trade then. Here's another example: Caribbean slaves made molasses from sugar. The molasses was shipped to the New England Colonies where it was made into rum and shipped across the Atlantic to Africa. The Rhode Island Colony alone had 20-30 rum distilleries (places where liquor is made) and at least 150 ships dedicated to trading with Africa for slaves. If you had been a sailor during the age of triangular trade, you'd probably cross the Atlantic Ocean seven or eight times a year!

Think about all the trade routes there are today and how fast goods can get from one continent to another. The next time you finish a candy bar, do some research about it. Trace the countries of origin of each ingredient and imagine how they traveled the world to get to you. How many triangles of trade exist now? Just thinking about it is mind-boggling!

title: Fort Mose
text:
Back in 1693, the King of Spain made a proclamation that slaves would be freed! Hooray, right? Wait, let's read the small print... there were three conditions:

1. Promise loyalty to Spain.

2. Convert to the Catholic religion.

3. Help build Castillo de San Marcos at St. Augustine.

Maybe this kind of freedom wasn't quite as free as it sounded. Still, many slaves agreed to the deal and ran away to Florida. They lived at a smaller fort two miles north of St. Augustine called Fort Mose (moh-say). This was the first settlement of free Africans in America. Slaves in the Southern, Middle and even New England Colonies heard about Fort Mose. The number of residents there grew as runaway slaves came from places north of Florida. Are you surprised that slaves in the colonies ran away to the South?

title: Benjamin Banneker (1731-1806)
text: Could a slave's child become a famous scientist? Well, that's exactly what became of Benjamin Banneker, who was the son of a slave in Maryland Colony. Benjamin became an astronomer who could predict eclipses. He was also an inventor who made irrigation systems and figured out crop rotations on farms, and a surveyor in the area that became Washington, D.C. Benjamin didn't stop at that, however. He was also a mathematician and wrote almanacs that were filled with poetry, essays and useful tables of information. How did he get his training? He mostly taught himself. Here's something you may not know about him: Benjamin studied the insides of a watch and then built a clock entirely of wood, gears and all!

title: What is Juneteenth?
text: Slaves in Texas celebrated on June 19, 1865, when they heard news of the Emancipation Proclamation. Juneteenth is a short way of saying "June nineteenth." Many people still celebrate this day every year with music, barbecues and strawberry soda. Why do you think it took two and a half years for the slaves in Texas to hear about the Emancipation Proclamation that helped free them on January 1, 1863?

title: Slavery and the Law
text: Have you heard of the Emancipation Proclamation? It was an executive order written by President Abraham Lincoln in 1863, and it helped put an end to most slavery in the United States. Unfortunately, it didn't happen until after slavery had already been around for about 250 years. The proclamation allowed slaves in some states to join the army and fight in the Civil War, which helped guarantee freedom for all. It didn't make slavery completely illegal, though. That didn't happen until 1865, when the 13th Amendment was added to the Constitution. By the way, some of the men who signed the Constitution in 1787 actually owned slaves, while others believed slavery was wrong. But the signers knew the Constitution wasn't perfect. That's what amendments like the 13th are for: to fix or improve our laws. This amendment officially abolished slavery and indentured servitude in our country. (And no, this doesn't apply to your parents making you do chores on Saturdays!)

title: Primary Sources - Slave Auctions and Runaway Slaves
text:
Look carefully at the pictures. These primary sources tell us something about what life was like for slaves in the colonies. Slaves were treated like property, and slave auctions took place often.

Posters put up by slave owners looking for runaway slaves were commonly seen in the late 1700s. Slave owners offered rewards for the return of a runaway slave. It is hard to believe that life could have been so different, isn't it? Use the pictures to answer these questions.

1. Why do you think some slave owners offered a reward for the return of a runaway slave?

2. How do you think runaway slaves felt when they saw the posters?

3. List four things (two for each picture) we can learn about slavery in the colonies by looking at these pictures. When you answer, think about people, places and events of the past.

4. Think of one question you have about one of the pictures. Work with a friend and do some research to see if you can answer your questions.

title: Triangle Trade Cycle Activity
text:
In order to understand how triangle trade “powered” itself, we have to be able to understand the cause and effect cycle. You will be constructing a four-page cause and effect pop-up book. You will need the following materials:

4 sheets of blank paper (any light color will do)

Scissors

Glue stick/Glue

Pencil

The four images featured on this page

Directions:

1. Fold one sheet of paper in half horizontally.

2. On the folded edge, estimate where the center is and make two one-inch cuts with your scissors.

3. Open the paper and gently push the center cut (tab) forward, bend the tab to make it look like a little chair.

4. Repeat steps 1 through 3 for the remaining sheets of paper and set aside.

5. Carefully cut out the four images for this activity.

6. Glue one image to one pop-up “chair” where the back of your calves would touch if you could sit in this “chair”.

7. Line up your four pop-up pages. Determine which event caused the next event and so on.

8. Carefully match up the outside bottom (cause) of one pop-up book to the outside top (effect) of the next pop-up. You will eventually glue all four pop-ups to form a rotating pop-up booklet that represents the cycle of triangle trade.

9. When the glue has dried, add in facts about each step of the triangle trade cycle. Be sure to write your name and date on one of the pages.

title: War in the New World: The French and Indian War
text:
By the 1750s, Great Britain and France were claiming more and more land in the New World. The two countries were bound to clash sooner or later. In 1754, these two powerful countries went to battle over control of an important piece of North American land, the Ohio River Valley.

Why We Fought

Great Britain

We needed the land of the Ohio River Valley. There were many settlers in our colonies who wanted to farm the rich soil there. They had come to the New World for just that reason. If the French wanted the land too, then they'd have a fight on their hands!

France

We had been trapping animals and trading furs for many years in Canada. We had the right to trap beaver in the Ohio River Valley too. We knew we could win this war against the British. No one beats the French - at trapping or at war!

Key Battle Points

Great Britain

Thousands of British soldiers fought side by side with the colonists. At first, things did not look good for our side at all. We lost many battles, but soon everything began going our way. We decided the best way to win the war would be to take control of Canada. In 1759, our troops captured the Canadian city of Quebec. We climbed 300 foot tall cliffs to overcome our foes (enemies). We continued to win battle after battle, ending with the capture of Montreal. We agreed to sign a peace treaty.

France

It was a good thing for us that we were on friendly terms with the American Indians! Because of that, many of the Indians fought on our side. It was easy to surprise the British. They were so easy to spot in their bright red coats! We won several major battles early in the war, but everything changed in 1759. In Quebec, the British defeated us and took over the city. By 1760, it was clear we had lost Canada. The war ended in 1763 when both sides agreed to sign the Treaty of Paris.

Advantages and Disadvantages

Great Britain

We had many more troops than the French. Each of our colonies had its own militia, or volunteer army. Each colony grew its own food, so our soldiers would not go hungry. One problem was that each of our colonies had its own government. Sometimes that caused arguments over small things that weren't all that important.

France

Because we had many settlements near the Ohio River Valley, we knew they would send help quickly if we needed it. They were easy to defend because they were all close together. The settlements were all under the control of one government, so they made decisions quickly. However, we had to have food shipped from France and we sometimes did not have enough for our troops.

After the War

Great Britain

The treaty gave us control of Canada. We also got the land between the Mississippi River and the Appalachian Mountains, the Ohio River Valley. Unfortunately, the war cost a lot of money. Since we spent most of the money on protecting the colonies, we had no choice but to require Americans to pay the debt. We had to raise their taxes, and they weren't happy about that.

France

We lost control of almost all the land we once claimed in North America. One good thing about the war was that we shared our battle techniques with the American Indians. Later, when the American colonists were fighting for their freedom from Great Britain, they used some of our ideas to help them beat the redcoats. That was almost like a victory for us!

title: Tension between the Colonies and Britain
text:
The Proclamation of 1763

After the French and Indian War, many British colonists settled land west of the Appalachian Mountains. The American Indians on these lands were not happy. They did not want European settlers taking the land and hunting the animals. American Indians attacked many colonists' forts and houses by 1763. Almost 2,000 settlers were killed. Great Britain knew it had to do something to protect the people and stop the fighting. The Proclamation of 1763 was its answer. According to this law, American Indians had a right to all the land west of the Appalachian Mountains. Settlers were not allowed to move there anymore. The law made many of the colonists really mad. Some of them ignored it and moved west anyway. More and more settlers began to talk to each other about not liking Britain's control. This was the first time a British law made the colonists angry, but it wouldn't be the last.

The Quartering Act

After the French and Indian War, Britain was still afraid the colonists would be attacked. Thousands of British soldiers stayed in the colonies to offer protection. Housing, feeding and supplying the soldiers cost a lot of money. Great Britain wanted the colonists to support the soldiers, so Parliament (branch of British government that made laws) passed a new law called the Quartering Act. The law said the colonists had to provide soldiers with places to live, or quarters. The colonists had to supply the soldiers with food, transportation and supplies like candles and fuel for lamps. Once again the colonists got mad about a British law. They did not believe they should have to support the British troops. They thought the British soldiers were rude and loud. They were also angry that the soldiers took part-time jobs away from colonists. Back then the American colonists did not have the right to elect representatives to Parliament. The colonists thought it was unfair that they had no representative to vote in Parliament.

The Stamp Act

Most American colonists had come to North America in search of wealth and freedom. However, it seemed that neither would be possible if Great Britain continued to have control over the settlers' daily lives. The British kept passing laws that the colonists thought were unfair. Britain passed The Stamp Act to help pay off its debts. Colonists would have to pay a tax on all printed papers. Every piece of paper the colonists used had to be marked with a large stamp to prove someone had paid taxes for that paper. Legal papers, newspapers, magazines and even playing cards were all taxed. The colonists were furious and refused to buy the stamps. Some of them protested, or spoke out against, the law while standing in the streets and town squares. A few colonists were so mad they even attacked the men who collected the stamp tax money for Britain.

In October 1765, nine colonies held a special meeting called the Stamp Act Congress. They wanted Parliament to know they didn't think it was fair for the colonists to pay taxes without having representatives to vote. The King of England and Parliament were surprised at how angry the colonists were. They repealed, or cancelled, the Stamp Act in 1766. However, Great Britain let the colonists know it was still Parliament's right to make colonists pay taxes.

Trouble in Boston

In 1770, colonists were still upset by the Quartering Act. Great Britain continued to tax colonists unfairly. Colonists believed the British soldiers were there to help collect taxes and keep peace, not to protect them from American Indians. Soldiers continued to live in colonial towns and cities, and they still did not get along with the colonists. In Boston, Massachusetts, the colonists often made fun of the soldiers. They laughed at the soldiers' red coats and called them "lobsterbacks." The British soldiers didn't always keep their tempers. They often went out of their way to hassle citizens they didn't like. Name-calling and street fights were common in Boston.

On March 5, 1770, the violence between the soldiers and colonists got out of hand. That night a group of Boston colonists began yelling at a British soldier guarding the Custom House, a tax collection building. Soon people were throwing trash, rocks, snowballs and ice at Captain Thomas Preston and seven other soldiers who had come to help him. No one is really sure what happened next. Perhaps the soldiers didn't hear a command correctly, or maybe were tired of having things thrown at them. The soldiers fired their muskets into the crowd. While the smoke from their guns was still in the air, five colonists lay dead. Six more were badly hurt.

The colonists called this awful event the Boston Massacre. A massacre is the murder of people who cannot defend themselves. The soldiers were put on trial for their actions. No lawyer wanted to represent them. John Adams, a local lawyer, finally agreed to take the case. Only two of the men were punished. Some of the people of Boston were very upset because they thought the soldiers did not get what they deserved. John Adams and Paul Revere made sure that news of the massacre spread throughout all 13 colonies. Colonists were more determined than ever to show Great Britain how angry they were. Unfortunately, Great Britain became even more determined to show how much control it had over the colonies. Trouble - and war - was in store for both sides.

title: Benjamin Franklin: Inventor, Scientist, Writer, Patriot
text:
When you think of the title "Founding Father" what comes to mind? We know many men as Founding Fathers. These men worked hard to gain America's freedom from Great Britain. One of them is Benjamin Franklin. When you hear his name you probably think of him as a very famous inventor or scientist. Of course, he did invent bifocal glasses, medical equipment, a wood burning stove, a lightning rod and the odometer (a tool for measuring distance traveled). His inventions and discoveries made life better for people.

Perhaps you think of Ben Franklin as a writer. After all, he wrote many different books and magazines. People enjoyed reading his advice on money and education. He also wrote many famous sayings people still use today. (Have you ever heard, "A penny saved is a penny earned"?) Franklin was also an excellent printer. This allowed him to make many copies of his books!

Most of all, Benjamin Franklin was highly respected and admired in colonial America. He was a true patriot! A patriot is someone who loves and defends his country. At first, Franklin wanted the colonies to try and work with Great Britain to solve their problems. He went to Great Britain to ask for fair treatment of the colonies. He stayed calm while he tried to persuade (convince) Parliament to repeal, or cancel, unfair laws. And he did help get the Stamp Act repealed. When Franklin finally realized Great Britain still believed they were right to tax the colonists, he came home. He was ready to help America fight for the right to govern themselves.

Another of Franklin's famous sayings was, "All mankind is divided into three classes: those that are immovable, those that are movable and those that move." Franklin wanted the American colonies to move towards independence.

title: Who was John Wise?
text: John Wise was a Colonial American minister who was indeed a very "wise" man. Wise was born and lived in Massachusetts his whole life. He studied at Harvard College and became the minister of a church in Ipswich, Massachusetts. This tall man often spoke forcefully about what he believed. He had strong opinions about how to organize the church. He preached about the democratic rights of people, and how they should have a say in government. One time he spoke out against unfair taxes, and other church leaders punished him by removing him as minister of the church. He had many ideas about how the church and the colonies could be better and stronger. His famous writings expressed ideas that our Founding Fathers later used in the Declaration of Independence.

title: Loyalists, Patriots and Neutralists
text:
As colonists began to argue about whether or not they should declare their independence, they started to take sides. Some people thought it was better for the colonies to stay under the rule of Great Britain. They wanted to remain loyal, or true, to the King of England. These people became known as Loyalists. Many Loyalists were rich landowners. Some of them had jobs in government or churches.

It was easy to think of a name for the people who did not like the way Great Britain treated the colonies - Patriots. They wanted the colonies to become an independent country that the King of England could not control. The Patriots gave speeches and wrote articles about the unfair treatment of the colonies.

Some colonists did not take sides. They were known as Neutralists. Which would you have been - Loyalist, Patriot or Neutralist? Talk about it with your class.

title: Causes and Effects of the French and Indian War
text:
Historians know it is important to try and understand what caused an event in history to happen. It’s also important to know what happened because of, or after, the event. This is an effect. The words “because,” “so” and “then” often show a cause-and-effect relationship.

Use information in this week’s issue to fill in the cause-and-effect chart below. As you look back at the articles, remember to look for words that show a cause and-effect relationship.
