title: Discover the Seven Wonders of America!
text:
If you traveled across America from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean, what landforms would you see along the way? Mountains? Plains? Plateaus? Lakes? Forests? You would see all of these and more! Our country has a wide variety of physical features that make it a beautiful and interesting place to live. This week, we will learn more about these features.

The United States can be divided into seven major areas, or regions. Each region has unique physical features. Each region also has its own climate (weather over a long period of time), economy (the way people make, spend and save money) and industry. Each has other characteristics that set it apart from the other regions, too.

Here’s a list of America’s seven regions. See if you can find them on the map and then keep reading to learn more about each one.

title: Mapping the News
text:
Have you ever heard or read a news report about a certain place and wondered where it is? Mapping the news can help. This is a fun way to learn geography and keep up with things that are going on in the world at the same time. Here’s how it works: Your teacher will put a world map on a bulletin board in your classroom or in the hall. Once a week, students can bring in news articles to share with the class. (Ask your parents to help you with that part, especially if you get your news articles from the Internet. Also, do some research before you get to class to get a general idea of where the place is located.) In class, talk about each article and the place where the event happened. Find that place on the world map and mark it with a pushpin or a sticker.

For example, let’s say your friend brings an article about a mountain climber who reaches the top of Mount Everest on the border between Tibet and Nepal. She already found out that those two countries are in south Asia. That will help you find Mount Everest more quickly.

Try mapping the news for several weeks. Then get into groups and make up a game that involves the places you mapped. Playing the game will help you remember what you learned. Have fun mapping the news!

title: USA’s Seven
text:
Read the description of each region below. Find your region on the map. What famous places are in your region? Look for other regions where you have lived or visited.

This is a map of the Continental United States. Do some research to find out in which regions the states of Alaska and Hawaii belong.

1. Pacific Coastal Plains

This region lies along the Pacific coastline from Alaska to Mexico. One physical feature of this region is that it has mountains bordering the ocean. There are more potentially active volcanoes in this region than in any other region in the Lower 48. The two main mountain ranges are the Cascade Mountains in the north and the Sierra Nevada Mountains in the south. The western valleys have fertile and rich land. Many high-quality fruits are grown there. Giant redwoods are an interesting feature in the northern Californian mountains. The San Andreas Fault, another feature of this region, sometimes causes earthquakes.

2. Western Plateau

East of the Pacific Coastal Plains and west of the Rocky Mountains lies the Western Plateau, or the Great Basin. This region stretches from Washington state to Mexico. The Western Plateau includes mountains, deserts and the Grand Canyon. Many places in this region are very dry, so not many crops grow there. In the north, farms are able to produce good crops through irrigation. Other areas have forested mountains, fertile farmlands and orchards. One famous part of this region is called the Colorado Plateau. Here you can see some of the world's most unusual and beautiful landforms.

3. Rocky Mountains

The Rocky Mountain range is the longest mountain range in North America. It begins in Canada and extends through central New Mexico. Many of the peaks are more than 12,000 feet high. Mount Elbert in Colorado is the tallest peak in the range at 14,433 feet. Crossing the Rockies was a major problem for settlers moving west in the 1800s.

An imaginary line called the Continental Divide passes through the Rockies. On the west side of the line, rivers and streams flow down toward the Pacific Ocean. On the east side of the line, rivers and streams flow down toward the Atlantic Ocean.

The lower parts of the Rocky Mountains are covered with trees. However, in the upper parts of the Rockies, only plants like grasses, mosses and lichens can grow.

4. Interior Plains

The Interior Plains is the largest region in the United States and it is located in the center of the country. The western part of this region has good grasslands for grazing cattle and rich soil for farming. Other parts of the region have oil and coal deposits. Today, the Mississippi River flows through the region, but it may surprise you to know that scientists think this area was once a large sea.

5. Atlantic Coastal Plains

This region extends from New England along the Atlantic coastline and the Appalachian foothills, down through Florida to the Gulf of Mexico. The gulf area has farms and grasslands. It also has large oil and natural gas deposits. The southern states also have good farmland. Farmers grow tobacco, peanuts, cotton and many other products.

6. Appalachian Region

This region begins in Maine and continues down into Alabama. Although the Appalachian Mountains are not as rugged as the Rockies, transportation through the Appalachians can still be difficult. Fortunately, large rivers cutting through the mountains have made some good places for people to build railroads and highways. Up in the mountains, minerals and coal are produced. In the valleys, farming is a major activity. Because forests cover these mountains, the lumber industry is a big part of the economy in this region.

7. Ozark Highlands

The Ozark Highlands are not very high at all! This area, including Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma and Arkansas, is best described as a plateau. The land is not good for farming but there are many forests filled with cedar, oak, hickory and pine trees. Underground caverns are an interesting feature of this region. You will also find many man-made water reservoirs in this area.

title: Sharing Public Space: Vitus Bering and Russian Colonies in Alaska
text:
Imagine traveling 6,000 miles over land with supplies for an expedition, and THEN sailing through frigid seas to look for a new world. This was the job given to Vitus Bering, a Danish navigator who sailed for the Russian navy. Peter the Great, czar (ruler) of Russia, asked Bering to explore the eastern coast of Russia. He was wondering if land connected Asia and North America.

Bering's first trip began in 1725. After spending three years getting his supplies to eastern Russia, Bering sailed along the coastline. He didn't see any land to the east, and he didn't realize he was sailing in the narrow passage between Russia and Alaska. This waterway is now called the Bering Strait.

Bering led another expedition in 1741. This time his ship landed on Kayak Island, off the coast of Alaska. They explored some of the Aleutian Islands and met the native people there, the Aleut. He was the first European to arrive in present-day Alaska.

Bering died before returning to Russia, but his voyages paved the way for Russian settlements in North America. Many fur traders came to the area. In 1799 the Russian government established a fur-trading operation in Alaska. Furs from foxes, sea otters and seals were very valuable.

Unfortunately, the Russians took advantage of the native people just as some Europeans had done in settling New England. The Russians took over their lands and forced them to hunt for furs. They also brought new diseases, which killed many natives.

Today, the Aleut people continue to live along the western coast of North America, and their population has grown. What might have been different if the Russians and the Aleut had shared public space fairly? Where in your community is there a debate over public land? How should such debates be handled?

title: Caravel
text: In the 1400s, the Portuguese built a ship that would carry explorers and traders all the way across the Atlantic Ocean. The ship they created was called a caravel. This boat was different from other boats of its time because it could sail very fast, it could sail into the wind and it could float in shallow water. It also had a unique feature: its sails were shaped like triangles. Columbus used a caravel when he went to explore the New World. The boats named the Niña and the Pinta were both caravels. The caravel was important because it allowed explorers to journey almost anywhere they wanted to go.

title: Two More Stars on the Flag!
text:
Alaska became the 49th state on January 3, 1959. Covering more than 650,000 square miles, it is our largest state. It shares a border with Canada.

Hawaii became the 50th state on August 21, 1959. It is the only state made up entirely of islands. Hawaii is in the Pacific Ocean, more than 2500 miles from California.

title: A New Country Heads West
text:
In 1776 a new nation was born. When the Revolutionary War was over, the United States began to grow and prosper. The people had a new government that guaranteed their liberties in the Bill of Rights. Many Americans began to look westward for the chance to make their dreams come true. Read this fiction story about 11-year-old William Pruitt, whose father was a silversmith and had great plans for his family to settle land west of their home in Virginia.

William could see how excited his father was about the idea to move west. A poster hanging in the window of the general store said there was plenty of land for the taking. All people had to do was claim it. William's father came home that day talking only about the westward adventure. It was all he had ever dreamed of.

A move west would be a difficult one, though. William's mother did not share her husband's excitement. The thought of crossing the Appalachian Mountains to claim land seemed foolish and dangerous to her. She carefully made her points to William's father.

"Please remember, Jacob. Less than 20 years ago Daniel Boone and his men started a settlement in Kentucky. The land was a brutal wilderness, and they had to hike through the dangerous brush with hardly any food at all. They met angry natives who were not happy to see white settlers on their land. And Boone's son was captured and killed by a group of Indians. I'm afraid a journey west might be the end of our family."

Taking his wife's hand into his own, William's father spoke calmly and firmly.

"Lydia, this is why we came to settle in America. We would never have had the chance to own land back in England. Here we have the freedom to follow our dreams. People say the land is fertile enough to grow any crop we choose. Maybe we'll even find riches like gold and silver. Yes, the journey will be dangerous, but we can conquer this land. It is our right to do so. We will head westward."

William knew from the serious tone of his father's voice that he had made a decision. The family's westward adventure would soon begin.

title: Eminent Domain: Public Good or Unfair to Property Owners?
text:
The U.S. government tried to order Brian Rainville to sell his Franklin, Vermont, farm. The government wanted to use Mr. Rainville's land to help protect the nation's border. In Lakewood, Ohio, the city government tried to order the Saleet family to sell their house. City leaders wanted to build a shopping center and new, higher-priced homes on the site so the city would make more money in taxes. The government of New London, Connecticut, supported a developer's plan to open new businesses, so homeowner Susette Kelo had to sell the land on which her home was built. She got to keep her house. How? Workers moved it to another piece of land. How can the government order U.S. citizens to sell their property?

Eminent domain is what can make that happen. The Fifth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution says that the government cannot take away someone's private property for use by the public without compensation (payment). Eminent domain allows the U.S. government to regulate (control) publicly owned property. That means sometimes people have to sell their property to improve communities for all people .

The judicial branch of government decides many cases of eminent domain. Courts hear the cases and decide if the Constitution supports the sale of the property. Sometimes the courts take the side of the government. Other times the courts side with the property owner. Usually one side or the other leaves court unhappy.

What do you think about eminent domain? Is it good for the public, or is it unfair to property owners?

title: Looking to the West
text:
Why Westward?

After the Revolutionary War ended in 1783, the United States found itself in control of all the land from the Atlantic Ocean to the Mississippi River. Some settlers who had been in America for many years were beginning to feel crowded in the colonies. They saw an opportunity to own more land and decided to head west to the other side of the Appalachian Mountains.

Some people looked across the mountains and saw plenty of natural resources, such as lumber and furs. They also saw business opportunities in those resources. They knew they would be able to sell goods to the people who stayed in the East and to the people who moved west. Some people moved west for adventure. Some liked the idea of being far away from other settlements, on their own in the vast wilderness.

American leaders also wanted the country to be strong and safe. Spain controlled Florida and much of the Southwest. France claimed much of the land west and northwest of the Mississippi River. England controlled the land to the north in Canada. If Americans settled these lands, it would be harder for foreign countries to continue to control them.

The Louisiana Purchase

By 1800 more and more settlers had crossed the Appalachians. Some had even moved as far west as the Mississippi River. The settlers needed supplies but the Appalachians were a big problem. It would be easier to ship goods up and down the Mississippi River to the port of New Orleans. From New Orleans people could get goods to or from the states along the Atlantic coast. The problem was that France owned New Orleans and all of the Louisiana Territory - more than 500 million acres!

President Thomas Jefferson offered to buy New Orleans from France. This would allow Americans to ship goods more easily. And France needed money to help pay for war with England. The French were ready to give up their land in North America. In 1803 French leader Napoleon Bonaparte agreed to sell not just New Orleans, but the entire Louisiana Territory for a very reasonable $15 million. The land doubled the size of the United States and only cost about 3 cents per acre.

The Louisiana Purchase was definitely a bargain for the United States, but it wasn't good for everyone living there. American Indians had already been pushed west by the settlers. Now even more were pushed off the land and forced to live on reservations (areas of land set aside by the U.S. government). Many died of starvation, harsh weather and disease.

The Lewis and Clark Expedition

When President Jefferson offered to buy the Louisiana Territory, he already had a plan to send a group of men to explore the unknown wilderness. In May 1804 two former soldiers led an expedition (a journey to explore new land) into the Louisiana Territory. Meriwether Lewis and William Clark were sent to explore the land, draw maps and study the plants, animals and American Indians living there. They were told to look for trading posts or settlements already established in the territory. Lewis and Clark also hoped to find the Northwest Passage. Remember those early explorers like John Cabot and Henry Hudson? People in Lewis and Clark's time were still convinced there was a waterway connecting the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.

About 40 other men joined Lewis and Clark on the expedition. They traveled up the Missouri River searching for another river that would take them to the Pacific. They were caught in the high, cold plateaus of what is now North Dakota in the winter of 1804-1805. There was little to eat, and the men were afraid they would die. They were saved by spending the winter with a group of American Indians. That winter they met a young Shoshone girl named Sacagawea. Later, she guided the men through the Rocky Mountains and translated for them when they met American Indians. At one point, she even saved the travel journals from being lost when a canoe overturned.

With Sacagawea's help, Lewis and Clark found the Salmon, Snake and Columbia rivers. They traveled these waterways and reached the Pacific Ocean in November 1805. On the way home, the men continued to map new discoveries and record information about over 300 new species of plants and animals. After returning to Missouri, the men were treated as heroes. They braved dangerous situations and survived to tell everyone about the new land the United States owned. Settlers now had maps and information that would make traveling through the Louisiana Territory easier. People could now move even farther west.

Manifest Destiny

Over time more and more Americans began to head into new territory to establish homes, farms, businesses and towns. They were proud of the United States. They felt it was their God-given right and their duty to spread the American way of life as far west as they could, no matter what the cost. If necessary, they would push other people, especially American Indians, out of the way. By the mid-1800s, this idea was known as Manifest Destiny. However, some people questioned it. Was Manifest Destiny more about spreading a good way of life or more about greed and controlling land and people? The United States held on to the idea of Manifest Destiny for many years to come.

title: President Thomas Jefferson, Anti-Federalist
text:
Most people would agree that Thomas Jefferson earned his place as one of the most important Founding Fathers of the United States of America. After all, he wrote the Declaration of Independence. The Louisiana Purchase is considered by many to be his greatest accomplishment after he became president. But the purchase was a difficult decision for him.

You see, Thomas Jefferson was an anti-federalist. That means he did not believe in having a strong federal, or national, government. Jefferson remembered the power King George had over the colonists, and he did not want the people of America to live that way again. Jefferson felt the national government should be strong when it dealt with foreign countries, but he believed that each state should make decisions in all other matters.

Jefferson also believed very strongly in the Constitution. He agreed that any power not given to the federal government belonged to the states or to the people. When the opportunity to buy the Louisiana Territory came up, Jefferson faced a tough decision. The Constitution did not give the federal government the specific right to make the purchase. However, Jefferson knew he did not have time to wait for an amendment to the Constitution. He had to act quickly. Jefferson approved the $15 million purchase. Luckily, most people in the United States agreed with Jefferson’s idea to buy the land. Without Thomas Jefferson, the history of our country might be very different!

title: Fur: Soft Gold of New Settlements
text:
People in North America had been trapping animals for their fur long before Lewis and Clark's expedition to the Northwest. The French, English and Dutch had been exploring and trapping since the 17th century. Many settlements started as trading posts for furs and other goods.

After Lewis and Clark mapped the area of the Rocky Mountains, fur trappers could better explore the land. Beaver pelts (skins) were especially valuable because it was not easy for European hunters to find beavers there. Beavers also had higher quality fur than some other animals. There were plenty of beavers in the Rocky Mountain region. People wanted the beaver pelts because they were waterproof and warm. They used the thick fur like money. They traded furs for weapons, blankets and food. People often wore beaver pelt hats and boots. Some trappers traded over 600 pelts in one season.

Soon many businesses saw a chance to make a lot of money. They hired young, strong trappers to head into the Northwest. People knew these trappers as "mountain men" because they could survive the extreme conditions of the Rocky Mountains. They often made friends with American Indians, who led the mountain men to the best hunting areas.

A business called the Rocky Mountain Fur Company started having gatherings called rendezvous. The gatherings were often held at trading posts, where the mountain men could trade their furs and buy supplies for the next year. Settlements sometimes formed around these fur trading posts and grew into successful towns and cities.

title: Before the War: Jefferson Defends the Louisiana Purchase
text:
"I know that the acquisition of Louisiana has been disapproved by some... The larger our association the less will it be shaken by local passions; and in any view is it not better that the opposite bank of the Mississippi should be settled by our own brethren and children than by strangers of another family?" - President Thomas Jefferson, 1803, talking about the purchase of the Louisiana Territory from France.

Buying the Louisiana Territory from France doubled the size of the United States. France had needed money, and the United States wanted land. Jefferson believed that the United States would be safer and stronger if the land west of the Mississippi belonged to us instead of a foreign country. To President Thomas Jefferson and many others, the Louisiana Purchase sounded like a win-win situation.

Citizens of the United States moved westward into the new territory. They built new settlements where they had plenty of space to farm the fertile land and start their own businesses. They used rivers like the Mississippi and Ohio to move goods. People were making good livings, and things seemed to be going well in the growing country.

Still, not everyone thought the Louisiana Purchase was a good idea. With so many people moving west, the biggest worry was that the land would eventually become new states. Why did some people think that was a problem? Because they were afraid the eastern states would lose some of their power. Jefferson reminded them that the United States now controlled the Mississippi River and the Port of New Orleans. Goods could be shipped to the port and then out of the United States. It would be good for the U.S. economy. He also said it would be better to have our own "brethren (brothers) and children" settle across the Mississippi River than strangers. President Jefferson worked hard to stay on friendly terms with foreign countries, especially Great Britain, France and Spain. He knew it was important to be able to continue to export goods overseas. (Export means to send something to another place.) And he wanted to stay out of disagreements between other countries.

Unfortunately, things did not go exactly as Jefferson hoped, and soon the United States found itself in the middle of a fight with Great Britain. By that time, James Madison was the president. Once again, we were at war with the country from which we had won our independence just a few decades earlier. How did the War of 1812 begin? What happened after the war was over? You'll find out inside this paper!

title: ‘Amanece, lo veis?’
text:
“The Star Spangled Banner” is the national anthem of our country. Americans take off their hats, hold their hands over their hearts and sing the anthem to honor the United States.

Not long ago Adam Kidron, a British music producer, recorded a Spanish language version of the anthem. “Nuestro Hymno” (“Our Anthem”) is sung by several artists, including Haitian singer Wyclef Jean.

Some people support the Spanish language version of the anthem. They believe since America is a country of immigrants it is fine to sing the song in another language. Some say the anthem’s themes of struggle, freedom and opportunity translate well into Spanish.

Others believe the national anthem should only be sung in English. They say it is disrespectful to the country to sing the national anthem in Spanish. Some people don’t like it because they believe singing the song in Spanish is a way to support illegal immigration.

What do you think?

title: The War of 1812
text:
Rumors of War

Just weeks after selling the Louisiana Territory to the United States, France was at war with Great Britain. The United States quickly made plans to keep doing business with both countries while staying out of the war itself. The United States depended on the money it made selling goods to European countries and could not afford to lose any of that business. So we kept selling food to both Great Britain and France. At first, Great Britain and France were OK with that plan. But soon both countries began to question whose side we were on. Great Britain and France began slowing down and sometimes stopping cargo ships (ships carrying goods) on the Atlantic Ocean. Many times British or French sailors searched the cargo areas of U.S. ships. Both countries wanted to make sure the United States wasn't supplying the other with weapons. Americans wanted to stay out of the war, but that was getting harder to do.

The Embargo Act of 1807

President Jefferson and his advisors decided that the United States had to do something to put an end to the bullying of our ships by Great Britain and France. He believed the United States should stop sending American supplies to both countries. That would teach them a lesson! So Congress passed the Embargo Act of 1807. An embargo is an order to stop ships from delivering goods. The law said that no goods could be shipped to any foreign port. The United States hoped that both France and Great Britain would be devastated without American supplies. Unfortunately the Embargo Act backfired. The two nations at war were able to get along just fine without U.S. goods. When the deliveries stopped, ships full of rotting food were left in American harbors. The people of the United States were very unhappy, and President Jefferson repealed (cancelled) the Embargo Act. U.S. ships began sailing again, but soon they were again being treated badly by the European countries. British ships continued capturing U.S. sailors and forcing them to fight for the British Navy. This practice was called impressment.

War Hawks Urge Mr. Madison to Start a War

James Madison was Thomas Jefferson's secretary of state. He knew a lot about history and government and was known as the "Father of the Constitution." He also helped write the Bill of Rights. In 1808 he succeeded, or followed, Jefferson to become the fourth president of the United States.

Our nation was not in good shape. The Embargo Act had left the United States feeling angry and upset. People lost a lot of money during this time. They also believed that many problems with American Indians were caused by the British. Everyone wanted the United States to be strong and proud again. Many Americans wanted the United States to declare another war against Great Britain.

A group of Congressmen called the War Hawks convinced Madison to declare war. Congress agreed, and in June 1812 the United States was again at war with Great Britain.

An End to War, But Not to Problems

The War of 1812 ended on Christmas Eve, 1814. Communication was slow in those days, and word of the end of the war didn't reach General Andrew Jackson in New Orleans. There, in early January 1815, he led an army of over 4,000 men. Some were regular U.S. soldiers, but others were frontiersmen from southern states, former slaves from Haiti and even pirate outlaws. They banded together against a British army of almost 8,000. When the Battle of New Orleans was over, 2,000 British soldiers had been killed, while the United States lost only 13 men.

Jackson's victory saved New Orleans even though the war had been over for days. The Treaty of Ghent was signed in February 1815, officially ending the war. What did Americans gain from the War of 1812? Something very important - the reputation as a world power.

Major Events of the War of 1812

June 1812 - United States declares war against Great Britain

July 1812 - First battle of the war as United States invades British-ruled Canada

August 1812 - U.S. troops surrender to British and American Indian forces at Detroit, Michigan

August 1812 - U.S. ship the USS Constitution defeats the British ship HMS Guerriere

November 1812 - James Madison re-elected president

December 1812 - The USS Constitution defeats the HMS Java

March 1813 - British Navy begins raids in the Chesapeake Bay area

April 1813 - Americans capture Toronto

May 1813 - British Navy blockades most middle and southern states in the United States

November 1813 - British offer to talk peace with the United States

April 1814 - British Navy blockades New England

July 1814 - British forces occupy Maine

August 1814 - U.S. banks and economy in serious trouble while peace talks begin

August 1814 - The British burn Washington, D.C.

September 1814 - Frances Scott Key writes “The Star Spangled Banner” at Fort McHenry

January 1815 - General Andrew Jackson and troops defeat the British at the Battle of New Orleans

February 1815 - Peace Treaty of Ghent ratified and President Madison declares the war at an end

title: Uncle Sam
text:
Everyone has seen him: A tall, white-haired gentleman with a white goatee on his chin. He usually wears a top hat and always dresses in red, white and blue. Of course, this is Uncle Sam!

Uncle Sam is a symbol that represents the United States of America. No one knows exactly how the character of Uncle Sam came into being, but he probably is based on a man named Samuel Wilson, who lived in the United States early in the 19th century.

According to legend, Samuel was a beef supplier for the U.S. Army during the War of 1812. When Wilson shipped the beef out in barrels from his company in New York, he labeled them "U.S." for United States. One of Wilson's employees joked once that U.S. stood for "Uncle Sam" Wilson. Soon Army men were talking about "Uncle Sam's" beef. This led to the idea that Uncle Sam stood for anything related to the U.S. government. Everyone agreed that Samuel Wilson was honest, fair and reliable. They also knew he loved and supported his country. He seemed like the perfect model for a character to represent the United States.

Did Samuel Wilson the beef packer look like the Uncle Sam character we know today? Not really. The Uncle Sam character today, an older man wearing a star-spangled suit, is the product of many artists and cartoonists over the years.

Along with the bald eagle and stars and stripes, Uncle Sam is an enduring, or long-lasting, symbol of our nation.

title: The Star-Spangled Banner
text:
The War of 1812 was a complicated one. There were many causes and unclear outcomes. One positive result of this war may have been a feeling of national pride. Americans had proved that the country was indeed a world power. This feeling of patriotism can be seen in "The Star-Spangled Banner," our country's national anthem, which was written during the war.

In September 1814, the United States and Great Britain fought a terrible battle near Baltimore, Maryland, at Fort McHenry. British ships attacked the fort from the harbor early in the morning. They blasted the fort with cannon fire. Rockets whizzed through the air and lit up the sky. The battle lasted through the night.

A lawyer named Francis Scott Key was on a ship in the harbor. He had been trying to help get an American prisoner freed. The British agreed to release the man, but not until the battle at Fort McHenry was over. All night long Key watched and waited for a sign that his nation had won a victory.

At dawn the Fort McHenry soldiers knew they were going to defeat the British. In celebration they raised a giant United States flag and played "Yankee Doodle." Key was eight miles away down the river, but he clearly saw the flag. He wrote the words to "The Star-Spangled Banner" as a poem to remember that night.

The poem was put to the music of a popular song of the day and quickly became a favorite of the people. In 1931 Congress voted to make "The Star-Spangled Banner" the national anthem for the United States of America.

title: The Annexation of Texas
text:
Following the War of 1812, the Industrial Revolution was in full progress in the United States. In many cities, industry changed the way people lived and worked. For some people though, the wilderness still called, and a land named Texas seemed the perfect place to be. In the 1820s, Mexico gained independence from Spain and took control of the Texas territory. Mexican officials realized they needed more Anglo settlers to come to Texas. What might life have been like then? Imagine that in 1845, 11-year-old James Young's family had been living in Mexican-controlled Texas for many years. Read James' journal entry about the day Texas became a part of the United States of America.

Dec. 29, 1845

Today, Pa says that the United States officially annexed (joined with) Texas, and we are now part of the United States. Texas President Anson Jones lowered the Texas flag this morning and the U.S. flag was raised high. Pa says it is what is best for us all, but I know everything has changed since he came to Texas with his parents in 1828.

Before that time, there were very few Anglos in Texas. Most people here were American Indian like the Apaches and Comanche. Pa's family lived in Virginia and wanted to own land. That would not be very easy to do in the United States. So, Pa's family came to Texas and settled on free land the Mexican government had promised them. In return, my grandfather promised to raise crops and animals on the fertile land. He also pledged, or promised, to pay taxes to the Mexican government and practice the Catholic religion. Like all the other settlers to Texas, Pa and his family promised to learn to speak Spanish and follow the Mexican laws.

By 1830, there were many Anglo families living in Texas. Soon the people weren't getting along with the Mexican government. Most of the people never learned to speak Spanish and didn't want to change religions just to please the Mexicans. The Mexicans passed new laws that made life even harder for settlers. Pa had just married Mama in 1833 when the settlers asked Mexico to let Texas have its own government. The settlers were not happy with Mexico's rules. Pa said when I was just a baby, fighting broke out between the powerful Mexican government and the Texas people. I have heard the stories of the battles in Gonzales and Goliad many times.

Of course, many know the story of the Texans who fought bravely against General Santa Anna at the Alamo. I always enjoy hearing Mama tell me about how she and Pa had to run away from the cruel general when they thought his men were coming to burn down our farm. I was too young to remember it all, but it sure sounds dangerous. I'll bet Pa was very brave. I know the Texans were shouting, "Remember the Alamo!" when General Sam Houston led an attack against the Mexicans at San Jacinto in April 1836.

Pa said many people probably cheered when the Texas flag was lowered and the U.S. flag was raised. Texas needs the money and the protection the United States can give. I know Texas might not be able to stand strong on its own right now. Like many other people though, I feel sad that the Republic of Texas is no longer. I just hope the Mexicans can accept that the United States is calling Texas its own.

Less than six months after Texas became a state, Congress declared war on Mexico. Turn the page and keep reading to find out what happened!

title: The United States Fights Mexico for Land
text:
The United States Fights Mexico for Land

The idea of Manifest Destiny was not a new one for the United States by the 19th century. After the United States purchased the Louisiana territory and Lewis and Clark explored and mapped the wilderness, many Americans wanted the chance to own land. They excitedly headed into the new territory to build homes, businesses and settlements. The people thought it was their job to spread their way of life as far as they could, even if it meant pushing people aside who were there first.

By the early 1800s, Americans heard about new land that Mexico held in the Southwest. Mexico was eager to have Anglo settlers. Officials were almost giving land in Texas away. Americans began moving into Texas by the thousands and by 1830, more than 20,000 Anglos had settled in the area. Though they had agreed to become Mexican citizens, many of the settlers never let go of the idea of Manifest Destiny. They became very upset that the Mexican government demanded they give up their own ways of living.

Texas as a Republic

The Texans ended up declaring their independence, and they fought a war with Mexico. From 1836-1845, Texas was an independent republic. They had defeated Mexico, but the Mexican culture lived on through the food, the customs, the names of the cities and the architecture of the buildings. Even though it was once a source of discord (disagreement), the Spanish language and Catholic religion are still very much a part of the Texas tradition today.

To Annex or Not?

Without the ability to raise money or form a powerful army, Texas turned to the United States for help. The answer was annexation. There were great debates about whether Texas should become part of the United States. Slavery was allowed in Texas, and many Northerners did not want another slave state. Also, the United States would have to take on the debts (money owed) that Texas had piled up. In the end, the United States decided to annex (join with) Texas, and Texas became the 28th state. The United States now had a very large state with an abundance (large amount) of excellent land with many resources.

Mexico Changes Its Mind

Mexico began to rethink its decision to give up so easily on Texas. The Mexican government suddenly wanted Texas back. The two countries did not agree on the southwestern boundary of Texas. Americans wanted the Rio Grande to be the border, but Mexico wanted it to be about 150 miles further northeast. This would greatly decrease the size of Texas. Tension grew between the neighboring countries.

The War is On!

The argument over the boundary of Texas continued. In 1846, U.S. President Polk sent the Army to protect the Rio Grande. The Mexicans tried to defend the land against U.S. General Zachary Taylor and his men. There was a small battle at Palo Alto, Texas. President Polk then went before the U.S. Congress and asked the members to declare war. The Mexican-American War began two days later on May 13, 1846.

The war continued for nearly two years. Many Americans were against the war. Some people felt the annexation of Texas would lead to war, and now they could say, "We told you so." People felt the United States was being too greedy for land. Others supported President Polk's war. They felt that the land was their Manifest Destiny, and many people joined the army to fight against the Mexicans. They fought to take land that they believed it was their right to have.

The battles were deadly as both sides fought fiercely. General Zachary Taylor led American troops into Mexico City. Even after they captured the capital, Mexico continued to fight. Soldiers also fought battles in Texas and California.

Mexico Surrenders

Mexico finally surrendered. In February 1848, officials signed the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo and ended the war. Mexico ceded (gave up) a great deal of territory. In fact, the country gave up about 55 percent of all its territory at the time. The United States now owned the entire present-day states of California, Nevada and Utah, as well as most of Arizona and New Mexico. They also got small parts of four other states. Mexico finally agreed that the Rio Grande would be the southern border of Texas. The United States agreed to pay Mexico $15 million for the cession.

After the War

Approximately 14,000 Americans lost their lives in the war. Nearly double that number of Mexicans were killed. But the end of the war did not end the bad feelings between the two countries. For many years, the two nations did not get along with one another and often fought in skirmishes (small battles).

The end of the Mexican-American War also brought many changes both to the nation and to people living in the Southwest. Americans poured into the new territories. They wanted to farm, ranch and mine for valuable metals and minerals. People began new settlements. Unfortunately, these newcomers did not always treat the people already living there very well. They treated many American Indians and former Mexican citizens very poorly. Sometimes Americans took over land that other people had already claimed. It's likely that not everyone agreed with the idea of Manifest Destiny. Who might have thought it was a bad idea? Why?

title: The Gadsden Purchase
text:
Five years after the end of the Mexican-American war, the United States set its sights on one additional piece of land. This strip of land was just south of the Gila River in present-day Arizona and New Mexico. It was the perfect pass through the mountains. A railroad system could easily be built to reach the Gulf of California. Mexico needed the money that the sale of the land would provide, so officials from the United States and Mexico began talks.

The U.S. Minister to Mexico, James Gadsden, helped put the deal together. The U.S. Congress agreed to pay Mexico $10 million for an amount of land that was about as big as the state of Pennsylvania. That was a lot of money for such a small area of land. Remember, Mexico got $15 million for about 55 percent of its territory it ceded to the United States after the war.

But the Gadsden Purchase made many Mexicans angry. They did not want to lose all claims to land north of the Rio Grande. The people were so angry that they removed General Santa Anna as dictator and banished him from the country. He was forced to leave Mexico forever. The Mexican people no longer trusted James Gadsden either. The United States had to replace him as minister to Mexico. Unfortunately, Gadsden died before workers completed the railroad route. But the Gadsden Purchase made it possible for railroad systems to begin criss-crossing the continent.

title: Forty-Niners Hit the Gold Mines
text:
In 1848, the Mexican-American War ended. At just about the same time, people discovered gold in the Sierra Nevada Mountains of California. Soon, news of the discovery spread to the United States. Even people in Europe and Asia heard about the possible chance to find a fortune. Suddenly forty-niners (people who rushed to California in 1849 to find gold) were leaving everything behind to head for the hills where they hoped to get rich quickly. The gold rush was on!

Miners found much of their treasure in rivers. They often spent long days panning for gold. First they scooped up dirt and rock from the riverbed in a large pan. Next, the miners swirled the pan around in the river water. Heavy gold would stay at the bottom of the pan while dirt and small rocks floated away.

Life for the miners was hard and lonely. Small communities began to form near large mining areas. However, miners often lived alone in tents or run-down cabins. Sometimes they did not have enough money to buy food or supplies. They often worked many days without finding any gold at all in their claims. A claim was the area of land in which each miner worked. Each miner had the right to all of the gold he found in his claim. Some of the forty-niners became very rich from the gold they found, but most of the miners gave up hope after a while. They returned home just as poor as when they had come to California.

At the end of the gold rush, many of the miners stayed in California. Some went to work for the railroads while others opened businesses or began farming. Many of them found more success after the rush ended.

title: Trail of Tears
text:
As the United States grew both in size and with people, settlers began claiming land that American Indian tribes had lived on for centuries. The white settlers felt they had the right to settle the land since it now belonged to the United States. But American Indians believed that they should be able to stay on the land since they had already been living there. Land battles broke out between the two groups and many people on both sides were killed.

When Andrew Jackson became U.S. president in 1829, he promised to solve the problem between the settlers and the American Indians. With his support, Congress passed the Indian Removal Act of 1830. This law said that the president had the power to move the American Indians away from their homes to an area west of the Mississippi River. This land was called Indian Territory.

The Chickasaw, Choctaw, Cherokee, Creek and Seminole tribes were the five major tribes affected by the Indian Removal Act. Some of these tribes agreed to sign a treaty giving them land in Indian Territory in exchange for the land they held east of the Mississippi. Other tribes, such as the Seminole, fought for their land for years before being forced to move west.

The Cherokee even took the battle to court. The Cherokee were a very advanced tribe that lived on the border between Georgia and Tennessee. They were successful farmers who raised many crops, along with large herds of cattle and horses. The Cherokee had their own alphabet, knew how to read and published their own newspaper. When the Cherokee took their case against the state of Georgia to court, they won. President Jackson chose not to enforce the ruling of the court, though. He moved the Cherokee off their land anyway.

The Trail of Tears is the name given to the terrible journey that 70,000 American Indians made when they were forced from their homeland to Indian Territory. During the journey, many Indians died. This included about 4,000 Cherokee, which was nearly one-fourth of the tribe. No one knows the total number of deaths from other tribes.

General Winfield Scott, the Army officer chosen to lead the Cherokee on the Trail of Tears, treated the tribes as kindly as possible. But the journey was rough and conditions were deadly. When the Trail of Tears ended in 1839, the spirit of many of the American Indians had been broken. Their way of life was destroyed and their hopes crushed. The United States had succeeded in taking American Indian land for its own.

title: Hungry? Ask a Robot!
text:
Have you ever watched a movie on the couch and wished that a robot could bring you a snack from the kitchen? Japanese and German scientists are working on that very thing!

The PR2 is programmed with a computerized version of common sense. It "knows" to look for food in the refrigerator. And it knows that if there is no food in the refrigerator, the place to look for food is a restaurant. The robot has maps of the building in its "brain," and is able to find its way through the building.

The robot is programmed with a semantic search program. That means the robot uses old information to help it understand new messages. You do something similar when you're in a new place. Think about the first time you walked into your classroom. What did you do the first time you had to throw something away? You looked for a trashcan by the front door. Needed to sharpen your pencil? You probably looked around at the walls to find a pencil sharpener. The robot operates in the same way.

Maybe in the future we'll have robots in school that can bring us lunch. I'd like turkey and cheese, please!

title: An Industrial Revolution Begins
text:
Can you imagine a world with few machines and no electricity or running water? Imagine working out in the hot sun or freezing cold all day long. Imagine having to grow or raise every bit of food your family ate. If you had lived in the United States in the early 19th century, you would not have had to imagine such a life. You would have been living it!

In the early 1800s, many people lived in the countryside. They farmed and raised animals. Their lives were very much like the lives of their grandparents. The work was hard and life itself was often a struggle. Around the time the United States was at war with Great Britain for the second time, life changed a lot for people in the United States We call this time of great change the Industrial Revolution. During this time, many people went from living and working on farms to living in cities and working in factories. The period of the Industrial Revolution continued in the United States well into the 20th century.

Eli Whitney’s Cotton Gin

The Industrial Revolution was a time when hundreds of new inventions and products made life easier for people. One invention that changed farmers’ lives was a special machine that made harvesting cotton easier. This machine was the cotton gin. Gin was a nickname for engine.

In the first half of the 1800s, many people farmed for a living. The most important southern plantation crop of all was cotton. The fertile soil and good weather was perfect for cotton farming. But it was also hard work. Cotton was not an easy plant to harvest, because workers had to separate the cottonseeds from the cotton fiber. At first, people did this difficult process by hand. It took a long time, so cotton farmers didn’t make a lot of money. Then in 1793, a man named Eli Whitney built a special machine called the cotton gin. Although Whitney got the patent for the cotton gin, not everyone believes he should get the credit. (Read more about it and have a class debate.) The cotton gin quickly separated the seeds from the cotton fiber. Farmers planted even more cotton than before, because each cotton gin could process nearly 55 pounds of cotton a day. Soon, farmers in the Southern United States grew and processed most of the world’s cotton. Large cotton plantations were located throughout the South. The plantations were large farms where slaves often worked. Cotton plantation owners planted more and more cotton, so they brought many more slaves to the South to help tend their larger cotton crops. Some believe that the invention of the cotton gin led to an increase in slavery.

War Brings Industrial Change

During the War of 1812, British ships would often blockade seaports. This meant that traders could not ship out and sell any goods. It also meant that no one could bring into the United States the things that people needed. But there was still a demand for the products. Americans began to realize they needed better systems of transportation and manufacturing to supply those demands.

Thanks to Eli Whitney’s cotton gin, cotton from Southern plantations could be quickly processed and shipped north for people to make into cloth. All that was needed was a way to quickly produce a large amount of cloth from the cotton. A man named Francis C. Lowell had visited British cloth factories in 1810. He had memorized how people built and operated the cloth manufacturing machines. Back in the United States, Lowell and several of his partners built power looms. These machines could easily turn cotton fiber into cloth. Lowell wanted to build factories that could produce cloth better and faster. He sold shares (portions) of ownership in his company for $1,000 each. The shareholder corporation worked. Lowell and his partners soon had plenty of money to open a factory. Many more textile factories began in the Northern United States. Lowell’s shares idea was also a hit, and many businesses in the United States use the same idea today.

Other industries began looking for ways to produce their goods and products quicker and more efficiently than ever. Soon the industrial revolution spread throughout the United States.

Life Won’t Ever Be the Same

The Industrial Revolution was a turning point for the United States. Everything about peoples’ lives changed quickly. Many families moved from farms to work at factories in cities. People were able to make their livings using simple machines. Improved methods of communication, healthcare and transportation soon followed.

Unfortunately, the Industrial Revolution also marked the beginning of a growing population. People flocked to the cities for work. These cities had to find ways to provide citizens with food, clean water, health facilities and natural resources such as coal. Cities quickly became dirty and overcrowded, and factories often used young children as workers. Factories were forced to burn large amounts of coal and oil that polluted the air and water.

The Industrial Revolution brought many changes, both good and bad, to the United States. One thing was certain. From that point on, the world had changed forever.

title: Supply and Demand
text:
One Christmas, 10-year-old Tyler knew exactly what he wanted to find under his Christmas tree. He really wanted a special sports game for his gaming system. All of Tyler’s friends wanted the game too. As the holiday got closer, Tyler started to worry. Every store in town was out of the game. The demand for the game was high. A lot of people wanted this special game. However, the supply of the game was low. There were not enough games for everyone who wanted to buy it.

Supply is the amount of a product that a business has for sale. Demand is how much people want to buy it. Usually if the price of an item is very high, the demand will be low. This results in a high supply. If the item goes on sale then the demand may increase and the supply would then decrease.

The best thing is when the demand is equal to the supply. Everyone who wants the product can make the purchase and businesses make money. On Christmas morning, Tyler found the sports game under his tree. It seems the video game store got a new supply of the game the evening before the big day. The supply and demand were equal and everyone was happy.

title: The Free Enterprise System
text:
It's Saturday afternoon and your mom has taken you and your best friend to spend the afternoon at the local mall. You can choose to eat lunch at McDonald's or get pizza. You can go ice skating or see a movie. Then for a special treat you can choose to get ice cream, cake or go to the candy shop. You are making economic choices when you choose what goods and services you will purchase with your money.

In the United States everyone can choose how to spend his/her own money. The government does not control a person's own personal spending. This is because the United States has a free enterprise economy. Sometimes a free enterprise economy is also called a free trade economy or capitalism. In our country all people have the freedom to work as much or as little as they choose in order to earn money. People may also spend or save whatever amounts of their money they wish.

Many of the ideas behind our free enterprise system had their beginnings during the period in history known as the Industrial Revolution of the 19th century. At this time many new businesses opened. People were excited to have the freedom to own and operate their own businesses.

The economic system of the United States is based on four important ideas:

Freedom of choice - All people can choose for themselves how to earn, spend and save their money.

Private property - People in the United States have the right to own property including homes and businesses.

Profit - Everyone who owns a business has the right to keep profits. That means if a business earns more money than it takes to run the business, then the leftover money, known as profit, belongs to the owner.

Owner control - The owner of a business controls and is responsible for his business at all times.

title: Westward Ho!
text:
By the mid 1800s, thousands of Americans had been encouraged to move westward. Western land was cheap and families needed very little money to build homes and start farms or ranches. Word spread through books, magazines and newspapers that the West was full of possibilities. After the discovery of gold in California in 1848, even more people raced west for the chance to earn their fortunes and live out their dreams. Even people from other countries wanted the opportunity for a better life in the American West.

Unfortunately, not everyone found westward expansion to be a positive experience. For many American Indians already living in the West, the expansion brought disruption, great hardship and even tragedy.

At first, the United States tried to maintain good relationships with the American Indian tribes who lived in the West. Both sides often signed treaties, or agreements. However, the settlers who were moving west often broke these agreements. Sometimes they took land from the American Indians. Many tribes lost land that had been their home for hundreds of years.

Settlers also seemed to have little respect for the American Indians' need for the buffalo. Tribes of the Great Plains depended on the buffalo for food, and often disturbed their migration patterns. The settlers only wanted the hides for trade and didn’t use any other part of the animal. It angered American Indians when they would find buffalo carcasses (dead bodies) rotting in the heat.

Some tribes tried to cooperate with the settlers. Other tribes were angered by such poor treatment and often fought back against the settlers. Workers also built railroads through American Indian territory. By the late 1800s, the United States had decided to try and remove all American Indians from their own lands in the West and place them on land in Oklahoma and South Dakota. The idea of living on government reservations made many tribes even angrier. The United States fought battles with the Sioux, the Nez Perce and the Navajo tribes. Many tribe members and U.S. soldiers were killed or injured. The tribes who were forced to live on reservations faced great problems, and many American Indians died of starvation or disease.

So the opportunities in the West held very little promise for American Indians. The anger and bad feelings between the U.S. government and American Indians continued well into the next century.

title: New People Come to a New Country
text:
Imagine packing up everything you own, traveling on a ship for months and beginning a new life in a different country. That is just what 60 million people around the world did from the early 1800s to 1930. About half of those people immigrated into the United States. Why would people choose to leave their home country? Well, there are many reasons. In the early 1800s, most immigrants to the United States came to find economic opportunity. In America, they had the chance to own land, homes and businesses. They could also work to make their family’s lives better. People came to the United States from countries all over the world during the 1800s, especially Europe and Asia. There were large groups of immigrants from Ireland, Germany and China and they usually arrived by ship. Let’s read and learn about some of their experiences.

Immigrants from Ireland

Life in Ireland during the 19th century was very difficult. There was a great deal of disease and starvation. The people were very poor. Poverty made many Irish citizens long to start a new life in America. But most were sad to leave their beautiful homeland.

The new life in America was not so easy either. Poor Irish were often forced to live in tenement houses. These run-down apartments were dirty, cold and dangerous, but they were affordable. Most Irish immigrants did not have money to move on to other cities, so they often stayed in the city where their ship had first landed. Many of the immigrants had been unsuccessful farmers in Ireland and did not wish to farm again. Instead, they wanted to work in factories in the cities. However, many employers looked down on the poor Irish immigrants. They spoke differently and couldn't read. Sometimes they were thought to be angry and even dangerous. Often signs hung in business windows saying, "No Irish Need Apply."

The Irish immigrants did not give up. They helped each other survive city life. Their strong beliefs in the Catholic church helped keep them close. Most of the men were actually ready and willing to work at the hard and dangerous jobs America needed. Many Irish men worked to build bridges, canals and railroads. Many also became police officers. Irish women found jobs as housekeepers and hotel cleaners. The signs in the business windows soon disappeared. The Irish immigrants proved they were smart and hard working. Each year when Irish-Americans in the United States celebrate St. Patrick's Day it is a reminder of how important the Irish immigrants have been to this country.

German Immigrants Find New Lives

Germans also faced hardships in their country during the 19th century. The German government was not very stable (secure) and taxes were very high. In addition, there was a lot of violence throughout the country. Germany seemed to be constantly at war with its neighbors. Many Germans immigrated to other countries to find better ways of life. While many Germans were sad to leave their homeland, they were also happy to be able to have a chance to live in peace.

Some Germans stayed in the first large U.S. city they visited. New York City and cities in Pennsylvania had large groups of German settlers as citizens. However, unlike the Irish immigrants, most Germans did not want to live in cities when they arrived in the United States. Many of them had saved money for a new life. They wanted to find land to settle that reminded them of the beautiful land they had left behind. Many German communities began after people migrated to the Midwest in search of good farmland.

Those Germans who chose not to farm found work as bakers, butchers, cabinetmakers and tailors. German women who worked outside the home found jobs as bakers, nurses, housecleaners and tailors. Most Germans practiced the Catholic or Lutheran religions. Along with the Irish, their culture and religion helped keep them together. German immigrants had an easier time fitting into the U.S. culture than the Irish did. Most Germans were skilled craftspeople and farmers. Many of them supported public education and spoke out against slavery. They seemed to have a lot in common with Americans. German difficulties came later in the early 20th century when much of the world feared Germany's leaders during World War I and World War II.

Chinese Immigrants

Tales of California gold reached China in 1851. Within one year, 25,000 Chinese immigrants had sailed to California to look for their own treasure. Most of these were poor people who hoped to get rich and return to China to buy farmland for their families.

When the Chinese arrived, they worked hard to invent new methods and tools for collecting hard-to-find gold. Some of the American miners in the area became jealous of their success. They often threatened the Chinese miners or used violence against them. The government also taxed the foreign miners.

Many of the Chinese immigrants found work building the first transcontinental railroad. They laid tracks across the United States. They were very good workers. Still, life was hard for the Chinese. They often received less pay for longer hours of work in very dangerous conditions. After the railroad was completed, many of the Chinese decided to stay in America. They worked as farmers and fishers. They opened stores and restaurants.

Some Americans didn't welcome the Chinese, partly because they looked different. They did not understand the Chinese culture or language, and they wanted the Chinese to leave America. Many Chinese were treated very badly and some were even murdered. In 1882, the U.S. government passed a law to keep Chinese people from immigrating into the country. For many years, the Chinese Exclusion Act made it much harder for people to come to America from China to live and work.

title: Liberty Enlightening the World
text:
The Statue of Liberty is often the first thing a U.S. immigrant sees of America. The amazing sculpture stands 151 feet and one inch high in the air (top of base to torch). It was given to the United States of America by the country of France in 1884.

A group of Frenchmen wanted to give the U.S. people a gift that would honor the democracy of the country. French sculptor Frederic-Auguste Bartholdi was chosen to design a statue. He imagined a huge sculpture of a woman holding a torch burning with the light of freedom. He created "Liberty Enlightening the World," also known as the Statue of Liberty.

For 21 years, the French people raised money to build the statue. In 1884, "Lady Liberty" was presented to the American people in a French ceremony. The statue was taken apart, placed in crates and shipped across the Atlantic Ocean for people to rebuild on Liberty Island in New York City. Americans paid for and built the pedestal for the statue to stand on. A poem called "The New Colossus" is found on a plaque at the statue's base. Its words have greeted millions of immigrants who have come to the United States since the statue was built to find freedom and a new life. Here are some of those words:

... Give me your tired, your poor, Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free, The wretched refuse of your teeming shore, Send these, the homeless, tempest-tossed to me, I lift my lamp beside the golden door! - Emma Lazarus, New York City, 1883

title: What is the best way to solve a problem?
text:
A problem is best handled with clear thinking. Here are six steps you can use the next time you have to find a solution to a problem.

Step One: Identify the problem - What issue needs to be solved?

Step Two: Gather information - What are all the facts about the situation?

Step Three: List and consider options - What are all the ways the problem can be solved?

Step Four: Think about the advantages and disadvantages of each option - What are the good and bad things about all the possible solutions?

Step Five: Choose a solution - What is the best way to solve the problem? Put the plan into action!

Step Six: Was the solution successful? - How well did the solution work? Should the same type of problem be solved a different way next time?

title: I Pledge Allegiance...
text:
A pledge is a promise, and allegiance is another word for loyalty. By reciting the Pledge of Allegiance each day, U.S. citizens are promising to remain faithful and true to our nation. The pledge is a reminder that every American, regardless of his or her race, religion or color, should be treated fairly under the laws of the nation.

Francis Bellamy, a Baptist minister from New York, wrote the Pledge of Allegiance. People first spoke the pledge at a special ceremony to honor the 400th anniversary of Columbus Day in 1892. A few changes have been made to the words over the years, but the ideas remain the same.

"I pledge Allegiance to the flag of the United States of America and to the Republic for which it stands, one nation under God, indivisible, with Liberty and Justice for all."

title: Industry vs. Agriculture
text:
The United States had grown a great deal by the beginning of the 1800s. Many people still lived on the eastern coast, but many also settled in the West and South. Settlers developed different ways of living in different areas of the country. People made money in various ways and lived in different types of homes. They also began to differ in their ways of thinking about topics such as slavery and states' rights. By the middle of the 19th century, Northerners and Southerners probably felt as though they were living in two separate countries.

Economic Differences

One difference between the two parts of the country was in the way people made money. The economies of the North and South led to bad feelings between the people who lived in some parts of the country.

For many years, people in the United States had made their livings in agriculture. Most families farmed and raised animals. In fact, about three-fourths of the country's population lived on farms in rural areas before the 1800s. However, the industrial revolution that spread from England to America had changed all of that.

Northern Economy

A growing system of manufacturing plants (factories) was very promising in the Northern states. People could find good jobs and support their families. Work in the factories was usually hard and often dangerous, but employers paid the workers well for their services. Immigrants from Europe and Asia also came to the North to work in the factories. By 1860, Northern cities were growing quickly. Much of the country's population lived and worked in the North. People also found jobs building new roads and railroads so that goods from factories could be shipped to other places. The Northern economy was strong.

Southern Economy

Life in the South was very different from that in the North. People in this region still made their livings mostly from agriculture, especially cotton. In fact, most Southerners depended on cotton for all of their income. After the invention of the cotton gin, people could harvest large amounts of cotton. But cotton plantations depended heavily on free slave labor. Though a lot of families did not own slaves on their small family-run farms, many people in the South accepted the idea of forcing African Americans into slavery. By 1860, there were about 4 million slaves in the South. About half of them worked on large cotton plantations. The economy of the South grew rapidly as cotton production increased. Cotton was often shipped to the North, and Northerners sold tools and other manufactured goods to Southern farmers.

To Tax or Not to Tax

The economies of these two areas were not the only differences that became clear in mid-1800s. The Northern industrial economy depended on reliable transportation systems to ship goods in and out of the region. This meant workers needed good roads and railroads.

Northerners supported tariffs (special taxes on imported goods) to pay for those systems. Tariffs went directly to the government. High tariffs meant that goods produced in the North would be cheaper to buy than heavily taxed goods from Europe or Asia. Northern factories would make lots of money.

Southerners generally wanted low tariffs. The South produced very few products on its own. Southerners had to import most manufactured goods from the North or overseas. If tariffs were high, then their cost of purchasing goods would also be high.

Slavery: the Great Difference

When the Founding Fathers wrote the Declaration of Independence in 1776, the phrase "all men are created equal" was an important idea. Yet that idea didn't seem to apply to thousands of slaves who were living in the colonies.

People first brought slaves to North America in the 1500s. Over the years, an estimated 350,000 to 450,000 Africans were brought by ship to the United States. In the South, slaves were sold at slave auctions. The enslaved people were considered property that could be bought, sold or traded at any time. Slaves had no rights and were not allowed to own property, marry or learn to read or write.

Some slaves lived in cities, but most lived and worked on Southern plantations. The work was very hard on the large farms. Often the slaves were treated very badly. Most of them had to work from sunup to sundown every day. They were often sold to different plantations, which broke families apart.

By the mid-1800s, slavery was against the law in the Northern United States. Southern states that made their money with cotton continued to allow slavery. Slavery was thought to be one of the most important parts of the Southern economy.

In 1860, people in the North and people in the South did not share the same idea about slavery at all. Southerners wanted new states in the country to allow slaves. Northerners wanted slavery to be against the law all over the United States. The differences between the North and the South became more distinct than ever before, and those differences would soon change the nation forever.

title: John Deere
text:
Much of the success of cotton plantations in the South was because of Eli Whitney's development of the cotton gin in 1793. But Whitney was not the only man whose ideas led to America's agricultural successes in the 1800s. America's farms also owe a great deal of gratitude to a man named John Deere.

This blacksmith left his home in Vermont in 1836 to start a new life in Illinois. After making the journey with only $73, he rented land and quickly opened up a new blacksmith shop. He hoped to make enough money to bring his wife and children from Vermont to live with him.

Local farmers in his shop often complained about how hard it was to break up the soil with regular plows. One day in 1837, John saw a broken saw blade at the mill. He asked the owner if he could have it. Within days, John Deere had invented a steel plow with the blade. The tool made it much easier for farmers to cut and turn over the hard prairie ground. Farmers everywhere heard of the new product. Within a few years, John Deere was selling 1,600 steel plows every year. American farmers could more easily plant and harvest crops.

John Deere was an excellent businessperson. He was always trying to find new ways to make better products for farmers. He often loaded plows onto wagons and took them to sell from farm to farm. People were impressed with his dedication and hard work. John Deere's company, Deere & Company, is a successful American tool business, even today.

title: Slave Families
text:
Slaves were considered the property of the man they had to call their master, or owner. This was true of slave children, too. For most slave children life was difficult, sad and lonely. A law passed in the late 1600s said that all children would have the same level of freedom as their mother. That meant if an African American woman was a slave, then all of her children were slaves as well.

Some slave families were separated. Fathers, mothers and children were sometimes sold to different plantation owners. However, some children were allowed to stay with their mother. If the mother of a child worked as a slave in the plantation fields, then the child usually worked in the fields as well. Young children were often expected to work all day in the hot sun. But if the mother worked as a house servant, then the slave children might be kept inside also. Slave children sometimes played with the white children of the plantation owners. But slave children weren't allowed to attend school because most slaves were not allowed to learn to read or write.

Life was especially hard for slave children. They often lived in small, dirty cabins that were either very cold or very hot. Most slaves had very little clothing or food and were often punished very cruelly. Slaves had little or no medical care, and diseases such as malaria often took their lives. Many of these children died before even reaching adulthood. The slaves bonded together to help each other deal with their terrible treatment. Children often gathered in the evenings with the adults to tell stories and sing songs. Adult slaves sometimes taught the children how to survive and avoid punishment from cruel masters. They used religion as a way to help them find the will to survive, which was a true test for slaves of all ages.

title: Population Charting
text:
In the 1800s the North and South were very different places to live. A manufacturing economy along with a large population of immigrants caused a growth in urban (city) development in the North. Because most people in the South lived and work on farms and plantations, it was known as a rural (country) population. The table shows the largest U.S. cities in 1860. Find and circle the 10 largest cities in 1860 on the U.S. map. Then use the information from the table and map to answer the questions on a separate piece of paper.

Top 10 Largest Cities in the United States, 1860

1. In which part of the United States were most of the largest cities located in 1860?

2. Why do you think these cities were in the top 10 in population?

3. Which city on the table is located in the South?

4. What do you know about this city that would support its place in the top 10 most populated cities?

5. What common geographic features do you notice about the 10 most populated U.S. cities in 1860?

6. Your teacher will give you a blank map of the United States. Work with a partner and use a classroom or online map to help you label the capital city of each state. Hint: Some of the cities in the chart above are capitals, and some are not.

title: Robert Smalls: A Brave Father and Civil War Hero
text:
What would you do if you and your family were going to be separated? Would you come up with a plan to stay together? That's exactly the situation in which Robert Smalls found himself. He knew that the only way to keep his family together was by escaping slavery. He thought of a plan and took action.

Robert was an enslaved member of the crew of the Planter, a Confederate ship. He decided to take over the ship and sail it to the Union Fleet at Fort Sumter and freedom!

He knew his plan was risky because he would have to get control of the ship and pick up his family and others hoping to escape. Then, he would have to sail the ship north past Confederate forces to the Union Fleet. Once there, he would have to convince the Union soldiers he was not an enemy.

Robert managed to get to the Union Fleet without a problem. He sailed right up to the fleet and quickly switched the flag on the ship from a Confederate flag to a white flag of surrender. The Union soldiers let the ship in and were amazed at what Robert had done.

Robert won freedom for his family, crew and others, but he didn't stop there. He went on to fight in the war and became a captain in the Union Army. After the war ended, he became a politician and served in the U.S. House of Representatives. What a brave hero!

title: The Roots of Conflict
text:
People who wanted to live in a democratic country founded the United States of America. They wanted a nation in which the people made decisions about who would lead the government and how the leaders would operate it.

At the Constitutional Convention in 1787, delegates spent a great deal of time planning how the government of the United States would work best. Not everyone agreed. The Founding Fathers disagreed about the amount of power the federal government should have. The Constitution cleared matters up a bit. It explained how the rights and responsibilities of the federal government differ from those of state governments.

Members of the Federalist party supported the idea of a strong central government. Members of another political party, the Democratic-Republicans, believed that states had the right to nullify (cancel or declare invalid) federal laws they believed were unconstitutional. They thought this allowed states the right to declare laws unacceptable.

At the beginning of the 19th century, many Southern states believed the federal government was too involved in states' business. They were especially concerned that the federal government might try to control slavery in the South. Southerners also accused the government of favoring the North.
