Tariffs (import/export taxes) helped the Northern manufacturing economy. Southerners felt the federal government was forgetting them.

As time went on, great differences were seen between the North and South. The economies of the two were different. The North made money in industry, while the South benefited from an agricultural economy. Most of the population in the North lived in large cities. The people in the South mostly lived on farms or in small towns. Many people in the North supported a strong federal government while most Southerners believed each state should have the right to make certain decisions for itself. The differences became more noticeable as the century went on. Soon it seemed that there could be no peaceful agreement or compromise between the North and the South. Would the disagreements lead to war?

title: Agriculture a Way of Life for Fewer in the U.S.
text:
When the United States began, most of its people were farmers. In 1860, the population of the United States was about 31 million. Almost half of that population listed their occupation (job) as "farmer" that year. Today, less than two percent of people earn their family's money by farming. There are about the same number of farms in the United States today as there were in 1860. This is very unusual because the total population has grown to well over 300 million people. Why do so few people choose agriculture as a way of life today? There are several important reasons.

Farming today involves a lot of work. With so many people to feed, farmers must operate their businesses with great care. Farmers say it takes a lot more than planting seeds to own a successful farm. The work is long and hard. Farmers must make many business decisions about the type of crops to plant, the machines to buy, how to pay taxes and how to meet payroll for the workers to run the farm. Crops often fail because of weather and other unpredictable situations. Farmers have to take many risks. Some seasons they make money and some seasons they don’t. Many people have tried to make a living by farming but later decided it isn't the life they want. However, the nation has plenty of excellent farm products. The U.S. is lucky to have enough farmers to produce the goods our nation needs to survive.

title: Compromises and Kansas
text:
The Missouri Compromise of 1820

The United States was still a young nation when President Thomas Jefferson approved the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. The land purchased from France nearly doubled the size of the country and included the Missouri Territory. In 1819, the Missouri Territory asked to become a new state. Immediately people became concerned. But why?

Missouri's state constitution allowed slavery. If it were to be admitted as a state, there would be 12 slave states and 11 free states. A free state was one in which slavery was not allowed. If Missouri became a new state, the balance of the United States' Congress would lean towards the South and slavery. People in the North were afraid of what might happen to the country if the slave states had more power than free states.

There were many debates in Congress about what to do with Missouri. Many people feared the United States might break apart. Then a senator from Kentucky named Henry Clay suggested a compromise. The situation could be settled if both sides gave up some of their demands.

Missouri was allowed to join the U.S. as a slave state. At the same time, Maine would also be admitted as a free state. The number of free and slave states would remain equal. Clay's plan also included an imaginary borderline across the western U.S. at 36 ° 30' north latitude, Missouri's southern boundary. Slavery wouldn't be allowed north of this line except in Missouri.

Clay's plan became known as the Missouri Compromise. The new plan began to make the people in the U.S. feel better, and it gave them hope that the problems with slavery could be solved for good. However, some Southerners were still concerned that Northerners might one day try to change the way they lived. For the next 30 years, it seemed the compromise had worked.

The Compromise of 1850

At the end of the Mexican-American War, the United States gained a large amount of land from Mexico in the West and Southwest regions. California was part of this land. In 1849, California asked to be admitted to the United States as a free state.

Once again, it was clear that a compromise would have to be reached. By that time, 15 states were free and 15 were slave states. Adding California would give more power to the North in Congress. In addition, much of California's land was below the 36 degrees 30' Missouri Compromise line. Remember that slavery was allowed south of the line. Some Southerners began to think about withdrawing their states from the Union if California joined as a free state.

Senator Clay from Kentucky came up with a way to settle the differences again. Clay offered several plans for new laws to help balance the power. First, California would be admitted as a free state. Second, people would not be allowed to sell slaves in Washington, D.C. These laws would make Northerners happy.

At the same time, people in Utah and New Mexico would be allowed to decide for themselves whether or not to allow slavery in their territories. In addition, Congress passed the Fugitive Slave Law. Northern officials would have to help Southerners capture fugitive (runaway) slaves. These two laws were aimed at pleasing Southerners.

The Compromise of 1850 was passed into law in September of that year. Even though Senator Clay and the other leaders worked to try and find a way to solve the differences the country had, they weren't successful. Many people in both parts of the country were more upset than ever. Southerners thought the North was trying to destroy slavery. Northerners thought the South would never be happy until slavery had spread to every state. Soon it became clear that the differences between the two groups were going to be difficult to overcome peacefully.

Kansas: The End of Compromise

The Compromise of 1850 did very little to bring peace to the nation. Instead, the compromise seemed to fuel the fire. This fire began to grow even stronger when the territories of Kansas and Nebraska wanted to become states.

Both territories were north of the 36 degrees 30’ Missouri Compromise line. According to law, both new states would be free from slavery. However, in 1854 a senator from Illinois named Stephen Douglas suggested a troubling plan. He believed the people in Kansas and Nebraska should be allowed to decide for themselves if they wanted to allow slavery. Congress agreed with Douglas, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act became a law.

Suddenly, the southern territory of Kansas became a battleground over states' rights and slavery. People who supported (approved of) slavery rushed to Kansas. People who opposed (were against) slavery also rushed there to voice their beliefs. Both groups wanted to vote in the election that would make the final slavery decision. The people argued with both words and weapons.

On election day, voters in Kansas approved a constitution that allowed slavery. The antislavery leaders believed the election had not been fair. Over 6,000 people had voted, but Kansas had only 3,000 voters. It was clear that some people who did not really live in Kansas had voted. The "free-soilers" (people who did not support slavery) set up their own political party in protest.

People on both sides of the issue became violent. There was fighting throughout the spring and summer of 1856. The issue was finally resolved (settled) when another election was held. In January 1861, Kansas was added as a free state. Neither the North nor the South was satisfied. The nation was now heading toward a war, one side against the other.

title: Abolitionists ‘Build’ an Underground Railroad
text:
Many Southerners felt that slavery was a necessary part of the Southern way of life and economy. Plantation owners used slaves to run their large farms. On the other side, many Northerners believed slavery was wrong. Northern abolitionists felt very strongly that all slavery should be abolished (ended) forever.

Some of those against slavery got together and organized the Underground Railroad. The Underground Railroad wasn't a real railroad and it wasn't underneath the ground. Instead, it was a name for a system of people and homes that secretly helped slaves escape to free states. Homes were known as stations. At each station, there were people, or "conductors," to help the slaves hide. They gave slaves food, clothing and a place to sleep. When it was safe, the conductors helped the slaves find their way to the next station.

Many slaves traveled from station to station until they felt they were safe. The Fugitive Slave Act allowed runaway slaves to be tracked into Northern states. Some of the slaves had to travel all the way to Canada before they felt they were free from slavery forever.

Most Northerners were not part of the Underground Railroad, but many Southerners became distrustful of them. Each group felt the other's ideas about slavery were wrong.

title: 1860: The Election of Abraham Lincoln
text:
By 1860, the United States was set to elect a new president. Northerners and Southerners both felt uneasy about how the election might affect the nation. Southern congressmen made it clear that unless an “acceptable” man was elected, their states would secede (withdraw from) the U.S.

The Republicans nominated (named as a candidate) a smart and thoughtful lawyer from Illinois named Abraham Lincoln. Lincoln was against slavery. He promised he would leave slavery alone in the South but would not let it spread into new territories. Most Southerners did not vote for Lincoln because of his views on slavery.

The Democratic Party seemed to fall apart in the months before the election. The party split into two separate groups. One group nominated the vice president of the United States, John C. Breckinridge, to be the next president. The other Democratic group wanted Senator Stephen Douglas of Illinois to be the next top leader of the nation. Douglas had previously run against Abraham Lincoln in a race for the Illinois Senate. Douglas argued with Lincoln and said that people in each state had the right to decide for themselves if they wanted to allow slavery. While Douglas won that election, Lincoln became well known as someone who would stand up against slavery.

On Nov. 6, 1860, Abraham Lincoln won the presidential election. Interestingly, the other two candidates outnumbered the peoples' vote for Lincoln, but Lincoln won the most votes from the Electoral College. He must have worried that the majority, or most of the nation's people, had not voted for him. He was sworn in as the 16th president of the United States of America. Lincoln’s election was the last straw for some states. The end of the country as it had been known was near.

title: Points of View from a Historical Perspective
text:
A person’s point of view is the way he or she looks at and thinks about an event. Different people often experience history in a variety of different ways. Not everyone who experiences a historical event feels or thinks the exact same way about it.

A number of things determine a person’s point of view. Life experiences (positive and negative), future needs and wants, and an emotional connection to the event all influence a person’s point of view.

After reading this week’s Studies Weekly, consider all the different points of view of people living in the United States during the mid-1800s. After reading each of the primary source statements below, add one or two sentences to support the speaker’s point of view.

I know no South, no North, no East, no West, to which I owe any allegiance. I owe allegiance to two sovereignty, and only two: one is the sovereignty of this Union, and the other is the sovereignty of the state of Kentucky.” —Senator Henry Clay

I am naturally anti-slavery. If slavery is not wrong, nothing is wrong. I can not remember when I did not so think, and feel. And yet I have never understood that the Presidency conferred upon me an unrestricted right to act officially upon this judgment and feeling.” —Abraham Lincoln

I shall see, this day … from the slave’s point of view. … What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July? I answer: a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.” —Frederick Douglass

title: The Union is Dissolved
text:
The presidential election of 1860 was the final push over the edge of discontent (unhappiness) for the Southern states. They were shocked at Abraham Lincoln's new position as U.S. president. Southern states did not waste any time waiting to see how the newly elected president might do as the nation's leader. They felt it was time for a big change.

Tension grew after Abraham Lincoln was elected president of the United States. Southern states felt the time was right to make a change. They were afraid that President Lincoln's election would lead to the end of their right to make their own decisions. They were especially concerned that the U.S. government would abolish, or do away with, their practice of owning slaves.

On Dec. 20, 1860, South Carolina's citizens voted and unanimously agreed "that the union now subsisting between South Carolina and other states under the name of the United States of America is hereby dissolved." With that declaration (announcement) South Carolina became the first of the Southern states to secede (break free) from the United States of America. Less than three weeks later, Mississippi became the second state to leave the U.S. By the end of January, the states of Florida, Alabama, Georgia and Louisiana had also left the Union. On Feb. 1, 1861, Texas became the seventh state to leave the Union. Not everyone in the South wanted the states to leave the Union, however. Some people known as cooperationists wanted the South to work out its differences with the North. They wanted the South to remain part of the Union.

However, the seven Southern states that had seceded by early 1861 wanted to protect what they thought was their right to own slaves. They wanted to have the freedom to make their own decisions. They formed the Confederate States of America. The Confederacy selected its own president-Jefferson Davis of Mississippi.

By April 1861 the lines of conflict were clearly drawn. Northern "Yanks" and Southern "Rebs" were set to fight against one another to protect their property, rights and values.

title: Quilted Controversy
text:
Is there one Civil War detail that has been kept "under cover" for over 150 years? That's what some historians think after studying slavery and the Underground Railroad from Civil War times.

Southern slaves often tried to escape to freedom in the North. Many received help from people who lived along the journey route. This group of people and the secret hideouts in their homes were known as the Underground Railroad. Thousands of slaves were able to reach freedom with help from the Underground Railroad. Historians want to learn more about how slaves knew where the "railroad" stops were located. Some historians think escaped slaves sewed secret information about safe houses into quilts. They believe that secret codes were sewn into the designs of the quilts. These special patterns may have given slaves the information they needed about where to hide or look for help.

Not everyone believes that the colorful bed linens helped the slaves. Some historians believe the idea that quilts guided runaway slaves on their path to freedom is just a tall tale. They say there is little evidence that slaves had such a patterned code. It is more likely that former slaves who had already escaped guided the slaves along the Underground Railroad. White landowners who disagreed with the idea of slavery also guided slaves to safety.

Historians are looking for facts and artifacts that prove or disprove this idea. Meanwhile, the story behind the secret-code quilts will surely continue to unfold.

title: The Blue and the Gray
text:
First Shots at Fort Sumter

The first states began to secede from the Union in December 1860. At that time, U.S. soldiers were stationed in South Carolina. Led by Major Robert Anderson, soldiers climbed into boats and took control of Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor. The people in Charleston were angry that the Union soldiers had taken the fort. They considered it a violation of their rights. The next day, Confederate forces took control of three nearby forts. They wanted to remove the Union soldiers from Southern soil.

The Union held control of Fort Sumter for almost four months. President Abraham Lincoln ordered that supplies be sent to the soldiers. The Confederates sent messengers by boat to speak with Major Anderson. They wanted him to surrender, but Anderson would not give up.

At 4:30 a.m. on April 12, 1861, the Confederates began firing upon Fort Sumter. The Civil War had officially begun. The attack lasted 34 hours. The Union soldiers fired back, but they were forced to surrender. Surprisingly, not one soldier on either side was killed in battle.

The Soldiers of War

Like it or not, the United States found itself in the middle of a war that neither side was prepared to fight. Both the North and the South needed to make improvements to their armies. Soldiers needed to be trained. Some men signed up voluntarily (on their own) while the government drafted others to serve in the military. When soldiers were drafted, they were ordered to fight whether they wanted to or not.

Northern men followed President Lincoln's request that they fight to keep the United States together. Eventually it became clear that the men of the North were also fighting for the freedom of slaves being held in the South. The Northern soldiers were mostly from poor farm families, and many were European immigrants. Eventually, African American men were also allowed to serve in the Union army and wore the Union blue uniforms.

Southerners believed they were fighting for their freedom to leave the Union. They wanted states to have the right to make their own decisions, and they were ready to defend the Southern way of life. They were willing to fight for the right to own slaves. Many of the Southern soldiers were poor farmers as well. They wore gray uniforms on the battlefield.

The Battle at Bull Run (also known as the Battle of Manassas)

In the summer of 1861, Northerners wanted President Lincoln to hit the Southerners with full force. Most people felt that the North would only need one major win to crush the South and bring the Union back together again. A plan was made for the Union to capture the city of Richmond, Virginia. In July, troops marched towards the city. The Union soldiers were not well trained. They moved slowly and did not follow orders well. The Confederates built up their defenses along Bull Run stream.

At first, the Union soldiers seemed to be winning the battle easily. A crowd of supporters even gathered to watch the battle. The people were excited to see the Union army defeat the Southern rebels. But the Union plan fell apart quickly. There was great confusion and panic. The Union troops started to retreat (move back). Many soldiers dropped their rifles and ran away.

By the end of the day, over 4,000 soldiers were dead. The Union knew that the Confederate soldiers were serious about fighting back. Everyone soon realized that the war was not going to come to a quick end. Both sides had shown they were in the war to win.

title: One War, Two Leaders
text:
Both the North and the South needed strong leaders for their troops. These leaders were Robert E. Lee and Ulysses S. Grant.

Robert E. Lee was born in Virginia to well-educated parents. His father was the governor of Virginia, and Robert's mother encouraged him to be religious and responsible. Robert received an education at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point where he graduated at the top of his class. He served in the Army after graduation and later served as superintendent of the school he had attended. During the Mexican-American War, Lee served as a quartermaster (Army officer). He was a smart man who carefully studied the military leaders he worked with. President Lincoln asked Robert E. Lee to head the Union troops at the beginning of the Civil War, but Lee felt he owed the South, especially his home state of Virginia, his allegiance (loyalty). He became leader of the Confederate States of America Army. After the Civil War, Lee became the president of Washington College in Virginia.

Ulysses S. Grant was born in Ohio. His parents were simple, hardworking people. Grant also attended the U.S. Military Academy at West Point like Lee, but Ulysses did not do well in school. He was, however, an excellent horseman and mathematician. During the Mexican-American War, Grant served as an engineer in the Army alongside General Robert E. Lee. Before President Lincoln chose Grant to lead the Union army, Grant worked as a farmer, real estate agent and cloth-store owner. Voters elected Grant president of the United States twice after the Civil War. He spent much of his presidency fighting for the civil rights of African Americans.

title: Jefferson Davis: President of the Confederate States of America
text:
Jefferson Davis was shocked to receive a letter on Feb. 10, 1861, informing him that people had chosen him as president of the Confederate States of America. Davis had not asked for such an honor.

Born in Kentucky in 1808, Jefferson Davis came from a long line of soldiers. His father and uncles had been soldiers in the Revolutionary War in 1776. His three older brothers fought in the War of 1812 with Andrew Jackson.

Jefferson Davis attended Transylvania University in Kentucky as a young man and was later appointed to West Point Military Academy. He served in the army for seven years. Davis was an excellent soldier and was admired for his character, leadership and bravery.

After Davis' first wife died, he moved to Mississippi and began growing cotton and studying law. He returned to the military when the United States became involved in the Mexican-American War. After the war, Davis represented Mississippi in the Senate and served a short time as the U.S. Secretary of War.

After Abraham Lincoln was elected, Mr. Davis hoped to be named leader of the Confederate forces. What Davis didn't know was that Confederate leaders had held a meeting. They wanted Jefferson Davis to serve in a more important position.

On Feb. 18, 1861, Jefferson Davis took the oath of office at an inauguration ceremony as the first (and only) president of the Confederate States of America. The job in front of Davis was a huge challenge. It soon proved even more difficult than anyone would have ever imagined.

title: The Emancipation Proclamation
text:
The first battles of the Civil War were small compared with battles that followed. By July of 1862, both the North and the South had suffered a heavy loss of soldiers. The Union had won few battles, and the end of the war was nowhere in sight.

President Lincoln was very concerned about how the war was unfolding. People urged the leader to abolish slavery. However, President Lincoln knew the war was about more than getting rid of slavery. He wanted to keep the Union together too. After a year of battles and decisions, Lincoln knew it was time to end slavery altogether.

President Lincoln met with his group of advisors (people who offer ideas and share opinions). They told him to wait until the North had won a major battle before announcing the end of slavery. This chance came in September 1862 after the Battle of Antietam in Maryland (also known as the Battle of Sharpsburg). Over 23,000 men were killed there. The Union Army forced the Confederates back into Virginia. The time was right for Lincoln to announce his plan.

On Sept. 22, 1862, President Lincoln made the Emancipation Proclamation. Lincoln warned the Southern states that most southern slaves would be forever free if the "rebellious states" did not rejoin the Union by January. Lincoln also announced former slaves were free to join the Union army.

There were mixed reactions to Lincoln's announcement. Some people thought the war was being fought only to free the slaves and not necessarily to bring the nation back together. Others felt the Emancipation Proclamation was the best thing that could have ever happened to bring the country together again. After Lincoln signed the Proclamation into law on Jan. 1, 1863, many slaves fled north to join Union forces.

The Emancipation Proclamation helped to free slaves, caused Southern plantation owners to lose workers and helped increase the number of soldiers fighting for the Union cause.

title: Comparing and Contrasting American Leaders
text:
Think about the North and South during the Civil War. Use information from this issue along with what you already know to compare and contrast the leaders of both sides. In each leader’s box, make notes about the man. Consider his background, leadership style, strengths and weaknesses.

On a separate piece of paper, write a paragraph about how the leaders were similar. Next, write a paragraph about how the leaders were different. Complete the assignment by filling in the blanks in the summary sentence below the chart.

Summary Sentence: Leaders of the North and South during the Civil War were alike in that they all ______________, but while Northern leaders ______________, Southern leaders______________.

title: The Boy is a Soldier
text:
Word of the Confederate attack on Fort Sumter in April 1861 spread quickly in the Northern states. President Abraham Lincoln called for men to pick up their arms (weapons) and join the fight against the Rebels. Some volunteers who reported for duty were young boys. Children as young as nine read newspaper headlines or heard adults talk about the fall of Fort Sumter. On both sides, there was a rush to join forces. Men and boys (and even some women) wanted to do their part to help.

The legal age to fight in battle was 18, but many boys were able to slip into an Army unit. There was no easy way to check on a young man's age. Documents to prove how old a person was, such as a driver's license or ID card, simply didn't exist. Some of the boys joined with their parents' permission, while others ran away from home without anyone knowing they joined the fight. Some boys even changed their names to keep their true age hidden.

Most Northern boys signed up because they wanted to be a part of the Yankee forces and not because they wanted to end slavery. Most of them wanted to experience a grand adventure far more interesting than the hard farm work back at home. Southern boys joined Rebel forces for the same sense of excitement. They also felt they needed to defend slavery and their Southern way of life against the large Northern army.

One of the easiest ways for a boy to enlist (join the military) was to be a musician. Drummers, buglers and fife (a type of flute) players were not part of the actual fighting forces. These small bands led the troops into battle by playing marching orders, and they often played to lift the spirits of weary soldiers.

The excitement the boys and young men felt when they signed up for battle quickly disappeared. The marching, training and fighting in battle was grueling (tough). There was little to eat and many of them became sick from diseases that spread quickly. Many soldiers died from disease while others died from battle wounds. Most soldiers made only about $13 a month for their hard and dangerous work. Unfortunately, many of the boys did not make it back home alive.

title: Behind the Lines and Back at Home
text:
The Battle of Gettysburg

In the beginning of the Civil War, many Southern victories kept the Union Army from capturing the Confederate capital at Richmond, Virginia. The South’s leader, Robert E. Lee, decided it was time to make a bold move. He wanted a victory on Northern soil because he was sure this would make the Union want to end the war once and for all.

Lee took his troops into Pennsylvania in June 1863. Union soldiers followed Lee and his Confederate troops and surprised them in the town of Gettysburg. The three-day battle that followed was a turning point in the war. Lee’s Confederate Army lost thousands of men and was forced to retreat (move back) to Virginia. The Confederate Army was never able to invade the North again.

On the Battlefield

Fighting in the Civil War was brutal. Most battles began with face-to-face attack on an open battlefield. A drummer would beat a drum slowly as a signal for the soldiers to move again into formations. The air was usually thick with black smoke as the soldiers walked in rows toward their enemy’s lines.

The soldiers shot at one another with rifles. Many fell dead within seconds of the start of battle. As the soldiers moved closer to one another, they usually switched to hand-to-hand combat. They used bayonets (long blades) that were fastened to the muzzles of their rifles. Dead and wounded soldiers lay on the battlefield at the end of the fighting. Sometimes, wounded people died on the battlefield waiting for help to arrive. Many soldiers died months or years later from wounds they got during the war.

On the Home Front

Half of all the men serving in the military during the Civil War were farmers back at home, and most of them could read and write. Letters sent back and forth between soldiers and their families helped keep everyone informed about what was going on.

Northerners wrote about a new income tax passed as part of the Internal Revenue Act of 1862. The government would use money from the tax to pay for the war. It turns out that the federal government spent approximately $2 million each day for war costs. The Northern economy was still strong, though. Workers continued to mine gold and silver in California, Nevada and Colorado. Factories expanded their businesses to produce war goods including rifles, ammunition, trains, blankets and shoes.

However, Northern citizens were angry about draft guidelines. The law allowed rich men to pay someone else to take their place on the battlefield. They could also choose to pay the government a fee to avoid serving in the military. Some people thought this was unfair. They felt everyone should be required to serve the country.

The South’s economy was based on agriculture, so it could not produce all the war materials its army needed. On top of that, the North had set up blockades at all Southern ports. This kept plantation owners from exporting cotton to sell in Europe. The South did not have the money to pay for a war. To solve the problem, the South simply printed $1 billion in paper money. But the true value of every Confederate dollar was only about five cents.

Most of the fighting took place in the South as well. Southerners lost property when Union troops marched through the territory. Sometimes soldiers stole property or burned homes and farms. Also, food was scarce and hard to find. Food that was available was very expensive. Most Southern families could not afford meat. Poor diets caused many Southerners to become ill.

From Gettysburg to Appomattox

Southern forces never recovered from the defeat at Gettysburg. At almost the same time, General Ulysses S. Grant and his soldiers had captured the Confederate fort at Vicksburg, a Southern city on the Mississippi River. With the North in control of this important waterway, the Confederacy was almost cut in half.

Grant took control of the entire Union Army and decided to attack the South in two states. With orders from Grant, General William Sherman marched through Georgia to the Atlantic Ocean. Grant himself led troops into Virginia to capture the capital of Richmond. Grant was determined to defeat the South at any cost. He believed the North could win if its Army just kept attacking. Sure enough, many Rebels realized they were in big trouble. A large number of them believed the war was lost, and they turned to head home.

The Final Surrender

On April 9, 1865, General Robert E. Lee surrendered to General Ulysses S. Grant in the parlor of a home near Appomatox Court House in Virginia. After four bloody years, the Civil War had ended.

Some describe Grant as a very kind and generous man for the treatment he offered to the defeated Southern soldiers. He allowed Lee’s officers to keep their weapons and all soldiers to return home. Grant also allowed soldiers to keep their own horses to be used at their homes. In addition, he ordered Union troops to share their food with Southern soldiers who were starving. When Union soldiers began to cheer at the word of surrender, Grant stopped them and exclaimed, “The war is over. The Rebels are our countrymen again.” Later, Grant wrote that at the moment of surrender he felt “sad and depressed” at the downfall of “a foe (enemy) who had fought so long and so valiantly (bravely).”

title: Civil War Secret Agents
text:
If you think spies are only found in good mystery books or in movies, then think again. Believe it or not, spies played an important role for both the North and South during the Civil War. Both sides knew the other was spying on them, but they also knew it was difficult to stop spies from infiltrating, or passing through, enemy lines to access secret information. Civil War spies didn't have all of the special technology that spies have today. They relied on good old-fashioned disguises and tricks to learn their secrets.

Some of the best Civil War spies were not even soldiers. They were women. One particularly clever Union spy was a woman named Sarah Emma Edmonds. Ms. Edmonds was a master of disguise. She first disguised herself as a man so that she could serve in the Union Army. As a spy, she "redisguised" herself as a woman or an African American man. When her secret was exposed, she spent the remainder of the war as a Union nurse.

The Confederacy had a woman spy named Nancy Hart. She disguised herself to track where Union soldiers were hiding out. She would then lead Confederate Rebels to their positions for an attack. Hart was captured, but she escaped when she tricked a guard into showing her his rifle. She grabbed the gun, shot the guard and headed out.

As long as there are wars, there will certainly be spies. The Civil War was no exception to this rule.

title: Women and the War
text:
Women did not sit and just wait and worry during the Civil War. They played important roles on both sides of the war. Without the help of women, both the North and the South would have had many more problems.

Some women disguised themselves as men and fought in the battles. Many more women worked on the battlefields as nurses. Some women worked as spies, but most women did their part back at home.

Many Northern women entered the workforce to take over jobs that had been held by men who were now off at war. Women worked in weapons factories, on farms, at government offices and in hospitals. Many of the women worked to earn money to help support the troops. Women earned about $50 million total to help the cause. In addition, Northern Women's Aid Societies provided blankets, clothing, medicine and other supplies to troops. Many of these women stayed on the job even after the war was over.

In the South, the women at home worked about as hard as the men on the battlefields. Women worked long and hard to sew uniforms, flags and blankets from fabric they found or made themselves. Women in the South also worked to produce weapons for troops. Some Southern women lost their lives filling rifle cartridges with gunpowder. They also helped tend to the wounded soldiers who returned home. Perhaps most importantly, Southern women kept farms, plantations and homes running as best they could despite the terrible wartime conditions.

Many have said the Civil War was a war between brothers. But given the number of women who were affected by the war, people can also say it was a war between sisters.

title: The Civil War Today!
text:
The Civil War began when Confederate troops attacked Union soldiers at Fort Sumter on April 12, 1861. The war lasted four years. The two sides fought over 50 major battles and hundreds of smaller clashes. The war ended after General Robert E. Lee surrendered to General Ulysses S. Grant on April 9, 1865.

2011 to 2015 marked the 150th anniversary of the Civil War. Many towns and communities took time to celebrate and remember this important part of our history. During those years, anyone who owned an iPad could “watch” the war happen using “The Civil War Today” app. The app showed users what had happened on that day 150 years ago. The app used pictures, maps and newspaper stories to show the events of the war one day at a time.

The anniversary has passed, but the app is still available. People with the app can look up any date during the war and read newspaper articles, letters soldiers wrote to their families and detailed descriptions of battles. If you or someone you know owns an iPad, ask for permission to look at “The Civil War Today” app. It can help you relive the drama of the Civil War with just the push of a button!

title: Summarizing Historical Information
text:
A summary is a short statement that tells all of the main ideas of an event. A historical event summary should tell the important ideas about what happened during a time in history. Small details and facts are not included. When writing a summary, it is sometimes helpful to think about all the big ideas first. Write down notes about these ideas. Then write a summary using the main details.

Read the information from this week’s lesson from the subtitle “The Final Surrender.” Use this information to fill in the summary chart. Then, use your notes to write a summary of three to five sentences about this time in American history.

title: Reconstructing a Nation
text:
After four years, the Civil War had ended. The North had defeated the South, and it was now time to put the country back together. Many disagreed about how to mend, or repair, the nation. Some members of Congress wanted to see the Confederates punished for their part in the war. However, President Lincoln wanted to reunite (bring together) the country quickly during a time called Reconstruction.

Under Lincoln's plan, 10 percent of the Confederate states' populations would need to swear loyalty (faithfulness) to the United States' government. After the people showed they would be faithful to the country, Congress would accept representatives from those states. After a state was represented in Congress, it would then be a part of the United States of America again.

Not everyone agreed with Lincoln's plan. Many Northerners were angry. They thought Lincoln was making it much too easy for Southern states to rejoin the Union. They argued that because of the Confederates, there had been far too much death and destruction. They thought the South needed to change its ways so such a terrible war would not happen again. But Lincoln stuck to his plan. He ignored Congress' Reconstruction advice. Congress wanted to take matters into its own hands, but Lincoln refused to sign a much stricter program into law.

While the president and Congress disagreed, problems only grew in the South. The war had devastated and destroyed most of what was once a successful area. Entire towns were burned to the ground. Farms were overgrown and abandoned. Soldiers returned from the war only to find their homes in ruins. Their families were sick, scattered or even dead. The people of the South were a broken group. Many were angry, and most were exhausted and scared about what the future might hold.

Slaves had been freed with the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863. Many freed slaves who were desperate for help had run away from their owners. They didn’t own land and very few of them could read or write. They needed food, clothing, shelter and medicine. Congress established the Freedmen's Bureau in March of 1865 to help the freed slaves adjust to life away from slavery. By the end of the war, millions of slaves were free and excited to begin their lives as American citizens.

The United States had so much healing to do after the Civil War. Unfortunately, it would be a long and bitter process. It was only made worse when the unimaginable happened just days after the South surrendered ...

title: One Nation Again
text:
The Civil War had been four long, bloody years. Neither side had planned on the war lasting as long as it did. When the fighting was finally over, it was time to return to normal life, but that wouldn't be easy.

Northerners were relieved the fighting had ended. During the Civil War, troops turned many of their cities into defense zones. They were filled with the hustle and bustle of soldiers and medical corps that were taking care of the injured. Now that both the North and South pledged peace, things could get back to normal. Northerners wanted to find a way to bring the nation together again. Most of them also wanted to make sure that all Americans would be guaranteed their civil rights from then on.

Southerners looked at their homes, land and communities with despair. Beautiful plantation mansions were destroyed. Soldiers had burned many to the ground. Fields where farmers grew crops were now overgrown with weeds. Industrial machines lay destroyed among the weeds. Nearly every village was devastated from the effects of a long, brutal war. Confederate soldiers returned home to find their families and communities shattered. White Southerners were tired, frustrated and angry at the whole situation.

Former slaves were experiencing their newfound freedom with joy. Many of them married, searched for family members and made plans for the future. Some of the freed slaves wanted to farm the land they knew so well. Others wanted to head north and start fresh, new lives.

A President's Death

During the Civil War, the nation had looked to President Lincoln as the leader. People hoped he would be able to guide the country through the Reconstruction. However, one devastating event destroyed the nation's hope. It was on the evening of April 14, 1865.

President Lincoln and his wife were attending a play at Ford's Theater in Washington, D.C. During the play, a wellknown actor and Confederate supporter, John Wilkes Booth, crept up behind the president and shot him in the back of the head. Soldiers carried Lincoln across the street to a boarding house where doctors tried to save the president's life. A crowd gathered to hear if doctors could save their leader.

President Abraham Lincoln died early in the morning on April 15. Federal troops later caught and killed President Lincoln's assassin (killer). Several other people had helped plan the murder as a way to punish Union leaders. Authorities later executed them for their part in the assassination of President Lincoln.

A New Plan

Vice President Andrew Johnson was immediately sworn in as the new U.S. president. He announced that he would continue with Lincoln's plan for Reconstruction. At first, Northerners were pleased with President Johnson's performance. However, they soon realized that while Johnson did not like the rich, white Southern plantation owners, he did not think the freed slaves should have equal rights. Many people became worried and angry. One group in Congress spoke up. The Radical Republicans believed African Americans should have the right to vote and own their own land.

The 13th Amendment

President Johnson's plan for new state governments to re-enter the Union was simple. The most important thing states had to do was to declare secession illegal and pass the 13th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. This amendment abolished (did away with) slavery forever in the United States. Many of the Southern states did not want to admit secession was wrong. Mississippi even refused to ratify the 13th Amendment for a long time. People in both regions of the country were not getting along with each other the way everyone had hoped they would.

Black Codes

Southern governments began passing laws called Black Codes that would return the freed African Americans to slavery. Under the laws, freed slaves were not allowed to vote or hold political office. If they wanted to travel, they needed permission from their white employer. Freed slaves were not even allowed to choose their own careers. If they wanted to work at any job besides farming, they needed permission to do so from a white judge. In addition to these unfair laws, many African Americans were the victims of violence. Many people worried another Civil War was on the way.

The 14th and 15th Amendments

President Johnson and Congress could not agree on how best to carry on the Reconstruction process. Congress was especially upset that Johnson did not support the Civil Rights Act that would give freed slaves basic human rights and protect them from unfair treatment. The Radical Republicans led the push to amend the Constitution again. In June 1866, Congress passed the 14th Amendment. Now all citizens, including African Americans, would have their civil rights protected.

By mid-1870, Congress had also realized that the freed slaves had little chance at living truly free lives unless they had the right to vote. It passed the 15th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution that guaranteed all men would have the right to vote. Women did not receive the right to vote until 1920.

Life in the New South

In the South, life was still far from normal even though the states were making changes. Free African Americans and former slaves became members of national and state governments. New state governments established public schools for both black and white children. Freed slaves learned to read and write. Agriculture and industry grew again. The South slowly made progress in rebuilding their communities. Eventually, Ulysses S. Grant replaced President Johnson. Rutherford B. Hayes then followed Grant. All of these men had to fight to continue bringing the U.S. back together again. It was many years before all people in the U.S. would truly have their civil rights protected as promised in the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments. Even today, the U.S. continues to work to provide freedom and equality to all citizens.

title: Sharecropping in the South
text: Eventually, Southern farmland was returned to the wealthy landowners and planters who had owned the land before the war started. Freed slaves and poor whites who wanted the chance to own their own farms found it difficult to raise enough money to buy land. They were forced to become sharecroppers. They rented land to grow crops and would give part of the crop to the landowner as payment for the land. Sharecropping was difficult work. Crops often failed in periods of poor weather or drought. Many sharecroppers found they could not pay their land rents and went into debt. Unfortunately, most Southern sharecroppers never had the chance to call any piece of land their own.

title: Hiram Revels: First African American Senator
text:
At the end of the Civil War, African Americans from the Southern states began to join local governments. By 1870, several black men had won positions in the federal government. Feb. 25, 1870, was an especially important day in U.S. history. On that day, 42-year-old Hiram Revels of Mississippi took the oath of office and became the first African American to serve in the U.S. Senate.

Revels was a teacher and a minister. During the Civil War, he had helped put together troops of African American soldiers, and he established schools for freed slaves in North Carolina. When he moved to Missi ssippi, citizens elected him to the state Senate. He was a strong leader whom his coworkers admired. When Mississippi was ready to re-enter the U.S. during Reconstruction, Revels took one of Mississippi's Senate seats.

Revels only served one year in the senate, but he spent his life working for the equal treatment of African Americans.

title: Carpetbaggers and Scalawags
text:
During the period known as Reconstruction, thousands of Northerners moved to the South. They wanted to take advantage of the opportunities that were available to make money. The South needed to be rebuilt. New industries and businesses were needed. Hired workers built factories that produced farm equipment and machinery. Mineral mines were opened. People replanted cotton and tobacco farms and operated them as big businesses.

Unfortunately, most Southerners did not like the "Yankee invaders." They called Northerners "carpetbaggers" because Northerners often arrived in the South carrying their belongings in cloth luggage bags. Southerners felt the Northern business people were trying to make money out of their difficult situation. They felt the carpetbaggers really cared more about making money for themselves rather than improving the lives of Southerners. In fact, most carpetbaggers weren't rich business people out to make money off the people of the South. Most were former soldiers who had set out to find opportunities that were not available in the North. Most of the anger the Southerners felt was because the carpetbaggers supported the rights of freed slaves.

"Scalawags" were Southerners who worked with carpetbaggers or supported the freed slaves. Many of these people were white Southerners who joined the Republican Party after the Civil War. Southerners considered the scalawags traitors to the South. Many of the so-called scalawags held positions in government during Reconstruction. They worked to make sure that state governments considered the equality of all citizens in the South when developing government plans for the states.

Many people still use the terms carpetbagger and scalawag in today's politics. A carpetbagger is used to describe a person who gets involved in someone else's business for his or her own personal gain. People today still consider scalawags as traitors.

title: Creating a Timeline
text:
Use information from the paragraph to construct a timeline of Reconstruction events of 1865.

The First Year of Reconstruction

Before the Civil War had officially ended, the U.S. Congress had already approved the 13th Amendment to the Constitution in January 1865. Ratified in December of that same year, the amendment abolished slavery forever in the United States. By March, Congress had started the Freedmen’s Bureau to provide newly emancipated slaves with assistance in finding food, shelter, education and jobs. Unfortunately, President Lincoln, who was responsible for the Emancipation Proclamation, did not live to see its results. On April 14, 1865, just five days after the end of the Civil War, a Confederate supporter named John Wilkes Booth assassinated him. Lincoln’s successor, Andrew Johnson, took charge of Reconstruction plans. He made them public in May. Reconstruction was not an easy process. Some states actually tried to find ways to bring slavery back to the South. In November of 1865, Mississippi enacted (passed) the Black Codes to limit the civil rights of freed slaves.

A Timeline of Reconstruction: 1865

title: Fake or Real News?
text:
Have you ever read something online, like on social media sites, that sounded fishy? Maybe it was real, but it could be fake news! The big danger, though, is news that sounds real but isn’t. Fake news is becoming common because anyone can post things online. Fake news can be in the form of a story. Fake news can be a photo or video that has been changed. The problem is that these fake items look real. Fake news can cause problems and it spreads misinformation.

Sam Wineburg, a professor, did some research. He found that 80 percent of students cannot tell the difference between real and fake news. Do you want to become a media-savvy person? You have to be able to find out if news is real or fake. How do you do that? You have to become a detective and search for the truth. You can learn about the author or company that posted the news. You have to think about the purpose of the news. Is there a hidden plan to get you to buy something or to make you think a certain way? Your teacher or a trusted adult can help you learn how to spot fake news. It takes a little time, but democracy depends on real information! Do your part and discover what is real and what is fake!

title: A New Era for a Reborn Nation
text:
A presidential election marked the end of the Reconstruction era in the United States. Voters elected (by compromise) Rutherford B. Hayes as president of the United States in 1876. This compromise, or agreement, meant that both the Republicans and Democrats had to give up some of their requests to get something in return. Neither Hayes nor his opponent, Samuel J. Tilden, had enough electoral college votes to win the presidency. A commission (group of people with given authority) came together to make a decision. This group of senators, representatives and Supreme Court justices decided that the Republican Hayes would be the 19th president. In compromise, Hayes agreed to remove all federal troops from the South. Now the North and the South could finally try to move past the effects from the terrible war that had torn the nation apart for 15 years.

Life for all U.S. citizens did not improve overnight. In the South, white Democrats gained control of most of the political offices after Reconstruction. African Americans had a difficult time entering politics at all. State officials did not always enforce the 14th and 15th Amendments (guaranteed citizenship and civil rights to all people). Unfortunately, a system of segregation, or separation of races, developed throughout much of the South.

Other changes in the U.S. happened as well. The American Industrial Revolution had started after the Revolutionary War and continued throughout the Civil War. This boom picked up after the war between the states ended. During this time, people created inventions and found new ways of manufacturing (making) products. The growth in industry and manufacturing resulted in even more people living and working in cities.

The slow pace of life in America sped up after the Civil War. Steamboats could quickly move goods and people longer distances over water. The West continued to grow with the completion of the transcontinental railroad. A trip across the U.S. that once took months now only took about a week.

In this issue, we'll explore the social, political and economic advances that continued to transform America as it headed into the twentieth century.

title: Is There Too Much Money in Politics?
text:
Candidates are spending huge amounts of money on political campaigns, more than ever before. There are many reasons for this, but a big reason is a decision made by the Supreme Court in 2010. In a decision called "Citizens United," the Supreme Court said corporations and unions could donate an unlimited amount of money to campaigns, but not directly to candidates. Many people think that this much money and secrecy in politics can only lead to trouble. Others are glad that the rules have changed.

A company or group with a lot of money can pay for commercials that support the candidate they like and criticize the other candidates. But some people say that the public doesn't know who those groups are. The groups might not be honest about what they want the candidate to do if he or she is elected. If the candidate is elected, then some believe that the groups will say, "We helped you win, now you change the laws to help our group get what we want."

Those who agree with the Supreme Court's decision say it's good to have fewer rules and less government involvement in campaigns. Many believe it doesn't matter who gives money, and politicians will do the jobs they were elected to do.

This year's political races will certainly be different because of the new rules. Watch the candidates' commercials and discuss them with your parents and teachers. What do YOU think about money and politics?

title: Industry, Communication and Transportation Take the Nation into a New Century
text:
Industry

The Industrial Revolution started in the United States after the Revolutionary War, and it continued well throughout the Civil War. Shipbuilding and the iron industry did well in the states. As the population of the country moved westward, agriculture, construction and mining industries grew also. By the time Reconstruction was over, the U.S. had become one of the largest and most competitive industrial nations in the world.

Before the Civil War, most people in the U.S. made their living in agricultural businesses. People owned or worked on small farms. Some worked in small family-owned businesses. After the war, industry grew much faster than agriculture. The population of cities increased quickly, especially in the North. Immigrants from all over the world flocked to the U.S. to find work and begin a better life for their families.

The demand, or need, for goods such as machinery and tools also grew quickly. Factories met this demand and supplied goods using powerdriven machinery both day and night. Machines now produced what had been hand-made goods. Small, familyowned businesses became large companies with the help of banks and investors. Investors gave money to businesses so companies could expand. Coal mining, steel production and clothing manufacturing were all big businesses.

Managers (people in charge of business) in the factories planned how the companies would operate, while workers took care of the machines. The work was often dangerous and difficult. Hard workers sometimes argued with companies to pay them better wages. They also asked for shorter working days and better conditions in which to do their jobs. The businesses made a lot of money for the owners, bankers and investors. Many of these people became very rich. The workers, though, did not always make a lot of money. Sometimes their families lived in very poor conditions. Problems between rich business owners and poor workers made some people feel unhappy with big business.

Communication

Even before the Civil War, developments in communication changed the way Americans sent and received information. In the 1830s, an American professor named Samuel F. B. Morse improved a way to use electromagnetic signals to send messages along wire that hung between poles. President Lincoln was interested in this communication technology and sent many telegraph messages during the war. Telegraph lines stretched from city to city. Communication was much easier and faster than sending letters by pony express or message carriers.

In the 1870s, as inventors Elisha Gray and Alexander Graham Bell worked on devices to improve telegraph service, they designed devices that could transmit speech electronically. Bell's design was patented first. The telephone uses electricity to transmit speech along wires. Wires between cities are used for voice communication. Now people in communities that were far apart could communicate easily.

As the nation entered the twentieth century, communication technology rapidly improved. Thomas Edison invented the phonograph. High-speed photography, film cameras, the radio, tape recordings, telephone answering machines and motion pictures were all invented before the 20th century was even one-fourth of the way over.

Transportation

After the Civil War, people began to move to different regions of the United States. Freed slaves could choose to live in the South or move to the North to work in factories. Northerners chose to either stay in their home regions or move south to farm. More and more people wanted to move west. This westward expansion was possible because of the development of the first transcontinental railroad.

The first talk about the possibility of a railroad connecting both the West and East regions of the U.S. began in the 1830s. Settlers moved westward to build homes, farms and communities. There had to be a way to transport goods and supplies back and forth between the East and West. Nearly everyone agreed a railroad was needed, but they didn't all agree on the route the rails should follow.

After much debate, people decided that the railroad route would follow the established Oregon, Mormon and California trails. The line began in Omaha, Nebraska, and followed the Platte River. It crossed over the Rocky Mountains at South Pass in Wyoming, and it then went through northern Utah and Nevada. From there the train crossed the Sierra Mountains to Sacramento, California. Workers laid more tracks to connect Denver, Colorado, and Salt Lake City, Utah, along with other cities not on the direct route. The Union Pacific Railroad built the line westward, and the Central Pacific Railroad built eastward. After six years, the two lines connected at Promontory Summit, Utah. A total of 1,777 miles of track was laid across the country.

Irish and Chinese immigrants, Mormons and Civil War veterans built the rails. White men working on the rails received higher pay than the immigrant workers did. The railroads also employed blacksmiths, bricklayers, carpenters, engineers, surveyors and cooks during the building process.

Workers officially completed the railroad on May 10, 1869. It changed the United States forever. The population of the western U.S. increased significantly. White settlers and freed slaves moved to the western region to farm, build homes, or start businesses. Railcars carried goods and supplies across the nation easily. Dangerous journeys west using wagons or stagecoaches were no longer necessary. Unfortunately, railroads also meant some American Indians were forced off their lands.

Railroads were responsible for more changes to the country than any other technological advance of the post-Civil War era. Indeed, many historians continue to argue that railroads are the most important invention ever created.

title: The Transcontinental Railroad and American Indians
text:
There is no doubt that the transcontinental railroad changed America forever. The railroad allowed people to travel and settle across the country. It easily shipped goods and supplies. People who had once grown all their own food and made all their own clothes were now able to buy supplies shipped on railroad cars. While the railroad brought the country closer together, it also brought many changes to the lives of American Indians of the West.

Railroad companies built tracks through a number of American Indian territories. One result of building the railroad was the loss of the buffalo herds that roamed freely. The American Indians depended on the buffalo for food, clothing and supplies. The railroads disrupted the everyday lives of the buffalo. In addition, many Americans on trains would often shoot the buffalo for fun as they rode past them. The buffalo then rotted on the ground. This angered many American Indians. By 1880, the buffalo had almost disappeared completely from the Great Plains. This left the American Indians without their most important food source.

Along with the end of the buffalo, American Indians often found themselves in arguments and battles with settlers. The settlers built homes and communities on American Indian territory. These two groups rarely lived together in peace. The U.S. tried to solve problems with the American Indians. Unfortunately, the United States’ only response was forcing American Indians onto reservations.

title: Leaders of Technology
text:
The United States quickly became an important industrial nation after the Civil War. There were many great business people and inventors who created machines and technology to help improve the economy. In 1876, the U.S. celebrated the Centennial Exposition. It was a celebration of the country's 100th anniversary. The main attraction at the exposition was Machinery Hall. This was where inventors from the United States displayed their inventions. Read on to learn more about two men and their important advances in technology.

Andrew Carnegie

Andrew Carnegie was born in Scotland. When he was 13 years old, he came to America and worked hard in a cotton mill. Once Carnegie saved enough money, he bought his own businesses. He soon made millions of dollars in the steel industry. He gave millions of dollars to charities in his later years.

Henry Ford

Henry Ford is best remembered for his work in designing and making the first automobiles in the country. He also perfected the assemblyline, conveyor-belt method of building cars. His ideas led to mass production of cars, and it changed the way people ran factories.

title: Main Idea and Details
text:
Look at the main ideas listed here after reading the article “Industry, Communication and Transportation Take the Nation into a New Century.” Then, find three details about each main idea and write them below the main idea.

1. The growth of industry following Reconstruction made the United States one of the most powerful industrial nations in the world.

2. Advances in communication technology brought big improvements to life in the United States.

3. The building of the first transcontinental railroad brought both positive and negative changes to the United States.

title: Writing Focus: Expository Writing/Informative-Main Idea-Detail
text: Authors often use the main idea-detail format of writing to inform readers of facts. Use information from this week’s lesson and ideas you organized in the activity to help you write. Compose three paragraphs explaining the growth of industry in the United States after Reconstruction. Be sure to write in complete sentences with each paragraph containing a main idea and at least three facts and details. Be sure to check for correct punctuation, grammar and spelling.

title: The United States Speeds into a New Century
text:
It was the "turn of the century." The 1800s faded into memory as the 1900s sped into view. America was becoming a world leader in industry. Its abundance (large amount) of natural resources and a manufacturing economy led by giant corporations helped the nation grow stronger and stronger. By 1910, the United States led the world in the production of iron, steel and oil. Miners also mined coal and gold in large amounts. The nation's agricultural, or farming, economy was also doing well. The transcontinental railroad system made shipping goods across the country easy. Goods and products were also being shipped to and traded with other countries all over the world.

Americans were working harder than ever to earn their living. People in rural, or country, areas were still struggling to get by. Life in overcrowded urban, or city, areas was also still difficult at times. However, most Americans were making larger incomes and spending more money than in previous decades. The increase in industry meant there were many more goods for people to buy. People shopped in new department stores and ordered goods from mail-order companies. In cities, people could even order goods using the telephone. Electricity was also reaching more and more people. People used Thomas Edison's electric light in more and more of their homes and businesses. Communities built hospitals, public schools and colleges, churches, libraries and theaters.

Immigrants continued to pour into the country from all over the world. These people wanted to live the "American dream." Millions of Europeans crowded into eastern coastal cities, while also branching out to farmland in the Midwest region of the country. Many found economic opportunities (new ways to make money) in the United States that they could have only dreamed about in their homelands.

Many Americans felt cheerful as the new century began. After all, the country had been through both the Civil War and Reconstruction. People had reason to believe that only good times were ahead. However, there were still citizens who believed the United States had room to improve.

In this issue, you will learn about people and groups who worked to make the United States of America a strong and fair country as it entered into the twentieth century.

title: Manufacturing Medicine Overseas May Put U.S. Citizens at Risk
text:
Remember the last time you had a fever? Your parents most likely went to the local drug store and bought medicine for you. After a couple of doses, you probably felt better. In the United States today, we know our medicine is safe. This is because the government created the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 1906.

The FDA works to make sure that companies make medicine that is safe and does its job. For over a hundred years, people in the United States have depended on the FDA to protect them from dangerous drugs.

Now, the FDA's job is becoming more difficult. This is because many medicine manufacturing companies are making their drugs in foreign countries. It is difficult to inspect all of the overseas factories and make sure they are following safety rules. FDA officials say that sometimes medicines made outside the United States are made with ingredients that don't work or are even dangerous. In fact, some factories are not as clean as they should be. FDA leaders say that the United States must work with the foreign governments to make sure people who take medicine will remain safe.

title: Turn of the Century Life
text:
The turn of the century brought many new and exciting changes to the country. Many of these changes happened because of the fast growth of industry and cities. Even though the wheels of change were turning quickly, some Americans held on to ideas from the previous century. Therefore, change in other areas didn't happen as quickly.

Technology in Cities

By 1900, four out of every 10 Americans lived in cities. In 1900, New York City had over 3 million residents. The cities of Chicago, Illinois and Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, had over 1 million residents each. Cities had to make advances to keep up with the challenges of an expanding population.

Cities were quickly running out of space to expand outward, so in 1900 cities began to build upward. Builders began constructing very tall buildings called skyscrapers to solve the problem of space in cities.

Cities also found ways to connect neighborhoods together. Networks of electric trolley cars and subway train stations made transporting people easier. More and more people were also brought together with telephones and radios.

Improving Public Education

After the Civil War, the United States made some effort to require children to attend school. Between 1865 and 1895, many states passed laws requiring children between the ages of eight and 14 to attend school for three to four months each year. The schools cost nothing to attend. However, these early schools were not successful. Some of the teachers weren't qualified, and it was difficult to get good books and materials.

As the country entered the 20th century, more and more people realized how important an education was to the future success of the country. By 1918, all American children were required to attend school at least through the elementary years. New schools were built, and high schools began to offer classes in different subjects such as math, science, government and social studies.

Unfortunately, the education a child received depended on the color of their skin. White children and African American children did not attend the same schools. Most African American children weren't allowed to attend high school or college. Many of these students were able to continue their education at schools started by African Americans. One such man was Booker T. Washington. After being freed from slavery, Mr. Washington became a teacher. He started Tuskegee University in Alabama, which is still open.

Segregation and Discrimination

The end of the Civil War did not end unfair treatment of African Americans. Discrimination, or unfair treatment, was common. In schools, theaters, restaurants and other public places, segregation was normal. African Americans were set apart from whites. They did not sit together on buses and trains. Most public places had separate restrooms and water fountains for each group.

Many Southern states continued to pass Black Codes. These laws made it difficult for African Americans to vote, own property or work at certain jobs. The legal system and police supported these unfair laws. Decades would pass before all of the unfair laws were repealed, or cancelled.

The Vote for Women

Women did not have the same rights as men at the turn of the century. Many believed that women should only be homemakers. Many believed women were only supposed to take care of their families and not take part in politics or speak out in public. The public considered married women under "control" of their husbands. Women weren't allowed to own property, sign contracts, attend college or work at high-paying professional jobs. Perhaps most importantly, women did not have the right to vote.

Of course, many people did not think women were being treated fairly. After all, the 14th and 15th Amendments to the U.S. Constitution guaranteed citizenship and the right to vote for all Americans - but not women.

Even before the Civil War, women wanted the chance to vote. They wanted the same opportunities as men. They wanted to go to college, own land and work as doctors and lawyers. By the 20th century, women were fighting for suffrage (the right to vote). Women began forming political groups. The National Women's Party, led by a young woman named Alice Paul, often marched in front of the White House demanding to vote. The suffragettes, as these women were known, were sometimes faced with both verbal and physical violence. Mrs. Paul was even sent to prison for seven months.

Finally, after many years of marching and fighting, the U.S. Congress passed the 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which gave women the right to vote.

title: Susan B. Anthony - Women’s Rights Leader
text:
Many important women worked to improve the quality of life for women in the beginning of the 20th century. One such woman was a Quaker named Susan B. Anthony. Anthony had worked as a schoolteacher before beginning her work for social reform (change). She supported the anti-slavery and women's rights movements. Anthony proved that women could be leaders in society. She along with many others wanted women to have the same rights as men, including the right to vote.

After the Civil War, Anthony and her fellow women's rights workers wanted both former slaves and women to have the right to vote. They were disappointed when the 14th and 15th Amendments to the Constitution did not talk about women at all. They didn't give up though. Anthony traveled all over the nation to convince people to support her cause. She was once arrested and fined $100 for voting illegally in a presidential election.

Women did not gain the right to vote during Susan B. Anthony's lifetime. The right came 14 years after her death. She did, however, influence many other Americans to continue with social reform. Thanks to Susan B. Anthony, women today don't have to think twice about casting their votes on election day.

title: The Progressive Era
text:
Business and industry grew fast in the first 20 years of the 20th century in the United States. Before the turn of the century, the government tried hard not to get too involved in private businesses. However, by 1900 many people felt businesses were getting too big and too greedy. They wanted the government to help control large industries and keep the free enterprise system fair.

These people called themselves Progressives. They asked the government to pass laws that would make sure businesses could compete with each other. The government passed laws that would prevent one large company, or corporation, from controlling a single industry. Many agencies were created to make sure businesses made and traded goods according to the laws.

During this time, Congress also passed the 16th Amendment to the Constitution. This amendment allowed the government to collect income taxes from citizens.

title: Henry Ford and Mass Production
text:
In 1913, car designer and manufacturer Henry Ford developed a new system of making cars in his factory. He began using a moving assembly line where each worker had one job to do in the car's assembly. Using this idea, factories made cars quicker than if they were assembled one car at a time. Ford believed that this mass production would make his company very successful.

Ford also had new and interesting ideas on how to treat workers in his car factory. He offered them up to $5 a day to work for him. At the time, this was a very large wage to be paid for a day's work. Ford wanted to be sure his own employees could afford to buy one of the cars they were helping to produce.

Today, Henry Ford's ideas about assembly lines and mass production of goods are still used at factories around the world.

title: Using Primary and Secondary Sources
text:
Historians must be able to gather information from many different sources as they study events and people in history. A primary source provides information from a person who was actually at the event. Letters, journals, newspaper articles, photographs or artifacts are all examples of primary sources. A secondary source of information comes from someone who was not at the event. Encyclopedia articles, biographies, textbooks and some Internet sites can be secondary sources.

Read the two pieces of information below related to the women’s rights movement for suffrage in the early 20th century. One is a primary source and the other is a secondary source. Identify each.

American History — Chapter 13

Women’s suffrage is the right for women to vote and hold political office. In the United States, women did not earn the right to vote until the 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution was ratified in 1920. The road to the Amendment was a long one for the women of America.

In 1848, the Seneca Falls Women’s Convention was held in Seneca Falls, New York. It was there that the idea of women’s suffrage was introduced to the American public. Several important women, including Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott, spoke at the conference. These activists began a 70-year struggle for women to have the right to vote in the United States of America.

Use information from the sources and this week’s issue to identify three cause-and-effect relationships about women’s suffrage. Complete the cause-and-effect chart below.

title: The United States Rises to a World Power
text:
At the beginning of the 20th century, Americans looked forward to a time of growth and prosperity. There were many new opportunities for people to find wealth and success. Industry was booming and America took pride in being a world leader.

In 1917 it was time for the United States to use its power and leadership. A war had been waging for control of Europe for over two years. The Allied Powers (France, Great Britain and Russia) were at war with the Central Powers (Germany and Austria Hungary). At first America was neutral, or uninvolved, in the war. The country did not support one side or the other. However, the United States was soon sending both money and supplies to help the Allies fight against Germany. It was clear to Americans that they would have to join the fight. On April 2, nineteen seventeen, the United States declared war against the Central Powers. American troops poured into Europe by the thousands. Courageous and strong, the U.S. soldiers played an important role in the war.
