By the fall of 1918, Germany's chances of a victory had been crushed.

The United States took the lead now in the war efforts. U.S. President Woodrow Wilson spent a great deal of time trying to find a way for all of the countries to come to a peaceful agreement and end the war. He wanted to make the world "safe for democracy." His plan, called Fourteen Points, created the League of Nations. This international organization would settle disagreements between countries. This way the world could prevent any more wars from occurring. Interestingly, the United States would never be a part of this group. Congress never approved the country's participation.

On Nov. 11, 1918, an armistice (agreement to stop fighting) was declared. The countries at war all agreed to stop fighting for a time. Leaders wanted to discuss peace. For six months, the countries at war discussed the issues during the Paris Peace Conference. World War I finally came to an end when the Treaty of Versailles was signed in France on June 28, 1919. Peace wouldn't last long though. Germany was never truly pleased with the way the war ended. They did not think they were being treated fairly. Within years that country's anger would lead to the rise of one of the most ruthless world leaders ever, Adolf Hitler.

title: Immunization Week Takes Shot at Saving Lives
text:
The United Nations (U.N.) is a group of 192 countries all working together to achieve peace and development in the world. The group's headquarters is located in New York City, New York. One way the group achieves its goals is through health education for the world's people.

Millions of people all over the world die each year from diseases that can be prevented with vaccines. Many people simply do not have access to the medicines they need to prevent diseases such as flu, measles, polio and tetanus. Others may not understand how the diseases are spread, treated and prevented.

Each year the U.N. marks Immunization Week throughout 180 countries and territories of the world. During this seven-day period, workers hold vaccination campaigns, training sessions and conferences to educate and treat people in regions of Africa, the Americas, the Eastern Mediterranean, Europe and Western Pacific.

The United Nations' World Health Organization believes that millions of lives can be saved during the week each year. Now that's a "shot" of good news!

title: Boom to Bust: The Roaring ‘20s to the Great Depression
text:
Flappers and Jazz

The 1920s was a colorful time in U.S. history. It was a time of new ideas and changes in the country. Radios were in almost every home. Charles Lindbergh flew the first solo plane flight across the Atlantic Ocean. Skyscrapers shot up all over the country. The people in the United States were changing too. Many of them wanted lives that were different from their parents’ and grandparents’ lives.

Some young people became free-spirited. Women, who had gained the right to vote in 1920, could now dress and act differently. Instead of long skirts and stockings, many young women wore short skirts and cut their hair. These women were known as flappers. They learned the latest dances and listened to jazz music. The mood of the country was confident. People bought more and more goods using credit (borrowed money). Soon, however, the happy times came crashing down.

Black Tuesday

Tuesday, October 29, 1929, was the end of a prosperous (successful) and optimistic (hopeful) time in the United States. During the 1920s, millions of people had bought shares of stock, or part ownership of companies. Stock prices continued to rise. People borrowed more and more money to buy more shares. On Black Tuesday, the prices of stocks fell sharply. Suddenly the shares were worth nothing. Many people lost everything they owned that day. The stock market had crashed, and the U.S. economy crashed along with it.

The Great Depression

The stock market crash was only the beginning of tough times for the country. Many banks lost money too. People worried that their money in the bank might not be safe, and they rushed to the banks to withdraw their funds. When banks were out of money, they closed their doors. Some of the banks began to go out of business. People who had deposited money in the banks were out of luck. There was no money left.

Many banks tried to get some of the money back they had let people borrow. They began to ask people to immediately pay back loans (money given with a promise to pay it back). Sometimes the banks took people’s homes and farms back when loans weren’t paid. People were left homeless and without a way to make money. Many felt the banks were being cruel to them.

Businesses were also affected by the economic hard time. Some businesses had also lost a lot of money in the stock market crash. Many of them had to cut back employees’ hours and reduce their pay. Many people lost their jobs altogether when businesses closed.

Within a few years, millions of Americans were out of work. Some of these people traveled on railroads from town to town looking for new jobs. Some businesses had more than 1,000 people apply for a single job opening. Farmers who had lost their land traveled all over the country to find work on other people’s farms.

The Dust Bowl

To make matters worse, 25,000 square miles in the southwestern Plains suffered terrible drought and severe windstorms. These windstorms were so bad they covered farmland with a blanket of dust. The Dust Bowl affected land in Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico and Colorado.

Farmland in these areas had been over plowed and overgrazed by animals for years before. Because the region was also in a drought and there was almost no rainfall for years, there was very little grass and few trees growing on the land. High winds blew the exposed topsoil away. Huge dust cloud storms blew across the land and destroyed everything in their paths.

Small farms were hardest hit. Many of the farmers were already in debt. They had borrowed money for seeds and tools to operate the farms. When crops didn’t grow, the farmers couldn’t repay the bank. Unfortunately, banks often had to foreclose on the farms. This meant the farmers no longer owned the land. Suddenly many farm families were left homeless and without a way to support their families.

Worldwide Effects

Though the Great Depression started in the United States, it quickly became a worldwide problem. After WWI, the United States helped many European countries pay their debts. When the American economy failed, there was no money to send to foreign countries. As a result, the western European countries fell into a period of economic depression too. Great Britain and Germany were the hardest hit.

The Great Depression lasted more than a decade. Unfortunately, it would take another great war to bring prosperity back to the world.

title: Life in a Hooverville
text:
As the Great Depression deepened so did the troubles of many Americans. Many families who were unable to pay rent or make house payments were forced to leave their homes. Some families who made their living on farms moved to cities, searching for better lives. Some city families even lost their homes. After being evicted (forced to leave), many of these families searched for public bread lines or soup kitchens for food. Cheese sandwiches, watereddown soup and oatmeal were typical free meals.

For shelter, many families shared run-down apartments. But even those were hard to find. Some people resorted to using scraps of lumber and cardboard boxes to build shacks in which to live. Soon small communities of these shack homes appeared. These new shantytown (shack town) areas were often called Hoovervilles. The name Hooverville was chosen in "honor" of President Herbert Hoover. Many blamed him for causing the Depression. Many workers sent their families to live with relatives while they stayed behind in the slums to look for work.

Hoovervilles had no electricity or running water, but they were often built near rivers. There was no garbage removal system, so trash piled up and rats ran wild. People living there stayed warm by covering themselves with "Hoover blankets," or newspapers. They used the restroom in "Hoover villas" or outside public toilets. The communities were dangerous and dirty, but for millions of out-of-work Americans they were home. Many Hoovervilles were often raided by local law enforcement and sometimes burned to the ground. The people who were living in the shacks were forced to wander to the next town. Life for Americans during the Great Depression was extremely difficult. Hoovervilles are just a small snapshot of the big picture of the United States during this sad time in history.

title: Why is Veterans’ Day celebrated in the United States?
text: World War I, the "war to end all wars," officially came to an end on June 28, 1919. However, the fighting stopped months earlier, on Nov. 11, 1918. Therefore, Nov. 11 became known as Armistice Day. The day was set aside for Americans to show their appreciation to the country's World War I heroes. The national celebrations included parades, speeches and public prayer meetings. After later wars in the 20th century, the name of the holiday was changed to Veterans Day. Today in the United States every Nov. 11 is set aside as a day of "celebration to honor America's veterans for their patriotism, love of country and willingness to serve and sacrifice for the common good."

title: Migrant Farm Workers in the Great Depression
text:
During the Great Depression, many found themselves out of work. People living in the Great Plains states lost their farms and businesses because of drought and the economic situation in the country. A great number of these people became migrant farm workers.

Migrant workers moved from place to place looking for work on large farms. Over 1 million people moved to California in the 1930s. These people hoped to find work easily because of the long growing season and variety of crops produced in the state.

There were so many families seeking work that jobs were still scarce (in limited supply) and wages were very low. Even with the entire family working, many migrant families struggled to pay for housing and food. Most families lived in very poor conditions. Life was difficult, dirty and without much hope. Life for migrant workers all over the United States did not improve until the 1940s when WWII ended the Great Depression.

title: Patriotism
text:
During World War I, feelings of patriotism grew strong in America thanks in part to a wonderful song written by George M. Cohan called "Over There." The popular piece became an anthem for liberty during WWI. Cohan is also famous for some other songs, including "You're a Grand Old Flag," "Give My Regards to Broadway," and "I'm a Yankee Doodle Dandy." Do you recognize these words (first verse and chorus)?

Over There
Johnnie, get your gun,
Get your gun, get your gun.
Take it on the run,
On the run, on the run.
Hear them calling, you and me,
Every son of liberty.
Hurry right away,
No delay, go today.
Make your daddy glad
To have had such a lad.
Tell your sweetheart not to pine,
To be proud her boy's in line.

Chorus
Over there, over there,
Send the word, send the word over there-
That the Yanks are coming,
The Yanks are coming,
The drums rum-tumming ev'rywhere.
So prepare, say a pray'r,
Send the word, send the word to beware.
We'll be over, we're coming over,
And we won't come back 'till it's over,
Over there.

title: Flowcharts
text: Read the article called “Boom to Bust: The Roaring ‘20s to a Great Depression.” Create a flowchart by writing complete sentences about the Great Depression in the United States. Be sure to write the events in the order that they happened during the 1920s and 1930s. Check your work for correct punctuation and spelling.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you are a farmer in the Dust Bowl during the Great Depression. Write a letter to your banker about your difficulties during the economic downturn. Persuade the banker to give you and your family more time to solve your problems before the bank forecloses on your home. Using complete sentences, give at least three reasons why your banker should give your family more time. Support all of your main ideas with at least three facts and details.

title: From Dust Bowl to New Deal
text:
The United States had fallen into terrible economic times when the stock market crashed in 1929. The country was in a Great Depression. Jobs and money were scarce. A long period of little rainfall affected the Midwest during this time too. The drought was made even worse when great wind and dust storms hit the same region. Many families abandoned their farms to look for work elsewhere. Emily Sarah's family owned a farm in the Dust Bowl. During the Great Depression they went searching for a better life and a New Deal.

Emily Sarah held Mama's hand tightly as she climbed into the old truck. She could see Papa trying to hold back tears as the truck sputtered away. Through the swirling dust and wind, Emi, as her Mama called her, could see the boarded up farmhouse getting smaller and smaller as they drove away. To Emi it seemed the road was leading away from her family's dreams.

Papa and Mama had tried as hard as they could to keep the farm. The crops just wouldn't grow in the dry soil. With no crops to sell, they were unable to pay back the money they had borrowed. Now the bank owned the farm. Sadly, Emi wondered if her family would ever be the same again. There was no farm, no home and no money. Some days there wasn't even much to eat. Papa said things would be better in California. He promised he would be able to find work on a farm there.

Mama had also reminded them that the United States had a new leader. President Franklin D. Roosevelt had been elected just months before. President Roosevelt declared that he had a "New Deal" for the country. He had new ideas and programs that would help people. Mama thought that Papa might even be able to find one of President Roosevelt's jobs for building roads or bridges.

Emily Sarah gripped Mama's hand even tighter. Maybe the road ahead would be better for her family. She smiled a thin-lipped smile in Papa's direction and he nodded at her. Maybe there was hope for them all.

title: Boom to Bust and Back Again
text:
You may have heard people compare the recent economic recession (2007-2009) to the Great Depression of the 1930s. But what some people call the "Great Recession" actually had more in common with a depression in the 1890s and something called "boom and bust."

In the early 1890s, the U.S. economy grew quickly ("boomed") but couldn't keep growing at that rate. When many companies and the housing market failed, there was an economic "bust." The railroad industry had been booming since the end of the Civil War, but in the 1890s more than 150 railroad companies closed. Other industries that depended on the railroads closed, and many people lost their jobs. Over 500 banks closed. Thousands of unemployed men marched to Washington, D.C., in 1894 to demand that the government take action to help families. Unemployment was over 10 percent for most of the 1890s. About one of every ten people had no job.

In the recent recession, the housing market slumped after several "boom" years. Some automakers went out of business and others filed for bankruptcy. The economy went "bust," just as it did in the 1890s. Hundreds of banks and thousands of businesses closed. The unemployment rate was about 8 percent - about one of every twelve people had no job.

Make a chart or Venn diagram that compares these two events in history.

title: A New Deal for the United States
text:
Franklin D. Roosevelt was elected president of the United States in 1932 when the nation was suffering and needing immediate help. Roosevelt wanted to put special programs into place to help all Americans quickly. He was especially concerned with "the forgotten man at the bottom of the economic pyramid." This included the working- class people who had lost everything after the stock market crashed in 1929. Roosevelt wanted to offer jobs to the millions of people who were out of work. He wanted to provide housing to those who had lost their homes when banks closed or foreclosed on farms and homes. He wanted the American people to regain their hope and confidence (feeling of trust or belief) in the nation and its government.

A New Deal is Born

During Roosevelt's presidential nomination acceptance speech he promised the American public, "I pledge you, I pledge myself, to a new deal for the American people." Within days after he was sworn in as president, Roosevelt addressed the nation over the radio to let them know of immediate changes and new programs that would help Americans.

President Roosevelt and Congress first developed a plan to reopen banks, provide money to the states to help citizens and establish programs to help get people back to work.

The government's new agencies and programs sometimes confused people. Many of them were known by their initials - the CCC, WPA, TVA and many more. So many, in fact, that people often referred to the New Deal programs as Roosevelt's Alphabet Soup. Despite the confusing names, there was no denying that the programs worked.

New Deal Programs Battle the Great Depression

Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC)

The CCC was one of Roosevelt's first programs. The purpose of the program was to put workers back on the job! Roosevelt did not want to hand out money to Americans. He wanted them to take pride in themselves by earning money through work. Thousands of young men joined the CCC to work on projects to better the nation. They planted trees, built roads and parks and fought forest fires.

Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA)

The TVA was a program to improve the lives of people who lived along the Tennessee River in the southeastern United States. Many companies hired workers to build dams and provide electrical service.

Federal Housing Administration (FHA)

Many people lost their homes during the Great Depression. The FHA was designed to help make it possible for people to borrow money to buy homes again.

Social Security Act (SSA)

The SSA provided direct help to needy citizens. Under the plan, the SSA made payments to all Americans who lost their jobs and could not find work. The government taxed the payments so workers could receive a pension at the age of 65. This meant when a person was too old to work they would still receive a monthly paycheck from the government.

Roosevelt's New Deal programs did improve life for many Americans. Not all of the programs were successful though. The government cancelled some of them after a short time. Others, like the TVA and Social Security, are still in existence. Just as in Roosevelt's era, government leaders today are still debating and making changes to programs that provide assistance to people.

title: Franklin D. Roosevelt: The Man Behind the New Deal
text:
In 1933 the United States was in the middle of the Great Depression. Businesses had closed. Some banks failed, and others had taken farms and homes away from families. Many workers lost their jobs, and most people had very little hope that things would get better. But in that same year, a man named Franklin Delano Roosevelt was sworn in as the new president of the United States. He brought hope and inspiration with him.

FDR, as he was called throughout his life, was an excellent example of how a man could overcome major life challenges. In the summer of 1921, Franklin developed a serious disease called polio. The disease made it difficult for him to walk or even stand. For the rest of his life, Franklin could not get around without help. He had to use a wheelchair or crutches everywhere he went. However, he did not let his disease slow him down or crush his dreams. Roosevelt was determined to live an active life with a purpose.

As president, Franklin D. Roosevelt faced many more challenges. One was finding a way to bring the country out of the Great Depression. His plan to develop programs that would help the poor and create jobs changed America. People all over the nation started feeling hopeful. They had confidence that President Roosevelt was leading the country in the right direction. They approved of his work so much they elected him president four times! He is the only U.S. president to serve more than two terms. The 22nd Amendment to the Constitution now limits a president to two terms.

In one famous speech Roosevelt told Americans, "The only thing we have to fear, is fear itself." Certainly Roosevelt believed this, and he lived his life as proof the statement was true in his own heart.

title: Famous Faces: The Making of Mount Rushmore
text:
A monument stands in the beautiful Black Hills of southwest South Dakota. It honors four of our nation's great leaders and celebrates American ideals of leadership, courage and strength. Mount Rushmore National Memorial is a giant mountainside carving of Presidents George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Abraham Lincoln's faces. Washington was chosen to represent the founding of America. Jefferson helped the country grow larger. Roosevelt represents the protection of America's great lands, and Lincoln brought the country together.

The U.S. Congress authorized the Mount Rushmore project to begin in August 1927. American sculptor Gutzon Borglum was the leader of the task. The granite carvings were created by hundreds of workers who used special drills and explosives to blast through the mountain rock. The work was difficult. Workers climbed hundreds of steps each day just to get to the site. Men hung dangerously by ropes to do most of the work.

After 14 years, presenters revealed the final creation. It had taken much longer than expected to finish the job. A great deal of time was spent waiting for the government to fund, or pay for, the work. The nation was in the middle of the Great Depression during most of the construction, and the government had difficulty providing the money workers needed to finish the carvings.

More than 3 million people visit Mount Rushmore each year, and it still represents to many the important values that make America the great nation it is today.

title: Art and the New Deal
text:
The largest of Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal agencies was the WPA, or Works Progress Administration. It was later renamed the Works Projects Administration. The agency was established in 1935 to carry out many different projects. Millions of Americans worked for the WPA and other government programs constructing parks, schools, airports and roads. The WPA also built many public buildings during its existence.

During the Great Depression, over 8 million U.S. citizens worked up to 30 hours a week for the agency. Many of the employees were women and young people. A job with the WPA helped many families survive during this terrible time. The agency also sponsored adult education and reading classes. In this way, many more people received the education they needed to be able to find jobs.

One job the Works Progress Administration created was for authors, who wrote tourist guidebooks. The guidebooks provided information on a state's history, agriculture and cities. The WPA also wanted to provide Americans the opportunity to see various works of art. The WPA hired artists to create paintings, sculptures and murals (wall paintings) for public buildings. Many of the nation's post office walls were painted with scenes from American history. Some of those paintings and murals still remain today in public buildings and museums.

The WPA also hired actors and musicians to perform in community cultural programs. At one time, 16,000 musicians were working for the WPA. They performed concerts and gave free music lessons to many people. Over 12,000 actors performed in WPA theaters across the country. They presented live theater performances to people who would have never had the chance to enjoy a play otherwise.

When the U.S. entered World War II, the economy began to grow again. The WPA was no longer needed. All WPA programs were discontinued in 1943, but they provided a great service to many Americans.

title: Clarity of Expression: FDR and the Four Freedoms
text:
For most people around the world, the years of economic depression and war between 1929 and 1945 were dark and dangerous. Resources such as food, clothing and fuel were in short supply. Families were often torn apart as parents looked for work, served in the armed forces, or as children were sent to safe, sheltered areas. It was a time of stress and hardship, when people desperately looked to leaders for safety and hope. In the United States, that leader was Franklin D. Roosevelt, our 32nd president who served from 1933 to 1945.

During that time of chaos, on Jan. 6, 1941, President Roosevelt delivered to Congress a historic speech, which we now call the Four Freedoms Speech. After years of economic depression, his words were not angry. When world war was happening, his tone was not fierce or mean. But knowing that there were still darker days of war to come for many, he spoke with passion about peace, good fortune, safety, and about the freedoms that humans everywhere deserve. “In the future days,” Roosevelt said, “we look forward to a world founded upon four essential human freedoms.” Even today those four freedoms are essential (important). Can you list them? They are: the freedom of speech and expression, the freedom of worship for every person, the freedom from wants such as hunger and lack of shelter and the freedom from fear.

How are we doing? Have we achieved those freedoms for everyone? Everywhere?

title: Point of View
text:
Read the following quotes by Presidents Herbert Hoover and Franklin D. Roosevelt. They are about the problems of the people before and during the Great Depression. Answer the questions below.

Herbert Hoover

“We in America today are nearer to the final triumph over poverty than ever before in the history of any land. The poorhouse is vanishing from among us.” –1928

“Economic depression cannot be cured by legislative action or executive pronouncement. Economic wounds must be healed by the action of the cells of the economic body—the producers and consumers themselves.” –1930

Franklin D. Roosevelt

“The test of our progress is not whether we add more to the abundance of those who have much; it is whether we provide enough for those who have too little.” –1937

“… true individual freedom cannot exist without economic security and independence. … People who are hungry and out of a job are the stuff of which dictatorships are made.” –1944

1. How did Herbert Hoover feel the United States economy was doing in 1928?

2. Who did Hoover believe was responsible for solving the nation’s economic problems in 1930? How do you know this?

3. What does Roosevelt say that lets readers know he believes a successful nation is one in which all people are taken care of?

4. What is Roosevelt trying to warn the country of in his 1944 quote?

title: A Strike in the Pacific
text:
Sixteen million men and women served in U.S. military forces during World War II. There are special stories about each and every one of these brave soldiers. What follows is one true story of courage, hope and honor from Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on Dec. 7, 1941.

William Fomby was born in Hamlin, Texas, in 1919. After high school, Billy, as his family called him, worked several jobs. Unfortunately, times were still hard in Texas. The Great Depression had consumed the nation for years. Good jobs were difficult to find even though FDR's New Deal programs were helping to improve life for Americans.

On Dec. 18, 1940, Billy decided to join the Navy. He would soon turn 21 and knew the U.S. government could draft him. Billy thought he would fit in better with the Navy than the Army, so he volunteered to sign up.

In early 1941, Navy recruit (new member) Bill Fomby reported for three months of basic training in San Diego, California. Afterward, he was assigned to his first job on board a large battleship named the USS Oklahoma. The ship was stationed in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, in the Pacific Ocean.

While on board, Bill cleaned and took care of the large guns. Bill was a hard worker and was liked by many officers on the ship. In fact, they suggested he work as a cook in the ship's kitchen so he could get a promotion.

While Bill was cleaning up after breakfast the morning of Dec. 7, 1941, he suddenly heard one of his fellow sailors shout from the deck, "Boy, they're having a lot of practice drills this morning! Planes are flying all over the place out here." The men watched for a while, thinking the U.S. was just having practice drills.

Suddenly, they heard cries of panic. "Man the anti-aircraft guns! This is a real air raid! No joke!" The Japanese were attacking! Bill ran to his weapons. Suddenly the ship was bombarded with torpedoes. Bill clung to ship ladders while trying to reach his gun. The violent shaking of the ship tossed the men like rag dolls. Within minutes the USS Oklahoma was sinking.

Bill realized there was nothing more he could do onboard the ship. It was going down quickly. Bill jumped 30 feet into the cold waters of the ocean. For what seemed like hours, he swam through heavy oil and fire. Bombs and torpedoes landed all around. Finally, he was pulled aboard another battleship named the USS Maryland. For hours, U.S. soldiers fought off the attack planes. Bill was exhausted and sick from swallowing oil and salt water, but he continued to fight. For days, the soldiers took care of the wounded and worked to clean and repair the military base.

Back home in Texas, Bill's family heard of the attack. They waited to find out if Billy was safe. On Dec. 12, the family received word that Bill was missing. On Dec. 15, a telegram arrived explaining that Bill was now thought to be dead. With great sadness, the family planned a memorial service for Dec. 22, 1941. That would have been Bill's 22nd birthday. On Christmas Day, the family didn't feel like celebrating. They sat quietly and thought about the dear son they had lost. Suddenly, late on Christmas morning, the family was startled by the telephone ringing. On the other end of the line was their beloved son, Billy, calling to wish them a Merry Christmas. Their courageous son was alive!

Bill Fomby continued to serve in the Navy for six more years. While being stationed all over the world, he worked clean up and rescue operations in Japan after the atomic bombs were dropped on the cities of Nagasaki and Hiroshima in August 1945. After being discharged in 1947, Bill returned to Texas to marry and start a family. William Fomby never thought of himself as a hero, but what a hero he is!

title: A Changing America in the Second World War
text:
By 1941, the United States was beginning to feel as though it just might pull itself out of the Great Depression. President Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal programs gave millions of Americans job opportunities. Jobs building roads, schools, bridges and parks were popping up all across the country. Rural areas began getting electricity and telephones. Air travel was also becoming common. Planes flew across the oceans of the world, and industry was beginning to grow again. However, in the background of America's climb to recovery was the war in Europe.

In 1939, Nazi Germany had invaded Poland. Because Great Britain and France promised to protect Poland, they immediately declared war. The nightmare of World War II had begun. Americans wanted no part in the war. In fact, President Roosevelt announced that the United States would stay out of the war. The people were so happy with this announcement that they re-elected the president to a third term in office in 1940.

'A Date Which Will Live in Infamy'

The United States tried to stay out of Europe's war, but it proved to be too difficult. Under FDR's leadership, the U.S. began sending aid to Great Britain. This angered Germany. Our country's relationship with Japan was also hanging in the balance when the U.S. put an embargo on shipments of oil and rice to Japan. This meant the U.S. would not allow trade of these products between the two countries.

At dawn on Dec. 7, 1941, over 300 Japanese planes surprised the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor. The attack killed 2,400 people in a matter of minutes. President Roosevelt said it was "a date which will live in infamy." By this, he meant the attack would always be remembered as a dishonor to America. Within days the U.S. was officially at war with Germany and Japan.

The Sacrifices of War

The United States knew immediately that Americans would have to pull together to win a victory overseas. Millions of men were drafted into, or forced to join, the army while others volunteered to join (offered to serve). Women were also very important to war efforts. Some women joined special units like the Women's Army Corps. Many women took over jobs left open when men went to war. Women often worked in factories building war supplies and equipment. The government encouraged some women with advertising posters. "If you've followed recipes exactly in making cakes, you can learn to load shells," one poster exclaimed. Twelve million women were already working at the beginning of the war. By the time the war had ended, more than 18 million women had joined the workforce. They drove trucks, built heavy equipment and assembled machine guns. For many women, this was the first time they had worked outside of the home.

The government developed new agencies to see that the production of military goods was a priority. To help meet the needs of the military, the U.S. government began rationing supplies the soldiers needed. This meant that items used for war, like rubber and gasoline, were limited for citizens at home. Meat, butter, coffee, sugar and shoes were among the items that had to be purchased with ration stamps. To help meet food needs, the government encouraged all Americans to plant Victory Gardens. The food people grew in these gardens would feed families at home and leave more food available for soldiers overseas.

The Battles Continue

The war dragged on into 1944. Soldiers fought battles in Europe, the Pacific, Asia and Northern Africa. The Allied powers (Great Britain, France and the Soviet Union) fought alongside the U.S. to keep Adolf Hitler and the Axis powers (Germany, Italy and Japan) from taking control of the world.

On June 6, 1944, war was raging in Europe as Allied leader General Dwight D. Eisenhower began a plan to free France from German control. On this day, forever known as D-Day, the U.S. landed in Normandy, France, with more than 5,000 vehicles and 150,000 troops. Over the next few months, thousands of U.S. soldiers were killed. By January 1945, the Germans had been defeated. It seemed the war might be coming to an end. Leaders began to meet and talk about what the world would look like when the war was over.

A Stunning Death, a New Leader and the End of the War

On April 12, 1945, the world was stunned when President Franklin D. Roosevelt died suddenly of a stroke. He was in his fourth term as president of the United States. The American people felt they had lost a hero.

Vice President Harry S. Truman took over the job as 33rd president of the United States. He had many decisions to make. The war was ending in Europe, but there was still a decision to be made about Japan. Either the United States could drop the first atomic bomb on a large Japanese city or thousands of American soldiers could invade Japan. President Truman chose to drop two bombs on Japan in order to save American lives. On Aug. 6, 1945, U.S. forces dropped an atomic bomb on the city of Hiroshima, Japan. After the Japanese still refused to surrender, the U.S. dropped a second bomb on the city of Nagasaki on Aug. 9, 1945. Over 200,000 people were killed in the two bombings. Less than a week later Japanese troops started to surrender and World War II was over at last.

title: Dedication and Determination
text:
The 442nd Infantry Regiment Goes For Broke

During WWII, one group clearly stood out as a brave group of soldiers. The 442nd Infantry Regiment was a group of Japanese American soldiers that served in the U.S. Army. They were stationed mainly in Europe. People knew the regiment to be an extremely dedicated and determined group of men. Many of them were part of families forced to move to Japanese relocation camps. These camps were virtual prisons for Japanese Americans. For part of World War II, the U.S. government feared that people of Japanese ancestry might side with Japan. As a result Japanese Americans weren't always treated fairly. The soldiers of the 442nd Infantry even had to take a loyalty test before joining the military. Nevertheless, the 442nd Infantry became one of the most highly decorated regiments in the history of the U.S. Armed Forces. They certainly lived up to their motto - "Go for Broke!"

The Tuskegee Airmen Fight for the Right to Fly

At a time when many people questioned the skill, courage and bravery of African American men, a group of very intelligent and skilled men emerged. They were the Tuskegee Airmen, the first African American military pilots in America. These men learned to pilot airplanes and trained in other military fields such as intelligence, meteorology and engine mechanics. However, people did not always treat the Tuskegee Airmen fairly. These men were often segregated and disrespected. They did not give up, though. They overcame prejudice to become some of the most highly respected fliers of World War II. In addition, the Tuskegee Airmen led the way for soldiers of all races to serve together for the good of the nation.

title: World War II and Its Unbreakable Code
text:
During World War II, the United States and Japan tried to keep secrets from one another. This was very difficult because both sides were able to break each other's secret codes. Japan kept winning many of the battles because U.S. secrets were lost. The U.S. wanted to develop an unbreakable code, or system of secret communication. A city engineer from Los Angeles, California, Philip Johnston, came up with the idea of using the American Indian Navajo language as a starting point for the code. He knew a code using the language would be difficult to break. Navajo has no alphabet, and most people cannot learn to speak it unless they are taught as children. A group of Navajo men worked to develop the code. They were called Navajo Code Talkers. Soon the U.S. was able to send secret messages back and forth among troops.

In Navajo code, military terms were often replaced with Navajo words for things they resembled, or looked like. For example, the word for "torpedo" was "lo-be-ca," which means fish shell in Navajo. Or, the Navajo word "ne-he-ma" for "our mother" was code for the word "America." Some Navajo words represented letters of the alphabet. For example, the Navajo word "be-la-sana" for the English word "apple" that started with the letter "A" simply represented the letter "A."

The Japanese were unable to crack the code no matter how hard they tried. However, the U.S. was still able to interpret Japan's secret messages. This meant the United States soon had the upper hand in battles. In the end, the Navajo Code Talkers' work saved many lives and ended World War II much faster.

title: America Changes Pace
text:
After World War II, millions of American soldiers returned home. Men and women were ready to pick up where they left off when the nation entered the war on Dec. 8, 1941. The people of America began working to make their lives even better than ever.

The country had changed dramatically in four years. War efforts brought many technological changes as well as advances in medicine and communication. During the war, special medicines called antibiotics were discovered. Medicines like penicillin help the body fight bacterial infections. Millions of lives were saved because of these antibiotics. Also, new medical procedures that were developed in war could be used at home to save lives too.

Changes in communication brought the people of the country closer together. Television became popular in the years following the war. Television made it possible for news to reach people almost as soon as it happened. Within 10 years after the war, most American homes had a television set, and many homes also had a telephone. Now people could communicate with each other quickly and easily.

Perhaps the greatest change for many of the returning soldiers was that they returned to a nation that had pulled itself out of the Great Depression. When they got home, the soldiers found jobs and other opportunities. Boys had gone to war, but they returned as men. Now they were ready to settle down. Some soldiers returned to the jobs they had before the war. Others decided to attend college. Many chose to start their families. The marriage and birth rates in the country soared. One of the most important things for these new families was finding a home to live in.

Veterans (people who served in the armed forces) were able to borrow money to buy homes. However, there weren't enough homes available for all the new families. One homebuilder thought he had the answer to the problem. William Levitt's company worked to build housing communities in several cities in the United States. These communities were called Levittowns. The first one was on Long Island in New York. The houses in Levittowns were fast and cheap to build. A family could buy a Levittown ranch for less than $8,000. Americans flocked to housing developments in the suburbs. These suburban areas were located outside big cities. They were smaller communities and offered families a different kind of life. Families who lived in Levittowns reported being extremely happy with their new lives.

Families in Levittowns settled down into their daily routines. The men worked while many women returned home to take care of the children. Some of the women decided to continue working outside of their homes. They liked to work and earn money for their families too. Families wanted to spend their money. Money had been scarce (in small supply) during the Great Depression. Now families had money to spend on extras like store-bought clothing, dinners at restaurants and appliances and furniture for their homes.

Extra money meant most families also owned an automobile. War technology had been used to make military vehicles like the Jeep. Now this technology was used to make cars sleeker and faster. Some of them even had air conditioning and radios. The automobile industry began to grow quickly in the country.

People describe the time immediately after World War II as a time when life was better for Americans. This was true for many people. However, it was also a time when it became clear that not all Americans were being treated fairly. African Americans and other minorities (smaller groups of people) were not always given equal opportunities. The country still had a long way to go before everyone was guaranteed the life and freedoms that were available here.

title: Two Wars and a Space Race
text:
The Korean War

Happier times in America were shattered five years after the end of World War II when the United States had to again send Americans to the battlefield. This time the war was in Asia. Since World War II, Korea was divided into two separate countries, North Korea and South Korea. On June 25, 1950, North Korean troops forced their way into South Korea. Their goal was to force the two countries to unite (join together).

Sixteen countries immediately sprang to help South Korea. The United States provided most of the troops. A few months later China entered the war and helped North Korea. At first, some U.S. military officials wanted to bomb China and end the war. President Harry Truman was afraid such an attack might start yet another world war, so he did not allow the bombing. Fighting continued and lasted almost three years. When a truce (an agreement to stop fighting) was declared in 1953, the two Korean countries remained divided after all.

The Cold War

Soon after World War II ended, a different war began. This war was not like the previous wars the United States had fought in. This war was known as a Cold War, and it wasn't really a war at all. The Cold War is the name given to the relationship that developed between the United States and Russia, which was now called the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR).

The two nations had been allies during World War II against Germany and Adolph Hitler. However, the U.S. and the USSR didn't always agree with each other on how to best fight battles. The Soviet Union, or USSR, was unaware of how dangerous the U.S. plan to drop atomic bombs on Japan would be. From then on, both sides didn't trust each other. They never fought against each other on the battlefield, but they often fought with words for their beliefs.

Both super powers began to try and find ways to show the other they were indeed the most superior nation in the world. Both began spending great amounts of money to develop technology such as computers and weapons. Both the U.S. and the Soviet Union continued to involve themselves in world politics. There were several times over the course of the 20th century that the two threatened each other with war. Another war, however, was taking place between the two countries, not on Earth but in space.

The Space Race Begins

After World War II, both the United States and the Soviet Union wanted to show each other how strong they were. They began to produce missiles and rockets that could be used during war times. Soon they began to think about building rockets to take people into outer space to explore the universe. The race to space was on!

At first it wasn't clear how the space race would be won. Neither the Americans nor the Soviets accomplished exactly what they had hoped to by going into space. Americans soon began focusing on a race to send people to the moon. They wanted to beat the Soviets to Earth's distant satellite. For many years Soviet officials claimed they wanted nothing to do with a space race. They kept their experiments top secret and did not share any failed attempts. Soviet officials only told people about successful missions.

On Oct. 4, 1957, Americans were shocked to find they had fallen behind in the space race. The Soviets launched an artificial satellite named Sputnik I. Americans feared that Soviets would use this technology to develop weapons that might one day be used to attack the United States. Americans wanted their government to spend more money and time on space technology. They wanted to catch up and then pass the Soviets in the race. Sure enough, in early 1958 America launched its own space satellite called Explorer I. After that the Soviets knew they weren't the only ones heading into space.

Space Race Results

The race to space resulted in improved technology for both the U.S. and the USSR. These technological advances improved life for all people on Earth. One invention was the jetliner. Engines that forced out a steady stream of air powered these types of planes. These planes, or airliners, could fly comfortably at nearly 600 miles per hour. People were able to travel all over the world quickly and safely. Weather satellites were also sent to orbit the Earth in outer space. These satellites used space race technology to help meteorologists (scientists who study weather) predict weather patterns and storms. Millions of lives have been saved because of the advanced storm forecasting provided by these satellites.

The First American in Space

It was only a 15 minute trip, but Alan B. Shepard Jr. made history on May 5, 1961, when he became the first American in space. The Navy test pilot was placed in a capsule and launched nearly 120 miles into space by a rocket. He remained weightless in space for five minutes before parachuting safely into the Atlantic Ocean some 300 miles away from the launch site in Florida.

The Soviets had launched the first artificial space satellite and only one month earlier had sent their own cosmonaut to orbit the Earth in a space capsule. The race was tightening now. Americans were certain their country could win the race and be the first to send someone to land on the moon.

title: Dwight David Eisenhower: General and President
text:
One of the most respected and admired military war heroes of World War II was a man named Dwight D. Eisenhower. Born in Texas and raised in Kansas, Eisenhower attended the U.S. Military Academy at West Point. He worked hard to show his intelligence and strategic planning as WWII raged across the Atlantic Ocean.

In 1942 Eisenhower was put in command of all U.S. troops in Europe. He was responsible for directing the Allied invasions of North Africa and Italy. Eisenhower became a national hero on D-Day, June 6, 1944, when he led more than 150,000 Allied troops from various countries as they stormed the beaches of Normandy, France. Eisenhower's ability to command the troops was a major factor in the Allied victory over Germany and Adolph Hitler.

After the war, General Eisenhower decided to enter the field of politics. At first, he wasn't quite sure he belonged in the running for president of the United States, but many Americans wouldn't have it any other way. His campaign slogan (saying or motto) was "I like Ike," which was Eisenhower's nickname. People all over the country wore campaign buttons and carried signs to persuade, or convince, others to vote for their hero. In 1952 and again in 1956, Dwight David Eisenhower was elected president of the United States of America.

title: Who is able to vote in local, state and national elections in the United States?
text:
In his State of the Union speech in 1954, President Dwight D. Eisenhower explained his support for allowing suffrage (the right to vote) for all American citizens age 18 and older. However, it took more than 16 years before the right to vote in federal, state and local elections was extended to those age 18 and up.

Some states did not think that 18 year olds should vote in state and local elections. There were many court cases held to decide whether the law was fair. Eventually it was decided that if people age 18 were old enough to be drafted into the military, then they were old enough to vote in all elections. Today any citizen 18 and older may vote in any election if they meet all other voting requirements for the election.

title: The Population Baby Boom
text:
After World War II, many young men eagerly returned home to the United States. The Great Depression was over and there were plenty of good jobs for people to find. The young men were also ready to marry and start families. So from 1946 to 1964 the number of children born in the country increased greatly. We call this time in history the baby boom.

In the U.S., almost 76 million babies were born in an 18-year period. For every 1,000 people in the United States there were almost 24 babies born in 1947. This number had increased from the 19 births per 1,000 people in 1932. The greater number of children born in the country increased the need for housing, schools and healthcare facilities.

The first baby boom children have now become grandparents. The birth rate in 2010 was about 13 children for every 1,000 people. Take a look at the chart to compare numbers.

title: One Giant Leap for Mankind
text:
Over the years, America has been built on technological inventions. Steamboats, railroads and automobiles changed the way people moved from place to place. As the United States rocketed into the 1960s, people were still in awe of the technological changes happening in the world. The U.S. and the Soviet Union were still neck and neck with each other to see who could be the first nation to claim outer space. The two countries sent rockets and explorers into space. The two world powers also continued their Cold War with one another. Together the rivals built up enough weapons to cause more damage than the atomic bombs in Japan. It seemed for a while that their disagreements might lead to yet another world war. During all the political and military drama between the two nations, however, one of the most important goals they still shared was getting the first human to the moon.

In 1961, President John F. Kennedy announced a big goal for the United States. He declared that by the end of the decade the U.S. would safely land an American on the moon. When Kennedy was assassinated, or killed for political reasons, in 1963, Americans wondered if the president's death would mean the death of the country's space program too. Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson took over as leader of the nation. He quickly announced that the space program would continue as planned.

Millions of dollars and hours of work were put into the Gemini program. When the last Gemini flight ended in 1966, the U.S. was able to take all the information they had gained and build even better rockets and larger spacecrafts. Americans planned the Apollo missions next.

For a while it seemed the space program might never be a true success. In January 1967, three U.S. astronauts died when their Apollo 1 space capsule caught fire during a preflight test. The deaths of Virgil Grissom, Edward White and Roger Chaffee stunned the nation. NASA (National Aeronautics and Space Administration) was in charge of the country's space program. NASA stopped all space missions for months in order to redesign space capsules and emergency procedures.

Late in 1968, the U.S. launched the Apollo 8 spacecraft. On board, the astronauts prepared to be the first to leave Earth's orbit. The spaceship was able to get close to the moon and orbit it 10 times. However, it did not land. With the success of Apollo 8, President Kennedy's promise to put a man on the moon seemed within reach now.

On July 16, 1969, a giant rocket was launched from Cape Kennedy in Florida. The rocket was as tall as a 28-story building and right on top was the Apollo 11 spacecraft. Three astronauts, Neil Armstrong, Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin Jr. and Michael Collins, were prepared to do what humans had never done before. They would land on the moon and make America the winner of the space race.

Millions of Americans watched on television as one of the greatest moments in history took place. On July 20, 1969, the Apollo 11 lunar module landed on the moon. Commander Neil Armstrong climbed down the ship's ladder and stepped onto the surface of the moon. "That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind," he said into his radio. The landing and return trip home to Earth went without any problems. Humans had conquered space travel.

The United States was proud to claim they were the first to get a man to the moon. Between 1969 and 1972 the country sent six manned missions to the moon. Twelve men walked on the surface of the moon.

For a moment the nation seemed to stop and celebrate its victory in space. However, turmoil back on Earth soon brought all of the celebrating to an end as the country experienced one of the most troubling of all eras.

title: Civil Rights for All Americans
text:
Lunch Counter Sit-Ins Mark a Milestone

On a cold February day in 1960, four African American college students decided to get a bite to eat. They left their college, North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University, and headed to a restaurant at a local store in the town of Greensboro, North Carolina.

No one paid attention to the young men as they entered the store. It was open to customers of all races. The restaurant in the store, however, was for white customers only. The four students sat down at the lunch counter and asked the server to take their order. The customers in the restaurant were shocked. The server reminded them the lunch counter was segregated and that African Americans were not allowed to eat there. The students were asked to leave.

The Civil War had ended almost 100 years earlier, but in the South people of different races were kept apart. African Americans were not allowed to sit with white people in theaters, restaurants, buses or in any public place. In 1960, however, civil rights leaders decided something had to be done about the unfair ways people of different races were being treated. They came up with a plan to have "sit-ins" at public places. The four college students sat at the lunch counter and refused to move.

When the store closed for the evening, the Greensboro students left peacefully. The following day, the group of four students brought more people to sit in at the lunch counter. The sit-in lasted for many days. Both African Americans and white people participated. Many people supported the sit-in, while others believed the students were trying to cause trouble. Some people called them bad names. In other cities across the South, thousands of people held the same types of demonstrations (public displays of opinion). Eventually, lunch counters in many cities finally became integrated and allowed people of any race to sit at them.

The sit-ins marked the rise of the civil rights movement in the United States. Civil rights are the freedoms and rights guaranteed to people. In our country, the U.S. Constitution and acts of Congress guarantee these rights.

March in Washington, D.C.

Near the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., a crowd of over 200,000 people listened to a message of hope from one of the greatest leaders of the civil rights movement. Millions more watched on television as Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. spoke with passion about civil rights on Aug. 28, 1963.

Dr. King's speech was the highlight of the march in Washington for civil rights, jobs and freedom. The crowd marched through the city streets carrying signs and demanding equal treatment for all people. They wanted new laws passed that would make sure African Americans were treated equally.

The people gathered in Washington and heard Dr. King describe his vision of America. He spoke of a nation in which people would not be judged by the color of their skin. Throughout his speech Dr. King said, "I have a dream!" It seemed that Dr. King's dream just might become reality.

In 1964, Congress passed the Civil Rights Act that ended discrimination in employment and education. People of different races could no longer be treated unjustly (unfairly). The act also made it against the law for hotels and restaurants to segregate based on the color of people's skin. Life in America did not change overnight for African Americans, but the country was on the right track.

The Assassination of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.

Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. worked for many years to bring racial equality to the people of the United States. His speeches and non-violent protests inspired many to work to improve the nation for all people.

Some people in the country did not agree with Dr. King. Some people still thought the country would be better if schools and businesses remained segregated. Some of these people wanted to hurt Dr. King. They didn't want him to speak out against discrimination.

Early in the evening of April 4, 1968, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. stepped out onto the balcony of a motel in Memphis, Tennessee. He was shot by a man hiding nearby. The 39-year-old minister was killed instantly.

Americans everywhere were stunned and saddened to learn of Dr. King's death. He had always spoken against violence and wanted everyone in America to enjoy freedom and equal treatment. People cried and marched in the streets to show their support of Dr. King and his family. Unfortunately, violence also broke out. People were outraged that Dr. King had been murdered. There were large riots in the streets as people showed their anger at the death of their hero.

Even today Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. is remembered as a man whose life symbolized freedom. He is admired and loved by all those who cherish their own freedom. Dr. King's "I Have a Dream" speech still inspires, or encourages, Americans today to continue to fight for equal rights for all citizens.

Civil Rights Today

Since the 1960s, many laws have been passed to help guarantee civil rights to all Americans. Many changes have helped make our nation a better place to live and work. There is still work to be done, though. Some groups including women, Hispanics, Asian Americans, people with disabilities and the homeless continue to try to improve equality for everyone.

title: Rosa Parks - Mother of the Civil Rights Movement
text:
A seamstress in Montgomery, Alabama, named Rosa Parks headed home after a long day of work one December day in 1955. The 42-year-old African American woman climbed aboard a city bus. Mrs. Parks took a seat and settled in for the ride home.

The first four rows of all the buses in Montgomery were reserved for white people. African Americans had to sit in the "colored" section, which was usually in the back of the bus. Mrs. Parks was used to the ways of the bus system. She knew that African Americans could sit in the middle rows until the white section was full. Then they had to move to seats in the back of the bus. If there were no available seats in the back, African Americans had to stand. Sometimes they were even forced to get off the bus to make room for white people.

On that December day, Mrs. Parks refused to obey the bus driver's order to give up her seat to a white passenger. She was arrested, tried and convicted (found guilty of breaking a law).

African Americans were very upset. They boycotted (refused to use) the city bus system. Led by a preacher named Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., people refused to ride the bus for over a year. Through it all, Rosa Parks remained a leader in the civil rights struggle. She continued working for equal rights for all people for over 40 years. Rosa Parks is remembered today as the "mother of the civil rights movement."

title: What was the Vietnam War?
text: In the 1950s the U.S. began sending support to South Vietnam, a country in Asia. By 1965 the U.S. was in the country fighting to help South Vietnam resist the Viet Cong rebels who were being supported by communist North Vietnam. Many Americans were against the war. There were anti-war demonstrations and rallies back in the U.S. For about nine years, American troops fought a war that seemed hopeless. Almost 60,000 Americans died in the war before America pulled out of the country in 1973. North Vietnam finally overtook the capital of South Vietnam in 1975 and the war was over. Today the Vietnam War is considered one of the nation's worst military disasters.

title: 1969: The End of an Era
text:
In 1961, President Kennedy promised Americans that the United States would land a man on the moon by the end of the decade. The promise was fulfilled on July 20, 1969, when Neil Armstrong stepped onto the moon's surface.

As 1969 ended the decade, it was clear that the nation had come through one of the greatest periods of change ever. World War II was long over. Families were settling into suburbs and working toward the American dream.

African Americans had joined together to fight for rights guaranteed to them by the U.S. Constitution. There was still a way to go, but the nation was on the right track.

The country was speeding into the 1970s, and it would be a bumpy ride!

text: Use information from the article called “Civil Rights for All Americans” in this week’s magazine to complete the Conclusion/Support notes below. Develop at least three conclusions about the civil rights movement. Explain the facts or information you read in this week’s magazine that support each of your ideas.

title: America Becomes a Superpower
text:
As the United States moved into the later part of the 20th century, the country was facing many domestic issues. A domestic issue is anything that concerns a country's internal affairs (operations). Tax rates, road construction and political elections are all examples of domestic issues that most nations face.

In the 1970s, Americans were still concerned with the effects of the U.S. involvement in the Vietnam War. Troops had been withdrawn in 1973, but many people were upset that the U.S. was a part of the Asian conflict. Americans were also still working to protect people's civil rights. In addition to these issues, there was a gas and oil shortage in the country.

In 1974, President Richard Nixon resigned (quit his job) as president when some of his close supporters broke into the headquarters of the Democratic National Committee. They were hoping to find information that might help President Nixon be re-elected. The president did not tell the truth about what had happened. Many people wanted the Senate to impeach President Nixon, or charge him with misconduct while he was in office. Nixon stepped down before he was placed on trial and removed from office if found guilty.

Despite the problems at home at the time, the U.S. continued to grow as an international superpower. As a superpower, the country had the ability to influence many world events during this same time. After World War II, the U.S. and the Soviet Union both became known as superpowers. The two countries had great military, economic, political and cultural power throughout the world. Sometimes the two superpowers agreed with one another, but more often the two countries disagreed on how world governments should run. Both countries supported many other nations around the world. They also kept a close watch on one another. They built up their supplies of nuclear weapons as protection. These weapons could release huge amounts of deadly energy and radiation if ever used.

In the late 20th century the Soviet Union fell apart. Today other nations are growing in power and military strength. However, the United States of America continues to work to help solve both domestic and international problems. We work to strengthen our standing as a great superpower in the world and our relationships with countries around the globe.

title: Who Has the Nukes?
text:
The world's two superpowers, the United States and the Soviet Union, spent many years of the 20th century developing powerful weapons. The nuclear devices created were powerful enough to destroy the world. But just how many countries today have access to these mighty arsenals (collections of weapons)?

The United States had hoped to keep the nuclear weapons technology all to itself after the atomic bomb was dropped on Japan to end World War II. However, the Soviet Union soon developed a nuclear weapons program following the end of the war. The United Kingdom, France and China also developed nuclear weapons. The exact number of nuclear weapons on Earth today is unknown, but experts believe it is probably less than 10,000.

The U.S. and other nations realized that nuclear technology would be very dangerous in the wrong hands. Many of these countries signed an agreement in 1968 to discontinue nuclear weapons production. The countries that already had weapons agreed not to use them.

Not all countries in the world signed or stuck to the agreement. India, Israel, Pakistan, Iran, Iraq, Libya, Syria and North Korea have all admitted they are working on nuclear technology or have weapons already. A few countries have also admitted they once pursued nuclear weapons but have given up the program.

Most of the world's nations understand how serious nuclear weapons technology is. They continue to work together to make sure the weapons are never used against each other.

title: Oil Today ... Gone Tomorrow
text:
The 20th century came in with a bang on Jan. 10, 1901. This was when the Lucas No. 1 oilrig blew drilling pipe, mud, gas and oil 100 feet high into the sky at Spindletop near Beaumont, Texas. From that moment on the United States of America was pulled from what was left of a rural agricultural economy and thrown right into a new era of industry.

Seventy years later the country couldn't remember a time when it didn't have all the oil and gas it needed. But that all came to a sudden halt from October 1973 to March 1974 when nearly every gas station in the country often displayed signs that said, "NO GAS TODAY!" Had all the oil and gasoline been drilled?

The gasoline shortage was a result of an oil embargo. An embargo is a ban on the trade of a certain commodity (valuable resource). The United States produced lots of petroleum products, but just not enough to supply the entire country's needs. Millions of barrels of oil were being bought from nations in the Middle East, a region in Asia. These countries controlled more than half of all of the world's petroleum. Petroleum is the material found in layers of the earth's rock that can be used to produce fuels such as oil and gasoline.

The Middle Eastern nations became angry at the United States because of its support of the country of Israel. They immediately stopped all shipments of petroleum to the United States and other western nations. Because of the low supply and high demand for petroleum products, the cost of gasoline and heating oil skyrocketed.

Drivers all across the United States had to wait for hours to purchase small amounts of gasoline for their cars. Sometimes the gasoline ran out. Oil used to heat buildings was also in short supply. During the cold winter months many schools and businesses were forced to cut hours or close altogether. Americans had to find ways to quickly adapt to the serious situation.

The crisis forced Americans to rethink the ways they used fuel. People drove less and shared rides with one another. The highway speed limits were reduced to help save gasoline. At home people burned wood and lowered their thermostats. Some people even began to try and find other energy sources. Solar energy collectors used energy from sunlight to heat homes and businesses.

The U.S. government introduced a plan to help make the country less dependent upon oil from foreign countries. The plan was called Project Independence. The goal was to find ways to improve energy use in the country. The U.S. wanted to get to a point where it no longer needed to purchase oil from another nation. Americans were asked to conserve energy, or to use it carefully to prevent waste or loss. The U.S. wanted to protect oil and gas from being used unwisely. The government also promised to use the nation's science, technology and industry to find ways to save oil and gas. Congress also approved the completion of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, which would carry oil from the Arctic region in Alaska to ice-free ports where it could be shipped to other parts of the country.

For a while it seemed Americans would join together to solve the oil embargo crisis. Unfortunately when the embargo ended, many people forgot about the plan. Today the United States still imports over 11 million barrels of oil each day from foreign countries.

title: Meltdown at Three Mile Island
text:
By the 1970s the American government knew that the nation's petroleum reserves (supplies) would one day be used up. Scientists needed to find new ways to produce energy for the nation. One promising energy source was the nuclear energy power plant. From 1968 to 1970 workers built a nuclear power plant near Harrisburg, Penn. It was named Three Mile Island Nuclear Power Plant. For years the plant operated without any problems, and it seemed the country might have found a clean and safe source of energy.

That all changed, however, on March 28, 1979, when the nuclear plant malfunctioned. Without warning a valve in the plant closed and the water supply to the nuclear reactor's cooling system was cut off. The plant overheated. The radioactive part of the plant began to melt down. Radioactive gases were released into the air. The gases were like those released when the atomic bomb was dropped on Japan during WWII. Scientists were afraid the gases might explode. They worried that thousands of people could be killed or injured.

Thousands of people for many miles around the plant were asked to leave the area. For nearly two weeks scientists watched the plant and waited for an explosion. Luckily such a traumatic event never happened. Some radioactive gases were released into the environment. The amount was very small, though. People were not put into danger. However, the damage to the power plant was severe. Even today the plant remains unusable.

After the accident people all over the United States began to question whether nuclear energy was really worth all of the possible problems. Very few nuclear energy power plants have been built or operated since the Three Mile Island disaster.

title: Super-Computers for the Superpower
text:
Keyboard ... monitor ... mouse ... laptop ... PC ... all of these terms might seem very familiar to you. You probably use a computer of some sort almost every day. You might have a computer you can use in your classroom. Maybe you even have a smart phone with a computer. Can you believe that before the 1970s there was no such thing as a personal computer? The only computers were room size machines that took enormous amounts of energy to operate. That all changed in 1977 when Apple Computer, Inc. first introduced the Apple II personal computer.

The first personal computer was smaller and cheaper than any of the larger computers that had been available before then. The new machines were perfect for businesses and families. The first computers were used mainly as word processors. They were also popular for game playing. Over time the personal computer has continued to change.

Today, nearly every person in America has access to a personal computer at home, school or work. They are smaller and cheaper than ever. Many people even have the same computer technology as part of their cell phones.

Computers today can be used to help people around the world communicate with one another. People can do their shopping and banking on their computers. It is even possible to get a college degree using a computer. Many people also use their computers to work from home. Computers can take us almost any place we need to go!

title: Ronald Reagan: From Hollywood to the White House
text:
Ronald Wilson Reagan grew up in a very poor family in Illinois. After high school he worked his way through Eureka College where he studied economics and sociology. Reagan also played on the school's football team and acted in school plays. After graduation he worked as a radio sports announcer. In the middle of the Great Depression, Reagan decided to take a chance on a new career. He went to Hollywood to try his hand at acting. Over the next 20 years, Ronald Reagan became one of the most respected actors of his time.

Reagan became involved with the actors' union in Hollywood. He even became president of the group. In the 1960s Reagan's ideas about what the government could do for the country changed. He switched from the Democratic to the Republican Party.

Reagan was an excellent speaker. He was also very likeable. The people of California elected him governor of the state two times. Soon people all over the nation began to talk about the confident California governor with the great ideas and patriotic outlook. In 1980 voters chose Ronald Reagan to represent his Republican Party in the race for president of the United States.

The country was facing difficult times. Reagan was elected as the 40th president of the United States with the hope he would improve the country. Reagan spent two terms (eight years) in office. He was the oldest person ever elected to the job.

During his time in office, most Americans felt confident about the country. They felt the country was strong and peaceful. Many people were certain the best person possible was leading the country. Today, many Americans still remember Ronald Reagan as a strong, patriotic leader who kept America on the path to success.
