Bartolomeu Dias and his crew were the first to make it to the southern tip of Africa, which he named the Cape of Good Hope. The year was 1488.

In 1497 and 1498, Vasco da Gama and his crew were the first to sail around Africa and through the Indian Ocean to the country of India. Only two of the four ships survived the voyage. Many of the crew died from thirst, scurvy and hunger.

Pedro Alvares Cabral, having been blown off course on his voyage around Africa, landed instead in South America in 1500. He discovered the area we know as Brazil.

Spain

Ferdinand Magellan, sailing for Spain (though he was born in Portugal), was the first to try to circumnavigate (travel all the way around) the Earth in 1519 to 1522. Sadly, Magellan and much of his crew died in the Philippines with the remainder of the crew completing the journey. Magellan renamed the South Sea "Mar Pacifico," or the Pacific Ocean. The word "pacific" means "peaceful."

Christopher Columbus: Unable to get Portugal to pay for his expedition, he convinced King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain to do so. He left in 1492 and reached the island of Hispaniola. To his dying day, Columbus was convinced he'd reached Asia, not realizing he'd actually discovered new lands for the people of Europe.

Ponce de Leon discovered Florida in 1513 while searching for the fountain of youth. The settlement St. Augustine became the first European settlement in the New World.

Hernando Cortes defeated the Aztec Empire of Mexico for Spain between 1519 and 1521.

Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca Empire in South America for Spain while Francisco Coronado, from 1540 to 1542, explored the southwestern United States. Hernando de Soto also made claims of North America for Spain.

Vasco Nunez de Balboa was the first European to see the South Sea, or the Pacific Ocean. Balboa claimed the ocean for Spain in 1513. American Indians helped him cut down vegetation in the Panama forest to reach the South Sea.

France

Giovanni Verrazano in 1524 and Jacques Cartier in 1534 made claims of much of the area of Canada for France. Both were unsuccessful in finding a route through North America to Asia. However, they mapped the land from North Carolina to Newfoundland and traveled what we now call the St. Lawrence River. A civil war in France in the mid-1500s ended their involvement in the Age of Exploration .

England

The leaders of England such as King Henry VII and Queen Elizabeth I hoped to find a northwest passage, a water route through North America to India. Although they were not successful in this effort, explorers did set up colonies in the new world.

John Cabot made his voyage to North America in 1497, claiming the area of Newfoundland for England.

Holland

Henry Hudson explored the Hudson River in 1609.

title: A Ship that Changed the World
text:
The invention of the automobile helped change the world. It enabled people to get from place to place much faster than by horse and buggy. During the Age of Exploration, a new type of ship revolutionized sea travel. It was called the caravel (also spelled carvel). It replaced the large, oar-driven galley ships that required lots of manpower. The caravel quickly became the sailing vessel of choice for many explorers, beginning in the 15th century.

Two of Christopher Columbus' ships, the Pinta and Nina, were caravels. Explorers such as Bartolomeu Diaz and Vasco da Gama also chose to sail caravels. Why was this ship so popular? First, it had two to three square or triangular masts that could sail into, or against, the wind. This made it a powerful, fast moving ship, about twice the speed of the oar-driven galley ships. It also required fewer men to operate, and with less crew, labor was cheaper and there was more space left for cargo.

The caravel could hold about 130 tons of supplies and a crew of about 20. With a length of only 65 feet, the caravel could sail upriver in more shallow waters without problem. Easy to maneuver, lighter than other ships of the time, the caravel was the ship that helped make the Age of Exploration successful.

title: Ethics: President Coolidge Rebuilds Bridge of Broken Trust
text:
Have you ever wondered how people acquire, or gain, power? In a representative democracy like the United States, a lot of that power comes from trust. We give our vote of confidence to leaders we have faith in. If those leaders betray our trust, then we are free to elect a new representative and the power shifts. But once trust is broken, it can be hard to rebuild.

One of the most famous betrayals of our public trust happened with President Harding's administration. With President Harding's sudden death in 1923, it was up to the new president to repair that bridge of trust. President Calvin Coolidge didn't waste time. He made it clear that no one in government would be above the law. "If there has been any crime," he said, "it must be prosecuted - no one will be shielded for any party, political or other reasons ... Every law will be enforced and every right of the people and government will be protected." And he meant it.

Investigators soon found that Secretary of the Interior, Albert Fall, was guilty of accepting bribes, or gifts, in exchange for the rights to a rich oil field in Wyoming called Teapot Dome. He was the first presidential advisor (helper) to serve time in prison for unlawful behavior. The Teapot Dome Scandal, as it became known, went down in history twice. It was first an example of broken trust, and again an example of how to rebuild it!

title: Let's Write
text: Answer the following questions: What was the most important invention of the Age of Exploration? What was the biggest challenge to the Age of Exploration? Who was the most innovative explorer? Write a paragraph explaining your opinions, and use evidence from the text to support your opinion.

title: Maya and Aztec and Inca, Oh My!
text:
When someone mentions pyramids, you probably think of Egypt. When you think of advances in mathematics and astronomy, you might remember the contributions of ancient India and Mesopotamia. Yet civilizations across the Atlantic Ocean flourished in ancient times, too. Cultures in the Western Hemisphere had writing and number systems, developed accurate solar calendars, studied eclipses, developed a place value for zero and built impressive cities with huge pyramids. Doctors performed brain surgery, cast broken bones, made false teeth from jade and turquoise and filled teeth with iron pyrite. The people of this part of the world were the first to develop chocolate, grow the potato and pop popcorn. In this issue, we will learn about three such civilizations - the Maya, Aztec and Inca.

Like other ancient civilizations we have previously studied, the Maya, Aztec and Inca were polytheistic (believing in many gods). They believed that happy gods rewarded their cultures by preventing floods, droughts and disease. To ensure that the gods looked down on people with good fortune, these civilizations practiced human sacrifices. Archaeologists continue to find Inca mummies in the frozen areas of the Andes Mountains in Peru. Many of the mummies are of children, who archaeologists believe the Inca often sacrificed to the gods. Historians believe Inca families thought it a tremendous honor to offer their child as a gift to the gods. The Inca would hold a feast in honor of the child to be sacrificed, where the child would be dressed in the finest clothing and jewelry. Then, celebrators usually gave the child a drink to make him or her go to sleep before the actual sacrifice.

Archaeologists have also found remains of stone ball courts in Mexican cities such as Copan. Historians believe the ball game was more than a sport - it was also a religious ceremony. Teams of two to three players would attempt to get a very hard rubber ball through a stone ring, and they couldn't use their hands or feet. With the rings 27 feet above the ground, scoring was difficult. The losing team was usually sacrificed to the gods.

Machu Picchu, Tenochtitlan, Copan and Tikal were important cities for these cultures. Montezuma and Pachacuti were important leaders. What do you already know about these civilizations? Let's begin our journey to learn more about the Maya, Aztec and Inca. It's easy - just turn the page.

title: Ancient Temple Discovered in Guatemala
text:
Imagine yourself in ancient Guatemala, 1,600 years ago, walking through the jungle. As you climb a hill, you see it: a huge temple, glowing red in the setting sun. Archaeologists from Brown University recently discovered this temple near El Zotz, Guatemala. The Temple of the Night Sun celebrates the sun god, who was very important in the Maya civilization.

During the first part of the excavation, archaeologists discovered a palace and tomb on Diablo Pyramid. Archaeologists were working on the tomb when they discovered some carvings behind that area. When they looked closely, they realized they were looking at a structure used for worship.

To decorate this temple, the Maya carved five-foot masks in stucco, a plaster-like substance. The masks show the different faces of the sun god as he moves through the day. He is portrayed as a shark and a jaguar. It is thought that the Maya carved gods near the tombs of their royalty to show the high power that their kings had. The structure was painted bright red and could be seen from 15 miles away. The Maya eventually built other structures over the temple, but the sun god faces are well preserved.

Researchers don't know why this temple was abandoned, but it wasn't used for very long. Archaeologists have just begun excavating the temple, so we'll learn a lot more about this amazing discovery.

title: Cultures of the Americas
text:
Maya

The Maya civilization flourished between A.D. 300 and 900. Influenced by an earlier group of people called the Olmec, the Maya culture peaked around A.D. 400 to 500. They became quite skilled in astronomy and created an accurate solar calendar based on 365 days. The Maya were mathematicians who developed a counting system based on the number 20. They also developed a place value for zero, using it long before the Arabs shared this concept with the Europeans. Most Maya were farmers who developed irrigation ditches to help raise crops such as corn (maize). The Maya developed a picture writing system. Sadly, the Spanish burned most of the Maya books, so much of their knowledge has been lost. And, like the ancient Egyptians, the Maya built wonderful pyramids as temples.

Many pyramids were in their largest city, Tikal (in Guatemala). Another important city was Copán (in Honduras), the cultural capital of the Maya Empire. Although many Maya cities were overgrown by jungles, roads connected the Maya cities where people traded items such as maize, feathers and cocoa beans.

The decline of the Maya civilization is a mystery. Was it drought, war or rebellion of the poor? Some Maya culture remains in parts of Mexico, such as the Yucatan Peninsula and much of Central America, where people still speak the Maya language.

Aztec

About 200 years after the Maya, the Aztec people came into the Valley of Mexico. In fact, they called themselves the Mexica, and Mexico got its name from them. They learned many of their ways from another group of people, the Toltec, who had also lived in the area.

Because other tribes had claimed the better farming land, the Aztec were forced to move to swampy areas near the shores of Lake Texcoco. Because they lived near water, they fished, built canoes for transportation and hunted wildlife in the area. Aztec also created floating gardens and built dams. They used irrigation systems and fertilizer to produce enough food to feed the large populations in their cities.

Their capital city of Tenochtitlan became the site of present-day Mexico City. The Aztec built a pyramid 135 feet high in the center of the city. Like the Maya and the Inca, the Aztec practiced human sacrifice, often at the top of the Tenochtitlan pyramid. They believed that sacrificing captured warriors to the main god, Huitzilopochtli (god of war and sun), would bring them good fortune.

The Aztec developed a calendar that revolved around their planting and harvesting seasons. They invented a game called Volador in which athletes dressed in colorful beaks and feathers and "flew" to the ground from the top of a long pole more than 60 feet high. That was like jumping off the fifth floor of a building. It was a very dangerous game but popular to watch. Another Aztec game was called Tlachtli, a cross between basketball and soccer. Popcorn (which the Inca enjoyed, too) was a popular treat among the Aztec, especially while watching games. The Aztec also used popcorn to decorate their headdresses and in their jewelry. Aztec liked wearing jewelry with gold and turquoise stones, and loved decorating with colorful feathers as well.

In the 1500s, Spanish troops brought horses, guns and dogs to fight the Aztec. They also brought a silent killer - disease. Many Aztec people died of the measles, a disease not native to them and against which they had no immunity. Other tribes who didn't like the Aztec sided with the Spanish. Eventually, invaders killed the Aztec emperor, Montezuma II, in 1520. The Aztec empire of about 5 million people ended after the Spanish took control, destroying much of Tenochtitlan and leaving it in ruins.

Inca

The Inca Empire, located in the Andes Mountains throughout the South American countries of Peru, Ecuador and Chile, began around A.D. 1430. At its greatest point in the 1520s, the Inca Empire stretched from present-day Chile to Colombia. The Inca called themselves the Children of the Sun.

Although the Inca had llamas, they didn't ride them but used them for carrying supplies. The Inca also didn't use the wheel and thus traveled along their many roads by foot. To connect their empire, the Inca built a massive road system where all roads led to the capital city, Cuzco. Everyone was required to speak the common language of Quechua. English words such as lima (as in the bean), llama, puma, vicuna, pampa and condor originate from Quechua. The Inca were polytheistic. To insure that the gods looked down on them in favor, the Inca practiced human sacrifice, especially of young children. As you read in the cover story, it was considered an honor to sacrifice your child for the good of the community.

The Inca practiced terraced farming, built aqueducts and invented the panpipe, a musical instrument. They developed a way to freeze dry food and used a calendar divided into 12 months, with 10 days in each week. When emperor Huayna Capac died in 1525, his sons Atahualpa and Huascar started a civil war as they fought for control. Atahualpa gained the victory by executing his brother in 1532, but his rule did not last long. Later that same year, the Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro and 200 men conquered the Inca Empire, which had been weakened by the civil war.

The Inca didn't have a written language but kept records using a series of knots, called quipu. They knotted short, differently colored wool onto longer cotton strings. The quipu hung down in a vertical direction. Different colors stood for different things. For example, four knots on yellow yarn might mean the amount of maize or gold. Quipus also recorded the births or deaths in a city, the number of llama, soldiers, etc. People brought along quipus as they traveled the many roads throughout the Inca Empire. Some people, called quipucamayoc, studied to read quipus so they could communicate with those from other cities.

title: Pachacuti (1438 - 1471)
text:
The founder of the Inca Empire was brave, even as a young man. He proved his bravery when the warriors of his father, King Viracocha, were losing a long battle. To save the royal family, King Viracocha decided to surrender. Viracocha's son, Pachacuti (whose name means Earth Shaker), knew that most of his father's people would be killed and refused to surrender. He asked the gods for help and led the soldiers to victory. After the battle, Pachacuti took power from his father, giving himself the title of Sapa Inca, or Emperor. He began his conquest of neighboring villages, offering membership in his Inca Empire to those who surrendered without resistance. He allowed local leaders to stay in power only if they were loyal to him. If people refused, Pachacuti's soldiers attacked.

Centered in the capital city of Cuzco, Pachacuti's strong central government directed everyone in his empire to practice the same religion and learn the same language, Quechua. He built one of the greatest road systems in the world in his empire. Information (carried by messengers), goods and people traveled on the roads across deserts and mountains to all parts of the empire. The Inca built bridges over rivers and gorges and dug tunnels through mountains. Their common language, religion and roads all helped to unite the people of Pachacuti's empire. Step (terraced) farming, irrigation and fertilizer produced more crops for the Inca. Under Pachacuti's rule, the people built schools and beautiful palaces. He was also responsible for the building of the famous city Machu Picchu, which means "Old Mountain" or "Old Peak" in the Quechua language. Located high up in the Andes Mountains, Machu Picchu's white granite stones have no mortar holding them together, yet the structure has stood for 500 years and even survived earthquakes.

title: Cocoa
text:
Do you like chocolate? Recent evidence suggests that Mesoamericans were consuming chocolate as far back as 1400 B.C. Cocoa beans were a very valuable gift, and people even used the beans as money. The Maya people called the beans xocoatl. The Aztec loved cocoa beans but were unable to grow the beans themselves. So, xocoatl became an important trading item for the Maya.

Eventually, the Aztec used the paste from the roasted cocoa beans and added vanilla, cinnamon and chili pepper to make a cold drink (called xocoatl or chocolatl) that only the wealthy could afford. They also added crushed flower petals and achiote seeds to make the drink red like blood. Aztec Emperor Montezuma (1480 - 1520) really liked his xocoatl. Many people think he guzzled more than 50 cups a day. Hernando Cortes took the beans and the xocoatl recipe back to Spain in 1519. Wealthy people in Spain began to sip the new concoction, but only in secret. Cocoa beans were scarce, and they didn't want to share the drink with others.

The Spanish began serving the beverage hot and without the chili pepper. Later, someone added sugar. It took about 100 years for cocoa beans to reach other countries in Europe. It continued to be something for the very wealthy. By 1657, the drink was served in London "chocolate houses." People said the chocolate had medicinal purposes, especially for stomach distress. It was not until 1847 that someone discovered another great use for chocolate - chocolate bars.

title: What are the Nazca lines?
text: Fly over the southern coast of Peru and you will see amazing artwork usually called the Nazca (or Nasca) lines. There are geometric shapes, spiders, hummingbirds, monkeys, whales, lizards - nearly 300 shapes and figures in all. Ancient artists created these works by removing reddish-colored pebbles to reveal the white earth underneath. The lines, which are ruler straight, make designs that cover about 193 square miles. Historians believed Nazca Indians created the artwork between 200 B.C. and A.D. 600, long before the Inca civilization began. The most amazing thing of all is that you can't see these pictures from the ground! How did they create these works of art centuries before such inventions as hot air balloons or airplanes? Why would ancient people create art that can't be seen from the ground? What do you think?

title: Mesoamerica
text:
Before Christopher Columbus arrived in the New World, the Olmec, Maya, Toltec, Zapotec, Teotihuacan and Aztec civilizations lived in a region called Mesoamerica. The word "meso" is Greek for middle. But just what and where was Mesoamerica? Historians include central Mexico, Belize, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, El Salvador and Guatemala in this region.

The main mountain range of Mesoamerica is the Sierra Madre range, with more than 83 volcanoes. The largest peak is a non-active, or dormant, volcano called Pico de Orizaba. It stands well over 18,000 feet tall. The highest active volcano is Popocatepetl, at just under 18,000 feet tall. Both volcanoes are in Mexico.

Mesoamerica now includes the second largest rainforest in the Americas, after the Amazon. With a great climate and rich volcanic soil, people started farming around 10,000 years ago. Corn, or maize, was the most abundant crop of Mesoamerica. Other early crops included peppers, squash and pumpkins.

title: Maya Math
text:
Pretend you are a Maya student and do some math. The Maya had three symbols for doing their arithmetic: a bar, a dot and a football shape for place value (zero). Based on 20, students wrote equations vertically, not horizontally. For example, to write 20, you’d make a dot over the football shape.

At the top, each dot = 20

In the second part, each dot = 1 and each bar = 5

The following example shows the number 27

Using the number key to help you get started, write the following numbers the Maya way. Be ready for the bigger numbers, though. They’re not on the chart, but you can figure them out if you think carefully. Once you get the hang of it, try writing simple math problems, trade them with a friend and write your answers in Maya numerals. Now you’re doing Maya math!

title: The Renaissance
text:
As we continue to travel through history, we enter a time known as the Renaissance. This word is French for "rebirth." Remember, the Middle Ages was a time in Europe when trade, travel and learning declined. Many ideas and inventions of the ancient Greeks and Romans had long been forgotten. The Renaissance was the time between 14th and 16th centuries when historians say there was a tremendous new interest in learning about the arts, science and more.

Can you remember some historical events that helped bring an end to the Middle Ages and sparked an interest in learning about the world? If you answered the Crusades, you are exactly right! Crusaders and pilgrims returned with stories of the people they met and their customs, clothing, foods and inventions. Also, ancient Greek and Roman ideas, mostly forgotten after barbaric tribes swept through Europe, were rediscovered.

Another event that helped bring about the Renaissance was the journey of Marco Polo to China in 1271. He returned from his travels 24 years later and wrote a book, "The Travels of Marco Polo." His stories about the Chinese people and their way of life encouraged others to venture out and explore new places. Johannes Gutenberg's printing press played a big part in shaping the Renaissance, as well. The printing press allowed books to be printed faster and at a lower cost, making them available to more people - not just the wealthy. More and more people began learning to read.

A movement called humanism began. Based on ancient Greek and Roman philosophy, humanists placed great value in individuals and believed that people should be free to think and discuss their ideas with others. Humanists were interested in astronomy, biology, math, botany and the human body. Like the ancient Greeks and Romans, people in the Renaissance believed that laws should be made - and changed when necessary - by the people. They believed art and literature could be done for enjoyment and not just for religious purposes. Such thinking brought many Renaissance people into conflict with the church. As we have read, the church was very powerful in the Middle Ages and taught that since God made the laws, they could not be changed. According to the church, questioning laws was going against God's will.

Who were some of the individuals that we think of when we think of the Renaissance? How did they make an impact on the world today? Let's turn the page and find out!

title: Rebirth of Learning
text:
The Renaissance began in the country of Italy. Why Italy? Many of the crusaders returned from the Holy Lands to cities such as Venice, Florence, Milan and Genoa. It was Italy whose ancient history had been "rediscovered," and where Marco Polo came from and returned to after his travels in China. Cities in Italy competed with one another to build more beautiful palaces, bridges, statues and more. This competition encouraged and promoted artisans of the time to create masterpieces that have endured throughout history.

Italy also had many wealthy merchants from the trading they established during and after the Crusades. Having more money to spend, many merchants became patrons, or supporters, of the arts. These wealthy patrons commissioned, or hired, people like Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo Buonarroti, Filippo Brunelleschi and others to create new works of art.

Artists

Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475 - 1564): The dome of St. Peter's Basilica in Vatican City, the Pieta sculpture and the Sistine Chapel paintings are just three works of this great Italian Renaissance artist. Michelangelo preferred sculpting to painting. He once said that statues are already inside selected pieces of stone and that it was his task to set the statues free. Michelangelo took four years to paint the biblical scenes on the Sistine Chapel ceiling, which is 44 feet wide and 132 feet long. Another one of his most famous works is the statue of David, which is more than 13 feet tall.

Sofonisba Anguissola (1532 - 1625): She was an Italian noblewoman who gained fame as a portrait painter. Anguissola spent almost two decades as court painter to King Philip II of Spain. She was the first female internationally known artist and was well acquainted with Michelangelo and Anthony van Dyck, both of whom recognized and respected her talent. After losing her sight in her older age, Sofonisba became a strong financial supporter of the arts.

Filippo Brunelleschi (1377 - 1446): He studied the dome of the Pantheon in Rome and won a competition to design a dome for the Cathedral of Florence - the first major dome built during the Renaissance. As Greek and Roman architecture regained popularity, Brunelleschi and other European architects designed and built structures with columns, arches and domes.

You'll read about the man many consider the greatest artist of the Renaissance (Leonardo da Vinci) in this week's "World Biography" article. Many other artists displayed their talent during the Renaissance, and you might like to learn more about some of them as well. Here's a list to get you started: Raphael Sanzio, Rembrandt van Rijn, Jan van Eyck and Albrecht Durer.

Writers

Francesco Petrarca "Petrarch" (1304 - 1374): Many call him the father of Humanism. Petrarch is credited with sparking an interest in people to learn new things. An Italian poet and scholar, Petrarch sought out books from people who traveled. He eventually built a library where people could come and study all the books he collected.

William Shakespeare (1564 - 1616): This famous English playwright wrote "Romeo and Juliet," "Hamlet," "Macbeth," "A Midsummer Night's Dream," "Much Ado About Nothing" and many more. Shakespeare was known as the Bard of Avon, since he was born and lived in Stratford-upon-Avon in England. Actors performed many of his plays in London's Globe Theater. Perhaps you have heard the following quotes of Shakespeare: "To be or not to be" or "Parting is such sweet sorrow."

Geoffrey Chaucer (c.1343 - 1400): He was a famous English writer and poet whose most famous work is "The Canterbury Tales," a story of 29 pilgrims on their way to the city of Canterbury to worship at the shrine of St. Thomas a Becket.

Miguel de Cervantes (1547 - 1616): Cervantes was a Spanish writer whose most famous work is "Don Quixote," a tale about a near-sighted Spanish nobleman who goes out to fight the injustices of his time. He died on exactly the same day as Shakespeare, April 23, 1616.

Dante Alighieri (1265 - 1321): This Italian poet from the city of Florence is most famous for the "Divine Comedy" (more than 14,000 lines of poetry). Before the Renaissance, authors wrote mostly about religion and mostly in Latin. Writers like Dante took on new topics including comedy, drama and adventure. Dante was also one of the first to write his work in the vernacular, or the everyday language of his people, instead of Latin.

Scientists

Nicolaus Copernicus (1473 - 1543): He was a famous Polish astronomer who published a new, shocking theory that the Earth moves around the sun. People at the time believed the sun moved around the Earth and did not want to believe Copernicus.

Isaac Newton (1642 - 1727): This English mathematician and physicist made many scientific discoveries. Newton's most famous discovery was probably the law of universal gravitation. Newton determined that gravity is the force that draws objects toward each other. Gravity explains why planets orbit the sun and why things fall to the earth. Historians say Newton developed the idea after sitting under an apple tree reading a book, when an apple fell to the ground near him.

Galileo Galilei (1564 - 1642): He was a famous Italian astronomer and mathematician who built one of the first telescopes, saw the phases of the moon (proving that the universe changes) and stated that the Milky Way is made up of individual stars. He also confirmed Copernicus' theory of the solar system, proved that objects fall at the same speed regardless of weight and much more.

title: Ah, Venice!
text:
When Attila the Hun invaded Italy during the fifth century, fleeing Italians ran to a nearby, watery lagoon to avoid the attacking Huns. That lagoon eventually became the city of Venice. By the ninth century, Venice was an independent state, and it became a trading center for all of Europe around the 1200s. By the time the Renaissance began, Venice had a large navy with hundreds of merchant ships and was a very wealthy and powerful city-state. When the people of Venice heard about Johannes Gutenberg's printing press in 1454, they couldn't wait to get this new technology. By 1482, Venice was the printing capital of the world.

Because it lies on the northern coast of the Adriatic Sea, Venice is often called the "Queen of the Adriatic." People know it as one of the most beautiful cities in the world, in part because it is an island city amid water. Venice consists of 118 islands with buildings constructed on wooden pilings. Except for narrow walkways throughout the city, people use boats to travel Venice's 160 canals. The narrow boats of Venice are called gondolas and are very popular, especially among tourists. Rowers compete in more than 100 races each year, and you can buy gondola-shaped pasta in shops. More than 400 arched bridges link the city's walkways and enable boats to glide underneath. Barely above sea level, Venice has had serious problems at times with flooding from high tides. Many of the buildings' foundations have eroded and sank into the Adriatic Sea, especially after people began digging wells in the 20th century. Today, many lower levels of the old homes in Venice have flooded, forcing owners to live on the upper floors.

title: Renaissance Man: Leonardo da Vinci
text:
Scientist, inventor, painter, sculptor - Leonardo da Vinci did it all. Born in 1452 in the village of Vinci (where he got his last name), da Vinci became one of the greatest painters of the Italian Renaissance. Two of his most famous paintings are the "Last Supper" and the "Mona Lisa."

Da Vinci was an impatient young man and a perfectionist, always thinking he could improve his works of art. Interested in the world around him, da Vinci kept a notebook tucked in his belt so that when he observed something or had an idea he could write it down. To make sure others didn't copy his ideas, da Vinci wrote backwards! (Try writing a sentence backwards. It's not easy.) To read his writings, one needs to hold the pages in front of a mirror.

Some of the ideas in his 5,000-page notebook include: a flying machine, an alarm clock, a helicopter, a parachute and a diving suit. Da Vinci also sketched what looks like an early automobile! Two huge springs helped power da Vinci's vehicle, and one could steer it with a tiller attached to wheels. To learn about the human body, da Vinci dissected human cadavers to study the workings of the muscles and other body organs. He did this during a time when authorities put to death anyone caught studying the insides of a body. Da Vinci, who died in 1519, once said, "Learning never exhausts the mind."

title: Did You Know?
text:
During the Renaissance, everyone over the age of 12 had to wear a hat in public.

People of the Renaissance liked playing a game similar to football. They used a "ball" made from a pig's bladder stuffed with peas! (Later the bladder was inflated.)

People knew forks, mostly two-tined, as "split spoons." Although there are examples of four- and five-tined forks from before the 1600s, the four-tined fork didn't become popular until the late 1800s.

The Lord of Florence, Piero de' Medici, commissioned 19-year-old Michelangelo to construct a snowman after a rare snowstorm in 1494.

People in the Renaissance bought "pilgrim-mirrors," small mirrors attached to a pin that they stuck in their hats. People believed that if you looked at religious objects, the mirrors captured the objects' powers and would benefit friends and family back home.

title: Gutenberg's Printing Press
text:
Communication increased rapidly after the invention of the printing press by a German man named Johannes Gutenberg. He based his invention on the ancient Chinese idea of block printing, and historians believe Gutenberg was the first European to develop this idea. Instead of printing from a carved wooden block of text, Gutenberg used individual letters that could be reused and moved around to form new words. Printers called this moveable type. Also, instead of carving letters on wood, which could warp, Gutenberg made metal blocks. Gutenberg's printing press enabled printers to produce books faster and cheaper. Until 1454, people had duplicated books by hand.

Historians estimate that before the printing press there were only about 30,000 books, which were very expensive. Just 50 years after Gutenberg invented the printing press, there were more than 9 million books. The first book printed on Gutenberg's printing press was the Bible. Historians believe printers manufactured about 200 copies and that parts of 48 copies of the Gutenberg Bible still exist today.

title: What was bloodletting?
text:
In the Middle Ages, people believed the body had four main fluids. Blood was one of these.

People thought illness resulted from these fluids being polluted or out of balance. Doctors believed that bleeding a person would remove impurities and help balance their fluids. Doctors would open a vein in a person's arm and let the blood fill a shallow bowl in an effort to cure many diseases. The practice was believed to be a reliable cure for many hundreds of years. It is still practiced in some cultures today. Modern doctors think U.S. President George Washington might have died prematurely from too much blood being taken during a bloodletting. However, doctors also suspect that bloodletting may actually have helped in some cases. Once blood is lost, the body kicks into overdrive and works to produce more blood, a process that can have positive effects.

title: Agility of Mind: Teddy Roosevelt Wins Nobel Peace Prize
text:
agile (adjective): able to move quickly and easily; ex.: as agile as a monkey, an agile mind.

Teddy Roosevelt was president of the United States from 1901 to 1909. He was also a great hunter, explorer, author, outdoorsman and soldier.

As a child Teddy was often sick and could not play sports. But he became a good problem solver. He wasn't afraid to put his thoughts into action or think of different solutions. If his first idea didn't work, he had the mental agility to change his mind quickly.

When Roosevelt was president, Japan and Russia were at war. He invited diplomats (official representatives) from Russia and Japan to Portsmouth, New Hampshire to talk about peace. At first, he didn't know how their problems could be solved but he acted quickly to get the diplomats together. He helped them compromise. After a lot of discussion, they worked out their differences and signed the Portsmouth Peace Treaty, an agreement that ended the war and saved many lives. President Roosevelt won the Nobel Peace Prize for helping end the war. His way of helping others solve problems is still used today.

Teddy Roosevelt had an important power skill - an agile mind. You can use this power skill when you act on your good ideas. Remember that an idea can be good without being perfect. People with agile minds often fail before they succeed. The ability to think on your feet, or think while doing, can help you find solutions that will benefit others.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you are the Mona Lisa portrait hanging in the Louvre in Paris, France. What do you notice as thousands of people crowd around to see you up-close? What do you hear? Do you smell anything funny? Are people taking lots of videos and pictures of you? Write about a day in your life as a famous painting, protected from air, flash photography and theft behind protective glass. Remember to write in the first person and check your writing for proper spelling, grammar and punctuation.

title: Movers and Shakers Change Religion
text:
Do you remember learning that during the Middle Ages the Catholic Church was extremely powerful? It collected taxes and selected and removed kings. It was the only Christian church in Western Europe for a long time. Things changed during a period we call the Reformation when people tried to reform, or make changes, in the Catholic Church. The Reformation happened during the humanist movement of the Renaissance. Basing their beliefs on ancient Greek and Roman philosophy, humanists placed great value in individuals rather than institutions.

People saw that some religious leaders were tremendously wealthy. Some clergy lived like kings in lavish palaces surrounded by beautiful art. The clergy gave their friends the best jobs while the church demanded higher taxes from its people. The church even offered indulgences in order to raise more money. An indulgence was money paid to the church to receive forgiveness for sins. Obviously, if you had money you were able to afford indulgences and forgiveness. Less fortunate people could not afford to pay for forgiveness. Some people began to question the power of the church and sought change.

In the 1370s, an English priest named John Wycliffe began to preach that the Bible was the source of all truth. Father Wycliffe said people should learn to read the Bible and not rely on the church to read it to them. He was called a heretic, a person who denies the church's teachings. As punishment, he was forced to retire from the priesthood. Father Wycliffe began translating the Bible from Latin to English, so the people of England could understand it. The church soon banned his translation, but his work helped spark the coming Reformation.

In the 1550s, the Catholic Church began a Counter-Reformation, in which it tried to regain its position of power in Europe. The church ended indulgences. A church court called an inquisition set out to find and condemn heretics. The inquisition charged those who questioned the church's teaching with being heretics and had them put to death. Many books were burned. During the Counter- Reformation, missionaries spread Catholic beliefs to other countries such as Vietnam, Japan and the Philippines. Missionaries also made efforts to strengthen the Catholic faith in France and Spain.

Eventually, after many bloody wars, European countries such as Germany, Netherlands and Scandinavia became predominately Protestant while countries such as Italy, Spain and France remained Catholic. This took power away from the Catholic church because it was no longer the only church in Europe. The Reformation made monarchs (kings and queens) more powerful. Teachers encouraged more people to learn to read so they could read the Bible themselves.

Turn the page to read about more of the movers and shakers who changed the world.

title: Galileo on Trial for Heresy!
text:
Dateline 1632: Extra! Extra! Read all about it! Catholic church arrests respected Italian scientist, brings Galileo Galilei to Rome for trial!

After building a better telescope, Galileo found evidence to support Nicolaus Copernicus' theory that the Earth isn't the center of the universe. Galileo had observed four objects moving around Jupiter. He suggested that if these moons revolved around Jupiter and not the Earth, then the Earth couldn't be the center of the universe. The church wanted Galileo to withdraw his scientific statements because they went against its teachings. The church had long stated that the Earth was the center of the universe, and everything revolved around it.

Galileo also got into trouble for his ideas about the Bible. Galileo said that although he understood the Bible's actual words, he wondered if people had made a mistake in interpreting its words. The church decreed that it would not tolerate such thinking. Only the clergy could interpret the Bible.

During his trial in 1632, Galileo was 68 years old and in poor health. He worried what his fate would be if he continued to argue with the church. Galileo remembered that in 1600, church authorities burned Giordano Bruno at the stake for declaring the Earth was not the center of the universe. Galileo conceded to the church's request and announced that he was wrong in his beliefs. The church spared his life and instead gave Galileo permanent house arrest as punishment. He stayed under house arrest until his death in 1642.

In 1992, the Catholic Church reversed the charges against Galileo.

title: Reformation and Church Reformers
text:
(1) Joan of Arc (1412-1431): The church burned at the stake many people accused of heresy, but a young woman named Joan is probably one of the most famous. Joan of Arc was born in Domrémy, France. While a young teen, Joan said she had visions of saints. She explained that these saints told her to help save France and its king, Charles VII, from the British. The French had been fighting the English for nearly 100 years, and France was losing. French soldiers supported Joan of Arc while she led thousands of troops into battle. She directed attacks and encouraged the soldiers to win. Her efforts led to a French victory over the English in Orleans.

Joan of Arc did not carry a weapon into battle—only a flag displaying religious pictures—as she led her troops on horseback. The English eventually captured Joan and put her on trial. They accused her of heresy. They brought many charges against Joan, but one of the most serious was that Joan claimed direct inspiration from God. The Catholic Church decreed that this was not possible. Joan of Arc also wore men’s clothes, which many thought was a crime against God. Authorities also accused her of practicing witchcraft. They found Joan guilty of heresy and burned her at the stake in 1431. In 1920, the Catholic Church made Joan a saint.

(2) Martin Luther (1483–1546): This German played a huge role in the Reformation. Martin was a young man studying law when he was caught in a vicious storm and nearly struck by lightning. He prayed and vowed to serve God if he survived, so he became a monk instead of a lawyer. Luther was a religious scholar. He thought the Bible should be in the everyday language of the people so that anyone who wanted to could read it. Luther thought the Bible contained the whole truth about God. The people did not need the clergy to tell them what the truth is.

Luther especially disliked the practice of indulgences. Luther wrote a list of 95 arguments (called Ninety-Five Theses) against the practice of indulgences, among other things. Historians say he posted them on a church door in Wittenberg, Germany. Because of Johannes Gutenberg’s invention of the printing press, printers copied Luther’s document fairly quickly and distributed it to many different people.

The church became worried after Luther’s actions. What if people thought they didn’t need priests and relied solely on the Bible? They might stop going to church, and the church would lose power and influence! The church responded by excommunicating Luther. Excommunication meant that Luther was kicked out of the church and could no longer be a monk—a very serious punishment. Fearing for his life, Luther went into hiding.

During his time in hiding, Martin Luther translated the Bible into German. Many people were able to read the Bible for the very first time. Many also agreed with Luther’s dislike of indulgences and his translation of the Bible into everyday languages of the people. Followers of Martin Luther who protested the practices of the church classified themselves as Protestants, or more specifically, Lutherans. Luther led the first branch of the Protestant Christian Church.

(3) John Calvin (1509-1564): Like Martin Luther, Calvin was another figure during the Reformation. A French religious scholar, Calvin left for Switzerland when Catholics began attacking Protestants for their different church views. John Calvin believed salvation came from faith and that the Bible was the source of religious truth. Calvin’s followers believed in the concept of predestination, which means that God determines eternal destiny. In other words, God already knows who will go to heaven, and nothing anyone does can change what God has already decided. Calvinism approved of dressing simply and disapproved of laughing in church, dancing, swearing and fighting. You might have heard of an English Protestant group that followed many of John Calvin’s ideas. They called themselves Puritans. As their term suggests, they wanted to purify, or cleanse the church of anything Catholic. Eventually, they left for Holland and then America in the early 1600s in search of religious freedom.

(4) King Henry VIII (1491-1547): This British monarch was a very strong supporter of the Catholic Church. Things changed when the king wanted to annul, or end, his marriage to Catherine of Aragon because she was unable to have a son to be the heir to the throne of England. When the pope refused to grant the king an annulment, King Henry VIII and England broke from the Catholic Church and founded the Church of England, or the Anglican Church. The king also took the land the Catholic Church owned and gave it to those loyal nobles who supported him and the Church of England. For religious leaders, remaining loyal to the pope and the Catholic Church was not an option. Those who did were put to death.

(5) Queen Mary I (1516-1558): As British monarch, Queen Mary tried to return the Catholic faith to power in England. Her regime persecuted and arrested Protestants, burning hundreds of people at the stake for their beliefs. It got so bad that many nicknamed her “Bloody Mary.”

(6) Queen Elizabeth I (1533-1603): Known as Good Queen Bess, Elizabeth was the daughter of Henry VIII and half sister of Mary I. After Mary I died, Elizabeth came to power. Queen Elizabeth was a Protestant and a member of the Anglican Church. She made the Protestant faith the main religion of England.

title: Germany
text:
While Italy was the origin of the Renaissance, Germany was the origin of the Reformation. It was in Germany in 1517 that Martin Luther first published his “Ninety-Five Theses,” the first call for changes in the Catholic Church.

About the size of Montana, Germany shares borders with Switzerland, France, Poland, Denmark, Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Czech Republic and Austria. It also borders both the North and Baltic seas, and the Bavarian Alps separate it from its neighbor, Austria. The Black Forest in southwest Germany is its largest wooded area with numerous pine and fir trees. Some famous German inventions include blue jeans (Levi Strauss), the Geiger counter (Hans Wilhelm Geiger) and X-rays (Wilhelm Konrad Roentgen). Many famous composers including Handel, Brahms, Bach and Beethoven were from Germany. So were the Grimm Brothers who were famous for their fairytales. Albert Einstein, one of the best-known scientists in history, was from Germany. Have you been to Disneyland and seen Sleeping Beauty’s castle? Its design is based on a famous castle in Germany— the Neuschwanstein Castle.

After World War II, the country was divided into East and West Germany. Berlin was also split, and Germans built a wall to separate East Berlin from West Berlin. However, Germans tore down the wall in 1989, and Germany’s capital city since the reunification of East and West Germany has been Berlin. It is also the country’s largest city.

Many English words came from the German language including kindergarten, noodle, poltergeist, sauerkraut, pretzel, schnitzel, gesundheit and delicatessen. While visiting Germany, you may see people wearing traditional clothing, a dirndl (women’s dress) and lederhosen (men’s leather shorts). For a souvenir, you can bring home a cuckoo clock, Hummel figurine or Steiff teddy bear!

title: William Tyndale
text:
Do you have a Bible in your home? There was a time in England when Bibles were not allowed, when owning a Bible meant death. Did you know that during this time, the Bible used in Europe was only printed in Latin? If you couldn't read Latin, you couldn't read the Bible, and some people thought this was wrong. You read about one such person - Father Wycliffe - in the cover story. William Tyndale agreed with Wycliffe's ideas, although he was born more than a century after Father Wycliffe died. Tyndale spent much of his life translating the Bible into English.

William Tyndale believed every person should be able to read the Bible in the vernacular, the everyday language of the people. He learned to read eight languages, including Greek and Hebrew. Eventually he left his home in England and traveled to Worms, Germany. It was here that Tyndale published The Worms New Testament Bible. At least 3,000 copies were printed after it was finished in 1526, and three are known to have survived to the present day.

Tyndale asked merchants going to England to sell his English Bibles there. Merchants smuggled the Bibles, wrapped in cloth, into England inside barrels of flour or rolls of wool. As government officials heard of the Bibles being sold, they confiscated and burned the books. However, Tyndale continued his work. He offered to return to England and face trial for his crime if King Henry VIII would permit people to read the English Bibles. The king refused. Bounty hunters tracked Tyndale down and delivered him to England to face trial. Finding him guilty, English officials burned him at the stake in 1536. Tyndale's last words were, "O God! Open the king of England's eyes!" Less than a year later, King Henry VIII reversed his ban, and the people of England were allowed to purchase and read Tyndale's English Bibles.

title: Where was tolerance during the Reformation?
text: During the Reformation, religious groups seemed to have forgotten two of God's teachings - "Love thy neighbor as thyself" and "Thou shall not kill." Protestants persecuted and killed Catholics, and Catholics did the same to Protestants. Religious fighters waged bloody wars for control of countries, and thousands of people died. In addition to Protestants and Catholics fighting each other, many people attacked Jews. They banished Jews who wouldn't convert to Christianity. Many Christians also burned Jewish holy books and Jewish places of worship, called synagogues. By 1516, religious crusaders had forced Jews to live in separate, walled areas called ghettos, in cities such as Venice and Rome. What does tolerance mean to you? Have you shown tolerance of someone who didn't share your views?

title: Actions and Reactions
text:
Every action has a reaction. For example, when Venice monopolized the spice trade, explorers searched for sea trade routes. Find a reaction to every action below. Write your answers on a separate piece of paper.

1. King Henry VIII did not allow the people of England to own Bibles. What was William Tyndale’s reaction?

2. Walt Disney viewed pictures of Germany’s Neuschwanstein Castle. What was Disney’s reaction?

3. The Catholic Church didn’t allow King Henry VIII to annul, or end, his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. What was the king’s reaction?

4. Puritans feared persecution of Queen Elizabeth I of England. How did they react?

5. Martin Luther didn’t like the Catholic Church’s policy of indulgences, the idea that you could atone (be forgiven) for sins by paying money. What was Luther’s reaction?

6. Bibles were published in the vernacular of the people. What was the result of this action?

title: Geography of Europe
text:
Use the map of Europe to help you answer the following questions:

1. Which river travels near the German city of Cologne?

2. King Henry VIII was a ruler of England. Which body of water separates England from France?

3. Which landlocked country touches France, Germany and Belgium?

4. Martin Luther was born in Germany. Germany and Netherlands border which body of water?

5. John Calvin was born in France. What is its capital city?

6. Calvin moved to Switzerland and lived in this town near the border of France.

7. King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella ruled Spain. Which mountain range borders Spain and France?

8. Which two countries in Europe border both the Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea?

9. Florence and Venice were important cities during the Renaissance. In which country are they located? What is the mountain range that travels down the spine of this country?

10. Which country in northern Europe is a peninsula? (Hint: Its capital is Copenhagen.) Define the term peninsula.

title: So Many Islands!
text:
Imagine the surprise of European explorers when they landed on island beaches in the Pacific, only to find the islands were already inhabited! From the Greek words "poly," meaning "many," and "nesos," meaning "islands," we get the word "Polynesia." Polynesia is made up of literally thousands of Pacific islands that are home to people of many different cultures. Can you think of some of the islands that make up Polynesia? If you said Tahiti, Fiji or the Hawaiian Islands, you'd be correct!

Most scientists sort the thousands of Pacific islands into three groups: Melanesia (south of the equator), Micronesia (north of the equator) and Polynesia (islands to the east). Polynesia also includes Australia, New Zealand and the Malay Archipelago. Geographers group these three island areas into one large region called Oceania. Many of the islands are actually the peaks of undersea volcanoes. Others are the remains of coral reefs. Many of the islands still have active volcanoes. With vast, open areas of ocean, the waves can get pretty big and cause lots of destruction when they hit island shores. Large storms, called tropical cyclones or hurricanes, sometimes cause much damage to this area of the world.

Historians believe those who settled the many islands in the Pacific originally came from Southeast Asia around 2,000 years ago. About two dozen people, their supplies, plants and livestock were all crammed aboard 60-foot, double canoes for their journey. The people called their canoes catamarans. These early seafarers didn't use compasses to guide their way. They relied on things in nature such as the stars, wind and flight patterns of birds to direct them through the Pacific Ocean. These brave travelers sailed great distances, "island hopping" as they went. Migrating first to the islands of Tonga and Samoa, these people eventually moved on to Hawaii. Later some migrated to Easter Island and then to the Society Islands and Tahiti. Ready to dive into the history of Oceania? Turn the page and jump in!

title: Research Shows Madagascar Was Founded by Women
text:
Picture an ancient ship full of explorers, searching for a new land. Many people would imagine that such a ship was filled with male passengers and crew. Though many explorers were men, scientists have discovered that the founders of Madagascar were a group of 30 women who traveled a long way from their home!

Madagascar is an island off the east coast of Africa in the Indian Ocean. The women's ship traveled 5,000 miles from Indonesia to Madagascar, stranding them there. How do scientists know this? DNA researchers have studied 3,000 blood samples of people from Indonesian islands and compared them to samples from 300 people from Madagascar (called the Malagasy).

They discovered that many Malagasy have an Indonesian gene in their DNA. This gene was passed down from generation to generation of Malagasy. Computer simulations have calculated that only 30 Indonesian women were responsible for beginning the Madagascar population about 1,200 years ago. Most people from Madagascar today have a mix of Indonesian and African DNA, and are descended from these 30 women.

Researchers have also been able to trace a special chromosome that is only found in men in the Malagasy people. Can you guess where it came from? If you guessed Indonesia, you are right! It looks like a few men as well as women sailed on that ship to Madagascar so long ago.

title: Oceania
text:
Palm trees, beautiful sandy beaches, waterfalls and tropical paradise. All these phrases might make you think of Polynesia. But living in paradise was also hard work in ancient times. Traditional Polynesians relied on fishing and growing fruits and vegetables to survive. Foods such as taro root, breadfruit, coconuts, yams and bananas were part of their diets. Let's discover more about the people of this region.

Aborigines

Oceania includes the country of Australia. The Aborigines of Australia have lived on the land for thousands of years. Historians date the Aborigines back 40,000 to 60,000 years and believe they migrated to Australia from Southeast Asia.

Australian Aborigines are hunters and gatherers. They believe some of their ancestors changed into rocks, rivers, the sky and other things in nature after dying. The spirits of these ancestors remain alive in these natural objects and are the reason Aborigines have a strong bond with nature. The world's largest rock, Ayers Rock (or Uluru), is especially important to the Aborigines. They believe the spirits who helped create the world live in this gigantic rock. The Aborigines call their creation story of the world Dreamtime.

The didgeridoo is a famous instrument of the Aborigines. They make these instruments from long pieces of bamboo, and its low, vibrating sounds are heard in many traditional ceremonies. The Aborigines don't have a written language but do have a strong oral tradition of telling stories through music.

When Europeans began settling Australia in 1788, they brought diseases such as chickenpox, measles, smallpox and influenza. With no immunity (ability to fight illnesses), much of the aboriginal population died. Others died in battles, fighting to keep their land from the Europeans.

Maori

Also part of Oceania is the country of New Zealand. It is home to an indigenous, or native, people called the Maori. Historians believe the Maori first came to the Polynesian area in canoes between A.D. 800 and 1300. Using currents and the stars and sun, they island hopped from Asia, until arriving in what they called Aotearoa, meaning, "Land of the Long White Cloud." Historians say these first people to the region saw a long white cloud covering the coast, which is why they named their new home Aotearoa.

The Maori language is similar to the Tahitian, Samoan and Hawaiian languages. Maori are famous for their full-facial tattoos, which they call ta moko. Although Maori males usually display ta moko, Maori females sometimes have them too, usually on their chin, nostrils and upper lip. In the Maori culture, one greets another with the hongi, or by pressing noses. With no written history, the Maori have passed down their rich culture through chants and songs.

A Dutch explorer, Abel Tasman, was the first European to come upon the New Zealand area in 1642. Captain James Cook from England came in 1769. As with American Indians, when Europeans started coming to New Zealand, they brought diseases for which the Maori didn't have immunity. Sadly, a large segment of the Maori population died.

Although most Maori have adopted Christianity, they once believed in many gods who represented the forces of nature - earth, sky and land. Maori believe their ancestors can be asked for help in time of need. Although most Maori have moved to cities, some do their best to continue the rich culture of the people who first settled New Zealand alongside the modern customs they have adopted.

Papua New Guinea

With high mountains and rough terrain in New Guinea, indigenous people of the area didn't have much contact with one another. Therefore, Papuans of New Guinea developed many different cultures. The first European to discover this area during the 16th century was Jorge De Meneses. He called the area "IIhas dos Papuas," or land of the fuzzy-haired people. In the 1800s, missionaries came in hopes of converting the Papuans of New Guinea to Christianity. Gold seekers came in the early 1900s.

Traveling further from the coastal areas, explorers came upon New Guinea tribes who lived an existence that hadn't changed in thousands of years. Many practiced headhunting and cannibalism (the practice of eating other humans). Tribes ate enemies from nearby villages. One of the most famous cannibalistic tribes on Papua was the Asmat. These people collected skulls and used them as pillows. Another tribe was the Purari Delta Tribe. The approximately 8,000 people of this tribe lived as hunters-gatherers and also practiced cannibalism. Tribal people used cannibalism as part of religious ceremonies, during which they believed they gained powers of the dead victim after eating the victim. As we have read previously, with culture contact most of these indigenous people changed their ways, adopting the customs of those who came to the island.

Did You Know?

"The Guinness Book of World Records" says the New Zealand Hill (North Island) called Taumatawhakatangihangakoauauotamateapokaiwhenuakitanatahu has the longest name of any place in the world.

New Zealanders invented bungee jumping.

Aborigines invented the boomerang. This wooden weapon returns to its thrower and was designed for hunting.

There are more islands in the Pacific than in all other oceans combined. (There are about 25,000 islands total.)

The Polynesian people created the sport of surfing.

title: Captain James Cook
text:
Perhaps the greatest explorer of the Pacific region was Captain James Cook. Cook, a British captain, made three important voyages between 1768 and 1779. While looking for the southern continent thought to exist, Cook explored the eastern shores of Australia and New Zealand. After enduring terrible weather, Cook eventually stopped searching for the continent saying it was out of reach of navigation. He also tried to find a northwest passage, sailing as far north as the coast of Oregon and discovering the Hawaiian Islands for Europeans. Cook called the islands the Sandwich Islands in honor of John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich. The Earl had sponsored the expedition. And, yes, it was in honor of this same man that the sandwich is named!

During his voyages, Cook and his crew collected animal and plant samples. They drew detailed maps of their voyages and learned the cultures of many people they encountered. On all his long voyages, Cook stressed to his crew the importance of proper nutrition, especially vitamin C. Cook knew that scurvy was a terrible disease that killed many sailors, and he believed it occurred from lack of proper nutrition. For this reason, Cook fed his crew lots of sauerkraut! He also made sure the crew practiced proper hygiene and ate fresh fruits and vegetables while at ports. For his efforts, very few of Cook's crew died.

Cook's most famous discovery was of the Hawaiian Islands. Sadly, this was where Cook's exploration ended. Apparently, someone stole one of Cook's boats. In return, his crew took the king of the island hostage. Fighting ensued, and Cook and several others of his crew were killed. A statue in his honor is on Hawaii's Big Island, and there is a monument to him on Kealakekua Bay where he was killed. Interestingly, the 25 square feet where the white stone monument stands officially belongs to the country of Great Britain and not the United States.

title: International Date Line
text:
The international date line is located in the Pacific Ocean region, mostly along the line of longitude at 180 degrees. Although it is not a line you can actually see (except on maps and globes), it is an important mark that helps keep track of days. The international date line runs vertically, from the eastern part of Russia and western part of Alaska, then west of Hawaii and east of New Zealand and finally to Antarctica. When you cross the international date line, you either gain or lose an entire day.

A scholar named Antonio Pigafetta sailed around the world with Ferdinand Magellan in 1519 and recorded the first actual acknowledgment of the effect of dates and travel, although the international date line didn’t exist back then. Of the 240 men who began the journey, only Pigafetta and 17 others made it back to Spain in 1522. Magellan was killed in a battle a year earlier. The international date line wasn’t put into place until 1884.

In 2011 the island nation of Samoa did an amazing thing— it lost an entire day! By moving the international date line to the east around the islands, Samoa is now closer in time to New Zealand and Australia. Samoa does a lot of trade and business with these countries, and they were always a day apart. Since the date line is an imaginary line, Samoa simply announced that the line was no longer where it had been. To make the switch, the country “skipped” Dec. 30, 2011. When they went to bed on December 29, they woke up on December 31. Imagine how you’d feel if your birthday was on December 30!

title: Great Barrier Reef
text:
The world's largest coral reef is found near Queensland in northeast Australia. It stretches about 1,250 miles through the Coral Sea. To understand the size of this reef, think of the distance between Miami, Florida and New York City.

The Great Barrier Reef is made of living coral that continues to grow on top of dead coral. Scientists say it may be more than 20 million years old. The reef is home to 1,500 species of fish, 400 species of coral and 500 species of seaweed. It is also home to the largest population of dugongs in the world. A dugong is a cousin of the manatee.

The Great Barrier Reef is the biggest structure made by organisms in the world. It is the only living thing that can be seen from outer space. The first European to discover this reef was English explorer Captain James Cook, who came upon it in an unusual way. In 1770, Captain Cook's wooden ship, the Endeavour, got stuck on it as they sailed along the coastline of Australia.

Today, this wonderful reef, one of the seven wonders of the natural world, is in danger. Sunscreen lotions, ship fuels, ships anchors and climate changes are threatening this beautiful reef's existence.

title: Mutiny!
text: In 1787, Captain William Bligh and his crew of 45 sailors traveled to Tahiti. After sailing 27,000 miles in 10 months, the ship, the HMS Bounty, reached the island. Their goal was to get breadfruit trees and bring them to the West Indies, where people could use the fruit as inexpensive food for their slaves. In 1789, the HMS Bounty's crew left Tahiti after spending several months on the island. First Mate Fletcher Christian and much of the crew took control of the ship in a mutiny. They said Captain Bligh had been unfairly harsh as their captain. And the mutineers had come to like Tahiti. Some had even married native women. They placed Captain Bligh and 17 loyal sailors on a small 23-foot launch with little food, no charts and only a broken sextant to navigate their way. It was a death sentence! The mutineers then sailed the HMS Bounty back to Tahiti. There they gathered supplies, and several Polynesian men and women sailed with them to the Pitcairn Islands while some of the crew stayed in Tahiti. When the crews of British ships hunted the mutineers down, they found the ones living in Tahiti. After they were taken back to England and tried for their crime, several mutineers were set free but three were hanged. British searchers never found First Mate Christian and those who had gone with him to the Pitcairn Islands. The colony they established survives to this day. Amazingly, Captain Bligh and his men survived a 3,618-mile journey to Timor and then home to England.

title: What are the moai?
text: Located about 2,200 miles from the South American country of Chile is Rapa Nui Island. We know it better as Easter Island. In 1722, Dutch Captain Jacob Roggeveen and his crew discovered this island. Giant rocks resembling faces line the coastline. Called moai, these structures stand 13 feet tall. And they are heavy, tipping the scales at 14 tons. Captain Roggeveen's crew found more than 600 stone moai, many of which are still left unfinished in nearby stone quarries today. Historians aren't sure how the inhabitants of the island were able to build such massive structures, which scientists believe were created around A.D. 1400 - 1600. Why did islanders take the time and energy to build the moai and line their island coast with them? And why did they suddenly stop building them? We may never know.

title: Aboriginal Dot Art
text: The Australian Aborigines created dot paintings using sticks or echidna quills. Traditional Aboriginal dot paintings usually told a story, such as about hunting or gathering food. Dot art drawings of fish, crocodiles, snakes, turtles, kangaroos and geometric shapes were also popular images. Do an Internet search to see examples of Aboriginal dot art. You can create your own dot art on a piece of paper or a smooth rock. Use a cotton swab or the tip of a paintbrush handle (not the brush end) and dip it into different color paints to make your very own dot art.

title: Let's Write
text: In the Eastern Highlands of Papua New Guinea lives an indigenous tribe called the Asaro Mudmen. They were once fierce warriors who scared their enemies by covering themselves with mud and scary masks made of gray clay. Today, many in this tribe continue this tradition for busloads of tourists who visit their villages in Papua New Guinea. More recently, automobile and soda companies have featured Asaro Mudmen in their commercials and advertisements. Write a paragraph expressing your opinion about how culture contact has changed the Asaro tribe. Remember to check for proper spelling, grammar and punctuation.

title: That's A Wrap!
text:
You may have thought, "Why do we have to learn this stuff?" as you read about all the world history topics we covered this year. It sure doesn't seem to have anything to do with your life today, does it? Your teacher might have told you that it is important to learn about the past, because history is the foundation of our present and future. Remember when you were little and sat in a circle while someone whispered something in your ear and then you passed the secret along to the person sitting next to you? Well, the history of the world is kind of like that game. People through the ages have passed down ideas that we still use today. You could say that in many ways the past really is our present. How? Let's see!

You wake up, look at the clock and see that it's time to get ready for school. Did you know that the ancient people of Mesopotamia, who lived in the present-day country of Iraq, developed a counting system based on the number 60? Sixty was the highest they could count using all the joints of their fingers and toes. It's the basis of our time system today.

You look at the kitchen calendar and see that it's Thursday. Well, thank the people of Mesopotamia again. They established a seven-day week. Now, take the name "Thursday." Would you believe Nordic people who lived long ago worshiped different gods on different days? "Tyr's day" became Tuesday, "Woden's Day" became Wednesday and "Thor's Day" became Thursday. Sticking with the calendar, have you ever wondered why there are 365 days in a year? The ancient Egyptians had 360 days in their calendar and added 5 extra days at the end of the year for a big celebration - 365 in all!

Next, you go into the bathroom and take a shower. Archaeologists excavated the earliest bathroom in a place called Orkney Islands, Scotland. Scientists dated the bathroom they found back to 8000 B.C. You grab a bar of soap. The ancient Phoenicians (of present day Lebanon) invented soap in about 600 B.C. They made their soap from goat fat and wood ash. Did you know people thought bathing once a month (and in some cultures, once a year) was sufficient? Thankfully, people no longer believe bathing is unhealthy! Do you think ancient people sang in the shower?

Now that you're all cleaned up and ready for your day, it's time to head for school. Turn the page and see how the past is not just part of your history class - it's part of every subject.

title: Wrapping it Up
text:
You arrive at school and open your math book. Thank Johannes Gutenberg from Germany! In the 1400s, he improved the Chinese idea of block printing and invented a printing press, which meant that books no longer had to be written and copied by hand. The printing press made books available to more people. Time to practice your math lessons, so take out some paper. People throughout the ages first wrote on clay tablets, then on weeds woven into a paper called "papyrus," then on wax coated tablets and finally, the Chinese invented the earliest paper that is the "granddaddy" of paper we use today.

Did you remember to write your name on the top of your paper? Thank the people who developed the writing system we use today. The earliest Phoenicians needed a quick way to record their trading activities and picture writing just wasn't the answer. So, they developed the first alphabet. They shared their alphabet with the ancient Greeks who, in turn, tweaked it a bit and passed it down to the Romans who then added their own flair (like capital letters), and the writing system eventually trickled down to us. What just fell onto the floor? Your pencil? Did you know that Germans used the earliest known pencil in the 16th century? And did you know the earliest pencils didn't have eraser tips? Someone developed erasers much later. Thank goodness!

Your mind begins to wander a bit during math class, and your eyes settle on a faded poster of someone skiing down a steep slope in the Rocky Mountains. The poster is taped to the white painted concrete wall of your classroom. Ancient Romans first used concrete in their construction. Oh, and that skier? Well, archaeologists discovered a really old picture of two men on skis in a rock cave in the country of Norway, which they've dated back to about 2000 B.C.

Time for gym class, and the class is bowling. Archaeologists have found a tomb in ancient Egypt with a bowling ball and nine bowling pins, which they've dated back to 3200 B.C. And, if you and your friends like to play kickball, think about this blast from the past: The Aztec were bouncing rubber balls as far back as the 15th century.

Did someone say lunch? Well, pick up that fork and thank someone from the country of Italy who lived during the 11th century. Before this time, people ate with their fingers. In fact, for many years people considered it poor manners to use that metal contraption called a fork. Now, drink up that chocolate milk and thank the Indian civilizations of Mesoamerica. These people used the cocoa plant for making a popular (although bitter-tasting) drink. It wasn't until many years later that someone thought to add sugar to the mixture. Oh, and the ancient people of India first used sugar in about 500 B.C.

Band lessons are next, and you pick up your music book. Once again the ancient Greeks and Romans are responsible for the first notation for music, although some historians believe the people of ancient Mesopotamia had music notation too. The Italians improved on musical notation in the ninth century.

Oh no! You can't remember where you left your glasses? How will you see to read Studies Weekly? The Chinese people invented eyeglasses. An Italian explorer named Marco Polo went to China and brought spectacles back to Europe in the 1200s. It was much later, in 1784, that Ben Franklin improved eyeglasses by inventing bifocals. And that kite he flew during an electrical storm? Well, that was another gift from the ancient Chinese, who first used their flying kites as a form of communication.

School's out, and you get back home. You decide to ride your bike for a while because the weather is great and you need a break before starting your homework. Someone in Scotland invented the first bicycle with pedals in 1839. Early bicycles had metal-rimmed tires, so they gave a pretty bumpy ride. (That's why bikes were nicknamed "bone shakers" at one time.) Later, someone thought to add rubber tires. After a snack and doing some homework, you can't wait to surf the Internet on your computer. Computers can't be connected to ancient times, can they? Actually, yes! Many historians trace the roots of the computer to a mechanical calculator developed by the ancient Greeks more than 2,000 years ago.

Let's thank the people of the past for making our present possible!

title: Test your World Culture I.Q.
text:
1. Famous for developing the first alphabet, these sea traders were also famous for their purple dye.

2. These people presented the world with ideas for trial by jury, democracy, the Olympics and much more.

3. Haiku, sumo wrestling, martial arts such as karate and jujitsu and paper folding art called origami came from this culture.

4. These people gave the world a counting system based on 60, the arch, the wheel, the seven-day week and one of the world’s oldest libraries.

5. These ancient people believed that to have life after death you needed your body preserved as a mummy. They left behind many possessions and hieroglyphic writings on papyrus.

6. These early people once lived in the land of Palestine. They were monotheistic, believing in only one God, and they developed a writing system called Hebrew.

7. Kites, paper, eyeglasses, fireworks, yo-yos — all were gifts to the world from these ancient people.

8. This culture developed a place value for zero, which Arabs learned then taught to the people of Europe. Hindus and Buddhists of this group of people believed in reincarnation and gave the world the activity called yoga.

9. Chocolate, the Nazca Lines, popcorn, potatoes, pyramids and Spanish conquest were part of the culture of these three ancient civilizations of the Americas.

10. Ancient people who lived in the western region of this continent established the kingdoms of Ghana, Mali and Songhai. They traded gold, salt, cloth, beads, ivory, kola beans and other items.

title: Test Your World Culture I.Q. Part II
text:
Who am I?
