title: America: New Life and New Riches Await
text:
If someone told you - you could find an endless pot of gold in a new and unknown land, would you believe it? The English did! Three ships, called the Discovery, Godspeed and Susan Constant, set sail for a land "filled with gold." At least, that's what the Spanish told them. The English sailed toward this new land hoping to find that gold and become very rich. In 1607, they landed at Chesapeake Bay, sailed the James River and built a settlement on a piece of land they named Jamestown.

The Discovery, Godspeed and Susan Constant carried 104 men and boys to the new land. No women or girls were among the passengers. What kind of person would go on such an adventure? One third of the men were wealthy Englishmen. These wealthy men, known as gentlemen, hoped to make even more money. They were looking for gold and some land to claim as their own. At least 12 of the men were craftsmen, men who had a useful skill or trade. These included a blacksmith, bricklayers, carpenters, a tailor, a barber and two doctors. Most of the men were laborers - unskilled workers. Many of the unskilled workers were poor. They were also hoping to make money and to start a new life in a new land. At least four boys made the journey, too.

The English also wanted to find a shorter water route to Asia. This route would open up trade and help England become wealthier. They hoped this water route began somewhere in the new land, and they wanted to be the first to find it.

The English had high hopes and big dreams. Would this new land be the start of a new life for these 104 settlers? Would they find gold or other riches? Would they find the water route to Asia? The answers are in this paper. Keep reading!

title: Jamestown Rediscovery
text:
The first settlement at Jamestown dates back to 1607. For many years, though, no one knew what happened to it. In fact, the park rangers at Jamestown told visitors that nothing was left of the fort.

In 1963, one of those visitors was a young college student who had hoped to see the fort. That young man was Bill Kelso. Kelso studied history and archaeology in college. He never forgot that the park ranger told him that Jamestown was gone. He believed that something of Jamestown must have survived and he wanted to prove it.

Thirty years later, he got his chance. In 1993, he was hired as an archaeologist at Jamestown. In the first dig, Kelso found a clay pipe and pieces of pottery that were from the early settlement. Since then, Kelso and his team of archaeologists have found more than a million artifacts. Kelso said the best part was finding a skeleton. They named the skeleton J.R., which stands for Jamestown Rediscovery. Other artifacts include a helmet, coins, a ring, copper and glass beads. The exciting news is that Kelso and his team are only half finished. There's much more to find and learn!

title: The English Colonize America
text:
Why Did the English Come To America?

In the 1500s and 1600s, England wanted to be powerful and rich. One way for a country to be powerful and rich was to find new land and set up colonies there. England knew about America. Explorers discovered it in the 1400s. Other European countries, such as Spain, already had land in America. Explorers from Spain said there was lots of gold in America, and the leaders of England wanted that gold. They also hoped to find a better trade route to the East - the "Northwest Passage." Two men from Jamestown, John Smith and Christopher Newport, sailed the James River looking for it, but they had to give up when they reached the fall line.

How Would American Land Help England Become Rich?

With a colony in America, England hoped to mine gold or silver or find other ways to make money. One way to make money was to find raw materials. Raw materials are objects found in nature used to make other things. For example, a tree is a raw material. Workers make furninture, boats and houses from trees. England did not have many trees. The leaders hoped the new colony would give them trees and other raw materials that were scarce in England.

Who Would Pay for the New Colony?

Setting up a colony costs a lot of money. Who would pay for the ships supplies and workers? Some wealthy Englishmen were looking for ways to become wealthier. They formed a business called the Virginia Company of London. These men became the stockholders. A stockholder is someone who owns part of a business and hopes to make money. These men agreed to pay for this new colony so they would make money on items sent back to England.

What Was the Name of the New Colony?

The king of England was King James I. He allowed the Virginia Company of London to set up this new colony. Three ships and 104 men sailed for the new land. On May 14, 1607, they chose the location of the new colony. They called it Jamestown in honor of King James. They also named the river that flowed near the colony after the king. They called it the James River.

What's an Economic Venture?

Jamestown was an economic venture. The stockholders hoped to make a lot of money for themselves and England - that's the economic part. A venture is a business that is risky or dangerous. The stockholders found 104 men willing to go on this trip. The men worried about many things. Would they have enough supplies? Would they run into terrible storms at sea? Would they find a good location for the colony? Would they find gold and silver? How would the native people treat them? How would they survive in a new land?

Who Was Willing to Take the Risks?

The men who went to Jamestown thought the chance of making lots of money was worth the risks. Many of the men were English "gentlemen." These men were already wealthy, but they hoped to make more money or find land of their own. Others on the trip included blacksmiths, bricklayers, some carpenters, two surgeons and laborers (workers with no special skills). Since Jamestown was set up to make money for the Virginia Company, the company paid all of the men who worked.

What Was Life Like at Jamestown?

Life at Jamestown was hard. Less than a year after the men landed, only 38 of them were still living. Many died from illness or hunger. They did not find gold and silver. They had a hard time getting enough food. The men worked hard to make money for the Virginia Company of London. They sent lumber, glass and furs back to England. None of these made much money. Five years later, they finally found something that did make money - tobacco. Through the hard times, though, the colony of Jamestown survived. It became the first permanent English settlement in North America.

title: How is a Lemonade Stand like Jamestown?
text:
Anyone who sets up a lemonade stand hopes to make money- just like the people who went to Jamestown. Imagine you are going to set up a lemonade stand. You need supplies and your parents agree to help you out. Your parents want you to pay them for the use of the supplies they give you. That makes them the stockholders in your company. They are going to give you a table, materials to make a sign and ingredients for the lemonade. You spend one morning getting ready. You are going to be the worker of the stand. After you pay your parents for supplies, you will pay yourself.

This sounds too easy to be like Jamestown! Even though setting up a lemonade stand seems easy, it still has risks. What could go wrong? Maybe you spend all the time and money getting ready and no customers show up. Maybe it starts to rain, your sign is ruined and you have to close up shop. If any of these things happen, you will not make any money. You will not be able to pay your parents for the supplies. You will not be able to pay yourself.

Having a lemonade stand is an economic venture, and so was Jamestown. When you set up a business, there are risks. At Jamestown, the risks were high. People lost their lives. It took five years for the colony to make money. For a lemonade stand, the risks are much lower. If you hang in there, you will make money. Best of all, it won't take you five years to do so!

title: A Tale of Two Men
text:
Three ships carried 104 men and boys to find new land for England. They sailed for 18 weeks before finding Jamestown. Some of the men kept journals. Read below the thoughts of two men the week before finding Jamestown.

From the journal of William Green, May 7, 1607: "We see land at last. The land is a welcome sight. Many of the men are sick. They are sick from the sea. My family did not want me to come. They are afraid I will die. The sea did not make me sick. I am sick with worry. I worry that I will not see my family again. They told me not to get on the ship. They said the land was not worth my life. If I make it, I will have 200 acres given to me. That land is for my family. That is why I came."

From the journal of Thomas Jordan, May 7, 1607: "The fresh, green trees are good to see. It has been seventeen long weeks on this boat. It will be worth it. I could not pay for this voyage. The Virginia Company is giving me this chance. I will work hard. They tell me that I will need to work for four to seven years. When the time is up, I will be free. Then I can work and make money. I cannot wait."

THINK ABOUT IT: Who was a "gentleman"? Who was a servant? How do you know? Who do you think will have to work the hardest in Jamestown and why?

title: Why is Jamestown called the first permanent English settlement?
text:
Jamestown was the first permanent English settlement in America. That means it was the first settlement that lasted.

Although life in Jamestown was very hard, the colony survived. Jamestown was not the first colony the English tried to set up.

Twice during the 1580s, the English tried to start a colony on Roanoke Island. The first group of colonists stayed for a year. They decided it was too much work so they returned to England.

Then, another group of colonists went to Roanoke. Roanoke has another name - "The Lost Colony." One of their leaders went back to England to get more supplies. He was not able to return to Roanoke for three years. When he returned, he never found any of the colonists. No one knows for sure what happened to them.

title: The Oyster
text: John Smith, one of the English leaders at Jamestown, wrote in 1608 that oysters “lay thick as stones” throughout the Chesapeake Bay. Almost 100 years later, another writer said that ships had to sail around the huge beds of oysters. An oyster is a soft-bodied animal that lives in a hard shell. The shell is oval and rough on the outside. Oysters can be found in both freshwater and saltwater. They attach themselves to rocks or other hard surfaces. Oysters stay close to each other and make oyster beds. Oysters do not move around. What does an oyster do? An oyster keeps the water clean. The oyster beds give other animals a place to live. The oyster is also food for many birds, fish and people. You will not see huge beds of oysters in the bay today. They do not “lay thick as stones” anymore. Oysters are few in number because of over-fishing, disease and water pollution.

title: Let's Write
text: This week you learned that the Virginia Company of London chose leaders for the new colony. Imagine you were on the ship that headed to Jamestown, and the Virginia Company of London chose you to be one of the leaders. Set up a journal and record your thoughts about your worries and hopes for the colony.

title: Jamestown Scramble
text: Directions: Unscramble the following Jamestown words using the clues to help you. You will find the answer to the Jamestown question by filling in the numbered blanks with the numbered letters. Use the articles in this issue to help you find the answers.

title: Get Ready! Get Set! Let’s go to Jamestown!
text:
Three ships, the Susan Constant, the Discovery and the Godspeed, carried 104 men and boys to the New World. The trip took four and a half months. The ships sailed over 6,000 miles. They landed on the coast of Virginia, today called Virginia Beach. Can you imagine what the men and boys were thinking when they arrived? Where would they sleep? What would they eat? How would the American Indians treat them? Would they find gold? Would they even survive?

The Virginia Company of London told them where to set up the colony. They were to travel upriver and find a safe location. Would they find the perfect place? They needed a place that would help keep them safe from attacks. They needed a place to dock their ships. They needed a water supply. When they found a strip of land they liked, they named it Jamestown. This was the first step in founding the new colony. Building a fort was the next step.

In less than a month, they built the fort. They cut down trees and removed branches and bark to make logs. They placed the logs upright in rows to make the walls of the fort. The shape of the fort was triangular. They called it Jamestown Fort. It became their home. But, was it home sweet home? They completed the fort on June 15, 1607 - just in time for summer. Virginia is hot and humid in the summertime. The colonists were not used to such weather and they didn't like it. Most of us don't like it, either, so we have air conditioners! The summer proved to be a hard time for the colony.

At least they had a place to live. Maybe it wasn't perfect, but it was home for now. Next, they had to find a way to make money. Would they find gold in Virginia? Would it grow in the trees or wash up on the beach? If they didn't find gold, would they find something else to make money for the company?

title: Jamestown: How, Where, When and Why?
text:
In last week's lesson, we learned about why the Virginia Company of London wanted to set up a colony in America. England was hoping to find wealth and stay a powerful country. In this week's lesson, we are going to find out why they chose the land they named Jamestown. Would this new colony bring England wealth and power?

The Virginia Company of London told the settlers to set up the colony off the coast of Virginia. The settlers sailed on three ships, the Discovery, Susan Constant and Godspeed, and arrived at Virginia. They reached the Chesapeake Bay and found four rivers. They named these rivers the Potomac, Rappahannock, York and James. After reaching the Chesapeake Bay, they put together a smaller boat called a shallop. They used the shallop to sail the rivers and other places along the bay. They tried to find a place that would keep them safe.

They found a place along the James River. The land they chose was a peninsula. A peninsula is a narrow piece of land that has water on three sides. They thought this land was a good, safe choice for three reasons. First, the water along this land was very deep. It was easy to dock ships in areas of deep water. Second, if the Spanish or American Indians did attack them, the land would be easy to defend. Finally, they thought this location had plenty of fresh water.

 On May 14, 1607, the men and boys went on land. They built a fort and named it Jamestown after their king, King James I. The fort was a triangle and had three sides. Each corner had a watchtower. A watchtower is a high place where someone can view the land. Why do you think they built watchtowers on each corner? Inside the fort, they built a church, a storehouse and houses.

But Jamestown was not the first settlement in the place we call Virginia. The colony was built smack in the middle of an American Indian empire that had been around for a long time. Powhatan was chief of the empire, which included a lot of land and power, and he lived in the village of Werowocomoco. Around 15,000 American Indians (also called Powhatan) farmed, hunted and traded across this wide area near the Chesapeake Bay.

Now that they had a place to live, they could work on making money for England and King James I. After all, King James I gave the Virginia Company of London a charter to start this new colony. A charter is a piece of paper giving rights, or permission, for something to happen. With the king's permission, the Virginia Company of London organized settlers to sail to the New World and start a colony. The charter also stated that anyone who went to the new colony would still be English. This meant that the Jamestown colonists would have the same rights in the New World that they had back in England. The Virginia Company of London would give the supplies needed. The colonists were workers for the Virginia Company of London. All the men needed to do was find gold.

However, there was no gold to find. There were many other problems for the colonists. While they were trying to find a way to make money, many of the colonists died. By January 1608, only 38 out of the 104 men and boys were still alive. That same month, the fort and most of their supplies burned in a fire. They tried making money with glass, silk and lumber. None of these made very much money for the company.

They also did not realize it would be hard to get fresh water. The water in the area was very brackish, which meant it was a little salty and not safe to drink. In times of drought, there was not enough fresh water for people. Another challenge was that many of the settlers were English gentlemen. They didn't really know how to do the work that would help the colony survive, and many did not want to work.

They didn't think they should have to build homes and a fort. They weren't prepared to hunt, fish, grow crops, fight natives, keep fires going, take care of the pigs, goats, cattle and horses they brought and … well, you get the picture. All of that was just too hard! They only came to the New World to grab as much gold as they could get their hands on. But they were out of luck.

Jamestown is a story of survival. At times, it was hard. Many of the early colonists lost their lives. Some of them did survive. Since some of them made it, that made Jamestown the first permanent English settlement. You might say that Jamestown is the birthplace of the United States. More and more settlements began in Virginia, and over time it became one of the original 13 states in our country. Today the Jamestown settlement is a popular tourist attraction in Virginia.

title: Jamestown: From Peninsula to Island
text:
In the 1600s, Jamestown was a peninsula. A peninsula is an area of land with water on three sides. It was connected to the mainland by a small strip of land called an isthmus. (It's kind of like the way your neck connects your head to your body.) In the 1800s, erosion washed away the isthmus. That's when Jamestown became an island. The land of Jamestown is rich with history. Once it was the home of government for the New World. Then, it became home to large plantations. During the Civil War, forts built on the island protected the river. Today, a bridge takes you to a five-mile road along the island of Jamestown.

What will you learn about on the island? There are 11 stops on the driving tour. Stop 1: Jamestown colonists made many bricks. They used bricks for wells, houses and walkways. Stop 2: A Civil War Fort was located here. Stop 3: Jamestown colonists dug a seven-foot pit in a hut. They filled the pit with ice and straw and stored food in it. Does this remind you of a modern appliance? Stop 4: One of the first doctors on the island used native plants as medicine. Stop 5: Jamestown potters used Tidewater clay to make pottery. Stop 6: Jamestown colonists traded with the American Indians, the Powhatan. Sometimes, trade was easy and other times, the colonists used guns. Stop 7: Tobacco grew at Jamestown. The seeds came from the West Indies. Stop 8: The Travis family graveyard exists here. At one time, Edward Travis owned almost half the island. Stop 9: The colonists tried to grow many different crops in Jamestown. Apples grew well. Bananas did not. Stop 10: Most of the trees were cleared at Jamestown and used for building homes, boats, barrels and firewood. Stop 11: Jamestown colonists used pitch (a sticky sap) that came from pine trees to help them build a small boat when they arrived. Today, we call this place Jamestown Island.

title: What is a shallop?
text: A shallop is a small wooden boat. In the 1600s, colonists used shallops for exploring coastal areas and trading with the American Indians. John Smith, one of the leaders of Jamestown, used a shallop to explore the Chesapeake Bay. He made many maps of the area after sailing around in a shallop. Colonists did not use shallops to sail on the Atlantic Ocean. Colonists brought the pieces of a shallop to the New World in the bottom of a bigger ship. When the colonists arrived, they put the shallop together and used it to sail on smaller bodies of water. Shallops measure 25 to 45 feet in length. They can hold up to 25 men and enough food for several days.

title: The Canada Goose
text:
What is a goose from Canada doing in the Chesapeake Bay? The Chesapeake Bay is a favorite place for birds flying south. It is a great place to stop and spend the winter. The bay also can serve as a place to stop and rest before going further south. The Canada Geese are the most abundant, or plentiful, birds in the bay.

Geese begin to arrive as early as September. Canada geese mark their arrival with their famous honking. The geese often fly in a V shape with the strongest geese in the front, or the point of the V. They fly at speeds up to 3 5 miles an hour. Geese have special bills shaped to help them eat plants they find underwater. The Chesapeake Bay does not have as many underwater plants as it once did, so many geese now eat grain they find in open fields. Canada Geese can live to be 2 5 years old.

title: Help a Rat and Learn to Run the Country This Year!
text:
Hey, kids! I'm Revere the Rat, but you can call me Rev. I'm your online Studies Weekly friend and I need your help. You can help me get great stuff by earning points while you learn. Just scan the code or go to www. studiesweekly .com and click on my picture.

Has your family ever bought something that came with an owner's manual? Cars, TVs and other things have an owner's manual, a book on how to use them. Your social studies class is the "owner's manual" for the United States of America. You'll learn about history, geography, government by the people, and much more, so you can do a good job of running our country someday.

In America rats can't vote, so "you the people" govern (run) the country. Someday you will be in charge of this country, and you'll choose leaders and representatives by voting. Then you can tell the representatives you help elect how you think the country should be run. In fact, Studies Weekly kids are so smart, that many of you will someday be mayors, senators, governors- maybe even the president!

For now you have two jobs: Learn about the country and how it works and earn points for me so I can get that great stuff I told you about. It's easy. Just scan or click and you're on your way!

title: Journey to Jamestown
text:
Directions: Look at the maps and answer these questions. If you need extra help, use classroom books or ask your teacher for permission to use the Internet. You may use another sheet of paper to write your answers on.

Label the following:

a. North America and Europe

b. England

c. Atlantic Ocean

d. the Chesapeake Bay

e. Jamestown, Virginia

f. James River

What direction did the ships sail from England to the Canary Isles?

What direction did the ships sail from the Canary Isles to the West Indies?

What direction did the ships sail from the West Indies to Jamestown?

The Virginia Company of London ordered the colonists to settle between the 34th and 41st northern lines of latitude.

a. What northern line of latitude is nearest to Jamestown?

b. Did the colonists follow the Company's orders?

Draw a dotted line to trace a direct route from England to Jamestown. This trip would have been about 4,000 miles long.

The trip the colonists took was 6,000 miles long. Why do you think the colonists took the southern route that they did?

Pretend you were the captain of one of the ships that sailed to Jamestown. Would you choose the 4,000-mile route or the 6,000-mile route. Why?

title: There’s Good News and Bad News
text:
This week’s lesson is full of good and bad news. Has anyone ever asked you, “What do you want to hear first, the good news or the bad news?” The early years of Jamestown were pretty much like that.

The good news is that England starts a colony. There is excitement in the air. The colonists hope to find gold and other goods to make money. The settlers know the bad news when they find that gold does not grow on trees. More bad news comes when they have a hard time finding things to make money.

The good news is Virginia Company of London keeps sending supplies. The colonists trade with the native people in order to get food. More colonists keep arriving at Jamestown. Then, a fire destroys much of their supplies and the storehouse. More bad news is that many colonists are dying, either from starvation or from illness. Many colonists do not want to work very hard at growing their own crops.

The good news is that John Smith becomes their leader. He tells them if they don’t work, they don’t eat. The colonists live thanks to his leadership. The bad news is that living near the native people becomes hard. There are many problems.

Perhaps the best news of all happens in 1619. The colonists form their own government. The colonists choose their own representatives from each town or plantation. The representatives meet at the Jamestown church. They called it the House of Burgesses. They make laws for the colony. They start democracy in America. The bad news is that this ends in 1624. The king of England makes Virginia a royal colony. The people of Virginia never forget what it was like to make their own laws. The good news is that one day this all changes. Today we have a democracy that no one can take away.

title: Jamestown and the House of Burgesses
text:
Let's review what we know so far about Jamestown. The king of England wrote a charter to start the new colony. The Virginia Company of London got the supplies, men and ships together. The 104 colonists landed in 1607. They built a fort on a peninsula and named it Jamestown. By January 1608, only 38 colonists were still alive. Many died from disease or hunger. Some died from attacks by the local American Indians, the Powhatan. In addition, in January 1608, the fort caught fire. Most of their supplies burned in the fire. More colonists arrived from England. Many of them died during the years of 1609 and 1610. Most of this sounds like bad news.

Didn't anything good happen at Jamestown? The answer is YES! In 1612, they finally found a crop that would make money - tobacco. It wasn't shiny and golden, but it did make money for Jamestown. They called it brown gold. Why do you think they called it brown gold?

As the colony started to make money, more colonists came to live in it. Most wanted to be planters and start a tobacco farm. As more people came to live in Virginia, the colonists needed rules and order. They needed to have rules that people could live by. Two groups made the rules. One group consisted of the governor and his council, or assistants. The other group represented each town or plantation of Virginia. The people on the town or plantation elected two men. Each man, or representative, was called a burgess. The second group, known as the House of Burgesses, elected 22 men. These two groups were Virginia's General Assembly.

The governor called the first meeting of the General Assembly in the summer of 1619. It was a hot, humid summer. They gathered in the church at Jamestown. What the first General Assembly did that summer is something we still talk about today. What did the first General Assembly do? The first thing they did was to set the price of tobacco. They passed laws to punish colonists who did wrong things. They wrote laws about how to treat the native people. They even passed a law that said the colony would build a university. Why is this important? The settlers were in control of their own government. This is more good news! The colonists of Jamestown made their own laws. Americans find these things important today. We value electing officials who help make our laws. We have the colonists of Jamestown to thank for starting this type of government for us.

Let's talk about one more piece of bad news. Not everyone took part in the House of Burgesses. What kind of people were elected to the House of Burgesses? Only men were. Only adult men who owned land were citizens. They were the only ones who could vote and become burgesses. The good news is that this changes- all Americans today are allowed to vote and become representatives if they so choose.

Democracy in America began that hot summer in Jamestown. In the 1640s, the House of Burgesses became its own legislative body and made laws for all of Virginia. Today, this system of government continues with the General Assembly of Virginia.

title: The Sturgeon
text: The Atlantic Sturgeon is one of the oldest fish in the Chesapeake Bay. The Atlantic sturgeon lives up to 60 years and can grow to be 15 feet and weigh 8 00 pounds. It is a bottom dweller, which means it lives near the bottom of the bay. The sturgeon was the first cash crop of the settlers at Jamestown. It did not make a lot of money for the settlers. Even though there were many sturgeon and they were easy to catch, the fish often spoiled when sent back to England. Colonists used it for their food supply. They also turned the skin of the sturgeon into leather and used it for clothing and book covers. During the time of Jamestown, colonists recorded sturgeon that jumped out of the water and landed on the ships' deck. Such a sight today is harder to see. Fewer sturgeon live in the bay because of over fishing and chemicals.

title: Virginia’s First Laws
text:
Below are some of the laws written during the summer of 1619 at Virginia's First General Assembly. The assembly wrote laws to help with growth of the economy and population.

1. All persons must attend church on Sunday. All persons must attend morning and afternoon services.

2. All persons must keep a year's supply of corn in stock.

3. No one will sell a dog to the Indians.

4. For swearing, a man will be spoken to three times. After the third time, a man will pay a fine to his church. A servant who swears will pay a fine to his master. A master may whip his servant. A servant may also admit his crime in church.

5. If a man gambles at dice or cards, he will lose all winnings and pay a fine. Some of the fine will go to the one who reports this crime. The rest of the fine will go to charity.

6. The Minister will warn anyone who is drunk. The second time, a drunk admits his crime in public. The third time, the drunk's legs are placed in leg irons for 12 hours and a fine must be paid.

7. Each man may trade with the Indians, except servants. Servants who trade with the Indians are whipped.

8. A man may not travel over 20 miles from his house or be absent for seven days unless the Governor knows.

Think and Discuss

What laws helped the colony to grow and why?

What laws seem silly today and why?

Some of the laws also give the punishment. What should the punishment be for someone who doesn't attend church? Or if a year's supply of corn is not kept? Or if travel is not known by the Governor?

What laws are about the economy?

What laws are about behavior?

title: What is a burgess?
text: We learned in this week's lesson a burgess is a representative. The word burgess first meant a freeman or citizen of an English town. Later, a burgess was a member of the English government who represented a town. When the colonists came to America, they used the word to describe a representative from a town or plantation. They used this word in England and continued to use it at Jamestown. The word comes from the Late Latin word "burgus," which meant fortified town. Do you see a small word that you recognize in fortified? If you said fort, you are correct! A fortified town protects the people against attack. That is kind of neat when you think about it: a burgess was a person who represented, or protected, the people's rights!

title: Responsibility
text:
Responsibility made Jamestown work. Colonists did not want to take responsibility at first. The colony was in trouble. The colonists learned about responsibility and the colony started to grow. You can learn a lot about responsibility from those early years at Jamestown.

Let's look at what that means with the letters that spell the word. R: Remember that your voice counts. E: Each person has a voice. S: Success depends on hard work. P: Put your best effort forward. O: One person can make a positive difference. N: Never give up. S: Solve problems. I: Include others. B: Be aware of your mistakes. I: Ideas that are positive are best. L: Learn from your mistakes. I: Improve after you make a mistake. T: Teamwork matters. Y: Your hard work can make a difference!

How can you apply this to your own life? Use your voice. If there is a problem, talk to a teacher or another adult. Talk to your friends and try to work things out. If you are having trouble in school, talk to your counselor or teachers. Make sure that you are working as hard as you can. Try to be positive and find something good in every one and thing. Be friends and friendly with all people. If you make a mistake, admit it, learn from it and try not to do it again. Remember to give your best effort all the time.

title: Early Virginia Laws
text:
We learned a lot about the laws written at Virginia’s First General Assembly. The laws below are shown exactly as they were written. Do the best you can to read the following laws. As you read, highlight words you know. The words below are an older form of English. After reading, match the laws written in modern English on the previous page with the ones below.

A. All persons whatsoever upon the Sabaoth daye shall frequente divine service and sermons both forenoon and afternoon.

This law matches number _______. (Sabaoth means Sunday)

B. For the reformation of swearing, every freeman and Mr. of a family after thrise admontion shall give 5s or the value upon present demaunde, to the use of the church where he dwelleth; and every servant afte the like admontion, excepte his Mr. discharge the fine, shalbe subject to whipping. Provided, that the payment of the fine notwithstanding, the said servant shall acknowledge his faulte publiquely in the Churche.

This law matches number ______.

C. Against gaming at dice and Cardes be it ordained by this present assembly that the winner or winners shall lose all his or their winninges and both winners and loosers shall forfaite ten shillings a man, one ten shillings whereof to go to the discoverer, and the rest to charitable and pious uses in the Incorporation where the faulte is comitted.

This law matches number ______.

D. Against drunkeness be it also decreed that if any private person be found culpable thereof, for the first time he is to be reprooved privately by the Minister, the second time publiquely, the thirde time to lye in boltes 12 howers in the house of the Provost Marshall and to paye his fee, and if he still continue in that vice, to undergo suche severe punishment as the Governor and Counsell of Estate shall thinke fitt to be inflicted on him.

This law matches number ______.

E. Read and circle the words you know in this law. Then, answer the questions below.

That no man shall purposely goe to any Indian townes, habitations or places or resortes without leave from the Governor or commander of that place wher he liveth, upon paine of paying 40 shillings to publique uses as aforesaid.

1. In the first part of the sentence, where is a man not allowed to go without approval?

2. Who can give approval?

3. What is the fine? (hint: a shilling is an English coin)

title: The New Pope
text:
The Catholic Church has about 1 billion members around the world, including about 66 million here in the United States. Catholics belong to a larger religious belief system called Christianity, which is based on the teachings of Jesus Christ. The pope is the head of the Catholic Church. In 2013, Pope Benedict XVI announced his retirement, and church leaders elected a new pope.

The new pope is Jorge Mario Bergoglio. Popes choose a new name when they are elected, and he will now be known as Pope Francis. Most popes have been European, but Pope Francis is from the Americas! He was born in Buenos Aires, Argentina, in 1936. He has dedicated most of his life to serving the poor and has lived a simple life.

The pope is not only the head of the Catholic Church, but he is also the head of the smallest country in the world! Vatican City is a tiny, 109-acre country located within the city of Rome, in Italy. Vatican City has its own flag and post office. The pope is the head of this country, but Vatican City doesn’t get involved in political disputes between other countries.

The pope’s main job is to encourage Catholics to follow the teachings of Jesus. He will visit countries all over the world and pray with people. Pope Francis will be a busy man!

title: Virginians Restore Slave Cemetery
text:
Cemeteries - not the kind of place you'd want to hang out, right? You may think of ghosts, ghouls and even zombies, but that's probably because you've watched too much television. For some Virginia volunteers, cemeteries are exactly the place to be. In fact, they've been in the cemetery for seven years now.

Why, you ask? Well, they're restoring the cemetery. It's an old slave cemetery that had been totally buried by grass and shrubs, surrounded by trees and almost completely forgotten about.

The Avoca Museum (www . avocamuseum . org) received a tip from a local resident that there may be a slave cemetery hidden in the area. With a little bit of careful research, a Sweet Briar College professor confirmed this tip in 2004.

Small, hand-hewn gravestones were scattered around the cemetery, but the stones had nothing written on them. This was probably due to a law passed in 1831 that made it illegal for slaves to read or write. The slaves either hadn't learned to write anything on the headstones, or didn't want to break the law by admitting they did know.

Most of what is known about the cemetery is from oral history, stories told from one generation to the next. From oral history, we know that the first person ever buried in this cemetery was an American Indian who had drowned in the Staunton River.

The topic of slavery is a sensitive one, and this restoration is meant to restore some dignity - an honor not given to the slaves in their lifetime. The people buried in this cemetery were an important part of Virginia's history and deserve a well-kept, dignified, final resting place.

title: Diversity at Jamestown II
text:
Why do you think the Virginia Company of London didn't send women to Jamestown in 1607? Were they worried that life would be too difficult for them? We know the early years of Jamestown were hard. But even before the Virginia Company sent 90 women, a few others came to the colony and survived.

English women arrive at Jamestown

Very few women lived in Jamestown in the first 13 years. Two English women - Mistress Forrest and her maid Anne Burras - arrived in 1608. The first Jamestown marriage of Anne Burras to John Laydon took place that same year. The Laydon family raised a family of four daughters. They named their first daughter Virginia. Having a family meant that Jamestown was not only a place to make money but also a place to call home. Still, for many years the settlers of Jamestown were mostly men.

In 1619, the Virginia Company gave many acres of land to the men of the colony. The men became tobacco planters. Tobacco made a lot of money for the colony. That same year, the men asked the Virginia Company to send English women to Jamestown. The Virginia Company agreed. They hoped the men would marry and have families. If men had wives and families, they were more likely to stay in Jamestown and grow tobacco. The Virginia Company knew this would help make Jamestown a more permanent settlement.

Ninety unmarried English women landed at Jamestown in 1620. A man who wished to marry gave 150 pounds of tobacco to the Virginia Company to pay for his wife's journey. Women and families helped the colony grow and become stronger. Over the next few years, more settlers came to Jamestown to grow tobacco. The men married, had families and made a home. Jamestown was indeed a permanent settlement.

Africans arrive at Jamestown

A different group of people arrived before the women, in 1619. About 20 Africans arrived on a ship called the White Lion in August of that year. In Africa, they were slaves and they were taken from their homeland against their will. It was not their choice to be slaves or to come to the New World.

There was no slavery in Jamestown at that time. Most planters had indentured servants from England. These servants worked for five to seven years without pay. English servants who came to Jamestown were often very poor. Working without pay for those years allowed them to pay back the money spent on their voyage. When the time was up, they would be free and could work for pay. The first Africans in Jamestown became indentured servants. They worked side by side with the English servants.

The first Africans who came to Jamestown worked in the tobacco fields. Planters wanted to grow as much tobacco as possible. The more tobacco a planter could grow, the more money he made. It takes a lot of hard work to grow tobacco, and planters needed help. Think about this: Planters want to make money with tobacco, but tobacco requires a lot of work. What did planters need more of? If you said more workers, you are right. As the colony began to grow, even more workers were needed. In 1620, more Africans arrived as indentured servants. By the 1660s, Africans who came to Jamestown could no longer earn their freedom — they were slaves for life.

title: Thoughts at Jamestown
text:
The following stories are historical fiction. The author is imagining what a woman and an African servant may have thought while living in Jamestown.

Laura Johnson: "What have I done? I came to the New World five years ago hoping for a better life. Is this better? There is dirt everywhere. When it rains, we have mud. It's hard to find food. Indians have killed many of our friends. Thomas, my husband, is very kind. He paid for my trip to the New World. We were married here. He is thankful that we have a family. He says that now Jamestown feels like home to him. He says Sara, Matthew, Michael, Allison and I make this his home. I worry one of us will get sick, and I pray it doesn't happen. We don't have the medicines that we did in England. Life will get better soon. At least, that is what I tell myself."

Jamal: "This is not my home. The people here are strangers to me. They make me work in the fields all day. I work and work and barely rest. I am always tired. They say I will be free in five more years. I do not know if I can survive that long. Long ago in my homeland I was free. Then war broke out and our enemies made me a slave. One day, strangers put me in chains and brought me here in a ship. I am still a slave. I want to go home to my family, but I fear I will never see them again."

Think about this:

1. What are Laura's feelings about Jamestown? What are Jamal's?

2. Which one is the most worried and why?

3. Which one is the most hopeful and why?

title: What is an indentured servant?
text: An indenture is a contract. A servant is a person who works for someone else. The colonists knew they had a lot of land and not enough people to work on it. Many people in England were poor and willing to do almost anything for a better life. They could not afford to pay for a trip to the New World. Some colonists agreed to pay their way, and the servants agreed to work for five to seven years to repay the cost of the trip. They only got a place to live and food to eat - no wages or salary. The work was very hard for servants, and punishments for breaking laws were severe. Many did not live long enough to earn their freedom. When they did, they received 25 acres of land, a year's supply of corn, a cow, a weapon and a new set of clothes.

title: Perseverance
text:
Very few women lived in Virginia during the early years of Jamestown. Most of their names are unknown. One of the few English women we know a little bit about is Temperance Flowerdew. She survived a hurricane on the way to Jamestown in the fall of 1609. Her first winter there was called the Starving Time. During that winter, many of the colonists died. Temperance lived. She returned to England in 1610. In 1619, she came back to Jamestown with her new husband, Governor George Yeardley. She survived an Indian attack that killed six people on their plantation. Through it all, Temperance helped the colony grow and do well.

How did she survive all the hardships? Temperance had perseverance. Perseverance is the ability to keep going even when the going gets tough. She never gave up!

title: Sharing Public Space: Vitus Bering and Russian Colonies in Alaska
text:
Imagine traveling 6,000 miles over land with supplies for an expedition, and THEN sailing through frigid seas to look for a new world. This was the job given to Vitus Bering, a Danish navigator who sailed for the Russian navy. Peter the Great, czar (ruler) of Russia, asked Bering to explore the eastern coast of Russia. He was wondering if land connected Asia and North America.

Bering's first trip began in 1725. After spending three years getting his supplies to eastern Russia, Bering sailed along the coastline. He didn't see any land to the east, and he didn't realize he was sailing in the narrow passage between Russia and Alaska. This waterway is now called the Bering Strait.

Bering led another expedition in 1741. This time his ship landed on Kayak Island, off the coast of Alaska. They explored some of the Aleutian Islands and met the native people there, the Aleut. He was the first European to arrive in present-day Alaska.

Bering died before returning to Russia, but his voyages paved the way for Russian settlements in North America. Many fur traders came to the area. In 1799 the Russian government established a fur-trading operation in Alaska. Furs from foxes, sea otters and seals were very valuable.

Unfortunately, the Russians took advantage of the native people just as some Europeans had done in settling New England. The Russians took over their lands and forced them to hunt for furs. They also brought new diseases, which killed many natives.

Today, the Aleut people continue to live along the western coast of North America, and their population has grown. What might have been different if the Russians and the Aleut had shared public space fairly? Where in your community is there a debate over public land? How should such debates be handled?
