title: Diversity at Jamestown
text:
The English settlers that were granted a charter in 1606 hoped to establish a thriving colony. After their establishment in 1607, American Indians, Africans and women became part of the diversity in colonial North America. Diversity means having many different kinds of people living in the same place. Let’s learn more about them.

Enslaved Africans and Indentured Servants

Jamestown started out as a colony of men and a few boys. In 1619, a group of approximately 20 captured Africans were brought and traded to colony officials for food. At first, they worked in the tobacco fields as indentured servants. They helped the Jamestown colony make money, but they did not get paid for their work. Indentured servants could earn their freedom after they worked for several years. However, sometimes these contracts were not honored and the periods of indentured servitude were extended. Many were not allowed to earn their freedom and were enslaved.

In 1662, slavery was recognized as law in the colony of Jamestown. After this, slavery became an institution. Enslaved Africans were brought to Jamestown and other colonies. They weren't allowed to earn their freedom the way the first groups could. They were enslaved for life.

American Indians

When the colonists came to Jamestown, there were about 25,000 Powhatan living in what is now Virginia. They lived in yehakins, or houses made from young trees that were lashed together in the shape of a barrel. When the English first arrived, the Powhatan helped them. Later, the English settlers increased their demand for food. This led to conflicts between the English settlers and the Powhatan. It was the marriage of Pocahontas to John Rolfe that brought peace to the area. This peace was short-lived.

Women in Jamestown

The first woman to help the colony was Pocahontas, who was an American Indian and a native Virginian. She brought food to the early settlers. She helped keep the peace between the settlers and the American Indians. After her marriage to the settler John Rolfe, there was a period of peace between the settlers and the Powhatan. This was known as the "Peace of Pocahontas."

In 1608, the first women from England began to arrive at Jamestown. One of them was Anne Burras. She was the first woman to marry in the colony. Her daughter, Virginia Laydon, was the first child to be born from English settlers in Jamestown.

Settlers believed that bringing women would help Jamestown become stable (likely to last). Women would become an important part of family life in the colonies. Even so, English women had few rights in the 1600s. Men held positions of authority in English society. Women's roles were mostly as caretakers and homemakers.

title: Hardships at Jamestown
text:
A group of men and boys head to the New World. They hope to find gold. They arrive safely but end up fighting for their lives. They don’t find gold. They don’t even have enough food. They worry about attacks. Many of the men die within a year. Sounds like a TV show, doesn’t it?

Episode 1: The English explorers leave for the new colony. They find it and name it Jamestown. It is on an island. It gives them a safe place to live. They build a fort. They can defend it against the Spanish or the native people. It is on a river. They have water. All is well, at least for now.

Episode 2: The summer heat sets in. The men start to get sick. They aren’t prepared for a hot, humid summer in Virginia. They aren’t prepared for the illnesses. Men start to die.

Episode 3: The men are workers for the Virginia Company. The workers need to find something that will make money for the company. They do not find gold. They try to make money in other ways. They fail many times.

Episode 4: The native people, the Powhatan, capture one of the leaders of Jamestown, John Smith. He meets Pocahontas, daughter of the Powhatan chief. Their friendship brings peace to the island for a while. Smith becomes president of Jamestown.

Episode 5: More men and supplies come from England. A fire breaks out. Many buildings and supplies burn.

Episode 6: Smith orders the men to work. He tells them they will not have food to eat if they don’t help with the work. An injury forces Smith to return to England.

Episode 7: A hard winter, known as “The Starving Time” happens next. Many men die. There is not enough food. There are many illnesses.

What will happen next? How many men will die? Will Jamestown be another Roanoke Island where the colonists are never heard from again? How long will peace last among the Powhatan and the settlers? What will the colony do without Smith? Will they ever make any money? Will they survive? Tune in to Page 2 to find out!

title: Survival: Jamestown
text:
In the past few weeks, we’ve learned life at Jamestown was hard. We also know the colony became permanent. So, why was life so hard at Jamestown? After all, the 104 men and boys came looking for gold and other treasures. Sounds exciting, doesn’t it? They followed the orders of the Virginia Company. They settled on a river so they would be safe and have water near them. The colonists hoped to succeed. Yet, a year later, only 38 of the first group of colonists were still alive. Why did so many die? Why was survival so hard?

One problem was the water supply. The good water supply they found turned out not to be so good. It was more like a swamp. The fresh water of the James River mixes with the salty water of the Chesapeake Bay. A mix of fresh and salt water is brackish water. People need fresh water to drink and stay healthy. When the settlers drank the water, they became ill. The diseases spread to the other colonists. There was no medicine to make them better.

Another problem was the fact that the men were not prepared to live in the wilderness. The English settlers did not have the skills needed to survive at Jamestown. About half of the men at Jamestown were English gentlemen. These men already had wealth and hoped for more. They did not want to work hard. The other half of the men and boys were laborers and skilled workers like blacksmiths. There weren’t enough workers to grow enough food. When their supplies ran low, they were not prepared to grow their own.

The men at Jamestown did not have a good leader at first. Many of the men fought over how to run the colony. The weather in Jamestown was hot and humid. The men were not used to such hot weather. The weather spoiled more of their food and made the men sick. The native people, the Powhatan, attacked the colonists. The men hoped supplies from England would arrive soon. However, Jamestown seemed hopeless.

The water supply and lack of food caused many settlers to die of starvation and disease. More than 50 men were dead, almost half of the colony, by the fall of 1607. A supply ship arrived in Jan. 1608. Only 38 men were still alive then. The men faced more problems when a fire burned many of their supplies and houses that same month. One of the leaders of Jamestown, John Smith, became friends with Pocahontas. Pocahontas was the daughter of Powhatan, the chief of the native people. Their friendship helped the Powhatan Indians to get along with the colonists of Jamestown.

Finally, things at Jamestown improved. The settlers rebuilt the fort, started a glass factory and planted 100 acres of corn. John Smith became president of the colony in Sept. 1608. Another supply ship arrived a month later. This time, the Virginia Company of London sent supplies, more workers and the first two women to live in the colony. Another leader of the colony, Christopher Newport, wanted the men to keep looking for gold. Smith didn’t think that was a good idea. He worried about the survival of the colony and said that if a colonist didn’t work, he wouldn’t eat. Smith taught the colonists to protect themselves against attacks from the native people. His leadership helped Jamestown succeed. A year later, a gunpowder explosion badly burned Smith. He went back to England to get treatment and never returned to Virginia.

title: Jamestown Economy
text:
Do you remember why the colonists went to Jamestown? They were supposed to make money for the Virginia Company of London. So, the next question is, did they ever make money? Let's look at the ways they tried.

They tried making money by making glass. The New World had everything they needed for a glass factory. It had wood for fire and sand to make the glass. In the fall of 1608, the Virginia Company sent over more men. Some of these men were glassblowers. We know two things about the glass factory. First, they shipped some glass back to England. Second, in a few years, they stopped using the glass factory since it didn't make enough money. By 1624, they gave up on making glass.

In 1619, the Virginia Company wanted the settlers to try growing flax. Flax is a plant used to make linen, a type of cloth. The fabric of linen is strong and dries fast. However, flax doesn't grow very well in the Coastal Plain of Virginia. Flax did not make any money for Jamestown.

The settlers attempted to raise silkworms, but also failed at that. The Virginia Company hoped the worms would make a lot of money for them. The rich people wanted silk and the company wanted the settlers to raise the worms that make silk. Silk needed more work than the colonists could give it. They gave up on silk, too.

Finally, the settlers started growing tobacco. It made money for the colonists and helped the colony to grow.

title: Tidewater: Stingray Point
text: John Smith was like a cat with nine lives. Many times, he almost lost his life, but always survived. One of those times happened when he was mapping the Chesapeake Bay. During the summer of 1608, Smith and a small crew sailed on a small, wooden boat called a shallop. One day, Smith was fishing where the Rappahannock River meets the Chesapeake Bay. A stingray's tail, which is poisonous, stung Smith in the back. His crew didn't think he would live and they dug a grave for him. Smith lived and ate the stingray for dinner that night. Stingray Point is the name of the place where Smith was hurt.

title: Ambition: John Smith
text: John Smith had ambition. That means he had a strong drive for success. He came to the colony and helped make it permanent. He didn't like the laziness of some men in the colony. He set out to search the Chesapeake Bay for food as well as to make maps of it. He hoped to find the Northwest Passage, a waterway to Asia. The passage didn't exist, but he did make many maps of the area. When he returned to Jamestown, the men chose him president of the colony. As president, he told the men, "He who does not work, does not eat!" John Smith's ambition helped him succeed at all of his jobs- explorer, mapmaker and president.

title: Was there medicine at Jamestown?
text: The colonists mostly used medicine made from plants. Europeans used plants for medicine for hundreds of years. The colonists used the new plants they found to cure different illnesses. Some of the plants they used included tobacco, Peruvian bark and ipecac. They used tobacco to treat lung problems. What would doctors think about this now? They used Peruvian bark to treat malaria, a disease passed on by mosquitoes. If someone ate something that might be poisonous, they took ipecac. Ipecac makes a person throw up. Does anyone use this type of medicine today? Doctors know tobacco is bad for you and they don’t use it as medicine. People in some places might use Peruvian bark to treat wounds. Doctors rarely use ipecac anymore.

title: Cownose Rays
text: Cownose rays are the most common type of ray in the Chesapeake Bay area. A cownose ray stung John Smith. Males grow to be about 35 inches wide and can weigh up to 26 pounds. Females grow to be around 28 inches and can weigh up to 34 pounds. Cownose rays spend most of the time at the bottom of the bay. They find food there in the mud and the sand. They eat oysters and clams. A pup is a baby cownose ray. A cownose usually doesn't sting anyone. If it does, the person may die, but it's not likely. A quick way to treat a sting is to clean the wound and soak it in very hot water. Why is it called the cownose ray? If you look at a cownose ray from above, it looks like it has a cow's jaw and nose.

title: Jamestown Timeline
text:
Timeline Questions: Use the information in this week’s lesson and the timeline to answer these questions.

1. Put these events in order from first to last:

_____ Smith becomes president of Jamestown.

_____ First supply ships arrive from England.

_____ King James grants charter.

_____ Settlers arrive at Jamestown.

_____Second supply ship arrives.

_____Fire burns the fort and supplies.

_____Three ships leave England for the New World.

2. When did King James grant a charter to start the colony?

3. What does the fire burn in Jan. 1608?

4. Other than president of Jamestown, what job did Smith have?

5. What are the names of the three ships that brought the first colonists to Jamestown?

6. Create a title for this timeline. Be creative and come up with something other than the Jamestown Timeline (or anything similar).

title: Highlight Five Words
text: As you read this week’s magazine, circle or highlight five words that are new to you. Write the words on a piece of paper. Try to figure out the meaning of the words by reading the other words and sentences around them. Write what you think the words mean and compare your definition to a dictionary definition.

title: Making the World a Kinder Place
text:
We sometimes wonder why bad things happen to innocent people. Although we may never understand it, we can do our best to keep things like this from happening in the future. When we do this, we are doing our part to make the world a kinder place, without anger and violence.

One way to do this is by making a plan to replace bullying and violence with kindness. The Cool to Be Kind (C2BK) program was developed to help students create programs in their classes and schools that are based on pro-kindness – doing nice things for others. Students look for ways to “pay it forward” each day. Paying it forward means that when someone thanks you for doing something nice, you ask that person to pay it forward by doing something nice for someone else. By paying it forward, kindness continues to spread across the world and people start thinking kinder thoughts and ways that they can help other people.

What are some ways you could practice paying it forward? How about doing yard work for an elderly neighbor for free? Or inviting a new student to eat lunch with you and your friends? What about giving up your seat on the bus to someone who looks tired, or helping someone pick up something they have dropped? Thinking kind thoughts and acting on them with acts of kindness is a simple change that you can do to change the world.

title: Two Worlds and 15 Miles
text:
American Indians lived in America for tens of thousands of years. The English set up Jamestown in 1607. Two different worlds met, and the lives of both groups changed forever.

Imagine what the meeting was like for an American Indian. Men arrived in big ships. These men wanted to trade. They had beads and trinkets. They also had guns. They wanted food from the American Indians. They spoke different languages. The Americans Indians might have thought: Why are these people here? Why do they dress the way they do? What are they building?

Now, imagine what the meeting was like for an English colonist. The English arrived on the East Coast of America. The bay was wide and there were plenty of oysters. They found land covered in trees. They knew the American Indians lived in this area. The English also knew the American Indians attacked the Spanish. The English might have thought: Are they going to attack us? Why do the men shave the sides of their heads? How are we going to trade with the American Indians?

The two groups met. Sometimes the meetings were friendly. They traded things, even though they didn’t speak the same words. The American Indians wanted copper and beads. The Jamestown colonists needed food.

Thanks to archaeology and journals, we know a lot about these groups. We know the colonists built a fort and named it Jamestown. More recently, archaeologists found the site of the local American Indians, the Powhatan Indians. Their main leader, Powhatan, lived at a village called Werowocomoco. Artifacts found at the site show the Powhatan and the colonists traded with each other.

These two sites are only 15 miles away from each other. But the two groups were worlds apart. We still have much to learn about each of these groups. Archaeologists continue digging at both sites. What will they find next? Will they learn more about Pocahontas and her father, Powhatan? What will they learn about John Smith and the other Jamestown colonists? Perhaps they will unlock the mysteries of these two groups.

title: The Powhatan and the English
text:
The Powhatan Indians lived in the Tidewater area of Virginia for many years. They respected the world in which they lived. They used the land, but did not believe they owned it. The Powhatan met the English settlers at Jamestown. The English believed they could own land. What would become of these two groups?

The two groups had good and bad times. The Powhatan Indians attacked the English several times the first year. At other times, the English traded with them. The English needed food and the Powhatan had lots of it. Virginia Indians measured their wealth by how much food they stored. Many of the English didn’t want to grow their own food, so they often wanted to trade with the Indians to get it.

The Powhatan attacked the English shortly after they built their fort. The English then made the fort stronger. By that time, many of the colonists had died of illness. The Powhatan Indians, instead of attacking, brought them food. The English needed food from the Powhatan many times. They wanted corn, venison and fish from the Powhatan. The Powhatan wanted metal and glass goods from the English. Metal goods helped the Powhatan Indians get and store food. They used the metal to make weapons, too. Glass beads showed an American Indian had a high rank in his tribe. Each group wanted something from the other. The English traded tools, pots, guns and other goods for food, furs and leather from the Powhatan.

The leader of the Powhatan was Wahunsonacock. His people called him Powhatan. Powhatan was the leader of more than 30 tribes when the settlers came to Jamestown. He had 100 wives and many children. One of his children, Pocahontas, helped the Powhatan get along with the settlers. Her real American Indian name was Matoaka, but her nickname was Pocahontas, which means playful girl. When the Powhatan Indians took John Smith captive, Pocahontas helped save his life. After feeding him, the Powhatan seemed ready to beat and kill him. Pocahontas stepped in and laid her head on his. Smith wrote about this in his journal and said she saved his life. Many historians believe this event was a ritual, and Smith’s life was not really in danger. A ritual is a ceremony or set of actions that is often repeated. People who knew Smith thought he loved to brag. He probably made this story sound more dramatic than it actually was. Most likely, Powhatan used this ritual to show his power over Smith and the colonists. We also know Pocahontas and Smith became friends after this event.

Their friendship brought a time of peace between the colonists and the Powhatan Indians. Another leader of Jamestown, John Rolfe, tried growing tobacco. The first type he grew came from the Powhatan. The colonists said it tasted awful. Rolfe then grew tobacco seeds from the Caribbean Islands. The colonists liked the taste of this type of tobacco much better. This tobacco became Jamestown’s first cash crop that really made any money. John Rolfe married Pocahontas and took her to England two years later. Pocahontas became ill in England and died.

During their marriage, times were peaceful. The marriage of John Rolfe and Pocahontas helped the Powhatan and the colonists get along with each other. Tobacco helped Jamestown make money. The time of peace ended when Pocahontas died. The Powhatan saw more and more colonists coming to stay and grow tobacco. They began attacking the colonists again. Many colonists died during an attack by the Powhatan in 1622.

title: The Big One
text:
Thomas walked along the river. He hoped to catch some fish. He planned to catch “the big one.” As he walked along, something caught his eye. It shone in the sun. He bent down to pick it up. It didn’t look like anything important. He almost threw the shiny thing in the water, but instead he decided to hold onto it. He slipped it into his pocket and kept on walking.

He reached his fishing spot and set up for the action. He cast his rod into the water and waited. He waited and waited. The fish were quiet today. He started digging in the sand. His hand hit a hard object. His fingers wrapped around it and pulled it up. It was a piece of something. It had marks on it. Thomas began to wonder. He wondered who made it and why it was here. Instead of throwing it in the water, he put that into his pocket too.

He returned home and put his fishing gear in the shed. Thomas sat on the front porch and waited for his dad to come home. When his dad arrived, he asked, “Did you catch the big one today, Thomas?” Thomas put his head down and said no. His dad said, “Don’t worry son, someday you will.”

After dinner that night, Thomas pulled the two objects out of his pocket and laid them on the table. His dad asked, “What do you have there?” Thomas replied, “Just some trash I found down near the river.” After looking at the items, his dad asked him if he knew that American Indians once lived on this land. Thomas had heard that they did, but never really believed it.

His dad said, “Thomas, I think you found things they used long ago. The shiny object looks like copper. American Indians wanted copper from the English colonists. Copper was like gold to them. That other piece looks like pottery. It is a broken piece now, but I bet that at one time, it was a pot to hold water or food.”

Thomas looked up at his dad. His dad told him, “Maybe you didn’t catch the big fish but I think you found something even more important. Something that helps us understand our history. That is a big catch.” Thomas smiled. He thought to himself that maybe he would go fishing again tomorrow.

title: Was Pocahontas a princess?
text: The Powhatan Indians did not have princesses like the English. The Powhatan did not think Pocahontas was a princess. Her father, Powhatan, was one of the most powerful chiefs on the East Coast. Another name for Powhatan was Chief Wahunsonacock. He was the chief ruler of the area. Pocahontas became friends with one of the leaders of Jamestown, John Smith. This friendship helped the colonists and the Powhatan Indians get along better. During hard times, she brought food to the sick colonists. She then married John Rolfe. She helped bring peace to the area for eight years. When she and her husband Rolfe visited England, they treated her like royalty. Pocahontas wasn't an English princess, but she was a princess in her own way.

title: White-tailed Deer
text:
Eastern Woodland Indians used deer for food and their skins for clothing. The white-tailed deer is the largest plant-eating animal in Virginia. The Jamestown colonists and the Powhatan found many deer to use. Deer live almost anywhere from forests and mountains to fields and beaches.

Males are called bucks. Bucks weigh 150 to 300 pounds. Bucks have antlers that fall off and grow again. You might find antlers in the forests of Virginia. Females are called does. Does weigh 90 to 200 pounds. Fawns are baby deer.

Colonists used deer in large numbers as they settled Virginia. Deer almost died out by 1900. After that, the laws for using deer changed. The number of deer has grown quickly since that time. There are almost 1 million more deer living in Virginia now than there were during the time of the Jamestown colony.

title: The Supreme Court and Citizens United
text:
The Supreme Court is one of the three branches of our United States government. The other two are the executive branch (the president) and legislative branch (Congress). It is the Supreme Court's job to decide if laws passed are constitutional.

For many years, laws have limited the amount of money that companies, unions and wealthy people could spend to support a candidate in an election. This was done because many believed that large amounts of money would make the voice of that corporation, union or wealthy person louder than the voice of regular people.

In 2010 the Supreme Court heard arguments on a case called "Citizens United." The nine justices of the Court ruled that limiting the amount of money a corporation, union or person could spend on an election was a violation of free speech. It was unconstitutional to limit that speech. As a result, many groups have set up "super PACs," or political action committees. These super PACs can collect as much money as possible and use it to help candidates win elections. Many people feel that super PACs will change the way political campaigns are run. As usual, people disagree on the subject of super PACs. Some people believe it is a good way for groups to get their messages across, and some believe that more money in politics will lead to more corruption.

Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/ for more Connections and Current Events articles.

title: Ethical Behavior: King Phillip's War
text:
Metacomet was an American Indian who lived in New England. His father, Massasoit, was the great Wampanoag chief who had welcomed the Pilgrims in 1620. Metacomet became sachem (chief) in 1662 and continued friendly relations with the colonists. He became known as "King Philip."

The American Indians and colonists had their differences, but overall things were peaceful. They depended on each other as trading partners. However, some Colonial leaders began making unfair demands on the Indian tribes. The colonists ignored previous agreements and expanded into Indian territories. They forced natives to sell their land. They even demanded that Metacomet's people surrender all their weapons.

Metacomet organized an army. He formed an alliance with other American Indian tribes. His goal was to force the Puritan colonists out of Indian territory. Puritans and some American Indians united to fight Metacomet's warriors. Colonel Benjamin Church formed the first American Ranger unit in Plymouth Colony.

Many bloody conflicts followed. Both sides attacked and burned towns. They killed and enslaved hundreds of people. They destroyed land, crops and livestock. Every Colony and tribe in New England suffered huge losses. One of Church's soldiers killed Metacomet in 1676, and the battles stopped shortly after. Historians call this period King Philip's War.

Both sides of this conflict chose to abandon ethical behavior instead of solving their problems peacefully. The war forever changed the way of life for colonists and American Indians in New England. Was there any chance this war might have been avoided? Have you experienced people ignoring ethical behavior in order to get what they want?

title: Pocahontas Saves John Smith
text:
John Smith wrote about a time when Pocahontas saved his life. Not everyone today believes the story is true, but it has become a Virginia legend. John Smith’s story starts when the Powhatan Indians take him to their chief. They share a meal together. Read the passage below to see what he said happened after that.

Having feasted him after their best barbarous manner they could, a long consultation

was held, but the conclusion was, two great stones were brought before Powhatan: then

as many as could laid hands on him, dragged him to them, and thereon laid his head,

and being ready with their clubs to beat out his brains, Pocahontas, the king’s dearest

daughter, when no entreaty could prevail, got his head in her arms, and laid her own

upon his to save his from death: whereat the emperor was contented he should live to

make him hatchets, and her bells, beads and copper; for they thought him as well of all

occupations as themselves.

In line 1, Smith talked about eating with the Powhatan. What word does he use to describe it?

In line 2, they give two stones to Powhatan. Read line 4 again. What will Powhatan use the stones and clubs for?

Smith writes about Pocahontas in line 4. In line 5, she made an “entreaty” or request that her father not kill Smith. When this doesn’t work, what does she do? Read lines 5 and 6 to find how she saves his life. Write what she does here:

In line 6, what word does Smith use to call Powhatan a ruler?

Powhatan lets Smith live. What will Smith do for Powhatan and Pocahontas?

Smith wrote about this event 15 years after it happened. Do you think he remembered it exactly as it happened and why?

title: Highlight the Adverbs
text: Use any color to highlight three relative adverbs (where, when, why) in this week’s magazine. Underline the clause that contains the relative adverb and circle the noun that the clause modifies.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you were one of the Powhatan Indians during the time John Smith lived in Jamestown. Write a journal entry about the Jamestown colonists. Be sure to include your thoughts and feelings about the fort, the colonists and John Smith. Do you like the colonists living at Jamestown? How are the lives of your people changing?

title: Hardships and Homesickness
text:
Read this passage and think about it: Someone takes you from your home. They take you far away. You end up in a place where most people don't speak your language. They make you do really hard work. You don't know where you are or how to get back to your family.

That is what happened to slaves. In the 1650s, slave traders brought 8,000 to 10,000 slaves to the colonies each year. Historians do not know the exact number of slaves brought to the colonies. They think the number is between 9 and 15 million total.

They called the journey from Africa to North America the middle passage. They chained slaves together in the bottom part of the ship. The slaves lived in terrible conditions. That is, if they lived. Many slaves had illnesses or did not get enough water to drink. Up to one third of all slaves on a slave ship died during the middle passage. Historians think this number is between 3 million and 5 million.

Slaves faced many hard times. The slave traders put shackles or handcuffs on them. Then, they chained male slaves to each other. They allowed women and children to go free if it looked as if they would not cause trouble. Many times, slaves didn't know each other. Slave traders took slaves away from their families.

Once they arrived in North America, they worked in the fields on large plantations. In Virginia, slaves mostly worked the tobacco plantations. In other colonies, slaves worked in rice, indigo and sugar cane fields. Later, cotton fields kept slave labor in high demand. Tobacco, rice, indigo and sugar cane were cash crops. These are crops that made money. Yet, slaves never saw any of the money.

Plantation owners bought and sold slaves. Slaves were considered the property of the owners. Colonies made a lot of money with slave labor. Slaves working in the tobacco fields made a lot of money for Virginia.

In this issue, we are going to learn about tobacco in Virginia and how slavery was part of the agriculture (farming) in the colony. Slavery takes away someone's rights. Slavery was a part of the colonial culture. Today, when we hear the words, "All men are created equal," we know that we mean it.

title: Local Markets: Supporting Virginia-Grown Eats!
text:
There was a time when Virginia-grown tobacco was the finest thing an Englishman could have. Imagine - something grown in Virginia travelling all around the world. In today's world, the fruits and vegetable you eat can come from just about anywhere: Chile, Argentina, Mexico, the Caribbean Islands, even as far away as Europe.

But wait, didn't we just decide that things grown in Virginia are already world class? Absolutely, and that's why local markets are springing up all over the state. There are many advantages to buying and eating locally grown produce - the food is fresher and doesn't need preservatives on it. Also, it doesn't travel thousands of miles (which is hard on the environment). Best of all, it keeps your friends and neighbors in business.

Not far away, the White House is even sponsoring a local market. The U.S. Department of Agriculture launched a small program in 2009 to support America's small farmers by promoting locally grown food. Programs like this will not only help the economics of America, but they should also get us all healthy.

Virginia grows all types of foods, and no matter what time of year it is, you'll find something good at your local market. Here's a sample menu of food you could eat in a day that comes right from your home state:

Breakfast: Buckwheat pancakes with maple syrup, eggs, grits and fresh bread with strawberry preserves.

Lunch: Virginia ham sandwich, green beans, corn on the cob and peach ice cream.

Snacks: Tortilla chips with salsa, roasted peanuts and fresh watermelon.

Dinner: Fresh seafood, ham, crab, mixed-greens salad with Vidalia onion dressing, mashed or roasted potatoes and blackberry cobbler.

Now that menu sounds like world-class eating!

title: Tobacco and Slavery
text:
Jamestown started in 1607. It had a rough start. Many colonists became sick and died. They had a hard time making money. They tried making glass, growing silk and raising flax for linen. None of these worked. They didn't want to spend the time or use enough people to make it work. Then, almost five years after the start of Jamestown, they finally found a crop that would make money - tobacco.

A cash crop is one that is grown to sell for money rather than for use by the growers. In 1610, John Rolfe came to Jamestown. He learned that the Powhatan people were growing a type of tobacco. Many of the colonists did not like this kind of tobacco. By 1612, Rolfe brought another type of tobacco to the colonies and started growing it. This tobacco was a huge hit and made Virginia a lot of money. Over the next few years, the colonists shipped 2,300 pounds of tobacco to England.

Tobacco made Virginia the wealthiest of all the colonies. By 1640, they had shipped 1.5 million pounds of tobacco to England. Jamestown became a permanent settlement thanks to tobacco. Virginia was an agricultural, or farming, colony. Its agriculture was all about tobacco. Some people called tobacco "brown gold." Tobacco leaves turn brown as they dry. They called it gold since it made so much money for Virginia.

Growing tobacco takes large amounts of land and a large labor force. The labor force doesn't need to be skilled. Planters used indentured servants from England to do the labor at first. Then, they used African slaves. Africans came to Virginia against their will. They worked on the plantations as the labor force of tobacco. As Virginia made more money with tobacco, the planters realized they needed more slave labor. For some, tobacco was brown gold. For slaves, tobacco was an evil weed.

In 1619, 20 Africans came to Jamestown. The colonists treated them as indentured servants. They could earn their freedom. That changed over time. By 1662, the law defined children by their mother. If the mother was a slave, then so was the child. The Virginia General Assembly wrote a law in 1705 that said all Africans in the colony are slaves for life. Tobacco planters depended on slaves working in the fields.

Growing and harvesting tobacco takes almost a whole year. What would a slave have to do? Land needed to be cleared. Seeds had to be started in containers. Then the small plants had to be moved to a prepared field. Slaves worked from sunrise to sundown. One slave took care of 10,000 to 20,000 plants of tobacco, which meant working on four acres of land. Slave children as young as 7 years old worked in the fields. A slave was punished severely for not working as he or she was told. Overseers, or the bosses of the slaves, punished slaves for not working or for running away. Sometimes, they sold slaves to other plantation owners and broke up families. Slavery was cruel and terrible.

In 1859, Virginia made $12 million from tobacco. Tobacco planters made a lot of money from tobacco. Tobacco needs a large work force to grow it. Tobacco planters used slave labor to grow the tobacco. Tobacco and slavery made up the economy of colonial Virginia.

title: Slavery and Tobacco Facts
text:
John Rolfe married Pocahontas in 1614. In 1616, they sailed for England. Rolfe hoped tobacco would make money for the colony. Pocahontas died during that trip. Rolfe returned to the colony and worked on tobacco growing. In 1618, he married Jane Pierce. Rolfe owned a tobacco plantation called Bermuda Hundred. Before he died in 1622, he doubled the amount of tobacco sent to England. Rolfe made Jamestown an economic success.

Tobacco Timeline

1604 - King James I wrote how tobacco is a “custom… dangerous to the lungs”

1612 - John Rolfe grew tobacco people liked

1613 - 200 pounds of tobacco were shipped to England

1616 - 2,300 pounds of tobacco were shipped to England

1619 - 20 Africans arrived at Jamestown

1621 - Anthony Johnson arrived at Jamestown

1625 - 23 slaves lived in Virginia

1630 - A half million pounds of tobacco were shipped to England

1640 - 1.5 million pounds of tobacco were shipped to England

1670 - Anthony Johnson died

1705 - Virginia Assembly said slavery is for life

1775 - 100 million pounds of tobacco shipped to England

1790 - 287,959 slaves lived in Virginia

1859 - Virginia made $12 million from tobacco

By 1640, this poem became popular for tobacco:

Life is a smoke! - If this be true,
Tobacco will thy Life renew;
Then fear not Death, nor killing care
Whilst we have best Virginia here.

title: Tobacco and Slavery
text: When John Rolfe started growing tobacco, he started a big business. Look at the chart and you will see the growth. In 1616, the first big shipment to England was 2,300 pounds of tobacco. There were no slaves in the colony then. The first Africans arrived in 1619. Indentured servants from England worked the fields in 1616. By 1790, Virginia had 292,627 slaves living in the colony. In the 1800s, Virginia made millions of dollars from tobacco. Remember how hard it was for the colonists to find something that made money? An interesting note about tobacco is that King James I very much disliked it. He described smoking as a "custom loathsome to the eye, hateful to the nose, harmful to the brain, dangerous to the lungs …"

title: Anthony Johnson: Courage
text: Anthony Johnson, an African, arrived in Virginia in 1621. He worked in the fields of a tobacco plantation. No laws defined slavery at this time. He was listed as a servant in colonial records. The Powhatan Indians attacked the colonists in 1622 and killed almost 350 people. On the plantation where Johnson worked, 52 out of the 56 people died. Johnson survived. Johnson had courage. He faced hard times, but was able to overcome them. He married a woman named Mary and they had four children. In the 1640s, they bought their freedom and their own land. By 1650, they had a farm of 250 acres. In 1665, they sold the land and moved to Maryland. They rented 300 acres of land. In 1670, Anthony died. Since he was African, the land was given back to England and not to his wife. Anthony's courage helped him succeed in a time that was very hard for Africans in America.

title: Why did slaves come from Africa?
text: Why did slaves come from Africa? Why not somewhere else? Why weren't American Indians slaves in the colonies? American Indians were slaves for the Spanish. But many of them died from illness that came from Europe. American Indians died by the thousands because of European sickness. Fewer Africans died from European sickness. There are other reasons why Africans were the slaves of choice. Africans knew about the labor needed in an farming society. Africans also knew how to work with metal. They knew how to work with iron and make tools. American Indians only used softer metals, such as copper, for decorations.

title: Tobacco Hornworm
text: The tobacco hornworm grows to a length of 4 inches. Can you guess what it eats? If you said tobacco leaves, you are right! It also eats the leaves of tomatoes, eggplant, peppers and potatoes. Since it doesn’t like the heat from the sun, it feeds on the underside of leaves. That makes them hard to see. During the summer, slaves walked up and down rows of tobacco looking for the tobacco hornworm. It could easily destroy a crop of tobacco. A slave removed the hornworm, threw it on the ground and stomped on it to kill it. How did it get its name? Its body is green, but it has a red colored horn on one end. The hornworm becomes a moth when it is an adult.

title: Let's Write
text: Choose the person you want to be: Anthony Johnson or his wife Mary Johnson. Now, pick your assignment. If you are Anthony, write your will. Make sure you write about who gets what—the land, animals, house, furniture and so on. Be sure to include a letter to the state of Maryland asking your wishes to be followed. If you are Mary, write a letter to Maryland asking for the land to be returned to your family and the reasons why.

text:
The slave trade is often called the triangular trade. Why do you think it was called triangular trade?

What continent did slaves come from?

What continent shipped tobacco to Europe?

What did Europe ship to Africa?

What direction did slave ships travel from Africa to North America?

The trip from Africa to North America was called the middle passage. Why do you think it was called the middle passage?

title: From Spoonbread to Shepherd’s Pie
text:
What do you believe? What is important to you as a person? Make a list of 10 things that are very important to you. If you need ideas to get started, think about how you feel about these: family, religion, clothing, traditions, food and where you live. Next, ask yourself why you believe these things. Does anyone you know share some of these beliefs? Did you come up with these beliefs on your own or did someone help you to believe in them?

If you find a group of people with similar ideas and beliefs, you have found a group of people who shares the same culture. Most likely, you share ideas and beliefs with your family and friends. That doesn’t mean that you are the same as everyone you know. It means that you have some ideas, beliefs and customs in common with them. Every state and country has a mix of different cultures.

Virginia began with the cultures of one group of people, the American Indians. Today, Virginia is a mix of many cultures. People from many different countries live and work together. It’s kind of like the way different ingredients come together to make your favorite dish. How did Virginia get to be a mix of cultures?

The first group of people who arrived from another country was the Jamestown settlers from England. The Africans came soon after the English. By living in the same areas, these three cultures learned from each other. As other Europeans arrived, such as the Germans and the Scotch-Irish, more cultures were brought to America.

The mix of cultures makes America and Virginia interesting. When we learn about other cultures, we learn about other types of food, clothing, buildings and beliefs. Have you ever tried spoonbread, sauerkraut, corned beef and cabbage or shepherd’s pie? If you have, then thank the cultures of Africa, Germany, the Scotch-Irish and English. If you haven’t had some of these foods, then give them a try!

title: The Culture of Colonial Virginia
text:
What is culture? It is the beliefs and customs shared by a group of people. Even though the American Indians were the first to live in Virginia, many tribes meant many cultures. Most American Indians in Virginia lived in the Tidewater, Piedmont and Appalachian Plateau areas. People from Europe moved to Virginia in the 1600s and the culture started to change. The colonists at Jamestown were the first immigrants. Immigrants are people who move from one country to live in another country. The immigrants brought their cultures with them and these cultures changed Virginia.

The first group from Europe was the English. Do you remember what life was like for the Jamestown settlers? Many of them died from starvation and disease at a young age. The first houses they built were simple. The houses had wooden walls and dirt floors. None of these houses lasted. As the settlement became permanent, so did the buildings. In the 1700s, they built stronger houses, and some of them still stand today. Some of the English became very rich because of slave labor. The tobacco planters built mansions because they made a lot of money. Furniture changed from simple items to works of art. Instead of pottery, they used silver. They painted the walls or covered them with wallpaper. The leaders of Virginia came from this rich group of people. The rich landowners controlled the colony. They ruled the poorer farmers, women and Africans.

The English people were Christians who followed the Church of England. They settled close to the coast in the Tidewater and Piedmont regions. Africans also settled in these areas because many of them were slaves on tobacco plantations. The Africans spoke many different languages when they got here, but they learned to speak English.

The fall line became a natural dividing line. Trading posts grew along the fall line. Richmond was a town along the fall line. The word Richmond is an English word that means “strong hill.” Richmond became a city in 1737. The people of Richmond mostly traded tobacco.

In the late 1600s, more people arrived. They migrated, or moved, from Pennsylvania to Virginia. They originally came from Germany and settled in Philadelphia. As they tried to migrate west to find good land, they found the land already in use. They followed a migration route called the Great Wagon Road to the Shenandoah Valley in Virginia. By 1790, almost one-third of all white Virginians were from Germany. How did the Germans change the culture? They built houses out of stones and logs. They built two-story barns called “bank barns.” They used stoves for heating instead of fireplaces. The food they ate included sauerkraut, scrapple and raisin pies. The Germans did not like slavery. They were Christians who built Lutheran churches.

Another group of people, the Scotch-Irish, arrived in Pennsylvania in the mid-1700s. They were Scottish people who had first moved to Ireland. Ireland was a country of unrest and fighting. After 1740, they moved to Virginia in the Shenandoah Valley. The Scotch-Irish people also used the Great Wagon Road to travel south to Virginia. They were the frontier people, those who lived in between the English and the American Indians. They settled in unclaimed land and farmed it. They also were Christians and built Presbyterian churches. Many of them also became trappers, men who hunted and sold animal skins. Roanoke, a city in the Shenandoah Valley, grew along the Great Wagon Road. The Algonquian Indians used shells to make beads. They called the beads wampum and used them to trade for other goods. The word Roanoke means “shell money.”

Virginia started with the culture of the American Indians. Today, Virginia includes the cultures of the American Indians, Europeans and Africans.

title: Valley and Ridge Region
text: This region has mountains on each side and valleys in between. The western border is the Alleghany Mountains and the eastern border is the Blue Ridge Mountains. The largest valley in between is the Shenandoah Valley. There are many things to do in this region. In Shenandoah National Park, there are more than 300 buildings listed on the National Register of Historic Places. A popular place to hike is Old Rag Mountain. Old Rag Mountain is made of granite that formed a billion years ago. Skyline Drive is a 105-mile drive along the top of the Blue Ridge Mountains. Skyline Drive is the only public road through the park. The whole drive takes about three hours since the driving speed is only 35 miles an hour. You might see deer, black bear or wild turkey.

title: Wade’s Mill
text: What if you lived on a frontier? Living on the frontier means living on land that is mostly unused. Where would you live? How would you make a living? Captain Joseph Kennedy faced these same questions in the 1770s. He was one of the earliest Scotch-Irish settlers of Virginia's frontier. Captain Kennedy was one of the first people to settle in the Shenandoah Valley. How did he make a living? He started a flour mill in 1750. The mill was part of the Kennedy family for more than 100 years. James Wade bought the mill in 1882. The Wade family used the mill for the next 100 years. The mill still works and is one of the few in the country that uses millstones to grind flour. The Young family owns it today and calls it Wade's Mill. It is on the National Register of Historic Places. Visit the store in Staunton, Virginia, or visit the Web site at wadesmill.com

title: What was so great about the Great Wagon Road?
text: It started out as the Great Warrior Path. The Iroquois Indians first made the path that was later used by settlers. The Iroquois used it for hunting and trading. The path stretched from the Great Lakes through Pennsylvania, western Maryland, the valley of Virginia, and then through North and South Carolina. The Scotch-Irish immigrants settled around Philadelphia. They followed the path to Virginia looking for cheaper land. They called the path the Great Philadelphia Wagon Road. They traveled in Conestoga Wagons, or covered wagons. What was great about it? It was the most traveled road in history at the time. It was also more than 700 miles long by 1775!

title: Black Bear
text:
The black bear is the only type of bear living in the Shenandoah National Park. Before the Europeans arrived, about 2 million black bears lived in North America. Today, the number is around 600,000. About 5,000 to 6,000 of those bears live in Virginia.

Male black bears are called boars. They grow up to 6 feet long, 3 feet tall and weigh as much as 300 pounds. Female black bears are called sows. They are much smaller and weigh up to 175 pounds.

If you are in the Shenandoah National Park and you see a black bear, what should you do? First, you need to keep your distance when you see one. Second, do not run, but move slowly away. Bears chase moving things. You can't run as fast as a bear. Bears run up to 35 miles an hour!

title: Main Idea & Details

title: Scherenschnitte
text:
Have you ever made a paper snowflake? If you have, then you made something like a craft the Germans started in the 1600s. The word scherenschnitte is a German word that means the art of paper cutting. The Germans pronounce this word as sharon-shnit-teh. The Germans brought this art form to America. They used it to decorate birth and marriage papers or to decorate their homes. You can make the paper cutting out of any color paper. At first, they used pictures cut from white paper placed on a dark background. Later, it switched to a black paper cutout placed on a white background. An easy way to begin is to draw a heart. Then, cut out a picture within the heart. Let’s try it!

Materials needed

Black or other colored paper

White paper for the background

Glue

Pencil

Scissors

Note about paper: For the paper cutout, a thin craft paper, such as origami or wrapping paper will work best. You can use any kind of paper for the background.

Directions

Cut the craft paper into an 8-inch square. Fold it in half and draw a half of a heart on one side.

Use a pencil to draw half of a picture inside the heart. Many times, the cutout pictures were things from nature. Carefully cut out the pattern that you drew, including the heart around the cutout.

Unfold the paper cutout and glue it to the background paper.

Now, you have a scherenschnitte! Use it to decorate a card or frame it!

title: A Census Full of Treasure
text:
On April 2, 2012, the government released the 1940 census. A census is a count of all the people in the United States, and it is done every 10 years. It also gives other information about citizens’ jobs, income, birthplace and education level. The government only releases a census’ records to the public after 72 years have passed. The 1940 census was the first one done after the Great Depression and World War I. It shows how these events caused people to move around and where immigrants went. You can find interesting facts about family members and famous people. For example, the future President Ronald Reagan paid $135 in rent in 1940!

The 1940 census was the last time census takers went door-to-door to personally interview people and write down the information. For the 1950 census the government started using census questionnaires sent through the mail.

The release of the 1940 census data is different from past years. This information was made digital and released through the Internet. There are more than 3.8 million pages of data in this census. Genealogists, or people who study family backgrounds, use this information to trace family history. Researchers, like historians, often use the census as a primary source of information.

So, was this release a success? Well, so many people tried to get the information on its first day of release that the server crashed! If you would like to learn more about your family history you can go to the 1940 census site at: www.1940census.archives.gov.

title: Moving Virginia
text:
Have you ever moved? If you have always lived in the same place, have you ever helped someone else move? Moving is a lot of work! Most people don't move just for the fun of it. What are some of the reasons people move? Maybe they move for a better job. They might move to be closer to family members. They might move to go to college. Whenever someone moves, they usually have a good reason for doing so.

Why would anyone move a capital city? Virginia changed its capital city three times! Did they have a good reason for moving it? Let's find out.

The first capital was Jamestown. The important buildings of Jamestown burned down several times. Not only that, but the people became sick from the water supply. The water was too salty and swamp-like. They decided to move the capital to a better location. They didn't move it too far, though. Williamsburg is less than 10 miles away from Jamestown.

Williamsburg was the second capital. Why isn't it still the capital? From 1704-1779, the state capital was Williamsburg. This location wasn't the best choice, though. Bad luck struck again when a fire broke out and burned down the main building. Even though some people wanted to move the capital again, they rebuilt at Williamsburg and stayed a little longer. The American Revolution started in 1775 near Boston, Massachusetts. The fighting spread to Virginia. Soon, people were afraid that Williamsburg was at risk of being attacked by the English. In 1779, the General Assembly voted to move the capital further inland. They chose Richmond as the new location.

They built the state capitol building on Shockoe Hill. It has a view of the James River. Thomas Jefferson designed the center of the building. The General Assembly started using the building in 1788. They added front steps and side wings in 1906. The Virginia Capitol survived some hard times. Much of Richmond burned during the Civil War, but not the capitol. The second floor collapsed in 1870 and killed 62 people. They called this the Capitol Disaster. The building survived the hard times. Every January, the General Assembly meets in the building to make decisions for the people of Virginia. The General Assembly is the oldest representative government in America. What started at Jamestown, and then moved to Williamsburg, continues today in Richmond.

title: Underground Additions to Virginia's Capitol
text:
When something is more than 200 years old, it usually needs a little attention. That was certainly the case with the Virginia state capitol building in Richmond.

The building was outdated, but it was also too small. But how could workers make it bigger and keep it looking the same? Well, they decided to renovate underground.

Since the capital of Virginia moved to Richmond in 1780, the capitol building has only been renovated twice: once in 1904 when the east and west wings were added, and again in 1962 to update the electrical system and add air-conditioning. Needless to say, the building was due for another upgrade.

This was no small upgrade, either. Work started in 2004 and cost more than $100 million. When the renovations were done, they had replaced all the mechanical, plumbing and water systems, upgraded the heating, air conditioning and electrical systems, protected the building from water and humidity damage, restored the original art and architectural features, cleaned up the exterior, and built an entire visitors center for the capitol - underground. That must have been dirty work.

Since the restoration, some important visitors have come to the capitol, including Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Phillip of England, President Barack Obama and even Thomas Jefferson (OK, OK it was just an actor portraying Thomas Jefferson).

If you'd like to see this magnificent building yourself, make a trip to Richmond or visit www.vacapitol.org to take a virtual tour.

title: Virginia’s Capitals
text:
Why three capitals?

Why did the capital of Virginia move so much? The capital changed places three times after several fires, a poor water supply and a need for a better location. Richmond became Virginia’s capital in 1780. Let’s find out what happened from 1607 to 1780 that caused the capital to change places three times.

Jamestown

Jamestown, the first permanent English settlement, was Virginia’s first capital. The first representative government met at Jamestown in 1619. The General Assembly began at Jamestown. Why isn’t Jamestown the capital today? There are a couple of good reasons. The colony started at Jamestown, but it wasn’t easy. Do you remember the problems they had? The drinking water was brackish, a mix of salt and fresh water. The colonists needed fresh water to stay healthy. The salty water caused many colonists to become ill. Then, there was fire. Not just one fire, but three. The first one happened in Jan. 1608. A new shipment of supplies had just arrived. Most of those supplies and the storehouse burned to the ground. In 1676, some of the colonists were unhappy with the government of the colony. The angry colonists burned down the church, statehouse and at least 16 houses. Twenty-two years later in 1698, the statehouse burned down again.

Williamsburg

Students at the College of William and Mary thought it was a good idea to move the capital. The College of William and Mary was located at the Middle Plantation about 10 miles away. The General Assembly agreed with them. They moved the capital to the Middle Plantation in 1699. They changed the name of the Middle Plantation to Williamsburg. After the move, Jamestown quickly changed. In 1716, the only buildings at Jamestown were a few houses, a church and a courthouse. Jamestown soon became fields for farming. Virginia was a strong colony, though. The 104 colonists who came to Jamestown in 1607 gave Virginia a place to begin. When the capital moved to Williamsburg, more than 60,000 people lived in the colony.

They built the first government building at Williamsburg by 1705. To avoid fire, the building did not have fireplaces. Without any heat, the colonists found the building cold and damp. In 1723, they added fireplaces and chimneys to the building. Almost 25 years later, the building caught fire and burned to the ground. Some people wanted to rebuild. Others wanted to move the capital to another place. They wanted the capital located near trade and transportation. They took a vote and decided to stay in Williamsburg and rebuild. The new building opened in 1753.

Many famous people made history in the building. This included Patrick Henry, George Washington and Thomas Jefferson. Many meetings and speeches that led to American independence from England took place in the building. The last time the General Assembly met in the building was in 1779. They decided to move the capital to Richmond.

Richmond

Why move the capital to Richmond? The colonists wanted independence from England. By 1779, the fight for independence from England was four years old. They thought Richmond was a safer place for a capital city. This location was away from the coast and safer from English attack. As people moved west into Virginia, people could get to Richmond more easily than to Williamsburg. Richmond was a trade city located on the James River. Richmond became the capital in 1780. All of these reasons made Richmond a good place for a capital.

title: Coastal Plain and Piedmont
text: The Virginia Capital Trail is a bike path that connects the three capital cities of the commonwealth. The trail is 54 miles long. The trail starts in Williamsburg at the Governor's Mansion. Then, it runs along the Colonial Parkway to Jamestown Island. The trail then heads west and follows Route 5. The colonists used that same road as they headed west into Virginia. Along Route 5, bikers and hikers pass homes of former presidents and battle sites of the American Revolution and the Civil War. The end of the path follows the James River and takes bikers to Richmond. Explore more than 400 years of history while riding along more than 50 miles of trail!

title: Thomas Jefferson
text: Thomas Jefferson designed the capitol building used by the Virginia General Assembly since 1788. Jefferson was a man of many talents. He started college at the age of 16, knew seven languages and wrote over 16,000 letters. Born in Albemarle County, Virginia, he attended the College of William and Mary and became a lawyer. He held elected positions such as representative to the House of Burgesses, governor of Virginia and president of the United States. Jefferson was the main writer for the Declaration of Independence. As the third president of the United States, Jefferson bought a large piece of land known as the Louisiana Purchase. It more than doubled the size of the United States. He started the University of Virginia. He sold his personal books that started the Library of Congress. He died on July 4, 1826, 50 years after the signing of the Declaration of Independence.

title: Is it capital or capitol?
text: You use the word "capital" when talking about a city. For example, the capital of Virginia is Richmond. You use the word "capitol" when talking about a government building. A capitol is the building where representatives meet to make decisions for the state. The General Assembly first met at the Jamestown Church. Starting in 1632, they met at the colonial governor's house. In 1641, the General Assembly bought the governor's house for 15,700 pounds of tobacco. That capitol burned down in 1656. Thomas Jefferson designed the capitol building for Richmond. When you see the word by itself with an uppercase first letter, such as Capitol, it usually means the building in Washington, D.C., where representatives make laws for the country.

title: Northern Gray Squirrel
text: If you visit the Virginia Capitol, you will most likely see a Northern Gray Squirrel. This squirrel grows to be between 14 and 21 inches long, which includes a 7-to-10-inch tail. Their color is gray to a yellowish brown, and their tails are outlined in white. They weigh just a little over a pound. Each squirrel family has about two litters of squirrels each year. Two to three baby squirrels make up a litter. Most Northern Gray Squirrels stay close to their home, which covers an area of 25 acres. They live in nests or in trees called dens. The squirrel's coat changes to a light gray during winter. These squirrels do not hibernate, but a bad storm could keep the squirrel in the den for several days.

title: Make a Capital City Flip Book
text:
Materials

8½-inch x 11-inch white paper
ruler
colored pencils or thin markers
scissors
optional: glue and construction paper

Directions

Fold an 8½-inch by 11-inch piece of paper in half lengthwise (a hotdog fold). Measure a strip of one inch along one of the wide ends. After marking the 1-inch strip, carefully cut the strip from the paper.

Place the folded paper in front of you, with the cut side closest to you. Measure the cut half into three smaller pieces: First, place the ruler along the 11-inch piece and mark it so you have three even pieces. Lightly draw a straight line from the cut edge to the folded edge. Use the scissors to cut along this line. Do not cut past the fold.

Place the folded paper in front of you, the three flaps facing you with the one-inch strip along the bottom. Now, you need colored pencils or thin markers to design your flap book.

In the 1-inch strip, write the title “Virginia’s Capital Cities.” Use color and creativity when you make your letters.

Write the names of the capitals, one on each of the cut flaps. On the first flap to your left, write Jamestown. On the middle flap, write Williamsburg. On the third flap, write Richmond. Use color and creativity when you make your letters.

Open the Jamestown flap. Write facts and draw pictures about Jamestown as the capital of Virginia. Use this issue to help you. Be sure to stay inside the area for Jamestown only.

Do the same for the Williamsburg and Richmond flaps.

To display your flap book, glue it to a piece of construction paper. You can also punch holes in the construction paper and place it in your notebook.
