title: The Age of Discovery and Colonization
text:
During the 15th and 16th centuries, European explorers started sailing all over the world. European kings wanted people to explore new areas to get more money for them and to help their country become more powerful in the world.

We have high tech instruments to help us sail the seas today, but back then they only had the sun and stars to figure out where they were going. Exploring and sailing was pretty dangerous.

So, why did they do it? Some were looking for adventure, many wanted to trade with other places, and some wanted to spread the word of God.

One thing many explorers wanted to do was find a shorter and faster way to get to Asia. People loved the things that came from Asia, especially countries like India and China.

Explorers knew that if they could find a shorter way to get there, they would be rich. The race was on to find a northwest passage!

The first explorers didn't know that a whole continent stood in the way. Their desire to find a northwest passage led them straight into what is now the United States, Canada and... well... all of North and South America.

title: Research Shows Madagascar Was Founded by Women
text:
Picture an ancient ship full of explorers, searching for a new land. Many people would imagine that such a ship was filled with male passengers and crew. Though many explorers were men, scientists have discovered that the founders of Madagascar were a group of 30 women who traveled a long way from their home!

Madagascar is an island off the east coast of Africa in the Indian Ocean. The women's ship traveled 5,000 miles from Indonesia to Madagascar, stranding them there. How do scientists know this? DNA researchers have studied 3,000 blood samples of people from Indonesian islands and compared them to samples from 300 people from Madagascar (called the Malagasy).

They discovered that many Malagasy have an Indonesian gene in their DNA. This gene was passed down from generation to generation of Malagasy. Computer simulations have calculated that only 30 Indonesian women were responsible for beginning the Madagascar population about 1,200 years ago. Most people from Madagascar today have a mix of Indonesian and African DNA, and are descended from these 30 women.

Researchers have also been able to trace a special chromosome that is only found in men in the Malagasy people. Can you guess where it came from? If you guessed Indonesia, you are right! It looks like a few men as well as women sailed on that ship to Madagascar so long ago.

title: The Age of Discovery and Colonization
text:
1. Columbus

Columbus was born in Italy in 1451. He was sure he could find a northwest passage, but he had trouble getting a king to give him money to do it. When he went to King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain, he got lucky. It took years, but he finally convinced them to finance the trip. They gave him three ships, the Nina, the Pinta and the Santa Maria. He thought he should be able to sail directly from Spain to India. What he didn’t know is that a whole continent stood in his way. That continent was North America. In 1492 Columbus landed in the Caribbean islands. He was so sure he had reached India, that he called the people who lived there “Indians.” When Columbus died he still thought he had found India. His discovery started a real rush by other European countries to send their own explorers to start colonies in the New World. Colonies were made of groups of people that would live in the New World, but stay loyal to their old country. That way the old country could have a port for trade.

2. Vasco Da Gama

Vasco Da Gama was an explorer from Portugal who found a way to get from Portugal to India in 1497. He wanted to trade for spices. He was the first person to sail around Africa to get to India. Until then people did not realize the Indian Ocean was actually connected to the Atlantic Ocean. One of his “friends” who was jealous of his popularity said Da Gama had committed treason against Spain. This meant he was trying to hurt Spain. He was hanged in 1519 for something he did not do.

3. Balboa

In 1510 Balboa, who was a Spanish explorer, set off on a great adventure. He was looking for gold in the new world, but ended up not only finding his treasure, but becoming the first European to see what would one day be called the Pacific Ocean. He claimed all the land that touched the ocean for Spain. Then, on a later trip, he started the very first European settlement in South America. The Spanish wanted to spread the word of God to the American Indians, so many Spanish missionaries came to the New World. Many Spanish people settled in areas that did “touch the ocean” as well as South America, and soon became the major group of people there.

4. Magellan

Ferdinand Magellan was born in Portugal in 1480. At first he did all of his exploring for the king of Portugal. But he got into a fight with the king because he wouldn’t give Magellan the money he needed to find a northwest passage to Asia. Magellan decided to sail for the king of Spain instead. In 1519 Magellan started his greatest trip. He sailed around the world! It took almost three years and was very difficult. As his boat sailed across the ocean first seen by Balboa, he gave it the name “Pacific” which means peaceful. The trip wasn’t so peaceful though. The men were so hungry that they ate rats and drank yellow, stinking water. It was so hard that out of the five ships that started the trip, only one made it back. To make matters worse, only 18 people survived out of 270. Even Magellan died because of a fight with Indians on one of the last islands they visited. As a result of Magellan’s trip around the globe, he proved for sure that the Earth was round. It also proved that the Americas were not part of Asia, but part of a totally new continent.

5. Henry Hudson

In 1609 Henry Hudson, from England, thought that if he went farther north, he could find a northwest passage to Asia. He worked for a company called The Dutch East India company, that wanted a shorter route to Asia. The company thought that if Hudson sailed around the Arctic Ocean, he would be able to get to the Pacific. However, ice stopped him, and he had to go south. He got to what is now New York and thought he could go up what is now called the Hudson River to get to the Pacific Ocean. That didn’t work because the river got too narrow and he had to turn back. He didn’t find a shorter way to Asia, but he did discover the Hudson River. Because of his discovery in the New World, many Dutch people came to start colonies. His discoveries also lead to more exploration of Canada.

Changes in the Americas

Once the European explorers came, things changed for the Indians. The Europeans taught them about a different religion, and brought horses, cattle and food they had never seen before. Many explorers conquered the people they met. That meant they fought each other and the explorers won. Then they told the Indians what to do. Many explorers also brought diseases that had never been in the new world before, and many Indians died. Over time, the American Indians lost their land and their way of life. Explorers changed things forever!

title: The Atlatl
text:
Atlatl is an Aztec word that means "spear thrower." Before the bow and arrow were invented, early American Indians used the atlatl to help them hunt animals for food. The atlatl was a special spear thrower that let the American Indians throw their spears farther and with more power than they could by using their arms alone.

Historians believe people have been using the atlatl for more than 40,000 years. The American Indians even used the atlatl as a weapon against the Spanish when they came to the New World in the late 1400s. The atlatl could throw a spear so hard that it could pierce the metal armor worn by the Spanish soldiers.

Today, many people have rediscovered the atlatl and have started having competitions to see who can use the atlatl to throw a spear the farthest and who can come closest to hitting the center of a target.

title: Madrid, Spain
text:
Italian born Christopher Columbus lived in Spain throughout some of his life. Spain is a very old country, and the Spanish people are proud of their history, music, art, food and entertainment.

Madrid is the capital of Spain and is one of its most beautiful and famous cities. People who live in Madrid today have a very pleasant way of life. They start their days a bit later than we do here in America, but they make up for their late start by staying up later as well!

In Spain, most schools are very challenging. The schools don't usually offer sports and clubs as American schools do. Instead, Spanish schools focus on studying and learning important subjects that will help children later in life. Children are still involved in sports and other activities, but these are done on their own after school.

Most young people in Spain live at home until they get married, so it isn't unusual to find young adults in their 20s and even older still living with their parents. Parents and older relatives are highly respected in Spain and are treated with honor. Mothers take great pride in their homes and keep them as clean and organized as possible.

Mealtimes are very important to the Spanish people, and they enjoy eating their meals together, with either friends or family. While Americans often eat on the run, the Spanish take their time and make their meals last as long as they can.

In the evenings, most young people go to the movies and spend time in the cafes with their friends. They stay out later than many American teenagers do, and their friends are a very important part of their lives.

Just as it was in Christopher Columbus's day, Spain is still a beautiful and exciting place to live. Children growing up in Madrid have plenty to see, do and enjoy.

title: Disagreements in the World
text:
When was the last time you had a fight or argument with someone? Was it today at lunch? How about last night with your mom or dad? Conflict means sharp disagreements, and disagreements often mean big arguments. But disagreements don't just happen between people. They can happen between states, countries and cultures.

People usually try to work together to achieve their goals. If you work with a group at school to finish a project, that's cooperation. Adults often work together to help their community. They may want to get better education for kids, get better laws in their community or find better ways to use energy. They work together to improve their lives and democracy. But sometimes, arguments start, and the purpose is lost because conflict and anger take over. Can you think of a time when this happened to you or a friend?

But sometimes, when an argument starts, it's really hard to stop it, or even keep control of what happens because of it. Your friend may not talk to you for a week, your mom may ground you, or a country could go to war.

That's what we're going to look at this week... conflict. The conflict could be personal, between cities or states, or even a war. It can end a friendship, alter a country and change the world.

title: Swedish Stonehenge or Burial Monument?
text:
Are you surprised to learn that scientists often disagree with each other? One scientist has a new idea and some facts to back it up. Other scientists say the idea is incorrect. Sometimes the argument ends with a change in scientific thinking. For example, paleontologists once thought dinosaurs were slow animals that dragged their tails behind them. Dr. Bob Bakker used fossil evidence to show that this was not true. He said dinosaurs were fast, smart and carried their tails high in the air. He was called crazy, but now his ideas have been scientifically proven. That's the way science works. Someone finds evidence that challenges current thinking, and over time that evidence is either shown to be false or proven to be true.

Something similar may be happening in Sweden. "Ale's Stones," found near a Swedish fishing village, are 59 large boulders arranged in the shape of a 220-foot ship. Archaeologists believe the arrangement is about 1,000 years old and was used as a burial monument. But a new research team now says the site is closer to 2,500 years old and was built to be an astronomical calendar. This would make Ale's Stones similar to Stonehenge in England. Other scientists disagree. They point to other small structures like Ale's Stones throughout Sweden that are between 500 and 1000 years old. Which side is right? Researchers will continue to investigate the site, but perhaps this scientific disagreement will end up changing what people believe about these ancient stones.

title: Conflict and Change
text:
Is conflict always a bad thing? Well, no it isn't. People will always have disagreements. The trick is to disagree without being disagreeable. That means that when you have a problem with another person you talk about the problem. You don't call them names, yell or get off the topic. It's possible to solve almost any problem if both people follow these simple rules. Unfortunately, it doesn't always happen.

What are some conflicts that we often see around us and in our world? One of the most dangerous kinds of conflicts is between nations. World War II was a conflict like that. When the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor the war began for the United States! Germany and Japan wanted to take over other countries, so many countries went to war to stop them from doing that. There are also political and cultural conflicts. The war in Iraq is a conflict that involves both political and cultural problems. Sometimes people from different cultures cannot see past their own point of view. Conflict happens because they would rather fight than talk about differences. The Twin Towers in New York City were attacked on 9/11 because the terrorists who drove the jet liners into the buildings didn't like policies the United States had in their country.

Conflict can involve political views. Sometimes the two political parties in the United States, the Republicans and Democrats, get angry with each other because they believe in different things. However, great things can get done when they work together. Many wars are fought over boundary lines. Sometimes people want to use natural barriers like rivers to divide areas, other times people want to make up where the lines will be. This caused such a problem in 1835 between Ohio and Michigan that they went to war with each other over where the boundary between the two states would be. Luckily it didn't last very long!

Water rights cause conflict too. For example, many states are concerned about how the Colorado River water is used. The states downstream don't like it when states upstream use too much water! Conflict comes from so many things! Where will a new prison be built? Should we drill oil in the Gulf of Mexico? What about oil spills? What is the best way to get rid of global warming? Conflict is everywhere. It's how we deal with it that makes the difference. It can give us a new beginning, or be the beginning of the end. It's up to us.

title: Differences in Primary and Secondary Sources
text:
When you do research sometimes you might want to get information from a primary source or “right from the horse’s mouth” (that’s an idiom that means directly from the person who said it).

This kind of information can come from diaries, newspapers, legal and historical writings and news magazines. Secondary sources are things that use primary sources for their information. That would be your textbook, encyclopedias and magazines. You can find both primary and secondary sources on the Internet.

Think of it this way, you tell me you bought a video game. That makes you the primary source for this information. Then I tell someone else you bought a video game. That makes me a secondary source because I used you for my information. Primary and secondary sources give you everything you need for research on anything!

title: What is a sister city?
text:
Did you know that some cities have sisters? A sister city is a city that has a special relationship with a city in a different country. The relationship is formed either legally, which means by law, or socially, which means by friendship. A sister city can also be known as a twin town.

After World War II, in 1947, people thought it would be a good idea to reach out to other communities and make friends with different kinds of people and learn about their culture. Kind of like what you do in your classroom! People also thought that it would help mend the wounds of war and help countries stop thinking of each other as enemies.

One result of having a sister city is that people want to visit their sister! It helps tourism and encourages trade when people visit places. It can also lead to more business for both cities.

Does the place you live have a sister city? Do some research and find out. If your city or town doesn’t have a sister, see if cities nearby do.

Where would you like your community to “twin”? Look at a map to help you decide.

title: My State is Great!
text:
This week it's YOUR turn to write the newspaper. That's right, you are going to write this week's newspaper all about your state. It's going to take some research, curiosity and a sharp pencil. This week the newspaper is your creation. Some of the things you are going to be writing about are landforms, imports and exports, geographic regions, your state symbols, and you even get to retell a folktale. So why wait another minute, let's get going.

Take a walk around your state

title: Write Your Own Current Event Article

title: No Other State is Like Mine
text:
Imports and Exports

Every state has special things that it grows or makes that it can sell to other places. That's called exporting. But there are things it can't make or grow as well. So people have to import those things. For example, most states need to import oranges. The climate in most of the United States isn't hot enough long enough to grow them. So we import them from Florida and California. Do some research and find out what your state exports and imports. What natural, human and capital (money) resources are needed to produce these things in your state? Then write about it.

What important landmarks and historical sites are in your state? Write about at least three of them on a piece of paper. Then draw one of them.

title: I Really Want That!
text:
There it is... the bike of your dreams! It's red, fast and begging to be yours. So how do you get it? You could beg your parents to buy it for you. That could work, but the bike costs a LOT of money. You probably couldn't even hope to get it until your birthday or Christmas, and then only if you were really lucky. So what now? You could ask your fairy godmother. Well, maybe not.

The truth is, you may have to save up enough money to get it yourself. Save? What's that all about? Saving up money for something you really want isn't always easy. What if you want to go out with your friends and spend money on fun stuff like a new CD or a new DVD? Maybe you just want to spend some money on a new toy for your dog. Can you save and spend money at the same time?

This week in World Community Studies Weekly we are going to talk about just how you could get that bike, MP3 player or whatever it is you really want. The truth is, with a good plan, you can get the things you want. But it does take a plan, and sometimes you have to give some things up that you don't want so very much to get that big thing you really want.

We're also going to talk about how you get money to buy what you want in the first place. That has to do with jobs. Having a job is a big way people get money. Kids can have jobs too. There are lots of ways to make money if you just take a good look around and see what other people need. People do lots of different jobs when they grow up too. Why is this so important? Well, hold on to your piggy bank and take a look inside. We'll decide if it's time to break that bank to get what you want, or save it for later.

title: What is a Personal Economic Choice?
text:
A personal economic choice is just a choice you make about what you want to do with your money. Are you going to save it, give it away or spend it? Some people spend every dime they have all the time. What is the problem with that? Well, it means that if there is something big they want to buy, they will never have the money to buy it.

Some people spend a lot of money on things that just don't last very long. We call those things non-durable goods. Durable is a word that means that something lasts a long time, so non-durable means it doesn't last long. Going out to eat is a non-durable good. It's lots of fun, but once you're done eating it's gone.

Think of a kid who spends all of his or her money buying snacks, going to the movies and on lots and lots of little toys that cost a dollar or two. Will that kid ever have enough money to buy that bike? The chances are that they won't. Even worse, they won't have anything to show for all the money they spent. The snacks will be gone, the movies will be forgotten, and the toys will break or be lost. That doesn't mean you can never buy things that are non-durable, but it does mean you need to think about your money and how you spend it. Giving up one thing for something else you want more is called an opportunity cost. There is a cost of not getting one thing, for the opportunity to get something else.

How do you get the things you really want? You make a budget. A budget is a spending plan. If you want that bike, you decide to save a certain amount of your money each week for the bike, then budget a smaller amount that you can spend for fun stuff. Having a budget doesn't mean you can't have fun, it means you have a plan to get the big things you really want.

It always helps to have a job. It takes money to get the things you want, so both kids and adults look for jobs to help them do that. People get jobs that they can do. Sometimes it takes a college education to do a job, sometimes it just takes some on-the-job training. We need people for lots of jobs to meet the needs of our country. We need people to drive trucks to deliver things we need to stores, to teach, to write books, to repair roads and on and on.

Some states or countries have a lot of people who are good at (or specialize) in one kind of job, like farming or making steel. When this happens, that state or country can trade their extra steel for something else they need. For example, one state may have lots of oranges, but not enough trees for lumber. Another state has lots of trees for lumber but no oranges. Trading with each other gives each state or country the things they need that they can't make or grow.

title: Ponds and Lakes
text:
We get a lot of our fresh water from ponds and lakes. A pond is a small body of water that has the same water temperature from top to bottom. It is shallow enough to allow rooted plants to grow from the bottom of the pond, which is usually mud. It is calm with no waves.

Lots of algae grow in ponds, which is great food for animals like fish. Dragonflies and mosquitoes and lots of other bugs love ponds! They need the calm water to lay their eggs and allow them to hatch. Frogs and toads lay their eggs in ponds too.

A lake, on the other hand, is too deep to have rooted plants growing in it, except at the edges. Sometimes lakes are so big they actually have waves.

A lake does not have the same temperature from top to bottom. In fact the sun cannot get all the way to the bottom, so lots of fish and animals live in the upper, warmer layer of water. Some lakes are so big that they rarely freeze in the winter. Lots of fish live in lakes, like bluegill, bass and catfish. It is very important to protect lakes and ponds because they are a great place to get fresh water. Many people make their living from lakes too. Many people fish to make money by selling the fish they catch. Others turn areas around lakes into great places to take a vacation.

title: Haym Salomon, Financial Hero
text:
In 1975, the U.S. Postal Service issued a stamp [right] honoring Haym Salomon as a “Financial Hero of the American Revolution,” yet many Americans have never heard of him. Who was Haym Salomon?

Haym Salomon was a Jewish immigrant from Poland who came to New York City in 1772. He became a successful financial broker (someone who arranges business transactions). Salomon sided with the patriots and joined the Sons of Liberty. The British arrested him as a spy. In jail he became an interpreter for German soldiers but secretly encouraged many to desert (leave the army). He was supposed to be executed, but he escaped. He set up a new business in Philadelphia.

Salomon could see that the Continental Congress was struggling to get money to support the war. American soldiers did not have enough pay, food or supplies. Salomon began raising money. He helped Robert Morris, the Superintendent of Finance, get loans from France and other countries. He often made personal loans to the government and to American leaders like James Madison, Thomas Jefferson and James Monroe. When George Washington needed money for the Battle of Yorktown, he said, “Send for Haym Salomon.” Salomon’s clear thinking, generosity and dedication helped our country win its independence.

The Treaty of Paris in 1783 ended the war, but the new country still had money problems. Salomon continued to help America raise money. He was also a strong leader in Philadelphia’s Congregation Mikveh Israel. He worked to overturn a law that kept non-Christians from holding office.

Now that you have learned Haym Salomon’s story, why do you think history has often overlooked him? How has clarity of thought led to a positive result in your life?

title: Fake or Real News
text:
Have you ever read something online, like on social media sites, that sounded fishy? Maybe it was real, but it could be fake news! The big danger, though, is news that sounds real but isn’t. Fake news is becoming common because anyone can post things online. Fake news can be in the form of a story. Fake news can be a photo or video that has been changed. The problem is that these fake items look real. Fake news can cause problems and it spreads misinformation.

Sam Wineburg, a professor, did some research. He found that 80 percent of students cannot tell the difference between real and fake news. Do you want to become a media-savvy person? You have to be able to find out if news is real or fake. How do you do that? You have to become a detective and search for the truth. You can learn about the author or company that posted the news. You have to think about the purpose of the news. Is there a hidden plan to get you to buy something or to make you think a certain way? Your teacher or a trusted adult can help you learn how to spot fake news. It takes a little time, but democracy depends on real information! Do your part and discover what is real and what is fake!

title: Changes to Your Environment
text:
Everything was going just fine, then BAM! You have a new baby brother. Everything was going just fine, then BAM! You're moving to a new city. Or maybe everything was going just fine, and BAM, your best friend has to move to a new state. Change happens all the time, and to everybody. Nothing stays the same for very long.

We say that change is inevitable (that means you can't stop it from happening) and it is universal, which means it happens everywhere.

Change isn't always bad. That new baby brother may turn out to be your best friend. Moving to a new city may be the best thing that ever happened to you. And your friend might just invite you to spend a few weeks with him or her this summer. Everything changes.

If it weren't for change we would never have gotten rid of slavery, invented the telephone or even video games. So, the big question is, how does change impact our lives? That's what we're going to look at this week in our World Community Studies Weekly newspaper.

People have made a lot of changes to the environment. Is that good or bad? What can we do to help the environment, anyway? What are we doing that hurts the environment? Why does that even matter? Well, "change" the page by looking inside to find a few of these answers!

title: How Clean is Our Water?
text:
The Environmental Protection Agency is an important part of our government. The job of the EPA is to protect people's health and the environment.

One part of the EPA's job is to make sure that the water in the United States is clean and safe. States have to test samples from bodies of water and report to the EPA every two years. The samples are rated good if the water is safe for whatever it's used for. If the tests show that the water isn't safe, it is rated impaired. (Impaired is another word for damaged.)

Recently, reports show that only 61 percent of our nation's rivers and streams are safe. Only 55 percent of our lakes, ponds and reservoirs are safe. But the worst news was for estuaries, the places where rivers meet the oceans. Less than half of them were rated good.

What can you do to help make our water cleaner? Conserve water, don't throw trash in storm drains and ask your parents to get rid of things like paint and pesticides properly. Your family could join a group that adopts a stream and volunteers to clean up trash. And keep learning about water and pollution. The more you know, the more you'll be able to help.

title: Humans and Their Environment
text:
People and the Weather

How do people impact (change) the environment? It’s hard to believe people, who are pretty small, can change the weather all over the world. But they can! There are a LOT of people on the Earth. When lots of people do things that can hurt the Earth, it’s hard for the Earth to clean it up fast enough. Things like exhaust from cars and factories make greenhouse gases that can cause global warming.

Urbanization

Urbanization means to make more and bigger cities. That means trees have to be cut down, there is less grass and green space, and pavement seems to be everywhere. We already have a built-in scrub brush that takes away greenhouse gases — trees and plants! Trees and plants actually clean the air for the Earth. The fewer plants and trees there are, the less air can be cleaned. So as more and more cities grow bigger and bigger it would help all of us to keep more trees and give more green space for people (and the air) to enjoy!

Clear Cutting

The Amazon Rain forest is one of the areas on our earth that makes the oxygen that you breathe. Unfortunately much of it is cut down every year. Almost one half of all the Earth’s species of animals and plants live there. In fact many of our medicines come from rain forest plants. Every time we lose acres of rain forest, we lose plants that might have cured a disease, and animals may become extinct. Here’s the good news! People have started to realize the wonderful resource the rain forest is to all of us. In recent years, clear cutting of trees (deforestation) has slowed down. The number of new trees being planted is growing slowly. People can make a difference.

Weather Changes

Weather is what happens outside from one minute to the next. It can change a lot from day to day. Climate is what happens with the weather over a lot of years. What kind of climate changes can people cause to happen? Well, greenhouse gases are causing a melting of ice at the poles. Snow and glaciers are melting on mountain tops, and the rate of animal extinctions (that’s when an entire species disappears) seems to be happening faster and faster. Some populations of animals are moving from areas they have lived in for thousands of years. When the oceans heat up there are stronger hurricanes, floods, droughts and crop failures. Wow! That all sounds pretty bad! But the good news is this — all of us together can stop global warming. You can walk instead of using a car for short trips, you can plant more trees, and you can write to our government and ask our representatives to do the things necessary to save our Earth. It’s up to all of us. We can change things for the better, or we can let change bring us more problems. Change is inevitable and universal. This is one kind of change we can control, if we really want to do it!

title: The First Car
text: Karl Benz built the first internal combustion engine for cars in 1885. By the way, that car only had three wheels. It also had gears and a water-cooled engine. Benz didn’t build his first four-wheeled car until 1891. In 1893 his company built a car called the Benz Velo—the world’s first car that didn’t cost much money to buy. By 1900, his company was the largest car maker in the world. Benz has been called a genius who invented the world’s first real car. So the next time you get into your SUV or car, remember Karl Benz!

title: How Coyote Stole Fire
text:
Long ago the earth was warm all the time. There was only summer and it was never cold. But change came and the weather turned colder. None of the animals worried about the cold except man. He had no fur and was afraid he would freeze! Coyote felt sorry for man and decided to help him. He even convinced the other animals to help him too. He had heard that the fire beings in the mountains had fire, but he knew they would never share any of it. So, he decided to go to the mountain and watch them closely.

When the fire beings heard coyote they yelled, "Who is that?" but when they saw him they said, "It's only stupid coyote, ignore him!" They sat back down and paid him no mind. Coyote watched closely. The next morning the Fire Being left the fire and went to wake up another Fire Being. For a while, no one was watching the fire at all - except Coyote. The next morning when the fire was not being watched, coyote grabbed a piece of fire and ran as fast as he could. The fire beings were furious and chased him. As they touched the end of his tail he tossed the fire to squirrel. Where the fire beings touched the coyote his tail turned white. It is white to this day. The fire the squirrel carried was so hot that it made her tail curl back, and it is still curled to this day. Squirrel threw the fire to frog. The fire beings grabbed him by the tail and broke it off. After that day, grown frogs have never had a tail. Finally frog threw the fire to the tree. Tree hid fire inside itself. The fire beings were furious, but could not get fire back. They gave up and went back to their mountain. But coyote was very clever and showed man how to rub two pieces of wood together to get the fire out of wood. Man has been grateful to coyote ever since!

title: Culture and Diversity - A Look At Africa
text:
Africa is surrounded by the Atlantic Ocean, the Indian Ocean, the Red Sea and the Mediterranean Sea. Many of the oldest civilizations started in Africa. There are 47 countries in Africa and six island nations around it. Only one other continent is bigger than Africa. Africa is also the home of the Sahara, which is the world’s biggest desert. About 500 years ago, Africa had many different cultures, cities and centers for learning. Later, the European traders began to take and colonize the land.

On a visit to Africa, you would see many wonderful sites such as huge and beautiful forests, grassy plains, deserts, mountains and powerful rivers. The people are just as diverse (different) as the land is. They come from many different cultures and backgrounds and speak many different languages. You would also be able to see both small villages and large cities in Africa. The weather you would see depends on what part of the continent you are visiting. It might be hot in the desert, but ice cold on the mountain tops.

Today, almost 900 million people live in Africa. Africa doesn’t have very many cities for the size of the continent, but it is one of the fastest growing places on Earth! There are big differences in how much money people have and the way they live.

Many aspects of African culture can be found in the United States. People with African heritage have faced many hardships in the U.S. The African ancestors of African Americans were brought to America in the early 1700s as enslaved people. They had no rights and were owned by someone else. After slavery was abolished, African Americans have fought and continue to fight for their rights in American society. African Americans have made and continue to make many contributions to our country.

title: Mali
text:
Mali is a country in West Africa that is mostly in the Sahara Desert. The southern part of Mali is where you find the Niger and Senegal rivers. It’s the only part of Mali where people can grow crops. The Niger River is as important to Mali as the Nile River is to Egypt. Have you ever had someone say as a joke that they were going to Timbuktu? Well, the real Timbuktu is actually in Mali!

Mali has a rich history, and a number of cultural groups live there. Although the people speak 32 different languages, French is the official language. Mali is home to the Bambara, Dogon and Fulani (Fula) people. The Bambara grow rice and peanuts and raise sheep and goats. The Dogon people are cliff dwellers who have kept their culture alive even though Mali has been invaded many times over the years. The Fulani are the largest group of nomads (people who move from place to place) in the world. Many speak more than one language because they travel through different African countries.

title: The Traffic Light
text:
In the early 1900s, it was not uncommon for there to be terrible accidents between the newly invented automobile and horse wagons.

Garrett A. Morgan decided to develop a traffic light signal. His invention looked like a T-shaped pole that had three positions - stop, go and stop in all positions. The traffic light used today has three circular signals. One of the signals is green for "go," another is yellow for "caution," and the last one is red for "stop." Another feature added to traffic lights is the use of an arrow, which tells a driver if it is safe to turn.

Today's traffic light also seems to know when a car is there. Actually, some lights are on a timer, so they change periodically. Other lights use detectors with everything from laser detectors to rubber hoses filled with air. When cars are detected, the length of the light changes so that traffic will move.

title: Anansi Looks for Wisdom
text:
Anansi the spider was not very wise. He was clever and could outwit other creatures, but he was not wise. He decided to take a large basket and collect as much wisdom as he could from the village people. He knocked on one door after another and asked the people for a little bit of their wisdom. Everyone laughed because they knew Anansi was not wise. So, they put a little of their wisdom into the basket.

When the basket was full, Anansi decided that he needed to hide his basket so no one would steal his wisdom. He found a tall tree and tied the basket to the front of himself so it would stay safe. He tried and tried, but could not get up the tree because the basket was in his way. He tried for hours but the basket always kept him from climbing that tree. Soon his young son came and saw what was going on. "Father", he said, "Why don't you tie the basket onto your back? Then you could climb the tree."

"Go home," yelled Anansi. But as soon as his son was out of sight he quickly tied the basket to his back and climbed to the top of the tree.

When he got to the top of the tree he yelled. "I'm still not wise! Even my little son is wiser than me! This wisdom is no good to me!" so he threw the wisdom in the basket to the four winds and watched it spread to every corner of the earth. And that is how wisdom came to the world.

title: What is a Culture Anyway?
text:
Culture is all the language, customs, food, art and music of a group of people. It also includes the many ways that people meet some important human needs. This might be how they get food, water, clothing and shelter. If you live in the desert, getting food and staying alive affects how you live. Trade can help with that. Trade caused many ancient civilizations to grow. They could trade things they didn’t need for things they needed. That’s where caravans (groups of people who wanted to trade) came in. Caravans from North Africa would travel through the Sahara to trade with West Africans. West Africans traded gold for salt. They used the salt to flavor and keep their food fresh. Let’s look at different cultures that have lived in or have come from Africa.

Nok

Nok was an ancient culture of West Africa that learned how to smelt (separate metal from) ore and how to use it to make things that they needed such as spears or plows. This Nok discovery was amazing and affected people all over the world!

Egypt

Egypt was the only society to last for thousands of years. Many other cultures became powerful, but were not as important as Egyptians. Ancient Egyptians understood math and knew how to build things better than anyone else ever did. They also used a paper-like substance called papyrus to write with hieroglyphs, one of the earliest forms of writing. The advances in their society included medicine, dentistry, and the start of a calendar.

Kush

Kush is also believed to be one of Africa’s early civilizations. The people of Kush came from Egypt. Their capital city was called Kerma, and it was an area of major trade between North and South Africa. Kush changed how government works because they elected a king from the royal family. During this time in history, the next king always came from the mother’s family. This led to women becoming queens, which was not done in any other major civilization at the time.

Ghana

The gold trade was done mainly by the ancient civilization of Ghana. Even though there were not many natural resources in Ghana, they still had a lot of skill in the use of iron. They used iron-tipped spears to control their neighbors, who were still using weapons made of stone. Ghana was able to collect taxes from traders who went through their territory. The name of their war chief was Ghana.

Timbuktu

Timbuktu started as one of the areas visited by early travelers and adventurers because it was a place where three big trade routes came together. Timbuktu got very rich and was the main place to trade in gold and salt across the Sahara in the 14th century. Timbuktu was not just a big center of trade. It also had a university.

title: People and Natural Disasters
text:
What's that you heard on the radio? A tornado's coming? What do you do? Where do you go? How do you stay safe? This week we're going to look at natural disasters. We'll talk about what causes them and how we can protect ourselves from them.

Our Changing Earth

The Earth is always changing. The continents on Earth are all moving. It's amazing to think that something as big as a continent could actually move, but they do. The land we live on is really the Earth's crust. This crust is floating on top of a very hot layer called the mantle which is nothing but hot, melted rock. Think of an egg. The shell would be the crust, the white part of the egg would be the mantle. What about the yolk? The center of the earth is even hotter than the mantle and is made of melted iron. The yolk would be the core or center of Earth.

When whole continents move, it is called continental drift. Scientists now think all the continents were once one big land mass many millions of years ago. They call this land mass Pangea. Slowly, pieces of this land mass have pulled apart and separated, becoming the continents we have today.

Sometimes all this moving land causes pressure to build up under the land. Sometimes it pushes one piece of land under or over another, sometimes it pulls land apart. When the pressure gets to be too much, the land moves a lot very quickly - that's what an earthquake is.

Change is inevitable and universal. This is especially true when it comes to the earth! So hang onto your hat and grab an umbrella! Rain, wind, tornados and hurricanes are waiting for you inside this week's issue!

title: Lend a Hand
text:
There are natural disasters happening all over the world at any given time. From fires and floods to earthquakes, tornados and hurricanes, disasters can destroy homes and communities in the blink of an eye.

What can you do to help? You might be surprised at the difference you can make in the life of someone going through a natural disaster. Take a look at the list below to see how you give relief to someone in need:

Organize a school fundraiser to raise money to send to disaster victims.

Talk to your church group about having a bake sale, fun run or other activity to raise money.

Donate clothing, canned food or household items to be sent to those in need.

Prepare hygiene kits (resealable plastic bags with a towel, washcloth, toothbrush and toothpaste, comb, soap, shampoo, deodorant, etc.) to send to disaster victims.

If you aren't sure how to get involved, where to send donations or even what to donate, check with a disaster relief organization such as the Red Cross, the Salvation Army, UNICEF or your local community center or health department. Every donation, whether large or small, helps relieve the suffering of those in need.

title: Shake it Up!
text:
Let’s get back to that earthquake! The surface of the Earth is like a big puzzle with huge pieces. Where the pieces meet are where things push and pull, which can cause earthquakes. The biggest place like that in the United States is along the Pacific coast. So, what do you do if you are in an earthquake? The first thing to do is have a disaster plan. Decide what heavy piece of furniture you will get under so things won’t fall on you. Finally, have a disaster kit ready that includes a first aid kit, water and food.

Hurricanes

A hurricane gives people lots of warning. The best thing to do is listen to the weather report and leave when they say it is time. A hurricane can be hundreds of miles across, but needs to have a wind speed of at least 74 miles per hour to be a hurricane. The problem with a hurricane is that since it forms over the ocean, when it hits land (called landfall) it brings LOTS of water with it! Some places that get lots of hurricanes even build their houses on stilts so the flood waters won’t destroy their homes. Areas that get hurricanes usually have evacuation routes, or ways to get away quickly.

We’re Not in Kansas Anymore!

So what about tornados? Tornados are actually the strongest storms on earth with winds that can go more than 300 miles an hour. A tornado usually happens when two different kinds of air hit each other, like warm and cold air. To keep safe in a tornado listen to TV and radio reports when the weather is bad. A tornado watch means the conditions are right for a tornado to form, but it hasn’t happened yet. A tornado warning means there is a tornado in the area. When this happens go to the lowest floor of your house and find a bathroom or closet with no windows. Lots of people buy insurance so if their property is damaged or destroyed they can replace it.

How Much Rain?

A drought is when there is less rain than normal over a long period of time. It can happen anywhere and can cause all kinds of problems including crop failures. Conserving water is always important, but especially during a drought. Washing cars and watering your lawn just has to wait for a good rain.

Flooding happens when rivers overflow, or there is too much water for any reason. Stay away from flood water. It moves very fast and is dangerous because you can get knocked down and caught in the water. Flood water can also be contaminated, which means it has dangerous stuff in it. This can cause disease which just adds to the problem.

The good news is that there are ways to prepare for disasters that may happen in your area. The key is to be prepared!

title: Preparing for Disasters
text:
Where lots of earthquakes happen, builders have done research and a lot of thinking about how to make buildings safer.

An earthquake has lots of energy. The trick is to keep some of that energy from shaking buildings. One way to do this is to put something under the building that can absorb (or take in) some of the energy from the earthquake.

Sometimes they use layers of rubber and steel between the building and the foundation to keep the up and down motion down, but still allow the building to go side to side. This helps keep buildings from falling down.

Another thing builders do is build a "sheer" wall. This is a wall made of concrete with steel bars in it to make it stronger. Science and technology make a big difference to our safety!

title: Pecos Bill and the Tornado
text:
Everybody knows that Pecos Bill could ride anything - until, that is, he tried to ride a tornado!

It was the only time he was thrown! He picked the meanest tornado he could find. That tornado whirled and twirled all the way from Kansas to Texas.

It tied rivers into knots and flattened the forests in its way. Bill didn't care. He was all calm-like and even spurred that old tornado every now and then just to make it mad.

Finally that tornado figured out old Pecos Bill wasn't going anywhere, so it took off for California and just rained itself out. There was so much water it washed out the Grand Canyon.

Finally, there wasn't much of it left and Pecos Bill fell like a bullet to the ground. He hit so hard he sank smack below sea level. We call that spot Death Valley today. Anyhow, that's how the rodeo got its start. But most cowboys just stick to riding broncos today!

title: Ancient Civilizations and the Resources They Used
text:
Do you know what resources are? Resources are anything that can be used. In this week's lesson, you'll learn about the kinds of resources that we have today and how we get those resources from one place to another. How did people in ancient times get and use their resources? Keep reading to find out.

Getting resources has been an important part of life since prehistoric times. The location of resources affected the lives of ancient people all over the world. They had to do whatever was necessary to get the resources they needed to survive.

Early people were nomads, people who wandered from place to place to find resources. They hunted animals to have meat. Wherever the animals traveled, the nomads followed. Along the way, they gathered plants like nuts and berries. When they were near water, they fished or caught other sea life. Animal skins provided clothing.

Archaic American Indians left cave paintings in some places that help us learn about their life. They were hunters, gatherers and fire builders. Their homes were also rock shelters. They made tools from stone and bones and used them to find food and to protect themselves.

As time went on, people began to settle in communities. They still hunted, fished and gathered wild plants. But they began to plant their own crops. That meant that having water was even more important. Most people settled near water - a creek, a river or an ocean. They learned how to use irrigation, a system of getting water to the fields of crops.

More than 4,000 years ago, people in the Indus Valley grew grains like wheat and barley. Each town had a large building to store the grain. The storage building was in the center of town so that everyone could have food.

In ancient China, Greece and Rome, people could buy many things they needed in the marketplace. But that was expensive, and not everyone could afford to shop there. Many people still had to grow their own food and make their own clothes.

There was not much wood in ancient Egypt, so the people who lived there built homes made of adobe (bricks made of mud and dried in the sun). The resources to build adobe houses were nearby and easy to get.

You may remember reading about the aqueducts of ancient Rome. The aqueducts were channels that carried water to every part of the city. Because the water was too far away, the Romans figured out a way to make sure that all the citizens had the water they needed.

As you can see, the location of resources influenced the way ancient people lived - where they settled, what kind of houses they built and what they ate.

title: Economy
text:
What Is An Economy?

What is economy? The businesses, jobs and resources in a community make up its economy. Read below to learn more about the way a community's economy works.

Resources

We live in a world with many resources. There are three kinds of resources - natural, human and capital. People have to make choices about how these resources are used.

Natural resources are things from nature like oil, wood, crops and water. Fish from Canada and elsewhere in the world will become food for people. This is also a natural resource. Natural resources will not last forever, so we must be sure to use them wisely.

Human resources are people - the workers who produce goods and provide services and the people who buy them. People who buy goods and services are called consumers.

Money is a capital resource. Buildings and machines are, too. When someone has an idea for a new business, she needs money to get started. Consumers need money to buy the goods and services they need and want.

Using Resources - Four Steps

1. Get the resources. Oil wells have to be dug, and oranges have to be picked. Many business owners borrow money from a bank. What happens when a resource is located far away? It has to be transported to the community by truck, train, ship or plane.

2. Develop the resources. Developing means changing the resources into a form that can be used. Oil has to be refined so that it is cleaner and safer to use. Oranges have to be juiced and bottled for consumers.

3. Distribute the goods and services. Producers of a product may be far away from their buyers. They will need suppliers who will carry their product who are closer to their buyers, and sellers who will sell the product.

4. Consumers buy the goods and services.

Where Are Resources?

The kinds of resources located in a community can change the way people live and work. If you live near oil wells, many people in your city or town may depend on the wells for their jobs. Gasoline may be cheaper there because it doesn't have to be shipped from far away. In a community that is near a large forest, there may be more buildings made of wood.

Getting, developing and distributing resources can cause noise and pollution in a community. The citizens need to work hard to make sure the air and water stay clean.

People who live near resources need to take care of them, and everyone needs to conserve the Earth's natural resources. That means we should protect them from harm and use them wisely so we do not run out.

title: The Crayon
text:
The first box of eight Crayola crayons was made in 1903. Before this time, there were other types of crayons, but they were expensive, greasy and hard to use. Binney and Smith, a company that made red barn paint, school pencils and "dustless" chalk, decided that it was time for children and teachers to have a crayon that made art projects fun.

Binney and Smith made special wax marking crayons used by businesses to label boxes. The company looked at these marking crayons and made some changes to make them perfect for children. Binney and Smith made the crayons smaller, added bright colors and made the wax stronger. The company then packaged the crayons in a box of eight colors: black, brown, yellow, orange, red, blue, green and purple. The box of Binney and Smith's Crayola crayons was a hit with both kids and teachers.

Today, Crayola makes crayons, paints, modeling clay and many other activity products. There are now more than 120 different colors of crayons, as well as markers that glitter, glow in the dark, smell like flowers, change color and even wash off walls. Look in your desk. You probably have Crayola crayons in there right now.

title: From Trees to Paper
text:
Where does paper come from? What kind of transformation does it undergo?

The very paper you're holding now was once a tree.

The process of getting paper starts out in a forest or tree farm. There, loggers harvest, or cut down, the trees to be used in a variety of goods - from paper to lumber. Some trees are grown specifically to produce paper, while sometimes scraps are used for paper making. Recycling old paper to make new paper is also becoming very common.

Once the trees are cut down, they're sent to a factory to be processed, where they're ground up and mixed with water and turned into pulp. The pulp is then dried, pressed into paper in the factory and put into big rolls.

The rolls of paper are then sold to the printer. The printer runs the paper through the printing press and the newspaper is printed.

The finished newspapers are then sent to the school, where you can read Studies Weekly.

title: Not Enough Food!
text:
Why do people leave home to move to another place? Why has this happened all through history? The reasons are many and have influenced people all over the world. One of the reasons is scarcity. Scarcity happens when there is not enough of something. All through history scarcity of food, water and other resources has forced people to make choices. Sometimes the choices were hard to make. Often, those choices changed people's lives forever.

The Irish Potato Famine

At one time, potatoes were a very important source of food for many people in Ireland. A blight (a plant disease) ruined the potato crops for several years between 1845 and 1850. Food became scarce. Many people had no way to earn money. This time in history is known as the Irish Potato Famine. (A famine happens when food is so scarce that people are starving.)

Some people were so hungry that they ate the rotten potatoes and got very sick. Almost 1 million people died from starvation or disease. Many people left Ireland, hoping to find a better life. It must have been hard to leave their homes.

One million people immigrated to England, the United States and Canada. The journey was very difficult. The ships were overcrowded and dirty. Food was scarce on the ships, too. People died of hunger and disease. Some people called the ships that left Ireland "coffin ships."

Famine in Africa

What causes famine? Crop diseases are sometimes the cause. Drought (a long period with no rain), floods and other weather problems can wipe out crops as well. In some places, food becomes scarce because of overpopulation (too many people living in the same area). Diseases can kill farm animals that provide meat, milk and eggs.

Many African countries have had famine. In 1889, drought, disease and locusts caused a terrible famine in Ethiopia. The Ethiopians called it "Ya Kifu Qan," which means "Cruel Days." People ate wild plants and tried to find cattle that were not sick. Some left their homes, looking for a place where there was no famine. Many people died.

The worst famine in Ethiopia's history happened in 1984 and 1985. Almost 1 million people died of starvation during that time. People all over the world donated money and food to help.

Scarcity of food is still a problem in parts of the world. In 2015, the United Nations said 795 million people around the world were not getting enough food to keep them healthy. Look inside to read more about the choices people make when resources are scarce.

title: Why Do People Move?
text:
People leave home for a lot of reasons. Often it is famine, or the need for food. Political reasons often cause people to leave their country. If a country is being run by leaders who are hurting the people who live there, many people will leave. Religious persecution makes people move as well. When people are not allowed to worship as they think they should, they will often move to a place that will allow them to believe the way they choose. This happened when the pilgrims moved to America.

Moving to another place can help people because there may be more food or jobs. They may also be safer and healthier. But immigrants, or people who move to another country to live, face problems, too. The first problem is language. If they do not speak the language of their new country, life can be very hard. They may have a difficult time finding a good job, even though better jobs may be one reason they moved to a new country. Their customs may also be different. Immigrants may wear different clothes or have different religions. Sometimes customs are so different from one culture to another that immigrants are treated unfairly because they do things differently. All of these were problems for immigrants who came to America in the 18th and 19th centuries. The same things are still problems for immigrants today.

Migration in the Western Hemisphere

Many things have caused lots of people to move in our hemisphere. When people think they can have a better life somewhere else, they are often willing to pick up everything and move. This happened during the Gold Rush days in 1848 in California. People all over our country moved to California to look for gold. Some were successful, but many were not.

Sometimes people have little choice about moving. They have to move if they are going to survive. Drought in the 1930s caused land in the plains of the United States to get so dry that huge dust storms covered the land. These storms were so bad they could cause the sky to darken for days. So much of it got into houses that layers of dirt would be all over the furniture. It was so bad that part of the United States got the nickname of The Dust Bowl. People couldn't grow crops anymore and many people went hungry. It caused millions of people to move to California to look for work so they could feed their families. It was such a terrible time in our history that a famous book was written about it called "The Grapes of Wrath."

Today we have many migrants coming from Mexico. These people are looking for what migrants have always looked for - a better life.

title: Email - Electronic Mail
text:
Do you have an email address? Does your family use Email to keep in touch with friends? You may be interested to know about how this way of communicating was invented.

Ray Tomlinson was one of the computer engineers who was hired by the U.S. government to build the first Internet in 1968. While working on this important project, Ray began experimenting with ways to leave messages for other computer engineers working on the same computer.

After figuring out a way to leave messages on the same computer, Ray eventually discovered a program that let him leave messages on other computers connected to the same network. A network is a group of computers connected to each other. This new way of sending messages was called Email because the mail was sent back and forth electronically, by computer. The “e” in “email” stands for “electronic.”

The first email message read, “QWERTYUIOP,” which is simply the top row of letters on a computer keyboard.

title: The Great Plains
text:
The Great Plains is a large area east of the Rocky Mountains that is very flat. It goes from Mexico to Canada and eastward to Illinois. It is primarily grassy with few trees. The soil is usually very good in the plains due to the abundant amount of grass material that grows there. It is a great place for growing crops like corn and wheat. This area was once the place where you would find herds of buffalo numbering in the millions.

Most of the Great Plains gets less than 24 inches of rain a year, making it a very dry place. That's not such a problem as long as the grass can hold the soil in place. However, during the 1920s and '30s farmers were not very careful when they planted their crops. They plowed too deep and in straight rows. They planted the same thing year after year too. This caused the soil to become depleted and not much good to grow crops at all. Since crops were only growing part of the year, the rest of the time wind erosion carried much of the top soil away. Then the droughts came. After a number of droughts the ground was so dry that gigantic dust storms covered huge areas of land. Crops died, which caused more wind erosion to take place. Now farmers understand how to plant their crops in a way that saves a valuable natural resource - our land.

title: Clarity of Expression: FDR and the Four Freedoms
text:
For most people around the world, the years of economic depression and war between 1929 and 1945 were dark and dangerous. Resources such as food, clothing and fuel were in short supply. Families were often torn apart as parents looked for work, served in the armed forces, or as children were sent to safe, sheltered areas. It was a time of stress and hardship, when people desperately looked to leaders for safety and hope. In the United States, that leader was Franklin D. Roosevelt, our 32nd president who served from 1933 to 1945.

During that time of chaos, on Jan. 6, 1941, President Roosevelt delivered to Congress a historic speech, which we now call the Four Freedoms Speech. After years of economic depression, his words were not angry. When world war was happening, his tone was not fierce or mean. But knowing that there were still darker days of war to come for many, he spoke with passion about peace, good fortune, safety, and about the freedoms that humans everywhere deserve. "In the future days," Roosevelt said, "we look forward to a world founded upon four essential human freedoms." Even today those four freedoms are essential (important). Can you list them? They are: the freedom of speech and expression, the freedom of worship for every person, the freedom from wants such as hunger and lack of shelter and the freedom from fear.

How are we doing? Have we achieved those freedoms for everyone? Everywhere?

To read or listen to the entire speech, with the permission of a parent or teacher go to: www.americanrhetoric.com To see the paintings by Norman Rockwell inspired by the Four Freedoms: www.archives.gov

title: Let’s Learn About Washington This Year!
text:
Welcome to Washington Studies Weekly! Hang on tight for the ride of a lifetime as we explore our state from top to bottom, start to finish, inside, outside, upside and downside. We'll climb the highest mountain, drop into the deepest hole, roam with the bison, hunt with the mountain men, build a boat, fly an airplane, discover gold and walk with the pioneers! This is Washington Studies Weekly, your weekly time capsule of historical events.

Each issue of the paper will include a current event on the front cover that discusses a real news item. Our cover story will help you get a head start on the week's history lesson. We will take you on a journey into the experiences of great people and great events with our cover stories.

And there's more. We will tell you about the Washington animals, birds, trees and plants. We will give you games, crafts and activities to enjoy and help you learn new words.

So, let's get started and jump right in. The water is fine—and so is the land. What land? Why, the land you're standing on. How did it get here?

Let's find out!
