title: Mountain Watching
text:
Hey, super sleuths, today you can join us in the pursuit of one of Washington's most infamous characters. Here are your clues:

The suspect is located in the Cascade Range.

The suspect is considered dangerous.

The suspect is half a million years old.

Suspect's description: Imagine two birthday cakes smashed together.

Can you solve the case? If you believe the suspect to be... Mount Rainier, you are one smart detective—case closed!

Mount Rainier is a mountain that gets a great deal of attention—not just because it is a big and beautiful landmark of Washington, but because it is an unpredictable mountain. Until Mount St. Helens erupted in 1980, many people thought of Mount Rainier as a harmless volcano. But, since then, they have come to realize that scientists are right—Mount Rainier is active and one of the most dangerous mountains in the United States!

It is not as active as Mount St. Helens, but is does experience at least 12 earthquakes at its highest point each year. Like many active volcanoes, an eruption could happen tomorrow or in 1,000 years. No one knows for sure.

In the meantime, much is being done to study the mountain, detect problems in time to warn people and teach nearby residents what to do in case of an emergency. They have already made plans to set up a one- of- a- kind monitoring system that can pick up the movement of large volcanic mudflows. Some towns have also set up monitoring systems that use special microphones to listen to the mountain's rumblings. Because we aren't sure exactly what to expect from it, Mount Rainier continues to be one of our most "watched" mountains.

title: Physical Features of Washington
text:
Let’s start our study of Washington this year by looking at how Washington’s physical features were formed, such as the rock far below our feet, the mountains, lakes, rivers and the basic land forms of Washington. It all began with the “Lost World” of ancient oceans and exploding volcanoes

What’s That Under Your Feet?

Have you ever wondered what lies deep beneath you and how it got there? The Pacific Northwest has a history filled with some of the most powerful and destructive forces on Earth. No one knows how many changes our state has seen over the ages. There have been times when we were buried under hundreds of feet of ancient oceans. Other times, the Earth’s crust buckled, sending great granite slabs into the sky to form mighty mountains. We probably had a great view of our neighbors from up there!

Let’s learn how our state was formed—a process we will follow from the very beginning!

Three Billion Years Ago

Our earliest mountains were worn down by wind and rain and washed into the sea. At least 10 more sets of mountains rose during the next 3 billion years. Our state was covered by ocean water during most of this time, but our various mountain ranges may have stood above the water to form islands. Those mountains didn’t last long.

Six Hundred Million Years Ago

About 600 million years ago, our first permanent layer of rock was formed. We call this rock igneous because it was formed by heat and fire. “Igneous” is a great word that comes from a Latin word meaning fire. (Ever heard of “ignite”? This is the same kind of word.) The igneous layer is 2 miles beneath us. (Don’t go digging; you’ll never find it!)

Two Hundred Million Years Ago

The Earth began to quiet down during this period. Around our state, there was a lot of volcanic activity, but plants were growing, and some ancient birds and mammals were roaming around the places that stood above the ancient oceans. Most of our state was still under water.

Sixty Million Years Ago

Suddenly, there occurred a great uprising of mountains to the east of Washington and Oregon. This became our new coastline, and oceans washed over our state for millions of years. Millions of small sea creatures died and formed a chalky layer of rock thousands of feet thick. We call this the sedimentary layer. “Sediment” is another great word. It means to sink or settle (like cookie crumbs in a glass of milk).

Fifteen Million Years Ago

Our third layer of rock was formed by molten granite, or lava, that oozed from cracks in the Earth’s crust. This oozing rock covered more than 200,000 square miles of the western United States with a layer more than 1 mile thick.

Thirteen Million Years Ago

The backbone for our Cascades to the west and northern Rocky Mountains popped up from the grinding, cracking action of the Earth’s crust.

Three Million Years Ago

Volcanic action began enlarging the Cascades to something close to what we see today.

Thirteen Thousand Years Ago

For millions of years, great sheets of ice would collect on the northern parts of the Earth. These sheets of ice are called glaciers. The long periods of time when the glaciers stayed around are called ice ages. The last great ice age was 4 million years ago. About 13,000 years ago, the last of the glaciers began melting away, and this ice age was over. Some animals became frozen in the ice. The mighty mammoth (similar to an elephant) has been found in many places where the glaciers once stood. The mammoths must have fallen into cracks in the ice while looking for water or food and were frozen solid. Scientists learn a lot by studying these beasts.

Today

Today, our state continues to change. The 1980 eruption of Mount Saint Helens is a good reminder of the power of the Earth’s buckling and heaving crust far below us. Thanks to the millions of years of collisions of natural forces inside and all around the Earth, today we have this beautiful and peaceful place. It is so green and exciting to explore, spreading out in all directions—a place we love to call home, sweet home.

Mountain Building in Washington

Teacher: Class, thousands of years ago, Washington might have been as flat as Kansas.

Students: If the land was all spread out flat, where did all of the mountains come from?

Teacher: The mountains came in several different ways. Down deep in the Earth, the rocks were squeezed into lava, which is hot, melted rock. Sometimes, this lava would find a crack and squirt out to form a volcano.

Students: Are there any active volcanoes in Washington now?

Teacher: New volcanoes were discovered on the sea bed off our coast. There are other kinds of volcanic mountains that are common in Washington. These were formed by lava pushing up through a crack. Instead of breaking through the crust, the lava would run between layers of rock and sand beneath the surface of the ground and form a sort of blister or huge hump in the ground.

Students: Are all mountains volcanoes?

Teacher: No, some mountains are made by the slipping of the Earth way down below the surface. When the Earth slips, we feel an earthquake. The cracks between huge blocks of Earth and rock are called “faults.” Fault-block mountains are made when one block is pushed up and another sinks down.

Students: Are there any more kinds of mountains in Washington?

Teacher: Yes, there are mountains we call folded mountains. Sometimes, the Earth was not only pushed up, but it also was shoved sideways. It is a lot like putting your finger on the back of your hand and pushing the skin along. Notice how the skin piles up to form tiny mountains?

title: The Five Natural Regions of Washington
text:
Our state would be very boring if it looked the same from top to bottom and side to side. Fortunately, Washington is home to a combination of landscapes ranging from sandy beaches to lush forests and from shadowy canyons to snowy mountain peaks. So how do we learn all about a state that is packed with so many unique features and differing climates? Perhaps the easiest way is to divide the map of Washington into smaller pieces, or regions, and discuss each region one at a time.

There are many ways we could divide the map into regions—we could label geographical regions, political regions, recreational regions and kids-who-eat-pizza regions. The list is endless! Currently, hundreds of maps picture our state differently depending upon the details they feature.

In Washington Studies Weekly, we will study what are called the five natural regions of Washington. These regions are divided geographically based on unique natural features, such as mountains or plains. The five natural regions of Washington are the Coastal Region (located on the West Coast), Western Lowlands (running north and south next to the Coastal Region), Cascade Mountains (running north and south along the Cascade Mountain Range), Northeastern Highlands (located in the state's northeastern corner) and Columbia Plateau (found in the southeastern corner). As we study these regions, you're sure to learn fascinating facts and divine details about each one.

title: Is the Ice Age over?
text: Winter never ended in North America eighteen thousand years ago. Thick ice sheets sprawled across most of Canada and down into Pennsylvania, central Illinois and Washington state. Mammoths, mastodons, short- faced bears and other mammals lived here. Eventually, the climate began to thaw. The glaciers melted, slowly at first, then with a rush. However, they're not completely gone yet. Interglacial Age sheets of ice are still found on Greenland and Antarctica. Some scientists believe that as long as we don't allow global warming to take place, some day the ice will return!

title: Petrified Wood
text: If you go shopping for some lumber, the salesperson might ask if you're looking for hardwood or softwood. Tell them you want genuine Washington rock wood and see what they say. Thousands of years ago, acres of cypress, oak, elm and ginkgo trees growing in swampy areas became covered over by massive lava flows and were otherwise trapped under water. Over time, water seeped into the wood and deposited silica as the wood fiber rotted away. After many years, a perfect duplication of the tree's shape and detail was created by the silica deposits - and it was as hard as rock. This is called petrifying. In 1975, Washington adopted petrified wood as its state gem because people liked to take small pieces, polish them and make jewelry. But don't try making a doghouse out of this Washington rock wood - you're guaranteed to break your saw and bend all your nails!

title: Cell Phone Safety
text:
Cell phones are great for staying in touch with family and friends, but there are times when they can become a distraction. One place where people can't afford to be distracted is behind the wheel of a car, yet using a cell phone while driving has become a way of life for many people. Talking on the phone while driving can be very dangerous. One study even showed that driving while on the phone is more dangerous than driving drunk. Drivers who use their cell phone take their eyes off the road to choose options and punch in numbers. It is impossible to drive safely without looking where you are going. Many cell phone users also get so involved in their conversations that they lose track of what is happening around them. Many things can distract a driver, including eating, looking at a map, applying makeup or taking care of children, but talking on the cell phone causes more accidents than any of these other distractions.

Because of the dangers of talking on the phone while driving, Washington has a law that makes it illegal to talk on a hand-held cell phone while behind the wheel of a car. Texting while driving has also been banned in many states—including Washington—and even more states have passed laws that limit teenagers from using cell phones while driving.

Communication is a good thing, but knowing where, when and how to do it safely is important for everyone.

title: How Do I Use the Library?
text:
One resource you may use your entire life is the library.

Use the Library’s Catalogs

The best way to find books in the library is to use its card or computer catalog system.

Card Catalog

A card catalog is a filing system where book information is stored on cards in drawers. They are organized alphabetically based on the information at the top of the card. Card catalogs contain three cards for each book: author, title, and subject cards. Each card contains the call number for a book, which is how you find it. If you wanted to find some books on dinosaurs, you would go to the “D” drawer and look for “dinosaurs.” Read the cards to decide which books would help you the most. Find the book’s call number in the upper left-hand corner of the card and write it down. A book on dinosaurs might have the call number 560.2. So, you would go to the part of the library where the 500 Science books are and look for 560.2.

Try It!

Find the drawer you need based on the topic you are researching. Write the letter(s) for that drawer here: _____

Look for cards that match your topic. Read them to decide which books would be most useful.

Write down the call numbers for those books here: __________, ___________

Find the section where your books are located based on the call numbers. Get the books you have selected and check them out.

Computer Catalog

To find materials with a computer catalog, you type keywords into the catalog system and do a search. If you type the word “dinosaur,” the computer will bring up all the books with “dinosaur” in the title or subject description. If the list is too long, be more specific by searching on, for example, “Jurassic dinosaur,” or “meat-eating dinosaur.”

title: Did Washington Have Dinosaurs?
text:
Chances of finding dinosaur bones in Washington are pretty remote. The problem is that our state is just too young—in fact, younger than the dinosaurs.

Are there any dinosaur bones in Washington? Scientists have found very few, and here's why—our state was totally covered by ocean water when the dinosaurs lived on the Earth. This is fairly recent and a rare find, but dinosaur bones have been found in Washington. In most other places on the Earth you will find some dinosaur bones, but there aren't many here. After the ocean water left our state, great lava flows spilled out across the ground. This killed any of the vegetation that might have started growing.

Even when the dinosaurs started dying out, we were still under water (about 60 million years ago). So, if no dinosaur could live here, what are all of these fossils we find? Aren't they dinosaur bones?

Most people would be surprised to learn that there are a lot of ancient animals that were not actual "dinosaurs." The word "dinosaur" is a combination of two Greek words meaning "terrible lizard" (deinos = terrible plus sauros = lizard). Scientists use the term to describe extinct gigantic reptiles. If the ancient animal you're thinking of doesn't fall into this category of being extinct, gigantic and reptilian, it is really not a dinosaur (gigantic reptile)—it is a "non-dinosaur."

Here are some examples of non-dinosaurs that once lived in our state:

Trilobites:

This group of animals lived around Washington 250 million years ago and belonged to a group that included horseshoe crabs, spiders, insects, shrimp and lobsters. If you go fossil (turned to rock) hunting in the right part of the state, you might find a fossilized trilobite.

Dimetrodon:

If you have some toy dinosaurs at home, chances are pretty good that you have a dimetrodon in the collection. This mammal-like creature has a fin along its back and has large, sharp fangs.

Mammoth:

Mammoths looked like super-sized elephants. Although you might see a mammoth pictured in your dinosaur book, or in the cartoons helping Fred Flintstone get a car wash, the mammoth is a prehistoric mammal and not a dinosaur. Mammoths arrived about 55 million years ago and were seen in Washington as recently as 9,500 B.C. Washington has adopted the Columbian Mammoth as its "official fossil."

Phobosuchus:

How about meeting up with a crocodile that is as long as your classroom (50 feet)? The skull of this meat eater was 6 feet long, and it probably ate any leftover dinosaurs that had not died out by 60 million years ago. Phobosuchus was not a dinosaur, just the biggest crocodile that ever walked the Earth!

title: Philanthropy and Values
text:
Maybe you have heard the word philanthropy before. What does it mean? It describes actions that people make for the good of other people. What ... is a value? It's a way of behaving that people believe is good- like believing it's good to be honest. Is honesty one of your values?

One way you can practice philanthropy today is to help yourself and others learn good values. How do you learn good values? You can learn them from your parents and grandparents, your teachers at school or church and other people you trust.

You can also learn them from people that have been recognized for doing good things for society. An easy way to learn about people that have done good things is to visit values.com. Values.com has lots of stories and short videos that highlight the traits that make each of us better people. They even have billboards on the highway to remind you about good values.

For example, you may have seen a billboard that looks like the one shown here.

This billboard is about Oral Lee Brown, who saved money from her job to send nineteen kids to college... all by herself! Wow! Isn't that cool? You can learn about lots of other people who practice philanthropy at values.com. Be sure to look for more of their "billboards" on Page 4 of Studies Weekly this year. We think they're so cool we want to remind you to check them out!

title: Five Geographic Regions of Washington
text:
It's important to know the shape of the land. Washington divides itself into five natural regions. Which do you live in?

Where in the World is Washington?

Washington is just a dot on the world. Can you see it? It doesn't look big, but it is very important. If you will study this article, you'll see how Washington fits into the world.

Natural Regions of Washington

A natural region is a part of the Earth that has one major kind of natural feature, such as mountains or plains, that makes that area unique.

1. Coastal Region

Washington's coastal plain, where our state meets the ocean, is narrow in the north, but widens to 30 miles at Gray's Harbor. It is a combination of great forests with trees hundreds of years old, the Olympic Mountains to the north, the Willapa Hills in the south and the valley of the Chehalis River. The Olympic Mountains are a rugged, eroded group of peaks that rise almost directly from sea level. They trap moisture-laden clouds from the ocean that dump 150-200 inches of rain per year on the thick forests— that's like pouring out 2 billion gallons of water on every acre! Heavy rainfall is common, as are mild winters and cool summers. Willapa Hills, just south of the Olympics, are low, rounded hills averaging 500 feet high, with dense forests. Along the coast are three excellent harbors: Gray's Harbor, Willapa Harbor and the mouth of the Columbia River.

2. Western Lowlands

This beautiful area varies in width between 25 and 60 miles and runs the whole length of Washington. It is guarded on the east by the Cascades and on the west by the Olympic Mountains and the Willapa Hills. The land is aptly called lowlands, as it averages only 100 feet above sea level, yet receives its share of rainfall at 20-40 inches a year. Rarely do temperatures rise above 90 or fall below freezing in this mild area. Thousands of years ago, ancient glaciers pushing down from Canada carved out the Puget Sound. Today, the Sound is an arm of the ocean and deep enough to hold the largest ocean-going ships in its harbors. At least 172 of its more than 300 islands are large enough for people to live on— Whidbey Island is the second largest island in the continental United States.

3. Cascade Mountains

The great range of Cascades divides the state from north to south into thirds- one third of the state on the ocean side and two thirds to the east. The Cascade Mountains are higher than the Olympics, averaging about 8,000 feet. Some of the highest mountain peaks in the United States are among the Cascades, and these are all volcanic cones— Mount Rainier, 14,408 feet; Mount Adams, 12,307 feet; Mount Baker, 10,827; Glacier Peak, 10,436 feet; and the remaining snowcapped slopes of Mount St. Helens. The Cascade range varies from 50 to 100 miles in width, with many rivers flowing down either side. The heaviest rain is on the west side, but enough rain makes it past the mountains to support forests on the east side.

4. Columbia Plateau

East of the Cascade Mountains, our state becomes a different country. Instead of lush, thick forests, there are vast stretches of lava flow that push out as far as the eye can see. This great central basin lies from 500 to 2,000 feet above sea level and is surrounded by a rim of higher lands. There is fertile soil on these lava flows, but too little rain to grow very much. In some places, it is almost like a desert, receiving as little as 6 inches of rain a year. Temperatures drop well below zero and rise above 100 degrees. Unusual land forms include the Grand Coulee and Moses Coulee (a coulee is a steep-walled, canyon-like trench that was created during the Ice Age when glaciers blocked the Columbia River, forcing it to take new paths), sand formations called potholes, the dry falls of the Grand Coulee, numerous deep canyons and petrified forests. The mighty Columbia River cuts through this area for 745 miles, falling 1,288 feet on its way to the ocean. This terrific drop makes it perfect for hydroelectric power plants. A plateau is flat land that has been pushed up from below.

5. Northeastern Highlands

From the Cascades eastward, our state is largely a range of low, round hills running up to the northern Rocky Mountains. This range is broken up by many north-south valleys, which are covered by pine with little undergrowth. The highlands range from 4,000 to 5,000 feet high with a few peaks rising to 7,000-8,000 feet. Rainfall averages 20-30 inches, enough to keep sagebrush and bunch grass growing. Where rivers flow into the valleys of the highlands, world-famous apples grow in abundance.

title: Birds Descended from Dinosaurs?
text: This is a trick question. While most people think that the animals listed on Page 1 are dinosaurs, those same people would probably also say that our delicate, little birds could not be at all similar to dinosaurs. But, according to scientists, that chicken you had for dinner has more similarities to the dinosaurs than any of the animals listed do. If you go to the park for the day, make sure your bucket of chicken isn't the petrified type—that would be one heavy bucket of extra-crispy!

title: What happened to the dinosaurs?
text:
The disappearance of dinosaurs 65 million years ago is one of science's greatest mysteries. There are no eye witnesses; there are no video tapes!

Changing climate, starvation, cosmic radiation, parasites, disease, erupting volcanoes and competition from new animals are just a few of the causes scientists guess at for the dinosaurs' sudden disappearance from the Earth.

Were mammals the problem? Some scientists say that small mammals appeared on the Earth and ate all the dinosaur eggs, and no more babies were hatched.

One important theory (scientific belief) says that the disappearance of the giant beasts started in Mexico near the Yucatan Peninsula. A comet or meteorite struck the area, causing huge forest fires 65 million years ago. The clouds of dust and ashes choked all living plants and animals.

Do you have a favorite theory as to why the dinosaurs of the world are no longer with us?

title: Whales
text:
Ever since the dinosaurs died out, the largest visitors ever to set fin on Washington's coast are the whales in all of their varieties. Whales can be spotted during their spring and fall migrations. They like to spend their summers in the cool Arctic and then move south to the tropics for the winter months. Washington is right in the middle of their migration route. These giants can swim against the current and need not fear any enemy. Among them are the gray, blue, piked, humpback, finback and sei whales.

Others joining the migration include the so-called killer whale and the Baird-beaked, Pacific-beaked and goose-beak whales. As the whales lumber along, their great movement in the water is marked by frequent geysers and spouts of water as the friendly creatures blow off air as they breathe. If you visit the coast during these migrations, you won't be the only curious on-looker as the whales go by. Families of dolphins also like to join the parade. And who knows? Maybe the whales and dolphins are looking at the funny-looking creatures with strange scales and hairy heads standing on the beach - you!

title: Promote Common Good
text:
What does common good have to do with you? Think about your way to school this morning. State police were patrolling the streets to make sure people obeyed speed limits and they helped when people had problems. Our state government helped pay for the roads you used. Another thing your government did for the common good was form strict safety rules for school buses. School buses are safer than trucks, minivans or cars. Before school even started this year, you may have bought school supplies. However, your state government pays for your bus, desk, computers and teachers' salaries. You can thank your government for that!

Do you buy your lunch at school? The government is promoting common good by passing laws that make sure your school lunch is healthy and safe. Speaking of healthy, remember when you were little and got lots of shots at the doctor's office? Well, the government is promoting common good through laws about vaccines too. They don't want kids coming to school spreading serious illnesses like measles or mumps! So, you have to get shots before starting school, which helps keep everyone healthier.

After lunch, you might go out to recess. Your government also had a hand in promoting common good out there too. They have an agency that makes safety rules for school playgrounds to help keep everyone safe while playing. After school, you might visit your local library for some information to help you with homework. Our government also helps support your libraries.

Can you think of other laws and rules that protect the common good?

title: How Do I Read a Map?
text:
Maps can tell you a great deal, from finding out which direction to travel to figuring out the elevation of an area or the amount of wheat produced in a state. Map reading is a valuable skill that you will use all your life.

Use a Grid and Legend

Most maps use symbols and marks to help you use them. Here are a few:

Scale — On a map you’ll often see: 1 inch = 1 mile. That means one inch on the map represents 1 mile of the land round you. Easy, huh?

Legend — What do those little pictures or symbols on a map mean? The legend is a box, usually in a corner of the map. It lists the symbols, then tells what they mean.

Grid — Many maps are arranged on a grid. See the lines going up and down the sides of the map? There are more lines at the top and bottom. Those grid lines help you locate places on the map. Grids have letters along the sides and numbers across the top and bottom.

Index — To use the grid to find a location, go to the map’s index. The index lists locations with a letter and a number for each location. Find the spot on the map where that letter and number cross. For example: House — D, 9

title: Washington’s Rivers
text:
Washington's rivers and lakes help water some of the richest soils on Earth. They also provide lush, safe homes for wildlife and scenic recreation for visitors. These water resources, along with the wondrous mountain ranges and vast desert plateaus, make Washington one of the most beautiful places to live.

Columbia River

The Columbia River system is the largest river in the west, draining 258,000 square miles of land. The Columbia River is 1,240 miles long, with 740 miles of that in the United States. A total of 11 hydroelectric dams mellow the Columbia's 1,290-foot drop with a series of giant stair steps.

Snake River

The Snake River is the largest tributary of the Columbia. (A tributary is a river that feeds into a larger river.) It flows into the Columbia at an average of 50,000 cubic feet (or 375,000 gallons) of water every second - about 1/5 of the Columbia's total flow. The 1,038-mile-long river begins at Yellowstone National Park and flows through the world's deepest gorge, Hells Canyon (7,900 feet deep). Several hydroelectric dams provide 7.1 million kilowatts to western states' power grids.

Yakima River

The Yakima River begins in the Cascades and flows 203 miles into the Columbia River. It helps irrigate 460,000 acres in one of Washington's most important farming and fruit-growing regions.

Okanogan River

The Okanogan River drains Okanogan Lake in British Columbia. Fort Okanogan became the first settlement in Washington when it was established along the riverbanks in 1811 by the Astor Fur Company.

title: The Peak That Popped
text:
Mount St. Helens is one of Washington's most famous mountains. It is more than just a pretty mountain peak, however. It is actually an active volcano! On May 18, 1980, an earthquake 1 mile below the mountain shook the ground. This caused the mountain to blow its top! The mountain that once climbed more than 9,000 feet into the air was cut down to just over 8,000 feet. Ash and rocks shot up and out of the mountain for nine hours. The eruption caused widespread damage and 57 people were killed.

Although it has been a long time since Mount St. Helens exploded, there are signs that the mountain is still rumbling and may erupt again. Scientists measure and record the many small earthquakes happening in the area to help predict when the volcano will growl once again.

Besides earthquakes, scientists have also discovered a large, fin-shaped rock growing out of the volcano's crater. The rock is now about 300 feet tall, but it is growing between 4 and 5 feet each day. This means that there is hot lava bubbling up under the rock, pushing higher and higher each day. Scientists believe that as the hot lava beneath the surface continues to push upward, it will keep building a new rock peak to replace the old one that was blown away when the volcano erupted.

Scientists hope that by watching Mount St. Helens very closely, they will be able to give people plenty of warning before she decides to erupt again. In the meantime, Mount St. Helens continues to be one of Washington's most famous and powerful mountains.

title: Lakes, Bays, Mountains and Rivers
text:
Puget Sound isn't a lake, but it is an inlet of the Pacific Ocean. It is one-fifth the size of Lake Erie. It has numerous islands and arms and is Washington's most significant body of water.

Lake Chelan is a glacial lake in the Cascades and is the largest natural lake in the state. Lake Chelan is in a glacial trough extending 55 miles into the Cascade Mountains. More than 1,500 feet deep, the lake bottom drops to 400 feet below sea level at its deepest point. This clear, blue lake is fed by 27 glaciers and 59 streams.

Franklin D. Roosevelt Lake, an artificial lake behind Grand Coulee Dam, is 151 miles long. It serves as storage for water that is used for hydroelectric power and irrigation.

Banks Lake, an artificial lake behind the Dry Falls Dam, has 91 miles of shoreline for uncrowded water enjoyment. Fishing season is open all year round.

Washington's Mountains

The Pacific Coast Range runs 5,500 miles along the western coast of the United States and Canada. The Willapa Hills are the lowest segment of the Pacific Coast mountains in Washington, and they don't reach higher than 3,110 feet.

The Olympic Mountains have some of the highest peaks of the Pacific Coast range - Mount Olympus is the highest at 7,954 feet. The range supports about 60 glaciers, and in some places it rains 140 inches a year.

The Cascade Range is largely volcanic and is studded with great cones such as Mount Adams and Mount St. Helens. Washington's highest peak is located here - Mount Rainier at 14,411 feet has 41 glaciers on its summit. The western slopes receive up to 100 inches of rain a year.

The Kettle River Range connects the Rocky Mountains (the Rockies cross a corner of Washington) to the Cascades, and it includes the Okanogan Mountains. A lot of gold has been found here!

The Puget Trough extends the length of the state and is very flat. The highest part rises only 500 feet.

The Columbia Plateau is a huge basin that was formed by massive lava flows. It includes some of the driest land in the northwest, receiving an average of 10 inches of rain per year. The Columbia and Snake rivers have cut deep trenches in the Columbia Plateau.

Palouse Hills in the southeastern corner of Washington is covered with very fertile, wind-blown dust (loess). Some of the richest wheat-growing land is found here.

title: The Cascades
text: The Cascades are a range of mountains that were once very active volcanoes. Two of the tallest are Mount Rainier in Washington, at 14,410 feet high, and Mount Hood in Oregon, at 11,245 feet high. This mighty range of mountains divides the Pacific Northwest into two major climactic zones: the high, dry lands of the vast interior plateau and the wet valleys and low, mountainous terrain of the coast. On the seaward side of the Cascades, wet air from the ocean gets trapped against the mountains and drops some 100-130 inches of annual precipitation. Farther west, the Puget-Willamette lowlands receive an average of 45-50 inches yearly. But, on the east side of the Cascades, where much of the moisture is blocked by the Cascades, it is a desert in some places. Only 10-12 inches of rain fall on average each year. Through this land of contrasts, the Columbia River flows 1,210 miles from its source in Canada to the Pacific.

title: Where is the tallest mountain in the world?
text: It is in Asia, on the border of two countries, Nepal and Tibet. This mountain is 29,035 feet high - that's like stacking up two Mount Rainiers. A long time ago, it was named Chomolungma, which means "Mountain-So-High-No-Bird-Can-Fly-Over-It." It now has the name of Mount Everest. Sure is a lot easier to say "Everest," isn't it? This mountain is so high that it has snow and ice all year, and blizzards bring high winds. It is very dangerous to climb.

title: The Beaver
text: The American beaver loves Washington's lush forests and streams. It is North America's largest rodent, weighing as much as some fourth graders (35-65 pounds) and is sometimes taller (3 to 4 feet, including its 16-inch flat tail). The beaver is like a miniature boat. Its large, webbed feet help propel it through the water while its broad, flat tail acts as the rudder. A beaver mates for life and can live up to 20 years. Beavers build dams with logs and sticks that they cut with their teeth. The dams create lakes where beavers may safely raise their families. A beaver always finishes a dam it starts, and beaver dams never break. The largest beaver dam is in Montana; it is 2,140 feet long, 12 feet high and 15-20 feet thick.

title: What Did Californios Think About Joining The United States?
text:
During history, there are often two sides to every story called viewpoints. What is good for one side is not always good for the other side. Historians often read both viewpoints to get an accurate understanding of a story.

The Californios were divided on their feelings when the Mexican-American War ended. Some were worried and others angry. Some were very happy to become a part of the United States. Additionally, there were American Indians who found themselves subject to a new government that they didn’t support. The American government had pushed them off of their lands, and many conflicts had occurred between the Mexicans and Americans and the American Indians.

Different Viewpoints

The following are three different viewpoints from Californians who lived during this U.S. takeover.

President of the Diputación

"Though I have complained loudly against Mexico, which for so many years has mistreated us, we preferred to undertake a life of shortages and uncertainty until Mexico won this lopsided contest." (reworded slightly for clarity) - Juan Bautista Alvarado

A U.S. Settler

"What foolishness it was for the natives of the Californias to attempt to stop the immigration from the United States to California. They might just as well attempt to arrest the thundering wheels of time or resist the mighty waters' flow." - Lansford W. Hastings

Mexican California Military Commander

"I am of the opinion that only one thing remains to be done, and that is to declare the annexation of our country to the United States. Only in this way will we be able to overcome the problems that hold us back from developing our resources." - Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo

What do these three viewpoints tell you about what was happening in California at the time? Was everyone happy about the situation? Can you think of another time in our nation’s history when there were different viewpoints?

title: Make a Rain Gauge
text:
Materials

a plastic bottle

scissors

bricks

a ruler

Ask an adult to help you cut the top half off the bottle.

Put it back on upside down.

Stand your rain gauge outside. Put bricks around it to hold it steady.

Each time it rains, measure how much rain has fallen.

title: How Do I Manage My Time?
text:
Feeling stressed? Not sure if you’ll have time to do all your homework? To keep up with your studies and have fun learning, you need to learn to manage your time. There are several techniques for managing your time. Here are some ideas:

Assignment book Find a small notebook (so that you can carry it around) to keep a list of your assignments. Write down each assignment as you get it, the class, the due date, the pages you need to read, the length of your paper and any other important facts. Review the day’s assignments before going home, and make sure you have all the materials to complete them. When the assignment is done, check it off.

Checklist When you have a big project that requires many steps, like a science project, research paper or presentation, it might be a good idea to use a checklist. That way, you know you’ve done everything you needed to. First, think of your final goal. Then, think about the steps you will need to take to reach that goal. How long will each step take? Finally, write down (your assignment notebook is a great place) the steps and the date that each should be completed. Be sure to list the steps in the order you will need to do them. And it’s never a bad idea to leave a couple extra days at the end in case some steps take longer than expected.

Reading methods There are many reading methods you can use to read effectively. We will discuss some of them in the future. Once you find one that you like, use it! You need to know what information is important and be able to take notes on it. If you are reading long stretches of text, take many breaks so that you do not get information overload. But make the breaks short enough that you don’t forget what you just read.

Study schedule Think about what time of day you do your best work. Is it in the morning before you go to school? After school in the afternoon? After dinner in the evening? Before bedtime? Pick a study schedule that works for you and stick to it. Choose a place that is quiet and free from distractions. If this is when and where you do your best work, then you will do a good job on your homework!

Try these time- management tools and use those that work for you. As you practice them, you will improve your study skills. And you will be forming good habits for your future schooling, college and work experience.

title: How’s the Weather up There?
text:
What’s the weather like in Washington? It’s hot. And it’s cold. It’s also rainy and dry, snowy and sunny, windy and calm, mild and extreme. The fact is, there are many different climates in our state. So whether you enjoy drizzling rains, blustery winds, or sunny days you’re sure to find weather you like in Washington. Weather is the temperature, moisture and wind in an area. Climate is normal weather over a period of time.

Along Washington’s coastline, pouring rain and toasty summer sun are both frequent visitors. Here you will find cool breezes that are perfect for launching a colorful kite, but you’ll also find raging winter storms complete with whipping winds and crashing waves.

Washington is also studded with towering mountains that are drenched by rain and blanketed by snow. Hiking and biking are popular activities during mild mountain summers, while skiers and snowboarders love swishing down our state’s many snowy slopes in wintertime.

The southeastern portion of our state is much drier than neighboring areas. Hills, plains, valleys and canyons create beautiful and assorted landscapes where temperatures can plummet below freezing or soar above 100 degrees.

Washington’s weather can swing wildly from one extreme to another. The hottest temperature ever recorded in our state was a blistering 118 degrees at Ice Harbor Dam on Aug. 5, 1961. The coldest temperature ever recorded was a chilly -48 at Mazama and Winthrop on Dec. 30, 1968. The summer of 2003 was the driest on record, while the most snowfall to pile up during a single winter occurred when 1,140 inches (that’s 95 feet!) of the white stuff covered Mount Baker ski area in 1998-1999.

Our state has also suffered its share of devastating weather. In 1993, a powerful windstorm blew through Washington. A brutal storm battered the coastline of Washington and Oregon in 1995, knocking out electrical power and leaving 1 million people in the dark. In 1996, floods (uncontrollable flowing water) that caused about $1 billion in damages and cost nine people their lives swamped the Pacific Northwest.

Fortunately, many communities are preparing themselves for the dangers and disasters severe Northwest weather can bring. Nearly two dozen Washington communities belong to the National Weather Service’s StormReady program, which arms cities with the knowledge and skills necessary to save lives and property during major weather events such as thunderstorms, floods, tornadoes and hurricanes (very strong winds more than 70 mph). A few communities along the coast also participate in the TsunamiReady program, which helps towns and counties in coastal areas prepare for and reduce the effects of tsunamis (soo-NAH-mes—huge sea waves caused by an underwater earthquake or volcanic eruption).

Another tool helping people prepare for and avoid dangerous weather conditions is the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Weather Radio. This special radio broadcasts weather information all across the country 24 hours a day, warning residents of approaching storms and other hazards such as volcanic eruptions or oil spills. September has been declared Weather Radio Awareness Month in Washington. Government officials hope that spreading the word about these lifesaving radios will help make them as common as smoke detectors in homes, businesses and schools.

So what’s the weather like in Washington? We have a little bit of every type of weather imaginable. Whether you’re searching for sunshine or rain, you’re sure to find the weather you like in Washington. Now you know what to say when your faraway friends ask, “How’s the weather up there?”

title: Cars That Run On Vegetable Oil?
text:
Washington has always been known as a clean, healthy place to live, but with more cars, trucks and buses driving on our roads, air pollution is becoming a real concern. Another problem is finding enough fuel to run all of these vehicles.

The United States realizes that there is only so much oil left to go around. Oil is a nonrenewable resource, which means that once we use it all up, it is gone forever and cannot be renewed, or made again. Before we run out of oil, our country is trying to find new, renewable energy sources, or sources of energy that can be used over and over again.

One Washington company is doing its part to give our country a renewable source of fuel for our vehicles. A Seattle company called Imperium Renewables makes a special fuel called biodiesel from vegetable oil. Biodiesel is made from canola oil and can be used in any diesel engine. Imperium Renewables buys most of its canola oil from Washington farmers who grow the rapeseed that is used to make canola oil. The company also buys canola oil from farmers in Canada and the Midwestern United States.

Besides being a good source of renewable energy, biodiesel is also much cleaner than regular gasoline or diesel fuel. Scientists say that biodiesel produces 78 percent less pollution than regular diesel fuel used to power our cars, trucks and buses. The United States currently uses about 63 billion gallons of regular diesel fuel each year. Think how much cleaner the air would be if all of this fuel were replaced with biodiesel fuel made right here in Washington!

Biodiesel seems to be the energy choice of the future. For now, it is a bit more expensive than regular diesel fuel, but Imperium Renewables hopes that the government will step in to help make the price more equal. The company also hopes that people will see how much better the new fuel is for our environment and use it to power their vehicles.

With a little help from companies like Seattle's Imperium Renewables, our country is well on its way to keeping our world running cleaner and longer than we ever thought possible.

title: Washington’s Weather
text:
Climate and Elevation:

We have learned that land closer to the ocean has a mild climate. Elevation is important to climate, too. The elevation of a place is how high or low it is compared to sea level (the level of the oceans). These maps shows the elevations and precipitation (rain, snow or other falling moisture) of Washington State.

Hey, Now That's Enlight(e)ning!

Question: How many thunderstorms are there each year?

Answer: There are about 2,000 thunderstorms rumbling around on our planet right this minute. About 16 million brew around the world each year.

Question: What are the odds of getting struck by lightning?

Answer: About a million to one - but you still need to go inside when a storm comes along!

Question: How many people die each year as a result of being struck by lightning?

Answer: 100-125. That makes lightning the second most deadly weather phenomenon. Flash floods are the worst. Lightning kills even more people than hurricanes or tornadoes!

Question: Are people always killed when they're struck by lightning?

Answer: About 2/3 of people struck by lightning survive. Even more could be saved if others would revive them with CPR instead of just standing around assuming they are dead.

Question: How can I protect myself from being struck by lightning?

Answer: Don't stand around wondering if the storm is going to pass. Take cover immediately. Lightning strikes without any warning!

Question: How can I tell how far away a storm is?

Answer: Count the seconds (thousand one, thousand two, etc.) between the time you see the flash and the time you hear the thunder. For every second you count, add 1,000 feet. So if the time between a flash of lightning and a crack of thunder is five seconds, that storm is about a mile away.

title: Western Lowlands
text: The Western Lowlands make a big region that is very low in elevation. There are mountains on the east of this area, and mountains lie to the west, but it is only 100 feet above sea level on the average. That is why it is called the Western Lowlands. Its climate is mild, meaning that temperatures are not very extreme: in the summer, it is usually below 90 degrees; and in the winter, it is usually above freezing. Why are the lowlands low? Well, scientists say that, thousands of years ago, glaciers carved out the lowlands and the Puget Sound. Glaciers are large rivers of ice. After the glaciers went away, ocean water filled up the Sound.

title: What is climate change?
text:
Climate change is a term we hear often in the news these days. Climatologists (scientists who study climate and weather) have figured out that over the past 100 years, Earth’s temperature has increased by over 1 degree Fahrenheit (nearly 1 degree Celsius). Climatologists say that starting in the late 1800s, since the beginning of the Industrial Revolution, we’ve created this increase by burning fossil fuels in our cars and in our electric power plants for industrial use.

The rate at which we burn fossil fuels releases more carbon dioxide into our atmosphere than can be absorbed by our “carbon sinks.” Carbon sinks are made up of physical features like peatlands, forests, grasslands and the ocean, which use the carbon we produce and neutralize its negative effects on the planet. But, because there are so many of us on Earth relying on fossil fuels, the global average temperature is expected to continue increasing by an additional 1-3.5 degrees by the year 2100.

You may be thinking, “1 or 2 degrees isn’t that much. How bad could climate change really be?” Well, let’s think about it. The human body normally maintains a body temperature of about 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit. Have you ever been sick with a fever? How did those extra few degrees make you feel? Did you get the chills even though you may have been covered by a blanket? Did you feel weak and achy all over? Maybe you couldn’t eat and felt sick to your stomach. Even though the fever may have been caused by a small germ or virus, those couple of degrees really threw your body off its normal rhythm, didn’t they? Climate change is like a fever for the whole of our planet.

Over the next few decades, unless we work together to lower Earth’s rising temperatures, we will see dramatic changes to our weather patterns. Heat waves, heavy rainfall, flooding and extreme drought in regions of Earth that aren’t used to these kinds of weather patterns. This can disrupt trade, agriculture and hurt many people and animals that live on Earth. Meetings are being held around the world to discuss the issue.

title: Tree Rings Tell About Past Weather
text:
Thick forests of tall trees shade Washington. Each year, these trees grow a new layer of wood just beneath their bark, forming a ring of new growth. You can tell roughly how old a tree is by counting the number of rings in its trunk. The rings of a tree also tell what the weather was like during the life of the tree - just like a wooden weather diary.

Because trees grow faster in mild, wet weather, they create a thicker ring in years with good weather. In years of drought, they grow more slowly and create a thinner ring. By studying a tree's rings, scientists can learn about past weather patterns. The rings tell which years brought either wet or dry weather to Washington's forests. They also tell scientists which years suffered forest fires, floods and extreme insect damage.

The science of studying the past by looking at tree rings is called dendrochronology. Tree rings can be studied by cutting open a dead tree's trunk or by drilling into the center of a live tree to remove a soda-straw-sized sample of wood. Although trees seem to be very quiet, they can tell us a great deal about Washington's weather!

title: Exchanging Goods and Services
text:
Think about walking home on a cold winter day. The wind is blowing hard. Just as your house comes into view, it starts to snow. You are freezing! Quickly, you bolt up your front steps. You stomp the snow off your boots as you enter the front door. You walk right to the kitchen and find your dad starting dinner. He asks you to help and gives you a can of tomato soup to open. You complain a little, not sure if your fingers are warm enough yet to move. You find the can opener and open the can. As the can spins around, you start to study it. You think of many questions about the can of soup. What part of the country did it come from? How was it made? At what store was it bought? How did it travel to the food store near your home? Who made the label? All of a sudden, that can of soup becomes more than the main menu for dinner tonight. You realize you are looking at a can of economics.

Economists ask all of these questions every day. Their job is to study the economy. They study what happens when manufacturers make and sell goods and services. They study the consumers who buy those goods and services. Producers make goods like soup. Your family, as the consumer, buys that good. On the other hand, if you provide a service for someone, such as mowing a neighbor's lawn, then the person paying you for the service becomes the consumer.

title: How Do I Take a Test?
text:
Do you get sweaty palms and butterflies in your stomach over the idea of taking a test? That happens to everyone at one time or another. Did you know test anxiety comes from a lack of self-confidence? How can you improve your self-confidence and improve your test-taking skills? The best way is to know the material very well. But here are some other important ideas that may help you:

Preview the test. What does it cover? How long is it?

Plan your time. Decide how much time you can spend on each section. Keep track of the time as you take the test.

Follow directions. Read all the directions and listen carefully to any directions read aloud.

Read the questions carefully. Look for keywords such as “when,” “where,” “why,” “different from,” “same as,” “before” and “after.”

Don’t get stuck on one question. If you can’t think of an answer, skip it and return to it later when you have finished the rest of the test.

Check your work. If you have time left after you finish the test, go back and double-check your work.

Use this list when getting ready for your next quiz. Practice good test-taking skills. You may want to use this list for the next few weeks until you have mastered the skills.

title: Weather Watch
text:
By scanning the sky for colors and other clues, people have tried to predict the weather since time began. Test these bits of ancient meteorology to see if they are really true.

A rose red sunset means fair skies are coming (“Red sky at night, sailor’s delight, red sky at morning, sailors take warning!”)

A pale yellow sunset means rain is on the way.

An evening rainbow predicts fair weather.

A morning rainbow in the west means rain.

A pre-dawn copper colored sky in the east means rain.

When the moon hangs in halo, there will be rain, especially if the halo is far from the moon.

text: As you read this week’s lesson, circle or highlight five verbs in any color. On a piece of paper, write a sentence for each verb using the progressive form (-ing).

title: Who Were the First Americans?
text:
When European explorers first "discovered" America, there were already thousands of American Indians living here. How did they get here? For many years, scientists believed that the first ancient ancestors of American Indians came to America from northern Asia. They believe these ancient people arrived about 12,000 years ago by hiking across a narrow strip of land that once bridged Asia and Alaska called Beringia, then eventually migrating across North and South America. But new information suggests that these ancient travelers might not have been the very first people to arrive in America.

In recent years, archaeologists in North and South America have discovered ancient tools, weapons, campsites and skeletons that are as old as, or even older than, artifacts from the landbridge travelers. As scientists studied these ancient bones, they discovered that they were very different from those people who walked the land bridge. So how did these early settlers arrive in America and where did they come from? Well they didn't travel here on a yellow school bus, that's for sure!

Scientists now wonder if some of the first people to arrive in America might have traveled here by boat from southern Asia, Australia, India, Japan or maybe even Europe, arriving long before the land-bridge travelers. These ancient people may have later died out or eventually joined the tribes of the land-bridge travelers, who became the ancestors of American Indians.

American Indians settled in Washington thousands of years ago. This land was like a fruitful garden containing thick forests, flowing rivers and an endless ocean to provide all the food and materials needed for survival. Many different tribes spread out to occupy different areas across Washington. Today, we sort these tribes into three main groups based on where they lived: Coastal Natives, Inland or River Natives and Plateau Natives.

Some of these early natives settled in villages, using thick cedar boards to build long houses (large homes that housed many families). Other tribes were constantly on the move. They packed up their homes and followed their food supply, moving to the forests to hunt deer, elk and birds or to the rivers to fish for slippery steelhead and trout. Early American Indians did not usually grow crops because delicious plants and roots grew all over Washington. They gathered huckleberries, onions, nuts, mushrooms, sunflowers, potatoes and other goodies. From the rivers, they harvested shiny salmon, and from the Pacific Ocean, they collected oysters, clams, shrimp and crabs. A few tribes even hunted whales. They carefully dried meats and plants, storing them in woven baskets for winter use. Trade was an important part of American Indian life. Natives would trade goods for other materials they could not get or that were unavailable in their area. Dried seafood, meats, whale oil, plants and medicines were traded between tribes. Northwestern tribes even traded with tribes from the plains to obtain bison meat and hides.

Early natives worked hard to survive, but they also loved to play. Many Washington tribes enjoyed stick games, wrestling, foot races and other competitive challenges. They often wagered on these games, betting valuable items such as meats, fish, colorful baskets, arrows and fishing nets.

Modern descendants of these early native tribes still live in Washington today. They are proud of their heritage and struggled to keep their native languages and traditions alive. They hope their ancient cultures will survive for many years to come.

title: A Neanderthal’s Best Friend
text:
Archaeologists in both Siberia and Belgium have found dog skulls that show wolves were well on their way to becoming domesticated dogs (pets or helpers for people) about 33,000 years ago. This means the change started about 14,000 years earlier than scientists once thought. How do we know the skulls were 33,000 years old? Scientists use a technique called carbon dating to figure it out. Carbon dating is a way to date things that were once alive by looking at how fast a certain type of carbon in the remains will decay.

This discovery also means that dogs were being domesticated in different areas of the world at the same time. The skulls show that people on two different continents were using dogs as pets or helpers.

Scientists once believed that cows, sheep and goats were domesticated first because they could provide meat and milk for prehistoric people. However, it seems dogs were domesticated first to give companionship and protection and to help during hunts.

Scientists don't think the dogs that were in Siberia or Belgium back then are the ancestors of our modern dog. Instead, they believe that many of these dogs died out during the Ice Age. Through DNA research, scientists have discovered that modern dogs come from the Middle East and East Asia. People and dogs have been best friends for a very long time!

title: Washington’s First Inhabitants
text:
The first people to live in Washington arrived about 12,000 years ago. These early people may have migrated from the mountain-desert regions of Utah and Nevada in search of a better life. Here in the Northwest, they found more than enough.

The Coastal People

Washington Coastal people lived off of the sea. They harvested the oceans for kelp, sea slugs, salmon, herring, halibut, dog salmon, whales and sea otters. From these, they obtained food, clothing, fishing line, ropes and tools. Their villages were usually near the sea, and their culture was built around sturdy cedar canoes, fishing and enduring the endless rains. They built nice villages, but also kept homes in the valleys, away from the winter ocean storms. Washington's Coastal tribes include Makah, Ozette, Quileute, Hoh, Quinault, Shoalwater and Chinook.

The Plateau and Plains People

Washington Plateau and Plains people had a harder time living in areas where food was scarce. Because of this constant search, these groups didn't settle and were always on the move, chasing the food. In early spring, the people had very little to eat - usually snails and slow rabbits. By May or June, they moved to the rivers to catch the spawning salmon. By fall, they left the rivers and stalked deer, elk, antelope and mountain goats. In preparation for winter, the women harvested nuts, berries and roots. Animal and fish flesh was dried and preserved. Some of Washington's Plateau and Plains tribes are Yakama, Spokane, Klickitat, Palouse, Walla Walla and Colville.

The Interior People

Washington Interior people didn't need the kind of strong, ocean-going canoes that the Coastal Natives used. Their canoes were shallower and designed for the more gentle currents of rivers. They became expert at catching salmon as they migrated from the ocean to spawn in the rivers. American Indians of the interior didn't cultivate the land because so much food grew freely around them. An occasional deer that wandered into camp was surrounded and killed for a feast. Their villages usually stayed in about the same place, so long as the food was there. Washington's Interior tribes include: Clallam, Lummi, Swinomish, Skagit, Tulalip, Puyallup, Muckleshoot, Nisqually, Chehalis, Cowlitz, Nooksack and Skykomish.

title: The Moon in Myth
text:
To the people living long ago, the moon was a god or goddess of special mystery and power.

Not only did the moon outshine the other nighttime lights, but it changed its shape and had its own strange motion in the sky. There were visible markings on the moon that fascinated people on every land for thousands of years.

Some said the markings were a rabbit; some said they resembled a frog. Other people said that the markings were a human face - A Man in the Moon.

In Scandinavia, however, there was no Man-in-the-Moon but instead two children and they were carrying between them a pail of water. Little of the myth remains except an old nursery rhyme:

Jack and Jill Went up the hill To fetch a pail of water...

Once, long before this myth became nursery rhyme, this story may have helped people remember how through the month the moon waxes (gets larger) to the full moon then wanes (gets smaller) to the new moon and increases to full again. You see, Jack gets his name from the Scandinavian word "jakka" - to increase, and Jill's name comes from "joila" - to dissolve.

Take this article with you on the next full moon and see if you can find the above markings.

title: Where Do American Indians Live Today?
text:
For thousands of years, Washington has been home to the colorful native cultures of American Indian tribes like the Makah, Yakama, Muckleshoot and Chinook. Many descendants of these tribes still live in Washington today.

According to the 2000 U.S. Census (a census is a count of U.S. population), there are currently 4.1 million American Indians living in the United States. Most live in the West. Washington ranks No. 7 on the list of states with the highest American Indian populations. When the census first started counting American Indians in 1860, only 426 natives were counted in Washington. Now more than 94,000 American Indians live in our state.

Today, most Washington American Indians live in or near the Western Lowlands and Cascade Mountains Regions. The counties with the highest American Indian populations are King, Yakama and Pierce counties. Snohomish, Spokane, Whatcom and Okanogan counties are also home to many American Indians.

Although they live in a modern world, Washington's American Indians are working hard to preserve their ancient cultures. Our state is dotted with museums that display pottery, jewelry, arrowheads and many other historical native artifacts. Several cultural centers are dedicated to teaching native languages, games, basket weaving and other cultural lessons. Tribes also hold gatherings called powwows, where members of different tribes dress in traditional regalia and perform tribal dances and songs. People from around the state and around the world enjoy learning more about native Washington cultures by visiting these interesting places and events.

title: Salmon Trout
text: Is that a salmon or a trout? Washington's juvenile Chinook salmon and rainbow trout look a lot alike. They can be found in many freshwater rivers, but only the salmon spends much of its adult life in the salty ocean. Can you tell the difference between a Chinook salmon and a rainbow trout?

title: How Do I Use a Dictionary?
text:
What does “native” mean? How do you pronounce “shaman”? To find the answers to these and many other questions, grab a dictionary. The dictionary just might be a student’s best friend. A dictionary lists and defines words.

Know Your ABCs

The words in a dictionary appear in alphabetical order. At the top of each page, two guidewords show the first and last words on that page. Guidewords help you find the word you need more quickly. For example, the word “tepee” might appear on a page with the guidewords “tension” and “territory” at the top of that page. Is your word followed by numbers? That means it has more than one definition. Look up the word “native” and see all the definitions for it.

After each word, you will find a letter that stands for a part of speech. For example, n. means “noun,” v. means “verb,” and adj. means “adjective.” Sometimes, one word can have two or more parts of speech. It depends on how it’s used in a sentence. Let’s show this with the word “hunt.” Look it up now in your dictionary.

What is the meaning of “hunt” as a verb?

Use “hunt” as a verb in a sentence.
