When you are an active reader, you are involved because you think about and respond to what you read. Here are some strategies to use for becoming an active reader.

Ask Questions

Ask yourself questions as you read. What kinds of questions should you ask? Well, any question that comes to mind as you are reading is a good question. But some questions you could ask follow:

How do I feel about what I am reading?

Do the characters' actions make sense to me?

Do the characters remind me of any people I know?

Do I understand the events that are happening?

Could similar things happen to me?

What do I hope will happen next?

What would I most like to ask this author?

Read As a Group

Sometimes, you can get a better idea of what to think about a book after talking to someone else about it. Discussion about books can make your reading more interesting because different people have different ideas about the same text. Follow these steps and try forming some discussion groups in your class.

Assemble a small group of interested readers. Include enough people to make the discussion interesting, but not so many that the group is hard to manage.

Pick a book that you all want to read.

Allow time for everyone to read it.

Write down a list of questions and ideas before the meeting.

Meet to discuss your reactions to the book. Before beginning, pick someone to lead the discussion.

Connect With the Words

Make a connection with what you read, even if you are reading about someone very different from you. Try putting yourself in different characters' shoes so that you will understand why they act the way they do. You can also make a connection with what you read by forming opinions about it.

Respond to Your Text

Keep a response journal where you can write your feelings, ideas, questions, reactions and thoughts about what you read. You can also note facts, copy quotations you liked, or talk about passages that you thought were well written.

Try these active reading strategies and you will get the most out of what you read.

title: Make an Astrolabe
text:
During his historic voyage, Christopher Columbus used simple instruments and his knowledge of the sun and stars to guide him. Follow these steps, and you will be able to determine your latitude in the same way.

Materials

Protractor

Rectangular piece of cardboard or index card big enough for the protractor to be traced on

String (about 10 inches)

Drinking straw

Metal washer or paper clip

Tape or glue, scissors

Fine-point marker

Atlas or globe

Directions

1. Lay the straight edge of the protractor against one edge of the cardboard. Trace the semi-circle edge, and cut out the cardboard along this curved line.

2. With the protractor as a guide, mark and number the degrees shown. Also, mark the vertex.

3.Tie one end of the string to the middle of the drinking straw. Use the tape or glue to hold it.

4.Tie the other end around the washer or paper clip.

5. Glue the straw just above the 90-degree marks with the string over the vertex.

6. On a clear night, take your astrolabe outside. Face north. (The sun sets on your left if you are facing north.) Find the Big Dipper and use the two stars farthest from the handle. They point to the last star in the Little Dipper’s handle. This is Polaris.

7. Look at Polaris through the straw. Try not to move anything and put your thumb over the weight (paper clip or washer) as it hangs. Go inside where it is light and read the number. Look on the globe or map to find your latitude. What do you notice about your astrolabe reading and your latitude?

title: Let's Write
text: You were a member of the Lewis and Clark expedition. Describe what your typical day was like. What things would you record in your journal?

title: Lewis and Clark Explore the Northwest
text:
The United States purchased the vast Louisiana Territory from France. President Jefferson was anxious to find out what the unexplored territory looked like. He sent his personal secretary, Meriwether Lewis, and his friend William Clark to explore it.

Journey Becomes Difficult

The journey became very hard. The party only had berries to eat. Another time, they only had bear grease and candles. Their moccasins were too thin and they feared freezing their feet off, but they pressed onward. The Nez Percé Indians in Idaho were very curious about York. York was an enslaved person who was forced to work for William Clark without pay. The American Indians had never seen an African American before. The American Indians were also amazed at what the white men would eat.

As they journeyed down the Columbia, they found European goods among the various tribes. Europeans had not traveled this far inland, but the American Indians had traded the goods upriver from the coast. By the time the party reached the ocean, everyone was very tired. They constructed Fort Clatsop for the winter of 1805-1806 and ate a native diet of berries and fish. Christmas was just another cold, rainy day as they forced themselves to eat spoiled elk and fish with a few roots.

Great Success

The Lewis and Clark expedition (a group with a special mission to perform) was a great success. They were welcomed back home the following year. They were called men "returned from the dead," as they were feared lost. Their journals, maps and friendly contacts with the American Indians opened up the area to safe passage for future travelers. This also strengthened America's claim on the western U.S. territory.

title: Westward Ho!
text:
The Oregon Trail was the long, hard path used by early pioneers to travel from the eastern United States to the Pacific Northwest. It was 2,000 miles long, and a wagon needed five or six months to make the journey. To make the trip easier, pioneers used a light-weight wagon called a "Prairie Schooner." These shorter, lighter wagons needed fewer animals to pull them.

The Oregon Trail began at Independence, Missouri, and ended in Oregon City. The trail was not a single road like today's freeways. In some places, the wagons spread out over large areas, coming together again to cross rivers or pass through canyons. This changed in 1843 with the "Great Migration," when a permanent cut was made in the prairie sod (grass and roots that cover the dirt) by the 900 people and 1,000 head of cattle who passed over that year. Other pioneers followed those ruts, which can still be seen today.

In 1805-06, Lewis and Clark were the first to map out a land route from east to west. This route was hard for people to follow until 1813, when Robert Stuart made a discovery. He was traveling the route backwards, from Oregon to the eastern United States, when he found a pass through the Rocky Mountains farther south than Lewis and Clark's. He named it "South Pass." In 1832, Capt. Benjamin de Bonneville took the first wagons over South Pass.

Two years later (1834), the missionaries came. They built forts and taught Christianity to fur traders and the American Indians. A Protestant missionary named Marcus Whitman settled near Walla Walla with his wife, Narcissa. They built a fort and used medicine and religion to help people. There were 15 other missions built, and these became stopping places for early pioneers.

Dr. John McLoughlin helped hundreds of these early pioneers with food, water and protection. He stood 6-feet 4-inches tall and had a full head of white hair. The American Indians called him "The Great White-Headed Eagle." His kindness and hard work encouraged early pioneers to make the journey on the Oregon Trail. It is estimated (judged, guessed) that 200,000 pioneers came west on the Oregon Trail. Grateful pioneers named McLoughlin the "Father of Oregon." He was British, but became a U.S. citizen in 1849.

Pioneer journals and diaries tell of a hard life on the trail. Pioneers broke camp at 4 a.m. and then walked all day until the sun went down. About one in 10 people died, mostly from accidents or disease. Boredom was a real problem, too. And if a group couldn't make the trip in six months, they risked getting caught in the snow as did the Donner Party in 1846. Out of 87 Donner pioneers, 40 of them froze to death in the snow.

Our pioneers didn't let death and hardship scare them. All along the trail, there were marriages, babies born, and holidays celebrated. It was a great time in our state's history, one to be very proud of. Do you have an ancestor who came here over the Oregon Trail?

title: Oldest Home in America?
text:
Researchers found an exciting clue to how early Americans lived in the Pacific Northwest. About 50 miles from Crater Lake, Oregon, a home site was discovered that is about 9,500 years old. Scientists say that the home site was preserved because it was buried beneath 2 feet of volcanic ash when Mount Mazama blew up about 7500 B.C. This is the same volcano that formed Crater Lake.

Researchers say that the home was in a shallow pit that measured about 14 feet by 16 feet. The stumps of five lodgepole pine support posts are there indicating that a tepee structure was erected above the pit.

In the middle of the floor is the fireplace, or hearth. The researchers sifted through the ashes and found the remains of hazelnuts, blackberries, choke cherries and other fruits and nuts. They also found obsidian tools that had blood on them. Obsidian is a dark natural glass formed from cooled molten lava. When the blood was analyzed, it turned out to be nothing more than part of dinner - rabbit blood.

Using DNA analysis, scientists learned that other blood stains on the rocks around the house are those of bear, bison (commonly called buffalo), sheep and deer or elk that were butchered. The researchers also found the remains of ponderosa pine and sagebrush wood. The early dwellers used the bark to make rope, matting, clothing and coverings for their tepee and floor.

The next oldest American Indian homes discovered in the area are about 7,500 years old. Researchers are calling this latest find the best discovery yet, showing how early Americans lived on a day-to-day basis in the Pacific Northwest. They know that people first arrived here about 11,000-13,000 years ago, but had little knowledge about their living arrangements and eating habits.

As strange as it may seem, the newly-discovered home site shows that the region around Crater Lake was once a great place to live. Forests, game and food were there before the volcano exploded. After the volcano, there was nothing but a bare, lifeless pumice desert. The eruption of the powerful volcano must have destroyed the lives of many American Indians.

title: The Oregon Trail
text:
The Oregon Trail brought the first permanent settlers to the Pacific Northwest. Pioneers settled in Idaho, Oregon and Washington. The trip took six months and cost $800-$1,000 per wagon. That was a lot for people earning only $1.50 a day. Was the trip worth the risk? Some people lost all their belongings, their wagons and sometimes their lives.

How to Play

Two to four people may play the game at one time.

Use a dice to determine which player goes first. The highest number wins. Move clockwise around the group.

Have each person find a token such as a coin, ring, plastic\figure or other small item different from the others.

Roll the die and move your token the number of spaces you spin or roll. Follow the instructions, if any, in the space. The first one to Oregon City is the winner.

title: Bartering in the Colonies
text:
Bartering is trading goods, but without the use of money. In early cultures, people were able to get many things they needed and wanted through bartering. Merchants would often travel with ships laden with goods. These goods were bartered for items that could be taken back. Then they would be either bartered for other goods or traded for money. People, towns and even countries bartered for items they did not produce or grow.

Bartering was easy as long as there was a simple trade between two people. However, sometimes bartering had to span several persons to get the goods wanted. Then it wasn't so easy. Suppose one merchant had a barrel of allspice. He wanted to trade with another merchant for some cloth. However, the merchant who had the cloth did not want or need a barrel of allspice. What do you think a good solution might have been? The people would barter for something they didn't need. They hoped they could later trade it for something they did need!

Bartering can be done with anything people value and assign a worth to. In Jamestown, tobacco was used. Colonists could pay with tobacco for items they needed but could not make or grow themselves. In New England, English fishermen worked on the coast years before the Pilgrims settled Plymouth. Fishing camps established along the coast eventually became the New Hampshire colony. First, the fishing camps began trading with the local American Indians. They traded their knives and supplies for furs. The camps became larger and larger until they turned into small towns. These small towns grew to be large trading centers. Eventually the New Hampshire area became a colony.

Another form of bartering was trade -offs. The same company that financed Jamestown also financed the Pilgrims' journey to the New World. However, the company asked the Pilgrims for seven years' worth of crops to pay back the money for the journey. This arrangement was required of anyone who wanted to come to America but couldn't afford it. People settled in areas where the natural resources would allow them to repay the company in crops. This was what is known as a trade-off. Although people didn't really want to give up seven years worth of crops, it was often the only way they could come to America. They were willing to trade something they didn't want to do (give crops) for something they wanted more (to be in America). This happens all the time, even to you. You may give up a few movies, so that you can buy a video game. Countries and all levels of governments do it as well. It's all a matter of deciding what is most important.

Bartering is still going on today. People, companies and even countries barter for things they need or want. Countries that raise great amounts of beef may barter with countries that grow large amounts of grain. Companies may trade services to support one another. Even children barter! When was the last time you tried talking someone out of a big chocolate chip cookie in exchange for your apple?

In Jamestown, Captain John Smith wrote about trading blue beads with the native tribes for food. The American Indians valued the glass beads, and the colonists needed food. Copper ornaments and beads were also highly prized by the chiefs of local tribes. At first, the Powhatan traded with other tribes to obtain copper. Over time, the Europeans gave copper beads and ornaments for barter. The Powhatan turned to the colonists for the copper items.

title: Keep Track of Information
text:
How will you keep track of all the good information you find while researching? Take notes! Here are some tips for taking research notes:

1. You will probably find that index cards are the best way to take notes. You can write one fact or quotation on each card and then organize and rearrange them based on how you want to write your report, give your presentation or study for your test.

2. Label your notes with subject headings.

3. Paraphrase and summarize information in your own words. Summarize information by writing the main ideas and most important supporting details. This will help you prevent plagiarism, which is copying writers' words without giving them credit.

4. If you like how a writer has said something, use a direct quotation. Be sure to record the quote exactly. Include punctuation and spelling just as written by the writer. Put quotation marks around the quote so that you know it is a quotation and not your summary.

5. Write down the title, author, publisher, city of publication, date and page numbers of each source after you have recorded the fact or quotation. This way, you can include this information in a bibliography, and you can go back and double check a quotation if you have questions.

6. Abbreviate the information you have researched to save time. Write in groups of words and phrases instead of complete sentences. Use abbreviations and symbols as long as you will remember what they mean. You can transfer the information into complete sentences later when you use it in your report or presentation. This will save you time when you start writing your report.

7. Organize your notes into the most useful order for you, your report or presentation. For example, you can organize them by subject or theme.

Try It!

Do some research on the subject you are currently studying in social studies. Use research notes to record the information you find. Use the research notes to write a report or make a presentation, depending on what your teacher assigns. Once you've organized your notes, write the report. Explain your ideas clearly and support them with details from your research. Be sure to follow all of the steps above!

title: Make a Compass
text:
Materials

magnet

large sewing needle

cork

glue

cup of water

Instructions

1. Stroke the needle with the magnet at least 30 times. Rub only in the direction of the sharp end.

2. Put a dab of glue on the center of the cork and put the needle in the glue as shown. Let glue dry.

3. Place the cork in the water and wait. Shortly, the sharp end of the needle will point to magnetic north.

Compass Rose

Color and cut out the compass pattern below. After you have determined where north is by using your compass, tape the compass rose to a table or desk with north in the correct position

title: Fun Facts
text: Alaska is home to both the northernmost and westernmost point in the United States. The northernmost is in Point Barrow and the westernmost is Cape Wrangell. It is also home to the highest point in the United States, Denali (Mount McKinley).

title: Let's Write
text: This week, write as if you were a farmer, moving into the big city of New York. Put yourself in the 1890s era and tell us why you moved to the city. Think about what you’ve learned in the paper that explains why people went to the cities. Describe the differences you will experience in the city compared to living on a farm.

title: Pushing the Rails West
text:
Building train tracks in America began in the east in 1825 and followed the frontier. The trains were often only 10 years behind the settlement of new areas. By 1850, there were tracks all over the eastern United States and a few scattered in the West, but there were no main lines to connect the East Coast with the West Coast.

Americans wanted the tracks to run near their favorite cities, something that would be impossible. This made it hard to decide what part of America an east-west line should run through. When the Civil War started and the Southern states left the Union, Congress decided to build tracks in the middle part and the north part of the country. Hence the Union Pacific and Central Pacific Railroad Companies were born (1862). In 1864, President Abraham Lincoln signed the act of Congress that permitted the Northern Pacific Railroad to be built. Our line began at Lake Superior (see your classroom map) and ended at Puget Sound.

While our railroad was being built, the first track to run the whole length of America was finished. The year was 1869. This track was built from two directions, with one company starting in California and the other company starting in Omaha, Nebraska. For six years, construction moved these tracks toward each other until they met at Promontory Point, Utah, where the famous "Golden Spike" was driven. Settlers began coming to the Pacific Coast by rail instead of the Oregon Trail. Why take six months by wagon when you could get there in only six days by train?

Building these large railroad lines took a lot of money and property. Congress helped the railroad companies by giving them millions of acres of land. Our Northern Pacific Railway Company received 44 million acres. The actual area reserved for track construction was 200 feet wide and more than 1,000 miles long. Our tracks ran over vast plains, rivers and mountains. The rest of the free land was used to obtain lumber, mine coal, sell, lease or house construction workers and provide for them. Many of these railway settlements later developed into towns and cities.

Our railroad took almost 20 years to complete because the company doing the work had problems, and the route was very difficult. At one time, 10,000 workers labored on the project. The last spike was finally driven in a place about 60 miles west of Helena, Montana. The day was Sept. 8, 1883.

At the west end, the track officially ended in Tacoma, Washington, but everyone wanted the track extended. People in Oregon built a line going south (Portland to San Francisco) so that they could hook up with the other east-west mainline. Another track was built north, from Portland to Puget Sound. A dozen other railroad companies were started in Washington and Oregon, but over time, most of these joined together to form fewer large companies.

The railroad is very important to our state. It has been used to move billions of dollars of lumber, fish, produce, cars and just about everything else - including people. Have you ever ridden a train?

title: All Aboard!
text:
While train travel has nearly become a thing of the past, there are still many people out there who enjoy a good, old-fashioned train ride. If you think that hopping a train would be a great way to relax and unwind, the Mount Rainier Scenic Railroad has a trip just for you.

The Mount Rainier Scenic Railroad Station is located in Mineral, Washington. Passengers board the train here and enjoy a journey through beautiful forests along the foothills of Mount Rainier. They also cross breathtaking bridges and then head back to civilization again. All trains are pulled by restored steam engine locomotives, making the ride a trip back in time to the days when steam engines were the fastest type of transportation available.

There are many special trips offered on the Mount Rainier Railroad each year. At Easter, guests can hop aboard the Bunny Hunt Eggspress, hot on the trail of the Easter Bunny. The ride includes an Easter Egg hunt, complete with eggs, goodies and prizes. At Christmas, passengers can take a trip on the Snowball Express, enjoying the Christmas spirit while chugging along the snow-covered hills of Mount Rainier.

The railroad also offers tours of its famous restoration shop. The shop restores steam locomotives for the Mount Rainier Scenic Railroad, as well as for other railroads throughout the Pacific Northwest.

Even though train travel isn't as popular as it once was, you can still enjoy a piece of railroad history by making a reservation on the Mount Rainier Scenic Railroad. All aboard!

title: Trappers & Traders Explore and Open New Territory
text:
This week, let's mention some important people who helped open up our land so that the trains could come.

Fur Trappers and Traders Pave the Way for Progress

Hundreds of early American and Canadian settlers came to trap furs. Companies were formed, groups were combined, and all kinds of money was spent because the fur business was making many people rich.

Hudson's Bay Company

In 1669, Britain gave the Hudson's Bay Company total control over the American fur trade. About 115 years later, the company expanded its operations to the western part of the continent. The company hired American Indians to do all the hunting and traded trinkets and cheap goods for the furs. It was hard for other fur trappers to compete. Everywhere a man turned, he heard that famous name, "Hudson's Bay Company."

Voyageurs were French-Canadians who trapped fur in Canada and transported furs for other trappers. They were very hard-working men who would paddle their birch-bark canoes 12-16 hours a day, travel over mountains, wade across lakes, hike for days with one or more 90-pound packs on their backs, live off the land and keep going in a blizzard. They dressed in colorful clothing and sang loud as they worked. Everyone knew about the voyageurs.

The Northwest Company

In 1784, a group of Scotsmen formed a trapping company and hired the voyageurs to work for them. The Scotsmen had a clever way of getting their furs. They would intercept the American Indians and buy their furs before they could sell them to the Hudson’s Bay Company. Several explorers were sent to find river routes to the Pacific Ocean. These men included Simon Fraser, who tried to survey the Columbia River and instead discovered the Fraser River in 1808; David Thompson, who founded four important trading posts and whose maps were so exact, they remained in use for 100 years; Alexander Mackenzie, the first European to travel across the continent by land and river in 1793; and Dr. John McLoughlin, who was Britain’s chief agent and the most powerful man in the region for 22 years.

Mountain Men

The Americans also sent trappers into the interior of the United States to find fur. These hearty men lived off the land, endured many hardships and often gathered together for a rendezvous to exchange information, goods, weapons, maps and ideas. Jedediah Smith and Jim Bridger are two famous mountain men.

The Pacific Fur Company

American businessman John Jacob Astor had a good idea. In 1811, he decided to find a place near the coast where his fur trappers could bring their furs. His ships would pick up the furs and leave supplies to maintain a fort. He established Fort Astoria, the first American trading post on the coast and site of today’s Astoria, Oregon.

title: Tacoma
text: This beautiful seaport and industrial center, built on an inlet of the Puget Sound, was the place where the Northern Pacific Railroad had its terminal. Its ideal location made it the perfect place to load products onto ships. In 1852, the first sawmill was built on the south shore of Commencement Bay. More sawmills were added, and the settlement grew up as "Old Tacoma." When the railroad came along, planners chose a place one mile south of "Old Tacoma" and named it "New Tacoma." The two towns were combined in 1884, and today Tacoma is the third largest city in Washington. It is at the center of a large forest-products industry, and many small ships and fishing boats are built there. Many residents work at the large Army and Air Force base nearby. Mount Rainier National Park is 56 miles away, and the Pacific Coast is 100 miles away. The city has railroad-repair shops, machine shops, chemical plants and food-processing plants. When ships pull out of the port of Tacoma, they are loaded down with manufactured goods, metals, lumber, wheat and fruit. If you plan to visit, save plenty of time to see the many museums.

title: Where is the world’s longest railway?
text: You will have to travel to Russia to see the world's longest railroad. The Trans- Siberian Railway from Moscow to Vladivostok is 5,777 miles long. In the United States, our longest single track is 1,780 miles long. This track was completed in 1869 when the Central Pacific Railroad built east from Sacramento, California, and the Union Pacific Railroad built west, meeting up at Promontory Summit, Utah.

title: Wood for Ties!
text: Building the railroads required a lot of wooden ties. We're not talking the kind of ties men wear to work - we're talking about a wooden timber 8 feet long and about 8 inches by 7 inches square. In England, they call them "sleepers" because the timber lies at rest under the rails. These ties were laid on gravel about 21 inches apart. In the Pacific Northwest, ties were cut from the center sections of Douglas fir trees. Ties had to be strong enough to hang onto the spikes that were driven into them to hold the rails. They had to endure the hot, blistering sun all summer long and freezing blizzards and deep snows, year after year. To keep the insects and weather from destroying the ties, they were soaked in three gallons of an oil made from tar. (Ever hear of creosote?) Each timber weighed more than 60 pounds. It took a lot of trees to make the ties for our Northern Pacific Railroad. Our first track from Puget Sound to Chicago required about 3 million ties. That's a lot of trees!

title: Timelines
text:
Timelines can be made for just about anything and for any time. A good place to start is with something or someone you know well... like yourself! What year was your first birthday? What year did you start kindergarten? Make a list of all the things you would like on your timeline. If you don't know when the event was, ask a parent to help you.

Next, get out a ruler and measure a straight line, with evenly spaced lines to mark years or months. Fill in your headings and draw some pictures that go with them. As you continue to grow, keep on adding to your timeline.

Historic Timelines

The timeline below is a historic timeline. It is about a person as well. What can you learn from this timeline? How old was Washington when he died? How long was Washington married when the Declaration of Independence was signed?

By marking the passage of time, we are able to have a clearer understanding of the life of an individual or an event in time.

Here are some other topics for timelines: the 19 70s, roller coasters, electric trains or Barbie dolls.

title: Clarity of Expression: Fred Rogers
text:
Do you like to give speeches? Can you convince others to understand your thoughts and opinions? Then maybe you have a gift for expressing yourself clearly, like Fred Rogers.

Fred Rogers was born in Pennsylvania on March 20, 1928. He graduated from college with a bachelor’s degree in music composition. When Rogers turned 35, he was ordained as a Presbyterian minister. He spent much of his life focusing on serving families and specifically children through film and television.

Rogers received several awards for the work he did on his show, “Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood.” He used puppets, songs, direct speech and imagined scenarios to help give kids ways of processing both traumatic and everyday events and relationships. He has successfully used these techniques to address death, assassination, disability and even racism.

This show aired on PBS (Public Broadcasting Service). This means that it was funded using donations, grants and public money. On May 1, 1969, Fred Rogers gave a speech to a select committee of Congress. During this time in history, the United States was involved in a war overseas. Many in the U.S. government felt that they needed to stop funding public broadcasting to help with the war effort.

In his speech, Rogers stressed the importance of investing in teaching kids constructive (positive) ways of dealing with anger, sadness and grief. This was something that he felt strongly about. During his speech, he said, “ ... I feel that if we in public television can only make it clear that feelings are mentionable and manageable, we will have done a great service for mental health.”

He spoke for a total of about six minutes, but by the end the chairman of the committee was convinced. PBS would receive the funding it needed to continue producing educational programming for children.

Do you think you have a good ability to express yourself clearly as Fred Rogers did? What topic do you feel strongly about?

title: How Do You Start a State?
text:
Have you ever wondered how our ancestors started Washington? It all began with a funeral.

In 1841, a very rich settler died. His name was Ewing Young. He had a lot of cattle and money, but no wife or children to inherit it. ("Inherit" means to receive as a gift the property of someone who dies.) The biggest problem was Young's cattle. The people couldn't just leave the cattle wandering around without an owner.

In those early days, the missions were the center of community activity. The Methodist Mission was asked to solve the problem of Young's cattle. The mission formed a committee that gave away Young's cattle to other settlers. But there were other problems, too. The settlers needed a sheriff, a judge and jury, and somebody who could record their land claims. Could this committee help them do that? For a couple of years, nothing happened.

Wolf Meetings

In 1843, the committee was again called to action. Wild animals were killing cattle and scaring the settlers. What could be done? The committee decided to ask everyone to donate money to a fund. This money was used to pay hunters a reward for killing a wolf, bear or mountain lion.The people met often to talk about animals, and their meetings became known as the "Wolf Meetings."

Later that spring (1843), the people at the Wolf Meetings decided to form a government. Twelve men were chosen to come up with a plan and report back. On May 2, 1843, a meeting was held to vote on the new government. American settlers and former employees of the Hudson's Bay Company met to vote in Champoeg (15 miles southwest of Portland, Oregon). The settlers approved the very first American government in the Pacific Northwest. On July 5, 1843, the new government was written down in a document called the "Organic Act of the Provisional Government of Oregon." Washington and Oregon were still a single territory at this time.

How did the Organic Act work? It allowed 640 acres of land for every family. However, you had to live on your land for one year and make improvements (build a barn, cut a road, etc.). The Organic Act did other things: It set the borders of the new territory; declared the territory an anti-slavery region; and established three branches of government. In 1845, the people chose George Abernathy as the first governor. There remained one last problem to solve: Will the U.S. Congress make the Oregon Territory a part of the United States?

Congress took a long time deciding. The Southern states hated the idea because they didn't want another anti-slavery region to join. And the Mexican War had everyone very worried. Finally, on Aug. 13, 1848, President Polk signed the bill making our region a part of the United States. He sent General Joseph Lane to be the first territorial governor. What about George Abernathy, the temporary governor? Abernathy stepped down so that Lane could take over.

Are we a state yet? Not at this point in our story. Before statehood, there needed to be a lot more growth and organization.

title: Kids Choose New State Amphibian
text:
Did you know that Washington now has an official state amphibian? In April 2007, Governor Chris Gregoire and the Washington State Legislature signed a law making the Pacific Chorus Frog our official state amphibian. Even though lawmakers voted in favor of the choice, it was actually a group of third graders from Keitlyn Watson's class at Boston Harbor Elementary School that came up with the idea.

Over the school year, the class did research to find out which amphibian would best represent Washington as our state amphibian. They read books, wrote reports, drew pictures and listened to recordings of the "song" (croak) of a Pacific Chorus Frog before making their final decision. With the help of their teacher, they also did research on what it takes for a bill to become a law. With the support of several representatives in the Washington State House of Representatives, the class brought a bill before the governor proposing that the Pacific Chorus Frog be chosen as the official state amphibian.

Wearing a "frog ring" on her hand, Governor Gregoire signed the bill into law, telling the children, "There, you got a bill passed and that's a really, really big deal. You made a law today."

The Pacific Chorus Frog, whose scientific name is Pseudacris regilla, is one of our state's smallest amphibians. It measures only 2 inches long, but has a beautiful voice that can be heard for long distances. The frog can be tan, brown, green or gray and has a black stripe through its eye and across its shoulder. The Pacific Chorus Frog can be found in all 39 of Washington's counties.

title: The Making of a Territory
text:
The boundaries of the Oregon territory were set by Congress in 1848. The Oregon territory was very large. It ranged from the Pacific Ocean along the 49th parallel to the crest of the Rocky Mountains. It included all of Washington, Oregon and Idaho, and parts of Wyoming and Montana. Over the years, the territory was broken up into individual states, as shown below.

Map 1

(Oregon Territory in 1848)

In 1848, Congress carved out a piece of the Northwest that was bigger than Texas—almost 290,000 square miles.

Map 2

(Oregon and Washington Territories in 1853)

In 1853, settlers in Washington became discouraged because they had to travel so far to participate in politics in Oregon. The Washington settlers thought the Oregon settlers south of the Columbia River didn’t pay enough attention to the Washington area. Congress voted that Washington should be a separate and new territory. Only 4,000 whites lived there at the time.

Map 3

(Washington Territory in 1859)

In 1859, Oregon was made a state. Congress didn’t want the state of Oregon to be so large, so they chopped off a big piece of land along the Snake River. This river became Oregon’s eastern border.

Map 4

(Pacific Northwest in 1868)

In 1868, Congress divided up the rest of the Pacific Northwest to make new states. Four new states took large pieces of the original Oregon territory. Washington and Montana became states in 1889, and Idaho and Wyoming became states in 1890.

title: Olympia
text: In 1846, Edmund Sylvester and Levi Lathrop Smith decided to call their little settlement Smithfield. In 1851, it became an important port for our territory, and people renamed it for the nearby Olympic Mountains. On Nov. 28, 1853, Washington territory was formed, and Olympia was chosen to become the capital. Washington territory was giant- it included northern Idaho and part of Montana. We didn't have many buildings in those days. In fact, our first territorial legislature met in the Gold Bar Restaurant for their regular meetings. In 1856, a wood- frame building was constructed on the site of our current capitol building, and the building served as Washington's capitol until 1902. Our permanent capitol building was started in 1893, but wasn't finished until 1928. That's a long time to work on a building! Olympia became the state capital of Washington. Olympia is a major port with many industries and oyster fishers. Its main business is government, and it’s a good place to visit all of those people we elect into office each year!

title: Mother Joseph
text:
Mother Joseph became one of the most important people in Washington territory. She is one of two Washington citizens with a statue in the nation's capitol. For years, she worked with other nuns in Canada, near her family's home. She mastered many skills including nursing, gardening, candle and soap making, weaving, sewing and carpentry. Mother Joseph also learned how to run a business.

She started seven hospitals, 12 schools and two orphanages. She helped build many of the buildings herself. Mother Joseph kept working until she was almost 80 years old. She was born with the name of Esther Pariseau.

title: Why do ponds and lakes freeze from the top down?
text: When the air temperature over lakes drops below freezing, the top of the lake will freeze. Ice expands when it freezes, making it lighter than water. The floating ice acts like a big blanket and helps prevent more of the lake from freezing. This is important because fish are living in the water and don't want to become frozen leftovers during the winter. We are lucky that ice floats. If ice were heavier than water, it would sink during the winter, and by spring, our lakes and oceans would be solid blocks of ice, and every creature in them would be dead.

title: Black Bear
text: One of the animals that caused the early settlers to come together and form a new government was the black bear. The black bear was a predatory animal that was destroying livestock and scaring the settlers. (See Cover Story.) This bear weighs about 300 pounds. Black bears can run very fast when they need to and are skilled tree climbers for their size and weight. Most black bears are timid. However, they would make dangerous enemies. They seldom attack humans unless they have been hurt or are defending their young. Black bears spend much of the winter sleeping in snug shelters (caves, hollow trees or holes dug into the ground). Cubs are born in midwinter weighing half a pound and measuring 7 to 9 inches long. They have very little hair, and their eyes are closed for about a month. They stay inside the den with Mom for about two months. Black bears live 15-25 years. If you venture into the forest, be kind to all animals, and they will be kind to you - but always keep your distance, especially when the animal is bigger than you! Here's a new word: What do you call a group of bears? A sleuth of bears!

title: What are Some Tricks to Spelling Correctly?
text:
Are there some words that you just have a hard time spelling, maybe every time you try to write them? Perhaps some guidelines will help you spell these words in the future.

Understanding the Code

Spelling is kind of like a code - it's a combination of letters that combine to form a word. And that code can sometimes be hard to crack. It is difficult to provide "rules" for spelling in the English language because not all words follow the rules. You can probably find an exception to every "rule" we provide here. But we wanted to give you these guidelines so that you could have a basic understanding of how spelling usually works.

"ie" and "ei" Words

You probably already know this one: I before E except after C or when sounded like A, as in "neighbor" and "weigh." If you follow this guideline, you will spell most of those "ei" and "ie" words correctly. Basically, a word is spelled with "ie" for the long "e" sound, except when the "e" follows the letter "c." When the vowel sound is a long "a," the word is usually spelled with "ei." Some exceptions to this rule are "either," "seize," and "weird." See if you can explain how each of these words follows the rule: Piece, Receive, Neighbor.

Plural Words

Generally, you make a word plural by adding "s" to the end. But, as you know, that is not the case with all words. Remember that there are exceptions to these guidelines.

If the word ends with "ch," "s," "sh," "ss," "x," "z," or "es," then you should add "es" rather than just "s" to make it plural. (buzzes, mosses)

For most nouns that end with a single "f," you change the "f" to "v" and add "es." ("leaf" becomes "leaves")

For most words that end with a consonant followed by "o," add "es." (heroes, potatoes)

Adding Endings to Words

Sometimes when you add an ending to a word, it's not as simple as adding "ed," "ing," "s," "est," or "er." You have to change the word before you can add the ending. Here are some guidelines for doing this successfully.

Before adding an ending to a word that ends with "y," check to see if a consonant comes before the "y." If the word ends with a consonant and "y," then change the "y" to "ie" before adding the ending. ("hurry" becomes "hurried")

If a word ends with "y" and has more than one syllable, change the "y" to "i" before adding "ness" or "ly." ("happy" becomes "happily")

For most one-syllable words that end with one vowel and one consonant, double the consonant before adding an ending that begins with a vowel. (thinnest, bigger)

For most two-syllable words that end with one vowel and one consonant, you double the consonant only if the accent falls on the second syllable. (referred, beginning) For words that end with a silent "e," drop the "e" when adding an ending that begins with a vowel. (riding, largest)

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend somebody just discovered a big piece of land south of where you live, and Congress wants you to make a state out of it. What will you call your state? Who will be the leader? What will you do if other states try to take your land away from you?

title: Population Timeline for Washington
text:
Washington’s population grew significantly after statehood. Study the population timeline and graph, and then answer the questions related to our state’s growing population.

1. Washington Territory was created in 1853. What was the population in the year depicted after 1853?

2. Washington became a state in 1889. What was the population in the year depicted after 1889?

3. What is the difference in population between 1860 and 1900?

4. Between what years was the largest population growth?

5. In what year did our population reach more than 1 million?

6. What is the earliest population depicted here?

7. What is the most recent population?

8. What is the difference in population between 1850 and 2000?

9. How much did Washington’s population grow between 1900 and 2000?

10. Did the population ever decrease?

(Information for this timeline was taken from the U.S. Census Bureau.)

Challenge: Look up today’s population and add it to the graph and timeline!

title: Big Land Squabbles
text:
New settlers went west to rule the land. They went to conquer all that lay in their path. And if the American Indians were in the way, they would help them become modern people. First came the missionaries. They hoped to convert the American Indians and show them how to raise their own crops and run their own farms. The American Indians didn't see it that way. The white settlers were intruders (not invited or welcome) on their sacred lands.

Outbreaks of violence began to occur. In 1847, some Cayuse murdered an American missionary, Marcus Whitman, his wife, and 12 others. Hundreds of American troops chased the Cayuse Indians to capture the murderers. They finally found five, and they were hanged for the murders. The fighting made some peaceful tribes join others who were at war. The Rogues, Klamaths, and Modocs fought for a long time, but they were beaten back by the whites.

By 1853, several tribes rose in anger and attacked more white settlements. An army fought the American Indians until, finally, a peace treaty (agreement between groups) was signed, and things were quiet for two years.

The new governor of the Washington Territory, Isaac Stevens, was sent to move the American Indians onto their reservations. In 1854, Stevens talked tribes into leaving Thurston and Pierce counties and parts of Mason and King counties (in Washington). At another meeting, Stevens convinced more than 5,000 American Indians to sign away 45,000 square miles of choice tribal land. The American Indians knew they were being cheated and began fighting again. One battle involved the Yakama and an American Army of 84 men. The Yakama killed five soldiers, wounded 17 and scattered the rest.

The last tragic fight was with the Nez Perces, the tribes who had first welcomed Lewis and Clark half a century before. The Nez Perces' reservation was agreed upon in a treaty, but later, it was cut in half and half again. Chief Joseph was angry at the lies and cheating. He led 300 men, 400 women and children, and 1,500 horses and cattle on an escape journey. They traveled 2,000 miles in four months, traveling through Montana, almost into Canada, and ending up at Yellowstone. Here, they were nearly subdued. However, they tricked the Army by running in circles around them and escaping up a narrow canyon that the Army could not follow. After crossing Yellowstone and the Missouri River, they were attacked and defeated in the Bitterroot Valley about 40 miles from the Canadian border.

At his surrender, Joseph spoke these beautiful words of peace: "All men were made by the same Great Spirit Chief. They are all brothers. Whenever the white men treat the Indian as they treat each other, then we shall have no more wars. We shall all be alike - brothers of one father and mother, with one sky above us, and one country around us, and one government for all. Then the Great Spirit Chief who rules above will smile upon this land and send rain to wash out the bloody spots made by brothers' hands upon the face of the Earth."

For better or worse, the Pacific Northwest was open for white settlers.

title: Lumber, Mining, and Agricultural Industries Grow
text:
Pioneers loved moving to Washington Territory. They found so many ways to make a living. Lumber was needed for homes and shipbuilding. Mining was needed for ores and coal. Agriculture was blossoming in ways nobody could have imagined.

Lumber

Nowhere in America was the lumber industry so rich as it was in the Pacific Northwest. Until sawmills came along, all lumber was cut by hand. By the 1880s, sawmills were producing more than 1 million board feet per day. (A board foot is one foot of finished lumber.) By the 1890s, the annual total topped 1 billion board feet. Major cities grew up around the sawmills. Logs were floated down rivers to the mills, and ships took the lumber to distant customers. In Oregon, the trains moved the lumber to the interior, where rapid (fast, quick) building was taking place. Logging camps and mills were producing $15 million in lumber a year. If Paul Bunyan, hero of the logging camps, were a real man, he’d be having a very hard time keeping up with the new steam- and water-powered logging machines. Timber was king!

Mining

The gold rush in California in 1847-1848 caused much excitement in the Pacific Northwest. People came back from California with pockets full of gold! Their riches helped create a demand for other products from Oregon and Washington—wheat, produce, timber and boats. The gold fever spread, and so did the treasure hunters. In the early 1860s, boomtowns sprang up everywhere. In the early 1860s, gold was discovered in several places in Idaho and Montana. But gold wasn’t the only important metal to be found. Big strikes of copper, silver, lead and zinc made many people rich. In Washington, coal became its major mining product. In Oregon, small pockets of low-grade coal were found. Both states tried to make steel, but couldn’t compete with the giant steel mills back east. Hundreds of small mining towns grew up around the richest mining sites. When Alaska’s gold rush started in the late 1890s, Seattle swelled. It became the launching place for people to sail to Alaska. What was the price for a ticket? It was $1,000 one way!

Agriculture

Farmers had many things to learn. In the western parts of the state, there was plenty of moisture, but crops wouldn’t grow well where old forests had been cleared. And in the east, things were just too dry. But the areas perfect for crops were quickly planted, such as the Willamette and Tualatin valleys in Oregon and along the same belt of good land in western Washington. The farmers’ biggest problem was lack of helpers. In the beginning, American Indians were hired to work the farms. As more settlers arrived, agriculture began to grow. By the 1840s, settlers were doing pretty well. One year, they sold 15,000 bushels of wheat, 2 million pounds of tallow, 1,000 barrels of wine and brandy, 200 ounces of gold, some soap and thousands of hides and furs—all homegrown, caught or mined. Things were looking up!

title: Kittitas County
text:
Coal isn't as glamorous as gold or diamonds, but it is just as important. Coal was spotted in the Pacific Northwest in the 1700s. Not until settlers came did anyone try digging it out. Various coal mines were opened up, many in the lowlands or along the Cascades, but most of them quickly were mined out and closed. In 1885, coal mines were opened in Kittitas County on the east side of the Cascades. When the Northern Pacific heard about the coal, it became very anxious to finish its Puget Sound extension so that it could get to the coal. Washington's coal mines are now closed, but they were an important source of income for our state.

Three important cities in Kittitas County include Ellensburg, Cle Elum and Roslyn. Ellensburg was once a neutral area where enemy American Indian tribes would come to fish and hunt in peace. It was once called Robber’s Roost by early settlers. It became famous for its dairying, potatoes and grains. Cle Elum is a town that started with a gold claim in 1883. When coal was discovered there in 1886, the money helped the town build its first sawmill, a school and a station for the Northern Pacific Railroad. Roslyn also popped up at this same time and was a very rich coal-mining town until the early 1960s.

title: How is Gold Formed?
text: Gold is an element. Elements cannot be broken down into simpler substances. Gold on the west coast of North America formed hundreds of millions of years ago. Hot liquid flowed through cracks in the Earth’s crust. As the liquid cooled, the gold particles stuck to each other. The other minerals around the gold cooled too, forming quartz. Some gold nuggets came to surface through river beds. Another way to get to gold was to mine the quartz. Much gold remains deep under the surface.

title: Beech Tree
text:
Washington is known for lumber, and one tree that is good for lumber is the beech tree. The beech tree can grow more than 50 feet tall with a 50-foot spread. Trees that grow in the forest can be up to 120 feet tall! The tree grows nice leaves and low branches, which provide an abundance of shade. The leaves turn to a bronze color and then a light tan in the autumn and often hold on late into the winter. The silvery-gray bark is often used for ornaments, and many birds, animals and even people eat the four tiny nuts that are on each bur of the tree. The wood is almost a white color and is used for furniture, cookware, tool handles, chairs and toys. It is very strong and resistant and was used for wheels in colonial times.

The beech grows slowly and does not require much cutting and pruning. Because they grow so slowly, they are often used as long-term projects to grow bonsai. This is also why young beech are often used in forest plantings.

title: What is Hydraulic Fracturing?
text:
People in the states of Colorado, Texas and Ohio have been feeling small earthquakes over the past few years. Some people are saying those quakes are the result of hydraulic fracturing.

Hydraulic fracturing is a way to get natural gas from underground rock formations up to the surface. We use natural gas for energy in homes and businesses. Water and chemicals are pumped underground through long, deep wells. The liquid causes fractures, or cracks, in the rock. Natural gas escapes through the cracks and gets piped up to the surface. Over 200,000 new wells have been drilled in the U.S. during the last 10 years.

The National Research Council released a report in 2012 that said hydraulic fracturing does not seem to be the culprit, but other human activity might be the problem. Some groups believe that it's the wastewater (leftover water and chemicals), not the fracturing itself that is causing the earthquakes. The wastewater from the process is either treated at a facility or sent deep underground. When the liquid is injected back into the ground, it can make the tectonic plates slip and rub against each other, causing earthquakes.

The companies doing the drilling say that they are following safety regulations and protecting their workers, the residents and the environment. Companies have been injecting waste liquids into the ground since the 1930s, and only recently has there been an increase in earthquakes. We will certainly be hearing more about hydraulic fracturing in the years to come.

Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/ for more Connections and Current Events articles.

title: President John Adams and the XYZ Affair
text:
Can you imagine following in the footsteps of George Washington? John Adams did. America's first president was greatly admired and respected for leading the troops in the Revolutionary War and helping to build our new country. When Adams became our second president in 1797, America was at peace. We had begun rebuilding our friendship with Great Britain. The former enemies were now buying and selling products from each other. Their ships crisscrossed the Atlantic with goods to trade.

Unfortunately, France was in the middle of its own revolution and was at war with Britain. France began capturing American trading ships to cut off supplies to their enemy. Some Americans were angry and wanted to declare war on France.

President Adams firmly believed in peaceful solutions. He sent a committee to France to work out the problem. The discussions did not go well. The Americans brought home a disturbing report. The three French delegates were angry at America for trading with Britain. They demanded that a large amount of money be paid to the French foreign minister as a bribe, along with a big loan.

When Adams sent the report to Congress, he disguised the names of the Frenchmen with the letters X, Y and Z. News of the "XYZ Affair" traveled across the nation. Many people were furious with France. Merchant ships from the United States and France were battling at sea in an undeclared war.

But Adams had confidence in his critical analysis of the situation. First, he called for Congress to build up America's armed forces. Then he sent new ambassadors to France who were able to work out a treaty that ended the fighting. The XYZ Affair was peacefully put to rest. When have you used critical analysis to help end an argument?

title: Let's Make a Timeline!
text:
It took many years to introduce new fruits and vegetables to the Pacific Northwest and add them to those already growing in our area. From the list below, fill in the blank timeline showing how the agriculture in our part of the United States got its start. The timeline entries below are mixed up. Put them in order on the lines in the timeline below. The first one has been done for you.

1792: AMERICAN INDIAN GARDENS (British explorers discover American Indian garden plots in which a now-extinct form of tobacco was grown.)

Centuries before 1600: CROP MANAGEMENT WITH FIRE (American Indians use fire to manage prairie lands where they grow berries, Garry oaks and camas.)

1823: EXPORTING PLANTS TO ENGLAND (Botanist David Douglas visits the Oregon territory and begins exporting to England about 150 trees, shrubs and plants, including his namesake, the Douglas fir.)

1790: FIRST GARDEN (Spanish explorers plant 19 crops in an experimental garden to see if Fort San Miguel at Friendly Bay can grow its own food.)

1829: FIRST PEACHES (Francis A. Lemont introduces peaches.)

1811: FIRST SUCCESSFUL GARDEN (The first successful garden is planted by employees of the Pacific Fur Company—founded by John Jacob Astor—near the mouth of the Columbia River. They harvested potatoes and turnips.)

1786: FIRST VEGETABLES (A British fur trader plants the first European vegetables in the Pacific Northwest.)

1789: POTATOES (Spanish explorers plant potatoes, onions, lettuce, cabbage, turnips and radishes at Nootka Sound.)

title: The Long Road to Statehood is Finished!
text:
Washington’s history was tied with Oregon’s since the very beginning. Do you remember when this changed? It was 1853 when Washington broke away from Oregon to became a territory of the United States.

From that time forward, we wanted to be our own state! But we had a hard time getting things organized. After Isaac Stevens's term as governor (leader of the state) ended in 1857, we had some strange people come to govern us. Most of them didn't like it here, and they quit or wouldn't do a good job. Congress punished them by saying, "If you don't spend more time at your office, we will reduce your pay!"

After 1872, we had four governors in a row who did a good job. We wanted local settlers to become our governors, not some out-of-staters from faraway Washington, D.C.

One of our problems was population. Congress wanted a territory to have 125,000 people before they would make it a state. We barely had a 10th of that. But other states were formed without that many people, including Oregon, so we were still hopeful.

In 1878, we made a hard push to become a state. Our forefathers wrote a new constitution, and local voters accepted it. But the U.S. Congress wouldn't respond, so nothing happened.

During the 1880s, we tried again. Many people didn't want us to be a state. Back in Washington, D.C., the Democrats were in power. They didn't want us because we were very Republican, and if we became a state, we would give the Republicans more voting power.

Finally, in 1888, the Democrats lost power in Washington, D.C., and the Republicans took over under President Harrison. The outgoing president decided to sign the bill that would let Washington, Montana and the Dakotas elect delegates. (A delegate is like your classroom president or representative—someone who represents all of the class members.) The delegates were to elect officers who would run our state. In the fall of 1889, we elected our state officers, voted on a new state constitution and were all ready to take over the running of our own government. The president finally said that we could move forward, and he formally declared us a state on Nov. 11, 1889.

When word got back that we were finally a state, there were celebrations and dancing in our streets! There were parades of wagons, horses, old pioneers and young people. And there were speeches, dinners and banquets all over the state. The old state capitol was decorated for the occasion of Statehood Day on Nov. 11, 1889. Everyone was so happy to finally be a state! On Nov. 18, the new governor was sworn in with more speeches, more celebrating, and then a great big cannon shot with a single “KA-BOOM!” This ended the Pioneer Era and marked the beginning of the new. After 200 years of struggle, the people of Washington State were in charge!

title: Puget Sound
text: Becoming a state meant we needed a way to grow our economy. Puget Sound County was the perfect place to help us grow because we have such deep harbors along the shoreline. This meant that sea-traveling ships could easily dock and take on products brought by train or drop them off for overland transport by train to other parts of the country. Deepwater ports are located at Olympia, Seattle and Tacoma. Even the Navy liked our ports and built a Naval shipyard at Bremerton. When people began settling around Puget Sound in the 1840s, our economy really grew because crops loved growing here. Puget Sound County has some of the best soil in the world for growing crops. The climate is controlled by a warm current that keeps winters mild with plenty of rainfall and fog. Many islands are in Puget Sound, the largest being Whidbey Island, Bainbridge Island and Vashon. Have you ever visited one of these islands? The Puget Sound region has become the most important economic center of Washington.

title: What is Washington's Most Recognized State Symbol?
text: The apple—Washington is the nation’s top apple-producing state. We grow more than half of all the apples eaten in America! It was appropriate during our centennial celebration year, 1989, to name the apple as the state fruit. On average, every American eats 10 pounds of our apples per year. We usually harvest about 3 million tons of apples every fall! It’s no wonder Washington is known as the apple-growing state!

title: Coastal Rhododendron
text: Perhaps you have seen them growing all around you. This strange word, “rhododendron,” comes from Greek and means “red tree.” This evergreen plant has large, beautiful blooms that appear in the spring in many colors, including lilac purple, white, red, light rose, apple-blossom pink, deep rose and rosy lilac. Rhododendrons can grow along the ground as ground cover or climb up trees and houses to more than 40 feet high. There are many different types of rhododendrons. They are part of a family of 10,000 different types! Rhododendrons love our state and are the perfect choice for a state flower. Do you have any growing where you live?

title: Symbols of Washington
text:
What are Washington State's symbols? This week, learn what they are and why they were chosen.

Washington State Facts and Trivia

Birthday: Nov. 11, 1889

Ranking: 42nd state

Capital: Olympia

State Nickname: Evergreen State - Mr. C. T. Conover, a pioneer Seattle realtor and historian, nicknamed Washington "The Evergreen State" for its large and beautiful evergreen forests. The nickname was adopted by the legislature in February 1893.

State Bird: Willow Goldfinch - In 1928, legislators let schoolchildren select the state bird, and the meadowlark won. Seven other states already had chosen the same bird, so a new vote was held in 1931. This time, the goldfinch was chosen. In 1951, children voted between the goldfinch and meadowlark, and they voted for the goldfinch.

State Fish: Steelhead Trout - Adopted in 1969

State Flower: Western or Coast Rhododendron - In 1892, before women had the right to vote, Washington women wanted to choose a state flower. They wanted to show it at the 1893 World's Fair in Chicago. The women narrowed the selection down to clover and the "rhodie." Voting booths were set up around the state for women to decide between the two. When the votes were counted, the rhododendron became the Washington State Flower.

State Gem: Petrified Wood - In 1975, petrified wood was adopted as the state gem. The best place to see petrified wood is the Ginkgo Petrified Forest State Park in Vantage.

State Tree: Western Hemlock - In 1946, an Oregon newspaper teased Washington for not having a state tree. The Portland Oregonian picked out the western hemlock (Tsuga heterophylla) for us, but Washington newspapers decided to choose their own and selected the popular western red cedar. State Representative George Adams of Mason County pleaded with the legislature to adopt the western hemlock. The hemlock, he said, would become "the backbone of this state's forest industry." Adams's bill passed the legislature and was signed into law in 1947.

Bordering States: Idaho and Oregon

Coastline: 157 miles

Flag: The state flag and the state seal are similar. The flag is the only state flag that is green and the only state flag that has a picture of a president. The law describing how the flag should look was passed in 1923.

Geology: Land area - 71,342 square miles; 18th largest in the United States

Highest Point: Mount Rainier - 14,410 feet

Inland Water: 1,627 square miles

Largest City: Seattle

Lowest Point: Pacific Coast

State Motto: "Al-ki" or "Alki" is an American Indian word meaning "by and by." This motto first appeared on the territorial seal designed by Lt. J. K. Duncan of Governor Stevens' surveying expedition. On one side, it pictures a log cabin and an immigrant wagon with a fir forest in the background; on the other side is a sheet of water being crossed by a steamer and sailing vessel, a city in perspective; the Goddess of Hope and an anchor are in the center. The figure is pointing at the word "Alki." According to Professor Edmond Meany, settlers from the schooner "Exact" first named their new settlement New York. The settlement was slower to grow than the New York on America's East Coast, so the name was changed to "New York-Alki," meaning "New York, bye and bye."

State Seal: In 1889, jeweler Charles Talcott designed our first state seal. Using a silver dollar, a postage stamp and an ink bottle, he fashioned the design. Talcott's brother, L. Grant Talcott, lettered the words, "The Seal of the State of Washington, 1889," and another brother, G. N. Talcott, cut the printing die.

State Dance: Square Dance - On April 17, 1979, the square dance became the official Washington State Dance. The square dance goes back many years. The old pioneers brought the dance with them when they moved here. It used to be called the "quadrille," a French word that means "square." Our pioneers liked "square" better. It's fun to learn and good exercise.

State Ship: "President Washington" - In 1983, the President Washington was declared the official state ship. It also is the first container ship ever adopted by a state. The ship is one of the largest container ships in the United States. It is 860 feet long and has a 43,000-horsepower diesel engine. And its giant propeller is 23 feet across and weighs 98,000 pounds.

State Grass: Blue-Bunch Wheatgrass - Next to apples, another very important symbol from eastern Washington is our blue-bunch wheatgrass. It was important to early pioneers to help them get started and remains today an important part of our agriculture industry. It was adopted by the 1989 legislature as the official state grass.

State Tartan: A tartan is a beautiful design of colors in a cloth that form lines up and down, back and forth, over a solid background color. Our tartan was designed for our centennial celebration by Vancouver, USA, Country Dancers Margaret McLeod van Nus and Frank Cannonita. The colors in our tartan represent different elements of our state as follows:

Green: The rich forests of Washington, the "Evergreen State"

Blue: The lakes, rivers and ocean

White: The snowcapped mountains

Red: Apple and cherry crops

Yellow: Wheat and grain crops

Black: The eruption of Mount St. Helens

State Fossil: Columbian Mammoth - In 1998, students from Windsor Elementary School near Cheney promoted the Columbian mammoth as our state fossil. These very large animals were relatives to our elephants and died out about 10,000 years ago. Their bones have been found in Washington.

Population: 6,664,195, 13th in the United States of America, as of 2009 (estimate).

State Song: "Washington, My Home" - This song was written by Helen Davis and arranged by Stuart Churchill, and it became the official state song in 1959. But, like the goldfinch, it had some stiff competition from another popular song. Back in 1909, "Washington Beloved" was adopted, sort of, by the legislature. Professor Edmond Meany, the historian, wrote the words, and Reginald de Koven, who also wrote "O, Promise Me" and other operettas, wrote the music. But this song was never formally introduced as a bill and so was not part of the state's code of law. When a state senator from South Bend introduced a bill in 1959 to make "Washington, My Home" our state song, it was approved unanimously. The lyrics are as follow:

"This is my country; God gave it to me; I will protect it, ever keep it free. Small towns and cities rest here in the sun, filled with our laughter. Thy will be done.

(refrain)

Washington, my home; Where ever I may roam; This is my land, my native land, Washington, my home. Our verdant forest green, Caressed by silv'ry stream. From mountain peak to fields of wheat, Washington, my home. There's peace you feel and understand. In this, our own beloved land. We greet the day with head held high, and forward ever is our cry. We'll happy ever be as people always free. For you and me a destiny; Washington, my home. For you and me a destiny; Washington, my home."

State Fruit: Washington is the nation's top appleproducing state. It was appropriate during our centennial celebration year, 1989, to name the apple as the state fruit. The apple trees in eastern Washington are one of the largest industries in our state and one of our most recognized symbols around the world.

State Capitol: The present state capitol building in Olympia, Washington, was first occupied by the legislature in March 1927. The design is reminiscent of the Acropolis in Athens, Greece. It is also closest in design to the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C.

title: Fake or Real News?
text:
Have you ever read something online, like on social media sites, that sounded fishy? Maybe it was real, but it could be fake news! The big danger, though, is news that sounds real but isn’t. Fake news is becoming common because anyone can post things online. Fake news can be in the form of a story. Fake news can be a photo or video that has been changed. The problem is that these fake items look real. Fake news can cause problems and it spreads misinformation.

Sam Wineburg, a professor, did some research. He found that 80 percent of students cannot tell the difference between real and fake news. Do you want to become a media-savvy person? You have to be able to find out if news is real or fake. How do you do that? You have to become a detective and search for the truth. You can learn about the author or company that posted the news. You have to think about the purpose of the news. Is there a hidden plan to get you to buy something or to make you think a certain way? Your teacher or a trusted adult can help you learn how to spot fake news. It takes a little time, but democracy depends on real information! Do your part and discover what is real and what is fake!

title: Counting on the Counties
text:
Is it okay to set up cities and counties before you become a state? Yes! Organizing our land into sections was needed long before we could become a state.

How would you divide Washington? Early pioneers had little to work with. There were no large cities, only towns, small settlements, or single-family farms, all separated by miles of wilderness. It was dangerous to spread out in those days because the American Indians were still fighting the new settlers. So, the early pioneers built their communities outward from a strong central fort or mission. When the first county lines were drawn, the land was divided up to include as many of these settlements as made sense.

The 1843 Organic Act divided the Pacific Northwest into four sections or districts. The first district was called Vancouver County (1844), and it was a very big piece of land. It covered all the territory north and west of the Columbia River. In 1845, the name was changed to Clark County, and its western part was broken off to form Lewis County. Both counties were named in honor of Lewis and Clark, who first passed through the area in 1805-1806.

By 1846, England decided that it did not want to fight a war with America over who owned the Pacific Northwest. England agreed to set the boundary between America and Canada at the 49th parallel. Our forefathers wanted the boundary to be 54 degrees 40', but that didn't happen.

When the American-Canadian border was approved, most people thought the Pacific Northwest would automatically become a territory of the United States. But this didn't happen for many more years.

During the 1840s and 1850s, two big things happened. First, pioneers came here by the thousands. They felt that it was a safe place to settle because borders were finally established. The second big thing was war with the American Indians. The American Indians didn't like all these strangers taking their land, and many American Indian wars broke out.

These were hard years on the early families that moved here. The men went around on snowshoes in the winter to gather wood and food. The women shivered in log cabins that were wet and leaked from the rain and snow, and some moved back to the ships that brought them here because the weather was so bad. When the weather warmed, the settlers could finish their homes and clear the land to plant farms. When new pioneers arrived, they, too, had to cut out their portion of the forest to build a home.

Thanks to the new county governments, pioneers began to find strength in numbers. They could combine their talents and resources to make towns, roads, and buildings that helped everyone. Every household could vote on things that were important for keeping the peace and helping everyone prosper.

This first decade of organization helped lay a foundation that to this day has proved very important and very helpful to our growth as a state. Do you know what county you live in? Do you know what city is the county seat (governing city of the county)? A county is a large section of a state that includes many cities.

title: Move Over, Brothers Grimm — New Fairy Tales Found
text:
There's a magical world out there full of elves, evil queens and beautiful princesses! If you enjoy "Cinderella," "Little Red Riding Hood" and "Rapunzel," you have already discovered the work of the Brothers Grimm. These German fairy tales and legends were collected by the Grimm brothers (left) and put into popular books about 200 years ago.

A new world of fairy-tale magic has just been revealed. Researchers found a collection of 500 stories gathered by Franz von Schonwerth, a German historian who did his work at the same time as the Grimm brothers. Because Schonwerth was a historian, he wrote the stories exactly as the German people told them to him. The Grimm brothers changed some of the stories to make them less frightening for children. The Grimm brothers admired Schonwerth's work. Jacob Grimm said, "Nowhere in the whole of Germany is anyone collecting (fairy tales) so accurately, thoroughly and with such a sensitive ear." Schonwerth's collection was never as popular as the Grimm brothers' books. His three volumes of stories collected dust for 150 years until they were rediscovered.

Schonwerth's collection includes a story of a beautiful girl who gets away from a witch by turning herself into a pond and another tale about a turnip princess. As soon as the stories are translated into English, you will have a whole new collection of fairy tales to read!
