title: Clark County
text: Clark County is the very first county ever formed in Washington. It was established in 1844, but later was made smaller, as parts were broken off to form other counties. The county seat is the city of Vancouver. Vancouver is the oldest city in all of Washington. It was founded in 1824 as a Hudson's Bay Company trading post. Vancouver lies on the banks of the Columbia River. A bridge links it to Portland, Oregon. The first steamboat (S. S. Beaver) to operate in the Pacific Northwest sailed to Vancouver from England in 1836. Its paddle wheels were lashed on its deck for the overseas journey and then attached after it arrived here. There are many jobs for people in Clark County. If you visited the docks one day, you would see the fruits of Clark County residents' hard work. You would see ships picking up all kinds of products such as farm goods, manufactured goods, lumber, grain, paper, steel cable, and canned foods. If you visit any part of Clark County, stop for lunch in any of the many parks and enjoy the large number of animals and birds that love Clark County.

title: Which Mountain is Most Dangerous in the Cascade Range?
text: Mount Rainier, the highest and one of the largest mountains in the Cascade Range of Washington, is probably the most dangerous mountain. It is a volcano that has not erupted since 1882, but is expected to erupt again in the next couple hundred years. It is also very dangerous because of how many people live below the volcano. Not only will an eruption cause ash and lava to come from the mountain, it will also cause tons of snow to avalanche down the mountain.

title: Woodchuck
text:
On Groundhog Day each year, the world turns its attention to the little town of Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania, and on a groundhog named Phil. (Here in Washington, we call groundhogs "woodchucks.") If he climbs out of his burrow on Gobbler's Knob and sees his shadow, the story goes, winter will be sticking around for another six weeks. Phil's an old hand at this prediction stuff. He or his ancestors (great-grandparents) have been doing it every year since Feb. 2, 1 8 8 7!

Punxsutawney Phil is a legend in his home state. There are groundhogs (woodchucks), in Washington, too. They are a rodent of the squirrel family. They are found in the woodlands and brush lands, are brown and have darker feet. Woodchucks are found in most of the United States except for the deep South.

title: Tacoma in Pierce County
text:
"Tacoma" - from the American Indian Word "Tacobet," Meaning "Many Waters"

Tacoma is a great place to work and live. It has an old but rich history of industry and work that today keeps the city strong and growing. It is one of the great landmark cities of the Pacific Northwest.

Tacoma was settled at the mouth of the Puyallup River, and with its great shipping port, it became a natural place to ship products in to and out of the Northwest. When the railroad arrived in Tacoma in 1873, people gave the city the nickname, "City of Destiny." It was a good name because the train brought fantastic prosperity to the city with new trade and transportation.

Many businesses settled in the Tacoma area. It soon became home to industries and businesses that made furniture, clothes, paints, bleaches, heavy machines and chemicals. Across America, Tacoma became known as the "lumber capital of America," because it was!

If you live in Tacoma, you already know some of the great landmarks that visitors will enjoy seeing: the Museum of Glass, the rebuilt Fort Nisqually and a tall totem pole, built by American Indians in 1903.

title: How Do I Read Nonfiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring. But it really isn't. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you will find it easier to understand - and maybe even fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will talk about cause and effect.

Cause/Effect

With this information pattern, writers organize their material to show how one thing leads to another. Cause is the reason why something happens. Effect is what happens as a result of the cause. Effects often turn into causes for different effects. Writers often use this pattern when they want to explain a chain of events.

One way to find the cause and effect of a passage is to make a Cause/Effect Diagram that allows you to show the cause and effect relationship graphically. You start by writing the cause of the events. Draw an arrow from the cause bubble pointing right, and then next to the arrow, write the effect of that cause. Draw a new arrow from the effect bubble pointing left and down and write the next effect. Draw the next arrow pointing right and continue in that manner until you have reached the final effect. See the sample diagram.

Try It!

Below is a passage about immigration to the United States. Read the passage. Then create a Cause/Effect Diagram that shows the causes and effects of immigration.

title: The Mountain Man Governor
text:
In the decade before the Civil War, most eastern states thought their governor should be a man of distinction and nobility ("nobility" means "famous family name"), familiar with the ways of etiquette and decorum (polite at parties) and proper in the presence of the aristocracy (upper-class, rich people). While Isaac I. Stevens had many of these qualities, he had one more trait- he was a tough, riding and fighting leader of soldiers who knew how to live off the land, eat his own horse if he had to, charge his enemies with drawn sword and guns a-blazing, and whip his soldiers into a driven, unified pillar of military might. And for all this, he hated to stand around to receive some medal for deeds done when there was work left to do!

Stevens was a great man. He was so energetic and driven, even his appointment as Washington's new territorial governor seemed too small a task to occupy all his time. In fact, he didn't want to waste his time simply traveling to Washington to become governor. He wanted to be more productive. So, he volunteered to lead an expedition to explore and survey a route for the future Northern Pacific Railroad while on his way to the Pacific Northwest!

Stevens was a smart man. He graduated at the top of his class at West Point (a military training academy) in 1839. He served with honor and glory in the Mexican War. When he was appointed governor of Washington, he left his job as chief assistant in the U.S. Survey Office in Washington, D.C.

Stevens began his surveying trip to the Pacific with 243 men. For six weeks, they explored the various mountains, looking for suitable passes the trains could use. He led his men over the Rocky Mountains on foot, with pack animals carrying their supplies. By November, he arrived in Olympia to start his new job.

There's a funny story about Stevens's arrival in town. The day's ride, mixed with torrential rain, made him look so grimy, dirty, and sloppy, the local people thought he was just some traveling bum and wouldn't let him into the main restaurant to eat. After he complained loudly, a cook let him eat kitchen leftovers in the back alley because they were all expecting the new governor and didn't want this dirty drifter to mess things up with his filth. When Stevens heard they were waiting for him, he argued his identity until they were convinced he was the new governor. All the important townspeople were quickly called, and he was the guest of honor in the very dining room he was forbidden to enter before. What about the great feast they had prepared? By that time, Stevens was too full from kitchen scraps and couldn't eat a bite.

Stevens immediately set about to get things organized. He called the first assembly of the legislature the next spring. He traveled all over the state making treaties with American Indians or fighting them if needed. Stevens ordered his survey party to assemble their notes on plants, animals, geography, and terrain so that the railroad could be started. And he personally traveled all over the state to explore passes around the Cascades, find river crossings, capture fugitives, and more.

When the Civil War started, Stevens had completed his term as governor and was in Washington, D.C., as an elected representative of Washington Territory. He was promoted to major general in the Union Army and fought in the Civil War. He was killed at the battle of Chantilly, on Sept. 1, 1862.

title: How About Those Apples?
text:
Whoever said that "An apple a day keeps the doctor away" must have been able to see into the future. For hundreds of years, people knew that apples were healthy, but scientists today continue to find more good reasons for us to eat the tasty fruit.

Researchers now believe that apples may help people lose weight, re-grow lost hair, and prevent strokes. They can also protect us from lung and heart disease, cancer, diabetes, and asthma. Not bad for a delicious fruit that you can take with you anywhere!

Here in Washington, we really love our apples. Washington is the country's number one apple producer, doing its part to help bring America's apple crop to around 216 million bushels each year. Each fall, Washington apple growers harvest between 10 and 12 billion apples, enough to circle the earth 12 times! Many of these apples are shipped to foreign countries, but each American eats about 19 pounds of apples each year.

U.S. apple growers are working hard to make sure that apples are anything but boring. Today, people want food that is easy, convenient and tastes great. You might not think an apple could get any more convenient, but apple growers have come up with some new ideas for making eating apples even easier than ever. How about selling pre-sliced apples in a bag? Other apple trends to watch for are kid-friendly apple products such as applesauce tubes and cups, as well as re-sealable apple juice bottles.

While the top selling apples are still the Red and Golden Delicious varieties, other popular apples include Fuji, Gala, Granny Smith, Braeburn and Jonagold. Everyone has their favorites, but once you try some of the new varieties, you may like them even better.

If you want a quick snack with a real health punch, now you know where to turn. Have you had your apple today?

title: Stevens County
text: Stevens County was part of the Oregon Territory long before Washington became a state. When Washington became an official territory of the United States in 1853, Stevens County was part of Walla Walla County. Ten years later, the territorial legislature made Stevens County an official county - the date was Jan. 20, 1863. It was named in honor of our first governor and delegate to Washington, D.C., Isaac I. Stevens. The following year, more land was included in Stevens County, and it grew to 25,000 square miles. In 1871, the legislature began to break off pieces, and by 1911, Stevens County became the size it is today. The county seat is Colville. Old Fort Colville, originally near Kettle Falls, was Hudson's Bay Company's major trading post for 30 years. In 1855, it became the scene of a major gold rush. Much silver and iron was also discovered, and mining remains a primary industry in Stevens County.

title: How Do Cats Purr, by Exhaling or Inhaling?
text: Do you have a cat staying warm indoors this winter? Have you ever listened to it purr? A cat does its purring the same way a lion roars or humans hum. It draws breath to make its vocal cords vibrate. Cats normally purr when they are happy or content. But this isn't always the case. Cats also purr when they are injured or in pain as a way of coping with the hurt. Some researchers believe that this kind of purring may be a form of self-hypnosis. This helps a cat comfort itself and show a good mood.

title: Mountain Lion
text: What animal has more names and nicknames than any other animal in the world? What animal can live almost anywhere, from deserts to the humid coast, from sea level to 10,000-foot-high mountains? And what animal eats deer, elk, mice, and grasshoppers and, if it isn't finished eating, buries its food and comes back for it later? If you guessed a mountain lion, or cougar, you are right! This graceful member of the cat family can be found in many parts of the North American and South American continents. It is the champion jumper among cats, able to leap 30 feet from a standing position and 18 feet straight up. It weighs 100-200 pounds with a 28-inch tail and grows to almost seven feet from head to tip of the tail. And they can live up to 18 years. They prefer their own territory (25-100 square miles) and only meet up with other mountain lions to have kittens. Because they kill livestock when there is a shortage of food, Washington and Oregon allow mountain lions to be hunted.

title: Spokane County
text:
Be sure to pack your swimming and biking gear!

A visit to Spokane is always fun, and without traveling too far in any direction, you can view an amazing future or stroll into the far distant past. A walk along the Spokane River Centennial Trail takes the visitor into places where evidence was discovered of life on the river that dates back 11,400 years. The river served people for thousands of years as a place for transportation and food. The Spokane Indians lived here until Europeans brought fur trading to the area in 1810, and they started settling the region in 1849. Today, you'll only need a bike to enjoy the Spokane River trail that stretches 39 miles from Spokane House to the far side of Coeur D'Alene Lake.

There are many small farming communities around Spokane. When the railroad arrived in 1881, people came looking to farm the land. Their farms grew into small communities around Spokane Valley. Today, most of these communities still have their charm as small-town communities, but the area is growing.

Spokane County is a great place for water sports. Within 50 miles from Spokane in any direction, you can find 76 lakes and four major rivers. Don't forget to bring what you need for fishing, swimming, boating and waterskiing. And when it gets cold, have fun snowmobiling, ice fishing and downhill skiing.

title: How Do I Read Nonfiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring. But it really isn't. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you will find it easier to understand - and maybe even fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will discuss classification.

Classification

With this pattern, the nonfiction piece is organized into categories or groups that share certain characteristics. In other words, the content is classified.

One idea for finding out how the content of a nonfiction piece is classified is to chart the information into categories. Charting information can help you see the categories graphically. You will also better remember the characteristics of each category.

Try It!

Here is a passage about the war between the states. Read the passage. Then chart the important information into categories.

title: Before the Civil War Came the Pig!
text:
One summer day in 1859, an American farmer named Lyman Cutler was tending his garden on San Juan Island. Suddenly, a big old pig from the British settlement wandered over for the third time that summer and started eating all the new potato plants. Cutler was so angry, he grabbed his gun and shot the pig. This nearly caused war! The British called for Cutler’s arrest, but local Americans protected him and asked for U.S. military protection. The British responded by sending a warship with soldiers, and more American troops were sent. Finally, the whole thing grew until more than 2,000 British and U.S. troops faced off to blow each other to pieces. The so-called “Pig War” ended after four months when troops were withdrawn, and peace was restored. No shots were ever fired, and the only casualty was the pig.

About a year after the Pig War, the Civil War started (1861). This was a terrible fight between the Southern states and the Northern states over issues of economy, states’ rights and slavery. With everyone’s attention focused on the fighting, life changed for the Washington-Oregon region.

There was no Red Cross during the Civil War, so women all over America were asked to prepare clothing and hospital supplies to help the wounded. It is said that women from the Pacific Northwest provided more supplies than women from any other state or territory in America.

In the middle of the war, when things were going badly on all sides, President Abraham Lincoln gave permission for railroads to be built to the West Coast. Even though there were no money, materials or workers to build the rails, Congress passed the bills so that people could begin making plans.

Most of the men teaching school had to leave their jobs to fight in the war. They were replaced by women teachers. During the Civil War, about 80 percent of teachers (up to 12th grade) were women. It has remained about the same ever since.

Many of the leading figures in the Civil War had ties to the Pacific Northwest. General Grant, for example, had been stationed as an Army officer at Fort Vancouver in 1853. Governor Stevens, who had been the governor of the Washington Territory and delegate to Congress, was a famous general for the Union troops.

Washington residents were very angry with the Confederates, especially after Captain James Waddell brought his Confederate ship, Shenandoah, into Washington waters and captured 38 merchant ships. He burned 30 of the ships. At the war’s end, Waddell fled to England to surrender his ship to the British. The British promptly returned the ship to the Americans.

People in Washington volunteered to protect the frontier from American Indian attacks and to guard the forts until regular troops returned.

For all the sadness, fighting and uncomfortable feelings the Civil War caused, our nation eventually healed. Both Oregon and Washington voted to accept the 13th Amendment to the Constitution, an amendment that banned slavery forever.

title: Honoring Civil War Heroes
text:
You may not have given much thought to the soldiers who fought in the Civil War, but one Washington group is committed to making sure these soldiers are never forgotten. The Washington Civil War Association (WCWA) is a group of citizens that works to honor their ancestors, from both the North and the South, who lived, fought, and died during the Civil War.

The WCWA wants to make sure that no one forgets the great men and women who lived the Civil War experience. One of the most important projects the group sponsors is the presentation of Civil War re-enactments. These re-enactments are presented for their families, friends, and visitors from all over Washington. A re-enactment is an event where members of the group join together to fight a pretend battle from Civil War history. Members of the group dress in uniforms and clothes just like those worn by soldiers and others from this time period. Members portray townspeople, infantry soldiers, cavalry (soldiers on horseback), navy officers, marines, engineers, surgeons, nurses, ministers, and cooks.

Going to a Civil War re-enactment can be fun, as well as educational. Visitors are allowed to watch the event to learn more about life during this period of our history. Black powder guns and cannons are used, but the weapons only fire blanks, so no one gets hurt. The guns are loud, however, so visitors may want to bring earplugs. Water bottles, umbrellas, camp chairs, sunscreen, and snacks are also good items to bring along.

The WCWA works hard to preserve the memory of those who were part of the Civil War.

title: San Juan County
text: This county is made of nothing but islands. The biggest island, San Juan, was shared between the British and the Americans. One day, a British pig wandered into an American’s potato garden and started eating the potatoes. The American shot the pig and almost started a war, later nicknamed the Pig War. From 1860 to 1872, the island was jointly occupied by both British and American troops. The leader of Germany, Kaiser Wilhelm I, was given the job to decide who owned the island. He picked America. San Juan is a whale watchers’ paradise! Visitors can take boat rides and drift out among the whales as they come by to feed and play. You can get into the water year round, too—by boating, swimming, scuba diving, kayaking and fishing. You may picnic there and look for any of the 200 species of birds that live there—eagles, falcons, owls, loons, ducks, woodpeckers, skylarks and more. The San Juan Island National Park was built where the Pig War occurred, a reminder that problems between nations can be worked out without killing—except for the dead pig, in this case. The county seat is Friday Harbor, at the south end of the island, and is a good place to start your visit.

title: What was Washington's Involvement in the Civil War?
text: One of Washington’s regiments—known as the First Regiment Infantry—was responsible for being at different forts throughout the western part of the United States. Responsibilities of the troops ranged from just being stationed at the fort to protecting immigrants and fighting Snake Indians. They were stationed often in Fort Walla Walla as well as Fort Vancouver in the Washington Territory. In April of 1862, they started being called out and were mustered out—which means they were discharged from the military—in December 1865.

title: Bald Eagle
text: The folks on San Juan Island say that the next best thing to whale watching is bald-eagle watching. These beautiful birds with their snowy white heads and dark bodies soar through the blue sky with grace and majesty. With about 90 pairs of nesting eagles on the island, San Juan has more eagles than any other county in all of Washington. According to Charlie Nash, a local eagle expert, the San Juan eagles nearly died out when a disease killed most of the rabbits on the island. Eagles depend on rabbits, as well as salmon in nearby rivers, as a main source of food. Eagles hatch in the late spring and are flying when they are about 12 weeks old. A young eagle doesn’t mature for about five or six years—that’s when its brown head feathers are replaced with white. The female is the larger of the pair and weighs 8 or 9 pounds. She has a wingspan of 6 or 7 feet. Eagles mate for life and typically have two or three eggs each year. They build two nests. When the first nest gets grungy and is infested with bugs, the eagle family moves to the other while the first airs out. Wouldn’t Mom and Dad like that idea for some of their kids?

title: Douglas County
text:
An amazing part of Douglas County's climate is the change in weather patterns. Depending on where you visit or live in this county, you could experience a completely different kind of season than your neighbors who might live only a few dozen miles away. For example, if you lived in Waterville, you could expect 43 inches of snow, on average. But move over to East Wenatchee, and you'd get less, about 28 inches. And the difference in temperatures is five degrees in summer or winter. Some of this change is because in one place, you're only 600 feet above sea level, and in another, you're more than 4,000 feet above sea level!

Badger Mountain Ski Hill is the place to go in the wintertime. Three towropes pull you to the top where skiers of all ages can find the easy slopes of Bunny Tow, or something more challenging on A Hill or B Hill. The runs are short, but fun.

Aside from being surrounded by the Columbia River and lakes, Douglas County sports hundreds of other water recreation and camping opportunities around the region. If you visit, watch out for some endangered or threatened fish and wildlife that have found a safe home in Douglas County. There are salmonid fish, the pygmy rabbit and sage grouse that need our help to survive as a species and to help increase their numbers.

title: How Do I Read Nonfiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring. But it really isn't. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you will find it easier to understand - and maybe even fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will discuss the main idea and supporting details.

Main Idea/Supporting Details

With this pattern, the writer presents a main idea and then backs it up with factual supporting details as evidence. You should be able to find this pattern when reading nonfiction because you probably already use it in your own writing.

One strategy for finding the main ideas and supporting details is to create an outline of what you are reading. With the outline, you will be able to see the main ideas at a glance. Use the main ideas as headings and the supporting details as subheadings in your outline.

Try It!

title: Washington Sprints to the Next Century
text:
What a race! After more than 200 years of exciting history, the people of Washington could hardly wait for the Civil War to end (1861-1865), so they could get this territory of ours on the fast track to statehood. (The Civil War is also called the War Between the States.)

Look at how fast people began moving here. In 1860, only 11,600 people lived here. In 10 years, that number doubled to 24,000. Ten years later, it tripled to 75,000. By 1890, we had 350,000 people living here. At the turn of the century, 518,000 called Washington their home. And what would you guess we had just 10 years after that? By 1910, we crossed the million mark with 1,141,000. In only 50 years, we grew from about 12,000 to almost 1,200,000.

The railroad was a big part of that. When the Northern Pacific Railroad was finished in 1883, people began pouring into our state. Naturally, there came problems with all the new-comers. In fact, thousands of Chinese workers who helped build the train tracks suddenly were out of work with the tracks all finished. They took all the jobs nobody else wanted (laundry, garbage, waiters and waitresses, etc.). But then bad times hit. In 1885, many settlers were out of work and felt that the Chinese had all the better-paying jobs. Terrible anti-Chinese riots broke out, and the governor had to declare martial law and call in U.S. troops to quiet things down.

Four years later, we became a state. Congress granted statehood on Feb. 22, 1889 (George Washington's birthday), and U.S. President Harrison made it official on Nov. 11, 1889.

There were plenty of jobs in our state, if people wanted them. Coal, for example, had been discovered in 1848 in the Cowlitz Valley and in 1860 in Bellingham Bay and near Seattle. Selling coal (a fossil fuel) didn't become important until 1885. By 1908, we were mining more than 3 million tons of coal a year.

People also worked at flour and gristmills. This work was bringing in $14 million a year by 1905, while slaughter and meat-packing houses were earning $6 million a year. We were also good at machine and metal fabrication work, earning about $3 million by the turn of the century.

Another huge business was our wheat crop. By 1909, Washington farmers could grow more than 36 million bushels of this grain, worth $33 million.

How do you water the land to do all this work? Western Washington had all the rain it needed. Elsewhere, we built reservoirs. In 1905, the Okanogan project funneled water from the Salmon River to irrigate 10,000 acres in Okanogan County. That same year, we created five reservoirs in Yakima to deliver valuable water to 600,000 acres.

Oh, and lest we forget, the fish! Salmon provided many jobs, especially after people invented a way to safely can salmon meat. By 1905, we were sending out almost 27 million pounds of salmon a year.

At last, we welcomed the new century of 1900. There was such a great feeling in our state-so much to do, so much growth, and so many places to visit, live, and enjoy. The sprint to the new century was worth every pioneer, dollar, fish, tree, or gold nugget carved out of our land. But not too far away was a great challenge that nobody wanted, even though they knew it was coming. As we will discuss in our next issue, headlines around the world cried out the news: world war!

title: Pend Oreille County
text:
The last county organized in Washington was Pend Oreille County, in 1911. The name “Pend Oreille” is pronounced “pond-er-ay.” It is a beautiful, lush county only 22 miles wide and 66 miles long. The second largest river in the state, the Pend Oreille River, flows north instead of south. The river flows into Canada before it joins the headwaters of the Columbia.

This is a great place to get lost! Miles of thick forest, 55 lakes, streams, rivers and mountains climbing up to 4,500 feet all joined to make Pend Oreille the place to camp, hike and explore. There also exist old logging camps, old mines (never enter without an adult!), pioneer homes and much more. And while you’re visiting, keep your eyes open for moose, bear, elk, deer, mountain goat, caribou, bighorn sheep and the rare (and probably lost) grizzly bear! Beautiful birds soar overhead and around the lakes, including the mighty eagle, osprey, geese, duck and heron. The cities and towns you will visit include Newport (the county seat), Cusick, Ione, Metaline and Metaline Falls.

title: Why do we say, “It’s raining cats and dogs?”
text: Old superstitions (strange beliefs) about weather, which go back for thousands of years, always included cats. A long time ago, people believed cats had a great influence on weather. Some people even believed witches changed their shape to cats and rode through storms. Others believed in a king of storms, a god called Odin, who was helped by a dog to produce wind. The cats came to represent down-pouring rain, and dogs represented strong gusts of wind.

title: Spotted Skunk
text: Here's a puzzle-What do these three things have in common: a skunk, your breath, and the natural gas that runs your furnace? If you guessed the smell, you are absolutely right! A chemical called mercaptan is produced by skunks in their spray. Bad breath includes mercaptan, and your local gas company adds mercaptan to natural gas so that you can tell if there's a gas leak. Everybody knows what skunk smells like. The spotted skunk is the most common variety in our plateau and desert areas. They grow to about 22 inches long; the female is smaller. They are most active at night when they go snooping for insects, seeds, and small animals. They like to build their dens under brush, homes, barns, and sometimes fallen trees or rocks. Like raccoons, skunks will invade your campsite for food if you're not careful when you go camping. Make sure you lock things up before going to bed. Close the cooler, put food away, and pick up your litter.

title: Woodrow Wilson and the Fourteen Points
text:
All presidents have important responsibilities, but few are more critical than those faced by presidents during times of war. While the United States was fighting in World War I, President Woodrow Wilson addressed Congress on Jan. 8, 1918. He presented a plan for peace called the Fourteen Points.

Woodrow Wilson was elected in 1912. World War I began in 1914 between Great Britain and Germany and other European nations. It was called The Great War. Everyone thought there would never be another war like it. President Wilson wanted to keep the United States out of the war. He tried to help Great Britain and Germany end the conflict. But when German submarines began sinking American ships, he asked Congress to declare war.

Wilson's Fourteen Points plan described his ideals for achieving world peace and democracy. He had consulted with a team of about 150 foreign policy advisors. He assured Americans that the war was being fought for good causes and would lead to peace in Europe. The Fourteen Points included free trade, freedom of the seas and returning territories taken in the war. Wilson also wanted to establish a League of Nations to protect the independence of "great and small states (nations) alike."

Wilson's Fourteen Points faced opposition from some people, but it was used as the basis for the German surrender at the end of the war. The Armistice took effect on "the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month" in 1918. America and other nations remember those who died by celebrating Armistice Day (now called Veterans Day) every November 11. Woodrow Wilson was awarded the 1919 Nobel Peace Prize, thanks to his clarity of expression. Why is it important for our leaders to be clear during times of war?

title: Okanogan County
text:
A great escape into the beauty of nature and the rugged days of the early West, Okanogan County is a wonderful place to visit. From snow-covered peaks to small towns, the visitor has plenty to choose from. Live theater, farmers markets, rodeos, festivals, galleries and history lurk just about everywhere. Hundreds of lakes, rivers and streams spread out across the land to tempt thousands to enjoy whitewater rafting, fishing, hiking, biking and rock climbing. And when the snow comes, get ready! There is plenty of opportunity to ski, snowboard, go snowshoeing or even try dog sledding.

Okanogan County didnt get its start as a tourist destination or haven for explorers. It drew early settlers because of its rich natural resources in timber, mining and ranching. David Thompson and other members of the North West Fur Company led the first white men to the area in 1811. On their trek to this county, they came upon two American Indian groups, the Nespelem and the Methow. Today, the county celebrates its early native history with annual events, shows and activities.

Mining was an important part of this countys beginnings. But besides mining various ores, todays explorers are hunting something else in the ground: fossils! Stonerose is a place you can visit where a great deal of fossilized plants, insects and fish have been found. Scientists have dated them as 50 million years old.

title: Let's Write
text: Suppose you lived in 1915, and you get hit by lightning and travel into the future to 2015. After a few days, you suddenly fizzle, pop, wheeze, go blurry and reappear in your own bed, back in 1915. Knowing what the future holds, what will you do differently? Who will you tell about computers, airplanes, space travel, medicine and digital watches? If you could bring one thing back from the future, what would it be? Why?

title: Washington's Early World Records
text:
Welcome to another terrific issue of Washington Studies Weekly! We finally made it to the 1900s. This century brought more fantastic change than anyone ever dreamed. Let's jump back 100 years and take a closer look at our own Washington world records of the first 20 years of the 1900s.

If someone wanted to write a book of Washington world records, the first 20 years of the 1900s would have been a good time to do it. In July 1900, the very first automobile ever to drive in Washington proudly coughed and wheezed its way down Seattle streets.

And then Mr. J. Willis Sayre decided to set a new world record traveling around the Earth the fastest. He left Seattle using trains, boats, cars, carriages, and just about anything that moved to complete a trip around the globe. He returned to Seattle 54 days, nine hours, and 42 minutes later - a new world record! That December, the Seattle Symphony Orchestra performed its first concert ever. And the following year, the first steel produced in King County rolled from its new steel mill.

Washington's harbors and shipyards were busy, too. In 1904, 55,000 people crowded the shoreline to watch the launching of the brand new battleship U.S.S. Nebraska. Meanwhile, the world's largest steam freighter, the Minnesota, left Seattle in January 1905 with the world's largest cargo for a maiden voyage to Asia. And America's fleet of battleships took its first round-the-world tour as a show of strength, stopping in Puget Sound in 1908.

In the summer of 1909, the famous Alaska-Yukon-Pacific Exposition officially opened. All of America was excited about this first national fair event. It celebrated the prosperity (wealth and growth) that had come since the 1897 Alaska gold rush. The first underwater cable from Washington to Alaska was laid so that people could communicate by telegraph.

In 1910, women were finally given the right to vote in Washington, and one of the largest buildings in the world was started. The 42-story Smith Tower took four years to complete, and only New York City had larger buildings.

This was the year when the very first powered airplane to fly in Washington took flight from a racetrack in Seattle. The demonstration came to a sudden stop two days later when the pilot dunked his plane into a pond. Nobody was seriously hurt, but historians wonder if in the crowd of observers there was William E. Boeing. Boeing would soon start one of the greatest aircraft and aerospace companies in the world.

In July 1914, Boeing enjoyed his first airplane ride with a friend who would join him in starting Boeing Aircraft Company. A month later, word came that Germany had declared war on Russia. The United States said that it would not take sides in the war. Things became so bad, America finally joined the war to help other nations under attack. The date was April 6, 1917. Twenty days later, Boeing won a government contract to build 50 training airplanes.

The First World War was not fought in America, but we were involved. Our whole country was involved. And Washington did its part helping us win!

title: Thirsty? Try Drinking... Water!
text:
When you work up a thirst, what do you reach for? Fruit juice? Soda pop? Sports drinks? Milk? How about a glass of water?

In the past, when kids got thirsty, they usually headed for the drinking fountain or the kitchen sink for a cool drink of water. Today, most kids grab a can of soda. National surveys show that in the late 1970s, kids drank an average of about five ounces of soda per day. Today, kids drink an average of between eight and 12 ounces of soda per day. Drinking this much soda adds about 200 calories per day to the diet of the average child, causing many children to become overweight. Drinking too much soda also causes children to drink less milk, water, and juice, drinks which are much better for their bodies.

Why choose water instead of soda? Water is the body's most important nutrient. Our bodies are about 60 to 65 percent water. Water brings nutrients to the body's cells and flushes out waste. Even though soda contains water, it also contains sugar, chemicals, and often, caffeine. These ingredients are difficult for the body to digest and often make us feel worse instead of better.

Drinking water is good for the body in many ways. It helps keep our body temperature steady, gets rid of waste, keeps our skin healthy, improves our digestion, helps us exercise and play longer without getting tired, and even helps us lose weight.

If you are used to drinking a lot of soda, do yourself a favor and give water a try. Try cutting out one soda per day and adding a glass or bottle of water instead. Soon, you may find that you actually enjoy the way water makes you feel. You may even want to get your parents to cut back on the soda along with you. Before long, your whole family may be enjoying the good health that drinking plenty of water provides.

title: World War I
text:
Washington During the First World War

When a war involves many countries, we call it a world war. The First World War involved 23 of the biggest countries in the world, including America. It started when Germany attacked Russia, and other nations quickly joined sides. The cost of the war was terrible. Almost 8 million soldiers died, and the cost in money was $200 billion. The First World War began in 1914 and ended in 1918. The state of Washington sent a total of 75,000 people to fight, and 2,000 of them were killed.

Victory Gardens

In most cities, people turned vacant lots and backyards into gardens. Growing our own food helped win the war in Europe by allowing large farm produce to flow overseas to troops and needy people. With husbands, fathers and sons off to war, women took on the burdens of the family farm or in factories. Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts watered and tended, as did families and communities. “Victory Gardens” sprang up everywhere with peas, beans and potatoes.

Labor

During the First World War, workers were frustrated. They had to work long days at dangerous jobs for pay that was different from place to place. Workers organized themselves into labor unions, and in 1919, they went on strike. This means they refused to go back to work until pay and the long working hours were made more fair. Companies and factories were forced to change because nobody would come work for them. The strike lasted five days and brought Seattle to a standstill. Another group of workers in Centralia were called the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW). They were viewed as unpatriotic by American Legion workers, who were celebrating the end of World War I. A fight broke out between the groups, and in a 10-minute shootout, seven people were killed, and 50 were wounded. This focused national attention on the labor movement in America.

Agriculture

The first change the war brought in Washington was on the farm. Most farm workers had gone to war. Others took higher-paying jobs in factories or in Canada, where pay was better. The farm problems were solved by our communities—women drove the tractors, high-school students donated after-school hours and college professors worked holidays and weekends. We built more meat-packing plants and dairy and poultry farms. Twenty new grain mills were built to make more flour.

Shipbuilding

Puget Sound was a perfect shipbuilding place. Its protected harbors were deep and ideal for the job. At the start of the war, there was only one shipyard that employed 200 people. A year later in 1916, it had grown to more than 6,000 workers. By 1918, there were seven shipyards in Seattle with 32,000 workers. Washington made 1/5 of the total ship production in the United States, and in 1919, it made 195 ships—more than any other state in America. Shipbuilding was an important source of jobs and income in the Pacific Northwest.

title: Centralia, Washington
text:
We’ve already mentioned Centralia as the site of a large riot in 1919 when armed members of the IWW fought with armed members of the American Legion. Seven were killed and 50 wounded in a 10-minute shootout. Today, Centralia is a friendly, historic city. Centralia is located halfway between Seattle and Portland and was first named Centerville. The town site was founded in 1850 by J. G. Cochran. Cochran and his wife had earlier adopted the son of an enslaved person. The child’s name was George Washington.

In 1875, George laid out the town site and founded the city of Centerville. He sold small lots at first, enlarging them later to attract more settlers. In 1891, the name was changed to Centralia. Hard times fell on the city, and George had to save it with his own money. Beautiful forests gave Centralia a strong lumber industry that continues today, along with dairying, poultry raising and fruit farming. Most of its buildings were built in the late 1800s. Centralia is a great place to visit, with antiques galore! You’ll find a treasure in one of the many antique shops!

title: When Was the Biggest Snow Storm in Seattle?
text: On Feb. 1, 1916, Seattle received a record of 21.5 inches of snow in a 24-hour period. That is almost 2 feet of snow in just one day! Many other parts of Washington were covered with 2 to 4 feet of snow. The winds howled and created snowdrifts that were as high as 5 feet, taller than many people were, especially people your age! Transportation was cut off during this time, and many parts of the region were in trouble. Overall, between January 31 and February 3 of 1916, Seattle received 33 inches of snow.

title: Pileated Woodpecker
text: Hey, who's that knocking on the door? If you're in the forest, that knocking sound is probably a pileated woodpecker. These big birds are very shy, and you won't see them too often, but you'll hear them a lot. Besides making noise to knock huge holes in both live and dead trees, this woodpecker has a loud call: "wuck a wuck a wuck a wuck a." This bird is black with a red crest and a white face. What are they looking for when they go pecking around? They want the ants, termites, and beetles that are living inside the fallen trees. The pileated woodpeckers are 16-19 inches long and love to live in mature forests. In fact, a healthy population of this bird means a forest's ecosystem is also healthy. Each bird needs about 1,000 acres. All this hunting and pecking helps break up decaying trees, speeding up the return of nutrients to the forest floor.

title: Reading and Writing
text:
Read the article carefully. Then answer the questions on a separate piece of paper. Be sure to write in complete sentences, with correct spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Zombies in Seattle?

If you suddenly found yourself in Seattle in the fall of 1918, you might think you were in a Hollywood zombie movie. Stores boarded up their doors, schools were closed and neighbors disappeared overnight. Sadly, this was all too real. In 1918 the flu was a serious illness. When soldiers got sick during World War I, they were sent on crowded trains to crowded hospitals. The ones didn’t need a hospital just went home and in the busy city streets, the virus spread easily. But it was not only in the U.S. People all over the world were getting sick. The flu of 1918 was a pandemic, which means it took place over a wide area and affected a large part of the population. So large, that by 1919 the flu had killed almost 6% of the world's population. That means about one in every seventeen people died!

People did not know what to do. A government document was issued telling people to "Beware of those who are coughing and sneezing, avoid crowded street cars, keep rooms well ventilated, and keep the feet dry." It also stated that the greatest danger was pneumonia. Pneumonia happens when the lungs become inflamed from bacteria or fill with fluid making it hard or impossible to breathe.

Perhaps the strangest part of this disease was the people it affected. Most flu viruses attack the very young and the elderly, whose immune systems are weaker. But the flu of 1918 attacked those between the ages of 20 and 40. At the Yakima Indian Agency, a Superintendent wrote to a parent whose child had died, "This plague attacked this school on the 13th of October. It was brought here at first by new students coming in and it spread rapidly until we had about 250 cases. The entire school stopped its regular activities and devoted itself absolutely to the care and nursing of the sick."

Today we have better medical care to fight illness, but we should always keep an eye out for deadly diseases!

title: Timelines
text:
Timelines can be made for just about anything and for any time. A good place to start is with something or someone you know well...like yourself! What year was your first birthday? What year did you start kindergarten? Make a list of all the things you would like on your timeline. If you don’t know when the event was, ask a parent or other relative to help you.

Next, get out a ruler, measure a straight line and add evenly spaced marks to show years or months. Fill in your headings and draw some pictures to go with them. You can add events to your timeline whenever you want to.

Multiple Perspectives

Historical events can have different points of view as well. For example, you and your friends have all been in class together today. Going to school may not seem like a historical event, but it’s part of history—your history! Even though you and your friends are in the same class, you have had different experiences getting to school and learning. Talk to some friends about their day and make a timeline of today using your classmates’ stories. How was their day different from your day? How was it the same?

title: Let's Write
text: Have you been downtown in our biggest city? Do you live near there? Write and tell us about your favorite things to visit in our state’s biggest city!

title: The Man Who Could Fly
text:
How would you like to build a rocket to the moon or ride in a balloon through the sky over Mars? Let’s look closer at one man’s dream of flying. His aircraft company helped land man on the moon, and someday, it will send us to Mars.

Yes, people had been floating around in balloons for years, but nobody had ever flown in a machine that was heavier than air. Wilbur and Orville Wright’s airplane flew only a few hundred feet along an ocean shore at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, but they had flown! And young William Boeing would never forget this amazing feat.

William moved to Grays Harbor, Washington, in 1903 and started buying and selling forest land. For him, the risky work proved profitable, and he made a large amount of money. He moved to Seattle in 1908. The idea of flying was stuck in his head. He wanted to fly and traveled to nearby air shows to convince the pilots to take him into the air. He wanted to know what it was like to fly, but no one would give him a ride.

William was disappointed, but he returned to Seattle determined to learn more about flying. For the next few years, William tried to learn all about airplanes. He found a friend who had taken some classes on how airplanes worked (aeronautics) at the famous Massachusetts Institute of Technology. This man was named George Conrad Westervelt.

One day, William and George had the chance of a lifetime. They went flying! The airplane was pretty scary, however. The pilot could only take one of them at a time, and both the pilot and his passenger had to sit on the wing! Said George afterwards, “I could never find any definite answer as to why it held together.” Both William and George became convinced they could build an airplane much better than the one they flew on.

In 1915, William went to California to learn how to fly. George stayed behind to design their very first airplane. They named their new plane the “B&W,” that stood for Boeing & Westervelt. It had two wings and floated on the water using pontoons.

The Boeing aircraft company, now one of the largest in the world, was finally started. In the 19th and 20th centuries, William’s company produced jet aircraft and giant passenger planes. The company helped land people on the moon and orbit the Earth in the space shuttle. In the future, Boeing may help send missions to Mars. And all this from the man who wanted to fly!

title: Boom to Bust and Back Again
text:
You may have heard people compare the recent economic recession (2007-2009) to the Great Depression of the 1930s. But what some people call the "Great Recession" actually had more in common with a depression in the 1890s and something called "boom and bust."

In the early 1890s, the U.S. economy grew quickly ("boomed") but couldn't keep growing at that rate. When many companies and the housing market failed, there was an economic "bust." The railroad industry had been booming since the end of the Civil War, but in the 1890s more than 150 railroad companies closed. Other industries that depended on the railroads closed, and many people lost their jobs. Over 500 banks closed. Thousands of unemployed men marched to Washington, D.C., in 1894 to demand that the government take action to help families. Unemployment was over 10 percent for most of the 1890s. About one of every ten people had no job.

In the recent recession, the housing market slumped after several "boom" years. Some automakers went out of business and others filed for bankruptcy. The economy went "bust," just as it did in the 1890s. Hundreds of banks and thousands of businesses closed. The unemployment rate was about 8 percent-about one of every twelve people had no job.

Make a chart or Venn diagram that compares these two events in history.

title: The Purpose of Government
text:
Citizens have responsibilities. Some examples of these are voting, paying taxes and obeying the laws. Did you realize that our state government has responsibilities to Washington citizens too? It’s true. It is similar to school. Just as you (the citizen) have responsibilities in your classroom, your teacher (the government) has certain responsibilities to you. This summer your teacher planned lessons, prepared materials, got the room ready for the first day of school and maybe even took a class to learn new ideas for teaching. Those are some of the responsibilities a teacher has for making learning interesting and fun each day! The government of our state has a purpose and responsibilities also.

What are some of the important purposes of government? Why is government necessary? Some important purposes of government are promoting the common good, protecting citizens’ rights and making sure everyone is treated equally under the law. (Common good means doing things that are good for everyone.) Government is necessary because without it we would have no laws or rules to follow. Can you imagine your classroom if everyone could do whatever they wanted? It would be hard for the students to learn anything. It is that way with our country too.

Stated simply, government decides how to manage a country, state or city. Although there are different levels of government, the main purpose of all government is to make laws and rules about things that effect everyone’s daily life. These laws and rules provide safety and security for everyone. The government makes sure that all citizens are treated fairly under these laws and that people’s rights are protected. To promote common good, our government provides services such as schools, police and fire departments, safe roads and other things that benefit all citizens. Our federal government provides many things for citizens of the United States, but state governments manage some things as well.

title: First the Roaring 20s, then the Great Depression of the 30s
text:
In our last newspaper we talked about the first 20 years of the 20th century, and the First World War. During the next 20 years, we had two important events occur in our state that you will want to remember. The first we call the Roaring Twenties. The second was the Great Depression. Ask your grandparents (or great-grandparents) about these-perhaps they are old enough to remember.

Roaring Twenties

The war was over, and Washington wanted to grow! We had almost 1,400,000 people in our state in 1920. Most of these newcomers settled west of the Cascades. Our number of farms now stood at 66,300. Lumber was still our number-one industry, with steel ship-building coming in second. But without a war, the country didn’t need ships. In a short time, our shipyards nearly collapsed. We had fewer than 1,000 workers in the shipyards by 1921, and about 150 vessels that were on order were suddenly canceled. People lost their jobs. The price for lumber was cut in half, and wheat dropped almost 2/3 of its war-time price. These were hard times.

Who could fix this mess? Many banks were started to loan people money so they could start businesses and build houses. Changes in our state government helped, too. Slowly, things started to get better. By the late 1920s, it appeared Washington was going to recover. The lumber industry was making enough to provide 1 million jobs, and the new train tunnel through the Cascades was finished, ending four years of amazing work (the tunnel is 8 miles long, cut through solid granite!). We also began planning for the Grand Coulee Dam on the Columbia, and thanks to modern airplanes, regular airplane trips were started from Seattle to British Columbia. Our 10th governor, a lumber millionaire named Roland Hartley, tried hard to build up our state. But then, disaster struck!

The Great Depression

In 1929, a panic spread across America. People who gave money to companies, to help the companies grow, wanted their money back. Most companies couldn’t give the money back, and thousands of companies began to die and go out of business. They had to lay off workers, close their doors and sell off their land and equipment to pay back the loans. It was a terrible time. In Washington, thousands lost their jobs. It was common to see long lines of people waiting just to get food so they wouldn’t starve. Wheat that sold for $2.04 a bushel during the war now sold for 34 cents per bushel. Lumber prices were slashed by 2/3. Farmers couldn’t afford to keep up with their orchards, and pulled up their apple and prune trees and burned them for fuel.

For 10 long years, we suffered. Everything became cheap but nobody had money or jobs to buy things. Many poor people wore rags and ate very little. Some labor unions (organized workers) tried to go on strike, but that only made things worse. By 1933, 1/5th of our state was getting welfare help just to stay alive.

The federal government finally stepped in to help. It gave enough money to give thousands of Washington workers a job. In 1935, approval was given to start the Grand Coulee Dam. The Bonneville Dam would be finished in 1937. By the end of the 1930s, people began to make a little money, and recovery seemed just around the corner. But the world wouldn’t settle for recovery. The world was about to break out in war, again. And for us, that meant more jobs.

title: From Seattle to Tranquility Base
text: Where is Tranquility Base? Isn't that some place on the moon? Yes, but we like to claim part of it for ourselves! Tranquility Base is the place where humans first set foot on the moon on July 20, 1969. The moon landing represented 10 years of hard work by Boeing and other aerospace ("fly" and "space") companies. With a little piece of Boeing still up there on the moon, we like to think we have a little claim there! And in honor of William Boeing, don't you agree it is fitting that we include part of the first landing spot on the moon as part of our state? This little plot of land, now covered with hundreds of footprints by the very first people to walk on the moon, is about 240,000 miles away. If you visit this outpost by spaceship, you will find the place very grey and very dusty. Your foot will sink into the dust about an inch. If you kick the dust, it doesn't scatter, but moves away from you in slow motion, because gravity on the moon is only 1/6th of what it is on Earth. You will have to wear a space suit because on the moon there is no air to breathe. There are plenty of mountains and craters, but nothing like our own snow-and tree-covered mountains. If you ever visit this far away Washington pretend "region," be sure to see the part of the lunar lander that is still there. Remember that our very own William Boeing is one reason we made it to the moon.

title: How does an airplane fly?
text: This puzzle is answered in the shape of the wing. Notice that bird and plane wings are curved on top and flat on the underside. When a wing moves through the air, the air passing over the top is thinned out, but the bottom air isn’t. What happens? The thicker (more dense) bottom air wants to push up, and that’s exactly what happens! Prove it yourself by holding a thin strip of paper close to your lips and blow across the TOP (not underneath) of the paper. Does the paper rise up? Yes! That’s how wings work. The propeller or engine gets the wings moving through the air fast enough until this bottom air is pushing strong enough to lift the aircraft, and off you go!

title: Peregrine Falcon
text: One of the fastest birds in the sky is the peregrine falcon. The peregrine has mastered the use of wings and speed better than most other birds. It will dive and strike in mid-air, killing its prey with a blow at speeds over 200 miles an hour. These medium-sized hawks have long pointed wings that are dark blue-gray, with pale undersides. The word “peregrine” means foreigner or traveler. It probably has this name because it migrates to warmer climates in winter and feeds all the way on other birds. They are about the size of crows, with wingspans of 40 inches. The females are larger than the males. Peregrines love to live along coast lines, mountain ranges and river valleys. They don’t like stick nests, and make their nests in gravel or in the side of a cliff. That’s why sometimes they’ll make a nest on a ledge of a skyscraper, tall tower or bridge. Peregrines are endangered because they ate so many other birds that had consumed pesticides (mostly DDT). The DDT made peregrine egg shells too soft, and babies couldn’t develop. If someone points out a nesting peregrine, stay far away! We must help peregrines regain their place in the world.
