title: Let's Write
text: Imagine it’s the year 2075, and trips to the moon are very common. You decide to save your money and buy a ticket to the new lunar city. Part of the tour is to visit the very first landing place at Tranquility Base. Describe what it’s like to visit the moon, walk around and see the sites. What would you need to live there? What would you do while on the moon? What things would you try to grow on the moon?

title: What are Homophones and Homographs?
text:
Homophones and homographs are the same but different! To find out the meaning of a word, carefully read the words and sentences surrounding it.

Homophones

Homophones are words that sound the same but have different spellings and different meanings. You can remember what a homophone is by remembering that a phone makes a sound, so a homophone sounds the same as another word.

It is important to know a homophone when you write it. If you need help with a homophone when you read or write, look it up in a dictionary. This will help you keep from making mistakes. For instance, would you write you have “bear hands” or “bare hands”?

Here are some common homophones:

Beat, beet

Earn, urn

Eye, I

Heal, heel, he’ll

Made, maid

Plain, plane

Rain, reign, rein

To, too, two

Homographs

These are words that are spelled the same but have different meanings. Sometimes they are pronounced differently even though they are spelled the same. You can remember what a homograph is by remembering that a graph is something you look at, so a homograph looks the same.

Here are some common homographs that are pronounced differently and have different meanings:

Bass: a low voice

Bass: a fish

Content: things found inside

Content: satisfied

Minute: 60 seconds

Minute: tiny

Try It!

The next time you are not sure which homophone or homograph to use, be sure you know the meaning of the word you are trying to use. This will help you spell it correctly. A dictionary will help you a lot!

title: That Terrible Day in December!
text:
December 7, 1941 was another sleepy Sunday morning in Washington. The newspaper delivery trucks were completing their rounds, dropping off bundles to young delivery boys and girls who were waiting with their bicycles. The milk trucks were finishing their rounds, leaving ice cold milk in boxes on front porches. A few early risers were stepping into the early darkness to enjoy the crisp damp air of the coming winter.

Far away to the west, a completely different morning was breaking over Hawaii. From far at sea, low to the horizon, a strange formation had gathered in the morning sky. As it approached, people watched from a distance. What were so many planes doing in the air at this time of day? Was it some exercise? Suddenly, it became very clear what the planes were doing. It was an attack!

Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, was the home of America's largest naval base on the Pacific. The 100 planes that attacked that morning were all from Japan. The Japanese came to destroy all of our biggest ships that were parked in the harbor. Immediately, the alarms sounded all over Hawaii, and the cry went out, "Pearl Harbor is under attack!"

Japanese fighting planes, torpedo bombers and dive bombers took only one hour and 55 minutes to empty their bombs and bullets. When it was over, five of our eight battleships were sunk, the other three were damaged. Five other ships were sunk and several damaged. About 325 of our planes on the ground were destroyed. Among the dead were 2,343 American sailors, soldiers and marines; 1,272 were wounded and 960 were missing. Many of the docks, repair facilities, hangers and runways were damaged or destroyed.

When word of the attack reached Washington, people began to panic, especially in our western cities. Instead of a day of rest, Sunday became a dark day of worry. Would the Japanese continue their attack along the Pacific Coast? Would they bomb Bremerton and Boeing facilities? No one knew what to expect.

When the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor, most countries in Europe were already at war. After Germany invaded Poland in 1939, Great Britain, France and Poland declared war on Germany. These three countries were the original Allies in WWII. Their enemies were known as the Axis. Germany, Italy and Japan were the three main Axis powers. By 1941, many countries had joined either the Allies or the Axis. Other countries stayed neutral (did not take sides).

Work with a partner to do some research about Europe in November 1941, just before Pearl Harbor was attacked. Make a list of Allied powers, Axis powers, neutral countries and countries that had been invaded by the Axis. Think of a way to show these countries on the map (colors, stripes, dots, etc.) and make a map key that explains the colors or markings on your map.

title: Washington Veterans Tell Their Stories
text:
As veterans (those who have served in the military) of foreign wars grow older, our country risks losing the stories of these brave soldiers forever. Thousands of war veterans die each week, and along with them go their stories. The Library of Congress' Veterans History Project hopes to record these amazing historical stories before the war veterans are no longer around to tell them.

So far, project participants have gathered more than 3,900 war stories from veterans of foreign wars. For many years, these veterans have kept their stories to themselves, not wanting to burden their families with their pain. As they age, however, many veterans feel the need to finally talk about their experiences and let someone know what war was really like.

Guy Stephens, a 78-year-old former school principal, told his interviewer about being rescued from a German prison camp where he was held as a prisoner of war, or POW. He says, "It's hard for POWs to talk to your family about combat or what you've experienced as a POW. There's something about POWs, we never talk about things. I told him things I've never told my family ... I don't know why."

Many Washington libraries have become involved in the project, including the Timberland Regional Library (TRL) in Southwest Washington. TRL was the first public library in Washington to become part of the Veterans History Project. The library has currently completed over 150 interviews with veterans. TRL plans to expand its program with the help of volunteers who are willing to interview veterans, as well as videotape their stories. By preserving the history of these brave soldiers, volunteers guarantee that these amazing stories will live on, even after the soldiers have passed away.

title: Washington Helps With the War
text:
As America prepared to fight World War II, Washington was called upon to provide a lot of help.

Fort Lewis, which had become a main training center during World War I, was again called to action. It became the second-largest camp in the whole country. Nearby rivers, lakes, air fields and mountains became training grounds where troops would practice flying, landing, climbing and bridge-building. After the surrender of Japan in August 1945, Washington found itself a much larger and very busy state. Here are some of the big changes we experienced during World War II.

The Hanford Works

All during World War II, America had been working on a new bomb that could destroy an entire city. This so-called atomic bomb was dropped on two Japanese cities, killing hundreds of thousands of people. This brought the war with Japan to an end. The bomb's main ingredient was a material called plutonium. The government decided to make the plutonium here in our state, but where could this super secret project be done? The small town of Hanford (436 people in 1940) was chosen. In a few short months, 51,000 people were brought to Hanford. Barracks and trailers were built to house the people, and almost overnight, Hanford became the fifth-largest city in Washington. Nearby Richland also grew from 200 to 15,000. By January 1945, the first plutonium was delivered for the bomb, and two months later, all the construction in Hanford and Richland was declared finished. A year later, after the war had ended, everybody moved out. These two cities almost became ghost towns.

Agriculture

Washington helped provide food during World War II, especially wheat. Wheat was our most important crop during World War II, but our state wanted to grow just about anything it could. Peaprocessing was expanded a lot. One food-packing company in Vancouver canned more than 650,000 cases of fruits and vegetables in one year. Our dairy, poultry and meat-packing businesses grew and enlarged at a very fast rate.

Shipbuilding

During the war many women filled the men's places in the factories and farms. A common term "Rosie Riveter" was used to describe the women workers. In fact, there were more women working in Washington than there were men. Our shipbuilding talent really shined during World War II. We ran 88 shipyards with 150,000 workers, around the clock. And we built just about everything, from patrol boats to mine-sweepers, destroyers, landing craft, tugs, barges, escort aircraft carriers, troopships and floating dry-docks. The crippled and damaged ships from Pearl Harbor were towed to Bremerton for repairs, and most went to sea again, stronger than before.

Aircraft

Since World War I, the Boeing aircraft company remained busy making planes. One month after the attack on Pearl Harbor, Boeing pumped out 60 of its B-17 Flying Fortress aircraft. With 45,000 workers making planes, and 200 other companies providing supplies, Boeing provided a steady stream of aircraft. A long-range bomber that could reach Japan was needed. Boeing built the B-29 that could fly 4,500 miles. Boeing built 2,766 of these. Fearing attack by Japanese bombers, Boeing covered its entire factory with grass and bushes. From the air, it looked like a small town with little houses and trees! Meanwhile, another airplane factory, Alcoa Aluminum Plant in Vancouver, built more than 14,500 bombers for the war!

title: Critical Analysis and Rumination: President Truman and The Atomic Bomb Decision
text:
rumination (noun): the act of giving serious thought and consideration to something

Adolf Hitler was defeated in May 1945 after years of war in Europe, and American troops would be coming home-wouldn’t they? Victory in Europe meant that some U.S. soldiers would be returning home. Others would go to the Pacific to face Japanese armies. Scientists in the U.S. had made a weapon that could certainly end the war with Japan, but it was so powerful that tens of thousands of people would be killed, including civilians (citizens not in the military). President Harry Truman had a decision to make that would greatly affect the world. What would the commander in chief do?

In the years leading up to President Truman’s decision, the Japanese had been a brutal enemy. They had killed thousands of Americans at sea and on Pacific islands, including the surprise attack on Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The president wondered how many more lives would be lost if we tried to end the war without the atomic bomb. What would happen if another country improved the weapon and used the bomb before we did? Would they use it on us?

President Truman tried several times without success to work out surrender with Japan. He then ordered atomic bombs to be dropped on the cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945. Within a week of the second attack, Japan did surrender, which put an end to World War II. Historians estimate that between 150,000 and 240,000 Japanese were killed from effects of the two bombings. They also estimate that thousands of American lives were saved. Do you think President Truman made the right decision?

title: Bremerton
text: Bremerton has seen a lot of the Navy since its beginning back in 1901. But even before, people recognized it as a perfect naval shipyard and harbor. It all started in 1891, when William Bremer sold 190 acres to the Navy. That same year, the Puget Sound Naval Station was established. The town of Bremerton was officially mapped out in 1901. After the city was settled, another dozen acres of coast line were donated so the Navy would have plenty to work with. During World War II, the town of Bremerton swelled to 80,000 people as workers arrived to build steel ships and submarines. The city’s 228 miles of shoreline make it ideal for many shipping activities. This is also the gateway to all the wonderful recreational areas of the Olympic Peninsula. People like living in this lush, rainy part of Washington. Bremerton is still home to the northern Pacific fleet. It’s a great place to learn about America’s great naval power and how it helps keep peace on the open oceans.

title: Who is Uncle Sam?
text: Ever since the War of 1812, Americans have looked to Uncle Sam as a symbol for the United States. Uncle Sam is a real person from Massachusetts named Samuel Wilson. He fought in the Revolutionary War. People who liked him, both family and business people, called him "Uncle Sam." In the War of 1812, his meat-packing business provided troops with pork and beef. He marked his boxes with a "U.S.," meaning "United States," but some thought it meant "Uncle Sam." People soon applied this term to ANYTHING supplied by the federal government. The image we identify as Uncle Sam evolved over the next 150 years.

title: Honey Bees
text: It’s hard to believe, but spring is just around the corner. With each warming day, you might notice a few bees flying around. Where do they come from and why are they out while it’s still cold? A beehive is usually only 2-3 miles away from a bee you might see, and as soon as it gets in the 40s, thousands of bees leave the hive to look for nectar. Honeybees are amazing insects. They are organized, hard working and very efficient. About 8 pounds of honey is eaten by bees to produce one pound of beeswax. In the winter, they huddle in their beehives in a great big ball of 20,000-30,000 bees. In the middle of this mass is the queen, staying nice and warm. During winter, they eat honey, and on the coldest nights, some of the bees on the outside of this ball will freeze. As the weather warms up, the hive becomes active. Worker bees clean out the dead bees, scrub the honeycomb clean, and the queen starts laying eggs. Workers go out looking for early blossoms. Nearly all the bees are female. They keep 5-10 males (drones) around just in case the queen is killed. If so, they feed a special royal jelly to a newly laid egg and grow a new queen. As bees gather nectar, they also spread plants’ pollen. This keeps all vegetation healthy and producing fruits. If you see a bee, don’t be scared. Be respectful. This is one hardworking insect!

title: Let's Write
text: Do you know someone who lived during the 1920s-1940s? Your great-grandparents would be good people to ask. Interview them about rationing, victory gardens and Prohibition. You’ll enjoy talking to them—we promise! Write an essay about what they told you.

title: Europe, November 1941
text:
When the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor, most countries in Europe were already at war. After Germany invaded Poland in 1939, Great Britain, France and Poland declared war on Germany. These three countries were the original Allies in WWII. Their enemies were known as the Axis. Germany, Italy and Japan were the three main Axis powers. By 1941, many countries had joined either the Allies or the Axis. Other countries stayed neutral (did not take sides).

Work with a partner to do some research about Europe in November 1941, just before Pearl Harbor was attacked. Make a list of Allied powers, Axis powers, neutral countries and countries that had been invaded by the Axis. Think of a way to show these countries on the map (colors, stripes, dots, etc.) and make a map key that explains the colors or markings on your map.

title: Welcome to the Future!
text:
The years since WWII make up our state’s modern period. During the modern period, Washington has stretched, grown, enlarged and shrunk in ways our forefathers could never have imagined.

Washington is smaller than its neighbors, Oregon and Idaho, but we have the largest population. Most of our residents live in the Seattle-Everett area and Tacoma, as well as cities along Puget Sound and our capital, Olympia. Spokane is our largest city east of the Cascades. It is the center hub (middle; center of activity) for what some people call our “inland empire.” By that they mean a massive working program in agriculture, forestry and mining that extends into Oregon, Idaho, Montana and southern British Columbia.

The Tri-Cities area (Richland-Kennewick-Pasco) is at the confluence (meeting place) of the Snake and the Columbia rivers. This forms a great transportation hub from which all kinds of commerce takes place: agriculture, manufacturing and the Hanford Site (an atomic energy installation).

A lot of our smaller towns are close to the earth – they work the timber, the wheat, the farming, the fish. Their horizons don’t include tall buildings, but hundreds of grain elevators, something we jokingly call prairie skyscrapers! And many food-processing plants are the heart of other settlements in farming areas. Many of our residents work in agriculture or in state or federal goverment agencies. Everybody is connected with 80,000 miles of roads, 5 million drivers and 3,000 miles of rails.

For a long time, our state grew by immigration – that is, from people moving into our state. In the 1950s, enough people were here that having babies became the biggest increase in our population. Which way is bringing more people to our state now? Do some research to find out!

We manufacture all sorts of things, from underwater submarines to the spacecraft that orbit the Earth. We have giant forests that provide timber, we have a giant fish and seafood industry, and broad and well-worked agriculture that includes all kinds of foods. We make aluminum, process oil and give tourists their money’s worth for each and every time they visit. We can fly you, drive you, boat you and ski you to all kinds of destinations. We will educate you, train you, give you culture, give you religion and a taste of the entire world without you leaving your own city borders. If you get sick, we can give you the world’s best treatment for healing. We’ll employ you, entertain you and give you all kinds of things on which you can spend your money. If you’re out of money, we’ll help you find a job, or if hard times remain, we will help you until you get back on your feet. Is there anything we don’t have and can’t do in our state? We doubt it!

title: Milk–What's Your Favorite Flavor?
text:
We all know that milk is good for us, but many children don’t enjoy the flavor of plain, white milk. Did you know that kids your age need at least 1,300 milligrams of calcium each day to keep their bones and teeth healthy? To get this much calcium, you would need to drink at least four glasses of milk. Many milk companies are trying to get children to drink more milk by making it a little more interesting. Milk is now available in nearly 50 flavors and is offered in plastic bottles with twist-on lids.

You have probably tried chocolate and strawberry milk, but how about orange cream, vanilla caramel, Milky Way or cookies and cream? Some dairies have even tried to make root beer milk! If you could choose one of these unusual flavors, would you choose milk instead of soda? Milk producers hope that your answer is “Yes!”

Several school districts across Washington now offer both chocolate and strawberry flavored milk, besides the usual white milk. Some schools are also serving their milk in plastic bottles rather than in cartons. More students choose to drink milk when it is flavored and when it is served in bottles rather than cartons.

Some parents worry that flavored milk may not be as healthy as white milk. Flavored milks have more sugar than white milk, but cup for cup, they provide the same amount of bone-building calcium and other nutrients as white milk, including protein, B vitamins, vitamin D and vitamin A.

No matter the flavor, milk is still one of the healthiest drinks around. What is your favorite flavor?

title: The Modern Period
text:
After World War II, our state started growing and Growing and GROWING!

Population

Washington’s population is around 7 million people. In recent years, our state has been growing by about one percent each year. When babies are born, our population grows. When people die, our population shrinks. Lately, there have been more births than deaths. In addition, more people have been moving into our state than have been moving out of our state. So, we’ve been growing! Check out the U.S. Census Bureau’s website. See how Washington compares to other states in population and growth.

Bridges

With all of our lakes and rivers, we have needed easier ways to get around our state. We’re known for our “floating” bridges. They’re anchored to the lake bottom but float on top of the water. Our first floating bridge was built on Lake Washington in 1939. Other famous bridges are the Evergreen Point Bridge and the Astoria-Megler Bridge. Can you think of any other famous bridges you have crossed?

Agriculture

We have about 38,000 farms and 15 million acres of farmland. Our hens lay almost 2 billion eggs in a year! Important crops are barley, fruit, potatoes and other vegetables. Our wheat harvest is usually strong as well. Wheat grows well in Washington, producing millions of bushels a year. What grows in your part of Washington?

Landscape

Our landscape keeps changing. If it isn’t a new building, road or community, it’s a volcano! Nobody goes to Seattle without noticing the Space Needle, the central attraction for the 1962 World’s Fair. In 1980, the whole world watched when Mount St. Helens erupted, sending a great cloud of dust that traveled thousands of miles in the atmosphere. And today, small volcanoes are rumbling on the ocean floor about 200 miles off the coast.

Laws

For a long time, some people were not allowed to enter public buildings because of their race or national origin. In 1953, we passed a new civil rights law that made access fair to everyone. For some kinds of work, women were not being paid the same as men doing the same job. In 1955, we passed a law so everyone received the same pay for the same work.

Shipping

We can’t say enough about our good harbors. A port is where ships dock to load and unload goods. Seattle and Tacoma are our largest ports, handling millions of tons of goods per year.

Electricity

Since 1920, more than 40 power dams have been constructed on the Columbia. Have you visited one? It’s worth doing — they are fantastic structures to see. With all of this inexpensive electricity, we do a lot of great things. But don’t forget to turn off the lights when you leave the room! Do a little research to find out how much electricity our state uses each year.

title: Governing the People
text:
A government is a system that keeps life running smoothly for people who live in a community. All levels of government make laws to keep citizens safe and protect the rights of the people. This week, we will learn how national, state, local and tribal governments help the citizens of Washington.

National Government

The national government governs the entire country. It makes laws, enforces them and collects taxes to pay for national projects. The national government prints money, supports the military, declares war, makes agreements with other nations, handles business between the states and runs the mail system.

State Government

Our state government leaders are chosen by Washington voters to run the state. The head of our state government is called the governor. It is the governor’s job to carry out the laws made by the legislators (lawmakers) of our state. The state of Washington also has courts that interpret, or explain, Washington’s laws. State governments collect taxes to pay for roads, hospitals, schools, water projects and other needs.

Local Government

Local means belonging to one community, so local government serves the people of a smaller area, such as a city or town. Local government looks at the needs of its citizens and makes decisions about how to meet these needs using tax money it collects from its citizens. Some of these needs include police and fire protection, garbage pick-up and public parks.

Tribal Governments

Another type of Washington government is called a tribal government. Tribal governments make rules or laws to care for local American Indian tribes and protect their rights. Tribal government leaders are often invited to join groups of leaders from nearby cities to work together on meeting the needs of the community and the tribes. Tribal government leaders from Washington’s 29 nationally recognized tribes also join state and national groups to help make sure that their tribes are being well represented and treated fairly.

title: Whitman County
text: Did you ever wonder who grows the most wheat in our state? Whitman County is usually the leader of the pack! Whitman County is nestled in the southeast part of our state, and is often known as the Palouse. The Palouse region extends from the Blue Mountains on the border of Washington and Oregon, into the gentle, rolling hills and river valleys that reach into the state of Idaho. There are never-ending wheat and grain fields as far as the eye can see. And wildlife everywhere - deer, raccoons and maybe a few owls perched in trees waiting for the dusk to bring out some nighttime feeding on mice. Look across the horizon and see hundred-year-old barns dotting the landscape between small communities where friendly folks wave at a passing stranger. Fishing, hunting, camping, museums, skiing, historical sites and more greet the visitor. The population in Whitman County is highly educated, with two universities, cultural opportunities, highly-rated grade schools and growing businesses with international connections. Colfax is the county seat. If you visit, bring a fishing pole! Visit the Revere Wildlife Area, and keep a look out for badgers, quail and rattlesnakes.

title: How many loaves of bread are in a bushel of wheat?
text: There are about 1 million kernels of wheat in a bushel! This wheat will make 42 pounds of white flour or 60 pounds of whole wheat flour. With the flour, bakers can make about 70 loaves of white bread or 90 loaves of whole wheat bread (one-pound loaves).

title: Wheat
text: Wheat is a grass-type plant. It belongs to the group of grains called cereals. Other important cereals are rice, oats, corn, barley and rye. Wheat is better for bread because the kernel has more gluten than other grains. Gluten is a stretchy material that, along with yeast, makes dough rise and become fluffy and edible. Farmers plant about 20 pounds of wheat per acre and harvest over 4,000 pounds of wheat! The new wheat plants grow best in mild, dry climates. They look like green grass and grow 2 to 5 feet tall. They turn golden brown when they are ripe. The leaves are long and slender, and the wheat heads hold 50-150 or more kernels. They also have coarse prickly hairs called beards. The kernels can be white, red, yellow or purple and are almost 1/4 inch long. Wheat is grown in the winter or spring. In Washington, our winter crop is mostly common white winter wheat - good for bread, rolls, tortillas and Asian noodles. Our spring crop is mostly soft white wheat - good for flat breads, cakes, pastries, crackers, muffins and snack foods.

title: Let's Write
text: In a few decades, Studies Weekly might be looking back to the early years of the new millennium. What kinds of articles do you think you might see? What will your children find interesting about the time you live in now? Think of new technologies, important events, changes in traditions, advances in the sciences or influential people. Be creative– you can’t go wrong!

title: What is Etymology (et-u-mall-u-jee)?
text:
It is History

It might sound like some scientific field or medical study, but etymology is the history of a word. Did you know that words can have histories too? Where did words come from? Did someone just wake up one day and decide to name things randomly? Most words came about for a reason, and knowing the history of a word can help you understand its meaning.

Word histories can be fascinating. Some root words came from the ancient Greek and Latin languages. Others were borrowed from other languages, such as Spanish, French and German. And new words are added all the time.

For example, the word “kindergarten” means “children’s garden” in German. The term was coined in 1840 by Friedrich Froebel to refer to his method of teaching young children.

Try It!

Here are some words and where they came from. Do some research and find out what each word originally meant, why it was invented and how its meaning has changed. Your community library should have an etymology dictionary, often called an Oxford English Dictionary. And you can find information on the Internet as well. One good site is http://www.etymonline.com/.

Here is an example of what a passage
might look like in an etymology resource:

1. Algebra—From Arabia

2. Route—From France

3. Zero—From Arabia

4. Bronco—From Mexico

5. Gorilla—From Africa

title: The Constitution - Mightier than the Sword!
text:
Have you heard someone say "The pen is mightier than the sword"? This means that things written down on a piece of paper can be more powerful than a person swinging a sharp sword. How can this be? Written words are easily more powerful than a sword. For example, a treaty can stop armies from fighting; a law can stop us from hurting others; a newspaper can help people find ways to solve problems without fighting.

A perfect example of this is a document called a constitution. A constitution is a body of laws that everybody agrees to obey. Our country has a constitution and our state has a constitution, and both protect our rights. What rights might those be? Here are some examples from our U.S. Constitution:

Right to Privacy (Fourth Amendment)

Can anybody walk into your house and start snooping through your closets and drawers, taking things, just because they felt like it? Our constitution says NO! because we all enjoy the right to privacy. Students in some states are forced to take drug tests to see if they are using drugs. Do you think this is a violation of the right to privacy? Do you think it is helpful in fighting the drug problems?

Freedom of Speech (First Amendment)

Can you say anything you want? Matt Fraser, a student in Washington state, gave a talk at a school assembly using indecent language causing the audience to hoot and holler. Angry teachers suspended him from school. Matt went to court saying the teachers violated his right to free speech. Was Matt right or wrong? The Supreme Court said Matt was wrong because free speech is protected only when the words don't hurt other people. A school, the court said, is a protected place where students, teachers and parents can expect protection from disruptive language.

Freedom of Religion (First Amendment)

Do you go to church or participate in a religious belief? If you do, you are free to practice any part of your religion so long as it doesn't hurt other people. If you don't practice a religion, nobody can force you to join a church or practice a religious observance.

Innocent until proven Guilty (Sixth Amendment)

In our country, a person can't be put in jail unless someone can prove the person is guilty of a crime. In other countries, people are sometimes thrown in jail and kept there until they can prove they are innocent. What do you think about this right?

Right to Bear Arms (Second Amendment)

In early America, England tried to take the guns from colonists as a way of keeping control over the people (such things continue in other countries even today!). When our Constitution was written, the right to keep a weapon by individuals was protected. Today, some people think this right refers only to a local militia or National Guard. Others want to ban guns, hoping that will reduce crime. What do you think?

Our U.S. and state constitutions protect many rights. They also provide a way to make new laws as we need them. Keep reading and learn more about it!

title: Student Pages Learn About State Government
text:
Imagine yourself on the floor of the Washington State Legislature, delivering an important message to one of our senators or representatives. Your page's uniform, a crisp white shirt and bright red jacket, lets everyone know you have a vital job to do. Does getting involved in the government and learning about it up close sound exciting? If you would like to see how our government really works, you may want to check into becoming a student page for the Washington State Legislature when you are a little older.

When the state legislature meets each January, about 50 teenagers are chosen to work as legislative pages. These young people present the flag, make deliveries, relay messages, pass out papers and run errands for the lawmakers while they are in session. Each student page serves for a total of five days and must spend at least two hours each day in Page School. Page School teaches the students about the government and how it works.

To become a student page, you must be at least 14 years old and under 17 years old. You must fill out an application and get permission from your parents and your school, since you will be missing at least a week of your regular classes. If you are chosen to be a student page, you will work from 7:45 a.m. until 5:00 p.m. and you will be paid $35 for each day you work.

Crystal, a former student page, said, "One of the important lessons that I learned in page school this week was that government affects my life everyday - probably more than I realize." If you think you would like to be a legislative page one day, start planning ahead now to take advantage of this great opportunity.

title: Sharing Public Space: Susan B. Anthony and Equal Rights for All
text:
From the time she was a young girl, Susan B. Anthony believed that what was open to one person should be open to all people. As a teacher, she felt that having separate schools for girls, boys and free African Americans was not fair. She believed that the minds of all genders and races were equal and that education should be equal, too.

As Susan grew older, she joined other fights as well. She hated slavery and thought working women should be paid more money. She began fighting for women's suffrage, or the right for women to vote. She once was arrested for voting illegally and was fined $100. She wouldn't pay the fine. She said, "Trust me that as I ignore all law to help the [enslaved], so will I ignore it all to protect an enslaved woman." Until women were allowed to vote, just like men, Susan felt they were no better off than the enslaved. She fought for this right until her death in 1906, but at that time, women still couldn't vote.

Susan's efforts finally paid off when the 19th Amendment to the Constitution was passed in 1920. It gave all American women the right to vote. In her honor, the amendment is also called the Susan B. Anthony Amendment.

Near the end of her life, Susan wrote, "The older I get, the greater power I seem to have to help the world; I am like a snowball - the further I am rolled the more I gain."

title: Our Constitution
text:
Our state constitution is a document that describes the basic laws, organization, and character of our government. It lays out a government where "we the people" rule and "we the people" have certain basic rights.

The American Way of Life!

Here are some of the rights we enjoy because of our state and federal constitutions. How many of these are important to you?

Right to worship God in your own way.

Right to free speech and free press (newspapers).

Right to gather in groups (assemble).

Right to ask for problems to be solved (the government must remain willing to fix problems).

Right to privacy in your home.

Right to no excessive bail (that means if you are jailed, the money paid to get out must match the crime).

Right to trial by jury.

Always innocent until proven guilty.

Right to freely move about the country and world (you are not trapped here!).

Right to own private property.

Right to free elections and secret ballots.

Right to work at any job, committee or group you choose.

Right to go on strike and bargain with employers and employees.

Right to go into business and make some money.

Right to bargain for goods and services in a free market.

Right to make contracts with people (the government can't undo contracts, if legally made).

Right to ask the government to serve and protect us, and referee our problems (military, police, agencies).

Right to one law for all (government can't make a law just for you - laws must apply fairly to everyone).

Something to Celebrate!

After reading the rights that are guaranteed to all U.S. citizens by both the U.S. Constitution and by our own state constitution, list some of the responsibilities you have as a citizen to maintain those rights.

(Two have been done for you.)

Freedom of speech means I also must not hurt others.

My right to vote means when I'm old enough, I should vote.

_________________________________________________________

_________________________________________________________

_________________________________________________________

Our Three-headed Eagle

Our state constitution is patterned after the national constitution which uses three branches of government. We are depicting this unique and dynamic form of government using a three-headed eagle. Each of these three branches of government has a special job to do as you can see below. Each branch also checks on each other to insure that we have a balanced government that lives by the laws of the Constitution.

The Executive Branch

This branch consists of the governor, attorney general and secretary of state. These men and women have the power to enforce the laws made by the legislature. Judges, the police and National Guard help them do this.

The Legislative Branch

This branch is called the state legislature. It makes up the laws or rules for us to follow. There are two parts to the legislature, the House of Representatives and the Senate. These men and women are chosen by the people of our state to represent them in making the laws.

The Judicial Branch

These men and women make up the Supreme Court of our state. They decide if the laws made by the legislature are constitutional. They also decide what punishment a person should receive for breaking the law.

title: Washington's State Capitol Building
text: Washington’s beautiful capitol building was completed in 1928. It stands 28 stories high and is the tallest domed masonry building in the United States. If you pay a visit to our capitol, be sure to count the steps out front. There are 42 broad granite steps leading to the entrance — symbolizing our place as the 42nd state in the Union. And then look around at the fine details on the outside of the building. It took 30 expert carvers to cut the many details of the building in sandstone, marble and wood. Around the base of the dome, you will see stone ox skulls to honor our early ox-cart pioneers. Inside the building you will see beautiful plaster ceilings with eagles and gold-covered rosettes. The doorknobs and railings all have our official state seal. A famous designer named Louis Comfort Tiffany helped decorate our capitol as one of his last major projects before he died. He designed the floor lamps, sconces and chandeliers. He created the giant 5-ton Angels of Mercy chandelier that hangs from a heavy 101-foot chain in the rotunda. More than half a million visitors come each year — how about you?

title: Where is our U.S. Constitution?
text: In a bomb shelter? That's right! Our actual U.S. Constitution is behind bullet-proof glass in the rotunda of the U.S. Archives in Washington, D.C. Along with the Declaration of Independence and other important documents, our Constitution shares space in a climate-controlled container. Each evening, after visitors leave, the container is lowered into a bomb-proof vault for protection. These precious documents are copied and spoken of all over the world, but the originals live part time in a bomb shelter!

title: Chokecherry or Wild Cherry
text:
Early settlers probably first learned that chokecherries can be used as medicine from the Americans Indians. These people used a bark tea for diarrhea and lung ailments. The settlers added the bark in cough medicines. The fruit can be used to make a delicious wild cherry-flavored jam or jelly. The fruit is sour by itself, which is why the cherries are called chokecherries.

Caution: The leaves and cherry pits are poisonous and can cause difficulty breathing, loss of balance and convulsions.

title: Fun Facts

title: Famous Washington Landmarks and Parklands
text:
The school year is about to end. We’ve had a lot of fun studying things about our state and the people who have lived here. Now it’s time to think about places to go and things to do when summer vacation arrives. Do you have any plans?

In this issue of Washington Studies Weekly, let’s take a look at places to visit in our beautiful state. You don’t have to travel far to have fun. Sometimes the greatest adventure can be in your own your own backyard.

What are your goals (tasks you wish to achieve)? While you are trying to decide, here are some ideas for places to visit and things to do. Jump in and let’s have fun!

Olympic Peninsula

What can you see in this amazing corner of our state? You can enjoy just about everything from beaches carved by stormy seas, jungle-like rain forests to mountain peaks capped with snow.

Walk through the Hoh Rain Forest and step back to dinosaur times as ancient trees tower over you, their barks draped in mosses and lichens. Gigantic ferns stretch their leafy branches in all directions. Take the 3/4th-mile Hall of Mosses Trail and find yourself in a delicious green fantasy land of beautiful forest and undisturbed nature.

Check out the beautiful beaches and walk past the amazing sea stacks that tower above you. Or, squat over pools from low tide waters and see starfish and shells unlike any in the world.

You don’t have to take a tent or camper when you visit the Olympic Peninsula. There are many lodges, hotels, bed-and-breakfast inns, cabins, shows, activities and food of every kind.

Makah Reservation

Don’t leave the Olympic Peninsula without visiting the most northwestern part of the continental United States! Take a walk on the the Cape Flattery trail. You can explore the beautiful coast, watch for many of the birds that live there, or the migratory birds who come by for a short visit. A Makah tribe member will be happy to take you and your family on a nice tour of the land. Stop by the Makah Museum to see some amazing artifacts.

Big City Life

Getting away from it all is fun, but getting into it all can also be an adventure. Our large cities such as Seattle, Bellevue and Tacoma are a delight. All of the history and culture that makes Washington an exciting and pleasant place to live can be found here.

Throughout these cities are museums, restaurants, the waterfront, Pike Place Market, Pioneer Square, the Space Needle, the Woodland Park Zoo, the Seattle Aquarium, the Seattle Art Museum, harbor cruises, boutiques, galleries, Washington State History Museum, charter fishing, boat tours, shops, farmers markets, freshwater marshes and grasslands and lots more!

Grays Harbor

Want to go fishing for tuna? July through October is when many people visit Grays Harbor and rent a deep-sea fishing boat. Most fishers reel in a whopper or two, and you can get it cleaned up and canned for taking home, too. If you’ve never seen a whale in person, this is the place!

You can hop aboard the “Lady Washington,” a replica (copy) of the first sailing ship to explore our coast, and go sailing through an area where millions of birds migrate. You might spot a blue heron, an osprey or other birds in this scenic area.

There are no shortages of beautiful forests in our state. The Quinault Rain Forest is a beautiful place to visit in June through August. The Quinault Ranger District offers free guided tours.

Stretch those legs and take the climb up the 133 iron steps of Washington’s tallest lighthouse. Now over a hundred years old, Grays Harbor lighthouse give a breathtaking view from on top.

Dragon Tracks?

What’s this legend of dragon tracks? According to some ancient legends, an island in Anderson Lake once was home to a dragon. Ask the local folks about 12 dragon tracks in Jefferson County. There’s also a fun “Tracking the Dragon” game that you can participate in.

Lewis and Clark Slept Here!

The Long Beach Peninsula is a beautiful spot where the Columbia empties into the Pacific. Fort Canby stands guard with two lighthouses to warn ships coming from either direction to beware there’s land ahead. The lighthouse on Cape Disappointment is our state’s oldest. Stop at the Lewis and Clark Interpretive Center and learn about their hard but exciting adventure to the Pacific, and their wet three-month stay over the winter of 1805-06.

Volcanoes– Living or Dead?

Washington has five active volcanoes. You can get a good close-up look at two of them. Mount St. Helens is south of Mount Rainier. Take any of the three entrances to this park and learn what happened when the volcano erupted on May 18, 1980, and blew off steam from 2004-2008. Mount Rainier National Park gets you up close to this huge mountain. It is visible from miles around. At the park you’ll see ancient trees, waterfalls, wildflowers and wildlife.

Do you think the nation’s longest beach is at Long Beach Peninsula? If you’re there in August, stick around for the International Kite Festival. You can also visit a kite museum and get a delicious lunch of oysters or other seafood.

Islands as Far as the Eye Can See

Whidbey Island is home to Fort Casey State Park where you can see the remains of the 1890 fort. Or, take a nice walk along the beach and then climb to the top of Admiralty Head lighthouse for a view you’ll never forget. Watch out for the birds! Three migration routes crisscross over Whidbey Island. You can also visit the little towns tucked away on the island and enjoy the quiet visit to the past at their bed and breakfast inns, seaside eateries and galleries.

Most of the more than 400 islands in the San Juan Islands group are part of a national wildlife refuge. San Juan, Orcas and Lopez are good places to visit. You can’t drive there, you have to take the ferry, seaplane or chartered boat or plane. If you go by boat, keep your camera ready. Chances are you’ll see orcas (killer whales), minke whales, porpoises, harbor seals, puffins or sea lions along the way. A large population of bald eagles also lives here. You can swim, bicycle, go kayaking, sleep on a floating bed-and-breakfast or just bask in the sea breeze.

title: Become a Fossil Hunter
text:
Millions of years ago, when water, wind and volcanoes were shaping the Earth, one of Washington's most beautiful areas was formed. Republic and the area surrounding this city is now home to the Stonerose Interpretive Center and the Boot Heel Fossil Site.

This area of our state is very rich in fossils. Fossils are skeletons or outlines of plants and animals preserved intact. The Boot Heel Fossil Site has fossils of insects, flowers, fish and other animals. These life forms lived near Republic millions of years ago.

Fossils tell a very important story. They tell what happened in Washington long before people were here to watch. They also tell stories of the changes that have occurred in the climate and how plants and animals have adjusted to make up for these changes.

If you visit the Stonerose Interpretive Center, you will be allowed to dig for your own fossils. You may bring your own tools, or you can rent some at the dig site. Visitors who dig for fossils are allowed to take up to three fossils home with them. Each fossil must be shown to a worker at the center, however, to make sure that it isn't an unusual fossil. If you happen to uncover a fossil that is of great scientific interest, you will have to leave it at the center so that it can be studied.

While at Stonerose, you will also want to visit the museum, which is filled with fossils that have been found at the Boot Heel Fossil Site. There you will learn more about fossils and the stories they tell.

If you want to know more about what Washington was like before humans arrived, plan a trip to the Stonerose Interpretive Center. You may even get to take a little piece of history home with you.

title: Regions With the Most...
text:
How would you like to visit the parts of our state that are the most (highest, hottest, southern, etc.)? If you do, here’s a checklist of places to visit. How many have you already visited?

Highest place – Mount Rainier at 14,410 feet (climb to the top of Mount Rainier with a stool, stand atop the stool, and YOU would be the highest place in Washington!)

Lowest place – The Pacific Coast.

Coldest place – Mazama (Okanogan County), -48 degrees in Dec. 1968.

Hottest place – Walla Walla County (South-central Washington), 118 degrees on July 1928.

Most Northern place – Our northern border with Canada is our most northern place, unless you sat in a boat on Ross Lake and drifted into Canada — and then YOU would be the northern-most part of Washington!

Most Southern place – Washougal and Cape Horn, two towns on the Columbia River, stand guard over our southern place.

Most Eastern place – The Snake River makes up part of our eastern border. The southeast corner of our state follows the Snake River east towards Idaho a few miles, our most eastern place.

Most Western place – Cape Flattery and nearby Cape Alava are our two most western outposts.

Most Intelligent Class – Yours, because you read Washington Studies Weekly!

title: How did Smallpox Bay get its name?
text:
Smallpox Bay, which is located at San Juan County Park, has a very interesting name. It received its name because of a very sad event: American Indians who caught smallpox tried to get rid of their fevers by diving into the freezing-cold waters.

By the time the European explorers began to colonize the islands, most of the American Indians were dead because of the diseases brought from the Europeans, such as smallpox.

title: Washington's Strangest Creature
text:
Try to guess this most strange of all creatures. It walks about on two legs, but sometimes all fours. It doesn't hibernate, but does prefer to stay in a shelter or den during winter, and will feed at any given time. It has a thick, heavy winter coat during the cold seasons that it sheds when spring returns. It doesn't like temperature extremes, and is happiest in the warm spring or summer sun.

It bears its young in litters of one, sometimes two, rarely more. It eats both meats and vegetables. It is very crafty and sneaky, and is one of the few creatures in Washington that uses tools. It is not typically nocturnal (active at night), although the older species tend to forage for food and seek companions well after darkness has set in. It has assorted skin colors, and the lighter-colored skins tend to darken when exposed to prolonged summer sun. It enjoys water, it lives in communities made up of families, and it is perhaps the smartest living thing in all of Washington.

So, just what is this strange creature? It is the mysterious and amazing Homo sapiens, also known as rug rat, or sugar-slurping-computer-savvy future terror behind the wheel of a suped-up sports car - YOU! ....the most sophisticated wildlife our state has known, and hopefully its greatest friend, too.

title: How Do I Listen to an Oral Presentation?
text:
Listen closely to your classmates when they give presentations. Pay attention. You can learn a lot from them. Your teacher may tell you to take notes. You may also be asked to make written comments. Also, it’s just plain polite to be a good listener!

1. Be an active listener. Don’t daydream. Focus on the speaker’s main idea. Listen for the way he or she ties details to that main idea. Take notes, either in your mind or on paper.

2. Your teacher may help you to evaluate (to examine and judge carefully) your classmates’ presentations. Keep in mind that being honest can help your classmates learn how to give better presentations.

3. You may not agree with everything the speaker says, but you should listen to his or her ideas.

4. Don’t interrupt your classmate unless he or she has asked for you to join in.

5. Think about the speaker’s conclusion. Is it logical?

Try It!

When your classmates give presentations, be a good listener. It will help them feel more comfortable. Make eye contact. Your evaluation will help them improve their future presentations. And you might learn something. Besides, you will want them to listen to you when it is your turn to give an oral presentation.

title: Own Your Own City
text:
How would you like to own your own city? You could be in charge of everything that goes on, who is hired, who is fired, what is built and what is not. You could be in charge of what movies they showed in the theater and get only those you liked, and you could be in charge so that your favorite ice cream store was built right next door to your house. But owning your own city would not be all fun and games.

Aside from having to pay for people to work in the city and take care of it, you’d have to make sure people were paying for their stores, houses and businesses and make sure that everything was running smoothly. You would have to worry about where the money to run your city came from. You would need to be a careful, thrifty manager of resources, such as money, materials or labor. You could not just open your wallet and pay for the people to fix the road that was damaged. You would have to have money. In order to have money, you would have to have a good economy, or way of using resources for capital gain. So how do you raise money for your city and create an economy? Your city economy needs to help move money to do the most good. People will produce things, distribute them and buy them. At each step, taxes can be gathered to help pay for your city’s government and services.

People in your city can sell things. Some places grow crops such as corn, carrots, apples or oranges. Instead of just eating these apples, they sell the apples to other cities, states and even countries. Sometimes, places will trade with another area for something that they need. If one city or state grows an abundance of corn but they are in need of wheat, and another city or state grows a great deal of wheat but is in need of corn, then the two will sometimes trade each other for what they need.

There are other ways to gain an economy, however. You can have industries move into your city. Some industries might make steel or automobiles, or maybe they will be agricultural industries and will grow crops. Some places take one industry and combine it with another in order to produce something completely different. If one industry grew cotton and harvested it, and another made that cotton into a material, then you could sell that to other places, or even start your own clothing industry in the same city! There are so many possibilities.

Another way to make money for your city might be something that does not involve growing or producing anything at all. Tourism is a big part of the economy for many places. People will come to an area, and they’ll spend money in restaurants, gift shops, hotels and tourist attractions. It may seem strange, but that is a way that some economies are run. As long as tourists still want to come, view your city and spend their money, then the economy can survive.

But think about what you want to build your city’s economy on. Several types of problems can come up in an agriculture industry or a tourist industry. The time of the year makes a big difference. Many places are only "tourist traps" during certain times of the year. These places have to hope that they make enough money during the tourist season to survive the rest of the year. The same goes for agricultural industries. Crops grow during a certain period, and so farmers have to either grow other crops during the off-season, or hope they make enough from that one crop to survive.

The economy is something that is very important to all communities. Without an economy, there is no way a city, state or country could survive.

title: Industries of Washington
text:
1. Coastal Region

The coast is abundant in oysters, fish and cranberries. Our state was once a major supplier of lumber to the world and was known for its deep-water harbors and ship building. Tourism is big here with bird watching, fishing, boat rides, whale watching and the many beautiful beaches and historic landmarks.

The northwestern region of Washington contains many forests used for lumber and paper production. Our forests also make beautiful places for people to visit and tour with the national parks that are located in the region.

2. Western Lowlands

The Puget Sound area is a large part of Washington’s industrial development. It holds many commercial and industrial cities such as Seattle, Tacoma and Everett. Seattle does a great deal of exporting and importing with Asia and is a passage to Alaska. It also is the center for making jet aircrafts, missiles and spacecrafts. Salmon, halibut, oyster and crabs, as well as irrigation farming and dairying, are big parts of the food processing industry.

3. Cascade Mountains

The south-central region contains a mixture of all that Washington offers: tourism, beautiful scenery and vineyards for winemaking, among others. There are also three volcanoes located in this region that also draw a great deal of tourists.

The Cascades offer a 400-mile self-guided tour across the mountains. Skiing, snowboarding and hiking are also very big in this region of mountains. There are also fields of tulips and waters full of salmon.

4. Northeastern Highlands

Much of eastern Washington is used for dry farming. Recently, however, many people have started irrigating from the river valleys east of the Cascades. It contains most of Washington’s vineyards for winemaking as well as apples, sweet cherries, pears and wheat. Other crops include corn, onions, potatoes, apricots, grapes and other fruits, nuts and vegetables. Dairy, sheep and poultry are also important.

5. Columbia Plateau

The northeastern part of this region includes the Grand Coulee Dam on the Columbia River, which is a major source of energy for Washington. The Grand Coulee Dam is used to make hydroelectricity, which is energy created from water.

title: What is Economy?
text:
The businesses, jobs and resources in a community make up its economy. Read below to learn more about the way a community’s economy works.

Resources

We live in a world with many resources. A resource is something that can be used. There are three kinds of resources—natural, human and capital.

Natural resources are things from nature like oil, wood and coal. Some of our natural resources will not last forever (like oil), so we must be sure to use them wisely.

Human resources are people—the workers who produce goods and provide services and the people who buy them. People who buy goods and services are called consumers.

A capital resource is money. When someone has an idea for a new business, he or she needs money to get started. Consumers need money to buy the goods and services they need and want.

Using Resources— Four Steps

1. Get the resources. Oil wells have to be dug, and trees have to be cut down. Many business owners borrow money from a bank. What happens when a resource is located far away? It has to be brought to the community by truck, train, ship or plane.

2. Develop the resources. “Developing” means “changing the resources into a form that can be used.” Oil has to be refined so that it is cleaner and safer to use. Trees have to be cut into lumber to be used for building.

3. Distribute the goods and services. Distributing goods and services means delivering them to consumers. Goods can be distributed in the same way that we get resources from far away.

4. Consumers buy the goods and services.

Where are Resources?

The kinds of resources located in a community can change the way people live and work. If you live near oil wells, many people in your city or town may depend on the wells for their jobs. Gasoline may be cheaper there because it doesn’t have to be shipped from far away. In a community that is near a large forest, there may be more buildings made of wood.

Getting, developing and distributing resources can cause noise and pollution in a community. The citizens need to work hard to make sure the air and water stay clean. People who live near resources need to take care of them, and everyone needs to conserve the Earth’s natural resources. That means we should protect them from harm and use them wisely so that we do not run out.

title: Wine-Producing Regions
text:
The Washington Wine Commission often says that Washington offers some of the most pristine water. But the water in Washington is not used only for drinking water. It is also often used in the almost 200 wineries in the state. Wine is a large part of the economy of Washington.

The three major wine-growing appellations - a name used to sell wine that shows that the grapes used are a specific kind - in the eastern part of Washington: the Walla Walla Valley, Yakima Valley and Puget Sound.

The Puget Sound Region is bordered by the Cascade Mountains, Mount Baker and Mount Rainier. It has a wonderful climate that rarely suffers from long, freezing weather in the winter and normally has long, warm summer growing seasons. The weather usually allows for early ripening.

The Walla Walla Appellation - which follows the Walla Walla River Valley and extends down into Oregon - has a long growing season. It also has a great deal of rain, which makes it an excellent area for growing grapes.

The Yakima Valley goes from the Cascade Mountains to the Kiona Hills, over 11,000 acres of vines. The Yakima River and the Roza and Sunnyside canals form an irrigation network that leads to the state’s highest percentage of vines per square mile.

So, as you can see, even in the same state, there can be enough difference in the regions to change how well the economy works.

title: Companies in Space
text:
Sometimes, the best way to do something new is to do it with someone. Many people like to be alone when they do things, but it can often be hard. It is not only people who choose to work together, but also sometimes businesses and companies think that it is a good idea to merge—or become one company by combining more than one.

Two companies that have decided to work as a team are the Boeing Company—which is known for making airliners—and the Northrop Grumman Corporation. They have worked together on designs for exploration vehicles and powerful telescopes. Think about these companies the next time you do a group project!

title: What is industry?
text: An industry is a group of businesses that have something in common. They can be based on what type of product they make or sell, the type of customers who buy from them, and the sort of marketplace they are competing in. You have probably heard of the "food industry" and the "computer industry." They are so named because that is what they produce and sell and whom they compete against.

title: Industrious
text:
If someone asked you if you were industrious, you would probably tell them no. After all, you are nothing like an industry or a business. You don’t make things that other people can use. You don’t work hard to get the things done that you need to be done. You don’t have to be taken care of…. Wait a minute. You do have these traits! These things do happen to you and do need to be done. Being industrious does not necessarily mean you are a building that produces items. It means that you do your work or study without complaint until it is complete.

Businesses and industries have to be industrious to survive. If they want to make money, make good products and keep out the competition, they have to make sure that they are doing the very best that they can do. If you purchase an item from a company and it does not work correctly, you may not ever go back to them. Industries have to make sure they do things right the first time. A business hopes to make money as well as do things well, but sometimes they try to “cut corners” and do things that cost less in order to make money. Sometimes it works, but often times it ruins a business. That is not being industrious.

You can be industrious, too. When your teacher gives you work to do at home or an assignment, make sure you do it without complaining. You should do work in a timely manner and make sure it is done correctly. If you do your work and chores with an industrious attitude, you will find that things go much more easily for you.
