title: Challenges on the Reservation
text:
The mission of The Governor's Office of Indian Affairs in Washington is to “[recognize] the importance of sovereignty, [affirm] the government-to-government relationship and principles identified in the Centennial Accord to promote and enhance tribal self-sufficiency and [serve] to assist the state in developing policies consistent with those principles.” There are 29 recognized tribes in Washington State. These tribes can be found in The Washington State Tribal Directory.

With permission, do some research online to find the list of tribes, as well as their websites. Many tribes are using technology to get information to their tribal members, such as events, help that is available, and jobs. Check it out!

title: Colonies Versus Tribal Homelands
text:
Imagine that you have your own bedroom in which you love to spend time. You decided what color to paint it and how to decorate it. This is your favorite place to study, read and hang out with friends. It has been your special place for as long as you can remember.

One day, you find out that your good friend is visiting from far away and will share your room. You are excited until your friend starts moving your stuff around. Your friend does not ask for permission before moving your bed to the other side of the room. You had put your bed there because you liked the way that you could see the trees through the window in the mornings. Now your friend’s bed has been brought in and placed there! Your bed is now far away from your favorite window on the far side of the room. Your friend needs room for clothes. They take your wardrobe out of your closet and put your clothes under your bed without asking. Now your closet is filled with your friend’s clothing, and yours are getting wrinkled! Finally, your friend moves everything off of your desk because your friend wants a place to study.

“Where am I going to work?” you ask. Your friend suggests that you can work at the kitchen table from now on and hands you a box filled with all the supplies that were taken off your desk. Your friend has taken advantage of your kindness. This makes you feel sad. You offered your friend a place to stay, and now, they have pushed you out of your favorite place in the world without giving you any say in the matter.

This encroachment is how the native tribes felt when the first visitors came to this land. These travelers believed they discovered the land of North and South America. However, more than 90 million indigenous men, women and children had lived here since time immemorial. Longer than humans have been able to record time and historical eras. Each of the nations had their own laws, government and way of life. They had made rules to follow when traveling through another nation’s land. The people of these tribes had taken care of the land for thousands of years. As more people colonized the land, tribes lost more and more of their homelands, or tribal regions, that predate Indian reservations. Our country expanded, but at whose cost?

title: Think and Review
text:
What is encroachment?

What are some of the lifeways of the tribes of your area?

Why do you think more people who were interested in tribal land would bring problems to the Yakama?

What is a treaty?

title: Homeland in the Heart
text:
You have learned that the native tribes in the Americas were subject to the encroachment, or gradual takeover, of their land by European colonists. These colonists came to this land thousands of years after the tribes had been established. Over time, many tribal nations gave much of their lands over in treaties, or written agreements, with settlers. The indigenous men, women and children were moved to smaller areas. They now lived a long way away from their homelands, on reservations.

Even though the tribal people lost their homelands, they did not lose their religions, languages and customs. The traditional ways in which tribal people had lived continued. This was because the people made sure to honor their history. They held on to their traditions and customs they practiced for thousands of years before the colonists forced them from their land. This perseverance and commitment are still apparent in the 29 American Indian nations that endure and live in Washington. These nations have their own tribal sovereignty. This means they have the right to govern themselves.

title: Changes on the Reservation
text:
When they arrived in the northwest, many non-Indians felt that they had more rights than the indigenous peoples. This is apparent in the way in which the tribes were treated. Settlers had little, if any, concern for their traditional ways of life. They were forced and tricked to live in reservations. That land was not in accord, or agreement, with their culture and beliefs.

One example of this is the Treaty with the Blackfeet or the Lame Bull Treaty of 1855. Governor Stevens wanted the Blackfeet to raise cattle. He did not understand the importance of the bison to the Blackfeet. After the treaty was signed, the Blackfeet tribe were given gifts of items that they had never seen. They had no use for these gifts. The Blackfeet agreed to share hunting grounds with neighboring tribes. However, within 10 years, the bison were completely gone. The land was being used for mining, which was against the treaty.

You have read in this issue about the Yakima Indian War that went on for three years. The Yakama fought against the broken terms of their treaty. The Yakama were defeated in 1858. Afterwards, the tribe was forced to live on a reservation. Non-Indian peoples tried to force the Yakama to give up their culture. They wanted the tribe to adapt to the culture of the settlers. This caused many problems for the tribe, including an increase in health problems. The building of roads and railroads through their reservation created even more problems for the Yakama.

Many treaties did not consider the beliefs and ways of life of the tribes who agreed to give away their land. Many Christian missionaries tried to force the native peoples to convert to Christianity. Treaties also often failed to ensure that reservation land was favorable to the tribes’ ways of life.

title: Research Activity
text:
Locate a list of local tribes in your area.

Create a map showing where these tribes were established. Include any geographic markers such as lakes on your map.

Using primary sources, compare and contrast the local tribes. Be sure to verify your sources.

Prepare thoughtful interview questions for one of the local tribes. With your teacher’s help, prepare for an interview. Ask how their tribe felt when white people came. Also, how has the land and environment changed? What beliefs does their tribe hold on to? Ask what a favorite legend is within their family. What other interests do you have in life and culture? What are you curious about?

Create a summary of your learning and a product you can share with the class. Show what you know about a local tribe.

title: Loss of Land and Sovereignty
text:
Some history has not been written down or captured in documents. Some has been passed through oral tradition. It is important to learn and know these oral histories as well. As one member of a tribe said, this is “the way we want it to be told, who we really are and will be tomorrow."

As Americans who study the American Revolution, we are drawn to the story of freedom and independence. We celebrate the outcome of this war with great pride. However, the tribal nations see the American Revolution as a massive destruction of tribal sovereignty. It was an end to freedom for them. It was an end to the way of life they had known since time immemorial.

The American Revolution was not only a war fought for independence, it was also a war for land. Tribes were trying to hang on to their land and to the life they had known. When the Declaration of Independence was written, it became clear to the tribes that they would not be celebrating independence at the end of the war. In fact, the Declaration of Independence actually refers to the American Indians as “merciless Indian savages.” It was obvious what these new Americans thought of them, and how little they cared about their needs, wants, culture or history. The tribes had no rights. They were not able to claim their own homeland. Their lives had been radically changed.

So, where did this perspective come from? Why did this group of people who were fighting hard for their own independence have such little regard for these tribal nations? During the war, these tribes were in survival mode. It was a fight or flight situation for them. They were desperate to find a way to protect both their people and their homelands. At times, they would fight with other tribes. You have to remember, each tribe was a distinct nation. Each nation had its allies, its enemies and its own strategies for survival. Each nation was fighting for its own land, its own culture and was in the mode of self-preservation.

At times during the war, they would side with the British. In survival mode, you side with those who will give you the best chance. Who would give them the best chance of keeping their land and continue to live in a way they were accustomed to? That is who they would side with.

As the American Revolution ended, the fight for independence actually began for the sovereign tribes. The borders were secured for the Americans, French and British who lived there. Treaties were signed with some groups, but those treaties were usually ignored. Some tribes had to move due to their loss of land. For example, the Shawnee of Ohio moved to Missouri. The Iroquois League split in two between New York and Ontario, Canada.

The behaviors of the tribal nations may have looked to some as “savage,” but how were their actions different from those early Americans fighting for their independence, freedom and rights? As the Revolutionary War ended, should it have provided rights and freedom to all in or near the 13 Colonies? Think of other groups whose perspective would have differed and why.

title: Analyzing Perspective
text:
One student sat studying with two letters in front of her. It amazed her how much information could come from two letters in history. One was written by Santana, Chief of the Kiowas and the other a letter to Professor Baird. The two letters had been written in the 1800s. Each gave a different perspective of a time when the tribes were losing their homelands. The letter written by Mr. Hornaday to the Professor was celebrating getting the “largest and finest” bison on the land. He goes on to discuss future plans to get more “skins” and to collect and store them for “future needs.” The mood and voice of this letter were of excitement, and the student didn’t sense any loss within the words.

She then shifted to the words of the Chief. He is looking back at a time when the land belonged to his ancestors. He speaks of the soldiers he now sees on this land. He speaks of their actions: “cut down my timber, they kill my bison” and he then shares that his “heart feels like bursting.” The mood of this letter is certainly different in mood and voice than Mr. Hornaday's.

She connects this analysis to what she had been taught, how the tribes felt a connection with nature and didn’t think anything should be taken from the land that will not be used. The differences in these voices spoke clearly to her, the perspective of these two groups of people were so very different. She wondered, could things have been different?

title: Let's Write
text: Think about the interview you made. Many ideas and beliefs of American Indians are told through legends. Write a legend that shares one of the stories you learned during your interview.

title: Along the Trails Today
text:
If you were to walk the Oregon Trail or Lewis and Clark Trail today, you will see mention of the tribes. One of the sites on the Lewis and Clark Trail is the Camp at Slaughter River. At this site, you will learn the explorers perspective of an event when they found the remains of 100 bison. It speaks of their assumption of how the tribe would have done this.

Of course, you will also find information on Sacagawea. One particular event is mentioned at the Beaverhead Rock site. There is a description of Sacagawea seeing her brother and an excited reunion. It also describes the interaction with Chief Cameahwait, the Shoshone tribe and some trading being done.

At Weippe Prairie, there is a description of a meeting with the Nez Perce nation. It also tells about their stay with this group. It shares an account of a good relationship with the nation and the explorers.

The Oregon Trail is not much different. Though there was a strong presence of tribal nations along the road, the stories of these people are not there. There are now times when the tribal people will come and speak, and share their stories. In the oral traditions that have been passed down for many years, they tell stories of people who were here long before the explorers and the settlers.

The missing pieces along these trails are the stories of those who called this land home. Though the nations are mentioned, their perspective is not shared. It is all told through the eyes and experiences of the explorers and settlers. One has to wonder how adding the voices of the tribal nations would add to the experience. They have a rich history on these lands. They have their own memorials that capture their culture, beliefs and language. To the explorers, this was an unknown wilderness, and they struggled on it. To the tribal nations, this was their homeland.

title: A Different Perspective
text:
One of the best ways to learn about your family history is to sit and listen to the stories that have been passed down through the years. You will find that the most important things are what is carried through generations of time. It is what makes your family unique and special. You may hear in your classrooms about historical events, but if you have a story from your family during that time period, their perspective will be the one you remember.

Tribal Homelands once dotted the Oregon Trail and the Lewis and Clark Trail. Stories from those homelands have been told over and over again, preserving a culture and tradition. They also give a different perspective of things that have occurred in history.

The Nez Perce are American Indians who believe that we are to respect all people and all things. It is a strong belief that people should only take from the land what they need, and nothing more. The Nez Perce signed a treaty in 1855 with the U.S. government. The Nez Perce used to occupy about 17 million acres of land in the northwest in Washington, Oregon, Idaho, Montana and parts of Wyoming. Before the treaty, they were able to roam and migrate from area to area. The treaty reduced the land to 7.5 million acres. Then gold was found on their reservation. The gold was not important to the tribe. They lived off the land, the animals, the birds, the fish and the vegetation. But it was important to others. So, in 1863, the U.S. government set up another meeting and another treaty was signed. The reservation was reduced from 7.5 million acres clear down to 750,000 acres! They lost 90 percent of their land base. Yet, Chief Joseph would say, “The Earth is the mother of all people, and all people should have equal rights upon it.”

Another perspective is about daily life for the Otoe Missouri, who lived along the Platte River in present-day Nebraska. This was not a sedentary tribe. Sometimes in competition for hunting grounds and other times for territory, they would war with another tribe. They lived in earth lodges. When hunting, they may have been in something more like a tipi. Yet, typically, people think of the plains with tipis and bison which was only a part of their lifestyle.

To truly get a clear picture of life in history, we must look through the eyes of all who lived within that time period.

title: A Trying Trade
text:
From 1808 until the 1840s, the fur trade escalated. It brought with it a wealth of new goods, foreign people and strange ideas.

The foreigners had a great demand for the fur. The Plains tribes either couldn’t keep up with demand or chose not to. In 1810, tribes from the Eastern Woodland migrated to the area. The Iroquois, Cree and Chippewa came to take advantage of this competition. This mixed cultures together. The competition brought unrest.

Ideas from the foreigners were very different from what the tribes had always known. They were introduced to new spiritual beliefs. There were marriages occurring between the different groups of people. People built relationships and families. This also brought with it access to wealth in Euro-American goods. New artistic styles and crafts spread among the many tribes.

The mixing of cultures caused both uncertainty and insecurity. Hostility between local tribes and foreign trappers was on the rise. Foreigners were also bringing in horses, guns and deadly disease. It brought changes that they had never seen before. These changes could be seen as both pros and cons. It was both an unsettling time and an exciting time.

title: Think and Review
text:
Why do you think there are such different perspectives in historical accounts? If both groups of people were there, why do they see things so differently?

How do primary sources help us analyze historical accounts?

If you could make changes on either the Lewis and Clark Trail or the Oregon Trail, what would they be, and why?

How do you think life would be different for the tribes today if they never lost land or their rights?

How would you describe life in your area 300 years ago?

title: Native Trappers
text:
As the white men entered, things changed. Hunting and trapping had long been survival tools, but settlers brought trade to North America.

During the time of fur trading, there was a lot of conflict. This happened not only between settlers and American Indians, but between tribes as well. The economy changed, and people were hunting just to sell the furs. The tribes were shocked as hunting increased. Animal populations fell. Some animals even disappeared in some places. By 1830, the beaver was gone from the Rocky Mountain streams.

With fewer beavers to hunt, many trappers looked to sea otters. Sea otters were found in the Northwest. The Chinese were willing to pay high prices for sea otter furs. The prices for the furs were raised by a huge margin. The furs were so desirable that the sea otter was overhunted. They nearly went extinct in the early 1900s.

The voices of the tribes give us a different perspective. They don't always agree with the usual story of what happened. Settlers also brought disease, pollution and destroyed natural habitats. They also introduced alcohol to the tribes. A whole culture was changing.

American Indians have always felt at one with nature and have great respect for it. They work to take care of it. During this time period, the environment around them changed. This affected their way of life greatly. It also interfered with their deep spiritual beliefs.

title: A Way of Life
text:
“My strength is from the fish; my blood is from the fish, from the roots and berries. The fish and game are the essence of my life. I was not brought from a foreign country and did not come here. I was put here by the Creator.”
—Chief Weninock, Yakama, 1915

Hello! My name is Tyee, and I am 12 years old. I am a member of the Chinook tribe. My family and I live with the rest of our tribe along the Columbia River. Our way of life is simple. It is not as bleak as you might think. We work hard. We rely on nature to take care of our needs. As we respect and honor the Earth, she nurtures us and gives us what we need.

I love spending time with my father, grandfather and the other men of our tribe. We hunt, fish, build canoes and make tools. When the work is finished, I also like playing my favorite game with my friends. We use a ball and sticks to play a game a lot like the one you call lacrosse.

The Columbia River is filled with salmon and other tasty fish. We use these fish for food. We also hunt sea creatures from our canoes. On the land, we hunt deer, elk and other animals. Our women gather berries and roots. They also collect clams, shellfish and seaweed for us to eat. The land and the water take good care of us!

Once, my father and uncles made a long trip across the mountains to hunt bison. The men took me with them. We killed bison to help feed our families. We killed only as many bison as we needed. I was taught that we use every part of the animal. We know that the Earth has provided the bison for our use, and not for us to waste. A 2,000-pound bison will give us around 800 pounds of meat. We use the bones and head to make utensils and tools. The bison skin is also very valuable to us. We tan the hide and use it to make robes, moccasins, teepees and clothing.

Because we know that the land takes care of us, we take care of her in return. We do our best to show respect for the Earth and everything in it. We only take what we need and always give thanks for what we receive. You may think that caring for the Earth is a new idea, but we have been doing it since time immemorial.

title: Let's Write
text: When the Northwest tribes were moved onto Indian Reservations, they were told that they would still be able to hunt and fish in their “usual and accustomed” spots. Imagine you are a member of one of the Northwest tribes. Explain your feelings when you find out that you will no longer be allowed to use the waters where your ancestors have fished for salmon since time immemorial.

title: Salmon Harvest
text:
Washington’s location near the ocean, along with the many freshwater rivers, lakes and streams found here, make our state the perfect home for all types of fish and water creatures. As we have learned in our studies this week, salmon fishing is an essential industry here. Take a look at the graph below and answer the questions. You may look back at the articles in this week’s student edition if you need help with some of the questions.

Since 1970, which year were the greatest number of Coho salmon caught in the state? How many were caught that year?

What year were the least number of Coho salmon caught since 1970? How many were caught that year?

Are more Coho or Chinook salmon caught in Washington?

In general, what has happened to the number of salmon caught since 1970?

Which species of salmon are making a comeback in Washington’s waterways?

Why do you think the harvest of salmon has increased or decreased in the state since 1970?

title: The Law of the Land
text:
American Indians commonly take the law of the land very simply. To non-tribal members, the law of the land means the laws passed by the local or national governments to rule the community and nation. To tribal members, the law of the land often means just that: the law of nature or the land on which they live. As long as they've been around, American Indians have lived in harmony with nature and have relied on the earth for their support. More than that, they have also seen themselves as stewards (caretakers) of the land. They built their homes in areas where nature offered them food, water and shelter. They did their best to take care of the plants, animals and waterways in the places where they lived.

Today, many American Indians find themselves in conflict over whether to obey the law of nature or the law of the land. Tribal leaders are working with state and government officials to help make sure that these two very different “laws of the land” are in harmony with each other.

title: Salmon Fisheries
text:
A salmon fishery is a fishing ground or area where fish are caught. Salmon fisheries are critical to the state of Washington, and to the people and tribes who live here. The tribal fisheries bring in more than $3 billion each year! That’s a lot of money! This cash is used to create jobs, pay taxes and bring in tourists. Salmon fishing along the Puget Sound alone brings in around $100 million each year.

Both state and tribal officials manage salmon fisheries. Both groups meet together to make decisions that will benefit those who fish for salmon and the salmon themselves. Many huge projects are now underway to help clean up the water. Improving the salmon habitats means that the fish will continue to thrive. Clean water makes life in the state better for everyone who lives here!

Salmon fisheries are about more than just money. They are also crucial to the way of life and culture of Northwest Indians and non-Indians alike. Salmon are tasty as well as healthy. Salmon have been the basis of the Northwestern Indians’ diet for as long as they've been around. Salmon are also a large part of the culture and beliefs of the tribes in our area.

Even those who don’t like to eat the fish enjoy the experience of fishing for salmon along our beautiful Northwest waterways. Outdoor adventurers come here to hike and fish and to feel nature in a way that can only be done here among our mountains, forests and fisheries.

Salmon fisheries are essential to Washington not just for economic reasons, but for cultural and religious reasons as well.

title: The Salmon
text:
Importance of Salmon to Northwest Tribes

For the Northwest Indians, salmon were, and still are, more than just a source of food. Salmon also play a role in their religion and culture. As part of the Covenant with the Creator, the Northwest tribes depend on salmon for life. They also promise to care for the fish and to help them return in the spring.

Each year, the tribes celebrate the return of the salmon with a unique ceremony. A legend passed down among the Northwest tribes says that before humans were placed on Earth, the Creator asked the plants and animals (who could talk at that time) to give gifts to the humans. Without their help, the pitiful humans would surely die. Salmon stepped forward and said that he would give his flesh to feed the humans. Water spoke up and said that Salmon could live in her. When the humans came, the Creator took the power of speech away from the plants and animals and gave it to the humans. Humans would now speak for nature since it could no longer speak for itself. Today, at special salmon ceremonies, water and salmon are always served first. This honors these two vital elements of nature. It reminds the tribe of its sacred trust to protect and speak up for the salmon.

Boldt Decision of 1974

When the U.S. government first signed treaties with the Northwest tribes, the American Indians gave up much of their land. However, they kept the right to hunt and fish in their “usual and accustomed” spots. Even if these places were no longer part of the reservation, these rights were upheld.

As more settlers came to the area, they told the tribes that they could only fish on the reservation. The settlers wanted all the fish and the money that came with them for themselves. Doing so went against the treaties that had been signed many years before.

In 1974, a U.S. federal judge named George Boldt made a ruling. He said that tribal members had the right to fish in the waterways. It did not matter whether or not they were located on the reservation. The Boldt Decision said that the Indians were entitled to half of the salmon in the rivers. It made them partners with the state of Washington in managing and protecting the salmon.

Acting Hand in Hand

The building of dams, pollution and overfishing caused the number of salmon in the Northwest to drop. By 1999, salmon were nowhere to be found in around 40 percent of areas where they once thrived. If something didn’t change soon, the salmon might become extinct.

In 1999, the Salmon Recovery Fund was created by the Washington State Congress. It gave money to help restore salmon habitats.

Later, the Salmon Recovery Act of 2005 was adopted. This law helps bring salmon and bull trout back to the Snohomish Basin. Then in 2008, the Columbia Basin Fish Accords were signed. These accords, or agreements, were made between several tribes and the U.S. government. The accords brought the federal and state government, along with the tribes, together to work for salmon recovery. The accords gave more than $900 million to bring the salmon back to life.

Salmon still struggle in the Northwest. Their numbers are increasing in our waterways. With many different groups working together, the future of our salmon looks brighter than it has in years.

title: Covenant with the Creator
text:
The feelings that American Indians have for the Earth are more than just the enjoyment of a beautiful sunset. They don't just hope that their favorite fishing spot won’t be disturbed by ATV trails. Tribes from all over North America believe that they were placed on the Earth by an all-powerful Creator. They believe that their people have been on the Earth forever. Or, as they like to say, since time immemorial.

They believe the Creator has given them a great gift. Tribal members believe that they have a sacred trust to care for the Earth. The natural resources found here are to be treated with respect. This sacred trust is often called the Covenant with the Creator. Some tribes have other names for this trust, but the meaning is the same. A covenant is a sacred promise between two people or groups. In this case, it is the American Indians' covenant, or promise, to take care of the land they have been given. In return, the Creator promises that the land will always provide for their needs.

The Covenant with the Creator helps us to understand the idea of sovereignty. Tribes rely on the land and are responsible for it. Their ancestors made this covenant with the Creator at the beginning of time. They still consider themselves to be bound by it today.

title: Boldt II
text:
In 1974, Judge George Boldt made the Boldt Decision. It said that the Northwest tribes had the right to fish on the rivers and waterways across the state, whether or not they were located on Indian reservations. It also said that the Indians had the right to protect the salmon’s habitat so that the fish would be preserved for generations to come.

In 2007, another case was brought before the courts. This case said that the state of Washington was breaking the law by not protecting the salmon’s habitat. The state had built more than 800 culverts (pipes) to carry water under roads and highways. These culverts often keep the fish from passing through. If the fish can’t swim through the culverts, they can’t live in their natural habitats or make their way to their spawning grounds.

Judge Ricardo Martinez ruled that the state of Washington was breaking the Boldt Decision. It wasn’t protecting the salmon and their natural habitat. He ordered the tribes and the state to work together to find a way to solve the problem. By 2013, they still hadn’t been able to agree on what should be done to restore the salmon’s habitat.

In 2013, Judge Martinez told the state of Washington that it had 17 years to fix or replace around 800 culverts along its waterways. The state believed that this ruling was unfair because it would cost too much money to fix all the pipes. The state also said that fixing the pipes wouldn't make much difference in the salmon habitat. They said there are other things that block the waterways as well.

The state decided to appeal the case (ask for a new trial). In May of 2017, the U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said “no” to the appeal and ordered the state to finish fixing the culverts. It will cost Washington around $1.88 billion to fix or replace the culverts. Hopefully, the project will help bring the salmon back to life.

title: Think and Review
text:
Explain what is meant by the Covenant with the Creator.

Why did Coyote steal fire from the Fire Beings?

Explain the Boldt Decision of 1974. What effect did this decision have on the Northwest tribes?

According to tribal legends, why are salmon so important to the American Indians and their way of life?

title: Earth’s Elements
text:
According to American Indian beliefs, earth, water, air and fire, the four elements of nature, all work together to provide for Earth’s creatures. The Northwest has plenty of these elements needed to sustain life. Earth is the symbol of stability. It nurtures and cares for all forms of life. Water is the great purifier. It heals, cleanses and restores. Air is the breath of life. It carries the spirit of nature. It is the symbol of language and song. Fire symbolizes both creation and destruction. It must be cared for and nurtured, or it will burn itself out.

How Coyote Stole Fire: An American Indian Legend

Coyote felt sorry for the humans. They had no fur to keep them warm. He decided to help the humans by stealing Fire. The Fire Beings lived on the top of a high mountain, guarding Fire and keeping it for themselves.

One night, Coyote stole a chunk of Fire and ran away with it in his mouth. A Fire Being snatched at Coyote, bleaching the end of his long tail white. Coyote tossed Fire to Squirrel just in time. Fire was so hot that it curled the end of squirrel’s tail. As the Fire Beings approached, Squirrel flung Fire to Chipmunk. A Fire Being grabbed at Chipmunk, leaving a wide scratch down the middle of his back. Chipmunk threw Fire to Frog, who hopped away until a Fire Being grabbed at his tail. The tail snapped off, and Frog tossed Fire to Wood, who swallowed it, quick as a wink. The Fire Beings tried and tried to get Fire out of Wood, but it was impossible. They gave up and returned to their mountaintop.

Coyote showed the humans how to get Fire out of Wood by rubbing two dry sticks together. Since that day, humans have had Fire to warm and cheer them.

title: Welcome to Washington Community Studies Weekly!
text:
Welcome to Washington Community Studies Weekly! This year, we will be learning about the great state of Washington and about our own local communities. We will be learning all about social studies, or the study of people, their history, their government, where they live and how they get along. We will find out what it means to be a part of a community and what we must do to be good citizens.

As part of our social studies lessons, we will learn about the history, geography, economics, government and culture of Washington. We will also study famous Americans, as well as famous people from our state, and learn how their efforts have improved our lives and shown good citizenship and values.

In this week's issue, we will learn more about what social studies is, why we study it and how Community Studies Weekly can help you learn more about your community, Washington, America and the world. Turn the page to find out more about what's in store for you this year from Community Studies Weekly and hang on for the ride of your life!

title: Philanthropy and Values
text:
Maybe you have heard the word "philanthropy" before. What does it mean? It describes actions that people make for the good of other people. What is a value? It's a way of behaving that people believe is good - like believing it's good to be honest. Is honesty one of your values?

One way you can practice philanthropy today is to help yourself and others learn good values. How do you learn good values? You can learn them from your parents and grandparents, your teachers at school or church and other people you trust.

You can also learn them from people that have been recognized for doing good things for society. An easy way to learn about people that have done good things is to visit values.com. Values.com has lots of stories and short videos that highlight the traits that make each of us better people. They even have billboards on the highway to remind you about good values.

For example, you may have seen a billboard that looks like the one shown here.

This billboard is about Oral Lee Brown, who saved money from her job to send 19 kids to college... all by herself! Wow! Isn't that cool? You can learn about lots of other people who practice philanthropy at values.com. Be sure to look for more of their "billboards" on Page 4 of Studies Weekly this year. We think they're so cool we want to remind you to check them out!

title: Community Members Have Things in Common
text:
The state of Washington is made up of hundreds of communities. A community is a group of any size whose members share certain things. For example, community members share the same location, which means that they live in or near the same place. Community members also share the same government, the same schools, the same parks, and often, the same history. Because community members live, work and play together each day, they build common memories. These common memories link members of a community together and help them to see the world in a similar way.

Studying Our Communities

This year, we will be studying the history of your community as part of our social studies units. Social studies is the study of history, geography, economics and civics. We will organize our studies this year in the following way:

Geography

Geography is the study of the Earth and its features, such as lakes, rivers, mountains and deserts. The first few weeks of Community Studies Weekly will focus on the geography of the land on which we live.

History

History is the story of our past, including our ancestors (those who came before us), our country and the changes that have brought us from where we were to where we are today. Community Studies Weekly will spend several weeks studying the history of our world, nation, state and communities.

Economics

Economics is the study of how things are made, bought, sold and used. We will discover how our communities provide for the needs of others, yet depend on others to provide for our needs as well.

Civics

Civics is the study of government and of how citizens get along with each other in a group. We will learn how our governments are organized, what it means to be a good citizen and how we can make our community a better place to live.

Our Washington History Brings Us Together

All of us living in Washington share an exciting and interesting history that stretches back hundreds of years. Our history includes all of the people who have called Washington their home, from the very first American Indians, to the early French and British settlers, to the hard-working farmers, pioneers and factory owners, to the business and technology heroes of our day. All of these people and events have left their mark on our state, and our goal this year is to learn about who they are and what they did to help build our great state of Washington.

United States Citizens Share Important Traditions and Beliefs

As citizens of the same country, we are members of an even larger community. Americans share many important traditions and beliefs. (A tradition is a custom or belief that is passed down from parents to children.)

As United States citizens, we are joined together by our belief in freedom, our respect for the founding fathers, our understanding of what our flag represents, our belief that all men and women are created equal and many more beliefs and ideas.

Celebrations Help Us Remember the Past

We also share in the celebrations that we hold each year to remind us of our American values. We will look at many of these celebrations and how they help us to pass the memories (things we remember) of one generation on to the next and make certain that we don't forget our past. We join together each year to celebrate Thanksgiving, the Fourth of July, Veterans' Day, Memorial Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day and many other occasions. These celebrations bring us together as members of a larger community and keep our important memories alive.

During our studies this year, we will explore what it means to be a member of a community. We will also find out more about Washington, what it was like in the past, what it is like today and what it may be like in the future. Join us for an unforgettable experience!

title: Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
text:
Here in the United States, we think of our own individual family unit of parents and children as our "family" and of our extended family members as "relatives." If you lived in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, your "family unit" would be much larger. In that country, "family" means parents, children, grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins!

In Riyadh, the extended family plays a very important role in the lives of young people. It even helps to choose whom a young person will marry and what his or her life will be like. In the past, the families of the bride and groom always arranged marriages in Riyadh. These arranged marriages still take place in Riyadh, but young people are now beginning to have more input in the choice of whom they wish to marry.

In Riyadh, women usually live with their parents until they get married. Men usually move out and start their own household when they get married. However, at least one son stays and lives with his parents to take care of them as they get older. If this son gets married, his wife and children will live with the husband's parents as well.

Large family groups are very important to the people of Riyadh, and they play a huge role in the lives of the young people as they grow up.

title: World Communities
text:
In each issue of Community Studies Weekly, we will visit cities and communities all over the world. On our journey, we will make stops in Europe, South America, Africa, Asia, and several places in between.

As we explore different world communities, we will discover that some things with which we are familiar here at home are pretty much the same everywhere we travel. We will also learn about things in other communities that are very different from what we are used to.

We will find out why people chose to build their communities where they did, what businesses help the community to survive, how the citizens of the community live, and what problems these communities face.

In addition, we will discover how modern inventions make it possible for communities all over the world to stay connected to each other. We will also learn how events in one community can influence communities half a world away.

Keep an eye on the World Communities column in each issue to learn more about places you may have heard of, and some you haven't! You may be surprised to learn that communities all over the world share many of your community's strengths, weaknesses, and challenges.

title: Dick Scobee
text:
In each issue of Washington Community Studies Weekly, we will be spotlighting a famous citizen from our state who has improved our lives in some way. This week, we will learn about astronaut Francis R. "Dick" Scobee.

Dick Scobee was born in Cle Elum, Washington, in 1939. Scobee joined the Air Force and became an airplane mechanic. He wanted to fly, however, so he took night classes and earned his college degree so that he could enter the Air Force pilot training program.

Eventually, Dick Scobee joined the NASA space program and served as the pilot of the fifth orbital flight of the space shuttle Challenger. During this seven-day mission, the crew proved that it was possible to use the shuttle to repair satellites already orbiting (circling) the Earth.

On Jan. 28, 1986, Dick Scobee and six other astronauts died when the Challenger exploded only 73 seconds after it was launched at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The shuttle exploded when one of the rocket boosters leaked and exploded.

Dick Scobee's courageous contributions to the space program make him one of our great Washington citizens and a hero.

title: Roman Aqueducts
text:
In Community Studies Weekly, you will learn more about great inventions and technology that have improved our lives in some way. In this week's issue, let's look at an ancient but interesting invention we know as the Roman Aqueducts.

Whenever a large group of people lives together, it needs a good water supply for drinking, washing and cleaning. Hundreds of years ago, most people lived in small villages where they were responsible for getting their own water from wells, springs or streams. In ancient Rome, however, the people knew that a large city needed a better way to get water. They tried many ideas and finally settled on a very creative way to move water: They used a system of aqueducts, or huge ditches to carry water from where it was available to where the people of the city could use it.

These large aqueducts were built both under and above ground and were made to slope downhill so that gravity would carry the water from a lake or river down to the city below. The water was often carried in pipes made from lead or terra cotta (baked clay), and the people living in the city could get water anytime they needed it. Many of these Roman aqueducts were built as early as 312 B.C. (more than 2,300 years ago) and are still being used today.

The invention of the aqueduct made it possible for people to live in large groups and still get the water they needed each day.

title: Anne Hutchinson
text:
We will also use Community Studies Weekly to study the biography, or life story, of an important American who has made a difference in the world. Anne Hutchinson is this week's American hero.

A strong, yet gentle, woman, Anne came to America in 1634. She left her home in England and settled at the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Anne held religious meetings in her home and taught some ideas that others didn't like. She told listeners that people were saved by the grace of God, rather than by any of their own good works. This idea upset the Puritan leaders in New England and made them angry. They believed that Anne was trying to destroy the religious beliefs, as well as the governing laws, of the community.

In 1637, Anne was put on trial by the General Court of Massachusetts. Governor John Winthrop and the rest of the court found Anne guilty of disobeying the Puritan ministers, and she was sent away from the colony. Anne and her family moved to what is now known as Portsmouth, Rhode Island, and later to Long Island, New York, where she and her family were killed in an American Indian attack on the settlement.

Anne is an example of individual courage. She stood up for her rights to follow her own religious beliefs no matter what those in the government thought of them. She knew that everyone has the right to believe what he or she wants and refused to back down from that belief.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: Choose one article from this week’s magazine and look for the nouns and verbs in each sentence. Circle or highlight the nouns in yellow and the verbs in green.

title: How Do We Get There From Here?
text:
Have you ever been on a long car trip with your family? How did your parents know what direction to go and what roads to take to get to where you were going? When people plan to drive long distances, or to new places, they use a map. A map helps them plan what route to take. A map can also show things to see along the way, or places to stop for food, gasoline and rest.

Maps come in all sizes and shapes. Flat maps show streets, cities and countries. Globes teach us about the shape of our world and on what part of the Earth everybody lives. Charts and graphs are like maps. They give us a lot of information about what goes on in places around the world. Who eats the most chocolate? How much money do people spend on video games? What direction does the wind blow in the northern Atlantic? What landforms are there in Australia? Maps, globes, charts and graphs help us to get a better picture of our world. These valuable tools make it easier for us to understand our community, our state, our nation and our world.

In this issue, we will learn about the maps, globes and other special tools that make studying our world easier. We will see how they are used to learn about history, geography and social studies.

title: Thank You, Mr. President!
text:
Helping others is a great way to make a difference in your community. It also makes you feel good! Do you know that you can earn an award from the president of the United States, just for helping out in your community?

In 2003, President George W. Bush started the President's Council on Service and Civic Participation. Many important business owners, actors, writers and journalists lead this group. They work to recognize kids who help others.

It is possible to earn three separate awards. The bronze award is given for 50-74 hours of community service in one year, the silver award for 75-99 hours of community service and the gold for 100 or more hours. When the award is given, the boy or girl will receive an official President's Volunteer Service Award pin, a certificate of achievement, a note of congratulations from the president of the United States and a letter from the President's Council on Service and Civic Participation. Anyone younger than the age of 14 can win these awards - and that includes you.

Once you start to volunteer, you can also earn the President's Call to Service Award. Kids earn this award after volunteering more than 4,000 hours of service during their lives. Think what a difference that many hours of service could make in your community!

Who can help you achieve this award? A service organization helps you keep track of your volunteer hours and then gives you the award once you have earned it. Some groups that give the award include select schools and churches, the Boy Scouts of America, Big Brothers and Big Sisters, America's Promise and the Girl Scouts of the USA.

If you are interested in earning the President's Service Award, talk to a teacher or club leader about getting involved. They can find out more by visiting https://www.presidentialserviceawards.gov. Any kid, young adult or family can win these awards, so that includes you.

title: Learning All About Maps
text:
In this issue, we will learn about maps and globes and how to use them to find places, measure distances and get important information. When you are finished with the Lesson, you will be ready to make your own map of Washington!

Globes and Maps

You have seen both round globes and flat maps of the world. What is the difference between the two? Both a round globe and a flat map of the world show the same cities, countries, oceans and landforms, but they are useful in different ways.

A globe is a round map of the world. A globe shows the Earth in its round form, just as it is in real life, only smaller. By using a globe, you can see how the Earth rotates, or turns, and where each country is in relation to other countries.

A flat map shows the same cities, countries, oceans and landforms as a globe, but it allows us to see the entire world all at once, rather than in pieces as with a globe. You can only see one side of a globe at a time, but when the globe is flattened out into a map, you can see everything all at one time.

Parts of a Map

Maps include more than just countries, cities, oceans and landforms. Maps also include many special tools that help you to find what you are looking for. Each map has a title at the top. The title of a map tells what location, or place, the map shows. Some maps that you may be using this year will be titled Map of the World, United States of America, Landforms of the United States or Map of Washington.

Compass Rose

All maps have a compass rose, or a drawing showing the directions on the map. The compass rose always shows the cardinal directions, which are north, south, east and west. North is always at the top of the compass rose, east is on the right, south is at the bottom and west is on the left.

The compass rose also shows something called the intermediate directions. Intermediate directions are the directions directly between the cardinal directions. The intermediate directions are northeast, southeast, southwest and northwest. By looking at the compass rose, you can find out exactly where each item on the map is located.

Legend

The legend of the map is a key that lists all of the symbols on a map. These symbols stand for things such as the streets, rivers, monuments, parks, buildings, capital cities and schools. The legend of the map helps you to know what each symbol on the map means.

Scale

Another tool used on a map is a scale. A map's scale shows the distance represented on the map. One inch on the map will be equal to an actual distance in miles. For example, an inch on the map may be equal to 1,000 real miles.

Grid System

Some maps use a grid system, or a system of numbered and lettered lines, to help you find places more easily. On a map that uses a grid system, there will be letters such as A, B, C, etc., running across the top of the map and numbers such as 1, 2, 3, etc., running down the side of the map. If you know that a certain city is located at point 2A on the map, you can find it easily using the grid system of the map.

In our study of history, geography and social studies this year, we will be using maps to help us find out where things are and how they relate to each other.

title: Strasbourg, France
text:
Strasbourg has been called the "City of Roads that Cross" because of its location in Europe. Located near the Rhine River, Strasbourg is a city where many major roads join. These roads link cities in France and Germany to the rest of Europe.

Because of its location, Strasbourg is a city that joins the eastern and western parts of Europe. In 1949, after World War II had ended, Strasbourg was chosen as the home of the Council of Europe. The job of the Council of Europe was to rebuild Europe after the war and bring all European nations together in peace. Strasbourg has long been known as a city that brings people together.

Although Strasbourg has often been caught in the middle when European countries have had disagreements, it stands today as a symbol of peace and represents the hope that all European countries can live together as friends.

title: Bill Gates
text:
Born in Seattle in 1955, Bill Gates used his computer skills to make himself the richest man in the world.

Gates first began programming computers while attending Lakeside School in North Seattle. He was only 13 years old at the time.

Gates later attended Harvard University, where he continued to develop his own computer software, or programs to make computers do what you want them to. In 1975, Gates started his own computer-software company called Microsoft and quit school to work on his business full time. He and his partner, Paul Allen, worked at creating software that would make computers useful to everyone, right in their own homes.

Microsoft developed a system (called MS-DOS) used to run personal computers. IBM first used this system in 1980, and soon, companies all over the world were using Gates' system to run their computers. At 31, Gates became the youngest person ever to become a billionaire by his own hard work.

Bill Gates still lives in the Seattle area and works to make computers and technology available to people all over the world. He is also very generous, and he and his wife have given away tens of millions of dollars to help other people around the world.

title: The Sextant
text:
The sextant was invented in both America and England at about the same time, around 1730. The sextant is a special gadget used to measure how high the sun or stars are above the horizon. These measurements (also called "readings") are then used to figure out a person's location on Earth. Using the sextant, people have been able to make accurate maps. They've also been able to navigate ships at sea and learn more about the sun, moon, and stars.

The sextant is a triangular frame attached to a telescope and a mirror. The sextant reflects the image of the sun in the mirror, and the user can measure how high in the sky the sun is found. This is a neat way to figure out where on Earth he or she is standing.

The sextant is one of the great inventions that helped early cartographers, or mapmakers, create maps that were more accurate than ever before.

title: John Melish
text:
Born in Scotland in 1771, John Melish moved to America in 1811. He had visited the United States several times and had made notes about his travels, drawing detailed maps of the places he visited. In 1812, Melish published a book called Travels in the United States of America, which included his first maps. These maps started Melish on his career as a famous cartographer, or mapmaker.

After coming to the United States, John Melish began making maps for a living. He was careful to make sure that his maps were of the highest quality. Later American cartographers used his maps as an example, and Melish is known for bringing the standards for American mapmaking to a higher level of accuracy and quality.

John Melish is one of America's great cartographers, and his maps are still collected and treasured by map lovers today.

title: Reason and Logic: Young George Washington, Surveyor and Mapmaker
text:
Most people know about George Washington. He was born in Virginia. He was a general during the American Revolution and our first president. But his earliest jobs, surveyor and cartographer (mapmaker), taught him skills and values he would use for the rest of his life. Using reason and logic to solve problems helped Washington become one of our country's most important leaders.

When Washington grew up, there were few roads or boundaries in much of the land. A surveyor's job was to measure and map the land. He had to make exact measurements for boundaries and physical features. This was a very big responsibility. People needed accurate maps and surveys for traveling and buying land.

At age 17, Washington traveled across the Blue Ridge Mountains to map and survey part of the frontier. He was the surveyor for the whole county, and that was an important job. When he led the Continental Army, it was even more important to have reliable maps. He established the job of Geographer and Surveyor General and appointed a man named Robert Erskine to this position. He gave Washington some information that was very helpful in making reasonable and logical battle plans and decisions.

You can use these same skills to make important decisions. Be sure you have the facts and information you need instead of acting on opinions and emotions. In what areas of your life are reason and logic very important?

title: Exchanging Goods and Services
text:
Think about walking home on a cold winter day. The wind is blowing hard. Just as your house comes into view, it starts to snow. You are freezing! Quickly, you bolt up your front steps. You stomp the snow off your boots as you enter the front door. You walk right to the kitchen and find your dad starting dinner. He asks you to help and gives you a can of tomato soup to open. You complain a little, not sure if your fingers are warm enough yet to move. You find the can opener and open the can. As the can spins around, you start to study it. You think of many questions about the can of soup. What part of the country did it come from? How was it made? At what store was it bought? How did it travel to the food store near your home? Who made the label? All of the sudden, that can of soup becomes more than the main menu of dinner tonight. You realize you are looking at a can of economics.

Economists ask all of these questions every day. Their job is to study the economy. They study the results of manufacturers making and selling goods and services. They study the consumers who buy those goods and services. In the case of the soup, producers make the soup. Your family, as the consumer, buys that good. On the other hand, if you provide a service for someone, such as mowing a neighbor's lawn, then the person paying you becomes the consumer.

Economists have two separate areas of study in economics: macroeconomics and microeconomics. Macroeconomics is the study of the economy as a whole. People who study macroeconomics ask questions about the entire nation and world. One example would be why gasoline prices have risen across the country. Microeconomics is the study of individual consumers and businesses. People who study microeconomics want to know things such as what prices you, as a consumer, would pay for your favorite video game. This year in Studies Weekly, we will be learning much more about our economy. We'll look at the roles of producers and consumers. Can you think of other ways you are a consumer?

title: Mapping Washington
text: Using the basic outline below, make a map of Washington. Label the capital city and the city where you live, and be sure to include a compass rose, legend, scale and simple grid system. Make sure that your compass rose includes both cardinal and intermediate directions. Include your school, park and any other important landmarks using symbols marked on the legend of your map. (You may look back at the map in the Lesson section of the newspaper to help you with this project.)

title: Where in the World Are We?
text:
Where are you right this minute? In your classroom, inside your school building, in a city in Washington? If you had to tell someone where your city is located, what would you say? If you happen to go to school in Olympia, you could say that it is located in Thurston County on the southern tip of the Puget Sound. This would tell the person your relative location, or where your city is located using landmarks. If you wanted to tell someone exactly where your city is located, or even exactly where your school can be found, you could give them your street address. Better yet, you could use the grid system that mapmakers use: longitude and latitude, or an absolute location. For example, Olympia can be found on a map at 47 degrees north latitude and 122 degrees west longitude.

In last week's issue, we learned about grid systems and how they help us find things on a map. In this week's issue, we will learn about latitude and longitude and about how these special lines help us to find any location on the Earth, no matter how large or how small. We will also learn about how the Earth is divided into sections, or hemispheres, and landmasses, or continents. We will use this information to help us find important places throughout the world. Look inside this issue and find out EXACTLY where you are!

title: Ryan’s Well
text:
Ryan Hreljac of Ontario, Canada, says that he is "just a normal boy," but many people think he is extraordinary. A few years ago, Ryan's first grade teacher told the class about children in Africa who were becoming sick from drinking polluted water. She explained that an organization called WaterCan provided wells for communities that could not afford them. Ryan did chores for four months to raise $70 to dig a well for people he had never met.

When Ryan and his mother took the money to WaterCan, they found out that he would actually need $700 to have enough for a well. That didn't stop Ryan. He just did more chores! His family and friends heard about how hard he was working and decided to help. Two newspapers published his story, and soon there was enough money to pay for the well.

Ryan wanted the well to be near a school. The Angolo Primary School in Northern Uganda was chosen as the site for the new well, because the nearest water supply of the school was a swamp three miles away. Two years later, Ryan and his family traveled to Africa to see the well that was named for him and to meet some of the children he had helped.

Ryan is still working and telling other people about the need for clean water. He helped raise $25,000 to buy a drill for Uganda, and today more than 30 communities there have clean water to drink, thanks to Ryan. It's amazing what "just a normal boy" can do!

title: Where in the World is Washington?
text:
Note: You may want to keep a globe or a world atlas (book of maps) handy as you study this week's lesson!

Hemispheres

Hundreds of years ago, mapmakers divided the Earth into sections to make finding places easier. They divided the globe into four hemispheres or sections. One line divides the Earth top to bottom, another around the middle. The line drawn around the middle of the Earth divides the Northern Hemisphere from the Southern Hemisphere like a belt. This line is called the equator. The line that divides the Eastern Hemisphere from the Western Hemisphere is called the prime meridian. This line runs through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, England. (See map.)

As you can see on the map, everything north of the equator is part of the Northern Hemisphere. This includes North America, Europe, most of Asia, northern South America and northern Africa. Everything south of the equator is part of the Southern Hemisphere, which includes Australia, Antarctica, most of South America, and southern Africa.

The Eastern Hemisphere, or everything east of the prime meridian, includes Asia, Africa, Europe and Australia. The Western Hemisphere, or everything west of the prime meridian, is made up of North America and South America, a small part of western Europe and western Africa.

Continents and Oceans

The world is also divided into seven continents, or large landmasses. The seven continents are Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America. Each of these continents is marked on the map.

On the map, you will see there are five major oceans: the Atlantic Ocean, the Indian Ocean, the Pacific Ocean, the Southern Ocean and the Arctic Ocean.

Using Latitude and Longitude to Divide the Earth

Now that we know how the world is divided and named, how can we pinpoint our location? Mapmakers decided to cover their maps with a series of numbered lines running up and down (north and south) and across (east and west). The lines that run across the globe are called parallels of latitude. (We usually just say "latitude.") The lines that run up and down the earth from north to south are called meridians of longitude. (We usually just say "longitude.") Think of the lines of longitude as being long enough (as in "long-itude") to stretch from the North Pole to the South Pole.

Each line of latitude and longitude has a number. Look at the world map and notice how the lines are labeled. The equator is 0 degrees latitude, and the prime meridian is 0 degrees longitude. The numbers on the latitude lines increase as you look both north and south. The numbers on the longitude lines increase as they go east and west.

To find a location on a map, all you need to know are the latitude and longitude numbers. Latitude numbers are always listed first, followed by longitude numbers. Can you find our nation's capital, Washington, D.C., at 38 degrees N 77 degrees W? (Use the compass rose to make sure that you are looking in the correct direction when finding north, south, east and west.) Using latitude and longitude numbers, you can find any place in the world!

title: Mexico City, Mexico
text:
Mexico City is one of the world's largest cities, with a population of about 20 million people. It is the capital of Mexico and is located in the center of that country.

Families living in Mexico City enjoy the hustle and bustle of a large city, but living with so many other people also brings problems such as pollution, or dirt and chemicals in the air.

Hundreds of factories and millions of cars, trucks, and buses pollute Mexico City's air every day. Families living there have learned to change the way they do things. If you lived in Mexico City, you would have to stay home from school on certain days during the winter because the air pollution was so bad. You would have to play indoors rather than outdoors until the air improved.

Families also have to plan their trips carefully because the city has special rules about which days families can use their cars. The government also encourages families to use the subway or to ride special low-pollution buses.

Mexico City is a fun and interesting place to live, but living there can be difficult because of the huge population, crowded streets and shops, and bad pollution. These problems are being worked on all the time, and one day, Mexico City hopes to become a better place to live.

title: The Randstad (Netherlands)
text:
There is a place in the Netherlands (Holland) called the Randstad. This isn't a city or community, but a huge, crowded metropolis in the heart of the Netherlands that is made up of that country's largest cities - Amsterdam, Den Haag, Rotterdam, and Utrecht. The population in this little area has grown to more than 7 million people. "Randstad" actually means "the Ring City," because these cities form a ring. In the middle of the ring is a beautiful area of farms and green valleys that is called Greenheart. However, there isn't much green left in Greenheart thanks to the growing cities. As you can imagine, with so many people living and working in this little area, there are many problems to deal with. It is difficult for anybody to find a comfortable place to live that isn't already a home for several others. The roads are crowded, terrible traffic jams occur daily, there is too little space for recreation, and there is a lot of pollution of the water, air, and soil.

The problem of too many people living in too small of an area is a big one for the people of the Randstad. Here in the United States, we solve our space problems by spreading out. In the Netherlands, the people don't have that option. They would have to move into the ocean! Overcrowding is a problem that people are working to solve.

title: Smohalla
text:
Smohalla was an American Indian prophet and chief of the Wanapum Tribe. Smohalla was born around 1815 and lived with his tribe in the Columbia River Valley of Washington. His followers, known as the Dreamers, considered him a prophet who spoke for God. He preached a religion of peace and of returning to ancient values that his people once followed.

Smohalla started out as a great warrior and medicine man (spiritual and physical healer) of his tribe. When the U.S. government started moving American Indians to reservations, Smohalla began preaching that the American Indians must return to their former way of life. He told his followers that they must preserve their traditions, their way of life, and their beliefs and that they should reject the influence of the white way of life. This created some difficulty for the U.S. government trying to force the American Indians to reservations, but no war broke out between the government and Smohalla's followers.

Smohalla's belief that the American Indians should hold onto their way of life had a great influence on the Wanapum Tribe and on other American Indians as well. His influence is still felt here in Washington.

title: Global Positioning System (GPS)
text:
GPS, or Global Positioning System, was invented by the United States Department of Defense and has been used since the mid-1980s. GPS is made up of 18 satellites that are orbiting (circling) the Earth in space. These satellites send information to stations on the ground, allowing scientists to take very specific measurements of different locations all over the Earth. With the newest GPS systems, scientists can pinpoint a place on the Earth to the nearest centimeter!

GPS has been used to measure the height of Mount Everest, to track submarines and ships, to follow cars and other vehicles as they travel and to make maps and movies. As GPS equipment becomes more affordable, everyday people all over the world will be able to find out exactly where they are at any given time. Wouldn't that be nice to have if you ever got lost in the woods or in a giant parking lot?

title: John Muir
text:
Do you enjoy nature? John Muir did. He was born in Scotland in 1838, grew up in Wisconsin and came to California in 1868. Muir was surprised and fascinated by the beauty of the California landscape. He was even more surprised that so many of the natural wonders there were being destroyed. So many of the large sequoia and redwood trees were being cut down! Muir decided to work to preserve California's beauty for those who would come later.

Muir persuaded Congress to pass a bill in 1890 that created Yosemite National Park. Muir also started the Sierra Club, a group that shared his goal of preserving the forests and other natural wonders of the Sierra Nevada Mountains. The Sierra Club is now a national organization that tries to help people balance the growth of cities and industry with the goal of protecting as much of nature as possible.

Muir believed that everything in nature was connected and that we must preserve the land in order to be at peace. His efforts have helped to keep America's natural wonders around for us to enjoy today.

title: Using Maps
text: Use the world map included in the Lesson (or a world atlas or globe) to answer the questions. On the world map below, find and label each of the following:

title: All About Borders
text:
Imagine that your family is driving home from a wonderful vacation. As you travel down the road, your mother says, "Keep your eyes open. We're about to cross the border into Washington!"

You watch closely, keeping your eyes on the road, but all you see as you cross the border, or line, between Oregon and Washington is a sign that says, "Welcome to Washington: The Evergreen State." That's it? Where is the state line? The line between the states is clearly marked on all the maps, so why was there nothing more than a sign at the border?

Unless the borders between states are formed by actual geographic land forms, such as rivers or mountain ranges, you can only see these border lines on maps. The borders drawn between states and countries are called political features and are man-made lines showing where different governments take control of the land. Some of the political features that divide the land are state and county lines, city limits, school-district boundaries and voting areas. Sometimes, these lines are drawn where a river runs or a mountain begins, but more often, they are drawn wherever government leaders decide is best.

If you look at a map of the United States, you will notice these political features, marked by lines, but you will see many physical features as well. Physical features are the land forms of the area, such as mountains, rivers, lakes and valleys. These physical features are also marked on maps.

In this week's lesson, we will learn more about the geography of the United States, its boundaries, its regions and its land forms. We will also learn more about where in the United States we can find Washington and where its borders are drawn. Grab a map, and let's get busy!

title: The Regions of the United States
text:
In last week's lesson, we learned about hemispheres, continents, and how to find things on a map. This week, we will find out more about where our communities, state, and nation are located.

Where is the United States Located?

The United States is located in the Northern and Western Hemispheres, on the continent of North America. Look at the map on Page 3 and notice that the country of Canada forms the northern border of the United States and the country of Mexico borders our nation to the south. The United States goes from the Pacific Ocean on the west to the Atlantic Ocean on the east. As the song says, America goes "from sea to shining sea."

Major Landforms of the United States

On the map below, notice that there are several important landforms marked. Let's learn more about them.

Rivers and Lakes

Some of our nation's biggest rivers include the Columbia River, the Mississippi River, the Missouri River and the Rio Grande. See if you can find these large rivers on the map.

Mountain Ranges

The largest mountain ranges in the United States are the Rocky Mountains, the Cascade Range, the Sierra Nevadas and the Appalachian Mountains.

There are other smaller mountain ranges that aren't marked on this map. We will talk about other landforms, such as plains, deserts and valleys in other issues of the newspaper.

Regions of the United States

The United States is divided up into five regions, or areas that share common landforms. A landform is a geological formation, such as a mountain range, a river or a desert. Each of these five regions shares the same types of landforms and climates. Climate is the kind of weather that a place has over a long period.

The five regions of the United States are the Midwest, the Northeast, the Southwest, the Southeast and the West. (These regions are marked for you on the map below.) The land in each of these regions shares certain landforms. Alaska and Hawaii are part of the West region. For example, the Midwest has beautiful, rolling prairies with rich, fertile farmland and warm summers with cool winters. The Southwest, however, is very dry and covered by areas of desert where most plants can't grow. Each region has its own landscape and climate.

Washington's Place in the United States

Washington is part of the Western Region of the United States. Some parts of the West are considered wasteland with very little plant life. Other parts are forested mountains and fertile farm and orchard areas. In the north, irrigated farms produce beautiful crops. Large, fertile valleys lie to the west. Farms in these valleys produce high-quality fruit.

Washington is bordered by Idaho to the east, Canada to the north, the Pacific Ocean to the west and Oregon to the south.

title: Reykjavik, Iceland
text:
Reykjavik is the capital city of Iceland. It is a city with about 200,000 people, and it is found in southwestern Iceland.

Most of the people in Iceland make their money by fishing. Cod, a type of fish, is one of Iceland's biggest exports, or goods sold to other countries.

The city of Reykjavik was built near some natural, underground hot springs. Reykjavik uses this natural hot water in an unusual way: It heats the city's homes, parking lots, and streets with this amazing natural resource!

The hot water is pumped to homes in Reykjavik through a long maze of pipes. The hot water runs under floors and keeps the homes warm and comfortable without the cost or mess of heating them with coal, gas, or electricity. Because the natural hot water is so easy to get, many people even use it to heat the sidewalks in front of their homes and businesses so that the snow will melt off without having to be shoveled. Parking lots all over the city have hot water pipes running under them as well so that they never need to be plowed when it snows.

Reykjavik uses its unusual natural resource, hot water, to conserve power, prevent pollution, and save work!

title: Thea Christiansen Foss
text:
Born in Norway, Thea Christiansen Foss was a young wife and mother in Tacoma during the summer of 1889. Her husband, Andrew Foss, was a carpenter and was away in the valley, building a shed. While sitting on the porch of her houseboat, Thea noticed an angry fisherman coming home from a fishing trip without any fish. She offered to buy his rowboat, and the fisherman sold it to her for $5. Soon, Thea had sold the rowboat for $15 and bought two more boats from unhappy fishermen.

Thea bought several boats, which she then rented out at a cost of 50 cents per day. By the time Andrew returned from his work, bringing his pay of $32, Thea had earned more than $41 renting out boats. Andrew and Thea decided to build rowboats and rent them out to fishermen, duck hunters and workers who needed rowboats to get to their jobs.
