Andrew and Thea quickly built a great business renting out rowboats. They began building and renting other types of boats as well. Foss Marine, the company started by Andrew and Thea, now has more than 1,000 people working for it. It is also the largest tugboat company on the West Coast.

Thea Foss came up with a great idea that provided a service for those in need and made her rich as well.

title: The Compass
text:
No matter where you stand on Earth, you can hold a compass in your hand and it will point toward the North Pole. The Earth has its own special magnetic field that pulls the compass needle, or magnetic pointer, toward the north. As long as you have a compass, you can always tell in which direction you are heading!

The compass was first invented in China more than 1,000 years ago. Chinese scientists found that a special type of iron ore, or rock, always lined itself up in a north-and-south position. They soon began using the ore to make magnets, which they then placed on a piece of a leaf and floated in a bowl of water. They marked the bowl with "north," "south," "east," and "west" and then watched the rock magnet to see which direction it pointed. The Chinese used this type of compass on their ships for hundreds of years to point them in the right direction during their journeys.

Are YOU headed in the right direction? Find a compass and check it out!

title: Benjamin Franklin
text:
Benjamin Franklin was a great inventor, writer, and leading founding father of the United States of America. Ben was born in 1706 in Boston, Massachusetts. He didn't go to school much, but he never stopped learning. Ben read constantly and taught himself algebra, geometry, history, science, navigation, and five foreign languages.

Benjamin Franklin served as a diplomat, or friendly representative, to France for many years. He also signed both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution of the United States. He believed that the United States should be a free nation, and he fought to make sure that it became one.

Ben was also a successful printer and publisher. He enjoyed doing scientific experiments in his free time and discovered many interesting facts about electricity. He invented the lightning rod, the Franklin stove, and bifocal eyeglasses.

"If you would not be forgotten as soon as you are dead and rotten, either write things worth reading, or do things worth the writing." - Benjamin Franklin

title: Historical Bookmarks
text:
Materials

8.5-inch-by-11-inch construction paper

Scissors

Crayons/markers

Pencils

Instructions

Fold a piece of 8.5-by-11-inch construction paper in half the long direction. Draw a famous historical person at the top of the folded piece of paper. Cut around it so that part of the face sticks above the edge of the paper.

Find a book in your library about the famous historical person you have chosen to draw. Look up some interesting facts about the person and choose a few to write on your bookmark.

Open your bookmark so the inside shows. Write the facts about your famous historical person on the inside of your bookmark.

You have a bookmark you can use in all your favorite books with information you can tell your friends and family about!

Extra Activity: You could also make a bookmark of your favorite sport or hobby and write information about that hobby on the inside. Say why you like that hobby or write little notes on any competitions you have won in this hobby. You could also make a bookmark of your favorite animal and then give information about that animal inside the bookmark. Have fun making your bookmarks!

title: Help a Rat and Learn to Run the Country This Year!
text:
Hey, kids! I'm Revere the Rat, but you can call me Rev. I'm your online Studies Weekly friend and I need your help. You can help me get great stuff by earning points while you learn. Just scan the code or go to www.studiesweekly.com and click on my picture.

Has your family ever bought something that came with an owner's manual? Cars, TVs and other things have an owner's manual, a book on how to use them. Your social studies class is the "owner's manual" for the United States of America. You'll learn about history, geography, government by the people, and much more, so you can do a good job of running our country someday.

In America rats can't vote, so "you the people" govern (run) the country. Someday you will be in charge of this country, and you'll choose leaders and representatives by voting. Then you can tell the representatives you help elect how you think the country should be run. In fact, Studies Weekly kids are so smart, that many of you will someday be mayors, senators, governors - maybe even the president!

For now you have two jobs: Learn about the country and how it works and earn points for me so I can get that great stuff I told you about. It's easy. Just scan or click and you're on your way!

title: Money
text:
When the English colonists first came to America, they brought some of the money they used back in England. They called their money shillings, pence and pounds. They soon found out it was of no use to them in the New World. The Native Americans didn’t care for their money. It didn’t mean anything to them. The Native Americans bartered with the colonists. As you can imagine, that became very hard. Therefore, the early colonists of Massachusetts started using wampum. Wampum consisted of purple and white shells. The purple ones were worth twice as much as the white ones. They used it the same way as money. Native Americans had traded wampum with seacoast tribes since the 1640s. Both the colonists and the Native Americans soon used it. This made for less trouble in the colonies. It was used in addition to bartering.

Economists like to say, “Money is what money does.” This was as true for the Native Americans and English colonists as it is for us today. Money has three main functions. First, it must be a way of exchange that people accept. This means that people have to agree on what they will use for money. Second, money must be a measure of value. This means that the people using the money must know how much the money is worth in their community. Last, money must be a store of value.

People should be able to save their money and use it later. Storing value is very hard when bartering. Often the goods or products people are trying to trade go bad before they can find someone in the market for them. For example, milk is hard to keep in hot weather. Bartering milk without a way to keep it cold for a long time would be very tricky.

Money must also be easy to carry. It must be sturdy, easy to recognize, and able to be broken down into smaller parts. Our U.S. money is small. It’s easy to carry and uniform, or all the same. People in the country accept it all over. You can divide it easily. This is nice for everyone because it is so easy. What if you lived in a country that used bowling balls for money? That wouldn’t work very well at all!

title: U.S. Landmarks
text: Below, you will find a map of the United States. Use the list of locations to label the map. (You may use the map included on pages 2 and 3 of the newspaper, or look online to find a map of the United States.)

title: Climate and Our Community
text:
As we have learned in other issues of Community Studies Weekly, the United States is divided into several different regions. All the land in these regions shares things that make it alike in certain ways. Just as the United States is divided into regions, the state of Washington is also divided into regions, or areas that share the same landforms and climates.

The climate of an area is what the weather has been like there over a long period of time. The climate of an area makes a difference as to which plants and animals - including humans - can live there. For example, the northwestern region of the United States is much too cool and wet for growing palm trees, and the southwestern region is much too hot and dry to grow blueberries. Each region of the United States and of Washington has the perfect climate for the plants and animals that live there. Each of these regions, along with its climate, landforms, plants and animals, is called an ecosystem.

In this week's issue, we will look at some of the different ecosystems in our state and how humans use and change these ecosystems in order to meet their needs. Join us for a look at Washington's ecosystems and how they help us enjoy a pleasant life.

title: YOU Can Make a Difference!
text:
In this world where people suffer from earthquakes, floods, wildfires and other natural disasters, it sometimes feels like there is nothing we can do to help. When disasters hit and people are in need, what can YOU do to make a difference? The answer is, plenty! Here is a list of some things that you and your friends can do to help or to raise money for those in need:

Call your local Red Cross or other service organization and ask if you and your friends can help pack boxes or sort items to be sent to disaster victims.

Hold a bake sale at your school. Ask parents to help you make treats to sell.

Organize a neighborhood garage sale. Clean out your room and sell toys, books and clothes you no longer use.

Help your school, club or neighborhood hold a carwash.

Put a large jar filled with small candies in your school office. Let your friends guess how many candies are in the jar, but charge each person $1 to make a guess. The winner gets the jar of candy and the money goes to help disaster victims.

Open a lemonade or hot chocolate stand in your neighborhood.

These are just a few of the ways you can help when a disaster happens. You can probably think of many more. The next time you hear of people in need, talk to your parents and find a way to get involved. You CAN make a difference!

title: Ecosystems: Natural Communities
text:
In earlier issues of Community Studies Weekly, we learned that a community is a group of any size whose members share certain things. The different regions, or ecosystems, of our state can also be called communities, as they share the same climate, plants, animals and landforms. These natural communities make our state interesting and help us get the things we need to survive.

Naming Different Natural Communities

Special words are used to describe how humans have settled the different natural communities of an area.

Wilderness is an area that is protected by the government so that the plants and animals that live there will not be hurt or destroyed. Wilderness areas can sometimes be used for hiking and outdoor adventures, but houses and businesses can't be built here.

Rural areas are natural communities where some humans have chosen to live, but where there are still large amounts of open space and where there aren't many houses, businesses or roads. If you live out in the country, you live in a rural area of Washington.

Suburban areas are communities that are found just outside the city borders of large cities. Most suburban areas are settled by people who have jobs in large cities, but would rather live in a community of houses and stores rather than in the middle of the city, surrounded by businesses, apartment buildings and traffic.

Urban areas are communities that are found in large cities. Urban areas usually have many apartments, businesses, factories, stores, schools, streets and people all located side by side in a small amount of space.

What type of area do you live in? Have you ever visited any other type of community? Where would you like to live, if you had a choice?

How Do Humans Change the Land to Meet Their Needs?

When people first began settling in Washington, all of the land was wilderness. How did the areas change over the years? People changed the land to meet their needs. When people came to settle an area, they needed water to survive. They dug wells and ditches to bring the water to where they needed it. They also needed shelter, so they built houses to keep out the sun, rain and weather.

Soon, people cut down trees and bushes to plant crops, built houses and roads and started stores and factories. When an area needed more workers, people quickly moved in, building more houses and turning the area into an urban community. When people got tired of living in large cities, they moved farther out and created a suburban community especially for houses and schools.

People changed their environments to take care of their needs and their wants. Today, people still choose to live where they can make a living and where they think life will be pleasant. We are still changing our environments to meet our needs.

title: Regions and Climate of Washington
text:
Washington is divided into five regions: the Coast, the Western Lowlands, the Columbia Plateau, the Cascade Mountains and the Okanogan Highlands.

The Coast Region runs the length of Washington's western border with the Pacific Ocean. The coast of Washington runs 157 miles from start to finish.

The Western Lowlands is only about 100 feet above sea level and is found between the Cascade and Olympic Mountains.

The Cascade Mountains average about 8,000 feet tall. Some of the peaks in this mountain range, such as Mt. Rainier, Mount Adams, Mount Baker and Glacier Peak, are more than 10,000 feet tall!

The Columbia Plateau lies east of the Cascade Mountains and is a dry area that is now good farmland, thanks to irrigation systems.

The Okanogan Highlands are found east of the Cascade Mountains and have perfect soil for growing Washington's famous apples.

Most of the people in Washington live near the ocean. In fact, three out of every four Washingtonians live west of the Cascades. About 75 percent of all Washingtonians live in cities, and only 25 percent live on farms or in small towns.

The climate of Washington is much milder in the western part of the state than in the eastern part. Seattle, located in the west, has a winter temperature of only about 41 degrees, but Spokane, in the east, averages a temperature of about 21 degrees in the winter. Summers in the west are mild, but in the east, the temperature has reached a record high of 118 degrees!

title: Rome, Italy
text:
Families have always been important in Rome, and while things have changed over the years, children still hold a special place in Italian family life.

In the past, Roman families had many children. Today, families are much smaller, usually with only one or two children per family. Roman parents today still treat their children with special care. Children in Rome are a part of all celebrations and events. Children go with their parents to restaurants and are allowed to stay up late and play in the piazza, or town square, while their parents visit at outdoor cafes. There are also several beautiful cathedrals, or churches, in Rome.

On warm evenings, parents and children dress up and go out for a passeggiata, or evening walk. They visit with neighbors and friends along the way and enjoy the time spent together.

In Rome, the father of the family is the head of the household and makes most of the decisions about money. The mother is in charge of the children and keeps the home running smoothly. Some of these responsibilities are changing now that more women are working at jobs outside the home, and men and women are starting to share some of the chores at home.

Rome is a wonderful place to grow up, as children are considered precious gifts to be treasured.

title: Vologda, Russia
text:
Vologda, Russia, is an oblast, or region of Russia a lot like a state here in America. Vologda has a cold climate with only about three months of summer weather each year. The winter temperatures often get as low as 42 degrees below zero! The summer temperatures can reach 80 degrees, but the summer weather doesn't last long.

For many years, residents of Vologda raised milk cows and beef cattle. The people of Vologda tried to farm, but the growing season is so short that the people of the area have looked for other ways to make a living.

Today, many people who live in Vologda work for mining and timber companies. Vologda now makes steel and other metal items, fertilizers and even cloth. The area also has one of the largest furniture factories in Russia. This factory makes furniture for schools. The factory builds desks, chairs and items for laboratories and gyms.

The people of Vologda have used their natural resources, such as metal ores and plenty of trees, to help provide for their needs. Although the area may be cold, the people there have still found a way to make a living, in spite of the freezing temperatures.

title: William Boeing
text:
The son of a wealthy Washington lumberman, William Boeing started his own lumber business in 1903. His business was very successful, but William found something he loved much more than wood: airplanes!

Boeing learned to fly in 1914 and was soon sure that he could build a better plane himself. With the help of a friend, George Conrad Westervelt, William designed and built the B and W, a special seaplane, or plane that took off and landed on the ocean.

Soon William started his own company to design and build airplanes. During World War I, the Boeing Airplane Company built planes used by the United States to fight the war. After the war, William's company built a plane that made history by flying from Seattle to Vancouver, starting the first international airmail route.

William soon formed Boeing Air Transport, or BAT. BAT flew all over the world, delivering mail. In addition to Boeing's transportation service, the company also built planes, engines and propellers.

William Boeing took his love of airplanes and used it to create a successful business. He is one of Washington's great businessmen.

title: The Band-Aid
text:
The year was 1920, and Josephine Dickson, the young wife of Earle Dickson, had a problem. She and Earle hadn't been married long. And as she worked hard to take care of the cooking, cleaning and other chores around the house, she couldn't help cutting, scraping and burning her fingers. Each time she hurt herself, she would have to get out the gauze and adhesive tape and try her best to bandage the cut.

Her husband worked for Johnson and Johnson, a company that made gauze and tape. Earle finally came up with the idea of making special bandages for his wife so that she would be able to bandage her wounds more easily. He cut small squares of gauze and placed the squares every couple of inches or so along a long strip of adhesive tape. Then all Josephine had to do when she hurt herself was to cut off a ready-made bandage and stick it on her wound.

Earle told his boss at Johnson and Johnson about his invention, and soon, the company began making and selling the very first Band-Aid brand adhesive bandages. Josephine's problem was solved, and ever since, the world has reached for a Band-Aid whenever a cut appears.

title: Harriet Tubman
text:
Harriet Tubman was one of the most successful "conductors" along the Underground Railroad during the 1800s. The Underground Railroad was a secret system for bringing slaves to freedom in the North.

Harriet was born into slavery in Bucktown, Maryland, in 1820. She escaped in 1849 and spent the rest of her life trying to help other black Americans find freedom. She helped as many as 300 slaves escape to freedom during her years with the Underground Railroad.

After the Civil War, Harriet went back to Auburn, New York, where she worked for better treatment for black Americans. She also worked to get more rights for women and older people. In 1908, Harriet started the Harriet Tubman Home for elderly (older) and homeless blacks.

Harriet Tubman died at the age of 93. She is still remembered for her work helping slaves to freedom.

title: Average Climate of the Continental United States
text: The Continental United States refers to the 48 states that are north of Mexico and south of Canada. This area has a variety of climates. On the map, use the key provided and color each of the climate regions the correct color. Label your state with a star. What type of climate do you have? Have fun learning about the climates of the United States!

title: Redmond
text:
When the first settlers came to Redmond in 1871, the biggest problem they faced was cutting down the trees in the area so that they would have a place to farm. The settlers soon realized that they could make more money by cutting down the trees and selling the lumber, or wood, than they could by farming. Redmond became a bustling city because of the very trees that had made it so hard for the first farmers to settle there. During the 1880s, many lumber and shingle mills opened in Redmond. Loggers, or men who worked cutting down trees, rushed to Redmond. These loggers needed places to live, food to eat and clothes to wear.

Business owners soon came to Redmond and opened hotels, restaurants, saloons and stores. By 1912, Redmond had become an official Washington city. After most of the trees in the area were cut down, the loggers moved on, and Redmond became a farming community. Farmers planted crops and ranchers raised milk cows and chickens. Today, Redmond is no longer a farming city, but is home to many large companies such as Microsoft, AT&T Wireless, Nintendo of America, Honeywell and Eddie Bauer. Redmond is also known for its good schools, its 34 beautiful city parks and its commitment to taking care of the environment.

title: Ancient Stone Tools Help Archaeologists Learn About the Earliest People in North America
text:
How do we learn about ancient peoples in the Americas? There is no time machine we can use to go back and see how they lived. Instead, we learn about how people lived in the past through clues left in the present. Sometimes ancient peoples left clues about how they saw the world in stories passed down to their descendants. They also left behind creations we still use. For example, corn only exists because of ancient American people who bred grasses into a new crop. We can also learn about ancient people through objects they made. Scientists called archeologists search for ancient objects, buildings, or even garbage heaps to learn about how people lived in the past.

Unfortunately, many of the clues disappear over time. Weather often wears away wood tools and buildings. Food decomposes. Clothing usually falls apart. Because stone wears away more slowly, stone clues are easier to find.

Studying stone tools has helped archeologists create theories about ancient Americans. Stone tools over 15,000 years old have been found in North and South America. These tools show people have lived on both continents since before the first cities in the world began. While there are still many questions about how they lived, the careful craftsmanship on their tools shows that ancient Americans used their ingenuity to survive. These early peoples prepared the way for hundreds of nations that developed later all across the Americas.

title: Studying History
text:
When it's time to study social studies each day, do you wonder why you have to spend so much time learning about things that happened many years ago? Studying history helps us to understand the things that are happening in our world every day. Studying history can also keep us from making some of the same mistakes that others before us have made.

Why is It Important to Study History?

History is the study of our past. It is important to study history to understand things that happened long ago. If we know what happened before, and why it happened, we can see how these events brought us to where we are today. As we study history, we learn what people and places were like before we were born. We see how these people and places changed from what they were once like into what we know today.

If we learn about the mistakes that others have made in the past, we can avoid making bad decisions in the future. For example, when we see the way the American Indians were treated by the early settlers, we are able to see the mistakes that were made, and we can learn to treat others fairly. As poet and author George Santayana once said, "Those who do not remember the past are condemned to repeat it."

Eras of History

To make it easier for us to keep track of when different things happened, history has been divided into eras, or periods of time. If we know when different events took place, we can understand how all these events fit together.

When we know that Columbus began the exploration of America during the Era of Exploration, for example, we understand that others were also exploring the earth at the same time.

Once people came to live in America, a new era called the Era of Colonization and Settlement began. To colonize an area means to settle it, or to build towns and cities. If we talk about things that happened during the Era of Colonization, we can see that these events will probably have a lot to do with building houses, getting along with the American Indians, planting crops and making new governments.

By dividing history into eras, it makes it easier for us to understand why things happened as they did and what made people act in certain ways.

title: Words to Live By
text:
Besides dividing history into eras, we also use special words to help us understand when things happened. These special words tell us if something happened millions, thousands, hundreds or even 10 years ago. These words can even help us talk about things that are happening right now!

Prehistoric

When we say that something is "prehistoric," we mean that it was around before people started writing history down. Dinosaurs lived in prehistoric times, which means either that no people were here to write about them or that those who were here didn't know how to write. "Pre" means "before," so "prehistoric" means "before history."

Ancient

"Ancient" means "very old," so when we say that something happened during ancient times, we know that it happened long ago. Many people use the word "ancient" to talk about history before the year A.D. 500.

Modern

The word "modern" is used to talk about things that have happened in the more recent past. Modern history talks about things that happened and people that lived several hundred years ago up to the present.

Contemporary

"Contemporary" means "living or happening at about the same time." You and your friends are contemporaries, which means that you live at the same time. Explorer Henry Hudson and Pocahontas were contemporaries, too, even if they didn't know each other, because they lived at the same time.

Circa

We use the word "circa" when we don't know exactly when something happened. "Circa" means "on or about a certain date." If we know that Betsy Ross made one of the first American flags, but we don't know exactly when she sewed it, we can say that Betsy Ross made the flag circa (or about) 1776.

title: Liverpool, England
text:
Liverpool is found on the River Mersey in western England, near the Irish Sea. During the 1700s, the shipping port at Liverpool was very busy. Ships from Liverpool also carried goods all over the world. Ships from Liverpool even carried slaves from Africa to the West Indies and North America.

When factories first started using machines to create things that people used to make by hand, Liverpool was at the heart of this new way of doing things. People came from all over England to get jobs in the new factories. They also found jobs working in the shipyards, helping to send the products made here to places all over the world.

During the 1800s, business was booming in Liverpool, and the city grew quickly. When World War II started, however, many German airplanes bombed the docks at Liverpool, damaging or destroying them. Many of the docks were rebuilt, but because of changes in the way shipping is done, Liverpool never became the great shipping city that it once was. Many people have lost their jobs, and unemployment is a big problem here. The way business is done has changed and so has the city of Liverpool. By studying the history of Liverpool, we can see how things that happened in the past made the city what it is today.

title: Mother Joseph
text:
When Esther Pariseau was 20 years old, she became a nun in the Catholic Church. When her father brought her to join the other nuns in Montreal, he told them, "I bring you my daughter, Esther, who wishes to dedicate herself to the religious life. She can read, write, figure accurately, sew, cook, spin, and do all manner of housework. She can even do carpentering, handling a hammer and saw as well as her father. She can also plan for others, and she succeeds in anything she undertakes."

Esther’s father knew her well. In 1856, Esther, or Mother Joseph as she was called as a nun, led a group of five missionaries to the Washington area. Mother Joseph was in charge of building 11 hospitals, seven schools, five American Indian schools, and two orphanages. Mother Joseph actually designed these buildings, raised the money to pay for them, and made sure they were built correctly.

She often climbed into the rafters to check that they were safe and bounced on the planks to test their strength. Mother Joseph died of a brain tumor in 1902, but her work is still remembered today. She is often called "The First Architect (building designer) of the Pacific Northwest."

title: The Ballpoint Pen
text:
When the Pilgrims wrote about their lives in America, they didn't have pens like those that we use today. They used pens made from feathers dipped in ink.

Later, people used fountain pens. These pens were messy and ran out of ink often, and their scratchy points made holes in the paper. Many people tried to make a pen that had its own ink stored inside, but the ink in these pens either clogged or leaked out all over.

In 1938, Ladislo and Georg Biro, two brothers from Hungary, came up with an idea to make the ink in a ballpoint pen flow more smoothly. They created a special rough ball at the end of the pen that worked like a sponge, sucking the ink into the point when someone wrote with it.

Other companies, like Papermate and Bic, improved the ballpoint pen and sold it for a price that everyone could afford. Today, most of us write with ballpoint pens, which are cheap, clean and easy to carry.

title: Pocahontas Saves Jamestown
text: Pocahontas, whose American Indian name was Matoaka, was the favorite daughter of Powhatan, a powerful chief of the Virginia Confederacy of Tribes. Captain John Smith, the leader of America's first English colony, wrote in his journal that Pocahontas saved his life. He had been captured by her father's warriors and was to be killed. Pocahontas also brought food to the people of Jamestown at times when they were starving. Pocahontas converted to Christianity and married John Rolfe, an English tobacco planter, who took her to England. "To convert" means "to join another religion." This marriage was the first alliance, or friendship, between the American Indians and the English settlers. Powhatan was happy about his daughter marrying an Englishman, and the king of England breathed much easier knowing he had a powerful ally (friend) such as Powhatan. Many English settlers moved to America because this marriage helped the English and the American Indians get along better. Pocahontas later moved to England and had a son, who moved back to America to raise his family. Pocahontas died in England in 1617.

title: Have a Debate
text:
Have you ever tried to convince someone who disagreed with you that you were right? Did you end up in a big, loud argument? There's a better way. It's called a debate. When you debate someone, you and your opponent both come prepared to discuss each side of an issue. The goal is to try to persuade people who are watching the debate to agree with you. This is a great way to practice the communication skills you'll be using more and more as you grow up.

Everyone in your class can play a part in the debate. First you have to choose a topic. Let's start with something simple. Read the book "The True Story of the Three Little Pigs" by Jon Scieszka. We all know the original story of the three little pigs, but this book gives us a very different version of what happened. Next, select two teams of students to debate this question: "Was the wolf guilty or was he framed?" One team will argue the wolf is guilty. The other will argue he was framed. Both teams need to use some of the techniques from the lesson to convince the audience of their point of view. No yelling or other aggressive behavior is allowed. Students who are not on the teams are the judges. After the debate, the judges talk about which team was most persuasive and why. Then they take a vote. The team with the most votes from the judges is the winning team.

For your next debate, you may want to choose a more serious issue such as school uniforms or an upcoming election in your area. For those topics you'll have to do more research than just reading a fairy tale.

title: People and Events in History
text: On the chart, there are different people and events from history listed down the side. Some of the special words we use to describe history are listed across the top. Find the word that describes the person or event and make an X in the correct box. The first one has been done for you. Good luck!

title: My Favorite Person or Event in History
text: Imagine that you could go visit any person or event in history. Draw a picture of where you would go or who you would visit. Tell why you chose that person or place. Good luck!

title: Let’s Visit Walla Walla!
text:
"Walla Walla" is an American Indian name that means, "many waters." Many American Indian tribes such as the Walla Walla, the Nez Perce, the Cayuse and the Umatilla once lived in the Walla Walla area. They gave the spot this name because of the many rivers and streams here. The famous explorers Lewis and Clark came to Walla Walla in 1805. Soon after their trip ended, fur trappers and traders came here to make money from the many furs that could be trapped in the area.

In 1836, Marcus and Narcissa Whitman came to Walla Walla to start a mission. Their goal was to bring their religion to the American Indians of the valley and to teach them to be Christians. A Christian is someone who believes in Jesus Christ and follows his teachings. The Whitmans built a mission near Walla Walla and worked with the Cayuse Indians for more than 10 years. Their mission was an important stopping place along the Oregon Trail. Many white settlers who were coming west stopped here to rest and spend the night.

As more settlers came to Walla Walla, the Cayuse and other American Indian tribes began to worry. They saw the settlers taking their land, and they didn't understand many of the things that the white people did. The white settlers also brought diseases with them that the American Indians had never seen. White settlers brought the measles to the Cayuse Indians, and more than half of the tribe died from the sickness. Finally, in 1847, the Cayuse Indians attacked the Whitman's mission. They killed both Marcus and Narcissa, as well as 11 others. When the United States government heard about the attack, they quickly made the Oregon Territory part of the United States. They did this to try to protect the white settlers from any more American Indian attacks. Today, a monument and visitors' center have been built on the site where the Whitman Mission once stood. The Whitman Mission National Historic Site is located seven miles west of Walla Walla.

title: Can Facebook Save Dying Languages?
text:
Can you say a few words in Siletz Dee-ni? No? How about saying "hello" in Aka? If you can't, you're not alone! These two languages and 3,500 more could become extinct by the end of this century. Almost 80 percent of the world's population now speaks only one percent of the world's 7,000 languages. This has happened because of globalization. Globalization means that countries are more connected through trade, money and workers. When countries work together, people must be able to communicate with each other. That means many people have to learn another language. English is the main language used throughout the world for business and the Internet.

Why is this a problem? When the last person who is able to speak a particular language dies, some of the knowledge that is found within that language dies with them. A language contains the history of its people, how they used their environment and their beliefs and ideas. Technology may just save many of these languages from extinction! With YouTube, Facebook and other forms of social media, languages that are spoken by even 5 or ten people can be taught to others around the world.

National Geographic has been working on the Enduring Voices Project. Its goals are to record native speakers of endangered languages into talking dictionaries and help communities learn ways to save their languages from extinction. What language do you want to help save?

title: American Indians in Washington
text:
The American Indians who lived in Washington and across America in the early days of this country lived together in tribes, or communities, much the same way we do today. Although each community was different from other communities in some ways, American Indian communities also shared many beliefs, values and ways of living in common. This week, we will look at some of the ways in which Washington tribes were both alike and different.

Water Gives Life

Because Washington is close to the ocean and has many rivers and streams, all of the American Indians living here ate a lot of fish and seafood. Salmon, clams, trout and even whale were important foods for all the Washington American Indian tribes. The Nooksack Indians used salmon for more than half of all the food they ate. The Nooksack people made fishing nets from cedar bark and nettle (a plant with sharp leaves) roots for catching salmon. They used these nets to catch salmon in the nearby rivers. They also traveled to Bellingham Bay to gather other types of seafood.

The Makah Indians also lived on seafood, but they were one of the few tribes to hunt whales. The Makah people made large whaling canoes out of hollowed-out trees and then paddled these canoes out to sea. Once the tribe had killed a whale, the men tied ropes to the whale and pulled it home behind their canoes. The tribe used the whale meat and blubber, or fat, for food throughout the year.

Settlers or Nomads

Some of our Washington American Indian tribes settled in villages and spent most of their time in one place. Other tribes were nomads, which means that they wandered from place to place, looking for food. The Washington tribes that lived in the middle of our state built villages and lived in one place. Tribes such as the Cowlitz and the Nooksack Indians lived in areas where there was plenty of food, so they didn't need to travel to look for more. They went on hunting and fishing trips, but always came back to their villages when the trips were over.

The Washington tribes living in the plains areas of our state had a harder time finding food. The Yakama and Palouse Indians were nomads, traveling from place to place, looking for food. They moved along the rivers, catching salmon. They also followed herds of deer, elk, antelope and mountain goats, searching for meat. In the fall, they gathered nuts, berries and roots. These tribes were always on the move, looking for new places to find food for their families.

Warriors or Peacemakers

Some Washington tribes were peaceful, while others lived for war. The Clallam people often blackened their faces with charcoal and attacked other tribes. They were fierce fighters who used knives and spears to attack their enemies. War was a way of life for the Clallam Indians.

The Nooksack Tribe was a much more peaceful tribe. They often traded with white fur trappers. They were also one of the few Washington tribes that didn't keep slaves.

title: Japanese Families
text:
When a Japanese husband and wife have a child, they stop calling each other by their first names. Instead, they call each other "otousan" (father) or "okaasan" (mother). They do this to show that being a parent is more important than being a husband or a wife.

Japanese parents teach their children that the group they belong to is much more important than each separate person is. The children must always do what is best for the group. Parents and teachers tell the children that they must behave well or it will make their families and their friends look bad.

Japanese children study hard and doing well in school is very important. Children go to school all day and into the evening. They eat lunch together in their classroom and spend part of their school day cleaning the rooms, halls, toilets and yards of the school.

Japanese children are taught to show great respect for their parents and grandparents. Many Japanese families have their grandparents living with them and the family takes care of them in their old age.

Japan is a great place to learn how to work, study and show respect for others.

title: Kenora, Ontario, Canada
text:
Kenora, a beautiful city in Ontario, Canada, was once the home of the Ojibwe Indian Tribe. The Ojibwe people settled here to be near Lake of the Woods, a good source of water and animals that came to drink there.

The first European to come to Kenora was a Frenchman named Jacques de Noyon. In 1688, de Noyon visited Lake of the Woods on a trip into the wilds of what was then an unknown area. He found the Ojibwe people and saw the large amounts of furs and skins they had gathered.

In 1836, the world-famous Hudson's Bay Company built a fur-trading post on the Winnipeg River. This post was later moved to the site of the present city of Kenora in 1860. When the railroad came through Kenora, the town began to grow. Businesses in the area used the railroad to send timber, fur and fish to people in the East.

Today, lumber and fish are still important to the city of Kenora. A large paper company uses the trees in Kenora to make all kinds of paper products. Fishing is also a popular sport in Kenora. People come from all over Canada and the United States to fish in Lake of the Woods. Tourists also come here to hunt, swim, water ski and boat.

The Ojibwe people came to Kenora because of the many furs, skins, fish and trees near Lake of the Woods. Many of the people who live in Kenora today came here for the very same reasons.

title: Chief Seattle
text: The city of Seattle, Washington, takes its name from the great Chief Seattle. When Seattle was still a young man, he became chief of the Suquamish Tribe living in Washington. He had fought many battles against other American Indian tribes and was a great warrior. The Suquamish Tribe loved to trade with the white settlers. When the Hudson's Bay Company built a trading post at Nisqually Prairie in 1832, Chief Seattle was very happy. The white people at the trading post were much more willing to trade with American Indians who shared their religion, so Chief Seattle and many of his tribe were baptized. They became Christians, or people who believed in Jesus Christ and followed his teachings. In 1850, another group of white settlers came to Elliot Bay. Chief Seattle asked an Indian agent (someone who was paid to help the natives and the Americans get along with each other) named Dr. David Maynard to build a store in Alki Point, near where the Suquamish Tribe lived. Dr. Maynard agreed, and out of respect for the chief, he changed the name of the town to Seattle. Later, the United States government moved the Suquamish Indians to a reservation, or an area of land set aside for the American Indians. Even on the reservation, Chief Seattle continued to try to get along with the white people. Chief Seattle was a peacemaker between the whites and the American Indians throughout his life.

title: The Atlatl
text:
"Atlatl" is an Aztec Indian word that means "spear thrower." Before the bow and arrow were invented, early American Indians used the atlatl to help them hunt animals for food. The atlatl was a special spear thrower that let the American Indians throw their spears farther and with more power than they could by using their arms alone.

Historians believe that people have been using the atlatl for more than 40,000 years. The American Indians even used the atlatl as a weapon against the Spanish when they came to the New World in the late 1400s. A spear thrown with an atlatl could pierce the metal armor worn by the Spanish soldiers.

Today, many people have rediscovered the atlatl. They hold competitions to see who can use the atlatl to throw a spear the farthest and who can come closest to hitting the center of a target.

title: Squanto
text:
Kidnapped by Spanish explorers as a young man and sold into slavery in Spain, Squanto managed to escape from slavery and return to his people. When he got back to America, he found that all of his tribe had died from smallpox, so he went to live in a nearby Wampanoag Indian village.

Squanto made friends with the settlers at the Plymouth settlement in Massachusetts and taught them to plant corn and to find and prepare seafood. Without his help, the Pilgrims might easily have starved to death.

Squanto also arranged a treaty, or an agreement, between the settlers and the local American Indians that helped the two groups get along with each other. This treaty remained unbroken for 50 years. Squanto performed many other acts of friendship for the English colonists before he died in 1622.

title: What is a Culture?
text:
The cultures that exist in the United States, Canada and Latin America today took a long time to evolve. They are still growing and changing. But what exactly is a culture? A culture is the combination of the way a specific group of people live, speak and act. The cultures that exist in these countries today developed through a long process of transculturation, or the passing of cultural traits between two or more cultures.

The indigenous people had their own unique cultures when the European settlers arrived. As the Europeans from various countries came over, they too had their own unique cultures. As various cultures blended, they began to evolve into the cultures we are familiar with today.

The ancient civilizations of North, Central and South America were advanced and well established when the Europeans arrived. The Europeans rarely valued the cultures of the native people. They wanted to assimilate the people into their own culture. Assimilation happens when people force other people to become like them. Some Europeans didn’t want to force the native people to be like them. They wanted to move the natives out so they could retain the land as their own and live without the influence of others. These attitudes eventually led to the dominance of the colonists’ culture over the indigenous cultures. But what happened to the other cultures? Did they totally disappear? No, they left their mark on our culture. Parts of the culture of American Indians can be found in the art, music and everyday lives of people everywhere. It isn’t uncommon to find someone with a dream catcher hanging in his or her window or on a car mirror. Many of the foods grown in the Americas were introduced by the natives and have remained a part of the American diet. Even some holidays and festivals can be traced back to indigenous people.

Similarly, since the arrival of the first settlers in the New World, millions more have migrated to these countries. They too have influenced those cultures. The existing cultures in the Americas is very different from the cultures of Great Britain, France and Spain which initially dominated this land. People from Africa, Asia and various parts of Europe have come, and all have contributed to the present culture. These immigrants quickly experienced cultural assimilation, and yet, to this day Scandinavian culture can be found in the names of towns all over the midwestern United States. A whole province of Canada speaks French instead of English. In Latin America, examples of beautiful Spanish and Portuguese architecture still abound.

People take pride in their cultures, or ethnicity. Ethnicity is the common background and history that a group of people share. The countries of the United States, Canada and Latin America have their own very well defined cultures. They also have very pluralistic cultures. Pluralism is when many specific cultures exist within the same country or area. This is what makes all countries such beautiful, rich places to live.

It is important to value the many things that make up the cultures of our countries. It is important to value diversity, as well as be proud of our unique and varied heritage.

title: Kennewick, Pasco, Richland
text:
The cities of Kennewick, Pasco and Richland are often called Washington's Tri-Cities. "Tri" means "three." These three cities were built at the spot where the Snake and Columbia Rivers join. Lewis and Clark, the famous men who first explored the West, came to the Tri-Cities area in 1805 and again in 1806. When Lewis and Clark traveled across the United States, they hardly ever knew exactly where they were. After all, no one had ever traveled that far across the country before! When Lewis and Clark finally got to what is now the Tri-Cities area, they finally recognized the Columbia River and knew exactly where they were.

Kennewick is a native word meaning "winter haven." The town was once an American Indian village where the Chemnapum Indians came to spend their winters. Today, Kennewick is the largest of the Tri-Cities. Kennewick is famous for being the place where a 9,200-year-old human skeleton was discovered. The skeleton was found in Kennewick's Columbia Park and is now called the "Kennewick Man."

Pasco was built near the spot where Lewis and Clark made their first camp in 1805. Today, Sacajawea State Park stands where the group spent time trading with the American Indians living here. Sacajawea was the American Indian woman who came with Lewis and Clark on their journey to help them find their way and to help them get along with any American Indians they might meet.

Richland started as a small farming town. During World War II, the city grew from about 1,500 people to more than 51,000 people when the government built the first nuclear reactor in Richland. The nuclear reactor was built to create weapons that could be used in the war. People came from all over the country to work at the Hanford Site, the place where the reactor was built.

The Tri-Cities of Washington were first explored by Lewis and Clark and later settled by people who found that Washington was a great place to live.

title: Celebrating An American Hero’s Trip Around the Earth
text:
It was 1957 when the Soviet Union launched the first spacecraft into orbit. Americans were shocked! The space race had just begun and we were already behind! In 1961 President John F. Kennedy announced that the U.S. planned to land a man on the moon by the end of the decade. The Russians responded by first launching a dog into orbit, and later two men. The race was on!

On Feb. 20, 1962, a Marine Corps fighter pilot from Ohio stepped up to put his life on the line. John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth. The success of his Mercury mission was one of the first steps to landing a man on the moon in July 1969.

John Glenn served as the U.S. senator from Ohio for 24 years, but he longed to go back into space. In 1998 at the age of 77 he was able to see that dream come true. He traveled on the space shuttle Discovery and became the oldest person to ever go into space! On Feb. 20th, 2012, America celebrated the 50th anniversary of John Glenn's first orbit. Mr. Glenn and the remaining members of the Mercury mission space team were given a hero's welcome at Cape Canaveral in Florida. Because of Mr. Glenn's service to our country as an astronaut and a senator, he has been called an American hero.

title: Explorers in Washington
text:
The first people who explored and settled in America and Washington came here for many different reasons. Some came here looking for gold and other ways to get rich. Others, like the Pilgrims, came here searching for a place to worship God in their own way. Some came to America hoping to find freedom from unfair governments. A few even came here hoping to find good health and a long life. This week, we will look at several different explorers and settlers to discover what they hoped to find when they came to America and Washington.

Christopher Columbus

When Columbus set out on his journey across the ocean, he hoped to find a new way to get to the Far East. If his plan worked, Spain would have a new way to get to China. Sailors could sail west and bring back all kinds of gold, spices and silks to sell in Europe. Columbus didn't realize that North and South America were blocking the way!

Juan Ponce de Leon

Ponce de Leon, a Spanish sailor, was an unusual explorer. He didn't sail west looking for gold, freedom or honor. He came looking for a way to stay young forever. Ponce de Leon had heard legends (stories that may or may not be true) about the Fountain of Youth. The Fountain of Youth was a spring that was supposed to make anyone who drank from it stay young and healthy forever. He explored the Bahamas, searching for this famous spring. Instead of finding the Fountain of Youth, Ponce de Leon became the first European to explore Florida.

Jacques Cartier

Jacques Cartier sailed northwest from France hoping to find a new trade route to Asia. A trade route is a pathway that can be used for traders to bring their goods back and forth. Like Columbus, Cartier wanted to find a new way to get to all the wealth and riches that could be found in China and other Asian countries. Cartier landed near the mouth of the St. Lawrence River. He thought that if he sailed up the river, he would reach the open sea. He hoped to reach Asia by using this waterway. In 1534, Cartier sailed up the St. Lawrence River and found that it never reached the ocean. His plans to sail to China were blocked by the American continent. He never found his trade route, but Cartier claimed Quebec for France.

Early Washington Explorers and Settlers

The Spanish explorers first came to the Washington area looking for gold. When they didn't find any, they left the Northwest alone and began looking for gold in other places.

After Captain George Vancouver explored Washington, a company called the Hudson's Bay Company started building forts in the area. The Hudson Bay Company was a fur-trading company that trapped and traded with the American Indians for fur. The company then took beaver, mink and otter fur back to Europe and made them into hats, coats and other fine clothes. The people who lived in France, England, Holland, Russia and Spain during the 1700s loved fur and were willing to pay a lot of money for clothes made of fur from North America. When Washington became part of the United States, the famous explorers Lewis and Clark came to the Northwest to see what the land here was like. Lewis and Clark told the United States government that the land in Washington was good for farming and that there were many good waterways (rivers and streams that can be used by boats) for fishing and shipping. When Americans heard this, many people loaded up their wagons and headed for the Northwest.

title: Timbuktu, Mali, Africa
text:
Timbuktu is a city in the Western African nation of Mali. You may have heard someone say something like, "Trash is scattered from here to Timbuktu," and wondered exactly what that meant. Timbuktu is in a very out-of-the-way place, far from other large cities. People often use the word "Timbuktu" to describe something that is far away, or out in the middle of nowhere.

Timbuktu wasn't always such an out-of-the-way place. The city of Timbuktu was once the center of learning, wealth and religion in Africa.

The city started in the 1100s as a camp for African nomads, or people who traveled from place to place. Later, as Mali became a rich African kingdom, Timbuktu became an important city for trading gold and salt. People came from all over northern Africa to trade in the wealthy city.

Besides the many traders who came to Timbuktu to do business, many wise men, artists and Muslims came here as well. Timbuktu was a beautiful city with large buildings, interesting people and wonderful places to eat and sleep.

Today, Timbuktu really is near the middle of nowhere. The famous city has crumbled, and its wealth is gone. Small traders still bring their camels, loaded down with salt, to the city to trade, but there is no longer any gold here to trade for. A few brave visitors still make the trip to Timbuktu, hoping to find out more about this city in the middle of nowhere.

title: George Vancouver
text:
George Vancouver was born in England in 1757. George joined the Royal Navy in 1771 and sailed to Hawaii with the famous Captain James Cook. After showing that he was both a good sailor and a good leader, Vancouver was given the job of commander of the ship Discovery. He sailed to Australia, New Zealand, the Hawaiian Islands, San Francisco and Alaska.

In 1791, Vancouver set out to make a map of the northwest coast of America. He was also looking for a Northwest Passage (a way to sail through North America) from Europe to China. Just like other explorers before him, Vancouver found that there was no way to sail through North America to get to China.

Vancouver also proved that Vancouver Island wasn't part of the mainland, but that it was actually an island. Between 1792 and 1794, Vancouver sailed around the island and made a map of the Pacific coastline of British Columbia.

Vancouver was a great explorer whose maps of our coast are still some of the best ever made. More than 50 places in the Pacific Northwest are named after him. Among these places are Vancouver Island; Vancouver, British Columbia and Vancouver, Washington.

title: The Zipper
text:
Most of the world's greatest inventions happened because someone had a problem that needed to be solved. The zipper is one invention created for this very reason.

Whitcomb L. Judson loved machines and gadgets. He spent much time tinkering with new ideas for making life easier.

Whitcomb had a friend with a problem. His friend had a stiff back that made it impossible for him to bend over and use both hands to hook up the hooks on his shoes. Whitcomb set out to solve this problem for his friend.

After working for a few weeks, Whitcomb came up with a special slide fastener that could be opened and closed with just one hand. By 1893, Whitcomb had received a patent, or license from the government giving him and only him the right to make and sell his new invention.

After a few years, other inventors came up with even better "hookless fasteners." Because they were so easy to "zip" up, the fasteners soon became known as zippers. By the 1920s, zippers were used in galoshes (rubber boots), clothing, luggage and bags. Today, the zipper is found on almost everything, from pants to dresses to tents. Whitcomb Judson's invention helped his friend and people everywhere who needed an easy way to open and close almost anything.

title: Cesar Chavez
text:
At the age of 10 years old, Cesar Chavez became a migrant worker when his father lost his farm in Yuma, Arizona. A migrant worker moves from place to place, working in the fields when the crops are ready. Cesar moved to California, working in the fields, orchards and vineyards to earn money for himself and his family. He joined many different groups that tried to help the migrant workers get more money, better houses and shorter working hours.

After years of work, Cesar Chavez started the United Farm Workers of America, the first successful farm workers' union in United States history. A union is a group that works for fair pay, safe places to work and good working hours for men and women working at the same type of job. The union started by Cesar Chavez is still around today and works to make sure that farm workers are treated fairly.

Cesar and his union started strikes against fruit and vegetable growers who refused to give farm workers fair pay, reasonable working hours, and safe places to live. A strike happens when workers refuse to come to work until the owners of the company promise to give them what they are asking for. These strikes made people across the nation aware of the needs of the farm workers and helped to bring important changes to the farm industry.

title: Sharing Public Space: Vitus Bering and Russian Colonies in Alaska
text:
Imagine traveling 6,000 miles over land with supplies for an expedition, and THEN sailing through frigid seas to look for a new world. This was the job given to Vitus Bering, a Danish navigator who sailed for the Russian navy. Peter the Great, czar (ruler) of Russia, asked Bering to explore the eastern coast of Russia. He was wondering if land connected Asia and North America.

Bering's first trip began in 1725. After spending three years getting his supplies to eastern Russia, Bering sailed along the coastline. He didn't see any land to the east, and he didn't realize he was sailing in the narrow passage between Russia and Alaska. This waterway is now called the Bering Strait.

Bering led another expedition in 1741. This time his ship landed on Kayak Island, off the coast of Alaska. They explored some of the Aleutian Islands and met the native people there, the Aleut. He was the first European to arrive in present-day Alaska.

Bering died before returning to Russia, but his voyages paved the way for Russian settlements in North America. Many fur traders came to the area. In 1799 the Russian government established a fur-trading operation in Alaska. Furs from foxes, sea otters and seals were very valuable.

Unfortunately, the Russians took advantage of the native people just as some Europeans had done in settling New England. The Russians took over their lands and forced them to hunt for furs. They also brought new diseases, which killed many natives.

Today, the Aleut people continue to live along the western coast of North America, and their population has grown. What might have been different if the Russians and the Aleut had shared public space fairly? Where in your community is there a debate over public land? How should such debates be handled?

title: Write Three Questions
text: After you read this week’s lesson, write three questions about the article on a piece of paper and trade questions with a friend. Circle or highlight the answers in the lesson. (CC ELA RI.3.1)

title: Vancouver
text:
In 1825, Dr. John McLoughlin (See Our State Heroes) moved the headquarters (main office) of the Hudson' Bay Company to a beautiful spot along the Columbia River. He called his new headquarters Fort Vancouver, after Captain George Vancouver, the man who had explored the area in 1792. Fort Vancouver became the center of all the fur trade in the Oregon and Washington Territory. The fort was a busy place, with fur traders and pioneers coming here every day to buy, sell and trade for furs and supplies. Someone once called Fort Vancouver the "New York of the Pacific" because it was so crowded and full of excitement.

When the Washington Territory became part of the United States, American soldiers came here and built the Vancouver Barracks. The community became the military base for most of the soldiers who came to the Pacific Northwest. In 1857, Vancouver became an official city. The first railroad line came east through the Washington side of the Columbia River Gorge in 1908 and the city began to grow like never before. The railroad made it possible to ship supplies by both land and sea, making Vancouver a great place to build a business. During World War I, Pearson Field was the site of one of the world's largest cut-up mills, or sawmills that cut lumber into smaller pieces. The cut-up mill cut large spruce trees into lumber used to build planes to help fight the war. Later, during World War II, Vancouver's Kaiser Shipyard built ships that helped America fight this war. When visiting Vancouver today, be sure to see the Fort Vancouver National Historic Site, Pearson Field and Officers Row.

title: Early Washington Communities
text:
In 1850, Congress passed the Donation Land Act. This law gave away land for free in the new Oregon Territory to any farm family that would stay and settle a claim for four years. A claim is a chunk of land staked out by a homesteader. This promise of free land brought thousands of people West. Many who came to the Oregon Territory began to settle in the new Washington Territory as well. Let's look at some of the first communities in what would later become the state of Washington. Most of Washington's first settler communities were built in the Puget Sound area. The eastern area took longer to settle. It was inhabited by American Indians and there wasn't as much rain as in the western side of the territory.

Seattle

Seattle was started in 1851 by a group of pioneers called the Denny Party from Illinois. They named the town after Chief Seathl, a Duwamish chief who had been kind to them. The town of Seattle struck it rich during the 1890s when many travelers stopped by on their way to Alaska to search for gold. People passing through Seattle bought pack mules, tents, wool pants, bacon, and many other supplies for the trip to Alaska.

Tacoma

In 1852, a man named Nichalas de Lin built a sawmill on the spot where Tacoma now stands. The sawmill was powered by water from the Puget Sound. Job Carr later made a claim to land in Tacoma and built a log house here. In 1869, a community called Old Town was planned on this spot. The name was later changed to Tacoma, which was close to the American Indian word for Mt. Rainier. Tacoma was nicknamed "City of Destiny" in 1873 when the Northern Pacific Railroad came to the city.

Olympia

Olympia was first settled in 1846 by Edmund Sylvester. He planned the community out very carefully. He made sure that Olympia had a town square, straight streets lined with trees, land for schools, and a spot for a capitol building. Olympia was a shipping town. Many logging and lumber companies used the port of Olympia to send their lumber to other parts of the country. Later, Olympia became the capital of Washington.

Centralia

Centralia was a community built by an African American man named George Washington (named after the first president). Washington was a formerly enslaved man who arrived in the Washington Territory with James and Hannah Cochran, the people who had enslaved him. The Cochrans had a land grant in the Washington Territory, but the government wouldn't give George Washington any land because he was African American. George worked hard as a lumberjack and a farmer. He earned enough money to buy the Cochrans' land and build his own community. He planned a city and sold lots for houses to families who wanted to settle here. Centralia grew into one of the most successful towns in Washington.

Port Townsend

The community of Port Townsend was built on the northern tip of Puget Sound. In 1853, the government customs house (place where people pay the taxes on the items they are shipping) was moved to Port Townsend. All ships that came to Puget Sound had to stop and register here. Because of all the sailors who stopped in Port Townsend, the community became a rough and wild place. Drinking, gambling, and fighting were daily activities in Port Townsend. Many people were afraid to visit because of the famous fights that often broke out in the taverns (bars or saloons) near the sea.

title: Athens, Greece
text:
Athens is a large city in the country of Greece. In Athens, the men are the leaders, both at home and in the government. The most important job of the women is still to take care of the home and raise the children. The men go to work and make money to take care of the family.

After work, Greek men usually meet at their favorite coffee houses to have some refreshments and visit with their friends. The women often get together with their friends as well. They go to church activities, let their children play together, join together to cook a meal or just visit.

Men are in charge of the money in the family. The women are in charge of the home and the children. Many women now have jobs and work outside their homes, but it is still the woman's job to run the household and raise the children. Women also have the right to own land, vote, hold jobs and speak out in public, just like women in the United States.

Athens is a large city with many modern buildings, as well as many ancient ruins.

title: Montreal, Quebec, Canada
text:
The famous French explorer Jacques Cartier arrived in what is now Montreal in 1535. About 100 years later, in May of 1642, the first French settlers came to Montreal. They shot guns to scare away any evil spirits that might already be living here and dedicated the island to the Virgin Mary. They named the spot "Ville-Marie," or the City of Mary. Over the years, Montreal was controlled by France, England and even the United States. Today, Montreal is part of the country of Canada.

Montreal has some neighborhoods in which most people speak French, and some neighborhoods in which most people speak English. There are strict laws about which languages can be used in business, in government and in schools. Many people have very strong feelings about which language should be used.

Today, Montreal is a famous meeting place for people from countries all over the world. Many conventions, or meetings of large groups of people, are held in Montreal each year. The city makes money from its airport, hotels, restaurants, convention centers and shopping malls.

title: John McLoughlin
text:
Dr. John McLoughlin stood six feet, four inches tall and had a full head of white hair. The American Indians called him "The Great White-Headed Eagle." His kindness and hard work helped early pioneers to make the journey on the Oregon Trail. About 200,000 pioneers came West on the Oregon Trail. Grateful pioneers named McLoughlin the "Father of Oregon."

Born in Quebec, Canada, in 1784, John became a doctor at the age of 18. He soon became the doctor for the North West Company, a fur-trading company that sent furs back to Europe. Later, he was made an agent for the Hudson's Bay Company. He chose Fort Vancouver as his headquarters, or main office, and helped many pioneers settle in the area. He also ran a trading post that sold supplies to the pioneers heading West and traded with the American Indians for furs.

John noticed the rich farming soil of the Willamette Valley and talked many pioneers into settling here instead of traveling farther west. He also made friends with the American Indians in the area and they had great respect for "The Great White-Headed Eagle." Dr. McLoughlin became a U.S. citizen in 1849 and died in 1857.

title: The Steamboat
text:
In 1787, John Fitch showed the first working steamboat to a crowd gathered near the Delaware River in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The first steamboat was 45 feet long and was pushed along by a steam engine that turned 12 paddles. When these paddles turned, the boat moved along the river.

In 1807, Robert Fulton created the first steamboat that could carry passengers and freight (a load of goods). His first steamboat, called the Clermont, traveled from New York Harbor, up the Hudson River, to Albany and back. Many people thought the steamboat would fail, and they were surprised when it was a success.

The steamboat made life much easier for people living near the rivers. It could bring people and goods up and down the rivers much more quickly than a wagon could bring them on land. It was also cheaper to travel by steamboat than by wagon. The invention of the steamboat helped Americans settle in new towns all over the country.

title: George Washington
text:
"First in war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen." - Henry Lee

George Washington was born in Westmoreland, Virginia, in 1732. His father died in 1743, and George went to live with his half brother, Lawrence, at Mount Vernon.

George wanted to be a sailor, but became a surveyor (someone who measures and marks the land) instead. After surveying for a short time, George joined the army and became a lieutenant colonel. He was only 22 years old, but he learned quickly and did very well. By 1755, George became a colonel and then the commander-in-chief of the Virginia militia (small army). George decided to quit the army for a while and began serving in the Virginia House of Burgesses.

When the Revolutionary War started, George was chosen as the commander-in-chief of the Continental Army. He was a great leader and helped the United States win its independence from England. His men loved him and respected him for his honesty and his leadership skills.

After the war ended, George served as president of the convention that wrote the U.S. Constitution, the paper that tells how our country should be run. He was later elected as the first president of the United States. Because he was our first president, he is often called "The Father of Our Country."

title: The Job of a Museum Director: ‘A Little Bit of Everything’
text:
The Campbell House Museum is beautiful Civil War-era home in St. Louis, Missouri. The wealthy Campbell family lived there from 1854 to 1938. Studies Weekly asked Andrew Hahn, the director of the museum, about his job.

SW: How is a house museum different from other types of museums?

AH: A house museum is different because it gives you an opportunity to get the full experience of the past. If you go to an art museum, you can see paintings from the past that may tell a story about history or a particular event. But when you come to a house museum, you get the full picture of what it was like to live in the past. When people come here, they get to experience what it was like to be welcomed into the house or to work in the house. The house was so well preserved, and the Campbells’ collection is still here. This is their house and how they lived in it.

SW: What does a museum director do?

AH: I do a little bit of everything. We have to raise money so that we can keep the doors open and pay the utility bills. I write the checks for all the bills, and I organize our volunteers who do most of the work at the house. We do research, so I look into the Campbell story and read old documents and newspapers that tell stories about the past. I even take out the trash!

title: How Can I Be a Critical Reader?
text:
Critical readers carefully examine what they read so they can make informed decisions about it. They might decide if they should believe what they read or if they like what they read.

Examine What You Read

There are many ways to be a critical reader, but they all involve looking at the text and thinking about what you read. Here are some strategies for being a critical reader.

Learn to Separate Fact from Opinion

Writers sometimes present their opinions as facts, so it is important to be able to tell the difference between facts and opinions. How do you tell a fact from an opinion? A fact is a statement that can be proven true. An opinion cannot be proven true in a way that everyone will agree on because it is a belief or judgment. Here are some questions you can ask to help you figure out if something is fact or opinion:

Can this be proven?

Is it generally agreed upon?

Could someone disagree with this?

Is this supported by facts or opinions?

Watch for Faulty Logic

Make sure the writer’s logic makes sense. Do the writer’s arguments make sense? Are they supported by evidence? Here is some faulty logic to watch out for:

Either/Or Thinking—When a writer says there are only two ways to think about a situation, he or she may be engaging in faulty logic. You need to think, “Are there more ways to think about this?” What is faulty about this statement: “No one should drive, or we will have too much pollution.”

Faulty Cause and Effect—When a writer claims that one event leads to another, but doesn’t show any clear connection between the two, then you are reading faulty cause and effect. What is faulty about this statement: “He passed the test because he ate beans.”

Overgeneralization—When the writer makes a statement that goes beyond what the evidence supports, he or she may be engaging in overgeneralization. Use of too many generalizing words such as “all,” “always,” “must,” “never” and “none” could be a sign of overgeneralization. What is faulty about this statement: “My cat likes water, so all cats like water.”

Identify the Writer’s Point of View

The point of view is the set of personal opinions that influence the way the author writes about a subject. You need to be able to recognize the writer’s point of view to figure out how it might have affected the writing.

Take note of sources. Are all the sources from one side of the issue, or are they balanced over many sides of the issue?

Ask what the writer is trying to say. How is this point of view supported? Do you agree with it? Why or why not?

Critical reading can be tough, but if you practice these strategies, you’ll be on your way!
Try these active reading strategies, and you will get the most out of what you read.
