title: Leavenworth
text:
Leavenworth, also known as Washington's Bavarian Village, is one of our most visited cities. The community has joined to create its own Alpine village that looks and feels just like something found in Germany or Austria. Visitors come from all over the country to spend their vacations in Leavenworth.

Although it may be hard to believe by looking at it, Leavenworth wasn't really settled by people from Germany or the Alps. The city was first settled by the Okanogan Investment Company in 1893 as a home for gold miners, fur trappers, farmers and lumberjacks. The city was named after the president of the company, Captain Charles Leavenworth.

When the railroad came to Leavenworth, the city became rich. Lumber mills, farmers and fur trappers sent their products all over the country using the railroad. Later, however, the rail lines were moved, and Leavenworth began to struggle. The sawmills closed down, and people lost their jobs.

Just when it looked like the city was about to fail, the citizens of Leavenworth had an unusual idea. They decided to use the natural beauty of the city to bring tourists, or people who travel for fun, to Leavenworth. Tourists usually spend plenty of money, and the people of Leavenworth needed new ways to earn a living.

The city worked to change Leavenworth into a lovely Bavarian village. (Bavaria is an area in Germany.) They remodeled stores and built new shops, hotels and restaurants. The city also began celebrating festivals such as the Autumn Leaf Festival in the fall, Maifest in the spring and the Christmas Lighting Ceremony in the winter. Leavenworth began advertising its Bavarian tourist community, and people came to see what it had to offer.

The hard work of the citizens of Leavenworth paid off. More than 1 million tourists come to Leavenworth each year to river raft, hike, camp, swim, fish, snowboard, ski and enjoy festivals such as Kinderfest and the Bavarian Ice Fest.

The citizens of Leavenworth worked together to save their city while making it an even better place to live. Plan a trip to Leavenworth to see why so many people enjoy spending time in Washington's beautiful Bavarian Village.

title: Boom to Bust and Back Again
text:
You may have heard people compare the recent economic recession (2007-2009) to the Great Depression of the 1930s. But what some people call the "Great Recession" actually had more in common with a depression in the 1890s and something called "boom and bust."

In the early 1890s, the U.S. economy grew quickly ("boomed") but couldn't keep growing at that rate. When many companies and the housing market failed, there was an economic "bust." The railroad industry had been booming since the end of the Civil War, but in the 1890s more than 150 railroad companies closed. Other industries that depended on the railroads closed, and many people lost their jobs. Over 500 banks closed. Thousands of unemployed men marched to Washington, D.C., in 1894 to demand that the government take action to help families. Unemployment was over 10 percent for most of the 1890s. About one of every ten people had no job.

In the recent recession, the housing market slumped after several "boom" years. Some automakers went out of business and others filed for bankruptcy. The economy went "bust," just as it did in the 1890s. Hundreds of banks and thousands of businesses closed. The unemployment rate was about 8 percent - about one of every twelve people had no job.

Make a chart or Venn diagram that compares these two events in history. (Teachers: You can find background information and activities that relate to this article at hnn.us)

title: Communities and Culture
text:
The United States is made up of people from all over the world. Americans speak many different languages, belong to many different religions, eat many different types of foods and wear many different types of clothes.

Why America?

Immigrants are people who leave their own countries to live in another. We know that people have been coming here for hundreds of years, but why have people chosen to leave their homes to settle in America?

Land for Sale

One very important reason the first immigrants came to America is that America had cheap land. Many immigrants, especially those from Europe, wanted the chance to own their own land. In Europe, land was very expensive, and only the very rich families could afford to have land of their own. In America, almost anyone could afford to buy land and use it any way he or she chose.

Religious Freedom

Another reason many immigrants chose to leave their countries to come to America was for religious freedom. During the 1800s, many people left Europe and Scandinavia because they were being forced to belong to the state church, and they didn't want to join.

Fair Government and Freedom

Still other immigrants left their countries to come to America because they didn't agree with the government in their home countries. In Germany, for example, boys were forced to join the military and were treated very badly. Many families chose to leave their country rather than have their sons serve as soldiers. Today, the governments of many countries have taken so much control over the lives of their citizens that these people often choose to come to America to find freedom. Many immigrants from Southeast Asia and some Latin American countries have come here to escape war and suffering in their homelands.

Finding a Better Life

Perhaps the most important reason people still choose to come to America is to find a better life. People come here searching for freedom, good jobs and a chance to make something of themselves. America has always welcomed these immigrants with open arms. Because of this, our country is full of rich cultural traditions. Our foods, clothes, music, religions, celebrations and even our words come from nations all over the world. Our immigrants have helped to make America great!

Who are the Washingtonians?

The first settlers in Washington were American Indians. Later, many Americans came here from the East, searching for their own land and a better way of life. As time went on, many immigrants came to Washington from China, Latin American countries, Japan, Korea and Vietnam. People from nearly every country in the world call Washington home. People from each of these countries bring with them their languages, clothing, foods and customs and share them with us to make Washington an even better place to live.

Celebrating the People of Washington

Throughout the year, many Washington cities hold special celebrations to honor the different cultures that are found here.

Each spring, Seattle holds the Cherry Blossom and Japanese Cultural Festival to celebrate the Japanese culture in Seattle. Many years ago, the Japanese government sent thousands of cherry trees to Seattle to make friends with the city. The festival includes arts and crafts, music and traditional Japanese foods.

In January, Leavenworth holds the Great Bavarian Ice Fest. This festival honors the German and Austrian cultures and brings in lots of tourists. The festival offers sleigh rides, snow-sculpting contests and dog-sled races.

Toppenish honors its American Indian heritage with the Toppenish Powwow and Rodeo each summer. The powwow opens with a special welcoming speech and a traditional American Indian dinner of salmon, deer, elk, roots and berries. During the festival, American Indians also compete in dance and drum contests. The festival is open to all those who want to come.

These are just a few of the many cultural festivals held in Washington each year. What celebrations does your community hold?

title: Santiago Sacatepequez, Guatemala
text:
In Guatemala and many other Latin American countries, November 1 is a very important holiday. November 1 is All Saints' Day, and the city of Santiago Sacatepequez, Guatemala, is the place to be for this colorful celebration.

All over the country of Guatemala, people celebrate All Saints' Day by visiting cemeteries and decorating the graves of their loved ones. But in Santiago Sacatepequez, they do something more. The people of this Guatemalan city design and make huge kites, some as large as elephants, and then fly them in the cemeteries of the city.

The people of Santiago Sacatepequez first started flying kites on All Saints' Day many years ago. Some say the reason they first started flying kites was that a magician in their city told them this would scare evil spirits away from the cemetery. He said the noise of the kites flying in the wind would frighten the evil spirits and keep them away.

Today, the people of Santiago Sacatepequez tie small messages for their dead loved ones onto the tails of their kites, hoping that their messages will reach the ones they love. Some people even write notes asking God for special favors and tie these onto the kites as well.

After flying their kites, the people of Santiago Sacatepequez join with their families to enjoy a meal in the cemetery. They eat a special dish called fiambre, which is a beautifully arranged platter full of cold meats, vegetables, olives and boiled eggs covered with a special sauce.

While many cities celebrate All Saints' Day, none do it quite like the city of Santiago Sacatepequez, Guatemala.

title: Bob Barker
text:
Have you ever watched "The Price is Right" on television? You may not know it, but the first host of the show spent more than three decades giving away money and prizes to lucky winners from all over the country. Bob Barker, who was born in Darrington, Washington, was the host of this popular television game show for more than 35 years. He retired from "The Price is Right" in June of 2007 at the age of 83.

Bob Barker is listed in the Guinness Book of World Records as television's "Most Durable Performer" because of the number of years that he spent on television. In 1956, Bob made his first appearance on television as the host of a new game show called "Truth or Consequences." This show was so popular that it stayed on the air for 18 years. When the show ended, Bob was chosen as the host for the new daytime game show, "The Price is Right." Bob was so good at talking to the audience members and making the contestants feel at home that no one else was ever considered for the job.

Bob didn't always plan to be a television star. He was trained as a fighter pilot in World War II and graduated from college with a degree in economics. During college, he got a job as a radio announcer to help earn money to pay for school. He was so good at talking to people that he decided to try to make a living with this skill. Bob's plan worked, and he has been on television for most of his life.

Bob also loves animals and he spends much of his free time working to see that they are treated kindly.

title: Velcro
text:
After walking his dog through the fields near his home in Switzerland one afternoon, George de Mestral noticed that both he and his dog had many burrs (prickly seed cases that stick to fur and clothing) stuck to them. Instead of just picking them off and throwing them away, George decided to look at the burrs under the microscope. When he did, George realized burrs are covered with small hooks. He then looked at his pants under the microscope and saw the cloth had soft loops that the hooks on the burrs could grab onto.

George had an idea. By creating the same types of hooks and loops on two different strips of material, George was sure that he could make a fastener that would be even better than a zipper. It could be used anywhere, and unlike the zipper, it would never jam, or get stuck.

Over the next eight years, George experimented with different types of cloth and finally came up with just the right combination. He decided to call his invention Velcro, using the first part of the French words for "velvet" (velour) and "hook" (crochet).

The first Velcro fastener was patented in 1955. Today, it can be found on everything from shoes and lunch bags to camping tents and sports equipment.

title: Sally Ride
text:
Sally Ride once dropped out of college to train for a career as a professional tennis player. After deciding she wasn't good enough to turn pro, she began attending Stanford University. While working on her doctoral degree in astrophysics (the study of planets and what they are made of), she read an article in the school paper saying that NASA was looking for astronauts, or people who would be trained to fly in space. More than 8,000 people applied for the astronaut program, and only 35 were accepted. Six of these 35 were women, and Sally Ride was one of these six.

Sally Ride joined the astronaut program and was trained in parachute jumping, water survival, gravity and weightlessness, radio communications, flying and navigation. In 1983, Dr. Sally Ride became the first American woman to fly in space when she boarded the space shuttle Challenger. She later became the director of the California Space Institute and a professor of physics at the University of California, San Diego.

Encouraging girls and women to study math and science was one of Sally Ride's greatest goals. She started Sally Ride Science to show girls that science and math are not just important things to know - they're fun!

Sally Ride died in 2012, but she will always be remembered as one of our highest-flying heroes.

title: How Do I Read Nonfiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring. But it really isn’t. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you will find it easier to understand—and maybe even fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will discuss comparison and contrast.

Comparison/Contrast

With this information pattern, the writer focuses on similarities and differences. When comparing subjects, writers use words such as “the equivalent of,” “like,” “the same as” and “similar.” Writers show contrast by using words such as “but,” “in contrast to,” “on the other hand” and “unlike.” The writer usually mentions both similarities and differences.

One way to find comparisons and contrasts is to use a Venn diagram. With a Venn diagram, you can easily see how information about your two subjects is alike and different. In the far left and far right bubbles, you write the differences of each of the two subjects. In the overlapping part, you write the similarities of the two.

Try It!

To the right is a passage about becoming a state of the United States. Read the passage. Then create a Venn diagram showing the similarities and differences in the subject.

title: Sao Paulo, Brazil
text:
Education in Brazil is very important! The children of Sao Paulo start primary (elementary) school when they turn seven years old, and most are finished with secondary school (high school) by the time they turn 14 years old. Other facts about education are: Brazilian children only go to school for four hours each day; schools are both public and private; all Brazilian children wear uniforms to school; there are many colleges and universities for those who want a higher education.

A short school day makes it possible for many Brazilian children to work to help support their families. A lot of jobs are found on farms helping grow coffee, soybeans, wheat, rice, corn, sugarcane, cocoa, citrus and beef. But, life isn’t all work! Brazilian children are able to spend some time being with their families, playing with their friends and watching or playing sports (Brazil’s two favorite sports are soccer and volleyball).

Sao Paulo has many cultural attractions. There are many museums, libraries, theaters, concert halls, historic buildings and parks. Many writers, artists and musicians make their home in the city; Sao Paulo has quite a few orchestras, bands, singers and dancers. Television, radio, newspapers and magazines keep the city and country informed. It seems there is something for everyone!

title: Let’s Learn About Utah This Year!
text:
We print this weekly paper for you with activities and lots of pictures, puzzles, games and craft activities to help you learn. There are several ways to make this newspaper more fun and exciting to read.

How to Use Utah Studies Weekly

Each issue will include a current event on the first page. This is an article about something happening or a place to visit in our state. Our cover article will give you a head start on this week's history lesson on the inside pages. Wildlife examines some of the flora and fauna native to our state; Arts and Crafts gives you instructions to make cool things; and the crossword puzzles will help you learn new words.

Arts and Crafts

This section is dedicated each week to help you use your imagination. Each week includes a fun new activity with step-by-step directions and colorful illustrations. We'll show you how to make maps of Utah, interesting fact cubes, historical bookmarks and much, much more. Here's the place to let your creativity shine.

Help Your Teacher

This newspaper is written to help you help yourself learn. If you go to your teacher or a neighbor to get all of the answers, you will slow down your own learning progress. Read it over at least three times and try to understand it before asking for help. If you do this, it won't be long before you can take care of yourself. It's a great feeling!

Studying Utah Geography

We are starting our study of Utah this year by finding out where Utah is in the world. We will learn how to find different locations on a map, including Utah and the Asian countries of China and Japan. We will then find out more about Utah's landforms (mountains, deserts, canyons, lakes and rivers) and compare and contrast the landforms of Utah, China and Japan.

title: Where in the World is Utah?
text:
While our state may seem large, if you look at a world map, you will see that Utah is actually a fairly small chunk of a very large earth. Utah is part of the United States of America, which is part of North America. North America belongs to the American continent, which is part of the Western Hemisphere. Hemispheres are sections that divide the earth in half from both north to south and east to west.

To find a location on the map, all you need to know are the latitude and longitude numbers. (If you need help remembering the difference between the two, see "This Week's Question" below.) Latitude numbers are always listed first, followed by longitude numbers. Using the map below, you will see how easy it is to find Utah if you know that it is at about 40 degrees N 111 degrees W.

Where in the World is Asia?

During our studies this year, we will also be learning about the continent of Asia. We will discover things that compare, or are the same, and things that contrast, or are different, from the state of Utah. In order to do this, we need to find out where in the world Asia is as well.

Asia is part of the Eastern Hemisphere and is also its own continent. Asia is the largest continent in the world and there are more people living here than on any other continent. Look at the map and see if you can find two of the largest countries in Asia. They are China, 40 degrees N 116 degrees E; and Japan, 35 degrees N 140 degrees E.

What are the Major Landforms of Utah, China and Japan?

Utah:

A landform is a natural feature of the earth's surface, such as a mountain, canyon, river, desert or island. Landforms are always caused by nature, so streets and highways are not landforms. Utah has many interesting landforms such as towering mountains, hot, dry deserts and clear, blue lakes.

Some of Utah's most impressive landforms are the Great Salt Lake, the Wasatch and Uinta mountain ranges, Bryce and Zion canyons, Timpanogos Cave and many of our beautiful river systems. Utah's highest point is King's Peak, part of the Uinta mountain range. The peak measures 13,528 feet above sea level. Utah's lowest point is located in the southwestern corner of the state at Beaver Dam Wash. This spot measures 2,350 feet above sea level. Many of Utah's landforms are considered tourist attractions because people come from all over the world to see them.

China:

China is also a land of interesting landforms. About one-third of the country of China is covered by mountains, but the land also has hills, valleys and plains. The tallest mountain in the world, Mount Everest, is located on the border between China and Nepal. This peak rises 29,035 feet in the air. The lowest point in China is found at Lake Ai-ting (Turpan Pendi), which measures 505 feet below sea level.

Tourists come from all over the world to see and try to climb Mount Everest. Some other famous landforms of China are the Yangtze River, the Yunnan Stone Forest and the Gobi Desert.

Japan:

The country of Japan is made up of four major islands, Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu. There are many other smaller islands that are part of Japan as well. About two-thirds of Japan is covered by volcanic (made by volcanoes) mountains. Mount Fuji, Japan's tallest point, is located on Honshu Island and is 12,388 feet tall. The lowest spot in Japan is Hachiro-gata, also on Honshu Island. Hachiro-gata is 13 feet below sea level.

Some of Japan's most visited landforms are the Sea of Japan, Mount Fuji and Matsushima Bay.

As you can see, Utah, China and Japan all have interesting landforms that make them special. All three have large mountains, but only China and Japan have access to the ocean. Learning more about the landforms of different locations helps us understand and appreciate them better.

title: Uintah County
text:
Named after Uintah Indians of the Ute Tribe
County Seat: Vernal
Population: 29,042

Uintah has become known as Utah's dinosaur land. North of Jensen, you can see the quarry where dinosaur bones are uncovered. You can see the bones of a Diplodocus as a specialist chips a dinosaur fossil from solid rock. A fossil is the remains or impression of a preshistoric plant or animal that has been turned to stone. Life-size dinosaur statues are on display at the Vernal Field House of Natural History. Other interesting things to see in Uintah County are the Ute Indian reservation, where you can visit the Ute headquarters and American Indian agency. You can see American Indians as they live today at Whiterocks, Ouray or Randlett. Bear dances and sun dances are held each year for the public.

title: What is the difference between latitude and longitude?
text:
The lines that run across the globe from east to west are called parallels of latitude. To help you remember that latitude runs across the earth from east to west, think of the rungs of a ladder (or "ladder-tude") running across the earth. The lines that run up and down the earth from north to south are called meridians of longitude. Think of the lines of longitude as being long enough (as in "long-itude") to stretch from the North Pole to the South Pole.

Each line of latitude and longitude has a number assigned to it that shows exactly where it is located. The equator is 0 degrees latitude and the prime meridian is 0 degrees longitude.

The numbers on the latitude lines increase as you look both north and south. The numbers on the longitude lines increase as they go both east and west. Learning the difference between latitude and longitude will make it easy for you to find any spot on the globe.

title: Giants Lived Here
text:
In the 1970s, at Dry Mesa Quarry in Colorado, just over the Utah border, a paleontologist named Jim Jensen from Brigham Young University led a team that discovered a petrified scapula, or shoulder blade bone, that measured 8 feet in length. At the time, it was the largest known bone to ever exist on a land animal. Jensen estimated that the dinosaur would have had to have been at least 50 feet tall. Imagine an animal being 50 feet tall! By comparison, a one-story house is about 20 feet tall to the point of the roof.

Before the discovery of this huge shoulder blade, the title of largest dinosaur belonged to the Brachiosaurus. Brachiosaurus was the same species of dinosaur as this new find. Without any official name, media outlets that reported on the find called this new dinosaur Supersaurus.

Over time, it has been discovered that this massive shoulder bone did not belong to a brand-new dinosaur. Paleontologists today are still debating if Supersaurus is a distinct species.

Many dinosaur fossils continue to be found in the United States and in other countries around the world. Recently in China in 2020, a complete fossil of a small burrowing dinosaur was found buried in volcanic soil. In Japan, a nearly-complete set of fossilized bones belonging to a large plant-eating dinosaur were found in 72 million-year-old marine deposits.

title: Head Flops
text:
Have you ever wanted to create 27 pictures by drawing three? Watch as one person gradually turns into another and another.

Materials

paper

pencils

scissors

crayons

Instructions

1. Fold a piece of 12-inch by 18-inch drawing paper in half lengthwise. Open it up. Fold the long sides of the paper into the middle crease you just created. (You will now have four long sections.) Unfold the paper and cut off one of the long sides. (See picture.)

2. Orient the paper so the fold lines are horizontal. Fold the paper into thirds as shown.

3. Cut the two fold lines on the two outside thirds of the page. Do not cut into the middle third. (See picture.)

4. In the middle third of the paper, draw ears, eyes and a nose in the center panel. Draw the mouth and chin in the lower panel and draw the forehead and hair in the top panel. You can draw a self portrait or a picture of a hero or a historical figure.

5. Fold the left-hand panels in and add different features, creating another complete face. Repeat this step with the righthand panels. You now have three complete faces.

6. Flip flop the sections and see how many different faces appear.

Extra Activity: You can turn your paper over and create 27 more faces.

title: A Neanderthal’s Best Friend
text:
Archeologists in both Siberia and Belgium have found dog skulls that show wolves were well on their way to becoming domesticated dogs (pets or helpers for people) about 33,000 years ago. This means the change started about 14,000 years earlier than scientists once thought. How do we know the skulls were 33,000 years old? Scientists use a technique called carbon dating to figure it out. Carbon dating is a way to date things that were once alive by looking at how fast a certain type of carbon in the remains will decay.

This discovery also means that dogs were being domesticated in different areas of the world at the same time. The skulls show that people on two different continents were using dogs as pets or helpers.

Scientists once believed that cows, sheep and goats were domesticated first because they could provide meat and milk for prehistoric people. However, it seems dogs were domesticated first to give companionship and protection and to help during hunts.

Scientists don’t think the dogs that were in Siberia or Belgium back then are the ancestors of our modern dog. Instead, they believe that many of these dogs died out during the Ice Age. Through DNA research, scientists have discovered that modern dogs come from the Middle East and East Asia. People and dogs have been best friends for a very long time!

text:
Climate is what the weather has been like in a certain place over a long period of time. The chart below compares the climates of Utah, China and Japan. title: Utah as Part of the West
text:
Utah is part of the Intermountain West, a group of seven western states including Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming. The Intermountain West is the name given to this region of the United States. A region is an area of land that has common features, such as location, climate and landforms.

Scenic Attractions of the Intermountain West

The states of the Intermountain West all have beautiful scenery that is enjoyed by people from all over the world. We will learn more about Utah's scenic attractions in other issues of this paper, but take a look below and see if you have ever visited any of these scenic attractions in our neighboring states.

Arizona - Utah's neighbor to the south, is famous for the Grand Canyon. The Grand Canyon, which measures up to 18 miles across and averages about 1 mile deep, is considered one of the Seven Natural Wonders of the World. Nearly 5 million people visit the Grand Canyon each year.

Colorado - Located directly to the east of Utah. One of Colorado's most exciting scenic attractions is Mesa Verde State Park. The park covers about 81 square miles and is filled with amazing archaeological sites. Visitors can climb ladders and explore actual cliff dwellings that once belonged to ancient people who lived there between 600 and 1300 A.D.

Idaho - Directly to the north of Utah is the state of Idaho. Idaho is well known as the home of Craters of the Moon National Monument, located near the city of Arco. The area is marked by three major lava fields covering almost half a million acres. The land looks a lot like the surface of the moon, which is how it got its name.

Nevada - Utah's western neighbor, Nevada, is home to Lake Tahoe, a very beautiful and popular scenic attraction. The lake is located in the Sierra Nevada mountains on the border between Nevada and California. It is one of the deepest and bluest lakes in the United States. The area also features restaurants, ski slopes and vacation cabins.

New Mexico - The southeastern tip of Utah touches the northwestern tip of the state of New Mexico. In the Guadalupe Mountains of New Mexico you will find Carlsbad Caverns, a National Park made up of at least 100 known caves. These caves are filled with fascinating geologic formations that began forming around 60 million years ago.

Wyoming - Just to the northeast of Utah is the state of Wyoming. Wyoming is home to the very first National Park in the United States - Yellowstone National Park. Yellowstone, which became a National Park in 1872, covers over 2 million acres in the states of Wyoming, Montana and Idaho. The land is marked by towering 10,000 to 14,000-foot mountains, free-roaming wildlife and geysers that shoot hot liquid into the air.

title: Philanthropy and Values
text:
Maybe you have heard the word "philanthropy" before. What does it mean? It describes actions that people make for the good of other people. What is a value? It's a way of behaving that people believe is good - like believing it's good to be honest. Is honesty one of your values?

One way you can practice philanthropy today is to help yourself and others learn good values. How do you learn good values? You can learn them from your parents and grandparents, your teachers at school or church and other people you trust.

You can also learn them from people that have been recognized for doing good things for society. An easy way to learn about people that have done good things is to visit values.com. Values.com has lots of stories and short videos that highlight the traits that make each of us better people. They even have billboards on the highway to remind you about good values.

For example, you may have seen a billboard that looks like the one shown here.

This billboard is about Oral Lee Brown, who saved money from her job to send 19 kids to college... all by herself! Wow! Isn't that cool? You can learn about lots of other people who practice philanthropy at values.com. Be sure to look for more of their "billboards" on Page 4 of Studies Weekly this year. We think they're so cool we want to remind you to check them out!

title: Utah’s Three Regions
text:
The photographs you see on this page look like what you would see in each of the three Utah regions. Study them and read about the regions. Which of the three regions do you like the best? Why? Which would be the best place to live?

1. Great Basin Region

About one third of Utah is called the Great Basin because, if seen from high in the air, it would look like a shallow bowl or basin. There are valleys and mountains within this huge basin, but they don't seem large. This region is a desert because the rainfall is less than 10 inches a year.

2. Rocky Mountain Region

The Rocky Mountains in Utah are two tall, beautiful ranges of mountains. The mountains in the Wasatch Range are the mountains that are the most familiar to us because most of Utah's people live along the foot of the Wasatch Range. These mountains were formed by being pushed upward in large blocks along fault lines. Fault lines are cracks between big blocks of Earth. The Uinta Range is the only range of mountains in the western hemisphere that runs east and west. A lot of the Uinta Mountains have been set aside as a primitive area.

3. Colorado Plateau Region

A plateau is a piece of land that is high and flat and has been formed by being lifted up. The Colorado Plateau is flat, but has some mountains that rise above it and some beautiful canyons that cut through it. The Colorado Plateau is known for its bright red, orange and yellow coloring as well as unusual rock formations. Many of Utah's national parks are found in this beautiful, colorful country.

title: Utah County
text:
An American Indian name for Utes or Yutas
County Seat: Provo
Population: 483,702

Utah County has outstanding scenery and is close to Utah's population centers. There are 30 or more developed camp and picnic grounds and trails for the hiker on and around the giant, sleeping princess of Timpanogos Mountain. Timpanogos Cave National Monument is reached through American Fork Canyon. Provo River is known for its large German brown trout fishing. Utah Lake is great for boating, fishing and water skiing. Brigham Young University has a great influence on the residents of Utah County. There are sports, dance, drama, music symposia and science programs such as the planetarium, Monte Bean Museum and more. Utah County is a top producer of fruit such as apples, pears and cherries. Newer industries include Novell, an international computer-networking company.

title: Where do honeybees go in the winter?
text: The honeybee queen and some of her workers live through the winter inside their hive. In the fall, the workers collect sticky gum from trees. They use this and a wax they secrete to seal cracks in their beehive and make it safe and warm. Then, when winter comes, they stay inside the hive. When it grows cold, the bees crowd together to keep warm. They move their bodies and wings to make heat. They eat honey that they have stored in honeycombs during the summer. Near winter's end, the queen bee begins laying eggs again. Soon the hive is busy with new worker bees making honey.

title: Map Legends
text:
To explore some of the interesting sites in Utah and the Intermountain West, it is important to know how to use a map. When starting off on a trip, you need to know which direction to head and which roads will take you to where you want to go. You also need to know how many miles it is from your home to the place you want to visit.

By looking at the legend on a map, it is easy to see how many miles you will have to travel to reach your destination. A map's legend is a special key that tells you the meaning of each symbol on the map. A legend often has symbols showing where campgrounds are located, whether a road is paved or not and which roads lead through national parks. The legend also shows how many miles are represented by one inch on the map. For example, an inch of highway on a state road map may be equal to 23 miles of actual highway on the road. By using a ruler to measure the length of the road you will travel, you can find out how many miles it is to your destination.

Take a look at a map and spend some time figuring out how far it is to many of the places you hope to visit. You will find that it really wouldn't take long to travel to some spectacular scenic attractions in Utah and her neighboring states.

title: Fact Cubes
text:
Materials

Instructions

title: Famous Mountains of Utah
text:
Utah is known all over the world for its many majestic mountains. Some Utah mountains, such as Mount Timpanogos, are the subject of beautiful legends. Others, such as Mount Carmel and Mount Nebo, were named after mountains mentioned in the Bible. Escalante Mountain, the La Sal Mountains, the San Francisco Mountains and the Sevier Range were named either after or by Fathers Dominguez and Escalante who explored Utah in the late 1700s.

Pilot Peak (in Nevada, but on the Utah border), Jedediah Mountain, Logan Peak and Kings Peak were all named for mountain men, government explorers and map makers. One Utah mountain, Big Rock Candy Mountain, was even named after a song once popular with school children all over the nation.

The Wasatch Mountain Range is also home to some of the greatest ski resorts around. Alta, Snowbird and Powder Mountain are all considered world-class ski areas. In fact, Utah is famous for having the "greatest snow on earth." In this week's issue, we will learn a few interesting stories surrounding some of Utah's famous mountains.

title: Utah Mountain Legends
text:
This week, we will learn just a few of the many interesting stories and legends surrounding Utah’s mountains. Take a look below to find out more about these amazing Utah peaks.

Creation Story of the Ute Tribe

Cultures the world over have unique stories about where they came from. These stories can tell us how these cultures understand themselves and the world around them. They can also tell us what a culture finds important, or what they value.

The Ute creation story is an oral tradition. That means that it wasn’t written down. People of the tribe told it to each other over many years, from generation to generation. Everyone told the story a little differently. If you read the story somewhere else, some things might be different from what you see here. What can you learn about the Ute people from this story? Before there were people on the Earth, there was the creator, Sinauf, who was half man and half wolf. He and his brothers, Coyote and Wolf, took care of the world.

One day, Sinauf made a magical bag. He put sticks in the bag, and the sticks became people. The people started to make noise. They attracted the curiosity of Coyote. He wanted to see what the people were doing. He took his knife and cut a small hole in the bag. As Coyote peered in, he saw and heard how the people spoke in many different languages. They had their different songs, too.

Sinauf threw the bag over his shoulder and began a journey to the high mountains. As he walked, people started jumping out of the hole that Coyote had made. Coyote tried to catch them and put them back in the bag as they jumped out, but he couldn’t. They came out in small groups, becoming many different bands and tribes.

Once Sinauf arrived at the tall mountain called Una-u-quich, he noticed that the bag had become lighter. He found the hole and realized that most of the people were gone. There were only a small number left in the bottom of the bag. They were a special people: the Ute people. Sinauf told them that they would be bravest and strongest of all the people who came from the bag. He put the people carefully in special places in the Rocky Mountains.

Big Rock Candy Mountain

Big Rock Candy Mountain is located in Sevier County, just five miles north of the city of Marysvale. The mountain is actually a cluster of colorful, knobby bumps of orange, red, yellow and white that look like pieces of hard candy.

This unusual looking mountain got its name from a practical joke played by Ken Olsen and some of his friends during the summer of 1929. A railroad brakeman named Harry “Haywire Mac” McClintock had just written a folk song called “Big Rock Candy Mountain.” As a joke, Ken put up a sign at the base of the mountain telling the world that this was the one and only Big Rock Candy Mountain from the popular song. The song told of a mountain made of candy near a spring of sweet lemonade where the lunches were free, the weather was warm and there was always time for a nap. It just so happens that there is also a spring near this unusual Utah mountain, so Ken Olsen put up another sign with the words “Lemonade Springs” to show that this spot was indeed the one described in the song.

People who lived in the area and travelers passing by on the highway loved the signs and the new names stuck. Today, Big Rock Candy Mountain is a popular tourist stop along U.S. Highway 89. There are restaurants, motels and even a resort that offers rafting, horseback riding and ATV rentals. Big Rock Candy Mountain does its best to live up to the imaginary mountain described in Haywire Mac’s folk song.

Mount Escalante

Mount Escalante is located in Iron County and it marks the spot where Fathers Dominguez and Escalante cast lots (which is a lot like flipping a coin) to decide whether to return home or continue on to the Spanish missions in California. The group decided to head home, which was a good thing, considering that they soon ran out of food and supplies and had to live off the land until they reached home. Although this isn’t one of Utah’s tallest or most famous mountain peaks, it is important because it honors those who first explored our great state. To visit the spot, you will need to travel about 30 miles northwest of Cedar City.

title: Summit County
text:
Means "Top of the Mountain"
County Seat: Coalville
Population: 35,541

Summit County...a land of variety! A land of year-round excitement! A land of quiet beauty and solitude! Park City is a multi-million-dollar resort built around a restored mining community. It is one of Utah's most popular and growing ski resorts and convention centers. The "Payday Ski Run" has been listed as one of the 10 best ski runs in the United States. Hunting is excellent throughout the open areas of the county. There is also a fish hatchery in Kamas. The industry consists mainly of agriculture, dairying and livestock (including mink ranching), mining and logging with saw mills. Places to note are the High Uintas, Rockport Lake and the Alpine Slide.

title: What is the tallest mountain in the world?
text:
The tallest mountain in the world is Mount Everest, an awe-inspiring peak marking the border between the Asian countries of Nepal and Tibet. The mountain measures 29,035 feet high - as tall as about 20 Empire State Buildings. Utah's tallest peak, Kings Peak, measures 13,528 feet tall, about half the size of Mount Everest.

As the tallest mountain in the world, Mount Everest attracts climbers from all over the world who want to prove their skills. Nearly 4,000 people have tried to climb Mount Everest, but only about 660 have reached the top. Mount Everest is covered in snow and ice all year and is so high that breathing at the top of the mountain is very difficult without extra oxygen.

title: Let’s Pick Wild Berries!
text:
The berries are ripe this week in Utah. Depending on your location, you should be able to find these three varieties along stream banks. Take a pail home to mom to have her help you make some delicious pioneer berry jelly.

Blue Elderberry

The sweetish, edible berries are used in preserves and pies. Lewis and Clark first reported Blue Elder as an "alder" with pale, sky-blue berries. Whistles can be made by removing the pith from the twigs. American Indians made flutes in a similar fashion. A remedy for fever has been concocted from the bark. You can find them in a thicket along streams.

Chokecherry

This is a shrub or small tree, often forming dense thickets, with dark red or blackish chokecherries. As the name suggests, the chokecherries are astringent (sharp or bitter tasting), especially when unripe. They can be made into a delicious jelly or preserve. However, the fruit stones are poisonous inside. If the leaves, wood or seeds are chewed, an acid is released which may cause terrible stomach pain.

Western Serviceberry

This tree also goes by the names "Saskatoon," "Western Shade Bush" and "Sarviceberry." The pioneers called it "Sarviceberry." The berries of this bush are eaten fresh, prepared in puddings, pies and muffins, and dried like raisins and currants. The serviceberry tree is usually small with several trunks and star-shaped, white flowers. The fruits are about a half inch in diameter like a small apple, purple or blackish, juicy and sweet, with several seeds.
