title: Make a Relief Map
text:
Maps that show mountains, rivers and other landforms are called relief maps. You can make one of your own using salt dough. You will need the following supplies:

Materials

mixing bowls

2 cups flour

1 cup salt

2 tablespoons cooking oil

3/4 cup water

watercolor paints

heavy cardboard

pencil

scissors

Instructions

1. Cut a piece of heavy cardboard from a shipping carton about 12 inches x 12 inches and trim the cardboard to fit the shape of Utah.

2. While looking at a map of Utah, form the mountains and plateaus out of salt dough (see recipe to the right).

3. Set aside to dry for a few days. After the map is dry, paint it with watercolors or poster paints. Use your watercolors to paint the mountains, rivers and valleys as follows: deserts=brown, woods=green, rivers=blue, mountains=purple, snow=white.

Salt Dough:

Mix two cups flour, 1/2 cup salt, and 3/4 cup water together to make a dough. Knead it three to four minutes. To make it more sticky, add a little water. To make it less sticky, add a little flour.

title: Trees of Utah
text:
See if you can discover which trees grow in Utah. You will find that different trees grow in the mountains than grow in the valleys. As you find a tree, check it off on the list.

High Peaks (Found in elevations over 8,000 feet)

Alpine Fir, Spruce

Upper Mountains (Found in elevations over 6,500 feet)

Blue Spruce, Engelmann Spruce, Quaking Aspen

Lower Mountains (Found in elevations over 5,000 feet)

Bigtooth Maple, Shrubby Maple, Scrub Oak, Sumac, Serviceberry

Foothills (Found in elevations over 4,000 feet)

Juniper, Chokecherry, Pinyon

Grasslands and Deserts (Found in elevations over 3,000 feet)

Creosote, Grasses, Sagebrush, Mesquite, Willows, Cottonwood, Red Birch, Mountain Alder

title: The Bear Lake Monster: Real, Imaginary or Tall Tale?
text:
By the time Joseph C. Rich's article about the Bear Lake Monster was published in the Deseret News on Aug. 3, 1868, the Bear Lake (a clear, turquoise-colored lake in northern Utah) settlements were already stirred up about the beast. Less than a month earlier, Rich explained, C. M. Johnson of South Eden had come face to face with a strange animal staring at him from the water. He said that it had "ears or bunches on the side of its head nearly as large as a pint cup." The beast seemed to be large enough to touch the bottom of the lake.

The next day, three women and one man saw a large creature in the lake. Then, on Sunday, a party of women and men returning from Fish Haven to St. Charles spotted four large creatures and six smaller ones in the lake nearly three miles away. One of the spectators, Thomas Sleight, said that the largest animal was "no less than 90 feet in length."

These reports had apparently convinced a lot of people that monsters ruled the lake. Few boats ventured out from Bear Lake's shore for several months after the scare. Too frightened to swim or fish in the lake, residents spent their leisure time watching from the shore for any signs of the monster.

When Lt. Samuel E. Tillman first heard about the monster, he decided to prove the story true or false. One foggy morning as he rode along the shore looking for his mules, he heard "a distinct clapping sound as of two solid bodies...quickly followed by sprays of water shooting up through the thin layer of fog."

What Tillman saw was strange enough: two bulls facing each other in water up to their sides, heads down and horns clashing. When water filled their nostrils, the bulls raised their heads up and blew out a spray.

Even today, some still claim to have seen a huge body rise momentarily from the lake and splash back into the water. Whether real or legendary, the Bear Lake Monster has lived on in campfire stories and incredible tales since the early days of settlement in the Bear Lake Valley.

Adapted from THE HISTORY BLAZER produced by the Utah State Historical Society

title: The Shrinking, Stinking Great Salt Lake
text:
The Great Salt Lake is called a terminal lake. It has no outlets to the oceans, and so its size depends on rain and snow fall. In times of drought, the lake shrinks. This drop in the water level produces large mud flats. The smell from the mud flats is called lake stink.

Lake stink is caused by the decay of plants and animal remains around the shore. Hundreds of birds, 19 varieties of reptiles and 64 species of mammals live near the lake, not to mention the brine shrimp, bacteria and algae. The brine in the water is heavy, so the water near the dirt is saltier than it is at the surface. This heavy brine traps the decay, remains and waste of plants and animals at the lake. Because there is no outlet in the lake, the waste and decay have no place to go. As it settles to the bottom, the heavy, salty brine covers it, and a gas is formed. As the water recedes and the dirt is exposed, the gas is released from the mud. This makes the air smell like stinky rotten eggs.

The sandy beaches of Antelope Island may look inviting, but you will find that this sand, besides often being smelly, is also very sticky. The reason for this "sticky sand" is that each particle of Antelope Island sand is actually a small particle of brine shrimp droppings surrounded by salt. Brine shrimp droppings covered with salt are very round, while most sand particles are sharp and pointed. These rounded particles attach to your skin very easily and make you feel sticky after a visit to the Great Salt Lake.

title: Lakes and Rivers of Utah
text:
Name the Rivers

Look for clues in the column below. Now look at the map on the right and see how many you can name. Some of the letters have been filled in to help you. Not all the rivers are on the map.

Bear River: Circles Bear Lake and empties into the Great Salt Lake

Colorado River: Large river that starts from the eastern edge of Utah and empties into Lake Powell, a man-made reservoir in southern Utah

Duchesne River: Only river in Utah that flows almost straight eastward; located in northeastern Utah.

Escalante River: Southern center of Utah; empties into Lake Powell

Fremont River: Joins with Muddy Creek to make the Dirty Devil River; empties into the Colorado River

Green River: Longest river in Utah- flows south out of Flaming Gorge, a reservoir along the northeastern edge of Utah

Jordan River: Flows north from Utah Lake to the Great Salt Lake

Paria River: Extreme south center of Utah; flows into the Colorado River

Provo River: Flows down Provo Canyon to Utah Lake

Price River: Originates near Price and flows to the Green River

San Juan River: Southeast corner of Utah; empties into Lake Powell

San Rafael River: Between the Price and Fremont rivers; empties into the Green River

Sevier River: Flows north from southwest Utah, curves around and empties into Lake Sevier (which used to be part of giant Lake Bonneville and is now usually dry)

Spanish Fork River: Flows down the Spanish Fork Canyon to Utah Lake

Virgin River: Southwest corner of Utah

Weber River: Flows down the Weber Canyon to the Great Salt Lake

If you live along the Wasatch Front, you may have noticed some flat shelves along the mountains. There may be anywhere from one to three of them. Can you see them in the photograph? Some of you may have your homes built on one of these shelves. They give you a great view of the valley below. These shelves are the remains of a huge lake. In fact, the lake existed in three different levels. Let's learn about it.

Lake Bonneville

Nearly half of Utah was once underwater. There are deposits of sand and gravel at the base of mountains to show at least three different levels at which the huge lake existed. These deposits are flat and level so, by using your imagination, you can see where this huge lake lay. The lake has been named Lake Bonneville after Capt. B. L. E. Bonneville, who first mapped the area.

Geologists tell us that somewhere in the north of the state, through an earthquake or some shifting of the earth, the lake's banks gave way, and most of the lake drained into the Pacific Ocean. Can you imagine what a flood that might have caused? All that remains now of Lake Bonneville are the Great Salt Lake, Utah Lake and Sevier Lake. Since the Great Salt Lake is what the geologists call a "sink," it doesn't have an outlet running out of it. The water enters the Great Salt Lake and either sinks into the ground or evaporates. After doing this for thousands of years, the mineral deposits keep building up so that now Salt Lake is very rich in minerals and salt. Utah Lake has remained fresh because it has an outlet as well as inlets.

title: Salt Lake County
text:
Named after the Great Salt Lake
County Seat: Salt Lake City
Population: 1,009,518

Salt Lake County has hundreds of attractions in the big city. Some are concerned with Utah history, such as Temple Square, the Mormon Tabernacle Choir and the "This is the Place" monument. Other attractions are the Hogle Zoo and Tracy Aviary (a bird zoo). You should see Trolley Square and Kennecott Copper mine, and by all means swim in the Great Salt Lake, the largest and saltiest inland sea in the Western Hemisphere, where some say that it is impossible to sink. The Salt Palace is a popular attraction for conventions and displays. The Symphony Hall and Triad Center are popular attractions, as is the Energy Solutions Arena, the home of the Utah Jazz, a professional basketball team. Salt Lake County was the home of much of the Olympics in 2002.

title: What is the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow?
text: According to old legends, there is a pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. Nobody, however, has ever found such a treasure, because a rainbow is really a circle, which means it has no end. The bottom half of the circle, hidden from the observer, lies below the horizon. Actually, a rainbow is really only a colored light created in the sky when the rays of the sun strike raindrops in the air. The raindrops are like prisms, which split the white sunlight into the many colors of the rainbow.

title: Critical Analysis: The Salem Witch Trial
text:
Can you imagine a group of children who did something terrible and then told an enormous lie about it? That is what began a shameful period in American history called the Salem Witch Trials.

In 1692, Salem Village, Massachusetts, was a strict Puritan community where children were expected to devote every minute to church, chores and studies. Toys and games were frowned upon. The minister Samuel Parris had a slave girl named Tituba. She entertained his daughter Betty and her friends with fortune-telling games and stories of magic. When Betty and some of the girls began to have strange symptoms like babbling and convulsions that doctors could not explain, they were declared victims of witchcraft. Tituba was beaten and jailed. Salem had laws against witchcraft. When the girls accused others in the community of being witches, terror gripped Salem and the girls became the center of attention.

Accused people did not get lawyers, but they were not put to death if they would confess and name other witches. Soon hundreds were thrown in jail. Prisoners were left there for months, and many got sick and died.

John Proctor was a wealthy farmer who spoke out against the witch hunt. But he was accused of witchcraft himself and hanged. Twenty people were executed before clear thinking ended these unfair trials in 1693.

The Salem witch trials were based on hysteria and fear rather than on critical analysis. Ann Putnam was one of the girls who accused people. She wrote an apology in 1706 saying, “… now I have … good reason to believe they were innocent persons. …” Think of a time in school when someone you know used critical analysis to solve a problem or make a decision and discuss it with your class.

title: Salt Lake County
text: Below, you will find some symbols of famous things to see and do in Salt Lake County. Beside each symbol, fill the blanks with the correct word. You may want to refer to the brief summary of Salt Lake County.

title: Great Salt Lake Life Forms
text:
Except for some spots very close to the mouths of the streams that empty into it, there are no fish living in the Great Salt Lake. The water in the ocean is about 3 percent salt, but the water in the Great Salt Lake averages about 13 percent salt. With water 10 percent more salty than that of the ocean, the Great Salt Lake is too salty for even the most hardy saltwater fish.

Two forms of life that CAN live in the extremely salty water of the Great Salt Lake are brine flies and brine shrimp. Brine means very salty water, so these creatures are well-named.

Brine flies are small, harmless flies that feed on algae, or green and red water plants. Brine shrimp are tiny creatures that live and lay their eggs in the Great Salt Lake. These shrimp and their eggs are used as food for fish grown in aquariums. Many tons of these tiny shrimp are harvested each year and sold as fish food all over the country and the world.

title: Utah Tribes Today
text:
Five major tribes have inhabited and continue to inhabit Utah: Ute, Dine' (Navajo), Paiute, Goshute and Shoshoni. All five tribes have managed not only to survive, but to progress despite their difficult past.

Ute

After several armed conflicts with the Mormon settlers in 1861, at the request of the Mormons through the Treaty of Spanish Fork, the Ute were forced by executive order of President Abraham Lincoln to leave their beloved, beautiful Provo Valley and relocate in the arid, bleak Uinta Basin. The Ute (tribal membership of 3,300 members) operate their own tribal government and oversee approximately 1.3 million acres of trust land. Tribal headquarters are in Fort Duchesne, Utah.

Dine' (Navajo)

After many clashes with settlers and a treaty that forced them to relocate, the Dine' were finally allowed to return to their sacred lands in 1868. The Utah Dine' are served by both the Navajo nation with headquarters in Window Rock, Arizona, and the Navajo-Utah Commission Office in Montezuma Creek, Utah. The population of Utah Dine' is nearing 7,000 enrolled members.

Goshute

The Goshute people exemplify the historic Great Basin desert way of life perhaps better than any other group does because of the nature of their territory. They have both benefited and suffered from their desert isolation. There are two bands of the Goshute nation - the Skull Valley Band of Goshute (tribal membership of 127) and the Confederated Tribes of the Goshute (tribal membership of 409).

Paiute

The Paiute bands in southern Utah consist of five bands: the Shivwits Band, Indian Peaks Band, Kanosh Band, Koosharem Band and Cedar Band. After years of bitter neglect and poverty, in 1980, through the efforts of Utah Senator Orrin Hatch, the Paiute were restored to federal recognition by the U.S. Congress. The southern band of Paiute now number approximately 709, and they are making great strides in economic development to return to their previous stature in Utah history. The southern band has its headquarters in Cedar City, Utah.

Shoshoni

At one time, the Shoshoni nation of Utah inhabited most of northwestern Utah. Compared to the large area where these people once lived, they now own only 187 acres (donated by the L.D.S. Church) and some private land held in trust by the Bureau of Indian Affairs. There are approximately 383 enrolled members in Idaho and Utah. The Northwestern Band has offices in Brigham City, Utah, and Blackfoot, Idaho.

title: A Battle with an Atlatl
text:
Prehistoric American Indians used an atlatl to hunt. But did you know that people today, who live in places like Minnesota, Montana and Utah, hunt with an atlatl, too? The ancient atlatl was about 14-30 inches long with a hook on the end. It looked like a giant crochet hook. There were two parts, the main shaft and the fore shaft. The fore shaft held a sharp stone or bone, like an arrowhead. Sometimes, there were feathers tied to the fore shaft to help it fly straighter and faster. The fore shaft, or dart as it is called, is what hits the animal. The hunter keeps the main shaft and uses it to reload another dart if a second shot is needed. Atlatls that are used today are made from the same design. The main shaft is made of hard maple wood, but the darts are usually made of aluminum.

The World Atlatl Association has members all over the world, from Scotland and Switzerland to the United States and Australia. There are hundreds of competitions in the United States and Europe every year. At the competitions, people see how far and how accurately they can throw darts using their atlatls. Some people can throw a dart farther than two football fields.

One of the best atlatl competitions in the country is in Utah. At the Fremont Indian State Park near Sevier, Utah, a ranger named Pete Weimer has organized the competition. It is a very difficult course, and the distances for throwing get longer and longer as the participants race around the mountains and hills. But everyone who comes has a great time.

Ranger Pete also loves to teach chldren to use the atlatl.

title: Prehistoric American Indians
text:
This week, let's look at the first people to live in Utah. Little is known about the very early people of Utah, and what is known is told to us by the things they left behind. Stone weapons and other simple objects have been found that are thought to have been made as long as 10,000 years ago.

As time went by, these early people learned to make baskets and pottery and came to be known as Basket Makers. They continued to progress and those who lived 1,200-1,500 years ago reached a very high level of civilization. These early people are now called the Anasazi, or "Ancient Ones."

Anasazi Basket Makers 300 - 500 A.D.

The American Indians of Utah developed a high culture more than 1,600 years ago. The center of their culture was in southeastern Utah around San Juan County. We call them the Basket Makers because of the perfection they attained in weaving baskets. They learned from the migrating tribes of Mexico to grow squash and corn. They raised turkeys and had dogs for pets. The Basket Makers made pit houses with a central fireplace. They used logs laid in mud to construct their homes. The most interesting thing about this group of people is the unique baskets they made. The Basket Makers worked beautiful designs and colors into the artistic and useful baskets they created.

Anasazi Pottery Makers

The need for improved storage containers was met by the invention of pottery. People began to raise vegetables in garden plots. Permanent villages were developed. The fact that this group of American Indians grew much of their food and had permanent houses meant that they had leisure time to develop art, crafts, rituals and religion. For example, archaeologists (people who study the past) have found kivas, or religious pits, where the father of an ancient American Indian family would worship. The American Indians eventually built villages called pueblos out of adobe bricks.

Prehistoric American Indians and the Atlatl

With a spear and a device called an atlatl - from the Aztec word meaning "spear thrower" - prehistoric (before written history) American Indians would approach two deer. Before the deer could run off, the American Indians would have sent their spears with great force to bring down one of them. No one knows when or where the atlatl was invented, but it was used widely in the southwestern part of our continent during this period. It gave the one throwing it a longer arm and much faster and harder throwing velocity.

title: Sevier County
text:
Named after the Sevier River, which flows northward for about 200 miles
County Seat: Richfield Population: 19,702

Clear Creek Canyon in Sevier County is well known for its beauty. There are many strange rock shapes and curious American Indian writings. A beautiful, new visitor center that features the Fremont Indians has been built there recently. Fish Lake is especially beautiful in the fall, when the aspens around the lake turn golden. The lake is 5 miles long, about 3/4 mile wide and 90 feet deep. Some large fish reside in the lake. Rainbow, brown, cutthroat and brook trout can all be caught at Fish Lake.

Richfield is the largest city in the area. People from several nearby counties come here to shop. Back in 1865, the Black Hawk War began in Manti. It lasted for seven years. Richfield, Salina and more than 25 other settlements were abandoned when the settlers moved into forts for protection. Violent conflicts occurred as settlers moved in and took land where American Indians had lived for hundreds of years. In 1868, a treaty of peace was signed, and the tribes in the area were forced to live on reservation. The Black Hawk Treaty Tree in Richfield remembers this treaty that ended the Black Hawk War. A famous folk song called “The Big Rock Candy Mountain” was written about the mountain with the same name in Sevier County. Do you think it is really made of candy?

title: Where did corn come from?
text:
In many American Indian languages, corn means "our life," or "our mother." Early American Indians ate corn at every meal and it was one of the most important foods in their diet.

Corn was first developed from an ancient wild grass called Teosinte. Early American Indians started growing Teosinte and cross-pollinating it with other plants to make it better and better. Over time, American Indians were able to develop the corn plant that we are familiar with today.

American Indians used the sweet, sugar-filled leaves of the young corn plant as a type of chewing gum. In the summer, they ate the fresh corn as a vegetable and in the fall, they dried the mature kernels and ground them into flour.

Corn, beans and squash, often called the "Three Sisters", were the three most important plants in American Indian diet.

title: Horned Toad
text:
The horned toad is really a lizard, not a toad. There are 14 different kinds in the United States. They are called horned toads or horny toads because their bodies have a flattened, toadlike shape. They grow from 2 1/2 to 6 1/2 inches long. Their bodies are covered with spines, and large, horn-like spines project from the back of their heads. Their spiny armor protects them from any attacking animals. When attacked, horned lizards sometimes squirt little streams of blood from their eyes. This ability may frighten off such enemies as coyotes.

Horned lizards live mainly in the Great Basin area of Utah. Their colors resemble their surroundings, making them difficult to find. These lizards move slowly and feed chiefly on insects, especially ants. Most horned lizards lay eggs, but in a few species, the young are born alive.

title: Etchings
text:
Materials

Crayons, including black

Stiff white paper

Black ink

Paintbrush

Nail or nail file

Instructions

1. Color your white piece of paper with light-colored crayons. Push hard on the crayons so that it leaves a thick layer of color all over the paper. Do different patches of color so that it is filled with all colors.

2. Cover over the patches of color with black crayon, or paint over them with two coats of black ink. Let the ink dry between the coats. Make sure all the patches are covered completely.

3. Take your nail or nail file, or anything with a pointy end, and scratch a picture on the black surface. You can scrape away the black crayon or ink, and, underneath, you should be able to see the colored layers peeking through.

4. Continue to scratch into the black ink or crayon until you’ve drawn the picture you had in mind. Hang your creation in your classroom or room at home.
Note: Be careful with the pointy object you use to create your etching. Do this activity with adult supervision.

title: Read the Petroglyphs
text:
Petroglyphs (American Indian writing that is carved in rock) and pictographs (American Indian writing that is painted onto stone) reached their highest form among the Fremont Indians of Utah. The Fremont Indians are thought to be a group of the Anasazis that migrated north and preferred to worship in their own homes.

Use the key to help you read the Fremont Indian petroglyphs. You will find words related to American Indians. Write each letter in the blank provided. (Note: This activity is just for fun. These particular symbols do not really stand for the letters indicated in the key. The early American Indians did not have an alphabet or written language. They communicated with pictures.)

title: How Utah Got Its Name
text:
The name Utah comes from the American Indians who dwelt here. Let's become better acquainted with these honest and peaceful people.

Four large groups of American Indians have occupied Utah since the time of white visitors to the area: Paiute, Ute, Goshute and Shoshone. Each of these groups has several divisions or tribes bearing such well-known tribal names as Timpiute, Uintah, Beaver, San Juan, Kaiparowits, Cedar and Kaibab.

Utah takes its name from the Ute tribe. Students of western history say that this name has been given many meanings, but members of the tribe say it means "people who live on the heights," "home on the mountain top," "high-up people" or "Mountain-Top Indians."

Life was hard in this region, and much of the time was spent gathering food. Most of the tribes in what is now Utah were not as warlike as the plains tribes to the east; nor were they as advanced and well developed as the more easterly tribes. Some of them had no chief and little tribal organization until the white men came.

Their most-used articles of clothing were rabbit-skin blankets. They had learned to use almost every shred of any animal they managed to kill. Basketry and pottery were important to American Indians of the area, and they became very skillful in weaving baskets.

When horses began to come into the country from the white men, the Ute quickly learned to make good use of them in hunting.

The Paiute lived in thatched tepees, while the Goshute lived in windbreaks without roofs. They were among the most primitive tribes of America. In southern Utah, reservoirs and canals with wooden gates show that the American Indians used irrigation successfully to grow crops.

The American Indians of Utah were noted for their honesty. It has been said that when a Mormon bishop from Minnesota visited them, he asked a chief if his belongings would be safe in his tent while he made a long trip. "Yes," the chief replied, "there is not a white man within 100 miles."

There is one more group of American Indians in southern Utah called the Navajo. They must have come from a long distance because they were unlike any of the nearer tribes. They were warlike and have always been a proud people. The Navajo are the largest group of American Indians remaining in the United States today. The great Navajo reservation is at the southern tip of Utah, south of the Colorado River and extending into Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona.

title: America’s Oldest Game
text:
The game of lacrosse has been around since the 15th century when American Indians first invented the sport. Lacrosse is a game where players use a stick with a net attached to toss a small rubber ball back and forth, trying to get it into a goal at the end of the field. Some people say that it is the fastest game on two feet.

In ancient times, American Indians played the game for fun, as well as for exercise. They were even known to play lacrosse against other tribes to settle arguments. Sometimes, these games ended in battles instead of celebrations. The number of players on each team varied, but there were sometimes as many as 1,000 players on each side! Today, there are only 10 players per team. American Indian lacrosse games could last two or three days, while today's games usually last about an hour.

Today, lacrosse is a growing sport in the United States. Many young people are becoming interested in the fast-pace and the skill of this ancient game. Students at colleges and universities play the sport, both on college teams and just for fun. Currently, lacrosse is played at over 500 colleges and universities in America. There are also over 1,400 high schools that offer lacrosse programs for their students. Women's lacrosse is becoming very popular with high school and college students as well.

If you think you have what it takes to play the exciting game of lacrosse, ask your parents to check to see if there are any youth programs in your city or county. You could start learning a game that has been around for centuries!

title: American Indians of Utah
text:
During the Utah pioneer period, there were five main groups of American Indians in Utah.

The Shoshone
(There are two spellings in the dictionary: Shoshone and Shoshoni)

The Shoshone Indians of northern Utah live in the areas of Box Elder, Cache and Rich counties. The Shoshone were mounted American Indians, owning many horses. They spent much of their time in Idaho or Wyoming because it was easy for them to move around. Chief Washakie was the most famous Shoshone in Utah history. The Shoshone built tepees of buffalo, elk and deer hides. They differed from the Ute tepees in that they were decorated. The hides were expertly sewn together and covered the pole frame to provide a warm home. Meat was the main diet of the Shoshone Indians. Meat was prepared by cooking it over coals or preserving it as jerky or pemmican. Jerky is strips of dried meat. Pemmican was made by pounding dried meat, dry seeds, berries and fat together. This was stored in leather pouches to be taken on long trips or used in the winter months.

The Goshute- "Digger Indians"

The Goshute were relatives of the Shoshone, who lived in the northern part of our state. They spoke a broken Shoshone language. They lived in the west- central part of our state and were called "Digger Indians" because they were often seen digging roots, bulbs, tubers, squirrels, gophers and snakes from the ground. Since the Goshute spent almost all of their time getting food, they didn't build very good homes. They built brush windbreaks that were temporary. It was like they were always on a camping trip, moving to where the food was best. During the winter months, caves and rock shelters were used. They ate mainly wild vegetation and wore very little clothing. During the winter, when it was cold, they wore fur robes made of jack rabbit hides. They didn't have a strong tribal structure, being more like families who worked together to harvest food or go on rabbit drives. Among the plants used for food were sunflower seeds, sedge bulbs, camas roots, serviceberries, yucca pods, cactus pears and arrowroot leaves. The pioneers were surprised to see them roast grasshoppers, crickets and ants. They frequently ground the roasted insects into a meal to be stored for winter.

The Paiute- "Gathering Indians"

The Paiute lived in southern Utah along the Virgin, Santa Clara and Muddy rivers. The Paiute were not strongly unified into bands like the Ute. Each small group had a chief who was more like the leader of a family. Neighboring camps joined together to conduct rabbit drives. These sometimes lasted 10 days and were under the direction of a "Rabbit Boss." Each day, a party of about 30 to 50 people would drive all the rabbits they could scare up into a semi-circular net that was about 4 feet high and more than 100 feet long. When the rabbits were caught in the mesh, they were harvested. Grasshoppers, lizards and tortoises were caught during the summer. Grasshoppers were considered a delicacy and were boiled and roasted. Pine nuts were gathered in the fall. They could be stored all winter. They did some fishing with double-barbed hooks of deer bone and they hunted large game. The meat was dried into strips for storage.

The Ute- "Mountain-Top" Indians

The Ute were a sturdy, vigorous race, with high cheekbones and a copper-colored skin. They were the largest Utah tribe. The women parted their long, coarse, black hair, but did not braid it. The men braided theirs. Most of them did not have beards, but a few of them did. Few people loved the outdoors as much as the Ute. Their legends were about their people and the forces of nature. The Ute lived close to the great outdoors, both figuratively and actually. They lived honorably and by the law of the tribe. There were eight main Ute bands. Each band had a definite district in which its members could hunt and fish. Each group moved around within its district during the summer hunting season. They learned from the plains American Indians about making the tepee, which they covered with deer, elk and buffalo hides. The Ute had horses, so they were able to get around much better than their neighbors. When they were ready to move, they would put their belongings onto a travois (frame of poles dragged behind a horse), another idea they borrowed from the plains American Indians. Horses were the most prized possessions of the Ute. The principal use of the horse was to hunt buffalo and large game.

The Navajo

It was believed that the original Navajo migrated from northwestern Canada in groups of nomadic hunters. The name Navajo means "Takers from the Field." The Navajo settled down in the Southwest and adopted many Pueblo practices. The typical Navajo home is called a hogan. It is built of timbers and poles that are covered with bark and dirt. Hogans are both well insulated and waterproof. The Navajo raise corn, squash, wheat, melons, tobacco and beans. The Navajo are best known for their ability to weave beautiful colors into their blankets and rugs. The shaman, or medicine man, cures illness by concerning himself with the causes of ailments, which he believes to be the spells of witches and evil spirits. The shaman makes a dry painting by drawing with various colors of sand. After smoothing the sand, he picks up a small amount of the desired color and, using his thumb and forefinger, lets the colored sand trickle onto the sand, forming the design he wants. When the design is complete, the sick person sits on the design while the shaman chants and shakes a rattle. The Navajo believe that the Holy People control their lives. The Holy People are the strange and powerful spirit beings who travel on the wind, sunbeams, rainbows and thunder. Every act of their day is an attempt to stay on the good side of the Holy People.

title: Piute County
text:
Named for the Piutes, a Shoshone American Indian Tribe
County Seat: Junction
Population: 1,341

Piute County, located in central southern Utah, is one of our smallest counties, both in size and in numbers of people who live here. The county is made up of a long, narrow valley with mountain ranges to the east and west. Mining was once a booming business in Piute County, where gold, silver and other valuable metals were uncovered, but the mines closed down long ago. Visitors can still see the remains of these mining towns by taking the "Canyons of Gold" driving tour that begins in Bullion Canyon. Another interesting tourist spot is the boyhood home of Butch Cassidy, a famous outlaw of the Old West. The small log cabin where the outlaw was raised still stands beneath a stand of cottonwood trees in Circleville. Piute County is also famous for its great year-round hunting and fishing opportunities. Piute State Park, Otter Creek Reservoir and the Tushar Mountains are beautiful places to get out and enjoy nature.

title: What is a shaman?
text: A shaman is an American Indian spiritual leader. Many American Indian tribes believe that the shaman is in direct contact with the World of Spirits and that he can heal the sick, predict the future and take dead souls to their final resting place. The shaman is highly respected and is usually given gifts to perform chants and heal the members of his tribe.

title: Travois and Bull Boat
text:
Utes used the travois to carry clothes, tepee coverings and belongings when tribes had to move. The original was pulled by dogs until the Europeans brought horses to the New World.

The bull boat was a bowl-shaped vessel of buffalo hides stretched over a framework of willow saplings. It aided in the transportation of large loads across rivers and lakes.

A bull boat was used to keep their belongings together.

title: Coyote
text:
Coyote are medium-sized wild dogs. They have a gray coat with a black stripe down the middle of the back and a black-tipped tail. Coyote hunt and eat whatever is handy and easy to get. They eat squirrel, rabbits and mice, but sometimes they gang up on larger animals, such as antelope or small deer. They will also eat insects and fruit.

Some coyotes form packs of three to eight. Others live alone until it is time to breed.

They have a very distinctive howl. Some think they sound ghostly, or supernatural, when they howl at the moon.

title: American Indian Storytelling and Drawing
text:
You will have fun telling this story to your family and friends. As you tell this story, draw each part on a paper or chalkboard. You can practice to make your drawing better each time.

The Big Fish

It was a bright, spring morning and two young American Indian braves sat beside a lake. "We should go fishing!" they said. So they climbed into their canoe that looked like this:

They paddled and paddled in their little canoe. They sailed east and they sailed west. They sailed north and they sailed south. But they didn't see one single fish! Quite suddenly they heard a big SPLASH. An enormous fish popped its head out of the water.

The fish had eaten up the bait the young brave had put on his fishing line. The fish began to swim away very fast. The big fish was very strong and he dragged the braves and the little canoe all around the lake. It was a frightening but exciting ride.

They even went down a waterfall just like this:

Finally the fish began to tire. It began to swim slower and slower. (Draw the line back from the "waterfall" slower as you tell this part). He swam very close to the canoe. Gulp! Oh my, but that was a big fish!

title: Piute County Word Search
text: There are eight words to help describe Piute County. Look in the maze of letters and find the eight words. They will read either across or down. You may want to refer to the brief summary of Piute County. Can you find: Piute, Junction, Butch Cassidy, Otter Creek, silver, gold, ghost towns and Tushar

title: Ute Snacks
text:
Was-Nah Corn and Cherry Snack

Serves eight to 10

It is important to let our children know that not all Americans have enjoyed sweet things in the forms that are so common today. This is such a treat . . . a treat from the American Indian community. It is made with truly American food products, though we will substitute Bing cherries for the chokecherries and butter for the buffalo kidney fat. We still have a dish that is close to a wonderful American Indian snack. The toasted cornmeal winds up tasting something like popcorn.

You’ll need:

2 cups cornmeal

1 cup seeded Bing cherries, fresh, frozen or canned

1/2 pound soft butter

2 cups brown sugar

What to do:

Place the cornmeal on a cookie sheet and toast it in a 325° oven until it begins to brown. Careful—this will not take long.

Drain the cherries well and chop them coarsely. Mix all the ingredients together well and chill in the refrigerator. To serve, simply dish out by the tablespoonful. It is eaten like candy.

Indian Bean Soup

Serves four

Beans and corn were some foods used by the Anasazi Indians.

You’ll need:

2 tablespoons butter or margarine

1 onion, chopped

1 15-ounce can black beans

1 cup water

2 teaspoons lemon juice

1/4 teaspoon allspice

1 tablespoon Worcestershire sauce

1 7-ounce can corn, drained

What to do:

1. Place the butter or margarine and onion in a large, microwave-safe bowl. Cover and microwave on HIGH for three minutes.

2. Add the remaining ingredients. Mix well.

3. Cover and microwave on HIGH for three to four minutes, stirring after each minute, until heated through.

title: Influential Native American Figures
text:
Tȟašúŋke Witkó (Crazy Horse)

Tȟašúŋke Witkó, also known as Crazy Horse, was an Oglala Lakota chief. Many believe he was born in what is now South Dakota around 1842. As a teenager, he was a skilled and well-known warrior among the Lakota.

During the 1860s, Crazy Horse participated in several battles against the U.S. Army to defend his people’s way of life. These conflicts ended with the signing of the Second Treaty of Fort Laramie in 1868. The treaty created the Great Sioux Reservation, which included the Black Hills of South Dakota. Crazy Horse and his people lived in the Black Hills, but they did not trust the terms of the treaty.

In 1874, gold was discovered in the Black Hills. Gold seekers traveled through Sioux lands and began prospecting for gold. Sioux leaders, including Crazy Horse, were angry at the U.S. government for violating the treaty. From 1876 to 1877, Crazy Horse participated in many battles during the Great Sioux War. On June 25, 1876, he and his warriors defeated the U.S. Army forces under the command of General George Armstrong Custer.

Tȟatȟáŋka Íyotake (Sitting Bull)

Sitting Bull was a leader for the Hunkpapa Lakota. He worked to help them maintain their independence. He was born in 1831 in present-day South Dakota. His birth name was Jumping Badger. When he was 14, he went with his father and came upon a group from a rival tribe. Jumping onto his horse, he started chasing them. He caught up with one warrior and tapped him with a coup stick. A coup stick is a thin wand, about three feet long. Tapping an opponent with a coup stick and getting away unharmed was considered an act of great bravery. That night at a ceremony, his father gave him the name Sitting Bull.

It was difficult being a Plains Native American during Sitting Bull’s lifetime. White settlers were taking over their land. Food was scarce because most of the buffalo had been killed. The U.S. government was forcing Native Americans to move onto reservations. Often, the land they were forced to use could not grow enough food to feed them.

Sitting Bull, along with other Native American leaders, led a series of attacks on U.S. forts and settlements. They wanted to regain their land. Sitting Bull became a well-known leader during this time. When the U.S. government offered him a treaty, he would not sign it. “I do not propose to sell any part of my country,” he said. He gathered thousands of people to his village.

Maȟpíya Lúta (Red Cloud)

Maȟpíya Lúta was a Native American leader, also known as Red Cloud. He was born in 1822, near present-day North Platte, Nebraska. He was a member of the Oglala Lakota.

Red Cloud became a leader when his people came into conflict with settlers who wanted the same land. In 1858, gold was discovered in Montana. The U.S. government started making a trail and building forts along the way. The trail crossed the land where Red Cloud’s tribe lived. The Oglala Lakota decided to defend their land in a war that was called “Red Cloud’s War.” His people won the war. The U.S. Army stopped trying to build the trail to Montana.

Red Cloud spoke out against the U.S. government’s broken promises. He traveled many times to Washington, D.C., and other cities in the East. He became a diplomat for his people. By the end of his life in 1909, Red Cloud was famous as a leader in both war and peace.

Heȟáka Sápa (Black Elk)

Heȟáka Sápa, also known as Black Elk, was a member of the Oglala Lakota. He was one of the most influential Native Americans. Born in the 1860s, he was the fourth male in his family to bear the name Black Elk.

At five years old, Black Elk started to have visions. When he turned nine years old, he got sick and had a vision of meeting with the Six Grandfathers. He felt uneasy from the vision and kept it a secret. He wanted to wait until he got older to see what it meant.

At 13 years old, Black Elk was a witness to the Battle of Little Bighorn (Greasy Grass). Even though the Native Americans won the battle, his tribe, along with others, were still at war with the United States Government. During this time, his visions became more apparent. He performed a ceremony in front of his tribe called the “Horse Dance.” It was in this dance that he reenacted his vision. After the ceremony, Black Elk became a healer and a holy man, or a man who saw visions.

Black Elk worked to heal his people. Many were left without food and were dying of different diseases. After the Massacre of Wounded Knee, Black Elk came to save as many as possible. After this conflict, Black Elk and his people surrendered to the U.S. government.

Black Elk’s legacy lives on as a leader in his tribe and people, speaking about Lakota traditions and customs, and seeing how traditions can be spread across all perspectives and viewpoints.

title: American Indian Chiefs
text:
This week, let's become acquainted with some of the famous chiefs and tribal leaders of early Utah.

1. Chief Washakie

Chief Washakie was one of the finest Shoshone chiefs. It was said that he never broke his word. He was chief for 60 years and became noted for the success of his people under his leadership.

Washakie lived in both Wyoming and Utah, leading his entire band to Utah during the summer months. Washakie and his tribe often received food from the Mormons and in return for this kindness, he and his people helped the Mormons any way they could. They helped the pioneers cross dangerous rivers and streams, joined them in looking for lost animals and treated them as friends. Because of this, the Mormons believed Chief Washakie to be one of the noblest American Indians they knew.

One time, 9,000 emigrants signed a paper commending this chief for his kind treatment. General Conner conferred upon him the title "Friend of Peace."

He was buried with military honors in the cemetery at Fort Washakie, Wyoming. In this same cemetery you will find another marble monument inscribed with the name, "Sacajawea," another great Shoshone Indian who once helped Lewis and Clark explore the West.

2. Chief Black Hawk

Chief Black Hawk is best known in Utah history as the Ute chief who led the warriors in nearly every raid or battle against the settlers during the Black Hawk War (1865 - 1867).

Chief Black Hawk was tall and stately, a fearless warrior who looked the part of a chief in every way. He was a real chief in appearance. His commanding appearance drew strong men to him. Some people claim that few trained generals have had greater influence over their men than Black Hawk had over his.

3. Chief Walker (Wakara)

The most powerful Ute chief in Utah at the time the pioneers came (about 1850) was Chief Wakara (also called Walker). He had become a war chief through his ability in war, his daring as a raider and his cleverness at trading. Chief Wakara was disturbed at the coming of the pioneers. The pioneers did not ask him if they could settle on American Indian lands. On the other hand, he hesitated to make war against the Mormons because he believed they had come in peace to teach their religion like Father Escalante and Dominguez. Besides, the pioneers could buy from or trade with him for his horses.

As the Mormons came to central Utah, Wakara led his people against them in the "Walker War." The American Indians were defeated after several "hit-and-run" attacks. Brigham Young signed a peace treaty with Wakara at Chicken Creek. Young asked only for peace and promised the American Indians that they would still be able to buy arms and ammunition for hunting. Wakara died on Jan. 29, 1855, an unhappy man. He was a fearless and respected leader and was buried as an honored chieftain.

4. Chief Kanosh

Another Ute chief who was friendly to the white settlers and helped the cause of peace was Chief Kanosh. He was the chief of the Pahvant Band, who lived in Millard County. Chief Kanosh and his band of 500 Pahvant Ute lived near the present city of Kanosh.

The early settlers tell us the story that Chief Kanosh visited the new, struggling colony of Fillmore and gave his word that he would protect them. He always kept his word. No chief did more during times of trouble between the whites and the American Indians in bringing about peace than Chief Kanosh.

Chief Kanosh was very intelligent. At the end of the Black Hawk War, 15 American Indian chiefs entered a treaty. Kanosh was the only one who could sign his name to the document.

Later in his life, he moved into the town of Kanosh after it was established, put on white man's clothes and fully adopted the white culture. Chief Kanosh died on Dec. 4, 1884. The white men and American Indian members of his Pahvant Band buried him in the Kanosh cemetery. The settlers of Utah lost one of their greatest friends and peacemakers.

5. Chief Ouray

Chief Ouray was a great chief of the Ute who lived in the eastern part of Utah. His mother was of the Uncompahgre Band of Ute, and his father was an Apache. He was born near Taos, New Mexico. He learned to speak not only Ute and Apache, but Spanish and English as well. He was highly intelligent and could express his thoughts and ideas clearly. Ouray made many trips to Washington, D.C., and President McKinley pronounced him "The most intelligent man I have ever conversed with." Kit Carson explained, "Ouray was able to see beyond the end of his nose."

There was much strife between the white settlers and the American Indians. Ouray's quick action and stern behavior saved many lives on both sides. He accomplished very much for his people by diplomacy and patience. He usually took his sweetheart, Chipeta, with him to Washington. She was treated as a queen. The Washington officials appointed Ouray chief of all the Utes.

On a buffalo hunt, a band of Sioux kidnapped Ouray's 5-year-old son, his only child. The governmental American Indian bureau found his son much later, but the son didn't recognize his father and wouldn't go with him. Ouray was very much hurt by this and carried this hurt all the rest of his life.

Ouray died at age 47 of a liver ailment. He was very much respected and loved by many people.

6. Chipeta

Chipeta married Ouray when she was only 16 years old. She was the only Ute woman ever allowed to sit in the council (group of leaders) meetings. Her people thought very highly of her. Many people said she was an extremely intelligent and dependable woman.

One time, she rode her horse through a swirling, flooded river to warn the white people living near her about an American Indian raiding party. She and Ouray did many good deeds. The government in Washington, D.C., often depended on the help they received from Ouray and Chipeta.

For many years, she was wealthy, but she spent her money taking care of orphan children. She became famous for her charity toward others. She outlived Chief Ouray by 40 years. She was so loved and appreciated that the people in the area around Grand Junction, Colorado, treated her as someone very special. She had always been friendly toward the white people.

Here is a part of a poem written as a tribute to Chipeta:

Chipeta

She is bravest and best of a persecuted race.
Give her a lodge on a mountain side,
And when she is gone on the hill provide
The queen of the Utes a resting place.

But give her a page in history, too.
Though she be rotting in humble shroud,
Write on the whitest of God's white clouds
Chipeta's name in eternal blue.

title: Juab County
text:
Comes from the Ute word that means "flat" or "level"
County Seat: Nephi
Population: 9,604

Juab County has a rich mining history, especially in and around the city of Eureka. The ore was so rich that shotgun guards were hired to protect it while it was being taken from the mine to the railroad. Most of the mines have now closed down, leaving only ghost towns behind. Rock hounding is still important in Juab County, though. Topaz Mountain contains topaz crystals, and petrified wood can be found in many areas. Paul Bunyan's Wood Pile, considered a natural wonder, is made up of hundreds of large, six-sided rock "poles." There is a national wildlife refuge near Fish Springs. Yuba Lake, Mona Reservoir and the White Sand Dunes are fun places to visit in Juab County. Nephi, a farming and stock-raising community, is the county seat and the largest city in Juab County. Juab county is also home to buffalo berries. Buffalo berries were used by the American Indians for food. They were dried or eaten fresh off of the bush. Often, they were boiled with flour to thicken them and used as a sauce.

title: How many American Indian tribes are there in the United States today?
text:
There are 116 American Indian tribes with at least 1,000 members living in the United States today. The 10 largest American Indian tribes are listed below.

1. Cherokee

2. Navajo

3. Chippewa

4. Sioux

5. Choctaw

6. Pueblo

7. Apache

8. Iroquois

9. Lumbee

10. Creek

title: American Indian Tools
text:
Obsidian

The ancient art of spear and arrowhead making began thousands of years ago. Before the bow and arrow were popular (about 1,000 B.C.), the spear was the primary weapon of the American Indians.

Flint or obsidian were the most common kinds of rocks that could be chipped into useful, sharp tools. Obsidian is sometimes called nature's glass.

Drums

American Indians took great pleasure in music. Every tribe had songs and music for religious ceremonies, games, dances and prayers.

Three kinds of drum construction:

1. Clay-pot drum (essentially a clay pot)
2. Water drum (tone is regulated by water level)
3. Ceremonial drum (suspended from stakes)

text:

text: Rock hounds seek topaz crystals and petrified wood in Juab County. Look at the crystals below and determine what other things are important in Juab County. Simply unscramble the words in each crystal and write them on the lines below. Some of the letters have been given to help you.

title: American Indian Sovereignty and Intergovernmental Cooperation
text:
Every nation in this world has a government. They make laws and have their own governing body. A nation is a group of people that lives in a certain area or territory. Nations often have the same history, culture, religion and language. The United States is a nation. American Indian tribes are nations, too! These tribes are nations that live within the U.S. and while part of it are also separate from it, having their own governing bodies and citizens.

Have you ever heard of the term sovereignty? This term applies to American Indian nations across the United States. A nation has its own government and rules. Sovereignty means that the American Indian nations have the power to govern themselves and that this right is inherent. That means they have the ability to make their own laws and govern themselves and that power existed far before the U.S. government was formed. The American Indian nations do not get their power from the U.S. government. They have the right to live their lives in the way they want to continue their lifestyle and culture.

Since the Nations have their own government, they and the U.S. government — local, state and national — have to work together to find solutions to many issues. This is known as intergovernmental cooperation. This is a big term for something unique in our country because the American Indian governments existed from “time immemorial,” which means something has existed since before the beginning of recorded time. American Indian governments exist today alongside the U.S. government. American Indians are both U.S. citizens and members of their respective Nations.

title: Father Escalante and the American Indian Boy
text:
On July 29, 1776, Fathers Dominguez and Escalante, along with eight companions, headed out from Santa Fe, New Mexico, to find a safe way to travel to Monterey, California. The Spanish government had asked the two Catholic fathers to make the expedition (trip into unknown territory to gain information) to record all they could about this unknown country. To make sure they didn't forget anything, Father Escalante kept a very complete journal, or record, of all they did and saw.

While most of Father Escalante's journal is filled with facts and observations, there is one subject that often brings out the softer side of this great explorer. At the beginning of the trip, an American Indian boy of the Laguna tribe begged to join the group. The fathers gave their permission and the boy, called "Joaquin," began to appear often in Father Escalante's writings.

A couple of months into the journey, the explorers made camp on the banks of the Green River, near what is now Dinosaur National Monument. The group stayed here overnight, letting their tired animals graze on the pastureland and enjoy some much-needed rest.

While the group camped here, Joaquin got restless and decided to ride a very spirited horse. As it galloped across the meadow, the horse tripped in a hole and fell. Instead of being angry, Father Escalante showed his love for the boy and patience with his mischief in the following account:

"We were frightened, thinking that the Laguna had been badly hurt by the fall because when he had recovered from his fright, he wept copious tears. But God was pleased that the only damage was that done to the horse, which completely broke its neck, leaving it useless."

Later that same month, on Sept. 23, 1776, the group arrived at Utah Lake, part of the Laguna Indians' territory. At first, some of the Laguna Indians came out to meet the group with their weapons ready, but when the tribe saw that Joaquin was traveling with them, they began to feel more friendly. Father Escalante writes:

"He [Joaquin] even refused to leave Father Dominguez, while sleeping at his side during the brief space of time that was left in this night. Such an attitude found in an Indian boy so far from civilization that he had never before seen fathers or Spaniards was an occasion for surprise, not only to his own people, but to us as well."

Father Escalante used his journal to record many stories and events that show the relationships Joaquin had with many members of the expedition. The fathers tried to teach the American Indian boy faith, courage and trust, and Joaquin responded with respect and love for the Spanish explorers. When other tribes saw the love Joaquin had for his companions, they judged the group more kindly. Because the fathers showed respect for everyone they encountered on their trip, they never had any difficulties with the tribes they met along the way.

title: Spanish Influence in Today’s Utah
text:
The Spanish came to Utah more than 200 years ago, but they made an impact that has lasted from that time to today.

The Spanish, of course, explored this place long before it was Utah. In fact, they were exploring the United States before it was the United States.

Utah's early history is all about the Spanish and American Indian heritage that still influences our state today. But where can you see this Spanish influence?

All over Utah there are towns, counties, rivers and lakes with Spanish-influenced names: Alta, Spanish Fork (named for the Escalante and Dominguez Expedition), Virgin, Escalante, La Verkin, Orofino, Santa Clara, San Rafael and La Sal. All these names came from the Spanish, although we may not pronounce the words like they did.

Spanish food? Well, there's Cafe Madrid in Salt Lake City. It's not a particularly old restaurant, but they are serving up traditional dishes such as paella (rice and seafood), Serrano ham and the Spanish tortilla (more like a potato omelet than a Mexican tortilla).

Spain may be a long way from here, and 200 years may seem like a long time. But everything from the green road signs displaying Spanish names down to the "Seedy Spaniard" summer 10k race in Spanish Fork shows that the influence of those early Spanish explorers is still here today.

title: First White Men in Utah
text:
For many long centuries, Utah, along with the rest of the Great Basin, was nothing more than a mysterious wilderness, known only to American Indians and wild beasts that haunted its valleys, canyons and deserts. The Spanish were settling California, but were afraid Russia or England would try to take it from them. They needed an overland route from Monterey, California, to Santa Fe, New Mexico, to allow them to defend California in case of an attack. The route the Spaniards took from Monterey to Santa Fe is called "The Old Spanish Trail."

Dominguez and Escalante Chosen to Lead Expedition (1776-1777)

The first expedition to Utah by white men was organized by Dominguez with the purpose of finding the most direct route from Monterey, California, to Santa Fe, New Mexico. Father Escalante, a Catholic priest (respected leader in the Catholic Church), had been dreaming of a mission to the American Indians for years, so when he was asked to go, he considered it his golden opportunity. (A mission is an education center with homes and buildings of the Catholic Church.) Father Dominguez was officially Escalante's superior, but actually he was a faithful follower of the more domineering Escalante. Ten persons, including the two fathers, made up the company.

Spanish See Utah's Possibilities

It was midsummer, July 29, 1776, shortly after our country declared its independence from Great Britain, that the little band left Santa Fe. Two months later, on Sept. 21, they crossed the divide, made their way down Spanish Fork Canyon and caught a glimpse of the fertile Utah Valley. Two days later, they were on the shores of Utah Lake. Father Escalante described in his most remarkable journal very vivid and accurate information concerning Utah and its possibilities.

Several of Utah's physical features, such as the La Sal Mountains, were given Spanish names as a result of Dominguez-Escalante expedition.

Fathers Befriend American Indians

They spent three days with the American Indians at Utah Lake. The fathers, or padres in Spanish, befriended the American Indians and preached their religion to them through an interpreter, or one who translates foreign languages. Many of these American Indians converted to Catholicism because Dominguez and Escalante begged them to come and live among them in the future. They also told the fathers that they could have all the land they wanted on which to settle and build houses. When they returned to Santa Fe, the American Revolution had begun as a result of the July 4 signing of the Declaration of Independence. Because Spain joined the side of the colonists, the fathers had to wait to return and start colonies in Utah.

title: Sanpete County
text:
"Sanpete" was originally called "Sanpitch," or "Sampichya" after the original Ute tribe living in the area.
County Seat: Manti
Population: 22,763

Sanpete is one of the top 10 turkey-producing counties in the United States. There are more than 10 million turkeys raised each year in Sanpete County. That averages out to nearly 10 turkeys per Utahn per year! Norbest, a leading turkey producer, has several modern processing plants in Sanpete. These plants prepare Norbest turkeys to be sold in stores. Snow College in Ephraim is a center for music and the arts. The Mormon Miracle Pageant, a religious production, is held on the Manti Temple grounds each July. Some popular recreation spots in Sanpete include Palisade Lake State Park, Maple Canyon and Skyline Drive. Sanpete Valley is also one of Utah's richest farming regions. It's tree-shaded towns, quaint old houses and scenic landscape give it a real pioneer flavor. The valley was one of the first Mormon colonies outside of the Salt Lake Valley.

title: What is “The Old Spanish Trail”?
text: The Old Spanish Trail started out as an ancient American Indian trade route, but was later mapped out by Spanish explorers such as Dominguez and Escalante. The route led from Santa Fe, New Mexico, to Los Angeles, California, and was used by many types of traders, from Spanish slave dealers to American horse traders. Today, the route is still marked in spots by deep wagon ruts where hundreds of traders once traveled.

title: Barn Owl
text:
Someone figured out that if all the offspring from one pair of field mice were allowed to live and reproduce, in four short years there would be mice 4 feet deep covering the whole state of Utah!

We can thank the owls, along with some other predators, for keeping this from happening. Some owls will eat several mice every night. The barn owl is one of these.

The barn owl is known by its heart-shaped face, small dark eyes and long legs. It only comes out at night, so we seldom get to see it. It nests in barns, abandoned buildings and tree cavities.

title: Make a Stamp
text:
Materials

Squares and rectangles of wood

Tempera or poster paints

A wide brush and large flat tray or cookie sheet

Pencil

Thick cardboard

Glue

Scissors

Paper for printing on

Instructions

1. On the thick cardboard, draw several simple shapes, like a heart, star, square or triangle, that you want to print. You can draw the same shape several times, or you can alternate shapes to make a pattern.

2. Cut out the shapes and glue them onto your blocks of wood. You can make a long design by gluing your shapes onto a long rectangular piece of wood, or you can make a single design by just gluing one shape onto a small square piece of wood. Let the glue dry.

3. Put a few spoonfuls of paint onto the large tray or cookie sheet. Use a different tray for every color you'd like to use. Spread the paint around with your paintbrush so that it covers the entire tray with a thin layer of paint.

4. To stamp, press your block of wood, with the shape side down, into the tray of paint. Make sure all of your shapes are covered with paint. Press your painted block on your piece of paper. Lift your block up, and there's your design on the paper.

5. Repeat Step 4 until you get the design you want. Let the paint on the paper dry. Hang on a wall or fridge when you're finished.

Extra Activity:
You could make a stamp of your name out of cardboard. Just write your name in block letters on the cardboard, cut them out and paste them onto a wood block. Use your stamp in the same way you did the shapes.

Try using different thick materials for the stamps, such as sponges. They create a different texture.

title: Jim Bridger: The Grand Ol’ Man
text:
When Jim Bridger was only 8 years old, his father moved the family from Richmond, Virginia, to St. Louis, Missouri. St. Louis was a bustling city full of fur traders returning from grand adventures out West. While listening to these men tell their tall tales, Jim decided that this was the life for him. At the age of 17, Jim Bridger joined a beaver-trapping expedition up the Upper Missouri River led by William Ashley and Andrew Henry.

While working for William Ashley, Jim came to what is now the state of Utah. He explored, trapped, traded and discovered that this was, indeed, the life for him. In 1824, when Jim was only 20 years old, he proved what a great explorer he had become when he set out on a journey to settle a bet. Jim and several of the other trappers in his group disagreed over where the Bear River led once it left the Cache Valley. Jim agreed to explore the river and find out where it ended up. He followed the river until in emptied into a huge lake of salt water, which he believed was an arm of the Pacific Ocean. Actually, Jim Bridger had become the first white man ever to set eyes on the Great Salt Lake.

Jim Bridger continued to explore the area, learning to speak Spanish, French and six American Indian languages so he could communicate with just about anyone he might meet during his travels. One of the famous men Jim Bridger met was Brigham Young, who was bringing his followers West to settle in Utah. Jim was worried that the group wouldn't be able to survive the harsh climate here and he told Brigham Young his concerns. He even promised the Mormon leader that he would pay him $1,000 for the first bushel of corn grown in the Salt Lake Valley. Jim was surprised to see what the Mormons were able to do once they brought water to the land!

One of Jim Bridger's greatest accomplishments came in 1850 when he discovered a shortcut through the Rocky Mountains. The shorter route was named "Bridger's Pass" and it proved to be a much better route than South Pass, used by travelers at the time. This pass was later used as an overland mail route and a Union Pacific Railroad Line. Today, Interstate 80 runs through Bridger's Pass.

Jim Bridger also started the American Fur Company, built Fort Bridger and served as a guide for many companies heading West. He is one of the most famous of all mountain men and is often called the "Grand Ol' Man of the Rockies."

title: Famous Trappers and Traders of Utah
text:
This week, we are going to read about the famous trappers who left their names on Utah towns, mountains, streams, forests and counties.

1. Jedediah S. Smith

Jedediah Smith did much exploring of Utah as he worked in a beaver-trapping company. He was the first white man after Escalante to explore Utah top to bottom. Along with two other men, he purchased the Rocky Mountain Fur Company. He drew the first map of the central Rockies and the Great Basin. Smith rediscovered the South Pass, making it well known to others. At one time, Smith met American Indian trappers who had been robbed and were lost. He agreed to guide them back to their post in exchange for all the furs they had trapped. He was famous for always carrying a Bible on his trips.

2. William Henry Ashley

Mountain men sometimes banded together to hunt for food. William Henry Ashley first organized the Rocky Mountain Fur Company along with Andrew Henry. He hired many of the famous mountain men (men who lived like American Indians) to trap fur for him. He was responsible for planning the huge "Trapper's Rendezvous" held in Utah each year. At the rendezvous, the trappers, or those who trapped fur-bearing animals, could trade or sell their furs without having to travel all the way back East. They also bought supplies and enjoyed themselves for a few days. Ashley was also the first recorded white man to boat down the Green River. It held many dangers and much excitement, but mountain men thrived on such things.

3. Peter Skene Ogden

Peter Skene Ogden was a tough mountain man. He was the leader of a number of Snake River expeditions. He worked for the Hudson's Bay Company, which was a British fur-trading company. There was rivalry between the American and British trappers over the trapping grounds. On his first expedition into Utah, an American company challenged him to a fight, but he remained calm and refused to open fire on them. He was a tough fighter, but not a foolish one. The city of Ogden was named after this great fur-trapping leader.

4. Etienne Provost

Etienne Provost was a French-Canadian who became a fur trapper in Utah. Provo City, Provo River and Provo Canyon were all named after him. He braved difficult times as all mountain men did. He was once invited to smoke the peace pipe with the Snake Indians. He and his men left their guns and knives as requested by the American Indians only to be attacked during the ceremony. Provost and three or four other men escaped, but many others were killed. The American Indians wanted to get revenge for injuries caused by other white explorers.

5. Jim Bridger

Jim Bridger, another fur-trapping mountain man, is credited with the discovery of the Great Salt Lake. After tasting the salty water, he decided it was an arm of the Pacific Ocean. Bridger started early in life as a trapper. He was an explorer as well and in his later life became a guide (one who helps others find their way). He established a trading post called Fort Bridger. Bridger knew the American Indian ways as well as any white person, and his wife was an American Indian woman. He was also famous for his tall tales.

title: Duchesne County
text:
Named after a French-Canadian Trapper
County Seat: Duchesne
Population: 14,371

Duchesne County's greatest claim to fame is the beautiful 5 High Uinta Mountains. These majestic mountains are home to Mirror Lake, Moon Lake and Grandaddy Lake, some of our state's most beautiful and popular camping and fishing spots. Starvation Reservoir is also found in Duchesne County. The High Uintas are great for backpacking and hiking trips. King's Peak, Utah's highest mountain at 13,498 feet, is also found in the Uinta Mountains. Once part of the huge Uintah and Ouray Indian Reservation, most of Duchesne County is now owned by individual Indians or controlled by the Ute Indian Tribe. These Indians make a living by farming and by raising cattle and sheep. Area farmers also produce potatoes, alfalfa and dairy products. The hunting and fishing are fantastic here, but if you want to hunt or fish on American Indian property, you will need to get a special permit. Duchesne is also home to many important natural resources such as oil, coal, natural gas, gravel, sand and gilsonite (a hard, tar-like substance used in making paints, asphalt, insulation, etc.). Oil and gas refining are Duschene County's largest industries.

title: What is meant by the term, “Mad as a Hatter?”
text: During the 1700 and 1800s, beaverfelt hats were very popular throughout Europe. In order to make the beaver pelts into hats, hatters, or hat makers, soaked the fur in mercury. Mercury is the heavy, silvery liquid that is used in thermometers. Mercury was used to soften up the pelts and make them easier to shape. The mercury also put off fumes that caused nerve damage to the hatter. Although people didn't understand why at the time, many hatters went mad, or crazy, from breathing these dangerous fumes each day.

title: Fur-Bearing Mammals
text: The fur-bearing mammals of Utah include: 1. beaver, 2. otter, 3. badger, 4. weasel and 5. mink. They are all prized for their furs, which bring top-market price. The most popular of these animals in the days of the fur trapper was the beaver. At one time, the beaver-felt hat was very fashionable in the East and in Europe. Because of this, large companies of fur trappers were sent to Utah to trap beavers. It is these trappers who explored and settled Utah.

title: New U.S. National Monuments
text:
Do you know how many national monuments there are in the United States? President Obama approved five new national monuments in March 2013. These and other U.S. monuments preserve national resources so that visitors can honor special people and events of the past.

One is the First State National Monument in Delaware. It’s the state’s first national park site, and it tells about the early settlement of the Delaware colony and how Delaware was the first state to ratify, or approve, the U.S. Constitution. Another is the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad National Monument in Maryland. It honors Ms. Tubman, who bravely helped slaves escape to freedom using the Underground Railroad. It is located on Maryland’s Eastern Shore. There is also the Rio Grande del Norte National Monument in New Mexico. It is an important habitat for many birds and wildlife, and it has a collection of petroglyphs (rock drawings or carvings) and other archaeological and cultural resources.

The Charles Young Buffalo Soldiers National Monument is in Wilberforce, Ohio. It preserves the home of Colonel Charles Young, who was an officer in the U.S. Army. He was the first African American to become a Colonel. And last, the San Juan Islands National Monument is in Washington State’s Puget Sound. It is a chain of islands, an archipelago, and there are 450 total! People can visit historic lighthouses and view cultural resources and fossils dating back 12,000 years.

President Theodore Roosevelt signed the Antiquities Act into law in 1906. Since then, 16 presidents have used this Act to preserve our national resources. Research the Antiquities Act online or at a library with the help of a trusted adult and find out how many national monuments there are in the United States. (Hint: There are over 100!) Which ones are most interesting to you? Have you ever visited any?

title: Clarity of Expression: Father Junípero Serra and the California Missions
text:
Do you like to give speeches? Can you convince others to see things your way? Then maybe you have a gift for expressing yourself clearly.

Father Junípero Serra was a Franciscan monk who some might call one of the “founding fathers” of California. He was born in Spain in 1713 and became a priest in his mid 20s. Many people noticed how well he spoke, or how clearly he expressed himself, during his powerful sermons, and he soon became a university professor.

Father Serra wanted to work as a Spanish missionary, so he first traveled to Mexico City in 1749. He started missionary work with the Sierra Gorda Indians. Soon he was made head of the Spanish missions in Baja (lower) California. Next, the Spanish governor asked him to start missions in Alta (upper) California. Father Serra personally built eight missions there and supervised the start of many more from San Diego to San Francisco.

Father Serra helped convert thousands of American Indians to Christianity. They lived and worked in the missions, but life was harsh. Many Indians died from overwork and diseases. But the missions kept going because of Father Serra’s preaching and care. His sermons were so dramatic that he would sometimes pound his chest with a stone or touch a lit torch to his chest.

Father Serra used his clarity of expression for what he thought was good. He argued with the Spanish army to get control of the missions. He even convinced Mexican officials to send more money and soldiers for his missions. Spanish colonists settled the area around the missions, which is all now the state of California.

Do you think you have a good ability to express yourself clearly as Father Serra did? What topic do you feel strongly about?
