title: Kit Carson: The Pathfinder’s Pathfinder
text:
Although he had no education and could neither read nor write, Kit Carson went on to become one of the greatest explorers and frontiersmen the West has ever known.

When Kit Carson was only 9 years old, his father died and Kit had to go to work in order to survive. He became an apprentice (someone who is legally required to work for someone until he learns a skill) to a saddle maker in Franklin, Missouri, but he hated the job. He ran away to Independence, Missouri, with hopes of joining in the excitement of the Western frontier. Independence was then known as the "jumping off point" for anyone wanting to head west because the Santa Fe and Oregon trails both started here.

When Carson got to Independence, he was thrilled to find traders and frontiersmen who told him exciting stories about life out west. Since Carson had run away from his job and had no education, he decided to join a wagon train and find out for himself what the frontier was really like.

After going west, Kit Carson became a fur trapper. He used Taos, New Mexico, as a base camp for his fur trapping expeditions and traveled from there all over the West. He learned all about the frontier regions from the Rocky Mountains to California.

Because he knew these regions so well, he became a guide for others who wanted to come here. Kit Carson was hired by the famous explorer John C. Fremont and helped guide him in his explorations through Oregon, California, the Central Rocky Mountains and the Great Basin. John Fremont was often called "The Pathfinder" because of the many routes he marked and the maps he made. Since Kit Carson served as Fremont's guide, he became known as "The Pathfinder's Pathfinder."

Together, Fremont and Carson mapped many important areas of Utah and the West. They found a new route over the Sierra Mountains which is now known as Carson Pass. Carson City, Nevada, is another spot that still carries Kit Carson's name.

Fremont wrote interesting articles and reports about his expeditions and he often mentioned Kit Carson and his amazing skills as a frontiersman. These articles told stories about Carson's adventures and when people read about them, Carson quickly became a national hero. One of Carson's interesting adventures involved a meeting with a couple of unfriendly bears. Two grizzly bears attacked Kit and he was able to climb a tree to get away from them. He dropped his gun, however, and had to stay in the tree for several hours until the bears decided to leave so he could climb down. Stories about Kit Carson grew and were exaggerated, or stretched, until many believed that Carson had super human abilities.

Kit Carson went on to serve as a wagon guide, an Indian agent and even a general in the U.S. Army. He served during the Civil War and also led a fight against the Navajo in the New Mexico area.

Kit Carson moved to Colorado after the Civil War ended. He planned to start a ranch in the area, but he died there in 1868. His body was later buried near his old home in Taos, New Mexico.

Kit Carson was a great Western pioneer who became famous for his exciting adventures on the wild frontier. People still remember this famous trapper, explorer and guide who ran away to explore the West and came to be known as "The Pathfinder's Pathfinder."

title: Weber County
text:
Named for John H. Weber, an early fur trapper killed by American Indians near the river that bears his name.
County Seat: Ogden
Population: 196,533

Weber County is Utah's second smallest county in size, but it has the third largest population, with nearly 290 people per square mile. In the days of the fur trappers, the Ogden area was known as Ogden's Hole. In trapper language, "hole" was another name for valley. Ogden's Hole was the original site of the area's trapper rendezvous, as well as many Shoshone Indian camps. Later, the railroad came to Ogden, making it the transportation center of the state. The center has since shifted to the Salt Lake area, now that trucks, busses and air freighters now serve many of our transportation needs. Ogden is known as home of the Browning Firearms Company and the Firearm Museum. John M. Browning invented the machine gun and made great improvements to rifles and pistols. His shop and many of his guns can still be seen at this Ogden museum. Popular recreational areas in Weber County include Snow Basin Ski Resort, Ogden Bay and Eccles Dinosaur Park.

title: Why do leaves change color?
text: When fall arrives in Utah, you can't help but notice the beautiful colored leaves that cover the mountainsides. What causes the leaves to change from green to shades of red, orange and yellow? Each year, as the temperature drops and the days shorten, a corky layer of cells forms at the joint between each leaf stem and twig. These cells cut off the flow of sap to the leaf. Without this flow of sap, chlorophyll, the special substance that turns leaves green, dies. The other pigments, or colors that aren't visible when chlorophyll is present, then get the chance to show their true colors, and what beautiful colors they are. The amounts and combinations of pigments in the leaves determine the stunning colors that paint our mountainsides each autumn.

title: Fur-Bearing Mammal Tracks
text: You may see these fur-bearing mammal tracks in the snow. There are several other tracks in Utah that you can look out for also. Next time you go out exploring, see if you can spot bobcat, deer, elk or brown bear tracks. There are many more, so have fun exploring.

title: Making the World a Kinder Place
text:
We sometimes wonder why bad things happen to innocent people. Although we may never understand it, we can do our best to keep things like this from happening in the future. When we do this, we are doing our part to make the world a kinder place, without anger and violence. One way to do this is by making a plan to replace bullying and violence with kindness. The Cool to Be Kind (C2BK) program was developed to help students create programs in their classes and schools that are based on pro-kindness – doing nice things for others. Students look for ways to “pay it forward” each day. Paying it forward means that when someone thanks you for doing something nice, you ask that person to pay it forward by doing something nice for someone else. By paying it forward, kindness continues to spread across the world and people start thinking kinder thoughts and ways that they can help other people. What are some ways you could practice paying it forward? How about doing yard work for an elderly neighbor for free? Or inviting a new student to eat lunch with you and your friends? What about giving up your seat on the bus to someone who looks tired, or helping someone pick up something they have dropped? Thinking kind thoughts and acting on them with acts of kindness is a simple change that you can do to change the world.

Teachers: Go to www.pifexperience.org to find out more about starting a C2BK program at your school!

title: Sharing Public Space: Vitus Bering and Russian Colonies in Alaska
text:
Imagine traveling 6,000 miles over land with supplies for an expedition, and THEN sailing through frigid seas to look for a new world. This was the job given to Vitus Bering, a Danish navigator who sailed for the Russian navy. Peter the Great, czar (ruler) of Russia, asked Bering to explore the eastern coast of Russia. He was wondering if land connected Asia and North America.

Bering’s first trip began in 1725. After spending three years getting his supplies to eastern Russia, Bering sailed along the coastline. He didn’t see any land to the east, and he didn’t realize he was sailing in the narrow passage between Russia and Alaska. This waterway is now called the Bering Strait.

Bering led another expedition in 1741. This time his ship landed on Kayak Island, off the coast of Alaska. They explored some of the Aleutian Islands and met the native people there, the Aleut. He was the first European to arrive in present-day Alaska.

Bering died before returning to Russia, but his voyages paved the way for Russian settlements in North America. Many fur traders came to the area. In 1799 the Russian government established a fur-trading operation in Alaska. Furs from foxes, sea otters and seals were very valuable.

Unfortunately, the Russians took advantage of the native people just as some Europeans had done in settling New England. The Russians took over their lands and forced them to hunt for furs. They also brought new diseases, which killed many natives.

Today, the Aleut people continue to live along the western coast of North America, and their population has grown. What might have been different if the Russians and the Aleut had shared public space fairly? Where in your community is there a debate over public land? How should such debates be handled?

title: Government Explorers
text:
This week, we will learn about the men who mapped, surveyed, studied and wrote about the new Utah frontier. They were explorers, people who had the courage to go where few had dared to go before.

When astronauts of today blast off into space, hoping to explore unknown frontiers, the world follows their adventures and can’t wait to see what new facts they will uncover. Just as astronauts are the explorers of today, government scouts were the explorers of yesterday. When early government explorers such as John C. Fremont set out on their journeys into the unknown Western frontier, the rest of the country awaited their return, anxious to find out what new and exciting information they would bring back. In this week’s newspaper, we will learn more about these early Utah heroes and find out more about their exciting accomplishments.

1. John Wesley Powell

John Wesley Powell, a former Army major who lost his right arm in battle, received money from the Smithsonian Institute and the government to explore the Green and Colorado rivers. Powell and his men traveled more than 800 miles by boat, studying the mountains and canyons along the way. Powell sent many reports to the government detailing the geology and the types of plant and animal life found in the area. He also studied the American Indians living along the Green and Colorado rivers. Powell was well known as a good leader and a thorough explorer. Lake Powell was later named after this man.

2. Howard Stansbury

Howard Stansbury was a U.S. topographical engineer, or mapmaker. He surveyed, or measured and mapped, the Salt Lake Valley and other regions throughout the state to find the best route for a railroad. He made a remarkably detailed study of the Great Salt Lake, mapping out the entire area. Stansbury Island, one of the islands in the Great Salt Lake, is named after him.

3. John C. Fremont

John C. Fremont was an important government explorer. He did not blaze (break a trail through unknown territory) new trails, but he made maps and reports of the trails that were already there. The charts and reports he made were extremely helpful to people immigrating to Utah and other parts of the West. Fremont was well educated and well qualified for the helpful work he did. He made several explorations of the Utah region. He was hard working and enthusiastic as well as patient and steady. Fremont had an interest in and knowledge of plant and animal life along the trails and studied and reported on the American Indian tribes and their habits.

4. Christopher (Kit) Carson

Christopher (Kit) Carson was a mountain man who led an interesting and exciting life. Kit served as a guide to Fremont on many of his expeditions (planned trips through unknown territories). During the time he was guiding half of Fremont’s group, he was sent to a peak across the Salt Flats to look for water at its base. There he found water, grass and wood. This peak became known as Pilot Peak, since it piloted, or guided, others across the Great Salt Lake Desert to the springs on the other side. Kit was also a soldier in the Mexican and Civil wars and an American Indian agent.

5. John Gunnison

John Gunnison was part of Howard Stansbury’s railroad survey expedition. Gunnison was later chosen as the leader of a return expedition to the Rocky Mountain area to survey for another railroad. On his return trip to the West, Gunnison and several of his men were massacred by a group of American Indians near the Sevier River in the Manti area. Since Gunnison had been a good friend to the Mormons and they were saddened by his death, they named the central Utah city of Gunnison after him.

6. Captain B. L. E. Bonneville

Historians agree that even though Captain B.L.E. Bonneville didn’t actually do a lot of original research, he did make one of the best early maps of the entire Great Basin region. Most of the information captain Bonneville used to make his maps came from mountain men and other explorers, but he was very talented at putting all the facts together to make accurate and useful maps. Ancient Lake Bonneville was named after him and he was the first to bring wagons west of the divide through South Pass. Washington Irving, a famous author, published a book called “The Adventures of Captain Bonneville,” which brought great fame to the captain and encouraged settlement in the far West.

title: Mountain Men in Utah
text:
People who own historical, old black-powder rifles like to get together with other antique gun-owners to show off their shooting skills. Nearly every weekend from Memorial Day to Labor Day, several black powder gun clubs sponsor competition shoots throughout the state of Utah. Shooting is open to anyone who has a primitive black-powder gun.

Family Events and Rendezvous

These shooting matches have grown into competitions for the whole family. They are much like the old mountain-man rendezvous of days gone by. There are tomahawk and knife-throwing contests for adults and children 8 years old and older. At some events, a special mortar gun is used to shoot candy into the air as the children scramble to get their share. There are also mountain man costume contests, American Indian fancy dancing demonstrations, evening square dancing for everyone and tall-tale telling competitions around the campfire. There is even a "Trader's Row" where handcrafted items are bartered for sale. In fact, you can barter for just about anything of interest to mountain man fans. Most of these local weekend rendezvous are attended by between 300-500 people.

Fort Bridger Rendezvous

The granddaddy of all local rendezvous takes place at the site of the original Fort Bridger in Wyoming, near the Utah-Wyoming border. It is a weekend-long event held each year on Labor Day weekend. The first Fort Bridger rendezvous was held in 1973 and the event has been growing steadily ever since. More than 20,000 people from Utah, Wyoming, Colorado, Idaho and Montana attend the event each year.

Many tourists and traders come in campers and trailers. Others set up primitive lodges (American Indian tepees) and dress in buckskin covered with colorful beads and trimmed in fur.

When and Where are Local Events Held?

Second Week of May - Dog Valley, west of Nephi

Memorial Day Weekend - Cache Valley, Sardine Canyon, Brigham City and Fort Buenaventura in Ogden

Fourth of July Weekend - Paiute Powwow in Cedar City

24th of July Weekend - Utah State Festival of the American West in Logan

First Weekend in August - Golden Spike at Pineview Reservoir in Ogden

Late August - Heber Canyon TNT (Traders 'n' Trappers) at Diamond Fork

Second Week of September - Depot Days in Eureka

Reliving Utah history is fun for the people who attend these events. It has become a fascinating hobby, as well as an educational pastime.

title: The Anasazi Free-Trappers: Mountain Men of Today
text:
If you thought the mountain men of Utah were dead and gone, think again. The Anasazi Free Trappers are alive and well- and sharpening their mountain man skills all year long.

The Anasazi Free Trappers are a St. George -based group of "true buck skinners." Buckskinners are people who dress, act and live like the mountain men of the early 1800s.

What sets this group of buckskinners apart is their constant devotion to their craft. While most buckskinners go to a "rendezvous" (or get together) once or twice a year, these Utah mountain men practice year round.

They have their own land (120 acres) near Pine Valley, Utah, set aside just for their own activities. They meet monthly to camp, visit and remember history by reenacting it.

They teach classes on bow making, gun smithing, hide tanning, weaving and more. They also have competitions for knife, spear and hatchet throwing, black powder shooting and archery. They are family oriented and include people of all ages in their activities.

These Free Trappers are regular people with regular jobs, but they have an appreciation for the hardship their ancestors endured while trying to make a living in one of the toughest environments around. And like their ancestors, these modern day mountain men are required to have only two things (besides a good costume): good manners and common sense.

title: The Mountain Man
text:
Between 1820 and 1840, a hardy and reckless group of men roamed the Utah mountain wilderness making a living as fur trappers. The mountain men loved to tell tall tales. Below are a few actual "mountain man" tall tales for you to read and enjoy.

Whoa, Molly!

Mountain men took special pride in their horses. There was one particular horse that had the reputation for being the fastest-stopping horse ever known. Her name was Molly, and if you hollered, "Whoa, Molly!" she would instantly screech to a halt wherever she was, not moving another inch.

Molly fell into the hands of an outlaw who used her to his advantage. He would steal from the American Indians or mountain men in the area and then ride away on Molly. When he was chased by his victims, the outlaw would jump Molly right off a cliff, but just before she crashed to the ground, he would shout, "Whoa, Molly!" and she would stop in midair. The outlaw would then gently step down off Molly, getting away from his pursuers every time.

Finally, some American Indians caught the outlaw and his famous horse. They tied the outlaw up and discussed what to do with Molly. They decided that if they killed the horse and ate her, they too would have her magical ability. They prepared Molly for the barbecue and readied for the feast that would give them the power to stop in midair.

None of the braves dared to eat before their chief, so each one took his first bite in hand, waiting for the chief to taste the meat. The chief put the meat in his mouth and the braves did the same. Then the chief chewed his meat and the braves did the same. Then the chief started to swallow his meat, and the braves did the same. It was then that the outlaw hollered, "Whoa, Molly!" Would you believe that all of those American Indians choked to death?

Ol' Gabe Grabs Some Fast Food

Most trappers and fur traders called Jim Bridger by his nickname, which was Ol' Gabe. One day, Ol' Gabe was riding through a valley on his way to Yellowstone Lake. He had traveled all day long and was tired and hungry. Ol' Gabe chose a camp site near a boiling hot spring and decided that a dinner of fresh trout would surely hit the spot. Ol' Gabe put his line into the spring and before he knew it, he felt a sharp tug on the line. He reeled in his catch, and to his surprise, he found that the heat from the spring had cooked the fish as he pulled it out of the water. His dinner was perfectly boiled and ready to eat. For some reason he never could quite explain, the hot water in this spring floated on top of the icy waters below. This way, the fish could live in the cold water below and be cooked as they were pulled through the hot water above, making this spring the original "fast food" place. From then on, this spot became Ol' Gabe's favorite fishing hole - especially when he was in a hurry!

Mountain Man Remedies

Mountain men didn't have doctors, nurses or hospitals to help them when they got sick or hurt. Instead, they used whatever was handy to treat illness and injury. Look below to see some of the remedies (medicines) that mountain men used when they weren't feeling their best.

Snakebites: the bite was cut crosswise and treated with milkweed, tobacco juice, whiskey or black mud.

Rattlesnake bite: drinking whiskey was supposed to stop the venom from working without making the person drunk.

Rashes: a mixture of molasses and sulphur was rubbed on the rash to stop the itch.

Earache: wood smoke was blown into the painful ear to stop the throbbing.

Sore throat: a strip of heavily-peppered fat was wrapped around the neck to take away the soreness.

Headaches: a band of rattlesnake rattlers was worn as a hatband to help get rid of the headache.

Bleeding: flour and turpentine were mixed together and rubbed on the wound.

Canker Sores: gunpowder was rubbed on the sores to help them heal faster.

Diarrhea: peppermint leaves were brewed into a tea to stop diarrhea.

The Cold Winter - By Jim Bridger

One winter, it snowed 70 days and 70 nights without stopping. The snow was 70 feet deep. Naturally this was a little hard on the buffalo. In fact, it killed them all, but the cold preserved the meat. When the spring thaw came, I tumbled all those frozen buffalo into the Salt Lake. That way, I had enough pickled buffalo for me and the whole Ute nation for years and years!

title: Cache County
text:
Named for the many furs "cached," or hidden, there by the fur trappers.
County Seat: Logan
Population: 91,391

Cache Valley, located in the far northern portion of Utah, marks the spot where many mountain men once cached, or hid, their furs. Mountain man Jim Bridger set out from the Cache Valley on a famous expedition that ended in his discovery of the Great Salt Lake. Today, Cache County is known for the many dairy herds that are raised here. Modern cheese processing plants make milk from these cows into many types of famous Cache Valley cheese. Condensed and evaporated milk is also produced at several plants in Cache Valley.

Cache County is also famous for its beautiful scenery. Logan Canyon offers fantastic fishing opportunities and breathtaking fall colors. It is also home to a 1,500-year-old Jardine juniper tree known as "Old Juniper."

Each winter, hundreds of visitors flock to Hardware Ranch in Blacksmith Fork Canyon to see wild game, particularly deer and elk, feeding on the ranch. Visitors ride horse-drawn sleighs around the nine-mile fenced feeding area where deer and elk are fed hay to help them survive the winter weather.

Utah State University in Logan was founded in 1888 as a school for training better farmers and forest rangers. Today, it is a well-known university that provides schooling in all kinds of subjects.

title: Can crickets tell the temperature?
text:
Yes! If you count cricket chirps, they will tell you the temperature. This is the way it's done:

Fahrenheit:

Count the number of chirps from one cricket (or many in unison) for exactly 15 seconds. Add 37 to that number. That will be the temperature in Fahrenheit.

Celsius:

This is a little harder. Count the chirps in 2 5 seconds, divide by 3 and add 4. There you have it!

Do you think you would hear a cricket chirping if it's below freezing (3 2 degrees Fahrenheit)? Why or why not?

title: Cache
text:
The fur trappers and mountain men were soon burdened with hundreds of furs that were difficult for them to carry around. They devised a way to hide the pelts (animal fur and skin).

They would dig a deep hole and line it with bark and stones. Then they would carefully place their furs into the hole and put logs over it. This creative hiding place was called a "cache." Cache County got its name from the hundreds of caches that were once found there.

title: Jim Bridger Comes to Life!
text:
An Art Project You Can Do

This art project makes a mysterious picture in which the eyes play the most important part. Remember the tall tales Jim Bridger used to tell us? Here is a tale we can tell about him! When you follow the directions, Bridger's eyes will appear to come alive and he watches you move around the room.

Directions

1. Carefully cut out the picture of Jim Bridger, along with the eye pieces.

2. Cut a slit in each of the eyes.

3. Glue each eye together in the form of a cone with the iris and pupil on the INSIDE.

4. After cutting out the eye slits, carefully glue the cones on the BACK of the picture.

5. Hang up the picture and watch Bridger's eyes follow you wherever you go!

title: Martha Hughes Cannon: "Pioneer" in Women's Rights
text:
The Mormon pioneers were the first white people to permanently settle in Utah. The members of this religious group, founded by Joseph Smith, were forced out of their homes in Illinois by their neighbors who didn't understand or agree with their beliefs. Under the direction of Brigham Young, the Mormons traveled to the Salt Lake Valley hoping to find safety and freedom from persecution (harassment and poor treatment). Life was hard for these early pioneers (people who explore or settle a new region), especially for the women who endured many hardships and who were expected to do work that had previously been done only by men. In this issue, we will learn more about many of the pioneer women who helped make Utah a comfortable, civilized place to live.

Martha Hughes Cannon, or "Mattie," as her friends called her, was born in Wales in 1857. Her family joined the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints when Mattie was very young and they soon decided to emigrate (leave their own country to settle permanently in another) to Utah. They arrived in Salt Lake in September 1861.

Mattie loved learning and decided at an early age that she wanted to become a doctor. There weren't many female doctors in the late 1800s, but Mattie didn't care. She knew that if she worked hard, she could achieve this goal. She studied hard and became a school teacher at the age of 14 years old, not because she loved to teach, but because she knew teaching would help her earn the money she needed for college. In order to pay for her education, she worked as both a school teacher and a typesetter while attending the University of Deseret in Salt Lake City.

After graduating from the University of Deseret in 1875 with a degree in chemistry, Mattie knew it was time to move on to bigger things. She entered the University of Michigan, where she studied for three years. She then graduated from the Auxiliary School of Medicine of the University of Pennsylvania and also received a diploma from the National School of Elocution and Oratory, where she learned to speak and communicate clearly, with proper pronunciation. Mattie planned to make a difference in the world and she wanted to be able to speak her mind in the most understandable way possible.

After finishing her education, Mattie returned to Salt Lake City and began working as a doctor at Deseret Hospital. While busy with her career, Mattie met and married Angus M. Cannon. By this time, Mattie was 27 years old and was likely seen as an "old maid" by most people at that time. Angus was 23 years older than Maddie and he already had three other wives. Mattie became his fourth plural wife and together, she and Angus had three children.

Mattie didn't let marriage and children stop her from staying active in the community. She believed women should be allowed to vote, and she worked hard to help bring them that right. She was also interested in politics. In 1896, she decided to run for the office of state senator as a democrat. She ran against several other candidates, including her own husband, and won the election, becoming the first woman in the entire United States to be elected as a state senator.

As a state senator, Mattie worked hard to pass laws that would protect those who couldn't protect themselves. She was also outspoken in favor of the right to practice polygamy (the practice of having more than one wife at a time) and believed it helped her to serve as she did. After all, with more than one wife in the family, they could take turns doing the household tasks, giving each wife more time to serve in the community. Mattie declared, "Somehow I know that women who stay home all the time have the most unpleasant homes there are. You give me a woman who thinks about something besides cook stoves and wash tubs and baby flannels, and I'll show you, nine times out of 10, a successful mother."

After serving two terms as a state senator, Mattie kept busy working for the health department and later, after the death of her husband, she moved to California. She practiced medicine here until her death in 1932. Martha Hughes Cannon was a woman of courage and ambition who never let the fact that she was a woman stop her from succeeding in areas where women weren't yet welcome.

title: 40 Years of the Oregon Trail Computer Game
text:
Before there was Wii, before there was PSP, before DS, Game Boy, Xbox, Nintendo 64, Playstation, Super Nintendo, regular Nintendo, Atari or even Pong, there was the Oregon Trail. Played by kids since 1 9 7 1, the Oregon Trail may be one of the longest running and most played games in history- and it's educational.

Created by a computer-programming history teacher, the Oregon Trail began as the most basic of computer games. The player had to make purchases - food, bullets, extra axles and wheels for the wagon, medicine and so on- and then set off on a journey on the Oregon Trail.

Along the way, the player would face different hardships, including disease and death. The Oregon Trail taught lots of life lessons to elementary students by using the game to show how pioneers may have had to face wild animal attacks, hunger, measles, typhoid, cholera, dysentery, exhaustion, diarrhea, broken legs and even drowning in swollen rivers.

Players could also hunt bison, deer, rabbits and squirrels to earn food for their family. Originally, to fire the gun, players had to type the words "BANG" or "POW" as quickly as they could. Later, players had to assign a direction to shoot with a keyboard and then fire. Years later, when the mouse became a standard way to control a computer, the player could mouse some crosshairs over their target.

As gaming evolved, so did the game. Working its way from Apple II computers to PCs to cell phone operating systems such as the iPhone and Palm, the Oregon Trail is as instructional today as it was in 1971.

title: Utah's Early Pioneer Women
text:
The women who came to Utah in its early days needed strong backs, quick minds and courageous spirits in order to overcome the many challenges that they would face on a daily basis. In this week's issue, we will learn about three of Utah's early pioneer women who had what it took to succeed under difficult circumstances.

Fanny Brooks: Businesswoman and Jewish Community Leader

When Fanny Brooks and her husband, Julius, settled in Salt Lake City in the 1860s, they weren't the usual Mormon immigrants. Fanny and Julius were members of the Jewish faith and had come to America from Germany. They had heard that Salt Lake City was full of business opportunities, so they came here to try their luck at running a boarding house. Fanny took in boarders, or people who paid to live in her house and eat her meals, and soon, she and Julius had a thriving business. Not long after this, Brigham Young, the leader of the Mormon Church, told all of the Latter-day Saints to do business only with other members of the church. Fanny was so upset that she made an appointment with Brigham Young to tell him how she felt. Fanny left the meeting with a smile on her face. She had convinced President Young to encourage church members to continue boarding at her house. Because of this experience, Fanny and Brigham Young became friends and the two often worked together to help the Jewish community in Salt Lake City. Because of his respect for Fanny, President Young later donated the land for a Jewish cemetery in Salt Lake City.

Fanny knew how to treat her customers right. She and her husband later bought a millinery (hat) shop, which she ran with great care. One day, when she was out running errands, her husband was left to deal with a difficult female customer. After she had looked at every hat in the shop and failed to find one she liked, Julius said, "My dear lady, if I had hats to make ugly ladies look pretty, I would be a millionaire and live in New York." As the angry customer was storming out the door, Fanny returned and calmed her down. Before the woman left, she had bought not just one, but three hats after Fanny told her how lovely she looked in each one.

Fanny Brooks knew how to smooth hurt feelings, solve problems and help people with different backgrounds and opinions learn to get along. She is one of our great pioneer women.

Hilda Anderson Erickson: Pioneer "Working Woman"

Today's women aren't the only ones who know how to balance a family and a career. Hilda Anderson came to Utah in 1866 at the age of 7 and had at least four different careers, along with the full time job of raising her two children.

Hilda was only 14 years old when she began her first career as a seamstress, or a woman who sews clothing for money. She did excellent work and could make an entire shirt or coat in one day, without the use of a sewing machine.

After Hilda got married, she and her husband moved to Deep Creek, Utah, near the Nevada border. She helped her husband run the farm, but she felt that the women in the area needed better medical care. She temporarily shipped her new baby off to her mother in Grantsville and spent the next year in Salt Lake, learning to be a midwife (a nurse who is trained to help women have babies). Once she finished her training, Hilda delivered every baby born in the Ibapah Valley over the next 20 years.

Hilda's next career began when she and her husband decided to build a small store to save other settlers the 100-mile-trip to Salt Lake City to buy supplies. Hilda bought the supplies, stocked the shelves, ran the store and opened her home to railroad workers who needed a place to stay. She even packed their lunches on work days.

Later in life, Hilda moved back to Grantsville and took a job for the Grantsville Farm Loan Association. She also served in many church and community positions and died at the age of 108, wearing out 11 cars in her travels around the state.

Mary Goble Pay: Courage During Hardship

Mary Goble Pay was only 11 years old when she and her family left England and made the long journey to the Salt Lake Valley. Her family made the final portion of their trip by handcart and when winter came early that year, Mary's feet were frozen.

When Mary finally made it to the Salt Lake Valley, her feet were so badly frozen that a doctor had to amputate, or cut off, all of her toes. Brigham Young promised young Mary that she would not lose any more of her feet, but the feet didn't heal properly and the flesh became infected. The doctor looked at her feet and told Mary that he must amputate both of them. She cried and refused, telling him that Brigham Young had promised her she wouldn't lose her feet. An old woman who lived in the area came to Mary and asked if she could help her. She made a special poultice, or warm, soft mass of herbs and plants, and put this poultice on Mary's feet each day. After three months of these treatments, Mary's feet were well.

The doctor saw Mary one day and said, "Well, Mary, I must say you have grit. I suppose your feet have rotted to the knee by this time." Mary told him that they were well and when he wouldn't believe her, she took off her shoes and socks and showed him. He couldn't believe his eyes!

Mary stretched and exercised her muscles each day until she was able to walk again. She went on to live a normal life, marrying and raising a large family.

title: Morgan County
text:
Named for Jedediah Morgan Grant, a Mormon pioneer
County Seat: Morgan
Population: 7,129

Morgan County is located in Northern Utah, near the Utah-Wyoming border. It is situated on one of the natural scenic pathways through the Wasatch Mountains. This route was once used by American Indians, fur trappers and pioneers as they traveled from place to place. Devil's Slide, an unusual and forbidding rock formation in Weber Canyon, has long been a natural landmark for travelers along this route.

Limestone is mined in Morgan County. It is then made into cement. Morgan is also home to the headquarters of Browning Arms, a company that makes many types of famous guns. Mink ranching is another profitable Morgan County business. The cool climate and high elevation helps the mink produce very fine and valuable furs.

Como Springs Resort is a popular Morgan County tourist attraction. These warm sulfur springs have been used for bathing and swimming since pioneer days.

Hunting is a popular sport in the county, especially for deer, pheasants, migratory fowl, chukars and rabbits. Trophy hunters flock to Lost Creek Lake State Park, hoping to bring home the big one.

title: What were common chores done by pioneer women?
text:

title: Silk Worms
text:
From 1855 until about 1905, the raising of silk worms was an important Utah industry. When the pioneers first arrived in Utah, Brigham Young wanted them to become self-sufficient as quickly as possible. He wanted the settlers to be able to raise their own crops and care for their own needs. Brigham Young believed raising silk worms would allow the pioneers to produce their own fine silks, as well as sell them in the East to earn much needed money.

Many pioneer women were given the job of raising silk worms. These women started out with a few ounces of silk worm eggs, which soon grew into three-inch worms that never seemed to stop eating. The silk worms ate pounds of mulberry leaves, which the women had to gather each day. Each silk worm then spun a cocoon, where the silk strands were located. Over a period of 48 hours, each silk worm produced 1,000 - 1,300 yards of silken fiber. The women then had to treat the cocoons to kill the worms inside, wash the cocoons, reel, or wind, the silk strands onto a cylinder, and then weave them into fine cloth.

Raising silk worms was a huge amount of work and after a few years, most pioneers gave up on the project. It was cheaper to buy silk from China than to spend the amount of time and effort it took to raise silk here in Utah.

title: A New Home
text:
It was the early 1840s, and violent mobs had forced the Mormon pioneers out of their homes in Nauvoo, Illinois. They were on their way to a new home somewhere in the West. Their wise leaders thought of a way to help these pioneer refugees make their way to the West. Read how Tommy and Betsy help carry out this plan.

Tommy turned over on the straw mattress in the bottom of the wagon box and pulled the patchwork quilt close around his ears. Any other morning, the bugle would have blown, and he would have been up, but the leaders had decided to stay in Garden Grove, and as a result he could stay in bed this one morning.

But the bugle blew crystal clear after all, right into Tommy's wagon box. Quickly, he put on his shoes, grabbed his coat and jumped out of the wagon. He met Father coming out of the tent.

"What's the matter?" Tommy asked.

"I don't know," replied his father. "Let's find out."

Together, they went over to the big bonfire where Brigham Young (the leader of the Mormon pioneers) was waiting for the men of the camp to gather. When they had all arrived, he began. "Today, the ground is in condition to plow. We can plant grain now, and by fall there will be a good harvest. If we're not still here, the pioneers coming after us will be able to harvest it. Those who are sick can stay here until they are better. Those who do not have enough food and clothing to go farther can stay here until they get what they need. The pioneers who come after us can use our houses until they are able to go on."

He paused, and the men were quiet, waiting for him to continue. "I have divided our camp into groups. One hundred will cut logs, 4 8 will build houses, 10 will build fences, 12 are to dig wells, and 10 will build bridges. The rest, numbering 175, will clear the land of brush, make some wooden plows and then plant grain."

As soon as Young had finished speaking, Tommy ran and told his mother about the new plan. "It's a wonderful way to help each other," she said. "Many of our friends in Nauvoo would start out west if they knew there was someplace along the way where they could get food and rest if they were sick."

"Maybe all our friends would come if they knew this," said Tommy wistfully, as he remembered the good times with the other boys back in Nauvoo.

"How can we let them know that there will be a house here for them?" asked Betsy, Tommy's sister.

"I think the leaders will let them know," Mother answered.

Just then, Father came into camp, very excited about his assignment. "I'm going to build houses," he said, "and, Tommy, you're going to help me!"

"Hooray!" said Tommy. Tommy's mother smiled as her two men walked off together.

The weeks that followed were busy ones. Every morning, the camp was awakened by the bugle. Everyone started to work as soon as breakfast was over and the morning prayers were said. Within two weeks, it was as if the little village, with all its houses, fences, bridges and wells, had been there for a long time. Around it were acres and acres of land that had been plowed, leveled and planted with wheat. Tommy and Betsy liked to imagine the pies and cakes they might have at harvest time. It had been a long time since they had tasted even a piece of bread made out of real flour instead of cornmeal. They were so tired of corn that sometimes they went to bed hungry rather than eat it.

Tommy was proud of the houses he helped build. They were made of logs stacked one on top of the other. (These early pioneer homes were log cabins.) His job was to fill the cracks between the logs with mud and grass. (Homes made out of mud were made from adobe.) It was a happy day when Tommy and Betsy moved with their father and mother into one of these houses. There was a fireplace at one end of a large room. Father made a table and some benches for the center of the room and a rough bed frame for one corner. Betsy and her mother made a rope spring by weaving a long, thin rope over the bed rails from front to back and from head to foot until the spring was woven into 3-inch squares.

"It makes the bed soft and jiggly," said Betsy when she sat on it.

"It's better than sleeping on hard boards," said Tommy, as he thought of his bed in the wagon box.

When everything was in place, Betsy looked around at her new home. A fire was burning in the fireplace, a potpie was simmering on the hearth, and a clean cloth was on the table, which had been set for supper. "It's a beautiful home," she said. "I hope we can live in it for a long time."

But Tommy and Betsy only lived in their house for three weeks. On June 1, Father told them, "We must leave in the morning for Council Bluffs. Brigham Young wants us to go there to build houses and plant crops as we have done here."

Tommy and Betsy looked sad. Mother tried to comfort them, saying, "It doesn't really matter where we live as long as we're together. It's the love that people have for each other that makes a home, not the place they live in."

When everything was packed and the family was ready to leave the next morning, they sat down for their last meal. Suddenly, there was the sound of wagons - many of them. "It must be a wagon train coming to join us," said Father. Instead of eating, the family went out on the road to greet the newcomers.

Tommy saw some friends in one of the wagons "Eliza, Elijah," he called. The newcomers turned and shouted for joy. Jumping out of the wagon, they ran to meet Betsy and Tommy.

Father invited Eliza and Elijah's family to supper. Mother made a bed so their mother could lie down. Betsy was glad she and her mother had made the rope springs so the bed would be more comfortable.

That night, before settling down in their wagon-box bed, Tommy said, "I'm glad Eliza and Elijah are going to live in our house."

"I am, too," said Betsy. "It is good that they have such a nice house to come home to."

This story is rewritten from a story by Mary Pratt Parrish. This is historical fiction, meaning that it is a fictitious story written about a true historical event. The Mormon pioneers really did build several settlements along the trail to the West where weary pioneer travelers could rest and eat. These settlements were called way stations.

title: Colonies Established by Brigham Young
text:
These are examples of the colonies (groups settling a new area) that were established by Brigham Young and the early pioneers. Did you know that Las Vegas was once a Mormon pioneer settlement? Brigham Young should see it now!

Brigham's Plan for Laying Out Streets and Towns

Brigham Young laid out the city of Salt Lake using the "two-coordinate system." He then told the surveyors who laid out other Utah towns to use the same system. This system made sure that the cities were planned in an orderly way and that addresses made sense and were easy to find.

Most Utah cities are laid out using the "two coordinate system." There are two main streets, usually called "Main" and "Center," and all other streets in the city are counted out from these two central streets. For example, the first street north of Main Street is called 100 North , or 1st North. The first street west of Center Street is called 100 West , or 1st West. The numbers increase as you travel away from Main Street or Center Street and decrease as you travel closer. By using this grid, it becomes very easy to find addresses using just two numbers, called coordinates.

Suppose you wanted to meet a friend someplace in "Utah Town." You could give your friend the coordinates, or numbers of 300 (or 3rd) East and 200 (or 2nd) North and your friend would know to meet you three streets east of Center Street and two streets north of Main Street.

(Note that 200 East is the same as 2nd East.)

title: Davis County
text:
Named for Captain Daniel C. Davis of the Mormon Battalion
County Seat: Farmington
Population: 238,994

If you enjoy amusement parks, you have probably visited Davis County, home of the Lagoon Amusement Park. The park includes roller coasters, adventure rides, arcade games and live entertainment. Pioneer Village and Lagoon-A-Beach Waterpark also add to the fun.

Davis County is Utah's smallest county in size, measuring only 630 square miles. Of these 630 miles, only 223 are made up of useable land, as the rest is either covered by the Great Salt Lake or Antelope Island. In spite of its small size, Davis County is the third largest county in Utah according to the number of people who live here. Because of its great location, right between Salt Lake and Ogden, and its rich farming soil, many people continue to make their homes here.

Hill Air Force Base, one of the largest military bases in the West, is located in Davis County. The base employs many military and non-military workers and is the largest employer in Davis County. At the Hill Aerospace Museum, visitors can view more than 80 military aircraft, missiles and aerospace vehicles.

Davis County is also home to several gasoline and oil refineries, which are located in the city of North Salt Lake.

Antelope Island State Park is another important Davis County attraction. There is a two-lane road that connects the mainland to this amazing island, where visitors will find hundreds of American bison, mule deer, antelope, coyotes, bobcats and game birds.

title: What was the cricket plague?
text:
Brigham Young and many of the other early pioneers returned to Illinois after they arrived in Utah. They helped to guide later groups of pioneers into Utah the following summer.

In 1847, the pioneers got a late start planting their crops, but they saved the marble-sized potatoes they harvested for seed for the next year. When they planted their crop in 1848, insects known as “Mormon crickets” swarmed on their precious harvest.

The pioneers fought hard with brooms, shovels, and fire to drive away the crickets, but the swarm came faster than they could fight. The pioneers were tired and discouraged. “We didn’t come here to starve,” they declared. “And we will not starve!” Soon after, they heard the noise of wings filling the sky. They saw flocks of gulls that landed and started eating the crickets. More gulls came until the crickets were destroyed. The California gull is now the state bird of Utah. On Temple Square in Salt Lake City, there is a monument to this bird that tells the story of the crickets and the gulls.

title: California Gull and Mormon Cricket
text:
The California Gull is probably the most easily recognized scavenger (one that lives on others' waste and leftovers) bird in Utah. Often called the seagull, it can be seen in freshly plowed fields, at garbage dumps and on the shores of the Great Salt Lake.

Our Utah seagulls aren't really "California" gulls at all, as they nest here in Utah. They do, however, spend their first winters in California before coming back to make their homes in Utah.

The Mormon cricket is a member of the katydid family and is related to the grasshopper. It ranges in color from dark brown to bluish black with antennae as long as its body, which can reach up to 5 inches in length!

The Mormon cricket lives in open fields and eats many plants, including grains and vegetables. Each cricket eats anywhere from 20 to 30 percent of its own body weight each day, with terrible results to fields and crops. It received its name from the cricket and gull incident in early pioneer Utah.

title: A Census Full of Treasure
text:
On April 2, 2012, the government released the 1940 census. A census is a count of all the people in the United States, and it is done every 10 years. It also gives other information about citizens’ jobs, income, birthplace and education level. The government only releases a census’ records to the public after 72 years have passed. The 1940 census was the first one done after the Great Depression and World War I. It shows how these events caused people to move around and where immigrants went. You can find interesting facts about family members and famous people. For example, the future President Ronald Reagan paid $135 in rent in 1940!

The 1940 census was the last time census takers went door-to-door to personally interview people and write down the information. For the 1950 census the government started using census questionnaires sent through the mail.

The release of the 1940 census data is different from past years. This information was made digital and released through the Internet. There are more than 3.8 million pages of data in this census. Genealogists, or people who study family backgrounds, use this information to trace family history. Researchers, like historians, often use the census as a primary source of information.

So, was this release a success? Well, so many people tried to get the information on its first day of release that the server crashed! If you would like to learn more about your family history you can go to the 1940 census site at: http://1940census.archives.gov/.

Reference: History News Network (hnn.us)

title: Porter Rockwell: “Samson of the West”
text:
"Have you heard of Porter Rockwell, the Mormon triggerite,
They say he hunts down outlaws when the moon is shining bright,
So if you rustle cattle, I'll tell you what to do,
Get the drop on Porter Rockwell, or he'll get the drop on you."

"Old Port Rockwell looks like a man, with a beard on his face and his hair in a braid,
But there's none in the West but Brigham who can look in his eyes and not be afraid."

These words come from some of the ballads (songs that tell a story) sung by many of the young cowboys, pioneers and even outlaws (people who didn't obey the law) about the famous Porter Rockwell. Porter was a close friend of the Mormon leaders Joseph Smith and Brigham Young. Joseph Smith once promised Porter that if he never cut his hair, no one could kill him. Because of this promise, Porter was sometimes called "Samson of the West" after a Bible character named Samson whose long hair gave him great strength.

Porter Rockwell lived at a time when outlaws didn't care much about the law and the person who was the best shot made his own laws. Those who were quick on the draw lived to fight another day, while those who hesitated were lost. The following story tells of a meeting between Porter Rockwell and Frank Slade, an outlaw who bet several men in California that he could shoot and kill Porter Rockwell. Porter was a U.S. marshal at the time this meeting took place.

At the south end of Salt Lake Valley, Porter Rockwell rode his wagon through the pass at the Point of the Mountain. He saw a familiar man on horseback.

"Excuse me, Mr. Rockwell. I mean to talk to you."

Porter glanced at him curiously, "Yeah?"

"My name is Frank Slade."

"What can I do for you?"

"Well I've come clear from California to settle something with you. And I've been following you longer than I care to admit."

"Oh? Why's that?"

"No particular reason - just to kill you." Slade pulled a revolver from behind his hat on the saddle horn.

Porter held back his surprise and kept his voice casual. "Why would you want to kill me?"

"A lot of people want to see you dead."

"Is that a fact?"

"A well-known fact."

"Well, I'm flattered," said Porter.

"You should be, but I reckon it's been worth my while. The wait I mean. I'll get a lot of money for this when I return."

"Thank goodness for that," Porter said. "I'd hate for you to have been following me around for free. When you're ready, let me know," Porter said.

"What're you talkin' about? I am ready!" said Slade.

Porter laughed and slapped his knee, "No, you're not."

"Don't tell me if I am or not," said Slade.

Porter said, "Well it is impossible to kill me - didn't you know that?"

Slade angered even further. "Frankly, I don't believe in your long hair protecting you - so don't tell me it's impossible to kill you."

"Actually," Porter said, "I wasn't referring to my hair protecting me - there's another reason you can't kill me."

"Why's that?"

Porter stared at Slade's pistol. "You can't kill a man without a firing pin!"

Slade's face flustered with panic He glanced down at his pistol. Rockwell was wrong! There was a firing pin! Slade, pleased, looked up again and found himself staring straight into Porter's revolver...then at the flash coming from the revolver...Within a few seconds, he was lying face down sprawled on the road.

Porter tipped his hat up with his pistol barrel and sighed. It seems he just couldn't even take a peaceful ride in the country anymore, he thought, without someone bothering him. He whistled to his team and wandered slowly on home.

Rewritten excerpt from a novel by Richard Lloyd Dewey titled "Rockwell, U.S. Marshal," Paramount Books

title: Keeping Utah’s History Alive Through Music
text:
Have you ever tried to Google your great-great-great grandpa? Most likely nothing came up. Have you ever looked on YouTube for some videos of pioneers crossing the plains? You wouldn't have much luck. So what did our pioneer ancestors do to record their lives? How do we know anything about them and what they did?

One way is with the help of Clive Romney. Romney is the founder of Utah Pioneer Heritage Arts, which has a goal to "turn the hearts of the children to their fathers through the arts." To help accomplish this goal, he created the "Heart of the Pioneer" program, which has been putting on assemblies for two years at more than 40 elementary schools across Utah.

These assemblies teach kids about their pioneer ancestors: how they lived, sang, danced, wrote and played. Romney and his "Willing Ensemble" will come to your school and in no time at all have you dancing the Virginia Reel, playing different pioneer games and learning the basics of writing poetry or song lyrics.

Once Romney saw some cabins built by Utah pioneer Archibald Gardner. "I was intrigued by some of the stories about the people that built the cabins on the Gardner Village site," he said. (Learn more about Gardner Village at gardnervillage.com.)

Romney wanted to know why these cabins were preserved. After some research into the stories, Clive hired three Utah songwriters to put those stories into songs. Those songs now tell the stories of people, the events and the history of a time before YouTube and Google. The songs also remind us of the great men and women who risked their lives to make ours better.

title: Pioneer Schools
text:
Learning was Very Important to the Pioneers

Brigham Young and the early pioneers believed learning was very important. Many of the pioneers were very well educated and brought books with them in their wagon trains. Sometimes, regular school lessons were held while traveling across the plains. The first school in Salt Lake was started soon after the pioneers arrived. Mary Jane Dilworth is recorded to have been the general school teacher, and she held classes in a tent until a one-room school cabin was built.

What were the Schools Like?

Children of all ages, from kindergarten through high school, attended school in the same room. The teacher gave the children assignments based on their age and ability. After the students learned their lessons, they then recited them in front of the class, showing what they had learned.

Instead of paper, which was expensive and hard to get, the students used slates, or

small chalkboards, and slate pencils, or chalk. Books were also hard to come by, so

families passed down their school books from child to child, and often from parents to children. When there weren't enough school books to go around, students shared with other children in the same grade or learned their reading, writing and spelling lessons using the Bible or other available books.

Students in Utah's early pioneer schools spent a lot of time memorizing and reciting. Teachers held regular spelling bees, poetry recitations and drama readings.

What is a Hornbook?

It wasn't really a book and certainly didn't have horns! What could it have been?

With few books available to the classroom, children often used a hornbook. A hornbook was a wooden paddle. On the front, a piece of paper was attached that had letters or lessons written upon it. A thin transparent sheet covered the paper to protect it, as it was used by many students through the years. The transparent sheet was made from the horn of an animal such as a cow, thus the name hornbook!

Eeeeeeasy Reading!

You've probably noticed by now that the English language we read, write and speak is very difficult at times. English words are often pronounced differently than the way they are spelled. They are also often spelled differently than we would expect. The Mormon pioneers lived far away from the rest of the world and there were many immigrants (people from other countries) who came to Utah needing to learn English quickly. To solve some of the problems with learning to speak, read and write English, the pioneers experimented with a new alphabet that was completely phonetic, meaning it was pronounced exactly as it was spelled. The new alphabet was called the Deseret Alphabet and was used in Utah schools for a time. Because it was very difficult to write the letters correctly, reading the Deseret Alphabet was sometimes a real challenge. By around 1 8 6 9, the Deseret Alphabet was rejected because it proved to be even harder to use than our standard English alphabet.

title: Beaver County
text:
Early pioneers named the area Beaver because of the thousands of beavers that lived there.
County Seat: Beaver
Population: 6,000

Beaver County is located between the Tushar Mountains on the east and the Nevada border on the west. The county seat is the city of Beaver and the only other large communities are the cities of Minersville and Milford.

The highest point in Beaver County is 12,169 feet above sea level. Because the area has such a high elevation, the growing season is very short. In spite of this, farmers still manage to grow good crops of potatoes and hay. Ranchers also raise cattle and produce fine dairy products.

Beaver County is known for its great hunting, fishing, hiking and motorsport opportunities. People come from miles around to enjoy the forests, lakes and streams of the Tushar Mountain Range. Areas such as Little Reservoir, Kent's Lake, LaBaron Lake, Big John's Flat and Puffer Lake are all popular outdoor areas.

Elk Meadows is also a popular outdoor spot with skiers from all over the state. The ski resort offers "bunny hills" for beginners, as well as heart-stopping advanced runs for experts.

Other interesting Beaver County attractions include the ghost town of Frisco and the Old Beaver County Courthouse. Frisco was once home to the Silver Horn Mine, which opened in 1800 and was one of the richest mines in history until a cave-in destroyed the mine. When the mine closed down, the town dried up. All that is left today is a skeleton of the historic old mining town. The Old Beaver County Courthouse was built in 1877 and has recently been restored. Visitors can now tour the historic old building.

title: Pioneer Craftsmen
text:
Because of the development of modern technology, the following skills have all but disappeared. But during pioneer times, life would have come to a halt without the skills of these great craftsmen.

Gunsmith

As the pioneers moved West, the demand for guns increased. The most famous rifle made at this time was the Kentucky rifle. These rifles were fired by a percussion cap. Kentucky rifles replaced the old flintlock rifles that were more difficult to use.

The gunsmith made his own gun barrels by wrapping hot iron around a straight iron rod. He then drove the rod back out of the formed barrel, making an accurate rifle that was easy to handle.

Cooper

Pioneer farmers needed barrels to store and move their food crops and other supplies such as flour, corn meal, molasses and grains. This made coopering, or barrel making, one of the most important trades. Coopers used mainly oak wood to create both "wet" and "dry" barrels. Wet barrels were used for holding liquids and dry barrels were used for holding dry items. In the picture, the cooper is assembling the staves, or slats, of the barrel before fastening the barrel together with hickory wood hoops. The hoops were circular pieces of wood that were slipped over the staves to keep them in place. A cooper could make as many as 10 dry barrels a day, while the wet barrels took a little longer, as they had to be made completely water tight.

Today, barrels made of iron or steel have replaced the oak barrels of the past, making coopering a nearly lost art.

Wheelwright and Wainwright

The wheelwright made and repaired wheels for wagons, carts, carriages and coaches. His partner is called a wainwright. The wainwright made the rest of the vehicle. Their most noteworthy product was the Conestoga covered wagon or prairie schooner. This wagon helped the Utah pioneers greatly in their westward migration. This wagon was invented by German immigrants who lived in the Conestoga Valley of Pennsylvania. It had a long, deep bed with a sag in the middle that made the load shift to the middle on inclines. This feature stabilized the load. From a distance, they resembled ships, with the covered part resembling sails and the bottom looking like a boat - thus the name prairie schooner (prairie ship).

title: Some Must Push, and Some Must Pull As We Go Marching up the Hill
text:
In 1855, thousands of people were leaving Europe for America because of war conditions. Many of these were converts to the Mormon religion. They came as far west as the Missouri rail lines, but most of them could not afford to buy oxen and carts for the long trip across the continent to Utah.

Brigham Young wrote, "They will be provided with handcarts on which to haul their provisions and clothing. We will send experienced men to aid them. They are expected to walk and draw their carts across the plains. Sufficient teams will be furnished to haul the aged, sick and those unable to walk. A few good cows will be sent along to furnish milk and some beef cattle...."

Within eight months after Brigham Young's statement, 750 handcart pioneers made the trip, many of them singing "The Handcart Song" as they hauled their simple, two-wheeled carts. The song says that "some must push and some must pull as we go marching up the hill" and it indeed took both pushing and pulling for the pioneers to haul their belongings out West. They were allowed only 17 pounds of baggage per person, and many prized belongings had to be left behind.

An early winter overtook two of the handcart parties in 1856; they were stalled by snow and almost completely without food. Rescue parties of volunteers gathered up supplies, which were contributed by the colonists of Utah. Some women contributed the clothes off their backs. The rescuers pushed across the snowy wastes to aid the starving handcart pullers.

When they reached the travelers, one rescuer reports, "The train was strung out for three or four miles. There were old men pulling and tugging at their carts, many of which were loaded with sick wives and children. We saw little children, six and eight years of age, struggling through the snow and mud. As night came on, the mud and snow froze to their clothing."

Altogether, in the period from 1850 to 1860, 4,000 people crossed the plains in handcart companies. One 73-year-old woman walked all the way from Iowa City to Salt Lake City.

title: Utah Immigrants Today
text:
Sometimes, when we talk about immigrants coming to the United States, we only think of people who arrived here 100 years ago or more. However, there are still immigrants coming to the United States today. The United States accepts millions of immigrants each year from all over the world, and many of those immigrants choose to settle in Utah. But the experience of today's immigrants is much different than that of immigrants who came to our state in the 19th and early 20th centuries.

First of all, we live in a world that is very much connected with the Internet, telephones, television and airplanes. One hundred or more years ago, immigrants had to travel across the ocean for weeks, sometimes months, before arriving in the United States. Today, immigrants can fly to America in a matter of hours. Once they arrive in the United States, instead of having to ride a horse, a train or a wagon, immigrants can now drive a car or take an airplane to get to Utah. How much easier it is for them!

Hundreds of years ago, immigrants came to Utah primarily to work in the coal mines. Today, immigrants to our state not only work in the coal mines but also are an integral part of the hospitality and service industry in places like hotels and restaurants. In addition, many immigrants are working as university professors, doctors and scientists.

Utah has become a temporary stopping point for many immigrants who are moving from California to other states, such as Wyoming, Montana and Colorado. However, not everyone is just passing through. Immigrants from Mexico make up the largest percentage of Utah's Hispanic population, and most of them make their home in Salt Lake County.

title: Mints
text:
You can easily tell a mint plant from any other plant because of its distinct aroma. (It really smells like mint!) All the mints found in Utah are fairly similar in appearance, with a square or four-sided stem. The early pioneers learned to use the herbs found naturally in Utah for medicines, teas and flavorings in their food. There were no stores during the first days and months in early Utah.

Try Making Some Horehound Candy!

This recipe was used by the pioneers to make horehound drops—which were commonly used as cough drops. Many people like the rustic "pioneer" flavor of horehound candy.

Recipe

Tea Water: Pour one cup of boiling water over 1/2 cup crushed horehound leaves. Steep until the tea is dark.
3/4 cup strong tea water
2 cups sugar and 1/3 cup corn syrup.
Boil to hard-crack stage (sets hard when dropped in cold water).
Form drops onto a cookie sheet. When cool, roll in sugar (to keep from being too sticky).

title: What is Dust, and Where Does it Come From?
text: Look around your classroom or at home for a flat surface that hasn't been touched for a week or two. It will be covered with a fine layer of dust. Believe it or not, most dust in a house or school is dead skin fragments from human bodies. (Yuck, that's YOU lying all over the place!) Other dust particles come from tobacco smoke, pollen, plants, factory smoke and soil. In 19 80, Mount St. Helens launched thousands of tons of dust into the air when it erupted. Dust can come from outer space, too. Could that thin layer of dust actually be millions of miniature UFOs all over the top of the piano? Who knows?

title: Kane County
text:
Named for Colonel Thomas L. Kane, who helped the Mormons through a difficult time during the "Mormon War"

County Seat: Kanab
Population: 6,300

Kane County is rich in unusual and colorful scenery. Hollywood filmmakers discovered this years ago and have made Kanab and Kane County the home of many Western movies. Several movie ghost towns are left from the filming of these movies. Both national and state parks can be found in abundance in Kane County. Part of both Zion and Bryce Canyon national parks are in Kane County. Also located in Kane County are Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park, Kodachrome Basin State Park, Navajo Lake, ancient cliff dwellings and miles of beautiful desert and mountain scenery. Much of Lake Powell is in Kane County. House-boating, fishing, waterskiing and exploring some breathtakingly beautiful scenery are the main attractions of Lake Powell. Some interesting historic sites in Kane County include the "Crossing of the Fathers" and "Hole in the Rock."

title: Many People Made Contributions to Pioneering Utah
text:
The Mormon contribution to the development of Utah was great. The Mormons made the first permanent homes, established irrigation, agriculture, cities, roads, government and some of the first businesses and developed natural resources. But the Mormons were not the only people to pioneer Utah. They came as merchants (people who manage goods and supplies), businessmen (people who run a business), soldiers (people who protect our country), teachers (someone who teaches in a school), religious leaders (people who serve in a church), explorers (those who travel through an unfamiliar area to learn about it), railroaders (people who build a railroad) and miners (people who mine for minerals).

It took people from all over the world to help build our state. These people included African Americans, Europeans, Latin Americans, American Indians, Japanese, Chinese, Jews, Greeks and others.
