title: Fake or Real News?
text:
Have you ever read something online, like on social media sites, that sounded fishy? Maybe it was real, but it could be fake news! The big danger, though, is news that sounds real but isn’t. Fake news is becoming common because anyone can post things online. Fake news can be in the form of a story. Fake news can be a photo or video that has been changed. The problem is that these fake items look real. Fake news can cause problems and it spreads misinformation.

Sam Wineburg, a professor, did some research. He found that 80 percent of students cannot tell the difference between real and fake news. Do you want to become a media-savvy person? You have to be able to find out if news is real or fake. How do you do that? You have to become a detective and search for the truth. You can learn about the author or company that posted the news. You have to think about the purpose of the news. Is there a hidden plan to get you to buy something or to make you think a certain way? Your teacher or a trusted adult can help you learn how to spot fake news. It takes a little time, but democracy depends on real information! Do your part and discover what is real and what is fake!

title: Utah Has Trouble Becoming a State
text:
On July 24, 1857, exactly 10 years after the pioneers first entered into the Salt Lake Valley, news came that 2,500 U.S. cavalrymen and artillery of the U.S. Army were about to march into Utah and take over. The pioneers were shocked!

They didn't have time to explain to the Army that there must be some mistake. Brigham Young issued a proclamation forbidding the troops to enter Utah. The troops came into Utah anyway. The pioneers remembered their troubles in Missouri and Illinois and were prepared to burn their own homes to the ground rather than allow the troops to have them.

President Buchanan sent Colonel Thomas L. Kane, a friend of the Mormons, to help work out the problem. Colonel Kane traveled at his own expense to talk to his good friend Brigham Young about the predicament, and they worked out a settlement. The people returned to their homes.

On another occasion, the U.S. government passed a law against polygamy (having more than one wife). Only a few Mormons had more than one wife, but Colonel Patrick Edward Conner and 300 troops were sent to Utah to force the Mormons to give up polygamy. All of the church's property was taken over by the government, and those practicing polygamy were put in prison. Finally, in 1890, the president of the Mormon Church, President Wilford Woodruff, issued a manifesto (a legal paper) saying that the Mormons were to give up polygamy. Soon after this decision, those in prison were released, and church property was returned.

During all of these trials and persecutions, Brigham Young and other Utah leaders were trying to help Utah become a state. (A state is an official area belonging to the United States.) They formed a government that they called the State of Deseret. They met for nine sessions in hopes that the U.S. Congress would make Utah a new state. Utah was far more ready for statehood than many other states that had been admitted earlier. Congress was very suspicious of Utah, however, because of the troubles and rumors that started the problems mentioned above. It was not until Jan. 4, 1896, that Utah at last became the 45th state of the United States.

title: See the Capitol, Play the Game
text:
Did you say "Beehives"? BINGO! Congratulations, you've just won Utah State Capitol Bingo! How do you play?

Step one: Get yourself on down to the Utah State Capitol— you know, the giant white building up on the hill in Salt Lake City, sitting in the middle of 40 acres of beautiful gardens, statues and monuments. The recently remodeled capitol now features earthquake- resistant construction that should keep it standing if the Wasatch fault slips a little. With the new features, it's the most expensive state capitol in the whole United States!

Step two: Get yourself attached to a guided tour, hosted by a volunteer who can tell you anything you want to know about the history of the building. Built in 1916 with materials gathered mostly from Utah, the Capitol is filled with history, artifacts and stories you'll want to hear as you're guided around.

Step three: Get your Utah State Capitol Bingo card ready! It's a cool card made up of pictures of things you'll have to find while hunting through the Capitol building. You can find the card in a printable form on the State Capitol website, utahstatecapitol.utah.gov.

Step four: Pay super-close attention to the details of the building. Some of the bingo items are pretty easy to see, like the 6,000-pound chandelier hanging from the ceiling. But watch for finer details, too, like the "Land and Community Niche" or the "Passing of the Wagons".

Step five: When you win, make sure all your friends know you are the all-knowing capitol expert—but don't shout! Sound really carries with all the marble flooring in the capitol. Plus, the Capitol is the real-live work place for Utah's elected officials, and they'd be jealous if they knew you got to play Utah State Capitol Bingo.

title: Local Government
text:
The U.S. Constitution explains the duties of the national and state governments. However, it does not tell about the duties of local governments. Many states have subdivisions of counties, cities, boroughs, towns, villages and even special districts. The state legislature and state constitution decide how many and what kinds of local governments there are.

Today, there are more than 85,000 local governments in the United States. Many times, these governments overlap and it can be very confusing. For instance, when a city is in a county, both have government officials. Sometimes, areas of jurisdiction, or control, overlap. It can make it hard to figure out which government should take action.

Sometimes, in large areas, counties and cities share services such as healthcare, fire, libraries, parks and recreation. Is the library nearest you a city library or a county library? Maybe it belongs to both!

title: Journey to Statehood
text:
This week, we will take a look at how Utah developed from a very large territory into the state we recognize today.

Religious Government

When the Mormons first settled in Utah, Brigham Young served as both the leader of the church and the leader of the government. In 1848, when the Mexican War ended, the US government bought a large amount of western land, including Utah, from Mexico. Since Utah was now part of the United States, the Mormons had to change the type of government they had been using to one that kept the church and the government separated.

State of Deseret

In 1849, Brigham Young and leaders from California met and organized a new government called the "State of Deseret." Brigham Young was elected as governor of the Deseret area.

Utah Territory

In 1850, the State of Deseret became the Utah Territory. Becoming a territory of the United States is one step before becoming an official state. Brigham Young remained the governor, or leader, of the territory. California, our neighbor to the west, became a state at this time, but Utah remained a territory and had to answer directly to the federal government.

Utah Wants to Be a State

The Mormons were unhappy with the government because the United States wanted Brigham Young to be a leader over the church and not over the territory. There are laws about having church and state separated. The people thought if they were made a state they could have their own constitution, or their own set of laws for governing themselves. Because the Mormons and the other citizens were becoming good friends, they worked together to show the government they could live peaceably as a state. On Jan. 4, 1896, Utah Territory became the State of Utah. Utah Territory was split, and parts went to Nevada, Wyoming and Colorado. Utah became the 45th state in our nation.

title: Millard County
text:
Named in honor of Millard Fillmore, the 13th U.S. president, who signed the act making Utah a territory in 1850
County Seat: Fillmore
Population: 12,500

Millard County is located in the middle-western part of our state, bordered by Nevada on the west and the Pahvant Mountain Range on the east.

Fillmore, the county seat of Millard County, served as the first capital of the Utah Territory from 1855 - 1856. It is located near the center of the state and was accessible from all parts of Utah. The legislature met there in the capitol building. After a few years, the capital was changed to Salt Lake City, which is closer to the highly populated areas of Utah. Inactive volcanoes and lava flows cover large areas of Millard County.

Millard County is a good place to find interesting and beautiful rocks. Topaz Mountain is known for its beautiful semi-precious topaz. There are also ice caves, hot springs and craters in Millard County.

Clear Lake is a waterfowl area in Millard that is managed by the Utah Fish and Game Commission. Birds such as the great blue herons, snowy egrets, ibis, ducks, geese, avocets, black-billed stilts and great white pelicans feed there.

Delta is famous for the alfalfa seed grown there. Nearly one-fourth of the alfalfa seed produced in the United States is grown in Delta. Lots of honey is produced in Delta. Besides making honey, the bees also do double-duty as they pollinate the alfalfa blossoms.

Plan a trip to Millard County to see what Utah's original capital city was like.

title: A Mini Field Trip of Capitol Hill
text:
1. State Capitol

Early pioneers located their capitol (government building) in Fillmore, Utah, because Fillmore is located in the center of the state. By 1865, they could see that Salt Lake City should be the capital because most of the people were settling in the Salt Lake Valley. Between 1856 and 1916, the legislature met in various buildings throughout Salt Lake City. There was not enough money to build a capitol building until March 1, 1911, nearly 15 years after Utah became a state. Utah received an unexpected $798,546 in inheritance taxes from Mrs. E.H. Harriman to settle the Harriman estate. The state then raised an additional $1-million bond and within two years, a site was chosen and the ground-breaking ceremony was held.

The Utah State Capitol is recognized as one of the finest examples of Renaissance revival architecture in the United States. The capitol building is situated on Salt Lake's northern foothills overlooking the city, valley and rugged Wasatch Mountains.

Upper Floors

Matching marble staircases lead from the main hall to the Supreme Court Chambers on the capitol's east side and to the House of Representatives on the west. The elegant Utah Senate Chambers is located on the north side. Outside the House Chamber on the third floor is an exact replica of the Liberty Bell, one of 53 given to the United States in 1950 by the mining and smelting industry. The replicas were bronzed and cast in France.

Ground Floor—Exhibition Hall

The entire state of Utah is represented through displays featuring a variety of scenic, recreational, educational, agricultural and industrial exhibits.

Main Hall

Throughout the main hall are statues, plaques and monuments of historical relevance to the people of Utah. Besides the rotunda and gold room, the main hall contains the executive branch of Utah government. The governor's office is in the northwestern corner, the lieutenant governor's office and secretary of state's office are in the northwest, and the attorney general's office is on the eastern side. The rotunda is a round room located 165 feet directly beneath the top of the capitol dome. The ceiling is decorated with sea gulls whose wingspans are 6 feet long. There are other historic murals, all done by Utah artists.

2. State Office Building

The office building is a six-story contemporary (today's style) gray building. It is connected to the capitol by a beautifully landscaped plaza.

3. Council Hall

Across the street and south of the capitol is one of the West's most historic buildings. The building was originally located in downtown Salt Lake City at 120 East First South and first served as the city hall and the meeting place for the territorial legislature. It is a fine example of Greek revival architecture.

4. Pioneer Memorial Museum

On the western side of the capitol building is a cream-colored reproduction of the Salt Lake Theater. This is actually a museum, operated by the Daughters of the Utah Pioneers. This building displays one of the largest and finest collections of authentic pioneer relics in the West. A carriage house is located directly behind the museum.

5. Mormon Battalion Monument

A bronze-and-granite monument honoring the 2,000-mile march of the Mormon Battalion from Council Bluffs, Iowa, to San Diego, California, during the Mexican War of 1846 is located in the southeastern section of the capitol grounds.

6. White Memorial Chapel

This LDS chapel was one of the first of its kind in Utah to include a steeple tower. It originally stood on Second Avenue, but was torn down and rebuilt on Capitol Hill in 1980. The church is now owned by the state and has been completely restored.

7. Governor's Mansion

Though eight blocks from Capitol Hill, the home of Utah's governor is an important part of our capitol field trip. This remarkable building is considered by historians, architects and artists to be one of Utah's most important landmarks. The mansion, as the home is called, was completed in 1902 and belonged to Thomas F. Kearns, a Park City mining magnate (a very wealthy owner) and US senator. In 1937, his widow deeded it to the state as the official residence of the governor. The building underwent a complete restoration after a 1993 Christmas tree fire. The 36-room house is lavishly decorated with exotic wood from throughout the world. African and Italian marble is used in the decoration. The grand staircase rises three stories to a domed ceiling and opens into a ballroom that looks like it's from the late 1800s.

title: The Constitution Protects Our Rights
text:
Let's look at some current human rights problems. After reading the following problems, you will see how the Constitution protects us and safeguards our freedoms. Inside Utah Studies Weekly this week, see how the Constitution organizes our government so that we the people make our own laws. (You'll learn how a bill becomes a law when it goes through Congress in next week's paper.) The Utah state constitution is patterned after the federal U.S. Constitution.

Freedom of Speech in School?

Matt Fraser Suspended for Disruptive Speech

A high school senior from Washington state named Matt Fraser delivered a speech in a student assembly nominating a friend for class vice president. He used words that had double meanings, which caused the audience to hoot and holler. The principal and other administrators told Matt that his speech was "indecent" and had violated a school rule against "disruptive behavior." As a result, he was suspended for three days from school.

Matt Goes to Court

Matt went to court and argued that the school had violated his right of free speech guaranteed under the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution. The school administration argued that high school students do not have full rights of free speech. Schools have a right "to maintain and enforce minimum standards of decency" by not allowing indecent and disruptive behavior such as Matt's speech.

Judges Agree with Matt

Judge Jack Turner from the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals heard all the arguments and judged in favor of Matt that the school had violated Matt's First Amendment rights. The school district appealed to a higher court at the state level, and again the state court agreed with Matt.

District Goes to U.S. Supreme Court

The nine justices of the U.S. Supreme Court do not hear just any case. They only have time to rule on important cases that involve the U.S. Constitution and the rights of citizens. Their decision is final. The school district (group made up of several schools located in the same general area) appealed to the Supreme Court. Chief Justice Warren Burger wrote the following: "While the Constitution does give freedom of speech to adults, it does not automatically give this right to children in a public school. This is because schools are special places where indecent or offensive conduct would disrupt the learning process. Surely, it is appropriate for schools to prohibit the use of vulgar and offensive terms in speeches." By a seven to two decision, the court overruled the two lower courts, saying that Matt's right of free speech had not been violated.

Ruling Still Debated (Discussed)

Some say that the ruling puts students' free speech in trouble and opens the way for school administration to clamp down on any expression by students, especially if they disagree with the official view.

The school board and others feel that this was an important victory for schools because the school should have the right to set standards for an orderly environment in which students can learn.

How do you feel? Which side would you take in a debate (a discussion about a topic)? Why?

Is Drug Testing Fair?

Because of dangerous, illegal drugs such as cocaine, crack, heroin, marijuana, and others, government officials are trying to have people tested for drugs. It is estimated that more than 2 6 million Americans are now using illegal drugs. The problem facing us is how can we stop this wave of drug abuse?

Many think the answer is to test people to find out if they are using drugs. The most common form of drug testing is through urinalysis. By analyzing a person's urine, an expert can determine if someone has used drugs even days before the test.

Drug Testing Now Being Used

Many of the nation's largest corporations are using some form of drug testing. The government currently tests about 1 million federal employees in sensitive government jobs.

Will Schools Do Drug Testing?

Many school districts and boards are doing some drug testing on students. They believe that it will cut down on student drug use, which is a great concern to parents and teachers.

Is Drug Testing a Violation of Constitutional Rights?

A large number of people think drug testing is in violation of the Fourth Amendment, which protects citizens' privacy by keeping the government from making "unreasonable searches and seizures."

Recent polls by magazines and newspapers claim that more than 72 percent of Americans are willing to submit to drug testing at work. One school system in Texas wants all children to submit to drug tests. Most parents support the plan. How do you feel about it?

title: How Government Works
text:
Government works similar to stacking blocks, and it all starts with you! You are a citizen of your community. Your community is part of a city, and a local government runs the city. The head of the city, the mayor, works out of city hall. Do you know where your city hall is?

The state government runs all of the combined local governments. The leader of the state government is the governor. The governor's office can be found at the state capitol. Voters in each state elect members of Congress. They meet in Washington, D.C., to take care of the federal government. The leader of the country is, of course, the president of the United States.

The United Nations is yet another block that we can add. It is a type of government made up of leaders from around the world. Wow! Many government leaders are members of the United Nations— but don't forget that the most important part of all of this is the citizens, including you!

title: Garfield County
text:
Named in honor of James A. Garfield, 20th President of the United States
County Seat: Panguitch
Population: 4,735

The Colorado River and Lake Powell border Garfield County to the east. Garfield County is the fifth-largest Utah county in size, but there are only about 4,000 people living here. Nearly 95 percent of the land in Garfield County is owned by the government, leaving only about five percent for those who make their homes here.

With huge forests and large amounts of grazing land, lumber production and cattle ranching are the county's top industries. Large amounts of oil are also produced in Garfield's Upper Valley Oil Field.

Garfield County is home to some of Utah's most beautiful scenery. Panguitch Lake, Bryce Canyon National Park and parts of Capitol Reef National Park and Glen Canyon National Recreation Area (including many miles of Lake Powell's shoreline), are all located in Garfield County. Red Canyon, Anasazi Indian Village State Park and Escalante Petrified Forest State Park are also located in Garfield County. Because of these exciting outdoor attractions, Garfield County is becoming a popular spot with tourists. Visitors love to fish, camp, hike, boat and swim in Garfield County.

The Henry Mountains, found in the northeastern section of the county, are very unusual. Often called dome or "mushroom" mountains, they have been described as "blue blisters on a desert landscape." Besides being interesting to look at, the Henry Mountains are filled with large numbers of longhorn sheep.

title: Golden Eagle
text:
The golden eagle is one of Utah's largest birds of prey. A bird of prey is a bird that eats other animals to stay alive. The golden eagle has a dark-brown body and a golden-brown neck. From head to tail, it measures about 3 feet long, with wings that can stretch up to 7 feet. The golden eagle weighs between 8 and 13 pounds. In addition to being large, the golden eagle is also strong. It can fly while carrying food that weighs as much as it does.

Golden eagles are meat-eaters. Usually, they fly high above the ground searching for rabbits, squirrels or groundhogs to eat. They have very good eyesight, which allows them to see prey while soaring high up in the sky. When they spot something they want to eat, they swoop down and catch it with their needle-sharp claws called "talons." Then they carry it to the top of a big tree or stony cliff to eat.

Each year between February and March, the female golden eagle lays up to three eggs. Before laying these eggs, the eagle builds a new nest or fixes up an old one. Favorite nests often become very large. In 1884, naturalist Denis Gale reported finding a nest that measured 10 feet across and 6 feet high!

Golden eagles can live 30 years or more. At one time, they were almost extinct from being killed or captured by hunters and falconers. Today, their numbers are growing, thanks to laws that protect them.

title: Constitutional Lawmaking
text:
Our state constitution is a piece of paper that states the basic laws, organization and character of our government. It describes a government that is divided into three parts or branches.

Our state constitution is patterned after our national Constitution. This week, we will look at two very important ideas from the Constitution. They are constitutional rights and constitutional lawmaking.

The Legislative Branch

This branch is made up of the state legislature. The legislature makes the laws, or rules for us to follow. There are two parts to the legislature: the House of Representatives and the Senate. The House of Representatives is made up of lawmakers who are elected to serve for two years. The Senate is made up of lawmakers who are elected to serve for four years. Senators and representatives are called legislators who are elected to make laws. These people are chosen by the citizens of our state to represent them in making laws.

The Executive Branch

This branch consists of the governor, attorney general and secretary of state. These people have the power to enforce the laws made by the legislature. The police and National Guard help them do this.

The Judicial Branch

These people make up the Supreme Court of our state. They decide if the laws made by the legislature are constitutional. They also decide what punishment a person should receive for breaking the law.

Constitutional Rights

Our State Bill of Rights

1. Worship in the church of your choice.

2. Say what you believe is right.

3. Print what you want to truthfully publish.

4. Own your own home.

5. Go to school.

6. Have guns within the law.

7. Vote when of age.

8. Have a trial by jury.

9. Don’t have to testify against oneself.

Our State Bill of Responsibilities

1. Obey the laws of the land.

2. Help correct things you disagree with.

3. Respect the rights of others.

4. Pay taxes.

5. Remain informed.

6. Defend your country.

7. Vote in elections.

8. Serve on a jury.

9. Help police and fire departments.

title: Were Our Founding Fathers Rich?
text:
Some of our modern presidential candidates have been very wealthy. It is interesting to compare these people’s fortunes to those of our founding fathers. For example, many people think that George Washington was our richest president. But is that true?

In letters to family and friends George Washington said he did not want to be president, but he was concerned that he didn’t have enough money to live out his retirement. In other words, he needed the job! Like other founding fathers after the war, he had land but no cash.

Washington owned a lot of land, but no one wanted to buy any of it. People who rented parts of his land didn’t have money to pay him. During the Revolution he refused to accept pay for being the commander of the Army. He fed his staff and paid spies with his own money. After the war, the government paid him back in Continental dollars, which were worthless. Washington even had to borrow money to get to the Constitutional Convention in 1787.

Thomas Jefferson once had to borrow money from one of his slaves. He died deeply in debt. When Alexander Hamilton died his family couldn’t afford to bury him. They collected donations for his burial.

Our founding fathers pledged their lives, their fortunes and their sacred honor for freedom. They lost most of their fortunes because of the war. Their wealth was not in money; it was in service.

title: Bill of Rights Roll Film
text:
Materials

half-gallon milk carton or box

two rods or pencils

long strip of butcher paper 3 inches wide

crayons or markers

tape

pen

scissors

colored paper or contact paper to cover the box

ruler

Directions

1. Prepare your box. Cut the top of the milk carton if that is what you use. Cover the box with construction or contact paper.

2. Make two 3.5-inch slits across the front of your box (horizontally) to let the roll movie pass in and out.

3. Poke holes in the sides for the pencils. Measure to make sure the pencils are straight.

4. Measure the distance between the two slits. This is how big your movie scenes can be.

5. Make a series of pictures (with captions) on the butcher paper, one for each of the 10 amendments listed in the Bill of Rights. (To find a copy of the Bill of Rights, look in an encyclopedia or online.) Make sure each picture fits in the size between the two slits (and is not bigger).

6. Tape one end of the paper to the bottom rod or pencil.

7. Roll the bottom pencil until the end is short enough to handle. Slip this end through the slits and tape it to the other rod.

8. Roll the pencils to see your Bill of Rights movie.

Extra Activity: You can make up 10 rights that you think everyone should have. Just make sure you write a caption for each.

title: Let's Write
text: Write two paragraphs about the freedoms and rights you have because of the Constitution. Use such words as “Bill of Rights,” “freedom of speech,” “freedom of religion,” “freedom of the press,” “freedom to gain an education,” and many others.

title: The Constitution Protects Our Rights
text:
The U.S. Constitution outlines the pattern for making laws in this country. Utah laws are made in the same way that national laws are made, following the Constitutional process.

When citizens or the government leaders who represent them see a need, they come up with a proposal for a law. This proposal is introduced into the Senate by one of our state legislators as a bill. A bill is a proposal or plan that may someday become a law. The bill must be debated, or discussed, in both the House and the Senate. If the bill makes it through both of these legislative groups, it is then sent on to the governor. The governor can either approve the bill and sign it into law or he can veto, or say "no" to, the bill. If the governor vetoes the bill, it can still become a law if two-thirds of the House and the Senate vote to override, or cancel, the governor's veto.

Our state legislature meets every January for a 60-day session. A special session can be called by the governor at any time to talk about unexpected problems that may come up throughout the year. Special sessions of the state legislature may last no longer than 30 days.

title: Some Silly Utah Laws
text:
Could you go to jail for carrying a violin in a paper bag? In Utah you could! Luckily for you, you probably don't ever run into that problem, but at some point in Utah history, lawmakers did and they had to make a law about it.

It's a lot easier to make laws than to remove them, and every state has some very old, very weird laws that are technically still in effect today! Here are a few of the stranger laws of Utah, or towns or counties within it:

It is illegal not to drink milk.

In Trout Creek, pharmacists may not sell gunpowder to cure headaches.

In Salt Lake County, Auctions may not be advertised by hiring trombone players to play on the street.

It is illegal to detonate any nuclear weapon.

It is against the law to fish from horseback.

It is illegal to cause a catastrophe.

In Provo, throwing snowballs will result in a $50 fine.

In Logan, Women may not swear.

The wording of these laws is more official sounding, of course, and sometimes a little context can explain a lot about why these laws exist, but it's funny to look back at hundreds of years of law making and laugh. Just remember to be careful how you carry your violin!

title: Civic Responsibility and You
text:
What is a civic responsibility? One of the most important responsibilities a citizen has is to vote. Other responsibilities include working for the common good, learning about things that are going on in your community, volunteering at local organizations and working to change things that you think are not right. How can fourth graders do those things?

You're too young to vote, but you can encourage the adults you know to go to the polling places on election days. Read or watch the local news to find out what is going on in your community. Is there an electronics recycling day coming up? That's a safe way to get rid of things like old computers and televisions that don't work anymore. Is a local food bank having a food drive at the mall? Ask your parents if you can take some canned goods to help.

Working for the Common Good

Americans come from lots of different backgrounds. But there are many things that we all agree on. One thing we all agree on is that we need to do things for the common good. Those are things that help all of us. We pay taxes to have parks, better schools and good roads. We give money to charities, volunteer to help others and help out when other people need us. What can you do to work for the common good in your community?

Making Changes

If you want to change something in your community, you need to go to the city council or your county commissioners. They are the people who make and change laws in your town or county. If you want to change things at the state level, you can write or e-mail your state senator or representative.

Thinking about changing things in the whole country? Contact your US senator or representative by logging on to congress.org. Lawmakers might not be able to get things changed right away. They might not even agree with what you want to change. But it's their job to listen to citizens—even fourth grade citizens who can't vote yet. Another way to try and get something changed is to start a petition. A petition is a written request to a government official signed by many citizens. You can also write letters to the editor in your local newspaper.

title: Making Utah Laws
text:
Each year, our Utah lawmakers meet together to make new laws to keep our state running smoothly. These laws are made according to the rules of our Utah constitution. As you study the chart and maps on this page, you will learn more about who makes our laws and how this process works.

State Senatorial Districts

The map shows the senatorial districts for Utah. There are 29 districts in all and 29 counties in Utah. However, the senatorial districts do not follow the county boundaries, as you can see on the map.

title: Washington County
text:
Named in honor of President George Washington
County Seat: St. George
Population: 90,354

Washington County is located in the far southwest corner of Utah and has the hottest climate in our state. The area is often called, "Utah's Dixie" because its warm weather is similar to the weather in America's southern states, which are also known as "Dixie." Washington County's first settlers raised cotton, silk, molasses and pecans, products also raised in the South.

Today, Utah's Dixie is a popular tourist center, especially with those who like to escape from the cold winter weather of areas farther north. St. George is full of hotels and motels for tourists who come to visit. People flock to Washington County to enjoy golf, hiking, bicycling and many other outdoor activities. In fact, many people choose to move to Washington County after retirement (stop working at their careers) because of the great weather and the many activities to enjoy. Washington County is full of condominiums and retirement villages that have been built especially for these people.

Zion National Park is located in the eastern part of Washington County. Zion is known for its beautiful solid-rock walls that rise up more than half a mile from the canyon floor. Snow Canyon State Park is a much smaller version of Zion and it is also popular with tourists.

Many tourists also come to Washington County to visit The Tuacahn Center, located in Ivins. Tuacahn offers a beautiful outdoor amphitheater where several different plays are presented throughout the year.

Because it has so much to offer, Washington County is growing very quickly. It is popular with visitors, as well as with those who want to make it their new home.

title: What is So Great About Gold?
text: Gold has been the favorite metal of humans ever since its discovery thousands of years ago. It is beautiful and lasts longer than any other metal. It is not affected by water, light or air. Gold is also very soft and easy to shape into useful things. It is so soft, in fact, that it is usually mixed with harder metals like silver to make it strong. Gold is used to make such things as coins, jewelry, dental fillings and gold leaf.

title: Elk
text:
Elk are some of the most handsome animals in Utah. The elk has a light-brown body, a dark-brown head and neck and a white tail end. They like to eat shrubs, weeds, grass and new tree growth - especially from willows and aspens. They live in the forests and meadows in the summer, and in the foothills and mountains in the winter.

Elk are one of the largest animals in Utah. A female elk is called a cow and usually weighs about 500 pounds. A male elk is called a bull. With his giant antlers, a bull can weigh as much as 1,000 pounds!

During the fall, a bull elk tries to gather several cows and form his own herd. He challenges other bulls to fight by giving high, whistle-like calls into the air. When the two bulls come together, they clash their huge antlers to see who is the strongest. They usually fight over cows or territory that they both want. The winner will take the cows and keep the territory. The loser will wander off to challenge another bull.

Many Utahns like to eat elk meat. However, elk can only be hunted during special hunts. Controlled hunts guarantee that there will be many elk for future Utahns to both see and eat.

title: Supply and Demand
text:
To an economist, a market includes everyone who buys or sells a certain good or service. That means all of the people who are buying or selling sweaters are in the sweater market. Everyone buying CDs is in the CD market. Everyone selling hot dogs is in the hot dog market. These markets are very important as economists study supply and demand. Supply is the amount of something being offered by producers for sale. Demand is a measure of how many consumers want to buy what producers are selling. Using the hot dog example, the companies and stores selling hot dogs are supplying them. The consumers who are willing to pay for hot dogs are demanding them.

Demand is more than "wanting" or "wishing" for something. If a person wishes to buy a hot dog, he or she is not in demand. Economists do not consider people in demand until they are willing and able to buy that hot dog. It is not demand until they have the money to actually pay for the hot dog. When they can purchase the hot dog, then they are in the hot dog market.

When economists study supply, they look at several things. They look at the product being sold. Next, they want to know who is selling it. Finally, they study the market for the product. They study prices being charged for a product and how much it costs a company to make that product.

When there is a greater demand for a product than producers can supply, a shortage occurs. Shortages usually mean that prices go up as people battle to buy it. When there is a greater supply of something than a demand for it, it is called a surplus. A surplus usually means that prices go down. The producers lower the price to boost the sales.

Can you think of a recent example of a shortage or surplus?

title: Let's Write

title: St. George
text: St. George is surrounded by beauty and a lush red color. It is also home to Brigham Young’s winter house, Dixie College and is in close proximity to Zion National Park.

title: The Emperor of Japan: A Leader Without Power
text:
In the United States, the official leader of our country is the president. In Utah, the official leader of our state is the governor. In Japan, the official leader of the country is the emperor. An emperor is a man who rules a country, or an empire. Often, an emperor is someone of royal blood, or someone whose ancestors also ruled the nation.

In years gone by, the emperor of Japan had power to make decisions and lead the country, but after Japan was defeated by the Allied Powers in World War II, the emperor lost all power. In 1947 Japan had a new Constitution. This constitution created a parliamentary government. The emperor of Japan now has a symbolic role and a new prime minister was chosen to run the government.

Even though he no longer has the power to run the country, the emperor of Japan is still a very important person. Japan has had an emperor since around 600 B.C. Japan is the only country that still has an emperor today. In the early history of Japan, the emperor was once considered to be a god who lived upon the earth in a human body. While the emperor of Japan is no longer thought of as a god, he is still honored as a respected member of an old, royal family. Japan's emperor has no real power to run the government. His job is to support the Prime Minister, and communicate new laws and treaties. He also meets with important leaders of the world and tries to build friendships between Japan and other nations. He is treated much like another famous monarch (royal leader), the king of England. He is also an example of a monarch who has no power when it comes to running the government, but who works to make things better for the citizens of his country.

Succession in Japan follows a hereditary system and only male children in the imperial family can take the throne. When the reigning emperor, Naruhito, passes away the title passes to the eldest male son. If the emperor does not have a male heir, the throne goes to the closest male relative within the imperial family. An heir is a person who will be given the power of another person after that person's death. Currently, the law excludes female members from being able to take the throne, even if they are the oldest child. There is a significant belief among many Japanese people that the law should be amended to allow the eldest daughter to become the head of state. However, the arrival of a male heir may diminish the urgency of this debate for now.

Japan's emperor and the royal family try to help the people of Japan in any way they can. The royal family makes visits to hospitals, retirement homes and schools for the handicapped. The emperor helps make the citizens of Japan aware of people in need and ways that they may be able to help.

title: Utah’s Japanese Obon Festival
text:
Are you looking for something to do? After all, it's summer, you're bored, and it's been ages since you've attended a 500 year old festival that honors the spirits of your deceased ancestors. Well, you're in luck!

The Japanese Obon festival happens every July in Salt Lake City's Buddhist Temple. The Obon Festival, or just "Bon," is a little like Memorial Day in the United States. The Japanese visit their cemeteries, leaving flowers and cleaning up around the graves.

The real draw of the Obon Festival is the dancing and music. The festival, which is like a big party in a lot of ways, features some pretty amazing traditional Japanese dancing. There are 13 different dances to participate in, and none of them are too challenging if you can pay attention and move gracefully. The dances also have cool names, like "Cherry Blossom" and "Refreshing Wind". The music includes "Taiko," which involves lots of different sized Japanese drums, and a great show, as well.

The Obon Festival is a great chance to see some authentic Japanese culture, do a little dancing and learn a little about Buddhist teachings as well.

title: Compare Governments of Utah and Japan
text:
Over the last several weeks, we have been learning about the governments of our nation and our state. Have you ever stopped to think that the governments of other nations may not be the same as ours? This week, we will be learning about the government of Japan. We will compare the governments of Utah and Japan, discovering how they are alike and how they are different.

Representative Republic vs. Constitutional Monarchy

Representative Republic

Utah's government is patterned after the US government. This type of government is called a representative republic. A representative republic is a government where the people have the power to make the laws and run the government. The people then choose representatives, or people whom they trust, to run the government for them. These representatives serve for a certain amount of time and are then replaced or re-elected when that time is up. This way, if the people who elected these representatives aren't pleased with the way they have run the government, they will replace them with others whom they believe will do a better job.

Constitutional Monarchy

Japan uses a type of government called a constitutional monarchy. A constitutional monarchy is a government where the monarch (the king, queen or emperor) is considered to be the head of the country and the country follows a written constitution that tells how it should be run. Many countries that are run by a constitutional monarchy also combine a type of representative democracy with this type of government. This makes it possible for the people to have a voice in running the country. Japan is one of these countries. The official head of the country of Japan is the emperor, but the government is actually run by the prime minister, his cabinet members and the legislature. These legislators are elected by the people to make laws and keep the country running smoothly.

Japan's Constitution

As we have learned over the last few weeks, Utah has a constitution that explains our rights and responsibilities as citizens of this state. Japan also has a constitution that explains these things.

Japan didn't always have such a document. In fact, until the late 1940s, Japan was run by an emperor and the people had no say in what happened in their country. After World War II, when Japan was defeated by the Allied Nations, Japan wrote a new constitution giving the people rights and powers to live with more freedom and protection than ever before.

This new constitution makes the following promises to the people of Japan:

Japan's Constitutional Rights

1. There will be complete sovereignty (supreme power) of the people to govern the country.
2. The rights of all citizens to enjoy human, individual freedoms will be guaranteed.
3. Japan will remain a peaceful nation and will not go to war.

Under the constitution, the citizens of Japan have the following responsibilities:

Japan's Constitutional Responsibilities

1. Citizens must work to earn a living.
2. Citizens must make sure that their children receive an education.
3. Citizens must pay taxes.

You may remember from our study of the constitutions of the United States and Utah that these documents guarantee some of these same rights, but we have many more individual rights promised to us, such as the right to own our own homes, to own guns and to worship in the churches of our choice. We also have many more responsibilities to fulfill, such as serving on a jury, voting in elections and defending our state and country in times of war.

Three Branches of Government:

Like Utah, Japan also divides its government into three parts, or branches. Japan's government also consists of the executive, the legislative and the judicial branches. While these three branches of government are basically the same in both countries, there are a few differences. Take a look at the charts to see how these governments differ.

title: Wasatch County
text:
An American Indian word meaning "Mountain Pass," or "Low Place in the High Mountains"
County Seat: Heber City
Population: 15,215

Wasatch County is located about 40 minutes southeast of Salt Lake City on the east slope of the Wasatch Mountain Range. The area was first settled by Mormon immigrants from Switzerland. The Swiss heritage of these early settlers is still celebrated in Wasatch County at the Swiss Days Festival held in Midway each fall.

Water is one of Wasatch County's greatest resources. Deer Creek Reservoir, Strawberry Reservoir and Jordanelle Reservoir are very popular recreation areas. In fact, Strawberry Reservoir is the most popular fishing spot in Utah! Fantastic fishing, water skiing, boating, wind surfing and jet skiing bring visitors from all over Utah to the reservoirs of Wasatch County. There are also wonderful opportunities for golfing, skiing, sailplaning and camping.

The Heber Valley was also chosen as the site for the cross-country and biathlon events during the 2002 Olympic Winter Games. The Heber Valley Railroad, the Homestead Resort and Soldier Hollow's day lodge are all popular tourist attractions. Cascade Springs is another beautiful spot for relaxing and enjoying Wasatch County's mountain scenery.

title: What is the Difference Between the Election of Utah’s Governor and the Election of Japan’s Prime Minister?
text:
In Utah, the governor is the head of the executive branch of government. The governor is elected by the people of the state to serve for a four- year period, or term. The governor is directly responsible to the people of the state of Utah.

In Japan, the head of the executive branch of government is the prime minister. He is not elected directly by the people, but is chosen by the members of the Diet, or legislature. The prime minister must already be a member of the Diet. After the prime minister is chosen, he then picks a cabinet to help him run the country. The prime minister and the cabinet run the country together and they are responsible to the legislature, not to the people of Japan. If at any time, the legislature stops supporting the prime minister and his cabinet, the prime minister must resign or call a general election to elect new representatives.

title: Quail
text:
Quail are small birds that live in many parts of the United States and North America. They are related to the partridge and the pheasant, and have spotted feathers.

Quail are very popular game birds, which means that people like to hunt them. One reason they are so popular is that the meat of the quail is quite delicious, and many people enjoy its flavor.

Quail build their nests on the ground, protected by tall plants. The female is in charge of most of the incubation, or keeping the eggs warm, and she also takes care of the baby birds once they hatch. The number of eggs produced at one time for hatching is called a clutch. Quail usually lay at least 12- 15 eggs per clutch.

It is easy to recognize the quail because of the crest on top of its head. The crest often flops down and looks like a "topknot" of hair. Quail eat insects and seeds, and travel in flocks called coveys. Quail can be found throughout the state of Utah.

title: Make Your Own Coat of Arms
text:
Many years ago, people would use a coat of arms to show which group or family they belonged to. They put their coat of arms up on flags in the territories they explored. A coat of arms was used as a symbol of one’s great achievements, goals and beliefs.

Believe it or not, we still use the concept of a coat of arms today. Each state has a state seal, and we have a national seal. They are used to show achievements, goals and beliefs of the country or region they represent.

Now, draw your own symbols for your coat of arms. You may wish to put decorations around it.

Symbols are very important to us. In fact, we can’t do without them. We go to school to learn about symbols. The words on a page are symbols of meanings or things. Pictures and icons are symbols too. Although some words are used on a coat of arms or seal, we mostly use pictures because they can be read at a glance by everyone, even those who don’t know how to read. Sometimes animals are used to stand for things. Colors can mean different things too. What does the red, white and blue of our flag stand for? On the presidential seal, what does the eagle, olive branch, arrows and stars mean? Another reason not to use words on symbols is the language problem. Can you read the Latin inscription on our country’s seal?

title: President John Adams and the XYZ Affair
text:
Can you imagine following in the footsteps of George Washington? John Adams did. America’s first president was greatly admired and respected for leading the troops in the Revolutionary War and helping to build our new country. When Adams became our second president in 1797, America was at peace. We had begun rebuilding our friendship with Great Britain. The former enemies were now buying and selling products from each other. Their ships crisscrossed the Atlantic with goods to trade.

Unfortunately, France was in the middle of its own revolution and was at war with Britain. France began capturing American trading ships to cut off supplies to their enemy. Some Americans were angry and wanted to declare war on France.

President Adams firmly believed in peaceful solutions. He sent a committee to France to work out the problem. The discussions did not go well. The Americans brought home a disturbing report. The three French delegates were angry at America for trading with Britain. They demanded that a large amount of money be paid to the French foreign minister as a bribe, along with a big loan.

When Adams sent the report to Congress, he disguised the names of the Frenchmen with the letters X, Y and Z. News of the “XYZ Affair” traveled across the nation. Many people were furious with France. Merchant ships from the United States and France were battling at sea in an undeclared war.

But Adams had confidence in his critical analysis of the situation. First, he called for Congress to build up America’s armed forces. Then he sent new ambassadors to France who were able to work out a treaty that ended the fighting. The XYZ Affair was peacefully put to rest. When have you used critical analysis to help end an argument?

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine that you are the emperor of Japan. Even though you don’t run the government, you have great influence in your country. What would you do to help make your country a better place? How would you make friendships with other countries? What would be your goals for solving some of Japan’s problems?

title: Kennecott Copper Mine: One Big Hole!
text:
If you were in outer space, looking down at Utah, what might you see? Why, you might see a giant hole in the ground where Utah's state mineral comes from. Yes, a very big hole indeed. It's the Kennecott Copper mine, and it's the world's largest man-made excavation hole. It's big enough, in fact, to be seen from outer space!

But you don't have to be in space to visit the copper mine—go ahead and drive right up to it and have a look! Kennecott invites visitors from the first of April to the end of October to come see the 3/4 of a mile deep pit.

Why would copper be our State Mineral? Copper is terribly useful for electronics, plumbing, roofing and pennies. And Utah just has tons of it! That one huge mine produces 13% of the country's copper needs: 300,000 tons of refined copper each year! While digging for all that copper, they also manage to get 400,000 ounces of gold, 4 million ounces of silver and 20 million pounds of molybdenum (used to make highstrength steel), just by chance!

The coolest thing you might see at the mine is the machinery. They have gigantic electric shovels that can scoop up 98 tons of rock in a single bite. That's like scooping up 50 cars! The shovels dump the rock into giant dump trucks - trucks that are 23 feet tall and weigh more than a jumbo jet. The driver sits two stories off the ground. It's like driving a building!

title: Two-Party System
text:
Two-Party System

In the United States, we elect our government leaders using the two-party system. This means that we have two main political parties, each with different goals and ideas it hopes to achieve.

Political parties are organized groups of voters with the same goals who try to put their ideas into action. They put these ideas into action by helping their candidates get elected to different offices in the government. A candidate is a person who has been nominated or chosen for election.

Both national and local political parties have a written plan explaining the things they want to achieve. This plan is called a platform. The platform has several planks, or specific ideas and goals to make the plan succeed. Usually, the platform wants to reform, or change something and make it better. For example, a political party may have a platform, or plan, to lower taxes. This party will choose a candidate who will work to reform the tax system and lower taxes.

Elections are held in order to let the people decide between the different platforms and candidates. Having at least two political parties to choose from creates a balance in our political (dealing with the government) system, just like the checks and balances of the three branches of government.

Usually, one political party is conservative, or wants to cut down on spending and save resources, and the other is liberal, or wants to put new programs and ideas into effect. Each political party also has many other ideas that it stands for and believes in and there are always members of each party who have their own ideas, but one party is usually conservative and the other liberal.

The Democratic and the Republican parties are the two major American political parties on both the local and the national levels. There are many other smaller political parties, but the Democratic and the Republican parties are the most powerful and the most well-known. These two parties compete against each other for support of their platforms, ideas and candidates.

Democrats and Republicans

What is the difference between these two parties? Each was formed with different beliefs and ideas about what is best for the citizens of this country. It is good to have the Democrats and the Republicans opposing each other with different viewpoints because even though they don't agree, both sides truly want what is best for the country. With two parties running the government, the citizens have a choice between different ways to solve some of our most difficult problems. Political parties work best when they share their ideas and work together to solve problems.

Compare Them Below

(Note that these are generalizations of what the political parties represent. There are always exceptions to these characteristics.)

The donkey is the symbol of the Democratic Party. This symbol was started by a famous cartoonist by the name of Thomas Nast during the early days of the party.

Democrats

(Tending to Be Liberal)
1. Favor laws that help the common man, or "blue-collar" workers (men and women who work in trades and industry for an hourly wage)
2. Support a strong central (federal) government to solve local and national problems
3. Work for government programs (such as Medicare, school lunch, food stamps and student college aid) that help the common people live better; favor a liberal spending policy to solve social problems and improve society.
4. In favor of increasing taxes to support federal programs

The elephant, also started by Nast, is the symbol of the Republican Party. The Republican Party is sometimes called the GOP, which stands for "Grand Old Party."

Republicans

(Tending to Be Conservative)
1. Favor laws that help the big-business executives and professional, or "white-collar" workers (men and women like doctors, lawyers, teachers and business executives who are paid by the job or are salaried by the year)
2. Support a strong local government (state and city) to solve problems
3. Conserve money spent on government programs
4. Usually for lower taxes, which stimulates business growth

title: Emery County
text:
Named in honor of George W. Emery, the governor of Utah Territory from 1875 to 1880
County Seat: Castle Dale
Population: 10,860

Emery County is located about 165 miles southeast of Salt Lake City. The county is full of wide-open spaces and unusual scenery. There are no large cities in Emery County, but those who live here say they like the small-town way of life. Most residents of Emery County work in the coal and uranium mines, at power plants or on farms.

Emery County is famous for raising juicy Green River watermelons and cantaloupes. The melons raised here are unusually sweet. Each year, people from all over the state look forward to the time when the first shipment of Green River melons arrives at their grocery stores.

Visitors to Emery County enjoy camping in Goblin Valley State Park. The area is full of incredible stone formations that look like goblins and monsters. Emery County is also home to the San Rafael Swell, a famous section of the Colorado Plateau. This high desert area is full of interesting geologic formations, such as towering mesas, buttes and pinnacles, along with rolling pastureland and barren desert floors.

Millsite Golf Course is another interesting attraction in Emery County. The golf course is built right next to the Millsite Dam. In fact, golfers tee off directly over the dam's spillway, making it one of the most unusual golf courses you will ever see.

Visitors to Emery County can also explore Temple Mountain, Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry and Sinbad Desert.

title: Pounded Plant Prints
text:
Materials

Several sheets of plain, ink-free newsprint

Just-picked leaves and flowers

100-percent cotton fabric

Washing soda

Hammer

Hard surface for hammering (such as a sidewalk or table)

Water

Soap

Paint brush

Bowl

Pan

Clothes line or dyer

Directions

1. Gather plants. Choose thin, flat leaves; juicy leaves do not work well. If you want to print flowers, choose small, bright flowers like pansies, violas and baby carnations. Remember, you never know how the dye is going to transfer to the fabric. The surprise is part of the fun.

2. Cover a hard surface with eight to 10 newsprint pages. Place a piece of fabric on the newsprint. We strongly recommend testing several plant parts on scrap pieces of fabric.

3. Place a leaf or flower on the fabric. Cover the plant with a double layer of newsprint.

4. Hammer the newsprint covering the plant. The tannin coloring in the plant will transfer to the fabric. Carefully lift your paper cover to see if your plant design is transferring to the cloth.

5. Dip cloth in a solution of 1/2 cup washing soda to 2 cups water. The green tannin of the leaves “fixes” successfully with the washing soda solution. After “fixing” the colors, wash your cotton in soapy water, rinse and dry. All flower petals “fix” differently. Many pinks and purples “fix” aqua and bright blue.

title: Students and Symbols: A Time for Change
text:
We have always used symbols to show pride and patriotic feelings for our country or state. Usually, those symbols don’t change. However, in 2014, a group of fourth graders in Utah felt that the Colorado blue spruce should not be the state tree. Instead, the students suggested the quaking aspen tree. The quaking aspen has a singular root system for a colony of trees. This reminded the students of Utah, a place where people work together to reach new heights. Their idea gained support from Senator Ralph Okerlund, who started the process of changing the symbol. He noted that the quaking aspen’s root system could also symbolize the state’s emphasis on family history and genealogy.

On March 26, 2014, Governor Gary R. Herbert sat at a desk made of quaking aspen. He signed the bill with pens made from the tree. The same fourth graders that started it all were even there to witness it. On May 13, 2014, the new Utah state tree officially became the quaking aspen.

The state tree is just one of our state symbols. Let’s learn about more symbols that help us remember our pride for Utah.

Utah State Flag

The state flag was officially adopted by our legislature in May 1913. The flag’s symbols and their meanings are listed here:

American eagle – U.S. national bird symbolizing allegiance to the United States protection in war and peace

American flag – Utah’s support to the nation

Beehive – state motto symbolizing industry

Sego lilies – state flower of Utah

1847 – the year pioneers came to the Salt Lake Valley

1896 – the year Utah gained statehood

Utah State Flower

The sego lily is Utah’s state flower. Hungry pioneers found they could eat the sego lily tuber, or root. The American Indians also ate parts of the sego lily, and Ute Indians agreed not to fight any battles on fields where these flowers grew. The sego lily, also known as the “mariposa lily” (butterfly lily) in other states, became our state flower on March 18, 1911.

Utah State Mammal

Utah’s state mammal is the elk, or wapiti. There is a rhyme that helps us say the name wapiti correctly. It is, “Hippity hoppity goes the wapiti.” “Wapiti” is an Algonquin name for “large American deer.” They are honored because they were so abundant, and the early inhabitants depended on them for food.

Utah State Bird

Hordes of crickets were destroying crops in Utah in 1848, but in came seagulls to save the first Mormon wheat crop. On Salt Lake’s LDS Temple Square stands a seagull monument. This is one of the only known monuments to a bird. And don’t kill a seagull in Utah because it is against the law!

Great Seal of Utah

One of the most familiar symbols in Utah is the beehive, which represents work and industry. It is on our state flag, state seal, state highway patrol cars and many other things. The beehive as a symbol of Utah is even older than statehood. It appeared as early as 1851 on the seal of the territory of Utah and Deseret. It comes from the Book of Mormon word “Deseret” meaning “honey bee.”

title: Buffalo Stampede!
text:
The following story comes from the daily journal of William Cody, better known as "Buffalo Bill." This adventure happened while he was working on a freight wagon train for Russell, Majors and Waddell. It took all summer long to haul a load of freight from the East to Utah and then make the return trip. One of the reasons it took so long to cross the country with teams of oxen (large cattle used for pulling wagons) is that the animals were strong, unpredictable and traveled at their own pace. The wagoneers had to be prepared for anything to happen at any time. Read the following experience as told in Buffalo Bill's own words.

"Nothing happened on the trip to delay or give us any trouble whatever, until the train struck the South Platte. Between the road and the river, we saw a large herd of buffalo grazing quietly, they having been down to the stream for a drink.

"Just at this time, we observed a party of returning Californians coming from the West. They, too, noticed the buffalo herd, and in another moment they were dashing down upon them urging their steeds to the greatest speed. The buffalo herd stampeded at once and broke for the hills; so hotly were they pursued by the hunters that about 500 of them rushed through our train pell-mell, frightening both men and oxen. Some of the wagons were turned clear 'round, and many of the terrified oxen attempted to run to the hills, with the heavy wagons attached to them. Others turned around so short that they broke the wagon tongues off. Nearly all the teams got entangled in their gearing and became wild and unruly, so that the perplexed drivers were unable to manage them.

"The buffalo, the cattle and the drivers were soon running in every direction, and the excitement upset nearly everybody and everything. Many of the cattle broke their yokes (wooden collars) and stampeded. One big buffalo bull became entangled in one of the heavy wagon-chains, and it is a fact that in his desperate efforts to free himself, he not only actually snapped the strong chain in two, but broke the ox-yoke to which it was attached, and the last seen of him he was running towards the hills with it hanging from his horns. A dozen other equally remarkable incidents happened during the short time that the frantic buffalo were playing havoc with our train, and when they had got through and left us, our outfit was very badly crippled and scattered. This caused us to go into camp and spend a day in replacing the broken tongues, and repairing other damages and gathering up our scattered ox-teams...." by William Cody (Buffalo Bill)

title: Take a Ride on the “Heber Creeper”
text:
There's a train in Provo canyon that gets robbed twice a day, and nobody ever does anything about it. Why? It's all part of the plan.

The Heber Valley Historic Railroad (or "Heber Creeper," as you've likely heard it called) is a railroad line that runs 28 miles between Heber to Provo. For nearly a hundred years, the Heber Creeper has been making its way up and down the canyon.

In the 1930s, before the highway was constructed, the Creeper carried agriculture and livestock—mostly sheep—from the higher, cooler country where things would grow later in the season down to the lower, warmer parts of the state where the days of fresh produce have passed. The Heber Creeper was part of the Provo branch of the Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad.

When the highway was finished, trucks replaced the train for moving things, and the train was almost abandoned. In 1968, the people of Utah cried out, and the train, with a little help from the State of Utah, was back in business - this time as a tourist attraction.

Today, the Heber Valley Historic Railroad carries 300 people at a time up and down the canyon all year. And the adventure changes each season. In the winter, you can ride the "North Pole Express". In October, ride up "Haunted Canyon." On Memorial Day, ride on "Thomas the Tank Engine". Other cool adventures offered by the rail line include horseback riding, river rafting, snow tubing, dinner trains, murder-mystery trains, bluegrass music trains and more!

Just beware, if you ride it—it's likely to get robbed (by actors dressed as bandits. It's all part of the fun of the ride), and you're apt to be taken hostage!

title: Moving Freight in the Old West
text:
A journey by stagecoach in the 1860s was always uncomfortable and often dangerous. John Butterfield built a mail and passenger service from Missouri to the Pacific Ocean in 1857.

Wells, Fargo & Co.

The freighting wagons were too slow for passengers and mail, so the stagecoach lines were developed. One of the most important stagecoach lines in the West was Wells, Fargo and Co. Stations were established along the way as rest stops for passengers. Gold shipments and vast amounts of money were shipped by stagecoach, which required an armed guard to ride "shotgun" along with the driver. There are hundreds of stories of adventure and excitement as the stage was robbed or harassed by outlaws or American Indians. Wells, Fargo and Co. still exists today as an armored-truck service to transport money to the banks.

How Freight was Shipped West

The following description comes from William Cody's (Buffalo Bill's) own journal, or autobiography. He worked for Russell, Majors and Waddell hauling freight across the prairies to the West.

"It might be interesting to the general reader to give a brief description of a freight train. The wagons used in those days by Russell, Majors and Waddell were known as the 'J. Murphy Wagons' made at St. Louis specially for the plains business. They were very large and were strongly built, being capable of carrying 7,000 pounds of freight (goods hauled by wagons) each. The wagon-boxes were very commodious (large), being as large as the rooms of an ordinary house and were covered with two heavy canvas sheets to protect the merchandise from the rain. These wagons were generally sent out from Leavenworth, each loaded with 6,000 pounds of freight and each drawn by several yokes of oxen in charge of one driver. A train consisted of 25 wagons, all in charge of one man, who was known as the wagon-master; then came the 'extra hand.' Next, the night herder; and lastly, the cavallard driver, whose duty it was to drive the lame and loose cattle. There were 31 men in all in a train. The men did their own cooking, being divided into messes of seven. One man cooked, another brought wood and water, another stood guard and so on, each having some duty to perform while getting meals. All were heavily armed with Colt (a well-known gun company of the time) pistols and Mississippi yagers (rifles), and every one always had his weapons handy so as to be prepared for any emergency.

The wagon-master, in the language of the plains (large flat area east of the Rockies), was called the 'bull-wagon boss;' the teamsters were known as 'bull-whackers' and the whole train was called a 'bull-outfit.' Everything at that time was called an 'outfit.' The men of the plains were always full of funny and exciting stories of their own experiences, and many an hour I spent in listening to the recitals of thrilling adventures and hairbreadth escapes.

Russell, Majors and Waddell had in their employ 250 trains, composed of 6,250 wagons, 75,000 oxen and about 8,000 men; their business reached to all the government frontier posts in the North and West to which they transported supplies, and they also carried freight as far south as New Mexico."

by William Cody (Buffalo Bill)

title: San Juan County
text:
Means "Saint John" in Spanish
County Seat: Monticello
Population: 14,500

San Juan County is Utah's largest county in area. It is in the southeastern corner of Utah, where Utah, Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona meet. It is the only place in the United States where four states meet in this way. This is why it is called the "Four Corners" area. Two national monuments have been created in San Juan to protect natural bridges. Natural Bridges National Monument and Rainbow Bridge National Monument are two natural bridges in San Juan County that are protected by the government. It protects some famous American Indian ruins and towers. There are several state parks such as Goosenecks of the San Juan, Newspaper Rock, Monument Valley and part of Dead Horse Point. Lake Powell has nearly 1,000 miles of shoreline in San Juan County. There are also two American Indian reservations in San Juan County, one Ute and the other Navajo.

title: What is the Largest Tree in the World?
text: American Forests in Washington, D.C., has a point system to determine the biggest tree. It includes how big around the trunk is, how tall and how far out the limbs reach. Based on this system, the world's largest known living tree is the General Sherman giant sequoia in California. It is 83 feet around and 275 feet tall and it weighs more than 6.167 tons (the same weight as 41 blue whales or 740 elephants).

title: Bobcat
text: The bobcat is a carnivore of the cat family. It is about 3 5 inches long and is brownish with black spots and stripes. Its tail has a black tip. The bobcat lives in shrubby and forested areas of Utah. It is nocturnal, meaning that it sleeps during the day and is awake at night. The bobcat is also found throughout most of North America and parts of Mexico.

title: Francis Hopkinson and the American Flag
text:
If you asked 100 people who designed the first American flag, 99 of them would probably say Betsy Ross, right? Many people would be surprised to learn that there are dissenting opinions about that.

The U.S. Postal Service issued this stamp [right] in 2000 with this passage printed on the back:

Francis Hopkinson Flag 1777

Continental Congress member Francis Hopkinson designed the first Stars and Stripes. His stars may have formed rows or a ring; the exact design is not known. In a resolution of June 14, 1777, they were said to represent “a new constellation.”

There has been an ongoing debate about who made the first flag. Did George Washington really ask Betsy Ross to make a flag from his design? There are no written records confirming it, so many historians believe this is a legend. However, Betsy Ross’ family has always insisted that the story is true. They do have papers showing that Betsy was paid to make flags for the new country for the rest of her life.

Francis Hopkinson’s defenders can’t prove his claims either. He was a delegate from New Jersey who signed the Declaration of Independence. He sent a bill to Congress asking for payment for designing the first flag and other projects. After a long debate, a Congressional committee refused payment but never claimed that the designs were not his.

America was founded on the freedom of its citizens to disagree with the government and with each other. Neither side in the flag debate has found absolute proof. The discussion will certainly continue, showing that the all-American values of debate and dissent are alive and well. What issues in your community are a source of debate and dissent?
