title: Riding the Pony Express
text:
Sally Johnson was waiting at one of the Pony Express stations for her brother Randy to change horses. It would be his last lap before he turned the mail over to the next Pony Express rider in Placerville, Utah. While she was waiting she decided to go berry picking with a large Native American friend named Suzy. A storm forced them to take cover in an abandoned log cabin. While they were there, they overheard two bad mail robbers planning to ambush Randy and steal the large money shipment he was carrying. Sally hurried back to the station to meet Randy and warn him of the danger.

It seemed no time at all before Sally heard the wild-coyote yell Randy always gave as he came down the trail toward the Pony Express Station (place along the trail to pick up fresh horses). Sally met him at the corral. While he pulled his saddle and blankets from the back of the pony and saddled the fresh horse, Sally poured out her story. Randy drank hot coffee and put the cookies Sally had made into a leather bag tied to his saddle.

"Good girl," he said, with a grin. "I'll take the cut-off. I meant to anyway after this storm. I'd rather face the smaller man on the upper trail than Black Jack at Arch Rock. Black Jack shoots too well. Now listen carefully," he said. "The express money is sewn inside the saddle. The bags that usually carry the mail are full of old letters. The real mail (letters) is rolled in my saddle blanket. I'll throw him the bags, and I may get through."

Randy handed Sally his now-empty cup. "You can see the Gap from here, Sal. Usually I make it in 20 minutes. The mud will slow me down. Give me a half hour. Saddle your horse as soon as I leave. Come out here where you can see clearly. I'll wave my hat. If you don't see me ride through the Gap in a half hour, you're to take the cut-off and find out why."

With one motion, he turned his horse, jumped into the saddle and was off down the trail.

"So long," he yelled, waving his hat as his pony plunged into the trees.

Sally saddled her horse. She changed her dress for a pair of Randy's doeskin trousers and a leather shirt. She pushed her curls into one of Randy's hats. She kept watching the clock on the wall. When there were just five minutes to go, she walked her horse out to the gate where she could see the Gap clearly. In her hand was her father's little minute glass. She watched the Gap, keeping half an eye on the sifting sand. Five times she turned the little glass. Then she jumped on her horse and started up the cut-off trail.

She found Randy on the main trail below the Gap. The short man she had seen at the cabin lay face down in a puddle of mud. Randy's horse was dead. Randy lay on the ground beside his horse, frantically trying to get the saddle blanket untied. As Sally rode onto the trail, he whirled away from the horse. "Never mind anything else. I can't get the saddle off. The horse is lying on it. Ride for all you are worth into Placerville. Turn the mail over to Rogers at the station."

"You're hurt," said Sally. "I can't leave you here in this mud."

"You're going to do as I say," Randy ordered.

Someone glided out of the woods. Sally thought it was Black Jack and her heart jumped.

"Old Suzy," Randy cried. "Good Old Suzy. Suzy is here!"

The large American Indian woman stopped and lifted Randy like a sack of meal across her shoulders. She carried him into the woods. When she came back, she had Randy's gun belt strapped about her wide waist. She took the saddle off Sally's horse. Then she pushed and pulled the dead horse until she had freed Randy's saddle. She and Sally put the saddle on Sally's horse. Sally worked frantically. She expected Black Jack to come down the trail any moment.

"Black Jack will come soon," said Old Suzy.

"What's keeping him?" asked Sally.

Old Suzy shrugged. "His horse is gone," she said. "He tied his horse by the tree. He went to Arch Rock and Suzy untied the reins and gave his horse a big slap." She smiled and her eyes were lost in a mass of lines.

Sally swung herself into the saddle. "Good Suzy," she said. Sally dug her heels into her horse's sides and started up the hill to the Gap. Two hours later, she galloped into the small mining town of Placerville and up to the Pony Express station.

"Thought you'd never get here," shouted the angry voice of the waiting rider. "You're an hour late." And then, "Why, it isn't Johnson. It's a girl. Who are you?"

"I'm Sally, Randy's sister," said Sally, sliding out of the saddle. "There was a hold-up. Randy's hurt and can't ride. The money's sewn inside the saddle, and the mail is rolled in the blanket." Her knees were trembling. She could hardly stand.

With a practiced hand, the rider slid the saddle onto his fresh horse.

"Have you got a place to stay?" he asked. "This town's pretty wild."

"I'll stay with the Strongs. They're cousins of ours," said Sally. He fastened the blanket behind his saddle, leaped on the horse and galloped away.

The rider waved and shouted, "You did good for a girl riding for the Pony Express (mail by horseback)!"

title: Boom to Bust and Back Again
text:
You may have heard people compare the recent economic recession (2007-2009) to the Great Depression of the 1930s. But what some people call the "Great Recession" actually had more in common with a depression in the 1890s and something called "boom and bust."

In the early 1890s, the U.S. economy grew quickly ("boomed"), but couldn't keep growing at that rate. When many companies and the housing market failed, there was an economic "bust." The railroad industry had been booming since the end of the Civil War, but in the 1890s more than 150 railroad companies closed. Other industries that depended on the railroads closed, and many people lost their jobs. Over 500 banks closed. Thousands of unemployed men marched to Washington, D.C., in 1894 to demand that the government take action to help families. Unemployment was over 10 percent for most of the 1890s. About one of every ten people had no job.

In the recent recession, the housing market slumped after several "boom" years. Some automakers went out of business and others filed for bankruptcy. The economy went "bust," just as it did in the 1890s. Hundreds of banks and thousands of businesses closed. The unemployment rate was about 8 percent - about one of every twelve people had no job.

Make a chart or Venn diagram that compares these two events in history.

title: Pony Express
text:
The account of the Pony Express, which carried mail between Missouri and California, is a famous chapter in the early days of the West. Pony Express riders were a group of men who were hired to carry the mail by horseback across much of our country. The daring deeds of this small group of riders will long be remembered. The Pony Express service began April 3, 1860, and was stopped on Oct. 24, 1861. It lasted about 19 months or until the telegraph line was completed. (The telegraph is an early method of sending messages electronically over wires.) The entire trail along which the horses galloped stretched from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California. It covered a distance of 1,966 miles. Over this distance, there were 190 relay stations, each located 10-15 miles apart. At the relay stations, riders changed horses. Home stations, where a new rider took over, were from 45 to 85 miles apart.

When California became a state in 1850, it was very difficult for the new state to keep in touch with the rest of the country on the East Coast. Sending messages between the two ends of the country was a real problem. Stagecoaches carried passengers and mail over this great distance, but it took them three weeks, traveling both day and night, to make the journey. The Pony Express riders covered about 250 miles a day. This distance was twice as far as a day's journey by stagecoach.

Before the Pony Express began its service, news from the eastern part of the United States traveled to Salt Lake City very slowly. It often took three months or more for news from the East to reach Utah. No wonder Utahns were thrilled with the idea of a new, speedy mail service!

In 1860, there were more than 500,000 white settlers living west of the Rocky Mountains. As the population grew, a faster mail service was needed. A large freighting firm, Russell, Majors and Waddell, was asked by our government to start the Pony Express. They started the first riders at the same time from St. Joseph, Missouri, going west and from Sacramento, California, riding east. This began on April 3, 1860.

The Pony Express riders followed the California Trail which had been traveled by wagon trains since the 1840's. From St. Joseph, this trail followed the Platte River over the Nebraska prairie and on to Wyoming. It passed famous posts and landmarks such as Scotts Bluff, Fort Kearny, Fort Laramie and Independence Rock. It crossed the Rocky Mountains at South Pass, Wyoming and continued on to Fort Bridger. From Fort Bridger, it came through the Wasatch Mountains into Salt Lake City. From here, it rounded the shore of the Great Salt Lake going south into Utah County and then across the western Utah Desert to Carson City, Nevada. At Carson City, it climbed the Sierra Nevada Mountains and came down their western slopes into Sacramento. From there, the mail was hurried to San Francisco by steamboat on the Sacramento River. The Pony Express route through Tooele County in western Utah was probably the most barren, uninhabited and dangerous part of the entire run. It covered mostly desert and American Indian territory.

About 100 riders were hired for the pony express. They were young, skinny, hardy and daring (fearless). The advertisement for riders in the newspaper described the kind of men the company was looking for: "Young, skinny, wiry fellows anxious for adventure and chance to see our great West. Must be expert riders willing to risk death daily." Riders were paid as much as $125 per month, a good salary (money paid to employees in exchange for service) at that time. Station men and assistants were paid $100 per month. Few riders were killed on the trail, but many station operators living in outlying posts were killed by unfriendly American Indians. Riders were small men but rode on the best horses that could be found. Many were purchased at Kimball's Ranch 18 miles east of Salt Lake City. They cost $200 each - a high price in those days.

During its nearly 19 months of service, the Pony Express and its riders made 308 runs, totaling 616,000 miles and carrying 34,753 letters. On Oct. 18, 1861, telegraph wires joining the East and West were connected at the telegraph office on Main Street in Salt Lake City. On Oct. 24, 1861, the Pony Express made its last run. The chatter of telegraph keys replaced the clatter of horses' hooves and the Pony Express became another frontier memory.

Today there are trail markers, monuments and a restored Pony Express station at Simpson Springs in Utah's western desert to mark the old trail. A relay is a method of carrying something from one station to another.

title: Tooele County
text:
Named either from the Tooelian Indians, or from the word "tule," which is the Spanish word for a type of bulrush found growing in the area.
County Seat: Tooele
Population: 40,730

Tooele County is the second largest county in Utah. The Tooele Ordinance Depot employs many people who live in Tooele County. It stores chemicals and ammunition and also repairs and overhauls army tanks, trucks and other military equipment. At Dugway Proving Grounds, many different types of weapons are tested and proven before they are used in combat.

Many thousands of sheep and cattle use Tooele's desert area for winter feeding. Hay and grains are raised, along with turkeys and chickens.

Tooele is also known for its mining. Many ghost towns remain from a bygone era. Famous ghost towns such as Mercur and Ophir are known for the gold and silver they once produced. Wagons carried the ore to the Great Salt Lake where it was loaded onto boats. The boats floated the ore to Corinne where it was loaded onto trains to be shipped to the smelter. A lot of mining still takes place in Tooele today. Salt companies take raw salt from the Great Salt Lake and refine it into table salt, rock salt, and salt for manufacturing. Rock hounds search Tooele County for interesting and valuable rocks such as marble, jasper, opal, agate, fossils and feldspar crystals.

Tooele is best known for the Bonneville Salt Flats. The surface of the salt flats is almost completely smooth, making it perfect for speed-testing all kinds of land vehicles. Nearly all of today's land vehicle speed records have been set at the Bonneville Salt Flats.

title: What is a Blue Moon?
text:
For the American Indians, time was measured by things in nature. The position of the sun and stars and the phases of the moon all helped them tell time.

The saying "blue moon" means a second full moon in one month. If there is a full moon on the first or second day of the month, there will be a second one later that month. This is called a blue moon.

This generally only happens about once every 33 months. Sometimes there are two blue moons in the same year. That usually happens every 19 years. The term “blue moon” means “once in a LONG while.” “Say, are you ever late for school?” You might reply, “Once in a blue moon!”

title: Pony Express Fun Facts
text:
183 men rode for the Pony Express during its 19 months of operation.

Riders earned $100 per month.

The average weight for a Pony Express rider was 120 pounds.

The youngest Pony Express rider was 11 years old.

The oldest Pony Express rider was in his mid - 40s.

New riders took over every 75–100 miles.

Riders got a fresh horse every 10–15 miles.

Horses traveled about 10 miles per hour.

There were about 165 stations along the Pony Express route.

The fastest Pony Express delivery took place in 7 days and 17 hours. The mail being carried was a copy of President Abraham Lincoln's inaugural address.

The price for sending mail on the Pony Express was $5.00 per 1/2 ounce at first. When the Pony Express stopped running, the price had dropped to $1. 00 per 1/2 ounce. (It actually cost the company $16.00 per 1/2 ounce to carry the mail.)

The record for the most miles ridden in one turn is 380 miles ridden by Bob Haslam.

The leather saddle bags used by the riders were called mochillas.

400 horses were used by the Pony Express. Thorough breds, mustangs, pintos and Morgans were the most common horses used.

The greatest dangers to the Pony Express riders were American Indians, outlaws, blizzards, desert-heat, wolves, mountain lions and panthers.

title: Tic-Tac-Know

title: Computers of the Future
text:
Entering the Communication Age

Many years ago, men like Thomas Edison, Eli Whitney, Alexander Graham Bell and hundreds of others invented machines that changed the world. Inventions such as the light bulb, the cotton gin and the telephone brought this country into the Machine Age, a time period when machines began making life easier than ever before. When computers were invented and became inexpensive enough that most people could afford to own one, the world entered the Information Age. Computers made it possible for people to get, organize, share and use information in ways they never thought possible. With the invention of the Internet, e- mail, cell phones and wireless computers, many believe that we are now entering the Communication Age, a time when computers make it possible for us to communicate instantly with people all over the world. But what will computers be like in the future?

New Computers Must Be Easy to Use

In the future, look for computers to become even easier to use. Even though they may be able to do amazing and complicated things, they must be easy for people to use or people won't buy them. Computer designers and programmers will develop computers that can be used by anyone with very little training.

More Information Will Be Available on the Internet

Do you still head for the library when you need to write a report on Jim Bridger, or do you flip on the computer and type "Jim Bridger" in the search box of your favorite search engine? On the Internet, you're sure to find information on nearly any topic your teacher assigns, but you may not find enough to write a really good report on every subject. The information on the Internet is growing every day and before long, you will be able to go online and find nearly all the information available at the best and most complete libraries.

Invisible Machines Await Your Command

Someday, you may see the computer disappear altogether and in its place, a voice-activated command center will tell hidden machines what tasks you would like them to perform. Instead of sitting at a keyboard and typing instructions or commands, you will simply code your voice to the computer and tell it what to do. The hidden computer will follow your instructions silently and quickly. If you need to write a report for school, just tell the computer what to write, along with how you want the finished report to look, and the printed copy will drop out of the slot, ready to be given to your teacher.

The Future is in Your Hands

Before you know it, you will be finished with school and ready to start a career. You, and others like you, will be the ones who decide the future of computers and other great inventions. What would you like the computers of the future to do? How would you like them to look? Where would you want to install them? The future is in your hands.

title: The Telegraph
text:
Transcontinental Telegraph Completed in Salt Lake City

One of the great problems the early pioneers had was communicating with the rest of the world. Even after the Pony Express began handling the mail, it still took at least 10 days to get news from the East. The completion of the transcontinental (stretching across the entire continent) telegraph in October 1861 changed all that, making it possible for Utah's settlers to receive messages from the East almost instantly.

In October 1861, the lines of the transcontinental telegraph were joined in Salt Lake City. Brigham Young was one of the first people to send a transcontinental message on the new telegraph. A telegraph is an electrical device that is used to send coded messages across special wires. The code used to send these messages was invented by a man named Samuel Morse. Morse Code, as it is called, is made up of a series of dots and dashes that represent different letters of the alphabet. (Go to this week's "Arts and Crafts" column to see how this code works.)

In order to get the telegraph line built, the United States government offered money to any company that would set the poles in the ground and string the wires across the country, connecting the East to the newly-settled West. Lines were built across the country, but the work moved slowly until two companies began racing to finish the job. On July 4, 1861, Edward Creighton began laying the telegraph line for the Pacific Telegraph Company of Nebraska. He started at Julesburg, Colorado, and headed toward Salt Lake City. On the very same day, James Gamble began digging telegraph post holes at Fort Churchill, Nevada, for the Overland Telegraph Company of California. Both companies headed for Salt Lake City as quickly as they could and on Oct. 20, 1861, the Pacific Telegraph Company from Nebraska won the race. Four days later, the Overland Telegraph Company arrived in Salt Lake City and on Oct. 26, the telegraph line was officially joined.

Utah was no longer cut off from the rest of the world. It could now receive messages from New York City or San Francisco in a matter of seconds. Being able to communicate quickly with the rest of the country helped the early pioneers remain up-to-date on the latest news in politics, inventions, entertainment, and even clothing styles. This new method of communication (the ability to present thoughts and ideas to others) helped Utah stay connected with the rest of the country and paved the way for it to eventually become its own state.

title: Wayne County
text:
Named for Wayne Robinson, son of William E. Robinson, a Utah state legislator. The boy was killed when thrown from a horse.
County Seat: Loa
Population: 2,500

Wayne Country is sometimes called Wayne wonderland because of its beautiful scenery. Capital Reef is made up of many strange and interesting formations. One of the most famous areas of the park is Cathedral Valley. Huge blocks of stone, looking very much like large cathedrals, or churches, stand above the valley, giving the area its name. There are also strange lava formations formed when hot lava was forced up through cracks in the Earth thousands of years ago. Boulder and Thousand Lake mountains tower above western Wayne County, while the eastern part of the county is home to Canyonlands National Park, as well as the Green and Colorado rivers. Though cattle and sheep have been raised successfully in Wayne County, beautiful scenery is the country's main attraction. Some crops such as potatoes, oats, barley, alfalfa, wheat and some fruits are also raised here.

title: Why Do We Say “It’s Raining Cats and Dogs”?
text: Old superstitions (strange beliefs) about weather, which go back for thousands of years, always included cats. A long time ago, people believed cats had a great influence on weather. Some people even believed witches changed their shape to cats and would ride through storms. Others believed in a king of storms, a god called Odin, who was helped by a dog to produce wind. The cats came to represent down-pouring rain, and dogs represented strong gusts of wind.

title: Wild Roots and Tubers
text:
You can get plenty of nourishment and good taste from the roots and tubers of 1. arrowhead, 2. cattail, 3. burdock and 4. Jerusalem artichoke.

If you are in a survival situation, you can peel and eat these tubers or roots raw. They are better boiled or roasted in the coals of your fire. For roasting, wrap the roots in several layers of large leaves that have been dipped in water. The wet leaves will steam and then roast the roots.

Caution: Be sure you know what plant you are dealing with before you try eating it. Some wild plants can make you very sick.

title: Agility of Mind: Teddy Roosevelt Wins Nobel Peace Prize
text:
agile (adjective): able to move quickly and easily; ex.: as agile as a monkey, an agile mind.

Teddy Roosevelt was president of the United States from 1901 to 1909. He was also a great hunter, explorer, author, outdoorsman and soldier.

As a child Teddy was often sick and could not play sports. But he became a good problem solver. He wasn’t afraid to put his thoughts into action or think of different solutions. If his first idea didn’t work, he had the mental agility to change his mind quickly.

When Roosevelt was president, Japan and Russia were at war. He invited diplomats (official representatives) from Russia and Japan to Portsmouth, New Hampshire to talk about peace. At first, he didn’t know how their problems could be solved but he acted quickly to get the diplomats together. He helped them compromise. After a lot of discussion, they worked out their differences and signed the Portsmouth Peace Treaty, an agreement that ended the war and saved many lives. President Roosevelt won the Nobel Peace Prize for helping end the war. His way of helping others solve problems is still used today.

Teddy Roosevelt had an important power skill—an agile mind. You can use this power skill when you act on your good ideas. Remember that an idea can be good without being perfect. People with agile minds often fail before they succeed. The ability to think on your feet, or think while doing, can help you find solutions that will benefit others.

title: The Railroads Are Coming!
text:
The completion of the transcontinental railroad marked the end of the pioneer era and the beginning of the Age of the Steam Engine in the United States.

The railroads are coming! The railroads are coming! The news spread across the United States in 1865. Men and women traveling in wagons brought the news west. They had heard the train whistles and had seen the tracks being laid. The Union Pacific Railroad (in the center of the United States) was laying track from Nebraska toward the Rocky Mountains. The Central Pacific Railroad was laying track eastward from California. Someday, the two lines would meet.

The cowboys were excited. They would be able to ship their cattle to the eastern markets by train. But the American Indians on the prairie were afraid. They watched as the trains rumbled by. They called the railroad the Iron Monster. The American Indians were afraid the railroad companies would take their land. They were right. The companies did take the land.

Building the railroad was not an easy job. There were no steam shovels or bulldozers in the 18 60s. All the digging, carrying, pushing and pulling had to be done without machines. Men used picks, shovels and mules. All supplies had to come from the East. Equipment for building the Union Pacific was shipped to the Missouri River by train. Then it went by boat, and then it was shipped on another train. The equipment then traveled by boat for a time and was then loaded onto another train.

The builders of the Central Pacific had even bigger problems. They were starting in California. But they too had to get their supplies from the East. Everything had to go by ship around the tip of South America and then up the coast to California. It was a trip of 15, 000 miles! For both companies, the hard work didn't stop when the supplies arrived. Rocks had to be cleared away and tunnels had to be drilled through the high mountains. In winter, snow fell. Sometimes the drifts in California were 100 feet deep.

Slowly, mile by mile, the building continued. Workers gave names such as Devil's Slide, Devil's Gate and Devil's Gulch to some of the places along the way. From these names, you can guess how rugged the country was and how hard these men thought their jobs were. At last, men building tracks from the East could see men building from the West. They met on May 10 , 18 69, in a little settlement called Promontory, Utah. The last two pieces of track were to be joined with gold and silver spikes. And what a celebration there would be!

On that great day, bands played and the crews from both companies gathered around to watch two important men drive in the last spikes. The president of the Central Pacific picked up a huge hammer. He swung it over his head and brought it down hard. He MISSED! The crowd laughed and cheered. Then the vice president of the Union Pacific swung. He missed too! There were more cheers and more laughs. Other men from both companies took their turns. At last the silver and the gold spikes were hammered down. Then, slowly, a Union Pacific train from the East and a Central Pacific train from the West chugged toward each other. The two engines met, and the crowds roared. Rails (heavy steel tracks) now reached across the country from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean. America had a transcontinental (goes across the continent) railway!

title: Railroad Fans Flock to Helper
text:
Did you know that there are hundreds of thousands of people all over the world who love the sound of train whistles, the smell of a steam engine and the sight of a locomotive chugging down the tracks? You may find it hard to believe, but at least 10,000 people each year visit the tiny Utah town of Helper to experience the excitement of railroad history for themselves.

SueAnn Martell, director of the Western Mining and Railroad Museum in Helper, says that while many Utahns have never heard of her museum, those who are serious about railroad history wouldn't miss the chance to stop in for a visit. "If you're a true railroad fan, you have to make one pilgrimage in your life to Helper," she says.

Helper is the logical spot for this interesting museum because it was once a booming railroad town. The Denver and Rio Grande Railroad came through the area in the early days of the steam locomotive. Trains would stop here to take on coal and water, as well as to hook up to special "helper" engines that would help them over Soldier Summit and into the Salt Lake Valley. Helper took its name from these important "helper" engines, and the town became a necessary stop for trains heading that way.

The Western Mining and Railroad Museum in Helper not only offers exhibits about the history of the great Rio Grande Railroad, but it also has rooms built to look just like a doctor's office, beauty shop, general store and other businesses that thrived during the height of coal mining in the area. Outside the museum, visitors can see trains such as Utah Railway Caboose No. 55, which was in operation from 1917 until the 1980s, and a Denver & Rio Grande snowplow, or "spreader," that was once used to push snow off the tracks leading to Soldier Summit.

The Helper Western Mining and Railroad Museum is a great resource for anyone interested in trains or in the history of the railroad. Talk to your parents about visiting this important Utah historic site.

title: Wedding of the Rails
text:
Few events in American history have captured the nation's imagination as did the building of the first transcontinental railroad and the celebration of its completion with the driving of a golden spike into a laurel tie at Promontory, Utah, on May 10, 1869. Two beautiful steam locomotives, the Jupiter of the Central Pacific Railway and No. 119 Rogers of the Union Pacific Railway nosed each other and touched pilots in remote Promontory, Utah. Not a person there doubted that this moment was among the nation's finest. The pioneer era was now over, the continent was bridged and the United States was now truly one nation.

To really capture the excitement that the whole nation felt at the Wedding of the Rails, imagine that you are watching your TV the day that Neil Armstrong stepped onto the moon. Or the day the Challenger returned from its maiden voyage victorious from space, mission accomplished. The same electrifying feeling was in the air. The entire nation was talking, writing and singing about trains. Model train-making was popular, and little pioneer children were asking for trains for Christmas. Store windows carried the train theme as they displayed their products for sale. School children memorized poems about trains and wrote about them in their school work.

The steam locomotive was the "Space Shuttle" of its day. It drove at unheard-of speed into a little known frontier carrying its payload of passengers and freight. The development of the locomotive ended the Pioneer Era and started the new era of the steam engine. Companies such as Rogers and Schenectady, which built steam locomotives, took great pride in decorating their engines and tenders with bright red paint, brass fittings and gold leaf trim. They also covered engines with hand painted oil paintings. These engines were exciting to look at and seemed almost alive as they puffed and breathed vapor while clanging into Promontory for the Wedding of the Rails.

The American steam locomotive was designed differently than the traditional British train. The British steam engine (locomotive run by steam) was built for long-established rail routes with little twisting or turning in the track. These giants traveled at about 35 miles per hour. The new American frontier, on the other hand, had hundreds of miles of twisting, mountainous terrain to cover. American steam locomotives were designed with little wheels in front that would follow the track easily, and travelled 60-75 miles per hour. Many of them burned wood as opposed to the British oil or coal. American locomotives had a striking appearance with their bright colors and brass or gold trim. They carried about 2,000 gallons of water which was used up about every 40 or 50 miles. Frequent stops were necessary to take on water.

Transcontinental Railroad

One of the greatest events to happen in Utah history was the Wedding of the Rails at Promontory, Utah. In 1861 Abraham Lincoln was made president of the United States. President Lincoln and many government leaders talked about a railroad that would stretch all the way across the United States from ocean to ocean. It would not be easy and would take millions of dollars to complete. Two companies decided to race to see which could lay the most track in the shortest amount of time. Since these companies were paid for every mile of track they laid, each wanted to lay as much track as possible. The Union Pacific started at Omaha, Nebraska. They used mostly Irish (people from Ireland) workmen. The Central Pacific started at Sacramento, California, (on the Pacific Coast) and used mostly Chinese (people from China) workers. The Central Pacific had the hardest job since they had to build lots of bridges and blast lots of mountain terrain. The companies met at Promontory Summit, Utah. The Union Pacific laid 1,086 miles of rails, and the Central Pacific laid 690 miles of rails. The first transcontinental (something that goes across the continent) railway was finished May 10, 1869. A golden spike was driven to celebrate the Wedding of the Rails. This marked the end of Utah's pioneer era, the time when the early settlers first came to Utah. Many changes came to our state along with the new railroad. Can you think of what some of those changes were?

title: Box Elder County
text:
Named after the many Box Elder trees growing there.
County Seat: Brigham City
Population: 44,000

Most of the people that live in Box Elder County live close to the mountains. The western part of Box Elder is mainly desert land used for dry farming and by cattle as a winter range. About a third of all dry land wheat raised in Utah is grown in Box Elder County. Besides wheat, the farmers of Box Elder County raise sugar beets, peaches, cherries, apples, watermelons, cantaloupes, tomatoes, potatoes and onions. The fruit stands along the highway south of Brigham City are famous for the delicious fruit and vegetables sold there.

One of the famous historic spots in Utah is found in Box Elder County. Promontory Summit, where the golden spike was driven in 1869, is at the north end of the Great Salt Lake about 30 miles west of Brigham City. The Golden Spike Celebration is held here every year to celebrate the last spike being driven into the laurel tie that joined the two railroads.

Bear River Bird Refuge, where that natural habitat of many local birds is protected, is located between Brigham City and Promontory. Box Elder County is also home to Willard Bay, part of the Great Salt Lake. The bay has been diked off so that the water there is fresh and no longer salty. Boating, waterskiing, swimming and fishing are all enjoyed at Willard Bay State Park.

title: “The Wedding of the Rails” by Lorraine S. Wilkinson
text:
It happened on the 10th of May in 1869, A wedding sealed with gold and silver nails, The place was Promontory, and the sun began to shine, For setting of the Wedding of the Rails,

The Central Pacific and Union Pacific, a huggin' and a chuggin' down their trails, They set a heavy pacin' while a racin' to the place; setting of the Wedding of the Rails.

One was pushing from the East, the other from the West, Their locomotives chuggin' right behind, With tampers 'n the layers 'n the spikers 'n the rest, The hardest workin' men you'd ever find.

The Central Pacific and Union Pacific, a huggin and a chuggin' down their trails. They set a heavy pacin' while a racin' to the place; setting of the Wedding of the Rails.

When the race was over great excitement filled the air, The Jupiter faced Rogers cross the track, The crowd was pushing to the front, they came from everywhere, And it was mighty hard to keep them back.

The Central Pacific and Union Pacific, a joinin' the transcontinental rails. They drove the precious golden spike into the laurel tie, history setting Wedding of the Rails.

They drove the precious golden spike into the laurel tie for setting of the Wedding of the Rails.

text: In 1869, the president of the United States, the state governors and other lawmakers wanted to bridge the gap between the East and the untamed wilderness of the West, so they had the transcontinental railroad built. Today, many government leaders are concerned about exploring a new frontier: outer space. In another hundred years, what “new frontier” will we need to explore? Write a page describing what you believe this new frontier will be.

title: Future Farmers of America: Teaching Kids About Farming
text:
How would you like to raise a calf, grow your own corn crop, run a landscaping business, build your own greenhouse or make and sell corsages and boutonnieres (flower arrangements) to your friends? These are just some of the creative and interesting projects that Utah high school students completed last year. The students had a chance to try their hand at these and many other projects when they joined FFA (Future Farmers of America) a club for high school students who want to learn about farming and other related businesses.

Future Farmers of America was started in 1928 in Kansas City, Missouri. The club has grown from a small group of Missouri students who wanted to learn how to become good farmers to a national organization with over 490,000 members. More than 3,000 of these members are from Utah, and FFA has 59 chapters in schools across the state.

In order to become of member of FFA, students must take at least one agricultural (farming) related class each year and must pay club dues of $5 per year. After joining the club, members must also do at least one at-home project throughout the year. In the past, most students chose to raise an animal, but today, members are choosing to do all types of outdoor and farm-related projects. Amanda Brown, an FFA member at Davis High School, learned to make and sell flowers arrangements as part of her individual project. "Now I can sell boutonnieres and corsages for homecoming," she said. "You can find basically anything you want to do."

One of the most exciting events of the year is the Utah State Fair. FFA members show off their projects and hope to earn prizes for their hard work. Members also run booths set up to let people know more about the club. At last year's fair, FFA members - dressed in their blue corduroy jackets - took turns volunteering at the FFA children's exhibits. At the Barnyard Friends exhibit, FFA members help children pet baby pigs, calves, lambs and chicks. Children were also allowed to plant seeds, grind wheat and drive toy tractors.

Besides learning about farming and agriculture, members of FFA can also earn scholarships and prize money to help them pay for college. Today, more farmers than ever before are going to college to prepare themselves to be the best farmers and ranchers they can be. FFA teaches students what careers are available in farming and how to prepare themselves for those careers.

If joining FFA sounds like fun, you may want to look into joining the 4-H Club right now. The 4-H Club is a club for children in the third through the 12th grades where members do projects in subjects that interest them. If you enjoy your experience in 4-H, you will probably be ready to become a member of FFA when you reach high school.

title: Give Goat Milk a Try
text:
If you are like most kids, you probably enjoy milk, cheese and other dairy products. If you are allergic to cow's milk, however, enjoying these delicious foods is impossible without a little creativity. The most common food allergy in the world is the allergy to cow's milk. For those who suffer from this allergy, eating even a small amount of dairy products made with cow's milk can cause diarrhea, asthma attacks, bloating and stomach cramps. The people at Drake Family Farms have a solution for those who love dairy products, but can't digest cow's milk.

Drake Family Farms, located in West Jordan, Utah, has been around for more than 100 years. For the last 20 years or so, Drake Family Farms has been in the goat business, raising goats specifically for milking. They then sell goat milk, goat cheese and even goat soap to those who have discovered the benefits of goat milk. Many of the people who buy goat milk and cheese from Drake Dairy Farms do so because they are allergic to regular cow's milk. Others prefer the taste, or believe that goat milk is more healthy for them.

The people at Drake Family Farms believe in selling the most healthy and natural products possible. Although their milk is pasteurized (made safe to eat by heating it to kill germs and bacteria), there are no preservatives, artificial flavors, artificial colors, pesticides or harmful chemicals used in their products. Their goal is to offer the best possible dairy products to those who care about their health.

Jeanette Drake, one of the owners of Drake Family Farms, also makes wonderful goat milk soaps and cheeses. The soaps come in a variety of scents such as rose petal, vanilla cream, cinnamon spice and milk chocolate mint. Some of the cheeses for sale by Drake Family Farms include chevre, queso blanco and fresh goat milk ricotta. Jeanette says that these cheeses are wonderful to snack on, but they are also great when added to salads, sandwiches and pasta.

If you or someone you know is allergic to cow's milk, or if you just want to give goat milk products a try, consider visiting Drake's Family Farm in West Jordan. You may find a new way to enjoy dairy products made from something other than cow's milk.

title: Utah’s Farming
text:
When the pioneers first came to Utah, they immediately planted crops. The crops they raised were watered by the cool mountain streams. There were no stores where they could buy things, so they had to rely on farming for their food and clothing. They had to be self-reliant, which means they had to provide for their own needs.

Most of the pioneers time was spent growing food, because if their crops failed, they had little to eat. When food became scarce, it was sometimes necessary for the pioneers to eat sego lily roots and to hunt wild game.

What Is Farming Like In Utah Today?

Since pioneer times, farming has remained an important means of earning a living in Utah. Many of the smaller towns in our state are farming communities. They rely on farming as a major source of income. Most of the farming is done in the valleys of the mountains near the foothills where the rich soil has washed down from the mountains. Many of the farms are small, made up of only a few hundred acres or less.

The main crops grown in Utah are wheat, alfalfa (hay), corn, sugar beets, (vegetables containing sweet juice that is made into sugar), tomatoes and other vegetables. Utah also produces fruit such as apples, peaches, apricots, cherries, pears and red raspberries. Utah's high altitude gives the apples and other fruit raised here an excellent flavor. Utah ships much of its fruit to other states by refrigerated trucks and rail cars.

title: Daggett County
text:
Daggett County was named for Elsworth Daggett who surveyed the canal which brought water from Henry's Fork to Daggett County farms.
County Seat: Manila
Population: 905

Daggett County is located on the northern slopes of the Uinta Mountains, is rich in wildlife and is an important cattle and sheep raising area. Flaming Gorge Dam and National Recreational Area have brought over a million visitors to Daggett County each year. Fishing, boating and water skiing are excellent on Flaming Gorge Reservoir, which is 91 miles long. Sheep Creek Canyon has good camping and some beautiful and unusual scenery. At Red Canyon Overlook you can stand at the edge of a deep canyon and look down at the water far below. The red cliffs and blue water are beautiful. The town of Dutch John was built to house the people who take care of the dam, the reservoir and the recreational area.

Hunting for deer, elk and rabbits is very good in Daggett County. Many rock collectors also come here every year to find beautiful rock specimens. Daggett County only has a population of a little more than 900 people, but it seems like a very busy place, especially during the summer when sports enthusiasts run the Green River in rafts. The Green River has also become the greatest fishing spot in Utah in recent years.

title: Ranching and Dairying in Utah
text:
Besides growing crops, Utah farming also includes ranching, or raising animals to sell, and dairying, or raising cows for their milk. Utah ranchers raise mainly cattle, sheep, turkeys, chickens and pigs. Utah ranchers raise more beef cattle than any other animals. Ranchers raise animals that support meat packing plants which process beef, lamb, turkey and chicken for sale to grocery stores around the country. Sanpete County is famous for the Norbest turkeys raised there. In fact, turkeys are Sanpete's main crop! Ranchers also raise chickens for the eggs they produce.

Utah also has many dairies throughout the state. These dairies raise cows for the milk they give. While all mammals produce milk, cows are the main source of milk used to make butter, sour cream, ice cream, yogurt and cheese. Cache Valley Cheese, made in Cache County, is famous all over the United States.

Sheep ranching also brings in a great deal of money to Utah each year. Sheep ranchers make money from selling both the wool and the meat from their animals. In the last few years, sheep ranchers have suffered heavy losses due to drought conditions on their rangelands. They have also lost many young lambs to predators (animals that live off of other animals) such as coyotes, or wolves. Both sheep and cattle graze in the mountains during the summer. They spend their winters in the valleys and western deserts.

title: A Man Goes To Jail For Growing Wheat Without Water!
text: A Nephi farmer, David Broadhead, was arrested for perjury (telling a lie) many years ago when he swore he had raised wheat without irrigation. This was completely unheard of in those days. He was placed in jail for a time, but was released after he furnished proof that what he said was true. He later renamed his homestead, "Perjury Farm." The practice of dry land farming caught on with other farmers because they found they could make money farming much of Utah's unused land in the drier valleys. What the old "Perjury Farm" owner had discovered was a system for growing wheat that was different from anything known. This is now known as "Winter Wheat" farming, or dry farming because the wheat is planted in the fall in time for it to sprout before the first snow storms cover it for the winter. When the spring rains come, the wheat continues growing until it reaches maturity. The wheat is then harvested in July, without ever needing any irrigation. Utah dry farmers grow a high-quality, hard, red wheat, which is very high in protein

title: It's Our Fault
text:
The Earth is our home. But the geography of Earth sometimes causes our home to be a not-so-safe place. Changes in the temperature in the atmosphere (called inversions) trap pollution in the air we breathe. Lightning strikes cause fires that destroy forests and sometimes neighborhoods. Flooding rivers can wash away a whole town. Strong earthquakes can damage or destroy buildings, roads and bridges.

The Wasatch Front in Utah is a great place to live. The scenery is beautiful and the mountains offer many opportunities to have fun—skiing, hiking, snowboarding— you name it! The people who live near the Wasatch mountain range have a constant water supply thanks to winter snows and spring thaws. But the mountains are along a fault, a break or crack below the Earth’s surface. Fault lines are where earthquakes happen, and the Wasatch Fault has had its share of earthquakes over the years. Look at the diagram below and to the right. To the right is a map of the Wasatch Fault. Below is a chart of earthquakes that have happened in different segments (parts) of the fault over the past 6,000 years. Only earthquakes that have caused the Earth’s surface to move and crack are shown. Use the diagram to help you answer these questions.

2. According to the diagram, which segment had the most recent earthquake?

3. Which two segments had earthquakes about 6,000 years ago?

4. On which segment has the most time passed since the last earthquake?

5. How many earthquakes does the diagram show altogether?

6. According to the diagram, how many earthquakes have happened less than 2,000 years ago?

title: Shakespearean Festival Center!
text:
The Shakespearean Festival continues in the beautiful Utah Shakespearean Festival Center in Iron County in Cedar City, Utah.

When the early pioneers began settling in Iron County, it wasn't long before they discovered its rich iron ore. Today, Iron County is the heart of Utah mining country, but it has also become famous for its high-quality entertainment. Cedar City, home of Utah's Shakespearean Festival, has put Iron County on the map as the center of world-class Shakespearean performances.

You can't put a price on the excitement and joy, laughter and tears which the Utah Shakespearean Festival creates. For over a quarter century, the festival has steadily grown to become one of the top theatres (the English way of spelling "theaters") of its kind anywhere in the world. As the festival has grown, so has the theatre itself. The Shakespearean Festival Center, located on the campus of Southern Utah University in Cedar City, is now one of the finest theatrical complexes in the country.

The Utah Shakespearean Festival was founded in 1961 by Fred Adams, a young actor who wanted to give Iron County tourists something to do in the evening once they were through exploring the beautiful area scenery. Fred came up with the idea of performing Shakespearean plays in an outdoor theatre on the campus of the college. The first three plays, "The Taming of the Shrew," "Hamlet" and "The Merchant of Venice," were presented in the summer of 1962 and the festival has continued ever since. In 1962, the plays were presented on an outdoor platform with a small backdrop behind it. Today, the outdoor plays are performed in the Adams Memorial Theatre, an authentic, open-air, Elizabethan playhouse patterned after the original Globe theatre used by Shakespeare. It is considered to be the finest theatre of its kind in the world.

The Randall L. Jones Theatre opened in 1989. This beautiful building is a more modern theatre for those who prefer indoor performances. In addition to the two large theatres, there are also sidewalk cafes, book shops, tea rooms, a memorial grove, the Center for Renaissance Studies, the Memorial Plaza and Fountain, an authentic clock tower and the Memorabilia and Sweet Shop.

More people than ever are flocking to the Utah Shakespearean Festival since it received the Tony Award for America's Outstanding Regional Theatre in 2000. People from all over the country come to Cedar City to see the award-winning festival. The festival opens each July with a parade and continues through most of September with daily (except Sunday) performances in both theatres. Iron County is still known for its mining activities, but it has also become famous as the home of the Utah Shakespearean Festival.

title: Become a Mining Engineer!
text:
Do you like math and science? Would you enjoy solving tough problems while inside a dark cave or while traveling deep inside a mine shaft? How would you like the opportunity to use your math and science skills while earning between $50,000 and $60,000 on your first year on the job? If this sounds like an ideal job to you, then you should think about becoming a mining engineer.

Mining engineers are in short supply right now, and there are more jobs available than there are people to fill them. During the 1980s, about 700 American students graduated from college each year as mining engineers. Today, only about 100 American students graduate in this field each year. At the University of Utah, between five and 10 students graduate from the mining engineering program each year. When they graduate, each of these students has four or five good job offers to choose from.

Why aren't more people interested in becoming mining engineers? Many students are afraid of the math and science they would have to learn, but others simply don't know about the career. Those who have heard of the job often think that it is dirty, dangerous and old-fashioned. Mike Nelson, associate professor of mining engineering at the University of Utah, says, "It certainly is not a business where you wear a suit and tie to work every day, but it's a very high-tech business now with a lot of intellectual challenge and opportunities to do interesting things."

Nelson also says that there are a lot of scholarships available to help students in the mining engineering program pay for their schooling. Students who are interested in this career can get help paying for school and go on to get a stable, high-paying job. With many other industries laying off their employees or cutting back on their pay, the field of mining engineering could be a good career choice. If you enjoy math and science and would like a job that offers good pay, along with a little adventure, you may want to look into becoming a mining engineer.

title: Utah’s Mining History
text:
Utah is rich in mineral resources. Our state has large deposits of copper, coal, iron, gold, silver, lead, uranium, zinc, salt, gypsum, potash, limestone, gilsonite, phosphates, oil shale and tar sands. Each of these items is very useful and can be used to make life better. Copper is used to conduct electricity, coal is burned to give off heat, iron is used for its strength, gold is used in jewelry, silver is used mainly for tableware, lead is used in computers and electronics, uranium is radioactive and is used in nuclear fuel, zinc is used to galvanize, or protect, other metals, salt is used for foods and in industry, potash is used as a fertilizer, limestone is used in cement, gilsonite is used in making asphalt, phosphates are used as preservatives, and shale oil and tar sands are used to make fuel.

When the pioneers first came to Utah, they had little interest in or time for mining (digging in the earth for ore and other materials). They were more concerned with surviving in the harsh wilderness. Most pioneers spent their time raising food and animals, using what they needed themselves and selling what they had left over. For the first few years that the pioneers were in Utah, farming was their main source of income.

How Did Utah Mining Get Started?

The pioneers first started mining by quarrying, or digging stone out of the mountainside. The pioneers began digging limestone from a quarry (a place where stone is found). The lime they found here was used in making mortar, a material used between bricks to keep them in place, and plaster, a mixture used to make the inside walls of their homes smooth. Old kilns, or brickbaking ovens, where pioneers once made lime, still dot the east bench of Salt Lake City. As the pioneers looked for more ways to become self-sufficient, or to take care of themselves, they began mining coal, lead, iron and salt. Clay was also mined and baked into bricks used for building their homes.

Mining Precious Metals

The Bingham brothers, Sanford and Thomas, first settled in Bingham Canyon in 1848. They later discovered minerals in Bingham Canyon, but mining didn't begin until 1863. These early miners dug mostly lead, silver and gold. As soon as the soldiers from Fort Douglas learned about the rich ores in Utah, hundreds of them began prospecting for gold and silver. They were organized into mining districts by Colonel Connor. He advertised rich strikes and many people flocked to Utah hoping to get rich. Lead and silver mining were Utah's most important mining interests in the beginning and mining towns such as Stockton, Ophir and Mercur sprang up almost overnight.

These towns were typical "boom towns," with miner's shacks and plenty of saloons and gambling halls. Mercur also had a school, which even had its own children's band. As the mines ran out of ore, most of these mining settlements faded away and became ghost towns.

The Railroad Opens the Way for Utah Mining

When the transcontinental railroad came to Utah, a new mining boom took place. With access to the railroad, miners could now haul their heavy ores easily and cheaply. A railroad was built in Bingham Canyon and a new way to mine the low-grade copper found here was born. Steam shovels were used to dig the copper ore out of the mountain and railroad cars were used to haul the ore to the smelter where it was refined into high-grade copper.

Utah Copper sold the mine to Kennecott Copper Corporation in 1936 and the mine went on to become the largest open-pit copper mine in the world. The mine looks like an oversized football stadium, with about 300,000 tons of copper being hauled out of the mountain each year. Kennecott Copper is one of the largest industries in Utah and has recently updated its mining techniques to compete with world production. The mine provides work for hundreds of Utahns and brings millions of dollars into Utah's economy each year.

title: Carbon County
text:
Carbon County got its name from the large deposits of coal (made mostly from carbon) found there.
County Seat: Price
Population: 21,000

Carbon County is rich in high grade coal. A fuel shortage in recent years made coal very popular again. Carbon County's coal contains very little sulphur, so it can be burned in industry to give off heat when other coal cannot.

Helper is the center of one of the largest railroad and coal mining areas in the West. It has a museum with displays and murals telling of early pioneer mining. Along with the museum is a large statue of "Big John," claimed to be the world's largest coal miner.

Castle Gate in Price Canyon was once one of Utah's oldest and best known coal mining towns, but the town has now disappeared. In 1974, those living here were forced to move when the company that owned the land where their houses stood sold it out from under them. The people of Castle Gate moved out and the houses were removed, leaving no sign of the once thriving mining town.

Price, the county seat, is home to the College of Eastern Utah. It also has a museum showing fossils and exhibits highlighting American Indian cultures.

title: The Famous Cornish Pump
text:
There is a famous folk tale told of an event that took place in Park City, Utah. Park City is another early Utah mining town. The mines in Park City were very rich, but they had a water problem. The mines were deep in the earth and a lot of water seeped into the mines. Cornish miners liked to work in the Park City mines. The cold, dripping water reminded them of the mines where they had worked in Cornwall, England.

To keep the Ontario Mine at Park City from filling with water, a huge pump was built. The flywheel weighed 70 tons and was 30 feet in diameter. The flywheel turned slowly, and a man could walk on the steps and oil it while it was turning and pumping water. It could pump 2,560 gallons per minute. The pump was known as the Cornish pump and was the pride of the Ontario Mine until one day it stopped working. The workers tried and tried to get it started while the water in the mine got deeper and deeper. When it seemed that nothing could get the giant flywheel turning again, the miners sent a messenger to another mine where a Scotchman worked. He knew about pumps.

The Scottish workman came quickly, bringing with him a huge sledgehammer. He climbed onto the giant flywheel. He placed his feet carefully. Then he swung the sledgehammer with all his strength. The hammer crashed against the wheel, sending echoes down the mine tunnel.

Slowly, very slowly, the 70-ton flywheel started turning. The miners cheered. The mine owners did not cheer, however, when the Scotchman presented his bill for $1,000.00. They wanted to know why it was so much. The Scotchman explained his bill this way:

"For hitting the wheel with a hammer...... $.50.
For knowing where to hit the wheel... $999.50."

title: Iron County
text:
Iron County was named for the iron ore found there.
County Seat: Parowan
Population: 34,000

Iron ore was discovered by an exploration party led by Parley P. Pratt in 1849. Since that time, Iron County has become the heart of Utah iron mining. In ancient times melted rock, or lava, flowed across this land as water might flow across it today. Interesting black lava rock formations are found throughout the county.

Brian Head is the highest point in Southwestern Utah at 11,315 feet above sea level. Many skiers come from Nevada and California to ski there. Brian Head overlooks Cedar Breaks National Monument. Cedar Breaks has the same type of formations and beauty as Bryce Canyon, but its coloring is lighter.

Southern Utah University is located in Cedar City. The famous Utah Shakespearean Festival is held here each summer and fall. The whole town dresses up for the occasion. There are parades, feasts and green shows, and plays by William Shakespeare are performed nightly in two beautiful theatres. Thousands of people come from near and far to enjoy this popular festival.

Many interesting ancient American Indian artifacts have been found in the diggings of Parowan Valley. Pit houses dating back 800 years before Columbus came to America have been discovered, along with storage bins, pottery, tools and bits of clothing. These artifacts can be seen on display at Southern Utah University in Cedar City.

title: Turning Lemons Into Lemonade
text:
The last time you asked your parents for money, what did they say? If their answer was "no," then you may have found yourself wishing that you had some money of your own. While having your own money to buy the things you want may seem like a dream for a kid your age, there are many creative ways for children to earn their own cash.

If you want to earn your own money, you need to find a way to offer a product (something you can sell) or a service (something you can do) that people would be willing to pay for. Once you find a need in your area, you can jump in and fill this need. You could sell lemonade, cookies or suckers, or you could offer to mow lawns, tend children or wash cars. If your product or service is something that people really need or want, they will be willing to pay you for it.

When deciding how much to charge for your product or service, you will need to think about several different things. If you are selling a product, you will need to figure out how much it costs you to make the item. If you charge $0.25 for an 8-ounce glass of lemonade, but it actually costs you $0.50 a glass for sugar and lemons, then you will lose money on each sale. You need to make sure you are making a profit, or that you are bringing in more money than you are spending on each item you sell.

If you are offering a service for sale, you need to take a look at how much time each job will take and how much you think your time is worth. You also need to find out how much others are charging to do the same job. If you offer to mow a neighbor's lawn for $20.00, but there is another person in the neighborhood who is willing to do it for $10.00, you may not get the job. On the other hand, if you offer to mow it for $10 and everyone else in the neighborhood is willing to pay $20.00, you won't be getting a fair price for your work. See what others are charging for the same job and decide what a fair price will be.

You may also want to see what you can do differently from other people in the same business. If there is a lemonade stand on the corner that serves only lemonade, you may want to offer brownies or cookies as well. If the other neighborhood yard care workers only mow lawns, you may want to offer edging, trimming and weeding services. Anything you can do to make your business different or special in some way will likely bring in more customers.

Once your business is making a profit, you will find that having your own money gives you a great feeling of accomplishment, not to mention the opportunity to get some things that you couldn't have bought without your own money.

title: Keeping it Here at Home
text:
Chances are you could go for a snack right now. Many Utah companies offer delicious foods that are sure to hit the spot when your stomach begins to rumble. Hundreds of these great Utah companies have joined together to create "Utah's Own," a group that reminds Utahns to buy Utah products whenever possible. Buying Utah's Own products gives customers great products while keeping the money they spend right here in our own state. Utah's Own slogan is, "Keeping it Here at Home, We're Utah's Own."

Buying Utah made and grown products is a good idea for many reasons. Utah products are fresh because they haven't been shipped long distances. They are often cheaper as well, since high shipping charges haven't been added. Buying Utah products also keeps the money you spend here at home and creates jobs for your parents, neighbors and friends.

title: Free Market System in Utah
text:
When the early pioneers first came to Utah, most of them were farmers who raised crops that their families needed to survive. As time went on, settlers looked for ways to make a living by filling the needs of the growing numbers of families who were making Utah their home. New businesses began springing up all over the valley and farming was no longer the only way to make a living. Today, business owners still keep their eyes open for products and services they can offer to people who will pay for them. Let's take a look at how businesses get started and what they need to do to succeed.

Getting Started

In order to open a business, the owner must have an idea of a product or service that he can offer to the public. Once he has done his research and believes that people will pay for what he has to offer, the business owner puts in his own money, and sometimes money he borrows from the bank, to buy the things he will need to open up his business. If he were opening up a candy factory, for example, he would need a building, along with large pots and pans, ovens, cooking utensils, candy molds and all of the ingredients to make the candy. He would also need to hire workers to help make the candy, wrap it, deliver it and sell it.

How Does a Business Make Money?

In order to make money, a business must bring in more money than it pays out. Take our candy company, for example. If it costs the company more money to buy ingredients, pay workers and put advertisements in the newspaper than the amount of money that candy sales bring in, the company will soon close down. If the candy sales bring in enough money to pay for all of the expenses, or costs of running the business, there will be money leftover at the end of the month and the company will make a profit. The more money leftover at the end of the month, the bigger the profit will be.

Making the Business Grow

Most businesses start out small and plan to grow larger in time. The candy maker may start out by making the candy himself in a small shop. If people like his candy and buy more than he can make himself, he may decide to hire one or two workers to help run his business. He may decide that the business will grow faster and make even better candy if he teaches each worker to do a specific job, instead of him trying to do all the jobs himself. Giving separate jobs to people who are good at them is called the division of labor. The candy maker may hire someone who is great at dipping chocolates to handle his chocolate department, while hiring someone with a college degree in accounting. An accountant can save the company money by helping them spend their money wisely and keep track of the company's money. As the business grows, the owner may begin offering new products and hiring more workers to make his ideas succeed. Many businesses grow so large that they need to store their products in warehouses until time for them to be shipped.

Taking Care of the Workers

As a business grows, the workers become more important than ever to the success of the company. Without the workers, no products could be made and no services delivered, causing the company to shut down. This is why it is so important for business owners to take good care of their workers.

Taking good care of the workers means making sure that they have what they need to do their jobs well. Workers should be hired to do something they are good at. They should also be given the proper equipment and supplies to do their jobs well.

Of course, workers must also be paid a fair wage, or payment for their work. If a company doesn't pay a worker what he is worth, the worker will soon quit and find a better job elsewhere. Most companies also offer certain benefits, or other advantages for working for the company. These benefits may be things like health insurance, bonuses, paid vacation time, sick leave and even discounts when they buy the company's products for themselves.

Companies that pay fair wages and offer good benefits to their workers often have better employees who stay with the company for many years, doing all they can to make the company a success. Workers who feel that they are treated well usually enjoy their jobs and have a better work ethic, or commitment to doing good work for the company, than those who believe that their employer isn't treating them fairly.

What Role Do You Play?

While you are still too young to work at many jobs, especially for a large company, you can still play an important role in the success of the businesses in your area. After all, even the most well-run company in the world wouldn't make any money if it didn't have any consumers to buy its products. A consumer is someone who consumes, or buys, products or services. You are a consumer when you buy candy, pizza, music, video games and clothes.

Consumers tell companies what they like, what they don't like, how much they are willing to pay for an item, and what type of quality they expect from the products they buy. If the candy company tries out a new recipe for gummy bears and the consumer - YOU - don't like it, then the company will have to go back to the old recipe if it wants to sell gummy bears. If your favorite pizza place decided to save money by using imitation cheese on its pizzas, you as the consumer have the power to either buy the pizza or go somewhere else if you don't like the new taste. If too many consumers don't like the quality of the pizza, the pizza place will have to go back to using real cheese or close down. On the other hand, if imitation cheese tastes just fine to you, then the pizza place can start using the cheaper "fake cheese" and make a larger profit. You, as the consumer, have the power to decide what you will and will not pay for.

title: Rich County
text:
Named for Charles C. Rich, a Mormon colonizer who helped settle the Bear Lake area.
County Seat: Randolph
Population: 2,000

Most of the land in Rich County is used for raising cattle and sheep. Hay is cut and stored in the summer so there will be feed for the cattle during the long, cold winter months. Rich County is Utah's unofficial cold spot. Weather reports often list either Randolph or Woodruff, two Rich County cities, as having the coldest temperatures in the state. Temperatures in these locations can plunge to as low as 65 degrees below zero!

Bear Lake is Rich County's most important tourist spot. Bear Lake is long and very deep. Half of the lake is found in Rich County and the other half is in our neighboring state of Idaho. Bear Lake is a rich blue-green color and is surrounded by cabins and summer homes.

In the summer, people flock to the lake to enjoy boating, water skiing, fishing and swimming. In the winter, ice fishing is a very popular sport. Bear Lake is the only place in the United States where the small Bonneville Cisco fish lives. The Cisco fish are caught during their two week spawning, or egg-laying, season. They are not caught with a hook and line, but with a dip net. These special nets are dipped down through holes in the ice and the unusual fish are scooped out of the freezing water. Fishermen also come to Bear Lake to ice fish for trout and white fish, but these fish are caught using a hook and line.

Summertime visitors to Bear Lake often take in a performance at the Pickleville Theater in Garden City. The playhouse was opened in 1977 and performs plays each summer from mid-June through Labor Day. The playhouse also offers a Western dinner, served up by the actors, before the show.

title: What Was America’s First Department Store?
text: America's first department store opened in Salt Lake City in 1868. The store's official name was Zions Cooperative Mercantile Institution, but it was known simply as "ZCMI." Brigham Young started the store so that members of the Salt Lake City community could trade with each other, getting the best prices possible on the things they needed to buy. He didn't want the new settlers to have to pay high prices to outsiders for goods shipped from the East. The first store sold all types of items, including clothes, wagons, farm equipment, sewing machines, carpets, shoes, groceries and medicines. By 1961, ZCMI had opened stores in malls throughout Salt Lake City, Provo, Ogden and Logan. By 1999, there were 14 ZCMI stores located throughout Utah. In December 1999, the May Department Stores bought ZCMI and changed its name to Meier and Frank. Meier and Frank was recently bought by Federated Department Stores, who changed the name to Macy's.
