title: Ethics: President Coolidge Rebuilds a Bridge of Broken Trust
text:
Have you ever wondered how people acquire, or gain, power? In a representative democracy like the United States, a lot of that power comes from trust. We give our vote of confidence to leaders we have faith in. If those leaders betray our trust, then we are free to elect a new representative and the power shifts. But once trust is broken, it can be hard to rebuild.

One of the most famous betrayals of our public trust happened with President Harding’s administration. With President Harding’s sudden death in 1923, it was up to the new president to repair that bridge of trust. President Calvin Coolidge didn’t waste time. He made it clear that no one in government would be above the law. “If there has been any crime,” he said, “it must be prosecuted—no one will be shielded for any party, political or other reasons ... Every law will be enforced and every right of the people and government will be protected.” And he meant it.

Investigators soon found that Secretary of the Interior, Albert Fall, was guilty of accepting bribes, or gifts, in exchange for the rights to a rich oil field in Wyoming called Teapot Dome. He was the first presidential advisor (helper) to serve time in prison for unlawful behavior. The Teapot Dome Scandal, as it became known, went down in history twice. It was first an example of broken trust, and again an example of how to rebuild it!

title: Chaps or Mary's Bloomers?
text: Delicate Arch - possibly the most famous natural span in the world - has had at least seven other names. The early names came from the free-standing arch's unusual shape. Since it looks like a bow-legged cowboy's pair of chaps, it has been called Chaps. It has also been known colorfully as Bloomers Arch, Schoolmarm's Pants, Old Maid's Bloomers and Mary's Bloomers. Just who Mary was - if she was a real person - is not known. Frank Beckwith made a scientific expedition to Arches National Park in 1934. He wrote an article about the arch in the February edition of Times Independent. He called the arch "Delicate Arch" and referred to the rare beauty and fragile nature of this masterpiece of delicately chiseled colored stone. His name stuck. It is officially called Delicate Arch today. Though there are many arches in the park, Delicate Arch has become the symbol for Arches National Park. You can also see Delicate Arch on the 1996 Utah Centennial license plates on many cars.

title: Climb Inside a Mountain
text:
Our state is full of beautiful scenery, from red rock formations rising out of hot desert sands to crystal blue mountain lakes surrounded by rugged peaks. There is truly something for everyone in the great outdoors of Utah. One place you and your family might enjoy exploring together is Timpanogos Cave National Monument, located up American Fork Canyon in Utah County.

Timpanogos Cave National Monument is actually a series of three caves inside the mountainside. The caves were discovered by Martin Hansen, an early American Fork settler who found the crevices by accident in 1887 while following the tracks of a mountain lion.

The caves are very popular with visitors from Utah, as well as those from out of state. To get to the caves, you must hike a paved, 1.5 mile trail. The trail is very steep, so no strollers, wheelchairs or other wheeled vehicles are allowed. The hike is free, but if you want to tour the caves at the top, you need to buy special permits at the visitor center at the base of the trail. Be sure to bring along plenty of water and a few snacks for the trail. You will also need a jacket, since it is only about 45 degrees inside the caves.

What will you see when you visit the caves? Spectacular rock formations including stalactites hanging from the ceiling like icicles, stalagmites rising up from the floor to meet them and other formations that look very much like draperies, drinking straws and popcorn.

The Timpanogos Cave Trail is open mid-May through mid-October, from 7:30 a.m. until 4:30 p.m. For more information, call the visitor center at (801) 756-5238.

title: Grand County
text:
Named after the Colorado River, which was once called the Grand River.
County Seat: Moab
Population: 8,500

Grand County's main attractions are the beautiful national parks such as Arches and Canyonlands National Parks. Roads lead from Moab to the Colorado River and across the lower elevations of the La Sal Mountains. Other roads reach out to Dead Horse Point and the Island in the Sky area of Canyonlands National Park. Breathtaking desert scenery and river scenery have attracted movie makers. Many famous Western movies and TV shows have been filmed near Moab. Boys and girls from Moab sometimes can earn money by being "extras" in the movies.

Moab was once called the uranium capital of the world. Grand County still mines uranium and has a mill there that processes it. Along the Colorado River there is beautiful scenery and dinosaur tracks and American Indian writings can be seen only a few feet from the road.

Cattle and sheep are raised throughout Grand County with alfalfa being grown on the ranches for winter cattle feeding. Moab valley grows peaches, apples and other fruit.

Boating on the Green and Colorado rivers has become popular in Grand County. In May the "friendship cruise" leaves the town of Green River in Emery County. Hundreds of boats go down the Green River to where it meets the Colorado River. The boats then go up the Colorado to Moab. Thousands of people cruise 196 miles of river to enjoy some of the most beautiful and unusual canyon scenery in the world. In June there is a "Marathon" boat race that covers the same route. The racers skim their boats down the Green River to where it meets the Colorado River. Here they turn upstream and finish at Moab. They find dinner, a bath and a bed for the tired racers. Prizes are awarded for the winners.

title: Archaeology and You
text:
Digging In

Why study archaeology? Why not! It is dirt-digging fun, with lots of story telling and mystery solving too.

Archaeology is the science of studying objects from the past in order to learn about people and human cultures of other times. Archaeologists are the people who search for these materials and they do it through a process called excavation. It sounds hard, but it's really just a fancy way of saying they dig a lot - and all over the place too! Just think, instead of working in an office, these people spend their days digging in places like the Wasatch Mountains or the Juke Box Cave in Utah. With all the stuff they have found in Utah, we know more about the American Indians who lived here thousands of years ago. The places where archaeologists dig are called sites.

They aren't just digging for any old thing though. They are digging for special things called artifacts and fossils. So what makes an artifact different from a fossil?

Artifacts are objects that were made, used or carried by humans that give us information about human behavior in the past. Pottery, stone tools and coins are just a few examples of artifacts. Fossils are remains or imprints of living things, like plants, animals and people. If you were to dig up an old dinosaur bone, you would have just found a fossil.

Artifacts and fossils help archaeologists piece together the past and tell the story of people and cultures that lived long before us.

Can You Dig It?

Each day it is important for us to take care of all the archaeological sites that let us keep learning about the past. Even though archaeology helps us learn about the past, it also helps us learn about the future.

Regular history gives us dates, names and events, but it does not always tell us how ordinary people lived, worked, ate or acted towards each other. This is why we must protect archaeology. It tells the story of past lives and cultures. We learn about the rise and fall of different groups of people and see what went wrong. Who knows? We may need to know this stuff for our own survival someday. By learning about other cultures and ways of life we are able to understand ourselves and other people better.

For example, fossils and artifacts helped us learn that people in Utah were hunters and gatherers for thousands of years. Once we learned this, lots of people wanted to study more about this way of life. By digging along the Wasatch Front in Utah, they learned even more about hunters and gatherers and how things changed when they switched to farming life.

If we don't protect the archaeological sites full of artifacts and fossils, we might lose important materials that would help us understand the past and the future of people from all over the world, including Utah. Plus, we have to save places for future archaeologists like you to dig.

title: Get Ready-Get Set-Go, Wisconsin!
text:
Welcome to Wisconsin Studies Weekly! Hang on tight for the ride of a lifetime. We'll explore our state from top to bottom, start to finish, inside, outside, upside and downside. We'll roam the ancient copper fields, explore lead mines, scuba dive through thousands of lakes and rivers, wander through deep forests, build a boat, race a car, fly an airplane, walk with the first pioneers and fly a spaceship to the moon. We'll feed the country, help fight its wars, work for lasting peace and stand up to defend the weak from the bullies. This is Wisconsin, land of the free, home of the brave, the greatest place on Earth to get the best hamburgers, chocolate and pizza the world has ever known!

Wisconsin Studies Weekly is your weekly time capsule of historical events. Learn about our state's roots, our beginnings that reach back thousands of years. Learn about the fantastic progress a state can make from the earliest days until freedom came to our borders. Learn how you can be a part of this great state and preserve its liberties, resources and beauty from now to a thousand years from now. This will be one of the most satisfying and exciting studies you will ever experience.

How to Use Wisconsin Studies Weekly

Each issue of Wisconsin Studies Weekly will include a current event on the front cover. This is a real news story about something important happening in our state or nation right now. Our cover story will help you get a head start on this week's history lesson. We will take you on a journey into the experiences of great people and great events with our cover stories.

And there's more: We will tell you about the jobs, skills and crafts early Wisconsin dwellers had and what principles guided their lives; the animals, birds, trees, and plants that live in our state and many other facts that will make your study of Wisconsin enjoyable and interesting.

And let's not forget the games, crafts, and activities! The crossword puzzles and word search games will help you learn new words. And we'll include other activities that are just plain fun.

So, lets get started! Turn the page and jump right in; the water is fine- and so is the land. What land? Why, the land you're standing on. And just where is that? Let's find out! (Hint- turn the page!)

title: Wisconsin in the World
text:
Where in the World is Wisconsin?

If you could fly into space aboard the space shuttle, our state would look like a green and brown smudge in the north- central United States. Getting closer, you would see that Wisconsin is surrounded mostly by natural boundaries. The Mississippi River forms the western border, and Lake Superior and Lake Michigan lie on the northern and eastern borders. Wisconsin's elevation slopes from an average 1, 700 feet on our flattened northern ridge to an average of 7 5 0 feet in the lowlands of the southeast. The highest points are about 1, 950 feet above sea level; the lowest, along the shore of Lake Michigan, is 5 8 0 feet.

Wisconsin is almost exactly the size of its neighboring states, Illinois and Iowa. Our land looks more different than any of the Great Lake states because of the effects of a glacier a long time ago. As the glacier melted over time, it left in its place thousands of lakes and great forests, covering two- thirds of the state. On the eastern border of Wisconsin is the Door Peninsula. A peninsula is a body of land almost surrounded by water.

Wisconsin is famous for timber and forest products, and our hillsides are loaded with important minerals. All of the work we do to use our land has made Wisconsin one of the great states in our nation. Can you find Wisconsin on a globe or map of America? Look at the maps on this page. Where do you live? What states are our neighbors?

Our Amazing State!

Wisconsin is the 20th largest state with 5,680,000 people.

Wisconsin's shores touch two of the five Great Lakes (the largest bodies of freshwater in America): Lake Michigan and Lake Superior.

Wisconsin leads the nation in production of green beans, beets, cabbage, and sweet corn.

Marathon County produces 9 5 percent of all ginseng in the country. Ginseng is a Chinese plant used for teas and other herbal preparation.

We are also one of the major beer- producing- and consuming- states in the nation, a reflection of our strong European heritage. Our fishing fleets bring in more fresh fish than any of the other Great Lakes states.

For almost 75 years, Wisconsin was the nation's leading dairy state. California recently passed us in this area.

In 1976, one of the 10 largest ore deposits in North America of zinc- copper massive sulfide was discovered in northern Wisconsin.

Our lumber mills produce more paper than any other state.

title: The first Wisconsin explorers were only two inches tall!
text: Who first discovered Wisconsin? Take a stroll down the sandy banks of Lake Michigan or Lake Superior, and you might step on one. Crustaceans, like the crab, shellfish, sea worms and seaweeds, were the first things to live here. These little creatures lived in the sea about a half a billion years ago, during the Cambrian period. The trilobite was the largest of these creatures. This creature was shaped like a beetle and stretched from 12 to 18 inches in length. That's one big creature, about the size from your elbow to the tip of your fingers. Trilobites were around for several million years. Soon, several neighbors moved in such as the "sea lilies." They sound fairly harmless, but sea lilies (or crinoids) were actually little animals growing at the top of slender stems. To catch food, they waved their petallike arms and scooped tiny sea animals into their mouths. Completing the Cambrian period were giant sea scorpions (eurypterids). Some of them were 6 feet long. That's about as long as a man is tall!

title: How thick is the Earth's crust?
text: Our Earth is made of mostly rock and metal. When the Earth was still a mass of molten rock, the lighter materials floated to the top. Today, the thinnest sections of the Earth's crust (the outer layer of the Earth) can be found at the bottom of our oceans, where it is only three miles thick. That's why there are many underwater volcanoes and earthquakes. The thickest crust is under the mountains and can be up to 45 miles thick. Compared to the rest of the Earth, the crust is very thin. If the Earth were the size of a baseball, the crust would be no thicker than a sheet of paper.

title: Where are Wisconsin's Dinosaurs?
text: When we talk about ancient times in Wisconsin, the question naturally comes up, "What kind of dinosaurs roamed our state?" Unfortunately, we'll never know. The problem has to do with old rocks and erosion. Millions of years ago, the eastern part of North America lifted up and became exposed to the weather. For millions of years, wind, rain and sun slowly destroyed, or eroded, the layers of rock that might have contained fossils of dinosaur life. The missing rock records cover about 3 00 million years of the geologic record. This includes the entire dinosaur period. Eons of rain, wind, and sun scraped it all away. By the time the glaciers came, we had deposits that were thousands of years old lying on top of rock 3 00 million years old, and nothing in between. People call this the "missing interval." So, there are no T. Rex teeth in our ancient landscapes. Our fossil record is either extremely old (before dinosaurs) or quite recent. We have plenty of fossils of mammoths, mastodons, giant beavers and musk ox, but little else.

title: Help a Rat and Learn to Run the Country This Year!
text:
Hey, kids! I’m Revere the Rat, but you can call me Rev. I’m your online Studies Weekly friend and I need your help. You can help me get great stuff by earning points while you learn. Just scan the code or go to www.studiesweekly.com and click on my picture.

In fact, Studies Weekly kids are so smart, that many of you will someday be mayors, senators, governors—maybe even the president!

For now you have two jobs: Learn about the country and how it works and earn points for me so I can get that great stuff I told you about. It’s easy. Just scan or click and you’re on your way!

title: Head Flops
text:
Have you ever wanted to create 27 pictures by drawing three? Watch as one person gradually turns into another and another.

Materials

paper

Instructions

title: How Do I Use the Library?
text:
One resource you may use your entire life is the library.

Use the Library’s Catalogs

The best way to find books in the library is to use its card or computer catalog system.

Card Catalog

A card catalog is a filing system where book information is stored on cards in drawers. They are organized alphabetically based on the information at the top of the card.

Card catalogs contain three cards for each book: author, title, and subject cards. Each card contains the call number for a book, which is how you find it.

If you wanted to find some books on dinosaurs, you would go to the “D” drawer and look for “dinosaurs.” Read the cards to decide which books would help you the most. Find the book’s call number in the upper left-hand corner of the card and write it down. A book on dinosaurs might have the call number 560.2. So, you would go to the part of the library where the 500 Science books are and look for 560.2.

Try It!

Use your library’s card catalog to find books on dinosaurs.

Find the drawer you need based on the topic you are researching. Write the letter(s) for that drawer here: ______________________________________________________

Look for cards that match your topic. Read them to decide which books would be most useful.

Write down the call numbers for those books here: ________________________________ , ____________________

Find the section where your books are located based on the call numbers. Get the books you have selected and check them out.

Computer Catalog

While some schools still have a card catalog, other schools (and most public libraries) have replaced it with a computer system. If you type the word “dinosaur,” the computer will bring up all the books with “dinosaur” in the title or subject description. If the list is too long, be more specific by searching, for example, “Jurassic dinosaur,” or “meat-eating dinosaur.”

title: How to Build a Paradise on Earth!
text:
Imagine that you could see a long, exciting movie about North America rising from the hot, molten mass of the Earth's crust and slowly becoming the land we know today. The opening scenes would show the continent (a large piece of the Earth's crust that is above the oceans) breaking away from other landmasses and gradually pushing toward the west. For ages, the oceans would wash over the barren lands, and then mighty mountains around the edges of the continent would bunch up and push above the waters. Rain and wind would wear the mountains down to sand, and the oceans would wash over them again. This amazing process would repeat over and over.

Finally, after a very long time, the whole land would rise above the sea, and the oceans would drain off. Our continent would be covered with layers of dead sea creatures, soil, and rocks.

Suddenly, volcanoes would explode to life and start building huge mountain ranges. Vegetation would start growing, and thick forests, swamps and jungles would appear. But then comes that ocean again, washing sand and dirt over the land to bury the forests. When the ocean finally left, new forests would start growing again.

But the land didn't stop moving and changing. As our continent continued drifting to the west, the large tectonic plates beneath our continent rubbed, ground and pushed into other parts of the Earth's crust. As these plates moved over each other, a lot of heat and destruction took place. This causes earthquakes and underwater volcanoes. These rumbles and tumbles are all part of our Earth's constant process of shifting and changing.

And then came the glaciers, sheets of ice. For many thousands of years, the giant mountains of ice age glaciers scraped across the top of the continent, digging out and smoothing down the landscape. As the glaciers retreated and melted, the changed landscape around our state suddenly had a whole new watershed system that fed five huge lakes - the Great Lakes!

After millions of years of volcanoes, glaciers, moving landmasses, storms, and earthquakes, we finally have this wonderful place of beauty and peace that millions of people love to call home. Warm sun, long and sculptured coastlines, magnificent forests and landscapes, spacious cities and the most fertile lands in the country - It's just about perfect. It is hard to believe such terrible forces were at work for so long to produce this beautiful state of ours. But the truth is, such forces are still at work! All of nature's change happens slowly and takes a very long time. Earthquakes and volcanoes come along once in a while to speed things up, but the bigger changes take ages.

Okay, the movie is over! Now, let's see how our state turned out. (Turn the page.)

title: Scientists Believe Volcanoes Caused a ‘Little Ice Age’
text:
An ice age usually lasts thousands of years. But between A. D. 13 00 and A. D. 19 00 the northern hemisphere experienced a cooling called the "Little Ice Age." The cooling was so intense that glaciers moved south, causing northern European towns to be destroyed. It was so cold that the Thames River in London and canals in the Netherlands froze! A scientist at the University of Colorado, using plant fossils from this period, may have discovered why this happened.

The plants died suddenly between 12 7 5 and 13 00. That's exactly when many volcanoes erupted. Fifty years later, volcanoes erupted again. Billions of tiny particles from the eruptions were in the atmosphere, reflecting the sun's heat away from the Earth. This caused the land to cool, the plants to die and the ice cap to grow. But there's more.

The growing ice cap sparked a feedback loop. A feedback loop causes something to happen over and over. First, the tiny particles stopped a lot of the sun's heat from reaching land. This cooling caused the ice cap to grow. The ice reflected more of the sun's heat back into the atmosphere. This caused more cooling. Finally, the glaciers became so large that they stopped the warmer ocean currents from melting the ice cap. Over centuries the glaciers grew to cover northern Europe.

Volcanic eruptions started the cooling, but it took the feedback loop to keep the "Little Ice Age" going for centuries!

title: Regions of Wisconsin
text:
Our beautiful state has 5 6 , 1 5 4 square miles of hills, mountains, low- lying land, swamps, rushing rivers, thousands of lakes, untouched forests, and great stretches of farmland. There are five natural regions in our state. A region is a section of our state set apart from others because it is different and unique. Let's find out more about these regions.

Lake Superior Lowland

The Lake Superior Lowland is a narrow shelf of lowlands on the shore of Lake Superior. Streams from the highlands divide this area into narrow valleys with bluffs and sandy beaches along the lake. There is iron in the east, but the lowland is used chiefly for grazing and hay production. The Apostle Islands are just off the central beaches. (Can you find and circle them on your map of Wisconsin?) Many people like to visit these beautiful islands in the summer time.

Central Plain

The Central Plain is a crescent- shaped region on a sandstone bed stretching across the center of the state. This area is known by its buttes and mesas. Buttes are steep- sided hills, and mesas are table- like lands. Because of the action of old glaciers, the region has flat- topped, sandy stretches, mounds and ridges that look like castles and thousands of acres of peat- filled swamp lands where cranberries grow. Hay and potatoes grow here. In the dells of the Wisconsin River, the glaciers carved the hard rock into deep canyons and odd rock formations.

Western Upland

The Western Upland is located in the southwest, a region of ridges and valleys etched by streams that have cut into the limestone and sandstone. This region wasn't smoothed over by glaciers, and so it has remained quite rugged. It stretches along the western boundary from St. Croix County to Rock County on the Illinois boundary. It is one of the most beautiful regions in the state. The rich pastures feed many dairy herds. This region produces butter as well as Swiss and Limburger cheese.

Northern Highland

The Northern Highland was once a range of very old mountains. As time passed, glaciers slid over the mountains and smoothed them out. A high plain was formed and was dotted with small lakes, marshes, stream beds and heavily forested hills. Cranberries love growing in the marshy sections of the northwestern and northern forests. The southern strip is mainly pasture land. It includes dairy farms and cheese factories, where several types of cheeses are made. In the north, the Gogebic Range and land along the Menominee River contain iron for mining. The upper Wisconsin River furnishes water power and is a perfect location for paper manufactures. It contains the state's highest point, Timms Hill (1, 9 5 1 feet [5 9 5 meters]) in Price County. Today, it is a favorite vacation land, and crowds come here to fish, ski and hike.

Eastern Ridges & Lowlands

The Eastern Ridges and Lowlands are formed by three broad, parallel limestone ridges, which run north to south and are separated by wide and shallow lowlands covering the eastern part of the state from Green Bay to the southern boundary. This region was once covered by glaciers. It contains Lake Winnebago, the Kettle Moraine, Horicon Marsh and the coastal and interior lowlands. The northern Fox River rapids provide the greatest water power in the state. The rapids are surrounded by forests, which have led to the establishment of the pulp and paper industry. This region is the greatest manufacturing region and most thickly populated part of Wisconsin.

title: Latitude and Longitude
text:
Map makers have come up with a good way to find things on our planet. It works very well. They made a globe of the Earth and carefully drew a giant grid (like a checkerboard) over the surface. The lines that run up and down (north and south) are called lines of longitude. Remember this word by noticing that longitude lines are very l- o- n- g. They are numbered in degrees. The starting place is called the prime meridian, which is zero degrees.

The lines that point left and right (east and west) are called lines of latitude. These are really giant circles that go horizontally all the way around the Earth. Each is numbered in degrees, beginning with the equator (the biggest circle!), which is in the middle and numbered zero degrees. Using this map, can you figure out your state's location by degrees longitude and latitude? Mark it with a dot.

You might also hear longitude lines called meridian lines and latitude lines called parallel lines. Take your pick; both are used worldwide.

A good way to find places on Earth is by using the latitude and longitude lines. Latitude lines run east and west. Longitude lines run north and south. Each line is numbered in degrees.

title: Where do things live?
text: Life on Earth is concentrated in a narrow, 12-mile layer of water, land and air. Birds, animals, plants, fish, ocean creatures and all living things are part of this region we call the biosphere. The highest point is Mt. Everest, where an occasional human climber can be found. The lowest point is the bottom of the ocean (almost 7 miles deep!), where a few worms and other creatures live. But that's not where the action is! Most life forms live from 10 feet underground to 100 feet above ground and in the top 300 feet of oceans and large bodies of water. If Earth were the size of a basketball, the biosphere would be thinner than paper.

title: Meet Wisconsin‛s Greatest Swimmers!
text: Fish love Wisconsin freshwater lakes. However, not all fish are lucky enough to swim in these beautiful lakes. Will the luckiest fish please splash their fins? Ladies and gentlemen, boys and girls, please meet the whitefish, herring, and lake trout. Whitefish are freshwater fish. They were found in North American lakes from the latitude of the Great Lakes and northward. Whitefish feed on insects and shellfish in moderately deep water most of the year. Herring are among the most valuable food fishes. Great numbers of them travel in schools and are easily captured by man. They feed on small organisms, mostly crustaceans, floating in the water. Lake trout are very tasty fish. They can live in saltwater and freshwater. They have red and light spots on a dark body.

title: Reason and Logic: Young George Washington, Surveyor and Mapmaker
text:
Most people know about George Washington. He was born in Virginia. He was a general during the American Revolution and our first president. But his earliest jobs, surveyor and cartographer (mapmaker), taught him skills and values he would use for the rest of his life. Using reason and logic to solve problems helped Washington become one of our country's most important leaders.

When Washington grew up, there were few roads or boundaries in much of the land. A surveyor's job was to measure and map the land. He had to make exact measurements for boundaries and physical features. This was a very big responsibility. People needed accurate maps and surveys for traveling and buying land.

At age 17, Washington traveled across the Blue Ridge Mountains to map and survey part of the frontier. He was the surveyor for the whole county, and that was an important job. When he led the Continental Army, it was even more important to have reliable maps. He established the job of Geographer and Surveyor General and appointed a man named Robert Erskine to this position. He gave Washington some information that was very helpful in making reasonable and logical battle plans and decisions.

You can use these same skills to make important decisions. Be sure you have the facts and information you need instead of acting on opinions and emotions. In what areas of your life are reason and logic very important?

title: How do I read a map?
text:
Maps can tell you a great deal, from finding out which direction to travel to figuring out the elevation of an area or the amount of wheat produced in a state. Map reading is a valuable skill that you will use all your life.

Use a Grid and Legend

Most maps use symbols and marks to help you use them. Here are a few:

Map scale— A map is a very small representation of a large area. So how do you know what a mile is on that small map? Using a map scale, you can see how the distances on a map relate to actual distances. If a map scale says, “1 inch = 1 mile,” then one inch on the map represents one mile in real life.

Legend—Have you ever seen little pictures or symbols on a map and wondered what they meant? Find out by looking at the legend. The legend is a box, usually in a corner of the map, that lists the symbols and then tells what they mean

Grid— Many maps are arranged on a grid, which means that you will see lines going up and down and back and forth on the top of the map. The grid helps you locate places on the map. Maps with grids usually also have letters along the sides and numbers across the top and bottom.

Index— To use the grid to find a location, go to the map’s index. There, you will find a list of places with a letter-number combination for each. Find the spot on the map where that letter and number cross, and you will find the location you were looking for.

title: Wisconsin’s Wonderland of Water and Forests
text:
Recycled water! Could you be drinking the water that your dog lapped up last week? Possibly. Water is always moving through a cycle that takes it from the Earth to the sky and back again. We call this the hydrologic cycle. ("Hydro" means "water.") The hydrologic cycle begins with the sun. The sun heats the Earth, and water begins changing from a liquid to vapor. This is called evaporation. The vapor is clean and rises high into the sky, leaving behind salt, pollution or other impurities it might have been mixed with.

The vapor meets up with other water vapors, and they combine to form clouds or fog. When the clouds cool down, the vapor turns back into liquid and falls to the ground as rain, snow, or hail. This is called precipitation. In some part of the country, large mountains stand in the way of clouds. When the clouds are stopped by the mountains, they drop much of their moisture through precipitation before moving on.

When the snow melts and rain falls, it trickles down the sides of mountains and hills. It gathers into cracks and low places and becomes creeks, streams and rivers. The little rivers join others and form huge rivers. And where does all this rushing water go? It goes to the lowest place it can find, usually rivers, lakes, or the ocean. Sometimes it just soaks into the ground.

Your local water company gathers water from underground, lakes, streams, or rivers. The water moves through a special cleaning system. Now water is safe to drink and bathe in, and it won't smell like your dog!

Forests

Trees also go through a cycle. Like people, trees are born as seeds, grow tall, reproduce and then die. These changes are all important to the ecosystem of the forest. The term "ecosystem" is a word that means "the total collection of living things, together with their non- living environment, in a particular area." The parts of a forest ecosystem include trees, bushes, herbs, animals, insects, fungi or 'trash burners,' the sun, wind, soil and rain.

Trees- especially hardwoods- undergo many changes over the course of the year. During the winter, when the temperature drops and the ground and water lie frozen, the trees don't grow or reproduce. They go dormant, almost like hibernating, or going to sleep. In the spring, the temperature increases, and the snow melts. There's plenty of water in the ground, and the sun shines brightly. Trees begin to grow and produce flowers and leaves.

Summer brings hot, sunny weather, but it's often a time of drought. Trees take this time to store food, using photosynthesis to control and preserve the new growth. Photosynthesis is the process by which plants make carbohydrates, or energy, from light and air.

When fall comes around, fruit ripens, and trees start preparing for winter. Days grow shorter, and the sun drops to the south. The air gets cold. Leaves can no longer carry out photosynthesis and start to turn red, orange and yellow.

When winter arrives, trees become dormant, and the cycle begins again. A tree's annual ring reveals the year's weather patterns. Trees have birthdays, too; just count the rings to see how old they are. And notice that during wet years the rings are thick because there was much growth. In dry years, the rings are narrow and close together because there was little growth. Do people have rings? No!

title: Fifth Graders Talk to Congressmen on Skype
text:
Have you ever thought about different ways to power your parents' cars? Fifth grade students at Columbus Elementary in Edwardsville, Ill., have been learning about other ways to power cars using alternative (substitute) fuels. In September 2011, Illinois Senator Bill Haine and Representative Dan Beiser visited the school to talk about the work being done to improve the environment and the use of "green" energy. Green energy is energy that produces less pollution. Fifth grade students from the entire school district "attended" the assembly. With the help of an internet video program called Skype, students from other schools were able to watch the assembly and ask the officials questions. After the assembly some students emailed questions to Sen. Haine and Rep. Beiser. Students were very excited to receive responses from the officials.

The teachers and students at Columbus Elementary are doing some amazing research when it comes to alternative energy. In fact, they are planning to run a diesel engine using vegetable oil instead of gas. Students are also learning how to reuse resources and are looking forward to turning used vegetable oil into hand soap. To learn more about alternative energy, visit www.benefits-of-recycling.com/alternativeenergyforkids.html.

Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/ for more Connections and Current Events articles.

title: Wisconsin’s Forests and Waterways
text:
River and Lake Facts

The name "Wisconsin" comes from an American Indian word for "gathering of the waters."

Our state has about 4 4, 000 miles of rivers and streams.

The river system associated with Lake Winnebago is the most important one draining into Lake Michigan from Wisconsin.

The Chippewa, St. Croix, Menominee, Wolf, and Wisconsin rivers have many rapids and falls that provide water power for state industries. The most valuable falls are in the northern Fox River.

Wisconsin has three drainage systems. One drains the eastern part of the state into Lake Michigan. A shorter system empties into Lake Superior. The largest system flows into the Mississippi. Only the Wisconsin River is suitable for shipping and water traffic.

Green Lake is the deepest of all the natural inland Wisconsin lakes, while Lake Wazee is the deepest man- made lake.

Wisconsin has about 15, 000 lakes.

Wisconsin's longest river is the Wisconsin River, one of several rivers that drain into the Mississippi. It is 4 3 0 miles long.

Wisconsin's many water resources have played an important part in the history of Wisconsin's economy. Waterways were important for the fur trade. Rivers powered the pioneers' machinery and helped transport their products. Today, the lakes and rivers are a source of electric power and a vital resource for the paper industry.

Wisconsin Forests are Faring Fantastically!

Before settlers came to Wisconsin, magnificent trees covered the countryside: Pine, hemlock, spruce, birch, maple and cedar in the north; ash, basswood, oak, cherry, elm, poplar, tamarack, hickory, maple and walnut in the south.

Evergreens, especially white pine, were thick in the farthest north. White pine resists rot and is good for river transport. It is also soft and strong, making it the wood of choice to build homes and farm buildings.

In the central portion of Wisconsin, the forests are a mix of evergreens and hardwoods.

Prairie grasslands filled most of the southern third of the state, interspersed with oak trees and other hardwoods.

Forests originally covered 30 million of the state's approximately 3 5 million acres. Today, forests cover about 4 6 percent of Wisconsin, a total that has remained the same since the first forest inventory in 19 3 6.

Over the past 40 years, the volume of wood in Wisconsin's forests has more than doubled. Landowners are cutting more timber, but are replanting trees and are growing more wood than they're cutting.

Our forests are a treasured natural asset that play an important role in our economy by providing wood for paper, furniture, buildings, and fuel, homes for wildlife, and beauty and recreation for visitors and people that live here.

title: Conservation
text:
Do you have a pet? If so, then you know how much care and work is needed to feed and clean it. In our world, nature gives us food to eat, water to drink and wash with, and a way to stay healthy. However, little actions by millions of people are making it hard for people in some parts of our world to find food and water and to live healthily.

A good Wisconsin citizen understands that our resources must be protected and conserved. You can help conserve resources by turning off the water when you brush your teeth, by putting garbage in a trash container, and by walking instead of asking someone to drive you. The candy wrapper, empty can or bottle, or plastic container that you might just toss to the four winds never goes away. Eventually, it collects somewhere and causes problems. A smart person knows that conserving and protecting resources will keep this Earth a safe place to live for ages to come. Nature does a lot to take care of us, but it can only do so much. The rest is up to us, if we want to stay here!

title: Is Daddy Longlegs a big spider?
text: They may resemble spiders, but Daddy Longlegs are neither spiders nor insects. Scientists call them "harvest men." They come from the same class as spiders, Arachnida, but are in a different order, phalangida. They have three body segments, and spiders have only two. They resemble watermelon seeds supported on eight long stilts, which may be up to 30 times as long as their bodies. They're gangly and fast-moving creatures. If the Daddy Longlegs is in danger of being caught, it can break off a portion of its legs and then escape. Daddy Longlegs can grow new legs to replace the broken ones. Daddy Longlegs spend considerable time cleaning their legs. Each leg is carefully held in its jaws and nibbled to clean the leg. These critters come out after twilight to search for dead insects or plant juices. As they move, their longest pair of legs touches the surface, sensing for food. If something edible is detected, the Daddy Longlegs grabs it and eats it. Daddy Longlegs live all over Wisconsin and are good for our environment.

title: Pine Cones: The perfect crib for baby trees
text: You wouldn't want to lick these cones. Pine cones don't necessarily come from pine trees. We use this term to refer to cones that come from many types of evergreens such as spruce, fir, pine, hemlock and cedar. We also call these trees conifers because they bear cones. Pine cones produce seeds, and without them trees couldn't reproduce. Each evergreen species pollinates at a different time of the year. To pollinate means to fertilize. When the tree is ready to be pollinated, it secretes fluid that collects between the scales of a female cone. At the same time, the male pine cone releases yellow pollen. The wind blows the pollen, carrying it to the fluid of a female cone. After pollination, the cone scales thicken until they are tightly pressed together. As the cone grows, it darkens, hardens and encloses the developing seeds. When the cone is mature and the timing is right, the cone dries out, pops open, and releases two seeds per scale, each with a tiny wing to guide its flight. Some pine cones open naturally; others may wait 10 -20 years and only open when exposed to intense fire.

title: Make a Rain Gauge
text:
Materials

1 plastic bottle

scissors

bricks

a ruler

Directions

1. Ask an adult to help you cut the top half off the bottle

2. Put it back on upside down and with the cap off.

3. Stand your rain guage outside. Put bricks around it to hold it steady.

4. Each time it rains measure how much rain has fallen, with your ruler.

title: How do I manage my time?
text:
Feeling stressed? Not sure if you’ll have time to do all your homework? To keep up with your studies and have fun learning, you need to learn to manage your time. There are several techniques for managing your time. Here are some ideas:

Assignment book—Find a small notebook (so that you can carry it around) to keep a list of your assignments. Write down each assignment as you get it, the class, the due date, the pages you need to read, the length of your paper, and any other important facts. Review the day’s assignments before going home, and make sure you have all the materials to complete them. When the assignment is done, check it off.

Checklist—When you have a big project that requires many steps, like a science project, research paper, or presentation, it might be a good idea to use a checklist. That way, you know you’ve done everything you needed to. First, think of your final goal. Then, think about the steps you will need to take to reach that goal. How long will each step take? Finally, write down (your assignment notebook is a great place) the steps and the date that each should be completed. Be sure to list the steps in the order you will need to do them. And it’s never a bad idea to leave a couple extra days at the end in case some steps take longer than expected.

Reading methods—There are many reading methods you can use to read effectively. We will discuss some of them in the future. Once you find one that you like, use it! You need to know what information is important and be able to take notes on it. If you are reading long stretches of text, take many breaks so that you do not get information overload. But make the breaks short enough that you don’t forget what you just read.

Study schedule—Think about what time of day you do your best work. Is it in the morning before you go to school? After school in the afternoon? After dinner in the evening? Before bedtime? Pick a study schedule that works for you and stick to it. Choose a place that is quiet and free from distractions. If this is when and where you do your best work, then you will do a good job on your homework!

Try these time-management tools, and use those that work for you. As you practice them, you will improve your study skills. And you will be forming good habits for your future schooling, college, and work experience.

title: Our State Has Everything If You Can Find It!
text:
Look around you at all the different things at your fingertips: plastic, wood, fiber, chalk, chemicals, machines, computers, lights, paint, flooring, metal, glass, corn, pizza, sodas, and candy bars. Natural gas and electricity keep you warm in winter, and air conditioning keeps you cool in summer. Your food is safe in the fridge. A car takes you wherever you need to go; a doctor can fix whatever is bothering you; and television, computer games and the radio work hard to keep you from doing homework at night.

None of these things was flown here by the Intergalactic Delivery Service. They were already right here on planet Earth. All we had to do was find them. Of course, what people really find are the raw materials needed to make things.

The Earth's natural resources provide everything we need to live and grow. There are even resources (supplies) here to help us fly off this planet and go live somewhere else or to destroy everything we've created to start all over again. What an amazing place we have. The role of the Earth's resources in our lives cannot be measured. Take away any part of the carefully balanced cycles of nature, and all life on Earth could stop (die). Add something that doesn't belong and we have the same problem.

Most of the Earth's resources lie in the top five miles of its crust. At the lowest depths are deposits of oil, gas and coal that we use for fuel. Many of our minerals are found deep in the ground, such as gold, silver and diamonds, just to mention a few.

On the surface of the Earth, we find our food: fish in the streams and oceans, animals, plants, fruits, vegetables and nuts on land. In the sky are the birds, clouds and an atmosphere that protects us from the harsh radiation of the sun and the occasional meteorite that streaks across the sky and burns up.

The wind keeps trees and plants strong, blows dead things around, sends seeds to new locations, and keeps the water cycle moving. The action of moisture on the planet breaks down everything and makes room for new things to grow. And high overhead is the great engine for all of this activity, the sun.

Wisconsin is a great place to live because our state has almost all the natural resources we need to do just about everything we want to do. Let's learn about our natural resources and how to protect them for future generations. After all, Wisconsin has just about everything if you can find it!

title: Crazy for Curds
text:
Does your cheese squeak? Many Wisconsin kids couldn't live without their cheese curds, also known as "squeaky cheese." What are cheese curds? They are the fresh curds that form in milk during the cheese-making process. They are about the size of a peanut in its shell, and they have a fresh, salty taste. Cheese curds are very popular here is Wisconsin, as well as in other states where cheese factories are located. The curds taste best when they are eaten fresh - only a few hours after they form. Fresh cheese curds squeak when you eat them, but the squeak disappears after about a day. If your curds don't squeak, you know they have been sitting around for a while!

It used to be that cheese curds were only available in locations where cheese was made. Now, however, fried cheese curds appear on different restaurant menus around the world. This makes the delicious little bites more popular than ever! The curds are vacuum packed to keep them fresh and then shipped to restaurants across the nation.

Shipping fresh cheese curds is a challenge. It is impossible to keep the squeak in squeaky cheese once it ages a bit. Some people put their cheese curds in the microwave for a second or two to recapture the squeak. But the cheese never tastes quite as good as it does fresh from the cheese vat. Although, vacuum-packed cheese curds can be the next best thing to fresh!

title: Wisconsin Climate & Resources
text:
Wisconsin Climate

Wisconsin weather is like an adventure that never ends. Did you know that we live on the edge of a seasonal weather system? It's like living with one foot in the ocean and the other on the sandy beach. In fact, that's just what it is. So many different weather patterns are swirling around us, it's hard to predict what will happen next. Our state experiences great thunderstorms and fantastic winds, as well as many floods, droughts, fires, and severe storms. Wisconsin also lies on the northern edge of the midwestern tornado belt. All this action makes this land a very exciting place to live.

We also have a very unique climate that scientists call a continental forest climate (average weather and temperature). That means we have severe winters and warm, humid summers. Humidity is moisture in the air. Wisconsin has higher humidity because of the moisture that rises off Lake Superior and Lake Michigan. The cold winter air combined with this lake moisture creates what skiers like best: snow! The northern counties receive an average of 100 inches of snow, while the southern counties are warmer and receive only 30 inches. Either way, we get a great deal of snow. The snow lies frozen until it's warm enough to melt and soak into the ground or drain into rivers and lakes.

Wisconsin Resources

Wisconsin corn grows best in the south because of the longer growing season. And, every year about two-thirds of the precipitation falls during the growing season (when there is no freezing). The average annual temperature of the south is 50 degrees Fahrenheit. Winter is the dominant season in the north, and on average it is 11 degrees colder. In fact, temperatures in Wisconsin can swing from 110 degrees on a hot day to 50 degrees below zero. Wisconsin usually experiences 30 to 40 major thunderstorms between May and August. All of this rain helps our crops to grow. We average 36 inches of rain a year.

Wisconsin's fertile (rich in nutrients) soils make our state one of the most important agricultural states in the nation. Our primary crops are corn, small grains, hay, and vegetables. Wisconsin is best known for its dairy farming. Wisconsin has many rich gifts in its land: forests, mineral deposits, thousands of lakes and rivers, excellent soil and plenty of wildlife. People have used these resources to build large businesses and industries. Wisconsin has the resources to create cereals, office furniture, chemicals, pharmaceuticals (drugs and medicines), iron, steel, paper and pulp, tools and machine-shop products, newspapers, refrigerators, and so much more.

Mapping and Research Activity

You may have noticed that not all of the counties on the Wisconsin Resources map have a symbol on them. Use the Internet and other resources to locate other resources found in Wisconsin.

title: Friendliness
text:
You know, just being friendly can make the difference between a bad day and a good day. The United States is home to some of the friendliest people around. Maybe that's why America has so many good days! Friendliness can turn driving in a car, riding on a bus, or taking a walk in your neighborhood into a pleasant memory all its own. Friendliness can make someone glad you were the one who answered the phone! Of course, some people choose to be unfriendly most of the time, but why would you want to do that?

After all, you hardly ever hear anyone say, "I just love coming over for a visit. You're all so nice and grumpy!"

Make friendliness one of your character traits, and anyone who ever visits you will go away feeling as warm as the sun!

title: How do we know what the climate was like millions of years ago?
text: All over the Earth are deep layers of ice, soil, sediments and rocks. Scientists have drilled thousands of feet into these layers for clues about our ancient atmosphere and climate. What they find is amazing. Bubbles of air trapped in ice tell us about the air that ancient creatures breathed. Spores and pollen tell us about the plants that lived nearby. Shells of plankton and layers of dust and clay tell us about ocean temperatures. Putting the information together gives us a good picture of what our world was like millions of years ago.

title: How Do I Take a Test?
text:
Test anxiety - sweaty palms, butterflies in the stomach, and brain cramps - has happened to everyone at one time or another. Did you know that test anxiety comes from a lack of self-confidence? How can you improve your self-confidence and improve your test taking? The best way is to know the material very well. But here are some important test-taking strategies that can help you:

1. Preview the test. See what it covers and how long it is.

2. Plan your time. After you finish previewing the test, you'll know how many questions there are. Decide how much time you can spend on each section. Keep track of the time as you take the test.

3. Follow directions. Don't start a section until you are sure of what you're supposed to do. Read all the directions and listen carefully to any directions read aloud.

4. Read the questions carefully. Look for keywords such as "when," "where," "why," "different from," "same as," "before," and "after." Have you ever misread a question that said, "What are NOT parts of climate?" instead of "What are parts of climate?" Reading the question carefully can help you avoid such mistakes.

5. Don't get stuck on one question. If you can't think of an answer, skip it and return to it later when you have finished the rest of the test.

6. Check your work. If you have time left after you finish the test, go back and double-check your work.

7. Learn from your mistakes. Once you get your test back, look at the questions you have answered incorrectly. Think of why you got each one wrong and then study the material again. Learn what your pitfalls are so that you do not make the same mistake again. If you do this, then next time, you'll get the answers right.

Use this list while taking this week's Studies Weekly quiz so that you can practice good test-taking skills. If your teacher approves, you may want to use this list for the next few weeks until you have mastered the skills.

title: Weather Watch
text:
By scanning the sky for colors and other clues, people have tried to predict the weather since time began. Test these bits of ancient meteorology to see if they are really true.

A rose red sunset means fair skies are coming (“Red sky at night, sailor’s delight, red sky at morning, sailors take warning!”)

A pale yellow sunset means rain is on the way.

An evening rainbow predicts fair weather.

A morning rainbow in the west means rain.

A pre-dawn copper colored sky in the east means rain.

When the moon hangs in halo, there will be rain, especially if the halo is far from the moon.

title: Meet the First People in Wisconsin
text:
Wisconsin has been a wonderful place to live for a very long time. The earliest dwellers arrived about 12,000 years ago. Scientists believe they came from other parts of North America and probably migrated to our state as the glaciers retreated and the climate improved. Early natives found our land cold and stony with great forests and sandy soil.

The first dwellers built their villages next to water. They made their homes out of trees and branches. They learned how to catch trout, sturgeon and muskellunge and trap the many kinds of wildlife that lived here. There was plenty of beaver, musk-ox, tapir and the mighty mastodon. Most families lived off of deer and moose, while those who farmed grew corn, squash and beans. And for anybody who went looking, Wisconsin offered plenty of fruits, berries, nuts and roots.

Early American Indians relied heavily on trees for just about everything. They knew how to weave bark to make sandals, baskets and mats. They also created many kinds of tools out of animal bones and stone. They used their tools to smooth and polish things, to punch holes or to chop. Their best transportation was the canoe. Some were large enough to hold between 10 and 15 people without tipping over. Their roads through our state were the rivers and lakes.

One of the earliest groups to live in Wisconsin discovered copper. They are called the Old Copper Indians. As early as 3,000 B.C., the Old Copper Indians were mining copper pits on several islands that could be reached only by canoe. Scientists have traced their copper artifacts among American Indians all over the eastern United States and even into South America. These artifacts include heavy copper tools, spear points, knives, axes, and harpoons.

The cultures that came next are called the Woodland Indians, the Middle Mississippian Indians, and the Hopewell Indians. These people began appearing in Wisconsin in about 800 B.C. They were the first to make clay pottery, store food and build burial mounds for their dead. The Hopewell were especially famous for their excellent pottery and beautiful weaving. One of the largest cities in the world was built by the Middle Mississippian people. And one of their most important river towns was Aztalan, a place we will talk about more in this week's geography lesson.

All of these people left behind many amazing artifacts that have kept scientists digging for years. More than 15,000 archaeological sites have been found in Wisconsin.

By the time the first French explorers paddled into Wisconsin in the 1600s, everything was changing. There were fewer people and fewer tribes. But those who remained watched with curiosity as the pale-skinned French explorers, with their strange language and clothing, wandered into the native peoples' ancient hunting grounds. No one knew it at the time, but this was the beginning of a long and painful change for Wisconsin's American Indians. It would begin when the secret of the lost paradise of Wisconsin was finally leaked out to all the world.

title: Tribe Talk
text:
Have you ever felt that miserable, sad feeling you get when you lose something that's really special and important to you? Many Wisconsin American Indian tribes are currently very sad because they are in danger of losing the cherished tribal languages their ancestors have spoken for hundreds of years. What happened to their native languages? Many died out years ago when sickness or warfare destroyed entire tribes. The English language replaced others. But today, many tribes are scrambling to revive their traditional native tongues.

Wisconsin's Oneida Tribe is working tirelessly to be sure their tribal language doesn't disappear forever. Today, teachers are teaching Oneida language classes in all tribal day cares, elementary schools, and high schools. Students are having fun as they learn their tribal language by reading stories and playing games such as bingo in the Oneida language. Adults are learning and refreshing their Oneida language skills through community classes and social gatherings.

Several special teachers and organizations are helping the Oneida Tribe revive their language by publishing Oneida reading and writing lessons, vocabulary lists, songs, a dictionary, and other educational materials. Similar materials are also helping Wisconsin Menominee, Ojibwa, Potawatomi, and Winnebago tribes restore their native languages.

Many tribes believe they can save their native languages if they can get their children involved in the excitement of learning their cultural heritage. Many children are catching on and are having fun greeting each other in their native language at school, at the park, or at the corner store. Some tribes are employing lively radio programs and rap music to charm youth with the beauty of their native languages.

American Indian languages are a beautiful and significant part of our nation's history, but unless tribes act quickly, their native tongues might fade away forever. Fortunately, American Indian tribes are working to make sure their tribal languages will survive for many years to come.

title: American Indians of Wisconsin
text:
Menominee (Omaeqnominniwuk)

Omaeqnominniwuk means "wild rice people." Wisconsin has been their home for more than 5,000 years. These Algonquian-speaking people were spread out over a 10-million-acre hunting range from Lake Michigan to the Yellow River. This area was rich in wild game, fish and wild rice. The Menominee call themselves Mamaceqtaw, or "the people." They were divided into two groups of clans - the Bears and the Thunderers. They became important fur trappers for the French.

Dakota (Santee Sioux)

Dakota means "friends or allies." This American Indian nation was a woodland group that was more advanced in warfare than their neighbors, the Ho-Chunk. They spoke Siouan and inhabited much of northern Wisconsin. The Dakota built easily moved villages and enjoyed hunting small game, fishing and gathering rice. The Dakota Wacipi ceremony, sometimes called a powwow, was held in the spring to celebrate the renewal of life. People gathered to sing, dance, renew old friendships and form new ones.

Ho-Chunk (Winnebago)

The Ho-Chunk (People of the Big Voice) were fishers and farmers. They grew corn, beans and squash. These Siouan speaking people lived in the southeastern part of Wisconsin. The Ho-Chunk had two special ceremonies. The Mankani took place in the summer and the Wagigo was a winter feast. The name Winnebago was what they were called by other American Indians. It means "People of the Dirty Water" and it probably described the lake the natives lived by in the 1600s.

Why does our map show four American Indian nations instead of three? The Ioway (Iowa) and the Ho-Chunk nations have so much in common, that many historians believe they were part of the same group at one time. No one knows for sure when the two groups split.

More American Indians Come to Wisconsin

The Iroquois were a powerful American Indian nation in the Northeastern United States. They wanted more territory for trapping and hoped to control the fur trade with the Europeans. In 1641, they started a war against other American Indian nations in the Northeast. The war drove many American Indians from Michigan into Wisconsin, as the Iroquois took their lands. During the Iroquois War the Potawatomi, Ojibwe (Chippewa), Ottawa (Odawa), Huron, Sauk (Sac), Meskwaki (Fox), Kickapoo, Miami, Mascouten and Illinois nations all moved to Wisconsin. Most of them moved further west as the European settlers moved in, but the Potawatomi and Ojibwe stayed here.

title: Mounds
text: Around 650 C.E., people of the Woodland and Hopewell cultures began to build effigy mounds out of dirt. They used these mounds for burial grounds and ceremonial centers. Sometimes these mounds were built in the shapes of animals, such as turtles, lizards, wildcats, and even people. They were about four feet high and sometimes several hundred feet long. The shape of the mounds may have symbolized tribes or clans. These cultures also created images by digging into the Earth. Cahokia Mound State Park in Collinsville, Illinois, across the Mississippi River from St. Louis, Missouri, has one of the largest platform mounds, covering 16 acres. These mounds were used for religious ceremonies and served as the center for commercial trade, farming, and artistry. The grounds of Mendota State Hospital in Madison, Wisconsin, are home to another large effigy mound. This mound is shaped like an eagle and has a 624-foot wingspan, making it the largest known surviving effigy mound in the state. Native Americans stopped building mounds around 1200 C.E. Since then, four-fifths of all Wisconsin mounds have been destroyed. Today, there are about 1,200 mounds remaining in Wisconsin. Recent laws now protect these mounds from being destroyed or damaged. The mounds are still considered sacred by Native Americans in Wisconsin.

title: Do we say Native American or American Indian?
text: Some individuals and some entire tribes of Native Americans prefer to be called American Indians. Some are offended by the name Indian because the name was a mistake that Christopher Columbus made when he sailed to America and thought he had reached India. It is considered correct to use the terms Native American, American Indian, Indian, or indigenous people, according to the tribes' website. Everyone agrees that we are all proud to be called Americans!

title: Aztalan
text: Aztalan is one of the most important archaeological sites in the United States. It is located by the Crawfish River right here in the great state of Wisconsin. Aztalan was built by the Mississippi culture of A.D. 900, making it more than 1,000 years old. The village is 21 acres in size. The earliest natives built a 10- to 12-foot high stockade, or fence of logs, surrounding the village. They put mud on the stockade and sculpted it to look like bricks. Inside, the American Indians built three pyramids 15 feet high. These pyramids were topped, meaning they had platforms on top that were about 50 square feet. They built watch towers at the corner of each pyramid. Steps led up to the platform through ornamented gates. The natives probably held religious ceremonies on these pyramids. Scientists also found remnants of vegetable seeds. These people were excellent farmers. They also made beautiful pottery and ornaments of stone, bone, shell, and copper. All this evidence tells us that these early natives were very smart and knew a lot about building, art and growing crops. We're not sure how these people died, but it looks like they were scattered, and their village burned down.

title: American Indian Nations in Wisconsin Today
text:
Today, six American Indian nations in Wisconsin are officially recognized by the U.S. government. Being officially recognized gives these groups some sovereignty, or the right to govern themselves. Members of these American Indian nations are citizens of two nations - the United States and an American Indian nation. They must obey the U.S. laws but they can also make some laws of their own.

This map shows where these six American Indian nations live in Wisconsin today. Use the map to help you answer the questions. You will need to do some extra research to find some answers.

2. Which nation has the largest area? In what part of the state is it located?

3. Which nations are also on the map inside? Compare the locations of those nations on the two maps and write a sentence about each nation's location then and today.

4. Why do two areas on the map show no American Indian nations? Do you think no American Indians live in those areas, or is there another reason?

5. Are any American Indian nations in Wisconsin not officially recognized by the U.S. government? Work with a partner and do some research to find the answer. On a separate piece of paper, write a paragraph or two to share the information you found.

title: The Moon in Myth
text:
To the people living long ago, the moon was a god or goddess of special mystery and power. Not only did the moon outshine the other nighttime lights, but it also changed its shape and had its own strange motion in the sky. The moon had visible markings on its face that fascinated people on every land for thousands upon thousands of years.

Some said the markings were a rabbit on the moon; some said it resembled a frog. Other people said the markings were a human face - a Man in the Moon. In Scandinavia, however, there was no Man in the Moon, but instead two children, and they were carrying between them a pail of water. Little of the myth remains except an old nursery rhyme:

Jack and Jill
Went up the hill
To fetch a pail of water...

Once, long before this myth became a nursery rhyme, this story may have helped people remember how, throughout the month, the moon waxes (gets larger) to the full moon, then wanes (gets smaller) to the new moon and increases to full again. You see, Jack gets his name from the Scandinavian word "jakka" - to increase, and Jill's name comes from "joila" - to dissolve.

Take this article with you on the next full moon and see if you can find the above markings.

title: The French Explore Wisconsin While Europe Fights
text:
Jean Nicolet and seven Huron men sat in the large canoe as it slowly worked its way through Lake Huron and into the Straits of Mackinac. He was moments away from becoming the first European to enter Lake Michigan and soon after to set foot onto Wisconsin soil. The year was 1634, and Nicolet knew a grand adventure lay before him. He anticipated great things from this new land: fur trading, settlements, farms and families. But on this historic day, there was only a vast wilderness to be explored. Suddenly, "land ho!" Wisconsin was in sight.

It took a long time for Europeans to discover and settle in our state. Part of the delay was because of wars in Europe. For 145 years, European countries fought to control Europe and the colonies in North America. As for Wisconsin, our state eventually became a frontier land of New France with some French forts and outposts built at important locations. New France was expanded to include the vast area of eastern Canada, the United States, and the Great Lakes region.

The 145 years of war started in 1618 with the Thirty Years War. The French couldn't spare a lot of money for its settlements in New France, but it encouraged fur traders. These hunters climbed, hiked, and paddled their way into the beautiful forest and lake lands of the eastern United States and Canada, and they hired local native people to help gather furs.

When the Thirty Years War ended in 1648, France emerged as the main European power. It had strong settlements at Quebec and Montreal, but it still depended on the fur trade for growth and expansion in the Americas. Expanding farther west fell to the missionaries and fur traders. Over the decades that followed, these rugged mountain men brought medicine, sanitation, housing, weapons, and cooking ideas to the American and Canadian Indians. By 1663, French King Louis XIV decided to step in and declared New France a royal province. He sent 3,000 settlers plus some soldiers and supplies to help New France grow.

But the fighting and squabbling among European powers was far from over. More wars erupted (hang on to your hat!): the King Williams War (1689-97), Queen Anne's War (1702-13) and King George's War (1744-48).

In 1749, the governor-general of New France ordered the northern United States to be cleared of all British, and he tried to restrict British settlements. This began yet another war in 1754 called the Nine Years War. Several native tribes were recruited to help the French (the French and Indian War). The fighting in Europe flared up two years later and was called the Seven Years War (1756-63). Are you tired of wars? So was everybody else. Finally, the fighting ended, and France was the loser. England and France signed the Paris Peace Treaty in 1763, and France had to surrender almost everything east of the Mississippi River. They were allowed to keep a couple of islands and the New Orleans area and their fishing rights in Canada.

What about Wisconsin? Our state was rarely a battle ground. However, the bodies of water surrounding our state were used as passageways during the war. The French built several strong forts along the Great Lakes and Mississippi River. A military post was established at Green Bay. When the dust settled in 1763, many French posts had to be abandoned, and the British moved in. Even though French troops were gone, the French citizens in these areas remained. At long last, Wisconsin was ready to grow!

title: Is There a Little French in You?
text:
When the Seven Years War ended in 1763, the French were forced to surrender a lot of land. However, their influence remained. If you look around you, you'll see there is something French just about everywhere:

Names: You name it, and there is probably a French connection. Many early American Indians carry French names: Iroquois, Algonquin, Sioux and others. Do you know anyone who drives a Chevrolet? The Frenchman, Louis Chevrolet, introduced a car called the Chevrolet Classic Six and started the Chevrolet company in 1911.

Food: Do you enjoy a croissant with butter?And what's dinner without some tasty hors d'oeuvres (appetizers) or a nice soufflé? This is a light egg dish that is baked until it puffs up. When the Titanic sank in 1912, many of the 1,581 who drowned picked their last meals from a French menu. Have you had filet mignons, consomme, chateau potatoes, pate de foie gras (a paste of fat, goose liver and truffles) or French vanilla ice cream? And don't forget pasteurized milk from Louis Pasteur!

Sports: The French have influenced Americans in the sports of bicycling and soccer. The greatest bicycle race in the world is the Tour de France.

Fashion: And what do the best dressed people wear? Paris fashions: Dior, Chanel and dozens more that set the standards in clothing, perfumes, makeup, shoes, accessories and more.

Music, art, literature, architecture and science have all been influenced by French inventors and innovators. Even the mighty skyline of New York City, with all of its skyscrapers, can be traced back to France. Alexandre Eiffel first showed how wrought iron could be used for buildings when he built the Eiffel Tower in 1889. The French also gave us the Statue of Liberty in 1884 as a gesture of goodwill and peace.

We could go on with more examples, but we don't have the room. Even though the French were defeated nearly 250 years ago, they are far from forgotten. And who knows: You might even have a little French in you. Adieu!

title: Early Explorers in Wisconsin
text:
Early explorers in Wisconsin began arriving in the 1600s. Many came by canoe (the main form of transportation in Wisconsin for 200 years). Others spent years carving a path overland through thick forests and swamps. And a lot paid for the adventure with their lives. Let's look at a few of the first.

Jean Nicolet (1598-1642)

At the urging of famous explorer Samuel de Champlain, Nicolet joined an expedition deep into Huron territory. In 1634, he boarded a large canoe with seven Huron men and paddled through the Straits of Mackinac to discover Lake Michigan. Nicolet hoped he had found the fabled Northwest Passage, but was disappointed when he learned it was just another large lake. He paddled to Green Bay, Wisconsin, becoming the first European to set foot on Wisconsin soil. He made friends with the Winnebago Tribe and then returned to Quebec.

Daniel Greysolon DuLhut (also Duluth) (1640-1710)

DuLhut sailed from France in 1674 and settled in Montreal, Canada. He set out with his brother La Tourette and six soldiers, becoming the first Canadian to explore the west. In 1679, he took possession of the Sioux country in the name of the king of France. DuLhut explored Lake Superior and the land near the Mississippi, Red and St. Lawrence rivers. He built Fort William and Fort La Tourette. During one expedition, he saved Father Hennepin from captivity, a feat that won him admiration and fear from the natives. DuLhut persuaded the natives to be loyal to France. This came in handy when the Iroquois began fighting in 1684 and 1687 to control the fur trade. For 30 years, DuLhut succeeded in keeping French control over the country west of the Great Lakes.

Pierre Radisson (1632-1710) / Medard Chouart des Groseilliers (1625-1698)

French-born explorers Radisson and Groseilliers set out for Lake Nipissing in 1658, searching for an inland Northwest Passage. To get there, they crossed what is now Wisconsin and the upper Mississippi River valley. On their way, they traded fur without a license. The French controlled all fur trade in this area at the time, and when they found Radisson and Groseilliers were trading without a license, the French took away all their furs. This made the two trappers very unhappy, and they offered their services to the English at Port Royal. Radisson established Port Nelson on Nelson River and returned to England with many furs. Later, these two helped establish the famous fur-trading giant, the Hudson Bay Company.

Robert La Salle (1643-1687)

La Salle arrived in Canada in 1666 and became a fur trader. In 1669-70, he explored the region south of lakes Ontario and Erie and even paddled on Lake Michigan along the eastern border of Wisconsin. He led an expedition down the Illinois and Mississippi rivers and claimed all the area watered by the Mississippi for France's King Louis XIV and named it "Louisiana." He established forts on the Saint Joseph and Illinois rivers. A few years later, during a search to find the mouth of the Mississippi to set up a colony, La Salle's men rebelled and murdered him near Brazos River (in Texas).

title: Journal of an Explorer
text: Pierre Radisson was an early French explorer and fur trader who traveled through Wisconsin. He was very impressed with the beauty of Wisconsin and wrote this description in his journal (circle the punctuation or words he used improperly or misspelled): "I can assure you I like noe country, as I have that wherein we wintered; for whatever a man could desire was to be had in great plenty; viz. staggs, fishes in abundance, and all sort of meat, corne enough...We embarked ourselves on the delightfullest lake in the world (Lake Michigan). I tooke notices of their cottages and of the journeys of our navigation, for because that the country was so pleasant, so beautiful and fruitfull that it grieved me to see that the world could not discover such inticing country to live in."

title: Bow and Arrow
text: American Indians used the bow and arrow to hunt and kill their food. It replaced the atlatl, which was used by earlier American Indians. They would sneak up on their prey, sometimes in disguise, so they could shoot from a short distance and not frighten their prey.

title: What is a “Voyageur”?
