text: Voyageurs were hardy French-Canadian canoe men who traveled the rivers and lakes in their birch-bark canoes, from the Great Lakes to the interior of the western United States and Canada. They were hired to transport furs and goods through rugged territory. They were known for their colorful clothing and tendency to sing as they journeyed.

title: New France
text:
As shown by these maps, by 1753, the French had expanded their claims across the central regions of North America, including the Great Lakes region. This area was called New France. At the end of the Seven Years War, France lost almost everything, and had to surrender its vast holdings to the Spanish and British. The maps to the right show the holdings of France, England and Spain as they stood before and after the Seven Years War.

France = blue

Britain = red

Spain = yellow

title: Clarity of Expression: Henry Hudson
text:
Henry Hudson was an English sea captain and explorer who started off as a failure. He sailed on two voyages for England to find a northeast water route to the rich spice trade in Asia. But both times the icy northern seas blocked his way. He had to return home defeated.

Sounds like the end of his career, right? It wasn't. Hudson next convinced the Dutch East India Company to hire him for exactly the same expedition. In 1609 Hudson and his crew sailed west across the Atlantic. He reached the New World, landing on the island we know today as Manhattan. He sailed inland up a wide river and explored the surrounding valley.

It wasn't a passage to Asia. But Hudson's explorations allowed the Dutch to claim the land and build a fur trading post there in 1614, before the Pilgrims arrived. A Dutch settlement called New Netherland soon followed.

Unfortunately, Hudson's last voyage ended in mutiny. He refused his crew's demands to return home, so the sailors took over the ship, setting Hudson adrift in a small boat. His fate is unknown, but his legacy is Hudson Bay, Hudson River, Hudson Valley and the Dutch settlement that became New York City.

Henry Hudson must have had excellent clarity of expression. He had to be able to explain clearly to the Dutch that his experience and determination made him the best man for the job, even though he was an Englishman and not a Dutchman.

Think about a time that you wanted to convince your parents or teachers to let you try something new. Did you beg and plead? Or did you give them a clear explanation of your reasons? Which way do you think works better?

title: How Do I Use a Dictionary
text:
What does "native" mean? How do you pronounce "shaman"? To find the answers to these and many other questions, grab a dictionary. The dictionary just might be a student's best friend. A dictionary lists and defines words.

Know Your ABCs

The words in a dictionary appear in alphabetical order. At the top of each page, two guidewords show the first and last words on that page. Guidewords help you find the word you need more quickly. For example, the word "tepee" might appear on a page with the guidewords "tension" and "territory" at the top of that page.

Is your word followed by numbers? That means it has more than one definition. Look up the word "native" and see all the definitions for it.

After each word, you will find a letter that stands for a part of speech. For example, n. means "noun," v. means "verb," and adj. means "adjective." Sometimes, one word can have two or more parts of speech. It depends on how it's used in a sentence. Let's show this with the word "hunt." Look it up now in your dictionary.

What is the meaning of "hunt" as a verb?

Use "hunt" as a verb in a sentence here:

What is the meaning of "hunt" as a noun?

title: Fur or Football?
text:
The young man sat around piles of blankets, beads, tools and different equipment. A few American Indians sat across from him, holding their fur out and pointing at different items. Sometimes the young man would trade the item for the fur, and sometimes he would barter or try to talk them into a different deal to benefit himself.

This young man is a fur trader from the 1600s. The scene describes what fur trading might have been like in those days. Fur trading was a large part of the lifestyles of American Indians and many European settlers, and it was a large part of the American economy in the 1600s. Beaver fur was one of the most desired objects for companies that made hats and other articles of clothing out of the fur. American Indians and other fur traders would bring fur into trading posts and trade for tools, equipment and other items they wanted or needed.

European Jean Nicolet explored Wisconsin in the early 1600s because he heard of bodies of water swarming with beaver. He established a trading post in Green Bay in 1634. Nearly 40 years later, explorers Marquette and Joliet claimed land southwest of Green Bay, along the Mississippi River, for France and called it Prairie Du Chien or "Prairie of the Dog."

Both establishments were the gathering place for fur trapping and trading in the upper Mississippi business. The Mississippi River and the Great Lakes were great places to trap animals for fur. They would use canoes made out of many different types of wood like birch bark. Fur trading in these areas helped form companies like Hudson's Bay Company.

Fur trading was the beginning of many other large cities like Chicago, Detroit, Albany, and St. Louis throughout the 19th century. Trapping and fur trading is still done today, but it has changed a lot since the 17th century. As you can see, it was one of the biggest reasons that people came to Wisconsin- even bigger than the Packers!

title: Tree Rings Tell an Ancient Story
text:
Could a city the size of New York City be destroyed by a drought? Many scientists believe that's what happened to a city called Angkor in what is now Cambodia. Angkor was the capital city of an empire that stretched from Myanmar (Burma) to Vietnam. This city of about 750,000 people lasted 600 years, from the ninth to the fifteenth century.

The Angkor area doesn't have the kind of summers and winters that many U.S. cities do. It has drought for about six months, and a rainy season for six months. Angkor had a complicated network of canals, reservoirs and dams to catch water during the rainy season so it could be used during droughts. The system worked well for almost 600 years.

Recently, scientists studied tree rings from 900-year-old trees near Angkor. The rings showed that year after year the droughts and the rains got more severe. Here's what scientists think may have happened: The reservoirs went completely dry during the drought seasons and the canals were badly damaged. The people of Angkor could no longer control one of their most important resources, water. Without water their civilization collapsed.

Isn't it amazing what you can learn from a tree?

title: Fur Trade Changes the Northeast
text:
The Fur Trade Changed Our Region in Four Important Ways:

Furs paid for exploration trips, making it profitable for more trappers to cross the ocean.

Fur hunters helped spread European culture into North America.

Traders and trappers came into friendly contact with American Indians (to trade instead of conquer).

Fur trading started international competition between nations, which led to territory disputes, then wars over boundaries, and the settlement of nations. Furs are important to our past!

Education

Most mountain men were not well educated in reading and writing, but they were very good at living off the land. They could make almost anything they needed from animal skins, rocks, trees, and plants. Usually, the only things they brought from the city were a few horses, a knife, a gun and some traps. They also brought a lot of courage.

Skills

Mountain men were mostly interested in beaver pelts (skins). Beaver pelts sold for six to eight dollars each. This was a lot of money back then. Pelts were sewn together to make warm clothing such as coats. Many beaver skins were sent to Europe, where beaver-skin hats were very popular with women. Trappers made a lot of money from selling beaver pelts.

Trapping

Fur trapping was very hard and lonely work. Because beaver skins were thickest and warmest during the cold months, mountain men had to do their trapping in the winter. Traps were set in or near icy streams where beavers lived, and the traps had to be checked often. Mountain men rode horses or hiked many miles through cold, deep snow. When a beaver was caught, the pelt (animal skin or hide with fur) had to be removed and stretched over a board until it dried. Scent glands had to be removed for baiting other beavers. Trappers kept very busy with their trap lines.

As soon as the snow melted, mountain men gathered their pelts and headed for a rendezvous. This was a gathering where trappers and traders could make exchanges. Each year, it was held in a different place in or around the Rocky Mountains. In later years, exchanges were made at trading posts.

Trading posts were like little stores in the middle of nowhere. Here, the trading post owner received wagonloads of supplies such as flour, sugar, gun powder, coffee and tobacco. He traded these for the trappers' furs. Most mountain men did not have money; they used their furs to buy the things they needed. Sometimes, American Indians also traded at the trading post. Trading post owners were more like storekeepers than mountain men.

1670- Hudson's Bay Company was formed by England and was granted sole fur-hunting rights in most of eastern Canada. The company built forts and trading posts. Most of the forts were captured by the French in 1686-1713, but were later surrendered back to the British. After more than 300 years, the Hudson's Bay Company finally dropped out of the fur trade in 1991.

1700s- Detroit, Michigan, became the center of fur trade in the Great Lakes area through the 1700s. French traders and American Indians brought their furs here to be bound and shipped to Montreal. From there, furs shipped overseas to France.

1741- Russia discovered Alaska's wealth in furs. Vitrus Bering (a Dane by birth) landed in Alaska and found a fortune in sea otter and beaver furs. Hundreds of Russian trappers followed in Bering's footsteps. In 20 years, Russians stripped the north of sea otters.

1763- Green Bay, La Pointe and Prairie du Chien became Wisconsin's most popular fur-trading sites under British rule.

1774- Spain tried to stop Russian expansion down the West Coast. Perez sailed to the Pacific Northwest to stake a claim for Spain.

1786- Britain tried to license the fur trade without much success.

1788- 1792 American trader Robert Gray sailed to the Pacific Northwest to stake a claim for America on the west coast. More than 85 American fur-trading ships followed over the following 15 years. Spanish and British traders couldn't compete with the American presence and withdrew.

1812- Demand for coastal fur died, and everyone's attention turned to the inland fur trade and the valuable beaver skin.

title: Canoes
text: During the fur-trading era, people didn't travel on roads because roads weren't paved like they are today. Instead, they traveled on rivers and streams in a little, narrow boat called a canoe. Canoes have been around for thousands of years. They come in many shapes and forms. Their invention made transportation, fur trading and fishing much easier and profitable. Bark canoes were very popular because they were lightweight and could be made from materials in forested areas. Sometimes, people used animal skins to wrap around the stick frames of their canoes. In the northeastern United States, birch bark was very popular. Canoes were also made by digging out the inside of a log. This was long, hard work, and the final canoe, called a dugout, was very heavy. The American Indians of the Pacific Coast made theirs from cedar, a wood that naturally resists water and rot. People would burn the inside of a log and use sharp-edged rocks or shells to scrape out the burned part. Another interesting canoe was made with planks that were carefully split from a log and sewn together with strands of animal hide. The cracks between the planks were filled with a substance like tar. A swift canoe could take travelers 150 miles or more after a long, hard day of paddling!

title: How big is your skin?
text: If you take your skin off and lay it out on the ground, it will measure 10-12 square feet and weigh about 4 pounds, depending on your size. By the time you're an adult, your skin covers more than 18 square feet and weighs about 6 pounds. Some adults wish their skin could get smaller, especially after eating all the Halloween goodies after a night of trick-or-treating.

title: Woofconsin: American Water Spaniel
text: Wisconsin has a pet! Do you know what it is? It's a dog, but not just any dog. This beautiful, brown-colored dog is called an American Water Spaniel. Officials named it the state dog in 1985. It's the only breed native to Wisconsin. This dog's hunting habits are perfect for Wisconsin's forests, lakes and fur-trapping industry. It's an eager hunter and excellent swimmer. Its dense coat of curly hair keep it warm in the cold winter months. This dog loves Wisconsin - woof!

title: Why should I follow directions
text:
Think about it. If someone took the time to write directions, then that person must want the directions to be followed. Have you ever heard the story of the test nobody passed because the students didn't read the directions? It was a long, 10-page test. And some students thought they did very well, getting most of the answers correct. But nobody passed. After the teacher had graded the tests, he pointed out the directions: "Write your name on the top of page 1 and hand the test in. Do not complete any of the questions." You can bet that those students wished they had followed the directions rather than do the whole 10-page test!

Reading directions carefully can mean the difference between an A in school and an F in school. It can mean the difference between doing your assignment correctly, and missing part of the assignment, or doing too much of an assignment. It can mean the difference between a delicious pan of muffins and a mess of burnt, yucky dough.

Read the directions to get an idea of what you're doing.

Make lists of any material or information you need. Go get it!

After you have everything you need, read the directions again carefully. Read them more than once, until you understand each step.

If you still have questions, ask your teacher or call the manufacturer of the product for help.

Follow the directions carefully, step by step.

If you follow these directions, you will have done your assignment correctly-or made a loaf of bread correctly-depending on what directions you were following.

Pemmican

2 cups buffalo jerky or beef jerky, shredded

1 cup dried choke berries or tart red cherries, chopped

6 Tablespoon tallow (beef fat) or butter, melted

Combine all ingredients and form into six patties. Refrigerate until serving.

title: Make Your Own Stamp
text:
Materials

Pencil

Thick cardboard

Glue

Scissors

Paper for printing on

Squares and rectangles of wood

Tempera or poster paints

A wide brush and large flat tray or cookie sheet

Directions

On the thick cardboard, draw several simple shapes, like a heart, star, square or triangle, that you want to print. You can draw the same shape several times, or you can alternate shapes to make a pattern.

Cut out the shapes and glue them onto your blocks of wood. You can make a long design by gluing your shapes onto a long rectangular piece of wood, or you can make a single design by just gluing one shape onto a small square piece of wood. Let the glue dry.

Put a few spoonfuls of paint onto the large tray or cookie sheet. Use a different tray for every color you’d like to use. Spread the paint around with your paintbrush so that it covers the entire tray with a thin layer of paint.

To stamp, press your block of wood, with the shape side down, into the tray of paint. Make sure all of your shapes are covered with paint. Press your painted block on your piece of paper. Lift your block up, and there’s your design on the paper!

Repeat step 4 until you get the design you want. Let the paint on the paper dry. Hang on a wall or fridge when you’re finished.

Extra Activity: You could make a stamp of your name out of cardboard. Just write your name in block letters on the cardboard, cut them out, and paste them onto a wood block. Use your stamp in the same way you did the shapes. Try using different thick materials for the stamps, such as sponges. They create a different texture.

title: Missionaries and Traders Explore Wisconsin
text:
As a young boy, Louis Hennepin dreamed of visiting far away places. He imagined circling the world, fighting pirates, dancing the Grizzly-Bear Dance with American Indians, hunting deer with bow and arrows, and sailing thunderous seas to exotic lands. By the mid-1600s, as he was reaching adulthood, he found an outlet for his dream. He decided to become a missionary (someone who preaches religion to people in other countries).

Louis enrolled in a missionary school for boys. Afterwards, he landed a great assignment to work at the docks. This was the perfect place from which to watch the great sea ships unfurl their mighty sails and ply the giant swells of the Atlantic Ocean (which many explorers crossed). It was here that he heard so many salty tales of voyages by ship masters and sailors. Sometimes, he was so enthralled with the stories that he would miss sleep and not eat. "I was very attentive to the accounts they gave of their encounters by sea," he wrote, "the perils they had gone through, and all the accidents which befell them in their long voyages."

In 1675, Louis received the exciting news that he was to leave his homeland of France and go to Canada as a missionary. At last, Louis would set out on his dream to travel the world.

Lucky for Louis, another important explorer was aboard the same ship. Robert La Salle was on his way to Fort Frontenac, a principle outpost of New France.

The trip to Quebec was dangerous. The ship was attacked by Turkish, Tunisian, and Algerian pirates, but they failed to ruin the voyage. Once in Canada, Louis began his job preaching. During the first four years, he took time out to go visit the nearby villages. In winter, such trips had to be made on snowshoes with his luggage strapped to a dog sled. Sometimes he would travel by canoe. When he reached these small native villages, he studied hard to learn the languages and customs of the people. He preached among the natives and made many friends.

One day, Louis was invited to join a large expedition lead by his old friend La Salle. They traveled through Lake Peoria and constructed Fort Creve-coeur. While La Salle departed for Quebec, Louis continued on a voyage of discovery. He traveled down the Illinois River and then up the Mississippi River. Louis took many notes, met many natives, and continued to preach. On one of his trips, he and two companions were captured by a band of Sioux. Fortunately, another French explorer was in the area. He was named Daniel DuLhut, and he was greatly respected by the natives. When DuLhut heard of the capture, he demanded their release, and they were let go. Louis and his companions joined DuLhut on his voyage down the Mississippi.

Louis had a grand experience in the Wisconsin area that lasted many years. After his mission ended, he went back to a monastery in France and wrote a book all about his journeys. This book was the first writing that described Wisconsin, and it caught the attention of many explorers. It wasn't long until one of the greatest secrets of the Great Lakes was finally in the open—Wisconsin!

title: Join the Club — Explore the World
text:
Does exploring the North Pole, climbing Mount Everest or landing on the moon sound exciting to you? Members of the world famous Explorers Club have done all these things - and many more!

The Explorers Club was started in New York City in 1904 and has been around ever since. The club's goal is to keep the spirit of exploration alive. It encourages its members to explore the land, sea, air and space and to teach others about science and the world around them. Many famous explorers have belonged to the Explorers Club, including Sir Edmund Hillary, the first person to climb to the top of Mount Everest; Robert Peary, the first person to explore the North Pole; Roald Amundsen, the first person to explore the South Pole; and Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, the first men to land on the moon.

Today, the club has more than 3,000 members in 60 countries around the world. Members of the club plan and carry out expeditions in interesting places around the globe. Each year, the Explorers Club gives special awards from the Youth Activities Fund to high school and college students who are interested in science and who have shown great talent in some way. These students sometimes get to go on special expeditions with members of the club.

If you are interested in finding out more about the Explorers Club, ask a parent or teacher to help you visit www.explorers.org.

title: Missionaries and Traders
text:
Marquette and Jolliet

Jacques Marquette, born in 1637, was a Catholic missionary and explorer. He came to Canada and learned the languages of the natives. He worked at the La Pointe Mission in Wisconsin. During this time, he met Louis Jolliet. Born in 1645, Louis Jolliet was a French-Canadian explorer raised in a Jesuit seminary. He became a great mapmaker and trader in the Great Lakes region. Along with five others, Jolliet and Marquette crossed Lake Michigan and explored the Fox, Mississippi, and Wisconsin rivers. Father Marquette preached among the Illinois American Indians until his death in 1675. Jolliet continued to explore until his death in 1700.

Fr. Rene Menard (1604-1661)

Menard went to work as a missionary among the Hurons and Nippisriens around the Quebec area and became the first missionary in Wisconsin. His home base was the Huron Mission, but this was destroyed by the American Indians. Menard moved on toward Three Rivers, but was captured in Cayugas and brutally treated by the Iroquois Indians. After hard labor among the natives, Menard became friends with the American Indians. In 1659, he started west to establish settlements with 300 Ottowas. His first stop was in Keeweenaw, and he tried to continue on to the Dacotahs, but never got there, and he was never heard of again. Researchers believe he was murdered at the first raid of the Menominee.

Nicolas Perrot (1644-1717)

Nicolas Perrot was born in France in 1644. He began his missionary work at a young age. When he arrived in New France, he lived at some missions for a short time before moving to live among the Fox and Potawatomi Tribes. Perrot learned many American Indian languages and was an interpreter. He did a lot of exploration and trading with many American Indian nations. Perrot and his group were the first French traders to visit the Algonquian tribes at Green Bay. Perrot was respected by the natives because he dealt with them fairly. He built several trading posts at Trempealeau, Lake Pepin, and at the mouth of the Wisconsin River, where he traded with the Sioux. Perrot was regarded as France's best representative among the American Indian tribes, who honored him with rights and privileges enjoyed by their own chiefs.

Fr. Claude Allouez (1622-1689)

A Jesuit missionary, Allouez sailed to Quebec in 1658. He was stationed at settlements along the St. Lawrence River. He traveled extensively through that territory and preached to the natives. Allouez established missions at Chequamegon and Green Bay and labored among the American Indians for 32 years. He's known as the "founder of Catholicism in the West." He preached the Catholic Gospel to 20 different tribes. No missionary did as much or traveled over a wider territory than did Allouez. At times, he had to prevent the American Indians from adoring him as a god; at other times, they were about to kill him. He died a natural death at age 69.

title: How Big Are the Great Lakes?
text: The Great Lakes cover over 94,000 square miles and contain about 6 quadrillion gallons of water. A lot of the Earth's available fresh water is contained in our Great Lakes. The lakes hold 1/5 of the Earth's fresh water and 9/10 of America's fresh water. The deepest lake is Lake Superior at 1,330 feet. Lake Erie's average depth is only 70 feet. If the Great Lakes were spread out over the entire 48 states, the country would be buried beneath nine feet of water, coast to coast!

title: What is the Algonquin language?
text: The word "Algonquin" is the name of a language the Ojibwa people spoke. Today, it refers to the group of similar languages spoken by native people who lived in Canada, New England, the Atlantic coastal region, the Great Lakes region, and westward to the Rocky Mountains. There are 13 Algonquin languages still spoken today. The language can be hard to understand because one Algonquin word can mean many English words. An example is "totem," meaning "his brother-sister relatives." The words take on different meanings depending on how they are used with other words and the ending or beginning of the word. Nearly all of Wisconsin's American Indians are of the Algonquin language group. Many of the early explorers, traders, and missionaries needed to learn this language so that they could communicate with the natives.

title: Trading Posts
text: Explorers, missionaries, and furtraders traveled all over Wisconsin. They built forts and trading posts along many rivers. The first trading post was established at Green Bay. By the 1800s, most of the posts were closed up and destroyed. Wisconsin still has many small shops that are good copies of the trading posts of old. Tourists can purchase American Indian jewelry, trinkets, pelts, and souvenir items. Today, Wisconsin is a member of a trading post that is much, MUCH bigger: the Wisconsin World Trade Center. This organization is set up so that businesses from Wisconsin can find companies to trade with from around the world. Typically, they trade money for goods, but once in a while they'll trade services for goods or goods for goods. Confused yet? It's much like the trading posts of the old days, but on a much larger scale. Do you think we'll ever have an Intergalactic Universal Trade Center where we can trade with planets, aliens, and stars? Maybe we can trade a space shuttle for a U.F.O.! What do you think?

title: Quadrorama
text:
Materials

Four 8-inch by 14-inch pieces of construction paper

Craft materials—construction paper, string, fabric scraps, cotton, markers and crayons

scissors

tape

ruler

glue

pencil

Directions

1. Fold the top left corner of a piece of 8x14 construction paper diagonally so that the top edge of the paper is flush with the right edge of the paper.

2. Fold the top right-hand corner diagonally so that it touches the lower point of the previous fold.

3. Fold the panel at the bottom to make a horizontal crease along the edge. (Fold it to the back.)

4. Open the paper up and cut along the lower left-hand diagonal crease to the center of the paper.

5. Pull point A over to point B so that the piece you cut is flush with the lower right-hand diagonal crease. Glue the base into place. This is one triorama.

6. When four trioramas are finished, glue them together to form a pyramid. From underneath, tape the four lower panels so that they form four corners. This is now called a quadrorama.

Design the Inside

1. Color and cut out the pictures on Page 4.

2. Glue the scenes inside each triorama.

3. Write a brief paragraph describing the scenes along the bottom flap. Make guiding lines by lightly drawing pencil lines after writing the paragraph.

4. You can decorate the scenes using any available craft materials to make the scene three dimensional.

Example Paragraph for Wool Carding

Carding Wool, 1770 — The manufacturer of woolen cloth began after sheep were sheared. The raw wool was cleaned of burrs and tangles and washed. It was then carded, or drawn between cards bearing stiff wire bristles. The carder would stroke the card across the wool until it was soft and fluffy.

title: Early American Trades
text:
This week is a good time to learn about early American trades.

The colonists could not easily buy everything they needed as they had in England. Many became tradesmen. They learned to make their own goods locally. Everything, from furniture, metal tools, glassware, cloth, and food, was produced locally. It would be fun to make a display of these skilled tradesmen and women to show in your classroom.

A good way to do this is to follow the directions on Page 3 for the quadrarama. First, make a “quad” as shown. Then draw or cut out the tradesmen’s pictures that are on this page. Next, color them and mount them with glue onto your quadrarama.

You will want to write about each of the trades so that those viewing them will learn something about early colonial America!

title: The Fight for Wisconsin Begins
text:
In the late 1600s, our territory began to look very inviting to a lot of people. Early explorers returned to Europe with stories of deep forests, rich game, and bounteous fur hunting that was just about everywhere. They told of a land of lakes, rivers, and timber - almost paradise!

The original settlers of Wisconsin, the American Indians, saw these newcomers and worried that their land would be overrun. They tried to protect their land and make friends with the new explorers at the same time. Things stayed quiet for many years.

And then the Iroquois in the eastern woodland areas made a bold move to take back land from both white and American Indian settlers. Many American Indian groups escaped the attacks by packing up their homes and moving to Wisconsin.

The French didn't like these changes in events. They were trying to settle the Great Lakes region, and these many tribes moving to Wisconsin made the French worry about wars with settlers. They also worried they wouldn't gain control over very important fur-trading routes on the Fox and Wisconsin Rivers. In 1706, the French decided to take action. They declared war on the local natives and tried to capture as much fur-hunting land as they could. These so-called Fox and Indian Wars killed many American Indians, and others were driven away. The French thought they finally had control. And then the British showed up.

Fighting between the French and British has a long history. They fought each other all over the world, especially in Africa, India, the Far East, and America. In America, things went against the French when the British joined with the Iroquois in the early 1700s to win Montreal, Ohio, the Great Lakes, and many other areas. But France also found some friends. Spain joined the French, but it was too little too late. The French began to lose, and the local tribes sided with the British to push the French and their friends farther west.

This tug of war involved a lot of land - all the way from Canada to the American colonies, over to Cuba, and clear across the Pacific to the Philippines. After a lot of long wars, the British finally won. The Paris Peace Treaty that everybody signed in 1763 forced the French to surrender all of its land in Canada and the Northwest and almost everything it had east of the Mississippi. And Spain had to give up Florida. Other lands changed hands, and mapmakers had to make a lot of changes on the world scene.

Many American Indians would not see these changes from the Wisconsin territory because they were moving out. By 1763, the Miami were in western Ohio, the Potawatomi were settling around what is now Chicago, and the Kickapoo had followed explorer Robert La Salle to the St. Louis area.

All that was left in Wisconsin were a few natives, some French settlers, and the trading posts at Mackinac and Green Bay. All seemed settled and quiet, but this was not so! In 20 short years, the sounds of freedom would rumble far to the east, and soon a new nation would be looking to Wisconsin to join the greatest experiment ever devised in freedom - the United States of America.

title: The Wisconsinites are Still Fighting for Land
text:
A recent survey showed that Wisconsin leads the nation in recycling. About 97 percent of Wisconsin households recycle, more than any other state in America.

Our state's emphasis on recycling and protecting our land is benefitting everyone who lives here. The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources is the state's leading agency for protecting and improving the state's land, water, and animal life, but it takes more than just this department.

Actually, it takes thousands of people, millions of hours and dollars, and a lot of dedicated effort.

Below is a list of what our Department of Natural Resources (DNR) does to keep our state looking good. Circle the things that affect the way you live today. You might be surprised at everything this department does. Protect the quality of air, land, water, fisheries, wildlife and forests:

Prevent and control pollution: This means the DNR helps stop bad things from getting into our water and air so that we don't drink or breathe anything dangerous.

Enforce conservation and environmental laws: Without laws, some citizens would throw garbage into our rivers and streams and burn fuel that is bad for the air we breathe. The DNR helps enforce littering and pollution laws.

Restore and protect habitat for all living things: Some habitats would be overrun if we didn't protect them with fences and trail paths. Sometimes, we need to restore wildlife and plant life. We do this by planting seeds and bringing animals back to the land.

Maintain parks, trails, hunting grounds, and other recreational areas: Tourists and residents love to visit the scenic places of Wisconsin, and thanks to hard efforts to keep these places clean and in good condition, millions of residents and tourists can enjoy them.

title: The Wars that Won Wisconsin
text:
Many of the important wars that helped our state become part of the new United States were part of international conflicts. Let's look at some of the highlights.

Fox and Indian Wars

These wars began when the American Indians closed the Fox-Wisconsin River trade route and demanded that people pay if they wanted to pass through. A Frenchman named Paul Marin didn't like this idea and sailed up the Fox River with soldiers and American Indians to challenge the people who had taken over. Fighting broke out, and by 1706, he had killed hundreds of Fox Indians. This was the first of many slaughters. In one battle, Marin and his men killed more than 1,000 natives. More peaceful American Indians didn't like the slaughter and fled west. The remaining Fox Indians fought back, killing any Frenchman in sight. The final war was fought in 1733 on a hill named Butte des Morts, "Hill of the Dead." After this bloody battle, the French decided to make peace and ended the Fox Wars. The Fox Wars pushed the fur trade to the southeast and also brought the French traders into conflict with the British. As the British tried to take more land, four wars broke out between them and the French.

King William's War (1689-1697)

The first British-French war in North America is called King William's War. Both French and British settlers gained the help of various natives and raided each other's settlements. The British also raided settlements in Canada. The French burned settlements in New York and Boston, destroyed homes in New Hampshire, and destroyed forts in Maine. The British fought back, capturing Port Royal in Nova Scotia and attacking Quebec. The two nations tried to make peace, but it was no use. A few years later, Queen Anne decided to go to war.

Queen Anne's War (1702-1713)

In the early 1700s, the British launched an attack across the settled parts of Canada and into parts of America to rid it of the French. At the same time, Spain took up arms against the British. In the end, the British attacked Quebec and won Hudson Bay (find this on your classroom map), the Spanish city of Saint Augustine in Florida, and other towns in the United States. The battles and raids ended in 1713, when the Utrecht Peace Treaty was signed. The French had to surrender most of their Canadian holdings to the British.

King George's War (1744-1748)

After several years of peace, small fights and conflicts broke out among the French and British. They both wanted to control North America. In 1744, the French destroyed a British fort at Nova Scotia and captured prisoners. In return, the British attacked the great French fort at Louisbourg. France tried to take it back twice, but was unsuccessful. At the end of the war in 1748, Louisbourg was returned to the French in return for British control of Madras, India. The settlement left both nations upset. Six years later, they returned for the last time to decide who would finally own the land and colonies in the French and Indian War.

The French and Indian War (1755-1763)

The French and Indian War was different from the previous wars. The earlier wars were fought over small areas such as military posts and land. The French and Indian War was part of a "great war for empire," a successful attempt by the British to win almost all the land in North America, the West Indies, and parts of India. Although the French and Indian War began in America, it expanded into Europe as the Seven Years' War (1756-1763). After the gun smoke settled and soldiers were buried, it was clear to everyone that the French had lost all their North American territory. This war also caused Britain to bear down hard on its American colonies, a change that eventually led to the American Revolution.

title: Charles de Langlade
text: Langlade County is named for a brave, skillful leader of the American Indians named Charles de Langlade. He was half Ottawa and half French. The natives called him Akewaugeketauso, meaning, "Fierce for the Land." Some people said he was the greatest soldier ever during the French and Indian War (1754-1760). As a boy, Langlade often sat on a buffalo-skin cloak in the lodge of his uncle, the Ottawa chief, and listened to tales of American Indian bravery. When he was only 10, he took part in an Ottawa war. The French officers recognized Langlade's military talent and friendship with the American Indians. They gave him a cadetship in the colonial army when he was 21. Langlade led Ottawa warriors against the Miami Indians in Ohio. The Ottawas demolished the Miami Tribe. In 1755, Langlade led a large force of American Indians against General Braddock's British army. Four horses were shot from under Braddock, and two from beneath his aide, George Washington. Braddock was mortally wounded as he signaled retreat, and the British fled for miles. Langlade continued to lead attacks until 1759, when the French lost Quebec, and the tide turned heavily in favor of the British. Altogether, he took part in 99 battles. As an old, balding, white-haired man, he used to tell his friends in Green Bay that he wished he could somehow get into just one more battle to make it an even 100.

title: Making Syrup
text: The "sweetest" time of the year in early Wisconsin was in the spring, when settlers made maple syrup. Nearly every family had its "sugar bush" or grove of maples, and a cabin to which the family moved at sugaring time. There, they began tapping trees and hanging buckets to gather sap. Early sap was the sweetest, and 30-35 gallons of it would boil down to one gallon of delicious syrup, perfect for crepes (pancakes) and candies. The steam from the boiling sap filled the air with a sweet maple-flavored scent that added to the enjoyment of the occasion. Today, automated tappers draw sap through tubs to giant collecting tanks for factory processing, and it still tastes delicious!

title: What types of weapons did early settlers use?
text: An important tool to settling the wild west of Wisconsin was the newly invented musket. This muzzleloader came around in the early 1700s. The British would arm the native people with guns to help harass the French or American settlers. Muzzleloaders had the bullet and gun powder forced down the end of the barrel. When the gun fired, it let out a thick cloud of smoke. Breech-loaders were loaded from the back of the gun. These weapons were dangerous but important tools for family defense and hunting in early Wisconsin.

title: Wild Turkey
text: Our turkeys love to strut their stuff, even in November. Our wild turkeys have excellent vision and hearing. Their field of view is 270 degrees. This is the main reason why most hunters have a hard time catching one. If you spook a turkey, it will sprint away at a top speed of 20 miles an hour or burst into flight at 50-55 miles an hour. Turkeys can adopt just about any place for home, but they love the grassy areas in hardwood forests the most. Turkeys spend the night in trees and fly to their roosts at sunset. At sunup, they fly to the ground to find crawling things for breakfast and continue eating until midday. They love to gobble and begin before sunrise and continue gobbling past lunchtime. During mating season, the males like to strut around to attract females. Do you know how to recognize the youngsters from the adults? A young turkey's middle tail feather is taller than the adult's, while the adult's feathers are all the same. Tracks in the mud are just the opposite. A middle toe that is four inches long is made by a full-grown adult gobbler.

title: Play Dough
text:
Materials

bowl

two cups of flour

one cup of salt

two tablespoons of cooking oil

3/4 cup water

food coloring

oven

poster or acrylic paints

Instructions

1. Mix the flour and salt together in a bowl.

2. Add the oil and a few drops of food coloring to the water.

3. Pour the water mixture slowly into the flour mixture, kneading with your hands until it becomes soft and doughy.

4. Create busts (statues from the chest up), statues, or figurines of historical characters from the dough.

5. You can dry your projects in a 250-degree oven for 1.5 to two hours, or you can let them air dry.

6. When the dough is dry, decorate the figurine with paint.

Note: This dough should not be eaten!

title: How Do I Read Tables?
text:
By learning to read tables, you can quickly compare and contrast data.

Use Categories

Tables are lists or boxes of information, organized into categories. Categories of information appear across the top and down the lefthand side. And the information in each column shows the data for these categories. Tables have labels and numbers. When reading a table, carefully read the title and labels so that you interpret the information correctly.

Try It!

Study the table below and then answer the questions that follow.

1. What does this table show?

2. Who traveled the shortest distance?

3. How far did John Cabot travel?

4. How far is it from France to Michigan?

5. How far did Jacques Cartier travel?

6. Who traveled 4,693 miles?

7. How far is it from England to Hawaii?

8. How far is it from Spain to Tampa Bay, Florida?

9. How far did Bernal Diaz del Castillo travel?

10. How far did Francis Drake travel?

11. Which trip is the longest, Spain to Peru or Spain to Mexico?

12. How far is it from Africa to Florida to Spain? (Hint: See Panfilo de Narvaez and Estevanico?)

title: The Great Lead Rush of the 1820s
text:
If it wasn't for the discovery of lead, Wisconsin might have been left alone for many years. Even though the land was beautiful and plentiful, few settlers found a reason to move into our territory. When lead was discovered in the 1820s, waves of settlers started moving in by the hundreds. For a short time, this "gray gold" was more important to settlers than furs or farming. Lead was used to make all kinds of things, including paint and bullets.

Mining lead in Wisconsin began long before the Europeans arrived. American Indians discovered lead in the southwestern part of Wisconsin, but didn't know how to extract it from ore. Two French explorers named Nicolas Perrot and Julien Dubuque showed them how to heat the ore and use the lead to make weapons and tools.

When the French eventually lost the Wisconsin territory and moved out, American Indians took over the mines. In 1804, the American Indians agreed to give the land to the U.S. government. By the 1820s, the miners began moving in, and the first mining operations began in 1822. Col. James A. Johnson and a crew of men worked the first mine in Galena, Illinois, which at the time was part of Wisconsin's lead district. As the mines developed, other miners caught wind of the huge lead finds and flowed into the region. Galena became a big mining town.

In 1824, the first permanent mining settlements in Wisconsin were made at New Diggings in Lafayette and Grant Counties. John Bonner was one of these miners. He started digging a shaft, and at only four feet down he found tons of lead. By the time he quit for the day, he had pulled out 17,000 pounds. He was rich! News such as this find attracted miners from the South, Kentucky, and Virginia.

Settlers formed "mining districts." One of the largest such districts in Wisconsin was Mineral Point. It quickly became one of the world's leading mining centers.

The earliest miners carted their lead to Galena for shipment down the Mississippi River. Later, the miners shipped it east to Milwaukee and then on to the Great Lakes. Lead was so valuable in Milwaukee that stores even accepted it for money.

The new settlers did not care if they invaded American Indian land while they were mining. This led to American Indian wars including the Red Bird War and Black Hawk War. The wars ended with many American Indians moving out of the territory and American settlers moving in.

The height of Wisconsin's lead-mining era was in the 1840s. Miners were producing 18 million pounds of lead per year, half of the national output. And then toward the late 1840s, the lead-mining boom began to die. Settlers had mined so much lead, it had lost its value and was cheaper than bread flour! Many miners decided to become farmers or take advantage of the great copper rush in Michigan in 1844 or the California gold rush in 1849.

Mining remained important to Wisconsin's economy during the First and Second World Wars, when strikes of zinc, copper, lead - and iron were found. These metals were used to make guns and cannons. Mining remains important to our state's economy even today. And thanks to these early efforts by miners, Wisconsin quickly expanded toward statehood.

title: Mining Wisconsin
text:
The discovery of lead brought many settlers to the Wisconsin region. After the lead began to disappear, miners dug for zinc, iron, and copper. The rich deposits of minerals made southwestern Wisconsin the longest-lived metallic-mining district in the United States.

Lead (1820s-1850s)

Lead is used in batteries, paint, glasswork, electric cables, plumbing, and ammunition. Lead is very dangerous if swallowed. It was once used to make water pipes, but this ended up contaminating the water and poisoning those who drank it. Today, we have laws to protect us from lead poisoning.

Zinc (1850s-1970s)

In the 1850s, some miners discovered zinc in lead mines. They began to dig for it. For a short period in the late 1800s, Mineral Point had one of the world's largest zinc smelters. A smelter is a machine that heats metals before it is poured into a mold. The zinc industry expanded during the World Wars, but had ended by the late 1970s. Its main use is to strengthen steel. Zinc is also used to make brass, car engines, tools, toys, rubber, fertilizers, and animal feed. It is important for our health.

Iron (1849-1983)

Iron mining began in Dodge County in 1849. Iron is the cheapest and most abundant, useful, and important of all metals. Today, we use it to make bridges, buildings, ships, trains, cars, machinery, refrigerators, airplanes, hardware, wire, nails, and bicycles.

Copper (1970-1997)

The United States acquired Wisconsin's Lake Superior shore in the 1842 Copper Treaty, but most copper deposits were discovered in Michigan. It was not until the 1970s that companies decided to mine copper from mines near Ladysmith and Crandon. More than half of the copper that is mined is used in the electric industry. Copper wire carries electric current for light, power, and telephones. It is also used to make coins and can be mixed with other metals to make bronze and brass.

title: Wisconsin Coat of Arms
text: Mining is a very important part of Wisconsin's heritage. Wisconsin's coat of arms has several symbols related to mining. A miner stands on the right holding a pick. On the shield, a triangular symbol represents a stack of lead bars. On top of the shield, a badger (the official state animal) symbolizes early lead miners who burrowed in underground mines and often lived in underground shelters. The miners' tools included the shovel, pick, gad or crowbar, drill, and blasting powder.

title: Helena Shot Tower
text: Lead was very important for ammunition. An early settler, Daniel Whitney of Helena, invented a way to turn lead into pellets, or shot. He built the Helena processing center, a tower, next to the Wisconsin River in 1830. Workers melted lead in a furnace and poured it from a pot into a deep hole in the ground. As it fell, the molten lead formed round balls, which hardened after hitting a pool of water at the bottom. Up to 5,000 pounds of pellets were produced each day. The pellets were shipped down the Mississippi River or loaded onto wagons to Lake Michigan ports. On their return trips, the wagons brought new settlers and supplies. The tower closed in 1861, because new rifles no longer required pellets.

title: Where was the largest diamond found, and how big was it?
text: The largest diamond ever unearthed in the United States was discovered in Murfreesboro, Arkansas. The 40.23-carat diamond is nicknamed "Uncle Sam." Diamonds were first discovered in Murfreesboro in 1906. More than 70,000 have been found. The area became a park in 1972 and is now known as 'Craters of Diamonds State Park." More than 22,000 diamonds have been carried home by visitors. Amethyst, garnet, jasper, agate, quartz, and more can also be found there.

title: Badger
text:
Wisconsin was once called the Badger State! Where did we get this name? Probably from early lead miners. Miners were nicknamed "badgers" because they lived in dugouts like the hillside burrows of the badgers. The badger is the official state animal.

Badgers have short, flat bodies with gray and white stripes on their heads and backs. Black markings appear on badgers' heads and faces. Badgers have several uses for their long, sharp claws. They dig underground burrows for shelter or fend off enemies, some much larger than they are. Badgers also use their claws to hunt for food. At night, badgers dig into smaller animals' burrows. Badgers eat mice, squirrels, or any other small animals they can catch.

title: Clarity of Expression: Father Junípero Serra and the California Missions
text:
Do you like to give speeches? Can you convince others to see things your way? Then maybe you have a gift for expressing yourself clearly.

Father Junípero Serra was a Franciscan monk who some might call one of the "founding fathers" of California. He was born in Spain in 1713 and became a priest in his mid 20s. Many people noticed how well he spoke, or how clearly he expressed himself, during his powerful sermons, and he soon became a university professor.

Father Serra wanted to work as a Spanish missionary, so he first traveled to Mexico City in 1749. He started missionary work with the Sierra Gorda Indians. Soon he was made head of the Spanish missions in Baja (lower) California. Next, the Spanish governor asked him to start missions in Alta (upper) California. Father Serra personally built eight missions there and supervised the start of many more from San Diego to San Francisco.

Father Serra helped convert thousands of American Indians to Christianity. They lived and worked in the missions, but life was harsh. Many Indians died from overwork and diseases. But the missions kept going because of Father Serra's preaching and care. His sermons were so dramatic that he would sometimes pound his chest with a stone or touch a lit torch to his chest.

Father Serra used his clarity of expression for what he thought was good. He argued with the Spanish army to get control of the missions. He even convinced Mexican officials to send more money and soldiers for his missions. Spanish colonists settled the area around the missions, which is all now the state of California.

Do you think you have a good ability to express yourself clearly as Father Serra did? What topic do you feel strongly about?

title: How Do I Use a Graph?
text:
Graphs present numerical amounts of something and show the relationship between sets of numbers.

Figure out What the Graph is Trying to Show

The type of graph used to present the information will depend on what is intended by showing the graph. Here is an explanation for some possible graphs.

Bar Graph

Bar graphs use bars of different length to show amounts. The bars can run either across the graph or up and down the graph. The categories and quantities of the items being compared run along the bottom and left-hand side of the graph. You can use a bar graph to show how the numbers compare.

Pictograph

Pictographs are like bar graphs, except that they use pictures or symbols instead of bars.

Pie Graph

Pie graphs, or circle graphs, use a circle to show 100 percent of something. The circle is divided into sections. Each section, or slice of the pie, represents a percentage of the group, or a part of the whole. You can use a circle graph to compare amounts by looking at how big each slice is.

Line Graph

Line graphs show trends over time. One side edge lists units of time, and another edge lists the amount being measured. Inside the graph, points are drawn to show where the two categories meet. A line connects the points to show the trend going upward or downward. You can use a line graph to see at a glance if a trend is going up or down.

Try It!

Create a graph using the data below. First, decide which type of graph would be the best way to present the information. Then create it, using the examples above for help.

Number of New Settlers in the United States

Pre-1790 = 875,000

1790-1820 = 270,000

1820-1880 = 9,830,000

1880-1930 = 22,100,000

1930-1965 = 3,630,000

1965-2000 = 10,020,000

title: Making the World a Kinder Place
text:
We sometimes wonder why bad things happen to innocent people. Although we may never understand it, we can do our best to keep things like this from happening in the future. When we do this, we are doing our part to make the world a kinder place, without anger and violence.

One way to do this is by making a plan to replace bullying and violence with kindness. The Cool to Be Kind (C2BK) program was developed to help students create programs in their classes and schools that are based on pro-kindness – doing nice things for others. Students look for ways to “pay it forward” each day. Paying it forward means that when someone thanks you for doing something nice, you ask that person to pay it forward by doing something nice for someone else. By paying it forward, kindness continues to spread across the world and people start thinking kinder thoughts and ways that they can help other people.

What are some ways you could practice paying it forward? How about doing yard work for an elderly neighbor for free? Or inviting a new student to eat lunch with you and your friends? What about giving up your seat on the bus to someone who looks tired, or helping someone pick up something they have dropped? Thinking kind thoughts and acting on them with acts of kindness is a simple change that you can do to change the world.

Teachers: Go to www.pifexperience.org to find out more about starting a C2BK program at your school!

title: Let's Write
text: One sunny day, you’re out with your friends on the shore of a lake, and you suddenly spot something gold poking out of the sand. You pick it up and realize it’s a very old coin. You wipe it off and discover it’s a gold coin from 500 years ago. Like most coins, the picture on the coin is a face of a king or queen, but oddly enough this coin has a picture of your face. Your friends come rushing over to see what you’ve discovered. They want to know why your face is on a 500-year-old golden coin. What do you tell them?

title: Black Hawk’s Final Stand
text:
Black Hawk was an American Indian warrior from the Fox-Sauk tribes. In the late 1700s, his people had become lead miners. They were doing very well at this industry and were trading lead for a prosperity that they had never before known.

When Wisconsin's Gov. Harrison learned about the vast lead holdings of the Fox-Sauk tribes in the rich Fever District, he decided to trade or buy the land so that American settlers could move in and mine it. The governor arranged two land-swap treaties, one in 1804 and another in 1816. Black Hawk and his followers thought that the treaties were unfair and refused to abide by the treaties or leave their land. Violence broke out, and the battles that followed became known as the Black Hawk War of 1832. This war is important because it was the last stand of the American Indians in Wisconsin.

Since 1823, white settlers had been invading Sauk and Fox land. The settlers harassed the American Indians to the point that the natives abandoned their land. A few settlers were mean-hearted, and they destroyed the American Indians' crops, burned their lodges, and beat the men. In 1829, Chief Keokuk took his people away on their usual winter hunt. While they were gone, some whites took over their village. When they returned, it was clear that they were outnumbered by the white settlers. Chief Keokuk decided he couldn't regain his village and led his people across the Mississippi into Iowa.

Black Hawk was part of that group, and he was very angry. When famine developed in Iowa in 1832, he decided to lead the people back across the Mississippi. News of the crossing spread panic among the white settlers. Regular soldiers and a militia were formed. Abraham Lincoln, who later served as president of the United States, was captain of one of these militia groups. Black Hawk did not want to fight, so he tried to surrender. However, some of the soldiers were half drunk, and they shot at the American Indians and killed them. There was no other choice but to go to war. Many small battles were fought during the summer of 1832. American Indians and settlers suffered many deaths and injuries.

Black Hawk led the band of warriors and their families northwest to the Wisconsin River. They were starving. The American soldiers picked up on the American Indian trail and overtook them as they were crossing the river near Prairie du Sac. Again, Black Hawk tried to surrender, but the American soldiers couldn't understand the American Indian language, and they killed many more. The natives retreated down the Wisconsin River, trying to get across to Iowa. The Americans intercepted them at Prairie do Chien, killed many of them, and captured others. Black Hawk and those who were not captured reached the Mississippi near the mouth of the Bad Axe River. The Americans met them there. Black Hawk again displayed a flag of peace, but the soldiers opened fire with guns and a cannon. Other soldiers came from behind, driving the American Indians into the river at bayonet point and shooting them as they tried to swim. In all, only about 150 of Black Hawk's 1,000 people survived.

Black Hawk was captured and kept at Jefferson Barracks. He was finally released after signing a peace treaty. He died in 1838 on an Iowa reservation. A year before his death, Black Hawk explained his stand in these simple words: "I liked my town, my cornfields, and the home of my people. I fought for them."

It was not only war that forced the American Indians to leave; it was also settlers, their illnesses (to which the natives were not immune), trade dependency, tribal disputes, and refugee migrations that weakened the tribes. This doesn't mean that white settlers were all bad, but mixing the cultures and different ways of living was hard on everyone. In the end, the settlers displaced the American Indians in just about every location they visited.

title: Horning On
text:
The Wisconsin Historical Museum, located on the Capitol Square in Madison, is full of interesting and amazing items. From military items such as swords, medals and uniforms to American Indian artifacts like moccasins, tools and baskets, the museum is full of history.

There is even an exhibit called "Odd Wisconsin" that displays items such as a 7-foot Bowie knife, a paper dress and the oldest pieces of toast in Wisconsin.

One interesting item on display at the museum is a powder horn used by a member of Colonel Dodge's militia during the Black Hawk War. Colonel Dodge was the head of the state militia that fought against Black Hawk at the Bad Axe River.

The powder horn carried black powder for a soldier's flintlock rifle. The soldier who owned it probably made it himself by hollowing out a cow horn. He then carved a piece of wood to fill the hole in the base of the horn and drilled a small hole in the pointed end for pouring the powder into the gun. The horn is about 7 inches long. It is also attached to a leather strap at each end so that the soldier could carry it over his shoulder.

If you are interested in taking a look at this Black Hawk War powder horn, plan a visit to the Wisconsin Historical Museum. You'll be glad you did!

title: Wisconsin Settlers
text:
With American Indians almost gone, a second great wave of settlers came to Wisconsin. (The first wave of settlers came during the lead rush.) These settlers came from New England, particularly New York. Most of them traveled through the newly built Erie Canal and settled along the shores of Michigan. These settlers worked hard to develop cities, towns, homes, and businesses.

1817

The first school was opened at Green Bay. Today, Wisconsin has hundreds of elementary, middle, and high schools and dozens of colleges and universities.

1821

The first steamer on the Upper Lakes appeared in Lake Michigan. Today, the Great Lakes steamships and steamboats carry iron ore, wheat, coal, and limestone.

1822

The government fur-trading factory system was discontinued.

1822

The lead rush begins.

1825

The Erie Canal was completed, making it possible for ships to sail from the east coast to the Great Lakes. A canal is a man-made waterway. Because there were no railroads at the time, traveling by ship was the fastest and most convenient way to get anywhere. Today, the canal is known as the New York State Barge Canal. Stretching from the Hudson River at Albany, New York, all the way to Lake Erie, this canal is a whopping 363 miles long!

1833

The first newspaper in Wisconsin was established at Green Bay. Today, one of the oldest surviving newspaper is the "Green Bay Press-Gazette," founded in 1866 as a weekly newspaper.

1846

Along the shore of Lake Michigan, Milwaukee served as the chief port of entry for settlers and became the first metropolis of Wisconsin in 1846. A metropolis is a large city and usually the main city of a state. Today, Milwaukee is the largest city in Wisconsin, known for its breweries and industries.

1846

The first mayor, Solomon Juneau, bought out the trading post and helped to establish Milwaukee City. Settlers continued to pour in from the east, buying land and establishing homes, towns, and marketplaces. The population grew rapidly from around 3,000 in 1830 to 11,683 in 1836. By this time, our state was still part of the Michigan territory. Settlers began calling for their own territory in the 1830s.

title: American Indian Reservations
text: Today, Wisconsin has 11 Federal American Indian Reservations. This map shows where the American Indian reservations are located and the major tribal offices. The major tribes or nations in Wisconsin include the Chippewa, Potawatomi, Ho-Chunk, Menominee, Oneida, and Munsee. The American Indians in our state have tried to help their children learn new things but not forget the old ways. If you have a chance to travel through a reservation area, be respectful. The people living there have a proud heritage that goes back thousands of years. You may one day enjoy asking an American Indian friend about his or her ancestors.

title: Log Cabins
text: When the settlers arrived in Wisconsin, they built homes called log cabins out of tree trunks. Cabins could be built by one person with a heavy ax and a hunting knife. Four walls made out of rough logs were laid horizontally and joined at the corners. The spaces between the logs were filled with mud and moss to protect against the wind. The roof was made out of flat pieces of wood. Usually, the cabin had only one door, hinged with wooden pegs. Windows were generally covered with greased paper, because no glass was available. The floor was made by beating down the dirt on which the cabin stood, or settlers made a floor out of the flat sides of halved logs. Log cabins were built as part of a community effort during social events. Many famous Americans were born in log cabins, such as Presidents William Henry Harrison, Abraham Lincoln, and Ulysses S. Grant.

title: Where do the states in our country gets their names?
text:
Half of the states in America take their names from American Indian words. Here are a few of them:

Arizona—From the Papago Tribe, "Arizona" means "little spring."

Connecticut—From the Mohegan Tribe, "Connecticut" means "long river."

Massachusetts—Means "big hill"

Michigan—From the Ottawa Tribe, this name means "big lake."

North and South Dakota—This Dakota Tribe word means "friendly ones."

Ohio—Means "beautiful river"

Wisconsin—An Algonquian river name meaning "gathering of the waters"

title: Black Hawk
text: Where do you think the American Indian warrior Black Hawk got his name? He was probably named after...you guessed it, a black hawk. Seventeen different kinds of hawks live in North America. These birds prey on mice, squirrels, and snakes for food. They have sharp eyesight and can see animals from a great distance. They pounce on their prey with lightning speed. They have sharp curved claws, powerful feet, and strong hooked beaks. Hawks swallow animals whole. Male and female hawks usually mate for life and keep the same nest year after year. Hawks are fairly silent birds and do not sing, but when they are upset or angry they utter piercing whistles, screams, and chattering calls.

title: How can I be an active reader?
text:
To get the most out of what you read, you should be an active reader.

Be Involved

When you are an active reader, you are involved because you think about and respond to what you read. Here are some strategies to use for becoming an active reader.

Ask Questions

Ask yourself questions as you read. What kinds of questions should you ask? Well, any question that comes to mind as you are reading is a good question. But some questions you could ask follow:

How do I feel about what I am reading?

Do the characters' actions make sense to me?

Do the characters remind me of any people I know?

Do I understand the events that are happening?

Could similar things happen to me?

What do I hope will happen next?

What would I most like to ask this author?

Read As a Group

Sometimes, you can get a better idea of what to think about a book after talking to someone else about it. Discussion about books can make your reading more interesting because different people have different ideas about the same text. Follow these steps and try forming some discussion groups in your class.

Assemble a small group of interested readers. Include enough people to make the discussion interesting, but not so many that the group is hard to manage.

Pick a book that you all want to read.

Allow time for everyone to read it.

Write down a list of questions and ideas before the meeting.

Meet to discuss your reactions to the book. Before beginning, pick someone to lead the discussion.

Connect With the Words

Make a connection with what you read, even if you are reading about someone very different from you. Try putting yourself in different characters' shoes so that you will understand why they act the way they do. You can also make a connection with what you read by forming opinions about it.

Respond to Your Text

Keep a response journal where you can write your feelings, ideas, questions, reactions, and thoughts about what you read. You can also note facts, copy quotations you liked, or talk about passages that you thought were well written.

Try these active reading strategies, and you will get the most out of what you read.

title: Weaving
text:
Materials

9-inch by 12-inch rectangle of thick cardboard

strips of cloth (quarter inch to half thick)

scissors

safety pin

Directions

1. Cut notches one-quarter inch apart into the nine-inch sides of the cardboard. Tie a strip of cloth to one corner of the cardboard, and then wrap it back and forth between the notches. Tie the other end of the strip at the corner of the rectangle diagonally across from the one you began with. You have now made your loom.

2. Attach another strip of cloth to the safety pin and close the pin. Begin weaving by threading the pin under the first strip at the top of your loom. Push the pin over the next strip, then under the one after it. Continue in this way, over and under, all the way across the loom.

3. When you reach the end of your loom, weave back the way you came, looping the cloth strips, as shown. This time, however, go under each strip you went over the first time, and go over each strip you went under.

4. Continue this for each row you want to weave, pulling the cloth strip over and under the loom. Make sure not to pull the strip too tight, or the edges of your final product will not be even.

5. Once you have woven a few rows, push the rows snugly together. If you come to the end of a strip of your weaving material and want to keep weaving, tie on a new strip with a strong double knot.

6. When you have finished weaving, be sure you are at the end of a row. Tie off each end of your cloth to the loom strip next to it, and lift both strip ends off the loom. To remove your work from the loom, bend down the tabs between the notches and slide the loom out. You can also break the loom by cutting it in half and removing the pieces.

title: Wisconsin Finally Becomes a Teritory!
text:
By the 1830s, settlers wanted to be in charge of the land they were farming, clearing, and developing. They were anxious for a territory of their own. They built cities, established small businesses and trades, and started families.

The requirements to become a territory included plenty of people. Wisconsin needed 12,000 people, a mark it finally reached in 1836. The Michigan territory was officially divided up to include a beautiful piece of land called the Wisconsin territory. From those early beginnings of only 12,000, our state has grown to almost 6 million people today.

Another requirement to become a territory was a designated capital city. Naturally, each settler wanted his or her town to be the chosen site. In the end, it was decided that Belmont would become the capital, but this choice didn't last long. Later that year, James Doty, who would serve as governor from 1841 to 1844, promised land to lawmakers if they would choose his city to become the permanent capital. At the close of 1836, Madison became Wisconsin's state capital.

The first governor of our territory was Henry Dodge. He served from 1836 to 1841. Dodge had been a pioneer soldier and a statesman for many years in the region, and many people liked him. However, leadership is hard to hang on to, and in 1841, James Doty replaced Dodge. But Dodge stayed busy as a delegate in Congress, and when he returned in 1845 he served another term as governor. Later, he became one of the first senators from Wisconsin to serve in the U.S. Senate.

A favorite settling place in Wisconsin was along the shores of Lake Michigan. Cities were soon established around major ports. As settlers poured into our territory, people began to wonder how the land should be divided up. Way back in 1785, a land ordinance guided the division of territories using an English grid system. Townships were formed by dividing the land into six square-mile areas. The towns were divided into 36 sections of one square mile each or 640 acres. The 16th section was set aside as a "school section." When the town was settled, the "school section" was sold to support the schools. In 1831, Lucius Lyon began mapping Wisconsin by marking a "point of beginning" on the Illinois border. He would inform settlers what land was for sale. This started the famous "land fever" in 1834-37, when more than 1 million acres were sold.

In 1841, Gov. James Doty looked for ways to make some money and help Wisconsin's economy. With the help of others, he convinced the settlers to build canals, railroads, toll roads, banks, and mining companies.

By 1848, the American Indians gave up the rest of their land. That same year, the long-awaited Canadian border was finally set. The citizen population was now booming and had increased tenfold since the establishment of Wisconsin Territory. The next important step was once a distant dream that had now neared reality - statehood!

title: Kindergarten Days
text:
Do you remember your first day at kindergarten? Were you excited or nervous? Could you already tie your shoes and write your name?

Kindergarten is important. It helps children do many things. They learn their letters and numbers. They learn to write their name and tell which crayon is blue and which one is green. And they learn to share and how to clean up a mess. Many children learn to read in kindergarten, too.

Have you ever wondered where the name kindergarten came from? The name came from Germany. In German, "kindergarten," means "children's garden." Although the name came from Germany, the very first kindergarten in the United States was held right here in Wisconsin. A woman named Margaret Schurz started it in Watertown, in 1856. She believed that young children needed an earlier start learning to read. The first kindergarten was for children from ages two to five.

In 1873, the public school in Manitowoc added kindergarten to the other classes that were taught. Now, almost every public elementary school in the United States has a kindergarten. In some states, children begin kindergarten at age four. In other states, they do not begin until they are five years old. In Wisconsin, some schools have the children begin at age four, and some wait until the children are five. Some schools have kindergarten for only half of the day. While there are many different types of kindergartens, all of them have one goal in mind: to help young children learn. Kindergarten is a great way for kids to learn and have fun at the same time.

title: Wisconsin Finally Becomes a Territory
text:
Let's take some time to look at what was happening in the country and world while Wisconsin was getting ready for statehood. Even though our territory was separated from many important and historical events, Wisconsin was really becoming a part of American history and didn't even know it!

The American Revolution

The War of Independence was fought in the east from 1775 to 1783. Wisconsin was passed from British hands to the American people when the war ended. A government was established according to the Constitution of the United States. In this form of government, the power would belong to the people instead of a king.

Britain signed the Treaty of Paris that ended the American Revolution. Under the treaty, Britain surrendered all the land east of the Mississippi River, a region called the Northwest Territory. It contained Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and the eastern part of Minnesota. However, many British remained in the area because the fur trade was a great business.

"Territory, Territory, Who Has My Territory?"

In 1800, the Wisconsin area became part of the Indiana Territory. In 1809, Wisconsin was traded to Illinois Territory.

In 1812, war again broke out between the United States and Britain. It was caused by disagreements over the rights of American shipping. During the War of 1812, most of Wisconsin's American Indians were on the British side. After the war, Americans began to settle in Wisconsin. The fur trade also came under American control at this time.

The Founders Create a Model Government Copied by All the States!

The Constitution of the United States is an important body of laws that run our federal government. It was ratified (accepted by the states) in 1787. The Constitution decides which powers belong to Congress, the president, and the courts. It is set up under a system called "checks and balances." That means that the three branches "check" on each other and "balance" the power so that no part of the government can take complete power from the others. The Constitution also spells out freedoms and liberties for U.S. citizens.

The Bill of Rights is a document containing the first 10 amendments, or corrections, to the Constitution of the United States. It was ratified in 1791. The Bill of Rights gives Americans liberties that the government cannot violate. Most states use the U.S. Constitution as a pattern for their own constitutions.

title: Belmont
text: Even though Belmont didn't remain the capital, it is a very important part of Wisconsin's heritage. The same buildings that lawmakers used 150 years ago still stand today. Although small and poorly insulated from the winter cold, these buildings were the site of a framework of law and order that would help Wisconsin become a state just 12 years later. To establish the laws necessary to become a state, the lawmakers met in these old buildings for 46 days and put 42 laws together. They organized a judicial system, called for roads and railroads, and most significantly established Madison as the permanent capital city. If you haven't visited this historic Belmont, then ask your parents to take you to the place where it all began.

title: Courage
text:
On Dec. 1, 1955, Rosa Parks had the courage to refuse to give up her seat to a white person on a crowded bus in Montgomery, Ala. She was arrested and tried. The result of the trial triggered a boycott (refusing to buy or use something), which was organized by Martin Luther King Jr. African Americans refused to ride the city bus until the laws were changed. It worked. Eventually, the laws were changed so that whites and blacks were allowed to sit together.

When Rosa died in October 2005, her casket was placed in the U.S. Capitol for two days so that people could pay their respects to her. Usually only the caskets of U.S. Presidents are placed in the Capitol. Rosa became the first woman to receive this honor.

The greatest kind of courage is to do what is right when others call you a coward or a chicken for doing it. It takes courage to stand up to people like that, but having courage will also help you be loyal, honest and responsible. Your parents, teachers, church leaders or good friends can help you prepare to deal with peer pressure and develop courage to face difficult situations.
