title: What did the state‛s capitol look like in the early days?
text: A settler traveling through Madison describes the state's capitol building in her journal: "Before leaving Madison, I must describe the capitol of Wisconsin, as I first saw it. It was a very small and squatty-looking house, having so much the appearance of an inverted wash bowl that it was called Doty's wash bowl. The dome of the present capitol covers the site of the old building. A common rail fence surrounded the grounds. The city in that early day was not crowded. The legislature was then the sole motive that brought people to Madison, and everyone was expected to entertain the members throughout the entire session."

title: The Many Trees of Wisconsin
text:
A long time ago, almost all of our state was covered in trees. The only real prairies or clearings were found in our southwest. Everywhere else, there were trees!

Wisconsin officials wanted to choose a state tree to honor Wisconsin's 100th birthday. They asked schoolchildren to vote on a tree. The students chose the sugar maple. In 1949, the Wisconsin government adopted the sugar maple as the state tree.

Sugar maples are medium-sized trees. A fully grown sugar maple can reach more than 100 feet tall. Sugar-maple leaves turn bright red in the autumn.

Wood from sugar maples is heavy and strong. Builders use the valuable wood for furniture, floors, and even wooden bowling pins. People harvest sap from sugar maples. The sap is boiled to make sweet maple syrup. Sugar maples make Wisconsin a beautiful place to live.

title: How can I be a critical reader?
text:
Critical readers carefully examine what they read so that they can make informed decisions about it. They might decide if they should believe what they read or if they like what they read.

Examine What You Read

There are many ways to be a critical reader, but they all involve looking at the text and thinking about what you read. Here are some strategies for being a critical reader.

Learn to Separate Fact from Opinion

Writers sometimes present their opinions as facts, so it is important to be able to tell the difference between facts and opinions. How do you tell a fact from an opinion? A fact is a statement that can be proven true. An opinion cannot be proven true in a way that everyone will agree on because it is a belief or judgment. Here are some questions you can ask to help you figure out if something is fact or opinion:

Can this be proven?

Is it generally agreed upon?

Could someone disagree with this?

Is this supported by facts or opinions?

Watch for Faulty Logic

Make sure the writer's logic makes sense. Do the writer's arguments make sense? Are they supported by evidence? Here is some faulty logic to watch out for:

Either/Or Thinking - When a writer says that there are only two ways to think about a situation, he or she may be engaging in faulty logic. You need to think, "Are there more ways to think about this?" What is faulty about this statement: "No one should drive, or we will have too much pollution."

Faulty Cause and Effect - When a writer claims that one event leads to another, but doesn't show any clear connection between the two, then you are reading faulty cause and effect. What is faulty about this statement: "He passed the test because he ate beans."

Overgeneralization - When the writer makes a statement that goes beyond what the evidence supports, he or she may be engaging in overgeneralization. Use of too many generalizing words such as "all," "always," "must," "never," and "none" could be a sign of overgeneralization. What is faulty about this statement: "My cat likes water, so all cats like water."

Identify the Writer's Point of View

The point of view is the set of personal opinions that influence the way the author writes about a subject. You need to be able to recognize the writer's point of view to figure out how it might have affected the writing.

Take note of sources. Are all the sources from one side of the issue, or are they balanced over many sides of the issue?

Ask what the writer is trying to say. How is this point of view supported? Do you agree with it? Why or why not?

Critical reading can be tough, but if you practice these strategies, you'll be on your way!

title: Language Arts Connection
text: Use any color to highlight three relative adverbs (where, when, why) in this week’s magazine. Underline the clause that contains the relative adverb and circle the noun that the clause modifies. (CC ELA L.4.1)

title: Accordion Book
text:
Materials

12-inch by 36-inch butcher paper

two pieces of cardboard or tag board

colored paper for covers

scissors

writing paper

glue

crayons

markers

Directions

1. Fold butcher paper in half lengthwise for strength. For a longer book, use a longer piece of butcher paper.

2. Fold the butcher paper accordion-style in two equal parts. The size of the resulting sections will determine what size of cardboard and writing paper you will use.

3. To make the book sturdy, glue a piece of cardboard or tag board inside each section.

4. To make a front cover, appropriately illustrate the front section or glue on a cover made from colored paper. Leave the last section as is or glue on a back cover. Now write out the information for the book and put it on the inside pages.

title: Immigrants Help Build a State
text:
Between the 1820s and 1920s, Wisconsin was buzzing with immigrants from foreign lands. Immigrants are people who leave their homelands to settle in new countries. Many came to farm the new land; others wanted to make money. Eastern cities overflowed with people who were looking for more space. The completion of the Erie Canal and the invention of steamboats allowed more settlers to move here. The construction of the National Road allowed a passageway into the beautiful West. Those who came from the South traveled up the Mississippi and usually stayed to mine lead in southwestern Wisconsin.

Yankees were the richest and most determined of the migrating groups to move to Wisconsin. These people came from New England and Great Britain. Many of Wisconsin's first politicians, doctors, and lawyers were Yankees. They made a living by purchasing the land and selling it to other immigrants.

By the 1840s, immigrants from other parts of Great Britain began to arrive. The Irish came here because a terrible potato famine was spreading across their country. The Scottish and Welsh came as missionaries to teach their Protestant faiths and begin farming communities. Many Scottish immigrants moved to Wisconsin from New York state.

Scandinavian immigrants began arriving in the 1830s. Scandinavia includes Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Iceland, and Finland. When the Norwegian people came to Wisconsin, they settled only with friends they had known from Norway. Because of this, the Norwegian people were able to hold onto their culture and traditions longer than any other group. By the time the Swedes arrived, most of the best agricultural land had already been settled. The Swedes changed course and moved to the northwest. They worked hard to build bridges, roads, ports, and mills. The Finns also arrived late and settled alongside the Swedes. The Icelanders and Danes settled mainly on Washington Island and became fishers, lumberjacks, and farmers.

German immigrants arrived in the 1840s. They liked Wisconsin because the weather and soil were similar to that in their homeland. Many came with money to establish homes, farms, and new businesses. When other groups decided to move farther west, the Germans stayed and formed the largest ethnic group in the state today. They played a major role in the switch from wheat to dairy and agriculture in the state.

The Poles didn't arrive until the 1870s. They founded their own newspapers, social clubs, and churches. Today, the Poles are the second largest ethnic group. Italians arrived in the 1890s mainly to work in the industries, mining, or lumbering jobs. Some worked only a few years before returning to Italy.

The first African Americans came during the fur-trade era of the 1700s. By the time of the 1820s lead rush, southern U.S. Army officers and lead miners brought in African American slaves. After Wisconsin became a territory in 1836, Gov. Henry Dodge freed the slaves and gave them land. In the 1850s, Wisconsin became known for opposing slavery.

By the 1900s, the population boom began to plateau, and settlers worked on establishing cities, governments, and family roots in this beautiful new state.

title: Can Facebook Save Dying Languages?
text:
Can you say a few words in Siletz Dee-ni? No? How about saying "hello" in Aka? If you can't, you're not alone! These two languages and 3,500 more could become extinct by the end of this century. Almost 80 percent of the world's population now speaks only one percent of the world's 7,000 languages. This has happened because of globalization. Globalization means that countries are more connected through trade, money and workers. When countries work together, people must be able to communicate with each other. That means many people have to learn another language. English is the main language used throughout the world for business and the Internet.

Why is this a problem? When the last person who is able to speak a particular language dies, some of the knowledge that is found within that language dies with them. A language contains the history of its people, how they used their environment and their beliefs and ideas. Technology may just save many of these languages from extinction! With YouTube, Facebook and other forms of social media, languages that are spoken by even 5 or ten people can be taught to others around the world.

National Geographic has been working on the Enduring Voices Project. Its goals are to record native speakers of endangered languages into talking dictionaries and help communities learn ways to save their languages from extinction. What language do you want to help save?

title: Wisconsin’s Heritage
text:
A wonderful part of Wisconsin's heritage are the histories, stories, struggles, and sacrifices of millions of immigrants who have built our wonderful state since the beginning. What ancestry can you claim in your lineage?

French

The French arrived in Wisconsin in the early 1600s and 1700s. They came to explore the land and make money from fur-trading. The French established many trading posts, ports, towns, and counties that today still carry French names, such as Fond du Lac and Marquette Counties.

African Americans

African Americans could be found in Wisconsin as early as the 1700s' fur-trading era. They were here in the 1820s as slaves, and more poured in after the abolition of slavery. For many African Americans, Wisconsin was a place of freedom and the first state to defy the fugitive law that was passed to punish escaping slaves. African Americans worked hard as farm laborers, and education was a priority.

Yankees

The Yankees migrated from the New England states and the British Isles in 1830. They were interested in buying and selling beautiful Wisconsin land. Yankees shaped the state's culture and landscape and founded Milwaukee, Green Bay, and Madison cities.

Swedes

A group of 12 families started a Swedish colony in 1841. The first wave came mainly to start a new life in America, not really sure what they would end up doing. Later, immigrants came for opportunities to buy land. The Swedes worked hard to build bridges, railroads, ports, and mills, primarily in northwestern Wisconsin.

Finnish

The Finns did not arrive until the 1880s. They came looking for land and settled next to the Swedes in northwestern Wisconsin. Finnish-style homes, barns, and saunas can still be found today. The Finnish enjoy potato soup, fish pie, and rye bread.

Irish

The Irish first arrived in 1840. A potato famine in Ireland forced many to immigrate. The Irish were hard workers. They farmed, built canals and railroads, and even formed Irish militias and regiments in the Civil War.

Germans

Germans began arriving around 1840. Their homeland was crowded, and many left because they couldn't get good jobs. Germans were among the first and the largest ethnic group to migrate to Wisconsin. They are known for their love of music, food, and the celebration of Oktoberfest.

Italians

The Italians arrived in the 1890s. They left their homeland due to poor growing conditions in their country. The Italians worked hard in the growing industries and gained a reputation for their wonderful cheeses.

Polish

The Polish people arrived in Milwaukee in the 1870s. They were very proud of their religious background and came in search of freedom. The Poles enjoy sausage, pork, and cabbage. They also introduced everyone else to the polka, their favorite dance.

Belgians

The Belgians and Dutch people settled in the 1850s. They came for better jobs and rich soil to farm, as well as to escape high taxes. They built many Catholic and Protestant churches. These people helped to established Sturgeon Bay, a location where ships of the Great Lakes are constructed.

Swiss

The Swiss established settlements in 1844. They came because of hardships and crowding in their homeland. Today, the Swiss are well known for their cheese and annual Heidi Festival.

title: Sturgeon Bay
text: Sturgeon Bay was settled as a lumbering community in the 1850s and was named after the sturgeon that could be found in the nearby lakes. It was known for its shipbuilding and cherry factories. Today, there are many businesses that run the best-equipped and staffed shipyards on the Great Lakes. It is home to the leading builders of self-unloading bulk carriers, double-hull tank barges, petroleum carriers, dredgers, and container ships. Sturgeon Bay is known as the "Shipbuilding Capital" of the Great Lakes.

title: A Few Wisconsin Immigrants
text:
Margaretha Meyer Schurz - (1832-1876) Born in Germany, Margaretha came to America in 1852. In 1856, she opened one of the first kindergartens in the United States at Watertown. She was also the wife of Carl Schurz, who was elected to Congress.

John Muir - (1838-1914) Born in Dunbar, Scotland, John immigrated with his family to Wisconsin in 1849. He was a talented writer and wrote about our rich scenic landscapes. Muir was perhaps this country's most famous and influential naturalist and conservationist. He helped create Yosemite National Park and was involved in the creation of the national parks at Sequoia, Mount Rainier, Petrified Forest, and the Grand Canyon.

Harry Houdini - (1874-1926) Houdini was the son of a rabbi who immigrated from Hungary to the United States and settled in Appleton, Wisconsin. He became a trapeze performer in circuses and in 1900 earned an international reputation for his daring feats and magical tricks. Houdini is remembered as one of the world's greatest magicians.

Golda Meir - (1898-1978) Though born in Kiev, Russia, she moved to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, with her family in 1906. In 1915, she joined the Labor Zionist Party and then moved to Tel Aviv shortly after. In 1969, Golda Meir was nominated by the Labor Party to be the prime minister of Israel. Many remember her as a compassionate and great leader.

title: What Wisconsin River Flows North?
text: No, this isn't a trick question! Nearly all rivers flow south, but a few flow north, and one of them is in Wisconsin. The Fox River has the unique reputation of having a northerly flow, but not completely. It moves around in all sorts of directions. It travels southwest before turning north to Lake Winnebago and out the north end of that lake on to Green Bay. It is a popular myth that all rivers flow south, and when you look at most of the world's rivers, that is true. But in a few places, rivers do flow north—the great Nile is one of the major rivers that doesn't flow south, and we claim the Fox River as being a northerner, too!

title: Where Are They Today?
text:
Most of Wisconsin's counties are home to one or more ethnic groups that boast a proud and early history in our state. Here is a list of the counties and areas where certain ethnic and national groups are concentrated. In the list, circle with red the county where you live, and circle your own family's national origins. Circle with blue the counties you have visited or driven through. Do these many nationalities live only in these counties, or are they now spread across our state?

French - Green Bay area, Fox River Valley

Yankees - Southwestern portion of the state, where lead was discovered

German - Milwaukee, Sheboygan, Sauk, Washington, and Ozaukee

Norwegian - Dunn, Barron, LaFayette, Vernon, Jackson, LaCrosse, Eau Claire, and Trempealeau

Swedish - Ashland, Burnett, Clark, Douglas, Polk, Price, and Oneida Counties

Swiss - New Glarus and nearby Monroe

Polish - Beaver Dam, Stevens Point, Pulaski, and Berlin, Trempealeau, Milwaukee, Arcadia, and Independence

Irish - Prairie du Chien, Patch Grove, and Bloomington

Black Americans - Pleasant Ridge, Milwaukee, Beloit

Finnish - Northern, Lake Superior region

Italian - Genoa, Campbellsport, Fond du Lac, and Plymouth

Belgium - Ootsburg, Cedar Grove, New Amsterdam, Union, and Brussels, Sturgeon Bay

title: Vitus Bering and Russian Colonies in Alaska
text:
Imagine traveling 6,000 miles over land with supplies for an expedition, and THEN sailing through frigid seas to look for a new world. This was the job given to Vitus Bering, a Danish navigator who sailed for the Russian navy. Peter the Great, czar (ruler) of Russia, asked Bering to explore the eastern coast of Russia. He was wondering if land connected Asia and North America.

Bering's first trip began in 1725. After spending three years getting his supplies to eastern Russia, Bering sailed along the coastline. He didn't see any land to the east, and he didn't realize he was sailing in the narrow passage between Russia and Alaska. This waterway is now called the Bering Strait.

Bering led another expedition in 1741. This time his ship landed on Kayak Island, off the coast of Alaska. They explored some of the Aleutian Islands and met the native people there, the Aleut. He was the first European to arrive in present-day Alaska.

Bering died before returning to Russia, but his voyages paved the way for Russian settlements in North America. Many fur traders came to the area. In 1799 the Russian government established a fur-trading operation in Alaska. Furs from foxes, sea otters and seals were very valuable.

Unfortunately, the Russians took advantage of the native people just as some Europeans had done in settling New England. The Russians took over their lands and forced them to hunt for furs. They also brought new diseases, which killed many natives.

Today, the Aleut people continue to live along the western coast of North America, and their population has grown. What might have been different if the Russians and the Aleut had shared public space fairly? Where in your community is there a debate over public land? How should such debates be handled?

title: How do I use a thesaurus?
text:
Do you use many of the same words when writing? Are you getting bored with those words? Do you wish you could think of a different word for "growth" so that you didn't use it so much in your writing? Well, look in the thesaurus.

Search for Synonyms

What is a thesaurus? Is it a kind of dinosaur? The word "thesaurus" almost looks like the name for some kind of dinosaur, doesn't it? But actually, a thesaurus is a book that provides synonyms (words that mean almost the same thing) for common words. Using a thesaurus is a great way to broaden your vocabulary with more interesting words.

A thesaurus is usually organized alphabetically. Some thesauri are similar to dictionaries because they give you the part of speech, definition and a sample sentence for a word. Sometimes, a thesaurus will give you directions to look under other entries. If you look up the word "growth," the thesaurus might say, "See change." This means that you need to look up the word "change" to get synonyms for "growth." Here is a description of the contents of a thesaurus.

Entry Word - The word you look up to find synonyms

Part-of-Speech Label - Tells you if the word is a noun, verb, adjective, etc.

Definition - Tells you what the entry word means

Example Sentence - Shows you how the entry word might be used in a sentence.

Synonyms - Words whose meanings are the same as or similar to the entry word

Antonyms - Words whose meanings are the opposite of the entry word

Try It!

Look up the word "grow" in a thesaurus. Write some of the synonyms here.

Look up each synonym for "grow" in the dictionary. Are the definitions for these words exactly the same as the definition for "grow"? How are they different? Use the lines below to write some of the definitions and discuss how they are different.

title: Statehood at Last!
text:
When Wisconsin was first made a territory in 1836, three of the borders were formed by bodies of water. Lake Michigan made up the eastern border, Lake Superior the northern border, and the Mississippi River the western. Officials negotiated to establish the Illinois border on the south.

To be made a state, Wisconsin needed a population of 60,000, a constitution, and permission from Congress.

Henry Dodge, who served as the territorial governor, had been pushing for statehood during his first term, 1836-1841. From 1841 to 1844, James Doty took the governor's seat and was also unsuccessful in obtaining statehood. Proposals continued to be defeated in 1840, 1841, and again in 1843. For the most part, people were afraid that there would be higher taxes under a state government. Dodge was once again elected governor in 1845. Finally, support for statehood grew when people heard that they could select the state officers, receive 500,000 acres of public lands for public schools and universities, and keep 5 percent of the net proceeds from the sales of all federal lands within its borders. The promises and rewards were enough to convince Wisconsin citizens. In April 1846, the people approved the move for statehood. By the time Wisconsin became a state, there were more than 155,000 people within its borders.

That same year, Wisconsin went about setting up a state government. Officials met together to write the state constitution, but some disagreements broke out over some of the laws. The first constitution was abandoned, and a second constitution was approved in December of 1847. Wisconsin was ready to become a state.

The formal congressional bill was passed and presented to U.S. Pres. Polk for his signature. Wisconsin finally became a state on May 29, 1848. The proclamation read, "That the state of Wisconsin be, and is hereby, admitted to be one of the United States of America, and is hereby admitted into the union on an equal footing with the original states in all respects whatever...." The beautiful state of Wisconsin was finally admitted, and the 30th star was added to the flag of the United States of America.

title: Cursive or Print
text:
Back in the 1800s when Wisconsin was made a state, school children spent a lot of time learning penmanship. Cursive writing was taught to all students and they often spent hours practicing until their handwriting was beautiful and easy to read.

Do you know how to write in cursive? Do you enjoy doing it? Most children still learn cursive in the third grade, but many teachers are spending less time on teaching this writing skill. As computers, palm pilots, and even cell phones take over, people spend more time typing on a keyboard or texting on a keypad than they do writing with an actual pen or pencil. This has led some teachers to believe that teaching cursive writing is a waste of time. There are other teachers, however, who believe that it is still important for their students to learn to make the loops and curlicues that form good cursive writing. Mary Bostrom, a second/third-grade teacher at John Muir Elementary in Madison, says that it is important for children to learn cursive because it is faster and easier to take notes using cursive. Some of her students agree and love writing in cursive rather than print. "I love writing in cursive because it's a lot faster than printing," said Andrea, one of Bostrom's students. "It almost feels like your pencil is floating along the pages."

Not all of Bostrom's students agree, however. Jacob says, "I don't like cursive because it is hard to read. All the loops make it weird. You get all the letters mixed up."

Many teachers find that they have a harder time reading their students' homework when it is written in cursive. Others believe that more time should be spent on teaching the students good keyboarding skills so that they can type most of their work. By the time students get to high school, teachers often require that their papers be typed on a computer.

Do you enjoy writing in cursive, or do you prefer to print? Whatever your opinion, the argument over whether or not to spend time teaching cursive in the schools is sure to continue for years to come.

title: Wisconsin State Facts and Trivia
text:
When Wisconsin became a state, people had no idea how populous and rich our state would become. After a while, people began to choose official state symbols, things for which our state was becoming famous. This week, let's learn what those symbols are.

State Nickname:

"The Badger State" - This nickname came from the early lead miners who lived in mines and dugout holes in Wisconsin's hills, similar to the burrowing of badgers.

State Bird:

School children chose the American robin as the state's bird in 1927. The choice was made official in 1949. Robins make Wisconsin their home in the summer months.

State Motto:

"Forward" - This motto means that the people of Wisconsin work for progress and change.

Origin of the State's Name:

Some people believe that the origin of the state's name came from a Native American, or Miami word ("Meskousing," "Miskonsing," or "Mescousin"), which means "river running" or "river running through a red place."

State Flag:

The flag is blue with the state's seal in the center. Several images on the seal represent important things. The badger is the state animal. A sailor represents those who work on the rivers and lakes. A miner stands for the mining business. Lead bars and fruit represent Wisconsin's natural resources.

State Flower:

An election of sorts to decide on a state flower was held on Arbor Day in 1909, making the wood violet our state flower. It was made official in 1949. The native flower is purple and grows in dark, shady places.

State Tree:

Government officials asked school children to vote on a state tree to honor Wisconsin's 100th birthday in 1949. The school children voted on the sugar maple.

State Animal:

The official state animal is the badger. It's used because it reminds us of Wisconsin's early lead miners.

State Dance:

The polka became the state dance in 1993.

State Beverage:

Milk became the official state beverage in 1986.

State Grain:

Corn was made the official state grain in 1991. Wisconsin grows more corn than any other state.

State Domestic Animal:

The dairy cow was chosen in 1971 because of Wisconsin's thousands of dairy farms and cheese factories.

Capital:

Madison - The capitol building sits on a hill that overlooks the city. It is built of granite and marble. Wisconsin has had three capitol buildings since 1838. The current building was finished in 1917.

Population:

More than 5,600,000 people live in Wisconsin.

Area:

Wisconsin is the 23rd largest state, covering 65,499 square miles.

Became a State:

Wisconsin became the 30th state on May 29, 1848.

title: Madison
text:
Madison is the capital of Wisconsin and the seat of Dane County. It is in the south-central part of the state, between lakes Mendota and Monona. Madison was founded by James Duane Doty in 1836 and was named for President James Madison. Industries appeared about 1850. The railroad arrived in 1854. The University of Wisconsin-Madison (1849) was established in this city and helped it to grow. Today, the city is booming with professionals, managers, and technical workers. Madison has more than 200 scenic parks, golf courses, play areas, and hiking trails. The city is filled with historic landmarks and buildings where our first pioneers organized to establish this great state.

Madison offers free outdoor concerts, the Farmers Market, art fairs, and parades. Ask your family to take a trip to Madison, where the dome of the capitol is one of the highest points in the city.

title: Birth of the Republican Party
text: Have you ever heard your parents speak about politics and mention Republicans, Democrats, Independents, and such? When people have certain views on governmental issues, they declare themselves as members of one of these political parties. Our political leaders who form the United States government usually take a stand primarily as Republicans or Democrats. Now that you know this, did you know that many believe that the birth of the Republican Party began right here in Wisconsin!? You can even visit the old schoolhouse where it all began in Ripon, Wisconsin, in 1854.

title: What is Wisconsin‛s most recognized symbol?
text: That's a tough question! Most people around the world recognize Wisconsin as America's dairy land. During football season, we're known as home to the Green Bay Packers. Some still refer to us as the "Badger State." And don't forget about our giant paper industry. Our state's location among the Great Lakes is another world-famous symbol that is instantly easy to recognize on the map. What is your vote for our most recognized symbol? Send your vote to symbol@historypaper.com.

title: American Robin
text:
The American robin has an orange or dull-reddish breast. The robin is one of the most well-known songbirds, especially in the eastern United States - although they are just about everywhere! Early settlers to America named it "robin" after a small European bird of the same name.

The robin loves to eat worms, insects, and berries. Perhaps you have seen a robin hunting for worms right after the sprinklers have forced the worms to the surface of your lawn. These birds make their nests with twigs, roots, paper, and mud. They lay four to six bluish-green eggs that take 12-14 days to hatch. The female keeps the eggs warm and safe while the male brings food. The birds may have two to three batches of eggs in a season.

The robin likes warmth in the winter and usually flies south. However, it can be found in cold places sometimes. If you see robins nearby, put out a little birdseed (away from where the cats can pounce) and help the birds raise a family in your yard. It's an amazing, wonderful thing to watch.

title: Lumberjacks, Lumber & Log Wars
text:
Do you know who the lumberjacks were? They were big, brawny, rugged men with red woolen shirts and pants cut off at the knee. These men cut down trees and sent them floating down rivers to lumbermills. They spent Saturday nights in rough lumber towns fighting, singing and story-telling. For fun, they would play a game called logrolling or "birling." Many of the early lumberjacks were Swedes, Norwegians, Irishmen and Germans. The lumberjacks helped create one of Wisconsin's most important industries, the paper-products industry.

In the 1800s, the northern half of the state was covered in conifer and pine, while the southern half was covered with oak. Early settlers depended on wood to build homes, carriages, furniture and railroad ties. Wood was also used to fuel fire and make paper.

Many settlers made a business out of chopping down trees and selling the wood. This was called commercial lumbering. In Wisconsin, commercial lumbering began in the 1830s and 1840s with the appearance of sawmills in the south. The industry grew fast between the 1850s and 1890s. As the supply of timber thinned out in the south, settlers found the best forestry in the northern part of the state.

Lucky for the lumberjacks, Wisconsin had many rivers that flowed south from the woods to the prairies where the wood was sold. The St. Croix, Chippewa, Black, Wisconsin, Wolf, and Menominee rivers provided transportation for the logs to mills and markets and provided power for the mills. Sometimes, lumberjacks fought over the rivers and timber. One famous conflict was called the "Beef Slough War." The Beef Slough was the name of a storage pond for logs. The Beef Slough company contracted to deliver 60 million feet of logs to the Mississippi in the spring of 1868. However, there was only one way they could get so many logs-by stealing them! A log-driving team of 75 of the toughest men were sent to bring logs down the Chippewa. They started cutting all the mill booms, opening the storage ponds and sending stolen logs down the Mississippi. The mill owners were furious, and the Beef Slough drivers were met by 200 rugged mill owners and the sheriff. The Beef Slough men were arrested for stealing. After a truce was arranged, they were released. Eventually the companies agreed upon a way to divide up the large amounts of lumber that floated down the river.

The introduction of trains and railroads helped logging to continue year round. Before the train, lumberjacks didn't work summers because there was not enough water in the rivers to transport logs. Trains helped move lumber that was too heavy to float in water, and they could transport lumber out of deep forests.

Lumbering peaked in the year 1892 at more than 4 billion board feet. Between 1899 and 1905, Wisconsin led the nation in lumber production. By 1900, Wisconsin had more than 250 furniture factories. The cities of the Fox and Wisconsin River valleys became major paper-manufacturing centers and remain so today.

Over-cutting, wasteful timber practices, and damaging fires caused the industry to slow down. Wisconsin has rules and laws for the lumber industry. Today, Wisconsin continues to be a leader in pulp and paper production.

title: Paper Products
text:
The papermaking process hasn't changed at least fundamentally since its discovery. But with almost two centuries of improvements and refinements, modern papermaking is a fascinating, high-tech industry today.

To tour the papermaking process, start with No. 1, and keep going until you've seen each section of the process!

1. Forestry

Typically, trees used for papermaking are specifically grown and harvested like a crop for that purpose. To meet tomorrow's demand, forest-products companies and private landowners in Wisconsin plant millions of new seedlings every year.

2. Debarking, Chipping and Recycling

To begin the process, logs are passed through a debarker, where the bark is removed, and through chippers, where spinning blades cut the wood into one-inch pieces. Those wood chips are then pressure-cooked with a mixture of water and chemicals in a digester.

3. Pulp Preparation

The pulp is washed, refined, cleaned and sometimes bleached, then turned to slush in the beater. Color dyes, coating and other additives are mixed in here, and the pulp slush is pumped into a moving wire screen.

4. Paper Formation

As the pulp travels down the screen, water is drained away and reused. The resulting crude paper sheet is squeezed between large rollers to remove most of the remaining water and ensure smoothness and uniform thickness. The semidry sheet is then run through heated dryer rollers to remove the remaining water.

Waste water is carefully cleaned and purified before its release or reuse. Fibers and chemicals are filtered out and burned to provide additional power for the paper mill.

Papermakers carefully test for things such as uniformity, color, surface, water resistance and ink-holding ability.

5. Paper Finishing

The finished paper is then wound into large rolls, which can be 30 feet wide and weigh close to 25 tons. A slitter cuts the paper into smaller, more manageable rolls, and the paper is ready for use.

Papermaking is one of the most capital-intensive industries in the nation, investing more than $100,000 in equipment for each employee. The largest papermaking machines are more than 32 feet wide and 500 feet long and can produce more than 1,000 miles of paper a day!

Highlights in the History of the Paper-Products Industry

The first paper created in Wisconsin was produced in Milwaukee and was used to publish a newspaper, The Milwaukee Sentinel & Gazette, on March 7, 1848. Three months later, Wisconsin became the 30th state.

The paper was made from rags at a mill near the Milwaukee and Menominee rivers. This small business produced 90 reams a week and was "enough to supply the entire press of the state."

Mills need a lot of fresh water to make paper. People built their mills and factories close to rivers such as the Wisconsin, Eau Claire and Peshtigo.

In 1872, the Keller groundwood process was introduced to the Fox River Valley. This was a process used to make paper from wood pulp. Suddenly, everyone was interested in becoming paper manufacturers using the revolutionary process.

In fewer than 80 years after commercial lumbering started, it began to decline. A big reason for this decline was that about 40 percent of Wisconsin's forest resources never arrived at the sawmills. It was lost because of fire or waste. In 1903 the state created the Forestry Commission. The legislature made new laws about cutting trees. These groups worked to help stop waste and preserve Wisconsin's resources.

Wisconsin's paper industry has seen many changes over the past 150 years and has grown into a huge industry, producing millions of tons of quality paper products and employing thousands of people.

Today, Wisconsin is the nation's No. 1 paper-manufacturing state, and papermaking is one of the most important parts of our state's economy.

title: Is Green Bay the “TP” Capital of the World?
text:
Green Bay is home to a Proctor and Gamble company that makes tissue products. Do you recognize the names Charmin, Bounty, Puffs, Bounce and Downy? These companies produce fabric conditioner, tissues, paper towels and toilet paper. Many even call Green Bay the Toilet Paper Capital of the World! Would you like to know the history of toilet paper?

We are not really sure when toilet paper was invented, but the first reference of a paper product used for this purpose was recorded in China.

In the late 1700s, women discreetly hid a small portion of tissue in a fan and called it "Madame's Double-Utility Fan."

The first recorded use of a roll of bath tissue versus sheets was in 1882 in New York State.

In the latter part of the 19th century, some bath tissue was manufactured and dispensed from a cabinet that contained a built-in knife or razor for cutting the desired amount of paper.

Today, the average person uses 20,805 sheets of bath tissue annually.

title: What kind of creature is attracted to forest fires?
text: Most animals panic and run away from forest fires. But one kind of beetle deliberately flies toward them. This beetle is called melanophila. Its name means "lover of blackness" because it likes charred wood. These beetles lay their eggs on burnt wood. They can detect fires from as far away as 12 miles by using special sensory organs on their midsection. Melanophila are the only living organisms known to seek out fire.

title: Logjams
text: Shipping logs down river was not an easy task. Many lumberjacks had jagged scars and bulging muscles as proof of their hard and dangerous job of log driving. Once in a while, "log traffic" became too crowded on the river, and it all piled up without moving, a problem they called a logjam. An 1869 logjam on the Chippewa River contained 150 million board feet of timber. It was backed up nearly 15 miles, and in some places, the logs were piled up 30 feet above the level of the river!

title: Paper Birch
text:
One of the most common and easy-to-recognize trees in the state of Wisconsin is the Betula papyrifera, better known as paper birch. It has a white, papery bark, which makes it easy to recognize. Dark brown "eyes" or branch scars are scattered on the trunk. In the winter, dangling flower clusters are seen on the tree. Paper birch grows rather quickly in the bare soil, but the tree doesn't live very long and is weak. This tree reaches 50-70 feet tall. It has oval leaves with jagged edges.

A variety of wildlife can be found in an aspen-birch or maplebeech-birch forest. Salamanders and small mammals are often found under fallen leaves, while hairy woodpeckers can be spotted perched on the side of the bark pecking for bugs.

These trees were used by American Indians to build canoes, wigwams, baskets, cups, bags and other useful items. Today, they are used to make decorative items, toothpicks, toys, flooring, firewood, interior finishing, and paper pulp.

title: How do I read non-fiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring. But it really isn't. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you will find it easier to understand - and maybe even fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/effect, (4) classification,(5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will talk about the problem and solution.

Problem/Solution

With this information pattern, the writer begins by stating a problem. Then the writer presents various solutions or ideas for solving the problem. This pattern is common in newspaper articles, as well as science and social studies texts.

One strategy for finding the problem and solution of a nonfiction passage is to create a cluster map. A cluster map will help you remember what you have read. Begin by writing the subject of the passage in the middle of a blank sheet of paper. On one side of the subject, write "problems." On the other side, write "solutions." Then write details you want to remember that illustrate the problems and solutions around these bubbles. Remember to draw lines connecting the problems to the word "problems" and connecting solutions to the word "solutions." This way, you show the connections between the information.

Try It!

To the right is a passage about transportation. Read the passage. Then create a cluster map showing the problems and solutions discussed in the passage.

Transportation was a major problem facing early settlers. Transportation in settled areas was largely confined to river bottoms. Although steamboats were common on the lower stretches of a number of rivers, some rivers were not deep enough for year-round transportation. Roads were poor, and people could not use them during wet weather. Ox carts could only travel a few miles a day and the cost of a wagon was 20 cents per mile.

People came up with many ideas to improve internal transportation, including river improvements, canals, and plank roads in addition to railroads. However, it was the railroads that made the development of the area possible, for many years, railroad growth and economic growth paralleled each other.

title: Fake or Real News?
text:
Have you ever read something online, like on social media sites, that sounded fishy? Maybe it was real, but it could be fake news! The big danger, though, is news that sounds real but isn’t. Fake news is becoming common because anyone can post things online. Fake news can be in the form of a story. Fake news can be a photo or video that has been changed. The problem is that these fake items look real. Fake news can cause problems and it spreads misinformation.

Sam Wineburg, a professor, did some research. He found that 80 percent of students cannot tell the difference between real and fake news. Do you want to become a media-savvy person? You have to be able to find out if news is real or fake. How do you do that? You have to become a detective and search for the truth. You can learn about the author or company that posted the news. You have to think about the purpose of the news. Is there a hidden plan to get you to buy something or to make you think a certain way? Your teacher or a trusted adult can help you learn how to spot fake news. It takes a little time, but democracy depends on real information! Do your part and discover what is real and what is fake!

title: Wisconsin’s Farmers Raise the Most of the Best!
text:
After early lumberjacks chopped and cleared out most of Wisconsin's timber, farmers were able to plow the soil and plant wheat. The first American farms were established in the 1830s, but long before that period, American Indians had been cultivating corn, squash, and beans.

By the 1840s, Wisconsin's best farming land had been plotted, surveyed and quickly bought up. Settlers built homes and fences, planted gardens, and grew wheat as their first cash crop. They also grew corn, hay and tobacco. The first farms were small, between 40 and 100 acres, and the soil was difficult to plow.

Wheat was an excellent crop because it required little attention after it was planted. Wisconsin became an important wheat-producing state because of all the settlers who came here, the excellent land, use of harvesting machines and demand for wheat during the Civil War.

Farm communities were close knit because the people lived near most of their relatives and relied upon each other for services and goods.

By 1850, there were more than 300,000 people living in Wisconsin. The demand for wheat and farm products was growing, and transporting farm goods became a problem. Even though ships were traveling the Mississippi River and Great Lakes, farmers were having a hard time getting crops from farms to ports. The problem was solved when the railroad came, and Wisconsin's wheat output ranked second in the nation.

Wheat production declined in the 1870s because the soil became exhausted. (Soil exhaustion is when the soil's nutrients are depleted because crops are planted in the soil year after year.) And then the terrible chinch bug invaded. The chinch bug drilled into the stalks of wheat to suck the juice, thereby destroying the crops of wheat. Farmers started looking for new crops. They tried hops and flax, but gave up in the 1860s. Other crops they tried included tobacco, sugar beets, sorghum, and cranberries. These crops caught on and today remain an important part of Wisconsin farms.

On some farms, farmers specialized in smaller crops that grew naturally in their areas. These "specialty crops" brought in needed income and included mint, hemp and honey production, maple syrup, berry-picking and wild-rice harvesting.

By the 1870s, farmers started growing barley, rye, soybeans, and buckwheat. Gardens and orchards on family farms began producing vegetables and fruit as cash crops in the late 1800s. Corn, oats and hay are still major crops today.

Before the Civil War ended, farming was changing. William Hoard, a newspaper editor, convinced farmers to switch to dairy products. It wasn't long after that when Wisconsin gained its great reputation as "America's Dairy Land."

text:

title: Wheat in Wisconsin
text:
When wheat was introduced in Wisconsin, farmers had very few tools. Harvesting was a long and difficult job. When new machines came along, farmers were happy to purchase these new inventions that would ease the task.

Reaper

Many Wisconsinites used the reaper built by George Esterly of New York in 1844. Two horses pulled the reaper, a blade cut the grain, and the grain fell into a bin. By 1861, 3,000 farmers were using reapers. Esterly built his prize-winning invention in Wisconsin!

Threshing

In 1844, J. I. Case, also a New Yorker, improved the standard thresher. This invention, when accompanied by two small horses, could thresh and separate grain before it was put into bags. Case built his threshers in Racine.

The threshing season was the busiest time of year. Families and neighbors gathered to help the farmers harvest. Threshing machines were passed from farm to farm as the harvesting crew helped their neighbors. The household of the farmer whose wheat was being threshed housed the entire threshing crew, and the farm wife baked chicken, biscuits, pies, cakes and puddings.

Binder

In 1878, the Appleby binder found its way to Wisconsin farms. This machine could bind bunches of grain and wrap them with twine. John Francis Appleby from Walworth County invented this machine, and the same basic principles are copied in today's grain-binding machines. Because of these new inventions, 16 percent of the wheat grown in the U.S. from 1840-1880 came from Wisconsin.

Livestock

Wisconsin farms were filled with all sorts of animal noises: cattle moos, sheep baas, pig oinks and horse neighs. Hog raising became very popular in Wisconsin because the pork brought in a good income. All these animals were important to Wisconsin farms, but it wasn't long before the cow would be crowned queen of them all. Many wheat farms changed to dairy farms.

Milling

After farmers harvested their wheat, they packaged it up in bags and took it to the mills, where it would be ground into flour. During the 1860s and 1870s, the milling industry in Wisconsin skyrocketed, and Milwaukee became an important grain port. When wheat was replaced with dairy cows, the milling industry was replaced with cheese factories.

Shipping

The Great Lakes made it possible for Wisconsin to become a major player in shipping goods to other markets. From the 1850s to the 1870s, the port cities and harbors grew and expanded. Products such as wheat, corn and livestock were shipped out. Wisconsin's ports also brought in farm machinery, fertilizer and livestock. Milwaukee alternated with Chicago as the greatest wheat-shipping port of the world.

Railroads

Railroads connected the countryside to cities and farms to markets. It brought immigrants to farm the land. It reached settlers who built farms far from the cities and allowed them to ship heavy loads to the market.

title: Milwaukee
text:
Milwaukee became an early center for businesses and industries. Milwaukee boasted of its flour mills in the 1840s, and nearby barley fields contributed to a growing brewing industry. The first brewery was opened by three Welshmen in 1840. Later, the Germans expanded the state's brewing industry.

For a short time in the 1860s, Milwaukee was the major flour-milling center in the Midwest. The city was also home to a major meat-packing industry, thanks to hogs raised in southern Wisconsin. Tanning companies were founded, and the city became the world's largest tanning center by 1872. In the 1860s, New England businessmen developed a clothing industry for men.

During the Civil War, this industry made uniforms for soldiers. In the 1860s, the metalworking industry was founded. Milwaukee Iron Company was established using iron and coal from mines to build iron rails. By 1873, the iron company was one of the city's largest employers and one of the country's most important ironworks. In the 1880s, factories were built that produced machinery, milling machines, farming and mining equipment and tools. Today, Milwaukee is Wisconsin's largest city with almost 600,000 people.

title: Can a cricket be used as a thermometer?
text: You bet! Early farmers noticed that crickets chirped faster when it was hot and slower when it cooled down. If you hear a cricket chirp and you have a watch, you can estimate the temperature where the cricket is. To do this, count the number of chirps in a 14-second period. Add 40 to the result, and you have a rough estimate of the Fahrenheit temperature of where the cricket is located.

title: First Hydroelectric Plant
text: A popular way to grind wheat for the past hundreds of years is the water mill. Water is used to turn a paddle wheel, and this wheel in turn moves a millstone that grinds wheat into flour. Scientists thought that if water could power machinery, could it also create electricity? Wisconsin scientists put their theory to the test. In 1882, the first plant in the United States to use waterpower to generate electricity was built on the Fox River in Appleton, Wisconsin. Such a factory is called a hydroelectric plant (factory). ("Hydro" means "water.") The electricity created from this plant was used in the early days for electric lighting and a streetcar line.

title: The Hog
text: Many of the first Wisconsin swine were tall, lean and longnecked. They were called the "prairie racers." These pigs were so lean that housewives had to grease the skillet before they fried the bacon. Beginning in the 1850s, the swine were crossbred for a new look - sleek, shapely and contented. Hogs grew quickly and readily provided meat, which was called pork. They were very profitable in the late 1800s and brought in enough money for families to pay off homes and land. Today, the hogs found on most farms are heavy, thick-skinned animals. A hog has a snout that helps it dig up vegetable roots. Hogs have an excellent sense of smell when looking for food. They can't see very well because their eyes are small and frequently bloodshot. A hog will squeal loudly if it is frightened or hurt. They can eat almost anything, but won't stuff themselves as other animals do. Many people think hogs are dirty, but actually hogs are very clean. Hogs like to wriggle in the mud because it keeps them cool and removes extra oil from their skin.

title: How do I read nonfiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring. But it really isn't. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you will find it easier to understand - and maybe even fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/ solution, (2) compare/ contrast, (3) cause/ effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/ supporting details. This week, we will discuss classification.

Classification

With this pattern, the nonfiction piece is organized into categories or groups that share certain characteristics. In other words, the content is classified.

One idea for finding out how the content of a nonfiction piece is classified is to chart the information into categories. Charting information can help you see the categories graphically. You will also better remember the characteristics of each category.

Try It!

Here is a passage about the War Between the States. Read the passage. Then chart the important information into categories.

The American Civil War was a war between the northern United States and the southern United States. The North was also called the Union and Yankees, and the South was also called the Confederacy and the Rebels. People in the North were generally abolitionists (against slavery) and did not want new states to be able to join the Union as slave states. Northern states also generally believed that states should have to follow some federal authority in order to keep the United States together. The ultimate goal of the North was to keep the Union together.

People in the South generally approved of slavery because it helped drive their economy and keep their cotton and keep their cotton businesses running. The South wanted new states to be able to decide if they would join the Union as pro-slavery or anti-slavery states. The south also believed in states’ rights, or the idea that states should be able to decided what they want by themselves, without the help of a federal government. Many pro-slavery states seceded from the United States during the Civil War. The pro-slavery state of Kentucky declared itself neutral throughout the war.

title: How to Make a Five-Pointed Star
text:
A five-pointed star is a symbol of our flag and nation. There is one star for each state on our flag.

Materials

Square Paper

Scissors

Directions

1. To make a five-pointed star, start by folding a square piece of paper in half as shown. To find the center, fold lightly in half (flap A to flap B) and unfold.

2. Next, use the found center as a pivot point and fold A over B as shown. The way to tell if you are folding the correct angle is to look at the flap on A. It should be twice as big as the B flap that is showing.

3. Fold B back over A. Now fold the piece with flaps A and B over the C section.

4. Cut at an angle on the dotted line as shown. Open it up, and the result will be a perfect five-pointed star.

Extra Activity: You can decorate your stars and use them to add some life to your classroom at school or bedroom at home.

title: Here Comes the Train!
text:
Building train tracks in America began in the eastern United States in the 1820s, and the frontier followed. The trains were often only 10 years behind the settlement of new areas. By 1850, there were tracks all over the eastern United States and a few scattered along the West Coast, but there were no main lines to connect the East Coast with the West Coast. That important project wasn't finished until after the Civil War, in 1869.

Americans wanted tracks to run near their favorite cities. Even in Wisconsin, settlers wanted tracks connecting their hometowns to Milwaukee or one of the Great Lakes. The coming of the train meant more business, more settlers, more trade and culture, and a much better life for everyone involved.

Railroad talk began with the lead miners in southwestern Wisconsin. They were looking for an easier way to transport lead to the Great Lakes. When the Wisconsin territory was organized in 1836, Henry Dodge suggested they begin a railroad line somewhere along the Mississippi, run it through the lead region and connect it to Lake Michigan. Officials liked the idea, but did not have the money to purchase supplies. Railroad construction wouldn't begin for another 15 years. Milwaukee & Mississippi Co. was the first to begin an east-west line in 1850. In 1859 Chicago and North Western Co. started building track from north to south.

Raising the money to build the line was difficult. Railroad builders couldn't afford the line themselves and wondered where they would get the money. They pled for money from the state and asked for federal grant loans and bank loans, but didn't receive much help. They decided to ask farmers, promising them railroad stock. In turn, farmers mortgaged their farms. When the lines weren't built and the railroad went bankrupt in 1857, farmers were left with worthless stock, and some even lost their farms. Many farmers tried to fight back, and violence broke out. Train depots (stops) were burned, and tracks were torn up. Slowly, the passion died as the rail responded by lowering railroad rates.

Wisconsin's basic railroad lines were completed before the outbreak of the Civil War. Construction stopped while the war was in progress, but by the end of 1860, the state had 891 miles of railway. Wisconsin passed the 1,000-mile mark in 1867 and more than doubled that number in the next six years. By 1890, the mileage reached 5,583 miles. By 1916, after World War I, the state's railroad mileage hit an all-time peak of 7,963 miles.

It took much work to open the interior of Wisconsin to settlers. But, it wasn't long after statehood that travelers from the East could move west without too much difficulty. A train ride might take several days to travel across the state, but this was a vast improvement over the period of weeks it once took on horseback.

title: Hobos Still Ride the Rails
text:
During the 1930s, when times were hard and jobs were nearly impossible to find, many men who were desperate for money began hopping on passing trains, riding them for free. They hoped that these trains would take them to places where they could find jobs and hope for a better future.

People like these who travel from place to place, never really settling down, are called hobos. When World War II started and the country had plenty of jobs, most of these hobos found work and settled down in towns across the country, but others enjoyed the traveling life and kept hopping trains. Today, more than 10,000 hobos still ride the rails, hitching a ride on trains taking them to their next adventure.

The life of a hobo can be hard, but those who choose to live this way say that they enjoy the freedom. They live in hobo camps along the railroad tracks and carry only what will fit in their backpacks, or "bindles," as they call them.

Some of these hobos have homes and many have families, but they choose to spend much of their time riding trains and working at any job they can find.

In the old days, the railroad companies could toss any hobo they found off the train while it was still moving. Today, the railroad companies wait to invite the hobo off the train until it has come to its next scheduled stop. If a hobo is caught riding the train for free a second time, he will be given a ticket for trespassing on private property.

Those who choose to live the life of a hobo claim to hear the train whistles calling them from afar. The loneliness, danger and discomfort of hobo life are all forgotten when the train whistle blows and another day's journey begins.

title: New Transportation Opens the State
text:
The railroad was part of a large, new transportation expansion that helped people settle the West. In the 1850s and 1860s, many new railroads, canals, roads and inventions helped Wisconsin to grow.

Railroad

In 1850, the first company to build a railroad in Wisconsin was the Milwaukee & Mississippi Railroad Co. After the company built five miles of track, citizens were given a ride over the line. People were so pleased and excited about the new track that they decided to grant the railroad the support it needed to continue. This line was the beginning of what later became the great Chicago, Milwaukee, St. Paul & Pacific Railroad.

Waterways

Wisconsin's earliest transportation system was its natural network of rivers and lakes. The Fox-Wisconsin waterway played an important part during settlement and economic development. Companies tried to control steamboat traffic by building locks, or water gates, on the river. Some even dreamed of building a canal between the Fox and Wisconsin rivers. Canal construction began in the 1850s, but was only built as far as Berlin.

Steamships

Robert Fulton's grand experiment with steam revolutionized river and lake travel in the 1820s and 1830s. Steamboats traveled the Fox-Wisconsin waterway for decades, but when the more affordable railroads arrived in 1850, the steamboat took second place.

Roads

Before any serious settlement of Wisconsin's interior could take place, roads had to be built. The first long roads in Wisconsin were developed to ship ore and metals from the lead district to the Great Lakes ports because it was easier to ship lead on the trains. The military built roads to connect forts, and the federal government funded a few roads during the Territorial Era. From 1849 to 1911, many Wisconsin citizens contributed their labor and tools to maintaining roads, instead of paying taxes. In the 1890s, the "Good Roads Movement" brought together groups of people interested in providing public funding of state roads. After the automobile was invented, the State Aid Road Law of 1911 began state funding for road construction.

title: First Town to Receive Rail, Waukesha
text: Waukesha was the first city to receive rail in 1851. Construction of the rail began in 1850 and started from Milwaukee. The 20-mile line was completed a few months later as the last tie was nailed down in Waukesha. Two hundred fifty citizens gathered to celebrate the official opening of the rail Feb. 25, 1851. The shiny, new locomotive, nicknamed "Bob Ellis," departed the depot at 11 a.m. It was received by cheering crowds as it arrived in Waukesha at 1 p.m. Waukesha lies in southeastern Wisconsin on the Fox River, immediately west of Milwaukee. It was settled in 1834 as "Prairieville," but was renamed Waukesha, which is Potawatomi for "by the little Fox." The city served as a station on the Underground Railroad for runaway slaves. It was an abolitionist center before the Civil War and published the anti-slavery newspaper American Freeman. From 1870 to 1915, it was a health resort complete with mud baths and mineral springs. Waukesha is also known for its limestone quarrying, industries, machine shops, and food-processing factories. Today, it is home to Carroll University (1846) and the University of Wisconsin (1966).

title: The Steam Locomotive
text:
George Stephenson and his son Robert built one of the first steam locomotives (early train engine), the famous Rocket. Stephenson also designed the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, one of the first railways during the early 1800s. The opening of the railway was the beginning of the Railway Era, which continued until World War I.

Locomotives increased in size and power, but their machinery remained the same. Horizontal cylinders were mounted beneath a boiler in the train's engine. A firebox was positioned at the rear, with a tender carrying the supplies of water and fuel. Before the invention of automobiles, railways were built across all the countries and continents of the world, opening markets and introducing industrial societies.

The steam locomotive came to America in the 1820s. The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad began building tracks in 1828. The locomotive "Tom Thumb" carried passengers in 1830. How much would a one-way ticket cost you? Nine cents! The locomotive was a big change in transportation technology.

title: Where is the world‛s longest railway?
text: You will have to travel to Russia to see the world's longest railroad. The Trans-Siberian Railway from Moscow to Vladivostok is 5,777 miles long. In the United States, our longest single track is 1,780 miles long. This track was completed in 1869 when the Central Pacific Railroad built east from Sacramento, California, and the Union Pacific Railroad built west met at Promontory Point, Utah.

title: Wood for Ties
text: Building the railroads required many wooden ties. We're not talking about the kind of ties men wear to work; we're talking about a wooden timber 8 feet long and about 8 inches by 7 inches square. In England, they call them "sleepers" because the timber lies at rest under the rails. These ties were laid on gravel about 21 inches apart. Ties had to be strong enough to hang onto the spikes that were driven into them to hold the rails. They had to endure the hot, blistering sun all summer and freezing blizzards and deep snows all winter, year after year. To keep the insects and weather from destroying the ties, they were soaked in three gallons of an oil made from tar. Each timber weighed more than 60 pounds. Our first railroad required almost 63,000 ties to go from Milwaukee to Waukesha. That's a lot of trees!

title: How do I read nonfiction?
text:
How do I read nonfiction?

Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring. But it really isn't. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you will find it easier to understand—and maybe even fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will talk about cause and effect.

Cause/Effect

With this information pattern, writers organize their material to show how one thing leads to another. Cause is the reason why something happens. Effect is what happens as a result of the cause. Effects often turn into causes for different effects. Writers often use this pattern when they want to explain a chain of events.

One way to find the cause and effect of a passage is to make a Cause/Effect Diagram that allows you to show the cause and effect relationship graphically. You start by writing the cause of the events. Draw an arrow from the cause bubble pointing right, and then next to the arrow, write the effect of that cause. Draw a new arrow from the effect bubble pointing left and down, and write the next effect. Draw the next arrow pointing right, and continue in that manner until you have reached the final effect. See the sample diagram below.

Try It!

To the right is a passage about immigration to the United States. Read the passage. Then create a Cause/Effect Diagram that shows the causes and effects of immigration.

There were many reasons why immigrants came to the United States. They came to find work, buy land and avoid religious persecution. Once they got here, immigrants faced an uncertain future. They moved to various states, seeking opportunities for jobs and food. Eventually, they settled into a particular state. They built farms or worked in one of the area’s industries.

Immigrants brought with them their customs and cultivated their cultural ideas, foods, arts and clothing. Many of the aspects of an immigrant’s culture are still practiced in the United States. Sometimes when an area had too many immigrants, such as big cities like New York, the immigrants moved to less populated states looking for work. This is one way that the rest of the United States was settled.

title: Wisconsin’s Dairy Land is the ‘Cream of the Crop’
text:
The cheese sprinkled on your pizza probably had its beginnings in your own backyard. Surprised? Probably not. Our state is referred to as "America's Dairy Land" because it is home to thousands of dairy farms (where cows are kept) and cheese factories. However, it was not always so.

In the 1840s, most farmers had a few dairy cows, but they were neglected, and their milk (baby cows’ food) was of poor quality. The first step in building an economy out of dairy products came in 1840 when Armine and Ann Pickett, started making butter from the milk of their cows and selling it. The idea caught on with the neighbors in Lake Mills. Soon, the factory system of dairying began. It was expanded to include cheese. New York, which had been the leading dairy state, helped introduce the factory system of cheese making. Chester Hazen built our state's first cheese factory in Fond du Lac County in 1864. Six years later, there were 45 to 50 factories in the state; today, there are over 100.

As the market for dairy products grew, people began to organize into associations. The first dairy workers' association in the state was formed in Fond du Lac County in 1870. The Wisconsin Dairymen's Association, was organized at Watertown in 1872. The association set standards for quality and price. They also talked the railroads into supporting the dairy market with more rail lines and new refrigerated cars.

By the end of the 1870s, Wisconsin cheese and dairy products were winning high honors at dairy shows. In 1912, A. T. Bruhn and J. L. Sammis, of Wisconsin University, found that pasteurization could be used to prepare milk before it was made into cheese. Pasteurization means to partially sterilize liquid by heating it.

The butter factory, also called a creamery, came into use in the 1870s, and Wisconsin butter soon won top-ranking status throughout the nation.

Wisconsin's delicious dairy products kept winning first prize all over the country. From the early 1900s and on, no one could match our quality. Well after WWII, our state's reputation for great products stayed strong.

Today, Wisconsin is the nation's leading producer of cheese with an average of 200 million pounds of cheese per month. The most popular types include American, cheddar, and mozzarella cheeses. For a long time, Wisconsin has also been the nation's leading producer of milk, but has dropped to second place after California. However, Californians don't make much cheese - they make ice cream and butter. Wisconsin doesn't make much ice cream, but it trails close behind in the butter industry watch out, California! Now, let's get back to our 200 million pounds of cheese. How much cheese is that? It's 100,000 tons or about 267 million pepperoni pizzas, 1,650,000,000 double-cheese burgers or 3,200,000,000 grilled-cheese sandwiches per month! So remember - when someone asks to take your picture, don't just say, "cheese." Instead, smile and say, "Wisconsin cheese."

title: Do Cows Give More Milk after Sleeping on a Waterbed?
text:
"It's been a long day," thought Bessie the cow after being milked one evening. "I think I'll just go in and get a good night's sleep on my waterbed." This may sound like the beginning of a fairy tale, but it could be happening on a dairy farm near you!

Dairy farmers know that happy cows give more and better-tasting milk. They also know that sleeping on a hard floor can cause knee and leg injuries that can sometimes make a cow unable to walk. Is a waterbed the answer? Maybe. Farmers are starting to think a cow-sized waterbed mattress might be every dairy cow's dream.

When a cow steps onto the waterbed, she feels the security of the cement floor below the mattress. When she lies down, the water in the mattress keeps her off the hard cement and protects her knees and her udder. Farmers have noticed that if there are not enough waterbeds for all the cows, they will wait in line to use it. Some research shows that cows that sleep on waterbeds sleep longer and have fewer knee and leg injuries. If cows sleep longer, they have more energy to make milk. Fewer leg injuries mean fewer trips to the vet.

The cows may be healthier in other ways too. Some researchers have found fewer white blood cells in cows that use waterbeds. White blood cells fight disease. More white blood cells indicate that the cow may be sick. Fewer white cells indicate a healthier cow. It looks as if better sleep helps cows as much as it helps people!

Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/ for more Connections and Current Events articles.

title: America's Dairy Land Today
text:
When farmers totaled up all the money they earned in one year from selling farm animals, dairy products and poultry, they made a total of $4.5 billion. That's a lot of money!

The dairy factories in the southeastern counties of Wisconsin produce milk for bottling. Cheese is manufactured in all regions of the state, but is highly concentrated in the eastern and central regions.

In total industrial output, dairy ranks as the state's second-largest industry.

You've heard of Kraft products, haven't you? Kraft has factories in Wisconsin, including one that makes Oscar Mayer products. Kraft and other companies help our state's economy by paying workers, purchasing raw materials and paying taxes every year to the state's economy in payroll, taxes, goods and services, and purchases for raw material.

Livestock

Livestock events are huge in Wisconsin. Have you ever been to the Wisconsin State Fair to see the dairy cows, pigs, chickens or other farm animals? Events such as the Wisconsin State Fair and the World Dairy Expo attract dairy professionals to Wisconsin from around the world. These events help Wisconsin's economy to grow.

Wisconsin leads the nation in the export of dairy products. Export means to send something to another country and sell it. Wisconsin exports almost 25 percent of the U.S. total. Do you know how much 25 percent is? Let's imagine that your mom has one cup of chocolate milk, and she gives half to you and half to your sister. Your friend comes over and wants chocolate milk, too, so you share half of yours. That's a fourth of a cup for your friend, or 25 percent. Out of all the dairy products exported in the United States, about a fourth comes from Wisconsin. What a great state!

Wisconsin is home to many farm animals, including pigs, chickens and, of course, cows. The dairy cows produce almost 3 billion gallons of milk each year. That’s enough to fill a 9-foot-deep Olympic-size swimming pool almost 11 times a day.

Genetics

Genetics is the talk of the future and can help improve newborn calves. Do you know what genes are? They are little messengers in our bodies that shape us into looking similar to our parents. Maybe you have the same blue eyes as your mom or blond hair like your dad. Cows have genetics, too. With the help of scientists, farmers are able to control the breeds of their farm animals by choosing the best genetics for a newborn calf. With better genetics, a cow can produce more and better milk. This whole process is called dairy genetics. Wisconsin leads the nation in the export of dairy genetics.

title: Wisconsin‛s Important Dairy Dates
text:
1851- First Wisconsin State Fair, Janesville, Wisconsin

1864- Wisconsin's first neighborhood cheese factory, Fond du Lac County, Wisconsin

1872- Wisconsin Dairymen's Association founded, Watertown, Wisconsin. William Dempster Hoard, governor of Wisconsin from 1889-1891 and founder of Hoard's Dairyman, had come from a New York dairy farm to Wisconsin in 1857. Hoard wanted the dairy cows to have the best care so that they would produce the best milk. Whenever he met with the dairy farmers, he would tell them to "speak to a cow as [they] would to a lady."

1874- Colby cheese invented, Colby, Wisconsin

1880- Wisconsin's first aboveground silo, Oconomowoc, Wisconsin. An important addition to dairying was the "silo," a machine that helped produce silage. Silage is green corn used to feed cows. Having silage available allowed for a longer feeding and milking season and, therefore, more milk!

1885- Rectangular butter churn patented, Fort Atkinson, Wisconsin

1890- Nation's first dairy school, University of Wisconsin

1890- Babcock test for measuring butterfat developed at University of Wisconsin, Dane, Wisconsin. Not all cow milk is the same - it varies in fat and quality content. Stephen Babcock of the University of Wisconsin wanted a standard for milk quality, so he invented the Babcock test. Presented in 1890, this test became the world standard for the simple measurement of butterfat content.

1933- Cold-pack method of cheese spread perfected, Kaukauna, Wisconsin

1986- Formation of Wisconsin Center for Dairy Research, Madison
