title: Where was cheese invented?
text: On the moon? Probably not. How about in the dairy section at the supermarket? Nope, not there, either. According to legend, cheese was discovered 4,000 years ago when an Arabian merchant journeyed across the desert carrying a supply of milk in a pouch. The lining of the pouch, combined with the heat of the sun, caused the milk to separate into curd and whey. That night, he drank the whey and nibbled on the curd. And as the story goes, our beloved cheese was born.

title: Cows on the Moooove Come to Wisconsin
text:
Like the immigrants who brought them, Wisconsin's various breeds of cattle come from around the world. A breed is a distinctive race or kind. The first purebred dairy sire in Wisconsin was named "Major." A sire is a male parent, and a dairy sire is a bull. Major was an Alderney breed registered in 1860.

Holsteins, brought from the Netherlands, make up 93 percent or almost all of the state's dairy herds. These cows may be most familiar to you with their white coats covered with black spots. A Holstein produces about six gallons of milk per day.

Jersey, the smallest of the dairy breeds, places a distant second in number, but produces a higher-fat milk than Holsteins-rich in cream. Jerseys have made their home in southwestern Wisconsin.

Brown Swiss, the more calm and obedient breed, is also a descendant of cattle raised in the mountains of Switzerland. These cows are much larger than Jerseys.

Guernsey, once found widely across the state, is now considered a minor breed. Their coats are similar to Holsteins in pattern, but are red and white in color. Guernseys, Jerseys and Alderneys originated on British Isles off the coast of France.

Ayrshire, originating in Scotland, is the least-numerous dairy cattle breed in the state. They are strong animals with coats of cherry red and white.

title: Salem Poor, a Brave and Gallant Soldier
text:
Do you know people who you admire because of their ethics? What actions show that a person can be counted on to do the right thing? History has very few details about Salem Poor, an African American soldier who fought in the Revolutionary War. However, 14 officers from the Battle of Bunker Hill signed a document presented to the General Court of Massachusetts. It recommended that a soldier named Salem Poor be rewarded for his heroism. He is described as "a Brave & gallant Soldier." That's strong proof of Salem Poor's ethics.

Salem Poor was born a slave in Massachusetts in the 1740s. He bought his freedom, married and had a son. When the war began, Poor left home to fight with the American colonists. Five times as many African Americans fought with the British because of promises of freedom. African Americans were not allowed to vote and faced many other types of discrimination.

For that reason, Salem Poor's award is even more remarkable. The details of his actions are unknown. The document reads "...to Set forth Particulars of his Conduct would be Tedious." But it does say "...under Our Own observation... we declare that... Salem Poor... behaved like an Experienced Officer, as Well as an Excellent Soldier." From 14 officers present at the battle, that's high praise indeed.

Some sources claim that Salem Poor shot and killed the British Lieutenant Colonel James Abercrombie at Bunker Hill. Other records show that he continued to fight in other battles. Like many African Americans of that time, exact details of both his birth and death remain a mystery. However, he was honored with a commemorative stamp in 1975.

To keep track of them, ranchers branded the cattle, which means they put a special symbol onto the animals’ bodies. title: The Constitution-Mightier Than the Sword!
text:
Have you heard someone say, "The pen is mightier than the sword"? This means that things written down on a piece of paper can be more powerful than a person swinging a sharp sword. How can this be? Written words are easily more powerful than a sword. For example, a treaty can stop armies from fighting; a law can stop us from entering war; a newspaper can help people find ways to solve problems without fighting.

A perfect example of this is a document called the Constitution. The Constitution is a body of laws that everyone agrees we should obey. Our country has a Constitution, and our state has a constitution, and both protect our rights. What rights might those be? Here are some examples from our U.S. Constitution:

Right to Privacy (Fourth Amendment) - Can people walk into your house and start snooping through your closets and drawers, taking things, just because they feel like it? Our Constitution says, "no!" because we all enjoy the right to privacy.

Freedom of Speech (First Amendment) - Can you say anything you want? Matt Fraser, a student in Washington state, gave a talk at a school assembly using bad words. Angry teachers suspended him from school. Matt went to court, saying the teachers violated his right to free speech. Was Matt right or wrong? The Supreme Court said that Matt was wrong because a school, the court said, is a protected place where students, teachers, and parents can expect protection from disruptive language.

Freedom of Religion (First Amendment) - Do you go to church or participate in a religious belief? If you do, you are free to practice any part of your religion as long as it doesn't hurt other people. If you don't practice a religion, nobody can force you to join a church or practice a religious observance.

Innocent Until Proven Guilty (Sixth Amendment) - In our country, a person can't be put in jail unless someone can prove that the person is guilty of a crime. In other countries, people are sometimes thrown in jail and kept there until they can prove they are innocent. What do you think about this right?

Wisconsin's 1848 state constitution closely models the U.S. Constitution. The state constitution includes laws on freedom of religion, election of judges and separation of powers. It supports a strong local government and limits state debt. Our preamble is similar to the nation's preamble: "We, the people of Wisconsin, grateful to almighty God for our freedom, in order to secure its blessings, form a more perfect government, ensure domestic tranquility, and promote the general welfare, do establish this constitution." Wisconsin founding fathers believed all people are born equal. They supported due process of law, which means that a citizen can expect fairness when he or she has broken the law. Wisconsin is known to have opposed slavery throughout history and celebrates February as African American History Month.

Our U.S. and state constitutions protect many rights. They also provide a way to make new laws as we need them. Turn inside and learn more about it!

title: Were Our Founding Fathers Rich?
text:
Some of our modern presidential candidates have been very wealthy. It is interesting to compare these people's fortunes to those of our founding fathers. For example, many people think that George Washington was our richest president. But is that true?

In letters to family and friends George Washington said he did not want to be president, but he was concerned that he didn't have enough money to live out his retirement. In other words, he needed the job! Like other founding fathers after the war, he had land but no cash.

Washington owned a lot of land, but no one wanted to buy any of it. People who rented parts of his land didn't have money to pay him. During the Revolution he refused to accept pay for being the commander of the Army. He fed his staff and paid spies with his own money. After the war, the government paid him back in Continental dollars, which were worthless. Washington even had to borrow money to get to the Constitutional Convention in 1787.

Thomas Jefferson once had to borrow money from one of his slaves. He died deeply in debt. When Alexander Hamilton died his family couldn't afford to bury him. They collected donations for his burial.

Our founding fathers pledged their lives, their fortunes and their sacred honor for freedom. They lost most of their fortunes because of the war. Their wealth was not in money; it was in service.

title: Our Constitution
text:
Our state constitution is patterned after our national Constitution. There are two great ideas to look at. They are constitutional rights and constitutional lawmaking.

Constitutional Lawmaking

Our state constitution is a document of paper that states the basic laws, organization, and character of our government. It describes a government that is divided into three parts or branches.

The Executive Branch

This branch consists of the governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, and secretary of state. These people have the power to enforce the laws made by the legislature. The police and National Guard help them do this.

The Legislative Branch

This branch is called the state legislature. It makes up the laws or rules governing us. There are two parts to the legislature: the House of Representatives and the Senate. These citizens are chosen by the people of our state to represent them in making the laws.

The Judicial Branch

These judges make up the Supreme Court of our state. They decide if the laws made by the legislature are constitutional. They also decide what punishment a person should receive for breaking the law.

Constitutional Rights

Our State Bill of Rights

Worship in the church of your choice.

Say what you believe is right.

Print what you want to publish.

Gather peacefully to petition (make a request to) the government.

Go to school.

Have guns within the law.

Vote when of age.

Have a trial by jury.

Don't have to testify against oneself

Our State Bill of Responsibilities

Obey the laws of the land.

Help correct things you disagree with.

Respect the rights of others.

Pay taxes.

Stay informed.

Defend your country.

Vote in elections.

Serve on a jury.

Help police and fire departments.

As an American Citizen

List as many rights as you can that are guaranteed to U.S. citizens by the Constitution.

As a Wisconsin Citizen

List as many rights as you can that are guaranteed to every Wisconsin state citizen by the constitution.

title: Who Are ‘The People?‛
text:
There are six levels in our government. The first is the individual, you. Your rights must be protected, and you must be willing to obey the law. That is the foundation of our entire Constitution.

Second is the family. The founders considered the family the most important part of organized society. It is inside the family circle that individuals find more satisfaction and growth than in any other part of society. This puts much responsibility on parents to do their very best at all times.

Third is the community. The community provides roads, schools, water, police protection, city courts, etc. and can tax people to pay for these.

Fourth is the county. The county is a group of cities. The county does those things the city does. However, it does these things for many cities, not just one.

Fifth is the state. The state establishes the law of the land (within state boundaries). It can tax, pass laws, build statewide roads, and provide government buildings. It can pass laws to make things fair for everyone who lives there. The states represent the feelings and desires of the people who live there.

Sixth is the nation. The national government keeps the whole country safe, but it has many controls on it. The founders did not want the national government ordering the states around like slaves. It has power to do some things, but not others. The national government is divided into three branches. If one branch does something wrong, the other two can make a correction.

title: Abraham Lincoln
text: On Nov. 19, 1863, Abraham Lincoln delivered a speech at the dedication of a national cemetery at the Gettysburg Battlefield. It expressed the resolve "that government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the Earth."

title: Where is our U.S. Constitution?
text: In a bomb shelter? That's right! Our actual U.S. Constitution is behind bulletproof glass in the rotunda of the National Archives Building in Washington, D.C. Along with the Declaration of Independence and other important documents, our Constitution shares space in a climate-controlled container, and each evening after visitors leave, the container is lowered into a bomb-proof vault for protection. These precious documents are copied and spoken of all over the world, but the originals live in a bomb shelter! Our state constitution is also closely protected and preserved so that it will last throughout history.

title: Symbol of the American Bald Eagle
text:
The U.S. Congress adopted the design for the Great Seal on June 20, 1782. The eagle was first introduced by William Barton. He chose the eagle because it is a symbol of supreme power and authority. Charles Thomson was the one who made the eagle the centerpiece of the Great Seal. The American bald eagle defends its nest and when anxious for his young, will spread out its wings, receive them and bear them upon its shoulders.

Joseph Campbell observed about the eagle, "He comes down, descending into the world of the pairs of opposites, the field of action. One mode of action is war, and the other is peace. So in one of his feet, the eagle holds 13 arrows. That's the principle of war. In the other, he holds a laurel [olive] branch with 13 leaves. That is the principle of peaceful conversation. The eagle is looking in the direction of the laurel [or peace]." What does the eagle represent? It represents what is indicated in this radiant sign above its head: glory. In the eagle's beak is the motto on a scroll, "E Pluribus Unum" - Out of Many, One - signifying many states becoming unified. These beautiful birds with their snowy white heads and dark bodies soar through the blue sky with grace and majesty as free as the citizens of the United States of America. Answering the eagle's call for unity, the united seal of America symbolizes one nation, under God. Look closely, and you will find this American symbol on money, stamps and flags all over our country.

title: Let's Write
text: You have learned about our Wisconsin Constitution. What rights does it give you? Would you like to be someone who runs for office? What would you do to make sure your freedoms were kept safe?

title: Wisconsin Sprints to the Next Century
text:
What a race! After almost 300 years of exciting history, the people of Wisconsin welcomed the new century of 1900 with open arms. We had come a long way since the first European settlers arrived. In those days, our state was a forest except for the south where there were a few small prairies. Timber was such an abundant resource that, by 1900, Wisconsin had more than 250 furniture factories and 3.4 billion board feet of timber annually. In fact, trees were being cut down so fast that by 1904, the state legislature saw the danger of our dwindling forests and formed laws to reforest the land.

Before the turn of the century, the University of Wisconsin College of Agriculture developed better hay seed and hybrid corn. Dairy cows grazed the fields where golden wheat used to grow. Farmers discovered inventions such as reapers, plows, planters and threshers that would help them sow and harvest crops. These inventions were so successful that farmers started cultivating crops in the northern counties. In the central and southeastern regions, more vegetable crops were grown, such as green peas, beans, cucumbers, beets, sweet corn, and cabbages. Today, Wisconsin remains among the top-ranked states in growing vegetables for canning. By the 1900s, Fox Valley played a major role in agriculture, particularly cheese making. The valley's meatpacking industry expanded into the 1900s, and its "packers" gave their name to a Green Bay football team.

Roads were cleared and paved as farmers looked for ways to transport their produce to the cities. In 1918, Wisconsin began to construct a state trunk highway system to connect every county seat.

In 1892, a local businessman boasted that Milwaukee had the "world's biggest iron foundry, the largest tannery and the largest brewery and manufactures the biggest engines." By 1910, metal production was the city's fourth-largest employer.

At the turn of the century, Ford Motor Company introduced the Model T for $850. On Dec. 17, 1903, brothers Wilbur and Orville Wright achieved the first piloted, powered airplane flight near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Their airplane remained in the air for 12 seconds and traveled 120 feet.

title: Has Amelia Earhart’s Plane Been Found?
text:
A research group that looks for historical aircraft has been trying to solve one of the greatest mysteries of the 20th century. What really happened to Amelia Earhart? Earhart was the first woman to try to fly around the world. She disappeared without a trace while flying over the Pacific Ocean in 1937.

Earhart and Fred Noonan, her navigator, could have landed somewhere near Gardner Island, now called Nikumaroro. Others believe they crashed into deep water. By using technology to study a 1937 photo of the island's shore, researchers may have new evidence in the case. The photo shows what may be the landing gear of her Lockheed Electra airplane sticking out of the water. This could mean Earhart and Noonan lived on the island for some time after the crash. Artifacts have also been found on the island that could have belonged to Earhart and Noonan.

The oceanographer who found the undersea wreckage of the Titanic says the photograph might be the clue that helps us find out what really happened. Underwater robotic submarines and mapping equipment will help the International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery look for the plane's remains. Perhaps an old photograph and new technology will help solve a 75-year-old mystery!

title: Entering the 20th Century
text:
Mining

From the 1880s to 1900s, ore mining expanded in the Gogebic Range in Wisconsin and Michigan. Enormous ore docks were constructed in Duluth, Superior and Ashland for shipping the ore to steel mills and manufacturing plants. By the 1930s, the Lake Superior ranges were producing two-thirds of the country's iron ore, which, along with coal and limestone, was the critical ingredient in steel making.

Technology and Progression

Commercial growth and new technology encouraged Lake Michigan and Lake Superior shipyards to build more ships. By 1900, the shipyards of Superior constructed two-thirds of all new ships used on the upper Great Lakes.

La Follette's election as governor in 1900 marked the start of the "Progressive Era." The Progressive and New Deal eras reigned from 1905 to 1935. Changes included workers' compensation and unemployment insurance.

In the early 20th century, Theodore Roosevelt became president following William McKinley's assassination. Our capitol building was built for the third time from 1906 to 1917.

Schools and Style

By the 1900s, the number of state school districts grew to 6,529. In 1911, the Board of Health began investigating water pollution, and in 1915, the state formed a conservation commission to oversee fish, game, forests and parks.

Women wore mostly dresses and skirts. In the year 1900, the style was a full skirt that fit tightly over the hips, a bodice that had very long sleeves, a high collar and a broad-shouldered look. Men wore knee knickers (pants that came to the knees), suspenders and button-up vests. Sleeve garters around the arms kept shirt sleeves from getting in the way. To complete the outfit, especially on a sunny day, they put on a derby or newsboy cap (hat).

Population and Growth

By 1900, Wisconsin's population was 2,069,042. The U.S. population was 75.9 million, and the average U.S. life expectancy was 47.3 years. The U.S. Census Bureau reported that seven of 10 Wisconsin residents were immigrants or had parents born in foreign countries.

In the midst of this blossoming century, a few citizens paused to consider the next 100 years. In 1901, a 14 year old from Milwaukee predicted, "In the year 2001, you will not see a single horse on Broadway, New York; only autos will be seen. The people of the Earth will be in close communication with Mars by being shot off in great cannons." Other predictions found in the New Year's Eve 1900 issue of the Oshkosh Daily Northwestern were that 100 years later death will be a matter of choice, people will be able to tolerate all human beliefs, wars will be no more and peace will reign over the whole Earth.

In 1936, Winston Churchill predicted, "We shall escape the absurdity of growing a whole chicken in order to eat the breast or wing by growing these parts separately...." In 1946, film producer Darryl F. Zanuck stated, "[Television] won't be able to hold onto any market it captures after the first six months. People will soon get tired of staring at a plywood box every night." How many of these predictions came true?

There was so much joy in our state in 1900 - so much to do, so much growth and so many places to visit, live in and enjoy. The sprint into the new century was worth every pioneer, every dollar and every fish, tree or copper nugget carved out of our land. But not far away was a great challenge that nobody wanted. As we will discuss in our next issue, headlines around the world cried out the terrible news: world war!

title: Robert M. La Follette Sr.
text: Robert M. La Follette Sr. changed the politics of Wisconsin in the 1900s. He helped bring about the Progressive Era. Born to Scots-Irish and French Huguenot parents in 1855, La Follette always wanted to make our world a better place. La Follette was interested in law. After college, he focused on a political career. La Follette was an excellent speaker, and people liked him. At age 41, he established a successful law practice in Madison. As the first governor of Wisconsin to be born in the state, La Follette also served three terms in the U.S. House of Representatives and in the U.S. Senate. He was a leader in social and economic reform. He believed that the government should reach out to experts - a "brain trust" - to help it serve the people. This trust helped Wisconsin make new laws to help workers who became injured on the job and provided minimum wage for working women and children. Years later, other states copied these laws. La Follette helped to make fair railroad laws. He was one of the founders of the Progressive Party. A Progressive Party meant public control of natural resources, public ownership of railways, and tax reduction. In 1924, La Follette ran for president, receiving nearly 5 million votes (a sixth of the total!) and winning Wisconsin. He wasn't elected as U.S. president, but we still celebrate him on Robert M. La Follette, Sr., Day every June 14. "To the character of the people of Wisconsin, I attribute the progress which we were able to make...." - Robert M. La Follette's autobiography (1912)

title: Tractor
text: The 1900s were the years of the tractor, a new monster machine with a traction engine, powered by gasoline. Farming would never be the same. Tractors were better than the steam engines of the past because they could do more. Gasoline was a cheaper fuel and more reliable. Tractors were very dependable and capable machines. It didn't take long for the American farmers to fall in love with the tractor. By 1915, already 25,000 tractors were in use on American farms. By 1920, the number skyrocketed to 246,000 tractors. Before rubber tires were invented in 1932, farm tractors had steel tires. Today, tractors are used in agriculture, construction and road building. We like to call them bulldozers, scrapers, and diggers.

title: What will life be like in 100 years?
text: In 1900, nobody could have imagined the huge changes in our world over the next 100 years. The U.S. Census Bureau predicts that by 2100, the U.S. population will double. The home will become the place where people work, learn, and worship. The Trend Journal calls it "home Zen." Sports television shows are broadcast holographically. Students will spend part of their time in schools and the rest at home, taking part in holographic classrooms. Tiny electronic microchips implanted in a person's arm could transmit messages to a computer that controls the heating and light systems of buildings. Of the world's 6,000 languages, 90 percent could be extinct by 2100.

title: YOU!
text:
What moves about on all fours, advances to two for most of its life and returns to three before it dies? The answer is you. As a baby learning to walk, you spent your day going about on hands and knees. When you learned to walk, you learned to run, skip, jump, race, trip and fall! When you get very old, you may need a cane or walking stick to get around.

More than 7 billion humans live on our planet. Every second, five are born, and two die. Our average life expectancy is in around 78, and many typically make it well into their 80s. People are living longer because of better nutrition, medical care and living conditions. That's why our world population has grown from 1 billion to 7 billion in fewer than 200 years.

Humans love to eat just about anything that tastes good, and we are pretty intelligent beings. We know how to use natural resources for food, clothing, shelter, defense, entertainment, energy, communication, medicine, knowledge, and a zillion other things.

With all of these great blessings of life, perhaps the most precious of all is a trusted friend. Humans both rich or poor are miserable, unhappy and lonely without a good friend. Make that your goal for the rest of this year, to be a trustworthy friend to all you meet, and help make this world of ours a more peaceful, helpful, and friendly place to live!

title: Why Should I Keep a Writer‛s Journal?
text:
Have you ever had to write something, but you did not know what to write about? Have you ever had a good story idea, but when you started to write the story, you realized that you could not remember the idea anymore? A writer's journal can help solve this problem.

Keep a Record

You can record your memories, observations, and thoughts in a writer's journal. You can even write colorful words and phrases or the events of the day in your journal. One very good use of your journal is free writing. Free writing is a kind of practice writing that allows you to sketch your thoughts and feelings without limits. Free writing can include single sentences or long strings of words that might not make sense to anyone else but you. You can even put drawings and diagrams in your journal. Just remember that no one else has to see your writer's journal - unless it is a class assignment, and then your teacher will want to see it.

Here are some tips for starting your writer's journal:

1. Find a special notebook to use as your writer's journal. You should use a notebook that appeals to you because it is your very own journal. Your teacher may have some Studies Weekly Student Journals that you can use. Color and draw on them so that they reflect your personality. You can also use a computer or index cards in a box for your journal.

2. You should write in your journal when you want to. You might want to write in it every day or just once a week. You might like to write at the same time every day so that you can have a routine. Just remember that the more you write in your journal, the more useful it will be to you.

3. Find a special, quiet place to do your journal writing. Make sure you have all the supplies you need to keep your journal: pencils, pens, markers, scissors, and glue.

4. Write whatever comes to your head, almost as if you are having a conversation with yourself. Do not worry about editing, rewriting, or spelling until later when you transfer something from your journal into a writing project.

Try It!

Start a writer's journal using the suggestions and tips we have provided. You will be amazed what you might discover about yourself.

Ideas for Your Writer’s Journal

1. Collect cartoons and articles to give you ideas for future writing projects.

2. Compose imaginary letters to people you wish you knew.

3. Record quotations, song lyrics, jokes, poems, or riddles.

4. Describe interesting people and places.

5. Keep learning notes—Take notes about your learning process. Record new facts and ideas you’ve learned in school, write about the progress you’ve made in class, and list questions you have about confusing content.

6. Record reading reactions—Explore ideas and feelings about what you have read. Write about your favorite character, predict what might happen next in the story, tell your opinion of the writer’s style, or summarize the story. You can even tell how the story relates to events in your own life. What is interesting about the story? What angers, amuses, or puzzles you?

6. Fold the bottom corners so that they meet on the middle line.

7. Fold the straight bottom up and then fold half of it down again.

8. Fold the top triangle down to make his head and turn over your frog.

title: World War and the Great Depression
text:
It was a brand new century in 1900, and Wisconsin was enjoying growth and success. Farming, manufacturing, wood products, and industries were bringing money, people, and prosperity to our state. And then things suddenly changed. Across the Atlantic, a terrible war was brewing.

When a war involves many countries, we call it a world war. The First World War (WWI) involved 23 of the largest countries in the world, including the United States. The war started when tensions in Europe flared up among Austria-Hungary, Serbia, Germany, France, and Belgium in 1914. England was the first to declare war on Germany, followed by the United States in 1917. Patriotic feelings were strong in Wisconsin. By 1917, hundreds of Wisconsin men had already traveled to Canada and joined the miliary to fight overseas in Europe.

WWI lasted from 1914 to 1918. In total, 8.5 million soldiers were killed, and more than $200 billion was spent to bring the war to an end. Much of the fighting took place on the smooth, rolling lowlands of Belgium and France. Ground troops had nothing to hide behind, so they dug huge networks of trenches. Soldiers lived in those trenches. They ate, slept, and died there. Anyone who ventured out and exposed himself to enemy fire was quickly killed.

Of the 125,000 Wisconsin men who joined the armed forces, 2,649 were killed during the war. Some of Wisconsin's National Guard were called to join Michigan units and head to France in January 1918. They fought in the major battles that finally broke Germany's back and ended the war later that year in November.

Wisconsin set up a State Council of Defense. This "little war cabinet" was made up of people from the government and other businesses. They helped citizens and the state prepare for the tough times ahead. Several other states copied this type of organization.

Wisconsin loaned $347 million for the war effort. Wisconsin Red Cross women knitted 500,000 garments and made 500 million surgical dressings (cloth that covers wounds). The state supplied 450 Red Cross nurses and sent hundreds of workers overseas. Wisconsin automobile companies produced cars, trucks and motorcycles for the armed forces.

Our state was very friendly to the soldiers who fought in the war. We were the first to aid the families of soldiers and give soldiers serving overseas the right to vote absentee.

Meanwhile, our state worked hard to support the war. Money was given to encourage farmers and city dwellers to plant gardens and increase farm harvests. Wisconsin farms produced 25 percent more food to supply to soldiers. About 15,000 school boys were hired to help plant and harvest these additional crops. Hundreds of factories worked 24 hours a day to provide materials and weapons for the war. As Wisconsin "dough boys" marched off to war, women took their places in farms, factories and offices.

Without a doubt, Wisconsin was a big supporter of and supplier for U.S. and Allied troops right through to the last shot fired and the victory ceremony ending World War I.

title: A Census Full of Treasure
text:
On April 2, 2012, the government released the 1940 census. A census is a count of all the people in the United States, and it is done every 10 years. It also gives other information about citizens' jobs, income, birthplace and education level. The government only releases a census' records to the public after 72 years have passed. The 1940 census was the first one done after the Great Depression and World War I. It shows how these events caused people to move around and where immigrants went. You can find interesting facts about family members and famous people. For example, the future President Ronald Reagan paid $135 in rent in 1940!

The 1940 census was the last time census takers went door-to-door to personally interview people and write down the information. For the 1950 census the government started using census questionnaires sent through the mail.

The release of the 1940 census data is different from past years. This information was made digital and released through the Internet. There are more than 3.8 million pages of data in this census. Genealogists, or people who study family backgrounds, use this information to trace family history. Researchers, like historians, often use the census as a primary source of information.

So, was this release a success? Well, so many people tried to get the information on its first day of release that the server crashed! If you would like to learn more about your family history you can go to the 1940 census site at: 1940census.archives.gov/.

title: The Day the Economy Stopped Working
text:
Can you imagine your parents, neighbors, and teachers losing their jobs? What if the local video and pizza shops, grocery store, hardware store, and movie theater closed their doors for lack of business? How would you eat? How would you learn? And how would you make money to stay warm in the winter or put food on the table? Unless you lived on a farm or in a fishing village, life would get very ugly very fast.

There is a terrible, dark period of history shortly after World War I. It was called the Great Depression. A depression is a slowdown in the economy for a long period. It was a time when money, jobs and food became scarce.

In 1929, a panic spread across the United States. People who gave money to companies to help them grow suddenly wanted their money back. In a flash, tens of millions of dollars were taken out of the American stock market, and fortunes turned to ashes. It was the great stock market crash of Oct. 29, 1929.

Most companies couldn't give the money back, and thousands of companies began to go out of business. They had to lay off workers, close their doors, and sell off their land and equipment to pay back the loans. Many poor people wore rags and ate very little. Some organized workers (unions) tried to go on strike, but that only made things worse. By 1935, hundreds of thousands of people were getting welfare help just to stay alive. Could it get any worse? Yes. A terrible drought had settled on the prairies, and few crops could grow. Farm prices were so low that many farmers were going bankrupt. People started losing jobs in 1929, and by 1933, nearly 25 percent of people were out of work. In North America in the 1930s, things looked mighty grim.

Getting Food

With so many out of work, the government and others set up soup kitchens. It was common in some places to see people in long lines for a little bread, trying to fend off starvation. Wheat selling for $2 or $3 a bushel during the war suddenly was worth only 38 cents or less a bushel. Lumber prices were slashed by 2/3. Farmers couldn't afford to keep up with their orchards and pulled up trees for fuel. Some families sold their cars to buy food. They then had to walk from town to town in search of food.

No Jobs

People lucky enough to have jobs had their wages cut time and time again. Some men out of work "bummed" rides on the trains and wandered about the country in search of work. In the coastal communities, people could catch fish for food, but they couldn't sell any for lack of buyers. Canadians poured across the border to the United States in search of work until the United States sealed the border to protect the few jobs that were available.

Trying to Solve the Problem

Fixing the Depression wasn't easy. These grim times seemed to go on without end. No one would expect that another world war would improve the economies of the Western world, but that's just what happened. Germany, Italy and Japan started threatening their neighbors and looking to conquer their way out of the Depression. Soon the United States would be at war again.

The Great Dust Bowl

During the so-called "Dirty '30s," long periods of no rain and poor soil management destroyed millions of acres of farmland in the prairies of the United States and Canada. The soil dried hard and cracked. The passing wind began cutting away, creating billowing clouds of dust that blew across the prairies. In some places, a barn could be buried in 3 to 6 feet of dust after just a week of blowing winds. Ruined farms sent farming families to the cities for work. Even in places where crops could grow, prices were so low that it wasn't worth harvesting them, or grasshopper plagues attacked the crops.

Prohibition

In 1919, the United States ratified the 18th Amendment, which made alcohol illegal. This was called "Prohibition." Beer was important to Wisconsin's economy, and Prohibition put many people out of work. Many people opposed Prohibition and smuggled alcoholic drinks from Canada or made their own. Thousands of homes were used to brew wine, beer and other drinks. In 1933, the 21st Amendment was passed, ending Prohibition, and things quieted down.

Women's Suffrage

In 1920, all females over age 21 won the right to vote in national elections thanks to the 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.

Workers Strike

As the grim poverty of the Depression settled in, people started strengthening their unions and organizing new ones. Sit-down strikes were organized to force companies to pay better wages. In 1937, several fights broke out between police and striking workers. In 1939, Governor Julius Heil took office, and his Employment Peace Act banned sit-down strikes, closed shops, and some forms of picketing and boycotts. The American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, born in the state in 1936, eventually became one of the nation's largest unions. Wisconsin became known as a state that supported unions.

title: The Roaring Twenties
text: The 1920s was an exciting time in the United States that is now known as the Roaring '20s. That's when dime novels, movies and dances became popular. A dance called "The Charleston" became all the rage at dance halls. Women during this time who broke free from the strict standards of the time became known as "flappers." Jazz also became popular and seemed to speak the soulful, deep sounds of the time. Louis Armstrong made jazz very popular during this era. He and his jazz band traveled to major cities all over the United States and Canada. During Prohibition, flappers and others met at illegal liquor establishments known as "blind pigs" or "speakeasies" to party and drink.

title: War Communications
text: During the war, it was important for commanders to be able to control, coordinate and direct huge armies. Commanders found this very difficult, especially when their armies were overseas. Remember, these commanders didn't have telephones, television, and the Internet as we do today. What they needed were signal and electrical communications. Field telephones and switchboards were soon developed and improved. Pole lines were constructed, and workers buried thousands of miles of telephone wire. Workers tried to protect the wire lines, but at times they were cut during intense artillery fire. Many thought the radio could be an easier way to communicate. Before the war began, radios were bulky and heavy. Engineers worked hard to develop smaller portable radios powered by batteries. There was only one problem: The enemy could also tune into the radio signal and listen to the message. So commanders used crypto-graphing or encoded messages. The easiest system of the time was visual signaling-flares, smoke and fire. Messengers carried communications by motorcycle, bicycle and automobile. Commanders even used homing pigeons and dogs to deliver documents. Communication was much slower than what we are used to, but through the years, engineers and scientists developed these tools into the amazing lightning-fast technology we enjoy today.

title: What were the Alphabet Soup Programs?
text: During the Great Depression, President Franklin Roosevelt and Congress started many programs to help people get jobs. These programs were usually referred to by initials, such as CCC for Civilian Conservation Corps or WPA for Works Progress Administration. With all the initials floating around, people nicknamed them the Alphabet Soup Programs.

title: Obedience
text:
You know what obedience means. It simply means obeying the rules or laws, and it's a very important character trait to have. Here's a basic example of when you should be obedient: "Look both ways before you cross the street." Everyone wants to avoid being run over by a car. That's a great benefit for keeping such a basic rule. Some rules are harder to keep than others, but most rules have a "built-in" benefit for obeying them.

Can you think of some other benefits of being obedient? What's the benefit of keeping the homework rule or of listening to your teachers? Great grades-and all the rewards that come with them!

Did you know that you can choose whether to obey the rules, but you cannot choose the consequences? That's right; if you keep a rule, whether you like it or not, you get to enjoy the benefits. Of course, that goes the other way, too. If you choose not to obey, then you must accept going without the benefits. Often, there's a penalty for not obeying the rules, like not being able to play with your friends because you didn't finish your chores. Can you think of other examples of benefits or penalties that come from obeying or disobeying rules?

title: Woodrow Wilson and the Fourteen Points
text:
All presidents have important responsibilities, but few are more critical than those faced by presidents during times of war. While the United States was fighting in World War I, President Woodrow Wilson addressed Congress on Jan. 8, 1918. He presented a plan for peace called the Fourteen Points.

Woodrow Wilson was elected in 1912. World War I began in 1914 between Great Britain and Germany and other European nations. It was called The Great War. Everyone thought there would never be another war like it. President Wilson wanted to keep the United States out of the war. He tried to help Great Britain and Germany end the conflict. But when German submarines began sinking American ships, he asked Congress to declare war.

Wilson's Fourteen Points plan described his ideals for achieving world peace and democracy. He had consulted with a team of about 150 foreign policy advisors. He assured Americans that the war was being fought for good causes and would lead to peace in Europe. The Fourteen Points included free trade, freedom of the seas and returning territories taken in the war. Wilson also wanted to establish a League of Nations to protect the independence of "great and small states (nations) alike."

Wilson's Fourteen Points faced opposition from some people, but it was used as the basis for the German surrender at the end of the war. The Armistice took effect on "the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month" in 1918. America and other nations remember those who died by celebrating Armistice Day (now called Veterans Day) every November 11. Woodrow Wilson was awarded the 1919 Nobel Peace Prize, thanks to his clarity of expression. Why is it important for our leaders to be clear during times of war?

title: How Do I Take Notes While Researching?
text:
If you haven't already, soon you will need to do some research to write a report, study for a test, or give a presentation.

Keep Track of Information

How will you keep track of all the good information you find while researching? Take notes! Here are some tips for taking research notes:

You will probably find that index cards are the best way to take notes. You can write one fact or quotation on each card and then organize and rearrange them based on how you want to write your report, give your presentation, or study for your test.

Label your notes with subject headings.

Paraphrase and summarize information in your own words. Summarize information by writing the main ideas and most important supporting details. This will help you prevent plagiarism, which is copying writers' words without giving them credit.

If you like how a writer has said something, use a direct quotation. Be sure to record the quote exactly. Include punctuation and spelling just as written by the writer. Put quotation marks around the quote so that you know it is a quotation and not your summary.

Write down the title, author, publisher, city of publication, date, and page numbers of each source after you have recorded the fact or quotation. This way, you can include this information in a bibliography, and you can go back and double check a quotation if you have questions.

Abbreviate the information you have researched to save time. Write in groups of words and phrases instead of complete sentences. Use abbreviations and symbols as long as you will remember what they mean. You can transfer the information into complete sentences later when you use it in your report or presentation.

Organize your notes into the most useful order for you, your report or presentation. For example, you can organize them by subject or theme.

Try It!

Do some research on the subject you are currently studying in social studies. Use research notes to record the information you find. Use the research notes to write a report or make a presentation, depending on what your teacher assigns. Be sure to always take organized research notes when doing any research. It will save you time in the future, when you start writing a report.

title: Let's Write
text: Have you been downtown in our biggest city? Do you live near there? Write and tell us about your favorite things to visit in our state’s biggest city!

title: That Terrible Day in December!
text:
Dec. 7, 1941, was another sleepy Sunday in Wisconsin. Families were coming home from church services, others were settling down after brunch with the Sunday paper and others were simply enjoying Sunday listening to music on the radio.

However, far away to the west, a completely different kind of morning was breaking over Hawaii. From miles away at sea, low to the horizon, a strange formation had gathered in the morning sky. As it approached, people watched from a distance. What were so many planes doing in the air at this time of day? Was it some kind of exercise? Suddenly, it became very clear what the planes were doing. It was an attack!

Pearl Harbor (Hawaii) was the home of America's largest naval base in the Pacific region. At 7:55 a.m. Hawaii time, 100 Japanese airplanes attacked American ships and people. Japan was officially at war with the United States.

Immediately, the alarms sounded all over Hawaii, and the cry went out, "Pearl Harbor is under attack!"

Japanese fighter planes, torpedo bombers and dive bombers took only one hour and 55 minutes to empty their bombs and bullets. When it was over, five of our eight battleships were sunk, the other three damaged. (Three were later repaired and went to war.) Five other ships were sunk and several damaged. About 325 Navy and Army planes on the ground were destroyed. Among the dead were 2,343 American sailors, soldiers and Marines; 1,272 were wounded, and 960 were missing. Many of the docks, repair facilities, hangars and runways were damaged or destroyed.

When word of the attack reached mainland U.S.A., panic and anger spread from coast to coast, especially along the western coastal cities where people feared a direct attack from the sea. Instead of a day of rest, Sunday became a dark day of worry. Would the Japanese continue their attack along the Pacific Coast? Would they bomb farther inland? No one knew what to expect.

And just like that, America was at war again.

Some historians believe there were never 20 years of peace between the end of World War I and the start of World War II. It was more like an armed truce. In 1939, Germany again attacked its neighbors and began a costly second attempt to take over Europe. America helped its allies for the first couple of years before jumping in with both feet to end Germany's threats and power in Europe. By 1942, the United States was heavily involved in two war zones: (1) in the Pacific against Japan and (2) in Europe against Germany and its friends.

And who was in the middle of all this fighting and trauma? It was Wisconsin, loaded with natural resources and the industrial might to become a mighty warrior during WWII!

title: Wisconsin Veterans Tell Their Stories
text:
As veterans (those who have served in the military) of foreign wars grow older, our country risks losing the stories of these brave soldiers forever. Thousands of war veterans die each week, and along with them go their stories. The Library of Congress' Veterans History Project hopes to record these amazing historical stories before the war veterans are no longer around to tell them.

Project participants have gathered thousands of war stories from veterans of foreign wars. For many years, these veterans have kept their stories to themselves, not wanting to burden their families with their pain. As they age, however, many veterans feel the need to finally talk about their experiences and let someone know what war was really like.

Guy Stephens, a 78-year-old former school principal, told his interviewer about being rescued from a German prison camp where he was held as a prisoner of war, or POW. He says, "It's hard for POWs to talk to your family about combat or what you've experienced as a POW. There's something about POWs, we never talk about things. I told him things I've never told my family. . . I don't know why."

Denise Fritz is a court reporter, or someone who records everything that happens in court, from Sheboygan. Denise was recently spotlighted by the Library of Congress for her work on the Veterans History Project. She volunteers her time to help transcribe, or write down, veterans' stories that have been recorded on video or audiotape. Denise says, "These stories are snapshots of individual veteran's personal experiences, and court reporters across the nation are transcribing them in an effort to preserve and share the history of our country." She hopes that more court reporters will get involved in the project and help make a record of these historic experiences.

By preserving the history of these brave soldiers, volunteers guarantee that these amazing stories will live on, even after the soldiers have passed away.

title: Wisconsin Helps Win World War II
text:
As America entered World War II, Wisconsin was called upon to provide a great deal of help.

Wisconsinites Donate Service and Blood

Wisconsin sent 350,000 soldiers to fight in WWII. Many who remained home gave their blood to Red Cross donor centers. Red Cross also trained thousands in first aid and home nursing and recruited nurses for the armed forces. The Red Cross sent many men and women overseas to work in hospitals, clubs and rest centers.

Factories and Manufacturing

The United States entered the war in 1941, but even before that, Wisconsin industries were hard at work. The factories in southeastern Wisconsin produced tanks and Army trucks instead of cars and farm equipment. Paper mills in the north made maps and books for soldiers. After World War II, the whole country saw a rise in manufacturing - Wisconsin, too. New farm machinery meant that fewer farm workers were needed. Many people moved to the cities, looking for work in the factories.

The 380,000 workers in war plants and shipyards produced more than $12 billion worth of war material. Wisconsin farms produced record quantities of dairy products, fruits and vegetables and eggs and poultry.

War Rations

The rationing system was a difficult job. Rationing meant that you could only have a certain amount of food, clothing, or fuel so that there would be enough to go around for everybody and nothing was wasted. Milwaukee did the best job at rationing their items. In fact, their record was so perfect that federal officials were sent here during the war to see how it was done.

When Wisconsin and the rest of America went to war, some things became hard to get. Tires and gasoline were rationed so that more materials could be reserved for the war effort overseas. Many people saved up their gas coupons so that they could afford a summer trip somewhere. Many of our highways that once were very busy had become quiet except for giant trucks, buses and other vehicles on official business. Even though no more personal cars were being produced, most people managed to keep their own vehicles running. Replacement parts were still allowed to be made and bought. All over the state, people were encouraged to save, not be wasteful and grow gardens to reduce the strain on food and food production needs.

Most citizens didn't complain even though they had given up many pleasures and liberties: food, clothing, fuel and gasoline. Instead, Wisconsinites faced rationing, the 35-mile speed limit, the midnight curfew on amusement places and the worst housing shortage in history. Some grumbled, and a few cheated, but the essential job was done.

News Flashes

The spring and summer of 1945 brought a series of startling news flashes: April 12, the death of President Roosevelt; May 1, Adolf Hitler's death: May 7, the surrender of Germany; Aug. 6, the dropping of the first atomic bomb on Hiroshima; and Aug. 14 - the news everyone had been praying for through four difficult years - the surrender of Japan.

Victory at Last!

World War II ended in 1945. Germany surrendered in May, followed by Japan in August. With each surrender, tens of thousands of men, women and children poured into the streets of Wisconsin cities to cheer, shout and celebrate.

title: Rosie the Riveter
text: During World War II, many women went to work for war-time industries including shipyards, steel mills, foundries, lumber mills, warehouses, offices, hospitals and day-care centers. They were welders, drafters, truck drivers, riveters and more. More than 6 million women across America left their chores and family at home to make the war-fighting effort a success. It was unusual in those days to have women doing that kind of work. A 1942 song called "Rosie the Riveter" became popular and provided the nickname for these women workers.

title: Atomic Bomb
text: Not long after Japan entered World War II, scientists began working on a powerful new bomb. Scientists knew that a powerful new energy source was available in the atom, and they wanted to release it for a new weapon. They called the new weapon the atomic bomb. The first atomic bomb was dropped on the Japanese city of Hiroshima on Aug. 6, 1945. A giant mushroom cloud rose many miles into the sky, as a terrible firestorm of heat, radiation and fire turned the city and tens of thousands of people to ashes in a mighty flash never before seen on Earth. Three days later, a second bomb was dropped on the seaport of Nagasaki, Japan. The Japanese immediately surrendered, and World War II was over. Nuclear weapons today are many times stronger than what was dropped on Japan.

title: Who is Uncle Sam?
text: Ever since the War of 1812, the make-believe character of Uncle Sam has become a symbol of the United States. Especially during World War II, much mention is made of Uncle Sam. So, who is Uncle Sam, anyway? Uncle Sam is based on a real person from Massachusetts named Samuel Wilson. He fought in the Revolutionary War. People who liked him called him Uncle Sam. In the War of 1812, his meat-packing business provided troops with pork and beef. He marked his boxes with a "U.S.," meaning, "United States," but those who knew him thought that it meant "Uncle Sam." The idea caught on, and people starting using the name "Uncle Sam" to mean the U.S. government. The image of "Uncle Sam" as a patriotic, bearded man in red, white and blue clothing evolved during the years that followed.

title: Wisconsin Men in History
text: Wisconsin gave to the American armed forces some of the most outstanding men of World War II. General Douglas MacArthur was the state's greatest military leader in the war. MacArthur grew up in Milwaukee as a boy. He came from a strong, valiant family that had been making history for three generations. After serving as the youngest chief of staff in American history, MacArthur became the field marshal of the Philippine Army. He prepared the Philippines for a probable attack by the Japanese. After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, they moved on to the Philippines. Although unable to hold back the Japanese, MacArthur's troops continued to fight courageously. Because of MacArthur's leadership, the Japanese never made use of Manila Bay, an important military post. After the war, MacArthur was given the Congressional Medal of Honor, the nation's highest military award, and was made supreme commander of Allied forces in Japan.

title: President Truman and The Atomic Bomb Decision
text:
rumination (noun): the act of giving serious thought and consideration to something

Adolf Hitler was defeated in May 1945 after years of war in Europe, and American troops would be coming home - wouldn't they? Victory in Europe meant that some U.S. soldiers would be returning home. Others would go to the Pacific to face Japanese armies. Scientists in the U.S. had made a weapon that could certainly end the war with Japan, but it was so powerful that tens of thousands of people would be killed, including civilians (citizens not in the military). President Harry Truman had a decision to make that would greatly affect the world. What would the commander in chief do?

In the years leading up to President Truman's decision, the Japanese had been a brutal enemy. They had killed thousands of Americans at sea and on Pacific islands, including the surprise attack on Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The president wondered how many more lives would be lost if we tried to end the war without the atomic bomb. What would happen if another country improved the weapon and used the bomb before we did? Would they use it on us?

President Truman tried several times without success to work out surrender with Japan. He then ordered atomic bombs to be dropped on the cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945. Within a week of the second attack, Japan did surrender, which put an end to World War II. Historians estimate that between 150,000 and 240,000 Japanese were killed from effects of the two bombings. They also estimate that thousands of American lives were saved. Do you think President Truman made the right decision?

title: What are Homophones and Homographs?
text:
Homophones and homographs are the same but different! To find out the meaning of a word, carefully read the words and sentences surrounding it.

Homophones

Homophones are words that sound the same but have different spellings and different meanings. You can remember what a homophone is by remembering that a phone makes a sound, so a homophone sounds the same as another word.

It is important to know a homophone when you write it. If you need help with a homophone when you read or write, look it up in a dictionary. This will help you keep from making mistakes. For instance, would you write you have "bear hands" or "bare hands"?

Here are some common homophones:

beat, beet

earn, urn

eye, I

heal, heel, he'll

made, maid

plain, plane

rain, reign, rein

to, too, two

Homographs

These are words that are spelled the same but have different meanings. Sometimes they are pronounced differently even though they are spelled the same. You can remember what a homograph is by remembering that a graph is something you look at, so a homograph looks the same.

Here are some common homographs that are pronounced differently and have different meanings:

bass: a low voice

bass: a fish

content: things found inside

content: satisfied

minute: 60 seconds

minute: tiny

Try It!

The next time you are not sure which homophone or homograph to use, be sure you know the meaning of the word you are trying to use. This will help you spell it correctly. A dictionary will help you a lot!

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you’re a kid in 2100 and you’re looking back 100 years. Your cyber teacher has given you an assignment to write about a technology that is no longer used, why it was replaced and what new technology replaced it. For instance, you could write about how wheels were replaced by anti-gravity thrusters. Pick anything we use now and tell us how it will be replaced in the future. Use your imagination!

title: Wisconsin Manufacturers Help Make the World Spin!
text:
It's hard to find something that isn't made in our state! Wisconsin has so many natural resources that people with all kinds of ideas, skills and craftsmanship have been pouring into our state for years. Agriculture, manufacturing and industry are a big part of Wisconsin's economy. Cheese, dairy products, cattle, hogs, vegetables, corn and cranberries make up the agricultural part of Wisconsin's economy. Auto manufacturing, machinery, food processing, paper products, electric equipment and fabricated metal products are the industrial side of Wisconsin's economy. Manufacturing is concerned mainly with the production of metal goods and with the processing of agricultural and forest products.

Iron is now rarely mined in Wisconsin, but there are many other minerals dug up that are important to the state's economy, such as sand and gravel, building and monumental stone and agricultural lime. Wisconsin is also home to one of the largest ore bodies of zinc-copper sulfide in North America, discovered in northern Wisconsin in 1975.

About 75 percent of our forests are hardwoods. However, the timber industries make most of their money from paper pulp that comes from aspen and pine. A great deal of timber is also used for fuel, especially after the energy crisis of the late 1970s.

There are plenty of delicious lake trout and whitefish in Lake Michigan. Commercial fishing is still a major industry in Wisconsin's portion of the Great Lakes. Anglers have worked hard to maintain and restock adequate numbers of lake trout, whitefish, lake herring, yellow perch and chub. Pacific coho, salmon and other game fish have been added to Lake Michigan, causing a boom in the sport-fishing industry. Sport fishing brings in more money to our state than commercial fishing.

Most of the state's electrical power is generated from coal-burning plants. A significant amount of electricity is produced in the state's three nuclear facilities, and a small percent comes from hydroelectric plants, or water-powered machines that make electricity.

Wisconsin's agriculture is mostly dairy farming, livestock and livestock products. About 60 percent comes from dairy products alone. Walk the streets of our cities and find hundreds of stores specializing in cheeses of all kinds and wide varieties of sausage. In addition, Wisconsin is one of the major beer-producing - and consuming - states in the nation, a reflection of its strong German heritage.

As we have studied Wisconsin over these past 23 weeks, the pattern should be clear: People settle where there are resources, water and avenues of transportation and communication. When early settlers built fur trading posts near main rivers and pathways, they probably didn't realize what these places would one day become. The early settlements grew into villages, towns and then cities. Wisconsin is unusual compared to other states because it has an abundance of all of these.

title: Boom to Bust and Back Again
text:
You may have heard people compare the recent economic recession (2007-2009) to the Great Depression of the 1930s. But what some people call the "Great Recession" actually had more in common with a depression in the 1890s and something called "boom and bust."

In the early 1890s, the U.S. economy grew quickly ("boomed") but couldn't keep growing at that rate. When many companies and the housing market failed, there was an economic "bust." The railroad industry had been booming since the end of the Civil War, but in the 1890s more than 150 railroad companies closed. Other industries that depended on the railroads closed, and many people lost their jobs. Over 500 banks closed. Thousands of unemployed men marched to Washington, D.C., in 1894 to demand that the government take action to help families. Unemployment was over 10 percent for most of the 1890s. About one of every ten people had no job.

In the recent recession, the housing market slumped after several "boom" years. Some automakers went out of business and others filed for bankruptcy. The economy went "bust," just as it did in the 1890s. Hundreds of banks and thousands of businesses closed. The unemployment rate was about 8 percent - about one of every twelve people had no job.

Make a chart or Venn diagram that compares these two events in history.
