1. My first home was northern Wisconsin. After I was shipped to factories in southeastern Wisconsin, I took on many shapes. I became paper, doors, cabinets and furniture. I’m an important resource to Wisconsin and the United States--so important that they replant me more often than they chop me down.

2. I play an important part in today’s technology. It tickles me to have electricity run through me. Scientists work with me to improve machinery and computers so that they run efficiently and faster. I have many parts and wires.

3. I love to play in the water. I have many great ancestors who have fought in WWII such as the USS Wisconsin. The Great Lakes are my backyard. I like to ship iron ore across the lakes to New York.

4. I love to feel the rush of the wind as I speed down the interstate on my wheels! People ride me to work, the hills and the lakes. I come in all shapes and sizes. Don’t forget your helmet!

5. I’m symbolic of the German heritage of Wisconsin. Some of the best is made right here in Milwaukee. I come in many different flavors, but you should leave me alone until you’re 21 and responsible. You can tour our facilities.

6. I’m important in the manufacturing industry. I’m made of metal, screws and wiring. Sometimes, they take me to the Gogebic Range to dig our iron ore. I’m also used to make paper-pulp products. An engineer put me together and turned me on. I got hot inside and have a great deal of power.

7. I’m everywhere you look. When you take your groceries to the car, I’m usually there. When you put leftover meals into containers, I’m usually there. When you use lotion bottles, I’m usually close by. When you blow up a water tube or an air mattress, I’m closer than you think. I’m good friends with Ziplock, Mattel Barbie and Legos. I’m man made.

8. Farmers need me to plant and harvest crops. I’m big, bulky and loud, and I burn a great deal of fuel. I love to play in the dirt and mud. My friends are bale choppers, conveyors, feeders and silo unloaders.

9. Monks used to copy the written language by hand. Books were all handwritten and expensive, but not today. We have machines that duplicate written documents. I’m one of those machines. I’ve duplicated thousands of pages. I’m important because I tell everyone the news and fashion trends.

title: Have You Ever Wondered How Door County Got its Name?
text: Dangerous currents lie between the Door Peninsula and Washington Island. Hundreds of ships were lost in this passage in Wisconsin's early history. The first French voyagers were afraid to travel this passage and named it Porte des Morts Passage or Death's Door Passage. Death's Door was the last reported sighting of the Griffin in 1679 when it encountered a violent storm on its way back to Niagara. An American Indian legend also claims that it named this peninsula. According to the legend, the Cape Indians were the first to live on the peninsula's northern tip. They were forced off by a huge army of Potawatomi Indians, and so they moved to Detroit Island. The Cape Indians plotted to get back their land and sent spies to the peninsula with instructions to light a fire at a safe landing point when the time to strike was good. Two spies were captured and tortured into revealing the plot. On a stormy night, the Potawatomi lighted a signal fire on top of a very steep bluff and waited. The Cape Indians saw the bogus signal and set out in their canoes just as the storm intensified. The few who survived the treacherous storm were met and killed by Potawatomis waiting on the shoreline. It was this American Indian tale of "death's door" that the legislature noted in giving Door County its name in 1851.

title: The Assembly Line
text: Meat-packing plants in Cincinnati, Ohio and Chicago, Illinois, were the first to use the assembly line idea in modern America. An overhead trolley moved an animal carcass at a steady pace through the plant using a powered chain or rope. Workers stayed in one place, performing their work while the carcass was in their area. Henry Ford used this principle to pull a car chassis at a steady pace past workers with piles of parts. The workers attached the parts before the chassis moved out of their area to the next station. By 1914, Ford's plant could produce a completed automobile every 93 minutes! Ford's ingenious ideas spread everywhere and helped industries get started in Wisconsin.

title: Where was the First Gasoline Station?
text: Gasoline is a byproduct of refining kerosene (an oil used for fuel). Most gasoline was only available near such refineries. People had to carry the gasoline in buckets to their vehicles. In 1907, the first station to deliver fuel opened in Seattle, Washington. A garden hose in an elevated 30-gallon tank let car owners "fill 'er up!" When word spread, more than 200 people a day bought gas at the makeshift gas station. The first drive-through gas station opened in Pittsburgh in 1913. Customers could buy "Good Gulf Gasoline." The station offered free air for tires, water for the radiator and a public bathroom. Today, America has more than 180,000 gas stations.

title: Honeybees
text: It's hard to believe, but spring is just around the corner. With each warming day, you might notice a few bees flying around. Where do they come from, and why are they out while it's still cold? A beehive is usually only two or three miles away from a bee you might see, and as soon as it gets in the 40s, thousands of bees leave the hive to look for nectar. Honeybees are amazing insects. They are organized, hard working and very efficient. In the winter, they huddle in their beehives in a great big ball of 20,000-30,000 bees. In the middle of this mass is the queen, staying nice and warm. During winter, they eat honey, and on the coldest nights, some of the bees on the outside of this ball will freeze. As the weather warms up, the hive becomes active. Worker bees clean out the dead bees and scrub the honeycomb clean, and the queen starts laying eggs. Workers go out looking for early blossoms. Nearly all the bees are female. They keep five to 10 drones (males) around just in case the queen is killed. If so, they feed a special royal jelly to a newly laid egg and grow a new queen. As bees gather nectar, they also spread plants' pollen. This keeps all vegetation healthy and producing fruits. If you see a bee, don't be scared. Be respectful. This is one hardworking insect!

title: What are Idioms?
text:
Have you ever heard an adult say, "I'm sorry, but we're up a creek on this one"? What did he mean? He was standing on dry ground when he said it! Well, you've just heard an idiom.

Idioms are Not Meant to Be Taken Literally

Idioms are sayings that mean something different from the literal meaning of their words. "Literal" means "following the exact wording." But idioms are not literal, so the words do not mean exactly what they say. Listen carefully for clues to figure out an idiom.

Try It!

The best way to learn what an idiom means is to learn it and use it in your own speech or writing. Ask someone what it means. Then use it in your own writing. Here are some idioms in sentences. See if you can figure out what they mean. Once you know what the idiom means, use it in your own sentence.

1. They were both so shy they had a hard time breaking the ice.

Use "breaking the ice" in your own sentence.

2. When it comes to modesty in dress, I have to draw the line somewhere.

Use "draw the line" in your own sentence.

3. By halftime, the game was in the bag.

Use "in the bag" in your own sentence.

4. Chris and I are in the same boat because neither of us have extra cash to spend on the field trip.

Use "in the same boat" in your own sentence.

5. Would someone lend me a hand with the dishes?

Use "lend me a hand" in your own sentence.

title: Let's Write
text: Do you know people who work in any of the industries mentioned in this issue? You’ll learn many new things from talking to them — and probably enjoy it too! Write an essay about what they told you.

title: Earth as an Apple
text:
Have an adult help you cut the apple with a knife.

Materials

Apple

Knife

Directions

1. Slice an apple into quarters. One-quarter of an apple represents the Earth’s land.

2. Slice one of the quarters into two. This 1/8 piece represents Earth’s land that is not swamps, deserts, or Polar Regions.

3. Cut the 1/8 piece into four 1/32 pieces. One of these pieces represents land that can be farmed. The rest is buried under cities, is too wet or too cold, or has poor soil.

4. Peel this 1/32 of the Earth’s surface carefully to represent the thin layer of topsoil that actually produces food.

Let this example remind us of how lucky we are to have the land we live on. Can you see how important it is to take good care of this valuable resource?

title: Touring the Greatest State in the Union!
text:
Wisconsin is a wonderful and beautiful state that is loaded with history, recreation, natural resources and wonders from border to border. Skiing, hiking, biking and fishing draw thousands of tourists each year. Tourism now ranks with manufacturing and agriculture as one of the major businesses in our state. Wisconsin has 117,000 acres of state parks for recreational use and millions of acres in national, state and county forests. Most of the public forests are in the north, and most of our parks are in the southeast, although there is a park within an hour's drive of any location.

Northern Wisconsin has just about everything the outdoor family dreams of: fishing, snowmobiling, skiing, snowshoeing, hiking, biking, lakes, forests, waterfalls, wildlife, wild flowers, birds, nature, camping and boating. About 90 percent of our 15,000 lakes are in the north, and they're loaded with fish. For those who want to explore off the mainland, take a sailboat to the Apostle Islands. Here, you'll also find the Penokee Range and Gogebic Range, great mineral sources. Sixty-two waterfalls adorn the crisp, cool forests and hillsides. For those hikers and bikers, the Ice Age Trail and North Country Trail are favorites.

Fishing is a wonderful pastime in Wisconsin. Pull out your pole and bait around October, and you’ll have a hard time keeping up with the catch! One angler gives this description of October fishing: “In the warmer months, fish are finicky and fickle, but in October, it’s like they take a stupid pill and bite at almost anything tempting that is put out for them!” For fish lovers, there are dozens of bait shops and fishing guides all over the state. Pontoons and fishing boats are always available to rent.

Wisconsin is a great place to see wildlife, particularly in the national forests and undisturbed land. In the spring, you just might see some fawns, or tiny black bear cubs following their mom across a road. If you like horses, there are riding stables in the Eagle River area. This is a wonderful way to enjoy the brilliant fall colors. Eagles, osprey, beaver dams and wilderness scenery add to the adventuresome outdoors. Trillium carpets the forest floors, and marsh marigolds rest in roadside waters. Even wild columbines sway in the wind among the rocky hills and cliff sides. Campers wake up to the songs of loons, eagles and great blue heron and the tap-tappity-tap of a pileated woodpecker.

Wisconsin is famous for a small red berry called a cranberry. The Warrens Cranberry Festival draws people from all over, every year. Visitors can tour cranberry bogs and wineries and watch the Cranberry Fest bakeoff. Bakers and cooks invent all sorts of foods with cranberries such as cranberry fritters, cranberry cheesecake, cranberry-sauerkraut meatballs, cranberry mustard and cranberry catsup.

Inside this issue of Wisconsin Studies Weekly is our County Connections Game. Make a spinner or bring some dice, gather some partners, and see who can be the first to travel our entire state! Along the way, we'll point out the beautiful landscapes to be seen. If you've been there, make sure you initial the county before you move ahead, lose a turn, or go backwards. You may wish to put a smiley face on the square that has your own county.

title: Discovering Nicolet
text:
In 1632, French explorer Jean Nicolet explored the "eastern shore" of Wisconsin. To honor Nicolet, 661,400 acres were set aside in 1933 as the Nicolet National Forest, a territory so big that it comes close to matching the size of Rhode Island.

The Nicolet is divided into four districts: Florence, Lakewood, Laona and Eagle River. The Nicolet includes 1,170 lakes, 580 miles of trout streams, 3,600 miles of back roads and 450 miles of snowmobile trails.

There are 960 plant species within the boundaries of Nicolet. Within any given four-square-mile area, you'll also find 64 species of wildlife, from fish to deer, bobcat, wild turkey and black bear.

If you hike, camp, or backpack, make sure you stop at the Lakewood ranger station. It has information about the forest's 22 campsites and other rustic camping spots. There's no end to the fun, or the trails. There are more than 800 miles of hiking, biking and skiing trails.

If you like to river raft, then you're in for the ride of a lifetime. The Wolf River starts out as a trickle about 25 miles south of the Michigan state line, then flows 223 miles to Lake Winnebago. The Wolf, like the animal for which it is named, has a wild personality. The river begins northeast of Antigo then curves south, eventually joining the lower Fox River and Lake Winnebago. You will notice that the river's gentle current changes without notice. It turns suddenly from calm water into a whitewater rollercoaster right before your eyes! The Wolf is at its snarliest as it dives nearly 1,000 feet, and then sails on through the canyons of the Menominee Indian Reservation near Shawano.

A segment of Wolf River, between Hollister and the Highway 64 bridge in Langlade, has been designated as a fly-fishing-only area.

If you're more of the type to enjoy Wolf River from a distance, there are many opportunities. Curl up on an overstuffed couch in one of the historic lodges near White Lake. From this lookout, you have a good view of the river and the feathery white rapids.

title: What is etymology (et-u-mall-u-jee)?
text:
It is History

It might sound like some scientific field or medical study, but etymology is the history of a word. Did you know that words can have histories, too? Where did words come from? Did someone just wake up one day and decide to name things randomly? Most words came about for a reason, and knowing the history of a word can help you understand its meaning.

Word histories can be fascinating. Some root words came from the ancient Greek and Latin languages. Others were borrowed from other languages, such as Spanish, French and German. And new words are added all the time.

For example, the word "kindergarten" means "children's garden" in German. The term was coined in 1840 by Friedrich Froebel to refer to his method of teaching young children.

Try It!

Below are some words and where they came from. Do some research and find out what each word originally meant, why it was invented and how its meaning has changed. Your community library should have an etymology dictionary, often called an Oxford English Dictionary. And you can find information on the Internet as well. One good site is http://www.etymonline.com/.

Here is an example of what a passage might look like in an etymology resource:

Algebra - From Arabia

Route - From France

Zero - From Arabia

Bronco - From Mexico

Gorilla - From Africa

title: Connecting Our Counties
text:
The largest of Wisconsin’s 72 counties is Marathon County at 1,545.1 square miles. Ozaukee County is the smallest with 232 square miles. Milwaukee County is ranked the highest in population density at 3,932.5 people per square mile, and Iron County has the lowest population density at 7.8 people per square mile.

Begin: Grant County, the most southwestern county of all, is our “Point of Beginnings.” The lead miners of the 1820s were among the first European settlers of Wisconsin. The state’s 1831 land survey began near Hazel Green. The first territorial government met at Belmont in 1836. Spin again or roll the dice to start your journey through the counties of Wisconsin!

How to Play

1. Two to four players can play the game at one time.

2. Make a spinner as shown above. It should have the numbers 1-6 on it. If you have dice, use one die.

3. Find a token, such as a coin, ring, plastic figure, or other small item.

4. Take turns flipping the spinner or rolling the die to see who is first. . . highest number wins. Move clockwise around the group.

5. On your turn, spin the spinner or roll the die and whichever number you get, move the token that number of spaces. Follow the instructions, if any, in the space. The first one to the finish line is the winner.

title: Birds and Mammals Love Wisconsin!
text:
Our state is the perfect home to millions of animals and birds. From black-capped chickadees darting from tree to tree, to wild black bears napping in the afternoon sun, creatures of all sorts and sizes love to call Wisconsin their home.

Just about every kind of animal can be found in Wisconsin. If not running wild in our wilderness areas, they can be found on farms and ranches and in zoos. Mammals are members of the highest class of animals. Mammals have backbones, milk glands to feed their young, and most (but not all) mammals have hair. Mammals include the largest animal, a sperm whale, and others such as the dog, cat, bat, elephant, hog, kangaroo, horse and humans! Birds are animals with feathers and wings.

Birds are the only animals with feathers, although some other animals, such as insects and bats, also have wings. Nearly all birds can fly, and all lay eggs where the babies develop outside of the mother's body.

Reptiles are animals with tough, dry skin covered with horny scales. Reptiles include turtles, lizards, snakes and alligators.

Fish are animals that live and breathe in water. They have gills for breathing, and most fish have fins for swimming and scales for protection.

When early explorers first visited our region, they hunted bear, fox, beaver and other furbearing animals. As more people moved into Wisconsin, many of the animals that lived in the wilds began to disappear. Hunters took them for food or fur, and lumberjacks took their homes by felling thousands of acres of trees.

By 1920, nearly all of our beaver, otters, muskrats and wild turkeys had all but vanished. People tried hard to start stronger programs of conservation to save our wild animals. Our timber industry worked hard to turn things around and began replanting thousands of acres with millions of trees. With a great deal of help and time, many wild animals began to return.

Among the thousands of species that breathe Wisconsin air, there are only 18 species on the threatened and endangered lists. In time, our state hopes to restore these animals to their habitat. With most species, you can find them in abundance. Every year, thousands of anglers fill up on the wonderful fish that swim in Lake Michigan and Lake Superior. Pike, sturgeon, muskellunge, walleye and trout are among the many game fish of Wisconsin's lakes and streams. The Lake Winnebago system contains the world's largest population of lake sturgeon, a living fossil fish.

White-tailed deer are found in most areas of Wisconsin, particularly in the northern cut-over areas, which supply tender shoots and twigs. Other mammals include black bear, badger, red and gray fox, porcupine, woodchuck, coyote, snowshoe hare, skunk, mink, beaver and muskrat. Among Wisconsin's game birds are pheasant, bobwhite, ruffed grouse and partridge. In recent years, the wild turkey has been reintroduced and is rapidly multiplying. Other common birds include the robin, wren, swallow, nuthatch and chickadee (has a distinctive call note).

title: Refill Not Landfill
text:
You probably know that drinking plenty of water is a great way to stay healthy. In the last few years, companies have started selling bottled water to make it easier for us to get a drink, even if we are away from home. While drinking lots of water is a great idea, buying lots of bottled water might not be. Have you ever stopped to think about where all of those empty plastic water bottles end up?

Nearly eight out of 10 plastic water bottles used each year in the United States end up in garbage. That is a lot of extra trash heading to the landfill. Plastic water bottles are made from oil products. In fact, it takes more than 1.5 million barrels of oil to make all the water bottles used in the United States each year. That is enough oil to run 100,000 cars for a year.

The answer isn't to stop drinking water, but to start using refillable containers instead. A refillable container is anything that you can refill, or use more than once. There are many types of refillable water bottles that you can use to carry water with you wherever you go. They are usually made of stainless steel or heavy-duty plastic. You can fill your container with water, wash it and use it again and again.

See just how easy it is to make a difference for our environment by choosing to use a refillable water bottle. If everyone did it, think how much nicer our world would be!

title: Wisconsin’s Wildlife
text:
It is difficult to imagine a place with more wildlife than Wisconsin. There are more varieties in our state than many other places in the world combined. Why? Because we still have a great deal of natural environment where animals can live in safety and raise families. Let's learn about a few creatures that love to call Wisconsin their home.

Wisconsin Mammals

Black Bear - Found throughout Wisconsin forests, these bears have thick, strong legs, big heads and small round ears. Wild black bears eat nuts, berries and insects. Black bears like to live alone, and some can weigh up to 310 pounds. Bears are smart and curious animals and can stand on their hind legs to smell and see better.

Gray Fox - The gray fox likes to live in wooded areas and among boulders on the slopes of rocky ridges in canyons and open desert. The gray fox is the only member of the dog family that can climb trees, usually to take a nap or in search of birds. It is fairly small and likes to hunt for small animals at night, but will also eat insects and berries.

Skunk - Best known for the stinky odor it produces, the spotted skunk gives warning by standing on its front feet and ejecting a spray. Skunks like to eat small mammals, birds, eggs and insects. Skunks typically adopt burrows or holes abandoned by other animals. They are very curious and will steal anything soft for their burrows.

Mink - Mink are members of the weasel family. They have long narrow bodies, short legs and relatively long tails. Mink make their homes in abandoned muskrat lodges and burrows along riverbanks and lake shores. A mink will often attack animals larger than itself. Mink feed on mice, small birds, frogs and fish.

Porcupine - The upper part of a porcupine is covered with thick, sharp, barbed quills mixed with longer, stiff guard hairs. Wild porcupines like to live in forests and eat twigs, leaves, flowers and seeds. Their hollow quills provide extra buoyancy in the water, making porcupines good swimmers. If a porcupine is cornered, it will attack by erecting all its quills and slapping the offender with its tail.

Woodchuck - The woodchuck, or groundhog, is a member of the squirrel family and lives in the woods or in brushy and rocky ravines. This rodent has short, powerful legs and a bushy tail. Woodchucks live in burrows and dig their tunnels three to six feet underground. Digging is done so rapidly that a small burrow can be finished in one day. Woodchucks play an important part in the lives of other animals by digging homes for skunks, foxes, weasels, opossums and rabbits.

Red Fox - The red fox has russet, or red-brown, fur, black ears and white fur on the under-parts. Red foxes tend to live near farmland, which provides them with a good ground and plenty of rats, squirrels, frogs and pheasants. It is afraid of humans and uses its keen sense to remain unseen. This fox is cunning and can adapt to most environments.

Coyote - Coyotes are members of the dog family. In size, the coyote is like a medium-sized collie dog. Coyotes can be found in low deserts and valleys or roaming in the mountains. The coyote frequently howls on bright, moonlit nights. The coyote's hearing is very sensitive, and its sense of smell is highly developed. Coyotes like to eat small mammals, insects, reptiles and fruit. They can run almost 40 mph.

Snowshoe Hare - The snowshoe hare has large hind feet covered in fur. These feet are perfect for jumping through deep snow, giving them the name "snowshoe." Snowshoe hares can be found in mixed spruce forests, wooded swamps and brushy areas. They feed on buds, twigs and leaves in the summer and needles, bark and buds of aspen and willow in the winter.

Beaver - The beaver is North America's largest rodent. It has a big body, webbed hind feet and a large flat tail. Beavers are found along rivers and small lakes. They have excellent engineering skills and spend much of their time building dams. They have a special digestive system that allows them to eat wood. The beaver also has a special respiratory system allowing it to stay underwater for 20 minutes.

Muskrat - Muskrats are excellent swimmers and thrive in lakes and rivers. Because they can tolerate some pollution in water, many are found living within large cities. Its entire body, with the exception of the tail and feet, is covered with waterproof, dark-brown fur. Its hairless tail helps it to swim. Muskrats live in large groups. They like to eat roots, stems and buds.

Wisconsin Game Birds

Pheasant - The common pheasant is also known as the ring-necked pheasant because of the white ring around the neck of males. Pheasants are colorful birds with feathers of red, purple, green and black. Pheasants live in open country, grain fields and prairie land. They nest on the ground and eat berries, seeds and worms.

Partridge - The species in this large family share plump bodies, short tails and short beaks, which they use to pick up seeds. They have strong breast muscles, which allow for explosive takeoffs to escape from predators. They prefer to run, and fly only short distances. Their habitats vary from rocky mountain slopes to forest floors, and only a few perch in trees.

Bobwhite - Named from the loud call of the male, the bobwhite is the most commonly hunted species of quail in the United States. These birds are reddish brown above and white on the belly. Bobwhites like to live in open country and grasslands. These birds gather in large groups of more than 100 and keep each other warm and protected by huddling in a circle. If frightened, they prefer to run from danger instead of fly.

Ruffed Grouse - The ruffed grouse is a member of the pheasant family and is about the size of a chicken. Because the grouse has short wings, it doesn't fly very much, but instead relies on camouflage and running for protection. This bird makes its home in coniferous forests, mountains and woodlands. The ruffed grouse likes to eat nuts, fruit and snails found on the forest floor.

Wild Turkey - The return of the wild turkey is one of the great success stories of wildlife management. After disappearing during Colonial times, the turkey is back and found in every state but Alaska. Wild turkeys are adapted to life on the ground and like to eat worms, insects and seeds. Because of their large, heavy bodies and short wings, they can fly only short distances.

Swallow - Swallows have long, pointed wings, round heads and small legs and feet. They like to eat flying insects and have short bills and wide mouths. There are many different species of swallow. The bank swallow is the smallest North American species. The largest is the purple martin. The cliff swallow and cave swallow build their nests in rows with mud pellets, sometimes on the outside walls of barns.

Nuthatch - These white-breasted birds have grayish-blue feathers on top and shiny black heads. The nuthatch is a climber and can move about using powerful feet and long claws. It climbs under branches and up and down tree trunks, searching for food. Nuthatches like to eat insects, larvae or eggs. Nuthatches live alone during the summer, but will join mixed flocks in the winter.

Wren - The wren is native to the North American continent. Most are small but highly vocal, and in many species, males and females sing duets. Wren have brown or black feathers on top and white below, sometimes with streaks or spots. Wrens either live in man-made bird boxes or build their own nests of twigs and grasses.

Chickadee - Chickadees are small North American birds with large heads, beady eyes and short bills. They can be found in forests and thickets throughout the northern United States and southern Canada. It's fun to watch these birds eat, either hopping from limb to limb or hanging upside down from a twig in search of food. These songbirds were named after their characteristic call note: "Chick-a-dee-dee."

Game Fish of Wisconsin's Lakes and Streams

Pike - These fish have long bodies, small scales, many bones and large, sharp-toothed jaws. They lurk in the weeds, preying upon fish, frogs and small mammals. Pike like to hunt alone, and they don't nest or tend eggs. Instead, they scatter their eggs about in the weeds, where the newly hatched try to find protection.

Walleye - The walleye is a spiny-rayed, freshwater fish that has a black dot on the first dorsal fin. This fish is native to the St. Lawrence, Great Lakes and Mississippi River basins. The walleye likes to eat crayfish and other fish. The walleye is considered to be an excellent game fish, reaching almost three feet long.

Muskellunge - This North American freshwater fish is found in the Great Lakes region and in the Northeast. It's an excellent game fish and can attain a length of eight feet and a weight of up to 100 pounds. The body is brown, spotted with black. It likes to eat other fish, ducklings and muskrats.

Trout - Brook trout are small fish that inhabit the cold, clear freshwater streams and mountain lakes. Some stay in lakes and streams for their entire lives, while some migrate to sea, returning only to lay their eggs or spawn. Most are greenish brown with red spots, but those at sea have shimmering dark blue backs and silver bellies. Brook trout like to eat water insects and crayfish.

Sturgeon - These giant fish can reach lengths of 13 feet. They feed on small animals and plants, which they swallow whole, because they don't have teeth. They like to live in coastal waters, rivers and seas of northern regions. The Atlantic sturgeon has been known to weigh up to 500 pounds.

title: Wisconsin Zoos
text: Have you visited a zoo in Wisconsin? Zoos are places to get up-close and personal with jaguars, parrots and hippopotamuses. The Henry Vilas Zoo offers free admission and was established on land donated by Colonel and Mrs. William Vilas in memory of their son. The Milwaukee County Zoo is Wisconsin's largest zoo and home to approximately 2,500 animals. Or make a trip to the North Eastern Wisconsin Zoo in Green Bay, which focuses on recreation, education and the conservation of selected endangered species. The Racine Zoo began in 1923 with a small collection of monkeys and goats. It has since expanded to cover 32 acres of Lake Michigan shoreline, providing homes for 250 animals. The Irvine Park Zoo was created in 1906 by William Irvine as a reserve that would enhance and protect the Chippewa Valley environment. Zoos make it possible to bring the "wild ones" home to Wisconsin land.

title: Endangered and Threatened Species
text:
Have you ever heard of the endangered- or threatened-species lists? Endangered means the species is in danger of extinction within the foreseeable future. "Threatened" refers to those animals and plants that are likely to become endangered within the foreseeable future. The Endangered Species Act established laws that would protect species from extinction. When the law was enacted, 109 species were listed for protection. Today, roughly 1,300 are on the list. A species is considered endangered or threatened because its habitat is being destroyed or overused for commercial, recreational or scientific use, disease and predation or other natural or man-made factors affecting its existence. Here are 18 endangered and threatened species in Wisconsin.

Indiana bat

Gray wolf

Piping plover

Kirtland's warbler

Higgins' eye pearly mussel

Winged maple leaf mussel

Sipper shell mussel

Karner blue butterfly

Hine's emerald dragonfly

Canadian lynx

Prairie vole

Wooly milkweed

Prairie bush clover

Dwarf lake iris

Fassett's locoweed

Northern wild monkshood
