title: What is the largest animal, and what is the smallest living organism?
text:
The blue whale is the largest animal living on Earth. It is also the loudest animal on Earth, even louder than a jet engine. Blue whales grow to be about 80 feet long and weigh 120 tons. Now that's huge!

Amoeba are among the smallest living organisms on the Earth. You can view them only through a microscope because they are unicellular. Unicellular means that their whole body is made up of one cell. Your body is made up of billions and trillions of cells.

title: Where do zoo animals come from?
text: About 99 percent of zoo mammals are bought, traded or loaned from other zoos around the country or the world. Some animals in captivity do well at having babies, and the young are happily adopted by other zoos. Sometimes, animals are donated by private owners. Some people try to steal or smuggle animals out of their home countries. When such people are caught, the animals are donated to a zoo if they cannot be returned to their natural habitat. Zoos often receive abused, neglected or confiscated wildlife. When such animals come to zoos, they are rarely kept very long before being sent to a safe animal sanctuary.

title: How Do I Give an Oral Presentation?
text:
Standing in front of a crowd and telling them what you think is not easy, but it can be done if you prepare well!

Preparing for an Oral Presentation

Know your audience. What you say should be directed toward them. Is it to be given in your classroom? This will make it easier!

How long should it be? If your teacher says 15 minutes, stick to the time.

What's the topic? Did your teacher assign it? Make sure you can cover it in within the time limit.

Make notes. Use index cards and put them in the order you want to use them. Index cards are not so large that they cover your face. You may write your presentation on numbered pieces of paper, but do not staple the pages.

Practice, practice and practice some more!

Making the Oral Presentation

Introduction - Get the audience's attention with the introduction. You can do this by asking a question, telling a story, using a quotation or making a statement. Once you have their attention, state your topic.

Body - State your main points and give information that supports your main points. You may ask rhetorical questions, (questions that don't need answers) use emotional words or repeat important information.

Conclusion - Repeat your main point. Conclude with something that leaves a lasting impression by asking a rhetorical question, making an emotional plea or using a quotation, story or statement.

Try It!

When you're asked to give an oral presentation, make sure you prepare well. Organize logically. Practice, practice, practice. Good luck!

title: Let's Write
text: If you had the chance to meet someone famous, who would you choose? Why? What would you ask him or her?

title: Famous Wisconsin People and Landmarks
text:
Wisconsin is the birthplace and home to many influential leaders and entertainers of our time. We celebrate these men and women by studying their history, naming buildings after them and building statues of them. We carry on the traditions they taught us and the ideals they lived up to. We remember them on certain holidays and read about them in school. We watch them on television and plaster posters of them on our bedroom walls. These are people who have made our lives better through technology, entertainment, music and literature. They governed the people, taught in schools and established societies. They helped to shape Wisconsin into a leading industrial state, a great-outdoors state and one of the top dairy states in the nation.

Some of these names you may already know. Others, you may be introduced to for the first time. Perhaps you will play an important role in the lives of others, and your name will be remembered as someone who did good for your country, a name that contributed to society, promising a better future for the next generation. Perhaps you'll be a great senator or governor. Maybe you'll educate millions on new space technology. Perhaps you'll teach small children math and science skills. Maybe you'll entertain America as one of the greatest actors or actresses who ever lived.

Historic landmarks are places where significant events occurred. Historic landmarks of our country include Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, where the Battle of Gettysburg took place during the Civil War. The Statue of Liberty, located in New York Harbor, was a gift from the people of France as a symbol of political freedom and democracy. And even the USS Arizona Visitor Center located on the Pearl Harbor Naval Base was built in memorial of those who died during the attack on Pearl Harbor during World War II. Today, these places are preserved and protected. When we visit these sites, we remember what took place there and why it's important in our lives today.

As we read about the famous men and women of Wisconsin and study the historical landmarks, decide which person is most like you. Are the landmarks important to you and why?

title: Seymour: Home of the Hamburger
text:
There are many interesting and unusual sites to see in Wisconsin, but there are few that are any more fun than the annual Burger Festival held in Seymour. Seymour is said to be the home of the first hamburger, invented by Charlie Nagreen in 1885. Charlie was selling meatballs at the Outagamie County Fair, but no one seemed to be buying them. Charlie realized that no one wanted to eat the messy meatballs while walking around the fair, so he quickly flattened out the meatballs, placed them between two slices of bread, and began selling the tasty new "hamburgers." The burgers were a hit and Charlie was known as "Hamburger Charlie" from that time on. To get more business, Charlie would often sing, "Hamburgers, hamburgers, hamburgers hot; onions in the middle, pickle on top. Makes your lips go flippity flop."

Today, Seymour calls itself the "Home of the Hamburger" and holds a Burger Festival on the first Saturday of each August. The festival is a great success and brings in visitors from all over. The festival includes a parade, a hamburger bun toss and, of course, a hamburger eating contest. While at the festival, be sure not to miss the very popular Ketchup Slide. Vivien Treml, a resident of Seymour, says, "You should really try the Ketchup Slide. That's where people pay to slide on a mixture of ketchup and water."

Several years ago, Seymour made it into the record books when it cooked up the world's largest hamburger as part of the annual Burger Festival. The burger weighed in at 8,266 pounds and was cooked on a grill the size of a two-car garage. The enormous grill is now on display at Seymour's Hamburger Hall of Fame, a museum in the city that shows off everything related to hamburgers.

If you love hamburgers, Seymour is the place for you. Plan a visit to this interesting city and see how Hamburger Charlie helped create one of the most popular sandwiches of all time, right here in Wisconsin.

title: Wisconsin People and Landmarks
text:
Pilots

In 1909, Arthur P. Warner, from Beloit, Wisconsin, bought the nation's first aeroplane and became Wisconsin's first pilot. Charles Lindbergh, known as the first man to fly across the Atlantic, attended the University of Wisconsin in Madison. Daniel C. Brandenstein, a NASA pilot from Watertown, was a crew member on three space shuttle missions. Admiral Marc A. Mitscher, from Hillsboro, was enlisted as a member of the International Aerospace Hall of Fame in 1989. Seventy years earlier, he served as a crew member on the first flight across the Atlantic in a Seaplane.

Sports

Bob Uecker was a sportscaster and baseball player, born in Milwaukee. Burleigh A. Grimes was a champ from Clear Lake and a National Baseball Hall of Fame pitcher for the New York Yankees, St. Louis Cardinals, Chicago Cubs, Boston Braves, Pittsburgh Pirates, New York Giants and Brooklyn Dodgers. The Green Bay Packers would have never made it to the Super Bowl without their Coach Vince Lombardi.

Movies and Television

You may not have heard of Robert Bloch from Milwaukee, but you've probably heard of the infamous Alfred Hitchcock thriller—"Psycho." Bloch wrote it. Harrison Ford attended college in Wisconsin before becoming a big star. John Hubley, a three-time Oscar winner, worked alongside Myron (Grim) Natwick. Both Wisconsinites animated Disney's "Snow White." Hubley animated other Disney films such as "Fantasia" and "Bambi." Natwick animated "Betty Boop." David Koepp, from Pewuakee, was the screenwriter of "Jurassic Park" in 1993 and "The Lost World" in 1997. Carl Laemmle lived in Oshkosh before starting Universal Pictures. Herbert Stothart, from Milwaukee, won an Oscar for composing the score to "The Wizard of Oz."

Architecture

Frank Lloyd Wright has made his artwork part of our nation's landscape. Born in the Richland Center in 1867, he designed more than 420 buildings. Wright is one of the most celebrated architects of our time.

Inventions and Technology

Before we had the computer, we had the typewriter thanks to Christopher Sholes, S. W. Soule and Carlos Glidden. These three inventors worked in Milwaukee designing various models of a typewriting machine. Sholes is given credit for having created the first workable typewriter, which he sold to the Remington Arms Company for $12,000 in 1873. Seymour R. Cray, from Chippewa Falls, developed the first commercial personal computer CDC 6600 and created many of the largest and fastest super-computers. Increase Allen Lapham, a scientist, was a strong influence in getting the U.S. government to set up the Weather Bureau in 1869. Lapham also explored Wisconsin American Indian mounds and helped establish Milwaukee-Downer College.

Vehicles

Don't forget Carl Eliason, from Sayner, who invented the snowmobile. And Harry Miller, from Menomonie, attached an engine to a bicycle, inventing the first motorcycle in 1898. The Pennington Victoria Automobile manufacturer, from Racine, invented the balloon tire. And Otto Zachow and William Besserdich, from Clintonville, developed the first successful four-wheel-drive automobile in 1908.

Food

George Hallaver, from Two Rivers, invented the ice cream sundae at Berner's Soda Fountain in 1881. Charlie Nagreen, a meatball vendor from Seymour, invented the hamburger in 1885.

Authors

Do you remember the children's classic "The Little Engine That Could," with those encouraging words, "I think I can. I think I can"? This story was written in 1912 by Frances Wiggins Ford from Footville. Do you ever watch "Little House on the Prairie?" It was inspired by Laura Ingalls Wilder, from Pepin, who wrote "Little House in the Big Woods."

Entertainers

Imagine monkeys with red vests, zebras with pink saddles and snarling tigers jumping through purple hoops. It's the circus! P. T. Barnum, from Delevan, co-founded Barnum & Bailey Circus in 1870. With the help of William Cameron Coup, also from Delevan, the three-ring circus was created. In 1884, the Ringling Brothers, Al, Charles, Alf, Otto and John, from Baraboo, also started a circus. The Ringling Brothers and Barnum & Bailey soon found each other and became the largest circus in the United States.

Household Names

Did you know that Dear Abby (Abigail Van Buren) and Ann Landers are from Eau Claire? These two women are celebrated for their advice columns in national newspapers. Millions seek their advice on relationships, business, etiquette and other problems. Oprah Winfrey, one of the most powerful talk-show hosts of a daytime talk show, spent her teen years in Milwaukee. There's an army of Barbie dolls today, but the original Barbie, the 11-inch fashion doll, was officially named Barbie Millicent Roberts. She was enrolled in the fictional Willows High School in Willows, Wisconsin.

Discoveries

E. V. McCollum, who studied at the University of Wisconsin, in Madison, discovered Vitamin A in 1913 and Vitamin D in 1916. Harry Steenbock, who also studied at the university, discovered in 1924 that Vitamin D is produced by exposure to the sun's ultra-violet rays. Roy Chapman Andrews, the world's top whale biologist, from Beloit, discovered the first known dinosaur eggs, huge fossil fields in Asia and evidence of the extinct land animal Baluchitherium.

Biggest and Largest

The Allen Bradley Clock Tower in Milwaukee has the largest four-faced clock in the world. The Biotron building at the University of Wisconsin in Madison, is the only laboratory in the world that can simulate any environmental condition. The House on the Rock Museum in Spring Green has the largest indoor carousel in the world. And the Soo Line Ore Dock, in Ashland, is the world's largest concrete dock and stretches 1,800 feet into Lake Superior.

title: Dedication to Work
text:
Success takes a great deal of endurance and work. Many of the great leaders and inventors of the past knew how to work hard. Abraham Lincoln was raised in poverty, but he became one of the nation's greatest presidents.

Franklin D. Roosevelt, also a president, had polio, but he was elected for four terms. Helen Keller, who went deaf and blind at an early age, graduated from college with honors, understood several languages and wrote several books. Before Albert Einstein became the most well-known scientist of the 20th century, his teachers called him a slow learner. Ludwig van Beethoven, who went deaf in his later years, continued to compose beautiful music. Winston Churchill, known as one of the greatest British leaders of the 20th century for his leadership during World War II, was labeled as dull, and he flunked the sixth grade.

A boy who loved to sketch was told that he had no talent. But he continued to draw, bringing entertainment to millions of people. His name is Walt Disney. These men and women worked hard through tough times.

title: Historical Markers
text:
Historic landmarks are special places, important people and memorable events that have helped make Wisconsin history. The first historical marker was placed near the Peshtigo Fire Cemetery. There are now about 500 markers throughout Wisconsin. New ones are added every year. If a person or a group wants a site to be recognized with a historical marker, they must complete a Wisconsin Historical Marker Application from the Wisconsin Historical Society. The Historical Markers Program coordinator reviews the application.

New applications are reviewed every three months by historians, archaeologists, preservationists and other professionals at the Historical Society. The cost of the marker is paid for by the people or group of people who nominate the site. They also pay for the installation of the marker, and they must agree to keep the marker in good condition. Official State of Wisconsin Historical Markers are informational signs with words that tell why the site is important. Each marker has the state animal, the badger, at the top of the marker with the words "Wisconsin Historical Marker" surrounding the badger.

title: Historic Landmarks
text:
Aztalan State Park near Lake Mills is the site of a former American Indian village. Old Wade House in Greenbush is a restored stagecoach inn and includes a museum of antique carriages, wagons and sleighs. Old World Wisconsin, near Eagle, is an outdoor museum containing examples of farmhouses erected by German, Norwegian, Danish and Finnish immigrants in the 19th century. These sites remind us of the people and events of the past. Many of these sites add to the beauty of Wisconsin's land and are well preserved and protected.

In Baraboo, you'll find the Ringling Brothers Circus Winter Quarters. With the purchase of the Barnum & Bailey Circus, they owned the largest circus in history.

The meetings held at the Little White Schoolhouse in Ripon were the first of those that led to the formation of the Republican Party.

The Pabst Theater in Milwaukee is the best-preserved German- American theater in the United States and is a reminder of the cultural role of Milwaukee.

The Milton House and the nearby log Goodrich Cabin served as stops on the Underground Railroad. Fugitive slaves could enter the cabin, open a trapdoor and make their way through a tunnel to the Milton House. The Goodrich family provided food, shelter and assistance to reach their next stop on their way to Canada and freedom. Constructed in 1828, the Astor Fur Warehouse made the city of Prairie Du Chien a prominent fur trading center.

title: President Ronald Reagan and the USSR
text:
Three decades ago a first class stamp cost fifteen cents. A Macintosh was not a computer; it was an apple that grew on a tree. And the United Soviet Socialist Republic (USSR or Soviet Union) was a threat to the safety and freedom of the United States and the world. All of those things were going on in 1981 when Ronald W. Reagan became our 40th president. President Reagan served for two terms, and by the time he left office in 1989 the world was becoming a much different place.

When President Reagan was first elected, the USSR had a communist government. Under communism, the government controls all industry, and the citizens do not have the same rights and freedoms as we have in America. The USSR and the United States were in what was called a Cold War. The two countries never actually went to war, but we came very close. President Reagan understood how dangerous the Cold War was for both countries and for the whole world.

Making the world a safe, free place for all people was one of President Reagan's main goals as president. He spent many years negotiating with Soviet leaders, especially Mikhail Gorbachev, to end the Cold War. In 1991, the USSR split into 15 different countries and the Cold War came to an end. Having clarity of thought means that you are able to think and understand things clearly. President Reagan's clarity of thought played a vital role in ending the Cold War.

title: How Do I Listen to an Oral Presentation?
text:
Listen closely to your classmates when they give presentations. Pay attention. You can learn a lot from them. Your teacher may tell you to take notes. You may also be asked to make written comments. Also, it's just plain polite to be a good listener!

Be an active listener. Don't daydream. Focus on the speaker's main idea. Listen for the way he or she ties details to that main idea. Take notes, either in your mind or on paper.

Your teacher may help you to evaluate (to examine and judge carefully) your classmates' presentations. Keep in mind that being honest can help your classmates learn how to give better presentations.

You may not agree with everything the speaker says, but you should listen to his or her ideas.

Don't interrupt your classmate unless he or she has asked for you to join in.

Think about the speaker's conclusion. Is it logical?

Try It!

When your classmates give presentations, be a good listener. It will help them feel more comfortable. Make eye contact. Your evaluation will help them improve their future presentations. And you might learn something. Besides, you will want them to listen to you when it is your turn to give an oral presentation.

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you are a travel agent in our state. Write about a place you would recommend that tourists see. Why do you think it’s a nice place to visit? What kinds of things will visitors learn at this place?

title: Edward M. Bannister
text: Edward Bannister changed the way people think about his people. Edward was a black man born in Canada. As a young man, he worked as a ship’s cook. After he moved to Boston, he worked as a barber. He took night classes to learn to paint. Then one day in 1867, he read an article in a newspaper. It said that people with his skin color could like art, but could not produce it. He didn’t believe that. He decided to prove it wasn’t true. He succeeded nine years later. He was the first African American to receive a national art award. After that, he could afford to paint full time. Sadly, most people still didn’t know about him until the 1960’s. Since then, many of his paintings have been found.

title: Wisconsin’s Amazing Legends and Lore
text:
Legends and lore are the sparkling threads of mystery and intrigue that are woven through the history of every civilization that has ever graced the Earth.

There are plenty of legends and lore among the residents of ancient and modern Wisconsin. Some are wonderfully true, and others are complete lies. A legend is a story that many people believe but that can't be easily proven. You've heard of the giant lumberman, Paul Bunyan. He is a good example of a great legend that grew up during the early days of the lumberjacks.

Whether legends are true or not, all societies enjoy their own collections of tales. Many are centuries old and have been passed from generation to generation. Such tales inspire greatness, encourage caution or wisdom or promise rewards for good living and correct choices. Other stories try to explain history. The Old Testament talks about a great flood that covered all the Earth and was survived by Noah and his family. Meanwhile, a Chippewa legend claims that a man named Nanabozho shot the Great Serpent with an arrow, and the dying serpent then caused an Earth-wide flood. And now scientists have discovered signs of human habitation on the bottom of the Black Sea, under 300 feet of sea water, certainly the ancient victims of a terrible and massive flood. So, what then is fact and what is legend?

As you might expect, legends and lore are subject to change. "Lore" is information about a particular subject. What may start as a true story, or local lore, sometimes becomes unbelievable as little details are changed or forgotten over time. Or what started as a great tall tale becomes truth for the same reasons. For a good example of both, go ask grandpa about what it was like walking to school when he was a boy. You might hear something like this: "Why, when I was your age, I had to walk to school in 10 feet of snow in my bare feet, and it was uphill both ways!" Discovering the truth is what makes legends so much fun to learn and investigate.

Some legends and lore are rumors made up to hurt people. Others are based on fact, such as some of Wisconsin's great sports stars who performed athletic feats unmatched by anyone since. Sometimes, great people are honored by being called "legends in their own time."

title: Does Bigfoot Live in Wisconsin?
text:
You have probably heard stories of Bigfoot, but did you know that there are people right here in Wisconsin who claim to have seen the huge monster? A team of researchers even spent some time here recently, hoping to find the hairy beast, but no one has ever been able to prove that Bigfoot really exists.

About 60 researchers from the Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization recently visited a marshy area of northern Wisconsin, hoping to see the mysterious monster. The researchers didn't find any evidence of Bigfoot, but they aren't giving up. Matt Moneymaker, head of the group, claims to have seen the monster dozens of times. He believes that there are up to 200 of the creatures living in Wisconsin and says that in the past, he has heard the monsters right here in our state. Describing a camping trip several years ago, Moneymaker says, "We definitely had some action there. At one point, they (Bigfoot) approached our tent. We heard them. They were around."

People who have seen Bigfoot say that it is a tall, hairy, very smelly creature that lives in the woods and only comes out at night. Legends of similar creatures are told all over the world. You may have heard stories about Sasquatch, Bigfoot or even MoMo, the Missouri Monster. If you have seen "Rudolph, the Red-Nosed Reindeer," you've heard of the Abominable Snowman, or Yeti, as it is called in Tibet.

No one knows for certain if these huge monsters are real, or if they live only in legends. Most researchers believe that Bigfoot is an imaginary monster based on legends, hoaxes and practical jokes. There are some, however, who believe that Bigfoot is real, so they continue to search for proof. Until someone proves for certain that Bigfoot doesn't really exist, there will be those who continue to search for this legendary beast - even right here in Wisconsin.

title: Wisconsin Legends and Lore
text:
There are many legends, tales, stories and events that add flavor and wonder to our state. People of all gifts and talents have added to our culture in ways that will never be forgotten. Let's look at a variety of legends in Wisconsin. We can't list them all, but here's a sampling.

The Legend of Wisconsin River

This river, 430 miles long, is swimming with tales, lore and legends of river men and entrepreneurs, stalwarts, scoundrels and dreamers. Stories of buried treasure, whether they were true or not, were told often enough to make searchers dig plenty of holes all over the area. The yellow-colored rock at Bogus Bluff, along Highway 60, was thought by some early settlers to contain gold. Rumors spread that cash was stashed in caves alongside the river. Many believed these tales and investigated the river for years.

Northern Lights

The aurora borealis, another name for the Northern Lights, have intrigued people since ancient times. The Eskimos and natives of North America have many explanations for the Northern Lights. Imagine living through a few months each year when the sun does not rise very high in the sky and there are hours of darkness. The Menominee Indians of Wisconsin explain these lights as torches used by great, friendly giants in the north, to spear fish at night.

Harry Houdini - Legendary Magician

Born in 1874, in Hungary, Harry Houdini is a familiar name to millions. When he was young his family sailed to the United States and settled in Appleton. Houdini began his career in 1882 as a trapeze performer. Soon he became world famous for his magic performances. He showed astounding ability in escaping from handcuffs, ropes, locked trunks and bonds of any sort. He left his library of magic, one of the most valuable in the world, to the Library of Congress.

Paul Bunyan and Babe

The tale of Paul Bunyan and his blue ox, Babe, is fascinating. Paul was born in Maine and arrived in Wisconsin in early manhood. His greatest logging camp was 40 miles from Rhinelander. Paul was a giant. His feet were enormous and left footprints forming the lakes of northern Wisconsin. Paul's voice was so strong that as a boy, he could kill a pond of bullfrogs with one "holler." Paul was a great hunter. He could shoot so far with his muzzle loader that he had to rub salt on the bullets to preserve the game until he got there. Babe was born the winter of the blue snow. Babe measured 42 ax handles across. For snacks, Babe ate 50 bales of hay. In the late 1800s, someone reported an ax found near Birchwood "with the pointed end embedded in the soil." The ax measured 28 inches long, 14 inches wide and 11 inches thick. It weighed 300 pounds! Could it have been Paul Bunyan's?

Green Bay Packers

The Green Bay Packers are a legendary team, winning 13 National Football League championships. That's more than any other franchise. They won three titles before 1933, when the NFL held its first championship game. They have won four Super Bowls. The Packers were founded by Curly Lambeau, who was a player, coach and vice president. He led the Packers to six world championships and is one of only five coaches to record more than 200 coaching victories in the NFL.

Mike Webster

Born in Tomahawk, Wisconsin, this Pro- Football Hall of Fame member played for the Pittsburgh Steelers and Kansas City Chiefs. He started in 150 consecutive regular season games and played in six AFC championship games. A player in four Super Bowl championship teams, he's received nine Pro-Bowl honors and six All-Pro honors.

Can Cows Be Tipped?

Is it possible to tip Wisconsin dairy cows? These beasts aren't easily toppled. Ranging from 1,500 pounds when fully grown to 500 pounds at a few months old, these animals are very alert, and it's almost impossible to walk up to a standing cow and have it remain asleep. Popular opinion says that cow tipping is a fun rumor. However, there are a few rope tricks that put pressure on the cow's spine and make it lie down peacefully. So if the cow was cooperative enough to let you wrap the rope around it, this might be perceived at a distance as cow tipping. So has cow tipping ever really been done? Probably. Is it done regularly? No.

Loch Ness Monster

For at least 1,500 years, a legend has held sway in the Scottish Highlands that Loch Ness is home to a mysterious aquatic animal. Some even claim that it has visited the Great Lakes. In Scottish folklore, large animals have been associated with many bodies of water, from small streams to the largest lakes. These water-horses, or water-kelpies, are said to have magical powers and evil intentions. Legend, lore or truth, you ask? Well, one agency has received more than 4,000 eyewitness accounts of the animal, described as a large creature with one or more humps, two fin-like arms and a long slender neck. Few can explain these sightings. One Loch Ness fan proposed that the monster was a plesiosaur, an ancient reptile that was thought to have gone extinct along with the dinosaurs some 65 million years ago. Or perhaps the sightings were optical illusions caused by boat wakes, wind slicks, floating logs, otters, ducks or swimming deer. The Loch Ness monster continues to stir up curiosity from children to marine biologists all around the world. Legend, lore or truth, what do you think?

Bigfoot

Bigfoot is described as an ape-like creature reportedly sighted hundreds of times in the United States and around the world since the mid-19th century. Standing 7-10 feet tall, with footprints 17 inches long and weighing more than 500 pounds, this creature is known for its enormous size and dark gray hair. Wisconsinites say that they have spotted this hairy beast by Black River and Rice Lake in Wisconsin. Could it really be a Sasquatch? Bigfoot? Yeti? Abominable Snowman? Or just a really tall, hairy guy carrying breakfast? Most scientists don't believe in the existence of such a creature because there are no artifacts, no bones, no dead bodies and no evidence. What do you think?

Gargoyle on the University of Wisconsin Law Building

Gargoyles graced the roof of the original University of Wisconsin Law Building, built on Bascom Hill in 1893. The building was torn down in 1962, and the dean preserved one of the gargoyles in storage. When the new building opened, Dean Young had it installed outside the main entrance. Over the next 30 years, the gargoyle once again watched over the school. Gargoyles originally appeared on French gothic cathedrals. From the beginning, they had at least two purposes: to drain rain water off the roof of the building and to scare away evil spirits. Perhaps this gargoyle should be credited with the good fortune of this law school and its graduates, or not. What do you think?

title: Ghost Towns
text: Have you ever roamed through the woods, or hiked across abandoned prairies, and stumbled upon a water well in the middle of nowhere? You probably walked into a ghost town (abandoned town). Wisconsin has five known ghost towns that were once villages settled during the lumbering industry. Donaldson in Vilas County was abandoned around 1920. All that is left are the steps of the old Donaldson School. La Crosse, on an island in the Mississippi River, was one of the first towns. After the jail was abandoned, people reported seeing ghosts at the jail. Strange paranormal activities have also been reported in Goodrich, a small town in Taylor County. All that remains is the foundation of an old school, an abandoned tavern and church. Witcome, in Shawano County, is still inhabited with 15 residents, a schoolhouse, a few homes and a bar (closed). Built in 1831, alongside the Mississippi River, Sinipee was for a short time a very busy area and shipping port. The town boasted a hotel where two future presidents stayed. The hotel foundation can still be seen.

title: Legend and Lore of Constellations
text:
Some of the oldest legends in the world are the constellations in the night sky. A constellation is a group of stars that form a shape most people recognize, such as a bear, a throne or a scorpion. They are totally imaginary things that the Greeks made up over the past 6,000 years. The real purpose for the constellations is to help us tell which stars are which. On a really dark night, you can see about 1,000 to 1,500 stars. According to some American Indian legends, the bowl of the Big Dipper is a giant bear and the stars of the handle are three warriors chasing it. The constellation is low in the sky in autumn, so it was said that the hunters had injured the bear and its blood caused the trees to change color to red.

The center of our galaxy, the Milky Way, lies in the direction of a constellation named Sagittarius. Hydra is the largest constellation on the sky. Hydra, also called the serpent of Lerna, was a beast with the body of a hound and 100 serpentine heads. As if this weren't bad enough, it also had poisonous breath and it was so hideous that it caused most people to die of fear from simply seeing it.

Constellations are very old and fun legends known around the world.

title: What is the most well known legend of our time?
text: This legend has many names and many heroes. It is one of the most well-loved and immortal stories of time. Some call it Camelot, Sword in the Stone, Arthurian legends, the Quest for the Holy Grail or the King and his Knights of the Round Table. To most it is known simply as the King Arthur Legend. The legend includes names such as Merlin, Guinevere, Lancelot, Galahad and Excalibur. Why has it become the favorite legend of time? To many, it is the allure of the "brief, shining moment" when chivalry was in style. Beautiful pieces of literature, film and music have been created about this legend. Perhaps it's because these very human characters feel and think in the way we do now. Some wish to be invincible knights, kings, beautiful princesses or wizards. The Arthurian legends are full of magic and wonder that capture the hearts of all ages.

title: Ever Been on a “Snipe Hunt”?
text: A well-known practical joke involves a group of people taking someone into the woods at night on a "snipe hunt." The person is told to lay in wait with a gunnysack to try to catch a snipe. After a few hours, this individual finally realizes he's been tricked - his "friends" have abandoned him in the woods, and there's really "no such thing as a snipe." But snipe ARE real birds. The Common Snipe was previously a popular game bird during the hunting days of the 1800's. But after a sudden drop in the snipe's population, the season was closed, and remained closed for 50 years. When it finally reopened, hunters had already turned their attention to larger game birds such as ducks, pheasants, grouse and others. Snipe hunting never again became popular, although most states still have a fall hunting season for this marsh bird.

title: How do I create an outline?
text:
You can use an outline to help you organize your nonfiction writing, especially when writing reports and research papers. An outline will help you effectively plan your writing.

Start with I, then II and III...

This list will help you create an outline:

Formal outlines have the main topics in Roman numerals (I, II, III...).

Subtopics are indented and listed with capital letters (A, B, C...).

Supporting details are indented more than subtopics and listed with Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3...).

More details that support those supporting details are indented more and listed with lowercase letters (a, b, c...).

You must have at least two items at each level.

To the right is a sample outline that someone might put together for a report on World War II.

Try It!

The next time you have to write a nonfiction piece, such as a report, write an outline first. You'll be amazed how it will help you organize your information and include all the important details.

title: Let's Write
text: Write about a legendary person who you feel has made a big impact on your life or our state. The person may be real or make believe. Explain why this person is so important and the things he or she has accomplished. How has your life been helped by this person?

title: Ojo de Dios
text:
This is an authentic and beautiful American Indian design.

Materials

popsicle sticks or tongue depressors

glue

yarn

pompoms

Directions

1. Find two popsicle sticks or tongue depressors. Glue them into a cross. Start the weaving by gluing the yarn to the back side of the sticks.

2. Start a crisscross pattern with the yarn. Continue to loop the yarn around the four ends of each stick. Keep the yarn fairly tight.

3. Continue the same pattern development, remembering to loop the yarn over each stick end in a like manner. Other colors may be added by tying new string to the old yarn. Make sure the knot is hidden behind the stick.

4. The work can be finished by tying the remaining yarn end onto the back of the design. Small pompoms can be attached to the end of the sticks.

Extra Activity

After you have mastered a small one, try a larger one!

title: History of Mapmaking
text:
Most people have seen a map or used one in their lifetime. What exactly is a map, and where did they begin? A map is a set of symbols that represents an area. Maps are the world reduced down to points, lines and areas, using resources like size, shape, texture, color, or pattern. A thin line will usually mean something very different from a thick one.

How do maps represent what the Earth, country, state, or city really looks like? Well, most mapmakers use symbols, points, lines and colors to show information about a certain place. Most maps have a legend, which shows what the symbols mean.

How old are maps? Evidence of mapmaking has been found in artifacts from all over the world. Ancient people carved lines and figures in clay, ivory, stone and even printed them on silk!

One of the earliest examples of a map comes from the Middle East. At a site in the ancient city of Nuzi (in present-day Iraq) archaeologists excavated (uncovered) a clay disk that dates from 6200 B.C. The small map shows a river and has place names written on it. Maps from ancient times have also been found in Egypt.

The Chinese were mapmakers as well. Silk maps found in tombs in the Hunan Province date from around the second century B.C. Also around that time, Greek geographer Eratosthenes was determining the circumference of the Earth. Eratosthenes knew that the Earth was round long before Columbus sailed the ocean blue! A Greek mathematician named Ptolemy was the first person to come up with the basic ideas of latitude and longitude. He used these ideas to make a map of the Earth around the year A.D 150. His maps and others that came later were added to and changed by explorers.

In the 1400s, a European named Martin Behaim created a globe that showed the world as Europeans knew it before the time of Columbus. Maps got more accurate as cartographers had better tools and technology available to them. What about maps today? You can type your destination into a smart phone, and within seconds have a detailed map of the area. Satellites and computers have made maps easier to use.

Maps are used for finding out which direction to go, what highway to take, or how many miles you are from somewhere else. They are also used to show where earthquakes occur, what the population density is - how many people per square mile - and where forests and deserts are.

As you can see, there are many uses for maps, and they have been around for a very long time. They may be changing the way they look, but maps will probably never go away because of how important they are in our lives.

title: Treasure Hunting
text:
"Got it!" shouts Tiffany Gonzales as she pulls a small container from the top of a fence. Tiffany is the advisor of the geocaching club at the University of Wisconsin-Stevens Point, and she has just found the "treasure" she has been looking for. She signs her name on a piece of paper inside the container, adds the date and puts the treasure back for someone else to find. Another geocaching adventure has come to an end.

What is geocaching? It is an amazing new form of treasure hunting that uses a GPS (Global Positioning System) device instead of a map to find different locations. "Geo" means geography and "caching" means hiding a treasure in a hidden place. Geocachers visit websites such as www.geocaching.com to get instructions for different treasure hunts in their area. They then use their GPS devices to guide them to the treasure. Sometimes, the treasure is nothing more than a recycled margarine tub with a geocache log and a pencil inside. Other times, the treasure may include prizes such as plastic toys, key chains or small whistles.

There are a few simple rules for geocachers:

Respect the environment.

Do not place caches on private property.

If you take something from the cache, leave something of equal value behind.

Write about your find in the cache logbook.

Never move a cache to a different spot.

To find out more about this great mapping activity, ask a teacher or parent to help you visit www.geocaching.com.

title: The Road Map
text:
1890s Horseless carriages were being invented around this time. The problem, however, was that there weren't any good roads to travel on, and the roads that were around had no route numbers. The maps that were used during this time were just as bad as the roads.

1900s There were many automobile manufacturers, and cars were being purchased by the wealthy people, but the roads were still terrible, and there were laws restricting the use of motorcars. Maps during this time were usually just used for route descriptions or photo guides. There were still no route numbers, so they were not very helpful. Photo route guides were often used to help early drivers navigate. Most maps were difficult to read.

1910s Roads were very expensive to build even in the early 1900s. Cars were not very popular, and no one wanted to pay taxes to have the roads built. In 1911, the American Automobile Association (AAA) began to publish some of their own road maps. They had route descriptions, which were a way of getting around, but you always had to keep an eye on the odometer (an instrument that shows how many miles have been traveled by a vehicle). Colorful signs were being put up all over, identifying major routes such as the Lincoln Highway, National Old Trail, Dixie Highway and others. The biggest news of the time was how Wisconsin was beginning a program to number its roads.

1920s Road surfacing had begun in the '20s, but the roads were still not paved. Maps, which were black and white before, began to use colors to indicate the best roads. The AAA published their first TourBook in 1926. That was the year that many roads received the U.S. Highway designation. The black-and-white shields that you see on highways today began to spring up everywhere. It was possible to travel from coast to coast by following the same route numbers between states.

1930s Although the Great Depression occurred during the 1930s, people were given work with paving roads. Road maps were improved as far as detail, color, readability and reliability. The AAA was sending out "pathfinders" to travel the roads, measure the distances and note construction, surface, etc.

1940s The Pennsylvania Turnpike opened in 1940, but World War II was also around the corner. Tourism almost ended. Gasoline was rationed, maps weren't printed and road building stopped. After the war, however, many families had a car, and travel was at an all-time high.

1950s People began to spend more time sitting at traffic lights than actually moving. President Eisenhower saw how the German Autobahns worked and how quickly vehicles and equipment could be moved. The National System of Interstate and Defense Highways was born. Initially, Route 66 was to be used for the military in the early Cold War era, but travel began to take over.

1960s The big changes of the 1960s were the new interstates. These roads limited entrances and exits to interchanges. There were no more traffic lights, restaurants, attractions, cabins, or other things along the road. Maps showed the interstates as proposed, under construction and completed. Maps were nearly in full color and showed parks, military bases and more. Such maps were issued for the World's Fairs and Olympic Games and even to help people visit the Civil War battlefields and historic sites.

1970s Travel grew quickly until 1973, when the oil supplies became a problem. Prices began to rise, and lines of vehicles could be found where gasoline was available. Things were stable again for a few years, but in 1979, the problems occurred again. More and more miles were added to the interstate system, and more maps were put out, becoming even easier to read.

1980s Increased use of trucking caused deterioration in the interstate system. By the 1980s, not many oil companies bothered with maps. If motorists wanted maps, they had to buy them, get them through the highway departments, or join AAA.

1990s to present The digital revolution is changing the way we look at maps, and it started in the 1990s. There is ever-increasing accuracy in maps. Maps can be printed from computer programs and the Internet. And Global Positioning Satellite systems allow in-vehicle navigation. People still use paper maps, however.

title: Outagamie County
text:
Outagamie County was created in 1851 after it was split from Brown County. Outagamie County covers only 640 square miles and is located in east-central Wisconsin. The region was once the hunting and fishing grounds for several American Indian tribes, including the Menominee, Outagamie and Winnebago. "Outagamie" is derived from an American Indian word meaning "dwellers on either shore" or "dwellers (people who live in a certain area) on the side of the stream."

In 1643, French explorer Jean Nicolet was the first European to the area. In 1837, Charles Grignon, a French fur trader, built his "mansion in the woods," which is still the oldest house in Outagamie County. Dutch, German, Polish, Irish and Laotian people soon followed.

There are around 175,000 residents within Outagamie County. Approximately one-fourth of the United States population lives within 500 miles of Outagamie County. The water from the nearby Fox River provided the beginning of what became, and still is, the world-renowned paper industry. The river provided the power for the first flour and wool mills in the area. They were later converted to paper mills for Kimberly-Clark, Appleton Papers, Wisconsin Tissue and Menasha Corporation. Because of this, the area has earned the nickname "the Paper Valley."

There are also plastics, printing and graphic arts, machinery, metals, electronics and food processing. Dairy and farming are the strong parts of the agribusiness of Outagamie County, as well as trade and service industries.

title: Global Positioning System
text:
Many people have been curious about who created Global (involving the whole Earth) Positioning Systems (GPS). Many different people, companies and fields of science created GPS.

On June 26, 1993, the United States Air Force launched the 24th Navstar satellite into orbit. This completed the network of satellites that were known as the Global Positioning System.

Trimble, a company that claims to be "a leading innovator of GPS technology," stated that the United States Department of Defense developed GPS for use at sea during the Cold War. The military needed a way to pinpoint the exact positions of surfaced submarines in a matter of seconds.

GPS uses the satellites—or "man-made-stars"—as reference points to calculate positions as accurate as a centimeter.

The final cost of developing this system, however, was $12 billion!

title: How does geography affect culture?
text: Land barriers like mountains, rivers, oceans and deserts, often separate people. When such a barrier is large, people often cannot get around it to visit other people. It is during times like this that people and cultures (social behaviors, arts, beliefs and other thoughts) find that it is hard to share their cultures or beliefs with anyone else. This is when groups often begin to develop distinctive languages, beliefs, ideas, etc. This often helps develop completely new cultures.

title: The Black Bear
text:
One of the largest concentrations (amounts of a specified thing) of black bears in North America is found on Stockton Island in Apostle Islands National Lakeshore. The black bears are the most numerous and widespread North American bears. Though the black color phase is most common, "black" bears can be brown or even white. Adult males usually weigh from 250 to 400 pounds, while females weigh between 150 and 225 pounds. They are omnivorous (eat both meat and plants) and depend a great deal on their sense of smell to find food. They can run up to 30 miles per hour and climb trees and they are great swimmers.

Studies have shown that, although black bears are classified as carnivores (flesh-eating animals), they are true omnivores. Vegetables are generally more than half of the bear's diet, with insects and other animals making up a small part. They particularly like fresh leaves, fruits, berries, nuts, roots and tubers (stubby, fleshy parts of a plant, like potatoes) and eat insects and small mammals when the opportunity presents itself.

title: Let's Write
text: Do you know someone who has an exciting career? Write about it.

title: How Do I Read Historical Fiction?
text:
Treat It As Art Full of Historical Facts

While nonfiction is about information, fiction is all about creativity. Reading fiction can be exciting and moving. When you read fiction, you are trying to understand a character deeply. Imagine the story as you read the words, reflecting on the events in the story and exploring the ideas and feelings created by the story.

Historical Fiction

Fictional pieces are imaginary stories, but they can be based on historical facts. Fictional stories based on historical facts are called “historical fiction.” When reading historical fiction, it is important that you understand which details are factual and which are fictional. Sometimes, you need to do background research on your story before you can understand the difference between fact and fiction in a story that is historical fiction. Fiction is the most popular genre of literature and ranges from short stories (a page or two) to novels (up to thousands of pages). Fiction has three basic elements: characters, plot and setting.

Characters

The characters are the people (or animals) in the story. In well-written fiction, the writer will describe what the characters look like, how they act, what they think and feel, what others say about them, what they talk about and many other details. Because of this, you will finish reading it and feel like you know some of the characters very well, like friends or family. Sometimes, they will seem like real-life people. Characters in historical fiction can help you understand what it felt like to live through that event or period. Most stories have a main character, or protagonist.

Plot

The plot is what happens in a novel or story. It is the sequence of events. Generally, fictional writing begins with a conflict, or a problem that needs to be resolved. The events that happen after the conflict is introduced are called the rising action. The rising action draws out the character’s problem. The story’s turning point is called the climax. This is when there is a dramatic shift in the story, especially regarding the conflict. In the end, the conflict is resolved or changed into a different conflict. This is called the falling action. You can illustrate how a story’s plot goes with a graph like this:

The plot in historical fiction will often follow a timeline of actual historical events, adding fictional details along the way.

Setting

The setting is the time and place in which the story happens. Stories can take place in the past, present or future and can last anywhere from one day to several years. Stories can also take place in a single room or city, or the action might happen in one big country or a planet. In historical fiction, the setting is, of course, in the past. If you imagine yourself in the setting of historical fiction, you will understand what conditions were like back then.

Theme

The theme of a fictional work is the idea that the author is examining in the work. The theme is a general topic, which allows the author to do a great deal of exploration.

Try It!

The next time you read a story or novel that is historical fiction, identify the main characters, the plot, the setting and the theme. You can even plot the theme as shown above. Think about the details in the story. Ask yourself which details are probably historical fact and which ones are fiction created by the author. Doing this will help you more fully understand the historical context being represented.

title: Physical Characteristics
text: Physical characteristics describe the natural environment of an area. Landscapes, plants, climate, and animals are physical characteristics. Bodies of water, including rivers, streams, lakes, and oceans, are also physical characteristics. Landforms are also a physical characteristic of an area. Some examples of landforms are mountains, plains, valleys, and deserts. These characteristics are all connected and help geographers describe different areas on the Earth’s surface. Physical characteristics are what make the Earth interesting and unique! A physical map shows the world's major physical features. Look at the physical map of the United States. Can you locate the rivers? Can you identify the surrounding oceans?

title: Physical Features of Florida
text:
Landforms are natural shapes that make up the Earth's surface. There are many types of landforms. They come in different shapes and sizes. Landforms are on the Earth's outer layer. This layer is called the crust. Most landforms take hundreds or thousands of years to form. The most common type of landforms located in Florida are hills, wetlands, rivers, lakes, bays, plains, and islands.

Hills

Hills are landforms that rise slightly above the land around them. Hills are smaller than mountains. The tallest point in Florida is Britton Hill, located in Defuniak Springs. It stands at 345 feet above sea level.

Wetlands

Wetlands are areas of land where water covers the soil at varying levels all year round. There are different types of wetlands in Florida. Swamps and marshes are common types of wetlands in Florida. Swamps are forested wetlands that include many different types of trees and vegetation. Marshes are wetlands that are dominated by grasses and reeds. There are freshwater and saltwater wetlands in Florida. The largest wetland in the state is the Florida Everglades, which is the largest marsh system in the United States.

Rivers

Rivers are large, flowing bodies of water that move across the land. Rivers often flow into other rivers or a larger body of water, such as a pond, lake, ocean, bay, gulf, or sea. Florida is home to over 1,700 rivers, which cover an area of 25,949 miles. The Apalachicola River is the longest river that flows through Florida, while the St. Johns River is the longest river contained within the borders of the state.

Lakes

A lake is a body of water with land on all sides. Lakes can be natural or human-made. Florida is home to over 30,000 lakes. The largest of the state’s lakes is Lake Okeechobee, covering 448,000 acres. Lake Okeechobee is the fourth-largest lake in the United States. It is a popular destination for tourists and Floridians alike.

Bays

A bay is a coastal body of water partially surrounded by land that feeds into a large body of water. Because it is surrounded on three sides by water, Florida is home to over 900 bays. Tampa Bay is the largest of Florida’s bays, encompassing 400 square miles.

Aquifers

Aquifers are a major physical feature of Florida. An aquifer is an underground reservoir of fresh water. Water is pumped from Florida’s many aquifers and supplies fresh water to millions of people throughout the state. There are two major aquifers in Florida. The Floridan Aquifer is the largest aquifer in the state, covering about 82,000 square miles, and extends into parts of Georgia, Alabama, and South Carolina.

The Biscayne Aquifer is much smaller than the Floridan Aquifer and only covers an area of 4,000 square miles. This aquifer supplies water to many major cities in south Florida, including Miami, Boca Raton, and Fort Lauderdale.

Plains

A plain is a large area of flat land with few to no trees. The plains of Florida are different from plains in other areas of the country. Unlike other plains in the United States, Florida’s plains have wet soil and are often marshy. Florida’s plains are located in the coastal and low-lying areas of the state.

Islands

An island is land that is surrounded on all sides by water. The state of Florida includes many different islands. Florida is primarily made up of the mainland areas, including the panhandle and peninsula. However, Florida also includes over 4,000 islands. The largest of Florida's island chains are the Florida Keys. The Florida Keys are made up of 1,700 islands, including Key West and Key Largo.

Limestone

Limestone is found throughout Florida. Thousands of years ago, following the last ice age, sea levels rose. Much of present-day Florida was underwater. As sea levels fell, the shells, coral, and sand that were left behind hardened into limestone. Limestone is usually white, but if it becomes polluted with other minerals, it will change color. If iron oxide mixes with limestone, it becomes brown, yellow, or red. If limestone and carbon mix together, the limestone becomes blue, black, or gray.

Limestone is used to make fertilizers and glass. It is also frequently used as a building material in items such as flooring, interior and exterior facings, and monuments. Limestone is soft when it is underground, but once it is exposed to the air, it hardens.

title: Regions of Florida
text:
Geographers organize the Earth into regions to help us learn about our world. A region is an area of land that has similar characteristics. Regions are often defined by their physical characteristics. Physical characteristics describe the natural environment of an area. Geographers divide Florida into six physical regions. These include the Western Uplands, Marianna Lowlands, Tallahassee Hills, Central Ridge Highlands, the Coastal Lowlands, and the Everglades. Each region has its own distinct and unique physical characteristics.

Western Uplands

Florida’s Western Uplands region includes the northern part of the Florida Panhandle, extending from the Perdido River in the western part of the state to the Apalachicola River in the central part of the panhandle. This region has the highest elevation of all of Florida’s physical regions. Because of this, the area has many hills and plateaus. A plateau is an area of high, flat land. The Western Uplands are home to Florida’s highest point. Britton Hill stands at 345 feet above sea level.

The soil and climate of the Western Uplands are ideal for growing crops and forest products. Pine forests cover much of the region, but large oak, magnolia, palm, and cypress trees also grow throughout the area. The soil of the Western Uplands region is ideal for growing many crops, including peanuts, corn, soybeans, wheat, and cotton. Farmers of the region also raise cattle and produce many dairy products, such as cheese, milk, and ice cream. Farmers of the Western Uplands region raise thousands of pigs, chickens, sheep, and goats.

Marianna Lowlands

The Marianna Lowlands are located east of the Western Uplands. The physical environment of the Marianna Lowlands is made up of low hills, small lakes, and sinkholes. Sinkholes form when excessive amounts of rain and groundwater move through the soil quickly. This causes open spaces and caverns to form underground. Eventually, the surface above these spaces collapses, causing a large hole to form in the ground.

One of the primary physical features of the Marianna Lowlands is the Florida Caverns, located in Marianna, Florida. These limestone caverns were formed millions of years ago. These large caverns are a popular tourist destination in the region. They are also home to many unique and rare species of plants and animals, including bats, cave salamanders, and blind cave crayfish.

Tallahassee Hills

The Tallahassee Hills region is located between the Apalachicola River and the Withlacoochee River. It stretches north from Tallahassee to the Georgia border. This region is the smallest of Florida’s six physical regions at 25 miles wide and 100 miles long. This area is characterized by low, rolling hills.

The Tallahassee Hills region is often called the Red Hills region. The Red Hills region extends north from Tallahassee to Thomasville, Georgia, encompassing 436,000 acres of pine forests and red clay fields. This area was once the center of cotton production in Florida due to its rich soil and moist red clay fields. Many of these former plantations have been converted into poultry farms that raise chickens, turkeys, and quail. Other parts of this region have been transformed into conservation areas for native plants and animals. Local conservation groups of the region are working hard to protect more than 60 threatened and endangered plant and animal species, including the endangered red-cockaded woodpecker and the gopher tortoise.

Central Ridge Highlands

The Central Ridge Highlands are located to the east of the Tallahassee Hills. This region encompasses much of the land in the central part of the state. It extends from the Okefenokee Swamp in the northern part of the state to Lake Okeechobee in the south. The geography of this area varies greatly throughout the region. The northern part of the region is only 150 feet above sea level, and the land is relatively flat. Areas of the western part of the region are very hilly, like the neighboring Tallahassee Hills region. The southern part of the region is characterized by grassy plains. It is also referred to as the Lake Region because of the number of lakes and sources of fresh water in the area.

The Central Ridge Highlands are home to many unique physical features. The Okefenokee Swamp is located in the northern part of the region. The Okefenokee Swamp is one of the largest swamps in the world and is the source of Florida’s Suwannee River. The Central Ridge Highlands region is also home to two national forests. The Osceola National Forest is located in the northern part of the region near the Georgia border. It is filled with thousands of acres of wetlands and pine forests. The Ocala National Forest is located in central Florida. It was the first of Florida’s national forests to be recognized by the federal government. This forest was designated a national forest in 1908 to protect Florida’s sand pine scrub forests.

Coastal Lowlands

The Coastal Lowlands are the largest of Florida’s physical regions. This region includes the coastal areas of the panhandle and the peninsula of the state. It runs along the Gulf of America and the Atlantic Ocean. This region extends inland from 10 to 60 miles in various areas of the state. The Coastal Lowlands also include the Florida Keys. This region consists of low-lying land with sandy soil.

The Coastal Lowlands region is home to Florida’s largest lake. Lake Okeechobee covers 730 square miles, making it the 10th-largest freshwater lake in the United States. It is home to hundreds of plant and animal species. Because of its abundant supply of fish, Lake Okeechobee is one of the state’s premier fishing destinations.

The economy of the Coastal Lowlands relies heavily on the region’s natural beauty and abundant resources. The natural wonders of this region, including its many beaches, islands, lakes, rivers, and coral reefs, attract thousands of tourists to the state each year. Fishing is also a major economic activity in this region. Commercial fishing boats and visitors catch thousands of pounds of fish, shrimp, oysters, and crabs in the waters of this region each year.

The Everglades

The Everglades is one of, if not the most, unique physical regions of Florida. The Everglades is made up of over one million acres of wetland. It is the largest mangrove ecosystem in the Western Hemisphere. This region is divided into different habitats, which include hardwood hammocks, pinelands, mangroves, ponds, sloughs (deep channels of fresh water), grassy wetlands, and forested wetlands. The abundant sources of fresh water in the region provide drinking water to one-third of Florida’s population.

These unique habitats are home to thousands of plant and animal species. Over 700 species of plants can be found in the Everglades, many of which are endangered or threatened. The Everglades is also home to 360 species of birds, 50 species of reptiles, 17 species of amphibians, about 300 species of fish, more than 40 species of mammals, and 5,000 different insect species. It is the only place in the world where alligators and crocodiles live side by side. It is also the home of the elusive Florida panther and the West Indian manatee, both of which are endangered species.

Thousands of tourists visit the Everglades each year to take in its natural wonders, hike, fish, enjoy water sports, and learn about the environment of the region.

title: Climate of Florida
text:
The climate of Florida varies depending on location. Most of the state has a humid, subtropical climate. Areas with a humid, subtropical climate have long, humid, hot summers and mild, wet winters. Humid climates have a high level of water vapor in the atmosphere.

The southern part of the state is divided into three different climate zones. Areas along the Atlantic Ocean have a tropical rainforest climate. Tropical rainforest climates are hot, humid, and wet all year long. The temperature does not vary much between the winter and summer months. Inland areas in the southern part of the state have a tropical savanna climate. Areas with a tropical savanna climate are often characterized by tall, grassy areas and hot, humid, wet weather conditions. The rest of south Florida has a tropical monsoon climate. This type of climate is similar to tropical rainforest and savanna climates. Areas in this climate zone are hot and humid year-round but receive less precipitation than other areas of the state.

Because of its hot, humid, and mostly sunny climate, Florida is known as the “Sunshine State.” Despite this nickname, Florida receives an average of 53 inches of rainfall each year. Florida’s climate makes the state a unique place to live in and visit. Average temperatures across the state range from the mid-50s to the mid-60s in the winter and the mid-80s in the summer. Because of the high levels of humidity, high temperatures in Florida often feel warmer than they actually are.
