title: The Creative People of North Carolina
text:
North Carolinians are very creative people. For hundreds of years, our state’s residents have created beautiful art, music, and crafts. They wanted to share their art with others, so they built museums and concert halls. They even founded schools to teach their creative skills to other people.

People from every part of the state and the country enjoy seeing paintings, sculptures, and photographs by North Carolina artists. One place they can go is the Green Hill Center for North Carolina Art in Greensboro. Green Hill Center was founded more than 25 years ago. In the Center is ArtQuest, a hands-on gallery for kids. A gallery is a place where artwork is shown and sometimes sold. Artists from North Carolina designed the ArtQuest exhibits. The gallery has a sculpting area and a place for birthday parties and other special events.

For music lovers, the North Carolina Symphony is worth a visit. The symphony was founded in 1932 and is an important part of our state's musical history. Its beautiful home, Meymandi Concert Hall, opened in 2001. Although the symphony is located in Raleigh-Durham, you can attend concerts in other parts of the state, too.

The Appalachian Heritage Crafters in Cherokee City is a group of people who enjoy making crafts. Crafts are useful items made by hand from clay, glass, metal, fibers, wood, and other materials. The crafters group wants to teach others about the beautiful crafts made by people who live in the Appalachian Mountains. They offer exhibits of North Carolina crafts and run a gift shop where people can buy handwoven clothing, toys, dolls, baskets, and many other items.

You may be a creative person too. Do you enjoy painting or working with clay? How about singing or playing an instrument? Whatever you like to do, North Carolina can show you how.

title: Art, Music, and Crafts of North Carolina
text:
Art

The Sawtooth Center for Visual Art was founded in 1945 in Winston-Salem. It is a gallery, museum, and art school. At Sawtooth, students aged four and up can learn to create art using their favorite medium. A medium is the material used to create art, like clay, paint, or metal.

James Barnhill is a North Carolina sculptor. A sculptor is someone who creates statues from clay, marble, bronze, or other materials. Barnhill was born in Asheville. He began drawing when he was only four. Today, he creates bronze sculptures. In 2001, he finished one of his most famous projects: a 10-foot sculpture of the Greensboro Four. The Greensboro Four were four students who sat at a Woolworth's counter to protest racial segregation. Barnhill has won many awards and honors for his artwork.

Jenean Hornbuckle is a Cherokee artist who paints mountain landscapes. Hornbuckle was born in North Carolina. She got her love of the mountains from her father and her Cherokee ancestors. Her beautiful landscapes have been displayed throughout our state. Hornbuckle also helped start the Seven Clans Art Guild. This group helps Cherokee artists show and sell their artwork.

Music

More than 200 years ago, the Moravians were known for performing excellent music. They sang and played instruments in church and gave concerts to entertain people. The Moravians are an important part of North Carolina’s musical history. From 1760 to 1840, they wrote hundreds of pieces of music. Today, you can still hear beautiful music sung and played by Moravians in our state.

Another traditional style of music popular in North Carolina is the blues. There are many different kinds of blues: Piedmont blues, Delta blues, jazz-blues, and rhythm and blues. During the 1950s, there was a musical group from Winston-Salem called the Five Royales. The Five Royales were one of the first rhythm and blues bands in the U.S. Today, you can hear the blues at festivals and concerts throughout North Carolina.

Old-time string-band music began as southern fiddle tunes. Surry County is a popular place to go in our state to hear this type of music. Old-time string-band music was featured in the movie O Brother, Where Art Thou? The movie sparked a new interest in the style.

Gospel music has deep roots in North Carolina and the South. James Vaughan, from Tennessee, usually gets the credit for making Southern gospel music popular throughout the U.S. He sang in a gospel quartet and ran a gospel music publishing company. He sent gospel quartets out on the road to give concerts. One of gospel's most famous singers, Shirley Caesar, started singing at a young age in her uncle's church in Winston-Salem.

The first settlers who came to the Carolinas in the 1600s often wrote songs about everyday life. Those songs inspired Bill and Charlie Monroe to create a new sound. This style became known as bluegrass music. Most people say that bluegrass really came together when a young North Carolina banjo player, Earl Scruggs, joined the Monroe brothers.

Crafts

Making crafts has been an important part of life in our state for centuries. Crafts are often beautiful, like art is. However, crafts differ from art because they are meant to be used. Until the mid-1800s, dishes, quilts, brooms, furniture, and other items were all handmade. Today, machines in factories make most things we use. But some people in North Carolina still take pride in making their own crafts.

The Penland School of Crafts is located in the Blue Ridge Mountains. Lucy Morgan founded the school in 1923. Soon, people were coming from all over the country to take classes at Penland. Today, the school offers classes in several mediums, from fibers to glass to metals.

The Cherokee people are famous for their beautiful crafts. Polly Rattler was born in Cherokee, North Carolina. As Rattler grew up, she watched her grandmother and other Cherokee elders make crafts. She quickly learned to make corn husk dolls, baskets, and beaded items. Rattler has demonstrated her creative skills to people across the country at powwows and festivals.

title: Ethical Behavior: King Philip's War
text:
Metacomet was an American Indian who lived in New England. His father, Massasoit, was the great Wampanoag chief who had welcomed the Pilgrims in 1620. Metacomet became sachem (chief) in 1662 and continued friendly relations with the colonists. He became known as "King Philip."

The American Indians and colonists had their differences, but overall things were peaceful. They depended on each other as trading partners. However, some colonial leaders began making unfair demands on the American Indian tribes. The colonists ignored previous agreements and expanded into Indian territories. They forced natives to sell their land. They even demanded that Metacomet's people surrender all their weapons.

Metacomet organized an army. He formed an alliance with other American Indian tribes. His goal was to force the Puritan colonists out of American Indian territory. Puritans and some American Indians united to fight Metacomet's warriors. Colonel Benjamin Church formed the first American Ranger unit in Plymouth Colony.

Many bloody conflicts followed. Both sides attacked and burned towns. They killed and enslaved hundreds of people. They destroyed land, crops, and livestock. Every colony and tribe in New England suffered huge losses. One of Church's soldiers killed Metacomet in 1676, and the battles stopped shortly after. Historians call this period King Philip's War.

Both sides of this conflict chose violence instead of solving their problems peacefully. The war forever changed the way of life for colonists and American Indians in New England.

title: North Carolina Culture
text:
Diversity

Diversity is a word that describes people's differences. These can be differences in race, religion, opinions, culture, etc. These differences are one of the reasons our state is a great place to live.

According to a recent count, about 61 percent of North Carolinians are Caucasian, or white Americans. African Americans make up about 12 percent of the state’s population. Nineteen percent are Hispanic, six percent are Asian, and American Indians make up a little more than one percent.

African Americans

After the U.S. won its freedom from England, people became increasingly dependent on slavery and the economic benefits it provided. In the North, many abolitionists argued that slavery was morally wrong. By the early 1800s, all the Northern states had made owning enslaved people illegal. But slavery in the South was ongoing. That was because the use of enslaved labor had helped make the South one of the richest places in the world.

On Jan. 1, 1863, President Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation. Emancipation means "freedom from slavery." Not all enslaved people were freed right away. It wasn't until the end of the Civil War that the South agreed to end slavery. In 1868, the U.S. Constitution was amended, or changed. The 14th Amendment promised freedom for all U.S. citizens, regardless of their race.

Being free didn't mean African Americans were treated equally. Jim Crow laws were put into place in the South around 1877. Jim Crow laws were used to segregate, or separate, white Americans and African Americans almost everywhere in public. It happened in schools, in restaurants, on buses, and at drinking fountains.

In 1960, four African American college students from Greensboro, North Carolina, protested segregation. The Greensboro Four sat at a Woolworth's lunch counter. The counter was supposed to be for white people only. After five months of sit-ins, Woolworth's and other stores in Greensboro finally agreed to end segregation. The Greensboro Four may have been inspired by Martin Luther King Jr. King was leading the Civil Rights Movement. The Civil Rights Movement was an effort to make segregation illegal and give African Americans equal rights under the law.

North Carolina's Native Peoples

Andrew Jackson and early white settlers drove many native peoples out of North Carolina. They were forced to relocate to Oklahoma. The march became known as “The Trail of Tears.” Many American Indians died from a lack of food, water, and shelter. It is estimated that over 4,000 died, nearly one-fifth of the Cherokee population. Today, there are about 130,000 people who make up North Carolina's American Indian community. They're in many different towns and come from lots of different tribes, like the Cherokee, Catawba, Creek, and Seminole.

The Eastern Band of Cherokee is the main group of American Indians in North Carolina. They have their own reservation and are officially recognized by the U.S. government. Most Cherokee live on or near their reservation, the Qualla Boundary, in the western part of our state. The Lumbee Tribe is also one of the largest tribes in North Carolina.

The history of the Eastern Band of Cherokee goes back to the days of the Trail of Tears. They refused to go west to Oklahoma, even though the U.S. Army tried to remove them through violence. They fought for their right to stay or hid in the mountains where no one could find them.

You may remember learning about Sequoyah. He was the Cherokee man who invented the first American Indian written language.

North Carolina's Hispanic Community

The word “Hispanic” is a name for people, cultures, or countries related to the Spanish language or Spain in general. When England was building and growing colonies in North America, Spain was doing the same thing in South America and Central America. That's why many South Americans speak Spanish and most people in North America speak English.

The Hispanic part of our population is the fastest-growing group overall. In the 2020 census, there were about 1,118,000 Hispanic people living in North Carolina. Experts believe there are many more Hispanic people living here who are non-documented immigrants. Some people immigrate to the United States without permission. There are many opportunities to earn money here. Most non-documented immigrants send much of the money they earn home to help their families. Because they don't get permission before they come, it's hard to know how many are here.

North Carolina's Asian Americans

The first immigrants and pioneers came to North Carolina in the colonial days. Most were from somewhere in Europe. Immigrants and pioneers are still coming to our state. Most immigrants are Hispanic or Asian.

Asian Americans are the second-largest group of immigrants coming to North Carolina. There are about 343,000 Asian Americans in our state. People from Japan or China make up a big part of the Asian American population in North Carolina. However, there are many other Asian immigrants, including Koreans, Asian Indians, Vietnamese, Filipinos, and many others.

title: Colonial Unrest - Solving Problems with Gunpowder
text:
How do you feel when people are mean to you? How do you treat people you don't like? There are many different ways to get people to understand that you don't like what they are doing. Some work better than others, and some don't work at all. Most people like to live peacefully with others. That's a good goal to have.

Immigrants Flock to North Carolina

In the early 1700s, people came to North Carolina for many reasons. Whether they were looking for rich soil, mild weather, available land, religious freedom, or adventure, thousands came from all parts of the world. Soon the backcountry was filled with immigrants, or people who left their homes and moved to another country. The backcountry was the western part of North Carolina, away from the coast. The backcountry of North Carolina is the mountainous region that is covered in forests. At that time, the backcountry hadn't been explored very much.

Many Germans came to the backcountry of North Carolina, too. They were Lutherans who were looking for religious freedom. Not many Germans held public office, probably because not many of them spoke English. Although they were from Germany, they were considered Loyalists, or people who were faithful to England.

In Scotland, the British government had defeated the Scottish Highlanders. Many of them decided they could not live in Scotland any more. Some of their distant cousins, Scots-Irish people called Ulster Scots, came to North Carolina with them. Here they drained swamps, cleared fields, planted crops, and herded cattle and sheep.

The Regulators

With all these new people in North Carolina , there were bound to be some disagreements. One big disagreement during colonial times was about regulation, or control, of the government. In 1765, a teacher named George Sims owed a few dollars in taxes. He couldn't pay, so he was taken to court. In front of the judge, George asked "all honest men" to oppose the cruel actions of the local government. By 1768, those "honest men" were organized into a group that called themselves Regulators. They fought violently against the government and destroyed the property of any government official they could find.

It Takes All Kinds

The Regulators had no official leaders. They were just a group of people who all felt the same way about the government, although many of them came from different backgrounds. But three men became well-known for organizing the Regulators.

Herman Husband could write and speak well. He wrote pamphlets and gave speeches to move the Regulators to action. Rednap Howell was another organizer. He was a schoolmaster who loved to write funny songs. His songs made fun of people in the government he didn't like. James Hunter believed that the way to get action from the government was to use force. People often called him the General of the Regulation.

These three men were very different, but they worked together to organize the Regulators. It takes all kinds of people to make big changes happen in a community.

Dishonest Government Officials

Most people in the Carolina colony in the mid-1700s thought the laws made by the king of England were fair and good. But the men who enforced the laws and collected the taxes made the people in Carolina's backcountry angry. The people of Carolina thought those men were thieves. They especially hated a man named Edmund Fanning. He was a judge and a colonel in the Carolina militia. (A militia is an organized army, made up of volunteers.) The colonists thought Edmund was a snobby rich man who hated the common people. One group of backcountry men dragged him out of his house and whipped him. They felt that was his punishment for the way he treated them.

Fanning wasn't the only one they hated. The colonists thought most of North Carolina's officials were rotten, and they had many reasons to think so. The officials collected twice as many taxes as the law called for, and they kept the extra for themselves.

The Battle of Alamance

After the Regulators were formed in 1768, the colonists lived through another four years of arguing and violence between the government and the backcountry farmers. In 1771, Governor Tryon decided to put a stop to the whole thing. He called out the Carolina militia to fight the Regulators.

The first battle happened on May 16, 1771, at Alamance. Things didn't look too good for the militia. The Regulators had almost twice as many men ready to fight. Governor Tryon gave the Regulators one last chance to leave peacefully, but they refused. He ordered his men to open fire, but at first, they didn't.

"Fire! Fire on them or on me!" he shouted. Shots rang out, and the battle began. The Regulators fought fiercely, but their weapons were not as good, and they weren't as well-trained as the militia, either.

When the battle ended, the militia members were surprised to see that they had won. The War of the Regulators was over.

The Regulators split. Some moved to other parts of the country. The governor pardoned some, but a few were executed for their crimes.

title: North Carolina's Natural Resources
text: Have you ever stopped to think about the power Mother Nature has over our everyday lives? One look at the weather ought to make it obvious! Nature determines a lot more than just whether or not you need to dress warmly to go to school. Modern technology has made this far less true than it used to be. However, it wasn't too long ago that Mother Nature determined what a person did for a living. If you lived in a place that was naturally good for raising cattle, that's what you did. If you lived by an ocean, you'd probably make your living in trade, transportation, or fishing. If you lived near a gold mine, you might spend your days digging in the dirt. Mother Nature has things pretty well figured out, and we ought to feel lucky. The natural world around us is brimming with all sorts of stuff to make life around here worth living. It would be a mistake to just kick back and let nature do all the work. To really make the most of North Carolina's natural resources takes many people. The work that people do to grow, harvest, mine, use, and sell what nature provides makes for one terrific North Carolina partnership.

title: North Carolina: America's Leader in Freedom
text:
Have you ever admired someone because that person was a good example? It seems like there are some people who set the pace for everyone around them. They're the ones the rest of us look up to and even try to be like sometimes. Maybe we just like their style. Maybe we admire the way they deal with problems or the way they treat people around them. Maybe we see them as real leaders with the power to make things better. It's sometimes the same with cities and states.

Take North Carolina, for instance. From time to time, the state has been a good role model, or leader, for other states to follow. Here's an example: During the Revolutionary War, it was North Carolina that led the way for America to become free, or independent, from England. Even today, car bumper stickers around the state read, "North Carolina, First in Freedom!" People say this with pride, and they have good reason. At one time, many colonists were fed up with high taxes and the lack of government representation in England. It was North Carolina who finally said so and did something about it.

North Carolina was the first to recommend independence from England. They were the first to win a battle against British troops. North Carolina was also the first to make plans for its own government that didn't include the royal crown. That's a lot of firsts for one state.

title: First in Freedom
text:
North Carolinians can be proud of their ancestors who didn't hesitate to fight for the right to be free.

The Halifax Resolves

Along the beautiful south bank of the Roanoke River lies the peaceful town of Halifax. The town was settled in the early 1700s. You can visit it today and see a slice of North Carolina history right before your eyes. But as early as the 1760s, it was an exciting and booming town. It was full of taverns, markets, boats, noise, and, most of all, people. In April 1776, North Carolina's provincial congress met in Halifax, a big town just right for making big decisions. On the agenda was independence from England. Out of that meeting came a document called the Halifax Resolves. Like most official documents, it was full of a lot of fancy words. At the heart of it all was a simple idea: North Carolina wanted independence (freedom from the British government). Other colonies followed North Carolina's lead. The Halifax Resolves was the first official act by any colony recommending independence from England.

North Carolina: Leading the Way to Freedom

The feelings of the colonists in America had been growing stronger for many years. People in North Carolina were talking about breaking away from Britain's rule as early as 100 years before the Revolutionary War. But things really got jumping around in the 1770s. In 1775, officials in Mecklenburg County learned that England considered North Carolina to be in rebellion.

The Mecklenburg County Committee of Safety drew up plans to run their own government. They declared that all laws that came from England were invalid. (That means they were not to be obeyed.) Mecklenburg County's plans (called the Mecklenburg Resolves) were one more step toward independence.

North Carolina Militia Wins First American Victory

By early 1776, England was doing everything it could to keep things in North Carolina under control. They won some support from Cherokee natives in the west. In the South, bands of Loyalists (people who favored English rule or were loyal to England), called Scovelites, were stirring up trouble. North Carolina Patriots (those in favor of American independence) looked surrounded. Finally, the situation exploded into battle. On February 27, 1,600 Scottish Highlanders who were loyal to England came face to face with North Carolina's militia. They met at Moore's Creek Bridge for a surprise ending. It was surprising because the Patriot minutemen actually won the battle. The spoils (property taken from the enemy) of that battle included 1,500 rifles and 150 swords. The spoils also included lots of medicine and supplies, and even a chest full of money. More than that, it prevented the royal army from having a stronghold in the South at the beginning of the Revolutionary War only a few months later.

A Neighborly Time to Live?

What would it have felt like to live in a North Carolina town during all this commotion? Sometimes it's easy to think that it might feel like a big, exciting, patriotic parade all the time, with you and all your neighbors and friends cheering for independence. However, in every North Carolina town, there were about as many Loyalists as there were Patriots. There were many different strong feelings in each town. It probably felt less and less like a parade and more like a big fight. Some experts have said that the feelings in most North Carolina communities during that time were probably a lot like the feelings during the Civil War. Even though this happened much later, it was a time where people who lived in the very same country fought against each other.

title: North Carolina Industries Span the World!
text:
Have you ever walked through your neighborhood and seen clouds of dust or felt the rumble of big tractors? Have you ever heard the pounding of hammers or the whirring of saws as a new home goes up for a family to live in? Have you ever seen fishing boats come in from the ocean with nets full of wriggling fish? Have you ever heard the honking of a semi-truck loaded high with chickens on their way to the market? Everywhere you look, you can see signs of industry. Products made, grown, found, or dug up right here in North Carolina find their way to other places.

Many people outside of North Carolina think our state is only about the tobacco industry. They’re only partly right. It’s true that tobacco keeps many people working in our state, but there’s much more to North Carolina’s industry than that. People all over the country wear clothes made from North Carolina cloth. They use products made from North Carolina chemicals and operate machines made in North Carolina. Sometimes, they might relax on fine North Carolina furniture, often without even knowing it. Some of these industries are new to the state. Others have been around as long as there have been people here. But they’re all important to North Carolinians and the world.

title: North Carolina’s Cash Crops
text:
Since its time as a colony, the economy of North Carolina has relied on farming. When settlers came to the state, they found good land and weather for farming. The colonists got to work planting and harvesting crops for trade.

The climate of North Carolina is warmer than England. English settlers found that they could grow crops in the colonies that they couldn’t grow back home. This helped them in trading, since they could grow things the English could not.

Tobacco was brought to the colonies from Spain. It needs a warm growing season and lots of sunshine to grow. It doesn't grow in places with cooler climates like England. The colonists found that the crop grew in their rich soil. Tobacco became a “cash crop." Cash crops are plants that can be grown and sold but not eaten. Farmers who grow cash crops have to buy food with money earned from their crops.

Cotton is another plant that grows in warm, sunny climates. Like tobacco, it is a cash crop. Many common products are made of cotton. Clothes, medical supplies, and even money are made of cotton!

Forest products were major exports in colonial times. Wooden ships needed lots of sticky tar and rosin to stop leaks. Tar and rosin could be found in the pine trees of the coastal region. The wood from the trees was also sold in the form of barrels and lumber.

Rice was a major product of the coastal region during times of slavery. Early settlers found that the swampy land of the coast was perfect for rice. Enslaved people drained swamps to make them into rice fields. The work was hard, but rice was a valuable crop. When slavery ended, rice became too expensive to grow. Today, very little rice is grown in the state.

title: State Government
text:
The governor is the leader of the state. The people in our state vote for the governor. The governor helps choose state leaders and make laws.

Who is the governor of your state?

title: The Declaration of Independence
text: The Declaration of Independence is an important document. It let Great Britain know we wanted to be our own country. It also explained important rights that everyone should have.

title: Models of the World
text:
The distance around the Earth is about 25,000 miles. In order to study it, we use a globe to represent it. A globe is a 3D model of the Earth. Globes show the location of water, land, and countries. A globe represents the size and shape of oceans and continents more accurately.

Maps are drawings of places. They show locations of features of the Earth and distances between places. They are usually flat. Maps also show the sizes and shapes of countries. However, they are not as accurate as globes. Globes are the same shape as the Earth. This makes it easier to represent shapes, distances, and sizes closer to how they really are on Earth. Shapes, distances, and sizes become distorted on a map. This is because a map is flat. It is not the same shape as the Earth.

title: Reading Maps
text:
A person who creates a map is called a cartographer. Like the author of a book, a cartographer has a point of view and a purpose. A cartographer decides what to include on a map. The title of the map tells us what the map is about.

There are map tools that we use to help us when using maps and globes. Map tools include the title, legend, compass rose, cardinal directions, and scale. A cartographer includes different map tools to help us read a map. The map’s legend explains what the symbols and colors on the map represent. Most maps have a compass rose. The compass rose is a symbol that shows the cardinal directions: north, south, east, and west.

Distance is how far it is from one place to another. You can tell the distance on a map by looking at the scale.

title: Thematic Maps
text:
There are many different kinds of maps.

A population map shows where people live.

A political map shows the dividing lines or borders that governments make between cities, states, and countries.

A physical map shows the natural features of a place, such as landforms, mountains, valleys, lakes, and streams.

A climate map shows whether a place is usually warm, cold, wet, or dry. Climate is the weather pattern of a place over many years.

An elevation map shows the height of a place in relation to sea level. It usually has contour lines or colors and numbers to represent height.

title: Scale Measurements
text:
The Earth is huge. We cannot carry it in our pockets. However, we can carry a map in our pockets. Since a map is so small, we can only put inches and centimeters on it. This means that we must use the inches and centimeters to represent the miles we travel in real life. That is why maps have scales. A scale shows us the relationship between a distance on a map and that distance on the ground.

The three most common map scales are linear, representative fraction, and verbal.

The linear scale is shown as a line. It is the most common. It looks like a ruler. It tells you that one inch or centimeter on a map represents a certain number of miles in real life.

The representative fraction shows the relationship of the distance on the map to the distance on Earth in a fraction. For example, it may show 1:25,000, which means that one unit on the map is 25,000 units in real life. This may also be expressed as 1/25,000.

The verbal scale writes the relationship of the distance on the map and the distance on Earth in words. For example, “One inch represents 16 miles.”

title: Effects of European Exploration
text:
The people of the Americas met their wants and needs using resources from the land around them. They had vibrant societies and extensive trade routes. They had art, history, and protection for their communities. They had governments and religion. They fed their families by hunting animals and gathering berries, nuts, and fruits. They cultivated crops of corn, squash, beans, tomatoes, potatoes, and some grains. They created tools from the resources around them. They traveled by walking or using boats on the waterways.

The Europeans used natural resources to create manufactured goods. Like Native Americans, they also had vibrant societies and extensive trade routes. They had art, history, and protection for their communities. They had governments and religion. They fed their families by farming and going to markets. The Europeans domesticated animals to keep on their farms. This meant they didn’t have to hunt for food. They had horses to help with the work on the farm and at the market. They cultivated grain crops of wheat, oats, and barley. The Europeans developed different modes of transportation. They used wagons and carts on land and ships on the sea. They manufactured goods out of metal and wood. They used many of their resources to help them explore new places across the ocean.

When these two societies met, there were intentional and unintentional consequences. The two groups traded ideas for the design of tools and transportation. The Europeans brought domesticated animals like pigs, chickens, and horses with them on their ships. The people of the Americas gave them plants, food, and precious metals. Sign language and gestures were used to help the two cultures communicate with each other.

Sometimes, Europeans and peoples of the Americas cooperated. Often, differences were misunderstood or treated with intolerance. Intolerance caused conflict that led to captivity and death for many people, especially among the Indigenous American peoples.

The introduction of domesticated animals in the Americas caused imbalance in the ecosystem. Pigs were turned loose to forage in the forests. The pigs multiplied until there were so many they depleted the vegetation. Other animals that depended on the same vegetation had nothing to eat.

The horse was a new animal to the Americas. The horse quickly became popular to help the people of the Americas in their everyday lives. They used horses for transportation and work. Horses became a valuable trade resource. The horses quickly multiplied. Descendants of these horses are still found on the East Coast and the western lands of the United States.

The most deadly exchange was invisible. The Europeans brought disease with them. They had developed immunity to many bacteria and viruses over the centuries. The people of the Americas had never been exposed to such diseases. Smallpox, tuberculosis, influenza, and other strains of disease were easily transmitted by unsuspecting people. Historians estimate that disease killed 90 percent of the native population within 150 years.

title: Scale
text: Distance is how far it is from one place to another. Maps can show the distance between two places. You can do this using a scale.

title: Physical Maps
text: A physical map shows us where natural features are located. Natural features are things like bodies of water and landforms. Bodies of water include rivers, lakes, and oceans. Landforms are things like mountains and plains.

title: Technology in Geography
text:
Technology has helped us create new types of maps. Satellites take pictures of the Earth. These pictures from space help us create better maps.

Radar images help weather forecasters track the weather. Radar images help us know if it will be rainy or sunny. Weather forecasters use this information to create weather forecast maps.

GPS Technology in our phones allows us to type in directions and follow a digital map.

title: What Happens When Governments Do Not Protect the Rights of the People?
text:
There are many forms and types of government throughout the world. Each type of government functions differently. Some governments gain authority from the people. They serve and protect their citizens’ unalienable, civil, and political rights. Other governments do not respect the rights of their citizens and do not allow them to have liberty and freedom.

The United States is a constitutional republic. The authority lies with the people. The written law of the Constitution is enforced by representatives chosen by the people. Some countries are ruled by a monarchy. A monarch’s authority comes from family inheritance. Subjects of a monarchy are loyal to the monarch. Monarchs are responsible for the safety, security, and welfare of their people. In an authoritarian government, such as a dictatorship or oligarchy, one person or a small group of people take authority by force. Citizens are expected to obey government leaders and have no role or say in government policies. In an authoritarian government, the rights of the people are not guaranteed.

There have been many instances in history when governments did not respect and honor the rights of the people. One example is Germany in the 1930s and 1940s. Authority was taken by one man, through his position in office, to control the actions of government. This government was known as the Third Reich. Historians refer to it as “Nazi government.” The Nazi government honored only the freedoms and liberties of the people they chose based on ethnicity and heritage. The Nazi government denied these same freedoms to specific groups based on their race, ethnicity, political beliefs, and religion.

The laws, policies, and actions of the Nazi government were intended to create the systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of European Jews and other groups from 1933 to 1945.

The purpose of government is to provide safety and security for those in the community from threats outside of the community, maintain justice and order within the community, and help the members of the community meet their wants and needs.

title: Segregation, Discrimination, and Persecution
text:
The Nazi government instituted policies and actions that discriminated against and segregated specific groups of people. Discrimination is the unfair treatment of people based on their race, age, gender, religion, abilities, or beliefs. Segregation is the forced separation of different groups of people in a country, state, or community based on race, age, gender, religion, abilities, or beliefs.

Unchecked discrimination and segregation can lead to persecution, or hostilities. The largest group targeted for such actions were Jews because of their race, religion, ethnicity, and beliefs. The Nazi government and its collaborators wanted to erase the Jewish population.

Laws and actions of the Nazi government against Jews were antisemitic. Antisemitism is prejudice against or hatred of Jews. Intense feelings of antisemitism led to the Holocaust. The Holocaust was the systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of European Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators between 1933 and 1945. The Holocaust is history’s most extreme example of antisemitism.

title: Compass Rose
text:
The compass rose is a symbol. It shows directions. The four main directions are called cardinal directions. They are north, south, east, and west.

There are other directions in between these directions. They are called intermediate directions. For example, northeast is between north and east. Southwest is between south and west.

title: The Government of the Third Reich
text:
After World War I, the nations of the world did their best to recover. In Europe, where much of the fighting had occurred, it was a time of change. Governments vowed to make sure a war of this size would never happen again. When there has been much tragedy, expense, and loss, people try to find reasons to explain why such things happened. The people of Germany were stunned when their government surrendered. The returning soldiers were trying to make sense of their service to their country’s leader, Kaiser Wilhelm. The Kaiser was removed and went into retirement. New leaders emerged.

One man became very popular because he wanted to place blame for the war, not rebuild and change. Adolf Hitler and the National Socialist German Workers’ Party, known as the Nazi Party, were loud in placing blame for Germany’s post-war situation. At first, they verbally attacked minorities. They targeted anyone who was not of German heritage. Hitler gained more and more popularity. He lashed out with old hatreds and misbeliefs against Jews. This specific population became the focus of prejudice, bias, and bigotry by the Nazi Party. The Nazis gradually stripped away rights from German citizens because they were Jewish. Legalized discrimination began slowly and gradually gained acceptance by communities of people who were not Jews.

Jews were not the only group of people who were segregated, discriminated against, and persecuted by the Nazi government. Various groups were singled out because of their ethnic backgrounds and race. Others were persecuted because of their political and religious beliefs. The Nazis also sponsored programs that discriminated against and persecuted people with emotional, mental, and physical disabilities.

The following is a timeline of the legalization of segregation, discrimination, and persecution of the Jews and other groups by the Nazi government.

1933

The Nazi government organized a boycott (not making purchases) of Jewish shops and businesses. Jewish civil servants, lawyers, and teachers were fired from their jobs. Jewish doctors and dentists were only permitted to see Jewish patients. Property ownership was legally restricted.

Books by Jewish authors were destroyed in large, public bonfires.

Laws were put in place to restrict the number of Jewish students in German schools.

The first concentration camp was established in Dachau to house opponents of the Nazi party (mainly Communists and Social Democrats) for their political beliefs.

1934

Jewish shops were marked with a yellow star on the front entrance. Jews also had to wear a yellow star on their outer clothing to identify themselves as Jewish.

Jews had to sit in separate seats on buses and trains. Many city councils banned them from public spaces.

Government offices were created in the Nazi regime to enforce laws targeting specific groups of people because of their gender, orientation, and physical and mental disabilities.

1935

The Nazi government passed the Nuremberg Race Laws. These laws were divided into two categories: the Reich Citizenship Law, and the Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honor. These laws:

Kept all Jews from participating in the government of the Third Reich. The law stripped Jews of all rights of being full German citizens.

Being a Jew was defined by an individual’s grandparents’ racial and religious community.

Jehovah’s Witnesses, a Christian religious group, was banned, and its followers were arrested.

The Nuremberg Race Laws were expanded to include people of Roma and African descent and other ethnic groups.

Consequences of the Nuremberg Race laws included arrest, imprisonment, and deportation to prison camps and work concentration camps.

1936

Nazi Germany hosted the 1936 Olympics. The eyes of the world were on Hitler and the government. There was no visible public persecution of Jews in Berlin during the Olympics, but it continued in other areas.

1937

Pope Pius, the leader of the Catholic Church, publicly criticized the hostile treatment of Catholics in Nazi Germany. In many areas of Germany, Nazi leaders shut down church services, confiscated church property, and imprisoned Catholic clergy.

1938

The Nuremberg Race Laws were expanded:

Jews were forced to change their middle names (men and boys had to take the middle name “Israel,” and women and girls were required to take the middle name “Sarah”).

Existing passports were invalidated. To make their passport valid, Jews were required to submit their passport to a government office and have them stamped with a “J” for Jew.

Jews were also ordered to register all wealth and property they owned. They could no longer work in jobs that handled money or any job outside of their homes.

Jewish children were forbidden to go to German schools and universities.

November 9: Kristallnacht (The Night of Broken Glass)

The Nazi government organized attacks on Jewish homes, businesses, and synagogues. During Kristallnacht, 400 synagogues and 7,500 shops were destroyed. Jews were forced to clean up the destruction and pay a fine to the government. The remaining Jewish property was then confiscated.

Jews were forced into ghettos, or areas in a city that have few resources and many people living in poor conditions.

1939

Germany occupied the Czech zone, known as Bohemia and Moravia. Antisemitic ideas and actions soon took root.

The Nazi government forced about 150,000 Jews to leave Germany and occupied areas. Jews were forced to pay a large “tax” before they could leave.

In March 1939, roughly 30,000 Jews were sent to concentration camps.

In September 1939, Germany invaded Poland. The Nazi government gave Polish authorities and their collaborators instructions to detain Polish Jews. Eventually, they began to deport Polish Jews and send them to concentration camps.

German authorities required Jews in the occupied areas of Poland to wear white armbands with a blue Star of David to identify themselves as Jewish.

1940-1945

Between 1940 and 1945, millions of people were murdered by the Nazi government and their collaborators.

title: Never Forget, Never Again: Why We Learn About the Holocaust
text:
Never Forget:

“For the survivor who chooses to testify, it is clear: his duty is to bear witness for the dead and for the living ... To forget the dead would be akin to killing them a second time.”

Elie Wiesel (Holocaust survivor, author, and Nobel Peace Prize winner)

“I have come to realize that my testimony carries so much more weight with them [people] than anything that they have read in a book or seen in a movie.”

Charles Middleberg (Holocaust survivor)

“I knew that I had to inform people of the greatest tragedy of human existence.”

Bill Zimmerspitz (Holocaust survivor)

“Even survivors from the camps … a lot of them can’t comprehend why, what happened … But you can tell people what happened …”

Jerry Meents (Holocaust survivor)

“Get rid of a four-letter word, that’s the first thing. That word is ‘hate.’ This word ‘hate,’ these four letters, were the cause of everything that the second world war was about. Intolerance and bullyism. This created a huge catastrophe. Many people lost their families and lost their lives.”

Norman Frajman (Holocaust survivor)

“It was the beginning of the end of survival ... of becoming a totally different human being... another world. That world was just faster and faster disappearing. I was constantly kept inside, I was not to go out. So I was like, inside forever. Any playing we did was inside. There was no outside anymore. The stories then were changing from Hitler invading to what's going to happen tomorrow? It was no longer next week or what we should have done a year ago. Now we were confronted with the Devil himself and no matter how I imagine how badly anyone perceived what was going to happen, it turned out infinitely greater so that we were instantly cut off from everything and instant brutality, orders, change. It was not a slower way of introducing you into that kind of existence. It was like the door shutting on you and that's it."

Ellis Lewin (Holocaust survivor)

"We would get up in the morning. To begin with we slept, worked, and wore the same clothes all the time. Every few months they would disinfect them. Every day we had to stand and be counted and they made us responsible [for each other]. So let's say one would want to run away and if you had a heart you'd say how can I endanger all, because then we would all suffer. You could sometimes stand for hours and for days. Dead or alive, everybody had to be counted."

"After the appell [roll-call], we would always march in fives. On both sides, the guards had dogs ... When you marched out, sometimes we never knew who would come back ..."

Itka Zygmuntowicz (Holocaust survivor)

Never Again:

“We must take sides. Neutrality helps the oppressor, never the victim. Silence encourages the tormentor, never the tormented.”

Elie Wiesel (Holocaust survivor, author, and Nobel Peace Prize winner)

“We never try to tell the tale to make people weep … If we decided to tell the tale, it is because we wanted the world to be a better world … and learn, and remember. What is our role? We must become the messengers’ messengers.”

Elie Wiesel (Holocaust survivor, author, and Nobel Peace Prize winner)

“I need to speak for all of those who can’t speak for themselves.”

Helene Bouton (Holocaust survivor)

“After being saved by a Righteous Rescuer, in the hope that my experience will be an incentive for students to realize that no matter how risky, they must always try to help people who are facing discrimination.”

Erna Anolik (Holocaust survivor)

“We must stay together. We must hold hands and stay together. There's not any room in our society, our community, for racism, for bigotry, for antisemitism. We must walk together. We must keep the faith and we must keep our eyes on the prize ...”

John R. Lewis (Former United States Representative and civil rights activist)

“I firmly believe that education is the best way to prevent the next Holocaust.”

Yossie Hollander (Son of Holocaust survivors, philanthropist, and founder of the “Echoes and Reflections” program)

“The Germans were the most civilized people in the world … They were great musicians, great thinkers, great philosophers. What we need to remember is that civilization is only skin deep. It takes very little to remove the surface and to be exposed to the darkest and most evil instincts in human beings.”

Noemi Mattis (Holocaust survivor)

title: Diving into Matter
text:
Read the articles and observe the diagram. Graph the data from the diagram. Then answer the questions.

Career Spotlight: Scientific Diver

Some scientists don’t work in a lab or an office. When it comes to scientific divers, their workplace is the wide ocean floor, filled with kelp, coral reefs, and creatures of all colors, shapes, and sizes. Scientific divers are specialized experts in scuba diving. They make observations and collect data in the deep blue sea to conduct their research. This can include counting organisms, taking samples and photographs, and setting up special underwater equipment.

Hanna Reed is a diving safety officer at the University of Southern California (USC). Growing up on the coasts of both St. Petersburg, Florida, and San Diego, California, Reed became passionate about humanity’s responsibility to care for the land and sea. She entered the Humboldt State University diving program when she was 18. After almost 10 years of teaching diving, she now runs the scientific diving classes at USC. Read the following interview to learn more about her experience in scientific diving.

Studies Weekly: Why did you decide to become a scientific diver?

Hanna Reed: I became a scientific diver because I have a passion for the ocean and making positive change for the health of our oceans and climate.

SW: What’s the best part about your job?

HR: When conducting surveys underwater, the dives are long and require extreme focus. It is quite special because after 20 minutes or so, I truly feel like “one” with the environment. As I am counting and identifying algae and marine life ... the animals become accustomed to my presence, and my breathing becomes calm and rhythmic. I become part of the seascape when I am down there, which at times can be truly magical.

SW: Tell me about how you safety check your equipment and air tank before a dive.

HR: Before I go on a dive, I do personal gear checks and a buddy check with my buddy. When I check my buddy's (or student's), we always check the air is on [and] the tank is secure. Then I move to the regulators (the part that you breathe from). I check their regulators by purging them, then move on to checking their dive computers and air pressure gauges. We make sure our weight we are wearing is “ditchable” in an emergency, make sure our inflator hoses work, then grab our masks and fins and head out to dive!

Studies Weekly made minor changes to the interview text to maintain consistency in grammar and style.

Packable Air

Scuba diving is only possible because of air. In order for humans to dive into the depths of the ocean without holding their breath, they need the help of tanks filled with air. Air is matter. That means it can be captured and pushed into containers, just like stuffing clothes into a small suitcase. However, unlike solid clothes, air is an invisible gas. Even though air is invisible, it has mass and can be weighed.

Like all forms of matter, gases can be measured. The air in a scuba tank, for example, is measured by the space it takes up. In science, the amount of space an object takes up is called its volume. Volume is calculated by multiplying an object’s length by its width by its height. Imagine a box that is one foot long, one foot wide, and one foot tall. Inside this box is air. You may not be able to see it, but it’s there! At one foot by one foot by one foot, the volume of the air in the box is one cubic foot. Anything that has volume also has weight. The air in the box weighs about .08 pounds. Now, imagine the amount of air in 77 of those boxes. About 77 cubic feet of air and other gases are squeezed into a scuba tank. That’s about as much air as would fit in a small closet! Using intense pressure to push air into scuba tanks is called compression. The result of compression is one heavy scuba tank. A standard aluminum tank, filled to its maximum capacity, is about 37 pounds. That’s about the same weight as a four-year-old! When the tank is empty, it only weighs about 31 pounds. That means about six pounds of air were compressed into the tank. As a diver uses the tank to breathe underwater, that air is used up. This causes both the weight of the tank and the pressure of the air inside to decrease. A gauge monitoring the pressure tells the diver how much air is left in the tank. That way, the diver can return to the surface safely before the air runs out!

title: European Exploration
text:
Gold, God, or Glory! Many Europeans were excited to hear stories about the great American Indian lands said to be filled with gold. There were many others excited to go there so that they could worship God as they believed. They also wanted to convert the Indigenous peoples. Some wanted lands, colonies, and the chance to become famous.

The French Find Friendly Native People

Giovanni da Verrazzano was a French explorer sent by King Francis I of France. He was searching for a new trade route to the Orient. The expedition explored the waterways between Cape Fear and Albemarle Sound. However, they made one major mistake: They thought the water on the other side of the narrow islands that line the coast of North Carolina was the Pacific Ocean, or the South Seas as it was called in those days.

They also had a frightening experience, which taught them how friendly the natives could be. Explorers told stories of fierce natives who cooked and ate their captives. So, when one of Verrazano's men was "captured" by American Indians in North Carolina, they got the scare of their lives. They watched from their boat as the American Indians built a great fire and removed their "captured" shipmate's clothes.

How did they "capture" him? He was the one man in Verrazzano's group who dared to approach the American Indians. He was afraid and about to return to the boat, when a huge wave washed him to the shore unconscious. The native people ran to help, carried him to higher ground and laid him in the sun. They took his clothes off and dried them near a huge fire they built. When he made signs that he wanted to return, they gave him back his clothes. With "... great love ... and many embracings (hugs)," they walked him back to his boat!

English "Seadogs" Dog the Spanish

The Spanish wrote that it took 60 Incan goldsmiths in Peru, working night and day for more than 90 days, to melt down all of the stolen artifacts into gold bricks. They did this to make it easier to ship the gold back to Spain.

In those days, there were many English "seadogs," like Sir Francis Drake, who sailed for one purpose: to steal as much gold as they could from the Spanish. It was tough for the Spanish to lose gold to the English. However, it was the Indigenous peoples of Mexico and South America who lost their gold to the Spanish.

Spanish Spy Out the New Land

Lucas Vázquez de Ayllón landed near Cape Fear with 600 people and 29 horses. This group wanted to start a new Spanish colony. Upon entering the mouth of Cape Fear River, one of their ships sank. Vázquez de Ayllón wasted no time building not one, but two ships to replace the one they lost. These were the first ships built in North America.

Vázquez de Ayllón sent explorers into the mainland along the coast. Quickly, they abandoned the Cape Fear area for a better place to the south. Soon, disease and hardships forced them to leave there. They headed back to the West Indies with only 150 people left out of the 600 that began the expedition.

Hernando de Soto

After finding shiploads of gold in South America, Hernando de Soto was determined to do the same in North America. He marched with 1,000 men from Florida all the way to North Carolina. Along the way, De Soto was responsible for the kidnapping, assault, enslavement, and deaths of thousands of Indigenous peoples in the areas he went through.

De Soto's expedition spent a whole month digging for gold in the North Carolina mountains. Not finding the gold they wanted, de Soto's men turned around and headed south. The only thing that de Soto found was the Mississippi River. De Soto died along the Mississippi with all but 300 of the 1,000 men who began the expedition.

Queen Elizabeth Goes for Gold

In England, Queen Elizabeth I ruled. Queen Elizabeth and her subjects were very excited to hear stories about Sir Francis Drake and other “seadogs” who plundered huge treasures of gold from their Spanish enemies. It was decided that England should try to take as much gold as possible from the Spanish so Spain would not become more powerful than England.

No one had a better plan than Walter Raleigh and his half brother, Sir Humphrey Gilbert. They wanted to set up a colony in America as their base. From this base, they could easily attack Spain's great treasure ships. In addition, they promised the queen that the colony would keep growing and produce more and more taxes from colonists. England would become wealthier. The plan was approved by the queen, but she made everyone promise not to tell the king of Spain. This was a private plan. "Officially," she only gave Raleigh and his brother permission to go "exploring."

Sir Gilbert Sinks at Sea

In 1583, Sir Humphrey Gilbert sailed to America with six ships. He took possession of the land in the name of the queen of England. After only one month, Gilbert decided to quit and go home. Sadly, on the way home, he drowned when his ship sank in a storm.

Gilbert's brother, Walter Raleigh, didn't quit so easily. He sent several expeditions to North Carolina in his attempt to set up the first English colony in North America.

title: Matter, Matter Everywhere
text:
Reading Strategy:

What is this passage mostly about? Underline two main ideas.

Highlight at least three key details that support the main ideas.

Look around your classroom. Everything you see — and even the things you can’t — is made of matter. And your classroom isn’t the only place with matter: matter makes up everything on Earth! Matter is made of particles so tiny that you can't see them. However, when these particles combine, they can create visible matter. Particles of matter can be organized into three states: solid, liquid, and gas. Think about an ice cube in a glass of soda. The ice cube and the glass are solid. Solids can hold their shape because their particles are packed tightly together and don’t have much room to move around. The soda is liquid. In liquids, the particles are still close together, but they are constantly moving, sliding past and bumping into each other. This explains why liquids don’t have a definite shape but instead take the shape of their container. The bubbles in the soda are gas. Particles move faster and farther away from each other in gases than they do in solids and liquids. Gas particles completely fill the container that they are in, whether that is a glass of soda, a balloon, or your classroom. They have lots of space between them, moving freely to hit and bounce off of each other.

We can see matter when there are enough particles close together, like in solids and liquids. When particles are farther apart, however, we cannot see them. We have to use our other senses to detect invisible matter, like gases. On windy days, you can feel the flow of air particles against you. Sometimes, they even carry dust and other materials, which can run into your body. Or have you ever wondered how the smell of baked bread spreads throughout your house? To smell, we use our noses to sense particles in the air. This means that the scent of bread is really bread particles moving through the air. You may not be able to see them, but your senses detect them. In what other ways have you observed the evidence of very small particles?

title: Continents and Oceans
text:
There are large areas of land on Earth. They are landforms called continents. There are seven continents in the world. These are Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America.

There are also large bodies of water on Earth. They are called oceans. The world has five oceans. They are the Arctic Ocean, Atlantic Ocean, Indian Ocean, Pacific Ocean, and Southern Ocean.

The poles are points at the top and bottom of the globe. The North Pole is the most northern point on Earth. The area around the North Pole is called the Arctic. The South Pole is the most southern point on Earth. The land around the South Pole is called Antarctica. It is also a continent.

title: Essential Question
text: How do maps help me locate things?

title: Locating Places
text: Mapmakers use imaginary lines. These lines divide a map into small squares. This makes finding a location easier. These squares form a grid. We label the grid with letters and numbers. It is called a coordinate grid.

title: Lines of Latitude
text: There are horizontal lines running east and west. These lines circle around the globe. They are called latitude lines.

title: Lines of Longitude
text: Vertical lines run around the Earth, going north to south. These are called longitude lines.

title: The Equator
text: One latitude line runs around the middle of the world. This line is called the Equator. The Equator divides the globe into halves. The halves are called the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere.

title: The Prime Meridian
text: A longitude line runs from the North Pole to the South Pole. It is called the Prime Meridian. It divides the world into two hemispheres. The hemisphere on the left is the Western Hemisphere. The one on the right is the Eastern Hemisphere.

title: GIS Technology
text:
Global Information Systems, also known as GIS, are a way of visualizing data on maps. As soon as people invented computers capable of doing it, they began using computers to map information. If you have data or information that matches locations on a map, you can use GIS to make a visual representation of that data on a map. Looking at the data overlaid on a map can reveal new relationships and patterns that might not have seemed obvious at first.

Without the ability to map data and visualize it, it can be difficult to understand what the data is representing. Trends and patterns in the data can often be missed if you do not understand the physical relationship between the various points of information. Any information that can be mapped can be visualized through GIS.

Many different careers rely on GIS data and visuals to do their work. City planners can use GIS to map the riders on public transportation like buses and subways to make sure their transportation plans meet people where they are. Biologists observe the presence of endangered species and plan protection strategies through the information they learn using GIS.

In Florida, archaeologists use GIS to map the presence of historical sites and artifacts. Archaeologists dig in the ground and dive in state waters looking for artifacts. They use GIS to make detailed digital models of the sites where they find these artifacts. Mapping the data through GIS allows them to visualize the entire site and find patterns they might otherwise miss. Recreating the site digitally also allows them to limit the amount they disturb the fragile historical sites.

County governments in the state use GIS data to identify areas threatened by the many hurricanes that develop in the waters off the coast. This helps them create and share evacuation routes with citizens. It also allows the counties to share other important information like flood zones and access to important services like fire stations and schools.

title: Chronological Thinking
text: Chronological means that we put events in the order they happened. We do this by thinking about what comes first, then next. We can keep track of chronological events by using a calendar. We can also use timelines. A calendar shows the days of the week. It also shows the months of the year in order. A calendar is a useful timeline that tracks the events of our lives and when they happened.

text: How can I talk about time?

title: Past, Present, Future
text: History tells the story of people and events that happened in the past. The things we did yesterday are in the past. The things we are doing today are in the present. The things we do tomorrow and as we grow up are in the future.

title: Timelines
text: A timeline shows events and dates in order. A timeline is divided into sections. Timelines show change over time. The space between events means that time has passed between the events. A timeline might show events that happened a long time ago. A timeline might show events that happened last week. You can create a timeline whenever you want to see events in order.

title: Historical Analysis
text: Many events in history can occur around the same period. The tools and items people used in the past become artifacts we can study. People, places, ideas, cultures, and technology change over time. Artifacts help us understand how people’s lives have changed over time. Historians analyze how much things have changed throughout history. They examine patterns to understand how and why things happened.

title: Past, Present, Future
text:
History tells the story of people and events that happened in the past. The things we did before are in the past. The things we are doing now are called the present. The things we will do later are called the future.

Chronological means that we put events in the order they happened. We do this by thinking about what came first, then next, and so on.

title: How Do We Keep Track of Time?
text:
One way to keep track of chronological events is using a calendar. A calendar shows the days of the week and months of the year. It can help us track the events of our lives and when they happened.

Time can be represented in days, months, years, decades, and centuries. These words help us understand when things happened.

A timeline is a list of events in chronological order. It starts with the earliest event and ends with the most recent event. Timelines can show change over time. A timeline might show events that happened a long time ago. A timeline might show events that happened last week.

When historians use timelines, they measure the time and label it. They often think about what was happening in the world at that same time. This allows them to provide context for a historical event or person.

title: Tribes of the Northeast
text:
Native Americans of the Northeast, or Eastern Woodlands, lived in a land rich in fresh water, including the Great Lakes. The land was also good for farming and had many types of trees and other plants.

Many tribes lived in the Eastern Woodlands. These included the Iroquois, Algonquin, Penobscot, Chippewa, Odawa, and Powhatan. They grew corn, beans, and squash. The tribes used all the natural resources around them to meet their basic needs. They used birch bark to build canoes and to cover their homes. They burned wood to stay warm and cook. They used tools for work and as weapons. The animals they hunted fed the people. The hides, or skins, were used to make clothes, containers, and bags. Everything was used, and nothing was wasted.

Eastern Woodland tribes lived in larger villages in the summer and smaller family groups in the winter. The houses were different from tribe to tribe. Some tribes lived in wigwams, which are small, dome-shaped homes. The Chippewa lived in wigwams. Tribes lived in wigwams when they moved to hunt, fish, and gather natural resources. Other tribes lived in larger, more permanent longhouses. The Iroquois lived in longhouses. Many people could live in a longhouse. The homes fit the lifestyles of each community.

title: Tribes of the West
text:
Many Native American tribes lived in the West. The West includes parts of Nevada, Idaho, Oregon, Utah, California, Colorado, Montana, and Wyoming. This area is very diverse, with mountains, rivers, coasts, and deserts.

Tribes relied on the region's abundant resources to establish a way of life. Many western tribes gathered, hunted, and fished for food. Coastal areas and the rivers of the Great Basin provided many fishing opportunities for native peoples. Tribes hunted large animals, such as bison, deer, and elk. They also gathered wild berries and nuts for food.

Many tribes followed large herds of animals and moved throughout the region. They lived in easy-to-move lodge homes, such as tepees or wickiups. A wickiup consisted of a wooden frame covered with woven leaves and brush. Some tribes lived along the Pacific coast.

Tribes of the Western region engaged in trade with one another. The tribes of the Great Basin traded shells, animal hides, furs, clothing, and baskets for other items. They used resources found in their environment for clothing. They traditionally wore furs in colder climates and seasons. In warmer areas and warmer parts of the year, they wore clothing made from bark, grasses, and animal skins.

Like other tribes, tribes of the West have a deep connection with their environment. Sacred sites that are important to the beliefs of the tribes, like mountains, sequoia trees, and rivers, are given special respect.

title: Tribes of the Southeast
text:
The Southeast region of the U.S. includes land from the Ohio River to the Gulf of America and from Texas to the Atlantic Ocean. The Native Americans who lived in this area had access to excellent soil for growing crops. Many of them were farmers. Corn was an important crop and was traded with other tribes. Southeastern tribes hunted and fished for their proteins. The land was also rich in plants that were made into medicines to help heal people. Because this area is a mixture of forests and grasslands, homes ranged from grass huts to wooden houses.

One of the largest tribes of the Southeast was the Creek tribe. Many early Creek tribes built large earthen mounds throughout the region. These mounds were part of large ceremonial complexes. The Creek lived in log cabins made from lumber, mud, and tree bark. Like other tribes, the Creek adapted to their environment and used the resources available where they settled. The Creek were expert farmers and planted crops such as corn, beans, and squash. They also hunted and fished for food.

title: The First Amendment
text:
"Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the government for a redress of grievances."

Religion

“Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion ...” The government shall make no law that makes its citizens practice a specific religion. This is known as the “Establishment Clause.” This means there is no established or official religion the United States government is making people follow.

“... or prohibiting the free exercise thereof ...” The government shall make no law that restricts citizens’ freedom to practice any religion. This is known as the “Free Exercise Clause.” This means the government cannot stop people from following their religion.

Speech

“Congress shall make no law ... abridging the freedom of speech ...” The government shall make no law that restricts freedom of speech. People have the right to speak freely, as long as it does not start violence.

Press

“Congress shall make no law ... abridging the freedom ... of the press …” The government shall make no law that restricts freedom of press, journalism, or news. Newspapers and journalists can write what they want about the government.

Assembly

“Congress shall make no law ... abridging the freedom ... or the right of the people peaceably to assemble ...” The government shall make no law that restricts freedom of assembly, or when people gather together to discuss politics or any other topic.

Petition

“Congress shall make no law ... abridging the freedom ... to petition the government for a redress of grievances.” The government shall make no law that prohibits its people from criticizing or asking the government to change.
