title: Ancient Civilizations in the Americas
text:
Before European exploration and colonization, thousands of Native Americans lived in the Americas and the Caribbean Islands. However, their ancestors were not originally from these regions. Historians, scientists, and archaeologists have developed many theories to explain how Native Americans first arrived in the Western Hemisphere.

For many years, researchers believed that the ancient ancestors of Native Americans came to America from Siberia, a region in northern Asia. They concluded that these people arrived about 12,000 years ago by hiking across a narrow strip of land that once bridged Asia and Alaska. This land bridge is known as the Bering Strait. From there, they settled in other areas of North America. Eventually, they migrated to Central and South America and the Caribbean Islands.

In recent years, however, archaeologists in North and South America have discovered ancient tools, weapons, campsites, and skeletons that are even older than artifacts from the land-bridge travelers. The bones, in particular, were very different from those linked to the people who crossed the land bridge. This new research suggests that a large group of migrants crossed the Bering Strait as early as 30,000 years ago. This larger group split into smaller tribes about 15,000 years ago. Some traveled south through the Americas.

Other researchers have proposed that the first people in the Americas traveled here by boat from southern Asia, Australia, India, Japan, or even Europe, arriving long before the land-bridge travelers. These people may have later died out. However, they also could have joined the Siberian tribes who migrated from Asia to Alaska via the Bering Strait. Combined, these groups represent the Native Americans’ earliest ancestors.

This week, you will be learning about some of the ancient civilizations of North America. Each of these civilizations had unique and distinct ways of life. Each had different types of economies, governments, and social and cultural practices. As you study each civilization, take notice of similarities and differences between each group.

Aztec

The Aztecs arrived in Mesoamerica around 1200 C.E. They built their capital city, Tenochtitlán, on artificial islands in the middle of Lake Texcoco. They had a sophisticated agricultural system using irrigation and “floating gardens” that allowed them to grow much of their own food. The Aztecs also formed political alliances with two neighboring tribes that helped to expand their empire. Today, the capital city of Tenochtitlán has become what is now Mexico City, Mexico.

Maya

The Maya Empire lasted for nearly 3,000 years, from 1800 B.C.E. to about 900 C.E. The empire covered parts of what are now Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, and Belize. The Maya were advanced mathematicians and agriculturalists. They knew how to rotate crops to keep farm soil from being overused. They used math to create complex architecture and accurate calendars. The Maya had a written hieroglyphic language and a sophisticated government system. This civilization existed between many independent city-states. Trade existed between the city-states. However, each settlement tended to manage its own people.

Mound Builders

The Mound Builders, also known as the Mississippians, lived in the Mississippi and Ohio river valleys from about 1000 to 1700 C.E. This culture received its name from the raised mounds found in the ruins of its ancient cities. The Mound Builders settled in places all over the eastern half of the U.S. Not much is known about the purpose of the mounds they built, but researchers believe they could have housed a settlement’s rulers. The mounds were also likely a central location for a Mississippian settlement.

Ancestral Pueblo

The Ancestral Pueblo lived around the Four-Corners region of the United States, from about 100 to 1600 C.E. This included parts of the states of modern Utah, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico. The Ancestral Pueblo built stone buildings and cliff dwellings that can still be seen today. By about 1300 C.E., however, the people seem to have vanished from the area. No one knows for sure what happened to the Ancestral Pueblo or where they went, but many scholars and historians believe that the modern Pueblo tribes are their descendents.

Inuit

Located in the Arctic Circle in Canada, Alaska, and Greenland, the people known as the Inuit lived farther north than any other people on Earth. With such a cold and harsh climate, the Inuit could not farm like other Native Americans. They relied on hunting, fishing, and gathering plants and shellfish for food. Like other Native Americans, the Inuit used dogs as a source of transportation. For fishing, however, they cut holes into the ice or made wood-carved kayaks. Many Inuit still live in the Arctic Circle today, but many live in modern houses. Those who can afford them use snowmobiles instead of dogs and sleds to travel and hunt.

title: Aztec
text:
The Aztec empire grew rapidly through the 14th century. Its people conquered neighboring peoples and built impressive, thriving cities. At its peak, the Aztec empire had a population of around five or six million, including conquered peoples. Tenochtítlan, the capital city of the Aztec empire, had a population of over 140,000, making it the most densely populated city to ever exist in Mesoamerica.

Government

Aztec society was incredibly advanced for its time. The Aztec government was a monarchy. It was ruled by a monarch, known as an emperor. The emperor worked with a council of four advisors to make all decisions for the empire. The empire was organized into provinces, which were required to pay a tribute to the emperor, depending on each province’s production. The Aztec government had many of the same systems and leadership roles that we have in our own society today, such as legal courts, a military, governors, tax collectors, postal and messenger services, and more.

Social Classes

The Aztecs had a social hierarchy in which individuals were identified as nobles, commoners, serfs, or enslaved people. The noble class was made up of government and military leaders, priests, and lords. The king was the highest rank in the nobility. Commoners were farmers and artisans. Serfs and enslaved people were the lowest-ranking people in the Aztec social structure. Even though there were four main rankings in the Aztec social structure, everyone in Aztec society who wasn’t in the noble class was considered a commoner.

Economy

Aztec agriculture was very successful because the Aztec were both farm laborers and experts in seeding and crop rotation. The Aztec were the first Mesoamerican group to extensively use chinampas, which look like gardens floating on water. This type of farming was necessary because they decided to build the great city of Tenochtitlán on a marshy island in the middle of Lake Texcoco.

Some of the crops the Aztecs grew would be sold at markets or exchanged as part of a trade. An empire as large as the Aztec also relied on products and crops grown outside of their area. The cotton they used in clothing, blankets, and armor couldn’t grow in the highlands. It would have been acquired from tribes they had conquered farther south. Cacao beans, their primary source of currency, didn’t grow in the region and needed to be acquired through trade.

Regional markets sold everyday goods: cloth, knives, medicine, produce, pottery, and gems. Government officials were on hand, not only to make sure the prices were fair but also to take their share of taxes. Crops, goods, or cacao beans were taken from all the merchants. A vast marketplace drew thousands of vendors and consumers each day.

Long-distance traders known as Pochteca were both a source of goods and a source of information. These traders would travel great distances over land to acquire goods for the nobility. This could have included special feathers or precious gems. While they were traveling, they would share information from different parts of the empire and even act as spies. These spies helped the Aztecs learn about their enemies’ defenses and made them easier to defeat.

title: Maya
text:
Some of the Maya’s great temples, pyramids, palaces, and residences still stand today, buried in the deep jungle. Historians have determined that the earliest Maya villages appeared around 2000 B.C.E. The Maya started out as farmers, but 2,000 years later, they were creating pyramids and making advancements in mathematics.

Social Classes

A class system existed in the Maya Empire. The ruler was at the top, had total power, and often also had the duties of a religious leader or priest. Governors from four royal families controlled the land; below the governors were the educated class, consisting of artists and architects. Near the bottom were the plebeians, including farmers, merchants, and laborers. Enslaved people, captives from wars, and their children were at the very bottom.

Government

The Maya had a legal system, which included a system for determining guilt, wooden cages to hold prisoners, and fines. At the height of Maya culture, the Maya had 18 separate states. These states each had smaller towns and villages, all of which were governed by a capital city. Half of the states were ruled by a single ruler, while the other half were governed by a council of members of the nobility. Leadership positions were passed down through family lines, or a member of the nobility was elected by the council and religious leaders.

Science

Maya cities included hundreds of homes and dozens of stepped pyramids. It took great engineering skill and mathematical knowledge to construct the well-built cities, the ruins of which have lasted millennia.

The Maya were very advanced in math. While we are comfortable using a base-10 system of mathematics, the Maya used base-5 or base-20. Instead of numerals, they used three symbols: zero: a shell shape; one: a dot; and five: a short line or bar. Armed with this knowledge and no instruments, they made extremely accurate observations of the stars. For example, we know a year has 365 and one-quarter days; the Maya measured it to 365.242 days. We know it takes 29.53059 days for the moon to orbit the Earth; the Maya measured it as 29.5308.

Agriculture

The Maya grew many crops and even domesticated animals, such as dogs and turkeys. They were great hunters and enjoyed deer, armadillos, wild pigs, rabbits, and monkeys. The deadly jaguar was very important to the Maya culture, and a jaguar pelt worn by a ruler was seen as a very high honor.

title: Mound Builders
text:
Around 1000 C.E., a people known as the Mississippians occupied much of the southeast region of the North American continent. Also called the Temple Mound Builders or the Mound Builders, no one knows for sure where they came from. They learned to work the land well enough to stay in one place and earned their nickname from the massive mounds they built within their villages.

The Mississippians are believed to have been organized into social orders or governments that included chiefs, warriors, workers, and even artists. Early accounts from Spanish explorers in the area describe powerful chiefs who lived in villages with large, earthen mounds and wooden defenses around the village perimeters.

Larger settlements extended rule over smaller villages. These smaller settlements existed on the borders of large trading centers. Less powerful chiefs paid tribute to the chiefs of the larger settlements. One of the largest settlements was found in Illinois. It was called Cahokia. The remnants of Cahokia stand today as the Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site.

Mississippian burial practices also suggest that they adhered to a social hierarchy. Poorer people were buried with basic tools or nothing at all. Those with wealth or more social standing were buried with rarer treasures, such as ornaments made of copper or shells. Burial mounds sometimes marked the resting places of families of higher rank.

Not only did the Mississippians have sophisticated social structures, but they were also noted for their advanced knowledge of agriculture. Corn was an important food source that encouraged year-round settlements and population growth. The Mississippians built their large villages in the flood plains of large rivers. The flood plains offered rich, well-drained soil that was good for growing corn, squash, and beans. Nearby fish and waterfowl were also readily available in these locations. Deer, raccoon, and turkey remained important sources of food, too.

What they couldn’t grow or make themselves, the Mississippians traded for. Goods moved all across the continent through extensive trade networks. Archaeologists have found late Mississippian artifacts hundreds of miles away from the villages where they started.

title: Ancestral Pueblo
text:
Not much is known about the structure of Ancestral Puebloan society. Formerly known as the Anasazi, the Ancestral Pueblo left behind no written records, and no knowledge remains about certain aspects of their society. We may not know what kind of government or social hierarchies they had, but we can glean some information from the buildings and artifacts they left behind.

The Ancestral Pueblo shifted from a hunter-gatherer society into an agricultural society between 500 and 750 C.E. Agriculture became the main staple of their economy. They built homes and public buildings out of sandstone, mortar, and wooden beams. One famous example of architecture left behind by the Ancestral Puebloans is the Cliff Palace in Mesa Verde National Park. The Cliff Palace has examples of dwelling places, storage rooms, and underground ceremonial chambers, called "kivas."

The Cliff Palace is the largest example of an Ancestral Puebloan settlement, but there are also other, smaller villages and settlements throughout Mesa Verde National Park. Some modern Native American groups believe they are descended from the Ancestral Pueblo who lived in the Cliff Palace and its surrounding villages. The Ancestral Pueblo are believed to have left the Mesa Verde area around 1200 C.E., but there is no conclusive evidence to tell us what happened to them. There are theories that they moved south, where their descendants still live today, while others claim there was a famine that wiped the people out entirely. Without any written records or physical evidence, there’s no way to know for sure exactly what happened or where they went.

title: Inuit
text:
Arctic tribes lived in parts of northern Canada, Alaska, and Greenland. The Inuit, Yuit, and Aleut are examples of Arctic tribes. The land of the Arctic and Subarctic regions remains frozen most of the year.

The people of the Canadian Arctic are known as the Inuit, which means “the people.” About 50,000 Inuits live in northern Canada today. This region is known as Inuit Nunaat, meaning “Inuit homeland.” The Inuit have always made their living through traditional means such as hunting, fishing, and trapping.

In the Arctic, food is not available in large amounts year-round. The native peoples who lived in this region had a very special understanding of how to get food in such a unique area. They traveled great distances to hunt animals like seals and caribou. They were also experts at fishing. Many tribal people gathered when a large animal, like a whale, was caught. They used all parts of the whale and its resources. When food was scarce, communities would organize into small units.

Arctic tribes used animal pelts to make their clothes. These kept them warm in the cold climate. Seal hides were very valuable because they were waterproof. Many Arctic tribes, like the Inuit, used dogs for transportation. For fishing, however, they made wood-carved kayaks. They also traveled on sleds and toboggans. Depending on the time of year, people either lived in tents made of animal skins or in underground dwellings made of wood or bone. Igloos were usually only temporary shelters built near hunting grounds during the winter months.

Women and children often gathered seaweed, sculpins, and clams to eat, while men hunted for game. Meat was the main staple in Arctic tribe diets. In Inuit culture, sharing food was an important and necessary part of everyday life for well-being and survival. Whatever food was caught was shared by all. This helped create a strong sense of community and ensured that no one went hungry.

There was no formally organized government in Inuit communities, but there were elders, leaders, and shamans who helped keep the peace, settle disputes, and work to create a united and harmonious way of life.

There were also oral laws that involved things like respecting wildlife and the environment and avoiding selfishness and fighting. The Inuit believed that breaking these laws would lead to bad consequences, such as bad winter storms, illness, or famine.

If a person caused an issue or broke one of the laws, they had to meet with the elders of the community to discuss their behavior and be encouraged to change and be better. If the person did not change, the same process was repeated until either the person changed their behavior or faced severe consequences. Love, patience, understanding, and talking peacefully were important tools used to maintain peace and solve problems.

These same practices are being woven into modern law enforcement in Inuit communities, even today.

title: Let's Learn About Kentucky This Year!
text:
Welcome to Kentucky Studies Weekly! Hang on tight for the ride of a lifetime as we explore our state from top to bottom, start to finish, inside, outside, upside, and downside. We'll climb the highest mountain, drop into the deepest hole, roam with the buffalo, hunt with the mountain men, build a boat, fly an airplane, discover gold, and walk with the pioneers! This is Kentucky Studies Weekly, your weekly time capsule of historical events.

Each issue of the paper will include a current event on the front cover that discusses a real news item. Our cover story will help you get a head start on this week's history lesson. We will take you on a journey into the experiences of great people and great events with our cover stories.

And there's more: We will tell you about the Kentucky animals, birds, trees, and plants. We will give you games, crafts, and activities to enjoy and help you learn new words.

This year you will travel back in time to discover the historical events that helped make Kentucky a great place to live. Are you ready for takeoff? Then turn the page, and let's start our Kentucky adventure!

title: Prehistoric Kentucky
text:
Where are Kentucky's Dinosaurs?

How can you talk about prehistoric life without talking about dinosaurs? The answer is simple: You can't! Scientists figure there were dinosaurs just about everywhere in North America long ago, but finding their remains takes real detective work, especially in the eastern United States. In western states, like Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado, and Utah, people sometimes find dinosaur bones, footprints, or even eggs, just lying on top of the ground! Here in the East, we have a lot more trees and vegetation than they do. All this vegetation has built up many layers of topsoil. Topsoil is great for growing stuff, but it's lousy for hunting dino fossils. To find fossils, you have to be lucky enough to find "cretaceous rock" poking out of the topsoil. Cretaceous rock was around when dinosaurs were alive, and Kentucky has very little of it.

Nevertheless, scientists have found remains of a few different kinds of dinosaurs. Two of the most commonly found in our area are the albertosaurus (more commonly known as the dryptosaurus) and the hadrosaur. Scientists think we'd find a lot more dino fossils if we could just lift up all the topsoil that covers most of the cretaceous rock. Of course, that's much too big of a job since in some places the cretaceous rock is buried nearly 20,000 feet down!

Say Cheese!

On this big, beautiful planet, animals come and animals go. Dinosaurs, mastodons, and giant sloths are all good examples of animals that were once here, but are now gone. But there are some animals that have outlasted them all! "Which animals are those?" you ask. Well, which animals swim great, have big ol' teeth, and get blockbuster movie jobs? Did you say sharks? If you did, you guessed correctly! Sharks haven't changed much in the millions of years since they first hit the ocean scene. They've still got big teeth and bad attitudes, and here's one more little detail: They still have cartilage skeletons (the rubbery stuff that you feel when you squash your nose flat). And here's the tricky thing about cartilage: While bones leave fossil remains for us to study, cartilage doesn't! Well, there is one part of a shark that does leave fossil remains, and it's the end of a shark you usually want to stay away from when he's alive: his teeth! Say "cheese!" (A great place to look for sharks' teeth in our state is in shale driveways. Good luck!)

Man: The Mighty Hunter?

How did humans contribute to the extinction of prehistoric animals, like mammoths and mastodons? This mystery takes detective work. For example, scientists have found man-made tools and weapons close to mammoth fossils. Did humans hunt these giant animals, or did they just happen to live where mammoths once lived? Until 1983, proof of humans hunting mammoths, such as a mastodon fossil with an arrow point stuck inside it, hadn't been found. Then in 1983, at Edisto Beach, South Carolina, a fossilized elephant rib was found. What was special about this rib? It had cut marks on it that were made by ancient stone-scraping tools. Hmmm . . . is this proof that ancient man hunted mammoths and mastodons?

Age of Mammals

The Age of Mammals spans about 65 million years, beginning with the death of dinosaurs and ending when recorded history began with man about 6,000 years ago.

Think of as many Kentucky mammals as you can. There are rabbit, squirrel, deer, plenty of rats and mice, and even some big carnivores. That's enough to fill your whole brain with mammals, isn't it? But scientists think that long ago there were as many as three times more mammal species than there are today! Imagine sloths as big as mini-vans, huge mammoths, saber-toothed tigers, and a few hornless rhinos. Where did they all go? Were they killed by comets or disease? Did they freeze to death during an ice age? Nobody knows for sure. Some scientists think that many of these mammals were destroyed by a new and interesting animal, which was brand new to the Kentucky scene: prehistoric man!

Prehistoric Elephants Throughout Kentucky!

For a good look at the remains of elephant ancestors, you can stay right here in Kentucky. At one time, there may have been more mammoths than any other mammal in Kentucky. Mammoths came in all shapes and sizes, and their fossil remains are found throughout most of Kentucky.

Prehistoric elephants evolved into a great variety of animals, some of them as big as houses! Modern elephants often have long, upward-curving tusks, but prehistoric elephants had tusks you wouldn't believe! Some were short and downward curving, like fangs. Others were as long as a car and straight as a spear. Some looped like a roller coaster, huge and round. Still others were shovel shaped, like a built-in spoon.

In some very cold places, like Siberia, nearly complete mammoths have been found frozen in the ice. Some of them even have hair and skin!

title: Friendliness
text:
You know, just being friendly can make the difference between a bad day and a good day. The United States is home to some of the friendliest people around. Maybe that's why America has so many good days! Friendliness can turn driving in a car, riding on a bus or taking a walk in your neighborhood into a pleasant memory all its own. Friendliness can make someone glad you were the one who answered the phone! Of course, some people choose to be unfriendly most of the time, but why would you want to do that? After all, you hardly ever hear anyone say, "I just love coming over for a visit. You're all so nice and grumpy!"

Make friendliness one of your character traits, and anyone who ever visits you will go away feeling as warm as the sun!

title: Time Traveler
text: I was a little nervous as I stepped into the strange machine. I'll admit that right up front! Oh sure, it was an honor to be the first kid to travel through time, but since it had never been done, can you blame me for having the jitters? Doctor Brown strapped me in, and then he sat down himself. With the push of a button, the journey began! At first, nothing happened. Then, outside the window, the lab fell down. Well, it didn't "fall" exactly; it sort of looked like it was being torn down in super-fast motion by a construction crew. Soon we were sitting in an empty lot, and the whole neighborhood started to disappear - just like the lab disappeared. In a moment, I knew what I was seeing: Outside the window, I was witnessing the whole history of this spot - only in high-speed rewind! In a moment, there was nothing but grass as far as I could see. Buffalo zipped by, going backwards. Snow gathered all around us. At times, it covered up the windows. Other times, we could see it falling upwards from the ground to the sky! One moment later, we were surrounded by water! The wind was blowing, and in the blink of an eye, mountains formed all around us. I gasped. The time capsule was being buried beneath layers and layers of heavy soil and rock! It was dark and frightening. "Don't worry! I expected this!" shouted Doctor Brown as he switched on powerful lights inside the craft. My knuckles were white from gripping the arms of my chair. Right against the window, I could see a rock that looked just like pictures of dinosaur bones I had seen. Before my eyes, the rock seemed to melt away, and in its place, I thought I saw a white bone forming. Moments later, the dirt began to blow away from the top of the window, and I could see the sun. The bone I was looking at now lay on the surface of a strange landscape, with great, green plants all around, and I could hear strange calls outside the time capsule. In an instant, other bones blew into view, joining the bone I was looking at. I stared in astonishment as muscles, cartilage, and finally skin formed around the bones. My hair stood on end as a huge dinosaur opened its eyes and stood up, staring right into our window! I had seen him die, decay and fossilize-only backwards! It was about then that I fainted. When I woke up, the face of my mother was staring down at me. "We were worried about you," she said, stroking my hair. "Doctor Brown told us what happened. Are you going to be all right?" I smiled, thinking about the amazing things I'd seen. "I'm going to be fine, Mom," I said. "But have I got a story for you!"

title: What happened to the dinosaurs?
text: It's been a long time since anyone has seen a real-life dinosaur. In fact, in the grand scope of history, scientists believe that humans missed dinosaurs by about 63 million years! But where did dinos go? Nobody knows for sure, but there are a couple of good theories (or ideas with evidence) about how the dinosaurs became extinct. Some scientists believe that at the end of the Cretaceous Period, about 65 million years ago, the world's shallow seas dried up, changing the climate around the whole planet. Summers became hotter, and winters cooler. Dinosaurs, without fur or feathers for protection, couldn't keep warm enough in the winter or cool enough in the summer to survive. Other scientists believe that a huge asteroid collided with the Earth, causing massive fires and darkening the Earth with smoke and dust for many months. Without light, plants died. Without plants, plant-eating dinosaurs died. Without plant-eating dinosaurs, meat-eating dinosaurs died. Another theory says that many dinosaurs did survive and evolved into birds. There's good evidence for all of these theories and many more. Maybe someday, you'll have a theory yourself!

title: Cottontail Rabbit
text: Did you know that a hare is different from a rabbit? When hares are born, they have hair on them and their eyes are open. Rabbits are born blind, and they have no hair. Another difference between them is that hares jump high, while rabbits run faster. The eastern cottontail rabbit grows about 13 inches to 16 inches long, from head to tail. Its name comes from its white tail, which looks like cotton. The cottontail makes its home in a vacant hole or bush. The female gives birth several times a year, with up to seven babies born each time. Cats, fox, hawks and owls are predators that help control the number of bunnies. During the day, cottontail rabbits usually hide in thick cover. The rabbit may be hard to see, but if you recognize and follow its tracks, you may catch a glimpse of one. "There goes Peter Cottontail, hopping down the bunny trail. . . ."

title: Woolly Mammoth
text:
How to make:

You will need some newspaper torn into small pieces, an old stocking, 12 pipe cleaners, wool yarn, two buttons, and a needle and thread.

1. Cut off the end of the stocking so it's about eight inches long. Then stuff it with newspaper. Put very little in the toe, and stuff the rest firmly.

2. Wind wool around the open end of the stocking to make the tail. Bind the toe end to make the trunk and head, as shown in the picture.

3. Join three pipe cleaners, and wrap them around the body behind the head. Tie in a knot underneath and leave the ends to make the legs. Repeat for the back legs.

4. Wind wool around a friend's hands, and then cut one side of the wool to make lots of pieces. Put the yarn over the mammoth's back, and stitch it onto the stocking.

5. Join two pipe cleaners, and poke them through the wool near the trunk. Make the ends the same length and twist them around each other. Do this again for the other tusk.

6. Sew on the buttons for eyes and a few short pieces of wool for the mammoth's ears. Then make sure the legs are the same length so that the mammoth will stand up.

title: Philanthropy and Values
text:
Maybe you have heard the word "philanthropy" before. What does it mean? It describes actions that people make for the good of other people. What is a value? It's a way of behaving that people believe is good - like believing it's good to be honest. Is honesty one of your values?

One way you can practice philanthropy today is to help yourself and others learn good values. How do you learn good values? You can learn them from your parents and grandparents, your teachers at school or church and other people you trust.

You can also learn them from people that have been recognized for doing good things for society. An easy way to learn about people that have done good things is to visit values.com. Values.com has lots of stories and short videos that highlight the traits that make each of us better people. They even have billboards on the highway to remind you about good values.

For example, you may have seen a billboard that looks like the one shown here.

This billboard is about Oral Lee Brown, who saved money from her job to send 19 kids to college... all by herself! Wow! Isn't that cool? You can learn about lots of other people who practice philanthropy at values.com. Be sure to look for more of their "billboards" on Page 4 of Studies Weekly this year. We think they're so cool we want to remind you to check them out!

title: Let's Write
text: You are living in Kentucky at the time that huge mammals roam the state. What is your favorite prehistoric mammal and why? Is it your pet? Is it scary looking? What does it eat? Can it do work for you? What does it look like?

title: What a Great Place to Live!
text:
The land under our state, with all its hills, mountains and cities, is like a giant pizza, with lots of great toppings! Read on and learn more . .

Welcome to another issue of Kentucky Studies Weekly. We're glad to have you back! This week, we're going to compare Kentucky to a giant pizza. Imagine that the toppings of this pizza are all of the cities and towns, parks and playgrounds, sidewalks and roads and schools and museums. Doesn't that sound tasty?

Now, think of what's underneath every great pizza: a great crust, right? If you scraped off all of Kentucky's amazing "toppings," what kind of crust do you think you'd find? A soft, thick, lumpy one? A thin, crisp, flat one? The truth is, when we're talking about Kentucky, there's a little of something for everyone!

On the state's eastern side, the crust is thick and bumpy. That's the Mountain Region. The Cumberland Mountains are there. They're part of a huge bunch of mountains called the Appalachians!

In the middle part of the state, look for everything from soft, rolling hills, to rich farmland, to deep, black coal deposits. There are lots of "toppings" throughout this part of Kentucky, with more cities and towns than on any other part of our pizza.

On the western edge of Kentucky, the crust might be just a bit soggy! There are a lot of rivers and swamps over there. Is your mouth watering yet? We hope so, because in this issue, we're going to take a look at the natural regions that make up our state.

The truth is, while one sidewalk or street may look very much like another, underneath it all is a tasty spread of land that changes from east to west, and from north to south. So let's serve ourselves a great big slice of Kentucky pizza - but please hold the anchovies!

title: Kentucky's Six Regions
text:
1) Jackson Purchase Region

If you like swamps, you owe yourself a visit to the wester-most tip of our fair state, which is known as the Jackson Purchase Region. The swamps are formed by all that water from the Mississippi River. In fact, there are THREE mighty rivers that form borders of this region! The other two are the Ohio River and the Tennessee River. Water, water everywhere, and it makes for some pretty good cotton growing! The Jackson Purchase area grows more cotton than any other place in the state!

2) Western Coal Field Region

Standing in the Western Coal Field Region of Kentucky, things might look a lot like the Pennyroyal Region, and you might not be able to tell the two apart - until you take a look under the surface! The rich farmland of the Pennyroyal goes pretty deep, but if you lift up just a bit of the Western Coal Field topsoil, what do you find? You probably guessed it already: COAL - and tons of it! Miles and miles of rich, black coal deposits. Nowadays, we don't use coal quite like we used to (to heat our homes), but power companies still use lots of it to make electricity. You do use electricity, don't you?

3) The Pennyroyal Region

Are there any bats reading this issue of Kentucky Studies Weekly? If so, listen up! The Pennyroyal Region might just be the region for you! It's the largest region in the state, and it covers much of Kentucky's southern border, but here's what might interest you bats: The Pennyroyal Region is full of underground springs and caves, including Mammoth Cave, one of the most visited caves in the whole darned world! The Pennyroyal Region also contains a huge piece of country called "The Barrens." It's called this because it doesn't have many trees, but a farmer can get pretty much anything to grow out of the ground there. Maybe, if he wanted trees, he could grow some giant carrots instead, and then he could just rest in the shade of their leafy tops!

4) The Knobs Region

The Knobs Region is the smallest region in the state. It wraps like a big horseshoe around the Bluegrass Region. How could we describe the Knobs? Well, it's full of rolling and rocky hills that aren't really tall enough to be called mountains. In fact, the best thing to call these hills might just be . . . hmmmm . . . KNOBS! The land in the valleys around the Knobs is great for farming, but the truth is, most places in Kentucky are the same way! You can hardly throw a rock anywhere in Kentucky without it landing on great farming soil!

5) The Bluegrass Region

You might be able to guess where Kentucky got its nickname, the Bluegrass State. The Bluegrass Region of Kentucky is covered with the stuff! People who study that kind of thing figure that Kentucky bluegrass grew first in far-away Eurasia, and it was somehow brought to Kentucky long before Europeans ever sailed the ocean blue and wound up here! The soil in bluegrass territory is rich and fertile ("fertile" soil means soil that can grow crops easily), and there are plenty of trees and water to go around. Maybe that's why people settled the Bluegrass Region so quickly, and maybe that's why so many people call it home today!

6) Eastern Mountains and Coal Fields Region

What do you think gave the Eastern Coal Field Region its name? It couldn't be that there's COAL there, could it? The eastern part of our state is just brimming with the black stuff that people counted on for so long to heat their homes! The region is also the home of the Cumberland Mountains, and the Cumberland Gap, where most of Kentucky's first settlers made their way into the state! The Cumberland Mountains are part of the Appalachians.

That's One Big Place!

Where's the biggest place you've ever been? Disney World? The Grand Canyon? There was once a place on Earth bigger than anywhere you've ever visited! We're talking bigger than Louisville, bigger than Kentucky, even bigger than all of North America! This huge place was called "Pangaea." This word means "one worldwide land." Pangaea was one huge continent! Imagine being able to travel over all the world's land without getting in a boat or a jet! What happened to this giant continent? Over millions of years, the land broke into huge sections and moved across the face of the planet to become the seven continents we know today. You may have visited some pretty big places, but you'll never visit a place as totally huge as Pangaea. But don't feel bad; nobody ever visited Pangaea. Scientists believe that the "worldwide land" broke into continents millions and millions of years before people ever lived on Earth!

States on Plates

What would the world look like without water? If you had a machine that could suck up all the world's oceans, you would see that the continents are resting on top of huge landmasses called "tectonic plates" that touch each other under the oceans. Scientists call the study of these plates "plate tectonics." There are often earthquakes where two plates rub against each other. For instance, there is a famous place in California called the "San Andreas Fault" that is right on the edge of one huge plate. Earthquakes happen there all the time! Where there are gaps or holes between plates, heat and molten rock from the Earth's core can leak out and become a volcano! Fortunately, Kentucky rarely gets any earthquakes. And when we do, they're usually not very bad. Whew!

title: Zaarg's Mysterious Discovery
text: Zaarg pulled a lever at the console of his hovering starship, and he slowly floated down through the moist, wispy clouds of a bright Kentucky morning. He was on his planet's fourth mission to this strange place, and he was sweating with excitement. A mystery awaited him - a mystery he was determined to solve. He missed his own planet as he imagined the view from his bedroom window, where a flat, silvery, metal surface covers his whole world. Zaarg sighed. When the blue planet had first appeared on their scopes, they had sent three missions, one by one, to find out just what this "Earth" place was made of. The first ship had brought back a sample from the surface of the planet. It was a sort of deep, brown, crumbly mess that didn't stick together well. The scientists of his planet had been pleased, but they wanted more. So it was that the second expedition to Earth had been sent, and what they found confused everyone. Their samples were big, roundish and hard. One of the scientists had struck one of the hard things with his hand and then howled in pain. Had the two explorers visited two different planets by mistake? A third expedition was in order, and when the spaceship went to Earth, it landed in some deep, blue liquid that seemed to rush past the explorer. He gathered some of it in a jar and flew home. The scientists placed the three samples side by side and scratched their heads. Surely, there must be some mistake. Was Earth soft, brown, and crumbly, or blue and wet, or full of roundish, hard things? There was only one way to solve the mystery. That was why Zaarg had been called. Now, light years from home, his ship touched down. He stepped proudly down the ramp. Then he tripped and fell over something hard and round, and he landed face-down in a puddle of something wet. He scrambled to his feet, and then he found that his star suit was covered with dark, crumbly stuff. Zaarg was dumb struck. "All three," he whispered in amazement. "This planet has all three!" He grabbed the hard thing that had caused his fall and hurried back to the cockpit of his ship, careful not to touch his suit and disturb his discoveries. No one saw his ship rise silently through the air and off toward his planet, but he knew that at home he would receive a hero's welcome. Through careful study and exploration, he had solved the mystery!

title: Northern Kentucky
text:
The largest city in northern Kentucky is called Covington, but it wasn't always that way. There was a time, in the 1700s, when the whole area was just wilderness. In those days, right where the Ohio River and Licking River met up at an area known as the Point, pioneers and explorers liked to get together for a rendezvous. By 1850, lots and lots of German and Irish immigrants had settled in the area, and Covington had become Kentucky's second-largest city!

About 100 miles to the east of Covington, there's another city called Ashland. Ashland was formed at about the same time Covington was making a name for itself (in the 1850s). Ashland caught the eye of ambitious industrialists, who saw that all around Ashland there were plenty of timber, coal and limestone, which were perfect for the manufacturing of pig iron. The area then dedicated itself to making the stuff!

title: Why Did Our Ancestors Move Here?
text: You know, the actual land in a state plays an important role in deciding what kinds of people live there and what they do for work and fun. It's true! For example, if the land in a state is rich and good for farming, it's not hard to guess that the place might be settled by farmers! If there's plenty of game, hunters and trappers might enjoy living there. If it's near water, especially an ocean, it might be a good place for fishermen. These days, some of that is changing because humans are getting better at creating environments that are exactly what they want, wherever they are. But you don't have to go back too many generations to find people who came to our state just because of what the land had to offer! Think about it for a moment. With what you now know about Kentucky's natural regions, what are some things that you think brought people here?

title: Firefly
text:
Do fireflies really have little, tiny light bulbs on their bodies that switch on and off? It may look like it, but their little lights are really produced by a chemical process that happens inside their bodies.

There are more than 1,500 different types of fireflies, but only about 50 kinds are found in the United States. They like warm, moist areas and are found mostly near creeks, marshlands and lowland areas. Did you know that fireflies, or lightning bugs, are members of the beetle family? Fireflies are dull brown or black when they're all grown up. Male fireflies use their light as a mating call to attract females. When the female blinks back in response, they live happily ever after - but for a very short time! The adult firefly lives only about three weeks. The female dies after depositing her eggs, and the male dies soon after.

title: Knitting for Charity - An American Tradition
text:
Did you know that, all across our country, people are knitting for charity? In homes, churches, schools and even prisons, they meet regularly to knit for people in need around the world. They knit hats for cancer victims, caps for premature babies, afghans for refugees, blankets for the homeless, socks for soldiers and blankets for shelter animals.

One charity knitting program, Afghans for Afghans, makes hats, mittens, sweaters, vests, socks and blankets to help keep schoolchildren in Afghanistan warm during the harsh winters. Another group, called Warm Up America, has distributed more than 250,000 blankets to people in need. One of their programs, called Caps to the Capital, collects knitted caps for newborns in developing nations.

The tradition of knitting for those in need actually started during the Revolutionary War when Martha Washington organized officers' wives into a group who knitted for the soldiers. Farm women also knitted socks and clothing, and many even rode to the battlefield themselves to deliver them!

During the Civil War, women across the country made socks, gloves, mufflers and blankets for soldiers. During World War I, John D. Rockefeller, a wealthy New York politician, welcomed knitters into his mansion. President Woodrow Wilson allowed sheep to graze on the White House lawn to provide some wool. Eleanor Roosevelt, America's First Lady during World War II, set an example for the country by knitting for soldiers. Today, there are many groups that still continue this noble tradition by knitting clothing, socks and blankets for our soldiers overseas.

title: Make a Relief Map of Kentucky
text:
Materials:

Corrugated cardboard

2 cups of flour

1/2 cup of salt

3/4 cup of water

Watercolors or poster paint

Salt Dough:

Mix 2 cups of flour, 1/2 cup of salt, and 3/4 cup of water together to make a dough. You will need to knead it for three to four minutes. If you need to make it more sticky, add a little more water. To make it less sticky, add a little more flour.

How to make:

1. Cut a piece of cardboard into a 12 inch x 12 inch square. Trim the cardboard to make the shape of Kentucky.

2. Form the different mountain and valley regions out of salt dough. (See recipe above.)

3. Let the map dry for a few days.

4. After the map is dry, paint it with watercolors or poster paint.

title: Let's Write
text: Write about building your own hotel in Kentucky. In which region would you build? Why there? In the back of your hotel, you must build a playground and swimming pool for children. What kinds of things will you put in the playground? What shape will your pool be?

title: Kentucky Rivers and Waterways
text:
Hey there, Kentucky adventurer! We think you'll love this issue of Kentucky Studies Weekly. But, to begin, here's a riddle for you. See if you can guess who, or what, is speaking. Good luck!

"Even though I live in Kentucky, I also have homes all over the world. You may not notice me, for sometimes I'm Kentucky's most silent resident. On the other hand, sometimes I make a lot of noise! When I am most wild, I could destroy a whole town with one swipe! Even so, cities and towns seem to spring up wherever I go, and people never get too far away from me if they can help it. It's been that way my whole life or at least since there have been cities and towns. Does that seem strange? Can you guess who I am? I don't mean to sound conceited, but pretty much everyone everywhere loves me. And it's not just people either; animals and plants seem to always look their best when I'm around. In fact, most of them would just shrivel up and die without me. What's my name? It depends on where you go. In some places they call me 'Ohio,' and in others, 'Licking.' Some people call me 'Green' or 'Rough.' Sometimes I'm ice cold; sometimes I'm salty; and sometimes I'm sweet. When I'm away, farmers hope I'll come back soon and bring my friends. Sailors mostly hope I'll keep quiet and friendly until they get home. Have you guessed who I am yet? Quick now; make a guess before I slip away!"

Did you guess who the mystery stranger was? If you guessed "water," you're one smart cookie! Water, water everywhere makes life spring up, green and beautiful, all over this great state of ours. Of course, too much water also brings its own challenges and problems. For example, America's most important river, the Mississippi River, provides water and causes flooding in all the states it runs through. It borders Kentucky on the west side. That's what we're all about this week in Kentucky Studies Weekly. "Water" we waiting for? Read on!

title: Creative Ways to Save Water
text:
How much H2O (water) have you used today? "Not much," you might say, but you have probably used more than you think. Did you take a shower, brush your teeth and flush the toilet this morning? If so, you were using water - gallons of it! Water goes into your orange juice and pancake mix. Water also cleans the dishes you used to eat your breakfast. It washed the clothes you are wearing and helped make the paper you are reading.

Here in Kentucky, and in the rest of our country, people are trying to find ways to use less water and reuse water. Sometimes people don't have enough water because of droughts (long periods of time with little or no rain). But the demand for water is also rising because the population is growing, and more people need water. You can do several simple things every day to conserve (avoid wasting) water:

Encourage your parents to fix dripping faucets.

Don't use the toilet as a trash can. Throw Kleenexes and other items in the waste basket so that you don't have to flush the toilet more times than is necessary.

Turn off the water when you brush your teeth. Doing this can save your family five to 10 gallons of water per day.

Keep a bottle of water in your refrigerator. Letting the tap run to cool drinking water wastes a lot of water.

Sweep leaves and other rubbish off your driveway instead of hosing down the driveway. Sweeping can save hundreds of gallons of water.

These suggestions may sound simple, but every drop counts. For more water-saving tips, visit www.americanwater.com.

title: Rivers and Waterways
text:
Kentucky Rivers

Kentucky is the home of some of America's most important rivers! The Ohio River flows for six hundred and sixty-four miles along the northern border of the state. Joining up with the Ohio at Carrollton, is the Kentucky River, which winds its way along for over two hundred and fifty miles. The Cumberland River flows from east to west for seven hundred miles, and then it drops off into Cumberland Falls, a waterfall that's the second biggest waterfall east of the Rocky Mountains. (It's one hundred and twenty-five feet wide and sixty-eight feet tall!) Only Niagara Falls on the Canada border is bigger! At Cumberland Falls, when the weather is right, you can see a rainbow by the light of the moon! It's worth staying up for, that's for sure! For many years, rivers were the best "roads" through the Kentucky wilderness. Some settlers came by wagon, and others came by boat because it was easiest!

Just Plain Fun

No one would ever deny that water has some important uses. Just ask any farmer, sailor, thirsty person or fish! But let's not forget one thing that water is great for: pure, clean fun! Kentucky is just plain FULL of ways to have fun in the water. So whether it's water-skiing at Rough River Dam, swimming at Lake Barkley, boating on Lake Malone or kayaking down the Cumberland River, Kentucky has plenty to go around!

Rollin' Like a River

If you have a ping-pong ball lying around, try this little experiment: Lay your hand flat on your desk or table with your palm facing up. Place the ping-pong ball in your open hand. What happens? Nothing? Gee, science is exciting, eh? But we're not done yet! Start over again, but this time, tilt your hand up like a hill. Place the ping-pong ball on the hill. This time, what happens? Did you see that? Wow! The ball rolled off! Now, before you think we here at Kentucky Studies Weekly have lost our marbles and rolled them down hills made out of hands, let's make a point for science. Gravity pulls things down a surface that is inclined (or tilted). Now, the same thing that's true for ping-pong balls is true for water, and all of Kentucky is on a slope - kind of like your tilted hand. The slope is called the Eastern Continental Divide. Kentucky is actually completely on the western slope of the divide. Any rain or snow that falls on the Kentucky side of the slope keeps on rolling down (a little like a ping-pong ball) west to the Gulf of Mexico. Water that falls on the eastern side (like in some parts of Tennessee, Virginia, Georgia and North Carolina) runs all the way into the Atlantic Ocean. In some places, a person can tell what part of the country he's in just by looking at the direction the water's running. Wow! You'll probably never look at your tilted hand in quite the same way again!

Kentucky Lakes

The big lakes in Kentucky are all man-made. How on Earth does a man make a lake, you ask? Does he make a huge bowl and pour water into it by the spoonful? Does he dig a hole deep enough to find water and then just let the water fill the hole? Nope! To make a lake, all you need is a river and the stuff to make a dam! Ever heard of Kentucky Lake? How about Lake Barkley or Lake Cumberland? These are all man-made lakes, formed when water began to stack up behind a dam someone built! They're some of the biggest lakes in the state and are made by folks like you and me. People make lakes for boating, fishing, swimming and playing, so relax and enjoy! And, if you run out of lakes before you're through having fun, don't worry! We'll make more!

title: Ethics: William Penn and the Pennsylvania Quakers
text:
William Penn spent less than five years in America, but he had a big impact on American history. His ethics (standards, values and principles) - especially his beliefs about freedom - had lasting effects on American democracy.

Penn was born in London in 1644. He was well educated and became interested in a religious group called the Society of Friends, or Quakers. They believed in equal rights for all and would not bow, remove their hats or take an oath to royalty.

Although Penn was raised in the Church of England, he agreed with the Quaker beliefs. He insisted on going to jail with his Quaker friends saying, "My prison shall be my grave before I will budge a jot; for I owe my conscience to no mortal man."

Some Quakers moved to America, but the Puritans in Massachusetts did not want them in their colony. King Charles II gave William Penn a land grant for territory in America to repay a debt owed to Penn's father. The colony was named Pennsylvania (Penn's Woods) in honor of William's father. Penn designed a city there named Philadelphia, meaning "city of brotherly love."

Penn wrote a constitution called "The Frame of Government." It guaranteed freedom of religion, trial by jury, fair taxes and many other liberties we take for granted today. Penn also established peaceful relations with the American Indians, buying land from them and writing successful peace treaties.

William Penn spent a lot of time in England, and he died there in 1718. He only lived in his colony for four years, but his ethics influenced Americans for generations to come. How might your life have been different without William Penn's constitution and the liberties he stood for?

title: Flatboat Adventure
text:
"This is it, Danny. This is what will take us to our new home!" Danny could hear his father's words - but just barely. From where he stood on the shore, all his attention was focused on the river. "Once you've ridden on a flatboat, Son, you'll never forget it!" Thirty yards out, getting closer and closer, Danny saw a boat, though he'd never seen one like it. Oh, he had seen boats before. He had visited the ocean once, and he had seen a tall-masted sailing ship, moving like a huge cloud across the face of the ocean. But this boat looked just like a big, wooden box. A man on the roof was steering it with a long pole. Danny wondered how it could float at all. He figured that if you dropped a log cabin in the river, it would sink to the bottom, yet that's pretty much what this looked like. "All aboard," said Papa with a smile, but it wasn't quite as simple as that. It took them what seemed like hours to load their things onto the wooden floor of the flatboat. Even Papa's horse came aboard! Once everything was aboard, Danny and his mother were helped up to the roof. A chair was waiting for Mama, but Danny walked around, inspecting the strange craft. He reached out to touch the long pole that worked the boat's rudder, but a man with a gruff voice told him to stay out of the way. He decided it might be safest to sit with Mama.

The trip up the river was quiet and smooth, but it took a long time. Danny napped for part of it. On either side of the river, he saw thick, green trees and the mud of the riverbank. Papa had been right; traveling on land through all that mud and those trees would have been nearly impossible! The river was the only smooth, flat road through this part of Kentucky. And here he was, Danny, king of the river! He hollered and heard his yell roll off in echoes over the forest. The men on the boat laughed, and some of them hollered as well. Danny's father stooped down with a grin to rumple Danny's hair. "Yes siree, Son. With you by my side, no land will be too wild for me to tame. Kentucky will be no match for us, eh? Just our family and the wilderness!" Danny felt like laughing out loud again. He hugged his father around the legs, and then they both put their arms around Mama. With their arms all around each other, they floated silently up the river, away from everything they'd ever known. They flowed, just like the slow and steady river, into the future.

title: Loyalty
text:
Are you a sports fan? Do you have a favorite team? I bet you jump and scream with joy when they win a game! What about when they lose? Does it make you gloomy? Chances are that you still say they're the best team ever, and you go back cheering even louder for their next game. That's called loyalty, and loyalty is a character trait that is what good kids are all about! It's cool to be loyal to your favorite team or even your favorite TV show, but it's much more important to be loyal to your family and friends!

It's easy to love the people around you when everything's going great, but what about when they make mistakes? Do you stick by them through thick and thin? If you do, I bet they're thankful! Your loyalty will help them tough out the rough times and celebrate the good times!

title: How can we conserve water?
text: It might be fun to look around your house for all the things you use water for and write them down. Have you ever boiled water to make a bowl of soup? Write it down! Have you ever turned on the tap for a drink of water? Or flushed a toilet? Or taken a bath? Gee, I sure hope so! Write them down. Now, once you have a nice long list, make another one. On this list, write down all the ways you might be able to use less water than you use now. Look at your first list to get some ideas. For example, would your bath get you less clean if you used an inch less water in the tub? It might save you a gallon or two every time you take a bath! Do you let the water run for a few seconds before you fill your cup? It might save water if you didn't! Can you think of any other examples? The truth is, the number of people in the world is growing and growing, but the amount of water on the Earth has always been and always will be the same! Conserving water (saving and preserving it) sounds like a dandy idea, doesn't it?

title: Black Bear
text:
Black bears have a reputation for being fierce and mean, but they're actually not a huge threat to people. At least they don't go hunting for "people sandwiches." The only time they attack humans is when they feel threatened or if their cubs are in danger. However, it is not safe to feed bears. Some tourists in Yellowstone National Park have found this out the hard way in years past.

Black bears are about 80 percent vegetarian. They love berries, and some have become pretty good at fishing.

Male bears can weigh up to about 350 pounds, and females weigh about 150 pounds. A female bear's cubs usually stay with her for about one and a half years before they're grown up. When the females grow up, they usually stay in the same territory as Mom. Male bears leave their mother's territory and search for a place of their own.

title: Kentucky's Climate and Resources
text:
Have you ever stopped to think about how much power Mother Nature has over our everyday lives? Think about it. You may want to wear a T-shirt and shorts today, but one gust of icy wind and a little hail from Mother Nature, and shazam! All of the sudden, it's long pants, a big coat and maybe even gloves for you! Mother Nature might decide for you whether you can go to the park or whether you have to stay inside. For people in some areas during big storms, Mother Nature might determine whether families can stay in their homes or whether they need to find somewhere safer! Though modern technology has made this far less true than it used to be, it wasn't too long ago that Mother Nature determined what a person did for a living! If you lived in a place that was naturally good for raising cattle, that's what you did! If you lived by an ocean, you'd probably make your living fishing or in trade or transportation. If you lived near a gold mine, you might spend your days digging in the dirt! Well, Mother Nature's got things pretty well figured out, and we ought to feel pretty lucky! But, more and more, we're realizing that while Kentucky has plenty of natural resources, like coal, crops and livestock, our state's most valuable resource isn't any of these at all. It's something far more important. Can you guess what it is? This resource will make the difference between a bright future and a gloomy one! It will make more of a difference around here than even the weather! See if you can guess what it is before you get to Page 2.

In this issue of Kentucky Studies Weekly, we're going to take a look at how Mother Nature affects our lives every day - even now. We'll read about climate and natural resources. These resources are all around us in the natural world and make things easier for humans! It's going to be quite a journey, so let's get started!

title: Scientists Believe Volcanoes Caused a 'Little Ice Age'
text:
An ice age usually lasts thousands of years. But between A.D. 1300 and A.D. 1900 the northern hemisphere experienced a cooling called the "Little Ice Age." The cooling was so intense that glaciers moved south, causing northern European towns to be destroyed. It was so cold that the Thames River in London and canals in the Netherlands froze! A scientist at the University of Colorado, using plant fossils from this period, may have discovered why this happened.

The plants died suddenly between 1275 and 1300. That's exactly when many volcanoes erupted. Fifty years later, volcanoes erupted again. Billions of tiny particles from the eruptions were in the atmosphere, reflecting the sun's heat away from the Earth. This caused the land to cool, the plants to die and the ice cap to grow. But there's more.

The growing ice cap sparked a feedback loop. A feedback loop causes something to happen over and over. First, the tiny particles stopped a lot of the sun's heat from reaching land. This cooling caused the ice cap to grow. The ice reflected more of the sun's heat back into the atmosphere. This caused more cooling. Finally, the glaciers became so large that they stopped the warmer ocean currents from melting the ice cap. Over centuries the glaciers grew to cover northern Europe.

Volcanic eruptions started the cooling, but it took the feedback loop to keep the "Little Ice Age" going for centuries!

Reference: History News Network (hnn.us)

title: Climate and Resources
text:
Kentucky's Natural Resources

What is a natural resource? If you check in a dictionary, you'll find that a natural resource is something that is "a natural source of supply, support or wealth" (Webster). Kentucky has lots of different sources of wealth. Just lift up a bit of Kentucky's topsoil, and what do you find? Vast mineral resources, including barite, clay, coal, fluorite, lead, limestone, natural gas and even oil. We could make a long list of all sorts of terrific uses for these things, but we'd be crazy to try in this little newspaper.

In addition to all the rich minerals under our topsoil, Kentucky has more than 110 species of trees. (There are fewer than 100 species in all of Europe.)

It appears that Mother Nature was generous when she put together the land of Kentucky.

Kentucky's Greatest Resource

Can you guess what Kentucky's greatest resource is? Is it the vast tobacco farms? Is it the sprawling forestlands that cover much of our state? Or is it possibly all the high-tech industries that we'll learn about later in Kentucky Studies Weekly? What about all the gold that is probably left from America's first gold rush? These are all valuable resources, but the honest to goodness truth is this: Kentucky's greatest resource is YOU - the rising generation. You are the teachers, engineers, doctors, scientists, entertainers, business people and workers of tomorrow's Kentucky. You are the hope of our land.

Kentucky's Climate

Climate, or weather, refers to the usual temperature, wind and rain in a certain area.

Foolproof Weather Test

Here's a simple test to tell what the weather's up to, and you can do it right now with this newspaper! Go on; take your newspaper outside. Stand there for a few minutes, holding your newspaper in front of you. Is the paper wet? If so, it's raining. Is the paper warm and dry? If so, the sun's probably shining. Is the paper moving around? It's windy. Is there white stuff on the paper? It's probably snowing (ha! ha!). If you'd rather stay inside, just check out your favorite weather forecaster on the news!

Uncertain Weather

Kentucky weather is never very certain. Some winters, we'll have a lot of snow. Other winters are as dry as a bone. Some springtimes are not rainy enough. Some are too rainy. When there's not enough rain, we call it a drought. Droughts can be scary times for farmers, who count on rain to grow their crops. On the other hand, when there's too much rain, Kentucky's rivers get too big for their britches. Kentucky has a history of serious floods. In 1937, for example, the Ohio River flooded, causing millions of dollars in damage and forcing thousands of people to leave their homes! Frankfort, Kentucky's capital, suffered the same kind of flooding in 1978. Many of your folks were alive for that one!

Round and Round You Go

Have you ever taken a ride on a merry-go-round? You get nowhere fast, but going around and around can make you giggle! Now imagine riding a merry-go-round that goes around and around at 250 miles an hour! That's just about as fast as some tornadoes go! Kentucky has had a few of those, and boy do they leave a mess! They're caused in part by hot weather, though even the smartest people will tell you that we don't know very much about 'em. One thing we do know is how much damage they cause! In 1974, a tornado touched down in Louisville. It was only on the ground for about 15 minutes, but even in such a short time, it left a trail of damage 12 miles long and killed 31 people! That's one of Mother Nature's tantrums that we could certainly do without!

title: Northern Kentucky
text: Northern Kentucky has come a long way since the first few cabins went up long ago. Today, the area is full of thousands of people and has all sorts of cool stuff to do! Would Kentucky's first settlers have ever dreamed that Ashland would be a place where thousands would gather to watch "the greatest amateur racing event in the world," a huge soapbox derby that is part of Ashland's "Summer Motion" celebration? Would they have guessed that in Newport there'd be an aquarium where visitors can enjoy sharks, alligators, jellyfish and even penguins - all in a million gallons of water? What would they have thought of the NASCAR speedway in Florence? People had big dreams for this place back when it was settled, and now we're seeing some of those dreams become reality. We're even seeing some things that our founding fathers never even dreamed of!

title: How do people prepare for weather?
text: You may have seen stories on the news about people leaving their towns during a hurricane or placing sandbags along rushing rivers to keep them from overflowing during the spring and summer. Nature is somewhat difficult to predict sometimes, and storms of all kinds, from light rain showers to mighty tornadoes, can come without warning! Some towns are more likely to experience certain kinds of storms than others are. People inland, for example, don't often experience hurricanes as people on the coast do. Towns often prepare for the kinds of weather surprises they might have. In coastal villages, sometimes houses are built high on stilts, to keep them above the crashing of huge waves during heavy storms. Cities in tornado country often have loud alarms in the center of town, alerting everyone of when to get ready for heavy weather. What about your town? Are there serious storms that sometimes surprise the people where you live? Your town may have certain plans already in place for extreme weather possibilities. Think right now, while the weather is calm, of some things you could do in your own home to be ready for the next weather surprise. It might save you some worry when the weather gets rough!

title: The Beaver
text: Did you know that beavers are rodents? They are the biggest rodents in North America. From nose to tail, beavers average three to four feet in length. They weigh 40 to 95 pounds. Now that's a big rodent! Beavers have webbed feet that help them swim, and they have long, sharp teeth that help them cut and chew wood. Because their incisor teeth never stop growing, beavers are always chewing trees to keep their teeth from growing too long! Beavers have two pairs of eyelids and two layers of fur. The outside layer has a special waterproof oil that allows them to dry quickly when they leave the water. Beaver fur has a built-in comb to keep tangles out. Beavers like to eat tree bark, water lilies, shrubs, bugs, twigs, leaves and roots. Yum, yum!

title: Weather Watch
text:
Since time began, people have tried to predict the weather by scanning the sky for colors and other clues. Test these bits of ancient meteorology to see if they are really true.

1. A rose-red sunset means fair skies are coming. A red sunrise means there will be a storm. ("Red sky at night, sailor's delight; red sky at morning, sailors take warning.")

2. A pale yellow sunset means rain is on the way.

3. An evening rainbow predicts fair weather.

4. A morning rainbow in the west means rain.

5. A pre-dawn copper-colored sky in the east means rain.

6. When the moon has a halo, there will be rain, especially if the halo is far from the moon.
