title: Tornado Safety
text:
Tornadoes are most common between March and August, but they can strike at any time. Tornadoes can develop anywhere but are most common in Arkansas, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Dakota, and Texas – an area commonly called “Tornado Alley.” Tornadoes are also most likely to develop between 3 pm and 9 pm but can happen at any time.

How Can I Stay Safe?

Before:

-Get an emergency kit

-Make an emergency plan

-Look for these warning signs

-dark greenish sky

-large hail

-loud roar sound, like a freight train

During:

If you are in a building:

-Get to the lowest level like a basement, or a cellar.

-Stay away from corners, windows, doors and outside walls.

-Don’t open any windows.

-Put on sturdy shoes.

-Protect your head.

If you are in a trailer or mobile home:

-Get out right away and get to the lowest floor of a building or storm shelter nearby.

If you are outside with no buildings nearby:

-Get into a vehicle and buckle your seatbelt, keep your head down below the windows and cover your head with your hands and a blanket or coat.

-If there are no vehicles, try to find a ditch or area lower than the ground and lie down in it.

After:

-Wear sturdy shoes or boots. You don’t want to step on broken glass, nails or other debris.

-Never get close to, or touch dangling or loose power lines because they could electrocute you.

-Text, don’t talk. Unless there’s a life-threatening emergency, send text messages to communicate so that you don’t tie up phone lines. These are needed by emergency workers. Also, texting may work even if cell phone calling services are down.

title: The First People in Kentucky
text:
Most scientists think the first people came to Kentucky as early as 10,000 B.C. That's about 12,000 years ago! We refer to those ancient people as Paleo Indians, but of course we have no idea what they called themselves. They came to North America during the Ice Age, probably following herds of animals traveling in search of food. During that time, low sea levels had dried up the land between Siberia and Alaska, and what is now the Bering Strait was then a huge land bridge at least as wide as the distance from Disney World to the Statue of Liberty! When the Ice Age ended, the land bridge was covered up with water again, and the people were here to stay.

When the first people arrived, the land was very different from the Kentucky of today. The plant life fed many large animals. Some of these animals weighed thousands of pounds. Herds of giant deer, camels, buffalo, sloths and huge mammoths - large, elephant-like animals - grazed on the prairies. Mastodons, which also looked like elephants, roamed the woodlands. They used their trunks to reach for leaves and tear off tree bark. Giant armadillos, some the size of a small car, searched for roots and insects to eat. Saber-tooth tigers stalked their prey (hunted animals).

The first Paleo Indians were hunters of big game. Because their lives depended on meat from wandering animals, these bands of hunters were nomadic, which means they had no permanent home but wandered about in search of food. Their shelters could be set up and taken down quickly. At night, the people camped near rivers or streams. During the day, they followed the great herds and hunted. Imagine how hard it was for these people to kill a giant mammoth! The animal stood as tall as a house and had tusks as long as a pickup truck. They used stone spears thrown by hand or from an atlatl to bring them down. To do their job they had to work as a team. From just one mammoth, a band got enough meat to last for months. Nothing went to waste. The hide was used to make clothing and shelters. The bones became tools and weapons.

title: Prehistoric Natives
text:
Kentuckians Natives Build Villages

Clues show that between six thousand and four thousand B.C., native tribes became larger and stayed in one place longer. This allowed them to build more permanent structures in which to live. They even traded with other villages.

One of the main reasons they were able to do this was that they had gradually learned how to farm. They still hunted for much of the food and other resources they needed, but as they grew their own food, they were less dependent on following the migrations of animals.

The main crops of these early natives are known as the Three Sisters. Centuries later, the grandchildren of these people who lived here when Europeans first arrived still maintain the Three Sisters as their most important crops: corn, beans and squash.

Basket Makers

The natives gathered berries and shellfish from six thousand to four thousand B.C. Basketry was important during this era, as the need for containers developed. Duck decoys made of reeds are known from this era and the natives made nets to catch fish and birds.

The Bow and Arrow

American Indians disguised themselves in deerskin in order to get close to living deer. The bow and arrow helped them kill their prey (hunted animals) from a greater distance than they could with the atlatl.

The Atlatl

With a spear and a device called an atlatl (at LAT uhl), ancient natives killed wild deer for their tribe. Atlatls were used almost everywhere in the Southeast during this time. The atlatl increased the natives' throwing power and accuracy.

The most important of all crops Three Sisters

The story goes that the Three Sisters were inside the wigwam. Who were these sisters? Actually, this is the natives' name for corn, bean and squash seeds.

The Three Sisters stayed inside all winter. But they wanted to come out and return to the fresh Earth. But they couldn’t come out yet. The ground was too hard and the earth too cold. If the Three Sisters came out they would surely die.

When would they be able to come out? The oak leaves would tell us. When they were the size of a red squirrel's foot, the earth would be ready for the Three Sisters.

The days got longer and the earth got warmer and softer. The oak leaves grew and grew. Eventually the leaves were the size of a red squirrel's foot and it was time for the Three sisters to come out. The seeds were then soaked in medicine. Animals hated the taste of the medicine and would not eat the fruit that grew from those seeds. The American Indians farmed the fields, making furrows for the Three Sisters. They placed the corn, bean and squash seeds into the ground.

By summer, the crops were healthy and thriving. They were all harvested to feed the people. Some seeds were then dried to be saved. They were then taken to the wigwam to be stored. Once again, the Three Sisters rested together through another long winter.

title: A Day in the Life of a Nomad
text:
Today's Kentucky Adventure was written by a fourth grader named Sarah Steele. Sarah is in Mr. Evan's class at Indian Trials Elementary School.

Once there was an American Indian girl named Little Eagle because she could see very far away. She came from the Paleo Tribe. One day, Little Eagle and her mother and father were traveling with the tribe, trying to find a mammoth herd, when they saw a big lake. The tribe decided to camp there for the night and send some scouts out to look for the herds. After the scouts left, Little Eagle decided to go exploring. She found an eagle's claw and laced it with some dried grass to make a necklace. She found some beautiful flowers and picked them for her mother. She saw a beautiful, turquoise butterfly land on the lake. Little Eagle was so still, it landed right on her arm! Little Eagle liked to climb trees. She decided to find the tallest tree, and when she climbed up the tree she saw a giant herd of mammoths! She climbed down the tree and raced back to their camp as fast as she could. When she got back and told everyone about it, some men went out to find the herd. They got a great big mammoth. It was delicious! It had been a very good day.

title: Courage
text:
On Dec. 1, 1955, Rosa Parks had the courage to refuse to give up her seat to a white person on a crowded bus in Montgomery, Alabama. She was arrested and tried. The result of the trial triggered a boycott (refusing to buy or use something), which was organized by Martin Luther King Jr. African Americans refused to ride the city bus until the laws were changed. It worked. Eventually, the laws were changed so that whites and blacks were allowed to sit together.

When Rosa died in October 2005, her casket was placed in the U.S. Capitol for two days so that people could pay their respects to her. Usually only the caskets of U.S. Presidents are placed in the Capitol. Rosa became the first woman to receive this honor.

The greatest kind of courage is to do what is right when others call you a coward or a chicken for doing it. It takes courage to stand up to people like that, but having courage will also help you be loyal, honest and responsible. Your parents, teachers, church leaders or good friends can help you prepare to deal with peer pressure and develop courage to face difficult situations.

title: “Native American” or “American Indian”?
text: Some individuals, and some entire tribes of American Indians, prefer to be called Native Americans. This is because they are offended by the name "Indian," because it was a mistake Christopher Columbus made when he landed in America and thought he had reached India. However, it is now considered correct to use the term "American Indian" to differentiate those in India from America's natives. Most everyone agrees that we are all proud to be called Americans. Even so, most American Indians like to be called by their tribal names.

title: Gray Squirrel
text:
Do you want to find out if there are any gray squirrels in your neighborhood? The best way to find out is to put a few saltine crackers in a dry place in your yard or around the outside of your house. Sometimes, they're even daring enough to come right up and take crackers from your hand.

This behavior is evidence that gray squirrels can adapt to suburbs as easily as they can to the hardwoods. Although, experts say that if given the choice, gray squirrels prefer the "untouched wilderness."

This little, furry friend is common all over Kentucky and seems to enjoy the Mississippi River bottoms as much as the eastern mountains.

They survive off acorns in the winter, but in the summer they spice things up with young, tender corn shoots, peanuts and bugs. Yum!

title: Ojo de Dios
text:
This is an authentic and beautiful American Indian design.

Materials

Popsicle sticks or tongue depressors

Glue

Yarn

Pompoms

Directions

1. Find two popsicle sticks or tongue depressors. Glue them into a cross. Start the weaving by gluing the yarn to the back side of the sticks.

2. Start a crisscross pattern with the yarn. Continue to loop the yarn around the four ends of each stick. Keep the yarn fairly tight.

3. Continue the same pattern development, remembering to loop the yarn over each stick end in a like manner. Other colors may be added by tying new string to the old yarn. Make sure the knot is hidden behind the stick.

4. The work can be finished by tying the remaining yarn end onto the back of the design. Small pompoms can be attached to the end of the sticks.

Extra Activity: After you have mastered a small one, try a larger one!

title: Pre-Columbian Natives of Kentucky
text:
What would you do if you woke up one morning and you weren't in the bed you fell asleep in? How would you feel if you looked around and saw none of your toys or games, but just dirt, trees and bushes? For thousands of years, that is what many children saw when they woke up. They did not have electronic games or a television or a VCR. Most children spent time working along with the adults.

Let's say that you fell asleep in your nice, cozy, warm bed last night and woke up this morning in the Woodland Period, which was from 1000 B.C. to A.D. 1000! You would find many unbelievable things. This period was the beginning of a time that introduced something amazing to the American Indians: pottery. If you had woken up in the Archaic or Paleo Indian period, you would have seen them using shells, baskets or gourds (shells of fruit) for holding and storing food, water and other materials. The Woodland people introduced pottery into the culture. It was extremely thick, fragile and very heavy, but it had many advantages. The pottery could be made waterproof for easier storage of water. It could also be used for cooking and storing food away from pests.

Besides pottery, what else would be different? After you woke up and ate with the others, you would begin your work. Depending on if you were a male or a female, you would either gather up a stone hoe or get your spear. The Woodland people were some of the first to begin gardening and harvesting crops such as corn and squash. The women would gather seeds and nuts as well as garden.

The men would hunt a variety of animals using a spear or an atlatl, which was a stick that helped them throw lightweight spears with much better accuracy and speed. They also developed the use of the bow and arrow.

After you hunted or gardened, you might help build one of the many mounds that the Woodland people built. Most religious or ceremonial occasions would be held in one of the enclosed mounds. There were other mounds used for burials. The dead would be placed in a log tomb and buried, having bracelets and copper and other items buried with them to show their status in society.

After a hard day's work and a good meal (possibly of rabbit and corn), you would settle down for a good night's sleep. Let's just hope you wake up in today's world so that you can finish reading the exciting information in this paper!

title: Pieces of the Past
text:
Kentucky is full of history and many people enjoy collecting bits and pieces of it. Some do this by reading old books and letters, but others like to dig into history and get their hands dirty. These people spend their free time looking for ancient artifacts, or objects that people made in the past.

The most common artifacts that people find in Kentucky are arrowheads. Ancient American Indians who once roamed our state left behind these arrowheads. People often find them near creeks, in plowed fields or in areas where American Indians are known to have settled. If you are searching for arrowheads on land that doesn't belong to you, make sure to get permission from the landowner before taking anything home.

What should you do if you find an arrowhead? Take it to a museum and ask the staff to identify it for you. Someone there can probably tell you what time period it is from and give you an idea of which American Indian tribe may have made it. Museums are full of arrowheads and most are not worth any money. However, if you happen to find one that is unusual or in perfect condition, it may be worth hundreds or even thousands of dollars to a collector!

Besides arrowheads, you may also find beads, bits of broken pottery, grinding stones or old cooking utensils. Searching for ancient artifacts is a fun way to learn more about the history of our great state. Dig in!

title: Pre-Columbian Natives
text:
Woodland Indians

Scientists organize American Indian history partly based on what native cultures learned how to do. For example, when the Archaic Indians learned to plant crops, create jewelry and clay dishes and build tricky traps to catch fish, their way of life changed so much that modern scientists have a whole different name for them. They call them the Woodland Indians. The Woodland period lasted a couple of thousand years, from 1000 B.C.E. to 1000 C.E. To the Woodland Tribes, growing crops and staying in one place for long periods of time was how they decided to live their lives. Now don't get us wrong; these people were still hunters, but instead of moving the whole tribe wherever the game went, they just sent out hunting parties for a few days, and the hunters brought back food for the village. It was easier to get the food to the tribe than to move the tribe to follow the food. This way of living gave the Woodland Indians more time to be creative and produce goods because they didn’t have to spend so much time moving around.

Mississippian Mound Builder

After 1000 C.E., the Woodland Tribes made room for a new group who moved into their territory. These new natives were called Mississippians. No one knows for sure where they first came from. They had learned to work the land well enough to stay in one place, but these people also traded with other villages for things they needed. Today's archaeologists have found Mississippian artifacts (handmade objects representing a certain stage of a culture) hundreds of miles away from the villages where they were created. Their villages were well organized with leaders, warriors, workers and even artists. The Mississippians mostly lived in huts built of cane (tall, thick stems of plants) covered with mud. They were skilled gardeners, too, and grew lots of beans, corn, squash and pumpkins.

What's a Mound Builder?

Some people have a different name for the Mississippians. They call them the mound builders. Many Mississippian villages were built to surround huge rectangular piles of dirt, or mounds. Each mound was built using thousands of bucket loads of dirt. Some were as high as 50 feet, and some of them still exist. Lots of people still wonder exactly what they were for, but here are a few things we're pretty sure of: First, it seems that some of the leaders of the village lived on top of some of the mounds. Another thing is that at least one mound in each village was known as the temple mound. The people performed rituals on its wide, flat surface. What kind of rituals? Here's an example: Every morning, one family in the village went to the temple mound and took a gift of food for the sun god.

Woodland Stone Petroglyphs

Here's something else that began to appear all over the rocks of Kentucky during the Woodland period: pictures carved into the stone. The pictures are called petroglyphs. That word comes from two smaller ones: "petro," meaning "rock," and "glyph," meaning "carved symbol." How'd the pictures get there? There are lots of theories. Many of the petroglyphs look like they were made by chipping, or pecking, the rock away with a pointed object. It's still a mystery just waiting for someone like you to solve!

Fort Ancient Natives

Mississippian villages were mainly in western Kentucky. In those days, eastern Kentucky was mostly inhabited by another group called the Fort Ancient natives. Their culture was a lot like the Mississippians, but there were some differences, too. For example, remember when we mentioned that the Mississippians were mound builders? Well, there are no mounds at Fort Ancient sites except for a few small burial mounds. Also, Fort Ancient pottery is not quite as decorated as some of that Mississippian pottery. They left many shell and bone tools and the ruins of many villages for us to wonder about! By the time Europeans arrived in Kentucky, the ancient people who had always lived here had grouped together into tribes with names of their own. The main tribe in Kentucky was the Shawnee. Historians think many of the tribes who lived here were destroyed by European diseases.

title: Raising the Sun
text: "Wake up!" whispered Mother loudly. She nudged me one more time. "Do you want to be late? You will not want the sun angry with you just because you slept in!" I sat up and rubbed my eyes. Through my blurred vision, I saw my mother standing at the other end of the room, smiling at me. "There's my strong young man," she said. "Your father is proud today, and I am, too." I stood and stretched my tired arms and legs. The world was still dark, and I could hear the crickets singing loudly. It was my first time to be the bearer of the sacrifice - to make the offering to the sun, hoping to entice it to rise. Mother had prepared a basket of maize and squash. She and Father joined me as I prepared myself. In the dark, I held the basket of food and walked slowly across the grass. Over the sound of the crickets, I heard my father speak to my mother: "It will be a good sacrifice today." I did not look back, but I felt his pride creep over me like a warm blanket, and I stood straighter as I walked away. It was early, but already I could see the smoke of the priest's fire on the temple mound. He had been up even earlier than I had. As I began to climb the steps to the top of the mound, I saw the priest's face more and more clearly. It was a kind face, but it was very stern. He had seen many sacrifices. He had greeted the sun on many days. Would he greet it today, too? Would my sacrifice be accepted by the sun? If the sun rose into the sky to light the day, we would know. Still, I was not sure I shared the confidence of my father. I handed the vegetables to the priest with shaking hands. He smiled and placed his hand over mine for a moment. "It's all right," he seemed to say. I felt a little better. The priest gently took the basket from my hands, and I watched as he placed the corn and squash into the fire. Soon, the burning smell came, and the black smoke wound its way upward. Higher it climbed, as an offering to the sun. Every day, one family in the village brought vegetables for the sacrifice. I wondered if they were always as tired as I seemed to be this morning. I closed my eyes and listened to the priest. He slowly said words, but I could not hear them all because I was so lost in thought. I closed my eyes slowly and tried to concentrate, but something stole my attention from the priest's words. My face felt warm, and through my closed eyelids, a warm, gentle light burned. My heart began to pound. Slowly, I lifted my eyelids, and I saw the sun - a bright ball of yellow fire, bursting on the horizon. My father had been right. This had been a good sacrifice, and morning had arrived.

title: Southeastern Kentucky
text: An army colonel named Christopher Gist wrote about the trail from Virginia into southeastern Kentucky. He said, "There was only one break. That Cumberland Gap was so narrow a wagon could not squeeze through it!" It was no joke, either. If you've visited the gap, you know for yourself just how narrow it is! But, no matter how narrow, it was the gateway to our grand state for those first brave explorers and settlers! And the history of southeastern Kentucky goes back even further than that! It was the home of the "Warriors Path," which was used by American Indians who traveled and camped there before Europeans ever set eyes on the place. As strangers started making Kentucky their home, the region became the home of the Daniel Boone Trace, later known as the Wilderness Road, along the Cumberland River. These days, southeastern Kentucky is one of the state's least populated areas. But what it lacks in Kentuckians it makes up for in rich wilderness and enough history for a dozen states!

title: How did little changes affect the early people of our state?
text: Little changes can sometimes make a big difference. Just as an experiment, switch your pencil from the hand you usually write with to the other hand. Try to write a letter or a poem. That wasn't a huge change, from one hand to the other, was it? But did it change how easy it was to write? Probably in a big way! Once upon a time, the early people of our state wandered from place to place, looking for plants and animals that were good to eat. Then, someone figured out how to grow some of those plants as crops. That little change allowed people to live in one place instead of moving around to where those plants naturally grew. It allowed them to establish villages. Creating villages meant creating governments and learning to live in communities. Over time, the little change of learning to grow crops led to huge changes in the lifestyle of the people!

title: Wild Turkey
text: Wild turkeys are classified as big game. With wingspans of four to five feet, wild turkeys can fly for short distances, but they mostly wander about on foot, looking for food with other turkeys. They eat fruits, buds, seeds, insects, nuts and acorns. Turkeys nest on the ground, but they roost at night in large trees. During the spring mating dance, males fan out their beautiful tails to attract females to a clearing. Usually, three to five females drop by to see what's going on. When the chicks are hatched, the males pay no attention to them. It's a good thing for the females that the young turkeys learn to look for food almost as soon as they're hatched. After only one month, the hatchlings can fly to Mama's favorite tree roost themselves. The turkey is mostly black with a red gullet, white head and red markings down the breast.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you live during the Woodland period. Where would you live? How would you spend your time? What do you do for fun? What do you worry about?

title: Upcycling
text:
upcycling(v.) – a process for recycling something into something better; When you upcycle, you recycle and reuse something for a new purpose.

You have read about how early American Indians used natural resources to survive. They used bison, traded fur and farmed. The American Indian way has always been “green.” This means that they used things in nature without hurting or polluting the environment. They used every part of an animal, vegetable or other food source and did not waste anything.

So what does that have to do with upcycling? Take a look at the following items that usually are thrown away, and upcycle them into useful things kids will like! The first ones are done for you. Use your imagination and be creative! (Just be sure to check with a responsible adult before digging for recyclables, and clean the items well!)

Here’s a real-world example: A student saved her juice pouches for about a month. She cleaned them and sewed them together to make a great new purse! She gave it to her aunt as a gift.

title: Exploring New Places!
text:
Have you ever wanted to climb Mt. Everest or maybe Mt. Kilimanjaro? Have you ever dreamed of discovering a new part of the world that no one has ever seen? A man by the name of Dr. Thomas Walker discovered a part of America that no one had ever seen before him. He did it by conquering a mountain no one had ever crossed.

Many explorers, including Hernando de Soto, Cabeza de Vaca and Christopher Columbus, had explored the eastern part of America in the early 1500s and 1600s. But no one had been able to explore west of the Appalachian Mountains. That was until Dr. Thomas Walker asked for a petition for 800,000 acres of land. He was granted the land and led an expedition to charter the land. They went on this expedition for four months. It led to the discovery of a gap in the mountain that he named the Cumberland Gap in honor of the Duke of Cumberland. The gap was worn down by wind and water and allowed passage from the east side of the Appalachian Mountains to the west side.

While on his expedition, he kept a journal of the animals he saw. He saw a large amount of bear, deer, turkey, buffalo and many other animals. He complained about the settlers damming up the streams for fish, because he believed they should be kept open for transportation uses.

Dr. Walker was able to open an entire new world for the expanding continent. If it was not for his bravery in attempting to cross the Appalachian Mountains, we may not have been able to get to the western side of the United States for a long time. We are sure he felt as proud standing on the other side of the mountains as a person would who just climbed to the peak of Everest - although probably a lot warmer.

How would it feel to explore something new, something that hardly anyone knew anything about? Those same questions may have been on the minds of the brave folks who first set sail for this continent hundreds of years ago, before you and I were around! What did those guys find? We thought you'd never ask! Go ahead - explore the rest of this issue of Kentucky Studies Weekly!

title: Southern Flying Squirrel
text:
This little critter proves that feathers aren't always necessary for flying.

It's easy to tell the difference between a flying squirrel and other types of squirrels. The flying squirrel has a pouch of skin (called a membrane) that goes from its front paws to its back paws. When the squirrel sticks out all four paws, its skin forms a parachute-like surface that allows it to glide through the air. Of course, flying squirrels can't take off from the ground or fly long distances like birds do, but they can use their tails to steer as they glide in a downward direction.

Southern flying squirrels are quite small. Adults are usually nine to 10 inches long, including the tail, and they weigh between two and four ounces. They have dark rings around their eyes (maybe from staying up all night) and dark borders on the edges of their flying membranes.

Flying squirrels are some of the most strict nocturnal mammals in Kentucky. They almost never come out during the day. It's believed that they are nocturnal because of the threat of hawks and other daytime predators.

If you're ever lucky enough to see one, just don't try to mimic the way it gets out of trees. YIKES!

title: Help a Rat and Learn to Run the Country This Year!
text:
Hey, kids! I’m Revere the Rat, but you can call me Rev. I’m your online Studies Weekly friend and I need your help. You can help me get great stuff by earning points while you learn. Just scan the code or go to www . studiesweekly . com and click on my picture.

Has your family ever bought something that came with an owner’s manual? Cars, TVs and other things have an owner’s manual, a book on how to use them. Your social studies class is the “owner’s manual” for the United States of America. You’ll learn about history, geography, government by the people, and much more, so you can do a good job of running our country someday.

In America rats can’t vote, so “you the people” govern (run) the country. Someday you will be in charge of this country, and you’ll choose leaders and representatives by voting. Then you can tell the representatives you help elect how you think the country should be run. In fact, Studies Weekly kids are so smart, that many of you will someday be mayors, senators, governors— maybe even the president!

For now you have two jobs: Learn about the country and how it works and earn points for me so I can get that great stuff I told you about. It’s easy. Just scan or click and you’re on your way!

title: Let's Write
text: Have you ever dreamed of discovering a new land that no one has ever seen? Imagine you are an explorer who gets to travel to a new land. What kind of animals do you find? What kind of plants grow there? What sort of people might live there? Write a description of your journey and of the new land.

title: Early Explorers
text:
The explorers came for gold, God and glory.

Discovering America

"In 1492, Columbus sailed the ocean blue!" Have you ever heard that rhyme? It's a good way to remember the name of the first European to set foot in America, as well as when he did it. But was Columbus the first? What about Leif Ericson and the Vikings? They were all sailing around before Columbus was even born. And what about that stone found here in Kentucky with the Jewish writing on it? The point is that sometimes, as we discover more about events in history, we find they may have happened much differently than people have always believed. There's always more to learn.

Claiming America

English Claims

John Cabot was about the same age as Columbus when he dreamed of sailing west. Luckily for Columbus, Spain gave him ships before England gave ships to Cabot. In 1497, only five years after Columbus "sailed the ocean blue," John Cabot sailed for the New World in English ships and claimed land for England.

Spanish Claims

Hernando De Soto left Spain to explore North America in 1539. His trip took him through what is now the southeastern United States. It made De Soto the first European (that we know of) to visit Kentucky.

French Claims

England and Spain weren't the only countries interested in the New World. Missionaries and explorers from France were interested, too. Perhaps the most famous of them all was an explorer named Robert Cavalier Sieur de La Salle. He sailed the Mississippi and claimed everything he saw for France - including Kentucky.

Land Companies Get Free Land!

In the early 1700s, when there were hardly any European Americans around here, the best way to get some land was to talk England's king or the local governor into giving you some! All you had to do was form a land company. A land company was a group of people who were interested in settling an area that hadn't already been explored. Here's a little about two land companies that made it into Kentucky history:

The Loyal Land Company:

These people talked the governor (not the king) into giving them 800,000 acres of land. The man they found to check out their new land wasn't a famous explorer at all, but a young doctor named Thomas Walker. In 1650, he passed through Caves Gap and into our home territory! These days, that gap is called the Cumberland Gap. Maybe you've heard of it. Have you ever heard of the Cumberland River? Walker named this river after his friend, the Duke of Cumberland. Within a few days' journey of Kentucky's beautiful Bluegrass Region, Walker climbed a tree and looked around. Everything looked pretty rugged. "Too rugged to settle," he thought, so he turned back. If only he would have kept going, he would have discovered the Bluegrass Region! This land company wasn't as successful as its owners had hoped it would be.

The Ohio Land Company

These people had a grant, or a gift, from England's government: 200,000 acres of land. All they had to do was get a hundred families to build homes on their land within seven years, and they'd get another 300,000 acres! They hired a man named Christopher Gist to explore the land, but his first trip was cut short to avoid fights with American Indians who were helping the French. So in 1753, Gist guided a young army major named George Washington to warn the French to get out of the area, or there'd be a fight!

title: Did You Know?
text:
Did you know that the “Happy Birthday to You” melody was written in Kentucky? Sisters Mildred and Patty Hill wrote the tune in 1893. It was originally called “Good Morning to All.” Then, in 1924, a man named Robert Coleman wrote the “Happy Birthday to You” lyrics to go along with the song.

When most people think of U.S. President Abraham Lincoln, they think of Illinois. However, Lincoln was born in Hodgenville, Kentucky.

The United States Bullion Depository in Fort Knox holds the biggest gold reserve in the whole world.

People don’t agree on where the name Kentucky comes from. It is generally believed that it originated from an American Indian name.

title: Two Different Worlds Meet
text:
Have you ever wondered what it might have been like to live in Kentucky before it was Kentucky? Before roads we've come to depend on? Before electricity? Before it was settled by immigrants from the Old World? We can only imagine! Unspoiled nature... abundant wildlife… Only the American Indians who lived in the area at that time knew what it was like.

In 1492, Christopher Columbus came to this “‘New World’. He brought a completely new culture to the Americas. The New World would never be the same. A few years later, Spanish explorers traveled through what is now the southern part of the United States. They were looking for riches, like gold and silver. They brought with them strange customs and serious diseases, like smallpox, typhus, measles, tuberculosis, chicken pox and influenza. The explorers had built up resistance to these diseases, but when the American Indians caught them, the illnesses spread rapidly and killed thousands of people. Entire villages were wiped out. The Spanish controlled this region of the world until 1682.

Then, French explorers claimed the area for France. The French were not looking for riches. Instead, they wanted to trade goods with the American Indians and strengthen French influence on them.

For almost 100 years, the British, the French and the Spanish struggled for control of the region. The French and Indian War was fought during this time. The British won the war and the French were forced to give up territories east of the Mississippi River, to Britain. Those territories west of the Mississippi were given to Spain.

The early history of the region was marked by great adventures of discovery and bloody fights for control of the region. It was a very difficult time for Kentucky’s American Indians. They endured many years of invasion from Europeans, many who hoped for a chance to take advantage of the riches and natural resources of the New World.

Can you imagine what it would be like to leave your home, your family and your country to travel to a mysterious, faraway place? Can you imagine what it would be like to have your entire way of life change because a new people moved to the land your family had been living on for generations? Life for many of these early people wasn’t easy but we can learn a lot from their stories!

title: A Tale of Two Sides
text:
Conflicts can happen at any moment. Some last for a short time. Others last months or years. It can be hard for people to settle a conflict.

Beginning in the 1500s, European settlers came to the Americas. At first, American Indians and the settlers worked together. The American Indians helped the settlers to grow crops and provided support during the winters. Europeans would trade with them, too. The American Indians were interested in the fabrics, tools and weapons that the settlers brought with them.

Over time, both groups began to fight over land. Settlers wanted to live in the resource-rich areas inhabited by the American Indians. Through treaties, the settlers slowly pushed the American Indians off their lands. European settlers also brought with them an invisible and deadly enemy: disease. Never having been exposed to smallpox and measles, American Indians had no immunity to these diseases like the Europeans did. This caused whole villages and tribes to become sick and even die.

Do you think it was possible for the settlers and American Indians to resolve their problems without fighting?

title: The French and Indian War
text:
Opening the Kentucky Frontier

Have you ever watched the ripples in a pool of water? Just tap the surface of the water with your finger, or drop a pebble (even a small one) into the pool and you'll see a ripple going out in a circle from the place where you (or the pebble) touched the water. How big will the ripple get? It depends, but even a tiny object thrown in the water can make a ripple as big as a swimming pool.

Sometimes, things in the world happen like that. Something may happen, even something very far away, and it can affect us. Here's an example: If you dropped your pencil on the floor and announced it to the class, pretty soon your classmates would be down on their hands and knees looking for your pencil. Even though they had nothing to do with dropping the pencil, they're still affected by it. So what are we getting at, anyway? We thought you'd never ask! In this issue of Kentucky Studies Weekly, we'll discuss something that happened outside of Kentucky, yet it changed how Kentucky was settled. What sort of something could have that much power over a place? Well, there are lots of powerful things that affect people and places, but this one was a war. England and France, two arguing neighbors, were both interested in certain parts of America at about the same time. They couldn’t reach an agreement and fought it out. It was the French, joined by the American Indians, against the English.

France was interested in the fur trade with the American Indians. The English were mostly interested in gaining land and sending European settlers to live on it. It all made for a tricky combination - so tricky, in fact, that war raged between the nations for years and years over who would be in charge of the land you're living on right now. The fighting went on everywhere - north, south, east, west and even in other countries. The "ripples" from the French and Indian War, as it was later called, affected Kentucky in some interesting ways. What were they? Turn the page and find out! Oh, by the way, it's not called the French and Indian War because the French and American Indians fought against each other. It's because the French and American Indians teamed up to fight the British.

title: Making the World a Kinder Place
text:
We sometimes wonder why bad things happen to innocent people. Although we may never understand it, we can do our best to keep things like this from happening in the future. When we do this, we are doing our part to make the world a kinder place, without anger and violence.

One way to do this is by making a plan to replace bullying and violence with kindness. The Cool to Be Kind (C2BK) program was developed to help students create programs in their classes and schools that are based on pro-kindness - doing nice things for others. Students look for ways to "pay it forward" each day. Paying it forward means that when someone thanks you for doing something nice, you ask that person to pay it forward by doing something nice for someone else. By paying it forward, kindness continues to spread across the world and people start thinking kinder thoughts and ways that they can help other people.

What are some ways you could practice paying it forward? How about doing yard work for an elderly neighbor for free? Or inviting a new student to eat lunch with you and your friends? What about giving up your seat on the bus to someone who looks tired, or helping someone pick up something they have dropped? Thinking kind thoughts and acting on them with acts of kindness is a simple change that you can do to change the world.

Teachers: Go to https://www.pifexperience.org/ to find out more about starting a C2BK program at your school!

title: French and Indian War: Western Lands
text:
Wars, Wars, Wars

Now don't get confused by this, but the French and Indian War wasn't the first war in America where the French and Indians fought against the English. In fact, it was the last! There were four of those wars in all, but we only use the name French and Indian War to describe the fourth one. Crazy, right? In Europe, they called it the Seven Years War. You may wonder what the other three were called. Here's the scoop: These wars ranged between 1689 and 1748 (59 years!), and it was the French and English lands in America they fought over. They were called King William's War, Queen Anne's War and King George's War. Can you think of anything those names have in common? For one thing, they're all names of English rulers. Another thing these wars had in common is that they were all won by England. Finally, these wars weren't just fought here in America. Because England and France are so near to each other in Europe, they took every opportunity to fight right there in their own backyards.

How Did the War Affect Kentucky?

There was fighting between Kentucky settlers and American Indians, but the French and Indian War was actually fought north of Kentucky. So why was it such a big deal, anyway? Well, just look at how Kentucky was set up during the time of the war. Some French explorers and trappers were doing business and making friends with the American Indians on the Kentucky frontier. (The frontier is land that hasn't been settled.) During that time, growing English colonies to the east of us were hesitant to head west into Kentucky land. When the war was over, though, it was pretty clear: England had taken the land! Suddenly, heading west didn't seem like trespassing. Folks came with confidence into this land that had once seemed "off limits." Another way the war affected Kentucky is that England didn't have enough money to pay its soldiers after the war. Instead, loyal soldiers were promised big land grants (gifts of land instead of money). Those grants brought people over the mountains and into Kentucky.

Why Fight a War?

So who wanted what anyway? Wars are usually fought for a reason, and taking a look at what each side wanted may clear things up a bit. What about France? They were getting rich trading French-made items with the natives for animal skins and furs. They didn't want to stop. The American Indians fought on the French side because they liked being able to trade with the French without giving up their favorite hunting lands. What about the English? Well, because they claimed to already own more or less all of the land in America anyway, their goal was to eventually settle all that land. They wanted to set up colonies and build new towns and cities, farther and farther west - maybe all the way to the Pacific Ocean.

The End of the War

The fighting in Europe and America wrapped up in 1763, when France, Spain and England signed an agreement called the Treaty of Paris. We won't talk much about what the treaty meant in other parts of the world, but in America, it changed things a lot. The French had to give England all their land east of the Mississippi River. That included Canada. What about the land west of the Mississippi? That all went to Spain. So much for England's idea about owning all of the New World. Before the war, they had claimed all the land from coast to coast - and 100 miles out to sea on either end. The English won the war, but they didn't end up with everything they wanted to own in the New World.

title: King Philip's War
text:
Metacomet was an American Indian who lived in New England. His father, Massasoit, was the great Wampanoag chief who had welcomed the Pilgrims in 1620. Metacomet became sachem (chief) in 1662 and continued friendly relations with the colonists. He became known as "King Philip."

The American Indians and colonists had their differences, but overall things were peaceful. They depended on each other as trading partners. However, some Colonial leaders began making unfair demands on the Indian tribes. The colonists ignored previous agreements and expanded into Indian territories. They forced natives to sell their land. They even demanded that Metacomet's people surrender all their weapons.

Metacomet organized an army. He formed an alliance with other American Indian tribes. His goal was to force the Puritan colonists out of Indian territory. Puritans and some American Indians united to fight Metacomet's warriors. Colonel Benjamin Church formed the first American Ranger unit in Plymouth Colony.

Many bloody conflicts followed. Both sides attacked and burned towns. They killed and enslaved hundreds of people. They destroyed land, crops and livestock. Every colony and tribe in New England suffered huge losses. One of Church's soldiers killed Metacomet in 1676, and the battles stopped shortly after. Historians call this period King Philip's War.

Both sides of this conflict chose to abandon ethical behavior instead of solving their problems peacefully. The war forever changed the way of life for colonists and American Indians in New England.

Was there any chance this war might have been avoided? Have you experienced people ignoring ethical behavior in order to get what they want?

title: The Other Side of the Mountains
text:
Jacob Adams was the blacksmith in his small Virginia town. Every day, his hammer pounded out rims for wagon wheels or horseshoes - things that would take people places. Every day, he looked past the flames of his forge, to the west, toward the mountains. What lay beyond those hills?

He longed to find out. Sometimes, trappers came into town, loaded with strange-looking carved figures, bone necklaces or clothes made of buckskin and furs. Jacob's only adventure was asking them about their business with the natives beyond the mountains in Kentucky. They told him stories, though he knew better than to believe more than half of them. "I'd go myself," he'd say to folks, "but we're at war with the French over there, and most of the natives have joined them." But, oh, how he would have loved to go! The war was old enough now that it was hardly news anymore. Clank, clank, clank went Jacob's hammer, as he tried not to think about what he might be missing. Then, one day, between clanks, a stranger came into his shop to get a wagon tongue repaired. They talked, and as they talked, Jacob's eyes widened.

"They say that the war is over, and all that land belongs to Britain," said the stranger, pointing to the mountains. "They signed a treaty that says so. Lots of folks are hitching up and heading through the Gap." Jacob's mind spun. Could it be that he might settle across the mountains with no danger of war?

He looked out at the frontier that had always been the edge of his world. He had opposed fighting the French, but now it had come to this and he wasn't so sure anymore. One thing was clear in his mind, though, and when the stranger left his shop with a new wagon tongue, Jacob turned to his forge again. Clank, clank, clank went the hammer. It was a wagon wheel this time. But there was a difference between this wheel and others he'd repaired or built. This one was for himself - a wheel that would take him to places he'd only dreamed about.

title: Southeastern Kentucky
text: A few weeks ago, we mentioned that southeastern Kentucky was the least populated area in the state. Even the biggest communities in the area have fewer than 20,000 people living in them. But the people who live here are happy to be surrounded by an almost constant celebration of Kentucky history. Take the Mountain Laurel Festival in Pineville, for example. The festival was created in memory of Dr. Thomas Walker, the first white man to build a house in our state. How about the Great American Dulcimer Convention, which has been going on every year for the last 20 years? People in the region are making history of their own, as well. For example, in 1945, when a coal mine at the Fourmile community left 20 men trapped inside, they were saved by the courage and clear thinking of a fellow miner named Bud Townes. He comforted his companions and kept everyone safe until they were rescued. He was hailed as a hero all over the state. That's southeastern Kentucky for you: big on history and making news at the same time!

title: What caused the Seven Years' War in the first place?
text: The war we know as the French and Indian War began in Europe in 1756. The "seven years" were the years between 1756 and 1763, when the Treaty of Paris was signed. But the war began as a tiny skirmish over a single province of Austria, called Silesia. A man named Frederick (usually called "Frederick the Great"), who was the king of a land called Prussia, had taken over rule of the province. Maria Theresa, ruler of Austria, wanted it back. Both Maria Theresa and Frederick the Great had many allies, and the argument over Silesia grew to include most of the nations of Europe. France was among Maria Theresa's allies and England was among Frederick's. That meant that England and France were pitted against each other on the battlefields of Europe and all over the world. And the funny thing is, when the dust from the Seven Years' War had settled, Silesia remained under Prussian rule, just like it had been before the war ever started.

title: Opossum
text: Opossums are Kentucky marsupials. That means the mom carries her babies in a pouch on her tummy. Opossums are found in nearly all parts of the state. The opossum has a furry body and feet with little fingers that look like human hands. Their tails are very long and hairless, sort of like a rat's tail, and their noses are very long, too. In fact, there are people who have mistaken a young opossum for a rodent. Opossums are also the only marsupials in North America. They have gray and white faces, black ears and black tails with white tips. They grow to be about 40 inches long.

title: Fun Facts
text: President Grover Cleveland can claim something that no other president can. He was the only president to serve two nonconsecutive (not in a row) terms. He was our 22nd and 24th president.

title: Let's Write
text: The year is 1762. One night, you overhear your parents talking and realize your dad wants to move to Kentucky as soon as the treaty with France is signed. This means you will have to say good-bye to all of your friends. You hope your dad changes his mind, but you know he seldom does—especially when he sounds as happy as he did while he was talking about moving to Kentucky. On the way to Kentucky, though, your family faces a pretty big problem. Write what happened and how you fixed the problem by yourself.

title: The First Who's and Where's
text:
The world around us is full of "firsts." Who was the first person in your family to have his or her tonsils taken out? Who was the first one of your friends to get stitches? Who was the first kid on your block to bring a pack of trading cards to school? What was the first pet you ever had? See what we mean? We could go on and on asking questions about firsts and coming up with answers that just might give us a pretty interesting picture of your life.

Some Kentucky firsts may always remain a mystery. For example, what color was the first dinosaur to scamper across the state? Who was the first human being to look out over the Kentucky wilderness? Like we said, the world may never know. But, this week in Kentucky Studies Weekly, we're going to look at some firsts that aren't so mysterious. Who was the first guy to set up a permanent settlement in Kentucky? Which white settler grew northern Kentucky's first corn crop? Where was Kentucky's first school? If you're looking for answers to these "first" questions, then you've come to the right place. We've got them! All you have to do is turn this first page and start reading the first words of the first article you see. Who can get there first? On your mark - get set - go!

title: Visit Historic Harrodsburg
text:
You can read all about Harrodsburg and fill your imagination with all sorts of good stuff, but the plain and simple truth is this: There's nothing quite like being there. So it's a good thing that in Kentucky, you can be there.

You heard correctly! These days, you can still visit the place where European Kentucky settlements first started. At Harrodsburg, you can see a full-size replica of Fort Harrod, Kentucky's first permanent European settlement. The original fort is long gone, but the replica stands in the same place. In Harrodsburg, you can also visit the Harrodsburg General Store, which was built around 1917. You can buy a piece of licorice and have a seat in a rocking chair on the porch. If you do, you may feel the history bug about to bite because the store sits right where Daniel Boone's cabin was built more than two centuries ago. We think you'll agree that when it comes to real-life history, it's tough to do better than a visit to Harrodsburg.

title: Harrodsburg
text:
Building Harrodsburg

James Harrod was an early European settler and Surveyor in Kentucky. Surveyors were adventurous men hired by land companies to go out into the wilderness and mark the boundaries of the company’s land. They explored the land and reported on what they found. As a surveyor, Harrod became a great woodsman just like Daniel Boone. In fact, he met Boone before he settled Harrodsburg.

In 1773, the same year Boone tried but failed to move his family to Kentucky, Harrod found just the right place for a Kentucky town. But building a town isn't a job for just one man - or even for just a few. Harrod returned to Pennsylvania hoping to get some men who would help him put a town in the Kentucky wilderness. By 1774, he found 31 such men, and they headed for Harrod's chosen spot. When they got there, they made plans to build a place named after their leader: Harrodstown. It didn't stay "Harrodstown" for long, though. Soon people called it "Harrodsburg".

Even though Harrod established Harrodsburg before Boone established Boonesborough, he and Boone were great friends and neighbors. After all, Boonesborough was only about 35 miles away. That's about a two-hour ride on a good horse.

Organizing Harrodsburg

Harrodsburg wasn't just a bunch of cabins sprawled out over the countryside. The plan was to build a town in the center of the settlement, with farmland all around it.

Each man would get half an acre in town (called a "town lot") to build a cabin and 10 acres outside of town (an "out lot") to farm. It seemed like a great idea, with plenty of farmland and beautiful Kentucky scenery for everyone. Before they finished more than a half dozen cabins, though, four of Harrod's men were attacked by American Indians because they stole the American Indians land. The settlers decided to leave the frontier and head for civilization. They were gone for a whole year.

A Great Place to Live

In 1775, James Harrod gathered his men and set off again. This time, they built a strong fort for the settlers to live in. It had high, log walls all around, and the cabins were inside the walls. That autumn, women and children started coming to "Fort Harrod." Soon, the first settlement in Kentucky became the home of the first school in Kentucky. But we're not through with "firsts" yet. Besides the first school in Kentucky, the first woolen mill and the first gristmill (a mill for grinding corn into flour) were built. Soon, the settlement was able to make its own cloth and food.

Hide and Seek

Daniel Boone was the most famous Kentucky pioneer, but there was a man named Simon Kenton who came to Kentucky in 1771, and some say he matched Boone at just about everything. One legend says that one day Boone was in the forest when he sensed that someone else was nearby. He took cover in the brush and snuck around for a couple of hours trying to get a good look.

There was just one problem: Whoever was out there was playing the same game. Around and around they went, sneaking from tree to tree, trying to see each other. Finally, Boone stood up from his hiding place and said, "Hey, is that you, Simon?" Kenton stood up with a big grin on his face and said, "Howdy, Boone."

A Safe Place

Fort Harrod was an important settlement in Kentucky for a lot of reasons. As one of the four major forts in Kentucky, it became a center for trade and a refuge for travelers and settlers who didn't feel that the open wilderness was safe.

title: Trustworthiness
text: Do you know what it means to be trustworthy? It's simple, really. Being trustworthy means that people can trust you. It means that if someone gives you a job to do, you do it. If someone tells you a secret, you keep it. If you say you're going to do something for someone, you follow through. It's easy to see that, when people are trustworthy, there are good feelings, understanding and peace. On the other hand, when people are not trustworthy, there are angry feelings, confusion and suspicion. Being trustworthy is important, but it's just one step on the road to being a great person.

title: Striped Skunk
text:
Striped skunks are the most numerous and well-known member of the weasel family. If beavers and minks had the same perfume as skunks, there would probably be a lot more of them around, too.

Most striped skunks are solid black with two white stripes on their backs. Skunks are good at finding food, but most people don't know they're almost blind. Skunks can only see about 2 feet in front of themselves.

Skunks are almost totally vegetarian, but they do eat meat sparingly (mice and birds).

Do you want to hear a true story about a pioneer and a skunk? Well, on the way out West, an old pioneer went hunting to get food for the people in his wagon train. There were just two problems: His old age had robbed him entirely of any sense of smell, and being an immigrant from a large European city, he had never seen a skunk. Imagine everyone's surprise when he joyfully returned to camp holding a skunk he had caught and killed with his bare hands. Imagine his surprise when everyone in the camp insisted he walk a half mile behind them for the rest of the trek!

title: Fun Facts
text: President Gerald Ford is the only president that was never elected. He was appointed to the vice president position by then-president Richard Nixon and then took over for Nixon after he resigned.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend that you grew up with Daniel Boone. You had all sorts of adventures together. Tell us about your adventures while hunting, fishing and tracking natives and “bars”... ahem, bears. What kinds of wild adventures did the two of you have? Make it a tall tale!

title: Three of The Bravest Frontier Women
text:
Most of the time when we think about the frontier, we think about grizzly mountain men. But there were lots of tough and brave women, too! Let’s learn about some of these women:

Molly Brant: She was the daughter of a Mohawk chief who grew up to be an influential American Indian leader.

Anne Bailey: She was a frontier scout and became a heroine when she delivered gunpowder to Fort Lee when their soldier’s supply was dangerously low.

Mary Donoho: She was the first European woman to settle in Santa Fe. She and her husband left Kentucky in 1833 and created the La Fonda Inn at the end of the Santa Fe Trail.

So next time you think that frontier life was just for men, think again!

title: American Indians in Harrodsburg
text:
Although settling in Harrodsburg was great for the colonists, it wasn’t great for those who lived there before them. The American Indians that inhabited that land felt as though these people were taking their land that they had worked so hard to maintain. The settlers were bringing their children, livestock and way of life into Kentucky. Unfortunately, there were many battles and wars between the settlers and the American Indians for the land.

Eventually, the American Indians were gradually forced to give up their land. Their numbers were depleted due to the diseases brought on by the settlers. There were many attempts to work together through treaties and peace offerings. One final treaty, The Treaty of Greenville, finally ended the fighting between the American Indians and the settlers in 1795. The contention between them was still there though. The American Indians still felt cheated. Their land was overrun by settlers. What once used to be their home, was now just a memory.

title: Daniel Boone's Early Years
text:
It's hard for anyone to see very far into the future. For example, it's tough for parents to see just what sort of grownups their kids will turn out to be. Do you see that boy, who's crashing through those trees? Some folks around here just shake their heads at him. Couldn't there be a better way to spend your time than tromping around the woods, looking for bears to hunt? And what if that kid ever found one? What would he do then?

Look, here he comes now, running out of the woods with great speed. Oh look, he’s being chased by a hive of bees! Knowing him, he probably gave their home a poke with a sharp stick, just to see what would happen. Serves him right, eh? You bet it does, especially since last month he went into town and took apart the doctor's wagon and put it back together again. What's so bad about that? When he put it back together, it was in the top of a 20-foot sycamore tree!

Yes indeed, it makes you wonder what kind of a grownup that kid will be. What's his name? It doesn't really matter, but if you must know, that's Squire Boone's boy, Daniel. He is quite an energetic and creative boy. While other kids are playing with frogs and swords made out of sticks, Daniel's out tracking wild animals and bears! What would he do if he ever caught up with one?

Well, in this issue of Kentucky Studies Weekly, we'll tell young Daniel's story. It's one that begins in Pennsylvania but ends up in a far-off place called Kentucky. Have you ever heard of it? There's not much in Kentucky but wild woods, but if you're patient and can wait until young Daniel grows up, you might get to know this great explorer and leader!

title: Modern Log Cabins
text:
Have you ever made a log cabin out of wooden blocks? In the early days of the Kentucky frontier, most settlers lived in log cabins. They used trees cut from the thick Kentucky forests to build their homes, stacking the logs together and filling any gaps with mud until they formed a cozy square home, just like you might have made with blocks (but probably without the mud).

These days, most homes are made from wood planks, brick, vinyl siding and stucco. But did you know that some people who have pioneering spirits like Daniel Boone still choose to live in log homes?

Modern log homes are a big business all across the United States. There are hundreds of builders and manufacturers who build nothing but log homes. They use some of the same techniques used by the early settlers in building log homes, but they also take advantage of modern-day technology.

While settlers had to use axes to cut and strip bark from logs, today's builders use electric saws. Settlers had to use oxen and wagons to move logs from the forests to their building site, but builders now use forklifts and trucks. And while settlers had to use trees of whatever shape they could find, today's builders can use machinery to trim all their logs to the same shape and size. The fact that people still love the home style of the early settlers shows that today we still appreciate the excitement and ways of the frontier.

title: Daniel Boone: History and Legend
text:
Daniel Boone’s Childhood Background

Daniel Boone was born to a family in Pennsylvania who belonged to a group called the Religious Society of Friends. You may be more familiar with the name most people called them: the Quakers. The Quakers came to America in the 1660s, looking for the freedom to worship God how they wanted. Twenty years later, and still 100 years or so before Daniel Boone’s time, there were 7,000 Quakers in Pennsylvania alone. They wouldn’t swear allegiance to the king, and they refused to fight any wars. That’s tough to do when you live in a country that spends a lot of time on the battlefield. What did being a Quaker teach young Daniel Boone? Well, for one thing, Daniel’s family believed that it was wrong to hurt other people—even if those people are your enemies. Later in his life, with native attacks and wars all around him, Boone had to make some tough choices.

Daniel Boone Joins the Army

By the time Daniel was 19, his family was ready to pull up stakes and leave Pennsylvania for good. They headed south, and they finally set up shop along the Yadkin River in what is now North Carolina. A couple of years later (in 1755), Daniel served under a British general named Edward Braddock during the French and Indian War. That might seem strange for a Quaker kid, but there you go. Some say that he mostly drove a wagon, and he even did that with the courage of a frontier hero.

Daniel Boone: Preparing for His Future

What would a colonial kid need to learn to grow up to be the mighty Daniel Boone? Daniel grew up in Pennsylvania, and he and his family lived out of town. Daniel’s father, Squire Boone (now don’t get confused; Daniel had a brother named Squire, too), was gone a lot, and young Daniel had to help his mama keep an eye on the place. Even as a kid, he was really good at tracking things that might want to make mischief on the farm, like bears, raccoons and foxes. He learned how to shoot and how to fix a gun when it was broken. Later, as a grownup explorer, he carried his gun, extra ammunition and tools to rebuild broken gun parts. In those days, it sometimes came down to huntin’ or starvin’, and young Daniel sure didn’t plan to starve.

Daniel Boone: A Bird out of a Cage

Today, our great nation stretches from sea to shining sea, and we’ve got just about as much elbow room as we can get. But in Daniel Boone’s day, most of the country was a big mystery. Only a narrow stretch of land on the East Coast was settled at all, and different countries fought to own most of the rest of the land. Living on just a little bit of land, with a great big continent stretching out to the West just beyond the frontier, must have been like living in a bird cage. Sooner or later, someone would have to break out and go see it all. Even when he was a kid, it was clear that Daniel Boone was just that someone.

Boone Comes to Kentucky

Daniel Boone loved Kentucky since he first heard about it from an old trapper named John Finley, who had traveled through the area trapping and trading with the natives. The more Boone heard, the more he fell in love with the place before he’d even seen it. When he finally did come to Kentucky, it didn’t disappoint him. He had plenty of hardships, and John Stuart, his traveling companion, was even killed by natives in 1771. But still, Boone longed for his family to live here. He called it a “second paradise.” The hardships didn’t go away, though. The first time he tried to bring his family to Kentucky, in 1773, his oldest son was killed by natives. But Boone still didn’t give up. Next week, we’ll learn how he finally settled his family in Boonesborough in 1775.

title: Fact Cubes
text:
Materials

square boxes, milk cartons

solid-color butcher or wrapping paper

tape or glue

crayons or markers

pencils

Instructions

1. Make a cube from a square box of any kind. You can also make a cube by cutting two milk cartons in half and then inserting the open square end of one into the open square end of the other.

2. Cover both cubes with butcher or wrapping paper. If you use wrapping paper, make sure that it isn't "coated," or you won't be able to draw or write on the paper without smearing the ink.

3. Write and illustrate facts about whatever subject that you choose. You could make a fact cube about your favorite animal or sport, or you could choose a subject in school to write about. For example, you could write what you have learned about the Earth from your science class, or you could copy one of your favorite poems you have learned in your English class.

4. Share your fact cube with family and friends and tell them about the facts you chose to write. Have fun!

Extra Activity: To improve your fact cube even more, you could have a parent help you type up the facts on your computer, print them out and paste them on the fact cube. You could also look on the Internet or in magazines to find pictures to print/cut out and paste on your fact cube. Make sure you always have an adult with you when working on the Internet.

title: Pennyroyal Region
text: When you're walking around Kentucky's Pennyroyal Region, there may be somebody (or something!) walking right underneath your feet, deep underground. Kentucky has about 3,000 caves, and one of them is the longest explored cave in the world: Mammoth Cave. Humans lived in this huge cave 4,000 years ago, leaving behind clothing, tools and bones that are marked in ways that suggest some humans may have eaten each other. They left the cave about A.D. 50, and this place stayed a secret until about 1800. Compared to that underground Kentucky history, everything happening after that, above ground, seems pretty new. For example, the natives and the English teamed up to fight the people of the brand-new United States of America, who wanted Kentucky added to their country. And the Civil War was fought when a large group of Confederates set up their own separate state capital in Bowling Green, elected their own governor, and tried to take Kentucky back out of the United States. Bowling Green became famous as a place for people who wanted to fight, but it began as a place for people who wanted to play. It was started by George and Robert Moore, who enjoyed bowling across the green meadows with hand-carved wooden balls. Although people have put on weddings, concerts and Shakespeare plays in Mammoth Cave, they haven't done much bowling.

title: What do we know about Daniel Boone's wife?
text: Plenty! When Daniel Boone was finished serving in the army under Edward Braddock, he married a beautiful young woman named Rebecca Bryan. She was his neighbor and only 17 years old. The Boone marriage was a good match. Rebecca was almost as tough and courageous of a pioneer as Daniel himself was! Daniel and Rebecca Boone had a big family: 10 children in all. Whenever it looked like too many people were settling in the area, Daniel always wanted to push deeper into the forest. His wife agreed with him every time, except for one. That time, Daniel wanted to move to Florida. In fact, he'd already purchased some land there! Rebecca didn't want to leave family and friends, and in the end, she got her way. In the end, they moved to Kentucky instead.

title: Fire Ants
text: Fire ants are found throughout the South. Did you know that fire ants can bundle tightly together in the water like a floating ball? If you ever see this ball in the water, stay as far away as you can. Fire ants swarm over any warm body they can find - your dog, your cat, your little brother or you! Their stings can be extremely painful or even deadly. Summer is a great time for outdoor activities, like exploring, playing in the grass, working in the garden or eating a picnic lunch outside. We have great weather, which can mean lots of great fun, but be very careful not to upset these fierce ants. If you get stung, tell a grownup right away. In the meantime, stick to hugging those "aunts" who are married to your uncles.

title: Let's Write
text: Write a story about an adventure you and Daniel have while exploring the woods between your homes.

title: The Cumberland Gap
text:
The Cumberland Gap is a pass that goes through the Appalachian Mountains. It cuts through Tennessee, Kentucky and Virginia. American Indians used the pass for a long time before European settlers discovered it.

In 1750, Dr. Thomas Walker put together the first expedition to explore what he called the Cumberland Gap. What an exciting time this was! These men would open up a whole new world to settlers seeking new lands.

In 1763, something happened that had a serious effect on many people in the area. The British put the Proclamation of 1763 in effect. The tribes nearby worried about the new settlers taking over their lands. This proclamation was designed to protect the rights of those tribes and the lands they claimed as their own. But the colonists didn't all see it that way. They thought that their rights were being threatened too, so the proclamation was often ignored as exploration took place. This was just a few years before the Revolutionary War.

In 1769, Daniel Boone explored the Cumberland Gap area. In 1775, a land spectator, Richard Henderson, sent Daniel Boone to explore parts of the Appalachian Mountains. Mr. Henderson wanted to buy some of the Cherokee lands. Little Carpenter, the Cherokee chief, agreed to sell him some land. The treaty they drew up became known as the Transylvania Treaty.

Daniel Boone blazed a trail through portions of the Cumberland Gap which became known as the Wilderness Trail. Once the purchase of the land became final, Boone and a group of ax men cut their way through a portion of Cumberland Gap. The land was rough and narrow. Boone's team made the trail easier to travel on, although still not something that was traveled easily. In time, the trail would be widened to allow wagons to move through. Thousands of settlers would use the Wilderness Trail as a gateway to the west and new lands. It brought many people into the Appalachian Mountains.

title: Boonesborough Beginnings
text:
Whoa! Get a hold of those reins! Somebody tie down that wagon cover! Whose dog is that, running around causing trouble? Make sure the children are aboard 'cause we're not coming back. All right, let's move. See that guy way up in front with a rifle on his shoulder? Yeah, the one leading that woman's horse by the bridle. That's Daniel Boone. He knows the way.

How does he know the way? Are you kidding? He's been through here before, maybe more than anyone else. He and his brother, Squire, entered this land at the head of the Big Sandy River in 1767 - just to have a look. We should be glad we're going with him now and not way back then. That winter was so hard that it forced them back home. You and I might never have made it.

The truth is, I think he would have stayed home for good if not for the winter that old John Finley spent at his place. All through the winter of 1768, Finley spent the days spinning stories for Daniel and his wife, Rebecca. By spring, Daniel was itching to head out again. Spring sure was different from winter. Buffalo roamed in herds all over the place, blossoms grew, and delicious fruit hung everywhere. Daniel was hooked. I tell you, we've got nothing to worry about. Like I said, Daniel Boone knows the way. Besides, it's his town we're headed for. Well, it's more of a fort really. At least I'm pretty sure it's his place. It's called Boonesborough, after all.

title: Who Owns History?
text:
When the Spanish explorers conquered the Inca Empire, they destroyed many of their beautiful cities. But the city of Machu Picchu was a hidden city, so it was not destroyed. Machu Picchu was built high in the Andes mountains so that its people could be closer to their gods. Today, Machu Picchu is a place many people go to see. Nearly half a million people visit "the Lost City of the Incas" every year.

Machu Picchu was discovered by Europeans in 1911 by professor Hiram Bingham from Yale University in Connecticut. He led three expeditions to Machu Picchu. Tourists who visit the Lost City can see ruins of palaces, temples, tombs and sundials, but they won't find very many tools, bowls or other small objects. That's partly because the president of Peru gave Hiram Bingham permission to take many objects back to Yale. However, many people believe that Hiram Bingham was supposed to bring the artifacts back once he was done studying them. The artifacts still have not been returned and the people of Peru say they are willing to sue Yale University to get them back.

Yale University disagrees that the artifacts were supposed to be returned, but they have offered to return some of the objects. How many artifacts are actually at Yale? The people of Peru say there are about 5,000; Yale University says they only have 250 artifacts. They say they have no mummies or gold objects and only a few silver objects. It is also possible that many artifacts had been stolen from Machu Picchu before Bingham even got there.

Everyone hopes the two sides can reach a compromise soon. Many people believe Yale University has taken good care of the artifacts and should get to keep taking good care of them. Many people believe all of the artifacts should be returned to their rightful home in Peru immediately. What do you think?

title: Settling Boonesborough
text:
Bound for Boonesborough

What do you do if you've got money to burn? If you're Judge Richard Henderson, and you're a buddy of Daniel Boone, you might just buy 1 million acres of Kentucky wilderness and then ask Boone to go settle it. To Daniel Boone, that sounded like an adventure. He set out in March 1775 with about 35 people to help him. Not long after Boone's group left, Henderson brought along some more willing settlers. Altogether, about 80 people (mostly men) set out to help settle the area. By June, they had a good start at building a fort. It was called Boonesborough, and you can probably guess who it was named after.
