When the fort was completed, there were 30 cabins built in a rectangle with high wooden walls in the spaces between the cabins. The cabins on each corner were two stories high, so riflemen could see what was going on.

Two Problems: Food Shortages and Few Wives

These first settlers of Boonesborough had a couple of big problems. First, within a couple of months, food was running low. Running low? How could that be? After all, when Boone first visited Kentucky, he saw nothing but bison in every direction. But the early settlers of Kentucky figured there were plenty of bison, so they shot as many as they wanted without thinking about it. Unfortunately, they wasted a lot of the meat. Soon, the bison got wise and moved on, and before long, hunters had to travel farther and farther to find food.

What was their other big problem? There weren’t enough women. Most of the men, including Boone, had left their wives at home or had moved without having a wife. Just like many of the others, Boone decided that his dream of a Kentucky settlement wouldn't be complete until his wife, Becky, came to live with him at Boonesborough. So in June, he and many other men headed back home to get their wives. Many men who didn’t have wives went to try and find women who would marry them and move back to the fort. By September of 1775 Boonesborough had almost 100 people living there.

These first settlers of Boonesborough and other settlements, like Harrodsburg (settled before Boonesborough), Logan's Station and Boiling Springs, were pioneers. They blazed the trail for others to follow. They proved that families could live safely on the other side of the mountains. It wasn't long before thousands of people rushed to Kentucky to start a new life.

Kentucky's First Laws

In Kentucky in the 1770s, people probably knew they were still officially ruled by England, but at the same time, the British government seemed pretty far away. Early Kentuckians felt they needed a government right there on the frontier to help keep things organized. On May 23, 1775, delegates representing the surrounding forts of Harrodsburg, Boiling Springs and Logan's Station met at Boonesborough in the shade of an elm tree and made some laws. They decided how to punish criminals, how to defend themselves from enemies, and especially how to hunt carefully so that the game (animals used for food) wouldn't all disappear.

Tough Women for a Tough Land

All his life, Daniel Boone dreamed of finding a place of his own, carving it out of the woods, clearing it to raise crops and working it hard to provide for the needs of his family. When it came time for him to find a wife, he looked for someone who wouldn't mind the hard life he had planned for himself. Rebecca Bryan wound up being the perfect match for old Daniel. She was brave and independent. Sometimes, Daniel was gone for weeks, or even months, hunting or exploring. While he was gone, Becky minded the farm by herself. Between working the farm, blazing a trail through the wilderness beside her husband and building Boonesborough, she lived a life as full of adventure as anyone could hope for. Sometimes, it must have been exciting, but most of the time it was probably just plain hard for both Rebecca and Daniel. And the same thing goes for all of those first pioneers who were brave enough to follow Daniel and Rebecca Boone to Boonesborough.

title: Perseverance
text:
It could be said that perseverance is the father of all other character traits. If you fail at courage, but try again; if you forget to be just or fair, but try again; if you lose your temper, but keep trying to do better; if all other character traits are not complete in your character, but you never give up in your effort to improve them, THEN you have perseverance. You've probably heard the old saying . . . "If at first you don't succeed, try, try again." That's perseverance.

Sir Winston Churchill, the English leader who helped his country win the war against Nazi Germany, said it this way: "Never, never, never, never give in!" Here's a poem about a common boy who became a millionaire because he had the character trait of perseverance (author unknown):

Bill Brown made a million - Bill Brown! Think of that!
A boy, you remember, as poor as a rat;
He hoed for the neighbors, did jobs by the day,
But Bill made a million, or near it, they say.
You can't understand it? Well, neither could I,
And then I remembered, and now I know why:
The bell might be ringing, the dinner horn blow,
But Bill always hoed to the end of the row.

Bill worked for my father, you maybe recall;
He wasn't a wonder - not that, not at all;
He couldn't out-hoe me, or cover more ground,
Or hoe any cleaner, or beat me around.
In fact, I was better in one way that I know:
One toot from the kitchen, and home I would go;
But Bill always hoed to the end of the row.

We used to get hungry out there in the corn.
When you talk about music, what equals a horn?
A horn yellin' dinner, tomatoes and beans,
And pork and potatoes and gravy and greens?
I ain't blamin' no one for quittin' on time,
To stop with the whistle, that ain't a crime.
But as for the million - well, this much I know:
That Bill always hoed to the end of the row.

title: Cottonmouth Snake
text: Don't you just love snakes? If you think we're crazy for even asking, then you're not alone. People have always had a good, healthy fear of snakes. While it is true that many snakes are harmless, and even make good pets, the cottonmouth is a good one to fear. Cottonmouths are also called water moccasins and can grow up to 4 feet long. The cottonmouth has a dark stripe through the eye and along the side of its head. Watch for dark cross bands down the body and color ranging from olive to black. The cottonmouth doesn't have a rattler to warn you. Its warning is a white mouth. Another way to tell them apart from other water snakes is the way they swim. Cottonmouths keep their heads way above the water when they swim. So watch out for cottonmouths. Their bites can be fatal!

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you’re best friends with Becky Boone. Your husband goes exploring and hunting with Boone all the time. Tell us what it’s like staying home on the wild frontier when the men are way. Do you visit Becky every day? Write a story about your adventures with Becky Boone.

title: Studying Perspectives
text:
A person’s point of view is the way he or she looks at and thinks about an event. Different people often experience history in a variety of different ways. Not everyone who experiences a historical event feels or thinks the exact same way about it.

A number of things determine a person’s point of view. Life experiences (positive and negative), future needs and wants, and an emotional connection to an event all influence a person’s point of view.

Different perspectives and points of view help us see the bigger picture. They help us to understand more than one side of a story. When you study history from multiple sides of a story, you can fully understand how different people experienced and felt through different periods of history. The more perspectives you can see from, the better you can understand what really happened in history!

title: Jemima Boone
text:
Life on the frontier was exciting and filled with many opportunities. It was also dangerous and filled with many perils.

In this week of Studies Weekly, you’ve been learning about the frontiersman and explorer, Daniel Boone. Here is a story about his daughter Jemima, and how she and her friends were kidnapped on the frontier!

One day, Jemima and her friends Francis and Elizabeth Callaway were canoeing in the river. They had been told that they needed to stay close to the fort and where the adults could keep track of them, but they didn’t listen.

Suddenly, a small band of Cherokee came and took Jemima and her friends! The Cherokee were upset that Daniel Boone had not been honoring treaties. One of the townspeople saw it happen from a distance and ran to get Daniel Boone, Jemima’s father. Once Boone heard the news, he gathered a group of men for a search party and ran to the riverbank where the girls had disappeared.

The men were experienced trackers and followed the trail left by the girls and the Cherokee. The girls were also very clever and left markers for the men to follow — bent branches, broken twigs and a trail of leaves and berries. They followed the trail for two days! The men were exhausted. By the third day, they saw a good sign — smoke from a fire!

The men tried to sneak up on the people around the fire, but they weren’t quiet enough and the small band of Cherokee ran away. However, much to Boone’s joy, they left Jemima Boone and her friends behind. Jemima and her friends were very thankful to be rescued and told the men that although the Cherokee had taken them, they had treated them well. The girls promised to obey the rules now that they could see that the rules would keep them safe!

title: What Was It Like Back Then?
text:
Hey, Kentucky history adventurers! At Kentucky Studies Weekly, we thought you'd enjoy a glimpse of the simple, happy life of the Kentucky frontier (unsettled territory) - way back before Kentucky was a state and way back before the United States of America was a country.

Life in those days must have been much less complicated than it is today. Imagine frontier children busily doing their chores, gathering eggs from the hens in the henhouse, helping their parents prepare and serve meals and then, when it's all done, relaxing with a bowl of popcorn and watching a movie. That must have been . . . What? What's that you say? No TV? No movies? Okay, our mistake. We'll start over.

Imagine yourself finishing up the simple daily chores of your frontier home when Mom looks in the fridge to find she's all out of ground beef and milk. She sends you on a quick trip on your four-wheeler down to the grocery store to pick up some milk for your . . . Now what? You're kidding! No grocery store? No fridge? What kind of place was this, anyway? Well, here's the answer: It was a new land full of hardship, but mostly it was a land full of LAND! Kentucky became the place to be for people who didn't mind lots of hard work, and who could stand the loneliness of frontier life. Those first farmers and other settlers started the ball rolling more than 200 years ago, and it hasn't stopped since. Kentucky is still the home of adventurous, hardworking folks like you. So what did they do in frontier Kentucky? Turn the page and find out. Go ahead; it's okay. This time, we're serious!

title: Kentucky Frontier Life
text:
Arkansas Land Fever!

In just 10 years, between 1810 and 1820, the U.S. Census (an official count of a population) showed record growth for Arkansas. The U.S. Census recorders only counted white and enslaved people. The American Indians were not counted at all even though they were living in Arkansas! In 1810, the population of white settlers and enslaved people in Arkansas was 1,062. By the time 1820 rolled around, the population of white and enslaved people in Arkansas was 15,000! Ten years later, in 1830, there were more than 30,000 people. That means the population doubled in just 10 years. That may not sound like a big deal to you, since Arkansas is now home to millions, but it was quite a start. Can you imagine if that happened today? Everything would be crowded! But what were all those folks after? Only one thing: LAND! In the East, the fields had been farmed until they were worn out, and the economy (overall business activity) wasn't so hot. People came to Arkansas and the surrounding states by wagons, flatboats, or even walking with all their stuff strapped to their backs. Arkansas held a lot of promise. Most of the newcomers were poor farmers, and just like the stars come out at night, cabins began to dot the Arkansas landscape.

Learnin' on the Frontier

What would it have been like to go to school on the frontier? Well, for one thing, at your school you probably have a chance to study all sorts of different things, like music, art, history and maybe even sports. But on the frontier, kids often went to school inside the forts where they lived, and they only learned the basic stuff: reading, writing and arithmetic! In some settlements, kids even had to go without ink and paper. How did they write anything down? These kids were creative! They wrote on smooth boards, using ink made out of the fluids inside the intestines of animals. Think about that the next time you write something down and be glad you go to school where you do!

Slavery in the South

Slavery existed in Latin America as early as 1515, when Spain and Portugal brought slaves to their colonies in the New World. In 1526, a Spanish colony was attempted in Georgia. The colony failed, but some of the 100 African slaves they brought with them might have escaped to live among the Seminole Indians. These were probably the first enslaved Africans to come to North America. Later, in 1619, a Dutch ship brought enslaved Africans to the Jamestown settlement in Virginia.

When settlers moved south to Arkansas, so did the practice of slavery. Unfortunately, slavery went on for hundreds of years in the South.

Let's Build a Cabin

Most people on the frontier lived in log cabins. They learned to help each other with the rough task of building their log homes. Everyone in a settlement turned out to help. The men cut down trees and whacked off the limbs with sharp axes. Then, they cut the trees into logs that were all the same length. After that, they cut deep notches in either end of each log so it would fit snugly on top of the log underneath it. Roofs were made from shorter trees cut into boards. Sometimes, they hammered wood pegs into the roof to hold it on. Other times, they just hefted a bunch of heavy rocks onto the roof to keep it where they wanted it. Kids helped, too! They mixed up batches of twigs, pebbles and mud to fill the spaces between the logs. There was no use having walls on a cabin if the rain and wind could go right in!

Frontier Creativity

Frontier homes contained just what a family needed, but not much more. There was usually only one room, with kitchen stuff in one end and beds in the other. Mattress tickings (coverings) were often made of burlap sacks sewn together and stuffed with hay or grass. If a family was fortunate, they might have a mattress ticking stuffed with soft cornhusks! For a blanket, they sometimes wrapped up in a bearskin or deerskin! What about a cradle for the baby? Sometimes, part of a hollow log served pretty well as a cradle. If a family was really lucky and had a stream outside, they could take a refreshing bath. Frontier folks were pretty darn creative when it came to making do with what they had.

Gettin' Hitched on the Frontier

Is anyone you know getting married soon? What would it be like to get married on the frontier (uncharted or unsettled territory)? Old journals (books that people write about their personal lives) tell us that everyone for miles around was invited to a wedding, and sometimes the celebration lasted two or three days. Many times, the wedding was outdoors - even in the winter. If it was too cold, big fires were lit to warm everyone up. After the bride and groom were married, there were shooting contests, music, hoedowns (square dances) and races, but it didn't stop there! They topped it all off with a huge dinner of meat they brought in from the forest: bear, venison (deer), wild turkeys and anything else they could hunt. After dinner, there was more dancing and singing. Sometimes, the celebration lasted all night. Some folks stayed and camped, and the celebration started up again in the morning. Weddings were happy times, when settlers got together and enjoyed each other's company for a while. It was a welcome break from the hard work of frontier life.

title: Famous Person Book
text:
Materials

12-inch by 18-inch piece of construction paper

6-inch by 6-inch piece of construction paper

Scissors

Glue

Crayons and markers

Instructions

1. Fold the piece of 12 by 18-inch paper into eight equal sections as shown in the picture.

2. (You don't have to label your sections as they are labeled here. We've done that to help you know which pieces to cut and fold.) Cut out sections E and H. Save these pieces for later.

3. Fold sections A and D into the center to make a vest or jacket. Glue pieces E and H on the back for arms, as shown in the picture.

4. Cut a head from the 6 by 6-inch piece of construction paper. Glue it to the top of sections B and C. To make pants for your famous person, cut a small triangle between sections F and G as shown. (Or you can cut the lower corners off these sections to create a skirt.)

5. Draw your famous person's face on the head. You can add hair and clothing. Add hands and shoes cut from paper scraps.

6. Open the flaps of the jacket and, on the inside, write something about your famous person. If you'd like, you can write a longer story or essay about your famous person on folded pieces of paper and then staple the pages into your famous person book.

Extra Activity: You can make your book about a family member or friend and give it to him or her as a gift.

title: Roads in the Woods
text: Come on through here," said James. He helped his cousin Sarah between the trees. "We'll be at the house in a minute. The road goes through here." "This is a road?" asked Sarah. She was growing tired, it was getting dark, and she had already torn her dress. Life had been different in Virginia. Since her family had moved to Kentucky, she'd only experienced one hardship after another. Her parents had told her that life in Kentucky would take some getting used to. One thing was for sure: She wasn't used to it yet! She grumpily followed James through the woods. "In Virginia, we had roads. This is nothing but a space between the trees, too narrow for us to even walk side by side!" Her cousin offered to carry her the last little bit. "I know it's tough, Sarah," he said, "but most of these roads are just native trails or paths made by soldiers." He grinned and said, "Maybe someday, they'll have roads just like they have in Virginia." Sarah scowled and complained, "I don't even know why I agreed to come out here with you. I hate it!" "Oh, come on," coaxed James. "Your mama just thought you might like to see a little of the place you live in. That's all." Sarah kept silent for a bit, and James kept quiet, too. Finally, Sarah spoke up again. "How can you tell what's the road and what's not the road, anyway? It looks just like forest to me." James pointed his finger and said, "See that bare place on the sycamore right there? Somebody's axe made that. The whole road is marked with them. See, there's another one." Sarah shrugged and replied, "So it's not that you're just smelling your way along?" James laughed, "No, ma'am! Here, you lead the way for a while!" He let her down, grabbed her by the arm, and pushed her in front of him. She was nervous for a bit, but soon she figured she could pick out the marked trees nearly as well as James. As she walked, she grew more and more confident. A smile even formed on her face. Soon, she could see the lights of the settlement ahead. She saw her family's cabin and her mother at the door, waiting for her. "Mother!" Sarah shouted and ran to her with a smile on her face. "Don't worry about me! I was just seeing some of the forest with James! If you need to go anywhere, take me along. I can find the road!" Yep, just like Sarah could see the lights shining from inside the cabin, she could imagine a day when this place wouldn't seem so strange to her. It would take some getting used to, but she knew she'd like it here someday.

title: Pennyroyal Region
text:
A big part of Kentucky is named after a mint plant that grows here. It's called the Pennyroyal Region. The people who live in one big city, Bowling Green, believe in getting people smart and getting them feeling better. You see, thousands of people work for Western Kentucky University and the local schools, and thousands work at the medical center. Many people work at the Corvette factory, too, so they must also believe in great-looking cars.

There's a lot to see in this part of Kentucky. You can go underground into Mammoth Cave, which stretches for 350 miles on five levels. (There may be 1,000 miles more we haven't even explored yet!)

One amazing place is Shakertown. Shakers are a group of people whose religion includes swaying and moving when they feel God is near them. Nine Shakers came to America in 1774 to find religious freedom. Some came as far west as South Union and built a beautiful community of thousands of acres and hundreds of peace-loving people. Their buildings and gardens, the tools, furniture and clothing they made were very simple, but they were very beautiful. A lot of it's there for people to see, even today. One of their beliefs was that men and women shouldn't have children, and partly because of this, the group got smaller and smaller. Finally, in 1922, the last western group of Shakers broke up. How many were left? Nine.

title: What kinds of toys did early Kentucky kids play with?
text: Kids in Kentucky probably didn't have as many toys as you do today. Children spent much time working or exploring Kentucky's forests with their friends. Those kids were as able as you are to use a straight stick for a toy sword or a gun. Kentucky's forests have probably seen many pretend battles between frontier kids over the years. Kentucky kids also enjoyed playing with other toys. Kentucky girls sometimes carried with them dolls made out of stuffed cornhusks. Boys looped string through large wooden buttons and spun them around like noisy buzz saws. And anyone walking along a Kentucky street might have had to jump out of the way of a herd of Kentucky youngsters racing old wagon hoops along with sticks!

title: Armadillo
text:
The armadillo is a mammal that's protected by bony plates all over the top of its body. When an armadillo senses danger, it hurries to its burrow. If that's too far away, it may dig a new hole. If there's no time for digging, it rolls into a ball and tucks its head and feet inside. In this position, it's about as safe as a turtle inside its shell.

The armadillo eats snakes, beetles, worms, snails, roots, fruit and sometimes dead animals - YUCK! An armadillo has strong claws and a long, narrow tongue. This helps it "pick and lick" its dinner. The nine-banded armadillo is found in the southern United States. It will grow about 2 feet long and weigh up to 15 pounds. The mother armadillo gives birth to four babies that are either all males or all females.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you are 10 years old and living in frontier Kentucky. Since you were 6, you’ve had a long list of chores to do. Write a 200-word story about all the chores you do each day. Are they hard? Do you mind doing them? What do you do after all your chores are done?

title: Living Like a Pioneer
text:
You've read or heard stories of pioneer life, right? Do you ever wonder what it was really like to be a child during that time, enjoying the freedom of the pioneer experience? For many teenagers, the dream of being a real pioneer can come true, at least for a few days. Young men and women from all over the world participate in pioneer treks each year.

Pioneer treks give young people a chance to see what traveling west in the 1800s would have been like. These treks take place in wilderness areas all over the world. Youth ages 14-18 dress in pioneer clothing and experience what it might have been like to make the long journey to a new home in the West. Most early pioneers traveled west in covered wagons, but many settlers carried all their things in small carts they pulled by hand, called handcarts. Youth pack a few supplies, pull their handcarts, set up tents, build campfires, cook pioneer food and even try their hands—or feet—at a little square dancing. What better way to find out what pioneer life was like than by trying it out firsthand!

Even though the young people aren't really walking 2,000 miles, the days they spend pulling their handcarts and living like pioneers give them a real taste of pioneer life. Trekkers come home tired, dirty and hungry, but also with a better appreciation for the courage and strength pioneers needed on the American frontier.

title: The Shot Heard Around the World
text:
The Revolutionary War in Kentucky

"Stand your ground, men. Don't fire unless fired upon, but if they mean to have a war, let it begin here!"

Those words, spoken by Captain John Parker to his band of minutemen, may have been the last words spoken before shots were fired at Lexington, Massachusetts, in April 1775. They may have been the last official words of peacetime, before the first gunshots of the American Revolution.

Now, it's true that Lexington is far north of Kentucky, but it's pretty clear that those shots and the war that followed them shook things up out here in our neck of the woods and all the way around the world. In this issue of Kentucky Studies Weekly, we'll learn how the war affected things here in Kentucky. Sometimes, it looked like we were part of the winning team, and sometimes, it didn't. Speaking of how "we" did, who were "we" in those days, anyway? Were we patriotic Americans or loyal British subjects? It was a real roller coaster!

As you read, you may want to imagine what it might have been like in Kentucky back then. It's easy to look back now and see that things went pretty well for America, but while the fighting was going on, did the folks around here feel like winners? Would you be frightened or worried at the sound of cannon fire? Would you have worried about your father or brother going off to battle? War is tough stuff, and it takes a pretty big dream to make it all worth it. Kentuckians have always been driven by dreams of freedom, justice and equality. Those are big dreams, and thanks to the dreamers of the American Revolution, who were willing to do more than just dream, we're still living those dreams today.

title: Kids Help Soldiers Phone Home
text:
Can you imagine spending thousands of dollars to call the people you love? Sounds pretty crazy, doesn't it? A couple of kids from Massachusetts think so too!

Last year, 13-year-old Brittany Bergquist and her 12-year-old brother, Robbie, heard about a soldier in Iraq who unknowingly racked up $7,600 in cell phone charges calling home.

They felt sorry for him and started saving their money to help him. This small act of kindness started a program called Cell Phones for Soldiers.

Brittany and Robbie have involved their families, classmates and organizations across the country in raising money to purchase calling cards and cell phones for soldiers in Afghanistan and Iraq.

So far they have sent more than 6,000 calling cards to the soldiers. They hope to raise $9 million to buy phones for the soldiers.

title: Critical Analysis: Henry Knox and the Cannons
text:
What does it take to be a good problem solver? Why is critical analysis, or careful judgment, so important? A bookseller from Boston named Henry Knox is an excellent example.

Knox was born in Boston in 1750. His father died when he was 12, so he left school to be a clerk in a bookstore. Later, Knox opened his own bookstore. He loved to read and learned a lot about military strategies and weapons from the books he read.

Knox sided with the American patriots and joined the Army in 1775. General George Washington soon noticed him because of his military knowledge.

The British forces were in Boston, and General Washington needed heavy artillery to force them out. Knox suggested bringing cannons from Fort Ticonderoga in northern New York down to Boston. This idea sounded impossible, but Washington trusted Knox's judgment.

Using heavy sleds drawn by oxen, Knox and his men traveled 300 miles. They brought over 50 cannons across snow-covered mountains and frozen rivers. They placed them overnight on a hill overlooking the harbor. When British Gen. William Howe saw this, he withdrew his troops. He said, "The rebels have done more in one night than my whole army would have done in a month."

Henry Knox used critical analysis again when he supervised Washington's famous crossing of the icy Delaware River. Knox stood on the shore shouting directions while boats moved troops, horses and weapons across. Washington's soldiers then won the Battle of Trenton. The next day they went back across the river with even more prisoners and supplies.

Washington promoted Henry Knox to brigadier general. When Washington became president, he made Knox the first secretary of war. Henry Knox used expert knowledge plus critical analysis to become a military mastermind. For what problem could you use your best judgment to solve?

title: The Fall of Israel Boone
text: "I'm nervous about this," said Daniel Boone, under his breath. The horses stamped at the ground, and the men readied their weapons. "Daniel Boone, nervous!" laughed Hugh McGary. "Surely, that's a joke! Besides, the tracks of those Indian raiders lead right to the river here. We've caught up with them! I say, charge and be done with it!" The worried look didn't leave Daniel's face. "This trail has been too easy to follow," he replied. "Something's up ahead that we're missing. I don't like it." McGary was getting annoyed. "And so, Mr. Boone, what do you think we should do?" he asked. Daniel replied, "I think we should break up, split into two groups, and try to get at them from both..." McGary interrupted him, "Nonsense! We're all here, right now, and we have more than enough men to walk out of here with a victory today! Let's go!" He turned to the men behind him. "Charge!" he shouted, and the men rushed forward across the river with a shout. The crowd pushed around Boone. There were so many men that he couldn't have held his ground even if he'd wanted to. Swept along with the rest, he turned to his son, Israel, who charged nervously beside him. "Come on, Son," he said. And then, louder, to his loyal militiamen, he cried, "On, men! This is it! We're all slaughtered now!" The words had just left his lips when the air was filled with smoke and noise from guns in the trees all around them. "I knew it!" shouted Boone. "It's an ambush! Retreat, men! There, through the trees to the left! Israel, go!" Israel fired again from his father's side. " I won't leave you, Pa," replied the boy. "Israel, I said run!" Boone fired again into the trees. "I won't, Pa. I won't leave your side, and don't you..." A shot rang out, clear among the rest, and Israel slipped to the ground at Daniel's feet. The father froze, not even able to speak. Then, almost in slow motion, Daniel fired again and again through the smoke of the battle, covering the retreat of his men, as they splashed back through the river that was growing redder by the second with the blood of Kentucky soldiers and poor Israel Boone.

title: Who was King George III?
text: King George III was the king of England during the American Revolutionary War. He became king in 1760, when his grandfather, George II, died. During much of the reign of George III, it seemed like England was always in the middle of big stuff. The American Revolution was just one of many different revolutions that involved King George in one way or another. The American Revolution cost England its colonies in America. But the French Revolution, which led to a war between England and France, nearly destroyed England altogether. In addition, the Industrial Revolution changed English society forever and almost doubled its population during George's reign. King George suffered from a disease that we now call porphyria. It struck at different times and sometimes made him appear to be mentally ill. In fact, by 1810, the disease had become so bad that many people thought he was insane.

title: Peregrine Falcon
text:
The peregrine falcon is one of the fastest Kentucky residents. It can reach speeds of more than 200 mph! That's faster than most small airplanes fly. They use this amazing speed to dive at other birds. Sometimes they knock their prey right out of the sky. But they never eat their prey until they've plucked all its feathers. Peregrines have been known to nest in large cities where pigeons are in great supply.

At one time, peregrine falcons were extremely endangered. There were fewer than 300 in the whole United States. But now, thanks to laws that outlawed certain pesticides, there are at least 1,600 pairs of peregrine falcons. In 1999, the peregrine falcon was officially removed from the endangered species list.

title: Let's Write
text: This week, pretend you’re living in Kentucky before the Revolutionary War. Your mother strongly believes it’s your family duty to be loyal to King George III of England. For several reasons, she changes her mind, and your family becomes patriots. Write a 200-word story telling us why she changed her mind.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: Use any color to circle or highlight three relative pronouns (who, whose, whom, which, that, etc.) in this week’s magazine. Underline the related noun. (CC ELA L.4.1)

title: American Revolution
text:
Whigs and Tories of the Revolution

Sometimes, during the revolution, even folks in the same town were loyal to opposite armies. Because they didn't wear T-shirts in their team colors, it might have been tough sometimes to tell the sides apart. After all, even the folks who supported the British were "Americans." Here's the lingo, plain and simple: The revolutionaries, all those who were against the British, were called Whigs. Now that's a goofy name! It's almost as goofy as the name for those folks who were loyal to the British. They were called Tories!

Henry Hamilton

The British were always on the lookout for ways to defeat the colonies. And though the action didn't get fierce way out here on the frontier right at first, British troops finally realized that folks in Kentucky weren’t backing down and had to be dealt with. How did they do it? Well, they hired the help of the only ones who knew Kentucky better than the settlers themselves: the local native tribes. In the summer of 1777, a lieutenant governor named Henry Hamilton, who was loyal to the British, coordinated attacks on European settlements. By the end of the year, Hamilton had 72 prisoners and had 129 settlers killed.

Kentucky's Last Battle

The last battle of the American Revolution was fought here in Kentucky on Aug. 19, 1782, and it didn't go well for Kentuckians. It was called the Battle of Blue Licks because it happened at the Lower Blue Licks crossing of the Licking River. A group of settlers, led by Daniel Boone and a guy named Hugh McGary, was attacked by a huge band of natives and British raiders. By the end of the day, there were 60 settlers dead, including Daniel Boone's son, Israel. Some say Boone's eyes filled with tears every time he talked about it, even years later. Some say he knew they'd lose the battle, even before it began. As McGary sounded the charge across the river, Boone turned to his men. "Come on," he told them, "We are all slaughtered now!"

George Rogers Clark: Hero

When you're talking about Kentucky people who were involved in the American Revolution, there's one guy you'd better not leave out. That's George Rogers Clark. George's younger brother William led a little trip called the Lewis and Clark expedition that you've probably heard of. But then, that's another story. Years before that expedition, right at the beginning of the American Revolution in 1775, George Rogers Clark was living in Kentucky when news reached him that Virginia's government (Kentucky was officially part of the Virginia colony back then) refused to send soldiers to help Kentucky defend itself. Clark gritted his teeth and said, "If a country's not worth protecting, it's not worth claiming!" He put together his own army of about 175 men, and with those brave followers and a bunch of borrowed supplies, he spent the years 1778 and 1779 capturing British strongholds, like Kaskaskia, Cahokia and Vincennes, in Illinois and Indiana. When he finally retired, some said that Clark had done more to save the western settlements (including Kentucky) than anyone else in the war.

The War Ends at Yorktown

The most important battle to end the Revolutionary War was fought at Yorktown, Virginia, almost a whole year before Kentucky's last battle. With the help of the French armies that joined his forces, George Washington trapped the main British army under General Cornwallis. This time, it was the British who were outnumbered. Though they were near the sea, their navy couldn't help them because the French fleet controlled the Chesapeake Bay. Hopelessly trapped, General Cornwallis asked for a temporary cease-fire, but General Washington demanded an immediate and unconditional surrender. At long last, the Revolutionary War was over. A new nation was finally free and independent.

title: Minutemen and Militia
text:
The terms minutemen and militia are often both used to describe the volunteer colonial soldiers during the Revolutionary War. But the minutemen and the militia were two different groups.

Almost every town in the colonies had its own militia. The men in these volunteer armies used their own weapons. They came from many different backgrounds. Many of these soldiers were farmers, shopkeepers, craftspeople and blacksmiths. Some of the men had military skills, but many were just ordinary citizens who wanted to protect their families' freedom.

The best soldiers from every militia were chosen to get special training. They were called minutemen because they had to be ready to fight at a minute's notice. The minutemen were usually the first to get to the battlefield. Then the regular militia came to back them up. Soon, the minutemen began to train under George Washington and became part of the Continental Army.

title: Frontier Transportation
text: Gee there! And, you! Get out of the way! There's a wagon coming through! Haw! Haw! Oh, wait! You're with us, aren't you? Well, this wagon's off on a trip across the country to Kentucky. Is your gear ready? Let's see here... What's this? X-Box? Sorry, you'll have to leave that behind. There's no electricity on the trail, anyway. That means you'll have to leave that electric guitar, too. Comic books? Afraid not. There's no room in the wagon! Besides, when we get on the flatboat at the Tennessee River, they'll get soggy. Star Wars action figures? You can bring one. Pick your favorite and stick it in your pocket. Who knows? It may come in handy on the trail if we have to trade something. Wait! What are you doing? You can't ride in the wagon! That's just for the beans, salt, tools, clothes and bacon. We've got pounds of it back there, so you'll have to walk. It's nothing personal, of course. Most of us are walking. Are those good shoes? Good. Don't worry about a thing. They finished cutting the road last year, and the whole trip shouldn't take more than a few weeks. Toss your gear in the back, spit in your hand and grab that switch (twig). You'll need it for the oxen. They won't get too cranky if you won't. But enough gabbing! Is everyone back there ready? Then let's hit the road! And we won't come back until we learn a little bit about how people get from place to place on the frontier.

title: Engineering is Fun with KEEN
text:
It took a lot of engineering expertise to bring us from the horse-and-wagon transportation of the early settlers to the car and jet transportation we use today. Engineering means using science and math to design and create products that work correctly.

To show kids across the state just how much fun engineering can be, the Kentucky Transportation Cabinet has developed a program called the Kentucky Engineering Exposure Network (KEEN). As part of KEEN, engineers bring fun experiments and exhibits to schools so kids can have hands-on experiences with transportation engineering.

For example, how would you and your classmates like to build cars with food items like pretzel sticks, rice cakes and peanut butter, and then race your creations? Or would you like to make boats out of aluminum foil and see whose boat can hold the most coins without sinking? Maybe you'd like to crawl into the cab of a dump trunk and honk the booming horn.

These are just some of the activities KEEN engineers can bring to your school. If your school hasn't been visited lately by a KEEN engineer, ask your teacher to contact your local transportation district office and ask about the program. Tell them you think engineering is keen!

title: From Buffalo Trails to the Railroad
text:
Following Buffalo

Suppose you're a buffalo, wandering with the rest of your herd through the forest. We bet you're not thinking that hundreds of settlers will build a road out of the path you just made. It's true! The early roads that took people from place to place by the hundreds began as buffalo trails, American Indian hunting trails, or paths made by traders with only a horse or two. When the official road builders came through, they figured it was easier to make a road where someone or something had already been - even if that someone or something was a buffalo like you!

5000-Pound Floating Convertible

If you were going on a long, cross-country trip, what would you like to ride in? A huge 4x4 with monster tires? A racy red convertible? A comfy sport utility vehicle? Well, top-of-the-line transportation in the pioneer days of Kentucky was quite a bit different. Have you ever heard of Conestoga wagons? They were named after the Conestoga Valley in Pennsylvania, where they were first built. How high-tech were they? Well, they didn't have CD players, but they did have some cool features. For example, the ends were higher than the middle, so all 5,000 pounds of cargo stayed in the center without rolling around. It had a few tricks up its sleeve, too. For example, once the wheels were taken off, the wagon became a 25-foot flatboat, ready to hit the river. Talk about convertible! Settlers used Conestoga wagons from the 1770s clear up to the 1850s. That's a long time for one rig to stay so popular.

"Gee" - That's One Way to Turn!

Just because a settler had a fancy Conestoga wagon, that was no excuse for him to be lazy and ride in it himself. No way! The wagon was for the supplies, and maybe some of the women and children if they were lucky. Wagons were mostly pulled by horses or mules, but oxen were the best for long trips. (See the front page of this issue.) Ox teams had to be driven from the ground. The driver would stand to the left of the team and yell out commands. When he wanted the oxen to turn away from him, he yelled, "Gee!" When he wanted them to turn toward him, he yelled, "Haw!" Just imagine, in the early 1800s, the roads of Kentucky must have echoed with cries of "Gee!" and "Haw!" You've never heard that before? Gee! - or is it "Haw"?

Fabulous Flatboats

Maybe you read the article about Conestoga wagons and said to yourself, "A wagon that turns into a flatboat? Cool! Uh... wait a minute. What's a flatboat?" Well, are you ever in luck! We're gonna tell you right here. When it came to river travel, flatboats were everybody's favorite. A flatboat was a large, flat, rectangular barge, with a sort of square house in the center. The house served as a floating fort in case the boat was attacked. Around the house, there was enough space for a couple of families and all of their supplies, including their wagons. And here's something more: When the river journey of a pioneer family was over, the flatboat stayed useful. Many families took flatboats apart and used the lumber to build their cabins.

Frontier Roads

If someone in frontier Kentucky asked for directions, it might not have done any good to say, "To get where you're going, you just take the Cumberland." There were only about 10 big roads in the whole state, and three of them had the name "Cumberland" in them. The poor guy asking directions might not know what was being talked about: the Cumberland Gap, the Cumberland Trace or the Cumberland Trail. Those roads kept pretty busy, as far as frontier traffic was concerned. The Cumberland Gap was the gateway to the West for all sorts of folks - even folks who weren't headed for Kentucky. The Cumberland Trace and the Cumberland Trail both connected Nashborough, Tennessee, with important Kentucky settlements, like Lexington and Falls of the Ohio. And if traveling a dusty road made their feet tired, settlers might have taken one of the other major "roads": the Ohio River. The Ohio brought as many people to Kentucky as dirt roads did. Boy, Mother Nature is some road builder!

Steam Power Moves Ahead

The "Gees!" and "Haws!" of oxen drivers and the happy songs of flatboat drivers were joined by other transportation sounds in the early 1800s. The first new sound was on the water. It was the sound of steamboats, puffing up and down the rivers, carrying more people and more stuff more quickly and comfortably than ever before. A few years later, in 1831, another sound began to chug its way across America. Can you guess what it was? Here's a hint: The surprised natives gave it the nickname Iron Horse. Have you guessed what it is yet? If not, we still think you can, we think you can, we think you can, we think you can. That's right! It was the railroad! First the steamboat, then the railroad, started changing how people got around in our country, and things have been getting bigger and faster ever since.

title: Danny's Boat Ride
text: "Papa, look! Fire!" Danny yelled. His father turned from the rudder of the flatboat and looked where Danny was pointing. Sure enough, there, around a bend in the river, huge puffs of white smoke rose into the air. "We ought to be safe out here in the water," said Danny's father. "No blaze could jump this river!" But even as he said it, the puffing smoke seemed to be moving down river, toward the bend Danny's family was nearing on their boat. How could that be? Danny couldn't tell for sure, because as near as he could tell, the smoke was still around the corner. The fire seemed to be right in the middle of where the river ought to be! He didn't understand. "Papa, there's no flame. Do you see a flame?" His father was silent. Then they both gasped. Around the corner, the hull of an enormous boat pulled slowly into view. It looked like a big building, floating there on the water. They'd never seen anything like it! Two tall pipes stuck up high above the roof of the huge boat, and out of the pipes blew great clouds of what looked like white smoke. "Papa, it wasn't a fire at all!" shouted Danny. "Sure, Son. But what is it?" The boat pulled out into the river just ahead of them. On its decks, people walked up and down. Some of them waved. Danny's father pulled the rudder hard to port, panicked to get out of the way of the monster boat. Other flatboats on the river did the same, and soon, the huge new ship had pulled alongside them, and then past them, as people laughed and waved, and huge wheels on the boat's sides churned the water. Danny had expected to see all sorts of new and interesting things on this trip, but seeing a steamboat beat everything he had ever imagined. His father seemed to think so, too, for as his gaze followed the giant steamer, the flatboat came to rest with a jolt on a sandbar. Danny whirled his arms to get his balance and nearly toppled into the river. Danny's mother came from inside the cabin hollering, "What on Earth could be going on out here? How'd we run a ground? And look at you two! You look like you've seen a ghost!" Danny and his father would have answered Danny's mother, but when they looked at each other, all they could do was laugh out loud.

title: Louisville
text:
In 1778, the explorer George Rogers Clark led a group of pioneers from Pennsylvania down the Ohio River. Those brave folks established Louisville in 1779. Twenty years later, its population was a whopping 350. It quickly became an important river-front community, harboring everything from steam-driven riverboats to huge ocean-going vessels. But river ports were only part of Louisville's story. By 1830, the area was one of the world's top producers of tobacco, causing the population to boom. By the mid-1800s, Louisville's handful of inhabitants had grown to 43,000! Even the Civil War couldn't stop people from coming here. By the end of the war, the area was well on its way to doubling the population once again, with nearly 100,000 citizens.

In those days, even though Louisville served as a supply depot for Union troops, and pretty much cut off trade with the rest of the South, there were plenty of folks who had strong feelings on both sides. It just goes to show that Louisville has always been a place for folks to speak their minds. Even Mother Nature sometimes has a say in things. In 1937, the Ohio River flooded the city. Since then, a big flood wall has protected the city, and Mother Nature has pretty much held her peace on the subject.

title: What happens when someone owns part of the land where the government wants to build a road?
text: Sometimes the government decides on a location for a road, railroad, bridge or dam that runs right across someone's private property. If that's ever the case, the government is allowed to take possession of the private property in order to use it for the public good. But they can't just up and take it without asking. The government must pay the owner "fair market price" for the land that it takes. That means that the government must pay the landowner whatever the land is worth. The law that gives the government the right to take private land for public use is called "eminent domain." It's a law that has been used repeatedly since the early days of Kentucky to make room for one transportation project or another. Folks who will travel those roads are usually happy about the law. Landowners who have to surrender their land sometimes aren't!

title: Gray Fox
text: The gray fox grows to be about 45 inches long. It has a grizzle-colored body and a black stripe down its tail. It is a nocturnal hunter in open forests and shrubby regions throughout most of the United States (not in the northwest quadrant) and Mexico. The gray fox is a member of the dog family and can even climb trees! It's a fast runner and can reach speeds of up to 28 mph. Female foxes have from two to seven babies in a litter in the spring. The babies are born blind and stay that way for about 10 days. The fox family stays together until winter, and then each go their separate ways. Foxes are usually solitary, or alone, during the winter months. They come back together to mate in the spring.
