title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you and your family are moving to Kentucky from Pennsylvania. It’s going to be a long walk alongside the Conestoga wagon that your dad just bought. He even decided to use oxen instead of horses to pull the wagon. You’ve never driven an ox before, but you think you’ll be able to learn quickly. Tell us about your journey. Do you miss your friends? How long does it take? When you arrive in Kentucky, do you buy a home, or do you have to build a cabin? Write about your adventure in 200 or fewer words.

title: Dividing the Land
text:
Land, land, land! You can walk on it, plant gardens on it, lie on it, wiggle your toes in it, climb up and down it, build a home on it, dig for gold in it, build a road on it and look for worms in it. In fact, this issue of Kentucky Studies Weekly is all about it!

We're going to look at how people divided the land in the years following the American Revolution. How did they decide which piece of land belonged to one person and which piece belonged to another? Did they get it for free? Where did towns begin and end? These are all good questions, and though we'd like to give you some good answers, it's a problem that Kentucky had a tough time dealing with. Rules about land and how to own it kept changing. In the beginning, folks could just go to a place, clear a few acres and build a cabin, and no one would bug them. Those people, who didn't have any legal claim to the land but who had lived on it for years became known as squatters. Later, as folks kept coming to the frontier, things had to get more organized. In 1776, the government divided the land like a pepperoni pizza. Anyone who had raised a corn crop in Kentucky was entitled to a 400-acre slice.

That's the size of a small town! By 1779, the rule had changed, and people who raised crops on Kentucky land could buy up to 400 acres at $2.25 an acre. Once they bought 400 acres, another $40 would get them 100 more acres if they wanted it. That's enough to make you rethink how you spend your allowance, isn't it? Go ahead, turn the page and "land" yourself a bunch of information on dirt, grass, creeks, roads, canyons and rocks and learn how people got a piece of it in the late 1700s.

title: Kentucky Land Problems
text:
Between outlaws in the Gap, government requirements and surveyor mistakes, some Kentuckians had a tough time owning a chunk of the Bluegrass State.

Fights Over No- Man's Land

No rule is perfect, and the rules for people obtaining land in Kentucky were certainly no exception! There were fights between neighbors that lasted generations because each side claimed to own the same land. You can bet that each neighbor had an accurate survey showing that the land was really his. In addition to the fights over claims of land that overlapped one another, the government was so eager to provide land warrants to so many new settlers who wanted them that it made a little mistake. No big deal, really, but if you add up all the land of the warrants issued in those days, you'd find that there were warrants issued for more land than Kentucky actually had. Oops!

Beware: Outlaws in the Gap

In the 1780s and 1790s, more people than ever were coming to live in Kentucky. They were pouring in through the Cumberland Gap by the wagon load, and they were floating in on the Ohio River. As the number of settlers grew, so did the number of greedy outlaws who were lying in wait for travelers to come by. The Cumberland Gap, because it was so narrow and there was no place to run, was especially handy for outlaws who wanted to ambush a wagon or two. Most people tried to travel in large groups, but some were still unlucky. The strange and frightening outlaw attacks didn't do much to stop the settlers from coming, but most settlers could have done without the added adventure of robbers on the trail.

Surveying Work: Better Nowadays

The days of deciding where one person's land ends and another person's land begins haven't ended. Even today, surveyors are very useful, and surveying is pretty exact work. Surveyors are well-trained, and they even use high-tech equipment to help them know exactly where to draw the lines. Surveyors in the 1780s weren't so lucky. They didn't have much experience. In fact, some of them couldn't even read or do math, and some were downright dishonest. Besides that, it was hard to say that someone's land ran from a certain tree to a certain bend in a stream when trees and streams had a way of looking the same or even changing. In the end, even after the surveys, people fought all the time over where the land boundaries were. Two famous examples are Daniel Boone and Simon Kenton. There's no question that they settled, worked, farmed and explored all kinds of land in these parts, but in the end, they lost all the acres they'd claimed because of sneaky surveyor mistakes.

Northwest Ordinance: Magic Numbers

All the time that Kentucky (which was then a county in Virginia called Fincastle) was trying to make room for new settlers, the United States was working hard on projects that would eventually make Kentucky a state. The biggest was called the Northwest Ordinance. It included the steps a territory had to follow to become a state. It was mostly created for land to the north of us, but it became the model for most states, even in the South. The Northwest Ordinance was full of magic numbers. Magic numbers? Sure! Let's explain: The first magic number was 5,000. When there were finally 5,000 free adult men in an area, something magical happened. Tah-dah! The area became an official U.S. territory, and they got to send a delegate (or someone to represent and speak for the territory) to Congress. Another magic number was 60,000. Once the population of a territory reached 60,000, the people could ask the U.S. government to make them a state.

Four Little Steps for Owning Kentucky Land

So many settlers were showing up in Kentucky every day that the government started making rules about obtaining land around here. Does that surprise you? In the end, they wound up creating four steps for anyone who wanted land. First, folks had to get a land warrant, or a piece of paper from the government that said that it was OK for them to get some land. Second, they had to give the government written details about where the land was and how much of it they wanted. Third, the government had to send a surveyor to the property to check it out officially. The surveyor would make notes and draw a map called a plat. Fourth, the surveyor's notes and the plat would have to be turned in at the nearest land office. After all that, you'd think people would have been too worn out to build a home or plow a field!

title: David Bushnell and the Turtle
text:
A submarine was used in the American Revolution? Absolutely. David Bushnell, American patriot and inventor, used reason and logic to build the first military submarine.

David Bushnell was born on a farm in Connecticut in 1740. He experimented with underwater explosives during college and built a submarine that would carry them. Bushnell's vessel was nicknamed "the Turtle" because it was shaped like two wooden turtle shells joined together, standing on end. Its hull filled with water to submerge and was pumped out by the operator to rise. Two propellers and a rudder were used to guide it.

Benjamin Franklin and others were impressed with Bushnell's invention. When British warships blockaded New York Harbor in 1776, the Turtle was called into action. The submarine operator was supposed to use a giant screw to attach the powder keg (called a mine) to the bottom of the British flagship, the HMS Eagle.

The plan seemed like a failure when the mine could not be fastened to the ship. However, the gunpowder made a frightening explosion underwater. The British quickly moved their warships from the area. Although it didn't work as planned, Bushnell's invention did have an effect on the British navy.

Bushnell then turned his skills to improving underwater mines. These were placed in harbors to protect American rivers and forts. General George Washington was pleased with Bushnell's work and gave him a commission (job) in the Army.

Today David Bushnell is given credit for inventing the first military submarine and for making valuable contributions to the American Revolution. You can visit a replica (an accurate model) of the Turtle in the Connecticut River Museum in Essex, Connecticut. By yourself or with a partner, think of a person who has used reason and logic to develop something that helped America.

title: Obedience
text:
You know what obedience means. It simply means obeying the rules or laws, and it's a very important character trait to have. Here's a basic example of when you should be obedient: Look both ways before you cross the street. Everyone wants to be safe around cars in the street. That's a great benefit for keeping such a basic rule. Some rules are harder to keep than others, but most rules have a built-in benefit for obeying them.

Can you think of some other benefits of being obedient? What's the benefit of keeping the homework rule or of listening to your teachers? Great grades and all the rewards that come with them!

Did you know that you can choose whether to obey the rules, but you cannot choose the consequences? That's right; if you keep a rule, whether you like it or not, you get to enjoy the benefits. Of course, that goes the other way, too. If you choose not to obey, then you must accept going without the benefits. Often there's a penalty for not obeying the rules, like not being able to play with your friends because you didn't finish your chores. Can you think of other examples of benefits or penalties that come from obeying or disobeying rules?

title: Why don't many people own hundreds of acres in Kentucky anymore?
text: It's true that the average Kentuckian doesn't own quite as much land as Kentucky's early settlers seemed to. There are probably some good reasons for that. For example, in the early days of Kentucky, a person had to grow much of the food he ate, which meant he needed ground to grow it on. Also, much of the business done in Kentucky dealt with products that people could grow themselves and then trade for other things that they needed. Owning an abundance of land was important to a person whose income depended on growing a crop. But that was then. Nowadays, most people don't need that much land. Food is available to most people without the need to grow it for themselves. Many different kinds of jobs don't require growing things out of the ground or owning land to hunt on. In some areas, there are so many people that owning lots and lots of land simply isn't practical. It's just one way that the face of Kentucky has changed over its many years of being our home!

title: The Bald Eagle
text:
Everyone has heard of the bald eagle, and we're sure you know that the bald eagle is our national bird. But, did you know that the government removed our majestic feathered friend from the endangered and threatened species list in 2007? It's true. Years and years of special protection have helped the bald eagle recover from a low of 417 nesting pairs in 1963 to 5,748 nesting pairs in 1999.

This amazing recovery is further proof of what we can do to improve our environment when we all work together and support wildlife protection laws.

Bruce Babbitt, secretary of the U.S. Interior, said, "Generations to come will not just see bald eagles on our coins, stamps and flagpoles; they will be able to look up in the sky and see our national symbol flying overhead."

Female bald eagles can grow to a wingspan of 8 feet. (Males are a little smaller.) They stay with the same mate their whole lives and build gigantic nests that can reach up to 20 feet across and weigh 4,000 pounds.

title: Let's Write
text: What would it have been like on the wagon trail through the Cumberland Gap in the 1780s? What would life have been like for an American Indian living near the Cumberland Gap in the 1780s?

title: Cumberland Settlements
text:
Life on the frontier was not easy. People came to the area because they wanted land for their families. While most of the land belonged to the Cherokee, Creek and Chickasaw, white settlers believed they had rights to the land as well. Many settlers traveled over the Cumberland Gap, which is a rough and steep pathway through the lower section of the Appalachian Mountains where Tennessee, Kentucky and Virginia meet. There were no roads, so new paths had to be cleared. Most traveled by horseback or on foot. Wagons were used to carry supplies. When possible, men would lead women and children by boat because it was a faster, safer and easier way to travel.

As more people settled on the frontier, trading businesses began to boom. Trade goods were moved down the Cumberland, Tennessee and Ohio rivers. After selling their products, merchants returned home on the Natchez Trace, a path that linked the Cumberland, Tennessee and Mississippi rivers. Merchants would sell things like corn, whiskey, tobacco and furs.

When families found a location they liked, they would clear the land of trees to make room for cabins and crops. The trees were then used to build log cabins. Spaces between the logs were filled in with mud or clay, called chinking. During the summer months, settlers would knock out the mud to allow for more airflow into the cabin.

Men and women lived very different lives. Men spent their time farming and hunting for food, while women took care of the home. Women spent many hours preparing food, sewing clothing and making soap. Music was an important form of entertainment for those living on the frontier. They sang hymns, played the fiddle and danced. Settlers also enjoyed telling tall tales. Education was important on the frontier as well, but it took time to build schools. Most children were taught to read and write at home before formal schools were opened.

title: Kentucky Hero: Mary Willie Arvin
text:
Mary Willie Arvin was born on April 21, 1879, in Henderson Kentucky. She became a nurse in 1904 and began working in Memphis, Tennessee. In June 1917 she and her unit of nurses were deployed to Pas-de-Calais, France, to aid the wounded from the first world war. She was such a dedicated and skilled nurse that she kept working to heal and calm the soldiers under her care even when the hospital she was working in was being bombed. General John Pershing wrote the following about one of those nights,

"My Dear Miss Arvin: Please accept my heartiest congratulations and sincere appreciation of the fine work you did on the night of June 30, 1918, when your hospital was a target of German airplane bombs. Your presence of mind and courage in quieting your patients was, under the circumstances, deserving of the highest praise. I am proud to have in the American Expeditionary Forces a nurse whose devotion to duty is of such high character as yours."

After the end of the war, Mary received medals from all three major allied countries, France, Great Britain and the United States. She was one of the first women to be awarded a purple heart. What a brave Kentucky hero!

title: Kentucky Becomes a State
text: It's tough to get two people to always agree on things. You may want to watch cartoons, and your big sister may want to watch the basketball game. You may want to eat dessert first, but Mom has other plans. If you increase the number of people in a house, sometimes it gets even trickier. Increase the number of people in an entire town, and it gets harder for everyone to agree on things. And let's not even think about a whole state's worth of people. Of course, a state's worth of people was just what Kentucky was in the 1780s and 1790s. We say "a state's worth of people," and not a "state," because, even though people were pouring in every day, Kentucky was still just a county in Virginia. Back then, many Kentuckians thought Virginians didn't care about what happened to Kentucky. Whenever Kentuckians had a big problem, they thought the Virginia government didn't even hear them or chose to ignore them. Have you ever been halfway through explaining something or telling a story to someone and realized he or she wasn't even listening? Well, that's how the leaders in Kentucky felt sometimes at government meetings in Virginia. Would we ever become a state? That might be pretty suspenseful stuff if you didn't already know how the story turned out. After all, are you living in the territory of Kentucky today? So it all worked out in the end, but what happened in the middle? We're glad you asked! In this issue of Kentucky Studies Weekly, you'll find some answers to that question. You'll be introduced to the years where Kentucky was part of Virginia. You'll know what the rules were, who wound up in charge of our baby state and more. Go ahead! Time is ticking by, and no one's getting any younger. Besides, the wait is over. Kentucky has now been a state for more than 200 years. That's why they call this history.

title: A "Capitol" Idea
text:
What's part French, part American, all Kentuckian and cost almost $2 million when it was built in 1910? That would be the Kentucky state capitol building. It was designed by a guy named Frank Mills Andrews, and he got so carried away with the project that his design was way too big for the space where they'd planned to put it. Luckily, there was a big old patch of ground in southern Frankfort that was just crying out for a capitol building to be built on it. And the state was glad to oblige. Kentucky had already been a state for more than 100 years, but it's never too late for a terrific capitol building, right?

Today, you can visit the place, and you might notice an interesting thing or two. The dome above the rotunda (the big, open place in the center of the building) is patterned after the dome in Napoleon's tomb in Paris, France. Below it, check out all the cool statues of famous Kentuckians. You'll probably recognize the guy in the middle. It's a statue of Abraham Lincoln, maybe the most famous Smart Kentuckian of them all.

The capitol building is open for tours every day until 4:30 p.m., but you may want to call first for a reservation. The phone number is (502) 564-3449.

title: Kentucky Statehood
text:
Waiting for Statehood

Kentucky didn't become a state until 1792, but people were thinking about it for a long time before then. Kentucky hero George Rogers Clark thought about it in 1776. Maybe ideas about independence from England got him thinking about independence from Virginia as well. Four years later, in 1780, more than 600 people who lived in Kentucky and Illinois signed a petition (formal request) asking the government to make a state along the Ohio Valley. But as much as they talked and thought about it, the time just wasn't right. Kentucky statehood had to wait just a few years longer.

Virginia's Too Far Away to Care

Why on Earth would Kentucky want to separate from Virginia, anyway? Virginia is full of nice folks, isn't it? Sure it is, but there was a problem with them running the show: They all lived so far away. Virginians concentrated on stuff that happened on the east side, but Kentuckians thought the Virginia government pretty much shrugged their shoulders at things that happened on the west side. For example, there was no problem with native warfare in the east, so the problem got ignored in the west. Virginia even forgot to deliver the mail to Kentucky. Sometimes laws got passed for Kentuckians to follow months before people in Kentucky ever found out about them. When the Spanish closed the Mississippi River to American boats (the main way for Kentucky products to get out and about), Virginia didn't lift a finger. Some people even compared Kentucky's complaints against Virginia to America's complaints against Great Britain.

Sharing the Same Raft

Have you ever thought about how much fun it would be to float down a big river on a homemade raft? Maybe you've seen a movie or heard stories about the adventures of Huck Finn, Tom Sawyer and their friend, Jim, as they floated down the Mississippi River. Or maybe the thought of being on a rickety old raft scares you. But what does floating down the river have to do with Kentucky becoming a state? Now that's a good question. And here's the answer: You see, before Kentucky became a state, it was like Kentucky and Virginia were both floating on the same raft, and the government of Virginia was in charge of steering. If there was a problem, they'd steer around it or something. Now let's pretend that you're with some friends going down the river, and they're always wanting to make stops where you don't want to stop. What would you do? Well, if the raft was big enough, you could split it up and make two rafts. And that's just what Kentucky did with Virginia, and we've been fine ever since.

After Nine Tries: The Virginia Compact

In the government, when folks want to get something big done, you can bet they'll call a meeting to talk it over first. When Kentucky began to talk about becoming its own state, they called a series of huge government meetings, called conventions, between 1784 and 1792 to work out the details. It took 10 conventions before Kentucky finally became a state! Finally, after nine of the 10 conventions and after six years of arguments, the time looked right for Kentucky's big separation. But there were certain things everyone had to agree on. Those things were all listed in a 1789 document called the Virginia Compact. Here were some of the things agreed on in the document: (1) Virginia would be released from all responsibility for Kentucky; (2) Kentucky would take responsibility for the cost of its American Indian wars; (3) Former land grants made by Virginia in Kentucky would still be good, and no one could kick those folks off their land; (4) A group of six men would settle any arguments that might arise over the rest of the things mentioned in the agreement. All in favor? There, now, that wasn't so bad, was it? They were finally on their way to statehood!

Kentucky: The 15th State

The big day turned out to be June 1, 1792. On that day, Kentucky became the 15th state in the grand old United States of America. The folks here had a lot of work ahead of them, but one of their first jobs was to elect a governor. They chose a man named Isaac Shelby. Shelby was a hero in the Revolutionary War. He won a battle against British General Patrick Ferguson at a place called King's Mountain. Some say that it was a big turning point for the South in the revolution. He was actually more interested in farming than in politics, but he was a man everyone admired because of his sound judgment and integrity. He had a sense of duty that just wouldn't quit, and maybe most importantly, he had the love and confidence of the people around him. Some people even compared him to George Washington.

title: The First Governor
text:
Governor Isaac Shelby sat thinking to himself. He had only a moment to think, and it would probably be the last moment he had all to himself for a long time. Even this moment wasn't ideal for thinking. The cheers and applause coming from just beyond the doors crowded his thoughts. Still, his mind was rolling images through his head like cannonballs. He thought about the Revolutionary War and how it had opened this new door for Kentucky and Kentuckians. He thought about King's Mountain. On that day, he hadn't felt grand at all, just desperate as he rode into British fire with the smell of blood and gunpowder in his nose.

Come to think of it, he didn't feel all that grand today, either. But Kentucky was a state now, and he was its governor.

Could he do it? Did he have enough experience? "It's the whole state of Kentucky," he said quietly to himself. "The whole darned thing. How can I judge wisely in such a place? Do I have the experience? Do I have the brain power?" He laughed and shook his head. "Probably not," he thought. Suddenly, the doors of the room opened, and the light and noise from beyond the doors was nearly blinding. "It must be time," he thought. "Now begins a journey for me and my state. There's no turning back now." The young man who had opened the doors spoke bashfully. "Governor Shelby," he said, "they're ready for you, sir." A sheepish grin half-appeared on the young man's face. "Of course, you can probably hear them without me saying so," he said, as he looked at the floor. Governor Shelby was silent for a moment more, and then he stood up. "Yes, of course," he said, "and why don't you and I face the new state together, shall we?" He placed a hand on the young man's shoulder. "We're both of the same sort, you and I," said the governor. "How so?" asked the youth. Governor Shelby looked beyond the doors and into the room of applauding people, and then he looked back at the young man. "Servants, both," he answered. Then he turned and, with the doorman, walked out to face the room full of Kentuckians as their governor.

title: Louisville
text:
Louisville has seemed to just grow and grow and GROW over the last couple hundred years. Well, we're here this week to tell you that it hasn't stopped. Today, the city covers about 65 square miles, which include almost five square miles of pure water. The heart of Louisville is in Jefferson County; in fact, Louisville is the county seat. But Louisville itself is the center of a huge metropolitan area (metropolitan means part of a big city) that stretches into Bullitt and Oldham counties and even into Clark, Floyd, Harrison and Scott counties in Indiana. Louisville can't be held back by anything as flimsy as a state line. Still, when people talk about downtown Louisville, they're talking about an area of a single mile square snugged right against the Ohio River, where most of the shops and businesses are.

The hard-working spirit that founded this terrific area hasn't died, either. The biggest employer in the area is UPS, hard at work with more than 16,000 people, getting important packages here and there. The Ford Motor Company also has a factory in the area. That's serious business!

People around here take their fun pretty seriously, too. The Kentucky Derby, one of the most famous horse races in the world, provides big fun for more than 100,000 visitors every year on the first Saturday in May - a tradition that's been around for more than 120 years.

title: Have the laws that govern Kentucky always been the same?
text: The laws that govern Kentucky have changed as the needs of the people have changed. Advances in business, technology, education, transportation and communication have required the modification of Kentucky law every once in awhile. The constitution of our state has changed a few times over the years. New Kentucky constitutions were adopted in 1792, 1799, and 1850. That's a new constitution every few years. But oddly enough, the constitution adopted by the state legislature in 1850 is the one we still have today. It must have been a good one, to stick around so long!

title: Wood Duck
text: One of the most beautiful birds in Kentucky is the wood duck. The wood duck is extremely colorful. The adult male has a pure white throat and foreneck, but his head is metallic green, violet and purple with two white stripes. The chest is a rich purplish chestnut. Its flanks are buff and its back a bronze green, metallic maroon, purple and blue. The female is somewhat less spectacular than the male. Areas around her bill, throat and eyes are white. The remainder of the head is gray with a crown and crest of metallic green. Her underside is white. These beautiful birds migrate in October to the Gulf of Mexico. They look for food in flooded timberland, swamps and occasionally open water. They feed by pecking on the surface of water. The male, or drake, protects his female and nest from other drakes. The female lays an average of 12 eggs. The drake must be on watch for raccoons, snakes and squirrels that like to eat duck eggs. The female cares for the young for five to six weeks. A female will accept younger displaced ducks into her brood.

title: Word Searching Fun!
text: One of this week’s vocabulary words is missing. See if you can find the rest of them after doing the crossword puzzle. Good luck!

title: Let's Write
text: Explain why state constitutions are changed every once in a while.

title: Kentucky and the War of 1812
text: Have you ever had a week with so many problems you couldn't see straight? If problems came one at a time, you could probably handle them like a pro. But as you probably know, problems sometimes come two or three or 12 or 25 at a time. How rude, eh? The first 15 years or so of the 1800s were a little like that. The United States was just a baby country back then, and you'd think the world would slow down long enough to let it get on its feet, wouldn't you? But, oh, no! There were problems to the left and problems to the right, right from the beginning. Here's an example or two: Way off in Europe, France and England were battling like cats and dogs. America didn't care who won those wars, but we did want to keep doing business with France. England didn't like that, of course, and attacked American ships on the way to Europe. Also, some adventurous American settlers wanted to stretch out into Canada on land owned by the British. Do you think that sat well with America's old enemy? It all led to another war between America and Britain, which was called the War of 1812. One thing's for sure: Kentucky has never been a state that lets little problems walk all over it. How did the war go in these parts? Well, it didn't really. Not a single battle was fought on Kentucky soil. So why would we include the War of 1812 in Kentucky Studies Weekly? Now you're asking our kind of question. Some of the answers are right here in this issue. So what are you waiting for? Let's go!

title: Jimmy Driftwood
text:
Have you ever heard of a high school history teacher named Jimmy Driftwood? He died on July 12, 1998, near Fayetteville, Arkansas. He was 91 years old and had lived a life just about as rich as Andrew Jackson's. Speaking of Andrew Jackson, why would we bring up a high school teacher from Arkansas in a Kentucky Studies Weekly issue?

Here's why: Mr. Driftwood (also known as James Morris) liked to write songs to help his students understand history better. One of these songs was liked by so many people that it was recorded by a singer named Johnny Horton in 1959. It was later voted one of the most loved songs in America. Who do you think the song was about? If you guessed Andrew Jackson, maybe you've heard the song before. Here's the chorus of Jimmy Driftwood's song "The Battle of New Orleans."

We fired our guns, and the British kept a coming. There wasn't nigh as many as there was a while ago. We fired once more, and they began to running, down the Mississippi to the Gulf of Mexico!

After Mr. Driftwood stopped teaching school, he spent the rest of his life sharing the music and stories of his mountain home with anyone who would listen. People all over the country remember and love his music and stories. For more information about Jimmy Driftwood, you can call the Jimmy Driftwood Barn and Folklore Hall of Fame at (870) 269- 8042.

title: The War of 1812
text:
Most soldiers who died in the war were from Kentucky.

War Hawks

The New England states were hesitant to go to war with England. They feared that their shipping trade would be completely shut down. But in the South, there were lots of folks who really wanted to go to war. They were tired of fighting native tribes that were armed with British guns. The leaders of those who wanted to go to war formed a powerful group in Congress called War Hawks. The top guys of that group included Kentucky's own Henry Clay. In those days, Clay was the speaker of the House of Representatives. His job put him in a good position to influence the government's top officials even the guy running for president of the United States, James Madison. Soon, with Madison in the White House, the War Hawks and the states they represented were demanding that President Madison declare war.

Score: British 1, United States zero

When America first entered the War of 1812, it had a brilliant plan: It would put troops in Canada and take over Great Britain's land there. America would then use their newly captured land to make deals with their British enemies. It was a great plan, too, but we'll never know how it would have gone because it never happened. Right from the beginning, the plan went haywire. They put a general named William Hull in charge of Detriot, one of the key positions in the plan. Hull was getting old, and he was also a little timid. Before anyone knew it, this key position that he was supposed to guard was in the hands of the British. Hey, that wasn't part of the plan! Any hopes of a quick victory faded right away, and much of the rest of the war was spent trying to get Detroit back.

Remember the Raisin!

Trying to get Detroit back under American control wasn't as easy as everyone thought it would be. First, we had to get there! The Army sent to do the job was commanded by a guy named William Henry Harrison (who later became president). Along the way, they tried to capture enemy supplies at a place called Frenchtown on the Raisin River. Instead, on Jan. 22, 1813, Harrison's 1,300 Kentucky soldiers found themselves outnumbered and outgunned by enemy Canadians and American Indians. They fought bravely, but by the end of the day, more than 400 Kentuckians were dead. Some of them were killed during the battle, but some, who had been wounded or taken prisoner, were slaughtered by natives after the battle was over. It was a tragic day, and from it came a Kentucky war cry that was heard during the rest of the war: "Remember the Raisin!"

The Battle of New Orleans

Jimmy Driftwood's folk song was written about the Battle of New Orleans. It was fought just a stone's throw away from Kentucky on the Mississippi River outside of New Orleans. It was Jan. 8, 1815, and General Andrew Jackson had heard that 7,500 British soldiers were coming through the swamps toward New Orleans, and he wanted to be ready. Sure, his 6,500 soldiers were outnumbered by 1,000 or more, but Jackson was pretty sure his frontier boys could take 'em. And he was right! Jackson's army chased those British soldiers out of New Orleans for good, and they did it in just a half hour. It was the last battle of the War of 1812, and it might not have been fought at all if someone had let Jackson know that the peace treaty had already been signed a couple of weeks earlier. Driftwood originally wrote about 300 verses to the song. Luckily, it was shortened!

Kentucky Troops Half Armed

The most famous battle of the War of 1812, the Battle of New Orleans, was a battle that probably should never have been fought. Some people called it the needless battle because it was fought after England had already signed the peace treaty that ended the war. Still, the battle of New Orleans made Andrew Jackson famous, and it made the hills of America ring with confidence in their brave soldiers. Between 400 and 500 Kentuckians fought in that battle, but our state legislature didn't have enough money to send weapons along with them. When they showed up, General Jackson was amazed at the poor condition of the Kentucky troops. He had his men hunt up as many guns as they could, but when they went into battle on Jan. 8, 1815, only about half of them were armed. Even so, at the end of the day, the Americans were victorious.

Kentucky Bleeds the Most in the War of 1812

Some people say the War of 1812 was nothing but a big misunderstanding. Many of its battles would have been avoided if only there had been better communication between the nations. Most people agree, though, that things weren't much different after the war than they were before. So what did America gain from the war? That's a good question, and the answer may surprise you. Mainly, what the United States gained from the war was confidence and unity. Kentucky soldiers, for example, gained a reputation all over the nation. People everywhere knew how dedicated Kentucky was to the USA. Though our state was never invaded, Kentucky sent 25,705 men to the conflict. The war cost America 1,876 lives, and 1,200 of them were from Kentucky.

title: Holiday Pop-up Card
text:
Materials

construction paper

scissors

crayons/markers

pencils

glue

writing paper

Directions

1. Fold a sheet of construction paper in half.

2. Make a tab by cutting two slits on the fold, in the middle of the paper, 1 inch apart. (See picture.)

3. Push the tab through to the inside.

4. Draw, color and cut out an object that will not extend beyond the page when it is folded in half (a small heart, for example).

5. Glue the object to the tab. Allow the glue to dry before proceeding.

6. Decorate your card and write someone a special message.

Extra Activity: You can use this technique to create a pop-up book about history. Have each student create a pop-up page from something in Studies Weekly. Put it together chronologically or by themes and see the scenes of history come to life.

title: Self-Discipline
text: Self-discipline is probably one of the hardest character traits to achieve. Do you know what it means to have self-discipline? Well, since it has the word self in it, you know that it has to do with something you do yourself. No one can have self-discipline for you. Self-discipline is being able to control your thoughts and actions in a way that helps you be a better person. It means that you'll have the control to do your homework even when your friends come and ask you to play a great game of ball outside. It means you'll go to bed on time even though there's a movie on that you really wanted to watch. Or it's when you've had three chocolate frogs already, but there are still a couple left. You'll have the strength to say, "I've had enough tonight. I'll save those for later." You need self-discipline in just about everything you do, including eating, sleeping, going to school and being at home - you name it! It's a great thing to have. By having it, you'll keep yourself healthy and strong, and you'll always do what's best for you in the end. Self-discipline is just one of the many character traits that make people in our state what they are today - a great bunch of people!

title: What does it mean when someone says a sailor was impressed?
text: To fight the war with France that led to the War of 1812, the British Navy was always in need of good sailors. In fact, they were suffering from a very severe shortage of seamen because many of their naval sailors had deserted the Navy to find work on American ships. To respond to the crisis, British ships claimed the right to stop ships on the open sea, search them for British-born crew, and then impress (or force) them back into British service. The United States was outraged to learn that even American citizens were often impressed into service in the British Navy. The British claimed that any instance of the impressment of American-born sailors was strictly a mistake, but the Americans weren't so sure. One thing's certain - the impressment of sailors didn't seem too neighborly, especially to the sailors being impressed.

title: River Otter
text:
River otters seem to have a childlike sense of fun and play. They'll slide down a muddy or snowy riverbank nose first with their arms at their sides. Then out they climb back to the top and do it again - over and over. Young otters have been seen chasing one another in the water or tackling each other on shore.

River otters have an amazing ability to hear. This is handy in case of danger. But they are actually at the top of their food chain and have no natural predators except people who hunt them for their fur. Because of this, otters have greatly dwindled in numbers over the years. Otters live in small, slow-moving rivers, wetlands or lakes.

Otters can hold their breath for up to six minutes and have been known to swim up to 1/4 mile underwater. If they're swimming under ice, they even know how to breathe from bubbles and trapped air. They're also deep swimmers at times. One otter was found swimming at a depth of 60 feet!

Otters can live up to about 15 years.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you were with Colonel Jackson on your way to fight the British in 1814. Describe what it was like to go to battle for the first time. Were you scared? Could you see the British soldiers marching toward you? How did they approach the battlefield? How did your regiment approach the battlefield? Did your regiment really hide until the very last second, like Driftwood’s song says? Were you injured in the battle? Were any of your fellow soldiers killed? Write a 200-word battlefield report!

title: Lucretia Hart Clay
text:
Lucretia Hart Clay is a prominent historical figure in Kentucky history. She is well known because of her roles as a wealthy heiress from a prominent family, as wife to Henry Clay, as mother of 11 children, as a local businesswoman and as the manager and hostess of Ashland, her home. She was born on March 18, 1781, in Hagerstown, Maryland to Colonel Thomas and Susanna (Gray) Hart. In 1784, Lucretia moved with her family to Kentucky and settled in Lexington. Lucretia and Henry married after a brief courtship on April 11, 1799.

Lucretia’s husband, Henry Clay, was a lawyer, congressman, senator, and secretary of state. He even ran for president, though he didn’t get elected. Because of Henry’s role in government, he spent many months away from Ashland and the management of their property fell to Lucretia, who operated it competently. In fact, under Lucretia’s management, Ashland became a social center where people wanted to visit. Lucretia and Henry entertained many prominent guests of the time at Ashland, such as Jefferson Davis, William Henry Harrison, Martin Van Buren, Daniel Webster, Mary Todd and possibly Abraham Lincoln. Lucretia even received guests such as Marquis de Lafayette, French general in the American Revolutionary War, in her husband’s absence on his behalf.

Henry and Lucretia Clay may have had different public roles in life, but they had similar traits. She was known for her generosity and kindness by the different accounts of people who stayed at Ashland, and Henry was nicknamed the “Great Compromiser” and the “Great Pacificator” for his ability to negotiate peace. While Henry Clay was one of the War Hawks who helped to embroil the U.S. in the War of 1812, he was also one of the men who negotiated for peace. In fact, he signed the Treaty of Ghent in Ghent, Belgium, on December 24, 1814, bringing the war to an end.

During Lucretia’s life, she knew joy and sorrow. While she was the mother of 11 children, five sons and six daughters, at the end of her life, she had only four. Lucretia died on April 7, 1864, at the age of 83 and was buried in Lexington, Kentucky.

title: Slavery in the South
text:
Slavery Outlawed in the North

One of the first anti-slavery movements was started by the Quakers in Pennsylvania before the American Revolution. In those days, most people in both the South and the North accepted the principle of slavery as a normal part of society. But when America won its freedom from England and became the land of the free, more and more people began to wonder why slavery still existed here. In 1777, the state of Vermont became the first state to make slavery against the law. Twenty-seven years later, in 1804, New Jersey became the last Northern state to outlaw slavery.

Missouri Compromise Keeps States Balanced

In 1803, the United States bought lots of land from France in a deal called the Louisiana Purchase. There was enough land for dozens of new states. But the question on everyone's lips in Kentucky and around the country was, "would the new states allow slavery?" It was an important question. There had always been the same number of states that allowed slavery as there were of states that didn't. Both sides wanted to keep it that way. In the end, they decided that states would only be allowed into the Union in pairs: one slave state with one free state. That would keep things equal. Today, we call that deal the Missouri Compromise because it was made when Missouri wanted to become a state.

Newspapers and Books Fight Against Slavery

In the 1800s, if you were one who thought slavery should be ended, people might call you an abolitionist. That name comes from the word abolish, which means "to put an end to." Starting in 1820, a man named Elihu Embree from Tennessee published a monthly paper called The Emancipator. There's another interesting word. It comes from emancipate, a word that means "to make free from slavery." Good name for an abolitionist newspaper, wouldn't you say? You might say that an abolitionist was someone in favor of emancipation, two great big words that dealt with one great big issue. Another famous newspaper of its time was called the North Star. It was published in New York by a man named Frederick Douglass, an African American who escaped slavery. Soon, abolitionists were getting the anti-slavery message out all over the South. The most famous anti-slavery publication wasn't a newspaper at all. It was a book named "Uncle Tom's Cabin" written by Harriet Beecher Stowe in 1852. More than 10,000 copies were sold in the first few days and more than 300,000 in the first year. The book made quite an impact.

The Underground Railroad

Imagine you're enslaved in the old South and you've decided to run away. How will you do it? Do you know the way? Where will you find food and shelter along the way? There weren't any hotels leaving the light on for folks back then. But there were other places throughout the South where people helped enslaved people escape to the North on what was called the Underground Railroad. It wasn't actually a railroad at all, but the nickname for a whole system of safe houses and secret routes that African Americans could use to escape slavery.

The most famous person to ride the Underground Railroad, and then help others do the same, was a woman named Harriet Tubman. After escaping slavery herself, Harriet risked her life 17 times on missions to free other enslaved people in the South. In the end, she helped more than 300 people escape slavery, including her parents.

Even people who escaped to Northern states like Ohio or Pennsylvania still weren't safe from slavery. You see, Congress passed a law in 1850 called the Fugitive Slave Act. Basically, it said that slave owners could hunt for runaways all over the country, even in the North. Most agents on the underground railroad tried to explain to runaways that even the North was a risky place to stay. They explained that if the enslaved people wanted real freedom, they'd have to go farther North all the way to Canada.

Kentucky Union Loyalty

When Abraham Lincoln was elected in 1860, some thought all the Southern states should leave the United States and form their own country. Within six weeks, seven of the Southern states decided to do just that. How about Kentucky? Did we jump on the bandwagon with the rest of our Southern neighbors? Not quite. Kentucky's governor, a guy named Beriah Magoffin, believed in states' rights to hold enslaved people and even to secede from the Union, but he wasn't convinced that Lincoln's election was that big of a deal. Delegates from other states tried to talk Magoffin into seceding, but Kentucky stayed neutral until September 1861. On September 10, a special meeting was held in Frankfort to vote on whether Kentucky should stay in the Union or join the Confederacy. They voted 71 to 26 to stay in the Union. But those who voted for the Confederacy felt so strongly about seceding that they formed their own Confederate government of Kentucky. On December 10, the Confederate States of America granted statehood to Kentucky's Confederate government. However, Kentucky's Confederate government could only operate if Confederate troops were nearby. Most of the time, their headquarters was located in an army tent. All the while, the "official" Kentucky government remained in the Union. Sound confusing? It was!

title: Milk Carton Log Cabin
text:
Build your own log cabin out of a milk carton!

Materials

Half-gallon waxed-paper milk or juice carton, emptied

Grease pencil

Scissors

Cardboard

Glue

Waxed paper scraps

Pretzel sticks

Cheerios or pasta

Acrylic paint

Water

Water container

Paper towels

Ruler

Instructions

1. Measure three inches down the side of the carton. At three inches, draw a line around the entire carton with a grease pencil.

2. Cut along the line and separate the top from the bottom. Discard the bottom. You will use the top.

3. Draw the outline of the door and windows with a grease pencil.

4. Cut out the windows and door. If they are too small for scissors, ask your teacher to use an X-acto knife and help you. You can leave one side of the door attached and fold it out so that it opens and closes.

5. Glue a piece of waxed paper over the inside of each window.

6. Glue the cabin to a cardboard base that is slightly bigger than the cabin. Let the pieces dry before proceeding.

7. Glue pretzel sticks along the base of the carton walls and build up. If necessary, cut the pretzels to fit around the door and windows.

8. Glue a stack of Cheerios or pasta together as a chimney. Glue this on the roof of the cabin.

9. Cover the roof with pretzels or acrylic paint.

Note: Watercolor and tempera paint will not stay on the waxed carton.

title: Southwest Kentucky
text:
Head with us down to southwestern Kentucky for a visit. The region is bordered on the west by the mighty Mississippi River, on the north by the great Ohio River and on the east by Kentucky Lake. The whole place used to be inhabited by the Chickasaw Indians, but after the Jackson Purchase (Remember reading about the purchase a few weeks ago?), small towns began to spring up - like Paducah, Mayfield and Murray. The area's access to important rivers made it a pretty handy place to control during the Civil War, and Ulysses S. Grant took over Paducah right from the beginning.

Southern Kentucky is famous for another milestone in the Civil War. Colonel Ed Murray, a local native, built the Monitor, a steel ship that fought in a famous Civil War battle. Folks from around here are proud of their rich heritage. One southwestern Kentuckian, Irvin S. Cobb, is famous for saying, "I would rather be born a homeless orphan in Paducah than duly certified twins anywhere else on Earth!"

title: When did slavery in America begin?
text: The enslavement of blacks in America began way before the United States was even its own nation. White men were holding slaves in the American colonies as early as the 1600s. Slavery flourished in the South because the large Southern plantations required many, many hands to work them. In the North, where the economy depended more on smaller farms and industry, slavery didn't have as much appeal. By 1860, just before the Civil War, there were more than 4 million slaves in the South. They made up one-third of the entire population of the slave-holding states combined. Slavery wasn't abolished until the 1860s. However, our nation's leaders, including Thomas Jefferson and George Washington (both of them Southerners), spoke out against slavery, saying that someday slavery would be outlawed. And they were right!

title: Barn Owl
text:
Barn owls are amazing hunters that prey on rodents in farmlands, especially near the edges of woods. Do you have a nickname? Barn owls have quite a few. They are called monkeyfaced owls because they look similar to monkeys, and ghost owls because they have an eerie, silent flight.

Barn owls have some very distinct yells. They have a very high pitched "shreee" scream which makes them very painful to listen to and, when captured or cornered, they can hiss like a snake and lay down on their backs and whip their sharp-taloned feet around.

If you are afraid of mice and rats, a barn owl may just be a perfect friend. A nesting pair of barn owls can eat thousands of rodents a year. These birds are such good hunters that they don't even require sight when hunting! They have ears positioned for maximum hearing and can swoop down and grab their prey through snow and grass with awesome accuracy. What a way to hunt!

title: Let's Write
text: This week you learned about fake news! Write a couple of paragraphs and create a fake news story so that you can see how easy it is to make something up. Then write about two ways you can check to see if something is fake news.

title: Fake or Real News?
text:
Have you ever read something online, like on social media sites, that sounded fishy? Maybe it was real, but it could be fake news! The big danger, though, is news that sounds real but isn’t. Fake news is becoming common because anyone can post things online. Fake news can be in the form of a story. Fake news can be a photo or video that has been changed. The problem is that these fake items look real. Fake news can cause problems and it spreads misinformation.

Sam Wineburg, a professor, did some research. He found that 80 percent of students cannot tell the difference between real and fake news. Do you want to become a media-savvy person? You have to be able to find out if news is real or fake. How do you do that? You have to become a detective and search for the truth. You can learn about the author or company that posted the news. You have to think about the purpose of the news. Is there a hidden plan to get you to buy something or to make you think a certain way? Your teacher or a trusted adult can help you learn how to spot fake news. It takes a little time, but democracy depends on real information! Do your part and discover what is real and what is fake!

title: Slavery and the Coming Conflict
text:
For hundreds of years, and right up to the middle of the 19th century, the states in the South allowed African Americans to been enslaved and do most of the work on the farm, in the shop or right at home. Slavery was big business in the South. Slavery made homes and businesses more productive. Farmers could grow and sell more crops. Free labor meant more money for those who owned enslaved people. The problem was, the states in the North believed slavery was just plain wrong and all people should be free. Many Northerners helped enslaved Africans escape. That made Southerners mad! Southerners felt that, regardless of whether slavery was right or wrong, the Yankees in the North had no right to tell them what they could or could not do. They believed their states' rights gave them the liberty to choose.

When Abraham Lincoln was elected president in 1860, the people in the Southern states got angry. They were sure Lincoln was going to end slavery. They were so mad that many Southern states began talking about seceding (leaving) the United States to make a new country. Trouble was brewing in our country, and the trouble was mostly over slavery. The differences between the North's ideas and the South's ideas were so strong that for a while it looked hopeless. Many people were certain the country's differences were too great.

title: Nothing Like a Train Ride
text:
The Underground Railroad was one approach abolitionist leaders used to end slavery. But it really wasn’t a railroad at all. There were no trains or tracks. There were no crossings or signal bells. There were no cars. Instead, the Underground Railroad was a system of roads, safe houses and helpers used to get enslaved people safely to freedom in Canada.

The Underground Railroad relied on people called “conductors.” You’ve read a little bit about Harriet Tubman in this issue of Studies Weekly. She was one of the most famous conductors after she escaped from slavery. Some conductors pretended to be enslaved. That way, they could easily get onto plantations and into homes. There, they’d lead people away, and help them get to safety.

It was a long way from slavery to freedom. As people traveled, they spent nights at homes, churches or schools. These places were called “stations.” The helpers who owned those places were called “station masters.” They gave food, clothes and rest to those bound for freedom.

There were stations all over the place. There were some in Topeka, Kansas and Tarrytown, New York. There were others in Reading, Pennsylvania and Worcester, Massachusetts. There were stations in lots of other places, too!

It took a lot of money to run the Underground Railroad! That’s why another group became important. These people were called “shareholders.” They had money, and they used it to keep things moving.

Everything about the Railroad was a secret. The brave men and women who worked as conductors, station masters and shareholders risked big trouble. After all, helping slaves escape was against the law. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 said that slaves must be returned to their masters, even if they were found in free territory. But for many people, the risks were worth it. It’s hard to say just how many people were helped by the Underground Railroad, but some think it’s more than 100,000!

title: The Word that Waged a War
text:
You probably know hundreds and hundreds of words. Some of them are big and long, like archaeologist, and some of them are short and simple, like cat. Here's one medium-sized word that caused the Civil War, the most deadly war ever fought by the United States. Are you ready for the word? The word is "secede." It's pronounced almost like "succeed," a word you probably know, but it means something completely different. Secede means "to leave or break away from something." How could that one little word start a great big war?

Well, secede is just what the slave-holding states in the Southern part of the United States wanted to do. They believed they had the right to break away from the rest of the Union and be their own country. Does that seem like a crazy idea? The people in the Northern states sure thought so, and when the Southern states seceded, it was only a matter of time before the first shot was fired. Kentucky even tried to stay neutral for a while. Eventually, Kentucky officially joined the Northern side. But there were a lot of Kentuckians who thought we should have joined the South and did it anyway.

Why did the South want to be its own country? That's a good question, and there are lots of different answers. But the main answer is that the Southern states allowed people to own slaves, and the Northern states did not. It was a big difference, and big differences can lead to big arguments. Solving big arguments sure is tough. It's tough enough to solve arguments between just two people; think of what it must take to solve an argument big enough for an entire nation. That's a lot to think about, but while you're thinking about it, go right ahead and read this issue of Kentucky Studies Weekly.

title: Secrets in the President's Pocket
text:
"The moment of truth has come. Is there or is there not an inscription?" These were the words of watchmaker George Thomas as he carefully took the back off Abraham Lincoln's pocket watch at the National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C. Just like a scene out of one of the "National Treasure" movies, the crowd gasped when Thomas revealed that there was indeed a secret message engraved inside Lincoln's watch.

Watchmaker Jonathan Dillon was fixing the president's watch when he heard that the first shots of the Civil War had been fired. For nearly 150 years, rumors said that when Dillon learned that the war had begun, he engraved a message on the inside of the watch.

Doug Stiles, a great-great grandson of the watchmaker, heard the story when he was young and wanted to check it out. He passed along the rumors to the museum and the directors decided to open the watch to see what was inside. Sure enough, the rumors were true!

So, what did the secret message say? The first line says: "April 13, 1861. Fort Sumter was attacked by the rebels on the above date. J. Dillon." A second line reads: "April 13, 1861. Thank God we have a government. Jonathan Dillon."

These words may not seem very mysterious, but just knowing that the rumors are true is important to many people. What was Doug Stiles' reaction to knowing that his great-great grandfather left an inscription on the president's watch? "My gosh, that was Lincoln's watch," he said, "and my ancestor put graffiti on it!"

title: The Civil War
text:
Lincoln Elected! South Carolina Fires the First Shot

One of the main starting points of the Civil War was when the country elected a new president in 18 60. All the Southern states were really upset that this man was elected because everyone knew he didn't like slavery. Can you guess the name of this new president? You got it! Abraham Lincoln. About one month after President Lincoln was elected, South Carolina became the first Southern state to secede from the Union. A few months later, the Southern armies fired their cannons at Fort Sumter in South Carolina. President Lincoln didn't like that a bit. The fort was owned by the U.S. government. After that, President Lincoln and Congress declared war on the rebellious Southern states.

Emancipation

New Year's Day in 18 63 was like no other New Year's Day ever. It was on this day that President Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation. The word emancipation means "freedom from slavery." Lincoln's proclamation freed the slaves on paper, but the real chains of slavery were broken on the bloodiest battlefields in America's history.

Kentuckians Make Tough Choices

Because it was right on the border between the North and the South, Kentucky didn't officially take sides for the first few years of the war. When Kentucky did finally take a side in 1861, it was with the Union (the group of states that did not secede). But that didn't keep the citizens of Kentucky from taking sides themselves. When it came right down to it, between 25, 000 and 40, 000 Kentuckians fought for the Confederacy, and about 1 00, 000 Kentuckians fought for the Union. Think about that. Citizens of the same state fought against each other. Citizens of the same town and even members of the same family fought against each other. Most of the soldiers were volunteers. That means they signed up on their own to fight for whichever side they believed in. But when the state finally decided to fight for the Union, many Kentuckians were drafted (asked to fight whether they wanted to or not). That may explain the difference in numbers between Kentucky's Confederate soldiers and Union soldiers.

What’s a Civil War Anyway?

The United States has fought a few wars since it became a nation more than 2 00 years ago wars like World War I and World War II, wars in Korea and Vietnam, and the Desert Storm war in the Persian Gulf. These wars were all fought by American troops in some other country and against someone else's government or army. There's a difference between that sort of war and a civil war. A civil war is a war between people in the same country. America's Civil War was a war that Americans fought, not against Canada, Mexico, France or England, but against other Americans.

The Battle of Perryville: Kentucky’s Bloodiest Civil War Battle

"The morning is half gone, and the Union boys are right in front of you! Why haven't your Southern troops attacked?"

General Bragg's words rang out in the Confederate camp just outside Perryville on Oct. 8, 18 62. They rang in the ears of 16, 000 Southern soldiers as they scurried to the ready, loading their guns and rubbing the sleep from their eyes. There were 22, 000 Union soldiers facing them across the battlefield, but they charged anyway. Through the afternoon, the Confederate underdogs pushed the Union boys back more than a mile, and by the end of the day, 8 45 Union soldiers and 5 10 Confederate soldiers lay dead, with thousands more wounded. The South might have celebrated their victory, but there was no time. More Union troops were on the way. The Southern soldiers withdrew, and they escaped the Union guns through the Cumberland Gap. The Battle of Perryville would live in memory as Kentucky's bloodiest Civil War battle.

Gibraltar of the West

How do you stop huge gunboats from traveling the river to fire on your troops and bring supplies to your enemies? You might try stringing a mile-long chain across the river. Of course, to do any good, the links in the chain would have to weigh 15 pounds a piece - and who has a chain that big? Well, the Confederate army made just such a chain. In 18 61 and 18 62, troops under Confederate Gen. Leonidas Polk put the chain in place near a 2 00-foot-high bluff at Columbus, Kentucky. The place came to be known as the Gibraltar of the West, after the small country that acts as a gateway to the Mediterranean Sea, because of all the other fortifications that were built there. Today, you can visit the site and check out the remains of the huge chain.

The War Ends: President Lincoln Is Assassinated

By April 18 65, the Union army was twice the size of the Confederate army. The main army of the South surrendered on April 9 in Virginia at the Appomattox Courthouse. On April 14, President Lincoln was assassinated by John Wilkes Booth with a gunshot to the head as he and his wife watched a play.

The war was over, but not the pain that war causes. Yes, it was the end of the war, but it was just the beginning of the long road toward healing the nation.

title: Francis Hopkinson and the American Flag
text:
If you asked 100 people who designed the first American flag, 99 of them would probably say Betsy Ross, right? Many people would be surprised to learn that there are dissenting opinions about that. The U.S. Postal Service issued this stamp [right] in 2000 with this passage printed on the back:

Francis Hopkinson Flag 1777

Continental Congress member Francis Hopkinson designed the first Stars and Stripes. His stars may have formed rows or a ring; the exact design is not known. In a resolution of June 14, 1777, they were said to represent "a new constellation."

There has been an ongoing debate about who made the first flag. Did George Washington really ask Betsy Ross to make a flag from his design? There are no written records confirming it, so many historians believe this is a legend. However, Betsy Ross' family has always insisted that the story is true. They do have papers showing that Betsy was paid to make flags for the new country for the rest of her life.

Francis Hopkinson's defenders can't prove his claims either. He was a delegate from New Jersey who signed the Declaration of Independence. He sent a bill to Congress asking for payment for designing the first flag and other projects. After a long debate, a Congressional committee refused payment but never claimed that the designs were not his.

America was founded on the freedom of its citizens to disagree with the government and with each other. Neither side in the flag debate has found absolute proof. The discussion will certainly continue, showing that the all-American values of debate and dissent are alive and well. What issues in your community are a source of debate and dissent?

title: Respect
text:
Part of being a happy and powerful person is showing proper respect. When we show respect to something or someone, we show honor.

Let's start with things. What are some things you respect? Do you show respect for the American flag? What about a loved one's grave? How about the laws of your country? Do you show respect for your body by not taking drugs or other harmful substances? Name three other things that you can show respect for: (Answers may vary.)

It's important to show common respect for all people. But people tend to honor or show the most respect to those who have done the most for them. This kind of respect comes from love and gratitude - just like your respect for a parent, grandparent or teacher who has always been kind and helpful.

How about people who have authority? Do you respect the principal of your school? What about a policeman? Do you respect your mom and dad?

We also show respect to heroes. Did you hear about the firemen who died rushing into the World Trade Center to save others? Do you show respect to heroes such as the men and women in our armed forces? Name three people you respect:

title: Why did John Wilkes Booth shoot President Lincoln?
text: John Wilkes Booth was angry with President Lincoln. He knew that slavery was ending, which was happy news for most people in Washington, D.C., but not good news for Booth. Booth approved of slavery and was convinced that it should stay. He also blamed Lincoln for the war. Anyway, Booth and others had had a plan to stop Lincoln for a long time. At first, they planned to kidnap him and then trade him for captured Confederate soldiers. But after the main Confederate army surrendered in 1865, Booth's plans turned to murder. And he didn't kill nearly as many people as he meant to! His murderous plans included killing Vice President Andrew Johnson, Gen. Ulysses S. Grant and Secretary of State William H. Seward as well. Booth only killed Lincoln, however, before he was cornered and shot in a barn where he was hiding after the assassination.

title: White-Tailed Deer
text:
The white-tail deer is one great survivor! While many species have become endangered because of loss of habitat, the white-tail deer keeps on thriving. Wildlife experts think there are about 12 million white-tail deer in the United States.

White-tail deer like to live in forests and wetlands the most, but they don't mind sneaking into your neighborhood at night, either. They eat grass, bark and leaves, but they also love fruits, veggies and flowers from your garden.

There are four kinds of deer in the United States: whitetail deer, mule deer, elk and caribou. The main difference is size. Elk and caribou are the largest, and white-tail deer are the smallest. White-tail deer are the most common deer in the eastern United States. They can run very fast and jump very high.
