title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you are a teenager living in Kentucky right at the beginning of the Civil War. Your family moved here two years ago from Ohio so that your father could run the local general store. You have lots of family in both places. It’s a crazy time to live anywhere in America. It looks like Kentucky will fight on the side of the North, and you have an older brother in Ohio who is going to fight for the Union. But many Kentuckians support the South. You’re 17 years old, and everyone expects you to serve in the Army. Write a 200-word story about how you decide which side to fight on. Do you come face to face with your brother at the Battle of Shiloh? Tell us what happens.

title: Choosing Sides: Brother Against Brother
text:
Kentucky tried to stay out of the Civil War. However, the Confederates wanted the border states of Missouri, Kentucky and Maryland to help them survive. Several battles were fought in the surrounding states. Kentucky’s population soon became divided between support for the North or for the South. It was sure to happen then that brother would have to fight against brother.

The Confederates invaded first. Kentucky called for Union help. The battle of Perryville would determine whether Kentucky would remain Union or Confederate. At 2:30 am on October 8, 1862, the Confederate troops (Army of the Mississippi) attacked. The Union forces (Army of the Ohio) held strong. Within 24 hours the Confederate troops were in full retreat towards Tennessee.

title: Kentucky's Reconstruction
text:
Have you ever built a fort in your living room out of couch cushions, blankets and kitchen chairs? What if you built a fort and felt pretty good about it, but your little brother came in and wanted his blanket back and wrecked the whole thing trying to get it out? Or what if your mom needed the kitchen chairs at dinner time? There goes all your hard work! What do you think you would do then? Would you go to your room and mope? Would you shrug your shoulders and go play video games? Would you build another fort right after dinner?

Well, think about this for a second: The Civil War ended in 1865, and the United States had to deal with a lot more than a broken-down living room fort. The whole country was torn apart! The people couldn't just turn their backs on the problem and mope, and there were no video games in those days. That left them with just one option: rebuild. Right away, people began to think of ways to make the nation better and stronger than ever before. That's why the time between 1865 and 1876 is called the Reconstruction.

Just like most big projects, some of the ideas for rebuilding the South were bad ones and some were good ones, but that's the rest of the story. So go ahead, open up this issue of Kentucky Studies Weekly and dig right in!

title: Starting Over
text:
Once the chains of slavery had fallen, the African Americans and the white Americans had to discover true freedom - the personal power to choose one's own destiny and circumstances.

Kentucky's After the War Blues

Just because Kentucky did its best to remain neutral during the war didn't mean we escaped all the fighting. In fact, Kentucky may have had it worse than other states. Both armies recruited around here, and sometimes one Kentucky citizen would find himself looking down the barrel of a gun held by his neighbor. Those bitter feelings continued after the war as well and took a long time to fade. In addition to all the human suffering during and after the war, here are some other ways the war affected us: After the war, there were 89,000 fewer horses in Kentucky than before the war.

There were also 37,000 fewer mules and 172,000 fewer cattle. In those days, if you lost your horses, mules and cattle, you had a hard time making a living. One Kentucky soldier returned home after the war and said that all he saw were "neglected farms, roads and paths overgrown with weeds and almost no business of any kind being carried on!"

Carpetbaggers and Scalawags

Here are a couple of words that will twist your tongue. The first word is carpetbagger. After the Civil War, things were pretty mixed up. Some Northerners came to live in the South thinking they could make a lot of money doing business with the desperate people in the Southern states. These Northerners were not very honest. They came to be known as carpetbaggers because they carried suitcases made of pieces of carpet.

The second word is scalawag. Almost the opposite of carpetbaggers, scalawags were Southerners who were rooting for the Northern states when the Civil War ended. It was a little like someone coming to one of your baseball games and sitting with your folks but cheering for the other team. Neither scalawags nor carpetbaggers were very popular, at least among white American people in Kentucky.

Kentucky and Delaware: Freedom at Last

Kentucky's position during the war caused some tricky problems for the state after the war was over. Here's an example: Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation, which freed the slaves in the South, officially applied only to states that were in rebellion. That didn't include Kentucky. As a result, Kentucky's slaves didn't know whether they were free or not. Some people said they were and encouraged them to leave their masters. But Kentucky's courts thought otherwise and told them they weren't free at all. In fact, because of that little detail, slavery remained legal in Kentucky and Delaware (another state in the same fix) longer than anywhere else in the nation. The Emancipation Proclamation was issued in 1863, but Kentucky's slaves didn't go free until December 1865 when the 13th amendment was passed.

What'll We Do Now?

Even though the Civil War brought freedom to those who had been slaves for so long, many African Americans were without work and places to live. Some white Americans tried to get them to go back to work on the plantation even though they were free. It was a real problem! After a while, many African Americans did choose to go back to work on plantations, but not as slaves. They became employees and were paid a share of the money the plantation made on its crops. It was a system known as sharecropping. This was one way former slaves made a living during the tough times after the war.

Fourteen for Freedom

In the year 1868, the U.S. Constitution was amended, or changed, to include citizenship, liberty and rights for all people, whether they were African Americans or white Americans. Amending the Constitution is a big deal. It had only happened 13 times before 1868. This was the 14th time - which is why it's called the 14th Amendment. It actually took many generations before African Americans were treated as equals, but the 14th Amendment was the first big step in the right direction.

title: Quadrorama
text:
Materials

Four 8-inch by 14-inch pieces of construction paper

Craft materials - construction paper, string, fabric scraps, cotton, markers and crayons

Scissors

Glue

Tape

Pencil

Ruler

Directions

1. Fold the top left corner of a piece of 8x14 construction paper diagonally so that the top edge of the paper is flush with the right edge of the paper.

2. Fold the top right-hand corner diagonally so that it touches the lower point of the previous fold.

3. Fold the panel at the bottom to make a horizontal crease along the edge. (Fold it to the back.)

4. Open the paper up and cut along the lower left-hand diagonal crease to the center of the paper.

5. Pull point A over to point B so that the piece you cut is flush with the lower right-hand diagonal crease. Glue the base into place. This is one triorama.

6. When four trioramas are finished, glue them together to form a pyramid. From underneath, tape the four lower panels so that they form four corners. This is now called a quadrorama.

7. Draw some historical figures or anything else that interests you. You may use a coloring book if you'd like.

8. Cut the figures out and glue each into a part of the quadorama. You should have four figures in the completed structure. Allow the glue to dry before proceeding.

9. Design the inside scenes of the quadorama using any available craft materials - construction paper, string, fabric scraps, cotton, markers, crayons - to make the scene three dimensional.

10. Write a brief paragraph describing the scenes along the bottom flap. Make guidelines for the words by lightly drawing straight pencil lines. These guidelines will keep the lines straight.

11. Hang the quadorama with a string or display it on a counter top.

title: Called to Teach
text:
George Wiggins wasn't looking for any trouble. He had moved to Kentucky just a few months ago to take a job as a school teacher. He accepted the job partly because he knew some of his students would be former slaves. They would need help getting on their feet after the war. The war - just thinking about the trouble his students would have experienced over the last few years made him shiver. Now that the war was over and the slaves had been freed, he thought that things would be different. But he was surprised sometimes, like when he caught people at the market whispering and looking at him strangely. One woman told him he should be ashamed of himself for teaching former slaves.

George couldn't stop thinking about it even though it was late at night and he should have been preparing his lessons for the next day. George sighed, then became startled at the sound of voices in the yard. He stood up and crossed the room to the backdoor. Was that smoke he smelled? George's eyes went wide. There behind his house, his barn was exploding into a huge burst of flame! Black smoke poured upward into the night sky. He hadn't time to wonder why or even to think about anything. He grabbed a blanket and ran across the yard toward the water trough. He had almost reached it when something struck the back of his head and knocked him to the ground. It was a rock the size of a large tomato. George reached up to feel blood on his head, hot and sticky. His vision blurred from smoke and pain, but through the blackness he thought he could make out white-robed figures, moving back and forth across the yard and shouting to one another. Anger swelled his heart, and he tried to get up, but dizziness drove him to the ground again. Tears came to his eyes, and he felt helpless. He had heard of the Ku Klux Klan, and he knew they terrorized newly freed slaves and those who were their friends. George had felt great fear when he thought of them. But lying on the ground beside his burning barn, his fear turned to anger, and he made a brave decision: If these men were so convinced that teaching former slaves to read and write was big trouble, then that was exactly what they were going to get from him - big trouble and plenty of it! Then with a loud crash, George's barn collapsed, where it burned for most of the night.

title: Southwest Kentucky
text:
Paducah is called the River City by some folks - and rightly so. There are more navigable river miles in and around Paducah than in any other inland city in the country. The rivers have always driven the area's economy. In fact, the oldest industry in Paducah is Paducah Marine Ways. The name has changed to Ingram Barge Lines, but it's the same company that has been building, maintaining and repairing boats since 1854.

Of course, there are other places to see in southwestern Kentucky as well. Try Murray, for example. It's a hop, skip and a jump away from the Land Between the Lakes recreation area, a huge wooded area between Barkley and Kentucky Lakes. While there, don't forget to hit the National Scouting Museum, combining history and computer robotics to give you a look at the Boy Scouts that you won't forget. Another place you might visit in southwest Kentucky is the town of Hopkinsville. If you go in early June, you might just be invited to a huge birthday party. Who's the birthday boy? Jefferson Davis, the first and last president of the Confederate States of America. He's been dead for a while now, but that's no reason to stop the party, right?

title: Freshwater Eel
text:
Freshwater eel are amazing and mysterious creatures. You can find them throughout the rivers and streams of Kentucky and beyond. Some eel have even been found as far inland as South Dakota. Freshwater eel all have one thing in common: When they are tiny eel larvae (eel babies), they set out on a long and difficult journey from the Sargasso Sea in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. Riding the current, they eventually find their way to the freshwater streams and rivers of North America and Europe.

Young eel will remain in freshwater for seven to 10 years before returning to the ocean. Eels have an amazing life span. One eel kept in an aquarium in Sweden lived for 88 years!

title: Smithsonian Dinosaurs Take a Break
text:
How do you move 10,000 dinosaur bones? Very carefully. The world-famous National Fossil Hall at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History is undergoing a huge renovation. In order to make the exhibition even better, workers took apart the collection piece by piece. The hall will be closed during renovation, but some dinosaur artifacts will be moved to other locations in the museum.

While the exhibition hall is being updated (it opened in 1910), paleontologists will be studying the dinosaur bones. They will take apart the dinosaur skeletons, clean them up and examine them. Paleontologists hope to learn more about the dinosaurs during this process and maybe even determine how old some of the fossils are. Recent research about dinosaurs will help the paleontologists put the skeletons back together accurately.

The new and improved hall will have a very large resident: an almost-complete skeleton of a T. rex, discovered in Montana. The museum has about 46 million fossils, so there will be plenty of other items to look at!

While you’re waiting for the exhibit to reopen (hopefully in 2019), do some research about your own dinosaurs. What dinosaurs lived near your area? Is there a natural history museum near you? If not, ask an adult to help you search for information on the Internet, so you can get your dinosaur fix.

title: Let's Write
text: You grew up in the South 140 years ago. It’s hard for you to remember what the Civil War was like because you were only 10 years old when it ended. But you do remember the Reconstruction. Write a 200-word story telling us what it was like back then. Can you remember damage to the farms? Do you remember helping your family and neighbors rebuild things? How about those carpetbaggers? Did your family hire them to help, or did you get by without them?

title: Madam C. J. Walker
text:
Sarah Breedlove McWilliams Walker was orphaned at age seven. She was the daughter of former slaves.

As a teen, Sarah began having problems with thinning hair. She tried mixing different ingredients to find something that might help. She used them on herself. She found something that worked!

Walker then moved to Denver, changed her name to Madam C.J. Walker and began selling her hair products to other black women. When she started, Walker walked door-to-door to make sales. Walker went across the U.S. and even to the Caribbean Islands, teaching women about hair care. Walker also taught women how to sell her products and make a living. Later she opened a beauticians’ college in Pittsburgh.

Walker came to employ thousands of “Walker Agents.” Her products and training took off, and Madam C.J. Walker became the first self-made African American female millionaire. Madam Walker will be remembered for creating not only her own success through hard work, but also for helping many other women succeed in sales and industry.

title: Transportation Today
text: Hey there, welcome to another issue of Kentucky Studies Weekly. This issue is all about moving around. Moving people and things from place to place is called transportation. This issue of Kentucky Studies Weekly was transported from your teacher's desk to your own! Kentucky people do plenty of transporting, and the truth is, they've found some pretty amazing ways to do it over the years. Just think of your trip to school this morning. You may have driven in a car from your house. On the other hand, you may have ridden with a lot of other kids in a big, yellow school bus. You may have whizzed down the road on a sleek aluminum scooter or a pair of roller blades. But (unless you walked, of course), there's a good chance that whatever transported you to school was something your great-great-grandparents had never heard of. Things in the world of transportation are changing every day. And that raises an interesting thought: How do you think your great-great-grandchildren will get to school? Will they have jet-powered skateboards that float above the ground? Will they travel in ultrafast school rockets that take kids to schools in outer space? Maybe they'll just hit a button and beam instantly to their school desks. The possibilities are enough to fuel the imaginations of scientists for as long as scientists are using their imaginations. Getting around has always been big fun and big business in Kentucky. To find out more about it all, transport this paper to the open position, and let's get going!

title: Faster Than the Speed of Light
text:
There's an exciting new plane flying around in the sky, and it's not just flying - it's speeding! NASA's new aircraft, the X-43A, is the fastest air-breathing engine that has ever flown. Its most recent test flight surpassed all expectations when the aircraft flew an amazing Mach 9.6, nearly 10 times the speed of sound. That's almost 7,000 miles per hour, or 2 miles per second. Can you imagine going that fast? The plane that set the record before the X-43A was the SR-71, which only flew at about Mach 3.2.

The X-43A has new engine technology that uses supersonic combustion ramjets, or scramjets. These kinds of engines use oxygen and fuel to combust at super fast rates to create amazing speed power. Rocket engines are much bigger and require a lot more storage for fuel, so they can't travel as light or fast as scramjets. Another reason the scramjets can go so fast is that they use a regular jet engine to get up to speeds of about Mach 4; then they break away from that engine and turn on their scramjet engines, which have few or no moving parts, and they're off to faster speeds than we've ever seen. This way they can use their engines more efficiently to reach top speeds.

So why would NASA build a plane that can go this fast? Well, NASA is hoping the X-43A will help them take things into space in a cheaper and faster way than rockets can. They're also hoping that this new technology will help make commercial planes, like the one you take to your grandma's at Christmas time, faster and more affordable to fly.

title: Transportation
text:
Kentucky's First Steamboats

Travelers on the great western rivers could see steamboats as early as 1811. In that same year, the New Madrid earthquake hit, and a great new comet appeared in the sky. But neither of those special effects by Mother Nature had quite as much effect on things around here as the steamboat. Suddenly, the rivers became the great highways of Kentucky, and people and their stuff traveled more quickly and in more comfort than ever before. Fire from the steamboat stacks belched up into the air. Huge wooden wheels churned up river water. The race was on for the best steamboats. Best meant fastest, biggest and most reliable. Keels got shorter, hulls got flatter, and machinery got faster. There was one problem: Some of the new machinery tended to blow up, turning steamboats into huge and deadly fireballs. Safety apparently wasn't on the agenda in those early days. At any rate, by 1859, steamboats ran on the Green River that could carry 10 tons of freight in only 8 inches of water.

Kentucky's First Trains

Whoo whoo! What makes that sound? An overgrown owl? Nope. This is the sound of the biggest thing to hit the world of transportation in centuries. It's the railroad! Big deal, you say? Well, in the middle of the 1800s, it was a big deal. It had never been easier or more reliable to get people and their things from one place to another - no more stagecoaches on bumpy or muddy roads, no more boats on dangerous rivers. This was style, and it hit the country in a big way. In our state, the first railroad was built in 1830. Folks called it the L and O, which was short for the Lexington and Ohio. By the turn of the 20th century, there were 1,500 miles of track in Kentucky, but that was only the beginning. Over the next 30 years, Kentucky got another 3,500 miles of track. That's more than 5,000 miles in all. More than 40 rail companies traveled those rails. Those tracks joined up with other tracks in other states, making it possible for people and things to go just about anywhere in the country on the rails.

Wilbur and Orville Wright Invent the Airplane

The idea behind airplanes is pretty old. Even Leonardo Da Vinci (a man who lived long ago) experimented with making models of flying machines. But, there were no working airplanes in the skies anywhere until Orville and Wilbur Wright perfected their glider and then built a special engine for it with the help of Charlie Taylor, their bicycle mechanic. The Wright brothers lived in Dayton, Ohio, but they went to Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, just to test their flying machines. The one shown here was a special glider designed just for their engine. It was fitted with special, carefully crafted propellers. The brothers flipped a coin, and Wilbur became the first guy ever to fly in a plane. Well, almost - the first flight failed in a crash before it ever got off the ground. Sometimes that happens. But on Dec. 17, 1903, Orville Wright (it was his turn) flew 120 feet while his brother stood by. The rest, of course, is history. What would Orville and Wilbur think of airplanes today? How would they feel standing in a modern airport? Well, anyone can get a taste of big-time air transportation in Kentucky just by visiting the airport. You don't even have to leave the ground. Airports these days are like small cities themselves. For example, at Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport, there are 93 different businesses, all in one airport. They include restaurants, shops, business offices, banks and more. Yes sir, we've come a long way since the Wright Brothers. Do you think they ever envisioned it being so big?

Henry Ford and the Automobile

Henry Ford figured out how to make a whole bunch of cars very quickly at a price anyone with a job could afford. After that, people could go anywhere.

His company produced and sold millions of Model Ts. He started out by building a car from scratch in his garage, but, in just a few decades, the automobile craze swept right through Kentucky and the rest of the nation. Why, in Kentucky alone, there were more than 46,000 motor vehicles by 1916.

Truckin' Across the USA

You may have been riding in a car on a freeway full of huge semitrucks and thought, "Gee, I wonder what's in those big trailers and where it's all going?" Well, just about anything you can imagine is in those big trailers. From cars to hogs, from corn to computer systems to schoolbooks, just about everything that gets around can get around in the back of one of those trucks. Where's it all going? Well, the answer to that question is simple, too: just about anywhere! After all, more than 80 percent of our state's cities get all of their goods delivered by semitrucks just like the ones you see on the freeway. In fact, because of all the trucks and modern highways, railroads and rivers, while still important, now play a lesser role in our state's transportation. Many of our modern communities don't even have a river or railroad nearby - something that would have been unthinkable 100 years ago.

The Skycar

A man named Dr. Paul Moller has been trying to fill Mr. Ford's shoes for the last 40 years. Dr. Moller dreams of building the first practical Skycar. So far, it's been mostly dreams. The Skycar has only flown about 15 feet above the ground.

Dr. Moller says that when his Skycar is finished, it will travel through the sky at about 350 mph, travel on roads at 25 mph, use unleaded gasoline, take off and land vertically and be completely safe. All you'll have to do is type in an address, and the Skycar will do the rest and take you where you want to go. Hopefully someday his dream will be a reality. Sometimes when we hear about new technology becoming available in the near future, we may have to wait a little bit longer than that for it to really happen.

Transportation in Style

There are lots of ways to get around, and some like to do it in real style - Corvette style, that is. Bowling Green, Kentucky, is the only place where that famous, speedy car is made, and folks know it! When the National Corvette Museum (also in Bowling Green) was dedicated, more than 4,000 Corvette owners showed up. They drove toward the museum in a huge caravan - Corvettes in all sorts of colors as far as the eye could see. It was quite a sight! And, speaking of transportation, just how far did those Corvette owners transport themselves for the big event? More than 250,000 miles all combined!

title: A New Invention
text:
"Tell these gentlemen what the clock says!" Alfonso shouted over the whirring of the computers and the rattling of the machinery around him. His assistant, Rufus, stepped from the group of frowning observers and ran to Alfonso's side. He glanced at the instrument panel attached to the cockpit of the machine. "9:15 a.m., April 15, 2007, boss!" he shouted into Alfonso's ear. Alfonso grinned behind his goggles and clicked a key on the panel. The engines sputtered to a stop, and the hangar was quiet again except for faint whistles and hums from the computers, still furiously calculating numbers and flashing displays on the monitors that surrounded Alfonso where he sat.

The room came alive with questions. Alfonso stood and quieted the crowd with the raise of a hand. "One at a time, please, one at a time." He pointed to a raised hand, and the man spoke: "Dr. Viajante," he said, "do you mean to tell us that this machine will actually transport you through time to this very spot, in the past?" Alfonso smiled. "That's exactly what I'm saying!" flashed Alfonso cheerfully.

Hands raised and voices clamored. Alfonso called on another bystander. "Dr. Viajante, nothing like this has ever been tried before. You realize that there are many who doubt that you can do it, don't you?" Alfonso stared at the floor for a moment, lost in thought. Then he spoke: "I realize that many are skeptical. But, remember Mr. Ford who created the automobile - a car that could move about without horses to pull it. Unthinkable! And, what about the Wright brothers and their airplane - a way to make wood, cloth, metal and even people travel through air? Never! And, when propellers were removed from airplanes and replaced with jet engines? Crazy! But, my friends, great men have made all those unthinkable things possible, even commonplace. Now watch me as I make the next unthinkable thing possible!"

The room exploded with waving hands and questioning voices, but Alfonso had already replaced his goggles and settled himself into the cockpit. He turned a key, and the machine sprang to life. Rattling and humming grew louder and louder with each passing second. Then Dr. Alfonso Viajante, with a quick smile at Rufus, pulled a lever. Rufus blinked. The room fell silent. The floor was bare where the doctor's machine had been. And, though no one in the room understood what they had seen and none of them dared guess where Dr. Viajante had gone, they all knew one thing: They had witnessed something unthinkable!

title: Responsibility
text:
To be able to respond is to be able to answer, or to be answerable. What does it mean to be answerable? It means that we are willing and able to answer, or respond, to our duties.

Here's a poem by Joy Allison about three children. Can you guess which one showed responsibility? Which one are you more like?

"I love you, Mother," said little John; Then, forgetting his work, his cap went on, And he was off to the garden swing, And left her the water and wood to bring.

"I love you, Mother," said rosy Nell - "I love you better than tongue can tell"; Then she teased and pouted full half the day, Till her mother rejoiced when she went to play.

"I love you, Mother," said little Fan; "Today I'll help you all I can; How glad I am that school doesn't keep!" So she rocked the baby till it fell asleep.

Then, stepping softly, she fetched the broom, And swept the floor and tidied the room; Busy and happy all day was she, Helpful and happy as a child could be.

"I love you, Mother," again they said, Three little children going to bed; How do you think that mother guessed Which of them really loved her best?

title: How does an airplane fly?
text: For hundreds of years, people tried to figure out how to put people in the air. They created all sorts of crazy contraptions in which to do it. Finally, the answer came simply in observing the flying creatures all around us: birds! The secret of flight, it turns out, is all in the wings. Airplane wings are shaped in the same way that birds' wings are: flat on the bottom and curved on the top. When the wing is traveling forward through the air, the air travels faster over the curved top than over the flat bottom. Fast air on top and slow air on the bottom creates air pressure beneath the wing that pushes it right into the air. It's like giant hands made of nothing but air, pushing the wing into the sky from below. And, of course, wherever the wind goes, the rest of the plane goes too. That answer came just by observing the creatures around us.

title: The Quail
text:
Most of the quail you'll see around here are called northern bobwhite quail. If the northern bobwhite ever went to a family reunion, it'd not only share the buffet table with turkeys, grouses and partridges (just in from the pear tree) but also with 44 other species of quail. They're all related!

The northern bobwhite is easy to spot. It's a small brown or gray bird with striking patterns of reddish-brown, blue, white, or black feathers. In the fall and winter, quail live in groups called coveys, which may contain up to 100 birds. When predators (like bigger birds) try to attack a covey, the quail freak out. They squawk like crazy and fly off in all directions like a big explosion. During the summer, the covey breaks up, and the quail lay eggs in nests on the ground. They protect their eggs by hiding them under a covering of grass.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you just finished building your own seaplane. It’s a safe, reliable airplane that can land on water or on the ground. You’ve been preparing for years for a trip. You could fly to Alaska or go out West to the Rocky Mountains. You could check out the deserts in the southwestern United States. One thing is for sure: You’ve decided to stay in the United States because this will be your first trip. When you return, please write to us and tell us about your trip. Where did you decide to go? What were your two favorite things that happened while you were away?

title: Communication Today
text:
Hey there, state studiers! Last week's issue was all about moving people and things around. We call that transportation. But there's a lot more to move around in this state than people and things.

This week, we're going to talk about moving ideas and information around. We call it communication, and Kentucky's full of it all the time. In fact, whether you know it or not, you're communicating right now just by reading the ideas and information in Kentucky Studies Weekly. If you spent some time talking to a friend before you came to class today - tah-dah! - you were doing it again. Using your voice is one of the oldest and most reliable forms of communication, but there are other ways as well. You could never yell loud enough where you live to be heard all the way across the state, or even across town. But, lucky for you and me, there are lots of ways to get your ideas from person to person - even if you're talking to someone on the other side of the world.

Here's one example of high-tech communications in your everyday life. Pretend you have a friend who just moved to China, and you want to tell him about the terrific new bike you just got for your birthday. It's too expensive to call him, and it will take days for him to receive a letter from you. You want to tell him right now. With high-tech communication, all you have to do is get on the computer, log on to your e-mail account and type away. He will receive your message in just a couple minutes. What a great way to communicate. This week we'll look at some of the ways we communicate, so turn the page, and let's get going!

title: Can Facebook Save Dying Languages
text:
Can you say a few words in Siletz Dee-ni? No? How about saying "hello" in Aka? If you can't, you're not alone! These two languages and 3,500 more could become extinct by the end of this century. Almost 80 percent of the world's population now speaks only one percent of the world's 7,000 languages. This has happened because of globalization. Globalization means that countries are more connected through trade, money and workers. When countries work together, people must be able to communicate with each other. That means many people have to learn another language. English is the main language used throughout the world for business and the Internet.

Why is this a problem? When the last person who is able to speak a particular language dies, some of the knowledge that is found within that language dies with them. A language contains the history of its people, how they used their environment and their beliefs and ideas. Technology may just save many of these languages from extinction! With YouTube, Facebook and other forms of social media, languages that are spoken by even 5 or ten people can be taught to others around the world.

National Geographic has been working on the Enduring Voices Project. Its goals are to record native speakers of endangered languages into talking dictionaries and help communities learn ways to save their languages from extinction. What language do you want to help save?

Reference: History News Network (hnn.us)

title: Communication Keeps the World Connected
text:
It's Great to Communicate

The simplest way to communicate is to open your mouth. Try it: Just get your voice going, and ideas start spilling out. When you want your ideas to stick around, write them down. People have been writing things for a long time, and recording ideas has kept information alive for thousands of years. Nowadays, we have a lot of stuff to help us communicate. Ever heard of a telephone or a fax machine? Or a newspaper or a mail carrier? Or how about a television? Add computers, modems and the Internet, and you can get any idea to almost anyone in the world. Now that's power. Kentucky is getting in on the communication action. Did you know there are dozens of daily newspapers and more weekly newspapers in Kentucky than we care to count? There are also TV stations, cable companies and thousands of Internet Web sites. Another great place to find and exchange ideas is the library. We have libraries all over the place in Kentucky. There's probably even one in your school. What it all means is that no matter who you are or where you're from, Kentucky is a great place to communicate.

E-mail: The New Pony Express

Technology exists today that allows people to communicate more quickly and with less expense than ever before in the history of the whole world. And you know what? Some of that technology is right at your fingertips. When was the last time you e-mailed anyone? Chances are that you or someone you know has access to this speedy way to communicate. The "e" in e-mail stands for electronic.

When you use e-mail, the information you type onto your computer screen is stored as an electronic code that can be sent to someone else's computer and decoded on that person's screen, just as you sent it. Those messages travel through the same wires that make your television or telephone work - the ones you see connected right to your house. Those wires send your messages faster than a mailman could ever dream of going. And, while there's nothing quite like getting a real-life paper letter in your mailbox, it's nice to know that communicating instantly with your faraway friends is just the touch of a button away, thanks to e-mail.

Telephones Keep Us Connected

Over the years, some of the most amazing travelers of all have been the voices of people talking on telephones. Since the very beginning of telephones, whenever someone made a phone call, that person's voice had to travel through long phone lines, all the way to the phone of the person she was talking to. Sometimes, those voice signals made trips of hundreds or even thousands of miles. But these days, the trips made by voices are even more amazing than that. It might be that the last time you made a long-distance phone call, your voice traveled for part of the way through phone wires and part of the way through outer space. You see, nowadays there are mighty satellites orbiting the Earth, built specially to receive messages from people making phone calls on Earth and then to beam those messages to their destinations at other places on Earth. The messages moved around by outer-space satellites include phone conversations, TV shows, radio broadcasts and much more. So, while your body may have stayed on the ground most of your life, it's a good bet that your voice has done some space travel.

title: Communications Hall of Fame
text:
Let's take a walk through the hall of fame of communications heroes. Whether or not these visionary men lived in our state, their work affects the way you communicate every single day. Every one of them deserves the thanks of anyone with something to say.

Samuel Morse

The telegraph was the first, fast method of two-way communication between long distances. Samuel Morse invented the telegraph in 1837. The telegraph quickly sent messages back and forth across electric lines using Morse code, a system of dots and dashes. An operator typed out a message and later decoded the answer.

Before the telegraph was invented, the fastest way to send a message was through horseback riders. You may have heard of the famous ride of Paul Revere, the man who warned the colonists the English Army was coming.

Christopher Sholes

Christopher Sholes forever changed personal communication when he invented the typewriter in 1868. Before the typewriter, letters had to be written by hand with pen and ink. In those days, anything that looked like it was printed by a machine had been slowly and carefully prepared by printing professionals, letter by letter, in a process that took hours for each page. After Mr. Christopher Sholes, anyone who owned a typewriter must have felt as if he owned his very own printing press.

Guglielmo Marconi

No list of communications heroes would be complete without a fella named Guglielmo Marconi. And, if that doesn't sound like your ordinary, everyday name, that's because Mr. Marconi was no ordinary, everyday guy. Marconi was born in 1874, and his experiments increased the distance that radio signals could be sent without wires - from the length of a room, to the length of a long hall, to the distance from his house to a nearby field, to several kilometers! He made his first two-kilometer transmission when he was just 21 years old. The Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company, formed in 1900, set the standard for wireless communications for years to come.

Alexander Graham Bell

"Watson, come over here. I need you." These were the very first words ever spoken over a telephone. Alexander Graham Bell said them in 1876 when he invented the first phone. Soon, folks were able to communicate faster and easier than ever before. Of course, these days, telephones are all over the place. Chances are that your teacher even has one in her purse.

title: One Slippery Night
text:
Sarah looked nervously out the window of the car. The rain was coming down harder every minute, and nighttime was setting in. Mom flicked on the headlights and turned the wipers up to full speed. A big truck thundered by, sending a shower of water spraying over the windshield. For just a moment, Sarah couldn't see out the windows. It made her a little frightened, as if she were underwater. Then the windshield cleared, and Sarah could see outside again. She looked through the storm and then said, "Mom?" "Yes," said her mother from the front seat. Sarah continued, "How are you doing on this slick, wet road? Are you all right?"

Mom didn't have time to answer. Another huge truck barreled by, showering the car with water. In the moment before the windshield went clear again, the car began to turn and slide. Mom gripped the steering wheel as the car spun slowly around on the slick road, sliding forward and off the shoulder to the right.

Sarah screamed. It seemed like this would be a big wreck, and they'd be in the center of it. But almost as soon as the sliding had started, it stopped again. The car rested, sprawled at an awkward angle on the gravel by the side of the road.

Mom shouted into the backseat, "Sarah, are you all right?" "Fine, Mom," replied Sarah. "I think we blew a tire," said Mom. "And the nearest phone's miles and miles from here."

Sarah began to cry. She felt like she and Mom were lost and alone in a broken car with the rain pouring down. "Sarah, honey, it's going to be all right," said Mom.

She reached into her purse and grabbed her cell phone. Quickly, she dialed a number. Then she spoke. Sarah thought by the way that Mom was talking that her dad was on the other end of the line. They spoke for a moment or so, and then Mom hung up and turned to Sarah.

"Everything's going to be all right. Dad's coming with a spare and the other car. Good thing I had my phone with me. You know, if this had happened 10 years ago, I wouldn't have had a phone in the car with me!"

Sarah smiled. Dad's coming, she thought, with a spare tire! That call was going to save them a whole lot of waiting in the rain. Suddenly, as surely as the rain outside washed down the gutters on the side of the road, Sarah's fears had been washed away too by Mom's handy phone.

Critical-Thinking Question: What might have happened in the story if Sarah's mom hadn't had a cell phone? How would our lives be different if we didn't have convenient ways of communicating? What things would change?

title: Owensboro
text:
It's funny how Mother Nature can shape the history of an area. Take the area around Owensboro, for example. The Ohio River flows just north of town and has helped form the history of this place. The river is what began to bring to this area the rich economy it enjoys today. And though the river is older than any humans can remember, the human history around here is pretty interesting too.

In the same region, the town of Henderson boasts the oldest city park west of the Alleghenies. James Audubon, the famous wildlife artist, roamed through the woods here before he had a bird society named after him. In nearby Elizabethtown, you'll find treelined streets once walked by George Armstrong Custer. You might even see where a fellow named Thomas Lincoln did carpentry work for people while he raised the future president of the United States. Can you guess which president that was?

title: How does communication affect business in our state?
text: The communication industry helps people do business in our state in many ways. Let's look at just one, for example. Businesses around here communicate what they offer to their customers by placing advertisements in newspapers, on the radio and in the middle of TV programs. You may think that those ads are annoying sometimes, especially when they come at the most exciting part of your favorite show. But the truth is, those commercials are an important part of letting you know about the business going on around you. In fact, they're important enough that businesses are willing to pay big bucks for just a little bit of advertising time. For example, if you want to put one 30-second commercial on television during a big television event (like the Super Bowl, for instance), you'd better have pretty deep pockets; it could cost you $1 million or even more!

title: The Pheasant
text:
If you want to see a bird with a real world-traveling history, just take a look at the nearest pheasant. These feathery friends were originally found only in Central Asia. Then, about 2,000 years ago, Romans traveling through Asia brought some pheasants to Europe. The pheasants you see around here are called ringnecks. They were first brought here in the 1800s.

Like many other types of birds, male pheasants are usually brightly colored with blue-green feathers on their heads and colorful bodies. Females, on the other hand, have dull-colored feathers to help them blend in with the grass around them. This makes it easier for them to protect their chicks.

Pheasants spend most of their time on the ground, but sometimes they take to the air for short, fast, noisy flights at up to 40 miles an hour. Maybe you've been walking through a field and scared a pheasant into the air. A scared pheasant will fly up so quickly and so loudly, it can scare the bee-jeebers out of you.

title: Let's Write
text: It’s the year 2035, and you have invented a new way to communicate. What is your invention and how does it work? How does it affect the world around you? How does it affect your state’s business and how you interact with people? Do you become famous from your invention? Write down everything you can about your invention!

title: Language Arts Connection
text: Use any color to circle or highlight three relative pronouns (who, whose, whom, which, that, etc.) in this week’s magazine. Underline the related noun. (CC ELA L.4.1)

title: Kentucky Industry and Agriculture
text:
Have you ever walked through your neighborhood and seen clouds of dust or heard the rumble of big tractors, the whirring of saws and the pounding of hammers as a new home goes up for a family to live in? Have you ever seen boats come up the Ohio River filled with all sorts of stuff stashed away in the holds? Have you ever heard the honking of a semitruck loaded high with chickens on their way to be fried? Everywhere you look, you can see signs of industry. Products made, grown, found or dug up right here in Kentucky are finding their way to other places.

Many people outside of Kentucky think our state is only about tobacco and race horses, but they're only partly right. It's true that raising and racing horses is a way of life for many Kentuckians, and tobacco is certainly a "cash crop" around here, but there's much more to Kentucky industry than that. People all over the country use steel forged over Kentucky coal fires, operate washing machines made in Kentucky and live in houses built from Kentucky wood—often without even knowing it. Some folks even live their lives with new hearts transplanted inside them here in Kentucky. In this issue of Kentucky Studies Weekly, we'll take a good look at just a few of the industries making life in Kentucky the way it is. Some of these industries are new to the state, and others have been around as long as there have been people here. But they're all important to the Bluegrass State and to the world.

title: Milk - What's Your Favorite Flavor?
text:
Kentucky produces more than 1.46 billion pounds of milk each year. Plain, ordinary white milk is still the most popular flavor, but Kentucky dairy farmers are getting very creative about the milk they sell. Chocolate, strawberry, vanilla, cookies and cream and even root beer milk are all making their way to tables across the state.

Why all the unusual flavors? Most children drink milk, but many kids don't drink enough. Kids your age need to drink at least four glasses of milk each day to get the calcium they need for healthy teeth and bones. Most kids don't drink nearly that much.

Have you tried some of the new milk flavors? You have probably tried chocolate and strawberry milk, but what about root beer, mango or strawberry-banana? Dairy producers hope that by adding new flavors to their milk, kids will drink more.

Flavored milk has a bit more sugar than plain white milk, but it is still very good for you. Flavored milk has the same important nutrients as white milk, including calcium, vitamin D, vitamin A, vitamin B12 and potassium. Many Kentucky schools are now offering flavored milk so kids will drink more of this healthy liquid.

No matter the flavor, milk is still one of the healthiest drinks around. What is your favorite flavor?

title: Industry and Agriculture
text:
Kentucky's Tourism

There's at least one industry in our state that depends on our place being interesting to people from other places. And when it all comes down to it, Kentucky must be a pretty interesting place. After all, tourists who visit here pump $1 billion into our state economy every year. And it's no wonder! With Civil War battlefields, 28 state parks, lakes for fishing and boating, terrific old homes and historical sites, Kentucky ought to please just about anyone who comes along. That's not to mention one-of-a-kind Kentucky attractions like the famous Mammoth Cave (brought to you by Mother Nature) and the Kentucky Derby (brought to you by some of the finest horses anywhere).

Kentucky's Famous Horses

What's the most exciting two minutes in sports? In other places, folks might say that it is the last two minutes of the Super Bowl or the last couple of free throws of the NBA playoffs. But here in Kentucky, we know better! Folks from the Bluegrass State know there's no bigger kick in the sports world than the Kentucky Derby. And don't let the grace and style of those horses fool you - they represent big industry in these parts. We're talking about the horse-raising industry, of course. Why do so many breeders of fine thoroughbreds like Kentucky so much? Well, it isn't for the scenery, though that's part of it. The soil in Kentucky's bluegrass region is full of phosphate. Phosphate is in the water and the grass as well. This may come as a surprise to you, but drinking that water and eating that grass make for terrifically strong bones. And terrifically strong bones make for terrifically fast racehorses. It just goes to show you, sometimes the key to big Kentucky industry is a gift from Mother Nature herself.

We Make Fast Cars

ZZZZZZooooooooooommmm! What was that speeding by, whipping your hair around your face like a high wind? A speeding bullet? A locomotive? A bird? A plane? Superman? Nope. It was a speedy Corvette, taking its owner on the ride of a lifetime. These classy cars are famous pretty much anywhere, and people have been paying big bucks for a long time just for the chance to drive one of these machines. You might see more of them in Kentucky than in most other places. That's not because more people drive them here; it's because Bowling Green, Kentucky, is the only place they're made - that's right, the only place on Earth.

Kentucky's Black Gold

Ever heard of a fellow named Jed Clampett? Well, one day he was shooting at some food, and up from the ground came a bubbling crude (oil, that is - black gold, Texas tea). Not everyone is as lucky as the Beverly Hillbillies stumbling across oil by accident. Folks in Kentucky have been drilling for the stuff on purpose since the 1800s. The problem is, these days folks are finding better and larger supplies of oil in other places around the world. What's a state to do when no one wants its oil? Better have a backup plan. And luckily Kentucky's Eastern Mountains are full of natural gas. There's plenty of demand for that. What happens when the natural gas runs out? Well, it hasn't happened yet, but who knows what Mother Nature's next underground surprise will be?

Don't Forget Service!

Some people don't have "things" like potatoes, pounds of hamburger, computer chips or truckloads of plastic bags to show for their work. Instead of things, some people produce happy, comfortable Kentuckians. Think about the bagger at the supermarket, or the police officer who helps keep you safe or even your schoolteacher. They don't produce products. Instead they provide what we call services.

The service industry is by far the biggest way for people to make a living in Kentucky. Maybe that's because it's so easy to find ways to serve people. Anything that helps make life around here more pleasant (everything except things, that is) can be called a service. Can you think of some other examples of service?

Kentucky Coal Mines

Here's another Kentucky industry you'll really dig: the mining industry. As early as 1750, folks have reported finding coal in the hills of our state. Later, in the 1800s, companies began to get organized mining the stuff. For all their organization, they stripped the land pretty bare, digging it all up and even cutting down whole forests, using the wood to build railroads to haul the stuff. But two things have happened since then that slow down the mining a bit. First, folks don't use anywhere near as much coal as they once did. Mines these days shut down when the demand for coal is low and then reopen when folks need more. Second, they're much more careful how they get the stuff. Before digging it up, they haul off the topsoil and store it safely away. Then, when the coal is all mined, they bring the topsoil back and smooth the ground over like nothing ever happened. Kentucky produces about 20 percent of all the coal used by the United States. The United States is a pretty big place, so coal is still a pretty big deal around here.

title: Sharing Public Space: Susan B. Anthony and Equal Rights for All
text:
From the time she was a young girl, Susan B. Anthony believed that what was open to one person should be open to all people. As a teacher, she felt that having separate schools for girls, boys and free African Americans was not fair. She believed that the minds of all genders and races were equal and that education should be equal, too.

As Susan grew older, she joined other fights as well. She hated slavery and thought working women should be paid more money. She began fighting for women's suffrage, or the right for women to vote. She once was arrested for voting illegally and was fined $100. She wouldn't pay the fine. She said, "Trust me that as I ignore all law to help the slave, so will I ignore it all to protect an enslaved woman." Until women were allowed to vote, just like men, Susan felt they were no better off than slaves. She fought for this right until her death in 1906, but at that time, women still couldn't vote.

Susan's efforts finally paid off when the 19th Amendment to the Constitution was passed in 1920. It gave all American women the right to vote. In her honor, the amendment is also called the Susan B. Anthony Amendment.

Near the end of her life, Susan wrote, "The older I get, the greater power I seem to have to help the world; I am like a snowball - the further I am rolled the more I gain."

title: Louisville Had Changed So Much
text:
Old Jack Davis didn't recognize much as he drove his slow wagon through the streets of Louisville. After all, he'd been living on his small farm in the Smoky Mountains for the last 30 years, and he hardly ever left the hills for anything. But now, here he was in Louisville, the town of his birth, to visit his daughter, Mary, and her husband. A new baby had been born, his first granddaughter, and Jack smiled when he thought of her. Jack reined up his team in front of his daughter's home, noticing the lights burning merrily in the windows. Mary saw him from the window and ran outside to gather her dear old father in her arms. She practically carried him through the front door, and then there were embraces and greetings from everyone. Other relatives and friends had gathered to celebrate the new birth. Then, from another room, Jack heard a baby's cry. The room fell silent. "Oh, Father, it sounds like little Anna is awake! You can see her!"

Mary led her father into the quiet dark of the baby's bedroom. Jack asked Mary for a candle to see the child, but she only laughed gently. Jack tiptoed toward the sound of the little cries. Suddenly, the room was filled with light. Jack jumped back and looked frantically at the ceiling, muttering something about lightning and how he hadn't even seen the storm coming. But the room stayed bright, lit steadily as a lamp. It was enough to turn Jack's attention away from his new granddaughter, as he wondered how the room could be lit so suddenly and so brightly with no lamp. It seemed brightest right around one glass ball, which was on the ceiling in the center of the room.

"Father, is something wrong?" Mary asked. "Where's the light coming from?" asked Jack, more confused by the minute. "Oh, Dad, I forgot. Louisville's got electricity these days. Watch this. I'll show you." She moved to the wall and pressed a button. There was a soft click, and suddenly the room was as dark as midnight. Jack couldn't help but shout out, "Hey!" which set the baby crying again.

"Oh, I'm coming, dear," said Mary, and with another "click," the room was bright again. Jack was shaking now, but he calmed down as Mary, smiling, handed little Anna to him. As he gazed into her tiny face and then up at the mysterious, bright glass bulb above him, Jack Davis knew that it was more than just his family that was changing. He had come back to the city where he'd been born, but he had found a strange new world.

title: Integrity
text: What does it mean to have integrity? It means that you make your actions match what you say and believe. Integrity is one of the most important character traits a person can have. Here’s an example. A man named Ascensión Franco Gonzales was walking in Los Angeles one evening in 2001 and came upon a bag of money. It was not just a couple of bucks, but $203,000! Gonzales thought about keeping the money, but in his heart he knew it was wrong. After he heard on the news that the money was missing from an armored car, a truck that transports money from big banks, he knew what he had to do. He returned the money, even though he could have kept it. Though he did not ask for a reward, he received $25,000 for returning the money! Gonzales showed integrity because he acted in the way that matched what he believed. He knew that keeping the money was wrong, so he gave it back. How can you show integrity in your life? You can clean up your room when you tell your mom you will. You can be honest with your friends and family. You can be kind to those around you because you know that it is wrong to tease and gossip. You can make your actions match what your parents and teachers have taught you, and then you can say that you have integrity!

title: Sometimes things go well in the world of industry. Was there ever a time when that wasn't so?
text:
Some of your ancestors remember living during a difficult time in our country called the Great Depression. It was a time of little money and few jobs. During the Depression, it was hard for many people to find homes to live in, clothes to wear or food to eat. The Great Depression hit the country in 1929 when the stock market collapsed. After that, the money people had invested in America's businesses became, quite suddenly, mostly worthless. The Great Depression lasted for about 12 years.

During this time, people were very careful not to waste anything. One out of every four people didn't have a job. Many business people, who were previously very wealthy, did anything they could to earn money, like selling apples or pencils on the streets. Things are different now, and it's a good thing! But any time the economy in our nation takes a little dip, some people get nervous, especially those who remember the Great Depression.

title: The Bobcat
text:
What sound does a bobcat make? Some people call it a "squall," and that's actually a pretty good description. If you say "squall" in a loud, hissing, whispery voice, you're making a bobcat sound - or as close to it as a human can get.

Bobcats live in swamps, mountains and wooded or shrubby areas. Once upon a time, you could find them all over North America, from Canada all the way to Mexico. Now, you can find them in the East and the West, but there are not many in the Midwest.

If you want to see a bobcat, we have some advice for you. Go to the zoo. In the wild, these critters are dangerous. If you happen to see one in the wild, it'll probably be at night. That's when they do most of their hanging around. Bobcats are great climbers and can swim as well.

Bobcats cause quite a stir among humans. Farmers tend to be angry at them because bobcats sometimes eat their livestock. Some people trap them to collect their skins. Wildlife-conservation groups are against that kind of thing. Most bobcats are too.

Do you like being an industry leader? What is your favorite product or service that your company offers to the public? Why do you think your business grew so fast?

title: The Wonderful Hall of Wonderful Women
text:
Welcome boys and girls to the Wonderful Hall of Wonderful Women, the place where you can find out about many of the great women who have helped make Kentucky such a great state. There are all kinds of women from many occupations. There are governmental women, athletic women, educational women and women who were involved in many different aspects of life.

As we take a stroll down the hallways, notice the pictures of these beautiful, powerful, intelligent and important women. All of them helped in one way or another to make Kentucky the state that it is today.

The first portrait we see here is Carolyn Bratt. Carolyn was born in Suffern, New York, and has lived in Kentucky for more than 30 years. She is known as a tireless fighter for civil rights in general and women's rights in particular. She obtained her law degree from Syracuse University College of Law in 1974 and joined the faculty at the University of Kentucky Law School in 1975. She was the first woman on the staff to earn the rank of full professor. She was one of the first women to practice law in Lexington and was one of the first women to serve as a faculty representative to the University of Kentucky Board of Trustees. She helped develop the University of Kentucky's policies on sexual harassment for staff, students and faculty.

Another portrait we see here is of Cynthia Beasley. Cynthia is the president and chief executive officer of ChangeMasters, Inc., a human resources firm in Lexington. Her company works in a variety of areas. She has volunteered countless hours to improve diversity (being different) and working conditions for minorities in Lexington. She has helped the Central Kentucky Chapter of the National Association of Women Business Owners with diversity training and has worked with the Lexington Chamber of Commerce to help minority businesses. She has a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of Kentucky, a master's degree in human resource development, and is working toward a doctorate degree from George Washington University.

Many other women have helped make Kentucky the great state it is and deserve to be in the Wonderful Hall of Wonderful Women, but we just don't have enough room for them all. So keep on turning the pages and find out about some of the great women of our great state.

title: Spotlight on Kentucky Women
text:
As we take the time this issue to learn all about famous Kentucky women in history, let's take a look at two important Web sites to learn more about women in the world and Kentucky.

The Kentucky Commission on Women (KCW) is a state agency that focuses on the improvement of women through services and information. It was started in 1968 after four years of studies showed that women in Kentucky really needed a permanent agency.

You can visit the Kentucky Commission on Women's Web site at www.women.ky.gov. This Web site includes links to events, meetings of special women's groups and even several state monuments and displays dedicated to Kentucky's wonderful women.

title: Great Kentucky Women
text:
1. Laura Clay: Leading the Way

Cassius M. Clay, the famous abolitionist, wasn't the only member of his family who knew how to fight for important causes. His daughter, Laura Clay, turned out to be pretty good at it too. When her parents divorced, Laura was troubled, but her confusion and anger didn't get her down for long. Instead, she turned it right around and used it to help fight against injustices toward women and children. That was a long time ago. After all, Laura Clay died in 1941. But even today, we're feeling the effects of her work and of the work of folks like her. What do you have to thank her for? Well, because of her, women have equal property rights with men. Women can vote for superintendents of schools. Women can even get into colleges that were once only for males. What thanks did Ms. Clay get during her lifetime? Well, in 1920, she received one vote from someone in the Democratic National Convention who wanted to nominate her as a candidate for president of the United States. It was the first time that had happened to a woman.

2. Mary Breckinridge: FNS Founder

For a long time, Leslie County had the highest childbirth death rate in the whole nation. But in 1881, a child was born- and survived- who would grow up and change all that. Her name was Mary Breckinridge, and she had a healing idea. She imagined rural Kentucky as a place where even the most isolated mothers could get help from a doctor, nurse, or midwife when they needed one. In 1925, she started the Kentucky Committee for Mothers and Babies. Nowadays, folks call it the FNS, or Frontier Nursing Service. Thanks to Breckinridge's plan, nurses were never more than six miles away from where someone might need them. The FNS served an area of 1,000 square miles and brought the death rate down to well below the national average. Mary Breckinridge died in 1965, but her legacy lives on in the FNS, which is still serving people in that same region today.

3. Patty Loveless: What a Voice

Patty Lee Ramey loved to sing and had a terrific voice. There was only one problem: She was so shy that when she sang for her family, she made them sit in the other room, within earshot but out of sight. Still, her shyness was no match for her dreams. Armed with a guitar and a handful of songs, she hit the road for Nashville. Though becoming a star is tougher than anybody thinks it is, Patty's move paid off in the end. Today, she has 14 Top-10 hits (7 of them are No. 1 hits) and fans from Tennessee to Timbuktu. These days, you and I know her as Patty Loveless, and anyone who has ever heard her voice coming out of the radio is sure glad she overcame her childhood case of shyness.

4. Mary Todd Lincoln: First Lady

Sometimes, it's just impossible to please everyone. Kentucky lady Mary Todd Lincoln, the wife of President Abraham Lincoln, understood this pretty well. When she entertained at the White House, folks said she was too extravagant. When she toned things down, other folks said she was shirking her social duty. During the years of the Civil War, Northerners suspected her of treason because she was from the South. Southerners, on the other hand, called her a traitor to her birth because she lived in the White House. That's tough stuff to go through. By all accounts, Mary Todd Lincoln had unwavering faith in her husband, and he had unwavering love for her. Here's what he had to say about her: "My wife is as handsome as when she was a girl, and I fell in love with her; and what is more, I have never fallen out."

5. Loretta Lynn: A Coal Miner's Daughter

The world may not know that Butcher Hollow, Kentucky, is the birthplace of one of the greatest country singers ever, but most folks know what Loretta Lynn's dad did for a living. A terrific song, a terrific book and a terrific movie all have the same name: "Coal Miner's Daughter". Though she's sung it 1,000 times or more, Loretta still gets a tear in her eye when she sings the song about her hometown and family. The road since then has been long and adventurous, and Loretta Lynn has shouldered her share of hard work. She kicked off her own career, taking records around to local radio stations herself and talking DJs into playing her songs. These days, she still loves singing the songs that made her a household name, but there's one difference. Now she doesn't have any trouble at all getting people to listen.

6. Martha Layne Collins: Governor

Martha Layne Collins wasn't always interested in politics. She was content for awhile to do a job that you get to see a little bit of every day - she was a schoolteacher! None of you would ever have had her for a teacher, though. She left teaching nearly 30 years ago to begin a long and successful career in politics. At first, she helped other people get elected, people like Governor Wendell Ford and Senator Walter Huddleston. But less than a decade later, in 1979, it was Martha Collins's turn to step into the spotlight. First, she was elected as Kentucky's lieutenant governor. Four years later, she was sitting in the governor's chair. Being elected governor is no small feat. She was only the third woman in the history of the United States to do it.

7. Georgia Davis Powers: Civil Rights Senator

What do you do to stand out if you're the only girl in a family of eight brothers? Well, if you're Georgia Davis Powers, you might just march with Martin Luther King Jr. as a civil rights activist. If that's not enough, you might become the first African American woman from Kentucky to serve as a member of the U.S. Senate. But if you were really like Georgia Davis Powers, those things would come only after a lot of other exciting things. For example, how many people do you know whose homes were blown away by a tornado? That happened to Georgia's family in 1925. In addition to her successful political career, she has worked as a telephone operator and a riveter as well as in 30 more jobs.

8. Diane Sawyer: America's Newswoman

Diane Sawyer was the anchorwoman for World News with Diane Sawyer on ABC. She was born in Glasgow, Kentucky, and was raised in Louisville. Did her life as a household face begin when she was crowned America's Junior Miss in 1963? Who knows? One thing's for sure: Her career as a journalist took her where few have gone before. Who else has interviewed women in a maximum-security prison? Who else has interviewed Cuban leader Fidel Castro? Who else has talked on national television with Michael Jackson? The list of her accomplishments goes on and on. But as famous or as powerful as her guests on television are, it's hard to become more famous than the woman doing the interviewing, Kentucky native Diane Sawyer.

title: Brittany's Hard Day
text:
Brittany stormed in the front door and slammed it behind her. It had been a lousy day at school, and she didn't want to talk about it. She threw her books in a pile on the living room floor and stomped up the stairs into her room. She flopped on the bed. Her face was hot, and she was glad no one had followed her up there. She was afraid if she started talking about her day, she wouldn't be able to keep the tears from flowing.

It seemed like a long time before there was a knock on her door. Her mother poked her head in. "Brittany, do you want to talk about..." Brittany interrupted her in an angry voice, "I don't want to talk about anything, Mom. Leave me alone, will ya!" Brittany heard the door shut softly behind her. She had half hoped her mom would stay. Maybe she didn't care about her either. Brittany couldn't hold it back any longer. Tears fell on her pillow, and she pounded a fist on the floor as she lay there. A moment more, and she had cried herself to sleep.

It was late in the afternoon when Brittany woke up. The house smelled terrific. She timidly left her room and went downstairs. Her schoolbooks were piled neatly on the coffee table. There was a tray of soft cookies on the counter in the kitchen, and beside them a note. "Brittany," it said, "Lisa's mom told me your lunch money was stolen. Bum deal, eh? I'm out in the garden. Have some cookies and come get me in plenty of time to use the movie tickets on the counter - sooner, if you'd like to talk. Love, Mom." There was a smile drawn below the signature.

For the first time that afternoon, Brittany smiled. She piled some cookies on a plate, got down a couple of glasses, filled them with milk, and arranged the whole thing on a tray. "Aw, Mom, you're a hero! You know that? A total hero!" she said as she walked out the door toward the garden, her smile growing bigger with each step.

Critical-Thinking Questions: Why was Brittany so upset? How did her mom handle the situation? Why was Brittany's mom a hero to her? How can you help someone who may be having a bad day?

title: Good Judgment
text: Have you ever felt sure you were right about something that your parents thought was wrong? Maybe you really think you should be allowed to stay up until 2 a.m. and eat all the popcorn, candy and ice cream you can. Sounds good to you, right? Well, you might rethink that decision when you wake up with a terrible stomachache from the sweets and very red eyes from not getting enough sleep. You might say you used bad judgment in that situation. Well, one great character trait to develop is good judgment. You could use good judgment by telling yourself you'll have one bowl of popcorn and one scoop of ice cream and stay up till 10 p.m. watching a good movie. That way, you won't be too tired to have a productive day tomorrow. But good judgment is used in lots of other situations, like choosing whom you hang out with, what kinds of movies you watch and books you read, what kind of language you use and pretty much every other decision you can make in your life. The key to good judgment is not necessarily going for the decision that will make you or those you want to impress happy but what will be best for you in the long run. It might take some work, but using good judgment definitely pays off in the end. Just ask the kid with the stomachache and droopy eyes. He's wishing he'd used a little better judgment!

title: When did women get the right to vote?
text:
Women fought for the right to vote for years and years before it was actually given to them. It's too bad it took so long, don't you think?

Voting is an important way for citizens in the United States to be involved in running the country, and women have worked hard right from the beginning to make this country a great one. Women all over the country were given the right to vote when the 19th Amendment to the Constitution was ratified (officially signed) into law in 1920. About time, right? The amendment reads like this: "The right of the citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any state on account of sex." That means that it doesn't matter whether you're a man or a woman. You can vote!

title: Raccoon
text:
The raccoon is a common animal in Kentucky. It is a nocturnal animal, which means that it likes to sleep during the day and prowl during the night. The raccoon is sometimes called "coon" for short.

The raccoon has a heavy, rounded body and a pointed face. Its front paws look like hands, and the raccoon uses them very much like we use our hands. The raccoon is also covered with heavy gray, brown and black fur, and it has a large, bushy tail with black rings along it. The raccoon is usually 1 and 1/2 to 2 and 1/2 feet long, and its tail adds another 8 to 12 inches to its length. The raccoon is sometimes compared to a robber because it has a black "mask" of fur around its eye area. It can be found stealing corn and other vegetables from the gardens of local farmers.

Raccoons are good climbers, and they often build their nests in hollow trees. They live mostly in wooded areas and feed along lakes and streams. They eat all kinds of foods, including nuts, seeds, fruits, eggs, insects, frogs and crayfish. When the raccoon is near water, it likes to wash its food by dipping it in water before eating it.

title: Pounded Plant Prints
text:
Materials

• plain, ink-free newsprint (several sheets)

• freshly picked leaves and flowers

• 100 percent cotton fabric

• washing soda

• a hard surface for hammering (sidewalk or sturdy table)

Instructions

1. Go outside and gather plants. Look for thin plants with flat leaves (plants with juicy leaves will not work).

2. Cover a hard surface with newsprint pages (eight to 10 will work best). Then place a piece of fabric on the newsprint.

3. Place a leaf or flower on the newsprint and cover the plant with a double layer of newsprint.

4. Hammer the newsprint that is covering the plant so the tannin coloring in the plant will transfer to the fabric. Carefully lift the paper cover to see if the plant design is transferring to the fabric.

5. Make a solution containing 1/2 cup washing soda and 2 cups of water. Dip the cloth into the solution. The washing soda will set the green tannin of the plant into the fabric. (All flower petals will set differently. Some pinks and purples will set aqua and bright blue.) After setting the colors, wash your fabric in soapy water, rinse it and let it dry.

title: Let's Write
text: The year is 2050. You go to the mailbox and find a letter from your school. Wow! What could it be? It’s been 40 years since you went to that school. You open the letter and find that your teacher from way back when you were a student is writing a book about all the students she ever taught. Your teacher wants you to send a 200-word article describing what your life has been like. Write about your career and your accomplishments. What have you done that has brought you the most happiness?

Try to figure out the meaning of the words by reading the other words and sentences around them. Write what you think the words mean and compare your definition to a dictionary definition.
