Markets bring consumers to producers and producers to consumers. Through these markets, exchange economies came to be. No one ever really invented an economy. It just happened as people traded with each other. As markets grew larger, many people began asking questions. Then they studied people as they traded for goods and services. That study is what we now know as economics.

One of these early economists was named Adam Smith. He was born in Scotland in 1723. He went to the University of Glasgow at the age of 14! That seems very young to be going to college now, but it was very common back then. He graduated, and then went on to Oxford University in England. He became a professor and began looking at exchange markets. Smith didn't know it, but he was really starting the study of economics. In 1776, he put out his book, "The Wealth of Nations." The book is about what he had found through 30 years of research.

Smith suggested that there was an "invisible hand" that guided trade in an economy. Think about sitting down to enjoy a nice bowl of tomato soup. Most people give little thought to all the steps and processes that go into putting that soup on your table. There are the tomato farmers and the soup makers. There are the marketing team who advertises the soup and the people who design the label. Don't forget the truckers who transport the soup. How about the grocery store that places it on the shelf? Who controls all of this? Is there someone leading each company? How does it all work?

According to the "invisible hand" theory, no one directly oversees companies trading with each other. Instead, markets bring people together. From that, producers find other producers to assist them. Then consumers are guided naturally to buy those products that they need. This process of trading in economy is known as voluntary exchange. When this is the main way of organizing production of goods and services, economists call it a market economy. These early ideas from Adam Smith still affect economists today, more than 200 years later. It is because of his work and study that Adam Smith is know as the Father of Economics.

title: What is Democracy?
text:
Democracy is government by the people. The word democracy comes from two Greek works. Demos means "the people," and kratos means "authority." The Greeks granted authority to the people to pass the laws. They used these two words to mean "government by the many." They did not want the government to be just a few people. They did not want the government to be a single ruler, such as a king or queen.

In those days, democracy was direct. The free people would gather to discuss and pass the laws. The people had a direct vote. Today, democracy in the United States is different. It is not direct. We just don't have room for everyone to gather in the town square. It would be nearly impossible for so many people to discuss ideas and to vote. Today, we practice representative democracy. We elect people to represent our ideas and to pass the laws. Each elected official discusses and votes for the laws of our country. Still, whichever form of democracy is used, it is government by the people. That includes you!

Sometimes during or after natural disasters, such as this ice storm in Maine in 1998, the government can help restore services.

title: Is the Earth getting hotter?
text:
It's getting hot out there, and scientists are worried. Some call it global warming. Others call it global climate change. The average temperature on Earth has gone up 1.4 degrees Fahrenheit since 1880. That may not seem like much, but it's causing other things to change, too. Arctic ice is melting fast. Polar bears and other animals could lose their habitat. Glaciers are disappearing, and coal reefs are dying. Some scientists blame global warming for the increase in extreme weather, too. They believe the changes are causing more storms, floods, wildfires and heat waves.

Most Scientists say it's our fault the Earth is getting hotter. Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide are trapping heat near the Earth. And those gases came from our cars and factories. People have cut down too many trees and caused too much pollution.

title: Beaver
text:
Did you know the beaver is the largest rodent in North America? It is 3 to 4 feet in length and weighs 40 to 95 pounds. They have a large flat tail about 16 inches long. They use their tail in water as a rudder to steer. On the land, they slap their tail on the ground as a warning of danger.

Beavers are excellent swimmers. They have webbed feet to help them swim better. They have two layers of fur. Beaver have a special oil to help them dry faster when they come out of the water.

A baby beaver is called a kit. Beaver usually have four kits. A beaver's family is called a colony.

Beavers live in lodges or burrows. They build a lodge out of branches and mud. They start at the bottom of a low creek and pile sticks upward. The whole colony works on a lodge.

A beaver has large, sharp teeth. The front teeth are always growing. By eating their favorite food, tree bark, and gnawing on trees as they build their lodges, their teeth are ground and worn so they don't become overgrown.

title: Make a Rain Gauge
text:
Materials

1 plastic bottle

scissors

bricks

a ruler

Directions

1. Ask an adult to help you cut the top half off the bottle.

2. Put it back on upside down and with the cap off.

3. Stand your rain guage outside. Put bricks around it to hold it steady.

4. Each time it rains measure how much rain has fallen, with your ruler.

title: Inferential Context Clues
text:
Did you ever ask someone the meaning of a word, only to have him answer, “Figure it out!” When you look again, there are no definite context clues. Now what? The fact is that the meaning is hidden in the rest of the words in that sentence. Sometimes, the meaning is tucked away in a whole paragraph. These are inferential context clues.

Below are three examples. Read the words around the vocabulary word and write what you think the new word may mean.

1. Brianna wanted a cookie, but the jar was out of reach. Jake, Brianna’s brother, climbed onto a chair and stretched his fingers around the jar. Just then, the chair tipped and Jake, the chair and the cookie jar came crashing to the floor. Brianna began to cry. As the noise and confusion mounted, their mother called out from the next room, “What’s all that commotion?”

Write what you think the word commotion means:

2. During a test in class, Spencer saw his best friend, Tyler, cheat. He told Tyler that if Tyler didn’t confess to the teacher, he would tell her what he saw. Standing up to Tyler took a great deal of fortitude on Spencer’s part.

Write what you think the word fortitude means:

3. Sometimes, we borrow words from other languages (exonymns). This vocabulary word is French and is sometimes followed by an exclamation point. Ashley said, “I cut a coupon from a magazine, mailed it in and — voilà! — here’s my new glow-in-the-dark lipstick!”

Write what you think the word voilà means:

title: Let's Write
text:
Some people say “If you want to see the weather in Maine change, just stick around for about half an hour.” That means our weather isn’t always predictable and must change a great deal.

Have you ever planned a family picnic, and just when you were about to eat, it began to pour? Did you spread the blanket out on your porch and have your picnic anyway?

In 200 words or less, write a story about an outing with family or friends that you planned, when suddenly the weather changed, and you had to be creative.

title: Fun Facts
text: Hawaii is home to the only royal palace in the United States. It is called Iolani and is located in Honolulu.

title: Buried Treasure in Maine
text:
The history of Maine is like a buried treasure. Much of what we know of Maine's early inhabitants comes from clues in the ground. Our history includes people who walked long distances, and plants that survived when other living things were not able to. Paleontologists are scientists who study prehistoric life forms. They have studied fossils to learn about these early forms of plant and animal life. Other clues come from artifacts (objects that people made in the past) found at burial sites. All of these things provide clues about what Maine used to be like. It also tells a little about the people who used to live here.

One of the most important ancient inhabitants of Maine is now Maine's state fossil, a plant called Pertica quadrifaria. Something peculiar about this plant is that it had no leaves! Obviously it didn't look quite like the plants that grow in gardens today. Pertica had branches. It probably grew to be about 6 feet tall. It lived about 390 million years ago. That was before dinosaurs or any animals ever saw the shores of Maine. Pertica was the largest known land plant of its time. There weren't any trees at that time. Actually, at the time that Pertica lived, there weren't any flowers, fruits or nuts either. Maybe there weren't even any insects!

Maine's motto is Dirigo which means, "I lead." Perhaps it brings to mind the Pertica. Before Pertica existed, the land was mostly barren and silent. Except for a few green rocks, the color green didn't exist on land. The climate then was very different. It was warmer, and there was not snow during the winter. Pertica was one of the first plants on our land. Without plants to eat, the animals never would have survived. These fossils, along with the study of the Earth's crust, are clues to life in ancient times.

Where are the dinosaurs? Sadly, there is a gap in the fossil record of Maine. No fossil-bearing rocks exist in Maine for the period from about 360 million years ago to about 1 million years ago. Because of this, no dinosaur fossils have ever been discovered in Maine.

Maine was once covered by the ocean so a lot of its others fossils, like brachiopods, coral and bivalvia, come from animals who were in the sea. Most of Maine's fossils date back from 500 to 360 million years ago, or even directly after the last ice age from 11,000 to 12,000 years ago. While it is rare, some fossil wood and fossils from mammoth, walrus and seal have been discovered in Maine.

title: Are Tar Pits Hiding Beneath U.S. Roads?
text:
If you live in Los Angeles, California, the answer may be yes. And those tar pits may contain the best-preserved fossils ever found! Near busy Wilshire Boulevard you can see the Le Brea Tar Pits. The area is still bubbling with the sticky tar that trapped animals up to 50,000 years ago. Scientists have found the bones of bears larger than any on Earth today, lions bigger than today's African lions and camels larger than the elephants you can see at a zoo. Over one million bones have been found in the pits so far. (No dinosaur bones have been found because they were already extinct.) And in 2006, 16 new tar deposits were found where a parking garage was being built at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. Some scientists think they will find a million bones there too.

The tar pits show that many large animals went extinct at about the same time. Why? Many scientists say evidence points to the climate change that took place at the end of the ice age. The large animals couldn't adjust fast enough to the warmer temperatures. At about that same time, man first migrated over the land bridge that used to exist between Asia and North America. Another theory is that man may have hunted many of these giants to extinction. What's underneath that road you were on when you came to school today? Maybe more than you think!

title: Productive Resources
text:
Productive resources are found in every good or service. Resources are the basic things used to make products in our community. Economists study resources a great deal and have put them into three groups. They help answer these three economic questions: How is a product made? What product is made? Who makes a product?

Natural Resources

Natural resources are unaltered or undisturbed gifts of nature. Fresh air, minerals, water and trees used for timber are all natural resources. They are things taken from the Earth that cannot be made any other way.

Human Resources

A secretary, a doctor, a mechanic and a teacher are all kinds of human resources. Human resources, or labor, require people to be creative. People must have skills and knowledge to help them put physical and mental effort into their work.

Capital Resources

The last type of resource can be found everywhere. Buildings, tools or machines people use to produce other goods and services are known as capital resources.

These productive resources are all around you every day. Let's say that you wanted to make cookies. Each of these resources would be very important. Most of what you put into the cookies - eggs, milk, sugar, salt and flour - would be natural resources. The human resource would be you making the effort to make the cookies. Lastly, your mixing bowl, measuring cups, spoon, baking sheet, mixer and oven would all be types of capital resources. All these things come together to make your product - yummy cookies! Can you think of other examples of natural, human and capital resources?

title: Other Fossils in Maine
text:
Most of Maine's fossil sites are in northern Maine. This is one of the few areas that contain sedimentary rocks (rock that is the deposited and hardened layers of dirt, silt, rock, etc.). These fossils range from 500 to 360 million years old. They are generally the shells of ocean animals. Some resemble modern clams, snails and coral. Crinoids are among Maine's most abundant animal fossils. These fossils sometimes look like plants. Some call them the "sea lily."

Scientists believe that all the land areas on the Earth were connected in a supercontinent. This was called Pangaea. This supercontinent gradually broke up and drifted apart. They believe that the continents we have today are a result of continental drift. This means the continents slowly drifted apart. This explains why the same kinds of dinosaurs are found all over the world. There have been some fossils found in Maine that have also been found on other continents.

The Age of Reptiles

The Age of Reptiles was a period in the Earth's history that began 200 million years ago. It ended 60 million years ago. Reptiles are cold-blooded creatures. They are closely related to crocodiles, snakes and lizards. Reptiles dominated the Earth for approximately 140 million years. We call this age of reptiles prehistoric. This means it was before any history was written down. The history of man has been recorded for about 6,000 years.

There were three main kinds of reptiles. Those on land were dinosaurs. Pterosaurs (TER oh sores) sailed through the air. One pterosaur you may have heard of is the pterodactyl. The oceans and seas swarmed with great sea serpents and lizards shaped like fish. These we call plesiosaurs (PLEEZ ee oh sores) and ichthyosaurs (IK thee oh sores).

Not all of these early creatures lived on the Earth for the entire 140 million years. Many went from birth to extinction at different times. Some of these dinosaurs really never saw each other.

The Age of Mammals

All of the dinosaurs disappeared mysteriously about 60 million years ago. Some scientists believe it happened suddenly. Others believe it happened over a long period of time. As the mountains built up, the climate changed. The Earth went through cold cycles. This caused ice to cover most of the world. The reptiles were cold-blooded. They did not adapt to a changing world climate. Mammals, on the other hand, are warm-blooded and produce their own heat. Plus they are covered with hair. They had bigger and much better brains for taking care of themselves. Some say they just had enough sense to come out of the cold!

The Age of Mammals lasted for 60 million years. It started with the mysterious death of the giant reptiles and went until humans started recording history. So far, humans are the only beings throughout Earth's history who have been intelligent enough to develop a written language.

title: Citizenship at Home
text:
Listening to others talk about their feelings is one way of being a good citizen at home. What if you accidentally broke your brother's new iPod? Would he feel angry? If he did, how might you be a good citizen?

A smart way to begin would be to listen carefully to how he felt about it. It is best not to interrupt. Next, in a kind voice, retell what you heard him say. Then apologize sincerely and ask what you might do to make it right. Everyone makes mistakes. You might choose to earn some extra money to repair it. Perhaps sharing something of yours would help to mend his feelings. By listening carefully and treating others fairly, we can encourage them to do the same.

title: Maclurites in the Capitol!
text:
Usually paleontologists look for fossils in the field. Lately, fossils have been discovered in the Maine State Capitol!

It seems that the floors in the capitol are black limestone tiles. They were installed during the west-wing construction from 1889 and 1890. More fossil-bearing limestone was added while the building was being remodeled in about 1909.

State geologists examined the stone tiles. They found that there are many of the snail-like mollusks known as maclurites. They were found in the stones. Further inspection revealed that there are at least four other fossil types in the floors as well.

Next time you visit the Maine State Capitol be sure to walk with your nose to the ground. See if you can spot those ancient fossils!

title: Why does oil come from the ground?
text: Scientists have learned that oil comes from organic material. That is something that was once alive! Dinosaur-type animals lived on the Earth for millions of years along with ancient plant life. Scientists naturally conclude that the remains of plants and animals over a period of millions of years created the oil. There are reserves that are beneath the ground. Since oil sources are limited, scientists are always looking for better ways to use it.

title: The Hummingbird
text:
Many skeletons of dinosaurs resemble features of the skeletons of birds today. Can you imagine the tiny hummingbird being related to a dinosaur? Well, the ruby throated hummingbird is the only species of hummingbird you can regularly see in Maine. They are metallic green on top and grayish or brownish white below. The males have a bright red throat. The females have a brownish white one. They are beautiful birds with long needle like bills. They have tongues that they use to feed on nectar.

Hummingbirds, or "hummers," are feisty birds in general. They make long, shrill calls when they scold. You can hear their calls as they chase other hummers away from their flowers or feeders. Sometimes a mother is protecting her nest.

Hummingbirds build their nests in either bushes or trees. The mother takes care of the young. She feeds the hatchlings small insects and nectar from flowers.

A hummer, unlike other birds, can fly backward, sideways or even hover. They hover over a flower when they drink its nectar. They are especially attracted to bright red and orange flowers. They might even investigate a red hat or a red bow in someone's hair! Have you ever seen a hummingbird?

title: Lady Deborah Moody, a Dangerous Woman?
text:
In 1643 Governor John Winthrop of Massachusetts Bay Colony wrote in his journal that Lady Deborah Moody was "a wise and anciently religious woman." But Winthrop's deputy-governor called her "a dangerous woman" and told the governor that Lady Moody shouldn't be allowed to remain in the colony. Why did he think she was dangerous?

Lady Moody's religious views didn't agree with the English church, so she moved to the American colonies after her husband died. She bought a large farm in Massachusetts. She was the first woman to own land in colonial America.

The Massachusetts Bay Colony was a Puritan community, and Lady Moody's opinions didn't agree with their ideas, either. For example, she and a group called the Anabaptists believed that adults, not babies, should be baptized. To avoid conflict, she moved again.

Lady Moody led a group of people who shared her beliefs to New Amsterdam. Under her planning and leadership, the town of Gravesend (today in Brooklyn, New York) got a government grant from the Dutch in 1645. It allowed freedom of worship and self-government, which was very unusual then. Lady Moody held meetings in her home to settle disagreements and welcomed Quaker missionaries who came to Gravesend.

Was Deborah Moody a dangerous woman? To people who expected her to "leave her opinions behind her" as the deputy-governor said, she was. Lady Moody became the only woman to settle a colony in the New World. As Governor Winthrop's journal also stated, "The Lady Moody ... appears to have been a lady of great worth."

A school in Brooklyn is named for Lady Deborah Moody. If you could name a school for someone like Deborah Moody, whom would you choose? Why?

title: Language Arts Connection
text: As you read this week’s lesson, circle or highlight five verbs in any color. On a piece of paper, write a sentence for each verb using the progressive form (-ing).

title: You found an old fossil!
text: As an amateur paleontologist, you are thrilled to be the first to discover the nearly complete fossilized skeleton of a dinosaur in Maine. In 200 words or less, write about your discovery. Be sure to include the era from which the dinosaur came, what you named it, and what the translation means. Describe what your new pal probably looked like, as well as its eating and traveling habits. You may even draw your dino, if you would like.

title: Maine’s Geographical Regions
text:
There are many things to learn about the great state of Maine. There are also many ways to study those things. Often the people who do the most studying are scientists and historians. They want to know about Maine's past. They want to know about the way things are right now so they can understand why things are the way they are. One way scientists study Maine is by dividing it into regions. One kind of region is called a physical region. A physical region is a part of the state that is physically different from the rest of the state. There are three major physical regions in Maine. The other kind of region is called a tourist region. These are the regions that people like to visit on their vacations.

Regions can be made up of many things, but they always have one thing that sets them apart from the other areas. What are some of the regions in Maine? Are they physical or tourist regions? Are there kinds of plants that only grow in those regions? Are there different languages spoken? Plants and language are only two of the many ways to define a region. Yet, they tend to be two of the most common.

The first of Maine's physical regions is the White Mountain region. This region takes up much of the western and central parts of Maine. This area of the state is the most rough and thickly forested region. The mountains here are usually between 2,500 and 4,000 feet high. Mount Katahdin, which is 5,267 feet high, is in this region in the central part of the state. The mountains are made mostly of granite that has been worn down by erosion.

The second region is the New England Upland. This region covers northern, eastern, and central Maine. It is the largest natural region in the state. This region is a rolling, heavily forested plateau. A plateau is a piece of land that rises up steeply, but is flat on top. The elevation here stays mostly between 1,100 and 1,250 feet. This region has many rivers and lakes. Unique to this region are eskers. These are long narrow ridges of earth and gravel. They were left after the glaciers.

Maine's last physical region is the Seaboard Lowland. This region lies between the New England Upland and the Atlantic Ocean. It is as narrow as 20 miles in some areas. It is as broad as 500 miles in others. The Seaboard has mostly gently rolling hills, but in some places there are rugged mountains and steep hills. Cadillac Mountain, for example, is on Mount Desert Island. It is the highest mountain on the Atlantic coast north of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. It rises 1,530 feet above sea level.

How does it help to divide Maine up into regions like this? It is helpful to study areas that have things in common. Scientists can learn about what happened to Maine a long time ago by studying what it looks like now. They can know what parts of Maine were, for example, covered by glaciers the longest. It is much easier to study changes in physical regions when the scientists can compare features of those regions.

title: Tree Rings Tell an Ancient Story
text:
Could a city the size of New York City be destroyed by a drought? Many scientists believe that's what happened to a city called Angkor in what is now Cambodia. Angkor was the capital city of an empire that stretched from Myanmar (Burma) to Vietnam. This city of about 750,000 people lasted 600 years, from the ninth to the fifteenth century.

The Angkor area doesn't have the kind of summers and winters that many U.S. cities do. It has drought for about six months, and a rainy season for six months. Angkor had a complicated network of canals, reservoirs and dams to catch water during the rainy season so it could be used during droughts. The system worked well for almost 600 years.

Recently, scientists studied tree rings from 900-year-old trees near Angkor. The rings showed that year after year the droughts and the rains got more severe. Here's what scientists think may have happened: The reservoirs went completely dry during the drought seasons and the canals were badly damaged. The people of Angkor could no longer control one of their most important resources, water. Without water their civilization collapsed.

Isn't it amazing what you can learn from a tree?

title: Maine’s Tourist Regions
text:
Another kind of region is the tourist region. Tourist regions are the different areas a person might like to visit on a vacation. If Maine is divided up into different tourist regions, people can decide where to visit. If the information about the regions is made available, people can look it up to decide where in Maine to go. There are eight major tourist regions in Maine.

Lakes and Mountains Region

In the Lakes and Mountains Region, there is a lot of unspoiled mountainland. This is a great place to hike or camp. During the fall, the wooded hillsides light up with many of the wonderful colors of nature. The snowscapes are snow-covered landscapes. Here, they are enough to enchant anyone.

Kennebec and Moose River Valleys Region

Next is the Kennebec and Moose River Valleys Region. Kennebec and Somerset Counties make up this region, which offers the best hiking in Maine. It includes the Maine State Museum and the historic Fort Western. There are many museums, libraries and recreational areas here. The region's wooded hills are among its greatest treasures.

Katahdin Moosehead Penquis Region

Penobscot and Piscataquis Counties make up the third tourist region. This is the Katahdin Moosehead Penquis Region. There's plenty of parkland here for everyone to enjoy! It includes the over 200,000 acre Baxter State Park. It also has Moosehead Lake, the largest lake in the Northeast. There you will also find Mount Katahdin, the tallest peak in Maine. There is also amazing white-water rafting on the Penobscot and Kennebec rivers.

Aroostook County Region

Another tourist region is Aroostook County. This is Maine's largest and northernmost county. Here the potato fields seem endless. As the fields blossom during the year, you can enjoy the view during a scenic ride. Many Mainers also enjoy fishing and canoeing. They often go in one of the region's 2,000 lakes, rivers and streams. Tourists can do the same!

Downeast and Acadia Region

Next is the Downeast Acadia Region. This region is made up of Hancock and Washington counties. One of the most beautiful things to see in Acadia is Acadia National Park. Its landscape was carved out by the glacier that used to sit on top of Maine. Other wonderful things to see are the dramatic tides at Cobscook and Passamaquoddy bays. This region offers some of the best lobster in the country. The coast boasts whale watching, puffin watching and sea kayaking.

Mid-Coast Region

The Mid-Coast Region has many seaside resorts and charming villages. It also has glacier-carved peninsulas. There are places that bring back the atmosphere of the early days of the United States. Here, you could hunt for antiques, find an auction, visit a museum or see a play.

Greater Portland Region

Next is the Greater Portland Region. This is in southern Maine. This area enjoys four distinct seasons. There are many things to do in each of them. Maine's metropolitan area is in this region. It is located on Casco Bay, which is a gateway to historic forts and lighthouses. There are fisherman, ferries and sightseeing cruises. There are also pleasure boats, restaurants and shops. It has some nice sandy beaches as well.

South Coast Region

Last, but not least, is the South Coast Region. The best white-sand beaches in Maine are here. Old villages line the shores. Much of Maine's marine history is found waiting here. There are many festivals and theaters. There are historical museums and other things to bring Maine's culture and history to the visitor.

title: Supply and Demand
text:
To an economist, a market includes everyone who buys or sells a certain good or service. That means all of the people who are buying or selling sweaters are in the sweater market. Everyone buying CDs is in the CD market. Everyone selling hot dogs is in the hot dog market. These markets are very important as economists study supply and demand. Supply is the amount of something being offered by producers for sale. Demand is a measure of how many consumers want to buy what producers are selling. Using the hot dog example, the companies and stores selling hot dogs are supplying them. The consumers who are willing to pay for hot dogs are demanding them.

Demand is more than "wanting" or "wishing" for something. If a person wishes to buy a hot dog, he or she is not in demand. Economists do not consider people in demand until they are willing and able to buy that hot dog. It is not demand until they have the money to actually pay for the hot dog. When they can purchase the hot dog, then they are in the hot dog market.

When economists study supply, they look at several things. They look at the product being sold. Next, they want to know who is selling it. Finally, they study the market for the product. They study prices being charged for a product and how much it costs a company to make that product.

When there is a greater demand for a product than producers can supply, a shortage occurs. Shortages usually mean that prices go up as people battle to buy it. When there is a greater supply of something than a demand for it, it is called a surplus. A surplus usually means that prices go down. The producers lower the price to boost the sales.

Can you think of a recent example of a shortage or surplus?

title: Citizenship in the Classroom
text:
Learning to be a good citizen in your classroom is important. It is a good way to make sure everyone has the chance to learn. When we understand the rules of our school and respect them, we are practicing good citizenship. It will help us to understand and respect the laws of our state. We will know how to respect the laws of the United States of America. When we are good citizens, it means we respect the rights of others. We are free to make choices about how we live and behave as long as our choices don't take away the freedoms of others.

When someone is noisy in the classroom, how does that take away your freedom? Good citizenship in the classroom means many things. You can also participate in activities or help others. List some ways that you may have been a good citizen in the last week.

title: Where is the tallest mountain in the world?
text:
The world’s tallest mountain (whose bottom is the surface of the Earth) is in Asia, on the border of two countries, Nepal and Tibet. This mountain is 29,028 feet high. Whew! A long time ago this mountain was called chomo-lungma which means “Mountain-so-high-no-bird-can-fly-over-it.”

The name was changed to Mount Everest in honor of Sir George Everest, a surveyor from India. It sure is a lot easier to say isn’t it?

The mountain is so high it has snow and ice all year long, and blizzards bring high winds. It is very dangerous to climb. Many have died trying, but many have also succeeded! Where is the tallest mountain in Maine?

title: Canada Goose
text:
The Canada Goose is the most commonly seen goose in Maine. It is often found in cities and parks and is highly adaptable to humans. All Canada geese have grayish-brown bodies, black heads and necks with a distinctive white patch like a chin strap. They grow from 22 inches to 40 inches.

They mate for life and both parents take care of the young. The goslings are a cute ball of yellow fluff with brown and black markings. They are adorable and you might want to hold one....but watch out! The parents will fiercely protect them.

The geese fly in a loose "V" formation when migrating at the change of seasons. The "V" formation helps them cut through the sky more easily. The head goose gets most of the wind pressure while the geese at the back get less pressure, making it easier to fly. The head goose tires easily, so they constantly change positions so that the work load is equal.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: Choose one article from this week’s magazine and read it again. Circle or highlight the main idea of the article in yellow. Circle or highlight three or more key details in green.

title: Synonyms
text:
Synonyms are words that have the same or almost the same meanings.

Learning synonyms for common words is important. Synonyms build your vocabulary. They can make your writing more interesting (alluring, compelling, fascinating) to read.

Below, you will find a common (ordinary, average, passable) fairy tale. Work with a partner to find synonyms for as many words as possible. Rewrite the fairytale using your favorite synonyms.

Do you want to find synonyms on the computer? Use this website to see what you can find: http://thesaurus.reference.com

Goldilocks and the Three Bears

Once upon a time, there were three bears. They lived in the forest in a cute little cottage. There was a big papa bear, a middle-sized mama bear, and a little baby bear. One chilly morning, mama bear stirred up some porridge. It was too hot to eat, so they went for a walk in the forest.

While they were out, Goldilocks came right in. She saw the porridge on the table and, forgetting her manners, sat down to eat.

“Wow,” said Goldilocks, “this big bowl is really hot.” She tasted the porridge in the middle-sized bowl. It was cold.

“Oh my heart,” she said, “this bowl of porridge is too cold.” Then she spied a little bowl. She took a little bite.

“Yummy!” she squeaked. It was just right. With a big smile on her face, she ate all of the porridge. It was just perfect for a crisp fall morning.

title: Let's Write
text: Keeping a journal of your travels is a great way to save your trip so you can enjoy it over and over. You’ve just returned from a long vacation through different regions of Maine. We’d like to know what you chose to write about in your journal. What regions did you visit and how long did you stay? What did you see that you liked? Did you like the food that you found to be a regional favorite? What sorts of things were going on in the regions that you visited? In 150 words or less, write an imaginary journal entry that tells about your visit to any region in Maine.

title: Maine’s First People
text:
Long before European settlers came to North America, American Indians already lived here. Tribes living in New England and surrounding areas belonged to the Algonquian family. Those that lived in Maine were known as the Wabanaki people. But a more accurate grouping would seperate them in two main groups: the Micmac and the Abenaki.

The Micmac are mostly found in Canada. In fact, there is only one recognized Micmac tribe in America. This is the Aroostook band in northern Maine that has about 1,000 members. In 1794, Great Britain and America entered into the Jay Treaty, which let the Micmac move freely across the Canada/U.S. border.

The original, and correct, spelling of the group is Mi’kmaq. (Today Micmac is the version most commonly used.) The name comes from a word in their own language that means “allies.” There are many other spellings and names for this group. One name was Matueswiskitchinuuk, which means “Porcupine Indians.” This was because they were very skilled at making porcupine quill arts and crafts.

The Micmac language is part of the Algonquian language family. Many Micmac still speak their own language at home, but may speak with different dialects. Dialects are variations of words and pronunciations. They vary enough from place to place that even Micmac from distant regions may find it hard to understand each other. The Micmac homeland was traditionally divided into seven hunting districts, each with its own chief. They added another district in 1860.

The second group, the Abenaki, call their homeland “Ndakinna,” which means “our land.” Their name is an Algonquian word meaning “people of the dawn.” The French often called them the Loup, or Wolves. Other names were Anagonges, Aquannaque and Bashaba.

The eastern Abenaki are concentrated in Maine. Although there are several groups, the United States officially only recognizes three Abenaki tribes, the Penobscot, Passamaquoddy and Houlton band of Maliseet.

Many epidemics, or wide-spread sicknesses, caused the Abenaki population to drastically decrease. Their numbers eventually dropped from 20,000 to 5,000. Many of the New England Algonquian natives mixed with the Abenaki. They can still be found together on their reservations.

title: Have American Indian Languages Disappeared?
text:
Before English was spoken on this continent, there were hundreds of other languages spoken by the American Indians. Many of those languages no longer exist. Many more of those languages are considered to be endangered, or dying. Linguists and American Indian leaders are beginning to work together to preserve some of these languages. They also want to save the culture of these native people.

Sapulpa is a small town in Oklahoma a few miles south of Tulsa. It has large populations of the Creek and Cherokee. They are descendants of the tribes that were moved to Oklahoma. This was a part of the treaties between the tribes and the U.S. government. From 1839, when the move ended, to the 1970s, it was forbidden for any American Indian language to be spoken in the schools. Students were punished if caught speaking their native tongue. As a result, the languages of these tribes have nearly died in their communities and homes.

The word "Sapulpa" means sweet potato in Creek. In recent years this small town has started a new language program at the high school. In this program, teachers are teaching students the Creek and Cherokee languages. About 120 of the 1,000 students are of Cherokee or Creek descent. Finding teachers who both write and speak these languages is difficult. One teacher's name is Woodrow Fourkiller. The American Indians of Oklahoma are excited to see two of their languages now being preserved. They are also glad it is being taught to their children once again. A scholar once wrote that "a culture that loses its language, loses its identity." The people of Sapulpa are trying to not let that happen.

title: The Algonquians
text:
Family History

Here in this village, a woman explains the family history to her daughter - but through the father's line only.

Marriage

This young man is explaining to this girl what he will do for her if she agrees to become his wife. In this culture, there wasn't much courtship or ceremony. Marriage was often just an agreement between two people to become man and wife. A man gave a woman an animal bone to show that he would provide for the family. She gave him an ear of corn as a vow that she would grow the crops. Some tribes allowed a man to have two wives as long as the women came from two different clans.

Wigwam

The women were in charge of building their shelters. The wigwams were constructed with thin young trees. They were bent into semicircles and set into the ground by the men. The bent trees were then covered with available materials. This included birch bark, animal skins, cornhusks and reeds or grasses. They were woven into mats. The cooking was done indoors in the winter time. A hole was left in the roof to allow the smoke to escape.

Learning for Survival

This young girl is watching her mother prepare an animal. It is being prepared for its many uses. Everyone helped in the way of life. "Woman's work" and "men's work" were well defined. There were times for play, but survival was the most important thing in the minds of all tribe members.

Deer, Elk and Moose

Wild game of any size was very useful to American Indians. They were used in every part of the country. They believed the Great Spirits had blessed them with these creatures for their survival. They never killed more than they could eat. The spirit of each animal had special meaning to them. They used all the parts of each animal for many things.The animal was used for food, shelter and clothing. It was also used for tools, toys and decorations.

Corn

This food was a staple of all tribes everywhere. When it was ground, as this woman is doing, it was used in bread, soup, ash cakes and foods for the trail. A favorite way to eat corn was right off the cob or as popcorn, as we do today.

Pottery and Baskets

The American Indian people made pottery from clay. This clay was powdered and mixed with shells, gravel or sand. They used the coil method. This was common to many American Indian cultures. Baskets were constructed mainly of reeds found near streams. They were often very beautiful in addition to being functional.

Canoes

In Maine, many American Indians built their canoes of the prized birch bark. What if there were no big birch trees? They constructed their canoes of the heavier elm, sycamore or hickory bark. Sometimes they made dugout canoes from logs. The canoes were so well designed that today the design is still used.

Home of the Shaman or Powwow

A spiritual leader is called a "Shaman" or "Powwow." One lived in every village. This man's magic helped him make journeys to the underworld. He went to visit the spirits of those who had died. By going into a trance, a shaman could visit the land of the spirits. He must not accept food from them. If he did, his spirit would be captured and his entranced body on Earth would die. It was the reports of these shaman that convinced the American Indians there was life after death. The name given to the Great Spirit by the natives was "Manitou."

Visitor

This is a visitor from the Piscataway tribe to a Nanticoke village. The people were peaceful and made all visitors, even white men, feel welcome. Are they speaking some Algonkian language they both know or using the more universal sign language?

Maple Sugar

This man is carrying back to camp the final batch of maple sugar. The tribe made this in the maple groves. This was a great treat. It was well loved by all people. A feast will be held soon to celebrate the end of winter. The same methods of sap gathering are used today. It is used to make fine maple syrup and candies.

Bow and Arrow

A wood craft learned from boyhood was bow and arrow making. Bows were made by eastern woodlands tribes from springy wood such as shagbark hickory, white ash, cedar or white oak. Even young boys became expert shots and were able to kill a bird in flight at a young age. Their lives depended on how well they could hunt.

Moccasins

This footwear is a true American Indian invention. Styles varied with the tribes, yet many were soft soled and came up to the ankles. Depending on the tribe, the tops could be puckered. They may have long side flaps reaching to the ground instead. Many were decorated with flattened porcupine quills. "Moccasin" is an Algonquian word we borrowed into English.

Dogs

These animals were as common among American Indian tribes as they are today. They were used as pets, beasts of burden, sacrifices to Manitou and, under extreme starvation circumstances, as food.

title: Scarcity
text:
Have you ever been to a movie house and wanted to see more than just one movie? Maybe you saw or heard ads on television or the radio that made you want to see two or three movies, but you only had time and money to see one. How did you decide which movie to go see? Was it a hard choice? Did you go to the one your friends wanted to see? Did you ask someone who had already seen the movies for advice?

From time to time, you have to make a choice about which movie to see. A society faces the same kind of challenge deciding how to use their resources. Our resources are scarce. That means there is a higher demand for them than a supply. Sometimes, time can be scarce. That's when people don't have enough time to do everything. Sometimes, money is scarce. That's when you want more candy than you can afford, or have the money to buy.

Because our resources are so scarce, people are always making choices about how to use them. Every time you make a choice about what to buy or how to spend your time, you are making a trade-off. Let's say that you decide to spend money on candy. Then you are making a trade-off of candy for money. You have less money, but more candy.

Economists also have a name for what you give up when you choose something else. An opportunity cost is what you do not get when you make a choice. There are opportunity costs in everything. When you woke up this morning, you may have decided to sleep in. If you did, what did you give up in doing so? Was it taking a shower or eating every bite of your breakfast? You could say that the opportunity cost of sleeping in was taking a shower or eating a nice breakfast. We have opportunity costs when we buy things, too. Let's say that you couldn't decide between buying a new DVD or a new book. You finally decide to buy the DVD. The opportunity cost of that DVD was the new book. What is the opportunity cost of going to school every day? Is it worth it?

title: Citizenship in the School
text:
Learning to be a good citizen at school is something to work on every day. By now, you have practiced good listening skills. You have also worked on good behavior in the classroom. There is another way to practice good citizenship. It begins right in your own school. You can begin by respecting the property of others. Property is anything that is owned by a group or individual.

The coat you are wearing is your property.

The desk where you sit is school property.

The school building may be state government property.

Respect for property can be shown in many ways. The first is to make sure you don't harm or destroy things. Another way to show respect is to let an adult know if you see property being damaged. A third way is to take part in repairing damaged property. It's great to take care of your things. It's great to show respect for the property of others.

title: Abenaki Grow Corn and Beans
text:
The Abenaki people relied on agriculture. This is also called farming. They grew mostly corn, beans and squash. This was a large part of their diet. As a result, their villages were usually near fertile floodplains of rivers. A floodplain is a place where high waters from the rivers leave a lot of rich soil. This soil is good for growing things. The Abenaki would also hunt, fish and gather other food to eat. In some places fish and seafood were more important. In areas of poor soil, fish were often used as fertilizer to enrich the soil for crops.

For most of the year the Abenaki lived in scattered bands of extended families. They were each of separate hunting territories. These hunting areas were inherited through the father's bloodline (patrilineal). In spring and summer, bands would gather at locations near rivers or the seacoast. This was for planting and fishing. Most Abenaki villages were fairly small. They averaged about 100 people. The Abenaki usually favored the dome-shaped, bark-covered wigwam during the warmer months. In the winter they moved farther inland. They then separated into small groups of conical, bark-covered wigwams. These were shaped like the buffalo-hide tepee of the plains.

title: Where does the word ‘toboggan’ come from?
text:
Many words in American English are borrowed from other languages. Toboggan is one of those words. The Micmac people spent a lot of time hunting in the winter because animals were easier to track that time of year. They used many things to help them get around in the snow. They had snowshoes to help them walk on top of the snow and sleds to help them ride on top of the snow. A particular kind of sled to help them pull things and get around is called a "taba'gan" in their language. This is where the English word "toboggan" comes from.

When was the last time you went tobogganing?

title: Golden Eagle
text:
The Golden Eagle is a magnificent flier and a fierce hunter. It is fast enough to take many of the smaller, ground animals on the fly. That means they pick them up off the ground while they are flying. They don't land on their prey and kill them on the ground. However, they cannot carry off the larger animals, and some have attacked animals as big as a deer.

An adult is 33 to 38 inches from head to tail. It can have a wingspan of up to 7.5 feet. They are dark brown in color with a golden brown head and neck.

They build nests out of large sticks usually on a rocky ledge or high up in a large tree. They like remote open areas, mountains and forests.

You would be most likely to spot this eagle in Maine during the winter since they migrate out of Canada for the winter time.

title: Antonyms
text:
Antonyms are words that have opposite meanings.

Antonyms are words that have the opposite meaning. What is the opposite of antonym? If you guessed synonym, you are exactly right. Just as with synonyms, antonyms are useful in reading and writing.

Below, you will see word pairs that are synonyms. Write at least one antonym for each word pair. Award yourself five points for every antonym you write.

Synonyms Antonyms

sell, market ______________________

ask, request ______________________

give, grant ______________________

whisper, murmur ______________________

light, glow ______________________

opinion, belief ______________________

praise, congratulate ______________________

solid, hard ______________________

You can find antonyms, as well as synonyms, in a thesaurus. Check it out.

title: Let's Write
text: You are an Eagle flying over an Abenaki Village. What did you just see? Fly back to a tall tree with your brother Wind for a better look. What is happening in the village? What kinds of things are the people doing? What time of year is it? What do their homes look like? What do you hear?

title: Arrival of Europeans Means Problems for the American Indians
text:
When the European settlers first came to America, life for the American Indians began to change very quickly. The settlers began spreading out on American Indians' land. Some bought the land, some just took it.

When the European settlers came to the new land, they brought their customs, tools and weapons with them. They also brought their foods, agriculture and diseases. All of these things affected the way American Indians lived. For many years after the European settlers arrived, the quality of life of most American Indians was very poor. When settlers first started coming to the new country, they took more and more of the land. They learned that many American Indian customs were different from their own, which made them uncomfortable. The Europeans thought the American Indians were less important and eventually pushed the native tribes away from their land and homes.

The Europeans forced the American Indians to live on land called a reserve. That name has changed to reservation, and now American Indians can choose to live there or not.

Today many American Indians live on reservations. A reservation is federally recognized land set aside for American Indians to use. Here they have the right to practice their native customs without interference from others, including the state governments. Because the reservations are run by tribal laws rather than state laws, some reservations may choose to have casinos to help earn money, even if gambling is illegal in that state. They can also use the land like their ancestors did years ago. They don't need fishing or hunting licenses and are free to farm and grow food as they wish.

Things haven't always been this way on the reservations. And many American Indians still don't think they have all the rights they should have. The only federally recognized Abenaki tribes in America are the Penobscot, Passamaquoddy and the Houlton band of Maliseet. The Aroostook band of Micmacs are also federally recognized in America. These tribes make up one big group called the Wabanaki people.

To be federally recognized, the U.S. government must agree that a group of natives is really a tribe and that they can have the same rights as other tribes, like the ones on reservations. Reservations are considered very important today because they offer American Indians a place to preserve and practice their culture.

title: America’s Oldest Game
text:
The game of lacrosse has been around since the 15th century when American Indians first invented the sport. Lacrosse is a game where players use a stick with a net attached to toss a small rubber ball back and forth, trying to get it into a goal at the end of the field. Some people say that it is the fastest game on two feet.

In ancient times, American Indians played the game for fun, as well as for exercise. They were even known to play lacrosse against other tribes to settle arguments. Sometimes, these games ended in battles instead of celebrations. The number of players on each team varied, but there were sometimes as many as 1,000 players on each side! Today, there are only 10 players per team. American Indian lacrosse games could last two or three days, while today's games usually last about an hour.

Today, lacrosse is a growing sport in the United States. Many young people are becoming interested in the fast-pace and the skill of this ancient game. Students at colleges and universities play the sport, both on college teams and just for fun. Currently, lacrosse is played at over 500 colleges and universities in America. There are also over 1,400 high schools that offer lacrosse programs for their students. Women's lacrosse is becoming very popular with high school and college students as well.

If you think you have what it takes to play the exciting game of lacrosse, ask your parents to check to see if there are any youth programs in your city or county. You could start learning a game that has been around for centuries!

title: Maine’s Heritage
text:
Today many American Indians make a living by making and selling the things their ancestors once used in everyday life.

Changes in American Indian Culture

The American Indian culture that has been shown in movies and on stage is very different than their real everyday life. Many people don't have a clear picture of what the Abenaki and Micmac tribes of Maine are really like. This is because many Americans were intrigued by the cultures they saw in movies. Tourists wanted to visit reservations and see American Indians making baskets or guiding hunting parties up and down the rivers. Very quickly, many natives had to change the way they looked and acted around others in order to support themselves. Many natives gave up hunting and fishing to make baskets and guide tourists. William Neptune, a former Passamaquoddy governor, said "Years ago we did not have to make baskets for a living. We hunted, but those days are gone." Many natives still make a living making baskets and catering to tourists.

Wabanaki Youth Program

The Wabanaki people have developed a program to help teach American Indian youth about their heritage. Knowing more about their background helps them develop strong confidence about who they are. The Wabanaki Youth program strives to promote greater understanding between natives and others. It allows the youth to have positive cultural experiences. It also helps them share those experiences with others. The sponsors of the program want young American Indians to learn about their heritage. It is important for them to know how their ancestors lived. Knowing the crafts that their tribes have practiced helps Wabanaki understand and appreciate the history of their people. Such a craft would be canoe making. Understanding their heritage brings pride. This will help the youth step forward and correct the wrong ideas that many people still have about American Indians.

Finally, the program encourages leadership. It does this by increasing communication between Youth Councils and Tribal Councils. The Wabanaki Youth program is a strong step forward in helping all people understand the native culture.

title: Bartering
text:
Bartering is trading goods, but without the use of money. In early cultures, people were able to get many things they needed and wanted through bartering. Merchants would often travel with ships laden with goods. These goods were bartered for items that could be taken back. Then they would be either bartered for other goods or traded for money. People, towns and even countries bartered for items they did not produce or grow.

Bartering was easy as long as there was a simple trade between two people. However, sometimes bartering had to span several persons to get the goods wanted. Then it wasn't so easy. Suppose one merchant had a barrel of allspice. He wanted to trade with another merchant for some cloth. However, the merchant who had the cloth did not want or need a barrel of allspice. What do you think a good solution might have been? The people would barter for something they didn't need. They hoped they could later trade it for something they did need!

Bartering is still going on today. People, companies and even countries barter for things they need or want. Countries that raise great amounts of beef may barter with countries that grow large amounts of grain. Companies may trade services to support one another. Even children barter! When was the last time you tried talking someone out of a big chocolate chip cookie in exchange for your apple?

In Jamestown, Captain John Smith wrote about trading blue beads with the native tribes for food. The American Indians valued the glass beads, and the colonists needed food. Copper ornaments and beads were also highly prized by the chiefs of local tribes. At first, the Powhatan traded with other tribes to obtain copper. Over time, the Europeans gave copper beads and ornaments for barter. The Powhatan turned to the colonists for the copper items.

title: Citizen in the Community
text:
What things do good citizens do in your community? It's the same as being a good citizen at home and at school!

Listening carefully is very important! We can listen carefully to the local news and read the paper. One idea is to write a letter with a solution to a community problem or concern.

We can respect the rights of others by keeping the laws of the state and country.

Picking up litter in the community is one great way to show respect for property. What are some others?

A good citizen is also one who performs acts of service for others in the community. It could be as simple as shoveling snow from your neighbor's path. How about planting seeds in a public garden?

Make a goal to do at least one service project in your community this year.

title: What does ‘Aboriginal title’ mean?
text: Aboriginal title is the right present-day American Indians have to use the land of their ancestors. They want to use it in the way that their ancestors did. On a reservation American Indians have aboriginal title to the land in the reservation. They may hunt, fish or farm without licenses from the state government. They may also practice their religion. They can follow their customs without outside interference. This allows American Indians to live more like their ancestors did. Having aboriginal title to land gives them more freedom. It gives them independence to honor their heritage.

title: The Bobcat
text:
The bobcat is a carnivore of the cat family. It is about 35 inches long and is brownish with black spots and stripes. The bobcat is an interesting looking fella, from the pointed tufts on the top of its ears to the black tipped, stubby tail. It lives in shrubby areas in the West or swamps and forests in the East. It is a nocturnal mammal, meaning it is active at night.

Rabbits are its usual food, although it will eat almost any mammal, bird or snake.

Rocky ledges, hollow logs or caves are its likely den sites. Kittens are born in the spring each year.
