text: Use any color to highlight three relative adverbs (where, when, why) in this week’s magazine. Underline the clause that contains the relative adverb and circle the noun that the clause modifies.

title: Fun Facts
text: President Franklin Delano Roosevelt was related by either blood or marriage to 11 other United States Presidents. Those presidents were: John Adams, John Quincy Adams, Ulysses Grant, William Henry Harrison, Benjamin Harrison, James Madison, Theodore Roosevelt, William Taft, Zachary Taylor, Martin Van Buren and George Washington.

title: Let's Write
text:
Write, in 200 words or less, about the life that American Indians in Maine lead today.

What is education for them like, on and off of the reservation? What do children do for fun on the reservations? Why are reservations so important to the culture of the American Indians? What rights do or should the people who live on a reservation have? What can be done to help American Indians and other people understand each other better?

title: Explorers Look for the Northwest Passage
text:
What is the Northwest Passage? Why were explorers looking for it? Did they ever find it?

An explorer is a person who journeys to the unknown for the purpose of discovery. Explorers often discovered places other than what they had hoped to find. Some, like Christopher Columbus, were mistaken about what they had found.

Thousands of years ago, people knew very little about far-off places. They grew all of their own food. They made everything they needed. They had no need to travel. However, as settlements grew and developed, so did the idea of trading with people in distant places. A desire to find new places for trading or to find better trade routes encouraged exploration.

One of the greatest goals of maritime explorers (explorers traveling by sea) was to find the Northwest Passage. This fabled passage was a route from Europe to China around the top of North America. Countries wanted a northern route because Spanish and Portuguese warships blocked the Southern routes around South America and Africa.

Giovanni da Verrazano was one of the many explorers looking for the Northwest Passage. He was an Italian explorer who worked for the French king, Francis I. In 1524, Verrazano sailed on his ship, the Dauphine, right to the mainland of North America. Then he traveled upward along the coast. Verrazano explored many bays and rivers. He hoped to find the Northwest Passage. While searching, Verrazano explored the coast of Maine. Verrazano met some angry natives when he sent an armed party to shore to explore in 1524.

title: Help a Rat and Learn to Run the Country This Year!
text:
Hey, kids! I’m Revere the Rat, but you can call me Rev. I’m your online Studies Weekly friend and I need your help. You can help me get great stuff by earning points while you learn. Just scan the code or go to www.studiesweekly.com and click on my picture.

Has your family ever bought something that came with an owner’s manual? Cars, TVs and other things have an owner’s manual, a book on how to use them. Your social studies class is the “owner’s manual” for the United States of America. You’ll learn about history, geography, government by the people, and much more, so you can do a good job of running our country someday.

In America rats can’t vote, so “you the people” govern (run) the country. Someday you will be in charge of this country, and you’ll choose leaders and representatives by voting. Then you can tell the representatives you help elect how you think the country should be run. In fact, Studies Weekly kids are so smart, that many of you will someday be mayors, senators, governors—maybe even the president!

For now you have two jobs: Learn about the country and how it works and earn points for me so I can get that great stuff I told you about. It’s easy. Just scan or click and you’re on your way!

title: Explorers
text:
Who was the first person to discover the American continents? Ancestors of American Indians probably first set foot on the Americas. Scientists think they crossed Beringia sometime between 10,000 and 45,000 years ago. They would have been the first to "discover" these lands. However, when we talk about the discovery of the Americas, we mean something different. We mean discovery by people from civilizations closer to our present day. One of the first sightings with written records was that of Christopher Columbus.

There are tales of other seafarers long before Columbus. These legends are found in the history of the Welsh, Irish and Phoenicians. Ancient China and Africa also have tales.

The Vikings

Discovery of artifacts leads historians to believe that people called Vikings also saw the North American continent. The Vikings came from the area of modern Scandinavia (northern Europe).

The Vikings were not actually explorers. They were raiders. Their small ships were swift. They sailed to coastal towns. They plundered and raided villages in Europe. The Vikings were skilled sailors. They steered their ships by observing the position of the sun in the daytime. They steered by the North Star at night.

The First Explorers of Maine

The first European to actually encounter the area of Maine was very possibly John Cabot (Giovanni Caboto) of Genoa. Cabot was sailing for the British king, Henry VII. Cabot reached Newfoundland or Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, in 1497. Not much is known about John Cabot, though he was the man who established England's claims to North America. No journals or logs written by Cabot or his men survive. Still, historians have been able to put together a version of his voyages to the Americas.

We don't know for certain where Cabot first saw land, but historians believe it was between the Cape of Labrador and Maine. When Cabot returned to England, he was rewarded by King Henry VII. Henry also approved a second voyage for Cabot. This time, Cabot planned to take people to colonize. Cabot set sail, but disappeared shortly after. He was never seen again. Twenty years after Cabot disappeared, the search for the Northwest Passage would begin.

Estevao Gomes of Portugal was another explorer who left behind some clues that he had been here. He named various places along the way. Today, Casco Bay and the Bay of Fundy are places that still retain those names. Gomes scouted the entire northeastern coast of this continent. He was trying to discover the Northwest Passage. He failed to find the passage, but he did take 58 natives hostage. He took them back to Spain. There he hoped to sell them as slaves. The king ordered their release. The information brought back by Gomes and later explorers helped Spanish mapmakers draw charts of the eastern coast of North America.

Giovanni da Verrazano, an Italian explorer, was hired by the French to search for the Northwest Passage. Like the others before him, he was not successful in his search. He did, however, explore the Atlantic coast of North America.

Sir Humphrey Gilbert explored the coast. Once again, he claimed his discoveries in the name of England. Later, the French explorer Samuel de Champlain made several voyages to North America. He explored the New England coastline in 1608. Champlain, along with the Sieur de Monts, attempted to colonize Maine.

Finders Keepers

Unlike the Vikings, later explorers made claims on the lands they discovered. They usually claimed the lands they saw in the name of their king or country. With each explorer doing so, it was like a game of Finders, Keepers. Claims of new lands often overlapped. They sometimes changed hands. Several claims of the same land would cause confusion for many years to come.

title: On Being Informed
text:
As good citizens, we should be informed about what is happening around us. We should read about current events. We must also understand our history. If we do not understand what has happened in the past, then we are doomed to repeat our mistakes in the future. You have been studying about American Indians. It is important to understand their history and culture. It is also important to understand what happens when two cultures come together. Combining cultures was both productive and tragic for the American Indians.

Change can happen only when we learn what went wrong and then commit to a better future. As you read this paper each week, you will learn the history of our state. You will learn about triumphs and tragedies. We hope you will take the lessons of history seriously. Good citizens must be informed about the present and the past. Being informed will help us to remain a self-governing and free people.

title: Money
text:
When the English colonists first came to America, they brought some of the money they used back in England. They called their money shillings, pence and pounds. They soon found out it was of no use to them in the New World. The American Indians didn't care for their money. It didn't mean anything to them. Instead, the American Indians bartered with the colonists. As you can imagine, that became very hard. So the early colonists of Massachusetts started using wampum. Wampum consisted of purple and white shells. The purple ones were worth twice as much as the white ones. They used it the same way as money. American Indians had traded wampum with seacoast tribes since the 1640s. Both the colonists and the American Indians soon used it. This made for less trouble in the colonies. It was used in addition to bartering.

Economists like to say, "Money is what money does." This was as true for the American Indians and English colonists as it is for us today. Money has three main functions. First, it must be a way of exchange that people accept. This means that people have to agree on what they will use for money. Second, money must be a measure of value. This means that the people using the money must know how much the money is worth in their community. Last, money must be a store of value.

People should be able to save their money and use it later. Storing value is very hard when bartering. Often the goods or products people are trying to trade go bad before they can find someone in the market for them. For example, milk is hard to keep in hot weather. Bartering milk without a way to keep it cold for a long time would be very tricky.

Money must also be easy to carry. It must be sturdy, easy to recognize and able to be broken down into smaller parts. Our U.S. money is small. It's easy to carry and uniform, or all the same. People in the country accept it all over. You can divide it easily. This is nice for everyone because it is so easy. What if you lived in a country that used bowling balls for money? That wouldn't work very well at all!

title: The Quadrant
text: Here, the captain is taking a sighting with a mariner's quadrant. The quadrant, the compass and the hourglass were the only instruments the early explorers used to find their position and sailing direction.

title: What is hardtack?
text: Hardtack is a very hard biscuit. It is made with flour, water and salt and then baked until, well, very hard! Explorers ate it as part of their meals while aboard ships. This was because voyages were very long, and there was no means to preserve food. Sailors usually ate hardtack and salted meat. Unfortunately, sometimes the hardtack became infested with beetles or maggots. The sailors would have to remove the bugs before eating the biscuits! What do you think? Would you have wanted to eat hardtack?

title: Eastern Bluebird
text:
The eastern bluebird is found in Maine. It has a beautiful melodious whistling that heralds the spring. Bluebirds are found in orchards, in farmyards and in open woodlands, often in family groups or small flocks.

They sit on conspicuous perches, from which they drop to the ground for insects. (When they perch, note how their shoulders hunch.) They also catch insects while flying. In fall and winter, bluebirds add berries to their diet.

You will find the bluebird nested in natural cavities or bird boxes.

The male has a bright, entirely blue back and a rusty throat and chest. The female has mostly gray coloring on her back. The young birds are spotted like a typical thrush.

title: A Suffix Celebration
text:
A suffix is a group of letters added to the end of a word that changes its meaning.

You are nearly done with Word Attack strategies. What better way to “end” it than to celebrate with suffixes?

Below, you will find a short list of common suffixes and their meanings. When you think you have them down, head to the activity below and strut your stuff!

1. ly (forms adverb)

2. er, or (one who, person)

3. ion, tion, ation, ition (state or quality of)

4. ible, able (is able)

5. ness (state or quality of)

6. ity, y (state or quality of)

7. ment (forms a noun from a verb)

8. ic (relating to, forms and adjective)

9. ful (full of)

10. less (without)

11. est (most)

12. ive, ative, itive (inclined to, forms an adjective)

A Suffix Celebration Exercise

Using the suffixes above, create as many words as possible from these base words: history, father, enjoy, desperate, smart, teach, window, talk, wonder, loyal, happy, comfort.

title: Let's Write
text:
A sailor on an explorer’s ship might be at sea for two or three years. All of his personal belongings as well as his tools had to be kept in a chest. A sailor’s chest was a very sturdy wooden box with a hinged lid. It was usually painted and often had the name of the sailor and a date painted on the front as well. Not only was the sailor’s chest used for storage, but also as a bench or table.

Imagine you are about to go on a voyage to explore a new land. You may be gone for many years. In fewer than 150 words, tell what you might take in your chest and what your duties might be on the long trip.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: As you read this week’s magazine, circle or highlight five words that are new to you. Write the words on a piece of paper. Try to figure out the meaning of the words by reading the other words and sentences around them. Write what you think the words mean and compare your definition to a dictionary definition.

title: Fun Facts
text: George W. Bush is not the only son of a president to become a president. John Quincy Adams, our sixth president, was the son of John Adams, our second president.

title: St. Croix Island for the French
text:
Colonizing a new land was risky and often resulted in the loss of many lives.

By 1524, explorers for both England and France had reached Maine. They saw Maine's riches, and both countries claimed the area. The French named their land Acadia. This included portions of Canada and Maine. Pierre du Gua Sieur de Monts was a Huguenot nobleman. He led an expedition to what is now Maine in 1604. Samuel de Champlain was the navigator. Together, the two founded a settlement on an island in the St. Croix river, near the Canadian border. It was the first permanent European settlement in Maine.The settlement was not far from the modern city of Calais. It was not a success. Though the Europeans worked hard to settle, they were unprepared for the harsh winter. The climate and temperatures were too extreme and the settlers suffered greatly. The river that surrounded the island was very salty and never froze well enough to travel across it, so the people were stranded. Supplies couldn't get out to the island, and people found it very difficult to get off. Almost half of the settlers died of scurvy. Scurvy is a fatal disease caused by a lack of Vitamin C. Half of the settlers - 79 people - died. When spring warmed the settlers up, they lost no time in abandoning the settlement. Many went on to Nova Scotia.

In spite of the failed attempt at colonization in Maine by the French, just three years later the British attempted a second colony. Captain George Popham established a British colony in Maine. It was named Popham. It was near Pemaquid. While there, the settlers held a type of thanksgiving service. They also built the first American ship, the Virginia. About a year after this colony began, Popham died and the other leader, Raleigh Gilbert, left to return to Europe. Once again, the colony was abandoned. It was because of lack of leadership more than from hardship. This did not discourage the British from trying again. They sent Captain John Smith. He tried to start a colony on Monhegan, but it failed as well.

In 1629, Edward Winslow headed to Maine from the struggling Plymouth Colony of Massachusetts. He carried supplies to trade with the American Indians for valuable fur which he sent to London. The venture was successful and the Pilgrims continued to trade for furs until 1636. Maine eventually became part of the Massachusetts Colony. Pilgrims and Puritans pushed northward to settle in the Maine region.

In 1759, Fort Pownall was built in Stockton Springs, then the area from Frankfort to Searsport was settled. In 1760, eight families lived in Castine, and a sawmill was built in Carver's Harbor on Vinalhaven. By the next year much of the land east of the Penobscot River was claimed, and the townships of Bucksport, Orland, Penobscot, Sedgwick, Blue Hill, Surry, Trenton, Sullivan, Mount Desert and Steuben were established. Within the next 10 years Camden, Belfast, Lincolnville and Bangor were settled. These towns covered a lot of ground, but didn't have many people. There were only seven families on Deer Isle, 10 on Mount Desert Island, five at Naskeag, in Brooklin, and one family with five sons on Islesboro. By 1772, only 12 families were living in Bangor.

title: Making the World a Kinder Place.
text:
We sometimes wonder why bad things happen to innocent people. Although we may never understand it, we can do our best to keep things like this from happening in the future. When we do this, we are doing our part to make the world a kinder place, without anger and violence.

One way to do this is by making a plan to replace bullying and violence with kindness. The Cool to Be Kind (C2BK) program was developed to help students create programs in their classes and schools that are based on pro-kindness – doing nice things for others. Students look for ways to “pay it forward” each day. Paying it forward means that when someone thanks you for doing something nice, you ask that person to pay it forward by doing something nice for someone else. By paying it forward, kindness continues to spread across the world and people start thinking kinder thoughts and ways that they can help other people.

What are some ways you could practice paying it forward? How about doing yard work for an elderly neighbor for free? Or inviting a new student to eat lunch with you and your friends? What about giving up your seat on the bus to someone who looks tired, or helping someone pick up something they have dropped? Thinking kind thoughts and acting on them with acts of kindness is a simple change that you can do to change the world.

Teachers: Go to https://www.pifexperience.org to find out more about starting a C2BK program at your school!

title: This Land is My Land!
text:
Winter wasn't the only hardship that colonists in Maine faced. When settlers arrived from different countries, they would often have charters that overlapped each other. A charter is a letter from the king that says a person has a right to settle in a certain part of a new place. The problem was that more than one country was sending people to Maine to settle. All of the kings felt they had a claim on the same land.

France gave Pierre du Gua, Sieur de Monts rights to the area from Newfoundland to New York City, including all of Maine. In 1613, he established a trading post in Castine, which he called Pentagoet. The British were dividing the same territory. The Puritans of the Massachusetts Bay Company settled much of southern Maine and claimed the land ranging up to the St. Croix River. Samuel Waldo also received permission to settle the area. The Pilgrims were granted trading rights up the Kennebec River to Cushnoc, where Augusta is today. In 1626, Governor William Bradford received a charter for his own trading post in Castine. This made the French angry and caused tension for a while between the French and English settlers in Castine.

Charters

At the end of this article is the partial text of the First Virginia Charter issued by King James I. It gave those named in the charter the authority to settle and colonize, in the name of King James I, all land located between 34 and 45 degrees latitude and 100 miles inland from the coast of the American continent.

George Popham, who was the nephew of the Lord Chief Justice of England, founded Fort St. George near the mouth of the Kennebec River. It was here that the first ocean-going ship was built on the American continent.

What did people do about all the overlapping charters that had been given out? They fought over the land. The French seized the British trading post in Castine and set up a Fort there to protect "their land." Between 1667 and 1676 Castine changed hands from the British to the French to the Dutch to the British again. In 1745, men from Kittery, joined by Samuel Waldo, defeated the French at Louisbourg, on Cape Breton Island. This defeat effectively ended the French claim to Maine. That didn't end the conflicts over land in America between the two countries, though, which continued on until after the French and Indian Wars.

How to Read a Charter: What it Really Means

Whew! Charters can be hard to understand. The documents are formal and patterned different than our documents today.

What does all of that information mean? Well, the first thing this charter states is the name of the person who is writing the charter-James, king of England, Scotland, France and Ireland. Next are the names of the people the charter is for. This lists the people who are being given authority to go live in this area. Do you recognize any of those names? It also states they are being given this privilege because they have been good subjects (or citizens). Next it gives them permission to make colonies in the area that was called Virginia at the time. This area included part of Maine. It lists the area they are allowed to settle by giving a north and south border in latitude. These men are given the right not only to settle on the mainland, but also on the islands that were off the coast of the land they were settling on. This would include places like Mount Desert Island.

James, by the grace of God [King of England, Scotland, France, and Ireland, Defender of the Faith], etc. Whereas our loving and well disposed subjects, Sir Thomas Gates and Sir George Somers, Knights; Richarde Hackluit, Clarke, Prebendarie of Westminster; and Edwarde Maria Winghfeilde, Thomas Hannam and Raleighe Gilberde, Esquiers; William Parker and George Popham, Gentlemen; and divers others of our loving subjects, have been humble suitors unto us that wee woulde vouchsafe unto them our license to make habitacion, plantacion and to deduce a colonie of sondrie of our people into that parte of America commonly called Virginia, and other parts and territories in America either appertaining unto us or which are not nowe actuallie possessed by anie Christian prince or people, scituate, lying and being all along the sea coastes between fower and thirtie degrees of northerly latitude from the equinoctiall line and five and fortie degrees of the same latitude and in the maine lande betweene the same fower and thirtie and five and fourtie degrees, and the ilandes thereunto adjacente or within one hundred miles of the coaste thereof;

title: Entrepreneurship (AWN tre pruh ner ship)
text:
Benjamin Franklin was one of the greatest entrepreneurs in history. An entrepreneur takes risks to create something or find a better way to do something. Ben Franklin was imaginative, creative and very smart. He was able to try many things. He was respected for the things he did. When he died in 1790, Franklin was known around the world as a businessman, politician, printer and inventor.

Franklin was born in 1706. Even as a little boy, he loved to read, write and collect books. He left school at the age of 10. By the time he was 12, he was helping as a printer for his older brother, James. When Franklin was 22, he owned his own printing press and started his own newspaper, the Pennsylvania Gazette. He also printed Poor Richard's Almanack. That book became one of the most popular books in the Colonies!

Franklin soon became one of the Colonies' busiest printers. He was named the official printer for Delaware, New Jersey and Maryland. He printed money and legal documents. Franklin made so much money that he retired when he was 42. He then became a full-time inventor. Franklin invented many things, including the lightning rod!

Franklin was very important in the Colonies. He started one of the first libraries in the United States with some of his friends. He signed the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. Franklin served as an ambassador from the Colonies to France. He was the oldest member of the Constitutional Convention!

Ben Franklin did many things to be considered an entrepreneur. Like Franklin, there are many entrepreneurs today. Do the names Bill Gates, George Lucas, Henry Ford and Oprah Winfrey mean anything to you? All of these people are entrepreneurs. They brought great ideas and business to our economy. Can you think of any entrepreneurs where you live?

title: Elections
text:
Our nation's form of government is called a democracy. This means we choose our leaders through voting. Voting is always held on the first Tuesday in November. We vote for different national or state officials. The time these officials remain in office is called a term. Terms may be for two, four or six years.

Who Can Vote?

Citizens of the United States of America can vote for the leaders of their country. They must be at least 18 years old. If you are voting for a state, city or county official, you must be a resident of that state, city or county.

Where Do We Go to Vote?

Voting booths are usually found at schools or other government buildings. People vote in the booth using a ballot, or piece of paper. Recently, some states have been using electronic voting systems. You may vote only once for each office, and you do not put your name on the ballot. This is called a secret ballot. The candidate receiving the majority of the votes is elected for that term.

title: West Quoddy Head
text: This lighthouse at West Quoddy Head in the Bay of Fundy is the eastern-most point in the United States.

title: Did the Vikings have settlements in Maine?
text:
Most historians would agree that the evidence found so far isn't enough to show there were any Viking settlements in Maine.

In 1979, a Norse (Viking) penny was found in a collection of American Indian artifacts at the Maine State Museum. The find was very rare, and it was the oldest European artifact to have been discovered in North America. It was dated during the period from 1066-1093 A.D. The silver penny was from the reign of the Viking King Olav Kyrre.

While it created a sensation when it was discovered, the Norse penny is believed to have found its way to Maine through a system of trades by native tribes. The penny probably was first traded with native peoples farther north in New Foundland.

title: Blueberry
text:
The blueberry grows very well in Maine. The cool moist climate here along with the perfect soil is ideal for growing these yummy berries.

Blueberries in Maine can be either the highbush or lowbush variety.

The highbush gets to be from 5 to 10 feet tall with leaves that are elliptical, smooth and green. Its blossoms are vase-shaped and vary in color from white to pink. The color of the berries varies from blue to blue-black. It grows best in swamps and moist woodlands

The lowbush gets to be from 3 to 15 inches tall with leaves that are bright green and shiny, and edges that resemble very fine teeth. Its blossoms also vary in color from white to pink. The berries are a blue-black color. It grows well in bogs, tundra and dry sandy flats.

title: What are Homophones and Homographs?
text:
Homophones and homographs are the same but different! To find out the meaning of a word, carefully read the words and sentences surrounding it.

Homophones

Homophones are words that sound the same but have different spellings and different meanings. You can remember what a homophone is by remembering that a phone makes a sound, so a homophone sounds the same as another word.

It is important to know a homophone when you write it. If you need help with a homophone when you read or write, look it up in a dictionary. This will help you keep from making mistakes. For instance, would you write you have “bear hands” or “bare hands”?

Here are some common homophones:

Beat, beet

Earn, urn

Eye, I

Heal, heel, he’ll

Made, maid

Plain, plane

Rain, reign, rein

To, too, two

Homographs

These are words that are spelled the same but have different meanings. Sometimes they are pronounced differently even though they are spelled the same. You can remember what a homograph is by remembering that a graph is something you look at, so a homograph looks the same.

Here are some common homographs that are pronounced differently and have different meanings:

Bass: a low voice

Bass: a fish

Content: things found inside

Content: satisfied

Minute: 60 seconds

Minute: tiny

Try It!

The next time you are not sure which homophone or homograph to use, be sure you know the meaning of the word you are trying to use. This will help you spell it correctly. A dictionary will help you a lot!

title: Let's Write
text:
You are one of the first people to receive a charter to settle in Maine. You sail over from England and find that there are already people from other countries living where you planned on making your colony. What will you do? Will you share the land? Look for another place to live? Fight for the land your king said you could have?

If you want to find another place for your colony, what will you look for? What should be near your settlement? If you decide to share, how do you split the land?

title: Sir Ferdinando Gorges Awards Land Grants in Maine
text:
You already know Maine was part of Massachusetts for a long time, and that it was not one of the original Colonies. In this issue we will look at how Maine became part of Massachusetts.

You recall that in the early days of colonization in America, governments sometimes granted overlapping charters to individuals or groups of people. This often caused disputes over the ownership of the land. Overlapping land claims were common in the areas around what are now Massachusetts and Maine. Some of these problems were a result of poorly written charters. Other problems occurred when one individual had rights to the land in a certain area, and another would have rights to the rivers that ran through that land. Still another might have rights to the coastline that was part of that land. This all contributed to the confusion.

To deal with land disputes, a council was formed by the British Parliament. The Council for New England was in charge of the land that included the Colonies of New Hampshire, Massachusetts, and parts of other areas that were not Colonies.

The council struggled to maintain control. Not all of the members lived in the Colonies, and money was short. It was not long before the Council for New England ended. The land should have been divided up between eight council members. That plan didn't work because England did not enforce it. Instead, almost all of the land went to two men - Sir Ferdinando Gorges and John Mason.

Gorges and Mason divided the land up between themselves and each took control of their pieces. Mason called his part of the land New Hampshire. He founded the Colony that would later become that state. Gorges called his section Maine. At this point Maine was a province, or a small body governed by another body. It was a province of far-away England. Though Gorges really was in control, he never actually went to Maine! Instead he tried to maintain authority by having others oversee the province. They were not very successful. Gorges finally authorized some patents to other people. A patent granted permission for an individual to use the land. While Gorges still owned the land, others lived there and worked the land. Over time these people began to claim rights to the land and often fought for it. For example, the patent that was given to George Cleeve in 1643 gave him the right to use the land that is now known as Portland, Maine. Later, George Cleeve appealed to the General Court of Maine to return to an earlier patent from 1630 that awarded him even more land. Gorges fought this additional land claim as it would take away from his own land. The court ruled in Cleeve's favor, but could not enforce its decisions because of the unrest at the time. Finally the court had to request Parliament's help. This and other land disputes slowed the growth of Maine.

Until this point, Maine had maintained an independent government since the Council for New England ended. At this point, the ruling body asked England for help. This helped England establish some power there and slowed the growth of Maine even more.

All this time, the Bay Colony (the company that founded Massachusetts) was growing quickly and gaining power. With Maine weakening, the Puritans of Massachusetts outsmarted Maine and purchased the area of Maine from the Gorges family for 1,250 pounds.

With that, Maine became part of the Massachusetts Bay Colony.

title: Has Amelia Earhart’s Plane Been Found?
text:
A research group that looks for historical aircraft has been trying to solve one of the greatest mysteries of the 20th century. What really happened to Amelia Earhart? Earhart was the first woman to try to fly around the world. She disappeared without a trace while flying over the Pacific Ocean in 1937.

Earhart and Fred Noonan, her navigator, could have landed somewhere near Gardner Island, now called Nikumaroro. Others believe they crashed into deep water. By using technology to study a 1937 photo of the island's shore, researchers may have new evidence in the case. The photo shows what may be the landing gear of her Lockheed Electra airplane sticking out of the water. This could mean Earhart and Noonan lived on the island for some time after the crash. Artifacts have also been found on the island that could have belonged to Earhart and Noonan.

The oceanographer who found the undersea wreckage of the Titanic says the photograph might be the clue that helps us find out what really happened. Underwater robotic submarines and mapping equipment will help the International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery look for the plane's remains. Perhaps an old photograph and new technology will help solve a 75-year-old mystery!

title: Massachusetts Attempts Annexation of Maine
text:
Massachusetts leaders knew Maine was important in helping the Colonies grow and never liked the idea of Maine having an independent government. So they decided to annex, or take over, Maine.

In 1652, an unclear statement in the Bay Colony charter helped Massachusetts leaders attempt to control parts of Maine. The charter gave Massachusetts the rights to the land up to three miles north of the Merrimac River. Some decided this border was three miles north of the source of the Merrimac River and straight across to the Bay Colony's border on the east, the sea. This new border took in some of Maine's southern colonies and created a conflict for many years.

In 1677, Massachusetts actually bought the rights to the land from Ferdinando Gorges' descendants for 1,250 pounds. This land was called York County and stayed that way until long after the Revolutionary War. During this time, the people of Maine were governed by the Massachusetts government. People who are now considered Mainers would have been from Massachusetts back then. What might be different today if Maine were still a part of Massachusetts?

In 1783, Maine's eastern boundary was fixed at the St. Croix River. Much later, on March 15, 1820, Maine was admitted to the Union as a free state and became the 23rd state. This is when Maine separated from Massachusetts and began governing itself.

Masonian Proprietors

Gorges and John Mason were two men who received a land patent for the province of Maine. They both wanted to colonize and settle the land. They divided the land between them - Gorges claimed the northern land that later became Maine (and was sold to Massachusetts), and Mason claimed the land that he named New Hampshire.

Mason's land included the 60 miles between the Merrimac and Piscataqua. But others strongly opposed this claim. For a long time Mason, and later his heirs, couldn't develop the land like they wanted. The case was settled in court, where it was decided that Mason's claim was good. Mason's descendants were finally able to settle the land freely, the way they had wanted to for a long time. They built cities and worked the land. The area slowly started looking like a colony rather than just a few scattered people. Still, the only people who really lived on the land were Mason's descendants and friends.

After all of that work, one of Mason's descendants sold the land to a group of 12 men known as the Masonian Proprietors. A proprietor is a person in charge of taking care of something or someplace. It was their job to watch over the land granted to Mason. Basically, they could decide who could and could not live in New Hampshire. They gave settlement permits to the people they wanted to live there. They gave out these permits and land titles for the undeveloped land until the area became settled and the population grew. Today this area is still known as New Hampshire.

title: What is Profit?
text:
Pretend you and your friends decide to be entrepreneurs for the day. You find a table in Jack's garage. Mary's mom helps you make some lemonade. Together, all three of you make a big sign that says, "Lemonade, 25 cents." You put all of your items on the sidewalk in front of your house and wait for your customers to come.

Soon people are lined up around the block for a taste of your delicious lemonade. You work quickly to serve your customers. Then you realize you are almost out of cups. Mary and her mom run to the store to buy some more. When they get back, you take the extra cups and keep on selling lemonade until there is no more. Together, everyone cleans up the lemonade stand. You start to count the money you've made.

You count it all up, and you have $6.00. Then you think about the extra cups that you had to buy. They cost $1.25. You give Mary's mom that amount from the money you made. Now you have $4.75. This new amount is your profit. Profit is the money a business makes after all of the expenses are paid. In this example, the extra cups that cost $1.25 are your only expense.

You and your friends have learned about profit motive today. Profit motive is the desire to benefit from the time and money people put into a business. In other words, you wanted to sell lemonade because you thought you could earn some money. In the same way, a business sells goods in hopes of earning a profit. Now the question is, what will you do with your profit?

title: Elected and Appointed Leaders
text:
Some of our government leaders are elected, and some are appointed. Do you know what the difference is between the two?

Elected leaders are chosen by the people. Citizens vote and elect a candidate, or person trying to get in office. These elections are often done by secret ballot. The president of the United States and our state governor are elected. The mayor of your city is also elected.

A person is appointed if people in charge choose him or her. They are selected, not elected. They usually work closely with elected leaders. Appointed officials often serve two to four terms.

We have examples of appointed officials all around us. The members of the U.S. president's Cabinet and Supreme Court justices are appointed leaders. There are also many appointed state and local leaders. There might even be examples in your classroom. If you have class leaders, did members of the class elect them or did your teacher appoint them?

title: What is secession?
text:
When a part of a country or group of people decides they don't want to belong to that country or group any longer, they withdraw, or secede.

Sometimes a state or group might not want to be part of the bigger country or group it belongs to. There are two major ways that secession has happened historically. One way is through a war. This is always tragic. Many people die, and the smaller government may lose after all.The American Revolution is a good example of a successful war of secession. The Civil War is an example of an unsuccessful war of secession.

The other way is to go through the laws of the land. In Maine, there are some laws that allow counties to secede from the state and explain how it must be done.

title: Eastern White Pine
text:
Beginning with the colonists, the eastern white pine has been one of the most important pines in North America. The white pine often grows to heights of 80 to 150 feet. When it is mature, the diameter of the trunk is 2 to 3 feet.

In the early Colonial days, trees with diameters of more than 2 feet were marked and reserved for England. Because they were tall and straight, they were prized as masts for ships.

The needles on the tree are soft and grow in groups of five. The cones from the tree contain the seeds. The scales on the cone are thin and never have prickles. The seeds are eaten by birds and small animals, while the bark is enjoyed by rabbits and porcupines.

title: What are Idioms?
text:
Have you ever heard an adult say, “I’m sorry, but we’re up a creek on this one”? What did he mean? He was standing on dry ground when he said it! Well, you’ve just heard an idiom.

Idioms are Not Meant to Be Taken Literally

Idioms are sayings that mean something different from the literal meaning of their words. “Literal” means “following the exact wording.” But idioms are not literal, so the words do not mean exactly what they say. Listen carefully for clues to figure out an idiom.

Try It!

The best way to learn what an idiom means is to learn it and use it in your own speech or writing. Ask someone what it means. Then use it in your own writing. Here are some idioms in sentences. See if you can figure out what they mean. Once you know what the idiom means, use it in your own sentence. Use another piece of paper if you need to.

1. They were both so shy they had a hard time breaking the ice.

Use “breaking the ice” in your own sentence.

2. When it comes to modesty in dress, I have to draw the line

somewhere.

Use “draw the line” in your own sentence.

3. By halftime, the game was in the bag.

Use “in the bag” in your own sentence.

4. Chris and I are in the same boat because neither of us have extra cash to spend on the field trip.

Use “in the same boat” in your own sentence.

5. Would someone lend me a hand with the dishes?

Use “lend me a hand” in your own sentence.

title: Let's Write
text: The United States controls many territories that are not actually states. One of these territories is Puerto Rico. People in both places have been talking for a long time about annexing Puerto Rico. If this happened, Puerto Rico would be the 51st state. We’d like you to do a little research on your own. Then write about the territory of Puerto Rico. Tell how it is the same as a state. Tell how it is different. Finally, tell why you think it should or should not become the 51st state.

title: Colonial Life in Maine
text:
When we talk about the 13 Colonies, Maine isn't on the list. During the Colonial period, from 1607 to 1763, Maine was part of Massachusetts. It was not until after the birth of our nation that Maine and Massachusetts separated.

While Maine is not listed by name, colonists certainly lived in the region that is now our great state of Maine. Let's discover what life was like in the Colonies.

Did you ever hear the tale of the City Mouse and the Country Mouse? Life was very different for these two fellows. So it was with the colonists. For example, Portland was a large, busy port city with many wealthy people as well as many poor people. A bustling city like Portland had more goods for people to purchase. Folks in the city usually had jobs as tradesmen or they owned businesses that catered to the needs of the population. Many found work in the shipping industry as well. For those who lived in towns and villages however, life was somewhat different. Let's take a look at what a typical town in the Maine region during the Colonial period would have been like.

The typical town in Maine was built up around the church, the school and other public buildings and stores. Several hundred families usually lived in one town and often enjoyed a public park, known as a village green or common. Does your town have a common or a green (park) today? Families strolled in the common and enjoyed the outdoors, just as you might today. Today however, cows are probably not found grazing there as well!

Most of the townspeople were farmers, and their fields and houses were scattered on the outskirts of the town. Colonial farm families raised much of their own food. What do you think they raised in their gardens? Beans, pumpkins, peas, corn and squash were favorites. Cornmeal mush was used to make a dish called hasty pudding which was eaten so often, children were commonly heard to complain about it.

There were no refrigerators then, so when a family butchered a pig or cow or hunted large game, they shared it with their neighbors. The colonists also traded food, such as eggs for milk or some other kind of treat. Apples were an important crop in this area of the Colonies. Cider was the most popular drink around, and it was served with each meal and generally used to drink in place of water.

Drawing the day's cider from the big barrel was often the job of the last child to wake for the day. Cider and beer were both common drinks for adults and children alike.

Who did all the work around the farms? The men generally built houses and out-buildings, cleared the fields and did the heavier farm chores. The women did the cooking, cleaning, clothes making and other household work. Women and children together did farm chores such as feeding livestock and planting and harvesting crops.

Much was expected of Colonial children. Besides going to school, they were still expected to help out with chores. Boys could be found in the fields with their fathers, and girls began at an early age to help around the house and supervise younger children.

What kind of clothes do you think Colonial children wore? Everyday clothes were often made from cloth made by their mothers. Flax was a plant grown on many farms. The flax was spun into a linen yarn by mothers and girls. It was then woven into a cloth on a large handloom. Finally it was cut and sewn, by hand, into the clothes for the family. You can imagine how exciting it must have been to have a new dress or shirt after all that work. Sunday clothes were probably fancier, made from European fabrics purchased in Portland or Boston. Some Colonial children had clothing made from deer or other animal hides, just like the American Indians.

A Colonial home was usually made from wood, with a fireplace being the center of the home. It kept the house warm, and was the place where families would gather after meals. Matches had not yet been invented, so it was very important to keep some embers burning; even if there was no need for a fire. If the fire went out, a child was sent with a fire pan to a neighbor's house to borrow some fire!

Though there was much work to be done, Colonial life was not all work. Often, chores were made into games. One such game was cornhusking. Everyone gathered to husk the corn. If a young man husked an ear with red kernels, he was lucky indeed. The red ear was his ticket to give each young girl a kiss! If a girl happened on a red ear, she was allowed to give her favorite young man a kiss. The colonists also enjoyed a variety of sports. Boys played football, though it was more like soccer than football today. Other popular sports included horse racing, target shooting and billiards.

Family entertainment included small traveling circuses or puppet shows, such as "Punch and Judy."

A favorite holiday was election day. Candidates would pass out election cakes and election beer to hopefully win votes.

What is your favorite holiday today?

title: Crazy Colonial Laws
text:
When visiting the 13 original Colonies, you should take heed, lest you be sentenced to some time in the stocks!

Did you know that a sea captain in Boston was sent to the stocks for kissing his wife in public on Sunday? Even after three years of being at sea, the poor guy was supposed to wait until Monday!

Though some laws in Colonial America may seem really weird to us today, they were often based on religious beliefs. Other laws may have been based on custom, superstition or unusual happenings.

Punishment was probably not too severe for many of these laws, but was surely embarrassing for the law-breaker.

Read on to find some fun and unusual Colonial laws:

It was once illegal in Boston to own a dog more than 10-inches high.

In Maine, you could not lead a bear around by a rope.

In Delaware, you'd be in trouble if you tried to pawn your wooden leg.

It was against the law to mistreat an oyster in Baltimore, Maryland.

In New Jersey, it was against the law to slurp your soup.

In Trenton, you could not throw a bad pickle on the street!

In Truro, Massachusetts, a young man could not get married until he killed either six blackbirds or three crows.

title: King Philip’s War
text:
Metacomet was an American Indian who lived in New England. His father, Massasoit, was the great Wampanoag chief who had welcomed the Pilgrims in 1620. Metacomet became sachem (chief) in 1662 and continued friendly relations with the colonists. He became known as "King Philip."

The American Indians and colonists had their differences, but overall things were peaceful. They depended on each other as trading partners. However, some Colonial leaders began making unfair demands on the Indian tribes. The colonists ignored previous agreements and expanded into Indian territories. They forced natives to sell their land. They even demanded that Metacomet's people surrender all their weapons.

Metacomet organized an army. He formed an alliance with other American Indian tribes. His goal was to force the Puritan colonists out of Indian territory. Puritans and some American Indians united to fight Metacomet's warriors. Colonel Benjamin Church formed the first American Ranger unit in Plymouth Colony.

Many bloody conflicts followed. Both sides attacked and burned towns. They killed and enslaved hundreds of people. They destroyed land, crops and livestock. Every Colony and tribe in New England suffered huge losses. One of Church's soldiers killed Metacomet in 1676, and the battles stopped shortly after. Historians call this period King Philip's War.

Both sides of this conflict chose to abandon ethical behavior instead of solving their problems peacefully. The war forever changed the way of life for colonists and American Indians in New England.

Was there any chance this war might have been avoided? Have you experienced people ignoring ethical behavior in order to get what they want?

title: Who Wore Wigs?
text: One item of dress that was fashionable in the mid-18th century was the wig. It was worn mainly by men and boys! Because head lice were a common problem, the person's real hair was cut very short. It was then covered by a wig. The wig was made of goat, horse or human hair.

title: Life in Early Maine
text:
Life in the larger towns was usually centered around the ports, rather than around the farm. People in these towns obtained many of the comforts in life from ships bringing merchandise into the harbor. Portland was the shipping center of Maine. Most of the things that were brought to Maine came into Portland, and most of the things that were sent out of Maine left from Portland.

The very wealthy families had large brick houses with fine furniture shipped from Europe. The wealthy had servants and possibly slaves. Wealthy men usually served as selectmen or other community leaders.

Towns like Portland also had a middle class, or people who were not terribly rich or poor, but lived comfortably. Most of these folks were tradesmen or shop owners. They probably owned a house made of wood and had a servant or two. An apprentice might be found living with them as well.

Port towns were also home to many poor people who were crowded together in small wooden buildings. Called "poorhouses" or "almshouses," local religious or town leaders provided meals and a place to stay.

Though there were not as many people as there are today, the towns usually occupied only a small area, and were often very crowded. Streets were usually narrow and winding.

The ports were usually the busiest places in these cities. A variety of ships were in and out on a regular basis. The children of Portland ate many of the same foods and played many of the same games as did their neighbors in the townships, though living near the port made it easier to obtain goods.

One of the reasons port towns like Portland were so crucial to Maine's economy was because of the shipbuilding industry. Maine had tall, straight trees that could be used to make the masts of ships. Shipbuilding quickly became one of the strongest industries in Maine, for the easiest place to build a ship is by the water!

title: The Role of Prices
text:
"And your total comes to $2.40."

You've shopped in many stores either with your parents or by yourself. Most products contain bar codes that tell the scanner what the price is for the item. The prices let you, the consumer, know how much money the store is willing to sell the item for. However, that's not the only purpose.

Prices have three main functions. First, prices help ration scarce goods. Things cost money, and money is a limited resource. We can't buy everything we want all of the time. Therefore, items need to be rationed, or spread out to many people.

Second, prices provide a reason for buyers to buy goods and sellers to sell them. Prices make the process of buying goods organized. They motivate sellers to provide more goods based on the idea of profit motive.

Finally, prices send signals about how a market is doing. Let's say that prices are too high, and no one is buying those goods. Then economists can study this and ask questions. They can find out what prices are in other markets. Then they decide what in this market made the price rise so high.

Economists can then figure out the price for the product. It should balance the amount of buyers who want to buy with the amount of sellers who want to sell. This price is called the market-clearing price, or the equilibrium price. By figuring out this price, both the buyers and sellers are happy, and goods continue to be sold.

Can you think of any other reasons prices are important to our economy?

title: What is a Citizen?
text:
A citizen is a person who is born in a country or who becomes a member of the country where he or she chooses to live. Citizens of the United States have many duties, rights and privileges.

Citizens should obey the laws and respect others. They have the duty to serve on juries and pay taxes. Men can be asked to serve in the armed forces during times of war. During times of peace, men and women can enlist, or volunteer, to serve our country in the military.

One right of U.S. citizens is to participate in government. Another right, protected by the Bill of Rights, is the freedom of religion. U.S. citizens are promised freedom of assembly, freedom of speech and freedom of press. They are also given the right to bear arms, or carry weapons.

The right to vote is very important to citizens. When citizens choose not to vote, they lose their voice in government. As a people, we need to take the right to vote more seriously. In the 2000 election, only 51 percent of Americans voted. By the 2008 election this number increased to 61 percent.

title: Colonial Sports
text: In addition to horse racing, boat racing, skating, sleighing, tennis, target shooting and billiards, (whew!) bowling on the green was a favorite pastime for the colonials.

title: Did many people live on the islands in Maine?
text: Yes, actually, by the middle of the 18th century people had already begun to move to the islands that Maine possesses. Why? Part of the reason was that it was easier to defend an island than it was to defend a town on the mainland. Or perhaps because it was easier to keep cows from running away (the water provided a natural fence). Anyhow, living on the islands had its challenges too. The land was very rocky and covered with only a thin layer of topsoil. The soil was usually very acidic, because of the many spruce trees that grew on the islands. This contributed to the poor soil conditions. It was also challenging to get back and forth to the port cities in the winter.

title: Indigo Bunting
text:
The indigo bunting is a small bird found in Maine as well as many other Eastern states. The male is indigo in color. Notice in the picture what a bright blue that is. He is blackish colored on his wings and tail and has a black-tipped beak. The female is a light brown with a white breast that has light streaks of brown at the throat.

The buntings build nests in bushes such as berry, rose or greenbrier. They may even nest in weeds or tangles of vines. The nests are woven with dry grass, bark, dry leaves and sometimes snake skins!

The male bunting is one of the few birds who gives a full singing performance at midday.

title: Let's Write
text: Traditions through the year are an important part of our society. Everyone, according to their heritage, may have different traditions. It is amazing how people do such different things, even on the same holiday. In 200 words or less, write about your favorite holiday or family tradition.

title: Slavery Comes to Maine
text:
The first slaves were brought in to help with farming, building and in the fur trade of the Dutch West India Company.

Slavery is owning another human being as property. The first slaves in Maine were brought to the area while it was still part of Massachusetts. These were not the first Africans to enter North America as slaves. Some historians believe at least one black slave accompanied Christopher Columbus on his voyage in 1492. The first Africans imported to the colonies arrived in Virginia in 1619. There were not any African slaves on the Mayflower or African residents in the early Plymouth Colony. The first mention of a black resident in Plymouth was on a list of men granted the right to bear arms for the town of Plymouth. One of the men was recorded as a blackamoor, a Colonial term used for Africans. There are not records of slaves in early Plymouth, but we know the ship, the Desire, arrived in the Boston area with a cargo that included slaves. The Desire was built in 1636 as a fishing vessel. But in 1638, it sailed from Salem Harbor to the West Indies under Captain Pierce and returned with African slaves.

For the most part, the two Massachusetts Colonies, including the area that became Maine, did not have slaves, but rather servants. This means that the Africans were given their freedom after 35 years of age. Some worked as house servants while others worked on fishing vessels or at the docks. Still others served apprenticeships. An apprentice is someone who works for a skilled craftsman in order to learn a trade or skill. Colonial apprentices usually worked for a certain period of time in return for training.

In 1641, Massachusetts, including Maine at the time, became the first Colony to legalize slavery, and by 1660 slavery had spread to all the Colonies. After 1660, Colonies began to enact harsh laws, or codes, that defined slavery and the slave trade. One law common to all Colonies was that black slaves now served for life. Children of slave women were also required to serve for life. These codes also said slaves could not carry weapons, receive an education, meet in groups of more than three or testify against masters in court. Slaves on small farms or in cities probably had more freedom than the plantation slaves in the Southern Colonies.

By the 1680s, slavery was practiced in full force in all of the Colonies. A French refugee in Massachusetts said of slaves, "there is not a house in Boston however small, that does not have one or two. There are those that have five or six."

By the early 1700s, Boston was the busiest harbor in the Colonies, and Colonial ship owners made fortunes in what is known as the Triangular Trade. Large sugar plantations in the West Indies were worked by African slaves. Massachusetts ships would sail to the islands to pick up molasses made from the sugar. The ship would then return to the Colonies with the molasses, where it was used to make rum. The ship would next sail to the west coast of Africa and use rum to trade for more slaves, which were then taken to the West Indies and traded for more molasses. At each leg of the trip, a handsome profit was made, encouraging the cycle.

Not all slaves went to the West Indies, however. Many were transported to the Colonies and auctioned at slave markets. Markets were often held in cities with large ports such as Boston, Salem, Portland and New York.

A slave market involved selling slaves. Notices were posted before slave ships landed, announcing the upcoming slave auction. Here men and women were lined up so the buyers could inspect their teeth and gums. They would feel muscles and look for skin diseases. The slaves had no control over what would happen. They might be sold to a master who was kind or to a cruel master who would work them hard, sometimes to death. By then, slaves were no longer treated as servants or laborers, but as chattel. Chattel is property that can be bought or sold with little emotion. It was not important to those purchasing slaves to keep families together. Husbands and wives were separated and often mothers never saw their children again.

Though Massachusetts was the first Colony to legalize slavery, in 1790 it was also the first to abolish it, and Maine abolished slavery along with it.

Sold Into Slavery

Slave labor in Maine grew rapidly as the Massachusetts Colony turned to the Triangular Trade. Though slavery in Massachusetts was different from the plantation slavery in the South, it was still slavery! How did the European slave traders obtain the slaves to bring to the Colonies?

One way was to wait near a river and kidnap small groups, who were then taken to a slave ship. More commonly though, one village or country would wage war on another, stealing members. These people were then enslaved by their enemies to use as property to trade with the Europeans for goods.

The more ships that arrived with goods to trade, the more the African society was disrupted as those societies captured more slaves from their neighbors. This slave trade degraded human life as never before, both in Africa and America.

America was not the only country to use slaves for labor. Some historians say the slave trade was as big then as the oil industry is today! Indeed, it was a global trade. The Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch, English and French were all involved in the slave trade. It is believed that during the 350 years of this slave trade, 10 million Africans were taken into slavery.

A Cruel Atlantic Journey

The passage for enslaved Africans to the Colonies was cruel and hard. Slave traders tried to get as many slaves as possible on a ship. Slaves were often chained together at the ankles and feet. Sometimes they had as little as 3 feet of space in which to move. They were forced to sleep on bare floors with no covering. There were no bathroom facilities, so there was much filth and disease. The air was suffocating. Some sailors at sea said they could smell a slave ship long before they could see one. About one in every 10 died during the passage, and a slave may have awakened to find himself chained to a corpse. Sometimes when food ran low on a voyage traders were known to throw slaves overboard. Many also died of disease before making it to America. It is impossible to imagine what it would have been like on a slave ship for the two months it took to cross the Atlantic Ocean.

title: Big Bang Meets Big Crunch
text:
Paul Steinhardt and Neil Turok are two scientists who recently came up with a theory about how the universe came to be. Almost everyone has heard of the Big Bang Theory, the idea that all matter was concentrated in one giant blob that suddenly exploded. But Paul and Neil think this theory doesn’t explain the whole story. The Big Bang Theory is based on the belief that one big explosion of matter was the beginning of all stars and planets. As the molten matter blew out into the cold of space, the globs and blobs began swirling and cooling into the universe as we see it today.

The Big Bang Theory leaves a few unanswered questions: What caused the first big explosion? Why is the universe still expanding? What happens when it stops expanding? What was the universe like before the Big Bang? Questions like these are the reasons Paul and Neil started working on a theory of their own. They think the universe goes through cycles of exploding apart and then pulling itself back together again. Like a stretching rubber band, extending and then shrinking, the universe will explode and contract, repeatedly. This means the universe is actually moving through a cycle, and it doesn’t have a beginning or an end. No beginning and no end? This idea could sure make your brain hurt! But don’t worry. Paul and Neil’s theory is only an idea. You’ll have plenty of time to think it over because it’s going to take a few hundred million years of observation and testing to see if it is actually correct.

title: Budgeting
text:
Making sure more money comes in than goes out

Have you ever asked your mom or dad for something, only to be told that it wasn't in the budget? A budget is a plan of how to manage your money. It has two main ideas.

First, you must think about how much money is coming in. Maybe you earn an allowance. Maybe you mow a neighbor's lawn to make money, also called income. If you earn money every week or month, like an allowance, then it is called a steady income.

Next, we look at how much is going out, or how much it costs you to live. Maybe you subscribe to a magazine or go to a movie every Friday night. These are types of expenses. Adults also have expenses. They pay bills every month to buy things we all need, like food, clothes and cars. These expenses come out of their income every month.

To make a budget, you must first look at your income (money coming in). Then add up all of your expenses (money going out). Now subtract the total amount of your expenses from your total income. This new number lets you know how much money you have for other things you want. This helps you plan and make wise choices when spending your money.

The goal of a budget is to try to balance your income with your expenses. It is best if your income is more than your expenses. That way, more money is coming in than going out. Now it is your turn to make a budget. Good luck!

title: U.S. Residents
text:
Simply living in the United States does not make you a citizen. Three different types of residents live in the United States today.

The first group of residents is made up of citizens. They include anyone born in the United States or babies born to citizens who are living abroad, or in a foreign country.

Throughout our country's history, there have been many immigrants. Immigrants, or aliens, are the second group of residents. These people come to live in a country where they were not born. They do not automatically become citizens and do not have the same rights. For example, they cannot vote. To become citizens, immigrants must apply and pass certain requirements. Then they can become naturalized citizens.

The third group of residents is made up of nationals.

Nationals are people born in American territories, such as Puerto Rico or Guam. They have all the protections of being U.S. citizens, but they do not have the full rights citizens have.

title: Slave Route
text: Study this map and you will see how much slavery was practiced throughout the world. As you can see most of the slaves went to South America and the West Indies.

title: Who was Henry “Box” Brown
text: Henry "Box" Brown was a very determined and clever slave. In 1849, he ordered a 3 foot x 2 foot x 8 foot box in Virginia. He put a jug of water and some biscuits inside. He also put in a bar to open the box. He then climbed in. A friend addressed the box to an abolitionist, someone who believed in freeing slaves. He lived in Philadelphia. After writing, "Handle with Care" and "This Side Up", the friend shipped him off. Twenty-seven hours later, he arrived in Philadelphia, a free man!

title: Dragons & Damsels
text:
Dragonflies and damselflies are similar in many ways. Both hunt as they fly by making a basket-like trap with their legs, where they catch mosquitoes and other insects.

The dragonflies are brown to black with transparent wings and often have bright rainbow markings. The damselfly has a thinner body that is often jewel colored and transparent wings that are darker. While the dragonfly rests with its wings straight out from its body, the damselfly rests with its wings folded slightly above its body.

Unlike most insects which either flap both wings together or only the back wings, these flies can beat their wings separately. That means one set of wings can be going down while the other goes up. You can see this happen if you watch very closely. These flies are great flyers! They can fly in loop-the-loops, hover and even fly backwards!

Dragonflies are considered fairly large insects today, but 300 million years ago they were much larger.

title: How Do I Use a Thesaurus?
text:
Do you use many of the same words over and over when writing? Are you getting bored with those same words? It’s time you learned to use a thesaurus!

Search for Synonyms

The word “thesaurus” almost looks like a name for a dinosaur, doesn’t it? It’s actually a book (it can be found online as well). This book or Web site provides synonyms (words similar in meaning) for common words. Using a thesaurus is a great way to broaden your vocabulary with more interesting words.

A thesaurus is usually alphabetical. Some are similar to dictionaries because they give you the part of speech, definition and sample sentences for words. Sometimes a thesaurus will give you directions to look up other entries. Here’s what you’ll find in a typical thesaurus.

Entry Word........................................... The word you look up to find synonyms

Part-of-Speech Label......................... Tells you if the word is a noun, verb, adjective, etc.

Definition............................................... Tells you what the entry word means

Example Sentence............................... Shows you how the entry word might be used in a sentence.

Synonyms............................................... Words whose meanings are the same as or similar to the entry word

Antonyms............................................... Words whose meanings are the opposite of the entry word

Try It!

Look up the word “grow” in a thesaurus. Write all the synonyms here.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: As you read this week’s magazine, circle or highlight five words that are new to you. Write the words on a piece of paper. Try to figure out the meaning of the words by reading the other words and sentences around them. Write what you think the words mean and compare your definition to a dictionary definition.

title: Let's Write
text:
Poetry is a good way to express emotion such as sadness, love and joy. Writing poetry about the slave trade is a good way to express your feelings about this dark time in history.

Write a poem expressing the way you feel about slavery or about how you imagine it was for those men, women and children who were enslaved.

title: Fighting the French and Indian War
text:
Sometimes students think this war was the French fighting the American Indians. But the French and the American Indians actually fought together against the English. While the French and English were fighting battles in the Colonies, they were also fighting in Europe. Because the Algonquian-speaking tribes were friendly with the French, they agreed to fight against the English - and also helped give this war its name. Really the French and Indian War was more of a group of wars including earlier ones like King Philip's War and Queen Anne's War.

Many countries wanted control of the new lands in North America for the wealth from the fur trade. France and England both claimed some of the same desired lands in the Ohio River Valley. Trying to control these lands, the French attacked many villages, including a number of townships in Massachusetts and what is now Maine.

Many towns in Maine were very important during the battles of the French and Indian War. Augusta, for example, is not just the capital of Maine and seat of Kennebec County, but was an important place during the wars. The first permanent structure here was Fort Western, which was used as a supply base during the French and Indian War.

Maine was still part of Massachusetts during the French and Indian War. Many of Maine's bravest men fought among thousands of men from Massachusetts for England in these wars. Five percent of the men that fought from Massachusetts were from the area that later became Maine.

Maine entered into the wars early, during the beginning of King Philip's war, and was involved in the fighting until the very end as they were so close to the border of Canada (which was where most of the French in the continent lived). By the end of King Philip's war, Maine had suffered a lot. Everything was destroyed except for three settlements: Kittery, York and Wells. The fighting in Maine was fierce, and began for reasons different than those of more southern areas of the Colonies. Many of the rich traders in Maine were notorious for cheating and tricking the natives during trades. The people in the area would also kidnap the natives and try to sell them as slaves. This made the natives very angry, and when war started in the Colonies the natives around Maine jumped right into the battle.

On Sept. 5, 1675, a group of natives raided Thomas Purchase's trading post above Penobscot Falls (this place is called Topsham today), and killed a few cattle. They did this in response to an order from the Colonial government for them to give up their weapons. On September 9, a group of Englishmen made an unprovoked attack on three Penobscot natives at someone's home. On September 12, the isolated home of Thomas Wakely at Falmouth (now Portland) was assaulted, leaving six people dead.

All of these attacks were made under the leadership of Squando, a Penobscot leader, and soon the Abenaki all throughout the Maine area were attacking British settlements. Squando hated the British because of something that happened years before. His wife and infant child were in a boat that some English men capsized on purpose. The English men did this to see if the rumor they had heard was true: that native children were born knowing how to swim. Squando's child died.

On September 18, a group of Penobscot, probably led by Squando, launched an attack that destroyed the mills belonging to Major William Phillips and almost captured the garrison that the English had retreated to. More than 25 settlers were killed during this month in battles with the natives. During the first phase of King Phillip's war in Maine more than 80 Mainers lost their lives.

Mainers continued to fight for their families, homes and businesses, in spite of their great losses early on. These efforts helped Great Britain win the French and Indian Wars.

title: The French and Indian Wars.....Again?
text:
There are many ways we can study history. We read about history in textbooks. We study newspapers and journals from the past. Historians look at drawings and photos too. Don't forget Maine Studies Weekly! There is also another way. Did you know that some people study history by reenactment?

Reenactment means to act out an event from the past. We can learn about history with facts and actors. When real people act out history, it is a way to understand more information.

There are many living history groups in the United States. Some are in historic villages. Others reenact battles. They choose battles fought in the United States. Who learns about history from reenactment? The actors themselves learn more about history. The people who are watching also do. It becomes a living textbook for the viewers.

The soldiers in these modern regiments try hard to re-live the battles as closely as possible. Of course, they do not really shoot at each other. They do use real muzzle loaders and wear replicas of uniforms. They eat the same kinds of food or go without. They may even be singing the same songs on lonely nights by a warm campfire.

title: French & Indian War
text:
Rogers' Rangers

Until the Europeans fought battles against the American Indians, they had always fought in long rows in open fields. But the American Indians hid behind rocks and trees to shoot at the enemy. So when the Europeans began fighting the American Indians, warfare began to change.

One man, Robert Rogers from New Hampshire, helped the British finally win the war. He organized a group of early colonists called Rogers' Rangers who chose to fight like the native people. These men not only shot at the enemy while hiding, but also engaged in warfare at night and in the wintertime, when battles had never been fought before. They were known to wear ice skates on ponds and to fight in snowshoes. The Rangers wore green outfits and developed tactics called Rogers' "Rules of Ranging." Some of these tactics are still used by Army Rangers and the Green Berets today.

Rogers and his men helped capture Crown Point and Ticonderoga - victories that also helped defeat the French in New York. The final battle in Quebec between British General Wolfe and French General Montcalm cut off French power in North America for good. The British and the French signed a peace treaty in 1763 that gave France's land in North America to the British and changed the map forever.

Standing Orders for Rogers' Rangers

Don't forget nothing.

Have your musket clean as a whistle, hatchet scoured, 60 rounds powder and ball and be ready to march at a minute's warning.

When you're on the march, act the way you would if you was sneaking up on a deer. See the enemy first.

Tell the truth about what you see and what you do. There is an army depending on us for correct information. You can lie all you please when you tell other folks about the Rangers, but don't ever lie to a Ranger or officer.

Don't ever take a chance you don't have to.

When we're on the march we march single file, far enough apart so one shot can't go through two men.

If we strike swamps, or soft ground, we spread out abreast, so it's hard to track us.

When we march, we keep moving till dark, so as to give the enemy the least possible chance at us.
