When we camp, half the party stays awake while the other half sleeps.

Results of the French and Indian War

Study the two maps on this page. You will see the results of the French and Indian War. Before the war, the French occupied a huge area in the center of America. After the war, the French were completely gone. The events that contributed to this huge change in America started because two countries had overlapping land claims in North America.

The French based their claims on the great explorer La Salle. He claimed the Mississippi River and all rivers that empty into it for France. The English based their claims on the original land grant of Virginia. The problem was some of that land overlapped the French claims.

The French believed they could strengthen their claims by building a string of forts. They buried lead plaques with the French claim written on them throughout the Ohio Valley. The English sent a messenger with a letter to explain to them their claim was wrong and they should leave. The messenger was 21-year-old George Washington. Instead of leaving, the French moved southward and captured an English fort. This started the French and Indian War.

It was called the French and Indian War because the Algonquian tribes at the time liked the French and joined their side.

The war was long and favored the French in the early years. However, the English finally won because of their great numbers and military strength.

The war took place in many of the Colonies. Most of the action and several important battles centered in New York, New Hampshire, Massachusetts and Pennsylvania.

title: Credit and Debt
text:
Trying not to spend more money than you have

You've made your budget, and you are trying to stick to it. You take care to plan what you will buy. You try to make sure that your income is greater than your expenses.

Then you see it - the bike you've always wanted! It is on sale for $55. You rush home and count all of the money in your piggy bank. You find you only have $30.

Discouraged, you decide to go talk to your dad about the situation. He agrees to loan you the remaining $25. He says he will take it out of your allowance for the next few weeks. You think this is a great idea! Together, you go down to the store and purchase your brand new bike.

Even though you most likely didn't know it, you just bought something on credit. Credit is money that is loaned and must be paid back. Usually, credit lenders require a fee, known as interest. The person who borrows money must pay back the money he or she owes. He or she also must pay some extra money for being able to borrow from the lender.

You are also now in debt. Debt is money you owe when you buy something by borrowing money. Although credit can help people in tight spots, it should be used carefully.

Sometimes, people just buy things on credit, usually with a credit card. They forget they have to pay the money back with interest. This can add up to huge amounts of debt that people have a hard time paying back. You should always remember that having things today and paying for them tomorrow is tricky business. Try to avoid it!

title: Becoming a U.S. Citizen
text:
People born in the United States are legal citizens of our country. People born in foreign countries can become U.S. citizens, too. This process is called naturalization.

To become a citizen, you must be at least 18 years old and have lived in the United States for at least five years. You must be loyal to the United States and be willing to pledge allegiance, or take an oath of loyalty. You must have a basic understanding of U.S. history, government and the Constitution. In addition, you must be able to speak, read and write basic English.

The process of becoming a citizen has three different steps. First, you must file an application. This includes being fingerprinted, taking photographs and providing legal documents. The next step is to take the naturalization exam. This test has two parts: an English test and a U.S. history and government exam.

The last step is to appear in court. You must go before a judge and ask to become a U.S. citizen. The judge listens to your reasons for wanting to become a citizen and makes the final decision. Once you are made a citizen, you have all the rights and duties of any other U.S. citizen!

title: Albany Congress
text:
There was unrest between the French and English during the War. England wanted a union between the Colonies and the English crown. Some Colonial leaders were thinking the same thing. They met in June 17 5 4 at Albany. Some members of the northern Colonies and Six Iroquois Nations met. They discussed the ideas of Benjamin Franklin. He suggested each Colony elect delegates for an American Continental Assembly. This would be presided over by a royal governor.

The plan was important. It was the first attempt to unify the Colonies. The British rejected the plan. They feared it would give colonists too much power. Later the Colonial assemblies also rejected the plan. They were not ready to give up individual independence to become one country. This did not happen until after the American Revolution. Many of Franklin's ideas for the Albany Congress would later be adopted in the Constitution.

title: Why do ponds and lakes freeze from the top down?
text:
When the air temperature above a lake drops below freezing the top of the lake will freeze. Water expands when it freezes. This makes ice lighter than water. The floating ice acts as a big blanket and helps prevent more of the lake from freezing.

Why is this important? Fish are living in the water and don't want to become frozen leftovers during the winter time! We are lucky ice floats. If ice were heavier, it would sink during winter. By spring, our lakes and oceans would be solid blocks of ice. Every creature in them would be dead.

title: Sugar Maple
text:
The sugar maple is found in several New England states and is the state tree of more than one state. No wonder, when it produces such a treat! Though red maples and silver maples also produce sugar, the sugar maple provides the best sugar.

The tree grows to be about 100 feet tall, with a tall straight trunk in the forest, and a fuller, more spreading type of a shape in a yard or a park.

The leaves are long and dark green. In the fall they turn a beautiful yellow and red. They produce "whirly-bird" type of seeds that twirl down with just a gentle breeze. The trunk is a light gray-brown and scaly with deep long furrows. The sugar maple grows in the northern forests. Maple trees do get tired and worn out after many, many years of tapping, but they are also important as a source of wood for beautiful furniture.

title: Fact vs. Opinion
text:
Right now you are reading a newspaper. A newspaper is a great place to find both facts and opinions.

Fact: A fact is a statement that can be proved. For instance, to say most oranges are orange in color can be proven. All you have to do is look at an orange to tell what color it is.

Opinion: An opinion is a belief held by someone. It cannot be proven by fact. For instance, to say, "red apples are sweeter than green apples" is an opinion. It depends on who's doing the tasting. Brian thinks red apples are sweeter. Brooke finds green apples the sweetest. They each have an opinion about the sweetness of apples.

Newspapers contain mostly facts on most of the pages. Certain pages are set aside for opinions. The editorial page contains letters to the editor, editorial cartoons and articles by the editors of that paper.

The purpose of the editorial page is to:

Make people think about events in the news

Try to get public officials to see your point of view

Give background and information about events in the news

Serve as a community "voice"

All your life you'll be reading books and articles. You'll also be doing a lot of writing for school and work. Get in the habit of asking yourself as you read or write, "Is this statement fact or opinion?" This habit will help you become a better thinker.

title: Change in Warfare
text: As the Europeans began to fight like the natives, warfare began to change. Colonists hid behind rocks and trees to shoot at the enemy rather than stand in the open.

title: Colonial Unrest on the Rise
text:
During the late 1600s the Colonies were beginning to form in the Americas. Each established economies based upon the materials that were available to them. Maine, as York County in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, was building an economy supported by shipbuilding. Maine had many tall, straight trees, including the prized white pine. The white pine trees were perfect for masts of sailing vessels. They were very important to the economy of Maine.

In 1691 the Parliament in London had declared that all white pine trees more than 24 inches (61 centimeters) in diameter belonged exclusively to the British crown. These wide trees were exactly the trees that were best for making the masts of ships. This decision by Great Britain made it extremely difficult to make money building ships in Maine. Because of the new law, Maine shipbuilders could only use these trees for masts on the ships they were building for the royal British ships.

This law outraged Mainers. They had been living in America for generations, and many of the colonists thought of Maine as their only home. They didn't feel like British people living in America, they felt more like American people living under British control. They had very little connection with their mother country, and many of them felt there was no connection at all. However, Great Britain had a different view. England saw the rich resources in Maine and the Colonies as a great source of money.

These differences in view points marked the beginning of the tension between the people of Maine and the British crown. It was these tensions that eventually led the people of Maine to join with the other Americans in fighting the Revolutionary War.

The white pines of Maine weren't the only things that Great Britain sought to exploit. To exploit means to take advantage of, or to use wrongfully. After the French and Indian Wars, England needed a way to pay for the wars they had just fought and decided to raise the colonists' taxes in order to do so. This was done without letting the Colonies have any part in the decision. The term for this act is "taxation without representation." It served to cause more tension between Maine and Great Britain. However, many people still relied on England for their livelihood, and they didn't want to break ties with Great Britain.

England also passed the Stamp Act, which required certain documents and items to have a stamp on them. The colonists had to buy these stamps from the British government, so this ended up being just another form of tax. Many felt this tax was ridiculous, and most people were upset that they still didn't have any say in decisions that were being made with regard to themselves. Another tax was established on tea, and it was one of the bigger money makers in the Colonies. This was one of the things which finally drove the Colonies into a state of unrest.

Maine and the other Colonies protested by burning tax collectors in effigy (making a dummy or likeness of an individual and hanging or burning it as a warning), signing petitions and boycotting British goods. This wasn't all! In 1774, a group of angry colonists from York County protested the new tea laws by burning a cargo of tea from the British East India Company. This was known as the York Tea Party, which happened after the better-known Boston Tea Party of 1773.

title: I Protest!
text:
While it has been over 230 years since the Boston Tea Party, the battle over taxes continues today. Many protesters (people who speak out against something they disagree with) call on our government each year to change our tax laws. They want taxes to be lowered and collected in more fair ways.

Why Reduce Taxes?

Tax protesters say the average worker spends two hours and 49 minutes of every eight-hour work day just to pay taxes. Tax protesters convince their legislators to write bills that would reduce and reform taxes. Government leaders then decide whether or not to pass these bills into law.

The Gas Bite

Have you noticed that when your parents fill up the car with gas, the price isn't always the same? Gas prices go up and down, but the price you pay isn't just for gas. About one third of the price for a tank of gas goes to the government in the form of taxes. This is just one of the taxes that many protesters are angry about.

The battle for tax change continues to this day, as bills are presented to our federal and local governments. Are these angry people breaking the law? No! They are exercising a right that our form of government allows: peaceful protest.

These are the same feelings American colonists had when the British forced taxes on them. Anger at taxes caused the Boston Tea Party. Do we need to throw tea in Boston Harbor to get the government's attention? No!

The biggest difference between Colonial days and today is that we can vote for our lawmakers and we have the right to not only visit with them about our concerns, but also to vote them out of office if we disagree with the decisions they make. The right to make our voices heard and to let our government leaders know how we feel is one of the freedoms our Founding Fathers were willing to fight for.

title: How Do I Give An Oral Presentation
text:
Standing in front of a crowd and telling them what you think is not easy, but it can be done if you prepare well!

Preparing for an Oral Presentation

Know your audience. What you say should be directed toward them. Is it to be given in your classroom? This will make it easier!

How long should it be? If your teacher says 15 minutes, stick to the time.

What's the topic? Did your teacher assign it? Make sure you can cover it within the time limit.

Make notes. Use index cards and put them in the order you want to use them. Index cards are not so large that they cover your face. You may write your presentation on numbered pieces of paper, but do not staple the pages.

Practice, practice and practice some more!

Making the Oral Presentation

Introduction - Get the audience's attention with the introduction. You can do this by asking a question, telling a story, using a quotation or making a statement. Once you have their attention, state your topic.

Body - State your main points and give information that support your main points. You may ask rhetorical questions, (questions that don't need answers) use emotional words or repeat important information.

Conclusion - Repeat your main point. Conclude with something that leaves a lasting impression by asking a rhetorical question, making an emotional plea or using a quotation, story or statement.

Try It!

When you're asked to give an oral presentation, make sure you prepare well. Organize logically. Practice, practice, practice. Good luck!

title: Patriotism Develops
text:
Liberty was something the colonists were beginning to value more as time went by. The Sons and Daughters of Liberty were organized to help preserve Colonial America's liberty.

The Patriotic Movement Begins in America

The Sons of Liberty planted a pine tree in the middle of a field. It is here they gathered and held many meetings. Many Colonies had similar trees. The tree was called a Liberty Tree or a Liberty Pole. These were honored as much as a flag. Several times the British soldiers destroyed the trees, causing more anger than ever before. On Jan. 19, 1770, shortly after another attack on their liberty pole, the Sons of Liberty in New York began to fight with the redcoats at Golden Hill. Men on both sides were injured. This was known as the Battle of Golden Hill. It was one of the first violent acts in the years before the Revolutionary War.

Who Were the Sons of Liberty?

In the fall of 1765, the Colonies united and formed a group called the Stamp Act Congress to fight the Stamp Act. Nine Colonies sent representatives to meet in New York City. The Congress expressed anger about the hated Stamp Act and said Americans would not be taxed without permission. Some Colonies formed groups called the Sons of Liberty. Women formed groups called the Daughters of Liberty. These groups became the strength behind the Colonial move to independence.

Stamp Act Inflames Patriots!

Sons of Liberty in York County in Maine, as in other places, pressured Stamp Act Agents to resign. Sometimes the agents were physically harmed. The Sons of Liberty in the picture to the left are burning in effigy the British stamp collectors. They also seized the stamps and burned them publicly. They had the support of many of the colonists in their attempt to stop the stamp tax.

When the English lawmakers realized how much trouble the Stamp Act was, it was repealed in 1766.

Tea Anyone?

The Tea Act was passed by Parliament in 1773. Not only did this tax all tea, but Parliament (a British law-making group) appointed its own merchants to sell the tea. They were creating a monopoly by selling directly to the Colonies. This left Colonial merchants at a loss, and forced the colonists to pay a tax they did not want to pay. Thousands of colonists responded by refusing to drink the tea. Others smuggled tea from other countries. Once again, many colonists' thoughts were of independence.

In response to the Tea Act, many "tea parties" occurred in the Colonies, where British cargoes of tea were destroyed. John Adams declared the Boston Tea Party to be the, "grandest event ever." These acts of defiance convinced the British that the colonists (particularly the Bostonians), no longer respected the law, and drastic measures were soon taken.

title: Banks
text:
Did you know temples were the first banks? Thousands of years ago, no one would steal from a temple. That's because they were afraid the gods would curse them. This made temples the safest place to store the costly metals people used for money. Some temples even made loans, giving money to people who promised to pay it back.

Do you know where the word bank comes from? Long ago, early Italian bankers used street benches to conduct their business. In time, the Italian word banca (bench) became the English word "bank." No matter what time era, or where you live, a bank has always been a business that deals with money. They hold money for customers, they make loans, and they provide other money-related services. There are three main types of banks.

The first is a commercial bank. These banks serve both businesses and individuals. They offer checking accounts, loans and saving accounts to their customers.

The second kind of bank is a savings bank. These banks are similar to commercial banks, but they mostly offer savings accounts and loans. They also offer mortgages. That's a special kind of loan for people trying to buy a house.

The third kind of bank is a credit union. Credit unions were started to help people borrow money. People in the same type of employment (a school district, for instance) put their savings together and loaned it to others within that organization. In other words, they operated their own banks. Today, credit unions provide many of the same services as commercial banks and savings banks. However, they are called non-profit organizations. This means all the members of the credit union share any profit that the organization makes.

title: How Government Works
text:
Government works similar to stacking blocks, and it all starts with you! You are a citizen of your community. Your community is part of a city, and a local government runs the city. The head of the city, the mayor, works out of city hall. Do you know where your city hall is?

The state government runs all of the combined local governments. The leader of the state government is the governor. The governor's office can be found at the state capitol. Voters in each state elect members of Congress. They meet in Washington, D.C., to take care of the federal government. The leader of the country is, of course, the president of the United States.

The United Nations is yet another block that we can add. It is a type of government made up of leaders from around the world. Wow! Many government leaders are members of the United Nations - but don't forget that the most important part of all of this is the citizens, including you!

title: Were there cowboys in the Colonies?
text:
The word cowboy was first used to name pro-British outlaws. They used the unusual method of distracting people by ringing a cowbell, then robbed them or stole animals from farmers and sold them to the British army.

Pro-patriot outlaws were called skinners. These skinners took all of a person's belongings, figuratively leaving them with only their bare skin.

title: Eastern Mole
text: Moles form a family within the order of insect eaters. This species is about 7 inches long. Its fur varies from gray to brown to golden and it has a hairless tail. Its large, sharp claws help it to dig underground. The mole lives in fields, meadows and gardens throughout most of the United States (not the extreme Northwest), from the Atlantic to the Rockies.

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you are in charge of collecting information for the local town crier. You were lucky enough to be present at the York Tea Party. Write about what you saw and how it made you feel. Do you want the things you say to make the other colonists angry, or would you like them to feel justified?

title: Language Arts Connection
text: As you read this week’s lesson, circle or highlight five verbs in any color. On a piece of paper, write a sentence for each verb using the progressive form (-ing).

title: Blows Must Decide!
text:
"The New England governments are in a state of rebellion, blows must decide whether they are to be a subject to this country or independent." (letter from King George III to Lord North, 18 Nov. 1774)

These are the words spoken about the unrest in the Colonies. The English believed using force was the only way to make the unruly Colonies pay taxes and obey the British laws. After the Boston Massacre and the Boston Tea Party, Parliament passed a series of acts called the Coercive Acts. These acts were meant to punish the colonists and make them pay for rebelling. The colonists called them the Intolerable Acts.

The acts closed trade in Boston and replaced governments with military officers. The Justice Act ruled that any British official would not be tried for crimes in America. Instead, they would be sent back to England where the judgment would be easier. The Quartering Act stated that the colonists must supply housing for soldiers within each Colony.

Because of these unjust acts, the Colonial leaders decided to meet and discuss these unfair acts. This meeting was called the First Continental Congress. Georgia was the only Colony to not participate. The congress agreed to boycott, or refuse, British goods. They even printed names of those who wore English clothing or drank tea in local newspapers to get them to join the boycott.

The Battles of Lexington and Concord

It looked like using military force was the only way to solve the problem. All 13 of the Colonies started storing guns and supplies, and volunteers began training for armed conflict. In April 1775, the British General Gage marched 700 men to Boston to destroy the patriots' military supplies at Concord, Massachusetts. Because they were armed, the Colonial minutemen were organized and waiting to stop the British. At Lexington, the patriots were ordered to leave. They began to, but then a shot rang out and the firing began. In this first battle of the Revolutionary War, eight colonists were killed and 10 were wounded. The Americans wounded one British soldier. As news of the battle spread, more patriots gathered near Concord. This time the Americans had more soldiers than the British. In the Battle of Concord the patriots killed or wounded nearly 300 of the British and lost about 100 of their own. The British retreated and the Battle of Concord became the first American victory.

It is important to remember that not everyone in America hated the British rule. After these two battles, the colonists divided into three groups. One group, called Whigs or patriots, wanted the Colonies to be free from British rule. About one third of the colonists were loyalists or Tories, who supported England. The last group of colonists were undecided and hoped the other two groups could work out their differences. Many families or households were split. Sometimes servants felt differently than the members of the household. Indeed, some of the Colonies seemed to be almost in a state of civil war as patriots and loyalists destroyed each other's property.

The Maine Battles

Maine was never the center of activity during the American Revolution, though it was right next to it. A few offensive actions did take place in the region that became Maine. American military leader Benedict Arnold brought an expedition 120 miles up the Kennebec River during his failed attempt to capture Quebec from the British in 1775. In that same year, the people of Machias captured a British frigate, the Margaretta. This was the first naval battle of the Revolutionary War. Afterward, Great Britain decided to strike back and punish Maine by capturing Castine, destroying Maine's ports and burning Falmouth (now Portland). When patriots sent 40 ships to recapture Castine, they were badly beaten due to problems with the weather and indecisive leadership. In the end, they burned the remaining boats to prevent Great Britain from capturing them. This is called the Penobscot Expedition, and it was one of the most disastrous events of the war. The coast of Maine was under British control for most of the war and became a haven for Loyalists.

title: The National Guard: Our Oldest Tradition
text:
The Army National Guard of the United States was authorized by Congress in 1933. But this military tradition actually began in the Massachusetts Colony in 1636. The first colonists formed regiments to protect their homes and families against attack. These regiments, the oldest in the U.S. Armed Forces, are known as the 101st Field Artillery, 101st Engineer Battalion and the 181st and 182nd Infantry Regiments.

Patterned after the English militia system, male colonists between the ages of 16 and 60 were expected to serve their country. There were no uniforms to speak of, and men often shared muskets, but they banded together anyhow.

During the 1770s, the Colonial militia began to ready themselves for battle. In Massachusetts, the militia proudly called themselves the minutemen, because they were said to be able to prepare for battle at a "minute's notice." Other Colonies began to adopt the idea of minutemen, but the best known were those from Massachusetts.

At the end of the Revolutionary War, the delegates who framed the Constitution realized the importance of the militia in protecting not only towns and states, but in defending the nation. The Militia Clause of the Constitution recognized this role, and the militia became the basis of today's National Guard.

title: Declaration of Independence
text:
After the first few battles of the Revolutionary War, most Americans were convinced it was time to separate from England.

Colonies Declare Their Independence

It was the summer of 1776. The Second Continental Congress met in Philadelphia to talk about independence. The Congress wanted to protest to the king. They wanted everyone to know the Colonies would govern themselves. But some of the members of Congress did not want to go to war. They argued for days. Then, they sent word home to their Colonies, "Discuss independence, and tell us how we should vote." Answers began coming in. Each time it was the same, "Vote for independence!" Richard Henry Lee of Virginia told the Congress, "These United Colonies are, and of right ought to be, free and independent states." The Congress decided to declare independence for the American Colonies. They chose Thomas Jefferson to write the document known as the Declaration of Independence. Jefferson worked hard for two weeks writing and rewriting. The first part of the Declaration explains men have certain rights that can't be taken away. The second part tells how the king refused to grant these rights. The Congress made the vote late on July 2, 1776. It was officially adopted on July 4, 1776. Some colonists may not have wanted independence. Even so, the Massachusetts delegates voted for independence. The Declaration was read to most of the Colonies within a few weeks.

title: Using Reason and Logic: Jury Duty
text:
Do you know any grown-ups who have served on a jury? U.S. citizens who are at least 18 years old are sometimes called to jury duty. It’s an important responsibility. A jury is a group of 12 people chosen to decide if a person being tried in court is guilty or innocent of a crime.

If you serve on a jury, you will have to come to court every day until both sides of the case have said everything they want to say.

Sometimes this might only be a few days, but some trials can go on for months! After the trial, a judge sends the jury to a special room to talk about what they saw and heard. Each jury member should practice reason and logic when talking with other members. They are helping to decide what happens to the person on trial.

For serious court cases, all 12 people on a jury have to agree. Even if the vote is 11 to 1, that’s enough for a “hung jury,” which means the case has to start all over with another trial and a different jury.

For some cases, the two sides can agree ahead of time if they will accept a majority (more than half) vote in the jury.

Juries are important because they help decide if someone who has been accused of a crime really did break the law. Jury members can only talk with each other about the case when they are deciding. So, if you know someone who has been called for jury duty, you can ask him or her what it was like after the trial!

title: Local Government
text:
The U.S. Constitution explains the duties of the national and state governments. However, it does not tell about the duties of local governments. Many states have subdivisions of counties, cities, boroughs, towns, villages and even special districts. The state legislature and state constitution decide how many and what kinds of local governments there are.

Today, there are about 90,000 local governments in the United States. Many times, these governments overlap, and it can be very confusing. For instance, when a city is in a county, both have government officials. Sometimes areas of jurisdiction, or control, overlap. It can make it hard to figure out which government should take action.

Sometimes, in large areas, counties and cities share services such as health care, fire, libraries, parks and recreation. Is the library nearest you a city library or a county library? Maybe it belongs to both!

title: Betsy Ross
text: There is a legend that Betsy Ross, who ran a shop on Arch Street in Philadelphia, was commissioned by George Washington himself to make the first American national flag. There is no historical proof to support the legend of Betsy Ross as creator of the first national flag. The day set aside each year to honor our flag is Flag Day, June 14.

title: What did Paul Revere do?
text: Paul Revere was a silversmith from Boston who discovered a British General was marching his troops on the towns of Lexington and Concord before they had actually arrived. Revere got his friend, Dr. Samuel Prescott, and they rode out to warn people. It was actually Dr. Prescott who got to Concord to warn them, not Revere. So why do people talk about Paul Revere and not Samuel Prescott? Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, a Mainer from Portland, wrote a poem about this event entitled "Paul Revere's Ride," that gave Revere, not Prescott, credit for the ride.

title: Bank Services
text:
Did you know you can do your banking without ever going to a bank? Many people prefer to use their computers at home or at their office to do their banking. This popular method is called online banking. It allows people to access their bank accounts online. It lets them do their banking right from home!

If you have ever done any type of business with a bank, you have made a transaction. The most common transactions are deposits and withdrawals. A deposit is any money that is put into a banking account. Most people make deposits with checks or cash. A withdrawal is money that you take from your banking account. In most cases, it is given to you as cash.

Pretend that your grandma gave you a $10 check for your birthday. You want to put it in your savings account. You take the check to the bank and fill out a deposit slip. The teller enters the information into the computer and gives you a receipt. You have just made a deposit. Later, you decide that it might be nice to take that same $10 and go to a movie. You go back down to the bank, fill out a withdrawal slip and give the paper to the teller. The teller asks for your ID. Then the teller gives you $10 in cash along with a receipt. You have made a withdrawal. Now that you have cash, you can enjoy your movie!

title: Whose side are you on?
text:
At first, patriots were colonists who wanted England to stop the taxes. As the conflict wore on, liberty meant more. The patriots no longer wanted to be British citizens. They just wanted to be Americans.

Loyalists were those who wanted to remain citizens of England. They stayed loyal for different reasons. Sometimes, it was because they were loyal to family members who still lived in England. Others were afraid that England was too powerful. Still, some believed a government run by "rich patriots" would be worse than the English crown. Finally, others who remained loyal to the king felt he had the right to rule the Colonies.

Did all of the colonists choose sides?

No! Many of the colonists tried to stay neutral (not choose a side). Some even changed sides as the war went on. Many families were split. Benjamin Franklin was a firm patriot. His son William Franklin was the royal governor of Massachusetts. He was a well-known loyalist.

title: Let's Write
text: Maine is a beautiful state. In 150 words or less, tell about a natural wonder in your region, county or city. Draw a picture of this Maine site to visit. Be sure to use a fine black marker, because pencil doesn’t copy well. Describe it so other students in Maine would love to visit this site!

title: Frigate Chesapeake Attacked!
text:
After the Revolutionary War, the United States of America became its own country. A new country always has lots of things to worry about. It didn't help that Great Britain treated the United States very poorly.

Before the War of 1812 (between Great Britain and the United States), Great Britain and France were at war. France's leader, Napoleon Bonaparte, closed all ports under his influence to British ships. In return, Great Britain forced all neutral ships to port in Great Britain. These ships had to pay duties before continuing to any ports closed to Great Britain. This was know as the Orders in Council and caused serious problems for America's economy.

Great Britain also started to impress American sailors. To impress means to force someone to serve on a ship from a country other than his or her own. Britain believed anyone who deserted British ships in American harbors, if found, should be forced to work on a British ship again. America thought this was a violation of an individual's rights. Between 1803 and 1810, about 5,000 Americans were forced to serve on British war ships. These sailors were only released when they proved they were Americans, which was hard to do. The impressed sailors usually served the British for a year or two before they were released.

Once the American commander of the Chesapeake, a frigate, or warship, refused to let his ship be searched for deserters. So the British attacked! Three Americans were killed, 18 were wounded and four men (three who were Americans) were taken on board the British ship, the Leopard.

The United States was fed up. More than anything else, these events pushed the United States toward the War of 1812. On June 18, 1812, Congress declared war on Great Britain.

Maine and the War of 1812

During the War of 1812, Bangor, Maine, saw its share of battles. In 1814, the British fought and beat American forces in the Battle of Hampden, which is just south of Bangor. The British then moved to Bangor and forced its selectmen, or officials, to surrender. Read on to see what happened.

On Sept. 3, 1814, a thick fog crept through the Penobscot Valley as militiamen from the greater Bangor area waited for the British. When the Americans heard the British coming sometime between 7 a.m. and 8 a.m., they began firing their guns. This time the British clearly had the upper hand, using two warships to bombard American troops on land. Once again, the British chased the Americans to Bangor. The British crushed the American forces, although casualties on both sides were light. One British trooper died, nine were wounded, and one went missing. One American trooper died, 11 were wounded, and one civilian died watching the battle. The British captured 80 Americans as prisoners of war.

The British forced the Bangor selectmen to surrender the town. Then the British looted shops and homes. They occupied the town for 30 hours. Before leaving, they threatened to burn ships in Bangor's harbor and unfinished ships on stocks. The Bangor selectmen feared the fires from the ships would spread into the town and destroy everything. They struck a deal with the British. They put up a bond and promised to deliver the ships by the end of November. The British eventually burned all but two ships, one brig, six schooners and three sloops. These they took, along with horses and cattle, back to their post in Castine, which they occupied until April 26, 1815.

title: Maine's War: The Aroostook War
text: Maine is special for many reasons. It has a unique history with lots of interesting events. One interesting fact about Maine is that it is one of the only states that has participated in a war in which no one was killed or hurt. That's right, no one! After the American Revolution, times weren't easy for the new states. Some old battles still lived on. One of those battles was the dispute over the border between Maine and Canada. Maine and New Brunswick both had economies that were supported largely by the lumber industry. The land in this area is rich in trees whose wood is good for lumber. There are also many broad rivers that flow through the area. This made transporting lumber much easier than hauling it over land. There was valuable land along that border. Whichever country won the border dispute was in a position to make a lot of money. In the late 1830s, lumber interests in the Canadian province of New Brunswick and in Maine both sought control of the area that is now Aroostook County. Maine and New Brunswick both sent troops to the area. The so-called Aroostook War ended without bloodshed in 1839. The boundary dispute wasn't over though. It continued on and was known as the Northeast Boundary Dispute. The boundary dispute was resolved by the Webster-Ashburton Treaty in 1842. The land was given to Maine.

title: War of 1812
text:
The Ships of War

During the War of 1812, naval warfare was very common and the favored type of battle. Maine was home to a successful shipbuilding industry and located on the coast, so it was often close to battles. Warfare on water was very different from traditional land warfare. People had to learn a whole new kind of fighting.

Navies in the early 1800s depended upon three main types of warships. The first type was the ship of the line, or line-of-battleship. Later it was known simply as the battleship. Weighing in at over 2,500 tons, ships of the line carried from 64 to 120 cannons. They were arranged on two or three levels, or gun decks. Slow and clumsy, these floating fortresses were unstoppable except by vessels of their own class.

Next in size was the frigate. Frigates were a thousand tons lighter than their big sisters. Frigates were called "the cavalry of the sea." These ships were swift and easy to handle, which made them popular. Frigates carried between 32 and 44 cannons set up on a single gun deck. Although they never fought ships of the line, these sleek, tall-masted beauties were excellent at scouting and hunting enemy ships.

A sloop, the last type of warship, mounted 16 to 24 light cannons. Depending upon the number of masts and arrangement of the sails, sloops might be known as brigs, brigantines or schooners. These lightweights were ideal for patrolling shallow offshore waters and blockading harbor entrances.

The Sailors of 1812

What was it like to be a sailor during the War of 1812? Unlike soldiers ashore, who wore uncomfortable uniforms, sailors (often called jack-tars) dressed comfortably so they could handle the ships. Sailors in both navies wore blue jackets and white trousers. They liked to braid their hair into a pigtail, which they greased with hog fat. They also usually wore a black scarf. Most sailors went barefoot, so the soles of their feet became as tough as old leather. Going barefoot gave a better grip on the slippery decks and made it easier to climb the masts when the sails had to be taken down and furled.

Officers, however, were gentlemen who wore high boots, tight breeches and blue coats loaded with gold braid and brass buttons. One of the duties of an officer on the ship was to provide a solid, steady crew to operate the big guns. Naval guns were larger and heavier than land cannons. They did not have to be dragged over the ground. Sailors had different jobs when it came to operating the two different kinds of cannons, long and short. Some sailors were called "powder monkeys." These were usually young boys. They were in charge of bringing fresh charges of powder to the gunners. They loaded it into the cannons along with rope wadding and shot before firing. A good cannon crew could load, fire and reload a cannon in a minute or less.

title: Making Money
text:
Have you ever wondered where money comes from? All of the paper money in the United States is printed at the Bureau of Engraving and Printing. It is located in Washington, D.C. Paper bills are made of a special blend of cotton and linen. This blend makes the paper much stronger than normal. It is illegal to make this blend of paper without the permission of the Bureau of Engraving and Printing.

Money is printed on sheets in sets of 30 bills. It is then cut apart and pressed. Then it is starched and bundled. Each bill is printed in different colors of ink. The ink is made from a special formula that only the Bureau knows how to make. The bills also have red and blue threads running throughout. You can't even see them. It would be very difficult to make money that is just the same.

Why can't just anybody print money? Well, when there are too many dollars in circulation (in use), the purchasing power of a dollar goes down. When the purchasing power is down, prices go up.

Purchasing power is a measure of how much the dollar is worth. If there is too much paper money out there, it is called inflation. What do you think deflation is? If you guessed it is when there is too little paper money, you guessed right! This causes product prices to fall. Lucky for us, the Federal Reserve watches the money each day. If it looks as if there is too much or too little, they can do things to fix it.

title: County Government
text:
A county in the United States is a tier of government. It is smaller than a state, but larger than a city. A county has governing powers over a clearly defined area. It is under state government. There are over 3,000 counties in the United States.

The structure or power of a county government varies from state to state. Most counties maintain city-like departments. They may have a business administration or a city council. There are also many sections to county governments. Fire departments, the police, parks and recreation and public works are all part of a county's structure.

Sometimes areas of jurisdiction, or control, overlap. For instance, a city is in a county, and both have government officials. It can be difficult to figure out which one should take action.

title: What was a jack-tar?
text:
A sailor in the War of 1812 was often called a "jack-tar." It didn't matter if he was American or British. Why were they called this?

A common word used for man, or guy, then was jack. Wooden ships were not waterproof on their own. They needed something put on them to seal the wood and keep the water from seeping through the boards. Many things could have been used. But, on the warships during the War of 1812, the paint of choice was a kind of tar. Sailors would spend days painting the ships with tar. When they were done, they smelled like the tar that waterproofed the ship, thus they were called "jack-tar."

title: River Otter
text:
River otters are members of the weasel family, as are minks. The river otter is the only member of the weasel family to have webbed feet and a strong, muscular tail.

River otters are very sociable and fun to watch. They wrestle, play and slide down river banks. They chirp, whistle, growl and even scream. The river otter can dive and swim expertly. They can swim about 7 miles per hour and can stay underwater for about two minutes. Unlike the muskrat or beaver, their sleek bodies hardly cause a ripple or a splash. When underwater, their ears and nose close up. Their whiskers help to sense prey, even when they can't see it.

The young are called cubs or kits. They are not good swimmers and are carried by the mother to the banks at about 12 weeks old.

In some states, river otters are a protected animal. They may be trapped or hunted during a limited season.

title: Why Should I Follow Directions?
text:
Why Should I Follow Directions?

Here's a really good story about why it's important to always follow directions. Once you read it, you'll never have trouble following directions again!

One time a teacher handed out a test to her students. It was a long 10-page test. At the end of class, some students thought they did very well. They got most of the questions correct. But nobody passed! After the teacher had graded the tests, she pointed out the directions at the top: "Write your name on the top of Page one and hand the test in. Do not complete any of the questions." You can bet those students wished they had read the directions!

Reading directions carefully can mean the difference between an "A" and an "F" in school. It can mean the difference between a delicious pan of muffins and a mess of burnt, yucky dough.

1. Read the directions from beginning to end before you do anything else.
2. Make a list of any material you will need. Gather it up!
3. After you have everything you need, read the directions again carefully. Do you understand every step?
4. Do you still have questions? Ask your teacher, parent or a friend for input.
5. Follow the directions carefully, step by step.

If you follow all these steps, you will do all your assignments correctly.

title: Let's Write
text: Most Americans didn’t like the British policies of impressment, but the British couldn’t understand American ideas. The British thought if they didn’t beat Napoleon, the freedom of the whole world was at stake. Many nations depended on Great Britain winning the war, and, to protect those nations, the British didn’t think impressing American sailors was too much of an inconvenience. Americans spoke of rights, but the British thought they were right! What do you think of impressment? Were the British right in what they did? Were the Americans right to be angry about impressments? Why or why not?

title: Maine Petitions for Statehood
text:
During the War of 1812 many things happened in Maine. The British took control of almost the entire shoreline, closing all the ports. Not only did this hurt Maine's economy, but it cost the lives and effort of many of the Mainers who were trying to defend the ports.

The British captured Eastport, Castine, Belfast and Bangor. Maine begged the Massachusetts government to send help. They never did. A similar thing had been happening all throughout the American Revolution. Massachusetts was either unwilling or unable to help and protect York County (Maine). This, however, was the final straw for Mainers. Other things had happened before that made them want to separate.

Maine and Massachusetts were very different. They based their industries on different things. Most of Massachusetts' money came from trading goods. Boston was one of the busiest trading centers in the new country. Maine also made a fair amount of money from trading. But Maine was the area where lumber was milled and ships were made. This is what made trading possible.

Maine was also more sparsely populated than the Boston area. By the time separation happened, Maine had 300,000 people living within its borders in 236 towns. It was spread out. Much of the land was used for harvesting trees and planting crops.

These reasons also fueled the desire of Mainers to become their own state. However, when the first talk of separation began, it was mostly those who lived inland and owned a lot of land that wanted separation. The merchants who lived on Maine's coast were quite happy being part of Massachusetts. They had more political influence in Maine than others. Maine did not petition for statehood until after the War of 1812.

The merchants soon changed their minds about staying unified with Massachusetts. They lacked support in defending Maine's ports.

Massachusetts did agree to allow Maine to petition for statehood. Now the decision needed to be made official by the Mainers. In the debate about statehood, many had feelings that Boston was too far away. Maybe Boston was too different to understand Maine's problems and way of life. They thought the government taxed them unfairly (like England did the Colonies), and showed little support for Maine. The decision was put to a vote in 1819, and the separatists won by a landslide.

Maine petitioned for statehood later that year. This posed an interesting problem which wasn't even resolved that year. During this time in the country there was a lot of debate about slave labor. Before Maine petitioned for statehood, there were 22 states. Eleven allowed slave owning and trading within their borders; 11 did not. The members of Congress were worried about upsetting that balance. Many Southern states depended on slave labor for their economy. It was based upon large plantations made successful by free slave labor. Many of the Northern states abhorred the practice and labeled it immoral. Between the two extremes, many had not decided.

Maine had never practiced slavery as a whole. In fact, only a few Mainers owned slaves. Maine did not want to allow slavery within its borders after it became a state. This started a battle in Congress that kept Maine from statehood for almost a year.

Finally, on March 15, 1820, Maine was admitted to the Union as the 23rd state as part of the Missouri Compromise.

title: A Census Full of Treasure
text:
On April 2, 2012, the government released the 1940 census. A census is a count of all the people in the United States, and it is done every 10 years. It also gives other information about citizens' jobs, income, birthplace and education level. The government only releases a census' records to the public after 72 years have passed. The 1940 census was the first one done after the Great Depression and World War I. It shows how these events caused people to move around and where immigrants went. You can find interesting facts about family members and famous people. For example, the future President Ronald Reagan paid $135 in rent in 1940!

The 1940 census was the last time census takers went door-to-door to personally interview people and write down the information. For the 1950 census the government started using census questionnaires sent through the mail.

The release of the 1940 census data is different from past years. This information was made digital and released through the Internet. There are more than 3.8 million pages of data in this census. Genealogists, or people who study family backgrounds, use this information to trace family history. Researchers, like historians, often use the census as a primary source of information.

So, was this release a success? Well, so many people tried to get the information on its first day of release that the server crashed! If you would like to learn more about your family history you can go to the 1940 census site at: 1940census.archives.gov/.

title: Separating From Massachusetts
text:
Doesn't Massachusetts Care?

Many Mainers thought Massachusetts didn't care about them. This wasn't just because Massachusetts didn't support Maine during the war. In fact, it was mostly because of Massachusetts' land policies.

Many Mainers thought Massachusetts favored absentee landowners over those who actually lived on and worked the land. What is an absentee landowner? He is a person who owns land he doesn't actually live on or near. An absentee landowner would often rent or lease that land to someone else. The renters would work and farm that land. They also paid the landowner a certain amount of their profits or crops.

After the war, Maine was struggling to recover, as was Massachusetts. Instead of giving help, Massachusetts (which was deeply in debt) began selling large pieces of land in Maine to wealthy investors. They used money from these sales to pay off their war debts. Selling this land in Maine devastated the Maine economy. In the late 1790s, after the Revolution and before the War of 1812, Massachusetts signed treaties with the Penobscot and Passamaquoddy Indians. This gave the state all but a small corner of their land. Indians also had some hunting and fishing rights. The state soon sold the American Indian lands at a huge profit, mainly to lumber companies.

Mainers were angry that Massachusetts would sell the Maine land just to make money. This anger began to fuel the landowners' cry for separation.

The Missouri Compromise

The Missouri Compromise was an agreement made in Congress. It kept a balance between slave-owning and free states in the country. The power of the government, at that time, was spread out over all the states. Many people on both sides of the issue feared an imbalance. The Missouri Compromise was a product of this fear. Its design was to preserve the balance between slave and free states. They would admit states in pairs, one slave state and one free state. Missouri was admitted as a slave state with Maine a free state. The Missouri Compromise set a line at about 36 degrees latitude north of the equator. North of this line in the Louisiana Purchase, slavery would not be allowed. This lasted until 1854, when the Kansas-Nebraska act changed it slightly.

title: Taxes
text:
You are standing in line at the grocery store. You have counted all of your change, and you have $1.03. It's just enough to buy the biggest pack of bubblegum you've ever seen in your life. The bubblegum costs $1.00. You get to the front of the line and the cashier rings it up. Your total comes to $1.06. What? That can't be right. You are three cents short. How did that happen? Then you remember about sales tax. Lucky for you, you find an extra nickel in your pocket and pay for your gum.

Taxes are sums of money that the government collects from people and businesses. They use this money to provide services for the citizens. There are many different kinds of taxes, like the sales tax you pay at the grocery store. Sales tax is a tax that is usually added to the price of your purchase for goods or a service.

There are three main types of taxes: progressive tax, regressive tax and proportional tax. A progressive tax can change. The tax depends on how much money a person makes. People that make more money pay more in taxes. People that make less money pay less in taxes. A proportional tax is the same tax for everyone. Regressive taxes are opposite of progressive taxes. This means that people with more income pay less in taxes and people with less income pay more in taxes. Which tax do you think is the most fair?

title: Write a Letter
text:
Even though you are not old enough to vote, you are old enough to write a letter to a government official. You can tell them how you feel about something.

The first thing to decide is who to write your letter to. Let's say you were writing a letter about your city's roller skating rink. You wouldn't write to the president of the United States, but to the mayor of your city. Likewise, a letter about health care issues wouldn't go to your school principal. You must write to the person who can help you.

Always write a government official in a formal way. Put your name and address in the upper right hand corner. Skip two lines and put the date. On the left put the official's name and address. Then open the letter by using the official's correct title. For example, "Dear Governor Smith." Be clear about the purpose of the letter. Be sure to thank the official for his or her time and attention.

Don't forget that letters to officials aren't always for asking. Sometimes they are for thanking them as well! A letter of thanks is helpful and surely appreciated.They want to know they are doing the right job for the voters of tomorrow!

title: What is a Ropewalk?
text:
Wherever there were ships, there had to be rope. Rope in the Colonial days had to be twisted by hand.

The work was done in very, very long sheds known as ropewalks. Many were as long as three city blocks.

Nearly all rope was made of hemp grown on American farms. The process of making it was really much like spinning yarn, although it looked different. In fact, the product of the first step in rope-making was called yarning.

The spinner would tie the head of the rope around his waist. The loose ends were fastened to hooks on a big spinning wheel. As the wheel turned, the yarn would wind together and form the rope.

title: Snowshoe Hare
text:
Snowshoe hare are rarely seen. They are one of the many mammals to inhabit our woods and back country.

This beautiful animal is shy and sweet. He blends in perfectly with his surroundings, because he's brown in the summer and pure white in the winter.

Snowshoes have about four litters per year. They have one to nine baby hare per litter. They are born fully furred, open-eyed and are able to hop around almost immediately. This is the opposite of rabbits, which are born naked and blind. Hares love to eat wild strawberry plants and the bark of maple, birch and willow trees.

These beautiful animals have natural enemies including the red fox, coyote and mink. Even the Great Horned Owl often attacks them. But their biggest killer is disease. They suffer from many kinds.

The hare has large furry feet. (Where do you think he got his name?) Look carefully to see if you can spot a hare next time your are out in the snow.

title: How Do I Read a Map?
text:
Maps can tell you a whole lot about the world. They show you which direction to travel and how to find an unknown place. But wouldn't you like to know how high the mountains are around you? And just where are those lakes and railroads? If you want to know all that and more, maps are for YOU!

These map functions will help you read a map:

Scale - On a map you'll often see: 1 inch = 1 mile. That means one inch on the map represents one mile of the land around you. Easy, huh?

Legend - What do those little pictures or symbols on a map mean? The legend is a box, usually in a corner of the map. It lists the symbols, then tells what they mean.

Grid - Many maps are arranged on a grid. See the lines going up and down the sides of the map? There are more lines at the top and bottom. Those grid lines help you locate places on the map. Grids have letters along the sides and numbers across the top and bottom.

Index - To use the grid to find a location, go to the map's index. The index lists locations with a letter and a number for each location. Find the spot on the map where that letter and number cross. For example: House - D, 9

title: The Eastern White Pine
text: The white pine timber was valuable for building ships and helped Maine to become an important shipbuilding state.

title: Let's Write
text:
Because of Maine’s unique situation of being part of a colony which it wasn’t geographically connected to, much of Maine’s history is unique when compared to the other Northeastern states.

There are certainly many other things that are unusual or unique to the history of Maine. Write and tell of some things that you know of from researching our great state of Maine. Perhaps they are things Maine did first or maybe some very old laws that are unusual today. Does Maine have a geographical feature or monument it is famous for?

title: Maine as a New State
text:
Maine is a state with rich history and meaning taught by the symbols it has chosen to represent it. Let's look at some of these symbols together.

State Flag

The coat of arms of the State of Maine is placed on a blue field of the same shade of blue in the U.S. flag. This flag was adopted by the legislature in 1909. It is interesting because it is actually not the flag design authorized by the original law. The original flag design was much more simple. It was on a light background with the state's tree, the eastern white pine, in the center, and a blue, five-pointed North Star in the upper left corner. Legislation that began in 1991 and 1997 by David Boice Martucci attempted to restore the flag design to its original form but has not yet been successful.

State Bird: The Chickadee (Parus atricapillus)

The chickadee was adopted by the legislature in 1927. The blacked-capped chickadee is a common sight in the woods and at backyard bird feeders throughout the state. It has a short, brownish-black bill, thick body and blended short feathers. Its tail is long, arched and rounded with 12 slender feathers. The whole upper part of its head and neck are pure black.

State Insect: Honeybee

The honeybee has helped the success of Maine farms since the earliest days of Maine. It goes from flower to flower gathering material to make honey and spreads pollen between the flowers in the process, allowing them to produce seeds which will grow into fruits which may be harvested.

State Flower: White Pine Cone & Tassel

Maine is the only state whose state flower is a pine cone. The cone of the white pine does flower, and is a rather pleasant pine cone itself, having a fragrant smell and no thorns.

State Tree: Eastern White Pine

The eastern white pine is a pagoda-shaped evergreen that reaches heights up to 250 feet. The white pine was coveted by all shipbuilders, because it made wonderful, tall masts. It was very important to the economy of early Maine.

State Soil: Chesuncook

Maine is one of only a few states with a state soil. Chesuncook is a kind of soil made from the sediment that was left behind by the glaciers that used to cover it, called glacial till. It is estimated that this soil covers 150,000 acres of Maine and occurs in altitudes between 300 and 2,500 feet above sea level. This soil is good for forests of trees such as red spruce, balsam fir, yellow birch, sugar maple, white ash and red maple. It is also very good for farming potatoes, oats and barley. Chesuncook was adopted as Maine's official state soil on April 16, 1999.

State Cat: Maine Coon Cat

The Maine coon cat is the oldest and largest breed that originated in America. It is known for its intelligence, good disposition and the delightful chirping or trilling sound it makes when it's happy. There are many legends about how the coon cat came to be, many of which are not possible, some of which could be true. One story credits Marie Antoinette, the queen of France. During the French Revolution, she smuggled her royal treasure, including six long-haired cats, to Wiscasset, Maine. When these cats bred with house cats here, the story says, the coon cat was born. Most breeders believe the coon cat was a cross between Angora and household cats brought to America by the colonists. The first mention of a Maine coon cat in literature was in 1861, a black and white cat named Captain Jenks.

State Seal

The state seal is a silver shield, on which can be found a pine tree with a moose lying at its foot. On the left side of the shield is a farmer resting on a scythe. On the right side, a seaman is resting on an anchor. In a banner below the shield the name "MAINE" is printed in all Roman capital letters. Above the shield is a banner containing the state motto, "Dirigo," in all capital letters, crowned by a five-pointed North Star. Colonel Isaac G. Reed of Waldoboro is credited with the seal's description and explanation based upon symbols suggested by Benjamin Vaughan of Hallowell, Maine.

title: Maine's State House
text:
Once Maine became a state, it needed to choose a capital and build a state house, or capitol building. Augusta was chosen as the state capital in 1827, and the cornerstone for the new state house was laid in 1829. The building, completed in 1832, was designed by Charles Bulfinch and was built of Hallowell granite.

The state house sits on a knoll above Augusta. It is a four-story building whose portico, or large, covered walkway supported by columns, rises to a height of 300 feet. The building has two 75-foot wings that spread out on either side of the portico.

In 1911, the building was enlarged using the designs of G. Henri Desmond. Most of the old building had to be destroyed and a new, higher dome was installed. Atop this dome stands a statue of Lady Wisdom, designed by W. Clark Noble.

To schedule a tour of the state house, call (207) 287-2301.

title: Maine's Constitution
text:
After Maine was finally cleared to become a state, the leaders took up the task of writing a state constitution. Delegates met in Portland for three weeks in October 1819 to draft it. William King, who later became Maine's first governor, presided over the convention. It turned out to be a document strongly rooted in political independence, religious freedom and popular control of the government.

Maine's constitution was, in some ways, very similar to the Constitution of the United States of America. It set up a government with three distinct departments - the legislative, the executive and the judicial - and specified that they were to be independent of each other to balance the power.

The state constitution recognized the right of American Indians residing on reservations in Maine to vote in all county, state and national elections. It states that those eligible to vote cannot be arrested while going to vote, voting or returning from voting, except for the most serious crimes. Also, no eligible voter can be kept from voting, except during times of war. These are just some things in Maine's state constitution.

The Constitutional Convention established Portland as a temporary capital. (The capital was moved to Augusta in 1832.) After having its constitution ratified, or accepted, Maine experienced a great economic boom as a new state that lasted throughout most of the 19th century.

Maine's First Governor

William King (1768-1852) was not the most educated man in his family. His half-brother, who was far more educated than he, participated in the U.S. Constitutional Convention. But King grew up to become a successful and influential politician.

William was the son of a wealthy merchant, but his father, Richard, died when William was a young boy. William had to leave his boarding school, Phillips Academy in Andover, Massachusetts, at the age of 13. He went to work in sawmills in Saco and Topsham, Maine.

Eventually his love of business led him to establish a shipbuilding and shipping business in Bath.

King organized Bath's first bank, helped fund Maine's first cotton mill in Brunswick in 1809 and owned a great deal of real estate, including Kingfield, Maine. King served on the Massachusetts General Court for several years, first as a representative for Topsham and Bath and later as a senator for Lincoln County. He worked extremely hard to secure Maine's separation from Massachusetts and won the governor's seat in 1820 by a landslide; 21,083 out of 22,014 votes were for him. This popularity earned him the nickname "Sultan."

title: International Trade
text:
You have learned so much about money. You have learned how it is used. You know how it is made. It would seem that using one form of money around the world would be a good way to trade. However, many countries have their own form of currency, or money. In fact, today there are about 140 different types of currency in the world! So how do countries trade with one another if their money is so different?

To solve this problem, countries have what is called the foreign exchange market. Here, dealers in different major cities like New York, Tokyo or London trade money between countries. They decide what the exchange rate should be. In other words - how many pesos, euros, francs or baht will it take to buy one United States dollar? The exchange rate is based on the ideas of supply and demand. For example, if people in the U.S. wanted to buy goods from Mexico, they would need Mexican pesos. This would create a demand for pesos. What happens when there is a greater demand for something? That's right, the value goes up. The value of the peso would then increase.

As the value of the currency goes up, so does the price of the goods. If the price goes too high, then the demand for that product goes down. When the demand is down, the value of the currency falls. It's a real economic roller coaster!

Have you ever thought of money as being weak or strong? Well, when the U.S. dollar has a high value, it is strong. It is usually strong when there is a great demand for American-made goods. The opposite can be true too. If the value of the dollar is low, then the American dollar is weak.

title: Governor
text:
According to the dictionary, a governor is an official who leads the government of a colony or state. Each state in the United States has a governor. He or she is elected by the citizens in that state. The governor is the chief executive. This means the governor is the leader of political and civic matters in that region.

Generally, governors work in a similar fashion to the president of the United States. They work in the executive branch of the state government. They have the power to veto bills. They can pardon people who have broken the law. Typically, governors serve in office for a term of four years. In New Hampshire and Vermont, they only serve two-year terms. Sometimes, someone in the U.S. Senate may suddenly die or be removed from office. The governor of that state has the ability to appoint someone to fill that office. The governor is also a military leader. He or she has control of the U.S. National Guard and State Defense Forces in the state. The governor can activate the National Guard in times of natural disaster or as directed by the president.

title: Was the Town of Lincoln, Maine, Named After Abraham Lincoln?
text:
Well in a word, no. Actually, the town of Lincoln was founded in 1829. Abraham Lincoln didn't even become president until 1861. The town of Lincoln, Maine, was named after Enoch Lincoln.

Enoch was an ambitious, talented young lawyer who was known for his character, scholarly pursuits, oration (speaking) skills and strong opposition to slavery. Enoch owned a private library that was considered to be one of the best in Maine. He was elected as governor of Maine and served two one-year terms. He was governor while the Northeastern Boundary issue was settled and when the location in Augusta was chosen for the new state house. He wrote a 2,000 line poem, "The Village," which was published in 1816, making him Maine's first poet.

title: Moose
text:
The moose is the largest deer-like animal in North America. The moose stands about 6 feet high and weighs about 1,000 pounds. The male has broad flattened antlers. Moose like the colder, northern climates. They are found from the northern United States up into Canada.

Moose can be found in moist lowlands around lakes where they feed on water plants. In the winter they stay closer to forests. Moose feed at night and the very early hours of the morning. One (or rarely two) young is born to the mother in the late spring. The young ones are called calves. Moose can run very fast. Never approach a moose, especially a cow with a calf.

title: How Do I Read Charts?
text:
By learning to read charts, you can quickly compare information.

Charts are very organized because they are used to compare data. They would be harder to understand if it was all jumbled together. That’s why charts use lists or boxes placed into categories. They appear at the top and down the left-hand side of every chart. You can easily see what information is being compared. You can also spot the differences and similarities. Using charts can help you understand information faster.
