title: Let's Write
text:
Enoch Lincoln wrote in his poem, “The Village,” “learn to love your country and its law.” What do you think he meant by that? What does it mean to you to “love your country?” Why is it also important to love the law? Who is that important to?

In fewer than 150 words, write why you love your country and how you support the law.

title: Slavery and Abolition
text:
In a previous issue of Maine Studies Weekly, we discussed the Atlantic Slave Trade and slavery in the Colonies. Let's review a few facts before we continue the story of slavery and abolition:

1641 - Massachusetts, including what is now Maine, became the first Colony to legalize slavery.

1680 - Slavery was in full force in all the Colonies.

1770 - The Triangular Trade made Boston the busiest harbor in the Colonies.

1789 - Massachusetts, including Maine, is the first colony to outlaw the selling of slaves.

1783 - Quork Walker, a slave in Barre, Massachusetts was awarded his freedom and fifty pounds in damages after his owner beat him.

1790 - There were no longer any slaves in Massachusetts or Maine.

Slavery was later abolished in all of the Northern states. The country was torn. Feelings of antislavery began to develop throughout Massachusetts and other states. Many states began to rise up against slavery. Many states thought slavery should continue.

Those who wished slavery to be abolished, or ended, were called abolitionists.

When states began making slavery illegal, they granted freedom to all former slaves who lived or came to live within their boundaries. Even though they were free, many former slaves still faced much hardship.

Sometimes slaves were awarded their freedom in courts. Others were given freedom after working for a long time. Most of the time, slaves became free by escaping. How did they escape? There were many ways. One very creative slave, Henry "Box" Brown, got in a box with some food and water and mailed himself to a free state!

A more common way to escape slavery was to travel the Underground Railroad. What was the Underground Railroad? It was a way of moving slaves to freedom in the North. Slaves would go from place to place until they got to the Northern states or all the way to Canada. The places these escaped slaves would go to were safe places: houses, churches or other buildings owned by free slaves, American Indians or sympathetic white Americans who were willing to hide them until it was safe to go on. The places that were safe for slaves to go to were called stations. The slaves were called packages (or passengers). People who helped the slaves get from place to place were called conductors. Those who ran the stations were called station masters. This was to protect slaves and the people who helped them when they had to talk about the activities of the Underground Railroad. This great movement peaked during the mid 1800s. It is estimated that between as many as 100,000 runaways reached freedom on the Underground Railroad.

Maine played a very important role in the Underground Railroad. Much of this has been learned only recently. Many communities and individuals knew about their local stations, but didn't know about each other. Maine was important to the Underground Railroad for many reasons: it shares a long border with Canada and it has many rivers that connect with each other and many coastal waterways. These were common means of transportation. Maine's shipping industry gave a lot of opportunity for stowaways. Currently there are 102 sites in 77 towns in Maine identified with the Underground Railroad. Many think this number falls short of identifying all the stations in Maine. The rest of this issue will look at two very important stations in Maine and their history.

title: A Slave No More!
text:
A letter written after the Civil War has shed light on the slave-master relationship. Jourdan Anderson was a slave who gained freedom when he and his family escaped to Ohio from Tennessee. In August 1865 his former owner, Colonel Anderson, wrote a letter asking Jourdan to come back to Tennessee to work on his farm.

The former slave's reply gave a clear message about his feelings. He said he hoped that God had opened the colonel's eyes to the wrongs done to slaves for generations. While he was glad his old master was alive, he was surprised that the Yankees hadn't hanged him yet. Jourdan wrote that there was one thing that might bring him back to Tennessee. He and his wife wanted to be paid for the 52 years of combined work that they provided as slaves (over $11,000). Without that, he said they had little faith in the colonel's promises. He ended by asking the colonel to give his best regards to a man named George Carter. Mr. Carter had apparently taken a pistol away from the colonel when he tried to shoot Jourdan...twice.

Reading letters and newspapers from the past can help us understand the people who lived during that time. Jourdan and his family may have once been slaves, but their spirits were not broken.

title: The Underground Railroad
text:
The Abyssinian Church

The Abyssinian Church in Portland, Maine, has long been known as a station for the Underground Railroad. In fact, there was never any doubt that it was. Why? Its members were African American. Many of them were mariners (people who worked on boats for a living). It was also a place of leadership in other parts of the abolition movement. This is definitely one of the most important stations in the country.

The Abyssinian Church was built in 1828. It is the oldest African American church in Maine and the third oldest in the United States. In addition to holding worship meetings, it housed a school for African-American children (because schools were still segregated, or separate, then). The church hosted many antislavery rallies. The members of the church would often hide runaway slaves in their homes or at the church.

In 1918, the church closed, and the building began to fall apart. Currently, the Committee to Restore the Abyssinian Church has begun the long process of restoring the building. It will be used as a cultural center and museum of African-American life in Maine.

The Holyoke House

The Holyoke House in Brewer, Maine, was perched on a bluff overlooking the powerful Penobscot River and the city of Bangor. This area was the lumber capital of the world. Many ships passed through there. In order to discover the Holyoke House connection to the Underground Railroad, the house had to be torn down.

Oral tradition had long claimed there was a tunnel that had been used by runaways to get from the river to the house. Then, in the 1950s, the owners figured out (by accident) that there was an underground room at the end of the tunnel. The room had been built for the runaways to stay in until they could go to an attic room in the house to hide. The tunnel still could not be found, though.

When the public learned about this, they petitioned for its preservation. They made claims of the house's historical significance. None of this outcry could save this beautiful home. It was demolished in 1995 to make way for a new bridge across what was once a water route to Canada.

In 1996, while working on the site, a bulldozer unearthed the tunnel. This discovery, in addition to an old slave-style shirt found tucked in the eaves in the attic room, prodded more research. Through this, much was learned about John Holyoke. He was a station master. Holyoke was a wealthy abolitionist who lived on one of the major waterways to Canada, the Penobscot River. This river was thick with piers and ships right below his house. The pier closest to the entrance of the tunnel was named Free Soil Wharf, after an anti-slavery party. The tunnel stretched 49 feet below the house to the wharf.

Harriet Tubman

The Underground Railroad wasn't a railroad as we think of it, but a group of people who secretly sheltered and moved runaway slaves to the safety of free states or to Canada. Many of the heroes of the Underground Railroad worked secretly and will never be known. No one is really sure how many slaves actually made it to freedom, perhaps as many as 100,000. Abolitionists, of many races, risked their freedom and even their lives to help ensure others were free as well.

Stories of spectacular escapes grew up around the Underground Railroad. A Maryland slave, Harriet Tubman, escaped and then risked her life by returning to the South to guide other slaves to freedom. She is referred to as a conductor. Runaway slaves, or passengers, sometimes hid in the woods. Along the Underground Railroad route runaway slaves would be guided by a conductor to homes and food provided by a station master. Frederik Douglass' home was one station on the Underground Railroad.

Frederick Douglass

Frederick Douglass was a runaway slave and a famous abolitionist. His story of hardship and cruelty was similar to many slaves' stories.

Douglass attended a meeting of the Anti-Slavery Society. Without preparation Douglass stood up and delivered a powerful speech. The members of the society were very impressed. They urged him to become an agent of the society and work full time for abolition. He was skilled at speaking and brought audiences to shame as he related stories from his days of slavery. It stirred people's hearts against slavery.

Douglass is also well known for his newspaper, the North Star. It was an anti-slavery newspaper in Rochester, New York. Douglass was a great abolitionist. He won many hearts for the cause of freedom.

title: Made in the U.S.A.
text:
Have you ever been surprised to see a sticker on something that says it was made in another country? Every country makes different kinds of goods. Countries trade with one another to get those goods. These goods are called imports. Imports are brought into one country, but they are for sale by another country.

Exports are just the opposite. A country sends products to other countries for sale. Let's say a car is made in Japan and then sold in the United States. In this case, Japan exported the car. The United States imported the car. It is a simple idea of in and out. Imports are brought in. Exports are sent out.

International trade can improve the standard of living for people around the world. A country can meet many needs through importing and exporting. Importing and exporting create new jobs. Yet, there are challenges too! Sometimes importing and exporting create competition at home.

Many times, things can be made for cheaper wages in other countries. Also, these countries are not subject to the same taxes that U.S. businesses pay. What is the effect? The prices of those products made in other countries may be much less than those same products made in the United States. Which products do you think people will want to buy?

Importing and exporting can be both helpful and harmful. We will learn about strategies used to control international trade in later issues. For now, can you name a product that is imported to the United States? Can you name one that is exported from the United States?

title: Lieutenant Governor
text:
A lieutenant governor is a state government official who supports the governor. He or she is also known as the deputy of the governor. This office is the second highest executive office in the state. This is similar to the vice-president of the United States. In 24 states, the lieutenant governor is elected at the same time as the governor. But in 18 states, the lieutenant governor is elected separately. This may result in the lieutenant governor being of a different political party than the governor.

The chief job of the lieutenant governor is to act as the governor when the governor is absent. The other duties of the lieutenant governor vary from state to state. In some states, they serve as chief election officials. In some, they are the speaker of the house in the state legislature. They may preside over the state senate. Maine is one of the states that does not have a lieutenant governor. If the governor is not able to serve, the president of the Maine State Senate fills the vacancy.

title: What Role Did the American Indians Play in the Underground Railroad?
text: The American Indians understood what it was like to be treated poorly by others. They sympathized with the escaping slaves. Often they would act as conductors for slaves. The American Indians would lead escaping slaves on trails through their land from place to place. They would try to stay out of the main areas of traffic. A safe haven on their land was provided. This way, the escaping slaves had a place to stay as they travelled. Without the help of the American Indians, there would have been much less success on the Underground Railroad.

title: The Wolf
text:
The wolf is a common symbol for many American Indian tribes. The largest clan of the Mahican tribe was the Wolf Clan.

The gray wolf lives in a pack, or a group. It will often stay with a pack all of its life. Though there are pack leaders, the pack will cooperate in hunting, caring for the young and defending their territory against other packs. Each wolf has a place in the pack and must fight for its rank.

Wolves can go many days without eating, and then eat as much as 20 pounds of meat at one time. Most are very agile and have incredible endurance. They can run very long distances and chase prey or plow through chest-high snow for long periods of time.

Fairy tales and cartoons would have you believe a wolf is aggressive, but there are few known cases of wolves attacking a human in the wild. Because wolves are very shy, it is rare that they will even come near humans.

title: How Do I Use a Graph?
text:
Graphs show numbers and tell what those numbers mean.

Types of Graphs

Bar Graph - Bar graphs use bars of different lengths to give information. The bars can run from left to right across the graph or from the bottom up. You can use a bar graph to show how numbers compare. Look at the bar graph about the U.S. population growth.

Pictograph - Pictographs are like bar graphs except they use pictures or symbols instead of bars. This pictograph shows different countries and how much ice cream they eat.

Pie Graph - Pie graphs use a circle to show 100 percent of something. The circle is divided into sections, or slices, of the pie. Each slice gives different information. Of the population in 2003, what percentage lived in China?

Line Graph - Line graphs show how information changes over time. One line shows units of time. Another line shows the information being measured. Inside the graph you'll see points that meet. You can use a line graph to see if the information is going up or down. This line graph shows the number of hurricanes since 1970. Have hurricanes increased or decreased?

title: Mob Rule
text: With no government, anarchy or mob rule can take over. In this situation it is survival of the fittest.

title: Let's Write
text:
Slavery was an ugly thing. Many people suffered and died because of the prejudices of others. Some people believed a person could be better than another person, or worth more, because of the color of his or her skin. Now we know that is not true, and almost everyone in America knows that slavery was wrong. What can be done to make sure slavery never comes back? What can be done to help change the attitudes of people who might not understand yet?

Write a poem about slavery in fewer than 200 words.

title: Abolition Movement In Maine
text:
In the last issue, you learned about the Underground Railroad and some important places in Maine that were connected with abolition. In this issue, you will learn more about people, organizations and events involved with abolition in Maine.

Perhaps one of the most important Mainers to the abolition movement was Harriet Beecher Stowe. She was an author who wrote a very important book, "Uncle Tom's Cabin." This book tells about the life of a man named Tom. Tom is a slave who leads an honorable life. The book brought to light many of the horrors of slavery. Harriet Beecher was born on June 14, 1811, in Litchfield, Connecticut. In 1836, she married Calvin Stowe. By the year 1850, they had moved to Maine. During the time before she moved to Maine, she had been exposed to slavery. Stowe did not agree with slavery. She wished something would be done to end the practice. Stowe didn't think she could do anything about it.

One Sunday, as she was sitting in church, she had a disturbing vision of a slave being beaten to death by his owner. This inspired her to write a story. Originally she did not intend for it to be a whole book. Once she started writing, she kept finding more to write. It ended up to be a very powerful and influential book. The story follows the life of a slave named Tom (and other characters) through slavery in early America to Tom's eventual death. A lot of the events in the book show many parts of the inhumanity of slavery.

After finishing the writing, Stowe wasn't sure if she should try to publish her book. When she went to her publisher he said it probably wouldn't sell. He agreed to try it anyway. Within the first week of its publication, 10,000 copies had been sold. Over the rest of the year, 290,000 more copies sold.

The book was adapted to the stage and played all over the North. Most of the showings were sold out. This was, of course, only true in the Northern states. In the South, many people hated the book. They called it one-sided and unfair.

One major heartache for Harriet was the disappearance of her son, also named Tom. He disappeared from a ship at Cape Horn in 1870. Until her death in 1896, she hoped he would return, but he never did. Her lasting legacy is her book "Uncle Tom's Cabin" which continues to be popular today. It is thought to be one of the strongest testaments against slavery in print.

The publishing of Stowe's book is only one of many important events having to do with abolition in Maine. Maine was the home of many of the first anti-slavery societies in the country. The first one in Maine was organized in Hallowell, at the house of Deacon Eben Dole, on Nov. 18, 1833. At the meeting five men were chosen to draft a constitution and nominate officers.

This anti-slavery society was followed by a state-wide anti-slavery society, with the first state convention being held in Augusta on Oct. 12, 1834. This society began annual meetings on Oct. 28, 1835.

These societies played a large role in preserving the freedom of African Americans in Maine. They pushed for abolition throughout the nation. They were among the first groups of brave people urging drastic changes in a new society.

title: Fighting Extremism with Education
text:
Extremism or radicalism means pushing an idea as far as it can go. Extremists are people who do this, and they often do not accept or tolerate other people’s ideas. They have hurt others and even killed because they didn’t agree with their beliefs.

Many brave individuals all over the world have dedicated their lives to fighting extremism by promoting education. Malala Yousafzai is one of these brave individuals. She believes that through education, people can learn to understand and accept one another.

Malala Yousafzai is a young Muslim woman. She was born and raised in Pakistan. In 2009, when Malala was 12 years old, the area of Pakistan she lived in was taken over by the Taliban. The Taliban are a religious extremist group who want to force their radical views onto other people. They believe that women should not receive an education, and Malala disagreed. When the Taliban came into her city and forbade girls from being able to attend school, she spoke up and campaigned for girls’ education. This put her in a lot of danger, but she did not let that stop her from speaking up for what she knew was right. At the age of 14, Malala was shot by a member of the Taliban and almost died.

On October 10, 2014, Malala was made a co-recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize for her dedication to education rights. More recently, in 2017, the United Nations named her the youngest ever official Messenger of Peace.

title: Important People and Events in Abolition
text:
An Important First

"[I] solemnly swear that [I] will do no falsehood nor consent to the doing of any in court. . . [I] will not wittingly or willingly promote or sue any false, groundless or unlawful suit nor give aid or consent to the same. . . [I] will delay no man for lucre or malice, but will conduct [myself] in the office of an attorney. . . according to the best of [my] knowledge and discretion, and with all good fidelity, as well as to the courts, as to [my] clients. So help [me] God."

This is an oath Maine residents take to become members of the bar, or lawyers. Until 1844, no person of color had taken this oath, or any oath to become a lawyer in the United States. On July 3, Macon Bolling Allen became the first African American lawyer in the United States. This was the first time the country's African American population had any representation in the courts. Many people considered this a big step towards the end of slavery.

Until then, the lawyer profession had been controlled by white men. Allen was soon joined by other African American lawyers, and they worked to make a difference. Here's something interesting: A short time after Allen became a lawyer, the U.S. Supreme Court made the Dred Scott decision. This decided that African Americans, both slave and free, could not become U.S. citizens and that slaves couldn't be taken from their owners. Allen and others helped influence the negative reaction to this decision. Because people did not agree with the decision, it was hard to keep official.

Student Anti-Slavery Society

The Anti-Slavery Society at Colby College has a very strange account of students causing hostile relations with administrators. This is recorded in the school's history.

The society began with the Literary Fraternity. It was organized so students could debate and pursue knowledge. They usually talked about important, current issues. Around 1833, those issues were often about slavery. They asked questions like, "Ought the government of the United States use force to compel South Carolina to submit to its laws, provided all other means prove ineffectual?" and "Ought Congress interfere with the abolition of slavery?" The students thought, in both cases, the correct answer was "Yes."

William Lloyd Garrison came to visit and speak to the students. He got them excited about abolition. Students decided that Independence Day should mark the beginning of their cause for freedom. They organized a meeting and wrote a constitution. They were excited, and the gathering got very loud. The college's president, Jeremiah Chaplin, could hear them across campus. He thought the students were drinking alcohol, which was strictly against the school's rules. This was a religious school. Many students were training to be ministers.

The next morning the president scolded the students for their behavior. He said they could not continue with the society. The students were upset and wanted Chaplin to take back his statements. He refused and the students left angry. The two groups could not agree, and later Chaplin resigned.

The next year, the students again tried to support abolition with the Colonization Society. This also failed. Finally in 1858, the faculty permitted the official Anti-Slavery Society.

title: Regulating Trade
text:
Every day, four friends make and bring their lunches to school. One day, they have an idea. They decide to specialize. Kate will always bring the sandwiches. Pete will bring juice for everyone. Maria decides to make cookies. Mike will bring fruit. Everything goes well at first. Everyone remembers and does their part. They meet each day and have a complete lunch. This continues for a while and is a great deal until Pete moves away. Maria also decides she does not want to trade anymore. All of a sudden, Kate and Mike have only half of a lunch! They have come to depend on everyone's contributions.

This is a pretend situation. It is an easy problem to solve. Each person just needs to pack a full lunch again. But countries, at times, have this same kind of problem. Exporting and importing can mean countries have access to many products. Some countries start to specialize in certain goods or services. As long as everyone is able to trade and the supply keeps up with the demand, everything works great. But if a certain country is unable to trade, the others may suffer.

The U.S. government tries to regulate the amounts of goods being imported and exported. This helps keep exchanges fair and balanced. The government uses tariffs, which are taxes on imports. If they want to encourage trade, they lower the tariffs on imports. If they want to discourage trade, they raise the tariff. They also set up quotas, which are limits on the amount of goods being imported. Why do you think there are limits?

title: How to Become President
text:
John Adams was the second president of the United States. He said, "No man who ever held the office of president would congratulate a friend on obtaining it."

Do you think being the president of the United States is hard? Most U.S. presidents actually enter the office after many years of public service. Some have served in other public offices. They may have served as a state governor or a U.S. senator.

In order to become president, a person has to win two elections. In the first election, a candidate must win the party's nomination to be a candidate at a national convention. Next, this person would need to win an election against the candidates from the other political parties. To win, it would be necessary to get the majority of the nation's electoral votes.

After the president has been elected, they are sworn into office in January. He or she serves for a four-year term. The president takes an oath that says, "I do solemnly swear that I will faithfully execute the office of president of the United States, and will to the best of my ability, preserve, protect and defend the Constitution of the United States." Do you know how many U.S. presidents there have been? How many presidents have there been in your lifetime?

title: Bill of Rights
text: The Bill of Rights (the first 10 amendments to the Constitution) guarantees everyone living under our Constitution some basic rights such as freedom of speech, religion, assembly, press, right to a trial by jury, freedom from unreasonable search and seizure and more.

title: What is Kwanzaa?
text: Kwanzaa is a holiday of the African culture. It celebrates the life and richness of the African people. There are seven days dedicated to seven goals, or Nguzo Saba, of Kwanzaa. The festival is fairly new. It was created in 1966. People who celebrate Kwanzaa hope it will inspire African Americans to learn about their culture and strengthen their communities and will help them learn about their African culture. Kwanzaa is Swahili for “first fruits of the harvest.”

title: Sassafras
text:
Sassafras (see if you can remember how to spell that one) is an important plant to both wildlife and people on the northeast coast.

For example, deer eat the aromatic (good smelling) twigs in the winter and the new leaf-buds in the spring. Bees love the flowers. Birds enjoy the glossy berries.

Today, the bark of the root is used to make teas. The leaves are ground to thicken food (like in Cajun cooking), and the aromatic wood is used to make furniture. Early Americans thought it healthy to have beds made of the fragrant wood.

In the North, sassafras is often more of a shrub than a tree. The leaves are three-lobed or sometimes mitten shaped. The twigs are a bright green, and the berries are shiny blue. The berries are especially fragrant when crushed. The leaves turn a brilliant red, orange and yellow in the fall.

title: Let's Write
text:
Abolitionists were very brave. They were people of all races in America who thought slavery was wrong and were willing to do something about it, even when that wasn’t the popular thing to do. Some were conductors on the Underground Railroad. Some were authors who wrote books, like Harriet Beecher Stowe. Some were people who went around and spoke about freedom and the equality of all people, like William Lloyd Garrison. All of these people faced danger and poor treatment because of what they did, but they were all very important to the abolition movement.

Imagine you are an abolitionist in early Maine. Tell how you helped end slavery. What you did doesn’t have to be something really big. It could just be helping a slave get to the next town or writing a small note expressing your feelings for a town meeting.

title: Women's Voices Are Heard!
text:
All of the women in Colonies, rich or poor, worked together. As society grew, their roles in society began to change. A Colonial woman could have been one of many things: a merchant's wife in New York, a slave in Virginia, an unpaid servant working for a family in Massachusetts or a farmer's wife with eight children to raise. Each of these women had one thing in common. They lived in America at a time when women had very few rights. Slave women had no rights. Married women had few. They were considered property of their husband. They could not pursue higher education. They could not own property or sign a legal document. They were not allowed to do any public speaking. In rare cases where divorce was allowed, they were not even allowed to keep their own children.

Life Changes After the War

Before the Revolutionary War, no colonists - male or female - had much of a say about major issues. Those things were decided for them in England. After the war, life changed for all men and women. New ideas of independence, freedom, equality and rights were everywhere!

The Constitutional Congress met in 1776. Abigail Adams (the wife of John Adams) wrote to ask him, "Remember the ladies." She hoped they would not put all of the power in the hands of men, with no representation for women.

Abigail Adams was far ahead of her time with her ideas about women. It would be another 150 years before women would have the right to vote!

Education for Women

The first big issue the women addressed was the right for women to have formal education. Until then, only wealthy families could pay for education of their children. Girls' academies taught young ladies how to entertain, play musical instruments, dance and sew. Girls were rarely educated in math, sciences, law or business.

Emma Hart Willard was a leader in education for women. Her father had given her wonderful education. She highly valued this. She became a teacher. Emma soon realized that women needed formal education. With help from some citizens in Troy, New York, she opened the Troy Female Seminary in 1821. It was the country's first high school for the education of young ladies.

By the 1840s, the country was quickly changing. No longer were women only servants or governesses. The new looms for weaving were run by women. More women began to work at mills or factories. As families moved westward, teachers were needed, and women began to fill that role. Most important, both men and women (black and white) became active in one the most important social changes of the times - abolition.

Most of the women who would become leaders in the women's movement learned their leadership skills from being involved in the abolitionist movement.

Among those early speakers against slavery were sisters named Sarah and Angelina Grimke. They were from a slave owning family in the South. They grew to hate slavery. They moved to Philadelphia and began to write essays. They spoke out against slavery. Women began to link slavery with the low position of women in society. From this thinking came women's suffrage.

title: League of Women Voters
text:
In November 1920, people in the United States were going to the polls to vote for the president. This was not something new, but something was very different. For the first time in history, women all across the country were allowed to vote!

After years of fighting for this right, Carrie Catt, (one of the leaders) did not think the work was done. She was concerned women would not know how to use their new right. She suggested a new organization be formed: The League of Women Voters. The League's first job was to get women out to vote. They telephoned women to remind them to vote. They also offered transportation to the polls and even babysat so women could go vote.

All of these efforts only helped a little. Very few women actually voted in that first election. But the League did not give up. They began to print pamphlets. These told about the people who were running. Later, they made new programs. They showed women how to use their political power. Those programs taught about communities, school board participation and how to start reforms and change social ideas.

The League of Women Voters still exists today. It has always been and still is a non-partisan organization. That is, it does not support any one political party.

The mission of the league today is much the same: to encourage participation in government and to influence public policies through education and support.

The league works today in four main areas: government, international relations, natural resources and social policy.

The LWV is not just for women. Anyone over the age of 18 can join. It is another way to help democracy work!

title: Women's Rights
text:
Seneca Falls is Site for First Women's Rights Convention

Suffrage means the right to vote. The women's suffrage movement began with the first women's rights convention. Its seeds had been planted years earlier at an antislavery convention.

In 1840, at the World Anti-Slavery Convention in London, some of the American delegates were women. At the last minute the convention ruled that only men could participate. The women were forced to watch the convention from a balcony. Two of those women were Elizabeth Cady Stanton of New York and Lucretia Mott of Massachusetts. They wondered what good it would do to be involved in worthy causes, like abolition, if they were not allowed to do anything because they were women.

The women wrote to each other regularly over the next several years. Later, the Stanton family moved to Seneca Falls. Mott was able to visit her there. The two women, along with three others, spent a day discussing women's rights. The women decided to call a public meeting about what rights women should have. Stanton put a notice in the newspaper for a meeting to be held five days later, on July 19 and 20, 1848.

She thought about what to say. There was so much that needed to change. She began by reading the Declaration of Independence. She thought of adding the word "woman" to each place it said "man"..."that all men and women are created equal..."

It was a very brave way of thinking for that time, but she did not stop there. Stanton was wise enough to know that some changes in women's issues would require a change in law. Women needed to be able to vote to change laws.

Allowing women to vote in 1848 was a truly shocking idea. Mott thought it was too soon for this idea. Stanton's husband, who usually supported her, threatened to leave town if she brought it up at the meeting. But Frederick Douglass, the famous abolitionist, sent a note saying he supported her and promised to speak at the convention. Stanton made up her mind. She would present a resolution about giving women a right to vote!

The day of the meeting arrived and Elizabeth Cady Stanton was surprised to have 300 people attend the meeting. The people at the convention voted on the issues. The right of women to vote was Resolution 9 and barely passed. The document, signed by 68 women and 32 men, was known as the Declaration of Principles.

Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott had no idea that one meeting would launch an organization that became the center of the women's suffrage movement. It would eventually change the lives of their daughters and granddaughters.

Among those who were present at that first meeting, only one - Charlotte Woodward - would live long enough to achieve their dream of women voting. Woodward voted in the election of November 1920.

Susan B. Anthony

The story of women's suffrage would not be complete without Susan B. Anthony. Susan was born in 1820 in Adams, Massachusetts. She was brought up in a Quaker family. They raised her to be socially active.

After the family business failed, Susan's family moved to Rochester, New York. There they became active in the antislavery movement.

Susan, as a woman, was not allowed to speak at public meetings. She was also angry because as a teacher she was being paid only one-fourth of a male teacher's salary.

She met Elizabeth Cady Stanton in 1851. She attended her first women's rights convention in Syracuse. Anthony and Stanton liked each other immediately. They began working together. Stanton was an excellent speaker. Anthony was very good at making things run. They were a good team and worked tirelessly together. The 19th Amendment was referred to as the Susan B. Anthony amendment because of Susan's sustained efforts to get it passed. Neither woman lived to see their dream come true.

title: Starting a Small Business
text:
Have you ever thought of starting up your very own business? Each day, thousands of people start their own businesses. They have many reasons for wanting to own their own businesses. They believe owning a business will make them more independent. They like to be the ones in charge. They like to build something of their very own. Many also feel the profit potential is greater than when working for someone else. The profit potential is the amount of money it is possible to make.

Most people start small businesses as sole proprietorships or partnerships. A sole proprietorship is a business owned by one person. Many businesses are sole proprietorships because they are not hard or costly to begin. They are usually very small. In this kind of business, the owner gets all of the profit, but also owns all of the debt. The owners have to deal with all the problems but enjoy all of the rewards.

A partnership is a business owned by two or more people. These are harder to form. In this type of business, both partners are in charge of the company. They share the debt and the profits. They share the problems and the rewards. Partners are able to bounce ideas off one another. They may be better able to expand their business.

One challenge of a partnership would be in cases where the partners do not get along. If for some reason the partners disagree on issues, the business may suffer.

Do you dream of owning your own business? If so, would you choose a partnership or a sole proprietorship?

title: Presidential Veto
text: The word veto is Latin. Its literal definition is "I forbid." A presidential veto is the ability of the president of the United States to stop a certain bill from becoming law. Many new ideas are presented to the president in the form of bills. Some of these bills are good. Some have very odd ideas attached to them. The president may veto them, or refuse to give his or her approval. However, the presidential veto is limited. If the president vetoes a bill that he or she does not approve of, it still has the chance of becoming a law. The bill would return to the House of Representatives and the Senate. Both houses must vote again. The Senate and House of Representatives need to pass the bill with a two-thirds majority. If they do, the bill becomes law, even if the president vetoed the bill first.

title: Amelia Bloomer
text: Amelia Bloomer wanted dress reform for women. She advocated trousers for women called bloomers which were worn under a dress at first. Later they were worn with a tunic.

title: What Are bloomers?
text:
Bloomers were the answer to comfortable dress for women in the 19th century. They were very loose-fitting pants. Banded below the knee, they were usually worn with a loose fitting tunic (shirt). Women in the 1800s wore skirts with as much as 5 yards of fabric just in the skirt. Under the skirt were layers of petticoats. Uncomfortable corsets were laced tightly and made their waists fit into very narrow waist bands. This was the fashion of the day.

This clothing was very uncomfortable and impractical for women who were taking care of children and doing chores. Even walking across a muddy street could be tiresome in the heavy clothing of the day. Amelia Bloomer introduced Elizabeth Cady Stanton to Susan B. Anthony. She attended the first women's rights convention at Seneca Falls. Bloomer became a convert to the women's rights crusade. She was a clothing reformer - she popularized the outfit that came to bear her name.

title: Barred Owl
text:
You'll find the barred owl in many wild places in Maine. There are many, many varieties of owls in the world. This one is distinctive by its call. It sounds like it's saying: "Who who who cooks for you? Who who who cooks for you all?" (Kinda makes you hungry, huh?)

This bird is round-headed, with brown eyes and a yellow bill. The face is whitish-brown with dark brown trim. The body is mottled brown and white. It loves wet areas and deep woods, and likes to nest in hollow tree cavities. These very gentle birds can often be seen and heard during the day and you'll find them dining on rodents, small mammals, birds, frogs and insects.

Did you know? If you wanted to see as well as an owl, your eyes would have to be the size of softballs! Would you like to hear a sound byte of this owl as well as several others? Go online to the following site and hear for yourself! www.allaboutbirds.org.

title: Margaret
text:
Margaret "Molly" Corbin

There are only two Revolutionary War soldiers buried near the Old Cadet Chapel in West Point Cemetery, and one of them is Margaret "Molly" Corbin. Who was this woman and why would she receive such a remarkable military honor?

Margaret was born in Pennsylvania in 1751. She was orphaned at age 5 when American Indians killed her father and kidnapped her mother. Margaret and her brother were away from home at the time. She married John Corbin when she was 21. John enlisted in the Continental Army when the Revolutionary War began. Wives sometimes went with their husbands to war. They helped with cooking and cared for wounded soldiers. Women often carried pitchers of water to pour on overheated cannons during battle. They were nicknamed "Molly Pitchers."

But Margaret did much more than that. When John was given the job of loading and firing a cannon, Margaret worked as his assistant right on the battlefield. In November 1776, the British army attacked Fort Washington where the Corbins were stationed. During the battle John was killed. Margaret immediately began loading and firing John's cannon by herself. What courage and quick thinking that must have taken! Margaret continued firing until she was wounded too.

Margaret was disabled for the rest of her life. Congress awarded her a lifelong pension (retirement pay) just as if she had been a soldier, something no woman had ever received.

In 1926 the Daughters of the American Revolution had Margaret's remains reburied in West Point Cemetery with full military honors. A memorial plaque also stands near the battle site in New York City. It reads "Capt. Molly Corbin...the first American woman to take a soldier's part in the War for Liberty." Think of a woman you know who demonstrates agility of mind. Who is she?

title: Let's Write
text: Congratulations! You just won a contest to spend one day in Washington, D.C., visiting with the representatives from your great state of Maine. You can tell them, ask them or thank them for anything you want. In 200 words or less, write about what you would say to make a difference as a representative of your state.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: Use any color to circle or highlight five words in this week’s magazine that have a prefix or suffix. On a piece of paper, write the words and the meaning of the prefixes or suffixes.

title: Temperance and Prohibition
text:
You probably don't hear about temperance and Prohibition much anymore, but they used to be hot topics. Temperance means abstaining from drinking alcoholic beverages. Some religions teach temperance. Although the U.S. government doesn't currently enforce temperance, that hasn't always been the case. Prohibition was a period of time when a law said alcohol was not allowed in the United States.

Alcoholic drinks have been around for a long time. We even have drawings from about 4200 B.C. of the fermentation process, which is how alcohol is formed. Alcohol was often used as a medicine. Sumerian physicians and pharmacists prescribed alcohol as early as 2100 B.C.

Around 1770 B.C., Hammurabi, the king of Babylonia, started regulating drinking houses and alcohol use. People soon noticed how alcohol affected their societies.

Throughout the United States' history, many groups have tried to make temperance a law. One group was the Total Abstinence Society, which was founded in Portland in 1815. By 1834, temperance groups in Maine had formed a state organization. These groups started pushing for all alcoholic drinks to be banned, except for specific purposes.

Why did people want temperance so badly? Some people had religious reasons. Others thought alcohol made people irresponsible, violent and unproductive. As the temperance movement grew, several other factors came into play.

The Civil War occurred during the early years of the Prohibition movement. Alcoholic beverages were banned, or prohibited, in the Union army. This was mostly because of wartime rationing. The available grain (used to make some types of alcohol) needed to be used to feed the troops, not to make liquor.

People also began to realize how harmful alcohol can be to a person's health. They discovered more scientific evidence and started magazines and periodicals like the Scientific Temperance Journal. School textbooks even talked about how human organs would rot away if a person drinks too much alcohol.

When America entered World War I, patriotism ran strong across the country. Americans pushed away anything considered foreign. Proponents (supporters) of Prohibition pointed out that many breweries were run by German-Americans. So alcohol became foreign, and Prohibition became patriotic.

During the war, the government took over railroads and factories, began a draft and controlled many liberties. It seemed natural that the government also control the issue of drinking. In 1919 Congress passed the law banning the production and use of most alcohol.

The Prohibition had far reaching effects in America in the political, economic and social environments. People became quite good at making and smuggling their own liquor. The laws were hard to enforce. The business around alcohol went underground, and our economy suffered. The U.S. ban on alcohol ended in 1933.

title: The Maine Law
text:
Maine is the First State to Outlaw Alcohol

Temperance laws did not just appear on the books one day in Maine. In fact, they developed over a long period of time. The first law that mentions drunkenness in America was made in 1619 in Colonial Virginia. If someone was found drunk in public three times, he or she had to spend 12 hours in a halter. Then, in 1650, the Puritans of the Massachusetts Bay Colony started punishing drunkards with whippings, fines and sitting in the stocks.

None of these laws seemed to matter, though. (During the early days of the 1800s, Americans drank almost three times the alcohol they did in the 1990s.)

In 1820, Maine became a state. It adopted the same laws about being drunk that Massachusetts had. They also made whipping a penalty for selling alcohol without a license. In 1821, Maine approved a law during its first legislative session which required posting names of common drunkards, or tipplers, in all licensed places. The law stated that liquor could not be sold to these people. Idleness and excessive drinking could cause a person to be banned from buying alcohol for a year.

In 1826, the sale of alcohol was banned on election days, dubbing them as, "occasions of great drunkenness and disturbance." Eight years later the sale of alcohol to minors and servants was prohibited. In 1837, the Maine Temperance Union tried to pass Prohibition legislation for the first time.

They finally succeeded in 1851, and Maine became the first state to outlaw the sale of all alcoholic beverages, except for, "medicinal, mechanical or manufacturing purposes."

The Father of Prohibition

Neal Dow is known as the father of Prohibition. He was born in 1804 to a Quaker family. The strict attitude of his family carried through into his own political and social opinions. Dow was the author of the Maine Law. This was the toughest statute against the sale and consumption of alcohol anywhere in the world. When the Civil War broke out, he was so well-known and popular that he was made a colonel when he offered his services. He gave the adjutant general and governor hourly bulletins. He offered advice, suggestions and demands and showed genuine concern for his men.

He made his regiment take a pledge of temperance, though some didn't strictly adhere to it. His regiment became known as the Temperance Regiment. Many mothers wanted their sons to join it. Dow prospered and was promoted to brigadier general. He saw some action at Port Hudson and was wounded and captured. He managed to make both his Confederate captors and fellow prisoners in Libby prison mad. He gave temperance tirades to starving and thirsty men.

He was finally released in exchange for Fitzhugh Lee. Dow went home to pursue his battle against alcohol. His popularity began to fall in 1855, when he ordered troops to fire upon citizens rioting outside the City Hall of Portland in pursuit of a stash of alcohol that was supposedly kept there.

title: A Business Plan
text:
Most people think writing reports ends when they graduate from school - but nothing could be further from the truth. In fact, people have to write for just about any kind of job. Business owners are encouraged to write down their ideas. They should report their work. It is especially important if they are starting a new business. This helps them to make a business plan. These plans can be long or they can be short. Generally, the more thought put into a business plan, the better the business works. This is because the owners have really focused and set goals.

Pretend you are starting a lemonade stand. The first part of your plan should include the basics of your business. First, what is your business and where will it be located? You will own a lemonade stand. It will be on the left corner of your driveway. Next, what do you need to get your business rolling? Do you need to buy a posterboard for a sign? Maybe you need to buy cups or lemonade mix? Don't forget a pitcher and a spoon! These are examples of start-up costs. Then, consider your target market. Are you trying to sell lemonade to older people or just kids? Are you going to advertise? What would be the cost of hanging flyers around your neighborhood? Consider if there is a demand for lemonade. Maybe you decide to only open your stand during the hottest months of the summer. This turns out nice because you are not in school. Now do some market research! Does your target market prefer lemonade or limeade?

These are all steps any company should include in their written business plan. The more details about the business, the better. With a good business plan, owners are ready to meet most challenges. It is one way to be great!

title: Impeachment
text:
The U. S. Constitution is a great system of checks and balances. This system prevents any person from gaining too much power. It also provides a way to remove people from public office who have committed crimes. This is the process of impeachment. To impeach is to charge, or accuse, a person in a high political office with a crime. The Constitution states that this is necessary in cases of "treason, bribery or other high crimes." The House of Representatives starts this process. Once they have created a resolution, then all the members vote on it. If a two-thirds majority is reached, then the resolution is given to the Senate. At this stage, the person is "impeached," or formally accused by the House of Representatives. Next, the Senate begins their debate.

It is in the form of a trial. Each side may call witnesses to testify. Finally, the Senate votes on the outcome. If two-thirds of the Senate agrees, then the accused official is immediately removed from office. Only three presidents in the history of the United States have been impeached. They are Andrew Johnson, Bill Clinton, and Donald Trump.

title: Bootlegger's Shores
text: Maine's rocky shores and thick forests were ideal for smugglers (bootleggers) who would bring illegal liquor (moonshine) into Maine and the United States.

title: What Groups Were Involved With the Rise of Prohibition in Maine?
text: As well as the Total Abstinence Society, there were other groups in Maine who supported and promoted Prohibition. The Woman's Christian Temperance Union fought for Prohibition. It also represented most reform groups of the day. Under the leadership of reformer Frances Willard, the WCTU took up the causes of suffrage, an eight-hour work day and prison reform. The group linked temperance with many other reforms and made it more attractive. In contrast, the Anti-Saloon League, founded in 1896, fought strictly for legal Prohibition of alcoholic beverages. They developed modern lobbying techniques which were hugely successful. They printed and distributed anti-drinking brochures. The League went to church members for support. They lobbied with both lawmakers and businessmen. They helped 25 states adopt Prohibition laws between 1900 and 1918.

title: Gray Squirrel
text:
The gray squirrel is a noisy little friend. Did you know that not all of that chatter is idle? Sometimes it has specific meanings: a rapid kuk, kuk, kuk means immediate danger. A longer, drawn-out ku-uu-k, sounded every few seconds, warns of less worrisome danger. A slow kuk-kuk-kuk means the danger has passed. The gray squirrels also send messages with their bushy tails!

Gray squirrels bear young in litters of two or three, twice a year. In late winter or spring, litters are usually born in tree hollows. Summer young can sometimes be found in leafy nests out along the end of a tree branch.

title: Using a Planner
text:
A planner can help you manage your time. It is a simple tool that will help you remember assignments.

Feeling stressed? Not sure if you'll have time to do all of your homework? To keep up with your studies and have fun learning, you need to learn to manage your time. A planner is a perfect tool to do this.

A planner is like a calendar. It will have days, weeks and months in it. You can look ahead in a planner to see what's due. You can also look at a day to see what you need to do. Planners help organize your time with just a little effort. Here are some ways to use a planner.

Write down assignments. Write down each assignment as you get it. You can include spelling lists, math homework and book titles. It's your planner, so put down what you need to know. With each assignment, be sure to include the due date and other requirements. When you're done with the assignment, check or cross it off.

Review your planner every day. To stay on top of things, review what you've written. You don't want to forget an important assignment! Look ahead to see what assignments are coming up. You can even start early on some of them. It's up to you to keep track of them.

Create a study schedule. Some people study well in the morning. Others do well in the afternoon or evening. When do you study best? Pick a schedule that works best for you. Block off some time in your planner. Then stick with it. Once you're done studying, check it off. You may need to choose a quiet place that is free from distractions.

You can use your planner to schedule other things as well, like soccer matches or music recitals. Planners can help you remember anything.

title: Let's Write
text:
Laws in every state are always changing. Some reflect the needs of the people at a particular time. Many laws like Prohibition are challenged and changed. Others are simply forgotten.

Here are a few of the forgotten laws in Maine that may seem strange today. You may not walk the street in Augusta playing a violin. You may not walk the streets in Portland with your shoes untied.

After you do some research, write about some other weird laws in Maine. Write a story of why someone made that law.

title: Maine's Republican Father
text:
About when Maine first became a state, only one political party really existed. A political party is a group of people who share the same ideas about how the government should be run. People were beginning to disagree with the one political party. Soon there were other ideas which led to other political parties, like the Republican Party.

In Maine's history, Hannibal Hamlin is known as the father of the Republican Party. Hamlin was born in 1809 in Paris Hill on his parents' farm. He worked on the farm and at various other jobs. He was a cook, wood cutter and a teacher. He worked as a land surveyor and then printer. Finally, he made his entrance into the world of law. He apprenticed as a law clerk under Samuel Fessenden, a well-known lawyer in Portland. Fessenden, like many Mainers, was an abolitionist.

When he completed his apprenticeship, Hamlin opened up his own law practice in Hampden. Soon he entered politics as a Democrat. So why is he known as the father of the Republican Party? Well, he served as a member of the state legislature and as speaker. He then served as one of Maine's Representatives to Congress and then in the U.S. Senate. In the Senate, he found himself in the middle of some turmoil. There were some problems within the Democratic party. They couldn't agree on the issue of slavery. Hamlin strongly opposed slavery. Others in the Democratic Party supported it. Members of the newly formed Republican Party, which opposed slavery, urged Hamlin to switch parties and run for governor. Hamlin told them that he felt he could serve his state better in Washington, D.C. than as the governor. He didn't decide to switch until the Republicans promised to let him return to the Senate afterward; then he agreed.

Hamlin served as the governor of Maine for only 48 days - from Jan. 8 to Feb. 25, 1857. He then returned to the Senate, as a Republican this time, to fill a vacancy. By resigning from the Democratic Party, he caught the attention of many people in Washington. They admired how he stood up against things he believed to be wrong. Because of this, three years later he was nominated to run as Abraham Lincoln's vice president. Hamlin didn't want this job, though. In fact, he didn't even know about it until some of his friends interrupted a card game to tell him so. Hamlin told his wife of the nomination, "I neither expected it or desired it, but it has been made and as a faithful man to the cause, it leaves me no alternative but to accept it." The cause Hamlin spoke of was the abolition of slavery.

Hamlin and Lincoln were not very close personally. In fact, they never even met until after they won the election. Hamlin was worried that he would not be able to contribute anything significant as the vice president. His fears were true in a way. Lincoln rarely turned to Hamlin for advice, and when Hamlin offered it, Lincoln held back. For example, Hamlin urged Lincoln to issue an emancipation proclamation immediately, but Lincoln held off. He feared that doing so would create discord in the Northern states. He worried it would fracture the Union. Lincoln waited until the Civil War took a turn for the worse to issue the proclamation.

Hamlin was a very astute (smart) politician. When the Republicans won the presidential election, Hamlin stated, "There's going to be a war, and a terrible one, just as surely as the sun will rise tomorrow." The Civil War went on during the Lincoln/Hamlin administration.

title: The Three Giants
text:
In the cover story, you learned about Hannibal Hamlin. Hamlin along with the following two men are known as Maine's three giants.

Representative Thomas B. Reed

Thomas B. Reed was a powerful leader who brought many new things to the House of Representatives. He was very serious about making sure things kept moving, so when he served as the speaker of the House, others gave him the nickname of "Czar" Reed. He also made many rules, known as Reed's Rules, that helped make it possible for a majority to effectively run the House of Representatives and make laws. His rules also gave the speaker of the House more authority and are still in use in Maine legislature.

Reed had a very sharp wit that stung or amused any who heard him. He once said of William McKinley that he had "the backbone of a chocolate eclair." Of another congressman, a gentleman who said he would rather be right than be president, "The gentlemen need not worry. He will never be either."

Reed had been described as, "a slow-moving, giant hulk of a barge dressed in black, out of whose collar arose an enormous, round, clean-shaven baby-face." His head was described as, "a casaba melon flowering from a fat, black stalk."

He was elected to the House of Representatives in 1876, just in time to see the controversy over the Hayes-Tilden election. It seemed that Congress had mishandled that election, and there were some changes to House rules to make rulings occur more quickly. In 1882, Reed helped establish strict limits on dilatory motions in election cases. A dilatory motion is one meant only to delay making a decision. Reed said, "Whenever it is imposed upon Congress to accomplish a certain work, it is the duty of the Speaker, who represents the House, to see that no factious opposition prevents the House from doing its duty."

Reed was elected as speaker of the house in 1890 and immediately began changing the way things worked. When it was time to adopt rules, as Congress opened, Reed chose not to adopt any special rules and to operate under general parliamentary procedures.

At the beginning of that year, the minority party decided to delay a vote on an elections case using a common strategy called the "disappearing quorum." The members would refuse to vote and were recorded as absent so the other votes wouldn't count. Reed directed the clerk to record the names of all present, even those not voting. He even locked the doors to prevent people from leaving! When one Representative challenged his methods, Reed said, "I am making a statement of fact that the gentleman from Kentucky is present, does he deny it?"

James G. Blaine: 20 Years in Congress

James G. Blaine began his professional life as a teacher in Washington, Pennsylvania. He was also writing for magazines and newspapers. In 1853 he moved to Kennebec, Maine, where he was to manage the Kennebec Journal. He very soon after accepted the control of the Portland Advertiser.

Blaine began his political career in 1858 when he was elected to the legislature and served there for four years. During his last term he was chosen as speaker of the House and performed the duties of that office well. It was in 1862 that Blaine was first elected to Congress. He began studying the rules of the House immediately and was soon known as an expert on rules and procedures. He was reelected again and again, and was made speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives in 1869. His rulings were always prompt and accurate.

Two days before the Republican convention of 1876 met, a report was presented to the House of Representatives that accused Blaine of certain improper actions as speaker. He responded to the charges but only partially corrected the damage that had been done. Even an energetic speech from a friend could not win Blaine the presidential nomination.

Blaine began serving in the Senate in 1877. He voted against the electoral commission bill, saying that it was unconstitutional. In 1880 he was again a candidate for the presidential nomination. He lost the Republican nomination to James Garfield. When Garfield won the presidential election, he asked Blaine to be the secretary of state.

In 1881 Blaine retired from the state department and began writing a book about his political career, called "Twenty years in Congress." The first volume was published in 1884 and the second in 1886. In 1887 he visited Europe for health and pleasure, and was well-liked by the leaders of many countries.

title: Your Growing Business
text:
Pretend you are the owner of a small company. Your business is making more money every year. You have a steady stream of business. Business is going so well that you decide it is time to expand your company.

You begin to research the options you have to help your company grow. You realize you need more money to get your ideas off the ground. You know you do not have enough to afford the expansion. You could borrow money from a bank. But then you will be in debt. Maybe you could borrow money from family or friends. But you would still be in debt. And what would happen if your business ideas failed?

Companies face the same kinds of problems every day. There is nothing wrong with borrowing money from a bank. But companies should only borrow money if they are sure they can pay the bank back. Many companies decide to finance businesses by taking on new owners. This means that some companies sell part of their business. They sell it as shares or stocks. You become a stockholder when you purchase a stock. Stockholders are actually owners of the company. Businesses use the money they get from selling the stocks to expand their business. They hope to create a better company that will yield more profit.

The company may give dividends to stockholders. Dividends are a percentage of the company's profit. This is one way for investors to earn money when purchasing stocks. But they can also make a lot of money by buying and selling stocks. Do you know anyone who has made money in the stock market?

title: Checks and Balances
text:
The men who created the Constitution were concerned about one branch of government having too much power. For this reason they planned a system of government that had several branches that shared power and checked on each other to give balance to our country.

State governments also have a government system of checks and balances. The state government has a legislature to make the laws. There is an executive branch to carry out the laws. There is a judicial branch that decides how we try lawbreakers.

Local governments often combine functions so the same group of public officials carries out all of the above jobs. Whichever way your local government is run, the voter elects most of the officials, so if they aren't doing a good job balancing power, the people may choose not to re-elect them.

title: From ‘The New Colossus‛
text:
Here at our sea-washed, sunset-gates shall stand
A mighty woman with a torch, whose flame
Is the imprisoned lightning, and her name
Mother of Exiles. From her beacon-hand
Glows world-wide welcome; her mild eyes command
The air-bridged harbor that twin-cities frame.
"Keep, ancient lands, your storied pomp!" cries she
With silent lips. "Give me your tired, your poor,
Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free,
The wretched refuse of your teeming shore.
Send these, the homeless, tempest-tossed to me,
I lift my lamp beside the golden door!"

by Emma Lazarus (inscribed on the Statue of Liberty)

title: What does “mark twain” mean?
text:
Mark Twain was the pen name of a writer by the name of Samuel Clemens. He heard the phrase while still in his early 20s. Clemens worked on Mississippi riverboats and eventually became a riverboat pilot. Clemens picked up a great deal from his life on the river, most particularly the pen name Mark Twain. The phrase was a cry used on steamboats to indicate a river depth of two fathoms, or 12 feet. Life on the river also gave Twain material for several of his books, including the raft scenes of "Adventures of Huckleberry Finn" and all of the material for his autobiographical "Life on the Mississippi."

Twain knew Thomas B. Reed and was very friendly to him, though he (Twain) didn't like Congress much at all. Reed and Twain enjoyed spending time on the river, playing cards (which Reed was apparently quite a bit better at), and arguing or discussing different points of interest. In spite of all his training in argumentation, Reed said he, "couldn't argue with a man like [Twain]."

title: Jack-in-the-Pulpit
text:
Jack-in-the-pulpit is a odd name for an odd little wildflower. It is found in the shady woodlands of the East.

Look at the picture to see the preacher in the pulpit in this flower. The "pulpit," or spathe, is green or purple, and the "jack," or spadix, is yellowish-green.

The plant blooms in April and May. It grows to be about 8 inches to 3 feet tall. Later in the season, the tiny flowers found inside the pulpit will turn into a cluster of bright red berries. The berries, along with all other parts of the plant, can sting when touched. If it gets on the lips or tongue it may cause swelling - so don't eat those berries!

American Indians were known to use the dried and prepared root which resembles a turnip. Another common name for this flower is Indian turnip.

title: Let's Write
text:
A fairy tale is a story that someone makes up and tells to others. Usually it involves things that couldn’t have happened, and sometimes even has a message for other people to learn. Not all fairy tales start with “Once upon a time...” Though some definitely do. Finish, in 200 words or less, the following fairy tale:

“Once upon a time there was a strange little man. He was a very funny man who often said things to make people laugh. One day, an evil king saw all the people who loved the little man and was jealous...”

title: Getting Organized
text:
Is your backpack overflowing with papers? Is your desk stuffed to the brim? It’s time to get organized!

We all need to be a little organized in life. We need to know where to put our assignments and where to find our homework. But getting organized will take some effort. It will take some practice to come up with a system that works for you. Here are some ways to become more organized.

Avoid Clutter. It’s very easy to collect clutter in your backpack and desk. Avoid doing this. It will be easier to find assignments. Have some folders where you can put school announcements or tests that have been graded. Throw anything away that has become outdated. Clean out your desk of all old assignments, broken pencils and dried-out markers.

Prepare your backpack the night before. By doing this, you’ll be ready to go. No more scrambling around in the morning. Put in your notebooks, textbooks and planner (if you have one).

Use one calendar. If you have a planner, you can use that. Write down when your assignments are due. Also, write down any other activities you have. Put down family activities, too! Write everything down so you can remember it.

Organize your notebooks. Color-code them if you need to. Choose one color for each subject. Now you can quickly spot the correct notebook. Also, write your name inside the notebook, in case it gets lost.

Choose a good study space. Make it clear to your family that this is where you’ll be studying. Have extra pens, pencils and paper in the area. It should have room for all of your books. It should also be away from distractions like the television.

Now that you have some ideas for getting organized, try some of them out. You may be surprised at what a difference it makes in your study habits!

title: Fake or Real News?
text:
Have you ever read something online, like on social media sites, that sounded fishy? Maybe it was real, but it could be fake news! The big danger, though, is news that sounds real but isn’t. Fake news is becoming common because anyone can post things online. Fake news can be in the form of a story. Fake news can be a photo or video that has been changed. The problem is that these fake items look real. Fake news can cause problems and it spreads misinformation.

Sam Wineburg, a professor, did some research. He found that 80 percent of students cannot tell the difference between real and fake news. Do you want to become a media-savvy person? You have to be able to find out if news is real or fake. How do you do that? You have to become a detective and search for the truth. You can learn about the author or company that posted the news. You have to think about the purpose of the news. Is there a hidden plan to get you to buy something or to make you think a certain way? Your teacher or a trusted adult can help you learn how to spot fake news. It takes a little time, but democracy depends on real information! Do your part and discover what is real and what is fake!

title: Better Transportation Changes America
text:
During the Industrial Revolution, lots of the new inventions were for transportation. Soon traveling from one place to another was easier and faster than ever before. New transportation changed how and where Americans lived.

Lots of people had ideas about how to change transportation. Some ideas were great, and some were, well, not so great. For any new idea to work, it had to have these qualities:

Meets a need

Works well and is reliable

Easy to fix and maintain

Affordable to most people

Some of the new ideas didn't have these qualities and didn't stay around very long. Take a minute to think about transportation for recreation, or for fun. Ask your parents what kind of transportation they used for fun when they were young. Maybe they used a scooter or roller skates. Maybe they had a stingray bike or skateboards. Are those things still around? Try to decide why or why not.

When transportation improves, it is not always just about the vehicles. Sometimes improvements are actually in the road, canal or rail. These things can all make traveling easier. Now let's look at some of the Industrial Revolution's new ideas for transportation. Remember to think about how they changed America and what is still used today.

The stagecoach was introduced to America around 1756. A man named Levi Pease is credited for beginning the first long-distance stage travel in 1784. The line ran from Boston to Worcester, Springfield, Hartford and New York.

In the 1770s, many engineers built stationary steam engines. Engines were used in machinery for factories, farms and mines and changed the face of the industry. In the 1770s, James Watt developed the first steam engine that could propel something. By the early 1800s, engineers made the steam engines small enough to mount on wheels but strong enough to turn the wheels. The locomotives were put on rails and eventually put stagecoaches out of business.

In 1807, the Clermont, Robert Fulton's steamboat, made its first run on the Hudson River. It traveled from New York to Albany. The Clermont wasn't the first steamboat, but was the first one to be commercially successful. By 1845, at least 100 steamboats chugged on the Hudson. They went about 5 miles per hour and made a terrible noise.

In 1825, the Erie Canal opened. This new waterway went from Albany to Buffalo and allowed boats to travel from the Atlantic Ocean to the Great Lakes. Barges were pulled along the canal by teams of horses or mules. The canal was a great success and became important to all of America. The Erie Canal actually helped settle the West.

As transportation became better, people moved farther apart, and trade between states and countries improved. Transportation helped change the country for sure!

title: The Stanley Steamer
text:
By the 1900s, many people lived in Maine. How did all of those people get around? Horse-drawn carriages were on their way out. Automobiles were about to change the face of the nation! Inventors had been experimenting with motorized carriages for several decades. The Pope Bicycle Company of Hartford built the first autos in Connecticut in 1895. These cars were electric. In fact, the first president of the United States to ride in an automobile (Teddy Roosevelt) rode in a Pope electric vehicle. In Massachusetts, Francis and Freelan Stanley became famous with their steam-powered automobile. They called it the Stanley Steamer. They made and sold this car from 1897 to 1927.

The Cadillac's self starter car eventually replaced the Stanley Steamer. The steamer continued to be popular for 20 more years, though. The steamer needed to be warmed up before it would run. It was a quiet car and had little vibration. People said it was easy to drive. It took a bit of practice to learn to work the valves which controlled the flow of water and steam. Under the hood was the valve which provided the pressure to the two cylinder engine. The engine was found under the floor.

Look at the picture of the Stanley Steamer (right). In what ways would travel in the Stanley Steamer have been different than traveling in your family car today?

title: Transportation in Maine
text:
Economy and social environment are linked to effective transportation

Over the years, transportation has changed a lot and helped make a lot of changes. The earliest important forms of transportation depended on the major bodies of water. Waterways help transport things up and down the coast and to the interior with ease and speed. Maine has been a state that thrives on its ports and waterways. The lumber industry has always been important to Maine, and the rivers were a great resource to help transport the felled trees. Today Maine has a well-developed transportation system. In fact, people in Maine now have lots of transportation options. But before we cover travel today, take a look at some ways it was done in the past.

Historic Trolleys

The first trolleys in Maine were built to help bring supplies and coal to and from the mills. Soon the trolleys started taking passengers and could move people all over New England. Today the Seashore Trolley Museum is a great place to visit to learn more about the history of travel in Maine. The museum opened with just one trolley car (No. 31) from the Biddeford and Saco Railroad. Now it has more than 250 transit vehicles.

The museum started after a group of young men decided to save and restore the trolley. They went to the trolley company to see how much it would cost to purchase one of the trolleys.

They were told they could have one for $300. This was more than they could afford, so they decided to visit the president of the company at home. When they arrived he was cutting his lawn, and he told them if they would finish cutting his lawn for him, he would sell them a car for $150. It was still a lot of money, but they were able to do it. Over the years the efforts of many people have made the museum into what it is today.

Maine Travel Today

There are now lots of ways to travel in Maine - airplanes, bicycles, motorcycles, trains, helicopters, even hot air balloons! You probably usually travel in a car. You may have even tried some of Maine's public transportation options.

Maine has several bus systems that help people travel within the state. Larger systems like those in Bangor and Portland have a variety of routes. Bangor and Portland also provide rail systems. These options help people move around, but also help them keep the environment clean.
