The busiest airport in Maine is the Portland International Jetport. More than 1 million people travel through here each year. Some of the major airlines are AirTran Airways, Delta, JetBlue and United Express.

title: The Stock Market
text:
When a company decides to sell shares, it first sells the stocks in a primary market. This is the first time stock is sold to the public. It is called an initial public offering (IPO). Then the stock moves to the secondary market, or the stock market. This means that the money made from selling the stock goes to the person selling it. It does not go to the original business.

There are many parts of the stock market. There are regional exchanges, which are smaller. They are like the exchanges in Los Angeles, Chicago and Boston. Some are large organized exchanges, like the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE). The New York Stock Exchange is located on Wall Street in New York City. The NYSE lists about 2,800 large and mid-sized companies. They are worth over $18 trillion!

Most stock markets have traders who make a living buying and selling stock. The NYSE has a trading floor where all of the shares are purchased. You have probably seen footage of Wall Street on the evening news. The news usually announces the day's Dow Jones Industrial Average. This is a mathematical calculation of 30 main stocks being sold. It gives a general overview of the market.

The stock market changes every day. It goes back to the concept of supply and demand. If a certain stock is popular, then the demand for that stock goes up. As the demand goes up, so does the price of the stock. If someone buys a stock at a low price and the price increases later, that person can make a profit. They can sell the same stock at the higher price. When prices keep going up, people call it a "bull market." People call it a "bear market" when the values keep dropping. Are we in a bull or bear market right now?

title: Symbols of Our Country
text:
Many of the symbols of our country, such as the flag of the United States and the eagle as the national bird, were chosen in the early days of our nation. Both of these are symbols of our great country. The first official national flag was adopted on June 14, 1777. It was considered to be a symbol of independence, freedom and democracy. The color red stands for hardiness and courage. The color blue stands for vigilance and justice. White stands for purity and innocence. There are 13 stripes that represent the original 13 Colonies and 50 stars on a field of blue representing the 50 states of America.

June 14 is celebrated as Flag Day. On that day people across the country hang the flag as a symbol of independence and freedom.

Our flag is called by many names such as Old Glory or the Stars and Stripes. Can you think of other nicknames?

title: Why did Tom Thumb race a horse?
text: In August 1830 two railroad cars pulled by a steam engine were set up to race against two railroad cars pulled by horse. Peter Cooper of New York built the steam engine which was named "Tom Thumb." This race was to prove that steam engines would be faster than the horse. Though the locomotive started out ahead and soon outdistanced the horse, a belt on the engine broke. The horse won the race! Even so, the B & O Railroad saw the value of the steam engine and decided to invest in it.

title: Northern Bayberry
text:
A shrub is a woody plant that is smaller than a tree. It has several stems instead of a trunk.

The northern bayberry is a shrub that grows along the Atlantic Coast. It has shiny, green leaves with jagged edges. The fruit grows in clumps of berries that have many black grains in the center covered with a greenish-white wax.

The leaves of the plant are very fragrant, but they are not what gives the well-known candles their fragrance; it's the berry.

To make candles, the berries are covered with boiling water and the wax covering them floats to the top. The delicious-smelling wax is then poured into candle molds or dipped to make a finished candle. It sounds simple, but it takes about four pounds of berries to make one candle.

title: Clarity of Expression: FDR and the Four Freedoms
text:
For most people around the world, the years of economic depression and war between 1929 and 1945 were dark and dangerous. Resources such as food, clothing and fuel were in short supply. Families were often torn apart as parents looked for work, served in the armed forces, or as children were sent to safe, sheltered areas. It was a time of stress and hardship, when people desperately looked to leaders for safety and hope. In the United States, that leader was Franklin D. Roosevelt, our 32nd president who served from 1933 to 1945.

During that time of chaos, on Jan. 6, 1941, President Roosevelt delivered to Congress a historic speech, which we now call the Four Freedoms Speech. After years of economic depression, his words were not angry. When world war was happening, his tone was not fierce or mean. But knowing that there were still darker days of war to come for many, he spoke with passion about peace, good fortune, safety, and about the freedoms that humans everywhere deserve. “In the future days,” Roosevelt said, “we look forward to a world founded upon four essential human freedoms.” Even today those four freedoms are essential (important). Can you list them? They are: the freedom of speech and expression, the freedom of worship for every person, the freedom from wants such as hunger and lack of shelter and the freedom from fear.

How are we doing? Have we achieved those freedoms for everyone? Everywhere?

To read or listen to the entire speech, with the permission of a parent or teacher go to: www. americanrhetoric. com. To see the paintings by Norman Rockwell inspired by the Four Freedoms: www. archives. gov.

title: The Wonderful Horse
text:
The era in the early 1800s was often called the Industrial Revolution because America grew rapidly and worked on new ideas in technology. But even with steam-powered vehicles and new railroads, people still needed the horse.

Horses pulled carriages and omnibuses (large buses used to carry many people within the city). They pulled stagecoaches between towns not yet connected by the steam railways. Even in areas serviced by the trains, horses were used to carry people and goods between the towns and the trains.

Later, horses help construct the famous Erie Canal. Afterwards, horses and mules pulled the barges full of people and goods along the canal.

In the Eastern United States, horses were largely replaced by railroads and farm machinery by the turn of the century. But in the West, horses remained important for stage transportation in rural areas for some time to come.

Stage horses in America lived hard but rewarding lives. They were usually treated with respect and were very well taken care of. The average life of a stagecoach horse in America was much longer than those in England, which averaged only three years at work. For instance, one horse working in California pulled about a quarter of a million miles while in harness for 15 years. What are some things horses are still used for today?

title: Steam Railroads
text: There are still some working steam railroads around today like this one in Utah. Most are tourist attractions.

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you are a famous scientist and you have been commissioned to develop a wonderful new form of transportation. In 150 words or less, tell of your invention and how and where it would take you.

title: Industrial Revolution . . . Good or Bad?
text:
Today, we think of the Industrial Revolution as a marvelous period of invention and progress. Indeed, many of the items that make life easier today had their beginnings during this time. The Industrial Revolution really began in Europe in the early 1700s. It did not reach the United States until after the Revolutionary War. New machines were developed in Europe and America. They began to change the way people lived, worked and thought. As new machines began to make manufacturing easier, more jobs became available in the cities. New transportation also changed the life of a farmer because goods could be shipped faster and over longer distances.

Maine, then a part of Massachusetts, relied heavily on foreign trade, and the Revolutionary War actually slowed maritime trade. Many businessmen began to look for other sources of wealth besides shipping.

Do you remember how Maine's state tree, the white pine, was used in shipbuilding? Well, the lumber industry was very important in Maine, so there were many sawmills in the area. Soon, water-powered factories began to spring up too. Textile mills and paper and leather production all became very common.

Maine grew a lot when it became a state. And lumbering, fishing and shipbuilding grew right along with it. Other industries, like ice harvesting, granite and lime quarrying and other mining industries started doing really well too. After Thomas Edison experimented with energy in the 1890s, Maine started using its rivers to make energy. The state built several hydroelectric plants, mainly along the Androscoggin, Kennebec, Penobscot and Saco rivers. Railroads also helped start industry in places like Androscoggin Valley. Between 1852 and 1866, eight cotton mills were built in Lewiston.

Before the Industrial Revolution, skilled craftsmen learned every single step involved in making an item. For instance, it might take a cobbler several days to make a pair of boots. It might have taken a smith an entire week to make a gun. With the growth of industry, mass production became more practical. This idea was to divide the jobs between many people to make one item. If each person only performed one step of the production, they could become faster and better. Less-skilled workers could also be used, making more workers available. This idea was called division of labor. It did much to speed up production. Many former craftsmen were unhappy about this new method, because it either meant they would lose their job, or at best they would have to repeat the same small task over and over.

Assembly lines were later introduced by Henry Ford. They were a brilliant new idea which made it possible to produce things faster with less expense. Ford's idea was to provide a moving belt that would bring the item to the worker. The worker could simply do their one small task, then the item would travel on to the next worker for the next step. The assembly line worked and actually made automobiles and countless other items less expensive. With this, average Americans could afford to buy things that were once too costly.

title: Whaling is a Hot Topic
text:
Shipbuilding was an important industry from the very earliest days of Colonial history. Whaling became nearly as profitable. Colonial sailors searched the waters, looking for the great sperm whales that swam up and down the Atlantic Coast. What products came from whales? Some common items were made from whale products. These included candles, lamp oil and soap. At the time of the Revolutionary War, some 360 whaling ships were recorded leaving Nantucket, New Bedford and Marblehead.

The Colonies were not the only place that whaling was a part of life, however. On the northwestern coast of North America, native tribes were also proficient at whaling, and the products were used by the members of the tribe. Later, an international ban on whale hunting stopped many nations from harvesting whales, but it remained a very touchy issue - especially between nations that use and sell whale products and people who wanted to protect whales.

In 1998, the Makah tribe and the U.S. government reached an agreement. This agreement allowed the Makah to harvest a few whales each year off the coast of Washington state. In May 1999, the Makah went whaling for the first time in 70 years.

Many people were unhappy with the agreement, and protesters were ready in May 2000 when the hunters were out. Some protesters on small watercraft tried to scare the hunters by buzzing their canoes. One woman was arrested because no one was allowed within 500 meters of the hunt.

Both sides were angry about the incident, and the anti-whaling folks were successful in a court of appeals.

For now the Makah have been ordered to stop their whaling until further studies have been completed about the impact of whaling on the Pacific Coast. What do you think should happen?

title: Early Industry in Maine
text:
Child Labor Increases

In the late 1880s, newcomers from southern and eastern Europe began to pour into New England. They came by the thousands. They filled positions that booming industrialization provided. Many Yankees were unhappy about the arrival of so many immigrants. It did not stop these families from coming. Over 12 million people eventually entered the United States through Ellis Island.

Because so many of them desperately needed work, they were willing to work for lower wages. The owners of factories shamefully took advantage of this. The manufacturing was done by men, women and children in dreadful conditions. Hours were much too long, and the work was hard. There were no laws which said children could not work. Children, often as young as 5 or 6 years of age, went to work long hours beside their desperate parents.

Factories encouraged child labor as the owners only needed to pay $1.50 or $2.50 for little ones. They were required to pay parents from $3.50 to $7.00 per day. Even though they were paid less, the children's hours were just as long and hard. Many children in the factories worked from 7:30 a.m. until 9:00 p.m. Others worked all through the night. If they began to fall asleep, cold water was dashed in their face to keep them working.

There were opponents of child labor, and many states did pass some early laws to stop it. With thousands of children working, however, these laws were hard to enforce.

In 1904, The National Child Labor Committee was formed. It began a drive to protect the children of the next generation.

Yankee Ingenuity

Maine soon became a key state for manufacturing. The can-do mentality of the time became known as "Yankee ingenuity."

In the years following the Civil War, our country experienced a boom in manufacturing. Maine boomed too. There was rapid progress in transportation along with frantic growth of industry. There was also a need to compensate for the suffering farming, fishing and shipping industries. This resulted in a great number of factories springing up in the state of Maine.

There were new factories everywhere. The need to fill them with workers opened up many jobs for anyone who would take them. This caused big changes in the workplace. Yankee girls in Lewiston's mills were among the first women to work in the industrial era.

Maine's industry continued to grow into the 20th century. Textile mills couldn't compete with those of the South, but the paper and pulp industry offset the losses. Large potato farms and dairy and poultry farms replaced the shrinking number of family farms.

Shipbuilding helped Maine to thrive. The new fast type of merchant ship called a "clipper" was built, along with many other ships, often in Maine.

title: Economics Competition
text:
Have you ever played on a sports team? Maybe you played soccer, basketball or baseball. If so, then you know the best way to become a winning team. Each player must play the best he or she can. Everyone must work together.

This same kind of competition is in a marketplace. Producers compete against each other. They try to give customers the best prices and products for their money. Monopolistic competition is when businesses offer similar products. The products are not identical, though. Each business can raise or lower its price. Each tries to reach a price where it can sell the most products. This is why economists call these businesses "price searchers."

An oligopoly is a market where a few (usually three to five) companies control the competition. They provide the most products. For example, airplane manufacturing is very hard and so only a few large companies compete against each other. When there is only one seller of a product, it is called a monopoly. No companies are making a product to use instead of this product, either. So there is no competition for the company. The company can charge whatever price it wants, because customers have to buy their product.

A monopsony is a market that has only one buyer. Sellers will compete with one another to make the best quality product. They try to offer this product at the best price. An example would be the U.S. government. They are the only buyers for aircraft carriers in this country. Businesses compete to make the best aircraft carriers. But there is only one buyer.

Now that you know about the different kinds of markets, can you decide which one you would prefer for a business you owned?

title: Liberty
text:
Liberty is the freedom to think, to rule or direct without being constrained by force. In the days before democratic government, people had to struggle to survive. It was often the strongest or the oldest who made the decisions for others.

The Greeks began a voting system that allowed some of the people to have a voice in decisions that affected them. Later, the Romans had a similar idea when it came to deciding about law cases.

For most of the next 2,000 years, however, kings and queens mostly ruled the world. Those rulers usually got their position by birth or war. Most people did not have the ability to choose their leaders or live without people forcing them to live a certain way.

Finally, people began to rebel against their leaders, just as the American Colonists rebelled against King George. After the Revolutionary War, the Colonists were free to set up a new government. They chose to establish a democracy so that they could have a voice in the decisions that affected their communities. This new freedom has often been described as liberty.

title: The Sewing Machine
text:
Can you imagine having to sew all of your own clothes with just a needle and thread? Before the invention of the sewing machine, that is exactly what clothing makers had to do.

In 1755, an American inventor named Charles T. Wiesenthal designed a double-pointed needle to make sewing faster. In 1830, a Frenchman named Barthelemy Thimonnier used this double-pointed needle to make the first sewing machine. He attached the needle to a rod connected to a wheel. When the wheel turned, the needle went up and down, sewing stitches.

By 1846, Elias Howe, an American inventor, had figured out how to make the first lock-stitch sewing machine. This machine pulled the stitches tight so they didn't come loose later. This machine was used in clothing factories to make sewing faster and easier.

In 1851, Isaac Merritt Singer, a Boston machine maker, built the first small sewing machine that could be used at home. He made it easy for people to have their very own sewing machines for making their own clothes at home. The Singer Sewing Machine Company went on to become the world's largest maker of home sewing machines.

Just think of all the time, money and energy saved by the invention of the sewing machine!

title: Is there a "Holy Mackerel?"
text:
Yes! There's one hanging right in the Senate Chambers of the Massachusetts statehouse. It is a wooden carving of a fish (referred to as the Holy Mackerel). In the House of Representatives hangs its neighbor, the Sacred Cod.

Fishing is the oldest industry in Massachusetts, and the codfish has been an unofficial state symbol since Colonial days. The first fish was destroyed in a fire in 1747, and a second met its doom during the Revolution. The current cod was carved in 1784. It has been in the House ever since, except when it was stolen briefly by some Harvard students who "cod-napped" it.

title: Black Walnut Tree
text:
Black walnut trees are usually found in bottom lands or growing on slopes. They grow to be 70 to 90 feet tall. Their leaves are found on a stem about 20 to 24 inches long. There are 15 to 23 lance-shaped leaves per stem.

The fruit of the black walnut tree is considered a treat, but can be a real challenge to get to. First, the sturdy outer husk must be crushed. As you peel the nut you may find it stains your fingers because the husk has a substance used in dye. At last you reach the inner shell, which is as hard as a rock, so hitting it several times with a hammer usually works! When you finally get to the dark, meaty nut inside, it's very tasty, and worth the work - unless you are planning on making a walnut pie! If so, you need to repeat the above procedure many, many times!

title: Good Handwriting
text:
It takes some time to develop good handwriting, but it’s well worth the effort.

Have you ever gotten a test back and lost points because your handwriting was too messy? Does your teacher have problems reading what you’ve written? Bad handwriting can lead to these situations. If no one can read your brilliant answer on the test, then it won’t help you get a good score. Most people think bad handwriting means a lack in organizational skills. If it’s difficult to read, people won’t take the time to decipher the handwriting.

Developing good handwriting takes patience and diligence. It takes a lot of practice to get those perfect letters. Here are some tips to get you started.

Take some time each day to practice writing out letters. The more you practice, the better your handwriting will become.

Practice in one notebook so you can compare how well you are doing.

It’s okay if you write slowly in the beginning. Focus on writing that can be read easily. Then move on to how fast you can write legibly.

Choose a pen or pencil that you like and gives you the best grip. You may want to try out different pens or pencils to find the one just for you.

Good handwriting is a great skill to have in this world. It’s needed when you take a test or write a paper in class. You’ll need it to write thank-you cards or to fill out invitations. And when you’re older, you’ll need it to fill out job applications.

In the end, good handwriting will help people understand what you’ve written. And that’s the most important part.

title: Children in the Workplace
text: Industry boomed during this era in Maine history. Sadly, children had to join the workplace at very young ages, some even as young as you.

title: Let's Write
text: The Industrial Revolution brought many changes to the United States. Some changes were good and some changes were hard. Pick a job such as a farmer, a merchant or a factory worker and tell what your life may have been like in the 1800s. You may want to read a book from your library about the Industrial Revolution.

title: Maine Honors Inventors
text:
After the Civil War, the United States experienced a huge growth in industry. A great number of inventions triggered this growth. These major inventions changed the lives of Americans forever. We are proud to showcase some Maine inventors who contributed to the growth of American industry, technology and medicine.

Hanson Crockett Gregory

Hanson Gregory was a teenager in Clam Cove, Maine, when he came up with something that is very popular even today - the ring-shaped doughnut. No one knows for sure exactly how Gregory's invention happened, but lots of stories tell different ideas.

When he was just 19, Gregory became Maine's youngest sea captain. Today many stories about the doughnut have to do with life on a ship. One story says the doughnut was invented when Gregory jammed one of his mother's cakes on the spoke of a ship's wheel during a storm. Another version tells that six men fell overboard and drowned after eating the cakes, so Gregory lightened the cakes by making a hole in the middle. Another tale says Gregory simply wanted the cakes to look like the life preservers on his boat.

The story passed down by Gregory's family says that in 1847, Gregory asked his mother why her fried cakes were so soggy in the middle. She didn't know but said the centers wouldn't cook like the outer areas did. So Hanson walked across the room and poked a fork through the center of some uncooked pieces of dough. "Here, Mom, fry these," he said.

The tale told by Gregory himself is slightly different from any of these. In an interview with the Boston Post, Gregory said that in 1847 he was on a schooner eating tough, greasy fried cakes and used the round cover of the ship's tin pepper box to cut a hole from the middle. He called it the "first hole ever seen by mortal eyes," adding, "Of course, a hole ain't so much, but it's the best part of the doughnut."

Maybe he came home that same year and also poked holes in his mother's cakes - no one really knows for sure. But, even though Gregory had a great career as a ship captain, he will always be known for inventing the doughnut. However, he had to prove it first.

In 1941, there was a big debate about who really invented the doughnut hole. The American Doughnut Corporation had a panel of celebrity judges in New York City help decide. A lawyer from Cape Cod claimed the hole was actually created when a Nauset Indian shot an arrow through a Pilgrim woman's fried cakes. He didn't have any proof and could only tell stories. Gregory's cousin, Fred Crockett, used letters and affidavits (signed documents) to prove Gregory was the real inventor.

Percy Lebaron Spencer

Percy Spencer invented several things, but you are probably most familiar with the microwave oven. Spencer worked at the Raytheon Company in 1941, which made magnetron tubes. Theses tubes make and send out microwaves (the actual waves, not the machine in your kitchen). At the time, the company was only making maybe 17 magnetrons a day. Spencer had some great ideas to make the machines in less time.

Later, Spencer noticed that the magnetron tubes heated things up. He came up with the idea for a microwave oven that quickly cooked food. The Raytheon Company liked the invention and started selling the oven to lots of people. Spencer's work changed the way millions of people cook their food! Do you have a microwave today?

Chester Greenwood

Chester Greenwood was born in Farmington, Maine, in 1858. When he was 15, he had a new pair of ice skates and was testing them out. But it was bitter cold outside, and he couldn't keep his ears warm. First he tried wrapping his head in a scarf, which didn't work so great. Finally he made two ear-shaped loops from wire and asked his grandmother to sew fur on them. This was just the beginning of earmuffs. Greenwood later patented an even better model that had a steel band to hold the sides in place. He named his invention "Greenwood's Champion Ear Protectors" and started a factory to make them. During World War I, he made a fortune selling earmuffs to U.S. soldiers. He also held patents for other inventions. In 1977, Maine's legislature made Dec. 21 "Chester Greenwood Day."

title: How Do Inventors Protect Their Ideas?
text:
What does someone do when they think of a really terrific idea? That idea can become intellectual property. To help people think of new ideas, the legal system developed the definition of intellectual property to protect people's new ideas. There are four kinds of intellectual property. One is a patent. A patent is a grant issued by the federal government. It gives the inventor the right to be the only one to make, use or sell the invention in the United States for a certain period of time.

A trademark is a logo, slogan, symbol or design made especially for a product or service. Can you think of a trademark for a well-known product?

A copyright protects the expression of ideas. That means if you wrote an awesome play or story, made a winning movie, took a fantastic picture or even made up a unique dance, it could be copyrighted. That way, only you had the right to reproduce it, or make copies.

A trade secret is something special a company knows or knows how to do. That something special may help them be a little ahead of their competition. A trade secret can be a chemical formula, a pattern for a machine or even a customer list.

Protecting a good idea is not a new idea. In fact, patenting began in Italy in 1421, 71 years before Columbus discovered the new world. Inventors who applied for patents wrote down all the details of their work. When it was approved, the patent office published them. This protected them from being copied for about 12 to 16 years.

A patent encourages invention. It publishes the latest technology for everyone to read. Many new ideas are built upon other ideas or inventions. Also, it gives the inventor time to profit from an idea before it can be copied.

Patents help ensure that everyone can benefit from good ideas. Do you have any good ideas?

title: Inventors and Inventions
text:
National Toy Hall of Fame

Did you know there is a National Toy Hall of Fame? The people who create toys for enjoyment and pleasure are inventors too!

Graduating from Yale medical college and winning an Olympic medal weren't enough for A.C. Gilbert. His next ambition was dreamed up as he rode the train between New York City and New Haven each day. He noticed crews building steel towers for electric wires and he thought of making toys out of steel girders as well. He experimented with cardboard cutouts until he was satisfied, then had a metal shop make the first set. In 1913, Gilbert introduced the Erector Set. Today, the Erector Set is part of the National Toy Hall of Fame.

One well-known hall-of-famer is the yo-yo. Did you know the yo-yo is the second oldest toy in the world? (Dolls are the oldest.) Many believe that the yo-yo originated thousands of years ago in China. But at the same time it was being played with in other cultures on separate continents. The first historical record of a yo-yo was in 500 B.C. in Greece.

The yo-yo we play with today has been around for 70 years, and more than 600 million have been sold!

The National Toy Hall of Fame encourages kids to invent toys too. How can you come up with an idea to invent a toy?

Here are some ideas:

Ask a friend.

Visit toy stores.

Brainstorm with a paper and pencil.

Make an accessory to go with an existing toy.

Make an existing toy easier to play with.

Make a toy to go with a popular TV show

The next step is to draw your design. Use a pencil and be sure to have an eraser on hand. After you are satisfied with your drawing, build it! (Then rebuild it and rebuild it, improving it each time!) Have friends and family play with it and make suggestions. Then rebuild it again.

After you have your final model, you must give it a name. It can be something that describes that toy or a simple word to describe what it does or how it sounds.

What's next? Submit it in a science fair or the Connecticut Invention Convention.

Maybe it will be the next inductee into the National Toy Hall of Fame!

No Shortage of Inventors in Maine

Maine's economy has been built somewhat around agriculture for a large portion of its history. Many of its inventions came around when industry started growing. The lumber industry, for example, faced some interesting challenges. Once a tree was harvested, the wood needed to be transported to a mill. This was no problem when the harvesting site and mill both existed near water, because the logs could be moved through the water fairly well. When a harvesting site was not near a suitable port or river, however, its lumber tended to be unused. In the early 1890s, James and Ira Peavey of Bangor, were working on a log hauler with a combustion engines that turned two large screws. This hauler worked well on ice and hard roads but not in snow.

Johnson Woodbury also had plans for a log hauler and shared them with a friend, Alvin Lombard. Woodbury never built the machine, but later Lombard came up with a machine that moves on a track that goes around two wheels. (Think about the tracks on a tank or snowmobile today.) This idea became the Lombard Log Hauler and helped the logging industry.

You've already learned about Chester Greenwood, but he also invented the steel-toothed rake used by millions of people in their yards and gardens.

These inventions show how a community's needs inspire individuals to create and invent. No invention becomes popular if people can't benefit from it.

title: Free Enterprise
text:
Have you ever heard the term free enterprise? What does it mean? Free enterprise refers to a market economy. When people in the market have their own ways to make and sell a product, it is called a market economy. The United States has a free enterprise system. Free enterprise markets only work if the laws of a country and the values of its citizens support them. If this type of market doesn't exist, then the system will fail.

Four pillars keep our free enterprise market standing. We will talk about the first two pillars today. They are private property and the price system.

Private Property - Do you own a bike, a board game or a CD player? Did you know that these things are considered your private property? That's right! This means that you are responsible for your own property. If you don't take good care of your things, no one else will. You must pay to have your things replaced or fixed.

Private property is the first pillar in the free enterprise system. It influences all of us to care for the things we own, or provides us with incentive. Incentive is what motivates us to make the decisions we make. If a business does not take care of its office building or breaks the equipment, it must pay to replace them. This gives the business incentive to take good care of the things it uses.

Price System - Prices provide guidance for producers and consumers. They show the market how much customers value the producer's goods. They also provide clues for economists about whether a market is healthy or not.

Prices also provide incentives for businesses and consumers. For example, most consumers try to shop for bargains if prices rise. Maybe consumers buy many packets of something because it is on sale. Can you think of other ways private property and the price system affect our economy?

title: World Organizations
text:
There is a group called the World Trade Organization that, like the United Nations, is a group composed of representatives from the governments of the states (or nations) that are members. The World Trade Organization (WTO) is the only international organization dealing with the global rules of trade between nations. Its main function is to ensure that trade flows as smoothly, predictably and freely as possible.

The United Nations has six departments. They work to solve problems that concern all of humanity.

The General Assembly addresses any important world problems and approves of the budget.

The Security Council has the job to maintain peace and security in the world. They help to settle international disputes by peaceful means.

The Economic and Social Council works at promoting economic growth and development of countries. They try to help countries solve problems relating to children, hunger, education, health and human rights.

The Trusteeship Council watches over the people living in U.N. territories.

The International Court of Justice settles legal cases between member states.

The Secretariat is the U.N. staff in New York, as well as additional staff throughout the world. They are drawn from 170 countries.

title: What is a penny farthing?
text:
Once in a while, the name of something doesn't tell us much about what it is. This is surely the case of the penny farthing.

The penny farthing is also known as an ordinary. It is a type of bicycle. It was made in the 19th century. It had a very large front wheel and a very small back wheel. The seat was mounted over the large wheel. This made it so it could only be ridden by long-legged people. Soon, more practical bikes were designed. Pedal power became the rage in America and Europe.

title: Worm Snake
text:
The worm snake is a very small species of snake. It rarely reaches more than 12 inches long.They are a very plain brown, with a reddish-pink belly. The worm snake has a pointed head and small eyes, with a sharp spine on the tip of its tail.

Worm snakes are carnivorous. That means they are flesh eating. Though they occasionally may eat a salamander, slug or fly larvae, they usually eat earthworms.

Where can you find a worm snake? In moist woodland areas, probably under a rock or a log.

Worm snakes are harmless to humans and they are endangered; if you see one you should leave it alone.

title: Can You Make an Invention?
text: This is our invention, the fly shooter. Now instead of swatting flies, you can just sit back, relax, aim your little swatter and fire away! Can you invent something? Submit your invention in a science fair or an invention convention.

title: How Do I Take a Test?
text:
Do you get sweaty palms and butterflies in your stomach over the idea of taking a test? That happens to everyone at one time or another. Did you know test anxiety comes from a lack of self-confidence? How can you improve your self-confidence and improve your test-taking skills? The best way is to know the material very well. But here are some other important ideas that may help you:

Preview the test. What does it cover? How long is it?

Plan your time. Decide how much time you can spend on each section. Keep track of the time as you take the test.

Follow directions. Read all the directions and listen carefully to any directions read aloud.

Read the questions carefully. Look for keywords such as “when,” “where,” “why,” “different from,” “same as,” “before” and “after.”

Don’t get stuck on one question. If you can’t think of an answer, skip it and return to it later when you have finished the rest of the test.

Check your work. If you have time left after you finish the test, go back and double-check your work.

Use this list while taking this week’s Studies Weekly quiz. Practice good test-taking skills. You may want to use this list for the next few weeks until you have mastered the skills.

title: Let's Write
text: Using the idea on Page 2 for the Fly Shooter, create your own invention on paper that will make life easier for someone. Use diagrams and notes to explain how your invention works. Remember to use a fine black marker, not a pencil.

title: The Three Branches of Maine Government
text:
Maine and the federal government both use the principle of checks and balances.

The men who labored to bring about the Constitution of the United States were often called the Founding Fathers. They were very concerned about the balance of power between the state and federal governments. Some of the delegates felt that under the Articles of Confederation, the states were united, but not really a nation. The Founders were concerned that powers be correctly distributed so as to best protect the rights of the individuals in this country. When the Founders completed the Constitution, the powers given to the national government were very important, but they were carefully selected. The Constitution lists only 20. These include:

powers relating to foreign affairs

war

national security

managing interstate commerce

national security

federal taxes

naturalization

patents

bankruptcy laws

federal land management

handling of federal finances

coinage of money

fixing weights and measures

setting up federal courts

establishing post offices

crime on the high seas

The national government has to coordinate national affairs, so it has more power than the state governments. But the states control their own affairs without help from the national government. James Inedell said of the new government, "When this government is adopted, there will be two governments to which we shall owe obedience - to the government of the Union, in certain defined cases - to our own state government in every other case."

Understanding the structure of our state government as it is set up in the Maine Constitution will help citizens to be informed of their rights. As in any state, the state constitution of Maine is the supreme law. It contains the rules and principles for this state.

Just as the federal government, Maine's government is divided into three branches, or departments. They include the executive branch, to administer the laws; the legislative branch, to make the laws; and the judicial branch, to interpret and apply the laws. Study the diagram to the left to see the branches of the Maine government and their related responsibilities.

title: Great Plates
text:
Maine first began using license plates on its vehicles in 1905. The first plates used black letters and numbers on a yellow background. Over the years, the colors and styles of our state's license plates have changed many times. In 1936, the state's first and only slogan, "Vacationland," was added to the bottom of the plate. For several years, a red Maine lobster was featured on a white background with blue lettering. Today's plate is white with black lettering and a picture of a chickadee, the state bird, on the left side.

Maine, like most states, also lets its citizens create special vanity plates for their cars, for an extra fee. This means that people can choose the letters and numbers that appear on their license plates, spelling out funny or catchy messages. For example, a dentist might choose to put "SMILE" on his plates, or someone who sells houses might put "SOLD" on hers. A Corvette was spotted with a license plate that read "2FAST4U," and a Star Wars fan chose "DRTHVDR" for his vanity plate. Have you seen any of these interesting license plates in your neighborhood? Start watching and you may be surprised at the funny messages you see! If you want to see more creative Maine license plates, ask a parent to help you visit http://emainehosting.com/MaineVanityPlates/series1.html.

title: Market Competition and Entrepreneurship
text:
Last week, we talked about the first two pillars of free enterprise. These pillars are private property (rights that allow us to own things) and the price system, which helps value and ration scarce goods. You might already know that there is more than one way to divide our resources among all of the consumers. One way is through market competition. It is the third pillar of the free enterprise system. This week we will finish talking about the last two pillars - market competition and entrepreneurship.

Market Competition - Do you remember when we talked about scarcity? Scarcity happens when products and resources are rare. Sometimes we want more of something than is available for us to have. Markets have this same kind of competition. Businesses compete every day for resources and products. They also compete for consumers!

Businesses create competition in the economy when they offer money for resources they want. Maybe they are offering money for machines they need. Or maybe they need skilled workers. Did you know that the more skills and education you have, the more companies will compete for you to work for them? Think of that! As you compete to get a job, companies are competing for the best-trained workers, too.

Businesses also compete for products and profit. They mostly do this by keeping their production prices low. They also do this by advertising (or telling people about) their products. Businesses compete with other businesses that have similar products.

Entrepreneurship - The last pillar under free enterprise is entrepreneurship. Remember good old Benjamin Franklin? Benjamin Franklin invented things and competed as a businessman. There are many entrepreneurs creating products and competing in our world today.

Entrepreneurs compete by thinking of better products for consumers. If people are unhappy with their breakfast cereal, an entrepreneur somewhere might come up with a way to improve their breakfast. Then the entrepreneur will turn around and use their product to compete with the other cereals. Entrepreneurs hope to make a profit competing with other companies. They use creativity and their incentive for profit to think up ideas that benefit everyone. What are some other ways entrepreneurs affect market competition in the economy?

title: United Nations and Preamble
text:
In previous issues, we talked about the Constitution of the United States and the Bill of Rights. The United Nations also has a Charter, or a constitution, that provides for the framework that governs what it may do. Read the preamble to that Charter and discuss how your class can contribute to world peace.

We the peoples of the United Nations, determined to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war, which twice in our lifetime has brought untold sorrow to mankind, and to reaffirm faith in fundamental rights in the dignity and worth of the human person, in the equal rights of men and women and of large and small, and to establish conditions under which justice and respect for the obligations arising from treaties and other sources of international law can be maintained and to promote social progress and better standards of life in larger freedom.

And to these ends . . . To practice tolerance and live together in peace with one another as good neighbors, and to unite our strength to maintain international peace and security and to ensure, by the acceptance of principles and the institution of methods, that armed force shall not be used, save in the common interest, and to employ international machinery for the promotion of the economic and social advancement of all peoples.

title: Governor Paul R. LePage
text:
Paul LePage, governor of the great state of Maine, is the oldest of 18 children. When he was only 11 years old, he left home to escape poverty and abuse. He lived on the streets of Lewiston, surviving on the money he earned as a shoeshine boy. As he grew up, he made a living by washing dishes, hauling Pepsi boxes and working at a meat packing plant.

Governor LePage learned early in life that if he were going to succeed, he would have to make it on his own. He lives by the motto, "If it is to be, it is up to me." He graduated from Husson University and later earned an MBA from the University of Maine. Getting a good education changed his life.

As governor, Paul LePage has big plans for public education. He hopes to offer students more technical classes that will lead to better jobs. He would even like to add an extra year of high school during which students could take college courses for free. Governor LePage said, "I want every Maine high school student, from their freshman year, to know they have options beyond high school and give them the tools to reach those aspirations (goals)."

Governor LePage's dog, Baxter, keeps tabs on Maine's first family and posts his opinions, with a little help from the first lady's assistant Paula Benoit, on Baxter Blogs at http://baxterblogs.wordpress.com/.

title: What's the Difference Between "Capitol" and "Capital?"
text:
We don't know why they made it so confusing for us, but the actual building is the CapiTOL. The city in which the CapiTOL is found is the CapiTAL. To help you remember, close your eyes and think of taking a trip to our CapiTAL on the long roads from your house to Trenton. Those roads are the sides of the letter "A."

Now think of the building itself. Your dad is looking for a parking place so you can all stop and go inside our beautiful CapiTOL building. The circles he keeps driving in to find a parking spot resemble the "O" in Capitol. Does that help?

title: White-Tailed Deer
text:
This guy lives all over the United States except most of the southwestern states. The underside of its tail (white, of course) acts as a flag to other animals. If the deer senses danger, it will spread its tail in the air as a warning to other deer. The bright tail also helps a fawn follow its mother in flight.

Two fawns, born in the spring, are the usual size of a brood. The young have red-brown fur flecked with white spots that disappear during their first winter. They like to eat green plants, acorns, twigs and all kinds of nuts.

Females have no antlers. Males begin growing them several months after birth. They shed them each winter and develop them again each spring and summer. It's a myth that one can tell the age of a deer by the size or number of points on the antlers. Antler size is determined by what the deer eats, not by its age.

title: Plagiarism
text:
Plagiarism is a long word and it’s hard to spell. But it’s very important you know and understand its meaning.

To plagiarize something is to steal another person’s writings, thoughts or inventions.

It means to take credit for that person’s ideas. This practice is dishonest, even if the writings have never been published. Another word for plagiarism is “copying.” In many schools, a student can be kicked out for plagiarizing. We should never steal another person’s ideas.

There are many ways to avoid plagiarism. Let’s look at some ideas you can use to become a writer who doesn’t plagiarize. By doing these things, you can always be confident in your work.

Paraphrase, or re-write in your own words. Read what several different writers say on the subject. Then write your version of what they’ve written.

Use quotations. It’s perfectly okay to state what another person has written on a subject. You just need to give credit to that person. Here’s an example: As Huckleberry Finn said to his buddy, Tom Sawyer, “.....”

Your opinion. What you think about a subject is what really matters. Read about the subject first. Then put down on paper what you truly feel about it!

Your teachers really want you to succeed. If you worry your writing is not what you’d like it to be, ask your teacher for advice. You will never lose marks for asking a teacher questions.

title: Maine Today
text:
Maine has such a notable past that it's sometimes hard to look at the future. With a history of about 400 years, major changes and exciting new developments don't come easy.

Maine's economy was initially focused around industries that have changed almost completely since the time that Maine became a state. It was originally one of the biggest shipbuilding centers in the United States. This industry has declined greatly as the big war and commerce ships are no longer wooden. (Maine's large forests were what made it a great place to construct ships.) After becoming a state, Maine enjoyed a great period of growth which gave birth to a number of other industries, including lumbering, ice harvesting - which remains one of Maine's big industries - and granite and lime quarrying. The discovery of methods which used flowing water to work in a factory changed the face of Maine's commerce a great deal. The state then enjoyed a greater market in the wood, textile, paper and leather industries along the state's water fronts.

Maine's economy continued to grow and take shape through the rest of the 19th century. Edison's discoveries gave yet another use for Maine's water resources - hydroelectric power. Family farms in Maine began dying as very large potato, dairy and poultry farms began to take their place.

Throughout the second half of the 20th century, Maine struggled to find a proper balance between resource-based industry and environmental protection. The state has come to rely heavily on tourism and small manufacturing enterprises, in addition to defense-related activities.

Currently, Maine has an economy based on many different things. It is the largest producer of wild blueberries in the United States. Potatoes are another important crop.

The wholesale-retail trade makes about 20 percent of Maine's economy. Wholesale is the sale of goods or services to businesses. Retail is the sale of goods and services to the consumer or individual buyer. That's you and me.

Maine waters are also popular for the harvesting of shellfish; around 90 million pounds of lobster are harvested annually. Maine is well known for its lobsters. Every year, Maine's coastal waters attract an increasing number of saltwater fishing enthusiasts.

You'll probably not be surprised to learn that we create many products from our trees. After all, about 90 percent of our state is forested! Products from our forests bring almost $2 billion into our economy.

With all of this going on what does Maine's economy look like today?

Maine exports over $3 billion dollars of goods to other countries, many of which are manufactured right here in our state. What kind of products does Maine produce? The top five on the list are electronic and electric equipment, paper products, lumber and wood products, seafood and industrial machinery.

As you read before, Maine has been successful at finding a good balance between industry and conservation (protection of the environment). Maine has over 500,000 acres of state and national parks. Have you visited one of our famous parks? Acadia National Park is one of the most visited parks in the country. You can start your walk on the Appalachian Trail at Baxter State Park. Maine also works to make neglected areas into parks. That's a lot of land for the state to protect! Talk with your class about how you can keep Maine a beautiful state.

title: Boom to Bust and Back Again
text:
You may have heard people compare the recent economic recession (2007-2009) to the Great Depression of the 1930s. But what some people call the "Great Recession" actually had more in common with a depression in the 1890s and something called "boom and bust."

In the early 1890s, the U.S. economy grew quickly ("boomed") but couldn't keep growing at that rate. When many companies and the housing market failed, there was an economic "bust." The railroad industry had been booming since the end of the Civil War, but in the 1890s more than 150 railroad companies closed. Other industries that depended on the railroads closed, and many people lost their jobs. Over 500 banks closed. Thousands of unemployed men marched to Washington, D.C., in 1894 to demand that the government take action to help families. Unemployment was over 10 percent for most of the 1890s. About one of every ten people had no job.

In the recent recession, the housing market slumped after several "boom" years. Some automakers went out of business and others filed for bankruptcy. The economy went "bust," just as it did in the 1890s. Hundreds of banks and thousands of businesses closed. The unemployment rate was about 8 percent - about one of every twelve people had no job.

Make a chart or Venn diagram that compares these two events in history.

title: Maine Conservation
text:
Brownfield Reclamation Sets the Pace

Have you ever gone by an old, rundown building or piece of property that is vacant (unused) and wondered why no one is using it, or why no one has tried to fix up that property? The reason that old or unused property is vacant may be because it is a brownfield. What is a brownfield? The term brownfield was coined by the United States Environmental Protection Agency. According to the EPA's definition, a brownfield, "is an abandoned, idled, or under-used industrial and commercial [facility] where expansion or redevelopment is complicated by real or perceived environmental contamination." What does that all mean? It means that a brownfield is a piece of property that is unused because there either is, or people believe there is, a danger such as chemical contamination or buildings that are so broken down they may fall apart.

These brownfields are becoming an increasingly important issue in environmentalism, because they are areas that have already been used, and probably have access to things like roads, water, sewage, etc. They are places that are no longer green or developed. People are beginning to run out of land, and cities are expanding at great rates; this is called urban sprawl. Reusing brownfields is one way to slow the rate of urban sprawl. Undeveloped places are called green fields, and there aren't as many of those left as there were a few years ago. It's important to preserve what is left.

So why aren't developers jumping to make use of the brownfields? The main reason is liability. If someone got hurt while fixing the property up, whose fault would it be? What if there was a chemical contamination that made people sick? Who would be responsible for that? It doesn't make sense to most people looking at buying properties to buy property that may have problems they don't know about. What are Maine officials doing about this? The Maine Department of Environmental Protection's Voluntary Response Actions Program represents the state's attempt to clarify liability and assign responsibility at brownfield sites. Through VRAP, an applicant may volunteer (at their cost) to investigate and reclaim a brownfield site in exchange for protections from DEP enforcement actions. At the federal level, the EPA regularly evaluates brownfield grant applications from around the country, picking the best applicants as pilot projects. The state has two very visible pilots, one located along Marginal Way in Portland, and the Bates Mill Complex in Lewiston.

Brownfield reclamation is just one way that people in Maine are working to help preserve the environment. Recently, the Federal Government granted an extra $1 million toward the purchase of thousands of acres on Tumbledown Mountain. The money was awarded to the Tumbledown Conservation Alliance, a group aiming to preserve some 30,000 acres on Tumbledown and around Mt. Blue State Park, and at bringing more public land ownership in Maine in general. In 1999 Maine voters approved a $50 million land bond to fund various projects.

Another way people are trying to protect Maine's natural resources is by protecting animals. The Wild Atlantic Salmon in Maine has recently received protection under the Endangered Species Act, making it illegal to take the fish for personal use. Currently, less than 10 percent of the population needed to sustain the population in Maine is returning to the state. The protection offered under the EPA would help this fish to grow in numbers.

title: Economics Review
text:
Congratulations! You now know about some basic economic concepts. You know about producers, the people who produce goods and services. You also know about consumers, the people who buy producers' products. You may even realize that you are a consumer. You know about the different types of resources, too (natural, human and capital).

You should understand the idea behind supply and demand and the role of prices in our economy. Supply affects demand. Demand can affect what is supplied. For example, if demand increases for a certain pair of shoes, then the producer will try to make more shoes. If the producer can't make more shoes, the price of the shoes would increase. The price helps to ration the shoes, because not everyone can afford to pay for the pair of shoes.

You should now have a general idea about trade-offs and opportunity costs. Remember, we make trade-offs every day. If we buy a candy bar, then we trade money for chocolate. We also make decisions involving opportunity costs every day. If we wake up late, we may not get to take our morning shower. This means the opportunity cost of sleeping in was getting to take a shower.

You know about money and its features. Remember, money should be used as way to exchange, a measure of value and a store of value. It should also be lightweight, durable, easily recognized and divisible. You know about banks, debt and credit. You know about income, budgets, profit, and profit motive. Every day we watch both microeconomics and macroeconomics in action. We see how they affect our world and how they affect each of us.

Some of you might own businesses someday. You might invest in the stock market at some point in your life. Who knows? Maybe some you of will be the greatest entrepreneurs of tomorrow. But even if you choose not to be a business owner, the economy will affect you every day for the rest of your life. It will determine what you eat, what you wear, and how you live. Good luck to all of you as you set out into the fascinating world of economics.

title: Treaties
text:
A diplomat is a person who has the job to handle relations between his or her country and other countries of the world. A diplomat is a specially trained person who is very skilled at dealing with tense and difficult feelings. The government of their country appoints most diplomats.

One of the things diplomats may do is write a treaty. A treaty is a signed agreement between two parties, or countries. A treaty is one way a nation can end a war or a disagreement. Do you remember learning about the Treaty of Paris in a previous issue of Studies Weekly? It was entered between the United States and Great Britain. Who were the diplomats? Was it favorable to the United States or Great Britain? Do you remember what the treaty accomplished?

title: What is biotechnology?
text: Biotechnology is the use of biological knowledge in industry. Biotechnology is a growing business. It involves genetic engineering (the use of plant and animal genes in custom-designed foods, drugs and fertilizers). Scientists, for example, have used genetic engineering to develop a very strong corn seed that is resistant to many diseases and severe drought. What other things do you think are explored in biotechnology?

title: Scarlet Tanager
text:
Visitors in Maine should look for the beautiful scarlet tanager. The brilliantly colored male gleams in the sunlight but is often difficult to see in the thick forest.

The female lays her three to four brown-spotted greenish eggs in a shallow nest. They like to hang around mostly oak and pine trees. You'll hear them make a call similar to a robin. It comes out sounding like a nasal chip-bang.

Would you be surprised to learn the most popular sport in America is not football or baseball? It's bird-watching! It gets people - kids too - out in open fields and walking through beautiful forests. You'll learn more than the sport of watching for birds. You'll learn a lot about trees and small animals too. And don't forget all that fresh air and exercise bird watchers get.

title: Taking Notes in Class
text:
Learning how to take good notes in class is very important.

Taking notes in class can be difficult. Sometimes it’s hard to concentrate and you can miss some information. Or you can’t read what you wrote. Other times, you’re not sure what information to write down. It’s important to learn how to take good notes. Without notes, taking tests is much harder! Here are some ways to take good notes in class.

Be ready. You don’t always need to have a pen in hand, but have your notebook open to a clean page. And have a pen or pencil nearby. When the teacher enters the room, you’re ready to begin.

Put the date and topic on top of the page. Knowing when you took the notes will help you study for tests. You can quickly flip through the pages and find the topic.

Don’t waste time writing what you already know. Notes help you remember what you learned in class. If you’re sure you know something, then don’t write it down. Let’s say you know George Washington was the first U.S. president. You don’t need to write it down. Instead, you can focus on his birth date, where he lived and what he did.

Make lists. Lists are easy to recognize and read. They organize the information. If you can make a list, you’ll likely remember the information later.

Remember, note taking will improve your learning. But your notes won’t make much sense if your eyes are always glued to the paper. Take some time to really listen to your teacher. Stop every now and then to listen and to watch your teacher. Write down the examples that are written on the board. By doing this, you’re sure to have success in class!

title: Did You Know?
text:
Maine is about 320 miles long and 210 miles wide, with a total area of 33,215 square miles; or about as big as all of the other five New England states combined.

Maine claims America’s first chartered town: York, 1641.

Maine is recognized as one of the most healthful states in the nation with summer temperatures averaging 70 degrees F and winter temperatures averaging 20 degrees F.

Maine has one county (Aroostook) so big (6,543 square miles) that it actually covers an area greater than the combined sizes of Connecticut and Rhode Island.

There are five federally recognized American Indian tribes living in Maine.

title: You Can Make A Difference!
text: Pollution control is always a community concern where a small area is inhabited by a very large population. Brainstorm with your classmates to think of places in your community that need to be cleaned up or protected from pollution. What are some ways you can make a difference? Make a list of your ideas, then develop a class pledge that tells of your commitment to protect the environment.

title: Farewell Fun!
text:
This is the final issue of Maine Studies Weekly for this school year. We hope you have enjoyed our paper and learned something as well. We have taken you back to the dinosaurs, met the American Indians who first lived here, explored with the European settlers and finally come back to present-day Maine. Together we have learned about our government and how to be a good citizen. You read about many famous people in Maine history, including women, inventors and leaders.

Well, our final issue is going to make it fun to review much of what we have talked about this year, but first, here are a few simple questions to get you warmed up.

• Who’s buried in Grant’s tomb?

• If there are two barbers in town and one has a bad haircut and one has a great haircut, to which do you go for your haircut?

• How many z’s are in a dozen?

• If a rooster lays an egg on the peak of your roof, which side will the egg roll down?

Now that you have thought about those for awhile, you are ready to move on to the questions and games on the following pages. We have crossword puzzles, word searches, multiple choice and true and false questions, fill in the blanks and matching quizzes.

We hope you have a great summer! Keep learning about our great state of Maine. Perhaps you will get to visit some places in Maine that you have never been to before. Or maybe you will be able to visit other areas in the world too.

OK! Are you ready? Turn the page and let’s get started.

title: Reason and Logic: The Marshall Plan
text:
When World War II ended in 1945, Europe was in ruin. Homes, schools and factories had been destroyed. Roads and railroad lines were gone and farmland was torn up by bombs. The war was over, but Europe still suffered. How would the United States respond to the pains of its European friends?

The United States could have left Europe to take care of itself, but Secretary of State George C. Marshall had other ideas. In 1947, he presented the Marshall Plan. The plan called for America to help Europe rebuild by giving money and materials. President Truman and Congress accepted the plan.

Over the next four years, the United States sent over $13 billion in money and supplies to countries throughout Europe. To explain why he thought it made sense for America to help, Marshall said, "In America we have not suffered the destruction of our homes, our towns, and our cities. We have not been enslaved for long periods, at the complete mercy of a conqueror. We have enjoyed freedom in its fullest sense." Many American soldiers lost their lives in the war. But our nation's cities, factories and farms were unharmed. What was our country's answer to the suffering in Europe when we had plenty of food, clothing, money and supplies? It was to give as much help as possible.

What did the United States gain by helping to rebuild Europe? It gained friendships, the ability to trade, and hope for a brighter future, in both Europe and America.
