title: Fun Facts
text:
A dog’s sense of smell is so good that it can tell the difference between a tub of water and a tub of water with a teaspoon of salt in it.

Want to know when it is going to rain? Look at a pine cone on a tree. The pine cone closes up when it is about to rain.

The longest city name in the world is officially Krungthep Mahanakhon Amorn Rattanakosin Mahintara Yudthaya Mahadilok Pohp Noparat Rajathanee Bureerom Udomrajniwes Mahasatarn Amorn Pimarn Avaltarnsatit Sakatattiya Visanukram Prasit. You may have heard of it, it is also called Bangkok, Thailand.

Typewriter is the longest word using only the letters on the top row of a keyboard, while stewardesses is the longest typed with just your left hand.

title: Let's Learn About Connecticut This Year!
text:
Welcome to Connecticut Studies Weekly. This year, we will learn all about our great state! We will learn about the people of Connecticut, both past and present. We will also learn about places, events and much more. The study of Connecticut is more than just history! It's social studies. Social studies includes many themes like history, geography, government, citizenship, economics and culture.

History is the study of people and events of the past. It begins with the first written records of people long ago. We study the past not because students need to learn a bunch of old facts. We learn of our history because it helps students understand how the world works and how human beings behave. Understanding this will help us to know just where we fit in the stream of time. Geography is the study of the Earth's surface. It is a study of the way the Earth looks and how it changes. What are some of the forces that change our Earth? If you named weather and climate, you are exactly right. People affect our environment as well.

Government is the way of ruling a country. It is a system of rules and laws. This year, we will examine the kinds of governments there are in the world. We will study how local, state and federal governments are organized. We'll look at who runs the governments and how they run governments.

Economics is the study of how people make decisions about resources. As we study economics, we learn how goods and resources are produced and consumed. We also learn how wealth is distributed in world communities.

Culture is a way of life shared by a group of people. It includes the values, traditions, customs, arts, history and folklore of that community. Cultures are different from place to place. They may change over time.

Wow, that's a great deal to learn, and we know just the place to start - right at the beginning! This week, we'll begin by learning about prehistoric Connecticut and the land.

So, turn the page, and hang on for the ride of your life as we explore Connecticut.

title: Tracking Dinosaurs: The first residents of Connecticut
text:
Paleontology is the study of the fossil remains of plant and animal life. Dinosaurs are part of this vast and interesting study. There are many ways a paleontologist finds information about dinosaurs. One way is to learn about them as they find bones and reconstruct the dinosaurs, but there are many other ways to learn about them as well. For example, a scientist can learn a lot from a footprint (or trace fossil).

While only partial skeletons for a few species of dinosaurs have been found in Connecticut, the Connecticut Valley is the home to the richest group of trace fossils in the world!

During the Jurassic Period, around 200 million years ago, there were mudflats in what is now the Connecticut Valley. Dinosaurs that patrolled these prehistoric beaches left more than 2,000 footprints that were fossilized.

One of the most famous footprint sites in Connecticut is Dinosaur State Park in Rocky Hill. There you will find many three-toed tracks. When Edward Hitchcock first discovered these tracks, the term dinosaur was not yet used. He imagined that the creature that made these tracks must have made a thunderous noise while walking. He called the creature Eubrontes, which is Greek for "true thunder." No one is sure what a Eubrontes looks like, but by comparing the tracks to others, many feel certain the Eubrontes is very similar to the Dilophosaurus. Because skeletal remains have been found for the Dilophosaurus, scientists believe that Eubrontes may have looked somewhat similar.

What can a paleontologist learn from a trace fossil? They can learn about behavior and size. For instance, they know if it was a walking or running dinosaur by the spacing between the footprints. By the depth and length of the footprint, scientists can tell if it was sitting or even swimming. They can also tell us if its tail was aloft or raised off the ground.

The prints of the dinosaur can also tell us if it's a theropod, meaning it walks on two legs, or a sauropod, meaning it walks on four legs.

Finally, the footprints can show the paleontologist the possible placement of bones.

title: One Big World
text:
We'll start our study of Connecticut this year by trying to imagine how Connecticut used to be millions of years ago. Before there were people living on the Earth, before there were animals like we know now, Connecticut existed in a tropical climate with great inland seas.

Worldwide Land

What’s the biggest place you’ve ever been? Disney World? The Grand Canyon? Some scientists believe that there was once a place on Earth bigger than any other place. This landmass was called Pangaea, which means “worldwide land.” Pangaea was one huge continent. Imagine being able to travel over all of the world’s land without getting in a boat or a jet! What happened to this giant continent? Over millions of years, the landmass divided and drifted apart over the face of the planet to become the continents we know today.

This explains why the same kinds of dinosaur fossils are found in different parts of the world.

Age of Reptiles

The Age of Reptiles was a period in Earth's history that began 200 million years ago and ended 60 million years ago. Reptiles are cold-blooded creatures like crocodiles, snakes and lizards. They dominated the Earth for approximately 140 million years. We call this age of prehistoric, or before any history was written down. The recorded history of people on Earth is just about 6,000 years old.

During the Age of Reptiles, there were three main kinds of reptiles. Those on the land were called dinosaurs. Pterosaurs (ter-ihsores) sailed through the tropical skies. The oceans and seas swarmed with great sea serpents and lizards shaped like fish called plesiosaurs (pleez-ee-oh-SORES).

Ice Age

The land of Connecticut was once buried in water, and many plants and animals lived in this watery world. Then the seas began to back away as land started to rise. Mountains rose out of the sea. The land left behind was an oozing swamp! Then the land was covered by water again. How many times this happened over hundreds of millions of years is unknown.

But then, much later, it became cold - very cold. Great glaciers grew in the north and pushed down into what is now the United States. Connecticut was completely covered over-even the highest peaks of the Northwest Uplands. As the glaciers grew, the sea level dropped. The great glaciers moved slowly. As they pushed through the mountains, they carved valleys and lakes. On the edges of the glaciers, rocks and woody materials were deposited. Then about 18,000 years ago, the whole process was put on rewind, and the sea level rose, once again, as the ice melted and formed glacial lakes such as Lake Hitchcock.

Age of Mammals

All of the dinosaurs disappeared mysteriously about 60 million years ago. Some scientists believe that it happened suddenly, and others believe that it happened over a long period of time. As the mountains were built up, the climate changed. The Earth went through cold cycles, which caused ice to form over most of the world. The reptiles were cold blooded and didn't adapt to a changing world climate. Mammals, on the other hand, make their own heat and are covered with hair. They are said to be warm-blooded. They had bigger and much better brains for taking care of themselves. One way to think of it is that they had enough sense to come in out of the cold.

The Age of Mammals was the 60-million year period from the mysterious death of the giant reptiles until recorded history began with people about 6,000 years ago.

title: Exchanging Goods and Services
text:
Think about walking home on a cold winter day. The wind is blowing hard. Just as your house comes into view, it starts to snow. You are freezing! Quickly, you bolt up your front steps. You stomp the snow off your boots as you enter the front door. You walk right to the kitchen and find your dad starting dinner. He asks you to help and gives you a can of tomato soup to open. You complain a little, not sure if your fingers are warm enough yet to move. You find the can opener and open the can. As the can spins around, you start to study it. You think of many questions about the can of soup. What part of the country did it come from? How was it made? At what store was it bought? How did it travel to the food store near your home? Who made the label? All of a sudden, that can of soup becomes more than the main menu of dinner tonight. You realize you are looking at a can of economics.

Economists ask all of these questions every day. Their job is to study the economy. They study the results of manufacturers making and selling goods and services. They study the consumers who buy those goods and services. In the case of the soup, producers make the soup. Your family, as the consumer, buys that good. On the other hand, if you provide a service for someone, such as mowing a neighbor's lawn, that person paying you for the service becomes the consumer.

Economists have two separate areas of study in economics: macroeconomics and microeconomics. Macroeconomics is the study of the economy as a whole. People who study macroeconomics ask questions about the entire nation and world. One example would be why gasoline prices have risen across the country. Microeconomics is the study of individual consumers and businesses. People who study microeconomics want to know things such as what prices you, as a consumer, would pay for your favorite video game. This year in Studies Weekly, we will be learning much more about our economy. We'll look at the roles of producers and consumers. Can you think of other ways you are a consumer?

title: It All Begins WIth You!
text:
History is a part of social studies. It is a very important part. Through lessons in history, we fashion our future. Another important part of social studies is learning about governments. The study of our government and of citizenship strengthens our country. We become the defenders of our democracy as we learn how governments work. We hold on to our freedoms as we learn about citizenship.

Just what is government? A government is the way in which a country, state, city or village is run. In every community, a government makes laws that citizens must obey. A government decides how to enforce those laws. Governments also decide how to protect their citizens. Governments are not all the same. The kind of government that Americans have is just one of many.

This year, we will learn about our government. We will learn what it does and why it is important. We will also focus on how to be good citizens in our homes, schools, and communities. At Studies Weekly, we know that "good government" begins with you!

title: Glaciers of Long Ago Shaped Connecticut!
text: Long ago, Connecticut was almost entirely covered by glaciers. The movement of these glaciers rounded off mountains, moved streams and rivers, and left us with hundreds of beautiful lakes and ponds.

title: Why is Oil in the Ground?
text: Scientists have learned that oil comes from organic material (that is something that was once alive). Since dinosaur- type animals lived on the Earth for millions of years, along with ancient plant life, we know the remains of plants and animals over a period of millions of years created the oil reserves that are beneath the ground. Because the source for oil is limited, scientists are always looking for better, more efficient ways to use it.

title: The Hummingbird
text:
Many skeletons of dinosaurs resemble features in the skeletons of birds today. Can you imagine the tiny hummingbird being related to a dinosaur?

You will most likely see ruby- throated hummingbirds in Connecticut. They are beautiful birds with long needle- like beaks. They are a metallic green. The males have a bright red throat; the females have a dingy white one.

"Hummers" are generally feisty birds, with a long, shrill call when they are scolding. Their calls are heard as they chase another hummer away from their flower or feeder. They migrate in early spring, with the males arriving first.

Hummingbirds' nests can be found in groups in a single bush or tree. The mother takes care of the young. She feeds the hatchlings small insects and nectar from flowers.

A hummer, unlike other birds, can fly backwards, sideways or even hover. They hover over a flower when they drink its nectar. They are especially attracted to bright red and orange flowers. It is not uncommon to have a hummingbird investigate a red hat or a red bow in someone's hair.

title: Direct Context Clues
text:
Direct context clues are words that say, “Look here!”

Learning how to guess words you don’t know is an important skill. If you learn how to guess what a word means, then you won’t have to read with your dictionary open all the time.

There are different strategies to guess word meaning. One way is to find other words or phrases nearby that point to the definition. We call those words or phrases direct context clues.

Below is a list of words that are often used to point to direct definitions. In items 1-5, circle the words from the list below. Underline the direct definition in each item.

is/are was/were
is/are called, means, or, such as
is/are known as different from
is/are like is/are similar to
unlike is/are considered

Mammoths lived during the Ice Age. A mammoth was something like a very large elephant. It sported very long tusks that curled on the ends.

The Spanish explorers used a very fast, three-masted ship. This ship is called a caravel. Because it was smaller, the caravel could be used to explore shallow coastal waters.

Do you want the thrill of your life? Then try the SkyScreamer out for size. The SkyScreamer is a 20-story-high swing ride found in the Texas Six Flags amusement park.

Jason’s bedroom is chaotic, unlike Harry’s room, which is tidy.

Check the BBC website for a list of monarchs, or rulers, of England.

title: Let's Write
text: As an amateur paleontologist, you are thrilled when you discover the nearly complete fossilized skeleton of a dinosaur. In 150 words or less, write about your discovery. Be sure to include the era from which the dinosaur came, what you named it and what the translation means. Describe what your new pal probably looked like, as well as its eating and traveling habits. You may even submit a black and white drawing of your dino if you would like.

title: The Anchisaurus
text:
Anchisaurus

AN-key-Sawr-us

Anchisaurus (meaning “near lizard”) was a sauropod (walked on four legs) from the early Jurassic period, about 200 million years ago.

Anchisaurus was 6 to 8 feet long and probably weighed from 75 to 100 pounds. It was a plant eater and could also walk on two legs.

Anchisaurus had a long neck, a long body, thin feet and a long tail. Its head was small and contained very sharp, leaf-shaped teeth.

Almost complete skeletons of adults and young Anchisaurus have been found in both Connecticut and Massachusetts. This dino is sometimes called the Yalesaurus.

title: Where in the World is Connecticut?
text:
We believe it's important to know how Connecticut looks on a map. This is so we can understand how the geography affects the history of our state.

Connecticut is the farthest south of the six New England states. New York is the giant neighbor to the west. Rhode Island is directly east. Massachusetts is the northern neighbor. Long Island Sound splashes against southern Connecticut.

Connecticut's landscape includes rolling hills, dense forests, and sparkling beaches. There is little flat, empty land in the 4,845 square miles of land in Connecticut. The best farmland in the state is found in the Central Connecticut Valley. Here, the Connecticut River runs through the Central Valley. It then crosses into the Eastern Upland where it empties into Long Island Sound.

Rivers and lakes play an important part in the history of Connecticut. Early inhabitants settled around waterways. This was because the land was often near a river. Some settlements grew near rivers or lakes. This was because they provided an efficient means of transporting goods. Today, Connecticut is dotted with about 6,000 lakes and ponds. Many were created by ancient glaciers thousands of years ago. The state's largest lake is Candlewood. It is a reservoir, or a lake that is a result of a dam constructed on a river. Lake Bantam is the largest natural lake in Connecticut. The major rivers in Connecticut include the Connecticut River, the Housatonic River and the Thames.

Whew! That was really a race through an amazingly diverse state! We will visit the topography (physical features) more in the next issue as we visit geographic regions of Connecticut.

title: Hurricanes: An “Eyeful” of Information
text:
Hurricanes are severe tropical storms. They form by gathering heat and energy through warm ocean waters. When the seawater evaporates, it adds power to the hurricane.

Hurricanes rotate in a counter-clockwise direction. This is around what is called the eye of the storm. It's hard to believe, but hurricane hunters fly directly into the eye of the storm. They do this to gather information. The hurricane hunters are part of the Air Force Reserve. They use the information from the storm to help predict the strength, size, and the direction of the hurricane. The plane ride can get pretty bumpy. The plane flies right into the storm. Sometimes, rain and clouds are so thick, crews can't even see the wings of the plane!

When hurricanes meet land, they bring with them heavy rains and strong winds. They have winds of at least 74 miles per hour. Heavy waves called storm surges are very dangerous. This is a good reason why you must stay away from the ocean during a hurricane warning or hurricane.

Hurricane season is from June 1 to November 30. Each hurricane is named by the National Weather Service. This helps with tracking the storm. Its name begins with a different letter of the alphabet, except for Q, U and Z. If a storm has been very big, then that name is retired. It is never to be used again.

title: Connecticut Rivers and Lakes
text:
People in Connecticut enjoy a variety of water sports. Grab your pencil and list as many as you can in one minute.

Waterways played an important part in the early settlement of Connecticut. Beaver was the most desirable of the furs for trade. It was plentiful near the Connecticut River. In addition, the Connecticut Valley boasted some of the most fertile farmland east of the Mississippi. Early colonists also valued the waterways as a quick and efficient means to transport goods for trade.

Plentiful Waters

In all, Connecticut has 8,400 miles of rivers and streams. As in the colonial era, access to waterways often determines where people live. It also determines what kinds of industries develop in a region. Lakes and rivers are a terrific source of recreation as well. Thousands of lakes and ponds are found in this lovely state. Many of those are “puddles” left behind by ancient glaciers. Other lakes are actually reservoirs, or man-made lakes. These are formed as a result of a dam.

Three major river systems have enabled people to move about. It has also allowed them to transport goods from one place to another. These three rivers are the Connecticut, the Housatonic and the Thames. Look on a map of Connecticut. Circle the one nearest to you. The Connecticut is the largest river in all of New England. It rises near the Canadian border moving southward. It then forms the border between New Hampshire and Vermont. It continues through western Massachusetts. Then it flows south through Connecticut. There, it empties into the Long Island Sound at Old Saybrook.

The Housatonic also crosses the entire state. It begins in Massachusetts, entering Connecticut at the northwest corner. It winds across the Western Upland. There it finally empties into the sound. Fishing is a major recreational activity along the entire length of the river and its tributaries. Trout, bass and perch abound—it is a fly-fisher’s heaven. The Thames flows into Long Island Sound at New London, after it flows through the Eastern Upland. The Thames has been the site of the Yale- Harvard rowing contests since 1878.

title: What is democracy?
text:
Democracy is government by the people. The word "democracy" comes from two Greek words. Demos means "the people," and kratos means "authority." The Greeks granted authority to the people to pass the laws. They used these two words to mean "government by the many." They did not want the government to be just a few people. They did not want the government to be a single ruler, such as a king or queen.

In those days, democracy was direct. The free people would gather to discuss and pass the laws. The people had a direct vote. Today, democracy in the United States is different. It is not direct. We just don't have room for everyone to gather in the town square. It would be nearly impossible for so many people to discuss ideas and to vote. Today, we practice representative democracy. We elect people to represent our ideas and to pass the laws. Each elected official discusses and votes for the laws of our country. Still, whichever form of democracy is used, it is still government by the people. That includes you!

title: The Bobcat
text:
The bobcat is a member of the cat family. It is a carnivore. It is about 3 5 inches long. It is brownish with black spots and stripes.

The bobcat is an interesting looking fellow. It has pointed tufts on the top of its ears. It also has a black tipped, stubby tail. It can be found across Connecticut, but the northwest part of the state has the highest population of bobcats. Bobcats are nocturnal mammals, meaning they are active at night. Bobcat attacks on humans are rare, but if you see one, be careful!

title: How Do Forecasters Predict Weather?
text:
People have always searched the skies for a way to predict the weather. You have probably heard sayings like, "Red sky at morning, sailors take warning; red sky at night, sailors delight." Seafarers and farmers have learned to read the winds and clouds for signs of incoming weather. Today we watch the news. We may even read the papers to see what meteorologists have to say. How do they know? They really don't know for sure. They are making predictions based on a lot of information. It isn't easy being the weather forecaster. Sometimes they are not the most popular people when the weather does unexpected things.

Forecasting is really an international effort. Thousands of weather stations are located around the world, on land and at sea. Each station monitors and records the weather at least four times a day. They measure air pressure, temperature and wind speed. They also measure cloud cover and precipitation.

Satellites and weather balloons do the work for us in the atmosphere. All of this information is sent back to the national weather bureaus. This is where it is plotted on charts and analyzed by meteorologists and computers. The information is then sent to newspapers and the local weather stations. Speed is everything in making accurate predictions. Without the technology we enjoy today, predicting the weather would be much less reliable.

Is it Climate or Weather?

You're lying on your back on the lawn watching the clouds above. The clouds form a horse, then a clown. Then it becomes a clown on a horse! What a great way to spend a lazy summer day. Suddenly, a brisk wind comes up. The sky turns dark, and you feel big warm drops of water on your face! Help! Your lazy summer day has been taken over by a cloudburst. What you've just experienced is a sudden change in the weather. The term weather refers to rain, snow, heat, cold, ice, etc. It changes from hour to hour, day to day and month to month. The weather is studied by a meteorologist.

The term climate describes the kind of weather a certain area has from year to year. Alaska has a much different climate than Hawaii. We think of Alaska's climate in the winter as freezing, snowy, and very cold. We think of Hawaii's winters as balmy, sunny and pleasant. Connecticut's climate varies. It changes from the warmer winters near the Atlantic coast to the colder regions in the mountainous areas. Climatologists are the folks who study climate and its many changes. They call our state moderate, as are many New England states. This means our climate is not terribly hot (like Nevada) or terribly cold (like Minnesota.) We are somewhere in the middle of these two extremes.
