title: Inferential Context Clues
text:
Did you ever ask someone the meaning of a word, only to have him answer, “Figure it out!” When you look again, there are no definite context clues. Now what? The fact is that the meaning is hidden in the rest of the words in that sentence. Sometimes, the meaning is tucked away in a whole paragraph. These are inferential context clues.

Below are three examples. Read the words around the vocabulary word and write what you think the new word may mean.

Brianna wanted a cookie, but the jar was out of reach. Jake, Brianna’s brother, climbed onto a chair and stretched his fingers around the jar. Just then, the chair tipped and Jake, the chair and the cookie jar came crashing to the floor. Brianna began to cry. As the noise and confusion mounted, their mother called out from the next room, “What’s all that commotion?”
Write what you think the word commotion means:

During a test in class, Spencer saw his best friend, Tyler, cheat. He told Tyler that if Tyler didn’t confess to the teacher, he would tell her what he saw. Standing up to Tyler took a great deal of fortitude on Spencer’s part.
Write what you think the word fortitude means:

Sometimes, we borrow words from other languages (exonymns). This vocabulary word is French and is sometimes followed by an exclamation point. Ashley said, “I cut a coupon from a magazine, mailed it in and — voilà! — here’s my new glow-in-the-dark lipstick!”
Write what you think the word voilà means:

title: Let's Write
text: You’ve been commissioned to write a short magazine article. It is to be of 100 words or less. Write about Connecticut lakes and rivers. Give a short history of how they were created. You might want to include the reasons that industry and cities are often found near bodies of water. Perhaps you can tell how water is used as a power resource.

title: Is the Earth getting hotter?
text:
It’s getting hot out there and scientists are worried. Some call it global warming. Others call it global climate change. The average temperature on Earth has gone up .9 degrees since 1880. That may not seem like much, but it’s causing other things to change, too. Arctic ice is melting fast. Polar bears and other animals could lose their habitat. Glaciers are disappearing, and coral reefs are dying. Some scientists blame global warming for the increase in extreme weather, too. They believe the changes are causing more storms, floods, wildfires and heat waves.

Most scientists say it’s our fault the Earth is getting hotter. Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide are trapping heat near the Earth. And those gases came from our cars and factories. People have cut down too many trees and caused too much pollution. We all need to work together to keep our Earth cool!

title: Geographically Speaking
text:
This week in Connecticut Studies Weekly, we will be learning about geographic regions in our state. Geography is the study of the Earth's surface and the way people use it. Geographers are the people who study geography. They study what makes one place different from another. Some of the special features we look at are those formed by Mother Nature. Physical features include landforms, bodies of water and other natural resources (things found in nature that are used by humans). To study the geography closely, we sometimes divide things into regions. A region can be made up of many things, but always has at least one thing that sets it apart from other areas. Can you think of regions in your town or school? Regions are described in many ways. How about landforms or plant life? Language or tourist sites might be other ways of determining regions. Let's learn together about some different kinds of regions in Connecticut!

Connecticut Physical Regions

1. Western Upland

Thirty thousand years ago, glaciers covered what is now Connecticut. As the glaciers melted, they dragged large rocks and chunks of soil along the ground, carving hills and ridges. The hills, valleys and lakes found in the Upland regions of Connecticut were carved by these ancient glaciers. The Taconic Mountains are in northwest Connecticut. Here, Mount Frissell towers 2,380 feet above sea level. The Housatonic and Naugatuck rivers flow through this region. Lake Candlewood (a manmade lake) and Bantam Lake are also located here.

2. Central Valley

The Connecticut Valley Lowland extends through the center of Connecticut and north into Massachusetts. Basalt ridges, including Hanging Hills, Mount Lamentation and Talcott Mountain, rise from 300 to 600 feet above the valley.

The Central Valley is home to Connecticut's best farmland. Green, fertile valleys make for a beautiful landscape. The Connecticut River, New England's largest river, runs through the Central Valley. Hartford, the state capital, lies on the western side of the Connecticut River.

3. Eastern Upland

The Eastern Upland consists of dense forest and gently sloping hills. A few of the hills rise as high as 1,200 feet. The land slopes gradually from northwest to southeast. The Eastern Upland covers most of eastern Connecticut. The entire upland stretches from Connecticut to Maine. Many creatures make the dense forest of the Eastern Upland their home. They include white-tailed deer, rabbits, beavers, minks and squirrels. Moose can occasionally be seen darting through the woods.

4. Coastal Lowlands

The Coastal Lowlands are part of a larger region of the same name that covers the New England coast. In Connecticut, the region is a narrow belt, from six to 16 miles wide, and runs for miles along the Connecticut coast. With beautiful sandy beaches breaking up the landscape, this region is a favorite recreation spot. The Coastal Lowlands are also home to many of the state's largest cities, such as Stamford, Bridgeport and New Haven. Many of those who live in this region travel to nearby New York City to work.

Woodlands

Connecticut was once almost entirely covered with woods. Today it is still one of the most heavily wooded states, with about 60 percent of the state covered in forest.

Trees are often the center of Connecticut's beautiful scenery. Trees such as maples, elms and oaks give a brilliant showing each fall.

Among the 30,000 acres of state parks is the Charles E. Wheeler Wildlife Management Area. It is located at the mouth of the Housatonic River where it empties into Long Island Sound. It is adjacent to the Smith Bird Sanctuary. Other trees that are plentiful in Connecticut include pines, cedars and hemlocks. Of course, the sugar maple is a favorite as Connecticuters produce 12,000 gallons of maple syrup each year. Try to visit all of these regions during the year!

title: Connecticut Regions
text:
Sometimes regions are formed as areas of tourism. There are four regions in Connecticut grouped this way.

Early summer mornings, chilly and bright, seem like the perfect time to get up in the wee hours to go on a family vacation. Everyone piles in the car, and it's never long before someone says, "Are we there yet?" Let's pile in and take a road trip around Connecticut. We'll learn of one historic site in each region and keep a journal of the things we see and do. What are we waiting for? Let's go!

1. Dear Journal,

After we visited the Danbury Railway Museum, we drove to Waterbury where we visited the Timexpo Museum. My mom says that Waterbury has always been a center for watch-making and clock-making. The Timexpo museum was pretty interesting.

There was a whole room full of clocks. One clock was a backward clock for a barber shop so when they looked in the mirror they could tell the time! I especially liked the time tunnel!! It was like stepping into a real-live social studies book. We saw displays of ancient civilizations.

Connecticut sure is a great place to visit!

2. Dear Journal,

Today I went with my classmates to visit the Barnum Museum. First, we learned about industry in Connecticut in the 19th Century. After that, we went to the third floor, and the fun really began. There were displays from Tom Thumb, a tiny man who performed with the P.T. Barnum circus.

We looked at a miniature circus carved from wood, with all the animals, performers and everything.

The best thing was the Clown Corner where we got to put on clown noses and shoes. Some of my friends put on clown make-up. It was great!

3. Dear Journal,

Today I visited the Nathan Hale Homestead in Coventry. Nathan Hale is our state hero. There was a special celebration called "Muster and Colonial Encampment."

There were old-looking tents and musket shooting. Boy, are those things noisy!

After we went for a wagon ride, we had a picnic lunch then went to play on the field. Everyone tried to walk on stilts, even my mom! It was a lot of fun.

Tomorrow we'll be visiting some other areas in the Northeast Region. We'll be going to Rocky Hill to the Dinosaur State Park. I hear that some of the dino footprints are 18 inches long! Now that's a big foot!

4. Dear Journal,

Today I visited the Submarine Force Museum. We were able to go onboard the Nautilus, a decomissioned nuclear submarine. My favorite part was the radar room, it was so cool!

In the museum we were also able to look through real periscopes. They had a display of several midget submarines, too. Finally, we went into a control room, just like in a real submarine. Wow! It was all pretty amazing.

We are on our way now to see some other great things in the Southeast Region. This afternoon we're going to the Mashantucket Pequot Museum.

title: Adam Smith
text:
Consumers and producers have been a big part of markets since the early civilizations. Markets are actually a way that people can trade with one another. Markets bring consumers to producers and producers to consumers. Through these markets, exchange economies came to be. No one ever really invented an economy. It just happened as people traded with each other. As markets grew larger, many people began asking questions. Then they studied people as they traded for goods and services. That study is what we now know as economics.

One of these early economists was named Adam Smith. He was born in Scotland in 1723. He went to the University of Glasgow at the age of 14! That seems very young to be going to college now, but it was very common back then. He graduated, and then went on to Oxford University in England. He became a professor and began looking at exchange markets. Smith didn't know it, but he was really starting the study of economics. In 1776, he put out his book, "The Wealth of Nations." The book is about what he had found through 30 years of research.

Smith suggested that there was an "invisible hand" that guided trade in an economy. Think about sitting down to enjoy a nice bowl of tomato soup. Most people give little thought to all the steps and processes that go into putting that soup on your table. There are the tomato farmers and the soup makers. There are the marketing teams who advertise the soup and the people who design the label. Don't forget the truckers who transport the soup. How about the grocery store that places it on the shelf? Who controls all of this? Is there someone leading each company? How does it all work?

According to the "invisible hand" theory, no one directly oversees companies trading with each other. Instead, markets bring people together. From that, producers find other producers to assist them. Then consumers are guided naturally to buy those products that they need. This process of trading in an economy is known as voluntary exchange. When this is the main way of organizing production of goods and services, economists call it a market economy. These early ideas from Adam Smith still affect economists today, more than 200 years later. It is because of his work and study that Adam Smith is known as the Father of Economics.

title: Citizenship at Home
text:
Listening to others talk about their feelings is one way of being a good citizen at home. What if you accidentally broke your brother's new iPod? Would he feel angry? If he did, how might you be a good citizen?

A smart way to begin would be to listen carefully to how he felt about it. It is best not to interrupt. Next, in a kind voice, retell what you heard him say. Then apologize sincerely and ask what you might do to make it right. Everyone makes mistakes. You might choose to earn some extra money to repair it. Perhaps sharing something of yours would help to mend his feelings. By listening carefully and treating others fairly, we can encourage them to do the same.

title: Reason and Logic: Young George Washington, Surveyor and Mapmaker
text:
Most people know about George Washington. He was born in Virginia. He was a general during the American Revolution and our first president. But his earliest jobs, surveyor and cartographer (mapmaker), taught him skills and values he would use for the rest of his life. Using reason and logic to solve problems helped Washington become one of our country's most important leaders.

When Washington grew up, there were few roads or boundaries in much of the land. A surveyor's job was to measure and map the land. He had to make exact measurements for boundaries and physical features. This was a very big responsibility. People needed accurate maps and surveys for traveling and buying land.

At age 17, Washington traveled across the Blue Ridge Mountains to map and survey part of the frontier. He was the surveyor for the whole county, and that was an important job. When he led the Continental Army, it was even more important to have reliable maps. He established the job of Geographer and Surveyor General and appointed a man named Robert Erskine to this position. He gave Washington some information that was very helpful in making reasonable and logical battle plans and decisions.

You can use these same skills to make important decisions. Be sure you have the facts and information you need instead of acting on opinions and emotions. In what areas of your life are reason and logic very important?

title: Keeping a Journal
text: Keeping a journal of your travels is a great way to save your trip so you can enjoy it over and over. Connecticut Studies Weekly invites you to draw a picture of a historical Connecticut site and tell about it in 50 words or less. Remember to use a black marker and don’t forget to sign your name.

title: Fun Facts
text: Idaho is home to the longest main street in the United States. You can visit it in Island Park and drive on it for 33 miles.

title: What is Succotash?
text:
Succotash is a word borrowed from the Algonquian language. It is a dish that contains lima beans and corn. If you haven’t had this tasty treat, you are in for a surprise. Ask a grown-up to help you make this recipe.

Succotash

2 cups fresh or frozen lima beans

2 cups fresh or frozen whole-kernel corn

2 tablespoons butter, 1 teaspoon salt, dash of pepper

1 teaspoon sugar, 1/2 cup water, 1/4 cup heavy cream

Cook fresh lima beans in boiling salted water until tender (if frozen beans are used, cook according to package instructions).

Mix cooked beans and corn with the butter, salt, pepper, sugar and water. Simmer on low heat for 10 to 15 minutes. Drain, then add cream and heat until hot, but do not boil.

(An authentic American Indian recipe would have you cook the corn and beans in bear grease. Succotash may have been one of the first recipes taught to the Pilgrims by Native Americans.)

title: The Moose
text: The moose is the largest member of the deer family in North America. It stands more than 6 feet high and weighs around 1,000 pounds. The male has broad, flattened antlers. Moose like the northern (colder) climates and are found in the northern states and Canada. They like moist lowlands around lakes where they feed on water plants in lakes and streams. In the winter they stay closer to forests. They feed at night and the very early hours of the morning. One (or rarely two) young is born to the mother in the late spring. The young are called calves. Moose can run very fast. Never approach a moose, especially a cow with a calf.

title: The Algonquians Welcome the Europeans!
text:
When Columbus landed in the New World, he thought he had found the East Indies, therefore, he called the people living there “Indians.” Even later, when the mistake was realized, the name stuck. Descendants of those “Indians” are often called American Indians. Sometimes they are called Native Americans because native means “belonging to by birth.”

The Algonquian-speaking tribes are those who share common languages. They lived throughout the Northeast at the time of the arrival of the Pilgrims. It was lucky for the first Europeans that the natives were kind and friendly. Tribal members welcomed them by teaching them how to survive in the new land. They taught them how to grow beans, squash and corn, and they helped the first settlers to learn about the land.

The Algonquians respected and shared the Earth and its resources. They hunted deer, moose, bear and beaver. Wild ducks and turkeys were also plentiful. They never hunted more than they needed and did not waste any part of the kill. While the men hunted, the women planted and harvested the crops. The main crop was yellow corn, called yokeag. Beans, squash and pumpkins were also grown. Tobacco was grown for religious purposes and was tended by the men.

Wigwam is the Algonquian word for home. Most wigwams were dome shaped. They had a hole in the center to let smoke from cooking fires escape. The men shaped the frames from young saplings (or tall young trees). The women then fastened woven mats or bark to the frame. Longhouses were constructed like the wigwams, but were much larger.

Just as nature provided shelter for the Algonquians, it provided clothing as well. Animal furs and skins were the materials used. Women wore long skirts of skins, and men wore a breechcloth. A breechcloth was a thin piece of hide put between the legs and draped over a belt. When it was cold, they donned robes of leather or fur. Beautifully crafted moccasins were worn by all to show respect for the Earth.

Algonquians used what we call a clan system. Many tribes were matrilineal. This means children in a family belonged to the mother’s family. They couldn’t belong to the mother’s and the father’s families. Even though a father lived with his wife and children, he belonged to a different clan.

Children were important members of the tribe. After chores were done, everyone played. A game like baseball was played with a stick for a bat and a pinecone for a ball. Darts were also played. With bird feathers attached, the darts would soar through the air. A favorite guessing game used four moccasins under which four objects were hidden. One object was marked, and teams tried to guess which moccasin hid the marked object.

In the winter tobogganing and snowsnake were favorite sports. In snowsnake, players threw long sticks down snow-covered hills. The player whose stick went the farthest won! Storytelling was enjoyed throughout the year. Members of the tribe told of heroes and history. Early American Indians had no books, so this was the only way for history to be passed on. Just as families in our society today work and play together, Algonquian families and communities worked and played together.

Though the Algonquians were a generous people and gave freely to the European settlers, they were treated poorly by many and driven from the land. Many died from diseases brought by early explorers and settlers. In addition, they were constantly at war with the mighty Iroquois nation (another group of many tribes with a different language family). The Algonquian–speaking tribes were nearly destroyed.

title: Philanthropy and Values
text:
Maybe you have heard the word “philanthropy” before. What does it mean? It describes actions that people make for the good of other people. What is a value? It’s a way of behaving that people believe is good—like believing it’s good to be honest. Is honesty one of your values?

One way you can practice philanthropy today is to help yourself and others learn good values. How do you learn good values? You can learn them from your parents and grandparents, your teachers at school or church and other people you trust.

You can also learn them from people that have been recognized for doing good things for society. An easy way to learn about people that have done good things is to visit values.com. Values.com has lots of stories and short videos that highlight the traits that make each of us better people. They even have billboards on the highway to remind you about good values.

For example, you may have seen a billboard that looks like the one shown here. This billboard is about Oral Lee Brown, who saved money from her job to send nineteen kids to college… all by herself! Wow! Isn’t that cool? You can learn about lots of other people who practice philanthropy at values.com. Be sure to look for more of their “billboards” on Page 4 of Studies Weekly this year. We think they’re so cool we want to remind you to check them out!

title: The Algonquians
text:
The main Algonquian–speaking tribes that resided in Connecticut were the Pequot, Mettabesic, Nipmuc and Mohegan.

Pequot

In the 1500s, the Pequot and the Mohegan were a single tribe numbering about 6,000. They were a well- organized and warlike tribe. (The name Pequot is derived from the Algonquin word “pekawatawog,” meaning destroyers.) During this time, they migrated to eastern Connecticut from the Hudson River Valley where they often dominated other tribes in the area.

After the smallpox epidemic of 1633-34 and their separation from the Mohegan, their numbers were reduced to about 4,000. The Pequot War further reduced their numbers to around 2,000. Those who were not killed were sold as slaves in the West Indies. Some of the captured women and children were taken as “servants” in colonial households. The Narragansett and Eastern Niantic were given other members of the Pequot tribe and a small band was exiled to Long Island and became subjects of the Nipmuc. The remaining Pequot were placed under the Mohegan tribe. The Mohegan treated the Pequot so badly that the English removed them in 1655. At this time, two reservations were established for the Pequot in 1666 and 1683. It is from this group that the two current tribes of Pequot in Connecticut evolved: the Mashantucket Pequot and the Paucatuck Pequot.

Mohegan

Sometime around 1500, the Mohegan and the Pequot left the Hudson River Valley in New York and moved to the Thames River Valley in southeastern Connecticut. The Mohegan, followers of Uncas, settled in the upper and western portions of the Thames River Valley, while the Pequot moved closer to the coast. The Mohegan tribes were close allies of the colonists, and perhaps it is through this association that the Mohegan were exposed to many diseases including smallpox, diphtheria, influenza and measles. By 1675 the Mohegan numbered less than 1,200, and their numbers continued to decline. Many of the Mohegan migrated to other states to live with the Oneida and Stockbridge tribes in New York. Others moved to Wisconsin. By 1920, there were only 22 of the Mohegan in Connecticut. The Mohegan tribe recently received Federal recognition. The tribe now claims about 1,700, and many of them live in Connecticut.

Nipmuc

No one is sure of the original numbers of the Nipmuc tribes, because some of the numbers may have been a part of the Pequot Confederacy. After the Pequot fought with the English, some of the survivors became part of the Nipmuc tribe. They occupied parts of Connecticut, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. After their defeat by the English, the Nipmuc fled west with the Mahican. Today, more than 1,400 Nipmuc live in Massachusetts and Wisconsin.

Mattabesic

The Algonquian tribes in Connecticut that lived west of the Connecticut River did not have a name to describe themselves. The name Mattabesic is the name of a single village and is often used to refer to each of the tribes/families who lived there. These included the Paugussett, Quiripi, Skeetambaugh, Wampano, Wappinger, Unocwa, Siwanoy and the Weawaug. In the years following the Pequot War, the lands of the Mattabesic tribes were taken by English settlement. While a few tribes were conquered by the Mohegan, others separated into small groups and moved to the Housatonic Valley where they were absorbed by the Paugussett tribes. By 1800, only 77 Mattabesic remained at the Golden Hill reservation. Currently, the Golden Hill Paugussett are recognized only by the state of Connecticut.

Smaller tribes of Connecticut were numerous. Many of those tribes included as few as 50 members. One rather small tribe was the Podunk, near what is now Hartford. To this day, people sometimes refer to a small town as “Podunk.”

The Pequot War

Like most wars, a series of events led to the Pequot War. These events caused many groups of people to harbor feelings of distrust and anger. Those groups involved in hostile encounters before the Pequot War included the English, the Dutch, the Pequots, the Mohegans and several other tribes native to the area that is now Connecticut.

The first incident that enraged the English took place before the war. It was the death of Captain John Stone in 1634. Earlier, Stone had been banished on penalty of death from the Plymouth and Massachusetts Bay colonies for various legal troubles. It is possible that Stone was killed as an act of revenge by the Pequot when their own grand sachem, “Tatobem” was killed by the Dutch. Tatobem’s death was, in turn, an act of revenge for murders committed by other Algonquin peoples.

Meanwhile, relationships between the Pequot and other tribes weren’t going so well, either. You remember that the Mohegans had previously broken away from the Pequot tribes. Both Uncas and Sassacus hoped to become the next chief sachem after Wopigwooit died. When the council chose Sassacus, Uncas and his followers eventually left the tribe and became known as the Mohegan. Relations between the two tribes became more strained as the Pequot favored the Dutch, while the Mohegan supported the English.

Each of these events led to a tragedy when a trader, John Oldam, was killed by some of the Niantic in 1636. What do you think happened then? More killings and raids by both the English and the Pequot were the result.

Finally, the English, along with their allies, the Mohegan, traveled to the fort where the Pequot resided, near what is now Hartford. In 1637 the Pequot fort was burned with over 500 of the Pequot inside. They were mostly women, children and the elders. Those who tried to escape were killed, and any survivors were sold as slaves or given to other tribes, including the Mohegans.

The Pequot War was a tragedy, and the first of many Indian wars in the colonies.

title: Productive Resources
text:
Productive resources are found in every good or service. Resources are the basic things used to make products in our community. Economists study resources a great deal and have put them into three groups. They help answer these three economic questions: How is a product made? What product is made? Who makes a product?

Natural Resources

Natural resources are unaltered or undisturbed gifts of nature. Fresh air, minerals, water, and trees used for timber are all natural resources. They are things taken from the Earth that cannot be made any other way.

Human Resources

A secretary, a doctor, a mechanic and a teacher are all kinds of human resources. Human resources, or labor, require people to be creative. People must have skills and knowledge to help them put physical and mental effort into their work.

Capital Resources

The last type of resource can be found everywhere. Buildings, tools, or machines people use to produce other goods and services are known as capital resources.

These productive resources are all around you every day. Let's say that you wanted to make cookies. Each of these resources would be very important. Most of what you put into the cookies -eggs, milk, sugar, salt, and flour- would be natural resources. The human resource would be you making the effort to make the cookies. Lastly, your mixing bowl, measuring cups, spoon, baking sheet, mixer, and oven would all be types of capital resources. All these things come together to make your product - yummy cookies! Can you think of other examples of natural, human, and capital resources?

title: Citizen in the Classroom
text:
Learning to be a good citizen in your classroom is important. It is a good way to make sure everyone has the chance to learn. When we understand the rules of our school and respect them, we are practicing good citizenship. It will help us understand and respect the laws of our state. We will know how to respect the laws of the United States of America. When we are good citizens, it means we respect the rights of others. We are free to make choices about how we live and behave as long as our choices don’t take away the freedoms of others.

When someone is noisy in the classroom, how does that take away your freedom? Good citizenship in the classroom means many things. You can also participate in activities or help others. List some ways that you may have been a good citizen in the last week.

title: The Sachem
text: An Algonquian tribe was an independent nation, with its own leaders. The leader of a tribe was called a sachem. The sachem was not chosen or elected, but inherited the title through birth. He had the authority to make rules and enforce punishments, provided council members agreed.

title: What is a powwow?
text:
A powwow (sometimes called a shaman) was the medicine man in an Algonquian tribe. The powwow's jobs included healing the sick and calling up spirits in ceremonies. He sometimes held a gathering, also called a powwow.

The people asked the powwow questions about the future or talked about problems. Today we often use the Algonquian word powwow to describe a discussion or a meeting.

title: The Wolf
text:
The wolf is a common symbol for many American Indian tribes. The wolf was used to represent many Algonquian clans.

The gray wolf lives in a pack, or a group. It will often stay with a pack all of its life. Though there are pack leaders, the pack will cooperate in hunting, caring for the young and defending their territory against other packs. Each wolf has a place in the pack and must fight for its rank.

Wolves can go many days without eating and then eat as much as 20 pounds of meat in one meal. Most are very athletic and have incredible endurance. They can run very long distances, chase prey and plow through chest–high snow for long periods of time.

Fairy tales and cartoons often portray wolves as aggressive. There are very few known cases of wild wolves attacking humans. Because wolves are very shy, it is rare that they will even come near people.

title: Let's Write
text: You can hardly wait for the powwow to begin. It is your first time to attend a gathering with the powwow, and you watch as he enters in special clothes and painted face. Some people dance and sing, others smoke a pipe. It is almost your turn to ask the powwow a question you have really been pondering. Write your question and then write the answer you think you would receive to your question.

title: Synonyms
text:
Synonyms are words that have the same or almost the same meanings.

Learning synonyms for common words is important. Synonyms build your vocabulary. They can make your writing more interesting (alluring, compelling, fascinating) to read.

Below, you will find a common (ordinary, average, passable) fairy tale. Work with a partner to find synonyms for as many words as possible. Rewrite the fairy tale using your favorite synonyms.

Do you want to find synonyms on the computer? Use this website to see what you can find: http://thesaurus.reference.com

Goldilocks and the Three Bears

Once upon a time, there were three bears. They lived in the forest in a cute little cottage. There was a big papa bear, a middle-sized mama bear and a little baby bear. One chilly morning, mama bear stirred up some porridge. It was too hot to eat, so they went for a walk in the forest.

While they were out, Goldilocks came right in. She saw the porridge on the table and, forgetting her manners, sat down to eat.

“Wow,” said Goldilocks, “this big bowl is really hot.” She tasted the porridge in the middle-sized bowl. It was cold.

“Oh my heart,” she said, “this bowl of porridge is too cold.” Then she spied a little bowl. She took a little bite.

“Yummy!” she squeaked. It was just right. With a big smile on her face, she ate all of the porridge. It was just perfect for a crisp fall morning.

title: Explorers Look for the Northwest Passage
text:
What is the Northwest Passage? Why were explorers looking for it? Did they ever find it?

An explorer is a person who journeys to the unknown for the purpose of discovery. Explorers often discovered places other than what they had hoped to find. Christopher Columbus was looking for a western route to India. Instead, he found the New World.

Thousands of years ago, people did not travel far from home. They grew their own food and made everything they needed. There was no need to travel. As settlements grew, so did the idea of trading with other people. A desire to find new places for trading encouraged exploration. Explorers were always looking for better and faster trade routes.

Maritime Explorers

One of the greatest goals of maritime explorers (explorers traveling by sea) was to find the Northwest Passage. This fabled passage was a route from Europe to China. It was thought to go over the top of North America. Some countries wanted a new northern route. Spanish and Portuguese warships blocked the routes around the south of South America and Africa. It was dangerous to travel the southern route.

Giovanni da Verrazano was one of the many explorers looking for the Northwest Passage. He was an Italian explorer. He was sent by the French king, Francis I and was a unique explorer. Verazzano wrote about the journey, and his brother made maps.

The French sent Champlain. The Dutch sent an English explorer by the name of Henry Hudson. None of these men found the Northwest Passage. They did explore many waterways and portions of the Americas. Many places in the east are named after them. The Hudson River, Lake Champlain and the Verrazano-Narrows Bridge are a few. Can you think of more?

title: Explorers Come to Connecticut
text:
The golden age of exploration began in the 15th century. Sailors from Europe ventured out and explored the world. They located routes across its oceans and continents. They defined the Earth's physical shape, size, and positions.

Dutch Navigator is First to Explore the Connecticut River

In 1613, a Dutch navigator, Adrian Block, arrived in New York. He sailed in a small ship called the Tiger. Block did some trading with the native tribes for fur. He then continued on the Hudson River until he anchored at what is now Manhattan. While there, the Tiger caught fire. Block's crew worked hard to save it, but it was destroyed.

With the help of the local tribes, the men built shelters that looked something like wigwams. Then they nestled in for the winter. Block and his crew were the first European settlers in New York.

In the spring of 1614, they cut down trees to build a new ship. They called it the Onrust, meaning "restless." This ship was too small to cross the ocean, but Block wanted to do some exploring. He hoped to find another ship. In the Onrust, Block sailed up the Connecticut River. He claimed what is now Connecticut for the Netherlands. He went on to Rhode Island as well. Block finally met with a larger ship. At last he and his men returned to the Netherlands.

In 1609 the Dutch sent Henry Hudson to find the Northwest Passage. Like the others, he did not find it, but instead found what is now the Hudson River. In 1610, he set out again and explored the Hudson Straight and the Hudson Bay on his ship the Half Moon. The Dutch were disappointed that Hudson did not find the Northwest Passage. However, they were happy because they realized that trading with the native people was a way to make a fortune.

Many new things were discovered in the New World as a result of explorers looking for the Northwest Passage. While many searched, it was not located for more than 200 years.

In 1817, the British government offered a large reward to anyone who might find it. Many explorers attempted again and again to find it. Many of them died in the attempt. Finally, in 1906, a Norwegian sailor named Roald Amundsen steamed through the passage after a three - year journey.

Who really discovered the Americas?

Who was the first person to discover the American continents? Ancestors of American Indians probably first set foot on the Americas. Scientists think they crossed Beringia sometime between 10,000 and 45,000 years ago. They would have been the first to "discover" these lands. However, when we talk about the discovery of the Americas, we mean something different. We mean discovery by people from civilizations closer to our present day. One of the first sightings with written records was that of Christopher Columbus.

There are tales of other seafarers long before Columbus. These legends are found in the history of the Welsh, Irish, and Phoenicians. Ancient China and Africa also have tales.

The Vikings

Discovery of artifacts leads historians to believe that people called Vikings also saw the North American continent. The Vikings came from the area of modern Scandinavia (northern Europe).

The Vikings were not actually explorers. They were raiders. Their small ships were swift. They sailed to coastal towns. They plundered and raided villages in Europe. The Vikings were skilled sailors. They steered their ships by observing the position of the sun in the daytime. They steered by the North Star at night.

Finders, Keepers

Unlike the Vikings, later explorers made claims on the lands they discovered. They usually claimed the lands they saw in the name of their king or country. With each explorer doing so, it was like a game of finders, keepers. Claims of new lands often overlapped and they sometimes changed hands. Several claims of the same land would be the source of confusion for many years to come.

title: Supply and Demand
text:
To an economist, a market includes everyone who buys or sells a certain good or service. That means all of the people who are buying or selling sweaters are in the sweater market. Everyone buying CDs is in the CD market. Everyone selling hot dogs is in the hot dog market. These markets are very important as economists study supply and demand. Supply is the amount of something being offered by producers for sale. Demand is a measure of how many consumers want to buy what producers are selling. Using the hot dog example, the companies and stores selling hot dogs are supplying them. The consumers who are willing to pay for hot dogs are demanding them.

Demand is more than “wanting” or “wishing” for something. If a person wishes to buy a hot dog, he or she is not in demand. Economists do not consider people in demand until they are willing and able to buy that hot dog. It is not demand until they have the money to actually pay for the hot dog. When they can purchase the hot dog, then they are in the hot dog market.

When economists study supply, they look at several things. They look at the product being sold. Next, they want to know who is selling it. Finally, they study the market for the product. They study prices being charged for a product and how much it costs a company to make that product.

When there is a greater demand for a product than producers can supply, a shortage occurs. Shortages usually mean prices go up as people battle to buy it. When there is a greater supply of something than a demand for it, it is called a surplus. A surplus usually means prices go down. The producers lower the price to boost the sales.

Can you think of a recent example of a shortage or surplus?

title: Citizen in the School
text:
Learning to be a good citizen at school is something to work on every day. By now, you have practiced good listening skills. You have also worked on good behavior in the classroom. There is another way to practice good citizenship. It begins right in your own school. You can begin by respecting the property of others. Property is anything that is owned by a group or individual.

The coat you are wearing is your property.

The desk where you sit is school property.

The school building may be state government property.

Respect for property can be shown in many ways. The first is to make sure you don't harm or destroy things. Another way to show respect is to let an adult know if you see property being damaged. A third way is to take part in repairing damaged property. It's great to take care of your things. It's great to show respect for the property of others.

title: The Quadrant
text: Here, the captain is taking a sighting with a mariner's quadrant. The quadrant, the compass, and the hourglass were the only instruments the early explorers used to find their position and sailing direction.

title: What is Hardtack?
text:
Hardtack is a very hard biscuit. It was used by explorers aboard ships for food. Voyages were very long. There were no means to preserve food. The food usually eaten by sailors was salted meat and hardtack. The hard biscuits often became infested with beetles or maggots, which had to be removed before the hardtack could be eaten!

Hardtack was made with flour, water and salt. It was baked until it became very hard. It wasn't very tasty, but it kept for a long time.

title: Canada Goose
text:
The Canada goose is the goose most commonly seen in New England. This goose is often found in cities and parks and is highly adaptable to humans. Each Canada goose has a grayish-brown body, a black head and neck and a sharp white patch like a chin strap. They grow from 22 inches to 40 inches.

The Canada goose mates for life. Both parents take care of the young. The goslings are cute balls of yellow fluff with brown and black markings. They are adorable, and you might want to hold one—but watch out! The parents will fiercely protect them.

The geese fly in a loose “V” formation when migrating at the change of seasons. The “V” formation helps them cut through the air more easily. The lead goose gets most of the wind pressure, while the geese at the back get less pressure, making it easier to fly. The lead goose tires easily, so the geese constantly change positions so the work load is equal. Keep your eyes (and ears) to the skies and listen for their loud “honk!”

title: Clarity of Expresssion: Henry Hudson
text:
Henry Hudson was an English sea captain and explorer who started off as a failure. He sailed on two voyages for England to find a northeast water route to the rich spice trade in Asia. But both times the icy northern seas blocked his way. He had to return home defeated.

Sounds like the end of his career, right? It wasn't. Hudson next convinced the Dutch East India Company to hire him for exactly the same expedition. In 1609 Hudson and his crew sailed west across the Atlantic. He reached the New World, landing on the island we know today as Manhattan. He sailed inland up a wide river and explored the surrounding valley.

It wasn't a passage to Asia. But Hudson's explorations allowed the Dutch to claim the land and build a fur trading post there in 1614, before the Pilgrims arrived. A Dutch settlement called New Netherland soon followed.

Unfortunately, Hudson's last voyage ended in mutiny. He refused his crew's demands to return home, so the sailors took over the ship, setting Hudson adrift in a small boat. His fate is unknown, but his legacy is Hudson Bay, Hudson River, Hudson Valley and the Dutch settlement that became New York City.

Henry Hudson must have had excellent clarity of expression. He had to be able to explain clearly to the Dutch that his experience and determination made him the best man for the job, even though he was an Englishman and not a Dutchman.

Think about a time that you wanted to convince your parents or teachers to let you try something new. Did you beg and plead? Or did you give them a clear explanation of your reasons? Which way do you think works better?

title: Help a Rat and Learn to Run the Country This Year!
text:
Hey, kids! I'm Revere the Rat, but you can call me Rev. I'm your online Studies Weekly friend and I need your help. You can help me get great stuff by earning points while you learn. Just scan the code or go to www.studiesweekly.com and click on my picture.

Has your family ever bought something that came with an owner's manual? Cars, TVs and other things have an owner's manual, a book on how to use them. Your social studies class is the "owner's manual" for the United States of America. You'll learn about history, geography, government by the people, and much more, so you can do a good job of running our country someday.

In America rats can't vote, so "you the people" govern (run) the country. Someday you will be in charge of this country, and you'll choose leaders and representatives by voting. Then you can tell the representatives you help elect how you think the country should be run. In fact, Studies Weekly kids are so smart, that many of you will someday be mayors, senators, governors - maybe even the president!

For now you have two jobs: Learn about the country and how it works and earn points for me so I can get that great stuff I told you about. It's easy. Just scan or click and you're on your way!

title: Let's Write
text: A sailor on an explorer’s ship might be at sea as long as two or three years. All of his personal belongings as well as his tools had to be kept in a chest. A sailor’s chest was a very sturdy wooden box with a hinged lid. It was usually painted and often had the name of the sailor and a date painted on the front. Not only was the sailor’s chest used for storage, but also as a bench or table. Imagine you are about to go on a voyage to explore a new land. You may be gone for many years. In fewer than 150 words, tell what you might take in your chest and what your duties might be on the long trip.

title: Dutch Send Colonists To New World
text:
Fur Trade and Colonization in a New World

Henry Hudson was an Englishman who was hired by the Dutch to look for the Northwest Passage, and like other explorers before him, he accidentally sailed to what is now the northeast coast of the United States. Upon his return to Europe, he sent a report to the Dutch of a land rich in furs and timber. The Dutch were anxious to acquire furs and soon prepared to send others in for trade. But the Dutch were not the only ones who had their sights set for this new land. France, Spain, England and Sweden did as well.

Five years after Hudson’s first voyage, Adriaen Block made his first voyage to the Americas. Unlike Hudson, Block’s destination was the northeast coast, and his purpose was to trade. Trade is exactly what Block did. His crew traded for furs with the natives along the Hudson River. While anchored offshore what is now New York City, Block’s boat caught fire. Block and his crew survived and swam to the shores of Manhattan Island. Here, friendly tribes helped Block and his crew build huts where they stayed for the season.

Block and his men quickly built a smaller ship. They named it the Onrust. Do you remember from last week’s magazine the meaning of this Dutch word? That’s right, it means “restless.” Why do you suppose that name was chosen? The Onrust wasn’t large enough to sail back to the Netherlands, but it was perfect for exploring. This is how they came to explore what is now Connecticut.

Block sailed along the southern coast of Connecticut, entering the mouth of the Connecticut River. Block continued to what is now northern Connecticut, then turned and headed back. Miraculously, they met a larger ship and returned to the Netherlands. After he returned to the Netherlands, he recorded his discoveries on a map. It is known as the “Adriaen Block Chart.” Based on the explorations of Hudson and Block, parts of what are now New York, Connecticut, New Jersey and Delaware were claimed by the Dutch and called New Netherlands.

The Dutch then sent settlers to the area that is now New York. They paid little heed to Connecticut except to send traders.

In 1633, the Dutch built a trading post near present–day Hartford. Can you guess why they built it there? Why do you suppose it was constructed near the river? The new fort was called the House of Hope. A few traders and soldiers lived at the fort.

The Dutch did not send people to build towns in Connecticut. The officials from the colonies in Massachusetts were anxious to settle Connecticut to prevent the Dutch from taking control over the rich fur trade the Connecticut River provided. Finally, some English settlers from Massachusetts relocated there. Men from the Massachusetts Colony were sent to build a fort just a few miles north of the House of Hope. Here they interfered with the steady trade the Dutch had enjoyed with the local tribes. Because the fort offered some protection, many people from the Massachusetts Colony began to move to Connecticut.

title: Can You Get There From Here?
text:
Could you give your grandmother directions to your local grocery store? Which street would you turn on to get to the park? Where is your doctor's office? Chances are you have been to these places many times, but would you know how to get there all by yourself? If you had a good map, you could find any of these places quickly and easily.

It is important to know where you are and how to get where you need to go. Making a map of your neighborhood can help you see exactly where each place is located and how to get there from anywhere in the area.

You can make a map of your neighborhood to help you find important places. Use a large piece of heavy paper, felt or craft foam. Start by marking your house, along with the street you live on. Be sure to mark the cardinal directions clearly on your map. Carefully label the streets in your neighborhood, along with other important landmarks, like farms, businesses, parks, churches and even an unusual tree or tire swing.

After you have finished your map, ask a parent or family member to help you test it out. Use your map to guide you to someplace in your neighborhood. Was your map helpful? Did you forget to mark anything?

Keep your map and add to it over time. You'll have fun and learn more about your neighborhood each time you do!

title: English Colonists Settle in Connecticut
text:
The Puritans of Massachusetts Have Their Eye on Connecticut

Windsor, Wethersfield and Hartford were called the Three River Towns.

The first permanent settlements in Connecticut were set up by the English. Many of those English settlers came from the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Some of the settlers were just looking for new opportunities. The fertile valleys along with the profitable fur trade attracted others. Still, some came to the Connecticut Valley because of religious intolerance in the Massachusetts Colonies. To understand why the English colonists wanted to settle in Connecticut, it is helpful to understand the conditions in England and in Massachusetts at the time.

In the early 1600s, people in England were not able to worship as they pleased. The king, Henry VIII, left the Catholic Church when it would not grant him the divorce he wanted. In response, the king formed his own church. He was of course the head of it. This church was known as the Church of England. Some people did not support the Church or openly spoke out against it. These people were often punished and lost their jobs and sometimes their lives.

There were still many English citizens who were unhappy with the Church of England. Some wanted to improve the Church but not leave it. They were known as Puritans. Those who actually quit the church were known as Separatists. To escape further persecution, many Puritans and Separatists fled England. They eventually founded two colonies in what is now Massachusetts. The Separatist group we know as the Pilgrims. They were the ones who founded Plymouth. The larger group of Puritans founded the Massachusetts Bay Colony and Boston.

While these two groups came to this country to escape religious intolerance, they in turn persecuted people. They punished those who disagreed with their religious views. Some individuals were expelled from the Massachusetts Bay Colony for their opinions and practices. Others left Massachusetts of their own free will. When the leaders of the Massachusetts Colony established a trading post north the House of Hope, many people took the opportunity to move.

Windsor

Connecticut’s first permanent settlement was Windsor. It was founded in 1633 around the English trading fort near the House of Hope. Windsor was at the confluence of the Farmington and Connecticut Rivers. The local native tribes first called this place Matianuck. Two years later, Reverend John Warham and 60 members of his congregation arrived. They renamed the place Dorchester. In 1637, the name was officially changed to Windsor. Windsor’s original land eventually became 20 other towns. Tobacco farming and later brickmaking became the main industries in Windsor.

Wethersfield

Wethersfield was settled just one year later in 1634. The colony was established by John Oldham. He had emigrated to Plymouth in 1623. In 1624 Oldham was banished. His opposition to the strict government was not acceped. Later, Oldham tried to establish the settlement of Cape Ann. He had no success. He also set up several of the settlements in the Massachusetts Bay colony. Finally, he set up Wethersfield. His murder would later be one of the events leading to the Pequot War.

Wethersfield is one of the oldest communities in America. If you visit, you will find many well-preserved buildings that are hundreds of years old!

Hartford

Hartford was permanently settled in 1635. Among its first colonists were the people led by the Reverend Thomas Hooker. He was from Newtown, Massachusetts. Hooker was very tolerant. He hoped to establish a community where people could have more peace. Hooker led a group of 100 people through the forest toward Connecticut in the spring of 1636. They had plenty of supplies and fresh milk from the cows they brought. Over the years Hartford grew to become an important trading center.

Old Saybrook

Old Saybrook was the fourth settlement. It was founded by a group of rich Englishmen. They called themselves the “Company of Lords and Gentlemen.” Saybrook was named for Lords Saye and Brook. Not many Lords came to live there. It was mainly a fort that housed a few soldiers and functioned as a trading post. In the spring of 1636, Windsor, Wethersfield and Hartford joined. They become the Connecticut Colony. They created a government called the Connecticut General Court.

title: Scarcity
text:
"Why do I never have enough money to buy all the candy I want?"

Have you ever been to a movie theater and wanted to see more than just one movie? Maybe you saw or heard ads on television or the radio that made you want to see two or three movies, but you only had time and money to see one. How did you decide which movie to go see? Was it a hard choice? Did you go to the one your friends wanted to see? Did you ask someone who had already seen the movies for advice?

From time to time, you have to make a choice about which movie to see. A society faces the same kind of challenge deciding how to use their resources. Our resources are scarce. That means there is a higher demand for them than a supply. Sometimes, time can be scarce. That’s when people don’t have enough time to do everything. Sometimes, money is scarce. That’s when you want more candy than you can afford or have the money to buy.

Because our resources are so scarce, people are always making choices about how to use them. Every time you make a choice about what to buy or how to spend your time, you are making a trade-off. Let’s say that you decide to spend money on candy. Then you are making a trade-off of candy for money. You have less money, but more candy.

Economists also have a name for what you give up when you choose something else. An opportunity cost is what you do not get when you make a choice. There are opportunity costs in everything. When you woke up this morning, you may have decided to sleep in. If you did, what did you give up in doing so? Was it taking a shower or eating every bite of your breakfast? You could say that the opportunity cost of sleeping in was taking a shower or eating a nice breakfast. We have opportunity costs when we buy things too. Let’s say that you couldn’t decide between buying a new DVD or a new book. You finally decide to buy the DVD. The opportunity cost of that DVD was the new book. What is the opportunity cost of going to school every day? Is it worth it?

title: Citizen in the Community
text:
What things do good citizens do in your community? It's the same as being a good citizen at home and at school!

Listening carefully is very important! We can listen carefully to the local news and read the paper. One idea is to write a letter with a solution to a community problem or concern.

We can respect the rights of others by keeping the laws of the state and country.

Picking up litter in the community is one great way to show respect for property. What are some others?

A good citizen is also one who performs acts of service for others in the community. It could be as simple as shoveling snow from your neighbor's path. How about planting seeds in a public garden?

Make a goal to do at least one service project in your community this year.

title: What colors are "Sadd?"
text:
When we think of Pilgrims and Puritans, we may think of them dressed in black. Black was mostly only worn by the members of the ruling class. The colors worn by the general people were called "sadd" colors.

In the 1600s, sadd did not mean "unhappy." It was a term used to show seriousness. Some of the sadd colors were, "liver color, tawny, russet and purple." Others were "deer colour, French green and orange."

title: Beaver
text:
Did you know the beaver is the largest rodent in North America? It is 3 to 4 feet in length and weighs 40 to 9 5 pounds. They have a large flat tail about 16 inches long. They use their tail in water as a rudder to steer. On the land, they slap their tail on the ground as a warning of danger.

Beavers are excellent swimmers. They have webbed feet to help them swim better. They have two layers of fur. Beaver fur has a special oil to help them dry faster when they come out of the water.

A baby beaver is called a kit. Beavers usually have four kits. A beaver’s family is called a colony.

Beavers live in lodges or burrows. They build a lodge out of branches and mud. They start at the bottom of a low creek and pile sticks upward. The whole colony works on a lodge.

A beaver has large, sharp teeth. The front teeth are ever growing. By eating their favorite food –tree bark –and gnawing on trees as they build their lodges, their teeth are worn down so they don’t become overgrown.

title: Thomas Hooker (1586-1647)
text:
Thomas Hooker was born in Leicestershire, England in 1586. During his lifetime, the Church of England was formed. Hooker was educated at Cambridge University in England. He went on to become a preacher and was well known.

When the Church of England became the official church, Hooker was troubled. He soon joined the group of Puritans who later fled to the Netherlands for safety and to freely pursue their religion.

After the Netherlands, Thomas Hooker ventured to the new land to join the Puritans. There he settled in Newtown, Massachusetts Colony in 1633, as a pastor. But once again, his liberal beliefs clashed with local authorities. Thomas Hooker had some basic ideas to which he held strong. He believed that each church should be independent, and that the people had a right to choose their magistrates (judges). He also felt that the people should be the ones to determine how much power the local authorities should have. Thomas Hooker’s ideas were well ahead of their time, for these were the same thoughts that the Founding Fathers had when they established the U.S. Constitution.

Hooker moved with his church members to Connecticut where he continued as a preacher.

Hooker’s ideas were written into the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut. Many people consider this plan for government to be the first written constitution.

title: Plenty of Prefixes
text:
A prefix is a group of letters added to the beginning of a word that changes its meaning.

You have learned many different strategies for learning vocabulary words. Learning what prefixes mean is another strategy to add to your bag of vocabulary tricks.

When you know what the parts of a word mean, you can put them all together, and then voila!—you know what the word means. Below is a short list of prefixes and their meanings. Study them and then complete the exercise.

Plenty of Prefixes Exercise

Using the prefixes below, create as many words as possible from these base words: fiction, standard, historic, compose, responsible, legal, applied, write, happy, agree, port, courage.

un (not, opposite)

re (again, back)

in, im, ir, il (not)

dis (not, opposite )

en, em (cause to)

non (not)

in, im (in or into)

trans (across)

mis (wrongly)

sub (under)

pre (before)

de (down, reverse)

title: Let's Write
text: You have just arrived by boat from the Netherlands. You are excited to reach your new home in America. You’ve heard about the American Indians who live here, and the wild and forested land. Write three to five short paragraphs in your journal or diary about your first days in America. Where did you sleep? How and where did you eat? What was it like? How was the boat trip?

title: Slavery Comes to Connecticut
text:
Slavery is owning another human being as property. The first slaves in Connecticut were not the first to enter North America as slaves. At least one black slave accompanied Christopher Columbus on his voyage in 1492. The first Africans imported to the Colonies arrived in Virginia in 1619.

It wasn’t long after the first settlements in Connecticut were founded that the first blacks come to the colony. Records show that there were black “servants” as early as 1660. There is some evidence that blacks lived in Connecticut as early as 1640. Many of the Africans were given their freedom after they reached their 20’s. Some worked as house servants. Others worked on fishing vessels or at the docks. Still others served apprenticeships. An apprentice is someone who works for a skilled worker in order to learn a trade or skill. Colonial apprentices usually worked for a certain period of time. They did this in return for training.

Blacks were not the only ones who were slaves. American Indians and some white criminals were also slaves. Colonists were nervous about enslaving the American Indians. This was because they were often troublesome and many ran away. The Africans had no place to run. They also had no one to rescue them.

Slavery grew rapidly in Connecticut. In 1680, there were only 30 slaves in Connecticut. By 1774, there were more than 6,500 black slaves. There were probably less than 10 free blacks at that time. The growth of black slavery in Connecticut prompted Puritan leaders to justify it. Some Puritan leaders reasoned that it was an opportunity for the slaves become Christians.

By 1660 slavery had spread to all the Colonies. After 1660, Colonies began to enact harsh laws, or codes. These laws defined slavery and the slave trade. One law common to all Colonies was that black slaves now served for life. Children of slave women were also required to serve for life. The codes in the Connecticut Colony also stated that slaves could not sell an item without permission. They could not strike a white person. They could not be out after 9 p.m. without a pass. If they used unseemly language, the punishment was a whipping. Slaves on small farms or in cities probably had more freedom than the plantation slaves in the Southern Colonies.

By the early 1700s, Connecticut harbors were busy indeed. One such harbor was Newport. Colonial shipowners made fortunes in what is known as the Triangular Trade. Large sugar plantations in the West Indies were worked by African slaves. Colonial ships would sail to the islands to pick up molasses made from the sugar.

CONTINUED IN CONNECTICUT LESSON

title: Connecticut Says, “I’m Sorry!”
text:
Imagine what it would have felt like to be a slave. You would not have had any control over your life, family or future. People practiced slavery in Connecticut for hundreds of years. In fact, by the mid 1700s, nearly 3% of the people living in our state were slaves. Recently, Connecticut's General Assembly formally apologized for having participated in slavery in the past.

The Senate voted 36 to 0 in favor of issuing this apology. Several senators said that they voted to apologize so that all Connecticut citizens would know that our state has not forgotten this sad history. Many are ashamed of the way our ancestors once treated our African American friends.

Connecticut became the second northern state to apologize for its part in slavery. New Jersey was the first. Five southern states - Alabama, Florida, Maryland, North Carolina and Virginia - have also issued official apologies. Not long before Connecticut's apology, the U.S. Congress also apologized to all African Americans for slavery. Congress also apologized for the racial discrimination they have suffered in America over the years.

Our state's lawmakers also made a promise to Connecticut citizens to do their best to get rid of all racial discrimination, or inequality, in our state. Many people feel that the apology was long overdue. But they also feel that it truly does make a difference to those who were wronged by slavery.

title: Slavery Comes to Connecticut
text:
(CONTINUED FROM COVER STORY)

Slaves were no longer treated as human beings, but as chattel, bought and sold with little emotion on the part of the owners.

The ship would then return to Connecticut with the molasses. Here it was used to make rum. The ship would then sail to the west coast of Africa and use rum to trade for more slaves. The slaves were then taken to the West Indies. They were traded for more molasses. At each leg of the trip, a big profit was made. This only encouraged the cycle.

Not all slaves went to the West Indies. Many were moved to the Colonies. There they were auctioned at slave markets. Markets were often held in cities with large ports. Such cities were Boston, Salem or New York.

A slave market involved selling slaves. Notices were posted before slave ships landed. The notices announced the upcoming slave auction. Here African men and women were lined up, so the buyers could inspect their teeth and gums. They would feel their muscles and look for skin diseases. The slaves had no control over what would happen. They might be sold to a master who was kind. They might be sold to someone who was a cruel master who would work them hard, sometimes to death. By then, slaves were no longer treated as servants or laborers. They were treated as chattel. Chattel is property that can be bought or sold with little emotion. It was not important to those purchasing slaves to keep families together. Husbands and wives were separated. Mothers often never saw their children again.

Though Connecticut had a huge population of African slaves, in 1785, it passed the Gradual Emancipation Acts. These acts provided that a slave be freed by the age of 21. Not until 1848 would emancipation (freedom) be declared.

title: People Abducted and Sold
text:
Slave labor in Connecticut grew rapidly as the Colony turned to the Triangular Trade. Slavery in Connecticut was different from the plantation slavery in the South. Yet, it was still slavery. How did the European slave traders obtain the slaves to bring to the Colonies? There were two ways:

One way was to wait near a river and kidnap small groups. They were then taken to a slave ship. More commonly though, one village or country would wage war on another. They would steal members of that neighboring village or country. These people were then enslaved by their enemies. They were to be used as property to trade with the Europeans for goods.

The more ships that arrived with goods to trade, the more the African society was disrupted. This slave trade demeaned human life as never before, both in Africa and America.

America was not the only country to use slaves for labor. Some historians say the slave trade was as big then as the oil industry is today! Indeed, it was a global trade. The Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch, English and French were all involved. It is believed that during the 350 years of this slave trade, 10 million Africans were taken into slavery.

A Cruel Atlantic Journey

The passage for enslaved Africans to the Colonies was cruel and hard. Slave traders tried to get as many slaves as possible on a ship. Slaves were often chained together at the ankles and feet. Sometimes they had as little as three feet of space to move. They were forced to sleep on bare floors with no covering. There were no bathroom facilities, so there was much filth and disease. The air was suffocating. Some sailors at sea said they could smell a slave ship long before they could see one. About one in every 10 slaves died during the passage. A slave may have awakened to find himself chained to a corpse. Sometimes when food ran low on a voyage, traders were known to throw many slaves overboard. Many also died of disease before making it to America. It took two months to cross the Atlantic Ocean.

title: Bartering
text:
"I'll give you three tennis balls for that frisbee!"

Bartering is trading goods, but without the use of money. In early cultures, people were able to get many things they needed and wanted through bartering. Merchants would often travel with ships laden with goods. These goods were bartered for items that could be taken back. Then they would be either bartered for other goods or traded for money. People, towns and even countries bartered for items they did not produce or grow.

Bartering was easy as long as there was a simple trade between two people. However, sometimes bartering had to span several persons to get the goods wanted. Then it wasn't so easy. Suppose one merchant had a barrel of allspice. He wanted to trade with another merchant for some cloth. However, the merchant who had the cloth did not want or need a barrel of allspice. What do you think a good solution might have been? The people would barter for something they didn't need. They hoped they could later trade it for something they did need!

Bartering is still going on today. People, companies and even countries barter for things they need or want. Countries that raise great amounts of beef may barter with countries that grow large amounts of grain. Companies may trade services to support one another. Even children barter! When was the last time you tried talking someone out of a big chocolate chip cookie in exchange for your apple?

In Jamestown, Captain John Smith wrote about trading blue beads with the native tribes for food. The American Indians valued the glass beads, and the colonists needed food. Copper ornaments and beads were also highly prized by the chiefs of local tribes. At first, the Powhatan traded with other tribes to obtain copper. Over time, the Europeans gave copper beads and ornaments for barter. The Powhatan turned to the colonists for the copper items.

title: On Being Informed
text:
As good citizens, we should be informed about what is happening around us. We should read about current events. We must also understand our history. If we do not understand what has happened in the past, then we are doomed to repeat our mistakes in the future. You have been studying about American Indians. It is important to understand their history and culture. It is also important to understand what happens when two cultures come together. Combining cultures was both productive and tragic for the American Indians.

Change can happen only when we learn what went wrong and then commit to a better future. As you read this paper each week, you will learn the history of our state. You will learn about triumphs and tragedies. We hope you will take the lessons of history seriously. Good citizens must be informed about the present and the past. Being informed will help us to remain a self-governing and free people.
