text: Study this map, and you will see how much slavery was practiced throughout the world. As you can see, most of the slaves went to South America and the West Indies.

title: Who was Henry "Box" Brown?
text: Henry "Box" Brown was a very determined and clever slave. In 1849, he ordered a 3 foot x 2 foot x 8 foot box in Virginia. He put a jug of water inside and some biscuits. He also put in a bar to open the box. He then climbed in. A friend addressed the box to an abolitionist, someone who believed in freeing slaves. He lived in Philadelphia. After writing, "Handle with Care" and "This Side Up", the friend shipped him off. Twenty seven hours later, he arrived in Philadelphia, a free man!

title: Sassafras
text:
Sassafras, see if you can remember how to spell that one! It is an important plant to both wildlife and people on the northeast coast.

For example, deer feed on the aromatic (good-smelling) twigs in the winter. They also eat the new leaf buds in the spring. Bees love the flowers. Birds enjoy the glossy berries.

The explorer Gosnold searched the New World for the bark of the root in the early 17th century. Today, the bark of the root is still used to make teas. The leaves are ground to thicken food (the filé in Cajun cooking.) The aromatic wood is used to make furniture. Early Americans thought it healthy to have beds made of the fragrant wood.

In the north, sassafras is often more of a shrub than a tree. The leaves are threelobed or sometimes mitten shaped. The twigs are a bright green. The berries are shiny blue. The berries are especially fragrant when crushed. The leaves turn a brilliant red, orange and yellow in the fall.

title: A Suffix Celebration
text:
A suffix is a group of letters added to the end of a word that changes its meaning.

You are nearly done with Word Attack strategies. What better way to “end” it than to celebrate with suffixes? Below, you will find a short list of common suffixes and their meanings. When you think you have them down, head to the activity below and strut your stuff!

ly (forms adverb)

er, or (one who, person)

ion, tion, ation, ition (state or quality of)

ible, able (is able)

ness (state or quality of)

ity, y (state or quality of)

ment (forms a noun from a verb)

ic (relating to, forms an adjective)

ful (full of)

less (without)

est (most)

ive, ative, itive (inclined to, forms an adjective)

A Suffix Celebration Exercise

Using the suffixes above, create as many words as possible from these base words: history, father, enjoy, desperate, smart, teach, window, talk, wonder, loyal, happy, comfort.

title: Let's Write
text: Poetry is a good way to express emotion such as sadness, love and joy. Writing poetry about the slave trade would be a good way to express your feelings about this dark time in history. Write a poem expressing the way you feel about slavery or about how you imagine it was for those men, women and children who were enslaved.

title: Connecticut Colony is Growing
text:
"The foundation of authority is laid, firstly, in the free consent of the people." - Thomas Hooker, 1638

After Thomas Hooker gave his famous sermon telling the people how they should establish their government, the Connecticut General Court went right to work. They made a set of laws based on Thomas Hooker's ideas. These laws were known as the Fundamental Orders. No one knows for sure who wrote the Orders, but it is likely that it was Roger Ludlow, who was the only lawyer in Connecticut at that time. The Fundamental Orders were unique in the Colonies.They allowed a great deal of freedom to the people. They were so popular, they lasted until 1662.

Meanwhile, southwest of the Connecticut Colony, the New Haven Colony was established by Theophilus Eaton and a Puritan minister, John Davenport. This Colony had laws and officials that were much stricter than Hooker's Connecticut Colony. Only members of the Puritan church could vote. The laws regulated the religious and moral lives of the colonists.

Both the Connecticut and New Haven Colonies attracted European settlers. Townships continued to spring up, and both Colonies grew. Most of the new settlers came from England and the Massachusetts Colony. As more people arrived the population of Connecticut grew from 1,500 to about 8,000. By 1650, the Connecticut Colony included nine townships, including Old Saybrook, which was sold to the Connecticut Colony in 1644. The New Haven Colony had gown to include seven townships.

As Connecticut continued to expand, the colonists continued to push onto the American Indian land. Since the Pequot were no longer a threat, it was much easier for the colonists to take land. The other local tribes were often taken advantage of in land deals throughout the Colonies. They were eventually pushed out of their ancestral homes. When the local tribes agreed to sell land, they thought it was an agreement to share the land. Owning land was a European practice, foreign to the American Indians. A number of Connecticut towns were built on land purchased from the local tribes for very small fees. For example, the colonists paid 24 coats, 12 spoons, 12 hatchets, 12 hoes, 24 knives, 12 bowls and four cases of scissors for this land. This deal was made during the winter months of November and December. Why do you think the native people agreed to this deal?

It was commonly believed that there was plenty of land for everyone. Unfortunately, the American Indians would eventually lose their homes.

A Charter from the King

When the Puritans of England were no longer in control of the government in England, the Puritans in the Colonies feared they could lose some of their lands. Connecticut Colony decided to obtain a charter from King Charles II. The colony sent John Winthrop Jr. to petition the king for the charter. Luckily, Winthrop was popular with the king and soon left England with the valuable papers that granted the Connecticut Colony all that it asked for. This included rights, privileges and new borders. As a result, New Haven colony was now swallowed up by the Connecticut Colony.

The new charter still had many of the features of the popular Fundamental Orders, and the local government was conducted as before. There was little interference from the English Crown. The Connecticut Colony was never self-sufficient. It engaged in trade with other colonies, local tribes and England. The colony continued to grow and prosper as people were drawn to the beautiful valleys and forests.

title: John Winthrop Jr., a Connecticut Pioneer
text:
John Winthrop, the founder of Massachusetts Colony, was the father of John Winthrop Jr. John Jr. was born in Groton, England in 1606. When John Jr. was 9 years old, his mother died. He was raised by his father and a loving stepmother.

John went to several schools in England, eventually winding up at Trinity college in Dublin, Ireland. He later studied law in England. He found he did not enjoy it, so he joined the English Navy. After his time in the navy, he traveled for one year throughout Europe. When he returned from Europe in 1629, John learned that his father was planning to lead a large following of Puritans from England to the New World. John Jr. stayed behind in England to take care of family business and the younger children. He married and eventually made his way to the Massachusetts Colony with his wife, Martha.

John was a gifted man and was often appointed to oversee various tasks. The first task was to found the town of Ipswich in Massachusetts. During a visit back to England in 1635, John was appointed to begin another new settlement - this time, in Connecticut. John set to work getting the town of Old Saybrook under way. While Saybrook was being colonized, John Jr. and his family lived mostly in Massachusetts and New York colonies.

In 1646, John Jr. was busy again getting people settled into a new township. This time, it would become the town of New London, Connecticut. The Winthrop family lived there from 1649 to 1655.

John Winthrop Jr. served the people of Connecticut his entire life. Unlike his father, whose views were often harsh, John Jr. was kind and tolerant of other ideas and religious views. He was well-loved by the people in the Connecticut Colony.

Three times, John Jr. tried to step down from office, but three times, the people begged him to stay. Winthrop was still governor of Connecticut when he died in 1676, at the age of 70.

title: King Philip's War
text:
Like his father before him, Metacomet was the grand Sachem of the Wampanoag. Massasoit was well-known for his kindness to the Pilgrims, who would surely have perished without his friendship.

After Massasoit's death, his son Metacomet followed a different path. He was known as King Philip among the colonists. He felt the time had come to defend his people after many years of conflict with the colonists. Metacomet spoke with other Algonquian leaders trying to form a strong alliance against the English. An alliance is several groups working together for one cause.

Unfortunately for Metacomet, many of the tribes were not willing to work together. The numbers of the native warriors stayed low. Metacomet was forced to continue his plans for war without the help of other tribes.

In June of 1675, colonists in Swansea, Massachusetts hanged three Wampanoags accused of killing a native spy. A Wampanoag warrior took revenge by killing cattle. In the process a colonist opened fire on the warrior. As a result, warriors poured into the area, killing settlers and burning the town.

At this point, the Nipmucs and Narragansett joined the Wampanoag. Other tribes, from as far away as what is today Maine, traveled to help. Fiftytwo of the 90 Colonial settlements were attacked. Twelve were totally destroyed.While most of the battles took place in Massachusetts and Rhode Island, the Connecticut Colony sent several hundred soldiers. Over 100 of their Mohegan allies joined in the defense of the Colonies.

In December 1675, a 1,000-man New England army, with many Connecticut troops, attacked a large native village in what is now Rhode Island. About 3,000 Narragansett people, adults and children, were burned to death. Those who tried to escape were shot. More Narragansett warriors were killed and wounded in what is known as the "Great Swamp Fight."

In 1676, Connecticut again sent 100 men, this time to finish off the war against the native tribes. They captured the Narragansett Chief Canonchet and offered his life in return for peace with his people. Canonchet refused, saying "Killing me will not end the war. Others were as forward for the war as myself, and I desire to hear no more about it. Have not the English burned my people in their houses?" He was executed in southeastern Connecticut.

The war continued for many long months. The last battles took place in Massachusetts. In August of 1676, Metacomet himself was killed when he was betrayed by one of his own warriors. Metacomet's wife and son, along with hundreds of other Algonquians, were sold as slaves. The defeat of the Algonquians in King Philip's War would be the last time any Algonquian tribe would be in a position of power or strength.

title: Who Gets Connecticut?
text:
When King Charles II granted the Charter to Connecticut Colony, he granted such a large tract of land that it was almost unbelievable.

The northern and southern borders of Connecticut Colony were to be the same as the state today. The eastern border included Rhode Island, but it was the western border that was a real surprise. King Charles extended the western border all the way to the Pacific Ocean. Whew! That's a mighty big piece of land. Take a look at the map and imagine what Connecticut would be like today had it remained that way. Instead of the third smallest state, it would be the third largest. It would include sections of what are now the states of New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Iowa, Nebraska, Wyoming, Utah, Nevada and California.

Of course, that didn't happen. Actually, the Connecticut Colony only tried to claim small portions beyond its borders of today. It did keep, however, the New Haven Colony, and many of the people of New Haven Colony were angry. Connecticut Colony officials tried to calm them. They agreed to leave New Haven churches alone and promised that New Haven would have a fair representation in the General Court. Many New Haven colonists, however, were ready to move, and some even threatened to fight. Events soon came about that changed their minds. In 1664 King Charles II gave a large piece of land to his brother James, the Duke of York. The problem was that this rather large chunk of land was already considered to be New Netherland, which included what is now New York and parts of Delaware and New Jersey. James then sent a fleet of ships to take over the land under Dutch rule. With little resistance, the area of New Netherland then passed to English rule.

Unfortunately for the people of Connecticut Colony, Charles II had given Connecticut to his brother James as well. Now, there were two different owners: the people of Connecticut Colony and the Duke of York.

Needless to say, the people of the newly formed Connecticut Colony were alarmed. Suddenly, the merging of Connecticut Colony and New Haven Colony didn't seem like such a bad idea. Their problems were much bigger now that they faced the possibility of once again being ruled by the English. In the year 1664, James, Duke of York, released his claim on Connecticut in exchange for Long Island.

Ten years after agreeing to release his claim on Connecticut, the Duke of York changed his mind and decided he wanted Connecticut back. In 1675, the duke sent Governor Andros to Connecticut to claim all of the land west of the Connecticut River for the duke. Andros attempted to take Old Saybrook by force, but the Connecticut leaders were prepared for him. Captain Bull at the Saybrook Fort firmly refused to surrender the fort to Andros, and Andros returned to New York.

In 1685, King Charles II died. His brother, James, then became King James II of England. One of the first things James II did was to try and disband the self-governing bodies of Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Plymouth and Rhode Island. He united these seven colonies and named them the Dominion of England. In an effort to control them, he sent Andros to seize the precious Connecticut Charter in 1687.

What exactly happened that night during the evening may never be known, but it is said that while the Connecticut leaders met with the representatives of King James II, the candles that lit the room that night were suddenly overturned. In the confusion of the darkness, Captain Joseph Wadsworth, who was standing outside the tavern, found himself with the Charter. He quickly hid it safely inside a majestic white oak on the Wyllys estate in Hartford. Wadsworth's quick thinking not only saved the Charter, but also preserved the rights of the colonists in Connecticut.

That is how the stately oak earned the name of the Charter Oak. It stood for another 150 years after. It was toppled in a storm on Aug. 21, 1856.

Today, the Charter Oak is an emblem of liberty proudly displayed on the State Quarter for Connecticut.

title: Money
text:
When the English colonists first came to America, they brought some of the money they used back in England. They called their money shillings, pence and pounds. They soon found out it was of no use to them in the New World. The American Indians didn't care for their money. It didn't mean anything to them. The American Indians bartered with the colonists. As you can imagine, that became very hard. Therefore, the early colonists of Massachusetts started using wampum. Wampum consisted of purple and white shells. The purple ones were worth twice as much as the white ones. They used it the same way as money. American Indians had traded wampum since the 1640s. The colonists and American Indians used wampum in addition to bartering. This made for less trouble in the colonies.

Economists like to say, "Money is what money does." This was as true for the American Indians and English colonists as it is for us today. Money has three main functions. First, it must be a way of exchange that people accept. This means people have to agree on what they will use for money. Second, money must be a measure of value. This means the people using the money must know how much the money is worth in their community. Last, money must be a store of value.

People should be able to save their money and use it later. Storing value is very hard when bartering. Often the goods or products people are trying to trade go bad before they can find someone in the market for them. For example, milk is hard to keep in hot weather. Bartering milk without a way to keep it cold for a long time would be very tricky.

Money must also be easy to carry. It must be sturdy, easy to recognize and able to be broken down into smaller parts. Our U.S. money is small. It's easy to carry and uniform, or all the same. People in the country accept it all over. You can divide it easily. This is nice for everyone because it is so easy. What if you lived in a country that used bowling balls for money? That wouldn't work very well at all!

title: Elections
text:
Elections

Our nation's form of government is called a democracy. This means we choose our leaders through voting. Voting is always held on the first Tuesday in November. We vote for different national or state officials. The time these officials remain in office is called a term. Terms may be for two, four or six years.

Who Can Vote?

Citizens of the United States of America can vote for the leaders of their country. They must be at least 18 years old. If you are voting for a state, city or county official, you must be a resident of that state, city or county.

Where Do We Go to Vote?

Voting booths are usually found at schools or other government buildings. People vote in the booth using a ballot, or piece of paper. Recently, some states have been using electronic voting systems. You may vote only once for each office, and you do not put your name on the ballot. This is called a secret ballot. The candidate receiving the majority of the votes is elected for that term.

title: Henry Whitfield House
text: A famous Connecticut landmark is this old stone house in Guilford. It was built for the Reverend Whitfield in 1639-1640. It is the oldest stone house still standing in all of New England. See if you can do some "mental math" to tell how old this house is today.

title: What is a charter?
text:
A charter is a written document issued by a ruler or a government to a person or group of people. The charter outlines agreements and grants certain rights.

In the days of European exploration, charters were issued by many kings in different countries, often for the same piece of land. When this happened, both countries believed they owned that land. Disputes were often settled in war or by sheer numbers.

Charters for new land were often given by kings or queens to individuals who were well-liked. If that individual was to fall out of favor, it was not uncommon for the ruler to issue a charter for the same land to some other individual.

Are there charters issued by rulers or governments today? Can you name one?

title: Mink
text:
Do you think of fur coats when you hear "mink"? Though some mink are still being trapped, ranch-raised mink supply most of the pelts today. Mink are members of the weasel family. They are fierce fighters and will scream, spit and hiss. Like other members of the weasel family (including skunks), they give off a strong odor when threatened.

Mink never live far from water, and they are excellent swimmers. They eat fish, rodents and snakes.

The mink will grow to be 11 to 20 inches long with a tail that is about 8 inches long. They are dark reddish-brown with a pale spot under their chins and white spots on their bellies.

Their young are born in the spring and are called kits.
