title: What are Homophones and Homographs?
text:
Homophones and homographs are the same but different! To find out the meaning of a word, carefully read the words and sentences surrounding it.

Homophones

Homophones are words that sound the same but have different spellings and different meanings. You can remember what a homophone is by remembering that a phone makes a sound, so a homophone sounds the same as another word.

It is important to know a homophone when you write it. If you need help with a homophone when you read or write, look it up in a dictionary. This will help you keep from making mistakes. For instance, would you write you have “bear hands” or “bare hands”?

Here are some common homophones:
Beat, beet
Earn, urn
Eye, I
Heal, heel, he’ll
Made, maid
Plain, plane
Rain, reign, rein
To, too, two

Homographs

These are words that are spelled the same but have different meanings. Sometimes they are pronounced differently even though they are spelled the same. You can remember what a homograph is by remembering that a graph is something you look at, so a homograph looks the same.

Here are some common homographs that are pronounced differently and have different meanings:

Bass: a low voice
Bass: a fish
Content: things found inside Content: satisfied
Minute: 60 seconds Minute: tiny

Try It!

The next time you are not sure which homophone or homograph to use, be sure you know the meaning of the word you are trying to use. This will help you spell it correctly. A dictionary will help you a lot!

title: Let's Write
text: You have been studying citizenship for many weeks now and hopefully you have practiced some good citizenship at home, in your classroom and also at school. Write about the things good citizens do. In fewer than 150 words tell about something you have done, or your class has done, to be better citizens.

title: Colonies Go to War!
text:
Nope, it wasn't the French fighting the Indians but actually the French fighting the English. War between France and England had been brewing off and on for some time in Europe. By 1754, the campaign spread to the Colonies. Because both France and England had begun colonizing North America at the same time, both countries considered future land claims in North America to be rightfully theirs. In 1689, France and England began fighting what would become a series of four wars. Some historians call this group of wars the Colonial Wars. They included King William's War (1689-1697); Queen Anne's War (1702-1713); King George's War (1744-1748) and the French and Indian War (1754-1763). To the colonists, this probably felt like one long war with several interruptions. Because the Algonquian tribes were friendly with the French and aided the French in the battles, the Colonial Wars are also called the French and Indian Wars.

The first of the wars, King William's War, began with an attack by French and Indian forces on Schenectady, New York. Quebec, a French colony, was then attacked by English forces. In the end, the French had some British lands, and the British had some French lands. The colonists wondered why they had fought at all when they heard that the Treaty of Ryswick had been signed. The treaty returned all land holdings to the ways they were before the war.

Queen Anne's War was a bit different from previous wars. This time the British did not leave the colonists to fight alone. The British sent troops, and the Colonial troops were asked to support them. Many of the Colonial troops resented this.

King George's War was fierce, but still did not settle the hostilities between France and England.

The ongoing war between France and England was not settled until the French and Indian War broke out in North America. This war concluded when the British finally succeeded in taking Quebec and Montreal. The Treaty of Paris was signed in 1763, giving control of the Canadian holdings to the English.

title: The French and Indian Wars...Again?
text:
There are many ways we can study history. We read about history in textbooks. We study newspapers and journals from the past. Historians look at drawings and photos too. Don't forget Connecticut Studies Weekly! There is another way. Did you know that some people study history by reenactment?

Reenactment means to act out an event from the past. We can learn about history with facts and actors. When real people act out history, it is a way to understand more information.

There are many living history groups in the United States. Some are in historic villages. Others reenact battles. They choose battles fought in the United States. Who learns about history from reenactment? The actors themselves learn more about history. The people who are watching do also. It becomes a living textbook for the viewers.

The soldiers in these modern regiments try hard to re-live the scenes of battles as closely as possible. Of course, they do not really shoot at each other. They do use real muzzle loaders and wear replicas of uniforms. They eat the same kinds of food or go without. They may even be singing the same songs on lonely nights by a warm campfire.

title: French & Indian War
text:
No Battles in Connecticut

The French and Indian Wars were fought over a period of 74 years. Though no battles were actually fought in Connecticut, Connecticut sent hundreds of soldiers to fight elsewhere.

During King William's War, that is just what happened. Connecticut sent a militia to neighboring New York, but they were surprised to find that New York's governor,

Benjamin Fletcher, wanted to command the Connecticut Militia. Of course, the Connecticut Militia had something to say to this: "No!" Governor Fletcher argued that since New York, and not Connecticut, was under attack, New York must provide the commander for the militia. The Connecticut folks held fast to their charter, and refused to have Governor Fletcher command their militia.

Furious, Governor Fletcher marched straight to Hartford to take command of the militia.Upon arriving, he ordered his aide to read the orders that placed Fletcher in charge. Each time the aide began to read the orders, however, the Connecticut soldiers began to beat their drums.

Fitz-John Winthrop was sent to England to petition the king to allow Connecticut to remain in charge of its own militia. The king agreed.

Connecticut finally agreed to provide 120 men to help fight King William's War under the command of the New York governor, but not the entire state militia.

Rogers' Rangers

Until the Europeans engaged in battles with the American Indians, they had always fought their battles in large rows in the open. But the native people of North America fought a different way. They hid behind rocks and trees to shoot at the enemy rather than stand in the open. As the Europeans began to fight like the natives, warfare began to change. Rangers were colonists who chose to fight like the native people. One of the most famous of these groups was known as Rogers' Rangers. These men not only shot at the enemy while hiding, but they engaged in warfare at night and wintertime when battles were not usually fought. They were known to wear ice skates on ponds and battle in snowshoes. The Rangers wore green outfits and developed tactics called "Rogers' Ranging Rules." These tactics are still in use by Army Rangers and Green Berets.

Standing Orders for Rogers' Rangers

Don't forget nothing.

Have your musket clean as a whistle, hatchet scoured, 60 rounds powder and ball and be ready to march at a minute's warning.

When you're on the march, act the way you would if you was sneaking up on a deer. See the enemy first.

Tell the truth about what you see and what you do. There is an army depending on us for correct information. You can lie all you please when you tell other folks about the Rangers, but don't ever lie to a Ranger or officer.

Don't ever take a chance you don't have to.

When we're on the march we march single file, far enough apart so one shot can't go through two men.

If we strike swamps, or soft ground, we spread out abreast, so it's hard to track us.

When we march, we keep moving till dark, so as to give the enemy the least possible chance at us.

When we camp, half the party stays awake while the other half sleeps.

title: Elected and Appointed Leaders
text:
Some of our government leaders are elected and some are appointed. Do you know what the difference is between the two?

Elected leaders are chosen by the people. Citizens vote and elect a candidate, or person trying to get in office. These elections are often done by secret ballot. The president of the United States and our state governor are elected. The mayor of your city is also elected.

A person is appointed if people in charge choose him or her. They are selected, not elected. They usually work closely with elected leaders. Appointed officials often serve two to four terms.

We have examples of appointed officials all around us. The members of the U.S. president's cabinet and Supreme Court justices are appointed leaders. There are also many appointed state and local leaders. There might even be examples in your classroom. If you have class leaders, did members of the class elect them, or did your teacher appoint them?

title: Albany Congress
text:
There was unrest between the French and English during the War. England wanted a union between the Colonies and the English crown. Some Colonial leaders were thinking the same thing. They met in June 1754 at Albany. Some members of the northern Colonies and Six Iroquois Nations met. They discussed the ideas of Benjamin Franklin. He suggested each Colony elect delegates for an American Continental Assembly. This would be presided over by a Royal Governor.

The plan was important. It was the first attempt to unify the Colonies. The British rejected the plan. They feared it would give colonists too much power. Later the Colonial Assemblies also rejected the plan. They were not ready to give up individual independence to become one country. This did not happen until after the American Revolution. Many of Franklin's ideas for the Albany Congress would later be adopted in the Constitution.

title: Entrepreneurship
text:
Benjamin Franklin was one of the greatest entrepreneurs in history. An entrepreneur takes risks to create something or find a better way to do something. Ben Franklin was imaginative, creative and very smart. He was able to try many things. He was respected for the things he did. When he died in 1790, Franklin was known around the world as a businessman, politician, printer and inventor.

Franklin was born in 1706. Even as a little boy, he loved to read, write and collect books. He left school at the age of 10. By the time he was 12, he was helping as a printer for his older brother, James. When Franklin was 22, he owned his own printing press and started his own newspaper, the Pennsylvania Gazette. He also printed Poor Richard's Almanack. That book became one of the most popular books in the Colonies!

Franklin soon became one of the Colonies' busiest printers. He was named the official printer for Delaware, New Jersey and Maryland. He printed money and legal documents. Franklin made so much money that he retired when he was 42. He then became a full-time inventor. Franklin invented many things, including the lightning rod!

Franklin was very important in the Colonies. He started one of the first libraries in the United States with some of his friends. He signed the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. Franklin served as an ambassador from the Colonies to France. He was the oldest member of the Constitutional Convention!

Ben Franklin did many things to be considered an entrepreneur. Like Franklin, there are many entrepreneurs today. Do the names Bill Gates, George Lucas, Henry Ford and Oprah Winfrey mean anything to you? All of these people are entrepreneurs. They brought great ideas and business to our economy. Can you think of any entrepreneurs where you live?

title: What do you call a group of ____?
text:
As you see a group of Canada Geese flying above, you might say "Look mom, a ________ of geese." What exactly do you call the group of honkers flying together up there? Why, a gaggle of geese, of course!

Animal groups have some unusual names, just like a gaggle (not a flock) of geese. For example: a twittering of magpies, a herd of cattle, an exaltation of larks, a pride of lions, a chatter of parakeets, a troop of monkeys and a swarm of bees.

There are hundreds of others, can you think of more?

title: The Beluga Whale
text:
Where can you see a beluga whale in Connecticut? Why, at the Mystic Aquarium in Mystic! There, among many other beautiful and exciting marine creatures, you can stand near a beluga and listen to the clicks and whistles which it uses to communicate. You can even touch it if you are lucky enough to get close.

Though belugas are found in the greatest numbers in the cold Arctic waters, about 400 are known to inhabit the upper St. Lawrence River. They also like the Hudson Bay and Hudson Strait. Beluga whales are known by two other names: white whales and canaries of the sea. A male beluga is called a bull, a female is a cow, and a baby is called a calf. A group of belugas is called a pod.

Belugas are born either a dark brownish or black and they have hair on their skin. When they are about five years old they turn a milky white. As adults they have no hair.

Belugas eat clams, squid, octopus, shrimp, crab, snails and worms! They are 11-15 feet long and weigh about 3,000 pounds as an adult.

Belugas are hunted by man, polar bears and killer whales. When they sense danger they warn others by making clicks and other sounds. It is because the unique noises they make that they are called the canaries of the sea.

title: Results of the French and Indian War
text:
Study the two maps on this page. You will see the results of the French and Indian War. Before the war, the French occupied a huge area in the center of America. After the war, the French were completely gone. The events that contributed to this huge change in America started because two countries had overlapping land claims in North America.

The French based their claims on the great explorer La Salle. He claimed the Mississippi River and all rivers that empty into it for France. The English based their claims on the original land grant of Virginia. The problem was some of that land overlapped the French claims.

The French believed they could strengthen their claims by building a string of forts. They buried lead plaques with the French claim written on them throughout the Ohio Valley. The English sent a messenger with a letter to explain to them their claim was wrong and they should leave. The messenger was 21-year-old George Washington. Instead of leaving, the French moved southward and captured an English fort. This started the French and Indian War.

It was called the French and Indian War because the Algonquian tribes at the time liked the French and joined their side.

The war was long and favored the French in the early years. However, the English finally won because of their great numbers and military strength.

The war took place in many of the Colonies. Most of the action and several important battles centered in New York, New Hampshire, Massachusetts and Pennsylvania.

title: What are Idioms?
text:
Have you ever heard an adult say, “I’m sorry, but we’re up a creek on this one”? What did he mean? He was standing on dry ground when he said it! Well, you’ve just heard an idiom.

Idioms are Not Meant to Be Taken Literally

Idioms are sayings that mean something different from the literal meaning of their words. “Literal” means “following the exact wording.” But idioms are not literal, so the words do not mean exactly what they say. Listen carefully for clues to figure out an idiom.

Try It!

The best way to learn what an idiom means is to learn it and use it in your own speech or writing. Ask someone what it means. Then use it in your own writing. Here are some idioms in sentences. See if you can figure out what they mean. Once you know what the idiom means, use it in your own sentence. Use another piece of paper if you need it.

1. They were both so shy they had a hard time breaking the ice
Use “breaking the ice” in your own sentence.

2. When it comes to modesty in dress, I have to draw the line somewhere.
Use “draw the line” in your own sentence.

3. By halftime, the game was in the bag.
Use “in the bag” in your own sentence.

4. Chris and I are in the same boat because neither of us have extra cash to spend on the field trip.
Use “in the same boat” in your own sentence.

5. Would someone lend me a hand with the dishes?
Use “lend me a hand” in your own sentence.

title: Let's Write
text: Connecticut is a beautiful state. Each region of the state is wonderful and unique. In 200 words or less, tell about your region, county or city. Write your description in an exciting and colorful way so that others will think your area is the greatest part of Connecticut!

title: Colonial Life in Connecticut
text:
By 1750, the Connecticut Colony had the fifth highest population in the colonies, with about 110,000 people. At that time, there were no large cities in Connecticut, but the population was spread throughout the Colony. Hartford and New Haven each only had about 3,000 residents at that time, and Middletown was the largest settlement with a population of about 5,600.

The typical town in Connecticut was built up around the church, the school and other public buildings and stores. In the center was the village common, or village green. Does your town have a common or a green (park) today? Families strolled in the common and enjoyed the outdoors, just as you might today. Today however, cows are probably not found grazing there as well!

Most of the townspeople were farmers, and their fields and houses were scattered on the outskirts of the town. When people from the farms needed to go to town, they often walked. Some families owned wagons or carriages which they used for special occasions such as church or gatherings.

Connecticut families raised much of their own food. What do you think they raised in their gardens? Beans, peas, pumpkins and squash were favorite vegetables. Grains such as corn, rye, barley and wheat were grown as well. Cornmeal mush was used to make a dish called hasty pudding, which was eaten so often children were commonly heard to complain about it.

There were no refrigerators in the 1700s, so when a family butchered a pig or cow or hunted large game, they shared it with their neighbors. The colonists also traded food, such as eggs for milk or some other kind of treat. Apples and pears were important crops in Colonial Connecticut. Cider was the most popular drink around, and it was served with each meal and generally used to drink in place of water. Drawing the day's cider from the big barrel was often the job of the last child to wake for the day. Though apple and pear cider were alcoholic, they were common drinks for adults and children alike, as water was not thought to be pure.

Who did all the work around the farms? The men generally built houses and out-buildings, cleared fields and did the heavier farm chores. The women did the cooking, cleaning, clothes making and other household work. Women and children together did farm chores such as feeding livestock and planting and harvesting crops.

Much was expected of Colonial children. Besides going to school, they were expected to help out with chores. Boys could be found in the fields with their fathers, and girls began at an early age to help around the house and supervise younger children.

What kind of clothes do you think Colonial children wore? Everyday clothes were often sewn from cloth made by their mothers. Flax was a plant grown on many Connecticut farms. The flax was spun into a linen yarn by mothers and girls. It was then woven into a cloth on a large handloom. Finally, it was cut and sewn, by hand, into clothes for the family. You can imagine how exciting it must have been to have a new dress or shirt after all that work! It was common to only have two sets of clothes, one for work and a nicer set for church. Wool was also spun and woven into cloth. Later, cotton yarn was introduced for weaving.

A Colonial home was usually made from wood, with a fireplace being the center of the home. It kept the house warm, and was the place where families would gather after meals. Matches had not yet been invented, so it was very important to keep some embers burning even if there was no need for a fire. If the fire went out, a child was sent with a fire pan to a neighbor's house to borrow some fire!

Though there was much work to be done, Colonial life was not all work. Often chores were made into games. One such game was cornhusking. Everyone gathered to husk the corn. If a young man husked an ear with red kernels, he was lucky indeed. The red ear was his ticket to give each young girl a kiss! If a girl happened on a red ear, she was allowed to give her favorite young man a kiss.

The colonists also enjoyed a variety of sports. Boys played football, though it was more like soccer than football today. Other popular sports included horse racing, target shooting and billiards.

Family entertainment included small traveling circuses, or puppet shows, such as "Punch and Judy."

Connecticut colonists enjoyed several holidays. Did you know that Connecticut has held Thanksgiving celebrations every year except one since 1649?

title: Crazy Colonial Laws
text:
When visiting the 13 original Colonies, you should take heed, lest you be sentenced to some time in the stocks!

Did you know that a sea captain in Boston was sent to the stocks for kissing his wife in public on Sunday? Even after three years of being at sea, the poor guy was supposed to wait until Monday!

Though some laws in Colonial America may seem really weird to us today, they were often based on religious beliefs. Other laws may have been based on custom, superstition or unusual happenings.

Punishment was probably not too severe for many of these laws, but was surely embarrassing for the law-breaker.

Read on to find some fun and unusual Colonial laws:

It was once illegal in Boston to own a dog more than 10 inches high.

In Maine, you could not lead a bear around by a rope.

In Delaware, you'd be in trouble if you tried to pawn your wooden leg.

It was against the law to mistreat an oyster in Baltimore, Maryland.

In New Jersey, it was against the law to slurp your soup.

In Trenton, you could not throw a bad pickle on the street!

In Truro, Massachusetts, a young man could not get married until he killed either six blackbirds or three crows.

title: What is a Citizen?
text:
A citizen is a person who is born in a country or who becomes a member of the country where he or she chooses to live. Citizens of the United States have many duties, rights and privileges.

Citizens should obey the laws and respect others. They have the duty to serve on juries and pay taxes. Men can be asked to serve in the armed forces during times of war. During times of peace, men and women can enlist, or volunteer to serve our country in the military.

One right of U.S. citizens is to participate in government. Another right, protected by the Bill of Rights, is the freedom of religion. U.S. citizens are promised freedom of assembly, freedom of speech and freedom of press. They are also given the right to bear arms, or carry weapons.

The right to vote is very important to citizens. When citizens choose not to vote, they lose their voice in government. As a people, we need to take the right to vote more seriously. In the 2000 election, only 51 percent of Americans voted. By the 2008 election this number increased to 61 percent.

title: Connecticut Farms
text:
Connecticut colonists brought pigs, sheep, chickens and cattle with them from England. Many colonists had a cow for milk and butter, sheep for wool and chickens for eggs.

These animals generally were not butchered unless there was a surplus or it was a very special occasion.

title: The Great Awakening
text:
Around the middle of the 1700s, many changes were taking place involving religion in the New England Colonies. Connecticut religious leaders were especially concerned as a series of religious revivals began to sweep through the Colonies. For many years, Congregationalists had been the main religious group in Connecticut.

Congregationalists were Separatists who believed congregations should be allowed to govern themselves. Many of the colonists became less committed to the strict Puritan ethics. They began to feel unhappy and restless and were eager to hear new ideas.

The Great Awakening was a religious movement that began in Europe. It reached the Colonies in the 1730s and spread to Connecticut by 1740. Traveling ministers preached dramatically powerful messages of repentance. These ministers traveled from place to place and preached to groups of people wherever they could. Sometimes they delivered sermons on the village green or in the streets. Sometimes, they were held at people's homes. These ministers "awakened" people to the idea that they should be personally involved in religion.

Many people began to leave the Congregationalist church and join the revivals. Those who remained conservative, the "Old Lights," wanted to keep things as they were, but the "New Lights" sought reform in worship. The Congregationalist leaders and the traveling ministers publicly opposed each other. Tension continued mounting in the Colony until 1742. Then, the General Assembly of Connecticut passed a new law that forbade traveling ministers from preaching in any congregation without the permission of the minister of that congregation.

While the Great Awakening did not last long, it brought about some social, religious and political changes in the colonies. By 1750, the law was repealed, partly because many people were anxious to hear new ideas. Many people left the Congregationalist church and joined the Church of England or became Quakers or Baptists.

title: What are pokes and yokes?
text:
Poke collars had a "poke" sticking out. They were put around the necks of cattle and oxen to prevent them from jumping over a fence.

Yokes were a kind of collar with a long bar going from side to side. They were often used with pairs of animals to help them pull a load. Commonly yoked animals are oxen, horses and donkeys.

title: What is Profit?
text:
Pretend you and your friends decide to be entrepreneurs for the day. You find a table in Jack's garage. Mary's mom helps you make some lemonade. Together, all three of you make a big sign that says, "Lemonade, 25 cents." You put all of your items on the sidewalk in front of your house and wait for your customers to come.

Soon people are lined up around the block for a taste of your delicious lemonade. You work quickly to serve your customers. Then you realize that you are almost out of cups. Mary and her mom run to the store to buy some more. When they get back, you take the extra cups and keep on selling lemonade until there is no more. Together, everyone cleans up the lemonade stand. You start to count the money you've made.

You count it all up, and you have $5.80. Then you think about the extra cups that you had to buy. They cost $1.25. You give Mary's mom that amount from the money you made. Now you have $4.55. This new amount is your profit. Profit is the money a business makes after all of the expenses are paid. In this example, the extra cups that cost $1.25 are your only expense.

You and your friends have learned about profit motive today. Profit motive is the desire to benefit from the time and money people put into a business. In other words, you wanted to sell lemonade because you thought you could earn some money. In the same way, a business sells goods in hopes of earning a profit. Now the question is, what will you do with your profit?

title: Golden Eagle
text:
The Golden eagle is a magnificent flier and a fierce hunter. They are fast enough to take many of the smaller quickmoving ground animals on the fly. That means they pick them up off the ground while they are flying instead of landing on them and killing them on the ground. They have been known to attack mammals up to the size of a deer, but they cannot carry off the larger animals.

The adult is from 30-41 inches from head to tail and can have a wingspan of up to 7 1/2 feet. They are dark brown in color with a golden brown head and neck.

They build nests out of large sticks usually on a rocky ledge or high up in a large tree. They like remote open areas, mountains and forests.

You would be most likely to spot this eagle in Connecticut during the winter since they migrate out of Canada for the winter time.

title: Vitus Bering and Russian Colonies in Alaska
text:
Imagine traveling 6,000 miles over land with supplies for an expedition, and THEN sailing through frigid seas to look for a new world. This was the job given to Vitus Bering, a Danish navigator who sailed for the Russian navy. Peter the Great, czar (ruler) of Russia, asked Bering to explore the eastern coast of Russia. He was wondering if land connected Asia and North America.

Bering's first trip began in 1725. After spending three years getting his supplies to eastern Russia, Bering sailed along the coastline. He didn't see any land to the east, and he didn't realize he was sailing in the narrow passage between Russia and Alaska. This waterway is now called the Bering Strait.

Bering led another expedition in 1741. This time his ship landed on Kayak Island, off the coast of Alaska. They explored some of the Aleutian Islands and met the native people there, the Aleut. He was the first European to arrive in present-day Alaska.

Bering died before returning to Russia, but his voyages paved the way for Russian settlements in North America. Many fur traders came to the area. In 1799 the Russian government established a fur-trading operation in Alaska. Furs from foxes, sea otters and seals were very valuable.

Unfortunately, the Russians took advantage of the native people just as some Europeans had done in settling New England. The Russians took over their lands and forced them to hunt for furs. They also brought new diseases, which killed many natives.

Today, the Aleut people continue to live along the western coast of North America, and their population has grown. What might have been different if the Russians and the Aleut had shared public space fairly? Where in your community is there a debate over public land? How should such debates be handled?

title: Let's Write
text: Traditions through the year are an important part of our society. Everyone, according to their heritage, may have different traditions. It is amazing how people do such different things, even on the same holiday. In fewer than 200 words, write about your favorite holiday or family tradition.

title: Shearing Wool
text: After the wool is sheared, it is cleaned, then carded before it is spun into yarn. This Colonial woman is carding the wool. It untangles the fibers and forms them into a web.

title: Yankee Peddlers
text:
It is 1750, and many young men are eagerly watching the harbor for approaching ships. As the ships drop anchor, the restless crowd swarms the sailors to look at the wares they have for sale. In the sailors' trunks and bags are pots, pans, pins, combs, needles, ribbons and sometimes even cloth. They are anxious to sell these goods for the highest price, and very soon the merchandise has gone from the sacks and trunks of the sailors to the packs of Yankee peddlers. The young peddlers then head for town where they offer their goods door to door. Sometimes they are paid in cash, and sometimes they trade for other items of value. When they are done in town, they head for farms. The farmers welcome the peddlers, as they also bring news from the larger cities and neighboring towns.

No one knows who the first Colonial peddler was, or where they came from. Many historians think the first peddlers probably came from the busy port cities in New England. Peddling became a trade, and soon young men were on their way to becoming wealthy. As the trade continued to grow, some of the peddlers became importers and paid for large quantities of items, then sold them to other peddlers who took them on the road. The number of peddlers continued to increase as the Colonies continued to grow. In addition to the thousands of colonists who lived in cities, many more lived in small settlements and lonely farmhouses from Maine to Georgia. These people needed those necessities they could not make or grow themselves, and the peddler was the person determined to go the distance.

The trade of peddling attracted many young men. If they didn't have the means to pursue an education or they didn't want to spend years as an apprentice, peddling was a trade they could enter immediately.

Colonial peddlers must have been fairly strong, as the peddler carried as much as he could contain in a sack. Small items were packed inside of other items, which went into yet bigger items. Everything was packed as tightly as possible into the largest bag he could carry. The peddler would then set off, on foot. Often, a trek would take several months.

Most peddlers travelled by foot. While a few in the mid-1700s may have been fortunate enough to own a horse or pack animal, there were very few roads. The peddler often walked on small footpaths, or made their own trails as they traveled to remote places. Bridges and public roads were scarce. It wasn't until after the Revolutionary War that improvements in roads were made, allowing the peddlers to use carts to carry their goods.

By that time, manufacturing in the Colonies, especially in Connecticut, had boomed. This increased the need for peddlers to carry the American products to the settlers in the new nation. Some peddlers carried a variety of products, while others specialized in one product such as clocks or tinware.

title: eBay: The Modern Peddler's Pack
text:
Computer technology has changed the way people do business all around the world. Today's peddlers are likely sitting in a comfortable chair as they sell and trade their wares. What about their peddler's pack? Why it's a computer!

Pierre Omidyar founded eBay in 1995. By 1998, Omidyar and his cofounder, Jeff Skoll, hired Meg Whitman. Whitman, a graduate of Harvard Business School, put together a team of experts to send the new company into the future. The mission of eBay today is to give people around the world a place to buy and sell practically anything. For tens of millions of eBay members from around the world, this is just what they do. Members buy and trade anything from antiques to books. They sell clothes and even automobiles.

What does eBay do that is different from just listing an item for sale online? eBay doesn't sell items directly to customers, but connects sellers and buyers as they negotiate their own terms of sale. eBay was one of the first sites to allow a seller to accept the highest bid for the item that was being sold. There was not a fixed price as in a classified ad. Today, buyers may have the option of submitting a bid, or buying an item at a listed price.

Here's how eBay works in today's marketplace:

The seller lists the item with eBay. He decides the amount of the opening bid and decides how many days (up to 10) bids will be accepted. The seller pays a small fee to eBay for listing his items.

Buyers search for items on eBay and bid on those they want to buy.

The person with the highest bid at the close of an auction is the winner.

The buyer and seller make arrangements for payment and shipping.

The seller pays a percentage of what he earned on the sale to eBay.

That's a pretty amazing way to connect people with similar interests as they seek to buy and sell merchandise. What other ways have computers and the Internet changed the way we do business today?

title: Colonial Goods
text:
The colonists could not easily buy their necessary goods and services from England because it was so far away. Many became tradesmen by learning to make their own goods locally. Everything from furniture, metal tools, glassware, cloth and food items were produced by local people and sold or traded to other colonists. As more colonists arrived, the demand for goods increased. More and more Connecticut colonists left farming and turned to manufacturing. In the early 1700s, 90 out of every 100 people farmed for a living. That gradually changed, and today, only four of every 100 Americans make their living by farming.

Connecticut became a leader in manufacturing for several reasons. Shrewd businessmen realized raw materials in Connecticut were abundant. There were plentiful forests where timber was harvested for building ships, homes and furniture. Iron and copper ore were made into tools and utensils. In addition, Connecticut's many waterways made transporting goods convenient.

Connecticut people led the way in establishing manufacturing centers independent of England. Some of these early businesses included the manufacture of tinware, steel and hats. Later, brassware, nails, chairs, silk cloth and clocks were also produced.

Wise Connecticut businessmen did not wait for customers to come to them, but hired others to take their products to the people. These traveling salesmen became known as Yankee peddlers.

The Peddler's Pack

Brooms in Colonial America were made by splitting a block of birch wood into many thin strips and tying them around a wooden handle.

Shortly after the Revolution, Levi Dickenson of Massachusetts made a superior broom of a special kind of corn. His brooms were soon a common item on the peddlers' wagons, and brooms could be seen waving like flags on the back of the load.

Clocks in Colonial America were not a common item. They were usually ordered by wealthy families and specially made. By the early 1800s, however, smaller clocks were made and peddlers carried clocks to homes throughout the new nation. From the early 1800s to the mid 1950s, Connecticut clockmakers made more clocks than anyone else in America, and many peddlers sold only clocks.

Pottery was much less breakable than china, and thus easier for the peddler to pack around. Most homes in Colonial American used pottery dishes.

Pottery was not made in the Colonies until after the Revolution. Much later, a finer pottery was made and sold in stores.

Bodkins were a type of needle used to poke holes in delicate fabrics. Bodkins, needles, pins and thread were always part of the peddlers' wares. Colonial women needed them for sewing clothes for the family.

Brassware in early Colonial times was made from sheets of rolled brass imported from England. Brass was popular among all colonists, and peddlers who carried a brass kettle or a pair of candlesticks were sure to sell them quickly.

After the Revolutionary War, Connecticut became a leader in the brass industry when the Porter brothers arrived from Europe and set up shop in Waterbury.

Tinware in early America was the mainstay of many a Yankee peddler. The shiny kitchen utensils, lanterns and even chandeliers were in demand by folks in all 13 Colonies.

Edward and William Pattison arrived in the Colonies from the British Isles in 1740. They began producing tinware in Berlin, Connecticut. At first the Pattison brothers made the tin items and sold them door to door. As the demand for items grew, they hired others to sell the tinware. No doubt, every Colonial peddler had tin items in their packs.

Soon tinsmiths began setting up shop in many other communities. These early tinsmiths used sheets of tin plate, imported from England. They snipped and hammered dozens of useful items for Colonial Americans.

Buttons in early Colonial times were often for decoration, and most articles of clothing had a button or two somewhere. These horn buttons were sure to be part of the Peddler's pack.

title: U.S. Residents
text:
Simply living in the United States does not make you a citizen. Three different types of residents live in the United States today.

The first group of residents is made up of citizens. They include anyone born in the United States or babies born to citizen parents who are living abroad, or in a foreign country.

Throughout our country's history, there have been many immigrants. Immigrants, or aliens, are the second group of residents. These people come to live in a country where they were not born. They do not automatically become citizens and do not have the same rights.

For example, they cannot vote. To become citizens, immigrants must apply and pass certain requirements. Then they can become naturalized citizens.

The third group of residents is made up of nationals.

Nationals are people born in American territories, such as Puerto Rico or Guam. They have all the protections of being U.S. citizens, but they do not have the full rights citizens have.

title: Peddler's Wagon
text:
As roads improved, peddlers began to use wagons for travel. Over the years, the peddler's wagon became more specialized. Every inch of possible space was used for the storage of goods. Small items were packed inside of larger items and stored in special compartments. Sturdier items were placed on hooks and nails on the outside of the wagons. Often times, a canopy frame was added for hanging even more items above the bed of the wagon.

By the early 1800s, and well into the 1900s, many peddlers only carried one type of item, such as tinware or clocks. Many peddlers repaired items as well as sold them, and workbenches with tools became a common item on the peddler's wagon.

title: What does the word "Yankee" mean?
text:
People of other countries often call any person from the United States a Yankee. In the southern United States, the word Yankee means a Northerner, or someone who comes from north of Mason and Dixon's Line. But most of the people of the United States use the word Yankee to mean a New Englander.

No one is sure where the word Yankee came from. Some dictionaries say it came from the Scottish word yankie, which means clever woman. Other dictionaries say it came from Janke, the Dutch equivalent of the English name Johnny. A pirate nicknamed Janke sailed in American waters in the 1680s. English colonists in New York spelled his name as it sounded to them, Yankey, and applied it to New Englanders as an insult for their sharp trading practices.

The word was widely used during the Revolutionary War in America (1775-1783), when British soldiers made fun of New England troops by calling them Yankees.

title: The Role of Prices
text:
"And your total comes to $2.40."

You've shopped in many stores either with your parents or by yourself. Most products contain bar codes that tell the scanner what the price is for the item. The prices let you, the consumer, know how much money the store is willing to sell the item for. However, that's not the only purpose.

Prices have three main functions. First, prices help ration scarce goods. Things cost money, and money is a limited resource. We can't buy everything we want all of the time. Therefore, items need to be rationed, or spread out to many people.

Second, prices provide a reason for buyers to buy goods and sellers to sell them. Prices make the process of buying goods organized. They motivate sellers to provide more goods based on the idea of profit motive.

Finally, prices send signals about how a market is doing. Let's say that prices are too high, and no one is buying those goods. Then economists can study this and ask questions. They can find out what prices are in other markets. Then they decide what in this market made the price rise so high.

Economists can then figure out the price for the product. It should balance the amount of buyers who want to buy with the amount of sellers who want to sell. This price is called the market-clearing price, or the equilibrium price. By figuring out this price, both the buyers and sellers are happy, and goods continue to be sold.

Can you think of any other reasons prices are important to our economy?

title: Eastern Bluebird
text:
The Eastern Bluebird has a beautiful melodious whistle that heralds spring. Bluebirds are found in orchards, farmyards, road sides and open woodlands. They are often in family groups or small flocks.

They sit on conspicuous perches, from which they drop to the ground for insects. (When they perch, note how their shoulders hunch.) They also catch insects while flying. In fall and winter bluebirds add berries to their diet.

You will find the bluebird nested in natural cavities or bird boxes.

The male has a bright blue back and a rusty throat and breast. The female has mostly gray coloring on her back. The young birds are spotted like a thrush.

title: How Do I Use a Thesaurus?
text:
Do you use many of the same words over and over when writing? Are you getting bored with those same words? It’s time you learned to use a thesaurus!

Search for Synonyms

The word “thesaurus” almost looks like a name for a dinosaur, doesn’t it? It’s actually a book (it can be found online as well). This book or website provides synonyms (words similar in meaning) for common words. Using a thesaurus is a great way to broaden your vocabulary with more interesting words.

A thesaurus is usually alphabetical. Some are similar to dictionaries because they give you the part of speech, definition and sample sentences for words. Sometimes a thesaurus will give you directions to look up other entries. Here’s what you’ll find in a typical thesaurus:

Entry Word---The word you look up to find synonyms

Part-of-Speech Label---Tells you if the word is a noun, verb, adjective, etc.

Definition---Tells you what the entry word means

Example Sentence---Shows you how the entry word might be used in a sentence.

Synonyms---Words whose meanings are the same as or similar to the entry word

Antonyms---Words whose meanings are the opposite of the entry word

Try It!

Look up the word “grow” in a thesaurus. Write all the synonyms here.

title: Let's Write
text:
After putting on your new tennis shoes you make an amazing discovery. You are able to fly while wearing them!

1. What color are your tennis shoes?

2. What do you have to do to your shoes in order to fly?

3. Name three places you would like to go while wearing your shoes.

4. Where are some places you would like to visit if you could go back in time with your flying tennis shoes?

My Trip Back in Time

Use your answers from the first four questions to finish this story:

With just a

_ _ _ _ _ _

of my

_ _ _ _ _ _

tennis shoes, I can fly anywhere I want. I found I can even fly back in time. My teacher assigned me to write about what New York was like back when the pirates walked the streets. I decided to go back in time and find out. You’ll never believe what I saw! Finish your story on a clean sheet of paper.

title: Education is Very Important in Connecticut
text:
He who ne'r learns his ABC

Forever will a Blockhead be

Be he who is to his books inclin'd

Will soon a golden treasure find.

This praise for good behavior is from the New England Primer, one of the first books used in the new Colonies. The Bible and the Book of Psalms were also used. Children were often tested at church on their studies during the week.

Schools in early America were very different than they are today. Let's look back 200 years to see how education has changed.

Education was extremely important to the first colonists in Massachusetts and Connecticut. By 1750, most children in Connecticut were able to receive some type of education. Connecticut had many one-room schoolhouses. Here children of all ages met in one room. Since it was impossible to have the same lesson for all ages, it was common for the students to work in groups, and older students usually helped tutor the younger children. The children learned reading from the New England Primer and the Bible. They learned arithmetic and worked especially hard on penmanship. Handwriting was considered very important, even more important than spelling! It was so important that before a teacher was hired, their penmanship was also inspected.

The New England Primer was used by several generations of children. Each letter of the alphabet had a little rhyme to go with it. Children memorized these and recited them out loud. Girls were usually only taught reading, writing and a little math. If a girl was fortunate to receive additional schooling, it was usually from a private tutor hired to teach her at home. Boys studied Latin and Greek in preparation for attending college. Attending college was still a luxury, however, and Yale had only 17 graduates in 1750.

There was no law that said children must go to school as there is today. Parents could decide when and for how long their children attended school. If a child's family lived on a farm, it was likely that they would only attend school in the winter when they weren't needed at home for chores.

By the time of the Revolution, many children attended a Dame school. This was a very simple school taught by an untrained woman in the community, often in a home. Owning books was unusual and paper was scarce. Without paper, many children wrote on thin pieces of bark to practice their letters.

The older students often did mental math (problems that did not require pen and paper). Such a math problem in the 19th century would have been something like this:

At the general store a man bought 5 yards of muslin at 12 cents a yard, a wooden bucket for 50 cents and three bags of barley at 6 cents a bag. How much must he pay the shopkeeper?

See if you can do that problem in your head!

As towns grew larger, they often hired a teacher for their children. All ages would attend one school. Classrooms were very strict. Teachers were allowed to punish children as they pleased. Whipping a misbehaving child with a switch was not uncommon. Some naughty children were locked in a closet for an hour as a punishment. Connecticut Studies Weekly knows that today schools are much different and depend on each person respecting the rights of others to learn.

title: Can Facebook Save Dying Languages?
text:
Can you say a few words in Siletz Dee-ni? No? How about saying "hello" in Aka? If you can't, you're not alone! These two languages and 3,500 more could become extinct by the end of this century. Almost 80 percent of the world's population now speaks only one percent of the world's 7,000 languages. This has happened because of globalization. Globalization means that countries are more connected through trade, money and workers. When countries work together, people must be able to communicate with each other. That means many people have to learn another language. English is the main language used throughout the world for business and the Internet.

Why is this a problem? When the last person who is able to speak a particular language dies, some of the knowledge that is found within that language dies with them. A language contains the history of its people, how they used their environment and their beliefs and ideas. Technology may just save many of these languages from extinction! With YouTube, Facebook and other forms of social media, languages that are spoken by even 5 or ten people can be taught to others around the world.

National Geographic has been working on the Enduring Voices Project. Its goals are to record native speakers of endangered languages into talking dictionaries and help communities learn ways to save their languages from extinction. What language do you want to help save?

title: Early Schools
text:
One-Room Schoolhouses

What did a schoolhouse in early America look like? If a child's family was wealthy, they probably attended a private school or an academy. The buildings and grounds of these schools were usually very nice and often very beautiful. Common schools were much different. They were usually just one-room schoolhouses and probably were in need of repairs.

The room was usually not more than 20 feet by 20 feet. (Measure that space in your classroom, and try to imagine what it would be like for students of all ages to spend all of their time together in that one space.) Near the entrance was a small hall with nails or hooks to hang coats and a small shelf for lunch pails. A bucket of water for washing hands stood here as well. The ceiling was very low, about 7 or 8 feet, and light came from the one or two windows at the sides. The desks went around three sides of the room, gently sloping down from the wall. Benches faced the teacher's desk. Children usually sat near others of their age. The teacher's desk was raised up on a small platform in the center of the room. It sat next to the stove that warmed the room on cold days.

Because all grades met in one classroom, the classroom could be a noisy place as children practiced reciting their verses aloud. A child's first instruction consisted of reciting letters. The teacher would call up one student at a time, while the others continued to practice or read. There was little (if any) paper and usually very few books. The Bible and New England Primer were used to learn letters and to learn to read. The rest of the subjects, like social studies, science and others, were designed and chosen by the teacher. All ages learned those lessons together.

There were many one-room schoolhouses in 18th century Connecticut. A few still remain and have been restored. Students can visit the schoolhouse in Norwalk. Actors dress up and describe what life was like in colonial times.

Yes, schools today are very different than the early American one-room schoolhouse. Aren't you glad?

title: Becoming a U.S. Citizen
text:
People born in the United States are legal citizens of our country. People born in foreign countries can become U.S. citizens, too. This process is called naturalization.

To become a citizen, you must be at least 18 years old and have lived in the United States for at least five years. You must be loyal to the United States and be willing to pledge allegiance, or take an oath of loyalty. You must have a basic understanding of U.S. history, government and the Constitution. In addition, you must be able to speak, read and write basic English.

The process of becoming a citizen has three different steps. First, you must file an application. This includes being fingerprinted, taking photographs and providing legal documents. The next step is to take the naturalization exam. This test has two parts: an English test and a U.S. history and government exam.

The last step is to appear in court. You must go before a judge and ask to become a U.S. citizen. The judge listens to your reasons for wanting to become a citizen and makes the final decision. Once you are made a citizen, you have all the rights and duties of any other U.S. citizen!

title: Ye Olde Books
text: How is this spelling book from the early 1800s different from the books you use in school today? How is it the same? Do you think studying out of this book would be fun or hard?

title: The Founding of Yale
text:
Connecticut has long been known for high-quality education. One of the best-known colleges in the country, Yale University, is found in New Haven, Connecticut. Yale actually began in Saybrook with only one student who was taught in the home of Rector Abraham Pierson. For the next 16 years, it moved from town to town and continued to be held in private homes.When the trustees of the school began to look for a permanent home, the colonists could not agree on where it should be located. Finally, it was decided that if New Haven contributed 2,000 English pounds, the college would be located there.

The trustees then asked Cotton Mather to approach a previous donor, Elihu Yale, for additional funding to build the college. Yale was persuaded to contribute, and in return the college was named for him. Yale did not actually donate money, but goods that could be sold to raise funds. He contributed numerous pieces of cloth, including calico, poplin, crepe and muslin. The colonists then sold the cloth (except for the black crepe which was made into tutors' robes) for 562 English pounds. While that may not seem like much today, Elihu Yale's gift was the largest received by Yale College for the next 100 years.

title: What is a Hornbook?
text:
It wasn't really a book and certainly didn't have horns! What could it have been?

With few books available to the classroom, children often used a hornbook. A hornbook was a wooden paddle. On the front, a piece of paper was attached that had letters or lessons written upon it. A thin transparent sheet covered the paper to protect it, as it was used by many students through the years. The transparent sheet was made from the horn of an animal such as a cow, thus the name hornbook!

title: Budgeting
text:
Have you ever asked your mom or dad for something, only to be told that it wasn't in the budget? A budget is a plan of how to manage your money. It has two main ideas.

First, you must think about how much money is coming in. Maybe you earn an allowance. Maybe you mow a neighbor's lawn to make money, also called income. If you earn money every week or month, like an allowance, then it is called a steady income.

Next, we look at how much is going out, or how much it costs you to live. Maybe you subscribe to a magazine or go to a movie every Friday night. These are types of expenses. Adults also have expenses. They pay bills every month to buy things we all need, like food, clothes and cars. These expenses come out of their income every month.

To make a budget, you must first look at your income (money coming in). Then add up all of your expenses (money going out). Now subtract the total amount of your expenses from your total income. This new number lets you know how much money you have for other things that you want. This helps you plan and make wise choices when spending your money.

The goal of a budget is to try to balance your income with your expenses. It is best if your income is more than your expenses. That way, more money is coming in than going out. Now it is your turn to make a budget. Good luck!

title: Barred Owl
text:
You'll find the barred owl in many wild places in Connecticut. There are many, many varieties of owls in the world. This one is known for its funny call. It sounds like it's saying, "Who, who, who cooks for you? Who, who, who cooks for you all?" (Kind of makes you hungry, huh?)

This bird is round headed, with large brown eyes. It has a yellow bill. The face and body are brown and white. It loves wet areas and deep woods. It likes to nest in hollow trees. This very gentle bird can often be seen and heard during the day. The barred owl can be found dining on rodents, small mammals, birds, frogs and insects at night.

Did you know that if you wanted to see as well as an owl sees, your eyes would have to be the size of softballs?

title: Fact vs. Opinion
text:
Right now you are reading a newspaper. A newspaper is a great place to find both facts and opinions.

Fact: A fact is a statement that can be proved. For instance, to say that most oranges are orange in color can be proven. All you have to do is look at an orange to tell what color it is.

Opinion: An opinion is a belief held by someone. It cannot be proven by fact. For instance, to say, “red apples are sweeter than green apples” is an opinion. It depends on who’s doing the tasting. Brian thinks red apples are sweeter. Brooke finds green apples the sweetest. They each have an opinion about the sweetness of apples.

Newspapers contain mostly facts on most of the pages. Certain pages are set aside for opinions. The editorial page contains letters to the editor, editorial cartoons and articles by the editors of that paper.

The purpose of the editorial page is to:

Make people think about events in the news

Try to get public officials to see your point of view

Give background and information about events in the news

Serve as a community "voice"

All your life you’ll be reading books and articles. You’ll also be doing a lot of writing for school and work. Get in the habit of asking yourself as you read or write, “Is this statement fact or opinion?” This habit will help you become a better thinker.

title: Shuffle the Brogue
text: The playground at early American schoolhouses was very different from yours. There were no swings or playground equipment and no grass or basketball courts. Children played outside and, with a bit of imagination, played games such as Fox and Geese with each other. One game children played was called Shuffle the Brogue. In this game one person was it. They stood alone in the middle while the other children made a circle around them, facing outward. Children passed a mitten, or a brogue, around the outside of the circle, and the child who was it tried to guess who had the brogue. If they were right, the person who was caught became it. You can play this game at recess just as they did centuries ago. Don’t forget to return the brogue to the owner at the end of the game!

title: Let's Write
text: Early schools used rhymes for teaching many things such a letters for writing or character values. Rhymes are often an easier way to memorize something. Choose a character value, such as honesty or courage. Make up a rhyme to teach about that value.

title: Colonial Unrest on the Rise
text:
For almost two centuries the people in the Colonies had lived under British rule. Slowly the colonists began to resent the English rule. Many of the early colonists regarded themselves as English people just living in another place. As time went on the colonists became more and more independent. The children and the grandchildren of those first colonists did not feel the loyalty to England their parents had. Most of them had never even seen England. Thousands of colonists came from countries other than England and had no ties with the country that ruled them.

By the mid 1700s, Connecticut Colony was home to over 100,000 people. For many, times had been good, and they lived a comfortable life. England regarded the Colonies as part of the British Empire and expected the colonists to be loyal to the king and work for Great Britain. However, most of the colonists were feeling quite separate from England. Some were even so bold as to call themselves "Americans."

England needed funds for the war being waged with other European countries, so it passed a series of laws that the colonists resented.

Colonies Begin Meeting Together

In 1754 nine of the Colonies met in Albany, New York. This group was called the Albany Congress. At this and other meetings the colonists found that they had some of the same problems and needs. They began to think of themselves as one people.

By the end of the Seven Years War, England was running out of money, and Parliament decided to tax the colonists. Some members in Parliament opposed the taxes because they thought it would cause discontent in the Colonies. They were right! "No taxation without representation," was a common call among the people.

The Parliament then passed the Sugar Act. It placed a tax on any molasses the Colonies received that wasn't from England. This made the colonists angry! Then in 1765 Parliament passed yet another tax called the Stamp Act. This required the colonists buy a special stamp to put on all legal papers. Even playing cards were taxed! The colonists were furious and protested in meetings. Many newspapers carried protests and broadsides, or papers posted on trees, that carried messages of anger. The Colonies soon realized they could make a stronger protest together than they could separately. In the fall of 1765, the Colonies united and formed a group called the Stamp Act Congress. Nine Colonies sent representatives to meet in New York City.

The Congress expressed anger about the hated Stamp Act and said Americans would not be taxed without permission. Some Colonies formed groups called the Sons of Liberty. Women formed groups called the Daughters of Liberty. These groups became the strength behind the Colonial move to independence.

The Sons of Liberty pressured Stamp Act Agents to resign. When the English lawmakers realized how much trouble the Stamp Act was, it was repealed in 1766.

Only one year later, in 1767, Parliament again decided to impose a tax on goods. The colonists became more determined to oppose what they felt was unjust rule.

Americans continued to riot and demonstrate against other tax laws. When British officers continued to be harassed regularly, British troops arrived in Boston to try and keep order.

The presence of British soldiers served to further agitate many of the colonists and trouble only increased.

title: Scientists Find "Tree Lobster"—Insect Thought to be Extinct for 80 Years!
text:
Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/ for more Connections and Current Events articles.

Off the coast of Australia lies Lord Howe Island, once the home of a huge bug called the "tree lobster." It's a stick insect, and it's related to walking sticks in North America. However, this bug is as large as a human hand and is the heaviest flightless stick insect in the world.

In 1918 a supply ship from England ran aground on the island. The ship carried more than people and cargo; it carried black rats. These rats escaped from the ship and discovered the tasty insects. Two years later the bugs were totally gone. For the next 80 years, scientists thought they were extinct.

In the 1960s mountain climbers told tales of large, dead bugs they found on a mountainous island called Ball's Pyramid, 13 miles from Lord Howe Island. The bug is nocturnal. Would you want to climb a steep mountain in the dark to look for giant insects? In 2001 two Australian scientists decided to look around. At 225 feet up the mountain they saw a single bush pushing out of the rock. There they found 24 of the tree lobsters hiding in the soil!

The scientists captured four bugs and began a breeding program to save the species. Today there are 700 adults in the captive population and over 11,000 eggs. The next step is to try to rid Lord Howe Island of rats and take the tree lobsters back home again!

title: Patriotism Develops
text:
Liberty was something the colonists were beginning to value more as time went by. The Sons and Daughters of Liberty were organized to help preserve Colonial America's liberty.

The Patriotic Movement Begins in America

The Sons of Liberty planted a pine tree in the middle of a field. It is here they gathered and held many meetings. Many Colonies had similar trees. The tree was called a Liberty Tree or a Liberty Pole. These were honored as much as a flag. Several times the British soldiers destroyed the trees, causing more anger than ever before. On Jan. 19, 1770, shortly after another attack on their liberty pole, the Sons of Liberty in New York began to fight with the redcoats at Golden Hill. Men on both sides were injured. This was known as the Battle of Golden Hill. It was one of the first violent acts in the years before the Revolutionary War.

The Boston Massacre

In Boston, Massachusetts, even more violence broke out. On March 5, 1770, British soldiers fired into an angry crowd. No one knows for sure if the first shot was fired on purpose, but it was followed by several shots fired into the crowd. Two men were killed and three that were wounded later died. The angry patriots called it the Boston Massacre.

Stamp Act Inflames Patriots!

The Sons of Liberty hung in effigy (a dummy or likeness of an individual) the British stamp collectors. They also seized the stamps and burned them publicly. They had the support of many of the colonists in their attempt to stop the stamp tax.

Tea Anyone?

The Tea Act was passed by Parliament in 1773. Not only did this tax all tea, but Parliament appointed its own merchants to sell the tea. They were creating a monopoly by selling directly to the Colonies. This left Colonial merchants at a loss, and forced the colonists to pay a tax they did not want to pay. Once again many colonists' thoughts were of independence.

On Dec. 16, 1773, about 7,000 Bostonians attended a town meeting where Sam Adams suddenly stood and declared, "This meeting can do nothing more to save the country!" These words were a signal to a band of men waiting outside. These Sons of Liberty were dressed as Mohawks and dumped the tea from English ships into the harbor. Sam Adam's cousin, John Adams, declared the Boston Tea Party the "grandest event ever."

This act of defiance convinced the British that the colonists (particularly the Bostonians) no longer respected the law, and Great Britain promptly ordered the ports of Boston closed until the tea was paid for.

title: Credit and Debt
text:
You've made your budget, and you are trying to stick to it. You take care to plan what you will buy. You try to make sure that your income is greater than your expenses.

Then you see it - the bike you've always wanted! It is on sale for $55. You rush home and count all of the money in your piggy bank. You find you only have $30.

Discouraged, you decide to go talk to your dad about the situation. He agrees to loan you the remaining $25. He says he will take it out of your allowance for the next few weeks. You think this is a great idea! Together, you go down to the store and purchase your brand new bike.

Even though you most likely didn't know it, you just bought something on credit. Credit is money that is loaned and must be paid back. Usually, credit lenders require a fee, known as interest. The person who borrows money must pay back the money he or she owes. He or she also must pay some extra money for being able to borrow from the lender.

You are also now in debt. Debt is money you owe when you buy something by borrowing money. Although credit can help people in tight spots, it should be used carefully.

Sometimes, people just buy things on credit, usually with a credit card. They forget that they have to pay the money back with interest. This can add up to huge amounts of debt that people have a hard time paying back. You should always remember that having things today and paying for them tomorrow is tricky business. Try to avoid it!

title: How Government Works
text:
Government works similar to stacking blocks, and it all starts with you! You are a citizen of your community. Your community is part of a city, and a local government runs the city. The head of the city, the mayor, works out of city hall. Do you know where your city hall is?

The state government runs all of the combined local governments. The leader of the state government is the governor. The governor's office can be found at the state capitol. Voters in each state elect members of Congress. They meet in Washington, D.C., to take care of the federal government. The leader of the country is, of course, the president of the United States.

The United Nations is yet another block that we can add. It is a type of government made up of leaders from around the world. Wow! Many government leaders are members of the United Nations - but don't forget that the most important part of all of this is the citizens, including you!

title: What is a Town Crier?
text:
Before newspapers came to the Colonies there was no shortage of news because every village had a town crier. He was an official who went about the village ringing a bell or banging a drum to call the townspeople to listen to his news.

After people gathered, the official would then declare the messages that officials believed all the people should know.

In addition to the town crier, there was often a watchman. The watchman roamed the streets at night to make sure all was well. It was also part of his job to call out the time on the hour and state the weather conditions. He might call out, "10:00 and a rough wind blows!"

title: Eastern Mole
text: Moles form a family within the order of insect eaters. This species is about 7 inches long. Its fur varies from gray to brown to golden and it has a hairless tail. Its large, sharp claws help it to dig underground. The mole lives in fields, meadows and gardens throughout most of the United States (not the extreme Northwest), from the Atlantic to the Rockies.

title: How Do I Give an Oral Presentation?
text:
Standing in front of a crowd and telling them what you think is not easy, but it can be done if you prepare well!

Preparing for an Oral Presentation

1. Know your audience. What you say should be directed toward them. Is it to be given in your classroom? This will make it easier!

2. How long should it be? If your teacher says 15 minutes, stick to the time.

3. What’s the topic? Did your teacher assign it? Make sure you can cover it in within the time limit.

4. Make notes. Use index cards and put them in the order you want to use them. Index cards are not so large that they cover your face. You may write your presentation on numbered pieces of paper, but do not staple the pages.

5. Practice, practice and practice some more!

Making the Oral Presentation

1. Introduction—Get the audience’s attention with the introduction. You can do this by asking a question, telling a story, using a quotation or making a statement. Once you have their attention, state your topic.

2. Body—State your main points and give information that supports your main points. You may ask rhetorical questions, (questions that don’t need answers) use emotional words or repeat important information.

3. Conclusion—Repeat your main point. Conclude with something that leaves a lasting impression by asking a rhetorical question, making an emotional plea or using a quotation, story or statement.

Try It!

When you’re asked to give an oral presentation, make sure you prepare well. Organize logically. Practice, practice, practice. Good luck!
