6. Who had more home runs, Ted Williams or Mark McGwire?

7. How many home runs did Mike Schmidt hit?

title: Harriet Beecher Stowe
text:
A native of Connecticut, Harriet was the author of one of the most popular novels in American history, “Uncle Tom’s Cabin.” Abraham Lincoln called Harriet “the little lady whose book started the Civil War.”

Harriet Beecher Stowe also wrote many works on domestic science and horticulture and published children’s stories and poems.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: As you read this week’s magazine, circle or highlight five words that are new to you. Write the words on a piece of paper. Try to figure out the meaning of the words by reading the other words and sentences around them. Write what you think the words mean and compare your definition to a dictionary definition.

title: Women's Voices Are Heard!
text:
At first all women in Colonies, rich or poor, worked together. As society grew their roles began to change. A Colonial woman could have been one of many: a merchant's wife in New York, a slave in Virginia, an unpaid servant working for a family in Connecticut, or a farmer's wife with many children to raise. Each of these women had one thing in common. They lived in America at a time when women had very few rights. Slave women had no rights. Married women only had a few. They were thought of as property of their husbands. They couldn't have higher education. They could not own property or sign a legal document. Women were not allowed to do any public speaking. In rare cases where divorce was allowed, they were not even allowed to keep their own children.

Life Changes After the War

Before the Revolutionary War, no colonists - male or female - had much of a say about major issues. Those things were decided for them in England. After the war, life changed for all men and women. New ideas of independence, freedom, equality and rights were everywhere.

The Constitutional Congress met in 1776. Abigail Adams (the wife of John Adams) wrote to remind him, "Remember the ladies." She hoped they would not put all of the power in the hands of men, without any thought for the women.

Abigail Adams was far ahead of her time with ideas about women. It would be another 150 years before women would have the right to vote!

Education for Women

The first important issue women addressed was the right to have higher, formal education. Until then, only wealthy families could pay for education for their children. Girls' academies taught young ladies how to entertain, play musical instruments, dance and sew. Girls were rarely educated in math, sciences, law or business.

Emma Hart Willard was a leader of education for women. Her father had given her a good education, which she valued. She became a teacher. Emma soon realized that women needed formal education. With help from some citizens in Troy, New York, she opened the Troy Female Seminary in 1821. It was the country's first high school for teaching young ladies.

By the 1840s, the country was changing. No longer were women only servants or governesses. The new looms for weaving were run by women. More women began to work at mills or factories. As families moved westward, teachers were needed, and women began to fill that role. Most important, both men and women (black and white) became active in one of the newest social changes of the times - abolition.

Many of the women who would become leaders in the women's movement learned their leadership and other skills from being in the abolitionist movement.

Among early speakers against slavery were sisters Sarah and Angelina Grimke. Their family owned slaves in the South. They grew to hate slavery. When they moved to Philadelphia, each of them began to write essays and speak against slavery. Women began to link slavery with the low position of women in society. From this thinking came women's suffrage.

title: Women's Rights
text:
The first national women's rights convention was held at Worcester, Massachusetts, in 1850.

Seneca Falls is Site for First Women's Rights Convention

Suffrage means the right to vote. The women's suffrage movement began with the first women's rights convention. Its seeds were planted years earlier at an anti-slavery convention.

In 1840, at the World Anti-Slavery Convention in London, some of the American delegates were women. At the last minute, the convention ruled that only men could participate. The women were forced to watch the convention from a balcony. Two of those women were Elizabeth Cady Stanton of New York and Lucretia Mott of Massachusetts. They wondered what good it would do them to be involved in worthy causes, like abolition, if they were not allowed to participate because they were women.

The two women wrote to each other for several years. The Stanton family moved to Seneca Falls. Now, Mott could visit Elizabeth there. These women, along with three others, spent a day discussing women's rights. The women decided to call a public meeting about women's rights. Elizabeth put a notice in the newspaper for a meeting to be held July 19 and 20, 1848.

Elizabeth Cady Stanton thought about what to say. There was so much that needed to change. She read the Declaration of Independence. She thought of adding the word "woman" to each place it said "man" - "that all men and women are created equal..."

It was a very brave way of thinking for that time, but she did not stop at that. Stanton was wise enough to know that some changes in women's issues would require a change in law. Women needed to be able to vote to change laws. Allowing women to vote in 1848 was a shocking idea. Mott felt it was too soon for this idea. Elizabeth's husband usually supported her. But he threatened to leave town if she was going to bring up this wild idea. Frederick Douglass, the famous abolitionist, sent a note saying he supported her. He promised to speak at the convention. Stanton made up her mind. She would call for the right of women to vote!

The day of the meeting arrived and Elizabeth Cady Stanton was surprised to have 300 people attend the meeting. The people at the convention voted on the issues. The right of women to vote was Resolution 9 and barely passed. The document, signed by 68 women and 32 men, was known as the Declaration of Principles.

Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott had no idea this meeting would launch an organization that would eventually change the lives of their daughters and granddaughters.

Among those who were present at that first meeting, only one, Charlotte Woodward, would live long enough to achieve Elizabeth's dream. Charlotte voted in the election of November 1920.

In 1867 a Connecticut woman named Frances Ellen Burr brought a petition for women's suffrage to the Connecticut House of Representatives. It was voted down 111 to 93, but the close margin (only 18 votes) showed the strong support for women's rights in Connecticut. In October 1869 in Greenwich, the first women's suffrage convention in the state was held and resulted in the formation of the Connecticut Women's Suffrage Association (CWSA), founded by Isabella Beecher Hooker (half-sister of Harriet Beecher Stowe). Hooker also organized the 1871 Suffragist Convention in Washington, D.C.

Susan B. Anthony

The story of women's suffrage would not be complete without Susan B. Anthony. Susan was born in 1820 in Adams, Massachusetts. She was brought up as a Quaker. She was raised to be socially active.

After the family business failed, Susan's family moved to Rochester, New York. They became active in the anti-slavery movement.

Susan had the frustrating experience of not being allowed to speak at public meetings. She was also angry, because as a teacher, she was being paid only one-fourth of a male teacher's salary.

She met Elizabeth Cady Stanton in 1851. Soon she attended her first Women's Rights convention in Syracuse. Anthony and Stanton liked each other right away. They began working together. Stanton was a good speaker. Susan B. Anthony was very good at making things run. They were a great team and worked tirelessly together. The 19th amendment was referred to as the Susan B. Anthony amendment, due to Susan's sustained efforts to get it passed. Neither woman lived to see their dream come true.

title: Presidential Veto
text: The word veto is Latin. Its literal definition is "I forbid." A presidential veto is the ability of the president of the United States to stop a certain bill from becoming law. Many new ideas are presented to the president in the form of bills. Some of these bills are good. Some have very odd ideas attached to them. The president may veto them, or refuse to give his or her approval. However, the presidential veto is limited. If the president vetoes a bill that he or she does not approve of, it still has the chance of becoming a law. The bill would return to the House of Representatives and the Senate. Both houses must vote again. The Senate and House of Representatives need to pass the bill with a two-thirds majority. If they do, the bill becomes law, even if the president vetoed the bill first.

title: What are bloomers?
text:
Bloomers were the answer to comfortable dress for women in the 19th century. They were very loose-fitting pants. Banded below the knee, they were usually worn with a loose fitting tunic (shirt). Women in the 1800s wore skirts with as much as 5 yards of fabric just in the skirt. Under the skirt were layers of petticoats. Uncomfortable corsets were laced tightly and made their waists fit into very narrow waist bands. This was the fashion of the day.

This clothing was very uncomfortable and impractical for women who were taking care of children and doing chores. Even walking across a muddy street could be tiresome in the heavy clothing of the day. Amelia Bloomer introduced Elizabeth Cady Stanton to Susan B. Anthony. She attended the first women's rights convention at Seneca Falls. Bloomer became a convert to the women's rights crusade. She was a clothing reformer - she popularized the outfit that came to bear her name.

Amelia Bloomer wanted dress reform for women. She advocated trousers for women called bloomers which were worn under a dress at first. Later they were worn with a tunic.

title: Regulating Trade
text:
Every day, four friends make and bring their lunches to school. One day, they have an idea. They decide to specialize. Kate will always bring the sandwiches. Pete will bring juice for everyone. Maria decides to make cookies. Mike will bring fruit. Everything goes well at first. Everyone remembers and does their part. They meet each day and have a complete lunch. This continues for a while and is a great deal until Pete moves away. What's more, Maria decides she does not want to trade anymore. All of a sudden, Kate and Mike have only half of a lunch! They have come to depend on everyone's contributions.

This is a pretend situation. It is an easy problem to solve. Each person just needs to pack a full lunch again. But countries, at times, have this same kind of problem. Exporting and importing can mean countries have access to many products. Some countries start to specialize in certain goods or services. As long as everyone is able to trade and the supply keeps up with the demand, everything works great. But if a certain country is unable to trade, the others may suffer.

The U.S. government tries to regulate the amounts of goods being imported and exported. This helps keep exchanges fair and balanced. The government uses tariffs, which are taxes on imports. If they want to encourage trade, they lower the tariffs on imports. If they want to discourage trade, they raise the tariff. They also set up quotas, which are limits on the amount of goods being imported. Why do you think there are limits?

title: Snowshoe Hare
text:
Snowshoe hares are rarely seen but are one of the many mammals to inhabit our woods and back country.

This beautiful animal is shy and sweet. They blend in perfectly with their surroundings, because they're brown in the summer and pure white in the winter.

Snowshoes give birth to about four litters per year with one to nine bunnies per litter. They are born fully furred, open-eyed and able to hop around almost immediately. This is the opposite of rabbits, which are born naked and blind. Hare love to eat wild strawberry plants and the bark of maple, birch and willow trees.

These beautiful animals have natural enemies including the red fox, coyote and mink. Even the great horned owl often attacks them. But the biggest killer is disease. The hare suffer from many kinds.

Hares have large furry hind feet. (Where do you think he got his name?) Look at the picture. Can you see the disguise for winter? From far away, it might be hard to catch sight of this crafty critter.

title: Margaret “Molly” Corbin
text:
There are only two Revolutionary War soldiers buried near the Old Cadet Chapel in West Point Cemetery, and one of them is Margaret "Molly" Corbin. Who was this woman and why would she receive such a remarkable military honor?

Margaret was born in Pennsylvania in 1751. She was orphaned at age 5 when American Indians killed her father and kidnapped her mother. Margaret and her brother were away from home at the time. She married John Corbin when she was 21. John enlisted in the Continental Army when the Revolutionary War began. Wives sometimes went with their husbands to war. They helped with cooking and cared for wounded soldiers. Women often carried pitchers of water to pour on overheated cannons during battle. They were nicknamed "Molly Pitchers."

But Margaret did much more than that. When John was given the job of loading and firing a cannon, Margaret worked as his assistant right on the battlefield. In November 1776, the British army attacked Fort Washington where the Corbins were stationed. During the battle John was killed. Margaret immediately began loading and firing John's cannon by herself. What courage and quick thinking that must have taken! Margaret continued firing until she was wounded too.

Margaret was disabled for the rest of her life. Congress awarded her a lifelong pension (retirement pay) just as if she had been a soldier, something no woman had ever received.

In 1926 the Daughters of the American Revolution had Margaret's remains reburied in West Point Cemetery with full military honors. A memorial plaque also stands near the battle site in New York City. It reads "Capt. Molly Corbin...the first American woman to take a soldier's part in the War for Liberty." Think of a woman you know who demonstrates agility of mind. Who is she?

title: Let's Write
text: Congratulations! You just won a contest to spend one day in Washington, D.C., visiting with the representatives from your great state of Connecticut. You can tell them, ask them or thank them for anything you want. In fewer than 200 words, write what you would like to say that might make a difference as a representative of your state.

text: Use any color to highlight three relative adverbs (where, when, why) in this week’s magazine. Underline the clause that contains the relative adverb and circle the noun that the clause modifies.

title: Fake or Real News?
text:
Have you ever read something online, like on social media sites, that sounded fishy? Maybe it was real, but it could be fake news! The big danger, though, is news that sounds real but isn’t. Fake news is becoming common because anyone can post things online. Fake news can be in the form of a story. Fake news can be a photo or video that has been changed. The problem is that these fake items look real. Fake news can cause problems and it spreads misinformation.

Sam Wineburg, a professor, did some research. He found that 80 percent of students cannot tell the difference between real and fake news. Do you want to become a media-savvy person? You have to be able to find out if news is real or fake. How do you do that? You have to become a detective and search for the truth. You can learn about the author or company that posted the news. You have to think about the purpose of the news. Is there a hidden plan to get you to buy something or to make you think a certain way? Your teacher or a trusted adult can help you learn how to spot fake news. It takes a little time, but democracy depends on real information! Do your part and discover what is real and what is fake!

title: Industrial Revolution...Good or Bad?
text:
The Industrial Revolution was a marvelous time of invention and progression. Indeed, many items that make life easier had their beginnings during this time. It really began in Europe in the early 1700s. It did not reach the United States until after the Revolutionary War. New machines, developed in Europe and America, began to change the way people lived, worked and thought. As new machines began to make manufacturing easier, more jobs became available in the cities. New methods in transportation also changed the life of the farmer. The speed and distance their goods could be shipped improved.

Connecticut relied heavily on foreign trade. The Revolutionary War actually slowed maritime trade. Many Connecticut businessmen began to look for other sources of wealth beside shipping.

Eli Whitney was born in Massachusetts. He moved to Connecticut and went to Yale University. Eli opened a firearms factory in New Haven. In 1798, he was awarded a contract from the U.S. government to produce 10,000 muskets. The United States was preparing for a possible war with France. To produce these weapons, he created a process whereby the parts for these muskets were interchangeable. They did not have to be assembled by a professional gunsmith. This enabled his workers to make the same part over and over again. It greatly increased the speed at which these weapons could be produced. The beginning of the mass production method of manufacturing had arrived.

The invention of machinery, like Whitney's cotton gin and Elias Howe's sewing machine, allowed workers to produce fabric and textiles. Sewing clothes and other things were made faster. This led to the building of large mills and factories. We have some in Willimantic, Connecticut. Today, most of these buildings are vacant. Some people are trying to preserve them as a museum.

How did the Industrial Revolution change manufacturing in the new nation during this time? Before this, skilled craftsmen learned every single step involved in making an item. For instance, it might take a cobbler several days to make a pair of boots. A smith may take an entire week to make a gun. With the growth of industry, mass production became practical. The idea was to divide the jobs between many people to make one item. If each person only performed one step of the production, they could become faster and better. Less skilled workers could also be used, making more workers available. This idea was called division of labor. It did much to speed up production. Many former craftsmen were unhappy about this new method. It might mean they would lose their job. At best they would have to repeat the same small task over and over.

Assembly lines were later introduced by Henry Ford. It was a brilliant new idea. This made it possible to produce things faster with less expense. His idea was to provide a moving belt that would bring the item to the worker. The worker would simply do their one small task, then the item would travel on to the next worker for the next step. The assembly line worked and actually made automobiles and countless other items less expensive. Average Americans could now afford to buy things that were once too costly.

title: Whaling is a Hot Topic
text:
Shipbuilding was an important industry from the very earliest days of Connecticut history. Whaling became nearly as profitable. Colonial sailors searched the waters, looking for the great sperm whales that swam up and down the Atlantic coasts. What products come from whales? Some everyday items were made from whale products including candles, lamp oil and soap. New London was third after New Bedford and Nantucket, Massachusetts, in whaling activity.

The Colonies were not the only place that whaling was a part of life. On the northwestern coast of North America, native tribes were also proficient at whaling. All the products were used by the members of the tribe. Later, an international ban on whale hunting stopped many nations from harvesting whales. It remained a very controversial issue - especially between nations that use and sell whale products and people who wanted to protect whales.

In 1998, the Makah tribe and the U.S. government reached an agreement allowing the Makah to harvest a few whales each year off the coast of Washington state. In May 1999, the Makah went whaling for the first time in 70 years.

Many people were unhappy with the arrangement. Protesters were ready when the hunters went out. Some protesters tried to scare the hunters by buzzing their canoes with small watercraft. One woman was arrested because no one was allowed within 500 meters of the hunt.

Both sides were angry about the incident. The anti-whaling folks were successful in a court of appeals.

For now, the Makah have been ordered to stop their whaling until further studies are completed about the impact of whaling on the Pacific coast.

title: Early Industry in Connecticut
text:
Because so many immigrants desperately needed work, they were willing to work for lower wages. The owners of factories shamefully took advantage of this.

Child Labor Increases

In the late 1880s, newcomers from southern and eastern Europe began to pour into New England. They came by the thousands. They filled positions that booming industrialization provided. Many Yankees and Connecticuters were unhappy about the arrival of so many immigrants. It did not stop these families from coming. Over 12 million people eventually entered the United States through Ellis Island.

Because so many of them desperately needed work, they were willing to work for lower wages. The owners of factories shamefully took advantage of this. The manufacturing was done by men, women and children in dreadful conditions. Hours were much too long, and the work was hard. There were no laws which said children could not work. Children, often as young as 5 or 6 years of age, went to work long hours beside their desperate parents.

Factories encouraged child labor as the owners only needed to pay $1.50 or $2.50 for little ones. They were required to pay adults from $3.50 to $7.00 per day. Even though they were paid less, the children's hours were just as long and hard. Many children in the factories worked from 7:30 a.m. until 9:00 p.m. Others worked all through the night. If they began to fall asleep, cold water was dashed in their face to keep them working.

There were opponents of child labor, and many states did pass some early laws to stop it. With thousands of children working, however, these laws were hard to enforce.

In 1904, The National Child Labor Committee was formed. It began a drive to protect the children of the next generation.

title: Impeachment
text:
The U. S. Constitution is a great system of checks and balances. This system prevents any person from gaining too much power. It also provides a way to remove people from public office who have committed crimes. This is the process of impeachment. To impeach is to charge, or accuse, a person in a high political office with a crime. The Constitution states that this is necessary in cases of "treason, bribery or other high crimes." The House of Representatives starts this process. Once they have created a resolution, then all the members vote on it. If a two-thirds majority is reached, then the resolution is given to the Senate. At this stage, the person is "impeached" or formally accused by the House of Representatives. Next, the Senate begins their debate.

It is in the form of a trial. Each side may call witnesses to testify. Finally, the Senate votes on the outcome. If two-thirds of the Senate agrees, then the accused official is immediately removed from office. Only three presidents in the history of the United States have been impeached. They are Andrew Johnson, Bill Clinton, and Donald Trump.

title: The Sewing Machine
text:
Can you imagine having to sew all of your own clothes with just a needle and thread? Before the invention of the sewing machine, that is exactly what clothing makers had to do.

In 1755, an American inventor named Charles T. Wiesenthal designed a doublepointed needle to make sewing faster. In 1830, a Frenchman named Barthelemy Thimonnier used this double-pointed needle to make the first sewing machine. He attached the needle to a rod connected to a wheel. When the wheel turned, the needle went up and down, sewing stitches.

By 1846, Elias Howe, an American inventor, had figured out how to make the first lock-stitch sewing machine. This machine pulled the stitches tight so they didn't come loose later. It was used in clothing factories to make sewing faster and easier.

In 1851, Isaac Merritt Singer, a Boston machine maker, built the first small sewing machine that could be used at home. He made it easy for people to have their very own sewing machines for making their own clothes at home. The Singer Sewing Machine Company went on to become the world's largest maker of home sewing machines.

Just think of all the time, money and energy saved by the invention of the sewing machine!

title: Yankee Ingenuity
text:
The "Connecticut Yankee" has long been a symbol of ingenuity and inventiveness.

After the Civil War, Connecticut (like the rest of the country) experienced a boom in manufacturing. Rapid progress in transportation, with frantic growth of industry, resulted in a great number of factories springing up in the state of Connecticut. Can you name any that began in your region during the Industrial Revolution?

The Willimantic Linen Company started business in 1854. It provided jobs for hundreds of people, including women and children. In 1898, American Thread Company bought the mills and continued to grow. Work days were 12 to 14 hours long. The employees were paid by how much work they finished rather than by the hour. After American Thread took over, the mills produced mainly thread. It produced up to 85,000 miles of thread a day at its peak. Mill No. 4 was the largest mill in the world for a time. Velcro was invented here in later years.

Shipbuilding also helped Connecticut thrive. The seaport Mystic lays claim to the construction of one of the fastest "clipper" ships ever to sail, the David Crockett.

title: Starting a Small Business
text:
Have you ever thought of starting up your very own business? Each day, thousands of people start their own businesses. They have many reasons for wanting to own their own businesses. They believe owning a business will make them more independent. They like to be the ones in charge. They like to build something of their very own. Many also feel the profit potential is greater than when working for someone else. The profit potential is the amount of money it is possible to make.

Most people start small businesses as sole proprietorships or partnerships. A sole proprietorship is a business owned by one person. Many businesses are sole proprietorships because they are not hard or costly to begin. They are usually very small. In this kind of business, the owner gets all of the profit, but also owns all of the debt. The owners have to deal with all the problems, but enjoy all of the rewards.

A partnership is a business owned by two or more people. These are harder to form. In this type of business, both partners are in charge of the company. They share the debt and the profits. They share the problems and the rewards. Partners are able to bounce ideas off one another. They may be better able to expand their business.

One challenge of a partnership would be in cases where the partners do not get along. If for some reason the partners disagree on issues, the business may suffer.

Do you dream of owning your own business? If so, would you choose a partnership or a sole proprietorship?

title: Was the Frisbee invented in Connecticut?
text:
Well, the Frisbee you see today was actually created in California. But the idea came from Connecticut!

For years students at Yale University in Bridgeport found it fun to toss empty pie tins (from the nearby Frisbie Pie Company) around the campus.

In 1948, a man named Walter Morrison saw this. He had an idea to manufacture a plastic disc and sell it. Around 1955, representatives from the Wham-o company saw his new toy. They liked it well enough to buy the rights from him. The rest is history.

It went through a few name changes like Pluto Platter and Pipco Crash before settling on Frisbee.

title: Black Walnut Tree
text:
Black walnut trees are usually found in bottom lands or growing on slopes. They grow to be 70 to 90 feet tall. Their leaves are found on a stem about 20 to 24 inches long. There are 15 to 23 lance shaped leaves per stem.

The fruit of the black walnut tree is considered a treat, but can be a real challenge to get to. First, the sturdy outer husk must be crushed. As you peel the nut you may find it stains your fingers because the husk has a substance used in dye. At last you reach the inner shell, which is as hard as a rock, so hitting it several times with a hammer usually works! When you finally get to the dark, meaty nut inside, it's very tasty and worth the work - unless you are planning on making a walnut pie! If so, you need to repeat the above procedure many, many times!

title: Using a Planner
text:
A planner can help you manage your time. It is a simple tool that will help you remember assignments.

Feeling stressed? Not sure if you’ll have time to do all of your homework? To keep up with your studies and have fun learning, you need to learn to manage your time. A planner is a perfect tool to do this.

A planner is like a calendar. It will have days, weeks and months in it. You can look ahead in a planner to see what’s due. You can also look at a day to see what you need to do. Planners help organize your time with just a little effort. Here are some ways to use a planner.

Write down assignments. Write down each assignment as you get it. You can include spelling lists, math homework and book titles. It’s your planner, so put down what you need to know. With each assignment, be sure to include the due date and other requirements. When you’re done with the assignment, check or cross it off.

Review your planner every day. To stay on top of things, review what you’ve written. You don’t want to forget an important assignment! Look ahead to see what assignments are coming up. You can even start early on some of them. It’s up to you to keep track of them.

Create a study schedule. Some people study well in the morning. Others do well in the afternoon or evening. When do you study best? Pick a schedule that works best for you. Block off some time in your planner. Then stick with it. Once you’re done studying, check it off. You may need to choose a quiet place that is free from distractions.

You can use your planner to schedule other things as well, like soccer matches or music recitals. Planners can help you remember anything.

title: Children in the Workplace
text: Industry boomed during this era in Connecticut history. Sadly, children had to join the workplace at very young ages, some even as young as you!

title: Let's Write
text: The Industrial Revolution brought many changes to the United States. Some changes were good and some changes were hard. Pick a job such as a farmer, a merchant or a factory worker and tell what your life may have been like in the 1800s. You may want to read a book from your library about the Industrial Revolution.

title: Fun Facts
text: McDonald’s sell more than 1/3 of all the restaurant french fries in the United States each year.

title: Connecticut Honors Inventors
text:
After the Civil War, the United States experienced a huge growth in industry. A great number of inventions triggered this growth. These major inventions changed the lives of Americans forever. We are proud to showcase some Connecticut inventors who contributed to the growth of American industry, technology and medicine.

Eli Whitney, 1, was born in Westboro, Massachusetts. He moved to Connecticut to go to Yale when he was a young man. Most of his work was done in Connecticut. He invented the cotton gin in 1793. This machine removed the seeds from cotton. It helped the United States to be the world's leading cotton producer. He started a firearms company in 1798. It made muskets for the government and pioneered the assembly-line type of manufacturing. This was a revolution in industry in the United States. It increased the speed at which things could be made.

Charles Goodyear, 2, was born in New Haven. He worked very hard at his idea. After many years and failures he discovered a way to vulcanize rubber. Rubber would melt in the summer and freeze and crack in the winter. Goodyear's invention made rubber more sturdy.

Elias Howe, 3, was born in Spencer, Massachusetts. He improved the sewing machine. He worked as a machinist in the textile mills in Lowell, Massachusetts. Elias was always fascinated by machinery. He patented the sewing machine before serving in the Civil War. He was with the 17th Connecticut volunteers. After the war he moved to Bridgeport and started his own sewing machine company. He lacked the talent for marketing though. Other people made money on his ideas. Howe later went to court to sue for rights on his patent. The court supported him, and Howe was awarded royalties on each machine sold.

Eli Terry, 4, was born in East Windsor, Connecticut. He went to work as a clockmaker at the age of 14. Around 1800 he developed a way to make clock gears for about $4 each. This was much cheaper than the previous cost of $20 each. This made the household clock affordable for most people.

David Bushnell, 5, of Saybrook, Connecticut, designed and built the first American submarine in 1776. The sub was named the Turtle. It was operated by only one man! It was used to try to sink the British ship Eagle. Unfortunately it did not work.

Samuel Colt, 6, was born in Hartford in 1814. He was fascinated by machinery. He liked to take things apart to see how they worked. He came up with the idea of a revolver while working on a sailing ship. A revolver is a pistol with a rotating cylinder that holds six bullets. This changed the hand gun from a single shot weapon to one that would fire six times! This changed the firearms industry forever.

George C. Blickensderfer, 7, born in Erie, Pennsylvania, moved to Stamford, Connecticut, when he was in his 30s. Blickensderfer invented the first portable typewriter.

Mary Kies, 8, was a Connecticut native. She was the first woman to be granted a patent. She developed a way to weave straw with silk to make better straw hats.

title: How Do Inventors Protect Their Ideas?
text:
What does someone do when they think of a really terrific idea? That idea can become intellectual property. To help people think of new ideas, the legal system developed the definition of intellectual property to protect people's new ideas. There are four kinds of intellectual property. One is a patent. A patent is a grant issued by the federal government. It gives the inventor the right to be the only one to make, use or sell the invention in the United States for a certain period of time.

A trademark is a logo, slogan, symbol or design made especially for a product or service. Can you think of a trademark for a well-known product?

A copyright protects the expression of ideas. That means if you wrote an awesome play or story, made a winning movie, took a fantastic picture or even made up a unique dance, it could be copyrighted. That way, only you had the right to reproduce it, or make copies.

A trade secret is something special a company knows or knows how to do. That something special may help them be a little ahead of their competition. A trade secret can be a chemical formula, a pattern for a machine or even a customer list.

Protecting a good idea is not a new idea. In fact, patenting began in Italy in 1421, 71 years before Columbus discovered the new world! Inventors who applied for patents wrote down all the details of their work. When it was approved, the patent office published them. This protected them from being copied for about 12 to 16 years.

A patent encourages invention. It publishes the latest technology for everyone to read. Many new ideas are built upon other ideas or inventions. Also, it gives the inventor time to profit from an idea before it can be copied.

Patents help ensure that everyone can benefit from good ideas. Do you have any good ideas?

title: Inventors and Inventions
text:
National Toy Hall of Fame

Did you know there is a National Toy Hall of Fame? The people who create toys for enjoyment and pleasure are inventors too!

Graduating from Yale medical college and winning an Olympic medal weren't enough for A.C. Gilbert. His next ambition was dreamed up as he rode the train between New York City and New Haven each day. He noticed crews building steel towers for electric wires and he thought of making toys out of steel girders as well. He experimented with cardboard cutouts until he was satisfied, then had a metal shop make the first set. In 1913, Gilbert introduced the Erector Set. Today, the Erector Set is part of the National Toy Hall of Fame.

One well-known hall-of-famer is the yo-yo. Did you know the yo-yo is the second oldest toy in the world? (Dolls are the oldest.) Many believe that the yo-yo originated thousands of years ago in China. But at the same time it was being played with in other cultures on separate continents. The first historical record of a yo-yo was in 500 B.C. in Greece.

The yo-yo we play with today has been around for 70 years, and more than 600 million have been sold!

The National Toy Hall of Fame encourages kids to invent toys too. How can you come up with an idea to invent a toy?

Here are some ideas:

Ask a friend.

Visit toy stores.

Brainstorm with a paper and pencil.

Make an accessory to go with an existing toy.

Make an existing toy easier to play with.

Make a toy to go with a popular TV show

The next step is to draw your design. Use a pencil and be sure to have an eraser on hand. After you are satisfied with your drawing, build it! (Then rebuild it and rebuild it, improving it each time!) Have friends and family play with it and make suggestions. Then rebuild it again.

After you have your final model, you must give it a name. It can be something that describes that toy or a simple word to describe what it does or how it sounds.

What's next? Submit it in a science fair or the Connecticut Invention Convention.

Maybe it will be the next inductee into the National Toy Hall of Fame!

Connecticut Leads in Technology

Sometimes inventions come about by accident, as in Goodyear's vulcanized rubber, but more often than not, inventions are a result of education and research.

Some colleges and universities try very hard to attract people who are creative and adventurous. Connecticut universities prepare students for high-tech business. The schools combine education and research in many different fields, such as medicine, communications, science and urban studies.

Connecticut has always been at the forefront of technological development and lays claim to some important firsts.

Igor Sikorsky developed the first practical helicopter, the V-300 (above), at his aircraft plant in Stratford.

The first commercial telephone exchange in the nation was installed in New Haven. It used switches instead of plug-in cords like the one above. It had 21 phones hooked up to it.

Connecticut has been at the forefront of the shipbuilding industry since Colonial times. These days are no different. In addition to building the first military submarine (the Turtle), the first nuclear submarine (the Nautilus) was built at the General Dynamics shipyard in Groton.

title: A Business Plan
text:
Most people think that writing reports ends when they graduate from school - but nothing could be further from the truth. In fact, people have to write for just about any kind of job there is. Owners are encouraged to write down their ideas. They should report their work. It is especially important if they are starting a new business. This helps them to make a business plan. These plans can be long or they can be short. Generally, the more thought put into a business plan, the better the business works. This is because the owners have really focused and set goals.

Pretend you are starting a lemonade stand. The first part of your plan should include the basics of your business. First, what is your business and where will it be located? You will own a lemonade stand. It will be on the left corner of your driveway. Next, what do you need to get your business rolling? Do you need to buy a poster-board for a sign? Maybe you need to buy cups or lemonade mix? Don't forget a pitcher and a spoon! These are examples of start-up costs. Then, consider your target market. Are you trying to sell lemonade to older people or just kids? Are you going to advertise? What would be the cost of hanging flyers around your neighborhood? Consider if there is a demand for lemonade. Maybe you decide to only open your stand during the hottest months of the summer. This turns out nice because you are not in school. Now do some market research! Does your target market prefer lemonade or limeade?

These are all steps any company should include in their written business plan. The more details about the business, the better. With a good business plan, owners are ready to meet most challenges. It is one way to be great!

title: Checks and Balances
text:
The men who created the Constitution were concerned about one branch of government having too much power. For this reason they planned a system of government that had several branches that shared power and checked on each other to give balance to our country.

State governments also have a government system of checks and balances. The state government has a legislature to make the laws. There is an executive branch to carry out the laws. There is a judicial branch that decides how we try lawbreakers.

Local governments often combine functions so the same group of public officials carries out all of the above jobs. Whichever way your local government is run, the voter elects most of the officials, so if they aren't doing a good job balancing power, the people may choose not to re-elect them.

title: What is a banana suitcase?
text:
Believe it or not, a banana suitcase is just exactly what it says - a suitcase to carry a banana. The inventor who filed the patent wanted a way to carry a banana without bruising the fruit. Now, that's a wacky patent!

title: Worm Snake
text:
The worm snake is a very small species of snake. It rarely reaches more than 12 inches long.They are a very plain brown, with a reddish-pink belly. The worm snake has a pointed head and small eyes, with a sharp spine on the tip of its tail.

Worm snakes are carnivorous. That means they are flesh eating. Though they occasionally may eat a salamander, slug or fly larvae, they usually eat earthworms.

Where can you find a worm snake? In moist woodland areas, probably under a rock or a log.

Worm snakes are harmless to humans and they are endangered; if you see one you should leave it alone.

title: Can You Make an Invention?
text: This is our invention, the fly shooter. Now instead of swatting flies, you can just sit back, relax, aim your little swatter and fire away! Can you invent something? Submit your invention in a science fair or an invention convention.

title: Getting Organized
text:
Is your backpack overflowing with papers? Is your desk stuffed to the brim? It’s time to get organized!

We all need to be a little organized in life. We need to know where to put our assignments and where to find our homework. But getting organized will take some effort. It will take some practice to come up with a system that works for you. Here are some ways to become more organized.

Avoid Clutter. It’s very easy to collect clutter in your backpack and desk. Avoid doing this. It will be easier to find assignments. Have some folders where you can put school announcements or tests that have been graded. Throw anything away that has become outdated. Clean out your desk of all old assignments, broken pencils and dried-out markers.

Prepare your backpack the night before. By doing this, you’ll be ready to go. No more scrambling around in the morning. Put in your notebooks, textbooks and planner (if you have one).

Use one calendar. If you have a planner, you can use that. Write down when your assignments are due. Also, write down any other activities you have. Put down family activities, too! Write everything down so you can remember it.

Organize your notebooks. Color-code them if you need to. Choose one color for each subject. Now you can quickly spot the correct notebook. Also, write your name inside the notebook, in case it gets lost.

Choose a good study space. Make it clear to your family that this is where you’ll be studying. Have extra pens, pencils and paper in the area. It should have room for all of your books. It should also be away from distractions like the television.

Now that you have some ideas for getting organized, try some of them out. You may be surprised at what a difference it makes in your study habits!

title: Let's Write
text: Using the idea on Page 2, the fly shooter, create your own invention on paper that will make life easier for someone. Use diagrams and notes to explain how your invention works. Remember to use a fine black marker, not a pencil.

title: Better Transportation Changes America
text:
Many of the inventions in the Industrial Revolution were applied to transportation. These changes made travel easier and faster. It changed the way Americans lived. It also changed where they lived.

The main methods of travel were horse power, water power and foot power before the Industrial Revolution. Many new inventions for moving people and goods made transportation easier. Some ideas were great and some just didn't make it. For any new idea to last, it had to have these qualities:

Did it meet a need?

Did it work well, and was it reliable?

Was it easy to fix and maintain?

Probably most important - could plenty of people afford to buy it?

Some of the ideas for transportation failed these tests. Many others were lasting contributions. What about transportation for recreation? Ask your parents what kind of transportation they used for fun when they were young. Maybe they used a scooter or roller skates? Ask them about their stingray bike or skateboards! Are those things still around? Why or why not?

Improvements in transportation were not always new types of trains, boats or cars. Sometimes it was an improvement in the road, the canal or rail. All of these improvements served to make travel easier.

Let's look at some of those new ideas for transportation which changed America. Ask yourself which things are still used today.

Stagecoaches were introduced to America by 1756. A man named Levi Pease is credited for making the first long distance stagecoach trail. The line was made in 1784. It ran from Boston through Worcester, Springfield and Hartford to New York.

Engineers built stationary steam engines in the 1770s. These new engines changed the face of industry! They were used in factories, farms and mines. In the 1770s, James Watt developed the first steam engine that could propel something. High pressure steam engines small enough to mount on wheels had been perfected by the 1800s. They were even strong enough to turn the wheels! The locomotives were put on rails. The new trains put stagecoaches out of business.

Robert Fulton's steamboat, the Clermont, made its first run on the Hudson River in 1807. It sailed from New York to Albany. Though not the first steamboat, Fulton's was the first to be commercially successful. At least 100 steamboats chugged on the Hudson by 1845. They went about 5 miles per hour and were said to make a terrible noise!

In 1825, the Erie Canal was opened. It allowed boats to travel from the Atlantic Ocean to the Great Lakes as it went from Albany to Buffalo. Barges were pulled by teams of horses or mules. The canal was a great success and important to all of America as it helped to settle the West.

As transportation grew better, people moved farther apart, and trade between states and countries improved. It affected the way our country was settled!

title: Boom to Bust and Back Again
text:
You may have heard people compare the recent economic recession (2007-2009) to the Great Depression of the 1930s. But what some people call the "Great Recession" actually had more in common with a depression in the 1890s and something called "boom and bust."

In the early 1890s, the U.S. economy grew quickly ("boomed") but couldn't keep growing at that rate. When many companies and the housing market failed, there was an economic "bust." The railroad industry had been booming since the end of the Civil War, but in the 1890s more than 150 railroad companies closed. Other industries that depended on the railroads closed, and many people lost their jobs. Over 500 banks closed. Thousands of unemployed men marched to Washington, D.C., in 1894 to demand that the government take action to help families. Unemployment was over 10 percent for most of the 1890s. About one of every ten people had no job.

In the recent recession, the housing market slumped after several "boom" years. Some automakers went out of business and others filed for bankruptcy. The economy went "bust," just as it did in the 1890s. Hundreds of banks and thousands of businesses closed. The unemployment rate was about 8 percent - about one of every twelve people had no job.

Make a chart or Venn diagram that compares these two events in history. (Teachers: You can find background information and activities that relate to this article at hnn.us)

title: Transportation in Connecticut
text:
Connecticut has a wealth of history in transportation. Some achievements include bridge construction, steam engines and new highways.

Inter-city transport was developed because of suburban growth. This included trains, trolleys and buses. Many towns had trolley service. Most towns stopped running them by 1935. Hartford's trolley ran until 1941!

Connecticut has an impressive network rail service. The New Haven Railroad carried passengers from Boston to New York. It went through New Haven and Hartford and had spurs (branches of tracks) that went to almost every town in Connecticut.

Connecticut also has a nice system of roads and highways. The state had thousands of miles of public roads by the mid-1990s. Currently there are about 300 Interstate, U.S. and state highways in our state. The interstate highway system is a network of expressways found in all 50 states. This system makes it possible to drive from coast to coast without stopping at a single traffic light.

Connecticut also has more than 150 airports and heliports. Bradley International Airport is the second-largest in New England after Boston's Logan Airport. Millions of travelers fly in and out of Bradley, which is 16 miles north of Hartford. Long Island is serviced by ferries which carry cars as well as passengers.

What are other ways that people and goods travel in the United States? Trucking competes with the railroads for the transportation of goods. While trucking moves goods, cars move people. Do you know that 90 percent of the households in our country own a car? Some own two or more.

There are many, many types of transportation today. Many things depend on our nation's transportation.

title: Your Growing Business
text:
Pretend you are the owner of a small company. Your business is making more money every year. You have a steady stream of business. Business is going so well that you decide it is time to expand your company.

You begin to research the options you have to help your company grow. You realize you need more money to get your ideas off the ground. You know you do not have enough to afford the expansion. You could borrow money from a bank. But then you will be in debt. Maybe you could borrow money from family or friends. But you would still be in debt. And what would happen if your business ideas failed?

Companies face the same kinds of problems every day. There is nothing wrong with borrowing money from a bank. But companies should only borrow money if they are sure they can pay the bank back. Many companies decide to finance businesses by taking on new owners. This means that some companies sell part of their business. They sell it as shares or stocks. You become a stockholder when you purchase a stock. Stockholders are actually owners of the company. Businesses use the money they get from selling the stocks to expand their business. They hope to create a better company that will yield more profit.

The company may give dividends to stockholders. Dividends are a percentage of the company's profit. This is one way for investors to earn money when purchasing stocks. But they can also make a lot of money by buying and selling stocks. Do you know anyone who has made money in the stock market?

title: Symbols of Our Country
text:
Many of the symbols of our country, such as the flag of the United States and the eagle as the national bird, were chosen in the early days of our nation. Both of these are symbols of our great country. The first official national flag was adopted on June 14, 1777. It was considered to be a symbol of independence, freedom and democracy. The color red stands for hardiness and courage. The color blue stands for vigilance and justice, while white stands for purity and innocence. There are 13 stripes that represent the original 13 Colonies and 50 stars on a field of blue representing the 50 states of America.

June 14 is celebrated as Flag Day. On that day people across the country hang the flag as a symbol of independence and freedom.

Our flag is called by many names such as Old Glory or the Stars and Stripes. Can you think of other nicknames?

title: Why did Tom Thumb race a horse?
text: In August 1830 two railroad cars pulled by a steam engine were set up to race against two railroad cars pulled by horse. Peter Cooper of New York built the steam engine which was named "Tom Thumb." This race was to prove that steam engines would be faster than the horse. Though the locomotive started out ahead and soon outdistanced the horse, a belt on the engine broke. The horse won the race! Even so, the B and O Railroad saw the value of the steam engine and decided to invest in it.

title: Northern Bayberry
text:
A shrub is a woody plant that is smaller than a tree. It has several stems instead of a trunk.

The northern bayberry is a shrub that grows along the Atlantic Coast. It has shiny, green leaves with jagged edges. The fruit grows in clumps of berries that have many black grains in the center covered with a greenish-white wax.

The leaves of the plant are very fragrant, but they are not what gives the well-known candles their fragrance; it's the berry.

To make candles, the berries are covered with boiling water and the wax covering them floats to the top. The delicious-smelling wax is then poured into candle molds or dipped to make a finished candle. It sounds simple, but it takes about 4 pounds of berries to make one candle.

title: The Wonderful Horse
text:
America saw rapid growth in the 1800s. There were many new ideas in technology. We call this the Industrial Revolution. Even with the introduction of steam-powered vehicles, the horse was still in great demand.

Horses pulled carriages and omnibuses. Omnibuses were large buses used to carry many people within the city. Horses pulled stagecoaches between towns not yet connected by the steam railways. Even in areas serviced by the trains, horses were used to carry people to the trains.

Horses helped with the construction of the Erie Canal. When that was finished, horses and mules pulled the barges along the canal.

In the eastern United States, horses were largely replaced by railroads and farm machinery by 1900. In the West, horses remained important for stage transportation for some time.

Stage horses in America lived hard, but rewarding, lives. They were usually treated with respect and were very well cared for. The average life of a stagecoach horse in America was much longer than those in England. Their horses averaged only three years of work. One horse working in California pulled almost a quarter of a million miles while in harness. The horse worked for 15 years! What are horses still used for today?

title: Ethics: President Coolidge Rebuilds a Bridge of Broken Trust
text:
Have you ever wondered how people acquire, or gain, power? In a representative democracy like the United States, a lot of that power comes from trust. We give our vote of confidence to leaders we have faith in. If those leaders betray our trust, then we are free to elect a new representative and the power shifts. But once trust is broken, it can be hard to rebuild.

One of the most famous betrayals of our public trust happened with President Harding's administration. With President Harding's sudden death in 1923, it was up to the new president to repair that bridge of trust. President Calvin Coolidge didn't waste time. He made it clear that no one in government would be above the law. "If there has been any crime," he said, "it must be prosecuted - no one will be shielded for any party, political or other reasons ... Every law will be enforced and every right of the people and government will be protected." And he meant it.

Investigators soon found that Secretary of the Interior, Albert Fall, was guilty of accepting bribes, or gifts, in exchange for the rights to a rich oil field in Wyoming called Teapot Dome. He was the first presidential advisor (helper) to serve time in prison for unlawful behavior. The Teapot Dome Scandal, as it became known, went down in history twice. It was first an example of broken trust, and again an example of how to rebuild it!

title: Steam Railroads
text: There are still some working steam railroads around today like this one in Utah. Most are tourist attractions.

title: Vernon Tunnel
text: Sometimes tunnels were the best way to get past an obstacle. In 1849, the Vernon tunnel was built to cross underneath some railroad tracks.

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you have succeeded in developing the car of the future. It’s amazingly fast and efficient. In fewer than 200 words, tell of your invention and how and where it would take you. Don’t forget to describe it and tell what it uses for fuel.

title: Millions Immigrate to America
text:
More than 6 million people immigrated to the United States from 1820 until the Civil War. To immigrate means to move to another country. The majority of these immigrants were from northern and western Europe. People immigrate for many reasons. Up until the Civil War people moved largely due to ad campaigns. America wanted to encourage people to come to the United States. These campaigns appealed to many who wanted a better life. The popular ballad below describes the campaign.

Of all the mighty nations in the East or in the West,

This glorious Yankee nation is the greatest and the best,

We have room for all creation and our banner is unfurled,

Here's a general invitation to the people of the world.

Come along, come along, make no delay,

Come from every nation, come from every way

Our lands are broad enough, don't be alarmed

For Uncle Sam is rich enough to give us all a farm.

People in many countries took the invitation. Soon Ellis Island became the main gateway for immigrants. Ships flying the flags of many countries could be seen on any day in New York Harbor.

The westward expansion of this country and this first major wave of immigration are linked. The larger America grew, the more people were needed to settle it. These immigrants brought energy and drive. They brought with them many skills. Farming, furniture making and weaving were some of them. They brought knowledge of medicine, science and law. Throughout our history, scientists and inventors have often been immigrants.

The early policy of this country concerning immigration was that anyone who wanted to come to America could. Things changed as each state decided how to handle its own immigration issues. Not all of the people in America were happy about the newcomers. One and a half million Europeans arrived in the 1850s! A wave of Irish came as they fled the potato famine in Ireland. They came and filled many of the jobs for common labor. They built bridges, roads and canals. Most were too poor to migrate westward so they crowded into Eastern cities like New York and Boston. Many Americans feared the loss of jobs. They also feared such large numbers of people from one heritage and culture. What a silly thing to be afraid of! Anti-foreign feelings began to flare.

New York state took over a large building in New York City in response. The building was named Castle Garden and it handled immigration. Immigration at Castle Garden was handled loosely. People who were criminals bribed corrupt officials to be admitted! Other immigrants became victims. Their belongings were easily stolen and they were hurried into poor work contracts.

Publicity about this finally made the federal government take over. President Benjamin Harris declared Ellis Island the Federal Immigration Center in April 1890. The world talked about Ellis Island as the gateway to the United States. Work to enlarge Ellis Island and to construct the facilities began. Finally the ceremonies to open Ellis Island were held. Ellis Island opened on Jan. 1, 1892.

The first immigrant to set foot on Ellis Island was Annie Moore of County Cork, Ireland. She was 15 years old! Annie and her two brothers were joining their parents. Their parents had come to America three long years before them!

The largest wave of immigration was between 1892 and 1901. Millions poured into Ellis Island during this time. More than 1,300,000 came to Ellis Island in 1907. On one single day, April 17, 1907, 11,000 awaited their turn to be processed.

Most people came to escape hard lives. These immigrants left behind poverty, religious persecution, hunger and despair. They had nothing to lose. Ellis Island became a symbol of hope. It lit their minds with dreams and gave them courage to face a new world.

title: Find Your Roots at Ellis Island
text:
Millions of immigrants were processed at Ellis Island between 1892 and 1954. Forty percent of Americans living today can trace their roots to ancestors who came through Ellis Island. How many of you have ancestors who came through Ellis Island?

Many of us want to know who our ancestors are and where they came from. Searching the records at Ellis Island could help. Many know their ancestors came through Ellis Island. It's much harder to find where their ancestors came from though. Without knowing that information, it is impossible to search further.

The search for your ancestors is called genealogy. The Statue of Liberty-Ellis Island Foundation made a new facility to provide help and guidance in that search. It is for adults and children who are doing genealogy work.

Hundreds of volunteers entered data into computers. The data shows 11 fields of information including:

Immigrant's given name (first name at birth)

Immigrant's surname (last name)

Ship's name

Port of origin (where the ship came from)

Arrival date

Number of the line the name appears on registry

Gender (male or female)

Marital status

Nationality

Last residence (town and county)

These records will help people who are doing genealogy work to find their ancestors.

The foundation has made a records search available to everyone online. You can search for a name by going to www.ellisisland.org.

title: Immigration and Migration
text:
Immigration to the Connecticut River Valley and surrounding areas didn't start in earnest until the 1890s. While a large part of the immigrants to places like Boston were Irish, most of the immigrants to Connecticut were from eastern Europe.

Ellis Island Immigration Center

Ellis Island is a symbol of America's immigrant heritage. Over 12 million people passed through Ellis Island from 1892 to 1954.

As the immigrants arrived by ship, hundreds of poor were confined below deck. Only first- and second-class passengers were on deck to see the Statue of Liberty. It was welcoming them to America. Those same passengers were the first to be processed, often right aboard ship. The others were ferried to Ellis Island. When they got there they were examined and questioned. Processing is the word used to describe the many examinations each person had to pass. They had to pass all of them before being let in. Not everyone was allowed. During those years, around 250,000 were sent back to their homeland.

The majority of those who came were men. Many came to America to find steady work. They would later send money for family members to follow. The countries they came from were numerous. Most claimed European ancestry. Others came from Asia, the West Indies and the Middle East.

Those who arrived often waited on barges for hours to be processed. They were told to drop their belongings in a large pile. The men were sent in one direction and the women and children went another. It was a frightening experience. Many wondered if they would be able to find each other again.

Medical Inspection

Medical inspection began as soon as they came into the registry room. Doctors watched carefully for signs of diseases. If the doctor found any signs, they would mark their clothing with chalk. "E" stood for eyes, "L" for lameness and "H" for heart. Those who had mental ailments were marked with and "X." Marked immigrants were pulled from the line and sent to examination rooms. There they were checked and tested. Many were sent to the hospital for care. Those who recovered were allowed to land. Those who did not were deported to their home country.

Immigrants Suffer Poor Living and Working Conditions

The labor force in Connecticut changed dramatically. Waves of immigrants replaced farm workers. Most immigrants were relieved to find work of any kind. They often took low pay, miserable working conditions and poor treatment.

With little money they settled in tenement houses. The tenement buildings were several stories. They often housed as many as 500 people! Several families often shared one apartment. Four or five families would have to share one bathroom. Laborers worked for small wages. Often entire families worked to be able to survive. Children as young as 6 years old went to work in factories.

The conditions in these factories were awful and the hours were long. Factories were overcrowded and nearly unbearable.

It wasn't long before workers began to discuss the need for better working conditions.

They formed labor unions to fight the factory owners for more freedom. A union is a group of people who join together to protect the rights and interests of the worker. The unions discussed a strike (walking off the job) to protest.

The owners of the Taftville Cotton Mill cut the pay of their workers twice in 1875. The workers weren't making much to begin with. They simply couldn't afford to work for less. The union called a strike. The company offered to restore part of the pay cut to those who had not taken part in the union. All 1,200 workers walked off the job. The company did not give in. They fired all the workers and evicted them from the company-owned housing. They hired "scabs." That is a union term for people who take the jobs of those on strike.

Sometimes the police had to be called out to protect company owners and those workers who were not on strike. The strikers' ability to support their families was at stake. Sometimes the strikers harmed those who chose to work during the strike.

The threat of strikes increased as more workers unionized. They wanted to create better working conditions for themselves. They wanted a higher standard of living for their families.

The first unions in Connecticut weren't very successful. It wasn't until the 1900s that unions began to impact working conditions for laborers.

title: The Stock Market
text:
When a company decides to sell shares, it first sells the stocks in a primary market. This is the first time stock is sold to the public. It is called an initial public offering (IPO). Then the stock moves to the secondary market, or the stock market. This means that the money made from selling the stock goes to the person selling it. It does not go to the original business.

There are many parts of the stock market. There are regional exchanges, which are smaller. They are like the exchanges in Los Angeles, Chicago and Boston. Some are large organized exchanges, like the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE). The New York Stock Exchange is located on Wall Street in New York City. The NYSE lists about 2,800 large and mid-sized companies. They are worth over $18 trillion!

Most stock markets have traders who make a living buying and selling stock. The NYSE has a trading floor where all of the shares are purchased. You have probably seen footage of Wall Street on the evening news. The news usually announces the day's Dow Jones Industrial Average. This is a mathematical calculation of 30 main stocks being sold. It gives a general overview of the market.

The stock market changes every day. It goes back to the concept of supply and demand. If a certain stock is popular, then the demand for that stock goes up. As the demand goes up, so does the price of the stock. If someone buys a stock at a low price and the price increases later, that person can make a profit. They can sell the same stock at the higher price. When prices keep going up, people call it a "bull market." People call it a "bear market" when the values keep dropping. Are we in a bull or bear market right now?

title: Liberty
text:
Liberty is the freedom to think, to rule or direct without being constrained by force. In the days before democratic government, people had to struggle to survive. It was often the strongest or the oldest who made the decisions for others.

The Greeks began a voting system that allowed some of the people to have a voice in decisions that affected them. Later, the Romans had a similar idea when it came to deciding about law cases.

For most of the next 2,000 years, however, kings and queens mostly ruled the world. Those rulers usually got their position by birth or war. Most people did not have the ability to choose their leaders or live without people forcing them to live a certain way.

Finally, people began to rebel against their leaders, just as the American Colonists rebelled against King George. After the Revolutionary War, the Colonists were free to set up a new government. They chose to establish a democracy so that they could have a voice in the decisions that affected their communities. This new freedom has often been described as liberty.

title: From ‘The New Colossus’
text:
Here at our sea-washed, sunset-gates shall stand

A mighty woman with a torch, whose flame

Is the imprisoned lightning, and her name

Mother of Exiles. From her beacon-hand

Glows world-wide welcome; her mild eyes command

The air-bridged harbor that twin-cities frame.

"Keep, ancient lands, your storied pomp!" cries she

With silent lips. "Give me your tired, your poor,

Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free,

The wretched refuse of your teeming shore.

Send these, the homeless, tempest-tossed to me,

I lift my lamp beside the golden door!"

by Emma Lazarus (inscribed on the Statue of Liberty)

title: Who was Sam Ellis?
text:
The famous Ellis Island is named for the New Yorker who came into possession of the island and owned it until his death.

Sam was a loyalist, and moved to New Jersey after the Revolution. Upon his death, the island changed hands within the Ellis family several times. Samuel Ellis Ryerson, a grandson, sold the island to John Berry, who sold the island to New York state. In 1808, New York sold it to the federal government.

Ellis Island was known by many names before it became Sam Ellis' island. It was called Kioshk by the American Indians, Oyster Island by the Dutch and Gibbet Island by the English. After the War of 1812, it was renamed Fort Gibson.

Eventually, by the time it was considered as a site for the immigration center, it was called Ellis Island.

title: Gray Squirrel
text:
The gray squirrel is a noisy little friend. Did you know that not all of that chatter is idle? Sometimes it has specific meanings: a rapid kuk, kuk, kuk means immediate danger; a longer drawn-out ku-u-u-k, sounded every few seconds warns of less worrisome danger; a slow kuk-kuk-kuk means the danger has passed. Gray squirrels also send messages with their bushy tails!

Gray squirrels bear young in litters of two or three, twice a year. In late winter or spring, litters are usually born in tree hollows. Summer young can sometimes be found in leafy nests out along the end of a tree branch.

title: Fun Facts
text: After cats eat, they always immediately bathe themselves to get the food scent off of them so that other predators won’t smell it and come after them.

title: Let's Write
text: Immigration did not end in 1954 with the close of Ellis Island. Some Connecticut Studies Weekly readers were born in other countries. Some of your parents, or grandparents, may have immigrated. In fewer than 150 words, tell of how life in the United States is different from the country from which you, your parents or ancestors came.

title: Good Handwriting
text:
It takes some time to develop good handwriting, but it’s well worth the effort.

Have you ever gotten a test back and lost points because of messiness? Does your teacher have problems reading what you’ve written? Bad handwriting can lead to these situations. If no one can read your brilliant answer on the test, then it won’t help you get a good score. Most people think bad handwriting means a lack in organizational skills. If it’s difficult to read, people won’t take the time to decipher the handwriting.

Developing good handwriting takes patience and diligence. It takes a lot of practice to get those perfect letters. Here are some tips to get you started.

Take some time each day to practice writing out letters. The more you practice, the better your handwriting will become.

Practice in one notebook so you can compare how well you are doing.

It’s okay if you write slowly in the beginning. Focus on writing that can be read easily. Then move on to how fast you can write legibly.

Choose a pen or pencil that you like and gives you the best grip. You may want to try out different pens or pencils to find the one just for you.

Good handwriting is a needed skill in this world. It’s needed when you take a test or write a paper in class. You’ll need it to write thank-you cards or to fill out invitations. And when you’re older, you’ll need it to fill out job applications. In the end, good handwriting will help people understand what you’ve written. And that’s the most important part.
