title: Connecticut in War and Peace
text:
The United States entered World War I in 1917. Thousands of Connecticuters entered the military to serve in the war. Connecticut had always been at the front of the line when it came to protecting the nation. It was no different this time! Connecticut fully met the challenge in the military. They also helped back home with support for the war effort.

Because of the great need for specialized products during wartime, the economy often shifts. Things like ammunition, guns, uniforms and tanks need to be made. This was the case with Connecticut. The state's industries churned out war materials at a fast pace. There were huge firearms and munitions factories in New Haven, Bridgeport and Hartford. These made Connecticut the country's leading munitions maker. Connecticut had produced 54 percent of the munitions for the United States by the end of World War I. This was really good news. It meant thousands of jobs and millions of dollars in income for the state.

With the end of the war came the end of military contracts. The end of the contracts meant fewer jobs. Soldiers were returning home and needed jobs. There were also many immigrants looking for jobs. There weren't enough jobs to go around, and it led to unrest in the workforce. Governor Holcomb created a 15,000-man Home Guard to keep the peace in 1917. Governor Holcomb was worried about unrest with the immigrants. The Home Guard was on alert throughout this period after the war. Tensions did not cease until the economy began to improve.

There was a huge change in the population of Connecticut by 1940. In 1900 the population of Connecticut was about 908,000. By 1940 the population was nearly double at 1,709,000! The population of Hartford alone went from 80,000 to 166,000 during this time. This increase was due largely to the immigration of Eastern Europeans. There were also high birth rates among these people.

During the 1930s the country was in the Great Depression. One-fourth of Connecticut men and women were out of work by 1933. Most of those who were still working were working for very low wages. Providing for families was not easy.

The Great Depression ended when the Japanese bombed Pearl Harbor. There was a flurry of wartime production. Once again, the state's factories pumped out submarines, machines, chemicals and ammunition.

The economy was strong after WWII. The products of the state were selling. The developing technology changed the way the people lived. The automobile market affected the way the population settled as well. Cars made it easy for people to travel long distances for work. People began leaving the cities and heading for the suburbs. All this meant more work for more people.

As industry and population continue to grow, Connecticut looks to its cleverness and spunk to solve the problems of the future.

title: Good Times, Bad Times
text:
My name is Lois Thompson and I was born in 1913 in Bridgeport. When my great-grandson, Thayne, was in fourth grade and studying the mid-20th century in social studies, he asked me if I knew anything about the Great Depression and the two World Wars. Ha! Do I know anything? Thayne honey, I lived through those events!

I remember my father coming home from World War I in 1918. I was 5 years old and my mother sure was happy! He told stories for many years about living in the trenches of France where most Connecticut soldiers were sent. The war was awful, but this country was really united.

Then came the Roaring '20s. There was lots of money and lots of food and I became a flapper. We danced the Charleston and wore dresses with fringe and long beads that flapped around. It was really fun! Then came Oct. 29, 1929.

The Great Depression

That date lives in the memories of all us who lived at that time. I was only 16, but I remember the stock market crashing. We were plunged immediately into the Great Depression. Our world caved in. Thousands of Americans lost their jobs. My father lost the bakery he owned and our home. Those were awful times. My family laughs at me now because I can't bear to throw anything away. Leftover feelings of my youth when I hardly owned anything, I guess.

I was 28 when the United States entered WWII in 1941. Then I was newly married and so sad to see my husband join the Navy. I didn't sit around and mope, though. I took a job in the munitions factory here in town. We women were proud of the work we did in the war effort. Many jobs were available then, though rationing was in force. My younger sister Jewel and I planted a Victory Garden. The war that killed so many of our young men also put an end to the Depression. We were so happy to see our husbands return in 1945.

Times are better now, but I often think back to the events of my youth. Those were sad as well as happy days. This country was more united then than now, and we appreciated even the little things.

Lois Thompson passed away in 1996 when she was 83 years old.

title: World War I to World War II
text:
World War I, the Great Depression and World War II were trying times for the United States of America. Many men and women died in the line of duty for their country. This week, let's take a look at how Connecticut fared through these trying times.

World War I

Leave Our Passenger Ships Alone!

War broke out in Europe in 1914. Many nations were fighting. The United States tried to stay neutral. Neutral means not helping one side or the other.

Germany would not stop attacking U.S. ships. Finally, the United States joined the Allied Powers in 1917. It was the United States, England, France, Italy and Russia fighting the Central Powers. The Central Powers were Germany, Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire.

Thousands of our sailors, soldiers and marines fought in the war. Most fought in France. Hundreds of women served as nurses. Our factories were used to make guns, ships and planes. Women worked in the factories as well. Connecticut became known as the "munitions state" because so many munitions factories were here.

The Allied Powers defeated the Central Powers in 1918, ending World War I.

Prohibition: A 13-Year Failure

No More Drinking in America!

Many religious leaders in the United States were convinced that alcohol was at the root of all crime. The 18th Amendment was added to our Constitution in 1920. It made liquor illegal. It didn't work though. People still bought it illegally. In fact, they drank even more.

Illegal bars called speakeasies opened. Sometimes drinkers made their own liquor at home. Many people died of alcohol poisoning this way. Mobsters took over the illegal liquor industry. Crime actually increased!

Finally, Prohibition was repealed, or taken back. Many people were happy to have their rights back.

The Great Depression

Oct. 29, 1929 - The Stock Market Crashes

What is the stock market, anyway? Stocks are shares, or parts, of ownership in a company. The Roaring Twenties were good times for this country. Many people bought stocks in several companies. They hoped to get even richer as the prices of these shares rose. In October 1929, for several reasons, the prices of stocks began to plunge. People grew worried. They began to sell their stocks that month.

On Oct. 29, the prices fell too low because so many people sold their stocks. The stock market had crashed. This was the beginning of many years of hard times for the people of this country. Many banks failed. Most people could not afford to buy things. Companies laid off workers. The Great Depression had begun. A depression is a time when people are out of work and business is slow.

Many families were divided as fathers and mothers left to work. Sometimes children were sent to live with relatives who could better care for them.

World War II

Dec. 7, 1941 - Pearl Harbor Day

In 1939, World War II had already begun. Germany was trying to conquer Europe. Once again the United states tried to stay neutral. The enemy persisted though. The Japanese entered the war. They bombed U.S. ships stationed in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii on Dec. 7, 1941. This forced the United States to action!

This time the Allied Forces were the United States, England, France and the USSR. The Axis Powers were Germany, Italy and Japan. During the war, Hitler killed millions of Jews. This is called the Holocaust.

More than a million American men and women served in this war. More than 210,000 of them were from Connecticut. The USS Cod was built at Electric Boat in Groton. It made seven successful war patrols in the Pacific during World War II, sinking more than 12 enemy vessels.

Miners and factory workers were sent back to work. They produced radios, uniforms and airplane engines. Because of the war, the Great Depression ended, but many Connecticuters were killed or wounded in World War II.

What does 'Rationing' Mean?

Rationing was done during WWII. It set up a fair distribution of meat, sugar, shoes, gasoline, tires and cars. The plants that made these items now concentrated on producing food for the soldiers and sailors. They also made ships, weapons, tanks and other war-time goods.

Coupon books full of ration tickets were issued to every family according to its size. People now needed two things to buy something. They had to have the money and the correct number of ration coupons!

Farmers were allowed extra coupons to purchase gasoline for farm vehicles. Connecticut farmers played an important role during WWII.

The motto for the folks back home was: "Use it up - Wear it out - Make it do - Or do without!"

title: Economics Competition
text:
Have you ever played on a sports team? Maybe you played soccer, basketball or baseball. If so, then you know the best way to become a winning team. Each player must play the best he or she can. Everyone must work together.

This same kind of competition is in a marketplace. Producers compete against each other. They try to give customers the best prices and products for their money. Monopolistic competition is when businesses offer similar products. The products are not identical, though. Each business can raise or lower its price. Each tries to reach a price where it can sell the most products. This is why economists call these businesses "price searchers."

An oligopoly is a market where a few (usually three to five) companies control the competition. They provide the most products. For example, airplane manufacturing is very hard and so only a few large companies compete against each other. When there is only one seller of a product, it is called a monopoly. No companies are making a product to use instead of this product, either. So there is no competition for the company. The company can charge whatever price it wants, because customers have to buy their product.

A monopsony is a market that has only one buyer. Sellers will compete with one another to make the best quality product. They try to offer this product at the best price. An example would be the U.S. government. They are the only buyers for aircraft carriers in this country. Businesses compete to make the best aircraft carriers. But there is only one buyer.

Now that you know about the different kinds of markets, can you decide which one you would prefer for a business you owned?

title: World Organizations
text:
There is a group called the World Trade Organization that, like the United Nations, is a group composed of representatives from the governments of the states (or nations) that are members. The World Trade Organization (WTO) is the only international organization dealing with the global rules of trade between nations. Its main function is to ensure that trade flows as smoothly, predictably and freely as possible.

The United Nations has six departments. They work to solve problems that concern all of humanity.

The General Assembly addresses any important world problems and approves of the budget.

The Security Council has the job to maintain peace and security in the world. They help to settle international disputes by peaceful means.

The Economic and Social Council works at promoting economic growth and development of countries. They try to help countries solve problems relating to children, hunger, education, health and human rights.

The Trusteeship Council watches over the people living in U.N. territories.

The International Court of Justice settles legal cases between member states.

The Secretariat is the U.N. staff in New York, as well as additional staff throughout the world. They are drawn from 170 countries.

title: Homefront Heroines
text:
The men who went off to fight were not the only heroes of World War II. Thousands of American women were called upon to join the war effort back home. They were defense workers. They built ships, aircraft and weapons. One such homefront operation was the Eldred National Munitions Company. It was in Pennsylvania. During the war, about 1,500 people worked there. About 95 percent of those people were women! They produced thousands of bombs, hand grenades and mortar shells.

You know how sparks fly between you and another person when you rub your foot on the carpet then touch their arm? That's called static electricity. The workers at this plant had to wear white cotton uniforms with rubber buttons and special shoes. The clothes were designed to reduce the risk of making static electricity. Those sparks could make the plant blow up! What a dangerous job.

Later they were given Army ordinance uniforms, which they proudly wore to places like church and parades. The women only earned between 35 and 50 cents per hour, the men 75 cents per hour. They were all proud to be part of the Allied Powers that defeated the Central Powers in World War II.

title: What is a Victory Garden?
text: Hundreds of thousands of Americans planted gardens during WWII to grow needed food. The more food we grew on our own, the more food produced by commercial farms could go to those fighting overseas. They were called Victory Gardens because the war had united all in a spirit of positive thinking. Throughout the country approximately 40 percent of all the produce eaten during the war years was grown in Victory Gardens.

title: Pawpaw Tree
text:
The pawpaw tree grows from 10- to 20-feet tall. It has leaves that are 5- to 10-inches long. It is a member of the custard apple family.

It has purplish flowers that bloom brightly in the spring and produces an edible fruit that ripens in the fall. The fruit is very tasty and the flavor is comparable to bananas or mangos. The fruit is eaten by people as well as opossums, raccoons, foxes, squirrels and many birds!

The pawpaw tree is not used for timber harvest, but its fibrous inner bark was used by American Indians to string fish and repair fish nets. It was also woven into cloth.

These trees like lots of moisture and grow best in bottomlands with rich, moist soil.

title: How do I Take a Test?
text:
Do you get sweaty palms and butterflies in your stomach over the idea of taking a test? That happens to everyone at one time or another. Did you know test anxiety comes from a lack of self-confidence? How can you improve your self-confidence and improve your test-taking skills? The best way is to know the material very well. But here are some other important ideas that may help you:

Preview the test. What does it cover? How long is it? Plan your time. Decide how much time you can spend on each section. Keep track of the time as you take the test. Follow directions. Read all the directions and listen carefully to any directions read aloud.

Read the questions carefully. Look for keywords such as “when,” “where,” “why,” “different from,” “same as,” “before” and “after.” Don’t get stuck on one question. If you can’t think of an answer, skip it and return to it later when you have finished the rest of the test. Check your work. If you have time left after you finish the test, go back and double-check your work.

Use this list while taking this week’s Studies Weekly quiz. Practice good test-taking skills. You may want to use this list for the next few weeks until you have mastered the skills.

title: Let's Write
text:
Here at Connecticut Studies Weekly, writing about history is definitely our favorite thing to do! There are so many awesome people and places to study. The hardest part is choosing which historic events to write about. We’d like to invite you to be a junior historian.

Begin your own history book by choosing five things from the past millennium to share with other students in Connecticut. You may choose to write about people, places or historic occasions. Tell about your choices and why you chose to highlight those particular historic events. There are endless possibilities just waiting for you!

title: Language Arts Connection
text: Use any color to highlight three relative adverbs (where, when, why) in this week’s magazine. Underline the clause that contains the relative adverb and circle the noun that the clause modifies. (CC ELA L.4.1)

title: Connecticut as a Cultural Center
text:
History is just one way to study people over time. Studying their ideas, artifacts, literature and values is another way to get to know the people of Connecticut long ago and to celebrate the people we are today.

The study of literature, art, music, languages, theater and philosophy are all part of what we call humanities. Things such as art bring joy and meaning to our lives. Let's explore some of the arts and leisure activities that make Connecticut such a great place to live.

Performing Arts

Theater, music and dance are considered performing arts.

The New Haven Symphony Orchestra is the fourth oldest in America. The New York Philharmonic, the Boston Symphony and the Chicago Symphony are older. It was formed in 1894 and gave its first concert in January 1895. The home for the NHSO is Yale's historic Woolsey Hall. They play there regularly. They also go on tours to other cities and states to play. The symphony plays traditional classical music most of the time. They have done some pop concerts from time to time. The symphony has over 70 professional musicians!

The Connecticut Ballet was founded in 1981. It performs at the Stamford Center for the Arts and in theaters all over the state. The Connecticut Ballet offers educational assemblies for schools and groups. Perhaps you will see one of their performances soon!

The Stamford Center for the Arts strives to make the best in the performing arts available to the public. They operate two theaters; the Palace Theater and the Rich Forum. Both are in downtown Stamford. If you have been to one of these theaters, you know that you may see a ballet or enjoy the symphony, plays, musicals and other performing arts.

Visual Arts

Those arts such as paintings or sculptures are called visual arts.

Willis S. Adams (1844-1921) was born in Suffield, Connecticut. His talent appeared at a young age. He told stories of how he would draw pictures in the dirt with the handle of the hoe when he should have been tending the garden.

Adams received an opportunity to go to Europe and study art. After that he returned to Connecticut. He became a well-known landscape artist. Some of his work has been on display at the Wadsworth Atheneum in Hartford.

Museums

Museums are also a great way to enjoy art. Many Connecticut counties have museums that contain various historical themes. A museum can feature just about anything. Museums such as the Connecticut Science Center feature special exhibits.

Other well-known Connecticut museums include the Wadsworth Atheneum in Hartford and the Florence Griswold Museum in Old Lyme.

The Wadsworth was established in 1842. It is America's oldest public art museum. Its permanent collection contains more than 50,000 pieces of art showing 5,000 years of history. Wow!

The transformation of the Griswold house into a museum started in 1899. Some artists approached Florence because her home looked like a perfect place for the artists to work. It quickly became the center of the art community. Today it is strictly a museum. The site is 11 acres in size! The museum holds summer art camps and other programs for kids. Bring your art supplies and sketch this beautiful house!

Have you visited one of these museums?

title: Born to Write
text:
Some people are just born storytellers. Samuel Clemens is one of the most beloved of all American storytellers. His wit and humor are woven throughout his collections. He wrote "Adventures of Huckleberry Finn," "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer," "The Prince and the Pauper" and "A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court."

Sam grew up in Hannibal, Missouri. He spent many hours watching the riverboats and barges float by. He daydreamed of adventures as a riverboat captain. His dreams were put on hold when his father died. He was only 11 at the time. Sam was apprenticed to a local newspaper printer the next year. He learned to set type and tried his hand at some reporting. He worked for several newspaper companies until he got a chance to apprentice on a riverboat. He worked on the Mississippi riverboat for two years and finally secured his license as a cub pilot.

With the start of the Civil War, traffic on the Mississippi was suspended. Sam found himself without a job. He traveled west. He found stories to tell wherever he went. He enjoyed writing of the humorous and unusual. He soon developed a style of his own.

Sam Clemens began using the pen name of Mark Twain. Sam traveled widely and wrote everything from newspaper columns to speeches. When he finally settled down, it was to marry Olivia Langdon. The Clemens' first child was Langdon. He died when only 2 years of age.

The Clemens family then moved to Hartford, Connecticut. Their second child, Suzy, was born shortly after that. They built a house near another famous author in Hartford. They lived next to Harriet Beecher Stowe.

Clemens wrote his most famous books while in Hartford. He enjoyed family life with his three daughters and wife. Clemens wrote, "There is no appreciation of my books that is so precious as the appreciation of my children."

Clemens closed the Hartford house and moved to Europe because of money problems. Sam was busy as a public lecturer. When Suzy returned to Hartford for a visit, she became ill and died there. Grief stricken, Olivia refused to return to the Hartford home, and it was eventually sold.

The home in Hartford has been restored today. People from around the country visit the home of the famous author. Have you read any of the books written by Samuel Clemens?

title: Connecticut Arts and Leisure
text:
The Children's Museum of Connecticut

An Interactive Museum for Kids of All Ages

The Children's Museum in West Hartford is the kid-picked favorite! It is loaded with fun learning experiences. The TCM is a great place to spend some time with your family. The center has many different exhibits. Let's visit some together.

Conny the Whale

Conny is a life-sized model of a sperm whale. The whale is Connecticut's state animal. It is 60 feet long, and children can climb inside of it. Be careful not to get swallowed up!

The Gengras Planetarium

Take a trip through the universe and explore its wonders in one of the planetarium shows. The star projector can show just about anyplace in the night sky.

Turtle Town

Try on a turtle shell, read about turtles and be amazed at the variety of turtles that are on display.

UTC Wildlife Sanctuary

Nearly 50 species of animals are here for kids to see. There are demonstrations on many of them. Kids can learn about the history of the animals and how they came to be at the Sanctuary.

Other Exhibits

In the Idea Zone you'll find a Lego race track, giant bubbles, a walk-in kaleidoscope and more. The World Weather Window lets you monitor weather conditions, practice forecasting and use the rooftop weather station. You can also measure the Earth's rotation with the Foucault Pendulum in the main lobby. Another favorite is the Kids' Corner, where you can freeze your shadow on the wall. Come explore this wonderful museum!

Connecticut for Kids

Let's look at some great things for kids to do in Connecticut today

1. The Mystic Aquarium is a great way to spend a day. You can get your hands right in the water. You can touch cownose rays as they glide through the water in the new touch pool. Other exhibits feature jellyfish, penguins, sea lions and beluga whales. Have an interactive experience in the 4-D movie theater.

2. Visit one of the largest dinosaur track sites in North America at Dinosaur State Park in Rocky Hill. Inside the dome you will find lots of dinosaur tracks. You will also see life-size dioramas of the Triassic and Jurassic periods. There are interactive displays too! Try the discovery room and reconstruct a geologic formation.

Outside are nature trails, an arboretum, picnic areas and a track casting area. You can even make your own dinosaur track casting. Call the park before you go to see what you need to bring.If you like books, they have thousands of books and manuals about aviation as well.

3. No list of kids' favorite-places-to-visit would be complete without a trip to the beach! Henry Hudson sailed the New England coastline. As he did he marveled at the long stretch of white sandy shoreline. People still enjoy this natural beauty 400 years later. Spend a day in the sun creating wonderful sandcastles or visit your favorite lighthouse. Don't forget your swimsuit!

4. Take a trip to Windsor Locks and visit the New England Air Museum. Learn about aviation history and technology with special attention to Connecticut contributions. There are many different aircraft on display. You can see the landmarks that changed aviation history! Learn about the men and women in the history of aviation. You can also hear first-hand stories from veterans who flew these aircraft.

5. Have you visited the Danbury Railway Museum? What a great place to visit to learn about the role railroads played in our history.

You can see the many pieces of original and restored engines, cars and cabooses. They even have a working turntable. You can take a short local ride on one of their trains as well. Be sure to visit the restored train station. There may even be a chance to work on the railroad!

title: Free Enterprise
text:
Have you ever heard the term "free enterprise?" What does it mean? Free enterprise refers to a market economy. When people in the market have their own ways to make and sell a product, it is called a market economy. The United States has a free enterprise system. Free enterprise markets only work if the laws of a country and the values of its citizens support them. If this type of market doesn't exist, then the system will fail.

Four pillars keep our free enterprise market standing. We will talk about the first two pillars today. They are private property and the price system.

Private Property - Do you own a bike, a board game or a CD player? Did you know that these things are considered your private property? That's right! This means that you are responsible for your own property. If you don't take good care of your things, no one else will. You must pay to have your things replaced or fixed.

Private property is the first pillar in the free enterprise system. It influences all of us to care for the things we own, or provides us with incentive. Incentive is what motivates us to make the decisions we make. If a business does not take care of its office building or breaks the equipment, it must pay to replace them. This gives the business incentive to take good care of the things it uses.

Price System - Prices provide guidance for producers and consumers. They show the market how much customers value the producer's goods. They also provide clues for economists about whether a market is healthy or not.

Prices also provide incentives for businesses and consumers. For example, most consumers try to shop for bargains if prices rise. Maybe consumers buy many packets of something because it is on sale. Can you think of other ways private property and the price system affect our economy?

title: United Nations and Preamble
text:
In previous issues, we talked about the Constitution of the United States and the Bill of Rights. The United Nations also has a Charter, or a constitution, that provides for the framework that governs what it may do. Read the preamble to that Charter and discuss how your class can contribute to world peace.

We the peoples of the United Nations, determined to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war, which twice in our lifetime has brought untold sorrow to mankind, and to reaffirm faith in fundamental rights in the dignity and worth of the human person, in the equal rights of men and women and of large and small, and to establish conditions under which justice and respect for the obligations arising from treaties and other sources of international law can be maintained and to promote social progress and better standards to life in larger freedom.

And to these ends . . .

To practice tolerance and live together in peace with one another as good neighbors, and to unite our strength to maintain international peace and security and to ensure, by the acceptance of principles and the institution of methods, that armed force shall not be used, save in the common interest, and to employ international machinery for the promotion of the economic and social advancement of all peoples.

title: Connecticut Hockey
text:
Are you a hockey fan? Connecticut has three professional hockey teams!

The Connecticut Whale competes in the Northeast Division of the American Hockey League. Home ice is the XL Center in Hartford.They are affiliated with the New York Rangers.

The Bridgeport Sound Tigers also compete in the Northeast Division. Home ice is at the Webster Bank Arena. They are affiliated with the New York Islanders.

Connecticut's newest team is the Danbury Whalers. They play in the Federal Hockey league at the Danbury Ice Arena. Cheer on one of our state's great hockey teams!

title: Who served the first hamburger?
text:
Well, according to some, it was Louis Lassen of New Haven, Connecticut. In 1900 at his luncheonette called Louis' Lunch, he ground up some beef scraps and served it between two slices of bread to a customer that was in a hurry and wanted to eat it on the run. The hamburger was born.

While there are some other claims to being the first, Louis' grandson Kenneth Lassen claims to have official documentation proving that his grandfather was first.

Today, you can still visit them for a tasty treat. They grill the burgers vertically on a gas grill and serve them between two slices of toast. Don't ask for ketchup or mustard, however; they don't believe it belongs on a hamburger!

title: Cottontail
text:
Did you know that a hare is different than a rabbit? Hares are born with hair on them and their eyes open. Rabbits are born blind and with no hair.

A cottontail is a rabbit. The eastern cottontail grows about 13 to 16 inches long. It has a white tail, which is where they get their name. The cottontail makes its home in a vacant hole or a bush. The female gives birth several times a year with up to seven young each time. Cats, foxes, hawks and owls are predators that help keep the bunny numbers down.

Another difference between rabbits and hares - rabbits have a smaller gait and are better runners. Hares, in contrast, can jump very high.

During the day, rabbits hide in thick cover. You may not be able to see them, but look for their tracks. Cottontails do not tame easily and generally do not make good pets.

title: Plagiarism
text:
Plagiarism is a long word and it’s hard to spell. But it’s very important you know and understand its meaning.

To plagiarize something is to steal another person’s writings, thoughts or inventions.

It means to take credit for that person’s ideas. This practice is dishonest, even if the writings have never been published. Another word for plagiarism is “copying.” In many schools, a student can be kicked out for plagiarizing. We should never steal another person’s ideas.

There are many ways to avoid plagiarism. Let’s look at some ideas you can use to become a writer who doesn’t plagiarize. By doing these things, you can always be confident in your work.

• Paraphrase, or re-write in your own words. Read what several different writers say on the subject. Then write your version of what they’ve written.

• Use quotations. It’s perfectly okay to state what another person has written on a subject. You just need to give credit to that person. Here’s an example: As Huckleberry Finn said to his buddy, Tom Sawyer, “. . . . .”

• Your opinion. What you think about a subject is what really matters. Read about the subject first. Then put down on paper what you truly feel about it!

Your teachers really want you to succeed. If you worry your writing is not what you’d like it to be, ask your teacher for advice. You will never lose marks for asking a teacher questions.

title: Connecticut Today
text:
"What a Difference a State Makes"

Connecticut's motto is "Qui Transtulit Sustinet." It means, "he who transplanted still sustains." It shows the positive attitude of our people as they step into the future while embracing their proud heritage. Connecticut has always been progressive. It has often led the nation in preparing for the future.

We have learned about the ingenuity of some Connecticut inventors. Our people continue in that tradition today. They strive to make things better for themselves, their state and their country. What does ingenuity mean? It is the quality of being creative.

Let's take a look at Connecticut's economy. Economy is the way a state makes and uses its goods and money. Connecticut has many types of businesses. They all work together to create a strong economy.

Connecticut is known for its insurance industry today. Many of the nation's largest and most successful insurance companies are located here.

Connecticut is near New York City, Philadelphia and other major cities. This makes a strong market for their manufactured goods. Look at the chart and see what percentage makes up Connecticut's industry. Industry refers to manufacturing businesses. You will see that about 20 percent of Connecticut's economy is supported by industry. What is being produced or made? The state makes many chemical products. Some of those include medicine, shampoo and paint. Connecticut also makes a lot of electronics and industrial equipment.

Praxair in Danbury produces industrial gases. United Technologies of Hartford makes parts for aircraft engines. International Paper Company of Stamford makes paper products. Other factories make computers, clothing, medical instruments and printed materials.

Before factories were built in Connecticut, many of its residents made a living from farming. Look at the graph: Less than one percent of Connecticut's production is from farming today. Connecticut is known for its peaches and pears, but it boasts other crops as well. Gardeners in greenhouses grow millions of roses each year. Connecticut is also home to many dairy farms.

Included in the agricultural section of the pie graph is the fishing industry. Did you know that Connecticut produces more oysters than any other state in the northeast region? Fishermen also bring in flounder, bass, crabs and lobsters.

Most of Connecticut's workforce can be found in the service industries. Look at the pie graph once again. General Services, Wholesale/Retail and Finance/Insurance/Real Estate combine to form about 80 percent of the pie graph. Wholesale is selling products to businesses. Retail is selling products to individual buyers. Service jobs are those in which workers help people. Service workers in Connecticut include government workers, salesclerks, waiters, doctors and real estate workers. Military personnel and researchers also have service jobs. Pfizer of Groton is one of the nation's leading pharmaceutical research companies. Many Connecticuters work on marvelous inventions and developments there.

Tourism is another leading service industry. Connecticut's seashore, lakes and parks are packed with visitors each summer. In the winter, ski slopes in the northwest are busy. Thousands of Connecticuters work in Connecticut's tourism industry.

It is because of the ingenuity of our people that Connecticut continues to progress. Connecticut workers are proud of their state!

title: Fact Finders
text:
The U.S. Census Bureau collects statistics about the people of this country. They do this every 10 years. Statistics are facts that are gathered to get information about a certain subject.

Fact finding is one of America's oldest activities. Did you know a census was taken in Virginia as early as 1600? It was used to count the people in the Colonies.

There was a great need for a census to be taken after the Revolutionary War. The first American census was taken in 1790. The census counted 3.9 million people in our newly formed country.

The need for information about people and their needs became more complex as time went on. The facts gathered help leaders understand what is happening. They also help us make plans for the future. The first questions about manufacturing were included in 1810. Questions about fisheries were added in 1840. Questions about taxation, income, crime and churches were added in 1850. By the 1880 and 1890 censuses there was a large variety of questions. It took almost a full decade to publish the results!

The census information is often gathered by mail. A person who asks questions may also stop at your house. Replies from people are used only to obtain statistical information. By law, the census takers or employees are not allowed to reveal any information about any one person, household or business.

title: Protecting Our Environment
text:
Connecticut is the third-smallest state. It is 29th in population. This means more people are living in a smaller area than many other states. Because of all the people, we need to conserve. Conservation means to protect our forests, rivers and other natural resources. We protect them by using them wisely.

Our people work hard at controlling pollution. Pollution is chemicals or dirt that get into the air or waterways. Years of efforts are paying off. The number of fish, such as striped bass, has increased. The fishing industry is improving as waters are cleaned up. There are also limits on how many fish you can catch.

Many Connecticut residents get their drinking water directly from groundwater. So you can see how important it is that we protect this resource.

For example, a few companies manufactured plastic moulding in Cheshire from 1966 to 1980. They polluted the ground with solvents and organic chemicals. These pollutants made their way into the water table. There they polluted the wells of the local residents. This meant we couldn't use our wells anymore. The people had to hook up to the municipal water system. This water came from a different source. It was also treated with chemicals.

Right now more than 90 percent of Connecticut's ground water is suitable for drinking without being treated. That's pretty good, but incidents of ground water contamination still happen. All of the drinking water comes from either the ground or rivers. It is very important to do what we can to keep it clean. Polluting one water source can also pollute another. We humans are not the only ones who drink this water either. Think of all the animals and fish who depend on water as well.

Protecting the Earth

Earth is an amazing planet. Its water, atmosphere and soil give life to hundreds of thousands species of flowering plants and more than a million species of animals. Humans are just one species, but it turns out that not all of us are good at sharing our planet. Many of the problems facing Earth's species are caused by people. American cars, factories, machines and chemicals are polluting the air, water and soil.

Although air pollution has decreased in the past 30 years, many areas in the United States still exceed the national standards set by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). The EPA also tests America's rivers, lakes and estuaries (coastal areas where freshwater and saltwater mix). Many of them are polluted by chemicals.

People are also responsible for the destruction of the habitats of many plants and animals. As Earth's population increases, people are sprawling out across the Earth and sometimes destroying places other species used to call home.

Have you heard the phrase "between a rock and a hard place"? In many ways people are between a rock and a hard place as they look for solutions to these problems. For example, people need cars to get around, but cars pollute the air. Another thing that makes finding answers a real challenge is that experts don't always agree about how to fix things. And many solutions would be very expensive.

That's the bad news. The good news is many thousands of people do know how to share our planet. They are working to find solutions to the problems we all face. Not only scientists, but also ordinary people like us can help.

Probably the most popular campaign to get people involved has been "Reduce, Reuse and Recycle." The three Rs stand for reducing the amount of packaging, reusing containers instead of throwing them away and recycling things like cans, bottles and papers. The goal is to decrease the amount of trash that is going into landfills, because we are running out of space. Each year, Americans generate more than hundreds of millions of tons of trash. What can you do? Reduce, reuse and recycle!

How are governments around the world helping to save the planet? Many governments have laws and regulations that help make things better. (Regulations are special rules that control the way things are done.) Some laws regulate how much pollution factories can put into the air or water.

Some rules protect plants and animals. Other rules protect wilderness areas. In many countries, there are laws that say companies that cut down trees must replace some or all of them with new trees. Governments have also made rules that required automobile manufacturers to build cars that get better gas mileage and produce less pollution.

title: Market Competition and Entrepreneurship
text:
Last week, we talked about the first two pillars of free enterprise. These pillars are private property (rights that allow us to own things) and the price system, which helps value and ration scarce goods. You might already know that there is more than one way to divide our resources among all of the consumers. One way is through market competition. It is the third pillar of the free enterprise system. This week we will finish talking about the last two pillars - market competition and entrepreneurship.

Market Competition - Do you remember when we talked about scarcity? Scarcity happens when products and resources are rare. Sometimes we want more of something than is available for us to have. Markets have this same kind of competition. Businesses compete every day for resources and products. They also compete for consumers!

Businesses create competition in the economy when they offer money for resources they want. Maybe they are offering money for machines they need. Or maybe they need skilled workers. Did you know that the more skills and education you have, the more companies will compete for you to work for them? Think of that! As you compete to get a job, companies are competing for the best-trained workers, too.

Businesses also compete for products and profit. They mostly do this by keeping their production prices low. They also do this by advertising (or telling people about) their products. Businesses compete with other businesses that have similar products.

Entrepreneurship - The last pillar under free enterprise is entrepreneurship. Remember good old Benjamin Franklin? Benjamin Franklin invented things and competed as a businessman. There are many entrepreneurs creating products and competing in our world today.

Entrepreneurs compete by thinking of better products for consumers. If people are unhappy with their breakfast cereal, an entrepreneur somewhere might come up with a way to improve their breakfast. Then the entrepreneur will turn around and use their product to compete with the other cereals. Entrepreneurs hope to make a profit competing with other companies. They use creativity and their incentive for profit to think up ideas that benefit everyone. What are some other ways entrepreneurs affect market competition in the economy?

title: Treaties
text:
A diplomat is a person who has the job to handle relations between his or her country and other countries of the world. A diplomat is a specially trained person who is very skilled at dealing with tense and difficult feelings. The government of their country appoints most diplomats.

One of the things diplomats may do is write a treaty. A treaty is a signed agreement between two parties, or countries. A treaty is one way a nation can end a war or a disagreement. Do you remember learning about the Treaty of Paris in a previous issue of Studies Weekly? It was entered between the United States and Great Britain. Who were the diplomats? Was it favorable to the United States or Great Britain? Do you remember what the treaty accomplished?

title: How big was the biggest iceberg?
text:
The biggest iceberg ever recorded broke off from the Ross Ice Shelf, Antarctica, in May 2000. It was 170 miles long and 25 miles wide. That's 4,250 square miles in area - almost as big as the whole state of Connecticut! (4,845 square miles). It was named B-15.

The process of an iceberg falling off an ice shelf or glacier is called calving. B-15 remained pretty much intact, calving a few smaller icebergs, until a powerful storm broke it into two smaller pieces in October 2003. Those two pieces were still very large.

Do some research to find out what other icebergs are forming.

title: American Black Bear
text:
Did you know the American black bear isn't always black? It can be light brown, beige, dark brown, cinnamon and even a blueish-gray color!

The black bear is a large mammal with a heavy body, short tail and rounded ears. It has four curved toes on each front foot and five on each back foot. Its curved claws help it to climb trees.

Bears can live to be 25 years old. They live under trees and bushes and can often be seen walking in streams and creek beds. Though they weigh between 125 and 600 pounds, they can run very fast - over 25 miles per hour!

Black bears have one to four cubs, with an average of two. The cubs are very tiny when born, have no hair and are blind.

title: Taking Notes in Class
text: Learning how to take good notes in class is very important. Taking notes in class can be difficult. Sometimes it’s hard to concentrate and you can miss some information. Or you can’t read what you wrote. Other times, you’re not sure what information to write down. It’s important to learn how to take good notes. Without notes, taking tests is much harder! Here are some ways to take good notes in class. Be ready. You don’t always need to have a pen in hand, but have your notebook open to a clean page. And have a pen or pencil nearby. When the teacher enters the room, you’re ready to begin. Put the date and topic on top of the page. Knowing when you took the notes will help you study for tests. You can quickly flip through the pages and find the topic. Don’t waste time writing what you already know. Notes help you remember what you learned in class. If you’re sure you know something, then don’t write it down. Let’s say you know George Washington was the first U.S. president. You don’t need to write it down. Instead, you can focus on his birth date, where he lived and what he did. Make lists. Lists are easy to recognize and read. They organize the information. If you can make a list, you’ll likely remember the information later. Remember, note taking will improve your learning. But your notes won’t make much sense if your eyes are always glued to the paper. Take some time to really listen to your teacher. Stop every now and then to listen and to watch your teacher. Write down the examples that are written on the board. By doing this, you’re sure to have success in class!

title: Let's Write
text: Pollution control is always a community concern where a small area is inhabited by a very large population such as in Connecticut. Brainstorm with your classmates to think of places in your community that need to be cleaned up or protected from pollution. What are some ways YOU can make a difference? Make a list of your ideas, then develop a class pledge that tells of your commitment to protect the environment.

title: Fun Facts
text: The longest city name in the world is officially Krungthep Mahanakhon Amorn Rattanakosin Mahintara Yudthaya Mahadilok Pohp Noparat Rajathanee Bureerom Udomrajniwes Mahasatarn Amorn Pimarn Avaltarnsatit Sakatattiya Visanukram Prasit. You may have heard of it, it is also called Bangkok, Thailand.

title: Farewell Fun!
text:
This is the final issue of Connecticut Studies Weekly for this school year. We hope you have enjoyed our paper and learned something as well. We have taken you back to the dinosaurs, met the American Indians who first lived here, learned about the European settlers and finally come back to present-day Connecticut. Together we have learned about our government and how to be a good citizen. You read about many famous people in Connecticut history, including women, inventors and leaders.

Well, our final issue is going to make it fun to review much of what we have talked about this year, but first...some things to think about. Here are a few simple questions to get your think tank warmed up.

Who's buried in Grant's tomb?

If there are two barbers in town and one has a bad haircut and one has a great haircut, to which do you go for your haircut?

How many z's are in a dozen?

If a rooster lays an egg on the peak of your roof, which side will the egg roll down?

Now that you have thought about those for awhile, you are ready to move on to the questions and games on the following pages. We have crossword puzzles, word searches, multiple choice and true and false questions, fill in the blanks and matching quizzes.

We hope you have a great summer! Keep learning about our great state of Connecticut. Perhaps you will get to visit some places in Connecticut that you have never been to before.

OK! Are you ready? Turn the page and let's get started.

title: Sharing Public Space: Susan B. Anthony and Equal Rights for All
text:
From the time she was a young girl, Susan B. Anthony believed that what was open to one person should be open to all people. As a teacher, she felt that having separate schools for girls, boys and free African Americans was not fair. She believed that the minds of all genders and races were equal and that education should be equal, too.

As Susan grew older, she joined other fights as well. She hated slavery and thought working women should be paid more money. She began fighting for women's suffrage, or the right for women to vote. She once was arrested for voting illegally and was fined $100. She wouldn't pay the fine. She said, "Trust me that as I ignore all law to help the slave, so will I ignore it all to protect an enslaved woman." Until women were allowed to vote, just like men, Susan felt they were no better off than slaves. She fought for this right until her death in 1906, but at that time, women still couldn't vote.

Susan's efforts finally paid off when the 19th Amendment to the Constitution was passed in 1920. It gave all American women the right to vote. In her honor, the amendment is also called the Susan B. Anthony Amendment.

title: La seguridad en las ciencias
text: Es importante estar protegidos en las ciencias. ¿Cómo estamos protegidos? Sigue las reglas y utiliza los instrumentos correctos. Eso te mantendrá protegido en las ciencias.

title: Protégete

Tienes que:

title: La Tierra
text: La Tierra es un planeta grande y redondo. La capa exterior de la Tierra es la corteza. Debajo de la corteza hay una capa llamada manto. En el centro de la Tierra se encuentra el núcleo. El núcleo está muy, muy caliente.

title: La corteza terrestre
text: La mayor parte de la corteza terrestre está cubierta por agua. Imagina que la Tierra es un pastel cortado en cuatro pedazos. Tres de esos pedazos estarían cubiertos de agua y el cuarto no. La corteza está hecha de rocas y tierra.

title: Continentes e islas
text: Los grandes trozos de tierra se llaman continentes. Un trozo de tierra con agua alrededor se llama isla.

title: Terremotos
text: La Tierra está siempre cambiando. Cuando la corteza se mueve, puede causar un terremoto. Los terremotos fuertes pueden causar muchos daños.

title: Volcanes
text: Los volcanes en erupción despiden lava muy caliente. Cuando la lava se enfría, forma tierra nueva.

title: Los geólogos

title: Haz y aprende
text:
¡Rompamos rocas!

Necesitas:

Una roca grande

Un martillo

Un calcetín largo

Un plato o bandeja

Una toalla

Una tabla de corte

Gafas de protección

Una lupa

Tienes que:

1. Doblar la toalla y colocarla sobre la mesa

2. Acomodar la tabla de corte sobre la toalla.

3. Poner la roca en el calcetín y ubicarla sobre la tabla de corte.

4. Colocarte las gafas de protección para cubrir tus ojos.

5. Golpear la roca con el martillo hasta que se rompa en pedazos. Puede que tengas que golpearla más de una vez.

6. Sacudir los pedazos de roca fuera del calcetín, sobre el plato.

7. Quitarte las gafas protectoras y observar los pedazos de roca con la lupa.

Cuéntale a tus amigos sobre la experiencia de romper las rocas. ¿Qué otras herramientas podrías usar para romperlas? Observa un pedazo de las rocas de tus amigos con una lupa. ¿En qué se parece al pedazo de tu roca? ¿En qué se diferencia?

title: Agua
text: La mayor parte del agua de la Tierra está en los océanos. Otra parte está en lagos, ríos y lagunas. También está en riachuelos y arroyos. Todos los seres vivos necesitan agua para sobrevivir.

title: Agua dulce, agua salada
text: El agua del océano es agua salada. Los humanos no podemos beberla. Los lagos, ríos y lagunas tienen agua dulce. Los arroyos y riachuelos también. Podemos tomar agua dulce si está limpia.

title: Agua líquida
text: Cuando el agua es líquida, podemos beberla. Pero el agua no siempre es líquida. Puede ser sólida o gaseosa.

title: Agua sólida
text: Cuando el agua está sólida, es hielo. El agua se convierte en sólido cuando se congela.

title: Agua gaseosa
text: El agua se convierte en gas cuando la hervimos. Puedes observar el gas. Es el vapor que está sobre el agua hirviendo.

title: Agua dentro de ti
text: El agua está en cada ser vivo. El agua está en las plantas. El agua está en los animales. ¡El agua esta dentro de ti!

4. Verter un poco del agua con sal en el platillo.

title: Tiempo
text: ¿Cómo está el tiempo hoy? ¿Está soleado o nublado? ¿Hace calor o frío? El tiempo es diferente en las distintas estaciones. El tiempo es diferente en las distintas partes del mundo.

title: El aire
text: Alrededor de la Tierra hay una capa de aire, casi como una sábana. Aquí es donde el tiempo toma forma. El aire está siempre moviéndose. El aire que se mueve se llama viento.

title: Las nubes
text: Los cirros son nubes livianas y plumosas. Los verás en el cielo a gran altura. Los estratos son nubes en capas planas. Los cúmulos son nubes de lluvia. Cuando los cúmulos se vuelven muy grandes, caen fuertes lluvias.

title: Tormentas
text: Una tormenta es algo que pasa cuando hay fuertes lluvias o nieve y mucho viento. Las tormentas pueden provocar relámpagos y truenos.

title: Desastres naturales
text: Algunas tormentas causan inundaciones. Los huracanes y los tornados son tormentas. Una ventisca es una tormenta de nieve.

title: En caso de tormenta
text: ¿Qué debes hacer para mantenerte seguro durante una tormenta? Ir a la habitación que se encuentre en el nivel más bajo de tu edificio. Mantenerte alejado de las ventanas. Si se acerca un huracán fuerte, es posible que tú y tu familia tengáis que ser evacuados. Eso quiere decir que tendréis que abandonar la ciudad o el pueblo e ir a un lugar seguro.

title: El espacio
text: Hay muchos objetos en el espacio. Las estrellas y los planetas están en el espacio. El sol y la luna están en el espacio. ¿Te gustaría ser astronauta algún día?

title: El ciclo de la luna
text: El modo en que vemos la luna tiene un patrón o ciclo. Estas imágenes muestran el patrón. El patrón o ciclo comienza cada 28 días. Cuando apenas puedes ver la luna, es luna nueva. Cuando la luna se ve como un círculo, es luna llena. ¿Puedes encontrar las medias lunas?

title: El color de las estrellas
text: Las estrellas pueden ser de diferentes colores. Las estrellas azules o blancas son las más brillantes y las de mayor temperatura. Las estrellas amarillas no tienen tanta temperatura. Nuestro sol es una estrella amarilla. Las estrellas rojas son más frías que otras estrellas.

title: El tamaño de las estrellas
text: Las estrellas pueden ser de diferentes tamaños. Las estrellas rojas son generalmente las más grandes.

title: Haz y aprende
text:
Una bebida patas arriba

La gravedad es lo que evita que las cosas vuelen al espacio. Mantiene el agua en el vaso, y te mantiene a ti en la Tierra. En el espacio no hay gravedad.

NECESITAS:

Un vaso de agua

Una silla

Un sorbete flexible

TIENES QUE:

1. Colocar el vaso de agua en el piso cerca de la silla.

2. Recostarte sobre la silla apoyando el estómago. La cabeza debe quedar del lado en el que está el agua. Pídele a un amigo que sostenga el sorbete.

3. Primero, trata de tomar un trago sin usar el sorbete.

4. Ahora, intenta tomar usándola.

¿QUÉ SUCEDE?

La gravedad te ayuda a comer y a beber. Te ayuda a empujar para que el alimento y la bebida pasen por el estómago. Cuando estás acostado en la silla, la gravedad trabaja en tu contra.

Es más fácil usar el sorbete.

title: El sol
text: El sol es importante para la vida en la Tierra. Nos da luz y calor. Sale y se pone todos los días.

title: La Tierra mueve
text: Desde la Tierra, parece que el sol se mueve por el cielo. Pero en realidad, es la Tierra la que se mueve. La Tierra rota, o gira, de la misma manera que el globo terráqueo de tu aula.

title: Día y noche
text: A medida que la Tierra rota, la luz del sol alcanza una parte distinta del mundo. Por ese motivo, cuando es de día en un lado de la Tierra, en el otro lado es de noche.

title: ¿Cuántos días tiene un año?
text: La Tierra se mueve alrededor del sol. Demora un año en dar toda una vuelta. ¿Cuántos días tiene un año?

title: ¿Cuántas horas tiene un día?
text: La Tierra demora 24 horas para realizar una rotación completa. Cada día tiene 24 horas.

title: Mira y aprende
text:
Cuando la luz del sol atraviesa una gota de lluvia, la luz cambia de dirección. Así se forman los arcoíris.

¿Sabes cuáles son los colores del arcoíris? Rojo, naranja, amarillo, verde, azul, añil y violeta son los colores del arcoíris.

title: Haz y aprende
text:
¿Cómo se forman los arcoíris?

NECESITAS:

Una caja de zapatos

Tijeras

Un papel blanco

Un vaso

Un día soleado

Agua

TIENES QUE:

1. Hacer un corte en un extremo de la caja de zapatos.

2. Colocar el papel en el fondo y los lados de la caja de zapatos. Quizás tengas que recortarlo para que encaje.

3. Colocar la caja en una ventana. Coloca el lado con el corte hacia el sol.

4. Llenar el vaso con agua. Luego colócalo en la caja al lado del corte.

5. ¿Ves un arcoíris en el papel?

¿QUÉ SUCEDE?

La luz del sol entra en la caja. Cuando la luz atraviesa el agua, cambia de dirección. Las distintas partes de la luz generan los colores del arcoíris.

title: ¿Has visto un arcoíris?
text:
Piensa en alguna vez en que hayas visto un arcoíris. A continuación, responde a las preguntas

2. ¿Qué crees que estaría pasando afuera antes de que lo vieras?

title: Seres vivientes
text: La Tierra es el hogar de muchos seres vivientes. ¿Qué necesitan los seres vivientes para sobrevivir? Los seres vivientes poseen diferentes características que les ayudan a sobrevivir.

title: Características de los seres vivientes
text: Los seres vivientes tienen características. Estas pueden ser partes del cuerpo, como antenas y oídos. A veces pueden ser cosas que los seres vivientes pueden hacer, como colgarse con la cola u obtener agua de raíces.

title: Características que ayudan
text: Los animales tienen características que les ayudan a obtener lo que necesitan. Algunos animales tienen garras y dientes afilados que les ayudan a capturar a otros animales para alimentarse. Los peces tienen branquias para poder respirar debajo del agua.

title: Alimento y agua
text: Los seres vivientes necesitan alimento y agua. Necesitan aire para respirar y un lugar donde vivir. ¿Cómo obtienes tú y tu familia lo que necesitan?

title: Las plantas
text: Las plantas tienen características que les ayudan a obtener lo que necesitan. Tienen raíces para obtener agua del suelo. La mayoría tiene hojas para almacenar luz del sol. La luz del sol le ayuda a las plantas a generar su propio alimento.

title: Mira y aprende
text:
Esta es una célula. Todos los seres vivientes están hechos de células.

Las células son demasiado pequeñas como para que podamos verlas. Los científicos usan microscopios para ver las células.

title: Haz y aprende
text:
Polinización

La polinización es el movimiento del polen de una planta a la otra.

NECESITAS:

Un filtro de café

Pegamento

Brillo de varios colores

Una pelota de espuma pequeña

Marcadores

Palillo de dientes

TIENES QUE:

1. Colorear el filtro de café. Ésa será tu flor.

2. Colorear la pelota de espuma y sujetar el palillo de dientes a la parte inferior. Ésa será tu abeja.

3. Tu maestra colocará una pequeña cantidad de pegamento y brillo en el centro de cada flor. Ese será el polen.

4. Luego, haz que tu abeja "vuele" sobre las flores de los demás compañeros y recoge el polen pasando la abeja por la mezcla de brillo y pegamento.

¿De qué modo cambió tu flor? ¿De qué modo cambió tu abeja?

title: Las plantas
text: Millones de plantas crecen en la Tierra. Las plantas viven en todos los lugares de nuestro planeta.

title: Semillas
text: La mayoría de las plantas comienzan siendo una semilla en el suelo. Las semillas necesitan agua y luz del sol para crecer.

title: Raíces
text: Las raíces crecen en el suelo. Los brotes crecen mirando hacia el sol.

title: Hojas
text: La planta sigue creciendo, y pronto podemos ver hojas.

title: Flores
text: Las plantas florecen.

title: Frutos
text: Las flores se convierten en frutos. Los frutos tienen semillas dentro.

title: Plantas nuevas
text: A partir de las semillas pueden crecer plantas nuevas.

title: Mira y aprende
text:
¿El tomate es una fruta o una verdura? Aquí te damos una pista: las frutas tienen semillas. Las verduras son partes de las plantas: raíces, tallos u hojas.

Si has dicho que el tomate es una fruta, ¡estás en lo cierto!

title: Haz y aprende
text:
¿Cómo hacen las plantas para obtener agua?

NECESITAS:

Un clavel blanco con tallo largo

Agua

Una taza medidora

Tijeras

Colorante para alimentos rojo y azul

2 vasos largos

TIENES QUE:

1. Pedirle a tu maestra que divida el tallo del clavel desde abajo hacia arriba, pero no entero.
2. Medir 1/2 taza de agua. Verterla en el vaso. Verter 1/2 taza de agua en el otro vaso.
3. Colocar colorante para alimentos rojo en una taza. Colocar colorante para alimentos azul en la otra taza. Trata de lograr colores muy oscuros.
4. Pon un lado del tallo en el agua roja. Pon el otro lado del tallo en el agua azul.
5. Deja la flor en el agua roja y en el agua azul durante dos días.

¿QUÉ SUCEDE? La mitad de la flor se tiñe de rojo y la otra mitad se tiñe de azul. El agua roja y el agua azul subieron por el tallo hasta la flor.

title: Fruta o verdura
text:
Escribe una F en el recuadro si la imagen muestra una fruta.
Escribe una V en el recuadro si la imagen muestra una verdura.

title: Los animales
text: Millones de animales viven en la Tierra. Los animales viven en todos los continentes. ¿En qué se parecen los animales? ¿En qué se diferencian?

title: Huevos
text: La mayoría de los animales nace de huevos. Otros huevos crecen dentro del cuerpo de la madre. Algunos huevos, crecen fuera.

title: El nacimiento de los animales
text: Algunos animales nacen vivos. A algunos animales se los empolla y nacen de huevos. Este pollito acaba de salir del huevo. Apenas nacen, los animales comienzan a crecer.

title: El refugio de los animales
text: Muchos animales usan las plantas como refugio. Los pájaros construyen sus nidos con ramitas, hojas y pasto. Las arañas tejen sus telas en arbustos y ramas.

title: Gallinas y gallos
text: Estos son pollos adultos. La hembra del pollo es la gallina. Las madres gallinas ponen huevos. El macho del pollo es el gallo. Los gallos son los papás.

title: Mira y aprende
text:
Los castores usan sus dientes afilados para talar árboles.

Usan árboles, palos y barro para construir diques y madrigueras. Las madrigueras son los hogares de los castores.

title: Haz y aprende
text:
El increíble huevo de goma

NECESITAS:

Un huevo crudo

Un tarro con tapa

Vinagre blanco

Una cinta métrica

TIENES QUE:

1. Medir el huevo con la cinta métrica. Anotar los números. ¿Cuántas pulgadas?
2. Contarles a tus amigos cómo se ve y cómo se siente el huevo.
3. Cuidadosamente, colocar el huevo en el tarro. Pon atención para no dejarlo caer.
4. Verter vinagre en el tarro hasta que el huevo quede cubierto.
5. Tapar el tarro.
6. Poner el tarro en un lugar seguro durante tres días. Chequearla todos los días.
7. Al cuarto día, saca el huevo de el tarro. Mídelo otra vez.

Anota los números. ¿Cuántas pulgadas? Cuéntales a tus amigos como se ve y cómo se siente el huevo.

¿QUÉ SUCEDIÓ?

El huevo se hizo más grande porque el agua del vinagre se metió dentro. La cáscara no está porque el vinagre la disolvió.

title: Ordenar los dibujos
text: Pon estas imágenes en orden escribiendo un número debajo de cada una.

title: Tu cuerpo
text: Las personas son criaturas fascinantes. Cada parte del cuerpo tiene un trabajo importante que hacer. Todas las partes trabajan juntas para que todo el cuerpo funcione como tiene que hacerlo.

title: Los sistemas
text: Un sistema es un conjunto de partes que funcionan juntas. Tienes diferentes sistemas en el cuerpo. Cada sistema realiza un trabajo diferente.

title: El sistema digestivo
text: La boca, dientes y lengua te ayudan a comer. Dentro del cuerpo, el estómago y otros órganos deshacen la comida. Pequeñas partículas de comida, demasiado pequeñas para que las veamos, van a los vasos sanguíneos.

title: El sistema circulatorio
text: El corazón bombea sangre. Los vasos sanguíneos llevan sangre a cada parte del cuerpo. Así es como el cuerpo obtiene el alimento y el oxígeno que necesita.

title: El sistema nervioso
text: El cerebro y los nervios son parte del sistema nervioso. Los nervios llevan los mensajes de las partes del cuerpo hasta el cerebro. También llevan mensajes desde el cerebro hasta las partes del cuerpo. Los mensajes ayudan a que el cuerpo funcione como tiene que hacerlo.

title: Mira y aprende
text:
El esqueleto es el marco del cuerpo. Los huesos se ven más o menos así:

Los huesos protegen los órganos. Trabajan con los músculos para ayudarte a moverte.

title: Haz y aprende
text:
Corazón trabajador

¿Cuántas veces late tu corazón en un minuto?

NECESITAS:

Cinta

Un reloj con segundero

2 embudos

Un tubo de goma de 3 pies

TIENES QUE:

1. Colocar los embudos en los extremos del tubo. Encintarlos firmemente en el lugar.

2. Colocar un embudo sobre tu corazón. Colocar el otro en tu oído. ¿Escuchas el corazón?

3. Hacer que un amigo controle por ti un minuto.

Cuenta los latidos de tu corazón. Anota aquí los números.

title: Los seres vivos crecen
text: Las plantas, los animales y las personas crecen. Conforme crecen, cambian. ¿Cómo has cambiado tú desde que naciste? Eres más alto y pesas más. Has aprendido muchas cosas nuevas, y aún sigues aprendiendo.

title: Las personas crecen
text: Las personas empiezan su vida como bebés. Crecen y se convierten en niños y aprenden a caminar y a hablar. Los niños se convierten en adolescentes y pueden aprender muchas cosas. Finalmente, se convierten en adultos.

title: Padres e hijos
text: Cuando los seres vivos dejan de crecer, pueden tener hijos. Un hijo se parece mucho a sus padres, aunque no es exactamente como ellos.

title: Cómo crecemos
text: ¿Cómo crecen los seres vivos? Necesitan energía. Las personas y los animales obtienen energía de los alimentos. Las plantas hacen su propia energía.

title: Nada vive para siempre
text: Los seres vivos no viven para siempre. Muchos insectos viven menos de un año, algunas personas viven 100 años o más, y algunos árboles pueden vivir cientos o incluso miles de años.

title: Mariposas - huevos
text: Una mariposa empieza como un huevo.

title: Mariposas - oruga
text: El huevo se convierte en una oruga.

title: Mariposas - crisálida
text: La oruga forma una crisálida.

title: Mariposas adultas
text: Una mariposa adulta sale de la crisálida.

title: Haz y aprende
text:
Mariposas

Lo que necesitas

1 pieza pequeña de pasta de forma redonda

1 pieza pequeña de pasta en forma de concha

1 pieza pequeña de pasta en forma de espiral

4 piezas de cartón

marcadores o crayones

pegamento

Qué hacer

1. Pega cada una de las piezas de pasta en una pieza cuadrada de cartón.

2. Escribe "huevo" bajo la pasta redonda.

3. Escribe "oruga" bajo la pasta en espiral.

4. Escribe "crisálida" bajo la pasta en forma de concha.

5. Usa los marcadores o crayones para dibujar una mariposa en la última pieza de cartón y escribe "mariposa" bajo tu dibujo.

6. Coloca las piezas de cartón en orden para mostrar el ciclo de vida de una mariposa.

title: Ordenar los dibujos
text: Coloca estas imágenes en orden. Escribe 1 bajo la imagen que muestra lo que sucede primero, escribe 2 bajo la imagen que muestra lo que sucede después y continúa así.

title: Mantente sano
text: ¿Cómo puedes mantenerte sano? Come los alimentos correctos para tener mucha energía, ejercita tu cuerpo todos los días para mantenerlo fuerte y duerme lo suficiente para descansar y estar alerta en la escuela.

title: Estar activo
text: Debes estar activo aproximadamente una hora todos los días. En la escuela, puedes divertirte en el recreo y en las clases de educación física. Los fines de semana, puedes practicar un deporte o tomar clases de danza. ¿Cómo te ejercitas?

title: Descansar
text: Tu cuerpo también necesita descansar. Todas las noches debes dormir al menos diez horas. Trata de irte a la cama y despertarte a la misma hora todos los días. Tus músculos estarán listos para hacer ejercicio. Tu cerebro estará listo para un gran día en la escuela.

title: No enfermarse
text: A nadie le gusta enfermarse. Puedes ayudar a que tu cuerpo esté sano. Lávate las manos con frecuencia, no compartas vasos ni cucharas con un amigo y que el doctor te haga una revisión una vez al año. Los doctores y las enfermeras pueden ayudarte a sanar si te lesionas o te enfermas. Los doctores y las enfermeras pueden trabajar en consultorios o en un hospital.

title: Comer bien
text:
Es importante comer los alimentos correctos. Los alimentos saludables te dan energía.

Las frutas y vegetales dan a tu cuerpo vitaminas y minerales. Puedes obtener las proteínas para tener músculos fuertes de la carne sin grasa y de las habichuelas. La leche baja en grasa, el queso y el yogur ayudan a mantener tus huesos y dientes fuertes.

title: Mira y aprende
text:
“Mi Plato” nos enseña cuáles alimentos debemos comer con frecuencia y cuáles alimentos debemos comer menos.

Encierra en un círculo “Sí” si la oración es verdadera. Encierra en un círculo “No” si no es verdadera.

La parte roja del plato representa las frutas.

SíNo

Debes comer más productos lácteos que vegetales.

SíNo

Comenta con tus amigos acerca de cómo “Mi Plato” nos puede ayudar a comer correctamente y a estar sanos.

title: Haz y aprende
text:
Yogur en un palillo

Lo que necesitas

Yogur bajo en grasa (de cualquier sabor de fruta)

un vaso de papel de 5 onzas

1 pequeño palillo de madera para manualidades

envoltura plástica

Qué hacer

1. Con una cuchara, llena 3/4 del vaso con yogur.

2. Usa el palillo de manualidades para hacer un hoyo en el centro de un trozo cuadrado pequeño de la envoltura plástica. Cubre el yogur con la envoltura plástica.

3. Mete el palillo de manualidades a través del hoyo de la envoltura plástica hasta el yogur. El palillo debe quedar parado derecho.

4. Pon el yogur en el congelador. Déjalo ahí toda la noche.

5. Saca el yogur del congelador. Quita la cubierta plástica y desprende el vaso de papel.

6. ¡Disfruta un alimento saludable!

title: Leyendo las etiquetas
text:
Usa las etiquetas del recipiente del yogur para responder las preguntas:

1. ¿Cuántas onzas hay en el recipiente?

2. ¿Cuántas onzas hay en una porción?

3. ¿Cuántas calorías hay en una porción?

4. ¿Cuántos gramos de grasa hay en una porción?

5. ¿Cuántos gramos de calcio hay en una porción?

6. ¿Cuántos gramos de proteínas hay en una porción?

title: Las familias
text: Todos los seres vivos dependen de otros seres vivos para sobrevivir. Muchas personas y animales dependen de sus familias. Las familias pueden ser grandes o pequeñas. Las familias son grupos de seres vivos que están relacionados de alguna forma.

title: Grupos de animales
text: Los científicos ponen a los animales en grupos. Los animales en los grupos son parecidos en algunas formas. Algunos grupos de animales se llaman familias.

title: Perros
text: Muchas personas tienen perros como mascotas. Los perros mascotas son parte de la misma familia de animales que los coyotes, los lobos y los zorros. Los científicos llaman a estos animales caninos. Los miembros de la familia de los perros tienen dientes grandes y comen principalmente carne. Algunos miembros de la familia de los perros cazan en grupos.

title: Lagartos
text: Hay muchos tipos diferentes de lagartos. Los geckos, iguanas, dragones de Komodo y monstruos de Gila son familias de lagartos. Muchos lagartos comen plantas e insectos. Los lagartos grandes comen animales como venados y otros lagartos. La mayoría de los lagartos no atacan a las personas. Los dragones de Komodo y los monstruos de Gila pueden ser peligrosos.

title: Pingüinos
text: Hay 17 tipos diferentes de pingüinos en la Tierra. Los pingüinos más grandes son los pingüinos emperador. Pueden crecer hasta casi cuatro pies de alto y pesar hasta 90 libras. Los pingüinos azules son los más pequeños, pueden crecer hasta 16 pulgadas de alto y solo pesan alrededor de dos libras. Los pingüinos comen peces, calamares y krill. El krill es parecido a los camarones.

title: Mira y aprende
text:
Algunos animales bebés se parecen mucho a sus padres, pero algunos animales bebés son muy diferentes a sus padres. Observa estas imágenes. ¿En qué se parece la rana bebé a una rana adulta? ¿En qué es diferente? Comenta con tus amigos en qué se parecen y en qué son diferentes.

Una rana bebé se llama renacuajo. Los renacuajos nacen de huevos.

title: Haz y aprende
text:
Los olores tienen sentido

Tu sentido del olfato es importante. Puedes reconocer el olor de una deliciosa pizza horneándose en la cocina, el perfume de tu mamá o las flores de tu jardín. El olfato también forma parte del gusto.

Lo que necesitas

frutas y verduras ralladas (tu maestro elegirá algunas).

platos pequeños de papel

una servilleta

cucharas o tenedores de plástico

una venda para los ojos

Qué hacer

1. Véndate los ojos. Asegúrate de no ver nada.

2. Tápate la nariz firmemente con una mano, para que no puedas oler los alimentos.

3. Tu maestro te dará un pequeño plato con un poco de alimento. Necesitas que un amigo te ayude con una cucharada de alimento.

4. Pon los alimentos en la boca, pero no los mastiques ni los tragues todavía. Hazlos girar con la lengua. ¿A qué te sabe?

5. Ahora, mastica y traga los alimentos o escúpelos en una servilleta, si lo deseas.

6. Sigue con la venda de los ojos puesta y con la nariz tapada y uno por uno, prueba los demás alimentos. ¿A qué te saben? ¿Cuántos alimentos pudiste reconocer?

title: Llena los espacios en blanco
text:
1. Todos los seres vivos______________ de otros seres vivos para sobrevivir.

2. Los lobos son parte de la familia de los______________.

3. Una rana bebé se llama___________________.

title: Hábitats
text: Los seres vivos necesitan un lugar donde vivir. Los lugares donde las plantas y los animales viven se llaman hábitats. Las plantas y los animales diferentes viven en hábitats diferentes. Los seres vivos tienen características especiales que les ayudan a sobrevivir en sus hábitats.

title: Características
text: El aspecto que una planta o un animal tiene te puede dar pistas acerca de su hábitat. Los seres vivos tienen características especiales que les ayudan a sobrevivir en diferentes lugares. Las plantas y los animales del océano tienen características que les ayudan a sobrevivir bajo el agua. Las plantas y los animales del desierto tienen características que les ayudan a sobrevivir con poca agua. Las plantas pueden tener características como tallos largos, flores coloridas u hojas anchas. Los animales pueden tener características como dientes y garras afiladas, grandes orejas o pelaje caliente.

title: Osos polares
text:
En el Ártico hace mucho frío y mucho viento casi todo el tiempo. Algunos animales que viven todo el año en ese lugar son blancos: Se confunden con la nieve.

Los osos polares tienen un grueso pelaje y una capa de grasa para mantenerse calientes. Las focas que viven en el Ártico también tienen pelaje y grasa.

title: Insecto palo
text:
Muchos insectos son de color marrón o verde. Así es difícil verlos entre las hojas, en las hierbas o en las ramas de los árboles. Esto les ayuda a estar seguros de otros animales que pueden comérselos.

Este insecto se llama insecto palo. Los insectos palo se cuelgan de las plantas durante el día y se comen las hojas en la noche.

title: Dientes de león
text: Los dientes de león son unas hierbas que tienen raíces muy profundas. Eso hace difícil que las personas puedan sacarlas de la tierra. En la selva, algunos árboles crecen hasta más de 100 pies de alto para poder obtener suficiente luz del sol. Los lirios acuáticos tienen hojas anchas que les ayudan a flotar en la superficie del agua. Las plantas de moras tienen espinas que las protegen de los animales que pueden comérselas.

title: Mira y aprende
text:
Observa esta imagen. El pez tiene branquias que le ayudan a respirar bajo el agua y tiene aletas que le ayudan a nadar.

¿Qué otras características pueden ayudar al pez a sobrevivir bajo el agua? Escribe tu respuesta.

title: Haz y aprende
text:
La grasa del oso polar

Los osos polares tienen una capa de grasa que les ayuda a mantenerse calientes. Este "guante de grasa" te mostrará cómo funciona.

Lo que necesitas (para el grupo completo)

1 bolsa de congelar de un cuarto, con cierre

1 guante desechable por estudiante

manteca de cocinar

una cuchara grande

un tazón grande de agua helada

Qué hacer

1. Tu maestro pondrá una cucharada grande de manteca de cocinar (la grasa) en la bolsa de congelar.

2. Todos tomarán turnos. Toquen el agua helada con una mano para ver qué tan fría está. ¡Brrr!

3. Ahora ponte el guante en la mano y después introduce la mano con el guante en la bolsa de congelar llena de grasa. A continuación introduce la mano dentro del tazón con agua helada.
