title: Mother Teresa - Caring for Others
text:
"Can I go to the slums now?" said the Catholic nun to the priest. It may have seemed like a strange question. Slums, after all, are not pleasant places. Slums are full of poverty, disease and violence. Who would spend time in the slums of India if they had a choice? Well, believe it or not, working in India's slums had been the greatest desire of one small Catholic nun for two difficult years.

The nun's name was Mother Teresa. But that hadn't always been her name. She was born in 1910, long before your grandparents. Her name back then was Agnes. Her father owned a construction company. The family was wealthy. Agnes's father gave food, clothing and shelter to the poor. He taught Agnes to always share what she had with the poor. Later, when Agnes became a nun, she cared for an ill, blind child. She loved the boy and called him "the crowning joy of [her] weary day's work."

When she became a nun, Agnes changed her name to Maria Teresa. Later, people would just call her Mother Teresa. Since she learned to love the poor when she was young, maybe it's no surprise that she decided to spend the rest of her life caring for the poor. She made that decision when she was 37 years old on a trip to recover from an illness. That's when she began asking her strange question, "Can I go to the slums now?"

What do you think Mother Teresa's life was like when she began working in the slums of India? To find out, just keep reading.

title: The Red Cross - American Heroes
text:
You could see them working in the rubble of the World Trade Center. After Hurricane Katrina, there they were, wading through the flooded streets of New Orleans. From time to time, you might see them in your very own neighborhood. Who are they? You might be able to guess the name of their organization. Here's a hint: The name is the same as the design on the sides of the white trucks they use when they're helping out at the scene of a disaster. If you guessed the Red Cross, good for you! Wherever there's a disaster, you can count on the American Red Cross to be there. It's been that way since 1881. That was the year Clara Barton formed the group we know as the Red Cross.

There are Red Cross organizations in other countries, too. Sometimes other countries use different symbols for their organizations. Most Islamic countries paint a red crescent on their trucks instead of a red cross.

Much of the work of the Red Cross is done by volunteers. A volunteer is a person who does a job without being paid. Red Cross volunteers help people, especially in times of war or natural disaster. They provide food, shelter and medical attention to people who need them.

They also help people get ready for disasters before they happen. They teach classes on how to prepare and how to prevent them from happening at all.

If you see the Red Cross in your neighborhood, they're probably having a blood drive. During a blood drive, healthy adults can donate some of their blood to help care for sick people everywhere. So why do the workers of the Red Cross do all that they do? They do it just because they care. Isn't that reason enough?

title: Legacy of Caring - Mother Teresa
text:
After her long wait, the priest could only bid her farewell. Mother Teresa's life changed forever that day. She left the school where she worked and went to a hospital. She didn't go there as a patient, but as a student. She wanted to learn how to treat the diseases that she would find among the poor in the slums.

Soon, however, she returned. Together with some of her fellow nuns, she formed an order called the Missionaries of Charity. The city gave Mother Teresa and her friends a building to use as a hospital. They named the place with a Bengali word that means Pure Heart. (Bengali is the language spoken by people who live in the state of Bengal in India.) To that building, Mother Teresa brought people from the streets who were sick and dying. There they gave them comfort, warmth and food. Many of the people who came to Pure Heart were people who had been rejected by their neighbors. Their illnesses had made them "untouchable." Other people would refuse to help them, but not Mother Teresa. She and her friends would help anyone who needed it, no matter how sick or poor.

Soon, something amazing began to happen. The Missionaries of Charity began to grow. Thousands of nuns wanted to help Mother Teresa with her work. Under her direction, they opened an orphanage, and then another and another. Soon, there were missions in dozens of countries. As Mother Teresa's work grew, so did her fame. She began to travel the world, teaching people how to care for one another. Governments and other organizations wanted to give her awards. The awards included the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979. The Nobel Peace Prize is one of the greatest honors anyone can receive. The people in charge of the award had prepared a great dinner party for Mother Teresa. But she asked them to cancel the dinner to save money. Mother Teresa told them that the money they saved could feed 400 poor children for a whole year.

Mother Teresa's work was difficult. She made sure to own only two saris. A sari is a loose robe worn often by people in India. With only two saris, she could teach the poor that they could remain clean and neat, even if they only had one change of clothing. People all over the world admired the work that Mother Teresa did. Millions of people were encouraged to perform acts of kindness. They were encouraged just by watching or hearing of the things that Mother Teresa did. And she inspired and encouraged the poor as well. Once, a very ill man died quietly as she watched over him. Right before he died, he said, "I have lived so long as an animal, but I am leaving this life as an angel."

Mother Teresa died in 1997. Fifteen thousand people went to her funeral in India. Millions more listened to the funeral on the radio or watched it on television. Today, tens of thousands of volunteers serve in Mother Teresa's orphanages and hospitals. Her legacy of caring lives on. With any luck, it always will.

title: Harriet Tubman - Courage and Caring
text: In 1849, Harriet Tubman ran for her life. What else could she do? She either had to run or be sold as a slave into the deep South. She traveled 90 miles, hiking through swamps and woodlands. Finally, as a free woman, she settled in Philadelphia. She worked there as a dishwasher. Happy ending, right? Not by a long shot! There were other people living in slavery that she cared about. So Harriet sneaked back into Maryland to rescue her sister's family. Then she went back again for her brothers. Again she went back and rescued her parents. Funny thing, caring for people. Soon, Harriet was caring about people she had never even met. Over the course of her life, she traveled secretly into slave country 19 times. Each time she rescued more slaves and brought them to freedom. All together, she rescued more than 300 people! She cared about her people very much, and kept on doing things to show it, right up until she died at age 93. We remember Harriet Tubman as a great American hero for the help she gave to others.

title: How Much Do You Care?
text:
How do you feel about your best friend? When she's happy, does it make you feel a little bit happy too? When she's sad, do you feel a little bit sad, and do you try to help her feel happy again? What about when she's trying to do something big like earning a black belt in karate? Do you help her feel excited about her goal? When the going gets tough, do you tell her to hang in there? If any of this describes how you feel about your best friend, it's probably because you care about her.

Caring about people, and being cared about, is where some of life's greatest happiness comes from. But what is it, exactly? Caring is making someone else's happiness important to you.

The dictionary says that caring is "watchful keeping; concern or attention." If you watch for trouble that might come to your little brother, and you want to keep him safe, that's caring. If you're concerned about your sister when she's sad, and you want to pay attention to her in a way that will make her happy, that's caring, too. The truth is, you probably know what it feels like. Have you ever given your mom a great big hug and told her you loved her? Have you ever given your cat a hug, just to make her happy? What a feeling! No doubt about it. Caring: it's where the good stuff is.

title: Maya Lin 1959 -
text:
One of the most important Asian American artists of our time is Maya Lin, the designer of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C. Lin designed the monument while attending Yale University. She entered her drawings in a nationwide contest that chose a design for a monument to honor those who died in the Vietnam War. Her design was chosen out of almost 1,500 entries!

Lin’s parents came to the United States from China in 1949, just before the Communist Party took control of China. Lin was born and raised in Athens, Ohio. Besides the Vietnam Veterans Memorial, she has designed many other sculptures and buildings across the nation.

title: Larry Itliong 1913-1977
text:
California farmers have always hired immigrants to work. During and after World War II, immigrants came to California looking for jobs. Many found jobs, but were treated badly. Living conditions were poor and pay was low.

During the 1960s, farm workers demanded better treatment. One was a Filipino named Larry Itliong, one of the first to make a plan for forcing the farm owners to change their ways. Itliong led the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee. He called for the Filipinos in Delano, California, to go on strike for better pay. A strike is when workers refuse to work until their demands are met.

There were two main groups of farm workers in Delano, the Filipinos and the Mexicans. At first, the Mexican workers ignored the strike. That was good news for the farm owners. The Mexicans kept working, so they didn’t need the Filipinos. The strike did no good. Larry Itliong went to ask Cesar Chavez, leader of the Mexican workers, to join the strike. The Filipinos and Mexicans joined together and refused to work until the owners promised to pay them more.

title: Honest Abe Lincoln
text:
You probably would have liked young Abraham Lincoln if you had known him. He was a great big tall kid, lanky and awkward. He liked to joke around, and he liked to work hard. He liked books and would sometimes walk miles and miles just to borrow one. One of his favorites was a little book about the life of George Washington. Stories of Washington and the Founding Fathers stirred Lincoln's imagination.

Lincoln was a good storyteller. People liked that about him and would often gather at the general store in the village to listen to his stories. He was also strong. By the time he was 20, he was 6 feet 4 inches tall. He still looked skinny and awkward, but he had a mighty chest and strong arms, perfect for the hard work of the frontier. It was tough to find him without an axe in his hand.

A strong kid like Lincoln could always find work. He threshed wheat, he cut and husked corn, and he split logs for fence rails. Much later in his life, when he ran for president, people called him "the railsplitter." That nickname didn't stick, but there was another that did: "Honest Abe." In fact, it stuck so hard that people still use it when they talk about Lincoln today.

How did Honest Abe go from being a railsplitter to being the leader of the United States during one of the most difficult times in history? How did his integrity, honesty and leadership change our country forever? Keep reading to find out.

title: Uniting a Country - Abraham Lincoln
text:
When Lincoln was a young man, he and a partner named William Berry bought a store together. The store didn't do well and closed after just a few months. What's more, his partner died, leaving Lincoln to pay the store's debts, about $1,100. It took him many years to do it, but Lincoln paid off the debt - every penny. People admired his integrity and began to call him by his famous nickname, Honest Abe.

As Lincoln got older, he did many interesting things. He was a lawyer for a while. Sometimes he was a success, and sometimes not. He ran for public offices many times. Sometimes he won, and sometimes he lost. But through the many ups and downs of his life, Lincoln always did what he believed to be right, no matter how difficult it was. That's what it means to have integrity.

Lincoln's integrity became ever more important after he was elected president of the United States. He served in the White House during the Civil War, one of the most difficult times in our nation's history. The Northern states and the Southern states fought against each other over questions of states' rights and slavery. By the end of his work as president, more than 600,000 soldiers would die.

During the war, two of Lincoln's strongest beliefs guided his actions. He believed it was not right for people to be slaves and that it was not right for the United States to be divided. There were many people in the country who disagreed with him. It made him unpopular, but he begged the Southern states to free their slaves. Later, in a famous document called the Emancipation Proclamation, he declared it unlawful for states that fought against the North to hold slaves.

After the war, there were deep hard feelings between people in the North and people in the South. Many in the North wanted to punish the Southern states for rebelling against the Union. But Lincoln was more interested in unity than in punishment. Although many people opposed him, he worked to welcome the South back to the Union and to ease the heavy burdens that war had placed upon the nation.

Sometimes it was very difficult for Lincoln to do what he believed was right. But he did it anyway. And in the end, Lincoln's integrity won over even his strongest enemies.

A few days after the surrender of the Southern troops, Lincoln was shot as he sat in Ford's Theater, enjoying a play with his wife. He died early the next morning, at about the same hour that you might spend getting ready for school. As his body was carried from Washington to Illinois by train, people lined the tracks, weeping for the man they called Father Abraham. Men who had been his opponents spoke out about his greatness - his kindness and his integrity. And today, people talk about Lincoln in the same way they talk about the Founding Fathers that he admired so much as a boy. Honest Abe has taken his place as one of the greatest Americans ever.

title: Galileo
text:
It was the year 1581, and young Galileo Galilei was miserable. His father was determined that Galileo should be a doctor and had sent him to study medicine at the University of Pisa. But Galileo didn't want to be a doctor. His real love was math, and finally, after four long years, he persuaded his father to let him leave the University to study mathematics.

For Galileo, it was as if a door had opened into a whole new world. As a mathematician, he studied scientific thought and astronomy. In those days, most people believed that the moon, the planets and everything else in the solar system revolved around the Earth. But in his studying, Galileo had a wild idea: What if the sun were really the center of the solar system? What if the Earth revolved around the sun, instead of the other way around? The more he studied, the more Galileo was convinced he was right.

But being right wasn't easy. It took integrity - enough integrity to stand up to many powerful enemies. In fact, because Galileo would not back down from his important new ideas about the solar system, he spent the last decade of his life under arrest. That might seem like a lousy way to go. But today, because of Galileo's integrity, we look back on him as one of the great heroes of science.

title: What is Integrity?
text:
Imagine for a moment that your teacher has passed out an important math test. It has lots of hard problems on it, and you're really worried. The truth is, you didn't study as hard as you should have. The kid next to you can tell how nervous you are. "Psst," he whispers. You look over. He has pushed his test over to the edge of his desk, right where you can see his answers. It's all up to you now. What happens next?

One kind of person might secretly copy the answers, thankful for the help. But another kind of person might whisper, "I appreciate it, but no thanks," and do the best she can on her own. That second kind of person has what people call integrity. Integrity is having the courage to do what you believe is right, even when it's difficult.

If you've ever hit a baseball through a glass window and then had the courage to confess that it was you, you've shown integrity. If you've ever said no when all the guys dare you to steal a candy bar from the store, you've shown integrity. If you've ever raked the leaves in the yard because you promised you would, even when it meant missing your favorite movie on TV, you've shown integrity.

Integrity is sometimes hard to develop. After all, who wants to be punished for breaking a window? Who wants to be made fun of for not taking a dare or miss a great movie just because of a bunch of dumb leaves? But as hard as it is, people who work to have integrity find that they can be counted on and trusted, no matter what happens. When things get tough, people look to them to know what's right.

title: Marco Polo
text: In 1295, a strange trio arrived in Italy. They were weary from years in foreign lands. But these were no foreigners. They had lived in Italy themselves, years ago. They were the Polos: Nicolo Polo and his brother Maffeo, along with Nicolo's son, Marco. Marco was 17 years old when they left Italy for China. Now he was 42. Their adventures had taken them to the courts of Kublai Kahn, the great Mongol ruler. They had seen more in 25 years than most men could in 25 lifetimes. Their story included incredible tales of great riches, strange animals and plants, odd and delicious things to eat and amazing natural wonders. Their story was so strange that not many believed it. Although many thought he was just making them up, Marco had the integrity to stick by his tales of their travels. Later, he decided to write them down in a book called "Description of the World." After Marco Polo died, Portuguese explorers found the strange lands described in his book. They discovered all his stories to be true. Having the integrity to stick by his stories paid off in more ways than one. Future explorers used Marco Polo's book to inspire and to guide them on international voyages for decades after his death.

title: Ruby Bridges
text:
Ruby Bridges was born in Mississippi in 1954. When she was only six years old, she helped change the world. You see, Ruby grew up in a time when schools were segregated. That meant that white children went to one school and black children went to a different school. A court case called Brown v. Board of Education in 1954 determined that schools could no longer be segregated. So, Ruby’s family thought she should be able to go to her neighborhood school in New Orleans instead of a school several miles away.

Only white children attended the nearby school. Ruby and other children had to take a special test in kindergarten to determine if they could go to the all-white schools the next year. Ruby was very bright and passed the test, so she headed off to first grade. White city leaders in New Orleans tried to delay Ruby’s entry into the white school, but they finally let her start there in November. Federal marshals were sent to the school with Ruby and her mother to make sure there was no trouble. When Ruby tried to go to class, an angry mob tried to keep her out. The marshals had to walk in front of and behind her to protect her. People were yelling at her. Ruby was brave. When Ruby finally got inside, none of the white children’s parents would allow their kids to be in class with her, so Ruby had a class to herself with the only teacher who would teach her, Barbara Henry. It was a very difficult year and the awful treatment continued day after day. By the next year, things had settled down, but the trouble had taken a toll on the Bridges family.

What does Ruby say about all this today? She says that she had no idea how people hated each other when she was six. She did not understand the concepts of racism and civil rights at the time. She didn’t understand what was going on at school.

Today, Ruby Bridges is at the heart of change and equality. She fights for civil rights so that no one will ever have to go through what she went through again.

title: Sacagawea - American Hero
text:
Sacagawea lived over 200 years ago, but she is still a great example of someone who showed true civic virtues. Civic virtues are habits or behaviors that help make communities better places to live. Civic virtues also help people get along better with each other and keep citizens safe and happy.

Sacagawea was a Shoshone Indian who was born around 1788 in what is now Lemhi County, Idaho. When she was about 11 years old, Hidatsa Indians captured her and took her to their village on the upper Missouri River. She married a French trader named Toussaint Charbonneau and then had her first child, a baby boy, in 1805. This young wife and mother was about to begin the adventure of a lifetime.

The famous explorers, Lewis and Clark, hired Sacagawea’s husband to travel with the Corps of Discovery on their journey west. President Thomas Jefferson formed the Corps of Discovery to explore and map the Louisiana Purchase. The United States had bought the 828,000 square miles of land from France. The explorers hired Toussaint Charbonneau as a translator to help change words from one language to another. Sacagawea and her two-month-old son came along too, and it’s a good thing they did!

Sacagawea made life better for the Corps of Discovery in many ways. First, having a woman with them showed the American Indians in the area that the Corps was not planning to attack. William Clark was one of the leaders of the expedition, and he wrote, “A woman with a party of men is a token of peace.”

Sacagawea also helped by cooking, sewing and washing clothes. She and her baby also softened the mood of the group at times and made the men more willing to compromise.

title: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. - Fighting for Fairness
text:
There was a time, and not so very long ago, when African Americans were treated much differently than they are today. Your grandparents may remember such a time. In many parts of the country, African Americans had to attend different schools than white Americans. They had to drink from different drinking fountains and eat at different restaurants. Any African American riding a bus had to give up his or her seat to a white American. That was the law. And if that weren't enough, African American families were often the victims of violent and hateful crimes. Sometimes people even got killed. The police and other leaders would often allow these things to happen.

Sound fair? If you say no way, you're not alone. Over the years, many people have fought to make the laws of our country fair to people of all races. Among them was a brave minister named Martin Luther King Jr. Dr. King came from a long line of ministers. His father and grandfather had been ministers. Dr. King himself was a gifted speaker. With his powerful words, he could persuade people to take action against the unfairness around them. His powerful words moved millions. Minds began to change all over the country and the world! But not everyone's mind was changed.

What do you do when you think something is unfair? Keep reading to find out how Dr. King led the fight for fairness for all Americans.

title: Writing for Fairness - Dr. Martin Luther King
text:
Many people fought against Dr. King. He was arrested time and time again for speaking out against laws that were unfair. Dr. King and his followers marched through cities in great numbers to let people know how they felt. Dr. King always demanded that the protests be peaceful. He did not want his supporters to lash out in violence, even against their enemies.

But those who fought against Dr. King were often less peaceful. They shot out windows in the homes of Dr. King's family and friends. They threw rocks at Dr. King when he went to speak. They sent him unkind notes and letters in the mail. Some of the notes promised Dr. King that he would be killed if he did not stop his work against unfair laws. The violence against him showed Dr. King that there was still a long way to go before people could call themselves equal. So he kept working. From city to city, Dr. King and his followers continued to speak out against unfairness toward African Americans.

In April 1963, he went to a city called Birmingham, in Alabama. There was trouble in Birmingham already, and some thought that Dr. King and his followers would be in danger if they went there. Sure enough, as they marched in protest against Birmingham's laws, Martin Luther King Jr. and a few others were arrested again. They were taken to Birmingham's jail. But they weren't jailed together in the same cell.

Dr. King was put in solitary confinement. That means he was completely alone. He was not allowed to call his family. He was not allowed to speak with a lawyer. It must have been lonely. But Dr. King continued his work, even from his jail cell. Outside the walls, he knew, were many who were trying to get his followers to stop their work. Others wanted to see unfair laws changed, but they wished Dr. King would wait for change to happen naturally, without so much marching or lecturing. He knew all of this. But what could he do, alone in his jail cell?

Then the answer came. Martin Luther King Jr. began to write. His jailers wouldn't give him nice paper or pens. He had no typewriter, but still he wrote. He scribbled on whatever scraps of paper he could find. He wrote in the margins of newspapers. Friends helped him sneak his writing, piece by piece, out of the Birmingham jail and off to where people could read it. The pieces, all together, made up one long letter, just under 7,000 words long. Today, we call that writing the Letter from Birmingham Jail. In the letter says, "When you have seen vicious mobs lynch your mothers and fathers at will and drown your brothers and sisters ...there comes a time when the cup of endurance runs over, and men are no longer willing to be plunged into the abyss of despair."

The letter filled Dr. King's followers with courage. It spoke to his enemies, perhaps with even more power than if he had been there to say those things to them in person. Nine days after he was arrested, Dr. King was released. His work in Birmingham continued. It continued even though police turned powerful fire hoses on his followers and attacked them with dogs. It continued even though the home of Dr. King's brother was bombed. And you know what? Dr. King's work continues even today, anytime someone stands up for fairness - even someone like you.

title: Taking Your Turn
text: Orville and Wilbur Wright stood on top of Kill Devil Hill at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Beside them was their amazing machine, the first airplane ever, ready for its first flight. And right there, on the very edge of making history, the brothers remembered an important lesson about fairness: they remembered to take turns. Wilbur took the first turn. He rode the plane down the track the brothers used as a runway. But something went wrong. The plane crashed without making much of a flight at all! Wilbur wasn't hurt, but it took them a few days to repair the plane. Then it was Orville's turn. This time, the plane rolled down the runway track and into history. Orville Wright became the first person to fly in an airplane. We'll always remember the Wright Brothers as the inventors of the world's first airplane. But we think it's only fair that we remember them as master turn-takers as well!

title: That's Not Fair
text:
Here's the deal: Your mom has some errands to run, and as she leaves she calls out, "Your big brother is in charge, and there are some cookies on a plate in the kitchen for you to share. See you in a little bit!" Before the door is even closed, your mouth is watering. Cookies! You run into the kitchen, and there they are - no ordinary cookies. These are six enormous chocolate-dipped, marshmallow-oozing, crunchy-chewy mom specials. You can't wait to get your hands on your share. Just then, your brother picks up the plate and starts for his room. "Hey, those are for us to share!" you remind him. "Oh, yeah," he says. He hands you one cookie, and disappears down the hall. You look at the cookie, and you can only shout, "One? Where's my fair share?" Your brother shouts back, through the closed door of his bedroom, "I got there first. Besides, I'm bigger." You wail out, "IT'S NOT FAIR!" And you're right. It isn't.

The dictionary says that fairness means "not favoring one more than any other." That means not favoring your brother with more cookies just because he's bigger or faster. You'll find opportunities to be fair on the playground, in the classroom, on the basketball court and more. If you're wondering whether or not you're playing fair, here's a good question to ask yourself: What if you were the other guy, and he was treating you the way you're treating him? If your brother were asking himself that question now, he'd be a lot more fun to eat cookies with!

title: The Supreme Court
text: Most people who commit crimes are tried and pronounced guilty or not guilty in a court. The court is usually in the city or state where the crime was committed. The job of the court is to decide fairly whether a person is guilty of a crime, and to fairly choose a punishment (called a "sentence") for a person who is found to be guilty. It's a big job, and the courts are under a lot of pressure to do it right. All the courts in America are important, but there's one court, the grand-daddy of all courts, whose fair decisions are watched by the whole nation. That court is called the U.S. Supreme Court. The Supreme Court today is made up of not one, but nine expert judges. When the Supreme Court judges a case, its decisions help other courts all over the nation decide their own cases fairly. Our country has always been concerned about the fairness of its laws. The U.S. Supreme Court has been dedicated to keeping things fair since it was created in 1789. That's well over two centuries!

title: The Blood, Sweat, and Tears Medgar Evers Put Into Life - He Put Into Everyone
text:
Medgar Evers became the Mississippi field secretary of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) in 1954. This was an extremely dangerous job to have during this time period because Medgar was to investigate and report all of the horrible things, like killings, that were happening around the state. He risked his life by digging into why African- Americans were being lynched, their houses being fire-bombed, or threatened by racists. He knew it was perilous work, but Medgar chose to work for equality, civil rights, fairness, and justice for African-Americans and all of the citizens of Mississippi.

Medgar’s wife, Myrlie Evers and their three young children, Darrell age 8, Reena age 7, and 3-year old Van were a happy, loving family living in Jackson, MS. Mississippi was not a safe place for African-Americans at the time, but Medgar had a way to make those around him feel safe. Medgar wanted to protect his family, his community, and neighborhood. When the community saw him standing up to the racist system, they began standing up, too. He served as a mentor to young protesters at Tougaloo College and across the state.

On June 12, 1963, Medgar arrived home late from a community church meeting when Byron De La Beckwith, a white man, shot Medgar in the back and sped off in a truck. Myrlie and her children were inside the house when they heard the gun shots. Myrlie and the two older children ran outside. The neighbors rushed him to a nearby hospital. At first, they turned him away because he was African- American. Finally, they allowed him in but it was too late. Medgar had lost too much blood and died.

The murder of Medgar Evers shocked people in Mississippi and around the world. However, he did not die in vain. His legacy continues to this day, stretching from his 1950s NAACP work to the passing of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 to the current Black Lives Matter movement.

“You can kill a man, but you cannot kill an idea.”

~ Medgar W. Evers July 2, 1925 - June 12, 1963

title: Susan B. Anthony 1820-1906
text:
From the time she was a young girl, Susan B. Anthony believed that what was open to one person should be open to all people. As a teacher, she felt that having separate schools for girls, boys and free African Americans was not fair. She believed that the minds of all genders and races were equal and that education should be equal, too.

As Susan grew older, she joined other fights as well. She hated slavery and thought working women should be paid more money. She began fighting for women’s suffrage, or the right for women to vote. She once was arrested for voting illegally and was fined $100. She wouldn’t pay the fine. She said, “Trust me that as I ignore all law to help the slave, so will I ignore it all to protect an enslaved woman.” Until women were allowed to vote, just like men, Susan felt they were no better off than slaves. She fought for this right until her death in 1906, but at that time, women still couldn’t vote.

Susan’s efforts finally paid off when the 19th Amendment to the Constitution was passed in 1920. It gave all American women the right to vote. In her honor, the amendment is also called the Susan B. Anthony Amendment.

title: Valley Forge - Perseverance
text:
Look around you in the world, and you may see people going through big, hard times or trying to do big, hard things. You may see people who seem to be able to hang in there, no matter how big the difficulties are. There's a word for that sort of hanging in there. The word is perseverance (pur-seh-veer'-unts). Perseverance means never giving up on what you set out to do, no matter how rough the road gets.

There are terrific examples of perseverance all around you. Here's one from before your time, or your parents' time or your grandparents' time, or even your great-great-great-great grandparents' time - a story about perseverance that may have changed the future of our nation. About 25 miles north of Pennsylvania, along a river called the Schuylkill (skool'-kill), is a place called Valley Forge. In the winter of 1777 and 1778 (during the Revolutionary War), George Washington lived in that valley with his army of 10,000 men.

The war was going badly in those days. Washington's troops had been defeated in battle after battle, and the government could not afford to give supplies and clothing to Washington's army. In the bitter cold, without enough clothing, shoes or food, General Washington watched nearly 2,500 soldiers grow weak and die. Many people would have given up. In fact, many soldiers did give up. Only the most loyal soldiers stayed with Washington as he persevered through the difficult winter.

If you were in Washington's army, what would you have done? Would you have given up and gone home to your family? Or would you have persevered and stayed at Valley Forge? Keep reading to find out what happened.

title: Pilot Perseverance
text:
Graphic novels can be really fun to read and these days there are a lot of them around. Recently Capstone Press published a graphic novel about Bessie Coleman, the first African American woman to get a pilot's license. Although Bessie lived about 100 years ago, this book makes learning about Bessie's life interesting and fun!

Bessie Coleman was born in 1892, but she's still a great example of perseverance today. She was one of 13 kids, and her father left the family when she was only nine. Bessie fought adversity her entire life because she was an African American woman. She faced racism because she was African American and faced discrimination because she was a woman. At that time, it was like having two strikes against her, because many people treated both African Americans and women as second-class citizens.

Bessie didn't let anyone tell her that she couldn't do what she dreamed of doing. She even moved to France so she could get her pilot's license, since women weren't allowed to get a license in America. Although she didn't live a long life, the time she spent on Earth was bright and filled with persistence.

You can read more about Bessie Coleman, and other famous people who persevered. Check out more graphic novel biographies at your local library or bookstore.

title: George Washington - The Father of America
text:
Though he still had the support of Congress, Washington's hard winter made some people doubt his ability to lead the army. Those people included men like Charles Lee and Horatio Gates. Lee and Gates each thought that they should have been the ones in charge of the army, instead of Washington. They spent a lot of time complaining about Washington's leadership while they sat down to fancy dinners in their warm homes. And in some cases, they did more than complain. A group of army officers and members of congress began to think of ways to remove Washington from command and to put Gates in his place.

Imagine yourself as General Washington. There you are, freezing at Valley Forge. Many of your men are sick. Many lay dying, and many have already died. Day after day, men leave your army, unable to bear the hardship. And on top of it all, the government won't send supplies. Instead of thanking you for your hard work under harsh conditions, some in the government are plotting to have you removed from command. Could you persevere through a winter like that? Washington did, though it's difficult to imagine how.

What was the fate of those men who persevered? What became of the men who remained loyal through the difficult winter? Washington spent the long, freezing days training those loyal men with the help of a man named Baron von Steuben (stoo'-ben). When spring came, Washington had an army that was well trained and ready to fight the war against England. Those who remained loyal to Washington helped him win the war.

Washington himself, after the war's difficulties, was so well loved by the people that they wanted to make him king. Instead, he served as our nation's first president - the only president in our country's history to be elected by a completely unanimous vote. Today, many people call George Washington the father of our country. They look to his courage and perseverance in much the same way that a child might look to its father for an example of how to live.

Valley Forge remains a special place for Americans. The Valley Forge National Historical Park now lies where Washington's camp was. People from all over the country (and even from all over the world) visit there to remember the perseverance of Washington and his troops - the perseverance that helped make our country free.

title: Perseverance is Hard Work
text: You may not have known it, but enjoying movies, listening to recordings of songs and using electric lights can all be traced back to the work of one guy. His name was Thomas Alva Edison, and he knew a little about perseverance. He was famous for saying, "Genius is 1 percent inspiration and 99 percent perspiration." By that, he meant that amazing people weren't amazing because they were inspired, but because they were willing to work hard. From his laboratories in New Jersey, Edison and his assistants invented some of the things that you and I use every day. Those inventions included the phonograph (the great-great-grandfather of today's CD players and MP3 players), the electric light bulb and the earliest motion picture projectors. Before he died in 1931, Edison held more than 10,000 patents on his ideas and discoveries. On the way to each successful invention, there were sometimes thousands of attempts that didn't work. But Thomas Edison didn't complain. He said once, "If I find 10,000 ways something won't work, I haven't failed. I am not discouraged because every wrong attempt... is often a step forward." That's perseverance!

title: Suzy‛s Tough Day
text: It's been a tough day for Suzy. First of all, it's her first day in a brand-new school. So far she doesn't have many friends. Her teacher pronounced her last name wrong, and some kids laughed. And to top it all off, Suzy accidentally dropped her lunch tray on the floor. Is Suzy going to make it around here? No doubt about it! Suzy just happens to have a character trait that's going to get her through all this just fine. It's called perseverance. Perseverance means hanging in there and doing your best, even when the going gets rough. Suzy's got it, and she's not alone. You can probably think of a time when you've shown perseverance yourself. Did you ever hang in there, patiently working on a big puzzle or a model airplane, even when it got complicated? That's perseverance! Did you ever keep a good attitude, even when you were in bed with a bad cold? That's perseverance, too! See, Suzy's not the only one who knows about perseverance. You've got it, too! And you know that a little first-day-of-school trouble is no match at all for someone like Suzy. Perseverance, along with a little help from good pals like you, is going to get her through just fine.

title: Astronaut Kalpana Chawla
text:
On Feb. 1, 2003, America watched in horror as the space shuttle Columbia broke apart over Texas while re-entering the Earth’s atmosphere. Kalpana Chawla was one of seven astronauts who died on board Columbia that day. She was an Asian American astronaut and the first Indian woman to fly in space.

Chawla was born and raised in India. After graduating from college she moved to the United States to study aerospace engineering. Chawla became an astronaut in 1995 and made her first flight in 1997.

In 2003, Chawla flew on the space shuttle Columbia as a mission specialist. During this mission, the crew conducted nearly 80 experiments on microgravity (zero gravity) and its effects on the health and safety of astronauts. After her death, Chawla was awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor.

title: Anne Sullivan’s Big Responsibility
text:
It was an August day in 1886, and Anne Sullivan sighed. She was thinking carefully about the letter she held in her hand. The letter invited Anne to accept a job caring for a 6-year-old girl. The girl was the daughter of a family named Keller. But this was no ordinary 6-year-old. The letter described her as “deaf-mute and blind.” Hmm. Caring for a handicapped little girl?

Blind? Anne knew something about that. She had begun to go blind herself when she was just 7 years old. She saw well enough now, but only after years of difficult operations. She could understand a blind child. But deaf? Mute? That meant that whoever the girl was, she couldn’t hear or talk either.

Anne sighed. She was only 20 years old and had barely finished school. Was she even ready to take on the responsibility of living out in the world on her own? Could she accept the responsibility of caring for such a child too? A lot would be expected of her. Her heart beat loudly in her chest as she made up her mind to accept the responsibility offered to her in the letter.

How would you feel if you were Anne Sullivan? Would you be nervous about meeting your new student? Turn the page and keep reading to find out what happens next.

title: Zora Neale Hurston
text: Do you like a good story? Well, there was one Florida woman who liked writing stories as much as she liked hearing them. Her name was Zora Neale Hurston. She grew up in Eatonville at the beginning of the 20th century. She described her hometown as “a pure Negro town—charter, mayor, council, town marshall, and all!” She paid close attention to the people at the local store when they told stories. Later, she lived in a lumber camp in Loughman. The workers around her, who came from all over the South, told folk stories, chanted work songs, spoke proverbs and sermons, recited children’s rhymes and sang the blues. Hurston tried to remember every story she heard. She used what she heard to write books. Her most famous books are “Their Eyes Were Watching God” and “Dust Tracks on a Road,” which is a story about her life. She also wrote poetry and more than 50 short stories. Isn’t it amazing what she did just by paying attention to what people around her were saying and doing? Hurston lived her last years as a poor servant. She died in 1960 and was buried in an unmarked grave.

title: Anne Sullivan's Big Responsibility
text:
Anne’s heart beat even more loudly as she approached the Keller home. And it jumped right into her throat when she met 6-year-old Helen Keller, the girl she would be responsible for. It seemed that Helen threw wild tantrums every few moments. She stamped and kicked whenever she didn’t get something that she wanted. She screamed and threw things whenever she was asked to do something she didn’t want to do. Her parents were afraid of upsetting her, and they quickly gave in to her tantrums. Anne had a sinking feeling as she watched the family. This was going to be an even bigger responsibility than she thought.

She rolled up her sleeves and went to work. The first step was to get Helen to obey her somehow. She asked Helen’s parents for a private place where she and Helen could work together alone. Helen’s parents gave Anne a little cottage. They allowed her to teach Helen there. The first night in the cottage, Helen wouldn’t get into bed at bedtime. Anne wrestled and argued with her for two hours before the exhausted child finally fell asleep. It hadn’t been a good day. But Anne had taken on the responsibility of teaching Helen. It was a big responsibility, and she wasn’t backing down. Tomorrow, she hoped, would be better. Maybe the day after that would be better still. But first, before any real work was done, she had to get Helen to listen to her. She had to get Helen to obey her as a teacher.

Little by little, Anne worked to convince Helen that she could be trusted. She began to speak to Helen by spelling out words in sign language. She kept her hand nestled safely inside Helen’s so that Helen could feel the shape of the signs and learn what they meant.

One day, Anne took Helen to the pump house. She pumped water over one of Helen’s hands while she made the signs that spelled water into Helen’s other hand. Something remarkable happened. “A new light came into her face,” wrote Anne. “All the way back to the house she was highly excited, and learned the name of every object she touched, so that in a few hours she had added 30 new words to her vocabulary.”

It seemed like a miracle, but day by day Helen began to understand the things that Anne was teaching her. Anne taught Helen to put her fingers on the lips of someone who was speaking. Helen felt the shape of the person’s mouth and felt the vibrations made by the sound. Finally, after much work, Helen the deaf-mute girl began to speak.

But even then, Anne’s feelings of responsibility toward her young friend didn’t end. She worked with Helen not for just a few more days or a few more months, but for 49 years! Helen graduated with honors from college. Anne Sullivan was there.

Helen began to speak in public. She toured the world telling her amazing story. Anne Sullivan was there wherever she went. In 1931, just a few years before Anne’s death, Temple University in Philadelphia wanted to honor Helen and Anne at a special ceremony.

Anne at first chose not to attend the ceremony, but she sneaked in at the last minute. When she entered the college auditorium, she saw everyone rise up from their seats in her honor.

What was she thinking as she watched them all standing there? Was she thinking of her childhood, a blind girl living in a poorhouse in Massachusetts? Was she thinking of her own eyesight, even now fading with each passing day? Perhaps she was simply counting the lives that had been changed since the day that she decided to accept a big responsibility and show up to care for a certain 6-year-old little girl. And perhaps in her counting of changed lives, she started with her own.

title: Never Give In
text: “Never give in. Never, never, never, never—in nothing great or small, large or petty—never give in!” The words rang out in England’s Harrow School in 1941. The man who said them was Winston Churchill, and tonight he had taken on a special responsibility: being the guest speaker at his old school. Outside the school walls, World War II raged. France had fallen to Hitler’s army. But somehow England had refused to give in. Many would say that Winston Churchill himself had kept England from falling. He was England’s prime minister, and he had taken upon himself the responsibility of filling the hearts of his countrymen with the courage to face their enemies. That’s quite a responsibility! But Churchill seemed up to it. Even though England was a tiny island nation, it couldn’t be beaten. Battered by bombs, England still stood strong. When the man responsible was asked how he did it, Churchill answered, “It was the nation and the race dwelling all round the globe that had the lion’s heart,” he said. “I had the luck to be called on to give the roar.”

title: We’re Counting on You
text:
Maybe it was tough to get up this morning and come to school. Most people have days like that. But here you are! You came anyway. Maybe a little something inside you said that school was where you ought to be today, whether you felt like getting out of bed or not. Some people would call that little something responsibility.

Responsibility is that character trait that makes a person reliable—able to be counted on. If your teacher can count on you to show up at school every day, or if your mom can count on you to put the dishes in the dishwasher after dinner, that’s responsibility. If your team can count on you to take care of third base during the big game, that’s responsibility, too.

Responsible people are good at taking care of the things that other people expect of them, but they are also good at taking care of things that they expect of themselves. Things expected by others might include getting your homework done or watching your baby brother. Things that you might expect of yourself might include practicing the piano, being on time to places you promised to be, or keeping yourself healthy by avoiding cigarettes, drugs and alcohol. Those may seem like a lot of assignments, but a responsible person like you can handle them all, no sweat!

title: Albert Einstein 1879-1955
text:
Little Albert Einstein was very special. Not only did he learn to play the violin before age 5, but he became the most famous scientist of modern time. Chances are that you have seen a picture of Einstein—you know, the happy-looking gentleman with frizzy hair. Perhaps you have even seen his great equation, E=MC2, and wondered what it meant. (Don’t worry. Most adults don’t understand it, either.)

Einstein was not afraid to ask questions. He wondered if Newton was right about space and time. His Theory of Relativity showed that Newton was not completely right about time and space. Basically, the Theory of Relativity showed that time and distance in the universe were different depending on where you stood.

That was just one of his revolutionary ideas that changed modern science. He came up with the idea that photons (particles of light) existed. He created the idea of energy and matter being related (his E=MC2 formula). He developed a system of counting and measuring atoms, a theory that light is both a particle and a wave, and many other great theories. Einstein even answered the question, “Why is the sky blue?”

When did he do all of this? Well, most of his great ideas came while he was working at a patent office in 1905. Einstein’s quest for knowledge about the universe inspired many more scientists to keep trying to answer those questions.

title: Gandhi—Changing the World
text:
If you told someone that you could speak a foreign language and that you had studied law in one of the world’s best universities, you might get a little respect. Maybe young Mohandas K. Gandhi expected a little of that same respect in 1893 as he left his home in India. After all, he had studied English until he could speak it well. He had been trained in London to be a lawyer. He was on his way to South Africa to do some legal work. But if Gandhi was looking for respect, he was in for a surprise.

In South Africa, nobody cared that he could speak English. Nobody cared that he had studied in a great London university. He was Indian, and that’s all that mattered. Indians in South Africa didn’t get much respect at all from the British and Dutch settlers who lived there. They were called names, made fun of and often much worse.

In his first few months in South Africa, Gandhi was asked to take off his turban in court. When he refused, the newspapers wrote about it. They called Gandhi an “unwelcome visitor.” When he traveled, he was told to sit in the third-class car of the train, even though he had a first-class ticket. When he refused, he was thrown off the train. Later, on a stagecoach, Gandhi was beaten because he wouldn’t move from his seat.

If you were treated so disrespectfully, how would you feel? Inside this paper you can read about how Gandhi felt and what he did to change things.

title: Senior Power
text:
Looking for someone to respect? Try someone who’s been around a while— someone who’s seen a bunch and knows a bunch. The mild-mannered senior citizens in your neighborhood may hold the key to decades and decades of wisdom and experience, all yours for the asking.

Wanna know what kids did for fun in the days before video games? Ask a senior! Wanna know how it felt to watch a man step on to the moon for the first time? Ask a senior!

And if you think they’re behind the times when it comes to our high-tech modern world, guess again. Senior citizens all over the country are finding ways to share their experience and their knowledge. They’re writing newspaper columns, hosting radio shows, managing Web sites and more. Have your parents introduce you to some of the senior citizens in your neighborhood or town. Give those folks a little respect. You never know what you’ll learn.

title: Peaceful Change - Mahatma Gandhi
text:
After being treated so badly, Gandhi felt thoughtful. He thought about the Indian people. He thought about the respect they deserved. As he thought, his life began to change.

He began to speak out in public for the rights of Indians in South Africa, and the world began to pay attention. Soon, people began to follow Gandhi as a leader.

But it wasn’t just respect for Indians that Gandhi was hoping for. He taught his followers to respect everyone, no matter who they were. In a war between the Dutch and the British, Gandhi organized more than a thousand Indians to care for wounded soldiers. Which side did they work for? Both sides! No matter which side a wounded soldier had fought for, he would receive care from Gandhi’s group, the Indian Ambulance Corps. In that war and others, Gandhi’s volunteers treated people who other doctors had refused.

Gandhi’s work began to make him famous all over the world. When he finally returned from South Africa to India in 1919, people called him Mahatma (a word that means Great Soul).

Gandhi found plenty of work to do in his home country. In those days, Britain ruled India. The British treated many Indians in the same way that Gandhi had been treated in South Africa. Gandhi worked first to gain respect for his people and then to gain independence, once and for all, for all of India.

When the British fought against Gandhi and his followers with guns and swords, Gandhi fought back only with his teachings. In 1919, an act of violence by Great Britain in India shocked the world. As a peaceful protest formed on the Sikh New Year in Jallianwala Bagh, General Dyer ordered his troops to open fire. Gandhi was shocked that soldiers would follow the orders to open fire on an obviously unarmed crowd. That act left 400 dead and 1,100 wounded, including women and children. Even then, Gandhi refused to allow his followers to use violence in their fight for independence.

But the British weren’t the only ones treating people badly. Indians themselves sometimes treated each other with great disrespect. They were especially cruel to the poor and outcast. They called those people untouchables.

Gandhi fought against the idea of untouchables. He did it by creating a community where people of all religions, races and social classes could live together, including untouchables. When people outside the community complained, he didn’t ask the untouchables to leave. In fact, he moved his people to a neighborhood in the city where even more untouchables could be a part of it.

Today, the world is still fighting many of the battles that Gandhi fought. For nearly 50 years after his death, Indians and blacks in South Africa were mistreated. Today, many Indians still avoid people that they call untouchable. And of course, right in your own school you see people disrespecting each other. But in a time filled with bad treatment and misunderstanding, Gandhi showed the whole world the awesome power of treating everyone around you with respect. Even his enemies came to admire his ideas.

How does the world feel today about Gandhi’s work? One summer Gandhi made a pair of sandals for Jan Smuts, a British general who considered himself Gandhi’s enemy. The general later said, “I have worn these sandals for many a summer since then, even though I may feel that I am not worthy to stand in the shoes of so great a man.” In the minds of most people around today, that about sums it up.

title: Pocahontas
text: When colonists from Europe came to America, they must have been quite a sight to the people who already lived here. These new European visitors wore strange clothes, used strange tools and spoke a strange language. Some were certain that the newcomers were enemies. Some of the newcomers thought the same thing about the natives. It was difficult for the colonists and the natives to respect each other. Often, the native tribes attacked the European settlers. Just as often, the European settlers treated the natives harshly. But one young American Indian girl believed the two groups could live together in peace. Her name was Pocahontas, a word that means playful one. She worked to keep peace between her people and the newcomers. Legend has it that once she even placed her own neck between her father’s stone club and the head of John Smith, the leader of the European settlers. Instead of being fearful of the people who had come to her land, Pocahontas respected them and even defended them from harm. That’s an example we could learn something from!

title: Respect and Understanding
text: Got any brothers or sisters? If so, chances are pretty good that while you’re alike in a lot of ways, you’ve also got your differences. You may not like the same toys or the same TV shows. You’ve probably learned that getting along with your brothers and sisters means trying to understand how they feel about their favorite toys or TV shows, even though you may feel differently about those same toys or TV shows. That’s an important character trait— understanding that the feelings, thoughts and beliefs of other people are important and valuable, even if they’re different from your own. People call that respect. You can have respect for people all around you. For example, you can show your teacher that you understand the importance and value of her work. Do it by obeying class rules and by trying hard to listen and participate. That’s respect! You can show your friends that you understand the importance and value of their feelings and ideas. Do it by not making fun of them, even when their ideas or beliefs are different than yours. That’s respect, too! Lots of nice things tend to come to those who show respect. One of the nicest is this: When people see how willing you are to respect them, they might just respect you right back.

title: Cesar Chavez 1927-1993
text:
At the age of 10, Cesar Chavez became a migrant worker when his father lost his farm in Yuma, Arizona. A migrant worker moves from place to place, working in the fields when the crops are ready.

Chavez moved to California, working in the fields, orchards and vineyards to help support his family. He later became involved in organizations that worked to help the migrant workers get better pay, better housing and better hours.

Cesar and his wife settled in San Jose. Eventually, Chavez founded the National Farm Workers Association, which later changed its name to the United Farm Workers of America. It was the first successful farm workers union in U.S. history. A union is a group of workers who join together to make sure they have fair pay and good working conditions. The union still exists today and works to make sure that farm workers are treated fairly.

Chavez organized strikes against fruit and vegetable growers who refused to give farm workers fair pay, reasonable working hours and safe places to live. A strike is a time when workers refuse to work until their demands are met. These strikes made people across the nation aware of the needs of the farm workers and helped bring important changes to the farm industry. Civil Rights Activist Dolores Huerta co-founded the United Farm Workers. She continues to speak out on social issues such as immigration, income inequality and rights for women and Latinos.

title: Do the Right Thing
text:
Have you ever heard of Honest Abe? His real name was Abraham Lincoln.

Abraham Lincoln was the 16th president of our country. He always tried his best to do the right thing, even when it was hard.

Abraham Lincoln always told the truth. That’s why people called him Honest Abe.

title: Springfield Illinois
text:
The people of Springfield, Illinois, are proud that Abraham Lincoln lived there. In 2005, they built a museum and library to help people remember him.

They had a big party on the day it opened. Former President Bush and his wife, Laura, came to the party.

title: Honest Abe—Tell the Truth!: Young Abraham Lincoln
text:
Abraham Lincoln was born in Kentucky on February 12, 1809. He worked hard to help his family. One of his jobs was to split logs for fences.

Abraham did not go to school very much. He taught himself most of the time.

Abraham loved to read, and he borrowed books from his neighbors. He always returned the books he borrowed.

title: Honest Abe—Tell the Truth!: Lincoln's Job
text:
Lincoln had many jobs before he became president. He worked on a boat and in a store. He was a postmaster and a lawyer, too.

There are lots of stories about his honesty. One story tells about a customer in the store where Lincoln worked. Lincoln made a mistake and didn’t give him the right change. He walked several miles to give the man the rest of the money.

No one knows for sure if that story is true. But people who knew Lincoln said that it sounded like something he would do.

title: Think About It
text:
It is very important to be responsible for the things we say and do. It isn’t always easy to do the right thing.

If you are not sure what you should say or do, think about it first. Ask yourself, “Is this the right thing to do?” or “Will I hurt someone’s feelings if I say that?”

title: This Week's Question
text:
What does being loyal mean?

Being loyal means being true to someone or something. When you say the Pledge of Allegiance, you are promising to be loyal to our country. When you stand up for a friend who is being bullied at recess, you are being loyal to your friend.

You can be loyal to your school, your soccer team and your town, too. What are some ways you are loyal?

title: Lost and Found
text:
“Recess!” someone yelled as the second graders hurried to get outside.

Chen walked down the hallway behind the students rushing to get to the playground. He saw a black wallet lying on the floor.

Chen leaned over and picked it up. He looked around to say something to one of his friends, but everyone was already out the door. No one else was in the hallway.

He opened the wallet and saw a driver’s license and some credit cards. There was money in the wallet, too. The name on the license was Thomas Carlson. He closed the wallet and headed toward the school office.

When Chen went into the office, Ms. Marshall smiled. Ms. Marshall was the school secretary.

“Hi, Ms. Marshall.” Chen said. “I found this in the hallway. The driver’s license says it belongs to a man named Thomas Carlson.” He gave Ms. Marshall the wallet.

Just then, a man came in the office. “Did anyone turn in a wallet? I must have dropped mine somewhere. I’m Thomas Carlson.”

“You’re in luck, Mr. Carlson. Chen just found it.” She handed him the wallet. “Here you go.”

“Thank you,” he said, taking the wallet. He took out a $20 bill and held it out to Chen. “You deserve a reward.”

“No, thanks, Mr. Carlson.” Chen said. “I can’t take any money. We’ve been talking about the Golden Rule in my class. It says to treat others the way you want to be treated. If I lost my wallet, I’d want someone to turn it in.”

“Thank you, Chen. It’s nice to meet someone so honest and responsible.” Mr. Carlson put the money back in his wallet. He held out his hand, and Chen shook it. “I came to the school today to enroll my son. He’s in second grade. We’re moving to our new house next week. I think this will be a great school for him.”

“I’m in second grade, too.” Chen said. He was glad he found Mr. Carlson’s wallet, and he couldn’t wait to make a new friend!

title: President Lincoln
text:
Being the president is a hard job. It was even harder for Lincoln.

Right after he was elected president, our country split into two parts and fought a terrible war against each other.

Lincoln did not want the country to be split. He believed we were stronger if we all stayed together.

title: What Would You Do?
text:
Pretend that you and your friend are playing in the living room at your house. You accidentally break a vase full of flowers. Your friend says, “Tell your mom your little brother broke it. He’s only 2. He won’t get in trouble.” You don’t want to get in trouble. What would you do?

You should tell your mom the truth. She may be disappointed that you broke the vase. But she will be proud of you for telling the truth.

If you blame your little brother, your conscience will bother you. Your conscience is the voice inside you that tells you when you do something wrong.

title: Be a Good Friend
text: Who takes care of us when we are sick or hurt? Our parents take care of us. We need doctors and nurses, too.

title: The Red Cross
text:
The Red Cross helps people in emergencies like hurricanes or fires. They give families food, clothes and a place to stay.

The Red Cross gives a special award to nurses who are very brave and do a lot to help others. This award is called the Florence Nightingale Medal.

title: Florence Nightingale—The Lady with the Lamp: Young Florence Nightingale
text:
Florence Nightingale was named after the city where she was born — Florence, Italy.

Florence did not go to school. Her father taught her at home. Florence liked learning about math and history. She learned how to speak six different languages!

title: Florence Nightingale—The Lady with the Lamp: Florence Goes to War
text:
Florence became a nurse because she wanted to help people. She cared about her patients very much. She worked hard to try and make her patients get better.

When Florence was a young woman, she went to a country far away. She helped take care of soldiers who were hurt during a terrible war. That is when she got her nickname, The Lady with the Lamp.

title: Think About It
text: There are lots of ways to be a good friend. Friends share things like snacks and games. Friends care about each other. You can listen to your friend when she tells you something important. You can say, “Good job!” when a friend does something they are proud of.

title: What is Compassion?
text:
Do you know anyone who lives in a city that was hit by a hurricane? You probably felt sad when you heard about the families who lost their homes. That means you had compassion.

Compassion is a big word that means caring about others. You can have compassion for your friends or family or people you have never met.

title: Mind Your Manners
text:
Jenna couldn’t believe she was meeting the governor. Twelve kids from all over the state were chosen for this special honor. Each one did something to help others. Jenna helped raise money for hurricane victims. The boy in line behind her, Garrett, volunteered at a food bank.

When it was her turn to shake the governor’s hand, Jenna reached out her left hand.

“Your other hand,” Garrett said, nudging Jenna. “You always shake hands with your right hand.”

“Oh. Sorry.” Jenna switched hands quickly.

Everyone went into a fancy dining room for lunch. Garrett and Jenna sat together at the long table. Garrett put his napkin in his lap, so Jenna did, too.

“Why do we need three forks?” Jenna asked.

Garrett pointed to the smaller fork on the left side of his plate. “That one is the salad fork. The bigger one next to it is for the main course, and the one at the top of your plate is the dessert fork.”

“Now you’re talking,” Jenna said. “I love dessert. How do you know all this stuff, anyway?”

“Etiquette class,” Garrett said. “My mom made me take it.”

“That’s like manners, right?” Jenna asked. “Did you drink tea with your little finger sticking out?”

Garrett laughed. “It wasn’t like that. It was actually kind of fun, but don’t tell my mom I said that.”

Everyone enjoyed lunch, especially the chocolate cake they had for dessert. Garrett helped Jenna when she wasn’t sure what to do. After lunch, the governor gave a short speech and thanked the kids for all the things they did to help others. Then a lady took them back to a room where their parents were waiting.

“How was lunch, Garrett?” his mom asked. “Did you mind your manners?”

“Lunch was great,” Garrett said. “And I didn’t just mind my manners. I minded Jenna’s manners, too!”

title: Nurse Nightingale
text:
Florence taught other nurses the right way to take care of patients. She wrote a book about being a good nurse.

Florence believed that all people should get good care when they were sick or injured. It didn’t matter whether they were rich or poor.

Florence will always be remembered as an excellent nurse and a kind and caring friend.

title: What Would You Do?
text:
Imagine that one of the boys in your class is sick and has to spend a few days in the hospital. You want to do something to make your friend feel better. What could you do?

You could send a get-well card to your friend. If you draw a picture or write a note in the card, it will make the card even more special.

When your friend comes back to school, you could tell him that you missed him and are glad he is back.

title: Florence Nightingale
text:
Florence Nightingale was one of the most famous nurses of all time. She lived in England a long time ago.

Florence lived most of her life before electric lights were invented. She carried an oil lamp. That’s why she was called The Lady with the Lamp.

title: Be a Good Citizen
text:
Do you know who is called The Father of Our Country? If you said George Washington, you’re right! He was the very first president of our country. Washington was a good citizen. He knew that all countries need laws.

The Constitution is the law of the United States. Good citizens obey the laws of their country, state and city. You can be a good citizen by obeying the rules at school and at home.

title: John Roberts
text:
John Roberts is the chief justice of the Supreme Court. (A justice is a judge.)

Justice Roberts has a very important job. He is the leader of the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court decides if laws agree with the Constitution.

title: George Washington — President and Patriot: Young George Washington
text:
George Washington was born in Virginia on February 22, 1732. His father died when George was 11.

George was a good student. He studied things like spelling, math, geography and handwriting. He also learned how to behave the way he should.

title: George Washington — President and Patriot: Washington Goes to War
text:
When George Washington was young, our country was part of England. Soon the people decided that they did not want to be part of England anymore.

The king of England sent his army to America, and the Revolutionary War began. George Washington was in charge of our army.

After many battles, the leader of the English army surrendered (gave up). The war was over!

title: Think About It
text:
Cooperating with others is very important. Cooperating means working together.

You can cooperate with your friends at school. You can cooperate with your family by setting the table and keeping your room clean.

Can you think of some other ways to cooperate?

title: What Is a Good Neighbor?
text:
A good neighbor is someone who cares about others. Good neighbors work hard to make their communities better places to live.

Neighbors are not just the people who live on your street. They are all of the people in your community, your state and even the world.

title: Saturday Service
text:
“Up and at ’em,” Monica’s dad called. “Come on, gang.”

“But it’s Saturday!” Monica yelled, pulling the covers over her head. She heard her dad knocking on the door of her brother’s room.

“Yes, and it’s also the day we promised to help clean up that empty lot over on Walnut Street, remember? We’re supposed to be there in an hour, so hurry up.”

Monica groaned. This is all Tyler’s fault, she thought. It was his idea for the family to help clean up an empty lot that was going to be turned into a playground.

After breakfast, Monica and her family walked to the lot. Her mom handed each of them a pair of work gloves. Mom said, “You can’t even see the ground under all this junk! This is going to take a lot of hard work.”

Several people were already there picking up trash. Two women came over to meet them. “Thanks for volunteering to help. How about if we put you on recycling duty?” one said.

Monica rolled her eyes. What a mess! She put on her gloves and got to work. This is going to take forever, she thought.

“Hey, everybody,” a voice called. “Lunch is served!”

Lunch? Monica looked at her watch. She couldn’t believe that four hours had gone by.

As the volunteers ate, Monica looked around at the lot. Most of the big things had been hauled away. She could even see the ground in a few places. Her back was tired, and she was sweating like crazy. But she was kind of glad she had come to help.

“Having fun yet?” Tyler asked, sitting down on the ground next to her.

“Nope,” said Monica. “Mom was right. This is really hard work. But when the new playground is built, everyone will be having fun.”

title: President Washington
text:
After the war, the people chose Washington to be our first president.

They chose him because he was a good citizen, a good leader, and a patriot. A patriot is someone who loves his or her country.

Washington was the president for eight years. Then he went to his home called Mount Vernon. He died in 1799 when he was 67 years old.

title: What Would You Do?
text:
You and your friend are drinking sodas in the park. When you are finished, you see a trash can but no recycling bin. Your friend wants to throw the bottles in the trash and go back to playing. You know that it’s important to recycle. What would you do?

You should look for a recycling bin even though it might take up some of your time for playing.

If you can’t find a recycling bin, you should carry the bottles with you and recycle them when you get home.
