title: Treat Everyone Fairly
text:
Imagine that you cannot see or hear. What would your life be like?

Helen Keller could not see or hear, but she never gave up. She graduated from college and wrote 11 books. She always wanted to be treated the same as everyone else.

In 1964, President Lyndon Johnson gave her a very special honor. It was the Medal of Freedom. The Medal of Freedom is the highest honor a U.S. citizen can receive.

title: Read the Dots
text:
How can you read if you can’t see the words? If you know Braille, you can feel the words with your fingers.

Braille is like a code that uses raised dots on a page. At first, the words may look like a bunch of bumps. Once you know the code, it’s just like reading any other book.

title: Helen Keller—Working for Equal Rights: Young Helen Keller
text:
Helen Keller was born on June 27, 1880. She and her family lived in Alabama.

When Helen was almost 2 years old, she got very sick. She became blind and deaf. That means she could not see or hear.

title: Helen Keller—Working for Equal Rights: Helen Meets Anne
text:
A wonderful person named Anne Sullivan came to teach Helen when she was 6. She taught Helen to spell words with hand signs. The first word Helen learned was water.

Many people did not believe Helen could ever learn to talk. But with Anne’s help, she did.

title: Think About It
text:
What should you do when someone tells you he is sorry? You should accept his apology. You can say, “It’s okay. I know you didn’t mean it.”

When you say that, you are forgiving your friend. Forgiving someone means that you are not angry anymore.

title: What Are Equal Rights?
text:
When people talk about equal rights, it means everyone should be treated the same. Everyone should have a chance to get a good education and a good job.

Everyone should be treated fairly. Their race, religion, gender and abilities should not matter.

title: Yes, I Can!
text:
“That’s the new girl,” said Maria. “Her name is Lucy.”

Robbie and Maria were waiting for their turn at kickball. Lucy was watching the game from her wheelchair.

“Do you think we should ask her to play?” asked Maria.

“How can she play kickball?” Robbie asked. “She’s in a wheelchair.”

“I don’t know,” said Maria. “Let’s go talk to her.”

Maria and Robbie walked over to Lucy.

“Hi, Lucy,” Maria said. “We wanted to ask you — ”

“About my wheelchair?” Lucy said. “I don’t mind telling you about it. I got hurt when I was really little, and I can’t move my legs.”

“We weren’t going to ask you about your wheelchair,” said Robbie. “We came over to see if you wanted to play kickball.”

“Really?” A big smile spread across Lucy’s face. “I love to play kickball.”

“Can you play?” asked Maria. “I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to hurt your feelings.”

“Yes, I can play,” Lucy said, “if you guys don’t mind changing the rules a little bit. I can hit the ball with my fist instead of kicking it.”

Lucy and Robbie got in line while Maria told the other kids that Lucy could use her hand to hit the ball.

When it was Lucy’s turn, Jack rolled the ball to home plate. Lucy smacked it hard with her fist, and started rolling her chair around the bases. She got to third base and beat the throw easily. All the kids cheered.

Just then the bell rang. Recess was over.

Jack called out, “Hey, Lucy! Tomorrow you’re on our team!”

title: Helen Becomes a Leader
text:
Helen was the first blind and deaf person ever to graduate from college.

Helen believed that everyone should have the same rights. She gave speeches all over the world about the rights of people who have different abilities.

Helen worked hard to make life better for blind and deaf people everywhere.

title: What Would You Do?
text:
Your team just won the big game. One of the kids on your team calls the other team a bunch of losers. You know that good sports should not say things that could hurt other people’s feelings. What would you do?

You could tell your friend that what he or she said was hurtful. You could remind your friend about the Golden Rule.

You could shake hands with the kids on the other team. Tell them they played a good game.

title: Respect All People
text:
What would life in America be like if people were not free?

A long time ago, African Americans in the South were not free. They were slaves. They dreamed of being free.

Harriet Tubman was a slave. She ran away to a state where slavery was not allowed. She helped more than 300 people escape from slavery.

title: UNICEF—United for Children
text:
UNICEF is the United Nations Children’s Fund. It is a group of people from many countries working together to help the world’s children. They believe children have rights, too.

The people of UNICEF help hungry kids get good food to eat. They help keep kids healthy and safe. They help all children get a good education.

title: Harriet Tubman — Respect and Courage: Young Harriet Tubman
text:
Harriet Tubman was born in Maryland. Her parents were slaves, so she was a slave, too.

Harriet’s life was very hard. She worked long hours on a farm, but she did not get paid for her work.

title: Harriet Tubman — Respect and Courage: Harriet Runs Away
text:
Harriet wanted to be free. She decided to run away.

One night, she sneaked away from the farm. She followed the North Star. Harriet walked many miles. A kind woman helped her.

Harriet went to Pennsylvania. She found a job where she was paid for her work.

title: Think About It
text: Everywhere you go, there are rules and laws. It is important to obey the rules and laws. It is important to respect the people who make the rules and help us follow them. Your parents and teachers make some of the rules. Crossing guards and police officers help us follow them.

title: America—One Nation, Many People
text:
Lots of different people live in America.

We don’t all look the same or speak the same language. We come from different places. But everyone deserves respect.

Our differences make America a great place to live!

title: America Is My Home
text:
Emil and his family were standing on the deck of the ship.

“There it is!” Emil’s mother called out. “The Statue of Liberty!”

“We’re in America!” Emil was excited but a little nervous, too. He wondered what life would be like in their new home.

The ship kept moving toward the huge statue. Emil could see Lady Liberty’s torch and crown.

The ship docked at an island near the statue. He heard his father say this was Ellis Island. People who wanted to make America their home had to come here first.

“Move along,” a man in a uniform said. Emil didn’t understand the words the man was saying. He only knew a few words of English.

Emil held his mother’s hand as they left the ship. The whole family saw a doctor who looked in their eyes, ears and throats. His parents had to answer many questions.

Finally, a man told them that everything was okay.

Emil and his family took a ferry boat to New York City. Emil looked at the Statue of Liberty again and again. He couldn’t believe they were in America.

“Come, Emil,” his mother said. “Help us look for your uncle.”

“Yes, Mother,” he said. He quickly spotted Uncle Kristo waving to them. “There he is!”

Uncle Kristo had come to America many months ago. He was going to help Emil’s father get a job in the factory where he worked. Emil’s family was going to live with Uncle Kristo for a while.

“Hello, everyone,” Uncle Kristo said. “I am glad to see you. Welcome to America.”

“Yes,” said Emil. “America is my home now. Hooray for America!”

title: Brave Harriet
text:
Harriet was worried about her family and other slaves. She went back to Maryland three times to get people from her family.

But she didn’t stop there. She kept going back, even though it was very dangerous.

Harriet made 19 trips to the South to help other people escape. Her courage and her respect for others make her a great American hero.

title: What Would You Do?
text:
Pretend a new girl comes to your class. She is from a different country, and she is still learning to speak English. At recess, some kids make fun of the way she talks. What would you do?

You could ask them to stop making fun of the her. Or you could ask a teacher to help.

Standing up for your friends shows that you respect them. You would be setting a good example for others.

title: Do Your Best
text:
If you’ve ever flown in an airplane, you can thank Wilbur and Orville Wright. They invented the first airplane.

It wasn’t easy. The Wright brothers had to try over and over again to get their flying machines to work.

When something went wrong, they tried to figure out why. Then they found a way to fix it.

title: What’s the Big Idea?
text: Kids have great ideas. Frank Epperson invented the popsicle when he was only 11 years old. When Leslie Scott was 15, she invented a popular game called Jenga. Do you have a great idea? With hard work and a little luck, your idea might be the next amazing invention.

title: The Wright Brothers—Never Give Up: Young Wilbur and Orville
text:
Wilbur and Orville Wright were brothers. They lived in Ohio.

When Wilbur and Orville were boys, their father brought home a toy helicopter. That’s when the boys started thinking about flying.

title: The Wright Brothers—Never Give Up: The Wrights at Work
text:
The Wright brothers opened a bicycle repair shop. They could build or fix almost anything.

Wilbur and Orville dreamed of flying. It took three tries, but they finally built a glider that flew. Next, they wanted to build an airplane with an engine.

title: Think About It
text:
What do you do when you have a bad day? Do you mope around feeling sorry for yourself? That won’t help at all.

Try looking on the bright side. Think about all the good things around you, like your family and friends. Soon you’ll be smiling again!

title: What is Confidence?
text:
Confidence is believing in yourself. It means you believe you can do something.

When your teacher asks you to do something you think will be hard, give it a try. If you believe you can do it, you probably can.

title: Mattie Makes It Work
text:
(This story is based on something that really happened. Margaret “Mattie” Knight lived in Maine in the 1800s. Back then, many boys and girls worked in factories and mills. The machines they worked with made their jobs very dangerous.)

Twelve-year-old Mattie Knight was really interested in machines. She loved making things, too. She made kites and sleds for her brothers. One day Mattie was at a mill where cloth was made.

“Oh, no!” someone yelled. “One of the boys just got hurt!”

Mattie was sorry that someone got hurt. She thought there must be a way to make the mills and factories safer for the people who worked there. She kept thinking about the problem.

“What if the machines stopped when something went wrong?” she thought. That was a good idea.

Mattie spent hours drawing pictures of things that would stop the machines. She built models to test her ideas. Finally, she came up with an idea she knew would work.

Mattie took her idea to the mill.

“I think your idea will work,” the mill owner said. “It will make the workers safer. It might even save someone’s life.”

Mattie did not make any money for her invention, but that was okay with her. She was proud that she had come up with an idea that helped people.

That wasn’t Mattie’s only good idea. Several years later she invented a machine that makes something we still use today. Mattie’s machine made the brown paper bags we use at the grocery store!

title: The Wright Brothers Fly!
text:
In 1903, the Wright brothers tested their first airplane. It flew, but it wasn’t perfect. They kept working on it.

The Wright brothers never gave up. They kept trying, even when things didn’t go their way.

Today millions of people fly in airplanes every day.

title: What Would You Do?
text:
Imagine that your soccer team won a trophy. Your parents say they’re proud of you. But your big sister says, “So what? I’ve already got lots of trophies.” You feel hurt. What would you say?

You could ask your sister not to say things that hurt your feelings.

You should be proud of winning a trophy with your team. Don’t let your sister’s mean words spoil your happy feelings.

title: Harry the Health Hound
text:
Hi, boys and girls! Welcome to Health Studies Weekly. I’m Harry the Health Hound, and I’m here to help you learn how to be healthy.

Not long ago I wasn’t healthy at all. I didn’t feel very good. I didn’t even want to play. But I was lucky. My family and friends helped me learn what to do to be healthy again. Now I feel great! I want to help you learn how to be healthy, too. It’s time to get started. On your mark...get set...read!

title: Good Food
text:
What foods do you like to eat? When I was a puppy, I only wanted to eat cookies. I loved cookies! My family helped me learn that no one can eat just cookies. They gave me good dog food to keep me healthy and help me grow.

Kids need healthy food too. Healthy food helps you grow. Foods like meat and beans help make your muscles strong. Foods like milk and cheese and broccoli help make your teeth and bones strong. Foods like fruits and vegetables give you vitamins and help keep you from getting sick.

title: Safety First!
text: Riding a bike can be lots of fun. But the fun stops if someone gets hurt. Do you wear a helmet when you ride your bike? Your helmet will help protect your head if you fall. Stay safe — wear your helmet every time you ride!

title: Keep Your Germs to Yourself
text: Everyone gets sick sometimes. The nurse at school told me when I am sick I need to keep my germs to myself! He said I should stay home when I am sick. He showed me how to sneeze or cough into the bend of my arm. If you do those things too, your germs won’t make your friends sick.

title: Rested and Ready
text:
Sleep is an amazing thing! It is like a little vacation for your body. Sleep helps your body stay well and helps you grow. Sleep helps your brain solve problems and remember what you learned that day.

How much sleep do kids need? Doctors say kids who are six to nine years old should get about 10 hours of sleep every night. If you do, you will wake up feeling rested and ready for a new day!

title: Harry's Health Hints!
text:
Eat a healthy breakfast every day.

Get 10 hours of sleep every night.

Always wear your helmet when you ride your bike.

Always sneeze or cough into the bend of your arm.

Stay home from school when you are sick.

Eat lots of fruits and veggies.

Only eat junk food once in a while.

title: Draw a Picture
text: In the box below, draw a picture of your favorite healthy breakfast.

title: Start the Day Right!
text:
Do you eat breakfast? It’s the most important meal of the day! Breakfast helps get your body going and keeps it going until lunchtime. Did you know that kids who eat breakfast every day get better grades in school? It’s true!

Your body is kind of like a car. Your body needs fuel, just like a car needs gas. Food is your body’s fuel. After 10 hours of sleep, your body needs breakfast to make it go. What can you eat? How about cereal with milk, a banana and a glass of orange juice? Pancakes topped with apples or blueberries are yummy and good for you too. What is your favorite healthy breakfast?

title: What is Junk Food?
text: Junk food is food with lots of sugar, fat or salt in it. Cake, candy, cookies and other sweet foods are junk food. Potato chips, French fries and other salty, fatty foods are junk food. Junk food isn’t very good for your body. If you eat too much of it, you might feel sick. Everybody likes a little junk food once in a while. Just don’t eat it every day.

title: Let's Be Healthy!
text:
Hi! It’s me, Harry the Health Hound. I’m here again to talk to you about being healthy. These are some of my good friends. Do they look familiar? You have friends just like them where you live.

Doctors and nurses help people who are sick or hurt. They do their best to help everyone stay healthy. In this paper you will read about other people who want to help you stay healthy. There are many people you can talk to about your health. Isn’t it great to know so many people care about you? Lucky you!

title: In Your Community
text:
Doctors and nurses often work in a hospital or a doctor’s office. Do your parents take you to the doctor’s office to get a check-up each year? You have probably been to see a doctor when you are sick, too. People who are very sick sometimes have to go to the hospital.

Your dentist takes care of your teeth and gums. You should go to the dentist twice a year to have your teeth cleaned. The dentist reminds you not to eat too many sweets or drink too much soda. Too much sugar can give you a cavity. That’s a hole in your tooth! Ouch!

title: Health Info
text:
Where can you find information about health? “Health Studies Weekly” is a great place to start! You can go to the library at your school or in your community. Libraries have many books that will help you learn about health. Look for special programs about health on TV and watch them with your family.

Ask your parents or teacher to help you look on the Internet. Check out kidshealth.org or kids.gov to learn about health, safety and fitness. Your parents or teacher might learn something, too!

title: What should you do when...
text: You get a cold? Stay home from school. Get extra sleep. Drink liquids like soup, water and juice. If your nose is stuffy or your throat is sore, ask your mom or dad for medicine that is made for children. Do not take aspirin. Throw away the tissues after you blow your nose. Wash your hands often. Do those things and you’ll be better before you know it!

title: Ready, Set, Get Healthy!
text:
Learning about health is just the first step. Next, you have to make a plan to stay healthy. Reading books and watching TV programs will give you lots to think about. Talk to your family about what you learned. Work together to come up with a plan that will help all of you stay healthy.

Now it’s time to put your plan into action. Don’t just make a list of things to do. Do them! Wear a helmet when you ride your bike, eat healthy food and visit the doctor for a check-up each year. Read Harry’s Health Hints on page 4 each week for some more great ideas!

title: Harry's Health Hints!
text:
Talk to people at home, at school and in your community. They care about your health.

Visit a doctor or nurse if you are sick or hurt.

Visit a dentist to keep your teeth and gums healthy.

Read “Health Studies Weekly” and books about health.

Watch TV programs about health with your family.

Make a plan to stay healthy. Put the plan into action!

Get lots of rest and drink plenty of liquids if you have a cold.

title: Let's Draw
text: Draw a picture of a person who works hard to help you stay healthy.

title: At Home
text: The people in your family care about your health. They take care of you when you are sick. They make sure you do things that will keep you healthy. They make sure you eat right, get plenty of sleep and stay safe. They remind you to brush your teeth twice a day and floss before you go to bed.

title: At School
text:
Your teacher cares about your health, too. If you have a question about health, you can ask your teacher. He will help you find the answer.

The school nurse takes care of you when you get sick at school. She has an office in the school. She calls your mom or dad if you need to go home. She puts band-aids on cuts and puts ice on bumps.

The school nurse helps you learn about staying healthy. She might come to your class to talk about things like washing your hands or eating healthy food.

title: Meet Cells and Systems
text:
Hey there! It’s me, Harry the Health Hound. This week you are going to learn about your body. Have you ever used blocks to make houses or towers? Cells are kind of like blocks. But they don’t make houses or towers. They make you! Every part of your body is made of cells. Cells are so small you can only see them with special tools called microscopes.

Systems are parts that work together. Your body has systems for eating, breathing, moving and much more! Turn the page to read about systems and how they work together to keep you healthy.

title: Breathing Air
text: Take a deep breath. Air comes into your body through your nose or your mouth. The air fills your lungs. Oxygen is part of air. You need oxygen to live. Now breathe out. Your body is getting rid of the things in air you don’t need. It keeps the oxygen. Your lungs move the oxygen into your blood.

title: Staying Well
text: Germs can make you sick. Your immune system helps protect you. White blood cells are an important part of your immune system. When a germ gets into your body, white blood cells go to work. White blood cells are like soldiers. Most of the time they fight off the germs before you even get sick!

title: Standing Tall
text: Inside you are lots of bones called a skeleton. Some bones are big, like the ones in your legs. Some bones are small, like the ones in your fingers and toes. Your bones hold up your body. You could not sit or stand without bones.

title: Getting Sick
text:
Sometimes the systems in your body do not work the way they should. When that happens, you can get sick. Sometimes your body just needs rest and time to get better. Sometimes you need to see a doctor to get well.

Your doctor might give you some medicine. Medicine can help get your systems working again. Never take any medicine unless a doctor, a nurse or a parent tells you it’s OK to take it.

title: Harry's Health Hints!
text:
Every part of your body is made of cells.

Systems are parts that work together.

Your lungs get oxygen from air and move it into your blood.

Your blood takes food and oxygen to every part of your body.

Your teeth, tongue, stomach, intestines and other organs help you eat. Your brain and muscles work together to help you move.

Your bones hold up your body.

Your immune system helps protect you from germs.

Never take medicine unless a doctor, nurse or parent tells you to take it.

title: Let's Draw
text: Draw a picture of your skeleton.

title: Pumping Blood
text: Next, the blood has to move to every part of your body. How does blood move? Your heart pumps it through your body. Your blood takes food and oxygen to every part. Put your hand on your chest. Can you feel your heart beating?

title: Eating Food
text: What happens when you take a bite of your favorite healthy food? Another system in your body goes to work! Your teeth chew the food and break it into tiny pieces. Your tongue pushes the food back and you swallow it down your throat. The next stop is your stomach. Your stomach breaks down the food into even smaller pieces. As the food goes through your body, it keeps breaking down. That way your body can get the things it needs. We call those things nutrients. Your intestines, liver and other organs help your body get the nutrients and get rid of the waste.

title: Moving Around
text: Eating gives you the energy to move around. Moving is a job for your brain and muscles. Let’s say you want to kick a ball. Your brain tells the muscles in your leg to move. It tells your eyes to watch where you kick. When your foot kicks the ball, your eyes and muscles tell the brain that you did just what it told you to do.

title: Meet Healthy Kids
text:
Hi, boys and girls! You know Harry the Health Hound. We are Harry’s friends, just like you! Harry helped us learn about being healthy. We have been reading Health Studies Weekly. We have learned a lot. You have been reading Health Studies Weekly, too. What have you learned about being healthy?

Being healthy doesn’t just happen. You have to make a lot of choices. This week, Harry is going to help you learn how to make healthy choices every day. Turn the page and keep reading. Harry is waiting for you inside!

title: Making Choices
text:
You make lots of choices every day. You choose books to read and games to play. You make choices about your health, too. You can make some choices by yourself. You can choose a healthy snack instead of junk food. You can choose to go outside and play kickball instead of staying inside to play a video game.

You might need some help making other healthy choices. Your parents are a big help! They remind you to brush your teeth twice a day. They hold your hand while you cross the street and teach you to look both ways.

Adults at your school can help you make choices. Your teacher can remind you to get some exercise at recess. The school nurse can remind you to wash your hands often. The principal might remind you not to run in the hallways.

Sometimes you have to let adults make the choices for you. When you are sick, the doctor chooses the medicine you need. Your parents choose your bedtime. They buckle you into a booster seat to keep you safe in the car. At school, the cooks fix a healthy lunch for you to eat. The principal and teachers make safety rules for you to follow.

title: Ask for Help
text:
Your parents and other health helpers want you to be healthy and happy. They can help you make healthy choices. They can help you solve problems. But they might not know you need help unless you tell them.

Are the letters on the board or in a book hard to read? Does one of your teeth hurt? Are you worried about something? Is someone being a bully on the playground? You can talk to your parents or your teacher about any problems you have.

title: Set a Goal
text:
Is there anything about your health that you would like to change? Maybe you would like to make better choices about the snacks you eat. The first thing to do is set a goal. A goal is something to work for.

Do you eat a snack every day? Your goal might be to only eat potato chips or a cookie once a week. On the other days you could eat fruit or veggies. Set a goal and stick to it!

Lots of people can help you set and reach your goal. Teachers, parents and doctors can teach you about healthy choices. They can remind you about your goal if you forget. Talk to your friends, too. You can help each other stick to your goals.

title: Harry's Health Hints!
text:
Choose healthy snacks instead of junk food.

Choose exercise instead of video games or TV.

Brush your teeth twice a day.

Cross the street with an adult and remember to look both ways.

Wash your hands often.

Walk in the hallways—don’t run.

Ask for help when you need it.

Set a goal and stick to it.

title: What Are Growing Pains?
text:
Read the story and answer the questions. Circle yes if the sentence tells something that is true. Circle no if the sentence tells something that is not true.

Have you ever had a hard time going to sleep because your legs hurt? Did anyone ever tell you those are “growing pains”? Growing pains do not happen because you grow. Growing pains happen because of all the things you did during the day, like running and jumping. The muscles in your legs get tired from all that work!

Kids between the ages of 3 and 12 are most likely to get growing pains. Having Mom or Dad rub your legs can help you feel better. Taking a warm (not hot) bath before you go to bed can help, too. And a nice, long hug never hurt either!

title: Start Now
text:
Now is a good time to learn about making healthy choices. Listen to what your parents and other health helpers say. Make healthy choices by yourself when you can. Ask for help when you need it.

When you grow up, you will have to make lots of choices on your own. The more you learn now, the easier those choices will be. Someday you may even have to make choices for your own kids!

title: Meet Halftime Harry
text:
Hi, boys and girls—Halftime Harry, here! Oops! You know me as Harry the Health Hound. My friends call me Halftime Harry because I love to play football. Why? Well, it’s lots of fun. And it helps me stay strong and fit.

Being fit means you feel good and are healthy enough to do the things you want to do. You need exercise to help you get fit and stay that way. Don’t be a couch potato! Go outside and run, jump and play. But first, turn the page and “catch” some more ideas about how to stay healthy.

title: Stay Strong
text:
Your body needs two things to help you stay strong. Harry just told you one — exercise. Doctors say kids need one hour of exercise every day. Exercise builds strong muscles. Did you know your heart is a muscle?

Exercise helps make your heart strong, too! Can you guess the other thing? If you said healthy food, you are right! Have you seen the food guide called “My Plate”? It shows you how much of each different kind of food you should eat every day.

title: Is Soda Good for You?
text: No. Soda is mostly water, sugar and color. (You may call it “pop” instead of “soda.”) Drinking too much can cause tooth decay. Soda fills you up so you don’t have much room for healthy food. It’s OK to drink a small glass of soda once in a while.

title: Is Milk Good for You?
text: Yes. There are things in milk that your body needs. The calcium and vitamin D in milk help keep your teeth and bones strong. You need 2 cups of milk every day. Yogurt and cheese are made from milk, so they count, too. You should choose low-fat milk, yogurt and cheese most of the time.

title: Smoking Stinks!
text:
It’s not a secret. Smoking is bad for you. It makes your breath and your clothes stink. It turns your teeth yellow. It costs a lot of money. But those aren’t the worst things about smoking. It hurts your heart and lungs. It makes it hard to breathe. It can cause cancer.

Sometimes kids start to smoke because their friends smoke. If your friends try to get you to smoke, they are not being good friends at all. Stay healthy! Choose not to smoke — ever!

title: Harry's Health Hints!
text:
Get one hour of exercise every day.

Use the “My Plate” guide to help you make healthy food choices.

Wash your hands often.

Get regular check-ups from the doctor and dentist.

Get your immunization shots.

Get plenty of sleep.

Never try to cook alone.

Learn how to swim.

Make sure your house has smoke alarms.

Choose milk instead of soda most of the time.

Choose not to smoke—ever!

title: Let's Draw
text: Draw a picture of you staying safe.

title: Stay Well
text:
No one likes to be sick! There are many things you can do to stay well. One very important thing to do is wash your hands often. Use plenty of soap and water. Wash every part of your hands, even the backs. Be sure to get plenty of sleep. Don’t share a cup or a glass with anyone. Get regular check-ups from your doctor and your dentist, too. Has your doctor ever given you a shot when you were not sick?

Some shots help keep you from getting sick. We call these shots immunizations. Remember when we learned about white blood cells in your immune system? Immunization shots and white blood cells work together to protect you from some germs.

title: Stay Safe
text:
There are many ways to stay safe. Learn how to swim. Do not try to pet a dog you do not know. Make sure your house has a smoke alarm on every floor. You and your family need a plan to get out of your house if there is a fire.

Cooking is fun as long as an adult is helping you. You can measure ingredients for cookies or tear lettuce into pieces for a salad. You should not try to take the cookies out of the oven or use a knife to slice veggies. Never try to cook alone!

You have learned some other ways to stay safe in other issues of “Health Studies Weekly.” How many can you remember?

title: Meet the Bully Tamer
text:
A bully is someone who is mean to others. A bully can make you feel small and weak. Here are some ways to tame bullies.

A bully loses power if you talk about what is going on. If a bully picks on you, talk to your friends. If you know someone who is being bullied, make friends with him or her. Bullies often pick on kids when no one else is around. Stick together!

You may feel like punching the bully in the nose, but don’t do it. It’s never OK to hurt someone, even if they hurt you first. If a bully hurts you, tell an adult right away.

title: Ask
text: One part of talking about health is asking questions. Asking questions helps you learn more. Any time you think of a question about health, ask a health helper. Remember, nurses, doctors, teachers and parents are all health helpers. They can help you find the answer to your questions.

title: Listen
text: Talking about health means knowing when to listen, too. If you are trying to help a friend, be sure to listen to what he has to say. Listen carefully to health helpers like doctors and nurses. Always listen to adults when they tell you something is dangerous. They don’t want you to get hurt.

title: Stand up for Health
text: Since you started reading “Health Studies Weekly” you have learned a lot about health. It’s time to share what you know. Work with your class and think of a plan to make your school a healthy school. Think about healthy food, exercise, safety and staying well. Maybe you can share your plan at a school assembly!

title: Keeping Secrets
text:
Sometimes it’s OK to keep a secret. If you know what your dad got your mom for her birthday, that’s a good secret to keep. But you should never keep a secret about something that makes you feel bad. What if a bully says he’ll hurt you if you tell on him? Tell an adult you trust even if you’re scared. Your parents and teachers want you to be safe. They will help you.

Remember what Harry said? A bully loses power if you talk to people about what is going on.

title: Harry's Health Hints!
text:
Tame a bully — tell an adult!

Stick together with your friends when a bully is around.

Ask questions about health.

Talk to adults about the way you feel.

Say no if someone tries to get you to do something you think is wrong.

If you are in danger, you should get away and tell an adult (and sometimes yell like crazy).

Never keep a secret about something that makes you feel bad.

Listen when adults say something is dangerous.

Make a plan for a healthy school.

title: Let's Draw
text: You have learned a lot in “Health Studies Weekly.” What do you need to change to be healthy? Draw a picture of what you want to change.

title: Talk, Part II
text: How do you feel? Are you worried or scared? Do you feel sad or hurt? When something is bothering you, you will feel better if you tell an adult you trust about the problem. It’s also a good idea to let people know when things are going right. Tell your parents when you feel great. It will make them feel great, too!

title: Keep Away from Danger!
text: What should you do when you are in danger? Get away fast and tell an adult you trust. If a friend tries to get you to do something you think is wrong, say no. Then walk away and talk to your parents or teacher about what happened. If someone you do not know asks you to get in a car, run away fast and yell like crazy!

title: Talk, Part I
text: What would you do if you saw a friend making a bad choice about health? You can’t make other people do things that are good for them, but you can let them know there is a better choice. If your friend always plays video games and doesn’t get much exercise, ask her to play an outside game with you.

title: What on Earth is Going on?
text:
You are about to begin a tour of the third largest continent - North America. Only Asia and Africa have more land. Can you name the three countries that share most of this continent? Have you ever visited outside of the United States?

If you named Canada, the United States and Mexico as the three major countries, you are right! These countries have much in common. Long before they were known as separate countries, they were home to many native people. Much later, Europeans would come to all three countries - Canada, the United States and Mexico. All three nations eventually won their independence from the European powers. Today, all three of these countries have democratic forms of government. That is, the people choose who their leaders will be through some method of voting.

What do these countries look like? Well among the three, there is almost every kind of landform possible. There are flat beaches and snow-covered peaks. There are rolling rivers and huge natural lakes. You will find desert cliffs and lush forests. There are canyons so deep that they seem to never end. All three countries are bordered by the Atlantic Ocean on the eastern coast and the Pacific Ocean on the western coast. The location between these two oceans gives these countries of North America the perfect opportunity to build trade with countries all over the world.

How about climate? Yes, you'll find that it can be steaming in the tropics, or frigid in the far northern tundras. Wet, dry, hot, cold - North America has it all.

Where do people live in North America? Most live in and around large cities, such as Mexico City, New York City or Montreal.

The three largest nations of North America even share problems, such as pollution and unemployment.

No matter where we go in North America, we can find children and adults who are similar in many ways. They worry about world peace and have grand dreams for the future. They feel afraid, sad or glad, just like you.

North America is a wonderful place, but just where is it, and what is it like?

As you read about North American geography, you will become geographers, or students of geography. Geography includes the study of the Earth's surface and the way people use it.

How to Use Massachusetts Studies Weekly - People and Places

Each issue of Studies Weekly will include connections articles on the front cover. This is a real news story about something important happening in our world right now. Our front-page story will help you get a head start on this week's topic in geography. We will take you on a journey to discover North America as never before. And there's more. We will send you a postcard, tell you of wildlife, test your skills and even help you with your homework.

The paper will focus on one of the five themes of geography, which help us to learn geography in a new and exciting way. You will discover the study of geography isn't just about maps. It's much, much more.

So, let's get started! Turn the page and jump right in. If you want to understand what on Earth is going on, you have to know where on Earth it's going on!

title: Philanthropy and Values
text:
Maybe you have heard the word "philanthropy" before. What does it mean? It describes actions that people make for the good of other people. What is a value? It's a way of behaving that people believe is good - like believing it's good to be honest. Is honesty one of your values?

One way you can practice philanthropy today is to help yourself and others learn good values. How do you learn good values? You can learn them from your parents and grandparents, your teachers at school or church and other people you trust.

You can also learn them from people that have been recognized for doing good things for society. An easy way to learn about people that have done good things is to visit values.com. Values.com has lots of stories and short videos that highlight the traits that make each of us better people. They even have billboards on the highway to remind you about good values.

For example, you may have seen a billboard that looks like the one shown here.

This billboard is about Oral Lee Brown, who saved money from her job to send 19 kids to college... all by herself! Wow! Isn't that cool? You can learn about lots of other people who practice philanthropy at values.com. Be sure to look for more of their "billboards" on Page 4 of Studies Weekly this year. We think they're so cool we want to remind you to check them out!

title: Reason and Logic: Young George Washington, Surveyor and Mapmaker
text:
Most people know about George Washington. He was born in Virginia. He was a general during the American Revolution and our first president. But his earliest jobs, surveyor and cartographer (mapmaker), taught him skills and values he would use for the rest of his life. Using reason and logic to solve problems helped Washington become one of our country's most important leaders.

When Washington grew up, there were few roads or boundaries in much of the land. A surveyor's job was to measure and map the land. He had to make exact measurements for boundaries and physical features. This was a very big responsibility. People needed accurate maps and surveys for traveling and buying land.

At age 17, Washington traveled across the Blue Ridge Mountains to map and survey part of the frontier. He was the surveyor for the whole county, and that was an important job. When he led the Continental Army, it was even more important to have reliable maps. He established the job of Geographer and Surveyor General and appointed a man named Robert Erskine to this position. He gave Washington some information that was very helpful in making reasonable and logical battle plans and decisions.

You can use these same skills to make important decisions. Be sure you have the facts and information you need instead of acting on opinions and emotions. In what areas of your life are reason and logic very important?

title: Geography
text:
Everything happens somewhere, and that's just what geography is about. But studying geography is more than just the location of things. It is the study of the Earth's surface and the ways humans interact with the environment.

This year, in North American geography, we will use the five themes of geography as a guide to help answer the following questions about a place.

These themes are:

location (Where is it?)

place (What is it like there?)

human interaction with the environment (How do people affect the place they live?)

movement (How and why do people, goods and information move from place to place?)

regions (What feature about this place makes it the same as another location?)

When we answer each of these questions about a place, we are studying geography.

1. Location

A location is something that can be found. You can tell someone where something is in many ways. You can give them coordinates on a map (like 6A, 12B), and they can know exactly where to find it. This is called absolute location. In conversation, you would probably use relative location to tell someone where something is located. For example, you might say, "The United States is between Canada and Mexico."

2. Place

Every place on Earth has something that makes it different from other places. There are many ways to describe what a place is like. We can talk about the climate. That is the kind of weather a place typically has from year to year. Physical features can also tell us what a place is like. Physical features include landforms, bodies of water and natural resources. The people who live in a location and their customs and cultures are also a way to tell about place.

3. Human-Environment Interaction

Geographers also study the way people interact with the environment. Sometimes, people change the land. For example, they might drain a wetland to build homes, or they might cut down trees for lumber.

Sometimes, the environment changes the way people live, or where they live. The environment can affect the kinds of clothes people wear, the jobs they have, and the food they eat. How do kids dress for school when they live in the far northern region of North America?

The environment also affects where people live. Throughout history, towns and cities were established near bodies of water. Fertile soil and waterways used for transportation and trade made these locations desirable places to live.

4. Movement

How do you get from one location to another? Perhaps you take a train or ride in a car. People around North America travel in many different ways. The theme of movement takes a look at how people, goods and information are moved.

In the days of the Pony Express, information traveled much slower than it does today with overnight express. Indeed, the age of technology has made it possible to send a message around the world at the push of a button.

Everywhere in North America, goods are moved from place to place. They are moved in many ways. Moving goods can be as simple as carrying a basket of peaches to market. It can be as modern as a jet.

We know people, goods and ideas move from location to location, but we must also study why they move to get the whole picture.

5. Regions

A region is a group of places that have at least one feature in common. Dividing large areas into regions makes it easier for geographers to study them.

A region can be described by physical features such as mountains or lowlands. It can be defined by a common language or culture. Another kind of region is a political region. Every continent has political divisions. Political regions can be countries, states, provinces or republics.

text:

title: What is a spelunker?
text:
Spelunkers (spee LUNG kerz) are people who explore caves. In North America, there are hundreds of caves. Some lie beneath the ground, and some can be entered through the sides of hills, cliffs or mountains.

Many caves have interesting lime formations such as stalactites (they drip from the tops of caves) and stalagmites (they start on the floors).

What kind of critters do you think make their homes in caves? If you guessed bats, you are right! Some species of bats live in a particular cave their entire lives. Other animals that live in caves include lizards and crayfish.

Sometimes, fish are found in caves that contain enough water or underground streams.

It all sounds so exciting - would you like to go spelunking?

title: American Bison
text:
Range - Western United States

The bison is one of the largest mammals on the North American continent. Hundreds of years ago, the bison were found on grassy plains from Alaska to northwest Mexico, across the United States almost to the Atlantic Ocean. As white settlers expanded across the continent, they reduced the number of bison until there were only 300 left in 1900. Today, the bison is protected and lives in wildlife parks in the United States.

The male reaches 5 to 6 feet tall and may weigh 2,000 to 3,000 pounds. The female is smaller and lighter. Both males and females have horns. Bison like to be well groomed and groom themselves daily. The animal rubs its head, neck and the sides of its body on tree trunks and branches. It also rolls, or wallows, in loose sand and dust. What would your parents say if you did that every day?

text:

b. Write what the focus of that theme of geography is and tell of things you might learn about while studying that theme.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: Use any color to circle or highlight three relative pronouns (who, whose, whom, which, that, etc.) in this week’s magazine. Underline the related noun.

title: My Amazing World of Maps
text:
Ask someone what they think of when you say the word "geography," and they'll probably say "map." Indeed, it is with the use of maps that we are able to explore the five themes of geography. So, what do you think this issue should be about? That's a cinch - maps, of course. This issue will explore basic map skills.

When you learn all about symbols and keys on a map, it's like learning a secret code. Before we discover keys and symbols, let's talk about what a map is and ways maps are useful to people in world communities.

Do you have a favorite photo that you love to look at often? Maybe it's a picture of your family or a group of friends. Are the people in the picture as big as they are in real life? Of course not, but they are proportionate. "Proportionate" is a big (but important) word that means the size of one object fits the size of another. Even though that photo is not life-size, it is nearly perfect. Often, the main purpose of a photo is to freeze an event or place. When we look at it later, we can remember it just as it really was. That is like a map. It should also be proportionate and nearly perfect in detail.

Some maps actually look like pictures taken from an airplane. Some are only an outline of a location like the map of the world below. Maps can show us land, water, roads and cities. They show us where things are and what they are shaped like. Some maps show us geographical features such as mountains and valleys. Other maps are designed to show industry. With the use of special cameras, some maps can even show us the ocean floor or the land under sheets of ice.

Have you ever looked at a road map? Road maps display the numbers of the highways to guide us as we travel.

title: When is a Ketchup Bottle Like a Bug-Eating Plant?
text:
Do you get frustrated trying to get ketchup from the bottle? Do you pound the bottom or hold your finger on a certain spot on the label? Well, scientists at Harvard University have created one of the most slippery materials ever, so the days of waiting for ketchup may be over! The material is called SLIPS, which stands for Slippery Liquid-Infused Porous Surface. SLIPS can repel, or not stick to, water- or oil-based liquids. The scientists call this "omniphobicity."

To create a material with omniphobicity, the Harvard researchers put a greasy film on a spongy layer of Teflon. Teflon is the nonstick coating on many pots and pans. The researchers got the idea to make this amazingly slippery surface from the pitcher plant, a plant that eats bugs. The pitcher plant grows in swamps and bogs around the world. One kind of pitcher plant becomes super slippery when it's wet because it locks a thin layer of water in the spongelike surface of its leaves. Insects cannot walk on the leaves and slide down into the plant's tube where they are trapped.

The scientists' new material can coat the inside of bottles and jars so all the food comes out easily. It can also coat airplane wings to help keep ice from forming on them. What other uses can you think of for this new material?

title: Map Symbols and Keys Unlock the Codes
text:
Map symbols help us read a map. A symbol on a map stands for something real. A fast way to find something on a map is to look for the symbol. What if you don't know what a symbol stands for? Then you need to look for the key. The key is a box of symbols and words that tell what they symbols mean. Look on a road map and find the key. Can you see a symbol for an airport? How many airports can you find?

Maps Show Directions

Looking at the directions on a map can tell you which way to go. These four directions are called north, south, east and west. The key is a box of symbols and words that tell what they symbols mean. cardinal directions. On most maps, north is at the top, south is at the bottom, east is on the right and west is on the left. A compass rose shows us the directions on a map.

title: Courage
text:
On Dec. 1, 1955, Rosa Parks had the courage to refuse to give up her seat to a white person on a crowded bus in Montgomery, Alabama. She was arrested and tried. The result of the trial triggered a boycott (refusing to buy or use something), which was organized by Martin Luther King Jr. African Americans refused to ride the city bus until the laws were changed. It worked. Eventually, the laws were changed so that whites and blacks were allowed to sit together.

When Rosa died in October 2005, her casket was placed in the U.S. Capitol for two days so that people could pay their respects to her. Usually only the caskets of U.S. Presidents are placed in the Capitol. Rosa became the first woman to receive this honor.

The greatest kind of courage is to do what is right when others call you a coward or a chicken for doing it. It takes courage to stand up to people like that, but having courage will also help you be loyal, honest and responsible. Your parents, teachers, church leaders or good friends can help you prepare to deal with peer pressure and develop courage to face difficult situations.

title: What is an isthmus?
text:
Do you know how to say this word: isthmus (is-mus)?

If you already knew how to say it, you probably know what it is. An isthmus is a thin strip of land that connects two larger pieces of land. It has water on two sides.

Look at a map of the world or a globe. Look for North America and South America. Can you find the isthmus there? It is called the Isthmus of Panama.

Many years ago, because the land was so narrow, a canal was built there so ships could go right from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific.

title: Capybara
text:
Range - South America

Without a doubt, the capybara is a rodent of unusual size! It is one of the largest rodents in the world. It weighs about 100 pounds. Whew, that's a big rodent! It is about 2 feet tall at the shoulder.

The capybara looks like a cross between a guinea pig and a hippopotamus. It is semi-aquatic (living close to water and sometimes found in water). It lives in groups along the riverbanks, where it eats grasses and other plants. The feet of the capybara are slightly webbed for swimming. Capybaras are said to be friendly critters, but they are a bit noisy - clicking, squeaking and grunting all day long.

title: Inferential Context Clues
text:
Did you ever ask someone the meaning of a word, only to have him answer, “Figure it out!” When you look again, there are no definite context clues. Now what? The fact is that the meaning is hidden in the rest of the words in that sentence. Sometimes, the meaning is tucked away in a whole paragraph. These are inferential context clues.

Below are three examples. Read the words around the vocabulary word and write what you think the new word may mean.

1. Brianna wanted a cookie, but the jar was out of reach. Jake, Brianna’s brother, climbed onto a chair and stretched his fingers around the jar. Just then, the chair tipped and Jake, the chair and the cookie jar came crashing to the floor. Brianna began to cry. As the noise and confusion mounted, their mother called out from the next room, “What’s all that commotion?”

Write what you think the word commotion means: ____________________

2. During a test in class, Spencer saw his best friend, Tyler, cheat. He told Tyler that if Tyler didn’t confess to the teacher, he would tell her what he saw. Standing up to Tyler took a great deal of fortitude on Spencer’s part. Write what you think the word fortitude means:

_________________________________________

_________________________________________

3. Sometimes, we borrow words from other languages (exonymns). This vocabulary word is French and is sometimes followed by an exclamation point. Ashley said, “I cut a coupon from a magazine, mailed it in and — voilà! — here's my new glow-in-the-dark lipstick!"

Write what you think the word voilà means: ______________________________

title: You Are Here, But Where is Here?
text:
Have you ever gone to a mall and looked at the store directory to find a store? It isn't much help if you don't know where you are in relationship to that store. When you talk about where someone or something is, you are describing location. In this issue of Studies Weekly, we will learn about two kinds of location - relative and absolute. Relative location tells us where something is in relation to another thing. For instance, you can say, "Canada is north of the United States," or even, "My friend is sitting near the window." Both of these descriptions give you a general location.

Absolute location, however, is much more specific. For example, if you were to describe where to find Boston, Massachusetts, you might say, "Boston is located at 42N, 72E." Absolute location gives the reader an exact location, meaning that latitude and longitude are always given.

To the right, you see a picture of the beach. The beach is laid out on a grid. The grid has numbers all around the sides. Follow the directions to answer the questions about location. Circle the location description if it is relative and underline it if it is absolute. Good luck!

title: Don’t Let Your Letters Become Nixies!
text:
Have you ever looked at someone's bad handwriting and wondered what it says? There are people who are paid by the U.S. Postal Service to do that every day. Their job is to decipher, or figure out the meaning of, the addresses of mail that the computerized mail sorter can't read. Postal employees in one of two Remote Encoding Centers (RECs) work to separate those addresses they can decipher and those they have to reject because they are completely unreadable. Each of these employees is supposed to work through 1,100 letters an hour!

The letters that are rejected are "nixies," or mail with unreadable or incorrect addresses. Some mail is sent to the Mail Recovery Center in Atlanta, Ga., if the envelope looks like it has money or important documents inside. But letters that don't seem important are sent to the shredder.

So how can we avoid having our letters shredded? Well, the computerized mail sorter is a technology, but so are pencils and paper. In fact, they are some of the simplest technology. We use these tools to learn and practice our handwriting, or penmanship. Most of us write our very best when we are in the fourth grade, and our handwriting does not usually get better as we get older. This is because as we write more, we write faster. People sometimes form opinions about us based on our handwriting, so good handwriting is still important. And grandma and grandpa really do want to get your letters, so write neatly!

title: Hemispheres
text:
Which End Is Up?

Using a globe, can you find the North and South Poles? Halfway between those poles is an imaginary line around the Earth called the equator. We call the top half the Northern Hemisphere and the bottom half the Southern Hemisphere.

The world can also be divided into Western and Eastern hemispheres. The Eastern Hemisphere is east of a line called the Prime Meridian. The Western Hemisphere is west of the Prime Meridian. Look at a map or globe to see the four hemispheres.

Latitude Attitudes

Look at the picture of the hemispheres. You will see lines running east-west (side to side). These lines are called lines of latitude, or parallels. These lines mark distances in degrees. If you can count by tens, you can name the lines of latitude. The equator is 0. The lines of latitude north of the equator are all named "north latitude." They go all the way up to the North Pole, which is 90 N latitude. All of the lines south of the equator are named "south latitude." They go all the way down to the South Pole, which is 90 S latitude. These lines are also called "parallels" because the distance between these lines (either north or south) always stays the same - all the way around the Earth.

Also in Figure 1, you will see lines that are running north-south (up and down). These imaginary lines are called meridians, or lines of longitude. These lines are different from the parallels because they are not the same distance apart, but they get closer and closer until they come together at the poles. Look on a globe and find the poles. See how the lines of longitude come together? The middle line, or the line that is 0, is called the prime meridian. Everything west of the prime meridian to 180 is named "west longitude." Everything east of the prime meridian to 180 is named "east longitude."

Lines of longitude are also used for measuring distances and for establishing time zones. Their most important function is, together with the lines of latitude, to pinpoint locations on Earth.

title: Compass
text:
The compass is every explorer's best friend. What is a compass? It is a tool that often looks like a pocket watch. It has a magnetic needle that can turn easily. The cardinal directions, north, east, south and west, are labeled on the face of the compass. It always points north because there are magnetic fields around the Earth. The needle lines up with those fields to give a pretty sure guide for the traveler. It takes some practice to know how to use a compass properly, so be sure to learn before your next camping trip!

Who invented the compass? The Chinese invented the first compass to use a magnetic needle. They were using their compass to explore the oceans of the world as early as the year A.D. 1000.

What are some ways to tell directions without a compass?

You can look for landmarks that you are familiar with. For example, you might remember that the tallest building in your town is north of you. Another way is to use the sun as your guide. Because the sun rises in the east (every single time), north is to the left of the sunrise. Finally, you can use the North Star, or Polaris, as your guide to north. It is in line with the Earth's axis, and so it always appears to remain in the same place - north!

title: Greetings from Canada!
text:
Population: 34 million
Capital City: Ottawa, Ontario

Dear Friends,

I'm in Alberta visiting my uncle. We did the coolest thing today. We went to the West Edmonton Mall. I couldn't believe my eyes!

This mall has everything. Besides stores, it has an indoor water park, an indoor amusement park with a triple-loop (scary) roller coaster, an indoor lake with bumper boats and even a miniature golf course.

We barely had time to shop. Yeah, this is my kind of mall!

After all that, we went to a place in the mall called Bourbon Street. It had all kinds of international restaurants. What kind of food do you think I ate?

Your friend,
Saba

title: What is a GPS
text:
GPS, or Global Positioning System, was invented by the United States Department of Defense and has been used since the mid-1980s. GPS is made up of 18 satellites that are orbiting (circling) the earth in space. These satellites send information to stations on the ground, allowing scientists to take very specific measurements of different locations all over the earth. With the newest GPS systems, scientists can pinpoint a place on the earth to the nearest centimeter!

GPS has been used to measure the height of Mount Everest, to track submarines and ships, to follow cars and other vehicles as they travel, and to make maps and movies. As GPS equipment becomes more affordable, people all over the world will be able to find out exactly where they are at any given time. Wouldn't that be nice to have if you ever got lost in the woods or in a giant parking lot?

title: Kodiak Bear
text:
Range: Most of North America, Alaska to Hudson Bay, south to northern Mexico

The Kodiak bear has a rich golden-brown coat. It can be 4 1/2 to 5 feet tall when down on all four legs. It is 8 to 9 1/2 feet from head to tail and is one of the largest land-living flesh-eaters in the world. The adult weighs from 800 to 1,600 pounds. Its head is exceptionally large. It has poor eyesight but a keen sense of smell and hearing. It lives on average about 20 to 25 years in the wild.

The Kodiak bear likes the coastline, Alpine meadows and open tundra. It likes to eat plants, bugs, small rodents, fish, berries, roots, bulbs, fungi and carrion (rotting meat).

It is not aggressive unless surprised or disturbed while hibernating. The female gives birth to two or three cubs between January and March. They will weigh about 1 1/2 pounds and are 11 to 12 inches in length. They are born with their eyes closed and are almost completely hairless.

text:

title: The Beginning of Time: When Was That Anyway?
text:
Our Earth is 4.5 billion years old, and our universe is probably a least 12 billion years old. It's very difficult to imagine such a long period of time. Most people mark the passing of time by counting the years. Even one year can seem like a very long time when you are waiting for a birthday or a special event. Let's explore the ways time has been measured through history.

No one really knows when early man began to keep time. We only have knowledge of time-keeping through written records and calendars of ancient civilizations. This is called historic time. Early humans probably only needed to keep track of simple units of time like days and seasons. For ancient peoples, the sun, moon and stars were their only clocks. The rising and the setting of the sun marked when they awoke and when they went to sleep. (Do you go to sleep when the sun sets?) Ancient people knew when a new month was beginning by observing the phases of the moon. Sometimes, they kept track of the passing months and years by carving scratches into sticks or pieces of bone. We know of this because archaeologists have found "calendar sticks" that may be more than 30,000 years old.

As civilizations developed, so did ways of keeping time. Early civilizations kept track of time by observing the movements of the sun or the moon, as well as the positions of the stars. Later, more sophisticated kinds of clocks and calendars were developed. As time marched on, so did the knowledge of measuring and calculating time. Today, time can be measured accurately within just a few fractions of a second. That's faster than you can blink!

Time, for all of its mystery, certainly controls our lives. You probably looked at the time as soon as you got up this morning. Some of you are probably sneaking a peek at the clock as you read this. Time tells us when to get up and when to go to school, when we go to recess or lunch and when we go home. It is hard to imagine a world without time devices, such as clocks and calendars.

Water Clock

Sundial

Aztec Calendar

Hourglass

Time Candle

Stonehenge

Clock Tower

Pocket Watch

title: Galileo: A Man out of Time
text:
In 1564, a tiny baby was born in Pisa, Italy. His father, a cloth merchant and musician, called him Galileo Galilei. His father schooled him at home until he was 11 years old. Then he was sent to school, where he thrived and grew. When he was 17, he entered the University of Pisa, where he studied mathematics and physics. He was very bright and entertained people with his amazing experiments. While a student, he read a letter from a friend who wrote that he watched a swinging light in the monastery, and it gave him the idea about pendulums. A pendulum is a weight that is hung in such a way that it can swing back and forth with a continuous rhythm. The clocks were not accurate at the time, and it was many, many years later that the 77-year-old Galileo (blind at this time) would think of the way to add the swinging pendulum to a clock to make it more accurate.

This was only one of Galileo's many bold, new ideas. It was another such idea that caused him to be imprisoned in his home. Galileo taught that the sun was the center of the universe, not the Earth, as people had believed for hundreds of years. As this idea was against the teachings of the Catholic Church, Galileo was soon summoned by the Pope. Galileo was condemned by the court to spend the rest of his life locked in his house under guard. After he died, his ideas lived on. Many years later, the church pardoned him and admitted he was absolutely right!

title: Ancient Calendars
text:
Lunar Calendars

The lunar month is the time taken for the moon to travel around the Earth - about 29 1/2 days. Until the 16th century, people believed that the Earth was the center of the universe. Therefore, religious calendars were always organized around the lunar month. The lunar year is 354 days.

The earliest written calendars were lunar. The Sumerians in Mesopotamia were probably the first to use a lunar calendar. Their calendar had only two seasons - summer and winter.

The ancient Egyptians also used a lunar calendar. The Egyptian calendar was 360 days. Because this didn't match the seasonal year, their year came up short, and they had to add extra days to make it up.

Around 1953 B.C., a rare celestial event happened. The sun, the moon and the five planets that look like bright stars all lined up in the eastern sky at dawn. Many historians believe that the Chinese began their lunar calendar at that time. They divided their year into 12 months of 24 days each. (How many days was the Chinese calendar?)

And so it goes, many lunar calendars with different numbers of months and often different numbers of days in each month. And they all had the same problem - they ran short of days each year.

By the time Julius Caesar came to rule in 46 B.C., the calendar needed some major adjustments, and Caesar ordered the lunar calendar to be replaced by a solar one.

Solar Calendars

The solar year is the time taken for the Earth to orbit around the sun. Around 2772 B.C., the Egyptians replaced their lunar calendar with the world's first solar calendar. In their new calendar, the Egyptians started each new year with the rising of the star Sirius.

Across the ocean in the Americas, Mayans began to watch the heavens, too. They mapped out the movements of not just the moon, but the sun, planets and stars. They were very good and figured that the length of a solar year should be 365.2420 days. Today, scientists have determined that the exact length of the solar year is 365.2422 days - almost exactly what the ancient Mayans figured! The Mayans had an interesting calendar. It included two cycles. One was a 260-day cycle used for religious purposes, and the other was the 365-day cycle. The larger wheel was a cycle of 20 days, while the smaller wheel had 13 days. Both wheels were like gears so that, as one turned, it turned the other also.

Ancient Clocks

After years and months, time is then divided into weeks and smaller units of days, hours, minutes and seconds. These are not natural divisions, but over thousands of years, people have adjusted these units until they work.

The very first "clocks" kept track of time by measuring shadows cast by the sun. The length of the shadow changed with the time of day. Sundials were used by the ancient Sumerians, Egyptians and Chinese. The problem with sun dials is that they can only show the time when the sun is shining.

Around 325 B.C., water clocks began to appear in Egypt. The water clocks work as water drips slowly, but steadily, from one container into another.

Burning candles that had markings on the side to count the hours were another way to measure time. Think of some challenges people may have faced using a candle for time.

An hourglass measures time by letting sand flow at a slow rate from one side of the glass bulb to the other. Have you ever used an hourglass before?

Around the 1300s, mechanical clocks began to be used in Europe, and around the 1600s, more accurate pendulum clocks were invented. Even with these improvements, early clocks were not very accurate, so scientists continued to think of better ways.

Early in the 1900s, quartz clocks were developed. These clocks were accurate enough to be used at sea, for communications systems and for other scientific purposes.

Finally, in 1967, atomic clocks were developed. They measure time by counting very regular vibrations - more than 9 billion a second! Atomic clocks are so accurate that they may only be off by one second in millions of years!

Time Zones

Look in the sky at noon, and you'll likely notice that the sun is directly overhead. Where is the sun for someone in California at exactly that same time? It's not directly overhead in California, is it? In fact, it's not 12 p.m. in California, either. It's only 9 a.m.

Because everyone on the planet wants the sun to be directly overhead at noon, there cannot be just one time zone. To solve the problem, scientists divided the world into 24 imaginary sections they call time zones. Each time zone is 15 degrees longitude, as the Earth turns 15 degrees longitude each hour. People in each time zone set their clocks accordingly.

In the 48 Continental United States, there are four zones: Eastern, Central, Mountain and Pacific. When it is noon in the Eastern time zone, then it's 11 a.m. in the Central zone, 10 a.m. in the Mountain zone and 9 a.m. in the Pacific zone. In which time zone is Massachusetts?

If you want to call your friend in Utah at 10 a.m. Mountain time, what time would it be in Massachusetts when you call?

title: Clarity of Expression: Henry Hudson
text:
Henry Hudson was an English sea captain and explorer who started off as a failure. He sailed on two voyages for England to find a northeast water route to the rich spice trade in Asia. But both times the icy northern seas blocked his way. He had to return home defeated.

Sounds like the end of his career, right? It wasn't. Hudson next convinced the Dutch East India Company to hire him for exactly the same expedition. In 1609 Hudson and his crew sailed west across the Atlantic. He reached the New World, landing on the island we know today as Manhattan. He sailed inland up a wide river and explored the surrounding valley.

It wasn't a passage to Asia. But Hudson's explorations allowed the Dutch to claim the land and build a fur trading post there in 1614, before the Pilgrims arrived. A Dutch settlement called New Netherland soon followed.

Unfortunately, Hudson's last voyage ended in mutiny. He refused his crew's demands to return home, so the sailors took over the ship, setting Hudson adrift in a small boat. His fate is unknown, but his legacy is Hudson Bay, Hudson River, Hudson Valley and the Dutch settlement that became New York City.

Henry Hudson must have had excellent clarity of expression. He had to be able to explain clearly to the Dutch that his experience and determination made him the best man for the job, even though he was an Englishman and not a Dutchman.

Think about a time that you wanted to convince your parents or teachers to let you try something new. Did you beg and plead? Or did you give them a clear explanation of your reasons? Which way do you think works better?

title: Justice and Fairness
text:
When you think of justice, do you think of our government, the Supreme Court or a courtroom full of people? Well, justice and fairness certainly are important in those places, but justice is also an important character trait for everyday life. Can you think of a time when you thought you were not treated fairly? Maybe you were not recognized for something you worked hard at, or maybe someone accused you of doing something you didn't do.

Wouldn't it be nice if everyone were treated fairly in this world? Well, you can start that right now. Do you treat your friends and family fairly? Do you ever cheat a little when you're playing cards or any other game? When you share something, do you always take the bigger half? What if a friend of yours was accused of stealing? Would you listen to both sides of the story or just assume that he or she was guilty because someone else said so? Doing those things isn't very just. Being fair in everything we do in our lives will help us build character. Others will trust us and know that we will treat them fairly.

title: Who is Father Time?
text:
Though the ancient Greeks and Egyptians worshipped time as a god, there were later views of time that were gloomier. The people of the Middle Ages pictured time as a figure who carried around an hourglass and a scythe (long, hooked blade). This figure was known as "Father Time," and his presence meant that someone would soon die. The hourglass meant that the sands of time had run out for the victim, and the scythe was meant as a symbol of a life cut short.

Today, the term "Father Time" is often used in connection with the New Year celebration.

title: Hoffman's Sloth
text:
Range: Central South America
Habitat: Mountainous tropical rain forests

Sloths spend a great deal of time hanging upside down in a tree. Sometimes, they even sleep this way! The sloths rarely leave the tree, feeding on leaves, blossoms and fruit. When the young are born, they cling to the mother for six to eight months, and then they remain in the same tree as the mother.

Sloths have rounded heads and flattened faces with tiny ears concealed under very dense, shaggy fur. Their hands and feet end in curved claws that are 3 to 4 inches in length. The basic colors of the sloth's coat are gray and brown. However, because of the humid atmosphere, a tinge of green algae may grow on the outer layers of hairs, making it blend in with the green of the trees.

title: Synonyms
text:
Synonyms are words that have the same or almost the same meanings.

Learning synonyms for common words is important. Synonyms build your vocabulary. They can make your writing more interesting (alluring, compelling, fascinating) to read.

Below, you will find a common (ordinary, average, passable) fairy tale. Work with a partner to find synonyms for as many words as possible. Rewrite the fairytale using your favorite synonyms.

Do you want to find synonyms on the computer? Use this Web site to see what you can find: thesaurus dot reference dot com

Goldilocks and the Three Bears

Once upon a time, there were three bears. They lived in the forest in a cute little cottage. There was a big papa bear, a middle-sized mama bear and a little baby bear. One chilly morning, mama bear stirred up some porridge. It was too hot to eat, so they went for a walk in the forest.

While they were out, Goldilocks came right in. She saw the porridge on the table and, forgetting her manners, sat down to eat.

“Wow,” said Goldilocks, “this big bowl is really hot.” She tasted the porridge in the middle-sized bowl. It was cold.

“Oh my heart,” she said, “this bowl of porridge is too cold.” Then she spied a little bowl. She took a little bite.

“Yummy!” she squeaked. It was just right. With a big smile on her face, she ate all of the porridge. It was just perfect for a crisp fall morning.
