text: Choose one article from this week’s magazine and read it again. Circle or highlight the main idea of the article in yellow. Circle or highlight three or more key details in green.

title: All the World’s Weather, Right Here at Home
text:
Weather refers to sunshine, rain, snow, heat, cold, ice, wind, etc. It changes from hour to hour, day to day and month to month. The weather is studied by a meteorologist. Climate is the weather patterns in an area from year to year. Climate is a combination of temperature, precipitation (rain and snowfall) and wind.

The wind could not have come at a worse time. The farms had failed - no water, no rain, no hope. With the ground plowed and seeds planted, it was all that some families could do to borrow a little money for food and shelter. After all, it was the Great Depression. People were losing their jobs, homes and farms by the thousands every day.

But that terrible wind - it would blow hard during the day, drying out the soil. The dust clouds were so thick, people went days without seeing the sun. When the wind stopped, the crops were buried beneath a foot or more of dust and dirt. Barns, old cars, cattle, wagons and horses were also buried. The dunes piled up 5, 10, 20 feet high. The Dustbowl lasted 10 long years, beginning in 1930, and grew worse each year. How could a family survive in a wilderness of blowing dust such as this?

Weather Patterns in the United States

Weather patterns in America not only change from season to season, but they go through cycles of seven to 10 or more years. The great Dust Bowl of the 1930s is a good example. Prior to the 1930s, the Great Plains enjoyed huge crops every year - until the drought came. This is just one weather pattern in our country.

To the south and along the East Coast, hurricane season is a routine, annual weather event that brings a lot of stormy weather. Sometimes, hurricanes will blow in from the sea and ruin coastal towns and lands. More often, heavy rainstorms drench the coastal areas.

To the north, winter is a shivering contest. Arctic temperatures plunge to 50 degrees or more below zero.

To the west, snow is important. The mountains collect enough snow to last most of the hot summer months. Melting snow fills rivers and streams. This water is used to irrigate crops.

Along the West Coast, warm Pacific air streams and currents keep the atmosphere comfortable and calm. There are no hurricanes here, but plenty of moisture. Places like coastal Washington and Oregon have more than 200 days of rain in a typical year. You have to like cloudy weather to enjoy the Pacific Northwest!

The great Southwest is redrock country. Here long periods of erosion by rivers and flash floods have carved the rocks into beautiful canyons. The southwest coast is a great place to pick grapefruit in January. Weather patterns in America are usually the same, year after year. That's why America's regions become famous for certain agricultures. You'll find oranges in California and Florida, but look for cattle in Texas, potatoes in Idaho and apples in Washington. Corn grows in Oklahoma and wheat in Kansas. Look for retired people in Arizona, boaters in Michigan and campers in Virginia. Each region of America is unique, colorful and a wonderful place to call home!

title: Climate and Vegetation of North America
text:
You just learned about North America's climate and weather patterns. Now, let's think about what different climates and biomes are on different parts of our continent. What about vegetation? You learned a lot on the front page of Studies Weekly. The maps on these pages will help you learn even more!

Climate and Vegetation

The world is made up of many different biomes. A biome is a very large area of the world's vegetation with a special climate and specific types of plants and animals. Let's explore the biomes and climates of the United States, Canada, Mexico and the Caribbean. Use the maps, map keys and information for each country. Remember, each map is not an exact copy of each area, and biomes cover large areas. For example, the state of Massachusetts is more than just a deciduous forest. We have coastal regions and mountainous areas.

The United States

Since the United States covers a large area of land, there are many different climate regions. The climate of the United States is mostly temperate (mild), but the climate in Hawaii and Florida is tropical (hot and humid with plenty of rainfall). The climate is arctic (extremely cold) in Alaska, semi-arid (partly dry) in the Great Plains west of the Mississippi River and arid (very dry with almost no rainfall) in the Great Basin area. The Great Basin is a desert area in the western United States that covers most of Nevada and parts of Utah, California, Idaho, Wyoming and Oregon.

Read about each biome in the list below. Then look at the U.S. biome map.

tundra: mostly flat land with no trees and always frozen soil

desert: an area of land that has sand, gravel or rock with little or no vegetation, no permanent bodies of water and little rainfall

grassland: land on which grass or low green plants are the main vegetation

temperate forest: forest that has four seasons where you will find both evergreen trees and deciduous trees

boreal forest: (also known as taiga) has coniferous trees, cold winters and warm summers

tropical forest: a forest with year-round temperatures about 70-75 degrees F found near the equator; tropical forests include rain forests (thick evergreen forests in areas of heavy rainfall), cloud forests (moist, foggy forests found on mountainsides), dry forests (forests that have a long dry season) and others.

Canada

Since Canada is located north of the continental United States, what do you think the climate and vegetation are like there? You probably know that it gets colder as you go north. The cold climate means most of Canada is forests and tundra. Canada covers a large part of the North American continent, so the climates differ, or vary, from one area to the next. The northern part of Canada has very cold temperatures and little rainfall. The middle areas of Canada have short summers and long, cold winters with lots of rainfall. Along the coastlines, the climate is mild and there are heavy rainfalls.

Read about each biome in the list below. Many places in North America have the same biomes. You may need to look back at other biome lists on these pages to find the definitions. The biome map of Canada shows where each biome is found.

boreal grassland: temperatures are higher than in the boreal forest; flat area with lots of grass

boreal barren: further north than the boreal forest; colder with a much shorter growing season and very little vegetation

Great Lakes: Lowlands located in the southern regions of Ontario and Quebec; location of the world's longest deep inland waterway

subalpine: low mountain areas

montane: high mountainous areas

Mexico

Mexico is our neighbor to the south of the continental United States. What type of climate and vegetation do you think would most likely be there? You probably know that it gets warmer as you get closer to the equator. The warmer climate means most of Mexico is deserts and rain forests. Although Mexico is smaller than the U.S. and Canada, it covers a lot of land and has several different biomes.

Read about each biome in the list below. Many places in North America have the same biomes. You may need to look back at other biome lists on these pages to find the definitions. The biome map of Mexico shows where each biome is found.

chaparral: thick group of bushes, shrubs and small trees

thorn forest: thick, shrub-like vegetation that is found usually between deserts and grassland areas

oak-pine forest: trees and vegetation located in dry, low mountain-like areas

The Caribbean

The Caribbean is south and east of the continental United States. It is made up of several island nations. The Bahamas, Cuba, Jamaica, Puerto Rico, Haiti and the Dominican Republic make up 90 percent of the land. Let's focus on those countries. What would you guess the climate and vegetation would most likely be in this part of the world? If you said, "hot with rain forests," then bingo - you win the prize! The Caribbean islands have mountains, montane forests, deserts and tropical rain forests.

Read about each biome in the list below. Many places in North America have the same biomes. You may need to look back at other biome lists on these pages to find the definitions. The biome map of the Caribbean shows where each biome is found.

mangrove forest: a forest of mangrove trees, a tree that grows in wet, salty soil near coastlines

wetlands: areas of standing water, such as swamps, marshes, etc.

title: Greetings from the United States! Grand Canyon, Arizona
text:
Dear Friends,

I've never felt so small in all my life as I did when I looked down at the Grand Canyon.

That's where we are this week in our tour of America. The Grand Canyon is in Arizona, and it is hot here!

We went on a tour of the canyon, and it wasn't in a car... guess what I rode on? A mule! At the end of the day, we could see over the Colorado River.

Wish you were here. It's really pretty!

Tawnysha

title: Why are the poles colder than the equator?
text:
To answer that question, think of a dark room where you are holding a flashlight a few inches above a flat surface. When you direct the light straight down on the surface, the light will be bright, and the pattern will be round.

Now, imagine that you tilt the flashlight and shine it at an angle on that same surface. There will be a change in the pattern and the brightness of the light. How do you think it will change? The patch of light becomes larger and oblong. The light is also weaker.

In a similar way, the sunlight is most intense at the equator because it strikes the Earth from directly overhead.

At the poles, the light strikes Earth at an angle and is spread across a wider area.

title: Gila Monster
text:
Range: Southern Nevada, western Arizona, southeastern California, and southwestern Utah to Sonora in Mexico

The Gila (HEE la) monster is one of only a handful of venomous lizards in the world. The venom of these colorful lizards is rarely fatal to humans, but when it bites, it bites hard and fast! This critter will hold on and chew as a way to inject venom into the wound.

The body of the Gila monster is pinkish in color, and the scales are spotted and blotched. The face is black.

The sluggish Gila is nocturnal and hunts primarily by scent. It can live months in the desert climates in times of drought because fat is stored in its tail. During a drought, it is likely to stay in a burrow for weeks at a time. It has sharp claws that are useful for digging into a protective shelter.

The Gila monster dines on rodents, eggs, other lizards, and baby mice and birds. It lays three to five eggs in damp sand from fall to winter.

title: Help a Rat and Learn to Run the Country This Year!
text:

title: A Nation's Treasures and Resources
text:
What is a natural resource? The natural resources of an area are the water, minerals, coal, oil, gas, living things and land that are found there. These are the treasures for the nation that possesses them. Because people depend so heavily on natural resources, they should understand them. Some important things to know are (1) how changing the amount used will affect them and (2) how those changes will affect the economy, environment and quality of life of the people who use them.

Some resources are called renewable resources. If we use them carefully, they probably won't run out. Things like water, trees and air are renewable resources. They grow back, or can be replaced.

Non-renewable Resources

Other resources, called non-renewable resources, can't be renewed or replaced. These resources include such things as coal, oil, gas, metals and jewels (gems). Coal, oil and gas are called fossil fuels. Fossil fuels are products of dead plants and animals over a very long period of time. It takes millions of years before decayed organisms are converted to gas or coal. People can't really replace them. Someday, they will be gone.

Right now, the major sources of energy in the United States, Canada and Latin America are coal, oil and natural gas. While there is concern that someday we will have used them up, there is also a problem of pollution.

Scientists have been working on other energy sources. They hope to develop resources that are both renewable and kinder to the environment. Solar electricity is energy from the sun. Hydroelectricity is generated from moving water. Geo-thermal electricity is generated from the Earth's heat. Nuclear energy is from the energy inside an atom. These are some of the other energy sources. It seems simple enough, so why don't we use these renewable resources for energy? Because it's very expensive to produce and use these resources, and because some just don't provide the same level of energy that fossil fuels do.

Another solution is to try to mix the use of a renewable resource with the use of a fossil fuel. This would use up less of the non-renewable resources and would produce more energy than trying to do it without the non-renewable resources.

Other Important Resources

Other resources are important, too. Metals have always been valued throughout history. Gold made explorers want to come to the western United States and into much of Latin America.

The rain forests are among Latin America's most important resources. People use the wood from the forests to build things such as homes and furniture. The tropical forests in the world, however, are home to many living creatures. It is a concern to many that they are disappearing at an alarming rate.

Water—the most important resource

Water is probably the most important natural resource because every single animal needs water to live. In the last few decades, many countries are making a huge effort to clean up this valuable resource. Can you think of water cleanup projects in your state?

Something important to know about natural resources is that when a nation has more of a resource than it needs, it can export it, or sell it, to countries that don't have enough. When European colonists first came to America, they sent a ton of wood back to Europe because there was a shortage. Selling things to other countries brings more money to a country. When a country has more money, it can take care of its people better!

title: Fifth Graders Talk to Congressmen on Skype
text:
Have you ever thought about different ways to power your parents' cars? Fifth grade students at Columbus Elementary in Edwardsville, Ill., have been learning about other ways to power cars using alternative (substitute) fuels. In September 2011, Illinois Senator Bill Haine and Representative Dan Beiser visited the school to talk about the work being done to improve the environment and the use of "green" energy. Green energy is energy that produces less pollution. Fifth grade students from the entire school district "attended" the assembly. With the help of an internet video program called Skype, students from other schools were able to watch the assembly and ask the officials questions. After the assembly some students emailed questions to Sen. Haine and Rep. Beiser. Students were very excited to receive responses from the officials.

The teachers and students at Columbus Elementary are doing some amazing research when it comes to alternative energy. In fact, they are planning to run a diesel engine using vegetable oil instead of gas. Students are also learning how to reuse resources and are looking forward to turning used vegetable oil into hand soap. To learn more about alternative energy, visit www.benefits-of-recycling.com.

title: Landforms of North America
text:
Brooks Range - Brooks range is in the most northern part of Alaska where it is very cold.

Alaska Range - These mountains of Alaska run from the Alaska Peninsula to the border of the Yukon in Canada. The highest point in North America is found in this range - Mount McKinley at 20,320 feet. The highest peak in Massachusetts is Mount Greylock at 3,491 feet. How many Mount Greylocks could you stack to equal Mount McKinley?

Rocky Mountains - The Rocky Mountains run through the three largest countries in North America: Mexico, the United States and Canada. The Rocky Mountains have more than 100 separate mountain ranges. Some of these include Absaroka, Big Horn, Laramie, Sacramento, Uinta and Zuni.

Sierra Nevada - This mountain range is in eastern California. It is about 400 miles long. The highest peak is Mount Whitney at 14,494 feet.

Sierra Madres - These mountains are much shorter than the Rockies and include two major ranges and one smaller one. They run parallel to both the Pacific coastline of Mexico and the Gulf of Mexico coastline. There are several peaks reaching more than 10,000 feet.

Coast Range - These mountains run along the Pacific Ocean coastline from California through Oregon, Washington, Canada and Alaska.

Canadian Shield - This is a very large plateau region that stretches from the Great Lakes area in the United States and covers much of northern and eastern Canada. The surfaces here are rough and rocky - not great for farming - and covered with evergreen forests. In the northernmost areas, along the Arctic Circle, it is a rocky, frozen tundra.

Cascades - This mountain range stretches from northeastern California across Oregon and Washington. This is where the volcano, Mount St. Helens, erupted on May 18, 1980. The eruption of Mount St. Helens in southwestern Washington state disrupted the lives of thousands and changed more than 200 square miles of rich forest into a gray, lifeless landscape. Now, more than 20 years later, the land around the mountain is slowly healing.

Appalachians - The beautiful Appalachians run from Alabama in the United States, up through the New England states, and then through the Canadian provinces of New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Quebec. They are about 1,500 miles in length. The famous Blue Ridge Mountains and the Pennsylvania Alleghenies are in this mountain range. The Catskills of New York, the Green Mountains of Vermont and the White Mountains of New Hampshire are also part of this range. Have you been camping in any of these ranges?

Great Plains - These well-known plains of North America slope gently from the Rockies to the edge of the Canadian Shield and to the western edges of the Appalachians. Put your finger on the map and trace the area that is the Great Plains. Minor hills and mountains are found in the Ozark Plateau of Missouri, as well as in the Boston Mountains and the Quachita Mountains of Arkansas. Much of the land in the Great Plains is flat and mostly treeless.

title: Greetings from Mexico!
text:
Population: 113 million
Capital City: Mexico City

Dear Friends,

We have been learning a lot of one of Mexico's first civilizations. The Omecs are known for creating giant head statues. Today, we visited the huge heads. If Celeste stood on my shoulders, she wouldn't even be able to reach the top. They are very tall. The Olmec heads are in LaVenta. The guide said that the Olmec moved these giant heads more than 100 miles to this site. I don't know how they did that. It's a mystery to me!

Tomorrow, we will be going to Acapulco. Aaaaahhhhh... the beach!

Wish you were here!
Omar

title: Is Hawaii part of North America?
text:
Look at a map or a globe. Hawaii is actually a string of 132 islands near the middle of the Pacific Ocean.

Hawaii is politically part of the United States - the 50th state. Geographically, however, it is not part of North America. In fact, the islands aren't considered part of any continent.

What is considered part of North America? Canada, Greenland, Mexico, the United States, all the countries of Central America and the island countries of the Caribbean.

title: Jaguar
text:
Range: Mexico through Central and South America to Argentina
Habitat: desert, grassy plains, forest and steaming jungles

Though it's covered with spots, the jaguar is stockier and more muscular than the leopard. It has a large head and very powerful jaws. The jaguar's color varies from almost white to orange-brown to black (with black spots). The chest is white, and it has uneven stripes on its belly. The jaguar's spots are a kind of rosette with a dot in the middle.

Though we classify the jaguar as one of the big cats, this feline seems to have no roar! The jaguar is usually solitary, and it hunts at night. It can run, swim or climb trees with ease. The jaguar can run very fast for short distances. Jaguars dine on many animals of the land and sea including fish, turtles, capybara, parrots, monkeys and sloths.

Female jaguars give birth to a litter of two to four kittens. Kittens are born with their eyes closed and are adorable to look at.

title: 'X' Marks the Landmark
text:
Did you know the United States spans (spreads across) the width of the whole North American continent? It also includes the islands of Hawaii and the frozen land west of Canada called Alaska. We share the continent of North America with two other countries, Canada and Mexico. We also share large bodies of water and a few physical features with the islands of the Caribbean. This week we'll learn about some of the physical features on the North American continent and in the Caribbean. We'll also talk about natural and man-made landmarks in the United States.

Let's start with physical features. What are they? Physical features are the natural parts of the Earth's surface. Some examples are lakes, rivers, oceans, mountains, deserts and plains. What are natural landmarks? Natural landmarks are well-known, or famous, geographic features that mark a certain place. Man-made landmarks are also well-known geographic places that identify a location. However, humans created these landmarks and they didn't form naturally. Take a look at the list of physical features, natural landmarks and man-made landmarks to the right. Use a red crayon to circle the ones you have heard of or seen. Then use a blue crayon to circle the ones you'd like to know more about.

Barry the Bigfoot

No one has ever met or talked to a creature we call Bigfoot. If one did exist, wouldn't it be great if it were friendly? Maybe if you were lost in the woods, a Bigfoot would help you find your way back home. Maybe you could name him Barry the Bigfoot and he could help you with your geography assignment! A Bigfoot would be an excellent guide to the Earth's physical features.

Barry might say something like this: "You seem like a nice kid. I think I'll help you with your Studies Weekly lesson. Let's look at some maps. We can identify physical features of North America and the Caribbean and find some important natural and man-made landmarks. Your job will be to use the map key and check off each one we find."

The Caribbean and North America are very large areas to investigate. Luckily, Barry is a very big guide. Now lace up those hiking boots, grab a pencil for Barry's checklist and turn the page to get started!

title: Yellowstone National Park
text: Yellowstone National Park in Wyoming is our country's first national park. It has some amazing geo-thermal (hot water under the ground) geysers and colorful boiling "mudpots." Old Faithful is the largest active geyser in the world.

title: Redwood National Park
text: Redwood National Parks are found near the coastline of California. Redwood National and State Parks are home to some of the world's tallest trees: old-growth coast redwoods. They can live to be 2,000 years old and grow to more than 300 feet tall. (A white pine in a New England forest is 30-70 feet tall.)

title: Physical Features and Landmarks
text:
Do you have your boots laced up? How about your sharpened pencil? If so, let's begin our journey...

Map #1 - Major Physical Features

Look at the map of North America. It's such a big place, that most maps can't show Hawaii where it is actually located. Hawaii is really much further out in the Pacific Ocean. Look at a globe to see where it is. Read the information below and use the symbols on the map to learn more about these major physical features. Find each area on the map as you complete this part of your journey.

Barry's Checklist #1 - Physical Features

Alaska Mountain Range: The mountains of Alaska extend from the Alaska Peninsula to the border of the Yukon Territory in Canada.

Sierra Madre Mountains: The Sierra Madre Mountains include two large mountain ranges and one smaller one. They are located in Mexico.

Rocky Mountains: The Rocky Mountains are about 3,000 miles long. They stretch from New Mexico up through the western United States and into British Columbia, Canada.

Appalachian Mountains: The Appalachians are about 1,500 miles long. They spread from central Alabama up through the New England states. They also stretch into the Canadian provinces (areas kind of like states) of New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Quebec.

Great Plains: The Great Plains of North America cover the land from just east of the Rockies to the western edges of the Appalachians. The land is mostly flat with large, treeless areas and shallow river valleys.

Mississippi River: The Mississippi is a major river of North America and the United States (over 2,300 miles long). It flows from northwestern Minnesota south to the Gulf of Mexico, just below the city of New Orleans.

Rio Grande: The Rio Grande is also one of the longest rivers in North America (over 1,800 miles long). It begins in southern Colorado and flows south. It flows through New Mexico and forms a natural border between Texas and Mexico. In Mexico, people call it the Rio Bravo del Norte.

The Great Lakes: The Great Lakes include Lake Huron, Lake Ontario, Lake Michigan, Lake Erie and Lake Superior. (Notice that the first letters of the names spells HOMES!) They are in the northeastern part of our country and form a border between the United States and Canada.

Kilauea Volcano: The Kilauea Volcano is an active volcano on the island of Hawaii. Scientists are recording eruptions of the Kilauea Volcano to this day.

OK, now you've explored a few major physical features like mountains, rivers and plains. Let's take a look at a few natural and man-made landmarks. Remember, landmarks are well-known, or famous, geographic features that mark a location.

Barry's Checklist #2 - Landmarks

Read the information below and use the map key to learn more about these natural and man-made landmarks. Which landmarks are natural? Which landmarks are man-made?

The Statue of Liberty: The Statue of Liberty is near New York City in the Upper New York Bay. France gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States as a gift in 1886.

Kennedy Space Center: Kennedy Space Center is located just south of Titusville, Florida. John Glenn, Neil Armstrong, Sally Ride and Jim Lovell are just a few of the brave men and women who have launched into space from Kennedy Space Center.

The Everglades: The Everglades are located across the southern part of Florida. This huge watershed has many habitats that provide shelter for plants and wildlife.

Dunn's River Falls: Dunn's River Falls is on the Caribbean island of Jamaica. People climb up the falls and enjoy the cool water splashing on them. They also enjoy swimming in the nearby lagoons (shallow ponds).

Aztec Pyramids: The Teotihuacán Aztec Pyramids are located in the Mexican highlands. Ancient Aztec were the native people of Mexico, and they built the pyramids.

Death Valley: Death Valley is in southeastern California and part of Nevada. This desert has many sand dunes, multicolored rock layers and snow-capped mountains. Death Valley also has water-fluted canyons (canyons with grooves carved by water) and wilderness that spreads across three million acres!

Mount McKinley: Mount McKinley is in Alaska. It is the highest mountain in North America. Mount McKinley is also known as Denali, which means "The Great One."

Gateway Arch: The Gateway Arch is in St. Louis, Missouri, next to the Mississippi River. The Arch is 630 feet high and is the tallest national monument in the United States.

Can you hear what Barry is saying? "Hey! You did a great job! You found some major physical features of North America and the Caribbean. You found some major landmarks. You even figured out which landmarks were man-made and which were natural. I'll be sending you an invitation to the Bigfoot Family Picnic soon, because I know you could find your way there!"

title: The Legend of Bigfoot
text:
Many things scare people. We have told stories of monsters, ghosts, vampires, giant squids and hairy creatures for many years. One of those scary, hairy creatures is Bigfoot. Sometimes people call Bigfoot a Sasquatch or Yeti. They call it Sasquatch in Canada. People in the Himalaya Mountains of Asia call it the Yeti, or Abominable Snowman. No matter what you call this half-human, half-ape creature, the stories say he's at least eight feet tall and weighs around 450 pounds. You wouldn't want to run into one of these guys at night - except for our friend Barry, of course!

Bigfoot is a mysterious creature of the woods, but does it really exist? Though the name of the beast changes from place to place, all the stories share the same basic ideas. For hundreds of years people have claimed to see this creature in every part of the world. People believe all Bigfoots, Sasquatches and Yetis are large, ape-like beasts. They sleep during the day, but come out to hunt for food at night. The main difference between the North American beasts and the Himalayan beasts is the color of their fur or hair. Bigfoot and Sasquatch are believed to have brown or black fur. Yetis, or Abominable Snowmen, are believed to have white fur. What do you think? Is Bigfoot real or just a legend?

title: 'My Vacation,' by Barry the Bigfoot
text:
Hi again! Would you like to know what I do on vacation? Here are some places I like to visit and things I like to do outside. I love to hike. Hiking is just like walking except you're climbing up hills or mountains. One of the best places I ever went hiking was in Oregon, near Mount Hood. I took some stunning pictures last summer of Mount Hood and Lost Lake. It's such a beautiful place! Since I wear a fur coat year-round, I really enjoy the summers there because snow is still on the ground. If I get too warm, I can take a nice swim in Lost Lake. You can go there and hike around the lake, climb up Mount Hood or go into the Timberline Lodge to enjoy hot cocoa. Sometimes I sneak into the lodge's kitchen at night and grab a cup of cocoa when no one's looking.

Another activity I really enjoy is swimming with friends. Not human friends - animal friends. They don't care if I'm really hairy and don't wear a swimsuit. Once I swam with a manatee and some fish when I vacationed in the Ellie Schiller Homosassa Springs Wildlife State Park. This park is on the west coast of Florida, just north of a big city named Tampa. There's a lot to do besides swimming. When I'm there, I love to hike, ride horses and watch people picnic. I even like to do a little bit of bird watching. People are not allowed to swim in the springs, which is good because so many plants and animals live there. The Homosassa Springs form the headwaters (small bodies of water at the start of a river) of the Homosassa River. Florida is my favorite place to visit during the winter. The temperature and weather are perfect, even for a furry fellow like me.

title: Let's Write
text: If you had the chance to create a landmark for your school, what would it be? How would your landmark represent your school? Think of a landmark that would make people want to travel long distances to see it, take pictures of it and maybe buy a t-shirt to remember their visit. Now design your landmark. Be sure to add lots of details, captions and labels. Color your landmark and describe its location so other people can find it.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: As you read this week’s magazine, circle or highlight five words that are new to you. Write the words on a piece of paper. Try to figure out the meaning of the words by reading the other words and sentences around them. Write what you think the words mean and compare your definition to a dictionary definition.

title: The First People: Who Were They, and Where Did They Come From?
text:
If you look at a map of the North Pacific Ocean, you'll find the Bering Sea. Alaska is on the east. The Aleutian Islands are to the south and to the west is Siberia. The Bering Straight connects the Chukchi Sea of the Arctic Ocean and the Bering Sea. It is a very narrow strip. Historians believe a long time ago, there wasn't water there, but a passage of land. During this period of time, approximately 20,000 years ago, men were hunters. When they needed food, they hunted it. Great herds of large mammals roamed the land, and where the herds went, so did those early humans. It is believed human beings used the Bering land bridge to enter the New World. The land bridge later disappeared when ice sheets and other glaciers melted, causing the sea level to rise. These early inhabitants did not stay in one place. They continued to depend on hunting for survival.

About 12,500 years ago, a band of wanderers known as the Clovis people lived in parts of North America and South America. Some believe the Clovis people are the ancestors of today's American Indians. The people, however, may not have been the first people in the Americas. Recently, archaeologists have found evidence that other people may have reached parts of North America and South America thousands of years earlier. Who these people were and where they came from remains a mystery.

Native people who lived in what is now central Mexico were the first to grow corn, squash and beans. They began to develop permanent settlements. The settlements grew and became great civilizations. The Olmec people were one of the greatest. They had cities and built pyramids, temples and other public buildings. The Aztec eventually became the most powerful people in Mexico. By A.D. 500, the Anasazi Indians were living in what is now the American Southwest. Their villages were constructed of stone. The Anasazi flourished for hundreds of years, but in the 1200s, they abandoned their villages and left everything behind.

Farther east, the Adena and the Hopewell people lived. These people built earthen mounds as forts, tombs and for religious reasons that aren't really understood today.

By the time the first Europeans arrived, historians believe there were anywhere from 2.5 million to 20 million people in what is now North America. These people were made up of individuals from many different tribes. Family groups had unique customs, languages and cultures. Indeed, this was not a "new world" to them. It was their home.

title: Horses in America
text: Thousands of years ago, there were horses in the Western Hemisphere. Know one knows why, but they disappeared. The American Indians of the 1600s had no knowledge of horses until they were brought over by Spanish conquistadors.

title: American Indians of the USA
text:
There were great differences in tribal customs, languages, dwellings, food and dress among the American Indians of the United States.

Who Was Here When the Europeans Arrived?

It is important to our study of the early United States to know who was here when the Europeans began colonizing. Much of the early history is concerned with conflicts between the settlers and American Indians.

Kwakiutl of Washington

American Indians of the Northwest built beautiful totems (large wooden carvings) to decorate their homes. They had a ritual for distributing their wealth called a potlatch. This was a feast and exchange of goods. The challenge was to match or top the rival clans with gifts, including blankets, food and ornaments.

Chumash Village Scene

There were about 300,000 American Indians in California when the Europeans arrived. They lived in small, independent groups. More than 100 different languages were spoken. The California natives were famous for their magnificent basketry. The skills of the coastal Chumash Tribe fishermen were well known. They used 25-foot canoes of driftwood or pine planks. They also gathered shellfish and hunted seals for their skins.

Inside the Anasazi Cliff Palace

(Anasazi means ancient ones.) There are 200 rooms and 23 ceremonial kivas. These Mesa Verde tribes cooperated on community water projects. They had observatories and made calendars. This pueblo, a rock-and-mortar home built into a cliff, was abandoned at the end of the Pueblo Period. We call these the Pueblo Indians.

The Dakota of the Plains

The Dakota like to be called Dakota, Lakota or Nakota which means "The Common People." Some people call the Dakota people the Sioux. The word "Sioux" means "Snake People" and was used against the Dakota as an insult. They don't like people to use that word today to identify them. The image of the Dakota is what many people think of when they hear the term "American Indian." That is because they lived in the Plains, rode horses, wore feathered headdresses and fringed shirts and lived in tepees. These people, who hunted the buffalo, worshiped the sun and buffalo as sacred powers.

A Caddo Farmer of Louisiana, Arkansas and Texas

The Caddo were forced to emigrate to Texas, where they were settled along the Brazos River. They were one of the tribes encountered by De Soto in his journey of exploration in 1541. They were farmers and raised corn, beans, melons, pumpkins, tobacco and squash. They lived in huts that looked like tall beehives. Villages had up to 700 people. The Caddo called newcomers Tayshas, as a friendly greeting. This eventually became the word Texas.

The Cherokee

The Cherokee lived in log houses in the southeast. They dyed cotton to make brightly colored clothing. They discovered spiraea, which is a plant medicine that contains aspirin. One of their favorite foods was bean dumplings. After the Revolutionary War, the culture of the Cherokee changed. They tried to live the life of the white man. They bought land and farmed it, learned to read and write and lived in towns. They even published their own newspaper. Despite all of this, the American government forced them to travel the Trail of Tears to relocate on land west of the Mississippi River.

Inside an Iroquois Long House

The New York state groups who joined together in the Iroquois League were noted for their longhouses of poles and bark. They were 50- to 150-foot dwellings built for a number of related families. The women did the farming while the men hunted in bands, built homes, traded and fought. There were other Iroquois-speaking tribes around the Great Lakes and along the East Coast. Though they spoke the same Iroquois language, they lived differently.

Building a Bark Canoe

This was a skill of American Indian tribes all over the northeastern part of North America. It took 10 to 20 days for two men and four women to finish a new canoe.

Timucua Indians

Some American Indian groups did war with each other. The Timucua made spears, shields and war clubs to use in battles with other American Indians. The word "timucua" actually means "my enemy." This group lived throughout Florida and southern Georgia. They wore tattoos.

American Indians Throwing the Atlatl

An atlatl is a tool for throwing spears. Thanks to the atlatl, ancient hunters were able to kill more deer, because it made their throws stronger. It also made it easier for the hunters to hit the target. Scientists believe the atlatl was used by ancient hunters on every continent except Antarctica.

title: Greetings from San Lorenzo, Mexico!
text:
Mexico Population: 114,975,406 Mexico Capital City: Mexico City

Dear Friends,

Today, we visited a kind of a temple built by the Maya Indians thousands of years ago. Look at the card, and you can see many steps leading up to the top of the temple. Whew! What a hike.

We also visited a place called San Lorenzo that the Olmec built. There were huge heads carved from rock. When I was on my dad's shoulders, I could barely see the top of one head. They are 9 feet tall.

This stuff is pretty cool. Maybe I'll be an archaeologist one day!

Your friend,
Pierre

title: Do We Say "Native American" or "American Indian"?
text: Some individuals and some entire tribes of American Indians prefer to be called American Indians. Some are offended by the name Indian because the name was a mistake that Christopher Columbus made when he sailed to America and thought he had reached India. It is considered correct to use the terms American Indian, Indian or indigenous people, according to the tribes' websites. Everyone agrees that we are all proud to be called Americans!

title: Ocelot
text:
Range - southern Texas, parts of Mexico, Central America through South America
Habitat: dry deciduous forests, flooded savannas, tropical rain forests

This fellow looks like he could be your household cat, but he's a bit bigger than that! The ocelot grows to weigh about 20-30 pounds.

The fur on the ocelot is spotted and blotched with black. No ocelot looks exactly like another. The ears are rounded with a large white spot on the back of each ear.

The ocelot does most of its hunting at night and sleeps in the leafy trees during the day for camouflage. Ocelots are generally solitary animals.

Ocelots like to dine on birds, rodents, snakes and lizards.

title: What are Homophones and Homographs?
text:
Homophones and homographs are the same but different! To find out the meaning of a word, carefully read the words and sentences surrounding it.

Homophones

Homophones are words that sound the same but have different spellings and different meanings. You can remember what a homophone is by remembering that a phone makes a sound, so a homophone sounds the same as another word.

It is important to know a homophone when you write it. If you need help with a homophone when you read or write, look it up in a dictionary. This will help you keep from making mistakes. For instance, would you write you have “bear hands” or “bare hands”?

Here are some common homophones:
beat, beet
earn, urn
eye, I
heal, heel, he’ll
made, maid
plain, plane
rain, reign, rein
to, too, two

Homographs

These are words that are spelled the same but have different meanings. Sometimes they are pronounced differently even though they are spelled the same. You can remember what a homograph is by remembering that a graph is something you look at, so a homograph looks the same.

Here are some common homographs that are pronounced differently and have different meanings:

bass: a low voice
bass: a fish
content: things found inside
content: satisfied
minute: 60 seconds
minute: tiny

Try It!

The next time you are not sure which homophone or homograph to use, be sure you know the meaning of the word you are trying to use. This will help you spell it correctly. A dictionary will help you a lot!

title: Big Bang Meets Big Crunch
text:
Paul Steinhardt and Neil Turok are two scientists who recently came up with a theory about how the universe came to be. Almost everyone has heard of the Big Bang Theory, the idea that all matter was concentrated in one giant blob that suddenly exploded. But Paul and Neil think this theory doesn’t explain the whole story. The Big Bang Theory is based on the belief that one big explosion of matter was the beginning of all stars and planets. As the molten matter blew out into the cold of space, the globs and blobs began swirling and cooling into the universe as we see it today.

The Big Bang Theory leaves a few unanswered questions: What caused the first big explosion? Why is the universe still expanding? What happens when it stops expanding? What was the universe like before the Big Bang? Questions like these are the reasons Paul and Neil started working on a theory of their own. They think the universe goes through cycles of exploding apart and then pulling itself back together again. Like a stretching rubber band, extending and then shrinking, the universe will explode and contract, repeatedly. This means the universe is actually moving through a cycle, and it doesn’t have a beginning or an end. No beginning and no end? This idea could sure make your brain hurt! But don’t worry. Paul and Neil’s theory is only an idea. You’ll have plenty of time to think it over because it’s going to take a few hundred million years of observation and testing to see if it is actually correct.

title: Let's Write
text: A fairy just visited you as you were falling asleep. She explained that she would send you anywhere you wanted to go, including back in time. You decided to visit an American Indian village of long ago. How was your trip? Use any five of these words to help you describe your trip: Iroquois, long house, Timucua, Caddo, Anasazi, Kwakiutl, totem, potlatch, atlatl, pueblo.

title: Choosing a Place to Live: How do we choose just the right place to live?
text:
People like to have choices about many things. They like to choose what to wear in the morning, what books they want to read and what to eat for lunch. People spend a lot of time shopping and choosing clothes they like to wear. They like to choose what church they go to, and they like to choose where to live.

What is it you like about the community where you live? Why do you think your family lives where it does?

There are many surveys conducted by cities and businesses that ask those same questions. They want to know why folks choose to live just where they do. Here are some of their answers:

They like to be near the city.

They want to stay near family members.

They want to live in the country.

They want to be close to schools.

They live there because of the kind of work they do.

They choose a place to live based on how much it costs to live there.

Sometimes people live in a certain place because their family has lived there for many generations, and they choose to stay.

People choose not only where to live but what kind of dwelling to live in. In one minute, name all of the different kinds of dwellings that people call home in the many communities in our world. Ready? Here are a few to get you started:

1. hogan (a round home made by Navajos in the Southwest)

2. brick (used as building material by many people for centuries.) Occasionally used by smart little pigs as well!

How did you do? Did you find that the places people around the world call home are just as different as the people who live in them? People choose the kind of dwelling they live in for many reasons. Perhaps one of the biggest factors (one of the things that causes something else) is the kind of climate they live in. Is it hot? Cold? Very rainy or a desert? Each of these things probably determines what kind of dwelling people choose to make. If you lived in a very rainy or snowy place, your house might be up on stilts. Can you guess why?

What is your home made of? Maybe it is an apartment or a highrise made of steel and concrete. If you live in an area where lumber is plentiful, maybe your home has wood siding. If you lived on a tropical island, maybe your home would have no walls, and only palm fronds for a roof.

Choosing a place to live is fun and exciting. Choosing the kind of home you will live in can depend upon the climate you live in, what kind of materials there are to build it and how much money it costs to build it. Whatever the reason, "there's no place like home!"

title: Warwick Castle
text:
Warwick Castle is considered by many to be one of the most beautiful castles in England. It was rebuilt in the 1600s, with the Great Hall dating to the 1300s.

Warwick Castle is one of hundreds of castles in Europe and Scandinavia.

Who do you think lived in castles of old?

title: What is a Census?
text:
In the year 2010, millions of Americans answered questions about their families, their ages and their income. We call that a census. The census is an official way to get a count of the population. That is the number of people living in a country or district. The census is a national event that has been carried out every 10 years since 1790. This is required by the U.S. Constitution. The government has to know how many people there are and where they live. One reason they need to know is to determine how many people should represent each state in Congress.

There are two ways that the census bureau gathers this information. For example, you may remember your parents receiving a pamphlet of questions in the mail. On the pamphlet, your parents answered questions about your family, including each family member's name and birthdate. After they complete all the questions, they mailed the pamphlet back to the census bureau to be counted. Another way the census bureau collects this information is by hiring census employees who go door to door asking people questions about their families. It is information from the census that contributes to decision making about issues such as housing, funding for programs, changes in education, healthcare and more.

The census results show us that some areas are densely populated. This means that a large population occupies a small area. The differences of population from one area to another are common. For example: The Netherlands is a fairly small country that has about 1,000 people per square mile; while Australia, a much larger country, has about six people per square mile. Which country is densely populated? If you said the Netherlands, you are right! Look at the map to find some other interesting facts about the number of people who live in different communities around our world.

Ancient People and the Fertile Crescent

Nearly 10,000 years ago, people began to settle down for the first time. Before this period of time, people were always on the move following the animals that they depended on for food. It wasn't until agriculture began to develop that they settled in one place. Agriculture refers to crops and animals raised on farms.

People began to discover certain plants could be grown. They began to rely on the steady supply of food from their crops and animals instead of moving from place to place.

Some of these earliest farmers settled in what is often called the Fertile Crescent. This is an area of land that is well watered by some rivers that flood each year, such as the Euphrates and Nile rivers. Here people grew wild wheat and barley. They kept goats, sheep, pigs and cattle.

People of today have many reasons for choosing a certain place to live. These early people settled in a region because of the water and rich soil.

Catal Huyuk was an early city that thrived about 8,000 years ago. Archaeologists have found many artifacts that the people who settled there left behind. They know from these artifacts that the people who lived there grew crops and raised cattle. They also found that this group of people were skilled metal workers, potters and woodworkers.

title: Population Density
text:
This is a population density map of Massachusetts. It shows the average number of people who live on one square mile of land. Places where more people live have a higher population density. Places where fewer people live have a lower population density. Use this map and other resources to help you answer these questions.

1. Which part of Massachusetts has the highest population density? Why?

2. Which part of Massachusetts has the lowest population density? Why?

3. Write how you would find the population density of your classroom.

title: Working for the Common Good
text:
Americans (that's you and I ) come from lots of different backgrounds. We look different, act differently and have different customs and traditions. Some of us celebrate Christmas, some of us celebrate Hanukkah and some of us don't celebrate any holidays at all.

But there are many things that we, as Americans, all agree on. We all believe in the value of a good education. A democracy cannot survive without citizens who are educated and able to make good decisions when they vote. We also agree that we need to do things for the common good. Things that are for the common good are things that help all of us. We are willing to pay taxes to have parks, better schools and good roads. It also means that we give money to charities, volunteer to help others and give aid when other people are in trouble. What can you do to work for the common good in your community?

title: Toco Toucan
text:
Range: Tropical South America
Habitat: Tropical forests

This extraordinary bird is one of the largest toucans, with a bright yellow beak and a blue ring around its eyes. Its beak is about as long as a banana. The beak contains many air-filled spaces that make it lighter than it looks. Scientists aren't sure why their beaks are so large. They are useful for reaching food, but may also help the birds recognize other members of their own species. Each species has its own beak colors.

Toco toucans hop along branches on their pale blue feet. Their feet have two toes that point forward and two that point backward. They love fruit, and they also eat small insects.

The toucan flies by first flapping its wings then closing them by its sides, causing it to dip up and down in the air.

title: Making the World a Kinder Place
text:
We sometimes wonder why bad things happen to innocent people. Although we may never understand it, we can do our best to keep things like this from happening in the future. When we do this, we are doing our part to make the world a kinder place, without anger and violence.

One way to do this is by making a plan to replace bullying and violence with kindness. The Cool to Be Kind (C2BK) program was developed to help students create programs in their classes and schools that are based on pro-kindness - doing nice things for others. Students look for ways to "pay it forward" each day. Paying it forward means that when someone thanks you for doing something nice, you ask that person to pay it forward by doing something nice for someone else. By paying it forward, kindness continues to spread across the world and people start thinking kinder thoughts and ways that they can help other people.

What are some ways you could practice paying it forward? How about doing yard work for an elderly neighbor for free? Or inviting a new student to eat lunch with you and your friends? What about giving up your seat on the bus to someone who looks tired, or helping someone pick up something they have dropped? Thinking kind thoughts and acting on them with acts of kindness is a simple change that you can do to change the world.

Teachers: Go to www.pifexperience.org to find out more about starting a C2BK program at your school!

title: What are Idioms?
text:
What are Idioms?

Have you ever heard an adult say, “I’m sorry, but we’re up a creek on this one”? What did he mean? He was standing on dry ground when he said it! Well, you’ve just heard an idiom.

Idioms are Not Meant to Be Taken Literally

Idioms are sayings that mean something different from the literal meaning of their words. “Literal” means “following the exact wording.” But idioms are not literal, so the words do not mean exactly what they say. Listen carefully for clues to figure out an idiom.

Try It!

The best way to learn what an idiom means is to learn it and use it in your own speech or writing. Ask someone what it means. Then use it in your own writing. Here are some idioms in sentences. See if you can figure out what they mean. Once you know what the idiom means, use it in your own sentence. Use another piece of paper if you need it.

1. They were both so shy they had a hard time breaking the ice. Use “breaking the ice” in your own sentence.

2. When it comes to modesty in dress, I have to draw the line somewhere. Use “draw the line” in your own sentence.

3. By halftime, the game was in the bag. Use “in the bag” in your own sentence.

4. Chris and I are in the same boat because neither of us have extra cash to spend on the field trip. Use “in the same boat” in your own sentence.

5. Would someone lend me a hand with the dishes? Use “lend me a hand” in your own sentence.

title: Let's Write
text: Everyone loves to tell about where they live. We want to know about your community and why you love to live just where you do. Write a paragraph about the community where you live. What is the climate like? What are the things you are proud of? What places do people like to visit when they come to your community?

2. Put a dab of glue on the center of the cork and put the needle in the glue as shown. Let glue dry.

title: Discover the Seven Wonders of America!
text:
If you traveled across America from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean, what landforms would you see along the way? Mountains? Plains? Plateaus? Lakes? Forests? You would see all of these and more! Our country has a wide variety of physical features that make it a beautiful and interesting place to live. This week, we will learn more about these features.

The United States can be divided into seven major areas, or regions. Each region has unique physical features. Each region also has its own climate (weather over a long period of time), economy (the way people make, spend and save money) and industry. Each has other characteristics that set it apart from the other regions, too.

Here's a list of America's seven regions. See if you can find them on the map and then keep reading to learn more about each one.

Pacific Coastal Plain

Western Plateau

Rocky Mountains

Interior Plains

Atlantic Coastal Plain

Appalachian Region

Ozark Highlands

title: USA's Seven Natural Regions
text:
Read the description of each region below. Find your region on the map. What famous places are in your region? Look for other regions where you have lived or visited.

This is a map of the Continental United States. Do some research to find out in which regions the states of Alaska and Hawaii belong.

1. Pacific Coastal Plains

This region lies along the Pacific coastline from Alaska to Mexico. One physical feature of this region is that it has mountains bordering the ocean. There are more potentially active volcanoes in this region than in any other region in the Lower 48. The two main mountain ranges are the Cascade Mountains in the north and the Sierra Nevada Mountains in the south. The western valleys have fertile and rich land. Many high-quality fruits are grown there. Giant redwoods are an interesting feature in the northern Californian mountains. The San Andreas Fault, another feature of this region, sometimes causes earthquakes.

2. Western Plateau

East of the Pacific Coastal Plains and west of the Rocky Mountains lies the Western Plateau, or the Great Basin. This region stretches from Washington state to Mexico. The Western Plateau includes mountains, deserts and the Grand Canyon. Many places in this region are very dry, so not many crops grow there. In the north, farms are able to produce good crops through irrigation. Other areas have forested mountains, fertile farmlands and orchards. One famous part of this region is called the Colorado Plateau. Here you can see some of the world's most unusual and beautiful landforms.

3. Rocky Mountains

The Rocky Mountain range is the biggest mountain range in North America. It begins in Canada and extends through central New Mexico. Many of the peaks are more than 12,000 feet high. Mount Elbert in Colorado is the tallest peak in the range at 14,433 feet. Crossing the Rockies was a major problem for settlers moving west in the 1800s.

An imaginary line called the Continental Divide passes through the Rockies. On the west side of the line, rivers and streams flow down toward the Pacific Ocean. On the east side of the line, rivers and streams flow down toward the Atlantic Ocean.

The lower parts of the Rocky Mountains are covered with trees. However, in the upper parts of the Rockies, only plants like grasses, mosses and lichens can grow.

4. Interior Plains

The Interior Plains is the largest region in the United States and it is located in the center of the country. The western part of this region has good grasslands for grazing cattle and rich soil for farming. Other parts of the region have oil and coal deposits. Today, the Mississippi River flows through the region, but it may surprise you to know that scientists think this area was once a large sea.

5. Atlantic Coastal Plains

This region extends from New England along the Atlantic coastline and the Appalachian foothills, down through Florida to the Gulf of Mexico. The gulf area has farms and grasslands. It also has large oil and natural gas deposits. The southern states also have good farmland. Farmers grow tobacco, peanuts, cotton and many other products.

6. Appalachian Region

This region begins in Maine and continues down into Alabama. Although the Appalachian Mountains are not as rugged as the Rockies, transportation through the Appalachians can still be difficult. Fortunately, large rivers cutting through the mountains have made some good places for people to build railroads and highways. Up in the mountains, minerals and coal are produced. In the valleys, farming is a major activity. Because forests cover these mountains, the lumber industry is a big part of the economy in this region.

7. Ozark Highlands

The Ozark Highlands are not very high at all! This area, including Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma and Arkansas, is best described as a plateau. The land is not good for farming but there are many forests filled with cedar, oak, hickory and pine trees. Underground caverns are an interesting feature of this region. You will also find many man-made water reservoirs in this area.

title: Mapping the News
text:
Have you ever heard or read a news report about a certain place and wondered where it is? Mapping the news can help. This is a fun way to learn geography and keep up with things that are going on in the world at the same time. Here's how it works: Your teacher will put a world map on a bulletin board in your classroom or in the hall. Once a week, students can bring in news articles to share with the class. (Ask your parents to help you with that part, especially if you get your news articles from the Internet. Also, do some research before you get to class to get a general idea of where the place is located.) In class, talk about each article and the place where the event happened. Find that place on the world map and mark it with a pushpin or a sticker.

For example, let's say your friend brings an article about a mountain climber who reaches the top of Mount Everest on the border between Tibet and Nepal. She already found out that those two countries are in south Asia. That will help you find Mount Everest more quickly.

Try mapping the news for several weeks. Then get into groups and make up a game that involves the places you mapped. Playing the game will help you remember what you learned. Have fun mapping the news!

title: Diversity
text: Just as there are many diverse regions in the United States, there are also many diverse kinds of people living here. The United States is home to people from many different countries. Why? People from around the world have decided to come here because they want to be Americans. Sometimes America is described as a large salad bowl. The different cultures and backgrounds of the people in our country are like the ingredients in a large salad. A salad with only lettuce isn't very exciting. But a salad with a combination of tomatoes, cucumbers, lettuce, carrots and other ingredients is delicious. The more ingredients, or diversity, the more flavorful our country will be! Here in America, we value the differences we have with others and learn from them. This diversity makes our country a unique and special place to live.

title: Which Is the Most Important River in America?
text: To answer this question, you have to ask other questions. Which river is the largest? Which carries the most trade? Which provides the most recreation? Which has the most important cities near it? Which has the richest history? The answer to all of these questions is the Mississippi River. A pageant of American history has passed up and down the Mississippi, the largest river in the United States and one of the greatest trade waterways in the world. It is affectionately and respectfully known as "Old Man River." The Mississippi and its chief tributary, the Missouri River, together make up the longest river system in the world. The Mississippi River was also the western border of the United States until the Louisiana Purchase.

title: Caravel
text: In the 1400s, the Portuguese built a ship that would carry explorers and traders all the way across the Atlantic Ocean. The ship they created was called a caravel. This boat was different from other boats of its time because it could sail very fast, it could sail into the wind and it could float in shallow water. It also had a unique feature: its sails were shaped like triangles. Columbus used a caravel when he went to explore the New World. The boats named the Niña and the Pinta were both caravels. The caravel was important because it allowed explorers to journey almost anywhere they wanted to go.

title: Sailing Down the River
text: Where do you think communities have formed for thousands of years? Near water, of course! Some of the most important reasons early communities formed near a source of water were that they needed it to drink and to grow crops. Communities along water were also able to use ships to exchange goods with others, or take part in commerce. Through trade people were able to acquire goods they could not produce. People still use water for these same purposes today.

title: Let's Write
text: Of all these states in the United States, which one would you like to visit? Why are you interested in visiting this location? What would you like to see on your trip? Write a paragraph or two explaining your reasons for choosing this location. You can do some extra research if your teacher gives you permission. Be sure to use correct grammar, spelling and punctuation.

title: The Largest State
text: Can you guess which state is the largest? If you guessed Alaska, you are right! It covers approximately 586,412 square miles. The smallest state is Rhode Island, which covers approximately 1,214 square miles. In 2010, more people lived in California than in any other state. The state with the smallest population in the year 2010 was Wyoming.

title: U.S. States and Capitals
text: Your teacher will give you a table to use for this activity. This map will help you write the state or capital city in the table. Make sure you spell each state and capital correctly!

title: Wildlife in Danger
text:
There are an extraordinary number of different animal species in our world. They are different sizes, shapes and colors. Did you know three quarters of all known animal species are insects? A third of all known insect species are beetles. While insects are plentiful, there are many species that are specially adapted to the habitats in which they live. Understanding what each species needs to survive helps scientists to know why they may be endangered. What does the term endangered species mean? If an animal species is considered to be endangered, it means they are in danger of extinction. In other words, endangered means there is still time for us to try and do something before they become extinct.

In some ways, extinction is a part of nature's scheme. Species have been vanishing since life began. No one is really certain how many species have disappeared. At certain times in the Earth's history, the rate of extinction has quickened. For example, when the dinosaurs disappeared some 65 million years ago. Now, the pace has jumped once again. Today the problem is mostly because humans are able to change the environment. They change it faster than the animals are able to adapt to the new living conditions. If we could control these forces of change, perhaps they would be less of a threat to the wildlife of our world.

What is the worst threat to wildlife?

The spotted owl only lives in ancient forests, or forests with trees more than 100 years old. Once, 15 million acres of ancient forest covered parts of North America. Now all but 10 percent of those forests have been cut down. The Mexican spotted owl lives in the old forests that provide a closed canopy for nesting. The old forests also provide uneven tree growth. This is unlike plantation forests where the trees are planted all at once. These ancient forests have fallen logs and decaying plantlife.They attract flying squirrels and other rodents which the spotted owl dines on. The closed canopy of the old trees also provides protection for the spotted owl. It is hidden from its enemy, the great horned owl. The great horned owl hunts in open spaces. Without a doubt, destruction of habitats is the greatest threat to wildlife today. Logging and clearing forests for farming contribute to habitat loss. Urban sprawl (growth of urban areas into rural areas) and wilderness recreation are problems too.

What can we do to help protect our environment? Turn to Page 2 and find out!

title: All About Earth Day
text:
"As the father of Earth Day, Gaylord Nelson inspired us to remember that the stewardship of our natural resources is the stewardship of the American Dream."

- President Bill Clinton 9/29/95

Earth Day was a dream-come-true for Senator Gaylord Nelson. After more than three decades, it has blossomed into a worldwide celebration. Gaylord Nelson had been worried. He believed there was a lack of concern about the environment. The people in our country had concerns about things such as air pollution and water pollution. They were concerned about our Earth. But, the U.S. government had not been able to give it time or attention. After several attempts to raise awareness, Nelson had an idea. He thought he should bring these concerns to college campuses and organize a demonstration. He thought students and other citizens might respond.

He couldn't have been more right. The response was electric and took off across the country like lightening. It became a nationwide effort. Rising concern about the environmental crisis swept our country. April 22, 1970, was the first Earth Day. More than 20 million people participated in demonstrations and activities. It was the biggest grassroots environmental movement in the history of our country. It helped people to voice their concerns. Soon the government responded by passing the Clean Air and Clean Water acts. By 1990, it was an international celebration. Over 200 million people in 141 countries participated.

Gaylord Nelson has always been passionate about the environment. After serving as a U.S. senator, Nelson left the Senate. He became director of the Wilderness Society in January 1981. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom Award in September 1995.

title: Want to Help? Here’s What YOU Can Do
text:
To be responsible for the environment and for the living creatures that depend on humans...well, that's a pretty huge job. It can't be handled by just one person. It requires communities of people just like you.

Environmental situations are always changing and it is important to keep up with current events. Here are some things you can do to learn about ways to protect our environment:

Get the facts about endangered species. A great resource is the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Check out their Web site at https://endangered.fws.gov/kids/

Look at current events in your local newspaper

Search online encyclopedias

Check your school library for magazines and books that talk about the environment and conservation.

Ask teachers and family members what they know about conservation.

Tell Others

If you care about the environment, make sure your voice is heard. It is so important to ask questions and express your views. Many students are worried that they can't make a difference, but adults need to know that you care about the future of our Earth. So, get on that computer and start typing! Ask your family and friends to write letters about environmental concerns as well. If you are concerned about the maintenance of National Parks, endangered species or the use of natural resources, then you can e-mail the Department of the Interior at webteam@ios.doi.gov.

You can also write to your senator or representative about your concerns or to give thanks.

Practice It

Once you have learned about endangered species and our environment, make a list of things you can do and commit to it! Hang it in a place where you can see it often or put it in your school notebook. The following are suggestions that you might want to put on your list:

Adopt an endangered species native to Massachusetts.

Find out how you can help and make a presentation to other schoolmates or family members.

For an endangered species list for Massachusetts, see www.state.ma.us/dfwele/dfw/nhesp/nhrare.htm.

The best way to learn about a subject is to experience it. As stewards of the Earth, we should take the time to enjoy beauty and peace of nature. Go outside and explore your school grounds. Pay attention to the trees, plants and wildlife you see in your state. How many can you identify? Take the time to notice the sights, sounds, and smells of nature when you have the opportunity to spend time in the wild. Want to do more?

Create a coloring book of nature for another class in your school.

Plant a tree

Plant a butterfly garden

Hang a birdfeeder

Refuse to buy products that are made from rare or endangered animals.

Keep the family dog contained at night so as not to disturb the local wildlife

When you are driving with your family along highways where wildlife may be present, remind adults to slow down and be on the lookout for wildlife. This will help to keep you safe as well.

Pick up litter and throw it away in proper trash bins

Make a class mural about endangered wildlife in Massachusetts. Ask your local library if they could display it for a month.

It's YOUR Future! Help Protect it Today

We create a lot of garbage, even when we don't mean to. Each time you eat at a fast food restaurant, pay attention to how much garbage they sell you with your food.

If it's not far, then don't take the car! Help conserve fuel.

If a 100-watt light bulb is on for half a day, every day, for a year, it can use enough electricity to burn almost 400 pounds of coal! What can you do? Turn off the lights when you are not using them or leaving a room.

When six-pack rings end up in the ocean, they are invisible to the sea creatures and birds. These animals can be hurt. You can help by snipping each of those circles apart before you throw them away.

What's the best thing to do with that empty soda pop bottle? That's right, recycle it!

Can you imagine if all the kids, in all the schools, in all our world communities recycled? We would really be helping our Earth.

If you don't have a recycling program in your school, talk to your principal to see if it would be a good idea to start one.

Stoves and ovens use a lot of energy! Here are some tips to conserve it:

Don't open the oven door too often

Cover pots

Bake with glass or ceramic pans

Adopt a piece of the Earth as your very own. It's your job to keep it free of litter. You can make a difference!

title: What Happens If We Use up All the World's Coal, Oil, and Natural Gas?
text:
Reduce, reuse and recycle- that's a wise saying when it comes to our natural resources. When it comes to the natural resources of coal, oil and gas, the only answer for now is to "reduce."

Coal, oil and gas are nonrenewable resources; once they're used up, we won't find any more. We would then have to do without them, or find a different source of energy to replace them. Scientists have been working for decades on other sources but haven't yet found things that are as easy to use, and cost about the same as these fossil fuels.

title: Black-Footed Ferret
text:
The black-footed ferret is currently considered the most endangered mammal in the United States. It originally inhabited the plains areas of the United States. As the plains were gradually plowed into farmland, the prairie dogs began to disappear. Farmers often poisoned large colonies of prairie dogs as they competed with the grazing livestock for food. The result was a drastic drop in the numbers of black-footed ferrets as well, for the main diet of the ferrets was the prairie dog.

It was thought the black-footed ferret was extinct until a ranch dog in Wyoming killed one in 1981. A colony of 130 ferrets was discovered, but disease soon eliminated all but 18 of that colony. The remaining 18 ferrets were taken into captivity to produce a bigger colony. Those ferrets in captivity have now reached about 2,600 in number and a few have been reintroduced into the wild in Wyoming, South Dakota and Montana.

The black-footed ferrets have long, slender bodies with short legs. The fur on the sides and back is generally a pale yellowish with lighter areas on the face, throat, chest and abdomen. The top of the head and middle of the back are dark brown, and the feet, tip of the tail and a mask across the face are black.

Ferrets generally give birth to a litter of four or five young in the late spring. The young ferrets are playful and jump and wrestle. They growl and hiss as they play or hunt. Ferrets are nocturnal and avoid humans, making them hard to observe.
