title: Agility of Mind: Teddy Roosevelt Wins Nobel Peace Prize
text:
agile (adjective): able to move quickly and easily; ex.: as agile as a monkey, an agile mind.

Teddy Roosevelt was president of the United States from 1901 to 1909. He was also a great hunter, explorer, author, outdoorsman and soldier.

As a child Teddy was often sick and could not play sports. But he became a good problem solver. He wasn't afraid to put his thoughts into action or think of different solutions. If his first idea didn't work, he had the mental agility to change his mind quickly.

When Roosevelt was president, Japan and Russia were at war. He invited diplomats (official representatives) from Russia and Japan to Portsmouth, New Hampshire to talk about peace. At first, he didn't know how their problems could be solved but he acted quickly to get the diplomats together. He helped them compromise. After a lot of discussion, they worked out their differences and signed the Portsmouth Peace Treaty, an agreement that ended the war and saved many lives. President Roosevelt won the Nobel Peace Prize for helping end the war. His way of helping others solve problems is still used today.

Teddy Roosevelt had an important power skill - an agile mind. You can use this power skill when you act on your good ideas. Remember that an idea can be good without being perfect. People with agile minds often fail before they succeed. The ability to think on your feet, or think while doing, can help you find solutions that will benefit others.

title: How do I Use a Thesaurus?
text:
Do you use many of the same words over and over when writing? Are you getting bored with those same words? It’s time you learned to use a thesaurus!

Search for Synonyms

The word “thesaurus” almost looks like a name for a dinosaur, doesn’t it? It’s actually a book (it can be found online as well). This book or website provides synonyms (words similar in meaning) for common words. Using a thesaurus is a great way to broaden your vocabulary with more interesting words.

A thesaurus is usually alphabetical. Some are similar to dictionaries because they give you the part of speech, definition and sample sentences for words. Sometimes a thesaurus will give you directions to look up other entries. Here’s what you’ll find in a typical thesaurus.

Entry Word ........................................... The word you look up to find synonyms

Part-of-Speech Label ......................... Tells you if the word is a noun, verb, adjective, etc.

Definition ............................................... Tells you what the entry word means

Example Sentence ............................... Shows you how the entry word might be used in a sentence.

Synonyms ............................................... Words whose meanings are the same as or similar to the entry word

Antonyms ............................................... Words whose meanings are the opposite of the entry word

Try It!

Look up the word “grow” in a thesaurus. Write all the synonyms here.

title: Our Monuments and Memorials
text:
Monument

A place that is designed and built as a lasting public tribute to a person, a group of people or an event.

Mount Rushmore is a massive sculpture of the faces of four American presidents: George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Abraham Lincoln. These faces are 60 feet high and are 500 feet up the mountainside.

The sculptor, Gutzon Borglum began drilling in 1927 and took nearly fourteen years to complete the monument.

The Washington Monument is now open to the public after several years of restoration. This monument, found in Washington, D.C., is a tribute to the most celebrated of all U.S. presidents -George Washington.

Made of white marble from several different quarries, the construction began in 1848. Interrupted by the Civil War and other problems, the monument was dedicated 40 years later in 1888.

Devils Tower National Monument is a familiar site to many from the movie "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," which featured the Tower as the landing spot for the alien mother ship.

The Tower and the land around it were dedicated as our nation's first national monument by President Teddy Roosevelt in 1906. Since that time, a president may decide that historic landmarks, historic or prehistoric structures, and other significant historic or scientific objects be national monuments.

Memorial

Something that is intended to remind people of a person who is dead, or an event in which people died. For example a statue, speech or special ceremony.

Fort McHenry is world famous as the birthplace of the United States' national anthem. Francis Scott Key, the young poet-lawyer, was inspired by the heroic defense of Fort McHenry by American forces during a British attack on Sept. 13 and 14, 1814.

The fort became a National Monument two years after Key's poem became this country's national anthem in 1933.

The Vietnam Veteran's Memorial (The Wall) is a somber wall made of shiny black granite. It is a memorial to honor the nearly 3 million men and women who served with the U.S. Armed Forces in the Vietnam War.

The Wall was dedicated more than 20 years ago. It has helped our country to mourn the loved ones lost and to help us remember the toils of war.

The Wall is the most visited memorial in Washington, D.C.

title: Memorial Day: How Do We Remember?
text:
Memorial day is a national holiday. It is observed each year on the last Monday in May. This day is set aside to honor the nation's armed services personnel who were killed in wartime. The holiday was originally called Decoration Day. It is traditionally a day of parades, ceremonies and speeches. Many people decorate the graves of loved ones with flowers and flags.

Memorial Day was first observed on May 30, 1868. It was ordered by John Alexander Logan for the purpose of decorating the graves of the American Civil War dead. He was a senator from Illinois and a war veteran.

Today many people feel Memorial Day has lost its meaning. Some feel it has become a camping and picnic holiday. To remind Americans of the true meaning of Memorial Day, the National Moment of Remembrance resolution was passed in December 2000. This resolution asks all Americans to "voluntarily and informally observe in their own way a moment of remembrance and respect. To pause from whatever they are doing for a moment of silence or listening to Taps. This should be done at 3 p.m. local time on Memorial Day."

title: Monuments and Memorials in World Communities
text:
The Taj Mahal

A visit to Agra, India would lead you to the Taj Mahal. It is a tomb for Mumtaz-i-Mahal, the beloved wife of Shah Jaham. Shah Jaham was an emperor of India long ago. He built the tomb to honor his favorite wife. The Shah had to build an entire city to house the 20,000 workers who constructed the tomb. It took 20 years to build the huge building of white marble and red sandstone. It is elaborate and one of the most beautiful man-made sights in the world.

Shwedagon Pagoda

A very long time ago, there was a great teacher and doctor. The people called him "the enlightened one" or Buddha. It is said that Buddha gave a token of eight hairs from his head to two brothers in exchange for some honey. These two brothers, Poo and Taupau, then built a shrine to Buddha.

Today you can visit that shrine in Myanmar (Burma). The Buddhists say it contains the eight precious hairs of Buddha.

A Journey to Mecca

Muslims try to make a hajj, or a journey to the city of Mecca in Saudi Arabia, at least once in their lifetime. After a Muslim makes a hajj, they are called a hajji, or a pilgrim.

At the Great Mosque in Mecca, there is a small box-shaped building called the Kaaba. The Kaaba holds the sacred black stone that Muslims believe God sent from heaven. Wherever Muslims live, they face the direction of the Kaaba when they pray.

Castel Sant' Angelo

This museum in Rome, Italy, was once a castle with a very interesting history. It was once a large tomb of the emperor Hadrian. It was later used as part of a wall to protect the city of Rome. Unfortunately, enemies destroyed the tomb along with Rome.

Legend says that a later generation of Romans was saved from a great sickness by the archangel Michael who appeared at the ruins of the tomb. The Romans built a chapel here to honor St. Michael. It was later made into a castle.

The Arizona

This monument is found above the place where the battleship Arizona sank in Pearl Harbor on Dec. 7, 1941. More than a thousand men were trapped inside the ship after Japanese planes bombed it in Pearl Harbor. The monument was built in memory of its crew and others who died during the invasion.

The United States Marine Memorial

This well-known statue is the United States Marine Memorial in Washington, D.C. It is a bronze statue designed by Felix W. de Weldon, based on the famous photo snapped by Joe Rosenthal at Iwo Jima during World War II.

Many people think the photo was posed, but film footage of soldiers lowering a smaller American flag earlier in the day, then raising a larger flag to replace it, verify that it actually happened. Iwo Jima was a fierce battle - 6,821 Marines were killed in action.

title: What Is a Gargoyle?
text:
If you see a spooky-looking critter on a building, don't worry! It's just a gargoyle.

A gargoyle is a water spout in the form of an unusually scary creature or human. They project from the gutter of a building and are made to "spout" water away from the building.

The word gargoyle comes from the Old French word gargouille, which means "to gargle." This is because the water seems to come out of its throat.

title: Northern Pike
text:
Range: Throughout the Northern Hemisphere

Habitat: Freshwater lakes and rivers

The northern pike waits quietly on the bottom of the lakes and rivers. SWOOSH! With a burst of sudden speed it moves quickly to grab its victim, usually a fish. With large eyes to spot movement and powerful jaws, the pike is strong enough to deal with animals up to a third of its own size. Pike are fierce predators. In the spring pike may also dine on young coot or duckling.

The pike has a very long body that is shaped like a cylinder. It has a long beak-like snout. It has large fins that are near to its tail. They grow to be up to 4 1/2 feet long.

title: Fact vs Opinion
text:
Right now you are reading a magazine. A magazine is a great place to find both facts and opinions.

Fact: A fact is a statement that can be proved. For instance, to say most oranges are orange in color can be proven. All you have to do is look at an orange to tell what color it is.

Opinion: An opinion is a belief held by someone. It cannot be proven by fact. For instance, to say, “red apples are sweeter than green apples” is an opinion. It depends on who’s doing the tasting. Brian thinks red apples are sweeter. Brooke finds green apples the sweetest. They each have an opinion about the sweetness of apples.

Newspapers contain mostly facts on most of the pages. Certain pages are set aside for opinions. The editorial page contains letters to the editor, editorial cartoons and articles by the editors of that paper.

The purpose of the editorial page is to:

Make people think about events in the news.

Try to get public officials to see your point of view.

Give background and information about events in the news.

Serve as a community “voice.”

All your life you’ll be reading books and articles. You’ll also be doing a lot of writing for school and work. Get in the habit of asking yourself as you read or write, “Is this statement fact or opinion?” This habit will help you become a better thinker.

title: Let's Write
text:
Often, monuments and memorials honor national heroes. Those who are honored have done something extraordinary for other human beings. Sometimes they have overcome great challenges. Monuments help us to remember them and honor them for their deeds.

Think about who you consider to be your hero and make a list of all the things that make that person extraordinary. After you have completed your list, use it as a guide to write a paragraph about this individual. When you are done, complete your work with a picture that illustrates your paragraph.

title: Dimensional Graphics
text:
To make dimensional graphic designs, begin by making a square, any size. The basic idea is not as difficult as it looks. It is simply a matter of drawing each line so it misses the oncoming corner. The closer together the lines, the better the results.

Materials

paper

pen or pencil

 ruler

tape or glue

crayons or markers

Directions

Start in a corner and use your ruler to draw the line to the next corner but miss it by a little bit.

Next, ricochet off of that corner and go to the next and miss it by a little bit.

Continue doing the ricochet thing to the next corner, and after a great deal of going in a circle, you’ll begin to see a pattern develop.

Extra Activity

After you do one design in a clockwise manner, try doing one with a counterclockwise pattern. Then put the two together. These patterns can be arranged and rearranged to make a number of fascinating designs. When color is added—wow!

title: All Aboard!
text:
Throughout history mankind has been restless to discover the unknown. The United States, Canada and Latin America have all been searched by explorers. As long ago as 986 A.D. Vikings from Greenland were blown off course and landed in Canada. They explored, but decided to go back to Greenland.

In 1492, one of the most famed explorers landed on the shores of what he thought was the East Indies. Christopher Columbus had actually landed on the shores of the Bahamas (islands in Latin America). Columbus was encouraged by his discoveries. He would make several more attempts to find a new trade route to Asia. He explored parts of what are North and South America in the process. The voyages of Columbus opened up the the Age of Exploration. Many European explorers such as Magellan, Juan Ponce de Leon, Giovanni Verrazano, Cortes and others soon followed.

One of the early explorers was Jaques Cartier. He was sent in 1534 by King Francis I of Spain. He was looking for land rumored to have "a great quantity of gold and other precious things." The search for gold and for a northern passage for ships across the Americas to the Pacific Ocean continued to drive explorers. Samuel de Champlain, Cabeza de Vaca, Simon Frasier, Don Juan de Orate and Henry Hudson searched the continent. They never did find the Northwest Passage, but sometimes they did find gold.

The early explorers of Latin America were mostly conquistadors and missionaries, (people sent for a religious cause). They explored and expanded European influence in America and established Christianity among the native people of South America. They also destroyed many cities full of people during wars while exploring the land.

The first explorers to what is now the United States came for a variety of reasons. Many came at the direction of European rulers to claim land and later establish colonies. The explorers included many of the famous trappers, like James Bridger, and famous explorers such as Lewis and Clark. These frontiersman pushed the boundaries of the United States westward.

The main explorers of Canada were the French, Spanish and English. All were in search of the Northwest Passage, a trade route through the Americas to the Pacific Ocean. This would give them an advantage in trading with other countries. Russian explorers sailed through the Bering Strait and began exploration and colonization of Alaska. It remained part of Russia until the sale of Alaska to the United States in 1867.

During the mid-1500s and 1600s Europeans began the colonization of North America. Among the first was the colony in Roanoke (in what is now eastern Virginia). It was established by Sir Walter Raleigh in 1584. This colony soon failed. Later in 1587, John White established the colony again. He left a few months later to get supplies from England. When he returned the colony had mysteriously been deserted. No one knows what happened to the colonists. Later the more fortunate colonies of Jamestown and Plymouth survived, learning from Roanoke's failure.

In Latin America an explorer named Don Juan de Onate moved north in 1598. He established a successful colony in what has become Santa Fe, New Mexico. In 1608 Samuel de Champlain established the first permanent French settlement in the New World. This was the colony of Quebec, which is now a French-speaking province in Canada.

title: Exploration Today
text:
The spirit of exploration didn't die when North and South America were discovered. It is alive today. It is driving people to search for answers to historic mysteries.

Thor Heyerdahl of Norway is a well-known explorer of modern day. While he did not discover new lands in faraway places, he spent much of his life proving that ancient cultures could have sailed to, and populated, the South Pacific.

In 1947, Thor Heyerdahl set sail aboard a balsawood raft called the Kon-Tiki. At that time, most scholars believed that Polynesia was populated by people from Asia. Heyerdahl, however, believed that people could have reached the islands much more easily from the Americas. He sailed over 4,000 miles on the Kon-Tiki. This voyage demonstrated that his theory was possible. He then led an expedition to the Easter islands. He wanted to prove that South Americans had been in the Pacific before Columbus crossed the Atlantic ocean.

In the 1960s and 1970s, Heyerdahl made three experimental voyages in reed ships modeled after ancient seacraft. The first two voyages traversed the Atlantic in the papyrus ships Ra I and Ra II. He wanted to show that such ancient craft were able to survive ocean voyages carrying both people and their ideas to far-flung lands. A third voyage was made on the Tigris. This was a reed ship which traveled from Iraq to the Red Sea. He wanted to show that contact was possible between the great ancient civilizations of Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley and Egypt.

title: Spanish Colonization of Latin America
text:
Spanish conquistadors conquered much of Latin America and it's native people. A conquistador was a person who was sent by the king to conquer a group of people. Most conquistadors had little interest in exploration, but they were often the first Europeans to enter a region where they conquered the people. Sometimes they remained to settle.

Conquistadors were a part of the Spanish culture for hundreds of years. They sought to dominate groups of people in both the Old World and the new. Those conquistadors who set out for the New World generally did so for one purpose. To obtain gold.

In their quest for gold, the conquistadors killed many native people. Sometimes entire empires were destroyed by the conquistadors. Some Europeans of the day considered conquistadors to be little more than land-locked pirates.

Hernando Cortes is one of the most famous conquistadors who conquered what is now central and southern Mexico. He encountered the Aztec empire in 1519. Their king was Montezuma II. His people were very friendly to Cortes and his group because they believed Cortes to be one of their gods, Quetzalcoatl, coming back to greet them.

The Aztec submitted to almost everything Cortes wanted. Cortes captured Montezuma and tried to rule the Aztec empire. When Montezuma died, Cortes then attacked the Aztec. By 1521 Cortes had killed all of them. His military triumphs led to 300 years of Spanish domination of Mexico and Central America.

Other conquistadors were sent to find the legendary "seven cities of gold" that were spoken of in native legends. No one ever found the seven cities of gold. The conquistadors did eventually conquer Latin America.

title: What is a Cosmonaut?
text:
A cosmonaut is a Russian astronaut. Just like our American astronauts, cosmonauts have to go through specialized training to join the ranks of other cosmonauts.

The cosmonauts train at the Yuri Gagarin Russian State Scientific Research Test Center of Cosmonauts Training, in Starry Town, near Moscow. Can you find that on a map?

Cosmonauts travel into space aboard vehicles called Soyuz. Unlike the space shuttles for American astronauts, these vehicles are not reusable.

Yuri A. Gagarin of the Soviet Union became the first person to travel in space. He orbited the Earth once in a Vostok capsule.

title: Atlantic Flying Fish
text:
Range: tropical and subtropical waters of the Atlantic Ocean

What, fish fly? Yes, this fellow can propel itself out of the water and glide for short distances (usually 50 yards or less) when trying to escape from a larger fish that is trying to eat it.

This fish is distinguished by its long pectoral fins. It lives near the shore in tropical and sub-tropical waters but near the surface in the open sea. Its length is normally 6 to 12 inches, though some have been known to get as long as 18 inches. Flyingfish eat smaller fish for dinner.

title: Ten Great Explorers of North America
text:
1. Amerigo Vespucci Italian

1499

Found the mouth of the Amazon River, new world maps were made from his writings; Americas were named after him

2. John Cabot Italian by birth but sailed in the name of England

1497

Set sail for Asia, but found Newfoundland off the coast of what is now Canada.

3. Ferdinand Magellan Portuguese

1505-1521

Led the first expedition to sail around the world; explored tip of South America and Phillipines

4. Hernando De Soto Spain

1539

Sailed in search of gold. Explored what is now Florida and the northeast coast.

5. Francis Drake English

1578

Searched the west coast of the United States for Northwest Passage and became second man to sail around the world

6. James Cook English

1759-1780

British naval officer who charted Canada’s St. Lawrence river and Newfoundland’s coast waters

7. Merriwether Lewis William Clark America

1806

Commissioned by President Thomas Jefferson to explore the Louisiana Territory; explored from St. Louis to Oregon coast.

8. James Bridger America

1822-1866

Trapper who explored as far west as Rocky Mountains; cut new wagon trails and surveyed for railroad

9. Roald Amundsen Norway

1906

First to successfully navigate the Northwest Passage. First to reach the South Pole. Flew over the North Pole.

title: How Do I Give an Oral Presentation?
text:
Standing in front of a crowd and telling them what you think is not easy, but it can be done if you prepare well!

Preparing for an Oral Presentation

Know your audience. What you say should be directed toward them. Is it to be given in your classroom? This will make it easier!

How long should it be? If your teacher says 15 minutes, stick to the time.

What’s the topic? Did your teacher assign it? Make sure you can cover it in within the time limit.

Make notes. Use index cards and put them in the order you want to use them. Index cards are not so large that they cover your face. You may write your presentation on numbered pieces of paper, but do not staple the pages.

Practice, practice and practice some more!

Making the Oral Presentation

Introduction—Get the audience’s attention with the introduction. You can do this by asking a question, telling a story, using a quotation or making a statement. Once you have their attention, state your topic.

Body—State your main points and give information that support your main points. You may ask rhetorical questions, (questions that don’t need answers) use emotional words or repeat important information.

Conclusion—Repeat your main point. Conclude with something that leaves a lasting impression by asking a rhetorical question, making an emotional plea or using a quotation, story or statement.

Try It!

When you’re asked to give an oral presentation, make sure you prepare well. Organize logically. Practice, practice, practice. Good luck!

title: Cabeza de Vaca
text: Cabeza de Vaca explored from Florida to the southwest. He and his group left the Karankawa Tribe. They walked all the way to what is now Mexico City. They crossed the southeastern corner of Arizona and claimed the land for Spain.

title: Explorers
text:
On Page 3 of this issue about exploration, you will see a chart listing only some of the famous explorers of North America. Choose one explorer of North America that is not on the chart.

write a paragraph about that explorer and where he/she went. What were his or her contributions?

title: Where is Everybody Going?
text:
America is considered by many to be like a giant salad a place where people from many countries and cultures combine to form a whole. In today's world people are able to travel much easier. Moving to a new country or even continent is more common. People move to a new country for many reasons. Some people move alone. Some move with their family. Others move with large groups of people. In this issue of Massachusetts Studies Weekly, we will see the reasons people move and where they are going.

As we study the shift of population throughout world communities, we are studying human migration. Migration is the act of moving from one place to another. The people who are planning to move to a new country are planning to emigrate, or leave. After they arrive in the new country, they are often called immigrants. An immigrant is a person who lives in a country in which they were not born. How many of you immigrated from another country? How many of you have parents or grandparents who are immigrants?

When we talk about immigrants, many people imagine boatloads of people arriving at Ellis Island. Indeed, that was a time in our history when millions of people came to the United States. But people immigrated here long before then. In fact, the first immigrants to this land walked here. People crossed the Beringia, a land bridge that no longer exists between Siberia and Alaska. That was 20,000 years ago. They are considered by many to be the ancestors of the Native Americans.

The first Europeans to come here (the early colonists) were also immigrants. They were born in another country and migrated to this continent.

After the forming of the United States Constitution, the first laws for becoming an American citizen were passed in 1790. One of the important things about American immigration policy is that an immigrant may become a citizen. Many countries allow immigrants to live and work in the country, but do not allow them to become citizens. They can't enjoy the rights and privileges of a citizen of that country.

The dream of freedom or individual liberty is a traditional reason why many people immigrate to the United States. American freedom attracts immigrants from every area of the globe. Many new immigrants find joy in common activities that other Americans may take for granted. Free speech, religious freedom, economic freedoms and rights to equal protection and equal opportunities are some of them.

Most immigrants that come to the United States settle in California, New York, Florida and Texas. The total number of immigrants in these states accounts for about half of the immigrant population in America today.

title: Paddling Across the Atlantic!
text:
Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/ for more Connections and Current Events articles.

Do you dream of becoming a big sports star or exploring Mars someday? When Gabor Rakonczay was a kid in Hungary, he dreamed of being alone in a ship on the ocean. It may seem unusual, but Gabor has made his dream come true!

On Dec. 21st 2011, 30-year-old Gabor set out from Portugal in his 24-foot canoe. His destination was the Caribbean island of Antigua, 3,500 miles away. No one had ever crossed the Atlantic alone in a canoe!

After 26 days at sea his canoe capsized (turned over). His communications equipment was ruined. For seven weeks he was totally alone with no way to let his wife know where he was. He didn't use a satellite tracking system because at the last minute the price went up and he couldn't afford it. Three different times he lit signal flares to get the attention of passing ships. But each time the waves were too high and the ships couldn't see his canoe.

His wife, Viktoria, never lost hope. She was sure he was ok and even posted entries on their website. Viktoria kept track of the weather conditions and estimated where Gabor might be.

On March 25th 2012, Gabor landed on the island of Antigua. It took 76 days to cross the Atlantic alone in his canoe. He was even three weeks ahead of schedule! Congratulations to Gabor Rakonczay on making a difficult journey through the Atlantic.

title: Where Did They Come From?
text:
Individuals, families or groups of people may leave their country because they choose to. Poor working or living conditions, war and harsh treatment because of religion or race are just some of the reasons people may flee their homeland. Long ago, native Africans were kidnapped and taken to other countries and continents. Upon arrival in the new country, they were sold as slaves. That was an instance of forced migration. Finally, others may have been expelled from their country. Some of America's early colonists were forced on ships bound for America because they were criminals in their native England.

Whatever the reason for going to a new country, those travelers must have felt some excitement and fear as they neared the shores of the new country, their new home. Have you ever moved to a new neighborhood where you were to attend a new school? Maybe you felt excited and a little scared too? The first immigrants to come to America were largely European. Immigrants from Germany, Sweden and Norway were very important in settling the middle section of America. When gold was discovered in California in 1849, thousands of people from many world communities rushed to try their luck.

The construction of the transcontinental railroad (across the continent) was the reason for another wave of immigration in the late 1870s. The California businessmen hired thousands of Chinese laborers. They built the railroad through the dangerous Sierra Nevada mountains. There were laws that kept the Chinese separate from the Americans. The immigrants lived only in certain sections of the city. Many cities have "Chinatowns" that are remnants from this time. Later, as our country experienced a depression, many American citizens began to resent the immigrants. Some Americans felt that jobs should first be given to American citizens. The Chinese were often hired because they were thought to be better workers. It was this growing resentment that caused the first immigration laws in the United States. These laws were made to restrict the number of immigrants who could enter the United States. Even with the immigration laws, more than 20 million people immigrated to the United States between 1880 and 1914! Even with the fears of many, these immigrants did become part of America. Many came with greatly needed skills. These immigrants brought their own cultures, foods and ideas. This is the story of the United States. This is who we are!

Where Did People Come From?

Not all people feel the same about immigration laws. Most Americans feel some immigration should be allowed. Some feel everyone should be allowed to enter America. There are also a few who feel no immigrants should be allowed to enter America.

Immigration laws have changed many times over the years. The laws today determine how many people may enter our country each year. They also determine who may enter our country. In 1990, immigration laws set the number of people allowed to immigrate to the United States each year to 675,000. Today, more Hispanic and Asian immigrants are arriving than European. It is predicted that by 2050, Hispanic races will make up one fourth of the American population.

There is another group of people who are allowed to enter our country each year - refugees. Refugees are people who are forced out of their homeland. They are no longer safe in their homeland because of dangerous conditions, or because their government has threatened them because of their actions or beliefs.

Refugees are counted separately from other immigrants. One goal of our refugee policy is to help refugees return to their homelands when it is safe for them to return. For many refugees, returning home is not possible and is not a solution to their problem.

What can we do to help refugees and other immigrants adjust to their new way of life in America? We can welcome them and be patient and helpful as they learn our language and learn about our customs. We can remember that it is often hard to adjust to a new life. We can value their native culture and customs. We can help them become part of our great country!

title: Is There a Circus in Piccadilly Circus?
text:
Is there a circus in Piccadilly Circus, or tin pans in Tin Pan Alley? Well, there is a circus in Piccadilly Circus. But it's not the kind of circus you are thinking of. The word "circus" can also mean a round, open area, just like the one that used to be on the outskirts of London. Now it is the center of a popular shopping district.

There are no tin pans in Tin Pan Alley. It is an area in New York City where song publishers have their offices. If you have a song to sell, Tin Pan Alley is the place to go. At one time, they say you could hear so many people playing pianos that it sounded "tinny." So that's why they call it Tin Pan Alley!

title: Kingfisher
text:
With its turquoise and orange plumage, this bird looks like it belongs in the tropics, but can be found in European countries, including Ireland. It grows up to 6 inches in length.

The kingfisher watches for food from a branch above the water. If it spots a fish, it quickly dives to catch it. It then flies back to its perch and stuns the fish against a branch. Finally ready to dine, the kingfisher swallows the fish head first.

The kingfisher uses its beak and claws to dig a burrow nest in the river bank. It is very clever and makes the burrow slope upward so rain or river water cannot get in the nest. Though the kingfisher doesn't use nesting materials, its nest soon becomes littered with fish bones.

title: Greetings from Colorado, U.S.A.
text:
Population: 5,116,796

Capital City: Denver

Dear Friends,

I thought I’d seen some cool old trains on other trips, but this one is the best! The Durango- Silverton train rides on some very narrow tracks up the mountain to an old mining town.

They let my dad and me go into the engine car and and see where they shovel the coal for fuel. It’s really noisy and hot.

The train used to run silver and gold ore out of the mines in the old days. A lot of passengers used to ride the train just to enjoy the scenery. We visited the Old Hundred mine in Galena. I even got to pan for gold.

Still panning and hoping!

Scott

title: Reason and Logic: The First Filipino Settlement in America
text:
Settlers in America often faced challenges while building new communities. In the 1760s, New Orleans was the capital of the Spanish colony of Louisiana. Sailors from the Philippines served on Spanish trading ships going between Manila, the capital of the Philippines, and Acapulco, Mexico.

Conditions on the ships were harsh, and Filipino sailors were often slaves. Some of them jumped ship (escaped) around 1765 and traveled to Louisiana. Once there they hid in the marshlands outside of New Orleans to avoid capture by the Spanish. They formed a colony of fishermen who lived and worked in the swamps and bayous.

These early Filipino settlers were called the Manilamen. Their first village was named Saint Malo. The Manilamen built their houses on stilts in the swamps. They developed a successful method of drying shrimp in the sun on raised platforms. The processed shrimp were exported as far away as Asia and South America.

The fishermen often sent money back to the Philippines so that more relatives could immigrate (move) to New Orleans. Manilamen's families did not stay in the fishing villages, but lived in homes in New Orleans. Their children would come to work on the platform during busy harvest times.

There were seven Filipino villages in all. Saint Malo was the first, and Manila Village was the largest. Hurricanes have destroyed all of the original villages, but their shrimp-drying legacy lives on. The Manilamen used reason and logic to survive in their environment, just as people do today.

Have you ever noticed where your school is built? Is it located on level land or a slope? Is it a one-story building or taller? What things make the location and design of your school building reasonable and logical?

title: Migration. . . It's for the Birds!
text:
Did you know that animals, birds, fish and insects migrate too? But they do it every year! Whew!

Usually animals migrate to colder places in the summer and warmer places in the winter.

How do animals find their way when they are traveling great distances? Well, we know birds find their way by the stars at night and by the sun during the day. People thought this was impossible until some migrating birds were put in cages inside a planetarium. When the operator turned the artificial sky around, the birds gathered at the sides of the cages nearest to the direction in which they would have been flying if the sky were real!

title: How Do I Listen to an Oral Presentation?
text:
Listen closely to your classmates when they give presentations. Pay attention. You can learn a lot from them. Your teacher may tell you to take notes. You may also be asked to make written comments. Also, it’s just plain polite to be a good listener!

Be an active listener. Don’t daydream. Focus on the speaker’s main idea. Listen for the way he or she ties details to that main idea. Take notes, either in your mind or on paper.

Your teacher may help you to evaluate (to examine and judge carefully) your classmates’ presentations. Keep in mind that being honest can help your classmates learn how to give better presentations.

You may not agree with everything the speaker says, but you should listen to his or her ideas.

Don’t interrupt your classmate unless he or she has asked for you to join in.

Think about the speaker’s conclusion. Is it logical?

Try It!

When your classmates give presentations, be a good listener. It will help them feel more comfortable. Make eye contact. Your evaluation will help them improve their future presentations. And you might learn something. Besides, you will want them to listen to you when it is your turn to give an oral presentation.

title: Let's Write
text: Immigration can be frightening and difficult until you learn the language of the new country. Many of you may have learned English as a second language. Or many of you may speak more than one language in your home. Share your nifty language skills with others. Write how to say the days of the week and the names of the months in a language other than English. Write the word in English first, then translate it to another language.

title: Moving Resources and People
text:
For thousands of years, small communities produced most of the things they needed. Later communities expanded and people began specializing in one thing. They would then trade with others. Soon trading became so common that some people did nothing but organize trade. These people were called merchants. The most famous early land merchants were the Babylonians and later the Arabs. These traders traveled on foot, rode donkeys or rode camels.

The Phoenicians were the chief sea traders of ancient times. They are known as being one of the first to use sails on boats. They made the sails from linen. These sails allowed them to harness wind power to travel faster.

Soon people began to travel to find and conquer new lands. They also wanted to find better trade routes. This led to a great period of sea exploration beginning in the 1400s. Can you think of one famous explorer of this time? The voyages of Columbus and other explorers opened a whole new world. Many new all-water trade routes were used by many countries. These trade routes opened the way for people to settle many new lands. One of these lands included our North American continent.

Today, there are many trade routes between world communities. In fact, it would be hard to count them all! Highways and railroads cover entire continents. Airplanes make it possible to transport goods around the world in a very short time. Huge ships carry goods on the world's oceans and waterways.

One of the most important things affecting world trade today is transportation. People need to transport goods easily and quickly. In the last two centuries, we have become much faster at transporting goods. Look at the map and see the time difference required for transportation between 1869 and the present. In 1869, the trip from London to San Francisco probably took about 138 days. That's about four and one-half months.

Today, improved transportation allows us to enjoy products and goods from around the world.

title: Fighting Extremism with Education
text:
Extremism or radicalism means pushing an idea as far as it can go. Extremists are people who do this, and they often do not accept or tolerate other people’s ideas. They have hurt others and even killed because they didn’t agree with their beliefs.

Many brave individuals all over the world have dedicated their lives to fighting extremism by promoting education. Malala Yousafzai is one of these brave individuals. She believes that through education, people can learn to understand and accept one another.

Malala Yousafzai is a young Muslim woman. She was born and raised in Pakistan. In 2009, when Malala was 12 years old, the area of Pakistan she lived in was taken over by the Taliban. The Taliban are a religious extremist group who want to force their radical views onto other people. They believe that women should not receive an education, and Malala disagreed. When the Taliban came into her city and forbade girls from being able to attend school, she spoke up and campaigned for girls’ education. This put her in a lot of danger, but she did not let that stop her from speaking up for what she knew was right. At the age of 14, Malala was shot by a member of the Taliban and almost died.

On October 10, 2014, Malala was made a co-recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize for her dedication to education rights. More recently, in 2017, the United Nations named her the youngest ever official Messenger of Peace.

title: Transporting People and Goods
text:
There are many different ways to transport cargo from one place to another. Some people carry goods with their hands, on their backs or in baskets on their heads. Other people use pack animals such as llamas or mules. Most countries use trains, planes, ships and trucks to transport goods. This cargo is taken from one world community to another.

Small Boats

This merchant sells her products from a boat at a floating market. She cannot travel far from home. She also cannot keep her products fresh for very long.

Using Ourselves

Sometimes, people carry goods themselves. People haul rice and vegetables. People pack small animals or produce. This woman is carrying a jar of water on her head. Let's hope she doesn't have far to go!

Cargo Ships

Some loads are too big for animals or people. They may even be too big for trucks. Huge ships travel over the ocean waters and can carry tons of cargo. They can carry products like steel, oil or even cars. Some have huge containers (gigantic metal boxes) that hold smaller items such as clothing. Enormous cranes lift these containers from ship to shore to be loaded onto trains or trucks.

Trucking

Large trucks move much of the cargo in our nation. Sometimes, they pick up the cargo right from the farm. Other times, they take goods from trains or ships to places that trains cannot go. Other names for these big trucks include semi-tractors, 18-wheelers and big-rigs.

Animals

Animals help haul loads too. Sometimes, they carry packs on their backs like the llama in this picture. What other animals can you name that carry packs of goods? Did you guess a mule or a horse? Camels or oxen?

Animals also pull carts or wagons full of goods. Sometimes they carry people. People in many world communities still use animals to carry packed goods or to pull wagons or carts.

Railroad

In 1869, a coast-to-coast railroad was completed. The Central and Pacific railroads met together at Promontory Point, Utah.

By the early 1900s, diesel trains had replaced most of the steam engines.

Each kind of railroad car carries a different kind of cargo. There are hoppers, flat cars and tankers. What kinds of goods are carried in these types of cars?

Airplanes

Small planes sometimes carry goods to people who live far from roads and cities.

Larger jets, like this C-17 Globe Master, are huge. Cargo jets carry things that must be transported quickly. They take mail, medicine, emergency supplies and even live lobsters!

title: Greetings from Victoria, Vancouver, Canada!
text:
Dear Friends,

Today, we took the ferry across the sound and visited the Victoria Butchart Gardens in Vancouver. I thought it was just going to be a bunch of flowers and was looking forward to a boring day. I was sure surprised. This is some garden!

There are some really unusual flowers, fountains and tons of roses. There was a Japanese garden too.

My favorite part? The fireworks, of course. We spread a blanket on the ground and watched fireworks set to music. I wish we had a park like this!

Your friend,

Jessie

title: Who invented roller skates?
text:
Have you ever wondered who the first person was to strap wheels onto their feet? It was probably the Dutch in the early 1700s. These ground skates, as they were called, were attached to their shoes. They weren't very safe, however. It was almost impossible to turn a corner. The wheels were set on a rigid sole.

Once a Belgium musician named Joseph Merlin wore a pair of similar skates to a fancy-dress ball in London. He rolled in playing a violin and crashed into a very expensive mirror. Oops!

title: David Bushnell and the Turtle
text:
A submarine was used in the American Revolution? Absolutely. David Bushnell, American patriot and inventor, used reason and logic to build the first military submarine.

David Bushnell was born on a farm in Connecticut in 1740. He experimented with underwater explosives during college and built a submarine that would carry them. Bushnell's vessel was nicknamed "the Turtle" because it was shaped like two wooden turtle shells joined together, standing on end. Its hull filled with water to submerge and was pumped out by the operator to rise. Two propellers and a rudder were used to guide it.

Benjamin Franklin and others were impressed with Bushnell's invention. When British warships blockaded New York Harbor in 1776, the Turtle was called into action. The submarine operator was supposed to use a giant screw to attach the powder keg (called a mine) to the bottom of the British flagship, the HMS Eagle.

The plan seemed like a failure when the mine could not be fastened to the ship. However, the gunpowder made a frightening explosion underwater. The British quickly moved their warships from the area. Although it didn't work as planned, Bushnell's invention did have an effect on the British navy.

Bushnell then turned his skills to improving underwater mines. These were placed in harbors to protect American rivers and forts. General George Washington was pleased with Bushnell's work and gave him a commission (job) in the Army.

Today David Bushnell is given credit for inventing the first military submarine and for making valuable contributions to the American Revolution. You can visit a replica (an accurate model) of the Turtle in the Connecticut River Museum in Essex, Connecticut. By yourself or with a partner, think of a person who has used reason and logic to develop something that helped America.

title: Hot Air Balloons
text:
Did you know that a duck, a sheep and a rooster were the first to take flight in a hot air balloon? The year was 1783, and it was a milestone in aviation.

A few months later in France, a hot air balloon (the Aerostat Reveillon) carrying Pilatre de Rozier rose to 250 feet. It stayed in the air for 15 minutes.

The science of ballooning has come a long way. The first solo transpacific balloon flight was made on Feb. 14–17, 1995. Steve Fossett launched from Seoul, Korea, and flew four long days to Mendham, Saskatchewan, Canada.

title: Why Should I Follow Directions?
text:
Here’s a really good story about why it’s important to always follow directions. Once you read it, you’ll never have trouble following directions again!

One time a teacher handed out a test to her students. It was a long 10-page test. At the end of class, some students thought they did very well. They got most of the questions correct. But nobody passed! After the teacher had graded the tests, she pointed out the directions at the top: “Write your name on the top of Page 1 and hand the test in. Do not complete any of the questions.” You can bet those students wished they had read the directions rather than finished the whole 10-page test!

Reading directions carefully can mean the difference between an A and an F in school. It can mean the difference between a delicious pan of muffins and a mess of burnt, yucky dough.

1. Read the directions from beginning to end before you do anything else.

2. Make a list of any material you will need. Gather it up!

3. After you have everything you need, read the directions again carefully. Do you understand every step?

4. Do you still have questions? Ask your teacher, parent or a friend for input.

5. Follow the directions carefully, step by step. If you follow all these steps, you will do all your assignments correctly. Or your muffins will be delicious!

title: Let's Write
text: There are many different ways to travel today. We can make our way to a destination in a plane, on a train, in a car or on a bike. Perhaps you’ve hiked to a favorite camping spot, or you have taken a trolley into a busy city district. Write a paragraph describing your trip and the way you traveled. Be sure to tell us how long it took you to get to your destination.

title: Wood Duck
text: One of the most beautiful birds in Illinois is the wood duck. The wood duck is extremely colorful. The adult male has a pure white throat and foreneck, but his head is metallic green, violet and purple with two white stripes. The chest is a rich purplish chestnut. Its flanks are buff and its back a bronze green, metallic maroon, purple and blue. The female is somewhat less spectacular than the male. Areas around her bill, throat and eyes are white. The remainder of the head is gray with a crown and crest of metallic green. Her underside is white. These beautiful birds migrate in October to southern Illinois and south to the Gulf of Mexico. They look for food in flooded timberland, swamps and occasionally open water. They feed by pecking on the surface of water. The male, or drake, protects his female and nest from other drakes. The female lays an average of 12 eggs. The drake must be on watch for raccoons, snakes and squirrels that like to eat duck eggs. The female cares for the young for five to six weeks. A female will accept younger displaced ducks into her brood.

title: It's a Small World
text:
By the year 2000, the world seemed a smaller place. People traveled more. News and radio broadcasts traveled around the world in seconds. Students connected with other students on the Internet. The exchange of information and ideas became global.

The world can seem like an awfully big place. More than 5.5 billion people live on the Earth today! With technology, the world seems to be shrinking. How so? Most of us depend on others from many different places to provide us with services, information and goods. There are networks in place to get things from one place to another. Last week we learned some of the ways that food, clothing and resources are transported. Ideas and information must be shared as well. Communication and technology are an important part of the study of movement within geography.

Communication happens when people share information. We communicate interpersonally. That means between two or more people. We use communications systems. These systems spread the information between large numbers of people. The Internet is a good example.

People communicate in many different ways. The way we communicate is not always a spoken or written message. For example, do you think you can tell how someone feels by watching their facial expressions? Can you tell how they feel by their body language? How can you tell if your best friend is upset? If your teacher is happy? We can also communicate through music, paintings or other forms of art.

Media is a word we use to describe communications systems that send information across a long distance. The mail was once the only way to send information. There were many obstacles that could prevent a message from getting to someone. Mountains, large rivers and oceans made it difficult to get information to others. Improvements in printing and the delivery of mail helped speed things up. Advances in technology in the 19th and 20th centuries really improved the speed of communication. Books, the telephone or the Internet are all good examples. Make a list of as many examples of media as you can.

We are able to connect with people around the world like never before. Technology makes it possible to share information with groups of people throughout the world. As the world becomes a smaller place, social geographers are anxious to see how it impacts the cultures of our world. How do you think things might continue to change?

title: Can Facebook Save Dying Languages?
text:
Can you say a few words in Siletz Dee-ni? No? How about saying "hello" in Aka? If you can't, you're not alone! These two languages and 3,500 more could become extinct by the end of this century. Almost 80 percent of the world's population now speaks only one percent of the world's 7,000 languages. This has happened because of globalization. Globalization means that countries are more connected through trade, money and workers. When countries work together, people must be able to communicate with each other. That means many people have to learn another language. English is the main language used throughout the world for business and the Internet.

Why is this a problem? When the last person who is able to speak a particular language dies, some of the knowledge that is found within that language dies with them. A language contains the history of its people, how they used their environment and their beliefs and ideas. Technology may just save many of these languages from extinction!

With YouTube, Facebook and other forms of social media, languages that are spoken by even 5 or ten people can be taught to others around the world. National Geographic has been working on the Enduring Voices Project. Its goals are to record native speakers of endangered languages into talking dictionaries and help communities learn ways to save their languages from extinction. What language do you want to help save?

title: Communication: Yesterday and Today
text:
The printing press was invented in the 15th century. Before that people shared ideas by word of mouth or by writing letters. Today we use books, newspapers, magazines, radio, television, films, telephones, emails and the World Wide Web to move information and ideas over long distances.

1. Dots and Dashes

Have you ever tried to send a secret, coded message to your friend? Well, in 1837, that's exactly what Samuel Morse allowed people to do! He found ways to improve the telegraph and then invented the Morse code. Morse's telegraph generated electrical signals using his code, which represents letters and numbers. Morse code is a system of dots and dashes that a sender taps into a telegraph. If you wanted to use Morse code to send a telegraph message to your friend saying "hello," it would look like this:

.... . .-.. .-.. ---

Can you figure out the code? Here's a hint: each letter is separated by a space. Now do you see it? Keep trying, and the next time you text your friend, remember Samuel Morse had the idea much earlier!

2. Number, Please

The first telephone was invented by Alexander Graham Bell. It took him many tries. Bell was finally able to send a human voice along wires on June 2, 1875. He built the first successful telephone almost one year later. Hundreds of calls were being made all over America within months.

The first operators for the telephone exchange were young men. These young men proved to be less than patient with telephone customers and were even known to pull pranks on callers.

In 1878, the Boston Telephone Despatch company began to hire women who proved to be more friendly with customers. By 1900, almost all operators were women.

The telephone changed communication more than any other invention of that century.

3. Marconi Makes Waves

Guglielmo Marconi was an Italian. He built a gadget that sent messages by radio waves in 1895. Marconi's new machine produced radio waves by making a strong electric spark.

Early radio sets were often known as the wireless because the signals were sent through the air. Wireless means something very different today.

Marconi sent the first signals across the Atlantic Ocean in 1901. Public radio programs began about 20 years later.

Unlike printed messages and telephones, families and groups gathered together to enjoy radio broadcasts.

4. Seeing is Believing

The name "television" comes from a Greek word meaning "far" and a Latin word meaning "to see." Thus, "television" means "to see far."

Television as we know it was not developed until the 1920s. It took some time to take off. Television didn't really begin to impact long distance communication until the 1940s.

Americans were fascinated with the idea of television There were a variety of things people could view in their homes! The demand for television sets was huge. There were no more than 10,000 sets in the country by 1945. This figure soared to about 6 million in 1950. By 1960 there were almost 60 million sets. In television's early days, people without a set would visit friends just to watch the television. Many stores placed television sets in windows. Crowds would gather on the sidewalk to watch programs.

5. The Age of Computers

Advances in computers have caused major changes throughout the world.

Governments, businesses, banks, schools and homes are all connected by a network. This network lets people access information almost anywhere. Young students like yourselves learn about computers in school. We use them to draft and edit papers like this one. We research and learn. We send emails and even take tests.

Modern technology has advanced so quickly in the last 50 years that it is difficult to guess what tomorrow may bring.

title: Obedience
text:
You know what obedience means. It simply means obeying the rules or laws, and it's a very important character trait to have. Some rules are harder to keep than others, but most rules have a built-in benefit for obeying them.

Can you think of some benefits of being obedient? What's the benefit of keeping the homework rule or listening to your teachers? Good grades — and all the rewards that come with them.

Did you know that you can choose whether to obey the rules, but you cannot choose the consequences? That's right. If you follow a rule, whether you like the rule or not, you get to enjoy the benefits. Of course, that goes the other way too. If you choose not to obey, then you must accept going without the benefits. Often there's a penalty for not obeying the rules, like not being able to play with your friends because you didn't finish your chores. Can you think of other examples of the benefits or consequences of obeying or disobeying rules?

Did you know that parents have to be obedient too? There are things they have to do for the benefit of everyone. One of these things is to pay taxes. If they choose not to pay taxes, there is a consequence. People who choose not to pay their taxes can get a big fine or even go to jail. It doesn't matter if you are a kid or an adult, there are always rules you need to follow.

title: What is Pong?
text:
Pong was the world's first commercially successful video game. Unbelievably simple by today's standards, in the early 1970s it provided hours of fun to those first kids (and adults) who were lucky enough to have the game system.

Pong is a sort of electronic Ping Pong game. Ask your parents or grandparents if they remember the game Pong.

Here are the rules to play Pong: (Just in case you want to step back in time.)

Find an old game — check top of the closet, the trunk in the attic or garage sales.

Press Start.

Move the cursor up and down to hit the white dot (the ball).

Play for hours!

title: Red Piranha
text:
Range: South America

Habitat: Rivers

The red piranha of South America grows to be about 12 inches long. It is not a large fish, but it is a dangerous one.

There are more than 50 species of piranhas living in the South American rivers. Did you know that many of them eat fruit. The red piranha is really a very dangerous hunter. It has a blunt face with a lower jaw that sticks out. Its razor-like top and bottom teeth fit together perfectly, like a puzzle, when it shuts its mouth. This is perfect for biting pieces of flesh out of animals much larger than itself. The red piranhas hunt in large schools, usually feeding on other fish. They do sometimes feed on large animals stranded in the water and have been known to attack humans. In the 1980s, more than 300 people died in a piranha attack after a boat overturned in a Brazilian river.

title: How Do I Read a Map?
text:
Maps can tell you a whole lot about the world. They show you which direction to travel and how to find an unknown place. But wouldn’t you like to know how high the mountains are around you? And just where are those lakes and railroads? If you want to know all that and more, maps are for YOU!

These map functions will help you read a map:

Scale — On a map you’ll often see: 1 inch = 1 mile. That means 1 inch on the map represents one mile of the land around you. Easy, huh?

Legend — What do those little pictures or symbols on a map mean? The legend is a box, usually in a corner of the map. It lists the symbols, then tells what they mean.

Grid — Many maps are arranged on a grid. See the lines going up and down the sides of the map? There are more lines at the top and bottom. Those grid lines help you locate places on the map. Grids have letters along the sides and numbers across the top and bottom.

Index — To use the grid to find a location, go to the map’s index. The index lists locations with a letter and a number for each location. Find the spot on the map where that letter and number cross. For example: House — D, 9

title: Reasons for Regions
text:
There are many different ways that we can divide our world into regions.

Our world is a very big place! There are so many countries and people. If you studied one country every day in school, you could not finish them all in one school year! Sometimes it is easier to understand a place if we divide it into regions. There are many different ways we can divide our world into regions. Think of some ways to divide land into regions. Here is a list to get you started: political (counties, states, countries, etc.), resources, climates, languages. Now it's your turn. What can you add to the list?

Look at the two regional maps below. They are both maps of Massachusetts. Map No. 1 divides the state into physical regions. Those are regions that have to do with geography and environment. Map No. 2 is divided into tourist regions. Those are regions that have things of special interest to tourists. Can you find which region you are in?

People in world communities might belong to several regions at the same time. For example, a student who lives in Quebec, Canada, lives in a French-speaking region. That student is also in the eastern region of North America. Both of those regions tell us something about the place where that student lives.

Regions often change over time. A farming community may become a part of a city. A small town may no longer be an industrial region if a new resource is found.

People in world communities live in many different kinds of regions, yet they share many things. They may all eat at the same restaurants. They may all wear denim jeans. People in different world regions share many things because of technology. Computers and televisions make it possible to share ideas and information with others almost everywhere in the world. Improvements in transportation also make it easier to stay connected to other regions in our world. Turn to Page 2 to discover the regions in our world.

title: Be a Citizen Scientist!
text:
Did you know that you could help scientists study how climate change affects plants and animals? You can become a citizen scientist with the National Phenology Network no matter how old you are!

The word "phenology" means the study of how timing affects plants and animals. Scientists observe things like when birds migrate, when flowers bloom or when insects swarm. There just aren't enough scientists to study all of the plants and animals in the country. That's where all of us come in!

By going to the National Phenology Network at www.usanpn.org you can sign up to follow a particular animal or plant in your own backyard. For example, you might sign up to monitor goldfinches in your yard. You would record what they are eating, how many you see at your bird feeder and where they build a nest. The site will show you how to register to be a citizen scientist, observe your chosen species and report what you have seen. All you need is Internet access. Anyone under the age of 13 needs an adult to register on the site for them. By contributing to the network you will be joining government agencies, universities and other professionals that use the data to monitor invasive species, manage wildlife and study the effects of climate change. All you have to do is be curious and observant!

Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/ for more Connections and Current Events articles.

title: Did London Bridge really fall down?
text:
Indeed it did, and not just once but over and over again.

The first London Bridge was made of stone. It was built across the Thames river in London and lasted for more than 600 years.

Eventually, due to accidents, traffic and the pounding river, the bridge wore out and was replaced with a stronger rock called granite. Over time, the granite began to crumble and sink, so once again, the people decided to replace it. This time with concrete.

The granite stones were taken apart piece by piece and shipped to the United States where they were put together again over a lake in Arizona.

title: Red-tailed Hawk
text:
Range: North America and as far south as the mountains of Panama

Habitat: Grasslands or marsh-shrub, very adaptable to different climates

The red-tailed hawk is one of the largest birds in North America usually weighing between 2 and 4 pounds. As with most raptors, the female is much larger than the male. The hawk's distinguishing feature is its red tail. It molts in the second year of life.

Like other raptors, the hawk has amazing eyesight, nearly eight times more powerful than a human! The main weapon of this beautiful bird is its talons. The hawk mostly preys upon small rodents.

Listen carefully next time you are in the wild for the wailing cry of the red-tailed hawk as it searches for food, "Klee-uk, klee-uk."
