title: Brazilian Drinking Straw Flute
text:
A Brazilian Indian may play a haunting tune on an end-blown flute. End-blown flutes are found in world communities in every continent, but are most common in South America and Asia. They have been used since historic times.

Materials

plastic drinking straw

colorful yarn

scissors

stickers

plastic gems

Directions

1. Flatten out about 1 inch of the end of the drinking straw. Crease the sides well so it lays flat.

2. With scissors, trim the flattened end to a “V” as shown in the illustration to make the flute reeds.

3. Glue on feathers, yarn, medallions, jewels or other festive materials.

4. Let it dry out before playing.

5. Blow hard! Sometimes you have to experiment with lengthening or shortening the reeds and with holding them in the mouth just right.

Hint: The shorter the straw is cut, the higher the sound will be and the easier it will be to blow.

title: Our National Symbols
text:
The Bald Eagle

Although Benjamin Franklin argued for the turkey, the bald eagle became our official national bird in 1782. The Founding Fathers chose the bald eagle because of its strength, long life, large size and because it is native to the United States. The bald eagle can fly as fast as 30 miles per hour and can dive at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour! The wingspan of a bald eagle can measure up to seven feet across, and it can live from three to 35 years in the wild. Eagles eat mainly fish and other small mammals. A bald eagle symbol appears on the Great Seal of the United States and on the back of many of our coins, including the silver dollar, the half dollar and the quarter.

The Rose

Lawmakers chose the rose as the official national flower in 1986. People have long considered the rose a symbol of love, beauty and peace. As a national symbol, the rose represents a love for our country. Roses are native to North America and come in many colors, particularly red, pink, white and yellow.

Red, White and Blue

Our official national colors are red, white and blue, and they are, of course, used on the U.S. flag! Red was chosen as a symbol of valor (courage), especially courage in battle. White is the symbol of purity and innocence (without guilt or sin). Blue represents vigilance (being alert of danger), perseverance (determination even when it’s difficult) and justice (fairness).

Liberty Bell

Although the Liberty Bell isn’t an official symbol of the U.S., many people throughout the world know it as a symbol of freedom. The 2,000-pound bell once hung in Independence Hall in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The bell rang out to call the citizens of Philadelphia to hear the first official reading of the Declaration of Independence in 1776. The Liberty Bell also rang to announce the beginning of the First Continental Congress in 1774 and the victory in the Battles of Lexington and Concord in 1775. The bell is now on display in the Liberty Bell Center in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

title: Presidential Trivia
text:
Barack Obama was elected the 44th U.S. president in November 2008. He will go down in history as the first African American to hold this office. Over the years, many remarkable men have served as president. Here are a few interesting facts about some of them:

• William Henry Harrison served only one month as president. Not long after his inauguration speech, he caught pneumonia and died 30 days later.

• At 6’ 4”, Abraham Lincoln was the tallest president. James Madison, at 5’ 4”, was the shortest.

• James Buchanan was the only president to never marry.

• Grover Cleveland is the only president to serve non-consecutive (out-of-order) terms. He served as both the 22nd and the 24th president. President Benjamin Harrison served as the 23rd.

• At 70 years old, Ronald Reagan was the oldest man to take office.

• At 42 years old, Theodore Roosevelt was the youngest man to take office.

• Four presidents were assassinated while in office: Abraham Lincoln, James Garfield, William McKinley and John Kennedy.

• Two father/son sets have served as U.S. presidents: John Adams and his son John Quincy Adams, and George H.W. Bush and his son George W. Bush.

title: Exploring the Great United States
text:
Geography

The United States covers 3,794,100 square miles and is the third largest country in the world, after Russia and Canada. It is bordered by the Atlantic Ocean to the east, the Pacific Ocean to the west, Canada to the north and Mexico to the south.

The U.S. has some of the most varied (different) and interesting geographic features of any country in the world. The eastern part of the country is made up of hills and low mountains, which are usually green and well watered. This area of the country receives around 40 inches of rain per year.

The middle section of the U.S. consists of flat, rolling prairies. Many know this area as the Great Plains. The Great Plains receive 10-20 inches of rain per year, and it is home to some of the most fertile (able to grow) farmland in the world. People sometimes call this area the breadbasket of the world, because the Great Plains produces a large amount of wheat, corn and barley. We use these grains to make most of the breads we eat.

The western part of the U.S. features rugged mountain peaks and a wide range of climates. The Northwest region is rainy and cool. The Southwest is hot and dry, with some areas receiving as little as three inches of rain per year.

Alaska and Hawaii are not connected geographically to the U.S., and they have their own unique geography and climates. Alaska is famous for its long, cold winters and Hawaii is known for its volcanic mountains, sandy beaches and warm weather.

The highest point in the United States is Alaska’s Mt. McKinley at 20,335 feet. America’s lowest point is California’s Death Valley at 282 feet below sea level.

Natural Resources

A natural resource is something useful that we find in nature. The U.S. is very rich in natural resources such as fresh water, fertile soil, oil, natural gas, timber, gold, silver, iron and other minerals. The U.S. also has a large supply of coal, accounting for about 27 percent of all the coal on Earth.

What does the U.S. do with all these amazing natural resources? Our rich soil is used to grow all types of grains, fruits and vegetables, as well as feed for cattle, horses and poultry. The U.S. also uses its oil and petroleum to produce gas to run cars and machinery. Workers also use oil and petroleum to make plastics and other useful items. Our nation uses iron and other metals to produce cars, trucks and vehicles sold throughout the world. We use our timber to produce lumber, furniture and paper products. The U.S. is also one of the top producers of cell phones, prescription drugs, medical equipment, airplanes and fertilizers.

National Monument and Treasures

A national monument is a landmark, geographic feature or historic site set aside by the national government for the public to visit and enjoy. A national treasure is a piece of architecture, a historic document, a landscape or artifact that historians consider important to our history. The U.S. is full of national monuments and treasures that you are probably very familiar with.

Mount Rushmore

Carved into Mount Rushmore in the Black Hills of South Dakota are the faces of four U.S. presidents: George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Abraham Lincoln. Sculptor Gutzon Borglum started creating this gigantic national monument in 1927 and (with help) it was completed in 1941. Millions of people visit this unique site each year, and it is one of our country’s most recognizable national monuments.

The Statue of Liberty

The Statue of Liberty is known around the world as a symbol of freedom and democracy. The statue was a gift of friendship from France to the U.S., and it was dedicated in October 1886. People sometimes call the Statue of Liberty “Lady Liberty.” It stands in New York Harbor to welcome all those who come to the U.S. seeking a new life. Sculptor Frederic-Auguste Bartholdi created the Statue of Liberty, which stands just over 305 feet from the ground to the tip of its torch. It is made of a thin copper “skin” shaped over an inner iron “skeleton.” In one hand there is the torch of freedom, and in the other hand there is a tablet representing the law.

The Grand Canyon

Located in northwestern Arizona, the Grand Canyon was named a national monument by President Theodore Roosevelt in 1908. Officials later changed it to a national park in 1919. The canyon measures 277 miles long and is up to 18 miles wide and 5,000 feet deep. The Grand Canyon is considered one of the Seven Wonders of the World, and more than 4 million people visit it each year. The views from the rim of the canyon are spectacular, but a trip down the trails to the canyon floor is even more breathtaking.

The Declaration of Independence

Thomas Jefferson wrote the original Declaration of Independence in 1776. Men such as John Hancock, Thomas Jefferson and Benjamin Franklin signed the Declaration, and it is on display in the Rotunda for the Charters of Freedom in Washington, D.C. The Declaration is badly faded because it wasn’t properly stored or preserved in its early days, but the fact that it still exists at all makes it one of our country’s great national treasures.

title: Spirit of Adventure
text: Americans are known for having a spirit of adventure, or the desires to take risks and try new things. That spirit was also in the early explorers and Pilgrims, the westward pioneers and great inventors and leaders throughout history. Men and women with adventurous spirits have made our country what it is today. It took great courage to break away from England and build a new nation. Then, our ancestors explored the wilderness, repaired a nation divided by slavery and spread out from sea to shining sea. We’ve also landed on the moon, explored space and recovered from foreign attacks on American soil. Americans’ spirit of adventure has made all of these accomplishments possible. Who knows where that spirit will lead us in years to come?

title: The Cell Phone
text:
Motorola employee Dr. Martin Cooper invented the first portable cell phone. He used his phone to make the first call on April 3, 1973. Motorola had been racing against Bell Laboratories throughout the 1960s and 70s, trying to come up with a cell phone that actually worked. Who did Dr. Cooper call on his new cell phone? Bell Labs, of course, to tell them the good news (for him and Motorola, at least) that he had finally won the race!

The first cell phone looked like a large brick and weighed two pounds. In 1983, Motorola started selling a business cell phone that weighed about one pound and cost around $4,000. Today, cell phones weigh about four ounces and are often given at no charge with the purchase of a service plan.

Cell phones make it possible to do business from anywhere, at any time and to stay in touch with family and friends no matter where they may be.

title: Look Down! Ocean Cartographer Marie Tharp (1920-2006)
text:
“Don’t look down!” is a line you may have heard in movies, usually while the heroes are walking on a narrow bridge over a dangerous pit. For Michigan native Marie Tharp, however, “looking down” is just part of the job.

During World War II when many men were off fighting, Marie’s college invited young women to join the geology department, and Marie accepted. She became interested in studying the bottom of the ocean. Unfortunately, this was during a time when women were not allowed to work “in the field.” Frustrated, Marie thought about quitting until her father encouraged her to find a way to do what she loved. Encouraged, she continued to follow her dream of exploring the ocean. Her hard work and determination paid off, and in 1965, she was able to join a cartographer named Bruce Heezen on an ocean expedition.

Together, Marie and Bruce completed several maps of the ocean floor, made discoveries about how the Earth’s tectonic plates and ridges fit together and sparked a new wave of interest in ocean exploration. Although she died in 2006, Marie Tharp remains an inspiration to many people to this day.

title: Theodore Roosevelt
text:
The 26th president of the United States was Theodore Roosevelt. He signed the National Monuments Act on June 8, 1906. This law gave the U.S. president the power to name landmarks, historic sites, places of scientific interest and geographic wonders as national monuments. The U.S. government would then control and protect these sites so that everyone could enjoy them.

Theodore Roosevelt was a nature lover and he wanted to be sure that important historic sites and natural wonders would be preserved for years to come. He established our first 18 national monuments, more than any other president to follow him has done. Some of the most famous national monuments that President Roosevelt named are the Grand Canyon, Arizona’s Petrified Forest, Washington’s Mount Olympus and Wyoming’s Devil’s Tower.

title: Let's Discover Canada's Physical Regions
text:
Canada's national motto, "From sea to sea," describes this vast land that stretches from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean. Canada is the second largest country in the world. This week, let's take a look at the eight regions of Canada and discover the wealth of beauty and geographical diversity.

Canada is a beautiful land. It is home to mountains, prairies and lakes. Many parts of Canada are undeveloped. This makes it a favorite stop for nature lovers from all over the world.

Canada is located north of the United States where it reaches so far north, it almost touches the North Pole. (brrrrrr!)

The southern border of Canada touches the United States.

Like the United States, the western border of Canada meets the Pacific Ocean and the eastern boarder meets the Atlantic. Canada's national motto, "From sea to sea," perfectly describes the land that stretches over half of North America.

With a country this vast, how can we best study the physical features? The most sensible way is to divide the country up into physical features that are similar. Those areas with similar physical features are regions, of course.

Look at the colored map key to the right of the map to locate the name of each region. How many regions do you see? Which region is the largest? Which region is the farthest north?

After you have studied them for a moment, find a partner and see who can name the most without looking at the map key. Give yourself an extra 25 points if you can spell them all correctly.

Some of the names sound familiar, and some are very different. To learn more about these eight beautiful regions, turn to pages 2 and 3.

title: From Hurley to Hockey
text:
No one is sure exactly when ice hockey began, but there is no question where it began. It began in Nova Scotia, Canada. Some folks think that it came from a popular field game in the early 1800s called hurley. They think it was adapted for the ice by students at King's College. It soon became a very popular winter sport and gradually spread from the East Coast to the West Coast.

In the 1870s, a group of college students at McGill University in Montreal was holding organized hockey games with a set of written rules. These rules were known as McGill's Rules. At this time, a wooden puck was substituted for a rubber ball, and the number of players was reduced from 11 to nine.

In 1885, Montreal became the site for the first national hockey organization. When the Amateur Hockey Association of Canada was founded, it reduced the number of players to only seven. A league was born that year with the formation of four teams in Ontario.

Ice hockey came to the United States in the 1890s. The first promoted game in the United States was between John Hopkins and Yale University in 1895. As ice hockey became popular, the United States also began a league. The Pro Hockey League was formed in 1903 in Michigan. It included teams from both Canada and the United States. The Pro Hockey League was short-lived though. The league ended in 1906. The National Hockey League (NHL) was formed in 1910 and remains in action today. How many NHL teams can you name?

Men's hockey was included in the Winter Olympic program for the first time in Chamonix in 1924. Women's hockey became an Olympic event at the 1998 Nagano Olympic Games.

title: Regions of Canada
text:
1. Cordilleran Region

This region is home to high mountain ranges. The most famous are the Canadian Rockies. Between mountain ranges are deep valleys and flat lands high above sea level called plateaus.

Canada's tallest mountain ranges are found in this area. The highest peak is over 19,000 feet! Most of the population in this region is found in the lowlands and plateaus near the warmer southern climates. This region is also known for its many rivers and mountain lakes.

2. Interior Plains

This region slopes upward from east to west as you approach the Rockies. It is an area of fertile soil known for its grain production, especially wheat. Farmers also raise cattle and other livestock in this region.

This entire region is generally flat. It does have a few low mountains, hills and even sand dunes. It also boasts many wide river valleys just like the one in this picture.

3. Hudson Bay Lowlands

These lowlands form a flat swampy region. Much of the region is covered by patchy forests and huge deposits of muskeg. Muskeg is an unusual soil formed from decaying plants. Muskeg is very wet but also very acidic. That makes it so trees don't grow well.

While there are not many permanent settlements here, the swampy habitat is home to many kinds of waterfowl.

4. St. Lawrence Lowlands

This region is noted for fertile river land and rolling lake shores. It also has some of the warmest weather in all of Canada.

Is it any surprise then that more than half of the total population of Canada lives here, in the smallest region?

5. Appalachian Highlands

This region was the first to be settled by the Europeans. It is known for the rolling hills of the Appalachian Mountains. It also has beautiful rivers and lakes. Small fishing villages are found along the rocky coastline.

6. Canadian Shield

This region is the largest in Canada. It completely surrounds Hudson Bay in the shape of a horseshoe.

This region is mostly rock with a shallow layer of topsoil. Long ago it was mountainous, but glaciers and wind have worn it down and carved deep rivers, lakes and valleys. This shield is known for its beautiful evergreen forests.

7. Arctic Lowlands

Because of the extreme cold of this region, not many folks live here. This region is one of permafrost, (when the ground is frozen year round). In the summer, the top of the soil thaws, leaving a wet, marshy surface. Not many plants grow here.

8. Innuitian Region

In the extreme north, mainly on Ellesmere Island, is the Innuitian Mountain system, where this region gets its name.

It is characterized by mountains, frozen seas and barren tundra. There are two seasons here — summer and winter. The Arctic winter is long, dark and very cold. Summer lasts only a few months.

title: Greetings from Yoho National Park!
text:
Dear Friends,

Today we visited Yoho National Park in British Columbia, Canada. It was so cool!

I saw Takakkaw Falls; it is one of the highest waterfalls in North America. The river comes right out from under a glacier at the top of the falls. Boy, is the water cold!

There are 28 mountain peaks in the park that are almost 10,000 feet high. We also saw hoodoos, a natural bridge, some mountain goats and some really neat railway tunnels called the spiral tunnels.

The name Yoho comes from a Cree word meaning awesome (and it sure is).

Your Friend,
Hilarie

title: What is mushing?
text:
Mushing means to travel by dogsled, and it's not for the weak or mild. It involves a lot of hard work, cold weather and dogs that demand careful care and attention. The reward is the wide-open spaces and beautiful scenery that Canada has to offer.

A team of dogs can pull a sled over lakes, up and down mountain ridges and over old logging trails in forested country. There are many beautiful things to see, but hold on because a dog team can travel up to 30 miles in one day.

title: North American Kestrel
text:
Range: From central Alaska to Nova Scotia and to central Mexico

Habitat: Open areas with scattered trees or structures for perching on to hunt, mostly rural areas but have been seen in some urban areas as well

The kestrel is a member of the falcon family. The adult is 9 to 12 inches long with a wing span of 20 to 24 inches. They weigh less than 1 pound. They have dark eyes and a notched beak. One way of identifying the kestrel is the black vertical stripe on each side of the face.

The male has blue-gray outer feathers, and the female has reddish-brown feathers. They eat insects, small mammals and reptiles.

They like to nest in holes in trees, cliffs, buildings or nest boxes. The female lays three to five eggs once each year in most areas. The male will sometimes share the responsibility of sitting on the eggs. The eggs begin to hatch about 30 days after being laid.

Kestrels can be found over the entire Continental United States and most of Canada.

title: Bernardo de Gálvez, Unsung Hero of the Revolution
text:
When American colonists fought for independence from Great Britain, many other countries were affected. Spain and France still held large territories in the New World and controlled the Mississippi River together. Bernardo de Galvez was a Spanish military officer who was governor of the Louisiana territory.

Galvez was sympathetic to the patriots' cause. He closed the port of New Orleans to British ships. Now the colonists could transport supplies for the Revolution safely along the Mississippi River. He also sent hundreds of horses to American forces. When Spain declared war on Great Britain, Galvez's army went into action. Galvez added American Indians, Creoles and free African Americans to his Spanish troops. He led attacks to capture British forts at Manchac, Baton Rouge, Natchez and Mobile. He fought a long battle in Pensacola to drive the British out of Florida, securing the southern border.

Galvez communicated directly with Thomas Jefferson, Patrick Henry and others. He helped draft the Treaty of Paris, which ended the American Revolution. Congress officially thanked Galvez for his service.

In 1974 Spain sent Erik I. Martel to Houston as Consul General. While preparing to move to America, Martel realized that he had never learned about Galvez and Spain's part in the American Revolution. He soon found that most Americans were not aware of it either. He helped create an organization named The Order of Granaderos de Galvez. These people were dedicated to "…setting the historical record straight," in Martel's words. The Granaderos y Damas de Galvez is still an active group. They give history presentations and march in parades while wearing authentic Spanish army uniforms. If you see these patriots, make sure to thank them for helping America win its freedom! Why is it important for America to work with allies (friendly countries)? How do countries help each other today?

title: How Do I Read Tables?
text:
By learning to read tables, you can quickly compare information. Tables have text and numbers. When reading a table, carefully read the text.

Try It!

2. Who hit the most home runs?

4. How many more home runs did Mark McGwire hit than Jimmie Foxx?

5. Who had 563 home runs?

6. Who had more home runs, Ted Williams or Willie Mays?

title: Let's Write
text:
This week we have looked at each of Canada’s eight regions and the physical characteristics that define those regions. 1. Write the name of one of Canada’s physical regions.

2. List at least three of the features of that region in Canada and tell how they are the same or different than the place where you live.

3. Write why you would like to visit that region in Canada and what you think you would enjoy seeing the most.

title: Natural Resources
text: Canada is a land rich in natural resources. The vast forests in the country provide raw materials for lumber, pulp for paper and other products. Jobs in the lumber industry provide jobs for 10 percent of Canada’s population. Alberta and the eastern coast are known for their wealth of oil and natural gas. Other minerals that are exported are nickel, silver and gold.

title: Let's Discover Mexico's Physical Regions
text:
Mexico is a beautiful country that ranges from desert to tropical. It is the northernmost country of Latin America. This week, let's take a look at the seven regions of Mexico and discover the wealth of beauty and geographical diversity.

Mexico is a beautiful land. It is also very rich in history. The ruins of ancient civilizations attract many tourists. The warm, sandy beaches bring visitors as well.

Mexico is the southernmost country on the North American continent. Mexico has water on two sides. The Gulf of California and the Pacific Ocean are to the west. The Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea lie to the east. The northern border is shared with the United States. Guatemala and Belize lie to the southeast. The country is shaped like a giant hook. The Yucatan Peninsula shapes the hook at the end.

Few other countries have so many climates that are so close together. The Sierra Madre Occidental and the Sierra Madre Oriental are the two mountain ranges in Mexico. Those ranges offer snow-capped mountains and volcanic peaks. Mexico also has high and rolling plateaus. It has tropical rain forests, dry deserts, famous beaches and fertile valleys.

To better study the physical features of Mexico, we will divide it into seven regions. These regions are based mainly on elevation. Look at the map key and find each of the regions. Study the regions for a moment. After you have done that, find a partner and see who can name all the regions without looking. Give yourself extra points if you can spell them all!

title: Monarchs of Mexico
text:
Each fall, people from Massachusetts to Mississippi see the gentle orange flutter of dozens, or even hundreds, of monarch butterflies. Did you know that these butterflies are on a journey? They are flying straight to the Transvolcanic Mountain Range near Mexico City. That is where they spend the winter.

The monarchs gather in huge colonies of hundreds of millions. They hang on the branches of the dense highland forests. They cluster so thick on the branches of fir trees that they look like clumps of dead leaves. Isn't it incredible that the butterflies know how to return to the same place year after year?

Jason Etheredge of the University of Kansas has been studying the monarch butterflies. He thinks that they can detect the magnetic fields of the Earth. He thinks they use it to find their way, much like a compass. The scientists gathered the butterflies in the fall when they were ready to migrate to test this theory. The team found that when there was no magnetic field, the butterflies flew in random directions. When the Earth's normal magnetic field was used, most of the monarchs flew towards the southwest. That is the same direction as Mexico. Under a reversed magnetic field they flew the opposite direction. They flew to the northeast!

While that answers the question of how they know where to go, there are still some unexplained mysteries. For example, the butterflies that migrate to Mexico are not the same generation that flew there the year before. In fact, probably three to five generations pass during the summer. So, who tells the great-grandchildren that southwest is the way to go?

Another puzzle is what prompts the butterflies' decision to migrate at all. When butterflies were collected in the summer months, they flew in random directions in the laboratory, no matter which magnetic field was used.

title: Regions of Mexico
text:
1. Baja California Peninsula

This region meets the United States on its north border. It is home to many cacti and is very arid (dry).

The peninsula has lots of mountains.It also has a narrow coastal plain.

Some folks say this is where the desert meets the sea. Indeed the beautiful coastal cities are becoming more and more popular with tourists.

2. The Pacific Lowlands

This region is found between the Pacific Ocean and the Sierra Madre Occidental range. The southern parts of the lowlands are lush and contain tropical forests. The irrigated northern region is nice for farming.

3. Southern Highlands

Southern Highlands are found just south of the Central Plateau. This region is made up of a number of steep mountain ranges, deep valleys and very high plateaus. The Sierra Madre del Sur range meets the sea and makes the rugged coastline known as the Mexican Riviera. Here you will find the famous cities of Acapulco and Puerto Vallarta.

4. Yucatan Peninsula

The Yucatan Peninsula is a limestone plateau. It has no rivers on its surface. The limestone dissolves in water. This allows the heavy rainfall to reach the sea through underground channels. Sometimes the roofs of the channels cave in. When this happens, it leaves great pits.

The northwestern part of the region is dry but turns to tropical rainforests in the south.

5. Chiapas Highlands

The Chiapas Highlands border Guatemala. This area receives lots of rain and is covered by tropical forests. The mountains in this region rise to more than 9,000 feet. Many of the American Indians live in this area. They are farmers, working on both small farms and on plantations.

6. Gulf Coast Plains

The Gulf Coast Plains lie between the Sierra Madre Oriental and the Gulf of Mexico. The plains are about 175 miles wide at the border with Texas. It becomes more narrow as it approaches Veracruz in the south. Then the plains widen again at the Isthmus of Tehuantepec.

The northern part of this region is dry. There is lots of rainfall in the southern part where there are tropical forests. The coastal areas are typically swampy lowlands with lots of lagoons.

7. Central Plateau

This region has an elevation of 3,000 feet in the north. As you go south it grows to 8,000 feet! Most of Mexico's major peaks and inactive volcanoes are located on this plateau. One of the highest peaks in Mexico is here. It is the Pico de Orizaba.

The capital of Mexico, Mexico City, is also found in the Central Plateau.

title: Greetings from Acapulco, Mexico!
text:
Hi there!

Today we went to Acapulco, Mexico. It is a very big city with lots of tourists. More than 1 million people live here.

There are lots of beaches. You can go deep sea fishing, scuba diving and swimming. The temperature here is about 90 degrees year round.

We saw the La Quebrada cliff divers. They dive into a narrow channel of shallow water from 150 feet up on the cliffs. I think they're nuts, but it sure was exciting.

Wish you were here!

Lacie

title: What is a prickly pear?
text:
A prickly pear is a type of cactus with flat pads and very long spines. Nopal is the name used for the type that can be eaten.

The pads of the green nopal are cut up and served as a delicious dish just as they were in ancient Mexico. It has been eaten as a vegetable since the Spanish arrival in Mexico. The Spanish explorers took the plant back to Spain, and they eventually spread throughout North Africa with the Moors.

The fruit of the black nopal is also called a prickly pear. It has a thorny skin and the thorns must be removed before eating. It tastes similar to a kiwi. The fruit is delicious and grows in these colors: yellow, purple, red, orange and green. It has many small seeds that need to be removed to fully enjoy and is very refreshing.

title: Greater Flamingo
text:
Range: northern South America, Mexican Yucatan, Africa, West Indies and (rarely) coastal southern United States

Habitat: salt water lagoons and mudflats or anywhere there is shallow salt water

The adult flamingo is a tall bird with long, pinkish legs and feet, bright pink outer feathers and a black tipped beak. It stands about 42 inches tall with a 60-inch wingspan and weighs about 8 pounds.

Flamingos live in shallow salt water areas. To eat, they stir up the mud with their feet, suck the muddy water through their beak and eat the algae, small shrimp and other organisms that are there.

The female lays a single egg in the spring in a mud nest, and both the female and the male will take turns incubating (sitting on) it. The egg will hatch in about 30 days.

Flamingos are usually found in very large flocks. They are easily scared and it is unlikely that you would be able to approach them.

title: Rubrics
text:
Rubrics tell you what is expected on an assignment. They can help you prepare for a project.

You have a big project coming up in your class on how to make chocolate chip cookies. You’re a little nervous because you haven’t made cookies before. Then your teacher hands out a rubric. A rubric? What’s that? It’s a scoring guide that lets you know what you should do to get a good grade. A rubric looks like a chart and is divided into specific categories. Here are some ways to use a rubric.

1. Look at the categories. They will tell you what you need to focus on for the project. If you’re making chocolate chip cookies, the teacher may want you to focus on the color, taste or the number of chocolate chips. The rubric should have these categories.

2. Look at what will give you a good grade. Once you know what to focus on, see what you need to do. This is often called the criteria. Do the cookies need to be a golden brown, or can they be a little crispy? Do your best to get that good grade.

3. If you have questions about the criteria, ask the teacher. Sometimes it’s not clear what something means. For the cookies, what is a golden-brown color? Don’t be afraid to ask questions.

4. You can evaluate your project before handing it in. You can use the rubric to mark off what you’ve done right. Let’s say your cookies turn out to be chewy and golden brown. But they don’t have many chocolate chips. You can mark off the first two because you’ve done them right. Then you can work on the third.

It’s really simple to use a rubric. By using a rubric, you will know what to do to receive a high score. You can be prepared for any project!

title: The Prickly Pear
text: The fruit of the black nopal, the prickly pear, is delicious. The thorns must be removed. Then after the tiny seeds are scraped, it is a delicious treat.

title: Stained Glass Window
text:
Materials

Teachers note: crayons can be shaved ahead of time, colors in separate containers. Plastic knives may be used instead; shaving will take longer.

waxed paper

scissors

crayons

utility knife (see teachers note)

glitter

pressing cloth

iron

black construction paper

glue

Directions

Cut two pieces of waxed paper, approximately 10” x 12”, into an interesting shape. Use an utility knife to shave pieces of crayons of different colors onto one of the waxed paper sheets. (Have a teacher or parent help you. These knives are very sharp.) Spread the shavings evenly over the waxed paper. Sprinkle colored glitter over the areas between the shavings.

Place the second piece of waxed paper over the first sheet that contains the crayon shavings and glitter. Place a pressing cloth over the two sheets of waxed paper and use a warm iron to pull across the top of the waxed paper to melt the crayons and to seal the two pieces of waxed paper together.

Cut a piece of black construction paper into various window shapes, and place it over your waxed paper creation. Place glue on the back side of your construction paper and glue your window to the waxed paper design.

Place the finished design against a window to let the outside light create a stained glass effect.

title: From Quebec to Canada
text:
Our Northern Neighbors

The first people to live in Canada probably came across Beringia from Asia 15,000 years ago. Their descendants became what we know as the native or indigenous people. Nearly 10,000 years later, the ancestors of the Inuit (sometimes called Eskimos) came across the same land bridge. They settled in the Arctic regions of Canada.

John Cabot was an Italian navigator in the service of the English crown. In 1497, he explored Canada's southeastern coast. His discoveries led to the opening of the European exploration of Canada. His discoveries put France in the lead. Another explorer, Champlain, later founded the settlement of Quebec along the St. Lawrence River.

Both France and England claimed land in Canada and were eager to obtain more land. There was a constant rivalry between the French and the English, both in Europe and in North America. Between 1689 and 1763, there were four wars between the French and the English fought in North America. The Treaty of Paris, signed in 1763, ended the fighting and turned most of the land over to England. England called the new territory that is now Canada, Quebec.

Other colonies developed, and Great Britain took control of them as well. So, how did Canada, as we know it today, come into being? In 1791, the Constitutional Act was approved by King George III of England and the British Parliament. It divided the British colonies into two groups, called Upper Canada and Lower Canada. This was the first time Canada was used as an official name.

This still wasn't the great country that is now Canada. It really started with a few people wanting to confederate, to join together, all the colonies in British North America. Support for this grew over time. Then in the 1860s, an American event actually hastened the process. It was the American Civil War. Why was it so significant? America had already been an independent country for quite some time. America was growing ever stronger. This concerned both Canada and Great Britain. They saw how quickly the United States had been expanding westward. They were worried that the Americans would try to annex British North America as their own. They also remembered the war that the United States started with them in 1812. The United States didn't really win that war, but now America was a stronger country. They knew that if the United States tried to overthrow them with their army, America might win. They didn't want to be Americans. In fact, many people who were loyal to Great Britain left the American Colonies when the Declaration of Independence was signed. They went to Canada. The Canadians believed the only way to be safe in their land was to unite. England had rejected the confederation of Canada before but this time decided to allow it.

In 1864, some of the colonies met in Charlottetown to talk about joining together. However, when they arrived, more colonies wanted to join. Others changed their minds and decided not to. The colonies decided to meet again in October 1864 in Quebec. This time, everyone was ready. Through debate at the Quebec conference, they created 72 resolutions. These resolutions were adopted by the colonies. They became the basis of the British North America Act in 1867. The British North America Act officially joined the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick into the Dominion of Canada. Later, in 1873, Prince Edward Island joined the union. Also during this time, the Northwestern Territory and the province of Manitoba were organized. In 1871, British Columbia joined the union. It wasn't until 1905 when Alberta and Saskatchewan joined the Dominion of Canada. Finally, in 1949, Newfoundland joined. That is the union that exists today.

title: A Canadian Victory
text:
The Dominion of Canada was created as a part of Great Britain. From 1867 until 1931, Canada had two active parts of the government in both Canada and England. In England were the queen and Parliament. The Canadian provinces had been given the power of self-government beginning with the Province of Canada and Nova Scotia in 1848. The other provinces quickly followed, but still, they weren't completely free. Every time the Canadian people wanted to amend, or change, their constitution, the English Parliament had to approve the change. This meant that even though Canada had a great deal of power to govern itself, it was still controlled by England.

In the late 1800s, Prime Minister Mackenzie began a policy that forced the English government to respect decisions made by Canadian provinces about their own affairs. This was the beginning of the road to independence. The last step to Canadian independence from Great Britain was taken in the early 1900s. In 1931, the Westminster Statute gave Canada complete power over amending its constitution. It no longer had to pass amendments through the British Parliament, making it completely independent of Great Britain. The queen of England is still technically the leader of Canada, but leaves all the ruling to the prime minister of Canada.

title: Canada Timeline
text:
A.D. 1000: Viking explorations

1497: Cabot explores southeast Canada, begins European exploration.

1534: Cartier (St. Lawrence River) and Champlain explore.

1605: Champlain establishes first successful New France colony at Port Royal.

1670: Hudson's Bay Trading Company is formed — the beaver trade contributes to the settlement of Canada and French-English rivalry.

1672: New France expanded by Frontenac — European powers are scrambling to establish dominance in all of North America.

1758: British capture Fort Loiusburg; French power declines.

1759: Battle on the Plains of Abraham: New France ends, and British North America begins.

1763: Treaty of Paris — The British claim French lands.

1774: Quebec Act provides civil and religious rights to French Canadians.

1775: Acadians are driven from Canada.

The Acadians were the French who settled lands now called the Maritime Provinces. These included present-day Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and parts of eastern Maine (in the present-day United States). The British had won control of much of the area by the 1760s. Thousands of French colonists were taken from their lands. Many were separated from their families. They were dispersed up and down the East Coast. Some fled north, to what is now Fredericton, New Brunswick. A generation later, some of those Acadians moved into the St. John Valley in Maine. The lands left behind were confiscated and given by the British crown to loyal British subjects.

1776: Many United Empire loyalists (those who wished to remain part of England) living in America flee to Canada/U.S. War of Independence.

1778: Captain Cooke explores West Coast.

1783: Britain loses the war with America, which redefines British claims in North America.

1791: Constitutional Act establishes Upper (Ontario) and Lower (Quebec) Canada. Fear that the United States would try to expand into Canada was, in part, responsible for the unification of Canada.

1793: Alexander Mackenzie travels west across Canada to the Pacific.

1808: Simon Fraser travels to Vancouver.

1812: War of 1812; Selkirk Settlement (Red River Colony) established.

1821: North West Company merges with Hudson's Bay Company to expand trade into Western frontier.

1837: Upper and Lower Canada rebel against colonial rule, but are suppressed.

1840: Act of the Union unites Upper and Lower Canada into the Province of Canada.

1849: Canada and U.S. boundary to Pacific is completed. Annexation Manifesto — A short-lived document drawn up by a group of Montreal businessmen, advocating that the Canadian colonies relinquish their ties with Britain and join the United States.

1849: Principle of Responsible Government established.

1867: Confederation

1870: Louis Riel forms provisional government.

1871: British Columbia joins the Confederation.

1873: North West Mounted Police formed.

1875: Western Indian Treaties signed.

1885: Canadian Pacific Railway completed. Saskatchewan's North-West Rebellion — Many feared the loss of land as settlers were encouraged by the government to move westward. The rebellion was squashed, and Riel, the leader, was hanged.

1897-1898: The Klondike Gold Rush

1900: Western immigration begins.

1917: Conscription Issue — As World War I progressed, Canadian volunteers declined, and conscription (draft) was put into place despite the strong opposition of French Canadians.

1929: Great Depression impacts all of North America.

1931: Statute of Westminster, signed by the British parliament, recognizes Canada and other self-governing dominions as independent nations.

1939: Canada declares war on Germany.

1949: New Foundland joins the Confederation.

1965: Official Canadian flag raised for the first time — On Feb. 15, 1965, Queen Elizabeth II proclaimed the Maple Leaf flag the official flag of Canada.

1969: Official Languages Act requires services for both French-and English-speaking communities.

1982: Canada Act — The Constitution Act ended British control over amendments to Canada's Constitution. The act included a new bill of rights.

1993: North America Free Trade Agreement is signed — NAFTA is a pact that unites Canada, Mexico and the United States in one of the world's largest free-trade zones. It takes effect in 1994.

1995: Canada votes "No" to Quebec sovereignty (establishing itself as an independent nation).

1999: Nunavut becomes the third territory of Canada.

title: Greetings from Regina, Saskatchewan!
text:
Hi there!

This time we visited Regina, Saskatchewan. It is the capital of Saskatchewan.

The training academy for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) is located here. We went to see it. They have a museum there too.

Near here are the cliffs that the Native Canadians used to herd buffalo (bison) to and force them over so that they would fall to their death. They are called Buffalo Jumps.

There are lots of trees and bushes here. It is really pretty and green.

Wish you were here!

Antoinette

title: What was the Klondike Gold Rush?
text:
The Yukon was a vast area known to few outside of the native people and a few traders, but it didn't take long to change things.

On Aug. 16, 1896, George Carmack, Dawson Charlie and Skookum Jim discovered a dime-size nugget of gold, and it didn't stop there. They quickly staked their claims, and a staking frenzy began. Folks from all over the Yukon and from Alaska came to try their luck.

The rest of the world didn't catch on until a steamship loaded with Klondike gold landed in San Francisco. News of the gold traveled like wildfire, and the population of the Yukon soared from 5,000 to 30,000 in just two short years.

The Klondike Gold Rush was the most publicized gold rush in history.

title: Canadian Lynx
text:
Range: Alaska, Canada, Northern United States, west mainland Europe, southern Siberia and Tibet

The lynx is a curious looking fellow with large tufts of fur on the ears. It has a furry ruff and is usually grayish-tan in color. The stubby tail is tipped in black. The lynx has unusually big feet which act as snowshoes, allowing swift movement in the deep snow. The lynx is nocturnal and solitary. It is an agile climber, swims well and travels with general ease. When it's racing, it's probably running after a snowshoe hare, its favorite meal.

An interesting relationship exits between the lynx and the hare. When the hare population is high (about every 10 years) the cats give birth to larger litters of kittens and the lynx population increases. After awhile the hare population declines, as does the number of lynx.

title: Using a Planner
text:
A planner can help you manage your time. It is a simple tool that will help you remember assignments.

Feeling stressed? Not sure if you’ll have time to do all of your homework? To keep up with your studies and have fun learning, you need to learn to manage your time. A planner is a perfect tool to do this. A planner is like a calendar. It will have days, weeks and months in it. You can look ahead in a planner to see what’s due. You can also look at a day to see what you need to do. Planners help organize your time with just a little effort. Here are some ways to use a planner.

Write down assignments. Write down each assignment as you get it. You can include spelling lists, math homework and book titles. It’s your planner, so put down what you need to know. With each assignment, be sure to include the due date and other requirements. When you’re done with the assignment, check or cross it off.

Review your planner every day. To stay on top of things, review what you’ve written. You don’t want to forget an important assignment! Look ahead to see what assignments are coming up. You can even start early on some of them. It’s up to you to keep track of them.

Create a study schedule. Some people study well in the morning. Others do well in the afternoon or evening. When do you study best? Pick a schedule that works best for you. Block off some time in your planner. Then stick with it. Once you’re done studying, check it off. You may need to choose a quiet place that is free from distractions.

You can use your planner to schedule other things as well, like soccer matches or music recitals. Planners can help you remember anything.
