title: Canada
text:
Canada's name is from the Huron-Iroquois word kanata. Kanata means "village." The French explorer Jacques Cartier used the word to describe a place near the St. Lawrence river. Today the name refers to that spacious country to the north.

Canada has an area of 3,849,953 square miles. It is the biggest country in the Western Hemisphere. Canada is also the second-largest country in the world. It is a beautiful country with many mountains and prairies. Canada also has tundras and lakes. Three oceans border Canada. They are the Atlantic, the Pacific and the Arctic. The southern border meets the United States. The Canada-U.S. border is the longest undefended national border.

Canada was covered by huge glaciers long ago. As they inched along, the force of their weight carved the land. Mountains, valleys and lakes were made. The glaciers melted and filled holes with meltwater. This made more lakes and rivers. Many plants, animals and people made Canada their home over time. Forests cover almost half of Canada. The other 40 percent is mountains and arctic areas. Most Canadians live in southern agricultural regions. They also live along the Atlantic and Pacific coasts.

Today, Canada is a federation of 10 provinces and three territories. Look at the map to find them all. The capital of Canada is Ottawa. The largest city is Toronto. Both cities are in Ontario. Canada is a self-governing nation. However, the Constitution Act of 1982 made the British monarch, Queen Elizabeth the II, also queen of Canada. King Charles III is now king of Canada.

Atlantic provinces include New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. They make up only five percent of Canada's land. Most of the people in those provinces are of British descent.

Quebec is very different from the rest of Canada. This is due to the French culture and language. Quebec was a French colony for more than 150 years. Then the English took control. Today about 80 percent of Quebec's population speak French.

Ontario shares four of the five Great Lakes with the United States. They are lakes Superior, Huron, Erie and Ontario. Ontario is the leading agricultural province. The largest city in Canada is Toronto. Toronto leads in manufacturing.

The Prairie provinces are Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. These three make up one-fifth of Canada's land area. Canada's Prairie provinces were isolated for hundreds of years. Canada's first transcontinental railroad was built in 1885. Later many thousands of people settled the fertile Canadian prairies.

British Columbia lies on the Pacific Ocean. The largest city in British Columbia is Vancouver. Vancouver is Canada's busiest port. The southern part of British Columbia has the mildest climate in Canada.

The territories include the Yukon, Northwest and Nunavut territories. They make up about one-third of the land in Canada. These territories are remote. The climates are very harsh. This makes the territories much less populated. They have a lot of mineral wealth.

title: A Night in an Ice Castle
text:
Canada is famous for its cold, frozen winters, but Quebec has found a way to make the most of its subzero temperatures. Each winter, business owners build a beautiful hotel made entirely of ice. Called the Hotel de Glace (French for "Ice Hotel"), this unique building is open for visitors and overnight guests from January through March.

The hotel looks like fairytale ice castle. Each room is furnished with furniture and decorations made completely of ice. There is even a bar where drinks are served in ice goblets that look just like crystal. Snacks of cold cuts and cheese are served on small ice plates.

The beds in the Hotel de Glace are made of ice as well. Ice beds are covered with deer skins and guests sleep in special sleeping bags made to keep out even the coldest temperatures. Because the hotel's ice walls are more than 4 feet thick, the temperatures in the bedrooms stay between 24 and 26 degrees, no matter how low the outdoor temperatures drop - and they often drop to as low as 20 degrees below zero!

The Hotel de Glace melts away when spring and summer come along, so it must be rebuilt each winter. It takes about 1,000 tons of snow and 500 tons of ice to build the hotel each year.

title: Canada’s Water Wonders
text:
Canada has an amazing number of lakes. It has more than 2 million. Canada's lakes and rivers make up about 15 percent of the world's fresh water volume. Its landscape is constantly being changed by water. The force of water changes the face of the Earth as rivers and glaciers carve out valleys. Water also pushes great amounts of soil, stone and sand over the surface. People have also used the force of moving water to generate power and electricity.

Water also influences where people live. Populations in Canada, and all over the world, are usually greater in places where there are rivers, lakes and coastlines. Rivers and lakes help provide water for irrigation. Mighty rivers and waterfalls also provide a source of power. It makes hydroelectric power. Rivers in Canada have played an important role in transporting goods and people to inland areas that were hard to reach. Don't forget the coastlines where busy shipping ports or fishing industries were found.

Oceans make up three of Canada's borders. Can you name the three oceans without peeking at the map? If you named the Arctic, Atlantic and Pacific, you are exactly right. Can you find them on the map? When you look at a map of the world all of the oceans seem to be connected. The oceans' boundaries were split by geographers.

Rivers are a part of Canada's rich heritage. Rivers nourished the natives and guided the early explorers. The rivers helped fur traders. They also helped the first European settlers. Today, Canadians use rivers for power, transportation and recreation. They are a beautiful part of Canada's land.

Rivers in Canada flow into five major ocean basins. They include the Pacific, Arctic, Atlantic, the Hudson Bay and the Gulf of Mexico. The longest river in Canada is the Mackenzie River. It is 1,060 miles long. The St. Lawrence River, the Nelson, the Churchill and the Fraser are next. Can you find these rivers on the map? The rivers that start in Canada make up 8 percent of the world's river flow into the ocean.

The St. Lawrence Seaway is the most important in Canada. It is the way that ships travel between the Atlantic Ocean and the Great Lakes. Busy port cities like Chicago in the United States and Toronto in Canada are found along the St. Lawrence Seaway.

It's hard to talk about rivers in Canada without mentioning waterfalls as well. Canada has more than 50 major waterfalls that are part of Canada's natural wonders. One of the most famous waterfalls in the world is shared by Canada and the United States. Niagara Falls is on the Niagara River. It is about halfway between Lakes Erie and Ontario. The Niagara River forms part of the U.S.- Canadian border. The mighty river carries water from four of the five Great Lakes. It then cascades over the falls. At the bottom the water travels 15 miles. Then it empties into Lake Ontario. Niagara Falls is the second-largest waterfall in the world. Victoria Falls in southern Africa is the largest.

Today a large portion of the Niagara River is diverted before it reaches the falls. Is moves on to hydroelectric plants. Both Canada and the United States depend on the great river as a source of hydroelectric power. The Niagara is not the only river to be used as a source of energy. Canada leads the world in hydroelectric power and the United States is second.

Lakes in Canada are more than plentiful. Lakes are bodies of water that are deep enough to contain water for long periods of time and which do not freeze to the bottom during the winter. They cover almost 9 percent of the landmass in Canada. The main lakes in Canada (from biggest to smallest) are Huron, Great Bear, Superior, Great Slave, Winnipeg, Erie and Ontario. Great Bear Lake is the largest lake that is entirely in Canada. The oldest rock in the world is thought to be Acasta gneiss, which is found east of Great Bear Lake.

The Great Lakes are the largest group of freshwater lakes in the world. The lakes are shared by Canada and the United States except for Lake Michigan which is entirely in the United States. The largest of the Great Lakes - Lake Superior - is the largest freshwater lake in the world. Scientists believe the Great Lakes were carved out by glaciers of long ago.

Glaciers are another important source of water in Canada. Canada contains the largest area of glaciers and icecaps outside of Greenland and the Antarctic. These glaciers contain a huge amount of fresh water.

The Rocky Mountain glaciers are the main source of fresh water for all of the Prairie provinces. As the water melts from glaciers it feeds the big river systems that crisscross the Plains.

title: Greetings from Quebec City, Quebec
text:
Dear Friends,

Greetings from the city of Quebec. We stayed at the hotel Chateau Frontenac. It is built on the highest point in the city and looks like it used to be a palace or something but, it's always been a hotel.

The city is almost 400 years old. It was founded by Samuel de Champlain in 1608. It started out as a trading post for furs. Some people speak English, but most speak French, the official language here. There are so many fun things to do here. It's like one big history lesson.

Your friend,

Lorelei

title: What is a toboggan?
text:
Indian hunters first built toboggans made of bark to carry game over the snow. The Inuit made toboggans of whalebone.

Today, we use toboggans to race down a snow-covered hill as fast as we can.

Toboggans are sleds without runners. They are made from strips of hickory, ash or maple. The front ends curl upward. The sled is usually 6 to 8 feet long. It can hold a team of up to six people. The one on the rear does all the steering. Toboggans have been recorded going as fast as 61 miles per hour.

title: Bighorn Sheep
text:
Range: Southwestern Canada to Western United States and Northern Mexico.

Habitat: Alpine to dry desert, likes cliffs.

The bighorn sheep lives in flocks. The flock has mostly females or ewes. There are only a few males or rams. The flock has lambs of all ages. Bighorn sheep have excellent hearing. They can detect danger from great distances. It likes the mountains because few predators can pursue the sure-footed sheep on rocky cliffs.

The sheep usually come down to the valleys when it snows to find food. They return to the mountains when the snow melts.

They are light to dark brown in color. The rams have large, curving horns. The babies are called lambs and will be full grown at 3 years old.

title: Reason and Logic: The Marshall Plan
text:
When World War II ended in 1945, Europe was in ruin. Homes, schools and factories had been destroyed. Roads and railroad lines were gone and farmland was torn up by bombs. The war was over, but Europe still suffered. How would the United States respond to the pains of its European friends?

The United States could have left Europe to take care of itself, but Secretary of State George C. Marshall had other ideas. In 1947, he presented the Marshall Plan. The plan called for America to help Europe rebuild by giving money and materials. President Truman and Congress accepted the plan.

Over the next four years, the United States sent over $13 billion in money and supplies to countries throughout Europe. To explain why he thought it made sense for America to help, Marshall said, "In America we have not suffered the destruction of our homes, our towns, and our cities. We have not been enslaved for long periods, at the complete mercy of a conqueror. We have enjoyed freedom in its fullest sense." Many American soldiers lost their lives in the war. But our nation's cities, factories and farms were unharmed. What was our country's answer to the suffering in Europe when we had plenty of food, clothing, money and supplies? It was to give as much help as possible.

What did the United States gain by helping to rebuild Europe? It gained friendships, the ability to trade, and hope for a brighter future, in both Europe and America.

title: The Flag of Canada
text: Dr. George Stanley from Ottawa designed the official flag of Canada in 1965. Red and white were declared the official colors of Canada by King George V of England in 1921. This is why red and white were chosen for the flag. The maple leaf in the center of the flag is Canada's official symbol. The two stripes on either side of the flag represent the Atlantic and the Pacific oceans. They border the east and west coasts. The flag represents the common values of Canadians. They are freedom, peace, respect, justice and tolerance.

title: Getting Organized
text:
Is your backpack overflowing with papers? Is your desk stuffed to the brim? It’s time to get organized!

We all need to be a little organized in life. We need to know where to put our assignments and where to find our homework. But getting organized will take some effort. It will take some practice to come up with a system that works for you. Here are some ways to become more organized.

Avoid Clutter. It’s very easy to collect clutter in your backpack and desk. Avoid doing this. It will be easier to find assignments. Have some folders where you can put school announcements or tests that have been graded. Throw anything away that has become outdated. Clean out your desk of all old assignments, broken pencils and dried-out markers.

Prepare your backpack the night before. By doing this, you’ll be ready to go. No more scrambling around in the morning. Put in your notebooks, textbooks and planner (if you have one).

Use one calendar. If you have a planner, you can use that. Write down when your assignments are due. Also, write down any other activities you have. Put down family activities, too! Write everything down so you can remember it.

Organize your notebooks. Color-code them if you need to. Choose one color for each subject. Now you can quickly spot the correct notebook. Also, write your name inside the notebook, in case it gets lost.

Choose a good study space. Make it clear to your family that this is where you’ll be studying. Have extra pens, pencils and paper in the area. It should have room for all of your books. It should also be away from distractions like the television.

Now that you have some ideas for getting organized, try some of them out. You may be surprised at what a difference it makes in your study habits!

title: Let's Write
text:
Have you ever hiked a mountain just to find a waterfall? If you have, you know that they are one of the many wonders of nature. There are many waterfalls in North America and they come in many shapes and sizes.

1. Name one waterfall in North America

2. Tell the size of the waterfall, and where it is located.

3. Tell some interesting facts about the waterfall. If you’ve had the opportunity to visit this waterfall, describe what it was like.

title: Canada: A Cultural Mosaic
text:
The United States is often called a melting pot. This means that America is a diverse nation. It is a culture that has grown from many cultures and customs.

Canadians refer to Canada as a cultural mosaic. The idea takes into account the people who have moved to Canada from all over the world. As they come together, they keep many of their customs and cultures.

Canada became the first country in the world with a policy on multiculturalism in 1971. This policy makes sure that all Canadians can nurture their culture and customs. They can take pride in their heritage and still belong to Canada.

Who are the Canadians? Today, Canadians can trace their roots to every continent. Native people of Canada have lived there for thousands of years. It has only been in the past 500 years that immigrants from all over the world made Canada their home.

The early arrivals in Canada were both the French and the British. These are the two founding nations of Canada. A small number of Chinese immigrated to work on the lines as the railroad developed.

Canada became the new home for many immigrants in the 1900s, just as in America. This new wave included people from other European countries such as the Ukraine, Germany, Poland, Greece, Ireland and Scandinavia. A flood of new immigrants streamed into Canada after World War II. A large number of them came from Italy. Many Asian and Indo-Chinese began to come later as well. More recently, many immigrants have come from South America and Africa.

One will find a variety of customs, religions and languages in Canada today. Canada's multiculturalism policy is designed to make sure all people in Canada can keep their cultural identities. This is one way to help ensure that all people are treated equally.

Where do you think the people in Canada live? Most of the people in Canada live in and around the major cities just as in the United States. Here they work for the federal and provincial governments. People also work in retail, service and manufacturing industries. The busy city life can be seen in the growing expressways and skyscrapers.

The farms of Canada are mostly owned by families. The largest farms are found in the Prairie provinces where grain is grown. Advanced machinery has made it possible for farmers to do all the work themselves. Technology has helped them to stay in touch with one another. It has also helped farmers with the rest of the business world.

The northern country of Canada has far fewer people. Many Indians and Inuit live in the harsher climates. Many still depend on hunting and fishing as a way of life. There are growing numbers of people that work for the government and in industry.

title: Proud of Two Languages: Nos Deux Langues, Notre Fierte
text:
Can you speak a language other than English? If so then you are bilingual. Bilingual is the ability to speak two languages. Bilingualism in Canada usually means one can speak both English and French. They are the two official languages of Canada.

The Canadian government put a policy in place in March 2003. It supports bilingualism. The Action Plan for Official Languages has three main areas. They include the education system, community programs and federal government.

Students in Canada will see some changes in their schools. Programs will be used to help reach the goals in the Action Plan. The Canadian government hopes to increase the number of students who are bilingual to 50 percent in the next 10 years. That means half of all students will speak both English and French. How many students in your class are bilingual? Is it 50 percent?

The Canadian government budgets hundreds of millions of dollars for community programs. The budget improves support in places where more than one language is spoken. New programs will include early childhood development and immigrant services.

The government is also taking steps to increase bilingualism. They are hiring more bilingual employees. Starting in 1988, all senior public servants were given until March 2003 to become bilingual. Those who did not pass the tests were transferred to lower-paying jobs. The government is also giving improved language instruction. Programs that help people maintain their language skills will also be added.

title: A Closer Look at Canada
text:
How are the lives of our northern neighbors different from ours? How are they the same?

Most Americans can describe Canada's landscape as well as our own. Maybe it's because they are like us in so many ways. Can you list three things that are the same about Americans and Canadians? You might have included dress, language, food, cars, hockey or baseball. How about dreams of peace and hope for a better future? Next, name three things that are different. If you find it hard to describe our northern neighbors, read on to get better acquainted.

Language

"Let me just put on a bunnyhug and grab my knapsack, then I'll meet you by the laneway." Hmmmm, that looks like English and sounds like English. Why couldn't you understand that sentence? Different dialects of one language often sound different. Dialects also use different words and phrases. Now, let's translate that to something you can understand. "Let me just put on my hoody and grab my backpack, then I'll meet you in the driveway."

Many Canadian words are different than American words, just as words used in Massachusetts may not be the same as words used in California. What do you call the thing a women carries that has handles and matches her shoes? Do you call it a purse or a pocketbook?

Below, you can read some words that are common in some or all Canadian provinces. See if you can guess what they are: (answers are in the teacher's materials)

a. pogo
b. candy floss
c. buttons
d. loonie
e. runners
f. hack
g. minty

Well, how did you do? In addition to using different words, Canadians are also known to say "eh" at the end of sentences. For example, "Pretty minty, eh?" They also say "eh" when they need something repeated.

What do Canadians call us? Well, America is referred to as South of the Border. We are known as the States, rather than as America or the United States.

Education

What do Canadian kids do in school? Pretty much the same thing that kids all over the world do. They study the same kinds of subjects. Math in Canada is very different from our own, however. Canadians use the metric system. Metric systems are based on the meter. A meter is a little longer than the American yard.

Not only are the math systems different, but signs and prices can be confusing for Americans if they don't know the metric system. You might see a sign on the freeway that reads 110km/h. You get ready to step on the gas - but hold on there. Translated to miles-per-hour, that means only 68.

If the weatherman in Canada said tomorrow would be sweltering at 40 degrees, you might think it odd. That means 40 degrees Celsius, not Fahrenheit. (Which would be 104 degrees to us, and that is hot!)

Education is the duty of each province in Canada. As in the United States, public education is paid by taxes and grants. Public education is free until a student completes high school. Elementary school is kindergarten through the eighth grade. From grades nine to 12 (or to grade 11 in Quebec and to grade 13 in Ontario), students attend high school. Students in the very far North or in rural areas may study through correspondence courses or computer courses.

Holidays

Many holidays in Canada are similar to U.S. holidays. A traditional Thanksgiving often includes a turkey and all the trimmings (but is celebrated the second week of October). Canadian children also celebrate Halloween with black cats, yummy candy and haunted houses on Oct. 31.

In Canada, public holidays include New Year's Day, Good Friday, Easter Monday, Queen's Birthday (also called Victoria Day, the Monday before May 25), Canada Day (July 1), Labour Day (the first Monday in September), Thanksgiving Day (the second Monday of October), Remembrance Day (Nov. 11) and Christmas (Dec. 25).

Everyone wears a bright red poppy pinned to their clothes on Remembrance Day. This day is to honor those who have served in the military. It also honors those who have given their lives in war. The red poppies are worn as a symbol of blood that was shed on the fields of battle. The green center reminds them of hope for a better future.

Christmas in Canada is not so different from in the United States. It is often a blend of many different customs. If each of you wrote about your holiday traditions, games and food, it would be difficult to find two that are just alike. It is the same in Canada.

One very special Christmas tradition is shared by Boston and Nova Scotia. The tradition began in December 1917, when two ships collided in the harbor near Halifax. There was a very large explosion and a tidal wave followed. A large portion of the north end of Halifax was destroyed. about 1,900 lives were lost, and 9,000 people were injured. Boston sent help to Nova Scotia in response to this tragedy. Doctors, nurses, medical supplies and food were given to the people of Halifax. Canadians send a special Christmas tree to Boston each year to show their thanks. A giant tree is always chosen. They pick one that is full and has even branches. The Canadians take great care in cutting and delivering it without damaging its beauty. Once the tree is up, thousands of Bostonians gather for the lighting. This is a reminder of their bond with Nova Scotia. The kindness of two communities in separate countries resulted in a holiday tradition of goodwill.

Recreation

Quebec City is where winter snow and ice become the stage for the Quebec Winter Carnival. The Carnaval de Quebec (car-na-val dew kay- BECK) is the largest winter carnival in Canada. More than 1 million people come to celebrate each year. It is held in February when it's very, very cold in Quebec.

Activities include snow sculptors (from around the world), a canoe race across the semi-frozen St. Lawrence and even a snow bath. In a snow bath, folks wear bathing suits and roll in the snow until they are too cold to continue.

The crowning of the Carnival Queen is the main event. There is a formal ball held in the evening. Huge firework displays make for a wonderful finale.

Fireworks are an important part of Canada Day. They are set off over the Parliament buildings in the capital city of Ottawa. Canada Day is on July 1 each year. It is Canada's birthday. This was the day when four provinces on the eastern side of the continent (Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario) agreed to join to form one country in 1867. They called it Canada. Six more provinces and three territories were added to Canada over time.

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police put on a show wearing their full dress uniform on this day. (They rarely wear these traditional uniforms.) In Ottawa, at the largest celebration, the mayor makes a speech. Then all the newcomers to the country receive their Canadian citizenship. Games, festivities and parties continue throughout the day. Many different kinds of traditional foods from all around the world are sold at food booths. Communities throughout Canada celebrate Canada Day in their own unique ways. It is a time for families to celebrate everything that makes being Canadian great.

Our northern neighbor, Canada, is unique and wonderful. Would you like to visit Canada? Would you visit Canada in the summer or the winter?

title: Greetings from Dawson, Northern Territory
text:
Dear Friends,

Yesterday we visited Dawson. It's a town that is from the gold rush days. It's right on the Yukon River.

The lady in the gift store said in the days of the gold rush there used to be 20 times as many people as there are here today.

It's weird to see people driving cars around because it looks like something right out of an old Western movie. I really keep expecting to see someone riding into town on a horse.

I tried panning for gold but I wasn't lucky.

Your friend,

(poor) Peter

title: What is an igloo?
text:
Mention the word "igloo," and most people think of a little round house made of snow and ice. "Igloo" is the Inuit name for shelter. Did you know that an igloo can be made of snow, rocks and dirt or animal skins? Today most Inuit have replaced igloos with prefabricated houses.

The snow domes that most people associate with the word igloo were actually only winter shelters. Some were temporary shelters, and some were used for the long winter months. The snow domes were constructed by carefully cutting blocks of snow and layering them in rounds that grew smaller, shaping a dome.

The opening of the snow dome is a tunnel that is much smaller than the dome. This design helps to keep the cold air out.

title: Cedar Waxwing
text:
Range: Central Canada to Central Mexico (including all of the United States)

Habitat: Scrub brush, open wooded areas, forest edges.

The cedar waxwing is a mostly light-brown bird with brownish gray wings. The tips of the wing feathers have red marks on them which resemble little globs of wax and they have a black band which goes from their eyes around the front of their face. The adult is 5 1/2 to 7 1/2 inches in length with an 11- to 11 1/2-inch wingspan.

They are voracious eaters and just love fruits and berries but also eat lots of worms and small insects. They are social birds and travel in flocks. Some will migrate south for the winter and some will not. They are often seen standing close together and passing a berry from one to another until one decides to eat it.

The female will nest and lay four to six eggs usually once a year in June, July or August. The female sits on the eggs for 10 to 12 days before they hatch.

title: Two Official Languages
text: This picture reflects the two official languages of Canada, French and English, that are used on signs around Canada. The building in the background is the Parliament building.

title: Keeping Deadlines
text:
Turning things in late only leads to stress. Take some time to stay ahead in your homework.

Every teacher will give you homework with a deadline. Sometimes, the homework is due the next day. When the project is big, it may be due in a few weeks. When that homework is given, it’s time to prepare yourself. You need to do a few things to turn that homework in on time. It’s all about keeping your deadlines.

Here are a few ways to stay ahead and keep on task.

1. Don’t procrastinate. Homework usually takes longer than you think it will. Start doing it as soon as possible. If you finish it early, you just have more time to make it better.

2. Break up big projects. Some projects may seem huge. Break them up into little pieces. Do you need to do some research for them? How about writing a report? Make a list of what you need to do. Try writing an outline for papers. Read a few chapters each day for a book report. Do something for the project every day before the deadline.

3. Keep a calendar with deadline dates. If you have a lot of homework, write down the deadlines on your calendar. Now you can see what’s due first. Find out which homework assignment will take the longest. Refer to the calendar often so you don’t forget.

title: Let's Write
text:
Winter in many North American communities is cold and snowy, but this doesn’t stop folks from enjoying the great outdoors.

1. List one winter activity that you do or would like to participate in.

2. Tell what kind of equipment and protection is needed to participate in this activity.

3. Write another paragraph describing how this activity is done and why you think it’s the best.

title: Mexico: Where the Past is the Present
text:
The first people who lived in Mexico are thought to have come from the north before 8000 B.C. They were hunters who traveled from place to place. They followed herds of buffalo, mammoths, mastodons and other large creatures that roamed the land.

The early inhabitants became farmers around 7000 B.C. They grew maize, avocados, beans, peppers, squashes and tomatoes. They also raised dogs and turkeys for food.

The cultures continued to develop. Large farm villages stood along Lake Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico by 1000 B.C. These people produced pottery and cloth. Religions were developing. Trade was carried on with other communities. The people began to build large flat-topped pyramids with temples on top. Some of the villages became religious centers. These villages spread across the land from the Valley of Mexico to the Gulf of Mexico. They also spread to the Pacific Ocean and down to what is now Guatemala. This area of land is often called Mesoamerica.

The Olmec was the first established culture in Mexico. It is quite mysterious. We know nothing of where they came from or what happened to them. They lived in Mexico between about 1200 B.C and 400 B.C. The Olmec had a counting system. They also carved dramatic stone heads.

The Classic Period of Mexico thrived between 250 A.D. and 900 A.D. Huge pyramids were dedicated to the sun and the moon at Teotihuacan, near what is now Mexico City. Teotihuacan was a city-state. It had a population of about 200,000 by 350 A.D. It influenced almost all of the Mesoamerican region.

The Maya culture thrived in southern Mexico and northern Guatemala. Maya were influenced by the Olmec. They also built temples and carved beautiful statues. The Maya people recorded important dates on pillars of stone using a kind of picture writing.

The Toltec and the Aztec empires were both important civilizations following the Classic Period.

The Toltec lived in the highlands of Mexico between 900 A.D. and 1200 A.D. The Toltec built a major city in the 900s. The ruins lie near what is now the town of Tula de Allende. It is about 45 miles north of Mexico City. The site is known as Tula.

The Aztec are probably the most well-known of Mexico's ancient cultures. They ruled a mighty empire during the 1400s and 1500s.

The center of Aztec civilization was the Valley of Mexico and included many cities and towns there. The largest city was the capital Tenochtitlan. It occupied an island in Lake Texcoco. Causeways, or raised earthen roads, linked the city to the mainland. On an island to the north stood the city of Tlatelolco. This was another great city. Both Tenochtitlan and Tlatelolco lay within the borders of what is now Mexico City. The present-day city covers much of the bed of Lake Texcoco. The lake was drained during the 1600s. The people of Tenochtitlan took over Tlatelolco. The two cities united in 1473. Tenochtitlan may have had a population of 200,000 to 300,000 when the Spaniards came in the 1500s. That was larger than any Spanish city in Europe.

When Hernando Cortes entered the Aztec capital, he and his troops were joined by Indians who were conquered by the Aztec. These tribes resented the Aztec's heavy taxes. Montezuma II was the Aztec ruler. He did not resist the Spaniards. Some scholars think he believed Cortes was the god Quetzalcoatl. An Aztec legend said Quetzalcoatl had sailed away to the east (where the Spaniards came from). Cortes entered Tenochtitlan. He made Montezuma a prisoner. When Montezuma died, the Aztec gave in to the Spanish.

title: Boom to Bust, and Back Again
text:
You may have heard people compare the recent economic recession (2007- 2009) to the Great Depression of the 1930s. But what some people call the "Great Recession" actually had more in common with a depression in the 1890s and something called "boom and bust."

In the early 1890s, the U.S. economy grew quickly ("boomed") but couldn't keep growing at that rate. When many companies and the housing market failed, there was an economic "bust." The railroad industry had been booming since the end of the Civil War, but in the 1890s more than 150 railroad companies closed. Other industries that depended on the railroads closed, and many people lost their jobs. Over 500 banks closed. Thousands of unemployed men marched to Washington, D.C., in 1894 to demand that the government take action to help families. Unemployment was over 10 percent for most of the 1890s. About one of every ten people had no job.

In the recent recession, the housing market slumped after several "boom" years. Some automakers went out of business and others filed for bankruptcy. The economy went "bust," just as it did in the 1890s. Hundreds of banks and thousands of businesses closed. The unemployment rate was about 8 percent - about one of every twelve people had no job.

Make a chart or Venn diagram that compares these two events in history. (Teachers: You can find background information and activities that relate to this article at hnn.us)

title: Mexico Timeline
text:
Pre-1500 A.D: Many American Indian groups have lived in the region for centuries.

1519-1521: Cortes conquers the Aztec Empire.

1540s: Spaniards discover silver in the northern part of the Spanish colony. The mines drew more immigrants, and estates were established where creoles ruled.

1808: French forces occupy Spain and imprison King Ferdinand.

1810: A priest named Hidalgo makes a speech known as the Grito de Dolores (Cry of Dolores) in which he calls for a rebellion so Mexico will be governed by Mexicans.

1813: Jose Maria Morelos, another priest, carries on the work of Hidalgo and forms a Congress that issues a call for independence and writes a constitution for a Mexican republic.

1819: Adams-Onis treaty; Spain and U.S. establish U.S.-Mexican border.

1821: Mexico wins independence from Spain.

1821: Flag of Mexico is created

1821: Mexico allows Stephen Austin to begin colonization of Texas.

1824: Mexico becomes a republic with Guadalupe Victoria as the first president.

1835-1836: Struggle over Texas independence includes the Battle of the Alamo and the Battle of San Jacinto. A treaty with Santa Anna establishes a new Texas that included what is now Texas and parts of present-day Colorado, Kansas, New Mexico, Oklahoma and Wyoming.

1846: Government of Mexico does not recognize Santa Anna's treaty, and Mexican soldiers attack U.S. soldiers who entered the area. The United States then declared war on Mexico.

1847: U.S. forces under General Winfield Scott enter Mexico City; peace negotiations with Mexico begin.

1848: Gold is discovered at Sutter's Mill in California, and as people swarm to the area, many set up camp on Mexican-held land, forcing the landowners out.

1848: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo brings the U.S.-Mexican War to an end. Mexico gives to the United States what is now California, Nevada and Utah, most of Arizona and parts of Colorado, New Mexico and Wyoming, and also recognizes Texas as independent. Mexico receives $15 million in payment.

1853: The Gadsden Purchase Treaty is signed, giving the United States what is now southern Arizona and New Mexico in return for $10 million.

1855: Liberal Government under Juarez begins Reform period

1862: France, Britain and Spain attempt to force Benito Juarez's government to repay debts owed. Even though Britain and Spain withdraw, the French remain, hoping to establish a new empire. On May 5 (Cinco de Mayo), soldiers defeat the French army in the Battle of Puebla.

1863: France occupies Mexico City.

1864-1867: Maximilian of Austria becomes the Emperor of Mexico.

1867: Maximilian is executed and Juarez regains power.

1872: Juarez dies and Sebastian Lerdo de Tejada is his successor.

1876-1880: Porfirio Diaz overthrows Lerdo and sets himself up as dictator.

1884-1911: Porfirio Diaz rules again.

1911: Francisco I. Madero leads a successful revolt and Diaz resigns and flees the country. Madero is elected president.

1913: General Victoriano Huerta seizes the government and Madero is murdered.

1914: President Woodrow Wilson sends troops to Veracruz, Mexico, in an effort to depose Victoriano Huerta, who soon resigns. Wilson actively supports Venustiano Carranza, a follower of Madero.

1916: General John J. Pershing leads 10,000 American soldiers into Mexican territory in retaliation for a raid on Columbus, New Mexico, by General Francisco "Pancho" Villa, a Mexican revolutionary. Pershing returned to the United States without capturing Villa. Because of this, U.S.-Mexico relations are strained.

1917: Revolutionary Constitution is adopted.

1920-1930: Revolutionary social and economic reforms, including land distribution

1942: Mexico enters the World War II on the side of the Allies. Mexico's contributions to the war were mostly economic. The country supplied raw materials, laborers and made war equipment in factories that the United States helped to set up.

1940-1960: Mexico's economy improves. Factories and production increase while the government expands highway, irrigation and railroad systems.

1970-1980: Inflation affects the Mexican economy.

1985: Earthquakes hit Mexico City and the surrounding area on Sept. 19 and 20. The quakes caused about 10,000 deaths and $5 billion in property damage.

1994: North America Free Trade Agreement goes into effect. NAFTA is a pact that unites Canada, Mexico and the United States in one of the world's largest free-trade zones.

title: Greetings from Cuernavaca, Morelos, Mexico
text:
Dear Friends,

Today we visited Cuernavaca. It is also known as the "City of the Eternal Spring" because of its year-round spring-type weather.

We saw the "Palacio de Cortes." Its construction was ordered by Hernando Cortes in 1522. When he had more money, he added on to the palace.

The city is beautiful with lots of flowers and old buildings. I also hear that lots of people come here to learn the Spanish language.

Your friend,

Paula

title: What was the Monroe Doctrine?
text:
The Monroe Doctrine was a set of declarations that warned the countries around the world that the United States recognized the new Latin American countries as free. The Monroe Doctrine also said the United States would protect the freedom of those countries.

Originally England had asked the United States to sign a joint agreement like the Monroe Doctrine stating the opinions of both England and the United States. The United States decided to sign their own declaration rather than jointly with England.

This didn't seem to make much difference in the attitudes of other countries towards the Latin American countries until the United States established a stronger Navy.

title: Wild Turkey
text:
Range: Colorado through Pennsylvania to Southern Mexico

This turkey is the wild version and the kind usually pictured in Thanksgiving displays.

You might be surprised to know that these fowl roost in trees, so look up next time you are strolling in the woodlands.

The turkey is very vocal and has many different calls which can be successfully reproduced by a human. The turkey was named by American Indians after its most obvious trait - "the one who gobbles!"

Turkeys feed on insects, berries, seeds and nuts.

When startled, they can fly for short distances but prefer to walk or run.

title: Ojo de Dios
text:
This is an authentic and beautiful American Indian design.

Materials

popsicle sticks or tongue depressors

glue

yarn

pompoms

Directions

1. Find two popsicle sticks or tongue depressors. Glue them into a cross. Start the weaving by gluing the yarn to the back side of the sticks.

2. Start a crisscross pattern with the yarn. Continue to loop the yarn around the four ends of each stick. Keep the yarn fairly tight.

3. Continue the same pattern development, remembering to loop the yarn over each stick end in a like manner. Other colors may be added by tying new string to the old yarn. Make sure the knot is hidden behind the stick.

4. The work can be finished by tying the remaining yarn end onto the back of the design. Small pompoms can be attached to the end of the sticks.

Extra Activity

After you have mastered a small one, try a larger one!

title: Let's Write
text:
Yipee! You’ve got some special glasses that let you translate records from ancient civilizations.

A. Write the name of the ancient civilization for which you will be translating.

B. Tell about the person who wrote the ancient record.

C. Describe the material used to write the message.

D. Translate the message for our readers.

title: Good Handwriting
text:
It takes some time to develop good handwriting, but it’s well worth the effort.

Have you ever gotten a test back and lost points because of messiness? Does your teacher have problems reading what you’ve written? Bad handwriting can lead to these situations. If no one can read your brilliant answer on the test, then it won’t help you get a good score. Most people think bad handwriting means a lack in organizational skills. If it’s difficult to read, people won’t take the time to decipher the handwriting.

Developing good handwriting takes patience and diligence. It takes a lot of practice to get those perfect letters. Here are some tips to get you started.

Take some time each day to practice writing out letters. The more you practice, the better your handwriting will become.

Practice in one notebook so you can compare how well you are doing.

It’s okay if you write slowly in the beginning. Focus on writing that can be read easily. Then move on to how fast you can write legibly.

Choose a pen or pencil that you like and gives you the best grip. You may want to try out different pens or pencils to find the one just for you.

Good handwriting is a needed skill in this world. It’s needed when you take a test or write a paper in class. You’ll need it to write thank-you cards or to fill out invitations. And when you’re older, you’ll need it to fill out job applications. In the end, good handwriting will help people understand what you’ve written. And that’s the most important part.

title: Early Art
text: Ancient civilizations of Mexico often painted elaborate scenes of everyday life in buildings. Sometimes they painted scenes on pottery as well.

title: Los Estados Unidos de Mexico
text:
Mexico is the fifth-largest country in the Western Hemisphere. Mexico is a federal republic. It has 31 states and one federal district. Can you see the capital of Mexico on the map below? It is number 21. Name two of the states that border the capital, Mexico City.

Mexico is a very long country. Its coastline is one of the longest in the world. The fishing industry has always been very important to the economy.

The marine life of the fisheries is varied. A day's catch can bring tuna, sardines, anchovies, red snapper, mullets and sharks. They might also harvest dogfish, shrimps, lobsters, abalone, oysters, clams, sea snails, octopuses and sea urchins.

Mexico is rich in mineral resources. It has smaller amounts of agricultural land. It is a quickly growing country. More than half the people live in the central core. Petroleum and tourism are important to the economy. Industry is growing in many parts of the country. Many people move to cities because of changes in resources and industry. More than two-thirds of the population have gone to cities. Mexico City is one of the largest metropolitan areas in the world. It has a population of almost 9 million! Guadalajara is a city in the state of Jalisco. It is the nation's second largest city. In spite of growing numbers in cities and great strides in the economy, most Mexicans are poor.

The traditional lifestyles of people in isolated areas are very different from those in cities. There are still many small villages. Here some American Indian people still live the way their ancestors did. This diversity in culture, landscape and climate is the thing that gives Mexico its colorful character.

title: Food for the Gods: Chocolate
text:
While the ancient Olmecs may have been the first to grow cacao trees, it is certain that the Aztec of Mexico harvested the fruit and seeds.

What's so special about cacao trees? We get chocolate from the seed of the cacao beans. The Latin name for this tree is Theobroma cacao, meaning "drink of the gods."

Chocolate was first a drink of the Aztec royalty and warriors. They ground the cacao beans then mixed them with ground corn and other seeds. They may have added honey or vanilla to sweeten the drink. The cocoa powder is very bitter.

The Aztec also used the cocoa beans as a form of money in religious rituals. Perhaps this is why the first seeds were brought to Spain. They thought they might grow "money trees." We know that the first cacao beans arrived in Spain in the 1500s.

The drink made from the cacao beans was a hit in Europe. It wasn't long before London began to sell chocolate drinks in shops. The Europeans added sugar, vanilla, cinnamon and milk to sweeten the bitter taste.

J.S. Fry and Sons, a British chocolate company, is thought to have developed solid eating chocolate. This was done by adding some of the cocoa butter to the chocolate liqueur. Daniel Peter of the Swiss chocolate company invented a way to produce milk chocolate. Today, cacao trees are grown on plantations in Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean Islands and West Africa.

The seeds are taken from the pods and dried for a few days. They are cleaned, roasted and shelled. Finally, the inside of the seed is pressed to remove the chocolate liquor. From this juice all chocolate products are made.

Today, chocolate is enjoyed by folks in communities around the world. There is chocolate candy, chocolate ice cream, chocolate cake and chocolate milk.

title: Mexico’s Water Wonders
text:
A drive from northern Mexico to the southernmost tip is a great trip. A traveler sees hundreds of miles of coastline. It is dotted with beautiful beaches and small fishing villages. Then the climb begins to move toward mountains. They are so green that it always seems to be spring. Still higher, one would find mountain peaks. Some would be capped with snow. Down the mountains there are rocky deserts. Heading inland it is far from green. The drive would end as the traveler enters lush tropical jungles.

There are but a few rivers that can be traveled by large boats in Mexico. The rivers lend their beauty to the Mexican landscape. Most of the rivers are short. They follow mountain ranges to coastlines. The longest river in Mexico is the Rio Bravo del Norte. Americans call it the Rio Grande. It forms more than half the border with the Unites States. Several important towns run the length of the Rio Bravo del Norte. On the Mexican side are the important cities of Ciudad Juárez and Chihuahua. Across the river in Texas are found Laredo and Brownsville.

The Rio Bravo del Norte is an important source of irrigation for the United States and Mexico. The water usage is regulated by a treaty between the two countries. The Rio Bravo is over appropriated. This means there are more users for the water than the river supply. Much of the river has been dry due to drought conditions. Ecologists fear that parts of the Rio Bravo will dry up unless rainfall is normal in the near future.

The rivers Yaqui and Santiago in the western part of Mexico flow into the Pacific Ocean. The eastern rivers like the Usumacinta and Moctezuma flow into the Gulf of Mexico.

There is a tributary of the Usumacinta River in the state of Chiapas to the far south. The water cascades and creates many beautiful waterfalls. The limestone also makes the water here a beautiful shade of blue. Many visitors take time to enjoy the falls in the Lacandon jungle. They also take a swim in the blue ponds of Agua Azul (blue water).

Also in the state of Chiapas is the Grijalva. It starts in Guatemala and flows down the mountains. It is navigable by boat in some places. This allows locals to transport goods by boat. Other rivers in Mexico are not useful for shipping goods. Those have been harnessed as a major source of hydroelectric power. Dams on these rivers also serve to help control the flooding.

The Infiernillo dam forms the country's largest reservoir. It is on the Balsas River which is southwest of Mexico City. The Lerma and Santiago rivers join farther north. They form the largest and most important river system in Mexico. There Lerma begins in the Sierra Madre Occidental. It then flows into Lake Chapala. The Santiago drains out of the lake. It empties into the Pacific Ocean in the state of Nayarit. It is a very important source of hydroelectric power.

Mexico doesn't have many large lakes. Lake Chapala is one of the largest lakes there. It is south of the city of Guadalajara. Other notable lakes are the Cuitzeo, Nezahualcoyotl and Angostura.

Many tourists visit the lakes in Mexico. They go to fish for prized striped bass. They are plentiful in many lakes.

One cannot talk of waterways and lakes in Mexico without telling of Xochimilco. It means "the place of the flower fields" in Nahuatl, the language spoken by the Aztec. Xochimilco was once a lakeside village connected to Tenochtitlán (the Aztec capital) by a causeway. Today it is the only part of Mexico City that has canals and floating gardens. That's right, "floating gardens," or chinampas are floating vegetable or flower gardens. They are used today just as the Aztec used them. These floating canals are first built by taking water plants with aquatic roots. Then they are covered with the soil dredged from the bottom of the canal.

Many scientists still marvel at the floating gardens. They are very efficient. Many tourists are excited about visiting the gardens. They ride in colorful boats on the canal in Mexico City.

Aside from the beauty of the canals, Mexico City is in trouble when it comes to water. With the huge increase in population, more people need more water. Mexico City has one of the most serious water management problems in the world. Portions of the city are starting to sink as increasing water is taken from the ground. City managers have begun to think of ways to solve the problem. They include ways to make the public more aware of the shortage.

title: Greetings from Guadalupe Canyon
text:
Dear Friends,

The drawings you see in this picture are ancient Indian drawings that we hiked to (here in Guadalupe Canyon). It seems like there are millions of caves here. It's pretty weird to think that we stood in caves where ancient Indians once stood.

I almost expected to see an Aztec warrior appear!

It's been pretty fun camping here. There are natural warm springs where we swim and relax each evening after a day of four-wheeling or exploring. It's all really beautiful. There are waterfalls and palm trees.

I like hanging out at the little store too. They have lots of chickens and a dog.

Your friend,

Arturo

title: What is a charro?
text:
Mexico has it's own kind of cowboys. They are called charros. The charros emerged early in colonial Mexico. They came when the Spaniards first began grazing cattle in Mexico.

Charros compete in competitions called a charreada. It is similar to a rodeo in the United States. The word rodeo came from Spanish. It means "round." Charros would circle around a group of cattle to separate them from the herd.

In a charreada, the charro demonstrates his skill in riding a horse. He will then show his skill using a lasso while riding. Finally, he must grab a wild bull by the tail and roll it over on its back.

The charro's costume is very formal and the rules are strict. Many towns in the ranching regions of Mexico hold a charreada every month.

title: Desert Tortoise
text:
Range: western Arizona, southern Utah, southern California and south to Sonora, Mexico.

Habitat: Deserts and other regions with harsh environmental conditions with extreme temperatures and very little moisture.

The desert tortoise is truly a steady creature. It travels about 20 feet per minute. That is, if it doesn't get sidetracked by a juicy plant along the way.

The carapace or shell on the desert tortoise is highly domed. The lower shields have prominent growth lines. Their forelimbs have really large scales. When they are drawn in they fill the entire front shell opening. This provides extra protection. The tail is very short. The head is small and rounded.

The desert tortoise is adapted well to desert life. It requires little drinking water to survive. Moisture comes from plant foods and is stored in two sacs found under the carapace.

A desert tortoise hibernates for the winter. Long burrows are where you might find one at that time.

title: Clarity of Thought: President Ronald Reagan and the USSR
text:
Three decades ago a first class stamp cost fifteen cents. A Macintosh was not a computer; it was an apple that grew on a tree. And the United Soviet Socialist Republic (USSR or Soviet Union) was a threat to the safety and freedom of the United States and the world. All of those things were going on in 1981 when Ronald W. Reagan became our 40th president. President Reagan served for two terms, and by the time he left office in 1989 the world was becoming a much different place.

When President Reagan was first elected, the USSR had a communist government. Under communism, the government controls all industry, and the citizens do not have the same rights and freedoms as we have in America. The USSR and the United States were in what was called a Cold War. The two countries never actually went to war, but we came very close. President Reagan understood how dangerous the Cold War was for both countries and for the whole world.

Making the world a safe, free place for all people was one of President Reagan's main goals as president. He spent many years negotiating with Soviet leaders, especially Mikhail Gorbachev, to end the Cold War. In 1991, the USSR split into 15 different countries and the Cold War came to an end. Having clarity of thought means that you are able to think and understand things clearly. President Reagan's clarity of thought played a vital role in ending the Cold War.

title: How Do I Take a Test?
text:
Do you get sweaty palms and butterflies in your stomach over the idea of taking a test? That happens to everyone at one time or another. Did you know test anxiety comes from a lack of self-confidence? How can you improve your self-confidence and improve your test-taking skills? The best way is to know the material very well. But here are some other important ideas that may help you:

Preview the test. What does it cover? How long is it?

Plan your time. Decide how much time you can spend on each section. Keep track of the time as you take the test.

Follow directions. Read all the directions and listen carefully to any directions read aloud.

Read the questions carefully. Look for keywords such as "when," "where," "why," "different from," "same as," "before" and "after."

Don't get stuck on one question. If you can't think of an answer, skip it and return to it later when you have finished the rest of the test.

Check your work. If you have time left after you finish the test, go back and double-check your work.

Use this list while taking this week's Studies Weekly quiz. Practice good test-taking skills. You may want to use this list for the next few weeks until you have mastered the skills.

title: Let's Write
text:
You are floating down the canals of Xochimilco, when suddenly you find yourself transported into the past.

You can’t believe your eyes—there must be 25,000 people in this bustling capital. All around you are people selling flowers, fruits, vegetables and colorful crafts.

You realize you must be in the ancient city of Tenochtitlán. You are enjoying the colors, sounds and smells of the busy markets of the Aztec.

You find a scrap of wood to write down the things you see.

Write a description of your adventure as if you were writing it in your diary.

title: Mexico: A Portrait of the People
text:
The population of modern Mexico is a mixture of Spanish and Indian ancestry. Do you recall the term "mestizos"? What does it mean? Today, six of every 10 Mexicans are mestizos. About 30 percent of the population are pure American Indians. Others are white, Asian or of African descent. The majority of Mexicans call themselves mestizos.

Much of Mexico's recent history has had a power struggle between the mestizos, American Indians and whites. Whites often boasted of their "pure Spanish" heritage. Many mestizos felt they were better than Indians. The American Indians viewed whites as invaders. They also felt mestizos were "impure." Today, many American Indians of Mexico are trying to unite. It is an effort to improve their status and living conditions.

Indians

Where do most of the American Indians, or indigenous people, of Mexico live? They are found mainly in southern Mexico. There are large populations of people of Maya descent in the states Oaxaca and Chiapas. The Yaqui, Mayo and Tarahumara are found in the north. Tribes like the Tarahumara keep much of the old way of life. They wear the traditional dress. They live in villages that have few, if any, modern conveniences we enjoy today.

The official language of Mexico is Spanish. About 60 native languages are still spoken. Most Mexicans who speak an indigenous language also speak Spanish. The most important indigenous language is Nahuatl. (See Page 4 to learn some Nahuatl words.)

Way of Life

The family is very important in the Mexican way of life. The whole family gathers for the midday meal. Sundays are a family day as well. Grandparents are deeply respected. They often live with children and grandchildren.

Mexicans who live in cities wear clothes not so different from those you wear. People in rural areas may wear more traditional clothing. Indigenous people wear their unique native costumes.

Children in cities of Mexico go to school. They enjoy many of the same things you do. They watch TV, go to movies, concerts and games. Do you know what the most popular sport in Mexico is? If you guessed soccer, you are right!

Life is not so easy for many people in Mexico. Most people in villages and rural areas are very poor. Almost half of Mexicans live in poverty. Many families have no electricity. Most don't have running water or plumbing for bathrooms. It is uncommon for villagers to have health care. Children are often unable to go to school. They must help support the family. As they grow older, many young people of villages are leaving to find work in cities and towns.

Almost every village and town has a marketplace. Every city in Mexico has one. Men, women and children take many things there. They bring clothes, food, lace, pictures, baskets and animals. They take whatever they wish to sell or trade and rent stalls. Goods are displayed on the ground too. People spend one day each week at the marketplace trading goods. At the marketplace people can catch up on news. They can also chat with friends. Children and adults look forward to the marketplace.

Mexico's culture is colorful and diverse. People are friendly. They are helpful from villages to cities.

Visitors to Mexico love to explore jungles, swim on beautiful beaches and shop in cities and towns.

Maybe someday you'll visit colorful Mexico too!

title: A Closer Look at Mexico
text:
How are the lives of our southern neighbors different from ours? How are they the same?

If you have the chance to visit Mexico, you'll feel welcome from your first "Bienvenidos!" to your last "hasta luego!" The friendly people of Mexico are one of its treasures. They are happy, gracious and expressive. They are very colorful people. Color seems to be everywhere from vibrant buildings to bright clothing and native crafts. Even the money of Mexico is full of color. Color reflects the past and present everywhere.

Are you ready to know more about our neighbors to the south? Read on to learn about this welcoming land of color, spirit and creative flair.

Language

Mexico is a land that combines the past and the present. Languages are no exception. Mexico has one of the largest indigenous populations in the Americas. It is no surprise that there is a variety of languages spoken. Spanish is the main one in Mexico. There are still 62 other living indigenous languages. Do you know what a living language is? It is a language used by people in a community every day. Latin is an example of a dead language.

How do Mexicans communicate with each other when there are so many languages? The country has an official language. Do you know what the official language of Mexico is? That's right, it's Spanish. It is spoken by 90 percent of the population.

Education

Most youth have to go to school until they are 18 in the United States. Mexican law requires all children from the age of six through 14 go to school. A child has six years of elementary school after kindergarten.

About 80 percent of students complete elementary school. They may attend basic secondary school after elementary. The dropout rate is very high. Only half of those students complete the required three years of basic secondary school. Those graduates may go on to one of Mexico's 10 public universities for more studies.

The oldest and largest Mexican university is the National Autonomous University of Mexico in Mexico City. The university became autonomous or free of government control in 1929. More than 325,000 students go to this university. There they study law, philosophy, medicine, science, music, political and social science, commerce, engineering, architecture and nursing.

Fiestas

In the words of a Mexican poet named Octavio Paz, "Fiestas are our only luxury." Mexico is a land where fiestas abound. You can visit any season of the year and enjoy a celebration. Many of the fiestas are community events. Some are to honor workers. In a fiesta to honor schoolteachers, for example, every student brings a gift for their teacher. On the day to honor postmen each household on a route offers food and drink to the letter carrier. Even the dead have their fiesta day, the Dia de los Muertos or Day of the Dead.

The Day of the Dead is held on Nov. 1 and 2. It is one of the largest festivals in all of Mexico. Many cities in the southwestern United States celebrate this holiday too.

The Day of the Dead is a mixture of ancient rituals and Christian holidays. This is like many of our modern holidays. The Aztecs were first to celebrate this holiday. They did so over two months. Skulls were used to honor the dead during the Aztec festivals. Aztec believed the dead came back to life during the months of the festival. An attempt to convert the American Indian people to Catholicism came with the Spanish conquest of the Aztec empire. Eventually traditional festivals and rituals were suppressed. This ritual refused to die. The Spaniards moved it to All Saints' Day in November to make the ritual more Christian. Today, the festival lasts for only one day and two nights. Some Aztec symbolism is still used. Aztec believed that yellow flowers were sacred to the dead. Bright yellow marigolds are used to decorate the graves of loved ones in Mexico today. They adorn alters created to honor those who died.

Special food and treats are made for the festival. For the Day of the Dead celebrations there are two kinds of traditional foods. They are calaveras and pan de muerto or "bread of the dead." Calaveras are candies molded of sugar in the shape of a skull. They are brightly decorated. Names of family members are written on the forehead of the skulls. The bread is also sweet. Often toy or candy skeletons are hidden inside. The person who finds the skeleton is lucky.

The families bring food for a picnic near the graves on the evening of the first day. Sometimes they stay in the cemetery through the night. There are two days for this celebration. Nov. 1 is thought to be the day for the souls of dead children to return. Nov. 2 is the day for the souls of adults. This is not a sad time. It is considered to be a happy time when all are reunited.

Carnival is a festival that is full of color and excitement. Carnival is celebrated in many Catholic countries. It is just before the traditional 40-day fast before Lent.

Carnival is a time when anything can happen in Mexico. People dress up in costumes for parades. They dance in the streets. There is music and bright floats. Best of all there are fireworks.

Women and children are known to have flower battles for Carnival. They line up and throw flowers at each other. They often throw them at spectators as well. Children dress as Mexican soldiers and conquistadores.

Sports

Fútbol, or "soccer," is the most popular sport in Mexico as in the rest of Latin America. Each village or town seems to boast a soccer field, a ball and players of all ages.

The Mexican soccer league has two championship tournaments each year. The most famous teams are the America and Cruz Azul from Mexico City and Guadalajara. These teams play major matches in Estadio Azteca. It is the largest stadium in Mexico and the first to host two World Cup finals.

Baseball and American football are becoming more popular in northern Mexico near the Mexico/U.S. border. Children play baseball in school as well as at the ball field.

A game that was developed in Mexico is called frontenis. This game is played using a tennis racket and a ball. Players bounce the ball off of a wall. The game of jai alai is also played against a wall. It requires great speed and flexibility. Players take turns firing the ball at the wall using wicker scoops called cestas. The ball flies out of the cesta at high speeds!

In the summer the Mexican leagues play baseball. Mexico won the Caribbean World Series in 2011.

Bullfighting is a sport in Mexico. It survived the Spanish colonial period. The largest bullfighting ring in the world is in Mexico City. It is called Plaza México.

Bulls are angered by men who pierce them between the shoulder blades in the Plaza México. The angry bull then charges. The matador has 16 minutes to kill the bull, then the fight is over. While the sport can often be cruel, it is seen by many Mexicans as an art form.

Food

Enchiladas, tacos and burritos are common Mexican food dishes. They are eaten in Mexico like hotdogs are in the United States.

The staple in Mexico is corn. It is the main ingredient used in tortillas. How many of your Mexican favorites use tortillas?

title: Greetings from Copper Canyon
text:
Dear Friends,

We are taking the train, El Chepe, through Copper Canyon on the way to Mazatlan.

What a ride! We have seen waterfalls and gone through tunnels galore. One of the tunnels was a horseshoe shape that climbed up the mountain at the same time. It was pretty exciting.

We've made many stops to visit small villages and do some camping. Today we've been in some really high mountains. Dad says the canyons here are deeper than those of the famous Grand Canyon found in the United States.

And I thought a train ride was going to be boring!

Your friend,

Melissa

title: What is a curandero?
text:
The health care systems in Mexico aren't always available in rural areas of Mexico. Many villages have a curandero or healer.

Curanderos are men or women who learned how to treat illness with special herbs and common foods. They treat many kinds of illnesses. Some are traditional. Others are not recognized by medical doctors.

Many American Indians in smaller villages think a person may be ill because they have been given the "evil eye" by another person. They believe when this happens only a curandero can help.

title: King Vulture
text:
Range: Southern Mexico through Northern Argentina

Habitat: Dense Tropical Forests

The king vulture is sometimes called the Mexican eagle. Colorful drawings of this bird are found in ancient Maya art. The king vulture is the largest of the seven species of North American or New World vultures. Ones in North America have a large nasal cavity at the top of the beak unlike Old World vultures. This is unique to birds of prey.

The weak feet of the king vulture are made for hopping as with other vultures. They are not for grasping live prey. These fellows generally eat carrion. Carrion is dead or decaying flesh.

The king vultures are solitary birds. If they are feeding, then there may be as many as 20 circling the remains. Other species of vultures are known to leave the remains of an animal when the king vulture comes. They continue to circle. They perch on a nearby tree until the king vulture has left.

The king vulture is light in color. The head and neck are colorful. It has very broad wings and a short tail. It doesn't have a voice box, but it can wheeze and whistle.

title: Plagiarism
text:
Plagiarism is a long word and it's hard to spell. But it's very important you know and understand its meaning.

To plagiarize something is to steal another person's writings, thoughts or inventions.

It means to take credit for that person's ideas. This practice is dishonest, even if the writings have never been published. Another word for plagiarism is "copying." In many schools, a student can be kicked out for plagiarizing. We should never steal another person's ideas.

There are many ways to avoid plagiarism. Let's look at some ideas you can use to become a writer who doesn't plagiarize. By doing these things, you can always be confident in your work.

Paraphrase, or re-write in your own words. Read what several different writers say on the subject. Then write your version of what they've written.

Use quotations. It's perfectly okay to state what another person has written on a subject. You just need to give credit to that person. Here's an example: As Huckleberry Finn said to his buddy, Tom Sawyer, ". . . . ."

Your opinion. What you think about a subject is what really matters. Read about the subject first. Then put down on paper what you truly feel about it!

Your teachers really want you to succeed. If you worry your writing is not what you'd like it to be, ask your teacher for advice. You will never lose marks for asking a teacher questions.

title: Youth Learning to Love Mariachi Music
text:
Have you ever tapped your feet to the lively, rhythmic beat of a mariachi band? Mariachi is a traditional Mexican music style featuring charming songs that are passed along from generation to generation. Lately, however, fewer children have been taught to play traditional mariachi instruments and songs. Today, a new organization called the Central California Alliance for the Preservation of Mariachi aims to preserve and revive mariachi music by teaching it to California’s youth.

CCAPM volunteers are bringing the magical music of mariachi to children by performing and teaching mariachi in local schools. They are also creating sheet music and teaching materials that schools and other organizations can use to teach mariachi. For advanced students, CCAPM offers an Honors Mariachi Music Program, which lets students study and perform with professional mariachi musicians.

CCAPM hopes to train young people in the art of authentic mariachi, while also teaching music history, discipline and the joy of performing. Performing mariachi bands traditionally include trumpets, accordion, violins and vihuelas (small five-string guitars). Performers are handsomely outfitted in colorful costumes decorated with detailed embroidery, shiny buttons and wide-brimmed sombreros. CCAPM students and their families are enjoying their participation in this rich slice of Mexican heritage.

Since CCAPM began, children’s interest in mariachi has skyrocketed. A few years ago, there were only two youth mariachi bands found in California’s Central Valley, and now there are about 20. CCAPM hopes to spread the love of mariachi not just across California, but across the United States and beyond!

title: Taking Notes in Class
text:
Learning how to take good notes in class is very important.

Taking notes in class can be difficult. Sometimes it’s hard to concentrate and you can miss some information. Or you can’t read what you wrote. Other times, you’re not sure what information to write down. It’s important to learn how to take good notes. Without notes, taking tests is much harder! Here are some ways to take good notes in class.

Be ready. You don’t always need to have a pen in hand, but have your notebook open to a clean page. And have a pen or pencil nearby. When the teacher enters the room, you’re ready to begin.

Put the date and topic on top of the page. Knowing when you took the notes will help you study for tests. You can quickly flip through the pages and find the topic.

Don’t waste time writing what you already know. Notes help you remember what you learned in class. If you’re sure you know something, then don’t write it down. Let’s say you know George Washington was the first U.S. president. You don’t need to write it down. Instead, you can focus on his birth date, where he lived and what he did.

Make lists. Lists are easy to recognize and read. They organize the information. If you can make a list, you’ll likely remember the information later.

Remember, note taking will improve your learning. But your notes won’t make much sense if your eyes are always glued to the paper. Take some time to really listen to your teacher. Stop every now and then to listen and to watch your teacher. Write down the examples that are written on the board. By doing this, you’re sure to have success in class!

title: Make an Astrolabe
text:
During his historic voyage, Christopher Columbus used simple instruments and his knowledge of the sun and stars to guide him. Follow these steps and you will be able to determine your latitude in the same way.

Materials

protractor

rectangular piece of

cardboard or index

card big enough for the

protractor to be traced on

string (about 10 inches)

drinking straw

metal washer or paper clip

tape or glue, scissors

fine-point marker

atlas or globe

Directions

Lay the straight edge of the protractor against one edge of the cardboard. Trace the semi-circle edge and cut out the cardboard along this curved line.

With the protractor as a guide, mark and number the degrees shown. Also, mark the vertex.

Tie one end of the string to the middle of the drinking straw. Use the tape or glue to hold it.

Tie the other end around the washer or paper clip.

Glue the straw just above the 90-degree marks with the string over the vertex.

On a clear night, take your astrolabe outside. Face north. (The sun sets on your left if you are facing north.) Find the Big Dipper and use the two stars farthest from the handle. They point to the last star in the Little Dipper’s handle. This is Polaris.

Look at Polaris through the straw. Try not to move anything and put your thumb over the weight (paper clip or washer) as it hangs. Go inside where it is light and read the number. Look on the globe or map to find your latitude. What do you notice about your astrolabe reading and your latitude?

title: Making Connections
text:
Think of the term making connections as if you were building a bridge. At one end of the bridge is the known. You already know some things about the subject. At the other end is the new. You don't know everything about the subject. Now let's pretend you are the bridge. Your goal is to use yourself to bridge the gap between the known and the new.

Read this paragraph and follow the instructions:

Almost everyone agrees there's nothing better tasting than a good old hamburger. Especially those you make at home. Different people like different toppings. Some like cheese, onion, pickles, bacon and tomatoes. Others like lettuce, ketchup, and mustard. There are other ways to make that hamburger even yummier. Just add things to the meat itself. You can do this before forming the meat into patties and frying it. Try some new ideas. Worcestershire sauce and grated onion make a zippy burger. Try a splash of soy sauce, powdered ginger and a little brown sugar for teriyaki burgers. You can also put in feta cheese, minced garlic and some Italian herbs. This adds a Mediterranean twist to your meat. Don't be shy—try them all!

Did you read anything that sounded familiar? (Almost everyone likes homemade hamburgers.) That's the known.

Did you read anything you hadn't heard before? (The taste of hamburgers can be changed by adding ingredients to the meat before frying.) That's called the new.

You become the bridge between the known and the new. You are making connections by relating information you already know about the subject to what you're reading.
