title: Let’s Learn About Maryland This Year!
text:
Welcome to Maryland Studies Weekly! Hang on tight for a terrific ride as we explore our state from top to bottom, start to finish, inside, outside, upside and downside. We'll climb the highest hills, drop into the deepest valleys and coast along the highways and byways of the grandest state in the union. We'll learn about our state's roots, our explorers, our legends and our leaders. But the people who really make our state great are the ordinary, everyday people- including kids like you! Together, we'll discover how you are an important part of our state and can develop your own Maryland pride.

How to Use Maryland Studies Weekly:

Each issue of Maryland Studies Weekly has lots of interesting articles. Our cover article gives you a head start on the week's history lesson found inside. The front page will also have a current event about important things happening in our state or around the world today. Every week you can find answers to common questions in the "This Week's Question." Our wildlife section will have lots of information about the flora and fauna in our state. "American Character" teaches important traits you should develop. There's even an arts and crafts section that will show you how to do some fun activities. Plus there's lots more!

So let's get started. Turn the page and jump right in. You'll have a great time this year.

title: Philanthropy and Values
text:
Maybe you have heard the word "philanthropy" before. What does it mean? It describes actions that people make for the good of other people. What is a value? It's a way of behaving that people believe is good - like believing it's good to be honest. Is honesty one of your values?

One way you can practice philanthropy today is to help yourself and others learn good values. How do you learn good values? You can learn them from your parents and grandparents, your teachers at school or church and other people you trust.

You can also learn them from people that have been recognized for doing good things for society. An easy way to learn about people that have done good things is to visit values.com. Values.com has lots of stories and short videos that highlight the traits that make each of us better people. They even have billboards on the highway to remind you about good values.

For example, you may have seen a billboard that looks like the one shown here.

This billboard is about Oral Lee Brown, who saved money from her job to send nineteen kids to college...all by herself! Wow! Isn't that cool? You can learn about lots of other people who practice philanthropy at values.com. Be sure to look for more of their "billboards" on Page 4 of Studies Weekly this year. We think they're so cool we want to remind you to check them out!

title: Did You Know?
text:
You have probably seen Maryland's colorful flag. But have you heard about the special connection it has to Sir George Calvert, the first Lord Baltimore? Calvert wanted to start a settlement in Maryland and made a request for the land. Unfortunately Calvert died two months before England granted the request in 1632. Two years later his son, Cecil, named and established the colony and became the second Lord Baltimore.

In 1904, Maryland adopted its colorful flag in honor of George Calvert and his family. It includes a coat of arms, or family symbol, for each side of Calvert's family. The black and gold sections represent the Crosslands (his mother's side), and the white and red sections represent the Calverts (his father's side).

title: Maryland Regions
text:
Where in the world are we? Before we can study Maryland history, we need to know a little about the place where we live.

Where in the World is Maryland?

The world is a big place! To better understand and describe where we live, we can think of the world as divided into parts. These parts are called hemispheres because imaginary lines divide our sphere (or globe) into halves. (Hemi means "half.") If you imagine a piece of string wrapped around our world from left to right, you would have a top half and a bottom half. An imaginary line called the equator does just that - the top half is called the Northern Hemisphere, and the bottom half is called the Southern Hemisphere. Now, imagine a string wrapped around the world from top to bottom. That line is called the prime meridian, and it divides the world into halves called the Eastern Hemisphere and Western Hemisphere. Can you figure out where Maryland is? Here's a clue: It is north of the equator and west of the prime meridian.

Baltimore City and Baltimore County?

We Marylanders keep everyone else in the United States stumped by having both a city and a county go by the same name. Well, that part's not actually so unusual; lots of states name their county seats after their counties - take York, Pennsylvania, for example. What is unusual, though, is that Baltimore City is not even in Baltimore County. In fact, it's not in any county! Baltimore City is an independent, or self-governing, city, meaning the mayor and city council make all the governing decisions.

Where are Maryland's Dinosaurs?

Most of North America's dinosaur fossils have been discovered in the Utah/Colorado/Wyoming area. But, believe it or not, Maryland has its own Dinosaur Alley! A C-shaped line of fossils curving from Cecil to Prince George's counties shows where Astrodon johnstoni, our official state dinosaur, lived more than 100 million years ago. At 40 feet tall and 60 feet long, and weighing 10 tons, the Astrodon could sure look scary. But it was an herbivore who loved munching the leaves in the treetops with its star-shaped teeth. You can learn more about this guy at the Maryland Science Center in Baltimore.

Counties of Maryland

On this map of Maryland counties, find your county. Color it red. Color all of the counties that border your county yellow.

Questions About Counties*

1. How many counties are there in Maryland? 24 (including Baltimore City)

2. What is the largest county by population? Montgomery - 972,000

3. What is the largest by square miles? Frederick - 663 square miles

4. What is the smallest by population? Kent - 20,100

5. What is the smallest by square miles? Calvert - 215 square miles

*Population figures from the national census

title: Friendliness
text:
Being friendly can make the difference between a bad day and a good day. If you are friendly to the people around you, you could make pleasant memories from everyday things like driving in a car, riding on a bus or even taking a walk in your neighborhood. Most people like being around others who are friendly and make them feel comfortable.

Of course, some people choose to be unfriendly most of the time. But why would you want to do that? Have you ever heard someone say, "I just love coming over for a visit. You're all so nice and grumpy"? Probably not. Most people like it more when you are friendly and welcoming.

Maryland is home to some of the friendliest people around. Make friendliness one of your character traits, and anyone who visits you will go away feeling upbeat and happy.

title: Map & Globe Making
text:
Before the 1400s, there weren't many attempts to make maps. However, by the late 1400s, a German merchant and navigator named Martin Behaim produced a globe that showed the world as Europeans knew it before Columbus' voyage. It didn't have the Americas on it because they hadn't been discovered yet; however, people knew that the world was a sphere (round).

During the 1600s and 1700s, the colonization of the New World created a need for a large number of new maps. The Spanish surveyed and mapped the lands that were under their control. English Captain John Smith published a map of Virginia's coastline and New England. Samuel de Champlain of France mapped the area of Maryland to the St. Lawrence River in Canada.

title: What do we mean by Old World and New World?
text: The eastern half of the world is usually called the Old World and includes Europe, Africa and Asia. It's called the Old World because we have written histories from people who lived in those areas first. The western half of the world is often called the New World. When people from the Old World began exploring for a better route to India, they found us - North America and South America! In their writings, they referred to these newly discovered lands as a new world.

title: Opossum
text:
If you are in Maryland's central region, you may see the opossum everywhere you look - in marshlands, forests, farmland and even residential areas. This animal is gray with a long, pointed nose and doesn't have hair on its ears or tail. Its tail is prehensile, which means it can wrap around objects like tree branches.

The opossum has quite a list of favorite snacks. It includes grasshoppers, caterpillars, mice, frogs, snakes, corn, acorns, blackberries and cherries. Sound good?

Female opossums give birth to one or two litters of babies a year. Each litter could have up to 17 babies. But here's the most unusual part - the babies are born as embryos, an early stage in the growth process. They are only about a half inch long. The babies nurse for about three months until they can survive on their own.

Have you heard someone say "playing 'possum"? Well that means playing dead and is how opposums stay safe from predators. When a predator is near, an opossum will roll onto its side, open its eyes and stare straight ahead. The predator thinks the opossum is already dead and goes away hungry. Pretty clever huh?

title: Milk Carton Log Cabin
text:
Build your own log cabin out of a milk carton!

Materials

Half-gallon waxed-paper milk or juice carton, emptied

Grease pencil

Scissors

Cardboard

Glue

Waxed-paper scraps

Pretzel sticks

Cheerios or pasta

Acrylic paint

Water

Water container

Paper towels

Ruler

Instructions

1. Measure three inches down the side of the carton. At three inches, draw a line around the entire carton with a grease pencil.

2. Cut along the line and separate the top from the bottom. Discard the bottom. You will use the top.

3. Draw the outline of the door and windows with a grease pencil.

4. Cut out the windows and door. If they are too small for scissors, ask your teacher to use an X-acto knife and help you. You can leave one side of the door attached and fold it out so that it opens and closes.

5. Glue a piece of waxed paper over the inside of each window.

6. Glue the cabin to a cardboard base that is slightly bigger than the cabin. Let the pieces dry before proceeding.

7. Glue pretzel sticks along the base of the carton walls and build up. If necessary, cut the pretzels to fit around the door and windows.

8. Glue a stack of Cheerios or pasta together as a chimney. Glue this on the roof of the cabin.

9. Cover the roof with pretzels or acrylic paint.

Note: Watercolor and tempera paint will not stay on the waxed carton.

title: How Do I Use the Library?
text:
Use the Library’s Catalogs

The best way to find books in the library is to use its card or computer catalog system. Find out what your library has and try it out.

Card Catalog

A card catalog is a filing system where book information is stored on cards in drawers. They are organized alphabetically based on the information at the top of the card.

Card catalogs contain three cards for each book: author, title and subject cards. Each card contains the call number for a book, which is how you find it.

If you wanted to find some books on dinosaurs, you would go to the “D” drawer and look for “dinosaurs.” Read the cards to decide which books would help you the most. Find the book’s call number in the upper left-hand corner of the card and write it down. A book on dinosaurs might have the call number 560.2. So, you would go to the part of the library where the 500 Science books are and look for 560.2.

Try It!

Use your library’s card catalog to find books on dinosaurs.

1. Find the drawer you need based on the topic you are researching. Write the letter(s) for that drawer.

2. Look for cards that match your topic. Read them to decide which books would be most useful.

3. Write down the call numbers for those books.

4. Find the section where your books are located based on the call numbers. Get the books you have selected and check them out.

Computer Catalog

While some schools still have a card catalog, other schools (and most public libraries) have replaced it with a computer system. To find materials with a computer catalog, you type keywords into the catalog system and do a search. If you type the word “dinosaur,” the computer will bring up all the books with “dinosaur” in the title or subject description. If the list is too long, be more specific by searching on, for example, “Jurassic dinosaur,” or “meat-eating dinosaur.”

Try It!

Use your library’s computer catalog to find books on dinosaurs.

1. Type the keyword for your topic into the catalog’s search field. Write the word you typed.

2. If too many books came up, narrow the search by adding keywords to the search field. Write the new series of words you typed.

3. Read the descriptions to decide which books would help you the most. Write down the call numbers for those books.:

4. Find the section where your books are located based on the call numbers. Get the books you have selected and check them out.

title: Unscramble Your Neighbors
text: Unscramble your neighbors and write the answers below.

title: Maryland: America in Miniature
text: Maybe you've heard our state called the Old Line State or the Free State. Well, another Maryland nickname is "America in Miniature." A miniature is a small copy. For example, a doll house is a miniature because it looks just like a real house - only much smaller. Maryland is also a miniature because it has almost everything our whole country has - and it's just a small state! In fact, even though Maryland is the 19th-largest state in terms of population, with 5,773,552 people, it is the 42nd largest in terms of size (12,407 square miles). Think of it like this: If you walked across America from east to west, you would start at the Atlantic Ocean, travel through some flatlands and then hit the Rocky Mountains. Your hike would probably take almost a whole year. If you walked across Maryland from east to west, you would start at the Atlantic Ocean, travel through some flatlands and then hit the Appalachian Mountains. Even if you took the longest route possible (238 miles), your hike would still only take you a few days. And even though the tallest mountain in our state - Backbone Mountain - is only 3,360 feet above sea level, it's still a mountain! Besides, look at all the other cool stuff we've got: beaches, marshes, hills, fields, forests, small streams, big rivers, farms, factories, big cities and small towns - all wrapped up into one package. You are lucky to be able to say, "I'm proud to be a Marylander," and "I'm proud to be an American."

title: The Living American Flag
text:
The American flag is a symbol of our country's heritage. Today the American Flag Foundation works to teach students about unity, patriotism and the importance of our flag.

Have you ever heard of a "living" flag? This is made up of people standing together, wearing our flag's colors, to form a large, living American flag. The first one was put together on Defenders' Day in 1914 to mark the 100th anniversary of Baltimore's victory in the War of 1812. It also marked the birth of our national anthem, "The Star-Spangled Banner."

About 6,500 school children helped make the first human American flag. The children wore red, white or blue hooded jackets and stood side by side, forming the shape of a flag. They were also each given a matching handkerchief to wave. This made the flag look like it was waving in the breeze.

Maryland school children have helped form another living American flag every year since 1983. Now they hold red, white or blue squares, and the flag is photographed from the air. Some kids get to hold one of the stars. Being a part of this experience helps children feel that they are a part of history and gives the flag a more personal meaning.

Each spring, the Living American Flag Committee travels to selected schools around the nation. It helps third, fourth and fifth grade students learn about our American Flag. Learn more about the program at www.americanflagfoundation.org.

title: Maryland’s Physical Regions
text:
A region is an area set apart from others because it is so different. Our state has three landform regions. Each has its own unique land features like flat terrain, hills and valleys or forested mountains.

That's One Big Place!

What's the biggest place you've ever visited? Disney World? The Grand Canyon? Some scientists believe there was once a place on the Earth bigger than any place you've ever been. We're talking bigger than Annapolis, bigger than Maryland, even bigger than all of North America! This huge place was called Pangaea, which means "worldwide land." Imagine being able to travel over all the world's land without getting into a boat or a jet! What happened to this giant continent? Over millions of years, the land broke up into sections and moved over the face of the planet to become the continents we know today. You may have visited some pretty big places, but you'll never visit a place as totally huge as Pangaea. Don't feel bad, though, because nobody ever visited Pangaea. Scientists believe the "worldwide land" broke up into continents millions of years before people ever lived on Earth.

States on Plates

What would the world look like with no water? If you had a machine that could suck up all of the world's oceans, you would see that the continents are resting on top of huge landmasses called tectonic plates. These plates are all touching each other under the oceans. The world is changing every day, little by little, as these huge plates rub against each other. When two plates start rubbing, earthquakes suddenly happen! We always think "California" when we hear "earthquake." But, earthquakes happen everywhere in the world - even in Maryland. That is how our planet gradually changes over time. Hey, California, we're "all shook up," too!

Appalachian Region

This area covers almost the entire western half of Maryland. Coal, natural gas and lumber are some of the natural resources the mountains provide. Because of the beautiful landscape, many Marylanders come here to relax. Camp David is also in this region.

Piedmont Plateau Region

Most Marylanders live in this area, which covers the central part of our state. The rolling land is very good for growing grains, fruits and vegetables. But large cities, including Baltimore, are here too. Factories, stores and offices keep this a busy region!

Atlantic Coastal Plain Region

The name of this region says it all: It's next to the Atlantic, it's made up mostly of coastline (31 miles along the Atlantic and an amazing 3,190 miles along the Chesapeake Bay), and the rest of the land is a flat plain. Annapolis, our state capital, lies in the central part of this region.

title: Recreational Regions
text: In our history lesson, we learned about Maryland's landform regions. But Maryland can also be divided into recreational regions- areas where there are cool, fun things to do and see. You can think of our state as made up of four parts: Western Maryland, Central Maryland, Southern Maryland and the Eastern Shore. Western Maryland lines up pretty well with the Appalachian Region, Central Maryland with the Piedmont Plateau, and Southern Maryland and the Eastern Shore with the Atlantic Coastal Plain. Because these regions differ in terms of the "lay of the land," people in Western Maryland have fun in ways very different from people along the Eastern Shore. But make no mistake- all Marylanders know how to have fun! Join us this year as we discover together what makes "America in Miniature" so exciting.

title: Why do we have seasons?
text: Seasons are periods of time when the Earth warms up (spring and summer) and cools off (fall and winter). This cycle occurs because the Earth's axis is slightly tilted. In the summer, our spinning Earth's Northern Hemisphere is closer to the sun than the Southern Hemisphere. In the winter, the Northern Hemisphere is farther away. This heating-cooling cycle creates changes in our weather. It gets colder outside. Trees become dormant (sleepy), drop their leaves and rest for a season. Snow or rain may fall in places that are normally very dry. Days are shorter, and nights are longer. Just imagine: If the Earth's axis were not tilted, we would have the same season all of the time!

title: Barred Owl
text:
The barred owl is just one of the wild animals living in our state. You can even find some of these animals at Maryland's Patuxent Wildlife Research Center, where scientists from around the world study how to protect our nation's wildlife.

This bird was named for the brown and white bars across its chest.

Barred owls love wet areas and deep woods. They eat rodents, small mammals, birds, frogs, insects and even skunks - their sense of smell is not so good! Most owls have yellow eyes, but the barred owl has dark-brown eyes. Like most owls, the barred owl can see very well both at night and during the day. A special inner eyelid filters out sunlight. Also, having both eyes in the front of their heads (rather than on the sides like most birds) allows them to have excellent depth perception. In order to see sideways, owls simply turn their heads almost all the way around. Did you know that if you wanted to see as well as an owl, your eyes would have to be the size of softballs?

title: William Penn and the Pennsylvania Quakers
text:
William Penn spent less than five years in America, but he had a big impact on American history. His ethics (standards, values and principles) - especially his beliefs about freedom - had lasting effects on American democracy.

Penn was born in London in 1644. He was well educated and became interested in a religious group called the Society of Friends, or Quakers. They believed in equal rights for all and would not bow, remove their hats or take an oath to royalty.

Although Penn was raised in the Church of England, he agreed with the Quaker beliefs. He insisted on going to jail with his Quaker friends saying, "My prison shall be my grave before I will budge a jot; for I owe my conscience to no mortal man."

Some Quakers moved to America, but the Puritans in Massachusetts did not want them in their colony. King Charles II gave William Penn a land grant for territory in America to repay a debt owed to Penn's father. The colony was named Pennsylvania (Penn's Woods) in honor of William's father. Penn designed a city there named Philadelphia, meaning "city of brotherly love."

Penn wrote a constitution called "The Frame of Government." It guaranteed freedom of religion, trial by jury, fair taxes and many other liberties we take for granted today. Penn also established peaceful relations with the American Indians, buying land from them and writing successful peace treaties.

William Penn spent a lot of time in England, and he died there in 1718. He only lived in his colony for four years, but his ethics influenced Americans for generations to come. How might your life have been different without William Penn's constitution and the liberties he stood for?

title: How Do I Read a Map?
text:
Maps can tell you a whole lot about the world. They show you which direction to travel and how to find an unknown place. But wouldn’t you like to know how high the mountains are around you? And just where are those lakes and railroads? If you want to know all that and more, maps are for you!

These map functions will help you read a map:

Scale — On a map you’ll often see: 1 inch = 1 mile. That means 1 inch on the map represents 1 mile of the land around you. Easy, huh?

Legend — What do those little pictures or symbols on a map mean? The legend is a box, usually in a corner of the map. It lists the symbols, then tells what they mean.

Grid — Many maps are arranged on a grid. See the lines going up and down the sides of the map? There are more lines at the top and bottom. Those grid lines help you locate places on the map. Grids have letters along the sides and numbers across the top and bottom.

Index — To use the grid to find a location, go to the map’s index. The index lists locations with a letter and a number for each location. Find the spot on the map where that letter and number cross. For example: House — D, 9

title: Adventure on the Potomac
text:
My name is Patawomeck. I am 10 years old. My father is the chief of our small Piscataway tribe. We have remained friendly with the white people and have taught them many things about surviving in this world. But European sicknesses have changed the great nation we once were, and our tribe only has a few members left.

As a small child, I learned that I was named for a great river west of here. It forms the boundary between what the white settlers call Maryland and Virginia. I am very excited because my family is finally taking a trip down the river like I have always dreamed of.

We put our canoes in the Potomac where it bends from flowing southeast to flowing directly south. My father calls this the narrowest neck of land between the Chesapeake Bay and the river. We cannot enter the river any farther north than this point, for the northern tribe - the Susquehannock - is our bitter enemy.

Our journey begins, and we paddle south for most of the day. From the lead canoe, my father cries, "The corner lies just ahead!" We follow the river as it turns directly west and passes through many sharp curves until it widens to double its size. My arms were tired from paddling, and I'm grateful the water calmed.

In the evening, we pull our canoes to shore. Wawasee, my dog, runs after my father and brothers to hunt wild turkey. Mother and I set up camp and haul the water needed for cooking. Supper included tochawhoughe - my favorite! Mother cooks this plant from the river's edge quite well - which is an art, because it can be poisonous if it's not cooked properly. We also have turtle soup and dried strawberries, all washed down with sassafras tea. I will sleep well, for my muscles are tired, and my stomach is full.

The next day, I wake to the smell of delicious corn cakes. After breakfast, we are back on the river. We will complete our journey today. We continue south and see a few settlements and white-faced children playing. I wonder if we play the same kinds of games. The river bends, then curves sharply, then narrows. My canoe speeds almost uncontrollably down the river. I work to keep it straight and follow my father. We are now traveling southeast. We see whippoorwills and sea gulls so we know we are near the bay.

I point out to my brothers river birches, maples and my favorite, the majestic white oak. Grandmother has taught me well and says I have the "eagle eye" of the Piscataway. This trip on the river has helped a lot too. Our journey will soon end when we reach St. Mary's City, but I will always remember the wonderful time I had. Most important, I am proud to have traveled this river for which I was named.

title: Maryland’s Waterways
text:
How Did We Get the Chesapeake Bay?

If you lived 15,000 years ago, your home might have been almost in the middle of the Chesapeake Bay! Of course, it wouldn't have been covered by water. That's because back then, the bay was no more than a river valley. The Susquehanna River used to flow all the way to the ocean. Then, at the end of our last ice age, melting glaciers flooded the river, forming an estuary, or place where the ocean's salt water mixes with the river's fresh water. The river flooded so much that the valley almost disappeared entirely. Fortunately for us beach bums, we still have the Eastern Shore and Delmarva Peninsula. We can swim, fish, boat and water-ski in the 200-mile-long bay. We can eat crabs, oysters, clams and mussels. More than 10,000 fishermen earn their living on the bay. Even the name "Chesepiooc" means "Great Shellfish Bay" in the Powhatan language.

What Good is Water?

No one would ever deny that water has some important uses; just ask any farmer, sailor or thirsty kid. Or ask a fish! Let's not forget that water is great for pure, clean fun! Maryland is full of ways to use water.

Keeping a Clean Chesapeake

We love our Chesapeake! So we need to care for and be respectful of our bay. Here are some ways you can help:

1. Conserve water: Take a "sea shower" like sailors do while at sea - get wet, turn off the water, soap up and rinse off! When we use too much water, too many chemicals are used to clean up our wastewater before it goes back into the bay.

2. Don't pollute: this is obviously a no-no, but even throwing too much stuff in the garbage overflows our landfills, which can then leak pollutants into our water.

3. Turn off those lights: When we use too much electricity, power plants produce more pollution.

4. Talk about it: Ask your parents to plant a tree. See if your brother could ride his bike to work instead of driving. Even take a walk in the park with a friend - the more you know about nature, the better you'll take care of it! For more ideas on how you can help, check out the Chesapeake Bay Foundation's website, www.cbf.org, and then click on Act.

Know Your Rivers

There are more than 50 rivers in Maryland. Here is a map of some of Maryland's rivers. Unscramble the names below, and then put the letter next to the correct name.

title: Central Maryland
text: The best way to learn about Maryland's waterways is to have fun! A good place to start is at the Riverfest in Laurel. On the banks of the Patuxent River, you can eat great food, take a guided nature walk, ride on a hay wagon or tour the Laurel Museum. And the admission is free! If you want to visit lots of places in one day, try Ed Kane's Water Taxi. Park the car for the day and take the blue and white water bus around to all your favorite places like Harborplace, the Maryland Science Center, the National Aquarium and Fell's Point. Another great choice in Baltimore City is Port Discovery, one of America's largest children's museums. Many of you already know about the three-story tree house, the kids' TV studio and the Egyptian expeditions. Finally, for all you ship builders, don't miss the U.S. Naval Academy Museum in Annapolis. Look for the ships made out of meat bones - you won't believe your eyes!

title: Is quicksand really dangerous?
text: Quicksand may look like regular sand but it sure doesn't act like it! If you step onto a sandy beach, you don't sink, do you? If you step onto quicksand, you will sink pretty quickly (hence the name). But don't worry, quicksand that sucks you under, never to be seen again, only exists in movies. In fact, quicksand rarely shows up in North America at all. Where it does, it's only a few inches deep. Even if you fell in, you wouldn't drown in it because quicksand is so dense (denser even than salt water) that you would actually float in it. Underground springs bubbling up into a sandy surface create the unusual sand/water mix we call quicksand. It does cause problems if solid ground is out of reach, but if you do happen to step in some, don't panic. Just roll to your back and float to the edge.

title: Canada Goose
text: When people speak of "wild geese," it's usually these familiar birds they have in mind. Look for them near almost any open water or marshland. We also commonly see and hear their flocks honking overhead in spring and fall. They are pretty easy to spot with their black heads, long necks and white throats. Canada geese mate for life, and the family group remains together for several months after hatching the young. A gander (male goose) protecting the nest is something you don't want to tangle with. His wings can deliver a surprisingly forceful blow— enough to knock down a human! But Canada geese are getting more used to being around humans. Some even nest in city parks. They are especially noticeable in late summer and early fall when they are molting (losing their feathers). Around November, most of these beautiful birds leave Maryland and head to Mexico. But many spend the winter at Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge in our own Dorchester County.

title: Make a Rain Gauge
text:
Materials

a plastic bottle

scissors

bricks

a ruler

1. Ask an adult to help you cut the top half off the bottle.

2. Put it back on upside down.

3. Stand your rain gauge outside. Put bricks around it to hold it steady.

4. Each time it rains, measure how much rain has fallen.

title: How Do I Manage My Time?
text:
Feeling stressed? Not sure if you’ll have time to do all your homework? To keep up with your studies and have fun learning, you need to learn to manage your time. Here are some ideas for managing your time:

Assignment Book

Find a small notebook (so that you can carry it around) to keep a list of your assignments. Write down each assignment as you get it, the class, the due date, the pages you need to read, the length of your paper and any other important facts. Review the day’s assignments before going home and make sure you have all the materials to complete them. When the assignment is done, check it off.

Checklist

When you have a big project that requires many steps, like a science project, research paper or presentation, it might be a good idea to use a checklist. That way, you know you’ve done everything you needed to. First, think of your final goal. Then, think about the steps you will need to take to reach that goal. How long will each step take? Finally, write down (your assignment notebook is a great place) the steps and the date that each should be completed. Be sure to list the steps in the order you will need to do them. And it’s never a bad idea to leave a couple extra days at the end in case some steps take longer than expected.

Reading Methods

There are many reading methods you can use to read effectively. We will discuss some of them in the future. Once you find one that you like, use it! You need to know what information is important and be able to take notes on it. If you are reading long stretches of text, take many breaks so that you do not get information overload. But make the breaks short enough that you don’t forget what you just read.

Study Schedule

Think about what time of day you do your best work. Is it in the morning before you go to school? After school in the afternoon? After dinner in the evening? Before bedtime? Pick a study schedule that works for you and stick to it. Choose a place that is quiet and free from distractions. If this is when and where you do your best work, then you will do a good job on your homework!

Try these time-management tools and use those that work for you. As you practice them, you will improve your study skills. And you will be forming good habits for your future schooling, college and work experience.

title: Damaging Droughts
text:
Have you ever thought of your life without food? Probably not. You can pretty easily go to the grocery store and buy a bag of chips or go to the gas station for a hot dog. But what would you do if the weather suddenly limited what foods you could eat?

Between 1930 and 1932, Maryland and the District of Columbia experienced their worst agricultural drought ever. There was 40 percent less rainfall than usual, and the estimated crop losses exceeded $40 million. Crops could not grow without rain, so many farmers lost their crops. Other droughts have happened more recently in Maryland, too.

Droughts are very damaging. The ground can become so dry that even if it does rain, the water just runs off it and can even lead to floods. The land can become barren and infertile so that it can't be used in the future.

Another thing a drought does is use up our water sources. During a drought, the supplies we have slowly diminish, and we often have laws to keep us from using too much water. A good habit to always practice is water conservation. Don't let the sink run when you brush your teeth. Turn it off while you brush and then turn it back on to rinse. Ask your parents if they can attach a water valve to your showerhead that you can turn off and on while you are showering. There are many different ways to control your usage of water. After all, you don't want to miss out on some of your favorite foods, do you?

title: Weather - It Matters
text:
What is Weather?

Weather is made up of:

1. Temperature - how hot or cold the air is

2. Precipitation - moisture (rain, snow, sleet or hail) that falls to the Earth (Take a look at the precipitation map on Page 4)

3. Wind - movement of air from high- to low-pressure areas

Foolproof Weather Test

Here's a simple test to tell what the weather's up to, and you can do it right now with this newspaper! Go on and take your newspaper outside. Stand there for a few minutes, holding your newspaper in front of you. Is the paper wet? If so, it's raining. Is the paper warm and dry? If so, the sun's probably shining. Is the paper moving around? It's windy. Is there white stuff on the paper? It's probably snowing. (Ha! Ha!) If you'd rather stay inside, just check out your favorite weather forecaster on the news!

Maryland's "Tornado Alley"

Most people think of the Midwest when they hear "Tornado Alley" (Oklahoma, Kansas and Nebraska). Here in Maryland, some scientists think the area between the Appalachians and the upper Eastern Shore is also particularly vulnerable to strong winds. Tornadoes form when cool, dry air collides with warm, moist air. The violent updraft creates a whirlwind. So, watch out! West Virginia's cool, dry air colliding with the Atlantic's warm, moist air provides the right ingredients for whipping up one whopper of a storm.

Is It Climate or Weather?

Pretend you're lying on your back on your lawn, watching the clouds above. What a great way to spend a lazy summer day. Suddenly, a brisk wind comes up, the sky turns dark, and you feel big, warm drops of water on your face. Help! The lazy summer day has been taken over by a cloudburst. The term weather refers to rain, snow, heat, cold, etc. It changes from hour to hour, day to day and month to month. The term climate, on the other hand, describes the kind of weather a particular area has year after year. Alaska, for instance, has a much different climate than Hawaii. We think of Alaska's climate as freezing, snowy and very cold. We think of Hawaii's climate as balmy, sunny and pleasant. Maryland's climate is altogether different. Climatologists call our state "temperate," meaning our climate is not terribly hot (like Hawaii) or terribly cold (like Alaska). We live somewhere in the middle of these two extremes.

I Want to Be a Weather Person!

The man or woman standing by the weather map on television isn't just any person off the street with a pretty face. These people have studied long and hard to get their degrees in meteorology, and they help us know what to do when the weather changes. Here are a couple of good weather-related words for you to know:

Meteorologist - a scientist who studies atmosphere, weather and weather forecasting

Climatologist - a scientist who studies climate and its many changes

Now, here's some homework: Why is a meteorologist a meteorologist and not a "weather-ologist"? Is it hard to become one of these scientists? Do some research and report to your class!

Hurricane Safety

The Maryland Emergency Management Agency (MEMA) says hurricanes don't come to our state very often. But recent examples, like Hurricane Isabel in 2003 and Hurricane Irene in 2011, helped cause a lot of damage to coastal areas like Ocean City. No matter where you live, there are some things you can do before or during a hurricane to stay safe.

1. Put together a disaster supply kit that has water, food and first-aid.

2. Keep trees and shrubs trimmed.

3. Listen to the radio or watch television for official weather information.

4. Follow instructions given by emergency officials.

5. Stay away from windows and doors, close all inside doors and block all outside doors.

6. Most important of all - stay inside! You are safer in your house than outside, where flying debris can hit you!

title: Loyalty
text:
Are you a sports fan? Do you have a favorite team? I bet you jump and scream with joy when they win a game! What about when they lose? Does it make you gloomy? Chances are that you still say they're the best team ever, and you go back cheering even louder for their next game. That's called loyalty, and loyalty is a character trait that is what good kids are all about! It's cool to be loyal to your favorite team or even your favorite TV show, but it's much more important to be loyal to your family and friends.

It's easy to love the people around you when everything's going great, but what about when they make mistakes? Do you stick by them through thick and thin? If you do, I bet they're thankful. Your loyalty will help them tough out the rough times and celebrate the good times.

title: Check Your Onions
text: Have you ever heard someone say about another person, "He really knows his onions"? This folksy compliment usually suggests that a person is smart and organized and has everything under control. The saying's origin is unclear, but one possible explanation might come from an old way of forecasting weather. In some parts of France, the interval between Christmas Day and January 6 was called "The Days of Fate." During these 12 days (also known as the Twelve Days of Christmas), French farmers used to follow a ritual to determine what the weather would be for the coming year. On Christmas Day, 12 onions were placed in a row, with a pinch of salt placed on top of each. Each onion stood for a month, the first one being January, the second one February, and so on. On January 6, the farmer checked all the onions. If the salt on any of the onions had melted, that meant that the month it represented would be a wet month. So if the fourth onion's salt melted, that meant that April would be a pretty rainy month. If the salt was still there, then April would probably be sunny. Like most folk traditions, forecasting the weather with onions might be worth trying just for fun. If you want accuracy, though, you would probably do just as well by guessing!

title: What is humidity?
text: Humidity is a measure of how much water there is in the air around us. If humidity is high (in other words, if there's a lot of moisture in the air), hot days seem hotter, and cold days seem colder. Why is that? The answer is actually a pretty simple one. Have you ever jumped into an 80-degree swimming pool on an 80-degree afternoon? Before you jumped in, the air probably felt nice and warm, but the pool might have surprised you for a moment with a burst of cold before you got accustomed to the water. That's because the more dense whatever you're moving around in is, the more you feel it! Water is denser than air, and so when you're in water, you feel its heat or cold more than if there's just air around you. Now, walking around Maryland isn't exactly like jumping into a swimming pool, and humid air isn't exactly the same as water, but since humid air is still more dense than dry air, you can rest assured that in Maryland humidity makes the heat feel hotter and the cold feel colder.

title: Bald Eagle
text: Ever wonder why the bald eagle isn't bald? During colonial times, the word "bald" meant white, not hairless. These majestic, white-headed birds were a common sight in the 1700s. Scientists estimate that there were more than 1 million in existence at that time. Now there are only about 70,000 bald eagles found throughout the United States; half of them are in Alaska. After nearly becoming extinct (no longer existing) during the 1960s, bald eagles are making a slow comeback. We are learning to use pesticides and other chemicals more cautiously, so the eagles are beginning to once again nest in areas around our state. They select high places to build their stick nests, and eaglets build their nests in the same area as their parents, who stay faithful to each other for their lifetimes. Many bald eagles do not migrate. They're real homebodies! Stories of eagles swooping down and carrying off babies and livestock are just that - stories. They can't carry anything heavier than 4 pounds. This bird became part of our national emblem in 1782.

title: Tornado Classification
text:
On Page 2 we learned that Maryland has its own "Tornado Alley." Let's read on to learn how tornadoes are classified and what kind of damage they might cause.

F0: (winds less than 73 mph) This type of tornado would only cause light damage. It might damage chimneys, break branches off trees, push over small trees or damage signs.

F1: (winds from 73 to 112 mph) This type of tornado would cause moderate damage. It might peel up the surface of roofs, push mobile homes off their foundation or blow moving cars off the road.

F2: (winds 113 to 157 mph) With higher winds, this type of tornado causes considerable damage. It might tear roofs off frame houses, demolish mobile homes, overturn boxcars, snap or uproot large trees or lift cars off the ground.

F3: (winds 158 to 206 mph) Now causing severe damage, this type of tornado may tear off roofs and walls of well-constructed homes, overturn whole trains, uproot most trees in a forest and lift up and throw heavy cars.

F4: (winds 207 to 260 mph) This type of tornado would cause devastating damage. It would level off well-constructed houses, blow away any structure with a weak foundation, throw cars and create other large missiles.

F5: (winds 261 to 318 mph) With the highest wind speed, this type of tornado would cause incredible damage. It may sweep away houses with strong frames, make cars fly through the air for more than 100 meters, debark trees and even badly damage steel structures.

(Information courtesy of the National Weather Service)

title: Help a Rat and Learn to Run the Country This Year!
text:
Hey, kids! I’m Revere the Rat, but you can call me Rev. I’m your online Studies Weekly friend and I need your help. You can help me get great stuff by earning points while you learn. Just scan the code or go to www.studiesweekly.com and click on my picture.

Has your family ever bought something that came with an owner’s manual? Cars, TVs and other things have an owner’s manual, a book on how to use them. Your social studies class is the “owner’s manual” for the United States of America. You’ll learn about history, geography, government by the people, and much more, so you can do a good job of running our country someday.

In America rats can’t vote, so “you the people” govern (run) the country. Someday you will be in charge of this country, and you’ll choose leaders and representatives by voting. Then you can tell the representatives you help elect how you think the country should be run. In fact, Studies Weekly kids are so smart, that many of you will someday be mayors, senators, governors— maybe even the president!

For now you have two jobs: Learn about the country and how it works and earn points for me so I can get that great stuff I told you about. It’s easy. Just scan or click and you’re on your way!

title: Weather Watch
text:
By scanning the sky for colors and other clues, people have tried to predict the weather since time began. Test these bits of ancient meteorology to see if they are really true.

1. A rose red sunset means fair skies are coming (“Red sky at night, sailors delight, red sky at morning, sailors take warning!”)

2. A pale yellow sunset means rain is on the way.

3. An evening rainbow predicts fair weather.

4. A morning rainbow in the west means rain.

5. A pre-dawn copper colored sky in the east means rain.

6. When the moon hangs in halo, there will be rain, especially if the halo is far from the moon.

title: Across the Icy Bridge
text:
More than 100 centuries ago, a small band of fur-clad hunters rested on the shores of a continent we now call Asia. The hunters were starving and very anxious to provide food for their children. They had wandered very far from their home.

The wild game that they hunted did not pause to rest. They continued eastward over a narrow strip of icy land to a far-off, unknown destination. The hunters, getting more desperate, kept up the chase. The animals continued southeast in their constant search of grazing land and to escape the hunters' spears. After many weeks, both the hunters and the hunted came to a halt. The lush, grassy valleys they stumbled into startled everyone. The hunters decided that these lovely lands would be a new home for their families.

Not realizing it, these ice age Asians had begun a whole new civilization and culture. Today, we call them Paleo Indians. "Paleo" means "ancient." They were among the first to travel from Asia to North America by an icy land route later named Beringia (named for Vitus Bering, a Danish explorer in the 1700s). At the end of the ice age, melting glaciers flooded the land. Thousands of years would pass before the great-great-great-grandchildren of the earliest Americans would travel south across a land later called Canada and a giant lake we call Michigan, and then down into the area now known as the Mid-Atlantic Seaboard. But travel they did, and eventually they became the Nanticoke, Piscataway, Shawnee and all the other American Indians of Maryland!

title: Ancient Rock Art
text:
When you were younger, did you ever get in trouble for drawing on your bedroom walls? Well, a long, long time ago people did draw on their walls - the walls of their caves. They even carved pictures right into the rock (don't try this at home)! Rock art from ancient people is scattered all over the United States. Archaeologists call drawings and paintings pictographs, from the word "picture." They call the carvings petroglyphs, a big word that comes from two smaller words: petro, meaning "rock," and glyph, meaning "carved symbol." Both types of art told of the events of the day and often included names of tribespeople. What was this art used for? Most archaeologists think the art helped the tribes record their history. Pictures of bison, weapons and humans seem to show what the natives were most concerned with: hunting food and surviving. Some archaeologists even think the pictures may have been used as a sort of target practice, helping the Indians know the best way to aim at their prey.

Petroglyphs are hard to find in Maryland because sites of ancient villages have been built on or made into quarries and mines. Some pictures have been spotted, though, around the northern tip of the Chesapeake Bay and in some underground caves around Calvert Cliffs. To make your own pictographs, ask your mom or dad for a piece of sandpaper (about 8 1/2 inches x 11inches). Decide on a simple drawing, maybe of an animal or just a design. Using bright crayons, draw your design right on the sandpaper. Press hard! Does it feel like you are drawing on a cave wall?

title: Early Marylanders
text:
For the next three weeks, we'll be learning about Maryland's native inhabitants. This week, let's take an overall look at the earliest Marylanders.

The Paleo Indians: (12,000-8000 B.C.)

When the first people arrived in Maryland, the land was very different from what it is today. The Paleo Indians hunted giant animals and were always on the move. Their main tools were spears and atlatls.

Mammoths and Mastodons

When the first people arrived around 12,000 B.C., the land was very different from the Maryland we know today. There was more rainfall. Moist grasslands covered much of the land. The plant life fed many large animals. Some of these animals weighed thousands of pounds. Herds of giant deer, camels, buffalo and mammoths - large, elephant-like animals - grazed on the plains. Mastodons, which also looked like elephants, roamed the woodlands. They used their trunks to reach for leaves and tear off tree bark. The Paleo Indians were big-game hunters. Because their lives depended on meat from wandering animals, these small bands of hunters were nomadic, meaning "always on the move." Their shelters, made of animal skins, could be set up and taken down quickly. At night, the people camped near rivers or streams. During the day, they followed the great herds and hunted. Imagine how hard it was to kill a mammoth! The animal stood as tall as a house and had tusks as long as a pickup truck. They threw stone-tipped spears using an atlatl - a tool that let hunters throw their spears from long distances. To do their job, they had to work as a team. From just one mammoth, a band got enough meat to last for months. Nothing went to waste; they used the hide to make clothing and shelters and the bones for tools and weapons. By 8000 B.C. most mammoths and mastodons had become extinct.

The Atlatl

Ancient Maryland natives hunted with a spear and this tool, named from the Aztec word meaning "spear thrower." No one knows exactly when the atlatl (at-LAT-uhl) was invented, but we know that it was thousands of years before the bow and arrow. We also know that the atlatl was used longer than any other weapon yet invented (even to the present). How did it work? Put simply, it made the spear spring forward. Just like a bow pushes an arrow through the air, the atlatl helped the hunter push the spear harder and farther.

The Archaic Indians: (8000-1000 B.C.)

By the time the Archaic Indians were around, the giant mammoths and mastodons were extinct. They instead hunted smaller game. They also came up with new inventions that helped their lifestyle.

The Great Bison

Nearly 30 million bison once roamed North America. The eastern bison, now extinct, provided ancient Marylanders with food, hides and bones to make weapons, tools and jewelry. Bison (also called buffalo) were the largest land animals on our continent. They weighed about 2,000 pounds (1 ton). American Indians still greatly respect this creature. An entire group of tribes - the Buffalo Nation - honor the animal each spring with a celebration of singing, dancing and storytelling.

Basket Makers

The Archaic people started gathering berries and shellfish along the Chesapeake Bay (about 5000 B.C.). They found that they needed somewhere to keep this food. So they invented good, strong containers. They also invented nets to catch fish and birds.

The Bow and Arrow

Around 1500 B.C., the Archaic people started using the bow and arrow. Sometimes American Indians disguised themselves in deerskins so they could get closer to their prey. The bow and arrow allowed hunters to hunt from even greater distances than the atlatl allowed.

title: The Moon in Myth
text:
To the people living long ago, the moon was a god or goddess of special mystery and power.

Not only did the moon outshine the other nighttime lights, but it changed its shape and had its own strange motion in the sky. There were visible markings on the moon that fascinated people on every land for thousands of years.

Some said the markings were a rabbit; some said they resembled a frog. Other people said the markings were a human face - A Man in the Moon.

In Scandinavia, however, there was no Man-in-the-Moon but instead two children and they were carrying between them a pail of water. Little of the myth remains except an old nursery rhyme:

Jack and Jill Went up the hill To fetch a pail of water...

Once, long before this myth became nursery rhyme, this story may have helped people remember how through the month the moon waxes (gets larger) to the full moon then wanes (gets smaller) to the new moon and increases to full again. You see, Jack gets his name from the Scandinavian word "jakka" - to increase, and Jill's name comes from "joila" - to dissolve.

Take this article with you on the next full moon and see if you can find the above markings.

title: Central Maryland
text: Our native Marylanders loved and respected nature. You can also learn to love Mother Earth by visiting some of these area attractions. (Plus, they're really fun, too!) Maryland is a beautiful state with many natural resources, parks and scenic sites to visit. Let's start in Frederick County at the Catoctin Mountain Orchard in Thurmont. Enjoy the taste of fresh strawberries, blackberries, raspberries and cherries. Best of all, you know that they're fresh, because you pick them yourself! In the fall, treat yourself to half a dozen different varieties of apples - all of them taste great. Down in Rockville in Montgomery County, don't miss Cabin John Regional Park, 500 acres of picnicking, nature hikes, tennis and even iceskating. More than half an acre of this park is dedicated to Action Playground, an obstacle course with tire bridges, slides and tunnels designed for kids ages 1 to 100. Also in Montgomery County, the Silver Spring Acorn (right) has the most unusual picnic gazebo ever. Find out why you can eat under an acorn and how Silver Spring got its name. Head on up toward Baltimore, and you will find Larriland Farms near Lisbon. Experience life during a simpler time with pick-your-own fruits, cut-your-own Christmas trees, campfire circles and hayrides. Get out and see Maryland!

title: Should we say “Native American” or “American Indian”?
text: Some individuals and some entire tribes of Native Americans prefer to be called American Indians. Others are offended by the name Indian because the name was a mistake Christopher Columbus made when he sailed to America and thought he had reached India. It is now considered correct to use the terms Native American or American Indian. Indigenous people is another term. Many people just want to be called by their tribal names. It is best to ask each person and use the term they prefer.

title: Wood Duck
text: One of the most beautiful birds in Maryland is the wood duck. The wood duck is extremely colorful. The adult male has a pure white throat and fore-neck, but his head is metallic green, violet and purple with two white stripes. His chest is a rich purplish chestnut, his flanks are buff, and his back is a bronze green, metallic maroon, purple and blue. The female is somewhat less spectacular than the male. Areas around her bill, throat and eyes are white. The remainder of the head is gray with a crown and crest of metallic green. Her underside is white. These beautiful birds migrate in October to southern Maryland and to the Gulf of Mexico. They look for food in flooded timberlands or swamps and occasionally in open water. The male, or drake, protects his female and nest from other drakes. The female lays an average of 12 eggs. The drake must be on watch for raccoons, snakes and squirrels that like to eat duck eggs. The female cares for the young for five to six weeks. She will accept younger, displaced ducks into her brood. Be on the lookout for these winged wonders.

title: American Indian Drawings
text:
This issue has a lot of information about the Paleo and Archaic Indian cultures. Pictured here are some samples of prehistoric drawings. Pictures drawn or painted onto rock are called pictographs, and those carved into rock are called petroglyphs. See if you can match the drawing with the word or phrase that most closely describes it. The answers are in the teacher’s materials.

2. Buzzard

title: Building 70-Foot Mounds
text:
How would you like to get your hands dirty and play in the mud? Grab a bucket and a ladder because we're going to explore the mounds of the Adena. These mound builders are mysterious people. But we know a few things about them. For example, they were very intelligent. They had to be smart to build the mounds they did.

The Adena people were believed to have been living in Ohio, West Virginia, Indiana, Kentucky and other present-day states from around 1000 B.C. to A.D. 100. They are believed to be the first people to domesticate plants for food, make pottery and built permanent villages. They did not have a good, strong way of construction, so they had to move ground by using buckets. So the Adena came up with a simple way of burying their dead.

When people would die, they would cremate them, put their ashes in a wooden tomb and bury them. Important people were buried in the flesh and had gifts such as flint, beads, pipes and copper ornaments buried with them.

Because the Earth was so hard to move in just buckets, they would bury people in layers. They buried one and put dirt and rocks on him or her, then buried another. As they buried more, the mounds would grow, even as high as 70 feet! Some mounds were formed in the shape of animals, such as the Great Serpent Mound, which is located near Hillsboro, Ohio and runs 1/4 of a mile long. Archaeologists believe the burial mounds found near the serpent show that the serpent itself was made by the Adena. But no burials have been found in the actual serpent.

There have been many artifacts (ancient cultural items) found in the Chesapeake Bay area, but archaeologists believe they were made in the Ohio Valley area, more than 500 miles away. They still don't know why the Adena people were on the eastern coast.

Though some facts about the Adena are unknown, we can still tell you a little about them. Open the paper and continue reading to learn more about the natives of this period.

title: Digging Inch by Inch
text:
Would you like to be an archaeologist? An archaeologist studies very old things like buildings, bones and tools. Archaeologists try to find out how people lived long ago.

If you were an archaeologist, you might work at the Grave Creek Mound in West Virginia. The Adena Indians made the burial mounds in this park hundreds of years ago. The Adena culture lasted for nearly 600 years, but the only things we know about them today came from what archaeologists found while digging in the grave mounds. For example, archaeologists know what kinds of food the Adena grew and ate. Archaeologists even discovered that the Adena people traveled and traded a great deal. Archaeologists know this because they found items from many different areas in the grave mounds. They found shells from the Gulf of Mexico, copper from the Minnesota area and mica (a sparkly rock) from North Carolina.

When archaeologists are digging, they use the "inch by inch" method. This means that they don't remove large amounts of dirt with shovels or machines, but move the dirt slowly, inch by inch. This means that they use small tools and brushes to move the dirt. They keep very detailed records and maps of everything they find. It takes a long time to do the work that carefully. They are careful because they know that every artifact they find can help us understand what ancient people did and how they lived.

title: Tribes of Maryland
text:
Cornfields, permanent villages and trading goods with neighboring tribes - these were some of the new experiences for our early Maryland natives.

The "Three Sisters"

Maize (corn), beans and squash, often called the "Three Sisters," were the most important foods to all American Indians. These vegetables grew well together because the beans weaved around and up the growing cornstalks, and the squash vines grew between the cornrows instead of weeds. The picture below shows the American Indian Shuffle Dance. A woman carrying the seeds of these vegetables leads a parade of the "Givers of Life" - women holding bread. They shuffle as they move around a cooking pot, rubbing the dirt with their feet to feel close to Mother Earth. This was a dance of deep gratitude.

The Eastern Woodland Indians

Scientists organize American Indian history partly based on the skills or industry among various native cultures. For example, when the Archaic Indians began to plant crops, create jewelry and clay dishes, and build tricky traps to catch fish, their way of life changed so much that modern scientists have a whole different name for them. They call them the Woodland Indians. The Woodland Period lasted 2,000 years, from 1000 B.C. to A.D. 1000. These natives and their families didn't follow herds of animals. Everybody wanted to grow crops and stay in one place for a long time. They were still hunters; but instead of moving the whole tribe wherever the food went, a hunting party left the village for a few days and returned with enough food for everyone. It seemed easier to bring the food to the tribe than to bring the tribe to the food.

Let's Make Moccasins

American Indians wore two kinds of moccasins: hard soled and soft soled. It was quite common for children your age to make moccasins for their elders. Almost all of them were made from soft, tanned animal skins. Many were decorated with beads and porcupine quills.

Wampum

When the white settlers first arrived, they often gave the natives salt, metal cookware or other things from Europe. In return, the American Indians would hand them belts or scarves made of highly polished beads.

The natives seemed to value these beads very highly, so the white people assumed they must be like coins or money. Later, wampum was used as money, but wampum is actually an ancient tradition among American Indians. Men used bone drills to pierce the beads, which were cut out of seashells. The beads were then strung together to make a belt. This was not a belt for holding up your pants, though! A wampum belt showed pictures of agreements, or treaties, between tribes. Beads were usually either white or purple - the more purple beads on the belt, the more important or serious the treaty. Some treaties were so serious, they were called covenants, meaning "solemn promises."

title: The Gift of Corn
text: One spring, a long, long time ago, a chief's son came of age. The chief told the boy that he must leave the village to find the spirit that would guide him through life. He could not eat or drink, and the guiding spirit would come to him in a dream. The boy went into the forest. By evening, he was very hungry, and his mouth was dry from thirst. His thoughts wandered, and he began to dream. He felt the sun on his skin as though it were midday. He opened his eyes and saw a tall stranger standing beside him. It was Corn Spirit. He was wearing a green robe. The spirit spoke. "I bring you a gift from the sun - a gift that you must worship above all others." Corn Spirit told the boy that he must wrestle with him and take from him his green robe. The boy must throw the spirit to the ground, and only then would he receive the gift. If the spirit lost, the boy must place the spirit in the rich soil of the spot where he fell. At the end of the third full moon, his gift would be ready to harvest. The boy was weak from hunger, but he swiftly took hold of Corn Spirit's arms and held tight. They wrestled with each other for three long days. At the end of the third day, the boy felt great strength fill his body. With one big tug, the boy was able to pull the robe from Corn Spirit. The boy followed the directions that the spirit had given him and buried him in the ground. After the third full moon, the boy returned to the spot where he had buried Corn Spirit. Waiting for him was a huge cornstalk with ears of corn ready to harvest. The spirit's gift was indeed great - food from a plant that the American Indians could grow to feed their tribes for many generations to come.

title: What crops did ancient American Indians grow?
text: Way back in 1500 B.C., a wild grass called teosinte grew in Mexico. As this wild grass was cultivated and cross-pollinated, it developed into the sweet corn natives later called maize. Squash and beans also found a place in ancient Maryland as these foods were brought in from neighboring tribes. Eventually, these vegetables were named the "Three Sisters" because they became the basic foods of most American Indian nations.

title: Oysters
text:
Oysters make their homes by attaching themselves to rocks, docks or other hard objects. Catching oysters is not really that hard, especially if you've been keeping an eye on where they live. You just pick them off the rock they're stuck on - kind of like picking corn. However, seafood merchants always wait to go oyster hunting at the right time of year. An easy way to remember when oysters are ready to be gathered for your dinner table is this: any month with an "R" in it is a good time to collect a basketful!

Early Marylanders ate so many oysters there are piles of empty shells, called middens, all around the Chesapeake Bay. Marylanders today still love their oysters. You can eat them fried, on sandwiches, in stew or even raw (just don't chew them)! But oysters are valued for more than just food. Inside an oyster's shell, the mantle, or skin-like membrane, takes lime and calcium particles out of the water and adds them to the hard shell. Sometimes sand flows into the oyster, which can be very painful. To protect himself, the oyster wraps his mantle around the sand grain and covers it with layers of the same lime and calcium he adds to his shell. The result is a small shimmery pearl that grows bigger the longer the oyster lives. Most pearls, while beautiful, are not perfectly round. The really valuable ones are made into expensive necklaces, bracelet, rings or wedding dresses. Oysters may be rather small critters, but we sure are glad so many of them call Maryland home!

title: Rumination and Contemplation: Bacon’s Rebellion
text:
rumination (n): a thought; a pondering

contemplation (n): a deep thought; reflection

Were you ever in a situation where you reacted quickly without thinking the problem through? What happened? Let's look at Bacon's Rebellion in Jamestown, Virginia, in 1676. As you read, think about whether the leaders used rumination and contemplation during the events.

Most people in the Virginia colony were farmers who had to deal with high taxes, low tobacco prices and problems trading with Europe. Hailstorms, floods and hurricanes destroyed many crops, and some American Indian groups attacked plantations.

Governor William Berkeley ignored the farmers' call for help, and a young Englishman stepped forward. Nathaniel Bacon asked for permission to lead the army to drive all Indians out of Virginia. Gov. Berkeley refused. He didn't want to upset the friendly Indians who traded with them. Bacon took a group of volunteer soldiers anyway and led a raid. They attacked American Indians who had not even been part of the earlier attacks.

Gov. Berkeley declared Bacon a rebel guilty of treason, but Bacon gathered almost 500 soldiers and took over Jamestown. They controlled the town from July to September of 1676. When Gov. Berkeley and his army took back control, Bacon was furious. His troops burned Jamestown to the ground.

Suddenly, Bacon got very sick and died. Gov. Berkeley arrested and hanged many of Bacon's men. However, King Charles II of England was not happy with Berkeley and chose a new governor.

Find examples when both leaders acted without rumination and contemplation. What might have been different if they had thought about the situation carefully? Imagine that you were Gov. Berkeley or Nathaniel Bacon. What would you have done differently?

title: How Do I Use a Dictionary?
text:
What does “native” mean? How do you pronounce “shaman”? To find the answers to these and many other questions, grab a dictionary. A dictionary lists and defines words. The dictionary can be a student’s best friend.

Know Your ABCs

The words in a dictionary appear in alphabetical order. At the top of each page, two guidewords show the first and last words on that page. Guidewords help you find the word you need more quickly. For example, the word “tepee” might appear on a page with the guidewords “tension” and “territory” at the top of that page.

Is your word followed by numbers? That means it has more than one definition. Look up the word “native” and see all the definitions for it.

After each word, you will find a letter that stands for a part of speech. For example, n. means “noun,” v. means “verb,” and adj. means “adjective.” Sometimes, one word can have two or more parts of speech. It depends on how it’s used in a sentence. Let’s show this with the word “hunt.” Look it up now in your dictionary.

What is the meaning of “hunt” as a verb? Use “hunt” as a verb in a sentence.

What is the meaning of “hunt” as a noun? Use “hunt” as a noun in a sentence.

title: Tocanum’s Great Adventure
text:
Tocanum is a Nanticoke boy. You may remember that the Nanticoke live along the eastern shore of the Chesapeake Bay. Tocanum has just turned 12 this spring and is now old enough to join the men for his first trip away from the tribe. He is very excited! The other men in his clan will leave the women and children at home and travel to the summer campsite. Here, they set up fish weirs, or traps. One kind of weir is a fence of sticks and brush placed across the mouth of the river. Tocanum knows that in the spring, salmon and other fish swim from the ocean into the bay and then up the river to spawn, or lay their eggs. A hole in the fish weir with a net behind it catches the fish as they swim through. Tocanum's father shows him how to paint his skin for both protection and decoration. Every day, they use grease from animal fat to protect themselves from the weather and insects. The men place hot stones in the sweat house and then pour water over the stones to make steam. Every evening Tocanum goes in for a sweat bath to clean the grease and paint from his body. It is hard to go from the blazing sun into a hut that is even hotter, but he has to prove he's a man.

The next lifesaving skill Tocanum learns is weapon making. His grandfather shows him how Nanticoke men use many different weapons for hunting. They make bows, arrows, clubs, traps and nets out of materials found in the Maryland forests. Arrowheads are made from sharp stone, wood, bone, copper and deer antlers. Tocanum is a very fast learner. He made 17 arrowheads his first day! Soon, he sees the women and children of the tribe off in the distance, traveling up the hill to join the men. They will plant crops and dry the meat and fish the men have caught. They will build wigwam homes from tree bark, bulrushes and other plants. They also build a special wigwam - a sweat house. Tocanum is anxious to show his mother his new skills, but he must not act too excited. After all, he's just spent one whole moon doing what all Nanticoke men do, hasn't he?

title: Please Pass the Sinzibukwud
text:
What tastes good on pancakes, granola, ice cream, fruit and in baked beans? The American Indians called it "sinzibukwud," but we call it maple syrup! Maple syrup is the sap from a sugar maple tree. There are many varieties of maple trees, and they all produce sap, but the sap from sugar maples tastes great!

Sap is juice that moves through the tree like blood moves through us. During the winter when it is cold, the tree stores sap in its trunk. In the spring, sap moves back to the branches and provides nourishment for the leaves. The sap for maple syrup is collected during the last part of winter. It works best to collect it on a warm day after a very cold night. Many tribes who lived in Maryland made maple syrup. When the early American settlers arrived, the American Indians taught them how to tap the maple trees, too. People who make maple syrup now do it very much the same way that the American Indians did it many years ago. A hole is drilled into the trunk of the sugar maple tree. A tube is put in the hole. The sap drips out of the tube and into a bucket. Then the sap is boiled and boiled and boiled. It takes nearly 40 gallons of sap to make one gallon of syrup. It takes a lot of time and work to make maple syrup, but the taste makes it worth the effort.

title: Early Maryland Scene
text:
This week, let's look at the Piscataway and Nanticoke tribes. What was daily life like for them?

Family History

Here in this village, a woman explains the family history to her daughter - but through the father's line only.

Marriage

This young man is explaining to this girl what he will do for her if she agrees to become his wife. In this culture, there wasn't much courtship or ceremony. Marriage was often just an agreement between two people to become man and wife. A man gave a woman an animal bone to show that he would provide for the family. She gave him an ear of corn as a vow that she would grow the crops. Some tribes allowed a man to have two wives as long as the women came from two different clans.

Wigwam

The women were in charge of building their shelters. The wigwams were constructed with thin young trees. They were bent into semi-circles and set into the ground by the men. The bent trees were then covered with available materials. This included birch bark, animal skins, cornhusks and reeds or grasses. They were woven into mats. The cooking was done indoors in the winter time. A hole was left in the roof to allow the smoke to escape.

Learning for Survival

This young girl is watching her mother prepare an animal. It is being prepared for its many uses. Everyone helped in the way of life. "Woman's work" and "men's work" were well defined. There were times for play, but survival was the most important thing in the minds of all tribe members.

Deer, Elk and Moose

Wild game of any size was very useful to American Indians. They were used in every part of the country. They believed the Great Spirits had blessed them with these creatures for their survival. They never killed more than they could eat. The spirit of each animal had special meaning to them. They used all the parts of each animal for many things.The animal was used for food, shelter and clothing. It was also used for tools, toys and decorations.

Corn

This food was a staple of all tribes everywhere. When it was ground, as this woman is doing, it was used in bread, soup, ash cakes and foods for the trail. A favorite way to eat corn was right off the cob or as popcorn, as we do today.

Pottery and Baskets

The American Indian people made pottery from clay. This clay was powdered and mixed with shells, gravel or sand. They used the coil method. This was common to many American Indian cultures. Baskets were constructed mainly of reeds found near streams. They were often very beautiful in addition to being functional.

Canoes

In Maryland, many American Indians built their canoes of the prized birch bark. What if there were no big birch trees? They constructed their canoes of the heavier elm, sycamore or hickory bark. Sometimes they made dugout canoes from logs. The canoes were so well designed that today the design is still used.

Home of the Shaman or Powwow

A spiritual leader is called a "Shaman" or "Powwow." One lived in every village. This man's magic helped him make journeys to the underworld. He went to visit the spirits of those who had died. By going into a trance, a shaman could visit the land of the spirits. He must not accept food from them. If he did, his spirit would be captured and his entranced body on Earth would die. It was the reports of these shaman which convinced the American Indians that there was life after death. The name given to the Great Spirit by the natives was "Manitou."

Visitor

This is a visitor from the Piscataway tribe to a Nanticoke village. The people were peaceful and made all visitors, even white men, feel welcome. Are they speaking some Algonquian language they both know or using the more universal sign language?

Maple Sugar

This man is carrying back to camp the final batch of maple sugar. The tribe made this in the maple groves. This was a great treat. It was well loved by all people.
