A feast will be held soon to celebrate the end of winter. The same methods of sap gathering are used today. It is used to make fine maple syrup and candies.

Bow and Arrow

A wood craft learned from boyhood was bow and arrow making. Bows were made by Eastern Woodlands tribes from springy wood such as shagbark hickory, white ash, cedar or white oak. Even young boys became expert shots and were able to kill a bird in flight at a young age. Their lives depended on how well they could hunt.

Moccasins

This footwear is a true American Indian invention. Styles varied with the tribes, yet, all were soft-soled and came up to the ankles. Depending on the tribe, the tops could be puckered. They may have long side flaps reaching to the ground instead. Many were decorated with flattened porcupine quills. "Moccasin" is an Algonquian word we borrowed into English.

Dogs

These animals were as common among American Indian tribes as they are today. They were used as pets, beasts of burden, sacrifices to Manitou and, under extreme starvation circumstances, as food.

title: Central Maryland
text: For our final look at this region, let's zip ahead in time from early Maryland to now. One of the best places to start is in Harford County at the Ladew Topiary Gardens. Let the gardeners "wow" you with their cute and comical tree sculptures. In the fall, check out Children's Day- a day of activities planned just for you. While you're in Harford County, hop over to Aberdeen, birthplace of record- breaker Cal Ripken Jr. Most Maryland kids already know the Ripkens are from Aberdeen, but did you know that they have built a baseball stadium? Ripken Stadium hosts youth tournaments and other events. The Ripken family loves the state of Maryland! Speaking of baseball, you can't call yourself a Marylander if you don't visit Oriole Park at Camden Yards (right). But don't just go see a game- take a tour of the stadium and learn lots of interesting tidbits. Did you know that the "warehouse" is the longest building east of the Mississippi? If you're up for some nature stuff, head out of the city to Oregon Ridge Park and Nature Center and visit Stubby, the resident pet opossum. If not, maybe you'd rather see the frogs, fish, bees and other fun animals. Have a great time!

title: What is a powwow?
text: Quite simply, a powwow is a meeting. Sometimes, American Indians would get together to talk about important things, like disagreements with other tribes, changes in weather, ways to improve trading or even war. Often a ceremonial dance was performed to invite the Great Spirit to participate in the discussion. Powwows were get-togethers, like parties or family reunions. People could renew old friendships and make new ones. Dances were again performed to invite the Great Spirit to join in the celebration.

title: Do You Have a Nose for Wildlife?
text:
No, we don't mean "Can you smell skunks?" It's easy to get excited about spotting various forms of wildlife in the woods of Maryland. There's so much to see and hear in our state. But developing the ability to identify wildlife by smell is a whole experience in itself. Here are some common forms of plant life for you to look (or sniff) for. They all have pleasant aromas:

1. wild cherry (bark)

2. spice bush (bark)

3. sweet fern (leaves)

4. hemlock (needles)

5. sassafras (bark)

6. wild mint (leaves)

7. sweet cicely (roots)

8. wild garlic (roots)

If you're in an area where picking small sprigs of plants is permitted, try an experiment. Pick some sprigs and take them home. Crush them slightly while they're fresh and put each in a different small paper bag. Make a game of testing your friends and family members to see how close they come to identifying at least eight plants by smell alone. Have additional sprigs in small plastic bags, and learn to identify them by sight as well. Have fun!

title: Why Should I Follow Directions?
text:
Here’s a really good story about why it’s important to always follow directions. Once you read it, you’ll never have trouble following directions again!

One time a teacher handed out a test to her students. It was a long 10-page test. At the end of class, some students thought they did very well. They got most of the questions correct. But nobody passed! After the teacher had graded the tests, she pointed out the directions at the top: “Write your name on the top of page one and hand the test in. Do not complete any of the questions.” You can bet those students wished they had read the directions rather than do the whole 10-page test!

Reading directions carefully can mean the difference between an A and an F in school. It can mean the difference between a delicious pan of muffins and a mess of burnt, yucky dough.

1. Read the directions from beginning to end before you do anything else.

2. Make a list of any material you will need. Gather it up!

3. After you have everything you need, read the directions again carefully. Do you understand every step?

4. Do you still have questions? Ask your teacher, parent or a friend for input.

5. Follow the directions carefully, step by step.

If you follow all these steps, you will do all your assignments correctly. Or your muffins will be delicious!

title: American Indian Sign Language
text: On this page, you will find some authentic American Indian sign language. Nearly all of the American Indian tribes could communicate using this sign language. It enabled them to have councils together. Many times they could work out their problems just with hand signals. Notice that sometimes several signs are used to stand for one word. Try putting some words together and sending messages to your friends across the room!

title: The Big Battle Over Maryland
text:
Did you know that three countries tried to claim Maryland? Each believed its explorer had discovered the land first. Let's take a closer look as three European powers raced to claim Maryland as their own. Your guides, Hank and Bill, will break down exactly what happened.

Hank: John Cabot, who sailed for England, claims he was the first to discover Maryland in 1498. But if you ask officials from France, they say he did not find it and shouldn't be allowed to claim it.

Bill: That's right. France claimed Giovanni da Verrazano saw Maryland first, in 1524. But it's hard to tell if he actually accomplished this.

Hank: Yes, everyone is having a hard time telling who can actually claim the land. But wait - here comes Pedro Menendez de Aviles from Spain. Now he claims Maryland should belong to Spain. Wow, this is becoming quite the battle!

Bill: Spain is being very active in colonizing the New World. England, however, is lagging behind.

Hank: Well, in 1580, the English have already settled Roanoke, Virginia. But they are having a tough time getting supplies because Spain is putting up a strong fight.

Bill: Spain is making things tough, but in 1607, England finally established a colony in Jamestown, Virginia.

Hank: That is an amazing move, Bill. But the American Indians and various illnesses are taking a toll on the Englishmen. They need to send their secret weapon, Captain John Smith, to Jamestown to map out Chesapeake Bay.

Bill: That's what they did, Hank! Plus, John Smith goes back to England to show King Charles I what he accomplished. And the king likes it! You'll have to stay tuned to find out what happens next.

Spain, France and England all claimed parts of Maryland and the surrounding area. Captain John Smith mapped the Chesapeake Bay area. After Maryland's charter was approved, the British sent people over to begin settling the land. On March 25, 1634, they landed on Maryland's shore and celebrated Maryland Day. They traveled and found land by a river called St. Mary's owned by the Yaocomico Indians. On March 27, the English settlers bought the land from them and named it St. Mary's City after the Virgin Mary.

title: Early Maryland Explorers
text:
Native Marylanders never “owned” land. They believed that you couldn’t own something you couldn’t take with you after death. They simply lived here and blended well with nature. The American Indians of Maryland were puzzled, therefore, by the activities of the early Europeans. New Americans thought differently than American Indians.

A Date, a Date, a Very Important Date!

It’s hard to remember dates when you’re studying history. Sometimes, the dates themselves are not as important as the order in which events fall. For example, one reason it is important to know that “’Twas in 1492, Columbus sailed the ocean blue,” is so you know it happened after people crossed the Bering Strait and before John Smith founded Jamestown. We’ve made a sort of timeline here so you can see how things changed over time as the early explorers came to our area. Think about the effects that one explorer’s findings may have had on the next. Ask yourself some questions like, why did Smith take the time to draw a map of the Chesapeake Bay region? Do you think it was important for explorers after him?

1498: John Cabot Sees the Chesapeake Bay from a Distance

Italian explorer working for England

Sailed along the eastern shore, looking for trade routes to Asia

1524: Giovanni da Verrazano Explores the Mouth of the Chesapeake

Italian explorer working for France

Looking for the Northwest Passage to China

1572: Pedro Menendez de Aviles Explores the Entire Bay

Sailor at age 14

Spanish admiral looking for more lands to conquer

1608: John Smith

English captain famous for founding the fi rst American colony at Jamestown, Virginia

First European to thoroughly explore (investigate something unknown) the Chesapeake Bay all the way up to the north end.

Cartographer (professional mapmaker); his map of the Chesapeake Bay was used as a settlers’ guide for decades.

1631: William Claiborne

Virginia’s Secretary of State

Set up a fur trading post on Kent Island

Established the fi rst Colonial settlement in Maryland

1634: Calverts Arrive

Land was granted by English government.

Started Maryland Colony

Permitted all religions to worship in peace

Claiborne’s Rebellion

When the Calverts came on the scene, William Claiborne was not too happy. He had set up his trading post to buy and sell goods with a legal license from England. But when King Charles set up the Calverts’ boundaries, Kent Island was included. So to whom did Kent Island belong? War broke out, and Claiborne lost. He left the island, but returned about 10 years later with some help. This time, he won—but not permanently. In 1657, the Calverts regained the island, and Claiborne returned to live out his days in Virginia.

title: Self-Discipline
text: Self-discipline is probably one of the hardest character traits to achieve. Do you know what it means to have self-discipline? Well, since it has the word "self" in it, you know that it has to do with something you do yourself. No one can have self-discipline for you. Self-discipline is being able to control your thoughts and actions in a way that helps you be a better person. It means that you'll have the control to do your homework even when your friends come and ask you to play a great game of ball outside. It means you'll go to bed on time even though there's a movie on that you really wanted to watch. Or it's when you've had three chocolate frogs already, but there are still a couple left. You'll have the strength to say, "I've had enough tonight. I'll save those for later!" You need self-discipline in just about everything you do, including eating, sleeping, at school and at home - you name it! It's a great thing to have. By having it, you'll keep yourself healthy, strong and always doing what's best for you in the end. Self-discipline is just one of the many character traits that make people in our state what they are today - a great bunch of people!

title: From John Smith's Own Account
text:
We couldn't possibly print a paper about Maryland's early explorers without mentioning the story of John Smith and Pocahontas. Many versions of the story abound, and some folks even question whether it happened at all. Read on and see what you think.

John Smith was exploring the Virginia wilderness. His relations with the American Indians were, for the most part, positive. He respected their way of life and was learning much about surviving in this beautiful but sometimes desolate place. On this expedition, however, Smith met up with some unfriendly natives. He tried to communicate his intentions, but went unheard. Powhatan, the American Indian chief, had had enough of the white people encroaching upon this land. Smith was to be an example to all who might follow: Come to America and face death. Powhatan intended to execute Smith. But someone saw something in Smith - something kind and good. Pocahontas, Powhatan's daughter, carefully approached her father about reconsidering. "Does John Smith really have to die?" she asked. Powhatan refused to listen. How could someone as young as Pocahontas understand what this man's death would mean? But she did understand the precious quality of every human life. And when the time came for Smith's execution, Pocahontas placed herself between her father's weapon and Smith's body. Her father saw that Pocahontas would protect this man's life with her own life, and he put down his weapon. Powhatan allowed Smith to return safely to Jamestown. Smith and Pocahontas remained friends, and a few months later, she even warned him of American Indians' plans to attack the settlement.

title: What makes a good place for a city?
text: While there are some new cities, most cities are pretty old. The location of a city depends mostly on what people needed way back when the city was founded. For example, during some of Maryland's wars, people needed safety from their enemies. People built settlements near military forts, mainly for security. When the war ended, people stuck around. Other people built settlements close to water, like on the banks of rivers or natural harbors. And, of course, in more recent history, wherever a railroad ran, sooner or later a city developed. Nowadays, airports and interstate highway systems set the pace for city growth. Towns along Interstate 83, for instance, have grown so much that sometimes you can't tell when you've left one town and gone into another. Some people even believe that in the future, when you drive north from Baltimore to Pennsylvania, it will seem like one big city. Can you think of other things that might make a place good for building a city?

title: Bottlenose Dolphin
text: Those of you who have visited the National Aquarium in Baltimore probably already know all about these intelligent mammals because you've seen them leaping at the dolphin show! They leap as high as 20 feet, clap their "hands," slap their flukes (tails) on the water and click, whistle and squeak their way into your heart. Though fun-loving and playful, bottle-nose dolphins are also very responsible parents. They have their babies every one to three years, keeping them with them for one year. Mothers get help from other female dolphins (we call them "aunties"), so dolphin young are well taken care of. Unfortunately, humans have been less responsible: Pollution and careless fishing have led to these dolphins being on the "vulnerable" list. This means that if our practices don't change, bottle-nose dolphins could become endangered or even extinct. But if we all do our part, we can protect these loveable animals from further harm. To learn fun facts, see a video, hear a recording and even make a postcard, visit www dot nationalgeographic dot com/kids. Another great site is, of course, the National Aquarium's site at www dot aqua dot org.

title: Sharing Public Space: Vitus Bering and Russian Colonies in Alaska
text:
Imagine traveling 6,000 miles over land with supplies for an expedition, and THEN sailing through frigid seas to look for a new world. This was the job given to Vitus Bering, a Danish navigator who sailed for the Russian navy. Peter the Great, czar (ruler) of Russia, asked Bering to explore the eastern coast of Russia. He was wondering if land connected Asia and North America.

Bering's first trip began in 1725. After spending three years getting his supplies to eastern Russia, Bering sailed along the coastline. He didn't see any land to the east, and he didn't realize he was sailing in the narrow passage between Russia and Alaska. This waterway is now called the Bering Strait.

Bering led another expedition in 1741. This time his ship landed on Kayak Island, off the coast of Alaska. They explored some of the Aleutian Islands and met the native people there, the Aleut. He was the first European to arrive in present-day Alaska.

Bering died before returning to Russia, but his voyages paved the way for Russian settlements in North America. Many fur traders came to the area. In 1799 the Russian government established a fur-trading operation in Alaska. Furs from foxes, sea otters and seals were very valuable.

Unfortunately, the Russians took advantage of the native people just as some Europeans had done in settling New England. The Russians took over their lands and forced them to hunt for furs. They also brought new diseases, which killed many natives.

Today, the Aleut people continue to live along the western coast of North America, and their population has grown. What might have been different if the Russians and the Aleut had shared public space fairly? Where in your community is there a debate over public land? How should such debates be handled?

title: Making the World a Kinder Place
text: We sometimes wonder why bad things happen to innocent people. Although we may never understand it, we can do our best to keep things like this from happening in the future. When we do this, we are doing our part to make the world a kinder place, without anger and violence. One way to do this is by making a plan to replace bullying and violence with kindness. The Cool to Be Kind (C2BK) program was developed to help students create programs in their classes and schools that are based on pro-kindness – doing nice things for others. Students look for ways to “pay it forward” each day. Paying it forward means that when someone thanks you for doing something nice, you ask that person to pay it forward by doing something nice for someone else. By paying it forward, kindness continues to spread across the world and people start thinking kinder thoughts and ways that they can help other people. What are some ways you could practice paying it forward? How about doing yard work for an elderly neighbor for free? Or inviting a new student to eat lunch with you and your friends? What about giving up your seat on the bus to someone who looks tired, or helping someone pick up something they have dropped? Thinking kind thoughts and acting on them with acts of kindness is a simple change that you can do to change the world.

title: How Do I Read Charts?
text:
By learning to read charts, you can quickly compare and contrast data.

Use Categories

Charts are lists or boxes of information organized into categories. Categories of information appear across the top and down the left-hand side. And the information in each column shows the hard data for these categories. Charts contain text and often have pictures. When reading a chart, carefully read the title and labels so you interpret the information correctly.

Try It!

1. What categories are covered in this chart?

2. List the tribes covered in this chart.

3. Which tribe is known for its birch-bark canoe?

4. Which tribe wore Mexican-style clothing?

5. How did the Cherokee get their food?

6. Where did the Inuit live?

7. Which tribe lived in a long house?

8. Where did the Algonquians and Iroquois live?

9. Which tribes wore buckskin?

10. Which tribes are known for their basketry?

title: We've Arrived, and We're Alive!
text:
Few children were aboard the Ark and the Dove, the two small sailing ships that arrived in the Colony March 25, 1634. One child was William Browne, only 10 years old, who was a servant indentured to Thomas Cornwallis. If we had William's journal today, it might read something like the following:

Jan. 28, 1634

Today is not much different from yesterday. And tomorrow probably won't be that much different from today. When we first started this voyage, I was excited to travel to a new land. I had heard wonderful stories about the green countryside, sandy beaches and even gold to be found in the place called "America." I'm still looking forward to the day when I will see that land, but after more than a month of sailing and a whole month of being sick, I'm wondering if that day will ever come. Mr. Calvert tries to keep our spirits up, but so many people are sick that he's worried about an epidemic breaking out. We've passed through so many storms that we have all had to stay below deck with the hatches closed for days on end. No one is sure how many of us are really here - I've heard some say around 140. Others say as many as 250. With no fresh air and nothing but salted - sometimes rotten - meat and bread to eat, I'm ready to set my feet firmly on dry land.

Sometime in Late February 1634

I'm losing count of what day it is. We've had a rough time of it. In a storm about a month ago, our ship, the Ark, became separated from our supply ship, the Dove. We all thought we were doomed. Thankfully, we were reunited near some islands in the Sea of the Antilles. Here we stocked up on clean water and fresh supplies. We are on our way again - quite a bit behind schedule - but on our way, nonetheless.

End of March 1634

I thought that this day would never come! We have arrived! When we first sailed into the bay, shouts of gladness arose from every passenger, and then we became silent in awe of this beautiful place. The shores of this land are so heavily wooded that we could see nothing beyond a few feet. We have since explored the land a bit and have been pleased to find the natives quite welcoming. St. Clement's Island (where we are now) is home to a fur trader named Henry Fleet. You can bet we had a heap of questions for him! This island is too small for us, so there is talk of trading with the Yaocomico tribespeople for some land they have closer to the bay. If we do settle there, Mr. Calvert will name the town St. Mary's City - after Mary, the mother of Jesus. Wherever we settle, I am grateful to be alive and feel sure we will prosper in a land we can really call our own. (St. Mary's City became Maryland's first capital.)

title: Back in Time
text:
Leonard Calvert and his family made their first home in St. Mary's, the original capital of the Maryland colony. Today St. Mary's, along with the Calverts' home and 800-acres of land, has been turned into a living history museum. There are lots of interesting things to do and see. Many of the buildings in St. Mary's are replicas, or models made to look the same, of the original buildings that stood here so long ago. Some buildings are actually built on the original foundations. You can also take a tour through the Maryland Dove, a typical coastal trading vessel of the mid-1600s. Visitors can learn a lot about what a 17th-century ship looked like. Next, you can visit a model of a small American Indian village with a long house like the ones the Yaocomicos built.

Historians have learned much about the way the early settlers lived from artifacts found in and around the city. Artifacts are objects that were made by people in the past. Most other places in Maryland have gone through many physical changes over the last 400 years, but St. Mary's has remained much the same as it was when the Calverts first settled here. Visitors to St. Mary's today can learn about the tobacco trade, take a peak at a real archaeological site, watch a militia drill, try their hands at churning butter and even shoot a real bow and arrow. The historic site is located in southern Maryland, about two hours from Washington, D.C.

title: Founding Maryland
text:
How do we keep all those Calverts straight? Let's look at them and some other people involved in the founding of this great place we call Maryland.

George Calvert

George Calvert loved to explore. But what he really loved was freedom - the freedom to worship in peace. King James loved George's loyalty, but could not allow him to stay in England. The king was the head of the Church of England, also called the Anglican Church. But George was a member of the Catholic Church, which was based in Rome, Italy. So the king gave George some land in Ireland and a new title, "Lord Baltimore." George had been interested in America for many years. First he tried to settle Newfoundland, but it was too rocky and cold. Then he tried Virginia, but that land had already been given to the Anglicans. Finally, a new king, King Charles, gave George some land from the Allegheny Mountains to the Delaware River. Unfortunately, Lord Baltimore died before he could see his new land.

Cecilius Calvert

Also known as the second Lord Baltimore, or simply Cecil, Cecilius Calvert inherited his father's (George's) land charter (document stating who can have what land). He named Maryland after the king's wife, Queen Henrietta Maria, and became the Colony's proprietor. Being the proprietor meant he was free to settle the land however he wanted: He made the rules, he chose the settlement's leaders, and he collected the settlers' taxes. He even had the right to give land to whomever he chose. Cecil was a good leader, but many of the landowners did not like the power he had over them. Even though Cecil was the settlement's proprietor for 43 years, he was never able to see his new land. Instead, he sent his younger brother, Leonard, on the Ark to help start the new Colony.

Leonard Calvert

Cecil told Leonard Calvert to do three things. First, Leonard was to make peace with the American Indians. Second, he was to allow the settlers to worship as they chose. In other words, there would be no official church in Maryland. Third, he was to make money! The crops the settlers planted wouldn't just be for themselves, but would be sold for a profit. Leonard became Maryland's first governor.

The Yaocomico

Leonard Calvert gave the natives knives, blankets, jewelry and axes. In return, the American Indians gave Leonard and his group the land along what is now known as the St. Mary's River. The Yaocomicos welcomed the colonists. They needed all the help they could get to defend their land, their families and their way of life against the Susquehannock in the north. They also taught the colonists fishing and hunting and guided them through the forests and marshes along the bay. The colonists and the American Indians got along well together, their villages side by side. In fact, Leonard's settlers ran into more trouble with their fellow Englishmen (remember Claiborne?) than with the natives.

Margaret Brent

Intelligent and strong, Margaret Brent was one of the first women in the New World to own land. Even though she never married, she was considered the head of her household. So, in 1638, Brent arrived in Maryland to claim her land grant. She was very careful with her money and made quite a profit in her tobacco-trade business. Governor Leonard Calvert was so impressed with her that right before he died, he named her the executor of his estate. This means she made sure his money and belongings went to the right people. In a way, this made her America's first female attorney! Feeling she had proven her ability to think and act responsibly, in 1648 Brent asked for the right to vote. She was denied, and in 1651, Brent moved to Virginia.

Indentured Servants

In England, some people were so poor that they could not afford to travel to America. So they signed an indenture, or paper saying that they would work for someone for between four and seven years. In return, their passage to the Colony was paid, they had a place to live and food to eat, and at the end of their service, they were given 50 acres of land.

Many important people came from these humble beginnings. Mathias de Sousa, who was half Portuguese and half African, became a sailor, a fur trader and an interpreter between the English and the American Indians. In 1642, de Sousa was elected to the Maryland Assembly.

Edward H. Nabb, an attorney who lived in Cambridge, Maryland, traced his ancestry back to indentured servants. Today, the Nabb family has become very prominent: The Nabb Research Center for Delmarva History and Culture is named after attorney Nabb.

title: Eastern Shore
text: With so much to do along the eastern shore of the Chesapeake, we'll just plunge in right at the top. Cecil County (named after that famous Calvert) is home to Fair Hills Natural and Environmental Center. Their outdoor-education school teaches students about forestry, wildflowers, bird watching, landscaping and entomology (the study of insects). To learn more about both plants and animals, head on over to the Plumpton Park Zoo (right), the second-largest zoo in Maryland. Who can resist exotic wildlife like Chinese deer, Persian sheep or Burmese pythons? If you're more of the "down-home" type, visit the Kent Museum in Kent County. Here you'll find old-time tractors, threshers, reapers and modern combines. Some are inside the museum, and some are outside - being used! Watch them work their wonders on wheat. For those of you interested in what those old-timers wore, drive down to see Millie Curtis in Talbot County. At her Museum of Costume, she'll probably greet you at the door wearing a ball gown from the 1890s or Mrs. Abraham Lincoln's apron. Finish the day with a beautiful sunset view of Oxford Harbor from the Tred Avon Ferry, one of the oldest ferries in America - in operation since 1683.

title: What is a skipjack?
text: A style of jeans? A playground game? Or maybe a new jump-rope rhyme? Actually, skipjack is a fairly old word, first coined in 1703. It is a small sailboat shaped like a flat "V" with sides that go straight up and down. One of the only places in the country to see them is at the sailboat races in Wicomico County. Every Labor Day weekend, pilots come from all over Maryland to participate in the run through the Tangier Sound. From a distance, these little boats look a bit like fish playing above the surface of the water. In fact, "skipjack" is also a name for a type of tuna known for jumping above the water!

title: Peregrine Falcon
text: If you see one of these flying after its prey, calling "WEE-chew, WEE-chew," watch out! This bird can dive at an incredible 180 miles per hour to catch its dinner. At 15 inches long, with a wingspan of around 40 inches, peregrines are one of the most beautiful birds of prey in our area. While perched, their wings reach all the way to the end of their tails, making them look a little like a man dressed up for his wedding. If you look closely enough, you can even see a black "cap" and white "shirt" (throat and breast). To top the look off, he comes complete with a mustache, too! Don't worry too much about these birds hurting you, though. They actually enjoy being around people. In Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, the arrival of the peregrines is a much-celebrated event. The birds make their nests on the window sills and ledges of the city's tall buildings. For food, the peregrines have plenty of pigeons to choose from. To learn more about the peregrine falcon or play some fun wildlife games, visit the Blackwater Refuge web site at www.friendsofblackwater.org/kids.html. And for a list of Maryland hot spots for bird watching, see https://www.camacdonald.com/birding/birding.htm.

title: Quadrorama
text:
Materials

Four 8-inch by 14-inch pieces of construction paper

Craft materials—construction paper, string, fabric scraps, cotton, markers and crayons

Scissors

Tape

Ruler

Glue

Pencil

Directions

1. Fold the top left corner of a piece of 8x14 construction paper diagonally so that the top edge of the paper is flush with the right edge of the paper.

2. Fold the top righthand corner diagonally so that it touches the lower point of the previous fold.

3. Fold the panel at the bottom to make a horizontal crease along the edge. (Fold it to the back.)

4. Open the paper up and cut along the lower left-hand diagonal crease to the center of the paper.

5. Pull point A over to point B so that the piece you cut is flush with the lower right-hand diagonal crease. Glue the base into place. This is one triorama.

6. When four trioramas are finished, glue them together to form a pyramid. From underneath, tape the four lower panels so that they form four corners. This is now called a quadrorama.

Design the Inside

1. Color and cut out the pictures on Page 4.

2. Glue the scenes inside each triorama.

3. Write a brief paragraph describing the scenes along the bottom fl ap. Make guiding lines by lightly drawing pencil lines after writing the paragraph.

4. You can decorate the scenes using any available craft materials to make the scene three dimensional.

title: Color your Quadrorama
text:
Early American Trades

The colonists could not easily buy their necessary goods and services from England because it was so far away. Many became tradesmen by learning to make their own goods locally. Everything from furniture, metal tools, glassware, cloth and food items were produced locally. It would be fun to make a display of these skilled tradesmen and women to show in your classroom.

A good way to do this is to follow the directions on Page 3 for the quadrarama. When you have made a “quad” as shown, draw or cut out the tradesmen’s pictures that are on this page. Next, color them and mount them with glue onto your quadrarama.

You will want to write about each of the trades so those viewing them will learn something about early colonial America!

title: Father Andrew White: Marylands First Reporter
text:
Born in London in 1579, Father Andrew suffered in both England and America for his beliefs. When the Protestants took over England and persecuted (hurt or killed because of religious beliefs) the Catholics, he risked death by becoming a missionary. In 1606, Father Andrew was banished from England. Staying mostly in France, he joined the Jesuits, or the Society of Jesus, a group of Catholics who worked hard to show others the truth about their religion. Then, in the late 1620s, George Calvert became friends with Father Andrew. This friendship continued with George's sons, Cecil and Leonard. Father Andrew wanted to serve a mission to the New World. So when Leonard set sail with the Ark and the Dove, Father Andrew naturally came too. He wrote down many of his thoughts along the way, and when the ships arrived at St. Clement's on March 25, 1634, he knelt with his companions to give thanks. Here he celebrated the first Catholic Mass held in the Colonies. He immediately fell in love with the land. He writes:

"We cannot set down a foot, but tread on strawberries, raspberries, fallen mulberry vines, acorns, walnuts, sassafras, etc. [The land] abounds with delicate springs, which are our best drink. Birds diversely feathered there are infinite, as eagles, swans, herons, geese, ducks. The place abounds not alone with profit, but also with pleasure."

Father Andrew also fell in love with the people: He wrote an Algonquian dictionary and translated certain scriptures into Algonquian for the Yaocomico. In 1645, Richard Ingle, a Puritan pirate, took over Maryland and shipped Father Andrew back to England in chains. Father Andrew begged to be returned to his "dear Marilanders," but was forced to remain in England where, in 1656, he died.

To see Father Andrew's original diary and read his entries in the original spelling, just type "A Briefe Relation of the Voyage unto Maryland" into your Internet search engine.

title: Respecting Religious Differences
text:
In the past, people often lived in communities with others of the same religion. They went to school, worked and worshiped with the same group of people. Today, most of our communities are made up of people from many different backgrounds, cultures and religions. Often, we live, work and play with people who don't share common religious beliefs. That is why it is important to be tolerant of different religious beliefs, even if we don't agree with them.

Today, many young people have friends with very different religious backgrounds and beliefs. Sometimes, children are invited to be part of special religious events in their friends' lives. At first, this may seem strange and even a little scary. Nicholas, a seventh-grader, was invited to several Jewish bar mitzvahs during the school year. A bar mitzvah is a special celebration held for Jewish boys when they turn 12 years old. The bar mitzvah is held to welcome the young men into the Jewish community. Nicholas, who is Catholic, wasn't sure how to act or what to expect when he was invited to his first bar mitzvah. He and his mother did some research and his mother even called the boy's parents to find out what the event would be like. This made Nicholas more comfortable and showed his friend that he cared enough about him to find out more about his religious beliefs.

Some children are nervous about attending events of a different religion because they are afraid that they will be asked to participate in some way that will go against their own religious beliefs. In most cases, visitors are not asked to be part of the ceremonies. Instead, they should be quiet and respectful while watching others participate. Knowing this makes going to a religious event with a friend less frightening.

Even if you don't agree with all of the religious beliefs of your friends, it is always important to show respect and tolerance for those beliefs. Religious tolerance is one of the most important reasons why Maryland was founded.

title: Religious Rivalries
text:
All this talk about religions can sure get confusing! Keep in mind these two ideas: First, at this time, most people were either Catholic or Protestant (which included the Anglicans, Puritans, Quakers, etc.); second, what happened in England affected what happened in Maryland. England sometimes had Catholic kings, sometimes Protestant kings and sometimes no king. Sometimes even the same king changed from Catholic to Protestant or from Protestant to Catholic! With all these changes in England, something was bound to change in the Colony. Let's see what happened.

What is a Protestant?

Many English Catholics loved their religion, but disagreed with the way their leaders handled things. They believed the priests were too powerful because they did not allow all members to read the Bible. The priests were afraid the common people would not understand the Bible the right way. But the common people believed they had the right to study it out for themselves. So they "protested," or strongly disagreed. They wanted a religion that was based more on what Jesus Christ started when he taught the apostles. These dissenters became known as "Protestants," or those who protest. They really did not intend to start a new church; they just wanted to reform the one they were in. However, many other Catholics disagreed with the Protestants so much that life became difficult for them - the Protestants decided to leave for America. But even in America, Protestants had problems. They did not agree with each other: Some, like the Puritans, believed the Catholic Church needed to be "purified." They were very strict in their customs. Others, like the Lutherans, focused more on following the Scriptures, but allowed people to decide for themselves how to best do that. Sometimes the Protestants argued with the Catholics, and sometimes they argued with each other. Sometimes, these arguments led to bloodshed.

The Toleration Act

Also known as the Act Concerning Religion, the Toleration Act was one of the most important things our early Maryland leaders did, both for our state and for our whole country. It was one of the first acts of religious toleration ever written in the English-speaking world, and it was passed in April of 1649. Written by Catholics, it allowed all Protestants to worship freely: "No person or persons whatsoever within this province . . . professing to believe in Jesus Christ shall from henceforth be any ways troubled . . . in respect of his or her religion." So all Christians, no matter how they practiced their faith, were protected. Unfortunately, those considered non-Christians - like those who practiced Judaism - suffered fines, whippings and even the death penalty. Maryland had come far, but still had a ways to go.

Quitrents: Something Else to Fight About

Quitrents are kind of like taxes. Each settler had to pay the proprietor, Cecil Calvert, two pence for every pound of tobacco grown on his land. Some settlers didn't mind the fee. They believed it was fair payment for using Calvert's land. Others, non-Catholics and Puritans especially, resented the fee. They believed if you cleared land and worked on it, you owned it - not Calvert. He lived in England and didn't do anything to clear, plant, cultivate or harvest the tobacco. The issue of quitrents continued to divide the Catholics and the Protestants, leading to other problems.

Richard Ingle Takes Over

A real-life pirate, Richard Ingle did not like Governor Leonard Calvert. Calvert (a Catholic) had convicted Ingle of piracy in 1642. So to get revenge, Ingle (a Puritan) took control of Maryland in February 1645, while Calvert was away in Virginia. Do you remember William Claiborne? He helped Ingle gain control of the Colony. Ingle demanded that the colonists be loyal to his new Puritan government. Ingle also sent Father Andrew White back to England and allowed Catholic property to be damaged or stolen. Not well-liked by the colonists, Ingle was forced to leave in August 1646 when Calvert returned to Maryland with an army.

Another Sign of Trouble

Around 1640, Sir Thomas Gerard (a Catholic), a wealthy landowner, Lord of St. Clement's and normally a good citizen, stole some Protestant books and the chapel keys from a building in St. Mary's used by both Catholics and Protestants. The theft made little sense because Gerard had earlier donated part of his land at St. Clement's to the Anglican Church (Protestant) to build a chapel. He did this because his own wife, Susanna Snow, was Anglican. Gerard was fined 500 pounds of tobacco, which was later used to pay Maryland's first Protestant minister. Why do you think he did it?

title: Respect
text:
Part of being a happy and powerful person is showing proper respect. When we show respect to something or someone, we show honor.

Let's start with things. What are some things you respect? Do you show respect for the American flag? How about the laws of your country? Do you show respect for your body by not taking drugs or other harmful substances? Name two other things that you can show respect for.

It's important to show common respect for all people. But people tend to honor or show the most respect to those who have done the most for them. This kind of respect comes from love and gratitude - like your respect for a parent, grandparent or teacher who has always been kind and helpful.

How about people who have authority? Do you respect the principal of your school? Policemen? Your mom and dad? We also show respect to heroes. Did you hear about the firefighters who died rushing into the World Trade Center to save others? Do you show respect to true heroes such as the men and women in our armed forces? Name two people you respect.

title: How Can the Bible be that Heavy?
text: Religious rivalries apparently continue beyond the grave. If you read ghost stories, you know that lots of weird things happen in or around churches. One such church in the Pocomoke Forest in Worcester County was so haunted that the townsfolk boarded it up and moved elsewhere. Like most churches, this one had a large, heavy Bible resting on the pulpit. The pastor used this Bible for his sermons. But for some reason, this Bible was destined never to leave the chapel. Many people have tried to remove it, but an odd thing happens: As the person starts walking toward the chapel doors, the Bible becomes heavier and heavier. Finally, overcome by the burden, the person drops the Bible to the floor and is unable to return it to the pulpit. And yet, when the next attempt is made, the Bible is always found back in its resting place at the pulpit!

title: What is the Right of Discovery and Conquest?
text: This means that anyone who discovers a new land or conquers the people living there has the right to own that land. From the 1400s to the 1800s, many explorers sailed to new lands, hoping to find riches, peace or freedom. It cost a lot of money to gather the ships, supplies and crew needed to make these long journeys. Usually companies, or groups of wealthy businessmen, gave money to support exploration. Because these voyages cost so much in time, money and even lives, nations believed this earned them the right to own whatever (or whomever) they discovered. Do explorers today claim this same right? Why or why not?

title: Blue Crab
text: It may seem weird to have a state crustacean, but every year more than 100,000 children used to write to the government asking for information about the blue crab for school projects! So, in 1989, Marylanders decided to make the Maryland blue crab a state symbol. The blue crab's scientific name, Callinectes sapidus, means "beautiful swimmer that is savory" (yummy!). To see how beautiful this crab is, go see the huge stained-glass sculpture on the upper level of BWI Airport. Or, to see real live crabs, check out the annual crab derby held at Crisfield, also known as the Crab Capital of the World. You can learn more about the blue crab's size, colors (yes, there are others besides blue!), places they live and things they eat at skipjack.net and the Maryland Department of Natural Resources web site (www.dnr.state.md.us). But this may be even more interesting: Fishermen have come up with all kinds of strange words to describe their catch. Female crabs are called "sooks"; male crabs are called "jimmies." See if you can find out what these terms mean: "peelers," "pink sign," "busting," "soft shells," "paper shell," "buckram," "hard shell," "sponge crab," "keeper," "doubler" and "picking."

title: How Do I Use a Graph?
text:
Graphs show numbers and then tell what those numbers mean.

Types of Graphs

Bar Graph — Bar graphs use bars of different lengths to give information. The bars can run from left to right across the graph or from the bottom up. You can use a bar graph to show how the numbers compare.

Look at the bar graph about the U.S. population growth.

Pictograph — Pictographs are like bar graphs except they use pictures or symbols instead of bars. This pictograph shows different countries and how much ice cream they eat.

Pie Graph — Pie graphs use a circle to show 100 percent of something. The circle is divided into sections, or slices, of the pie. Each slice gives different information.

Of the population in 2003, what percentage lived in China?

Line Graph — Line graphs show how information changes over time. One line shows units of time. Another line shows the information being measured. Inside the graph you’ll see points that meet. You can use a line graph to see if the information is going up or down.

This line graph shows the number of hurricanes since 1970. Have hurricanes increased or decreased?

title: Bill of Rights Roll Film
text:
Materials

half-gallon milk carton or box

two rods or pencils

long strip of butcher paper 3 inches wide

crayons or markers

tape

pen

scissors

colored paper or contact paper to cover the box

ruler

Directions

1. Prepare your box. Cut the top of the milk carton if that is what you use. Cover the box with construction or contact paper.

2. Make two 3.5-inch slits across the front of your box (horizontally) to let the roll movie pass in and out.

3. Poke holes in the sides for the pencils. Measure to make sure the pencils are straight.

4. Measure the distance between the two slits. This is how big your movie scenes can be.

5. Make a series of pictures (with captions) on the butcher paper, one for each of the 10 amendments listed in the Bill of Rights. (To fi nd a copy of the Bill of Rights, look in an encyclopedia or online.) Make sure each picture fi ts in the size between the two slits (and is not bigger).

6. Tape one end of the paper to the bottom rod or pencil.

7. Roll the bottom pencil until the end is short enough to handle. Slip this end through the slits and tape it to the other rod.

8. Roll the pencils to see your Bill of Rights movie.

Extra Activity: You can make up 10 rights that you think everyone should have. Just make sure you write a caption for each.

title: Create a Graph
text: Create a graph using the data below. First, decide which type of graph would be the best way to present the information. Then create it, using the examples above for help.

title: Joshuas First Day of School: A Letter from 1696
text:
Dear Grandmamma,

I just can't wait! Tomorrow's the big day. Papa is going to take Nathaniel and me to Annapolis to start our first day at King William's School. I know I'm only 10, but I feel so grown up. Nathaniel feels the same way I do, but a little scared. I must admit - I will miss my family back home. I may even miss playing marbles and leapfrog with little Sarah. I feel especially sad about leaving our comfortable schoolhouse and the best teacher on this side of the Alleghenies, Miss Pickering. She has taught me so much about my numbers and letters. I still remember the little rhyme she taught us about the letter "M": "The moon giveth light in the time of the night."

One thing I will certainly not miss is my hornbook!* At King William's, instead of looking at the same piece of paper day after day, we get to use lots and lots of paper - and we can write on it as much as we want! I am also really looking forward to seeing King William's library. You know how I love to read. I will miss hearing Papa's voice reading Bible stories to us while we sit by the fire. But being able to read more than one book - it will seem like heaven! Because I will have so many other books to choose from, I am handing down my New England Primer to Sarah.

Well, I must finish packing and get to bed early, for we will rise early tomorrow morning. I promise I will write to you all about my first day at King William's.

Sincerely,

Joshua

* A hornbook was a flat piece of wood with one sheet of paper glued to it. Because paper was so expensive, a thin see-through layer made from horn covered the paper to protect it. Hornbooks usually contained the alphabet, Roman numerals, and the Ten Commandments or Lord's Prayer.

title: King Williams Free School
text:
King William's "Free" School was not actually "free" at all. Colonists paid taxes to support the school. The term "free" refers to the school's original Latin motto. The Latin translation of the motto is "I make free adults out of children by means of books and balance." A group of Maryland citizens decided that while it was good for children to learn from the Bible, they also needed to learn from the world's greatest authors. They felt that children needed a balance. King William's School worked hard to give all youth, no matter what religion, a good education.

In 1784, the original King William's School became St. John's College. St. John's, located in Annapolis, is the third oldest college in the United States. Four of the founders of the college, William Paca, Charles Carroll, Thomas Stone and Samuel Chase, had signed the Declaration of Independence and they were very interested in building a college that would train fine young citizens of this new country. Today, students from across the country study at St. John's, receiving a balanced education while focusing on books written by the world's greatest authors. Education has always been very important to the people of Maryland and St. John's College continues this tradition today.

title: A Class System
text:
From the late 1600s to the mid-1700s, everyday life in the Colony was, in some ways, not much different from today. People worked, ate their meals and celebrated birthdays just like we do, just in different ways. Let's take a look!

Class, in Colonial Maryland, did not have anything to do with school. If you were rich, you were in the upper class, or gentry. If you were poor, you were in the lower class. If you were somewhere in between, you were in the middle class. Class wasn't really a place you went to, like a classroom; it was a way of defining who you were and what you were allowed to do. Here are some examples:

1. If you are in the gentry, your father owns a large plantation or farm. Or maybe he is a doctor or a lawyer. You live in a large house with beautiful furniture and paintings. You have servants to tidy up your room or drive you around in a carriage. Also, you go to the best schools or have a tutor to teach you at home. You enjoy visiting with your friends and going to see plays.

2. If you are in the middle class, your father owns a small farm or store. Or he works as a blacksmith or shoemaker. Your mother makes candles and soap to sell and helps your father at his work. Your home is not large, but it is comfortable. You help your parents at work and at home, and when you can, you study - mostly from the Bible. Your father can vote and even helps the mayor with some of his duties. Most colonists were in the middle class.

3. If you are in the lower class, both your mother and father work hard in the fields harvesting tobacco. Sometimes, your mother works inside the "big house," serving meals to the owner and his family. Your house has only one room and no windows. You really only use it for sleeping because you are out working in the fields or doing laundry with the other children. You do not know how to read or write. Your parents cannot vote.

Houses

Most Colonial houses had two rooms with a hallway in the middle. Above the rooms were sleeping lofts, usually not tall enough to stand up in, but cozy for bedtime. There were no stairs, just a ladder. A fireplace (sometimes two - one at each end of the house) provided heat for warmth and for cooking. Windows were simply open squares, which could be covered with wooden shutters. Only the gentry could afford glass.

Furniture

A table made of wooden planks, a storage chest, a bench or two and straw-stuffed mattresses were about all the colonists had in their homes. Usually, they just laid their mattresses on the floor when it was time to sleep. Some families made bed frames by stringing rope between boards. This way, they could fit another mattress or bed frame underneath, which they pulled out at night for the children. This was called a trundle bed. Most furniture was similar to the types they had in England, but some colonists made new designs popular. For example, do you know what Benjamin Franklin made by putting curved wooden pieces on the bottoms of chair legs? A rocking chair!

Clothes

Only the very wealthy purchased pre-made clothing. Colonial women used a spinning wheel to make flax or fleece into long threads. Then they wove the threads together to make a large piece of cloth. If they wanted to add color, they used crushed nuts or berries to dye the cloth. Linsey-woolsey, cloth woven from both flax (linen) and fleece (wool), lasted through the long hot summers and chilly winters. Men wore long linen shirts and wool pants called breeches. They were shorter than men's pants today, so they also wore very long stockings called leggings. For shoes, they wore leather shoes and moccasins or even went barefoot (if they were working in the fields). Women wore long, thin dresses called shifts, petticoats and thicker linen or wool dresses - all at the same time, even in the summer! In the winter, they wore hooded capes to keep warm.

Food

Mush, hoecakes, hominy and succotash - do you have any idea what these things are? After the early years, the colonists actually had plenty to eat. Cheese and mush for breakfast, ham stew with turnips and carrots for lunch (the main meal of the day) and buttered bread and cheese for supper made up a typical day's fare. The most important vegetables were corn, beans and squash. For meat, they usually ate pork or chicken; sometimes, after a good hunt, they had turkey or squirrel. They enjoyed apples, pears, berries and all sorts of fruits. To wash it all down, they brewed their own beer or cider, milked a cow or goat or, for special occasions, had some wine imported from England. The colonists very rarely drank water because they were afraid it would make them sick.

Fun

Though early Marylanders worked hard, they also knew how to have fun. One of their favorite pastimes was dancing. You could find colonists doing reels and jigs at local fairs, weddings, holiday celebrations and frolics - parties that combined work and play. Everyone worked together to build a church, for example, and then they had relay races, contests of strength, dancing and lots of food!

title: Eastern Shore
text: One of the most fascinating sights to see in Maryland - the 460-year-old wye oak in Talbot County - no longer stands. On June 5, 2002, a violent storm blew the state tree over. But scientists hope to be able to clone the grand, old oak with some DNA they gathered from the fallen tree. We also have the beautiful Wye Oak Sculpture to remind us of our state tree. Back in 1984, a 70,000-pound limb fell, and sculptor Steven Weitzman carved part of it into two children planting a sapling. Go see the sculpture at Martinak State Park in Caroline County. While you're there, go fishing, rent a boat and play on the playground, or camp overnight in a year-round cabin. If you'd like to learn about one of Maryland's most famous and important people, Harriet Tubman, stop by the Underground Railroad: Harriet Tubman Museum in Dorchester County. You can also visit her birthplace on nearby Green Briar Road. West of Cambridge, you can see an old one-room schoolhouse, a farmhouse, a country store and, best of all, the Spocott Windmill. Originally built in 1850, the windmill was destroyed in a blizzard in 1888. In 1972, builders reconstructed the windmill for people to visit.

title: What is an acre?
text: In the olden days, an acre was the amount of land a yoke of oxen could plow in one day. So what happened if your oxen were young "teenagers" who could plow twice the land that the old oxen could? People finally agreed that the ox thing didn't work and decided to measure an acre differently. Different units of measurement were used then. An acre was measured by surveyors using a standard chain - consisting of 100 links. The chain was 66 feet long. An acre was the area of land one chain by 10 chains, or 66 feet by 660 feet, or 43,560 square feet. Below is an acre (in red) in relation to a football field.

title: Diamondback Terrapin
text:
The diamondback terrapins earned their name from the beautiful diamond shapes on their shells. They have been Maryland's state reptile since 1994 and are the official mascot of the University of Maryland.

These animals have strong, webbed feet. They mostly eat snails, crabs, fish and various plants. The adult males are smaller than females in weight and length. In the winter, these animals hibernate in mud up to 12 feet under water.

Maryland is doing a lot to keep these animals around. The diamondback terrapins were once hunted almost to extinction. Laws now protect them, but there are other threats. Female diamondbacks lay their eggs in sandy beaches. When the beaches disappear, the terrapins disappear too! People are now building houses and stores so close to water that these animals need a little help. Some kids just like you have raised money to help protect the species. Others have raised terrapins and released them into the water.

title: How Can I Be an Active Reader?
text:
To get the most out of what you read, you should be an active reader.

Be Involved

When you are an active reader, you are involved because you think about and respond to what you read. Here are some strategies to use for becoming an active reader.

Ask Questions

Ask yourself questions as you read. What kinds of questions should you ask? Well, any question that comes to mind as you are reading is a good question. But some questions you could ask follow:

-How do I feel about what I am reading?

-Do the characters’ actions make sense to me?

-Do the characters remind me of any people I know?

-Do I understand the events that are happening?

-Could similar things happen to me?

-What do I hope will happen next?

-What would I most like to ask this author?

Read As a Group

Sometimes, you can get a better idea of what to think about a book after talking to someone else about it. Discussion about books can make your reading more interesting because different people have different ideas about the same text. Follow these steps and try forming some discussion groups in your class.

-Assemble a small group of interested readers. Include enough people to make the discussion interesting, but not so many that the group is hard to manage. -Pick a book that you all want to read.

-Allow time for everyone to read it.

-Write down a list of questions and ideas before the meeting.

-Meet to discuss your reactions to the book. Before beginning, pick someone to lead the discussion.

Connect With the Words

Make a connection with what you read, even if you are reading about someone very different from you. Try putting yourself in different characters’ shoes so you will understand why they act the way they do. You can also make a connection with what you read by forming opinions about it.

Respond to Your Text

Keep a response journal where you can write your feelings, ideas, questions, reactions and thoughts about what you read. You can also note facts, copy quotations you liked or talk about passages that you thought were well written.

Try these active reading strategies, and you will get the most out of what you read.

title: Lets Have a Tea Party!
text:
The citizens of the Colonies were angry. England's King George and his Parliament were trying to sneak taxes upon the colonists, which they had been resisting for months. The tax on tea hurt the most - tea was the colonists' favorite beverage. The time was ripe to do something drastic!

Britain's East India Tea Company was almost bankrupt (completely out of money). The owners had lots of tea they couldn't sell. England wanted to help this tea company and at the same time tax the American Colonies. Parliament passed the Tea Act, which allowed the tea company to sell tea directly to the Colonies. Colonists were not allowed to purchase any tea that didn't have the British Parliament seal on the package. The colonists loved their tea, but they didn't like being forced to buy British tea only!

Samuel Adams and his Sons of Liberty proclaimed that the tea importers were "enemies of America" and vowed to stop them. Colonial women organized and refused to buy English tea. They drank coffee instead.

When tea ships arrived in Boston Harbor, the colonists demanded they turn around and go right back to England. The captains refused. It was time for the Sons of Liberty to take action!

On Dec. 16, 1773, that loyal group of patriots disguised themselves as a local tribe of Mohawk Indians. They stealthily boarded the three tea ships. Very quietly, they dumped hundreds of chests of tea into the Boston Harbor.

But Boston wasn't the only place to react against the tea tax. Marylanders were angry too. One man was forced to burn his own ship full of tea from England, rather than pay the tea tax. As the news spread through the Colonies, similar incidents took place in Pennsylvania, New York and South Carolina.

This was the first big act against "Mother England" that would lead to the American Revolution. The colonies were about to become their own Country!

title: Replaying the Revolution
text:
There are lots of ways we can study history. We can read books, watch historical movies or study newspapers from the past. (Reading Maryland Studies Weekly helps too!) Did you know that some people study history by reliving it? The word "re-enact" means "to act out the past." You've already learned about living museums, where people dress, talk and act like the colonists. In a re-enactment, a specific event - like an important battle - is acted out. Using documents like newspapers, diaries, letters and journals, historians put together details of that event. Then, rather than just imagining how the battle might have gone, real people "replay" the battle (without the ammunition, of course).

There are many members of living-history groups in the United States who have fun re-enacting various battles. Re-enactments help us understand how events might have actually taken place. For those of us watching, a re-enactment is like a living textbook right before our eyes! Seeing the sweat on the uniformed soldier's brow, hearing the blast of the old-time muzzleloaders and smelling the food cooking over an open fire sends us back in time. You may even hear the soldiers singing old war songs to lighten their spirits.

Maryland re-enactors from around the state reproduce battles from different wars throughout the year. Many of the battles re-enacted are from the Revolutionary War.

title: Rumors of War
text:
The more England tried to control the colonists, the more the colonists fought for what they believed in: freedom. Read on to find out what events led to that fated "shot heard 'round the world."

The French and Indian War (1754-1763)

It was France and the American Indians against England and the colonists. And it was a war over land: Who should have what? In the end, England and the Colonies won land all the way to the Mississippi River. But the colonists really gained a lot more than land - they gained training for an even bigger war. The French and Indian War was a kind of preview to events yet to come.

September 1774

The French and Indian War had ended. The 13 British Colonies were at peace again. Some of the "redcoats" had gone back to England. Some were still stationed in Annapolis. Maryland had been a Colony for more than 100 years.

March 1775

The British government was beginning to realize that they had big bills to pay. After all, they bought uniforms and food for the war, paid soldiers' salaries and shipped armies from England to the Colonies. What happened next? Let's imagine an interview with a colonist - maybe he can answer some of our questions.

Who is the King, and What Does He Want to Do About His War Debts?

His name is King George III, and he wants to start a tax system here. Naturally, we have to pay for the goods we use and the food we eat. But the king wants to tax us to pay his debts for a war he started! Ridiculous!

But Why Not Pay Taxes?

Taxes help pay for clearing roads, keeping bridges safe, paying government workers . . . those kinds of things, don't they?

Not the way King George wants to do it. Parliament - that's the name for England's government - refuses to let anyone from the Colonies vote on any tax matters. They expect us to give them our money and let them decide how to spend it. With no one to represent us in Parliament, we have no say over how our money is used. We call that "taxation without representation."

What Exactly Does the King Want to Tax?

Pretty much anything we can't make ourselves - sugar, tea, lead, paint and printed materials. And we're still housing and feeding the redcoats in Annapolis too!

What Are You Going to do About It?

We're pretty upset. The people of Annapolis have agreed not to buy any more goods from England until Parliament ends this taxation without representation. You should see us! We're wearing our old clothes, and we've even stopped drinking tea! Our wives have come up with new recipes for other drinks, so we're doing fine.

Do You Think This Will Lead to War?

I'm sure of it. The tea parties caused Parliament to pass a series of laws we're calling the Intolerable Acts. These acts have closed Boston Harbor. Worse yet, King George has sent a military commander to rule in place of our Colonial governor. More troops are on the way. The people of Boston have had to close down their shops and businesses and are literally starving. Maryland citizens have banded together with other Colonies to send food and supplies to Massachusetts. That's one good thing that's come out of all this - we are united.

Have You Heard any Rumors About Organizing an Army?

Oh, definitely. We're gathering guns and ammunition and storing them in the towns of Lexington and Concord. Sam Adams has organized groups called the minutemen. These are men and boys who are trained to leave their farms or shops and, "in a minute," take up arms against England.

April 1775

British General Thomas Gage got the news of guns and ammunition being stored. He sent soldiers to seize the weapons in Concord and capture Sam Adams and John Hancock, who were in Lexington. When the colonists learned that the British were marching toward Lexington, a dedicated silversmith by the name of Paul Revere raced through the night and warned Adams and Hancock. The two leaders fled Lexington just in time.

As the church bells tolled, the town's minutemen gathered on Lexington's village green. About 65 minutemen were waiting for the British when they arrived at Lexington Green at dawn on April 19, 1775. British Major John Pitcairn ordered them to put down their guns. The colonists were terribly outnumbered. Men and boys began to run for home. Then someone fired a shot - no one knows from which side. The British began firing on the minutemen, killing eight and wounding 10.

Because this first shot of the American Revolution changed so many lives and so many boundaries over the next few years, it is often referred to as "the shot heard 'round the world."

Who was Peggy Stewart?

Actually, maybe what we should ask is, what was the Peggy Stewart? It was a tea-toting ship named for Anthony Stewart's daughter. In October of 1774, the Peggy Stewart arrived in Annapolis Harbor carrying 2,000 pounds of tea. Stewart, the ship's owner, planned to pay the British tea tax even though many of his neighbors disapproved. More people found out about his plan and threatened him, demanding he either burn his ship loaded with the tea or be hanged right in his own front yard. Because of his concern for his family's safety, he agreed to burn the ship, but asked if he could unload the tea first. He was refused. The citizens insisted on him running his own ship aground, lighting the torch and burning ship, tea and all to complete destruction. The punishment was harsh, but historians agree that this act, along with similar acts in other Colonies, showed England we really meant business.

title: Responsibility
text:
To be able to respond is to be able to answer, or to be answerable. What does it mean to be "answerable?" It means that we are willing and able to answer, or respond, to our duties. Here's a poem by Joy Allison about three children. Can you guess which one showed responsibility? Which one are you more like?

"I love you, Mother," said little John;

Then, forgetting his work, his cap went on,

And he was off to the garden swing,

And left her the water and wood to bring.

"I love you, Mother," said rosy Nell -

"I love you better than tongue can tell";

Then she teased and pouted full half the day,

Till her mother rejoiced when she went to play.

"I love you, Mother," said little Fan;

"Today I'll help you all I can; How glad I am that school doesn't keep!"

So she rocked the baby till it fell asleep.

Then, stepping softly, she fetched the broom,

And swept the floor and tidied the room;

Busy and happy all day was she, Helpful and happy as a child could be.

"I love you, Mother," again they said,

Three little children going to bed;

How do you think that mother guessed

Which of them really loved her best?

title: The Liberty Tree
text: Have you ever heard of the Liberty Tree? If you have toured any of the historic buildings in Annapolis, then you have probably seen the tree engraved on the Historic Foundation's plaque found at the entrance. During the Revolution, patriots who met to make plans against the British would often gather under a favorite tree in the community - these meeting places became known as "liberty trees." Samuel Chase, a Maryland signer of the Declaration of Independence, conducted his planning meetings under a tulip poplar on the campus of King William's School (which is now St. John's College). That Liberty Tree survived until 1999.

title: What is the Correct Name: England, Britain, Great Britain or United Kingdom?
text: These names are often confused. Britain is an island with three countries: England, Scotland and Wales. In 1707, these three became one that was named Great Britain. When northern Ireland became part of Great Britain, the name was changed to the United Kingdom. The word British applies to anyone from the United Kingdom.

title: Humpback Whale
text: A long time ago, sailors named this whale "humpback" because of the way the animal arches its back as it dives into the water. Another trick is the "spin-and-crash," where the whale leaps up out of the water, spins around and does a "back-flop" that can be heard for miles around. Though only about 50 feet long (medium sized by whale standards), humpbacks eat a ton of food, or 1 million calories, each day! And they do it with no teeth! Instead of teeth, humpbacks use filters called baleen plates to let in only the smaller fish, which they swallow whole. Humpbacks can be seen in all the oceans of the world. They migrate to warm waters to give birth and nurse their calves. In warm water, they also sing songs made up of sound patterns lasting around 20 minutes that they repeat over and over again for about a year. The following year, they make up a new song. Scientists can tell the difference between two similar humpbacks by looking at the tail, or flukes, for different-colored patterns. See if you can spot the differences by looking up more information at www.aqua.org

title: Fact Cubes
text:
Materials

square boxes, milk cartons

solid-color butcher or wrapping paper

tape or glue

crayons or markers

pencils

Instructions

1. Make a cube from a square box of any kind. You can also make a cube by cutting two milk cartons in half and then inserting the open square end of one into the open square end of the other.

2. Cover both cubes with butcher or wrapping paper. If you use wrapping paper, make sure that it isn’t “coated,” or you won’t be able to draw or write on the paper without smearing the ink.

3. Write and illustrate facts about whatever subject that you choose. You could make a fact cube about your favorite animal or sport, or you could choose a subject in school to write about. For example, you could write what you have learned about the Earth from your science class, or you could copy one of your favorite poems you have learned in your English class.

4. Share your fact cube with family and friends and tell them about the facts you chose to write. Have fun!

Extra Activity: To improve your fact cube even more, you could have a parent help you type up the facts on your computer, print them out and paste them on the fact cube. You could also look on the Internet or in magazines to find pictures to print/cut out and paste on your fact cube. Make sure you always have an adult with you when working on the Internet.

title: Mapping & Charting
text:
Physical features are natural parts of the Earth's surface. Human-made features have been built by people to improve their environment.
