Mount Rushmore

Now think about Maryland! Name a physical and human-made feature close to you.

Physical feature

Human-made feature

title: How Can I Be a Critical Reader?
text:
Critical readers carefully examine what they read so they can make informed decisions about it. They might decide if they should believe what they read or if they like what they read.

Examine What You Read

There are many ways to be a critical reader, but they all involve looking at the text and thinking about what you read. Here are some strategies for being a critical reader.

Learn to Separate Fact from Opinion

Writers sometimes present their opinions as facts, so it is important to be able to tell the difference between facts and opinions. How do you tell a fact from an opinion? A fact is a statement that can be proven true. An opinion cannot be proven true in a way that everyone will agree on because it is a belief or judgment. Here are some questions you can ask to help you figure out if something is fact or opinion:

Can this be proven?

Is it generally agreed upon?

Could someone disagree with this?

Is this supported by facts or opinions?

Watch for Faulty Logic

Make sure the writer’s logic makes sense. Do the writer’s arguments make sense? Are they supported by evidence? Here is some faulty logic to watch out for:

Either/Or Thinking—When a writer says there are only two ways to think about a situation, he or she may be engaging in faulty logic. You need to think, “Are there more ways to think about this?” What is faulty about this statement: “No one should drive, or we will have too much pollution.”

Faulty Cause and Effect—When a writer claims that one event leads to another, but doesn’t show any clear connection between the two, then you are reading faulty cause and effect. What is faulty about this statement: “He passed the test because he ate beans.”

Overgeneralization—When the writer makes a statement that goes beyond what the evidence supports, he or she may be engaging in overgeneralization. Use of too many generalizing words such as “all,” “always,” “must,” “never” and “none” could be a sign of overgeneralization. What is faulty about this statement: “My cat likes water, so all cats like water.”

Identify the Writer’s Point of View

The point of view is the set of personal opinions that influence the way the author writes about a subject. You need to be able to recognize the writer’s point of view to figure out how it might have affected the writing.

Take note of sources. Are all the sources from one side of the issue, or are they balanced over many sides of the issue?

Ask what the writer is trying to say. How is this point of view supported? Do you agree with it? Why or why not?

Critical reading can be tough, but if you practice these strategies, you’ll be on your way!
Try these active reading strategies, and you will get the most out of what you read.

title: We Declare Our Independence
text:
You may wonder why we read and write so much about the history of the United States during this time, when the rest of the year we talk about the history of Maryland. There are two reasons. First, if the 13 Colonies had not won independence, there would be no Maryland. The second reason is that Maryland played a major role in supporting the colonists' cause. In fact, four of the signers of the Declaration of Independence were from the great Colony of Maryland.

The Declaration is a famed document known throughout the entire world today, but in the 1770s, there was really nothing like it known to our humble forefathers. Try to imagine Thomas Jefferson, an honest and intelligent young man, sitting up night after night in his candlelit room, struggling over every word of this most important work. He wanted to make England understand how serious we were about being free. He wanted the colonists to sound united, clear and unwavering. Jefferson wanted to declare proudly our desire for independence. He wrote and rewrote. Finally, after more than two weeks, he was finished. On July 2, Jefferson's paper was read to Congress.

Now imagine that you are a member of Congress. You need to decide whether to put your name to Jefferson's paper. You know that doing so shows that you agree that the Colonies should be free to govern themselves. Signing will be considered treason, or betrayal, to Parliament, and the punishment could be death. Our forefathers were brave and unselfish men, willing to face even death for their beliefs. But they were also simple men - fathers, brothers and husbands. Charles Carroll worked hard to prevent British goods from entering the Colonies. He was the only Catholic to sign the Declaration of Independence. About 10 years later, he helped ratify the Constitution in Maryland. At his death in 1832 at 95 years of age, he was the oldest and last of the signers of the Declaration. Samuel Chase was born in a Maryland farmhouse. He fled from Annapolis officials while active in the Sons of Liberty. After the Revolution, he helped Charles Carroll get the Constitution ratified and served as the chief judge in Baltimore County. William Paca traveled a lot, but came home to Maryland when some Marylanders did not support our independence. He successfully changed their minds, and Maryland voted to support Jefferson's document. Though Thomas Stone struggled with his desire to compromise with England and remain a Colony, he eventually supported independence and signed the Declaration. In 1784, he served as president of Congress for one year.

Thanks to these great men and others, the Declaration of Independence was adopted on July 4, 1776. Our new country was about to be born.

title: Signing your "John Hancock"
text:
Have you ever heard the expression, Sign your John Hancock"? It means sign your name, nice and big! That saying comes from the signing of the Declaration of Independence. You see, there really was a man named John Hancock! Here is how a "John Hancock" became the nickname for a signature.

At the Second Continental Congress in 1776, Thomas Jefferson presented the Declaration of Independence for all of the representatives to read and approve. After it was approved, all of the representatives signed it at the bottom.

Signing the Declaration of Independence was serious. It meant you were declaring yourself to be an enemy of Great Britain. There was a reward offered for arresting someone signing the Declaration of Independence. The British troops could arrest you and might even kill you for signing it! Obviously, the signers were very brave.

The first person to sign the Declaration of Independence was John Hancock. Did he sign it in tiny letters or over in a corner somewhere? No! He signed his name with bold, strong writing and even wrote a flourish, or decoration, under his name. In fact, his name is bigger than all the others. As he signed, he said, "The British ministry can read that name without spectacles; let them double their reward." By his words and actions, John Hancock was telling the world that he was not afraid to stand up for America's freedom.

And ever since then, a signature has been nicknamed a "John Hancock."

title: Freedom for Maryland
text:
While no major battles were fought on Maryland soil, many of her citizens gave their all to see freedom. Let's take a look at some of our heroes and heroines of the Revolution.

Mary Katherine Goddard

While being at the battle's front was dangerous work, back here at home, a Baltimore pioneer was fighting a battle too. Mary Katherine Goddard started and became chief editor of the Maryland Journal, Baltimore's first newspaper. She believed that Marylanders should know the truth about what was happening in the war. Some people disagreed with her and even stormed into her office twice, trying to stop her from publishing letters from her readers. She reported on America's desire for freedom and the battles of Concord and Lexington. But she is most famous for publishing the first full copy of the Declaration of Independence that included all the signers' names. She even paid riders to carry copies of the Declaration to all the Colonies. Thanks to Mary Katherine, everyday citizens could read how we declared our independence and rally to the cause of freedom from England's tyranny.

Tench Tilghman

This man was one of the most unselfish, dedicated Revolutionary heroes known throughout Maryland. He was born on Christmas Day, 1744, the first of 12 children: six boys and six girls. He served as George Washington's aide for five years - without asking for any pay! In 1781, Washington rewarded him with a regular paycheck (including what was owed him) calling him his "faithful assistant." At the end of the war, messengers were sent to Congress in Philadelphia bringing news of the British surrender at Yorktown, Virginia. But Congress insisted on waiting to hear the news from Colonel Tilghman himself, for they knew they could trust him to bring the truth. And bring it he did, in full uniform along with his dress sword, which he had worn at Valley Forge. He answered questions they had about the final battle, after which they rewarded him with a horse, a new dress sword and a festival in the streets of Philadelphia in his honor. You can see Colonel Tilghman's swords on display at the State House in Annapolis; they were donated to Maryland by his great-great granddaughter. You can also see one of the swords in the famous painting of him with George Washington and Lafayette.

Tench Tilghman died in 1786, after being married less than three years, leaving his wife, Anna Marie, with two small daughters, Anna and Elizabeth. In a letter to Tench's father, Washington mourned his death by saying, "While living, no man could be more esteemed, and since dead, none more lamented than Colonel Tilghman."

John Shaw

One of the most memorable contributions to the war effort did not involve a battle at all. John Shaw, who made beautiful furniture that can still be seen in the State House today, also made two flags for the revolution. One flew over the State House for the Annapolis Convention, and one flew over the president of the Continental Congress's home. Neither of these flags still exists, but you can see a replica hanging in the State House that was presented by the Daughters of the American Revolution in 1983.

If we don't have the original flags, how could we know what they looked like to make a replica? In 1983, 200 years after the flags flew, old receipts were found at the Maryland State Archives. They turned out to be receipts for the materials Shaw used to make the original flags!

Paris and Its Many Treaties

A treaty is a peace agreement, usually written. You will hear the phrase "Treaty of Paris" often in your study of history. How many Treaties of Paris have there been? Many - but the big years were 1763, 1783, 1856 and 1898.

Why Paris?

France was the economic center of the world for several hundred years. That means most major decisions about trade were made in meetings, or conventions, in the largest western European city - Paris. But the French language was used all over the world. So even treaties that were written in other countries were written in French. Two treaties were important during this time in U.S. history:

Treaty of 1763

After the French and Indian War - which was a branch of the Seven Years' War in Europe - England, France and Spain signed documents agreeing to the following terms:

1. France gives up Canada and all land east of the Mississippi River.

2. England gains all land previously claimed by France.

3. Spain trades Florida for Cuba.

4. Spain gains Louisiana.

England was the big winner in this treaty. Was the country now on its way to becoming a worldwide empire?

Treaty of 1783

Just 20 years later, following the American Revolution, another treaty took place in the French capital. This time, the signers were Great Britain and the new United States of America. The treaty recognized the complete independence of the 13 former Colonies.

Mystery Men

These five men were representatives at the Treaty of Paris from our new country. Just for fun, see if you can match their names to their faces (Answers in Teacher’s Materials):

A. Benjamin Franklin

B. William Franklin (secretary and Ben’s grandson)

C. John Adams

D. John Jay

E. Henry Laurens

title: Eastern Shore
text:
If you get a little overwhelmed by jungle-sized zoos, try the smaller Salisbury Zoological Park. Bring a picnic to share in the shade and see about 400 native Marylanders (in the form of animals, that is). Best of all, admission is free! For those who love to combine their love of animals with their love of art, the Ward Museum of Wildfowl Art shows bird carvings, oil paintings and American Indian art while overlooking a waterfront setting. To learn more about our state boundaries, visit the monument marking the Mason-Dixon Line. Also called the Middle Point Monument because it marks the exact middle of the Delmarva Peninsula, the stone bears the Penn and Calvert families' coats of arms.

In Worcester County, the best part of the Taylor House Museum is Calvin B. Taylor's desk. A wise banker, C. B. Taylor had a special desk made with hidden doors. Find out more by touring the house! At the Assateague Island National Seashore, you can learn to catch crabs and clams, actually touch some marine life or explore the island. But the best part is seeing the Chincoteague ponies. Two herds of wild ponies, one on the Maryland side and one on the Virginia side, live here. Finally, Ocean City may seem like a strange place to visit in the winter, but for the best tree trimming, beach lighting and Christmas decorating around, go to the eastern shore. Don't miss the Christmas parade!

title: Where is the Declaration of Independence?
text: In a bomb shelter? That's right! Our actual Declaration of Independence is behind bulletproof glass in the rotunda of the U.S. Archives in Washington, D.C. Along with the U.S. Constitution and other important documents, our Declaration shares space in a climate-controlled container. Each evening, after visitors leave, the container is lowered into a bombproof vault for protection. These precious documents are copied and spoken of all over the world. We keep the originals safe and sound so our children and grandchildren will be able to see the important writings that make our world what it is today. See photos of the original declaration at the Online Exhibit Hall of the National Archives at www.nara.gov.

title: Maryland's Strangest Creature
text:
Try to guess this most strange of all creatures. It walks about on two legs, but sometimes all fours. It doesn't hibernate, but does prefer to stay in a shelter or den during the winter and will feed at any given time. This creature has a thick, heavy winter coat during the cold seasons that it sheds when spring returns. It doesn't like temperature extremes and is happiest in the warm spring or summer sun.

It bears its young in litters of one, sometimes two, but rarely more. The creature eats both meats and vegetables. It is very crafty and sneaky and is one of the few creatures in Maryland that uses tools. It is not typically nocturnal; however, the older members tend to forage for food and seek companions well after darkness has set in. This creature has assorted skin colors, and the lighter-colored skins tend to darken when exposed to prolonged sunlight. It enjoys water; it lives in communities made up of families; and it is perhaps the smartest living thing in all of Maryland.

So, just what is this strange creature? It is the mysterious and amazing Homo sapien, also known as "rug rat" or sugar-slurping, computer-savvy future maniac behind the wheel of a souped-up sports car: YOU! You are the most sophisticated wildlife our state has ever known - and, hopefully, its greatest friend too!

title: Movie History Book
text:
Materials

scissors

4-inch by 10- inch writing paper

pencil or pen

stapler

glue

crayons or markers

two sheets of 9-inch by 12-inch construction paper for the cover

Instructions

1. Divide a sheet of 9-inch by 12-inch construction paper in half and make two slits in the top half. (Make the slits the same width as the filmstrip pictures on Page 4.)

2. On the 4-inch by 10-inch strips of paper, write about each event that is depicted in the pictures on Page 4. You can get the information from your Studies Weekly, textbook, library or Internet. Your teacher may have some books you can use as resources. Staple the story as shown, making sure you keep the strips in chronological order.

3. Cut out the movie strips from Page 4 and glue them together in chronological order. Color the illustrations.

4. Starting from the back, pull the movie strip up through slit A and down through slit B. (For easy storage of the book, fold back the strip so that it does not extend beyond the page.)

5. Staple the cover at the top and write the title and your name on the front.

title: From Bartering to Dollars and Cents
text:
Bartering is trading goods, but without the use of money. In early cultures, people were able to get many things they needed and wanted through bartering. Merchants would often travel with ships laden with goods. These goods were bartered for items that communities could not produce or grow.

In Jamestown, Captain John Smith wrote about trading blue beads with the native tribes for food. The American Indians valued the glass beads, and the colonists needed food. Colonists were not allowed to make their own coins; they had to use England’s. But there was always a shortage of coins, so people bartered. In Maryland, tobacco was often used as a good for trading. Each Colony set their own rates for trading goods and many had their own paper money. Can you imagine how confusing that got? After the Revolutionary War, the Treasury Department developed a common currency that all states used.

Bartering is still going on today. People, companies and countries barter for things they need or want. Countries that raise great amounts of beef may barter with countries that grow large amounts of grain. Companies may trade services to support one another. Even children barter! When was the last time you tried talking someone out of a big chocolate chip cookie in exchange for your apple?

title: Summer in Philadelphia
text:
Timothy Duncan was from Maryland, but he had come to Philadelphia to visit his grandmother, as he sometimes did during the summer. This summer, however, the summer of 1787, Philadelphia seemed different. There was a feeling of mystery in the streets, and people talked in hushed tones about politics and government. One evening, he heard his uncles whispering. One of them said, "Well, I really don't think there's anything to this talk of new government. They say that the delegates just fight all the time. But I tell you, I expected big changes after we threw England out of here, and where are the changes now?"

Timothy had been too young to remember the Revolutionary War, but people sure talked about it now! They were always complaining that the American government wasn't much better than the British one, and they wondered what they had fought for. Everyone in town seemed to know that behind the locked doors of the brick building in the middle of town, big things were happening - big changes for the new country's government.

Timothy watched the building every morning and evening. In the morning, tired, grumbling gentlemen walked in. And in the evening, tired, grumbling gentlemen walked out. Day after day, it was the same. Then, one day, he could hear the sound of applause and shouts of "Hurrah!" He looked around to see if there was a parade coming, but the street was quiet. The people standing outside turned wondering faces toward the brick building. Suddenly, Timothy realized that the applause must have been coming from inside!

The roar grew as the doors burst open, and a stream of happy faces flowed from the building - the same faces that had seemed stern and frowning for so many weeks. Timothy recognized Benjamin Franklin from a picture he had seen, and he was sure he saw General George Washington. He also saw James McHenry, Daniel Carroll and others from Maryland. He found himself cheering right along with them. Timothy didn't fully understand the change, but something was in the air - something new and good. He heard some of the men talking to one another, and some of them used the word "constitution." Timothy didn't know exactly what that meant, but when he heard it, something made him glad to be a Marylander - glad, in fact, to be an American.

title: Were Our Founding Fathers Rich?
text:
Some of our modern presidential candidates have been very wealthy. It is interesting to compare these people's fortunes to those of our founding fathers. For example, many people think that George Washington was our richest president. But is that true?

In letters to family and friends George Washington said he did not want to be president, but he was concerned that he didn't have enough money to live out his retirement. In other words, he needed the job! Like other founding fathers after the war, he had land but no cash.

Washington owned a lot of land, but no one wanted to buy any of it. People who rented parts of his land didn't have money to pay him. During the Revolution he refused to accept pay for being the commander of the Army. He fed his staff and paid spies with his own money. After the war, the government paid him back in Continental dollars, which were worthless. Washington even had to borrow money to get to the Constitutional Convention in 1787.

Thomas Jefferson once had to borrow money from one of his slaves. He died deeply in debt. When Alexander Hamilton died his family couldn't afford to bury him. They collected donations for his burial.

Our founding fathers pledged their lives, their fortunes and their sacred honor for freedom. They lost most of their fortunes because of the war. Their wealth was not in money; it was in service.

title: Constitution
text:
Our forefathers discovered that declaring and gaining our independence was only the beginning of a long, hard road.

Statehood Had Its Problems

The war for independence was finally over. Now there was nothing but peace, prosperity, lots of food and plenty of money for everyone, right? Well, not exactly. Independence was brand new to our forefathers, and they weren't quite sure what to do with it. Our newfound freedom came with a lot of responsibility - we had to form our own government, make our own laws and pay our own debts. A group of volunteers representing their own states' interests met to try to take care of some of these things. They called themselves the Continental Congress and drew up some rules called the Articles of Confederation. These rules gave the federal government (government of the country as a whole) control over dealing with other countries, getting mail from state to state and everything that had to do with war. The individual state governments would be in charge of just about everything else. The rules also said that the states had to be friendly with each other.

These seem like pretty good rules, don't they? Unfortunately, there were still some problems: Some people wanted a stronger government with more control; others were afraid a strong national government would grow too strong and become as controlling as England's - or worse. States argued about which trade rules should be followed. There were also problems between neighbors who had fought on opposite sides during the war.

How the Constitution Changed Us

The Articles of Confederation helped us get off to a good start, but too many things were still unclear. After six years of trying to make them work, pretty much everyone agreed that there ought to be a better way. That "better way" was worked out and was called the U.S. Constitution. How much better was it? Well, it has kept things more or less shipshape around here for well more than 200 years. Many other countries around the world that are going through their own independence look to the U.S. Constitution for guidance in making their own sets of laws.

The Signing of the Constitution

On a hot summer day in 1787, 55 representatives from different states met in Philadelphia to talk about a new government. By the time they were done, they had drawn up a constitution that organized a strong national government kept in check by power given to the people. But it was not an easy road! Men disagreed on what the new government should be like. Sometimes feelings were so intense that delegates stormed out, refusing to compromise. Then they came back the next day, cooled off and were ready to try again. As if the combination of hot tempers and hot weather weren't enough, the delegates decided they didn't want people on the street to know how tough things were going in "Constitution Hall," so they kept all the doors and windows shut. No wonder they shouted for joy when they were done.

Under the Articles of Confederation: Under the Constitution:

Congress had to ask states for money Congress could tax people

Congress had no control over trade between states Congress could control trade between states

Congress had no way to settle arguments between states There were courts to settle arguents between states

title: Good Judgement
text: Have you ever felt certain that you were right about something that your parents thought was wrong? Maybe you really think you should be allowed to stay up until 2 a.m. and eat all the popcorn, candy and ice cream you can. Sounds good to you, right? Well, you might rethink that decision when you wake up with a terrible stomachache from the sweets and very red eyes from not getting enough sleep. You might say you used "bad judgment" in that situation. Well, one great character trait to develop is good judgment. You could use good judgment by telling yourself you'll have one bowl of popcorn and one scoop of ice cream and stay up till 10 p.m. watching a good movie. That way, you won't be too tired to have a productive day tomorrow! But good judgment is used in lots of other situations, like choosing whom you hang out with, what kinds of movies you watch and books you read, what kind of language you use and pretty much every other decision you can make in your life! The key to good judgment is not necessarily going for the decision that will make you or those you want to impress happy, but what will be best for you in the long run. It might take some work, but using good judgment definitely pays off in the end! Just ask the kid with the stomachache and droopy eyes. He's wishing he'd used a little better judgment!

title: Scientist at Heart
text:
He was born on a Maryland farm to a poor family. He loved to learn and continued his education as long as he could - until he was 15. He was very mechanically gifted. One time, he borrowed a watch, took it apart piece by piece, studied each piece to see how it worked and then put it back together perfectly. A little later, based one what he had learned from the watch, he built a wooden clock that kept exact time and struck on the hour. It kept the time until it was destroyed in a fire 40 years later.

Thomas Jefferson, the secretary of state, heard about this man's brilliance and assigned him to help survey the land for our nation's capital - Washington, D.C. At the age of 60, this man used his knowledge of math to help create the boundaries of the new capital city.

This man also wrote important books, which Jefferson himself then sent to the French Academy in Paris. That was something really special for an African American. For Benjamin Banneker, one of America's first scientific geniuses, was born the son of a slave.

title: Where does the word
text: Our language has some words that are fairly new, like "computer" and "microchip," and some words that have been around a really long time. Some of our oldest words come from Latin, which is no longer spoken as a native language. Centuries ago, Latin (spoken by the Romans) influenced nearly every other written and spoken language. The Romans especially liked to talk and write about law; so many of our words about government come from Latin. If you take the word "legislation" apart, you will actually see two Latin words: "legis" means law, and "latio" means to bring. Put them together, and you get "law to bring," or "to bring about laws." And that's exactly what "legislation" means: "to bring about, or pass, laws." Neat, huh?

title: Seashells
text: If you've ever walked along the beach, here's one form of wildlife you just can't miss. Seashells aren't really a form of wildlife, but they are what's left when the wildlife leaves. Seashells come in all shapes, colors and sizes. Some of the largest come from horseshoe crabs. A lot of times, when you see this kind of shell, the wildlife is still inside, so keep your distance! Some of the smallest shells look like tiny pebbles, but if you look closely, you'll see the place where the shellfish once lived. Why are there so many shells on the beach? Most shells are washed ashore during winter tides. Also, heavy storms bring shells in from deep under the surface of the water. Wherever you go, you're bound to find plenty to collect. For a great collection, look for unbroken, empty shells or large pieces of unscratched shell. But most important, choose the ones you like best!

title: Dissent and Debate: Sam Adams and the Committees of Correspondence
text:
When reading about the American Revolution, we might think everyone in the Colonies felt the same way. American colonists definitely had strong opinions, but they did not always agree.

Most colonists were angry about Great Britain’s actions. The Boston Tea Party protested taxes on tea, right? But some merchants needed to trade with Britain to get the items they sold in their stores. They didn’t want to boycott, or refuse to buy, British goods. Colonists in rural areas didn’t want to go to war because they needed British soldiers to protect them from unfriendly Indian attacks. There were dissenting, or differing, opinions in those days, just like today.

News in the Colonies was hard to get during the late 1700s. People carried letters and pamphlets by horseback or on boats. Samuel Adams was one of the leaders of the Boston Tea Party, and he found a powerful way to organize and share the colonists’ different points of view.

In 1772, Adams formed a Committee of Correspondence in Boston. This group wrote about what the Colony thought of Great Britain’s actions. Their letters traveled to all parts of the Massachusetts Colony, keeping the colonists up to date. The letters also went to the other Colonies and even to some foreign countries. Soon most colonists agreed about the need to rebel against the British.

Within a year, 11 of the 13 Colonies also set up Committees of Correspondence. These committees led the way in electing delegates for the First Continental Congress.

The Committees of Correspondence also show the value of debate and dissent. What steps do you take when someone is treating you unfairly? Do you argue or complain? Maybe next time you’ll think of Samuel Adams and put your ideas in writing!

3. While still folded in the “hamburger” way, fold it the hot dog way again. Now unfold the “hot dog” way and cut halfway up the middle folded line, from the folded side.

title: Preamble Booklet
text:
Follow the instructions on Page 3 for each of the sets of figures shown here. You can staple the three little booklets together and have the complete preamble with instructions for hand gestures.

The preamble explains the reason for and goals of the Constitution of the United States and was written by Gouverneur Morris. He was responsible for much of the wording of the Constitution because he was very skilled at writing.

title: Capture on the High Seas
text:
The year was 1810, and I was just a youngster - a boy of only 15. My father was a shipbuilder in Maryland's busiest shipyard at Fells Point. I spent a lot of time with my dad down at the Baltimore harbor watching him work. Was I impressed with all those big, beautiful sailing ships? You'd better believe I was! I was so impressed, in fact, that the first chance I got, I lied about my age - I was a pretty big lad, you see - and got myself into the U.S. Navy as a seaman. I was pretty proud of myself. I worked hard aboard the U.S.S. Baltimore to prove my abilities to my superiors. On our days off, they let us wear anything we wanted. I loved sitting on the bowsprit (a large spar projecting from the front of the ship), talking to old timers about their adventures on the seas of the world.

June 17 is a day I will always remember. I was on duty, scrubbing the decks as usual. Suddenly, we increased our speed. The captain was sailing away from a quickly approaching British vessel off the starboard (right) side. The Baltimore tried to outrun the other ship, but we lost the race. Almost before we realized what was happening, the Brits had sidled up to our ship, placed planks between their railing and ours and overrun our deck. I was shocked - it happened so fast! Several men pointed their pistols at the officers and ordered a dozen deck hands off the ship - including me! We were marched across the planks and onto the British ships at gunpoint. At the time, I thought myself the victim of a simple kidnapping. I know now there's another word for it - impressment.

What did they want from us? Military service, that's what! I was used to working hard, but the British forced us to fight their enemies, the French, in battles on the high seas. They had been at war with the French for years. We were very unhappy and looked forward to the day when we would be back aboard the Baltimore with our buddies.

Impressment by the British was the last straw. Forced service became the main crime for which the U.S. Congress declared war one more time upon Great Britain. We'd gained our independence from that country more than 35 years earlier, but our grievances with each other never seemed to end. This new war, declared in 1812, was later referred to as, appropriately, the War of 1812.

Maryland's Unsung Hero

Commodore Joshua Barney sailed as a privateer and served as a commodore in both the French and American navies. Although largely forgotten, he was one of the most clever officers of the American sailing navy. He was a natural seaman and a leader of extraordinary courage. Barney organized a Chesapeake flotilla (small boats and barges) and, on June 26, 1814, successfully fought off two huge, heavily armed British ships that were determined to take Baltimore. The commodore was then ordered by the Navy to leave his flotilla and join the ragged forces in Washington, D.C., to defend our nation's capital. Barney's 1,500 men successfully fought off four attacks by a British force of 5,000 at the Battle of Blandensburg. In the end, however, Barney was forced to surrender. British General Ross was so impressed by the bravery of Commodore Barney and his flotilla men that he immediately paroled them.

title: Visit Fort McHenry!
text:
The War of 1812 marked its bicentennial, or 200th birthday, in 2012. Baltimore Harbor is one of the most significant sites of the final war between the United States of America and its mother country, Great Britain. For two days in September 1814, during the Battle of Baltimore, Fort McHenry was bombarded with enemy fire for 25 hours. The star-shaped fort, the guardian of Baltimore's harbor, valiantly defended her country.

Have you visited this famous historic site? If you have, you may know that it is a tradition that any newly designed American flag is flown first over Fort McHenry. This way, the new flag is flown over the same "ramparts," or watch towers, seen by Francis Scott Key before it is flown anywhere else. If you haven't visited Fort McHenry, you are missing a vital part of our state's history. Plan a visit to this great national monument and historic shrine to learn more about the history of Maryland and the United States.

title: The War of 1812
text:
The War of 1812 was one of our country's least-popular wars. Nevertheless, it was fought valiantly. Maryland was in the thick of several battles.

Why Another War with Great Britain?

In 1776, America won its independence from England. But, even though the war was over, the British never really left America. They still wanted our land! The Americans and the British argued constantly over borders - the northwest area around the Great Lakes and areas in Baltimore, New Orleans and Washington, D.C. England and France had border problems as well. Those two countries were at war from 1792 to 1814. France controlled most of Europe, and England ruled the oceans with its ships. Britain was short of sailors for its navy, however, so it just captured American sailors right off our ships! This made our Congress angry! Now it was time to fight! The United States declared war. The War of 1812 was fought from June 1812 to the spring of 1815. Many Marylanders were involved in battles. During one battle, the British burned down the White House. A peace treaty was finally signed by both sides in Ghent, Belgium, in December 1814. In the end, both sides ended up pretty much with the land they started with. The War of 1812 was considered a draw - neither side really won.

Oh, Say Can You See

Francis Scott Key was born on Aug. 1, 1779, in western Maryland. His family was very wealthy and owned an estate called Terra Rubra. Key went to law school in Annapolis and became an attorney in Georgetown, a suburb of Washington, D.C. He was a deeply religious man. At one time, he nearly gave up his law practice to become a minister. During the War of 1812, Dr. William Beanes, a close friend of Key, was taken prisoner by the British Royal Navy. Key and another friend immediately left for Baltimore. They boarded the British ship to see if their friend could be released. They were still at sea, about eight miles from shore, when the British attacked Fort McHenry. After about 25 hours of continuous bombing, the British decided to leave. They were unable to destroy the fort as they had hoped. Realizing that the British had ceased the attack, Key looked toward the fort to see if the flag was still there. It was flying high! Quickly, he wrote down the words to a poem forming in his head. He named it "Defense of Fort McHenry." It was renamed "The Star-Spangled Banner" and became a popular patriotic song. It was written in 1814, but didn't become our national anthem until 1931.

The Successful Battle That Shouldn't Have Happened

The war ended with the Treaty of Ghent in December 1814. Unfortunately, in the 1800s, there were no phones, faxes or fast communication of any kind. There was no way to inform Colonel Andrew Jackson that the war was over! A battle took place in New Orleans a month after the war ended and eventually became better known than the war itself. This was due to a wildly popular song from the early 1960s. You may even know it. Ask any teacher, parent, or grandparent you know to sing "The Battle of New Orleans," and they will immediately burst into song. We promise!

In 1814 we took a little trip
along with Colonel Jackson
down the mighty Mississip.
We took a little bacon, and
we took a little beans,
And we caught the bloody British
in the town of New Orleans.

We fired our guns
and the British kept a' comin'
There wasn't nigh as many
as there was awhile ago.
We fired once more, and
they began to run
on down the Mississippi
to the Gulf of Mexico.

The Chasseur

This is the Baltimore clipper schooner Chasseur. It was a famous privateer brig built in 1813. She mounted 14 guns and was brilliantly successful as a commerce raider in the War of 1812.

What was a Privateer?

Many writers lump the words "privateer," "pirate" and "buccaneer" all in the same category. Only two of those occupations were illegal. Pirates have been around for centuries - and still are! They board ships and steal money and other possessions, and sometimes they steal the ships themselves. Today's pirates are most likely to be involved in drug trafficking. Buccaneers were not as bad as pirates. They were British, French or Dutch sea adventurers during the 1600s who harassed Spanish ships and settlements. Usually escaped servants, former soldiers or loggers, they ran their ships in an organized way. Buccaneers founded the South Sea Company.

Privateers were different. Privateering was a legal occupation. Until its end in the late 1800s, it was generally respected. Privateers operated only in wartime and only against enemy ships. They were, in many ways, in the same business as the Navy, which likewise paid its sailors and officers from the proceeds of captured ships. During the War of 1812, more than 300 ships were taken by the United States within six months! They were seized by both naval vessels and privateering vessels.

title: Trustworthiness
text: Do you know what it means to be trustworthy? It's simple really. Being trustworthy means that people can trust you! It means that if someone gives you a job to do, you do it! If someone tells you a secret, you keep it! If you say you're going to do something for someone, you follow through! It's easy to see that, when people are trustworthy, there are good feelings, understanding and peace. On the other hand, when people are not trustworthy, there are angry feelings, confusion and suspicion! Being trustworthy is important, but it's just one step on the road to being a great person.

title: The Town That Fooled the British
text: St. Michaels is known as "the town that fooled the British." The tale may not have even happened, but it's been around for so long that people who live in St. Michaels will swear to its truthfulness. It happened during the War of 1812. The town was an important shipbuilding center. They built privateer ships, blockade runners and naval barges. The British knew the town built these valuable ships, so they decided to destroy the shipyard and all the boats currently under construction. The residents of St. Michaels had been warned in advance, however. In the early morning darkness of Aug. 10, 1813, several British barges lined up in the harbor outside the town, loaded with cannons and many other weapons. They immediately began firing at the lights of downtown St. Michaels as well as at the lights in the shipyard. The British then crept away in the night, confident that they'd destroyed all the ships along with the town itself. But the joke was on the British. Because the citizens of the town had been warned, they'd placed lanterns in the tops of trees and on the tops of the ships' masts in the shipyard. The British, aiming at what they thought were the lights of the town and the shipyard, overshot their cannon, and the balls went right over the town! Only one house was struck. Today it's called the "Cannonball House." And St. Michaels is called "the town that fooled the British."

title: What is the “1812 Overture?”
text: It's a beautiful piece of music by a famous, brilliant Russian composer, Tchaikovsky (chi-KOFF-ski). He's the same man who composed "The Nutcracker Suite." You've heard the overture many times, and you'll continue to hear it - The piece is almost always played at the conclusion of Fourth of July celebrations all over the country. In larger concerts, actual cannons are fired during the performance. It sounds so "American" that many people assume the bold piece was written with our War of 1812 in mind. Not so! At the same time that we were fighting Great Britain, France's General Napoleon Bonaparte was invading Russia. Tchaikovsky composed the piece in 1882 to celebrate the 70th anniversary of Russia's victory in that invasion. (Ask your teacher to play the "1812 Overture.")

title: Black-eyed Susan
text: The black-eyed Susan is Maryland's state flower. A group of women citizens chose the flower in 1896. It became the official state flower in 1918. The black-eyed Susan shares the black and yellow colors of the Calvert coat of arms. The flower's petals are yellow, and its center is black and 2 to 3 inches in width. The name of the flower in Latin means "rough; hairy." The black-eyed Susan is a member of the daisy or sunflower family. This wildflower can grow up to 3 feet tall. Its leaves are sometimes 6 inches long. The black-eyed Susan needs lots of sun and blooms in late summer. Its flowers grow separately or in pairs. Sometimes, the flower is 6 inches wide. It's found mostly in fields and roadsides in every part of Maryland. It's a very hardy flower - It grows in all types of soil. And Free Staters are not the only folks who enjoy this bright, sunny flower. It grows wild throughout the eastern United States and as far west as the Rocky Mountains.

title: How Do I Read Nonfiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring. But it really isn’t. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you will find it easier to understand—and maybe even fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will talk about the problem and solution pattern.

Problem/Solution

With this information pattern, the writer begins by stating a problem. Then the writer presents various solutions or ideas for solving the problem. This pattern is common in newspaper articles, as well as science and social studies texts.

One strategy for finding the problem and solution of a nonfiction passage is to create a cluster map. A cluster map will help you remember what you have read. Begin by writing the subject of the passage in the middle of a blank sheet of paper. On one side of the subject, write “problems.” On the other side, write “solutions.” Then write details you want to remember that illustrate the problems and solutions around these bubbles. Remember to draw lines connecting the problems to the word “problems” and connecting solutions to the word “solutions.” This way, you show how the information connects.

Try It!

To the right is a passage about transportation. Read the passage. Then create a cluster map showing the problems and solutions discussed in the passage. The cluster map has been started for you.

title: Let's Write
text: Tell about your huge tree house that you and your friends have built. What furniture does it have? Who is allowed inside?

title: Fun Facts
text: The word “bookkeeper” is the only word in the English language with double letter combinations, three times in a row.

title: Moving People and Things
text: Hey there! Welcome to another issue of Maryland Studies Weekly! This issue is all about moving around. Moving people and things from place to place is called transportation. Even this paper was probably transported from your teacher's desk to your own. Maryland folks do plenty of transporting, and over the years, they've found some pretty amazing ways to do it! Just think of your trip to school this morning. Your mom may have driven you in a car. Or, you may have ridden with a lot of other kids in a big, yellow school bus. You may have whizzed down the road on a sleek aluminum scooter or a pair of roller blades. But whatever transported you to school, there's a good chance your great- great-grandparents never heard of it (unless, of course, you walked to school)! Things in the transportation world are changing every day. And, that raises an interesting question: how do you think your great-great-grandchildren will get to school? Will they have jet-powered skateboards that float above the ground? Will they travel in ultra-fast school rockets that take kids to schools in outer space? Maybe they'll just hit a button and beam instantly to their school desks. The possibilities are enough to fuel the imaginations of scientists for as long as scientists are using their imaginations. Getting around has always been big fun and big business in Maryland. To find out more about it all, transport this paper to the open position, and let's get going!

title: Maryland’s Transportation
text:
Colonial Roads

You probably know the names of a dozen different streets in your town alone. But think about this for a second: When Maryland was first being settled, there were only a few big wagon roads on the whole state! The biggest one around here was the National Road, which began in Cumberland and eventually went west through other states like Pennsylvania and Ohio until it got all the way to Illinois. Of course, if wagon travel wasn't your style, you could hop aboard a boat and travel along one of Maryland's rivers, like the Patapsco, the Potomac or the Patuxent. In the early days, most of the towns were built along rivers, wagon roads or railroads. Traveling a river is a good way to let the road do the work for awhile. In fact, if you compare the number of rivers in early Maryland to the number of roads, it looked like Mother Nature was even better at building "roads" than we were!

The Maryland Canal System

Man-made canals provided another form of transportation for early Marylanders. Since rivers didn't always go where people needed them to go, workers dug "channels" for the river water to flow through. Canal digging was extremely difficult, and life for the workers and their families was equally hard. Often two or three families lived together in one small hut, with no clean water to drink or bathe in. Many people died of what they called "ague," or malaria, a disease carried by mosquitoes in swampy areas.

But the work paid off: canals made travel much easier and faster. People could visit far-off relatives or even move far off themselves if they wanted to! Each canal had a towpath where a mule rigged to the boat would walk, dragging the boat alongside. Mule drivers were 14- to 18-year-old boys. Maryland's two canals were the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal - nicknamed the C&O - and the Chesapeake and Delaware Canal. This canal connected two bays and is still used today.

Maryland's First Train

Whoo-whoooooo! What makes that sound? An overgrown owl? Nope. That's the sound of the biggest thing to hit the world of transportation in centuries - the railroad! "Big deal" you say? Well, in the early 1800s, the railroad was a big deal. Never before had there been an easier or more reliable way to get people and their things from one place to another. No more stagecoaches on bumpy, muddy roads. No more boats on dangerous rivers. This was traveling in style, and it hit the country in a big way. The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, also known as the B & O, was built quickly, reaching from Baltimore to Cumberland in 1832. This was quite a distance for the time period. For the B & O was not only Maryland's first railroad - it was the first railroad built in the whole United States!

Henry Ford and the Automobile

Around 1903, Henry Ford figured out how to make a whole bunch of cars very quickly, at a price anyone with a job could afford. After that, people could go anywhere the roads went. The Ford Motor Company produced and sold nearly 36 million cars and trucks from 1903 to 1950. He started out by building a car in his barn, but in just a few decades, the automobile craze swept right through Maryland and the rest of the nation.

Space Vacations?

Transportation into space is getting more common all the time. The space shuttle launches barely even make the news nowadays. What does that mean for you? Well, the time isn't far off when space travel could be for regular people like you and me. In fact, one guy, a wealthy American businessman named Dennis Tito paid the Russian government to make him the first space tourist! Have you heard of anyone else rich or famous taking a trip into space? Who knows? Maybe space travel could be the next big transportation business!

title: Western Maryland
text: This region has only three counties! So this week we'll take an in-depth look at Maryland's westernmost county, Garrett County. We've already talked about the largest lake in Maryland, Deep Creek Lake. Don't miss the swimming, hiking, boating and waterskiing available in this beautiful area. If you prefer winter skiing, be sure to hit the slopes here - they get more snow than any other mountains in the East except for New Hampshire. If you like learning about transportation, visit the La Vale Toll Gate House, along the old National Road, the only tollhouse left in Maryland. Find out what the toll was for everyone back in the 1830s, including animals! For more on transportation, walk along the old C&O Canal (right). No longer in operation, the towpath has been restored into a bike/hike trail 184 miles long! While here, stop by the only town in the country named Accident. Of course, there's an interesting story that goes along with the name, but you'll have to go there to learn more. Probably the most fascinating and unusual spot here is the Cranesville Sub-Arctic Swamp. Here we are, way south of the Arctic Circle, growing things like tamarack, sundew and creeping snowberry. Visit this "frost pocket" and report what you found to your class.

title: What is the longest road in the world?
text: Most would name the Pan American Highway the longest road. It covers 15,600 miles from Prudhoe Bay, Alaska to Tierra del Fuego, Argentina. It spans 14 countries and two continents. If you want to meet someone who knows every single mile of the highway on a very personal level, read the web site created by Emmanuel Gentinetta of Sonora, California. He traveled the highway on a bicycle over a nine-month period in 1999. Read the complete report at www.bikeitsolo.com.

title: Christmas Bird Count
text:
"Four calling birds, three French hens, two turtledoves and a partridge in a pear tree . . ." Sounds like a pretty good Christmas Bird Count, doesn't it? Actually, it goes like this:

In 1900 ornithologist (scientist who studies birds) Frank Chapman was disturbed by the slaughter of birds in an annual holiday event call the "side hunt." The team that shot the most birds and other small animals was the winner. As a protest, Chapman organized 27 friends in 25 locations on Christmas Day. Instead of shooting birds, they counted them! The bird count has continued to this day, and Maryland participates too.

Here are the count rules: each bird count is a circle 15 miles in diameter. Bird counters cover as much of the area as possible within a 24-hour calendar day. Over 45,000 people from all 50 states, every Canadian province, the Caribbean, Central and South America and the Pacific Islands participate in about 1,700 counts held during a two-three week period. To help with the bird count in Maryland, you need to contact your local bird-watching club. Make sure the club is registered with the National Audubon Society, or its numbers won't count. Look on the Internet for a club near you. The Christmas Bird Count has become the largest and longest-running wildlife survey ever undertaken.

title: How Do I Read Nonfiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring. But it really isn’t. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you will find it easier to understand—and maybe even fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will discuss comparison and contrast.

Comparison/Contrast

With this information pattern, the writer focuses on similarities and differences. When comparing subjects, writers use words such as “the equivalent of,” “like,” “the same as” and “similar.” Writers show contrast by using words such as “but,” “in contrast to,” “on the other hand” and “unlike.” The writer usually mentions both similarities and differences.

One way to find comparisons and contrasts is to use a Venn diagram. With a Venn diagram, you can easily see how information about your two subjects is alike and different. In the far left and far right bubbles, you write the differences of each of the two subjects. In the overlapping part, you write the similarities of the two.

Try It!

To the right is a passage about becoming a state of the United States. Read the passage. Then create a Venn diagram showing the similarities and differences in the subject.

title: Maryland Industries Span the Entire World!
text:
Have you ever walked through your neighborhood and seen clouds of dust or heard the rumble of big tractors, the whirring of saws and the pounding of hammers as a new home goes up for a family to live in? Have you ever seen fishing boats come in off the ocean with nets full of wriggling fish, bound for dinner on your table? Have you ever heard the honking of a big lumber truck, loaded high with heavy boards to be made into homes, offices or doghouses? Everywhere you look, you can see signs of INDUSTRY! Industry is the products and services that bring money into a community. Products made, grown, found, or dug up right here in Maryland are finding their way to other places. We even send stuff as far away as Canada, Japan, Germany, Taiwan, Egypt, the United Kingdom and Belgium!

There are a lot of people outside of Maryland who think that our state is only about crabs and American history. They're only half right! It's true that fish and tourism make up a big part of Maryland's economy, but there's much more to Maryland industry than that. People all over the world are heating their homes with Maryland coal, picnicking with Maryland corn on the cob and celebrating with Maryland Christmas trees, most times without even knowing it! In this issue of Maryland Studies Weekly, we'll take a good look at just a few of the industries that make life in Maryland the way it is. Some of these industries are new to the state, and others have been around as long as people have settled here. But they're all important to Marylanders and the world.

title: Maryland’s Industry “There is no Treasure Without Toil”
text:
Maryland Tourism

There's at least one industry in our state that depends on being interesting to people from other places. And Maryland must be a pretty interesting place. After all, tourists who visit here (from another place) pump a lot of money into our state economy every year. Even though Ocean City seems to be the center of the tourist industry in Maryland, our state has plenty of theme parks, national forests, state parks and historic sites to keep folks happy, even far away from the beach. In addition to the money tourism generates for the state, tourism also supplies a whole heap of jobs.

Aquaculture - What's That?

There are all kinds of crops that grow in good soil, that's for sure. But lately Maryland farmers have been experimenting with stuff you can grow in water! They call it aquaculture instead of agriculture. Here's how it works: Farmers dig holes in flat land and fill the holes with water. Then they fill the water with baby catfish called fingerlings and feed them like crazy. Once the catfish are big enough, they're as easy to harvest as any vegetable garden! People who research what kinds of fish can be "farmed" in Maryland are called studiers. Recently, Maryland farmers have begun raising fish in tanks of water rather than the man-made ponds. This way, Marylanders can enjoy fresh fish all year 'round. More than 150 aqua-farms across the state annually raise 80,000 pounds of catfish, 237,000 pounds of rock fish and a whopping 1 million pounds of tilapia! Even water plants for aquariums are raised on aqua-farms.

O Christmas Tree, O Christmas Tree

Once upon a time, families hiked out to their local woods and cut down their own fresh tree for traditional tree-trimming celebrations. Today, we can go down to the corner parking lot and pick a nearly-perfect, just-the-right-height, already-cut-for-us tree (for a modest fee, of course). But did you ever wonder where all those Christmas trees came from? Believe it or not, people own farms that, instead of growing wheat, corn or soybeans, grow Christmas trees!

Harvesting at Christmastime is hard work, but Christmas tree farming is a year-round endeavor. A tree begins as a seed in a greenhouse. At about two years of age, the seedling is transplanted, or moved and replanted to the farmer's field. Throughout the next seven years, the farmer takes great care to prune, feed and nurture the tree until it reaches the desired height and fullness. This is not an easy job, for dangers like the wrong amount of sun or rain, bad weather like hail or wind, destructive insects or disease threaten to cut the tree's life short. Sometimes, people even steal trees from farms.

But despite the difficulties, most Christmas tree farmers enjoy the satisfaction of knowing that they produce a great symbol for many Maryland families.

Maryland's Mining

Most of the time when you hear about coal mining, you probably think of Pennsylvania or West Virginia, but Western Maryland has also been mining since the early 1800s. At first, coal was mined just for local use - for heating homes and powering the early trains. By 1820, coal was transported east to Cumberland, then shipped along the Potomac River and sold to more distant customers. Between 1900 and 1918, Western Maryland produced nearly 5 million tons of coal a year! The deep mines dug during this time period used gravity drainage so the mines wouldn't fill with water. This caused people's drinking water (from streams and underground springs) to be polluted with acid and toxic minerals. So today, work is being done to reclaim the land used for deep mining. This means finding ways to make the land safer and more beautiful.

Don't Forget Service

Some people don't have things to show for their work - things like potatoes, pounds of hamburger, computer chips or truckloads of plastic bags. Instead of things, some people produce happy, comfortable Marylanders. Think about the bagger at the supermarket, the police officer who keeps you safe or even your school teacher! These people don't produce products. Instead they provide a service.

The service industry is by far the way most people make a living in Maryland. More than 75 percent of Maryland's money comes from service-related work! Maybe that's because it's really not that hard to find ways to serve people. Anything that helps make life a little more pleasant can be called a service. Can you think of some examples?

title: Integrity
text: What does it mean to have integrity? It means that you make your actions match what you say and believe. Integrity is one of the most important character traits a person can have. Here's an example. A poor Mexican immigrant, Ascension Franco Gonzales, was walking in Los Angeles one evening in 2001 and came upon a bag of money - not just a couple of bucks, but $203,000! Gonzales thought about keeping the money but knew in his heart that it was wrong. After he heard on the news that the money was missing from an armored car, a truck that transports money from big banks, he knew what he had to do. He returned the money, even though he could have kept it. Though he did not ask for a reward, he received $25,000 for returning the money. Gonzales showed integrity because he acted in the way that matched what he believed. He knew that keeping the money was wrong, so he gave it back. How can you show integrity in your life? You can clean up your room when you tell your mom you will. You can be honest with your friends and family. You can be kind to those around you because you know that it is wrong to tease and gossip. You can make your actions match what your parents and teachers have taught you, and then you can say that you have integrity!

title: Grave Full of Gold
text: Pat was sorry to see his friend's life end like this. They had been buddies for about four years. It all started when a guy named Joe was telling some tall tales down at the local tavern. He claimed to have found gold while wading in Crumpton Creek. Of course, no one believed him. Whoever heard of gold in Maryland? But Pat had a funny feeling about this, like just maybe it could be true. So after all the other men left the table, Pat stepped over to Joe to ask some more questions. Joe offered to show Pat where he found the gold. The two men headed over to Crumpton Creek. Sure enough, when Joe drew his pan up out of the water, sand-like grains glinted in the sunlight! Pat and Joe had been prospecting together ever since. Now, four years later, Pat sadly stood by the side of Joe's grave. At least Joe had died doing what he loved best - searching the hills for gold. As Pat bent his head for the minister's prayer, he saw a familiar glint in the pile of dirt beside Joe's grave. Could it be? Pat stooped closer to the earth, cupped the soil in his hands and examined it closely. Gold! Pat jumped up, staked a claim around Joe's grave and then proceeded to give his own prayer of thanks. He wondered, "If you're watching, Joe, thanks a million!"

title: Has gold ever been found in Maryland?
text: Yes! In 1849, gold was found on Samuel Ellicott's farm in Montgomery County. Then, during the Civil War, some soldiers who were washing their dishes in a stream near Great Falls discovered some gold slivers in their pans. But don't go rushing out to your yard to start digging. Gold has been found all along the Piedmont Plateau, but in very small quantities. Small fibers, wires or sheets might be seen within other rocks. Some of Maryland's copper mines have also found traces of gold. But if you want to strike it rich, you're going to have to move out west! (Or maybe you can just bum a few dollars off your parents.)

title: Albino Animals
text: An albino animal is one that was born without color to its hair or fur. Most American Indian tribes believed albino animals had a special spirit. These animals were not to be hunted or killed. Because the albino lacked a natural ability to blend into its environment, it was unfair game for the native hunter. American Indians believed anyone who did hunt these creatures would be cursed. For instance, Maryland Indians believed that if an albino squirrel were hunted and killed, the hunter would lose his hunting abilities. If an albino deer were killed, the hunter would later lose his life in a freak hunting accident. Among all tribes, the albino animal had spirit connections. One of the strongest among the Plains tribes was the white buffalo, a definite symbol of great wisdom. Today, all hunters respect the American Indian customs concerning albino animals.

title: Earth as an Apple
text:
Have an adult help you cut the apple with a knife.

Materials

Apple

Knife

Directions

1. Slice an apple into quarters. One-quarter of an apple represents the Earth's land.

2. Slice one of the quarters into two. This 1/8 piece represents Earth's land that is not swamps, deserts or polar regions.

3. Cut the 1/8 piece into four 1/32 pieces. One of these pieces represents land that can be farmed. The rest is buried under cities, is too wet or too cold or has poor soil.

4. Peel this 1/32 of the Earth's surface carefully to represent the thin layer of topsoil that actually produces food.

Let this example remind us of how lucky we are to have the land we live on. Can you see how important it is to take good care of this valuable resource?

title: Specialization and Interdependence
text:
Imagine a day in the life of a bread baker. First, the baker buys the wheat seeds. Then he plants the seeds and takes care of the farm until the wheat is ready to be harvested. After harvesting the wheat, the baker grinds it into flour. He uses the flour to make the dough and then bakes the bread. But he is not done yet! After the bread is baked, he has to package it, write the advertisements and manage the store that sells the bread. How could one person possibly do all those tasks? That poor bread baker would not have a very successful business because he would be exhausted and too busy focusing on things besides baking the bread. That is exactly why businesses specialize to produce one type of product or provide one certain service.

Thanks to specialization, today’s bread baker is only responsible for making the dough and baking his delicious bread. So, who does the rest of the work? Many other people including farmers, mill workers, people in the packaging factory, advertisers and store employees all play an important role in getting the bread to the consumers. They each specialize, or do one specific job, to make the product—bread. Specializing allows companies to make more product in less time and improves the quality of the product. Because one specific worker (or a small group of workers) focuses on each step of production, the baker has more time to focus on his special talent, bread baking.

So what would happen if one of the people along the way didn’t do his or her job well or didn’t do it at all? What if the packaging factory didn’t make any bags for the bread? The bread would get stale before it made it to the store. Then no one would buy the bread, and the farmer, baker, mill workers, advertisers and store employees would all lose income. All the workers in the process are interdependent. That means each worker relies or depends on the others for help or resources to make the final product.

When you think of specialization and interdependence, you might picture an assembly line. Each worker on the line has a job to do before the product moves on to the next worker. This increases the amount of product made because each person is responsible for only one part or phase of production. Therefore the work gets done more quickly. The worker gets faster and more efficient at his or her job by only focusing on that one duty. In an assembly line it is very important that each worker does his or her part. Everyone else is counting on the other people to help get to the finish. Now that takes cooperation!

title: How Do I Read Nonfiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring. But it really isn’t. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you will find it easier to understand—and maybe even fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/ effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will talk about cause and effect

Cause/Effect

With this information pattern, writers organize their material to show how one thing leads to another. Cause is the reason why something happens. Effect is what happens as a result of the cause. Effects often turn into causes for different effects. Writers often use this pattern when they want to explain a chain of events.

One way to find the cause and effect of a passage is to make a Cause/Effect Diagram that allows you to show the cause and effect relationship graphically. You start by writing the cause of the events. Draw an arrow from the cause bubble pointing right, and then next to the arrow, write the effect of that cause. Draw a new arrow from the effect bubble pointing left and down and write the next effect. Draw the next arrow pointing right and continue in that manner until you have reached the final effect. See the sample diagram below.

Try It!

To the right is a passage about immigration to the United States. Read the passage. Then create a Cause/Effect Diagram that shows the causes and effects of immigration.

title: Fake or Real News?
text:
Have you ever read something online, like on social media sites, that sounded fishy? Maybe it was real, but it could be fake news! The big danger, though, is news that sounds real but isn’t. Fake news is becoming common because anyone can post things online. Fake news can be in the form of a story. Fake news can be a photo or video that has been changed. The problem is that these fake items look real. Fake news can cause problems and it spreads misinformation.

Sam Wineburg, a professor, did some research. He found that 80 percent of students cannot tell the difference between real and fake news. Do you want to become a media-savvy person? You have to be able to find out if news is real or fake. How do you do that? You have to become a detective and search for the truth. You can learn about the author or company that posted the news. You have to think about the purpose of the news. Is there a hidden plan to get you to buy something or to make you think a certain way? Your teacher or a trusted adult can help you learn how to spot fake news. It takes a little time, but democracy depends on real information! Do your part and discover what is real and what is fake!

title: Movin’ Down the Line
text:
"Quick! Put out the light!" Josiah's words were hushed and frantic, and his wife, Letty, swiftly and silently sprang up to blow out the lamp's flame. There were voices outside the window - the loud laughter of drunken men - and the sound of heavy boots tromping on the wooden floor of the front porch. The night was moonless, and Josiah strained to peer through a crack in the curtain.

Suddenly, the sound of a gunshot rattled the whole house, from the rafters to the windows to the floorboards! Letty spread herself flat on the floor, her heart beating hard against her ribs. Josiah crawled to where she was and whispered in her ear, "Don't be afraid, Letty. They ain't lookin' for anything. They're just drunk and shootin' off in the air for show. See there, can you hear the laughin'?" Outside, but further down the road now, loud laughter rang out, and then another gunshot. Still, Letty covered her head. Josiah stayed with her on the floor until the voices had faded completely. Then he stood, crossed the room, moved the big rug and grabbed the notch in the floorboard beneath it. He pulled up the board, and there was the secret cellar and two frightened pairs of eyes.

"Up you come, friends. The danger was nothin' after all. Just a couple a' drunks on their way home." Out of the cellar, with a "Much obliged, Josiah," climbed Samuel and then, with Samuel's help, his little son, David.

"Of course," said Josiah, "It don't look as safe as all that here tonight. Sometimes when there's a big party in town, those drunks come prowlin' around the yard. You and your boy had best get on to the next house. I'll show you the way. It'll be dangerous getting there, but you'll be safer."

Samuel looked at the face of his son. Dangerous? No danger could be too great, as long as he could take his boy to a place where he could grow up to be a free man. He turned to Josiah, "We're ready." He took David by the hand. "Let's go."

Josiah started out the door but turned to Letty before he disappeared. "You'll wait up for me, now won't ya?" Letty nodded. Josiah smiled for a moment, and then three shadows slipped silently into the night.

title: Historic Maryland Safe House
text:
Cooling Springs Farm is a great place to go to learn more about Maryland's role in the Underground Railroad. The Underground Railroad was a system of secret routes used by escaping slaves that led from the South to the Northern United States or Canada. Cooling Springs Farm is located about three miles north of the Potomac River in Frederick County, Maryland. It is one of only a small number of Underground Railroad "safe houses" that still exists in this part of the country.

During the Civil War, Cooling Springs Farm was owned by Ezra and Margaret Michael. Margaret came from an abolitionist family who wanted to abolish, or get rid of, slavery in the United States. Margaret and her husband used the farm's Spring House as a safe house for slaves traveling along the Underground Railroad. Runaway slaves could hide in the safe house until they were able to continue their journey along the railroad.

The Michaels also founded nearby St. Paul's Episcopal Church, a church that allowed blacks and whites to worship together. During the time that he ran the safe house, Ezra was a judge who followed the law during the day, but who chose to follow a "higher law" at night, when he helped slaves escape from their masters.

Tours of Cooling Springs Farm and the Spring House are available to those who are interested in learning more about the Civil War. Cooling Springs Farm is now owned by Peter and Vicki Michael, who are more than happy to welcome visitors if they call ahead. If you visit, you will learn all about the Underground Railroad and how one Maryland family helped many desperate slaves escape to freedom during the Civil War.

title: Slavery in Maryland
text:
You may ask why we study the awful events of this time. But understanding how we became a nation of slave-owners will help us to never repeat the mistakes of our ancestors.

How Did Slavery Start?

The first slaves were brought into the Colonies in 1619, when Jamestown was just beginning. Most black people came to the Colonies from West Africa. English or American slave ships dropped anchor off the west coast of Africa, and the captains went aboard to buy slaves. A native chief who had captured slaves to sell talked with the captains, and they agreed on a price. After the slaves were loaded onto the ships, the slave traders crossed the Atlantic to the West Indies, or to one of the Southern Colonies, where the human cargo was sold for high prices.

All of the Colonies had slaves at first. But as time passed, slavery increased in the South, where plantations thrived on the labor slaves provided. Northerners did not depend on slave labor and felt more strongly about the immorality of keeping slaves.

From the beginning of a slave's journey, life was difficult. Slave traders crowded men, women and children into dark, narrow spaces on their ships. Many were kept chained to the deck. Without room to move or fresh air to breath, many died. On a ship carrying 400 slaves, as many as 40 may die on the voyage. The slave trade was so cruel that the United States stopped after 1801. But slavery continued until well past the middle of the century.

The Media Fights Slavery

Today's televisions, movies, newspapers, websites and radios can be used to persuade people to think a certain way. In the 19th century, books, brochures and newspapers were used in the same way to convince people that slavery was wrong.

Starting in 1820, a man named Elihu Embree from Tennessee published a monthly paper called The Emancipator. "Emancipate" means "to make free."

Abolitionists were people who wanted to emancipate slaves, or abolish (get rid of) slavery. Many abolitionists voiced their opinions through their writing. And the effect was remarkable: thousands of U.S. citizens came to understand the awful existence of slavery. They summoned up their courage and became a united front, helping many slaves to freedom.

Harriet Beecher Stowe

The writer who had the most effect on the abolitionist movement was Harriet Beecher Stowe, the wife of a Cincinnati minister. She wrote "Uncle Tom's Cabin" in 1852 and created a storm across the country. Her stories were based on the experiences of Josiah Henson, a Maryland slave, and made slavery more real to her readers.
