She sold more than 10,000 copies of her book in the first few days and more than 300,000 in the first year. The book convinced almost every Northerner to act kinder to African Americans. One person who escaped slavery said, "Since the book has come out, everybody is good to us. We find friends everywhere." People in the South were angry about the book. Later, President Abraham Lincoln introduced her as "the lady who started the Civil War."

Frederick Douglass

Frederick Douglas was born a slave but later became a famous abolitionist. He learned to read and write, which most slaves weren't allowed to do. But he also suffered numerous beatings and neglect, which was typical for most slaves at the time.

Douglass tried to escape several times and eventually fled to Massachusetts. He went to a meeting of the American Anti-Slavery Society where he was asked to speak. His words were so powerful that from then on, he was famous. Douglass traveled in America, Europe and Canada with his message that slavery was evil and should be abolished. He also published a newspaper called The North Star.

The Underground Railroad

You've decided to escape. Where will you go? How will you get food and shelter along the way? Who is it safe to talk to? Abolitionists knew slaves needed help, so they acted as "conductors" along the way to freedom. The system of safe houses, secret codes and hidden routes was called the Underground Railroad, based on something said by a slave owner who couldn't figure out how the slaves were escaping. He remarked that, "Theah mus' be an underground railroad outta heah!"

Harriet Tubman

By far, the most famous of all conductors on the Underground Railroad was a woman of great faith and a legend in her own time - Harriet Tubman. She was 28 years old in 1849 when she escaped from her master in Maryland and traveled on the Underground Railroad to Pennsylvania. She lived in Philadelphia for two years and worked hard to earn enough money to rent a tiny apartment and furnish it. Then she bought a set of men's clothes and returned to Maryland with the intention of helping her husband escape with her back to Philadelphia. Upon her arrival in Maryland, she was shocked to learn he'd married someone else. Harriet was heartbroken. But her faith and prayers saw her through, and she determined to help fellow slaves escape like she had. She risked her life 19 times on missions to free other slaves, helping over 300 people to safety. Two of those people were her own aging parents. For her brave deeds, she was nicknamed "Black Moses - the Deliverer." The South offered a $40,000 reward to anyone who could stop her. Thankfully, Harriet Tubman was never captured.

title: Western Maryland
text: Destination: Allegany County! Two mountain ranges in one county - wow! If you like the outdoors, you've come to the right place. Probably the best way to see it all is to take a ride on the Western Maryland Scenic Railroad (right). Riding a vintage 1916 locomotive along 17 miles of mountain scenery, you'll see the Cumberland Narrows, Bone Cave, the Brush Mountain Tunnel and, at the end of the ride, the Thrasher Carriage Collection. Transportation buffs can't miss the Transportation & Industrial Museum. Find out why rails and trails are so important to this great county. For something a little out of the ordinary, spend an afternoon at Constitution Park, the mibster capital of America. Marble players here are the best! But if marbles is not your game, try baseball, swimming, horseshoes, basketball, tennis or badminton - this place has it all. Have fun!

title: Does slavery still exist in the world today?
text: Unfortunately, many countries still use slave labor to work in farms, in factories or in homes. In some countries, masters are kind; in others, some are very cruel. The difference seems to be in the way the masters view the slaves: if they perceive them as people too, they are more kind to them than masters who see their slaves as less than people. Slavery no longer exists in the United States. The best way to make sure slavery never returns is to treat others as you would like to be treated.

title: White- Tailed Deer
text: This beautiful white-tailed animal is found in all 23 counties of Maryland. The deer feeds on twigs, leaves, forbs (weed plants), fruits and nuts. Breeding begins in September and fawns (baby deer) are born seven months later. The fawns are hidden for the first two weeks but follow the mother as soon as possible. The buck's majestic antlers are shed between December and March, and a new rack is grown every year. They usually appear in May. The deer loses its hair twice a year. On the sad side, there are many car/deer collisions every year. The deer's enemy is the coyote, wild dog, bobcat and cougar. The deer is very destructive to farmers' crops and home gardens. Hunting keeps the population down. The white-tailed deer is named for its large distinctive feature - that large, beautiful tail (or flag) - often the only thing you see as it bounds away from you in the woods.

title: Salem Poor, a Brave and Gallant Soldier
text:
Do you know people who you admire because of their ethics? What actions show that a person can be counted on to do the right thing? History has very few details about Salem Poor, an African American soldier who fought in the Revolutionary War. However, 14 officers from the Battle of Bunker Hill signed a document presented to the General Court of Massachusetts. It recommended that a soldier named Salem Poor be rewarded for his heroism. He is described as “a Brave & gallant Soldier.” That’s strong proof of Salem Poor’s ethics.

Salem Poor was born a slave in Massachusetts in the 1740s. He bought his freedom, married and had a son. When the war began, Poor left home to fight with the American colonists. Five times as many African Americans fought with the British because of promises of freedom. African Americans were not allowed to vote and faced many other types of discrimination.

For that reason, Salem Poor’s award is even more remarkable. The details of his actions are unknown. The document reads “…to Set forth Particulars of his Conduct would be Tedious.” But it does say “…under Our Own observation…we declare that… Salem Poor… behaved like an Experienced Officer, as Well as an Excellent Soldier.” From 14 officers present at the battle, that’s high praise indeed.

Some sources claim that Salem Poor shot and killed the British Lieutenant Colonel James Abercrombie at Bunker Hill. Other records show that he continued to fight in other battles. Like many African Americans of that time, exact details of both his birth and death remain a mystery. However, he was honored with a commemorative stamp in 1975.

title: How Do I Read Nonfiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring. But it really isn’t. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you will find it easier to understand—and maybe even fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/ effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will discuss classification.

Classification

With this pattern, the nonfiction piece is organized into categories or groups that share certain characteristics. In other words, the content is classified.

One idea for finding out how the content of a nonfiction piece is classified is to chart the information into categories. Charting information can help you see the categories graphically. You will also better remember the characteristics of each category.

Try It!

Here is a passage about the war between the states. Read the passage. Then chart the important information into categories.

title: Let's Write
text: Go to the Internet or phone book and find out who your state senator or representative is. Write him or her a letter about an issue important to you or your family. Suggest a specific solution.

title: Brother Against Brother
text:
Ben stared angrily out the kitchen window, across the yard and over the two hundred acres of Maryland he shared with his brother, Thomas. He heard Thomas shouting behind him and then the sound of his fist slamming down on the kitchen table. He wasn't listening though. In fact, Ben was ignoring his brother on purpose. He watched as five slaves moved slowly down the furrows in the field. They had come with the farm, most of them as part of the inheritance. As he watched them working in the sun, his brother's words grew louder and louder: "But Ben, the times are changing! You must realize it. The time for supporting the Union has come. Surely you can see that slavery is not the right way? Perhaps it never was . . . Ben? Ben! Ben, are you listening to me?"

Ben could ignore his brother no longer. He turned, and as he spoke, it was difficult to keep his voice from trembling. "Thomas," he said, "The way we live is the way our father lived and his father before him. The Union has no right to tell us what to do with our land, our laws and our slaves."

"Our slaves?" interrupted Thomas. "They're people, brother! I can see that now. Why can't you?" Ben turned back to the window. "There's nothing more to talk about, Thomas. If you turn your back on Maryland now, you'll betray everything we've worked for. You'll - " The kitchen door slammed shut. A few seconds later, Ben saw Thomas striding across the yard. Ben walked to the front door, ready to go after his brother. Thomas turned and stood for a moment. As they watched each other, they exchanged no words. Then Thomas turned and disappeared across the field. Ben couldn't explain, but somehow he knew that if he and Thomas ever saw each other again, it wouldn't be from opposite sides of the yard, or across the kitchen table. The next time he would see his brother, it would be from the opposite side of a battlefield.

title: The Civil War
text:
It was called “The Civil War” or “The War Between the States.” The bloodiest one-day battle of all was fought on Maryland soil, at Antietam.

What is a Civil War?

The United States has fought a few wars since it became a nation more than 200 years ago—wars like World War I and World War II and wars in Korea, Vietnam and the Persian Gulf. These wars were all fought by American troops in some other country, against someone else’s government or armies. A civil war, on the other hand, is a war between people that live in the same country. America’s Civil War was fought not against Canada, Mexico, France or England, but against America. It was Americans fighting Americans.

What Caused the Civil War?

Why would brother fight brother, father fight son, and people of the same nation rise up against their neighbors? This question is harder to answer than simply, “They were fighting over slavery.” The North thought slavery was wrong and it was a reason for war, but it didn’t cause the war.

States’ Rights or Federal Rule?

How much power does each state have to govern itself? The South claimed that each state’s leaders could decide for themselves how to carry on their business. This was called states’ rights. They said, “If we need slaves to help us earn a living, then we have a right to own slaves. If we want to leave the United States and form our own country, we have the right to do it.” The North claimed that a central leadership should make decisions about what individual states can and cannot do. They felt that federal rule (or central rule) was best and that states should stay together to form one country. The South said, “We’ll leave the Union and form our own country and army.” President Lincoln said, “Don’t leave—we must preserve the Union.” South Carolina voted to secede, meaning to leave and form their own separate country. The new leaders demanded that Fort Sumter, which was in the Confederacy (South), be turned over to its new, separate government. President Lincoln would not agree to it.

The South took the fort by force. Cannons were fired—the war had begun. It now became a contest to see who would win. Would it be state’s rights for the South or federal rule for the North?

Maryland Battles

Our state was in the worst position it could be in: right in the middle. We became known as a border state and many, many battles were fought on Maryland soil. There were seven major confl icts: Boonsboro, Folck’s Mill, Hancock, Monocacy, South Mountain, Williamsport and the bloodiest of all—Antietam. With so many soldiers coming into our state, Maryland residents had to make some big changes. Farmers’ fields were crushed from army camps, orchards were raided for their fruit, wells dried up after providing drinks for so many thirsty soldiers, and homes and churches were overfilled with wounded men needing medical attention. After the war was over, many people took what was left of their homes and moved elsewhere to start a new life.

Antietam

From Sept. 16-18, 1862, the Union’s Major General George B. McClellan fought with the South’s General Robert E. Lee. At times, the Union (states that wanted to say together) seemed to be winning. Then Lee would smash into them with unexpected force. Despite his relatively few numbers (the Union outnumbered the South two to one), Lee charged with all his troops, while McClellan held back a quarter of his soldiers. The result was not only the single bloodiest day in the Civil War, but the single bloodiest day in our nation’s military history. The death toll was a staggering 23,100 soldiers. Who won? No one. Lee ordered his troops to retreat back to Virginia without gaining one inch of ground.

The Angels of Antietam

The country’s men fought bravely in battle, but many women helped out as well. On Sept. 17, one woman arrived with a covered wagon filled with medical supplies from Washington, D.C. She set up a mini-hospital at the Poffenberger Farm on Monument Road. Soldiers knew where to go for the best soup, the cleanest water and the most compassionate care on the battlefield. Years later, in 1881, she would start the American Red Cross, but for now she was known simply as “the angel of the battlefield”—Clara Barton.

Another woman at Antietam was Franklin Thompson. Well, her real name was Sarah Emma Edmonds. Hundreds of women, feeling the need to save their country, disguised themselves as male soldiers during the Civil War. Sarah was the only woman who managed to do so successfully at Antietam. She served a full two years as a man in the 2nd Michigan Infantry, then later as a Union spy who got through Confederate lines 11 times without getting caught! Women who lived in or near Antietam also served as angels during the battle. Mary Bedinger Mitchell was only 12 years old in 1862. Her family’s farm, now known as Rosebrake, was just 3 miles from the battlefront. She recorded her experiences as she and nearly every other woman in the area aided the wounded. In her writings, she describes the noise, dirt, yelling and fighting first-hand: “An ever-present sense of anguish, dread, pity and, I fear, hatred— these are my recollections of Antietam.”

title: Courage
text:
On Dec. 1, 1955, Rosa Parks had the courage to refuse to give up her seat to a white person on a crowded bus in Montgomery, Alabama. She was arrested and tried. The result of the trial triggered a boycott (refusing to buy or use something), which was organized by Martin Luther King Jr. African Americans refused to ride the city bus until the laws were changed. It worked. Eventually, the laws were changed so that whites and African Americans were allowed to sit together.

When Rosa died in October 2005, her casket was placed in the U.S. Capitol for two days so that people could pay their respects to her. Usually only the caskets of U.S. presidents are placed in the Capitol. Rosa became the first woman to receive this honor.

The greatest kind of courage is to do what is right when others call you a coward or a chicken for doing it. It takes courage to stand up to people like that, but having courage will also help you be loyal, honest and responsible. Your parents, teachers, church leaders or good friends can help you prepare to deal with peer pressure and develop courage to face difficult situations.

title: Wat Bowie
text: Wat Bowie, a spy for the South, had escaped from a Washington, D.C. prison. Search parties were everywhere. One morning, around a campfire built with wood from a local farmer's fence, five men were startled by a tall man stumbling into their camp. They didn't realize it was Wat, but he sure realized who they were! Being the smart spy that he was, he came up with a plan to trick the search party. He pretended to be the farmer who owned the land they were on. "What do you think you're doing, burnin' my fence up! I know there's a war going on, but look around ya, there's plenty of good dry wood on the ground." The men apologized, after which they all had a good-natured conversation. Eventually, talk turned to the outlaw: "Have you seen Wat Bowie?" one of the men asked the "farmer." "He's tall, with brown hair and a mustache, and blue eyes." The group quieted as they realized how closely the farmer matched the description. Bowie didn't miss a beat: "Yes, I heard tell that renegade was here just a few days ago. They say he went on to the next county. I hear he's from up north a bit, so I'd imagine that's where he's goin'." Bowie stood slowly and said with a smile, "I sure am relieved to have met up with you here on my land! Anyplace else, I might a' been in some trouble. Folks do say I look a lot like the man." Bowie said his goodbyes and walked purposely away.

title: How many people were killed in the Civil War?
text: The Civil War was our nation's most devastating and deadly war. More Americans were killed during the Civil War than during all other wars combined. The war lasted between 1861 and 1865, during which we lost 600,000 soldiers. How can you comprehend that many? If each grave were 6 feet long and the graves touched end to end, they would cover a distance of more than 680 miles. That would be like driving from Baltimore to Canada. Traveling at 65 mph, it would take over 10 hours to drive by all those graves. What a great price our country paid to stay united and free from slavery.

title: Baltimore Oriole
text: As you know, the Baltimore Orioles are the best baseball team in the United States, featuring such "birds" as Cal Ripken, Eddie Murray and Jim Palmer. Oh, wait! This is supposed to be a wildlife article. While the ball players may do some pretty wild things, we don't think most naturalists would consider them "wildlife." The team's name does, however, come from one of the most beautiful birds in Maryland's skies. About 8 inches long, orioles eat fruit, nuts and bugs. They drink nectar from flowers. Parents keep their clutch, or group of eggs, safe in a grass nest hanging from a tree branch. Why are they called Baltimore Orioles? Legend has it that way back in 1629, George Calvert - also known as Lord Baltimore - came upon flocks of orioles while he was exploring the Chesapeake Bay. He fell in love with the black and gold birds, and some say he designed his coat of arms based on their coloring.

title: The Civil War Today!
text:
The Civil War began when Confederate troops attacked Union soldiers at Fort Sumter on April 12, 1861. The war lasted four years. The two sides fought over 50 major battles and hundreds of smaller clashes. The war ended after General Robert E. Lee surrendered to General Ulysses S. Grant on April 9, 1865.

2011 to 2015 marked the 150th anniversary of the Civil War. Many towns and communities took time to celebrate and remember this important part of our history. During those years, anyone who owned an iPad could “watch” the war happen using “The Civil War Today” app. The app showed users what had happened on that day 150 years ago. The app used pictures, maps and newspaper stories to show the events of the war one day at a time.

The anniversary has passed, but the app is still available. People with the app can look up any date during the war and read newspaper articles, letters soldiers wrote to their families and detailed descriptions of battles. If you or someone you know owns an iPad, ask for permission to look at “The Civil War Today” app. It can help you relive the drama of the Civil War with just the push of a button!

title: Pounded Plant Prints
text:
Materials

Several sheets of plain, ink-free newsprint

Just-picked leaves and flowers

Hammer

100-percent cotton fabric

Washing soda

Hard surface for hammering (such as a sidewalk or table)

Water

Soap

Paint brush

Bowl

Pan

Clothes line or dryer

Directions

1. Gather planets. Choose thin, flat leaves; juicy leaves do not work well. If you want to print flowers, choose small, bright flowers like pansies, violas, and baby carnations. Remember, you never know how the dye is going to transfer to the fabric. The surprise is part of the fun.

2. Cover a hard surface with eight to 10 newsprint pages. Place a piece of fabric on the newsprint. We strongly recommend testing several plant parts on scrap pieces of fabric.

3. Place a leaf or flower on the fabric. Cover the plant with a double layer of newsprint.

4. Hammer the newsprint covering the plant. The tannin coloring in the plant will transfer to the fabric. Carefully lift your paper cover to see if your plant design is transferring to the cloth.

5. Dip cloth in a solution of 1/2 cup washing soda to 2 cups water. The green tannin of the leaves “fixes” successfully with the washing soda solution. After “fixing” the colors, wash your cotton in soapy water, rinse and dry. All flower petals “fix” differently. Many pinks and purples “fix” aqua and bright blue.

title: Maryland Civil War Battles
text:
Look at this map of major Civil War battles in Maryland and answer the questions.

1. In what area of the state did most of the battles take place?

2. Which battle took place farthest south?

3. Which battle site is almost directly east of Folck’s Mill?

4. Place a “U” by South Mountain for a Union victory. Place a “C” by Monocacy for a Confederate victory. The remaining battles had no clear winner. Why do you suppose neither side claimed victory in these battles?

title: How Do I Read Nonfiction?
text:
Some people think that nonfiction literature is hard to read. Others think it is boring. But it really isn’t. Not all nonfiction tells a story, but it does have patterns.

Find the Pattern

If you will learn the patterns most common to nonfiction literature, you will find it easier to understand—and maybe even fun to read. Here are five of the most common patterns in nonfiction literature: (1) problem/solution, (2) compare/contrast, (3) cause/ effect, (4) classification, (5) main idea/supporting details. This week, we will discuss the main idea and supporting details.

Main Idea/Supporting Details

With this pattern, the writer presents a main idea and then backs it up with factual supporting details as evidence. You should be able to find this pattern when reading nonfiction because you probably already use it in your own writing.

One strategy for finding the main ideas and supporting details is to create an outline of what you are reading. With the outline, you will be able to see the main ideas at a glance. Use the main ideas as headings and the supporting details as subheadings in your outline.

Try It!

To the right is a passage about the Great Depression. Read the passage. Then outline the information in the passage so that the main ideas are the headings, and the supporting details are the subheadings.

title: Maryland’s Reconstruction
text:
Have you ever built a fort in your living room out of couch cushions, blankets and kitchen chairs? What if you built a fort and felt pretty good about it, but your little brother came in and wanted his blanket back and wrecked the whole thing trying to get it? Or what if your mom needed the kitchen chairs for dinnertime? There goes all your hard work! What do you think you would do then? Would you go to your room and mope? Would you shrug your shoulders and go play video games? Would you build another fort right after dinner?

Well, think about this for a second: the Civil War ended in 1865, and the United States had to deal with a lot more than a broken-down living room fort. The whole country was torn apart! The people couldn't just turn their backs on the problem and mope, and there were no video games in those days, so that left them with just one option: rebuild. Right away, people began to think of ways to make the nation better and stronger than ever before. That's why the time between 1865 and 1877 is sometimes called the "Reconstruction."

Just like most big projects, some of the ideas for rebuilding Maryland were bad ones, and some were good ones, but that's the rest of the story! So go ahead, open up this issue of Maryland Studies Weekly and dig right in!

title: Secrets in the President’s Pocket
text:
"The moment of truth has come. Is there or is there not an inscription?" These were the words of watchmaker George Thomas as he carefully took the back off Abraham Lincoln’s pocket watch at the National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C. Just like a scene out of one of the "National Treasure" movies, the crowd gasped when Thomas revealed that there was indeed a secret message engraved inside Lincoln’s watch.

Watchmaker Jonathan Dillon was fixing the president’s watch when he heard that the first shots of the Civil War had been fired. For nearly 150 years, rumors said that when Dillon learned that the war had begun, he engraved a message on the inside of the watch.

Doug Stiles, a great-great grandson of the watchmaker, heard the story when he was young and wanted to check it out. He passed along the rumors to the museum, and the directors decided to open the watch to see what was inside. Sure enough, the rumors were true!

So, what did the secret message say? The first line says: "April 13, 1861. Fort Sumter was attacked by the rebels on the above date. J. Dillon." A second line reads: "April 13, 1861. Thank God we have a government. Jonathan Dillon."

These words may not seem very mysterious, but just knowing that the rumors are true is important to many people. What was Doug Stiles’ reaction to knowing that his great-great grandfather left an inscription on the president’s watch? "My gosh, that was Lincoln’s watch," he said, "and my ancestor put graffiti on it!"

title: Reconstruction and New Cultures
text:
Once the chains of slavery had fallen, the African Americans and the European Americans had to discover true freedom - the personal power to choose one's own destiny and circumstances.

What'll We Do Now?

Even though the Civil War brought freedom to those who had been slaves for so long, many African Americans were without work and a place to live. Some European Americans tried to get them to go back to work on the plantations, even though they were free. It was a real problem! African Americans did choose to go back to work on plantations, but not as slaves. They became employees and were paid a share of the money the plantation owner made on his crops. It was a system known as sharecropping. This was one way former slaves made a living during the tough times after the war.

Fourteen for Freedom

In the year 1868, the U.S. Constitution was amended, or changed, to include citizenship, liberty and rights for all people, whether they were African American or European American. Amending the Constitution is a big deal! It had only happened 13 times before 1868. This was the 14th time - which is why it's called the 14th Amendment. It actually took many generations before African Americans were treated as equals. But the 14th Amendment was the first big step in the right direction!

Culture Explosion!

Our rich heritage of many nationalities and languages really took off during the end of the 1800s. New inventions opened up lots of opportunities for work. Thousands of immigrants came from all over the world to settle in the boomtowns of Maryland. Polish, Czech, Russian, Ukrainian, Greek, Hungarian, Lithuanian, Irish, German and Italian men, women and children brought their language, their religion and their crafts to America. While tensions between ethnic groups sometimes made it difficult to hold onto those cultural values, most families continued with their time-honored traditions - many of which still exist today. Growth and change were happening fast, and Marylanders did more than keep up - they led the pack! Immigrants coming to Maryland had to work hard, but they could count on a better chance for a better life and freedom to worship, speak, write and feel as they chose. In fact, freedom was their main reason for moving permanently to the United States.

Our German Heritage

For reasons from crop failures to overpopulation to religious persecution, Germans came to Maryland by the hundreds of thousands. Because of anti-Semitic (or anti-Jewish) laws in Germany, many German immigrants were of the Jewish faith. But the Germans in Maryland were the largest ethnic group to contain great numbers of all three Western religions - Catholicism, Protestantism and Judaism. Germans also left their home country after the ravages of war. In 1848, thousands of Germans unhappy with their government sailed to Maryland. They later came to be known as the "48ers." By 1870, more than half of the immigrants in Baltimore were from Germany. Ships carrying Maryland products to Germany returned carrying German families, mostly from the town of Bremen, in Northern Germany. These ships brought more German immigrants through Baltimore than any other port in America, including New York. In 1876, the Johns Hopkins University was founded in Baltimore. The school was modeled after the German system of education and almost all of its professors were German. Many universities today are patterned after Johns Hopkins. The year 1882 saw the most incoming Germans - 250,630 arrived in Baltimore.

Our Italian Heritage

Many of the beautiful sculptures done in our nation's capital were actually done by Italian artists. The most famous were Giovanni Andrei and Giuseppe Franzoni. Thomas Jefferson, who had an eye for great architecture, brought the sculptors here to America in the 1790s. But most Italian immigrants came to America without a job already in place. Starvation, overpopulation and the desire to choose their own leaders led them to our land of opportunity. From the end of the Revolutionary War to 1880, 70,000 Italians immigrated to America. That same year, a "Little Italy" in Baltimore appeared. So many Italians - craftsmen, musicians, teachers and mostly farmers who sold their produce at city markets - settled in the growing city that their own area was named "Little Italy."

title: Western Maryland
text: What an honor - to live in the first county to be named after George Washington. First stop: The Washington Monument in Washington Monument State Park (right). Not to be confused with the one in D.C., this is the first one built to honor our nation's first president. Climb to the summit and get a great view of the valley below! If you like camping on the "wild" side, you've got to go to Maple Tree Campground - so named because you camp out in a maple tree! If you've always wanted to sleep out in a tree house, here's your chance. While you're doing the outdoors thing, be sure to hike a bit of the Appalachian Trail, the most famous (and probably longest!) trail in the country. You geologists who love learning about how these mountains were formed should spend some time at Sideling Hill. When workers blasted through 360 feet of rock, they found millions of years' worth of history - right in the rock! See all the layers and read the displays about how they were formed. Happy traveling!

title: Is it Scot or Scotch?
text: You see the word "Scotch" everywhere. Most often the word is used to describe someone who was born in Scotland. "Scotch" is actually a type of whiskey. Also, it is the brand name of cellophane tape made by the 3M Company. "Scot," or "Scotsman," on the other hand, is the correct way to describe a person who comes from Scotland. Old textbooks use "Scotch" and the newer ones use "Scot or "Scottish." Most Scotsmen prefer "Scot" rather than "Scotch."

title: Large White Trillium
text: Everyone knows all about the red carnation, but how often do you hear about the large white trillium? The trillium is a showy plant. Its favorite month is May. Each stem of this plant bears three leaves, and the large white flower turns pink as it ages. It blooms from April to June in shady woods and thickets, reaching 8"-18" in height. It's not always wild, however; you can cultivate it in your garden. You'll see many trilliums when you visit the sloping hillsides and open woodland areas of Maryland. It's found in nearly every county in the state. American Indians used trilliums to make some of their medicine. The trillium is also the official flower of the province of Ontario in Canada.

title: Magnetic Money Clip
text:
Materials

One-dollar bill

Two metal paper clips

Directions

1. Explain to your friends that you have the power to magnetize the paper clips so that they will link themselves together in midair.

2. Fold the right side of the dollar bill over about a third of the way. (George Washington’s picture will be covered.) Do not crease the fold. Clip the two layers of the bill together, with the top of the paper clip at the top of the bill. As you do this, explain that George Washington did this trick first, and because every dollar bill has his picture, it contains some of that same magic.

3. Turn the bill over and fold a third of the other side, still without creasing your fold. Slide the other paper clip onto the top of the bill, but clip only two layers together. Both of your paper clips should frame the number one that appears on the front and back of the dollar bill.

4. Hold the edges of the bill and pull them quickly but firmly apart. As you do this, say some patriotic magic words such as, “By the dawn’s early light.”

If you have clipped the bill properly, the clips will leap into the air and fall to the ground attached to each other. Show the clips to your friends, and be sure to thank George Washington.

title: Why Should I Keep a Writer’s Journal?
text:
Have you ever had to write something, but you did not know what to write about? Have you ever had a good story idea, but when you started to write the story, you realized that you could not remember the idea anymore? A writer’s journal can help solve this problem.

Keep a Record

You can record your memories, observations and thoughts in a writer’s journal. You can even write colorful words and phrases or the events of the day in your journal. One very good use of your journal is free writing. Free writing is a kind of practice writing that allows you to sketch your thoughts and feelings without limits. Free writing can include single sentences or long strings of words that might not make sense to anyone else but you. You can even put drawings and diagrams in your journal. Just remember that no one else has to see your writer’s journal—unless it is a class assignment, and then your teacher will want to see it.

Here are some tips for starting your writer’s journal:

1. Find a special notebook to use as your writer’s journal. You should use a notebook that appeals to you because it is your very own journal. Your teacher may have some Studies Weekly Student Journals that you can use. Color and draw on them so that they reflect your personality. You can also use a computer or index cards in a box for your journal.

2. You should write in your journal when you want to. You might want to write in it every day or just once a week. You might like to write at the same time every day so you have a routine. Just remember that the more you write in your journal, the more useful it will be to you.

3. Find a special, quiet place to do your journal writing. Make sure you have all the supplies you need to keep your journal: pencils, pens, markers, scissors and glue.

4. Write whatever comes to your head, almost as if you are having a conversation with yourself. Do not worry about editing, rewriting or spelling until later when you transfer something from your journal into a writing project.

Try It!

Start a writer’s journal using the suggestions and tips we have provided. You will be amazed what you might discover about yourself.

Ideas for Your Writer’s Journal

1. Collect cartoons and articles to give you ideas for future writing projects.

2. Compose imaginary letters to people you wish you knew.

3. Record quotations, song lyrics, jokes, poems or riddles.

4. Describe interesting people and places.

5. Keep learning notes—Take notes about your learning process. Record new facts and ideas you’ve learned in school, write about the progress you’ve made in class and list questions you have about confusing content.

6. Record reading reactions—Explore ideas and feelings about what you have read. Write about your favorite character, predict what might happen next in the story, tell your opinion of the writer’s style or summarize the story. You can even tell how the story relates to events in your own life. What is interesting about the story? What angers, amuses or puzzles you?

title: Let's Write
text: What do you suppose your state will be like in 100 years? What will the world be like? List your predictions.

title: Fun Facts
text: The first hard drive available in the Apple computers were only a few megabytes. That is about the size of two mp3 downloads!

title: Baltimore: City of the Future
text:
So far in Maryland Studies Weekly, we've learned how things used to be here in Maryland. It's been fun and interesting talking about prehistoric mammals, land forms, wars, railroads, flags and, most importantly, people. What would history be without people's stories? In this issue we'll learn about a place where a lot of diverse people live. Diverse means from different backgrounds, having different religions, different cultures or even different languages! Today, Baltimore is one of the most diverse cities in the United States. Back in the 1800s, Baltimore was also a gathering place for people from all walks of life. Let's take a look at how this great city got started:

1729 - Baltimore Town is founded.

1800 - New banks, new stores; a harbor filled with ship builders, sailors, captains and fishermen makes Baltimore Maryland's economic center.

1807 - The College of Medicine of Maryland is started. It is later renamed the University of Maryland.

1818 - More tourists and more visitors mean more inns, more places to eat and more wagons: The National Road joins an already-existing road from Baltimore to Cumberland to lead west.

1828 - The first U.S. railroad, the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad (B&O) is built.

Late 1800s - Baltimore leads the nation in the Industrial Revolution, when there were major changes about how things are made. People in factories can food, sew clothes and put together machinery in faster, more efficient way.

Early 1900s - City water pipes bring water to all residents. Trolleys and a few cars hit the streets. In the Port of Baltimore, steamships rather than sailing ships become a more common sight. Goods are shipped here from all over the world.

title: Reduce! Reuse! Recycle!
text:
The Industrial Revolution brought a lot of great changes to Baltimore and to our state. But some of those changes were not for the better. Factories produced dirty air and water, cars emitted toxic fumes, and steamships clouded the air with pollution. This continued for many years. Now every person can participate in keeping our water, land and air clean and beautiful. Reduce, reuse and recycle!

Reduce means to "cut down on." You can do your part to reduce waste by using less of things whenever you can. Try using fewer paper towels to dry your hands, or use an electric air dryer. At home, use a cloth towel that can be washed again and again rather than paper towels that are thrown away. Many companies are also trying to reduce and make less waste by using less packaging materials. Have you noticed that some cereals are now sold in bags rather than boxes? To help reduce trash and waste, you can also reuse. This means that you should use items over and over before tossing them in the trash. Fix things that break instead of just throwing them away. When using a paper cup, write your name on it and use it all day long. Use empty plastic containers to store paperclips, marbles, or other small items. By reusing items again and again, you keep them from ending up in the land fill.

At home and at school, you should also be recycling as many items as possible. You can recycle plastic and glass bottles, aluminum soda cans and used paper. If your school does not have a recycling program, ask your teacher or principal about starting one. Talk to your parents about saving newspapers, junk mail and other items for recycling. If everyone does a little to help clean up our world, it can make a big difference!

To learn more about recycling, contact your local city government office and ask what you can do to get started. You will be surprised at how easy it is to help make Maryland a more beautiful place to live.

title: Famous Baltimoreans
text:
What would our city be without her people? Early Baltimoreans shaped the way we live today: the way we go to church, the way we study at school, the way we read, and even the way we treat each other. Let’s take a glimpse at some folks in the late 1800s who moved Baltimore into place as the City of the Future.

1. Rabbi Abraham Rice

Rabbi Rice was born in Bavaria. When he arrived in the United States in 1840, he was one of the first Rabbis in America. For the next nine years he led the Baltimore Hebrew Congregation. He also started an all-day, German-Jewish school — the first in the United States. When he heard that Jews in Israel were starving because of a war, he made sure shipments of food and clothing got to them.

2. Elizabeth Seton

Elizabeth Seton established the first Catholic school in America. But first, she had a pretty difficult life for a while. Her husband, William provided well for their family while they lived in New York. After some financial difficulties though, he became very ill. The family traveled to Italy, hoping the clean air and sunshine would revive his spirit. Unfortunately, he passed away, leaving Elizabeth with five small children. Soon after this, Elizabeth found out about the Catholic religion. She believed strongly in its doctrines and converted, even though her family told her not to. They were so angry with her that they would not help her support her children. She started a school in her home to help make some money. The school was a great success and she was invited by a Bishop in Maryland to come start a school in Baltimore, which she did. The school grew rapidly, as well as a charitable organization called the Sisters of Charity.

Today, many schools are named after Elizabeth Seton, even a school for homeschoolers — the Seton Home Study School. In September 1975, Elizabeth was granted sainthood, making her the first native-born American to be given such an honor.

3. Johns Hopkins

Johns Hopkins was a young man from Anne Arundel County who did not get to attend college, but who did have a quick mind and a generous heart. Though he had very little education, he knew how to manage money and became a great financier. He helped finance the B&O Railroad and then became director in 1847. In a time when people died from what are now relatively harmless diseases, Hopkins saw the need for medical research. Shortly before his death, Hopkins donated $7 million to begin a free hospital and university. It now bears his name — Johns Hopkins.

4. Roberta Sheridan

You might think that things were better for African Americans after the Civil War, but in some ways they weren’t. While young African American children were now allowed to go to school, their teachers were all white — no African American teachers were allowed. All that changed when a little lady from Colvin Street believed she could make a difference. With the help of Frederick Douglass and others, Roberta Sheridan began teaching at the Waverly School, becoming the first African American teacher in Baltimore City and in Maryland.

5. Isaac Myers

This expert ship-builder knew freedom meant more than just not being a slave — it meant equality. Before the Civil War, the shipping industry traditionally hired people from all backgrounds. But, when more white people moved into Baltimore after the war, many African Americans were fired to make room for the white workers. Isaac Myers became angry at this inequality and, with 15 others, organized the Chesapeake Marine Railway and Dry Dock Company — a workplace committed to fair hiring practices. He also helped organized African American workers into unions so they could help themselves gain the rights they needed. Isaac Myers was also one of the most important people involved in organizing the Republican Party in Baltimore — he believed political power came through economic, or financial, power.

6. Harry Cummings

Having an education wasn’t common at this time. But Harry Cummings worked hard until he graduated from the University of Maryland Law School in 1889 — as one of the first African American men to do so. Just one year later, he ran for the Baltimore City Council — and won! He was the first African American elected to the council. Through his position and determination, he helped other African Americans get scholarships so they too could gain the value of an education. In 1904, he gave a speech to gather support for a new presidential candidate. The candidate won the election — he was Theodore Roosevelt.

7. Enoch Pratt

Like Johns Hopkins, Enoch Pratt was a great businessman and philanthropist (one who gives to charitable causes). Born in Massachusetts, Pratt moved to Baltimore as a young man selling horseshoes to the army during the Civil War. He later became a banker and director of several transportation companies. He mostly educated himself through reading. To allow others the same opportunity, he opened the first free public library in Maryland — the Enoch Pratt Free Library. He believed books were for all people — rich or poor, black or white — and donated nearly $1 million to the library with the condition that it would always stay free to all. Soon after the library opened, it expanded to four branches. Today it has 25. Who was the first African American to get a Pratt library card? Harry Cummings!

title: Edgar Allan Poe’s Death: A “Purr”-fect Puzzle
text:
Famous mystery and horror writer, Edgar Allan Poe lived in Baltimore the last few years of his life, editing and writing for local magazines. Like his writings, Poe's death was shrouded in mystery: Baltimore newspapers reported doctors saying, "We have no idea what killed him, but the poor guy sure had gone bananas." Around Sept. 28, 1849, Poe disappeared without a trace. Five days later, he turned up at a Baltimore tavern in Little Italy. His clothes were dirty, his speech was gibberish and he seemed dazed and confused. He was taken to the hospital at Washington Medical College. After four days of sometimes muttering to imaginary beings in his room, sometimes lying in a coma and sometimes seeming quite normal, he passed away. He was only 40 years old.

Until recently, many believed Poe had drunk himself to death - he was a known alcoholic. But that didn't make sense because medical records showed he had quit drinking several months before. Also, the tavern owners and the doctors both described Poe as being unwilling to drink anything - alcohol or water - even in the hospital.

About three years ago, Baltimore Doctor R. Michael Benitez compared Poe's confusion, hallucinations and periods of seeming normal to what is known today about diseases like viruses, epilepsy and other infections. The conclusion was almost unbelievable - rabies! But how did he get it? Back in the 1800s, there were no pet immunizations for rabies. Poe loved cats and had several in his house. Who could have known that a simple nip from his pet could have caused such a mysterious and deathly illness?

title: How does the government get money to run our cities?
text: Our leaders decide how many new roads to build, libraries to renovate and museums to repair based on taxes your parents pay. Without the money from taxes, our government wouldn't be able to do much! You may have noticed that when you buy something at the store, there is a sales tax added on to the price of the items you buy. There is also a tax charged on the money people earn - income tax. So when you hear people complain about paying taxes, remember that the money collected in taxes is used to run our city!

title: Raven
text: Besides being the name of Baltimore's great football team (as inspired by Edgar Allan Poe's poem, "The Raven"), the raven is a beautiful but rare bird in Maryland. Only 20 nests are seen each year. After our NFL team won the Superbowl in January 2001, many fans believed the raven should be promoted to state bird along with the Baltimore Oriole. It didn't happen, though, perhaps because, like Poe, the bird has always been surrounded by mystery. Ravens are glossy, shiny black and can be confused for blackbirds or crows, which are usually considered nuisances. Ravens, however, stay away from people. They build their nests high in trees or on cliff walls along old abandoned mines. They are also quite large, growing to a length of 26 inches with a 4-foot wingspan. Despite the superstitions about ravens, they can be pets much like parrots. They can even be taught to mimic human speech.

title: The New Houdini
text:
Materials

Two pieces of string or rope (4 feet long each)

One door with two doorknobs

Directions

Tie loops into both ends of both pieces of string, using strong double knots that won't slip. The loops should be big enough for you to put your hands into easily.

Put each loop of the first string on the doorknobs of an open door, as shown.

Put your right wrist through one of the loops on the second piece of string. Pass the other end of that piece through the opening created by the string that's hanging between the two doorknobs and then put your left wrist through the empty loop.

Show your friends how you are "handcuffed" to the door. Ask one of them if he or she can free you without taking the loops off your wrists.

When they have all given up, explain that you are the new Houdini and can escape from anything. Take the middle of the string that is attached to the door and hold it together in a loop.

Push this loop through the handcuff on your right wrist, and then pull the loop over your right hand.

Pull away from the door, allowing the handcuff on your right hand to slide over the loop attached to the door. You're free!

title: Margaret “Molly” Corbin
text:
There are only two Revolutionary War soldiers buried near the Old Cadet Chapel in West Point Cemetery, and one of them is Margaret “Molly” Corbin. Who was this woman and why would she receive such a remarkable military honor?

Margaret was born in Pennsylvania in 1751. She was orphaned at age 5 when American Indians killed her father and kidnapped her mother. Margaret and her brother were away from home at the time. She married John Corbin when she was 21. John enlisted in the Continental Army when the Revolutionary War began. Wives sometimes went with their husbands to war. They helped with cooking and cared for wounded soldiers. Women often carried pitchers of water to pour on overheated cannons during battle. They were nicknamed “Molly Pitchers.”

But Margaret did much more than that. When John was given the job of loading and firing a cannon, Margaret worked as his assistant right on the battlefield. In November 1776, the British army attacked Fort Washington where the Corbins were stationed. During the battle John was killed. Margaret immediately began loading and firing John’s cannon by herself. What courage and quick thinking that must have taken! Margaret continued firing until she was wounded too.

Margaret was disabled for the rest of her life. Congress awarded her a lifelong pension (retirement pay) just as if she had been a soldier, something no woman had ever received.

In 1926 the Daughters of the American Revolution had Margaret’s remains reburied in West Point Cemetery with full military honors. A memorial plaque also stands near the battle site in New York City. It reads “Capt. Molly Corbin…the first American woman to take a soldier’s part in the War for Liberty.” Think of a woman you know who demonstrates agility of mind. Who is she?

title: How Do I Take Notes While Researching?
text:
If you haven’t already, soon you will need to do some research to write a report, study for a test or give a presentation.

Keep Track of Information

How will you keep track of all the good information you fi nd while researching? Take notes! Here are some tips for taking research notes:

1. You will probably find that index cards are the best way to take notes. You can write one fact or quotation on each card and then organize and rearrange them based on how you want to write your report, give your presentation or study for your test.

2. Label your notes with subject headings.

3. Paraphrase and summarize information in your own words. Summarize information by writing the main ideas and most important supporting details. This will help you prevent plagiarism, which is copying writers’ words without giving them credit.

4. If you like how a writer has said something, use a direct quotation. Be sure to record the quote exactly. Include punctuation and spelling just as written by the writer. Put quotation marks around the quote so that you know it is a quotation and not your summary.

5. Write down the title, author, publisher, city of publication, date and page numbers of each source after you have recorded the fact or quotation. This way, you can include this information in a bibliography, and you can go back and double check a quotation if you have questions.

6. Abbreviate the information you have researched to save time. Write in groups of words and phrases instead of complete sentences. Use abbreviations and symbols as long as you will remember what they mean. You can transfer the information into complete sentences later when you use it in your report or presentation.

7. Organize your notes into the most useful order for you, your report or presentation. For example, you can organize them by subject or theme.

Try It!

Do some research on the subject you are currently studying in social studies. Use research notes to record the information you find. Use the research notes to write a report or make a presentation, depending on what your teacher assigns. Be sure to always take organized research notes when doing any research. It will save you time in the future, when you start writing a report.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you’re on a mission to Earth from another planet. Part of your mission is to check out the planet and report back to your home world if you find places where your friends can live. You find a city in our state that you know everyone back home will just love. Tell us the name of the city you like best, and write a description that will make your friends and relatives back home want to go there to live.

title: Taking a Look Back
text:
Hey there, Marylander adventurers! This might seem a little late, but welcome to the 21st century! You've actually been living in this latest millennium for a while now. Still, you are probably pretty impressed by all the amazing, modern things that make life in Maryland easier. Today's hospitals, schools, grocery stores, movie theaters and theme parks all seem pretty cutting-edge.

But did you know that people had the same attitude a hundred years ago about their "modern" society? Man, what will people think of your modern lives in another hundred years? By then the future folks will probably think everything about your life seems old-fashioned. Let's imagine going back in time to see what we think about the past.

Go back about 15 years. There aren't any DVD or MP3 players, and most people aren't connected to the Internet. Travel back to 1990. Now only very wealthy people have cell phones. Add another 10 years, and nobody has a VCR. Go back another four or five years, and there are no video games. Next, jump about 20 years to the early 1950s. Now the coolest technology in town is probably your neighbor's new black-and-white television. Travel back another 10 years, and everyone in America is probably listening to a radio show each night. Finally, let's travel all the way to the year 1900 - more than a century ago!

Look around carefully. You'll see folks going to work, studying at school, and having fun. In some ways, they're just like you. But there are differences, too. Look at the way they are dressed, for example. Look at their toys and their tools. Look at the way they play sports. Look at the movies they see. (Do they even have movies?) And as you look around, remember - to them, this is modern living! Here at Maryland Studies Weekly, we thought it might be fun to celebrate the beginning of this century with a look back at the way the last one started. Turn the page, and come along!

title: The 1900 House
text:
The closest thing to time travel without actually having a real time machine might just be the grand adventure the Bowler family had in a beautiful old Victorian house! What's more, their adventure was right on screen, for millions of folks to check out! What was so special about this family and some old house? Was it haunted? Was there buried treasure under the floorboards? Or was it something even stranger?

The Bowlers were one of 400 families who applied to participate in a public television program called, "The 1900 House." On this show, one of today's families was "transported" back in time to the year 1900. Paul, his wife Joyce and four of their children took on the challenge of living as a typical family of the 1900s. The Bowler family had to wear clothes from the year 1900, as well as cook, do laundry, and care for their family just as people from this era would have done. And to top it all off, they had to do all this while television camera crews filmed everything they did.

Does this sound like fun to you? Do you think it would be easy? If so, think again! Imagine life without a bottle of shampoo close by; no Big Mac and fries anywhere in sight; and your favorite television show - forget it! The Bowlers found out just what it was like to live a part of history. They spent three months living in the 1900 House, without any of the modern conveniences that we take for granted. At the end of their experience they had a greater appreciation for all the trials their great-grandparents went through and were more than happy to "travel" back to the 21st century.

title: Into the 20th Century
text:
Do you ever wonder what kids in the 22nd century will think of your "modern" way of life?

Take a second to think about your cars, movie theaters, restaurants and even toys. Things are pretty different today than they may have been 100 years ago. Learning about the past helps us understand how things changed over time. So let's learn a little more about the early 1900s and what life was like back them.

U. S. Presidents

In 1900 President William McKinley was serving as the leader of the United States. He was elected for a second term in office, but unfortunately, his term ended without warning. A young man named Leon Czolgosz shot McKinley in the chest on Sept. 6, 1901.

Theodore Roosevelt was the vice president, so he was next in line to become president. Roosevelt was on vacation in Vermont, and he traveled to visit the president. McKinley appeared to be getting better, so Roosevelt returned to his vacation. However, McKinley soon died from his injuries. On Sept. 14, wearing a borrowed high hat that was the wrong size, Roosevelt was sworn in as the 26th president of the United States.

Transportation

When did you last take a ride in a car? Was it really exciting? It was probably pretty ordinary - rides in cars these days usually are. But in 1900, riding in a car was one of the most exciting things you could do. Many people had never even seen a car. People had lots of names for a car, like horseless carriage, motocycle, petrocar, locomobile and even names like mocle and mobe (pronounced like "moe-bee"). Many people in those days were worried about cars hurting people, so there were lots of traffic rules. In some places, an adult had to walk (or ride a horse) in front of a motorcar, waving a red flag and telling everyone to get out of the way. There were only 8,000 cars in the whole country, but they were selling quickly and becoming really popular. By the end of the decade, there were about 460,000 cars in the country. Today, there are more than 100 million.

Health

Think for a second about what you'd say are the biggest health problems in America today. Would you say cancer or AIDS? Maybe even the common cold? Doctors and scientists are still working to find treatments for these illnesses, but there's been a lot of progress over the last century. Some of the diseases that were really dangerous during the early 1900s aren't really a problem anymore. You probably don't have any friends that have to stay home from school because they have beriberi, rickets or scurvy. Maybe you haven't even heard about those diseases! Vitamins were discovered around 1906, and now we can take them to prevent these diseases. Even a balanced diet with lots of nutritious foods goes a long way toward staying healthy.

In the early 1900s, one of the biggest diseases was yellow fever. Not many people catch it today. A man named Walter Reed believed that sick mosquitoes caused the disease. But he had to prove it and needed volunteers to agree to be bitten by the sick mosquitoes. People were a little nervous, but it was the only way to test his idea. Today Reed is respected for his work. His gravestone reads: "He gave man control over that dreadful scourge, yellow fever."

Everyday Fun

Today you might spend an afternoon playing video games with your friends or jumping on the trampoline. But in 1900, bored Maryland kids got ideas from the "Handy Books" by a man named Dan Beard. These books has instructions - complete with pictures - for making all kinds of things, like boomerangs, razor-edged battle kites, Robinson Crusoe rafts, dolls made from corn husks, beeswax candles, walnut shell candleholders and even telephones made from tin cans. Kids could make everything from items they probably already have around the house. Well, with just a little imagination. Beard once said, "I'd rather be an American boy than president of the United States or anything else in the world."

Movies

Have you ever been really excited for a big blockbuster movie with special effects to finally make it to theaters? You've got to admit, movie producers can do some pretty cool things. Well it all started somewhere, so let's take a look back at the first movie with special effects.

In 1902, a man named Georges Méliès in Paris was filming a carriage passing by when his camera jammed. By the time he fixed the camera, the carriage was long gone. But a hearse was cruising by, so he filmed that instead. Then when he viewed his film, Méliès noticed something strange: a carriage rolled into view, and then - presto! - it seemed to change into a hearse as it drove off. This discovery led to a lot of trick photography that was used in movies.

Does that sound pretty simple? Well, movies back then were pretty simple. For example, the first movie with a storyline, "The Great Train Robbery," came out in 1903. It was only 11 minutes long. You might not think that's super cool, but folks in 1903 went nuts! In fact, there was one close-up shot of a bandit aiming and firing right at the camera. Movie-goers were so thrilled, they wanted to watch the scene over and over again.

Restaurants

When you are in the mood for something good to eat, where do you go? Do you grab a hamburger at a fast food place down the road? Do you find a chocolate-coated ice cream bar in the freezer? If you had lived in 1900, you'd probably head to the drug store. You wouldn't even think of that today! But at the drug store, you could buy a tall glass of plain soda for just a nickel. Add another nickel, and you could add ice cream. With just one more nickel, you could get something fancy, like a cantaloupe sundae, a grape lemonade or an chocolate egg cream. Plus, you'd have some change left over!

title: Southern Maryland
text: Our first stop in Southern Maryland is quiet Calvert County. Nature, water, lighthouses and even fossils await! For an interesting and unusual picnic, visit Annmarie Garden on St. John, where you'll see large and small sculptures and beautiful gardens all in one place. Situated on the St. John Creek, the gardens host special events like Halloween in the Garden, and Garden in Lights for the holidays. If you like lighthouses, you already know there are plenty in Maryland. One of the most famous is the Drum Point Lighthouse. Here you can climb up the stairs (watch your head, parents!), shimmy through the "trapdoor" and enter into a hexagon-shaped cottage - on stilts! Nature lovers won't want to miss the Flag Ponds Nature Park and Calvert Cliffs State Park. Both have great hiking trails, places to picnic, fish and swim. At Flag Ponds you can journey on a boardwalk through the wetlands, and at Calvert Cliffs, don't forget to dig for those fossils. Who knows? With more than 600 species of 15 million-year-old bones to choose from, you're bound to find something! Finally, for a not-so-quiet day, take everyone to the Chesapeake Beach Water Park where you'll enjoy a children's pool, 12-foot long alligators and snakes (pretend!), a seashell slide and a lazy river.

title: How does a cellular phone work?
text: In a cellular phone system the area covered by the system is divided into circular sections, or cells. Each cell has a transceiver (or transmitter and receiver) that is connected to the telephone company's central switching office. The transceiver has only enough power to reach a certain distance. A cellular phone has a built-in radio transmitter and receiver, but instead of linking to your telephone line, it links to the transceiver of the cell you're in. This in turn links to the central switching office and the telephone company. A computer in the switching office keeps track of the cell you are in and can automatically switch the link to another one if you change cells mid-call. This allows you to talk over long distances without interference or being cut off.

title: White Oak: Our State Tree
text:
The white oak tree has lightly colored bark which makes it easy to recognize. It is found in many parts of Illinois, Wisconsin and Michigan, all along the Eastern seaboard from Maine to northern Florida, and of course, in Maryland! The white oak can live as long as 800 years. It grows in the thick forest and is usually around 80 feet tall. The bark on the white oak is sometimes 2 inches thick. The wood is so beautiful and strong that it is often used to build boats, barrels, hardwood floors and even sculptures.

As you probably already know, acorns come from oak trees. Acorns are shaped like capsules with little helmets on their heads. More than 180 forest critters like white oak acorns better than any other kind of acorns. This is because white oak acorns are sweeter and more easily digested. Just ask any squirrel!

Not long ago, you could go see one of the largest white oaks in the world at Wye Mills, Md. It was more than 100 feet tall and 450 years old! Unfortunately, on June 6, 2002, a raging thunderstorm destroyed this symbol of our state tree.

title: Sharing Public Space: Susan B. Anthony and Equal Rights for All
text:
From the time she was a young girl, Susan B. Anthony believed that what was open to one person should be open to all people. As a teacher, she felt that having separate schools for girls, boys and free African Americans was not fair. She believed that the minds of all genders and races were equal and that education should be equal, too.

As Susan grew older, she joined other fights as well. She hated slavery and thought working women should be paid more money. She began fighting for women's suffrage, or the right for women to vote. She once was arrested for voting illegally and was fined $100. She wouldn't pay the fine. She said, "Trust me that as I ignore all law to help the slave, so will I ignore it all to protect an enslaved woman." Until women were allowed to vote, just like men, Susan felt they were no better off than slaves. She fought for this right until her death in 1906, but at that time, women still couldn't vote.

Susan's efforts finally paid off when the 19th Amendment to the Constitution was passed in 1920. It gave all American women the right to vote. In her honor, the amendment is also called the Susan B. Anthony Amendment.

title: What are Homophones and Homographs?
text:
Homophones and homographs are the same but different! To find out the meaning of a word, carefully read the words and sentences surrounding it.

Homophones

Homophones are words that sound the same but have different spellings and different meanings. You can remember what a homophone is by remembering that a phone makes a sound, so a homophone sounds the same as another word. It is important to know a homophone when you write it. If you need help with a homophone when you read or write, look it up in a dictionary. This will help you keep from making mistakes. For instance, would you write you have “bear hands” or “bare hands”? Here are some common homophones:

Beat, beet

earn, urn

eye, I

heal, heel, he’ll

made, maid

plain, plane

rain, reign, rein

to, too, two

Homographs

These are words that are spelled the same but have different meanings. Sometimes they are pronounced differently even though they are spelled the same. You can remember what a homograph is by remembering that a graph is something you look at, so a homograph looks the same. Here are some common homographs that are pronounced differently and have different meanings:

bass: a low voice

bass: a fish

content: things found inside

content: satisfied

minute: 60 seconds

minute: tiny

Try It!

The next time you are not sure which homophone or homograph to use, be sure you know the meaning of the word you are trying to use. This will help you spell it correctly. A dictionary will help you a lot!

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you’re a kid in the 22nd century and you’re looking back about 100 years. Your cyber teacher has given you an assignment to write about a technology that is no longer used, why it was replaced and what new technology replaced it. For instance, you could write about how wheels were replaced by anti-gravity thrusters. Pick anything we use now and tell us how it will be replaced in the future. Use your imagination!

title: The Roaring Twenties
text:
My name is Lois Thompson, and I was born in 1913 in Harford County. When my great-grandson, Thayne, was in the fourth grade and studying the 20th century in social studies, he asked if I knew anything about the Great Depression and the two world wars. Do I know anything? You bet I do - I lived those events.

I remember my father coming home from World War I in 1918. I was just 5 years old, and my mother sure was happy. The war was awful, but our country was really united. Then came the Roaring '20s. During this time, there was lots of money and food, and I became a flapper. We went to "talkies," danced the Charleston and wore dresses with fringe and long beads. It was fun!

But everything changed on Oct. 29, 1929.

The Great Depression

That date - Oct. 29, 1929 - is one that we "old-timers" will always remember. I was only 16, but I still remember the stock market crash. We were plunged immediately into the Great Depression. Our world caved in. Thousands of Americans lost their jobs. My father lost our home and the bakery he owned. Those were awful times. Even years after the Depression, I still couldn't bear to throw anything away. It was probably because of my leftover memories of my youth when I hardly owned anything. Our governor at the time, Albert Ritchie, worked hard to help find jobs for people like my father. Franklin D. Roosevelt became president in 1933. He also acted to provide food and jobs for Marylanders. My father finally was offered a job working on the National Road.

I was 28 when the United States entered WWII in 1941. By then, I was married and so sad to see my husband leave with the Navy. I didn't sit around and mope, though. I took a job at the Aberdeen Proving Grounds. We women were proud of the work we did in the war effort. Many jobs were available then, though rationing was in force. My younger sister Jewel and I planted a Victory Garden. The war that killed so many of our young men also put an end to the Great Depression. We were so happy to see our husbands return in 1945.

Times are better now, but I often think back to the events of my youth. Those days were hard but America was so united, and our values were firmly in place.

Lois Thompson passed away in 1996 when she was 83 years old.

title: Welcome Home!
text:
During the '20s, '30s and '40s, people were thrilled to have such incredible luxuries as indoor plumbing, electric lights, radio and washing machines. Today, our homes have become filled with gadgets that our great-grandparents could never have imagined. Technology has taken over, especially when it comes to our homes.

Many of today's new houses are filled with gadgets that make life more comfortable than ever before. There are showers that come on automatically and adjust to the proper temperature while the homeowner is still getting out of bed. Tubs can be programmed to fill themselves with warm, bubbly water just in time for the lady of the house to arrive home from work. Air conditioners and furnaces can be set to come on half an hour before you get home from school, making the house comfortable to welcome you home.

If you hate the annoying beep of your alarm clock, there is a gadget that will automatically open your blinds to wake you in the morning. Meghan Henning, a spokeswoman for the Consumer Electronics Association, says, "In the morning, instead of setting your alarm, you set the drapes to open so you wake up to natural light and the sound of music playing." What a pleasant way to greet the day!

A lot of the new technology used in today's houses can also be operated by remote control. "You carry this panel about the size of a credit card and you can turn on anything in your kitchen with it," says Henning. Some of the appliances can even be turned on while you are at work or school.

Other popular uses of technology in today's homes include wireless Internet access, sound systems that deliver music of your choice anywhere in the house and home theater rooms that include programmable popcorn makers.

Things have really changed since the '20s, '30s, and '40s. Technology is a way of life for families of the 21st century, making today's homes more comfortable than ever before.

title: World War I, The Great Depression and World War II
text:
World War I, the Great Depression and World War II were difficult times for the United States of America. Many men and women died in the line of duty for their country. This week let's take a look at how Maryland fared through these trying times.

World War I

In 1914, war broke out in Europe among many fighting nations. The United States tried to stay neutral, meaning we did not take one side or the other. But Germany would not stop blowing up our ships! Finally we had enough and joined the Allied Powers in 1917. The United States, England, France, Russia and Italy fought against the Central Powers: Germany, Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire. About 60,000 Maryland sailors, soldiers and marines fought in the war. Hundreds of women served as nurses. Back home, Bethlehem Steel Company helped make a lot of the ships for the U.S. Navy. Fort Meade and the Aberdeen Proving Grounds in Maryland opened as places to train soldiers and test weapons. To do their part to support the war, women worked in the factories and offices. In 1918, the Allied Powers finally defeated the Central Powers and ended the war.

Prohibition: 14-Year Failure

Many religious leaders in the United States were convinced that drinking alcohol was the root of all crime in this country. In 1919, the 18th Amendment made it illegal to buy and sell liquor. But it didn't work - people just started smuggling alcohol. Illegal bars called "speakeasies" opened, usually in someone's basement or behind a store. Sometimes drinkers even made their own liquor at home, and many people died of alcohol poisoning. Also, mobsters took over the illegal liquor industry, and crime actually increased! Finally, in 1933, Prohibition was repealed (officially taken back).

The Great Depression

You've learned that the stock market crashed on Oct. 29, 1929. But just what is the stock market, and how does it crash? Stocks are shares, or parts, of ownership in various companies. During the Roaring '20s many people bought stock in companies. They hoped the price of those shares would rise and that they'd get rich. But in October 1929, stock prices began to fall for several reasons. People started to worry and wanted to quickly sell their stocks.

So many people sold their stocks so quickly that prices fell to the very bottom. The stock market had crashed, or completely broken down. For many years the people of our country faced hard times. Many banks had no money left and had to close their doors. Companies had to fire lots of workers. Most people could not afford to even buy basic things. Eight out of 10 Maryland miners and steelworkers didn't have work. Our country's economy suffered the most during the Great Depression.

World War II

By 1939, World War II had already begun in Europe. Germany and Japan had started attacking and invading other countries, and it looked like there was no stopping them. The United States tried to stay neutral, but, again, the enemy would not allow that. On Dec. 7, 1941, the Japanese bombed the U.S. station in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. Suddenly the United States was right in the middle of another world war.

This time the "good guys," or Allied Forces, were the United States, England, France and later, Russia. The "bad guys," or Axis Powers, were Germany, Italy and Japan. Adolf Hitler of Germany was truly the worst of the bad guys. You'll learn in years to come about the Holocaust when Hitler treated Jews and others very horribly during this awful war.

Almost a quarter of a million Maryland men and women served in this war. Miners and steelworkers were no longer unemployed. They worked long and hard. They produced coal, steel, cement, ships, food, clothing and weapons. The Great Depression had ended, and nearly everyone had important work to do. Unfortunately, the war also took many lives - many Marylanders were killed or wounded trying to fight for what they knew was right.

What is Rationing?
