Rationing was done during World War II to establish a fair distribution of meat, sugar, shoes, gasoline, tires and automobiles. The plants that manufactured these items needed to concentrate on producing food for soldiers and sailors. Some of these same factories also manufactured ships, weapons, tanks and other items to fight the war.

The government issued coupon books full of ration tickets to every family, according to its size. So you not only had to have the money to purchase an item, you also had to have the correct number of ration coupons. Farmers were allowed extra coupons to purchase gasoline and vehicles because they had to grow the food to feed those who were fighting as well as those at home. Maryland farmers played an important role during WWII.

Each family had enough ration tickets - but just enough. There could be no wastefulness. The best way for Marylanders to help us win the war was to abide by this motto: "Use it up, wear it out. Make it do, or do without!"

Planned Communities

As you have already learned, cities usually start as small towns along a river or road. The horse trails through the town gradually turn into wagon trails, then roads. Smaller homes are built first, then are replaced through the years by larger homes. This is how most cities grow. But can you imagine a city being built within just a few short years? During the Depression, one of President Roosevelt's ideas to help people find work was to build planned communities. How wide the roads are going to be, how close the houses will be to each other, how big the houses will be, where to put the stores . . . everything is planned out before it is built. In 1936, construction began on Greenbelt, Maryland. It was a very pleasant place to live, with playgrounds, schools and homes all laid out in an orderly manner - all connected by sidewalks. Many people wanted to live in Greenbelt, so there was an application process. Greenbelt had some problems, as does any new idea. But, in general, it was so well liked that other communities patterned their plans after Greenbelt's plans. One you might know about is Columbia - hailed as one of the best in the country!

title: Rosie the Riveter
text:
The men who went off to fight the Nazis (Hitler's Germans) were not the only heroes of World War II. Back home, thousands of American women were called upon to join the war effort too. They worked as defense workers to build ships, aircraft and weapons. Women made thousands of bombs, grenades and mortar shells.

But life was not easy in these new roles for women. Factory work was hard and sometimes dangerous. Here's just one example: you know how sparks fly between you and another person when you rub your feet on the carpet and then touch your friend's arm? That's called "static electricity." The workers at some factories had to wear white cotton uniforms with rubber buttons and special shoes, all designed to reduce the risk of making static electricity, because those sparks would make the plant blow up. What a dangerous job!

Also, some of the men who stayed home during the war did not care for working alongside women. So many communities began putting up posters of a strong, hard-working woman. They called her "Rosie the Riveter." Seeing Rosie on posters, billboards and flyers encouraged many women to keep up the good work, despite the hardships.

title: What is a Victory Garden?
text: Hundreds of thousands of Marylanders planted gardens during WWII to grow needed food. If families grew the food they needed in their own backyard, the big farms could send more food to those fighting overseas. These family gardens were called Victory Gardens because the war had united all citizens in a spirit of positive thinking - thinking of victory. Throughout the country, approximately 40 percent of all the produce we ate during the war years was grown in Victory Gardens. Some of those same gardens remain today. They're devoted mostly to flowering plants and are kept as WWII memorials. Tourists all over the country visit them.

title: Know Your Animal Tracks
text: It's a beautiful day and you're hiking through the woods of Maryland with your family. You spy animal tracks in the soft dirt. Your big sister shouts, "A skunk has been here!" How did she know that? Somewhere - in school, in Girl Scouts, in her church youth group or from hiking with your family - she studied animal tracking and now she knows more than you do! Don't let it happen again! For starters, you can study this page. There are many more sources available for animal track identification. Have fun learning to become a real Daniel or Danielle Boone!

title: Dimensional Graphics
text:
To make dimensional graphic designs, begin by making a square, any size. The basic idea is not as difficult as it looks. It is simply a matter of drawing each line so it misses the oncoming corner. The closer together the lines, the better the results.

Materials

paper

pen or pencil

ruler

tape or glue

crayons or markers

Directions

1. Start in a corner and use your ruler to draw the line to the next corner but miss it by a little bit.

2. Next, ricochet off of that corner and go to the next and miss it by a little bit.

3. Continue doing the ricochet thing to the next corner, and after a great deal of going in a circle, you'll begin to see a pattern develop.

Extra Activity

After you do one design in a clockwise manner, try doing one with a counterclockwise pattern. Then put the two together. These patterns can be arranged and rearranged to make a number of fascinating designs. When color is added - wow!

title: What are Idioms?
text:
Have you ever heard an adult say, “I’m sorry, but we’re up a creek on this one”? What did he mean? He was standing on dry ground when he said it! Well, you’ve just heard an idiom.

Idioms are Not Meant to Be Taken Literally

Idioms are sayings that mean something different from the literal meaning of their words. “Literal” means “following the exact wording.” But idioms are not literal, so the words do not mean exactly what they say. Listen carefully for clues to figure out an idiom.

Try It!

The best way to learn what an idiom means is to learn it and use it in your own speech or writing. Ask someone what it means. Then use it in your own writing. Here are some idioms in sentences. See if you can figure out what they mean. Once you know what the idiom means, use it in your own sentence.

1. They were both so shy they had a hard time breaking the ice. Use “breaking the ice” in your own sentence.

2. When it comes to modesty in dress, I have to draw the line somewhere. Use “draw the line” in your own sentence.

3. By halftime, the game was in the bag. Use “in the bag” in your own sentence.

4. Chris and I are in the same boat because neither of us have extra cash to spend on the fi eld trip. Use “in the same boat” in your own sentence.

5. Would someone lend me a hand with the dishes? Use “lend me a hand” in your own sentence.

title: Let's Write
text: Do you know someone who lived during the trying times mentioned in this issue? Your grandparents or great-grandparents would be good people to ask. Interview them about rationing, victory gardens or Prohibition. Did your family lose anyone in either of those wars? You’ll learn many new things from talking to them— and probably enjoy it too! Write an essay about what they told you.

title: Thurgood Marshall and Brown vs. the Board of Education
text:
In the early 1950s, African American and white children attended separate schools - they were segregated. One little girl in Topeka, Kansas - Linda Brown - had to walk a mile through a railroad switchyard to get to school. The school that was closer to her house was for white children only. Her father decided to try to register her in the closer school so she wouldn't have to walk so far. But because she was African American, the principal turned her away.

An attorney from Baltimore, Thurgood Marshall, led the NAACP's legal department. He organized countless witnesses and evidence showing that having separate schools sent a false message to African American children: that they weren't good enough to attend school with white children. Also, he showed how segregation was unconstitutional because it separated people based solely on the color of their skin. This ran directly counter to the 14th Amendment, which granted African American Americans equal rights under the law. A relatively new organization, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), along with several other parents, came to the aid of the Browns. They were unsuccessful in getting the school district or the local courts to reconsider. So they took their case to the Supreme Court - the highest court in America!

In May of 1954, the U.S. Supreme Court agreed, stating, "Segregated schools are not equal and cannot be made equal, and hence [African American children] are deprived of the equal protection of the laws." Attorney Marshall had argued his case well. He kept working for civil rights for African American Americans and made a big difference. He even became a Supreme Court justice himself - the first African American member of the same court who upheld him in Brown vs. Board of Education.

title: Boom to Bust and Back Again
text:
You may have heard people compare the recent economic recession (2007-2009) to the Great Depression of the 1930s. But what some people call the "Great Recession" actually had more in common with a depression in the 1890s and something called "boom and bust."

In the early 1890s, the U.S. economy grew quickly ("boomed") but couldn't keep growing at that rate. When many companies and the housing market failed, there was an economic "bust." The railroad industry had been booming since the end of the Civil War, but in the 1890s more than 150 railroad companies closed. Other industries that depended on the railroads closed, and many people lost their jobs. Over 500 banks closed. Thousands of unemployed men marched to Washington, D.C., in 1894 to demand that the government take action to help families. Unemployment was over 10 percent for most of the 1890s. About one of every ten people had no job.

In the recent recession, the housing market slumped after several "boom" years. Some automakers went out of business and others filed for bankruptcy. The economy went "bust," just as it did in the 1890s. Hundreds of banks and thousands of businesses closed. The unemployment rate was about 8 percent - about one of every twelve people had no job.

Make a chart or Venn diagram that compares these two events in history. (Teachers: You can find background information and activities that relate to this article at hnn.us)

title: The 1950s to the 1970s
text:
Much has happened during this 30-year period in Maryland's history. Universities, golf courses, high schools, state parks, housing - everyone seemed to be building, building, building! See what more you can find out about these fascinating decades. (A decade is a period of 10 years.)

The 1950s

Chesapeake Bay Bridge

If you lived before July 30, 1952, and wanted to travel between the eastern and western shores of the Chesapeake Bay, you would have only two very slow choices. You could either take a long ferry boat ride or travel 130 miles over land north of the bay. But the Chesapeake Bay Bridge (also known as the William Preston Lane Jr. Memorial Bridge) was built in 1952 and cut the trip down to 4.3 miles. Now traveling from one side to the other was fast and easy. Once the bridge opened, the number of people crossing it doubled each year for the first decade. In 1973 a second bridge, identical to the first, opened. Today, more than 65,000 vehicles cross each bridge every day.

Friendship International Airport

On June 24, 1950, President Harry S. Truman dedicated the Friendship International Airport on a 3,200-acre site in Anne Arundel County. In 1973, the airport was renamed the Baltimore-Washington International airport (or BWI), and today it's known as BWI Thurgood Marshall Airport. BWI is one of America's busiest airports. Over 20 million airline passengers pass through the airport each year! It even has one runway that is almost 2 miles long. It also provides a bike trail that goes all the way around the site - 12.5 miles in length. No other airport in the United States can boast that achievement!

The Baltimore Orioles

The Baltimore Orioles started in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, in 1901 and moved to St. Louis, Missouri, in 1902. Back then they were known as the Browns. The Browns stayed in St. Louis until 1954, when they finally moved to Baltimore and became known as the Orioles.

The Orioles have had many top players, including Cal Ripken, who played in more consecutive games than anyone in history. When Cal finally took a night off, he had played in every Oriole game for over 16 years - 2,632 games in a row!

But did you know there was another Baltimore Orioles team? In 1914, the Baltimore Orioles were a part of the minor International League. On April 22 of that year, a 19-year-old rookie named Babe Ruth played his first professional baseball game. Babe had grown up in Baltimore and played his first game as a pitcher, helping his team beat Buffalo 6-0.

The 1960s

The Race Riots

Unlike many states during the 1960s, many Maryland schools, restaurants, public restrooms and apartments were open to people of every skin color. But suddenly people started thinking that African American citizens should not have equal rights. They started getting upset if an African American person was eating at a restaurant they believed should be only for white people. Sometimes people started fighting each other. There were even riots, when lots of people of both races started fighting, breaking windows, setting fires or destroying property. The rioting was so bad in Cambridge that the Maryland National Guard came to help calm things down. After Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in April 1968, there were riots in Baltimore and Washington, D.C. Even the University of Maryland, the first university south of the Mason-Dixon line to admit both African American and white students, canceled classes for a few days. In the end, moderates, people willing to negotiate, found ways to provide better jobs and schools for all people.

Columbia: a Planned Community

In 1963, a man by the name of James W. Rouse announced his plan to develop some farmland between Baltimore and Washington. There was nothing unusual about that. Maryland needed more houses. In just 10 years, the population of this small area had increased by 1 million people! But the development Rouse had in mind was just a little different: he would build a city with shopping centers, parks, ponds, schools and houses - everything a community needed. Other builders were building just houses, whose owners had to travel great distances to get to the stores and other places they needed.

More importantly, Rouse believed that everyone should be able to own a house, rich or poor. So he designed his city in such a way that people of all different incomes, races and religions could enjoy a better life together. Today, Columbia has 99,000 people - people who enjoy an easy commute to work in either Baltimore or Washington. Nine villages, 14,000 acres (5,300 acres are open space, never to be built on), and many pathways make Columbia a great place to live!

The 1970s

Modern Education

Ever wonder why you have to take all those tests in school? Well, it all really began in the early 1970s when businesses began complaining that their workers did not know basic reading, writing and math skills. So in 1977, the Maryland Board of Education created a program called "Project Basic." Together with 30 other states facing the same problems, Maryland decided on several areas that teachers could focus on in the classroom to help their students grow into more prepared adults. And before you could graduate from high school, you had to take tests that showed you really knew the right stuff! So, the next time you have to take that dreaded test, remember that you're on the road to becoming a great adult!

Washington Metro

Welcome to the second-busiest rail transit system in America! The Washington Metro has 103 miles of track and is the fastest way to get to Baltimore (or Washington or Fairfax, Virginia) from just about anywhere in Maryland. The idea for the system started in the 1950s. Workers started laying track in 1969, and the first part opened in 1976.

Today people leave their cars in large parking lots by Metro stations, hop on a train and let someone else drive them to work. Some teenagers even take the Metro to high school. The best feature of the system is that it helps cut down on car pollution.

Some people don't like certain things about the system. In a recent survey, people said their least favorite part was the escalators. Some think the station names are confusing. One station has a particularly long name: the U Street/African Amer Civil War Memorial/Cardozo station. However, everyone still agrees that life without the Washington Metro would be a lot more hectic.

title: Southern Maryland
text: Our second stop in Southern Maryland is in Charles County. If you like crabs, there are some great places to eat in Popes Creek. But for you historians out there, this place's claim to fame is Popes Creek Road, the road John Wilkes Booth took after assassinating Abraham Lincoln. Farther north in Charles County is Dr. Samuel A. Mudd's house, home of the doctor who treated Booth's injuries. If you like to fish but don't want to go through the hassle of getting a license, try Friendship Landing. Here you can fish for free, or go kayaking or canoeing. Fossil hunters, check out Purse State Park. You'll find some great fossils and seashells for your collections. For July 4, don't miss the Charles County Fairgrounds' grand fireworks display in La Plata. Finally, relax by biking, hiking or even in-line skating any of the county's many neighborhood trails.

title: Why do people riot?
text: It sounds like a horrible thing - and it is - but many times riots occur because people are at the "end of their rope," so to speak. Often rioters are normal, law-abiding citizens who have tried every other means possible to have laws changed to what they believe is right. But when they are with groups of other people who feel the same frustration, that frustration gets the better of them and they lose control. This frustration does not make rioting right, but is does help us to understand why it happens. What do you think are some better solutions?

title: Wild Turkey
text: The eastern wild turkey is a bird that once flourished in the woodlands of Maryland. It was eventually eliminated, however. But because of re-introductions and careful management, the Maryland Department of Natural Resources has restored this regal bird to much of the state. A good place in this region to view it is at Maines Pond near Freetown. In May and June, watch for hen turkeys leading broods of young birds (poults) into the grassy areas to feed on insects. Adult turkeys eat mostly seeds, fruits, and nuts, but poults need the high-protein content of insects. This bird grows to a length of 34 inches. It is too large to be easily confused with any other Maryland bird. It has a very large body with a small head, rounded wings and a long tail. The turkey is a ground-dwelling bird. Its head is unfeathered and often bluish in color. One group of people really loves this bird - hunters! Does this mean you can go out and shoot your own bird for that Thanksgiving dinner? Better check Maryland laws for hunting season rules!

title: Fairness Collage
text:
We are lucky to be living today when children of all races can travel, play and learn together. You can find many illustrations of racial equality in today's magazines and catalogs.

Materials

discarded magazines and catalogs

paper or poster board - 9 inches x 12 inches or larger

scissors

glue or glue stick

pencils, markers, colored pencils

Search through discarded magazines and catalogs to find pictures that can show examples of justice. These could be pictures of children sharing classrooms or playgrounds, children playing together on sports teams or maybe children talking and working together.

Directions

Gather pictures showing racial equality and fairness for all children.

Look for interesting letters and headlines that you can use for titles and captions.

Cut out the pictures, letters and words.

Glue the pictures on the paper or posterboard.

Add titles, descriptions and captions. You can use markers to write your own, or you can glue letters and words to your collage.

title: What is Etymology (et-u-mall-u-jee)?
text:
It is History

It might sound like some scientific field or medical study, but etymology is the history of a word. Did you know that words can have histories too? Where did words come from? Did someone just wake up one day and decide to name things randomly? Most words came about for a reason, and knowing the history of a word can help you understand its meaning.

Word histories can be fascinating. Some root words came from the ancient Greek and Latin languages. Others were borrowed from other languages, such as Spanish, French and German. And new words are added all the time.

For example, the word “kindergarten” means “children’s garden” in German. The term was coined in 1840 by Friedrich Froebel to refer to his method of teaching young children.

Try It!

Here are some words and where they came from. Do some research and find out what each word originally meant, why it was invented and how its meaning has changed. Your community library should have an etymology dictionary, often called an Oxford English Dictionary. And you can find information on the Internet as well. One good site is http://www. etymonline.com/.

Here is an example of what a passage might look like in an etymology resource:

1. Algebra—From Arabia

2. Route—From France

3. Zero—From Arabia

4. Bronco—From Mexico

5. Gorilla—From Africa

title: Let's Write
text: In a few decades, Studies Weekly might be looking back to the early years of the new millennium. What kinds of articles do you think you might see? What will your children find interesting about the time you live in now? Think of new technologies, important events, changes in traditions, advances in the sciences or influential people. Be creative— you can’t go wrong!

title: Taking a Closer Look at the U.S. Constitution
text:
Do you know where the U.S. Constitution was signed? At the bottom, of course! Seriously, the Constitution was signed in Pennsylvania. Just how much do you know about the U.S. Constitution? Let's take a closer look at this grand old document.

A constitution is a written list describing the duties of government and the rights of people. The U.S. Constitution is the supreme law of our country and the blueprint for our government. It defines the basic responsibilities of the federal (national) government, organizes the three branches of government (legislative, executive and judicial) and guarantees our basic rights. Whew! That's a great deal of work!

The Constitution also performs a tricky juggling act, balancing government powers in order to protect both the demands of the many and the rights of the few. It binds the 50 states together with a central government, while still allowing individual states to govern themselves. You could think of the Constitution as a police officer who lays down the law, or as your own personal bodyguard who daily defends your freedoms.

The U.S. Constitution was born during the hot summer of 1787, when 55 representatives from the original states met at Independence Hall in Philadelphia to create a new government for our young nation. Hammering out a constitution was no easy task. These representatives came from different backgrounds - there were lawyers, farmers, merchants and teachers, to name a few - and they each brought very different ideas with them. A great deal of arguing and grumbling occurred. There were conflicts between big and small states and Northern and Southern states, and there were disagreements about the size and power of the federal government. But the representatives' common goal was to build a stronger country, and their conflicts cooled into compromises (an agreement in which each side gives up a little). The Constitution of the United States was the result of their efforts. It was approved by a majority of the states in 1788 and took effect in 1789.

Our country has been governed by the Constitution for more than 200 years, making it the world's oldest written constitution still in effect. But that doesn't mean it has always remained the same. Over the years, the Constitution has occasionally been amended (added to or adjusted) to further explain government's responsibilities and to increase protection of our freedoms.

Shortly after the Constitution took effect, a group of 10 amendments was added. These first 10 amendments are known as the Bill of Rights. They list several basic freedoms that cannot be taken away from any U.S. citizen, such as freedom of speech, freedom of the press, freedom of religion, freedom of peaceful assembly and many other rights that allow each of us to live our lives the way we want.

The Constitution is only amended to correct very rare and critical issues. For example, the 13th Amendment (adopted in 1865) outlawed slavery in the United States. And the 19th Amendment (added in 1920) guaranteed the right to vote to women across the country. So far, the Constitution has been amended 27 times.

The Constitution of the United States is not just some dusty old document penned on crumbling parchment paper. It is a respected, powerful guardian that provides the government organization and the freedoms that make the United States of America one of the greatest countries in the world.

title: Maryland State Government
text:
Government by the People for the People

Like each of the 50 states, Maryland has its own state government. It operates out of Maryland's capital, Annapolis. This is where the governor, the head of Maryland's government, works. The governor runs more than 20 different agencies or departments. In Maryland, citizens elect a new governor for a term of four years. A term is the length of time an elected official stays in office. Citizens can elect the same governor for a second term but not for longer - the same rules as for the U.S. president.

The governor makes decisions about how the state should be run. He or she decides on such things as new laws and how to spend state money. He also appoints people to certain positions in the government. Maryland also has a lieutenant governor who also is elected to office. This person helps the governor run the state and leads the meetings of the state senate. Also, if anything ever happened to the governor, or if he was given another assignment by the president, the lieutenant governor would act in the governor's place until the governor's term was over.

The Executive Branch

This branch of government manages and makes decisions. The governor is the head of the executive branch. The governor carries out the Maryland state laws and decides how to run the state. He or she decides on things such as new laws and how to spend state money. The governor also gets to choose people who help run the state. Dozens of state departments and agencies report to the governor, such as the attorney general, the departments of agriculture, education and health services. The governor certainly keeps busy! The governor also has veto power. This means he or she can say no to any bill. A bill is an idea for a new law.

Maryland also has a lieutenant governor who is elected into office. This person helps the governor run the state and leads the state senate meetings. If anything ever happened to the governor, or if the governor received an assignment from the U.S. president, the lieutenant governor would fill in until the end of the term. In Maryland, citizens elect a new governor for a term of four years. A term is the length of time an elected official stays in office. Citizens can elect the same governor for a second term but not for longer - the same rules as for the U.S. president.

The Judicial Branch

The judicial branch's job is to interpret or explain what the laws of our state mean. This branch is made up of judges and courts. Maryland's highest court is called the Court of Appeals. The Court of Appeals has seven justices who look over very important court cases from lower Maryland courts. The justices decide if the lower courts handled cases properly. They also review any laws passed by the General Assembly and make sure they are constitutional, or that they agree with the state constitution. The Court of Appeals will reject a law if it doesn't agree with the constitution.

The Legislative Branch

The legislative branch makes the laws. This branch includes the General Assembly, which is made up of two parts: the Senate and the House of Representatives. These elected officials write bills and vote to decide if these bill should become laws.

There are representatives for every Maryland citizen in the legislative branch. Do you know who your senator or delegate is? There is certainly a lot you can learn about Maryland's government, isn't there?

From an Idea to a Law

Here's an example of how a kid just like you was responsible for an idea becoming a law in Ohio, a state not too far from us!

In 1991, Jacob Mercer, a fourth-grader in Fairborn, near Dayton, discovered that Ohio did not have a state reptile. The Buckeye State had a state flower, a state animal, even a state drink (tomato juice) - but no reptile.

Jacob suggested that the black racer be made Ohio's state reptile. He shared his idea with his state senator, Merle Grace Kearns. Senator Kearns agreed to introduce a bill in the Senate. The bill became known as Senate Bill 250. Jacob even gave a speech before the Senate - and they approved the bill! Then they sent the bill to the House of Representatives. The members of the House listened to discussions about the bill and approved it. Then the bill was approved by (then) Governor Voinovich.

On Aug. 25, 1995, the bill became a law and now Ohio has a state reptile - the black racer! (Can you think of an idea you'd like to see become a law in Maryland?)

title: Bill Hill
text: Bill Hill - This illustration explains how bills become laws in Maryland. All laws start out as bills, which are usually written by Senators or members of the House of Delegates. A bill can be introduced by citizens, special-interest groups or the governor. Even schoolchildren have introduced bills into Congress that were then voted into law.

title: The Three-Legged Stool
text:
Pretend you won a contest that lets you be the Maryland governor for just one day. You start by sending your whole school to Disney World for spring break. Then you order the state police to arrest that bully down the street from you. Next, you order the school cafeteria to supply ice cream sundaes for afternoon break every day. Wow! That sounds like fun!

Have you ever tried to sit on a two-legged stool? You can't. You'd tip over. Your stool needs at least three legs. The founders of our U.S. government had the same idea. They created a three-legged government - with legislative, executive and judicial branches. The three legs form a system of checks and balances. If you, as governor, sent your school to Disney World, the people in Congress would gang up on you. They would go to the state Supreme Court and complain, "That's the craziest, dumbest idea we ever heard!" The court would agree. This is how all three branches work together to balance and keep each other in "check."

title: Two-Party System
text:
Which are best - Democrats or Republicans? This is a hard question to answer, because both parties have good qualities. While the two belief systems often seem to oppose each other, the ideal government operates best when Republicans and Democrats work together for the common good while still keeping their individual personalities - much like the ideal marriage. Look again at the eagle to your left. Can you imagine this bid with only one wing? It takes both the left wing and the right wing for this mighty bird to take flight!

Democratic Party

Thomas Jefferson founded the Democratic Party in 1792. The Populist Party was the popular party of that time. The new party was called the "party of the common man" and its official name was the Democratic-Republicans. In 1800, Thomas Jefferson was elected as the first Democratic president. The name was shortened to Democratic Party. The donkey is the symbol used to represent the Democratic Party.

Republican Party

This party is nicknamed the GOP for "Grand Old Party." It was founded in 1854 when the issue of slavery forced a division between the existing Whig and Democratic-Republican parties. The new party was founded on the idea of keeping government out of people's social and financial lives. Abraham Lincoln was the party's first president. This elephant is the symbol used to represent the Republican Party.

title: Governor Larry Hogan
text:
Lawrence J. Hogan, Jr. was elected governor of Maryland in November 2014. When he took office a few months later, he knew he had a big job to do.

Governors make important choices about how to spend tax money in their state. They have to decide how much should go to schools, police or farms. Before tax money can be spent, state leaders meet to talk about what the state needs and how much money they have to spend. Governor Hogan works with people all over our state to see what needs to be done.

Larry Hogan was born in 1956 and grew up in Landover. His father was also a politician. As a young man, Hogan helped his father run for office. After Hogan finished college, he started working for his father in Maryland. His father left politics a few years later, and Hogan started his own real estate company.

As time passed, Hogan decided he wanted to be involved in government again. Since taking office in 2015, Hogan has worked to cut taxes and bring jobs into our state. Governor Hogan and his wife, Yumi, have three daughters named Julie, Jaymi and Kim.”

title: Let's Write
text:
1. Use a semicolon to join parts of a compound sentence when a conjunction like “or,” “but,” or “and” is not used. (I am not sick today; I should go to school.”

2. Use a semicolon to join independent clauses that are subdivided by commas, even if a conjunction is used. (I love dodge ball, jump rope and hopscotch; but we could not go out today because of the weather.)

3. Use semicolons to join parts of a series that contain commas within them. (On our trip, we want to visit Omaha, Nebraska; Kansas City, Missouri; and Chicago, Illinois.)

Use semicolons where appropriate in this week’s Let’s Write.

If you had the chance to meet someone famous, who would you choose? Why? What would you ask him or her?

title: How Do I Give an Oral Presentation?
text:
Standing in front of a crowd and telling them what you think is not easy, but it can be done if you prepare well!

Preparing for an Oral Presentation

1. Know your audience. What you say should be directed toward them. Is it to be given in your classroom? This will make it easier!

2. How long should it be? If your teacher says 15 minutes, stick to the time.

3. What’s the topic? Did your teacher assign it? Make sure you can cover it in within the time limit.

4. Make notes. Use index cards and put them in the order you want to use them. Index cards are not so large that they cover your face. You may write your presentation on numbered pieces of paper, but do not staple the pages.

5. Practice, practice and practice some more!

Making the Oral Presentation

1. Introduction—Get the audience’s attention with the introduction. You can do this by asking a question, telling a story, using a quotation or making a statement. Once you have their attention, state your topic.

2. Body—State your main points and give information that support your main points. You may ask rhetorical questions, (questions that don’t need answers) use emotional words or repeat important information.

3. Conclusion—Repeat your main point. Conclude with something that leaves a lasting impression by asking a rhetorical question, making an emotional plea or using a quotation, story or statement.

Try It!

When you’re asked to give an oral presentation, make sure you prepare well. Organize logically. Practice, practice, practice. Good luck!

title: Amazing Maryland Women
text:
Welcome back to Maryland Studies Weekly, the paper that teaches you all about what great men have done to make Maryland the amazing state it is today. There have been some amazing men in this state all throughout history. Hey, wait a second - men aren't the only people in the world! What about the women? Aren't there any females in the story of Maryland's history?

Where would all those men be without women in the first place? Women have been working, thinking, fighting, writing and exploring right from the beginning to make this a great state in a great country. And they're still doing it!

We've discussed several great Maryland women in prior issues. We talked about American Indian women, Queen Henrietta Maria and Margaret Brent in the fall issues. Then there were Mary Katherine Goddard, Harriet Tubman and Harriet Beecher Stowe, the legendary writer who helped many people see the horrors of slavery. Clara Barton, Sarah Emma Edmonds, Mary Bedinger Mitchell and their Civil War sisters taught us how to stand behind our nation. And where would Baltimore be without Elizabeth Seton and Roberta Sheridan?

Women all over Maryland today are flying planes, fighting fires, writing books, taking care of families, running companies, making laws, arresting bad guys and selling cars. This week in Maryland Studies Weekly you'll meet some women who have helped put our state on the map. Some of them are Maryland natives. Other women proudly say, "I wasn't born in Maryland, but I got here as fast as I could!"

title: Research Shows Madagascar Was Founded by Women
text:
Picture an ancient ship full of explorers, searching for a new land. Many people would imagine that such a ship was filled with male passengers and crew. Though many explorers were men, scientists have discovered that the founders of Madagascar were a group of 30 women who traveled a long way from their home!

Madagascar is an island off the east coast of Africa in the Indian Ocean. The women's ship traveled 5,000 miles from Indonesia to Madagascar, stranding them there. How do scientists know this? DNA researchers have studied 3,000 blood samples of people from Indonesian islands and compared them to samples from 300 people from Madagascar (called the Malagasy).

They discovered that many Malagasy have an Indonesian gene in their DNA. This gene was passed down from generation to generation of Malagasy. Computer simulations have calculated that only 30 Indonesian women were responsible for beginning the Madagascar population about 1,200 years ago. Most people from Madagascar today have a mix of Indonesian and African DNA, and are descended from these 30 women.

Researchers have also been able to trace a special chromosome that is only found in men in the Malagasy people. Can you guess where it came from? If you guessed Indonesia, you are right! It looks like a few men as well as women sailed on that ship to Madagascar so long ago.

Reference: History News Network (hnn.us)

title: Maryland's Great Women
text:
Here are a few past and present great Maryland women. Who knows? Maybe some of the girls in your class will turn out to be featured as "great women of Maryland"!

Rachel Carson

Rachel Carson (1907 - 1964) was a writer and scientist who specialized in the study of nature. During the Depression, she wrote radio scripts for the U.S. Bureau of Fisheries and articles for the Baltimore Sun. Later, she became editor-in-chief of all publications for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Rachel became concerned about a chemical called DDT that was sprayed on crops to kill bugs. In 1962, she wrote "Silent Spring," a book that tells of the dangers of DDT. She also wrote several children's books, which often showed how we humans are but a small part of the whole Earth and yet what we do (for good or bad) can have irreversible effects. Two of the best-known books are "The Sea Around Us" and "Silent Spring." She once said, "The more clearly we can focus our attention on the wonders and realities of the universe about us, the less taste we shall have for destruction."

Connie Chung

Connie Chung has been in the spotlight since 1993, as a major newscaster for such well-known TV shows as "CBS Evening News" and "20/20." But she has actually been working on TV since 1971, when she started in the Washington, D.C. area for CBS.

She is the daughter of Chinese immigrant parents and has nine brothers and sisters! She was the only one of the 10 children born in the United States. Connie graduated from the University of Maryland and has won numerous awards, including three Emmy awards.

Dr. Helen Taussig

Helen was born in 1898. When she was growing up, her father did not have much hope for her future. Her mother died when she was 11, and young Helen fought tuberculosis, as well as dyslexia, a learning disability that makes reading difficult. This led to some very poor grades. But she eventually taught herself to read, and accomplishments followed quickly. Helen got her medical degree from Johns Hopkins and did a great deal of research on heart problems, especially in babies. She was one of the pioneers of open-heart surgery, using her special skills of observation and touch to understand better the relationship of the heart to the health of newborn babies. She discovered a method to help blue babies, babies born with a bluish color because they are not getting enough oxygen. This operation has since been used to save tens of thousands of babies. Dr. Taussig passed away in 1986.

Annie Oakley

Some of you may have heard of the musical "Annie Get Your Gun" - the story of a backwoods girl who became a celebrity due to her expert shooting. Well, the story is true! One of the most amazing shooters in history was ... a woman! Born in 1860, Annie Oakley, who lived in Cambridge for several years, was well known for her amazing prowess with a rifle. She toured all over the country and around Europe, with Buffalo Bill Cody. The show included not only her talents, but also those of cowboys, American Indians and storytellers. Once Annie even shot the ashes off the cigar of a dignitary! Annie's husband was a good friend with Thomas Edison, so guess who became one of the first stars of motion pictures? Annie performed her shooting skills so that Edison could try to track the bullets on film.

Lizette Reese

Lizette Woodworth Reese was a poet born in 1856 in Waverly, Maryland. She taught school at the Western High School in Baltimore for over 20 years. She started her career as a poet in 1874 and published until 1886, after which she took a 24-year break from poetry! After that, her pen again flowed with verse, with books and poems being published even until 1936 (a year after her death). One of her most interesting quotes was "The old faiths light their candles all about, but burly Truth comes by and puts them out." Talk about what that means with a partner.

Billie Holliday

Billie Holliday was one of the greatest jazz singers of all time. Legend has it her singing career began when she heard the music of Louis Armstrong and Bessie Smith played on a Victrola (an old-time record player). She was busy scrubbing floors in Baltimore, but knew good music when she heard it. Billie went on to sing with famous jazz musicians like Count Basie, Artie Shaw and Benny Goodman and even wrote some of her own songs. Her favorite was "God Bless the Child." She recorded over 200 songs, but never made any money from these records! One of her trademarks was the white gardenias she wore in her hair. Sadly, Billie's music was silenced when she died at the young age of 44.

title: Shoshana Cardin
text: Named one of America's 100 Most Influential Women, Shoshana Cardin (born in 1926) has helped hundreds of people better understand Jewish heritage. She is a strong leader and has met with many famous and important people like past presidents George Bush (U.S.) and Mikhail Gorbachev (USSR). Meeting people like that can be scary, but legend tells us that Ms. Cardin had a special experience that to this day gives her courage when meeting new people. In her early days of teaching, she was assigned a particularly difficult class. Many teachers had already quit because these students were so mean. When Ms. Cardin told the class that she was to be their new teacher, one very feisty boy retorted, "Don't worry, we'll get rid of you too - just like we did all the others!" Ms. Cardin walked slowly up to his desk and asked, "What did you say?" He smirked and replied, "I'll bet anyone in this room a nickel that I'm not afraid to punch your lights out!" The room was silent. Ms. Cardin walked back to her desk, pulled her purse out of the drawer, dug around a bit and found a nickel. She quietly put the nickel on the kid's desk. He couldn't believe it. All he could do was stare at her. She never had problems with him again. Later in life, Ms. Cardin was quoted as saying, "The reason why I had the courage to meet with all of those famous people is because of that student." Sometimes we never know what good can come out of such bad situations.

title: Striped Bass
text: When the striped bass, also called rock fish, was named the state fish in 1965, the General Assembly had this to say: "In [our] judgment . . . it is a simple act of justice and of equity that this fine old Maryland fish should be honored by being designated the official fish of the State of Maryland." If you ever go fishing you know rock fish are not hard to spot - green on the back, silver on the sides and a white belly with long, dark stripes from head to tail (hence the name striped bass). Rock fish swim in the ocean but they lay their eggs in fresh water rivers and streams in late spring. They can live as long as 30 years! People love to fish for striped bass - their size and strength make them a challenge to catch. The record has not been beaten since 1995 when one was caught in the Chesapeake Bay weighing 67 pounds, 8 ounces!

title: Ojo de Dios
text:
This is an authentic and beautiful American Indian design.

Materials

popsicle sticks or tongue depressors

glue

yarn

pompoms

Directions

Find two popsicle sticks or tongue depressors. Glue them into a cross. Start the weaving by gluing the yarn to the back side of the sticks.

Start a crisscross pattern with the yarn. Continue to loop the yarn around the four ends of each stick. Keep the yarn fairly tight.

Continue the same pattern development, remembering to loop the yarn over each stick end in a like manner. Other colors may be added by tying new string to the old yarn. Make sure the knot is hidden behind the stick.

The work can be finished by tying the remaining yarn end onto the back of the design. Small pompoms can be attached to the end of the sticks.

Extra Activity

After you have mastered a small one, try a larger one!

title: How Do I Listen to an Oral Presentation?
text:
Listen closely to your classmates when they give presentations. Pay attention. You can learn a lot from them. Your teacher may tell you to take notes. You may also be asked to make written comments. Also, it’s just plain polite to be a good listener!

1. Be an active listener. Don’t daydream. Focus on the speaker’s main idea. Listen for the way he or she ties details to that main idea. Take notes, either in your mind or on paper.

2. Your teacher may help you to evaluate (to examine and judge carefully) your classmates’ presentations. Keep in mind that being honest can help your classmates learn how to give better presentations.

3. You may not agree with everything the speaker says, but you should listen to his or her ideas.

4. Don’t interrupt your classmate unless he or she has asked for you to join in.

5. Think about the speaker’s conclusion. Is it logical?

Try It!

When your classmates give presentations, be a good listener. It will help them feel more comfortable. Make eye contact. Your evaluation will help them improve their future presentations. And you might learn something. Besides, you will want them to listen to you when it is your turn to give an oral presentation.

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you are a travel agent in our state. Write about a place you would recommend that tourists see. Why do you think it’s a nice place to visit? What kinds of things will visitor learn at this place?

title: The Building Blocks
text:
Last week in Maryland Studies Weekly, we learned about some very amazing Maryland women who have made a difference in our society. Now it's time to learn more about the men. All of these amazing people, both men and women, are great examples of some of the things you can do too!

What do you want to be when you grow up? Do you like the excitement of a life in the big city, doing business with the big guys? Would you rather own a restaurant, cooking up the best grub east of the Mississippi? Maybe you'd like to write detective novels, books that will make people all across the country shiver into the late night hours, as they curl up in a cozy blanket and sip from a mug of hot cocoa. Would you like to feel the power of a million sticks of dynamite blast off beneath you, in perfect control, as you fly into orbit?

Well, whatever your dreams, you're not alone. People from Maryland have been reaching their dreams since there was a Maryland to dream in. Some have followed their dreams to become successful in business. Some delight us in movies on the silver screen. Still others help us live healthier happier lives by studying, experimenting and inventing. Some have become famous politicians, making laws to keep things rolling around here, and one grew up to be vice-president of the United States (Spiro Agnew). And while doing all of this, most have become parents and helped their families grow.

It's been a long time since we've gone to war, or colonized a strange new land, or sent brave explorers far into uncharted territory. In our modern times, the people of Maryland have time to think, write, act, invent, coach and play like never before. This is a time bursting with new ideas, and some of these ideas are kind of surprising. In this issue of Maryland Studies Weekly, we'll meet some Maryland folks who are finding ways to make us laugh, cry, think and cheer! All over Maryland, people are reaching for their dreams. Hey, dreaming is what we're made for! So come along and enjoy this week's ride with Maryland Studies Weekly!

title: Operation Hero Miles
text:
Several years ago, Maryland Congressman C.A. Dutch Ruppersberger went to the Baltimore Washington International Airport to meet a group of soldiers. These soldiers were coming home from Iraq and Afghanistan for two weeks of R and R, or Rest and Relaxation. While visiting with the soldiers, he found out that the military paid for their soldiers to travel to Baltimore, but that they then had to pay for their flights from Baltimore to their hometowns. Some soldiers who lived on the West Coast had to pay as much as $1,000 for a plane ticket home. Congressman Ruppersberger felt this was wrong, and he promised to do something about it.

It wasn't long before the congressman came up with a way to pay for the soldiers' plane tickets without asking the government to come up with more money. Operation Hero Miles, as the plan is called, asks ordinary citizens to donate their unused frequent flier miles to soldiers who are returning home on leave. Frequent flier miles are passes that can be used to fly for free. People can donate their frequent flier miles quickly and easily by visiting an Internet website.

Operation Hero Miles has made it possible for soldiers to visit their families, as well as for families to visit their wounded soldiers. A mother from Wisconsin was able to fly to Washington, D.C., to visit her daughter who had been injured in Iraq. A young father from Arkansas used Operation Hero Miles to fly home from Iraq for his newborn daughter's surgery. One young soldier from Colorado used the program to fly home to spend Christmas with his new wife. Operation Hero Miles makes life easier for our American soldiers serving throughout the world.

Thanks to Congressman Ruppersberger, hundreds of American soldiers and their families have been reunited during a very stressful time in their lives. The program is now a permanent part of our government's plan to take care of its soldiers.

title: Maryland’s Leading Men
text:
Here are a few of Maryland's great men of the past and present. Who will be our great men of the future?

1. Francis Scott Key

The words to our national anthem were written by Marylander Francis Scott Key during a battle of the War of 1812. In September 1814, the U.S. and Great Britain fought a terrible battle near Baltimore at Fort McHenry. Key was on a ship in Baltimore harbor, waiting for a sign that his nation had won a victory. At dawn the Fort McHenry soldiers raised a giant United States flag. Key saw the flag and wrote the words to "The Star-Spangled Banner" as a poem. The poem was put to the music of a popular song of the day and quickly became a favorite of the people. In 1931 Congress voted to make "The Star-Spangled Banner" the national anthem for the United States of America.

2. Eubie Blake

Eubie Blake (1883-1983) was a ragtime composer and musician who was born in Baltimore. Eubie's music career covered over 80 years, starting when he learned to play organ at age 4, until the release of his final album when he was 86! In fact, he died only five days after his 100th birthday. Blake wrote "The Charleston Rag," his best known number, when he was only 16 years old, while playing in bars in the Baltimore area. He continued to play this song, and many others, until he was 99. When his last record was released in 1969, he became very popular with a whole new generation, and toured for several years, playing music and lecturing on his life. Eubie received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1981.

3. Matthew Henson

Who was the first person to reach the North Pole? You might say "Admiral Peary," but did you know that Matthew Henson, his assistant on the trip, was from Maryland? Peary once said, "Henson must go all the way. I can't make it there without him."

In 1896, the explorers went to retrieve several meteorites they had found on earlier North Pole trips. The men spent years trying to get to the North Pole, but by 1908 were starting to think they were too old to continue. (Peary was 50, and Henson was 40.) But on their final trip in 1909, they finally made it! They crossed more than 400 miles in 16 days, using only their sleds.

4. Lefty Grove

Lefty Grove was born as Robert Moses Grove in 1900 in Lonaconing, Maryland. He was only the 11th pitcher ever to be able to win 300 baseball games. He also won four pitching titles, seven strikeout titles and four World Series games over his 17 years in the Major Leagues. After this excellent career, Lefty was easily inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1947. He had won 300 games, while only losing 141. He also struck out 2,266 batters in the almost 4,000 innings he pitched. In fact, he struck out 116 players his very first year as a major league pitcher!

5. Sugar Ray Leonard

Sugar Ray Leonard is one of the most agile and talented boxers in the world, and he comes from Maryland. While only 5 feet 9 inches tall and weighing 147 pounds (when he was boxing), he was a definite challenge in the ring. In 1976, he was the Gold Medal winner in the Olympics, in the light welterweight division. He also won the world title in 1979, followed by four more titles, facing challenges in some of the best boxing matches of all time. Sugar Ray's final record when he lost his title in 1991 was 36 wins, two losses, and one tie. His wins included 25 knockouts! Leonard tried one more time for a comeback in 1997, but was unable to overcome Hector Camacho. He did remain in the world of sports, becoming a commentator for television.

title: Our Great Writers
text:
Great Maryland men have done all kinds of things. But it seems like lots of them have been authors. Let's take a look at just a few of Maryland's great writers.

Tom Clancy (1947- )

If you drive through Huntingtown, Md., you might see a street sign warning you about a Tank Crossing. Yes, this is near the home of Tom Clancy, the author who wrote such novels as "Hunt for Red October" (his first novel) and "Patriot Games." He so much loves to learn about wartime history that he has a World War II tank in his front lawn! Clancy went to Loyola College and began his career as an insurance salesman. Before his first novel, he wrote very little. But he worked on a novel in his spare time and has now sold over 5 million paperbacks, hundreds of thousands of hardback books and several movies.

F. Scott Fitzgerald (1896-1940)

Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was named for his distant cousin, who wrote the national anthem. He went to many schools to become a writer, and published many articles, scripts and lyrics before his first novel ("This Side of Paradise") appeared in 1919. Possibly, his most famous novel was "The Great Gatsby."

Ogden Nash (1902-1971)

Ogden Nash wrote over 1,500 poems, which were interesting and unique. Rather than a narrative approach, his style was light and often humorous. His mind was very sharp, but he had to work very hard at his poetry. Although he was born in New York, he felt at home in Maryland! He once wrote, "I could have loved New York had I not loved Balti-more."

James M. Cain (1892-1977)

James Cain was born in Annapolis. He wrote crime fiction and once described his writing by saying "I merely try to write as the character would write." One of his most successful novels was "The Postman Always Rings Twice," which was made into a very popular movie.

Dashiell Hammett (1894-1961)

Born in Maryland, Dashiell started his career with Pinkerton National Detective Agency and then the Army before becoming a writer. He published several novels before hitting the big time with "The Maltese Falcon," a mystery that introduced Sam Spade, one of the most famous fictional detectives in literature.

H. L. Mencken (1880-1956)

H. L. Mencken was born in Baltimore and was one of the great intellectual writers of the 20th century. In fact, another journalist described him as "the greatest of all American journalists." His best-known work is "The American Language," often described as the best description of the American language (no small task). He is also well known for his articles and critical writings.

title: Southern Maryland
text: Our third visit to Southern Maryland is to St. Mary's County, located at the southernmost tip of Maryland. Although many people visit St. Mary's every year, it still seems like the country. At the beginning of this school year, we learned about historic St. Mary's City. Here, be sure to visit one of the oldest plantations in the country, Sotterley Plantation. It is a working plantation, so be prepared to get your hands dirty! At the St. Clements Island Potomac River Museum, you can see where the first European settlers landed. Many people have worked together to reconstruct the Maryland Dove so it looks just like the one so long ago. For an unusual stop, check out Buzzy's Country Store, filled with the usual stuff, but look up! His ceiling is covered with more than 400 hats from all over the world - even Russia. Finally, submarine fans won't want to miss the Black Panther, a German World War II submarine covered with rubber, which at the time made it undetectable to the enemy. The picture to the right is the Black Panther in 1949, shortly before it sank. If you want to see it today, you better bring diving gear, because it is underwater.

title: What’s the difference between ‘great’ and ‘famous?’
text: Have you ever wondered why you can't be famous? It does seem like it would be cool. Well, there is a big difference between being great and being famous. Many famous folks aren't so great, and many great people aren't very famous. Chances are, you're not one of the famous ones (not many are, to tell the truth), but we bet there's a person or two who thinks you're great! So, which would you rather be?

title: Salamander
text:
You're walking around your backyard after an all-night rainstorm, and what do you spy slithering along the ground? It has soft, smooth skin, four legs, a slender body and a loooong tail. Is it a lizard? Is it a frog? Wait a minute - it's a salamander!

And this one sure isn't trying to hide from anyone! Salamanders come in many different shapes, sizes, and colors. The giant salamander, which lives in China and Japan, is an enormous 5 feet long! Salamanders, like lizards, can grow new body parts if their original parts get pulled off. They are lizard shaped, but they have smooth, rather than scaly, skin. Like frogs, salamanders are amphibians. Even though they are born in water with gills, they later grow lungs and move onto land.

The yellow-spotted variety is found throughout Indiana in low-lying, moist woodlands near swamps, ponds and creeks. You'll see them only in early spring, and they are nocturnal. Some salamanders live in trees, some in water and some may live in your backyard!

title: Your Name Becomes a Work of Art
text:
Materials

4 1/2-inch by 11-inch drawing paper

Crayons

Scissor handles or ruler (for rubbing the back of the paper)

Directions

Fold the paper lengthwise and unfold.

Write your name with a crayon on the fold (large as shown).

Refold the paper so that the name is sandwiched between the two halves.

Use the scissor handles to transfer the crayoned image to the other side of the folded paper.

Do a little touch-up work and color the design.

Extra Activity

After you understand the basic design idea, you may want to try other ideas.

title: How Do I Create an Outline?
text:
You can use an outline to help you organize your nonfiction writing, especially when writing reports and research papers. An outline will help you effectively plan your writing.

Start with I, Then II and III…

This list will help you create an outline:

1. Formal outlines have the main topics in Roman numerals (I, II, III…).

2. Subtopics are indented and listed with capital letters (A, B, C…).

3. Supporting details are indented more than subtopics and listed with Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3…).

4. More details that support those supporting details are indented more and listed with lowercase letters (a, b, c…).

5. You must have at least two items at each level.

Below is a sample outline that someone might put together for a report on World War II.

The Two Wars Fought During World War II
I. Background Information (Main Topic)
A. Germany’s defeat in World War I
B. Japan’s need for more land

II. The War with Germany
A. Adolf Hitler
1. The Nazis
2. The supreme race
3. The Holocaust
a. Jews
b. Other races targeted by the Nazis
B. Germany’s pride

III. The War with Japan
A. The attack on Pearl Harbor
B. The atomic bomb
1. Hiroshima
2. Nagasaki

IV. The End of World War II
A. Germany’s defeat
B. Japan’s surrender

Try It!

The next time you have to write a nonfiction piece, such as a report, write an outline first. You’ll be amazed how it will help you organize your information and be sure to include all the important details.

title: Let's Write
text: There are many important men in your life. They’re probably people like your dad, your teacher, your leaders at church, or uncles and grandpas. Write an essay and tell us all about one of them!

title: Fun Final Focus for Maryland
text:
Well, here it is (sniff), the very last issue of Maryland Studies Weekly. What a ride it's been! You've hunted with American Indians and traced the paths of the first explorers. You've sailed on the high seas and been in the middle of scary battles. You've witnessed the riches of farmland and the misery of slavery and war. You've met many great Maryland men and women and learned so much that your brains will never be the same again!

So now that you've had a year of Maryland history, you know all there is to know, right? Well, close. One thing that's so great about our state is the chance you have to keep learning. All around, you have places to visit that teach you more, remind you about what you've already learned and that are just plain fun!

Have you ever gone on a field trip with your class or a vacation with your family that you just weren't excited about? Maybe a museum, a battlefield or historical house? But then, once you got there and started learning some cool stuff, it wasn't so bad was it? Learning can be like that - it takes some hard work, but in the end, it can really be fun too.

In this final issue of Maryland Studies Weekly, we're going to go on a few "field trips." We'll get just a little taste of what's out there, sometimes right next door. We promise a fun ride for all. And who knows - maybe with a little hint from you, your school just might try one of these trips for real!

title: Maryland’s Attractions
text:
This might be the last issue of Maryland Studies Weekly for the year, but you can still keep learning about this great state. There are dozens of ways to keep learning. Let's read on about some of the fun places you can visit and explore.

Western Maryland

Deep Creek Lake Discovery Center

Use a microscope to investigate underwater life. Feel the bones of creatures long extinct. Compare the size of your hand with a real black bear paw print. If any of this sounds interesting to you, then this place is for you. If you remember, Deep Creek Lake is the largest lake in Maryland - one that still has a lot you can explore. The Discovery Center is a great place to start. Teachers here will introduce you to the lake and the area around it. Then you can hike, bird-watch, pick wildflowers, swim, water ski - whatever! Just think, over a hundred years ago, people here were mining for coal - things are a little different now, aren't they?

Central Maryland

The B and O Railroad Museum

We already learned a little bit about the United States' first railroad in our transportation issue. But the best place to get the lowdown on the B and O is the museum located on Pratt Street in Baltimore. You'll hear stories about what life was like when the railroad was being built, how much money it cost, what people in Maryland really thought about this new-fangled way of traveling, what kind of seats it had, what kind of food was served, how hot/cold the train was - you get the idea! Sometimes the museum has special programs and plays, plus you'll actually get to see real stuff from the 1800s.

Eastern Region

Ocean City

Everybody knows that Ocean City is the hip spot of the Eastern Shore. And everybody knows that sandcastles, catching the waves and getting a little tan (not too much!) are what Ocean City is all about. But did you also know that there are TONS of other fun things to do? How about some kite flying? Or mini-golf? Maybe the go-carts or the arcades are more your style. Amusement parks, water slides and the best darn French fries east of the Mississippi - who could ask for more!

Southern Region

St. Clement's Island-Potomac River Museum

Before you say, "Oh, no! Not another museum!" just wait until you hear about this one. Imagine a museum on an island, and the only way you can get there is by boat. Well, this is it! Remember reading about George Calvert, the First Lord Baltimore? And the treacherous voyage of the Ark and the Dove? And Father Andrew White's journal entry when he arrived in the new land? And how the American Indians helped the English "get settled" in their new home? This museum has it all, and more. Visit "The Little Red Schoolhouse" and step back in time almost 200 years ago. Take a look at the artifacts archaeologists have dug up - they tell us a lot about life along the Potomac River. Do some imaginary shopping at the country store. You'll see what a few cents could buy you way back in 1890. Finally, you'll know where those first colonists landed in 1634 by the large white cross on the island. This is the same place they had the first Roman Catholic Mass in the English Colonies. Learn a bunch, but most importantly - have fun!

Appalachian Trail

We've looked at many fun things to do in lots of regions, but by far the most favorite is the Appalachian Trail. The trail actually snakes through a large part of the East Coast, but 40 miles of it is in western Maryland, along the South Mountain ridge. Part of it even follows the C and O Canal Towpath, where you'll see both bicyclists and hikers. People from all over the world come to hike the Maryland portion of the Appalachian Trail, known for its beauty and diversity. Amateur (new at it) hikers come to enjoy the spectacular views. More experienced hikers bring their backpacks and sleeping bags and make a four-day trip out of it. Civil War buffs can find plenty of history along our part of the trail, especially where it nears Antietam (remember learning about the bloodiest single day of the Civil War?). Archaeologists are studying the trail along Fox Gap, looking for more clues from the past. And Boy Scouts a little older than you often come to pass off their 50-mile hike merit badge. There's something here for everyone!

title: A Circle of Love
text:
"For the free and the brave, we should all take a hand,

To form a circle of love for those who fight in the sand."

(From a poem written by 11-year-old Jenessa Largent of Minnesota)

When Jenessa's Uncle Mike was sent to fight in the war in Iraq, she wanted to do something to let him and other soldiers know that they were not forgotten. She designed a bracelet to wear until her Uncle Mike comes home. The yellow beads on her bracelet are there because someone she loves is "in harm's way," or in danger. The red, white and blue hearts stand for love and the U.S.A.

Jenessa wants to give her bracelets to all the families whose loved ones are fighting for our country anywhere in the world. She's getting a great deal of help from her family, friends and even strangers. So far, they have sent 36,000 bracelets to people all over the world, and they haven't charged anyone a penny! Jenessa and her helpers are working hard to fill orders for thousands more bracelets as well.

Jenessa says her bracelets are a symbol of hope for a future where there is no terrorism, and children all over the world are safe. The men and women of the military are her heroes. At Studies Weekly, we think Jenessa is a hero too!

title: Where does the word “museum” come from?
text: The Muses were Greek goddesses who helped people who were interested in science or art. They were Zeus's daughters, and their mother was named Mnemosyne, which means "memory." So it makes sense that a MUS-eum is a safe place where we keep and study artifacts, stories, journals and pictures - things usually scientific or artistic - which will help us to remember things from the past. How do museums help you remember the past?

title: Baltimore Checkerspot Butterfly
text: In 1973, several people got together and decided we needed a state insect. They chose the checkerspot butterfly as their favorite. Which is no surprise - the black-and-gold wings, "Maryland's colors," are the same colors that are on our state flag, our state bird (the Baltimore Oriole), and our state flower (the black-eyed Susan). Just like most butterflies, checkerspots choose only one kind of plant to eat, lay their eggs on, and hatch from - a pink-and-white flower called the Turtlehead. In summer, the black-and-gold caterpillars turn into beautiful butterflies. When people first suggested the checkerspot, they didn't like the term "State Insect." So they decided to call it our "Arthropodic Emblem." Arthropod is a fancy name for an animal that's soft on the inside and hard on the outside. Unfortunately, they didn't realize that we already had a state arthropod - the blue crab! So the blue crab was called the "State Crustacean" - and the checkerspot? Well, she was called our "State Insect." Imagine that.

title: Ethics: President Coolidge Rebuilds a Bridge of Broken Trust
text:
Have you ever wondered how people acquire, or gain, power? In a representative democracy like the United States, a lot of that power comes from trust. We give our vote of confidence to leaders we have faith in. If those leaders betray our trust, then we are free to elect a new representative and the power shifts. But once trust is broken, it can be hard to rebuild.

One of the most famous betrayals of our public trust happened with President Harding's administration. With President Harding's sudden death in 1923, it was up to the new president to repair that bridge of trust. President Calvin Coolidge didn't waste time. He made it clear that no one in government would be above the law. "If there has been any crime," he said, "it must be prosecuted - no one will be shielded for any party, political or other reasons ... Every law will be enforced and every right of the people and government will be protected." And he meant it.

Investigators soon found that Secretary of the Interior, Albert Fall, was guilty of accepting bribes, or gifts, in exchange for the rights to a rich oil field in Wyoming called Teapot Dome. He was the first presidential advisor (helper) to serve time in prison for unlawful behavior. The Teapot Dome Scandal, as it became known, went down in history twice. It was first an example of broken trust, and again an example of how to rebuild it!

title: How Do I Read Historical Fiction?
text:
Treat It As Art Full of Historical Facts

While nonfiction is about information, fiction is all about creativity. Reading fiction can be exciting and moving. When you read fiction, you are trying to understand a character deeply, imagining the story as you read the words, reflecting on the events in the story and exploring the ideas and feelings created by the story.

Historical Fiction

Fictional pieces are imaginary stories, but they can be based on historical facts. Fictional stories based on historical facts are called “historical fiction.” When reading historical fiction, it is important that you understand which details are factual and which are fictional. Sometimes, you need to do background research on your story before you can understand the difference between fact and fiction in a story that is historical fiction. Fiction is the most popular genre of literature and ranges from short stories (a page or two) to novels (up to thousands of pages). Fiction has three basic elements: characters, plot and setting.

Characters

The characters are the people (or animals) in the story. In well-written fiction, the writer will describe what the characters look like, how they act, what they think and feel, what others say about them, what they talk about and many other details. Because of this, you will finish reading it and feel like you know some of the characters very well, like friends or family. Sometimes, they will seem like reallife people. Characters in historical fiction can help you understand what it felt like to live through that event or period. Most stories have a main character, or protagonist.

Plot

The plot is what happens in a novel or story. It is the sequence of events. Generally, fictional writing begins with a conflict, or a problem that needs to be resolved. The events that happen after the conflict is introduced are called the rising action. The rising action draws out the character’s problem. The story’s turning point is called the climax. This is when there is a dramatic shift in the story, especially regarding the conflict. In the end, the conflict is resolved or changed into a different conflict. This is called the falling action. You can illustrate how a story’s plot goes with a graph like this: The plot in historical fiction will often follow a timeline of actual historical events, adding fictional details along the way.

Setting

The setting is the time and place in which the story happens. Stories can take place in the past, present or future and can last anywhere from one day to several years. Stories can also take place in a single room or city, or the action might happen in one big country or a planet. In historical fiction, the setting is, of course, in the past. If you imagine yourself in the setting of historical fiction, you will understand what conditions were like back then.

Theme

The theme of a fictional work is the idea that the author is examining in the work. The theme is a general topic, which allows the author to do a great deal of exploration.

Try It!

The next time you read a story or novel that is historical fiction, identify the main characters, the plot, the setting and the theme. You can even plot the theme as shown above. Think about the details in the story. Ask yourself which details are probably historical fact and which ones are fiction created by the author. Doing this will help you more fully understand the historical context being represented.
