title: Proud to Be an American
text:
Welcome to Massachusetts Studies Weekly, a magazine designed especially for fifth-grade students just like you. This year, we will be studying about our great country and the history of how it came to be.

History is a story just waiting to be told. It is a way of reviewing the past to help us better understand the present, so future generations will continue to enjoy the freedoms and privileges that we have today.

Understanding the events of the past helps us develop an appreciation for those people who forged the way for us. As we learn about the exciting events and the tragic ones, the heroes and the villains, we will develop a sense of pride and awe in our heritage. We will understand what it means to be an American.

The following are the features you can look forward to each week in the American History series of Massachusetts Studies Weekly:

Feature Article

This feature introduces you to the main topic and the facts and ideas that are important for you to know in our timeline of American history.

Connections

The Connections article focuses on events outside the scope of our studies. They may be events that occurred one week ago or events that occurred 100 years ago.

History Lesson

This feature allows the reader to step back in time as events unfold in the story of our nation.

Government

The government of the United States begins with you! You are the foundation of our government. This feature explores the various levels of government, their functions, and how you fit in to the scheme of things.

Economics

Everyone likes money, but it is important to know more than the basics of earning and spending. This feature is just the ticket to get you started.

This Week's Question

This is the place to look for weird and crazy facts that make learning so much fun.

In Other Words

Over time, people use word choices to convey an idea. Sometimes, they don't seem to make sense because they have historical roots that we may not know about. So get on the bandwagon and strut your stuff.

Vocabulary and Word Games

This section gives you a chance to review the new vocabulary introduced in each week's features. While you read, it's a good idea to highlight (with a crayon or colored pencil) words that are new. If you don't know what they mean...try not to ask, but discover on your own by looking for clues in the reading or using your old friend, the dictionary.

Let's Write

Each week, Let's Write lists some instructions, or a writing prompt, for you to write an article. Sometimes, you will be asked to write about something you read in the paper, or an idea connected to the history lesson. Other times, you are asked to write a creative piece that requires you to use your imagination. Occasionally, you may be asked to write about a drawing or diagram.

Well, welcome to the family of Massachusetts Studies Weekly. We hope you enjoy this course of study as you embark on a journey to learn of your heritage and to find out what it means to be an American.

Fun Facts About America

Hawaii is the newest state in the United States. It became a state in 1959.

Alaska is the biggest state in the United States.

Alaska has the smallest population in the United States.

In 1776, there were only 13 colonies in the United States.

Each state has its own flag, and some of them tell you about the history of the state.

Baseball, basketball, football, volleyball and water skiing all originated in the United States.

New York is the largest city in the United States with a population of 8,084,316.

Lake Chargoggagoggmanchauggauggagoggchaubunagungamaugg is a lake found in the United States. Do you know where this lake is located? Do some research to find out where this lake is and what the name means.

title: How do Political Parties Choose a Presidential Candidate?
text:
During presidential elections you will hear people talking about caucuses, primaries and conventions. What are they talking about? It's all about which candidate from each political party will be picked to run as the official candidate of their party.

A caucus is a community event where people talk about who will be their party's candidate for president. Each person at the caucus gets to vote for a delegate to go to their party's convention. They vote for delegates who support the presidential candidate they want to be the official candidate in the election in November. Usually, only people who are registered members of a party can attend a caucus and vote for delegates. Today, 10 states hold caucuses. In most states that hold caucuses, the majority of delegates they choose support the same candidate, but the delegates sometimes are divided between two or more candidates. That can make the convention pretty interesting!

Most states hold primary elections instead of caucuses. In a primary election, people who are registered to vote can cast a vote for the person they want to be the next president. Delegates who go to the election will vote for a candidate based on the results of the primary. Primaries can be open or closed. In an open primary anyone can vote for a candidate from any party. In a closed primary, only registered members of each party can vote for a candidate from that party.

A few months before the election, each party holds a convention to nominate the person who will be their candidate for president. Delegates from caucus states and primary states get together to nominate the official candidate for their party. You can watch the republican and democratic conventions on TV. The voting is usually a voice vote, so if you watch, you can see the delegates from your state cast their votes. Will your state's delegates vote your favorite candidate? Tune in to the conventions later this year to find out!

Teachers: This is a Studies Weekly/History News Network Spotlight article. Find a link to background information, lesson plans and more at www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/

title: The Place Where We Live
text:
Long ago, cartographers (mapmakers) divided our world into two halves-- the Eastern Hemisphere (that's where they lived), and the unknown, backside of the planet, or Western Hemisphere. Many years after explorers reached the Western Hemisphere, they discovered two continents: North America and South America. We live on the North American continent.

Our Shape

The North Americans continent is shaped similar to a triangle, with the widest part in the northeast and the narrowest to the southwest.

Our Size

Our continent is the third largest. It stretches approximately 5,000 miles from top to bottom, and about 5,000 miles from side to side. Its top is close to 500 miles from the North Pole, and its bottom is close to 500 miles from the equator. In all, we have 9,355,000 square miles of land.

Our Age

We live on the oldest continent in the world. Our continent is about 2.6 billion years old.

Our Land

We have many mountain ranges with beautiful, volcanic peaks. A giant slab of rock called the Canadian Shield is on the largest parts of our continent. Large mountain ranges to the east and west frame the central Great Plains and lowlands. Our highest spot is Mount McKinley in Alaska (20,320 feet tall). The lowest spot is Death Valley in California (282 feet below sea level).

Our Water

We have thousands of lakes, streams and rivers. In the Pacific Northwest, it can rain 150 inches a year, and in the Wild West, they can receive less than five inches of rain in a year. The East enjoys rain nearly every month, while the middle regions often go months without rain.

Borders

Canada is to our north, and Mexico to our south, and the continent is surrounded by oceans - the Arctic Ocean to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to our east, and the large Pacific Ocean to our west. The toasty-warm Caribbean Sea covers our southern coastline. We have 37,000 miles of coastline--That's enough to wrap around the Earth 1 1/2 times.

Resources

You name it, and we probably have it. Our rich natural resources have helped us do an abundance of good in the world. Our citizens enjoy a very high standard of living in history. As a nation, we help others around the planet with food, manufactured goods, and medical and military aid.

title: Exchanging Goods and Services
text:
Think about walking home on a cold winter day. The wind is blowing hard. Just as your house comes into view, it starts to snow. You are freezing! Quickly, you bolt up your front steps. You stomp the snow off your boots as you enter the front door. You walk right to the kitchen and find your dad starting dinner. He asks you to help and gives you a can of tomato soup to open. You complain a little, not sure if your fingers are warm enough yet to move. You find the can opener and open the can. As the can spins around, you start to study it. You think of many questions about the can of soup. What part of the country did it come from? How was it made? At what store was it bought? How did it travel to the food store near your home? Who made the label? Suddenly, that can of soup becomes more than the main menu of dinner tonight. You realize you are looking at a can of economics.

Economists ask all of these questions every day. Their job is to study the economy. They study the results of manufacturers making and selling goods and services. They study the consumers who buy those goods and services. In the case of the soup, producers make the soup. Your family, as the consumer, buys that good. On the other hand, if you provide a service for someone, such as mowing a neighbor's lawn, then that person paying you for the service becomes the consumer.

Economists have two separate areas of study in economics: macroeconomics and microeconomics. Macroeconomics is the study of the economy as a whole. People who study macroeconomics ask questions about the entire nation and world. One example would be why gasoline prices have risen across the country. Microeconomics is the study of individual consumers and businesses. People who study microeconomics want to know things such as what prices you, as a consumer, would pay for your favorite video game. This year in Studies Weekly, we will be learning much more about our economy. We'll look at the roles of producers and consumers. Can you think of other ways you are a consumer?

title: It All Begins With You!
text:
History is a part of social studies. It is a very important part. Through lessons in history, we fashion our future. Another important part of social studies is learning about governments. The study of our government and of citizenship strengthens our country. We become the defenders of our democracy as we learn how governments work. We hold on to our freedoms as we learn about citizenship.

Just what is government? A government is the way in which a country, state, city or village is run. In every community, a government makes laws that citizens must obey. A government decides how to enforce those laws. Governments also decide how to protect their citizens. Governments are not all the same. The kind of government that Americans have is just one of many.

This year, we will learn about our government. We will learn what it does and why it is important. We will also focus on how to be good citizens in our homes, schools and communities. At Studies Weekly, we know that "good government" begins with you!

title: Actions speak louder than words
text:
Sometimes people say one thing but then do another. In other words, we can tell what they really mean by watching what they do.

"My brother says that he really hates cartoons," Jacob said sadly. "Every afternoon, when I'm watching them, he wants to change the channel."

"But," said Sam, "last Saturday morning, I saw him watching the same cartoons. He looked like he really liked them."

"Well," Jacob said, "maybe he really loves the cartoons, but wants to watch something else that's on at the same time. They say, 'Actions speak louder than words.'"

title: What is a dialect?
text:
Have you noticed that, while we all speak English, not everyone sounds the same when talking? For instance, if a person is from a southwestern state (Utah, Nevada, Arizona, California), then it is likely that he or she pronounces the words "naughty" and "knotty" the same way. How about you? Do you say those exactly the same?

The different ways people pronounce words, and even sometimes the words themselves, can be a clue to where a person is from. Do you call the fizzy stuff that you drink that comes in a can "soda," "pop," or "soda pop?" Depending on where you are from (or where your parents are from), you may say any one of those things.

That's what a dialect is. But let's take it a step farther. What if you say a word differently than anyone in your family? We call that an idiolect. That means it's your very own, personal dialect.

title: The Compass
text:
The compass is every explorer's best friend. It is a tool that often looks like a pocket watch. It has a magnetic needle that can turn easily. The cardinal directions - north, east, south and west - are labeled on the face of the compass. It always points north because there are magnetic fields around the Earth. The needle lines up with those fields to guide the traveler. It takes some practice to know how to use a compass, so be sure to learn before your next camping trip!

Who invented the compass? The Chinese invented the first compass to use a magnetic needle. They were using their compass to explore the oceans as early as 2,000 years ago.

What are some other ways to tell your directions? You can look for landmarks with which you are familiar. For example, you might remember that the tallest building in your town is north of you. Another way is to use the sun as your guide. Because the sun rises in the east, north is to the left of the sunrise. Finally, you can use the North Star, or Polaris. It is in line with the Earth's axis, so it always appears to remain in the north.

title: Direct Context Clues
text:
Direct context clues are words that say, “Look here!”

Learning how to guess words you don’t know is an important skill. If you learn how to guess what a word means, then you won’t have to read with your dictionary open all the time.

There are different strategies to guess word meaning. One way is to find other words or phrases nearby that point to the definition. We call those words or phrases direct context clues.

Below is a list of words that are often used to point to direct definitions. In items 1-5, circle the words from the list below. Underline the direct definition in each item.

is/are was/were

is/are called, means, or, such as

is/are known as, different from

is/are like is/are similar to

unlike is/are considered

1. Mammoths lived during the Ice Age. A mammoth was something like a very large elephant. It sported very long tusks that curled on the ends.

2. The Spanish explorers used a very fast, three-masted ship. This ship is called a caravel. Because it was smaller, the caravel could be used to explore shallow coastal waters.

3. Do you want the thrill of your life? Then try the SkyScreamer out for size. The SkyScreamer is a 20-story-high swing ride found in the Texas Six Flags amusement park.

4. Jason’s bedroom is chaotic, unlike Harry’s room, which is tidy.

5. Check the BBC website for a list of monarchs, or rulers, of England.

text:
The name of the feature article is “Proud to Be an American.”

A. Write the title “Proud to Be an American” as the title of your article.

B. Interview an adult and ask him or her why he or she is proud to be an American.

title: Massachusetts Students are Going Places!
text:
This week in Massachusetts Studies Weekly, we will learn about maps. To fully understand what happened in history, we need to know where it happened and how to find it on a map. After you have completed this issue, you will have added some serious map skills to those you have learned in previous years. So, let's get going. We have places to go!

Mercator

The lines on this map are equally spaced, like a checkerboard. See how the lines on the equal-area and interrupted projection maps are curved? Because of the evenly spaced lines, it is easier to use a Mercator map for navigation. It isn't a very accurate world map, however, because the scale isn't proportionate (when the size of one object fits the size of another). Look at Greenland on the Mercator map. It looks bigger than the continent of South America.

Flat Maps

A projection map is a way of showing the round Earth on a flat piece of paper. This is sort of like peeling an orange in one piece and laying it out flat. The kinds of projection maps shown here are equal area and interrupted.

Globes

When you want something realistic, the map of choice would be the globe. The globe is a very accurate way to represent our Earth. One disadvantage is that you can only see half of the globe at a time. Another disadvantage is that it's pretty hard to fold a globe into your backpack and take it home to study.

Topographical Maps

Topography is a word that means the physical things of the Earth's surface. These kinds of maps show physical features, like oceans and mountain ranges. They can also show us how high a mountain is or how deep the ocean is. Who might use a physical map?

title: Can You Get There From Here?
text:
Could you give your grandmother directions to your local grocery store? Which street would you turn on to get to the park? Where is your doctor's office? Chances are you have been to these places many times, but would you know how to get there all by yourself? If you had a good map, you could find any of these places quickly and easily.

It is important to know where you are and how to get where you need to go. Making a map of your neighborhood can help you see exactly where each place is located and how to get there from anywhere in the area.

You can make a map of your neighborhood to help you find important places. Use a large piece of heavy paper, felt or craft foam. Start by marking your house, along with the street you live on. Be sure to mark the cardinal directions clearly on your map. Carefully label the streets in your neighborhood, along with other important landmarks, like farms, businesses, parks, churches and even an unusual tree or tire swing.

After you have finished your map, ask a parent or family member to help you test it out. Use your map to guide you to someplace in your neighborhood. Was your map helpful? Did you forget to mark anything?

Keep your map and add to it over time. You'll have fun and learn more about your neighborhood each time you do!

title: Hemispheres
text:
Which End Is Up?

Can you find the North and South poles on the globe? Halfway between those poles is an imaginary line around the Earth called the equator. We call the top half the Northern Hemisphere and the bottom half the Southern Hemisphere.

The world can also be divided into the Western and Eastern hemispheres. This is done by grouping continents. The Eastern Hemisphere is made up of Europe, Asia, Australia, Africa and half of Antarctica. The Western Hemisphere is made up of North America, South America and half of Antarctica. Look at the flat representations of the hemispheres in Figure 1 or look at a globe to see the four hemispheres, then answer the questions below.

1. Write all the names of the continents (or parts of continents) that are found in each hemisphere.

Northern

Southern

Eastern

Western

2. Find the equator and trace it with a red crayon or colored pencil.

3. In which hemispheres is the United States located?

4. In which hemispheres do you find the Indian Ocean?

Latitude Attitudes

Look at figure 1. You will see lines running east-west (side to side). These lines are called lines of latitude, or parallels. These lines mark distances in degrees. If you can count by tens, you can name the lines of latitude. The equator is 0°. The lines of latitude north of the equator are all named north latitude. They go all the way up to the North Pole, which is 90° N latitude. All of the lines south of the equator are named south latitude. They go all the way down to the South Pole, which is 90° S latitude. These lines are also called parallels because the distance between a line of latitude and another (either north or south) always stays the same, all the way around the Earth.

Also in Figure 1, you will see lines that are running north-south (up and down). These imaginary lines are called meridians, or lines of longitude. These lines are different from the parallels because they are not the same distance apart, but they get closer and closer until they come together at the poles. Look on a globe and find the poles. See how the lines of longitude come together? The middle line, or the line that is 0°, is called the prime meridian. Everything west of the prime meridian to 180° is named west longitude, and everything east of the prime meridian to 180° is named east longitude.

Lines of longitude are also used for measuring distances and for establishing time zones. Their most important function is, together with the lines of latitude, to pinpoint locations on Earth.

1. 45°N, -105°W

2. -28°S, 135°E

3. 50°N, 30°E

4. 45°N, 105°E

5. -15°S, -60°W

6. 0°, 20°E

title: Adam Smith
text:
Consumers and producers have been a big part of markets since the early civilizations. Markets are actually a way that people can trade with one another. Markets bring consumers to producers and producers to consumers. Through these markets, exchange economies came to be. No one ever really invented an economy. It just happened as people traded with each other. As markets grew larger, many people began asking questions. Then they studied people as they traded for goods and services. That study is what we now know as economics.

One of these early economists was named Adam Smith. He was born in Scotland in 1723. He went to the University of Glasgow at the age of 14! That seems very young to be going to college now, but it was very common back then. He graduated, and then went on to Oxford University in England. He became a professor and began looking at exchange markets. Smith didn't know it, but he was really starting the study of economics. In 1776, he put out his book, "The Wealth of Nations." The book is about what he had found through 30 years of research.

Smith suggested that there was an "invisible hand" that guided trade in an economy. Think about sitting down to enjoy a nice bowl of tomato soup. Most people give little thought to all the steps and processes that go into putting that soup on your table. There are the tomato farmers and the soup makers. There's the marketing team who advertises the soup and the people who design the label. Don't forget the truckers who transport the soup. How about the grocery store that places it on the shelf? Who controls all of this? Is there someone leading each company? How does it all work?

According to the "invisible hand" theory, no one directly oversees companies trading with each other. Instead, markets bring people together. From that, producers find other producers to assist them. Then consumers are guided naturally to buy those products that they need. This process of trading in an economy is known as voluntary exchange. When this is the main way of organizing production of goods and services, economists call it a market economy. These early ideas from Adam Smith still affect economists today, more than 200 years later. It is because of his work and study that Adam Smith is known as the Father of Economics.

title: What is Democracy?
text:
Democracy is government by the people. The word "democracy" comes from two Greek words. Demos means "the people," and kratos means "authority." The Greeks granted authority to the people to pass the laws. They used these two words to mean "government by the many." They did not want the government to be just a few people or a single ruler, such as a king or queen.

In those days, democracy was direct. The free people would gather to discuss and pass the laws. The people had a direct vote. Today, democracy in the United States is different. It is not direct. We just don't have room for everyone to gather in the town square. It would be nearly impossible for so many people to discuss ideas and to vote. Today, we practice representative democracy. We elect people to represent our ideas and to pass the laws. Each elected official discusses and votes for the laws of our country. Still, whichever form of democracy is used, it is government by the people. That includes you!

title: Two heads are better than one
text:
This saying is used when a person is having trouble with something. In other words, he or she often needs a second person to help.

Jessie was searching the Internet for information about the population of Mexico City. "Ryan," she said to her friend, "I can't find a site that has this information. Can you think of some different words I can use to search?"

"Hmmmm," said Ryan. "How about 'countries' and 'capital cities'?"

"That's a good idea," Jessie answered. "Let's see what it brings up...oh, perfect! You are so great. Thanks for your help."

"No problem," he replied, "I guess two heads are better than one."

title: What is the difference between seas and oceans?
text:
When you look at a map of the world, it looks like the seas are really part of the ocean. Well, you're right. They are!

There are five oceans that cover three-fourths of the world. They are the Atlantic, Pacific, Indian, Southern and Arctic oceans.

Seas are sections of oceans but are partly cut off from them by stretches of land.

Look at a globe or a map of the world. Can you find the South China Sea? ( Hint: Try at about 115 E. longitude and 15 N. latitude.) It is part of the Pacific Ocean, which is the largest ocean on the planet.

Here are some names of other seas for you to locate. Work with a partner and when you have found them, write the map coordinates on the lines.

1. Caribbean Sea

2. Bering Sea

3. Tasman Sea

4. Arabian Sea

5. Sea of Japan

title: Global Positioning System
text:
What would you do if you went on a hike and got lost? You would be able to find out where you were if you had a Global Positioning System, or GPS.

The early Global Positioning Systems were very large and could only locate your position within 50 feet. Later, Charles Counselman, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, made them about the size of a backpack. He also improved the technology so that you could determine your location to within just a centimeter! Today’s GPS receivers are small enough to fit in your pocket. Many cars come with a GPS and a computer program that gives you directions to wherever you are going. In 2002 a GPS helped save nine coal miners who were trapped underground for more than three days.

title: Inferential Context Clues
text:
Did you ever ask someone the meaning of a word, only to have him answer, “Figure it out!” When you look again, there are no definite context clues. Now what? The fact is that the meaning is hidden in the rest of the words in that sentence. Sometimes, the meaning is tucked away in a whole paragraph. These are inferential context clues.

Below are three examples. Read the words around the vocabulary word and write what you think the new word may mean.

1. Brianna wanted a cookie, but the jar was out of reach. Jake, Brianna’s brother, climbed onto a chair and stretched his fingers around the jar. Just then, the chair tipped and Jake, the chair and the cookie jar came crashing to the floor. Brianna began to cry. As the noise and confusion mounted, their mother called out from the next room, “What’s all that commotion?”

Write what you think the word commotion means:

2. During a test in class, Spencer saw his best friend, Tyler, cheat. He told Tyler that if Tyler didn’t confess to the teacher, he would tell her what he saw. Standing up to Tyler took a great deal of fortitude on Spencer’s part.

Write what you think the word fortitude means:

3. Sometimes, we borrow words from other languages (exonymns). This vocabulary word is French and is sometimes followed by an exclamation point. Ashley said, “I cut a coupon from a magazine, mailed it in and — voilà! — here’s my new glow-in-the-dark lipstick!”

Write what you think the word voilà means:

title: Let's Write
text: You have just won a trip around the world, and you get to plan the trip yourself. You are allowed to choose up to 15 destinations. Write about the adventures that happened on your trip around the world, but don’t tell the name of the destinations you chose. Use only the coordinates of your destinations. Other classmates will be able to practice their new map skills using your coordinates. Don’t forget to list the answers separately.

title: Mapping Our World
text:
Anciently, many civilizations used maps and developed the kinds of maps they created in different ways. For example, the Aztec used footprints to represent roads in pictures. Early Inuit carved ivory coastal maps. The Inca built relief maps on clay tablets. Some historians believe the Chinese may have been using maps since as early as the seventh century B.C.

People who make maps are called cartographers. Early cartographers were artists, and some had more training in the science of creating maps than others.

Some of the earliest mapmaking comes from the Babylonians in about 600 B.C. They kept records on clay tablets. Some clay tablets showed lines of property ownership. Babylonians showed the Earth as a flat, round disk.

About this same time period, the Chinese painted maps on squares of silk. There was a great deal of information available on these maps, such as certain symbols for cities and accurate depictions of rivers. Compared to other ancient maps, the Chinese maps were very accurate.

By 250 B.C., a Greek man by the name of Eratosthenes made some major contributions to cartography. He measured the circumference of the Earth and was surprisingly close to what we know it is today. He also used a grid to show locations of places, much the way we use latitude and longitude today.

After Eratosthenes (about A.D. 150), Ptolemy drew a map of the world using different calculations. Unfortunately, his calculations were off, and Ptolemy figured Earth to be 3/4 of its actual size. However Ptolemy was far ahead of his time. He proposed a system of projections and a coordinate system that we still use today.

After Ptolemy, little progress was made in cartography for several centuries. By the 15th century, cartography boomed in Europe. As Portuguese sailors discovered new lands, the royalty commissioned maps to be made of those discoveries. Spain and Portugal sent many explorers during this time, and rulers were frantic to show maps of their newly claimed lands. In addition to the surge in exploration, the printing press was invented in the mid-1500s, and maps were more readily available.

In the 1600s, Gerardus Mercator created the Mercator projection map. This flat map allowed sailors to plot their destinations on fixed lines.

By the 17th and 18th centuries, scientific advances helped cartography improve even more. One of the important advances during that era occurred when Sir Isaac Newton proposed that the Earth was not a perfect sphere. His idea was that the Earth bulges at the equator and flattens at the poles. He was right! The Earth is a spheroid.

Today, cartographers rely on many means to map and chart the surface of our planet. They use satellites and aerial photos for accurate pictures of the Earth. They use sonar and computers for oceans. What do you think is used to map the moon, Mars or space?

Cartographers for the past and today have generated images of the places we live. They have used tools and calculations to show us the unknown.

title: Mapping the Final Frontier
text:
Only about 15 percent of the ocean floor has been mapped, so that leaves a great deal of work for cartographers to do. That’s just what the cartographers aboard the USNS Bruce C. Heezen are doing these days.

This ship is the U.S. Navy’s newest oceanographic survey ship. It is equipped with sonar, bathymetry (a device that measures the depth of the water) and computers that record the water temperature. It is also designed to examine the ocean floor and determine what the seabed is made of.

The Navy is excited about the information that the Heezen can collect. The military uses a lot of the information to predict the weather and plan submarine exercises. Boat owners also enjoy more reliable weather information and better coastline maps that the Heezen’s data make possible.

The Heezen has recently assisted with some other interesting projects as well. It was used to rebuild oyster beds off the Gulf coast and sometimes pinpoints shipwrecks for recreational divers.

The ship is named for marine scientist Bruce C. Heezen. He was a pioneer in the study of plate tectonics and is best known as a co-creator of some of the best ocean maps in the world.

title: Timeline of Maps
text:
Who needs cartographers in the 21st century? Why, everyone does! Cartographers today do much more than chart explorations. With maps, we can understand what a place looks like and even what land features are found in that area. Maps can show us where people live or where they are going (not to mention, how to get there). Maps are used by many companies today. They can project where most of their products are sold and how to improve sales. Maps can assist scientists as they study diseases and other healthcare issues. They are also used by climatologists as they track weather patterns. How many more uses for maps can you name?

Cartographers today are highly skilled. They have to have a broad knowledge base to be able to accurately create maps of many kinds. Some of the subjects that cartographers need to know include math, geology, biology, chemistry and physics. Cartographers also study social sciences, archaeology and anthropology. Wow! What a list! Would you like to become a cartographer?

The Compass Rose

The compass rose is a small drawing that shows directions on a map. Its tips point to the four cardinal, or main, directions: north, south, east and west (N, S, E and W). It also shows the intermediate, or in-between, directions: northwest, northeast, southwest and southeast (NW, NE, SW and SE).

Compass roses were used extensively by Portuguese mapmakers. They placed them on the map to indicate directions, but they were also used for navigation.

Some compass roses were ornate, and others were plain. Circle your favorite compass rose.

title: Productive Resources
text:
Productive resources are found in every good or service. Resources are the basic things used to make products in our community. Economists study resources a great deal and have put them into three groups. They help answer these three economic questions: How is a product made? What product is made? Who makes a product?

Natural Resources

Natural resources are unaltered or undisturbed gifts of nature. Fresh air, minerals, water and trees used for timber are all natural resources. They are things taken from the Earth that cannot be made any other way.

Human Resources

A secretary, a doctor, a mechanic and a teacher are all kinds of human resources. Human resources, or labor, require people to be creative. People must have skills and knowledge to help them put physical and mental effort into their work.

Capital Resources

The last type of resource can be found everywhere. Buildings, tools or machines people use to produce other goods and services are known as capital resources.

These productive resources are all around you every day. Let's say that you wanted to make cookies. Each of these resources would be very important. Most of what you put into the cookies - eggs, milk, sugar, salt and flour - would be natural resources. The human resource would be you making the effort to make the cookies. Lastly, your mixing bowl, measuring cups, spoon, baking sheet, mixer and oven would all be types of capital resources. All these things come together to make your product - yummy cookies! Can you think of other examples of natural, human and capital resources?

title: Citizenship at Home
text:
Listening to others talk about their feelings is one way of being a good citizen at home. What if you accidentally broke your brother's new MP3 player? Would he feel angry? If he did, how might you be a good citizen?

A smart way to begin would be to listen carefully to how he felt about it. It is best not to interrupt. Next, in a kind voice, retell what you heard him say. Then apologize sincerely and ask what you might do to make it right. Everyone makes mistakes. You might choose to earn some extra money to repair it. Perhaps sharing something of yours would help to mend his feelings. By listening carefully and treating others fairly, we can encourage them to do the same.

title: Give the devil his due
text:
This saying means that even if we don't like someone, we can give him or her credit for the things he or she has accomplished. In other words, find something positive about that person.

"I thought I was going to faint before I finished the mile run today," said Wendy. "That crazy coach works us too hard!"

"Yeah," replied April, "but every year, he has a winning team. I guess you have to give the devil his due!"

title: Where do you find volcanoes?
text:
Pick any place on the globe. If you could travel there, do you think you would find a volcano? Well, probably not, because most volcanoes, especially active ones, are found in only a few narrow bands across the face of the Earth.

Why do most volcanoes appear in "narrow bands?" Volcanoes occur near the edges of the large plates that comprise the solid surface of Earth. The explosive volcanoes, or the active ones, are found where plates are crunching together. The quieter volcanoes are found mostly where plates are coming apart. These would be volcanoes in Hawaii or Iceland.

Many of the world's active volcanoes are located around the edges of the Pacific Ocean: the West Coast of the Americas, the eastern coast of Siberia, Japan, the Philippines, Indonesia, an island chain in the New Zealand area, Africa, Italy and Hawaii.

Some volcanoes are found underwater on the floor of the oceans. As the hot lava is expelled, it is cooled and then slowly shifts apart.

Thanks to satellites, we also know that there are volcanoes on many moons in our solar system.

title: Astrolabe
text:
Sea travelers figured out how to find out where they were by using the North Star as a guide. The North Star is always to the north. So by looking at where the North Star was above the horizon, they could determine their latitude. The latitude tells you how far north or south of the equator you are. People used to use their arms and fingers and "shoot" at the star to measure how far up the North Star is.

Eventually, people invented tools to help find out where they were. The astrolabe was a tool sailors often used to figure out latitude. People also used it to tell the time, day or night.

title: Reason and Logic: Young George Washington, Surveyor and Mapmaker
text:
Most people know about George Washington. He was born in Virginia. He was a general during the American Revolution and our first president. But his earliest jobs, surveyor and cartographer (mapmaker), taught him skills and values he would use for the rest of his life. Using reason and logic to solve problems helped Washington become one of our country's most important leaders.

When Washington grew up, there were few roads or boundaries in much of the land. A surveyor's job was to measure and map the land. He had to make exact measurements for boundaries and physical features. This was a very big responsibility. People needed accurate maps and surveys for traveling and buying land.

At age 17, Washington traveled across the Blue Ridge Mountains to map and survey part of the frontier. He was the surveyor for the whole county, and that was an important job. When he led the Continental Army, it was even more important to have reliable maps. He established the job of Geographer and Surveyor General and appointed a man named Robert Erskine to this position. He gave Washington some information that was very helpful in making reasonable and logical battle plans and decisions.

You can use these same skills to make important decisions. Be sure you have the facts and information you need instead of acting on opinions and emotions. In what areas of your life are reason and logic very important?

title: Maps Through Time
text:
Study the two maps from the 17th, and 19th centuries (above).

A. Using a present-day map of the same area, compare and contrast it with one of the maps above.

B. Explain what advances in cartography have improved maps since the 17th century.

title: What is time?
text:
Time is what keeps everything from happening at once. That’s how one British clockmaker defines time. For ages, people have tried to define time, measure it and divide it. Today, we have a pretty good way to mark the passage of time with calendars and clocks.

How do we talk about events of the past? Things that happened in the past are known as history. Historical events are usually described in the order in which they happened. Another way of saying that is in chronological order. When we put events in order, it links them together as if they were a chain. It is a way of linking the past with the present.

A timeline is a handy way to show events and happenings in chronological order. A timeline can cover any length of time from a day to many millions of years. For example, you may wish to make a timeline of what you will do today starting at 6:00 a.m. and ending at 9:00 p.m. That could be a short timeline. Perhaps you would rather make an historic timeline of prehistoric life. That could cover millions of years. There are some great timelines on the Internet, or there are many history books that have timelines in them. Take a look at a few and decide what you like. When you know what you like, it’s time to do some research.

To research the subject you have chosen, start by visiting the Internet. The Internet is a great source for information and for good examples of timelines on just about any subject you can think of. Encyclopedias are also good places to find information, people, and events. You may also choose to look at almanacs, newspapers and magazine for more information on your topic. So, what are we waiting for? Let’s make a timeline!

title: The Time Machine
text:
Where would you go to if you could turn back the clock?

Put on your seat belts and get ready to roll....Where should we go? We could go forward or backward into time, witness history as it unfolds or be part of history in the making! If you think time travel is unlikely, you are not alone. On the other hand, if you think time travel is possible, you are not alone either.

Several decades ago, a famous science fiction author wrote a book titled "The Time Machine." This author, H. G. Wells, wrote of a mysterious machine created by a man. The machine could go forward or backward in time. The book was a huge success, and films and remakes have been based on the book. What is it about time travel that's so curious? What would your time machine look like? Would it be all black and polished brass like the machine of H. G. Wells?

Maybe it would be like a speedy sports car with a flux capacitor, like in the movie, "Back to the Future."

Scientists really haven't been very serious about the notion of time travel. When one famous scientist named Carl Sagan decided to write a science fiction book, he wrote a theory of time travel into his book. What was special about Sagan's theory? It wasn't the idea of the machine itself (a simple chair), but it was the journey through a worm hole that sparked the curiosity of other scientists.

So, what does this very smart group of scientists say? Is it possible or not? Well, some say, "Yes!" and some say, "No!" For now, we'll just have to be content with reading and writing about time travel.

title: Timelines
text:
Timelines can be made for just about anything and for any time. A good place to start is with something or someone you know well... like yourself! What year was your first birthday? What year did you start kindergarten? Make a list of all the events you would like on your timeline. If you don’t know when the event was, ask a parent to help you.

Next, use a ruler to measure a straight line with evenly spaced lines to mark years and months. Fill in your headings and draw some pictures that go with them. As you continue to grow, keep on adding to your timeline.

Historic Timelines

The timeline to the right is a historic timeline. It is also about a person. What can you learn from this timeline? How old was George Washington when he died? How long was he married when the Declaration of Independence was signed?

By marking the passage of time, we are able to have a clearer understanding of the life of an individual or an event in time.

Here are some other topics for timelines: the 1970s, roller coasters, electric trains or Barbie dolls.

title: Supply and Demand
text:
To an economist, a market includes everyone who buys or sells a certain good or service. That means that all of the people who buy or sell sweaters are in the sweater market. Everyone wanting to buy CDs is in the CD market. Everyone wanting a hot dog is in the hot dog market. These markets become very important as economists study supply and demand. Supply is the amount of something being offered by producers for consumers to buy. Demand is a measure of how many consumers want to buy what producers are offering. Let's take the sweater, for example. The companies and stores selling sweaters are supplying them. The consumers who are willing to pay for sweaters are demanding them.

Demand is not the same as someone wanting or wishing for something. If a person wishes to buy a new bike, he or she really is not demanding it. Economists do not think people are demanding something until they are willing and able to buy that bike, or until they have the money to actually pay for the bike. When they can purchase the bike, then they are in the bike market.

When economists study supply, they look at the product being offered. They also look at who is offering it and at the market for the product. They study prices being charged for a product. Economists find out how much it costs a company to make that product. When there is a greater demand for a product than producers can supply, a shortage occurs. A shortage often means that prices go up for that product as people compete to buy it. When there is a greater supply for something than a demand for it, it is called a surplus. A surplus often means that prices go down. That's because producers are unable to sell that product because there is less demand.

Can you think of recent examples of a shortage and a surplus?

title: Citizenship in the Classroom
text:
Learning to be a good citizen in your classroom is important. It is a good way to make sure everyone has the chance to learn. When we understand the rules of our school and respect them, we are practicing good citizenship. It will help us understand and respect the laws of our state. We will know how to respect the laws of the United States of America. When we are good citizens, it means we respect the rights of others. We are free to make choices about how we live and behave as long as our choices don't take away the freedoms of others.

When someone is noisy in the classroom, how does that take away your freedom? Good citizenship in the classroom means many things. You can also participate in activities or help others. List some ways that you may have been a good citizen in the classroom during the last week.

title: A feather in your cap
text:
"Wow! Look at your timeline. You've done something you can really be proud of!" That's what this expression means. It means that you are happy to have completed a task well. So, go ahead and shine.

Will had been working hard to earn a scholarship for one of the best universities in the country. As a junior in high school, he was excited when the principal announced he had just won first place in the regional science fair.

"Good job, Will!" said the principal. "That is a real feather in your cap. It will help you to earn that scholarship."

title: What does “e pluribus unum” mean?
text:
If you look closely at U.S. coins, you will see the phrase "e pluribus unum" printed on the back of quarters, dimes, nickels and pennies. This translates to mean "One out of many."

This refers to America as one nation with many peoples and cultures. This does not mean that we are all the same, but that we share the same values of freedom and democracy that bind us as a nation.

title: Ancient Calendars
text:
The Earth goes around the sun every 365 and slightly less than a quarter day. In fact it's 11 minutes and 14 seconds less. For thousands of years people have tried to keep track of time with a calendar that uses the rotation of the Earth around the sun as a guide. The problem is that pesky extra time. If you don't keep track of it right, you could end up with spring starting when the calendar says July! That's a problem. Here is how some people in history have tried to keep track of time.

The Aztec and Mayan calendars are based on two cycles. The first cycle was used by the priests for devotion. It had 260 days. These days were broken into 20 periods of 13 days each. The second cycle was 365 days. The two together made a 52-year century called a Calendar Round. The actual calendar used by the Aztec was carved about 1479. It weighs almost 25 tons, is 12 feet across and 3 feet thick! How would you like to hang THAT on your wall?

The Julian calendar is made up of 365 days with one leap year day every four years. It is also divided into 12 months. It was started by Julius Caesar in 46 B.C. The problem with the Julian calendar was that it didn't take the slightly less than a quarter day into account. So it was slightly off every year.

By 1582 people realized the Julian calendar was 10 days off of the actual time of year! It was time for a better calendar! The Gregorian calendar was the answer.

The Gregorian calendar is the calendar we use today. It's a lot like the Julian calendar except it takes that extra time into account. It's a little complicated, but by skipping leap year three times in a 400-year cycle, it works out just right!

title: Synonyms
text:
Synonyms are words that have the same or almost the same meanings.

Learning synonyms for common words is important. Synonyms build your vocabulary. They can make your writing more interesting (alluring, compelling, fascinating) to read.

Below, you will find a common (ordinary, average, passable) fairy tale. Work with a partner to find synonyms for as many words as possible. Rewrite the fairytale using your favorite synonyms.

Do you want to find synonyms on the computer? Use this Web site to see what you can find: thesaurus.reference.com

Goldilocks and the Three Bears

Once upon a time, there were three bears. They lived in the forest in a cute little cottage. There was a big papa bear, a middle-sized mama bear and a little baby bear. One chilly morning, mama bear stirred up some porridge. It was too hot to eat, so they went for a walk in the forest.

While they were out, Goldilocks came right in. She saw the porridge on the table and, forgetting her manners, sat down to eat.

“Wow,” said Goldilocks, “this big bowl is really hot.” She tasted the porridge in the middle-sized bowl. It was cold.

“Oh my heart,” she said, “this bowl of porridge is too cold.” Then she spied a little bowl. She took a little bite.

“Yummy!” she squeaked. It was just right. With a big smile on her face, she ate all of the porridge. It was just perfect for a crisp fall morning.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: Choose one article from this week’s magazine and read it again. Circle or highlight two or more main ideas of the article in yellow. Circle or highlight three or more key details in green. On a piece of paper, write a summary statement about the article.

title: Let's Write
text: You have been chosen to be the passenger in a time machine traveling into your own past. Write a paragraph telling other readers if you think it would be OK to make events in the past change. What would happen if you did change them? Would the present and the future still be the same? Tell us about your choices and the decision you made.

title: Old World Meets New World
text:
From the dawn of time, mankind has been restless to explore beyond the horizons. The earliest explorers ventured to new places as they hunted for food. Later, as civilizations evolved, exploration was often a result of trade. During some periods of history, exploration was born of one country's desire to conquer other countries and people in an effort to expand their empires. In some instances, religion became the driving force as people desired to convert all of humankind to Christianity.

Who do most Americans think of when they hear the words "explorers" and "discovery"? They probably think of Christopher Columbus, but few people actually know much about Columbus and his voyages across the Atlantic Ocean to a new world.

Christened "Cristoforo Cololmbo" at birth, he was born in Genoa in 1451. Columbus joined a ship's crew as a youth and claimed to have sailed as far away as Iceland. Perhaps it was hearing tales of earlier explorers and debates about what lay beyond Europe that first sparked his desire to explore.

Christopher returned from his travels and settled in Portugal, where he married. His wife died giving birth to their first child, a son named Diego. But adventures of the sea called, and it wasn't long before Christopher was planning a new voyage.

Many people today mistakenly believe that Christopher Columbus came up with the idea that the Earth was round and tried to convince the rest of the world. This fact had been known for centuries! As early as the sixth century B.C.E., Greek scholars determined our Earth to be round. While Columbus didn't come up with the idea, he was aware of the fact. Columbus went to King John II of Portugal and asked him to fund a voyage to Japan. At the time, many explorers were going around the continent of Africa to make their way into Asian territory. Columbus believed that if they sailed west across the Atlantic Ocean instead, the journey would be shorter and much easier. King John, however, promptly turned him down. He correctly believed that Columbus had miscalculated the distance and was reluctant to fund any more explorers at the time.

Christopher then tried to persuade the Duke of Medina Sidonia, but was turned down once again. Columbus was at last given audience with Queen Isabella of Spain. She did not immediately agree to provide the funds for the voyage. But after nearly six years, she decided to commission Columbus "Admiral of the Ocean Sea" and set him up with three ships, supplies and crews.

Columbus set sail from Palos on Aug. 3, 1492. He was in command of three ships, the Niña, Pinta and Santa Maria. Columbus was the captain of the Santa Maria.

For the first six weeks of the voyage, the winds were favorable, and all went well. Then, between Sept. 20 and 30, the winds died out, and the ships were still. The crews began to fidget and grumble as they feared the unknown.

Just when things were getting really tense, land was sighted on Oct. 12, 1492. What the lookout on the Santa Maria had sighted was an island that Columbus christened San Salvador.

The relieved crews were greeted by friendly Arawak tribespeople. Believing that he had reached Asia, Columbus, of course, called the local natives "Indians." He then sailed on to Cuba in hopes of finding the Mongol emperor of China, Khan. When he arrived in Cuba, he did not find the great palace he was expecting, so off they went again. This time, they landed in the present-day Dominican Republic. It was there that a storm destroyed the Santa Maria, and Columbus and crew completed their voyage on the Niña.

Columbus next stopped at the Canary Islands to replenish. While there, he sent a letter to his friend in Spain. The letter told of his discovery of "a great many islands, inhabited by numberless people." He then claimed all the land and the resources in the name of Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand.

Columbus realized he did not find what he was looking for, but he insisted (until his death) that he had found a new route to the East. He would make three more voyages to the New World and visit parts of South and Central America.

While Columbus wasn't the first person from the Old World to set eyes on the New World, he was the first person to write about it. The fact that Columbus actually never set foot on the North American continent in any of his voyages does not lessen the importance of his travels. It was Columbus's letter from February 1493 that brought the New World to the Old World and set into motion American history as we know it.

title: CubeStormer Robot Beats Record for Solving Rubik’s Cube
text:
How fast are you at solving the Rubik’s cube? Have you ever tried to solve this puzzle? Well, so many people have tried that there are international tournaments where people compete to solve this puzzle the fastest. They are called speedcubers. So far, Feliks Zemdegs of Australia has the world record of solving the 3 x 3 Rubik’s cube at 5.66 seconds. Pretty cool, huh?

Some people have even invented robots that solve the Rubik’s cube. Friends Mike Dobson and David Gilday created a robot they named the CubeStormer. It is made of Legos®, controlled by a laptop computer and can solve the Rubik’s cube in less than 12 seconds. But Mr. Dobson and Mr. Gilday wanted something even faster, so they invented the CubeStormer II. It is also made of Legos® but is controlled by a smartphone. The phone uses a special application (app) to take a picture of the puzzle cube, solve the puzzle in the phone and then transfer the solution to the robot to fix the cube. The really fun part is that this robot solves the Rubik’s cube in 5.35 seconds. That beats the official human world record!

With permission, check out this online video of the CubeStormer II solving the Rubik’s cube in 5.35 seconds: https://www.youtube.com/user/RoboticSolutions. What do you think? Would you like to try your hand at speedcubing? What about building robots that solve puzzles? The possibilities are mind-boggling!

title: Exploration Begins
text:
From A.D. 500 to about A.D. 1400, Europe didn't grow very much. We call this period the Dark Ages, the Middle Ages or the Medieval period. You've probably seen movies depicting this period, when there were knights, castles, lords, peasants and kings. People didn't travel much in those days, and as a result, even the kings knew almost nothing of the world outside of their own small kingdoms. It wasn't until a few explorers left Europe and brought word back to their fellow Europeans of the wonders of the Orient, that men cared about exploring new worlds. This week, let's learn how these few men paved the way for the Age of Exploration to begin.

Viking Adventures in A.D. 1000

Historians believe that one of the first groups of Europeans to visit North America that we know of were the Vikings. A Viking ship from Greenland was blown off course and accidentally discovered the new land. Leif Erikson landed on Labrador or Newfoundland and called the place Vinland because of the many grapes growing there. Later, Leif's brother, Thorvald, established a colony in Vinland. He and his crew spent two years exploring the coast and fighting the indigenous people whom they called "skraelings." (This is what they called them in their sagas or stories.) These indigenous people eventually forced the Vikings to abandon the Vinland settlement and return to Greenland. The Vikings were not interested in returning to Newfoundland, and news of the New World discovery did not reach Europe at this time, so Europe was still in the dark about the American continents.

Marco Polo Introduces Asia to Europe!

Marco Polo was the son of an explorer. His father, Niccolo, and uncle, Maffeo, made the long and treacherous trek to China. Here, they stayed for many years until their return to their home of Venice. When Niccolo returned to China in 1271, he took his son, Marco, with him. Marco stayed in China for 20 years and served the Mongol ruler of China, Kublai Khan.

When Marco Polo finally returned to Venice, it was to find his country at war. Upon his return, he was imprisoned in Genoa. While in Genoa, Marco spoke of the wonders of Mongol China. He told of worms that spun silk, black stones that burned, water clocks and paper money. He spoke of a great wall and a grand canal. All of these things were unheard of in Europe. A fellow prisoner was a writer and wrote a book of Marco's adventures.

As the tales were passed around, people became eager to visit Asia. The desire to see and bring back these treasures gave Europeans the exploring spirit. There was much talk of finding the best and fastest trade route to Asia.

Later, an explorer named Christopher Columbus would be inspired by this book and seek to find the shortest route to Asia.

Henry the Navigator Launches the Age of Exploration

Prince Henry of Portugal was the son of King John I. He became interested in Africa early in his life. Before he was 18 years old, the young prince sent ships to explore the coast of Africa. By the time he was 24, Prince Henry had decided to devote his life to learning more about Africa and the far-off lands of the Indies.

Prince Henry traveled to Sagres, a lonely spot at the southwestern tip of Portugal. There, he built a small village high on a cliff, overlooking a harbor. He studied navigation and sailing for about 40 years and started a school to teach what he learned about navigation and sailing.

He invited mapmakers, scientists and navigators to come to his school. Prince Henry's scholars trained the sailors to use compasses, astrolabes and other important navigating instruments. They also taught them many other skills necessary for exploration on the high seas. The studious prince became known as Henry the Navigator. The "Age of Exploration," which he started, lasted for more than 200 years.

Year after year, Prince Henry sent out ships to sail the vast Atlantic Ocean. He actually only went on two voyages, but funded many more. His ships sailed farther and farther along the coast of Africa. Often, his sailors stopped to explore the land along the coast. They claimed these lands for Portugal.

title: Scarcity
text:
Have you ever been to a movie house and wanted to see more than just one movie? Maybe you saw or heard ads on television or the radio that made you want to see two or three movies, but you only had time and money to see one. How did you decide which movie to go see? Was it a hard choice? Did you go to the one your friends wanted to see? Did you ask someone who had already seen the movies for advice?

From time to time, you have to make a choice about which movie to see. A society faces the same kind of challenge deciding how to use their resources. Our resources are scarce. That means there is a higher demand for them than a supply. No matter how much of something is being supplied, people always want more. Sometimes, time can be scarce. That's when people don't have enough time to do everything. Sometimes, money is scarce. That's when you want more candy than you can afford or have the money to buy.

Because our resources are so scarce, people are always making choices about how to use them. Every time you make a choice about what to buy or how to spend your time, you are making a trade-off. Let's say that you decide to spend money on candy. Then you are making a trade-off of candy for money. You have less money, but more candy.

Economists also have a name for what you give up when you choose something else. An opportunity cost is what you do not get when you make a choice. There are opportunity costs in everything. When you woke up this morning, you may have decided to sleep in. If you did, what did you give up in doing so? Was it taking a shower or eating every bite of your breakfast? You could say that the opportunity cost of sleeping in was taking a shower or eating a nice breakfast. We have opportunity costs when we buy things, too.

Let's say that you couldn't decide between buying a new DVD or a new book. You finally decide to buy the DVD. The opportunity cost of that DVD was the new book. What is the opportunity cost of going to school every day? Is it worth it?

title: Citizenship in the School
text:
Learning to be a good citizen at school is something to work on every day. By now, you have practiced good listening skills. You have also worked on good behavior in the classroom. There is another way to practice good citizenship. It begins right in your own school. You can begin by respecting the property of others. Property is anything that is owned by a group or individual.

The coat you are wearing is your property.

The desk where you sit is school property.

The school building is government property.

Respect for property can be shown in many ways. The first is to make sure you don't harm or destroy things. Another way to show respect is to let an adult know if you see property being damaged. A third way is to take part in repairing damaged property. It's great to take care of your things. It's great to show respect for the property of others.

title: Don't beat around the bush
text:
We say this when someone is avoiding talking about something. If you tell someone not to beat around the bush, you are saying, Get to the point.

"Did you do your math homework?" asked Ricky's teacher.

"Well, I started it, but I got stuck, so I took a break. Then my sister came home and my mom made us a snack. And then when I started working on math again, my little brother was crying and...."

"Ricky, don't beat around the bush," said his teacher. "I'd just like a 'yes' or a 'no,' please."

title: Were there any women explorers?
text: As rough as exploring was, we often assume that explorers were all males. There were, however, female explorers. In 17 6 9, Isabel Godin des Odonais became the first woman to descend the Amazon. She went with a small party including some members of her own family. Along the way they faced extreme weather, wild animals, illness and hostile natives. Eventually, everyone but Isabel was killed. She was left alone to fend for herself, and she did. She stayed for 2 1 days by herself in the jungle until she was found and was finally able to return home.

title: The Printing Press
text:
Before the printing press, the only way to make more than one copy of anything written was to do it by hand. This was a very long and difficult task, and it often took years for one person to copy a large book.

Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg, a German printer, invented the first printing press with moveable type. He made a mold, or pattern, of each letter of the alphabet and would set the type, or arrange the letters, to spell out what he wanted to print. He then used a large press with a screw that could be tightened or loosened to push the ink-covered type up against a piece of paper. This made a copy of the page.

Gutenberg's printing press made it possible to print many copies of written works quickly and easily. More importantly, it made it possible to spread important information to citizens all over the world.

title: Antonyms
text:
Antonyms are words that have opposite meanings.

Antonyms are words that have the opposite meaning. What is the opposite of antonym? If you guessed synonym, you are exactly right. Just as with synonyms, antonyms are useful in reading and writing.

Below, you will see word pairs that are synonyms. Write at least one antonym for each word pair.

1. sell, market

2. ask, request

3. give, grant

4. whisper, murmur

5. light, glow

6. opinion, belief

7. praise, congratulate

8. solid, hard

You can find antonyms, as well as synonyms, in a thesaurus. Check it out.

title: Let's Write
text:
Cristoforo Cololmbo

When Christopher Columbus set sail from Spain on Aug. 3, 1492, he brought with him on board the ship a scholar who spoke Arabic.

A. Write a paragraph explaining why you think Christopher Columbus thought this was necessary.

B. Explain your thoughts about whether or not Christopher Columbus’ voyage was successful. Tell us why you think so.

title: World Cultures and Civilizations
text:
The story of humankind begins a long, long time ago, in a time we will call prehistoric time. "Prehistoric" is the word used to describe the time before people began writing. Imagine a people who hunted and gathered plants for their daily food. At night, they huddled around fires in caves to keep warm. These people made their own tools out of sticks and stones. They made clothing from animal skins sewn together with needles fashioned from bones. The most important task for these prehistoric people would have been the daily hunt for food. As the animals moved from place to place, the people had to follow.

Today, most people don't need to move around to hunt and survive. People have learned how to farm, and they produce goods that can be sold. Cities and countries have grown because people settle in one place, and people can communicate by writing. These changes - settling in one place, growing food, making and selling goods and communicating by writing - are ways that show when a group of people has become a civilization. Civilizations began to form when the prehistoric peoples learned to grow large amounts of food. With plenty of food, they no longer needed to move around, so they settled in one place. As more people joined them, cities and towns grew, and civilizations were born. As towns and cities grew, not all people farmed. Some were soldiers, and some made tools, clothing or jewelry. Still others became musicians, teachers or scholars. Each civilization developed a culture of its own. Culture is a word used to describe the arts, beliefs and customs of a group of people in a certain time. Culture is something that is passed from one generation to another.

Turn the page to learn about some of the ancient (very old) civilizations and their cultures.

title: Respect for the “Write” Stuff
text:
Scholars have recently learned new information about ancient scribes. While studying the Mayans' writing system, they have reached some new conclusions. They believe that writing was not just used for spreading news and information, but it was also used for gaining and keeping power.

In the Mayan civilization, there were many city-states, each one ruled by a king. Each king had a scribe whose job it was to help the king be powerful by showing that power through writing and through pictures. For example, the scribe might draw a picture showing a king standing on the backs of a people he had defeated in battle. That kind of picture, and the story that was written with it, were to show other people how mighty the king was. If a people feared a king, they were likely to be loyal to him.

Much of what scholars have learned about scribes in all of the ancient civilizations comes from pictures or statues of them. Scribes are shown sitting near the king wearing fine clothes. They have writing tools near them, and they are described in writing as "the keepers of the royal library."

A scribe in ancient civilization had to go through years of training and was highly respected.

title: Ancient Civilizations
text:
Maya Civilization

The Maya lived in Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and Honduras. Archeologists have found evidence that the Maya existed in those countries from 1000 B.C. until A.D. 1519. Their society was divided into four classes or groups - kings, priests, common people and slaves. The Maya are known for many amazing achievements. They studied astronomy, the science of celestial objects. They were especially interested in the sun. They built a pyramid calendar that had four stairways with 91 steps in each and a platform at the top. (4 x 91 steps = 364 + 1 platform = 365 days)

Another cool thing about the Maya is that they were really good at math. They used a dot for ones and bars for fives. They even had a symbol for zero (right).

Most Maya made their living as farmers. They grew corn, which they called maize, and lived in small villages. Priests lived in the large cities. The common people like the farmers only went to the cities for special ceremonies and festivals.

Inca Civilization

One of the greatest empires of all time lasted only about 100 years, from 1438 to 1532. The Inca lived in South America. Their cities and villages stretched from Columbia to Chile in the Andes Mountains. The Inca were strong, smart people. They survived at high elevations in the mountains, as well as in the desert and the Amazon Rain Forest.

The Inca built an incredible system of roads that has amazed engineers for centuries. They paved the roads with flat stones and built stone walls to keep people from falling off cliffs as they traveled. They built stone temples by carving the stones to fit together perfectly. They didn't even need mortar to hold the stones together.

Farming was an important part of Inca life. The people raised more than 70 different kinds of crops including corn, potatoes, squash, beans, peppers, peanuts, tomatoes and grains. They built huge buildings to store food for times of famine (when there is not enough food). They ate mostly fish and vegetables and not much meat.

The Inca used a 12-month calendar and a number system based on the number 10. Their spoken language was called Quechua, but they did not have a written language. They believed in many gods. The most powerful was Inti, the Sun God. The Inca were known for their gold (which they called the sweat of the sun) and their silver (which they called the tears of the moon).

Aztec Civilization

If you've ever been to Mexico City, you visited a city that was built on the site of the capital of the Aztec civilization. The Aztec people called it Tenochtitlan. Tenochtitlan was one of 300 cities in the Aztec civilization. About 15 million Aztec people lived in central Mexico during the 14th, 15th and 16th centuries.

The Aztec grew corn, chili peppers, squash, tomatoes, beans and other crops on their farms. They ground the corn to make tortillas, one of their main foods. They hunted rabbits, deer, ducks and geese for meat. And they get the credit for discovering one of our favorite foods - chocolate! They used cocoa beans to flavor their food and to make candy and beverages.

The number system used by the Aztec people was based on the number 20, and their calendar had 18 months of 20 days (360 days). But they knew there were 365 days in each year, so they added five special days to the calendar. They called the special days Nemontemi, or Days of Sacrifice.

Aztec homes were low, wide houses made of adobe (sun-dried bricks). They built small temples on mounds. The mounds also helped protect the Aztec from attacks by enemies. The Aztec are known for their beautiful sculptures. They created these beautiful pieces of art to please their gods.

title: Citizenship in the Community
text:
What things do good citizens do in your community? It's the same as being a good citizen at home and at school!

Listening carefully is very important! We can listen carefully to the local news and read the paper. One idea is to write a letter with a solution to a community problem or concern.

We can respect the rights of others by keeping the laws of the state and country.

Picking up litter in the community is one great way to show respect for property. What are some others?

A good citizen is also one who performs acts of service for others in the community. It could be as simple as shoveling snow from your neighbor's path.

How about planting seeds in a public garden?

Make a goal to do at least one service project in your community this year.

title: Touch and go
text:
People say this when they talk about something that is a little unsure. In other words, they just don't know what is going to happen.

It is down to the final two contestants in the spelling bee. Each of them has missed a word, but the opponent wasn't able to spell it either. Both of the contestants have been confident about all of the words up until now.

Cory has just been asked to spell the word "Portuguese." "P-O-R-T-U-G-U..." Cory says, and then he stops to think. The audience members are holding their breath, and Cory's mom is crossing her fingers.

Cory's mom leans over and whispers to his dad, "It's touch and go from here."

title: What is a Chunnel?
text:
Chunnel is the nickname used for the Channel Tunnel. This amazing tunnel is an undersea rail link that connects France to Great Britain. (And we thought the rides at Disney World were cool!)

The Chunnel took seven years to build. It includes two rail tracks. Trains take 35 minutes to pass through the tunnel. Travelers can now journey from London to Paris in about three hours when using the Chunnel. That's a pretty quick trip!

title: The Slabbing Saw
text:
Even though we aren't sure exactly how the ancient Egyptians built their pyramids, we do know that they used special tools. In order to cut the stone used in these amazing buildings, the Egyptians had to use a large, sharp cutting tool. One of the important tools used by the Egyptians to cut rock was a slabbing saw. A slabbing saw was a rectangle-shaped saw with a straight, wooden handle and a jagged blade made of copper or bronze.

Ancient Egyptians used slabbing saws to cut both wood and rock. The saw was meant to be pulled, not pushed, through the wood or rock, and most of these saws were about six feet long. Without these large saws, the pyramid builders wouldn't have been able to cut the rock into the proper sizes and shapes.

How do we know that the pyramid builders used these types of saws? Archaeologists have discovered saw marks on many of the rocks used to build the pyramids. They have also found pictures of these slabbing saws in Egyptian art.

Today, stonecutters use powerful saws with strong, long-lasting, jeweled blades to cut though tough rock, but in ancient times, the slabbing saw was the best tool available for the job.

title: Plenty of Prefixes
text:
A prefix is a group of letters added to the beginning of a word that changes its meaning.

You have learned many different strategies for learning vocabulary words. Learning what prefixes mean is another strategy to add to your bag of vocabulary tricks.

When you know what the parts of a word mean, you can put them all together, and then voila!—you know what the word means.

Below is a short list of prefixes and their meanings. Study them and then complete the exercise.

Plenty of Prefixes Exercise

Using the prefixes below, create as many words as possible from these base words: fiction, standard, historic, compose, responsible, legal, applied, write, happy, agree, port, courage

1. un (not, opposite)

2. re (again, back)

3. in, im, ir, il (not)

4. dis (not, opposite )

5. en, em (cause to)

6. non (not)

7. in, im (in or into)

8. trans (across)

9. mis (wrongly)

10. sub (under)

11. pre (before)

12. de (down, reverse)
