text:
Yippee!

You have some special glasses that let you translate records from ancient civilizations.

A. Write the name of the ancient civilization for which you will be translating.

B. Tell about the person who wrote the ancient record.

C. Describe the material used to write the message.

D. Translate the message for our readers.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: As you read this week’s lesson, use any color to circle or highlight five verbs. On a piece of paper, write a sentence for each verb using the perfect form (past tense plus helping verb: I have walked. She has swung.).

title: Fun Facts
text: President Franklin Delano Roosevelt was related by either blood or marriage to 11 other United States Presidents. Those presidents were: John Adams, John Quincy Adams, Ulysses Grant, William Henry Harrison, Benjamin Harrison, James Madison, Theodore Roosevelt, William Taft, Zachary Taylor, Martin Van Buren and George Washington.

title: The Treaty of Tordesillas
text:
Spain and Portugal did not exist until the late 1300s. That is to say, the people were there and the language also, but their were no political boundaries. Portugal was the first to unite as a country. As a new country, Portugal turned to the sea. After Prince Henry the Navigator, Portugal improved knowledge, instruments and even ships in the quest for a new trade route to Asia.

Spain was born with the marriage of Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile. (Remember those royal people? They funded the voyages of Christopher Columbus.) When Columbus returned from his first voyage, he brought news of new lands.

Portugal was worried, because while they had very nearly reached India, Spain had already found Asia (or so Christopher Columbus said).

It was the Pope who settled the problem with a papal decree. He divided the world between the two countries, and they agreed (but who asked the natives?). This division was called the Treaty of Tordesillas. While the Portuguese focused much of their energy on sailing around Africa, the Spanish focused on obtaining gold from the Americas.

The Treaty of Tordesillas not only divided the land, but also gave Spain and Portugal the opportunity to control the water routes. As a result, other countries were forced to find new trade routes. Many countries began to look for a passage around the top of North America. The search for the Northwest Passage led England, the Netherlands and France to push forward as they sought to establish better trade routes.

Risky Business

The first trade routes were overland. It was a long and treacherous journey for merchants. Merchants would do almost anything to get to the spices and treasures found in the East.

As navigation improved, many Old World countries turned to maritime (sea) routes in hopes of finding shorter ways to bring goods home.

The need for better trade routes ushered in the Age of Exploration and Discovery; and that discovery, in turn, expanded trade.

A trade route is a pathway, real or imaginary, that people use over and over to deliver or obtain goods.

It was the search for new trade routes that led to the Age of Exploration. Those voyages of Old World explorers opened up the eyes of Europeans to a whole new world. Many new maritime trade routes were quickly established, and the race was on. The rival countries of Spain and Portugal pushed forward quickly. When the rest of the Old World countries saw the treasures and heard of the adventures. They were anxious to catch up. Soon, most of the major European countries were in on the race to discover new trade routes.

Maritime trade was expensive, however, and Columbus wasn't the only one who had a hard time convincing royalty to sponsor ships and supplies. Even when they were able to convince someone to sponsor the voyage, there was no guarantee they would successfully reach their destination. Many attempts failed, and countless numbers of sailors died trying to find new passageways for trade.

Trade companies were soon established, and commercial empires led to colonial empires.

title: Technology Improves World Trade
text:
Distributing goods and services today takes much less time than it did 100, or even 50, years ago. Today, we can take something to the post office, and just like magic, it will arrive at its destination tomorrow. Computers, telephones, jets, trains and trucks - all of these things make trade between world communities seem like a miracle.

While many improvements in transportation have been notable, one of the most significant accomplishments has been the development of the jet engine.

It was a race to see who would complete the jet engine first, as Hans Von Ohain was working in Germany, Sir Frank Whittle was frantically trying to complete one in England. Both men completed their first experimental engines in the mid-1930s.

Then, in February of 1937, Von Ohain was ready to test the He S-1 turbojet. It was tested using hydrogen fuel. Von Ohain reported to the public that the engine fully met all expectations. Because the tests went so well, the engine design program sped up, and on Aug. 27, 1939, the first jet-powered airplane (the He-178) was successfully flown.

Back in England, Frank Whittle's test didn't go as well. Everything began as planned, but when he began to give it more fuel, it went out of control, and everyone except Whittle ran for their lives. After stopping the engine, the cause of the problem was found and finally fixed. Whittle completed his jet-powered airplane (the ES 28/39) in 1941, and it completed a successful test run on May 15, 1941.

The development of the jet engine drastically changed transportation and the time it took to move people and goods all around the world.

title: Focus on Explorers
text:
Magellan's Crew Sails Around the World

In 1519, Ferdinand Magellan took five ships and over 200 men to venture around the world. In 1520, he went around the tip of South America, crossed the Pacific and discovered the Philippine Islands. Here, he was wounded in a skirmish and died. Survivors continued to Borneo and the Spice Islands. In 1522, the convoy's last remaining ship limped into harbor at Seville with only 18 men alive. Magellan's trip around the globe took three years and 12 days and cost the lives of more than 200 men.

Spanish Explore and Colonize the Americas

In 1539, an explorer named Coronado in search of the "Seven Lost Cities of Cibola" traveled through the southwestern United States and stumbled on the magnificent Grand Canyon.

Spain and Portugal tried hard to take advantage of the new economies opened up in the Americas and Asia. By 1575, there were over 575,000 Spaniards in hundreds of Spanish settlements all over South America and on the major islands in the West Indies. The Portuguese were not as rich or numerous as the Spanish, but they still became wealthy from the new trade. The only strong investment in a Portuguese settlement was in Brazil where they flourished. They built trading posts and forts along the coasts of Africa, India and in the East Indies, Java and Sumatra. Portugal used its African trading posts to launch a slave trade business. Although slavery had been practiced in every generation somewhere in the world since the beginning of humanity, this particular episode that began in the 1500s took hundreds of years and millions of lives to finally abolish.

Spain was larger and richer than Portugal, and early on it sent explorers to Santo Domingo in the West Indies. From there, settlers spread out all over the mainland in all directions. In 1577, Sir Francis Drake started a trip around the world and became rich by attacking Spanish ships loaded with treasures. Drake pulled into England in 1588 much richer than when he left.

England and France Explore and Colonize the Americas

While Spain and Portugal were getting rich, England, France and the Dutch watched from the sidelines. They wanted part of the action. The English were the first to venture out, and in the beginning, they worked hard to take control of the open seas. They defeated the Spanish Armada in 1588, and for the next 100 years, they developed a rich overseas trade. In 1607, their first permanent colony was established at Jamestown, Virginia. By 1733, they had 13 well-established colonies on the mainland of America and several island possessions in the West Indies.

The French were not too far behind. In 1534, Jacques Cartier was sailing on behalf of France when he ventured up the St. Lawrence River. He declared all the land he found to be New France. In 1608, Samuel de Champlain sailed up the St. Lawrence River and founded Quebec, the capital of New France. Montreal came along after.

title: Money
text:
When the English colonists first came to America, they brought some of the money they used back in England. They called their money shillings, pence and pounds. They soon found out it was of no use to them in the New World. The American Indians didn't care for their money. It didn't mean anything to them. The American Indians bartered with the colonists. As you can imagine, that became very hard. Therefore, the early colonists of Massachusetts started using wampum. Wampum consisted of purple and white shells. The purple ones were worth twice as much as the white ones. They used it the same way as money. American Indians had traded wampum with seacoast tribes since the 1640s. Both the colonists and the American Indians soon used it. This made for less trouble in the colonies. It was used in addition to bartering.

Economists like to say, "Money is what money does." This was as true for the American Indians and English colonists as it is for us today. Money has three main functions. First, it must be a way of exchange that people accept. This means that people have to agree on what they will use for money. Second, money must be a measure of value. This means that the people using the money must know how much the money is worth in their community. Last, money must be a store of value. People should be able to save their money and use it later. Storing value is very hard when bartering. Often the goods or products people are trying to trade go bad before they can find someone in the market for them. For example, milk is hard to keep in hot weather. Bartering milk without a way to keep it cold for a long time would be very tricky.

Money must also be easy to carry. It must be sturdy, easy to recognize and able to be broken down into smaller parts. Our U.S. money is small. It's easy to carry and uniform, or all the same. People in the country accept it all over. You can divide it easily. This is nice for everyone because it is so easy. What if you lived in a country that used bowling balls for money? That wouldn't work very well at all!

title: Sir Francis Drake
text:
Pirate or explorer? Sir Francis Drake was both. Drake, an Englishman, began as an apprentice to a ship's master. He always dreamed of sailing the high seas. At the age of 23, his dream came true when he joined a slave-trading expedition.

At that time, England was arguing with Spain and Portugal about who owned the land and seas of the New World. Drake became a "sea dog" for England. A sea dog attacked ships of other countries. There were many sea dogs on the ocean at this time. Drake mostly attacked ships from Spain. Spain considered him a pirate, but the Queen of England thought he was doing a good job. She made him a knight, which gave him the name Sir Francis Drake. Drake began exploring in 1577 when he set out on what would become a three-year voyage around the world. He was the first Englishman to sail all the way around the world. When he returned to England, he was a hero!

Sir Francis Drake died in 1595 at age 62. He was buried at sea.

title: Missed the boat
text:
This saying is used when someone misses an opportunity to do something. In other words, they just didn't think about a plan.

"Did you hear that the tickets to the concert went on sale yesterday?" Jacob asked. "I'm on my way to buy ours now."

"Hey," said Sam sadly, "you can forget that idea. They sold out of tickets this morning."

"What?" Jacob moaned. "I guess I should have gone to stand in line like you suggested. Boy, I really missed the boat."

title: What is hardtack?
text: Hardtack is a very hard biscuit that was used by explorers aboard ships for food. Voyages were very long, and there was no means to preserve food. The food usually eaten by sailors was salted meat and hardtack. The hard biscuits often became infested with beetles or maggots, which had to be removed before the hardtack could be eaten! Hardtack was made with flour, water and salt. It was baked until very hard.

title: The ATM
text:
Years ago the only way to take money out of the bank was to walk into a bank and fill out a form. This wasn't always easy, because most banks closed before people got off work. But things are different now thanks to technology! We have Automatic Teller Machines (ATMs) almost everywhere that work like little banks. Thanks to ATMs we can take our money out anytime we want. We just put our ATM card in the machine and punch in the amount of money we need. Of course, the machines are only giving us our own money. If there is no more money in your account, the ATM can't give you any cash.

An ATM card is a card the bank gives you that allows you to take money out of your bank account even if the bank is closed. When you put in your card, you also have to type in a number, sort of like a password. If you lose your card, that number helps protect your money from thieves. Without the right password, the card will not work. Most ATM cards are also debit cards. You can use them to buy things almost anywhere. The money comes right out of your bank account, and you don't have to pay interest the way you do if you use a credit card.

title: Clarity of Expression: Henry Hudson
text:
Henry Hudson was an English sea captain and explorer who started off as a failure. He sailed on two voyages for England to find a northeast water route to the rich spice trade in Asia. But both times the icy northern seas blocked his way. He had to return home defeated.

Sounds like the end of his career, right? It wasn't. Hudson next convinced the Dutch East India Company to hire him for exactly the same expedition. In 1609 Hudson and his crew sailed west across the Atlantic. He reached the New World, landing on the island we know today as Manhattan. He sailed inland up a wide river and explored the surrounding valley.

It wasn't a passage to Asia. But Hudson's explorations allowed the Dutch to claim the land and build a fur trading post there in 1614, before the Pilgrims arrived. A Dutch settlement called New Netherland soon followed.

Unfortunately, Hudson's last voyage ended in mutiny. He refused his crew's demands to return home, so the sailors took over the ship, setting Hudson adrift in a small boat. His fate is unknown, but his legacy is Hudson Bay, Hudson River, Hudson Valley and the Dutch settlement that became New York City.

Henry Hudson must have had excellent clarity of expression. He had to be able to explain clearly to the Dutch that his experience and determination made him the best man for the job, even though he was an Englishman and not a Dutchman.

Think about a time that you wanted to convince your parents or teachers to let you try something new. Did you beg and plead? Or did you give them a clear explanation of your reasons? Which way do you think works better?

title: Let's Write
text: A sailor on an explorer’s ship might be at sea as long as two or three years. All of his personal belongings as well as his tools had to be kept in a chest. A sailor’s chest was a very sturdy wooden box with a hinged lid. It was usually painted and often had the name of the sailor and a date painted on the front as well. Not only was the sailor’s chest used for storage, but also as a bench or table. Imagine you are about to go on a voyage to explore a new land. You may be gone for many years. Write a paragraph telling what you might take in your chest and what your duties might be on the long trip.

title: A Suffix Celebration
text:
A suffix is a group of letters added to the end of a word that changes its meaning.

You are nearly done with Word Attack strategies. What better way to “end” it than to celebrate with suffixes?

Below, you will find a short list of common suffixes and their meanings. When you think you have them down, head to the activity below, and strut your stuff!

1. ly (forms adverb)

2. er, or (one who, person)

3. ion, tion, ation, ition (state or quality of)

4. ible, able (is able)

5. ness (state or quality of)

6. ity, y (state or quality of)

7. ment (forms a noun from a verb)

8. ic (relating to, forms and adjective)

9. ful (full of)

10. less (without)

11. est (most)

12. ive, ative, itive (inclined to, forms an adjective)

A Suffix Celebration Exercise

Using the suffixes above, create as many words as possible from these base words: history, father, enjoy, desperate, smart, teach, window, talk, wonder, loyal, happy, comfort.

title: Culture Clash
text:
Centuries before Europeans came to the Americas, there were great civilizations—the civilizations of the Maya, the Inca and the Aztec. Less than 50 years after Columbus sighted the Americas, Spanish and Portuguese explorers and conquistadors had conquered these mighty civilizations.

In the years after the voyage of Christopher Columbus, numerous Spanish explorers traveled to Central America. They were seeking one thing—treasure. When the Spanish explorers arrived, they found three great civilizations in the Americas. They were the Maya, the Inca and the Aztec.

The Spanish encounter with these civilizations was devastating. The conquistadors (Spanish conquerors) did not understand or value the culture and customs of the people they encountered. In their quest to obtain riches, especially gold, they were responsible for the decline and final destruction of these civilizations.

These civilizations were a mixture of many tribes and nations. They were founded on the shoulders of other civilizations before them. They had spectacular cities and well-established governments. These civilizations were masters of many art forms. Their cultures were based largely on religious beliefs. Mesoamerica is the name given to one of two areas in the Americas that had advanced civilizations. The people built temples and pyramids. They had writing systems and calendars. They had established forms of trade with distant neighbors and large markets. The people even had ball games (that were for religious purposes).

Mesoamerica has three periods—the Pre-classic, the Classic and the Post-classic. These periods span the period of time from 2000 B.C. until the Spanish conquest in the 1500s.

The Olmec were the dominant culture in the Pre-classic period. When we think of the Olmec people, we probably remember the large stone heads they carved. The Olmec also used heiroglyphics (picture writing), and they developed calenders. The rise of the Olmec civilization was about 1200 B.C. and continued until their gradual decline in about A.D. 200. They were taken over by other tribes coming into the area. The Olmec are thought of as the "mother of the Mesoamerican civilization."

The Classic period saw the rise of the city Teotihuacán and the Maya culture. The Maya had a great knowledge of astronomy. The strength of the Maya gradually declined until the early 1500s. They were almost completely overtaken by the Spanish conquerors.

The Post-classic period was the time when the Aztec and the Toltec enjoyed their greatest power. The Toltec flourished from A.D. 900 to A.D. 1187. The Toltec influenced the Maya in many ways. As nomads migrated to the area, the Toltec civilization began to wane. Finally, it was completely taken over by the Aztec.

The Aztec founded the great city of Tenochtitlán. This became the capital of the Aztec Empire. Montezuma was their leader from 1440 to 1469. Under his leadership the Aztec warriors conquered neighboring cities and forced them to pay tributes to the Aztec rulers. When Montezuma II became the ruler in 1502, the Aztec Empire was at the height of its power.

It was an Aztec legend that set the stage for the fall of the empire. The Aztec believed a god they called Quetzalcoatl had left their presence and gone eastward. He was to someday return.

When the Spanish conquistador Hernando Cortes landed on the eastern coast of Mexico, Montezuma probably believed he was Quetzalcoatl returning. Montezuma made no effort to resist the advancing Spaniards. In fact, he welcomed them. As the Spaniards began to pillage the cities for gold, the Aztec resisted, and Montezuma died that year. His successor, Cuahtemoc, surrendered to the Spaniards, as the Aztec were no match for the guns, horses and armor of the conquistadors. The Spaniards destroyed the cities. New cities were built over the ruins of the old.

The Inca Empire was also on the rise in the Post-classic era. It was not part of Mesoamerica. It was in the Andes in South America. The Inca Empire was huge. The government was well-organized and was able to control all of the area for a very long time. Though they seemed to have no writing system, their civilization was surprisingly advanced.

When Huayna Capa, the ruler of the Inca, died in 1527, rival groups of followers of his two sons, Huascar and Atahualpa, fought to gain control of the empire. Civil war broke out and ended with Atahualpa ordering the execution of Huascar.

Enter the Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro. He went to the Americas specifically to obtain gold and fortune. When he found the fabulously wealthy Inca Empire, he was able to take it over with only 168 soldiers. The Inca Empire was an easy target because it had been weakened by the civil war, as well as epidemic. When Pizarro executed Huascar, the Inca no longer had a leader. They were easy prey.

The Spanish tried to wipe out the culture and customs of those early civilizations. But, there is evidence of them, even today, in the customs, language, architecture and traditions of the people of Mexico, Central America and parts of South America.

title: A Neanderthal’s Best Friend
text:
Archeologists in both Siberia and Belgium have found dog skulls that show wolves were well on their way to becoming domesticated dogs (pets or helpers for people) about 33,000 years ago. This means the change started about 14,000 years earlier than scientists once thought. How do we know the skulls were 33,000 years old? Scientists use a technique called carbon dating to figure it out. Carbon dating is a way to date things that were once alive by looking at how fast a certain type of carbon in the remains will decay.

This discovery also means that dogs were being domesticated in different areas of the world at the same time. The skulls show that people on two different continents were using dogs as pets or helpers.

Scientists once believed that cows, sheep and goats were domesticated first because they could provide meat and milk for prehistoric people. However, it seems dogs were domesticated first to give companionship and protection and to help during hunts.

Scientists don't think the dogs that were in Siberia or Belgium back then are the ancestors of our modern dog. Instead, they believe that many of these dogs died out during the Ice Age. Through DNA research, scientists have discovered that modern dogs come from the Middle East and East Asia. People and dogs have been best friends for a very long time!

title: Ancient American Civilizations
text:
During the Middle Ages, three large empires rose in the Americas. Today, their ancient pyramids, roads and cities are still being discovered and explored.

The Maya

The Maya appeared in the Americas as early as 1500 B.C. They expanded south from southern Mexico through Guatemala, Honduras and into northern Belize. By A.D. 200, they had developed into a great civilization with ornate temples, steep pyramids and palaces. The Maya Empire grew to 40 cities with at least 2 million people. They also had their own calendar and mathematics and could predict eclipses. They invented their own picture form of writing and made paper from the inner bark of wild fig trees. Around A.D. 900, some unknown catastrophe occurred, and the Maya Empire suddenly dwindled away. Some believe it was due to war or something destroyed their natural resources.

Aztec

The Aztec were a poor, wandering group of hunters and gatherers who moved from the north into Mexico around the mid-1100s. In A.D. 1325, they built their capital city of Tenochtitlan and expanded into central Mexico. They cultivated every square foot of land and watered it with a huge network of canals and ditches. They became a rich and populous empire and adopted the ideas of people they conquered. The military dominated their society. They believed in human sacrifice. Some scholars estimate they sacrificed about 20,000 captives on their altars in a year. They had a marvelous calendar that had a solar year of 365 days, a sacred year of 260 days and a long cycle that was 52 years. The Aztec's power vanished beginning in the late 1400s when subjected people revolted. The Spanish finished the job in the early 1500s.

Inca

The Inca existed about the same time as the Aztec, but they lived in the Andes Mountains area. They worshiped the sun, and even their name, "Inca," means "children of the sun." The Inca left no written records, so very little is known about their beginnings. In the A.D. 1100s, the Inca built their capital city at Cuzco ("City of the Sun") in Peru. In the 1400s, they began conquering nearby villages and expanded to a great power by 1500. They built many palaces, cities and irrigation systems that still stand today. Their economy was agricultural. Today, visitors to Peru might be surprised to see guinea pig, a delicious protein source that dates back hundreds of years, on their dinner plate. The Inca grew potatoes, corn (maize), tomatoes, squash, nuts, cocoa, cotton and chili peppers. They loved to eat guinea pigs and raised llamas, ducks and dogs. They, too, believed in human sacrifice and tolerated other religions among their conquered subjects.

Toltec

The Toltec invaded central Mexico around A.D. 650. In A.D. 900, they built Tula, their capital city, about 50 miles north of Mexico City. From here, they ruled their empire of city-states until about A.D. 1200. Tula became the Toltec's center of power, culture and wealth. They believed in a god named Quetzalcoatl (feathered serpent god). Their religion included human sacrifice, worship of the sun and a sacred ball game. The Toltec became famous for beautiful artwork in stone and metal, giant statues, carved human and animal standard-bearers and serpent columns. Their culture spread farther south into Central and South America. In the mid-1100s, they were invaded. Among the attackers was a group called the Aztec.

title: Entrepreneurship
text:
Benjamin Franklin was one of the greatest entrepreneurs in history. An entrepreneur takes risks to create something or find a better way to do something. Ben Franklin was imaginative, creative and very smart. He was able to try many things. He was respected for the things he did. When he died in 1790, Franklin was known around the world as a businessman, politician, printer and inventor.

Franklin was born in 1706. Even as a little boy, he loved to read, write and collect books. He left school at the age of 10. By the time he was 12, he was helping as a printer for his older brother, James. When Franklin was 22, he owned his own printing press and started his own newspaper, the Pennsylvania Gazette. He also printed Poor Richard's Almanack. That book became one of the most popular books in the Colonies!

Franklin soon became one of the Colonies' busiest printers. He was named the official printer for Delaware, New Jersey and Maryland. He printed money and legal documents. Franklin made so much money that he retired when he was 42. He then became a full-time inventor. Franklin invented many things, including the lightning rod!

Franklin was very important in the Colonies. He started one of the first libraries in the United States with some of his friends. He signed the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. Franklin served as an ambassador from the Colonies to France. He was the oldest member of the Constitutional Convention!

Ben Franklin did many things to be considered an entrepreneur. Like Franklin, there are many entrepreneurs today. Do the names Bill Gates, George Lucas, Henry Ford and Oprah Winfrey mean anything to you? All of these people are entrepreneurs. They brought great ideas and business to our economy. Can you think of any entrepreneurs where you live?

title: Elections
text:
Elections

Our nation's form of government is called a democracy. This means we choose our leaders through voting. Voting is always held on the first Tuesday in November. We vote for different national or state officials. The time these officials remain in office is called a term. Terms may be for two, four or six years.

Who Can Vote?

Citizens of the United States of America can vote for the leaders of their country. They must be at least 18 years old. If you are voting for a state, city or county official, you must be a resident of that state, city or county.

Where Do We Go to Vote?

Voting booths are usually found at schools or other government buildings. People vote in the booth using a ballot, or piece of paper. Recently, some states have been using electronic voting systems. You may vote only once for each office, and you do not put your name on the ballot. This is called a secret ballot. The candidate receiving the majority of the votes is elected for that term.

title: A Fly on the Wall
text:
This saying is usually used to mean that you wish you could be someplace, but unobserved.

Or in other words... be invisible!

Darrell has a birthday coming up, and he's really hoping for a bike. He's been working extra hard to earn money to pay for half.

"I think mom and dad are talking about your birthday present," said Leslie. "But they shut the door, so I'm not sure."

"Oh, man," Darrell groaned, "I wish I was a fly on the wall. The suspense is really killing me."

title: What Is an Ear Flare?
text:
The Aztec, Inca and Maya adorned their bodies in many ways as a show of social standing. They wore necklaces, elaborate headdresses and ear flares (also called earplugs). These were enormous earrings sometimes inlaid with elaborate designs.

Many of the artifacts of these ancient civilizations depict the ornate jewelry and feathered head-dresses.

title: The Loom
text:
Looms were developed in ancient times when civilizations had finally developed. People had time and resources to spend on better-quality items like cloth. The cloth created on looms allowed people to wear clothing rather than crude animal hides or plant fibers. And fine linens were a status symbol of the wealthy.

One of the oldest known depictions of the loom dates from 5000 B.C. It is on a pottery dish found at Badari, Egypt.

The early loom was horizontal and made from wood. The yarns were lifted with two little sticks. Vertical looms with heavier wooden frames came into use later. The weaver sat in front of the loom on a little stool in order to weave cloth.

Early weavers produced linen. By 3000 B.C., Egyptian linen was fine and delicate.

In modern times, looms became high-powered machines that could produce quality cloth quickly and without as much work from people.

title: Let's Write
text:
The title of the feature article is “Culture Clash.” It tells of the decline of the Aztec, Inca and Maya cultures.

A. Write a paragraph that tells what a “culture clash” is.

B. Discuss the difference in the cultures of the Mesoamericans and the Spanish. How did those differences contribute to the destruction of the ancient Mesoamericans?

title: What are Homophones and Homographs?
text:
Homophones and homographs are the same but different! To find out the meaning of a word, carefully read the words and sentences surrounding it.

Homophones

Homophones are words that sound the same but have different spellings and different meanings. You can remember what a homophone is by remembering that a phone makes a sound, so a homophone sounds the same as another word.

It is important to know a homophone when you write it. If you need help with a homophone when you read or write, look it up in a dictionary. This will help you keep from making mistakes. For instance, would you write you have “bear hands” or “bare hands”?

Here are some common homophones:

beat, beet
earn, urn
eye, I
heal, heel, he’ll
made, maid
plain, plane
rain, reign, rein
to, too, two

Homographs

These are words that are spelled the same but have different meanings. Sometimes they are pronounced differently even though they are spelled the same. You can remember what a homograph is by remembering that a graph is something you look at, so a homograph looks the same.

Here are some common homographs that are pronounced differently and have different meanings:

bass: a low voice; bass: a fish
content: things found inside; content: satisfied
minute: 60 seconds; minute: tiny

Try It!

The next time you are not sure which homophone or homograph to use, be sure you know the meaning of the word you are trying to use. This will help you spell it correctly. A dictionary will help you a lot!

title: How John Smith Saved Jamestown!
text:
John Smith was in big trouble. There he sat in the middle of the wilderness of Virginia, miles from the struggling new colony of Jamestown and about to be killed! He was a captured prisoner of Chief Powhatan's tribe, and several warriors stood over him with clubs ready to crush his head.

John Smith must have begged for a miracle and, thank heavens, got his wish. Just as Chief Powhatan was about to order his warriors to kill John Smith, the chief's 13-year-old daughter Pocahontas threw herself into the scene. She pleaded for his life. The chief spared John Smith and ordered him to be released.

The story of Pocahontas and John Smith is very famous, but no one really knows much about it. The original story is only 27 words long. The rest is all pretend. In real life, Pocahontas married John Rolfe. She converted to Christianity and followed Rolfe to England where she became very famous. They had a son named Thomas. She became sick with smallpox and died.

John Smith was born in Willoughby, England, in 1580. He grew up on his family's farm and went to work for a rich merchant before leaving for a life of adventure. He traveled far and wide. He fought wars and served time as a prisoner of war. John Smith traveled through Crete, Egypt, Greece, Rome, Venice, Transylvania, Russia and Hungary. By the time he returned home, he was only 24. Was that enough adventure? Not at all! Right away, he signed up for a trip to America.

On May 14, 1607, his ship landed in the wilderness of Virginia. The new colonists named their little outpost Jamestown. Jamestown would become the first permanent settlement in America. The leaders set up the colony as a commune where everyone shared everything equally. Things progressed at first, but the problem with people is that nobody works the same. Some are hard workers, but some are lazy. The gold-hungry men spent their time looking for treasure and came home to eat the food the others had worked hard to get. This made the hard-workers feel cheated. That winter, food was scarce, and people became weak. Almost half of the colonists died.

John Smith finally took over and fixed things. He told the lazy men, "He that will not work shall not eat!" Under John Smith's leadership, the people built 20 homes, dug a well and began regular fishing. They also expanded the fort and started a community farm. They gave up the commune idea in favor of private ownership and free enterprise where each man owned a plot of land to work himself. The people liked this idea. They worked hard because the land was theirs. This saved the colony!

In 1609, John Smith had an accident with a gunpowder bag. It caught fire and burned his leg so badly he returned to England. Without his leadership, Jamestown suffered its worst winter. All hope seemed lost until a financial miracle occurred. Another settler named John Rolfe discovered tobacco grew well in Virginia. Suddenly the little Jamestown colony had something to sell. Many people heard the news and began sailing for Jamestown.

As for John Smith, he did not return to America until 1614. He landed far to the north of Jamestown and mapped Massachusetts Bay before returning home for good.

For the last 15 years of his life, he drew maps and wrote books describing his adventures. He published his last book the very year he died in 1631. He was 51 years old.

title: Stone Tools Help Archaeologists Learn About Early People
text:
How do we learn about ancient peoples in the Americas? There is no time machine we can use to go back and see how they lived. Instead, we learn about how people lived in the past through clues left in the present. Sometimes ancient peoples left clues about how they saw the world in stories passed down to their descendants. They also left behind creations we still use. For example, corn only exists because of ancient American people who bred grasses into a new crop. We can also learn about ancient people through objects they made. Scientists called archaeologists search for ancient objects, buildings, or even garbage heaps to learn about how people lived in the past.

Unfortunately, many of the clues disappear over time. Weather often wears away wood tools and buildings. Food decomposes. Clothing usually falls apart. Because stone wears away more slowly, stone clues are easier to find.

Studying stone tools has helped archaeologists create theories about ancient Americans. Stone tools over 15,000 years old have been found in North and South America. These tools show people have lived on both continents since before the first cities in the world began. While there are still many questions about how they lived, the careful craftsmanship on their tools shows that ancient Americans used their ingenuity to survive. These early peoples prepared the way for hundreds of nations that developed later all across the Americas.

title: Roanoke Colony Vanishes!
text:
Drama, intrigue and mystery surround the first attempts of the English to establish colonies in the New World. One attempt ended as a mystery that has never been solved.

Today, Roanoke Island appears much as it did more than 400 years ago. The narrow island lies between the Outer Banks and mainland Virginia. Unlike other islands nearby, Roanoke Island hosts thick marshlands. It also has many live oaks that are teeming with wildlife. Sir Walter Raleigh of England thought it was a great location for a settlement. He sent captains Philip Amadas and Arthur Barlowe to explore the North American coast. This exploration party landed above Roanoke Island in North Carolina in July 1584. The explorers went by boat to Roanoke Island where they encountered an American Indian village. They described Roanoke as a "most pleasant and fertile ground." The explorers claimed the land for Queen Elizabeth of England.

1585 – The First Expedition and Settlement

The reports of the beautiful Roanoke pleased both Raleigh and Queen Elizabeth herself. She called the new possession "Virginia."

The next spring, Raleigh sent a colony of 108 to Roanoke Island. Sir Richard Grenville commanded this expedition. The colony was established on the northern end of the island, and Ralph Lane was made governor. The group was a mix of gentlemen, soldiers and craftsmen. There appears to have been no women among this first group of settlers.

After the colonists were somewhat settled, Grenville returned to England for supplies. While the colonists remained friendly with the native tribes, they seemed to manage well. As hostilities grew, the fish traps began to be robbed or destroyed. Food began to be scarce, and groups of men were sent at intervals to the mainland to try to survive on oysters and native foods. Meanwhile, Grenville was delayed with supplies. The colonists began to feel desperate. When the fleet of Sir Francis Drake was anchored nearby on their way to England, the colonists took the opportunity to return to England with him.

Grenville returned shortly after in search of the colonists, and when he was unable to find them, he left 15 men to hold the island in the name of the queen.

The Lost Colony of 1587

Sir Walter Raleigh once again organized a colonial expedition of 117 persons. This group included women, children and those who were called "planters." John White was appointed governor of this colony. During the first year, the colony began to run short of food, and once again, there were battles with the native tribes. Governor White returned to England for help. Before he left, he instructed the colonists to leave a message if they decided to move to a different location. A war between England and Spain delayed his return for three years. When the rescue party finally arrived, they found no one there. As they searched the ruined cabins, they found that everyone had vanished! Only one clue was found. Carved on a tree was the word "Croatoan," and the letters "CRO" were on a nearby tree. Could they have moved to Croatoan? Though many parties searched, the colonists' location was never discovered. The mystery of what happened to the missing colony has never been solved.

First English Child Born in America!

The new little colony of Roanoke was the scene of a happy event. On Aug. 18, 1587, Eleanor White Dare gave birth to a baby girl. Governor John White explained in his journal why his new granddaughter was named Virginia Dare: "Eleanor, daughter of the governor and wife to Ananias Dare was delivered of a daughter in Roanoke, and because this child was the first Christian born in Virginia, she was named Virginia."

Harriot and White

Luckily for history, there were two men in Raleigh's colony who were more interested in recording what they saw of the world around them than in prospecting for gold or collecting skins and pelts. One was a scientist named Thomas Harriot. The other man was John White, who was a professional artist. Working closely together, the two partners made an honest and accurate record of the people who lived in the region.

Harriot was quite impressed with the American Indian cornfields. Unlike the white settlers, who would later tear down vast forests to create fields for planting, the American Indians were conservationists. They planted their crops in natural clearings. Harriot also noted with surprise that the American Indians could get high yields without fertilizer. One reason for this was that the Roanokes, unlike European farmers, allowed bean vines to grow free and wild among their corn. Although this puzzled Harriot, it is known today that the bean plants introduced nitrogen to the soil at root level so the cornstalks were continually fertilized.

Harriot noted that the American Indians cultivated and smoked a plant they called uppowoc. They first dried and ground the uppowoc leaves. Then they used clay pipes to suck the smoke into the stomach and head. Uppowoc turned out to be tobacco. Harriot thought tobacco had medicinal qualities.

Because he believed this, he used it for the rest of his life. Sadly, Thomas Harriot was one of the first documented cases of a smoker who died of cancer.

title: What is Profit?
text:
Pretend you and your friends decide to be entrepreneurs for the day. You find a table in Jack's garage. Mary's mom helps you make some lemonade. Together, all three of you make a big sign that says, "Lemonade, 10 cents." You put all of your items on the sidewalk in front of your house and wait for your customers to come.

Soon people are lined up around the block for a taste of your delicious lemonade. You work quickly to serve your customers. Then you realize you are almost out of cups. Mary and her mom run to the store to buy some more. When they get back, you take the extra cups and keep on selling lemonade until there is no more. Together, everyone cleans up the lemonade stand. You start to count the money you've made.

You count it all up, and you have $5.80. Then you think about the extra cups that you had to buy. They cost $1.25. You give Mary's mom that amount from the money you made. Now you have $4.55. This new amount is your profit. Profit is the money a business makes after all of the expenses are paid. In this example, the extra cups that cost $1.25 are your only expense.

You and your friends have learned about profit motive today. Profit motive is the desire to benefit from the time and money people put into a business. In other words, you wanted to sell lemonade because you thought you could earn some money. In the same way, a business sells goods in hopes of earning a profit. Now the question is, what will you do with your profit?

title: Elected and Appointed Leaders
text:
Some of our government leaders are elected, and some are appointed. Do you know what the difference is between the two?

Elected leaders are chosen by the people. Citizens vote and elect a candidate, or person trying to get in office. These elections are often done by secret ballot. The president of the United States and our state governor are elected. The mayor of your city is also elected.

A person is appointed if people in charge choose him or her. They are selected, not elected. They usually work closely with elected leaders. Appointed officials often serve two to four terms.

We have examples of appointed officials all around us. The members of the U.S. president's Cabinet and Supreme Court justices are appointed leaders. There are also many appointed state and local leaders. There might even be examples in your classroom. If you have class leaders, did members of the class elect them, or did your teacher appoint them?

title: A Little Elbow Grease
text:
This is what people say when they are describing a situation where a little extra work is needed. Or in other words...something might require someone to put in a little physical effort.

It is the last week before Christmas break, and Mr. Cordell has asked the class to get ready to scrub their desks.

"Oh no," groans Mandy, "my desk is so dirty. It even has little pieces of tape stuck on it from that last art project."

Mr. Cordell overhears Mandy's comment and replies with a smile.

"Don't worry, Mandy. That desk just needs a good scraper and a little elbow grease, and it will be clean in no time."

title: How Is the Real Story of Pocahontas Different From a Popular Movie Version?
text: It is believed John Smith and Pocahontas had a father-and-daughter relationship during John Smith's stay at Jamestown. She was only about 12 or 13 years old at the time. Her original name was Mataoka. She came to visit the colonists often and would playfully turn handsprings and somersaults in the streets of Jamestown. Her nickname, Pocahontas, meant "child who can never be found because she is always off playing somewhere." Pocahontas did fall in love with John Rolfe, who was a wealthy tobacco planter. They were married in what was referred to as the social event of the century. Her father was pleased to hear about the marriage and made a peace pledge to the colonists. As news reached London, the king and queen were pleased because this union ensured their colony would be successful. Thousands of English people made plans to move to the colony because the threat of war with local American Indians was removed.

title: Pit Sawyer
text: So what was one of the first jobs of settlers in Jamestown? Building houses! The settlers probably used a pit saw to make boards for the houses. Working a pit saw took two people working together as a team. One stood on top of the log and the other one stood in a dug-out pit. They mounted the log on a frame. Then the two people sawed back and forth using a two-handed saw. Many years later, water-powered lumber mills were invented. These mills made this work much easier. But the early settlers in Jamestown had to do it the hard way!

title: Jamestown Today
text: This 1639 church tower is one of the few remnants of the Jamestown settlement visible today.

title: Let's Write
text: Traditions through the years are an important part of our society. Everyone, according to his or her heritage, may have different traditions. It is amazing how people do such different things, even on the same holiday. Write a story about your favorite holiday or family tradition.

title: What are Idioms?
text:
Have you ever heard an adult say, “I’m sorry, but we’re up a creek on this one”? What did he mean? He was standing on dry ground when he said it! Well, you’ve just heard an idiom.

Idioms are Not Meant to Be Taken Literally

Idioms are sayings that mean something different from the literal meaning of their words. “Literal” means “following the exact wording.” But idioms are not literal, so the words do not mean exactly what they say. Listen carefully for clues to figure out an idiom.

Try It!

The best way to learn what an idiom means is to learn it and use it in your own speech or writing. Ask someone what it means. Then use it in your own writing. Here are some idioms in sentences. See if you can figure out what they mean. Once you know what the idiom means, use it in your own sentence. Use another piece of paper if you need it.

They were both so shy they had a hard time breaking the ice. Use “breaking the ice” in your own sentence.

When it comes to modesty in dress, I have to draw the line somewhere. Use “draw the line” in your own sentence.

By halftime, the game was in the bag. Use “in the bag” in your own sentence.

Chris and I are in the same boat because neither of us have extra cash to spend on the field trip. Use “in the same boat” in your own sentence.

Would someone lend me a hand with the dishes? Use “lend me a hand” in your own sentence.

title: The Real Story of Thanksgiving
text:
Thanksgiving Day is a special holiday to many Americans. It is a day of giving thanks for all the blessings our nation has received. This tradition dates back over 300 years ago when the Pilgrims were trying to get their colony started in Plymouth, Massachusetts. Here is their story.

The Pilgrims lived in England. More than anything else, they wanted freedom of religion. They wanted to worship God in their own way. The Church of England did not approve of the Pilgrims and persecuted them (treated them badly). The Pilgrims decided they were tired of the persecution and moved to the Netherlands in 1609. This was a great idea for awhile. But after 11 years, they saw their children speaking Dutch and learning the Dutch ways, and they longed to be back in England. They decided it was time to go to America and start over.

With the backing of a London company, the Pilgrims sailed for the New World. On Nov. 11, 1620, they finally dropped anchor at Provincetown, Massachusetts. After explorers checked out the area, they decided it wasn’t what they wanted, and they sailed on to what is now Plymouth, Massachusetts.

Plymouth was deserted. The remains of an old Indian village were there, but no sign of any inhabitants. Smallpox had killed most of the American Indians a few years before, so the Pilgrims felt free to move in and start their new lives.

That first winter was hard. Almost half of the 102 people died. By spring, the Pilgrims didn’t know if they could survive another year.

And then a wonderful thing happened. Two English-speaking natives came to visit. Samoset was the first. He came by to say hello and said his friend spoke good English. A week later, Samoset brought Squanto to the Pilgrim’s village. The Pilgrims learned Squanto had been kidnapped 15 years earlier and was taken to England where he learned English.

A short time later, Samoset and Squanto announced the best news of all-Chief Massasoit was coming to visit. Massasoit was determined to make friends with the Pilgrims. He didn't want any fighting to break out, as had happened in other places. Massasoit worked hard. He told his people to teach the Pilgrims how to plant, fish and cook so they could survive. Thanks to this great man, peace lasted among the Pilgrims and the Indians for more than 50 years.

After a summer of good crops, the Pilgrims felt happy with their new home. Their leader, Governor William Bradford, suggested they hold a feast of thanksgiving. The people liked the idea, and in early October they made preparations. They caught wild turkeys, waterfowl, fish and seafood. They gathered fruits, berries and squash. They collected nuts, herbs and seasonings. When all was ready, they invited Chief Massasoit to join them. He brought 90 of his men and five freshly-killed deer.

For three days the people talked, ate, drank and made merry. It was a good ending to the summer and a good beginning for the coming winter.

The Pilgrims never held another day of thanksgiving. However, many Americans copied their example. During the Revolutionary War, our forefathers held a day of thanksgiving on eight different occasions. George Washington ordered a national day of thanksgiving on Nov. 26, 1789. During the Civil War in 1863, Abraham Lincoln declared Thanksgiving Day an official national holiday. He set aside the last Thursday of November "as a day of thanksgiving and praise to our beneficent Father." Today we observe Thanksgiving on the fourth Thursday of November.

title: The Parchment That Saved Plymouth
text:
The Mayflower Compact is only 166 words long and is one of the most famous documents from early American history. It is the first document to set up a government in America. The amazing part of this story is that the Mayflower Compact came about by accident! Here's what happened. . .

When the Pilgrims first came to America, they landed at a place in Massachusetts called Provincetown. This area was part of the Virginia Territory. The Virginia Territory was huge and covered a large section of the Northeast. It was controlled by the English, and everyone who lived there had to obey English laws. The Pilgrims decided this wasn't the place for them, and they sailed farther north to Plymouth, Massachusetts. Plymouth was outside of English control, and there were no laws for new settlers to follow.

The Mayflower carried two groups of people: Pilgrims, who were seeking religious freedom, and non-Pilgrims, who only wanted to begin a new life in America.

When the Pilgrims ordered their ship to Plymouth, the non-Pilgrims were worried. Some of them thought, "What are these people going to force us to do? Will we have to live their religion and be their slaves?" These fears led to arguing, and arguing led to fights, and fights almost led to mutiny (mutiny means taking over a ship by force). Something had to be done and fast.

One of the Pilgrim leaders, a man named William Brewster, knew there had to be some kind of agreement. He ordered all the men to meet him on the ship to look at a document he had been writing. The document stated there would be a new law for everyone to follow. They would unite themselves into one community, and everyone would share in the leadership. They would agree to pass laws that seemed good for the whole colony. They would agree to obey whatever laws were passed.

The men took the document and read it. They talked about it and asked questions. After a long discussion, they all agreed this was the best solution to their problems. Each man took the quill pen and signed his name to the document. When it was done, they all smiled and shook hands. The document was called the Mayflower Compact.

The important part of the Mayflower Compact that students must not forget is the idea of self-government. Self-government happens when people meet together and pass laws that everyone can agree upon. The settlers at Plymouth knew they could make laws that would be fair, wise and sincere because everyone would be involved. They would govern themselves.

The settlers lived up to the Mayflower Compact and the colony survived. One year later, a man named John Pierce expanded the Mayflower Compact so the English government could support it. The Mayflower Compact remained the constitution of Plymouth for more than 70 years.

title: The New England Colonies
text:
These New England Colonies were nearly all started by people looking for religious freedom.

1. New Hampshire Settled by Fishermen

For many years before the Pilgrims settled at Plymouth, English fishermen visited the excellent fishing waters of New England. They set up small fishing camps in the little harbors and bays. The American Indians came to these fishing camps and wanted to trade furs for knives and supplies. Fur trading became profitable. Some of these fur trading camps grew into small towns. After awhile, the towns became larger trading centers. New Hampshire was one of these kinds of settlements.

2. Pilgrims Land at Plymouth

A group of people from England disagreed with some religious practices. They did not believe in the costly robes worn by the ministers or in fancy church services. They wanted simple, plain church services. Because they wanted to "purify" the Church of England, they became known as Puritans. Some Puritans broke away from the Church altogether. They were known as Separatists.

A group of those Separatists decided to move to Holland where freedom of religion was allowed. Because they made a pilgrimage far from home they were later known as Pilgrims.

They were not happy in Holland because they loved England and wanted to bring up their children in English ways. Finally, they planned to go to America and set up their own colony. English merchants provided a ship, the Mayflower, in exchange for seven years of the Pilgrims' profits from the new colony. They began their voyage with 102 passengers, including children. After a nine-week voyage, they arrived at Cape Cod.

Before looking for a place to settle, the men gathered in a cabin of the Mayflower and made a set of rules to govern the colony. The rules were called the Mayflower Compact. They all signed the compact, and John Carver was elected as the first governor.

3. Massachusetts Bay Colony Settled by Puritans

A wealthy group of Puritans who stayed in England decided to go to America for religious freedom. In 1629, 10 years after the Pilgrims landed, more than 1,000 Puritans set out for the New World. Their fleet of ships was loaded with farming tools, weapons, cows, pigs, spinning wheels, furniture and books. They sailed north of Plymouth and set up eight small towns. The largest was Boston. All of these settlements together were called the Massachusetts Bay Colony.

Food was scarce the first winter and many died, but Governor John Winthrop encouraged farming, fur trading, hunting and fishing.

This persuaded about 18,000 more Puritans to join them and soon they were thriving.

While people of other religions could live in the Puritan colonies, only those who were Puritans could vote. Also, to be accepted in the colony, its settlers had to agree with and follow the Puritan leaders. The Puritan leaders were a stern, honest, hardworking and God-fearing people. They were intolerant. If they did not like someone, they asked that person to leave the settlement. Others were publicly whipped or left sitting in the stocks. One of the greatest threats to the Puritans were individuals who were considered "free thinkers."

4. Rhode Island Exhibits True Religious Freedom

Roger Williams, a Puritan minister, was not satisfied with the Puritan colony of Massachusetts. When he spoke out against the Puritan Church, the leaders planned to send him back to England. He escaped and spent the winter with Chief Massasoit a few miles to the south. Other settlers who were not happy with the Puritan way of life joined him. They bought land from the natives and built homes near springs of clear, pure water. They named the place Providence because they believed God had provided it for them. Many people found refuge in Rhode Island. There they could worship as they chose.

5. "Fundamental Orders" Governs Connecticut

Thomas Hooker was the minister of a Puritan Church near Boston. He had heard reports from farmers along the Connecticut River of the rich soil there. It was much better farmland than the rough, rocky land of most of New England. About 100 of Hooker's church members decided to go with him to the Connecticut Valley. They sold their homes and loaded their horses with all the tools and supplies they could carry. They made the difficult 100-mile trip. They were thankful when they finally came to the Connecticut River.

In 1636, they started a colony near the Dutch fort at Hartford. Within a few years, more than 1,000 settlers had followed them to the Connecticut Valley. Reverend Thomas Hooker wrote the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut, the first constitution written in America. The colony received a royal charter in 1662.

title: The Role of Prices
text:
"And your total comes to $2.40."

You've shopped in many stores either with your parents or by yourself. Most products contain bar codes that tell the scanner what the price is for the item. The prices let you, the consumer, know how much money the store is willing to sell the item for. However, that's not the only purpose.

Prices have three main functions. First, prices help ration scarce goods. Things cost money, and money is a limited resource. We can't buy everything we want all of the time. Therefore, items need to be rationed, or spread out to many people.

Second, prices provide a reason for buyers to buy goods and sellers to sell them. Prices make the process of buying goods organized. They motivate sellers to provide more goods based on the idea of profit motive.

Finally, prices send signals about how a market is doing. Let's say that prices are too high, and no one is buying those goods. Then economists can study this and ask questions. They can find out what prices are in other markets. Then they decide what in this market made the price rise so high.

Economists can then figure out the price for the product. It should balance the amount of buyers who want to buy with the amount of sellers who want to sell. This price is called the market-clearing price, or the equilibrium price. By figuring out this price, both the buyers and sellers are happy, and goods continue to be sold.

Can you think of any other reasons prices are important to our economy?

title: What is a Citizen?
text:
A citizen is a person who is born in a country or who becomes a member of the country where he or she chooses to live. Citizens of the United States have many duties, rights and privileges.

Citizens should obey the laws and respect others. They have the duty to serve on juries and pay taxes. Men can be asked to serve in the armed forces during times of war. During times of peace, men and women can enlist, or volunteer to serve our country in the military.

One right of U.S. citizens is to participate in government. Another right, protected by the Bill of Rights, is the freedom of religion. U.S. citizens are promised freedom of assembly, freedom of speech and freedom of press. They are also given the right to bear arms, or carry weapons.

The right to vote is very important to citizens. When citizens choose not to vote, they lose their voice in government. As a people, we need to take the right to vote more seriously. In past elections, only about 50 percent of Americans have voted. This could be a big problem if citizens don't start taking action!

title: Down in the dumps
text:
This is what people say when they are feeling discouraged or sad about something.

Emilie's brother Brent was moving away to college. She helped him go shopping for his new apartment. She helped him sort through his things in his room. Finally, she watched as he packed his bags.

She waved goodbye through teary eyes as he was driving away. She already felt lonely.

The phone rang, and Emilie answered glumly, "Hello?"

"Oh, Hi Em," said her best friend Erinn. "You sound awful! What's up?"

"Well, I'm just feeling down in the dumps because Brent left for college today," she replied.

title: Why Did the Puritans Use the Pillory and Stocks?
text:
Puritans used the pillory and stocks to punish smaller offenses within the colony. This device had holes for the person's head and two hands. A person would be put in the pillory or stocks when they missed church or acted disorderly. For a few humiliating hours, a person would be on display for everyone to see that they had broken a rule.

Some believe that we still use a similar kind of punishment today. We print the names and pictures of criminals in the newspaper. Sometimes their faces are even on television.

Do you think this was a good way to punish people? Why or why not? Would it work today? How is this different or similar to the way people are punished today?

title: Bow and Arrow
text: American Indians used the bow and arrow to hunt and kill their food. It replaced the atlatl, which was used by earlier American Indians. They would sneak up on their prey, sometimes in disguise, so they could shoot from a short distance and not frighten their prey.

title: How Do I Use a Dictionary?
text:
What does “native” mean? How do you pronounce “shaman”? To find the answers to these and many other questions, grab a dictionary. The dictionary just might be a student’s best friend. A dictionary lists and defines words.

Know Your ABCs

The words in a dictionary appear in alphabetical order. At the top of each page, two guidewords show the first and last words on that page. Guidewords help you find the word you need more quickly. For example, the word “tepee” might appear on a page with the guidewords “tension” and “territory” at the top of that page.

Is your word followed by numbers? That means it has more than one definition. Look up the word “native” and see all the definitions for it.

After each word, you will find a letter that stands for a part of speech. For example, n. means “noun,” v. means “verb” and adj. means “adjective.” Sometimes, one word can have two or more parts of speech. It depends on how it’s used in a sentence. Let’s show this with the word “hunt.” Look it up now in your dictionary.

title: Let's Write
text: Think of the Thanksgiving when you went to grandma’s and grandpa’s, or the whole family came to your house. Tell about the fun things you did. Did you play games, watch a special show, sing together or shop together? How was the trip? Did you get sick, eat too much or do homework all of the time? Does your family always have a turkey? Do you sometimes have a goose or duck? Describe your favorite dessert—is it pumpkin pie, a special boiled raisin bread or banana splits? Do you watch the parades on TV and ball games?

title: The Dutch Discover Manhattan
text:
It was 1609, and Henry Hudson was the first to sail a ship up the river that would later carry his name. The interesting surprise that made Hudson so excited about this river was that the water was salty. To an adventurer like Henry Hudson, that meant the river might connect to oceans. It might be the secret route to the Pacific everyone was trying to find.

"Hey, you there!" he called again. "Another bucket of water. Is it yet salty?" A bucket was quickly lowered over the side and drawn up. "Hey, captain! It’s as salty as the back of a deep sea whale." "Then sail on!" Hudson continued his sharp lookout. But as the day wore on, disappointment replaced excitement. The water had become fresh and the channel had become shallow.

This was not a route to the Pacific Ocean, he decided. This was just another river.

Hudson was not discouraged because he also noticed that the beautiful wooded forests in the region were filled with fur-bearing animals. And the harbor at the mouth of the river was one of the best he had ever seen. He decided they had found a suitable place to live. He turned his ship around and began hunting for a place to build a settlement.

The banks of the Hudson River made ideal places to build trading posts. The Dutch dropped anchor and almost immediately started up a lively trade with the American Indians. They swapped trinkets and beads for beautiful furs. The years passed, and the fur trade became very profitable. In 1624, the first Dutch colonists came to settle the region. The harbor area became their capital and they named it New Amsterdam. They started building small villages that were patterned after their homes in Europe.

One day, some colonists decided to put a trading post on Manhattan Island. Several of them packed their goods and crossed the river. Their Dutch leader, Peter Minuit, was worried that the new settlers might be attacked. He decided to buy the island from the American Indians. He approached some natives living on the island and offered them $24 in beads and trinkets. The Indians accepted, and the island was considered sold.

Over the years, the communities around Manhattan grew and prospered. Settlers from many different lands came to live there. These included the English, French, Swedes, Irish, Germans, Norwegians and Danes.

About 40 years later, the English began to take control of the eastern region, including the Dutch settlements in New York. The English claimed the land was theirs because John Cabot had been there more than 100 years earlier. The Dutch didn’t like this.

With English war ships in the harbor, the captain met with the Dutch leader, Peter Stuyvesant, and gave him a letter demanding they surrender New Amsterdam. Stuyvesant was a very stubborn man and disliked by the colonists. He took the letter from the English captain and tore it to shreds, saying he’d rather fight than leave. Unfortunately for Stuyvesant, the settlers refused to fight and allowed the English to take over the land.

The English renamed the area New York. Today, New York City is one of the most important cities in the entire world. And what about the Dutch? Some of New York’s most important neighborhoods are still known by their original Dutch names.

title: Magnificent Manhattan
text:
Manhattan is an amazing major, magnificent, mega city! There are over 1.5 million people living on 23 square miles, plus millions more who come to the city each day for their jobs. This fantastic concentration of businesses, arts, money, entertainment and transportation make Manhattan a one-of-a-kind place. The Dutch wouldn't have believed it could happen when they first arrived in 1624.

Manhattan is a cauldron of clashing cultures. There are the high-finance people of Wall Street; the international flavors and languages of Chinatown, Little Italy and Yorkville where pockets of Czechs, Germans and Hungarians live, and Inwood, where Irish taverns serve as gathering places for the Irish population. Spread throughout the island are pockets of races and nationalities representing just about every corner of the Earth. There's Harlem, Greenwich Village, East Village, Soho (taken from "south of Houston Street") and neighborhoods that are separated by only a city block but could be as different as Peru is from China.

Manhattan is the home of big banking and finance. It has Wall Street, one of the busiest beehives of money and stocks in the world. Banks, insurance companies and giant corporations keep their headquarters here. The pulse of America's economy beats in the buildings of Manhattan.

Manhattan is also the home of the arts: Broadway, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Metropolitan Opera House and the Museum of Modern Art. At the Lower East Side, there is a concentration of struggling writers and artists. In Greenwich Village there are many successful writers and artists.

Manhattan still has some green among all those buildings. There's famous Central Park. You can find a few of Manhattan's remaining forest areas in Inwood. Grassy open areas help the Irish keep alive their national sport of hurling or Gaelic football. Sports courts are provided for activities like bocciball games in Little Italy, or good old-fashioned American basketball. Many children enjoy an easy summer evening playing stickball among friends on a quiet neighborhood street or empty lot.

Residents of Manhattan don't really need a car, since the subway system links passengers to all sorts of bus and train connections throughout the city. Jump on a subway and you become one of about 7 million passengers who ride the tunnels each and every day.

Manhattan has a little of everything and a lot of everything! The island was once valued by the Dutch at $24. Today, it is worth tens of millions of dollars an acre. If you have never visited Manhattan, you should make plans to go there someday. Magnificent Manhattan Island has become one of the modern wonders of the world.

title: The Middle Colonies
text:
The Middle Colonies were settled by colonists from several countries in Europe, including groups seeking religious freedom.

Dutch colonists brought their cattle, horses and other livestock to Manhattan Island in 1625. That year, the colonists built Fort Amsterdam and began laying out a town on Manhattan Island. They named the town New Amsterdam after the city of Amsterdam in the Netherlands.

Peter Minuit, the new governor, wanted to make sure there would be no trouble with the natives over the ownership of Manhattan Island. He met with some Indians who were in the area and offered to buy Manhattan from them. The Indians accepted cloth, knives, beads and trinkets worth about $24.

Today, you could spend nearly that much just parking the family car in the city for a few hours!

1. Quakers Settle Pennsylvania

A group known as the Quakers were persecuted in England because its members refused to bow to the king, take part in war or support the Church of England. Thousands were thrown in jail. A rich young Englishman named William Penn became a Quaker. When his father died, William inherited his father's wealth. This included a large sum of money that the king owed Penn's father. William Penn offered to take land in America in place of the money owed him. The king granted Penn a huge piece of land on the banks of the Delaware River. There were many trees, so they called it Pennsylvania, which means "Penn's woods". Here Penn started a new colony. He advertised that there would be freedom of worship for all who believed in God.

Philadelphia, or the "City of Brotherly Love," one of the largest settlements. Many of the settlers were Quakers, but people of other religions and from every country were welcome.

2. Maryland: A Refuge for Roman Catholics

The Roman Catholics were treated poorly in England because of their religious beliefs. Finally, one of the Catholic leaders, Lord Baltimore, decided the Catholics should have a colony in America. Lord Baltimore asked the king for permission to start a colony north of the Virginia settlements. In 1634, 200 settlers of Lord Baltimore's colony settled in Chesapeake Bay. They bought the land from the Indians who had cleared it. Soon the settlers began planting their crops.

The settlement was named Maryland after the English Queen Henrietta Maria, the wife of Charles I, who gave the land to Lord Baltimore.

Protestants also came to live in Maryland because there was religious freedom there. Settlers of all faiths were welcome in Maryland.

3. New Amsterdam Becomes New York!

In 1624, the first Dutch colonists came to America. They started a trading post on Manhattan Island at the mouth of the Hudson River. This settlement was called New Amsterdam. Because of its good harbor, it became the capital of the colony. In 1647, Peter Stuyvesant became the governor of New Amsterdam. He was unique because he had a wooden leg. He did a good job of cleaning and organizing the city. He was not well-liked by the people of New Amsterdam, however, because he ruled harshly and refused to let the people take any part in the government. In 1664, the English declared New Amsterdam belonged to them. They sent four warships to seize it. A message was sent to Peter Stuyvesant demanding the Dutch surrender. Stuyvesant flew into a rage, but the colonists refused to fight. They knew they were outnumbered and desired to keep peace.

4. York Gives Personal Friends New Jersey

The story of how the colony of New Jersey began starts with its neighbor colony New York. At the time the English took New York from the Dutch, the Duke of York rewarded two faithful friends and supporters by giving them New Jersey. His friends, Lord Berkeley and Sir George Carteret, had defended the English island of Jersey for the king, so the Duke of York named the land grant "New Jersey." The eastern shore of this New Jersey territory was settled largely by a group of religious people called Congregationalists. The western side was sold to another group of religious people called the Quakers. This led to the dividing of the colony into East and West Jersey. The settlers in West Jersey developed large plantations while in East Jersey the land holdings were smaller. New Jersey became a royal colony in 1702.

5. Swedish Colonists Settle Delaware

A group of Swedish settlers sailed into Delaware Bay to start a new colony. They found a good harbor protected from the wind and ocean waves. The settlers brought tools and supplies with them to the New World. They planned to build a fort to protect themselves and homes to live in. They wanted to farm the land. They bought the land from the native, and built a fort named Fort Christina for the Swedish queen. Wilmington, Delaware, now stands on the site of this original fort.

The Swedes liked to work hard. They cut down trees and built some of the first log cabins in America. Later, many settlers built log cabins modeled after those first built by the Swedes.

The colony changed hands several times. First the Dutch made it a part of New York. When the English captured New York, Delaware was given to William Penn so he would have access to the ocean for trading purposes. Later in 1704, Delaware became its own colony.

title: Budgeting
text:
Making sure more money comes in than goes out

Have you ever asked your mom or dad for something, only to be told that it wasn't in the budget? A budget is a plan of how to manage your money. It has two main ideas.

First, you must think about how much money is coming in. Maybe you earn an allowance. Maybe you mow a neighbor's lawn to make money, called income. If you earn money every week or month, like an allowance, then it is called a steady income.

Next, we look at how much is going out, or how much it costs you to live. Maybe you subscribe to a magazine or go to a movie every Friday night. These are types of expenses. Adults also have expenses. They pay bills every month to buy things we all need, like food, clothes and cars. These expenses come out of their income every month.

To make a budget, you must first look at your income (money coming in). Then add up all of your expenses (money going out). Now subtract the total amount of your expenses from your total income. This new number lets you know how much money you have for other things that you want. This helps you plan and make wise choices when spending your money.

The goal of a budget is to try to balance your income with your expenses. It is best if your income is more than your expenses. That way, more money is coming in than going out. Now it is your turn to make a budget. Good luck!

title: U.S. Residents
text:
