Simply living in the United States does not make you a citizen. Three different types of residents live in the United States today.

The first group of residents is made up of citizens. They include anyone born in the United States or babies born to citizens who are living abroad, or in a foreign county.

Throughout our country's history, there have been many immigrants. Immigrants, or aliens, are the second group of residents. These people come to live in a country where they were not born. They do not automatically become citizens and do not have the same rights. For example, they cannot vote. To become citizens, immigrants must apply and pass certain requirements. Then they can become naturalized citizens.

The third group of residents is made up of nationals.

Nationals are people born in American territories, such as Puerto Rico or Guam. They have all the protections of being U.S. citizens, but they do not have the full rights citizens have.

title: I've got my wires crossed
text:
This is what people say when they are describing a feeling of confusion. Or in other words... I must have mixed some things up!

Tom was waiting for what seemed like forever. His stomach was starting to turn. Where was everyone? Just then, Coach North walked in with a puzzled look.

"Are you waiting for someone, Tom?"

Now Tom is really confused. "Isn't today the start of volleyball?" he asked weakly.

"Volleyball? No, that starts NEXT Monday," replied coach North.

"Oh, I guess I must have got my wires crossed," said Tom.

title: What is religious freedom?
text:
Religious freedom is the freedom to worship how, where or what you choose to worship. In America we have had religious freedom all of our lives, so it is difficult to understand what it would be like not to have it.

Many of the groups that migrated to America were searching for this freedom. In England they were told what church they had to join. Thousands were put in jail for not attending or supporting the Church of England.

The Puritans tried to purify the official Church of England. One group of Puritans, the Pilgrims, separated themselves from England. Another group (later Puritans) set up a colony in America with the idea of being an example to England of what a pure church should be like.

The Quakers, Catholics, French Huguenots and others all came to America to have the right to religious freedom. This freedom to worship has been a motivating factor for change throughout the world's history.

title: The Atlatl
text:
Atlatl is an Aztec Indian word that means “spear thrower.” Before the bow and arrow was invented, early American Indians used the atlatl to help them hunt animals for food. The atlatl was a special spear thrower that let the American Indians throw their spears farther and with more power than they could by using their arms alone.

Historians believe people have been using the atlatl for more than 40,000 years. The American Indians even used the atlatl as a weapon against the Spanish when they came to the New World in the late 1400s. The atlatl could throw a spear so hard it could pierce the metal armor worn by the Spanish soldiers.

Today, many people have rediscovered the atlatl and have started having competitions to see who can use the atlatl to throw a spear the farthest and who can come closest to hitting the center of a target.

title: Vitus Bering and Russian Colonies in Alaska
text:
Imagine traveling 6,000 miles over land with supplies for an expedition, and THEN sailing through frigid seas to look for a new world. This was the job given to Vitus Bering, a Danish navigator who sailed for the Russian navy. Peter the Great, czar (ruler) of Russia, asked Bering to explore the eastern coast of Russia. He was wondering if land connected Asia and North America.

Bering’s first trip began in 1725. After spending three years getting his supplies to eastern Russia, Bering sailed along the coastline. He didn’t see any land to the east, and he didn’t realize he was sailing in the narrow passage between Russia and Alaska. This waterway is now called the Bering Strait.

Bering led another expedition in 1741. This time his ship landed on Kayak Island, off the coast of Alaska. They explored some of the Aleutian Islands and met the native people there, the Aleut. He was the first European to arrive in present-day Alaska.

Bering died before returning to Russia, but his voyages paved the way for Russian settlements in North America. Many fur traders came to the area. In 1799 the Russian government established a fur-trading operation in Alaska. Furs from foxes, sea otters and seals were very valuable.

Unfortunately, the Russians took advantage of the native people just as some Europeans had done in settling New England. The Russians took over their lands and forced them to hunt for furs. They also brought new diseases, which killed many natives.

Today, the Aleut people continue to live along the western coast of North America, and their population has grown. What might have been different if the Russians and the Aleut had shared public space fairly? Where in your community is there a debate over public land? How should such debates be handled?

title: Let's Write
text:
While Peter Stuyvesant accomplished many things in New Netherland, he was not well liked.

1. List two or more reasons why you think he was not well liked.

2. Tell us what qualities a good leader should have.

3. Tell us whether or not you believe those qualities are important for leaders today.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: As you read this week’s magazine, use any color to circle or highlight five words that are new to you. On a piece of paper, write the words and what you think each one means based on the context in which it is used. Compare your definition to a dictionary definition.

title: A Place to Call Their Own
text:
If somebody gave you a piece of land, what would you do with it? Would you sell it or maybe dig for gold? Would you build a house, a skyscraper, a flower shop or a rocket-launch pad? Would you plant apple trees or wheat, daisies or potatoes? Would you build a zoo, make a giant swimming pool and invite your friends or build the world's fastest roller coaster ride and charge $5 a person?

If you had your own land, you could do just about anything you could imagine.

Land has always been important to people. They need it to live on, to grow food, to play on, to travel on and to spread out cattle, crops, timber and communities. Most of us at one time or another have said, "All I want is a little place I can call my own."

One of the biggest reasons people came to America in the 1600s was to have a little place they could call their own. The poor people wanted to make a little money by farming their own land. Those people who were persecuted wanted to build a community where they could live in peace. The rich merchants in England, Spain and France wanted to make more money by putting people to work for them on cheap land in America.

After the disaster at Roanoke and the horrible time at Jamestown a lot of people wondered if having a little land was worth dying for, and then things started looking better.

In 1612, John Rolfe harvested the first crop of high-grade tobacco in Virginia. This proved the new land could earn somebody a lot of money in the farming business. Six years later, in 1618, settlers were offered 50 acres of American land for free! All they had to do was work the land for seven years and give back all the crops except enough to live on.

And then the British started giving away huge chunks of land to their governors and leaders in America as a reward. New settlers had to work for the big land owners just to survive. This frustration helped kindle the flames of revolution 150 years later.

The history of America is a history of land. Our biggest wars have been over land. Our largest law books deal with land. Our form of government is based on land ownership. Even our Declaration of Independence and Constitution outline the right to own property and how it is used for life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.

If you were given a piece of the United States, what would you do with it? You can choose from over 3 million square miles, but choose wisely! If you want a high place, go to one of the the highest communities in America at Climax, Colorado (11,360 feet above sea level). Or try out Calipatria, California, one of our lowest communities at 184 feet below sea level. If you like rain, move to Mount Waialeale, Hawaii, where you'll get an average 460 inches of water every year! That's like getting about three-quarters of a gallon of water dumped on every square foot every day!

During our study of U.S. history, you will learn about the importance of land to the growth of our country. If you were given a piece of land as large as your school or home, what would you do with it?

title: Tobacco – A Good Seed Gone Bad
text:
Tobacco has been growing in the Americas since 6000 B.C. Early Americans started using it for healing and religious purposes about 2,000 years ago. Even today people use it to dress wounds and kill toothache pain by chewing it.

When Columbus first met Caribbean natives in 1492, he was given smoldering tobacco as a gift. He didn't know what it was, but he did notice it had a nice smell. Then he saw the natives inhaling the smoke through a Y-shaped pipe they called a tabaca.

Tobacco was eventually taken to Europe. It became very popular - not for smoking, but for curing medical problems. A Spanish doctor wrote a book in 1571 that included tobacco as a wonderful natural herb. He said it could cure 36 health problems. In 1588, Thomas Harriot told people that a good way to get their daily dose of tobacco was to smoke it using a pipe in the nose. Harriot later died of nose cancer. His death is one of the first known tobacco-caused deaths.

In the 1600s, tobacco was so popular people used its leaves as money. "It's as good as gold," they said.

In 1826, scientists learned that the main ingredient of tobacco is a deadly poison. They called it nicotine. People discovered they could use nicotine to kill insects and pests and found it could also be used as a sheep dip. A person with tetanus or strychnine poisoning could be saved with a dose of nicotine. It was also used to treat high blood pressure.

However, nicotine is dangerous when inhaled while smoking. Smokers enjoy this habit because the tobacco calms their nerves. Actually, this is the nicotine acting in their bodies. Smokers quickly become addicted (trapped in the habit of smoking).

Tobacco has large, broad leaves that grow almost 4 feet long. The plant stands anywhere from 2 to 8 feet tall. Even though tobacco is a tropical plant, it is grown all over the world where conditions are right.

Tobacco is credited with saving the colonies in Virginia. John Rolfe planted South American tobacco and reaped a wonderful harvest. Farmers in Virginia and North Carolina became very rich. Today, tobacco products make up a multi-billion dollar industry. In the 1980s, American tobacco companies produced close to 600 billion cigarettes a year. That number has dropped in recent years because people don't want to risk good health for a smoke. More than 400,000 people die each year from using tobacco. Tobacco-related medical costs run more than $70 billion.

Many smokers hooked on tobacco are afraid for their health and try to quit. Two-thirds of all smokers try to quit each year. Among those who do quit, 75 percent go back and start up again. That's how powerful the smoking habit can be.

Nicotine isn't the only drug in cigarettes. Another 4,000 chemicals have been identified in American tobacco products. Cigarette smoke also deposits a sticky tar that clogs the air sacs in the lungs. People who smoke a long time may have trouble breathing. Many find they get sick more often than non-smokers. Smoking greatly increases the risk of lung cancer and heart disease.

Tobacco can be a helpful plant when used the right way. Used the wrong way, it kills. In schools all over America, students of all backgrounds are standing together against smoking. When it comes to drugs of any kind, including tobacco, be smart and don't start.

title: The Southern Colonies
text:
While the New England and Middle Colonies were established principally by people from England searching for religious freedom, the South was established by people who were motivated by other reasons. Read about these southern colonies and discover what their motivation was.

1. Slavery in the Colonies

Slavery existed in Latin America for a century before it was introduced into North America. As early as 1515, Spain and Portugal brought slaves to their colonies in the New World.

On Aug. 20, 1619, a Dutch ship anchored in the harbor of Jamestown, Virginia. The captain claimed he was short of food and wanted to sell some of his cargo of Africans, so the little colony purchased 20 of them. They were not slaves, however, but indentured servants, as were many whites, who eventually worked out their obligation and gained their freedom.

In early Jamestown, Africans who had worked out their freedom apparently were treated pretty much the same as white people. Some of them purchased indentured servants and even slaves. In the first case of a runaway slave on record, the slave had a black master.

2 & 3. Carolina Becomes Two Colonies!

South Carolina started out as simply "Carolina." Both North and South Carolina were one region. This region was later divided into two royal provinces, North Carolina and South Carolina. This was done to make colonial government more effective. Eight proprietors, or businessmen, were given the responsibility of governing Carolina. These eight men were more interested in making money than governing the colony. They had many problems until the colony was divided into two colonies in 1729. Both of the Carolinas were named "Carolina" in honor of King Charles I. The Carolina colony later became North Carolina and South Carolina.

4. Debtors Find Their Fortune in Colonial Georgia!

General James Oglethorpe had a friend who was put in an English prison because he could not pay his debts. This friend was kept in prison until he died. Oglethorpe wanted to do something to help these unfortunate people. He went to the king. King George gave him some land and told him to start a colony for debtors and poor people in America.

The king was concerned that the Spanish would claim and settle the area if England didn't stake a claim first. In 1733, a little band of 130 colonists sailed up the Savannah River into the new territory. They made a settlement that later became the city of Savannah. They named the colony Georgia in honor of their king. The little colony was the beginning of one of the original 13 English colonies.

title: Credit and Debt
text:
Trying not to spend more money than you have

You've made your budget, and you are trying to stick to it. You take care to plan what you will buy. You try to make sure that your income is greater than your expenses.

Then you see it - the bike you've always wanted! It is on sale for $55. You rush home and count all of the money in your piggy bank. You find you only have $30.

Discouraged, you decide to go talk to your dad about the situation. He agrees to loan you the remaining $25. He says he will take it out of your allowance for the next few weeks. You think this is a great idea! Together, you go down to the store and purchase your brand new bike.

Even though you most likely didn't know it, you just bought something on credit. Credit is money that is loaned and must be paid back. Usually, credit lenders require a fee, known as interest. The person who borrows money must pay back the money he or she owes. He or she also must pay some extra money for being able to borrow from the lender.

You are also now in debt. Debt is money you owe when you buy something by borrowing money. Although credit can help people in tight spots, it should be used carefully.

Sometimes, people just buy things on credit, usually with a credit card. They forget they have to pay the money back with interest. This can add up to huge amounts of debt that people have a hard time paying back. You should always remember that having things today and paying for them tomorrow is tricky business. Try to avoid it!

title: Becoming a U.S. Citizen
text:
People born in the United States are legal citizens of our country. People born in foreign countries can become U.S. citizens, too. This process is called naturalization.

To become a citizen, you must be at least 18 years old and have lived in the United States for at least five years. You must be loyal to the United States and be willing to pledge allegiance, or take an oath of loyalty. You must have a basic understanding of U.S. history, government and the Constitution. In addition, you must be able to speak, read and write basic English.

The process of becoming a citizen has three different steps. First, you must file an application. This includes being fingerprinted, taking photographs and providing legal documents. The next step is to take the naturalization exam. This test has two parts: an English test and a U.S. history and government exam.

The last step is to appear in court. You must go before a judge and ask to become a U.S. citizen. The judge listens to your reasons for wanting to become a citizen and makes the final decision. Once you are made a citizen, you have all the rights and duties of any other U.S. citizen!

title: It really caught my eye
text:
This is what people say as they are describing a situation when something attracted their attention. Or in other words... something was really noticeable.

Jasmine is excited to wear her new jacket to school. She hopes her friends will like it as well as she does.

When she finds her friends before school starts, she is smiling with excitement.

"Hey guys, what do you think?" She asks.

"Wow, that's a really cool jacket, Jasmine. I'll bet you spent all day shopping for a find like that," said Lizzie.

"Oh good, you like it then. Actually, I found it in that new department store. It really caught my eye, and the price was right, so my mom said I could get it," said Jasmine.

title: What was an indentured slave?
text:
Some of the slaves who came to America were on a contract either for their ticket to America or some other arrangement. This contract was for a specified number of years. When the contract was finished, the indentured servant was allowed to go free. These servants were any nationality or skin color.

Unfortunately, many slaves were captured against their will and brought to America under terrible circumstances to serve a lifetime of servitude. These slaves were not allowed to learn to read or write to keep them dependent on their slave masters. Most slave masters treated their slaves well. Others were cruel.

title: The Cotton Gin
text: The word "gin" is old English for "engine." Eli Whitney invented his cotton gin in 1794 to remove cotton seeds from cotton fibers. Removing seeds by hand had always been a hard, difficult job that made cotton expensive to produce. Whitney's cotton gin used wire brushes to pull the cotton and seeds apart quickly and easily. The simple machine made cotton production very affordable, and cotton soon replaced tobacco as the No. 1 crop in the South. Whitney never made much money off his invention because people stole his ideas and made their own.

title: Fact vs. Opinion
text:
Right now you are reading a magazine. A magazine is a great place to find both facts and opinions.

Fact: A fact is a statement that can be proved. For instance, to say that most oranges are orange in color can be proven. All you have to do is look at an orange to tell what color it is.

Opinion: An opinion is a belief held by someone. It cannot be proven by fact. For instance, to say, “red apples are sweeter than green apples” is an opinion. It depends on who’s doing the tasting. Brian thinks red apples are sweeter. Brooke finds green apples the sweetest. They each have an opinion about the sweetness of apples.

Newspapers contain mostly facts on most of the pages. Certain pages are set aside for opinions. The editorial page contains letters to the editor, editorial cartoons and articles by the editors of that paper.

The purpose of the editorial page is to:

Make people think about events in the news

Try to get public officials to see your point of view

Give background and information about events in the news

Serve as a community “voice”

All your life you’ll be reading books and articles. You’ll also be doing a lot of writing for school and work. Get in the habit of asking yourself as you read or write, “Is this statement fact or opinion?” This habit will help you become a better thinker.

title: Portrait of Colonial America
text:
A colony is a settlement that is started by people outside their native land and is ruled by individuals or rulers from the native land. The colonial period in American history began with the first settlement at Roanoke in the late 1500s and ended at the time of the Revolution in 1775. During that period of about 175 years, colonial life changed in many ways. The first colonists were trailblazers and focused on survival in the new land. By the end of the colonial era, many of the colonists were wealthy and lived quite comfortably.

Population of the 13 Colonies increase rapidly during the late 1600s and 1700s. By 1700, about 250,000 people lived in the English colonies. By 1775, the population had grown to about 2.5 million people. Virginia was the largest colony with about 450,000 people. The immigrants to the Colonies come from many countries.

Social classes in the Colonies developed as the trade and industry of the Colonies began to grow. Social classes determined much of the colonists' lives, including what they wore, what they ate, how they traveled, where they sat in church and even determined their right to vote.

The gentry formed the wealthiest, best-educated class of people. Those who were considered gentry may have been merchants, doctors, lawyers or ministers. Those who owned large farms or plantations were also considered gentry. Most gentry had servants and many owned slaves. They had time for social functions such as plays and parties.

The middling sort or middle class was made of folks who ran shops, small farms, small business or were ordinary tradesmen, such as a tinsmith or a cooper. Both men and women in middle-class families helped to earn income and provide for the family. The men in the middle class could vote, and some held minor public positions.

The lower sort or lower class included common laborers, sailors, indentured servants and other servants and slaves. Most of the individuals in the lower class did not own property. They often could not read or write and usually were not allowed to vote.

Colonial houses were often made of wood as trees were plentiful. In some areas, rich clay made it possible to construct homes made of brick. The fireplace was a very important feature in all colonial homes. It was used for cooking and heating. Fireplaces in small homes were 4 feet high and 8 or 10 feet wide. They took up a good portion of the home. In the South, where the climate was warm, fireplaces were usually outside of the home. An average colonial home had a hall or main room that was about 16 feet by 20 feet. Compare that to the size of your classroom. Some homes had a loft for sleeping, but most of the family activities were held in the hall. If the average family consisted of eight people, do you think it was crowded?

Food in the Colonies changed with the seasons because they weren't able to store and preserve food for long periods of time as we do today. Corn and beans, introduced by the American Indians, became staples for the colonists. Other vegetables such as carrots, turnips, onions and parsnips were common as well. A mix of vegetables was put into a pot and left to cook over the fire for hours. The result was a kind of thick, not very flavorful soup. It was usually eaten at midday, and the cold leftovers were eaten for supper in the evening. Wild game and fowl were common meats. If a family was lucky, they had a cow for milk and chickens for eggs.

Colonial children led lives very different than you. Younger children were watched by older children, and when they reached the age of 6, they were expected to begin helping with the chores. Girls helped with household chores and younger children, and boys worked outdoors with their fathers. In poor families, children were often apprenticed to craftsmen and left their family home to live with the master craftsman. What do you think colonial children did for fun? Imagine a world with no TV, computers, video games or even books. Common games for colonial children included hopscotch, marbles, tag, tops, hoop rolling and cratch cradle (cat's cradle.) Girls made dolls from cornhusks, and boys used dried cobs as blocks.

title: Boston in Colonial America
text:
Life in colonial Boston was a little different than life in the busy Massachusetts city today. Back them, most Bostonians depended on ships sailing into the Boston Harbor to bring them all the comforts of life.

The very wealthy families had large brick houses with fine furniture shipped from Europe. The wealthy had servants and slaves. Wealthy men usually served as selectmen or other community leaders.

Boston also had a middle class, or people who were not terribly rich or poor, but lived comfortably. Most of these folks were tradesmen or shop owners. They probably owned a house made of wood and had a servant or two. An apprentice might be found living with them as well.

Boston was also home to many poor people who were crowded together in small, wooden buildings. They were the ones who suffered most from malnutrition and disease. Death among the very young was more common.

Not only did fewer people live in colonial Boston, but the city itself was also much smaller. The streets were narrow and winding and often crowded with people. Some of the original Boston street names are still used today. You may have heard of historic Milk, Beacon, Water, Essex and Summer streets.

Just as today, one of Boston's busiest areas is the port at the city's eastern edge. A variety of ships came in and out on a regular basis. Children in colonial Boston lived similar lives to the children in other colonial towns. They often had better health, however, because Boston Harbor made it easier for them to get the supplies they needed.

In the 1750s, there were some young folks living in Boston who would one day be famous: Paul Revere was 15, John Hancock was 13 and Sam Adams was 28. What can you tell your classmates about these famous Bostonians?

title: Skilled Craftsmen in the Colonies
text:
Early American Trades

The colonists could not easily buy their necessary goods and services from England because it was so far away. Many became tradesmen by learning to make their own goods locally. Everything from furniture, metal tools, glassware, clothware and food items were produced and used locally.

As more colonists arrived, the demand for goods increased. While some of these trades were common during colonial America, they aren't so common in today's world.

1. Pit Sawyer

Two sawyers worked as a team to operate a large-framed pit saw. A tree trunk was mounted on trestles and was sawed by the two men, one standing in the pit below and the other on top of the log. With the pit saw, the sawyers cut beams and boards for houses and ship construction in the days before the introduction of water-powered lumber mills, which could produce these products more quickly and efficiently.

2. The Blacksmith

During the early colonial era of the United States, pig iron was manufactured in Massachusetts and Connecticut. This key industry enabled the Colonies to become independent of England. These furnaces furnished raw materials for the blacksmith, who, in turn, provided metal tools for use by craftsmen and farmers. The blacksmith made everything that could be made of iron by hand: weapons, cooking utensils, horseshoes, cutlery and padlocks. Even today the all-purpose blacksmith can be seen in some rural communities.

3. The Basketmaker

Not much was required for the basketmaker to begin production: an ax, a few wedges, a large knife and a supply of saplings (young trees.)

Both men and women of the colony made baskets. Many made their own baskets at home, while a few made a living out of it.

The weaving and plaiting required for basketmaking required both nimble fingers and strength.

4. The Glassblower

Glassblowing was one of the first businesses the colonists formed in the New World. Not long after their arrival in Jamestown, John Smith sent for Dutch and Polish glassblowers to start a business in the new colony.

All that is required to make glass is sand, soda ash, pot ash, lime and high heat. With miles of beaches, Smith hoped to create a profitable business. Soon, glass items were made and shipped back to England to sell. However, the business did not do well and was eventually discontinued.

5. The Spinning Wheel

The simplest type of spinning wheel was the wool wheel, shown here. The spinner had to stand up when operating it. She held the wool in her left hand and rotated the wheel with her right hand. As the spindle began to turn with the wheel, she pulled the wool into a long, thin strip that twisted into thread or yarn as it ran onto the spindle. It took many turns of the wheel before the spindle was full of yarn.

6. The Wheelwright

The local wheelwright was responsible for producing the wheels for carriages, wagons and riding chairs.

The wheelwright was a master in precise woodwork as he created the joints for hubs, spokes and the rim. Each wheel had to be perfectly round. The wheels were then bound with an iron hoop.

Wheelwrights required physical strength and good measuring skills. Often the wheelwright acted as a blacksmith as well if he produced his own iron hoop.

7. The Cooper

Farmers, especially those in the South, needed millions of barrels per year to store and export crops and commodities such as flour, cornmeal and molasses. This made coopering one of the most prevalent (widespread or popular) trades in colonial America. Mainly using oak, coopers made barrels, kegs, buckets, tubs and tankards. There were both "dry" and "wet" barrels. The wet barrels were the hardest to make because they had to hold liquid without leaking.

title: Banks
text:
Did you know temples were some of the first banks? Thousands of years ago, no one would steal from a temple. That's because they were afraid the gods would curse them. This made temples the safest place to store the costly metals people used for money. Some temples even made loans, giving money to people who promised to pay it back.

Do you know where the word bank comes from? Long ago, early Italian bankers used street benches to conduct their business. In time, the Italian word banca (bench) became the English word "bank." No matter what time era, or where you live, a bank has always been a business that deals with money. They hold money for customers, they make loans, and they provide other money-related services. There are three main types of banks.

The first is a commercial bank. These banks serve both businesses and individuals. They offer checking accounts, loans and saving accounts to their customers.

The second kind of bank is a savings bank. These banks are similar to commercial banks, but they mostly offer savings accounts and loans. They also offer mortgages. That's a special kind of loan for people trying to buy a house.

The third kind of bank is a credit union. Credit unions were started to help people borrow money. People in the same type of employment (a school district, for instance) put their savings together and loaned it to others within that organization. In other words, they operated their own banks. Today, credit unions provide many of the same services as commercial banks and savings banks. However, they are called non-profit organizations. This means that all the members of the credit union share any profit that the organization makes.

title: How Government Works
text:
Government works similar to stacking blocks, and it all starts with you! You are a citizen of your community. Your community is part of a city, and a local government runs the city. The head of the city, the mayor, works out of city hall. Do you know where your city hall is?

The state government runs all of the combined local governments. The leader of the state government is the governor. The governor's office can be found at the state capitol. Voters in each state elect members of Congress. They meet in Washington, D.C., to take care of the federal government. The leader of the country is, of course, the president of the United States.

The United Nations is yet another block we can add. It is a type of government made up of leaders from around the world. Wow! Many government leaders are members of the United Nations - but don't forget that the most important part of all of this is the citizens, including you!

title: What are pokes and yokes?
text:
Poke collars had a "poke" sticking out. They were put around the necks of cattle and oxen to prevent them from jumping over a fence.

Yokes were a kind of collar with a long bar going from side to side. They were often used with pairs of animals to help them pull a load. Commonly yoked animals are oxen, horses and donkeys.

title: The Silversmith
text: Because there were few safe places to keep money, wealthy colonists often had their silver coins converted into household silver such as tankards, bowls, teapots and tableware. Silver objects could be marked with an owner's name or initials for greater security. In this picture, the silversmith on the right is pouring molten silver into a crucible, or mold. The smiths on the left are beating out a silver plate on an anvil.

title: I'm all ears!
text:
That's a funny picture to conjure up, but what people are really trying to say is they are eager to listen.

Carina has been working on her science fair project for weeks. It is a model of how a lightswitch works. She is so proud that she has done all of the research and work herself, but it isn't working like it should.

Carina's uncle Trevor has been watching her project with interest, and is aware that all is not going as it should.

"Hey, it looks like you could use a few pointers. I think I know some things you can try to get your project finished," Trevor said.

"Great," replied Carina. "I'm all ears."

title: How Do I Give an Oral Presentation?
text:
Standing in front of a crowd and telling them what you think is not easy, but it can be done if you prepare well!

Preparing for an Oral Presentation

Know your audience. What you say should be directed toward them. Is it to be given in your classroom? This will make it easier!

How long should it be? If your teacher says 15 minutes, stick to the time.

What’s the topic? Did your teacher assign it? Make sure you can cover it within the time limit.

Make notes. Use index cards and put them in the order you want to use them. Index cards are not so large that they cover your face. You may write your presentation on numbered pieces of paper, but do not staple the pages.

Practice, practice and practice some more!

Making the Oral Presentation

Introduction Get the audience’s attention with the introduction. You can do this by asking a question, telling a story, using a quotation or making a statement. Once you have their attention, state your topic.

Body State your main points and give information that support your main points. You may ask rhetorical questions, (questions that don’t need answers) use emotional words or repeat important information.

Conclusion Repeat your main point. Conclude with. something that leaves a lasting impression by asking a rhetorical question, making an emotional plea or using a quotation, story or statement.

Try It! When you’re asked to give an oral presentation, make sure you prepare well. Organize logically. Practice, practice, practice. Good luck!

title: Let's Write
text: The year is 1770, and you are a child in a middle-class colonial family. You’ve lived comfortably your whole life on a family farm in Pennsylvania. You have just been invited to spend the holidays with your wealthier cousins in the busy city of Boston. You can hardly believe your parents have agreed to let you go. Write a journal entry that tells how you feel about this holiday adventure. Make a list of things you hope to do. Compare the lifestyles of Bostonian gentry and Pennsylvania farmers.

title: Slavery in the Thirteen Colonies
text:
Slavery is owning another human being as property. The first slaves in the Colonies were not the first Africans to enter North America as slaves. Some historians believe that at least one black slave accompanied Christopher Columbus on his voyage in 1492. The first Africans imported to the Colonies arrived in Virginia in 1619. For years and years, Africans continued to be imported to Virginia and the rest of the Colonies. The first slaves worked side by side in the fields and in households as indentured servants. An indentured servant was an individual who agreed to work for a certain number of years in return for passage to the Colonies. At first, the slaves were treated much the same as indentured servants, but over time they lost more and more privileges. It is also important to remember that indentured servants usually chose to come to the Colonies, while the African slaves were kidnapped and forced to leave their home, family and way of life.

In 1641 Massachusetts became the first colony to legalize slavery. By 1660 slavery had spread to all the Colonies. After 1660, Colonies began to write harsh laws, or codes, that defined slavery and the slave trade. One law common to all Colonies was that black slaves now served for life. Children of slave women were also required to serve for life. These codes established that slaves could not carry weapons, receive an education, meet in groups of more than three or testify against masters in court. Slaves on small farms or in cities probably had more freedom than the plantation slaves in the Southern Colonies.

In 1630, there were only about 60 Africans in the Colonies. By 1760, the numbers of Africans had grown to over 325,000. As the Colonies became a nation the practice of slavery continued. By the time of the Civil War, 100 years later, the number of African slaves neared 4 million. Most historians agree that from 1619 to 1860, 15 million Africans were taken from their homelands and sold into bondage throughout the New World. However, many slaves never completed the journey. Many died of illnesses, starvation and abuse. Still others committed suicide by refusing to eat or jumping overboard.

The period of time in which slavery was practiced is a dark time in history. There were, from the start, individuals who opposed it. By the time the Colonies achieved independence, some of the states had outlawed slavery. The Quakers in Pennsylvania particularly opposed it and actively helped slaves escape to free states. Individuals in many Northern states helped to run what is known today as the Underground Railroad. This was not a real railroad, but a series of secret hiding places. Conductors, both free blacks and whites, were those individuals who took escaping slaves from one location to another. Through the Underground Railroad, slaves were transported to freedom in the Northern states, while others escaped to Canada, where slavery was not allowed.

Slavery would not be completely abolished in America until after the Civil War ended in 1865. Through the 13th Amendment to the Constitution, slavery was abolished in the United States forever.

While slavery was finally outlawed, it was not an end to racial discrimination. Generations of African Americans were subject to ridicule, torture and death. In the 1950s and 1960s, the civil rights movement helped African Americans to achiever more power and true liberty in the United States.

title: A Slave No More!
text:
A letter written after the Civil War has shed light on the slave-master relationship. Jourdan Anderson was a slave who gained freedom when he and his family escaped to Ohio from Tennessee. In August 1865 his former owner, Colonel Anderson, wrote a letter asking Jourdan to come back to Tennessee to work on his farm.

The former slave's reply gave a clear message about his feelings. He said he hoped that God had opened the colonel's eyes to the wrongs done to slaves for generations. While he was glad his old master was alive, he was surprised that the Yankees hadn't hung him yet. Jourdan wrote that there was one thing that might bring him back to Tennessee. He and his wife wanted to be paid for the 52 years of combined work that they provided as slaves (over $11,000). Without that, he said they had little faith in the colonel's promises. He ended by asking the colonel to give his best regards to a man named George Carter. Mr. Carter had apparently taken a pistol away from the colonel when he tried to shoot Jourdan...twice.

Reading letters and newspapers from the past can help us understand the people who lived during that time. Jourdan and his family may have once been slaves, but their spirits were not broken.

title: Slavery Comes to Massachusetts
text:
The first slaves were brought in to help with farming, building and in the fur trade of the Dutch West India Company.

By the early 1700s, Boston was the busiest harbor in the Colonies, and Colonial shipowners made fortunes in what is known as the Triangular Trade. Large sugar plantations in the West Indies were worked by African slaves. Colonial ships would sail to the islands to pick up molasses made from the sugar. The ships would then return to the Colonies with the molasses, where it was used to make rum. Next, the ship would sail to the west coast of Africa and use rum to trade for more slaves, which were then taken to the West Indies and traded for more molasses. At each leg of the trip, a handsome profit was made, encouraging the cycle.

Not all slaves went to the West Indies, however. Many were transported to the Colonies and auctioned at slave markets. Markets were often held in cities with large ports such as Boston, Salem or New York.

A slave market involved selling slaves. Notices were posted before slave ships landed, announcing the upcoming slave auction. Here, African men and women were lined up so the buyers could inspect their teeth and gums. They would feel their muscles and look for skin diseases. The slaves had no control over what would happen. They might be sold to a master who was kind or to a cruel master who would work them hard, sometimes to death. By then, slaves were no longer treated as servants or laborers, but as chattel. Chattel is property that can be bought or sold with little emotion. It was not important to those purchasing slaves to keep families together. Husbands and wives were separated. Many mothers never saw their children again.

Though Massachusetts was the first colony to legalize slavery, in 1790 it was also the first to abolish it.

Sold into Slavery!

Slave labor in the Colonies grew rapidly as the merchants turned to the Triangular Trade. Though slavery in the North was different from the plantation slavery in the South, it was still slavery! How did the European slave traders obtain the slaves to bring to the Colonies?

One way was to wait near a river and kidnap small groups, who were then taken to a slave ship. More commonly though, one village or country would wage war on another, stealing members of that neighboring village or country. These people were then enslaved by their enemies to use as property to trade with the Europeans for goods.

The more ships that arrived with goods to trade, the more the African society was disrupted as those societies captured more slaves from their neighbors. This slave trade degraded human life as never before, both in Africa and America.

America was not the only country to use slaves for labor. Some historians say the slave trade was as big then as the oil industry is today! Indeed, it was a global trade. The Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch, English and French were all involved in the slave trade. It is believed that during the 350 years of this slave trade more than 10 million Africans became slaves.

A Cruel Atlantic Journey

The passage for enslaved Africans to the Colonies was cruel and hard. Slave traders tried to get as many slaves as possible on a ship. Slaves were often chained together at the ankles and feet. Sometimes they had as little as 3 feet of space in which to move. They were forced to sleep on bare floors with no covering. There were no bathroom facilities, so there was much filth and disease. The air was suffocating. Some sailors at sea said they could smell a slave ship long before they could see one. About one in every 10 died during the passage, and a slave may have awakened to find himself chained to a corpse. Sometimes when food ran low on a voyage traders were known to throw many slaves overboard. Many also died of disease before making it to America. Study the picture of the slave ship. It is impossible to imagine what it would have been like on a slave ship for the two months it took to cross the Atlantic Ocean.

title: Bank Services
text:
Did you know you can do your banking without ever going to a bank? Many people prefer to use their computers at home or at their office to do their banking. This popular method is called online banking. It allows people to access their bank accounts online. It lets them do their banking right from home!

If you have ever done any type of business with a bank, you have made a transaction. The most common transactions are deposits and withdrawals. A deposit is any money that is put into a banking account. Most people make deposits with checks or cash. A withdrawal is money that you take from your banking account. In most cases, it is given to you as cash.

Pretend your grandma gave you a $10 check for your birthday. You want to put it in your savings account. You take the check to the bank and fill out a deposit slip. The teller enters the information into the computer and gives you a receipt. You have just made a deposit. Later, you decide it might be nice to take that same $10 and go to a movie. You go back down to the bank, fill out a withdrawal slip and give the paper to the teller. The teller asks for your ID. Then the teller gives you $10 in cash along with a receipt. You have made a withdrawal. Now that you have cash, you can enjoy your movie!

title: Local Government
text:
The U.S. Constitution explains the duties of the national and state governments. However, it does not tell about the duties of local governments. Many states have subdivisions of counties, cities, boroughs, towns, villages and even special districts. The state legislature and state constitution decide how many and what kinds of local governments there are.

Today, there are about 90,000 local governments in the United States. Many times, these governments overlap, and it can be very confusing. For instance, when a city is in a county, both have government officials. Sometimes, areas of jurisdiction, or control, overlap. It can make it hard to figure out which government should take action.

Sometimes, in large areas, counties and cities share services such as healthcare, fire, libraries, parks and recreation. Is the library nearest to you a city library or a county library? Maybe it belongs to both!

title: I'm fed up!
text:
This is what people say when they are feeling frustrated or out of patience.

It was time for lunch, and Randy hurries to the lunchroom. On the way, he meets Cory who asks to borrow some money for lunch.

"Cory, I can't believe you are asking. I remind you everyday to bring your lunch tomorrow. I even called you this morning and told you to remember to bring your lunch. I think you are just too careless." said Randy in frustration.

"So, does that mean you aren't going to lend me some money?" asked Cory.

"Hey, you know, I think the answer is 'no', I'm just fed up with your attitude about it, and maybe if I say 'no', you'll have a reason to try harder," Randy replied.

title: Who was Henry “Box” Brown
text: Henry "Box" Brown was a very determined and clever slave. In 1849, he ordered a 3 foot x 2 foot x 8 foot box in Virginia. He put a jug of water and some biscuits inside. He also put in a bar to open the box. He then climbed in. A friend addressed the box to an abolitionist, someone who believed in freeing slaves. He lived in Philadelphia. After writing, "Handle with Care" and "This Side Up," the friend shipped him off. Twenty-seven hours later, he arrived in Philadelphia, a free man!

title: The Gunsmith
text: As pioneers moved west and explorers such as Lewis and Clark moved into unknown territory, the demand for rifles increased. The best known firearm manufactured at this time was the Kentucky rifle. The gunsmith made his own gun barrels by wrapping hot iron bands around a cylindrical rod, then driving the rod back out of the formed barrel. In the late 19th century, mass-production methods replaced traditional gunsmithing.

title: Reason and Logic: The First Filipino Settlement in America
text:
Settlers in America often faced challenges while building new communities. In the 1760s, New Orleans was the capital of the Spanish colony of Louisiana. Sailors from the Philippines served on Spanish trading ships going between Manila, the capital of the Philippines, and Acapulco, Mexico.

Conditions on the ships were harsh, and Filipino sailors were often slaves. Some of them jumped ship (escaped) around 1765 and traveled to Louisiana. Once there they hid in the marshlands outside of New Orleans to avoid capture by the Spanish. They formed a colony of fishermen who lived and worked in the swamps and bayous.

These early Filipino settlers were called the Manilamen. Their first village was named Saint Malo. The Manilamen built their houses on stilts in the swamps. They developed a successful method of drying shrimp in the sun on raised platforms. The processed shrimp were exported as far away as Asia and South America.

The fishermen often sent money back to the Philippines so that more relatives could immigrate (move) to New Orleans. Manilamen’s families did not stay in the fishing villages, but lived in homes in New Orleans. Their children would come to work on the platform during busy harvest times.

There were seven Filipino villages in all. Saint Malo was the first, and Manila Village was the largest. Hurricanes have destroyed all of the original villages, but their shrimp-drying legacy lives on. The Manilamen used reason and logic to survive in their environment, just as people do today.

Have you ever noticed where your school is built? Is it located on level land or a slope? Is it a one-story building or taller? What things make the location and design of your school building reasonable and logical?

title: Let's Write
text: Poetry is a good way to express emotion such as sadness, love and joy. Writing poetry about the slave trade would be a good way to express your feelings about this dark time in history. Write a poem expressing the way you feel about slavery or about how you imagine it was for those men, women and children who were enslaved.

title: Education in the Colonies
text:
He who ne'r learns his ABC,
Forever will a Blockhead be.
Be he who is to his books inclin'd,
Will soon a golden treasure find.

This praise for good behavior is from "The New England Primer," one of the first books used in the new Colonies. The Bible and the Book of Psalms were also used. Children were often tested at church on the things they studied through the week.

Schools in colonial days were very different than they are today. Let's look back 200 years to see how education has changed.

Our own state of Massachusetts has a proud history as a leader in education. The first public secondary school in the Colonies, Boston Latin School, was founded in 1635. It is the oldest existing school in the United States. Its purpose was to prepare young men for university entrance. In 1972 the Boston Latin School was made coeducational, meaning both boys and girls could attend.

The year after Boston Latin was founded, Harvard became the first college. In 1635, the English High School became the first public high school in the nation.

Because education was extremely important to the Massachusetts colonists, a law was enacted in 1642 requiring the teaching of reading and writing. By 1647, every town of 50 or more was required to have a school funded by taxes. In 1852, Massachusetts was the first state to require mandatory attendance in school, and in 1854 a law was passed providing free textbooks. This was important, because now every child, rich or poor, could be educated.

Early textbooks in the Colonies were very different than textbooks today. "The New England Primer" was used by several generations of children. Each letter of the alphabet had a short rhyme to go with it. Children memorized these and recited them out loud.

Before the mandatory attendance law of 1852, parents could decide when and for how long their children attended school. If a child's family lived on a farm, it was likely that they would only attend school in the winter when they weren't needed at home for chores.

In very small colonial townships, many children attended a dame school. This was a very simple school taught by an untrained woman in the community, often in a home. Owning books was unusual, and paper was scarce. Many children wrote on thin pieces of bark to practice their letters.

As they got older, children often did mental math (problems that did not require pen and paper). Such a math problem in the 19th century would have been something like this:

At the general store a man bought five yards of muslin at 12 cents a yard, a wooden bucket for 50 cents and three bags of barley at 6 cents a bag. How much must he pay the shopkeeper?

See if you can do that problem in your head! As towns grew larger, they hired a teacher for their children. All ages would attend one school. Classrooms were very strict. Teachers were allowed to punish children as they pleased. Whipping a misbehaving child with a switch was not uncommon. Some naughty children were locked in a closet for an hour as a punishment. Massachusetts Studies Weekly knows that today schools are much different and depend on each person respecting the rights of others.

title: Education? He’s the Mann!
text:
In the early 1800s Horace Mann, a native of Massachusetts, began to teach new ideas to Americans about education. He said schools should be free to everyone. He believed our nation needed people to be well educated to become a strong nation. Not everyone agreed with Horace Mann. Some thought the nation would grow faster if children were working or learning trades. They believed time in school was wasted. Mr. Mann's ideas were slow to catch on, but finally the nation began to respond.

Today, Massachusetts boasts more than 1,800 elementary and secondary schools. More than 120 colleges and universities make Massachusetts one of the greatest learning centers of the world.

Over 400,000 students attend one of the many universities in Massachusetts. Today, about 50 colleges and universities flourish in the Boston area.

The state of Massachusetts has many fine teachers and administrators who are dedicated to making sure that education is the very best for every student. They are dedicated to YOU!

title: Early Education
text:
One-Room Schoolhouses

What did a schoolhouse in early America look like? If a child's family was wealthy, they probably attended a private school or an academy. The buildings and grounds of these schools were usually very nice and often very beautiful. Common schools were quite different. They were usually just one-room schoolhouses and probably were in need of repairs. The room was usually about 20 feet by 20 feet. (Measure that space in your classroom and try to imagine what it would be like for the whole class to spend all of its time together in that one space). Near the entrance was a small hall with nails or hooks to hang coats and a small shelf for lunch pails. A bucket of water for washing hands stood there as well. The ceiling was very low, about 7 or 8 feet, and light came from the one or two windows at the sides. The desks went around three sides of the room, gently sloping down from the wall. Benches faced the teacher's desk. Children usually sat near others of their age. The teacher's desk was raised up on a small platform in the center of the room. It sat next to the stove that warmed the room on cold days.

Because all grades met in one classroom, the classroom could be a noisy place as children practiced reciting their verses aloud. There was little paper and few books. The Bible was used as a teaching text, "The New England Primer" was used to learn letters and to learn to read. The rest of the subjects, like social studies, science and others, were designed and chosen by the teacher. All ages learned those lessons together.

Yes, schools today are very different than the early American one-room schoolhouse. Aren't you glad?

Colleges

Only young men in the Colonies attended colleges. While there were no universities in the Colonies (such as Harvard and Dartmouth) some wealthy families sent their sons to England to complete their education.

Many of the universities were started by churches to train young men as ministers.

School Systems in the Colonies

Many Colonies believed education was for everybody. The Dutch in New Amsterdam, the New England Colonies and the Quakers in Pennsylvania all believed strongly in education. In many of the Colonies, girls did not attend public school. Instead they were given lessons at home by their parents or a tutor.

The first school in Pennsylvania began in 1683. The school taught reading, writing and accounting (keeping financial records). Most Quaker communities provided schools of one sort or another for their children (both boys and girls.) More advanced subjects such as classic languages, history and literature were offered at the Friends Public School. At the Friends Public School, all children were able to attend. Tuition was free for those who were poor. The Friends Public School was founded in 1689. They hold classes there to this day. The school is now called William Penn Charter School.

The Southern Colonies did not have community schools. The large farms were too far apart to make it practical. Wealthy families hired tutors, but the poor were often unable to obtain a formal education.

School children in the Colonies commonly read from the Bible. In addition, many New England families brought their own books from England. The books pictured on the left had pictures to go with the short phrases and showed the students how to properly write their letters.

The first printing press at Harvard University in 1638 helped to bring printed materials to a greater number of students and adults.

Benjamin Franklin is known to have started the first circulating library in the Colonies, where people were allowed to borrow books.

title: Making Money
text:
Have you ever wondered where money comes from? All of the paper money in the United States is printed at the Bureau of Engraving and Printing. It is located in Washington, D.C. Paper bills are made of a special blend of cotton and linen. This blend makes the paper much stronger than normal. It is illegal to make this blend of paper without the permission of the Bureau of Engraving and Printing.

Money is printed on sheets in sets of 30 bills. It is then cut apart and pressed. Then it is starched and bundled. Each bill is printed in different colors of ink. The ink is made from a special formula that only the bureau knows how to make. The bills also have red and blue threads running throughout. You can't even see them. It would be very difficult to make money that is just the same.

Why can't just anybody print money? Well, when there are too many dollars in circulation (in use), the purchasing power of a dollar goes down. When the purchasing power is down, prices go up.

Purchasing power is a measure of how much the dollar is worth. If there is too much paper money out there, it is called inflation. What do you think deflation is? If you guessed it is when there is too little paper money, you guessed right! This causes product prices to fall. Lucky for us, the Federal Reserve watches the money each day. If it looks as if there is too much or too little, they can do things to fix it.

title: County Government
text:
A county in the United States is a tier of government. It is smaller than a state, but larger than a city. A county has governing powers over a clearly defined area. It is under state government. There are over 3,000 counties in the United States.

The structure or power of a county government varies from state to state. Most counties maintain city-like departments, though. They may have a business administration or a city council. There are also many sections to county governments. Fire departments, the police, parks and recreation and public works are all part of a county's structure.

Sometimes areas of jurisdiction, or control, overlap. For instance, a city is in a county, and both have government officials. It can be difficult to figure out which one should take action.

County governments have one vital role in the government. This role is the election process. People vote for those running for office in their county. Counties have the job of registering voters, holding elections and ensuring voting accuracy.

title: Easy as pie
text:
This is the expression people sometimes use when they are describing how simple a task was to complete.

Layne had spent several days preparing for the spelling test. The words on this test were names of holidays, and some of them were hard for him to remember. Each afternoon this week, his sister Linnea had helped him study, and all the hard work paid off! He was proud to show Linnea his paper with 100 percent!

"Wow!" Linnea said. "Was it as hard as you thought is was going to be?"

"No," replied Layne. "I guess all that studying really helped. It was as easy as pie!"

"Well, good for you!" Linnea replied.

title: What is a Hornbook?
text:
It wasn't really a book and certainly didn't have horns! What could it have been?

With few books available to the classroom, children often used a hornbook. A hornbook was a wooden paddle. On the front, a piece of paper was attached that had letters or lessons written upon it. A thin transparent sheet covered the paper to protect it, as it was used by many students through the years. The transparent sheet was made from the horn of an animal such as a cow, thus the name hornbook!

title: The Abacus
text:
The word "technology" can be defined as using science to solve problems. Many ancient civilizations solved some of their problems using science.

About 2,500 years ago, a counting tool called an abacus was invented. It was especially helpful to merchants (people who sold goods) who needed a way to figure out the price of a customer's purchases. No one knows who invented the abacus, but it was used by many ancient cultures. The oldest known abacus was found on the island of Salamis, off the coast of Greece. It is made of marble and is more than 2,000 years old.

The type of abacus that you may have seen first came into use in China about 800 years ago. It is still used by many store owners in China, and Asian children learn how to use it in school. Blind children in many countries are taught to use an abacus because they cannot see to write on paper. Some people say you can solve math problems faster with an abacus than with pencil and paper.

title: Going “Old School”
text:
You might know that one of the oldest wooden schoolhouses is in St. Augustine, Florida. Well, two of the oldest colleges in the United States are Harvard and Yale, and they both started in the New England colonies. Harvard University started in the Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1636. A colonist named John Harvard left his library and half of his estate to the school. Yale University began in 1701 in the Connecticut Colony. A Welsh merchant named Elihu Yale donated property and money to this school. He wanted to preserve the tradition of European education in the New World.

If you think that Pilgrims and Puritans loved education, then you are correct! They thought that learning to read and studying the classical languages of Latin and Greek were extremely important. The two schools continued to develop, and today many people consider Harvard and Yale two of the finest universities in the world. Many Nobel laureates (award-winners), U.S. presidents and Supreme Court justices graduated from these schools. The universities also enjoy a rivalry that goes back centuries! Look at the table to learn a bit more about these famous American institutions.

title: Fighting Extremism with Education
text:
Extremism or radicalism means pushing an idea as far as it can go. Extremists are people who do this, and they often do not accept or tolerate other people’s ideas. They have hurt others and even killed because they didn’t agree with their beliefs.

Many brave individuals all over the world have dedicated their lives to fighting extremism by promoting education. Malala Yousafzai is one of these brave individuals. She believes that through education, people can learn to understand and accept one another.

Malala Yousafzai is a young Muslim woman. She was born and raised in Pakistan. In 2009, when Malala was 12 years old, the area of Pakistan she lived in was taken over by the Taliban. The Taliban are a religious extremist group who want to force their radical views onto other people. They believe that women should not receive an education, and Malala disagreed. When the Taliban came into her city and forbade girls from being able to attend school, she spoke up and campaigned for girls’ education. This put her in a lot of danger, but she did not let that stop her from speaking up for what she knew was right. At the age of 14, Malala was shot by a member of the Taliban and almost died.

On October 10, 2014, Malala was made a co-recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize for her dedication to education rights. More recently, in 2017, the United Nations named her the youngest ever official Messenger of Peace.

title: Take Me to Your Leader
text:
Government is one of the oldest and most important institutions in the world. From earliest times, some kind of government has been a part of civilization. This is because every community needs someone to make and enforce decisions.

During the 1600s, 12 Colonies were established on the North American continent. They went north from South Carolina. In the early 1730s, a group of trustees established the 13th Colony, Georgia. These Colonies did not think of themselves as one country yet. There were many groups of people with very different ideas. As a result, there was not one government or one leader, but 13. While each group of colonists set up their own laws, they all still considered themselves to be under English rule. You might think of the 13 colonies as children who had left home to seek their fortune in a new land.

There were two kinds of Colonies. There were chartered Colonies and proprietary Colonies. Proprietary Colonies were awarded their land either by being loyal to the English crown or because the crown owed them a great deal of money. In other words, a proprietary Colony was a gift to an individual or group of individuals. A chartered Colony was granted to companies who had petitioned the crown for land rights in the New World. These two types of Colonies were governed in different ways. Proprietors were given several guidelines that established the supreme power of the king and Parliament. They were somewhat free to set up their own rules, as long as they didn't interfere with the laws of England.

Chartered Colonies usually enjoyed less interference from the crown. They were often able to trade more freely.

In 1624, the English king started to convert the Colonies into royal Colonies. This means that the Colonies were controlled by the crown. Connecticut and Rhode Island were the only two Colonies that remained charter Colonies. Delaware, Maryland and Pennsylvania remained proprietary. The remaining eight Colonies were converted into royal Colonies.

During the colonial era, the Colonies had a governor, a legislature, a governor's council and a court system. In proprietary Colonies, the proprietors appointed the governor. In the Colonies of Connecticut and Rhode Island, the voters elected the governor, and in the royal Colonies, the crown appointed the governor. These colonial governments could pass laws and tax the people. The governor could veto laws. The governor could also call or dismiss the legislature.

The colonial governments weren't the only ones who could pass laws. The British Parliament also passed laws, especially those that were connected with trade. This practice would cause many of the colonists to resent the crown and would prove to be the beginnings of colonial unrest, eventually leading to the War for Independence.

title: The Magna Carta
text:
The Magna Carta was a charter that changed the ideas of government in England. The charter was signed as English barons forced King John to approve the charter in A.D. 1215 in London. In the charter, the king granted many rights to the English ruling class. It clearly limited the power of the king and made it clear that even the crown must obey the law.

There were 63 articles, most of which addressed the king's need to recognize local authority. One law granted the church freedom from royal interference. A few of the articles guaranteed rights to residents of towns. Ordinary people, however, were not mentioned in the charter even though they made up most of England's population.

The Magna Carta did not end the struggles of power between the crown and the barons. Centuries later, in the 1600s, members of Parliament used the Magna Carta, once again, as a way to check the powers of the kings. The members of Parliament used the charter as a legal support. They argued that there could be no laws or taxation without the consent of Parliament. They demanded that individuals be guaranteed a trial by jury and wanted protection against unfair imprisonment.

In the 1700s, the colonists carried the English ideas about political rights to the North American Colonies. These ideas eventually became part of the framework for the U.S. Constitution.

title: Colonial Governments
text:
1. New York - This area was originally settled by the Dutch and was known as New Netherland. In 1664, King Charles II of England decided to claim the territory between Virginia and New England, and New Netherland was taken over by English forces. This was given to the king's brother, the Duke of York.

One of the Middle Colonies, New York originally started as a proprietary colony, but in 1685 became a royal colony.

2. Pennsylvania - William Penn was granted much of what is now Pennsylvania. The crown owed his father a large debt. This deal settled that debt. Penn was a Quaker. He formed a colony to harbor the Society of Friends (Quakers).

Pennsylvania was a proprietary colony. It was a Middle colony.

3. Virginia - Sir Walter Raleigh was a favorite of the crown. He was granted a charter to settle what we know as Virginia. The settlers of Jamestown hoped to make money in the New World. The year was hard and many people did not survive the harsh conditions.

Virginia is grouped with the Southern Colonies. It started out as a corporate Colony but became a royal colony in 1624.

4. Georgia - Georgia was taken from Spanish control. It was then granted to James Edward Oglethorpe, an English general.

Georgia was a Southern colony. It started out as a proprietary colony but became a royal colony in 1752.

5. Maryland - Charles I granted a Maryland Charter to Lord Baltimore in 1632. Lord Baltimore's son, Leonard Calvert, led a group of settlers there in 1633.

Maryland was a proprietary colony. It was one of the Southern colonies.

6. North Carolina - Virginia colonists settled this region. In 1691, the northern Carolina region was recognized by the crown. It was then called "North Carolina" for the first time.

North Carolina started out as a proprietary colony, but became a royal colony in 1729. It was one of the Southern colonies.

7. South Carolina - King Charles II created the colony of Carolina in 1663. He granted the territory to his loyal supporters. He gave them what we now call North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia. The Virginia settlers challenged the charter. They thought it was unfair, and the region was split.

South Carolina started out as a proprietary colony, but became a royal colony in 1729. It was one of the Southern colonies.

8. New Hampshire - John Wheelwright was banished from Boston. When he left he founded New Hampshire. The settlers there signed a document in 1639 that was very similar to the Mayflower Compact.

It was a New England colony. It started out as a proprietary colony and later became a royal colony in 1679.

9. Massachusetts - The Pilgrims were the first English colonists to permanently settle in New England. They stayed in what is now Massachusetts. Puritans settled in the town we call Salem not long after the pilgrims in 1628. John Winthrop carried the Massachusetts Bay Charter for this settlement. The topmost green area on the map is Maine. It became part of the Massachusetts Bay Colony later on. So did the Plymouth Colony founded by the Pilgrims.

Massachusetts was a New England colony which started out as a charter colony. In 1691 it became a royal colony.

10. Rhode Island - Rhode Island was settled when Roger Williams was driven from Massachusetts for religious differences. He spent the winter with local American Indians. He then bought some land from them. That area is now Providence. Rhode Island was a liberal colony. Those seeking religious freedom from Puritan rule found safety there.

Rhode Island was a New England colony and was established as a charter colony.

11. Connecticut - Thomas Hooker was forced out of Massachusetts. He left because of religious intolerance. He took a group of followers and established Hartford. Connecticut obtained a Royal Charter under John Winthrop Jr. in 1662.

Connecticut was a New England colony. It was also a charter colony.

12. New Jersey - When the Duke of York gained control of the the lands between Virginia and New England, he made a proprietary grant to Sir George Carteret and Lord Berkeley. These men named New Jersey for Carteret, who was the governor of the Isle of Jersey.

One of the Middle colonies, New Jersey started out as a proprietary colony, but became a royal colony in 1702.

13. Delaware - After a failed Dutch settlement, Peter Minuit led a group of Swedish settlers to the Delaware River area under a grant from the New Sweden Company. The Dutch took control over the Swedish, then the English obtained Delaware from the Dutch. Delaware was briefly awarded to William Penn, but his control didn't last, and Delaware became independent in 1701. Delaware was a proprietary colony. It was part of the Middle colonies.

title: Taxes
text:
You are standing in line at the grocery store. You have counted all of your change, and you have $1.03. It's just enough to buy the biggest pack of bubblegum you've ever seen in your life. The bubblegum costs $1.00. You get to the front of the line and the cashier rings it up. Your total comes to $1.06. What? That can't be right. You are three cents short. How did that happen? Then you remember about sales tax. Lucky for you, you find an extra nickel in your pocket and pay for your gum.

Taxes are sums of money that the government collects from people and businesses. They use this money to provide services for the citizens. There are many different kinds of taxes, like the sales tax you pay at the grocery store. Sales tax is a tax that is usually added to the price of your purchase for goods or a service.

There are three main types of taxes: progressive tax, regressive tax and proportional tax. A progressive tax can change. The tax depends on how much money a person makes. People that make more money pay more in taxes. People that make less money pay less in taxes. A proportional tax is the same tax for everyone. Regressive taxes are opposite of progressive taxes. This means that people with more income pay less in taxes and people with less income pay more in taxes. Which tax do you think is the most fair?

title: Write a Letter
text:
Even though you are not old enough to vote, you are old enough to write a letter to a government official. You can tell them how you feel about something.

The first thing to decide is who to write your letter to. Let's say you were writing a letter about your city's roller skating rink. You wouldn't write to the president of the United States, but to the mayor of your city. Likewise, a letter about healthcare issues wouldn't go to your school principal. You must write to the person who can help you.

Always write a government official in a formal way. Put your name and address in the upper right hand corner. Skip two lines and put the date. On the left put the official's name and address. Then open the letter by using the official's correct title. For example, "Dear Governor Smith."

Be clear about the purpose of the letter. Be sure to thank the official for his or her time and attention.

Don't forget that letters to officials aren't always for asking. Sometimes they are for thanking them as well! A letter of thanks is helpful and appreciated. They want to know they are doing the right job for the voters of tomorrow!

title: Eat crow
text:
This is what people say when they are describing a situation when they have to take back something they said.

Miriam was excited about the track and field meet. She was part of the cross country team and was feeling like she was in better form then ever before. She bragged to her teammates that this time - she was going to be way ahead of everyone else.

The day of the meet dawned, and Miriam woke up to find she had a cold. She just wasn't feeling herself. She decided to participate anyway. Miriam had to eat crow when she came in last place.

title: Did London Bridge really fall down?
text:
Indeed it did, and not just once but over and over again.

The first London Bridge was made of stone. It was built across the Thames river in London and lasted for more than 600 years.

Eventually, due to accidents, traffic and the pounding river, the bridge wore out and was replaced with a stronger rock called granite. Over time, the granite began to crumble and sink, so once again, the people decided to replace it. This time with concrete.

The granite stones were taken apart piece by piece and shipped to the United States where they were put together again over a lake in Arizona.

title: Voting Machine
text:
Some state laws now require that every polling site in the state have at least one touch-screen voting machine that can be used by voters who have physical disabilities.
