Markets have this same kind of competition. Businesses compete every day for resources and products. They also compete for consumers.

Businesses create competition in the economy when they offer money for resources they want. Maybe they are offering money for machines they need. Or maybe they need skilled workers. Did you know that the more skills and education you have, the more companies will compete for you to work for them? Think of that! As you compete to get a job, companies are competing for the besttrained workers, too.

Businesses also compete for products and profit. They mostly do this by keeping their production prices low. They also do this by advertising (or telling people about) their products. Businesses compete with other businesses that have similar products.

Entrepreneurship - The last pillar under free enterprise is entrepreneurship. Remember good old Benjamin Franklin? Benjamin Franklin invented things and competed as a businessman. There are many entrepreneurs creating products and competing in our world today.

Entrepreneurs compete by thinking of better products for consumers. If people are unhappy with their breakfast cereal, an entrepreneur somewhere might come up with a way to improve their breakfast. Then the entrepreneur will turn around and use their product to compete with the other cereals. Entrepreneurs hope to make a profit competing with other companies. They use creativity and their incentive for profit to think up ideas that benefit everyone. What are some other ways entrepreneurs affect market competition in the economy?

title: United Nations and Preamble
text:
In previous issues, we talked about the Constitution of the United States and the Bill of Rights. The United Nations also has a Charter, or a constitution, that provides for the framework that governs what it may do. Read the preamble to that Charter and discuss how your class can contribute to world peace.

We the peoples of the United Nations, determined to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war, which twice in our lifetime has brought untold sorrow to mankind, and to reaffirm faith in fundamental rights in the dignity and worth of the human person, in the equal rights of men and women and of large and small, and to establish conditions under which justice and respect for the obligations arising from treaties and other sources of international law can be maintained and to promote social progress and better standards to life in larger freedom.
And to these ends . . .
To practice tolerance and live together in peace with one another as good neighbors, and to unite our strength to maintain international peace and security and to ensure, by the acceptance of principles and the institution of methods, that armed force shall not be used, save in the common interest, and to employ international machinery for the promotion of the economic and social advancement of all peoples.

title: Break the Ice
text:
Have you ever been in a new situation or been around a new person at school? It can be uncomfortable. Breaking the ice means that someone does something to make you more comfortable.

Jane sat down by a new girl in the lunch room. She decided to break the ice and said, "Hey you're new here, what's your name?"

title: Map and Globe Making
text:
Before the 1400s, there weren't many attempts to make maps. However, by the late 1400s, a German merchant and navigator named Martin Behaim produced a globe that showed the world as Europeans knew it before Columbus' voyage. It didn't have the Americas on it because they hadn't been discovered yet; however, people knew that the world was a sphere (round).

During the 1600s and 1700s, the colonization of the New World created a need for a large number of new maps. The Spanish surveyed and mapped the lands that were under their control. English Captain John Smith published a map of Virginia's coastline and New England. Samuel Champlain of France mapped the area of Maryland to the St. Lawrence River in Canada.

title: The Value of Debate and Dissent: W.E.B. Du Bois and Booker T. Washington
text:
Disagreements can be unpleasant and cause hard feelings. So what can you do? Have a debate! A debate is a chance for you and your friend to explain your point of view. If you understand why your friend sees things differently, it's easier to respect his or her point of view, even if you don't agree with it.

Booker T. Washington and William Edward Burghardt (W.E.B.) Du Bois were two great American leaders. Both men were African Americans, but Washington was born a slave in 1856 and Du Bois was born free in 1868. Each man spent his life working to improve the lives of African Americans, but they disagreed about the best way to do it.

U.S. laws between 1876 and 1965 said that blacks and whites should be separate but equal. Washington believed that if African Americans worked hard, eventually they would no longer be separate. They would be accepted as citizens with the same rights white people had. Du Bois dissented, or disagreed. He wanted people to protest and fight for the laws to be changed. He worried that Washington's advice would hold African Americans back instead of helping them. The debates and struggle for civil rights went on for years, but both men are remembered as great leaders.

Read the quotes below and have a class discussion about what they mean.

"In all things that are purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress." -Booker T. Washington

"But we do not merely protest; we make renewed demand for freedom in that vast kingdom of the human spirit ..." -W.E.B. Du Bois

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you were a member of the Lewis and Clark expedition. Describe what your typical day was like. How would you travel? What things would you record in your journal? How would you eat? What would you do when it became cold and rainy? How would you dress yourself when your clothes wore out?

title: Jedediah Smith Fills in the Blanks
text:
Gentle yet tough, Jedediah Smith set out to explore the territory - every bit of it! He became one of the great frontiersmen of American history. He kept a detailed journal which gives historians a peek into the life of a mountain man.

Jed studied his maps. Southwest of the Great Salt Lake was an unknown land, a big blank space on the map. Jed wanted to fill in that white space. Jed left Bear Lake with 17 men, and headed south into the unexplored territory. The men rode southwest through a country of sand and bare hills. The hot sun beat down on them every day. Many of the rivers the men crossed were nearly dry. Horses and mules began to die from lack of grass and water.

When the men reached the Colorado River, they crossed it and rode along its bank. The men were worn-out and half-starved. Several begged Jed to turn back.

"We must keep going," said Jed. "I promise you we'll reach an American Indian village soon."

In a short while, the hungry men reached a Mojave village on the Colorado River. They all shook their heads in amazement.

"How in thunder did Jed ever know we'd find a village so soon?" asked one of the men.

"Jed has a feeling for the country," said Art Black. "Those eyes of his seem to see through mountains."

Jedediah led the trappers across the hot Mojave Desert and over the snowcapped San Bernardino Mountains. All the while, he made careful notes of what he saw and which pass to take so that he might fill in the white space on the maps when he returned.

They reached California (which was then part of Mexico). After a brief visit with the governor of California, Jedediah started on the return trip to Utah.

As the desert stretched before them, their eyes ached and their throats burned with thirst.

One of his men fell and said he couldn't go on. Jed buried him up to his neck in sand to protect him from the sun. "I'll find water," said Jed. A few miles ahead they found a flowing spring. He had plenty of water for his men. They rested there for a day then started walking again. In eight days, ragged, hungry men reached the rendezvous at Bear Lake. The trappers looked in amazement at Jed, Robert, Silas and the other men. It was hard to believe that they had really crossed the Great Salt Lake Desert. No white man had ever done it.

Jed carefully filled in the white space on the map with the notes he had taken on their long and dangerous journey.

title: Texas Rangers
text:
The Texas Ranger's story began on Aug. 5, 1823. Stephen F. Austin realized the need for a body of men to protect his new and struggling colony. The story continued through the Mexican-American War. The Rangers again proved their valor as riders and fighters. Have you ever watched "Walker, Texas Ranger," starring martial arts expert Chuck Norris? Well, your parents and grandparents had a Texas Ranger TV hero as well!

Ask them about "The Lone Ranger." This was a fictional story of a man who wore a mask, rode a horse named Silver and had a faithful American Indian friend named Tonto. The older folks in your family will remember the theme song of the series and will be able to hum it if you ask them. Tell them you know the music is the overture from the "William Tell" opera by Rossini. They will be impressed.

Many books, movies and television shows have been inspired by the Rangers over the years. The Rangers are part of the history of the Old West, and part of its mythology. The Rangers traveled by horse 150 years ago. Today they're much more likely to travel by helicopter or car, although they'll still be found riding horseback at special events.

They dress as they need to. A Ranger in Dallas might wear a suit and tie while a Ranger assigned to a rural area would likely choose Western wear. During normal, every day activity, Rangers are still expected to wear western boots and have their badges pinned to their shirts.

title: Settling Texas Territory and the West
text:
Settlers Flock to Texas Territory

Moses Austin opened the way for pioneers in Texas. Austin found south-eastern Texas much to his liking. He persuaded the Mexican government to give him a large grant of land. After Moses Austin's death, his son Stephen Austin encouraged many pioneers to settle in Texas. He made speeches and wrote letters praising Texas as the finest region in the whole world. He promised that good land could be purchased for just 12 cents an acre. Hundreds of pioneer families rushed to Texas in covered wagons. The first settlement was called Austin, now the capital of Texas. Because of his efforts, Stephen Austin is called the father of Texas.

The pioneers were unhappy under Mexico's rule. The colonists spoke a different language. They also worshiped in a different religion and were not allowed to rule themselves. The Mexican government passed very strict laws for its colonists. It feared the colonists would become too strong to be governed. The laws forbade any more pioneers to enter Texas and raised taxes. These laws also required the settlers to give up their guns. When Stephen Austin went to Mexico to see what could be done, he was held in jail for many months. All these things angered the colonists.

Alamo Falls to Santa Anna

When Santa Anna made himself a dictator in Mexico, the colonists demanded their independence. Santa Anna made plans to punish the daring rebels. With several thousand soldiers, he set out to do this.

One group of about 200 men carried ammunition and supplies to San Antonio's old Spanish mission, the Alamo. It had high walls nearly 3 feet thick. Two of the men were famous. One was James Bowie, inventor of the Bowie hunting knife. The other was Davy Crockett, the famous frontiersman from Tennessee.

Santa Anna expected an easy victory, but had a surprise in store. Day after day, the brave Texans held the fort. Santa Anna led about 2,000 soldiers against the Alamo. The 200 defenders were able to hold the Alamo for 12 days, but at last, the struggle became hopeless. Santa Anna's troops finally broke into the fort. They captured the five weary Texans who were still alive. Santa Anna ordered them shot.

The Battle of the Alamo ended in defeat for the Texans. Yet it spurred others on to later victory. "Remember the Alamo," became the battle cry of Sam Houston's army, who soon retaliated.

Remember the Alamo!

The Texas army was retreating from the Mexican army until General Sam Houston thought the time was right for an attack. On April 21, 1836, near San Jacinto, the Mexican army was taking its afternoon siesta (nap) when the Texans launched a surprise attack. The Texans rushed forward, crying, "Remember the Alamo!" The battle lasted 18 minutes. More than 600 Mexicans were killed and 700 taken prisoner, including Santa Anna. General Santa Anna was forced to sign a paper that gave Texas its independence. In 1836, Sam Houston became the first president of the Republic of Texas. Because its flag had one star, Texas was nicknamed the "Lone Star Republic." It remained a republic for more than nine years. Many of its settlers longed to be citizens of the United States once again during that time. This desire led to statehood in 1845.

Jim Beckwourth Becomes Chief

Jim Beckwourth is a famous African American mountain man and trapper who lived in the West while he trapped furs. Jim fought the Blackfeet to gain back some horses they had stolen. He killed many of the Blackfeet and the Crow tribe saw him do it. This was a great victory for the Crow because the Blackfeet were their enemies. The Crow made Jim a hero. They took him into their camp and made him one of their leaders. He taught them how to trap furs and trade them at the trading post.

John Charles Fremont: The Pathfinder

John C. Fremont, "The Pathfinder," was always on the move. Born in Georgia, he moved throughout the South while his father made a living teaching French and dancing. Fremont eloped with 17-year-old Jessie Benton, daughter of the powerful Senator Thomas Hart Benton in 1841. Benton was impressed with his adventurous son-in-law. He persuaded Congress to fund expeditions for Fremont to explore. The areas included the Oregon country, Rocky Mountains and northern California. Fremont's vivid descriptions heightened American interest in acquiring these territories.

Fremont was amazed by California's wealth and scenic beauty. He hoped to gain control of the region for the United States. The Mexican authorities sensed his plans and ordered him to leave. Instead, Fremont led a group of American settlers in a revolt that set up the Bear Flag Republic in the summer of 1846. Fremont purchased land in California, which amassed a fortune from the gold found there. When California gained statehood in 1850, he became its first U.S. senator. Fremont was also chosen as the Republican presidential candidate in 1856, but he lost to James Buchanan.

Kit Carson: The Pathfinder's Pathfinder

On the riverboat returning from Saint Louis, Kit made a new friend. This friendship became very important. It helped shape the history of the American West.

Kit was standing on deck when a stranger spoke to him. "I'm John Fremont," he said. "They tell me you're the famous Indian scout, Kit Carson."

"Not very famous," mumbled Kit.

"I'm going West to map the Oregon country for the government," Fremont said. "I'm going to need help. Are you interested?"

"I can't read or write," said Kit. "I don't own a compass or a watch. What help would I be?" Fremont laughed. "I hear your mind is a map. They say you know every stream, canyon and mountain in the West. I want you to act as my guide. I'll pay you $100 a month."

Thus began the famous friendship. With Kit as his guide, Fremont explored and mapped the Oregon Trail. Kit saved Fremont's life several times. Fremont was deeply grateful.

title: Economics Review
text:
Congratulations! You now know about some basic economic concepts. You know about producers, the people who produce goods and services. You also know about consumers, the people who buy producers' products. You may even realize that you are a consumer! You know about the different types of resources, too (natural, human and capital)!

You should understand the idea behind supply and demand and the role of prices in our economy. Supply affects demand. Demand can affect what is supplied. For example, if demand increases for a certain pair of shoes, then the producer will try to make more shoes. If the producer can't make more shoes, the price of the shoes would increase. The price helps to ration the shoes, because not everyone can afford to pay for the pair of shoes.

You should now have a general idea about trade-offs and opportunity costs. Remember, we make trade-offs every day. If we buy a candy bar, then we trade money for chocolate. We also make decisions involving opportunity costs every day. If we wake up late, we may not get to take our morning shower. This means the opportunity cost of sleeping in was getting to take a shower.

You know about money and its features. Remember, money should be used as a way to exchange, a measure of value and a store of value. It should also be lightweight, durable, easily recognized and divisible. You know about banks, debt and credit. You know about income, budgets, profit and profit motive. Everyday we watch both microeconomics and macroeconomics in action. We see how they affect our world and how they affect each of us.

Some of you might own businesses someday. You might invest in the stock market at some point in your life. Who knows? Maybe some of you will be the greatest entrepreneurs of tomorrow. But even if you choose not to be a business owner, the economy will affect you every day for the rest of your life. It will determine what you eat, what you wear, and how you live. Good luck to all of you as you set out into the fascinating world of economics.

title: Treaties
text:
A diplomat is a person who has the job to handle relations between his or her country and other countries of the world. A diplomat is a specially trained person who is very skilled at dealing with tense and difficult feelings. The government of their country appoints most diplomats.

One of the things diplomats may do is write a treaty. A treaty is a signed agreement between two parties, or countries. A treaty is one way a nation can end a war or a disagreement. Do you remember learning about the Treaty of Paris in a previous issue of Studies Weekly? It was entered between the United States and Great Britain. Who were the diplomats? Was it favorable to the United States or Great Britain? Do you remember what the treaty accomplished?

title: Don't Put All Your Eggs in One Basket
text:
If you plan something and don't make any backup plans, you take a chance on losing everything if something goes wrong. Think of someone collecting eggs in one basket. If they drop it, then the eggs are all gone.

Arturo planned to have his birthday party at the beach. Joey said, "I heard it's supposed to rain. Don't put all your eggs in one basket. We should plan something indoors just in case."

title: Bells
text:
Bells have been used since the time of the ancient Greeks and are still being used today. Bells are most often used to communicate something. They can be used to mark the hour, warn people of danger or signal that someone is waiting on the phone line. Bells can even call people to worship, or let them know that a funeral is about to begin. Bells are also used as musical instruments and at celebrations.

The process used to make a bell determines how it will sound when it is finished. Most bells are made by pouring liquid-hot metal into bell-shaped molds. The type and amount of metal used in the mixture is very important to the sound that the bell will have after it cools and hardens. The mixture of metals must also make the bell very strong or it will crack when it is rung. The Liberty Bell, now a symbol of our nation, was made in England at the beginning of the Revolutionary War. Since this famous bell wasn't made of strong metal, it has cracked and been repaired several times over the years.

Most of the bells we use today, such as school bells and fire alarms, are electronic, but they still communicate many of the same messages as the handmade bells of the past.

title: Taking Notes in Class
text:
Learning how to take good notes in class is very important.

Taking notes in class can be difficult. Sometimes it's hard to concentrate and you can miss some information. Or you can't read what you wrote. Other times, you're not sure what information to write down. It's important to learn how to take good notes. Without notes, taking tests is much harder! Here are some ways to take good notes in class.

Be ready. You don't always need to have a pen in hand, but have your notebook open to a clean page. And have a pen or pencil nearby. When the teacher enters the room, you're ready to begin.

Put the date and topic on top of the page. Knowing when you took the notes will help you study for tests. You can quickly flip through the pages and find the topic.

Don't waste time writing what you already know. Notes help you remember what you learned in class. If you're sure you know something, then don't write it down. Let's say you know George Washington was the first U.S. president. You don't need to write it down. Instead, you can focus on his birth date, where he lived and what he did.

Make lists. Lists are easy to recognize and read. They organize the information. If you can make a list, you'll likely remember the information later.

Remember, note taking will improve your learning. But your notes won't make much sense if your eyes are always glued to the paper. Take some time to really listen to your teacher. Stop every now and then to listen and to watch your teacher. Write down the examples that are written on the board. By doing this, you're sure to have success in class!

title: Let's Write
text:
Texas Rangers, like all lawmen, are public servants. They have special responsibilities. They are:

1. Protect the life and property of Texans by enforcing the criminal statutes

2. Suppress riots and insurrections

3. Investigate major crimes

4. Apprehend fugitives from justice

Now write about the lawmen of Massachusetts. After you’ve done some research, or interviewed an officer of the law, write about what they do for the citizens of Massachusetts. Don’t forget to write if they are a ranger, sheriff or police officer.

title: Fun Facts
text: A dog’s sense of smell is so good that it can tell the difference between a tub of water and a tub of water with a teaspoon of salt in it.

title: Millions Immigrate to America
text:
During the 1840s and 1850s, four million immigrants flooded into the United States. Sometimes there were 5,000 immigrants a day. Many immigrants came from Ireland. A disease rotted the potato crop in Europe in 1845 and this loss caused a famine, especially in Ireland. Irish peasants depended on the potato for food. Famine and death came to Ireland. The Irish had already started to immigrate to America. The numbers ballooned after potato crops were destroyed. Some 1.25 million Irish had arrived by 1854. The journey was often paid for by relatives who left Ireland earlier.

Once in America, the Irish stayed in the great port cities of Boston, New York, Philadelphia and Baltimore. The populations of these cities were one-quarter Irish by 1850. There were more Irish in America than in Ireland by 1900.

They had little money, education and few skills. The Irish survived at first by doing unskilled work. Women took in washing and sewing. They also worked as cooks and servants. Men found jobs on construction gangs. They built the nation's roads, canals and railroads. These newcomers were often paid less than a dollar a day. A newspaper declared in 1850, "Waterpower, steam power and Irish power" run the United States. "The last works hardest of all." The Irish later became skilled and professional workers.

The church was also a powerful force in Irish neighborhoods. Almost all the Irish immigrants of the 1850s were Catholics. In addition to its religious tasks, the Catholic Church ran schools in which young Catholics were educated.

With the acceptance of each immigrant group, American culture expanded. The Germans probably had the greatest influence on American culture. They were the largest immigrant group in the 1800s. Most arrived in the United States with skills as farmers or artisans.

German immigrants settled both in cities and on farms. A very large number moved to the midwestern states of Ohio, Illinois, Wisconsin and Missouri. The German immigrants often built new industries. In doing so, they made their names household words. They included names like Steinway (pianos), Bausch and Lomb (eyeglasses), Heinz (processed foods) and Levi Strauss (clothing).

Much of German culture became part of American culture. The traditions of the Christmas tree, marching bands, musical societies, gymnasiums and kindergartens all began in Germany. Foods like the hamburger and frankfurter also came from Germany.

Newcomers from many lands helped the American economy grow rapidly. Irish workers kept northern factories humming. Crafts workers from Britain and Germany brought useful skills to America. Each group left its imprint on American life. Irish immigrants brought their lively music and dances. German immigrants brought the custom of decorating the Christmas tree. Immigrants from other nations enriched America with their languages, foods and customs.

title: Success is in the Jeans
text:
The gold rush drew many people to San Francisco. But not all of them wanted gold - that is, not from digging in the ground. Many people saw in the gold rush an opportunity to open shops to supply the gold hunters. One such man was Levi Strauss, a Jewish settler from Germany who arrived in San Francisco in 1853. He opened a business to buy goods from the eastern United States and sell them to shop keepers in California.

In 1873, one of Levi's customers, Jacob Davis, joined him in the business of making very strong pants. These pants had metal rivets placed in the locations where most pants rip at the pocket, at the base of the button fly, and in other places. The new pants were perfect for the goldminers in San Francisco. Over the years, Levi Strauss & Company grew so big that it had to open several new factories to make the pants. After a long and successful career making pants, Levi died on Sept. 6, 1902. He was 72 years old. But that didn't stop his company from growing.

Today, Levi Strauss & Company makes the most famous denim jeans in the world. It is the only garment created in the 1800s that is still worn today. In the 1880s, a pair of Levi's sold for around $1.50 a pair. Today, a pair of men's Levi's jeans cost around $50. Levi's are now sold in more than 30,000 stores in 110 countries.

Have you ever worn a pair of Levi jeans? Have your parents?

The 501® jeans are made in 108 sizes and 20 finishes/fabrics. A typical pair requires 1 3/4 yards of denim, 213 yards of thread, five buttons and five rivets. Each year, the company uses 1,250,000 miles of thread to make these jeans. (That's enough thread to wrap around the world more than 50 times!)

There are 37 separate sewing operations used to make a pair of 501® jeans. The pieces of fabric are cut with electric saws from a bolt of denim. These saws cut through 120 layers of cloth at one time. Almost 60 pairs of jeans can be made from one bolt of fabric.

This amazing garment has been worn by presidents, kings, movie stars, actors, actresses, farmers, miners, teenagers, fourth graders, dogs and dolls! They are just about everywhere. The next time you put on a pair of jeans, whether they are the official Levi's brand or not, you can still see the influence of the great gold rush pantmaker, Levi Strauss.

title: The Mexican-American War
text:
After a war with Mexico and the building of the transcontinental railway, gold was discovered in California. Westward expansion exploded!

Statehood Causes Bad Feelings

When Texas became the 28th state, it triggered a war with Mexico. Statehood caused bad feelings in Mexico. Mexico had not agreed to the independence of the Texas republic. Mexico felt that the United States had taken over a large area of land that did not belong to it. Mexico quarreled with Texas over its Rio Grande boundary. Mexico insisted that it owned the lands on both sides of the river. This boundary dispute started the war in 1846.

Some battles of the war were fought in Mexico and some took place in the southwestern United States. The United States defeated its neighbor after two years. A peace treaty was signed, but bad feelings remained. Mexico was unfriendly toward the United States because of these feelings for a long time. The treaty gave the United States an enormous region of about 500,000 square miles. We have carved out parts of Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona. The entire states of California, Nevada and Utah are from these Mexican lands. We paid Mexico $15 million for the Southwest. The United States bought a strip of land from Mexico a few years later. It is now occupied by the southern parts of Arizona and New Mexico. This area was known as the Gadsden Purchase.

Gold in California

Thousands Struck with Gold Fever

Captain John Sutter owned a 49,000 acre ranch in the beautiful Sacramento Valley. Sutter's ranch was a prosperous one. Captain Sutter had hired James Marshall and other workmen to build a sawmill on a stream in a wooded canyon. Marshall noticed bits of yellow gravel glistening in a streambed. He took it to Sutter thinking it might be gold. The two men agreed to keep their discovery a secret. The news soon leaked out. Excited farm workers quit their plowing. Stockmen left their cattle to hurry to the streambed.

As the news spread to San Francisco, strange things began to happen. Businesses closed, sailors deserted ships and soon only a few people remained in San Francisco. The news of gold traveled across the country before long. Men everywhere dreamed of making a fortune out West. Thousands had gold fever by 1849. These people were called the "forty-niners," because 1849 was the year when gold fever was at its peak. Some traveled overland while some crowded onto ships which sailed down around South America and back up the Pacific Coast. California grew to a population of over 100,000 people within a year.

Wedding of the Rails at Promontory, Utah

One of the greatest events to happen in U.S. history was the "Wedding of the Rails" at Promontory, Utah. Abraham Lincoln was president of the United States in 1861. President Lincoln and many government leaders talked about a railroad that would stretch all the way across the United States from ocean to ocean. It would not be easy and would take millions of dollars to complete. Two companies decided to race to see which could lay the most track, since they were paid for every mile they laid.

The Union Pacific started at Omaha, Nebraska. They used mostly Irish workmen. The Central Pacific started at Sacramento, California, and used mostly Chinese workers. The Central Pacific had the hardest job since they had to build lots of bridges and blast lots of mountain terrain. They met at Promontory Summit, Utah. The Union Pacific laid 1,086 miles of rails and the Central Pacific laid 690 miles of rails. The first transcontinental railway was finished May 10, 1869. A golden spike was driven into a laurel tie to celebrate the "Wedding of the Rails." Two beautiful steam locomotives were built, the Jupiter of the Central Pacific Railway and No. 119 Rogers of the Union Pacific Railway. They nosed each other and touched pilots in remote Promontory, Utah. Not a person there doubted that this moment was among the nation's finest. The pioneer era was over now. The continent was bridged and the United States was now truly one nation.

Oregon Trail

Settlers Stream into Oregon Territory

Dozens of fur trappers explored and blazed trails through the Oregon territory. Missionaries and fur trappers wrote letters back to their families about how wonderful the Oregon country was. Such letters were passed around and some were published in newspapers. Thousands of people heard about the faraway Oregon country. Many decided to move there.

Men like Kit Carson, James Beckwourth and John Fremont were pathfinders and trailblazers. They helped mark the great Oregon Trail. The Oregon Trail began at Independence, Missouri. The long trip to Oregon took nearly five months. Mountain men were often hired to guide the wagon trains to the Oregon territory.

England and the United States both claimed the Oregon Country. Both had explorers and settlements claiming the land. Neither country was willing to give up its claim. Some thought there should be a war. Others urged a wiser way like talking things over at a conference or meeting. The two parties finally agreed on a compromise. Both parties had to give up a part of what was wanted. The northern part became Canadian British Columbia. The southern part became the states of Washington, Oregon and Idaho.

Mormons Colonize West

Religious Leader Says, "This is the Place."

The Mormons were looking for a new home. They were members of a religious group organized by a young man named Joseph Smith. At first they lived in New York state, but because of their different beliefs and ways of living, they were treated unkindly. Finally, they were forced out of the community. The Mormons were determined to worship God in their own way, so they moved west to Ohio, Illinois and later to Missouri. The story was always the same.

Finally, Brigham Young, leader of the Mormons, and 143 pioneers set out from Missouri to the West. They looked for a place where they could rear their families in peace. They reached the western side of the Wasatch Mountains in the great Rockies. They looked down on the Great Salt Lake and Brigham Young said, "This is the place! Here we shall build our homes." The new land did not look inviting to many of the pioneers. Still, the Mormons had faith in their leaders.

The Mormons were rewarded as they developed a system of irrigation. The men flooded their fields with water by damming streams that rushed down from the mountains. The valleys began to develop into lush, green farms and orchards. Brigham Young became known as the Great Colonizer. He had organized over 300 new colonies that spread over Utah, Idaho, Nevada, Arizona and California.

title: Farewell
text:
Thank you for joining us for economics this year. It is very important for students to have a good understanding of this principle.

As you leave school and become working citizens, one of the most important things you can do is be responsible spenders. Budgets will be very important. If you can learn to live on a budget, it's not so important how much money you make. You will be able to be self-reliant and responsible.

As you go on in life with these good habits, you can be successful in whatever you choose to do. Perhaps your good habits and attitudes will help you to make our country a better place to live.

title: Knock Down the Wall
text:
In 1989 the Berlin Wall was destroyed. It had served as the boundary between the countries of East Germany and West Germany. These two countries joined together to make one country with one kind of government in 1990. Before East Germany had a communist government. West Germany had a democratic government. The people of East Germany wanted a democracy, or government made by the people of the country. And they finally got it. This kind of boundary change can be called confederation. Neither East Germany nor West Germany changed in size or location, but they joined together to form one country. Confederation is the opposite of boundary changes by division.

Canada is another example of boundary changes by confederation. Originally the area that is now Canada was simply a few colonies that were all neighbors. Between the years of 1867 and 1905 these colonies joined together, one by one, to form what is now Canada.

title: He Who Hesitates is Lost
text:
If you wait (or hesitate) before you do something, the opportunity may pass you by. People say this to try to get someone to do something or talk about a lost opportunity.

Jeff was sad because he missed a bike trip with his friends. His mother said, "You need to make up your mind sooner; he who hesitates is lost!"

title: What does the poem “The New Colossus” Mean?
text:
If you understand a couple of things about history, you'll find "The New Colossus" by Emma Lazarus a very emotional poem. First, one of the seven great wonders of the ancient world was the Great Colossus (a human statue) that stood over the harbor in ancient Greece. It stood with its feet on each side of the harbor as the ships would navigate under it.

The other thing to understand is the reference to America's willingness to take in refugees from other countries. "Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses (of people) yearning to breathe free. The wretched refuse (cast-offs) of your teeming shore (crowded country). Send these the tempest-tossed (weather-beaten), I lift my lamp beside the golden door."

The Statue of Liberty quickly came to represent the hopes and opportunities that the United States held for immigrants.

title: Tools of the Gold Rush
text:
Gold is heavier than dirt. Most gold-mining tools were made to separate loose gold from other rocks and dirt. Miners scooped up a little sand and dirt and dumped it into one of their separating tools. They poured water over it, swished it around and poured off the mud and water. The heavy gold stayed at the bottom.

Gold Pans: A shallow pan was filled with sandy dirt from a stream. Water was swished around to wash out the mud. The heavier gold stayed at the bottom.

The Long Tom: A stream of water was diverted into a long wooden box where miners put their dirt. The mud washed out, and the remaining rocks were picked through for gold.

The Rocker: Two wooden boxes were used to separate gold from dirt. The top box received a shovelful of dirt. One miner poured water over the dirt, while the other miner rocked the top box back and forth to shake the sand and mud down. A screen kept the big rocks out. The heavy gold fell through to the second box while the mud washed away.

title: Making Connections
text:
Think of the term "making connections" as if you were building a bridge. At one end of the bridge is the known. You already know some things about the subject. At the other end is the new. You don't know everything about the subject. Now let's pretend you are the bridge. Your goal is to use yourself to bridge the gap between the known and the new.

Read this paragraph and follow the instructions:

Almost everyone agrees there's nothing better tasting than a good old hamburger. Especially those you make at home. Different people like different toppings. Some like cheese, onion, pickles, bacon and tomatoes. Others like lettuce, ketchup and mustard. There are other ways to make that hamburger even yummier. Just add things to the meat itself. You can do this before forming the meat into patties and frying it. Try some new ideas. Worcestershire sauce and grated onion make a zippy burger. Try a splash of soy sauce, powdered ginger and a little brown sugar for teriyaki burgers. You can also put in feta cheese, minced garlic and some Italian herbs. This adds a Mediterranean twist to your meat. Don't be shy - try them all!

Did you read anything that sounded familiar? (Almost everyone likes homemade hamburgers.) That's the known.

Did you read anything you hadn't heard before? (The taste of hamburgers can be changed by adding ingredients to the meat before frying.) That's called the new.

You become the bridge between the known and the new. You are making connections by relating information you already know about the subject to what you're reading.

title: Top 10
text:
Well, here it is, nearly the end of the school year. You’ve learned so many new things, and you’ve had some great fun. In fact, you probably think that you have the best school in the whole state of Massachusetts. We’d like to give you the chance to write why.

First, number your paper from one to 10, then begin your list of the top 10 reasons you have the best school of all.

Finally, now that you are older and wiser, include some sage advice for next year’s fifth grade class. That’s the way to pass on a little of that school spirit!

title: Let’s Learn About Massachusetts This Year!
text:
Welcome to Massachusetts Studies Weekly. This year, we will learn all about our great state! We will learn about the people of Massachusetts, both past and present. We will also learn about places, events and much, much more. The study of Massachusetts is more than just history! It's social studies. Social studies includes many themes. Massachusetts Studies Weekly includes history, geography, government, citizenship, economics and culture.

History is the study of people and events of the past. It begins with the first written records of people long ago. We study the past not because students need to learn a bunch of old facts. We learn about our history because it helps students understand how the world works and how human beings behave. Understanding this will help us know just where we fit in the stream of time.

Geography is the study of the Earth's surface. It is a study of the way the Earth looks and how it changes. What are some of the forces that change our Earth? If you named weather and climate, you are exactly right. People affect our environment as well.

Government is the way of ruling a country. It is a system of rules and laws. This year, we will examine the kinds of governments there are in the world. We will study how local, state and federal governments are organized. We'll look at who runs the governments and how they run governments.

Economics is the study of how people make decisions about resources. As we study economics, we learn how goods and resources are produced and consumed. We also learn how wealth is distributed in world communities.

Culture is a way of life shared by a group of people. It includes the values, traditions, customs, arts, history and folklore of that community. Cultures are different from place to place. They may change over time.

Wow, that's a great deal to learn, and we know just the place to start– right at the beginning! This week, we'll begin by learning about prehistoric Massachusetts and the land.

So, turn the page, and hang on for the ride of your life as we explore Massachusetts.

title: Philanthropy and Values
text:
Maybe you have heard the word "philanthropy" before. What does it mean? It describes actions that people make for the good of other people. What is a value? It's a way of behaving that people believe is good- like believing it's good to be honest. Is honesty one of your values?

One way you can practice philanthropy today is to help yourself and others learn good values. How do you learn good values? You can learn them from your parents and grandparents, your teachers at school or church and other people you trust.

You can also learn them from people that have been recognized for doing good things for society. An easy way to learn about people that have done good things is to visit values.com. Values.com has lots of stories and short videos that highlight the traits that make each of us better people. They even have billboards on the highway to remind you about good values.

For example, you may have seen a billboard that looks like the one shown here.

This billboard is about Oral Lee Brown, who saved money from her job to send 19 kids to college... all by herself! Wow! Isn't that cool? You can learn about lots of other people who practice philanthropy at values.com. Be sure to look for more of their "billboards" on Page 4 of Studies Weekly this year. We think they're so cool we want to remind you to check them out!

title: Plymouth, Massachusetts
text:
Plymouth is the county seat of Plymouth County. It is found in southeastern Massachusetts, on Plymouth Bay.

Since the arrival of the Pilgrims nearly four centuries ago, Plymouth has grown. It was once a small settlement. Now it is a large community with more than 50,000 people.

Did you know there are 365 ponds and lakes in Plymouth county? One for each day of the year!

There are also some really beautiful public beaches and a working town wharf. There are acres of parks and many historic landmarks. Don't forget to visit a replica of the Mayflower called the Mayflower II.

You can also visit famous Plymouth Rock and learn the story of the landing of the Pilgrims. Then travel on to the Plymouth Plantation. Don't forget to visit the Ocean Spray Cranberry World for a "tangy" tour. And when that's all said and done, perhaps you'd like to stop for a little whale watching.

title: Why is oil in the ground?
text: Scientists have learned that oil comes from organic material. It takes millions of years before it becomes oil. Organic material is something that was once alive! Dinosaurs lived on the Earth for millions of years. There were also many plants. Scientists believe that the remains of those plants and animals were the beginning of the oil reserves. These reserves are beneath the ground. Because we cannot make more oil, scientists are always looking for better ways to use it.

title: The Hummingbird
text:
Did you know that some dinosaurs and humming birds have something in common? They both have very light, hollow bones.

Ruby- throated hummingbirds are the only species of hummingbird in Massachusetts. They are beautiful birds with long, slender beaks. They are a shiny green. The males have a bright red throat. "Hummers" are often feisty birds. They have a shrill call when they are scolding. Their calls are heard as they chase other hummers away from a flower or feeder.

A hummer, unlike other birds, can fly backwards or sideways or they can hover. They hover over a flower when they drink the nectar. They especially like bright red and orange flowers. Have you seen a hummingbird lately?

title: Massachusetts Geography
text:
It is important to know how Massachusetts looks on a map. This helps us understand how geography affects the history of our state.

Where in the World is Massachusetts?

Massachusetts is one of the New England states. The eastern border is shaped by the Atlantic Ocean. A part of the southern border is also shaped by the Atlantic Ocean. Connecticut and Rhode Island make up the rest of the southern border. To the west of Massachusetts lies New York. Northward are Vermont and New Hampshire. The coastline of our state has hundreds of inlets and bays. It is no surprise its nickname is The Bay State! To the southeast lie the state’s two largest islands, Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard. The Elizabeth Islands are a group of many smaller islands.

The area of Massachusetts is 7,838 square miles. This makes Massachusetts 45th in size among all of the states. Boston is the capital and the largest city in Massachusetts.

The land of Massachusetts is very diverse. What an exciting place for us to live!

How Do Forecasters Predict Weather?

People have always searched the skies. They are looking for a way to predict the weather. Predict means to tell about a future event based on knowledge.

You have probably heard sayings like, “Red sky at morning— sailors take warning. Red sky at night— sailor’s delight.” In the past, sailors and farmers watched the winds and clouds to predict weather. Today we watch the news or read the papers to see what the weather forecaster says. How do the forecasters know? They really don’t know for sure. They are making predictions based on a lot of facts. It isn’t easy being the weather forecaster. Sometimes the weather plays tricks. Forecasting is really the effort of many people working together. There are thousands of weather stations around the world. Some are on the land. Some are at sea. Each station watches and records the weather at least four times a day. They measure many things like wind speed, cloud cover and temperature.

Satellites help with forecasting too. They send information back to the busy national weather stations. At the stations, it is plotted on charts. It is studied by weather experts. The information is quickly sent on to radio and television stations. Speed is everything when it comes to being right about the weather.

Is it Climate or Weather?

You’re lying on your back on the lawn watching the clouds above. The clouds form a horse, then a clown, then a clown on a horse! What a great way to spend a lazy summer day. Suddenly, a brisk wind comes up and the sky turns dark. You feel big warm drops of water on your face! Help! Your lazy summer day has been taken over by a cloudburst. What you’ve just experienced is a sudden change in the weather. The word weather refers to sunshine, rain, snow, heat, cold, ice and wind. It changes from hour to hour, day to day, and month to month. The weather is studied by a meteorologist.

The word climate, on the other hand, describes the kind of weather a certain area has from year to year. Alaska, for instance, has a much different climate than Hawaii. We think of Alaska’s climate in the winter as snowy and very cold. We think of Hawaii’s winters as sunny and pleasant. In Massachusetts, climate varies. There are the warmer winters near the Atlantic coast, but it is cold in the mountains. Climatologists are the folks who study climate and its many changes. They call our state moderate. This means our climate is not terribly hot (like Nevada) or terribly cold (like Minnesota). We are somewhere in the middle.

title: Direct Context Clues
text:
Direct context clues are words that say, “Look here!”

Learning how to guess words you don’t know is an important skill. If you learn how to guess what a word means, then you won’t have to read with your dictionary open all the time.

There are different strategies to guess word meaning. One way is to find other words or phrases nearby that point to the definition. We call those words or phrases direct context clues.

Below is a list of words that are often used to point to direct definitions. In items 1-5, circle the words from the list below. Underline the direct definition in each item.

is/are, was/were

is/are called, means, or, such as

is/are known as, different from

is/are like, is/are similar to

unlike, is/are considered

1. Mammoths lived during the Ice Age. A mammoth was something like a very large elephant. It sported very long tusks that curled on the ends.

2. The Spanish explorers used a very fast, three-masted ship. This ship is called a caravel. Because it was smaller, the caravel could be used to explore shallow coastal waters.

3. Do you want the thrill of your life? Then try the SkyScreamer out for size. The SkyScreamer is a 20-story-high swing ride found in the Texas Six Flags amusement park.

4. Jason’s bedroom is chaotic, unlike Harry’s room, which is tidy.

5. Check the BBC website for a list of monarchs, or rulers, of England.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you have a friend who doesn’t live in Massachusetts and has never been to Massachusetts. Write a friendly letter to him or her describing the geography, climate and one of your favorite things to do in Massachusetts.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: Choose one article from this week’s magazine and look for the nouns and verbs in each sentence. Circle or highlight the nouns in yellow and the verbs in green.

title: Exchanging Goods and Services
text:
Think about walking home on a cold winter day. Just as your house comes into view, it starts to snow. You are freezing! Quickly, you bolt up your front steps. You stomp the snow off your boots as you enter the front door. You walk right to the kitchen and find your dad starting lunch. He asks you to help and gives you a can of tomato soup to open. You find the can opener and open the can. As the can spins around, you start to study it. You think of many questions about the can of soup. How was it made? Where was it made? How did it travel to the food store near your home? Suddenly, that can of soup becomes more than the main menu for lunch. You realize you are looking at a can of economics.

Economists ask all of these questions every day. Their job is to study the economy. They study the results of the making and selling of goods and services. The folks who make goods are producers. Those who buy those goods and services are called consumers.

Economists want to learn everything they can about both groups.

In the case of the can of soup, producers in New Jersey made and packaged the soup. Your family bought that soup, so they are the consumers.

If you help your grandma weed her garden, and she pays you, your grandma is the consumer. She paid for services provided by you.

This year in Studies Weekly, we will be learning much more about our economy. We'll look at the roles of producers and consumers. Can you think of other ways you are a consumer? Can you think of other ways you are the producer?

title: Groton, Massachusetts
text:
Groton is a lovely New England village in the northeastern region of Massachusetts. It is famous for its rolling countryside, apple orchards, family farms and historical homesteads. Just driving down the road makes a person feel like they might be back in the colonial times!

Groton is the home of two very famous private schools: The Lawrence Academy and the Groton School. Did you know that former President Theodore Roosevelt sent his sons to study at the Groton School?

Groton has also hosted the National Shepley Hill Horse Trials for over 25 years. This brings many visitors from across New England every year.

Come visit Groton soon!

title: What is a molasses flood?
text:
It wasn't a flooded river that caused the destruction, but truly, a flood of molasses! On Jan. 15, 1919, a huge steel tank full of more than 2 million gallons of molasses suddenly burst. The sticky goo poured through Boston. Twenty-one people died in the Molasses Flood.

When the flood finally came to a halt, a layer of sticky ooze 3 feet thick covered much of Boston. Molasses could be smelled for months. Some say, on hot days, the smell of molasses still lingers in the air!

title: The Moose
text: The moose is one of the largest animals in Massachusetts or America. It stands more than 6 feet high and weighs around 1,000 pounds. The male has broad, flat antlers. Moose like the northern (colder) climates and are found in the northern United States and Canada. They like the moist lowlands around lakes where they feed on water plants. In the winter they stay closer to forests. One or two young are born in the late spring. The young are called calves. Moose can run fast. Never approach a moose, especially a cow (female moose) with a calf.

title: Geographically Speaking...
text:
This week we will learn about geographic regions in our state. Geography is the study of the Earth’s surface and the way we use it. Geographers are the people who study geography. Some of the special features they study are those formed by changes that happen in nature. Some people say that Mother Nature has formed landforms and bodies of water. They also include other natural resources, or things in nature which are used by humans.

We sometimes divide areas into regions to study them more easily. A region can be made up of many things. However, it always has at least one thing which sets it apart from other areas. Can you think of regions in our state? Regions are described in many ways. How about a regions for kinds of trees. Maybe regions for tourist sites?

Let’s learn together about the four regions in Massachusetts.

Massachusetts Physical Regions

1. The Western New England Upland

The Western New England Upland runs westward from the Connecticut River Valley to the Berkshire Valley. The region is mostly made up of the Berkshire Hills. In fact, the Western Upland region is often referred to as the Berkshire Hills. It is here you will find Mount Greylock. Mount Greylock is the highest point in Massachusetts at 3,491 feet.

At the western edge of this region is the Taconic Range. It is very narrow. This mountain range includes Mount Everett. It measures at 2,602 feet in height.

2. The Connecticut Valley Lowland

The Connecticut Valley Lowland region runs from the northern border of Massachusetts to the northern border of Connecticut.

The beautiful Connecticut River flows through the center of the valley. The Connecticut River Valley is known for its rich soil. Some say it is the best in Massachusetts.

Because of its fertile soil, farmers here raise fruit trees and corn. There are also ranches with livestock.

3. Eastern New England Upland

To the east of the Connecticut River Valley we find the Eastern New England Upland. It stretches from Maine to Massachusetts. The Eastern Upland is a hilly region. It is part of the White Mountains of New Hampshire. There are also several monadnocks in this region. A monadnock is a mountain made of rock. It is not part of a range— it stands alone.

4. Coastal Lowlands

Moving to the southeastern side of Massachusetts, we enjoy the Coastal Lowlands. The Coastal Lowlands run the entire New England coastline. They cover more than one-third of the state. They include Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard. The Elizabeth Islands are here too. Can you find them all on a map of Massachusetts?

The Great Blue Hill is also located in this region. It is south of Boston. It rises to 635 feet and is a unique landmark.

title: Massachusetts Tourist Regions
text:
Sometimes regions are formed as areas of tourism. There are six regions in Massachusetts grouped this way.

The Massachusetts Road Trip!

Early summer mornings, chilly and bright, seem like the perfect time to get up and start the family vacation. Everyone piles in the car. It’s never long before someone says, “Are we there yet?”

Let’s pile in and take a road trip around Massachusetts. We’ll learn about one historic site in each region. We’ll keep a travel journal of the things we see and do. What are we waiting for? Let’s go!

1. The Mohawk trail in Western Massachusetts is our first stop. It is one of the oldest scenic routes in the country. It was once a footpath used by American Indians. Today, it is a beautiful highway with lots of cool shops and places to visit.

2. Visiting the Old Sturbridge Village in the Central Massachusetts region was great fun! We spent the whole day visiting shops and houses. Everything seemed old, like stepping into another time. Even the sounds and smells were different.

3. In the North of Boston region, we stopped to visit the Hancock-Clarke House. In 1775, John Hancock and Samuel Adams were guests of Jonas Clarke. Paul Revere stopped at the house to warn Hancock and Adams of the approaching British on his famous midnight ride.

4. Visiting the Boston Tea Party was great fun. This ship, the Brig Beaver II, is found in the Boston Cambridge Region. We were able to throw a “bag of tea” into the harbor, just like the real Boston Tea Party. You can also visit “Old Ironsides,” the USS Constitution.

5. Plymouth Plantations and the Mayflower II are found in the South of Boston Region. It was awesome to visit the Mayflower II. As the ship’s bell was rung, it was not hard to imagine being aboard for the long, hard journey.

6. Our final stop is Cape Cod and the Islands. Here we took a tour of many lighthouses, learning the history of each one. Pictured here is my favorite, the Brant Point Lighthouse. It was the second American lighthouse built in 1856.

title: Inferential Context Clues
text:
Did you ever ask someone the meaning of a word, only to have him answer, “Figure it out!” When you look again, there are no definite context clues. Now what? The fact is that the meaning is hidden in the rest of the words in that sentence. Sometimes, the meaning is tucked away in a whole paragraph. These are inferential context clues.

Below are three examples. Read the words around the vocabulary word and write what you think the new word may mean.

1. Brianna wanted a cookie, but the jar was out of reach. Jake, Brianna’s brother, climbed onto a chair and stretched his fingers around the jar. Just then, the chair tipped and Jake, the chair and the cookie jar came crashing to the floor. Brianna began to cry. As the noise and confusion mounted, their mother called out from the next room, “What’s all that commotion?”

Write what you think the word commotion means:

________________________________________

________________________________________

2. During a test in class, Spencer saw his best friend, Tyler, cheat. He told Tyler that if Tyler didn’t confess to the teacher, he would tell her what he saw. Standing up to Tyler took a great deal of fortitude on Spencer’s part.

Write what you think the word fortitude means:

3. Sometimes, we borrow words from other languages (exonymns). This vocabulary word is French and is sometimes followed by an exclamation point. Ashley said, “I cut a coupon from a magazine, mailed it in and — voilà! — here’s my new glow-in-the-dark lipstick!”

title: Carving out Massachusetts
text:
A glacier is a slowly-moving mass of ice.

Long ago, Massachusetts was nearly covered by glaciers. The movement of these heavy glaciers rounded off mountains. The glacier movement carved out streams and rivers. They left us with hundreds of beautiful lakes and ponds. Today, there are more than 1,100 lakes and ponds in our great state. How many can you name?

title: Algonquians Welcome Europeans to America
text:
When Columbus first landed in the New World, he thought he had found the East Indies. He called the people living there "Indians." The name stuck! Some descendants of those Indians like to be called "Native Americans," because native means "belonging to by birth." Others like to be called American Indians.

The Algonquian people lived in the northeast when the Pilgrims arrived. The Pilgrims were lucky that the natives were kind and friendly. Tribal members welcomed them and taught them how to survive in the new land. Though the tribes had their own days of thanksgiving, it was an Algonquian tribe that shared the first Thanksgiving feast in America.

The Algonquians respected and shared the Earth. They hunted deer, moose, bear, beaver, wild ducks and turkey. They never hunted for more than they needed and did not waste any part of the kill. While the men hunted, the women planted the crops. The main crop was yellow corn, called yokeag. Beans, squash and pumpkins were also grown.

Wigwam is the Algonquian word for home. Most wigwams were dome shaped. They had a hole in the center to let smoke from cooking fires escape. The men shaped the frames from young saplings, or tall young trees. The women then fastened woven mats or bark to the frame.

What did the Algonquians wear? Animal furs and skins were used for clothes. Women wore long skirts of skins, and men wore only a breechcloth. A breechcloth was a thin piece of hide put between the legs and draped over a belt. When it was cold, they wore robes of leather or fur. They wore beautiful moccasins to show respect for the Earth.

Algonquians used what we call a clan system. Many tribes were matrilineal. That meant children in a family belonged to the mother's family. They couldn't belong to both the mother's and father's families.

Children were important members of the tribe. After chores were done, everyone could play. A game like baseball was played with a stick for a bat, and a pine cone for a ball. Darts were also played. With bird feathers attached, the darts would soar through the air. In the winter, tobogganing and snowsnake were favorite sports. In snowsnake, players threw long sticks down snowcovered hills. The player whose stick went the farthest won! Storytelling was enjoyed by all. Members of the tribe told of heroes and history. There were no books, so this was the only way for history to be passed on.

Though the Algonquians gave freely to the European settlers, they were treated poorly by many colonists, driven from the land and nearly destroyed.

title: Mahican-Mohawk Trail
text:
Long before white settlers began to build roads, American Indians had worn trails between villages. The main form of travel for the tribes of the northeast was foot travel. Runners took messages between villages. Some ran up to 100 miles in one day! Foot trails grew wider as natives hunted and traded with other tribes.

One of these Mahican-Mohawk trails, going from the Valley of Massachusetts to the Hudson River Valley, is being recreated as a hiking trail. Plans for the trail call for 100 miles of marked hiking trail. Sometimes the trail will be a dirt road. In other places the new trail will be paved. The finished trail will go from Deerfield, Massachusetts, to Schaghticoke, New York.

Currently there are 34 miles of trail completed. Some parts of the trail are used for riding bikes, snowmobile riding, horseback riding and paddling. For more information about Mahican-Mohawk Trail visit www.mass.gov.

title: The Algonquians
text:
The main Algonquian-speaking tribes that resided in Massachusetts were the Nauset, Nipmuc, Pocomtuc, Wampanoag and the Massachusett. In the map you will see some of the Algonquian-speaking tribes that lived in Massachusetts.

Massachusett

In the early 1600s there may have been as many as 3,000 Massachusett living around Boston Bay. When the first people from Europe arrived, they brought new diseases. Many of the Massachusett died. Only about 800 were there when the Pilgrims arrived in 1620. There are some descendants who are still living near the cities of Canton, Mattapan and Mansfield.

Nipmuc

No one is sure how many Nipmuc tribes there were. Some of the Nipmuc tribes may have been part of the Pequot Confederacy. After the Pequot were destroyed by the English, the freed people became known as the Nipmuc. War and disease caused many to die. Others were scattered. Today two groups of Nipmuc live in Massachusetts.

Pocomtuc

Perhaps close to 5,000 Pocomtuc lived in the Connecticut River Valley in 1600. Most were destroyed during King Philip's War. Many of the Pocomtuc fled to join the Mahican village in New York. Others joined the Western Abenaki. Today, we believe the Abenaki in Vermont include descendants of the Pocomtuc.

Nauset

The Nauset have never been a very large tribe. Smallpox caused the numbers to grow even smaller. After King Philip's War, members of other tribes joined the Nauset, near Mashpee.

Wampanoag

The Wampanoag were one of the main New England tribes. They numbered nearly 12,000 in 1600. The 40 or so villages were divided between the mainland and the offshore islands. After the spread of disease, there were only about 2,000 left on the mainland. Only 400 of the Wampanoag remained after King Philip's War. Today there are five organized bands in Massachusetts. Drifting Goose, the Grand Sachem (chief or leader), formed a council of chiefs.

Today, the Wampanoag children have a day off from school in October to celebrate Cranberry Day. The tribe meets in the cranberry bog to pray and harvest cranberries, after which the tribe and other members of the community meet at the town hall for feasting and dancing.

title: Adam Smith
text:
Consumers and producers have always been important to markets. Markets are actually a way that people can trade with one another. Markets bring consumers to producers and producers to consumers. Through these markets, exchange economies came to be. No one ever really invented an economy. It just happened as people traded with each other. As markets grew larger, many people began asking questions. Then they studied people as they traded for goods and services. That study is what we now know as economics.

One of these early economists was named Adam Smith. He began looking at exchange markets. Smith didn't know it, but he was really starting the study of economics. In 1776, he put out his book, "The Wealth of Nations."

Smith suggested that there was an "invisible hand" that guided trade in an economy. Think about sitting down to enjoy a nice bowl of tomato soup. There are the tomato farmers and the soup makers. There are the marketing team who advertises the soup and the people who design the label. Don't forget the truckers who transport the soup. How about the grocery store that places it on the shelf? Who is in charge of all this? According to Smith, no one is in charge of trade. Instead, markets bring people together. This process of trading in an economy is known as voluntary exchange. These early ideas from Adam Smith still affect economists today, more than 200 years later. It is because of his work and study that Adam Smith is known as the father of economics.

title: Ipswich, Massachusetts
text:
Ipswich was formed in 1633 and is one of the oldest towns in the history of the United States. The town is located in the middle of the North Shore. It is approximately 33 square miles! There are many different things to see. There are marshes, beaches, dunes, forests, farms and fields.

A trip to Ipswich will surely include many historical houses. In fact, there are more than 40 houses that were built before 1725.

Many folks stop to take a tour of the Whipple house. This home is one of the oldest houses still standing in New England. The 17th-century garden is a surprise with over 60 different plants.

Ipswich is well known for fresh clams that are processed at a nearby plant. Yummy! Do you like clams?

title: What is a powwow?
text:
A powwow (sometimes called a shaman) was the medicine man in an Algonquian tribe. The powwow's jobs included healing the sick and calling up spirits in ceremonies. He sometimes held a gathering, also called a powwow.

The people asked the powwow questions about the future or talked about problems. Today we often use the Algonquian word powwow to describe a discussion or a meeting.

title: The Wolf
text:
The wolf is a symbol for many American Indian tribes. The gray wolf lives in a pack, or a group. It will often stay with a pack all of its life. Though there are pack leaders, the pack will work together. Together, they hunt, care for the young and defend their territory.

Wolves can go many days without eating and then eat as much as 20 pounds of meat in one meal. Most are able to run for a long time for great distances.

Fairytales and cartoons would have you believe a wolf is aggressive. In fact, wolves are very shy. It is rare that they will even come near a human.

title: King Philip's War
text:
Like his father before him, Metacomet was the grand Sachem of the Wampanoag. Massasoit, his father, tried hard to work peacefully with the Europeans. After Massasoit died, his son Metacomet followed a different path. The colonists called Metacomet by the name King Philip. He felt that the time had come to defend his people. Metacomet spoke with other tribal leaders. He wanted to form a strong alliance (several groups working together for one cause) against the English.

Unfortunately for Metacomet, many of the tribes did not join him. Metacomet was forced to continue his plans for war without much help.

The War Begins

In June of 1675 some colonists in Massachusetts hanged three Wampanoag. They were accused of spying. A warrior took revenge by killing cattle. In the process, a colonist opened fire on that warrior. This sent more warriors pouring into the area. They killed settlers and burned towns.

At this point, the Nipmucs and Narragansett joined the Wampanoag. Other tribes, from as far away as what is today Maine, traveled to help fight against the colonists. Twelve colonial towns were destroyed. Forty more were attacked.

New England sent armies to fight back. For a few months, no one could tell who would win the war.

A Truce is Signed

The war continued for eight long months. The last battles took place in Deerfield and Bridgewater. In August of 1676, Metacomet himself was killed. He was betrayed by one of his own warriors. Many more were killed before a truce was finally signed. Metacomet's wife and son, along with hundreds of others, were sold as slaves. The defeat of the Algonquians in King Philip's War would be the last. Never again would any Algonquian tribe be in a position of power.

title: Building on Base Words
text:
A base word is the basic word. As you create new words from a base word, they are all related.

Base words are used to make other words you use every day. Derivations are those words created by adding parts to the base word. Here’s an exercise to make you think. For each group of derivations, write the base word in the blank space. In the future, when you’re reading on your own, try to think what the base word is for many of the words you read.

title: Let's Write
text: You can hardly wait for the powwow to begin. It is your first time to attend a gathering with the powwow. You watch as he enters in special clothes with a painted face. Some people dance and sing, others smoke a pipe. It is almost your turn to ask the powwow a question you have really been pondering. Write your question and then the answer you think you would receive to your question.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: As you read this week’s cover story, circle or highlight all of the adjectives in yellow and all of the adverbs in green.

title: Explorers Look But Don’t Stay
text:
An explorer is a person who journeys to the unknown for the purpose of discovery. What were explorers looking for? Did they ever find it? Explorers have often discovered places other than what they hoped to find. Sometimes, like Christopher Columbus, they were mistaken about what they found.

Six thousand years ago, people knew very little about what lay more than a few days' journey from their homes. They grew all of their own food and made everything they needed. They had no need to travel. However, as settlements grew, so did the idea of trading with other people. Because people wanted to trade, they began looking for new trade routes. Trade was one reason people began to explore new lands.

One of the greatest goals of early maritime (having to do with the sea) explorers was to find the Northwest Passage. The fabled passage was a route from Europe to China around the north of North America. Some countries wanted to find a new northern route. Spanish and Portuguese warships blocked the routes around the south of South America and Africa, limiting trade. Look at a world map, and trace the southern route.

Giovanni de Verrazano was one of the explorers looking for the Northwest Passage. He was an Italian explorer who served the French king, Francis I. In 1524, Verrazano sailed on his ship, the Dauphine. He sailed right to the mainland of North America! He then traveled north along the coast. He may have been the first European to see this part of North America. Some historians think Verrazano met two Wampanoag chiefs in his travels. Verrazano was a unique explorer because he wrote about what he saw, and his brother drew maps.

title: Dighton Rock...We’re Still Waiting!
text:
Historians think Dighton Rock is the place that everyone wanted to leave a message, like a bulletin board for ancient Americans. No one knows for sure.

As early as 1677, colonial scholars such as the famous Cotton Mather, Ezra Stiles and Dean Barkeley tried to decipher the message. Mather copied the engravings and sent the drawings to the Royal Society in London. He hoped they would decode them. We are still hoping for answers!

In 1837, Carl Rafin, a Danish scholar, read Roman numerals and the name "Thorfinn Karlsefni" on the stone. Some folks believe Thorfinn was supposed to have sailed to America from Greenland in the year 1010. However, in the 20th century, Edmund Burke Delabarre announced that part of the message read "Miguel Cortereal by will of God, here Chief of the Indians - 1511."

The famous rock was moved to dry land a few years ago by Massachusetts. To protect it from winter and weather, a building was constructed around it.

Dighton Rock has been endlessly studied. We hope that someday we'll know what all the jumbled writing really means.

title: Explorers Come to Massachusetts
text:
Up until 1492 when Columbus bumped into the New World, Europeans did not know about the New World or the people living there. They were motivated to explore new lands because they wanted to find a sea route to the rich Eastern lands of China and India. After the discoveries of Columbus, a race began. Everyone wanted to find a passage around America. The exploration of Massachusetts started with Europeans looking for the Northwest Passage.

Cortereal before Verrazano?

Historians in recent years feel that Miguel Cortereal of Portugal may have arrived at the New England coast some 20 years before Verrazano. Cortereal's ship wrecked on the coast in 1502. Because of the inscription on Dighton Rock, (which some historians believe translates as "Miguel Cortereal by will of God, here Chief of the Indians - 1511") it gives scholars the idea that Cortereal may have lived with the American Indians for nine years. Some think he may even have become a chief for a time!

Gosnold names Martha's Vineyard

The first European explorer that we know lived here for a bit was Bartholomew Gosnold. Gosnold was an Englishman who arrived in 1602. Gosnold was not in search of the Northwest Passage. He was searching for sassafras for use as a medicine. He and his crew sailed along the eastern coast. They stopped at a long peninsula shaped like a hook. Look at a map. Can you guess where he might have been? Because of the large numbers of codfish his crew caught, they named it Cape Cod. That is still the name today. Gosnold named Martha's Vineyard after his daughter, Martha. He even explored and named the Elizabeth Islands, stopping at what is now Cuttyhunk. There they built a fort. Gosnold liked Massachusetts so well he thought about leaving 20 crew members behind to colonize, but he did not have enough supplies. Gosnold and his crew returned to England laden with sassafras and furs. Because furs were valuable in Europe, many abandoned the search for the Northwest Passage and came looking for beaver. Soon permanent colonies would be found all along the coast.

John Smith of Jamestown

While the King of England was busy colonizing the New World, other explorers continued to map the Massachusetts region. A few years after Champlain (a French explorer) sailed the coast, John Smith of the Jamestown colony in Virginia did the same. Smith published "A Description of New England." He told in detail of the region of Massachusetts. He called it "paradise" and said, "could I have but means to transport a colony, I would rather live here than anywhere."

It was Smith who first used the name of Massachusetts on a map. He named it after the American Indian tribe, the Massachusett, of course. The word Massachusetts is thought to mean "the place of the great hill." Do you think that great hill is the Great Blue Hill south of Boston?

title: Productive Resources
text:
Productive resources are found in every good or service. Resources are the basic things used to make products in our community. Economists put them into three groups.

Natural Resources

Natural resources are gifts of nature. Fresh air, water and trees used for timber are all natural resources. They are things taken from the Earth that cannot be made any other way.

Human Resources
