A secretary, a doctor, a mechanic and a teacher are all kinds of human resources. Human resources, or labor, require people to be creative. People must have skills and knowledge to provide a service.

Capital Resources

The last type of resource can be found everywhere. Buildings, tools or machines people use to produce other goods and services are known as capital resources.

These productive resources are all around you every day. Let's say that you wanted to make cookies. Each of these resources would be very important. Most of what you put into the cookies - eggs, milk, sugar, salt and flour - would be natural resources. The human resource would be you making the effort to make the cookies. Lastly, your mixing bowl, measuring cups, spoon, baking sheet, mixer and oven would all be types of capital resources. All these things come together to make your product - yummy cookies! Can you think of other examples of natural, human and capital resources?

title: Fall River, Massachusetts
text:
Fall River is a town located in southeastern Massachusetts. It is one of the largest centers for cotton textiles in the country. The name Fall River actually comes from the American Indian word Quequechan. This means "falling water." This is a perfect name for this town. It is located right where the Taunton River flows into the Mount Hope Bay!

While in Fall River, many folks stop to see the USS Massachusetts. This ship is located in Battleship Cove. The USS Massachusetts was also known as "Big Mamie." It was one of the heaviest battleships of its time. It was launched in 1941 and served the U.S. Navy until 1946. In June 1965, the ship's old crew and many Massachusetts school children raised enough money to take her to Battleship Cove. Here she rests and welcomes visitors from all over the world.

title: What is hardtack?
text:
Hardtack is a very hard biscuit. It was used by explorers aboard ships for food. Voyages were very long and there was no way to preserve food. Sailors commonly ate salted meat and hardtack for their meals.

The hard biscuits often became infested with beetles or maggots. These had to be picked off by the diner before the hardtack could be eaten! Hardtack was made with flour, water and salt. It was baked until very hard.

title: Sassafras
text:
Sassafras is an important plant to both wildlife and people on the northeast coast.

For example, deer feed on the aromatic (good smelling) twigs in the winter. Bees love the flowers, and birds enjoy the glossy berries.

It was the bark of the root that brought Gosnold searching. Today, the bark of the root is still used to make teas. The leaves are ground to thicken food - the file in Cajun cooking. The aromatic wood is used to make furniture. Early Americans thought it was healthy to have beds made of the fragrant wood.

The leaves are three lobed, or sometimes mitten shaped. The twigs are a bright green and the berries are shiny blue. The berries are especially fragrant when crushed. The leaves turn a brilliant red, orange and yellow in the fall.

title: Synonyms
text:
Synonyms are words that have the same or almost the same meanings.

Learning synonyms for common words is important. Synonyms build your vocabulary. They can make your writing more interesting (alluring, compelling, fascinating) to read.

Below, you will find a common (ordinary, average, passable) fairy tale. Work with a partner to find synonyms for as many words as possible. Rewrite the fairytale using your favorite synonyms.

Do you want to find synonyms on the computer? Use this Web site to see what you can find: http://thesaurus.reference.com

Goldilocks and the Three Bears

Once upon a time, there were three bears. They lived in the forest in a cute little cottage. There was a big papa bear, a middle-sized mama bear and a little baby bear. One chilly morning, mama bear stirred up some porridge. It was too hot to eat, so they went for a walk in the forest.

While they were out, Goldilocks came right in. She saw the porridge on the table and, forgetting her manners, sat down to eat.

“Wow,” said Goldilocks, “this big bowl is really hot.” She tasted the porridge in the middle-sized bowl. It was cold.

“Oh my heart,” she said, “this bowl of porridge is too cold.” Then she spied a little bowl. She took a little bite.

“Yummy!” she squeaked. It was just right. With a big smile on her face, she ate all of the porridge. It was just perfect for a crisp fall morning.

title: Let's Write
text: A sailor on an explorer’s ship might be at sea for as long as two or three years. All of his personal belongings as well as his tools had to be kept in a chest. A sailor’s chest was a very sturdy wooden box with a hinged lid. It was usually painted and often had the name of the sailor and a date painted on the front. A sailor’s chest was used for storage and as a bench or table. Imagine you are about to go on a voyage to explore a new land. You may be gone for many years. In 150 words or less, tell what you might take in your chest and what your duties might be on the long trip.

title: Separatists Flee to a New Land
text:
Europeans were drawn to America for many reasons: some for adventure, some in the hopes of obtaining wealth and still others for religious ideas. Today, it may be difficult to imagine why religion, or a desire for wealth, would drive people to make a dangerous journey to a land where they had few comforts and lacked even food. It was their dream – a dream of a better future – that inspired the journey to this new land.

The story of the Pilgrims really began when King Henry VIII of England wanted to get a divorce. He was unhappy when the Pope did not grant it. So Henry created a new church. He named it the Church of England. Next, Henry placed himself as the head of the new church. Many people in England were unhappy with the new church. Some folks in England wanted to purify it. These people were known as Puritans. Others felt the only way to be happy was to separate from the Church of England. Those who wanted to separate from the church were known as Separatists.

A Journey to Holland

A group of Separatists we want to learn about lived in Scrooby, England. In 1608, a small band of Separatists from Scrooby fled to Holland. They lived in Holland for nearly 12 years. They were unhappy in a strange country. Some of the Separatists decided to travel to the New World. They wanted to begin a colony of their own.

Return to England

A small ship, the Speedwell, carried them to England. Here, they joined another group of Separatists. To help pay for the voyage, passage on the ship was sold to others. Others were traveling to the New World for adventure. The Separatists called themselves Saints. They called the other passengers Strangers. Finally, 102 passengers, both Saints and Strangers, were ready to leave for the New World. Trouble soon followed when the Speedwell began to leak. They turned back for repairs. At last, all 102 passengers boarded a second ship – the Mayflower. The Mayflower sailed on Sept. 16, 1620. The tiny ship was cramped and crowded. There was not enough fresh water for all. Dried meat with hardtack was the usual meal. The ship faced many storms. One storm almost washed a passenger named John Howland overboard!

The Pilgrims Land in Plymouth

The Mayflower sailed for 65 days. Finally, on Nov. 19, the Separatists spotted Cape Cod. They did not land here. They went on to Plymouth Harbor. Here they made their historic landing on Dec. 21, 1620.

So when did they become known as Pilgrims instead of Separatists? A pilgrim is a person who begins a holy journey. William Bradford kept a journal. He first wrote the term "Pilgrim" to describe the Separatists. They did not call themselves Pilgrims. We use that term today to describe those Separatists of long ago.

title: Clarity of Thought: William Bradford and the Mayflower Compact
text:
Imagine that someday you join a group that is going to start the first colony on the moon. What is one of the first things you might need? If you said a set of rules or laws to live by, you'd be thinking clearly. That's exactly what William Bradford helped write for the Pilgrims in 1620.

William Bradford decided early in his life that he did not agree with the Church of England, and this was the only church the English laws allowed in those days. He joined a separatist church, one that had separated from the Church of England. Bradford wanted to avoid being arrested and put in prison, so he led a group of church members and moved to the Netherlands. But they faced persecution for their religion there too.

In 1620, the separatists returned to England to meet others with their beliefs and sail for the New World on a ship called the Mayflower. The group received a patent (land grant) from the king of England to establish the first permanent colony in Virginia. The Mayflower was blown off course and landed near Cape Cod instead of Virginia. William Bradford and the other leaders of the colony decided that they needed to write an agreement for all people to have protection and to keep the peace. This unique document, signed by 41 men, is called The Mayflower Compact.

William Bradford was later elected governor of the colony over 30 times, so his clarity of thought must have been well respected. The Mayflower Compact has been called the inspiration for the U.S. Constitution. Look it up. Rewrite it in your own words to see how it reads in today's language. Would you have signed it? Why or why not?

title: Plymouth Colony a Success!
text:
Plymouth colony was a success. The colonists wanted to stay in one place. They did not leave their homes to seek riches. They did not journey around the world to trade. Plymouth Colony was a success because of great leaders and friends, including Squanto, Massasoit and William Bradford. Let's read together about each of these great leaders.

The Mayflower Compact

The Mayflower Compact was an agreement drawn up by the men aboard the Mayflower. The Separatists feared that there would be trouble with the Strangers. So they all signed a pledge to work together. The Mayflower Compact was that pledge. It was the first agreement for self-government in the New World. The group then elected John Carver to be the first governor in Plymouth Colony.

Building Plymouth Colony

The colonists began building right away. They were worried because it was winter. On Christmas Day in 1620, the Pilgrims began felling (cutting down) trees to construct a common house (a combination church/fort). A few small houses were built. Most of the colonists spent the first winter on the Mayflower.

Conditions were really terrible during the first winter in Plymouth. Many colonists were sick. They did not have enough food. Only 50 of the colonists were alive at the end of that first winter.

Help Arrives

Early in the spring of 1621, the nearby native people watched the Pilgrims closely. Samoset was an English-speaking Algonquian. He entered Plymouth and said, "Welcome, Englishmen." They were surprised to hear Samoset speak English! Samoset visited that day. He stayed the night with Elizabeth and Steven Hopkins. Early the next day, he left. He returned with another native who spoke English even better. His name was Squanto.

Squanto and Massasoit

Squanto lived in England for many years. It was there that he learned to speak English so well. Later, Squanto was captured as a slave. He was gone for many years. While he was away, his whole tribe was wiped out by sickness. When he returned, he lived near Plymouth. This is where his people had once lived.

With the help of Squanto, the Pilgrim leaders finally met with Massasoit. He was the leader of the Wampanoag tribe. Governor Carver was happy that Massasoit wanted peace. Both leaders agreed their people would not carry weapons. They also pledged to protect one another from enemies. This peace agreement lasted more than 50 years.

1. William Bradford (1590-1657)

Governor John Carver died suddenly. It was shortly after the Pilgrims settled Plymouth Colony. The colonists elected William Bradford as the new governor.

Bradford was orphaned by the age of 7. He later lived with two uncles in Austerfield, England. As a young man, Bradford walked 16 miles to attend a Puritan church. That's a very long walk! He later joined the Separatists of Scrooby and traveled to Holland. While in Holland, Bradford married a young woman named Dorothy. They had one son by the name of John. When the colonists set sail for the New World, John was left behind. He probably stayed in Holland with his grandparents. John would later join his father in Plymouth.

After the Mayflower arrived, William and a few others explored the coastline. They were searching for a place to live. While William was away, his young wife fell overboard and drowned. He returned to the ship to learn of Dorothy's death. He was very sad. William spent the rest of his life serving Plymouth Colony. The people loved Bradford and elected him to serve many years as governor - 31 years in all!

2. Squanto (Late 1500s-1622)

When Squanto returned to his native land after his capture, he found all of his people to be gone. He was the last surviving Patuxet. He went to live with his neighbors, the Wampanoags. There is no doubt that Squanto saved the Pilgrim colony from perishing. He taught the people how to farm and fish in this strange new land. Squanto was very important to the success of the colony. William Bradford called him a "special instrument sent of God."

Squanto lived with the Pilgrims for the last two years of his life. He died of an illness on a trading voyage with William Bradford. Bradford greatly mourned his "especial friend."

3. Massasoit (about 1580-1661)

Massasoit was born in the village of Pokanoket, in what is now Rhode Island. He was also known as Ousamequin, or "Yellow Feather." He became the chief of the Wampanoag people. He was kind and trusting. He helped the Pilgrims thrive in the new land. They lived many peaceful years with the Wampanoag. Massasoit was a firm friend of the Pilgrims until his death in 1661.

title: Supply and Demand
text:
To an economist, a market includes everyone who buys or sells a good or service. That means all of the people who are buying or selling sweaters are in the sweater market. Everyone buying CDs is in the CD market. Everyone selling hot dogs is in the hot dog market. These markets are very important as economists study supply and demand. Supply is the amount of an item for sale. Demand is a measure of how many consumers want to buy what is being sold. Using the hot dog example, the companies and stores selling hot dogs are supplying them. The consumers who are willing to pay for hot dogs are demanding them.

Demand is more than "wanting" or "wishing" for a hot dog. It is not demand until a person has the money to pay for the hot dog. When they can buy the hot dog, then they are in the hot dog market.

When there is a greater demand for a product than producers can supply, a shortage occurs. Shortages usually mean that prices go up as people battle to buy it. When there is a greater supply of something than a demand for it, it is called a surplus. A surplus usually means that prices go down. The producers lower the price to boost the sales.

Can you think of a recent example of a shortage or surplus?

title: Westborough, Massachusetts
text:
On Nov. 18, 1717, Westborough began as the 100th town in Massachusetts. At the time, it had 27 families living there. Now there are more than 18,000 people living there.

Westborough has many old American Indian trails. Experts say some may be 7,000 years old! In 1633, a man named John Oldham explored these trails. He paved the way for settlers searching for good farmland. These families settled near Lake Chauncey in the late 1600s. They built large farms, mills and taverns along the Assabet River.

A number of famous people had their start in Westborough. Eli Whitney, the inventor of the cotton gin, was born here in 1765. Olympians Nikki Stone, 1998 gold medal winner in aerial skiing and Ashley Hayden, 2002 eighth place in women's luge, are both from Westborough. Can you name any famous people from your hometown?

title: What colors are “Sadd?”
text:
When we think of Pilgrims, we probably imagine them dressed in black. Black was usually only worn by those of the ruling class. The colors worn by most people were called sadd colors.

In the 1600s, sadd did not mean "unhappy". It meant "reverent" or "serious". Some of the sadd colors were liver color, tawny and russet. Purple, deer color, French green and orange were others.

Can you find sadd colors in your crayon box?

title: Barred Owl
text:
You'll find the barred owl in many wild places in Massachusetts. There are many, many varieties of owls in the world. This one is known for its funny call. It sounds like it's saying, "Who, who, who cooks for you? Who, who, who cooks for you all?" (Kind of makes you hungry, huh?)

This bird is round headed, with large brown eyes. It has a yellow bill. The face and body are brown and white. It loves wet areas and deep woods. It likes to nest in hollow trees. This very gentle bird can often be seen and heard during the day. The barred owl can be found dining on rodents, small mammals, birds, frogs and insects at night.

Did you know that if you wanted to see as well as an owl sees, your eyes would have to be the size of softballs?

Would you like to hear a sound byte of this owl? Go online to the following site and hear for yourself! www.owlshill.org

title: Help a Rat and Learn to Run the Country This Year!
text:
Hey, kids! I’m Revere the Rat, but you can call me Rev. I’m your online Studies Weekly friend and I need your help. You can help me get great stuff by earning points while you learn. Just scan the code or go to www.studiesweekly.com and click on my picture.

Has your family ever bought something that came with an owner’s manual? Cars, TVs and other things have an owner’s manual, a book on how to use them. Your social studies class is the “owner’s manual” for the United States of America. You’ll learn about history, geography, government by the people, and much more, so you can do a good job of running our country someday.

In America rats can’t vote, so “you the people” govern (run) the country. Someday you will be in charge of this country, and you’ll choose leaders and representatives by voting. Then you can tell the representatives you help elect how you think the country should be run. In fact, Studies Weekly kids are so smart, that many of you will someday be mayors, senators, governors—maybe even the president!

For now you have two jobs: Learn about the country and how it works and earn points for me so I can get that great stuff I told you about. It’s easy. Just scan or click and you’re on your way!

title: The Flying Tennis Shoes
text:
After putting on your new tennis shoes for the first time, you make an amazing discovery. You are able to fly while wearing them!

1. What color are your tennis shoes?

2. What do you have to do to your tennis shoes in order to fly?

3. Name three places you would like to visit while wearing your wonderful tennis shoes.

4. What are some places you would like to visit if you could go back in time with your flying tennis shoes?

My Trip Back in Time

Use the sentences below to finish this story: With just a __________________ of my _______________ tennis shoes, I can fly anywhere I want. I found I can even fly back in time. My teacher assigned me to write about what Massachusetts was like in Plymouth Colony. I decided to go back in time and find out. You’ll never believe what I saw.

Finish your story on a larger sheet of paper.

title: The City on a Hill
text:
Eight Years after the Pilgrims came to Massachusetts, the first of the Puritans came. There are several differences between the Pilgrims and the Puritans. Yet both groups came from England seeking religious freedom.

The Pilgrims were Puritans too. But what made the Pilgrims of 1620 different was that they were Separatists. As you remember from last week, they rebelled against the Church of England and left it. The Puritans, on the other hand, did not desire to leave the Church of England. They felt it could be "purified" from within.

It was still hard to please the king. So the Puritans continued to suffer. King Charles disliked them. He took away their property and their jobs. In some cases he put them in prison. As things were getting worse, a large group of Puritans asked King Charles for permission to leave England. They wanted to begin a colony. They wanted to settle in the bay region of Massachusetts. Happily, King Charles sent them on their way!

Unlike the Pilgrims of Plymouth colony, these Puritans were wealthy. They were also well-educated. Since they were wealthy, they had plenty of supplies and food to take to the new colony. In 1628 John Endicott led the first group of about 50 Puritans. He led them to the Massachusetts Bay region. They settled quickly. They named the first town Salem. The Puritans still in England heard that the new colony was truly safe. They then prepared to follow. The largest group to make the journey was led by John Winthrop. He was a London lawyer. In 1630, Winthrop led nearly 1,000 Puritans to a new life in the Massachusetts Bay Colony. This group came on 11 ships carrying passengers and supplies. What do you think the Puritans packed on those ships? Supplies included oatmeal, butter, cheese and many other foods. Animals such as pigs, goats and chickens were on the ship. Crates of tools, guns, clothes and blankets were all shipped. They also brought many books along.

Another important difference between the Puritans and the Pilgrims was their tolerance. The Pilgrims believed that one should be allowed to live and worship as chosen. The Puritans believed God had chosen them to show the world how to live. It was on the voyage to Massachusetts Bay that Winthrop said "We must consider that we shall be a city on a hill, the eyes of all the world upon us." These strict beliefs allowed few differences. Winthrop was governor for 20 years. He ran the colony with very strict rules.

As Salem grew, the Puritans began to spread out. Groups of Puritans soon settled at Lynn and Dorchester. They also lived in Medford and Watertown. Winthrop led about 800 followers. They settled across the Charles River. This settlement was known as Boston.

The Massachusetts Bay Colony was a theocracy. The laws and government were determined by religion. Those who disagreed with leaders about religious ideas were considered lawbreakers and were banished and sometimes executed.

With time, the idea of a "city on a hill" broke down. It was hard to enforce all of the rules and laws. Many of younger people wanted land more than religion. As people became richer, leaders felt that the people forgot the old ideals. The dream of the perfect city slowly died.

Puritan leaders such as William Bradford, John Winthrop, Endicott and others built a better city than they knew. Many of the ideas on which the colonies were founded are still around today. For example, today we remain a generous nations with many different religious groups. Our forefathers believed in a strong education, as do we. Finally, like the Puritans, we believe in working hard. With hard work, they could build a wonderful life. We too believe that if we work hard, we can have a wonderful life.

All of these ideas together lead us to wonder if the "city on a hill" did not totally disappear. Maybe some parts lived on to shape the values of America today.

title: Massachusetts: First in Line
text:
The Puritans considered the study of the Bible by all people to be very important. Education was highly valued. Their love of learning led to many important "firsts" in this country.

In 1635, the Puritans started the Boston Latin School. It was the first public school in our country. This led to the establishment of the first college in 1638. Originally called Newtowne, it was later changed to Harvard. The first library was started at Harvard. Today this library is the oldest one in the United States.

The first English language book to be published in America, "The Bay Psalm Book," was published by Stephen Daye in 1640. This was done on the first printing press in the American colonies. Whew! A lot of important firsts were happening in Massachusetts!

Here are some other interesting Massachusetts firsts:

the first post office in the colonies

the first free public school

the first public park

the first American lighthouse

the first volleyball game

the first World Series in Boston in 1903

the first American subway system

the first English book published in America was the "Bay Psalm Book."

title: The Puritans
text:
During the 1640s, Puritans began sending out missionaries to preach Christianity to the local tribes.

Praying Towns

The Puritans firmly believed that everyone should have the same religious beliefs. This included the American Indians. The Puritans began sending missionaries to preach to the native tribes. The leading Puritan missionary among the American Indians was John Eliot. Eliot learned the language of the people. He labored among them for more than 20 years.

In 1646, Eliot first preached to these native peoples at a site he later referred to as Nonantum. This means "Place of Rejoicing." It is now known as Newton, Massachusetts.

In 1651, Eliot established the settlement of Natick. It was for the new converts. Much of the Natick land was donated. It was referred to by the new converts as a "Place of Hills."

Eliot went on to establish seven new towns. They were all in the Nipmuc area. Later, there would be 14 towns in all. The towns were referred to as Praying Towns. The people were known as Praying Indians. In the Praying Towns, the native converts were required to forsake their native language. They also had to change their ceremonies, beliefs, dress and customs. In other words, they had to become Puritans.

To assist in their religious education, Eliot worked out a written language for the Algonquian language. He did this with the help of some tribal members. He spent 12 years translating the Bible into that language. Eliot's Algonquian Bible was the first Bible printed in the American colonies.

Metacomet was a chieftain and a fighter. He was known as King Philip. He liked to strut through the streets of Boston in his best clothes. King Philip thought it his duty to do something about the settlers coming. He convinced other tribes to join him in a war. This war bears his name. Many people, including Metacomet himself, lost their lives in King Philip’s War.

Where did the Praying Towns go? At the start of King Philip's War, many of the colonists resented the natives. It did not matter if they were converts. Elders, women and children fled to safety in other areas. Many of the local people were moved to Deer Island. Large numbers of the people died of cold and starvation there.

In spite of the cruel treatment, many of the men from the Praying Towns remained loyal to the English during King Philip's War. Some even acted as spies.

After the war, the native converts returned to the towns. They found them destroyed. Many moved, and after Eliot's death, most of the praying towns were gone.

Puritans Intolerant of Other Religious Views!

Some of the colonists did not believe what the Puritans did. They were punished for this. Many of the colonists fled the Massachusetts Bay Colony. They wanted religious freedom. They ended up in areas in what are now Rhode Island, Connecticut and Maine. Some even went to the more tolerant Plymouth Colony.

Roger Williams

There was a young man with very bold ideas Williams was a clergyman living in Salem. He did not agree with the Puritans' ideas. Williams preached that everyone should have the right to have their own religious ideas. He also claimed that the American Indians were the true owners of the land. In 1635, Williams was ordered to leave Massachusetts Bay colony. Leaders said he was spreading "new and dangerous opinions." Williams and his wife escaped to the woods. During the winter, they lived with a local tribe.

In 1636, Roger Williams bought some land from the Narragansett tribe. Williams began a settlement by the name of Providence. It was located in the Rhode Island area. It was the first American town to promise religious freedom.

Anne Hutchinson

Anne was also banished for her religious views. Hutchinson held meetings in her home. She questioned some of the Puritan teachings.

Like Williams, Hutchinson and her family were banished. They also went to what is now Rhode Island where they founded Portsmouth.

Mary Dyer

Mary Dyer was a follower of Anne Hutchinson. After some time in Portsmouth, Dyer returned to England. She went there on a political mission. She became a member of the Society of Friends, or Quakers.

When she returned to New England, Mary was marched off to jail with others. Mary's husband, William, asked for her freedom. Endicott allowed her freedom if she would be silent.

Mary, however, was anything but silent. She returned to Boston to preach. Mary was arrested along with two men. The men were hanged. Just minutes before the rope was put around her neck, Mary was pardoned. She was warned never to return.

Mary felt strongly about religious freedom. She returned to protest the deaths of Quakers. Mary was arrested again. This time she was hanged.

Boston was in shock at the execution of a woman. The execution of Quakers was stopped. However, they still suffered persecution.

title: Scarcity
text:
You just earned some money to go to a movie. There are many movies you want to see, but you only have enough money to see one. It's a hard choice. What do you do?

A society faces the same kind of challenge deciding how to use their resources. Our resources are scarce. That means there is a higher demand for them than a supply. Sometimes, time can be scarce. That's when people don't have enough time to do everything. Sometimes, money is scarce. That's when you want more candy than you can afford, or have the money to buy.

Because our resources are so scarce, people are always making choices about how to use them. Every time you make a choice about what to buy or how to spend your time, you are making a trade-off. Let's say that you decide to spend money on candy. Then you are making a trade-off of candy for money. You have less money, but more candy.

Economists also have a name for what you give up when you choose something else. An opportunity cost is what you do not get when you make a choice. There are opportunity costs in everything. When you woke up this morning, you may have decided to sleep in. If you did, what did you give up in doing so? Was it taking a shower or eating every bite of your breakfast? You could say that the opportunity cost of sleeping in was taking a shower or eating a nice breakfast. We have opportunity costs when we buy things, too. Let's say that you couldn't decide between buying a new DVD or a new book. You finally decide to buy the DVD. The opportunity cost of that DVD was the new book. What is the opportunity cost of going to school every day? Is it worth it?

title: Townsend, Massachusetts
text:
Townsend is a city in Middlesex County in north central Massachusetts. This town has all four seasons every year. This gives visitors and residents a chance to enjoy year-round activities. Many people enjoy biking, hiking and sailing. Others enjoy skiing, sledding and swimming.

Townsend began in 1732 and was named after Viscount Charles Townshend. He was a British cabinet minister. Around 1780 the town clerks started spelling Townsend without the "h." They still spell it that way today.

A fun place to visit is Townsend Harbor. This is where one of the first mills was built in 1733. For fishermen, the Squannacook River offers freshwater fishing year-round. Many folks visit Joslinville Tavern. Here, passengers on the first New Hampshire stagecoach stopped to eat on their journey.

title: What is a blue moon?
text:
For the American Indians, time was measured by things in nature. The position of the sun and stars and the phases of the moon all helped them tell time.

The saying "blue moon" means a second full moon in one month. If there is a full moon on the first or second day of the month, there will be a second one later that month. This is called a blue moon.

This generally only happens about once every 2 1/2 years. The last blue moon was in August 2012. The next blue moon will be in July 2015. The term "blue moon" means "once in a LONG while."

Say, are you ever late for school? You might reply, "Once in a blue moon!"

title: American Black Bear
text:
Did you know the American Black Bear isn't always black? It can be light brown, beige, dark brown, cinnamon and even a blueish-gray color!

The black bear is a large mammal with a heavy body, short tail and rounded ears. It has four curved toes on each front foot, and five on each back foot. Its curved claws help it to climb trees. Bears can live to be 25 years old. They live under trees and bushes and can often be seen walking in streams and creek beds. Though they can weigh between 125 and 600 pounds, they can run very fast, up to 35 miles an hour!

Black bears have one to four cubs, with an average of two. The cubs are very tiny when born, have no hair and are blind.

title: Ethics: William Penn and the Pennsylvania Quakers
text:
William Penn spent less than five years in America, but he had a big impact on American history. His ethics (standards, values and principles) - especially his beliefs about freedom - had lasting effects on American democracy.

Penn was born in London in 1644. He was well educated and became interested in a religious group called the Society of Friends, or Quakers. They believed in equal rights for all and would not bow, remove their hats or take an oath to royalty.

Although Penn was raised in the Church of England, he agreed with the Quaker beliefs. He insisted on going to jail with his Quaker friends saying, "My prison shall be my grave before I will budge a jot; for I owe my conscience to no mortal man."

Some Quakers moved to America, but the Puritans in Massachusetts did not want them in their colony. King Charles II gave William Penn a land grant for territory in America to repay a debt owed to Penn's father. The colony was named Pennsylvania (Penn's Woods) in honor of William's father. Penn designed a city there named Philadelphia, meaning "city of brotherly love."

Penn wrote a constitution called "The Frame of Government." It guaranteed freedom of religion, trial by jury, fair taxes and many other liberties we take for granted today. Penn also established peaceful relations with the American Indians, buying land from them and writing successful peace treaties.

William Penn spent a lot of time in England, and he died there in 1718. He only lived in his colony for four years, but his ethics influenced Americans for generations to come. How might your life have been different without William Penn's constitution and the liberties he stood for?

title: Let's Write
text: This week’s issue deals with people who fought for their religious freedom. Do you know of people in your family, church or community who had to fight for religious freedom? Did they have to move to another place for what they believed? Write your story on a separate piece of paper.

title: Fur Trade for Profit
text:
While the early explorers did not find the Northwest Passage, they did find lands rich in fur-bearing animals. They were excited to find beaver, mink and otter. In Europe, it was stylish to wear furs and beaver felt hats. Europe's beaver and other fur-bearing animals were now scarce (in short supply), and explorers quickly found that money could be made from the fur trade in North America. The fur trade, more than anything else, led to the exploration of the wilderness north of Mexico. Because of the fur trade, the native people became involved in a global market for the first time. A global market means that products are bought and sold with other countries throughout the world. Other countries involved with the fur trade were the French, Dutch, English, Russian and Spanish.

Early in the 1600s, the French traders set up trading posts on the St. Lawrence River. Around that same time, the Dutch began trading on the Hudson River, building posts in what is now Manhattan and Albany. Soon they were joined by a third group. This London group traded on the Hudson Bay. Can you find these locations on a map of North America?

Although the governments of those countries wanted people to colonize, it did not happen quickly. Many of those who went to colonize were drawn to the fur trade because of the money they could make.

So, how did the Pilgrims get mixed up in the booming fur trade? After Captain Smith traveled the coast of New England and traded trinkets for a wealth of furs to take back to England, he told English leaders to send more colonists to the New World. Many countries wanted to harvest the fur, fish and wood along the coast. The need for settlers opened the way for the Pilgrims to go to the New World. Their wish to travel to this country to start a new colony did not include the desire to trade for fur. But they had no money to make the voyage, so they became part of a business deal.

Thomas Weston, an English merchant, organized a group of other merchants to pay for this voyage. They put up the money to pay for a ship stocked with food and other supplies. Among those supplies were cloth, beads, knives and other items meant for trade with the American Indians. In exchange for the ship and supplies, the Pilgrims agreed to work hard and send back ships filled with goods, including the prized beaver pelts. The English merchants promised the colonists they would send them food, clothing and more items for trade.

After the first rough winter in the new land, the Pilgrims badly needed food and supplies for themselves and for trading. They waited, but the supplies never came. Finally, in 1621, a small group of the colonists, along with Squanto, went north in a small ship. This trip was a lucky voyage for them. They returned to Plymouth with many beaver pelts to send back to England. In November they loaded two hogsheads, or barrels, of pelts onto the Fortune. The ship was also loaded with lumber and sent on its way. They hoped the goods would pay off some of their debt and earn some much needed supplies.

The Fortune was attacked by a French pirate ship at sea. It never returned to England. The Pilgrims were devastated! It would be another year before they could get enough pelts to send a second shipment. They had a hard year of trapping and trading. The second shipment arrived successfully, and after that, shipments of furs to England were regularly sent.

title: Furry Friends May Land Behind Bars
text:
Though beavers almost faced extinction 200 years ago, they are now thriving in many states. But, in some cases their nibbling habits are a worry for their human neighbors.

Not long ago, some of our furry friends became the center of attention in our nation's capital when they began chewing on the wrong trees! Beavers were gnawing on the famous cherry trees of Washington, D.C. The 3,000 or so trees were a gift from Japan to the United States in 1912. They are now the focus of the famous Cherry Blossom Festival each year.

When park workers noticed 30 or 40 trees with teeth marks, they began to suspect our beaver friends. It is hard to catch sight of the little guys, so workers began to set traps for them. Finally, several of the beaver ended up behind bars and were sent to a place where the trees weren't so famous!

Have you seen beaver or signs of them in your community?

title: The Fur Trade Expands
text:
Although governments wanted to encourage colonization, it did not happen quickly. Many of those who went to colonize were drawn to the fur trade because of the money they could make.

The Undertakers

By 1627, the colonists at Plymouth were tired of being in debt to the English merchants. So, a few of the Pilgrim leaders formed their own trading company. Among the group were William Brewster, Isaac Allerton, Myles Standish, Edward Winslow and John Alden. These men made sure they were the only ones in Plymouth Colony who could deal in the fur trade for six years. Because of the deal, they undertook (or tried) to pay off the colony's debt to the English merchants. That's why they were called the Undertakers.

The Undertakers were clever and bold. They pushed their fur trade into the northern wilderness of what is now Maine. They set up a booming trade with the Abanaki tribe and had storehouses and posts in the Connecticut River Valley.

The Undertakers made huge profits. Before long, they paid off their debt to the English merchants. They could then bring over more of their congregation, as well as food and supplies for the colony.

During this six-year period, the Undertakers bought more property for themselves. They became rich men.

Making Felt Hats

When the hatters used heat and steam to produce the hats, they made a dangerous mercury vapor. If a hatter was exposed to this for a long time, he experienced problems with his nervous system. His muscles would twitch and it would soon become hard to walk, think and even swallow. Many hatters eventually died of this mercury poisoning.

The Beaver Boom

Never in the history of North America has one small animal had such an impact. Symbols and paintings of the beaver can still be found today.

Because of European fashions, beaver fur became very popular. Rivers and lakes are plentiful in the Northeast, and there were many beaver to be found nearby.

Take a look at these interesting beaver facts:

The Hudson Bay Company, a powerful trading company, put a picture of the buck-toothed rodent on its coat of arms.

The Dutch West India Company also picked the beaver as a symbol for its official seal.

In 1678, the governor of New France suggested that the beaver be included on its coat of arms.

In 1690, to celebrate France's defense of Quebec, a medal was made. It showed a woman, representing France, with a beaver at her feet. The beaver represented Canada.

In 1851, the beaver again became a national symbol when it appeared on the first postage stamp in Canada. It was called the "Three Penny Beaver."

Despite all of the recognition and honor, the beaver was close to extinction by the mid-1800s. It is estimated that there were more than 6 million beavers in North America before the fur trade began. During the peak of the fur trade, the beaver was close to being wiped out. Luckily, by the 1850s, silk hats had replaced felt ones in European fashion, and the need for beaver pelts went away. Today, thanks in part to conservation and silk hats, the beaver is alive and well throughout the country.

title: Bartering
text:
"I'll give you three tennis balls for that frisbee!"

Bartering is trading goods, but without the use of money. People of long ago were able to get many things they needed and wanted. They bartered with people near and far. Merchants would often travel with ships laden with goods. These goods were bartered for items that could be taken back. Then they would be either bartered for other goods or traded for money. People, towns and even countries bartered for items they did not produce or grow.

Bartering was easy as long as there was a simple trade between two people. However, sometimes bartering had to span several persons to get the goods wanted. Then it wasn't so easy. Suppose one merchant had a barrel of apples. He wanted to trade with another merchant for some cloth. However, the merchant who had the cloth did not want or need a barrel of apples. What do you think a good solution might have been? The people would barter for something they didn't need. They hoped they could later trade it for something they did need!

Bartering is still going on today. People, companies and even countries barter for things they need or want. Even children barter! When was the last time you tried talking someone out of a big chocolate chip cookie in exchange for your apple?

title: Gloucester, Massachusetts
text:
Folks love to visit the Hammond Castle in Gloucester. The castle was built by John Hays Hammond Jr. in 1926. He built it like the medieval castles he saw while visiting Europe. The Hammond Castle gives tours to many people every year. Visitors can go through the indoor courtyard, dining room, bedrooms, gardens and towers. A bonus is the great view of the Atlantic.

Gloucester Harbor is also a favorite place to stop. Artists travel many miles just to paint this beautiful harbor. The Gloucester Harbor is one of the top fishing ports in the entire Northeast!

Gloucester has a history full of famous artists. The famous painters Winslow Homer, Edward Hopper and Fitzhugh Lane all said Gloucester had a pure light which made everything they painted even more beautiful. Maybe you could try painting the harbor or the shore on your next visit!

title: Who invented the graham cracker?
text:
Did you ever wonder, while dipping this crunchy creation into milk, who invented this treat? Why, Dr. Sylvester Graham, of course!

Graham who lived near Mill River, had some unpopular ideas for his time. He told people to eat less meat, more whole-wheat products, more fruits and vegetables and to exercise every day. Many people thought his ideas were foolish. So, the dedicated Dr. Graham made delicious crackers to tempt the public to have healthier habits.

But, what about s'mores and cheesecake with graham cracker crusts? Do you wonder what Dr. Graham would think if he knew what his cracker has been used for?

title: Mink
text:
Do you think of fur coats when you hear "mink"? Though some mink are still being trapped, ranch-raised mink supply most of the pelts today. Mink are members of the weasel family. They are fierce fighters and will scream, spit and hiss. Like other members of the weasel family (such as skunks), they give off a strong odor when threatened. Mink never live far from water and they are excellent swimmers. They eat fish, rodents and snakes.

Mink will grow to be 11 to 20 inches long. Sometimes they are dark reddish-brown and have a pale spot under their chins and white spots on their bellies. Their young are born in the spring and are called kits.

title: A Suffix Celebration
text:
A suffix is a group of letters added to the end of a word that changes its meaning.

You are nearly done with Word Attack strategies. What better way to “end” it than to celebrate with suffixes?

Below, you will find a short list of common suffixes and their meanings. When you think you have them down, head to the activity below and strut your stuff!

1. ly (forms adverb)

2. er, or (one who, person)

3. ion, tion, ation, ition (state or quality of)

4. ible, able (is able)

5. ness (state or quality of)

6. ity, y (state or quality of)

7. ment (forms a noun from a verb)

8. ic (relating to, forms and adjective)

9. ful (full of)

10. less (without)

11. est (most)

12. ive, ative, itive (inclined to, forms an adjective)

A Suffix Celebration Exercise

Using the suffixes above, create as many words as possible from these base words: history, father, enjoy, desperate, smart, teach, window, talk, wonder, loyal, happy, comfort.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: After you read this week’s lesson, write three questions about the article on a piece of paper and trade questions with a friend. Circle or highlight the answers in the lesson.

title: Beaver Fur Hats
text:
From 1550 until 1850, felt hats were very fashionable in much of Europe. Beaver fur was thought to be better than wool or other furs for making felt. By the late 1500s, the beaver was extinct in Western Europe. The North American fur trade became a new source of fur, keeping the fashion alive for another 200 years.

How were beaver pelts made into fine hats for gentlemen? The people who produced hats were called hatters. It was a hard job!

First, the hatters would lay the pelt on their knee, and using their thumb and a knife, they would pull out all the long hairs until only the beaver wool remained.

The hats were not made from the pelts, but from felt made from the beaver wool. Felt is fur or wool pressed together in layers again and again. It isn’t woven like cloth.

In order to make the wool better, it was brushed with nitrate of mercury to make it rougher. After it dried, it was shaved off the pelt. After many steps, the fibers were cleaned and pressed together until a sheet of felt was made. It was then cut and shaped into a hat using steam and heat. Next it was dyed and waterproofed. Finally, a ribbon was added, and a lining was sewn into the hat.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend you are a fur trader. What items would you trade your furs for? Write a paragraph describing what items you would need to survive and how many beaver pelts each item would cost.

title: Massachusetts Colonies Become One!
text:
King Philip's War was mostly over in 1676. About 1,000 colonists had died in the war. Several thousand American Indians were killed. Some who were not killed escaped. They went to live with other tribes in New York and Canada. Still, others were captured and sold as slaves in the West Indies. Metacomet's wife and children were among those sold into slavery.

The colonists were happy to have the American Indians gone. They felt it gave them more land to own. Many people came to the colonies because they wanted land of their own. Plymouth Colony was growing quickly. Massachusetts Bay Colony had nearly 10 times as many people as Plymouth.

By now, many people had lived in the Colonies their whole life. They did not think of themselves as part of distant England. English rulers did not live in the colonies. The colonists did not like laws made by people who lived far away. There were many problems between the Colonies and England. One of the biggest problems was about trade.

The English Take Control of Trade with the Colonies

The English crown did not wish the Colonies to trade with anyone other than England. The colonists, on the other hand, wanted to trade with other countries. Those countries were willing to pay higher prices for the goods. What sort of goods do you think the Colonies produced for trade? Some of the early products from the Massachusetts Colonies were dried codfish and other seafood. There were farm crops, furs and cloth. There was also lumber, shoes and whale products. They produced iron ore and candles. As trade grew, the colonists began building their own ships. The ship owners carried the goods across the ocean. They made a fortune. A so-called Triangular Trade began. African slaves tended large sugar plantations in the West Indies. Molasses was made from that sugar. The molasses was then sent to Boston where it was used to make rum. The rum was sold to England. The profits were used to buy more slaves in Africa. The slaves would then be taken to the sugar plantations in the West Indies. Look at a map or globe. Trace the triangle shape of the trade route with your finger.

title: Shiver Me Timbers!
text:
"The Whydah is out there and I'm going to find it."

That's what Barry Clifford said as a young man while on the beach at Wellfleet. Decades later, Clifford's dream came true. After a very long search, the fabled pirate ship was finally found.

Samuel "Black Sam" Bellamy was the captain of the Whydah, a pirate ship. Bellamy attacked ships off the New England coast. When the ship sank in 1717, Bellamy drowned. Those who were rescued were hanged. Boston leaders didn't take kindly to pirates.

In 1984, Clifford began recovering the Whydah. At first a cannon and coin were found. However, these items weren't enough to prove that the sunken ship was the Whydah. A short time later, something exciting happened. The ship's bell was recovered. Inscribed on the bell were the words "The Whydah Galley 1716." This made the Whydah the first known pirate shipwreck to be recovered. Clifford has since been involved in other great discoveries. He continues on missions to find more pirate shipwrecks. Today you can visit the Whydah Museum at the end of MacMillan Wharf in Provincetown.

title: Massachusetts Colonies
text:
Trouble in the Colonies

The English were angry that the colonists were selling goods to other countries. They passed a series of Navigation Acts. These trade laws made it hard for the colonists to trade with any country except England. The colonists were not about to give up their huge profits. They instead turned to smuggling. Smuggling is sneaking something in or out of a country illegally. Boston became a haven for smugglers.

Early in the 1680s, King Charles II threatened the colonists. He told them to obey the Navigation Acts or he would take away their prized Charter. The colonists ignored the threat and continued the practice of smuggling goods. So, in 1684, Charles II nullified the Charter. This meant Massachusetts could no longer govern itself.

Two Colonies Become One

In 1686, England's next king, James II, combined the two Colonies to become one. Then, he added the Colonies of New Hampshire and Rhode Island. He also added Connecticut, New Jersey and New York. The huge new region was called the Dominion of New England. Edmund Andros was sent by King James as Royal Governor of the newly formed Dominion of New England.

Andros was not well-liked. As luck would have it, King James II was overthrown in England. The colonists wasted no time in sending Andros back to England. New Englanders used this chance to once again set up their own government.

However, the new rulers of England, William III and Mary II, would not let Massachusetts go back to its old way of ruling itself. In 1691 they again made Massachusetts a royal colony. At this time Massachusetts Bay Colony was combined with the Plymouth Colony to form the Massachusetts Colony, which had Boston as its capital.

Biography: Edmund Andros (1637-1714)

Edmund Andros worked as a page in the royal household. He was faithful to the crown. As a reward, he was made the governor of New York and New Jersey Colonies. Although Andros was skilled, he was not well-liked by the colonists. Some accused him of being crooked. He was recalled to England in 1681.

Andros returned to America in 1686 when King James II made him Royal Governor. He was in charge of the Dominion of New England. He tried hard to enforce the Navigation Acts. This made the colonists angry. The colonists were really angered when he allowed Anglican meetings to be held in their new land. The meetings were held in the South Meeting House in Boston.

When King James II was overthrown in England, the colonists wasted no time. They sent Andros back to England. In England, he was tried and released. Andros later served as governor or lieutenant governor of Virginia, Maryland and Guernsey.

title: Money
text:
When the English colonists first came to America, they brought some of the money they used back in England. They called their money shillings, pence and pounds. They soon found out it was of no use to them in the New World. The American Indians didn't care for their money. It didn't mean anything to them. The American Indians bartered with the colonists. As you can imagine, that became very hard. Therefore, the early colonists of Massachusetts started using wampum. Wampum consisted of purple and white shells. The purple ones were worth twice as much as the white ones. They used it the same way as money. American Indians had traded wampum since the 1640s. The colonists and American Indians used wampum in addition to bartering. This made for less trouble in the colonies.

Economists like to say, "Money is what money does." This was as true for the American Indians and English colonists as it is for us today. Money has three main functions. First, it must be a way of exchange that people accept. This means that people have to agree on what they will use for money. Second, money must be a measure of value. This means that the people using the money must know how much the money is worth in their community. Last, money must be a store of value.

People should be able to save their money and use it later. Storing value is very hard when bartering. Often the goods or products people are trying to trade go bad before they can find someone in the market for them. For example, milk is hard to keep in hot weather. Bartering milk without a way to keep it cold for a long time would be very tricky.

Money must also be easy to carry. It must be sturdy, easy to recognize and able to be broken down into smaller parts. Our U.S. money is small. It's easy to carry and uniform, or all the same. People in the country accept it all over. You can divide it easily. This is nice for everyone because it is so easy. What if you lived in a country that used bowling balls for money? That wouldn't work very well at all!

title: Cotuit, Massachusetts
text:
Cotuit is found in Barnstable County. It is one of 15 towns in the Cape Cod area. Cotuit hosts many visitors every year. People travel to Cape Cod each summer to see the beaches and play in the water.

One of the most famous Cotuit attractions is the Cahoon Museum of American Art. The museum is located in the old home of Ralph and Martha Cahoon. During the 37 years they lived there, they painted countless pictures. Ralph created pictures of sailors, mermaids, ships, lighthouses and hot-air balloons. Martha liked painting children, animals and the outdoors.

You can see their paintings and many others in Cotuit.

title: Were there ever any female pirates?
text: Plundering doesn't sound like a lady's work, but history tells of at least two lassies that sailed the open seas and pillaged with the worst of them. They were Mary Read and Anne Bonny. The two were shipmates and spent much of their time dressed like men. Both were found guilty of robbery but were not killed. No one knows for sure what happened to them after that. Some people say they died in prison. Others think they escaped and lived the rest of their lives in Louisiana with their babies. Can you imagine the bedtime stories in that house?

title: Jack-in-the-Pulpit
text:
Jack-in-the-Pulpit is a odd name for an odd little wildflower. It is found in the shady woodlands of the east.

Look at the picture to see the preacher in the pulpit in this flower. The "pulpit," or spathe, is green or purple, and the "jack," or spadix, is yellowish-green.

The plant blooms in April and May. It grows to be about 8 inches to 3 feet tall. Later in the season, the tiny flowers found inside the pulpit will turn into a cluster of bright red berries. The berries, along with all other parts of the plant, can sting when touched. If it gets on the lips or tongue it may cause swelling - so don't eat those berries!

American Indians were known to use the dried and prepared root which resembles a turnip. Another common name for this flower is "Indian turnip."

title: Navigation Acts
text:
The Navigation Acts were a series of tax laws. They made it difficult for the colonists to trade legally with any non-English country. One of the laws stated that all goods for overseas trade had to be carried on ships owned by the British. Another said that threequarters of a ships' crew had to be British. The British wanted the colonists to buy goods only from them. However, the colonists wanted to buy goods from countries that gave them the best deals.

Smuggling

Many colonists ignored the Navigation Acts. They smuggled goods to and from non-English countries. They unloaded the smuggled goods in the middle of the night or in secret places. Few people felt it was wrong to buy or sell smuggled good. They felt the Navigation Acts were wrong.

Privateering and Piracy

Piracy was another way that colonists obtained goods cheaply. Pirates and privateers robbed ships belonging to enemy nations. They brought the goods to colonial ports where they were sold to wealthy merchants. The merchants in turn sold the goods at low prices to the townspeople. Except for the shipowners who had been robbed, just about everyone gained. The pirate captains made a fortune from the merchants who bought the stolen goods. During the late 1600s pirates were a common sight on New York City's streets. In Massachusetts, however, pirates were not so welcome and were hanged if caught.

title: What are Homophones and Homographs?
text:
Homophones and homographs are the same but different! To find out the meaning of a word, carefully read the words and sentences surrounding it.

Homophones

Homophones are words that sound the same but have different spellings and different meanings. You can remember what a homophone is by remembering that a phone makes a sound, so a homophone sounds the same as another word.

It is important to know a homophone when you write it. If you need help with a homophone when you read or write, look it up in a dictionary. This will help you keep from making mistakes. For instance, would you write you have “bear hands” or “bare hands”?

Here are some common homophones:

Beat, beet

Earn, urn

Eye, I

Heal, heel, he’ll

Made, maid

Plain, plane

Rain, reign, rein

To, too, two

Homographs

These are words that are spelled the same but have different meanings. Sometimes they are pronounced differently even though they are spelled the same. You can remember what a homograph is by remembering that a graph is something you look at, so a homograph looks the same.

Here are some common homographs that are pronounced differently and have different meanings:

Bass: a low voice Bass: a fish

Content: things found inside Content: satisfied

Minute: 60 seconds Minute: tiny

Try It!

The next time you are not sure which homophone or homograph to use, be sure you know the meaning of the word you are trying to use. This will help you spell it correctly. A dictionary will help you a lot!

title: Let's Write
text: While visiting the old Massachusetts Colony of long ago, I heard a strange laughing sound coming from behind a barrel. When I went to look, I saw the strangest creature sitting on the dock. How big was it?What color was it? How many legs did it have? Any wings? Describe its body and face. What was it covered with (fur, fins, feathers, pizza sauce)? What was it doing? Where did it come from? How many were there? Why was it laughing?

title: Seals
text:
In 1629, King Charles I granted a charter to the Massachusetts Bay Colony. The charter included the use of a seal. Seals of long ago were made by an impression in a soft blob of wax. The purpose of the seal was to show the document with the seal was authentic.

From 1686 to 1689, Governor Edmund Andros used a seal with two sides, one showing King James II, and the other showing a lion and a unicorn of the royal coat of arms.

title: Slavery Comes to Massachusetts!
text:
Slavery is owning another human being as property. The first African slaves in Massachusetts were not the first slaves in North America. Some historians believe that at least one black slave came with Christopher Columbus on his voyage in 1492. The first Africans arrived in Virginia Colony in 1619.

Were there African slaves on the Mayflower? No, there were not. There were no Africans living in early Plymouth Colony. The first mention of a black person living in Plymouth was in a list of men. These men were granted the right to bear arms for the town of Plymouth. On the list was the word "blackamoor." That was the colonial term used for Africans.

Though there are not records of slaves in early Plymouth, we do know the ship Desire, arrived in Boston with slaves. The Desire was built in 1636 in Marblehead. In 1638 it sailed from Salem Harbor to the West Indies and returned to Boston with African slaves.

For the most part the two Massachusetts colonies had no slaves - but had servants. Servants were given their freedom after 25 years of age. Some worked as house servants, while others worked on fishing vessels or at the docks. Still others served as apprentices. An apprentice is a kind of student of a trade. The apprentice works for a skilled worker to learn that trade or skill.

In 1641 Massachusetts became the first colony to make slavery legal. By 1660 slavery had spread to all the colonies. After 1660 colonies began to write harsh laws, or slave codes, about slavery. These codes made one big change: Black slaves now served for life. Children of slave women served for life. With these codes, slaves could not carry weapons. They were not educated. Slaves could not meet in groups of more than three. Slaves were not allowed to testify in court.

By the 1680s, slavery was practiced in all of the colonies.

CONTINUED IN THIS WEEKS LESSON

title: Amistad Replica Tours Former Slave Ports
text:
In 1839, 53 Africans were illegally kidnapped from West Africa. They were from the region now known as Sierra Leon. They were all sold into slavery. They were then taken to Cuba. There, they were "classified" as native Cuban-born slaves. The slaves were then transferred to the schooner l'Amistad for transport. They went to another part of the island, where they would be illegally purchased. As they went to the new place, a 25-year-old rice farmer led the other kidnapped people in a revolt. His name was Sengbe Pieh or "Cinque" to his captors. They then tried to return to their homeland. Instead, crew members took them to Connecticut. This was where the Untied States Naval Revenue Cutter USS Washington towed them to New London. The Africans were then jailed and charged with murder. Former President John Quincy Adams argued their case before the U.S. Supreme Court. He won the case. Two years after they were abducted, the surviving 35 prisoners were returned to their homeland.

The Amistad story is an amazing story of the struggle for human rights, a struggle that continues to the present in many places throughout the world. In March 2000, a replica of the Amistad was launched in Connecticut. The mission of this schooner is to tell the story of the Amistad. It is also to educate people about human rights. The new Amistad was christened with water from Cuba, Long Island and Sierra Leone. These were the places where the slaves were taken. After it was christened, a silver bell tolled for each of the ship's 53 captives.

The name "Amistad" translates to friendship. This is just what the crew and staff hope it will achieve. In an effort to educate others, the Amistad visits ports nationally and internationally. It acts as an ambassador for friendship. It has become a floating classroom and monument to the many souls that were broken or lost as a result of the transatlantic slave trade.

title: Slavery Comes to Massachusetts
text:
The first slaves were brought in to help with farming, building and in the fur trade of the Dutch West India Company.

A French refugee in Massachusetts said of slaves, "there is not a house in Boston however small, that does not have one or two. There are those that have five or six."

By the early 1700s, Boston was the busiest harbor in the colonies. Shipowners made fortunes in what is known as the Triangular Trade. Large sugar plantations in the West Indies were worked by African slaves. Massachusetts ships sailed to the islands to pick up molasses made from the sugar. The ship would then return to Boston with the molasses. In Boston, it was used to make rum. The ship would then sail to the west coast of Africa. Here rum was traded for more slaves. The slaves were then taken to the West Indies and traded for more molasses. Everyone made money at each leg of the triangle. This caused people to continue the trade.

Not all slaves went to the West Indies. Many were shipped to the colonies. Here they were auctioned, or sold, at slave markets.

A slave market involved selling slaves. Notices were posted before slave ships landed. They announced the upcoming slave auction. Here African men and women were lined up. Buyers inspected their teeth and gums. Buyers felt their muscles and looked for skin diseases. The slaves had no control over what would happen. Slaves might be sold to a master who was kind. They might be sold to a cruel master who would work them hard, sometimes to death. By then, slaves were no longer treated as servants or laborers, but as chattel. Chattel is property that can be bought or sold with little feeling. It was not important to buyers to keep families together. Husbands and wives were separated. Children never saw their mothers again.

Though Massachusetts was the first colony to legalize slavery, in 1790 it was also the first to end it.

Sold Into Slavery!

Slave labor in Massachusetts grew quickly. How did the slave traders get the slaves to come to the colonies? One way was to wait near a river and kidnap small groups. The groups were then taken to a slave ship. But, it was more common for one village to wage war on another, taking prisoners. The prisoners were then enslaved by their enemies. They were later sold to slave ships for goods.

The more ships that arrived with goods to trade, the more the African way of life changed. This slave trade degraded human life as never before.

America was not the only country to use slaves for labor. Indeed, it was a global trade. The Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch, English and French were all involved in the slave trade. It is believed that during the 350 years of this slave trade, more than 10 million Africans were taken into slavery.

A Cruel Atlantic Journey

The passage for enslaved Africans to the colonies was cruel and hard. Slave traders tried to get as many slaves as possible on a ship. Slaves were often chained together at the ankles and feet. Sometimes they had as little as 3 feet of space in which to move. They were forced to sleep on bare floors. There were no bathrooms, so there was filth and disease. The air was horrible. Some sailors at sea said they could smell a slave ship long before they could see one. About one in every 10 died during the passage. A slave may have awakened to find himself chained to a corpse. Sometimes when food ran low on a voyage traders were known to throw some slaves overboard. Many also died of disease before making it to America. It is impossible to imagine what it would have been like on a slave ship for the two months it took to cross the Atlantic Ocean.

title: Entrepreneurship
text:
Benjamin Franklin was one of the greatest entrepreneurs in history. An entrepreneur takes risks to create something or find a better way to do something. Ben Franklin was imaginative, creative and very smart. He was able to try many things. He was respected for the things he did. When he died in 1790, Franklin was known around the world as a businessman, politician, printer and inventor.

Franklin was born in 1706. Even as a little boy, he loved to read, write and collect books. He left school at the age of 10. By the time he was 12, he was helping as a printer for his older brother, James. When Franklin was 22, he owned his own printing press and started his own newspaper, the Pennsylvania Gazette. He also printed Poor Richard's Almanack. That book became one of the most popular books in the colonies!

Franklin soon became one of the colonies' busiest printers. He was named the official printer for Delaware, New Jersey and Maryland. He printed money and legal documents. Franklin made so much money that he retired when he was 42. He then became a full-time inventor. Franklin invented many things, including the lightning rod!

Franklin was very important in the colonies. He started one of the first libraries in the United States with some of his friends. He signed the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. Franklin served as an ambassador from the colonies to France. He was the oldest member of the Constitutional Convention!

Ben Franklin did many things to be considered an entrepreneur. Like Franklin, there are many entrepreneurs today. Do the names Bill Gates, George Lucas, Henry Ford and Oprah Winfrey mean anything to you? All of these people are entrepreneurs. They brought great ideas and business to our economy. Can you think of any entrepreneurs where you live?

title: Danvers, Massachusetts
text:
Danvers was once known as Salem Village. Salem Village was the place of many of the witch trials of 1692. It did not become a township until 1757.

If you ever go to Danvers, make sure you check out the old Israel Putnam House. In 1692, Joseph Putnam lived in this house. He worked the 100-acre farm around it. He spoke against the witch trials happening in what was then Salem Village.

In the 1850's, Daniel Putnam owned the house and had a cobbler shop. The most famous Putnam to have lived there was Israel Putnam. He commanded troops in the Battle of Bunker Hill. It was a fight of the Revolutionary War.

Today, this house is the location of the Danvers Museum. If you take a tour, you can learn all about the Salem Witch Trial. You will also learn about the Putnam family and the local history of Danvers!

title: Who was Henry “Box” Brown?
text: Henry "Box" Brown was a very determined and clever enslaved man. In 1849, he ordered a 3 foot x 2 foot x 8 foot box in Virginia. He put a jug of water and some biscuits inside. He also put in a bar to open the box. He then climbed in. A friend addressed the box to an abolitionist, someone who believed in freeing enslaved people. He lived in Philadelphia. After writing "Handle with Care" and "This Side Up", the friend shipped him off. Twenty-seven hours later, he arrived in Philadelphia, a free man!

title: Beaver
text:
Did you know the beaver is the largest rodent in North America? It is 3 to 4 feet in length and weighs 40 to 95 pounds. It has a large flat tail about 16 inches long. It uses its tail in the water as a rudder to steer. On the land, the beaver slaps its tail on the ground as a warning of danger.

Beavers are excellent swimmers. They have webbed feet to help them swim better. They have two layers of fur. Beavers have a special oil to help them dry faster when they come out of the water.

A baby beaver is called a kit. Beavers usually have four kits. A beaver's family is called a colony. Beavers live in lodges or burrows. They build a lodge out of branches and mud. They start at the bottom of a low creek and pile sticks upward. The whole colony works on a lodge.

A beaver has large, sharp teeth. The front teeth are always growing. By eating their favorite food - tree bark - and gnawing on trees as they build their lodges, their teeth are ground and worn down so they don't become overgrown.

title: What are Idioms?
text:
Have you ever heard an adult say, “I’m sorry, but we’re up a creek on this one”? What did he mean? He was standing on dry ground when he said it! Well, you’ve just heard an idiom.

Idioms are sayings that mean something different from the literal meaning of their words. “Literal” means “following the exact wording.” But idioms are not literal, so the words do not mean exactly what they say. Listen carefully for clues to figure out an idiom.

The best way to learn what an idiom means is to learn it and use it in your own speech or writing. Ask someone what it means. Then use it in your own writing. Here are some idioms in sentences. See if you can figure out what they mean. Once you know what the idiom means, use it in your own sentence. Use a seperate piece of paper if you need to.

They were both so shy they had a hard time breaking the ice. Use “breaking the ice” in your own sentence.

When it comes to modesty in dress, I have to draw the line somewhere. Use “draw the line” in your own sentence.

By halftime, the game was in the bag. Use “in the bag” in your own sentence.

Chris and I are in the same boat because neither of us have extra cash to spend on the field trip. Use “in the same boat” in your own sentence.

Would someone lend me a hand with the dishes? Use “lend me a hand” in your own sentence.

title: Let's Write
text: Poetry is a good way to express emotion such as sadness, love and joy. Writing poetry about the slave trade would be a good way to express your feelings about this dark time in history. Write a poem about how you feel about slavery, or about how you imagine it was for those men, women and children who were enslaved.

title: Colonial Life in Massachusetts
text:
By 1750, Massachusetts had more than 300 towns. At that time 200,000 people made Massachusetts their home. Boston was the largest city with approximately 20,000 people. Boston was a busy port where both the very rich and the very poor lived. Many of the smaller towns in Massachusetts were different than large cities like Boston.

Towns

The typical town in Massachusetts was built around the church, the school and stores. Several hundred families usually lived in one town. The families often enjoyed a public park, known as a village green or common. Does your town have a common or a green (park) today? Families strolled in the common and enjoyed the outdoors just as people do today. One thing is surely different. Today, cows are probably not found grazing there as well!

Most of the townspeople were farmers. Their fields and houses were scattered outside of town. Farm families raised most of their own food. What do you think they raised in their gardens? Beans, pumpkins, peas, corn and squash were some of the favorites. Cornmeal mush was used to make a dish called hasty pudding. Hasty pudding was eaten so often, children often grew tired of it.

There were no refrigerators then. When a family butchered a pig or cow or hunted large game, they shared it with their neighbors. They also traded food, such as eggs for milk or some other kind of treat. Apples were an important crop in early Massachusetts. Cider was one of the most popular drinks around. It was served with most meals in place of water. Drawing the day's cider from the big barrel was often the job of the last child to wake for the day.

Who did all the work around the farms? The men built houses and out-buildings. They cleared fields and did the heavier farm chores. The women did the cooking, cleaning and other household work. The women made the clothes, including spinning and weaving the cloth. Women and children fed the livestock and planted crops.

CONTINUED IN THIS WEEKS LESSON

title: Colonial Life in Massachusetts
text:
Colonial life in Massachusetts varied somewhat between the townships and Boston.

Colonial children had much to do. Besides going to school, they still helped out with chores. Boys could be found in the fields with their fathers. Girls began at an early age to help around the house and watch younger children.

What kind of clothes do you think the children wore? Everyday clothes were often sewn from cloth made by their mothers. Flax was a plant grown on many Massachusetts farms. The flax was spun into a linen yarn by mothers and girls. It was then woven into cloth on a large handloom. Finally, it was cut and sewn, by hand, into clothes for the family. You can imagine how exciting it must have been to have a new dress or shirt after all that work! Sunday clothes were probably fancier, made from fine fabrics purchased in Boston.

Some colonial children had clothing made from deer or other animal hides, just like the American Indians.

A colonial home was usually made from wood, with a fireplace in the center of the home. It kept the house warm and was the place where families would gather after meals.
