Matches had not yet been invented, so it was very important to keep some embers burning, even if there was no need for a fire. If the fire went out, a child was sent with a fire pan to a neighbor's house to borrow some fire.

Though there was much work to be done, colonial life was not all work. Often chores were made into games. One such game was cornhusking. Everyone gathered to husk the corn. If a young man husked an ear with red kernels, he was lucky indeed. The red ear was his ticket to give each young girl a kiss! If a girl happened on a red ear, she was allowed to give her favorite young man a kiss.

The colonists also enjoyed a variety of sports. Boys played football, though it was more like soccer than football today. Other popular sports included horse racing, ninepins (bowling), target shooting and billiards.

Families enjoyed small traveling circuses, or puppet shows, such as "Punch and Judy."

A favorite holiday was election day. Candidates would pass out election cakes and election beer to win votes.

What is your favorite holiday today?

title: Life in Boston
text:
Life in Boston was different than in smaller towns and villages. The Bostonians were able to buy many of life's comforts from the busy Boston Harbor.

The very wealthy families had large brick houses with fine furniture. They also had servants and slaves. Wealthy men usually served as selectmen or other community leaders.

Boston also had a middle class. The middle class was made of the people who were not terribly rich or poor, but lived comfortably. Most of these folks were tradesmen or shop owners. They probably owned a house made of wood and had a servant or two. An apprentice might be found living with them as well.

Boston was also home to many poor people who were crowded together in small wooden buildings. They were the ones who suffered most from hunger and disease.

Colonial Boston was a crowded place. Streets were usually narrow and winding. Some of those Boston streets still have their original names today: Milk, Beacon, Water, Essex and Summer.

Just as today, one of Boston's busiest areas was the port at the city's eastern edge. A great many ships were in and out. The children of Boston ate many of the same foods and played many of the same games as their neighbors in the townships.

In the 1750s, there were some young folks living in Boston who would one day be famous: Paul Revere was 15, John Hancock was 13, and Sam Adams was 28. What else do you know about these famous Bostonians?

title: What is Profit?
text:
Entrepreneurs for the day. You find a table in Jack's garage. Mary's mom helps you make some lemonade. Together, all three of you make a big sign that says "Lemonade, 25 cents." You put all of your items on the sidewalk in front of your house and wait for your customers to come.

Soon people are lined up around the block for a taste of your delicious lemonade. You work quickly to serve your customers. Then you realize you are almost out of cups. Mary and her mom run to the store to buy some more. When they get back, you take the extra cups and keep on selling lemonade until there is no more. Together, everyone cleans up the lemonade stand. You start to count the money you've made.

You count it all up, and you have $5.80. Then you think about the extra cups that you had to buy. They cost $1.25. You give Mary's mom that amount from the money you made. Now you have $4.55. This new amount is your profit. Profit is the money a business makes after all of the expenses are paid. In this example, the extra cups that cost $1.25 are your only expense.

You and your friends have learned about profit motive today. Profit motive is the desire to benefit from the time and money people put into a business. In other words, you wanted to sell lemonade because you thought you could earn some money. In the same way, a business sells goods in hopes of earning a profit. Now the question is, what will you do with your profit?

title: Great Barrington, Massachusetts
text:
Great Barrington is located in a beautiful valley along the Berkshire River. The valley was named by the Mohicans, who were the first settlers. They called it the "Housatonic Valley." This word was described many years later by a Stockbridge Indian who came to visit the land. He pointed to the full moon rising over the East Mountain in Great Barrington and explained the word "Housatonic" meant " over the mountain."

A settlement was soon founded called Housatonnuck. Later, Great Barrington was founded here. It was along the main trail from Fort Orange (now Albany, New York) to Massachusetts Bay. Many visitors traveled the trail beside Great Barrington. In fact, the Dutch nicknamed it "the New England Path."

title: Where is Beantown?
text: Puritan laws were strict and often very exact. For example, no one was allowed to work or play on Sunday. Since cooking on Sunday was considered a sin, women made Sunday's dinner on Saturday night. The common dish was beans, thus earning Boston the nickname of "Beantown." Does your family have a favorite recipe for Boston baked beans?

title: American Cranberry
text:
Wild cranberries were among the first native foods that the Pilgrims learned to love. They are called cranberries because the flower is said to resemble the head of a crane. Cranberries were one of the first New World crops grown for trade.

The American cranberry is usually about 8-12 inches in height. It bears an unusual pink flower. It is found in moist, sandy meadows and bogs. Blooms are everywhere from June through October.

According to American Indian myth, a dove carried the first cranberry from heaven to Earth in its beak. The cranberry surely seems heaven-sent for Massachusetts. Massachusetts is one of the top cranberry producers in the nation. There is a growing demand for the tasty berry. More and more berries have been harvested in the last two decades.

title: The Job of a Museum Director: ‘A Little Bit of Everything’
text:
The Campbell House Museum is a beautiful Civil War-era home in St. Louis, Missouri. The wealthy Campbell family lived there from 1854 to 1938. Studies Weekly asked Andrew Hahn, the director of the museum, about his job.

Studies Weekly: How is a house museum different from other types of museums?

Andrew Hahn: A house museum is different because it gives you an opportunity to get the full experience of the past. If you go to an art museum, you can see paintings from the past that may tell a story about history or a particular event. But when you come to a house museum, you get the full picture of what it was like to live in the past. When people come here, they get to experience what it was like to be welcomed into the house or to work in the house.

The house was so well preserved, and the Campbells’ collection is still here. This is their house and how they lived in it.

Studies Weekly: What does a museum director do?

Andrew Hahn: I do a little bit of everything. We have to raise money so that we can keep the doors open and pay the utility bills. I write the checks for all the bills, and I organize our volunteers who do most of the work at the house. We do research, so I look into the Campbell story and read old documents and newspapers that tell stories about the past. I even take out the trash! ￼

title: How Do I Use a Dictionary?
text:
What does “native” mean? How do you pronounce “shaman”? To find the answers to these and many other questions, grab a dictionary. The dictionary just might be a student’s best friend. A dictionary lists and defines words.

Know Your ABCs

The words in a dictionary appear in alphabetical order. At the top of each page, two guidewords show the first and last words on that page. Guidewords help you find the word you need more quickly. For example, the word “tepee” might appear on a page with the guidewords “tension” and “territory” at the top of that page.

Is your word followed by numbers? That means it has more than one definition. Look up the word “native” and see all the definitions for it. Write some of them here:

After each word, you will find a letter that stands for a part of speech. For example, n. means “noun,” v. means “verb,” and adj. means “adjective.” Sometimes, one word can have two or more parts of speech. It depends on how it’s used in a sentence. Let’s show this with the word “hunt.” Look it up now in your dictionary.

What is the meaning of “hunt” as a verb? Use “hunt” as a verb in a sentence here:

What is the meaning of “hunt” as a noun? Use “hunt” as a noun in a sentence here:

title: Who Wore Wigs?
text: One item of dress that was fashionable in the mid-18th century was the wig. It was worn mainly by men and boys! Because head lice were a common problem, the person’s real hair was cut very short. It was then covered by a wig. The wig was made of goat, horse or human hair.

title: Let's Write
text: Traditions through the year are an important part of our society. Everyone, according to their heritage, may have different traditions. It is amazing how people do such different things, even on the same holiday. Write a story about your favorite holiday or family tradition.

title: Massachusetts Goes to War!
text:
French and Indian War Is Fought!

Nope, it wasn't the French fighting the Indians, but the French fighting the English. They were fighting on two continents at the same time. The French were fighting the English in North America and in Europe. So, how do the Indians fit in? The Algonquian tribes were friendly with the French. They agreed to help them fight. It was the French and Indians fighting against the British. In America, this war was known as the French and Indian War. In Europe, this same war was considered part of the Seven Years War.

Many countries wanted control in North America. There was money to be made in the fur trade. France and England both claimed the beaver-rich lands in the Ohio River Valley. To gain control of these lands, the French attacked many villages in Massachusetts and other Colonies. The town of Deerfield was burned in 1704 by French soldiers and their Algonquian allies. About 50 of the townspeople were killed. Over 100 were captured. As they were marched to New France, 20 more died.

Thousands of men from Massachusetts fought for England in this war. In 1690 a Massachusetts regiment was under the command of Sir William Phips. They captured Port Royal (now Annapolis Royal) in Nova Scotia. Can you find Annapolis Royal on a map?

Colonel Ephraim Williams Jr. was the commander at Fort Massachusetts. He led his troops to the battlefield from the fort. The troops marched to the French fort of Crown Point. It was a successful victory over the French, although Williams died in the attack. Massachusetts was re-named Williamstown in 1765 in his honor.

These efforts of the Massachusetts soldier helped Great Britain to win the French and Indian War. This was very important to the Colonies. It was also important in Europe.

title: The French and Indian Wars... Again?
text:
There are many ways we can study history. We read about history in textbooks. We study newspapers and journals from the past. Historians look at drawings and photos too. Don't forget Massachusetts Studies Weekly! There is also another way. Did you know that some people study history by reenactment?

Reenactment means to act out an event from the past. We can learn about history with facts and actors. When real people act out history, it is a way to understand more information.

There are many living history groups in the United States. Some are in historic villages. Others reenact battles. They choose battles fought in the United States. Who learns about history from reenactment? The actors themselves learn more about history. The people who are watching also do. It becomes a living textbook for the viewers.

The soldiers in these modern regiments try hard to re-live the battles as closely as possible. Of course, they do not really shoot at each other. They do use real muzzle loaders and wear replicas of uniforms. They eat the same kinds of food or go without. They may even be singing the same songs on lonely nights by a warm campfire.

title: French and Indian War
text:
Rogers' Rangers

A New Hampshire man named Robert Rogers helped the British win the war. He helped the British capture Crown Point. He helped to capture Ticonderoga. Both were important victories. The final battle was fought in Quebec between British General James Wolfe and French General Marquis de Montcal. It cut off French power in North America for good. A peace treaty between England and France was signed in 1763. The land held by the French in North America was given to the British. It changed the map forever.

Until the colonists fought against American Indians, they had always fought their battles in large rows and in the open. The American Indians fought a different way. They hid behind rocks and trees to shoot at the enemy. They did not stand in the open. As the colonists began to fight like the natives, warfare began to change.

Rangers were early colonists who chose to fight as the native people. One of the most famous of these groups was known as Rogers' Rangers. These men shot at the enemy while hiding. They also waged war at night and in the wintertime. That was something new! They were known to wear ice skates while fighting on ponds. They battled in snowshoes. The Rangers wore green outfits and developed tactics called "Rogers' Ranging Rules." These tactics are still in use by Army Rangers and Green Berets.

Results of the French and Indian War

Study the two maps on this page. You will see the results of the French and Indian War. Before the war, the French occupied a huge area in the center of America. After the war, the French were completely gone. The events that contributed to this huge change in America started because two countries had overlapping land claims in North America.

The French based their claims on the great explorer Robert de La Salle. He claimed the Mississippi River and all rivers that empty into it for France. The English based their claims on the original land grant of Virginia. The problem was some of the land overlapped the French claims.

The French believed they could strengthen their claims by building a string of forts. They buried lead plaques with the French claim written on them throughout the Ohio Valley. The English sent a messenger with a letter to explain to them their claim was wrong and they should leave. The messenger was young 21-year-old George Washington. Instead of leaving, the French moved southward and captured an English fort. This started the French and Indian War.

It was called the French and Indian War because the Algonquian tribes at the time liked the French and joined their side.

The war was long and favored the French in the early years.However, the English finally won because of their great numbers and military strength.

The war took place in all of the Colonies. Most of the action and several important battles centered in New York, New Hampshire, Massachusetts and Pennsylvania.

title: The Role of Prices
text:
"And your total comes to $2.40."

You've shopped in many stores either with your parents or by yourself. Most products contain bar codes that tell the scanner what the price is for the item. The prices let you, the consumer, know how much money the store is willing to sell the item for. However, that's not the only purpose.

Prices have three main functions. First, prices help ration scarce goods. Things cost money, and money is a limited resource. We can't buy everything we want all the time. Therefore, items need to be rationed, or spread out to many people.

Second, prices provide a reason for buyers to buy goods and sellers to sell them. Prices make the process of buying goods organized. They motivate sellers to provide more goods based on the idea of profit motive.

Finally, prices send signals about how a market is doing. Let's say prices are too high, and no one is buying those goods. Then economists can study this and ask questions. They can find out what prices are in other markets. Then they decide what in this market made the price rise so high.

Economists can then figure out the price for the product. It should balance the amount of buyers who want to buy with the amount of sellers who want to sell. This price is called the market-clearing price, or the equilibrium price. By figuring out this price, both the buyers and sellers are happy, and goods continue to be sold.

Can you think of any other reasons prices are important to our economy?

title: Nantucket, Massachusetts
text:
Nantucket is the only place in North America that is an island, a county and a town. It was first settled by about 1,500 of the Wampanoag tribe. In 1659, the island was purchased for 30 pounds and two beaver hats!

The nine Englishmen who bought it planned to raise sheep on the island. Here, they could escape the strict Puritans on the mainland.

In 1672, the islanders invited whalers to move to the island. The whaling industry soon found a home on the island. Whaling continued strong for over 100 years! In fact, Nantucket was known as "The Whaling Capital of the World." It became the third largest city in Massachusetts.

Today, Nantucket has more than 800 houses built before the Civil War still standing. People have nicknamed the island "The Little Gray Lady of the Sea" because of the fog and the many gray shingled roofs on the island.

title: Why do ponds and lakes freeze from the top down?
text:
When the air temperature above a lake drops below freezing the top of the lake will freeze. Ice expands when it freezes. This makes it lighter than water. The floating ice acts as a big blanket and helps prevent more of the lake from freezing.

Why is this important? Fish are living in the water and don't want to become frozen leftovers during the winter time! We are lucky ice floats. If ice were heavier, it would sink during winter. By spring, our lakes and oceans would be solid blocks of ice. Every creature in them would be dead.

title: Sugar Maple
text:
The sugar maple is found in several New England states. No wonder, when it produces such a treat! Though red maples and silver maples also produce sugar, the sugar maple provides the best sugar.

The tree grows to be about 100- feet tall in the forest. In a yard or park it has a fuller, more spreading type of a shape. Its leaves are long and dark green. In the fall they turn a beautiful yellow and red. They produce "whirly-bird" seeds that twirl down with just a gentle breeze. The straight trunk is a light gray-brown. The trunk is scaly with deep long furrows (grooves). It grows in the northern forests. Maple trees do get tired and worn out after many, many years of tapping. They are also important as a source of wood for beautiful furniture.

title: How Do I Use a Thesaurus?
text:
Do you use many of the same words over and over when writing? Are you getting bored with those same words? It’s time you learned to use a thesaurus!

Search for Synonyms

The word “thesaurus” almost looks like a name for a dinosaur, doesn’t it? It’s actually a book (it can be found online as well). This book or website provides synonyms (words similar in meaning) for common words. Using a thesaurus is a great way to broaden your vocabulary with more interesting words.

A thesaurus is usually alphabetical. Some are similar to dictionaries because they give you the part of speech, definition and sample sentences for words. Sometimes a thesaurus will give you directions to look up other entries. Here’s what you’ll find in a typical thesaurus.

Entry Word...........................................The word you look up to find synonyms

Part-of-Speech Label.......................Tells you if the word is a noun, verb, adjective, etc.

Definition...............................................Tells you what the entry word means

Example Sentence.............................Shows you how the entry word might be used in a sentence.

Synonyms..............................................Words whose meanings are the same as or similar to the entry word

Antonyms...............................................Words whose meanings are the opposite of the entry word

Try It!

Look up the word “grow” in a thesaurus. Write all the synonyms here.

title: Let's Write
text: ￼Massachusetts is a big and beautiful state. Each region of the state is wonderful and unique. Write a paragraph telling about your region, county or city. Describe it so other students in Massachusetts would love to visit!

title: Change in Warfare
text: As the Europeans began to fight like the natives, warfare began to change. Colonists hid behind rocks and trees to shoot at the enemy rather than stand in the open.

title: Colonial Unrest on the Rise
text:
By the mid 1700s, the Massachusetts Colony was home to many people. For many, times had been good. England considered the Colonies to be part of the British Empire.The colonists were expected to be loyal to the king. Many colonists did not feel loyal to the king. They felt as if they were separate from England. Some even called themselves "Americans." This did not please the king. In addition, England needed funds to pay for costly wars. So, a series of new laws were passed. The colonists were unhappy with the new laws.

The Albany Congress

In 1754, leaders from seven of the Colonies met in Albany, New York. This group was called the Albany Congress. At this meeting, the colonists found they had some of the same problems. They began to think of themselves as a united people. It was then the British Parliament decided to tax the colonists. Some members in Parliament voted against the taxes. They thought it would cause trouble in the Colonies. They were right!

The Sugar Act

The first tax was called the Sugar Act. It was a tax on any molasses the Colonies received that wasn't from England. This made the colonists angry! Some began to say, "No taxation without representation!"

The Stamp Act

In 1765, Parliament passed another tax. It was called the Stamp Act. This required the colonists to buy a special stamp to put on all legal papers. Even playing cards were taxed! The colonists were fuming. They protested in meetings. Many newspapers carried protests. Broadsides, or papers posted on trees, carried messages of anger.

The Stamp Act Congress

The colonists knew they could make a stronger protest by joining together. In the fall of 1765, the Colonies united. They formed a group called the Stamp Act Congress. Nine colonies sent leaders to meet in New York City. The Congress expressed anger about the hated Stamp Act. They believed Americans should not be taxed without permission. With Massachusetts in the lead, some Colonies formed groups called the Sons of Liberty. The women formed groups called the Daughters of Liberty. These groups helped the Colonies move toward independence.

The Sons of Liberty pressured Stamp Act agents to resign. When the English lawmakers understood how much trouble the Stamp Act was, it was repealed, or ended, in 1766.

Only one year later, in 1767, Parliament placed another tax on goods. The angry colonists decided to oppose this.

Colonists continued to riot and protest against other tax laws. British officials sent for help. British troops arrived in Boston to try and keep order.

The presence of British soldiers only served to make the colonists more angry. Massachusetts became a hotbed of angry colonists.

title: Don’t Let Your Letters Become Nixies!
text:
Have you ever looked at someone's bad handwriting and wondered what it says? There are people who are paid by the U.S. Postal Service to do that every day. Their job is to decipher, or figure out the meaning of, the addresses of mail that the computerized mail sorter can't read. Postal employees in one of two Remote Encoding Centers (RECs) work to separate those addresses they can decipher and those they have to reject because they are completely unreadable. Each of these employees is supposed to work through 1,100 letters an hour!

The letters that are rejected are "nixies," or mail with unreadable or incorrect addresses. Some mail is sent to the Mail Recovery Center in Atlanta, Ga., if the envelope looks like it has money or important documents inside. But letters that don't seem important are sent to the shredder.

So how can we avoid having our letters shredded? Well, the computerized mail sorter is a technology, but so are pencils and paper. In fact, they are some of the simplest technology. We use these tools to learn and practice our handwriting, or penmanship. Most of us write our very best when we are in the fourth grade, and our handwriting does not usually get better as we get older. This is because as we write more, we write faster. People sometimes form opinions about us based on our handwriting, so good handwriting is still important. And grandma and grandpa really do want to get your letters, so write neatly!

title: Sharing Public Space: Vitus Bering and Russian Colonies in Alaska
text:
Imagine traveling 6,000 miles over land with supplies for an expedition, and THEN sailing through frigid seas to look for a new world. This was the job given to Vitus Bering, a Danish navigator who sailed for the Russian navy. Peter the Great, czar (ruler) of Russia, asked Bering to explore the eastern coast of Russia. He was wondering if land connected Asia and North America.

Bering's first trip began in 1725. After spending three years getting his supplies to eastern Russia, Bering sailed along the coastline. He didn't see any land to the east, and he didn't realize he was sailing in the narrow passage between Russia and Alaska. This waterway is now called the Bering Strait.

Bering led another expedition in 1741. This time his ship landed on Kayak Island, off the coast of Alaska. They explored some of the Aleutian Islands and met the native people there, the Aleut. He was the first European to arrive in present-day Alaska.

Bering died before returning to Russia, but his voyages paved the way for Russian settlements in North America. Many fur traders came to the area. In 1799 the Russian government established a fur-trading operation in Alaska. Furs from foxes, sea otters and seals were very valuable.

Unfortunately, the Russians took advantage of the native people just as some Europeans had done in settling New England. The Russians took over their lands and forced them to hunt for furs. They also brought new diseases, which killed many natives.

Today, the Aleut people continue to live along the western coast of North America, and their population has grown. What might have been different if the Russians and the Aleut had shared public space fairly? Where in your community is there a debate over public land? How should such debates be handled?

title: Patriotism Develops
text:
Liberty was something the colonists were beginning to value more as time went by. The Sons and Daughters of Liberty were organized to help preserve colonial America's liberty.

The Patriotic Movement Begins in America

The Sons of Liberty planted a pine tree in the middle of a field. It is here they gathered and held many meetings. Many Colonies had similar trees. The tree was called a Liberty Tree or a Liberty Pole. These were honored as much as a flag. Several times the British soldiers destroyed the trees, causing more anger than ever before. On Jan. 19, 1770, shortly after another attack on their liberty pole, the Sons of Liberty in New York began to fight with the redcoats at Golden Hill. Men on both sides were injured. This was known as the Battle of Golden Hill. It was one of the first violent acts in the years before the Revolutionary War.

The Boston Massacre

On March 5, 1770, British soldiers fired into an angry Massachusetts crowd. No one knows for sure if the first shot was fired on purpose. It was followed by several more shots. Two men were killed. Three that were wounded later died. The angry patriots called it the Boston Massacre. It is still known by that name today. The Boston Massacre put Bostonians in a fighting mood.

Stamp Act Inflames Patriots!

The Sons of Liberty hung effigies (stuffed dummies that look like actual people) of British stamp collectors. They also seized the stamps and burned them publically. They attempted to stop the Stamp Act. Many colonists were happy they did.

Tea Anyone?

The Tea Act was passed in 1773. It was another tax. It was a tax on all tea. The Tea Act allowed only British merchants to sell tea. This left colonial merchants at a loss. It also forced the colonists to pay a tax they did not want to pay. So, many colonists quit drinking tea. Others smuggled tea from other countries. Once again, many colonists thought of independence. On Dec. 16, 1773, about 7,000 Bostonians attended a town meeting. At the meeting, Samuel Adams suddenly stood and declared, "This meeting can do nothing more to save the country!" These words were a signal to a band of men waiting outside. These Sons of Liberty were dressed as American Indians. They dumped the tea from English ships into the harbor. Samuel Adam's cousin, John Adams, declared the "Tea Party" the "grandest event ever."

The tea party was a surprise to England. It convinced the king that the colonists no longer respected English law. England promptly ordered the ports of Boston closed. England ordered the colonists to pay for the tea. It wasn't long before other colonies had their own "tea parties." Sometimes the tea was thrown into the water. Other times it was burned.

title: Budgeting - Making sure more money comes in than goes out
text:
Have you ever asked your mom or dad for something, only to be told that it wasn't in the budget? A budget is a plan of how to manage your money. It has two main ideas.

First, you must think about how much money is coming in. Maybe you earn an allowance. Maybe you mow a neighbor's lawn to make money, also called income. If you earn money every week or month, like an allowance, then it is called a steady income.

Next, we look at how much is going out, or how much it costs you to live. Maybe you subscribe to a magazine or go to a movie every Friday night. These are types of expenses. Adults also have expenses. They pay bills every month to buy things we all need, like food, clothes and cars. These expenses come out of their income every month.

To make a budget, you must first look at your income (money coming in). Then add up all of your expenses (money going out). Now subtract the total amount of your expenses from your total income. This new number lets you know how much money you have for other things that you want. This helps you plan and make wise choices when spending your money.

The goal of a budget is to try to balance your income with your expenses. It is best if your income is more than your expenses. That way, more money is coming in than going out. Now it is your turn to make a budget. Good luck!

title: East Falmouth, Massachusetts
text:
The town of East Falmouth is located on Cape Cod. It is part of Barnstable County. At one time, the village was the strawberry growing capital of the world. Today, there is a strawberry festival every June on the Village Green. The community also has many strawberry farms. Farmers allow you to pick your very own strawberries. What a treat!

Every August since 1973, the town holds the Falmouth Road Race. Runners from average joggers to some of the best runners in the world are invited to come. Nearly 10,000 runners come together. They begin early in the morning on Water Street.

They race through the town. They finish 7 miles later at Falmouth Heights Beach. Then, a huge party is held for all of the runners. Are you practicing for the next year's race yet?

title: What is a town crier?
text:
Before newspapers came to the Colonies there was no shortage of news because most villages had a town crier. He was an official who went about the village ringing a bell or banging a drum to call the townspeople to listen to important news.

After people gathered, the town crier would then declare the messages officials thought all the people should know.

In addition to the town crier, there was often a watchman. The watchman roamed the streets at night to make sure all was well. It was also part of his job to call out the time on the hour and state the weather conditions. He might call out, "10:00 and a rough wind blows!"

title: Eastern Mole
text: Moles form a family within the order of insect eaters. This species is about 7 inches long. Its fur varies from gray to brown to golden and it has a hairless tail. Its large, sharp claws help it to dig underground. The mole lives in fields, meadows and gardens throughout most of the United States (not the extreme Northwest), from the Atlantic to the Rockies.

title: Let's Write
text: The colonists in Massachusetts Bay are buzzing about the latest taxes. They think it’s time to tell the king of England how they feel. Imagine you have been chosen to write a broadside in colonial Massachusetts. Your township wants you to make a list. The list should include five reasons the colonist are angry with the British crown. After you have written the list of complaints, write a list of requests that you will make for the people of Massachusetts.

title: Blows Must Decide!
text:
"The New England governments are in a state of rebellion, blows must decide whether they are to be a subject to this country or independent." (Letter from King George III to Lord North, 18 Nov. 1774)

What do you think King George III meant when he said "blows must decide?" He meant British soldiers would force the colonists to obey English law. To do this, more acts were passed by Parliament. They first passed the Coercive Acts. They wanted to force the colonists to pay taxes. The colonists called them the Intolerable Acts. These acts closed trade in Boston. They also removed colonial leaders and replaced them with British military officers. Next was the Justice Act. This ruled any British official would not be judged for crimes in America. Instead, they were sent back to England where judgment would be easier. The last was the Quartering Act. With this act, the colonists had to supply places for the soldiers to be quartered, or housed. The colonists were angry. The colonial leaders decided it was time to meet in 1744. A group of delegates came from all of the Colonies except Georgia. This group was known as the First Continental Congress. The delegates agreed the colonists needed to resist. They decided the colonists should boycott, or refuse, English goods. Some people continued to wear English clothing. Some still drank English tea. When they did, they were named in local newspapers.

The Midnight Ride of Paul Revere

By 1775, the colonists of Massachusetts were ready to fight. Knowing this, British General Gage ordered his troops to march. They marched on the towns of Lexington and Concord.

Paul Revere was a Boston silversmith. He learned of the advance. He decided to act. Late at night, on April 18, 1775, Revere and his friend William Dawes set out for Lexington. They wanted to warn the American leaders of the attack. At midnight, the two men reached Lexington. Here, Dr. Samuel Prescott joined them. The plan was to continue to Concord. Before they could, Revere and Dawes were arrested. Only Dr. Prescott made it past the British soldiers to warn the colonial leaders of their approach. Revere and Dawes were able to alert many people along the way. However, it was really Prescott who succeeded in warning the troops. He prepared the rebels at Concord for the British attack. Much later, in 1863, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow penned a famous poem, "Paul Revere's Ride." Because of this poem, some people thought Paul Revere was the "midnight rider."

The Battles of Lexington and Concord

As the Colonies continued to rebel, England sent more forces. All 13 of the Colonies began storing guns. Volunteers began to drill for war. On April 19, 1775, General Gage marched 700 men from Boston. They were going to destroy the patriots' military supplies at Concord. The patriots were ready to fight. At Lexington, the patriots were ordered to leave. They began to, but then a shot rang out. The firing began. In this first battle, eight colonists were killed, and 10 were wounded. The patriots wounded one British soldier. As news of the battle spread, more patriots gathered near Concord. This time, the Americans had more soldiers than the British. The Battle of Concord followed later that day. The patriots killed or wounded nearly 300 of the British. They lost about 100 of their own. The British retreated. The Battle of Concord was an American victory.

Looking back, we know these two battles were important. They were the beginning of the Revolutionary War. But, in the spring of 1775, only a few colonists were ready to fight. Many colonists felt these were just small conflicts.

Not everyone in America hated British rule. After these two battles, the colonists divided into two groups. One group was called Whigs, or Patriots. They wanted the Colonies to be free from British rule. About one third of the colonists were loyalists, or Tories. They supported England. Many families or households were split. Sometimes servants felt differently than the members of the household. Sometimes fathers chose a different side than their sons.

title: The National Guard: Our Oldest Tradition
text:
The Army National Guard of the U.S. was authorized by Congress in 1933. But this military tradition actually began in the Massachusetts Colony in 1636. The first colonists formed regiments to protect their homes and families against attack. These regiments, the oldest in the U.S. Armed Forces, are known as the 101st Field Artillery, 101st Engineer Battalion, and the 181st and 182nd Infantry Regiments.

Patterned after the English militia system, male colonists between the ages of 16 and 60 were expected to serve their country. There were no uniforms to speak of, and men often shared muskets, but they banded together anyhow.

During the 1770s, the colonial militia began to ready themselves for battle. In Massachusetts, the militia proudly called themselves the minutemen, because they were said to be able to prepare for battle at a "minute's notice." Other Colonies began to adopt the idea of minutemen, but the best known were those from Massachusetts.

At the end of the Revolutionary War, the delegates who framed the Constitution realized the importance of the militia in protecting not only towns and states, but in defending the nation. The Militia Clause of the Constitution recognized this role, and the militia became the basis of today's National Guard.

title: Declaration of Independence
text:
After the first few battles of the Revolutionary War, most Americans were convinced it was time to separate from England.

It was the summer of 1776. The Second Continental Congress met in Philadelphia. They met to talk about independence. The Congress wanted to protest to the king. They wanted everyone to know the Colonies would govern themselves. But, some of the members of Congress did not want to go to war. They argued for days. Then, they sent word home to their Colonies, "Discuss independence, and tell us how we should vote." Answers began coming in. Each time it was the same, "Vote for independence!" Richard Henry Lee of Virginia told the Congress, "These United Colonies are, and of right ought to be, free and independent states." The Congress decided to declare the American Colonies independent. A document needed to be written. Thomas Jefferson was chosen to do the writing. He worked hard for two weeks writing and rewriting. This famous document was the Declaration of Independence.

The first part of the Declaration explains men have certain rights that can't be taken away. The second part tells how the king refused to grant these rights. Those who signed declared these truths to be understood by everyone. The Congress made the vote late on July 2, 1776. It was officially adopted on July 4, 1776. Some colonists may not have wanted independence. Even so, the Massachusetts delegates voted for independence. The Declaration was read to most of the Colonies within a few weeks.

title: Whose side are you on?
text:
At first, Patriots were colonists who wanted England to stop the taxes. As the conflict wore on, liberty meant more. The Patriots no longer wanted to be British citizens. They just wanted to be Americans.

Loyalists were those who wanted to remain citizens of England. They stayed loyal for different reasons. Sometimes, it was because they were loyal to family members who still lived in England. Others were afraid England was too powerful. Still, some believed a government run by "rich patriots" would be worse than the English crown. Finally, others who remained loyal to the king felt he had the right to rule the Colonies.

Did all of the colonists choose sides?

No! Many of the colonists tried to stay neutral (not choose a side). Some even changed sides as the war went on. Many families were split. Benjamin Franklin was a firm Patriot. His son William Franklin was the royal governor of Massachusetts. He was a well-known Loyalist.

title: Bourne, Massachusetts
text:
Bourne, Massachusetts, is home to the widest sea-level canal in the world! The canal has three beautiful bridges spanning over it. Here you will find the Sagamore Bridge, the Bourne Bridge and the Cape Cod Canal Railroad Bridge. If you ever visit, you can run, walk, bike or rollerblade on paths along each side of the canal. What a view!

Bourne City has more shoreline than most cities in the state. While you are here, check out Buzzards Bay, Cape Cod Bay, Monument Beach, Mashnee Island, Gray Gables, Sagamore Beach or a number of others. You can visit the Aptucxet Trading Post at Monument Beach. This trading post was used long ago by Indians and Pilgrims. They would meet together and barter for things they needed.

Every year, the city of Bourne holds an annual Scallop Festival in September. Come see the whole town come together and celebrate. Oh by the way, does your town have an official city color? They do! Purple is the official city color of Bourne.

title: Who wants a turkey for the national bird?
text:
It is 1784, and our nation's leaders cannot agree on something. They cannot agree on which bird should be the national bird. It was Benjamin Franklin who argued against the eagle as the symbol. He really preferred a turkey! (gobble!)

Does the turkey seem like an odd choice? Franklin pointed out that the turkey was an intelligent and noble bird. It also sustained the first colonists in the New World. He believed the bald eagle should not be the choice because it was a scavenger. Obviously, the vote was for the eagle that stands proudly as a symbol of our nation today.

title: Indigo Bunting
text:
The indigo bunting is a small bird found in Massachusetts as well as many other Eastern states. The male is indigo in color. Notice in the picture what a bright blue that is. He is blackish colored on his wings and tail and has a black-tipped beak. The female is a light brown with a white breast that has light streaks of brown at the throat.

The buntings build nests in bushes such as berry, rose or greenbrier. They may even nest in weeds or tangles of vines. The nests are woven with dry grass, bark, dry leaves and sometimes snake skins!

The male bunting is one of the few birds who gives a full singing performance at midday.

title: How Do I Give an Oral Presentation?
text:
Standing in front of a crowd and telling them what you think is not easy, but it can be done if you prepare well!

Preparing for an Oral Presentation

1. Know your audience. What you say should be directed toward them. Is it to be given in your classroom? This will make it easier!

2. How long should it be? If your teacher says 15 minutes, stick to the time.

3. What’s the topic? Did your teacher assign it? Make sure you can cover it within the time limit.

4. Make notes. Use index cards and put them in the order you want to use them. Index cards are not so large that they cover your face. You may write your presentation on numbered pieces of paper, but do not staple the pages.

5. Practice, practice and practice some more!

Making the Oral Presentation

1. Introduction—Get the audience’s attention with the introduction. You can do this by asking a question, telling a story, using a quotation or making a statement. Once you have their attention, state your topic.

2. Body—State your main points and give information that support your main points. You may ask rhetorical questions, (questions that don’t need answers) use emotional words or repeat important information.

3. Conclusion—Repeat your main point. Conclude with something that leaves a lasting impression by asking a rhetorical question, making an emotional plea or using a quotation, story or statement.

Try It!

When you’re asked to give an oral presentation, make sure you prepare well. Organize logically. Practice, practice, practice. Good luck!

title: Let's Write
text: Massachusetts is a beautiful state. Write a paragraph telling about a natural wonder in your region. Draw a picture of your favorite Massachusetts nature site to visit. Be sure to use a fine black marker, as pencil doesn’t print well. Describe it so that other students in Massachusetts would love to visit there!

title: Massachusetts Goes to War!
text:
Massachusetts plays an important role in the War for Independence!

Many colonists expected the fighting to begin in Massachusetts. Today, we know the battles of Lexington and Concord were the first battles of the Revolutionary War. In 1776, many colonists thought those battles would be the end of the fighting. Just the same, the colonial militia fought bravely in the first battles at Lexington and Concord.

Not everyone supported independence. Some still favored English rule. Nearly 100,000 people left the Colonies. Some went to England. Others moved to Canada. Those who remained were called loyalists.

Electing a Leader

After the battles of Lexington and Concord, the Second Continental Congress came together in Philadelphia. John Hancock of Massachusetts was elected president of the Congress. One of the first tasks of Congress was to select a leader for the American troops. George Washington was elected by a solid vote.

The Battle of Bunker Hill

England wanted to crush the rebellion. More British troops were sent toward Massachusetts. On June 17, 1775, the first major battle of the Revolutionary War was fought. It was in Massachusetts again.

The American leaders learned the British planned to take the two hills across the Charles River from Boston. Colonel William Prescott was ordered to take a thousand men to Bunker Hill. He hoped to beat the British to the hill. That night, Prescott took his men to Breed's Hill instead. Breed's Hill was closer to Boston. The troops worked through the night to fortify (protect and strengthen) the hill. In the morning, the redcoats were surprised when they marched toward the hill. As the British came near, Prescott is said to have told his troops, "Men you are all marksmen - don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes."

The British marched toward their enemy in rows. The colonists were scattered in many hiding places.

(CONTINUED IN THIS WEEKS LESSON)

title: Can Facebook Save Dying Languages?
text:
Can you say a few words in Siletz Dee-ni? No? How about saying "hello" in Aka? If you can't, you're not alone! These two languages and 3,500 more could become extinct by the end of this century. Almost 80 percent of the world's population now speaks only one percent of the world's 7,000 languages. This has happened because of globalization. Globalization means that countries are more connected through trade, money and workers. When countries work together, people must be able to communicate with each other. That means many people have to learn another language. English is the main language used throughout the world for business and the Internet.

Why is this a problem? When the last person who is able to speak a particular language dies, some of the knowledge that is found within that language dies with them. A language contains the history of its people, how they used their environment and their beliefs and ideas. Technology may just save many of these languages from extinction! With YouTube, Facebook and other forms of social media, languages that are spoken by even 5 or ten people can be taught to others around the world.

National Geographic has been working on the Enduring Voices Project. Its goals are to record native speakers of endangered languages into talking dictionaries and help communities learn ways to save their languages from extinction. What language do you want to help save?

title: Reason and Logic: The First Filipino Settlement in America
text:
Settlers in America often faced challenges while building new communities. In the 1760s, New Orleans was the capital of the Spanish colony of Louisiana. Sailors from the Philippines served on Spanish trading ships going between Manila, the capital of the Philippines, and Acapulco, Mexico.

Conditions on the ships were harsh, and Filipino sailors were often slaves. Some of them jumped ship (escaped) around 1765 and traveled to Louisiana. Once there they hid in the marshlands outside of New Orleans to avoid capture by the Spanish. They formed a colony of fishermen who lived and worked in the swamps and bayous.

These early Filipino settlers were called the Manilamen. Their first village was named Saint Malo. The Manilamen built their houses on stilts in the swamps. They developed a successful method of drying shrimp in the sun on raised platforms. The processed shrimp were exported as far away as Asia and South America.

The fishermen often sent money back to the Philippines so that more relatives could immigrate (move) to New Orleans. Manilamen's families did not stay in the fishing villages, but lived in homes in New Orleans. Their children would come to work on the platform during busy harvest times. There were seven Filipino villages in all. Saint Malo was the first, and Manila Village was the largest. Hurricanes have destroyed all of the original villages, but their shrimp-drying legacy lives on. The Manilamen used reason and logic to survive in their environment, just as people do today.

Have you ever noticed where your school is built? Is it located on level land or a slope? Is it a one-story building or taller? What things make the location and design of your school building reasonable and logical?

title: War for Independence
text:
First they declared their independence from Great Britain, then they had to fight for it!

The British marched toward their enemy in rows. The colonists were scattered in many hiding places. The British got close to the colonists, and the Patriots fired. The British were forced to retreat while leaving hundreds of bleeding soldiers behind.

The British repeated the attack. The results were the same. The British tried for a third time. Now, the Americans were running out of gun powder. With no gunpowder, they were forced to retreat.

The Battle of Bunker Hill was really fought at Breed's Hill. It was one of the worst battles of the Revolution. The British called this battle a victory because they captured the hills. Even so, they lost many more men.

George Washington arrived after the Battle of Bunker Hill. He trained the troops. In the spring they were ready. Washington led his troops to Dorchester Heights. He aimed his cannons at the British below. Remembering the Battle of Bunker Hill, the British fled.

There would be many more battles. They took place in different colonies. The only other battle that took place in Massachusetts was in September 1778. The British burned New Bedford. New Bedford was an important port. Here, American ships attacked British vessels.

Nearly 90,000 Bay Staters took part in the Revolutionary War. They helped the colonists travel the road to freedom.

The Turtle

It was a dark night on Sept. 6, 1776. The American Turtle was quietly launched. The Turtle was the first submarine ever to be used in combat. It was created by David Bushnell of Connecticut. He and a friend designed the submarine. The Turtle was assigned to attach a bomb to the side of a British war ship. The one-man submarine was only designed to carry the bomb and then flee.

Ezra Lee piloted the first attempt. He was unable to attach the bomb because the ship was metal. The screw would not go in. He was spotted by the British, and they took chase. The bomb was released in the water, causing a huge explosion. Though the mission failed to plant the bomb, it concerned the British. They decided to move the fleet.

Today you may see a working model of the Turtle in the Connecticut River Museum.

The Execution of Nathan Hale

On Sept. 21, 1776, Nathan Hale was captured. He was a spy behind the British lines on Long Island. He was condemned and hanged the next morning. These were his last words: "I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country." He was an inspiration to the rest of Washington's army.

Saratoga— Turning Point in the War!

After the victories at Freeman's farm and Bemis Heights, British General John Burgoyne was surrounded. He was forced to surrender at Saratoga, New York, on Oct. 17, 1777. This was the best American victory of the entire war. It encouraged France to enter into an alliance with the Americans. This, in turn, lead to the final victory.

title: Banks
text:
Did you know that temples were the first banks? Thousands of years ago, no one would steal from a temple. That's because they were afraid the gods would curse them. This made temples the safest place to store the costly metals people used for money. Some temples even made loans, giving money to people who promised to pay it back.

Do you know where the word bank comes from? Long ago, early Italian bankers used street benches to conduct their business. In time, the Italian word banca (bench) became the English word "bank." No matter what time era, or where you live, a bank has always been a business that deals with money. They hold money for customers, they make loans, and they provide other money-related services. There are three main types of banks.

The first is a commercial bank. These banks serve both businesses and individuals. They offer checking accounts, loans and saving accounts to their customers.

The second kind of bank is a savings bank. These banks are similar to commercial banks, but they mostly offer savings accounts and loans. They also offer mortgages. That's a special kind of loan for people trying to buy a house.

The third kind of bank is a credit union. Credit unions were started to help people borrow money. People in the same type of employment (a school district, for instance) put their savings together and loaned it to others within that organization. In other words, they operated their own banks. Today, credit unions provide many of the same services as commercial banks and savings banks. However, they are called non-profit organizations. This means that all the members of the credit union share any profit that the organization makes.

title: Boston, Massachusetts
text:
Boston is the capital of Massachusetts. It is found in Suffolk County by the eastern seaboard. Today, the population is about 6 1 8, 000 people. It wasn't always that way! Boston was founded in 16 30. It was actually named after Boston, England- a place where many of the Pilgrims came from.

In Boston's early days, the city was made up mostly of English Puritans. Boston became a main port for ships going to England or the West Indies. It played a big part in the Revolutionary War. Boston was the site of the Boston Tea Party and the Boston Massacre. It was the city where Paul Revere began his famous ride.

In the 19 00s, Boston became a main center for business and learning. Today, many top universities, such as Harvard and MIT, are found here. Boston is also a major cultural center. If you visit, check out the Boston Symphony or the Boston Pops Orchestra!

title: What is a Purple Heart?
text: The purple heart is a badge that some soldiers are awarded. George Washington felt the most outstanding soldiers should receive some type of award. In 17 8 2, he started giving the Badge of Military Merit. This later became known as the Purple Heart. Today, this medal is given to any soldier wounded in battle. Do you know a family member or friend who has received a purple heart?

title: Dragons and Damsels
text:
Dragonflies and damselflies are similar in many ways. Both hunt as they fly by making a basket -like trap with their legs, where they catch mosquitoes and other insects.

The dragonflies are brown to black with transparent wings and often have bright rainbow markings. The damselfly has a thinner body that is often jewel colored and transparent wings that are darker. While the dragonfly rests with its wings straight out from its body, the damselfly rests with its wings folded slightly above its body.

Unlike most insects which either flap both wings together or only the back wings, these flies can beat their wings separately. That means one set of wings can be going down while the other goes up. You can see this happen if you watch very closely. These flies are great flyers! They can fly in loop-the-loops, hover and even fly backwards!

Dragonflies are considered fairly large insects today, but 300 million years ago they were much larger.

title: Molly Pitcher
text: Washington's army left Valley Forge in Pennsylvania. They were heading for New York. On the way they engaged the British at Monmouth, New Jersey. It was here that "Molly Pitcher" (Mary Hays McCauley) took over her husband's gunner position when he fainted from the heat. She served the cannon throughout the fight. She became a legend in the Continental army. It was here she earned her nickname "Molly Pitcher." Some say she carried the water pitcher to serve the troops during battle.

title: Let's Write
text: Many men, women and families gave up so much for the freedom we enjoy today. Research a man, woman or family in the Revolutionary War and write about their contributions.

title: Cornwallis Surrenders at Yorktown!
text:
Yorktown, Virginia was the final battle of the Revolutionary War

On Oct. 19, 17 8 1, British General George Cornwallis and his men lost to General George Washington and his army. The colonists were sure of victory after this great battle. Then, on Nov. 2 5, 17 8 3, General Washington's army won back New York from the British. The British began to evacuate, or leave. Evacuation Day was a wonderful day for many colonists. Now the British were gone, and the new country, the United States of America, was finally free!

A New Government

In 17 8 1, the Second Continental Congress met once again to draft a new set of rules. They wrote the Articles of Confederation.

The Articles called for a "firm league of friendship" between the states. But each state was to remain separate- more like 13 little countries. This caused some problems. For several years after the Revolution ended, it seemed as if the new country would fall apart. The national government was very weak. Most of the power was given to the states. Things were confusing! The states bickered with each other. For example, the states each began printing their own money. The U. S. government had no power to collect taxes. Tensions grew, and it began to seem like the new country might not stay united. What could be done for the new country they fought so hard for?

Shays' Rebellion

The new nation was held loosely together by the Articles of Confederation and a very weak national government. One event that convinced American leaders that a change was due was Shays' Rebellion.

Led by Daniel Shays, the farmers were protesting high taxes and unfair laws that placed debtors in prison. The U. S. militia was not big enough to squash the rebellion, so the Massachusetts militia finally had to do it. The American leaders worried this rebellion was probably the first of many. They took steps to form a stronger federal government.

title: Francis Hopkinson and the American Flag
text:
If you asked 100 people who designed the first American flag, 99 of them would probably say Betsy Ross, right? Many people would be surprised to learn that there are dissenting opinions about that.

The U.S. Postal Service issued this stamp [right] in 2000 with this passage printed on the back:

Francis Hopkinson Flag 1777

Continental Congress member Francis Hopkinson designed the first Stars and Stripes. His stars may have formed rows or a ring; the exact design is not known. In a resolution of June 14, 1777, they were said to represent “a new constellation.”

There has been an ongoing debate about who made the first flag. Did George Washington really ask Betsy Ross to make a flag from his design? There are no written records confirming it, so many historians believe this is a legend. However, Betsy Ross’ family has always insisted that the story is true. They do have papers showing that Betsy was paid to make flags for the new country for the rest of her life.

Francis Hopkinson’s defenders can’t prove his claims either. He was a delegate from New Jersey who signed the Declaration of Independence. He sent a bill to Congress asking for payment for designing the first flag and other projects. After a long debate, a Congressional committee refused payment but never claimed that the designs were not his.

America was founded on the freedom of its citizens to disagree with the government and with each other. Neither side in the flag debate has found absolute proof. The discussion will certainly continue, showing that the all-American values of debate and dissent are alive and well. What issues in your community are a source of debate and dissent?

title: Bank Services
text:
Did you know you can do your banking without ever going to a bank? Many people prefer to use their computers at home or at their office to do their banking. This popular method is called online banking. It allows people to access their bank accounts online. It lets them do their banking right from home!

If you have ever done any type of business with a bank, you have made a transaction. The most common transactions are deposits and withdrawals. A deposit is any money that is put into a banking account. Most people make deposits with checks or cash. A withdrawal is money that you take from your banking account. In most cases, it is given to you as cash.

Pretend that your grandma gave you a $10 check for your birthday. You want to put it in your savings account. You take the check to the bank and fill out a deposit slip. The teller enters the information into the computer and gives you a receipt. You have just made a deposit. Later, you decide that it might be nice to take that same $10 and go to a movie. You go back down to the bank, fill out a withdrawal slip and give the paper to the teller. The teller asks for your ID. Then the teller gives you $10 in cash along with a receipt. You have made a withdrawal. Now that you have cash, you can enjoy your movie!

title: Effects of the Revolutionary War
text:
After the war, the states began to face the problems of a new country without a strong set of laws to govern it. The 13 new states were being guided by 13 different steering wheels. This caused many quarrels. It looked as if there might be some serious trouble

The Constitutional Convention

A new group gathered in Philadelphia at the Constitutional Convention. Every state except Rhode Island was there. The men who represented Massachusetts included Elbridge Gerry, Nathaniel Gorham, Rufus King and Caleb Strong. George Washington was in charge of the meeting.

Writing a new constitution for the United States was not easy. The delegates knew there would be many arguments. They decided to keep the meetings private. They shut all of the windows and locked the doors. The members of the Convention argued about everything! It took four months of meetings to write the Constitution. Many of the states were afraid the bigger states would have too many votes. They worried large states would have too much control over things like taxes, armies and religion.

The delegates worked very hard to create a form of government that would be fair.

When it was finally done, many of the delegates were upset that it did not contain a Bill of Rights. Many of the states had a Bill of Rights as part of their own state's constitution. They wanted rules that would protect the rights of the people. These were rights such as the right to speak or print whatever they wanted. They knew a Bill of Rights was very important.

Massachusetts would not approve the Constitution for a while because they wanted a Bill of Rights. Massachusetts finally approved when they knew a Bill of Rights would soon be added. The Bill of Rights finally went into effect in December 17 9 1. Massachusetts, the site of the Pilgrim colonies, the scene of the first Revolutionary War battle, the home of Squanto, Paul Revere, Sam Adams and John Adams, became the sixth state when it ratified the Constitution on Feb. 6, 17 8 8.

Hooray for Massachusetts! Happy Birthday America!

title: Salem, Massachusetts
text:
Salem started out as a small fishing village. American Indians who lived there before the English came called it Naumkeag. This meant "comfort haven." The English changed the name of the town in 1629 to Salem. Salem is the Hebrew word for peace.

Salem is probably most famous for the witch trials that took place in 1692. The English settlers of Salem were very superstitious. They believed in witches and witchcraft. Sadly, some men and women began to tell stories about some of the other people in the village. The officials in the town arrested people. They held trials. Many people were killed. This was a sad time in our history.

Visitors to Salem get the chance to visit the Witch Trial Memorial. This memorial reminds us of the terrible things that happened in Salem. It also reminds everyone about the lessons of understanding. It is a lesson about tolerance. We can learn from the witch trials of 1692.

title: What is a Chinese Sedan Chair?
text: When the Constitutional Convention was called, Benjamin Franklin arrived in the most colorful way of all. By the time Franklin was 81 years of age, he had aches and pains, especially in his legs. It was extremely hard for him to walk or ride. Even a bumpy carriage ride caused him great discomfort. Creative as always, Franklin came in a Chinese sedan chair. He lived in Philadelphia where the convention was being held, so he didn't have far to go. The sedan is a covered seat that sits on two long poles. It was carried by four prisoners from the jail in Philadelphia!

title: River Otter
text:
River otters are members of the weasel family. The river otter is the only member of the weasel family to have webbed feet and a very strong tail.

River otters are very sociable and enjoyable to watch. They wrestle, play and slide down riverbanks. They chirp, whistle, growl and even scream. The river otters can dive and swim very well. They can swim about 7 miles per hour. They can stay underwater for about two minutes. Unlike the muskrat or beaver, they hardly cause a ripple or a splash. When underwater, their ears and noses close up. Their whiskers help to sense prey, even when they can't see it.

The young are called cubs or kits. They are not good swimmers. Kits are carried by the mother to the banks when they are about two months old.

In some states, river otters are a protected animal. They may only be trapped or hunted during a limited season.

title: Start the Music!
text:
Music during the American Revolution played many roles. Songs were sung by the British and Americans alike. They told of loyalty, victories or sometimes were created to poke fun at the enemy. Yankee Doodle was originally sung by the loyalists to taunt the patriots, but the patriots changed the words to suit their tastes, and it became popular with the colonists as well.

West Point, the military academy in New York state, is home to the Hellcats. The Hellcats is a group of 12 buglers and drummers that traces its history back to the Continental fifers (flute players) and drummers who were part of the original minutemen. The bugles were later added because army commanders liked the big sound of the bugle. It could be used to give camp and battlefield commands. Today, the Hellcats play for reveille and retreat. They play for marching drills and every day in the mess hall. They rally support at the Army/Navy football games as well. The Hellcats also have the sad task of performing “Taps” during West Point funerals. Each year, a bugler also plays at the tombs of presidents Ulysses S. Grant and Franklin D. Roosevelt at the anniversary of their deaths. The Hellcats have instruments designed and handmade especially to play traditional American military music and provide us with a piece of living history.

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you have an opportunity to write a new law for the state of Massachusetts. It could be anything from wearing purple tennis shoes on Tuesdays to having computers in every school in Massachusetts. Write a paragraph describing a new law and tell why you think it’s important.

title: The New Congress vs. The Old Congress
text:
The men who wrote the Constitution gave the new Congress enough power to solve the problems that the old Congress could not solve.

Under the Articles of Confederation:

Under the Constitution:

Congress had to ask states for money Congress could tax people

Congress had no control over trade between states Congress could control trade between states

Congress had no way to settle arguments between states There were courts to settle arguments between states

title: Fake or Real News?
text:
Have you ever read something online, like on social media sites, that sounded fishy? Maybe it was real, but it could be fake news! The big danger, though, is news that sounds real but isn’t. Fake news is becoming common because anyone can post things online. Fake news can be in the form of a story. Fake news can be a photo or video that has been changed. The problem is that these fake items look real. Fake news can cause problems and it spreads misinformation.

Sam Wineburg, a professor, did some research. He found that 80 percent of students cannot tell the difference between real and fake news. Do you want to become a media-savvy person? You have to be able to find out if news is real or fake. How do you do that? You have to become a detective and search for the truth. You can learn about the author or company that posted the news. You have to think about the purpose of the news. Is there a hidden plan to get you to buy something or to make you think a certain way? Your teacher or a trusted adult can help you learn how to spot fake news. It takes a little time, but democracy depends on real information! Do your part and discover what is real and what is fake!

title: Massachusetts as a New State
text:
In 17 7 8, the people of Massachusetts wanted a new constitution for the state. When it was completed, it was presented to the people, but they rejected it. A new convention was then organized to write the new constitution.

John Adams was a strong leader at this convention. The new constitution was largely his creation. The people were happy with the new constitution because it included some very important ideas. It included a bill of rights and a system of checks and balances. These were things that would later be included in the Constitution of the United States. The state constitution was accepted in June 17 80.

Though Massachusetts and many other states had adopted state constitutions, the new nation was still very weak. Many states, including Massachusetts, suffered an economic depression. (A depression is a time when wages are low, business is slow and many people are out of work.) Some people wanted to raise taxes to pay off war debts. Those who suffered most were the farmers of western Massachusetts. When Daniel Shays led a rebellious mob of fearful farmers in protest, both state and federal governments decided to make some changes.

In 17 8 7, the Constitution of the United States was drafted. However, Massachusetts, New York and other states refused to ratify it. Leaders in Massachusetts were concerned because the Constitution did not contain a Bill of Rights. When leaders of the convention agreed to add it later, Massachusetts delegates were ready to sign! The Bay State, our state nickname, ratified the Constitution on Feb. 6, 17 8 8, becoming the sixth state of the union.

During the early years of the United States, there were two political parties. Massachusetts largely supported the Federalist Party. The Federalists favored a strong central government while the Democratic- Republican Party favored more powerful state governments. John Adams, a Federalist, served as the nation's first vice- president and in 17 9 7 became the second president of the United States.

While many businesses in Massachusetts suffered, the sea provided the key to better business. Trade with other nations, fishing, whaling and shipbuilding were all important for our state and our new nation.

During the War for Independence, many sea merchants had supplied their own ships to fight the powerful British Navy. Many vessels were lost and others were damaged in battle. Soon shipyards were to be found all along the coast of our state. Here ships were repaired and new ships were built.

It was in the 17 80s that Americans opened new trade routes to China. Because of the growing shipbuilding industry in Massachusetts, Salem became America's main port for the China trade.

Shipyards provided vessels for trade. They also supplied America's new Navy. President Washington requested a new fleet to help merchant ships fight pirates.

In 17 8 7, Boston launched one of the new ships. It was called the USS Constitution. It later became known as "Old Ironsides."

The Massachusetts whaling industry also grew into a prosperous successful business for many. Whalers from Nantucket and New Bedford were often gone on whaling voyages for two to three years at a time. The harvested mammal provided whale oil from melted down blubber. Whale oil was used for oil lamps and for oiling machines and gears. Whalebones were also valuable for the production of ladies' corsets and umbrellas.

title: Where is Old Ironsides?
text:
The USS Constitution and five other frigates (warships) were commissioned by President George Washington in 1794. All of them were designed by Joshua Humphrey. Each was built at a different site. The Constitution was built by Edmond Hart's shipyard in Boston.

It was made from more than 1,500 trees, felled from Georgia to Maine. It was armed with cannons cast in Rhode Island and fitted with copper hardware made by Paul Revere. This vessel became a truly national ship. The Constitution first put to sea in 1798. It has remained a part of the U.S. Navy for over 200 years.

Before the War of 1812, the Constitution was part of a fleet sent by President Thomas Jefferson to protect American ships from attack by Barbary pirates.

The battle fought with H.M.S. Guerriere, just months after the War of 1812 began, is where the Constitution began her journey of fame. At some point in the battle, someone was said to have seen a shot bounce off the side of the Constitution They shouted "Huzzah her sides are made of iron." And so was born the nickname of "Old Ironsides."

After many years of service, she was restored to her original condition. Under tow, the Constitution went from Bar Harbor, Maine, to Bellingham, Washington, on tour in 1931.

In 1992, Old Ironsides was again docked for major repairs, and in July 1997, she sailed for the first time in 116 years.

In 1998, naval vessels and tall ships from around the world came to Boston Harbor to honor the Constitution. Old Ironsides is the oldest commissioned warship afloat in the world.

title: Making Money
text:
Have you ever wondered where money comes from? All of the paper money in the United States is printed at the Bureau of Engraving and Printing. It is located in Washington, D.C. Paper bills are made of a special blend of cotton and linen. This blend makes the paper much stronger than normal. It is illegal to make this blend of paper without the permission of the Bureau of Engraving and Printing.

Money is printed on sheets in sets of 30 bills. It is then cut apart and pressed. Then it is starched and bundled. Each bill is printed in different colors of ink. The ink is made from a special formula that only the Bureau knows how to make. The bills also have red and blue threads running throughout. You can't even see them. It would be very difficult to make money that is just the same.

Why can't just anybody print money? Well, when there are too many dollars in circulation (in use), the purchasing power of a dollar goes down. When the purchasing power is down, prices go up.

Purchasing power is a measure of how much the dollar is worth. If there is too much paper money out there, it is called inflation. What do you think deflation is? If you guessed it is when there is too little paper money, you guessed right! This causes product prices to fall. Lucky for us, the Federal Reserve watches the money each day. If it looks as if there is too much or too little, they can do things to fix it.

title: Celebrate Massachusetts Statehood With Some Famous Faces
