text: There are still some working steam railroads around today like this one in Utah. Most are tourist attractions.

title: Getting Organized
text:
Is your backpack overflowing with papers? Is your desk stuffed to the brim? It’s time to get organized!

We all need to be a little organized in life. We need to know where to put our assignments and where to find our homework. But getting organized will take some effort. It will take some practice to come up with a system that works for you. Here are some ways to become more organized. Avoid Clutter. It’s very easy to collect clutter in your backpack and desk. Avoid doing this. It will be easier to find assignments. Have some folders where you can put school announcements or tests that have been graded. Throw anything away that has become outdated. Clean out your desk of all old assignments, broken pencils and dried-out markers. Prepare your backpack the night before. By doing this, you’ll be ready to go. No more scrambling around in the morning. Put in your notebooks, textbooks and planner (if you have one). Use one calendar. If you have a planner, you can use that. Write down when your assignments are due. Also, write down any other activities you have. Put down family activities, too! Write everything down so you can remember it. Organize your notebooks. Color-code them if you need to. Choose one color for each subject. Now you can quickly spot the correct notebook. Also, write your name inside the notebook, in case it gets lost. Choose a good study space. Make it clear to your family that this is where you’ll be studying. Have extra pens, pencils and paper in the area. It should have room for all of your books. It should also be away from distractions like the television. Now that you have some ideas for getting organized, try some of them out. You may be surprised at what a difference it makes in your study habits!

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you are a famous scientist and you have been commissioned to develop a wonderful new form of transportation. In fewer than 150 words, tell of your invention and how and where it would take you. Don’t forget to describe it and tell what it uses for fuel.

title: The Wonderful Horse
text: The early 1800s in the United States saw rapid growth and many new ideas in technology. This was called the Industrial Revolution. There were new steam-powered cars. There were new railroads. Even still, the horse was in great demand for travel. Horses pulled carriages and omnibuses. An omnibus was a large bus used to carry many people within the city. Horses also pulled stagecoaches. Not all towns were connected by the steam railways yet. Horses were also used to carry people between the towns and the trains. Horses also helped make the Erie Canal. They pulled supplies to the workers. Horses helped when the Erie Canal was finished. They pulled the barges full of people along the canal. Horses were largely replaced by railroads and farm machinery in the eastern United States. But, horses were still important in the West. They were used there for travel by stage. Stage horses in America lived hard lives. They were usually treated with respect. They were very well cared for. The average life of a stagecoach horse in America was much longer than those in England. The horses averaged only three years of work in England. A horse working in California pulled almost a quarter of a million miles while in harness. The horse may have worked for about 15 years. What are some things horses are still used for today? Have you ridden a horse?

title: Millions Immigrate to America
text:
More than 6 million people immigrated to the United States between the 1820s and the Civil War. Immigrate means that people move to a country where they were not born. Most of these early immigrants were from northern and western Europe. People immigrate for many reasons. It was largely due to ad programs before the 1850s. Americans wanted people to move here. Many Europeans had very hard lives in their home countries. The ads looked good to many people who wanted a better life. The popular ballad below describes the campaign.

Of all the mighty nations in the East or in the West,
O This glorious Yankee nation is the greatest and the best,
We have room for all creation and our banner is unfurled,
Here's a general invitation to the people of the world.
Come along, come along, make no delay,
Come from every nation, come from every way
Our lands they are broad enough, don't be alarmed
For Uncle Sam is rich enough to give us all a farm.

People in many countries took that invitation. Soon Ellis Island became the main gateway for immigrants. Many ships could be seen on any given day on New York Harbor. The ships were all from different countries!

The westward movement was helped by the surge of new people. The larger America grew, the more people were needed to settle it. These immigrants brought energy and drive. They also brought many skills. Many of the people were farmers. There were also merchants and furniture makers. They brought knowledge with them, too. They brought new medicine. They brought new ideas about science and law. The United States wouldn't be the same without them!

At first, anyone who desired to come to America was allowed. This didn't last very long though. Not all of the people in America were happy about the newcomers. About 1.5 million Europeans arrived in the 1850s. A wave of Irish followed the Germans and Poles. They wanted to escape the potato famine in Ireland. Many people died because of the famine. The people came and filled many jobs. They worked to build bridges, roads and canals. Most crowded into Eastern cities like New York and Boston. They were too poor to move westward. Many Americans feared the loss of their jobs. They also feared such large numbers of foreign people. Antiforeign feelings began to grow.

New York state took over a large building in New York City to handle all the new people. The building was Castle Garden. Immigration at Castle Garden was handled loosely. Some people who came were very sick. Some were even criminals. They bribed corrupt officials to be allowed entrance. Other immigrants became victims. Their belongings were easily stolen. They were often hurried into poor work contracts as well.

The U.S. government took over to help solve these problems. President Benjamin Harrison declared Ellis Island the Federal Immigration Center in April 1890. The ceremonies to open Ellis Island were held on Jan. 1, 1892.

The first immigrant to set foot on Ellis Island was Annie Moore. She was from County Cork, Ireland, and she was only 15. Annie and her two brothers were joining their parents. Their parents had come to America three long years before them.

The largest wave of immigration was between 1892 and 1901. Millions poured into Ellis Island during this time. These people left behind poverty, hunger and despair. They had nothing to lose. Ellis Island became a symbol of hope.

title: Find Your Roots at Ellis Island
text:
Millions of immigrants were processed at Ellis Island between 1892 and 1954. Forty percent of Americans living today can trace their roots to ancestors who came through Ellis Island. How many of you have ancestors who came through Ellis Island?

Many of us want to know who our ancestors are and where they came from. Searching the records at Ellis Island could help. Many know their ancestors came through Ellis Island. It's much harder to find where their ancestors came from though. Without knowing that information, it is impossible to search further.

The search for your ancestors is called genealogy. The Statue of Liberty-Ellis Island Foundation made a new facility to provide help and guidance in that search. It is for adults and children who are doing genealogy work.

Hundreds of volunteers entered data into computers. The data shows 11 fields of information including:

Immigrant's given name (first name at birth)

Immigrant's surname (last name)

Ship's name

Port of origin (where the ship came from)

Arrival date

Number of the line the name appears on registry

Gender (male or female)

Marital status

Nationality

Last residence (town and county)

These records will help people who are doing genealogy work to find their ancestors.

The foundation has made a records search available to everyone online. You can search for a name by going to www.ellisisland.org.

title: Immigrants Come to Massachusetts
text:
By the 1840s, nearly one-half of Boston was populated by Irish immigrants. Leaving famine in their homelands, they arrived looking for work in the growing factories of Massachusetts. Immigrants also came to Massachusetts from Poland, Russia, Greece, Scandinavia, Slovakia, Germany, Canada, Italy and Portugal.

Ellis Island Immigration Center

Ellis Island is a symbol of America's immigrant heritage. Over 12 million people passed through Ellis Island from 1892 to 1954.

As the immigrants arrived by ship, hundreds of poor were confined below deck. Only first- and second-class passengers were on deck to see the Statue of Liberty. It was welcoming them to America. Those same passengers were the first to be processed, often right aboard ship. The others were ferried to Ellis Island. When they got there they were examined and questioned. Processing is the word used to describe the many examinations each person had to pass. They had to pass all of them before being let in. Not everyone was allowed. During those years, around 250,000 were sent back to their homeland.

The majority of those who came were men. Many came to America to find steady work. They would later send money for family members to follow. The countries they came from were numerous. Most claimed European ancestry. Others came from Asia, the West Indies and the Middle East.

Those who arrived often waited on barges for hours to be processed. They were told to drop their belongings in a large pile. The men were sent in one direction and the women and children went another. It was a frightening experience. Many wondered if they would be able to find each other again.

Medical Inspection

Medical inspection began as soon as they came into the Registry Room. Doctors watched carefully for signs of diseases. If the doctor found any signs, they would mark their clothing with chalk. "E" stood for eyes, "L" for lameness, or "H" for heart. Those who had mental ailments were marked with an "X." Marked immigrants were pulled from the line and sent to examination rooms. There they were checked and tested. Many were sent to the hospital for care. Those who recovered were allowed to land. Those who did not were deported to their home country.

Immigrants Suffer Poor Living and Working Conditions

Most immigrants were happy to find work of any kind. This changed the labor force greatly. The new people took low paying jobs. They often settled for bad working conditions and poor treatment.

The people settled in tenement houses. These houses were several stories high. They often housed as many as 500 people. Many families shared one apartment. Four or five families would share one bathroom. Laborers worked for small wages. Whole families worked just to survive. Children as young as 6 were sent to work.

The conditions in these factories were usually awful. The hours were long too. The buildings were very overcrowded. It wasn't long before workers got fed up. They began to discuss the need for better working conditions.

They formed labor unions to fight the factory owners for more freedom. A union is a group of people who join together to protect the rights of the worker. The unions discussed a strike to protest their treatment. A strike meant that they would all walk out and stop working.

The Lawrence strike in 1912 was the most notable in Massachusetts history. It began over a pay cut. The workers were mostly young women from 14 to 18. They were already hurting from lack of food and sleep. Some of these young women walked off the job. Twenty thousand people joined the strike on Jan. 12, 1912. The factory owners were angry about the strike. They asked the city for help.The city called for state troopers to come in. A young man and a young woman were killed when this happened. Strikers began to send their children out of town for safety. These fleeing children brought national attention to the strike, so the local government declared that no more children would be allowed to leave. People around the country began to support the strikers.

The strike was successful, and in March the owners increased their pay.

title: Your Growing Business
text:
Pretend you are the owner of a small company. Your business is making more money every year. You have a steady stream of business. Business is going so well that you decide it is time to expand your company.

You begin to research the options you have to help your company grow. You realize you need more money to get your ideas off the ground. You know you do not have enough to afford the expansion. You could borrow money from a bank. But then you will be in debt. Maybe you could borrow money from family or friends. But you would still be in debt. And what would happen if your business ideas failed?

Companies face the same kinds of problems every day. There is nothing wrong with borrowing money from a bank. But companies should only borrow money if they are sure they can pay the bank back. Many companies decide to finance businesses by taking on new owners. This means that some companies sell part of their business. They sell it as shares or stocks. You become a stockholder when you purchase a stock. Stockholders are actually owners of the company. Businesses use the money they get from selling the stocks to expand their business. They hope to create a better company that will yield more profit.

The company may give dividends to stockholders. Dividends are a percentage of the company's profit. This is one way for investors to earn money when purchasing stocks. But they can also make a lot of money by buying and selling stocks. Do you know anyone who has made money in the stock market?

title: Worcester, Massachusetts
text:
Worcester is the second-largest city in all of New England. It has a population of about 180,000. It is also home to nine colleges and universities. The city hosts the University of Massachusetts Medical Center and the Massachusetts Biotechnology Research Park.

Worcester's growth really started during the Industrial Revolution. Many immigrants came from Europe and the Middle East to work in factories. The population was about 20 percent Swedish at the start of World War I. There was even a Swedish newspaper called Svea. It was read just as much as the English papers.

The Worcester Lunch Car Company made over 650 diner cars between 1906 and 1961. Some of the cars are still being used today. That is why Worcester is sometimes referred to as the diner capital of the world. While in town, order that diner burger or meat loaf and give it a try.

title: Who was Sam Ellis?
text:
The famous Ellis Island is named for the New Yorker who came into possession of the island and owned it until his death.

Sam was a loyalist, and moved to New Jersey after the Revolution. Upon his death, the island changed hands within the Ellis family several times. Samuel Ellis Ryerson, a grandson, sold the island to John Berry, who sold the island to New York state. In 1808, New York sold it to the federal government.

Ellis Island was known by many names before it became Sam Ellis' island. It was called Kioshk by the American Indians, Oyster Island by the Dutch and Gibbet Island by the English. After the War of 1812, it was renamed Fort Gibson.

Eventually, by the time it was considered as a site for the immigration center, it was called Ellis Island.

title: Gray Squirrel
text:
The gray squirrel is a noisy little friend. Did you know that not all of that chatter is idle? Sometimes it has specific meanings: a rapid kuk, kuk, kuk means immediate danger; a longer, drawn-out ku-uu- k, sounded every few seconds warns of less worrisome danger; a slow kuk-kuk-kuk means the danger has passed. Gray squirrels also send messages with their bushy tails.

Gray squirrels bear young in litters of two or three, twice a year. In late winter or spring, litters are usually born in tree hollows. Summer young can sometimes be found in leafy nests out along the end of a tree branch.

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you have succeeded in developing the car of the future. It's amazingly fast and efficient. In fewer than 200 words, tell of your invention and how and where it would take you. Don't forget to describe it and tell what it uses for fuel.

title: Keeping Deadlines
text:
Turning things in late only leads to stress. Take some time to stay ahead in your homework.

Every teacher will give you homework with a deadline. Sometimes, the homework is due the next day. When the project is big, it may be due in a few weeks. When that homework is given, it’s time to prepare yourself. You need to do a few things to turn that homework in on time. It’s all about keeping your deadlines.

Here are a few ways to stay ahead and keep on task.

1. Don’t procrastinate. Homework usually takes longer than you think it will. Start doing it as soon as possible. If you finish it early, you just have more time to make it better.

2. Break up big projects. Some projects may seem huge. Break them up into little pieces. Do you need to do some research for them? How about writing a report? Make a list of what you need to do. Try writing an outline for papers. Read a few chapters each day for a book report. Do something for the project every day before the deadline.

3. Keep a calendar with deadline dates. If you have a lot of homework, write down the deadlines on your calendar. Now you can see what’s due first. Find out which homework assignment will take the longest. Refer to the calendar often so you don’t forget.

title: Massachusetts Honors Inventors
text:
The United States had a huge growth in industry after the Civil War. Many inventions triggered this growth. These major inventions changed the lives of Americans forever. Massachusetts Studies Weekly - State History is proud to showcase some Massachusetts inventors. They helped the growth of American industry, technology and medicine.

Samuel Morse, 1, was born in what is now Boston. He invented the telegraph. It was an early way to send a message over long distances. A code was tapped out with a series of taps. Slow taps are called dashes. Quick taps are called dots. Each letter of the alphabet has a pattern of dots and/or dashes. The word "so" would be.

Alexander Graham Bell, 2, did many things in his life. He is best known for his patent on the telephone. Bell taught at Boston University for a bit. Do you think computers will one day replace telephones? Why or why not?

Robert Goddard, 3, dreamed of rockets and trips in outer space when he was young. He was raised in Worcester. He launched the world's first liquid-fuel rocket in 1926.

Fannie Farmer, 4, did not invent cooking. She was the first to use standard measurements in printed food recipes. This made cooking more uniform. Think of Fannie next time you ask someone for a recipe.

Eli Whitney, 5, was born in Westborough. He made the cotton gin in 1793. This machine took out seeds from cotton. It made the United States the world's leading cotton producer.

Edwin Land, 6, had 537 patents. That's more than any other person beside Thomas Edison. Land was founder of the Polaroid camera. He made the first instant-picture camera.

Ruth Wakefield, 7, is the legend who came up with chocolate chip cookies. Wakefield baked chocolate butter cookies at her Toll House Inn. Ruth was at the inn when she saw she was out of baker's chocolate. There was a chocolate bar handy so she cut it into small pieces. Wakefield was surprised when the chocolate didn't melt through the cookie. It held its shape! Isn't your mouth just watering? Today chocolate chip cookies are the best-selling cookies in the the United States.

Jan Ernest Matzeliger, 8, of Lynn, Massachusetts, dreamed of making a machine that could make shoes. Folks laughed at this former sailor. They said, "It can't be done!" He secretly worked on it for 10 years. Jan patented his machine. It could produce thousands of pairs of shoes in one day.

Elias Howe, 9, of Spencer built the first sewing machine. He did not market his own idea as well as Singer. Other companies stole his ideas too. Howe later went to court to sue for rights on his patent. The court was on his side. Howe was given royalties on each machine sold.

title: Clarity of Expression: FDR and the Four Freedoms
text:
For most people around the world, the years of economic depression and war between 1929 and 1945 were dark and dangerous. Resources such as food, clothing and fuel were in short supply. Families were often torn apart as parents looked for work, served in the armed forces, or as children were sent to safe, sheltered areas. It was a time of stress and hardship, when people desperately looked to leaders for safety and hope. In the United States, that leader was Franklin D. Roosevelt, our 32nd president who served from 1933 to 1945.

During that time of chaos, on Jan. 6, 1941, President Roosevelt delivered to Congress a historic speech, which we now call the Four Freedoms Speech. After years of economic depression, his words were not angry. When world war was happening, his tone was not fierce or mean. But knowing that there were still darker days of war to come for many, he spoke with passion about peace, good fortune, safety, and about the freedoms that humans everywhere deserve. "In the future days," Roosevelt said, "we look forward to a world founded upon four essential human freedoms." Even today those four freedoms are essential (important). Can you list them? They are: the freedom of speech and expression, the freedom of worship for every person, the freedom from wants such as hunger and lack of shelter and the freedom from fear.

How are we doing? Have we achieved those freedoms for everyone? Everywhere?

To read or listen to the entire speech, with the permission of a parent or teacher go www.americanrhetoric.com. To see the paintings by Norman Rockwell inspired by the Four Freedoms go www.archives.gov

title: How Do Inventors Protect Their Ideas?
text:
What does someone do when they think of a really terrific idea? That idea can become intellectual property. To help people think of new ideas, the legal system developed the definition of intellectual property to protect people's new ideas. There are four kinds of intellectual property. One is a patent. A patent is a grant issued by the federal government. It gives the inventor the right to be the only one to make, use or sell the invention in the United States for a certain period of time.

A trademark is a logo, slogan, symbol or design made especially for a product or service. Can you think of a trademark for a wellknown product?

A copyright protects the expression of ideas. That means if you wrote an awesome play or story, made a winning movie, took a fantastic picture or even made up a unique dance, it could be copyrighted. That way, only you had the right to reproduce it, or make copies.

A trade secret is something special a company knows or knows how to do. That something special may help them be a little ahead of their competition. A trade secret can be a chemical formula, a pattern for a machine or even a customer list.

Protecting a good idea is not a new idea. In fact, patenting began in Italy in 1421, 71 years before Columbus discovered the new world. Inventors who applied for patents wrote down all the details of their work. When it was approved, the patent office published them. This protected them from being copied for about 12 to 16 years.

A patent encourages invention. It publishes the latest technology for everyone to read. Many new ideas are built upon other ideas or inventions. Also, it gives the inventor time to profit from an idea before it can be copied.

Patents help to ensure that everyone can benefit from good ideas. Do you have any good ideas?

title: Inventors and Inventions
text:
National Toy Hall of Fame

Did you know there is a National Toy Hall of Fame? The people who create toys for enjoyment and pleasure are inventors too.

Graduating from Yale Medical College, then winning an Olympic medal weren't enough for A.C. Gilbert. His next ambition was dreamed up as he rode the train between New York City and New Haven each day. He noticed crews building steel towers for electric wires and he thought of making toys out of steel girders as well. He experimented with cardboard cutouts until he was satisfied, then had a metal shop make the first set. In 1913, Gilbert introduced the Erector Set. Today, the Erector Set is part of the National Toy Hall of Fame.

One well-known Hall of Famer is the yo-yo. Did you know the yo-yo is the second oldest toy in the world? (Dolls are the oldest.) Many believe that the yo-yo originated thousands of years ago in China. But at the same time it was being played with in other cultures on separate continents. The first historical record of a yo-yo was in 500 B.C. in Greece.

The yo-yo we play with today has been around for 70 years, and more than 600 million have been sold! The National Toy Hall of Fame encourages kids to invent toys too. How can you come up with an idea to invent a toy? Here are some ideas:

Ask a friend.

Visit toy stores.

Brainstorm with a paper and pencil.

Make an accessory to go with an existing toy.

Make an existing toy easier to play with.

Make a toy to go with a popular TV show.

The next step is to draw your design. Use a pencil and be sure to have an eraser on hand. After you are satisfied with your drawing, build it! (Then rebuild it and rebuild it, improving it each time!) Have friends and family play with it and make suggestions. Then rebuild it again.

After you have your final model, you must give it a name. It can be something that describes that toy, or a simple word to describe what it does or how it sounds.

What's next? Submit it in a science fair or to an invention convention.

Maybe it will be the next inductee into the National Toy Hall of Fame!

Massachusetts Leads in Technology

Sometimes inventions are by accident, like Ruth Wakefield's Toll House cookies. More often than not inventions are a result of education and research.

Some colleges and universities try very hard to attract people who are creative and adventurous. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology prepares students for high-tech business. The school combines education and research in many fields. They include medicine, communications, science and urban studies.

Is it any wonder then that most production in Massachusetts is of scientific equipment and measuring devices? Factories in the Boston area make equipment used for automatic machines. They also make equipment used in science labs.

Massachusetts is a leader in high-tech manufacturing today. That and many fine universities attract people interested in high-tech careers. Some of the best engineers and programmers in the world come out of Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

Many of the most recent inventions are high-tech. What kind of inventions will be created in the next decade? How many of you would like to become inventors?

title: The Stock Market
text:
When a company decides to sell shares, it first sells the stocks in a primary market. This is the first time stock is sold to the public. It is called an initial public offering (IPO). Then the stock moves to the secondary market, or the stock market. This means that the money made from selling the stock goes to the person selling it. It does not go to the original business.

There are many parts of the stock market. There are regional exchanges, which are smaller. They are like the exchanges in Los Angeles, Chicago and Boston. Some are large organized exchanges, like the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE). The New York Stock Exchange is located on Wall Street in New York City. The NYSE lists over 2,800 large and mid-sized companies. They are worth over $18 trillion.

Most stock markets have traders who make a living buying and selling stock. The NYSE has a trading floor where all of the shares are purchased. You have probably seen footage of Wall Street on the evening news. The news usually announces the day's Dow Jones Industrial Average. This is a mathematical calculation of 30 main stocks being sold. It gives a general overview of the market.

The stock market changes every day. It goes back to the concept of supply and demand. If a certain stock is popular, then the demand for that stock goes up. As the demand goes up, so does the price of the stock. If someone buys a stock at a low price and the price increases later, that person can make a profit. They can sell the same stock at the higher price. When prices keep going up, people call it a "bull market." People call it a "bear market" when the values keep dropping. Are we in a bull or bear market right now?

title: Franklin, Massachusetts
text:
Franklin was originally part of the town of Wrentham, which was settled in 1676. The settlers began to farm and graze animals there. They soon saw that waterpower was the best way to earn a living. Soon there were cotton mills, shoe factories and felt makers that relied on waterpower.

The city renamed itself Franklin on Feb. 16, 1778. This was done in honor of Benjamin Franklin. Ambassador Franklin was honored by this tribute. He sent the town a library of 116 books. It became the country's first public library. Franklin was also known for manufacturing straw bonnets.

Franklin has about 31,000 people living there today. As you might guess, the town of Franklin celebrates Ben Franklin's birthday each year. It is a time for the whole town to honor Benjamin Franklin's life, teachings, wisdom and gifts he gave to Franklin and all America.

title: What is a penny farthing?
text:
Once in a while, the name of something doesn't tell us much about what it is. This is surely the case of the penny farthing.

The penny farthing is also known as an ordinary. It is a type of bicycle. It was made in the 19th century. It had a very large front wheel and a very small back wheel. The seat was mounted over the large wheel. This made it so it could only be ridden by long-legged people. Soon, more practical bikes were designed. Pedal power became the rage in America and Europe.

title: Worm Snake
text:
The worm snake is a very small species of snake. It rarely reaches more than 12 inches long. They are a very plain brown, with a reddish-pink belly. The worm snake has a pointed head and small eyes, with a sharp spine on the tip of its tail.

Worm snakes are carnivorous. That means they are flesh eating. Though they occasionally may eat a salamander, slug or fly larvae, they usually eat earthworms.

Where can you find a worm snake? Look in moist woodland areas, probably under a rock or a log.

Worm snakes are harmless to humans and they are endangered; if you see one you should leave it alone.

title: Can You Make an Invention?
text: This is our invention, the fly gun. Now instead of swatting flies, you can just sit back and relax and aim your little swatter and fire away! Can you invent something? Submit your invention in a science fair or an invention convention.

text: Using the idea on the left, the fly gun, create your own invention on paper that will make life easier for someone. Use diagrams and notes to explain how your invention works. Remember to use a fine black marker, not a pencil.

title: The Three Branches of Massachusetts Government
text:
Both the federal government and Massachusetts use the principle of checks and balances.

The men who wrote the Constitution of the United States were called the Founding Fathers. They were very concerned about the balance of power between the state and federal governments. Some believed that under the Articles of Confederation, we were united states, but not really a nation. The Founders wanted the powers to be correctly divided to protect the rights of each person in this country. When the Founders completed the Constitution, the powers given to the national government were very important. They were carefully selected. The Constitution lists only 20. These include:

powers relating to foreign affairs

war

managing interstate commerce

national security

federal taxes

naturalization

patents

bankruptcy laws

federal land management

handling of federal finances

coinage of money

fixing weights and measures

setting up federal courts

establishing post offices

crime on the high seas

The Founders placed the national government over states to coordinate national affairs. They still wanted the states to control their own affairs with no help from the national government. James Inedell said of the new government, "When this government is adopted, there will be two governments to which we shall owe obedience - to the government of the Union, in certain defined cases - to our own state government in every other case."

It is important to know how a state government works. It helps people to know their rights. The state constitution of Massachusetts is the law. It contains the rules for our state. The constitution of Massachusetts was called "a glorious covenant." It was written in 1780. It is the world's oldest written constitution still in use.

The federal government has three branches that work together to carry out laws. Our state government is the very same. Those branches are the executive branch, the legislative branch and the judicial branch. Study the diagram to the left to see the branches of the Massachusetts government. The chart also show you what their jobs are.

title: The State House Today
text:
Did you know that the Massachusetts State House with the golden dome wasn't the first State House? The old State House can still be seen today! It is at the corner of Washington and State streets. It was built in 1713. It was used as the home for the Royal government of the Colony of Massachusetts. It became the home of the government of the state of Massachusetts after the Revolution.

It wasn't long before state leaders decided a larger State House was needed. The new site was chosen near Beacon Hill. Charles Bulfinch was the designer. He was a native of our state.

The new State House was finished on Jan. 11, 1798. It was one of the greatest buildings in the country. It is a red-brick building with white columns, topped with a large dome. The Paul Revere Company covered the dome with copper when the roof became leaky. The dome was gilded with real gold leaf in 1874.

The original Bulfinch State House is still the central part of the building. Many rooms have been added though. Would you like to take a tour? Go to http://www.sec.state.ma.us/trs/trsbo/trstour.htm. There you will learn about each room in the State House. All the art was done by kids.

title: Governor Charlie Baker
text:
Massachusetts has had over 70 governors. The first was John Hancock. Today, our governor is Charlie Baker.

Governor Baker grew up in Needham, Massachusetts. He went to Harvard for college and started to work helping businesses improve. He decided to help our state. Charlie Baker was elected governor in 2014.

Governor Baker works hard to make Massachusetts a great place to live. He is trying to help schools and create more jobs for people who live here. Baker is working to pass laws that will make our towns and cities safer.

Charlie Baker and his wife, Lauren, live in Swampscott. Their three children are Charlie, AJ and Caroline.

title: Massachusetts Government
text:
Massachusetts Constitution Bingo

The players in this game must write the words listed on their Bingo board in the boxes. There are 16 boxes and there are 20 words, so four of the words will not be used. Write the words in any box that you choose, in any order you choose. The game leader will read one clue at a time. The players must find the answer to that question and cross out or color the box that has the answer. The first one to get four boxes crossed out in a row, diagonally, vertically or horizontally, is the winner and shouts BINGO! You can get more mileage from the bingo board by making x's for the first game, o's for the second game, then color in the third game. Another variation is to play "blackout." The first to completely fill the board wins.

Words And Definitions

Unconstitutional - something that is contrary to the Constitution

Senator - member of the legislature, there are 40 members

Representative - member of the legislature, there are 160 members

Taxes - money citizens pay to fund government

Executive - branch of government that enforces laws

Legislative - the branch of the government that makes the laws

Judicial - branch of government that decides if laws are constitutional

Amendments - changes or additions to a constitution

Veto - governor rejects a bill passed by the legislature

Governor - the top official in the executive branch

Ratify - approval of a bill by the legislature

Freedom - the most important guaranteed right in our Constitution

Citizenship - the position of membership in a state or country

Document - the piece of paper on which the Constitution is written

Supreme Court - there are seven justices in this court of the judicial branch

Lieutenant Governor - becomes the acting governor in the event that the governor cannot fulfill duties

Election - the act of voting people into office

General Court - otherwise known as the legislature, is made up of the senators and representatives

Appeals Court - this court in the judicial branch hears cases from people who are requesting a change in the court's decision.

1780 - the year that the Massachusetts Constitution was adopted

title: Economics Competition
text:
Have you ever played on a sports team? Maybe you played soccer, basketball or baseball. If so, then you know the best way to become a winning team. Each player must play the best he or she can. Everyone must work together.

This same kind of competition is in a marketplace. Producers compete against each other. They try to give customers the best prices and products for their money. Monopolistic competition is when businesses offer similar products. The products are not identical, though. Each business can raise or lower its price. Each tries to reach a price where it can sell the most products. This is why economists call these businesses "price searchers."

An oligopoly is a market where a few (usually three to five) companies control the competition. They provide the most products. For example, airplane manufacturing is very hard and so only a few large companies compete against each other. When there is only one seller of a product, it is called a monopoly. No companies are making a product to use instead of this product, so there is no competition.The company can charge whatever price it wants, because customers have to buy their product.

A monopsony is a market that has only one buyer. Sellers will compete with one another to make the best quality product. They try to offer this product at the best price. An example would be the U.S. government. They are the only buyers for aircraft carriers in this country. Businesses compete to make the best aircraft carriers. But there is only one buyer.

Now that you know about the different kinds of markets, can you decide which one you would prefer for a business you owned?

title: Amesbury, Massachusetts
text:
Welcome to the town of Amesbury, Massachusetts! It is located along the Merrimack River. Amesbury is famous for its textile industry, not farming. This is due to the many mills that were built along the Powow River Falls in the early 1800s.

Amesbury is often called Carriage Town. There used to be a lot of carriage-making shops in the town. Beginning in the 1840s, thousands of carriages were made here. Look for some on display as you walk around town.

Amesbury was also the home to the Merrimac Hat Company. It was founded in 1838.

Do you like peanut butter? Then you would have loved Hoyt's Buffalo Brand Peanut Butter Kisses. The kisses were the nation's number one candy for a time.

If you ever visit Amesbury be sure to see "The Doughboy." He rests in front of Amesbury Middle School on Main Street. The statue was made by Leonard Craske. It is a tribute to all the Amesbury soldiers who fought in World War I. You shouldn't miss it.

title: What’s the difference between “capitol” and “capital?”
text:
We don't know why they made it so confusing for us, but the actual building is the capiTOL. The city in which the capiTOL is found is the capiTAL. To help you remember, close your eyes and think of taking a trip to our capiTAL on the long roads from your house to Boston. Those roads are the sides of the letter "A."

Now think of the building itself. Your dad is looking for a parking place so you can all stop and go inside our beautiful capiTOL. The circles he keeps driving in to find a parking spot resemble the "O" in capitol. Does that help?

title: White-Tailed Deer
text:
This guy lives all over the United States except most of southwestern states. The underside of its tail (white, of course!) acts as a flag to other animals. If the deer senses danger, it will spread its tail in the air as a warning to other deer. The bright tail also helps a fawn follow its mother in flight.

Two fawns, born in the spring, are the usual size of a brood. The young have redbrown fur flecked with white spots that disappear during their first winter. They like to eat green plants, acorns, twigs and all kinds of nuts.

Females have no antlers. Males begin growing them several months after birth. They shed them each winter and develop them again each spring and summer. It's a myth that one can tell the age of a deer by the size or number of points on the antlers. Antler size is determined by what the deer eats, not by its age.

title: Let's Write
text:
Here at Massachusetts Studies Weekly, writing about history is definitely our favorite thing to do. The hardest part is choosing which historic events to write about. We’d like to invite you to be a junior historian.

In fewer than 150 words, choose five things from the past to share with other students in Massachusetts. You may choose to write about people, places or historic events. Tell about your choices and why you chose those special events.

title: How Do I Take a Test?
text:
Do you get sweaty palms and butterflies in your stomach over the idea of taking a test? That happens to everyone at one time or another. Did you know test anxiety comes from a lack of self-confidence? How can you improve your self-confidence and improve your test-taking skills? The best way is to know the material very well. But here are some other important ideas that may help you:

Preview the test. What does it cover? How long is it? Plan your time. Decide how much time you can spend on each section. Keep track of the time as you take the test. Follow directions. Read all the directions and listen carefully to any directions read aloud. Read the questions carefully. Look for keywords such as “when,” “where,” “why,” “different from,” “same as,” “before” and “after.” Don’t get stuck on one question. If you can’t think of an answer, skip it and return to it later when you have finished the rest of the test. Check your work. If you have time left after you finish the test, go back and double-check your work. Use this list while taking this week’s Studies Weekly quiz. Practice good test-taking skills. You may want to use this list for the next few weeks until you have mastered the skills.

title: Massachusetts as a Cultural Center
text:
History is just one way to study people over time. Studying their ideas, artifacts, literature and their values is another way to get to know the people of Massachusetts long ago and to celebrate the people we are today.

The study of literature, art, music, languages and theater are all part of what we call humanities. The arts bring joy and meaning to our lives. Let's explore some of the arts that make Massachusetts such a great place to live.

Performing Arts

Massachusetts boasts several opera companies and two major symphony orchestras. It also has major dance companies and several professional theater companies.

The Boston Symphony Orchestra (BSO) and the Boston Pops Orchestra are known throughout the world. Have you been to Tanglewood for a summer concert? Tanglewood is the summer home of the BSO. It's fun to sit out on the lawn and listen to the "1812 Overture." They might even use fireworks under the stars.

Ballet is a performing art that many enjoy. "The Nutcracker" is performed each year by the Boston Ballet. Travel to Lee to attend the Jacob's Pillow Dance Festival. Leading dance companies have performed there for more than 50 years.

The Williamstown Theatre Festival, Chester Theatre Company and the Berkshire Theatre Festival in Stockbridge present plays throughout the summer. What plays have you seen lately? You may have even done a bit of acting, singing or dancing yourself. Did you know that the Watertown Children's Theatre features about 100 children from ages 5 to 15? They all act and sing in musicals. They also perform for schools for the deaf. The words are interpreted into American Sign Language.

Maybe you've had the chance to see a wooden performer? Puppet shows are staged yearround at the Puppet Showplace Theatre in Brookline.

Visual Arts

Visual Arts are an important part of our lives. Massachusetts is the birthplace and workplace of several famous artists.

You may have visited the Whistler House Museum of Art. It is the birthplace of artist James McNeill Whistler. He is best known for his painting, "Whistler's Mother."

You can see the works of two more famous Bostonian artists at the Museum of Fine Arts. John Singleton Copley was born in Boston in 1738. He is known as America's first great portrait painter. His portraits of John Hancock and Paul Revere hang in the Museum of Fine Arts.

John Singer Sargent lived about 100 years after Copley. He studied in France. There, he worked with the French artist Claude Monet. He returned to Boston at the peak of his career. Much of the decorative painting in the Museum of Fine Arts was done by Sargent.

Museums

Massachusetts has been a cultural center since its early days. The state has many museums. Not all museums are just for looking. Some are for doing things. The Boston Children's Museum is just the place for hands-on activities. Have you been there? Boston's Museum of Science also provides some hands-on activities. It also has a planetarium. Maybe you can go see one of the star tours. The New England Aquarium is a live museum. Stop by to visit more than 2,000 species of marine life.

title: Kershner Conducts the Pops at 18
text:
Imagine conducting the Boston Pops at 18 years old. That dream came true for young Braeden Kershner. He was an 18-year-old high school senior from Goose Creek, South Carolina.

Braeden was a music student. He played more than a dozen different instruments. His dream to conduct the Pops came true in South Carolina.The Boston Pops were on a two-week swing tour there.

Kershner had to plan well in advance for this to happen. He contacted the Pops one year prior to his debut. He was told that the donation price to be a guest conductor was $10,000. WOW! How could one teenager earn so much money? Braeden decided to give it his best shot! He worked the third shift at the Waffle- House. During the summer he mowed lawns. He delivered pizzas and tutored music students. Braeden contacted the office of the Pops after many months. He told them he had raised half of the money needed to conduct. The officials of the Boston Pops were very impressed. The fund raising department decided to help out. Mr. Kershner was able to conduct after all! The Pops even agreed that Braeden Kershner should keep his hard-earned money to use for college.

title: Massachusetts Sports
text:
What do Massachusetts folks do for fun? The people here do plenty. The state is home to many famous sports teams. A few sports were even invented here. Volleyball was invented in Holyoke in 1895. Basketball was played for the first time in 1891. Peach baskets were hung 10 feet high on a gym balcony. Players tossed a ball in the basket and the rest is history. Today we can enjoy basketball at its finest. Head to the TD Garden to watch the Boston Celtics.

The Celtics are a legendary basketball team. They have 36 Hall of Famers and 17 NBA Championships! The Celtics have more banners than any other NBA team except the Los Angeles Lakers who also have 17.

The Bruins are our hockey team. It was the first American NHL team when they formed in 1924. They captured the first of six Stanley Cups in 1929.

The Boston Red Sox are our baseball team. The team began more than 100 years ago. They were also called the Americans and the Pilgrims. The first games only cost 25 cents to attend! "Big Papi" David Ortiz led the Sox against the New York Yankees and helped end the "Curse of the Bambino,ˮ bringing Boston two more titles, for a total of seven.

The New England Patriots are the NFL football team from Massachusetts. The Patriots were organized in 1959. They first played on the Boston University Field. The team moved to Fenway Park in 1963. They moved to Gillette Stadium in 1971. It seats more than 68,000 people. How many people are in your class? How many of your classes would it take to fill up the Gillette Stadium? The Patriots are winners of six Super Bowls thanks to superstar Tom Brady.

title: Massachusetts For Kids
text:
The Higgins Armory Museum - Worcester

At Higgins Armory you can actually try on a helmet or full suit of armor (if you're big enough). There might be some big enough for your mom or dad. Higgins Armory has a really amazing collection. It's not something you come across very often. The Castle Quest has costumes for everyone. You could be a prince or princess. You could even be a queen or king.

Butterfly Place at Papillon Park - Westford

Papillon means "butterfly" in French. This is the place to go see the butterflies. It is a huge solar dome with many kinds of plants to please our friends. There are hundreds of butterflies there. They flutter above flowers and through plants. They will even fly right up to you. See how many kinds of butterflies you can identify.

Museum of Science - Boston

This is a huge museum. School children visit from Massachusetts every year. Maybe you have been there already. The museum is found at the mouth of the Charles River. It includes over 6,000 interactive things for you to do. Explore the world of X-rays, check out fossils and take a ride in the simulator. There is a vertical maze too. You can even see a live animal show. What's your favorite?

The Bridge of Flowers - Shelburne

Just off of Route 2 in Shelburne Falls is the Bridge of Flowers. It is very beautiful in July and August. It's a nice place to take a stroll with your family. The bridge is a 400-foot retired trolley bridge. It has been fully planted with many flowers. While you are there you should visit the Salmon Falls. They have the country's most glacial potholes. The potholes were formed by glaciers from the Ice Age.

Lantern Tour - Legends and Lore - Plymouth

Plymouth has much to offer for the whole family. A historian would be in heaven! A different twist on the historical tour is the Lantern Tour. It goes through the streets of Plymouth. You carry your own punched tin lantern as you walk through Plymouth. As you walk you will learn the chilling legends of Plymouth.

title: Free Enterprise
text:
Have you ever heard the term free enterprise? What does it mean? Free enterprise refers to a market economy. When people in the market have their own ways to make and sell a product, it is called a market economy. The United States has a free enterprise system. Free enterprise markets only work if the laws of a country and the values of its citizens support them. If this type of market doesn't exist, then the system will fail.

Four pillars keep our free enterprise market standing. We will talk about the first two pillars today. They are private property and the price system.

Private Property - Do you own a bike, a board game or a CD player? Did you know that these things are considered your private property? That's right! This means that you are responsible for your own property. If you don't take good care of your things, no one else will. You must pay to have your things replaced or fixed.

Private property is the first pillar in the free enterprise system. It influences all of us to care for the things we own, or provides us with incentive. Incentive is what motivates us to make the decisions we make. If a business does not take care of its office building or breaks the equipment, it must pay to replace them. This gives the business incentive to take good care of the things it uses.

Price System - Prices provide guidance for producers and consumers. They show the market how much customers value the producer's goods. They also provide clues for economists about whether a market is healthy or not.

Prices also provide incentives for businesses and consumers. For example, most consumers try to shop for bargains if prices rise. Maybe consumers buy many packets of something because it is on sale. Can you think of other ways private property and the price system affect our economy?

title: Brockton, Massachusetts
text:
Did you know Brockton, Massachusetts, is known as the "City of Champions?" That's right! Brockton is the hometown of two world boxing champs. Rocky Marciano and "Marvelous" Marvin Hagler are both from there.

Rocky was the World Heavyweight Champion from 1952 to 1956. He is the only champion in history to have a perfect record. He never lost a single match. "He was a man of courage inside the ring. Outside, he was kind and gentle." said Jersey Joe Walcott. Joe lost his title to Marciano.

"Marvelous" Marvin Hagler became the Middleweight Champion of the World in 1980. He won the title in Wembly, England. Both athletes are greatly loved in Brockton. There are tributes scattered around the city.

Brockton is one of the two county seats of Plymouth County. Come visit this city of champions!

title: What is a pugilist?
text: A pugilist (pyu-juh-list) is a person who boxes. Did you know that Rocky Marciano of Brockton, Massachusetts, was the only undefeated, heavyweight champion in boxing history? Marciano, who died in 1969, began his boxing career while serving in the U.S. Army during World War II. By 1952, he had become the heavyweight champion. When he retired in 1956, he had a record of 49-0, with 43 knockouts! This famous Massachusetts pugilist is considered one of the hardest punchers in boxing history.

title: The Bobcat
text:
Don't count on seeing this critter near the highways or houses. Try the forests of Massachusetts instead.

The bobcat is a carnivore. It is in the cat family. It is about 35 inches long. The cat is brown with black spots and stripes. The bobcat is an interesting looking fella. It has pointed tufts on the top its ears. It also has a black-tipped and stubby tail. It lives in shrubby areas in the west. Here it lives in swamps and forests. The bobcat is nocturnal. That means it is active at night.

title: Let's Write
text:
Have you ever written a poem? Then you know how hard it can be to find words that rhyme and still have the meaning you desire for your poem. This week we would like to practice rhyming by a fill-in-the-blank exercise. Just find the word or words that rhyme with the phrases below. Roses are red, violets are blue, ________________________________
I think I saw, a thing _____ ____.
One - two, ____ ____ ____
Three - four, ____ ____ ____.

title: Plagiarism
text:
Plagiarism is a long word and it’s hard to spell. But it’s very important you know and understand its meaning.

To plagiarize something is to steal another person’s writings, thoughts or inventions.

It means to take credit for that person’s ideas. This practice is dishonest, even if the writings have never been published. Another word for plagiarism is “copying.” In many schools, a student can be kicked out for plagiarizing. We should never steal another person’s ideas. There are many ways to avoid plagiarism. Let’s look at some ideas you can use to become a writer who doesn’t plagiarize. By doing these things, you can always be confident in your work.

• Paraphrase, or re-write in your own words. Read what several different writers say on the subject. Then write your version of what they’ve written.

• Use quotations. It’s perfectly okay to state what another person has written on a subject. You just need to give credit to that person. Here’s an example: As Huckleberry Finn said to his buddy, Tom Sawyer, “. . . . .”

• Your opinion. What you think about a subject is what really matters. Read about the subject first. Then put down on paper what you truly feel about it!

Your teachers really want you to succeed. If you worry your writing is not what you’d like it to be, ask your teacher for advice. You will never lose marks for asking a teacher questions.

title: Massachusetts Today
text:
Massachusetts has a very rich past. It is sometimes hard to look to our future. The state is nearly 400 years old!

High-tech industries will be a big part of our future. The business is drawn here due to the fine universities. These schools for higher learning began about 400 years ago! Let's look at the state today. We will compare the work force and environment of today to the past.

Massachusetts led the Industrial Revolution long ago. Manufacturing was the most important industry in Massachusetts for about 100 years. The machines used for making shoes wore out and broke down. Better machines and parts were built as a result. Machine industries sprang up in Boston, Springfield and Worcester. The textile and shoe industries began to move south in the 1920s. They were looking for cheaper labor. Look at the graph. See how much of the workforce is part of the manufacturing industry today. You can see it makes up 22 percent of the whole economy. The state's manufacturing is focused on machinery. We produce many computers and office machines. Other industries include printing and paper goods. The state also has a large transportation industry. Chemicals, plastic goods and processed food are also made here.

It's hard for Massachusetts to compete with the farms of the Midwest. Less than 14 percent of the state is farmland today. Farms here tend to be small. There isn't much room for a farm in the city. Cranberries are the second-biggest crop in the state. What do you think is first? Flowers and shrubs.

What about farming the ocean? There used to be many fishing boats sailing our waters. Now sea scallops make up a big part of Massachusetts' fishing industry. Farming and fishing together only make up 1 percent of the economy. Massachusetts is still a leading fishing state though. New Bedford, Gloucester and Boston are some of the busiest fishing ports in the country.

Look at the graph. What is the largest percent of the state's economy? It is called the service industry. You will see three sections on the map called Wholesale/Retail, Finance/Insurance and General Services. These three things combine to form the services industry. They make up more than three-quarters of the total.

There are many different fields of service. Service includes education, healthcare and law. There is also wholesale and retail, government and finance. Wholesale trade is selling goods to businesses. Retail trade is selling goods to a private buyer like you or me.

Tourism is a huge industry too. It provides a great deal of income for the state. People come here to see history. There is plenty to see in Boston alone. Tourists come to see Plymouth or Salem. Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard are hot spots as well. Tourists visit many of our many beaches too. Try Cape Ann and Cape Cod for fun vacation spots.

Massachusetts today is like a treasure chest. It is rich in culture and history. Bay Staters are proud to be building a future as grand as the past.

title: Boom to Bust and Back Again
text:
You may have heard people compare the recent economic recession (2007-2009) to the Great Depression of the 1930s. But what some people call the "Great Recession" actually had more in common with a depression in the 1890s and something called "boom and bust."

In the early 1890s, the U.S. economy grew quickly ("boomed") but couldn't keep growing at that rate. When many companies and the housing market failed, there was an economic "bust." The railroad industry had been booming since the end of the Civil War, but in the 1890s more than 150 railroad companies closed. Other industries that depended on the railroads closed, and many people lost their jobs. Over 500 banks closed. Thousands of unemployed men marched to Washington, D.C., in 1894 to demand that the government take action to help families. Unemployment was over 10 percent for most of the 1890s. About one of every ten people had no job.

In the recent recession, the housing market slumped after several "boom" years. Some automakers went out of business and others filed for bankruptcy. The economy went "bust," just as it did in the 1890s. Hundreds of banks and thousands of businesses closed. The unemployment rate was about 8 percent - about one of every twelve people had no job.

Make a chart or Venn diagram that compares these two events in history. (Teachers: You can find background information and activities that relate to this article at hnn.us)

title: Massachusetts Conservation
text:
Massachusetts is one of the smallest states in the country. It has many people though. It has more people than all but 13 other states. There are a lot of people in a small space. We must have a plan to conserve our natural resources. Conservation is the wise use of these resources. We need to protect our forests, rivers and minerals.

Several state organizations were reorganized in 1990. The Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) was born. The DEP is in charge of water and air quality. They also take care of the cities' waste.

Air Quality

Few of the state's counties met the air standards for the federal government before 1990.

Our state made the control of toxic air pollutants a must in 1986. Companies had to reduce their pollution. The toxic gases being released into the air were lowered by about one-half in the 1990s. Springfield, Lowell and Boston face the greatest challenge. They are heavily populated. The towns are also home to many industries. Air quality is getting better though. Thanks to new state laws we can all breathe easy in the future.

Waste Management

The "right to know" law was passed in 1984. It was one of the first in the nation. The law makes a business provide lists of the toxins they release each year. Many of our laws about toxic wastes are more strict than the federal laws.

Massachusetts was also one of the first states to address the problem of household hazardous wastes. These wastes include paint thinner and used motor oil. Ask your parents to tell you the right way they dispose of these things.

Water Quality

The state's biggest conservation challenge has been Boston Harbor. Boston Harbor has been very polluted for a long time. It was one of the worst in the country.

Untreated sewage filled the harbor. It came from homes and factories near the harbor. Two new sewage plants were built in the 1950s. The problem did not go away though. Fish from the harbor became poisoned. In 1984, 14,000 workers in the fishing industry lost their jobs. The Massachusetts Water Resource Authority (MWRA) was organized in 1984. It was formed to clean up the water. The clean-up was well underway by the early 1990s. Boston Harbor has improved a lot today. There is still much to be done.

The people have have had to think of many new ways to help. Environmental issues are still a problem. Efforts to restore the land never stop. Our state has the power to show the nation the way to a more healthy environment.

title: Market Competition and Entrepreneurship
text:
Last week, we talked about the first two pillars of free enterprise. These pillars are private property (rights that allow us to own things) and the price system, which helps value and ration scarce goods. You might already know that there is more than one way to divide our resources among all of the consumers. One way is through market competition. It is the third pillar of the free enterprise system. This week we will finish talking about the last two pillars - market competition and entrepreneurship.

Market Competition - Do you remember when we talked about scarcity? Scarcity happens when products and resources are rare. Sometimes we want more of something than is available for us to have. Markets have this same kind of competition. Businesses compete every day for resources and products. They also compete for consumers.

Businesses create competition in the economy when they offer money for resources they want. Maybe they are offering money for machines they need. Or maybe they need skilled workers. Did you know that the more skills and education you have, the more companies will compete for you to work for them? Think of that! As you compete to get a job, companies are competing for the best-trained workers, too.

Businesses also compete for products and profit. They mostly do this by keeping their production prices low. They also do this by advertising (or telling people about) their products. Businesses compete with other businesses that have similar products.

Entrepreneurship - The last pillar under free enterprise is entrepreneurship. Remember good old Benjamin Franklin? Benjamin Franklin invented things and competed as a businessman. There are many entrepreneurs creating products and competing in our world today.

Entrepreneurs compete by thinking of better products for consumers. If people are unhappy with their breakfast cereal, an entrepreneur somewhere might come up with a way to improve their breakfast. Then the entrepreneur will turn around and use their product to compete with the other cereals. Entrepreneurs hope to make a profit competing with other companies. They use creativity and their incentive for profit to think up ideas that benefit everyone. What are some other ways entrepreneurs affect market competition in the economy?

title: Springfield, Massachusetts
text:
Springfield, Massachusetts, became a town in 1636. That makes it one of the oldest cities in the country. It is in Hampden County. Springfield is pretty big. There are about 153,000 people there.

Springfield played a big role in history. The Armory made weapons during the Revolutionary War. There are many railways in the town. Immigrants came to lay the tracks for these rails. They also worked in the many factories.

Springfield City Hall was rebuilt in the early 1900s. There was a huge fire. The fire was started by a monkey. The monkey got loose during a City Hall Fair. It ran and tipped over an oil lamp which started the fire.

Springfield is the birth place of Theodor Seuss Geisel. You may know him as Dr. Seuss. This author wrote many books before he passed away. Have you read "Green Eggs and Ham?" Or maybe you read "The Cat in the Hat?" He also wrote "How the Grinch Stole Christmas!" The Dr. Seuss National Memorial Sculpture Garden is right in Springfield.

title: What is biotechnology?
text: Biotechnology is the use of biological knowledge in industry. Biotechnology is a growing business in Massachusetts. It involves genetic engineering (the use of plant and animal genes in custom-designed foods, drugs and fertilizers). Scientists, for example, have used genetic engineering to develop a very strong corn seed that is resistant to many diseases and severe drought. What other things do you think are explored in biotechnology?

title: Eastern Box Turtle
text:
Although most kinds of turtles can withdraw into their shells, the box turtle is different because the bottom of its shell, called the plastron, is hinged. The bottom shell can go upward to meet the top shell, completely closing it off!

In Massachusetts, box turtles can be found in forests, fields and floodplains. What would you look for if you were looking for a box turtle? They are not very large, only about 4-8 inches in length. The top shell makes a high dome that is a brown to black color. Lines or spots on the shell can be olive, orange or yellow. The plastron is light in color and can be plain or blotched, with hinges.

The box turtles are well known for their long life span. Although some turtles have reportedly lived for more than a hundred years, we do not know for sure if that is true. Some individuals have scratched dates on the backs of their shells. We don't know if those dates were right. They may have been a joke! "Growth rings" on the shells are not a reliable way to tell either. What do we know for sure about box turtles? They, like other turtles, are truly slooooowww!

title: Let's Write
text:
You Can Make A Difference!

Pollution control is always a community concern where a small area is inhabited by a very large population, such as in Massachusetts. Brainstorm with your classmates to think of places in your community that need to be cleaned up or protected from pollution. What are some ways you can make a difference? Make a list of your ideas, then develop a class pledge that tells of your commitment to protect the environment.

title: Taking Notes in Class
text:
Learning how to take good notes in class is very important.

Taking notes in class can be difficult. Sometimes it’s hard to concentrate and you can miss some information. Or you can’t read what you wrote. Other times, you’re not sure what information to write down. It’s important to learn how to take good notes. Without notes, taking tests is much harder! Here are some ways to take good notes in class.

Be ready. You don’t always need to have a pen in hand, but have your notebook open to a clean page. And have a pen or pencil nearby. When the teacher enters the room, you’re ready to begin. Put the date and topic on top of the page. Knowing when you took the notes will help you study for tests. You can quickly flip through the pages and find the topic.

Don’t waste time writing what you already know. Notes help you remember what you learned in class. If you’re sure you know something, then don’t write it down. Let’s say you know George Washington was the first U.S. president. You don’t need to write it down. Instead, you can focus on his birth date, where he lived and what he did.

Make lists. Lists are easy to recognize and read. They organize the information. If you can make a list, you’ll likely remember the information later.

Remember, note taking will improve your learning. But your notes won’t make much sense if your eyes are always glued to the paper. Take some time to really listen to your teacher. Stop every now and then to listen and to watch your teacher. Write down the examples that are written on the board. By doing this, you’re sure to have success in class!

title: Farewell Fun!
text:
This is the final issue of Massachusetts Studies Weekly - State History this year. That sure went by fast! We hope you have enjoyed our paper. You may have even learned something to boot! We have taken you back to the dinosaurs. You learned about the American Indians who first lived here. You read on through the European settlers and into present-day Massachusetts. Together we have learned much. You read about many famous people in Massachusetts history. There were many famous leaders and inventors.

Well...our final issue is going to be just for fun! It will be a good review from the past year. There are some things to think about first. Here are some questions to get you warmed up.

If there are two barbers in town and one has a bad haircut and one has a great haircut, to which do you go for your haircut?

Now that you've thought about those for awhile, you are all warmed up for games on the following pages! We have crossword puzzles, word searches, multiple choice and true and false questions. There are some fill in the blanks and matching quizzes as well.

We hope you have a great summer. Keep learning about our great state of Massachusetts. Maybe you will get to visit somewhere you have never been this year.

title: Critical Analysis and Rumination: President Truman and The Atomic Bomb Decision
text:
rumination (noun): the act of giving serious thought and consideration to something

Adolf Hitler was defeated in May 1945 after years of war in Europe, and American troops would be coming home - wouldn't they? Victory in Europe meant that some U.S. soldiers would be returning home. Others would go to the Pacific to face Japanese armies. Scientists in the U.S. had made a weapon that could certainly end the war with Japan, but it was so powerful that tens of thousands of people would be killed, including civilians (citizens not in the military). President Harry Truman had a decision to make that would greatly affect the world. What would the commander in chief do?

In the years leading up to President Truman's decision, the Japanese had been a brutal enemy. They had killed thousands of Americans at sea and on Pacific islands, including the surprise attack on Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The president wondered how many more lives would be lost if we tried to end the war without the atomic bomb. What would happen if another country improved the weapon and used the bomb before we did? Would they use it on us?

President Truman tried several times without success to work out surrender with Japan. He then ordered atomic bombs to be dropped on the cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945. Within a week of the second attack, Japan did surrender, which put an end to World War II. Historians estimate that between 150,000 and 240,000 Japanese were killed from effects of the two bombings. They also estimate that thousands of American lives were saved. Do you think President Truman made the right decision?
