title: Your Adventure of a Lifetime!
text:
Welcome to Iowa Studies Weekly. Hang on tight for the ride of a lifetime. We will explore our country from top to bottom, start to finish, inside, outside, upside and downside. We'll climb the highest mountain, drop into the deepest hole, roam with the buffalo, hunt with the mountain men, build a boat, fly an airplane, discover gold, walk with the settlers and put an Iowan into outer space. Iowa is the most wonderful place to live on this whole planet.

Iowa Studies Weekly is your time machine into the past. Come along for the trip as we make stops to learn about our state's roots - our beginnings that reach back thousands of years. Learn about the fantastic progress we have made in such a short time since we became a state. This will be one of the most satisfying and exciting studies you will ever experience as we learn about Iowa.

Each issue of Iowa Studies Weekly will include a connections article on the front cover. This is a real news story about something important happening in our state or nation right now. Our cover story will help you get a head start on the week's history lesson. We like to take you on a journey into the experiences of great people and great events with our cover stories.

And there's more. We will tell you about the jobs, skills and crafts that early Iowa dwellers had, what principles guided their lives, the animals, birds, trees and plants that live in our state, and many other facts that will make your study of Iowa enjoyable and interesting.

And let's not forget the games, crafts, and activities! Many of these crossword puzzles and word search games will help you learn new words. And we'll include other activities that are just plain fun. So, let's get started! Turn the page and jump right in. The water is fine - and so is the land. What land? Why, the land you're standing on. And just where is that? Let's find out. (Hint - Turn the page!)

title: Philanthropy and Values
text:
Maybe you have heard the word "philanthropy" before. What does it mean? It describes actions that people make for the good of other people. What is a value? It's a way of behaving that people believe is good like believing it's good to be honest. Is honesty one of your values?

One way you can practice philanthropy today is to help yourself and others learn good values. How do you learn good values? You can learn them from your parents and grandparents, your teachers at school or church and other people you trust.

You can also learn them from people that have been recognized for doing good things for society. An easy way to learn about people that have done good things is to visit values. com Values. com has lots of stories and short videos that highlight the traits that make each of us better people. They even have billboards on the highway to remind you about good values.

For example, you may have seen a billboard that looks like the one shown here.

This billboard is about Oral Lee Brown, who saved money from her job to send 19 kids to college... all by herself! Wow! Isn't that cool? You can learn about lots of other people who practice philanthropy at values. com. Be sure to look for more of their "billboards" on Page 4 of Studies Weekly this year. We think they're so cool we want to remind you to check them out!

title: The Earth
text:
Did you know that scientists believe the Earth is nearly 5 billion years old? This is especially amazing when we realize that people have only lived in Iowa for around 12 thousand years. What has been happening to the Earth during the last 5 billion years? The Earth has been slowly changing until it finally became the land we are familiar with today.

Geologists, or scientists who study the history and structure of the Earth, have discovered many things about the land we now call home. Geologists have uncovered many secrets about how the Earth developed by looking at the land itself. By studying the layers of rock that make up our state, geologists can tell a lot about the Earth and what caused it to become the way it is today.

Most scientists believe that the Earth was once a huge ball of liquid lava, or molten rock. As this red hot lava started to cool, large sheets of rock were formed on the surface, with liquid lava underneath. These huge sheets of rock, called plates, slowly drifted apart at the rate of about one inch each year. Eventually, these plates moved into the places they occupy today and are now known as continents. From clues they have found in the rocks, many scientists believe that Iowa was once a mountain area and was located to the south of the equator, in a warm, tropical climate. It was then that some major forces of nature began to mold and form the land we now live on. The forces of water, ice and fire all played a part in forming the Iowa landscape.

Fire

After the last glacier finally melted, the land dried out, and trees began to grow. Forests of spruce, pine, oak, hickory and walnut began to take over the area. The climate continued to get warmer and drier, and grasses began to grow between the trees. As less rain fell, many of the trees that needed more water died. However, the grasses could survive with little water, and they spread rapidly across the land. About 4 thousand years ago, the climate changed again, and more moisture fell. More trees grew, and the grass and trees began to compete for places to grow. The grasses had a powerful friend to help them in their battle against the forests, however. Fire is much more deadly to the trees of the forests than it is to the grasses of the prairies. Prairie grasses grow back the next spring, even if they have been burned by fire. Trees that have been badly burned usually die. As fires burned across the land of Iowa (usually started by lightning), the forests were damaged the most, leaving the grasses to grow and create the prairies for which we are now so famous. As you can see, the forces of nature have been at work for billions of years to create the beautiful state of Iowa. The forces of wind, sun and water are still at work, slowly changing the land today just as they have in the past.

Water

A warm ocean once covered the entire eastern United States. Scientists believe that around 5 hundred million years ago, Iowa was at the bottom of the sea. Over time, the land at the bottom of this shallow sea collected layers of sand and seashells. This later hardened into a layer of sandstone rock that still exists today as our state. Limestone, another rock that lies under much of Iowa's soil, was also formed when the land was underwater. There are rich limestone deposits throughout Iowa, especially in the central portion.

Since the sea that covered Iowa was shallow, plants and trees eventually started growing in swamps near the banks of this ocean. When these plants died, more grew in their places, and as each plant died, it formed a new layer at the bottom of the sea. Mud covered these layers of dead plants, and very slowly, these layers changed into coal. The land we call Iowa still has large deposits of coal.

The saltwater from Iowa's ancient sea also left another mineral behind. As the water from the sea dried up, large deposits of salt were left behind, and this salt eventually became gypsum. Gypsum is still found in Iowa today, and it is mined to make wallboard, plaster and cement.

Ice

After the water dried up and the land dried out, more changes started to occur. Between 2 million and 3 million years ago, the weather became cooler. Layers of snow fell to the ground that didn't melt.

Instead, the snow stayed year round and piled up until it turned into huge ice sheets. These ice sheets became thick and heavy, eventually joining together to form enormous glaciers. A glacier is a thick sheet of moving ice and snow. In some places, these glaciers were more than a mile thick!

These huge glaciers started moving outward, smoothing and flattening everything in their path. The mountains that once covered the land were crushed into loose boulders, sand and gravel. As the glaciers pushed along the loose rocks, they acted like sandpaper, flattening and smoothing the land beneath them. When the ice melted, it dumped its load of rocks and sand, forming mounds, hills and ridges. During the Ice Age, the climate cooled down and warmed up at least four times. Each time a new ice sheet moved across the land, it flattened our state a bit more. Each new glacier also left a new deposit of sand and silt (called loess) on the Earth, creating a deep, rich soil that would later become some of the best farmland in the world. This area of Iowa is called the Loess Hills.

title: Geode State Park
text:
Geode State Park is named after the state rock of Iowa. It is one of the best places in the world to search for beautiful geode formations. Geode State Park is located in southeastern Iowa in Henry County, about 20 miles west of Burlington.

Geode State Park is one of the most popular picnicking spots in southeastern Iowa. People come from miles around to enjoy the scenery and relax. The park also offers swimming, boating and fishing in Lake Geode. This man made lake was built in 1950 and has become famous for its excellent fishing. The lake is a great fishing spot for largemouth bass, bluegill, crappie, channel catfish, bullhead, red eared sunfish and tiger muskie.

There are also many campsites at Geode State Park. The campground area has a large display of geodes that have been collected in the park. Many visitors come here to see the natural wonders that gave the park its name.

Geode State Park also offers several hiking trails around the lake. Part of one trail has been made into a nature trail. There is even a printed pamphlet that visitors can use to guide them along the trail. This pamphlet tells about different plants, animals and formations that hikers may notice as they explore the trail.

Visit Geode State Park, and you may get to see a real geode up close!

title: How thick is the Earth’s crust?
text: Our Earth is made of mostly rock and metal. When the Earth was still a mass of molten rock, the lighter materials floated to the top. Today, the thinnest sections of the Earth's crust (the outer layer of the Earth) can be found at the bottom of our oceans, where it is only three miles thick. That's why there are many underwater volcanoes and earthquakes. The thickest crust is under the mountains and can be up to 43 miles thick. Compared to the rest of the Earth, the crust is very thin. If the Earth were the size of a baseball, the crust would be no thicker than a sheet of paper.

title: Geode
text:
The geode is not considered part of Iowa's wildlife, but plays an important role in making Iowa what it is today. The geode was chosen as the official state rock of Iowa in 19 6 7. A geode is a rare and beautiful rock found in the state of Iowa. Geodes are round in shape and are usually about four inches in diameter. They have a rock hard outer shell with a spectacular surprise inside. When a geode is carefully cut in half, a sparkling cave of mineral crystals is revealed. These mineral crystals are made up of quartz and calcite in several beautiful colors.

The word "geode" means "earth like" in Latin. These rocks were named geodes because they are round, like the Earth. They are also formed in layers and have a center, or core, just like the Earth.

Southeastern Iowa is one of the best places in the world to find and collect geodes. We even have a state park named after this famous rock. Geode State Park is located in Henry County and is a great place to look for samples of our state rock.

title: Reason and Logic: Young George Washington, Surveyor and Mapmaker
text:
Most people know about George Washington. He was born in Virginia. He was a general during the American Revolution and our first president. But his earliest jobs, surveyor and cartographer (mapmaker), taught him skills and values he would use for the rest of his life. Using reason and logic to solve problems helped Washington become one of our country's most important leaders.

When Washington grew up, there were few roads or boundaries in much of the land. A surveyor's job was to measure and map the land. He had to make exact measurements for boundaries and physical features. This was a very big responsibility. People needed accurate maps and surveys for traveling and buying land.

At age 17, Washington traveled across the Blue Ridge Mountains to map and survey part of the frontier. He was the surveyor for the whole county, and that was an important job. When he led the Continental Army, it was even more important to have reliable maps. He established the job of Geographer and Surveyor General and appointed a man named Robert Erskine to this position. He gave Washington some information that was very helpful in making reasonable and logical battle plans and decisions.

You can use these same skills to make important decisions. Be sure you have the facts and information you need instead of acting on opinions and emotions. In what areas of your life are reason and logic very important?

title: The Mississippi - Our Great Water Highway
text:
Does it seem strange to you that a landlocked state like Iowa would use ships or barges to transport goods from one place to another? Although Iowa may be nowhere near the ocean, we still rely on riverboats as one of our main sources of transportation. Riverboating comes easy for us because the nation's greatest water highway, the Mississippi River, forms the eastern border of our state.

The Mississippi River is 2,348 miles long and is the second longest river in the United States. It has been used as a great water highway since the days of the American Indian canoe, linking the middle portion of the United States with the rest of the nation.

In the early 1800s, the government of the United States decided that the Mississippi River would take responsibility for maintaining the Mississippi River system for boat traffic. The Lower Mississippi River was always deep enough to carry riverboats, but during the hot summer months or long dry spells, many parts of the Upper Mississippi River became too shallow for the larger boats. To keep the entire river system open during all seasons of the year, the Army Corps of Engineers set out to create and maintain a river channel that would be at least nine feet deep and 400 feet wide from St. Louis, Mo., to St. Paul, Minn.

In 1930, the Army Corps of Engineers began the task of building a system of 29 locks and dams between St. Louis and St. Paul. These dams took about 10 years to build, and most were completed by 1940. Each dam holds back the water in the river to create a lake-sized pool of water nine feet deep - deep enough to safely carry the large riverboats and barges. Locks, sections of the river closed off with gates, raise and lower the ships from one water level to another and allow the boats to travel the Mississippi even during times when the river is low.

Today, most of the traffic on the Mississippi River is river barges. These barges are towed along the river by powerful diesel engines. Each towboat is made up of 12-15 barges carrying up to 22,500 tons of freight.

Each year, an average of 175 million tons of freight is moved along the Upper Mississippi River. Grain is the most popular item transported on the river, including corn, wheat, oats, barley and rye. These grains are loaded onto the large barges by grain elevators (located near the river) and shipped to New Orleans, where the grain is then loaded onto ships to be sent to foreign countries across the ocean. Other items shipped on the Mississippi River include gasoline, kerosene, fuel oil, coal, fertilizers, sulfur, cement, sugar and molasses. We are lucky to have the Mississippi River forming our eastern border. We have easy access to America's largest water highway!

title: Do Cows Give More Milk after Sleeping on a Waterbed?
text:
"It's been a long day," thought Bessie the cow after being milked one evening. "I think I'll just go in and get a good night's sleep on my waterbed." This may sound like the beginning of a fairy tale, but it could be happening on a dairy farm near you!

Dairy farmers know that happy cows give more and better-tasting milk. They also know that sleeping on a hard floor can cause knee and leg injuries that can sometimes make a cow unable to walk. Is a waterbed the answer? Maybe. Farmers are starting to think a cow-sized waterbed mattress might be every dairy cow's dream.

When a cow steps onto the waterbed, she feels the security of the cement floor below the mattress. When she lies down, the water in the mattress keeps her off the hard cement and protects her knees and her udder. Farmers have noticed that if there are not enough waterbeds for all the cows, they will wait in line to use it. Some research shows that cows that sleep on waterbeds sleep longer and have fewer knee and leg injuries. If cows sleep longer, they have more energy to make milk. Fewer leg injuries mean fewer trips to the vet.

The cows may be healthier in other ways too. Some researchers have found fewer white blood cells in cows that use waterbeds. White blood cells fight disease. More white blood cells indicate that the cow may be sick. Fewer white cells indicate a healthier cow. It looks as if better sleep helps cows as much as it helps people! Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/ for more Connections and Current Events articles.

title: Waterways of Iowa
text:
Did you know that Iowa is the only state that is bordered by two navigable rivers? Navigable means that the rivers can be navigated, or sailed upon. Iowa's entire eastern border is made up of part of the Mississippi River, and on the west, the Big Sioux River joins the Missouri River at Sioux City and makes up the rest of our eastern border. The Mississippi and the Missouri Rivers are the two longest rivers in the United States, and parts of both of these huge rivers make up our state's borders!

The Missouri River

The Missouri River is sometimes called "The Big Muddy" because of its brown, murky water. The American Indians who lived here more than three hundred years ago nicknamed the Missouri "The Big Muddy," and because the name fits so well, we still use it today.

The Big Muddy has its source, or beginning, far away from Missouri in the tops of the Rocky Mountains. From its beginning, the mighty Missouri winds its way some 2,000 500 40 miles, cutting across Missouri, and finally joins the Mississippi near St. Louis at a point called the mouth of the Missouri. The mouth of a river is the place where it empties into a larger body of water.

Great Rivers Help Iowa Grow

How do the Missouri and Mississippi Rivers affect life in Iowa? For many years, before the railroad began connecting the different regions of the United States, the rivers played a vital role in transporting goods and passengers from one place to another. These rivers were the country's first highways. Although trains, planes, and trucks are now used most often for carrying people and goods across the country, the rivers are still widely used for the transportation of goods such as grain, coal, steel, petroleum and cement. These items are transported by river barges. A barge is a large, flat boat that is perfect for transport on Iowa's huge rivers. Iowa also has other large rivers, such as the Big Sioux, the Little Sioux, the Floyd, the Raccoon and the Des Moines Rivers. A low ridge in central Iowa marks the division between the rivers of Iowa. Those to the west of this ridge, including the Big and Little Sioux and the Floyd, empty into the Missouri River. Those to the east of this ridge, including the Raccoon and the Des Moines, empty into the Mississippi River. Iowa also has many beautiful lakes. All of our natural lakes are small, but many of them are quite pretty. Northwest Iowa has the five lakes that are often called Iowa's "Great Lakes." These lakes are the small, glacier formed lakes called Spirit Lake, Storm Lake, Clear Lake, West Okoboji Lake and East Okoboji Lake.

Some of our state's man made lakes include Coralville Lake, Lake Red Rock, Saylorville Lake and Rathbun Lake. These large lakes were created by damming rivers such as the Iowa, the Des Moines, and the Chariton. They are very popular recreational sites for the people of Iowa. These lakes provide great fishing, swimming, boating and water sports. People also enjoy visiting these lakes for picnics and to see the beautiful scenery.

The Mississippi River

The Mississippi River also has many nicknames. Two of its most common nicknames are the "Father of Waters," because of its enormous size, and also "Old Man River," because of the river's age and the respect people have for it.

The Mississippi is the second longest and has the largest water volume in the United States. It runs 2,000 300 40 8 miles from the Great Lakes in the north to the Gulf of Mexico in the south. Tributaries of the Mississippi, or smaller rivers that flow into it, drain most of the land from the Rocky Mountains all the way to the Appalachian Mountains. The Mississippi River is a huge river system that collects water from the land and empties it into the sea.

title: Dubuque
text:
Dubuque is located in northeastern Iowa and is one of the Mississippi River's busy port cities. The city is named after Julien Dubuque, a French Canadian lead miner who settled here in 17 80 8. Dubuque is famous as a shipping center. Dubuque also has factories that make furniture, snow removal equipment, construction materials, and cars and trucks.

If you get a chance to visit Dubuque, you will find many interesting things to see and do. The National Farm Toy Museum near Dubuque displays all types of farm toys and collector's items. Dubuque is considered the farm toy capital of the world for good reason! You may also be interested in seeing the site where the 19 80 8 movie "Field of Dreams" was filmed. Here, you can practice pitching and batting on the baseball diamond set in the middle of an Iowa cornfield.

The beautiful Mississippi River is the focus of many of the things to do in Dubuque. You can visit the Mississippi River Museum and see exhibits exploring more than 3 hundred years of river history. There are even life size, hands on displays showing what life was like on the mighty Mississippi.

If you really want to get to know the Mississippi River, you can even sail down the river on one of Dubuque's riverboats or paddleboats. These are boats that offer tours of the river and provide food and entertainment during the trip.

Dubuque also offers beautiful caves to visit and explore. Crystal Lake Cave and Spook Cave are both located near Dubuque and are interesting places to visit. Dubuque has something for everyone!

title: What is a river barge?
text: A barge is a large, flat-bottomed boat used for transporting goods. Most barges are towed on a waterway, but there are some barges that are self-propelled, meaning they run on their own power. Years ago, the barges carrying goods on the Mississippi River were towed by men, horses, or mules. Today, this towing is done by a tugboat or by other self-propelled barges. Barges have been around a long time. They were even used on the Nile in ancient Egypt and in Europe for carrying royalty and other important people.

title: Largemouth Bass
text:
The largemouth bass is a member of the sunfish family. It is also one of the black basses, which is a group that includes the largemouth, smallmouth and spotted bass.

The largemouth bass is easy to recognize. It has many dark spots that form a horizontal stripe down its middle, a spiny dorsal fin, and a very large mouth that extends past its eye. The largemouth bass is between 10 and 20 inches long and weighs anywhere from five to eight pounds. Largemouth bass are the largest of the sunfish.

The largemouth bass is found throughout Iowa in slow moving or standing water. It does not normally like to live in dirty or muddy water. It likes to hide in the water beneath trees, logs, weeds and stumps.

The largemouth bass spawns from mid April to the end of May, and its eggs hatch in less than a week. The male largemouth bass watches the young until they are ready to venture out on their own.

The largemouth bass is a very popular game fish in Iowa, and fishermen consider themselves lucky to catch an Iowa largemouth bass.

title: Milk Carton Log Cabin
text:
Build your own log cabin out of a milk carton!

Materials

Half-gallon waxed-paper milk or juice carton, emptied

Grease pencil

Scissors

Cardboard

Glue

Waxed paper scraps

Pretzel sticks

Cheerios or pasta

Acrylic paint

Water

Water container

Paper towels

Ruler

Instructions

1. Measure three inches down the side of the carton. At three inches, draw a line around the entire carton with a grease pencil.

2. Cut along the line and separate the top from the bottom. Discard the bottom. You will use the top.

3. Draw the outline of the door and windows with a grease pencil.

4. Cut out the windows and door. If they are too small for scissors, ask your teacher to use an X-acto knife and help you. You can leave one side of the door attached and fold it out so that it opens and closes.

5. Glue a piece of waxed paper over the inside of each window.

6. Glue the cabin to a cardboard base that is slightly bigger than the cabin. Let the pieces dry before proceeding.

7. Glue pretzel sticks along the base of the carton walls and build up. If necessary, cut the pretzels to fit around the door and windows.

8. Glue a stack of Cheerios or pasta together as a chimney. Glue this on the roof of the cabin.

9. Cover the roof with pretzels or acrylic paint.

Note: Watercolor and tempera paint will not stay on the waxed carton.

title: The Cardiff Giant
text:
Did you know that one of the 19th century's greatest hoaxes, or tricks, got its start in the state of Iowa? Would you believe that the hoax all began with a large slab of gypsum, one of Iowa's most plentiful minerals? Exactly what was this hoax, and what did it have to do with Iowa?

In the spring of 1868, a New York cigar maker named George Hull was in Ackley, Iowa, visiting his sister. While he was there, he stopped at a religious revival, or outdoor meeting. The preacher was talking about the first book in the Bible and how it spoke of "giants" who used to live on the Earth. Hull, who didn't believe in the Bible and thought that the notion of giants walking the Earth was just plain silly, decided to see how many people would believe in a "real" giant.

Hull went to Fort Dodge, where gypsum is mined, and asked for a large block of gypsum. He purchased a 5-ton, 12-foot-long block of the soft, pale stone for the price of one barrel of beer. He then loaded the block onto a train and took it to Chicago, storing the stone in a barn belonging to one of his friends.

Later, Hull hired an artist and a stonecutter to make a huge, naked giant out of the block of gypsum. For four months, the men worked on the giant, and when it was completed, they placed it in an enormous copper box, labeled it "machinery," and shipped it to Binghamton, New York, where Hull lived.

After giving it some careful thought, Hull decided that the perfect place to bury the giant would be on his cousin's farm in Cardiff, New York. The men buried the giant on the farm, and a year later, William Newell, Hull's cousin, hired two men to dig a well on his farm. He told the men just where to dig, and imagine their surprise when they uncovered a huge, stone giant! The giant was "discovered" on October 16, 1869.

Word of the amazing discovery at the Newell farm spread quickly, and the very first weekend after the giant was found, more than 1,000 people had come to see the giant for a price of 50 cents each. Scientists and paleontologists of the time came to see the giant. Some said it was a fossil, while others claimed that it was an ancient statue. People flocked to see the remarkable discovery and to make their own opinions about what the giant actually was.

Eventually, a famous New York sculptor named Eratus Dow Palmer was able to convince people that the giant was a fraud. The giant was proven to be carved out of gypsum, and chisel marks were discovered in some spots. Still, people paid to see the giant.

In December of 1869, Hull finally confessed that the giant was a fake and that he had created the whole scheme. In less than two months, Hull had made a total of more than $100,000 from the Cardiff Giant. As much as he enjoyed the money, Hull may have enjoyed fooling so many people even more.

The Cardiff Giant spent many years in Independence, Iowa, and later stood in Des Moines in the home of publisher Gardner Cowles. The giant is now on exhibit at the New York State Historical Association's Farmers' Museum in Cooperstown, New York. That is how a piece of Iowa became part of one of the greatest hoaxes of the 19th century.

title: Fifth Graders Talk to Congressmen on Skype
text:
Have you ever thought about different ways to power your parents’ cars? Fifth grade students at Columbus Elementary in Edwardsville, Ill., have been learning about other ways to power cars using alternative (substitute) fuels. In September 2011, Illinois Senator Bill Haine and Representative Dan Beiser visited the school to talk about the work being done to improve the environment and the use of “green” energy. Green energy is energy that produces less pollution. Fifth grade students from the entire school district “attended” the assembly. With the help of an internet video program called Skype, students from other schools were able to watch the assembly and ask the officials questions. After the assembly some students emailed questions to Sen. Haine and Rep. Beiser. Students were very excited to receive responses from the officials.

The teachers and students at Columbus Elementary are doing some amazing research when it comes to alternative energy. In fact, they are planning to run a diesel engine using vegetable oil instead of gas. Students are also learning how to reuse resources and are looking forward to turning used vegetable oil into hand soap. To learn more about alternative energy,

title: Iowa’s Natural Resources
text:
Iowa is a land rich in beauty. We have many useful natural resources, such as limestone, coal and gypsum, but Iowa's most important and valuable resource is the land itself. Let's explore some of our state's important natural resources (things that are useful found in nature).

Limestone

Limestone rock lies under much of Iowa. This limestone was formed at the bottom of the prehistoric sea that once covered our state. Limestone is the sandy, sedimentary rock that makes up the beautiful cliffs along the Mississippi and Upper Iowa Rivers. Iowa's beautiful and mysterious caves are also made up of limestone.

Wildlife

Our state was once a haven for wildlife of all kinds. Before the early settlers began building cities and plowing the land, Iowa was home to herds of bison, elk and deer. There were and still are otters in many of Iowa's rivers and streams. Although some of these animals have disappeared from the landscape, others still remain.

Iowa provides nesting grounds for many types of birds. Our state provides a home for quails, pheasants and wild turkeys. Canada geese rest in our fields on their way to other climates when the seasons change. There are even horned owls and bald eagles in our state.

Our state is still home to the beaver, chipmunk, coyote, deer, fox, gopher, mink, muskrat, opossum, rabbit, raccoon, rattlesnake, squirrel and skunk. There are also many fish in our rivers, lakes and streams, including the bass, bluegill, carp, crappie, northern pike, perch, sucker and walleye.

With proper care and responsible use, our natural resources will continue to make Iowa a beautiful and productive place to live.

Coal

In central and southern Iowa, another important mineral was formed beneath the ancient sea that once covered the land. When plants and trees growing along the tropical seashore died and fell, more plants grew over them. When the water covered these dead plants and mud settled on top, the dead plants slowly turned into coal. Coal mining was once a very big business in southern and central Iowa at the time that coal was used to fuel trains and heat homes. Now that other sources of energy have become more popular, coal mining has become less important to our state, but some coal is still mined in these areas.

Gypsum

When the prehistoric sea finally dried up, it left behind large deposits of salt. The salt that was left behind eventually hardened into gypsum, a rock found in large quantities in the central portion of Iowa. Today, gypsum is mined around Fort Dodge and is used to make wallboard, plaster and cement. Cement manufacturers in Mason City use large amounts of Iowa gypsum for making cement.

Soil

There is no question that our state's most famous and valuable natural resource is its rich and fertile soil. Because of this rich, black topsoil, Iowa has become known as the land of never ending cornfields.

The fertile soil of Iowa was formed over thousands of years by the grasses that grew here. These grasses grew and matured every summer, died off in the fall and left their roots to decay over the winter. These decaying roots became the rich, black soil that has made Iowa so famous. Scientists believe that it takes 4 hunnerd years to produce one inch of new soil. When the settlers first plowed the prairies of our state, the topsoil was 16 inches deep! That means that our fertile Iowa dirt has been in the making for a very long time!

During the droughts (long periods of time without rain, snow or other moisture) of the 19 thirties, the rich Iowa soil dried up and began to blow away because there was no water. Without the prairie grasses to keep the soil in place, much of our fertile soil was lost. In fact, Iowa's topsoil is now only about six to eight inches deep, about half what it was when the first settlers began to farm the land.

Farmers today use many new soil conservation programs to protect this valuable resource and keep it from being destroyed.

title: Maquoketa Caves
text:
Maquoketa Caves are a series of unique and beautiful caves, limestone formations and bluffs located in east central Iowa. Maquoketa Caves State Park is located just eight miles from the city of Maquoketa and offers visitors a wonderful trip back through time. The caves and the surrounding area give us a glimpse into what the Earth may have looked like in Iowa thousands of years ago.

The park contains more caves than any other state park in Iowa. There is also a system of trails linking all of the caves, formations and overlooks so that it is easy to see all the sites. Some of the most spectacular attractions are Dancehall Cave, Dugout Cave, Natural Bridge and Balanced Rock.

The caves were first discovered in the 18 30s by some of Iowa's early settlers, but the land wasn't purchased for the park until 19 2 1. Most of the park's facilities were built during the 19 30s, including a stone lodge, the Dancehall Cave walkway system, a stone picnic circle and several picnic shelters along the trail. A new visitor's center has also been completed that offers information about geology, history and a "video tour" for those who are unable to hike to the caves. The park also offers picnicking, camping, hiking and cave exploration.

Maquoketa Caves is open all year and offers unique experiences during each season. Spring wildflowers, beautiful summer greenery, colorful fall leaves and blankets of winter snow all give the park a different look. If you haven't visited Maquoketa Caves, you may want to plan a visit soon!

title: How much of Iowa’s land is devoted to agriculture?
text: Nearly 90 percent of Iowa's total land is devoted to farming or agriculture (industry of farming). Because of the rich, fertile farmland that makes up our great state, farming is how many Iowans make their living. Today, Iowa is among the leading producers of corn, hay, oats and soybeans. It is also a major producer of beef and is the No. 1 producer of pork in the United States.

title: Gypsum
text:
Gypsum is not considered part of Iowa's wildlife, but plays an important role in making Iowa what it is today. Gypsum is one of the most common sulfate mineral. The ancient sea that used to cover Iowa left behind large deposits of salt, which later turned into the mineral known as gypsum.

A type of gypsum called alabaster is used to make vases, boxes and ornaments. Satin spar, another type of gypsum, is used in jewelry. Gypsum is most commonly used to make a powder called plaster of Paris. Plaster of Paris is created by heating the gypsum so that all of the water evaporates, leaving behind a fine, white powder. This powder is then used to make molds for statues, ceramics, and dental plates and casts for broken bones. Gypsum is also used to make wallboard and cement.

Gypsum is mined today in and around Fort Dodge. Much of the gypsum mined there is sent to Mason City for use in Iowa's cement plants.

title: Climate and Weather
text:
The summer of 1993 marks the year of one of the greatest natural disasters (destruction caused by the forces of nature) ever to hit the United States. Much of the Midwest experienced the worst flooding ever recorded in the United States. In the flood area, damages totaled more than $15 billion, and 50 people died. Thousands were left homeless for months, and hundreds of levees (embankment of dirt used to prevent overflowing)failed. Those people who lived in Iowa at the time of the Great Flood will never forget it. What caused the Great Flood of 1993? The simple answer is that it started to rain and just wouldn't stop. From April 1 through August 31, precipitation (rainfall) amounts approached 48 inches in Iowa, about 30-36 inches above normal. Throughout the Midwest, rainfall amounts were 200-350 percent of normal rates. Many locations received rain every day between late June and late July. The rain kept falling. The rivers kept rising, and the water had nowhere to go but up and over the banks, flooding everything in its path.

The damage caused by the flooding will never be forgotten. Tens of thousands of people were evacuated during that summer, and some were never able to return to their homes. Most of those who returned were greeted by water- and mud-soaked homes, damaged and destroyed property, and some faced unemployment as well. Some businesses that were heavily damaged in the floods shut their doors forever, leaving their employees without work. At least 75 towns were totally covered by floodwaters. More than 15 million acres of farmland were flooded, and because of the sand left when the water dried up, some of these lands will not be useable for farming for many years to come.

Life on the river was completely shut down during the Great Flood of 1993. Barge traffic on both the Missouri and the Mississippi Rivers was stopped for two months. Bridges were out. Highways and roads were closed, and 10 airports were flooded. All railroad traffic was at a standstill. There were also many sewage and water treatment plants that were destroyed, making it difficult or impossible to get clean water. The people of the Midwest, including Iowa, experienced difficulties that are impossible to imagine if you have never experienced them yourself.

The people of Iowa are hard working and hardy, and many of those who lived through the flood simply dug out of the mud and rebuilt their lives. Others moved away, but still more set to work helping their neighbors clean up and rebuild. Many who had lost everything were grateful to have made it through the flood with their lives and focused on helping others who were also in need. The people of Iowa hope that they will never again see a flood like the Great Flood of 1993, but if they do, they will likely dry off, shovel out, and start all over again.

title: Scientists Believe Volcanoes Caused a ‘Little Ice Age’
text:
An ice age usually lasts thousands of years. But between A. D. 13 100 and A. D. 19 100 the northern hemisphere experienced a cooling called the "Little Ice Age." The cooling was so intense that glaciers moved south, causing northern European towns to be destroyed. It was so cold that the Thames River in London and canals in the Netherlands froze! A scientist at the University of Colorado, using plant fossils from this period, may have discovered why this happened.

The plants died suddenly between 12 70 5 and 13 100. That's exactly when many volcanoes erupted. Fifty years later, volcanoes erupted again. Billions of tiny particles from the eruptions were in the atmosphere, reflecting the sun's heat away from the Earth. This caused the land to cool, the plants to die and the ice cap to grow. But there's more.

The growing ice cap sparked a feedback loop. A feedback loop causes something to happen over and over. First, the tiny particles stopped a lot of the sun's heat from reaching land. This cooling caused the ice cap to grow. The ice reflected more of the sun's heat back into the atmosphere. This caused more cooling. Finally, the glaciers became so large that they stopped the warmer ocean currents from melting the ice cap. Over centuries the glaciers grew to cover northern Europe.

Volcanic eruptions started the cooling, but it took the feedback loop to keep the "Little Ice Age" going for centuries!

title: Iowa's Climate
text:
When it comes to our climate and weather, Iowa is a land of extremes. The climate of a region is the weather pattern in that area over a period of many years. Iowa's climate can be very harsh and dramatic at times. In fact, the temperature sometimes drops as much as 50 degrees in a single day!

The first white settlers who came to Iowa came expecting a moderate, healthy climate. Glenda Riley, a well known historian, has said "maybe there was some logic which assumed that if Iowa was good for corn, it was good for people." Those settlers who came here expecting mild weather were soon in for a rude awakening.

Iowa is prone to harsh winters, sweltering summers and exciting storms any time of the year. The coldest temperature ever recorded in Iowa was minus forty 7 degrees Fahrenheit in Washta, Iowa, located in the northwest part of our state. This temperature was recorded on January 12, 19 twelve. The hottest temperature ever recorded was 1 hundred 18 degrees Fahrenheit on July 20, 19 3 four, in Keokuk. Keokuk is located in the southern tip of Iowa.

Normal temperatures for an Iowa winter average in the low to mid 30s for a daytime high temperature and in the low to mid teens at night. It is not uncommon, however, for Iowa to experience temperatures below zero, especially when the wind chill factor is taken into consideration.

During the summer months, Iowa's temperatures average in the high 80s during the day and get down in the mid 60s at night. These hot days and warm nights are perfect for growing corn!

Iowa is especially famous for its spectacular storms. Iowa boasts some of the fiercest blizzards, the most amazing thunderstorms, the scariest tornadoes and some of the most powerful funnel clouds anywhere in the United States.

Tornadoes

A tornado is caused by the same conditions that cause thunderstorms. When the warm updraft meets the cold downdraft, sometimes the winds begin blowing in opposite directions around the updraft, and a "twister" begins. These winds blow violently, causing destruction and damage wherever they touch down. Each year, Iowa is hit with an average of forty 8 tornadoes more for its size than any other state. Iowa also experiences about 1 hundred funnel clouds each year as well. Funnel clouds are like tornadoes, but they aren't as powerful. Tornadoes often take roofs off of houses and buildings, pull trees directly out of the ground, and even pick up cars, animals and people. The force of the wind is so strong that it can even drive a straw straight into a plank.

Blizzards

A blizzard is a heavy snowfall that is joined by fierce, bitter, arctic winds. Iowa's blizzards pile snow on the ground, snarl traffic and injure livestock. Many farmers plant trees around their property to break the wind and keep the snow from creating enormous drifts. Blizzards still cause problems for ranchers, and animals are often lost if they are caught in a blizzard. A late blizzard in April of 19 seventy 3 caught people off guard, killing 14 people and freezing millions of dollars worth of livestock.

Precipitation

Precipitation is the amount of moisture that falls to the ground in an area each year. This moisture can fall in the form of rain, hail, sleet or snow. Iowa averages between 2 6 to 3 8 inches of precipitation per year. When a flood year occurs, our state may receive much more than this. In nineteen 9 3, during the year of the Great Flood, Iowa received 4 8 inches of rain between April 1 and August 30 1. No wonder the state was flooded!

Thunderstorms

Thunderstorms are common in Iowa, especially during the months between April and September. In fact, Iowa averages forty 5 6 5 thunderstorms during this time. These thunderstorms are caused by warm updrafts of wind, which collide with, or crash into, cold downdrafts.

title: Keokuk
text:
Keokuk is located in the southeastern tip of Iowa, right on the mighty Mississippi River. Keokuk is named after Chief Keokuk, an elected leader of the Sauk Indians, who made their home here in southeast Iowa. Chief Keokuk's burial site is located in Rand Park on a beautiful overlook with the Mississippi River below.

Keokuk is also the site of the first national cemetery west of the Mississippi River. This cemetery was used during the Civil War to bury soldiers who died as a result of their wounds. There were seven Civil War hospitals located in Keokuk during the war. Hospital boats were used to transport the wounded soldiers up the Mississippi River to these hospitals for treatment. If the soldiers didn't survive, they were buried in what is now known as Keokuk's National Cemetery.

Visitors to Keokuk enjoy taking a tour of Lock and Dam 19, first built in 19 13. The lock was replaced in 19 5 7 and is one of the longest locks on the river, measuring 1, 200 feet across. Visitors can watch boats move through the structure from dusk to dawn. Visitors can also view the hydroelectric plant near the dam.

Tourists also enjoy many beautiful, old Victorian homes that can be seen on a walking tour of Keokuk. The George M. Verity Riverboat Museum is also a popular tourist attraction.

title: What is the wind-chill factor?
text: The wind chill factor is a measurement that is used to figure out how much colder the wind makes a temperature feel to your bare skin. For example, the thermometer may say that it is 14 degrees Fahrenheit outside, but if a cold wind is blowing, the wind may make it feel much colder. That would mean that, with the wind chill factor taken into consideration, the temperature could actually feel more like 20 degrees Fahrenheit below zero!

title: The Bald Eagle
text:
The bald eagle, Haliaetus leucocephalus, is a member of the hawk family. Eagles are very large birds with a wingspan of up to seven and one half feet. They have long beaks, nearly as long as their heads, which they use to grasp and eat fish.

The eagle is a solitary bird, meaning that it likes to live alone. It mates for life and usually produces two eaglets, or baby eagles, at a time. Eaglets do not develop adult markings until they are three years old. They are protected by their parents until they reach this age. The eagle uses the same nest year after year, continuing to rebuild and repair its nest as needed.

Eagles are native to North America and live near water. Iowa has many bald eagles living near its rivers. Eagles eat mainly dead fish and rodents, often stealing their food from other birds.

The American bald eagle became the national emblem of the United States in 17 8 2 and is protected by law. It is illegal to harm or even possess a bald eagle in the United States, except for some aviaries and zoos.

title: Iowa’s Famous Effigy Mounds
text:
Some of Iowa's most interesting and famous reminders of its early inhabitants are its historic effigy mounds. These mounds were built somewhere between A.D. 300 and 1600 in certain areas of southern and southwestern Wisconsin, as well as in parts of Minnesota, Iowa and Illinois. One of the largest known effigy (made to look like a living creature) mounds is located in southwestern Ohio and is formed in the shape of a gigantic snake holding an egg in its mouth. This mound has been named the Great Serpent Mound.

What is an effigy mound? Ancient American Indians who lived in Iowa and other parts of the Midwest built large mounds of Earth as part of their culture. Most of the mounds found throughout North America are cone-shaped (conical) or rectangular (linear), but a few mounds, mainly those found along the Mississippi River Bluffs, are shaped like birds, bears, lizards and sometimes even humans. These special mounds are called effigy mounds.

The people who constructed these amazing mounds of Earth are called the Woodland people. They were ancient American Indians who lived here long before any Europeans arrived in Iowa. The effigy mounds they built survive today as a reminder that we are not the first people to call Iowa home.

The mounds built by other ancient people in North America are believed to have been used in religious ceremonies or as burial grounds, or as the foundation for temples. Less is known about what the effigy mounds were used for, but some were used as burial mounds by the Woodland people.

To build an effigy mound, early American Indians dug out the soil around an outline of the shape they planned to make. Often, burials were included in these trenches dug to outline the shape of the mound. Later, dirt was built up inside the outline to resemble the bird or animal that had been outlined earlier.

Archaeologists believe that the Woodland people lived in small family groups during the cold winters, living in rock shelters and caves. When spring came, the small groups would come together in the river valleys and construct the effigy mounds together. Some believe that the mounds were built to keep the people in touch with nature. Others believe that the mounds were markers to show that the territory belonged to certain groups.

Other types of mounds frequently contain artifacts buried with the dead, but the Woodland people who constructed the effigy mounds didn't include such items. Some interesting pottery samples have been found in the effigy mounds, but there are rarely any of the intricately-made artifacts found in other types of mounds. The effigy mounds are also much shorter than the typical mounds built by earlier cultures. Earlier mounds often reached heights of several meters tall, but the effigy mounds are usually less than one meter high.

Effigy mounds are some of the last mounds to be built by the early American Indians. Later groups occasionally buried their dead in mounds that were already built, but few built new mounds, and the tradition died out. You can see some of Iowa's famous effigy mounds at Effigy Mounds National Monument, located near Harpers Ferry.

title: Can You Dig It?
text:
Archaeologists are scientists who dig up and study artifacts left by people who lived long ago. Artifacts are the things these people left behind, such as buildings, tools, pottery, graves, etc.

Dave Stanley is an archaeology graduate student from Cedar Rapids. He started Bear Creek Archaeology in Cresco in 1983. There's a law that says an archaeology team must survey, or inspect, a site before any government construction project can begin. Archaeologists must make sure that any construction won't disturb or destroy buried artifacts. So Bear Creek Archaeology keeps very busy!

Each job that the archaeologists do is different. Sometimes, the survey can be completed by poking holes in the ground. Other times, the ground must be excavated, or dug up, with expensive equipment. No matter how the survey is done, the goal is to find out if there are any historical artifacts on the site that will put it on the National Register of Historic Places. If the archaeologists find such artifacts, the company planning to build on the site must have the artifacts carefully removed and preserved. If the Bear Creek archaeologists don't find any artifacts, then the construction can continue as planned.

Since 1983, Bear Creek Archaeology has surveyed over 100,000 acres. It has identified more than 2,000 new archaeological sites. One of the most interesting projects the company has worked on was near Muscatine for the Department of Transportation. The department planned to add new lanes to Highway 61, and Bear Creek did a survey before the project began. Bear Creek found more than 60,000 artifacts there. Scientists found artifacts that were more than 4,500 years old!

Bear Creek Archaeology is one of the few archaeology companies in Iowa, and as long as there are construction projects planned, the company should have plenty of work!

title: Iowa’s First People
text:
The first people to call Iowa home probably entered the Mississippi Valley thousands of years ago. We don't know exactly when they got here, who they were, where they were from, or what they called themselves because they didn't write their history down for us. Because they came here without a written history, we call them prehistoric American Indians, or Americans who were here before history was recorded.

While there may be a lot of things that we don't know about Iowa's first people, there are some things we have discovered through studying artifacts that these first American Indians left behind. Archaeologists are scientists who dig up the remains of people and things that existed long ago and study them; these remains are called artifacts, and by studying them, archaeologists have learned a lot about the first people of Iowa. They have found many clues that have helped them to piece together a brief history of our state's first inhabitants.

Archaeologists believe that the first people living in America came here from Asia more than 20,000 years ago. These early people traveled here by walking across a bridge of land that once connected Asia and North America. This strip of land is called the Bering Strait and is now covered by the Bering Sea. Scientists believe that these first American Indians were nomads, meaning that they didn't stay in one place for long, but traveled around in search of animals to hunt for food. These early hunters crossed the strip of land from Asia to North America, searching for more game to hunt. They probably never knew that they had crossed into a new continent, but they continued to spread south throughout North America and South America.

The first American Indians found large beasts in the Iowa area and hunted them for food. The mastodon and the mammoth (both animals resembling elephants) were huge mammals that the early American Indians used for food. These animals were large and slow, but difficult to kill. To hunt them, it appears that the early people of Iowa chased them into large bogs or muddy swamps. When the beasts got stuck in the mud, the hunters could kill them with their spears. Archaeologists know this because they have found American Indian spear points near the bones of the ancient mastodons and mammoths.

Eventually, the American Indians killed all of the big game, and their lifestyle began to change. They had to learn to hunt and kill small animals, and they also began to gather wild plants, berries and nuts to survive. These people often lived in caves where archaeologists have found many early American Indian artifacts. They have found needles made of bone, probably used for making clothes, and also small nets and bags. Scientists think that the nets were used for trapping animals for food and that the bags were used for storing seeds and nuts. One of the oldest artifacts from this period ever found in Iowa is a small flute. The flute is made from the bone of a bird and was found near the city of Cherokee in northwest Iowa.

Later, the early American Indians created villages and towns. They planted crops for food and began burying their dead in large effigy mounds in northeast Iowa.

The Woodland people were probably the first to plant small gardens in Iowa. They continued to gather food from the forests, but they planted a few crops in their villages as well.

The Woodland people are also well known for their pottery. These early American Indians molded pots from clay and then baked them for several hours in a hot fire. They often decorated their pottery with designs made by pressing rope into the wet clay before it was fired. Archaeologists can often tell one American Indian group from another by the differences in the pottery they made.

By the time the first French explorers arrived in Iowa, the early American Indians were gone. The only things left were their mounds and other artifacts. There are still many things we don't know about these early people of Iowa, but thanks to the things they left behind, we are learning more all the time.

title: Effigy Mounds National Monument
text:
There are prehistoric American Indian mounds found from the Midwest to the Atlantic seaboard, but did you know that the area in and around Effigy Mounds National Monument is the only place where mounds constructed in the shapes of mammals, birds, and reptiles can be found?

Effigy Mounds National Monument is located in northeast Iowa near Harpers Ferry. Effigy Mounds National Monument became a national monument in 19 fourty nine and covers over 2wenty 5ive hundred00 acres. The park contains over 1 hundred 90 prehistoric American Indian mounds, and 3 1 of these are animal effigies. An effigy mound is a mound that is made in the shape of an animal or bird, rather than the more common cone or rectangular shape. The mounds in the park were built by the Eastern Woodland Indians from about 5 hundred00 B. C. to A. D. 13 hunred00.

The park has a visitor's center near the entrance. In the visitor's center, tourists will find an information desk, museum exhibits and auditorium for lectures. The park offers ranger guided tours, hikes and even prehistoric tool demonstrations.

Each September to October, Effigy Mounds National Monument also hosts the annual Hawk Watch. Visitors can come to the park and view the many hawks and other birds of prey that make this area their home. Skilled bird watchers come every year during the Hawk Watch and bring their spotting scopes and binoculars to help visitors view the hawks for themselves.

If you want to see a piece of Iowa's ancient history, or if you want to take a look at some of our native wildlife, plan a trip to Effigy Mounds National Monument!

title: Why do we call the earliest people of Iowa “Prehistoric” American Indians?
text: We call them "prehistoric" American Indians because they lived at a time before their people started writing down their history. "Pre" means "before," so "prehistoric" means "before history." It isn't that the early American Indians didn't have a history; of course they did! It is just that we don't know exactly what that history is because they didn't write it down for us. We study their artifacts and the things they left behind and write their history as well as we can with the facts we have.

title: The Oak Tree
text:
Do you know which tree has been designated as Iowa's official state tree? If you guessed it was the oak tree, you're right! The oak tree is a member of the Quercus family and is famous for its strength and its long life. The oak tree became Iowa's official state tree in 1961.

Oak trees are native to Iowa, which means that they can be found growing wild here in our state. Oaks are prized for their beautiful, hardwood lumber. Oak is used in construction and shipbuilding and is popular for furniture, flooring, barrels, railroad ties and tool handles.

Oak trees are also prized for their acorns. Acorns are an important part of the diet of many animals and birds. Iowa wildlife that feed on acorns include turkeys, pheasants, quail, wood ducks, raccoons, squirrels, chipmunks, blue jays and many types of woodpeckers.

While oak trees are useful in producing lumber and acorns, they are probably most loved for their beauty and for the shade they produce. Oaks are beautiful growing in our woodlands, parks, and cities. You may even have an oak tree growing in your own backyard!

title: Etchings
text:
Materials

Crayons, including black

Stiff white paper

Black ink

Paintbrush

Nail or nail file

Instructions

1. Color your white piece of paper with light-colored crayons. Push hard on the crayons so that it leaves a thick layer of color all over the paper. Do different patches of color so that it is filled with all colors.

2. Cover over the patches of color with black crayon, or paint over them with two coats of black ink. Let the ink dry between the coats. Make sure all the patches are covered completely.

3. Take your nail or nail file, or anything with a pointy end, and scratch a picture on the black surface. You can scrape away the black crayon or ink, and, underneath, you should be able to see the colored layers peeking through.

Continue to scratch into the black ink or crayon until you’ve drawn the picture you had in mind. Hang your creation in your classroom or room at home.

Note: Be careful with the pointy object you use to create your etching. Do this activity with adult supervision.

title: Types of Mounds
text:
There are 206 prehistoric mounds found in Effigy Mounds National Monument. These mounds come in many different shapes and sizes. The four most common types of mounds are conical, linear, compound and animal effigy. Using what you know about effigy mounds, correctly label each type of mound found at the monument.

Now that you have labeled each mound correctly, it’s your turn to design your own mound. On a separate sheet of paper, design your own effigy mound. Be sure to give it a name and tell why it is important.

When you’re done, share your mound with the class!

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend that you belong to one of the mound-building tribes. Describe how to build a mound and what it will be used for. What is the mound made of? How big is it? Who is in charge of planning the mound? Who does the work to build it? Use your imagination and have fun!

title: What Did the Early American Indians Give to Us?
text:
We have learned that Iowa's first people were American Indians who hunted, farmed, and settled here long before white people claimed the land as their own. Although it has been many years since the early American Indians roamed the land, Iowa still retains many reminders of their presence.

The names of many of our rivers, lakes and cities are American Indian names. The counties of Sioux, Winnebago, Pottawattamie and Sac are all named after American Indian tribes. The names for the Missouri, Mississippi, and Big and Little Sioux Rivers are all American Indian names as well.

We use many American Indian words without even realizing that they are not our own. Tomahawk, papoose, hominy and wigwam are all American Indian words that we know the meanings of and use from time to time.

Did you know that the name of our state, Iowa, is also an American Indian word? "Iowa" is an American Indian word that means "beautiful land." This is the name that one of the early Iowa tribes called itself: Ioway. A young army lieutenant named Albert M. Lea called the land "Iowa" after the Ioway tribe living here when he arrived. Because the American Indians were the first people to live here, it is natural for us to call our state after them.

What other things do we have to remind us of the early American Indians of our state? Many of the foods we eat every day come from the American Indian culture. Did you know that corn, potatoes, squash, pumpkins, beans and tomatoes were all crops that were grown by the American Indians? Corn bread is also a popular food that was first introduced to us by the American Indians. Hominy and succotash are also foods that you may have eaten which were first eaten by Iowa's early inhabitants. Hominy is made from hulled and dried kernels of corn, which are then boiled. Succotash is a vegetable dish made from cooked corn, lima beans and tomatoes.

Some other things that are familiar to us today, but that we have borrowed from the American Indians are the canoe, the hammock, and the tobacco pipe. American Indian clothing has also become popular at times. Have you ever worn moccasins, a vest or shirt with fringe, or a parka? Each of these items was worn first by the Americans Indian.

Even though the early American Indian tribes no longer live here as they once did, the influence of these people lives on in our state. Whenever we say "Iowa," wear a pair of moccasins, or eat a piece of corn bread, we can remember the people who first called Iowa home.

text:

title: Iowa Tribes
text:
Ioway

The Ioway tribe is one of the first Iowa tribes to have contact with Europeans. The French explorers who first met members of the Ioway tribe called the land after the American Indians who lived here. Iowa is named after this early American Indian tribe.

The Ioway people were some of Iowa's first farmers. They were not nomads, as many of the earlier tribes had been, but lived in the same place for years at a time. The Ioways built houses of willow poles and elm bark, leaving a small hole in the roof to be used as a chimney. The women planted vegetables each spring and cared for them throughout the summer. They grew beans, squash, and corn. The Ioway people were the first to grow corn in the rich Iowa soil. The Ioways used corn in many ways. They ground it into meal and made corn bread from it. They cooked the corn with meat in their stew pots, and they even roasted the ears over the fire and ate it from the cob.

In 1677, when the Ioways first came in contact with European explorers and traders, their way of life changed forever. Up until this time, the Ioways had made everything they used, but after finding that they could trade with the Europeans, they began to depend on this trade to get things they wanted and needed. The Ioways traded animal skins for iron kettles, glass beads, metal knives, cotton cloth and European guns. The Ioways liked the new things they were able to get from the Europeans, so they began to hunt more than ever before so that they would have plenty of skins to trade for the things they wanted. Animals became more scarce, and the tribe began to look for better hunting grounds. They continued to move farther south and west, always searching for better hunting grounds.

Sauk

The Sauk tribe once lived in northern Michigan, while the Mesquakie had settled along the Fox River in Wisconsin. Together, these two tribes drove away the Illinois Indians and settled along the Mississippi and Wapsipinicon Rivers. These two tribes controlled the hunting grounds in western Illinois and eastern Iowa.

The Sauk people settled in a large village called Saukenuk on the east side of the Mississippi River at the mouth of the Rock River. This village was once the home of thousands of Sauk Indians. They fished and gathered nuts, berries and fruit from the forest. The women were in charge of planting and caring for large gardens of beans, pumpkins and squash, as well as hundreds of acres of corn.

In the summer, most of the Sauk left the village for a huge hunting expedition. They hunted for buffalo and elk throughout western Iowa and returned in the fall. With fresh meat from a successful hunt, the Sauk celebrated with feasts, horse races and games. They also traded meat and skins with traders for needed supplies. The women were busy preparing the meat and skins, drying vegetables from their gardens and storing food for the winter.

As winter approached, the Sauk left for their cold-weather homes. They took some food and buried the rest in deep pits. When the cold weather ended and spring came again, the Sauk returned to their village and planted crops for a new season.

Mesquakie

The Mesquakie tribe is also called the Fox tribe. "Mesquakie" means "red Earth people." The Mesquakie also lived in permanent villages, just like the Sauk. The women planted and cared for gardens, and the men went on yearly hunts across the prairie.

The Mesquakie Tribe was made up of family groups called clans. Each clan participated in special religious ceremonies and helped govern the tribe. The Mesquakie also had a religious organization called the Grand Medicine Society made up of medicine men who were believed to have the power to heal the sick. These medicine men supposedly used supernatural powers to help the tribe and make sure that it was protected. These medicine men often used special objects to help work their magic.

The Mesquakie people were eventually forced out of Iowa and moved to Kansas, but they missed their homes. Many Mesquakie families joined together and bought 80 acres of land near the town of Tama in central Iowa. The Mesquakie still call this area home today.

title: Mines of Spain Recreation Area
text:
Located along the south edge of the city of Dubuque, near the mouth of Catfish Creek, the Mines of Spain State Recreation Area was first inhabited by the Mesquakie tribe. The Mesquakie tribe carried on the fur trade with the French traders from this site. They also worked the lead mines in the area.

The Mines of Spain Recreation Area was dedicated in 19 80 1 and became a National Historic Landmark in 19 90 3. It is made up of 13 80 acres of mostly rugged, wooded bluff land. The area has also been designated as one of Iowa's "Watchable Wildlife Areas," which means that it is a good place to view interesting wildlife species in their natural habitats. You can see many types of rare species in the Mines of Spain, including the bobcat, red shouldered hawk, flying squirrel and bald eagle.

The E. B. Lyons Interpretive Center is located inside the park. It acts as a visitor information center and a park office. The center is open all year and provides information about the native prairies, woodland flower gardens and hiking trails in the area.

Another feature of the area is the Horseshoe Bluff Interpretive Area. This is a horseshoe shaped dolomite rock quarry that allows visitors to see the interesting geological layers that make up the land in the area. There is also a 15 acre wetland with two "floating trails" that visitors can raft or boat down to view the wildlife in the wetlands.

The Mines of Spain Recreation Area also offers hiking and cross country ski trails. There are four miles of groomed ski trails and 12 miles of hiking trails. The park offers five different nature walks, and trapping, archery and limited firearm hunting are also permitted in the park.

title: Do we say “Native American” or “American Indian”?
text: Some individuals and some entire tribes of Native Americans prefer to be called American Indians. Some are offended by the name Indian because the name was a mistake that Christopher Columbus made when he sailed to America and thought he had reached India. It is considered correct to use the terms Native American, American Indian, Indian or indigenous people, according to the tribes' websites. Everyone agrees that we are all proud to be called Americans!

title: Blue Jay
text:
One of Iowa's most beautiful and familiar birds is the blue jay. The scientific name for the blue jay is Cyanocitta cristata, and it is a native of central and eastern North America. The blue jay is closely related to the crow, the raven and the magpie.

The blue jay is a large bird that usually measures about a foot long. It is a very showy bird and is easy to spot because of its size and its striking color. The upper parts of the blue jay, including the crest, are a grayish violet-blue. The rest of the bird is a bright, vivid blue. The wings and tail are the brightest blue of all, with black and white markings. There is a ring of black around the neck of the blue jay, and the under parts of the bird are gray and white.

The blue jay is also known for its loud, boisterous cry. It often imitates the cry of other birds as well, especially that of the hawk.

The diet of the blue jay consists of large insects, seeds and nuts. They especially enjoy eating acorns and beechnuts. The blue jay is also known to eat small baby birds and eggs.

title: Famous Person Book
text:
Materials

12-inch–by–18-inch piece of construction paper

6-inch–by–6-inch piece of construction paper

scissors

glue

crayons and markers

Instructions

1. Fold the piece of 12-by-18–inch paper into eight equal sections as shown in the picture.

2. (You don’t have to label your sections as they are labeled here. We’ve done that to help you know which pieces to cut and fold.) Cut out sections E and H. Save these pieces for later.

3. Fold sections A and D into the center to make a vest or jacket. Glue pieces E and H on the back for arms, as shown in the
picture.

4. Cut a head from the 6-by-6–inch piece of
construction paper. Glue it to the top of sections B and C. To make pants for your famous person, cut a small triangle between sections F and G as shown. (Or you can cut the lower corners off these sections to create a skirt.)

5. Draw your famous person’s face on the head. You can add hair and clothing. Add hands and shoes cut from paper scraps.

6. Open the flaps of the jacket and, on the inside, write something about your famous person. If you’d like, you can write a longer story or essay about your famous person on folded pieces of paper and then staple the pages into your famous person book.

Extra Activity: You can make your book about a family member or friend and give it to him or her as a gift.
