title: Father Jacques Marquette
text:
One of the earliest French explorers of the Iowa area was Father Jacques Marquette. Father Marquette was a Catholic priest who explored the area with fellow explorer Louis Jolliet. These two Frenchmen were the first Europeans to see the land of Iowa. Jacques Marquette was born on June 10, 16 30 7, in Laon, Aisne, France. He began his training as a Jesuit priest when he was 17 years old, and before long, he knew exactly what he wanted to do with his life. He had heard about the excitement and adventure in faraway lands, and he wanted to see it for himself. Marquette wrote, "Would that I be ordered to set out for foreign lands. This has been the object of my thoughts since my earliest childhood." In 16 60 6, Marquette got his wish when he was assigned to the Catholic missions in Canada.

While working as a missionary in Canada, Father Marquette met a French trader named Louis Jolliet. Jolliet wanted to explore the land to the south and find new American Indian tribes to trade with for furs. When Father Marquette heard about Jolliet's interest in exploring the area, he was excited about the possibility of going along. He hoped to convert new American Indian tribes to Catholicism. The two men spent a lot of time talking to the American Indians living in the Great Lakes area about the land located to the west and south. These American Indians told Marquette and Jolliet about a river they called the Mississippi, which in their language meant, "The Father of the Waters." This river fascinated Marquette and Jolliet, and they decided to set off on a journey down this great and unexplored river.

The two men left from St. Ignace, on Green Bay, where Father Marquette had served as a missionary since 16 70. They had with them a crew of five men, and they traveled in two birch bark canoes. The date was May 17, 16 70 3. They found the Mississippi River with help from their American Indian guides and began paddling down the huge and mysterious river.

As Marquette and Jolliet traveled down the river, they were careful to record everything they saw, from the giant catfish in the river to the wild turkeys and buffalo along the banks. They took notes describing each American Indian tribe they found and each twist and turn of the river they noticed. Near the spot where the Missouri and Mississippi Rivers join, the group met and visited with some American Indians from the Missouri tribe. These Missouri people warned Marquette and Jolliet that the American Indian tribes farther down the river were dangerous and unfriendly. Jolliet and Marquette were also afraid to travel farther down the river because they knew that they might accidentally enter land that had been claimed by Spain. The Frenchmen were afraid that the Spanish might capture or kill them. Marquette and Jolliet decided that it would be better for them to turn back than to risk their lives.

By the time the Frenchmen turned back, they had already explored an area that no European had ever seen before. They had also discovered that the Mississippi River did not lead to the Pacific Ocean, but that it lead to the Gulf of Mexico, something that no one had known for certain.

After they returned to Canada, Father Marquette drew a detailed map of the Mississippi River and described the lands they had seen. Marquette described the land of Iowa as "treeless," but he also said that "no better soil can be found, either for corn, or for vines, or for any other fruit whatever."

Marquette later traveled south again and founded a Catholic mission among the Illinois tribe. On his way back to Canada, he became ill and died at the age of 30 8.

title: Leave No Trace
text:
There are 83 state parks and recreation areas in Iowa. They are great places to camp, hike, and spend time with your family and friends. If everyone is careful when visiting the parks, the wildlife will be protected and the land will stay clean.

The National Parks Council has asked us to "Leave No Trace" when we camp and hike. That means don't let other people know you were there because of something you did. Here are six ways to "leave no trace" when you are camping or hiking:

1. Travel on trails that are already made.

2. Dispose of trash the right way-in a trash can! Did you know that it takes 2 years for an orange peel to biodegrade? (That means that it will take 2 years before it will rot enough to turn back into dirt.) It takes 90 years for an aluminum can to biodegrade and 1 million years for it to happen to a glass jar!

3. Leave nature the way you found it. Do not take rocks or sticks home with you, and don't pick the flowers.

4. Don't feed the animals. If you feed them they will lose their fear of people. Our food is not good for them. If they are not afraid of people and they like people food, they will start to hunt for it. Then they will become a nuisance or even dangerous to hikers and campers.

5. Don't build a fire unless there is a pit already built for it. If there is no pit where you are camping, then make sure you clean up the pit you build before you leave.

6. Tell yourself, "Take only pictures and leave only footprints."

title: Entrepreneurship
text:
Benjamin Franklin was one of the greatest entrepreneurs in history. An entrepreneur takes risks to create something or find a better way to do something. Ben Franklin was imaginative, creative and very smart. He was able to try many things. He was respected for the things he did. When he died in 17 90, Franklin was known around the world as a businessman, politician, printer and inventor.

Franklin was born in 17 06. Even as a little boy, he loved to read, write and collect books. He left school at the age of 10. By the time he was 12, he was helping as a printer for his older brother, James. When Franklin was 20 2, he owned his own printing press and started his own newspaper, the Pennsylvania Gazette. He also printed Poor Richard's Almanack. That book became one of the most popular books in the colonies!

Franklin soon became one of the colonies' busiest printers. He was named the official printer for Delaware, New Jersery and Maryland. He printed money and legal documents. Franklin made so much money that he retired when was 40 2. He then became a full-time inventor.

Franklin was very important in the colonies. He started one of the first libraries in the United States with some of his friends. He signed the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. Franklin served as an ambassador from the colonies to France. He was the oldest member of the Constitutional Convention!

Ben Franklin did many things to be considered an entrepreneur. Like Franklin, there are many entrepreneurs today. Do the names Bill Gates, George Lucas, Henry Ford and Oprah Winfrey mean anything to you? All of these people are entrepreneurs. They brought great ideas and business to our economy. Can you think of any entrepreneurs where you live?

title: Iowa’s Explorers
text:
The French, English and Spanish were all important explorers of the New World, including Iowa.

French

After the discovery of the Americas, the French had watched Spain get rich from the gold and silver they had found in the New World, and they, too, wanted some of the wealth. France sent explorers to North America, hoping that they would discover gold as well.

The early French explorers arrived in Canada, but found no gold or silver there. They did find something of great value there, however. Wealthy French men and women loved to wear fancy clothing and hats made from the furs of beaver, mink and otter. These furs and skins were widely available in North America. The American Indians of the area trapped and skinned these animals, so the French made friends with these American Indians and found ways to get them to trade the furs with them. The Frenchmen traded tools, cloth, beads and guns with the American Indians for these valuable furs and then sent the furs home to France for a good price. Eventually, the French wanted to explore the land to the south and west, hoping to find more furs and more American Indians willing to trade with them.

Louis Jolliet was one of these French fur traders who wanted to explore the land to the south, hoping to find more furs and more friendly American Indians. He also hoped to find a waterway (a body of water that can be sailed or floated down) that would lead to the Pacific Ocean. He joined with the Catholic missionary Father Jacques Marquette on a journey down the mighty Mississippi River, and the two became the first Europeans to explore the Mississippi. (See cover story on the front page.)

After the famous expedition of Jolliet and Marquette, another French explorer decided to make the same trip. Robert de La Salle planned to explore the Mississippi River and build a series of forts and trading posts along its banks. He set out in January of 16 80 2 to explore the river and the land around it, claiming everything he saw in the name of the King of France, King Louis XIV. La Salle called the region "Louisiana," in honor of the king. At this time, Louisiana included all the land from the Rocky Mountains to the Appalachian Mountains and from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico.

The French explorers who first came to the Iowa area came for two main reasons: to expand the fur trade and to convert the American Indians to Christianity. Both the French fur traders and the Catholic missionaries helped to explore and eventually settle the land we now call Iowa.

English

The English didn't agree with the claims that the French made to the land in the Mississippi River area. They also claimed the land, not for fur trading or mining, but for settlements (small communities where groups of people lives together). The English had already settled colonies along the Atlantic Coast and wanted to expand their colonies even farther. The Appalachian Mountains had been a barrier to this expansion in the past, but now the English were ready to claim the Mississippi River area.

In 17 50 6, the English and the French went to war over the right to claim parts of North America as their own. The English won control over most of the land that had once been held by the French.

Spanish

When the French saw that the English were winning the war, they secretly gave their lands to Spain. The French hated the English and would rather give their land to the Spanish than see England take control of it. The Spanish became the owners of the land west of the Mississippi. By this time, Spain had already been in the Americas for many years. After the discovery of the New World, or the Americas, Spain sent many explorers here searching for gold and other wealth. Spain found gold and silver in Mexico and parts of South America, and it became a wealthy nation.

The English soon forgot about both the French and the Spanish, however, as they developed bigger problems. In 17 70 6, the American colonies declared their independence from England, and the American Revolution­ occupied all the thoughts and resources of the British.

After the Revolutionary War ended, the boundaries (borders marking the end of a territory) of the United States were drawn up with the Mississippi River becoming the western border of the new nation. Iowa, therefore, was not part of the original United States, but was still part of the Spanish Empire.

title: Pikes Peak State Park
text:
Pikes Peak State Park marks the spot where Jolliet and Marquette first reached Iowa. Located in northeastern Iowa near McGregor, Pikes Peak State Park is the highest bluff on the Mississippi River. From the 5 hundred00 foot bluff, you can see the Wisconsin and the Mississippi Rivers to the south and the twin suspension bridges connecting Iowa and Wisconsin to the north.

Pikes Peak was named for the explorer Zebulon Pike, who explored the Mississippi River Valley in 18 05. It became a state park in 19 30 5.

Today, Pikes Peak State Park offers many activities for those who enjoy the outdoors. Because the land has never been developed with houses and businesses, visitors can view the land much as it would have looked hundreds of years ago when Jolliet and Marquette first saw it. There are many picnic sites in the park, as well as several overlook areas. From these areas, visitors can view several effigy mounds built by the ancient American Indians who once lived in the area. The park also offers overnight camping.

Pikes Peak is also well known for its hiking trails. Along the trails, hikers will see wooded bluffs, beautiful valleys, walls of Decorah limestone and even fossil remains of prehistoric sea creatures. There are also six permanent Volkssport Trails, which are trails meant for use by the entire family. Families often use these trails, carrying their infants on their backs or pushing them in strollers. There are also several portions of the park trail system that allow mountain biking.

To see what Iowa looked like before settlers began changing the face of the land, plan a visit to Pikes Peak State Park.

title: Who was the first European to settle in Iowa?
text: The first European to settle in Iowa was Julien Dubuque. Dubuque was born in Canada in 1762, and he arrived in Iowa in 17 80 8. He received a large land grant from the Spanish and married the daughter of a Mesquakie chief. He successfully mined lead in the Iowa area for several years. The city of Dubuque is named after this man.

title: Opossum
text:
The opossum is the only marsupial to make its home in North America. Marsupial means that the female of the species has a pouch in which to carry and nurse her young.

The opossum is about the size of a house cat, measuring about 40 3 inches long. The opossum's tail makes up about half of these 40 3 inches. The opossum is gray to black in color with black eyes, black ears, and a pointed nose. The opossum's nose, feet, and tail are pink. Opossums are famous for their prehensile tail. Prehensile means that the tail is adapted for grabbing and holding onto things.

The opossum likes to live alone and is nocturnal, meaning that it sleeps in the daytime and roams around at night. The opossum is a slow animal and often goes into a state of shock when frightened. This state causes the opossum to "play dead," which is why we use the term, "playing 'possum" when describing someone who is faking or pretending to be asleep.

The opossum eats insects, snails, rodents, berries, fruit and occasionally snakes, eggs, corn or other vegetables. The opossum rarely lives longer than one year in its natural environment and is often killed by cars, dogs, cats, owls and other wildlife.

title: Clarity of Expression: Henry Hudson
text:
Henry Hudson was an English sea captain and explorer who started off as a failure. He sailed on two voyages for England to find a northeast water route to the rich spice trade in Asia. But both times the icy northern seas blocked his way. He had to return home defeated.

Sounds like the end of his career, right? It wasn't. Hudson next convinced the Dutch East India Company to hire him for exactly the same expedition. In 16 09 Hudson and his crew sailed west across the Atlantic. He reached the New World, landing on the island we know today as Manhattan. He sailed inland up a wide river and explored the surrounding valley.

It wasn't a passage to Asia. But Hudson's explorations allowed the Dutch to claim the land and build a fur trading post there in 16 14, before the Pilgrims arrived. A Dutch settlement called New Netherland soon followed.

Unfortunately, Hudson's last voyage ended in mutiny. He refused his crew's demands to return home, so the sailors took over the ship, setting Hudson adrift in a small boat. His fate is unknown, but his legacy is Hudson Bay, Hudson River, Hudson Valley and the Dutch settlement that became New York City.

Henry Hudson must have had excellent clarity of expression. He had to be able to explain clearly to the Dutch that his experience and determination made him the best man for the job, even though he was an Englishman and not a Dutchman.

Think about a time that you wanted to convince your parents or teachers to let you try something new. Did you beg and plead? Or did you give them a clear explanation of your reasons? Which way do you think works better?

title: Language Arts Connection
text: As you read this week’s lesson, use any color to circle or highlight five verbs. On a piece of paper, write a sentence for each verb using the perfect form (past tense + helping verb: I have walked. She has swung.). (CC ELA L.5.1)

title: James Monroe
text:
James Monroe was one of our country's great statesmen. He was especially important to Iowa because he was charged with making the Louisiana Purchase, which included Iowa land.

Monroe served as president of the United States from 1817 to 1825 during what was later called the "Era of Good Feelings." It was called this because it was a time when the new country of America was beginning to feel good about itself and to have success in many areas. The political party that President Monroe was a member of, the Democratic-Republican Party, ruled almost without opposition. People were beginning to leave the colonies to settle the lands to the west, roads and canals were being built, and most of all, people had begun to think of themselves not just as New Yorkers or Virginians, but as Americans. America as a nation was growing and becoming more powerful.

Before Monroe became president, he served his home state of Virginia as a congressional representative and later as governor. He also served his country as a U.S. Senator. While serving in Congress, he became very interested in the lands to the west of the Mississippi River. During 1784, Monroe took a trip through the West. He went up the Hudson River, saw the Great Lakes, and returned down the Ohio River. After this visit, Monroe was more interested than ever in making these lands part of the United States.

Monroe is not only famous for serving his country here at home, but also for his work as a diplomatic minister to France. (A diplomatic minister is someone who represents his nation to another for the purpose of promoting good relations.) Monroe had been serving as a U.S. Senator from Virginia when he was asked to go to France and try to improve relations between the United States and France. France was unhappy with the United States because it felt that the United States was too friendly with Great Britain, France's greatest enemy. Monroe went to France in 1794 to see what he could do. While he served as a minister to France, some people thought that he showed too much love for France. He often gave speeches that were very much in favor of France and not in favor of Great Britain. Eventually, he was called back from France because the United States was afraid that the things Monroe was telling the French would upset the British. The United States was hoping to remain friendly with both France and Great Britain.

Although Monroe was called home from France because he seemed to be too friendly with the French, this good relationship would come in handy a few years later. In 1803, Monroe was sent back to France when the United States was ready to make what has been called the largest real-estate deal in history, the Louisiana Purchase. Monroe joined United States Diplomat Robert Livingston in France and helped to figure out the terms of the agreement. Monroe's good relationship with the French and his interest in expanding the United States westward helped to make the Louisiana Purchase a wonderful deal for America.

By the time he died in 1831, Monroe had given more than 40 years to public service. He spent his life doing what he considered to be his duty in helping to make the United States a strong, honorable, and lasting country.

title: Is There Too Much Money in Politics?
text:
Candidates are spending huge amounts of money on political campaigns, more than ever before. There are many reasons for this, but a big reason is a decision made by the Supreme Court in 2010. In a decision called "Citizens United," the Supreme Court said corporations and unions could donate an unlimited amount of money to campaigns, but not directly to candidates. Many people think that this much money and secrecy in politics can only lead to trouble. Others are glad that the rules have changed.

A company or group with a lot of money can pay for commercials that support the candidate they like and criticize the other candidates. But some people say that the public doesn't know who those groups are. The groups might not be honest about what they want the candidate to do if he or she is elected. If the candidate is elected, then some believe that the groups will say, "We helped you win, now you change the laws to help our group get what we want."

Those who agree with the Supreme Court's decision say it's good to have fewer rules and less government involvement in campaigns. Many believe it doesn't matter who gives money, and politicians will do the jobs they were elected to do.

Political races will certainly be different because of the new rules. Watch the candidates' commercials and discuss them with your parents and teachers. What do YOU think about money and politics?

title: Louisiana Purchase - Iowa
text:
By the late 1700s, Spain had taken control of the Iowa area, although some French settlers still lived there. In 1800, however, the Spanish made a deal with France to give control of the area back to France. France traded the region of Tuscany, in Europe, to Spain for the Louisiana region in North America. Spain was more interested in getting control of Tuscany, and France was very anxious to get back control of the Louisiana Territory to keep it out of the hands of Great Britain, its greatest enemy. Napoleon, the leader of France, was planning to make France a powerful nation by gaining control of some important lands.

New Orleans Trade Problems

When the United States heard about this new development, they were worried because when the French were in control of the port of New Orleans once before, they had closed it to the Americans. This made it impossible for them to float their goods down the Mississippi River and sell them in New Orleans. The western traders wanted the United States government to help them keep the port of New Orleans open for trade.

President Thomas Jefferson decided to talk to the French and try to solve the problem. He asked Robert Livingston, the American minister to France, to talk to the French government about the Mississippi River. He also sent James Monroe, the former American minister to France, and told these two men to offer to buy New Orleans and West Florida from France as well.

United States Doubles in Size

When Livingston and Monroe visited with Napoleon about the problem, they were surprised to have Napoleon offer to sell the entire Louisiana Territory to the United States. Napoleon had lost interest in trying to hang on to land in America, and he was also in great need of money, as he was still trying to revive a war against Great Britain. He also wanted to make sure that the Louisiana Territory never ended up under British control, as the British were despised enemies of the French. Because he wanted to resolve the problem quickly, Napoleon offered to sell the entire Louisiana Territory, about 375 million acres, to the United States for the unbelievably low price of $15 million.

Livingston and Monroe were surprised, but they quickly worked out an agreement, and the treaty (an agreement between nations) for the Louisiana Purchase was signed on April 30, 1803. Neither of the American representatives had been told that they could spend that much money, or buy that much land, but when the opportunity came, they couldn't refuse. President Jefferson later approved their actions, and most people in the United States were happy with the purchase of the new western lands. This purchase doubled the size of the United States at the price of only a few cents per acre. The United States made a great bargain!

U.S. Flag Raised

On Dec. 20, 1803, the French flag was lowered at New Orleans, and the American flag was raised. A few months later, another flag-raising ceremony was held, this time in St. Louis. On March 9, 1804, Captain Amos Stoddard accepted the transfer of Upper Louisiana from France to the United States. The American flag was raised for the first time over the area on this date.

Moses Austin, the colonizer of Texas, wrote in his journal around 1797, "It is Not possible a Country which has with in its self everything to make its settlers Rich and Happy can remain unoticed [sic] by the American people." (Spelling and capitalization as originally written.) The words of Austin proved to be true as Americans began to flood this new area in search of fertile soil, wide open spaces, and the adventure of a new land.

title: Old Fort Madison
text:
In 1808, the first United States military post on the upper Mississippi River was built in what is now Iowa. Settlers called the fort Fort Madison after President James Madison. Soldiers of the First Regiment U.S. Infantry built it to protect the government "factory," or trading post in the area, and to keep the American frontier safe.

After continual American Indian attacks and trouble during the War of 1812, the commander ordered that the fort be abandoned in 1813. The soldiers who fled the fort set fire to it as they left, because they did not want the American Indians in the area to use it for their own protection.

In 1983, the city of Fort Madison received two government grants to help rebuild the historic fort. Today, the fort has been restored to nearly the same location where it once stood. It offers many activities to help visitors see what life would have been like at the frontier fort in the old days.

Visitors are greeted by guides wearing clothing much like that worn during the early 1800s. The guides help visitors tour the old fort and offer them opportunities to see firsthand what frontier life was all about. Visitors can try a taste of home-baked bread, lift an authentic musket, and try their hand at dipping candles.

There are also many special events held at the fort throughout the year, including a special Children's Day each August, a Military History Reunion each June, and a Trade Fair and Re-enactment of the Siege of Fort Madison in September.

title: How many states were eventually carved out of the land that the United States bought from France as part of the Louisiana Purchase?
text: The Louisiana Purchase was eventually divided into 13 states or parts of states. These states were Louisiana, Arkansas, Missouri, Iowa, North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas, Wyoming, Minnesota, Oklahoma, Colorado, and Montana.

title: Raccoon
text:
The raccoon is a common animal in Iowa. It is a nocturnal animal, which means that it likes to sleep during the day and prowl during the night. The raccoon is sometimes called "coon" for short.

The raccoon has a heavy, rounded body and a pointed face. Its front paws look like hands, and the raccoon uses them very much like we use our hands. The raccoon is also covered with heavy gray, brown, and black fur, and it has a large, bushy tail with black rings along it. The raccoon is usually one and one-half to two and one-half feet long, and its tail adds another eight to 12 inches to its length. It is sometimes compared to a robber because it has a black "mask" of fur around its eye area. It can also be found stealing corn and other vegetables from the gardens of local farmers.

Raccoons are good climbers, and they often build their nests in hollow trees. They live mostly in wooded areas and feed along lakes and streams. They eat all kinds of foods, including nuts, seeds, fruits, eggs, insects, frogs, and crayfish. When the raccoon is near water, it likes to "wash" its food by dipping it in water before eating it.

title: An 'Interest'ing Way to Make Money
text:
Why do people save money? Some people save up to buy something special; others save money for emergencies, like getting sick or needing a new roof after a storm. Many people save money for retirement, the time when they don't have to work anymore. Those are all good reasons for saving money.

But there's another reason to save money. Did you know there are ways to make your money grow faster by letting someone else use it for a while? That's called investing. How does that work? Let's take a look.

Imagine that you put $1 each week in a piggy bank or cookie jar. At the end of one year, you will have $52. Sounds pretty good, right?

But if you put $1 each week in a savings account, the bank will pay you interest. Interest is the money you get for letting the bank use your money for a while. The bank invests your money in things like real estate (homes, farms and land) or the stock market, and your money makes more money. You get some, and the bank keeps some. So, at the end of one year, instead of having $52 you might have $53 or $54.

There are many ways to earn interest on your money. You don't have to let the bank invest your money for you. You can invest in things like real estate or the stock market on your own. There are lots of other choices, too.

How do you know where to invest? You can do research to find out which investments are right for you. Or you can get some help from a financial planner, a person who gives people advice about how to invest money.

Are you getting "interested"? Then start saving!

title: Fun Facts
text: Four presidential candidates won the popular vote but lost the election (due to the electoral college system): Andrew Jackson in 1824, Samuel J. Tilden in 1876, Grover Cleveland in 1888, and Al Gore in 2000.

title: Lewis and Clark Explore a Strange and Forbidding Land!
text:
Welcome to another terrific issue of Iowa Studies Weekly! This week, our adventures take us back in time over 200 years to the land of the Rocky Mountains and beyond to the Pacific Ocean. We know all about this land today, but back in 1803 it seemed like a distant new world. No European Americans had ever been there. President Thomas Jefferson wondered if dinosaurs might still exist in the area. Exploring these lands seemed as unknown and scary to people then as sending a man to Mars may seem to us today. Come with us as we meet the two brave men chosen to lead the "Corps of Discovery," as they were called, into this strange and forbidding new land.

So who were Meriwether Lewis and William Clark? These were really great men—brave and smart—and they loved adventure. They were friends of President Thomas Jefferson who were appointed to explore a huge chunk of land called the Louisiana Purchase. In 1803, this was the latest addition to America’s backyard, but no one knew for sure what was there. Lewis and Clark were given the job to find out. They were to follow the Missouri River to its source and, from there, try to get to the Pacific Ocean. They accomplished their goal, but not without near starvation, one death, dangerous encounters all the way, and much sickness and hardship.

Sacagawea Joins the Expedition

The party of about 40 departed in May 1804 from St. Louis. By late fall, they reached North Dakota, where they wintered. Their French guide had brought with him his wife, an American Indian woman named Sacagawea. She was a Shoshone and knew much about the country. She also helped negotiate with American Indians as an interpreter. Her first baby, Jean-Baptiste, was born at camp, and Clark nicknamed him Pompey. During a difficult journey over the Bitterroot Mountains, the group stumbled onto Sacagawea’s home tribe and family. There was dancing, crying and hugging when she found her brother, friends and relatives, whom she hadn’t seen since she was a little girl.

title: Join the Club — Explore the World
text:
Does exploring the North Pole, climbing Mount Everest or landing on the moon sound exciting to you? Members of the world famous Explorers Club have done all these things—and many more!

The Explorers Club was started in New York City in 1904 and has been around ever since. The club’s goal is to keep the spirit of exploration alive. It encourages its members to explore the land, sea, air and space and to teach others about science and the world around them. Many famous explorers have belonged to the Explorers Club, including Sir Edmund Hillary, the first person to climb to the top of Mount Everest; Robert Peary, the first person to explore the North Pole; Roald Amundsen, the first person to explore the South Pole; and Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, the first men to land on the moon.

Today, the club has more than 3,000 members in 60 countries around the world. Members of the club plan and carry out expeditions in interesting places around the globe. Each year, the Explorers Club gives special awards from the Youth Activities Fund to high school and college students who are interested in science and who have shown great talent in some way. These students sometimes get to go on special expeditions with members of the club.

If you are interested in finding out more about the Explorers Club, ask a parent or teacher to help you visit www.explorers.org.

title: Explorers
text:
The United States purchased the vast Louisiana Territory from France. President Jefferson was anxious to find out what the unexplored territory looked like. He sent his personal secretary, Meriwether Lewis, and his friend William Clark to explore it.

Journey Becomes Difficult

The journey became very hard. The party only had berries to eat. Another time, they only had bear grease and candles. Their moccasins were too thin, and they feared freezing their feet off, but they pressed onward.

The Nez Perce Indians in Idaho were very curious about Clark's African American helper, York. The American Indians would wet their fingers to rub off the color, thinking York was painted to ward off some spirit. The American Indians were also amazed that the white men would eat dogs. This was done because the constant diet of salmon was so tiring. Here's where our otherwise close and agreeable Lewis and Clark differed—Lewis enjoyed dog meat; Clark couldn't stand it!

As they journeyed down the Columbia, they found European goods among the various tribes. Europeans had not traveled this far inland, but the American Indians had traded the goods upriver from the coast. On Nov. 7, 1805, the explorers had their first view of the Pacific Ocean. By the time the party reached the ocean, everyone was very tired. They constructed Fort Clatsop for the winter and ate a native diet of berries and fish. Christmas was just another cold and rainy day as they forced themselves to eat spoiled elk, spoiled fish, and a few roots.

Great Success

The Lewis and Clark expedition was a great success. They were welcomed back home the following year as if they had returned from the dead, because they were feared lost. Their journals, maps, and friendly contacts with the American Indians opened up the area to safe passage for future travelers and strengthened America's claim on the western United States territory.

title: DeSoto National Wildlife Refuge
text:
DeSoto National Wildlife Refuge is located in west-central Iowa. The refuge is made up of 8,362 acres of important wildlife lands. These lands are used mainly as a stopover for migrating ducks and geese on their way south each winter and north again each spring. During a typical year, as many as 200,000 snow and blue geese use the refuge as a place to rest and feed during their migrations. There are also around 125,000 ducks that use the refuge during their migrations.

October and November are the months when the refuge sees the greatest number of waterfowl in the area. In early March, the refuge fills up again as the birds return from their winter homes. During these periods, visitors can see not only geese and ducks, but bald eagles, warblers, gulls, and shorebirds as well.

The DeSoto National Wildlife Refuge offers wonderful bird viewing from the DeSoto Visitor Center. Another great way to see the wildlife in the area is to take the 12-mile Wildlife Drive. This drive winds along DeSoto Lake, through the woods and grasslands, and near several freshwater ponds and the Missouri River.

Visitors can also visit the pond where the hull of the Bertrand steamboat is buried. The site also offers displays that explain the history of the steamboat on the Missouri River and what happened to the Bertrand.

There are several walking trails in the DeSoto National Wildlife Refuge. The Missouri Meander is located near the DeSoto Visitor Center and provides a 900-foot paved trail, followed by a footbridge and a 7/8-mile woodchipped trail through the woods and along DeSoto Lake. Fall is the perfect time to visit DeSoto National Wildlife Refuge!

title: Can crickets tell temperatures?
text: Yes! If you can count cricket chirps, you can tell the temperature. Count the number of cricket chirps from one cricket (or a group chirping in unison) for exactly 15 seconds, and then add 37. That will be the temperature in Fahrenheit. Celsius is a little harder. Count the chirps in 25 seconds, divide by three, add four, and that will be the temperature in Celsius.

title: Beaver
text:
Have you ever seen a beaver before? If you have, you are very lucky. Beavers don't like to be seen. Beavers are reddish-brown animals that look like big, chubby rats. Their tails are wide and flat, and their back feet are webbed like ducks'. This makes them very good swimmers.

Beavers like to live in ponds in the mountains. When there isn't a pond, though, they make one. They have very sharp front teeth, which they use to cut down trees. Then they drag the trees into a stream and make a dam. It takes many days and many logs to get the job done, but when the beavers finish, a new pond is made.

After building a dam, beavers make a den where they can hide from predators and have their families. (Predators are animals that like to eat other animals.) On the outside, the den looks like a pile of logs resting in the middle of the pond. But on the inside, there is a warm, safe room. The entrances to the den are under the water. This also helps protect the beavers.

There are many beavers in Iowa. Be sure to watch closely if you are near a river or stream. Chances are, you will see a beaver - or at least his dam.

title: Lewis and Clark Trail
text:
On the map you will see that Lewis and Clark not only explored the Louisiana Purchase, but also land belonging to Spain and Britain. Because Lewis and Clark wanted to find a water route to the Pacific Ocean, their journey took them through the Louisiana Purchase and beyond, all the way to the West Coast. Use the map to answer the following questions:

From which city did Lewis and Clark leave on their journey west?

Where did the Lewis and Clark Expedition spend the winter of 1804-1805?

Which country owned the land just south of the Louisiana Purchase?

Near which Oregon city did Lewis and Clark finally reach the Pacific Ocean?

Sacagawea met her brother in a village of _______________________ Indians.

Which country owned the land just north of the Louisiana Purchase?

title: Fun Facts
text: Alaska is home to both the northernmost and westernmost point in the United States. The northernmost is in Point Barrow and the westernmost is Cape Wrangell. It is also home to the highest point in the United States (Mt. McKinley).

title: Early Settlers Come to Iowa for Cheap Land
text:
Most of the settlers who came to Iowa in the beginning came for one thing: inexpensive land. Most of these settlers who came were from the northeastern United States, the states of Ohio or Indiana, or from Europe. They had heard of the rich, fertile soil available at reasonable prices in Iowa and wanted to come and get their share of the bargains.

Once the early settlers made it to Iowa, how was the land divided up fairly? The federal government had come up with a system that made buying land orderly and kept the boundaries of each piece of land secure.

The federal government sent men to survey the land of Iowa. To survey means to measure the land and map it out on paper. The survey conducted by the government marked out public townships that were six miles square. These six square miles were then marked out into 36 sections. Each of these sections contained 640 acres. An acre is made up of about 43,560 square feet. This is about the size of a football field. The area that makes up the state of Iowa took the men hired by the federal government about 20 years to survey!

Once the survey of the land was completed, the government set up a land office where it sold land to settlers. The land was sold by auction, which means that people bid on the land they wanted to buy. If the government accepted the bid, then the land was sold to the bidder. Most settlers bought 80 acres at a time, usually paying about $1.25 per acre. For about $100, most settlers were able to purchase enough land to farm and make a living. This doesn't seem like much money to us today, but in the 1830s and 1840s, this was still a lot of money. Many settlers only had a few dollars to their names when they made it to Iowa, and they often had to work and save for years just to earn enough to buy land.

There were also other ways that settlers could get land. The very early settlers were often able to use "squatter's rights" in order to claim the land. If the settlers arrived before the survey was completed, they could mark their own boundaries and settle the land on their own. If they settled the land, they earned the right to keep it. Most settlers came to Iowa after the surveys were completed, but there were some settlers who were able to get their land by squatting on it.

Another way that Iowa settlers were able to get land was to buy it from the railroads. The government gave land to the railroads to encourage them to build new railroad lines on the frontier. The railroads then sold most of this land in order to raise money to build more lines. Many people bought land from the railroads, but it was not cheap. It often cost as much as $8 to $10 per acre to buy railroad land.

Finally, there were settlers who were able to get land in Iowa by serving in the military. The government didn't often have much extra money to pay soldiers, so they would offer them land instead. Soldiers who served in the Black Hawk War and the Civil War were often paid with 120 acres of land in Iowa.

No matter how they got it, the early settlers of Iowa were happy and grateful to have land of their own and a place to call home.

title: Were Our Founding Fathers Rich?
text:
Some of our modern presidential candidates have been very wealthy. It is interesting to compare these people's fortunes to those of our founding fathers. For example, many people think that George Washington was our richest president. But is that true?

In letters to family and friends George Washington said he did not want to be president, but he was concerned that he didn't have enough money to live out his retirement. In other words, he needed the job! Like other founding fathers after the war, he had land but no cash.

Washington owned a lot of land, but no one wanted to buy any of it. People who rented parts of his land didn't have money to pay him. During the Revolution he refused to accept pay for being the commander of the Army. He fed his staff and paid spies with his own money. After the war, the government paid him back in Continental dollars, which were worthless. Washington even had to borrow money to get to the Constitutional Convention in 1787.

Thomas Jefferson once had to borrow money from one of his slaves. He died deeply in debt. When Alexander Hamilton died his family couldn't afford to bury him. They collected donations for his burial.

Our founding fathers pledged their lives, their fortunes and their sacred honor for freedom. They lost most of their fortunes because of the war. Their wealth was not in money; it was in service.

title: Early Settlers
text:
After the Louisiana Purchase was final, settlers began flocking to the new area to the West, hoping to find rich, fertile ground at reasonable prices. Settlers began arriving in Iowa and soon sent letters to friends and relatives, urging them to come as well. Many people took the advice of these first settlers, and between 1833 and 1870, nearly 1 million people came to Iowa. By 1870, nearly the entire state of Iowa had been settled.

Getting to Iowa

Before the Civil War, most of Iowa's settlers came from the northeastern United States, particularly from the states of Ohio and Indiana. There were also some southerners from Kentucky, Virginia, and Missouri. Many Europeans also came to Iowa, most coming from Holland, the British Isles, the Scandinavian countries, and Germany.

How did these early settlers get to Iowa? They obviously didn't just jump in their cars and head west. Most people came to Iowa over a long period of time, using several different means of transportation.

Those who came from Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Indiana usually came by covered wagon. Later, once the railroad was finished, many settlers came as far as they could by rail. Some settlers would take a stagecoach, then a steamboat, the railroad, and, finally, they would hire a wagon and a team of horses to take them to their final destinations in Iowa.

The European immigrants who came to Iowa had an even longer and more difficult journey ahead of them. They traveled on either sailing ships or steamships from a port in either Bristol, England, or Amsterdam, Holland. The trip to America usually lasted about six weeks, and the voyage was often very unpleasant. People often suffered from seasickness during the trip, which was always made worse if a storm came up. Storms could also delay the arrival of the ship in America.

Most of these immigrants (people who leave their countries to make homes in another) landed in New Orleans, where they then boarded steamboats that would take them up the Mississippi River. This trip usually took another three weeks, and then, finally, the immigrants arrived in one of Iowa's river cities.

Adjusting to the Prairie

When the early settlers finally arrived in Iowa, they had to get used to the new land. Most new settlers had come from areas where trees were plentiful and where wood was used for almost everything. Wood was used to build log cabins, to fuel their fires, to build their furniture, and to form their fences.

Iowa, however, had very few trees, and the new settlers had to find new materials to replace the wood they were used to using. There was plenty of tall grass, but not a tree to be seen in many areas. Settlers would go to the rivers and streams, where trees grew near their banks, to find enough timber (lumber) to build their log cabins. For fuel and fencing, however, the new settlers had to use some imagination.

The settlers discovered that dried prairie grass could be used as a fuel for their fires if it was tied into tight knots. The children were set to work tying knots in the dry grass. They could usually provide enough fuel for an entire day by spending an hour each morning tying knots. Some families used corncobs and cow chips, or dried cow manure, for fuel. Some settlers who had settled in southern Iowa found coal along the riverbanks and used this for their fires.

For fencing, some settlers stacked rocks and built walls from them. Others discovered that Osage orange, a fast-growing Iowa plant, could make a thick, fence-like hedge.

Once the pioneers started moving into northwest Iowa, they discovered that not only were trees scarce here, they were practically non-existent. There wasn't even enough timber to use for making log cabins. These settlers finally started using chunks of the prairie itself to build their houses. These sod houses, called "soddies," were built by mowing about an acre of grass, then cutting the sod into strips about three to six inches thick and a foot wide. These strips were then stacked on top of each other, forming the outside walls of the house. The door and windows were framed of lumber, and the roof was made by laying pieces of timber over the top of the walls and covering them with strips of sod, grass side up. In the spring, the roof would turn green, and prairie flowers would often bloom right on top of the roof.

These sod houses were warm in the winter and cool in the summer, although they were a bit dirty and could rain mud in a fierce rainstorm. The best part about a sod house was that it could be built with materials readily available to the settlers, and an average soddy only cost about $1500.

The early Iowa settlers were a hardy group of people, willing to work hard and to make do with what was available. Although the prairie may have seemed strange to them at first, with its lack of timber and mountains, the settlers soon adjusted to their new home and made the prairie a pleasant place to live.

title: Hayden Prairie
text:
Hayden Prairie is located in northeastern Iowa, in Howard County. It is one of the few native prairies left in our state. The prairie is named after Dr. Ada Hayden, a botany professor at Iowa State University who worked hard to see that at least some of Iowa's beautiful prairies were preserved and protected.

Dr. Hayden was concerned that the tall-grass prairies of Iowa were rapidly disappearing. She persuaded the Iowa Academy of Science to give her the money to buy a prairie site to be kept as it was and preserved for future generations. In 1944, the academy gave Dr. Hayden a grant of $100, and she used it to buy a 240-acre block of prairie ground in Howard County. After Dr. Hayden died in 1950, the land was named Hayden Prairie after her. In 1965, Hayden Prairie, became a National Natural Landmark and was dedicated as a state preserve in 1968.

Hayden Prairie is a wonderful place to see what most of Iowa looked like when the early settlers first arrived. More than 80 percent of our state was covered with tall prairie grasses like those of Hayden Prairie before it was tilled by settlers. Visitors to Hayden Prairie can see big blue stem, Indian grass, northern drop seed, blue joint, and slough grasses native to the early Iowa prairies.

The best times to visit Hayden Prairie are in the spring and again in the fall. Various wildflowers are in bloom during both of these seasons, and the prairie is a beautiful sight to behold!

title: What were some of the problems of living in a “soddy”?
text: "Soddies" were cool in the summer and warm in the winter, but the early settlers who lived in these houses had to get used to some rather unpleasant things. Insects and snakes often lived in the roofs of a sod house and would sometimes drop down into the home when they were least expected, especially during rainstorms. One man remembers having to hold an umbrella over the stove during rainstorms so that no bugs would fall into the food.

title: Osage Orange
text:
Osage orange is a thorny, shrub-like tree that is native to North America. It is a member of the mulberry family. Osage orange gets its name from the Osage Indians, who once used the bright orange wood from this tree to make their bows. Osage orange also gets its name because the large, round fruits that grow on the trees resemble oranges. The fruit of the Osage orange may look like an orange, but it can't be eaten. The Osage orange trees were planted close together throughout the prairie to form natural fences. The trees were planted and then cut back often to encourage them to grow in thick clumps rather than as tall, straight trees. The goal was to create a hedge that was "horse high, bull strong, and hog tight." Osage orange was perfect for creating fences where no lumber was available.

Osage orange is still used as an ornamental hedge tree today. Its wood is also used to make railroad ties and fence posts, for fuel, and as a source of yellow dye.

title: Reason and Logic: The First Filipino Settlement in America
text:
Settlers in America often faced challenges while building new communities. In the 1760s, New Orleans was the capital of the Spanish colony of Louisiana. Sailors from the Philippines served on Spanish trading ships going between Manila, the capital of the Philippines, and Acapulco, Mexico.

Conditions on the ships were harsh, and Filipino sailors were often slaves. Some of them jumped ship (escaped) around 1765 and traveled to Louisiana. Once there they hid in the marshlands outside of New Orleans to avoid capture by the Spanish. They formed a colony of fishermen who lived and worked in the swamps and bayous.

These early Filipino settlers were called the Manilamen. Their first village was named Saint Malo. The Manilamen built their houses on stilts in the swamps. They developed a successful method of drying shrimp in the sun on raised platforms. The processed shrimp were exported as far away as Asia and South America.

The fishermen often sent money back to the Philippines so that more relatives could immigrate (move) to New Orleans. Manilamen's families did not stay in the fishing villages, but lived in homes in New Orleans. Their children would come to work on the platform during busy harvest times.

There were seven Filipino villages in all. Saint Malo was the first, and Manila Village was the largest. Hurricanes have destroyed all of the original villages, but their shrimp-drying legacy lives on. The Manilamen used reason and logic to survive in their environment, just as people do today.

Have you ever noticed where your school is built? Is it located on level land or a slope? Is it a one-story building or taller? What things make the location and design of your school building reasonable and logical?

title: Pioneer Homes
text:
The first task of the early Iowa pioneers was to build shelter for themselves and their families. It was important to get a house built as quickly as possible to escape the unpredictable and often harsh weather of Iowa. What were these early pioneer homes like?

The first houses built by the pioneers in Iowa were very small. Most settlers, if they could find the wood, built log cabins. These cabins were about 16 feet by 18 feet. Most of the living rooms in our houses today are bigger than that!

These log cabins usually had only one room, with a loft (open attic) overhead where the children slept in the summer. During the winter, the unheated loft was too cold to sleep in, so the children would sleep on straw pallets (thin mattresses) in front of the fireplace.

The heart of the early pioneer cabins was the fireplace. A large fireplace along one wall of the cabin provided heat, light, and a place for cooking meals. On winter evenings, the family would gather in front of the fire to keep warm and to see to do tasks such as mending and sewing.

Since the pioneer cabins were almost always small, they were always crowded. The family had no room for extras, and only very basic furniture was used. Most cabins had at least one bed, a cupboard for storing dishes, a table, and a few chairs or stools. The typical pioneer family often had a spinning wheel and a loom for weaving cloth, but these were only set up when they were needed, as they took up a lot of space.

The early pioneer cabins were difficult places to live in during the winter. The wind often blew in through the cracks between the logs, and the walls were not insulated, as our walls are today. The pioneers tried to close up the spaces between the logs when they built their homes by pushing bits of wood into the cracks, then sealing them up with a mixture of mud or clay, but there were still spots where the wind blew through. Some cabins had wooden floors, which helped keep out the cold, but many had only dirt floors. Dirt floors froze once winter came, and walking on these floors was a very chilly experience! Sometimes, the pioneer women who lived in these cabins would stand on a block of wood to do their housework so that their feet wouldn't become too cold.

During the winter, when the weather became deathly cold outside, many pioneer families simply went to bed to keep warm. Snuggling under the blankets was often the only way to keep from being frozen!

Where there wasn't enough wood available to build log cabins, Iowa pioneers built "soddies," or homes made of strips of the tough Iowa sod. Many families lived in these soddies for years before building homes of wood. These houses made of dirt and grass were warm in the winter and fairly cool in the summer. Soddies were small, just like the log cabins, and they offered a few challenges that log cabins didn't, such as streams of mud from the ceiling during rainstorms and falling bugs and snakes on occasion.

The pioneers who first settled in Iowa were quick to build shelters for themselves and their families. Their homes were much smaller and less comfortable than the homes we live in today, but they kept out the weather well enough, and the pioneers were grateful to have them.

title: Joplin Works to Rebuild After a Deadly Tornado
text:
On May 22, 2011, a tornado hit the city of Joplin, Missouri. It wasn't just any tornado. It was a monstrous EF-5, with winds over 200 miles an hour. This huge tornado was almost a mile wide and cut a path over 22 miles long. It crushed almost 1/3 of the city, killed 162 people and destroyed almost 8,000 buildings. It is considered one of the deadliest tornadoes in over 50 years.

Joplin is working hard to rebuild. Think about all of the parts that make a city work. In addition to houses and businesses, cities need electricity, sewers, roads, hospitals, parks and government buildings. In January 2012 federal and civic organizations in Joplin got together to give the "ok" to a plan called Joplin Area - Next Steps Plan. The plan outlined how to replace what was destroyed in the tornado. 4,000 building permits have been given to homeowners so they can begin construction on new homes. After the tornado hit, 530 businesses were either destroyed or badly damaged. The good news is that 420 of those businesses have reopened. Work has begun on a new hospital. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) is helping to clean up waste and keep the area safe for residents.

The people of Joplin will never forget that terrible day. Recovering from something this devastating is difficult, but Joplin is showing how it's done!

Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents for more Connections and Current Events articles.

title: Pioneer Life
text:
The men and women who first settled in Iowa were hardy people willing to work hard to make a living on the new frontier. These men and women, and their children, didn’t enjoy an easy life, but through their hard work they were able to build homes, farms, and lives in the land we now call our own.

What was life like for the early pioneers here in Iowa? Busy! Men, women, and children had their own special jobs to do, and there wasn't much time left over for play. In those days, there were certain jobs that only men did and certain jobs that were only for women. Both worked very hard.

Men's Work

In the early days of Iowa, the main role of the man was to provide for the needs of the family by planting crops, taking care of livestock, and selling any extra in town. The most important work of the farmer was to break the hard Iowa sod and then plant and care for the crops. With the invention of the steel plowshare in 1837, plowing the sod became easier for the pioneer men. Even with the better plows, plowing the Iowa prairie for the first time was hard, backbreaking work. Several oxen harnessed to yokes (wooden frames) had to be used just to pull the plow through the tangle of grass roots that made up the top layer of soil. Men said that when the sod was plowed for the first time, it sounded like guns going off or like cloth ripping. The grass roots made loud popping sounds when they were ripped apart with the plow.

Iowa farmers usually planted 40 of their 80 acres in crops. The main crop was corn, followed by oats and barley. Corn was used both to feed the family and to feed animals. Oats and barley were usually used as feed for the livestock on the farm. Farmers also planted wheat to be ground into flour for making bread or to sell to bring in some extra money. Hay was also grown to feed the animals during the winter months.

Taking care of the livestock was also considered men's work. Farmers usually raised hogs, both for food and for sale, as well as cows, for meat and milk, and horses and oxen for transportation and farm work. The men were in charge of butchering the hogs or beef for the family, usually during the cold winter months so that the meat would stay frozen and not spoil. Many times, neighbors would get together to help each other with the butchering, as it was a big and messy job. The pioneer men butchered the meat, and the women were in charge of preparing and preserving it. They were careful not to waste any part of the animal, as food was always scarce.

Women's Work

The early pioneer women of Iowa were in charge of preparing food, providing clothing, and caring for the health of the family. While the husband took care of the crops in the fields, the wife was in charge of planting, caring for, and harvesting the household garden. This garden was very large, often a half acre in size. The women would plant carrots, radishes, lettuce, pumpkins, beans, and especially potatoes.

During the summer, the women and children would weed and care for the garden. When fall came, they would harvest the vegetables and preserve them for winter. Vegetables had to be dried or preserved to make sure they wouldn't rot before winter ended. The women stored carrots, potatoes, and other vegetables in root cellars between layers of straw or sawdust to keep them cold, but not frozen, throughout the winter.

Pioneer women also did the cooking for the family. During the spring and summer, the family ate a lot of fresh vegetables and fruits from their gardens, but during the winter, fresh vegetables were hard to come by. The pioneer women fixed corn in many ways. They made johnny cakes, hominy, corn bread, and mush. The women also served salt pork at nearly every meal during the winter. Salt pork is made by cooking and salting the pork, then sealing it in big barrels to keep it from spoiling during the winter. Many pioneer families got very tired of eating salt pork day after day.

Pioneer women were also in charge of clothing the family. The woman of the house often had to make her own cloth by spinning yarn from the wool of her own sheep. She then had to weave the cloth on her own loom, cut out the pieces, and sew pants, shirts, and dresses, by hand, for her family.

Women also had to mend the clothing and, perhaps even more difficult, wash it. Without water nearby, it was very difficult to wash the family's laundry. The water had to be hauled by hand to the house and then heated on the stove or outside before the clothes could be washed. The clothes then had to be washed on a washboard and hung out to dry. It often took all of one or two days to do the wash for the week. Because it was so hard to do the laundry, clothes weren't washed as often as they are now. Until the clothes were really filthy, they were simply worn and worn again.

The health of the family was also the responsibility of the woman. She often planted special herbs in her garden for making tea to treat colds and flu. She also knew how to care for infections, burns, and other wounds, as well as how to deliver babies and care for the dying. Because doctors were very hard to find on the frontier, the women took care of the needs of their own families as best they could.

title: Living History Farms
text:
To see what pioneer life would have been like here in Iowa, plan a trip to the Living History Farms in Urbandale. Living History Farms is a 500-acre outdoor museum in central Iowa that allows visitors to see what life was like for Iowa farmers during different historic periods. Those who visit the farms are allowed to wander through the different exhibits at their own pace and to learn about the farms from workers dressed as real pioneer farmers of the period. A complete tour of the farms can last from three to four hours.

Living History Farms shows what farm life would have been like in various time periods. These different periods are shown in the 1700 Ioway Indian Farm, the 1850 Pioneer Farm, the 1875 Town of Walnut Hill, and the 1900 Horse-powered Farm. Each of these areas is set up as authentically as possible, and visitors can get a real feel for what life was like during that period of time. For example, the 1850 Pioneer Farm has a cabin, a barn, outbuildings, and fenced and plowed fields. The fields are planted with corn, wheat, and potatoes, just as they were during pioneer times. Oxen are still used for the heavy work on the farm, and there are horses, hogs, cows, sheep, and chickens on the farm as well.

Throughout the year, many special events are held at the Living History Farms. There are Halloween and Christmas celebrations, historic baseball games, an annual family Easter party, an annual quilt show, and other events. The Living History Farms is a wonderful place to see what pioneer life was really like.

title: Who invented the first large steel plowshare?
text: John Deere, an American blacksmith from Vermont, invented the first large steel plowshare in 1837. The plows used by farmers before this were hard to handle and weren't strong enough to cut through the stubborn Iowa sod. John Deere's new plow was able to plow deep, wide furrows without getting stuck in the tangle of grass roots beneath the surface. The polished steel of the plowshare (cutting blade) slid through the dirt, making plowing much easier and faster for the Iowa farmer.

title: Goldenrod
text:
Goldenrod is a weedy herb that is native to most of North America. It is a pretty plant with a long, straight stem and clusters of small yellow flowers at the top. Goldenrod blooms in late summer and early autumn, adding beauty to fields and roadsides throughout Iowa.

The goldenrod plant has been used for years to make teas and other soothing tonics. Its bright yellow flowers have also been used to make dye for coloring cloth. There are even certain types of goldenrod that contain latex.

Goldenrod was once considered one of the main causes of hay fever, but scientists have discovered that this isn't true after all. Goldenrod and ragweed bloom at the same time, but goldenrod is much more noticeable, so it was blamed for causing allergies when the ragweed was really to blame.

Goldenrod blooms freely throughout the state of Iowa and was even suggested as our nation's state flower. It is currently the state flower of Kentucky, and Nebraska.
