title: Old Capitol
text:
When Iowa's first territorial governor, Robert Lucas, took office, he chose Burlington as the new state capital. After setting up his office there, however, he soon found that Burlington was too far southeast to be a convenient place for the capital. A new capital was chosen and named Iowa City. This new spot was chosen because of its convenient location on the Iowa River and because of its beautiful, sloping hills.

In 1840, construction began on the building that would be the Iowa State Capitol Building. It would give the territorial government, and later the state government, a place to call home. The building has since come to be called Old Capitol, and it still stands in Iowa City today.

John Francis Rague, a famous architect (one who designs buildings) of his day, had already designed the Illinois State Capitol Building, and he was chosen to design the new Iowa capitol as well. On Independence Day, July 4, 1840, construction on the new capitol building began. Just nine days later, Rague resigned from the project and left Chauncey Swan, an Iowa territorial government commissioner, to head the project.

The capitol was built of huge blocks of Devonian limestone taken from the bluffs along the Iowa River. Most of these blocks weighed four tons each! After the blocks were cut from the bluffs, they were floated on barges down the Iowa River to Iowa City. The large limestone blocks were then loaded onto wagons and hauled by oxen to the capitol building itself. This was no small task for the workers of that day, with no modern equipment to help them.

The wood in the building, including the floor joists, roof trusses, and supporting beams, came from oak trees growing in the area. Most of these beams and trusses were cut and shaped by hand by skilled craftsmen. A very unusual spiral staircase was also fashioned by the woodworkers of the day.

By December of 1842, the workmen had completed four rooms of the Old Capitol, and the Iowa Legislative Assembly moved in. The government continued to use the building while it was under construction, and it was not completely finished until after the state capital had been moved to Des Moines in 1857.

When the state government moved to Des Moines, the State University of Iowa moved into the newly completed building. A library and a museum of natural history were opened in 1857 and 1858, and from 1857 to 1863, the Old Capitol was home to the entire university. All of its offices, classrooms, its chapel, an armory, and even a fire station were located in the Old Capitol.

For a time during and after the Civil War, the building was somewhat neglected. Later, between 1921 and 1924, however, Old Capitol was renovated and repaired. Unfortunately, in November 2001 part of the Old Capitol caught fire. But there have been ongoing restoration projects to repair the building's structure and contents. The Old Capitol is still the center of the University of Iowa's campus. It is home to some university offices and is a beautiful reminder of Iowa's heritage and history.

title: The Job of a Museum Director: ‘A Little Bit of Everything’
text:
The Campbell House Museum a is beautiful Civil War-era home in St. Louis, Missouri. The wealthy Campbell family lived there from 1854 to 1938. Studies Weekly asked Andrew Hahn, the director of the museum, about his job.

SW: How is a house museum different from other types of museums?

AH: A house museum is different because it gives you an opportunity to get the full experience of the past. If you go to an art museum, you can see paintings from the past that may tell a story about history or a particular event. But when you come to a house museum, you get the full picture of what it was like to live in the past. When people come here, they get to experience what it was like to be welcomed into the house or to work in the house. The house was so well preserved, and the Campbells' collection is still here. This is their house and how they lived in it.

SW: What does a museum director do?

AH: I do a little bit of everything. We have to raise money so that we can keep the doors open and pay the utility bills. I write the checks for all the bills, and I organize our volunteers who do most of the work at the house. We do research, so I look into the Campbell story and read old documents and newspapers that tell stories about the past. I even take out the trash!

title: Iowa Gains Statehood
text:
Once the early settlers started arriving in Iowa, they needed to set up a government to keep the newly settled communities running smoothly. They needed to make laws and have someone there to make sure the laws were followed. The new settlers wanted to have someone represent them in the U.S. Congress and make their wishes known. The people of Iowa also wanted to get some help from the U.S. government with things like building roads and paying for schools. Iowa needed to become a state.

Iowa Territory

When the Louisiana Purchase became part of the United States in 1803, Iowa became part of a large district of the United States. A district is a part of the United States with very few people living in it. A district governor was appointed by the president of the United States, and the Army helped to make sure that people obeyed the laws of the land.

As more people came to the new frontier, the area was divided into territories. A territory had more people living in it than did a district, and the people of a territory had more rights to govern themselves. The president of the United States appointed a governor of the territory, and the settlers were allowed to elect their own legislature to make laws for the territory.

In 1834, Iowa became part of the very large Michigan Territory. This territory included the present-day states of Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, and parts of North and South Dakota. In 1836, Michigan became its own state, and the rest of the territory was then called the Wisconsin Territory.

As more and more settlers arrived in what is now Iowa, the people felt that they should be able to govern themselves. They didn't want someone from Wisconsin or Minnesota making their laws, so they asked to be made their own territory. In 1838, the Iowa Territory was created out of the western part of the Wisconsin Territory. The Iowa Territory included Iowa, southern Minnesota, and parts of North and South Dakota.

The first governor of the Iowa Territory was Robert Lucas. He was appointed governor by President Martin Van Buren in 1838. Gov. Lucas was a stern man with definite ideas about what he wanted to do. On the first day he arrived in Burlington, Gov. Lucas got right to work. He set a date for the election of the men who would serve in the territorial legislature and began looking for a capital city. The capital city is the city where the government offices are located. It was the governor's job to choose a city to serve as the capital of the new territory, and he looked at many locations before making his choice. After considering Dubuque and Davenport, Gov. Lucas finally chose Burlington and began setting up the new territorial government there. The capital was soon moved to Iowa City, however, as the legislature felt that it was in a better location.

Iowa Becomes a State

Governor Lucas was in a hurry for Iowa to become a state, but most of the Iowa settlers wanted to wait until there were more people living here. That didn't take long, with settlers moving in by the thousands, and in 1844, the people of Iowa voted to begin applying for statehood.

In order to become a state, the people of Iowa had to first draw up their own state constitution. A constitution is a document that describes the basic laws of the state and explains the rights of the people, the responsibilities of the government, and what powers belong to each branch of government.

A constitutional convention was held in Iowa City, and the group drew up a new state constitution. The new constitution told how the government should work, and it also set the boundaries for the new state. The boundaries set by this constitution would have made Iowa larger than it is today, extending its northern border into Minnesota.

Before Iowa could become a state, it had to submit its constitution to the U.S. Congress in Washington and get its approval. Congress looked at the new constitution and decided that the borders of the state of Iowa should be changed. Iowa would be admitted as a "free state," meaning that it didn't allow slavery within its borders. The northern states were afraid that the southern "slave states," or states where slavery was allowed, were going to outnumber the free states, and they would try to force their ideas on the entire country.

To preserve this "balance of power" between the free states and the slave states, Congress decided to cut the new state of Iowa in half and try to bring in two "free states" rather than just one. The people of Iowa didn't like this new plan because it made their new state too small. The voters of Iowa rejected the plan and went back to work to create new borders that would make both Congress and Iowans happy.

A new plan, using the Iowa borders we know today, was submitted to Congress in 1846. On December 28, 1846, President James K. Polk signed a law making Iowa the 29th state of the Union. Iowa was a state and had the right to make its own laws, as well as to send representatives to Congress in Washington to help make the laws of the nation. Iowa was on its way!

title: Burlington
text:
Burlington became the first capital of the Iowa Territory in 1838. Since it is located right on the Mississippi River, the early settlement of Burlington was able to attract many types of businesses and tradesmen. Burlington is now home to over 25,000 people.

The city of Burlington is famous for having what Ripley's Believe It or Not has called the "Crookedest Street in the World." Snake Alley in Burlington is a great place to test your driving skills, in a car or on a bicycle! The street winds down a hill, dropping 58 feet in a distance of 275 feet of roadway. There are five half curves and two quarter curves in the road, making it a real challenge to use.

Burlington is also home to many interesting historical museums. The Des Moines County Heritage Center contains displays from the Des Moines County Historical Society, including a "Roads, Rails, and River" exhibit and items belonging to the early citizens of Burlington. The Phelps House Museum, at the top of Snake Alley, is an old Victorian house with furnishings dating back as far as 1774. It houses an interesting medical display, as the house was once used as the first Protestant hospital in Burlington.

Burlington also sponsors many fun events throughout the year, including the docking of the Mississippi, Delta, and American Queen steamboats each summer. There is always something to do and see in Burlington.

title: Why was the Capital at Iowa City Moved to Des Moines?
text: Iowa City is located in eastern Iowa, and as more people began settling in western Iowa, Iowa City wasn't convenient for them to reach to do business. Des Moines, located in the middle of Iowa, seemed to be a better spot for the capital, as it would be easier for most of the settlers to get to when they needed to visit the capital. Des Moines became the capital of Iowa in 1857.

title: Chipmunk
text:
The chipmunk is a small member of the rodent family that is native to North America, including Iowa. The chipmunk is about five to six inches long, with another four to five inches of tail. It has reddish-brown fur and black-and-white stripes along its back. The chipmunk also has large cheek pouches, where it carries its food.

Chipmunks build underground burrows under stone walls or trees. They store food for the winter in these burrows and go underground around the end of October. Chipmunks hibernate but instead of storing fat on their bodies they will take from their piles of food to eat at times during the winter

The chipmunk's diet consists of nuts, seeds, berries, and insects. They also enjoy eating bird's eggs, if they get the chance. Although there are a lot of chipmunks, they don't usually invade homes or cause problems for farmers, as do mice.

Chipmunks have their babies in early spring, and each female usually produces a litter of three to five babies. By July, the young chipmunks are fully grown and will have their own litters the following spring.

Even though chipmunks are members of the rodent family, most people like them much better than they like mice or rats. What do you think of chipmunks?

title: Sharing Public Space: Vitus Bering and Russian Colonies in Alaska
text:
Imagine traveling 6,000 miles over land with supplies for an expedition, and THEN sailing through frigid seas to look for a new world. This was the job given to Vitus Bering, a Danish navigator who sailed for the Russian navy. Peter the Great, czar (ruler) of Russia, asked Bering to explore the eastern coast of Russia. He was wondering if land connected Asia and North America.

Bering’s first trip began in 1725. After spending three years getting his supplies to eastern Russia, Bering sailed along the coastline. He didn’t see any land to the east, and he didn’t realize he was sailing in the narrow passage between Russia and Alaska. This waterway is now called the Bering Strait.

Bering led another expedition in 1741. This time his ship landed on Kayak Island, off the coast of Alaska. They explored some of the Aleutian Islands and met the native people there, the Aleut. He was the first European to arrive in present-day Alaska.

Bering died before returning to Russia, but his voyages paved the way for Russian settlements in North America. Many fur traders came to the area. In 1799 the Russian government established a fur-trading operation in Alaska. Furs from foxes, sea otters and seals were very valuable.

Unfortunately, the Russians took advantage of the native people just as some Europeans had done in settling New England. The Russians took over their lands and forced them to hunt for furs. They also brought new diseases, which killed many natives.

Today, the Aleut people continue to live along the western coast of North America, and their population has grown. What might have been different if the Russians and the Aleut had shared public space fairly? Where in your community is there a debate over public land? How should such debates be handled?

title: Language Arts Connection
text: Choose one article from this week’s magazine and read it again. Circle or highlight two or more main ideas of the article in yellow. Circle or highlight three or more key details in green. On a piece of paper, write a summary statement about the article.

title: The Underground Railroad
text:
When Iowa became a state in 1846, it was brought into the Union as a free state. This meant that slavery was not allowed within the state of Iowa. Many Iowans believed that it wasn't enough for Iowa to be a free state. They wanted to make sure that all African American people living in slavery were released and able to live in freedom. Those who believed that all slaves should be freed were called abolitionists, meaning that they wanted to abolish, or get rid of, slavery.

Many Iowa abolitionists helped runaway slaves escape to freedom using a system called the Underground Railroad. The Underground Railroad was not a real railroad, but a secret system for helping slaves get from one point to another on their way to freedom in Canada. Once runaway slaves escaped to Canada, they could no longer be reclaimed by their owners, and they would be free.

Railroad terms were used to describe the system of getting the runaway slaves from place to place. For example, a "conductor" on the Underground Railroad was someone who helped the runaway slaves escape. A "station" was a safe house or hiding place along the road to freedom.

No one knows for sure how many Iowans worked on the Underground Railroad, because it was against the law to help runaway slaves. If you were caught helping a runaway slave escape, the penalty was up to six months in jail and a fine of $1,000. Because helping runaway slaves was illegal, most abolitionists didn't keep written records of how many slaves they helped. Even the messages sent between "conductors" and other workers on the Underground Railroad were sent in code to make sure that there would be no written proof of what they were doing. One message sent between "stations" said, "Dear Sir. By tomorrow evening's mail, you will receive two volumes of the 'Irrepressible Conflict' bound in African American. After perusal, please forward." This message meant that there would be two runaway slaves arriving at the "station" the next evening and that the conductor was to help the runaways to the next station.

William Maxson, an abolitionist farmer who lived in Springdale, used to hide runaway slaves in empty potato sacks. He would put the runaways into the empty sacks and load them into his wagon. He would then take them to the train station and load them on the train to be transported to safety. Once, while at the train depot, one of the potato sacks sneezed, but luckily for him, the ticket agent chose to ignore it and allow the "potatoes" to be loaded onto the train.

Reverend John Todd, a Congregational minister, also worked hard as part of the Underground Railroad. He lived in Tabor, near the Missouri River, and often helped runaway slaves flee to safety. Once, Reverend Todd dressed an African American woman in his wife's clothing, her face covered by a heavy veil, and traveled with her by buggy, taking her across the state to the next point along the Underground Railroad. They were forced to travel at night on the back roads, hoping that no one would discover them.

Although no one knows exactly how many Iowans worked on the Underground Railroad or how many runaway slaves were helped to safety, we do know that many Iowans risked their lives to help save their fellowmen. The Underground Railroad is a part of Iowa's rich history of helping those in need.

title: A Slave No More!
text:
A letter written after the Civil War has shed light on the slave-master relationship. Jourdan Anderson was a slave who gained freedom when he and his family escaped to Ohio from Tennessee. In August 1865 his former owner, Colonel Anderson, wrote a letter asking Jourdan to come back to Tennessee to work on his farm.

The former slave’s reply gave a clear message about his feelings. He said he hoped that God had opened the colonel’s eyes to the wrongs done to slaves for generations. While he was glad his old master was alive, he was surprised that the Yankees hadn’t hung him yet. Jourdan wrote that there was one thing that might bring him back to Tennessee. He and his wife wanted to be paid for the 52 years of combined work that they provided as slaves (over $11,000). Without that, he said they had little faith in the colonel’s promises. He ended by asking the colonel to give his best regards to a man named George Carter. Mr. Carter had apparently taken a pistol away from the colonel when he tried to shoot Jourdan... twice.

Reading letters and newspapers from the past can help us understand the people who lived during that time. Jourdan and his family may have once been slaves, but their spirits were not broken.

title: Slavery in Iowa
text:
Although Iowa never allowed slavery within its borders, those African Americans who lived here before the Civil War were not treated as equal to whites. There were only a small number of African Americans living in Iowa before the Civil War, they didn’t have any legal rights or protections. African American members of society couldn’t vote, attend public schools, associate freely with whites, or run for public office.

Abolitionists

Today, this type of attitude toward African Americans is known as racism (the feeling that one's own race is better than someone else's race), but in those days, most people believed that African Americans and whites should live separately. There were abolitionists who wanted to rescue the slaves from slavery, but many of these people didn't want the African Americans to go to school with their children. They believed that there should be separate schools for African Americans and whites and that the two races should keep to themselves. Harriet Tubman and Frederick Douglass fought to end slavery and bring equal rights to African Americans.

Rights

Even though Iowa was a free state, the laws made by the first leaders of Iowa did not give rights and freedoms to African Americans. When Iowa joined the Union as a free state, only four out of the 25 states allowed African American men to vote. Most of the government leaders in Iowa had come from states where slavery was legal and where African Americans weren't allowed the same rights as whites. It seemed normal and reasonable to these early Iowa leaders to make laws discriminating against African Americans. The first Territorial Legislature concluded in 1839, after having made laws against the ownership of land by African Americans, laws against marriages between people of different races, laws against African Americans voting, and laws against any African American being allowed to move into Iowa without papers proving that he or she was a free person. As unfair as these laws are, they were accepted as normal when they were made.

Riots

In 1860, a riot (a violent disturbance with many people involved) erupted in Grinnell over whether African Americans could be allowed to go to school with whites. There were four African Americans who had been rescued from slavery and who were anxious to receive an education. A school meeting was held, and the group voted on the question, "Shall colored pupils be received in our schools?" The group voted to allow the African Americans to attend the school, but there were still many who angrily demanded that the African Americans not be allowed to join. One man said, "They shall never enter those doors unless over my dead body."

After the meeting, the community was divided over whether the African Americans would be allowed to go to school or not. Men from both sides brought knives and guns, and both sides were ready to use them. In the end, the African Americans were convinced not to try to join the school at the moment, and the school was closed for three weeks in the hopes that tempers would cool down.

Feelings Change

When the Quakers and the Congregationalists began arriving in Iowa, feelings about rights and freedoms for African Americans began to change. The Quakers and the Congregationalists were religious groups who believed that slavery was wrong and that basic freedoms and rights should be granted to all people, not just to whites. The beliefs of these new settlers helped to change some of the "black laws" over time, but even then, African Americans weren't allowed to vote in Iowa until 1868. As early as 1847, the Iowa General Assembly passed a law stating that public schools would be open and free to all white people living in the district who were between the ages of five and 21. In 1858, the General Assembly passed another law stating that there must be separate schools provided for white and African American children. By 1875, African American children were attending public schools along with white children. Even though slavery wasn't actually practiced in Iowa, those African Americans who lived in Iowa during its early days didn't enjoy much freedom. It took years of struggle before African Americans began to enjoy the same freedoms as their white neighbors.

title: Grinnell
text:
Grinnell is located just east of Des Moines in central Iowa. Josiah Bushnell Grinnell, a Congregational clergyman and a well-known abolitionist, founded the city in 1854. It was once a frequently used stop on the Underground Railroad, and it offered shelter and protection to many runaway slaves during the Civil War.

Grinnell is home to one of Iowa's great schools, Grinnell College. The college is well known for being a great place to study and to have fun.

Each August, Grinnell holds its annual Happy Days, a celebration of the city. There are crafts, an antique-car show, a carnival, lots of food, and fun for everyone. A highlight of the celebration each year is the annual Happy Days T-shirt Sale. A new design is offered for sale each year, and citizens make sure they don't miss adding that year's design to their collection.

Grinnell is also home to the Merchant's Bank, originally designed by the famous architect Louis Sullivan in 1914. The bank has been called the "Jewel Box" of Sullivan's bank designs and was designated as a historic landmark in 1976.

Grinnell Historical Museum displays items once belonging to J. B. Grinnell. Visitors to Grinnell can also view J. B. Grinnell's Long Home, which once served as a station along the Underground Railroad. Grinnell is full of history and many friendly people willing to share that history with visitors.

title: If Iowa was a “Free State,” why weren’t slaves who escaped to Iowa considered free?
text: Iowa was a free state, which meant that it was illegal for anyone to hold slaves within the state. However, a law passed by the federal government stated that escaped slaves had to be returned to their owners, so if a slave escaped to Iowa, he or she was still a slave and had to be sent back. Abolitionists who helped slaves escape to Canada were breaking the law by not returning the runaway slaves to their owners.

title: Pallid Sturgeon
text:
An interesting inhabitant of some of Iowa's rivers is the pallid sturgeon. This enormous creature is often considered one of the ugliest fish in North America. It evolved from fish that lived in Iowa during the late Cretaceous Period, about 70 million years ago.

The pallid sturgeon still looks a bit like its prehistoric ancestors, with a flat, shovel-shaped snout, bony plates, and a long, reptile-like tail. It has a toothless mouth, located under its snout, which it uses to suck small fish and other foods from the river bottom. It lives in the Missouri River system, from central Montana to St. Louis, and in the Mississippi River from St. Louis to the Gulf of Mexico.

The pallid sturgeon has survived for millions of years in the natural river systems, but since the building of dams on the rivers, the population has become so small that the fish has been added to the endangered species list. This means that, due to human-made changes in its environment, the pallid sturgeon is now in danger of becoming extinct.

title: What should I do with my money
text:
Most people have lots of questions about money. Where's the safest place to keep it? How do you make your money grow? Where can you get extra money to buy a house or a car? The answers to many questions about money can be found at financial institutions like banks, credit unions and investment companies.

Financial institutions provide important and valuable services to people. They help keep your money safe by providing checking and savings accounts. (That way you don't have to keep your money under your mattress!) They offer ways to invest your money so that it will grow. When you put money into stocks, bonds or mutual funds, you may earn interest (money you get for letting someone else use your money for awhile). If you need extra money for a house, car or just about anything else, financial institutions will loan you money. When you get a loan, you have to pay interest because you are borrowing someone else's money for awhile.

Still have questions about money? Ask your parents if you can go with them the next time they go to the bank. Someone there will be glad to help. After all, you might be a future customer.

title: Primary Sources- Slave Auctions and Runaway Slaves
text:
Look carefully at the pictures. These primary sources tell us something about what life was like for slaves in the new America. Slaves were treated like property, and slave auctions often took place.

It was common for slave owners looking for runaway slaves to put up posters in the early 1800s. Slave owners offered rewards for the return of runaway slaves. It is hard to believe that life could have been so different, isn’t it? Use the pictures to answer these questions.

title: Annie Wittenmyer: Making a Difference in War
text:
Nearly all of the soldiers in the Civil War were men, but women still found ways to provide service during this great and terrible war. One woman who served as valiantly as any man during the Civil War was Annie Wittenmyer.

Wittenmyer had always had a great interest in helping the poor, the sick, and those who were unable to help themselves. When she and her husband moved to Keokuk in 1850, Mrs. Wittenmyer found that there were no free public schools available there. She immediately hired a school teacher, paying the teacher with her own money, and started a free school for poor children. She also joined with some women from her church and provided meals and clothes for children who didn't have what they needed.

Mrs. Wittenmyer's husband died just as the Civil War broke out. Her husband left her with quite a bit of money, so she joined the Keokuk Soldier's Aid Society and began to use her money to provide for the care of soldiers wounded in the war.

Near the beginning of the Civil War, Mrs. Wittenmyer went to Sedalia, Missouri, to help take care of her brother, who had been wounded in the war. When the nurses brought him his breakfast, Mrs. Wittenmyer was astonished at what poor food the sick were given. For breakfast, her brother had received a cup of cold coffee, one piece of greasy bacon, and one slice of bread. She decided then and there that she would do something to make sure that the wounded and sick soldiers received good, wholesome food.

Mrs. Wittenmyer began writing letters to the leaders of the Union Army, telling them of the poor food the soldiers were receiving and begging them to make improvements. She also told every woman she knew about the terrible conditions and asked them to send food to the hospitals for the wounded. Word spread quickly, and soon there was a large group of women organized to make sure that the wounded received healthy, satisfying meals. These women also worked together to collect bandages and blankets to be given to the wounded soldiers.

Mrs. Wittenmyer set up special diet kitchens at Army hospitals during the war. She set up her first diet kitchen in a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee, and then began training other women to help her. By the end of the war, Mrs. Wittenmyer's ideas about providing healthy food for wounded soldiers had been put into use by the entire Army medical department.

After the Civil War ended, Mrs. Wittenmyer didn't stop working to help those in need. She continued to work for the Iowa Orphans' Home Association, she became editor of the magazine Christian Woman, she became a member of the "Woman's Crusade," which worked to get rid of alcoholic drinks, and she was elected president of the Woman's Relief Corps. She worked to make sure that Civil War nurses received pensions, or money from the government, to live on in their old age. In 1898, Mrs. Wittenmyer, who had used up most of her own money helping others, received a pension from the government for all her work helping Civil War soldiers. Wittenmyer may not have fought on the battlefield, but she was truly one of the great soldiers of the Civil War.

title: Research Shows Madagascar Was Founded by Women
text:
Picture an ancient ship full of explorers, searching for a new land. Many people would imagine that such a ship was filled with male passengers and crew. Though many explorers were men, scientists have discovered that the founders of Madagascar were a group of 30 women who traveled a long way from their home!

Madagascar is an island off the east coast of Africa in the Indian Ocean. The women's ship traveled 5,000 miles from Indonesia to Madagascar, stranding them there. How do scientists know this? DNA researchers have studied 3,000 blood samples of people from Indonesian islands and compared them to samples from 300 people from Madagascar (called the Malagasy).

They discovered that many Malagasy have an Indonesian gene in their DNA. This gene was passed down from generation to generation of Malagasy. Computer simulations have calculated that only 30 Indonesian women were responsible for beginning the Madagascar population about 1,200 years ago. Most people from Madagascar today have a mix of Indonesian and African DNA, and are descended from these 30 women.

Researchers have also been able to trace a special chromosome that is only found in men in the Malagasy people. Can you guess where it came from? If you guessed Indonesia, you are right! It looks like a few men as well as women sailed on that ship to Madagascar so long ago.

title: The Civil War
text:
The Dissolving of the Union

In 1860, a lawyer from Illinois named Abraham Lincoln was elected president of the United States. President Lincoln did not believe that each state had the right to decide for itself whether to allow slavery. Lincoln didn't want slavery to be allowed in any of the new states that were being formed in the West. He believed that slavery was wrong.

Most southerners didn't agree with President Lincoln and felt that they had the right to decide about slavery for themselves. They were also afraid that if slavery were to end, they would lose their way of life. Very few southerners voted for Lincoln, but because there were more northerners who opposed slavery than there were southerners who supported it, these northerners voted for Lincoln, and he won the election.

After Lincoln became president, many southerners were afraid that slavery would be outlawed in all the states of the Union. They were afraid that the national government was getting too powerful and that the states would no longer have any say about how they were governed. They were afraid that they were losing their states' rights.

Because many southerners were afraid of what would happen when Lincoln was president, some southern states met together and began to talk about forming their own country. South Carolina was the first state to decide to leave, or secede from, the Union. Soon after South Carolina left the United States, other southern states followed until 11 states had left the Union. The states that left the Union were Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, Florida, Tennessee, South Carolina, North Carolina, and Virginia. These states formed a new country called the Confederate States of America.

Civil War Begins

Soon, America was involved in the Civil War. A civil war is a war fought between people of the same country. The war began in April of 1861, and President Lincoln asked for 75,000 men to join the Union Army. Many men were eager to volunteer, and most believed that the war would be over by Christmas. How wrong they were!

The Union Army wore blue coats, and they fought to keep the United States together and to free the slaves. The Confederate army wore gray coats, and they fought for their rights to break away from the United States and to preserve slavery. The Union soldiers were often called "Yankees," or "Yanks," and the Confederate soldiers were called "Rebels," or "Rebs."

Most people in Iowa supported the war and believed that it was necessary in order to free the slaves and preserve the United States, but there were some who did not. Some Iowans believed that the South had the right to break away from the Union and set up its own government. Others believed that all war was wrong, no matter what the cause. There were still others who were afraid that if the war ended slavery, many freed slaves would come to Iowa looking for work and take jobs away from white people. Those who were against the Civil War were called Copperheads, after the poisonous snake. The supporters of the war said that these Copperheads were snakes who were trying to destroy the Union. They received a lot of pressure from Iowans who supported the war to change their minds.

The Beginning of the End

After much fighting, death, and destruction, President Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation in September of 1862. This was a document stating that as of Jan. 1, 1863, all slaves in the rebellious Confederate states would be free. It also said that all former slaves were free to join the Union Army. It took nearly two more years for all slaves to gain their freedom, but finally, January 31, 1865, Congress passed the 13th Amendment, which abolished slavery in the United States.

The war didn't end by Christmas, as most people had hoped. It was a long, bloody war in which more than 600,000 Americans died. About 13,000 Iowans were killed in the Civil War. Many Iowa soldiers died in battle, but a greater number of them died from disease. Many of these soldiers died in Confederate prison camps. These camps were usually terrible places to live, with no shelter and very little food. Many of the soldiers in these camps died from lack of food, exposure, and disease. The Civil War finally ended April 9, 1865. The Confederacy surrendered to the United States, and both sides agreed to stop fighting. With the end of the war came the end of slavery in America as well. The United States faced the huge task of bringing the Union back together and rebuilding a strong and united nation.

title: Bellevue
text:
Halfway between Dubuque and Clinton, right on the Mississippi River, is the beautiful city of Bellevue. The city was founded before the Civil War, and many Iowa soldiers headed out by ship from Bellevue on their way to the war.

The name Bellevue means, "beautiful view," and that is exactly what you will find when you visit Bellevue. The city offers an amazing view of the mighty Mississippi River, along with wooded hills and bluffs along the river's edge.

Bellevue's population always increases during the summer months, when many tourists come to the area to enjoy all kinds of outdoor activities. Visitors and residents enjoy great fishing, boating, and canoeing, as well as beautiful strolls along the river. Those who are interested in bird watching may even be able to see an eagle in flight, if they watch closely.

Bellevue State Park is a great place to visit as well. The park offers a famous butterfly sanctuary and gardens planted with special butterfly-attracting plants. The butterflies in the park are breathtaking!

The park also offers walking trails lined with trees and plant life, as well as hiking trails from which hikers can see several conical American Indian burial mounds that were made in between 500 B.C. and A.D. 1300. These same trails are used by cross-country skiers in the winter when snow covers the park.

Bellevue is one of Iowa's scenic, old river towns that indeed offers visitors a "beautiful view."

title: What did Iowa women do to help during the Civil War?
text: Women in Iowa had to help during the war in many ways. Because their husbands, fathers, and brothers were away fighting in battle, many women had to take care of the farms and businesses on their own. They also rolled bandages for those who were injured and fed and clothed wounded soldiers, nursing them back to health. Some even visited the battlefields to find the soldiers who had been wounded.

title: Scarcity
text: During the Civil War, people did not have very much money. It was not easy to get food and other things that people needed. Instead of farming or working to make money, most men were fighting in the war. People had to use the little money they did have wisely. They could not buy everything they wanted. When people cannot have everything they want and they have to make choices about what to buy, there is scarcity. Have your parents ever said, "We can’t afford that," when you asked them to buy something? Because of scarcity, your parents have to choose carefully how to spend their money. If you only had enough money to buy one thing, would you buy a toy or a CD? You would choose what you wanted the most because there is scarcity and you can’t have it all. Next time you hear, "We can’t afford that," remember that scarcity causes your parents to make important choices about how to spend money.

title: George Washington Carver
text:
When the Civil War ended, things began to change for African Americans in Iowa. African American men were given the right to vote and to serve in the Iowa state legislature. African American children were given the right to attend school along with white children. Still, African Americans weren't treated as well as their white neighbors. Many restaurants refused to serve them, and there were many employers who wouldn't hire them. Life was especially difficult for those African Americans who had no education. George Washington Carver was one African American man who knew that getting an education would help him to succeed.

George Washington Carver had been born into slavery, but he overcame the odds against him and became a famous scientist. He was born to slave parents in Diamond Grove, Missouri, around 1864, but was raised by his owners, Moses and Susan Carver. George's father had died in an accident shortly before George was born, and his mother was kidnapped by Confederate night raiders. When the slaves were freed in 1865, the Carvers continued to raise George and care for him. They taught him to read and write, and when he was around 11 years old, they sent him to a school for African American children in Neosho, Missouri.

Education was very important to George, and he did everything he could to make sure that he could go to school. He was always interested in plants and was a fantastic student. He worked many odd jobs over the years to make enough money to pay for his schooling.

After finishing high school in Kansas, George tried to attend college, but was told he couldn't because of his race. He applied at Simpson College in Indianola, Iowa, and was accepted. George showed great talent as a painter, but he had always loved plants, so he decided to study agriculture (the science of farming) instead of art. In 1891, he transferred to Iowa State Agricultural College, now Iowa State University, in Ames. He earned his bachelor's degree in agriculture in 1894 and his master's degree in 1896.

After graduating from college, George was approached by Booker T. Washington, the founder of the Tuskegee Institute, an agricultural college for African Americans. Mr. Washington wanted George to come and teach at the school. George moved to Alabama, where the school was located, and soon became head of the Tuskegee agricultural department.

While teaching at Tuskegee, George began doing research into how farming could be made more productive. He studied soil conservation, crop rotation, and other ways to improve farming. George tried very hard to pass what he learned on to African American farmers and to help them learn to succeed in farming. He traveled around the South teaching African American farmers all he could about managing the land and raising better crops.

After 1914, George began doing research on the peanut. He developed more than 300 products made from the peanut, including a milk substitute, face powder, printer's ink and soap. George Washington Carver is still remembered today for his research on peanuts.

George spent much of his time and money trying to help African American students and farmers to succeed. He never married, and in 1940, he gave his entire life savings, nearly $33,000, to the Tuskegee Institute to help the college continue to teach African American students. George Washington Carver realized that education was the key to success for the African Americans, and he never stopped trying to bring the opportunity for education to his people.

title: Quail
text:
Quail are small birds that live in many parts of the United States and North America. They are related to the partridge, pheasant, and grouse and have mottled, or spotted, feathers.

Quail reproduce very successfully, usually laying 12-15 eggs per clutch. A clutch is the number of eggs produced at one time for hatching. Quail build their nests on the ground, protected by tall plants. The female is in charge of most of the incubation, or keeping the eggs warm, and she also takes care of the baby birds once they hatch.

Quail are very popular game birds, which means that people like to hunt them. One reason they are so popular is that the meat of the quail is quite delicious, and many people enjoy its flavor.

Quail are easy to recognize because of the crests on top of their heads. These often flop down and look like "topknots" of hair. Quail eat insects and seeds and travel in flocks called coveys.

title: What did most African American people want more than anything else after the Civil War ended?
text: They wanted an education. Even though all African Americans were legally free citizens after the war, they still didn't have the same rights and freedoms that white people did. They wanted to be able to get good jobs, have nice homes, and enjoy the same kind of life that white people did, but they knew that they would need an education in order to do that. After the Civil War ended, African Americans tried to establish schools for themselves and their children as quickly as possible.

title: Cass County
text:
Cass County is located in southwest Iowa and includes the communities of Anita, Atlantic, Cumberland, Griswold, Lewis, Lyman, Marne, Massena, and Wiota. Cass County is an agricultural leader, and the farmers of this area grow mainly corn and soybeans. They also raise livestock.

There are many interesting places to visit in Cass County, including portions of the Oregon and Mormon Pioneer Trails, an actual station of the Underground Railroad, and Lewis, the "birthplace of Kool-Aid."

Visitors will especially enjoy seeing the Hitchcock house, once used as a station on the Underground Railroad. Built by Rev. George B. Hitchcock and his wife, Caroline, in 1856, the home was built as the couple's "dream home" with a beautiful view of the Nishnabotna River. Rev. Hitchcock, a Congregationalist minister, had determined when he built the house that it would be used to hide slaves who were running away from their owners. With the safety of the runaway slaves in mind, Hitchcock made the walls of the house more than 18 inches thick and also included a secret room in the basement where slaves could hide and rest before continuing on their journey. The Hitchcocks placed a lit candle in the window when it was safe for slaves to come to the house. The Hitchcock house is located just west of the town of Lewis and offers tours to visitors.

Besides its historical attractions, Cass County also offers great camping, fishing, swimming, and annual festivals.

title: Recovery
text:
After the Civil War ended on April 9, 1865, people hoped that life would soon return to normal. There was a lot to do after the war in order to repair all of the damage that had been done. Many homes, farms, buildings, railroads, and bridges had been destroyed during the war, both by Civil War battles fought in our nation and by guerrilla raids on people and property. Guerrillas were soldiers who didn't belong to either the Union or Confederate armies. They hid in the bushes and attacked those they felt to be their enemies.

Rebuilding Our Nation!

When the war ended, the nation began working hard to rebuild. This time period, just after the war, is called "Reconstruction," which means "to build again." The people of Iowa worked hard to rebuild what they had once had before the war. The North and the South worked hard to bring our nation back together. Luckily, no Civil War battles were fought in Iowa, but other parts of the nation had been severely damaged by the fighting during the war.

Even more difficult to repair than the damage to homes and property was the damage to people's lives and feelings. Those who had fought for the Union believed that they had been right all along, and the fact that the North had won the war proved them right. Those who had fought for the Confederacy felt that they had been right and that it was terribly wrong that the South had lost the war. It was very difficult for neighbors who had been on opposite sides of the war to understand each other and to get over the bad feelings they felt toward each other.

Lincoln is Assassinated!

After the war ended, many northerners felt that the South should be punished for seceding from the Union. Some of these people were called Radicals, and they believed that those who had supported the Confederacy should not be allowed to vote or to run for a political office. President Lincoln disagreed with the Radicals. He believed that the South had suffered enough and that it was time to stop being angry and to enjoy peace. He wanted the country to pull together again as a strong unit.

President Lincoln was shot and killed just after the war ended. He and his wife had gone to see a play at Ford's Theater in Washington, D.C., and John Wilkes Booth shot and killed President Lincoln while he and his wife were watching the play. Booth was an actor who was angry with President Lincoln because Booth had wanted the South to win the war.

After President Lincoln's death, Vice President Andrew Johnson became the president. The Radicals didn't like him, and they pushed hard to have their own way when it came to the treatment of the South. The Radicals became more powerful and passed many laws to punish the South.

Democrat or Republican?

In Iowa, the Republican Party became very strong during and after the Civil War. Before the war, most people in Iowa supported the Democratic Party. But because most Democrats believed in slavery and Iowa was a free state, the Democratic Party began to lose power here. The Republican Party didn't want slavery to spread outside the South. It also said that slavery could remain in the South if those living there wanted it to. This view was popular before the Civil War, and the Republican Party began to take control of Iowa. After the war, Iowa became a very strong Republican state.

The state of Iowa was very fortunate that no Civil War battles were fought here. Our homes, businesses, and farms weren't destroyed, as those of many other people living in the South and states that bordered the South were. After the war, Iowa grew very quickly, and more people than ever before came to settle here. Soon the last portion of Iowa to be settled, the northwest portion of the state, was experiencing growth as people from all over began to pour in. New settlers saw Iowa as a great place to start new farms and businesses, and our state grew as never before. Four new railroads were soon completed, and Iowa became a great place to do business.

title: Woodrow Wilson and the Fourteen Points
text:
All presidents have important responsibilities, but few are more critical than those faced by presidents during times of war. While the United States was fighting in World War I, President Woodrow Wilson addressed Congress on Jan. 8, 1918. He presented a plan for peace called the Fourteen Points.

Woodrow Wilson was elected in 1912. World War I began in 1914 between Great Britain and Germany and other European nations. It was called The Great War. Everyone thought there would never be another war like it. President Wilson wanted to keep the United States out of the war. He tried to help Great Britain and Germany end the conflict. But when German submarines began sinking American ships, he asked Congress to declare war.

Wilson's Fourteen Points plan described his ideals for achieving world peace and democracy. He had consulted with a team of about 150 foreign policy advisors. He assured Americans that the war was being fought for good causes and would lead to peace in Europe. The Fourteen Points included free trade, freedom of the seas and returning territories taken in the war. Wilson also wanted to establish a League of Nations to protect the independence of "great and small states (nations) alike."

Wilson's Fourteen Points faced opposition from some people, but it was used as the basis for the German surrender at the end of the war. The Armistice took effect on "the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month" in 1918. America and other nations remember those who died by celebrating Armistice Day (now called Veterans Day) every November 11. Woodrow Wilson was awarded the 1919 Nobel Peace Prize, thanks to his clarity of expression. Why is it important for our leaders to be clear during times of war?
