title: “How May I Direct Your Call?”
text:
When Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone, he forever changed the way people communicated with each other. Most people who saw the telephone in use for the very first time were convinced that it was something they could use.

Iowans were quick to take advantage of the new technology (scientific knowledge used to create new inventions) that allowed them to speak to each other with this amazing gadget. Iowans wanted to install the new machines as quickly as possible, but the first telephones were more difficult to use than the ones we use today. These telephones were connected to each other by wires that could only connect phones at each end of the wire. For example, a rich Des Moines businessman ran a telephone line from his home to his office, and the telephone worked great—except that it could only be used to communicate between the house and the office, not with any other residents of Des Moines.

This problem was solved when telephone companies began installing phones in homes and businesses and then connecting all the phone lines to a switchboard located in a central location. People would then call the switchboard and ask to be connected to a certain phone number. A telephone operator sat at the switchboard and answered calls, connecting the phone line of the person who called with the phone line belonging to the person he or she wanted to talk to. The telephone operator could connect the caller with anyone else who was connected to the system.

The first telephone operators were young men in their teens. These young men answered calls and made connections, but it was soon discovered that many of these young men were unreliable and often rude to their customers. To correct the problem, telephone companies began hiring young women who had good manners and polite voices as telephone operators. The New England Bell Company in Boston hired the first young woman. Other companies began hiring women as well, and the job of a telephone operator was "for women only" until the late 1960s.

Telephone operators held very responsible positions, as their duties included more than just connecting calls as they came in. If a fire broke out, the citizens of the community called the operator, and it was her job to sound the alarm and call the fire department. If someone was sick, the family called the operator and expected her to locate the doctor as quickly as possible. If a woman couldn't find her husband, the operator received a call, and she did her best to find him. When someone wanted to know the correct time of day, the operator supplied this information as well.

Hired operators were expected to be in the office, taking calls, between 8:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m. After these hours, the telephone system was often shut down, although some offices provided an apartment behind the office where a night operator lived and answered emergency calls.

When we use the telephone today, we rarely talk to an operator because computers now manage the telephone systems, and an operator is rarely needed. Our calls go through quickly, but we may be missing some of the personal service provided by the friendly voice of the calm and efficient telephone operator.

title: Can Facebook Save Dying Languages?
text:
Can you say a few words in Siletz Dee-ni? No? How about saying "hello" in Aka? If you can't, you're not alone! These two languages and 3,500 more could become extinct by the end of this century. Almost 80 percent of the world's population now speaks only one percent of the world's 7,000 languages. This has happened because of globalization. Globalization means that countries are more connected through trade, money and workers. When countries work together, people must be able to communicate with each other. That means many people have to learn another language. English is the main language used throughout the world for business and the Internet.

Why is this a problem? When the last person who is able to speak a particular language dies, some of the knowledge that is found within that language dies with them. A language contains the history of its people, how they used their environment and their beliefs and ideas. Technology may just save many of these languages from extinction! With YouTube, Facebook and other forms of social media, languages that are spoken by even 5 or ten people can be taught to others around the world.

National Geographic has been working on the Enduring Voices Project. Its goals are to record native speakers of endangered languages into talking dictionaries and help communities learn ways to save their languages from extinction. What language do you want to help save?

Reference: History News Network (hnn.us)

title: Black Walnut
text:
The black walnut, or Juglans nigra, is a tree that is used for both its fruits, or nuts, and its lumber. The black walnut is native to the central and eastern parts of the United States and Canada and it thrives here in Iowa.

Although its nuts are delicious, they are also hard to remove from the shell, so most people who want to harvest walnuts for eating plant the English walnut tree instead. The black walnut is grown more for its lumber than its nuts.

The lumber of the black walnut is very hard and durable. It is used for furniture, wall paneling, gunstocks, musical instruments, and cabinets. Since colonial times, the wood of the black walnut has been the most popular cabinet wood in the United States.

The black walnut is also a beautiful tree that grows tall and gives wonderful shade. You may have noticed the black walnut in many places around your own neighborhood.

title: How did Iowa pay for improving its roads once automobiles started using them?
text: Iowa needed to improve its dirt roads by adding gravel or oil once people started driving automobiles on them, but where did the money to do this come from? Iowa began putting a tax on gasoline to help pay for improving its roads. That way, those who bought gasoline to run their cars were the same ones who paid for the roads. Those who drove on the roads the most also bought the most gasoline and paid the most for improving the roads.

title: Newton
text:
Newton is located near the very center of Iowa, about 30 minutes from Des Moines. Newton has many interesting attractions, including the Jasper County Museum. This museum displays artifacts of Jasper County and includes a unique sculpture showing the history of the county. The museum also houses the Maytag Historical Museum, home of the Maytag washer. Fred Maytag, a Newton resident, developed the first motorized washing machine, and the museum has many original items on display.

If you enjoy museums of a different type, you may be interested in Newton's own International Wrestling Institute and Museum. This museum is dedicated to wrestlers and those who love the sport, with displays depicting the history of wrestling.

Visitors to Newton also enjoy a stop at the Maytag Dairy Farms, home of the world-famous Maytag Blue Cheese. Maytag Dairy Farms invites visitors to their cheese shop that overlooks the cheese plant below.

The farm offers a 20-minute video showing the making of the special blue cheese. Visitors can also enjoy delicious free samples of unique Maytag Blue Cheese at the end of their visit.

Newton also offers tours of the historic old mansion called La Corsette Maison Inn. This home was built in 1909 and originally belonged to August Bergman, an early Iowa state senator. The inn now offers tours, gourmet dinners, and overnight stays.

Take a trip to Newton for a taste of cheese, a look at an old washing machine, and an overnight stay at a historic mansion. You'll be glad you did!

title: Great Inventions in Iowa
text:
As the 1800s came to an end and the 20th century began, an amazing number of new inventions sprang up across the country. These new inventions improved the quality of life for people throughout Iowa and helped them to connect more easily with people throughout the nation.

The Telephone

Alexander Graham Bell made the very first telephone call on March 10, 1876. He then exhibited his amazing new machine at the Philadelphia Exhibition the following summer, allowing thousands of visitors to try the newest technology for themselves. The telephone was an immediate success, and people everywhere were anxious to use the invention in their daily lives.

Frederick M. Hubbell, a rich Iowa businessman, was one of the first Iowans to install a personal telephone connecting his home to his office. Soon, telephone companies opened offering telephone service throughout Iowa. Farmers who lived too far outside the cities to receive telephone service joined together with their neighbors and installed their own telephone lines so that they, too, could enjoy this new invention.

Because these phone lines often ran for long distances and could be quite expensive, many farm families connected their phones to the same telephone line. This system was called a party line, and as many as 15 homes would sometimes share the same telephone line. This meant that people in one house could listen in on the telephone conversations going on in 14 other homes, so people had to be careful about what information they shared over the phone if they wanted to protect their privacy.

By 1920, Iowa farms were more likely to have a telephone than farms in any other state in the Union. Iowans were excited about this amazing invention that allowed them to communicate with their friends and neighbors with such ease.

Electricity

Thomas Edison began building large generators that could produce huge amounts of electricity around 1882. Soon, cities all over the country were building their own generators to produce electricity for themselves. In other cities, private companies built power plants and sold the power to the citizens in the area.

Electricity was first used to run lights in Iowa homes. Before electricity, kerosene lamps lighted most Iowa homes. These lamps gave off a very dim light, and the lamps' chimneys had to be cleaned often to remove black soot. Electric lights were much brighter, and the light they produced was clean and easy to use. After connecting their homes to electricity, Iowa families soon added other electrical appliances as well. Housewives were thrilled with the invention of the electric iron because it was light and stayed hot during the entire ironing session. Before electricity, women ironed with heavy sadirons that were heated on the stove. One iron was left heating on the stove while another was used to iron the clothes. When the iron she was using cooled down, the woman would take the hot iron from the stove and put the cool one there to reheat.

Electric vacuum cleaners made cleaning the rugs and carpets much easier, electric toasters helped speed up breakfast preparations, and refrigerators kept food fresh and easy to get to.

In the 1890s, Fred Maytag, a resident of Newton, began experimenting with the crank washing machines of the time and added a gasoline motor. Soon women throughout Iowa and all over America were using his incredible electric washing machines. Doing the laundry had once been one of the housewife's most difficult and time-consuming tasks, but with this new machine, laundry was no longer hard labor.

The Automobile

By around 1900, the automobile was being marketed by several different inventors. The first automobiles were very different from those we know today, and it took time before all the bugs were worked out of the horseless carriage (nickname for the first cars because you didn't need a horse to drive them). The first cars were heavy, often getting bogged down on muddy roads, and the engines were very unreliable, breaking down often. The first cars were also noisy, hard to steer, and very expensive. In 1900, the first automobiles offered for sale cost between $6,000 and $7,000—about four or five times more money than most men made in an entire year. Automobiles were only for the rich and the brave in those early years.

As the years went by, automobiles became more dependable, lighter, easier to handle, and less expensive. As the price came down, many Iowa families became interested in owning their own cars. With a car, families could travel to visit family, take a trip to town to do some shopping, or drive to church when a horse and buggy would take too long to make the trip worthwhile.

The Model T, developed by Henry Ford, became the most popular automobile with the average American family. Often called the Tin Lizzie, it cost between $250 and $900 and was very dependable. All of these Model T Fords looked exactly alike, and Henry Ford said that customers could have the car in any color they wanted, "so long as it's black." The customers didn't seem to mind, however, and the Model T could be seen in front of homes all over Iowa.

Now, it is rare to find any adult in Iowa who doesn't own his or her own car. The automobile is one of the most important inventions of the 20th century because it has made it possible for people to travel faster, farther, and more easily than could ever have been imagined before its invention. The automobile helps us work, play, and keep in touch with the world around us.

title: Graphing Activity
text:
People can protect their inventions by applying for a patent. A patent is an official document that gives a person or company the right to be the only one that makes or sells a product for a certain period of time. Study the line graph of patents given during the 1800s, and then answer the questions.

1. In which year did the number of patents begin to increase?

2. How many patents were issued in 1830?

3. During which years did the number of patents that were issued drop from 200 to 150?

4. What is the highest number of patents issued?

5. Think About It—Do you think the number of patents increased or decreased during the Civil War? Why?

title: The Sullivan Brothers
text:
During World War II, many families sent their sons off to war to do their part in bringing peace to the world. Many of these families lost a son, sometimes even two sons, but the Sullivan family from Waterloo, Iowa, suffered the almost unbelievable tragedy of losing five of their sons in the war.

Thomas and Alleta Sullivan were the parents of six children, five boys and one girl. Thomas was a freight conductor on the Illinois Central Railroad and Anna stayed at home to raise the family. When news of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor reached Waterloo, the Sullivan boys were brought to attention. One of their old friends had been killed in the bombing. After talking it over, the Sullivan boys decided to enlist (join the military voluntarily) together, hoping to do their part to avenge the death of a pal. On Jan. 3, 1942, all five Sullivan brothers enlisted in the Navy, requesting that they be allowed to serve together on the same ship. The brothers were close and before they enlisted, all five brothers had worked together at the Rath Packing company in Waterloo. It wasn't long before George, 27; Francis "Frank," 26; Joseph "Red," 24; Madison "Matt," 23; and Albert "Al," 20, were on their way to war.

Despite Navy policy against allowing brothers to serve on the same ship, the Sullivans were allowed to serve together on the USS Juneau. The ship was involved in a vicious enemy attack while sailing just off the Solomon Islands on Nov. 13, 1942. A Japanese submarine launched a torpedo that struck the ship, exploding immediately and sinking the wounded vessel. Nearly 700 men serving aboard the USS Juneau died in the attack. Only 11 men survived. None of the Sullivan brothers were among the survivors.

Frank, Joe, and Matt died instantly in the explosion. Albert tried to swim to safety, only to drown the day after the attack. George, who was badly wounded in the attack, managed to climb into a life raft. He survived for another four or five days before slipping overboard into the shark-filled waters.

It took until January for the Sullivans' parents to receive the official word that all five of their sons had been killed in action. President Franklin and first lady Eleanor Roosevelt wrote a personal letter to the Sullivans, telling them how sorry they were for the loss of their sons. The Sullivans were left with only one child, their daughter Genevieve, out of their original six children.

The Sullivan brothers have become a symbol of courage and patriotism since their tragic deaths. A ship was soon named after the brothers, the Hollywood movie, "The Fighting Sullivans," has told their story, and in 1995, a new ship was once again named in honor of these famous Iowans. Like so many other young men before them, the Sullivan brothers from Waterloo, Iowa, gave their lives to protect the freedom of this country.

title: Iowa Veterans Tell Their Stories
text:
As veterans (those who have served in the military) of foreign wars grow older, our country risks losing the stories of these brave soldiers forever. Thousands of war veterans die each week, and along with them go their stories. The Library of Congress' Veterans History Project hopes to record these amazing historical stories before the war veterans are no longer around to tell them.

Project participants have gathered thousands of war stories from veterans of foreign wars. Many veterans find it hard to talk about war, but it is often helpful for them to share their stories. For many years, these veterans have kept their stories to themselves, not wanting to burden their families with their pain. As they age, however, some veterans feel the need to finally talk about their experiences and let someone know what war was really like.

Iowan Stub Jessen served in World War II from 1942 to 1945. He was one of 2,000 prisoners forced to march for 128 days. The prisoners marched for about 950 miles, from Luxembourg to Brunswick, Germany. Jessen said, "The worst part about being a prisoner was the hunger part." Jessen lost 65 pounds on the march because they were only fed a piece of bread every few days. Telling his story is important to Stub because now he knows that his experiences mean something to all Americans.

The Veterans History Project uses volunteers instead of professional interviewers to talk with the veterans and record their stories. Many young people have gotten involved in the project, including Boy Scouts, Girl Scouts and members of service clubs. Kids just like you can help collect and preserve stories for the Veterans History Project. By preserving the history of these brave soldiers, we can guarantee that their amazing stories will live on, even after the soldiers have passed away.

title: Rattlesnake
text: The rattlesnake is one Iowa resident that you don't want to meet up with by accident. These poisonous reptiles are known for their rattle that makes a very distinct sound. The rattlesnake uses its rattle to warn other animals of its presence. This way, it doesn't have to waste its venom on potential enemies. The rattle is made up of hard segments. Each time the snake sheds its skin, a new segment is added to the rattle. Rattlesnakes like to eat small animals such as mice and birds, but they do not like to chase their prey. They would much rather coil up in a cool, shady spot and wait for their lunch to walk by. When a small creature does come along, the rattlesnake will jump out and bite it. Rattlesnakes have glands (small sacs) inside their cheeks, which are filled with venom (poison). When the rattlesnake bites an animal, venom comes out of its fangs and begins to kill the animal. The venom causes the animal's lungs and heart to slow down as it destroys tissue in the animal's body. After a rattlesnake bites an animal, it lets the animal run away and die. Later, the rattlesnake will find the dead animal by smelling it with its tongue.

title: What was the “Manhattan Project?”
text: The Manhattan Project was the code name used for a secret project to develop the atomic bomb. During World War II, scientists in America worked together secretly to create and perfect the atomic bomb. The atomic bomb was then dropped on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, causing Japan to surrender to the United States.

title: West Branch
text:
West Branch, located in eastern Iowa, is the birthplace of the only Iowan ever to serve as president of the United States. Herbert Hoover was our 31st president, and he was born in West Branch. This city is now the home of the Herbert Hoover Presidential Library and Museum and the Herbert Hoover National Historic Site. The Herbert Hoover Presidential Library and Museum opened in 1962 and has had over 3 million visitors since that time.

During World War I, many Europeans were left without food to eat and President Woodrow Wilson asked Herbert Hoover to be in charge of getting food to these starving families. Herbert Hoover did such a good job with this effort that he gained the respect of both Europeans and Americans. In 1928, Hoover was elected President of the United States. Besides the Hoover artifacts, West Branch is also famous for the Secrest 1883 Octagonal Barn. This barn is one of the oldest and largest round barns in the United States. Tours of the barn and the old farm on which it is located are available. The barn is also rented out for parties and receptions.

West Branch isn't one of Iowa's largest cities, but it offers some of our most interesting and famous historical displays and papers.

title: WWI, WWII and The Great Depression
text:
World War I

The beginning of the 20th century was an exciting time for our state and our nation. Farms and factories were growing and new inventions were springing up everywhere. Life looked good to Iowans, but something happened then that changed the entire world.

In 1914, a war started in Europe that would change the lives of people in Iowa, half a world away. At first, this war was fought between Britain, Russia, and some other smaller nations, who were called the Allied Powers, and Germany, Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria, and Turkey, who were called the Central Powers. The United States tried to stay out of the war, but eventually, America joined the Allied Powers.

The German navy had come up with a new and dangerous weapon. When American ships sailed in the Atlantic Ocean, German U-boats, special boats that could travel underwater, would sometimes sneak up on them and attack. Some Americans were even killed in U-boat attacks. U-boats are what we now call submarines. Because the Germans refused to stop attacking American ships with their new weapon, President Woodrow Wilson decided to declare war on Germany. The United States joined the Allied Powers and became part of what was then called the Great War. We now know this war as World War I.

Iowans helped to win the war in many ways. The United States sent troops to Europe to help fight the Central Powers and over 114,000 Iowans were part of these troops. Almost 2,000 Iowans were killed in action and another 1,600 died of other causes. Iowans at home helped by raising food to be sent to the Allied forces in Europe. Because of the efforts of those in Europe and those at home, the Allied Powers won the war in 1918.

The Great Depression

After the World War I ended, life was exciting and good here in Iowa. Most people had jobs and could afford to buy many of the new gadgets that were being invented. Many people bought their first automobiles in the 1920s, and people began to travel as never before. People filled their homes with new gadgets and women were given the right to vote. A few even began taking jobs outside the home. It was an exciting time to be alive! This period of time is known as the Roaring 20s. Things changed for all Americans with the stock market crash of 1929. Many people had hoped to make money in the stock market and had bought stock in a lot of companies. When the prices of the stock dropped, people lost money. Soon, businesses and banks throughout the country closed their doors. People lost their jobs and had no money to pay rent, buy food, or provide for their families. Many people were forced to stand in soup lines, or long lines where they could receive free food.

President Franklin D. Roosevelt came up with some new programs meant to help those who were out of work. He called his plan the New Deal, and it helped those who were unemployed by giving them jobs doing things that the government needed done anyway. The New Deal gave people jobs repairing and building roads, building government buildings such as post offices, city halls, courthouses, and schools, and even planting trees and building dams. These jobs helped those who were out of work support their families and got them back on their feet.

World War II

In 1939, another great war began in Europe. This time the Axis Powers, led by Germany, Italy, and Japan, went to war against the Allies, led by Great Britain, France, China, and the Soviet Union. Again, the United States was determined to stay out of the war, but something happened on Dec. 7, 1941, which left America no choice but to join the war. On this date, Japanese airplanes dropped bombs on the United States naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. Hundreds of Americans were killed and many American ships were sunk. After the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, the United States declared war on Japan and the other Axis countries.

Iowa did its part in helping to win World War II, as this war was called. A total of 263,000 men and women from Iowa served in World War II, but those who stayed at home helped with the war effort as well. Farmers had to produce extra food to feed those at home and those away fighting the war. Factories that had made cars now made airplanes and tanks instead. Iowa women who had once stayed at home now entered the work force. With many of the men off fighting the war, thousands of women were forced to take over their jobs, doing work that they had never done before. Women worked in factories, making airplanes and tanks, and did other jobs that had been reserved for men only.

Finally, after four years of fighting, the Allies won the war. Over 225,000 Iowans served in the military, and 8,398 died in service to our country. Japan was the last of the Axis powers to give up the fight. They signed the final terms of surrender on board the battleship USS Missouri on Sept. 2, 1945. Iowans breathed a sigh of relief and looked forward to better times.

title: Meet Governor Terry Branstad
text:
Do you know who the 39th governor of Iowa was? Do you know who our governor is now? If you said "Terry Branstad," then you would be correct both times! Governor Branstad is the youngest governor ever to be elected and the longest-serving governor in our history. He first took office in 1983 when he was 37 years old and served for 16 years. But that won't be the grand total because he's not finished yet! Governor Branstad was elected our 42nd governor in 2010 and will serve at least four more years. That's 20 years (so far) working as the governor for the Hawkeye State.

Terry Edward Branstad was born and educated right here in Iowa. After graduating from high school and college, Governor Branstad served in the U.S. Army and also went to law school. As governor, he has been a leader in education in our state. In 2001, President Bush appointed him to lead the President's Commission for Excellence in Special Education. This group had the important job of finding ways to improve the quality of education for students with disabilities. Next, Des Moines University offered him a position as president. In 2009, Branstad decided to run for office again, and was elected to his fifth term.

If you have questions for Governor Branstad or for Lieutenant Governor Kim Reynolds, you can ask your parents or teacher to help you reach them through the government website: ltgovernor.iowa.gov/contact/. But we can report the answer to one interesting question already. Governor Branstad's favorite food at the Iowa State Fair is a pork chop on a stick!

title: The Supreme Court and Citizens United
text:
The Supreme Court is one of the three branches of our United States government. The other two are the executive branch (the president) and legislative branch (Congress). It is the Supreme Court's job to decide if laws passed are constitutional.

For many years, laws have limited the amount of money that companies, unions and wealthy people could spend to support a candidate in an election. This was done because many believed that large amounts of money would make the voice of that corporation, union or wealthy person louder than the voice of regular people.

In 2010 the Supreme Court heard arguments on a case called "Citizens United." The nine justices of the Court ruled that limiting the amount of money a corporation, union or person could spend on an election was a violation of free speech. It was unconstitutional to limit that speech. As a result, many groups have set up "super PACs," or political action committees. These super PACs can collect as much money as possible and use it to help candidates win elections. Many people feel that super PACs will change the way political campaigns are run. As usual, people disagree on the subject of super PACs. Some people believe it is a good way for groups to get their messages across, and some believe that more money in politics will lead to more corruption.

Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/ for more Connections and Current Events articles.

title: The Wild Rose
text:
The rose, or Rosa, is a familiar plant that is prized for its beautiful, sweet-smelling flowers. It is part of the same scientific family of plants as the raspberry, blackberry, dewberry, loganberry, almond, apricot, cherry, nectarine, peach and plum.

The wild rose plant is thorny, with stipules (small, paired leaves at the base of the larger leaves), and flowers made up of five sets of parts. The rose flower is one of the most beautiful and popular flowers of all time. The rose is a native of North America, which means it is found growing here naturally. Iowa has a great climate for growing roses, as it is humid and neither too cold nor too hot. The wild rose is the state flower of Iowa and it can be found growing in fields and along roadsides in shades of white, yellow, pink, and red.

Roses are used primarily for their beautiful flowers, but they are also used to make sweet perfumes, light-tasting jellies, and in hedges and landscaping.

title: How does the government get money to run our state?
text: The government gets its money from taxes. Without money, the government wouldn't be able to do much! You may have noticed that when you buy something at the store, there is a sales tax added on to the price of the items you buy. There is also an income tax charged on the money people earn. A property tax is charged on property, homes, cars, etc. When you hear people complaining about taxes, remember that the money collected in taxes is used to run our government.

title: Terrace Hill
text:
Benjamin Franklin Allen was Iowa's first millionaire, and he built Terrace Hill for his family in 1869. The estate originally cost $250,000 and included the mansion house and a carriage house located on 30 acres of land in Des Moines, overlooking the Raccoon River valley. William Boyington, a popular architect during the 1800s, designed Terrace Hill. The mansion measures 18,000 square feet and included many unusually modern features for its time. The house had hot and cold running water, gas lights, an elevator, and indoor bathrooms.

In 1971, Terrace Hill was given to the state of Iowa by F. M. Hubbell, who was then the owner of the historic mansion. The mansion is now used as the home of Iowa's governor and his family.

The governor and his family live on the third floor of the mansion and have private quarters there. The rest of the mansion is open to the public for tours. Guided tours are offered March through December, Tuesdays through Saturdays. Since Terrace Hill was opened to the public in 1978, nearly 500,000 people from countries all over the world have visited the beautiful old house. Each year, school children from throughout the state take field trips to Terrace Hill to tour the mansion and learn more about Iowa history.

title: Iowa State Government
text:
The state of Iowa has a constitution that is patterned after the U.S. Constitution. A constitution is a plan for how the government should work. Our constitution tells about the three different branches of our government and explains how they work. It also tells about the rights of the citizens of the state of Iowa. Our government is divided into three branches or parts. These three branches share the power of governing so that one person or one group of people won't become too powerful and force its will upon others.

A Bicameral Congress

After much debate during the 1787 Constitutional Convention, the Connecticut Compromise was proposed. Congress would be bicameral, which means that it would be divided into two houses. Any law made for the nation would have to pass through both houses.

The first house is the Senate, and it has two senators from each state, no matter how big or small a state's population. In this way each state has equal representation. The second house is the House of Representatives, and it has representation in proportion to each state's population. In this way the states with larger populations have more representatives in Congress than states with smaller populations.

The Executive Branch

The governor is the head of the executive branch of government in our state. The governor's job is to carry out the laws of the state of Iowa. Our state's governor is elected by the people and serves for a term of four years. A term is the length of time that an elected official stays in office. The governor chooses people to work with him or her to help run the state. The governor also has veto power. This means he or she has the right to refuse to sign any bill. A bill is a proposal for a law.

The Legislative Branch

The legislative branch makes the laws. The legislative branch is called the General Assembly and it is made up of two parts: the Senate and the House of Representatives. There are 50 state senators and 100 representatives. State senators and representatives are elected by the people of Iowa. State senators serve four-year terms and representatives serve two-year terms. These elected officials write bills and then vote on whether or not these bills should become laws.

The Judicial Branch

The job of the judicial branch of Iowa's state government is to interpret, or explain, the laws of our state. The judicial branch is made up of judges and courts. The highest court in Iowa and the United States is called the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court consists of nine judges. These judges review the most important cases from the other courts in Iowa and decide if they have been handled correctly. They also review all laws passed by the General Assembly to see if they are constitutional, or that they agree with our state's constitution. If the law doesn't agree with the constitution, then the Supreme Court rejects the law. The state of Iowa also has a state court of appeals, with six judges handling cases that the Supreme Court is too busy to deal with. The district courts handle most of the cases in Iowa. The district court system is made up of 108 judges and 135 magistrates. The court system in Iowa handles cases of crimes that are brought to court. They also handle disagreements over property and money.

Each of the three branches of government in our state keeps track of the other branches and makes sure that things are running as the constitution says they should. The executive branch keeps an eye on the legislative and judicial branches. The legislative branch passes laws that keep the executive and the judicial branches in order, and the judicial branch makes sure that everything the executive branch and the legislative branches do is legal. This principle is called the system of checks and balances. Each branch of government checks on the other branches and the power of government is balanced between each branch.

title: Bill of Rights Roll Film
text:
Materials

half-gallon milk carton or box

two rods or pencils

long strip of butcher paper 3 inches wide

crayons or markers

tape

pen

scissors

colored paper or contact paper to cover the box

ruler

Directions

1. Prepare your box. Cut the top of the milk carton if that is what you use. Cover the box with construction or contact paper.

2. Make two 3.5-inch slits across the front of your box (horizontally) to let the roll movie pass in and out.

3. Poke holes in the sides for the pencils. Measure to make sure the pencils are straight.

4. Measure the distance between the two slits. This is how big your movie scenes can be.

5. Make a series of pictures (with captions) on the butcher paper, one for each of the 10 amendments listed in the Bill of Rights. (To find a copy of the Bill of Rights, look in an encyclopedia or online.) Make sure each picture fits in the size between the two slits (and is not bigger).

6. Tape one end of the paper to the bottom rod or pencil.

7. Roll the bottom pencil until the end is short enough to handle. Slip this end through the slits and tape it to the other rod.

8. Roll the pencils to see your Bill of Rights movie.

Extra Activity: You can make up 10 rights that you think everyone should have. Just make sure you write a caption for each.

title: The Constitution Protects Our Rights
text:
Let's look at some current human rights problems. After reading the following problems you will see how the U.S. Constitution protects us and safeguards our freedoms. Inside this issue of Iowa Studies Weekly, see how the Constitution organizes our government so that we the people make our own laws. The Iowa State Constitution is patterned after the U.S. Constitution.

Is Drug Testing Fair?

In the United States today it is estimated that more than 22 million Americans use illegal drugs such as cocaine, heroin and marijuana. One of the greatest problems our country faces is how to stop this wave of drug abuse.

Many think the answer is to test people to find out if they are using drugs. The most common form of drug testing is through urinalysis. By analyzing a person's urine, an expert can determine if someone has used drugs even days before the test.

Many of the nation's largest corporations are using some form of drug testing. The government wanted to test about 1 million federal employees in sensitive government jobs.

Employers are not the only ones who think drug testing might be needed. Many school districts and boards are doing some drug testing on students. They believe it will cut down on student drug use, which is a great concern to parents and teachers.

However, not everyone believes the drug testing is supported by the U.S. Constitution. A large number of people think drug testing is in violation of the Fourth Amendment, which protects citizens' privacy by keeping the government from making "unreasonable searches and seizures." An amendment is a change to an existing law.

Some polls by magazines and newspapers claim that over 72 percent of Americans are willing to submit to drug testing at work. One school system in Texas wants all children to submit to a drug test. Many parents support the plan. How do you feel about it?

Freedom of Speech in School?

In 1983, a Washington high school senior named Matt Fraser delivered a speech in a student assembly. Fraser's speech contained language that caused the students in the audience to laugh loudly and holler out. The principal and other administrators told Matt that his speech was "indecent" and that he had violated a school rule against "disruptive behavior." Fraser was then suspended from school for three days.

Fraser and his parents did not think the school had treated him fairly. Matt went to court and argued that the school had violated his right of free speech guaranteed under the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. The school administration argued that high school students do not have full rights of free speech. Schools have a right "to maintain and enforce minimum standards of decency" by not allowing indecent and disruptive behavior such as Matt's speech.

Judge Jack Turner from the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals heard all the arguments and judged in favor of Matt that the school had violated Matt's First Amendment rights. The school district appealed to a higher court at the state level and again the state court agreed with Matt.

The nine justices of the U.S. Supreme Court do not hear just any case. They only have time to rule on important cases that involve the U.S. Constitution and the rights of citizens. Their decision is final. The school district appealed to the Supreme Court. Chief Justice Warren Burger wrote the following: "While the Constitution does give freedom of speech to adults, it does not automatically give this right to children in a public school. This is because schools are special places where indecent or offensive conduct would disrupt the learning process.

Surely it is appropriate for schools to prohibit the use of vulgar and offensive terms in speeches." By a 7-2 decision, the court overruled the two lower courts, saying that Matt's right of free speech had not been violated.

Some say the ruling put student free speech in trouble and opens the way for school administration to clamp down on any expression by students, especially if they disagree with officials views. The school board and others feel this was an important victory for schools because the school should have the right to set standards for an orderly environment in which students can learn. How do you feel? Which side would you take? Why?

Are School Uniforms Good?

In three public schools in Baltimore, Maryland, all the children dress alike. They wear school uniforms.

Public-school children have always been free to dress as they wish. For private school children, however, this is not new. Private school students often wear special school clothes. The children are not forced to wear the uniform in Maryland; almost all of them want to.

Recently, a committee of parents presented the plan to a principal of one of the schools. After meeting with the parents several times, about 97 percent of the parents supported the idea of the children wearing uniforms. The Baltimore school system approved the project and a local designer designed and produced the uniforms for about $30 each.

Some teachers think it would be good if children wore uniforms because their clothing is often distracting to their learning. Some children like to wear short dresses or cut off pants or tee shirts with distracting slogans on them. Some children compete to be the best and frequently look down on others who can't buy expensive brand name clothing.

Not everyone approves of school uniforms. Some people believe that making children wear uniforms is not fair. They argue that uniforms make it impossible for children to have their own identities. Some people even think that uniforms violate the civil rights of students. What do you think? Would uniforms improve your school?

title: The White-Tailed Deer
text: The white-tailed deer is one of Iowa's native mammals. Its scientific name is Odocoileus virginianus and it is a member of the same family as the mule deer, the elk, and the moose. The white-tailed deer is about three to three and one-half feet tall at the shoulder. The male white-tailed deer, or buck, weighs up to 400 pounds and the female, or doe, weighs up to 200 pounds. The buck has antlers, or branched horns that he sheds once each year. This means that his antlers drop off and are re-grown later on. White-tailed deer are usually shy and spend most of their days eating. They are herbivores, which means that they eat only plants. They especially enjoy eating grass, leaves, bark, and acorns. White-tailed deer babies are called fawns, and they are born each spring, usually in May or June. The deer often travel in herds and the doe keeps her fawn with her while it is young.

title: What requirements must you meet to be able to vote in Iowa?
text:
To vote in Iowa, you must:

1. Be a citizen of the United States.

2. Be a resident of Iowa.

3. Be at least 18 years old.

4. Not have been convicted of a felony (or have had your rights restored).

5. Not currently be judged "mentally incompetent" by a court. (Incompetent means that you are not mentally able to function in society.)

6. Give up the right to vote in any other place.

7. Not be in prison.

title: The Iowa State Capitol
text:
The Iowa State Capitol building is located in Des Moines and was built between 1871 and 1886. The Capitol originally cost $2,873,294.59 when it was completed in 1886. It is considered one of America's finest examples of 19th century architecture.

There are 29 different types of marble used in the Capitol, along with many beautiful works of art, detailed carvings in both wood and stone, and interesting antique fixtures. There are delicate chandeliers throughout the building, with a large number used to light the House Chamber. There are 5,600 crystals in each of the chandeliers in this room!

The most amazing feature of the Iowa State Capitol is probably the huge dome. The dome is 275 feet above the ground and has a diameter of 80 feet. The dome is made of steel and bricks and is covered with a layer of real 24-carat gold leaf. It cost $3,500 to gild, or put gold leaf on the dome in 1886. When the dome was re-gilded in 1998, it cost nearly $400,000 to apply new gold leaf! The gold leaf is only about 1/250,000th of an inch thick across the dome. This spectacular dome glistens in the sun and can be seen from many miles away. The Iowa State Capitol is one of Iowa's most impressive and recognized state landmarks. It is visited each year by school children throughout the state, as well as people from all over the world.

title: Constitutional Rights
text:
Our state constitution is patterned after our U.S. Constitution. There are two great ideas to look at, they are: Constitutional Lawmaking and Constitutional Rights.

Constitutional Lawmaking

Our state constitution is a document that states the basic laws, organization, and character of our government. It describes a government that is divided into three parts, or branches.

The Legislative Branch

This branch is called the state legislature. The Iowa State Constitution states that the legislature writes the bills that could become laws for citizens to follow. The legislature is bicameral. This means it consists of two parts, the House of Representatives and the Senate. Representatives are elected to represent a certain number of people. These leaders are chosen by the people of our state to represent them when making the laws. Senators are elected to represent a certain district, or area of the state made for political purposes.

All laws begin as bills, or legislation for Congress to consider. When Congress approves a bill, it becomes a law.

The Executive Branch

This branch of state government consists of the governor, attorney general and secretary of state. These people have the duty to enforce the laws passed by the legislature. The police and National Guard help them with this responsibility.

The governor also has a special power that helps this branch check on the legislative branch. If the legislature has voted to make a bill a law, but the governor does not think the law is best for the people of the state, then the governor may veto the law. This means he or she refuses to sign the bill into law. The legislature must then go back and discuss the bill further and vote again. It is often difficult for the legislature to pass a law that has been vetoed by the governor. This is one way power is balanced between the branches.

The Judicial Branch

Judges make up the Supreme Court of our state. They decide if the laws made by the legislature are constitutional. They also decide what punishment a person should receive for breaking the law.

Our State Bill of Rights

1. Worship in the church of your choice.

2. Say what you believe is right.

3. Print what you want to publish.

4. Own your own home.

5. Go to school.

6. Have guns within the law.

7. Vote when of age.

8. Have a trial by jury.

9. Don’t have to testify against oneself.

Our State Bill of Responsibilities

1. Obey the laws of the land.

2. Help correct things you disagree with.

3. Respect the rights of others.

4. Pay taxes.

5. Stay informed.

6. Defend your country.

7. Vote in elections.

8. Serve on a jury.

9. Help police and fire departments.

As an American Citizen

List as many rights as you can that are guaranteed to U.S. citizens by the Constitution

As an Iowa Citizen

List as many rights as you can that are guaranteed to every Iowa State Citizen by the Constitution.

title: How Many Delegates to Win a Nomination?
text:
Have you heard candidates for president talk about "delegates"? That's because the Republican candidates for president compete against each other to get as many delegates as possible. Why? The candidate with at least 1,191 delegates will become the Republican candidate for president!

A delegate is a person who is chosen to represent the state they are from at the Republican or Democratic conventions. They are people who are active in their party in some way. About 2,300 delegates go to the Republican National Convention, held in August, to officially nominate a candidate.

Each state has delegates that can be won in a primary election or caucus. The results of the primary or caucus determine how many delegates the candidate wins. For example, in Ohio Mitt Romney came in first with about 456,000 votes and got 35 delegates. Rick Santorum came in second with about 446,000 votes and got 21 delegates. Neither Newt Gingrich nor Ron Paul won delegates in Ohio because they didn't get enough votes.

A state's population is one important factor that determines the number of delegates a state has. States with larger populations get more delegates.

In most election years, a candidate has already won enough delegates by the time the convention begins. If no candidate has the 1,191 delegates needed by the time of the Republican convention, it will be up to the delegates to make the final decision. After the conventions are over, the race for the White House is on!

title: Branch Out and Learn More
text:
Many websites are excellent sources for research information. However, not all websites give all the facts. In fact, some websites are biased. They present only one point of view. Other websites include facts, opinions and some advertisements. With some practice you can learn to find excellent online sources by reading information from the search page. Study the information from the online search below and then answer the questions.

1. Which link would you use if you wanted to find out more about women who have served or are currently serving on the U.S. Supreme Court?

2. Which website would you use if you wanted to know the address of your city’s congressman/woman in Washington, D.C.?

3. Which website is most likely written by someone biased about the branches of government?

4. Which website would you use if you wanted non-biased information about all three branches of government?

text: Write two paragraphs about the freedoms and rights you have because of the Constitution. Use such words as: “Bill of Rights,” “Freedom of Speech,” “Freedom of Religion,” “Freedom of the Press,” “Freedom to Gain an Education” and many others.

title: John Deere - Iowa's Largest Manufacturing Company
text:
John Deere, who was born in Vermont in 1804, developed the world's first self-scouring (self-cleaning) steel plow in 1837. Farmers who had come west during the 1800s brought with them the old cast-iron plows they had used in New England. These plows worked fine in the sandy New England soil, but were very difficult to use in the rich, heavy soil of the Midwest. The soil stuck to the blade of the New England plows and had to be scraped by hand every few feet. This made for very slow plowing indeed.

John Deere was a blacksmith by trade and after seeing the problems that the Midwestern farmers struggled with, he set out to create a plow that would stand up to the rich, black earth of the Midwest.

After studying the problem, John Deere was convinced that if he made a plowshare of highly polished steel and shaped it in just the right way, the blade would scour, or clean, itself with each turn of the soil. In 1837, using the steel from a broken saw blade, Deere created just such a plowshare. News of the invention spread quickly across the prairie and John Deere was in business.

John Deere's first factory was built in Grand Detour, Ill., but was later moved to Moline, Ill., home of the company's headquarters today. In those days, it was the custom of the blacksmith to wait for an order from a customer before manufacturing the tools. With the success of his new invention, John Deere started doing things in just the opposite way. He would manufacture a supply of plows and then take them out into the country and sell them to the farmers of the area. Farm products and machinery are still manufactured this way today. Salespeople often visit farmers to show them new products that may be of use to them.

In 1918, the John Deere Company bought a factory in Waterloo and began making tractors here in Iowa. In 1918, very few farmers owned tractors, but just 20 years later, it was rare to find a farmer without one. John Deere also began manufacturing plows, corn planters, cultivators, and harrows at its Waterloo factory.

The John Deere Company still has its headquarters in Moline, Illinois, but most of the manufacturing of its farm equipment is done here in Iowa. John Deere has factories in Dubuque, Ottumwa, Waterloo, and Ankeny and the company employs nearly 10,000 Iowa workers. John Deere is currently the leading producer of farm equipment in the world. It is also a major producer of construction, forestry, and lawn care equipment. The trademark yellow and green of a John Deere tractor has come to represent quality and durability throughout the world.

title: When is a Ketchup Bottle Like a Bug-Eating Plant?
text:
Do you get frustrated trying to get ketchup from the bottle? Do you pound the bottom or hold your finger on a certain spot on the label? Well, scientists at Harvard University have created one of the most slippery materials ever, so the days of waiting for ketchup may be over! The material is called SLIPS, which stands for Slippery Liquid-Infused Porous Surface. SLIPS can repel, or not stick to, water- or oil-based liquids. The scientists call this "omniphobicity."

To create a material with omniphobicity, the Harvard researchers put a greasy film on a spongy layer of Teflon®. Teflon®is the nonstick coating on many pots and pans. The researchers got the idea to make this amazingly slippery surface from the pitcher plant, a plant that eats bugs. The pitcher plant grows in swamps and bogs around the world. One kind of pitcher plant becomes super slippery when it's wet because it locks a thin layer of water in the sponge-like surface of its leaves. Insects cannot walk on the leaves and slide down into the plant's tube where they are trapped.

The scientists' new material can coat the inside of bottles and jars so all the food comes out easily. It can also coat airplane wings to help keep ice from forming on them. What other uses can you think of for this new material?

title: Corn
text:
The name corn is given to the largest cereal crop of any region. In England, corn means wheat. In Scotland and Ireland, corn means oats. In the United States, corn means Indian corn, or maize. Most of the corn grown in the United States is grown in the Corn Belt, which includes the states of Missouri, Indiana, Illinois, Ohio, Kansas, Iowa, and Nebraska.

More than half of the corn grown in the United States each year is grown for animal feed. The rest of the corn is used as a vegetable for humans, either canned, frozen, or fresh. It is also ground into cornmeal or corn flour and made into corn bread, tortillas, and breakfast cereals. Corn is also used for hominy, mush, and grits. The corn kernel can also be pressed to get starch, sugar, and oil.

Iowa's number-one crop is corn. Our state produces over 1.5 billion bushels of corn a year.

title: How much milk does a dairy cow produce in her lifetime? What happens to all of this milk?
text: An average milk cow produces nearly 200,000 glasses of milk in her lifetime. She weighs in at about 1,400 pounds and drinks between 25 and 50 gallons of water each day. That's nearly a bathtub full! About 40 percent of the milk produced in the United States is sold as drinking milk. Another 17 percent is made into butter. The rest is used to make cheese, ice cream, yogurt, sour cream, and other dairy products.

title: Sioux City
text:
Sioux City is located in the center of what is often called "America's Heartland." Sioux City sits right at the spot where Iowa, Nebraska, and South Dakota all come together, and this tri-state area is often called Siouxland.

Sioux City is a great place to live because it has a very low cost of living, very low crime rates, and good health care and education systems.

Sioux City is the headquarters for many national companies. You may be familiar with some of these companies: Sioux Honey Association, Metz Baking Company, Aalfs Manufacturing, Terra Industries, Inc., and Great West Casualty Company.

Sioux City is a great place to visit. The Mid America Air Museum offers displays of all types of aircraft. Some of the most popular full-sized aircraft are the Huey Helicopter, the Bob Cat, the Cherokee II, and the Boredom Fighter. The Sioux City Public Museum is a great place to learn about the history of Sioux City. It also offers exhibits about American Indian life and natural history.

The Dorothy Pecaut Nature Center is dedicated to preserving and appreciating the amazing Loess Hills. The center offers educational lectures and exhibits describing the wildlife of the area, and a wonderful system of trails for visitors to do their own exploring. There are several miles of trails that can be used for horseback riding, bicycling, cross country skiing, snowmobiling, and hiking.

Come to Sioux City and find out what life is like in the middle of America's Heartland!

title: Farming, Business, and Industry Today
text:
Iowa's economy is one of the healthiest in the nation, because our state makes its money in many different ways. The economy of a state is the way in which it uses its resources to make money. The state of Iowa gets its money from farming, manufacturing, and service industries. Our state leaders make sure that even if farmers have a bad year, other Iowa industries can make up some of the difference and keep the state from experiencing a depression.

Farming

About 90 percent of all the land in Iowa is used for some type of farming. Iowa is the top producer in the nation of both corn and hogs. Iowa also exports, or ships out to sell for a profit, more grain than any other state in the union.

Iowa gets about 55 percent of its farm income from livestock (animals that are raised for a profit) and about 45 percent from crops (cultivated plants). Hogs, sheep, and cattle are all important livestock products for our state. Iowa farmers produce about 17.3 million hogs each year. In fact, our state provides 28 percent of all U.S. pork. Farmers here also raise about 235,000 sheep and 3.8 million cattle every year, as well as millions of turkeys, chickens and dairy cows.

Iowa has been the leading producer of corn in the United States for several years. Farmers have produced about 2.1 billion bushels of corn every year. Our state is also one of the top producers of soybeans. Each year, workers provide about 525 million bushels of soybeans for our nation. Iowa is also one of the top five states for producing sheep and cattle each year. Iowa's livestock farmers also raise chickens, turkeys, and dairy cattle.

As the leading producer of corn in the United States, Iowa produces 1.5 billion bushels, or one-fifth of the nation's corn each year. Iowa is also the nation's second largest producer of soybeans. Our state produces nearly 300 million bushels of soybeans each year. Most of these soybeans are made into animal feed, but soybeans are also used to make oil, margarine, nondairy cheese, soy sauce, paint, fertilizer, and glues. Iowa is also one of the nation's top producers of oats and hay.

Manufacturing

Nearly all of Iowa's manufacturing companies are connected to farming in some way. Manufacturing is the process of making raw materials into a finished product. Iowa's largest manufacturing industry is food processing. There are factories throughout the state that take products from Iowa farmers and process them so that they can be shipped all over the world and used by people there. There are factories in Iowa that process corn, making it into corn oil, cornstarch, popcorn, corn flakes, corn meal, and many other items.

Meat packing is also a major industry here in Iowa. Since our state produces so many hogs, we naturally must process much of this pork before selling it throughout the world. Sausages and hot dogs are two of the most popular items processed in Iowa's meat packing plants. The sausage stuffing machines in these meat packing plants can stuff about 30,000 sausage links per hour!

Iowa is also home to many milk processing plants. These plants heat, purify, and package milk from our state's many dairy farms. Cheese, yogurt, and cottage cheese are also processed in Iowa milk processing plants. Iowa is one of the top producers of cheese in the United States.

After food processing, Iowa's second most important manufacturing industry is the production of machinery. Most of this machinery is farm equipment, once again showing that nearly all of Iowa's manufacturing businesses are somehow connected to farming. The John Deere Company is one of Iowa's largest employers. This company has factories in Waterloo, Des Moines, and Davenport and produces farm machinery such as tractors, harvesters, combines, etc.

Service Industries

Service industries produce more money for our state than both farming and manufacturing combined. Our state makes over $30 billion each year from service industries, which are industries where workers serve other people rather than produce a product. One out of every two workers in Iowa works in the service industry.

There are many types of service industries. Salespeople, grocery store clerks, bankers, insurance agents, department store executives, doctors, nurses, and restaurant workers all work in the service industry. Iowa is well known for its large number of insurance companies and our state has many people who work in the real estate business as well. Many of Iowa's salespeople sell agricultural products, processed foods, and farm machinery. Because our state has a good balance between agricultural, manufacturing, and service jobs, our economy is healthy and our unemployment rate is low.

title: Clarity of Thought: President Ronald Reagan and the USSR
text:
Three decades ago a first class stamp cost fifteen cents. A Macintosh was not a computer; it was an apple that grew on a tree. And the United Soviet Socialist Republic (USSR or Soviet Union) was a threat to the safety and freedom of the United States and the world. All of those things were going on in 1981 when Ronald W. Reagan became our 40th president. President Reagan served for two terms, and by the time he left office in 1989 the world was becoming a much different place.

When President Reagan was first elected, the USSR had a communist government. Under communism, the government controls all industry, and the citizens do not have the same rights and freedoms as we have in America. The USSR and the United States were in what was called a Cold War. The two countries never actually went to war, but we came very close. President Reagan understood how dangerous the Cold War was for both countries and for the whole world.

Making the world a safe, free place for all people was one of President Reagan's main goals as president. He spent many years negotiating with Soviet leaders, especially Mikhail Gorbachev, to end the Cold War. In 1991, the USSR split into 15 different countries and the Cold War came to an end. Having clarity of thought means that you are able to think and understand things clearly. President Reagan's clarity of thought played a vital role in ending the Cold War.

title: RAGBRAI Keeps Citizens in Touch With the Real Iowa
text:
Have you ever heard the word RAGBRAI? Do you have any idea what RAGBRAI is? Most people in Iowa have heard the word, but to those outside our state, it may sound a bit strange. RAGBRAI is the name of a huge bicycle ride across the state of Iowa. This ride is held each summer and has become one of the most popular recreational events in our state. RAGBRAI, or the Register's Annual Great Bicycle Ride Across Iowa, is sponsored by the Des Moines Register, a large daily newspaper with its headquarters in Des Moines. The event first began as a few friends taking a pleasant bike ride across the state. John Karras, a feature writer and copy editor for the Register, suggested that Don Kaul, author of a column in the Register, ride his bike across Iowa and write articles about the interesting things he learned on his ride. Kaul liked the idea, but suggested that Karras ride along with him. The two men presented their idea to the managing editor of the Register and when he agreed, the two started making plans.

Kaul and Karras decided to invite a few "friends" along for the ride as well. This meant that they opened their ride up to anyone who wanted to go with them. This first ride was scheduled for August 26-August 31, 1973. The ride began at Sioux City and made overnight stops in Storm Lake, Fort Dodge, Ames, Des Moines, and Williamsburg. The ride then concluded in Davenport on August 31.

The ride was announced in the newspaper only six weeks before it was scheduled to begin, but even so, about 300 people showed up for the start of the ride. At one point during the ride, there were about 500 people riding along with the group, but only about 114 actually rode the entire distance of that first event.

Readers of the Register wrote letters and made phone calls saying how much they would love to participate in another event such as this first RAGBRAI. Many suggested that it would be better to hold the event earlier in the summer, before school started, so children and teachers could participate as well.

With such a positive response to the first RAGBRAI, the Des Moines Register decided to sponsor a second RAGBRAI the following year, this time in early August. The event was even more popular the second time around and a decision was made to make the bicycle ride an annual event. RAGBRAI has now become so popular that a limit of 8,500 riders per week has been set, both to protect the riders from injury and to make the ride easier to control. In the years since RAGBRAI began, bicyclists have visited 780 Iowa towns, spent the nights in 125 different cities, and ridden through all 99 of Iowa's counties. RAGBRAI is now one of Iowa's most popular recreational events and is a great way for Iowans to get a better look at the state in which they live.

title: Boom to Bust and Back Again
text:
You may have heard people compare the recent economic recession (2007-2009) to the Great Depression of the 1930s. But what some people call the "Great Recession" actually had more in common with a depression in the 1890s and something called "boom and bust."

In the early 1890s, the U.S. economy grew quickly ("boomed") but couldn't keep growing at that rate. When many companies and the housing market failed, there was an economic "bust." The railroad industry had been booming since the end of the Civil War, but in the 1890s more than 150 railroad companies closed. Other industries that depended on the railroads closed, and many people lost their jobs. Over 500 banks closed. Thousands of unemployed men marched to Washington, D.C., in 1894 to demand that the government take action to help families. Unemployment was over 10 percent for most of the 1890s. About one of every ten people had no job.

In the recent recession, the housing market slumped after several "boom" years. Some automakers went out of business and others filed for bankruptcy. The economy went "bust," just as it did in the 1890s. Hundreds of banks and thousands of businesses closed. The unemployment rate was about 8 percent - about one of every twelve people had no job.

Make a chart or Venn diagram that compares these two events in history.

title: Western Meadowlark
text:
This brightly-colored songbird is found all over Iowa, but especially in grasslands and open fields. It can sing many different tunes and has a loud voice. It isn't hard to identify the Western Meadowlark with its very distinct and colorful markings. The head and wings are streaked with dark black, and on its bright yellow chest is a black "V" bib. Unlike many species of birds, the male and female Meadowlark look alike. These birds are omnivores, meaning that they eat meat and plants. They enjoy dining on grain, seeds, insects, worms, snails, spiders, and even road kill.

Together the male and female build a nest in a small hole in the ground using grass, pine needles, and horsehair for building materials. The female lays three to seven spotted white eggs in each clutch (a set of eggs laid at one time). She then sits on the eggs for 13-14 days. Once the eggs hatch, both parents care for the fledglings. Believe it or not, the baby birds are ready to leave the nest before they are two weeks old! This special bird isn't only popular here in Iowa. The Western Meadowlark is the state bird of Kansas, Nebraska, Montana, North Dakota, Oregon, and Wyoming!

title: Why is Iowa nicknamed “The Hawkeye State”?
text:
James G. Edwards was a newspaper publisher, and he was one of the men to suggest the nickname, "Hawkeye." It was in honor of American Indian Chief Black Hawk. This was in 18 38, before Iowa even became a state.

The name stuck and Iowa has been calling itself "The Hawkeye State" ever since.

title: National Hot Air Balloon Classic, Indianola
text:
Each summer, the city of Indianola sponsors the National Hot Air Balloon Classic. Indianola is located just 12 miles south of Des Moines, and it comes alive with color as the enormous balloons launch from a huge field in the city.

Nearly 100 hot air balloon pilots launch their crafts, and people from all over the Midwest gather to watch. There is nothing quite like the sight of these balloons of all shapes and colors filling the Iowa sky! New events have been added to the balloon classic over the years and there are now activities offered for all ages and tastes. As part of the balloon festival, Indianola now offers a 5K race, a car and truck show, a parade, family fishing, a bathtub race, and a new and improved fireworks display.

If you have ever wanted to see what it would be like to go up in a hot air balloon, come to the balloon classic and find out! The festival offers hot air balloon rides every morning and evening during the event (if the weather is good). For those who are a bit less adventurous, the festival also gives tethered balloon rides, which means that you can ride in a hot air balloon that stays tied to the ground with long, strong ropes. Another popular event during the National Hot Air Balloon Classic is the Nite Glo Extravaganza. For this activity, the balloons are launched at night and the sky is filled with what looks like hundreds of enormous light bulbs burning brightly in the darkness. Plan a trip to Indianola this summer and take a peek for yourself!

title: Recreation and Places to See Iowa
text:
What do you do after a hard day at school? What do your parents do to relax after a long day at work? On the weekends, does your family do something special for fun? During the summer or on holidays, does your family go on vacation? The things that we do to relax and refresh our minds and bodies is called recreation. Recreation is what we do when we play! Iowa is a great place to live if you like to play.

State Parks

Iowa has more than 80 state parks and recreation areas. About 10 million people visit our parks and recreation areas each year. A state park is land set aside by the state government to be protected for all people to enjoy. Have you ever visited one of Iowa's state parks to enjoy nature? People from our state and from all over the world come to Iowa to hike, watch birds and wildlife, and view the beautiful scenery.

Hunting and Fishing

Native Iowans and tourists from all over enjoy hunting and fishing in Iowa's hills, forests, rivers, and lakes. Fishers enjoy successful fishing for largemouth, smallmouth and hybrid bass, crappie, bluegill, perch, channel catfish, flathead and blues. Hunters love to come to Iowa for many types of large and small game, but Iowa is especially famous for its white-tail deer and wild turkeys. Hunters also come to Iowa for pheasant, ducks, geese, and quail. Iowa is a great place for those who enjoy the outdoors.

Sports

Sports are an important form of recreation in Iowa. Whether you play sports, watch them, or do both, our state has plenty of activities to go around.

Many people in Iowa enjoy playing all types of sports. We play basketball, baseball, soccer, football, and many others. We also enjoy rodeo and just about any other sport you can think of. Although Iowa has no professional sports teams, Iowans love to follow college and high school sports. Many Iowans love the University of Iowa Hawkeyes and enjoy watching them play in the challenging Big Ten athletic conference. Girls' sports are also very popular with Iowans, especially girls' basketball.

Historic Sites

Our state offers many interesting historic sites to visit. Historic sites are places where important events took place in our past. Many people who are interested in the history of our nation visit important frontier sites in our state. The Western Historic Trails Center in Council Bluffs is dedicated to preserving the history of westward trails such as the Oregon, Mormon, and California Trails, and it has always been a popular tourist attraction. People also come to Iowa to see historic American Indian sites such as Toolesboro Indian Mounds, where many ancient American Indian mounds still stand today. Tourists (people who travel for pleasure) interested in history also enjoy visiting the Herbert Hoover Presidential Library in West Branch, home of the only Iowan ever to serve as president of the United States (so far).

Museums

Iowa's museums are also popular recreation spots. Our state has many museums with displays about ancient American Indians, modern art, famous citizens of Iowa, science, history, and just about anything else you might be interested in. Museums that focus on science are popular places to visit. Two are the Science Center of Iowa in Des Moines and the University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics Medical Museum. Other museums that present the history of transportation are also fun to visit. Many people go to the Iowa Great Lakes Maritime Museum in Okoboji, the Airpower Museum in Ottumwa and the Fred W. Woodward Riverboat Museum in Dubuque. Iowa also has many interesting and educational art museums. The University of Iowa Museum of Art, Iowa State University's Art on Campus, Brunnier Art Museum, and the Figge Art Museum are great places to view some of Iowa's fine art.

Festivals and Holiday Celebrations

Iowans enjoy celebrating holidays and remembering their heritage with special events. There are hundreds of festivals throughout the year in nearly every town and city in Iowa. Have you heard of or been to any of these events: the Sac City Kiwanis Kite Tournament, Waterfest Weekend in Sioux City, the Cedar Basin Jazz Festival, the Gus Macker 3-on-3 Basketball Tournament or the Tanager Place Summer Fest? Iowa certainly has its share of exciting annual festivals and parties. Most Iowa cities decorate for special holidays, hold parades and fairs (events held to show off the talents and products of the people from a specific area), and get together to enjoy each other's company as often as possible.
