title: Grant Wood Capturing Iowa With His Brush
text:
When Grant Wood was only three years old, he was already showing his talent as an artist. His mother loved to tell a story about Grant as a young boy. It was when he had drawn a group of half-circles on a piece of paper and told her that it was a chicken. She first had trouble finding a chicken in the pattern. Later, as she looked at the hens scratching in their own yard, she realized that the shapes Grant had drawn exactly matched the markings on the hens. It was then that she knew for certain that young Grant had an eye for detail and that he would someday become a great artist.

Grant Wood was born on Feb. 13, 1891, on a small farm in Anamosa, Iowa. When Grant was 10 years old, his father died and his family moved to Cedar Rapids. In high school he painted scenery for plays and made drawings for the yearbook. Grant knew he wanted to be an artist, and the night following his high school graduation, he left for Minneapolis to go to art school.

After art school, Grant Wood returned to Cedar Rapids and began teaching school. He later served in the Army as a camouflage painter, once again taught art in the Cedar Rapids public schools, and made several trips to Europe to perfect his painting skills.

(Camouflage is material used to hide things by making them blend into their surroundings.)

In 1929, Grant was visiting the small town of Eldon, Iowa, when a simple white house caught his eye. The home had a Gothic-style window in its upper gable that held his attention at once. Grant made a sketch of the window, along with two people standing in front of the house, one holding a pitchfork. When Grant returned home, he decided to use the sketch as the basis for a painting. He asked his dentist, Dr. B. H. McKeeby, to pose as the farmer and his own sister, Nan, to pose as the farmer's daughter. After finishing the painting, Grant sent it to an exhibition at the Art Institute of Chicago. He won a bronze medal, along with a $300 prize, for the painting and quickly became famous. Grant called his painting "American Gothic" and the portrait of the plain, serious Iowa farmers is still his most famous work.

Grant Wood also had a sense of humor, and he enjoyed poking fun at American traditions in some of his work. His painting titled "Parson Weems' Fable" makes fun of the legend that George Washington couldn't tell a lie about cutting down the cherry tree. The story was actually made up by a pastor named Parson Mason L. Weems and never really occurred at all. Grant Wood painted the adult head of George Washington on the body of a six-year-old boy holding an ax in front of a cherry tree. Grant also painted Parson Weems standing by, watching. The painting is another of his most famous and popular works.

Grant Wood died in 1942 in Iowa City. He is known as one of America's most outstanding regional painters, which means that he painted scenes, people, and values of a particular region of the United States. He is one of the very few artists who helped present what the Midwest is all about to the rest of the nation and the world. Grant Wood captured the Iowa landscape and its people as no other artist could. Grant Wood's paintings are still very popular today and for many people, his work captures the true beauty, color, and strength that are Iowa.

title: A Census Full of Treasure
text:
On April 2, 2012, the government released the 1940 census. A census is a count of all the people in the United States, and it is done every 10 years. It also gives other information about citizens’ jobs, income, birthplace and education level. The government only releases a census’ records to the public after 72 years have passed. The 1940 census was the first one done after the Great Depression and World War I. It shows how these events caused people to move around and where immigrants went. You can find interesting facts about family members and famous people. For example, the future President Ronald Reagan paid $135 in rent in 1940!

The 1940 census was the last time census takers went door-to-door to personally interview people and write down the information. For the 1950 census the government started using census questionnaires sent through the mail.
The release of the 1940 census data is different from past years. This information was made digital and released through the Internet. There are more than 3.8 million pages of data in this census. Genealogists, or people who study family backgrounds, use this information to trace family history. Researchers, like historians, often use the census as a primary source of information.

So, was this release a success? Well, so many people tried to get the information on its first day of release that the server crashed! If you would like to learn more about your family history you can go to the 1940 census site at: 1940census.archives.gov.

title: Woodrow Wilson
text:
The Wilson Family Bible says that Thomas Woodrow Wilson was born at 12 o'clock, in the wee morning moments of Dec. 29, 1856. Woodrow Wilson himself saw it differently. He always celebrated his birthday on the 28th of December.

Woodrow Wilson was the third of four children. When he was a child, people called him "Tommy." He used this nickname until he graduated from college. Then he went by "Woodrow," his middle name.

Wilson struggled with dyslexia, and he was 10 years old before he learned to read. He quickly became a scholar, though. Through hard work and determination he succeeded in school and eventually went on to earn his Ph.D. in history and political science.

Wilson eventually served as the governor of New Jersey and the president of Princeton University before he ran for president of the United States. World War I was Wilson's biggest obstacle during his presidency. However, he won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1919 for his efforts to end the war and for establishing a group called the League of Nations. Also during his term in office, President Wilson allowed sheep to graze on the White House lawn. Their wool was sold to raise money for the Red Cross.Wilson was also the first president to cross the Atlantic ocean while in office. Woodrow Wilson was also president when Amendment 19 was passed, giving women the right to vote. Wilson died in his sleep in 1924, just three years after leaving the White House. He is the only U.S. president to be buried in Washington, D.C.

title: Muskrat
text:
The muskrat is a member of the rodent family and is sometimes called the "musquash," its American Indian name. It is found in marshes, quiet streams, and small ponds throughout Iowa. The muskrat looks like a large rat with a long, flattened tail. It is about 10 to 14 inches long, not counting another 10 inches of tail, and is about five inches tall at the shoulder. It weighs between two and three pounds and has partially webbed hind feet. The muskrat has shiny brown outer fur and a dense, thick undercoat. The muskrat lives alone in burrows or huts that are often built out of cattails.

Muskrats don't build dams or cut down trees like beavers. They swim by paddling with their hind feet and they eat plants and water animals. The chief enemy of the muskrat is the mink, which eats young muskrats. The female muskrat bears several litters of between two and six muskrats per year. Muskrat fur is sometimes used for making coats and it is often dyed to look like other more expensive furs, such as seal or mink. Musk taken from the glands of the muskrat is also used in making perfumes.

title: Who was the first female lawyer in the United States?
text: Arabella "Belle" Babb Mansfield was the first woman lawyer in the United States. Arabella was born near Burlington, Iowa, and graduated from Iowa Wesleyan University in 1866. She taught political science, history, and English at Simpson College and later studied law with her husband. She applied for admission to the Iowa bar in 1869 and after taking her examination, the professor who gave her the test said that she was the best example for proving that women could join the law profession that he had ever seen. She was then certified as the first female lawyer in the United States. Belle never did practice law, but she studied it and taught instead.

title: Eldon
text:
Eldon is the home of the famous American Gothic House, which Grant Wood used in his painting of the same name. The house has become a popular tourist attraction, but private citizens own and live in the house, so visitors are only able to look at and take pictures of the outside of the building. The State Historical Society of Iowa rents the house to people. You can research to find out who is the current resident!

Other popular attractions in the Eldon area are the Fox Hills and the Eldon Wildlife Management Areas. The Fox Hills Wildlife Area covers 1, 3 4 3 acres of trees and rolling hills, populated by deer, turkeys and squirrels. The Eldon Wildlife Area covers 1, 2 90 acres of woods and open fields and also offers several well-stocked fishing ponds. Catfish, walleyes, bullheads, crappies, bluegills and sunfish, along with bass, are very popular game fish in these areas.

An interesting historical site is also located near Eldon. The final battleground of the Sac-Fox and the Ioway tribes is found on the flat prairie land not far from the city. The battle was held in 18 24 and the Sac-Fox destroyed nearly all of the Ioway tribe in this bloody battle.

Many bald eagles make their home in Eldon and the surrounding area, especially during the months of December, January, and February. Visitors enjoy coming to Eldon during these months for a glimpse of the huge and beautiful birds.

title: Famous Iowans
text:
Most people think of Iowa's greatest asset as its rich, fertile soil, but the great land we live on wouldn't be worth much without the people who live here. The people of Iowa come in all shapes, sizes, and colors. Each person adds his or her own color and flavor to our state, making Iowa what it is today. Take a look at just a few of Iowa's great citizens from the past and the present!

Amelia Earhart (1898-1937)

Amelia Earhart was born in Atchison, Kansas, but grew up in Des Moines. Earhart grew up to be the first woman to fly across the Atlantic Ocean, the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean, the first woman to fly solo between Hawaii and California, and the first woman to fly solo across the continental United States. Earhart disappeared near Howland Island in the South Pacific in July of 1937 as she attempted an around-the-world flight. The mystery of what really happened to her has never been solved. (A solo flight is a flight made alone.)

Herbert Hoover (1874-1964)

Born in West Branch, Herbert Hoover became the 31st president of the United States in 1929. People called him the "Great Engineer" at the beginning of his career, when he managed mines in Australia. Hoover went on to become Secretary of Commerce for Presidents Harding and Coolidge. When voters elected him president, Hoover won all but eight states, and this made his victory a huge Republican success.

William Frawley (1887-1966)

Actor William Frawley was born in Burlington. He is well known for playing Fred Mertz, the crabby next-door neighbor of Lucy and Ricky Ricardo on the classic TV series, "I Love Lucy." Frawley's role as Fred Mertz won him five Emmy nominations. He also worked as a vaudeville performer and had small roles in over 100 movies. (Vaudeville is entertainment with many different short acts.)

Shawn Johnson (1992-present)

Gymnast Shawn Johnson was born in Des Moines in 1992. When she was 16 years old she won four gold medals in the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing, China. She also won three silver medals. In 2009 Johnson competed on the TV show "Dancing With the Stars" and earned even more praise. She unfortunately tore a major knee ligament in 2010 while skiing and announced later that she was retiring from competitive gymnastics.

Carrie Chapman Catt (1859-1947)

Carrie Chapman Catt helped form the Iowa Woman Suffrage Association and was very involved in social reform. Raised near Charles City, Carrie graduated from Iowa State University at the top of her all-male (except for her!) class. She was superintendent of the Mason City schools for many years and led the campaign to ratify the 19th Amendment to the Constitution in 1920, guaranteeing women the right to vote.

The Ringling Brothers (late 1800s-1936)

The seven Ringling Brothers, sons of August and Salome Ringling, grew up in McGregor. In 1870, a traveling circus came to the town and the brothers were fascinated by the show. Five of them soon began putting on their own backyard circuses and by 1882, they had created their first professional show. By 1889, all seven Ringling Brothers had put their circus on train cars and were traveling the Midwest with their popular show. In 1907, the brothers bought then later joined with Barnum and Bailey, creating the popular Ringling Brothers and Barnum and Bailey Circus.

Johnny Carson (1925-2005)

Johnny Carson was born in Corning and became a very popular entertainer and talk show host. He hosted the famous Tonight Show for 30 years before retiring and passing the job along to Jay Leno.

Lee de Forest (1873-1961)

Born in Council Bluffs, this inventor was known as the "Father of Radio" to many. He invented special transmitting and receiving devices used by U.S. Navy ships. He also developed wireless telephones that the military used, and his inventions helped begin the first radio news broadcasts. Bess Streeter Aldrich (1881-1954)

Born in Cedar Falls, Bess was a talented writer who wrote most of her stories and novels while also taking care of her active family. She is well known for her touching portrayals of Iowa pioneers. Her works include 160 short stories and 13 novels. Some of her better known works include "A Lantern in Her Hand," "Miss Bishop," and "Spring Came on Forever."

Henry Agard Wallace (1888-1965)

Henry Wallace was born in Adair County, and he became a U.S. politician. He served as Secretary of Agriculture and then vice president for President Franklin D. Roosevelt. He also developed a hardier and more productive type of corn seed, which he introduced to farmers throughout the Midwest to help them increase their corn yields.

Elijah Wood (1981-present)

Actor Elijah Wood was born in Cedar Rapids and is the second of three children. He moved with his family to Los Angeles and began acting when he was eight years old. Elijah has had a number of small parts in films, but he is most famous for his role as Frodo Baggins in "The Lord of the Rings" movie trilogy.

title: Mike Fink
text:
Mike Fink is one of the Mississippi Valley's famous American folk heroes. A folk hero is someone who may or may not be a real person. A folk hero is famous because he or she is able to do things that require super-human strength, intelligence, or other remarkable abilities. Mike Fink was a real person who was born in the 1770s in Fort Pitt (now Pittsburgh), Pennsylvania. He was a larger-than-life keelboat captain who piloted boats on the Mississippi and Ohio rivers. He was famous for his drinking, fighting, joking, and shooting. Because he often had adventures and then bragged about them, adding a little to them each time, Mike Fink's abilities became exaggerated and he became a folk hero. There are many stories told about the strength and abilities of Mr. Mike Fink. Here are two that you might enjoy!

Mike Fink and the Indians

Mike Fink once saw a band of roving Indians sneak into a cave. This cave was cool and protected, so a poor widow used it as a "refrigerator" to keep her food fresh. The widow used the cave as a storage place for her milk, cream, meat, and cheese so when Mike saw the Indians slip into the cave, he knew that they were up to no good. They were planning to steal all of the food they could carry. Mike watched the thieves until they were all safely inside. He then fastened the door shut on the outside and the Indians were trapped. Mike then proceeded to play a trick on the American Indians, which scared them away. Mike thought the trick worthy of a hearty laugh and figured that the Indians would not be sneaking around the widow's cave again anytime soon.

Mike Fink Catches a Moose

It was late fall when Mike Fink and some of his friends went on a moose hunt. Moose hunting was often dangerous, as the huge animals were likely to charge and trample a hunter to death if cornered. Mike set out far ahead of his hunting companions and when darkness fell, Mike was nowhere to be found. Mike's fellow hunters lit signal fires, hoping to direct him back to camp, but still no sign of Mike. Suddenly, the hunters heard the cry of a man, along with the wild snorting of a moose. They quickly climbed to the top of a cliff and looked over the edge. There they saw below them Mike Fink clinging to the horns of an enormous moose that was swimming through the river toward a distant island. Mike held on with amazing strength, and once the animal reached the shore, the real battle began. The moose shook Mike from his horns and immediately tried to dash him to bits. Mike had both his rifle and his pistols, but they were wet and would not fire. Mike quickly used the butt of his rifle to strike the moose, but on his second swing, the rifle shattered when it struck the moose's heavy antlers. The moose swung his gigantic head at Mike, but Mike ducked just in time and pulled out his long hunting knife. He plunged the knife into the moose's neck and the battle was over. Mike Fink had done what no other man could do: wrestle a moose and kill him without the use of a single bullet.

*A moose is a large, hoofed mammal of the deer family.

title: Iowa Legends - Fact or Fiction?
text:
Is there really an enormous turtle living in Mason City's Big Blue Pond? Many people who live in the area swear that there is. What about Bigfoot? Does he really wander through Floyd, Franklin, Hamilton, and Humboldt counties, frightening Iowans who happen to see him? And then there's the Mugwump, a marsh monster that some people claim lives in Ventura Marsh. Do you think he is real?

These are just a few of the Iowa legends that have been passed around our state for years. A legend is a story that may or may not be true, but which is passed along from person to person anyway. While many people believe these stories to be true, no one has ever been able to prove that they are.

Jim Wahl, a biologist with the Iowa Department of Natural Resources in Clear Lake, has heard stories of a huge turtle living in Big Blue Pond, but he isn't a believer. He says, "I've heard rumors that there's one as big as the hood of a Volkswagen, but I don't believe it."

Biologist Ron Andrews has never seen any proof that Bigfoot exists, but he would like to believe. Bigfoot is a large, hairy, smelly monster that people claim to have seen wandering throughout Iowa. Andrews says, "I keep hoping I might see him someday. Whenever I see a Bigfoot pamphlet, I always pick it up."

Ken Borrill remembers an old fisherman telling him stories about the Mugwump when he was a kid. Says Borrill, "He always told us it came out at night. Just spooky stories. In fact, I tease my granddaughters about the Mugwump every once in a while." The Mugwump is a big, hairy monster that some say still lives in the Ventura Marsh.

What do you think of these Iowa legends? Are YOU a believer?

title: The Chigger
text: Have you ever been bitten by a chigger? If you live in Iowa, especially if you enjoy getting out in nature, you are sure to have had this experience. Chiggers are the tiny, six-legged, reddish larva of the harvest mite. They live throughout the world and are very common in the southern and midwestern portion of the United States. They are usually found in low, damp areas where there is a lot of plant growth. They like shrubs and small trees as well. They are even common in the lawns around homes in some areas. Chiggers are a nuisance to humans, as they attach themselves to our skin and bite us, causing an itchy, red welt. The chigger sucks the cell tissue and fluid out of the host that it is attached to and injects its saliva into the bite. The saliva of the chigger is what causes the itchy reaction. Chiggers may not be the most pleasant insects, but they are natives of Iowa and will probably stay here as long as we do.

title: What is a “ring-tailed roarer”?
text: A ring-tailed roarer was the frontier name for the folk heroes of the American West. Men like Davy Crockett, Daniel Boone, and Mike Fink are some examples of ring-tailed roarers. They were said to be bigger, stronger, and smarter than any other pioneer. They could "shoot straighter, fight harder, and yell louder" than anyone else on the face of the earth. Only America could give birth to a creature such as the ring-tailed roarer.

title: The Mathias Ham House
text: Located on the north end of Dubuque, the Ham House is a historic gothic mansion with a majestic view of the Mississippi River. The mansion was first built in 1840 by Mathias Ham as a small stone cottage. Ham, his wife, and children lived here until 1856, when Mathias's first wife died. A few years later, Mathias remarried and began adding on to the cottage, eventually turning it into a 23-room mansion. The family became one of the most respected and well-known families in the area. Eventually, Mathias' second wife passed away and Mathias himself followed several years later. When the rest of the family moved away, Mathias' daughter, Sarah, stayed on alone in the house. It is at this point that the legends of the Ham House begin. Late one night, someone broke into the house. Sarah, in bed, heard the intruder coming toward her room. She took out her pistol and fired two shots through the door. Later, a trail of blood was found leading out of the house and down to the river. The body of a river pirate was found on the muddy banks of the Mississippi. Ever since this time, legends have spread that this river pirate continues to haunt the house and the riverbank nearby. Stories are told of mysterious lights that move along the riverbank at night, supposedly carried by the pirate planning his revenge. The Mathias Ham House is now used as a museum and workers there still tell of windows opening by themselves, phantom footsteps, and lights flickering on and off, just as they have for over 100 years.

title: Legends and Lore of Iowa
text:
Iowa has a rich history made up of interesting people and amazing events.

Over the years, people have preserved this history by telling the stories of our past to each other and passing our heritage along. Some stories that we pass along are factual, which means that the people in the stories are real and the events are described just as they really happened. Other stories that have been passed along have been exaggerated, or added to, as each person has told the story. By the time a story has been passed along over many years, the final result might not be anything like a true, factual story. These types of stories are known as legends or folk tales.

Legends

Legends are often about people who have actually lived and places that actually exist. The stories about theses people and places have just been exaggerated, or added to, until they are nearly unbelievable. Other times, legends are told about people or places that may not exist at all.

Many tales are told about a real man who became a legend in the Mississippi River Valley and throughout the entire United States. Davy Crockett was born in eastern Tennessee in 1786. He spent much of his life exploring the wilderness in the West and even served in the U.S. House of Representatives. He became famous not only for the things he actually did, but also for the things that people SAID he did. In the following story, see if you can decide which things could have happened and which must only be a part of the legend of Davy Crockett.

Davy Crockett Teaches the Steamboat a Little Patriotism

One morning, Davy Crockett got up feeling very ornery and cantankerous. He decided to go over to the Mighty Mississippi to take a ride on one of the river's famous steamboats to cheer himself up. He brought his pet bear, Death Hug, along for the ride.

Along the way, Davy and Death Hug met up with a well-known heroic sailor named Ben Hardin and the three of them continued on to the Mississippi River. When they got to the gangplank to buy their tickets for the steamboat, the captain shook his head and said, "No bears allowed." Well, this kind of attitude toward his best friend didn't set well with Davy and he hollered in his loudest voice, "Maybe you ain't heard that this here is the United States of America, where every citizen, human or bearlike, has the right to ride in a steamboat!"

Davy Crockett's speech made no difference to the captain, and he still refused to let the men board the ship with the bear along. Davy was so angry that he vowed to show the captain just what a couple of true American heroes and a bear could do.

Davy, Ben, and Death Hug went into the forest nearby and cut down a tree. They made two 10-foot paddles, hollowed out the log like a canoe, and launched themselves into the Mississippi.

The next thing the captain of the steamboat knew, along came the strangest water vessel he had ever seen. Davy and Ben were both paddling for all they were worth, puffing huge billows of smoke out of their lit pipes. The contraption passed the unpatriotic steamboat in a blur of smoke and motion, leaving the captain wondering what on earth had happened. Davy Crockett crowed with joy, shouting, "Well, boys, I guess we taught that locomotive river town a little bit of patriotism (love for one's country). There's nothing a steamboat can do that American brains and brawn, human or bearlike, can't do better."

(This story is taken from the book "Big Men, Big Country" by Paul Robert Walker.)

title: Superstitions
text:
Superstitions are also part of our heritage in Iowa. In days gone by, many people used superstitions to explain things that they didn’t understand. Superstitions cannot be proven true; in fact, most superstitions can be proved false, but people from the past often believed them anyway. Many people still believe certain superstitions to be true. How many of these superstitions have you heard of? Do you believe any of them?

If you break a mirror, you will have seven years of bad luck.

A horseshoe hung above a doorway brings good luck, but you must hang it facing upward or the luck will run out.

If you use the same pencil to take a test that you used to study for that test, the pencil will remember the answers.

If the palm of your left hand itches, it means you will soon be paying out money.

If the palm of your right hand itches, it means you will soon be getting money.

If you bite your tongue while eating, you have recently told a lie.

Cover your mouth when you sneeze so that your soul doesn‛t escape.

Don‛t rock an empty rocking chair because it invites evil spirits into your house.

Don‛t step on a crack in the sidewalk or you will break your mother‛s back.

When you make your bed, don‛t interrupt your work or you will have a restless sleep that night.

title: Welcome to Kentucky Community Studies Weekly!
text:
Welcome to Kentucky Community Studies Weekly! This year, we will be learning about the great state of Kentucky and about our own local communities. We will be learning all about social studies, or the study of people, their history, their government, where they live, and how they get along. We will find out what it means to be a part of a community and what we must do to be good citizens (members of a community or country).

As part of our social studies lessons, we will learn about the history, geography, economics, government, and culture of Kentucky. We will also study famous Americans and Kentuckians, learn how their efforts have improved our lives, and how they showed good citizenship and values.

In this week's magazine, we will learn more about what social studies is, why we study it, and how Kentucky Community Studies Weekly can help you learn more about your community, Kentucky, America, and the world. Turn the page to find out more about what's in store for you this year from Kentucky Community Studies Weekly and hang on for the ride of your life!

title: Tree Rings Tell an Ancient Story
text:
Could a city the size of New York City be destroyed by a drought? Many scientists believe that's what happened to a city called Angkor in what is now Cambodia. Angkor was the capital city of an empire that stretched from Myanmar (Burma) to Vietnam. This city of about 750,000 people lasted 600 years, from the ninth to the fifteenth century.

The Angkor area doesn't have the kind of summers and winters that many U.S. cities do. It has drought for about six months, and a rainy season for six months. Angkor had a complicated network of canals, reservoirs and dams to catch water during the rainy season so it could be used during droughts. The system worked well for almost 600 years.

Recently, scientists studied tree rings from 900-year-old trees near Angkor. The rings showed that year after year the droughts and the rains got more severe. Here's what scientists think may have happened: The reservoirs went completely dry during the drought seasons and the canals were badly damaged. The people of Angkor could no longer control one of their most important resources, water. Without water their civilization collapsed.

Isn't it amazing what you can learn from a tree?

title: Community Members Have Things in Common
text:
What Is a Community?

Kentucky is made up of hundreds of communities. A community is a group of people who have certain things in common. For example, community members share the same location, which means that they live in or near the same place. Community members also share the same government, the same schools, the same parks, and often, the same history. Because community members live, work, and play together each day, they build common memories. These common memories link members of a community together and help them to see the world in a similar way.

Studying Our Communities

This year, we will be studying the history of your community as part of our social studies units. Social studies is the study of history, geography, economics, and civics. We will organize our studies this year in the following way:

Geography

Geography is the study of the Earth and its features, such as lakes, rivers, mountains, and deserts. The first few weeks of Community Studies Weekly will focus on the geography of the land that we live on.

History

History is the story of our past, including our ancestors (those who came before us), our country, and the changes that have brought us from where we were to where we are today. Kentucky Community Studies Weekly will spend several weeks studying the history of our world, nation, state, and communities.

Economics

Economics is the study of how things are made, bought, sold, and used. We will discover how our communities provide for the needs of others, yet depend on others to provide for our needs as well.

Civics

Civics is the study of government and of how citizens get along with each other in a group. We will learn how our governments are organized, what it means to be a good citizen, and how we can make our community a better place to live.

Our Kentucky History Brings Us Together

All of us living in Kentucky share an exciting and interesting history that stretches back hundreds of years. Our history includes all of the people who have called Kentucky their home. These include the first American Indians, the early French and British settlers, the hard-working farmers, pioneers and factory owners, and the business and technology heroes of our day. All of these people and events have left their mark on our state, and our goal this year is to learn about who they are and what they did to help build our great state of Kentucky.

United States Citizens Share Important Traditions and Beliefs

As citizens of the same country, we are members of an even larger community. Americans share many important traditions and beliefs. (A tradition is a custom or belief that is passed down from parents to children.)

As United States citizens, we are joined together by our belief in freedom, our respect for the founding fathers, our understanding of what our flag represents, our belief that all men and women are created equal, and many more beliefs and ideas.

Celebrations Help Us Remember the Past

We also share in the celebrations that we hold each year to remind us of our American values. We will look at many of these celebrations and how they help us to pass the memories (things we remember) of one generation on to the next and make certain that we don't forget our past. We join together each year to celebrate Thanksgiving, the Fourth of July, Veterans Day, Memorial Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, and many other occasions. These celebrations bring us together as members of a larger community and keep our important memories alive.

During our studies this year, we will explore what it means to be a member of a community. We will also find out more about Kentucky, what it was like in the past, what it is like today, and what it may be like in the future. Join us for an unforgettable experience!

title: Our Cities
text:
In each magazine of Kentucky Community Studies Weekly, we will visit cities and communities all over the world. On our journey, we will make stops in Europe, South America, Africa, Asia, and several places in between.

As we explore different world communities, we will discover that some things with which we are familiar here at home are pretty much the same everywhere we travel. We will also learn about things in other communities that are very different from what we are used to. We will find out why people chose to build their communities where they did, what businesses help the community to survive, how the citizens of the community live, and what problems these communities face.

Also, we will discover how modern inventions make it possible for communities all over the world to stay connected to each other. We will also learn how events in one community can influence communities half a world away.

Keep an eye on the World Communities column in each magazine to learn more about places you may have heard of, and some you haven't! You may be surprised to learn that communities all over the world share many of your community's strengths, weaknesses, and challenges.

title: Daniel Carter Beard
text:
Although he was born in Ohio, "Uncle Dan," as most boys called him, grew up in Covington, Kentucky. As a child, he loved the outdoors and learned the stories of Daniel Boone and the American pioneers.

Uncle Dan became an illustrator and drew pictures for both magazines and books. He also wrote several books about nature, animals, and pioneers.

Daniel Carter Beard is best known as one of the founders of the Boy Scouts of America. He was always interested in working with boys and teaching them about nature and their heritage, so he formed a boys' club called "The Boy Pioneers" in 1905. When he heard about a program in England called the Boy Scouts, he helped to bring it to America, calling it the Boy Scouts of America.

Uncle Dan worked hard to help boys learn to love and respect nature, to develop good values, and to grow into honorable men. Daniel Carter Beard is one of our great Kentucky citizens.

title: Roman Aqueducts
text:
Whenever a large group of people lives together, it needs a good water supply for drinking, washing, and cleaning. Hundreds of years ago, most people lived in small villages where they were responsible for getting their own water from wells, springs, or streams. In ancient Rome, however, the people knew that a large city needed a better way to get water.

They tried many ideas and finally settled on a very creative way to move water. They used a system of aqueducts, or huge ditches to carry water from where it was available to where the people of the city could use it.

These large aqueducts were built both under and above ground and were made to slope downhill so that gravity would carry the water from a lake or river down to the city below. The water was often carried in pipes made from lead or terra cotta (baked clay), and the people living in the city could get water anytime they needed it. Many of these Roman aqueducts were built as early as 312 B.C. (more than 2,300 years ago) and are still being used today.

The invention of the aqueduct made it possible for people to live in large groups and still get the water they needed each day.

title: Anne Hutchinson
text:
We will also use Kentucky Community Studies Weekly to study the biography, or life story, of an important American who has made a difference in the world.

A strong, yet gentle, woman, Anne came to America in 1634. She left her home in England and settled at the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Anne held religious meetings in her home and taught some ideas that others didn't like. She told listeners that people were saved by the grace of God, rather than by any of their own good works. This idea angered the Puritan leaders in New England. They believed that Anne was trying to destroy the religious beliefs, as well as the governing laws, of the community.

In 1637, Anne was put on trial by the General Court of Massachusetts. Governor John Winthrop and the rest of the court found Anne guilty of disobeying the Puritan ministers, and she was sent away from the colony. Anne and her family moved to what is now known as Portsmouth, Rhode Island, and later to Long Island, New York, where she and her family were killed in an American Indian attack on the settlement.

Anne is an example of individual courage. She stood up for her rights to follow her own religious beliefs no matter what those in the government thought of them. She knew that everyone has the right to believe what he or she wants and refused to back down from that belief.

title: Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
text:
Here in the United States, we think of our own individual family unit of parents and children as our "family" and of our extended family members as "relatives." If you lived in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, your "family unit" would be much larger. In that country, "family" means parents, children, grandparents, aunts, uncles, and cousins!

In Riyadh, the extended family plays a very important role in the lives of young people. It even helps to choose whom a young person will marry and what his or her life will be like. In the past, the families of the bride and groom always arranged marriages in Riyadh. These arranged marriages still take place in Riyadh, but young people are now beginning to have more input in the choice of whom they wish to marry.

In Riyadh, women usually live with their parents until they get married. Men usually move out and start their own household when they get married. However, at least one son stays and lives with his parents to take care of them as they get older. If this son gets married, his wife and children will live with his parents as well.

Large family groups are very important to the people of Riyadh, and they play a huge role in the lives of the young people as they grow up.

title: My Favorite Celebration
text: Draw a picture of a favorite holiday celebration that you have had with your friends or family. What did you do? Did you have a special dinner? Who was there? Put all of these things in your picture!

title: Kentucky History Timeline
text:
In each issue of Kentucky Community Studies Weekly, you will find maps, charts, graphs, and tables that will help you get a clear picture of the topic covered in that week’s magazine. A timeline is a list of events in order of the earliest to the most recent. This timeline is a brief timeline of Kentucky’s history. Can you add an event to the timeline?

Kentucky History Timeline

1739 – American Indians lived in Kentucky.

1750 –Thomas Walker explores Kentucky and goes through the Cumberland Gap.

1763 – France gives up the area including Kentucky to Britain.

1776 – The Declaration of Independence is signed.

1792 – Kentucky becomes the 15th state.

1813-1814 – Creek Indian War

1875 – The first Kentucky Derby race takes place at Churchill Downs.

1891 –The current state constitution is adopted.

1900 – Governor William Goebel was assassinated.

title: How Do We Get There From Here?
text:
Have you ever been on a long car trip with your family? How did your parents know what direction to go and what roads to take to get to where you were going? When people plan to drive long distances, or to new places, they use a map. A map helps them plan what route to take. A map can also show things to see along the way, or places to stop for food, gasoline, and rest.

Maps come in all sizes and shapes. Flat maps show streets, cities, and countries. Globes teach us about the shape of our world and on what part of the Earth everybody lives. Charts and graphs are like maps. They give us a lot of information about what goes on in places around the world. Who eats the most chocolate? How much money do people spend on video games? What direction does the wind blow in the northern Atlantic? What landforms are there in Australia? Maps, globes, charts, and graphs help us to get a better picture of our world. These valuable tools make it easier for us to understand our community, our state, our nation, and our world.

In this magazine, we will learn about the maps, globes, and other special tools that make studying our world easier. We will see how they are used to learn about history, geography, and social studies.

title: Maps and Globes
text:
In this magazine, we will learn about maps and globes and how to use them to find places, measure distances, and get important information. When you are finished with the Lesson, you will be ready to make your own map of Kentucky!

Globes and Maps

You have seen both round globes and flat maps of the world. What is the difference between the two? Both a round globe and a flat map of the world show the same cities, countries, oceans, and landforms, but they are useful in different ways.

A globe is a round map of the world. A globe shows the Earth in its round form, just as it is in real life, only smaller. By using a globe, you can see how the Earth rotates, or turns, and where each country is in relation to other countries.

A flat map shows the same cities, countries, oceans, and landforms as a globe, but it allows us to see the entire world all at once, rather than in pieces as with a globe. You can only see one side of a globe at a time, but when the globe is flattened out into a map, you can see everything all at one time.

Parts of a Map

Maps include more than just countries, cities, oceans, and landforms. Maps also include many special tools that help you to find what you are looking for. Each map has a title at the top. The title of a map tells what location, or place, the map shows. Some maps that you may be using this year will be titled Map of the World, United States of America, Landforms of the United States, or Map of Kentucky.

Compass Rose

All maps have a compass rose, or a drawing showing the directions on the map. The compass rose always shows the cardinal directions, which are north, south, east, and west. North is always at the top of the compass rose, east is on the right, south is at the bottom, and west is on the left.

The compass rose also shows the intermediate directions. Intermediate directions are the directions directly between the cardinal directions. The intermediate directions are northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest. By looking at the compass rose, you can find out exactly where each item on the map is located.

Legend

The legend of the map is a key that lists all of the symbols on a map. These symbols stand for things such as the streets, rivers, monuments, parks, buildings, capital cities, and schools. The legend of the map helps you to know what each symbol on the map means.

Scale

Another tool used on a map is a scale. A map's scale shows the distance represented on the map. One inch on the map will be equal to an actual distance in miles. For example, an inch on the map may be equal to 1,000 real miles.

Grid System

Some maps use a grid system, or a system of numbered and lettered lines, to help you find places more easily. On a map that uses a grid system, there will be letters such as A, B, C, etc., running across the top of the map and numbers such as 1, 2, 3, etc., running down the side of the map. If you know that a certain city is located at point 2A on the map, you can find it easily using the grid system of the map.

In our study of history, geography, and social studies this year, we will be using maps to help us find out where things are and how they relate to each other.

title: Strasbourg, France
text:
Strasbourg has been called the "City of Roads that Cross" because of its location in Europe. Located near the Rhine River, Strasbourg is a city where many major roads join. These roads link cities in France and Germany to the rest of Europe.

Because of its location, Strasbourg is a city that joins the eastern and western parts of Europe. In 1949, after World War II had ended, Strasbourg was chosen as the home of the Council of Europe. The job of the Council of Europe was to rebuild Europe after the war and bring all European nations together in peace. Strasbourg has long been known as a city that brings people together.

Although Strasbourg has often been caught in the middle when European countries have had disagreements, it stands today as a symbol of peace and represents the hope that all European countries can live together as friends.

title: Casey Jones
text:
Probably the most famous American train engineer of all time, John Luther "Casey" Jones was born in 1863. As a boy, Casey lived in Cayce, Kentucky. He is known for his courage in saving a trainload of passengers, giving his own life instead.

Casey Jones was an engineer for the Illinois Central Railroad. He was very proud of the fact that he always brought his trains in on time. Because of his skill as an engineer, he was given the assignment of driving the Cannon Ball express train from Memphis, Tennessee, to Canton, Mississippi. This run was a dangerous one, and many accidents had already happened here.

On April 30, 1900, Casey Jones saw a train parked on the tracks ahead. He had no time to stop his speeding locomotive. He told his fireman to jump, and he slammed on the brakes. Casey's train crashed into the train ahead, killing Casey, but saving the lives of all the passengers in the cars behind.

Monuments honoring Casey Jones now stand at Cayce, Kentucky, and Jackson, Tennessee. A popular poem called "The Ballad of Casey Jones" was also written about his bravery.

title: The Sextant
text:
The sextant was invented in both America and England at about the same time, around 1730. The sextant is a special gadget used to measure how high the sun or stars are above the horizon. These measurements (also called "readings") are then used to figure out a person's location on Earth. Using the sextant, people have been able to make accurate maps. They've also been able to navigate ships at sea and learn more about the sun, moon, and stars.

The sextant is a triangular frame attached to a telescope and a mirror. The sextant reflects the image of the sun in the mirror, and the user can measure how high in the sky the sun is found. This is a neat way to figure out where on Earth he or she is standing.

The sextant is one of the great inventions that helped early cartographers, or mapmakers, create maps that were more accurate than ever before.

title: John Melish
text:
Born in Scotland in 1771, John Melish moved to America in 1811. He had visited the United States several times and had made notes about his travels, drawing detailed maps of the places he visited. In 1812, Melish published a book called Travels in the United States of America, which included his first maps. These maps started Melish on his career as a famous cartographer, or mapmaker.

After coming to the United States, John Melish began making maps for a living. He was careful to make sure that his maps were of the highest quality. Later American cartographers used his maps as an example, and Melish is known for bringing the standards for American mapmaking to a higher level of accuracy and quality.

John Melish is one of America's great cartographers, and his maps are still collected and treasured by map lovers today.

title: Banks
text:
Did you know temples were the first banks? Thousands of years ago, no one would steal from a temple. That's because they were afraid the gods would curse them. This made temples the safest place to store the costly metals people used for money. Some temples even made loans, giving money to people who promised to pay it back.

Do you know where the word "bank" comes from? Long ago, early Italian bankers used street benches to conduct their business. In time, the Italian word "banca" (bench) became the English word "bank." No matter what time era, or where you live, a bank has always been a business that deals with money. They hold money for customers, they make loans, and they provide other money-related services. There are three main types of banks.

The first is a commercial bank. These banks serve both businesses and individuals. They offer checking accounts, loans and saving accounts to their customers.

The second kind of bank is a savings bank. These banks are similar to commercial banks, but they mostly offer savings accounts and loans. They also offer mortgages. That's a special kind of loan for people trying to buy a house.

The third kind of bank is a credit union. Credit unions were started to help people borrow money. People in the same type of employment (a school district, for instance) put their savings together and loaned it to others within that organization. In other words, they operated their own banks. Today, credit unions provide many of the same services as commercial banks and savings banks. However, they are called non-profit organizations. This means all the members of the credit union share any profit that the organization makes.

title: Where in the World Are We?
text:
Where are you right this minute? In your classroom, inside your school building, in a city in Kentucky? If you had to tell someone where your city is located, what would you say? If you happen to go to school in Frankfort, you could say that it is located in north-central Kentucky, at the western edge of the state's Bluegrass Region. This would tell the person your relative location, or where your city is located using landmarks. If you wanted to tell someone exactly where your city is located, or even exactly where your school can be found, you could give them your street address. Better yet, you could use the grid system that mapmakers use: longitude and latitude, or an absolute location. For example, Frankfort can be found on a map at 38 degrees north latitude and 84 degrees west longitude.

In last week's magazine, we learned about grid systems and how they help us find things on a map. This week we will learn about latitude and longitude and how these special lines help us to find any location on Earth, no matter how large or how small. We will also learn about how the Earth is divided into sections, or hemispheres, and landmasses, or continents. We will use this information to help us find important places throughout the world. Look inside this magazine and find out EXACTLY where you are!

title: Can You Get There From Here?
text:
Could you give your grandmother directions to your local grocery store? Which street would you turn on to get to the park? Where is your doctor's office? Chances are you have been to these places many times, but would you know how to get there all by yourself? If you had a good map, you could find any of these places quickly and easily.

It is important to know where you are and how to get where you need to go. Making a map of your neighborhood can help you see exactly where each place is located and how to get there from anywhere in the area.

You can make a map of your neighborhood to help you find important places. Use a large piece of heavy paper, felt or craft foam. Start by marking your house, along with the street you live on. Be sure to mark the cardinal directions clearly on your map. Carefully label the streets in your neighborhood, along with other important landmarks, like farms, businesses, parks, churches and even an unusual tree or tire swing.

After you have finished your map, ask a parent or family member to help you test it out. Use your map to guide you to someplace in your neighborhood. Was your map helpful? Did you forget to mark anything?

Keep your map and add to it over time. You'll have fun and learn more about your neighborhood each time you do!

title: Where in the World is Kentucky?
text:
Note: You may want to keep a globe or a world atlas (book of maps) handy as you study this week's lesson! Dividing the Earth

Hemispheres

Hundreds of years ago, mapmakers divided the Earth into sections to make finding places easier. They divided the globe into four hemispheres or sections. One line divides the Earth top to bottom, another around the middle. The line drawn around the middle of the Earth divides the Northern Hemisphere from the Southern Hemisphere like a belt. This line is called the equator. The line that divides the Eastern Hemisphere from the Western Hemisphere is called the prime meridian. This line runs through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, England.

As you can see on the map, everything north of the equator is part of the Northern Hemisphere. This includes North America, Europe, most of Asia, northern South America, and northern Africa. Everything south of the equator is part of the Southern Hemisphere, which includes Australia, Antarctica, most of South America, and southern Africa.

The Eastern Hemisphere, or everything east of the prime meridian, includes Asia, Africa, Europe and Australia. The Western Hemisphere, or everything west of the prime meridian, is made up of North America and South America, a small part of western Europe and western Africa.

Continents and Oceans

The world is also divided into seven continents, or large landmasses. The seven continents are Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America. Each of these continents is marked on the map.

On the map, you will see there are five major oceans: the Atlantic Ocean, the Indian Ocean, the Pacific Ocean, the Southern Ocean and the Arctic Ocean.

Using Latitude and Longitude to Divide the Earth

Now that we know how the world is divided and named, how can we pinpoint our location? Mapmakers decided to cover their maps with a series of numbered lines running up and down (north and south) and across (east and west). The lines that run across the globe are called parallels of latitude. (We usually just say "latitude.") The lines that run up and down the Earth from north to south are called meridians of longitude. (We usually just say "longitude.") Think of the lines of longitude as being long enough (as in "long-itude") to stretch from the North Pole to the South Pole.

Each line of latitude and longitude has a number. Look at the world map and notice how the lines are labeled. The equator is 0 degrees latitude, and the prime meridian is 0 degrees longitude. The numbers on the latitude lines increase as you look both north and south. The numbers on the longitude lines increase as they go east and west.

To find a location on the map, all you need to know are the latitude and longitude numbers. Latitude numbers are always listed first, followed by longitude numbers. Can you find our nation's capital, Washington, D.C., at 38 degrees N, 77 degrees W? (Use the compass rose to make sure that you are looking in the correct direction when finding north, south, east, and west.) Using latitude and longitude numbers, you can find any place in the world!

title: The Randstad (Netherlands)
text:
There is a place in the Netherlands (Holland) called the Randstad. This isn't a city or community, but a huge, crowded metropolis in the heart of the Netherlands that is made up of that country's largest cities - Amsterdam, Den Haag, Rotterdam, and Utrecht. The population in this little area has grown to more than 7 million people. "Randstad" actually means "the Ring City," because these cities form a ring. In the middle of the ring is a beautiful area of farms and green valleys that is called Greenheart. However, there isn't much green left in Greenheart thanks to the growing cities. As you can imagine, with so many people living and working in this little area, there are many problems to deal with. It is difficult for anybody to find a comfortable place to live that isn't already a home for several others. The roads are crowded, terrible traffic jams occur daily, there is too little space for recreation, and there is a lot of pollution of the water, air, and soil.

The problem of too many people living in too small of an area is a big one for the people of the Randstad. Here in the United States, we solve our space problems by spreading out. In the Netherlands, the people don't have that option. They would have to move into the ocean! Overcrowding is a problem that people are working to solve.

title: Alben W. Barkley
text:
Alben W. Barkley was born in Graves County, Kentucky, in 1877, to a poor tobacco farmer. From such humble beginnings, he worked and studied hard and went on to become vice president of the United States under President Harry S. Truman.

Barkley loved to study law. He attended law school, became a lawyer, and worked as a judge in McCracken County for several years. He decided to run for public office and work on state and national laws. Barkley ran for Congress and served as a representative and later a senator from Kentucky for more than 20 years.

In 1948, Harry Truman chose Alben Barkley to run for vice president when he ran for president. When they were elected, President Truman chose to make Barkley an important part of his presidency. He appointed him to the National Security Council and asked his advice about many important government problems.

After leaving the office of vice president, Barkley was again elected as a senator from Kentucky. He was a very popular and well-loved senator who worked hard for the rights of the citizens of Kentucky.

title: Global Positioning System (GPS)
text:
GPS, or Global Positioning System, was invented by the United States Department of Defense and has been used since the mid-1980s. GPS is made up of 18 satellites that are orbiting (circling) the Earth in space. These satellites send information to stations on the ground, allowing scientists to take very specific measurements of different locations all over the Earth. With the newest GPS systems, scientists can pinpoint a place on the Earth to the nearest centimeter!

GPS has been used to measure the height of Mount Everest, to track submarines and ships, to follow cars and other vehicles as they travel, and to make maps. As GPS equipment becomes more affordable, everyday people all over the world will be able to find out exactly where they are at any given time. Wouldn’t that be nice to have if you ever got lost in the woods or a giant parking lot?

title: John Muir
text:
Do you enjoy nature? John Muir did. He was born in Scotland in 1838, grew up in Wisconsin and came to California in 1868. Muir was surprised and fascinated by the beauty of the California landscape. He was even more surprised that so many of the natural wonders there were being destroyed. So many of the large sequoia and redwood trees were being cut down! Muir decided to work to preserve California's beauty for those who would come later.

Muir persuaded Congress to pass a bill in 1890 that created Yosemite National Park. Muir also started the Sierra Club, a group that shared his goal of preserving the forests and other natural wonders of the Sierra Nevada Mountains. The Sierra Club is now a national organization that tries to help people balance the growth of cities and industry with the goal of protecting as much of nature as possible.

Muir believed that everything in nature was connected and that we must preserve the land in order to be at peace. His efforts have helped to keep America's natural wonders around for us to enjoy today.

title: Mexico City, Mexico
text:
Mexico City is one of the world's largest cities, with a population of about 20 million people. It is the capital of Mexico and is located in the center of that country.

Families living in Mexico City enjoy the hustle and bustle of a large city, but living with so many other people also brings problems such as pollution, or dirt and chemicals in the air.

Hundreds of factories and millions of cars, trucks, and buses pollute Mexico City's air every day. Families living there have learned to change the way they do things. If you lived in Mexico City, you would have to stay home from school on certain days during the winter because the air pollution was so bad. You would have to play indoors rather than outdoors until the air improved.

Families also have to plan their trips carefully because the city has special rules about which days families can use their cars. The government also encourages families to use the subway or to ride special low-pollution buses.

Mexico City is a fun and interesting place to live, but living there can be difficult because of the huge population, crowded streets and shops, and bad pollution. These problems are being worked on all the time, and one day, Mexico City hopes to become a better place to live.

title: All About Borders
text:
Imagine that your family is driving home from a wonderful vacation. As you travel down the road, your mother says, "Keep your eyes open. We're about to cross the border into Kentucky!

You watch closely, keeping your eyes on the road, but all you see as you cross the border, or line, between Tennessee and Kentucky is a sign that says, "Welcome to Kentucky: Unbridled Spirit." That's it? Where is the state line? The line between the states is clearly marked on all the maps, so why was there nothing more than a sign at the border?

Unless the borders between states are formed by actual geographic landforms, such as rivers or mountain ranges, you can only see these border lines on maps. The borders drawn between states and countries are called political features and are man-made lines showing where different governments take control of the land. Some of the political features that divide the land are state and county lines, city limits, school-district boundaries, and voting areas. Sometimes, these lines are drawn where a river runs or a mountain begins, but more often, they are drawn wherever government leaders decide is best.

If you look at a map of the United States, you will notice these political features, marked by lines, but you will see many physical features as well. Physical features are the landforms of the area, such as mountains, rivers, lakes and valleys. These physical features are also marked on maps.

In this week's lesson, we will learn more about the geography of the United States, its boundaries, its regions and its landforms. We will also learn more about where in the United States we can find Kentucky and where its borders are drawn. Grab a map, and let's get busy!

title: CubeStormer Robot Beats Record for Solving Rubiks Cube
text:
How fast are you at solving the Rubik's cube? Have you ever tried to solve this puzzle? Well, so many people have tried that there are international tournaments where people compete to solve this puzzle the fastest. They are called speedcubers. So far, Feliks Zemdegs of Australia has the world record of solving the 3 x 3 Rubik's cube at 5.66 seconds. Pretty cool, huh?

Some people have even invented robots that solve the Rubik's cube. Friends Mike Dobson and David Gilday created a robot they named the CubeStormer. It is made of Legos®, controlled by a laptop computer and can solve the Rubik's cube in less than 12 seconds. But Mr. Dobson and Mr. Gilday wanted something even faster, so they invented the CubeStormer II. It is also made of Legos® but is controlled by a smartphone. The phone uses a special application (app) to take a picture of the puzzle cube, solve the puzzle in the phone and then transfer the solution to the robot to fix the cube. The really fun part is that this robot solves the Rubik's cube in 5.35 seconds. That beats the official human world record!

With permission, check out this online video of the CubeStormer II solving the Rubik's cube in 5.35 seconds: www.youtube.com/user/RoboticSolutions. What do you think? Would you like to try your hand at speedcubing? What about building robots that solve puzzles? The possibilities are mind-boggling!

title: The Regions of the United States
text:
In last week's lesson, we learned about hemispheres, continents, and how to find things on a map. This week, we will find out more about where our communities, state, and nation are located.

Where is the United States Located?

The United States is located in the Northern and Western hemispheres, on the continent of North America. Look at the map and notice that the country of Canada forms the northern border of the United States and the country of Mexico borders our nation to the south. The United States goes from the Pacific Ocean on the west to the Atlantic Ocean on the east. As the song says, America goes "from sea to shining sea."

Major Landforms of the United States

On the other map, notice that there are several important landforms marked.

Rivers and Lakes

Some of our nation's biggest rivers include the Columbia River, the Mississippi River, the Missouri River, and the Rio Grande. See if you can find these large rivers on the map. The map also shows the Great Lakes, made up of Lake Superior, Lake Michigan, Lake Huron, Lake Erie, and Lake Ontario. These lakes are found at the northern part of the United States, near Canada.

Mountain Ranges

The largest mountain ranges in the United States are the Rocky Mountains, the Cascade Range, the Sierra Nevadas, and the Appalachian Mountains. There are other smaller mountain ranges that aren't marked on this map. We will talk about other landforms, such as plains, deserts, and valleys, in other issues of the magazine.

Regions of the United States

The United States is divided up into five regions, or areas that share common landforms. A landform is a geological formation, such as a mountain range, a river or a desert. Each of these five regions shares the same types of landforms and climates. Climate is the kind of weather that a place has over a long period.

The five regions of the United States are the Midwest, the Northeast, the Southwest, the Southeast, and the West. (These regions are marked for you on the map) The land in each of these regions shares certain landforms. For example, the Midwest has beautiful, rolling prairies with rich, fertile farmland and warm summers with cool winters. The Southwest, however, is very dry and covered by areas of desert where most plants can't grow. Each region has its own landscape and climate.

Kentucky's Place in the United States

Kentucky is part of the southeastern region of the United States. The Southeast has rolling hills, rugged mountains, and valleys with rich soil for farming. Several large rivers, as well as beautiful forests, cut through the mountains.

Kentucky is bordered by Virginia and West Virginia to the east, Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois to the north, Missouri to the west, and Tennessee to the south.

title: Reykjavik, Iceland
text:
Reykjavik is the capital city of Iceland. It is a city with about 200,000 people, and it is found in southwestern Iceland.

Most of the people in Iceland make their money by fishing. Cod, a type of fish, is one of Iceland's biggest exports, or goods sold to other countries.

The city of Reykjavik was built near some natural, underground hot springs. Reykjavik uses this natural hot water in an unusual way: It heats the city's homes, parking lots, and streets with this amazing natural resource!

The hot water is pumped to homes in Reykjavik through a long maze of pipes. The hot water runs under floors and keeps the homes warm and comfortable without the cost or mess of heating them with coal, gas, or electricity. Because the natural hot water is so easy to get, many people even use it to heat the sidewalks in front of their homes and businesses so that the snow will melt off without having to be shoveled. Parking lots all over the city have hot water pipes running under them as well so that they never need to be plowed when it snows.

Reykjavik uses its unusual natural resource, hot water, to conserve power, prevent pollution, and save work!

title: Martha Layne Collins
text:
Martha Layne Collins grew up in Bagdad, KY, and went on to become the third American woman ever to be elected as governor.

Martha started out as a schoolteacher. After helping others get elected to the government, she wanted to try for a position. She ran for the office of Kentucky Supreme Court Clerk in 1975 and won! She was then elected as lieutenant governor in 1979 and then governor of Kentucky in 1983.

After her term was over, Martha Collins used her experience as a teacher to help make education better throughout the state of Kentucky. She also worked to bring more businesses to our state, and her work helped to bring a new Toyota automobile plant to Georgetown.

After leaving the governor's office, Martha Collins became president of St. Catharine College and worked for the University of Louisville's School of Business, the University of Kentucky, and Georgetown College.

Martha Layne Collins used her skills to make our state a better place to live.

title: The Compass
text:
No matter where you stand on Earth, you can hold a compass in your hand and it will point toward the North Pole. The Earth has its own special magnetic field that pulls the compass needle, or magnetic pointer, toward the north. As long as you have a compass, you can always tell in which direction you are heading!

The compass was first invented in China more than 1,000 years ago. Chinese scientists found that a special type of iron ore, or rock, always lined itself up in a north-and-south position. They soon began using the ore to make magnets, which they then placed on a piece of a leaf and floated in a bowl of water. They marked the bowl with "north," "south," "east," and "west" and then watched the rock magnet to see which direction it pointed. The Chinese used this type of compass on their ships for hundreds of years to point them in the right direction during their journeys.

Are YOU headed in the right direction? Find a compass and check it out!

title: Benjamin Franklin
text:
Benjamin Franklin was a great inventor, writer, and leading founding father of the United States of America. Ben was born in 1706 in Boston, Massachusetts. He didn't go to school much, but he never stopped learning. Ben read constantly and taught himself algebra, geometry, history, science, navigation, and five foreign languages.

Benjamin Franklin served as a diplomat, or friendly representative, to France for many years. He also signed both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution of the United States. He believed that the United States should be a free nation, and he fought to make sure that it became one.

Ben was also a successful printer and publisher. He enjoyed doing scientific experiments in his free time and discovered many interesting facts about electricity. He invented the lightning rod, the Franklin stove, and bifocal eyeglasses.

"If you would not be forgotten as soon as you are dead and rotten, either write things worth reading, or do things worth the writing." - Benjamin Franklin

title: Reason and Logic: Young George Washington, Surveyor and Mapmaker
text:
Most people know about George Washington. He was born in Virginia. He was a general during the American Revolution and our first president. But his earliest jobs, surveyor and cartographer (mapmaker), taught him skills and values he would use for the rest of his life. Using reason and logic to solve problems helped Washington become one of our country's most important leaders.

When Washington grew up, there were few roads or boundaries in much of the land. A surveyor's job was to measure and map the land. He had to make exact measurements for boundaries and physical features. This was a very big responsibility. People needed accurate maps and surveys for traveling and buying land.

At age 17, Washington traveled across the Blue Ridge Mountains to map and survey part of the frontier. He was the surveyor for the whole county, and that was an important job. When he led the Continental Army, it was even more important to have reliable maps. He established the job of Geographer and Surveyor General and appointed a man named Robert Erskine to this position. He gave Washington some information that was very helpful in making reasonable and logical battle plans and decisions.

You can use these same skills to make important decisions. Be sure you have the facts and information you need instead of acting on opinions and emotions. In what areas of your life are reason and logic very important?
