title: Climate and Our Community
text:
As we have learned in other issues of Kentucky Community Studies Weekly, the United States is divided into several different regions. All the land in these regions shares things that make it alike in certain ways. Just as the United States is divided into regions, Kentucky is also divided into regions, or areas that share the same landforms and climates. The climate of an area is what the weather has been like there over a long period of time.

The climate of an area makes a difference as to which plants and animals - including humans - can live there. For example, the northwestern region of the United States is much too cool and wet for growing palm trees, and the southwestern region is much too hot and dry to grow blueberries. Each region of the United States and of Kentucky has the perfect climate for the plants and animals that live there. Each of these regions, along with its climate, landforms, plants, and animals, is called an ecosystem.

In this week’s issue, we will look at some of the different ecosystems in our state and how humans use and change these ecosystems in order to meet their needs. Join us for a look at Kentucky’s ecosystems and how they help us enjoy a pleasant life.

title: Scientists Believe Volcanoes Caused a "Little Ice Age"
text:
An ice age usually lasts thousands of years. But between A.D. 1300 and A.D. 1900 the northern hemisphere experienced a cooling called the "Little Ice Age." The cooling was so intense that glaciers moved south, causing northern European towns to be destroyed. It was so cold that the Thames River in London and canals in the Netherlands froze! A scientist at the University of Colorado, using plant fossils from this period, may have discovered why this happened.

The plants died suddenly between 1275 and 1300. That's exactly when many volcanoes erupted. Fifty years later, volcanoes erupted again. Billions of tiny particles from the eruptions were in the atmosphere, reflecting the sun's heat away from the Earth. This caused the land to cool, the plants to die and the ice cap to grow. But there's more.

The growing ice cap sparked a feedback loop. A feedback loop causes something to happen over and over. First, the tiny particles stopped a lot of the sun's heat from reaching land. This cooling caused the ice cap to grow. The ice reflected more of the sun's heat back into the atmosphere. This caused more cooling. Finally, the glaciers became so large that they stopped the warmer ocean currents from melting the ice cap. Over centuries the glaciers grew to cover northern Europe.

Volcanic eruptions started the cooling, but it took the feedback loop to keep the "Little Ice Age" going for centuries!

title: Ecosystems: Natural Communities
text:
In earlier issues of Kentucky Community Studies Weekly, we learned that a community is a group of any size whose members share certain things. The different regions, or ecosystems, of our state can also be called communities, as they share the same climate, plants, animals, and landforms. These natural communities make our state interesting and help us get the things we need to survive.

Regions and Climate of Kentucky

Kentucky is divided up into six regions: the Jackson Purchase Region, the Western Coal Field Region, the Pennyroyal Region, the Knobs Region, the Bluegrass Region, and the Eastern Mountains and Coal Fields Region.

The Jackson Purchase Region: Found at the far western tip of the state, this region is full of swamps. The Jackson Purchase area also grows more cotton than any other place in the state.

Western Coal Field Region: This Kentucky region is full of coal. This coal is mined and sold to power companies, who burn it to make electricity.

The Pennyroyal Region: The Pennyroyal Region is full of underground springs and caves, including Mammoth Cave, one of the most visited caves in the world. "The Barrens" is also part of this region. This is a large piece of flat land without many trees growing on it. This area has some very good farmland, in spite of its name.

The Knobs Region: This is the smallest region in the state. The Knobs Region is full of rolling and rocky hills that look like knobs, which is how the region got its name. Even with all the bumps and hills, this region still has great farming soil.

The Bluegrass Region: The soil in bluegrass territory is rich and can grow crops easily. There are also plenty of trees and water to go around. These are two good reasons why so many people call the Bluegrass Region home today.

Eastern Mountains and Coal Fields Region: This region is the home of the Cumberland Mountains and the Cumberland Gap, where most of Kentucky's first settlers made their way into the state. The Cumberland Mountains are part of the Appalachians. The land in this region is also full of coal, just like the Western Coal Field Region.

Most of the people who live in Kentucky now live in cities and towns. Only about one-fifth of all Kentuckians still live in the rural mountain areas of the state. People moved away from the mountains to find jobs and take care of their families.

Kentucky's climate is mild and comfortable and healthy during most of the year. The average temperature during the summer months is 85 to 88 degrees, and during the winter, the normal high temperature averages between 27 and 30 degrees. Winters can get cold, however, and the temperatures sometimes drop below 0 degrees.

Naming Different Natural Communities

Special words are used to describe how humans have settled the different natural communities of an area.

Wilderness is an area that is protected by the government so that the plants and animals that live there will not be hurt or destroyed. Wilderness areas can sometimes be used for hiking and outdoor adventures, but houses and businesses can't be built here.

Rural areas are natural communities where some humans have chosen to live, but where there are still large amounts of open space and where there aren't many houses, businesses, or roads. If you live out in the country, you live in a rural area of Kentucky.

Suburban areas are communities that are found just outside the borders of large cities. Most suburban areas are settled by people who have jobs in large cities, but would rather live in a community of houses and stores rather than in the middle of the city, surrounded by businesses, apartment buildings, and traffic.

Urban areas are communities that are found in large cities. Urban areas usually have many apartments, businesses, factories, stores, schools, streets, and people all located side by side in a small amount of space.

What type of area do you live in? Have you ever visited any other type of community? Where would you like to live, if you had a choice?

How Do Humans Change the Land to Meet Their Needs?

When people first began settling in Kentucky, all of the land was wilderness. How did the areas change over the years? People changed the land to meet their needs. When people came to settle an area, they needed water to survive. They dug wells and ditches to bring the water to where they needed it. They also needed shelter, so they built houses to keep out the sun, rain, and weather.

Soon, people cut down trees and bushes to plant crops, built houses and roads, and started stores and factories. When an area needed more workers, people quickly moved in, building more houses and turning the area into an urban community. When people got tired of living in large cities, they moved farther out and created a suburban community especially for houses and schools. People changed their environments to take care of their needs and their wants. Today, people still choose to live where they can make a living and where they think life will be pleasant. We are still changing our environments to meet our needs.

title: Vologda, Russia
text:
Vologda, Russia, is an oblast, or region of Russia a lot like a state here in America. Vologda has a cold climate with only about three months of summer weather each year. The winter temperatures often get as low as 42 degrees below zero! The summer temperatures can reach 80 degrees, but the summer weather doesn't last long.

For many years, residents of Vologda raised milk cows and beef cattle. The people of Vologda tried to farm, but the growing season is so short that the people of the area have looked for other ways to make a living.

Today, many people who live in Vologda work for mining and timber companies. Vologda now makes steel and other metal items, fertilizers, and even cloth. The area also has one of the largest furniture factories in Russia. This factory makes furniture for schools. The factory builds desks, chairs, and items for laboratories and gyms.

The people of Vologda have used their natural resources, such as metal ores and plenty of trees, to help provide for their needs. Although the area may be cold, the people there have still found a way to make a living, in spite of the freezing temperatures.

title: Maurice Rabb
text:
Do you enjoy taking pictures with a camera? What do you like to take pictures of? How about the inside of someone's eye? You have probably never even thought of taking a picture of the inside of an eyeball, but Maurice Rabb has done just that!

Born in Kentucky in 1932, Maurice Rabb graduated from the University of Louisville as a medical doctor in 1958. He became an ophthalmologist, or a doctor who treats diseases of the eye. He went on to do research to help those who have trouble with their eyes.

Maurice is most famous for his work in photographing, or taking pictures of, the inside of the eyeball. He developed a way to take pictures of the eye so that doctors could study diseases and injuries and find better ways to help heal these problems.

Maurice was also the director of the Illinois Eye Bank and head of the research laboratory of the University of Illinois. He was also given special awards from the University of Louisville for his work.

title: The Band-Aid
text:
The year was 1920, and Josephine Dickson, the young wife of Earle Dickson, had a problem. She and Earle hadn't been married long. And as she worked hard to take care of the cooking, cleaning, and other chores around the house, she couldn't help cutting, scraping, and burning her fingers. Each time she hurt herself, she would have to get out the gauze and adhesive tape and try her best to bandage the cut.

Her husband worked for Johnson and Johnson, a company that made gauze and tape. Earle finally came up with the idea of making special bandages for his wife so that she would be able to bandage her wounds more easily. He cut small squares of gauze and placed the squares every couple of inches or so along a long strip of adhesive tape. Then all Josephine had to do when she hurt herself was to cut off a ready-made bandage and stick it on her wound.

Earle told his boss at Johnson and Johnson about his invention, and soon, the company began making and selling the very first Band-Aid brand adhesive bandages. Josephine's problem was solved, and ever since, the world has reached for a Band-Aid whenever a cut appears.

title: Harriet Tubman
text:
Harriet Tubman was one of the most successful "conductors" along the Underground Railroad during the 1800s. The Underground Railroad was a secret system for bringing slaves to freedom in the North.

Harriet was born into slavery in Bucktown, Maryland, in 1820. She escaped in 1849 and spent the rest of her life trying to help other black Americans find freedom. She helped as many as 300 slaves escape to freedom during her years with the Underground Railroad.

After the Civil War, Harriet went back to Auburn, New York, where she worked for better treatment for African Americans. She also worked to get more rights for women and older people. In 1908, Harriet started the Harriet Tubman Home for elderly (older) and homeless blacks.

Harriet Tubman died at the age of 93. She is still remembered for her work helping slaves to freedom.

title: Rome, Italy
text:
Families have always been important in Rome, and while things have changed over the years, children still hold a special place in Italian family life.

In the past, Roman families had many children. Today, families are much smaller, usually with only one or two children per family. Roman parents today still treat their children with special care. Children in Rome are a part of all celebrations and events. Children go with their parents to restaurants and are allowed to stay up late and play in the piazza, or town square, while their parents visit at outdoor cafés. There are also several beautiful cathedrals, or churches, in Rome.

On warm evenings, parents and children dress up and go out for a passeggiata, or evening walk. They visit with neighbors and friends along the way and enjoy the time spent together.

In Rome, the father of the family is the head of the household and makes most of the decisions about money. The mother is in charge of the children and keeps the home running smoothly. Some of these responsibilities are changing now that more women are working at jobs outside the home, and men and women are starting to share some of the chores at home.

Rome is a wonderful place to grow up, as children are considered precious gifts to be treasured.

title: Elizabethtown
text:
"Elizabethtown, Strong and Growing Since 1779" is the motto of one of Kentucky's historic cities.

Captain Thomas Helm, Colonel Andrew Hynes and Colonel Samuel Haycraft first settled the area. These men built forts, each fort located one mile apart, in what is now Hardin County. These three forts formed a triangle and were meant to protect these settlements from American Indian attacks.

Within a few years, many businessmen and their families came to settle in Hardin County, and Colonel Hynes set aside 30 acres for a town. He divided the land into streets and building lots and called the spot Elizabethtown, after his wife, Elizabeth Hynes.

One of Elizabethtown's most well known settlers is Thomas Lincoln. Thomas married Nancy Hanks, and they built a cabin in Elizabethtown. Their daughter, Sarah, was born here, and the family then moved to Sinking Spring Farm, where their son, Abraham Lincoln, was born.

The family moved to Indiana for a time, and Thomas's wife became sick and died. The family later moved back to Elizabethtown, where Thomas married Sarah Bush Johnston. Sarah raised Abraham Lincoln, one of the greatest presidents our country has ever known.

Visitors can still see and tour the Lincoln Heritage House, where the famous Lincoln family once lived.

title: Ancient Stone Tools Help Archaeologists Learn about the Earliest People in North America
text:
How do we learn about ancient peoples in the Americas? There is no time machine we can use to go back and see how they lived. Instead, we learn about how people lived in the past through clues left in the present. Sometimes ancient peoples left clues about how they saw the world in stories passed down to their descendants. They also left behind creations we still use. For example, corn only exists because of ancient American people who bred grasses into a new crop. We can also learn about ancient people through objects they made. Scientists called archeologists search for ancient objects, buildings, or even garbage heaps to learn about how people lived in the past.

Unfortunately, many of the clues disappear over time. Weather often wears away wood tools and buildings. Food decomposes. Clothing usually falls apart. Because stone wears away more slowly, stone clues are easier to find.

Studying stone tools has helped archeologists create theories about ancient Americans. Stone tools over 15,000 years old have been found in North and South America. These tools show people have lived on both continents since before the first cities in the world began. While there are still many questions about how they lived, the careful craftsmanship on their tools shows that ancient Americans used their ingenuity to survive. These early peoples prepared the way for hundreds of nations that developed later all across the Americas.

title: Studying History
text:
When it's time to study social studies each day, do you wonder why you have to spend so much time learning about things that happened many years ago? Studying history helps us to understand the things that are happening in our world every day. Studying history can also keep us from making some of the same mistakes that others before us have made.

Why Is It Important to Study History?

History is the study of our past. It is important to study history to understand things that happened long ago. If we know what happened before, and why it happened, we can see how these events brought us to where we are today.

As we study history, we learn what people and places were like before we were born. We see how these people and places changed from what they were once like into what we know today.

If we learn about the mistakes that others have made in the past, we can avoid making bad decisions in the future. For example, when we see the way the American Indians were treated by the early settlers, we are able to see the mistakes that were made, and we can learn to treat others fairly. As poet and author George Santayana once said, "Those who do not remember the past are condemned to repeat it."

Eras of History

To make it easier for us to keep track of when different things happened, history has been divided into eras, or periods of time. If we know when different events took place, we can understand how all these events fit together.

When we know that Columbus began the exploration of America during the Era of Exploration, for example, we understand that others were also exploring the Earth at the same time.

Once people came to live in America, a new era called the Era of Colonization and Settlement began. To colonize an area means to settle it, or to build towns and cities. If we talk about things that happened during the Era of Colonization, we can see that these events will probably have a lot to do with building houses, getting along with the American Indians, planting crops and making new governments.

By dividing history into eras, it makes it easier for us to understand why things happened as they did and what made people act in certain ways.

Besides dividing history into eras, we also use special words to help us understand when things happened. These special words tell us if something happened millions, thousands, hundreds or even 10 years ago. These words can even help us talk about things that are happening right now!

Prehistoric

When we say that something is "prehistoric," we mean that it was around before people started writing history down. Dinosaurs lived in prehistoric times, which means either that no people were here to write about them or that those who were here didn't know how to write. "Pre" means "before," so "prehistoric" means "before history."

Ancient

"Ancient" means "very old," so when we say that something happened during ancient times, we know that it happened long ago. Many people use the word "ancient" to talk about history before the year A.D. 500.

Modern

The word "modern" is used to talk about things that have happened in the more recent past. Modern history talks about things that happened and people that lived several hundred years ago up to the present.

Contemporary

"Contemporary" means "living or happening at about the same time." You and your friends are contemporaries, which means that you live at the same time. Explorer Henry Hudson and Pocahontas were contemporaries, too, even if they didn't know each other, because they lived at the same time.

Circa

We use the word "circa" when we don't know exactly when something happened. "Circa" means "on or about a certain date." If we know that Betsy Ross made one of the first American flags, but we don't know exactly when she sewed it, we can say that Betsy Ross made the flag circa (or about) 1776.

title: Liverpool, England
text:
Liverpool is found on the River Mersey in western England, near the Irish Sea. During the 1700s, the shipping port at Liverpool was very busy. Ships from Liverpool also carried goods all over the world. Ships from Liverpool even carried slaves from Africa to the West Indies and North America.

When factories first started using machines to create things that people used to make by hand, Liverpool was at the heart of this new way of doing things. People came from all over England to get jobs in the new factories. They also found jobs working in the shipyards, helping to send the products made here to places all over the world.

During the 1800s, business was booming in Liverpool, and the city grew quickly. When World War II started, however, many German airplanes bombed the docks at Liverpool, damaging or destroying them. Many of the docks were rebuilt, but because of changes in the way shipping is done, Liverpool never became the great shipping city that it once was. Many people have lost their jobs, and unemployment is a big problem here. The way business is done has changed and so has the city of Liverpool. By studying the history of Liverpool, we can see how things that happened in the past made the city what it is today.

title: Enid Yandell
text:
Did you know that many of the famous statues of Daniel Boone found in Kentucky were made by a woman? Enid Yandell, one of the few female sculptors (people who make statues) of her time, created many of the most famous statues of Daniel Boone.

Enid was born in Louisville in 1871 to a very rich family. During this time wealthy women were expected to let the men take care of them. Enid broke this rule when she left for France on her own to learn the art of sculpting.

Enid studied sculpting with a very famous French sculptor, August Rodin, and came back to America to begin her work. She practiced until she was an excellent sculptor and made many statues that now stand in Kentucky. Her statues of Daniel Boone can be found on the campus of Eastern Kentucky University and at the entrance to Louisville’s Cherokee Park. She also sculpted Hogan’s Fountain in Louisville.

Enid was successful with her artwork and was one of the first women admitted to the National Sculpture Society. She also worked for women’s voting rights and helped the American Red Cross. This wonderful Kentuckian died in 1934 and is buried in Louisville.

title: The Ballpoint Pen
text:
When the Pilgrims wrote about their lives in America, they didn't have pens like those that we use today. They used pens made from feathers dipped in ink.

Later, people used fountain pens. These pens were messy and ran out of ink often, and their scratchy points made holes in the paper. Many people tried to make a pen that had its own ink stored inside, but the ink in these pens either clogged or leaked out all over.

In 1938, Ladislo and Georg Biro, two brothers from Hungary, came up with an idea to make the ink in a ballpoint pen flow more smoothly. They created a special rough ball at the end of the pen that worked like a sponge, sucking the ink into the point when someone wrote with it.

Other companies, like Papermate and Bic, improved the ballpoint pen and sold it for a price that everyone could afford. Today, most of us write with ballpoint pens, which are cheap, clean and easy to carry.

title: Pocahontas Saves Jamestown
text: Pocahontas, whose American Indian name was Matoaka, was the favorite daughter of Powhatan, a powerful chief of the Virginian Confederacy of Tribes. Captain John Smith, the leader of America’s first English colony, wrote in his journal that Pocahontas saved his life. He had been captured by her father’s warriors and was to be killed. Pocahontas also brought food to the people of Jamestown at times when they were starving. Pocahontas converted to Christianity and married John Rolfe, an English tobacco planter, who took her to England. "To convert" means "to join another religion." This marriage was the first alliance, or friendship, between the American Indians and the English settlers. Powhatan was happy about his daughter marrying an Englishman, and the king of England breathed much easier knowing he had a powerful ally (friend) such as Powhatan. Many English settlers moved to America because this marriage helped the English and the American Indians get along better. Pocahontas later moved to England and had a son, who moved back to America to raise his family. Pocahontas died in England in 1617.

title: Eskippakithiki—Indian Old Fields
text:
Many years ago, the eastern part of Clark County was the site of an American Indian village called Eskippakithiki. This unusual name is a Shawnee Indian word that means, "Place of Blue Licks." The Shawnee Indians chose this name because of the salt deposits near Lulbegrud Creek. The American Indians liked this spot because many animals came here to drink the water and lick the salt. This made Eskippakithiki a good place to hunt and trap animals.

The Shawnee Indians were the only American Indians who dared to settle in Eskippakithiki because all other American Indians agreed the land here was to be used as a hunting ground by all tribes. The Shawnees came here and planted corn, tobacco, potatoes, beans, pumpkins and sunflowers.

Eskippakithiki covered about 3,500 acres of flat meadowland between Lulbegrud Creek and Howard's Creek. The Iroquois Indians who came to Eskippakithiki to trade with the Shawnee called the place "Ken-ta-ki," which means, "flat meadowlands." The Iroquois also called the river they followed to get to this place "Ken-ta-ki," and soon, white settlers began calling the spot "Kentucky."

The Shawnees lived in the village of Eskippakithiki from 1718 until about 1754. The American Indians of the area fought many battles over who should control the land, but when the white traders and settlers began coming in, the Shawnees left.

Today, the area is called Indian Old Fields, after the American Indians who once farmed here. A monument and an old American Indian burial mound can be found near what is now Goffs Corner in Clark County, Kentucky.

title: American Indians in Kentucky
text:
The American Indians who lived in Kentucky and across America in the early days of this country lived together in tribes, or communities, much the same way we do today. Although each community was different from other communities in some ways, American Indian communities also shared many beliefs, values and ways of living in common. This week, we will look at how the tribes of Kentucky were the same in some ways and different in others. Two of the most important tribes in the Kentucky area were the Shawnee and the Cherokee.

Shared Beliefs of the Kentucky American Indian Tribes

Belief in a Great Spirit

Both tribes had a strong belief in the Great Spirit, who watched over them and all the Earth.

The Shawnee asked the Great Spirit for help with their crops each year. In the spring, the Shawnee did a spring bread dance, asking that their crops would grow well so that they would have bread to eat. When the crops began to grow, the Shawnee did the green corn dance, thanking the Great Spirit for the corn. In the fall, it was time for the autumn bread dance to thank the Great Spirit for the good harvest they had received.

The Cherokee also believed in the Great Spirit. They believed each creature in nature had a spirit of its own and that animals and birds were sacred. The Cherokee believed in order to show respect for nature, they should only kill the animals they needed for food.

The Cherokee also celebrated the Busk, or green corn festival. This festival thanked the Great Spirit for the corn, rain, sun and a good harvest. The Cherokee did not eat the corn until they had thanked the Great Spirit for helping it to grow.

Houses and Gardens

Both the Shawnee and the Cherokee Tribes built houses for their families and planted crops to feed them.

During the summers, the Shawnee gathered together in large villages. They built long houses, which were between 50 and 150 feet long and shared by many families. These houses were made of wooden frames covered with bark. Each family had a small section of the house where they slept and kept their belongings.

The Shawnee also planted cornfields, and the women took care of the corn throughout the summer. The men hunted and fished to get food for the village.

The Cherokee built houses out of wattle and daub. These houses were shaped like a half circle and were made from a frame of branches woven together and covered with mud. A wattle-and-daub house looked a lot like a basket turned upside-down.

The Cherokee women planted corn, beans and squash and gathered wild plants. The men hunted and fished.

Differences Between Tribes

Wanderers and Farmers

The Shawnee Tribe was a wandering tribe, which means that they didn't settle in one place for long. They traveled around, looking for the best hunting grounds and following the movement of the animals. They settled in large villages for the summer months, but when fall came, they moved to small hunting camps as they looked for meat.

The Cherokee was a more sedentary tribe. This means that they settled in one place and didn't travel much. They built houses, planted crops, and returned home after going on hunting trips around the area.

Patriarchal Versus Matriarchal Tribes

The Shawnee was a patriarchal tribe. "Pater" means "father," so the fathers, or men of the tribe, ruled. The chiefs of the tribe were men, and they were chosen from the great families of the tribe.

The Cherokee tribe was a matriarchal tribe. "Mater" means "mother." This means the women were the leaders of the tribe and made most of the decisions about what should happen. The Cherokee chiefs were men, but the mothers of the tribe chose them.

Kentucky American Indian tribes were different in many ways, but they all lived in communities, built houses for their families, grew crops to survive and believed in a Great Spirit that watched over them.

title: Japanese Families
text:
When a Japanese husband and wife have a child, they stop calling each other by their first names. Instead, they call each other "otousan" (father) or "okaasan" (mother). They do this to show that being a parent is more important than being a husband or a wife.

Japanese parents teach their children that the group they belong to is much more important than each separate person is. The children must always do what is best for the group. Parents and teachers tell the children that they must behave well or it will make their families and their friends look bad.

Japanese children study hard and doing well in school is very important. Children go to school all day and into the evening. They eat lunch together in their classroom and spend part of their school day cleaning the rooms, halls, toilets and yards of the school.

Japanese children are taught to show great respect for their parents and grandparents. Many Japanese families have their grandparents living with them and the family takes care of them in their old age.

Japan is a great place to learn how to work, study and show respect for others.

title: Kenora, Ontario, Canada
text:
Kenora, a beautiful city in Ontario, Canada, was once the home of the Ojibwe Indian Tribe. The Ojibwe people settled here to be near Lake of the Woods, a good source of water and animals that came to drink there.

The first European to come to Kenora was a Frenchman named Jacques de Noyon. In 1688, de Noyon visited Lake of the Woods on a trip into the wilds of what was then an unknown area. He found the Ojibwe people and saw the large amounts of furs and skins they had gathered.

In 1836, the world-famous Hudson's Bay Company built a fur-trading post on the Winnipeg River. This post was later moved to the site of the present city of Kenora in 1860. When the railroad came through Kenora, the town began to grow. Businesses in the area used the railroad to send timber, fur and fish to people in the East.

Today, lumber and fish are still important to the city of Kenora. A large paper company uses the trees in Kenora to make all kinds of paper products. Fishing is also a popular sport in Kenora. People come from all over Canada and the United States to fish in Lake of the Woods. Tourists also come here to hunt, swim, water ski and boat.

The Ojibwe people came to Kenora because of the many furs, skins, fish and trees near Lake of the Woods. Many of the people who live in Kenora today came here for the very same reasons.

title: Chief Cornstalk
text:
Chief Cornstalk was a great Shawnee chief who lived in the area that is now Virginia, West Virginia and Kentucky. He was born around 1720.

Chief Cornstalk led his warriors in many battles with the white settlers. After fighting for many years, he was tired and told his tribe that it was time to make peace with the white people. Chief Cornstalk's tribe wanted to keep fighting, but Chief Cornstalk went to the Americans at Point Pleasant (now West Virginia) and told them he wanted peace.

Chief Cornstalk promised to give all of Kentucky to the Americans and that he and his tribe would not cross into Kentucky again. He also warned the Americans that many of his tribe wanted to join the British and fight with them against the Americans. He told them he was afraid his tribe would force him "to run with the stream," or fight with them. The Americans decided to keep Chief Cornstalk with them to protect him from having to fight.

While the Americans were protecting Chief Cornstalk, some of the settlers who were angry with the American Indians crept in one night and murdered Chief Cornstalk. The governor offered a reward for anyone who caught the murderers, but no one ever found out who had killed the brave chief.

title: The Atlatl
text:
Atlatl is an Aztec Indian word that means "spear thrower." Before the bow and arrow were invented, early American Indians used the atlatl to help them hunt animals for food. The atlatl was a special spear thrower that let the American Indians throw their spears farther and with more power than they could by using their arms alone. Historians believe that people have been using the atlatl for more than 40,000 years. The American Indians even used the atlatl as a weapon against the Spanish when they came to the New World in the late 1400s. A spear thrown with an atlatl could pierce the metal armor worn by the Spanish soldiers.

Today, many people have rediscovered the atlatl. They hold competitions to see who can use the atlatl to throw a spear the farthest and who can come closest to hitting the center of a target.

title: Squanto
text:
Kidnapped by Spanish explorers as a young man and sold into slavery in Spain, Squanto managed to escape from slavery and return to his people. When he got back to America, he found that all of his tribe had died from smallpox, so he went to live in a nearby Wampanoag Indian village.

Squanto made friends with the settlers at the Plymouth settlement in Massachusetts and taught them to plant corn and to find and prepare seafood. Without his help, the Pilgrims might easily have starved to death.

Squanto also arranged a treaty, or an agreement, between the settlers and the local American Indians that helped the two groups get along with each other. This treaty remained unbroken for 50 years. Squanto performed many other acts of friendship for the English colonists before he died in 1622.

title: Can Facebook Save Dying Languages?
text:
Can you say a few words in Siletz Dee-ni? No? How about saying "hello" in Aka? If you can't, you're not alone! These two languages and 3,500 more could become extinct by the end of this century. Almost 80 percent of the world's population now speaks only one percent of the world's 7,000 languages. This has happened because of globalization. Globalization means that countries are more connected through trade, money and workers. When countries work together, people must be able to communicate with each other. That means many people have to learn another language. English is the main language used throughout the world for business and the Internet.

Why is this a problem? When the last person who is able to speak a particular language dies, some of the knowledge that is found within that language dies with them. A language contains the history of its people, how they used their environment and their beliefs and ideas. Technology may just save many of these languages from extinction! With YouTube, Facebook and other forms of social media, languages that are spoken by even 5 or ten people can be taught to others around the world.

National Geographic has been working on the Enduring Voices Project. Its goals are to record native speakers of endangered languages into talking dictionaries and help communities learn ways to save their languages from extinction. What language do you want to help save?

title: Paducah
text:
In 1795, General George Rogers Clark claimed 37,000 acres at the mouth of the Tennessee River as his own. General Clark was a famous Revolutionary War general and the brother of William Clark, the explorer who traveled with Meriwether Lewis.

After General Clark died, his brother William planned a town on the land that General Clark had owned. William Clark named the new town Paducah after Chief Paduke. Chief Paduke was a legendary leader of a sub-tribe of Chickasaw Indians called Padouca Indians. This tribe once hunted and lived on the land where the town now stands.

People first came to Paducah because it was close to the place where the Ohio and the Tennessee rivers joined. This spot was the perfect place to build a town because the river made their lives much easier. Settlers in Paducah used the river for transportation and in their businesses. Paducah Marine Ways, a company that made barges, became the town's most important business when it opened its doors in 1854. Barges became an important part of the city's economy.

Today, there are many interesting sites to see in Paducah. There are museums and galleries in Market House Square. You can visit Civil War sites and learn about life on the river at the River Discovery Center.

Visitors to Paducah can also see the last steam engine, or "Iron Horse," used by the railroad in this part of Kentucky. Paducah is one of Kentucky's oldest and most interesting cities.

title: Celebrating An American Hero’s Trip Around the Earth
text:
It was 1957 when the Soviet Union launched the first spacecraft into orbit. Americans were shocked! The space race had just begun and we were already behind! In 1961 President John F. Kennedy announced that the U.S. planned to land a man on the moon by the end of the decade. The Russians responded by first launching a dog into orbit, and later two men. The race was on!

On Feb. 20, 1962, a Marine Corps fighter pilot from Ohio stepped up to put his life on the line. John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth. The success of his Mercury mission was one of the first steps to landing a man on the moon in July 1969.

John Glenn served as the U.S. senator from Ohio for 24 years, but he longed to go back into space. In 1998 at the age of 77 he was able to see that dream come true. He traveled on the space shuttle Discovery and became the oldest person to ever go into space! On Feb. 20th, 2012, America celebrated the 50th anniversary of John Glenn's first orbit. Mr. Glenn and the remaining members of the Mercury mission space team were given a hero's welcome at Cape Canaveral in Florida. Because of Mr. Glenn's service to our country as an astronaut and a senator, he has been called an American hero.

title: Explorers in Kentucky
text:
The first people who explored and settled in America and Kentucky came here for many different reasons. Some came here looking for gold and other ways to get rich. Others, like the Pilgrims, came here searching for a place to worship God in their own way. Some came to America hoping to find freedom from unfair governments. A few even came here hoping to find good health and a long life. This week, we will look at several different explorers and settlers to discover what they hoped to find when they came to America and Kentucky.

Juan Ponce de Leon

Ponce de Leon, a Spanish sailor, was an unusual explorer. He didn't sail west looking for gold, freedom or honor. He came looking for a way to stay young forever.

Ponce de Leon had heard legends (stories that may or may not be true) about the Fountain of Youth. The Fountain of Youth was a spring that was supposed to make anyone who drank from it stay young and healthy forever. He explored the Bahamas, searching for this famous spring. Instead of finding the Fountain of Youth, Ponce de Leon became the first European to explore Florida.

Jacques Cartier

Jacques Cartier sailed northwest from France hoping to find a new trade route to Asia. A trade route is a pathway that can be used for traders to bring their goods back and forth. Like Columbus, Cartier wanted to find a new way to get to all the wealth and riches that could be found in China and other Asian countries.

Cartier landed near the mouth of the St. Lawrence River. He thought that if he sailed up the river, he would reach the open sea. He hoped to reach Asia by using this waterway. In 1534, Cartier sailed up the St. Lawrence River and found that it never reached the ocean. His plans to sail to China were blocked by the American continent. He never found his trade route, but Cartier claimed Quebec for France.

Early Kentucky Explorers and Settlers

The land that we now call Kentucky was first claimed by the Spanish, then the French and then the English. In 1750, a man named Dr. Thomas Walker, a surveyor for the Loyal Land company, came through the Cumberland Gap. Dr. Walker and his group built a supply post near what is now Barbourville. When they returned to Virginia, they told everyone about the great hunting they had found in Kentucky. They also spoke of the good soil and plentiful water for farming.

Soon, mountain men, hunters and fur trappers such as Daniel Boone came to Kentucky and found the hunting to be just as good as Walker had promised. Settlers began coming to Kentucky to hunt and trap animals and to farm the land.

The first settlers came to America and Kentucky for many different reasons. Those who had the courage to stay did their best to make their dreams come true here in a new and sometimes frightening land.

Christopher Columbus

When Columbus set out on his journey across the ocean, he hoped to find a new way to get to the Far East. If his plan worked, Spain would have a new way to get to China. Sailors could sail west and bring back all kinds of gold, spices and silks to sell in Europe. Columbus didn't realize that North and South America were blocking the way!

title: Timbuktu, Mali, Africa
text:
Timbuktu is a city in the Western African nation of Mali. You may have heard someone say something like, “Trash is scattered from here to Timbuktu,” and wondered exactly what that meant. Timbuktu is in a very out-of-the-way place, far from other large cities. People often use the word ”Timbuktu” to describe something that is far away, or out in the middle of nowhere. Timbuktu wasn’t always such an out-of-the-way place. The city of Timbuktu was once the center of learning, wealth and religion in Africa.

The city started in the 1100s as a camp for African nomads, or people who traveled from place to place. Later, as Mali became a rich African kingdom, Timbuktu became an important city for trading gold and salt. People came from all over northern Africa to trade in the wealthy city.

Besides the many traders who came to Timbuktu to do business, many wise men, artists and members of the Muslim religion came here as well. Timbuktu was a beautiful city with large buildings, interesting people and wonderful places to eat and sleep.

Today, Timbuktu really is near the middle of nowhere. The famous city has crumbled, and its wealth is gone. Small traders still bring their camels, loaded down with salt, to the city to trade, but there is no longer any gold here to trade for. A few brave visitors still make the trip to Timbuktu, hoping to find out more about this city in the middle of nowhere.

title: James Harrod
text:
Some of Kentucky’s earliest settlers were surveyors. James Harrod was one of these surveyors. Surveyors were men hired by land companies to go out into the wilderness and mark the borders of the company’s land. They explored the land and reported on what they found.

While exploring the Kentucky area in 1773, James found just the right place to build a town. He went back to Pennsylvania, hoping to get some men to help him start a town in the Kentucky wilderness. By 1774, James had rounded up 31 men who were willing to go to Kentucky. The men bought supplies and headed for the spot James Harrod had chosen.

When they got to Kentucky, they made plans to build a town called Harrodstown, after their leader. The name was soon changed to "Harrodsburg." James and his men began building the town in the center of the Bluegrass Region in 1774. Harrodsburg became Kentucky’s very first permanent settlement.

James Harrod and Daniel Boone were good friends, and both had hoped to be the first to build a town in Kentucky. Although James built Harrodsburg before Daniel Boone finished Boonesborough, he and Daniel stayed great friends and neighbors. The towns of Harrodsburg and Boonesborough are only about 35 miles apart.

title: The Zipper
text:
Most of the world's greatest inventions happened because someone had a problem that needed to be solved. The zipper is one invention created for this very reason.

Whitcomb L. Judson loved machines and gadgets. He spent much time tinkering with new ideas for making life easier.

Whitcomb had a friend with a problem. His friend had a stiff back that made it impossible for him to bend over and use both hands to hook up the hooks on his shoes. Whitcomb set out to solve this problem for his friend.

After working for a few weeks, Whitcomb came up with a special slide fastener that could be opened and closed with just one hand. By 1893, Whitcomb had received a patent, or license from the government giving him and only him the right to make and sell his new invention.

After a few years, other inventors came up with even better "hookless fasteners." Because they were so easy to "zip" up, the fasteners soon became known as zippers. By the 1920s, zippers were used in galoshes (rubber boots), clothing, luggage and bags. Today, the zipper is found on almost everything, from pants to dresses to tents. Whitcomb Judson's invention helped his friend and people everywhere who needed an easy way to open and close almost anything.

title: Cesar Chavez
text:
At the age of 10 years old, Cesar Chavez became a migrant worker when his father lost his farm in Yuma, Arizona. A migrant worker moves from place to place, working in the fields when the crops are ready. Cesar moved to California, working in the fields, orchards and vineyards to earn money for himself and his family. He joined many different groups that tried to help the migrant workers get more money, better houses and shorter working hours.

After years of work, Cesar Chavez started the United Farm Workers of America, the first successful farm workers' union in United States history. A union is a group that works for fair pay, safe places to work and good working hours for men and women working at the same type of job. The union started by Cesar Chavez is still around today and works to make sure that farm workers are treated fairly.

Cesar and his union started strikes against fruit and vegetable growers who refused to give farm workers fair pay, reasonable working hours, and safe places to live. A strike happens when workers refuse to come to work until the owners of the company promise to give them what they are asking for. These strikes made people across the nation aware of the needs of the farm workers and helped to bring important changes to the farm industry.

title: Sharing Public Space: Vitus Bering and Russian Colonies in Alaska
text:
Imagine traveling 6,000 miles over land with supplies for an expedition, and THEN sailing through frigid seas to look for a new world. This was the job given to Vitus Bering, a Danish navigator who sailed for the Russian navy. Peter the Great, czar (ruler) of Russia, asked Bering to explore the eastern coast of Russia. He was wondering if land connected Asia and North America.

Bering's first trip began in 1725. After spending three years getting his supplies to eastern Russia, Bering sailed along the coastline. He didn't see any land to the east, and he didn't realize he was sailing in the narrow passage between Russia and Alaska. This waterway is now called the Bering Strait.

Bering led another expedition in 1741. This time his ship landed on Kayak Island, off the coast of Alaska. They explored some of the Aleutian Islands and met the native people there, the Aleut. He was the first European to arrive in present-day Alaska.

Bering died before returning to Russia, but his voyages paved the way for Russian settlements in North America. Many fur traders came to the area. In 1799 the Russian government established a fur-trading operation in Alaska. Furs from foxes, sea otters and seals were very valuable.

Unfortunately, the Russians took advantage of the native people just as some Europeans had done in settling New England. The Russians took over their lands and forced them to hunt for furs. They also brought new diseases, which killed many natives.

Today, the Aleut people continue to live along the western coast of North America, and their population has grown. What might have been different if the Russians and the Aleut had shared public space fairly? Where in your community is there a debate over public land? How should such debates be handled?

title: Harrodsburg
text:
Harrodsburg was the first permanent English settlement west of the Allegheny Mountains. James Harrod was a surveyor who brought a group of men to the area in 1774. He laid out a town with houses in the center and farmland around the outside. Each man got half an acre inside the town for his house and yard and another 10 acres outside the town to farm.

Harrodsburg was not only the first permanent settlement. It also had the first school, the first gristmill (mill for grinding corn or wheat into flour), and the first woolen mill (mill for making wool into cloth) in Kentucky!

Harrodsburg had much trouble with American Indians at first. Many early settlers were attacked by American Indians, and the whole town packed up and left Harrodsburg until they felt that it was safe to come back. They were gone for a whole year. But when they came back, they built a strong fort to protect the settlers from American Indian attacks.

Today, Harrodsburg is a great place to find out about the early history of our state. The original Fort Harrod is gone, but a new fort, built to look just like the old one, has been built in its place. At Fort Harrod State Park, you can also learn about basket making, weaving, doll making, blacksmithing, broom making and woodworking. Workers at the park dress in clothes just like the early settlers used to wear. They teach visitors what life was like in Harrodsburg hundreds of years ago.

A visit to the Harrodsburg General Store will also give you a taste of history. You can buy old-fashioned candy, sit in a rocking chair on the porch and think about what Kentucky was like when it was first being settled.

title: The Job of a Museum Director: ‘A Little Bit of Everything’
text:
The Campbell House Museum is beautiful Civil War-era home in St. Louis, Missouri. The wealthy Campbell family lived there from 1854 to 1938. Studies Weekly asked Andrew Hahn, the director of the museum, about his job.

SW: How is a house museum different from other types of museums?

AH: A house museum is different because it gives you an opportunity to get the full experience of the past. If you go to an art museum, you can see paintings from the past that may tell a story about history or a particular event. But when you come to a house museum, you get the full picture of what it was like to live in the past. When people come here, they get to experience what it was like to be welcomed into the house or to work in the house. The house was so well preserved, and the Campbells' collection is still here. This is their house and how they lived in it.

SW: What does a museum director do?

AH: I do a little bit of everything. We have to raise money so that we can keep the doors open and pay the utility bills. I write the checks for all the bills, and I organize our volunteers who do most of the work at the house. We do research, so I look into the Campbell story and read old documents and newspapers that tell stories about the past. I even take out the trash!

title: Early Kentucky Communities
text:
When people heard about the wonderful farmland, the streams full of fish and the woods full of animals, they came to Kentucky. They built cabins, farms and, later, communities. What things in these early communities were the same as they are in your community today? What things were different?

Boonesborough and Harrodsburg

After Daniel Boone and his friends built a trail from Virginia to Kentucky, many groups of settlers came to the area. Boonesborough and Harrodsburg were both settled around 1775. Both small villages were surrounded by forts to protect them from unfriendly American Indians. By joining together in small communities, Kentucky’s early settlers could protect themselves from American Indian attacks and other dangers. They could also help each other with the work that needed to be done on the new frontier.

Lexington

Lexington was started by Robert Patterson and a group of settlers from Harrodsburg. Once the fighting with the American Indians died down, settlers in Kentucky felt free to build new, larger towns without forts around them. Lexington was one of these new communities.

Lexington was known for its horse racing. At first, men raced their horses right down the middle of the town’s main streets. When the town leaders decided this was too dangerous, they passed a law against these races, and a special race track called Red Mile was built.

Lexington was also the home of The Kentucky Gazette, the first newspaper in Kentucky. Transylvania University, the first college west of the Allegheny Mountains, was also built in Lexington.

Pleasant Hill

Some Kentucky communities were built for special reasons. Pleasant Hill, not far from Harrodsburg or Lexington, was built by a religious group called the Shakers. The Shakers danced, sang and shook their bodies when they worshiped. Because of all this shaking, the members of the group were called Shakers.

The Shakers built a community where everyone was expected to obey the rules of the group. They all lived together in large dorm-style buildings. No one was allowed to get married or have children, and all people had to work hard to make the community better.

Before long, the Shakers had built more than 250 buildings and had more than 5,000 acres of beautiful farmland in Pleasant Hill. Pleasant Hill was a strong Kentucky community for more than 100 years, until the Shakers began to move away from the town. Many Shakers got tired of the hard work and the lonely life here and wanted to join the world again. The settlement was divided up and sold. Today, Pleasant Hill has been rebuilt as a historic visitor’s site.

Danville

This community was started in 1787. It is often called the "City of Firsts," because of the many "firsts" that happened here. Danville was a busy town on the Kentucky frontier. It was the site of the first courthouse and the first post office in Kentucky. Danville was also the first capital of Kentucky when it hadn’t yet become a state. When Kentucky was ready to become a state in 1792, special conventions, or meetings, were held to decide what the government of the new state should be like. At these conventions, many people thought Danville should stay on as the capital, but Lexington was chosen instead. Later, the capital was moved to Frankfort.

title: Athens, Greece
text:
Athens is a large city in the country of Greece. In Athens, the men are the leaders, both at home and in the government. The most important job of the women is still to take care of the home and raise the children. The men go to work and make money to take care of the family.

After work, Greek men usually meet at their favorite coffee houses to have some refreshments and visit with their friends. The women often get together with their friends as well. They go to church activities, let their children play together, join together to cook a meal or just visit.

Men are in charge of the money in the family. The women are in charge of the home and the children. Many women now have jobs and work outside their homes, but it is still the woman's job to run the household and raise the children. Women also have the right to own land, vote, hold jobs and speak out in public, just like women in the United States.

title: Montreal, Quebec, Canada
text:
The famous French explorer Jacques Cartier arrived in what is now Montreal in 1535. About 100 years later, in May of 1642, the first French settlers came to Montreal. They shot guns to scare away any evil spirits that might already be living here and dedicated the island to the Virgin Mary. They named the spot "Ville-Marie," or the City of Mary. Over the years, Montreal was controlled by France, England and even the United States. Today, Montreal is part of the country of Canada.

Montreal has some neighborhoods in which most people speak French, and some neighborhoods in which most people speak English. There are strict laws about which languages can be used in business, in government and in schools. Many people have very strong feelings about which language should be used.

Today, Montreal is a famous meeting place for people from countries all over the world. Many conventions, or meetings of large groups of people, are held in Montreal each year. The city makes money from its airport, hotels, restaurants, convention centers and shopping malls.

title: Daniel Boone
text:
"I have never been lost, but I will admit to being confused for several weeks." - Daniel Boone

Born near Reading, Pennsylvania, Daniel was one of the greatest American trailblazers of all time. A trailblazer is someone who goes first and makes a path for others to follow.

In 1769, a friend of Daniel's named John Findley asked him to help him blaze a trail to Kentucky. Boone, Findley and five other men set out along the small trails and pathways leading through the Cumberland Gap in the Appalachian Mountains into Kentucky. They found a "hunter's paradise" filled with buffalo, deer, wild turkey and meadows that were perfect for farming. Daniel was so excited about this new land that he promised to bring his family back here to live.

A few years later, Daniel and 30 other woodsmen were hired to build what became known as the Wilderness Road into the heart of Kentucky. By 1775, Daniel had built a fort and a small town called Boonesborough. He soon moved his family here to live.

When Kentucky became part of the United States, Daniel lost all his land. His son, Daniel Morgan Boone, had moved to St. Charles, Missouri, and he invited his parents to come and live there. Daniel and his wife Rebecca went to Missouri, where Daniel became a judge. Daniel died in Missouri, but his body was later buried in Kentucky, the hunter's paradise that he loved so much.

title: The Steamboat
text:
In 1787, John Fitch showed the first working steamboat to a crowd gathered near the Delaware River in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The first steamboat was 45 feet long and was pushed along by a steam engine that turned 12 paddles. When these paddles turned, the boat moved along the river.

In 1807, Robert Fulton created the first steamboat that could carry passengers and freight (a load of goods). His first steamboat, called the Clermont, traveled from New York Harbor, up the Hudson River, to Albany and back. Many people thought the steamboat would fail, and they were surprised when it was a success.

The steamboat made life much easier for people living near the rivers. It could bring people and goods up and down the rivers much more quickly than a wagon could bring them on land. It was also cheaper to travel by steamboat than by wagon. The invention of the steamboat helped Americans settle in new towns all over the country.

title: George Washington
text:
"First in war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen." - Henry Lee

George Washington was born in Westmoreland, Virginia, in 1732. His father died in 1743, and George went to live with his half brother, Lawrence, at Mount Vernon.

George wanted to be a sailor, but became a surveyor (someone who measures and marks the land) instead. After surveying for a short time, George joined the army and became a lieutenant colonel. He was only 22 years old, but he learned quickly and did very well. By 1755, George became a colonel and then the commander-in-chief of the Virginia militia (small army). George decided to quit the army for a while and began serving in the Virginia House of Burgesses.

When the Revolutionary War started, George was chosen as the commander-in-chief of the Continental Army. He was a great leader and helped the United States win its independence from England. His men loved him and respected him for his honesty and his leadership skills.

After the war ended, George served as president of the convention that wrote the U.S. Constitution, the paper that tells how our country should be run. He was later elected as the first president of the United States. Because he was our first president, he is often called "The Father of Our Country."

title: Draw a Community
text: Imagine that you live in a new community in our state. Which community would you live in? Would you live in Boonesborough and Harrodsburg, Lexington, Pleasant Hill or Danville? Draw yourself in one of these early Kentucky communities.

title: Danville
text:
The community of Danville is about 35 miles southwest of Lexington. It first became a town in 1787. The community is proud of the many "firsts" that happened here. Danville was the site of the first courthouse in Kentucky and the first United States Post Office west of the Allegheny Mountains. Danville was also the first capital of Kentucky and the place where the first successful abdominal surgery was done. (See Our State Heroes.) And, Danville was even the place where the first Kentucky Constitutional Convention was held in 1792.

Danville has always believed that education is very important. The first law school in the West was built here in 1799. Danville also opened the School for the Deaf in 1823.

Danville was one of the first Kentucky communities to build schools for African Americans. A home school (a school where the students lived and went to school) for African Americans was established around 1850. African Americans went to public schools in Danville as well. The Danville Freedmen School, run by Boyle County, began as a one-room schoolhouse and became a large high school.

Today, the city of Danville is home to about 16,000 people. The community has well-planned roads, good doctors and even its own college, Centre College, built in 1819.

There are plenty of interesting historic sites to see in Danville. Visitors can take a tour of the McDowell House where Dr. Ephraim McDowell performed his famous surgery. They can also see the first post office west of the Alleghenies when they visit Constitution Square. Historic Penn's Store is the oldest country store in America run by the same family. Visitors can still gather around its potbellied stove while talking over the things they have done that day. Perryville Battlefield, the site of a famous Civil War battle, is another great site to see. To find out more about what Kentucky was like during its early years, plan a trip to Danville.

title: Joplin Works to Rebuild After a Deadly Tornado
text:
Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/ for more Connections and Current Events articles.

On May 22, 2011, a tornado hit the city of Joplin, Missouri. It wasn’t just any tornado. It was a monstrous EF-5, with winds over 200 miles an hour. This huge tornado was almost a mile wide and cut a path over 22 miles long. It crushed almost 1/3 of the city, killed 162 people and destroyed almost 8,000 buildings. It is considered one of the deadliest tornadoes in over 50 years.

Joplin is working hard to rebuild. Think about all of the parts that make a city work. In addition to houses and businesses, cities need electricity, sewers, roads, hospitals, parks and government buildings. In January 2012 federal and civic organizations in Joplin got together to give the "ok" to a plan called Joplin Area - Next Steps Plan. The plan outlined how to replace what was destroyed in the tornado. 4,000 building permits have been given to homeowners so they can begin construction on new homes. After the tornado hit, 530 businesses were either destroyed or badly damaged. The good news is that 420 of those businesses have reopened. Work has begun on a new hospital. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) is helping to clean up waste and keep the area safe for residents.

The people of Joplin will never forget that terrible day. Recovering from something this devastating is difficult, but Joplin is showing how it’s done!

title: Organizing History
text:
As we study the history of Kentucky, America and the world, we find that there are many things to think about. Have you ever wondered how we know what happened long ago? Or why things happened in the order they did? Or why people see the same event in different ways? This week, we will be learning how to find out what happened in the past, how to organize these events and why different people see the same event in different ways.

Thinking "Chronologically"

When we study history, it is important for us to be able to ask, "What happened first?" "What happened next?" and "What happened last?"

Putting events in order of when they happened is called organizing them chronologically. Chronological order is a lot like ABC order. Only instead of organizing a list of words by which letter they start with, you organize a list of events in order from which happened first to which happened last.

Using a timeline makes it easy to see which things happened first and happened later. A timeline is a list of events, starting with the first and ending with the last.

Look at the timeline below. It shows some of the events that happened during the Civil War. You will see that the timeline is in chronological order, with the events that caused the war at the beginning and Lincoln's death at the end.

Primary or Secondary

When we try to find out what happened in the past, we need to look in many different places. We can read journals, letters and reports. We can also look at pictures, read books, watch movies and listen to people tell about their experiences. All these different places to get information are called sources.

Each of these sources can be put into one of two groups: primary sources and secondary sources. Primary sources are actual records that have survived from the past, such as letters, journals, photographs and articles of clothing. Primary sources come from people who actually lived through an event. Primary means "first," or "main," so primary sources are usually the first places we should research when trying to find out what happened.

Secondary sources are created sometime after an event has happened by people who weren't actually there. Secondary means "less important," or "coming later," so we usually look at secondary sources after we have already looked at the primary sources first. Some secondary sources are textbooks, history books, research papers and movies.

Both primary and secondary sources are good places to look for information when we are studying the past.

Point of View

When we study history, we also notice that our sources don't always agree on what happened, why it happened or why it is important. If two people were part of the same event in history, how could they tell different stories about this event?

Each person who tells a story has a different point of view about what happened. Point of view is the way that a person sees things.

When we study the Civil War, we notice that those in the North had a different point of view from those in the South. We also see that those who owned slaves had a different point of view from those who were held as slaves.

If this seems strange to you at first, think about your life today. Do you have a different point of view about some things than your parents? Do you think you have a different point of view about what happened on September 11 than someone who lives in Africa, Afghanistan or France? Do you think that you see the Civil War differently than a child who actually lived through it?

When we read what different people have written about things that happened in the past, we need to look at what their point of view was. Then we can understand the things they say.

title: Chihuahua, Mexico
text:
Chihuahua is the capital of the state of Chihuahua, Mexico. Chihuahua is in the northern part of Mexico, in a little valley surrounded by hills.

Chihuahua is known for playing a part in many of the changes that have happened in Mexico's government over the years. During the Revolution of 1810, Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla, a famous priest who fought against the government, was put in prison in Chihuahua. The brave priest was held for 98 days and was fed only bread and water. He was later executed, or killed, for trying to get rid of the Mexican government. The night before he was executed, he wrote a poem on his cell wall thanking his guard for being so kind to him. Today, a flame is kept burning on the patio of the Government Palace to remind those who visit of the price Hidalgo y Costilla paid for their liberty.

Chihuahua was also part of another Mexican revolution, fought more than 100 years later. The famous bandit Pancho Villa fought to get rid of a government that he felt treated the people unfairly. He had a home in Chihuahua where he often hid from the Mexican army. The mansion still stands, and many visitors tour here. The car that Pancho Villa was in when he was shot to death is also on display.

Chihuahua is a city where visitors can see the past and the present, all at the same time!

title: Dr. Ephraim McDowell
text:
Ephraim McDowell was a pioneer in the field of medicine. A pioneer is someone who goes ahead of others and explores the unknown. Dr. McDowell was the first doctor to successfully take out an abdominal tumor (in the abdomen, or mid-section).

Ephraim came to Kentucky with his family when he was 12 years old. He studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh in Scotland. This was the best medical school in the world at the time.

In 1795, Ephraim came back to Kentucky and set up an office in Danville. In 1809, he was called to Green County to see a patient named Jane Crawford. Mrs. Crawford thought that she was expecting twins, but when Ephraim examined her, he found that she really had a huge tumor, or growth. He told her to come back to his office in Danville and he would try to remove it.

On Christmas morning 1809, Ephraim McDowell performed the surgery, the first of its kind in the world! The surgery was done without any pain killers, and the tumor weighed 22 pounds.

Strangely enough, Ephraim McDowell died in 1830 from what doctors now believe was appendicitis. If someone had operated on Dr. McDowell, his life may have been saved.

title: The Sewing Machine
text:
Can you imagine having to sew all of your own clothes with just a needle and thread? Before the invention of the sewing machine, that is exactly what clothing makers had to do.

In 1755, an American inventor named Charles T. Wiesenthal designed a double-pointed needle, with a sharp point on each end, to make sewing faster. In 1830, a Frenchman named Barthelemy Thimonnier used this double-pointed needle to make the first sewing machine. He attached the needle to a rod connected to a wheel. When the wheel turned, the needle went up and down, sewing stitches.

By 1846, Elias Howe, an American inventor, had figured out how to make the first lock-stitch sewing machine. This machine pulled the stitches tight so they didn’t come loose later. It was used in clothing factories to make sewing faster and easier.

In 1851, Isaac Merritt Singer, a Boston machine maker, built the first small sewing machine that could be used at home. He made it easy for people to have their very own sewing machines for making their own clothes at home. The Singer Sewing Machine Company went on to become the world’s largest maker of home sewing machines.

Just think of all the time, money and energy saved by the invention of the sewing machine!

title: Jonas Salk
text:
Jonas Salk was born in New York City in 1914. After graduating from medical school, he became a professor of epidemiology (the study of diseases and how to control them) at the University of Michigan. He later began teaching at the University of Pittsburgh, where he made the first polio vaccine. Polio is a disease that attacks the nervous system, often leaving its victims paralyzed. A vaccine is a special medicine that keeps people from getting certain diseases. The polio vaccine was first given to children in 1953, and it turned out to be a great success. Today, babies and children regularly get the polio vaccine to protect them from this terrible disease.

In 1963 Dr. Salk built the Institute for Biological Studies in La Jolla, California, to study diseases and ways to stop them. He left his home in Pittsburgh and spent the next 30 years in the San Diego area trying to find ways to protect people from contagious illnesses, or sicknesses that can be passed from person to person. He died in 1995.

Dr. Jonas Salk made the world a better place by fighting the germs that make us sick.

title: Scarcity
text:
Have you ever been to a movie theater and wanted to see more than just one movie? Maybe you saw or heard ads on television or the radio that made you want to see two or three movies, but you only had time and money to see one. How did you decide which movie to go see? Was it a hard choice? Did you go to the one your friends wanted to see? Did you ask someone who had already seen the movies for advice?

From time to time, you have to make a choice about which movie to see. A society faces the same kind of challenge deciding how to use their resources. Our resources are scarce. That means there is a higher demand for them than a supply. No matter how much of something is being supplied, people always want more. Sometimes, time can be scarce. That's when people don't have enough time to do everything. Sometimes, money is scarce. That's when you want more candy than you can afford or have the money to buy.

Because our resources are so scarce, people are always making choices about how to use them. Every time you make a choice about what to buy or how to spend your time, you are making a trade-off. Let's say that you decide to spend money on candy. Then you are making a trade-off of candy for money. You have less money, but more candy.

Economists also have a name for what you give up when you choose something else. An opportunity cost is what you do not get when you make a choice. There are opportunity costs in everything. When you woke up this morning, you may have decided to sleep in. If you did, what did you give up in doing so? Was it taking a shower or eating every bite of your breakfast? You could say that the opportunity cost of sleeping in was taking a shower or eating a nice breakfast. We have opportunity costs when we buy things too. Let's say that you couldn't decide between buying a new DVD or a new book. You finally decide to buy the DVD. The opportunity cost of that DVD was the new book. What is the opportunity cost of going to school every day? Is it worth it?

title: Timeline
text:

The events listed are mixed up, so it is your job to put them in chronological order. On the lines to the right, make a timeline by listing the events in Kentucky history in order of first to last.
