If you go to google.com and type in health information, how many hits do you think you'll get? You will get millions of hits. That is amazing and a little bit scary. Do you think all those millions of people and organizations who created those Web sites actually know the truth about health? How do you decide which Web sites are accurate? Anyone can create a Web site about anything - how to be different by wearing your underwear inside out, why people should eat seven cans of beans each day - anything. Does reading something on the Internet make it true? Of course not. Any one of those millions of health information Web sites could contain mistakes or things that are not true.

So, how do you make your way through the millions of Web sites to find the best health information? That's a great question. First of all, remember that not everyone who creates a Web site knows what he or she is talking about. Not everything out there is accurate. Next, look at the web address. If the ending of the URL is .org instead of .com, it means that the site comes from a non-profit organization instead of a business. Both may have Web sites with accurate information, but remember that a business is probably hoping to sell you something. There is no guarantee a non-profit Web site is 100 percent accurate, but it's often a reliable source of information. Look for organizations whose names you have heard before.

If the Web site is a ".com" Web site, find out who created it. Did this health information come from a group of trusted doctors? Then it's probably more credible (believable) than a Web site created by a group of people who are not health professionals. Be especially careful of Web sites selling items that claim to improve your health. These people have a reason to try to convince you they're correct. They want your money.

Look for Web sites endorsed by government agencies such as the Food and Drug Administration or that have been created by health care professionals. Then, take the information you find on the Internet and compare it with other resources. Go to your local library and look up information about healthcare in books and magazines.

No matter what information you find, talk to your doctor and ask his or her opinion. Although the Internet can be a terrific source of information, it can also be misleading. It's important not to fall into traps others have set for you.

title: Spit Test
text: Your spit may be more important in health diagnoses than you thought. U.S. researchers can now identify all of the 1,166 proteins in human saliva (spit). This means that most of the proteins found in saliva are also found in a patient's blood and some proteins match proteins that play a role in a variety of diseases. So how does that affect you? Well, when you go to the doctor in the future, you could possibly only have to spit into a cup instead of having blood taken. Can our saliva tell doctors if we have cancer, heart disease or diabetes? Some researchers believe doctors will be able to easily and inexpensively diagnose diseases in this way in the future. It has already been proven that saliva testing can detect oral cancer and HIV infection. However, only 23 people participated in the latest study that suggests saliva could replace blood testing. Before we can definitely say this new kind of testing is in our future, researchers will have to complete many more hours of studies with thousands more participants.

title: Advertising - How Healthy Is it?
text:
So you've decided to start living a healthier lifestyle. Good for you! You want to get healthy, eat right, exercise and take care of your body. Where do you start? How do you know which products and services are really good for you and which ones aren't? Welcome to the world of advertising. Everywhere you turn, there is someone who wants your money and is willing to manipulate you to get it. (Manipulate means to use clever or unfair ways to get someone to do something.) It may sound tricky, but it's the way advertising often works. Knowing how advertisers manipulate people can help you figure out what is true and what isn't.

Vitamins and Minerals

If you feel a cold coming on, should you take extra zinc or vitamin C? Many people believe strongly that these substances can help you fight a cold. Although it really may work for some people, scientists have not yet proven that vitamin C and zinc are cures for the common cold.

Some people think that since vitamins and minerals are necessary for our health, taking a lot of them will make you even healthier. This isn't true. Too much of anything, even vitamins and minerals, can hurt your body.

There are a lot of companies out there that would like you to believe that taking their supplements will make you healthier. Supplements are products some people take hoping to improve their health. Before people take supplements, they should check the company's claims to find out whether they've been proven or not. They should also talk to their doctors about the supplements. Most doctors agree that the best way to get the vitamins and minerals you need is to eat well-balanced meals every day.

Exercise Equipment

Alright. You're ready to exercise regularly to get in shape. That's wonderful! But where do you start? Do you go out and buy weights or a treadmill or a stationary bicycle? Which brands are best? Although your parents may be interested in buying this type of equipment, there are plenty of terrific ways to get the exercise you need without buying expensive equipment.

Which of these suggestions sound like fun ways to get your exercise? Playing soccer, basketball or football with friends? How about a game of dodgeball, kickball or hopscotch? Do you enjoy riding your bicycle, jumping rope, doing cartwheels, walking your dog or roller skating? You can get your daily exercise by doing any activity that involves moving instead of sitting in front of a TV or video game. Just get outside, climb a tree, build a snowman or run around the yard. And do it every day.

Smart Snacking

Don't let the advertisers manipulate you into eating lots of foods that aren't good for you. Choosing healthy foods is a much better idea. Once again, how do you know if something is really healthy or not? Are all natural (not artificial) products healthy? Just because something has natural on the label doesn't mean it's good for you. There are "natural" fruit drinks out there that are loaded with added sugar. Too much sugar can cause health problems like cavities and obesity.

Read the ingredients on the food label. The ingredients are listed in order from the most to the least. If sugar or corn syrup is the first ingredient on the list, you know there is more sugar than fruit juice in that drink. For some healthy snack ideas, visit kidshealth.org/kid/recipes/index.html. There's a long list of fun, healthy and easy-to-make snacks for kids.

No matter what area of your health or lifestyle you want to improve, don't fall into the traps many advertisers leave for you. Do your own research, ask opinions and double check with your doctor or school nurse if you have any questions.

title: Safe Surfing
text:
How safe is it to surf the Web? Almost everyone knows not to enter chat rooms or give out personal information when you're online, but do you know why?

When your parents were growing up, adults warned them not to take candy from strangers or talk to people they didn't know. That was their parents' way of making sure dangerous people didn't harm them. Your parents or teachers have probably talked to you about things like that, too.

Today, with computers and the Internet in our lives, it is an even bigger challenge for adults to keep dangerous people away from children. Unfortunately, there are some mean people out there on the World Wide Web, and you don't want them to know anything about you. Even if you only give out your name and a little more information, such as your city or where your parents work, someone dangerous might be able to find out where you live. The Internet can be a wonderful tool that connects the world in seconds and lets us communicate with people far away. However, it also makes it easier for dangerous people to find children.

So be safe! Get permission from your parents or teacher before you log on to any Internet site. Never give out any private information about yourself, even information you don't think is important. Stay away from chat rooms - not everyone on the Internet is who they say they are. Be smart and protect yourself at all times.

title: The President’s Challenge
text:
What is the President's Challenge? It began as a way for the president of the United States to get children to be more physically active. Now it's grown into dozens of programs that help citizens of any age get into shape.

If you're already active, you can join the Presidential Champions. Kids who are just starting may want to begin with the Active Lifestyle group.

It's simple. Just choose an activity that interests you. There are suggestions at the Web site listed below. Activities range from traditional sports, such as baseball, tennis, volleyball and basketball, to games like darts and croquet. You can even shovel snow, jump on the trampoline or do work around the house.

The Web site below has more than 100 options. Keep track of your activity either online or on paper. Once you've reached your goal, your online activity log will automatically remind you you've earned an award.

You can order it online or by mail. There is a small fee for each award. Then continue with the next level of challenges and earn more awards.

The awards are bronze, silver and gold medals, depending on your level of activity.

Many students do the President's Challenge in their physical education classes at school.

Go to presidentschallenge.org/home_kids to learn more about this exciting challenge.

title: Epi-Pens are Lifesavers
text:
How many of you know someone who is allergic to something? Probably everyone can answer "yes" to that question. But have you ever heard of the term anaphylaxis? That is a serious allergic reaction that can cause a person to stop breathing. What happens when someone who has a life-threatening peanut allergy accidentally eats one or comes into contact with a peanut product? The reaction may start with tingling or itching in the mouth. Hives, swelling, vomiting, cramping and difficulty breathing may follow. In the worst cases, the person may stop breathing and even die if he or she does not get treatment immediately.

Many people with life-threatening allergies carry an Epi-pen with them at all times. Inside this pen-shaped cylinder is the medicine needed to help save someone's life in the event of an allergic reaction emergency.

It's a good idea for everyone to know how to handle an allergic reaction emergency and how to use an Epi-pen. Go to epipen.com and click on "How to Use the Epi-pen." Watch the video carefully. After you watch, use magic markers (with the lids on) as pretend Epi-pens. Get into groups of four and take turns practicing what you would do if a friend had a severe allergic reaction and needed you to use the Epi-pen. Being prepared now, when there isn't an emergency, will help you handle the situation should it ever arise.

title: Healthy Web Sites
text:
This week you've learned how to find reliable information on the Internet and how to stay safe while you're surfing the Web. Take a look at the URLs for the Web sites below. Do you see the letters "gov" in the first three? That means those sites come from the U.S. government. The last one is an "edu" Web site. That means it is the Web site of a school. This one comes from Wake Forest University Medical School. All of these sites provide reliable information about staying healthy.

epa.gov/kids/ - At this Web site you can learn about the environment and ways to protect it. They also have a safe way for you to join the EPA Kids Club. Your parents can sign a form and send it in by mail. That way your personal information isn't on the Internet.

fda.gov/oc/opacom/kids/default - The U.S. Food and Drug Administration created this Web site just for kids. Learn about vaccines, mad cow disease, food safety and other interesting topics. Games and puzzles make this a fun place to get important health information.

www1.wfubmc.edu/Nutrition/Count+Your+Calories/dtd.htm - Want to know exactly how many calories are in your favorite fast foods? Go to this Web site and click on one of the 15 fast food restaurants. The information you find will help you make healthier fast food choices.

title: Writing Connection
text: Imagine you work for an advertising company. Create an imaginary health product and write an advertisement for that item. Don’t forget to include catchy headlines, vivid verbs and strong adjectives. You may want to include a testimonial in your ad. A testimonial is a quote from someone who thinks the product is worth buying. Focus on your strongest selling points, and end by telling the reader what to do. Maybe they need to “call now” or “click here to order.” Share your ads with the class and see if your friends can decide what techniques you used to manipulate them into wanting to buy your product

title: Making Healthy Choices
text:
Every day you make decisions that affect your life. Some decisions, such as what color socks to wear, are not as important as other decisions, like how often to exercise or eating healthier foods. Decisions about what to eat or drink and whether or not to exercise can affect your health. That makes them very important decisions. Before you make any important decision in life, it's important to follow these four basic steps.

First, look at all the choices you have. If you're hungry and you see a bag of potato chips, some pretzels and a chocolate bar in the pantry, you know you have at least three choices. Check the refrigerator and see what other choices you have. Hmmm. An apple, a hunk of chocolate cake and a bag of carrot sticks are some of the things you see in the fridge.

Next, think about the pros and cons of each choice. Pros are the good things that could happen, and cons are the bad things. Which of the snacks are best for your body? Which might cause cavities in your teeth or contain unhealthy fats? Picture what could happen if you eat that chocolate bar instead of the carrot sticks. Could you end up with a filling in one of your teeth?

Now it's time to make the best choice. You will usually know in your gut which is the best choice, especially after you've looked at all the options and considered all the possible results.

Finally, think about the actual result of your choice. Let's say you picked the carrot sticks. They're tasty, and you probably feel pretty good about your choice. You're probably not worrying about your next visit with the dentist. Remember to think about both the short-term and long-term results. Eating healthy foods can give you more energy right away and improve your health throughout your life. Chocolate bars taste good, but it's better to save treats like that for special occasions instead of having them as an everyday snack.

As you get older, you'll be faced with more and more difficult choices to make. Following these basic decision-making steps will help you make the choices that are best for you.

title: Put Down that Salt Shaker!
text:
Yum! Yum! Who doesn't love to shake salt onto popcorn, corn on the cob and mashed potatoes? And don't those salty pretzels and potato chips taste delicious? There's no doubt about it. We love our salt, and we need some salt to stay healthy. But too much salt can cause high blood pressure, and that can be very bad for your heart.

"I don't add much salt to my food," you may say. That may be true. However, have you looked at the back of the boxes and cans of the foods you eat? There's an awful lot of salt in foods like soup, lunchmeat, snacks and crackers. More than three-fourths of the salt we eat comes from processed (already cooked) foods.

How much salt do you need? The U.S. government recommends that you eat no more than 2,400 milligrams of sodium each day. That's about a teaspoon of salt. If you have one cup of chicken noodle soup and some peanut butter crackers for lunch, you are eating more than half of the salt you need in just that one meal.

One great way to eat less salt is to eat more fresh fruits and veggies. They're naturally low in sodium. OK, so you don't think veggies taste as good as chips. Try to learn to like more veggies. Your heart will thank you for it!

title: Test Your Decision-Making Ability
text:
Making choices - it's what life is all about. Now that you're nearing the end of elementary school, it's going to be more and more important for you to be able to make healthy choices for yourself. We already talked about the four steps to follow when you have a choice to make. All four steps are important, but many people forget step two - weighing the pros and cons of each choice. And that's why many people fail to make the best choice. They don't consider what will happen after they smoke tobacco, drink alcohol or try illegal drugs. There are consequences for almost every important decision we make.

Take tobacco, for example. A friend offers you a cigarette. What do you do? Imagine what would happen if you smoke it and what would happen if you didn't. If you didn't, perhaps someone would laugh at you, or maybe they'd just say, "OK." If you do smoke the cigarette, you have willingly decided to put toxins (poisons) into your body that will do it great harm. Weigh the choices and decide what the best outcome would be for you.

Here's another one. You're spending the night at a friend's house, and she wants to try one of her dad's beers. What do you do? What are all your choices? You can say, "yes," or you can say, "no." You could talk to her about why you don't think you should drink. You could talk to her parents. Are there any other choices you could make in this situation? What do you think will happen if you drink the beer? What if you don't? What if you talk to her or her parents? Now, what do you think the best choice would be?

OK. Here's one more situation to think about. Marijuana is the most widely-used illegal drug in the United States. Your brother's friend, who you think is super cool, offers you some. What do you do? Consider all your choices and their outcomes. If you choose to smoke it, do you know that you will be making changes to your brain? Is it worth it? No one thinks they will get cancer or bronchitis from smoking marijuana, but it could happen. Most people think the really bad things only happen to someone else. What are your other choices in this situation? Could you tell your brother's friend you thought he was too cool to make such a bad choice and suggest he not smoke marijuana? Could you tell your brother? Maybe you need to discuss whether or not your brother is making the right choices, too.

No matter how old you are, you will always be faced with choices that could affect your health and change your life. Get into the habit now of using the four-step method to decide the best outcome for you and your health.

Making Safe Choices at Home

Are there toxic chemicals in your home? Most of you will say, "Of course not. I don't live near a toxic waste dump!" Believe it or not, there are some dangerous chemicals that can be found in almost all homes.

For example, do you have extra strength cleaners in your bathroom? Mild cleansers are much safer to use. Some of the chemicals found in bathroom cleaners can burn your skin or damage your brain and nerve cells if you are exposed to them for a long time. Never use bathroom cleaners with the doors closed.

Certainly there's nothing dangerous in the kitchen, right? Wrong. When you heat foods in the microwave, it's better to use ceramic or glass dishes. Some plastic dishes can leach (leak) chemicals into the foods you are microwaving. What about the paint on the walls and baseboards? Old paint may contain lead, which can cause brain damage if children accidentally eat some of the paint chips. New paint could have dangerous solvents. The best paints are those listed as no-VOC paints. (VOC stands for Volatile Organic Compounds.)

Do you have an old computer you want to get rid of? Although leaving it in your home may not harm you, it is much better to send it to a recycler than to dispose of (to get rid of) it in the trash. Why? Because computers may contain lead and other dangerous metals. If you throw them in the garbage can, they will end up in our landfills, allowing the dangerous metals to leach into our soil and water system. In most places it's against the law to put computers, monitors and other electronic equipment in your regular trash.

For more information about dangerous chemicals, go to: checnet.org/healthehouse/home/home.asp. Click on the virtual house, scroll over the different rooms and discover what hazards may be found in your home. You'll also learn how to dispose of the hazards without harming yourself or the environment.

title: Louis Pasteur
text:
Louis Pasteur was one of the most important scientists in the field of health. He proved disease is caused by germs that are spread through the air. Now, this may seem obvious to you and me, but before Pasteur came along, doctors didn't really know what caused people to get sick. No one knew about germs. He was the first to prove diseases spread from person to person because germs travel through the air. That's quite an accomplishment!

Pasteur was born on Dec. 27, 1822, and died on Sept. 28, 1895. Quick math question: How old was he when he died? Remember, he didn't have a chance to celebrate his birthday during the year he died. Pasteur is also famous for showing people how to keep milk from going bad. This process became known as pasteurization. Pasteurization is a process in which the liquid is heated first to kill any germs and bacteria that may be in it.

That's not all. Pasteur also developed a vaccine to prevent rabies in dogs and people. Rabies is a disease that affects the nervous system and can kill people. The only way to get rabies is to be bitten by an infected animal. Thanks to Pasteur, our pets don't usually have rabies, because they are vaccinated (given shots) when they are young. And people who do get rabies (from wild animals or pets that haven't been vaccinated) can be treated with the medicine he developed.

Are you interested in learning more about Louis Pasteur or other scientists? There's lots more information at your school or hometown library. Keep practicing, experimenting, observing and studying science. Who knows? Maybe you could make a discovery that could save lives, just like Louis Pasteur! You can start with the "In the Lab" experiment.

title: Growing Up
text:
You're a fourth grader now! You are growing intellectually (what you know), emotionally (the way you feel) and physically (how you look).

Have you ever seen pictures of yourself when you were a baby? You've changed a lot since then, haven't you? You've learned to walk and talk and read and do many more wonderful things. Now you're entering adolescence, and you will begin to look and act more like an adult.

As your body changes, you may discover that you need to wash your face more often to keep from getting pimples. You may need to begin wearing deodorant. Good hygiene makes you (and the people around you) more comfortable, and it helps keep you healthy. And remember that everyone's body changes at a different rate, so it's important to respect others as you notice some ways they've changed. If you do, they'll respect you in return.

To help your body adjust to the changes, you'll need to take care of each system in your body. Eat healthy food for your digestive system. Exercise every day so your skeletal and muscular systems stay strong. Protect your respiratory system and your circulatory system by not smoking or taking part in other risky behaviors.

At this stage of your life, your emotions will change, as well. Sometimes it may seem as if you don't have much control over your feelings. You may be sad one minute and really angry the next. Talking to an adult or a good friend can help you feel better.

Growing up can sometimes be a little scary, but it can also be exciting. People change - little by little - every day throughout their lives. It's all part of being, well, a human being!

title: Pasteurization
text:
Why was Louis Pasteur so sure germs were in the air? You can conduct your own experiment to test his theory. (NOTE: You should skip this experiment if you're allergic to mold.)

Materials

soap and water

2 bendable straws

a slice of bread

a paper towel

bathtub caulk

an oven

a clean plastic water bottle with a push-pull closable cap

Directions

Wash and dry your hands well.

Break the valve off the push-pull closeable part of the bottle cap. You may want to try tapping it with a heavy pan to break it off more easily.

Put the long end of the bendable straw into the long end of the other straw to make a really long straw.

Then, put one of the short ends (the end near the bendable part) in the bottle cap.

Using the caulk, seal the straw in the bottle cap and then seal the straws together. Make sure you leave both ends open for air. Let the caulk set overnight and become firm.

The next day, tear a piece of the bread off and drop it into the bottle.

Next, tear the paper towel in half, get it wet and put it into the bottle also.

Screw the top on tightly and bend the straws so that they make a tube that comes up and out of the bottle, down toward the table and then back up again.

Put the bottle in a shallow pan of water and set the oven as close to 167 degrees Fahrenheit as you can (a low setting). Leave the pan and bottle in the oven for at least an hour.

After an hour, take the bottle out of the oven (get an adult to help you with this) and put it in a warm area for a few days. You may need to support the end of the straw that is coming out of the bottle with a stack of books.

Observe (watch) the bread. What has happened?

Take the top off the bottle and set it aside for a few more days. What happens now?

At first, you'll see that no mold will grow in the bottle because there's hardly any airflow to carry the germs into the bottle and to the bread. After you open the bottle, the mold can get in and grow. This experiment is similar to the ones Louis Pasteur did to prove that germs are in the air.

title: Recipe for Health
text:
Use the list of ingredients below to create your own recipe. You don't have to use all the ingredients, but you can't use anything that's not on the list. Be sure you give the directions in order and include measurements. After you write your first draft, trade with a friend to see if your directions make sense before you write the final recipe. Don't forget to name your new dish.

At the end of the recipe, explain why you selected the foods you did. What benefits will someone get from eating this new creation of yours? You may need to do a little research to find out what some of the foods will do for your health.

Choices for ingredients:

beans (protein and zinc to help your body grow and develop normally)

eggs, parsley or red meat (iron to reduce stress)

kiwi, tomatoes, strawberries, zucchini or bell peppers (vitamin C)

fish (vitamin E)

cabbage and carrots (antioxidants to prevent disease)

olive oil (good for the nervous system and healthy brain cells)

milk (calcium to build strong bones and teeth)

bananas (potassium)

You may add garlic, salt and/or pepper for flavor if you want to.

title: Writing Connection
text: Your parents are helping you plan your birthday party. They give you three choices. Choice one is you can invite three friends to spend the day at the local amusement park with you. The second option is to invite six friends to go to the movies and out for pizza. Choice three allows you to have 10 friends over for a sleepover at your house. Using the four basic rules of making decisions, think about the possible outcomes of all three choices and make a list for each one. Then, decide what is best for you. Write down your choice and explain why you made that choice. Share your ideas with your classmates and talk about why different people made different choices.

title: Risky Behaviors
text:
Which do you think is more dangerous: getting a tattoo or getting your body pierced? Which do you think could harm you the most: using drugs or trying tobacco? If you had a choice, would you rather share a can of Coke with someone or skip washing your hands in the restroom? Believe it or not, every single one of these risky behaviors can harm your health in one way or another.

Take getting your ears pierced, for example. You might say, "How could getting my ears pierced harm my health? Even some babies have their ears pierced! You just go to the mall, plop down your $25, and it's over in two minutes." Is it really that simple? Actually, it's not. There are lots of things to think about if you decide to get your ears pierced. First, you should only have your ears pierced by a licensed professional. Never have a friend pierce your ears. Next, ask whether the equipment is sterile (germ-free). If it's not, you could get an infection. You don't want to deal with a nasty infection in the holes in your ears (or anywhere else you might be thinking about getting pierced). If an infection takes hold, the area will get red and swollen. Eventually you could get a fever. Failing to take care of an infection could lead to serious illness, deformity and even death in rare cases. Ask your parents or guardians for permission before getting a piercing. Together you can talk to your family doctor and research all the dangers. Make sure you keep the pierced area extremely clean afterward.

Believe it or not, tattoos have something in common with piercing. A tattoo is a lot of punctures made deep inside your skin and filled with ink. Anytime you have a puncture wound on your body, you are increasing your risk for infection. Many states require tattoo artists to get a license and use sterile equipment. Getting a tattoo with equipment that isn't sterile could give you a severe skin irritation, a viral infection like hepatitis or a bacterial skin infection. And don't forget that it's almost impossible to remove a tattoo completely. A doctor has to remove several layers of skin or take off the tattoo with a scalpel. At best, that part of your skin will probably be discolored permanently. At worst, you'll be left with a scar. Either way, it's a painful process.

What about sharing a soda, not washing your hands and using drugs? Look inside for more information about these risky behaviors that can harm your health.

title: Can Your Food Make You Sick?
text: "Don't eat some peanut butter products. They could make you sick!" Peanut butter is just one type of food that has been recalled recently because of food poisoning scares. What is food poisoning anyway, and how does it make us sick? Food poisoning happens when people eat food that has been infected with organisms that can make people sick. There are more than 250 different diseases that can cause food poisoning. The most common of these include salmonella, shigella, E. coli and botulism. How do you know if you have eaten food that is "poisoned" with these viruses? You may have a fever, stomach pain, vomiting and diarrhea, among other symptoms. If bacteria grow on food, it can lead to food poisoning. You are most likely to find food poisoning in foods such as meat and dairy products. Although the food supply in the United States is probably the safest in the world, it is still possible to get food poisoning if food isn't kept as sanitary as it should be. Most people recover from food poisoning, especially if they see their doctor when it gets bad. However, babies, young children and the elderly are in more danger when afflicted with food poisoning. These groups of people have much more difficulty recovering from any type of illness.

title: More Risky Behaviors
text:
Accepting Responsibility for Your Actions

You may only be 9 or 10 years old, but you are already responsible for your own actions. Accepting this responsibility is a big part of growing up. Accepting responsibility means you can take credit for the good things that happen, but you also must take the blame for the bad things that happen because of your choices and actions. If you choose to walk away from a fight, you can take at least some of the credit for not causing harm to yourself or others. If you choose to eat a salad instead of fried chicken, you can take credit for keeping your body healthy. On the other hand, if you choose to give in to peer pressure and begin smoking cigarettes, you must take the blame for doing harm to your body. It is no one's fault but your own. Since you are responsible, you need to know the risks you face as you make choices. We've already talked about tattoos and body piercing. Here are a few other risky behaviors that can put your health in jeopardy.

To Smoke or Not to Smoke

Imagine this: You're walking down the sidewalk with a friend. He picks up a half-smoked cigarette from the ground, pulls a lighter out of his pocket, and suggests the two of you smoke it. You have two choices here - say "yes" or say "no." Before you decide, you need to understand all the possible consequences of your choice. What will your body be exposed to if you smoke the cigarette? Nicotine, tar and other cancer-causing agents will be flowing through your bloodstream and making your body sick. Think about this, too. How safe is it to put anything in your mouth that your friend found on the street? You have no idea who touched it before or whose mouth was on it. If you choose not to smoke, there are also consequences. On the plus side, you won't be putting all those poisons in your body. But don't stick around if your friend lights up. Second-hand smoke is dangerous, too. Another consequence is your friend may make fun of you. Do you have the courage to stick to what you know is right?

Picking Up Germs

Have you ever been in a rush to get to lunch and decide to skip washing your hands? That's a really bad idea. There are millions of germs in bathrooms, on everything from the toilet handle to the doorknob. Get a few on your hands and then touch your eyes or mouth, and you've just infected yourself with any number of viruses. The same goes for sharing a soda with a friend. Although your friend may seem healthy, she may be carrying a virus that just hasn't shown any symptoms yet. You both could end up sick. Is that worth a sip of a soda?

Illegal Drugs

Maybe no one has ever tried to get you to use illegal drugs. But there's a good chance it will happen someday. On average, people who smoke marijuana started when they were only about 14. Some kids get their first drink of alcohol before they are 12. (Remember alcohol is an illegal drug if you're not 21.) Taking illegal drugs can cause many health problems, from a chronic (never-ending) cough to heart attacks. It can shorten your lifespan by many years. Many illegal drugs cause emotional problems like mood swings, low self-esteem and depression. Most of them are highly addictive. Start taking illegal drugs and, before you know it, you may find that it's very, very hard to stop. Say "no" the first time and every time someone tries to get you to try illegal drugs. It might just save your life.

As you enter adolescence, you will find yourself faced with more and more risky choices every day. When it happens, consider the consequences and accept responsibility for your choices. After all, that is what will someday make you the strong, healthy adult you want to be.

Choose Healthy Character

Every choice you make has a consequence. When you choose to stay away from things like smoking and illegal drugs, you are not just protecting your health. You are also helping to keep your character healthy, too. A healthy character is just as important as a healthy body and a healthy mind. What is healthy character? Good question!

Having a healthy character means many things. It means being honest and responsible every day. Someone with a healthy character has the courage and self-discipline to make the right choices, whether you are saying no to risky behaviors or choosing to do your homework before you sit down in front of the TV. It's also important to know how to compare choices and consider the consequences of each choice you have. If you can do that, you are showing good judgment, another part of a healthy character. Do you treat everyone with respect and kindness? If so, your character is strong and healthy.

What are some of the consequences of making the wrong choices about character? One consequence is you may get a bad reputation. Your reputation is the opinion others have of you. If you are not honest and responsible, people will not think they can trust you. What if you don't have enough self-discipline to get your homework done every day? Your teacher will be upset, your grades will suffer and your next report card won't make your parents happy. Do you sometimes forget to treat others with respect and kindness? We all have bad days and may say some things we don't really mean. But if you are always forgetting the Golden Rule, you may not have many friends. People may even think you are a bully.

title: Are You a Bully?
text:
When you hear your parents or teachers talking about how to handle bullies, have you ever considered the possibility you may be the bully they are talking about? Answer these questions and see whether your actions and decisions make you a bully.

1) A classmate is laughing at a girl who is back to school after having head lice. What do you do?

(a) Laugh along with him. It's funny.

(b) Ignore the situation and try not to make eye contact with anyone.

(c) Tell him to cut it out.

2) As the teasing continues, several more students join in and begin scratching their heads as if they have lice. What do you do?

(a) Join the teasing. It's even funnier now.

(b) Walk to the other side of the room to get a book so you're not caught up in the situation. They're not teasing you, so it doesn't really matter.

(c) Tell the teacher about the teasing.

3) The teacher calls the class together and has a long discussion about treating each other with respect. What do you do?

(a) Laugh with your friends later about the discussion.

(b) Tell everyone exactly what you heard the other kids saying about the poor girl who had lice. Make sure you include every detail so everyone knows the entire story.

(c) Feel glad the teacher is addressing the issue and hope that the teasing will end.

Give yourself three points for every (a) you chose, two points for every (b) and one point for every (c).

If your total was three or four you are not a bully. Pat yourself on the back and keep up the great work.

If your total was five or six, you chose mostly (b) answers. That makes you a bystander bully. You are allowing the bullying to happen, and you refuse to help in any way. By turning away and avoiding the situation, you are not just telling the bullies you don't care what they do. You are saying what they are doing is OK. How will it feel when no one is there to stand up for you when you are being bullied?

If your score was seven or higher, you probably already know you are a bully. You push others around to make yourself feel better. Believe it or not, bullies are often weak people who only feel good about themselves when they ridicule (make fun of) others. Talk to a school counselor or a teacher and to get some ideas about how to control your anger. Take up a new sport or hobby. Maybe you'll build your self-esteem and you won't need to bring others down to feel better about yourself. Apologize to those you've bullied and make an effort to be kinder in the future.

Some people think being a bully means they're strong and tough. That's not true. Bullies have little self-esteem and are actually weak. Bystander bullies usually just don't want to get involved. Where would we be if Abraham Lincoln, Martin Luther King Jr. and Mother Theresa had decided not to get involved? Make an effort, starting today, not to be any kind of bully. It's your choice. Choose wisely.

title: Caffeine Addiction
text:
Did you know that most of us put something in our body nearly every day that is considered a legal drug? Caffeine can be found in most soft drinks and is considered a stimulant, which is a drug that speeds up your body processes. When you drink or eat something with a lot of caffeine in it, you may feel a rush, followed by a surge of energy. Caffeine causes your heart to pump faster and your breathing to quicken. It can even be addictive, although certainly not as addictive as cocaine or many other illegal drugs.

Would you notice a difference if you cut caffeinated drinks out of your diet? Let's perform an experiment and see. For the next week, stop drinking all drinks that contain caffeine. That means no tea or coffee, and you'll need to check the label for soft drinks. Don't drink any caffeinated beverages at all. (Caffeine can also be found in foods such as chocolate, but we'll just focus on the drinks for now.)

Each day, make notes in a journal about how you feel. Anytime you crave a cola, notice what time it is, so you can write it down. Are you having frequent headaches? This is often a side affect of reducing caffeine in the diet. Keep track of your headaches in your journal, too. Are you feeling irritable, restless or sleepy? People who have given up caffeine often have those feelings. If you experience those things, write about it in your journal.

Use the chart below to keep track of your cravings and any other problems you experience. Put a tally mark in the appropriate box to indicate what you are feeling. At the end of seven days, check your chart. Did you find that the problems showed up less often after a few days without caffeine? Try drinking some caffeine now. Do you notice the affect on your body?

title: Prefixes and Suffixes
text:
Knowing the meaning of prefixes and suffixes of different words can really help you understand what the word means. For example, thermo means heat and meter means a device for measuring, so a thermometer is a device for measuring heat.

Use the beginnings and endings of the words below and try putting them together to make words that make sense. Look up your words in the dictionary. Do they exist or did you create a new word?

Beginnings:

pedi - foot

bio - life

ortho - straight

tachy - fast

pachy - thick

stereo - solid or three-dimensional

phono - sound or voice

geo - Earth

Endings:

pod - foot

pterous - having wings

phage - eater

phagous - eating

morph - one having a certain form

morphic - being shaped like

genous or genic - making

lith - stone

phone - device for listening

title: Math Connection
text: Every time you shake someone’s hand, you transfer germs. So, let’s do a math problem to discover just how “germy” your hands could get. If six people are at a meeting, and each person shakes hands with every other person only once, what is the total number of handshakes that will take place? How will you find the answer? Work with a partner and try to figure out the answer before reading ahead. There are many correct ways to find the answer. Here’s one way: Person A shakes 5 hands, person B shakes 4 hands (because she already shook hands with person A), person C shakes 3 hands, and so on. So, 5 + 4 + 3 + 2+1=15. Now, try the same problem with eight people and 10 people. Can you predict the solution for 12 people? If you transfer 100 germs every time you shake hands, how many germs will you have transferred by the end of the meeting in each problem? What other ways can you think of to solve this problem and still get the correct answer?

title: How to Handle Stress
text:
Some grown-ups may be surprised to realize kids are stressed too. What stresses you out? Divorce? Moving? A new school? The loss of a beloved pet? Poor grades? Conflicts at school? A lot of problems kids deal with every day cause stress.

What happens to your body when you're stressed? Well, you've probably felt most of these symptoms before a big test. Your muscles may tense up, you may start sweating, and your heartbeat may increase. If this happens now and then, it's not such a big deal, but feeling stressed often can be really unhealthy for your body and mind.

How can you handle stress? There are lots of ways to help deal with things that are stressing you out. Exercise is an excellent way to handle stress. Go for a walk or play a game of soccer. Exercising for 20 to 30 minutes will help balance your stressed-out brain. Find something you enjoy that gets you moving!

Writing your feelings in a journal can relieve a lot of stress. If you're upset, worried, or anxious about something, you may feel as if you have no one to talk to. You do.

Get out your journal (just a regular school notebook will do) and write down everything you're thinking and feeling, even if it involves expressing anger toward someone you love. Something almost magical happens when you write your feelings down on paper. It will feel as if a burden has been lifted from your shoulders.

It's normal to be stressed now and then. If you're always feeling this way and you can't control it yourself, be sure to tell a teacher, parent or guardian so they can help you.

Don't try to handle everything on your own.

title: Divorce Emotions
text:
Everyone knows someone whose parents are divorced. Maybe you thought it would never happen to you, but it's happening now. Perhaps your parents recently split up, or they've been divorced for awhile but it still hurts. Just because it happens to a lot of kids doesn't mean it's easy to accept when it happens to you. How can you handle the range of emotions you feel when your parents tell you they are splitting up?

The first thing to do (and one of the hardest) is to realize you are not the reason your parents are getting divorced. Even though it affects you, it's not your fault. Your parents' marriage was between them, and their divorce is between them. You may feel as if you could have done something to prevent it, but you really couldn't. Take the pressure off yourself. If you are having trouble accepting this fact, talk to your parents about how you're feeling, so they can reassure you.

Another good idea is to find some friends whose parents are divorced. The kids who are going through this right now will be able to relate to your feelings and help you talk things through. The friends who went through this awhile ago can give you advice about how things may change and help you understand some things may actually be better after the divorce.

You can also talk with teachers and the counselor at your school. They are there to help you cope with difficult problems such as this. Most counselors can loan you some terrific books that may help you understand your feelings better. They may be able to help you meet some other students who are having a tough time dealing with their parents' divorce, too.

Write your feelings in a journal. Getting your feelings out through writing can really help make you feel much better. If you're angry at your parents (and it's OK to feel angry for a little while), then write down everything you wish you could say to them, even if it's not so nice. Then tear the paper into tiny little pieces and throw it away. You will feel better because you got your angry emotions out, but you didn't hurt your parents while doing it.

There are actually good things about people getting a divorce. Most people don't get a divorce unless there are serious problems in the marriage, and you've probably witnessed some of these problems. You may have had to watch or listen to your parents argue. Once your parents separate, you probably won't have to go through that anymore. After some time goes by, many divorced parents become more cordial (friendly) with one another, and life is much more enjoyable for everyone.

Both your parents love you, no matter how they may feel about each other at the time of the divorce. Never forget how important you are to both of them. Your parents are not divorcing you; they are divorcing each other. The time you spend with each parent will be precious to all of you. Yes, it's true that you may no longer experience outings with both your parents together, but you'll be creating new memories with each parent separately.

Most importantly, don't forget that things will get better as time goes on, as long as you continue to express yourself and your emotions in a healthy manner.

title: How to Deal with a Bully
text:
Everyone knows someone who likes to bully others. Maybe it's someone in your class who tries to cut in line every day at lunch. It could be someone on the playground who is always calling other people names or telling them what to do. A bully may try to take your seat on the bus when you are trying to relax after a long day at school. Bullies are always pushing people around.

How should you handle a bully? The most important thing to do is stop and think. You are in charge of your actions, not the bully. You can decide what to do.

You may feel like punching the bully in the nose. But if you hit another person, there will be consequences. Remember, it's OK to feel angry, but it's not OK to hurt someone else, even if he or she hurt you first. You can tell the bully to stop what he's doing. You can walk or run away and find an adult. Try not to cry, if you can help it. Bullies love making people cry. And whatever you do, don't try to get even with the bully. That makes you a bully, too.

title: Sibling Rivalry
text:
A sibling is a brother or sister. How do you feel about your siblings? If you're like most kids, some days you love them and other days you may wish you were an only child. Brothers and sisters can sometimes be bossy, demanding, whiny and annoying.

Rivalry is competition. You may compete with your brothers and sisters to see who gets better grades in school, who plays soccer better or who gets the last slice of pizza. Sometimes you may feel as if you're competing with them for your parents' time and attention. Sibling rivalry can get complicated, and sometimes things don't seem fair.

When it comes to siblings, you may feel proud, jealous, angry and irritated all at once. That's a lot of confusing feelings to sort out! Although you will probably admit that you love your siblings, there are times when you may need a break from them. That's OK. Everyone needs some alone time. Try talking with your parents and letting them know that you need some quiet time now and then without your siblings.

Hang in there when things aren't going too well with your siblings. Believe it or not, in 10 years or so you may find that your brother or sister is your best friend.

title: Rules for Resolving Conflicts
text:
1. Attack the problem, not the person.
2. Listen with an open mind.
3. No hitting, teasing or name-calling allowed.
4. Focus on the problem, not on the person.
5. Treat the other person's feelings with respect.
6. Take responsibility for your actions.

Cut out these rules and paste them on an index card (or just copy them on the card). Keep the card in your desk to help you remember what to do when you have a conflict with another person.

title: The History of Sign Language
text:
You may have seen someone using sign language to communicate now and then. Isn't it an amazing language? It's the ultimate in nonverbal communication. Believe it or not, the creation of a formal sign language took many twists and turns over the past centuries.

Until the middle of the 1700s, deaf people really didn't go to school. The deaf in Paris, France and London, England, formed their own groups, and each city created its own sign language they shared with others in the city. In 1755, Charles Michel, a French priest, began the National Institution for the Deaf in Paris. As the students arrived at school, he realized they could already communicate through their own sign language. This became known as French Sign Language (FSL).

In 1817, a brilliant deaf man named Laurent Clerc and a teacher named Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet opened a school for the deaf in Hartford, Connecticut. The school became known as the American School for the Deaf and is still around today. These two men began teaching the students using FSL, but some of their American students had already created their own sign language. Over time, FSL evolved (changed gradually) into what is now known as American Sign Language (ASL).

title: Nonverbal Communication
text:
Here's a great team-building exercise that shows the importance of nonverbal communication. All you need for this activity is a few friends and some space. Move the desks and tables to the sides of your classroom or go outside if the weather is good.

Directions

Get into groups of eight or 10 students.

Each student must join right hands with one other student in the group, but it can't be someone who is standing right next to you.

Join left hands with a different person who is not standing next to you.

Try to untangle yourself from each other without letting go of hands and without talking. Use facial expressions and other nonverbal communication to try to move people where they should. You may need to loosen your grip on someone's hand to twist or turn, or even step over or under people.

The first group to untangle everyone and end up in a straight line is the winner.

title: Peace is a Choice
text:
Two goats meet on a narrow bridge. They have a choice. They can choose peace: One goat can back up and let the other pass. Or they can choose war: They fight until one is knocked off the bridge.

Think of these goats the next time you are dealing with a conflict with someone. Who will choose peace and move aside? Peace is a choice, but you must decide you want it. Then, you must work toward it.

The story of the two goats is a Russian folktale. If you want to read more stories like this one, go to the library and look for "Peace Tales" by Margaret Read MacDonald.

title: Recipe for A Good Friend
text: What’s your recipe for a good friend? Maybe you’d start with four cups of kindness and mix in a cup of humor. A few tablespoons of responsibility might be important, so that she doesn’t get you in trouble. How much listening skill does your recipe call for? Is listening more important than kindness? Write your own recipe for a good friend. List the ingredients (and amounts) you think every good friend should have. After you’ve created your own recipe, look back over it and see how many of those qualities you have. How can your recipe help you be a better friend to those around you?

title: Influencing Others
text:
What does it mean to influence others? When you influence others, you have an effect on their decisions. The effect can be good or bad. You can influence them to make the right choice or you can try to get them to make the wrong choice. Has anyone ever tried to get you to do something you know you shouldn't do? How did they try to convince you it was OK to break the rules? Did it work? That person was a negative influence. A real friend would try to be a positive influence. She would try to help you make the right choice.

Think about how others influence you. Do your parents, friends and teachers do or say things that try to get you to act in a certain manner? Of course, they do. As a matter of fact, it's your parents' and teachers' job to be a positive influence on you. Sometimes their influence is as simple as a look or as complicated as a long discussion about how to behave in public. It's important to listen to the people who have a positive influence on you and to ignore the ones who are trying to get you to do the wrong thing.

Now think about how you influence others. Maybe you've done something subtle (not really obvious), like laughing when your friends act silly in class. When you laugh, aren't you telling them it's OK to be silly when they should be listening? If you choose not to laugh, you may be a positive influence on your friends. You might even help them learn something!

If you think your influence won't make much of a difference, you're wrong. Look inside for the story of Mattie Stepanek, who only lived to be 14 but was a positive influence on millions. You'll also learn some ways you can be a positive influence, too.

title: Living with Diabetes
text:
What does famous pop singer Nick Jonas have in common with more than 18 million Americans? Diabetes. In 2005, Nick Jonas lost 15 pounds in two weeks, drank water constantly and was not acting the way he usually did. After going to the doctor, he was told he had Type 1 diabetes.

About 8 percent of the population (more than 23 million children and adults) have diabetes. So what is diabetes? Well, there are really two types, although both have the same basic problem. The people with this disease have too much sugar (glucose) in their blood. The first, called juvenile diabetes, got its name because children seemed to get it most often. It's now called Type 1 diabetes. This kind of diabetes occurs when the immune system attacks the cells that make insulin. Without insulin, you get diabetes because your body can't process glucose. The other kind is called Type 2 diabetes. With this kind, your body doesn't make enough insulin, or your body can't use it correctly. Type 2 diabetes is usually found in people who are overweight. This type is increasingly occurring in children since so many more children have become obese.

Signs of diabetes include being extremely thirsty, having to go to the bathroom a lot and quickly losing weight. Some people even have blurry vision or are extremely tired.

There is no cure for diabetes, so people who have it must control it by eating right, using medicine and exercising.

title: Be a Positive Influence
text:
Believe it or not, you influence others everyday without even saying a word. Your laugh, your scowl and your gestures all influence others. If you want to get better at being a positive influence on others, you just have to work on a few skills. Many adults spend lots of money going to workshops and buying books about how to influence people. Here are a few ideas you can use. Share them with your parents, too!

Be a Good Listener

The first step to being a strong positive influence is to be a good listener. Be patient and really listen to what others are saying. When you are talking with someone, it's important to understand that person's point of view. You need to know why they are feeling a certain way or have a certain opinion. Here's an example: Your teacher assigned some extra homework for tonight, and your friend is furious. He says he's just not going to do the assignment, and you want to try to change his mind. Start by trying to find out why he is so angry. Does he have something to do after school that will make it difficult to complete the assignment? Maybe it's because he knows his parents will be busy tonight and won't be able to help him. Is he angry because he isn't sure how to do the homework? Understanding his point of view not only helps you influence him, but also it creates a positive atmosphere between the two of you.

Be Assertive, Not Aggressive

Another way to be a strong positive influence is to be assertive without being aggressive. What's the difference? When you are assertive you act in a confident manner. You are showing the person you know what you are talking about, and you believe in yourself and your opinion. Being aggressive is when you act in an angry or threatening manner if someone doesn't do what you believe he should do. Let's go back to your friend who says he won't do the extra homework. An assertive response would be telling him how important it is and why you believe doing it will help him in class. An aggressive response would be to yell and stomp your feet, make fun of him for not being able to do the homework or threaten to hurt him if he doesn't do it.

Try a Different Approach

Being a positive influence also means being able to try a different approach if your first idea isn't working. This can be a very difficult skill to learn. You don't want to change your opinion, of course. However, if you find that you are having a negative impact on the person you are talking to, you may want to change your approach. For example, if your friend is still refusing to do his homework, perhaps you should look at it from another angle. Are you being too pushy? That's not influencing; that's forcing. Try changing the way you're talking to him. Maybe you should take a break and pick up the conversation later. Appeal to his sense of responsibility or offer to help him complete his homework on the bus. Being able to change your techniques will help you become a stronger positive influence on those around you.

Are you ready to give it a try? Get together with a classmate and act out the situation we talked about in this lesson. Take turns being the person who doesn't want to do the homework and the person who tries to be a positive influence. Practice being a good listener, acting in an assertive manner and thinking of different ways to approach the problem.

title: Support Your Local Farmer
text:
What can you do right now to stand up for health? There are a lot of ideas, but let's start with something easy - food. It's good to know where the food you eat came from. Look at the signs in the produce department at the grocery store. Some fruits and vegetables come from thousands of miles away. That means they were picked several days ago - maybe weeks ago. The farmers who grew them may have used pesticides to keep insects away or herbicides to keep out the weeds.

If you have a Farmer's Market nearby, shop there for some of your food. It's almost always fresher than the produce you find in the grocery stores, and you can actually talk with the person who grew it. You can find out if the farmer used chemicals to get rid of insects or if the food is organic. (Organic food is grown without man-made chemicals.) You're also supporting small, local farmers by buying their food. Visit local farms where you can pick your own fruit and vegetables. It's lots of fun, your family gets healthy food, and it helps the farmer make a living.

Stand up for healthy food. Become involved and ask questions. After all, what you put in your body is up to you.

title: Mattie Stepanek
text:
Mattie Stepanek was a young man who suffered from a rare, incurable form of muscular dystrophy. Muscular dystrophy is a disease that causes your muscles (including your heart) to waste away. It's hereditary, so it often runs in families.

Mattie was born in 1990, and died one month before his 14th birthday in 2004. By the time he was 3 years old, he was writing poetry. His brother Jaime had died, and Mattie was angry and sad. He turned those feelings into beautiful poetry that helped him feel better. All of his older siblings died from the same disease he had. Jaime was the third. His mother also had the disease.

By age 6, Mattie had written several hundred poems. But he didn't stop there. He kept writing and eventually six books of his inspiring poetry were published. Millions of people around the world have read and loved his poetry. Mattie was the National Goodwill Ambassador for the Muscular Dystrophy Association.

Before he died, Mattie said he wanted to be remembered as "a poet, a peacemaker and a philosopher who played." Mattie Stepanek took the short time he had in life and used every second of it to spread his belief we should love each other and live in peace. And he started when he was only 3. If you don't think you're old enough to make a difference in the world, think again.

title: Have a Debate
text:
Have you ever tried to convince someone who disagreed with you that you were right? Did you end up in a big, loud argument? There's a better way. It's called a debate. When you debate someone, you and your opponent both come prepared to discuss each side of an issue. The goal is to try to persuade people who are watching the debate to agree with you. This is a great way to practice the communication skills you'll be using more and more as you grow up.

Everyone in your class can play a part in the debate. First you have to choose a topic. Let's start with something simple. Read the book "The True Story of the Three Little Pigs" by Jon Scieszka. We all know the original story of the three little pigs, but this book gives us a very different version of what happened. Next, select two teams of students to debate this question: "Was the wolf guilty or was he framed?" One team will argue the wolf is guilty. The other will argue he was framed. Both teams need to use some of the techniques from the lesson to convince the audience of their point of view. No yelling or other aggressive behavior is allowed. Students who are not on the teams are the judges. After the debate, the judges talk about which team was most persuasive and why. Then they take a vote. The team with the most votes from the judges is the winning team.

For your next debate, you may want to choose a more serious issue such as school uniforms or an upcoming election in your area. For those topics you'll have to do more research than just reading a fairy tale.

title: An Irresistible Force
text:
We've been talking a lot about influences in this issue of Health Studies Weekly and how important it is to resist those negative forces that try to get us to make the wrong choices. Did you know there's one force that no one on Earth can resist? Luckily, it's not a negative force. Have you guessed what we mean? It's gravity, of course. Here are a couple of activities that will show you the power of this irresistible force!

Materials

a straight-backed chair

Directions

Sit down in the chair and put your back up against the back of the chair. You have to be sitting up perfectly straight.

Fold your arms across your chest.

Stand up - one catch, though. You can't lean forward. Just stand straight up.

What Happens

It is impossible to stand up. When you sit with your arms across your chest, your center of gravity is over the seat of the chair, not over your feet. In order to stand up, you have to lean forward, so that your center of gravity is over your feet. Your center of gravity is the average location of your weight. When most of your weight is over the seat of the chair, you can't stand up. Leaning forward puts most of your weight over your feet.

Now try this one:

Materials

a glass of water

a bendable straw

a straight-backed chair

Directions

Place the glass of water (without the straw) on the floor near one side of the chair.

Lie face down across the seat of the chair, so that your head is hanging over on the side where the water is. Hold the straw in your hand.

Pick up the glass and try to take a drink without using the straw.

Now try using the straw to take a drink.

What Happens

When you are standing or sitting, gravity helps you eat and drink. It helps pull the food downward toward your stomach. When you are lying across the chair, gravity is working against you. It helps to use the straw, because you are putting pressure on the water, sucking it into your mouth. Once the water is in your mouth, your muscles help you swallow it.

title: Math Connection
text:
Anna decides to plant a vegetable garden in her backyard. She will plant 12 rectangular sections. Anna decides 1/3 of the garden will be tomatoes. She decides to plant half as many cucumbers as tomatoes, and she will plant onions in the rest of the garden. (Anna really likes onions.) Use the information above to figure out what fraction of the garden will be cucumbers and what fraction of the garden will be onions. It might help to draw a picture of Anna’s garden on a separate piece of paper. Write your answers below:

Cucumbers ____________ Onions _____________

title: Exercise Your Way to Good Health
text:
How much do you exercise everyday? Do you ride your bike to school? Do you play soccer with your friends in the evening? Do you take your dog for a walk now and then? Regular exercise doesn't have to mean jogging three miles a day or working out at the local gym. You can get the daily exercise your body needs simply by playing with your friends. What if you're alone? Turn on some music and dance. See how long you can keep a balloon in the air without letting it touch the floor. Practice hopscotch. See how many jumping jacks you can do or how long you can hop on one foot. All of these fun games are exercise, and all of them help your body in a variety of ways.

There are two basic types of exercise - aerobic exercise and anaerobic exercise. Aerobic exercise increases your heart rate and usually lasts for 20 minutes or more. Activities such as cycling, swimming or running are good aerobic exercises. As your heart rate increases and you breathe harder and faster, your muscles get the oxygen they need to continue working. Aerobic exercise can reduce stress and perk you up when you feel tired in the middle of the day. Because it gets your blood moving faster, you feel more energetic.

Anaerobic exercise works your muscles really hard for a short period of time. Examples of anaerobic exercise would be doing chin-ups or carrying something heavy. These types of exercises build strong muscles.

Both types of exercise are important to your body. However, before doing any type of exercise it's important to warm up and stretch your muscles. A warm-up should include a slow version of the main activity you plan to do (such as jogging or swimming). The warm-up helps prepare your heart for the more difficult exercise that is coming. Without it you are more likely to suffer muscle and joint injuries.

After exercising, you'll need to cool down. A cool-down allows your heart rate to return to normal. Finish your main activity at a slower pace and then stretch your muscles again just as you did during your warm-up.

Now it's time to exercise your brain by reading the rest of Health Studies Weekly. Warm up with the "Current Event" article, then move to the articles inside.

title: Kicking the Smoking Habit
text:
Everyone knows someone who smokes and has tried to quit. But quitting is really hard. It's also hard for the people who care about them, because you wish you could help them. Everyone knows it's unhealthy to smoke. So, why is it so hard for people to kick the habit?

Smokers become addicted to nicotine. When smokers try to stop, they become depressed and have headaches or other symptoms. Believe it or not, there are things that you can do to help them give up cigarettes.

First of all, understand that it is hard for people to quit smoking. Many people quit and start smoking again several times before they quit for good. Don't make them feel bad when their plans to quit don't work. Tell them that you know they can do it if they just keep trying. Reward that person for trying to quit. Make a card telling them how proud you are of them.

Smokers often crave cigarettes right after eating. You can help take someone's mind off cigarettes. Volunteer to take a walk or play a game of cards with someone who's trying to quit.

Most importantly, continue to support your loved one no matter how many times he or she may start smoking again. One of these days, with your support, your mom or grandpa or brother or aunt may give up smoking forever. Won't that be great?

title: The Benefits of Exercise
text:
How exactly does exercise benefit your body? Different exercises provide different benefits to the systems that keep our bodies going strong. In addition to giving you more energy and making you feel good, exercise helps your body function better. Here are some ways exercise helps keep us strong and healthy.

Immune System

This is the system that defends your body against infections. Exercise helps your immune system protect your body. According to some studies, regular exercise has been shown to increase the number of cells that fight bacteria in your body. So the more you exercise, the less likely you are to become ill. However, it's important to remember that if you're already sick, exercise may do you more harm than good. Your body needs to rest to fight the infection, and exercising during an illness can sometimes cause you to be sick longer.

Respiratory System

Your respiratory system includes all the parts of your body that help you get oxygen - your lungs, blood vessels, trachea (windpipe) and more. When you breathe in, your diaphragm (a sheet of muscle below your lungs) moves down toward your stomach. Your ribcage expands. When you breathe out, your diaphragm relaxes and moves up. Your ribcage gets smaller again. About 75 percent of the work of breathing is done by your diaphragm, and the rest is done by your ribs. Aerobic exercise makes your diaphragm and the muscles around your ribs stronger. And that helps you breathe better.

Circulatory System

The circulatory system consists mainly of your heart, veins and arteries. When you take air into your lungs, it goes to air sacs where your blood absorbs the oxygen. The blood then carries oxygen to all the cells of your body. When you exercise regularly, the air sacs in your lungs stay open all the time. That way, your lungs take in extra air every time you breathe. Your organs (such as your heart and brain) receive more oxygen and work better.

The circulatory system is sometimes called the cardiovascular system. (Cardio is a prefix that means having to do with the heart.) Your heart is a muscle that pumps blood to all the cells in your body every second of your life. When you exercise, your heart beats harder and faster. Because it's a muscle, exercising makes the heart stronger. Every time your heart beats, it is pumping blood throughout your body. A strong heart pumps more blood with each beat than a weak heart. Because your body is receiving more oxygen and nutrients from this strong heart, your entire body works better.

title: The Human Life Cycle
text:
You probably learned about the life cycle of a butterfly. People have a life cycle, too. It's much slower and not nearly as extreme as a butterfly's, but it's real and it's happening to you right now.

Before you were born, you were in the first stage of the human life cycle, which is the prenatal stage. Infancy is the second stage. During this time you depend completely on others to take care of you. Next comes childhood, which lasts for about 10 years. Most fifth graders are in the adolescence stage. This takes place from about age 12 to age 18. This is an extremely important stage of life because you are changing physically, emotionally and intellectually. Adolescence can be a confusing and difficult time for many teenagers. You're caught between being a child and being an adult. Your body is changing and growing, and your emotions may seem to be going a little crazy as well.

Everyone grows and changes at a different rate. If you have classmates who aren't as tall or as grown-up looking as you are, it's important to remember that we're all different. Be considerate of others' feelings and don't make fun of anyone who is growing more quickly or more slowly than you are.

Around age 18, you enter the adulthood stage. You'll spend most of your life in this stage. Old age is the final stage, and you'll enter that as you near the end of your life.

Sometimes knowing what is happening to your body helps you to understand everything better. For more information, check out https://kidshealth.org/teen/ and learn about how other kids are dealing with the changes that are happening.

title: Avoiding Illness
text:
How can you keep from getting sick? Everyone gets sick at one time or another, but there are actions you can take that will reduce your chances of contracting certain illnesses.

First and foremost, cleanliness is the most important way to stay healthy. Bathe or shower daily and always wash your hands after using the restroom. If you keep your hands clean, germs will be less likely to travel from your hands to your eyes, nose or mouth where they can enter your body and make you sick. If you're unable to wash your hands for some reason, try to keep your hands away from your face so you'll be less likely to transfer any germs into your body.

Vaccinations are shots that include weakened or dead microbes (microscopic organisms) that cause the disease that you want to prevent. By injecting these microbes into your system, your body is able to build up immunity (resistance) to the disease. Most children receive vaccinations when they are young for such diseases as measles, mumps, polio and rubella (also known as German measles). Some vaccines aren't given until children reach the age of 11 or 12. Others, such as tetanus shots, require booster shots every few years to continue to work. It's important to make sure your vaccinations are all up-to-date.

Exercising, eating nutritious foods and keeping a positive attitude are also ways to keep your body healthy and to keep the risk of illness at bay. Even laughing is good for your body according to some research. It results in better breathing, more immune cells and an increase in endorphins (a natural painkiller). So, take time to wash your hands, get your vaccinations and laugh at a joke. You'll be feeling better in no time!

title: Water, Water Everywhere
text:
Water. H2O. Two parts hydrogen and one part oxygen. Next to air, water is the item we need most to survive. The human brain is made up of 95 percent water. Our blood is about 82 percent water. Water is important to all living things on Earth, including plants and animals. Here's a fun experiment to help you understand how difficult it can be for plants and animals to survive in the desert.

Materials

sponges

water

a balance scale

some basic information about desert plants and animals (Visit desertusa.com)

Directions

1. Saturate (fill with liquid) your sponge with water. The sponge will represent a desert animal, such as a coyote, that has limited water available.

2. You must help your "animal" conserve that water. For the next 24 hours, take care of your "animal" in a way that will allow it to keep as much water as possible in its system. Your "animal" must be in the open for at least four hours during that time to "feed." You can only use natural items to help you - no plastic wrap or aluminum foil.

3. Weigh your "animal" at the beginning of the experiment. After 24 hours, weigh it again to see how much water it lost.

4. Keep a control sponge you saturated with water out in the open for the entire 24 hours to use for comparison.

How much water were you able to conserve compared to the control sponge? What are some ways you conserved water? Did you store your "animal" in a cool, shady spot? Did you allow your "animal" plenty of "rest" so as not to waste water?

title: Brain Food
text:
Many people consider the brain to be one of the most interesting organs in the body. Recently researchers have noticed a close relationship between the workings of the brain and our diet. Believe it or not, what and how we eat really does affect our brains.

Protein (which is found in foods like meat, nuts and beans) helps you stay alert and allows you to remember things better. Eat some protein before heading to school in the morning.
