Complex carbohydrates (such as vegetables, fruits and whole-grain breads) give you a sense of relaxation. If you’re feeling nervous and need to relax, have a roll and some veggies.

Fats (which are found in dairy, meat and oils) are important for the formation of memory and for the overall health of your brain and nerves.

Simple carbohydrates (such as the sugar in those cookies you love so much) give you a quick energy boost. But that boost fades away quickly, and you’re left feeling sluggish.

The brain needs 180 grams of carbohydrates per day. How much is that? A small banana contains about 21 grams. If you have a peanut butter and banana sandwich for lunch, you’re almost halfway there. Don’t skimp on the healthy food - feed your brain!

title: Writing Connection
text: Select a healthy food you already like. You may choose oranges, broccoli, carrots or anything else good for people to eat. Write a story from the point of view of that food. Why should someone choose you as part of their healthy eating plan? Why do some people not want to try you? What vitamins and minerals do you give to the person who chooses you? (You may need to do a little research to find out.) Try to convince the reader to eat the food you chose. After you write and edit the article, draw a picture to go along with it. Share the stories with your friends and see if you were able to convince anyone to try a new food.

title: Health Information
text:
Take a look around your school cafeteria. How healthy are your meals? Do they meet government nutrition standards? Do you have vending machines filled with unhealthy snacks and drinks in them? Is lunch being served at odd hours, such as 10 a.m., when students aren't really hungry, or 2 p.m. when all you hear in class is growling stomachs? The biggest question of all is this: What can you do to make your school a healthy eating environment?

Actually, there are quite a few things students can do to make their schools healthier. The first step is to gather a group of people who are interested in making the same changes you are. The more adults you can get in this group, the better. Perhaps there are teachers and food service workers who agree with your opinions. The only way to find out is to ask, so start talking.

As a group, look at the areas that need improvement in your cafeteria. Do the foods sold represent all of the five major food groups? Do all students have lunch periods long enough to enjoy eating healthy foods with friends? Are these lunch periods as close to the middle of the day as possible? Are new foods served in new ways to meet the taste preferences of a diverse (different) group of students? What changes do you believe can and should be made to meet these needs?

After you have made a list of things to change, develop an action plan. Decide what materials and resources you will need to make those changes. Spread the word - tell others in the community about your plans. Invite them to join the team and help put the plan into action. Still not sure you can make such changes? Read this week's lesson to find out about other schools that made changes and became healthy success stories.

title: Spit Test
text: Your spit may be more important in health diagnoses than you thought. U.S. researchers can now identify all of the 1,166 proteins in human saliva (spit). This means that most of the proteins found in saliva are also found in a patient’s blood and some proteins match proteins that play a role in a variety of diseases. So how does that affect you? Well, when you go to the doctor in the future, you could possibly only have to spit into a cup instead of having blood taken. Can our saliva tell doctors if we have cancer, heart disease or diabetes? Some researchers believe doctors will be able to easily and inexpensively diagnose diseases in this way in the future. It has already been proven that saliva testing can detect oral cancer and HIV infection. However, only 23 people participated in the latest study that suggests saliva could replace blood testing. Before we can definitely say this new kind of testing is in our future, researchers will have to complete many more hours of studies with thousands more participants.

title: Healthy Students Learn More
text:
Feed Your Body

Your school should be a reliable source of information about health. Most schools do a good job in the classroom, but the food they serve doesn't always set a good example for students. What sort of simple changes have schools around the country made to help their students become healthier eaters?

Byfield Elementary School in Bristol, Rhode Island, removed sweetened drinks and ice cream from their menu. They replaced those items with water, 100 percent fruit juice and frozen yogurt. Parents, teachers, students and administrators worked together to make classroom parties healthier. Chips and sweetened drinks are no longer allowed at classroom events. Instead, graham crackers, cheese trays and 100 percent fruit juice are served, and the students love it! Every teacher keeps pretzels and animal crackers in the classroom. But the school isn't stopping there. They have plans to include soup-and-salad lunches and morning milk service in the classrooms. They also plan to introduce "Dairy Dollars," a program in which students can earn coupons redeemable for milk and yogurt.

There are 370 students in the Ennis Montana public schools. The Ennis School Board decided in 2002 to keep their students healthy by removing candy vending machines from the school. Next, the school replaced soda with water and juice in the beverage machines. Instead of a sign on the front of the machine advertising soft drinks, the school used pictures of children being active. Food service workers added a salad bar to the school's lunch menu, and they hope to increase the fresh fruit and vegetable options in the future.

These are just a few of the many, many success stories you can find at fns.usda.gov/tn. Students, parents and teachers all around the country are working hard to make our schools healthier.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture is a part of our government that helps make sure kids get healthy meals at school. They have created a new award to recognize schools that are helping make students healthier. Does your school provide a healthy nutrition environment? Do your school meals meet the government's dietary guidelines? Do students have the opportunity to be physically active during school hours? Do they learn about nutrition? If you answered "yes" to these questions, then your school may qualify for either a Silver or Gold Team Nutrition Award. Visit teamnutrition.usda.gov, and click on "Healthy Schools" to take the challenge. Tell your principal about the Web site, too.

Feed Your Brain

What you eat - and when you eat it - has a direct effect on your performance during the school day. That is all the more reason for schools to get behind groups who want to make the school environment healthier.

For example, did you know that if you eat snacks that contain simple carbohydrates like sugar, the energy you get doesn't last very long? You'll probably find yourself getting tired not long after you eat sugary snacks. Foods that contain complex carbohydrates - such as whole grains and vegetables - give you energy that lasts longer.

Drinking too much caffeine, which is found in colas and other drinks, can make it very difficult to concentrate. That's not good for solving those tough math problems. So, cut out the sodas and stick to water or 100 percent fruit juices, especially during the school day.

Many studies have clearly shown that the nutrition we put in our bodies affects our brains. Some schools that have made healthy changes can boast (to speak proudly) that their students are receiving better scores on tests and there are fewer discipline problems. Could you learn more and better during the school day if you put better foods into your body? There's only one way to find out.

title: Accidents and Emergencies
text:
Think back to the last time you hurt yourself. Did you fall while skateboarding or playing soccer? We all have accidents now and then, but there are some accidents that are more likely to occur during childhood. Sometimes just knowing what they are will help you prevent them from happening.

Two of the most common causes of childhood injuries are fires and handguns. What can you do to prevent these from happening to you? OK, you've heard it before, but we'll say it again. Don't play with matches or lighters and don't let anyone around you play with them. A fire can happen instantly, and you don't want to be caught in one. Make sure your family has a fire escape plan. You should have two different ways to get out of the house and you should decide on a place to meet once you are outside. Every year hundreds of children are injured or killed while playing with handguns. Don't ever play with guns. Even if you think a gun is not loaded, don't touch it. If you're wrong and someone gets hurt, you can't take it back.

Try to prepare yourself for any emergency that may happen. First, you need to recognize what is an emergency and what isn't. For example, if you get a small cut that stops bleeding pretty quickly, that's probably not an emergency, right? However, if you knock a candle over and something catches on fire, that is an emergency. Call 911 anytime an emergency occurs. Stay calm and tell them where you are and what happened. They'll send help right away.

Go to the library and check out some books about first aid. Better yet, call your local Red Cross and take a first aid class. Knowing what to do could save someone's life.

title: Flu Shot
text:
Not another shot! Yes, for some of us, flu season means getting a flu shot. Flu is short for influenza, a viral illness that can make some people extremely sick. Flu causes fever, aches, chills and fatigue (feeling tired). The symptoms come on suddenly.

Who should get a flu shot? Getting a flu shot isn't required, like a vaccine. However, people who are more likely to get really ill during flu season should get the shot. Children between the ages of 6 months and 5 years old should get a flu shot. Older children who suffer from HIV, diabetes, asthma, kidney disease or anemia should also get a flu shot. If you suffer from any of these diseases, your body is already at a disadvantage, and fighting off the flu will be extra difficult for you. You should also get a flu shot if you live with someone who shouldn't get the flu. That includes small babies, pregnant women or people who are older than 65.

Because the flu virus changes every year, you'll need to get a new shot each year if you want to avoid the flu. The flu vaccine is grown inside eggs, so if you are allergic to eggs, you should NEVER get a flu shot. This could cause you much more harm than good.

Even if you choose not to get a flu shot, you can make sure you keep the virus away by washing your hands often and keeping the things around you clean. And if you do get the flu, stay home so that you don't spread it to others.

title: Fun With Food Dyes
text:
Today, companies use chemical dyes to make all kinds of things we buy more colorful. But what did people use long ago, before chemical dyes were invented? Plants! Here's an experiment you can perform to create a natural vegetable dye.

You'll need a grater, raw beets, a large bowl, a large saucepan (not aluminum), water, white cotton fabric, a long-handled wooden spoon, rubber kitchen gloves and newspaper.

Beets can stain your hands and clothes, so wear old clothes and gloves. Grate three or four beets and put them in the saucepan with a quart or so of water. With an adult's help, boil the liquid and let it simmer for half an hour. Add more water as the mixture boils, so that the water level stays the same. After half an hour, turn off the heat and carefully put the cotton fabric in the hot liquid. Every few minutes, use the long-handled wooden spoon to move the fabric around. Make sure it is completely wet everywhere.

Once the dye has cooled (about an hour later), put on the gloves and carefully take out the cloth. Rinse the cloth in a bowl of warm water and hang it up to dry with newspaper underneath it to catch drips. The next morning, you'll have a piece of pink fabric instead of white cotton.

Did all of your material change color? Dyes from beets will only stain natural fabrics like wool and cotton. If there are any man-made fibers in the cloth, that part will stay white.

What other plants do you think would work? Do some research and try again. What about coffee, tea or grated carrots? What if you decide to remove the color? Try soaking the cloth in vinegar, lemon juice or baking soda. How well did it work?

title: Stacking Up
text:
Sport stacking is quickly becoming the hottest new P.E. activity in the country.

The sport has become so popular the 2006 World Stacking Championship was shown on ESPN.

What exactly is sport stacking? First of all, it's fun. Just stack and un-stack - stackers say, "up-stack" and "down-stack" - the plastic cups in a particular way as quickly as possible. Sounds simple, right? But it takes a lot of practice to get really fast.

Why is sport stacking part of so many P.E. programs? This sport helps improve your hand-eye coordination and speed. Stacking uses both sides of your body and your brain, and that improves your concentration.

Once you get started, you may find it hard to stop.

You can compete against others or against yourself, trying to beat your own best time. The more you practice, the faster you get.

Want to know more? Visit: speedstacks.com. Then talk to your P.E. teacher about adding sport stacking to the P.E. program at your school.

title: Writing Connection
text: How healthy is your environment? Is there smog floating over your city? Is your drinking water safe? What about the rivers or streams nearby? Are they clean? No matter where you live, there are environmental concerns that can and will affect your health. Go to scorecard.org. Type in your zip code, and you’ll see what — and who — is polluting your county. Learn what hazards (dangers) are in your drinking water and air and make a list of the biggest polluters in your area. Write a letter to those companies or individuals asking them how they plan to make the local environment healthier.

title: Making Healthy Choices
text:
"Do I look fat in this outfit?" How many of you have said that or heard someone else say it? In most schools today, there are two kinds of problems involving weight. One is more students are obsessed about gaining weight, when they don't need to be. These people worry all the time about what they eat. Many harm their bodies by dieting and exercising way more than they should. The other problem is more students are obese (overweight by more than 20 percent). Many of them choose not to exercise, and they eat lots of unhealthy foods. Obesity causes many health problems, ranging from diabetes to heart disease.

Both kinds of people harm their bodies by not taking care of them. Do you see how we need to find a happy medium between these two issues? You are in control of your body, and you are the one who will choose how healthy you can become. This week we'll look at the choices you have and how to decide what is best for you.

Sometimes it's as simple as choosing the healthiest option when you have two or more choices. For example, instead of sugary cereals, try eating whole grain versions that have more fiber. Choose a whole-wheat bagel rather than a doughnut. Then, instead of slathering the bagel with regular cream cheese, use just one tablespoon of reduced-fat cream cheese. For snacks, choose low-fat yogurt instead of a cookie, or pick real fruit instead of a fruit roll-up. Replace the meat in your lasagna with spinach or roasted veggies. Choose a baked potato topped with fat-free ranch dressing in place of fries. Ask for broiled chicken, not fried. Cutting back on fast food can save you a lot of needless calories. Make one or two more nutritious choices each day, and you'll be on your way to being a healthier person.

Today, write down one change you plan to make to improve your eating habits. Perhaps you just want to drink water or milk instead of soda each day. Start with a small change and before long you might just see big results.

title: Put Down That Salt Shaker!
text:
Yum! Yum! Who doesn't love to shake salt onto popcorn, corn on the cob and mashed potatoes? And don't those salty pretzels and potato chips taste delicious? There's no doubt about it. We love our salt, and we need some salt to stay healthy. But too much salt can cause high blood pressure, and that can be very bad for your heart.

"I don't add much salt to my food," you may say. That may be true. However, have you looked at the back of the boxes and cans of the foods you eat? There's an awful lot of salt in foods like soup, lunchmeat, snacks and crackers. More than three-fourths of the salt we eat comes from processed (already cooked) foods.

How much salt do you need? The U.S. government recommends that you eat no more than 2,400 milligrams of sodium each day. That's about a teaspoon of salt. If you have one cup of chicken noodle soup and some peanut butter crackers for lunch, you are eating more than half of the salt you need in just that one meal.

One great way to eat less salt is to eat more fresh fruits and veggies. They're naturally low in sodium. OK, so you don't think veggies taste as good as chips. Try to learn to like more veggies. Your heart will thank you for it.

title: Making Healthy Choices: Nutrition and Weight
text:
Calories

What are calories, anyway? We all know that if we want to lose weight we have to eat fewer calories, and if we want to gain weight we have to eat more calories. So, what is a calorie? A calorie is basically a measure of energy. Without energy we can't move or do anything, so calories aren't bad. We need them to live. Some people try to lose weight by cutting out all of a certain food group like carbohydrates or fat. Your body needs a balance of all the food groups - even some fats - to work properly. Controlling your weight depends on a good balance of the calories we take in and the calories we burn while exercising and doing our daily activities. If we eat more calories than we are burning, then we'll put on weight. If we eat fewer calories than we burn, we lose weight. It's really as simple as that.

How many calories should we eat each day? It depends on your age and gender, how much you exercise and other health factors. One pound of body fat has about 3,500 calories of potential energy in it. So, if you eat just 500 calories fewer than you burn each day, you will lose about five pounds of body weight in 35 days. However, it's really not necessary for most fifth-graders to count calories. Making some of the healthy choices we talked about on Page 1 is more important. Don't worry about counting calories unless your doctor has told you to.

Eating Disorders

Some people become obsessed about weight and feel as if they're overweight even when they are not. If you find yourself feeling this way, you should talk to a trusted adult about your concerns, because those feelings could lead to serious illnesses. Anorexia Nervosa is an eating disorder that causes people to believe they are overweight and to almost stop eating altogether. They often feel anxious or depressed. No matter how thin they become, they still feel overweight. Bulimia Nervosa causes people to binge and purge. That means that they'll eat a large amount of food and then vomit afterwards. The food is not in their bodies long enough to absorb any of the nutrients. If a person's weight is too low, his or her internal organs become damaged and often fail. Admitting there is a problem is the first step to recovery. There are many doctors and hospitals that specialize in helping children and adults recover from eating disorders.

Body Mass Index

On the other end of the spectrum, we have children who are overweight. This can cause damage to your body as well. Right now it is estimated that around 15 percent of children in the United States are overweight. What does it mean to be overweight? Doctors today use something called the Body Mass Index (BMI) to decide whether a person is overweight or obese. You can go to kidshealth.org/kid/exercise/weight/bmi.html to find out what your body mass index is. Enter your birth date and your weight, and the computer will calculate your BMI. Then, look on the chart to see if you are underweight, healthy or overweight. Keep in mind, however, you really need to talk with your doctor for more specific information about your own weight and health.

The Perfect Body

No matter what advertisers want us to believe, there is no perfect body weight. Experts agree that there is a range of healthy weights for each person based on age and height. In other words, everyone is built differently, so not everyone can (or should) weigh the same. If you are worried about your weight, always check with your doctor before you try to lose or gain any pounds.

The bottom line is we need to eat healthy foods and get some exercise everyday. Don't obsess over weight, but don't make a meal out of potato chips, either. Find your happy medium. And if you need help, ask your parent, doctor, teacher or school nurse for help. That's what they're there for!

title: Saving the Planet
text:
We need to stop pollution! You've probably been hearing that your whole life. What is pollution, anyway? Pollution is when a chemical interferes with the health of the environment. Pollution can occur in many ways. Imagine an oil tanker is traveling across the ocean. It hits some rocks near the coast and the tank gets a hole in it. What do you think happens to the oil? It goes into the ocean. That is water pollution. The oil can kill wildlife and harm the natural habitat.

Factories cause air pollution when they burn coal or oil. Even you can cause pollution. Have you ever poured motor oil or paint thinner on the ground or thrown cans of paint in the trash? Those items contain dangerous chemicals. When you don't dispose of things like that properly, the chemicals seep into the ground and pollute our drinking water.

Not only does pollution cause us to waste natural resources, but it's also bad for our health. Pollution has been linked to asthma, cancer, birth defects, bronchitis and other diseases.

So, is it hopeless? No way! There are a lot of things you can do. You can purchase environmentally safe products. That means, try to buy items that aren't packed in Styrofoam or plastic. Talk to your parents about buying the "green" cleaners instead of the ones with strong chemicals that hurt the earth. According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, each of us uses enough paper each year to equal a 100-foot tree. Wow! Imagine if we all recycled that paper. We could save a lot of trees! You really can make a difference through reducing, reusing and recycling.

Help teach others, including your family, how they can help as well. If we all work together, we really can save the world.

title: Setting Realistic Goals
text:
So you've made the choice to get healthier. Good for you! Now what do you do? One of the most important things to do is to set realistic goals for yourself. Realistic goals are goals that are actually possible. If you've never lifted weights before, then you're not likely to be able to lift 75 pounds 15 times when you first start.

Take a few minutes to write down some realistic goals. Start with fitness and decide when you will find time to exercise for at least 30 minutes each day. Write down several times when this would work for you. Maybe you could get up 30 minutes earlier or do your exercise as soon as you get home from school.

Next, list some steps to help you meet that goal. Perhaps you want to choose something different to do each day (soccer, biking, walking, etc.) to keep yourself interested. Plan what you'll do each day. Monitor your progress by making a chart and hanging it in a convenient place. Every time you exercise, mark the day and the length of time on your chart.

The last, and very important, step is to evaluate your progress. Perhaps you're noticing that you're not getting much exercise on the days when you have piano lessons. Make a change so that you can still do both. Maybe you could skip an after-school TV show or ride your bike to school on those days. After you've completed setting your goals for fitness, you can use this same system to set goals for any number of things - better nutrition, better grades, anything you want. It's all up for grabs. Just set your goal and keep working at it.

title: Digestion
text:
What happens to your food after you eat it? We know that the body digests the food, or breaks it down, but what does "breaking down the food" mean? Here's an experiment that will help you better understand what happens to food while it's traveling through your body.

Materials

a tomato

cloth about 8-10 inches square

2 large bowls of warm water

laundry detergent that contains enzymes. Enzymes are proteins that help break down food in the digestive system. Laundry detergent that contains enzymes helps break down food stains on clothing.

Directions

Squeeze the tomato and let the juice run onto both pieces of cloth. Leave the cloth until the juice has dried.

Add a scoop of laundry detergent to one of the bowls of warm water and put one of the stained cloths into that bowl.

Put the other stained cloth into the other bowl, but don't add any detergent.

Observe what happens to the stained cloth in each bowl.

What happens?

In the bowl with the laundry detergent, you can see the enzymes breaking down the stain. This is what happens to the food in our bodies.

What happens to our food after it's digested? After the enzymes break down the food into a sort of soupy liquid, the material moves to the small intestine where the nutrients are absorbed into the blood. The broken down food we don't need goes on to the large intestine. It takes about 24 hours for food to be completely digested. The food stays in the stomach for about four hours, and then it spends about six hours in the small intestine. For the next 14 hours or so, the food is in the large intestine until it leaves our bodies as waste.

title: Prefixes and Suffixes
text:
Knowing the meaning of prefixes and suffixes of different words can really help you understand what the word means. For example, thermo means heat and meter means a device for measuring, so a thermometer is a device for measuring heat.

Use the beginnings and endings of the words below and try putting them together to make words that make sense. Look up your words in the dictionary. Do they exist or did you create a new word?

Beginnings:

crypto - hidden

hydro - water

tele - far away

hemo - blood

micro - small

chrono - time

cyano - blue

Endings:

kinesis - movement

phobia - fear of

graph - something that writes

gram - something written

mania - craving

maniac - someone who craves

scope - device for viewing

logy - study of

sophy - science of

philia - love of

title: Math Connection
text:
Did you know that human beings breathe about six quarts of air every minute? A quart is a unit of volume equal to four cups, or 32 ounces. There are 4 quarts in a gallon. Let’s check your math skills. Use the information below to help figure out the answers to the questions below:

1 quart = 32 ounces 1 quart = ¼ of a gallon

1) How many ounces are in 6 quarts of air?

2) How many gallons of air does a person breath each minute?

3) Assuming you breathe 6 quarts of air every minute, how many quarts of air will you breathe in (a) two minutes? (b) 10 minutes? (c) one hour?

4) How many quarts of air are being breathed in and out in one minute in your classroom?

title: Who Influences Your Health
text:
Several of the kids in your class have come down with laryngitis, and you're worried that you might get it, too. (Laryngitis is an inflammation of the larynx that makes speaking very painful and often impossible.) You want to find out how to avoid laryngitis. Where can you get the information you need?

If you ask your brother, will he tell you to (a) talk to the family doctor or (b) look it up on the Internet? If your brother is a member of Generation Y (someone 25 or younger), he'll probably suggest looking it up on the Internet. Generation Yers have grown up with the Internet at their fingertips. They feel comfortable going online and sifting through thousands, if not millions of hits about a particular topic.

What would your father tell you? If he was born between 1965 and 1980, he's a member of Generation X. Although he may search the Internet for information, your father would be less likely to take that information at face value. The Internet wasn't around much until he was an adult, so he might be a little skeptical. He may ask his doctor if the information he found is true.

What about your grandmother? She might tell you to call your family doctor. People who grew up in the 40s and 50s are used to getting most of their health information from their doctors. Back then, many doctors even made house calls. That means they would visit you at home when you were sick. Imagine that! No waiting in crowded waiting rooms or sitting in doctors' offices for hours. People your grandmother's age put a lot of faith in those who treated and cared for them and would probably be less likely to believe anyone except their own doctor.

Age is one factor that influences what people believe about health. People are also influenced by their gender (whether you're a man or woman). Women are more likely to see their doctors when they are sick. Men are less likely to admit they have diseases like depression. Culture also influences people's health behavior. In this week's lesson, we're going to learn about some approaches to healthy living from a variety of cultures.

title: Can Your Food Make You Sick
text: "Don't eat some peanut butter products. They could make you sick!" Peanut butter is just one type of food that has been recalled recently because of food poisoning scares. What is food poisoning anyway, and how does it make us sick? Food poisoning happens when people eat food that has been infected with organisms that can make people sick. There are more than 250 different diseases that can cause food poisoning. The most common of these include salmonella, shigella, E. coli and botulism. How do you know if you have eaten food that is "poisoned" with these viruses? You may have a fever, stomach pain, vomiting and diarrhea, among other symptoms. If bacteria grow on food, it can lead to food poisoning. You are most likely to find food poisoning in foods such as meat and dairy products. Although the food supply in the United States is probably the safest in the world, it is still possible to get food poisoning if food isn't kept as sanitary as it should be. Most people recover from food poisoning, especially if they see their doctor when it gets bad. However, babies, young children and the elderly are in more danger when afflicted with food poisoning. These groups of people have much more difficulty recovering from any type of illness.

title: Healthy Living: Alternative Approaches
text:
The alarm goes off and you feel a rocket blast off inside your head as you lift it off the pillow. You heave yourself out of bed feeling tired, listless and foggy. Your nose is stuffed up and your throat is scratchy and sore. Ugh. You have a cold. What can you do to feel better? Your mom or dad will probably give you some over-the-counter medicine (medicine you don't need a prescription for) and maybe a glass of orange juice. But many cultures take a different approach to colds and other illnesses. Here are a few alternative ideas.

Folk Remedies

Folk remedies are the ideas and practices ordinary people have used throughout time. Some of these remedies are hundreds, even thousands, of years old. They have stood the test of time for many people. What folk remedies are popular for curing a cold?

You could start with Echinacea, an herb sold in pill or capsule form in the United States. Or try sipping a hot, fragrant tea. You could make the tea with many plants like elder, mint, thyme, catnip, garlic, onions, mustard or a combination of two or more of them.

If you are a member of an American Indian nation and you practice the beliefs of your ancestors, you might drink some wild ginger root tea or tea made from the leaves of the boneset plant. Folk remedies are catching on in some unlikely places. Some medical schools are studying boneset and other herbs as a method for healing colds and flu.

Ancient Chinese Methods

Maybe folk remedies aren't your cup of tea. Don't worry. There are plenty of choices left. If you're not afraid of needles, then acupuncture may be for you. Acupuncture involves inserting very thin needles into the skin at specific pressure points. Heat and herbs must also be applied in this ancient Chinese remedy. It is important to have a licensed, trained acupuncturist insert the needles in the proper spot and leave them there for five or 10 minutes. The Chinese also believe in massage therapy, herbal medicine and food therapy (eating certain foods to cure various illnesses), as well.

Ayurvedic Medicine

Let's move on to India and learn about Ayurvedic medicine. In this alternative medicine, ailments are cured through the use of herbs and special foods. Treatment involves restoring "balance" to the mind and body. Those who practice this type of medicine believe you can restore balance by eating a specific type of food and by meditating. Meditation involves getting negative thoughts out of your mind and focusing on breathing and relaxing.

Hypnosis

Hypnosis is used by many people for everything from boosting your immune system to quitting smoking. When you are hypnotized, you go into a relaxed, trance-like state that allows your subconscious mind to be influenced by suggestions made by the hypnotist. Can a hypnotist make you jump around and act like a chicken if you don't want to? No way. Even when you are under hypnosis, you are still in control of your actions.

There are dozens of other alternative approaches to healthy living, including aromatherapy, music therapy, reflexology and many more. (Do some research if any of those sound interesting.) Some alternative approaches to healthy living may seem very different to you, and you may be skeptical about whether they really work. It's always interesting to learn about different ideas, even though you may not want to try them for yourself.

title: Don't Believe Everything You See
text:
Can you believe everything you see on television? If something is not true, they wouldn't be allowed to put it on TV or in magazines, right? Wrong. Believe it or not, there are some things in the mass media (television, newspapers, magazines and radio) that are not always accurate (correct).

Take, for example, infomercials. Do you know what those are? OK. It's Saturday morning and you're flipping through the channels looking for the newest episode of "The Suite Life of Zack and Cody." You pause for a moment on a show that looks like a cooking show. What are they doing? They're showing you how wonderful this amazing new food chopper is. This show is an infomercial. If you look at the word, you'll see part of the word information and part of the word commercial.

Infomercials look like regular TV programs such as talk shows or cooking shows, and they last 30 minutes or longer. But they are really just extra-long commercials. They are designed to sell you a product and that is it. There are hundreds and hundreds of infomercials for products that include everything from pills that claim to help you lose weight to creams that promise to grow hair on your Grandpa's bald spot. Although these programs look like well-researched news shows, it's important to understand that, just like a 30-second commercial, the object behind this 30-minute program is to get you to spend your money on their product. Before spending your money on anything you see on TV, do your research. Check with an organization like Consumer Reports to see if their product really does what it claims to do.

title: Do the Right Thing
text:
Have you ever had a conversation something like this one?

"Come on. Let's go play basketball."

"Nah. I have to do my homework."

"Forget your homework. Just tell the teacher you lost it or something."

Do you know the right thing to do? Of course you do. By the time you're 10 or 11 years old, you know you should finish your homework before you go outside to play. You know lying is wrong. Will you do what is right? That depends on how strong you are, how comfortable you are with yourself and how willing you are to build your character into something you can be proud of.

An American writer named H. Jackson Brown once said, "Our character is what we do when we think no one is looking." And it's true. Chances are pretty good no one is looking at you and your friend talking about playing basketball. No one will know if you lie about your homework or not. What do you do? What you decide will help shape your character - the distinctive qualities that make you special.

You will always have positive and negative influences in your life. Those influences are everywhere you go. It's up to you to know the difference between the influences you should listen to and those you should ignore. Even if no one is looking.

title: Take a Poll
text:
What is a poll? No, not pole, like the kind that holds up telephone wires. A poll is a survey of people's opinions. You hear a lot about polls in election years. Pollsters (people who ask the questions) ask people who they will vote for or what they think about a certain issue. They often share the results by using graphs or charts. For example, if Mikey and Jessica are both running for class president, you could take a poll. First, you'd ask as many people as possible who they would vote for if they had to vote today. Then, you could create a graph that showed the results of your poll. Although polls can be very informative, they don't guarantee that a certain person will win, especially if the percentages were fairly equal. Maybe 50 percent said they'd vote for Jessica, 49 percent said they'd vote for Mikey, and 1 percent had not yet decided. That would make it a very close race. Also, some people may change their minds before they actually vote and that could change the final outcome.

Let's take a poll to find out which places people trust most to get health information.

Directions

1. Create a sheet on which you will keep your notes. Fold a sheet of paper so that you have five columns. At the top of the columns write "Name," "Doctor," "Internet," "Friends/Family" and "Television."

2. Ask 25 people of different ages and gender where they think they can get the most accurate health information. Give them these choices: (1) a doctor; (2) the Internet; (3) their friends or family; (4) television. Be sure you ask some students, some adults, some males and some females the same question and make a tally mark in the correct column.

3. After you tally all the responses, create a chart or graph that shows what you learned. Pie charts or bar graphs work well.

4. Because you asked 25 people, it will also be easy to convert your figures into a percentage. Since 25 times four is 100, you can multiply your answers by four to find the percentage. For example, if 17 people said they trusted doctors most, then multiply 17 x 4, which equals 68. So, 68 percent of the people you polled would choose a doctor.

5. Create an eye-catching poster that includes your graph or chart. It should also show how many males and females you asked and their approximate ages. (You might want to divide them into age ranges something like this: ages 8-15; ages 16-25; ages 26-50; ages 50 and older. Tell how many people in each age range you polled.)

6. Present your poster to your class. Compare and contrast your results with the results your classmates got.

title: Healthy Menus
text:
Create an entire menu for three days (breakfast, lunch, after-school snack and dinner) based on healthy foods available at the grocery store. You may want to ask a parent to take you to the grocery store. Walk through the aisles and make a list of foods you think would make healthy meals. (The assignment is to write a menu, so you don't have to actually buy the food.) Be sure you look at the nutrition label on the back of the box. How much is a serving? How many calories are in each serving?

A healthy menu needs to include the recommended amounts of calories and nutrients for someone your age. You may need to do a little research by checking out the food guide called "My Plate" (www.choosemyplate.gov). It's all about balance. You don't want to eat too few calories, or you'll get hungry before it's time for the next meal. However, you don't want to overeat either. You need fruits and vegetables, but you don't have to pick kumquats and rutabagas unless you like them.

You don't have to plan to cook all the meals from scratch, either. Take a look at the frozen foods section. Want pepperoni pizza or chicken nuggets for dinner one night? That's fine, but find out which brand is lowest in fat and put that one on your list. After creating your three-day menu, write a brief summary explaining why you chose certain brands over others and why you think this is a healthy menu.

Do the meals you've planned sound good to you? Maybe you should go ahead and follow it for a few days!

title: Writing Connection
text: Use the brochure template in your favorite word processing program to create a brochure about places where students in your area can safely find health information. (If you don’t have access to a computer, you can turn a sheet of paper sideways and fold it into thirds to make the brochure.) Start by giving your brochure a title. Include addresses and phone numbers of local hospitals, health care centers, doctors and even your school nurse. Locate and research some reliable Web sites and list them in the brochure, as well. Remember to include graphics to make your brochure more interesting.

title: Watch What You Don't Say
text:
Picture this: You're sitting in social studies class, thinking about anything but the Revolutionary War, and your friend is trying to talk to you from across the classroom to tell you she thinks all this Revolutionary War stuff is crazy. How does she do this without using words? You'll probably see her make the "crazy" symbol by twirling her finger in circles by the side of her head. You laugh quietly so your teacher doesn't catch you. How did you understand what your friend meant? Most kids learn that sign when they're young. By fifth grade, pretty much everyone knows that sign, don't they?

What if you lived in Argentina? Would your friend's sign mean the same thing? Actually, that same movement in Argentina means you have a telephone call.

Signs that mean one thing to us can mean something completely different in another country. For example, how do you tell your friend that her hair looks good without talking? You could make the OK sign by making a circle out of your thumb and forefinger. Guess what? In France that means zero and in Japan that is the sign for money.

What about thumbs up? That always means good job, right? Nope. In Germany and Japan that signal means one. If you want only one order of fries in Germany, give the thumbs up sign.

OK. But everyone knows that a nod means yes and a shake of your head means no. Isn't that true all over the world? Actually, in a few places those signs mean the opposite! If you wanted to tell someone in Bulgaria that you want to try the Shopska Salad (a favorite in Bulgaria) then shake your head to say, "Yes, please."

Nonverbal communication (communicating without using words) can mean different things in different places. So, don't just be careful what you say, be careful what you don't say. Otherwise your friends may not know whether you're trying to tell them they have a telephone call, or you think they're crazy.

title: Sibling Rivalry
text:
A sibling is a brother or sister. How do you feel about your siblings? If you're like most kids, some days you love them and other days you may wish you were an only child. Brothers and sisters can sometimes be bossy, demanding, whiny and annoying.

Rivalry is competition. You may compete with your brothers and sisters to see who gets better grades in school, who plays soccer better, or who gets the last slice of pizza. Sometimes you may feel as if you're competing with them for your parents' time and attention. Sibling rivalry can get complicated, and sometimes things don't seem fair.

When it comes to siblings, you may feel proud, jealous, angry and irritated all at once. That's a lot of confusing feelings to sort out! Although you will probably admit that you love your siblings, there are times when you may need a break from them. That's OK. Everyone needs some alone time. Try talking with your parents and letting them know that you need some quiet time now and then without your siblings.

Hang in there when things aren't going too well with your siblings. Believe it or not, in 10 years or so you may find that your brother or sister is your best friend.

title: Nonverbal Communication
text:
Every day we communicate without saying a word, and sometimes we don't even know it. That's nonverbal communication - communicating without using words. Instead of words, your body language - gestures, facial expressions, body movements and posture - does the talking for you.

When you roll your eyes at someone, what are you saying? That depends on the context - the other things that are happening at that time.

If your teacher tells you to put your feet under your desk and you roll your eyes, the context says you are not taking your teacher seriously.

However, if your teacher says you are a wonderful student and you roll your eyes, you might be saying you are a little embarrassed by the compliment.

Rolling your eyes is body language that says a lot without using any words.

Can you think of any other times when people communicate without words? What makes that kind of communication so confusing?

Remember the story on Page 1? Different people interpret (to explain or understand) nonverbal communication differently.

Did you know the way you sit or stand can say a lot to the people around you?

If you sit with your arms crossed and legs crossed in your classroom, what are you telling others?

Sitting that way may be seen as aggressive behavior. You are telling other students to stay away - that you don't want anyone close to you. Your teacher may think you are not interested in what he or she is teaching.

The wrong kind of body language can put you in danger. Think about the way you walk down the sidewalk on your way to the bus stop or to a friend's house.

Do you look at the ground as you walk? If so, you may be telling others around you that you are not self-confident, and it might make some people think it would be easy to try to hurt you.

Do you avoid looking people in the eye? That could tell those around you that you are too shy to yell or fight back if someone tried to hurt you.

The right kind of body language can help keep you safe. When you walk, look ahead and notice the people and places around you. Walk with confidence, so someone interested in harming you will decide not to waste their time.

If you walk with confidence, you will be less likely to become a victim. Criminals will choose someone who looks like an easy target, not someone who looks confident.

So the next time you're simply sitting in your seat or walking down the street (Hey, that rhymes!), realize others are making decisions about you simply based on what your body language, or nonverbal communication, is telling them.

Be aware your body can speak for you when your mouth isn't even open. And be careful what it is telling others about you.

title: How to Say No to Drugs
text:
Everyone tells you drugs are bad for you and you should say "no" when someone offers them to you. You know they're right about saying "no" to cigarettes, beer and illegal drugs.

But how do you say "no" when you are afraid others are going to make fun of you?

First, make sure the other person knows you really mean NO. Don't sound unsure about it - make it clear. Simply say, "No way!" Humor is another option that works. You could say, "Sorry. I'm on a drug-free diet." Maybe you would feel more comfortable if you say why you aren't interested. Tell them, "My coach says smoking will really hurt my game."

Or, you can find the solution that works best with your personality. Think about how you feel most comfortable saying no and practice it at home and in your head. Then, when the time comes (and it probably will), you'll know what to say, and you'll be ready to say it.

Whatever you do, stand firm. You are in charge of your body, and you don't want to make bad choices just because someone else tells you to.

title: Rules for Resolving Conflicts
text:
1. Attack the problem, not the person.

2. Listen with an open mind.

3. No hitting, teasing or name-calling allowed.

4. Focus on the problem, not on the person.

5. Treat the other person's feelings with respect.

6. Take responsibility for your actions.

Cut out these rules and paste them on an index card (or just copy them on the card). Keep the card in your desk to help you remember what to do when you have a conflict with another person.

title: Say What You Mean - Kindly
text:
Expressing yourself, whether verbally or nonverbally, can be difficult for both adults and children. It's important to learn how to express your feelings to others in a way that won't hurt their feelings.

For example, let's say a friend tells you that he knows for a fact that Jell-O is made of ground-up bones. Your initial reaction may be to say, "That's so dumb and so are you." However, this will immediately put your friend on the defensive. So, say something that isn't so "in-your-face." A good response would be, "Well, I've heard that story before, and I checked it out on the Internet. I really don't think it's accurate." Or a simple, "I see it differently" would do.

If someone tries to gossip about a friend, respond with this kind but clear remark: "I'm uncomfortable talking about Brandon when he's not here." That puts an end to the situation, tells people how you feel and doesn't make anyone else feel silly or hurt. Believe it or not, it is possible to express your ideas without hurting other people's feelings.

title: Say It Silently
text:
How easy do you think it would be to go an entire day using only nonverbal communication to convey your thoughts and feelings to others? It may be more difficult than you think. Before you try to make it through an entire day, first try to play a typical board game without saying a word. All you need is a few friends and a Monopoly game.

Gather in groups of four or five around the Monopoly game board. Start by making sure all the players are familiar with the rules. (It's OK to talk for that part of the activity.) Next, try to play a game of Monopoly without speaking at all. An entire game would take too long, of course. Just play for about 15-20 minutes, and you'll see how hard it is for everyone to let the other players know what they need or want. How did you do it? Did you create your own type of sign language to help communicate with each other? Do you think it was harder to understand others, or harder to make others understand you?

title: Peace is a Choice
text:
Two goats meet on a narrow bridge. They have a choice. They can choose peace: One goat can back up and let the other pass. Or they can choose war: They fight until one is knocked off the bridge.

Think of these goats the next time you are dealing with a conflict with someone. Who will choose peace and move aside? Peace is a choice, but you must decide you want it. Then, you must work toward it.

The story of the two goats is a Russian folktale. If you want to read more stories like this one, go to the library and look for "Peace Tales" by Margaret Read MacDonald.

title: Writing Connection
text: Sign language is a way for people who cannot hear or speak to communicate. It’s easy to learn the sign language alphabet. Check it out at funbrain.com/signs/. Level 1 shows you the signs for each letter of the alphabet. After you’ve practiced a while, try level 2. It will quiz you on the signs. (You can also look for a book on sign language in the library.) Once you know all the letters, practice with a friend by signing words to each other. Before long, your classroom might become a very quiet place!

title: Working Together to Save Lives
text:
If you try to push a huge boulder up a hill, you won't get very far, right? What if you have a friend help you push? What if you have several friends help you push? Hey! The boulder is moving. Why? Because you are working together to push the rock. When we work together, we can make an incredible change in the world around us. We can make the world a healthier, happier and safer place.

That's exactly what we do when we band together to help each other. The Red Cross, the American Heart Association, Susan G. Komen for the Cure, the American Cancer Society and the World Health Organization are just a few of the many, many organizations that work together to help us all live fuller, happier and longer lives.

Because these organizations are willing to take on the burden of raising money and educating the public, we are all much better off. Without them, our world would not be as healthy or as safe as it is now.

Many organizations started with just one person. Clara Barton volunteered to serve as a nurse during the Civil War and later founded the American Red Cross. Nancy Brinker promised her dying sister, Susan G. Komen, she would do all she could to end breast cancer forever.

Drop one pebble in the water and watch the ripples spread out in all directions. People like Clara, Nancy and many others are like that pebble. Each of them helped the world become a better place. One person is all it takes. One person to care. One person to try. One person to make a difference.

Inside you'll read about some of the organizations that work together to make all of us healthier. When you're finished reading, ask yourself this question: "What will I do today, tomorrow and in the future to make this world a healthier, happier place?"

title: Living With Diabetes
text:
What does famous pop singer Nick Jonas have in common with more than 18 million Americans? Diabetes. In 2005, Nick Jonas lost 15 pounds in two weeks, drank water constantly and was not acting the way he usually did. After going to the doctor, he was told he had Type 1 diabetes.

About 8 percent of the population (more than 23 million children and adults) have diabetes. So what is diabetes? Well, there are really two types, although both have the same basic problem. The people with this disease have too much sugar (glucose) in their blood. The first, called juvenile diabetes, got its name because children seemed to get it most often. It's now called Type 1 diabetes. This kind of diabetes occurs when the immune system attacks the cells that make insulin. Without insulin, you get diabetes because your body can't process glucose. The other kind is called Type 2 diabetes. With this kind, your body doesn't make enough insulin, or your body can't use it correctly. Type 2 diabetes is usually found in people who are overweight. This type is increasingly occurring in children since so many more children have become obese.

Signs of diabetes include being extremely thirsty, having to go to the bathroom a lot and quickly losing weight. Some people even have blurry vision or are extremely tired.

There is no cure for diabetes, so people who have it must control it by eating right, using medicine and exercising.

title: Organizations Help Protect Our Health
text:
Susan G. Komen for the Cure

Nancy Brinker's sister, Susan G. Komen, was dying of breast cancer. Nancy promised Susan she would work hard to find a cure for this disease. To keep her promise, Nancy founded the Susan G. Komen Foundation. Since 1982, the foundation has raised nearly $1 billion for research and education. Their most popular fundraiser is the Race for the Cure, which takes place in cities all across America every year.

When the organization began, the five-year survival rate for breast cancer patients was only 74 percent. Today, 98 percent of breast cancer patients are still alive after five years. In 1982, only 30 percent of women got mammograms (tests to detect breast cancer). Now 75 percent of women are tested. A lot of the credit for the improvements goes to the foundation now called Susan G. Komen for the Cure. What began as a promise by one woman is now helping millions of women survive.

American Heart Association

As long ago as 1924, a group of doctors was concerned about the lack of information about heart disease. To raise awareness of this dangerous condition, they formed the American Heart Association. By 1949, the association began its first national fundraising campaign and was able to raise more than $2.7 million in donations. That was an incredible amount of money back then. (That's an incredible amount of money even today!)

Over time, the American Heart Association became a voluntary health organization instead of a society of doctors and scientists. People began to learn about the dangers of heart disease. They found that they could extend their lives by taking care of their bodies. Visit their Web site at www.americanheart.org, and you'll find healthy heart information for people of all ages - even children. The site also lists warning signs of heart disease, different kinds of heart diseases and conditions and places to find more information. Thanks to the American Heart Association, people all over our country are taking better care of their hearts and living longer.

World Health Organization (WHO)

In 1948, the United Nations established the World Health Organization to help all people reach the highest possible level of health. The main goal of the WHO is to fight disease and promote better health throughout the world. WHO also shares information, sets global health standards, works with governments to strengthen national health programs and keeps track of contagious diseases. They provide vaccinations against many diseases. In 1980, they announced their vaccinations against smallpox (a contagious and deadly disease) had succeeded in eliminating the disease completely.

The American Cancer Society

The American Cancer Society (ACS) is dedicated to eliminating all types of cancer. That is a big dream, but it's one they believe will come true someday. The organization was formed in 1913. Back then people hardly ever discussed the "c" word - cancer. People were so frightened and confused by this deadly disease, information about it was almost never discussed in public. The only way to beat a disease is to learn about it, and talking about cancer was the first step. In 1947, the American Cancer Society began a public information campaign warning people of some common signs of cancer. These included unusual bleeding, change in a wart or mole, and a sore that didn't heal, among others. Over the years, the ACS has warned people that smoking causes cancer and taught us the importance of annual physical exams in preventing this disease. Although we have come a long way in the treatment of cancer, we still have not found a cure. If you're thinking about being a doctor or scientist someday, your work and research might help find a cure.

title: Clara Barton - Volunteer Nurse
text:
At a time in history when women were not recognized as important members of society, Clara Barton stepped forward and made a difference in the world.

Clara Barton was born in 1821. By the time she was only 11 years old, she was already practicing the art of nursing by helping her brother survive a serious illness. During the Civil War, Clara learned many wounded soldiers died because there weren’t enough medical supplies to care for them. She was sad about so many needless deaths and wanted to make a difference for future soldiers.

Clara began by raising money to purchase medical supplies. Later she traveled with the soldiers and helped make sure they received the medical attention they needed. After the war, she helped many soldiers locate family members. She also helped find soldiers who were listed as missing in action.

In 1881, Clara Barton founded the American Red Cross, which is alive and well today. For more than 125 years, the Red Cross has helped Americans survive floods, hurricanes and other natural disasters.

The Red Cross has been there to help us through the difficult times of war. The people of the Red Cross are also working hard to educate others about health and safety. Would you like to take baby-sitting classes? Call the Red Cross. They can also teach you CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation), a technique that can help get a person’s heart and lungs to start working after they have stopped.

At the Red Cross, you can volunteer to help others, donate blood or give money to help victims of natural disasters. One person started it, others joined her, and now millions of people around the world get help when they need it.

title: Access for Everyone
text:
At one time, people with disabilities didn’t have the same rights as others in this country. Disabled Americans had a harder time finding jobs, getting into buildings with stairs and using public transportation. The Americans with Disabilities Act was passed in 1990. The law says employers cannot discriminate against disabled persons. It also says public buildings have to provide access for people who are in wheelchairs or who cannot walk up and down stairs. Ramps and elevators are now required in all public buildings. Buses and other vehicles for public transportation must have lifts for wheelchairs. Telephone companies must provide special equipment for deaf users to type and send messages.

Thanks to people who rightly believed all Americans - including those with disabilities - deserved equal treatment, we now have a law that guarantees this. One law made a difference for millions of others. What will you do to make the world a better place to live?

title: Start Your Own Organization
text:
Ever heard of Turkeys 4 America? It’s an organization started by kids. Yes, kids - just like you! Every Thanksgiving since 1996, Danny and Betsy Nally have asked people to donate turkeys and money to feed the hungry. Danny and Betsy are the founders of this amazing organization. At first, they went door to door, asking their neighbors, friends, and church members to donate. Now they have a Web site (www.turkeysrus.com) and a toll-free phone number (1-866-2turkey). Since the project began, they have collected enough food to feed more than 320,000 people. Imagine that! A brother and sister with an idea to help others have created an entire organization. Who says you can’t make a difference as a kid?

What would you like to do to help others? Start small - just some food for a family in need or a pair of gloves for someone who is homeless - and your idea could end up taking on a life of its own. It might just grow and grow until it became something as great as Turkeys 4 America or even the American Cancer Society. What could you do? How would you like to help? What will you need to make your idea work? Make some lists. Think of a name for your organization. Who knows? Your small idea may turn out to be a big help!

title: Research
text:
In this Mini-Lab, you'll do some research to learn more about the parts of the human body. Who knows? Your knowledge could help you become the next scientist to discover a cure for a disease!

Imagine you are an organ of the human body. Select which organ you would like to be (kidney, heart, lungs, etc.) and use books and the Internet to do your research. Find out about the things that organ does to keep the body going and the bad habits that can harm it.

Now imagine the person whose body you are part of is doing something that could harm you. Maybe you're the heart, and the person has never exercised a day in her life. Or perhaps you're the lungs and the person started smoking. What if you were the skin and the person never uses sunscreen? In your letter, explain why you are important to the body. List the reasons the person should change his or her behavior. Do your best to convince the person to start doing things differently to keep you healthy.

title: Math Connection
text:
You’ve decided to try to raise money for a local homeless shelter by having a walk-a-thon at your school. Can you figure out how much money you might make using the information given?

1. If you have 100 students walk five miles each, how many miles will they walk in all?

2. If those 100 students received pledges for $1 per mile, how much money would they collect in all?

3. What if 250 students walk five miles each? How far will they walk in all?

4. Of those 250 students, half get pledges of $1 per mile and the other half get pledges of $2 per mile. How much money will they collect altogether? Write your own set of word problems involving a fundraiser and give them to a friend to solve.

title: Kinds of Health
text:
Physical Health

A person in good physical health is free from disease and has greater ability to heal from injury and recover from illness. Some of the key areas to focus on for good physical health are exercise, nutrition and health care.

Exercise

Kids who exercise regularly have stronger muscles and bones. They are less likely to become overweight because exercise helps control body fat. People who exercise tend to have a better outlook on life, too.

When you play a sport, you are likely to use the three elements of fitness: endurance, strength and flexibility. For example, soccer players must have good endurance to run up and down the field for long periods of time. Kicking the ball hard enough to get past the goalie requires leg strength. And the goalie will need to have considerable flexibility to block that shot. Try to work in all these elements in your exercise.

The National Association for Sport and Physical Education (NASPE) recommends one hour a day of moderate to vigorous exercise for school-age children. So, how does a busy person fit in that much exercise?

If you are on a sports team, you get the chance to exercise regularly. Your physical education classes ensure that you have some exercise several times a week. There are other ways to get exercise, too. Try walking over to a friend's house instead of getting a ride. Volunteer to do some outdoor chores (you will get extra points from your parents, too!). You can even exercise while you are watching TV.

Besides enjoying the health benefits of regular exercise, kids who are physically fit sleep better and are better able to handle physical and emotional challenges - from running to catch a bus to studying for a test.

Nutrition

Our bodies need the proper balance of nutrients to perform optimally. Fats, protein and carbohydrates provide the body with energy. Vitamins and minerals make your body work properly. But how much of each does a person need to be healthy?

You've seen the food plate. This graphic organizer puts food into groups and recommends daily amounts to be eaten. Each day we should eat from each of the groups. Grains contain carbohydrates for energy and fiber for good digestion. Fruits and vegetables should be eaten often for the vitamins and minerals as well as for simple carbohydrates and fiber. Dairy products are recommended for calcium and protein. Meats and beans will provide protein for proper growth of cells.

Whatever you choose, try to avoid foods from each group that have a lot of fat and sugar. For example, potatoes are very nutritious, but French fries contain more fat than what is healthy for you. Whole-grain cereals are good for you, but those that are highly sweetened will carry more calories than you need without providing any additional nutrients.

Health Care

Good health care can keep you well and help you get well quickly. Your parents should see to it that you get regular doctor's visits, and you can help support your own health by following doctor's orders. Your doctor probably asks you questions about your lifestyle and makes recommendations for how you can be healthy. Take her advice. Following your doctor's advice about exercise and nutrition are a good idea. Keeping current with immunizations will keep you from getting diseases like measles, mumps and diphtheria.

When you are sick, your doctor might prescribe some medicine, perhaps an antibiotic (a drug that kills bacteria) for an ear infection or strep throat. Be sure you take all of your medicine according to the instructions - even if you are feeling better. Doing so will ensure that you are well and that the infection will not return.

Did you know that good dental health is important to your overall physical health? Brushing your teeth not only cleans your teeth and helps prevent tooth decay, but it helps your gums. The gums and bones supporting the teeth need care. Poor brushing and flossing cause gingivitis, a gum disease. When gingivitis isn't treated, it can lead to periodontitis, a disease which can result in tooth loss.

Emotional Health

People with good emotional (having to do with feelings) health are in control of their thoughts and behaviors. They feel positive about themselves and have good relationships with other people. They can deal with their problems. They care about others and their well-being.

We all get angry every now and then. We may feel sad also. These unpleasant feelings are normal and are not signs of poor emotional health unless they are out of control. When you feel that you are having difficulty with your feelings and that they are getting in the way of doing your best, find someone to talk to. Your mom or dad, a teacher or counselor, or a good friend or older sibling can help you see that your feelings are normal. That understanding can help relieve the stress you may be feeling.

You can also use exercise to deal with troubling feelings. Exercise helps your body produce chemicals called endorphins that make you feel better. Exercise is good for emotional health as well as physical health.

Intellectual Health

Intellectual health is when you regularly increase your knowledge and improve your skills. Beyond school, you can improve your intellectual health by participating in cultural and community activities.

Your local newspaper and your school can inform you of opportunities in your community to improve your intellectual health. Use these resources to find out where you can go to learn another language or to audition for a play or to participate in a service project. Go to the library or use the internet to find out about something new. Try a new kind of puzzle. Turn off the TV, or switch to a program on science or history.

People who are intellectually healthy are open to new ideas, think critically and seek out new challenges. They have a sense of humor and an idea of their place in the world. They are creative and curious and never stop learning. An intellectually healthy person can use what is learned in the classroom to understand better what happens outside the classroom.

As you get older, you will find yourself better able to solve problems, be creative, and learn more complex and difficult ideas and skills. Your interests will change. You will become more curious. You have more intellectual ability than you know.

title: Being Healthy is Important
text:
What does being healthy mean to you? Many of us would agree that being healthy means feeling good each day when we wake up. Others would say that being healthy is simply not being sick. Most, however, agree that health can be described in different ways. The World Health Organization (WHO) gives this definition of health: "Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity." Lately, this statement has been updated to include the ability to lead a "socially and economically productive life."

Being healthy is important. A healthy person is better able to lead a longer, happy, productive life. How can you stay healthy? Observing some simple rules and following certain practices can help increase your chances of staying healthy. Many of us already have daily routines that keep us going strong, but each of us should look for and change habits that may interfere with being as healthy as possible.

It is true that no matter what good habits we develop and practice, sickness and injury are likely to happen at some time or another. Our behavior plays a part in being healthy. For example, if you play a contact sport, your chances of injury are increased. Stress can lead to a greater chance of getting sick. And, of course, pollutants and toxins in your environment (everything around you) can also make you sick. Genetics is also a factor. You are you largely because of the genes you inherited from your parents. Those genes determine to some degree how healthy you will be. Some people have heritable diseases that affect their health. Others simply are born with a weaker immune system that makes it more likely that they will get sick. Despite the influence of the environment and your family history, there are many things each of us can do to stay healthy.

In this issue of Health Studies Weekly you will learn about the different kinds of health and how they are interrelated in the lives of young people. You will also read about infection, how to avoid getting sick and how to protect yourself from injury. The first step in staying healthy is an easy one - just turn the page!

title: Hidden Effects of Triclosan
text:
We have been told to use hand sanitizer to kill germs that can cause illness. These products are inexpensive, easy to use, and claim to kill most of the bacteria they come in contact with. Sounds great, doesn't it?

Triclosan is one of the chemicals used in hand sanitizers. Some cutting boards and even toothbrushes are impregnated with this product to kill bacteria. But, Triclosan may be harmful to the environment.

University of Minnesota chemist Kristopher McNeill conducted a study on Triclosan. McNeill and his team found that when you put Triclosan in natural water and shine sunlight on it, it converts into a dioxin. This pollutant is very toxic. Dioxin can be formed by natural processes such as forest fires and volcanic eruptions, but it is mostly formed by industrial processes such as paper bleaching and manufacturing pesticides.

So, why is Triclosan a concern? Well, McNeill says Triclosan is washed into streams and rivers through treated human waste water. He and his colleagues found that up to 12 percent of this Triclosan gets converted into a form of dioxin. This form isn't dangerous to humans, but it could have negative effects on plants and other animals. Studies have shown disastrous effects on the bullfrog. There are concerns about reduced fertility and hatching rates, birth defects and immune system problems.

This study shows that just because something is beneficial in one form doesn't mean it stays that way. There are other compounds we use that break down into harmful components over time.

"I think this is a good example of a compound doing something maybe a little bit unexpected," says McNeill.

So how should we protect ourselves from germs? Most experts recommend 20 seconds of washing with good old soap and water.

title: Protecting Yourself from Injury is No Accident
text:
The number one killer of kids in this country is accidental injury. Accidents involving automobiles, water and recreational activities, such as bike-riding and sports, cause thousands of deaths per year. You can help protect yourself from these injuries.

When riding in a car, wear a seat belt - even when you are going a short distance. Wearing a seat belt dramatically increases a person's chances of survival in a car accident.

Drowning is the second-leading cause of accidental death of kids in America. Swim only in safe areas where an adult - preferably a life guard - is present. Know your limitations. If you are not a strong swimmer, don't jump into the deep end of the pool.

In 2006, 770 people were killed while riding their bicycles. Of those people who were killed, 95 percent were not wearing helmets. It is a simple fact that wearing a helmet can save your life. Always wear a helmet while playing baseball and football and while riding bikes, skateboards and scooters.

title: Avoiding Infection
text:
Being healthy means practicing good habits to avoid infection. Usually when you are sick, it's because of an infection caused by bacteria, viruses or some other pathogen. There are treatments for most infections, but it is better to just avoid them.

Follow these simple rules:

Avoid raw eggs and undercooked meat. Proper cooking kills bacteria that cause illness.

Wash fruits and vegetables. This cleans off bacteria, viruses and pesticides that could make you sick.

Get your shots. It hurts for a minute, but shots can keep you from getting diseases that can hurt for a long time.

Avoid wild animals. Unlike our pets, wild animals can carry bacteria and diseases like rabies. Let wildlife centers care for injured or abandoned birds and bunnies.

Avoid insect bites. Insect repellent can keep you from getting diseases like Lyme disease and West Nile Virus, serious diseases carried by ticks and mosquitoes.

Relax. Find time to take it easy and enjoy yourself. Lowering stress can make you less likely to get sick.

title: How does the environment affect health?
text:
Exercise and good nutrition are necessary for good health, especially when our environment contains factors that can make us sick. Some studies show that almost 20 percent of our illnesses are related to factors in our environment.

Pollution can lead to health concerns. Air pollution and second-hand smoke from cigarettes can cause asthma attacks. Water pollution can make drinking water unsafe. Noise pollution can lead to greater stress.

Even nature can affect health. Pollen causes allergic people to spend weeks in misery. The sun's rays can cause skin problems, including cancer. Bites from disease-carrying insects have made many people sick.

Is there anything you can do to avoid environmental factors associated with poor health? We will probably not be able to completely eliminate toxins from our environment, but we can take steps to control our risk.

Wear protective clothing and sunscreen outside. Avoid places that allow smoking. Use earphones and listen to soothing music to reduce stress. Talk to your family about buying water and air filters for your home.

title: Alexander Fleming
text:
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish biologist and pharmacologist best known for his discovery of the antibiotic substance penicillin. The discovery earned him the Nobel Prize in 1945.

His most famous work was the result of an accident. Fleming had built a reputation as a scientist and researcher, but he was a bit messy. He had been studying a bacterium called staphylococcus. In 1928, he left on a family vacation, leaving his cultures of the bacteria on a bench in a corner.
