When he returned he found that one culture was contaminated with a fungus, and all the colonies of bacteria around it had died. Fleming identified the mold that contaminated the cultures as a Penicillium fungus.

Fleming recognized the disease-fighting potential of penicillin. His tests showed a positive anti-bacterial effect on the bacteria that cause scarlet fever, pneumonia, meningitis and diphtheria.

Today, if you go to the doctor for strep throat, you may get a prescription for penicillin.

title: Using the Food Guide “My Plate”
text:
Knowing what and how much to eat is very important. It can be a challenge to change your habits to meet the requirements of a healthy diet.

For three days record what you eat at each meal and between meals. Be accurate. If you eat a hot dog, count it as meat, but count the bun as a grain. If you butter your toast, record the bread as a grain and write down the butter as well. Of course, a bowl of cereal contains foods from two groups - milk and grains.

You might have to do a little math. When you look at the package, you can tell that hot dog is about 2 ounces of meat (16 oz. package divided by 8 hot dogs equals 2 oz.).

Compare your findings to this chart that lists serving recommendations for children ages 9-13. How do you match up? What foods should you eat more of? Which foods should be scaled back? Make a list of foods you need to increase and those that you need to decrease.

title: What Do You Know About Health?
text:
"No, thanks. I don't want to get sick."

Charlie had just offered his friend, Thomas, a bite of his ham sandwich.

"Don't worry. I'm not sick," said Charlie.

"Yeah," said Thomas, "but I don't want to get swine flu from that pork!"

Thomas has been influenced by something he heard about swine flu. He might have heard it from a friend or he might have just made a guess because swine is another name for pig. He may not even remember where he heard it. That's too bad, because he is wrong! Swine flu is caused by a virus and not found in cooked pig meat.

How do you know what you know about health? Have you been taught about nutrition and exercise at school? Have you learned from your friends how to stay healthy? Perhaps you have picked up some good (and bad) health habits of family members. Some of what you know about health might have come from TV, radio, the Internet and other media sources.

"Bundle up before you go out. You don't want to catch a cold."

Many of us have been influenced to believe that the common cold is caused by exposure to cold temperatures. It just isn't so! You may have been under that impression, but colds are caused by the rhinovirus. It doesn't matter how cold it is, you won't catch a cold without a virus. You might feel pretty uncomfortable, though!

Mark Twain once said, "It ain't what you don't know that gets you into trouble. It's what you know for sure that just ain't so." The great American author and humorist was not necessarily talking about health, but it may be a good idea to pay attention to his warning. What do we accept as fact that might be untrue or inaccurate? And where did we get that information in the first place?

Twain also said, "Be careful about reading health books. You may die of a misprint." Much information about health is available to you at school, from the media, from your family and friends and on the Internet. Some of that information is confusing, misleading or just plain wrong. Claims may be made that do not have any scientific evidence.

One of the skills a responsible, successful person has is the ability to evaluate the quality of information that he or she learns from different sources. A first step in leading a healthy life is learning how to distinguish between healthy and unhealthy influences. In this issue of Health Studies Weekly, you will learn about some of the factors in our lives that influence our thinking and practices about health.

title: CDC: Keeping an Eye on Influenza
text:
For months we have heard about H1N1, sometimes known as the swine flu. So much information has been out there that it is hard to know what to believe. News of possible epidemics can cause a lot of worry and stress.

One of the jobs our government has is to protect the health of the public. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is the agency charged with that duty. When the outbreak of H1N1 was first recognized in the spring of 2009, the CDC began gathering data from other countries and from individual states. The data were used to conclude that H1N1 was causing more problems for people under the age of 25.

The CDC developed recommendations for people to help them avoid getting sick. Following the directions provided by the CDC should reduce the number of cases of H1N1 and of seasonal flu, a different type of influenza that comes around every year. The CDC offers these suggestions:

Cover your nose and mouth with a tissue when you cough or sneeze. Throw the tissue in the trash after you use it.

Wash your hands often with soap and water. If soap and water are not available, use an alcohol-based hand rub.

Avoid touching your eyes, nose and mouth. Germs spread this way.

Try to avoid close contact with sick people.

title: Health Influences
text:
Your family, friends and teachers care about you very much. You probably know quite a few people who help you to understand and make the right choices for your health. Let's look at some of the influences in your life that can help you on your quest for good health. We'll look at influences that might be confusing or misleading too. An influence is something or someone with the power to affect you.

Family

Moms, dads and other family members are influenced by many of the same health factors as you are. In the last issue of Health Studies Weekly, you read about some factors that can cause illness and injury. Your family may have ways of doing things that help you reduce the possibility of illness and injury. Do your mom and dad, for instance, tell you to eat your vegetables? Do your parents tell you to turn off the TV and go outside? Do they make you wear a helmet when you get on your bike? Maybe you can think of other things that your mom or dad expect of you that might be related to good health.

Ellen is 11 years old. She has learned a lot about health at school and from her parents. She knows some of the basics of good nutrition and exercise. She wonders why her mom does not exercise regularly. She questions her older brother about eating a lot of junk food. She wishes her dad would give up smoking. What should Ellen make of these influences?

It's a tricky question. Humans aren't perfect, and parents are human, too! You want to be healthy, and you want to respect the choices others make. Your parents probably have talked to you about taking care of yourself; however, making the right choices every day is difficult. Many adults make choices even though they are aware of the potential risks and dangers involved. It is important for Ellen and all younger people to realize that parents' behaviors are very influential. However, you need to make health choices that are right for you. Learn all you can so you can make informed choices about your health.

Peers

How do your friends and classmates influence your health? Well, health is partly about choices, and your peers heavily influence your everyday choices. You are at an age when you care a lot about what your friends think, say and do. You are concerned with their opinion of you. This is normal. Sharing activities with friends is a way to fit in and form good relationships. It is important to recognize that your friends - like anyone - may not always choose what is best for their health. Some kids make choices because they want to be liked or to fit in. Peer pressure can make some kids want to go along with the crowd. In some cases they leave their common sense behind so they can be a part of the group.

Do you know one of the main reasons kids smoke their first cigarette? That's right - peer pressure. In fact, if your best friend smokes, you are 13 times more likely to smoke than if you hang around friends who do not smoke. To make matters worse, a person who starts smoking in middle school will have a more difficult time quitting and have more health-related problems than a person who starts smoking as an adult. Choose your friends carefully, and remember that you do not have to make the same choices - especially the bad ones - as your friends.

School

How does your school influence your health? Well, teachers present lessons on nutrition, exercise, body systems and other health topics. Posters in the cafeteria tell about the benefits of eating according to the food plate. Your P.E. teachers ensure that you have exercise several times a week. School is a great place to get honest answers about health. Teachers, counselors and nurses provide useful lessons and may be able to point you in the right direction for more information.

Doctors

Regular check-ups with your doctor are important in maintaining good health and catching problems early on. Your doctor is also a good source of the latest health information available. Most physicians keep up with current health issues and can help you sort out what you learn from your friends and the media.

Public Health Organizations

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is one of the major parts of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). The HHS is the U.S. government's main agency for protecting the health of all Americans. The CDC is responsible for disease prevention and control, environmental health and health promotion and education activities designed to improve the health of the people of the United States. Local health agencies, such as county health departments, often work with the HHS and CDC to provide information and services that are available to you and other people living in your area.

Media

"Don't believe everything you see on TV!" This warning goes for movies, magazine ads and the Internet, as well as any other media. We get countless messages every day about what is "cool" and how to make our lives better. It is important to realize, though, that these messages most often come from people and companies whose goals are to entertain or to sell products.

Tobacco companies once used famous movie stars, Santa Claus and an American president in their ads to sell cigarettes. Some even featured doctors and sent the message that cigarettes were actually healthy! We know today that cigarette smoking causes many health problems, including cancer, heart disease and emphysema. It is important to not be fooled by messages in the media.

title: Peer Influences
text:
Your friends inspire you to do good things, but they can also persuade you to make poor choices. Your parents and teachers have probably told you to be careful about peer pressure. When people your age try to influence how you act, it is called peer pressure. Peer pressure is not necessarily bad. If you try out for a team because your friends encourage you, then it's a good thing. However, sometimes a friend tries to get you to do something you know is not good.

A person sometimes pressures a friend because he or she wants to try something new, but doesn't want to try it alone. Consider Jason and his best friend, Michael. An older brother offered them beers. Michael knows that they shouldn't drink the beers. He is curious, though, and a little nervous. Michael figures that if Jason is with him, everything will be all right. How do you think Jason should deal with the pressure that Michael is putting on him?

title: Media Messages
text:
A commercial shows beautiful people enjoying time together sipping a well-known brand of soft drink. The women are thin and beautiful. The men are tall and muscular. They all have perfect teeth, hair and clothes. The message is implied: buy this soft drink, and you will be happy and good looking.

That's kind of silly, of course, but it is not the only message. Notice there are no normal looking people in the commercial - people you would see at school or the grocery store. You are presented with a distorted, unrealistic picture of what people look like. Most people don't look like that, and it's okay not to - it's even normal!

People are exposed to perhaps hundreds of ads a day depending on how much TV they watch. This bombardment is bound to have an impact on people's perception of what is real and normal. Pay attention to your own views of what is normal and don't let ads give you unrealistic perceptions.

title: How does culture affect health?
text:
America is a multicultural (reflecting many different ethnic or cultural groups) society. People emigrated from other lands and brought parts of their homeland's culture with them. This includes views of health that are different from the mainstream. For example, the Hmong brought from their native country of Laos the belief that health is spiritual as well as physical. They may be distrustful of medical care that does not address spiritual issues.

Sometimes language can lead to misconceptions (somthing you think you know, which is not true) about health care and illness. In some African American communities, hypertension is interpreted as high pertension, or just tension. Some feel that avoiding emotional situations will treat the condition. Medical science, on the other hand, considers hypertension a serious condition that requires medication and changes in behavior and diet.

Some Latinos go to healers who might use prayer, massage and diet changes to treat illnesses. While none of this is harmful and may be beneficial, some diseases might be more effectively treated with conventional medical practices.

title: Improve Your Body Image
text:
Look around you. People come in a lot of different sizes, colors and shapes. Body image is what you think about your appearance. Your body is your own. Enjoy the wonderful things it can do!

Change what you can and accept what you can't. That sounds simple - but it is hard. You can make positive changes to some parts of your body. You can change your diet and your activity level to affect your weight, muscle size and strength. Try a new hairstyle or clothes.

Train yourself to block out those negative thoughts you are having about your appearance. Try to recognize how the media are making the problem worse by showing you what they think you should look like. Those commercials and ads are just trying to get you to buy something!

title: Mixed Messages
text:
Earlier in this paper, you read about the messages about health that you get from various sources. You listen to the words of your parents, your read the information in pamphlets and you see news reports. However, you also observe the behavior of your friends and family, and sometimes the actions do not match the words. Mixed messages can be very confusing. Let’s see if you can recognize the multiple messages transmitted in the following scenarios.

Joe has learned in school and from his parents that cigarette smoking causes cancer, heart disease and lung disease. In ads in a sports magazine he sees young, happy and apparently healthy people smoking.

Message 1:

Message 2:

Anthony’s mom and dad talked to him about alcohol. They wanted him to know that some of the older kids in the neighborhood have been drinking. Anthony knows that he should never get into a car with anyone who has been drinking. But Anthony’s parents had a party on Saturday night. The guests were drinking, and the friends left to drive home.

Message 1:

Message 2:

Kayla has always been considered pretty. She dresses nicely and is well groomed. Her friend shows her a fashion magazine with models that are considerably taller and thinner than Kayla.

Message 1:

Message 2:

Joanna, like many teenagers, is insecure about how she looks. Her parents tell her she is pretty just how she is. Yet they are constantly telling her to watch what she eats, especially high calorie food.

Message 1:

Message 2:

What is the best way to deal with mixed messages?

title: Let's Investigate
text: Keep a journal of your healthy choices over the course of a few days. For example, if you choose an apple for a snack instead of a candy bar, that is a healthy choice. Some decisions might be for fun but have health benefits, like playing soccer with friends. Then, examine each choice and see if you can tell how you were influenced to make the choice. Do you seem to be more heavily influenced by media or school? Friends or family? Understanding these influences can help you make healthier choices in the future.

title: Making Healthy Choices
text:
"Well, that was stupid!"

"What was I thinking?"

"It seemed like a good idea at the time!" Sound familiar? Of course it does! We all have done things that we regret. It seems to be human nature to make poor choices occasionally.

What makes our actions regrettable? Sometimes we do things that seem like fun at the time. Perhaps we later realized there were consequences we hadn't considered. Maybe the result of our actions was something unpleasant. Sometimes we make decisions without enough information. Hopefully, the outcome of our actions was not too damaging or embarrassing.

Andrew is a smoker. At age 19, he has been smoking for six years. He is addicted to nicotine, and he has experienced health problems as a result. He has developed a nasty cough, and he cannot keep up in sports with his friends like he used to. A significant amount of Andrew's income from his part-time job goes to buying cigarettes.

We all know that smoking is bad for your health. We know that cigarettes are an expensive habit as well. Smoking a pack a day can cost a person over $1,500 every year! People who smoke also have other effects not related to their health, such as smelly clothes and hair, yellowed teeth and fingernails, and wrinkled skin. So, why did Andrew choose to start smoking?

Well, Andrew says that it was "stupid" to start. He made a poor choice when he was young, and he became addicted. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) lists nicotine as one of the most addictive drugs ever used. Andrew had heard that cigarettes were addictive, but he did not understand how hard it would be to overcome the addiction.

Would Andrew have made a different choice had he known all the information? Possibly. His decision might have been affected by other influences, including a need to fit in with other people. There are often several factors that influence our decisions. Fortunately, most of the decisions we make do not have such serious long-term consequences.

Nearly every decision has alternate choices, and many have short-term and long-term effects. In this issue, you will read about how to use a decision making process that can help you make good health choices. You will learn how to analyze the possible effects of your decisions. You will also read about how a simple choice can have a long lasting impact on your life.

title: The Vegetarian Choice
text:
How do we save the planet from global warming? Become a vegetarian! A vegetarian is a person who does not eat meat, fish or poultry. He or she eats mostly plant-based food. Some vegetarians choose not to eat anything that comes from animals, such as milk, eggs and cheese.

An expert in climate change, Lord Stern of the United Kingdom encourages his fellow citizens to become vegetarians in order to reduce the greenhouse gases that scientists believe contribute to global warming. Cattle produce methane gas during digestion. The emissions of methane gas add to other greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide. Methane is found to be 23 times more powerful a greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide. Data from the United Nations suggest that raising cattle for beef is responsible for about 18 percent of carbon emissions around the world. Destruction of forestland for cattle ranching reduces the number of carbon absorbing trees. Growing feed such as soybeans and corn for cattle uses a lot of energy and water. Cattle producers are not happy with Lord Stern. They point out that there is no alternative to methane producing animals.

The American Dietetic Association concludes that there are health benefits to a vegetarian diet as well. A vegetarian diet that is well planned can lower rates of obesity, Type 2 diabetes, heart disease and some cancers. The choice to become a vegetarian is one that can have an impact on your health and on the health of the planet.

title: A Six-Step Decision Making Process
text:
Paper or plastic? Pen or pencil? The green shirt or the blue one? Do you want fries with that?

Experts say the average person makes thousands of decisions each day - 200 of them are about food alone! Some are small and unimportant, like "Should I brush my teeth or comb my hair first?" Others are significant and may have a big impact for several days, weeks or years like, "Should I smoke that cigarette?"

We are confronted with situations that require us to make a quick decision with little time to think it over. However, often we have the opportunity to consider our decisions carefully. Even though we make so many decisions, most of us have had no training on how to make good decisions. Approaching problems using the following six step decision making process can help you make good choices about your health as well as in many other parts of your life!

Abby has been feeling down lately. She can't quite put her finger on what is wrong. She feels like she doesn't have the energy she used to have. Her appetite has been weak, and she lacks the enthusiasm she is used to. Abby is encouraged by her teacher to use a decision-making process.

First, Abby will state the problem. She needs to make sure she understands fully what the problem or question is about. "I want to feel better" might not be specific enough. She can focus her efforts better if she targets a behavior or situation. "I want to have more energy" gives her more focus.

Next, Abby will brainstorm courses of action that she can take. She has several options. In her health classes and from other influences in her life, Abby has learned about some practices that lead to good health. She considers changing her diet, exercising more and sleeping longer. She also thinks about whether she should go to the doctor for a check-up. Abby recognizes that any of these alternatives might be worthwhile. She also knows that not choosing one of the options is a choice. The brainstorming process should be done without taking the time to evaluate the alternatives. The purpose is to get as many ideas out as possible. Taking time to judge each one could slow down the process and rule out ideas that might be useful.

Now it's time for Abby to evaluate the options. Each option may have benefits, but some might not be right at this time. Abby needs to decide whether she has the time, money or information to take a certain action. Changing your diet for the better requires information. Going to the doctor costs money. She should also evaluate her current situation to see if she already is doing a fair job of it. For example, since Abby already gets nine hours of sleep each night, perhaps sleeping longer is not a reasonable option at this time. Evaluating an option should include looking at the likely positive effects, but also the possible negative consequences. Going to bed earlier, for example, may make Abby feel more rested the next day, but she would have less time to finish her homework and participate in extracurricular activities.

Based on her evaluation of the options, Abby has decided to change her diet. So, she will make a plan of action. She is going to list the steps that she will take to improve the way she eats. Her first step is to record what she eats each day. Her second step is to study the food plate to see if she is getting the recommended amounts of each food group. Abby learns that the potato chips she eats for a snack is providing her with extra calories but no nutritional benefit. Next, she changes her habits by asking her mom to stop buying the chips and begin buying toasted almonds, a much healthier alternative. A plan of action can include several steps, a list of materials or supplies and a timeline. Abby recognizes that results may not happen overnight, so her timeline needs to be at least a few weeks.

After a reasonable amount of time Abby will evaluate the plan. She will check her progress toward her goal of increasing her energy. She will try to assess whether she feels like she has more energy now than before her dietary changes. If she does, she will want to take steps to make these changes more permanent. She would probably want her healthy eating to become a habit.

If Abby has not seen improvement in her energy level, it may be time to modify, or change, the plan. This step will require Abby to examine what parts of her plan are likely not helping and identify other steps to improve the plan. She might need more information about some of the food she includes in her diet. There are numerous foods that are called healthful even though they pack a lot of empty calories. If she is having trouble meeting the demands of her plan, Abby might need to make some changes so that her plan is one she can follow. Of course, it is possible that Abby just needs to give her plan more time, but a plan may need to be abandoned or replaced with another. If Abby's diet changes have not helped her energy level, she should examine her other health choices, such as exercise or seeing her doctor.

title: The Sun: Friend or Foe?
text:
Being in the sun can be fun in the summertime! The sun is also a significant source of vitamin D, a nutrient necessary for good health. However, too much sun exposure causes sunburn. People who have been sunburned five times in their early lives have doubled their chances of getting skin cancer when they get older.

So, do you go out in the sun or avoid it completely? Well, let's consider the latest information before making a decision. We need vitamin D, but during the summer you can get enough vitamin D with just 10 minutes exposure, too little time for sunburn. There are vitamin D supplements and foods rich in vitamin D, like salmon and vitamin D-enriched milk and yogurt. Your favorite breakfast cereal may even have vitamin D added. What do you think is the healthiest choice?

title: Defense Mechanisms
text:
Choices affect emotional health. A defense mechanism is a process that people use - most often without realizing it - to deal with difficult social or emotional situations. They can be helpful and sometimes harmful.

Randy is angry at his brother for borrowing his football and losing it. Randy responded by stomping off to the park and throwing rocks at trees for half an hour. He felt a little better. The helpful side of his choice was that he got over his anger without hurting his brother. On the other hand, he did not deal with it in a way that would help his brother become more responsible and trustworthy.

Jordan cannot seem to get better than a C in math no matter how hard she works. So, she decided that she would get As in all of her other classes. It's probably good that Jordan does not dwell on her troubles and feel bad about herself; however, she may not be doing all she can for her math success, like getting a tutor.

title: Should I choose organic or regular food?
text:
Organic foods are those grown without synthetic fertilizers and pesticides. Organic foods represent just 1 to 2 percent of the food sales around the world, and the cost of the food is generally 10 to 40 percent higher. They are better for the environment, though. Organic farms use less energy and produce less waste. They release no pesticides and fertilizer into the environment. Organic farms are better at sustaining diverse ecosystems.

However, whether organic food is better for you is not clear. Pesticide residue on regular food is clearly not good for you, but there has been no scientific evidence to support organic food as a better nutritional choice. (In some tests, organic food was judged to taste better.) Organic foods may not benefit you directly, but they are a good choice for the health of the environment.

title: Analyzing Consequences
text:
Part of good decision making involves the ability to analyze the short-term and long-term impacts of decisions. Some decisions have significant short-term consequences but little long-term effects. Others have little short-term impact but effects that might be felt for years to come. Some of these decisions involve a little bit of luck.

Luis is at the river with friends. A buddy dares him to jump off a cliff into the river. What are the short- and long-term consequences? If he takes the dare, his friends will think he is cool - for a few hours or days. If he refuses, Luis might be teased for a few minutes. These are short-term consequences.

Luis probably likes the idea of being cool, but he knows there are risks. If he jumps, he could be seriously injured, changing his life forever. The threat of a spinal cord injury is very scary to him. What would you do?

title: Careful with Cholesterol!
text:
Cholesterol is a fat-like substance that occurs naturally in your body. Your body needs it to work properly. If you have too much of it, however, it can stick to the walls of your arteries and restrict blood flow. Cholesterol is usually more of a concern for adults than for kids, but your choices now may affect the way you eat later in life. How can you make choices to limit your intake of cholesterol? Well, today’s nutrition labels on foods list the amount of cholesterol. The recommended daily amount of cholesterol is not more than 300 mg. Take a look at the chart of common foods and the amounts of cholesterol they contain. Then, answer the questions to see if you can choose a healthier way to eat!

1. What could you put on bread instead of butter to reduce you cholesterol intake?

2. Which would have more cholesterol: a grilled cheese sandwich with 2 tsp butter and 2 ounces of cheese or a piece of chicken?

3. Which main course would have the least cholesterol: salmon, pork, beef or eggs?

4. Why do you think whole milk products have more cholesterol than skim or lowfat products?

5. Which is a better alternative to reduce cholesterol: a baked potato with 2 tsp of butter or a baked potato with 4 Tbsp of sour cream?

6. What do all of the foods with some cholesterol content have in common?

title: Let's Investigate
text:
Think of a choice you have to make. Choose one that is more complex than, say, what color socks to wear. Here are some examples:

• How much time after school should I spend watching T.V.?

• How can I get a better grade in math?

• What are some ways I can fit more exercise into my busy schedule?

Use the six-step decision making process to guide you in your choice. Write down your thoughts and actions. You might find that some of the steps of the process are not necessary every time for every decision.

title: Where Do You Get Your Information?
text:
Do hand sanitizers really help prevent disease?

Mikayla thought of this question as she was using a popular alcohol-based hand sanitizer. She had heard that it was a good idea to use these products to stop the spread of disease and infection. Her teachers recommended this practice frequently. One even stood at the door to his classroom with a bottle of hand sanitizer and gave each student a squirt before class started. However, Mikayla wondered if this information was accurate and reliable (dependable or true).

Mikayla had learned that viruses, microscopic disease-causing agents, cause colds, flu and other infections. She noticed the hand sanitizer bottle contained the phrase "decreases number of bacteria on the skin." She wondered, "Are bacteria and viruses similar? Are they controlled in the same way?" Mikayla wondered whether hand sanitizers were effective against both bacteria and viruses or just against bacteria, as the label says.

Mikayla asked her friends about hand sanitizers. She got mixed information. One friend said that sanitizers kill germs. This brought up another question, "What are germs?" Another friend said that washing your hands with soap and water is just as good. Mikayla wonders if it matters what kind of soap you use to wash your hands.

Mikayla's parents told her that it's important to be careful to not touch your eyes and mouth because they are entryways for germs. They said they don't know about the effectiveness of hand sanitizers, but why not use them just to be safe?

Trying to find the answer to her question just raised more questions and gave Mikayla conflicting answers. How can a person find accurate and reliable answers to questions related to health? How can a person distinguish between fact and fiction? Truth and myth?

In this issue of Health Studies Weekly, you will learn about some sources of reliable, accurate health information. You will learn some skills that will help you determine whether the source of your information can be trusted.

title: Feeling SAD?
text:
Have you ever noticed feeling sad during the wintertime? If you have, you might have experienced SAD, or Seasonal Affective Disorder. Seasonal Affective Disorder is a form of depression that is correlated with the shortening of the daylight hours. People who have SAD have symptoms of depression and fatigue during the winter. They enjoy their favorite activities less. They may sleep more and overeat. They socialize less and have difficulty concentrating. These symptoms begin to ease and go away when spring returns and daylight becomes longer again.

Experts are not certain what causes SAD. Some believe the depression is triggered by the brain's response to less daylight. A leading theory is that sunlight might have something to do with the production of two key hormones, melatonin and serotonin. Briefly, these two chemicals regulate a person's energy and mood. Melatonin is produced more when there is less light, and serotonin is produced less in the same conditions. When these two hormones are out of balance, a person's mood can be affected.

SAD can be treated with more light exposure, by talking to a therapist or by taking medication. People with SAD find that when they travel to sunny areas, they do not experience their symptoms. This is more evidence for the theory that SAD is related to light exposure.

title: Information You Can Trust
text:
The Department of Health and Human Services is a cabinet department of the U.S. government. Its job is to protect the health of all Americans. The motto is "Improving the health, safety and well-being of America." The HHS is a huge organization with a huge job. Ten regional offices serve different parts of the country, and many different agencies focus on particular health issues or services. In this article you will learn about the job of this important department and how to get up to date health information that you can trust.

Some of the agencies overseen by HHS may not be of interest to most kids in school, such as the Administration on Aging and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, but others work directly to improve the health of young people.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is an agency that affects kids directly. It works to protect the health and safety of all Americans. The CDC focuses on raising awareness of threats to your health, such as the H1N1 influenza. Your doctor and school nurse receive recommendations from the CDC on how to prevent spread of disease. This information is passed on to you.

Julio's family planned a trip to Peru where he was born. Julio found out he had to get some shots before he left. This information came to him from his doctor through the CDC. It appears that there is a significantly higher risk of diseases such as typhoid, yellow fever and malaria in parts of South America. The CDC carefully researches the risks involved in international travel and communicates this information and their recommendations through doctors and their Web site.

When the H1N1 virus began making people sick, the CDC began tracking outbreaks of the illness months before most people had heard anything about it. The center gathered information through careful research. It developed a vaccine to prevent infection, and recommended to the public how to avoid infection. You can go to the CDC Web site for information on vaccinations, how to avoid getting sick and what to do if you get sick. There are even videos on some topics.

The CDC also works to promote good health for you and the environment, and provides information on staying safe. For example, Maggie is a good soccer player but she recently missed a few games because of a concussion, a brain injury caused by a bump or blow to the head that can change the way your brain normally works. Information about concussions is available to coaches, athletes and parents as well as anyone who wants to stay safe while playing sports.

The Food and Drug Administration

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is an important agency that affects your health and safety. The FDA protects your health by assuring the medicines for you (and your pets) are safe and effective. They also oversee the safety of the nation's food supply.

Have you heard of concerns about high fructose corn syrup? Is it something you should worry about? Have you heard that you should avoid trans fats? What are they and why should you avoid them? Are there other foods that have dangers you should be aware of? The FDA has a lot of information available on their Web site.

The FDA regulates tobacco products. The department recently banned the manufacture and sale of cigarettes flavored with candy or fruit. The FDA realized that these flavorings would make cigarettes more attractive to children, and more people would become addicted to cigarettes at a younger age. Another product at which the FDA is looking carefully is the electronic cigarette. Makers of this product claim that these "e-cigarettes" are a safer alternative to smoking. The FDA has strong concerns about the safety of this product and is making the information available to consumers. They are not yet banned.

Lead is a useful but dangerous product. The metal has been added to gasoline, paint and industrial chemicals. Concerns about leaded paint were raised when the dangers of lead became known. Small children sometimes eat leaded paint chips. Breathing in the dust of old leaded paint is also a danger. Lead poisoning can cause damage to several important organs and result in learning disabilities and behavior disorders in children. The FDA banned leaded paint in 1978.

National Institutes of Health

Doctors diagnosed Travis with asthma when he was 7 years old. Asthma is a condition that affects a person's bronchial tubes. These tubes lead from the windpipe into the lungs. For kids with asthma, breathing can be a lot more difficult because their airways are very sensitive. Since asthma symptoms and severity are not the same for everyone, Travis and his parents worked with his doctor to develop a treatment and prevention program that fits his condition. With his doctor's guidance, Travis manages his asthma with some lifestyle changes and an inhaler for when he has an attack.

Do you have asthma or know anyone who does? Has anyone in your family been affected by cancer? How about heart disease, stroke or arthritis? The National Institutes of Health employ scientists and doctors who work to understand these diseases. The mission of NIH is to research diseases and their treatments.

Travis's doctor was able to help Travis manage his asthma largely because of the research done by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, a division of the National Institutes of Health. There are more than 20 other institutes that perform research on various diseases and provide doctors and patients important health information that can improve and even save lives.

title: Look for the Nutrition Facts Label
text:
The FDA provides consumers with a lot of important nutritional information every day. How do you read these food labels? First, look at the serving size at the top of the label. The information on the label is for one serving.

Next, count the calories, the units of energy contained in the food. As a rule of thumb, when you compare foods, 400 or more calories per serving is high. The nutrition label information is based on a 2,000 calorie diet, so a single serving of 400 calories is 20 percent of your calories for the whole day. Of course, depending on your age, size, health and activity level, your calorie needs may be higher or lower.

A column on the right lists "% Daily Value." This number tells you the percentage of that nutrient (substance that provides nourishment for growth) one serving of the food accounts for in a day. If you choose a food high in fat, it would be wise to choose lower fat foods for the rest of the day.

Now, look at the nutrients and choose wisely. Opt for foods that are lower (5 percent) in trans fats, saturated fats, cholesterol and sodium. Select foods that are higher (20 percent) in potassium, fiber, vitamins A and C, iron and calcium.

The label does not list "% Daily Value" for trans fats or sugars. The FDA has no recommended amounts of these nutrients. You should avoid trans fats because they raise cholesterol. Limit your intake of sugar because it adds unneeded calories.

Daily values for protein are not required, unless the product is listed as "high in protein" or is meant for children under 4 years old. Current scientific evidence is that protein intake is not a concern among Americans older than 4 years old.

title: When should I go to the doctor?
text:
Let's consider three common complaints: cough, sore throat and fever.

Allergies, an infection or foreign objects such as dust all can cause coughs. If your cough lasts longer than a week or is very painful, see your doctor, especially if you cough up any blood. Don't delay.

Viruses often cause sore throats. These infections run their course, and you usually do not need to see a doctor. However, sometimes bacteria, like streptococcus, cause sore throats that need to be treated with antibiotics (drugs that kill bacteria). If your throat is sore for several days and does not seem to be a symptom of a cold, call your doctor.

Fevers are signs of infection. Sometimes, though, a fever may last only a day or so, and you begin to feel better. Most physicians agree that if you have a fever over 101 °F that lasts for three days, you should call your pediatrician. Of course, if you have trouble breathing, call the doctor immediately!

title: Your School Nurse
text:
Mitchell skinned his knee at recess. Tamia's throat had begun to feel sore. Emma needed to take an antibiotic at noon. They all went to their school nurse.

Your school nurse can help you when you need it, but she (or he) is also a quick and reliable source of health information available to you nearly every day. Nurses are trained not only to give you direct health care, but also to provide health information to students, teachers and parents. School nurses pay attention to health trends and treatments so they can provide up-to-date information to help you stay well. School nurses often help develop health curriculum by lending their professional skills, knowledge and experience to the process.

So, if you have an injury or illness, your nurse can help. For your health questions, go to your school nurse to get the facts and an informed opinion.

title: Evaluate Internet Information
text:
A recent search on the Internet for “Health Information” yielded over 190 million possible Web sites! How can you tell which ones have reliable information? Follow the five Ws of Web site evaluation: Who, What, When, Where, Why.

Who wrote the Web site? Is the author a physician, nutritionist, scientist or nurse? If so, the information is probably more reliable than if the author is not an expert. Take care to see if the author represents a company that sells a product—the information may not be balanced.

What is the purpose of the site? What does the author have in mind? If the author is trying to inform readers of health issues, the site is probably reliable. Be careful of an author who might be trying to sell a product or convince you to adopt a certain viewpoint. Consult other sources for a balanced viewpoint.

When was the site created? When was it last updated? There are constant new discoveries and research that change recommendations for good health. Don’t trust a site that has not been updated within the last year. Look for more current information.

Where does it come from? As you read in the main article, the HHS has numerous agencies, centers and institutes that are responsible for protecting and promoting health. Their Web sites are generally very reliable, current and supported by expert research. Web sites from universities are also fairly reliable, but they may be written for college students or professionals.

Why should I use this information? Why is this Web site better than others? Make sure that the Web site provides the information you want for your purposes. Consult a few other reliable Web sites before making any decisions about your health.

Get on the Internet and find a reliable Web site about a health topic of your choice.

title: Let's Investigate
text:
You don’t have to go all the way to the Department of Health and Human Services to get the health information you want. Your state, county or city has health departments that can provide you with many of the health resources available at the federal level.

Develop a question that is of interest to you. If you have a health issue, such as asthma or eczema, this could be your focus. Maybe you are an athlete and have a sport-related question. Maybe you have a question about a disease that afflicts one of your friends or family members. You can also use the Internet, your school nurse or family doctor to find reliable answers to your question. Report back to your class how you found your information.

title: Ready, Set, … Goal!
text:
Molly gets up a little early every morning and does 20 minutes of yoga. Sari has asked his mom to buy an air popper to make popcorn, his favorite snack. Billy always remembers to put on his helmet and pads before he steps on his skateboard. Ruby tries her best to stick to her bedtime schedule so she gets enough sleep.

What do these kids have in common? They've taken steps toward healthy living. Healthy living is a worthwhile goal (something toward which you are working), but as these kids know, it takes a little bit of effort.

Molly would like to sleep in a little longer on most days, but she enjoys the benefits of her daily yoga routine. The increased flexibility and strength make her feel better and help her compete more effectively on her volleyball team. Sari knows that movie theater popcorn can have a lot of butter and calories, so he chooses popcorn with no fat. Sometimes it's a hassle and takes a little more time, but Billy realizes that putting on his protective gear protects him and allows him to enjoy his favorite hobby for a long time. Ruby understands that getting enough sleep is important to succeed in school and gives her the energy she needs to tackle the challenges of the day.

Each of these kids has adopted personal health practices. You can too. Start by taking a good look at your health. How do you feel? How do you look? Can you do the physical and mental tasks that you need and want to do? This is a type of health assessment. Perhaps you will identify an area you would like to improve. Maybe you will want to improve your nutrition. Maybe you will want to become more physically fit. You might identify some ways to protect yourself from risks such as injury and infection. Progress in one area often means gains in another.

Once you have identified an area for improvement, you will need to set a goal. The main lesson inside this paper offers suggestions for developing a health goal. Read it to begin your quest for a healthier life.

A healthier lifestyle is possible for you. It is up to you to take responsibility for your health. This paper contains articles and activities that can give you guidance as you move toward healthy living. Are you ready for the challenge?

title: Healthy Living for You and the Environment
text:
Healthy living isn't just about you - it affects the whole planet. Raising the food that we eat produces a lot of carbon dioxide that is released into the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide, of course, is a greenhouse gas most scientists believe is responsible for global warming. Production of meat - especially beef - produces a lot of carbon dioxide, as well as methane, another greenhouse gas.

We have to feed cattle. The trucks carrying cattle feed give off carbon dioxide when they burn gasoline. Manure the cattle produce gives off methane. Each animal must be slaughtered and processed. All of this takes energy and produces greenhouse gases.

By the time you are served a half-pound hamburger, greenhouse gases equal to almost 20 times the burger's weight in carbon dioxide have been released into the environment, according to scientists. Also, cutting our beef consumption in half would not put nutrition at risk, because Americans eat twice the amount of beef than is recommended by the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

Other meats have much less impact on the environment. Scientists report that substituting chicken for beef would reduce greenhouse gases that meat production releases by more than half. Pork production also harms the environment less than does beef.

All meats do more harm than vegetables. The growing and consumption of a pound of potatoes, for example, sends less than .25 pounds of carbon dioxide into the air. So, a diet with more vegetables and less meat may contribute to healthy living in more ways than one!

title: Set Goals and Achieve Them!
text:
You get older every day. You can do a lot more things than you used to when you were a little kid. You also have more responsibilities and decisions to make.

Your parents still make a lot of decisions for you, and this will continue for years to come. However, you can start to make some decisions and set goals for yourself. It's a great idea to set health goals for yourself so that you can live a healthy life.

Goal setting for Good Health

Jordan wants to be an athlete. He knows that athletics keep a person fit and healthy. Being part of a team can increase a person's social and mental health as well. Like many boys his age, Jordan would like to play in the NBA or NFL someday. Is this a good goal?

Well, most very good athletes do not make it into professional sports, so perhaps Jordan's goal is not realistic, or practical. That doesn't mean he shouldn't try - he should just try to make a more realistic goal at this age. So, Jordan adjusts his goal: he wants to make the seventh grade basketball team next fall.

Is Jordan's goal realistic? For a good athlete who is willing to work hard, it is a realistic goal. Jordan needs to answer another important question: Is his goal specific, or precise and definite? Had Jordan said he wanted to be a good athlete, his goal would not have been very specific. It's hard to measure. Also, there are athletes in many different sports. Making the basketball team is specific. It is clear, easy to measure and as Jordan will find out, his goal requires him to take specific steps along the way.

Sometimes people fail to achieve their goals because they do not care enough about the goal to stick with it when the going gets tough. So, Jordan should ask himself, "Why do I want to achieve this goal?" and, "Is this goal for me or for someone else?" Jordan finds this an easy one to answer. He loves basketball and wants to play on the team for himself.

Okay, so Jordan has a realistic, specific goal for himself. Now comes the hard part: How will he do it? Practice? Of course, but Jordan may need some guidance to help him know how and what to practice. This leads to another question, "Who will help me?"

Jordan asks his P.E. teacher for help. Mr. Holmes teaches Jordan some drills that he can do to improve his ball handling skills. He also tells Jordan that he's observed some skill areas that Jordan needs to improve. With this advice from his teacher, Jordan develops a plan to sharpen his basketball skills.

Before he starts, Jordan should also know what obstacles might get in the way of his goal. Knowing about these problems ahead of time can help Jordan make a plan to deal with them. Jordan knows he sometimes has trouble balancing schoolwork, chores at home and hanging out with his friends. He decides he needs to make a workout schedule and watch less TV to make time for additional basketball practice.

When should Jordan start? He answers this question for himself. He can start next week for a half an hour each day. When school is out for the summer, Jordan can increase his practice time to an hour or more.

Next week comes, and Jordan begins his practice routine. Things are going pretty well: he practices drills and does conditioning exercises to increase his endurance and his strength. So far, Jordan is keeping up with his schoolwork and chores. The tryouts for the team are a long way off. Can he stay on track? What if Jordan starts to get behind in his work? What if he begins to find his training program boring? It might be hard for him to stay motivated.

Fortunately, Jordan has planned ahead. He came up with a few strategies, or plans to achieve a result, to keep himself on track and motivated. If he begins to slack off, he will imagine the first game of the season when the players are introduced and he trots out on the basketball court. He can visualize his mom and dad in the stands cheering. If he starts to get bored with practicing, he plans to get together with some of the kids in his neighborhood for some two on two or three on three. That will give him a chance to try out his new skills and help him identify areas he needs to work on. Jordan has even promised himself a visit to the ice cream shop if he can make 10 free throws in a row.

Jordan has a goal setting program that will help him achieve his goal. It's not a guarantee, but Jordan is on the right track for success in improving his health and his self esteem.

title: Healthy Snacking
text:
Healthy living requires some choices, and you have choices when you reach for a snack after school. Snacking is actually a good thing when done right. Satisfying your hunger provides the nutrients a growing body needs. Those nutrients keep your energy level up. If you eat too many calories, however, your body will store the extra as body fat.

Choose snacks that are high in complex carbohydrates (like whole grains) and protein. These have fewer calories. Avoid those high in simple carbohydrates (sugars) and fats. These will satisfy your hunger now but you will pay later with a quick drop in energy.

Ask your parents to buy whole wheat pretzels, raisins, low fat yogurt and low fat graham crackers. Hummus on pita is a good snack. Fruits and vegetables are always a great snack. Look at Food Nutrition Labels to make sure your snack is a healthy one.

title: Personal Health Practices
text:
Take a good look at your personal health practices. It's probably a good idea to assess your current health practices to help identify areas that need work. Do you wear your seat belt in the car? Do you wear protective gear when engaging in potentially dangerous activities, such as sports and bike riding? Risk is a part of everyday life. However, some risk factors can be lowered or even eliminated. For example, smokers can give up smoking. What about you? Can you think of risk behaviors you can change?

Now, what about fitness and nutrition? Are you active? You can keep weight under control and reduce the chance of disease with a reasonable amount of regular physical activity. You can do the same with a balanced diet that limits calories from fats and sugars. A healthy diet also provides your body with the energy it needs for proper growth and development.

title: How can I develop bigger muscles?
text: Your favorite pro athletes have strong, well developed muscles. You may want to have big, powerful muscles, too. Pro athletes lift weights to achieve those big muscles. Until you reach puberty (a stage of rapid physical growth and reproductive development), however, no amount of weightlifting will produce those results. In fact, weightlifting can damage young tendons and muscles. At your age, you should work on toning and strengthening. Any physical activity will help your muscles stay toned, firm and strong. P.E. class and sports will help. You can do some push ups and sit ups also. Stay away from pumping iron until you are a little older. In the meantime, make sure you eat a balanced diet and get plenty of sleep. Those are activities the pros do that you can do, too.

title: Staying Fit Without Sports
text:
"Playing sports isn't my thing."

Some of us do not like sports very much. Marcy tried playing soccer when she was 7 years old, and then again when she was 8. She didn't like it. She played baseball for a few years, but she didn't care for it enough to pick up her glove except for a practice or a game. She never really got the hang of basketball. How could Marcy stay fit?

Any physical activity will strengthen muscles. Vigorous activity will exercise your heart, a very important muscle. With Marcy's parents' help, she found some things she wanted to do to stay in shape without playing on a team. She began taking karate lessons. She went with her family on hikes in the woods. When she got older, she started mowing the lawn.

Staying active is very important for healthy living. Can you think of other activities that will keep you fit?

title: Are You Active Enough?
text:
Part of healthy living is including enough physical activity. Most kids get a good amount of physical activity on a regular basis. How do you know if you are active enough?

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that kids get 60 minutes or more a day of physical activity. The activity should be from three types of physical activity: aerobic, bone strengthening and muscle strengthening. Aerobic activity, such as skating, running, swimming and bike riding, should be most of the 60 minutes daily. Muscle strengthening activity includes push ups and chin ups, as well as gymnastics, rock climbing and tree climbing. Bone strengthening exercises include running and jumping rope, and sports such as basketball, volleyball and tennis. Bone strengthening occurs when the bones are stressed during physical activity.

Keep track of your activity to see whether you are meeting recommendations for a healthy lifestyle. Use a table like the one shown here to record your daily activities.

Look at your results for the week.

Did you meet, exceed or fall short of the recommendations for physical activity of 60 minutes a day?

Does the information you collected reflect a normal week?

Approximately how much of your activity is from aerobic exercise?

Reflect on your level of physical activity. How can you improve your fitness level?

title: Let's Investigate
text: Now it’s your turn. Set a goal that you want to achieve to improve your healthy living. Keep it simple for now. Make sure your goal is specific and realistic. Use the internet or a health book to find out ways you can achieve your goal. Identify those around you who can be depended upon for help. Report back to your class on the steps toward your goal. Ask for feedback. Revise your plan so that it is a “recipe for success.” Now, you just have to get started on your way to a healthier lifestyle!

title: Stand Up for Health
text:
Kayla sat in her sixth grade class listening to every word Officer Russell said about the dangers of tobacco. He warned of the serious health risks associated with nicotine addiction. Kayla took the information to heart. She wondered why anyone would ever start smoking cigarettes. "I will never touch a cigarette," she thought to herself. Yet, two years later, behind the school building, there stood Kayla, smoking a cigarette. What happened to Kayla's strong stance against smoking?

Kayla had met some new kids in seventh grade. They were in the "cool" crowd. Kayla was flattered that one of the girls, Gina, asked her to hang out. They met after school one day. Kayla was shocked that Gina pulled out a pack of cigarettes. Gina offered one to Kayla, and she stammered, "Uh, I don't think so." The next day, Kayla thought Gina seemed much less friendly to her. After a few weeks, Kayla saw Gina hanging out with her friends in the parking lot of a nearby fast food restaurant. Kayla approached and, to her own surprise said, "Hey, do you have a cigarette?"

Gina never forced Kayla to smoke. But she did use peer pressure by ignoring her. Kayla made a choice. She chose friendship over health. Her choice will affect her physical health, but Kayla needs to examine her emotional health. Emotionally healthy people are good at making healthy choices in the face of peer pressure.

Kayla is not unusual. Peer pressure causes kids to make all kinds of choices that are bad for them. If Kayla had been aware of the dangers of peer pressure and had been ready to deal with it, she would have been more likely to stand up for her own health.

Standing up for health means understanding what is important to you and using effective communication skills to advocate for your health. You will learn about good communication skills later in this paper. You will also learn about self advocacy, or standing up for yourself. You will also read about conflict management skills. These will help you resolve conflicts and resist peer pressure that can affect your health in a negative way.

title: Stand Up for Healthy School Lunches
text:
Curly fries. Chicken rings. Fried mozzarella cheese sticks. These high fat, high-calorie items are not healthy. Why do schools that teach about healthy choices offer such unhealthy foods in their school cafeteria? It's simple: because kids buy them.

Most schools used to run their own cafeterias, and the school district employed managers and cooks to choose and prepare the food. Many school districts today hire independent, private companies to provide food for the schools. It's a business, and a business makes money when people buy the product.

A few years ago, voters in Berkeley, California, voted to fix the problem. The School Lunch Initiative (SLI) is a program designed to connect school subjects with food. Students are involved in activities that include growing, preparing, serving and enjoying food. SLI provides all students with healthy meals made from local ingredients.

At Martin Luther King Jr. Middle School in Berkeley, each student participates in the Edible Schoolyard. Classes taught in the one acre garden teach about plant life cycles, community values and the pleasures of work. Kitchen classes allow kids to prepare and eat delicious and nutritious meals from foods they have grown in the garden.

People are standing up for healthy choices in school cafeterias!

title: Prepare for Peer Pressure
text:
Your friends have quite a lot of influence over you. Think about it: how often do you consider your friends before you make a choice? You might choose an outdoor activity because your friends are involved. You might even join a team because of your friends. Where you hang out after school and with who depends a lot on your friends.

When friends try to get you to do something, we call it peer pressure. Friends can have a positive influence over you, but they can also influence you in negative ways. Making good decisions requires you to be able to resist negative peer pressure.

Negative Peer Pressure

In the cover story you learned about Kayla, a student who gave in to peer pressure and started smoking. Only about one of every 10 middle school students smokes. But nearly all middle school students make choices because of peer pressure. Some of those choices may be good, but others - whether it is substance abuse, risky behaviors or participating in illegal activities - are bad. Friends who make these choices are not necessarily bad people. They might just be curious and want you to join in. Your participation in the activity makes it easier and more fun for them. How can you prepare yourself to handle peer pressure?

Avoid Peer Pressure

Avoid negative peer pressure. This is the most important strategy. Hang out with people who have the same values as you do. Values are those parts of life that you feel strongly about - enough to stand up for - like freedom, honesty and good health. You and your friends like hanging out together partly because you like the same things, whether it is sports, fashion, video games or a hobby. Kayla's mistake was to choose to be with someone who had different values than hers. After all, studies show that you are twice as likely to smoke if you have friends that smoke.

Sometimes, friends change. Nick and Dominic used to do everything together. They met in kindergarten and were best friends throughout elementary school. Then, when they found themselves on different teams at their new middle school, Nick and Dominic began to see less of each other. Each made new friends. Nick noticed that Dominic was starting to get in trouble at school. Dominic and some of his new buddies were seen more often in the office with the assistant principal. Dominic's grades fell. He began to brag to Nick about skipping class, spray-painting graffiti on the school building and even stealing food from the cafeteria.

How can Nick stay friends with Dominic and resist the peer pressure to participate in Dominic's risky behaviors? It helps that they are in different classes in school. That way Nick is able to avoid some peer pressure. But, Nick may have to choose one day between his friendship with Dominic and Nick's own values.

Handling Peer Pressure

Meeting people with values different from yours is not a bad thing. You learn new ideas from different people, and some of those ideas make you feel even stronger about your own values. You can show respect for other people's values without changing yours.

What if you are in a situation where someone pressures you to try something that is against your values? A firm, confident "No" is often enough. But sometimes the response will be, "Why not?" You can answer this question best if you are prepared. Practice a well rehearsed response. For example, when Maggie's friend offered her a beer, Maggie wanted to say that she didn't think it was a good decision for her health and that she didn't want to get into trouble. She would have liked to have said that she didn't think she needed to drink alcohol to have a good time. What Maggie said, though, was "No" and then "I'm allergic." Maggie didn't tell the truth, but she avoided the beer and the awkwardness of not fitting in.

Paul used another strategy. When some friends invited him to join them at a fast food restaurant for some fries and soft drinks, Paul instead invited them over to his house for some popcorn and sport drinks. He saved fat, calories and money with this alternative.

Sometimes it is best to simply leave a situation. You need to know your limits and the consequences of your choices. Matt was hanging out in Austin's backyard with other friends. Austin came out of the house with some fireworks and matches. Even though Austin knew it was illegal to light fireworks in their city, he said, "Don't worry: the cops are too busy to catch us." Matt was very uncomfortable because it was illegal and because he thought of his cousin who was once severely burned when he was playing with matches. Matt left, saying, "I need to do my chores or I won't be able to meet you guys tomorrow."

You can remember refusal skills with the acronym STOP:

S - Say no in a firm voice

T - Tell why not

O - Offer a different choice

P - Promptly leave

There is "safety in numbers." That means it is safer to be with a friend who shares the same values as you do when you are faced with negative peer pressure. It is hard to be the only one to say no, so a friend can be a support for you as the two of you try to make the right choice.

Be prepared for peer pressure. Nearly everyone experiences it at some time or another. Try your best to avoid risky situations, and be ready to deal with peer pressure when it happens.

title: Communicate Skillfully
text:
Learn to use good communication skills: they help you stand up for your health!

Understand that communication is the exchange of meaning between a sender and a receiver.

Be honest, patient, sincere, respectful and accepting.

Make eye contact. It shows interest and respect.

Be aware of your body language. For example, arms folded across the chest can seem that you are not receptive to the other person's ideas.

Have courage. Say what you think. Be confident that your opinions are valuable.

Speak clearly and in an appropriate tone of voice. This shows respect and reduces misunderstandings.

Practice. We get better at most things by practicing.

Listen! Show the other person that you understand by summing up what you have heard. Your partner knows you are interested and can help clear up misunderstandings.

title: Conflict Resolution
text:
"Hey, give that back! It's mine!"

How do you handle conflict, or disagreement? It happens all the time. People who are emotionally healthy do a good job of conflict resolution (solution to a problem). There are positive and negative ways of managing conflict. Let's focus on the positive ways - you can talk it out, ignore it or get help.

Talk it out: It is often the best way. Make sure you have a positive attitude, listen carefully and are honest. Being respectful will encourage the other person to be positive also.

Ignore it: It does not resolve the conflict, but this may be a good choice if the conflict is likely a one-time occurrence that does not have any really serious consequences.

Get help: Sometimes it is clear that you and the other person cannot resolve it on your own. You might be too angry to speak respectfully and honestly.

title: Is smoking one cigarette dangerous?
text:
If you smoke one cigarette, your hair and breath will smell. Your mouth will feel dry, and you might feel a burning sensation in your lungs and windpipe. You'll probably cough and maybe feel nauseous, but one cigarette will not likely cause any long-term health problems.

The problem is addiction. Tobacco contains a highly addictive substance called nicotine. New smokers can start to feel addicted after just one cigarette. Another often follows that one cigarette. And another.

Every day, over 3,800 kids under age 18 try their first cigarette. Almost 1,000 of them get addicted and become daily smokers. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about half of them will die someday from heart disease, cancer, emphysema or other effects of smoking. So, a cigarette today may not seem like a bad thing, but it can lead to a lifetime of health problems and an early death.

title: Self Advocacy
text:
Self-advocacy is like learning how to steer the boat of life!

Step One: Self-Assessment

The first step is to identify what you need to be healthy and successful. Pay attention to how you feel, how you get along with others and how you perform in school. Perhaps you feel tired in class, or frustrated in math.

Step Two: Identify Help

Who should you turn to? Sometimes it’s as simple as talking to your parents or your teacher. But they are busy, so it may take some effort.

Step Three: Take Action

Now that you've identified your need and who can help, make it happen. Approaching your teacher may be more successful if you say, "I would like help on reducing fractions," rather than, "I’m not good in math."

Step Four: Evaluate

Did your actions help you with your problem? If they didn’t, you should try again. If they did, congratulations: you successfully advocated for yourself!

title: Practice Peer Pressure Prevention
text:
In small groups, discuss the following scenarios and create a skit, draw a comic strip or write a story. Demonstrate effective, healthy ways of dealing with peer pressure. Present these to your classmates.

You walk to school with a friend. Your friend asks you to skip school.

You are taking a test. Your friend is cheating and offers the answers to you.

There's a substitute in your social studies class. She is having trouble controlling the class. Your friends make noises and throw paper wads around the room.

It's been snowing. One of your friends says it would be fun to throw snowballs at passing cars.

While walking home from school, your friend shows you a pack of cigarettes and offers you one.

You've been invited over to a friend's house to study for tomorrow's science test. When you get there, your friend and others are playing video games and texting other friends. You really need to study.

While hanging out with some of the popular kids, one of them points to a girl/boy and says, "Look at those clothes and that hair. We're ignoring her/him."

You are at your friend's house, and no parents are home. Your friend offers you a drink of beer.

After seeing your classmates' treatment of these scenarios, can you identify the strategies used to deal with peer pressure? In the presentations, how effective were the strategies? What alternate suggestions do you have? How realistic do think the strategies were?

title: Let's Investigate
text: Anthropologist Margaret Mead once said, “Never doubt that a small group of thoughtful, committed people could change the world. Indeed, it’s the only thing that ever has.” Look around you—at yourself, your school, your community and your environment. What about your world could be changed? It’s okay to start small. That’s a good way to build your confidence. Talk to a trusted adult about a problem. See if you can find out the cause of the problem, attempted solutions and possible obstacles. Who knows what effect you could have on the world!

title: Our Bodies' Systems
text:
Hello. It's good to see you. It's me, Discovery Dan, on a quest to learn about some of the important systems in the human body. We have many basic systems in our bodies, but you probably already knew that. What is a body system, anyway? Well, a system is a group of different parts working together to make one large part work well. Your body can be divided into several systems that help your entire body function smoothly.

Here's a list of some of the systems you and I rely on to get us through each day:

Skeletal System- This system pretty much holds your body together and allows you to move. This is important - no bones about it!

Circulatory System - I like this system a lot because it's like your friendly neighborhood letter carrier and trash collector put together. The circulatory system delivers necessary items all over your body and carries away the waste products (things you don't need).

Digestive System - Without this system in place we couldn't turn the food we eat into the energy we need to live and grow.

Respiratory System - Oxygen in, carbon dioxide out. We all need oxygen to survive, and this is the system that allows us to breathe it in.

Nervous System - This is the control center of your body. It's responsible for everything your body does. The senses you're familiar with (touch, taste, sight, hearing and smelling) are an important part of the nervous system. Different parts of our body send signals to the brain to let us know what we're sensing.

Immune System - Most doctors (and lots of other folks) would say the immune system is an important part of our bodies. Without this system, we wouldn't be able to avoid catching a disease or get better when we do become sick.

Endocrine System - Ever heard of this one? It's actually more important than you may guess. This system works with the nervous system to control the body's growth.

Muscular System - This system works with the skeletal system to help your body move. Without your muscles, you couldn't even turn the page, which is what you need to do to read the rest of Health Studies Weekly.

title: Kicking the Smoking Habit
text:
Everyone knows someone who smokes and has tried to quit. But quitting is really hard. It's also hard for the people who care about them, because you wish you could help them. Everyone knows it's unhealthy to smoke. So, why is it so hard for people to kick the habit?

Smokers become addicted to nicotine. When smokers try to stop, they become depressed and have headaches or other symptoms. Believe it or not, there are things that you can do to help them give up cigarettes.

First of all, understand that it is hard for people to quit smoking. Many people quit and start smoking again several times before they quit for good. Don't make them feel bad when their plans to quit don't work. Tell them that you know they can do it if they just keep trying. Reward that person for trying to quit. Make a card telling them how proud you are of them.

Smokers often crave cigarettes right after eating. You can help take someone's mind off cigarettes. Volunteer to take a walk or play a game of cards with someone who's trying to quit.

Most importantly, continue to support your loved one no matter how many times he or she may start smoking again. One of these days, with your support, your mom or grandpa or brother or aunt may give up smoking forever. Won't that be great?

title: Healthy Systems for a Healthy Life
text:
Each of the systems mentioned on the front page is equally important to your physical health. Without even one of these systems, your body would have a difficult time functioning as it should. Just as every student is an important part of your classroom, every system is an important part of your body.

Let's talk about some of these systems and find out how we can take good care of them so our bodies will stay in tip-top condition.

Imagine how difficult life would be if our sense organs no longer worked properly. At the very least, think how awful it would be to never again be able to taste melted chocolate!

Did you know your senses can be affected by brain injuries? You can keep your brain protected by fastening your safety belt when riding in the car and wearing your helmet when playing sports.

Your bones and joints make up your skeletal system. Joints are made up of ligaments, cartilage and tendons. You can take care of your bones by eating food rich in calcium (like milk, yogurt or cheese) and by warming up and cooling down before and after exercise.

The circulatory system consists mostly of your veins, arteries and capillaries (tiny blood vessels). Without the circulatory system, your blood wouldn't get to your heart.

How can you take care of this system? Don't ever smoke! Smoking narrows the blood vessels, making it more difficult for the blood to make its way through the system to the heart.

What good would food do us if we didn't have the digestive system to break the food down? This system includes a variety of body parts, including the stomach and the esophagus (the tube leading to your stomach from your mouth).

Try to drink at least six to eight glasses of water a day to help food move through your digestive system.
