Take a deep breath! Aahh. Doesn't that feel good? That's your respiratory system at work bringing in fresh oxygen to your lungs and discarding carbon dioxide. This is another body system that is harmed if you smoke or if you inhale someone else's smoke.

Your brain and your spinal cord are parts of your nervous system. The fact that your body takes in oxygen regularly - without you thinking, "Breathe, breathe, breathe" - is due to the nervous system.

Don't ever take any illegal drugs. Many drugs can affect your brain cells, which control the nervous system.

A-a-achoo! I think I'm getting a cold. Have you ever felt that way? Thanks to your immune system (which includes important body parts like the tonsils and spleen) your body is able to fight off infections, and you'll get better. Help your body fight disease by keeping up with your immunization shots.

You know, I think you're even taller than you were the last time I saw you. That's because of your endocrine system, which controls your body's ability to grow properly. Some drugs (such as steroids) can harm your endocrine system.

Thanks to all the muscles in your body (more than 600 of them) you are able to move your bones, which are connected to your muscles.

Taking a quick five-minute walk each day and doing stretches before challenging work-outs, will help keep your muscles in terrific shape.

So, now you have it - a run-down on our bodies' systems and how they keep us going. Amazing, aren't we? Is there one system that's the most important? No way! Take care of them all so that your body continues to work at its best.

title: Taste Bud Tester
text:
What do you know about your taste buds - besides the fact that without them eating would not be nearly as much fun! We used to believe that the location of the taste buds on your tongue focused on the flavor that bud tasted. For example, we used to think the front edge of your tongue detected only the sweet flavors you taste in candy. However, new evidence has proven what we used to believe about the tongue map (sour taste buds were located on the sides, bitter on the back, sweet on the front, etc.) is now incorrect. Scientists now believe all our taste buds on our tongue can detect all flavors, although it is still possible some taste buds are more sensitive to certain flavors than others.

Here's an experiment you can do to test just where the different taste buds are located. You will need a teaspoon of salt, a teaspoon of sugar, a teaspoon of lemon juice, a teaspoon of ground coffee, four paper cups, a marker and four craft sticks.

Put each food item in a separate paper cup and label each cup with what is inside of it. Wet a craft stick and dip it into the cup with the lemon juice. Place the stick on the tip, back and sides of your tongue. Can you taste the lemon juice on all sides of your tongue? Is there a location where you can taste the sour lemon juice more strongly than others? Repeat this with each item, using different craft sticks for each item. Where do you get the strongest taste of the salt, the sweetness of the sugar and the bitterness of the coffee? Or, do you simply taste all the flavors on all parts of your mouth? Take notes and perhaps you can be the next scientist to shed more light on the taste bud mystery.

Interesting fact: An adult's tongue has about 10,000 taste buds. Babies' tongues usually have more taste buds than that, and as we grow older the number of taste buds decreases.

title: Recipe for Good Health
text:
Did you know if you add a lot of fruit and vegetables to your diet, you're more likely to stay healthier longer? If you eat at least five or more servings of fruit and vegetables each day, you could reduce your risk of heart disease and cancer. Fruits and vegetables have lots of vitamins, minerals and fiber, and they are also low in fat.

Surprise! Did you know that a tomato is a fruit, not a vegetable? The fruit is formed around the seeds of the plant to protect them. This makes a tomato a fruit! Vegetables are usually parts of the plant. For example, carrots are the root of the plant, and celery is the stem.

Here's a terrific recipe for Pineapple-Raisin-Sunflower Salad that will help you get some healthy fruits and vegetables in your diet.

Ingredients:

2 lettuce leaves

2 slices canned pineapple rings

1/2 cup low-fat (2 percent) cottage cheese

1/3 cup raisins

1 tablespoon sunflower seeds

Put the lettuce leaves on a plate and lay one pineapple ring in the center of the lettuce. Cut the second pineapple ring into eight equal pieces and place those pieces around the pineapple ring so they look like flower petals. Put a scoop of cottage cheese in the center of the pineapple ring and decorate the cottage cheese with the raisins to look like the center of a sunflower. Sprinkle the salad with sunflower seeds. You can use any dried fruits instead of raisins. This makes a healthy and beautiful side dish for lunch or dinner.

title: Childhood Illnesses - Can You Avoid Them?
text:
Children experience many illnesses every year, but not nearly as many as their parents and grandparents got. For example, until about 10 years ago most children got chicken pox. Chicken pox is a viral infection that causes a rash and fever. In 1995, scientists discovered a vaccine for the disease. Now, many children who receive the chicken pox vaccine never get chicken pox. So, what sort of diseases do you still get?

Well, everyone gets colds every year. As a matter of fact, most children will have six to 10 colds every school year. There are more than 200 different viruses that cause colds. You can reduce your risk of getting sick by washing your hands often and keeping your hands away from your eyes, nose and mouth.

Almost every year many students suffer from the flu, strep throat or allergies. Some of these illnesses can be safely treated at home, but it's important to see a doctor if you have a fever for more than a few days or if you're in constant pain. Any time you're in doubt about your health, it's always a good idea to get to a doctor as soon as possible.

title: How Do Lungs Work?
text:
The lungs help supply oxygen-rich blood throughout our body. How do our lungs really work? You and I aren't able to look inside each other's bodies and watch the lungs expand with air. So, create a model of your lung with a clear plastic bottle (like a soda bottle), two balloons, a rubber band and tape.

Have an adult cut the bottle in half across the middle using a pocketknife. Then, take one of the balloons and cover the neck of the bottle with it (the end that the cap was on). Tie the rubber band around the balloon so it's tight. Take the other balloon and cut it open. Then, stretch that rubber material over the cut end of the bottle and tape it into place so it's secure. Now, let's see how your lungs work. Using your finger, gently push the rubber piece at the bottom into the bottle. What happens to the balloon at the top of the bottle? It should expand. This is basically how our lungs work.

The bottle represents our lungs and the rubber piece tied to the cut portion is the diaphragm (a muscle located just below the lungs). When we blow air out of our lungs, the diaphragm curves upward, which causes increased air pressure inside the chest cavity, forcing air out. When we breathe in, the diaphragm flattens. You can see this happening when you take your finger off the rubber on the bottom of the bottle and the balloon on the neck of the bottle relaxes.

title: Writing Connection
text:
Have you ever had to try to persuade (convince) someone to do something they may not want to do? Being able to write a persuasive letter is something you’ll use time and time again in your life.

Practice the art of persuasion by writing an imaginary letter. Address the letter to the school board asking them to put healthier foods in the lunchroom and to replace the junk food in the vending machines with healthy snacks. Tell them why it’s important for growing children to have healthy alternatives. Explain what is wrong with a lot of the food they offer at school and how it can negatively affect students’ health and bodies.

title: Learning About Health
text:
Quick, what's your favorite fast food restaurant? Did you say McDonald's or Burger King? Was it because they sell children's meals that include toys? Was it because they offer play areas for children? Have you seen their commercials on TV?

What's your favorite candy? How about cereal? How did you first hear about them? If you're like most kids, you get a lot of information about food from TV commercials. The average kid watches about 40,000 commercials each year - commercials that advertise candy, toys and fast food. Think about how many commercials you watch in one night. How many of those commercials are for foods that are bad for you?

Try keeping a tally of how many commercials you see and what they are for. Hey! That means you get to actually watch TV for homework! Before you begin, get a sheet of paper and divide it into five columns. At the top of the columns write the words candy, cereal, toys, fast food and other. When a commercial comes on, mark a tally in the correct column. Do this for one to two hours. At the end of the time period, add up how many commercials you saw and how many were in each column. Most commercials are about 30 seconds long. If two commercials total one minute, how many minutes did you spend watching commercials during that time?

Children don't usually realize how often they are targeted by companies that make commercials. You probably don't see commercials for toys and candy on the news channels your mom and dad watch. Companies know the people who watch children's television are - what else? - children. You will probably watch their commercials and then ask your parents to buy you the things they advertise. Did you realize they were doing that to you on purpose?

Not all commercials are trying to get you to ask your parents to buy things. Have you seen the commercials on the Disney Channel for VERB? You know that a verb is an action word, right? VERB is a program that wants kids to be active - to get out and exercise. Commercials like the ones for VERB are called Public Service Announcements (PSAs), because they aren't trying to get you to buy anything. They are helping you learn something important.

Now it's time to make like a verb and do something. Turn the page to learn more about advertising techniques that are directed specifically toward you.

title: What Is Autism?
text:
Autism is a disorder that affects a person's brain. A child with autism may have a hard time talking to others, making friends and understanding the things he sees or hears. He may have habits that seem strange, like rocking back and forth or saying words over and over. Some children with autism only have minor symptoms and others have more serious types of this disorder. For children with the most serious types, each day can be a challenge. Doctors don't know what causes autism.

It's important to treat people who have autism with kindness and understanding. You can also take an active part in the fight against autism, like Michala Riggle, a student in Louisville, Kentucky. Her brother, Evan, improved after getting treated by doctors at Kosair Children's Hospital. Michala wanted other kids to get good treatment, too. She decided to make and sell bracelets to raise money for doctors to study autism. So far, she's raised more than $200,000.

You can help, even if you don't raise thousands of dollars. Start by being kind to anyone who seems different from you, whether they have autism or not. Take time to learn about the disorder. Check out library books or ask an adult to help you find information on the Internet. Learning about something is the first step to changing it.

title: Advertising Techniques
text:
Television Commercials

Do you think it's a coincidence that candy commercials feature cartoon characters such as SpongeBob or Scooby-Doo? Of course not. The advertisers do that on purpose. Aren't you more likely to want a snack shaped like a favorite cartoon character than a plain snack? Believe it or not, advertisers use specific techniques like that to get you to buy their products.

When you watch a commercial, ask yourself what the advertiser is doing to try to get you to buy the product. Is there a celebrity endorsing the product? (Endorse means saying you think something is good in order to sell it.) Do you think the famous people in commercials really use this product or were they just paid to say they do?

How do the actors who are using the product look? Are they trying to make you think that if you use the product you'll be happier, prettier or more popular? You probably already know the people in these commercials are being paid to pretend they love these products.

Are there large groups of children playing with the toys and eating the food? Does the commercial make you feel as if you will be left out if you don't also get their toy or eat their food? This technique is used to make you believe you will be "one of the group" if you buy the product.

Are the commercials focusing on music and sound to make you want to buy something? Turn your back to the TV and just listen to the sound. What visual techniques are being used to make you want to buy the item? Are there flashing lights or special effects? Try turning the sound off and just watching the screen.

Talk about each of these techniques with your class. Find out how many students in your class have talked their parents into buying something they saw in a commercial. Why do you think the advertiser's techniques work so well? Which ones do you think work best?

Public Service Announcements

What about Public Service Announcements? Think you've never seen one? You've heard of Smokey Bear, right? He's the star of a Public Service Announcement that has been popular for more than 50 years. This famous PSA teaches us how to prevent wildfires. What about the Crash Test Dummies, who teach us to buckle up, or McGruff the Crime Dog telling us to "take a bite out of crime"? You may see a celebrity reminding people about the importance of reading or staying away from harmful things like drugs and tobacco. All of these are Public Service Announcements.

PSAs help us learn about safety and health. Can you think of other PSAs you have seen? Brainstorm a list with your class. Public Service Announcements actually use many of the same techniques that advertisers use when they try to get you to eat their fast food or buy their toys. The difference is that the PSAs are giving you information that is important to your health and well-being.

Do you have any new ideas for PSAs? Can you think of a great slogan (a phrase that people will remember) to get kids to not try drugs, to exercise more or to eat more fruits and vegetables? Try the lab experiment in this paper and see if you and your friends can create your own terrific PSA.

title: Create a PSA
text:
There are many health issues children (and adults, too) need to learn about. Public Service Announcements are great ways to tell people about the dangers of too much fast food, the importance of exercise and more.

Imagine you are working for a company creating a one-minute PSA for your local television station. Working in groups of four or five, pick a topic you think is important. Any idea that is healthy for your body, brain or feelings would make a good PSA. Brainstorm several ideas with your group, then take a vote.

Once your group has selected the subject, focus on the way you are going to get the audience's attention. What is the best way to reach children your age? Create a rap song? Write a one-minute play? Make up a slogan? You can use more than one of these ideas. Remember, you want to use the same techniques advertisers use to sell you toys or fast food, but you want to give your audience a healthy message.

Next, write your PSA and practice it with your group. Then perform it for your class. Your class can be your focus group. Focus groups are people who try out products or watch commercials before they are made public. Ask your focus group what they liked and what they think should be changed. You don't have to make changes, if your group doesn't want to.

Finally, have your teacher or a parent volunteer record your group as you perform the PSA. Perhaps your teacher and principal could arrange an assembly to share the PSAs with the whole school. Use your creativity to help make others healthier.

title: Turn On the TV
text:
For clear, accurate information about health news, you can turn to - or at least turn on - your television. You may not find accurate information by watching commercials, but many local and national news stations have up-to-date information about health news. You can learn about what's new in the health care, exercise equipment, nutrition information and more.

News stations often have special health segments about a variety of topics on their nightly broadcasts. You can also check out weekly news programs such as "60 Minutes" or "Dateline" for health information. Staying home sick one morning? Turn on one of the morning news programs like the "Today Show" on NBC or the "Early Show" on CBS. They have regular features that will give you the latest information about health issues such as eating a healthy diet, staying fit and even keeping your pets healthy. Not sure when they're on TV? Check out cbsnews.com or msnbc.msn.com. Both have links to all of their news programs and a schedule of when they are on.

Interested in health news in your community? Most local news stations air health segments. They often interview local doctors and talk about health issues facing the people in your city. Visit your local news Web site or watch the news one evening to learn more.

It's always important to double-check any information you receive, even those from news stories. You can usually feel pretty confident when you get information from a reputable news show. News agencies check their facts and do lots of research before airing stories about health.

title: Public Health
text:
The health of the people who live in a community, state or nation is called public health. Organizations such as the National Institutes of Health, the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention are supported by the government. Their job is to help keep the public healthy.

At the National Institutes of Health, researchers are working on new medicines to help sick people. The Food and Drug Administration makes sure the medicines we take and foods we eat are safe. Keeping track of how diseases spread is the job of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The information they gather lets hospitals, doctors and other health-care workers know what type of diseases are being spread and what to look for when sick people come to see them.

There are many other organizations that help keep us healthy. You may have heard of groups such as the American Cancer Society or the American Heart Association. You can find out more about the people who help keep us safe and healthy by going to kidshealth.org.

title: Reading Nutrition Charts - How Much Fat?
text:
Have you seen the nutrition charts on food packages? Those charts tell us what's in the food we are eating. Laws say companies that sell food products have to give us that information. Nutrition charts list the number of calories in a serving and how much protein, carbohydrates and fat it contains. Most list the amount of vitamins and minerals (if any) you will get from that food.

You've probably heard a lot of people talking about the fat in our food. We all need some fat in the things we eat. But how much fat is too much? Health experts suggest no more than 30 percent of our daily calories should come from fat. When you add up the total calories in everything you eat each day, 30 percent or less should be fat.

Most third-graders can eat 72 grams of fat per day. (A gram is a metric unit of measurement that equals 0.035 ounces.) Here's how we came up with that number: Experts recommend third-graders eat about 2,400 calories a day. Thirty percent of 2,400 is 720, so 720 of your daily calories can come from fat. Fat is usually about 10 calories per gram, and 720 divided by 10 equals 72. That means you can eat up to 72 grams of fat each day.

Conduct a fat-finding experiment. Go to your kitchen and choose five packages of your favorite foods. Put them on the table so that you can look at them. (If you choose any frozen foods, use them first and get them back in the freezer quickly. Don't let them start to thaw.)

On the table on this page, write down the name of each food, its serving size and the number of grams of fat a serving contains. In some foods, one serving may have eight grams of fat, while other foods may only have one gram of fat per serving.

After you finish filling in the chart, compare the foods. Which has the least and which has the most fat? Don't forget serving sizes will vary. Write about what you discovered in your journal. Think about the other foods you eat each day. How can you be sure you are eating what is most nutritious?

title: Writing Connection
text:
Imagine you are a celebrity and you’ve been asked to endorse a product. Write a commercial for that product.

Remember — you’ll be the star of the commercial. The product you endorse can be real or something you made up. You can ask some of your friends to be in the commercial, too. Practice a few times, then perform your commercial for the class.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: As you read this week’s magazine, circle or highlight five words that are new to you. Write the words on a piece of paper. Try to figure out the meaning of the words by reading the words and sentences around them. Write what you think the words mean and compare your definition to a dictionary definition.

title: Making Healthy Choices
text:
Your body is growing and changing. This is an important time in your body's development, because you are approaching the time doctors call adolescence. That's the time in your life between ages 10 and 19. The choices you make during those years will affect the way you grow and develop.

You know you should eat right and exercise, but have you ever thought about how much time you spend in front of the television screen? Get a notebook and keep track of how much time you spend watching TV for one week. Then, add up the total number of hours. You might be surprised when you see the total. Did you watch some shows you really wouldn't have minded missing? What else could you have done during that time that may have been a better choice?

The choices you make about how much TV to watch can also affect your health. Some people believe watching too much television can be harmful to the development of your brain, your social skills and even your eyes and ears. Believe it or not, your body is getting you ready to become an adult. It's important now to spend as much of your free time as possible developing your mind and body. Watching lots of television might be relaxing, but it's not good for you.

After tracking your TV time for a week, see if you can cut that number in half the next week. If that is too much for you, just try to cut down by a few hours. What could you do during that time instead of watching television? You could play outside, read a book, build a birdhouse, play cards or a board game, make a card for someone, write a letter, draw a picture, ride your bike, bake cookies - the list could go on and on. What other fun activities can you think of? Try to cut back a little bit at a time and see if you feel better at home and at school. You probably won't miss TV as much as you think you will, especially if you keep busy doing other fun things.

This week we're going to learn about the stages of growth that human beings go through, some of which you are experiencing right now. Turn the page, and you'll see what you've got to look forward to.

title: Put Down that Salt Shaker!
text:
Yum! Yum! Who doesn't love to shake salt onto popcorn, corn on the cob and mashed potatoes? And don't those salty pretzels and potato chips taste delicious? There's no doubt about it. We love our salt, and we need some salt to stay healthy. But too much salt can cause high blood pressure, and that can be very bad for your heart.

"I don't add much salt to my food," you may say. That may be true. However, have you looked at the back of the boxes and cans of the foods you eat? There's an awful lot of salt in foods like soup, lunchmeat, snacks and crackers. More than threefourths of the salt we eat comes from processed (already cooked) foods.

How much salt do you need? The U.S. government recommends that you eat no more than 2,400 milligrams of sodium each day. That's about a teaspoon of salt. If you have one cup of chicken noodle soup and some peanut butter crackers for lunch, you are eating more than half of the salt you need in just that one meal.

One great way to eat less salt is to eat more fresh fruits and veggies. They're naturally low in sodium. OK, so you don't think veggies taste as good as chips. Try to learn to like more veggies. Your heart will thank you for it.

title: Human Development
text:
I'll bet you've learned in science class about the stages a caterpillar goes through on its way to becoming a butterfly. Perhaps you've also talked about frogs and other animals and how they change as they grow into adulthood. Well, did you know you're an animal (a mammal) that also goes through growth in a variety of stages? Right now, you have already passed through two of those stages, and you will soon leave the third. There are five stages in all, so you're about halfway there.

The Prenatal Stage

The first stage of development is one you don't even remember. It's called the prenatal stage, the time before birth. It began while you were in your mother's womb and continued until you were born. During this stage you changed the most. While you were inside your mother's body you developed all the body parts, organs and systems you would need to live.

Infancy

The second stage of development, which you probably don't remember either, is called infancy. Infancy lasts from the time you were born until you were about 2 years old. During this period, you experienced a growth spurt (a time when you change quickly). Your body became much bigger and stronger. You learned to talk, sit up, crawl and walk.

Childhood

You're getting close to the end of the third stage of development, which is called childhood. This stage lasts from the time you're 2 years old until you are about 10. You continue to grow during this time period, although it happens more slowly than all the growth your body has done in earlier years. You get taller and stronger, and you learn to communicate better. Think of all the things you've learned since you were 2 years old! You can now read and write, add, subtract, draw, dance, play soccer and much more!

Adolescence

From about age 10 to 19 is the stage called adolescence. This is the final growth spurt of your life. During this time you'll go through a lot of physical and emotional changes. You may have mood swings that cause you to be really happy one day and down in the dumps the next. Your body will continue to change as you become an adult.

Adulthood

The final growth stage is adulthood. During this time, you won't have any more growth spurts but you will continue to grow. You'll grow emotionally, intellectually and socially during this time. (Growing intellectually means you continue to learn.) Older adults are in the final stage of life. You may know some elderly people, and you may have noticed that they are no longer as physically fit as some younger people are. Although some of our physical abilities decline (get less strong) as we get older, it's still important to continue practicing the same good health habits as always.

No matter what stage of development you're in, keep exercising and making good choices. Your body will reward you in the end.

title: Health Careers
text:
Are you interested in health and nutrition? Perhaps you could make a career out of your interest. The most rewarding jobs are the ones people really enjoy doing, so find something you love and learn more about it. There are more than 250 different health-related careers - far more than just doctors, nurses and dentists. Here are some health-related jobs that may interest you:

Athletic Trainers - These people work with athletes to help them stay in shape and train for upcoming sports events. They also help them get back in shape after an injury.

Radiologic Technologist - Have you ever had an x-ray taken? That's what these people do. They are qualified to operate the machinery that takes the "pictures" of your bones.

Physical Therapist - Anyone who has ever been in an accident can tell you how important these people are. They help you learn to get around again after you've hurt yourself. If the accident leaves your arm or leg permanently damaged, a physical therapist helps you learn to make changes that will help you live with your new situation.

Optometrist - If you're having trouble seeing, you might want to go to this doctor. An optometrist is someone who is qualified to check vision and prescribe glasses

These are just a few ideas. Want to know more? Go to your library and do some research. Check out "Career Ideas for Kids who like Science" by Diane Lindsey Reeves. This is a terrific book that just might help you decide what you want to be when you get to the fifth stage of development - adulthood.

title: Clean and Healthy
text:
It's the end of a long, hot school day and you plop down right next to your friend on the bus. Your friend makes a face and scoots closer to the window. What's up?

Keeping your body clean is an important part of staying healthy. Not only is it more enjoyable for those around you, but it also helps you feel good about yourself. So, where do we start? Well, let's start with washing our hands. Are they clean? Is there dirt under your nails? Make sure you're always washing your hands well before eating and after using the restroom. This will also kill any germs on your hands and will keep you healthier.

What else could cause odor? Clothes get stained and they need to be changed every day. Does someone in your household smoke? Smoke gets into your clothes and, although you may not notice it, others can detect the strong smell of smoke in your clothes and on your body. See if you can arrange for family members to smoke outside. (This is also healthier for your lungs.)

We all know that we sweat. As we get older, the odor of our sweat can get worse. Most kids will ask their parents to buy them deodorant in about third or fourth grade. Some older kids may choose to use perfume, but it's more important that you stay clean. Spraying perfume on a dirty body will only make things worse.

Halitosis (hal-uh-toe-sis) is the medical name for bad breath. Bad breath can be caused by forgetting to brush your teeth or eating strong smelling foods (like garlic or onions). Make sure you brush your teeth twice a day to keep your breath fresh. If bad breath continues, ask your parents to take you to the doctor. Sometimes halitosis can be a sign of a medical problem.

No one likes to be near a dirty person or someone who stinks. You're old enough now to take charge of your body and keep it clean and healthy. Lather up!

title: Seeing Germs
text:
"Wash your hands." We all hear it everyday from our parents and teachers. Why? They tell us that because it will keep us from getting sick. Washing your hands helps keep the germs from getting into your body. How do adults know there are germs on your hands? They can't see them, right? Here's an experiment you can do to actually SEE the germs on your hands.

Materials

a paper towel

2 plastic sandwich bags

dirt

2 slices of bread

Directions

1. Tear the paper towel in half.

2. Wet each half of the towel and put one piece into each plastic bag.

3. Rub your fingers in the dirt.

4. Touch your dirty fingers to one slice of bread and put that slice in one of the bags along with the wet towel. Close it tightly.

5. Wash your hands well with soap and water. Take a full minute to make sure you get them completely clean. Sing "Happy Birthday" or watch the second hand on the clock, so you know when you've been washing at least a minute.

6. Touch the second slice of bread with your clean fingers and put it in the second bag. Seal that bag, too.

7. Keep an eye on the bread during the next several days.

What happens?

What do you see in each bag after a few days? The bread you touched with your clean hands will probably look fine, but there will be mold growing on the dirty bread. There's your proof that washing your hands washes away not only dirt, but also germs. Now, go wash your hands and get rid of some germs!

title: Growth Timeline
text:
Create a pictograph timeline to show how you've grown and changed already in your life. Find photos that show you as a baby, a toddler and at several different ages in your childhood. Try to end with a recent picture. Turn a sheet of paper sideways and use a ruler to draw a straight line from left to right. Near the beginning of the line, write the month, day and year you were born. Paste a newborn picture here, if you have one. Paste the other pictures along the time line and write the date and your age underneath each. You can also add some milestones you may not have pictures of. Do you know when you first walked?

Write that on the timeline. When did you head off to kindergarten? That's another great milestone to include.

On a separate sheet of paper, write a paragraph comparing and contrasting the way you look now and the way you looked in the earliest picture. In what ways have you changed? Do you see similarities in your face?

If you like, you can extend the timeline and draw pictures of how you think you'll look as you go through adolescence and adulthood. Think about how you might change both mentally and physically.

title: Writing Connection
text: Imagine a friend of yours has e-mailed you to tell you that she just got glasses. She thinks she picked cool frames and is ready to wear them to school, but she’s afraid some of the other kids will make fun of her. Write an imaginary letter back to her telling her why she shouldn’t worry about wearing her new glasses to school tomorrow. What will you say to make her feel better? Do you have suggestions about what she could say if someone does make fun of her? Remember to list some reasons why it’s important for her to wear her glasses, even if she is uncomfortable at first.

title: Who Helps Us Make the Right Choices?
text:
Each day of your life you're asked to make choices that affect your health. Will you have the French fries or the applesauce? Will you play on the computer or walk the dog? Will you drink milk or soda? Do you make these choices all by yourself? Not really. Even though you may think you're deciding on your own, you're often letting others influence your choice. For example, if all your friends are getting a soda instead of milk, you may be more likely to drink a soda, right? You don't want to be the only one left out. If your class attends an assembly about how important it is to exercise, will you be more likely to participate in P.E.? There's a good chance you will. If you hear your parents say smoking caused your grandfather's heart attack, will that affect your decision about cigarettes? It should.

You don't live in a vacuum. When we say vacuum, we're not talking about the thing that sucks up dirt off the floor. A vacuum is also a state of complete emptiness. It's impossible to live your life every day and not be affected by a person you meet, a newspaper article you read or a show you watch on TV.

How do these things alter (change) the decisions you make? That depends on who shares the information and how important that person's opinion is to you. Who do you listen to more often - your best friend or your best friend's younger brother? Chances are you care more about your friend's opinion than her brother's. It also depends on how much you trust the one who tells you something. Most students are more likely to believe something their teacher says than something they overheard an older kid say in the hallway. It's easier to trust your teacher than someone you may not know very well.

Many things influence the decisions we make, sometimes for better and sometimes for worse. Remember that, and you'll nearly always choose what is best for you, no matter what others say.

title: Three Cheers for Ears!
text:
Here's a riddle for you: What am I? You have two of me - one on each side of your head. I'm an ear, of course. How often do you really think about your ears and how to take care of them? Usually we forget all about our ears until we get an ear infection. But taking good care of our ears is very important.

Never, ever, ever put anything inside your ear. Even something as soft as a cotton swab can hurt your eardrum or ear canal. Only clean the outside of your ears. Earwax may seem gross, but there's a reason you have some in your ears. It helps protect them. If there's too much wax in your ears, it will usually come out on its own or you can ask your doctor to remove it safely.

You also need to protect your ears when you are at loud concerts or near anything that makes loud noises (like lawn mowers, airplanes or racecars). Wear earplugs so you don't hurt your hearing. If you're wearing headphones for your MP3 player, don't turn up the music too loudly. Any loud noise can cause temporary or even permanent hearing loss. Instead of ignoring our ears, we need to give them three cheers. Just make sure you cheer quietly!

title: Risky vs. Safe
text:
Risky behaviors are the things people do that could hurt them in some way. Safe behaviors are just the opposite. They are the things people do that probably won't hurt them. Risky behaviors are things like not wearing a bicycle helmet, smoking cigarettes or drinking alcohol. Wearing your helmet and staying away from cigarettes and alcohol are safe behaviors. Comparing risky and safe behaviors will help you make the right choices.

Riding a Bicycle

Do you wear your helmet every time you get on your bicycle, even if you are just going a few blocks? If not, that's risky. Each year thousands of people get head injuries during bicycle accidents. Many of them are serious enough to cause them to spend some time in the hospital, and some cause permanent brain damage. More than 500 people died in 2005 from head injuries they got in a bicycle accident. Choose safety. Wear your helmet every time you get on your bicycle.

Smoking Cigarettes

People who smoke cigarettes are taking lots of risks. Cigarettes give you bad breath, turn your teeth yellow and make your clothes stink. They make it harder for you to taste and smell. Smoking is addictive, too. Once you start, it's hard to stop. The longer you smoke, the greater your health risks are. You'll get colds more often, and before you know it, you'll have a cough that won't go away. It will become harder and harder to breathe. Eventually, smoking causes diseases like heart disease and cancer. And those diseases are killers.

The safest behavior is never to start smoking at all. You'll smell better, and you'll save lots of money. If you know someone who smokes, ask her to quit. Within eight hours of quitting, she'll cut the nicotine and carbon monoxide in her body by half. Two days after she stops, her senses of taste and smell will improve, and there is no more nicotine in her body. After three days, she'll find it easier to breathe. Over time, she will reduce her risk of heart disease and lung cancer. Is that amazing or what? When you stop smoking, your body starts healing itself right away!

Drinking Alcohol

Choosing to drink alcohol is another risky behavior. It can make you sick to your stomach and cause you to feel terrible even the next morning. Alcohol hurts your ability to make good decisions and sometimes makes people do embarrassing things they wouldn't normally do. You probably know that it's illegal to drink alcohol until you're at least 21 years old. When teenagers drink, they are breaking the law. They run the risk of being caught and maybe spending time in jail. Alcohol can be addictive, just as cigarettes are. When drinking alcohol becomes an addiction, it's hard to stop, even if you want to. Alcohol has many serious health risks. It can cause heart failure and brain damage. Over time, alcohol can do serious damage to your liver. Scars form on your liver, and it doesn't work the way it's supposed to. If your liver stops working altogether, you will die.

Choosing not to drink will help keep you out of trouble. You'll stay in control of your body and be able to make good decisions. People who don't drink alcohol are less likely to be overweight, and their blood pressure is usually lower. Saying no to alcohol keeps your liver healthy. It may even save your life.

You have the power to make either the risky choice or the safe choice. Look how the safe choices outweigh the risky choices in the examples we just talked about. Isn't it clear now which behavior you should choose?

title: Emergency!
text:
"It's an emergency!" How many times have you said that? Maybe it's really important to you, but is it really an emergency? A true medical emergency means that someone needs medical help immediately. Let's look at some examples and decide if they are true emergencies or not.

1. Your friend is eating at lunch and starts choking. Is this a true emergency? Yes! Get help right away.

2. Your little sister trips running down the stairs. She tumbles down the steps and lands at the bottom. She's not moving. Is this a true emergency? Yes! Call an adult or 911 right away.

3. You're running outside and you trip and skin your elbow. Is this an emergency? No, it's not. You may need a band-aid, but your life isn't at risk.

So what do you do if you find yourself in an emergency situation? First of all, take a deep breath and try to calm down a little. You can't be much help if you're not thinking clearly. If there's an adult around, get an adult immediately. If there's no adult around, call 911 and ask for help. Stay on the line and tell the operator where you are and what is happening.

There are also First Aid techniques you can learn that could help you save someone's life. Your local Red Cross can teach you how to perform the Heimlich maneuver on a choking victim and other First Aid techniques. If you're interested in learning more, ask your teacher to contact your local Red Cross and ask for a volunteer to visit your classroom to discuss First Aid. Who knows? Perhaps it could help you save someone's life someday.

title: All Kinds of Families
text:
If someone asked you to think of a dog, what kind of dog would come to mind? Do you think everyone would picture the same dog? Probably not. We would most likely think of different breeds, sizes and colors of dogs. The same thing would happen when different people think of a family. All families are different. Some children live with two parents, and some live with one.
Sometimes kids live with their grandparents or other relatives. Other kids are foster children, which means they live with a family that is not related to them. Isn't it great that there are so many different types of families?

Families can change, too. Do you have a younger brother or sister? When he or she was born, your family changed. Happy things like a new baby or someone getting married can change families. Sad things like a death in the family or a divorce can change families, too.

Different families have different cultures. Your friends' families may celebrate different holidays, worship in different ways or speak a second language. Ask your friends about traditions their families have. Learning about other cultures is fun and it helps everyone respect our differences.

What is your job in the family? You don't think you have a job? Sure you do! Everyone has responsibilities, or jobs, in their family. Most kids have chores like making the bed or clearing the table. Maybe you're an older child and you're responsible for being a good role model for a younger child. Everyone's responsibilities are important.

Although you may argue or disagree now and then, it's important to remember that families need each other for love and support. There is no other family on Earth exactly like yours. They are special, just like you.

title: Exercise Programs
text:
Why should you exercise? Well, for one thing, it makes your heart happy. If your heart is happy, then the rest of your body is happy. When you exercise, your heart gets more and more practice at taking oxygen through your bloodstream to the rest of your body. The more you exercise, the healthier your body is. Your organs get oxygen and your heart (which is a muscle) gets stronger. What could be better?

How healthy can your heart become in the next two weeks? Let's find out. Before you start this project, make sure you check with your parents. It can be dangerous for people with certain health risks to exercise without a doctor's consent.

First, take your resting pulse. Remember how to do that? Count how many times your heart beats in one minute. Use the chart below or make your own chart to keep track of your progress.

Now it's time to begin your exercise program. Doing 20 minutes of exercise each day is a good way to start. You can do any aerobic exercise you enjoy, such as jumping rope, walking in place or doing jumping jacks. (Aerobic exercise speeds up your heart rate.) You can do a different aerobic exercise each day or stick to the same one.

Each day, take your pulse just before and just after you exercise. Did your resting heart rate change after one week of exercising? If not, keep exercising for another week or two and see what happens. (You may want to increase your exercise time to 30 minutes, too.) After your body gets used to exercising every day, you'll find that your resting heart rate will be lower. For example, instead of 95 beats per minute, it may drop to 80 beats per minute. That is great news for your heart and your body. Keep up the exercise and see how healthy you can be.

title: Finding Your Heart Rate
text:
The number of times your heart beats in one minute is called your heart rate. For kids your age, the average heart rate is between 80 and 110 beats per minute. (But everyone is different.) Here's a way to find out your heart rate.

Materials

a cardboard tube from an empty paper towel roll

a friend

a stopwatch

a pencil

a notebook

Directions

1. Put one end of the tube near the center of your friend's chest where his heart is. Listen through the other end of the tube. Can you hear his heart beating?

2. Start the stopwatch and count the number of beats you hear in one minute.

3. Record the number of beats in your notebook.

4. Have your friend listen to your heart and record your heart rate.

Is the number of beats different for you than for your friend? Do you think your heart rates would be different if you exercised for one minute before? Make a prediction, then try it and see. Write the results in the notebook. Talk to several other classmates and see how your heart rates compare.

Fun Fact: Did you know that each time your heart beats it releases some electricity? Doctors can measure this electricity using an ECG (electrocardiogram) machine. These machines help doctors learn if their patients' hearts are beating properly.

title: Writing Connection
text:
Most people celebrate the big things that happen in their lives, but all of the good things that happen are important, even if they seem small. Keep track of everything that is worth celebrating by starting a Success Journal.

What is a success? It’s something you have been working toward that you’ve managed to achieve. It could be anything from writing a paragraph in cursive to getting along better with your siblings. Keep a notebook and a pen or pencil next to your bed. At the end of each day, write down at least one success you had at school, at home or anywhere. Any success, no matter how small, is worth celebrating.

The next time you are feeling down, go back and read some entries in your Success Journal. Look at all you’ve accomplished! There is no one quite like you, and you should be very proud of all your successes — big or small.

title: Good Listeners
text:
One of the best assets of a good friend is being a great listener. (An asset is something valuable or good.) When you're going through a tough time, doesn't it help to sit down with a friend and tell that person about what's upsetting you? If you show your friends you can be a good listener, they will be there to listen when you need someone to talk with, too. How do you learn to be a good listener?

Be sure you always make eye contact with the person who is talking to you. There's nothing more annoying than talking to someone and having him looking around the room or watching the clock.

Let your friend know you're listening by repeating some of the points he made. Say them in a different way, so that you aren't just copying his words. Imagine your friend tells you he broke his brother's favorite toy because his brother tattled on him. You may want to say something like, "It sounds like you were feeling hurt." This will let him know you're listening to him and may help him express his angry feelings better the next time he's upset with his brother.

Ask your friend about his feelings. It's wonderful to have someone care about how you feel. Sometimes all we need when we're upset is for someone to listen to how we feel about the situation.

Don't give your friend any advice at the beginning of the conversation. If you do, your friend won't get the chance to express all his feelings. It's important to let him get all his emotions out. After he's finished telling you all about the problem, you can help him brainstorm some solutions. You may not be able to decide on a solution right away, but just talking the problem out will really help your friend - and you, too.

title: Sibling Rivalry
text:
A sibling is a brother or sister. How do you feel about your siblings? If you're like most kids, some days you love them and other days you may wish you were an only child. Brothers and sisters can sometimes be bossy, demanding, whiny and annoying.

Rivalry is competition. You may compete with your brothers and sisters to see who gets better grades in school, who plays soccer better or who gets the last slice of pizza. Sometimes you may feel as if you're competing with them for your parents' time and attention. Sibling rivalry can get complicated, and sometimes things don't seem fair.

When it comes to siblings, you may feel proud, jealous, angry and irritated all at once. That's a lot of confusing feelings to sort out! Although you will probably admit that you love your siblings, there are times when you may need a break from them. That's OK. Everyone needs some alone time. Try talking with your parents and letting them know that you need some quiet time now and then without your siblings.

Hang in there when things aren't going too well with your siblings. Believe it or not, in 10 years or so you may find that your brother or sister is your best friend.

title: Im So Mad, I Could Scream!
text:
Your teacher just took away your recess. She accused you of talking when the person behind you was the one making noise. You're angry because now you're being punished for something you didn't do.

What do you do now? There are a lot of choices. However, if you lose your temper, throw your crayon box and storm out of the room, you are not handling your anger well. Not only will you get in more trouble, but the teacher will also be less likely to listen to your side of the story because of the way you acted. Now she'll be focused on what she did see you do and not so worried about what she thought you did.

How do you keep from losing your temper? This is something that even some adults have trouble with, but it is an important thing to learn. First, you need to understand that it's OK to feel angry. Anger is a natural emotion everyone feels sometimes. But how you handle the anger may not be OK.

When we're in danger, our bodies react by giving us a lot of energy to help get us out of danger. The same thing happens when you're angry. That energy is rushing through your body almost like a ticking time bomb. You may feel as if you are about to explode. Here are some tricks to defuse (to calm down) your anger.

The first thing to do is check your body language. Are you making fists? Is your jaw tight and locked? Get control physically by breathing in and out slowly. You are in control of your body. Close your eyes and visualize something calming such as waves on the ocean or snowcapped mountains or flowers waving in the breeze. (Visualize means to picture something in your mind.)

Give yourself a time-out if you need it. If you're allowed to go to the restroom without asking, do that. If you can't leave your seat, try counting slowly to 25.

Visualizing how you want to handle the situation may help you calm down, too. Imagine yourself explaining the truth to your teacher and picture her believing you. This will help put you in a positive mood instead of an angry one.

Sometimes teachers are too busy to handle students' concerns at that exact moment. Write your teacher a note when you have free time, explaining what you believe really happened and ask her to talk with you when she has time. Most teachers will be willing to listen to your side of the story and will appreciate the way you controlled your anger.

Remember - even if things don't work out the way you want them to, it's important to get your anger under control. Losing your temper, saying things you shouldn't or acting in a violent manner will only cause more problems in the long run. This is a skill that takes a lot of practice, so keep working on it every time you get angry. Before long, you'll be handling your anger better than some adults do! Then you can teach them how to do it.

title: How to Say You're Sorry
text:
Have you ever had a big argument with a friend? Maybe you wanted to apologize but you felt so uncomfortable that you didn't know how to say you're sorry. What's a good way to apologize?

The first thing to do is admit that you did or said something wrong. It takes two to argue, so both of you have to admit you did something hurtful. Your friend is probably feeling guilty about the argument and missing you, too. Neither of you wants to be the first to say something, but remember - the first person to speak up is the bravest.

It's best to make your apology when no one else is around. If your friend is surrounded by other people, she may want to continue the argument just to put on a show. Or she may be embarrassed if you talk about it in front of others.

Most importantly, make the effort. A good friend is worth hanging on to.

title: Rules for Resolving Conflicts
text:
1. Attack the problem, not the person.
2. Listen with an open mind.
3. No hitting, teasing or name-calling allowed.
4. Focus on the problem, not on the person.
5. Treat the other person's feelings with respect.
6. Take responsibility for your actions.

Cut out these rules and paste them on an index card (or just copy them on the card). Keep the card in your desk to help you remember what to do when you have a conflict with another person.

title: One Day in Peace
text: Go to www.cultureofpeace.com and read the online picture book called "One Day in Peace." It's available in 21 languages. Then write down some ways you can work for peace in your school, home or neighborhood. What little things can you do to help move the hope of peace along? Say, "Excuse me?" Open the door for someone? Hold your temper until you calm down? Only you can decide how to help change the world.

title: Peace is a Choice
text:
Two goats meet on a narrow bridge. They have a choice. They can choose peace: One goat can back up and let the other pass. Or they can choose war: They fight until one is knocked off the bridge.

Think of these goats the next time you are dealing with a conflict with someone. Who will choose peace and move aside? Peace is a choice, but you must decide you want it. Then, you must work toward it.

The story of the two goats is a Russian folktale. If you want to read more stories like this one, go to the library and look for "Peace Tales" by Margaret Read MacDonald.

title: Nonverbal Communication
text:
How easy do you think it would be to go an entire day using only nonverbal communication (communicating without words) to "talk" with others? It may be more difficult than you think. Before you try to make it through a whole day with no words, try this activity. You'll need a deck of playing cards.

Gather in groups of five or six and sit in a circle facing each other. You'll be playing "Go Fish," a card game you've probably played before. If not, ask someone in your group to explain the rules ahead of time or check with your teacher.

When you play, instead of asking out loud for a card, you'll need to hold up the correct number of fingers to let the other players know what you're looking for. But what about aces and face cards? Make up some signals that will stand for those cards. Once everyone knows what the signals are, play the game but don't talk at all. (It's actually much harder than it sounds.) If you want, add a rule that says anyone who talks has to skip a turn.

title: Writing Connection
text: Have you ever had a hard time apologizing to someone? If it’s too hard to apologize to your friend in person, you can write a letter. Make sure you admit what you did wrong and let your friend know you feel bad about it. Give it a try right now. Imagine you and a friend had a big argument, and now you want to apologize. Write your friend a note and tell him or her you are sorry. If you ever need to write a real apology letter, you’ll know just what to do.

title: It's OK to Ask for Help
text:
Ever have one of those days when everything goes wrong? Your mom and your step-dad got into a huge argument while you were getting ready for school. You hate it when they yell. You nearly missed the bus, and when you got to school you realized you left your homework on the kitchen table. Then your friend reminds you about the big math test you have to take, and you forgot to study! What do you do?

Anytime you have problems you feel are too big for you to handle, it's important to ask for help. No one solves every problem that comes their way on their own. Everyone needs help sometimes - adults, children, your parents - even the President of the United States has an entire group of people who help him make decisions.

The first thing to remember is that it's OK to ask for help. Asking for help doesn't make you weak or dumb. It actually shows you're strong enough and smart enough to know when you can't handle something alone. Think about this: What might happen if you don't ask for help? Will anything get better or will it more likely get worse?

Next, decide who might be able to help you. Talking to your parents is a great place to start. After all, it's their job to take care of you, and part of that job is helping you with problems. Teachers are always willing to try to help you handle any problems you're having at school or at home. The school counselor and the principal are glad to listen and to help you figure out what to do. Doctors are also good people to ask for help. They know a lot about kids' health - both physical and mental. Stand up for your health. Ask for help whenever you need it.

title: Healing Broken Bones
text:
Have you ever known anyone who had a cast on an arm or leg? If it's not you who broke a bone, a cast can seem pretty cool! It's kind of like an autograph book that you wear. Not long ago, casts were really heavy and itchy and they were always white. Today, they're much lighter and they come in lots of fun colors and designs.

How does all of this work? If you think you broke a bone, you get an x-ray. If the x-ray shows a broken bone, your doctor will set the bone, so it will heal the right way. Setting the bone puts it in the right position.

Next, your doctor may decide you need a cast. A cast is like a hard bandage that helps keep the bone from moving around. The doctor wraps cotton around your arm or leg to protect your skin. Then she puts a layer of wet fiberglass bandages around the cotton. (Fiberglass is pretty much what it sounds like. It's a type of fiber made of glass.) The cast dries quickly, but you may have to keep it on for a few weeks. When it's time to take off the cast, your doctor will use a special saw. Don't worry. You won't get hurt. You end up with a cool souvenir - one that reminds you to be careful with your bones!

title: Understanding What Doctors Say
text:
Have you ever gone to the doctor and listened to her using words like diagnosis and tonsillitis? She may tell your dad that you need to have a test - a test with a name you can't even pronounce. You can't stand up for your health if you don't understand what the doctor is saying. Keep reading to learn some words and parts of words that will help you know what doctors are talking about.

Diseases and Conditions

Viruses and bacteria are those nasty germs that make you sick. Inflammation is the swelling, redness, pain and burning you feel when part of your body is hurt or infected with germs. Sometimes doctors use the suffix -itis on the end of a word. That suffix means inflammation. If your doctor says you have tonsillitis, she means there is inflammation in your tonsils. If you've ever had a rash, the doctor might have called it dermatitis. Derma means skin, so dermatitis is a skin inflammation. Here's another one: -osis means disease. You may have heard commercials about medicine for osteoporosis. If you know that osteo means bone, you can figure out that osteoporosis is a disease of the bones.

Making a Diagnosis

Do you see the suffix -osis in diagnosis? You know that it has something to do with disease, right? When a doctor makes a diagnosis, she is looking for a disease. The best diagnosis is that you don't have a disease at all! But how does she know whether you have a disease? Your doctor has many special tools to look at and listen to your body. She may use an otoscope to look in your ears or a stethoscope to listen to your heart. An instrument with scope in its name is one that helps your doctor "see" what's going on. You've probably had your temperature taken with a thermometer, too. An instrument with meter in its name is one that measures something. Thermo means heat, so a thermometer is an instrument that measures heat. It tells the doctor if you have a fever. Hey! This isn't so hard after all, is it?

Tests and Machines

Doctors always want to be sure they make the right diagnosis. Sometimes that means the patient has to take a test. If you fall off your bike, you may need a test that lets the doctor see inside your body . Some tests are done by machines that use special cameras to take pictures of your bones or organs. If your doctor thinks you may have broken your arm when you fell, she will probably have you get an x-ray to find out for sure. If you weren't wearing a helmet, you may get a test called a CAT scan that looks at one section of your brain at a time. (Always wear your helmet when you're riding a bike!) If you don't understand something a doctor says, ask her to say it in a different way. If you aren't sure what a certain instrument does, ask the doctor to explain it. The more you know, the more you can stand up for your health.

title: Germs - Yuck!
text:
"Eww, you have germs!" you might say when a classmate sneezes. What are germs anyway? How do we spread germs and is there a way to keep from getting them? Germs are tiny organisms (living things) that cause disease. Once the germs get in your body, they produce toxins (poisons) that make you sick. Depending on the type of germ, it could give you a sore throat, a fever or even cause vomiting.

So how do these little creatures get into your body? First of all, remember that they are so tiny that we can't even see them without a microscope. Germs can be spread through the air. If someone sneezes and doesn't cover his or her mouth, the germs could be spread to others. Some germs, especially viruses, can live for a long time on the surface of objects. For example, let's say someone has the flu and sneezes. He covers his mouth, but doesn't wash his hands. Then he goes outside. He touched the doorknob to go outside, right? So you come along a little while later and touch the same doorknob to go outside. Now the virus is on your hands. If you put your hands near your eyes, nose or mouth, the virus can get into your body.

How do we fight these mighty germs? Soap and water is the magic weapon. Wash your hands every time you cough or sneeze and after playing outside. Always wash your hands before you eat and after you use the restroom. Make sure you don't spread disease to others either. Use a tissue when you cough or sneeze and throw it in the trash, so someone else doesn't have to pick it up and get germs.

Wouldn't it be great to get through the entire school year without getting sick once? Try to keep as many germs from entering your body as you can by using that awesome weapon - soap and water.

title: What Can You Do About Pollution?
text:
How many different types of pollution can you think of? There may be more than you think. There's air pollution (outside and inside), land pollution (trash and chemicals like fertilizers), water pollution (Have you seen what floats in some of our lakes and rivers? Yuck!) and noise pollution (Loud, unwanted noises can harm your ears.), just to mention a few. So, who cares, right? Well, all these pollutions can affect your health and well being. For example, air pollution can cause short-term effects such as headaches or allergies. It can also cause long-term effects such as lung cancer and heart disease. We are also harming other living things on our planet. Water pollution kills animals and harms our natural resources.

So, what can we do about it? There are a lot of things that you can do to slow down the effects of pollution on our planet. First of all, remember the three R's: Reduce, Reuse and Recycle. Reduce your waste by not throwing as many things in the trash. Reuse things you don't need anymore. Can you give away that old toy instead of tossing it in the trashcan? Plastic, paper and aluminum can all be easily recycled.

You can also choose to purchase environmentally safe products. Look at the glass cleaner you have at home. Does it have ammonia in it? That could be harmful to your health. Look for products that list all the ingredients. If there is a long list of chemicals, that product could be harmful to you. It's not too hard to find "green" products that are safer for us and for the environment. But don't throw those old products in the trash or down the drain! That waste is hazardous and can cause land and water pollution. Your local department of public works can tell you where and how to dispose of those things properly.

Take charge of your health and the health of your planet. Everyone needs to work together to make our planet pollution free.

title: Take a Poll
text:
Take a Poll

Who would you turn to when you have a question and really need to talk with someone you trust? Who do you think most people would trust? There's a way to know what people think. Create your own poll (a survey of the public) to find out.

Materials

2 sheets of paper

a pen or pencil

Poll Question

If you could only choose one person from this list, which one would you choose to talk to about a personal problem you were having?

Directions

1. Make a list of choices. You could include parent, doctor, teacher, friend or anyone else. (Just for fun, throw in some different possibilities such as your plumber or Hannah Montana.)

2. Hit the hallways and ask students and adults the poll question.

3. Write the answers given by students on one piece of paper and the answers given by adults on the other.

4. Graph the results of your poll. Compare the graph of the adult answers to the graph of the student answers.

Is there a difference between the students' choices and the adults' choices? If you didn't find very much difference, why do you think that is so? Write a paragraph explaining your findings and why you believe the majority of people chose the person they did.

title: Make a Pinhole Camera
text:
This week you learned that some machines use special cameras that take photographs of the inside of our bodies. Those machines are really complicated, but here's a way to see how a camera works.

Materials

scissors

ruler

shoebox

clear tape

aluminum foil

waxed paper

a straight pin

table

lamp

another object of any kind

Directions

1. Cut a one-inch square in the end of the shoebox and tape a piece of foil over the hole.

2. Cut the opposite end of the shoebox off completely.

3. Tape a piece of waxed paper over the open end of the shoebox.

4. Put the lid on the shoebox and tape it down.

5. Use the straight pin to make a small hole in the center of the foil.

6. Set the lamp on the table and turn it on. Set the object in front of the lamp.

7. Point the pinhole end of the shoebox at the lamp.

8. Look at the waxed paper.

What Happens

You should see an image of the object showing up on the waxed paper. (The image will be upside down.) If the waxed paper were film, you would have been able to take the picture.

If you want to know more, do some research to answer these questions. Why do you think this works and how? How does light travel? What causes the image to be upside down?
