title: Welcome to Missouri Community Studies Weekly!
text:
This year we're going to learn about what makes a community tick and how we all work together to make it a pretty great place to live!

Welcome to Missouri Community Studies Weekly! This year, we will be learning about the great state of Missouri and about our own local communities. We will be learning all about social studies, or the study of people, their history, their government, where they live and how they get along. We will find out what it means to be a part of a community and what we must do to be good citizens.

As part of our social studies lessons, we will learn about the history, geography, economics, government and culture of Missouri. We will also study famous Americans and Missourians, learn how their efforts have improved our lives, and how they showed good citizenship and values.

In this week's issue, we will learn more about what social studies is, why we study it and how Missouri Community Studies Weekly can help you learn more about your community, Missouri, America and the world. Turn the page to find out more about what's in store for you this year from Missouri Community Studies Weekly and hang on for the ride of your life!

title: Philanthropy and Values
text:
Maybe you have heard the word "philanthropy" before. What does it mean? It describes actions that people make for the good of other people. What is a value? It's a way of behaving that people believe is good - like believing it's good to be honest. Is honesty one of your values?

One way you can practice philanthropy today is to help yourself and others learn good values. How do you learn good values? You can learn them from your parents and grandparents, your teachers at school or church and other people you trust.

You can also learn them from people that have been recognized for doing good things for society. An easy way to learn about people that have done good things is to visit values.com. Values.com has lots of stories and short videos that highlight the traits that make each of us better people. They even have billboards on the highway to remind you about good values.

For example, you may have seen a billboard that looks like the one shown here.

This billboard is about Oral Lee Brown, who saved money from her job to send 19 kids to college... all by herself! Wow! Isn't that cool? You can learn about lots of other people who practice philanthropy at values.com. Be sure to look for more of their "billboards" on Page 4 of Studies Weekly this year. We think they're so cool we want to remind you to check them out!

title: Community Members Have Things in Common
text:
The state of Missouri is made up of hundreds of communities. A community is a group of any size whose members share certain things. For example, community members share the same location, which means that they live in or near the same place. Community members also share the same government, the same schools, the same parks, and often, the same history. Because community members live, work and play together each day, they build common memories. These common memories link members of a community together and help them to see the world in a similar way.

Studying Our Communities

This year, we will be studying the history of your community as part of our social studies units. Social studies is the study of geography, history, economics and civics. We will organize our studies this year in the following way:

Geography

Geography is the study of the Earth and its features, such as lakes, rivers, mountains and deserts. The first few weeks of Community Studies Weekly will focus on the geography of the land on which we live.

History

History is the story of our past, including our ancestors (those who came before us), our country and the changes that have brought us from where we were to where we are today. Community Studies Weekly will spend several weeks studying the history of our world, nation, state and communities.

Economics

Economics is the study of how things are made, bought, sold and used. We will discover how our communities provide for the needs of others, yet depend on others to provide for our needs as well.

Civics

Civics is the study of government and of how citizens get along with each other in a group. We will learn how our governments are organized, what it means to be a good citizen and how we can make our community a better place to live.

Our Missouri History Brings Us Together

All of us living in Missouri share an exciting and interesting history that stretches back hundreds of years. Our history includes all of the people who have called Missouri their home, from the very first American Indians, to the early French and British settlers, to the hard-working farmers, pioneers and factory owners, to the business and technology heroes of our day. All of these people and events have left their mark on our state, and our goal this year is to learn about who they are and what they did to help build our great state of Missouri.

United States Citizens Share Important Traditions and Beliefs

As citizens of the same country, we are members of an even larger community. Americans share many important traditions and beliefs. (A tradition is a custom or belief that is passed down from parents to children.)

As United States citizens, we are joined together by our belief in freedom, our respect for the founding fathers, our understanding of what our flag represents, our belief that all men and women are created equal and many more beliefs and ideas.

Celebrations Help Us Remember the Past

We also share in the celebrations that we hold each year to remind us of our American values. We will look at many of these celebrations and how they help us to pass the memories (things we remember) of one generation on to the next and make certain that we don't forget our past. We join together each year to celebrate Thanksgiving, the Fourth of July, Veterans Day, Memorial Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, and many other occasions. These celebrations bring us together as members of a larger community and keep our important memories alive.

During our studies this year, we will explore what it means to be a member of a community. We will also find out more about Missouri, what it was like in the past, what it is like today and what it may be like in the future. Join us for an unforgettable experience!

title: Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
text:
Here in the United States, we think of our own individual family unit of parents and children as our "family" and of our extended family members as "relatives." If you lived in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, your "family unit" would be much larger. In that country, "family" means parents, children, grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins!

In Riyadh, the extended family plays a very important role in the lives of young people. It even helps to choose whom a young person will marry and what his or her life will be like. In the past, the families of the bride and groom always arranged marriages in Riyadh. These arranged marriages still take place in Riyadh, but young people are now beginning to have more input in the choice of whom they wish to marry.

In Riyadh, women usually live with their parents until they get married. Men usually move out and start their own household when they get married. However, at least one son stays and lives with his parents to take care of them as they get older. If this son gets married, his wife and children will live with the husband's parents as well.

Large family groups are very important to the people of Riyadh, and they play a huge role in the lives of the young people as they grow up.

title: Edwin Hubble
text:
In each issue of Missouri Community Studies Weekly, we will be spotlighting a famous citizen from our state who has improved our lives in some way. This week, we will be learning about Edwin Hubble, one of the greatest astronomers (one who studies the universe) in history.

Edwin Hubble was born in Marshfield, Missouri, in 1889. He attended the University of Chicago and later went to Oxford University in England to study law. He discovered that astronomy, or the study of the universe, was much more interesting to him than the law, so he returned to Chicago and graduated from the Yerkes Observatory in 1917 with a Ph.D.

Hubble did research to prove that galaxies are really "island universes," or that each galaxy is made up of millions of groups of stars. Hubble also created a system for organizing information about each galaxy that has been discovered. His greatest discovery is known as the Hubble Constant, which shows that the speed a galaxy is traveling is connected to how far it is from us. NASA named the Hubble Space Telescope after him, which orbits our Earth and is used to see deep into space.

Edwin Hubble is one of the greatest astronomers of all time and is also one of our great Missouri citizens.

title: Roman Aqueducts
text:
In Community Studies Weekly, you will learn more about great inventions and technology that have improved our lives in some way. Today, let's look at an ancient but interesting invention we know as the Roman Aqueducts.

Whenever a large group of people lives together, it needs a good water supply for drinking, washing and cleaning. Hundreds of years ago, most people lived in small villages where they were responsible for getting their own water from wells, springs, or streams. In ancient Rome, however, the people knew that a large city needed a better way to get water. They tried many ideas and finally settled on a very creative way to move water: They used a system of aqueducts, or huge ditches to carry water from where it was available to where the people of the city could use it.

These large aqueducts were built both under and above ground and were made to slope downhill so that gravity would carry the water from a lake or river down to the city below. The water was often carried in pipes made from lead or terra cotta (baked clay), and the people living in the city could get water anytime they needed it. Many of these Roman aqueducts were built as early as 312 B.C. (more than 2,300 years ago) and are still being used today.

The invention of the aqueduct made it possible for people to live in large groups and still get the water they needed each day.

title: Anne Hutchinson
text:
We will also use Community Studies Weekly to study the biography, or life story, of an important American who has made a difference in the world. Anne Hutchinson is this week's American hero.

A strong, yet gentle, woman, Anne came to America in 1634. She left her home in England and settled at the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Anne held religious meetings in her home and taught some ideas that others didn't like. She told listeners that people were saved by the grace of God, rather than by any of their own good works. This idea upset the Puritan leaders in New England and made them angry. They believed that Anne was trying to destroy the religious beliefs, as well as the governing laws, of the community.

In 1637, Anne was put on trial by the General Court of Massachusetts. Governor John Winthrop and the rest of the court found Anne guilty of disobeying the Puritan ministers, and she was sent away from the colony. Anne and her family moved to what is now known as Portsmouth, Rhode Island, and later to Long Island, New York.

Anne is an example of individual courage. She stood up for her rights to follow her own religious beliefs no matter what those in the government thought of them. She knew that everyone has the right to believe what he or she wants and refused to back down from that belief.

title: World Communities
text:
In each issue of Community Studies Weekly, we will visit cities and communities all over the world. On our journey, we will make stops in Europe, South America, Africa, Asia and several places in between.

As we explore different world communities, we will discover that some things with which we are familiar here at home are pretty much the same everywhere we travel. We will also learn about things in other communities that are very different from what we are used to.

We will find out why people chose to build their communities where they did, what businesses help the community to survive, how the citizens of the community live, and what problems these communities face.

In addition, we will discover how modern inventions make it possible for communities all over the world to stay connected to each other. We will also learn how events in one community can influence communities half a world away.

Keep an eye on the World Communities column in each issue to learn more about places you may have heard of, and some you haven't! You may be surprised to learn that communities all over the world share many of your community's strengths, weaknesses and challenges.

title: Timeline
text:
In each issue of Missouri Community Studies Weekly, you will find maps, charts, graphs and tables that will help you get a clear picture of the topic covered in that week’s newspaper. In this week’s issue, you will find a timeline of important events in Missouri state history. A timeline is a list of events in order of the earliest to the most recent. Take a look below at a brief timeline of the history of the state of Missouri.

Missouri History Timeline

1682 — Explorer Cavalier claims Louisiana Territory for France.

1724 — Fort Orleans is built on the Missouri River, and is later abandoned.

1803 — The United States buys the Louisiana Territory from France.

1821 — Missouri becomes the 24th state, with St. Charles as its temporary capital.

1826 — State legislature meets in Jefferson City.

1861 — The Battle of Wilson’s Creek is fought.

1873 — The first public kindergarten in the country opens.

1901 — The first state fair is held in Sedalia.

1945 — Harry S. Truman becomes 33rd president of the United States.

1965 — The Gateway Arch is completed in St. Louis.

1993 — The Great Flood damages many Missouri farms, homes and businesses.

2011 — Tornado destroys much of Joplin.

title: Let's Write
text: You and your friends have decided to build a tree house. You decide the rules for it. Describe what you have built and what materials were used. Where did you build it? How did you build it? How long did it take? What furniture does it have? Who is allowed inside? What kind of rules do you make? Anything else special about your creation? Be specific in your details.

title: How Do We Get There From Here?
text:
Have you ever been on a long car trip with your family? How did your parents know what direction to go and what roads to take to get to where you were going? When people plan to drive long distances, or to new places, they use a map. A map helps them plan what route to take. A map can also show things to see along the way, or places to stop for food, gasoline and rest.

Maps come in all sizes and shapes. Flat maps show streets, cities and countries. Globes teach us about the shape of our world and on what part of the Earth everybody lives. Charts and graphs are like maps. They give us a lot of information about what goes on in places around the world. Who eats the most chocolate? How much money do people spend on video games? What direction does the wind blow in the northern Atlantic? What landforms are there in Australia? Maps, globes, charts and graphs help us to get a better picture of our world. These valuable tools make it easier for us to understand our community, our state, our nation and our world.

In this issue, we will learn about the maps, globes and other special tools that make studying our world easier. We will see how they are used to learn about history, geography and social studies.

title: When is a Ketchup Bottle Like a Bug-Eating Plant?
text:
Do you get frustrated trying to get ketchup from the bottle? Do you pound the bottom or hold your finger on a certain spot on the label? Well, scientists at Harvard University have created one of the most slippery materials ever, so the days of waiting for ketchup may be over! The material is called SLIPS, which stands for Slippery Liquid-Infused Porous Surface. SLIPS can repel, or not stick to, water- or oil-based liquids. The scientists call this "omniphobicity."

To create a material with omniphobicity, the Harvard researchers put a greasy film on a spongy layer of Teflon®. Teflon® is the nonstick coating on many pots and pans. The researchers got the idea to make this amazingly slippery surface from the pitcher plant, a plant that eats bugs. The pitcher plant grows in swamps and bogs around the world. One kind of pitcher plant becomes super slippery when it's wet because it locks a thin layer of water in the sponge-like surface of its leaves. Insects cannot walk on the leaves and slide down into the plant's tube where they are trapped.

The scientists' new material can coat the inside of bottles and jars so all the food comes out easily. It can also coat airplane wings to help keep ice from forming on them. What other uses can you think of for this new material?

title: All About Maps
text:
In this issue, we will learn about maps and globes and how to use them to find places, measure distances and get important information. When you are finished with the Lesson, you will be ready to make your own map of Missouri!

Globes and Maps

You have seen both round globes and flat maps of the world. What is the difference between the two? Both a round globe and a flat map of the world show the same cities, countries, oceans and landforms, but they are useful in different ways.

A globe is a round map of the world. A globe shows the Earth in its round form, just as it is in real life, only smaller. By using a globe, you can see how the Earth rotates, or turns, and where each country is in relation to other countries.

A flat map shows the same cities, countries, oceans and landforms as a globe, but it allows us to see the entire world all at once, rather than in pieces as with a globe. You can only see one side of a globe at a time, but when the globe is flattened out into a map, you can see everything all at one time.

Parts of a Map

Maps include more than just countries, cities, oceans and landforms. Maps also include many special tools that help you to find what you are looking for. Each map has a title at the top. The title of a map tells what location, or place, the map shows. Some maps that you may be using this year will be titled Map of the World, United States of America, Landforms of the United States or Map of Missouri.

Compass Rose

All maps have a compass rose, or a drawing showing the directions on the map. The compass rose always shows the cardinal directions, which are north, south, east and west. North is always at the top of the compass rose, east is on the right, south is at the bottom and west is on the left.

The compass rose also shows something called the intermediate directions. Intermediate directions are the directions directly between the cardinal directions. The intermediate directions are northeast, southeast, southwest and northwest. By looking at the compass rose, you can find out exactly where each item on the map is located.

Legend

The legend of the map is a key that lists all of the symbols on a map. These symbols stand for things such as the streets, rivers, monuments, parks, buildings, capital cities and schools. The legend of the map helps you to know what each symbol on the map means.

Scale

Another tool used on a map is a scale. A map's scale shows the distance represented on the map. One inch on the map will be equal to an actual distance in miles. For example, an inch on the map may be equal to 1,000 real miles.

Grid System

Some maps use a grid system, or a system of numbered and lettered lines, to help you find places more easily. On a map that uses a grid system, there will be letters such as A, B, C, etc., running across the top of the map and numbers such as 1, 2, 3, etc., running down the side of the map. If you know that a certain city is located at point 2A on the map, you can find it easily using the grid system of the map.

In our study of history, geography and social studies this year, we will be using maps to help us find out where things are and how they relate to each other.

After you read this week’s lesson, write three questions about the article on a piece of paper and trade questions with a friend. Circle or highlight the answers in the lesson. (CC ELA RI.3.1)

title: Strasbourg, France
text:
Strasbourg has been called the "City of Roads that Cross" because of its location in Europe. Located near the Rhine River, Strasbourg is a city where many major roads join. These roads link cities in France and Germany to the rest of Europe.

Because of its location, Strasbourg is a city that joins the eastern and western parts of Europe. In 1949, after World War II had ended, Strasbourg was chosen as the home of the Council of Europe. The job of the Council of Europe was to rebuild Europe after the war and bring all European nations together in peace. Strasbourg has long been known as a city that brings people together.

Although Strasbourg has often been caught in the middle when European countries have had disagreements, it stands today as a symbol of peace and represents the hope that all European countries can live together as friends.

title: Thomas Hart Benton
text:
Born in Neosho in 1889, Thomas Hart Benton was named after his famous great-uncle, Senator Thomas Hart Benton. His father was also a well-known lawyer and served in the United States House of Representatives. This Thomas Benton isn't famous for government service, however. Instead, he made his mark in the world using a paintbrush. Thomas Benton is known for his beautiful paintings showing everyday life in Missouri. His artwork captures the spirit and beauty of life in small-town America.

Benton went to art schools in Chicago and Paris. By the 1930s, Tom Benton had become the most important mural painter in America. A mural is a work of art painted directly on a wall or ceiling. He painted murals on the walls of buildings throughout the Midwest and on the East Coast. One of his most famous murals, "A Social History of the State of Missouri," can still be seen on the wall of the House Lounge of the Missouri State Capitol.

title: The Sextant
text:
The sextant was invented in both America and England at about the same time, around 1730. The sextant is a special gadget used to measure how high the sun or stars are above the horizon. These measurements (also called "readings") are then used to figure out a person's location on the Earth. Using the sextant, people have been able to make accurate maps. They've also been able to navigate ships at sea and learn more about the sun, moon and stars.

The sextant is a triangular frame attached to a telescope and a mirror. The sextant reflects the image of the sun in the mirror, and the user can measure how high in the sky the sun is found, a neat way to figure out where on Earth he or she is standing.

The sextant is one of the great inventions that helped early cartographers, or mapmakers, to create maps that were more accurate than ever before.

title: John Melish
text:
Born in Scotland in 1771, John Melish moved to America in 1811. He had visited the United States several times and had made notes about his travels, drawing detailed maps of the places he visited. In 1812, Melish published a book called "Travels in the United States of America," which included his first maps. These maps started Melish on his career as a famous cartographer, or mapmaker.

After coming to the United States, John Melish began making maps for a living. He took pains to make sure that his maps were of the highest quality. Later American cartographers used his maps as an example, and Melish is known for bringing the standards for American mapmaking to a higher level of accuracy and quality.

John Melish is one of America's great cartographers, and his maps are still collected and treasured by map lovers today.

title: Famous Person Book
text:
Materials

6-by-6-inch piece of construction paper

scissors

glue

crayons and markers

Instructions

1. Fold the piece of 12- by-18-inch paper into eight equal sections as shown in the picture.

2. (You don't have to label your sections as they are labeled here. We did that to help you know which pieces to cut and fold.) Cut out sections E and H. Save these pieces for later.

3. Fold sections A and D into the center to make a vest or jacket. Glue pieces E and H on the back for arms, as shown in the picture.

4. Cut a head from the 6-by-6-inch piece of construction paper. Glue it to the top of sections B and C. To make pants for your famous person, cut a small triangle between sections F and G as shown. (Or you can cut the lower corners off these sections to create a skirt.)

5. Draw your famous person's face on the head. You can add hair and clothing. Add hands and shoes cut from paper scraps.

6. Open the flaps of the jacket and, on the inside, write something about your famous person. If you'd like, you can write a longer story or essay about your famous person on folded pieces of paper. Then staple the pages into your famous person book.

title: Mapping Missouri
text: Using the basic outline to the right, make a map of Missouri. Label the capital city and the city where you live, and be sure to include a compass rose, legend, scale and simple grid system. Make sure that your compass rose includes both cardinal and intermediate directions. Include your school, park and any other important landmarks using symbols marked on the legend of your map. (You may look back at the map in the Lesson section of the newspaper to help you with this project.)

title: Where in the World Are We?
text:
Where are you right this minute? In your classroom, inside your school building, in a city in Missouri? If you had to tell someone where your city is located, what would you say? If you happen to go to school in Jefferson City, you could say that it is located along the Missouri River, near the very center of the state of Missouri. This would tell the person your relative location, or where your city is located using landmarks. If you wanted to tell someone exactly where your city is located, or even exactly where your school can be found, you could give them your street address. Better yet, you could use the grid system that mapmakers use: longitude and latitude, or an absolute location. For example, Jefferson City can be found on a map at 38 degrees north latitude and 92 degrees west longitude.

In last week's issue, we learned about grid systems and how they help us find things on a map. In this week's issue, we will learn about latitude and longitude and about how these special lines help us to find any location on the earth, no matter how large or how small. We will also learn about how the earth is divided into sections, or hemispheres, and landmasses, or continents. We will use this information to help us find important places throughout the world. Look inside this issue and find out EXACTLY where you are!

title: A Neanderthal’s Best Friend
text:
Archeologists in both Siberia and Belgium have found dog skulls that show wolves were well on their way to becoming domesticated dogs (pets or helpers for people) about 33,000 years ago. This means the change started about 14,000 years earlier than scientists once thought. How do we know the skulls were 33,000 years old? Scientists use a technique called carbon dating to figure it out. Carbon dating is a way to date things that were once alive by looking at how fast a certain type of carbon in the remains will decay.

This discovery also means that dogs were being domesticated in different areas of the world at the same time. The skulls show that people on two different continents were using dogs as pets or helpers.

Scientists once believed that cows, sheep and goats were domesticated first because they could provide meat and milk for prehistoric people. However, it seems dogs were domesticated first to give companionship and protection and to help during hunts.

Scientists don't think the dogs that were in Siberia or Belgium back then are the ancestors of our modern dog. Instead, they believe that many of these dogs died out during the Ice Age. Through DNA research, scientists have discovered that modern dogs come from the Middle East and East Asia. People and dogs have been best friends for a very long time!

title: Reason and Logic: Young George Washington, Surveyor and Mapmaker
text:
Most people know about George Washington. He was born in Virginia. He was a general during the American Revolution and our first president. But his earliest jobs, surveyor and cartographer (mapmaker), taught him skills and values he would use for the rest of his life. Using reason and logic to solve problems helped Washington become one of our country's most important leaders.

When Washington grew up, there were few roads or boundaries in much of the land. A surveyor's job was to measure and map the land. He had to make exact measurements for boundaries and physical features. This was a very big responsibility. People needed accurate maps and surveys for traveling and buying land.

At age 17, Washington traveled across the Blue Ridge Mountains to map and survey part of the frontier. He was the surveyor for the whole county, and that was an important job. When he led the Continental Army, it was even more important to have reliable maps. He established the job of Geographer and Surveyor General and appointed a man named Robert Erskine to this position. He gave Washington some information that was very helpful in making reasonable and logical battle plans and decisions.

You can use these same skills to make important decisions. Be sure you have the facts and information you need instead of acting on opinions and emotions. In what areas of your life are reason and logic very important?

title: Where in the World is Missouri?
text:
Dividing the Earth Hemispheres

Hundreds of years ago, mapmakers divided the Earth into sections to make finding places easier. They divided the globe into four hemispheres or sections. One line divides the Earth top to bottom, another around the middle. The line drawn around the middle of the Earth divides the Northern Hemisphere from the Southern Hemisphere like a belt. This line is called the equator. The line that divides the Eastern Hemisphere from the Western Hemisphere is called the prime meridian. This line runs through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, England. (See map.)

As you can see on the map, everything north of the equator is part of the Northern Hemisphere. This includes North America, Europe, most of Asia, northern South America and northern Africa. Everything south of the equator is part of the Southern Hemisphere, which includes Australia, Antarctica, most of South America and southern Africa.

The Eastern Hemisphere, or everything east of the prime meridian, includes Australia, Asia, most of Europe and Africa and half of Antarctica. The Western Hemisphere, or everything west of the prime meridian, is made up of North America, South America, half of Antarctica, a small part of western Europe and western Africa.

Continents and Oceans

The world is also divided into seven continents, or large landmasses. The seven continents are Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America. Each of these continents is marked on the map.

The oceans cover about 70 percent of the Earth. On the map, you will see there are five major oceans: the Atlantic Ocean, the Indian Ocean, the Pacific Ocean, the Southern Ocean and the Arctic Ocean.

Using Latitude and Longitude to Divide the Earth

Now that we know how the world is divided and named, how can we pinpoint our location? Mapmakers decided to cover their maps with a series of numbered lines running up and down (north and south) and across (east and west). The lines that run across the globe are called parallels of latitude. (We usually just say "latitude.") Think of the lines of latitude as the rungs of a ladder (as in "ladder-tude"). The lines that run up and down the Earth from north to south are called meridians of longitude. (We usually just say "longitude.") Think of the lines of longitude as being long enough (as in "long-itude") to stretch from the North Pole to the South Pole.

Each line of latitude and longitude has a number. Look at the world map and notice how the lines are labeled. The equator is 0 degrees latitude, and the prime meridian is 0 degrees longitude. The numbers on the latitude lines increase as you look both north and south. The numbers on the longitude lines increase as they go east and west.

To find a location on the map, all you need to know are the latitude and longitude numbers. Latitude numbers are always listed first, followed by longitude numbers. Can you find our nation's capital, Washington, D.C., at 38 degrees N 77 degrees W? (Use the compass rose to make sure that you are looking in the correct direction when finding north, south, east and west.) Using latitude and longitude numbers, you can find any place in the world!

title: The Randstad (Netherlands)
text:
There is a place in the Netherlands (Holland) called the Randstad. This isn't a city or community, but a huge, crowded metropolis in the heart of the Netherlands that is made up of that country's largest cities - Amsterdam, Den Haag, Rotterdam and Utrecht. The population in this little area has grown to more than 7 million people. "Randstad" actually means "the Ring City," because these cities form a ring. In the middle of the ring is a beautiful area of farms and green valleys that is called Greenheart. However, there isn't much green left in Greenheart thanks to the growing cities. As you can imagine, with so many people living and working in this little area, there are many problems to deal with. It is difficult for anybody to find a comfortable place to live that isn't already a home for several others. The roads are crowded, terrible traffic jams occur daily, there is too little space for recreation and there is a lot of pollution of the water, air and soil.

The problem of too many people living in too small of an area is a big one for the people of the Randstad. Here in the United States, we solve our space problems by spreading out. In the Netherlands, the people don't have that option. They would have to move into the ocean! Overcrowding is a problem that people are working to solve so that Randstad can become again the livable "ring city" it once was.

title: Martha Jane Cannary
text:
Martha Jane Cannary, better known as Calamity Jane, made a name for herself by doing things that women didn't normally do at the time. Born in Princeton, Missouri, in 1852, Calamity Jane spent her life traveling through the unsettled territories of Arizona and the Dakotas, wearing men's clothing, riding horses and shooting rifles.

Before she reached the age of 20, Calamity Jane was hired as a scout under the famous General Custer. She was a skilled horsewoman, a crack shot with a rifle and fearless in the face of danger.

Buffalo Bill tells the following story about Calamity Jane: The stage was surrounded by Indians, and the driver, Jack McCall, was wounded by an arrow. Although the other six passengers were men, not one of them had nerve enough to take the ribbons [reins]. Seeing the situation, Jane mounted the driver's seat without a moment's hesitation and brought the stage safely and in good time to Wild Birch.

Missourians can claim the spirited and fearless Calamity Jane as one of their own.

title: Global Positioning System (GPS)
text:
GPS, or Global Positioning System, was invented by the United States Department of Defense and has been used since the mid-1980s. GPS is made up of 18 satellites that are orbiting (circling) the Earth in space. These satellites send information to stations on the ground, allowing scientists to take very specific measurements of different locations all over the Earth. With the newest GPS systems, scientists can pinpoint a place on the Earth to the nearest centimeter!

GPS has been used to measure the height of Mount Everest, to track submarines and ships, to follow cars and other vehicles as they travel and to make maps and movies. As GPS equipment becomes more affordable, everyday people all over the world will be able to find out exactly where they are at any given time. Wouldn't that be nice to have if you ever got lost in the woods or in a giant parking lot?

title: John Muir
text:
Do you enjoy nature? John Muir did. He was born in Scotland in 1838, grew up in Wisconsin and came to California in 1868. Muir was surprised and fascinated by the beauty of the California landscape. He was even more surprised that so many of the natural wonders there were being destroyed. So many of the large sequoia and redwood trees were being cut down! Muir decided to work to preserve California's beauty for those who would come later. Muir persuaded Congress to pass a bill in 1890 that created Yosemite National Park. Muir also started the Sierra Club, a group that shared his goal of preserving the forests and other natural wonders of the Sierra Nevada Mountains. The Sierra Club is now a national organization that tries to help people balance the growth of cities and industry with the goal of protecting as much of nature as possible.

Muir believed that everything in nature was connected and that we must preserve the land in order to be at peace. His efforts have helped to keep America's natural wonders around for us to enjoy today.

title: Mexico City, Mexico
text:
Mexico City is one of the most populated cities in the whole world! There are about 20 million people living in the urban area." It is the capital of Mexico and is located in the center of that country.

Families living in Mexico City enjoy the hustle and bustle of a large city, but living with so many other people also brings problems such as pollution, or dirt and chemicals in the air.

Hundreds of factories and millions of cars, trucks and buses pollute Mexico City's air every day. Families living there have learned to change the way they do things. If you lived in Mexico City, you would have to stay home from school on certain days during the winter because the air pollution was so bad. You would have to play indoors rather than outdoors until the air improved.

Families also have to plan their trips carefully because the city has special rules about which days families can use their cars. The government also encourages families to use the subway or to ride special low-pollution buses.

Mexico City is a fun and interesting place to live, but living there can be difficult because of the huge population, crowded streets and shops, and bad pollution. These problems are being worked on all the time, and one day, Mexico City hopes to become a better place to live.

title: All About Borders
text:
Imagine that your family is driving home from a wonderful vacation. As you travel down the road, your mother says, "Keep your eyes open. We're about to cross the border into Missouri!" You watch closely, keeping your eyes on the road, but all you see as you cross the border, or line, between Kansas and Missouri is a sign that says, "Welcome to Missouri: The Show-Me State." That's it? Where is the state line? The line between the states is clearly marked on all the maps, so why was there nothing more than a sign at the border?

Unless the borders between states are formed by actual geographic landforms, such as rivers or mountain ranges, you can only see these border lines on maps. The borders drawn between states and countries are called political features and are man-made lines showing where different governments take control of the land. Some of the political features that divide the land are state and county lines, city limits, school district boundaries and voting areas. Sometimes, these lines are drawn where a river runs or a mountain begins, but more often, they are drawn wherever government leaders decide is best.

If you look at a map of the United States, you will notice these political features, marked by lines, but you will see many physical features as well. Physical features are the landforms of the area, such as mountains, rivers, lakes and valleys. These physical features are also marked on maps.

In this week's lesson, we will learn more about the geography of the United States, its boundaries, its regions and its landforms. We will also learn more about where in the United States we can find Missouri and where its borders are drawn. Grab a map, and let's get busy!

title: Do Cows Give More Milk after Sleeping on a Waterbed?
text:
"It's been a long day," thought Bessie the cow after being milked one evening. "I think I'll just go in and get a good night's sleep on my waterbed." This may sound like the beginning of a fairy tale, but it could be happening on a dairy farm near you!

Dairy farmers know that happy cows give more and better-tasting milk. They also know that sleeping on a hard floor can cause knee and leg injuries that can sometimes make a cow unable to walk. Is a waterbed the answer? Maybe. Farmers are starting to think a cow-sized waterbed mattress might be every dairy cow's dream.

When a cow steps onto the waterbed, she feels the security of the cement floor below the mattress. When she lies down, the water in the mattress keeps her off the hard cement and protects her knees and her udder. Farmers have noticed that if there are not enough waterbeds for all the cows, they will wait in line to use it. Some research shows that cows that sleep on waterbeds sleep longer and have fewer knee and leg injuries. If cows sleep longer, they have more energy to make milk. Fewer leg injuries mean fewer trips to the vet.

The cows may be healthier in other ways too. Some researchers have found fewer white blood cells in cows that use waterbeds. White blood cells fight disease. More white blood cells indicate that the cow may be sick. Fewer white cells indicate a healthier cow. It looks as if better sleep helps cows as much as it helps people!

title: The Regions of the United States
text:
In last week's lesson, we learned about hemispheres, continents, and how to find things on a map. This week, we will find out more about where our communities, state, and nation are located.

Where is the United States Located?

The United States is located in the Northern and Western Hemispheres, on the continent of North America. Look at the map on Page 3 and notice that the country of Canada forms the northern border of the United States and the country of Mexico borders our nation to the south. The United States goes from the Pacific Ocean on the west to the Atlantic Ocean on the east. As the song says, America goes "from sea to shining sea."

Major Landforms of the United States

On the map below, notice that there are several important landforms marked. Let's learn more about them.

Rivers and Lakes

Some of our nation's biggest rivers include the Columbia River, the Mississippi River, the Missouri River and the Rio Grande. See if you can find these large rivers on the map.

Mountain Ranges

The largest mountain ranges in the United States are the Rocky Mountains, the Cascade Range, the Sierra Nevadas and the Appalachian Mountains.

There are other smaller mountain ranges that aren't marked on this map. We will talk about other landforms, such as plains, deserts and valleys in other issues of the newspaper.

Regions of the United States

The United States is divided up into five regions, or areas that share common landforms. A landform is a geological formation, such as a mountain range, a river or a desert. Each of these five regions shares the same types of landforms and climates. Climate is the kind of weather that a place has over a long period.

The five regions of the United States are the Midwest, the Northeast, the Southwest, the Southeast and the West. (These regions are marked for you on the U.S. map.) The land in each of these regions shares certain landforms. Alaska and Hawaii are part of the West region. For example, the Midwest has beautiful, rolling prairies with rich, fertile farmland and warm summers with cool winters. The Southwest, however, is very dry and covered by areas of desert where most plants can't grow. Each region has its own landscape and climate.

Missouri's Place in the United States

Missouri is part of the Midwest Region of the United States. The Midwest is the largest region in the United States. It is made up of grassy plains, forested areas, and rich farmland. The Midwest includes most of the middle states on the map.

Missouri is bordered by Kentucky, Illinois, and Tennessee to the east, Iowa to the north, Nebraska, Kansas, and Oklahoma to the west, and Arkansas to the south.

title: Reykjavik, Iceland
text:
Reykjavik is the capital city of Iceland. It is a city with about 200,000 people, and it is found in southwestern Iceland.

Most of the people in Iceland make their money by fishing. Cod, a type of fish, is one of Iceland's biggest exports, or goods sold to other countries.

The city of Reykjavik was built near some natural, underground hot springs. Reykjavik uses this natural hot water in an unusual way: It heats the city's homes, parking lots and streets with this amazing natural resource!

The hot water is pumped to homes in Reykjavik through a long maze of pipes. The hot water runs under floors and keeps the homes warm and comfortable without the cost or mess of heating them with coal, gas or electricity. Because the natural hot water is so easy to get, many people even use it to heat the sidewalks in front of their homes and businesses so that the snow will melt off without having to be shoveled. Parking lots all over the city have hot water pipes running under them as well so that they never need to be plowed when it snows.

Reykjavik uses its unusual natural resource, hot water, to conserve power, prevent pollution and save work!

title: Langston Hughes
text:
Langston Hughes, born in Joplin in 1902, used his talents as a writer to show the world what life was like for African Americans living in America's large cities. He wrote novels, stories, songs, poems, speeches and children's books, all from the point of view of an African American.

Langston's father left when he was young, and Langston spent time living with his mother and grandmother. He found his writing talents early and published his first book when he was only 19.

Hughes became known as part of the Harlem Renaissance, a group of African American authors who wrote about the hardships they faced. Unlike many of the other authors included in the Harlem Renaissance, Hughes often used humor to make his point.

Like many of the others in his family, Langston Hughes worked for equal treatment of African Americans and whites and for a better way of life for everyone. He is remembered for his courage in fighting for equal rights, as well as for his writing abilities.

title: The Compass
text:
No matter where you stand on Earth, you can hold a compass in your hand and it will point toward the North Pole. The Earth has its own special magnetic field that pulls the compass needle, or magnetic pointer, toward the north. As long as you have a compass, you can always tell in which direction you are heading!

The compass was first invented in China more than 1,000 years ago. Chinese scientists found that a special type of iron ore, or rock, always lined itself up in a north-and-south position. They soon began using the ore to make "magnets," which they then placed on a piece of a leaf and floated in a bowl of water. They marked the bowl with "north," "south," "east" and "west" and then watched the rock "magnet" to see which direction it pointed. The Chinese used this type of compass on their ships for hundreds of years to point them in the right direction during their journeys.

Are YOU headed in the right direction? Find a compass and check it out!

title: Benjamin Franklin
text:
Benjamin Franklin was a great inventor, writer and leading founding father of the United States of America. Ben was born in 1706 in Boston, Massachusetts. He didn't go to school much, but he never stopped learning. Ben read constantly and taught himself algebra, geometry, history, science, navigation and five foreign languages.

Benjamin Franklin served as a diplomat, or friendly representative, to France for many years. He also signed both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution of the United States. He believed that the United States should be a free nation, and he fought to make sure that it became one.

Ben was also a successful printer and publisher. He enjoyed doing scientific experiments in his free time and discovered many interesting facts about electricity. He invented the lightning rod, the Franklin stove and bifocal eyeglasses.

"If you would not be forgotten as soon as you are dead and rotten, either write things worth reading, or do things worth the writing."

--Benjamin Franklin

text:

1. Fold a piece of 8.5-by-11-inch construction paper in half the long direction. Draw a famous historical person at the top of the folded piece of paper. Cut around it so that part of the face sticks above the edge of the paper.

title: Climate and Our Community
text:
As we have learned in other issues of Community Studies Weekly, the United States is divided into several different regions. All the land in these regions shares things that make it alike in certain ways. Just as the United States is divided into regions, the state of Missouri is also divided into regions, or areas that share the same landforms and climates.

The climate of an area is what the weather has been like there over a long period of time. The climate of an area makes a difference as to which plants and animals—including humans—can live there. For example, the northwestern region of the United States is much too cool and wet for growing palm trees, and the southwestern region is much too hot and dry to grow blueberries. Each region of the United States and of Missouri has the perfect climate for the plants and animals that live there. Each of these regions, along with its climate, landforms, plants, and animals is called an ecosystem.

In this week's issue, we will look at some of the different ecosystems in our state and how humans use and change these ecosystems in order to meet their needs. Join us for a look at Missouri's ecosystems and how they help us enjoy a pleasant life.

title: Fifth Graders Talk to Congressmen on Skype
text:
Have you ever thought about different ways to power your parents' cars? Fifth grade students at Columbus Elementary in Edwardsville, Ill., have been learning about other ways to power cars using alternative (substitute) fuels. In September 2011, Illinois Senator Bill Haine and Representative Dan Beiser visited the school to talk about the work being done to improve the environment and the use of "green" energy. Green energy is energy that produces less pollution. Fifth grade students from the entire school district "attended" the assembly. With the help of an internet video program called Skype, students from other schools were able to watch the assembly and ask the officials questions. After the assembly some students emailed questions to Sen. Haine and Rep. Beiser. Students were very excited to receive responses from the officials.

The teachers and students at Columbus Elementary are doing some amazing research when it comes to alternative energy. In fact, they are planning to run a diesel engine using vegetable oil instead of gas. Students are also learning how to reuse resources and are looking forward to turning used vegetable oil into hand soap.

title: Ecosystems: Natural Communities
text:
In earlier issues of Community Studies Weekly, we learned that a community is a group of any size whose members share certain things. The different regions, or ecosystems, of our state can also be called communities, as they share the same climate, plants, animals and landforms. These natural communities make our state interesting and help us get the things we need to survive.

Naming Different Natural Communities

Special words are used to describe how humans have settled the different natural communities of an area.

Wilderness is an area that is protected by the government so that the plants and animals that live there will not be hurt or destroyed. Wilderness areas can sometimes be used for hiking and outdoor adventures, but houses and businesses can't be built here.

Rural areas are natural communities where some humans have chosen to live, but where there are still large amounts of open space and where there aren't many houses, businesses or roads. If you live out in the country, you live in a rural area of Missouri.

Suburban areas are communities that are found just outside the city borders of large cities. Most suburban areas are settled by people who have jobs in large cities, but would rather live in a community of houses and stores rather than in the middle of the city, surrounded by businesses, apartment buildings and traffic.

Urban areas are communities that are found in large cities. Urban areas usually have many apartments, businesses, factories, stores, schools, streets and people all located side by side in a small amount of space.

What type of area do you live in? Have you ever visited any other type of community? Where would you like to live, if you had a choice?

How Do Humans Change the Land to Meet Their Needs?

When people first began settling in Missouri, all of the land was wilderness. How did the areas change over the years? People changed the land to meet their needs. When people came to settle an area, they needed water to survive. They dug wells and ditches to bring the water to where they needed it. They also needed shelter, so they built houses to keep out the sun, rain and weather.

Soon, people cut down trees and bushes to plant crops, built houses and roads and started stores and factories. When an area needed more workers, people quickly moved in, building more houses and turning the area into an urban community. When people got tired of living in large cities, they moved farther out and created a suburban community especially for houses and schools.

People changed their environments to take care of their needs and their wants. Today, people still choose to live where they can make a living and where they think life will be pleasant. We are still changing our environments to meet our needs.

Regions and Climate of Missouri

Missouri is made up of four regions. These regions are the Northern Plains, the Western Plains, the Ozark Highlands and the Southeast Lowlands.

1. The Northern Plains Region was formed by prehistoric glaciers. It is made up of gently rolling, rounded hills and shallow valleys, called plains. Because the soil here is fertile, or good for growing crops, many farmers make this region their home.

2. The Western Plains Region is located to the south of the Missouri River along the border between Missouri and Kansas. This region is made up of flat, rolling prairie land, with only a few low hills and almost no trees. These prairies are perfect for growing grain, which is what the farmers of this region do, along with raising cattle.

3. The Ozark Highlands Region is the largest region in our state. The land in this region is rocky, and the soil is thin, so there isn't a lot of farming in the Ozark Highlands. Although the land may not be rich for farming, it is rich in minerals, or substances brought out of the earth by mining. Lead, zinc, iron, sand, clay, limestone and gravel are all important minerals taken from this region.

4. The Southeast Lowlands Region is the smallest region in the state. Since the land is very low and flat in this region, the region was once an enormous swamp. To drain the land, 1,500 miles of ditches and canals (man-made ditches or waterways) were built, and the land became dry enough to farm. This land is now unusually rich farmland that grows wonderful cotton, corn, wheat, soybeans and rice.

title: Vologda, Russia
text:
Vologda, Russia, is an oblast, or region of Russia a lot like a state here in America. Vologda has a cold climate with only about three months of summer weather each year. The winter temperatures often get as low as 42 degrees below zero! The summer temperatures can reach 80 degrees, but the summer weather doesn't last long.

For many years, residents of Vologda raised milk cows and beef cattle. The people of Vologda tried to farm, but the growing season is so short that the people of the area have looked for other ways to make a living.

Today, many people who live in Vologda work for mining and timber companies. Vologda now makes steel and other metal items, fertilizers and even cloth. The area also has one of the largest furniture factories in Russia. This factory makes furniture for schools. The factory builds desks, chairs and items for laboratories and gyms.

The people of Vologda have used their natural resources, such as metal ores and plenty of trees, to help provide for their needs. Although the area may be cold, the people there have still found a way to make a living, in spite of the freezing temperatures.

title: Harriet Tubman
text:
Harriet Tubman was one of the most successful "conductors" along the Underground Railroad during the 1800s. The Underground Railroad was a secret system for bringing slaves to freedom in the North.

Harriet was born into slavery in Bucktown, Maryland, in 1820. She escaped in 1849 and spent the rest of her life trying to help other African Americans find freedom. She helped as many as 300 slaves escape to freedom during her years with the Underground Railroad.

After the Civil War, Harriet went back to Auburn, New York, where she worked for better treatment for African Americans. She also worked to get more rights for women and older people. In 1908, Harriet started the Harriet Tubman Home for elderly (older) and homeless African Americans.

Harriet Tubman died at the age of 93. She is still remembered for her work helping slaves to freedom.

title: Band-Aid
text:
The year was 1920, and Josephine Dickson, the young wife of Earle Dickson, had a problem. She and Earle hadn't been married long. And as she worked hard to take care of the cooking, cleaning and other chores around the house, she couldn't help cutting, scraping and burning her fingers. Each time she hurt herself, she would have to get out the gauze and adhesive tape and try her best to bandage the cut.

Her husband worked for Johnson and Johnson, a company that made gauze and tape. Earle finally came up with the idea of making special bandages for his wife so that she would be able to bandage her wounds more easily. He cut small squares of gauze and placed the squares every couple of inches or so along a long strip of adhesive tape. Then all Josephine had to do when she hurt herself was to cut off a ready-made bandage and stick it on her wound.

Earle told his boss at Johnson and Johnson about his invention, and soon, the company began making and selling the very first Band-Aid brand adhesive bandages. Josephine's problem was solved, and ever since, the world has reached for a Band-Aid whenever a cut appears.

title: Walter Cronkite
text:
Born in St. Joseph in 1916, Walter Cronkite is one of the most famous news reporters ever to be on television. He has often been called "The Most Trusted Man in America" because of the honest and serious way that he told the news of the day.

Walter started out writing for his college newspaper in Houston, Texas, and later went to work doing news and sports for a radio station in Kansas City.

During World War II, he went to Europe and wrote stories about the war. When television got its start, Walter was there as well. In 1954, he moved to New York City and became the anchorman, or main news reporter, for the first CBS evening news program.

Walter spent 60 years of his life working as a news reporter. He wrote and told the nation about important events such as World War II, the first man to walk on the moon, the assassination of President Kennedy and the Vietnam War. He always ended his news broadcasts by saying, "And that's the way it is," telling the world that he had reported the news just as it really was.

Missouri is proud to call "The Most Trusted Man in America" one of its own.

title: Rome, Italy
text:
Families have always been important in Rome, and while things have changed over the years, children still hold a special place in Italian family life.

In the past, Roman families had many children. Today, families are much smaller, usually with only one or two children per family. Roman parents today still treat their children with special care. Children in Rome are a part of all celebrations and events. Children go with their parents to restaurants and are allowed to stay up late and play in the piazza, or town square, while their parents visit at outdoor cafés.

On warm evenings, parents and children dress up and go out for a passeggiata, or evening walk. They visit with neighbors and friends along the way and enjoy the time spent together.

In Rome, the father of the family is the head of the household and makes most of the decisions about money. The mother is in charge of the children and keeps the home running smoothly. Some of these responsibilities are changing now that more women are working at jobs outside the home, and men and women are starting to share some of the chores at home. Rome is a wonderful place to grow up, as children are considered precious gifts to be treasured.

There are several ancient buildings in Rome like these remains of the Roman Colosseum.

title: Average Climate of the Continental United States
text: The Continental United States refers to the 48 states that are north of Mexico and south of Canada. This area has a variety of climates. On the map, finish the key provided and color each of the climate regions the correct color. Label your state with a star. What type of climate do you have? Have fun learning about the climates of the United States!

title: Jump Off St. Joseph
text:
St. Joseph is located on the Missouri River along the western border of our state. St. Joseph is famous for being one of the "jumping off" points for the trip west, as well as for being the home of the Pony Express. It was founded in 1826 by Joseph Robidoux and became a city in 1843.

The St. Joseph of today is a safe and pleasant city with many things to see. The Patee House, a grand hotel built in 1858, is a wonderful place to visit. Many travelers heading West spent a night or two here while waiting for their trains to arrive. It is also the building where Russell, Majors and Waddell had their office when they started the Pony Express in 1860.

The St. Joseph Museum is also a great place to learn more about our state. Some of the most popular exhibits are "Indians of the Northwest Coast," "Wagons West," and "The Upland Forest."

The Jesse James House is another site that brings visitors from across the state as well as across the nation. Bob Ford shot and killed Jesse James in this house in 1882. Ford was a member of the James gang who killed Jesse James to collect a $10,000 reward offered by Governor Tom Crittenden.

The Society of Memories Doll Museum, founded in 1968, is also an interesting place to visit. The museum has a collection of beautiful, rare dolls that are on display for all to see.

The floods of 1993 heavily damaged St. Joseph, and many businesses were forced to shut down. St. Joseph is now attracting new businesses and is still a wonderful place to visit to learn more about Missouri's great history.

title: Stone Tools Help Archaeologists Learn About Early People
text:
How do we learn about ancient peoples in the Americas? There is no time machine we can use to go back and see how they lived. Instead, we learn about how people lived in the past through clues left in the present. Sometimes ancient peoples left clues about how they saw the world in stories passed down to their descendants. They also left behind creations we still use. For example, corn only exists because of ancient American people who bred grasses into a new crop. We can also learn about ancient people through objects they made. Scientists called archeologists search for ancient objects, buildings, or even garbage heaps to learn about how people lived in the past.

Unfortunately, many of the clues disappear over time. Weather often wears away wood tools and buildings. Food decomposes. Clothing usually falls apart. Because stone wears away more slowly, stone clues are easier to find.

Studying stone tools has helped archeologists create theories about ancient Americans. Stone tools over 15,000 years old have been found in North and South America. These tools show people have lived on both continents since before the first cities in the world began. While there are still many questions about how they lived, the careful craftsmanship on their tools shows that ancient Americans used their ingenuity to survive. These early peoples prepared the way for hundreds of nations that developed later all across the Americas.

title: Studying History
text:
When it's time to study social studies each day, do you wonder why you have to spend so much time learning about things that happened many years ago? Studying history helps us to understand the things that are happening in our world every day. Studying history can also keep us from making some of the same mistakes that others before us have made.

Why is It Important to Study History?

History is the study of our past. It is important to study history to understand things that happened long ago. If we know what happened before, and why it happened, we can see how these events brought us to where we are today. As we study history, we learn what people and places were like before we were born. We see how these people and places changed from what they were once like into what we know today.

If we learn about the mistakes that others have made in the past, we can avoid making bad decisions in the future. For example, when we see the way the American Indians were treated by the early settlers, we are able to see the mistakes that were made, and we can learn to treat others fairly. As poet and author George Santayana once said, "Those who do not remember the past are condemned to repeat it."

Eras of History

To make it easier for us to keep track of when different things happened, history has been divided into eras, or periods of time. If we know when different events took place, we can understand how all these events fit together.

When we know that Columbus began the exploration of America during the Era of Exploration, for example, we understand that others were also exploring the earth at the same time.

Once people came to live in America, a new era called the Era of Colonization and Settlement began. To colonize an area means to settle it, or to build towns and cities. If we talk about things that happened during the Era of Colonization, we can see that these events will probably have a lot to do with building houses, getting along with the American Indians, planting crops and making new governments.

By dividing history into eras, it makes it easier for us to understand why things happened as they did and what made people act in certain ways.

title: Words To Live By
text:
Besides dividing history into eras, we also use special words to help us understand when things happened. These special words tell us if something happened millions, thousands, hundreds or even 10 years ago. These words can even help us talk about things that are happening right now!

Prehistoric

When we say that something is "prehistoric," we mean that it was around before people started writing history down. Dinosaurs lived in prehistoric times, which means either that no people were here to write about them or that those who were here didn't know how to write. "Pre" means "before," so "prehistoric" means "before history."

Ancient

"Ancient" means "very old," so when we say that something happened during ancient times, we know that it happened long ago. Many people use the word "ancient" to talk about history before the year A.D. 500.

Circa

We use the word "circa" when we don't know exactly when something happened. "Circa" means "on or about a certain date." If we know that Betsy Ross made one of the first American flags, but we don't know exactly when she sewed it, we can say that Betsy Ross made the flag circa (or about) 1776.

Modern

The word "modern" is used to talk about things that have happened in the more recent past. Modern history talks about things that happened and people that lived several hundred years ago up to the present.

Contemporary

"Contemporary" means "living or happening at about the same time." You and your friends are contemporaries, which means that you live at the same time. Explorer Henry Hudson and Pocahontas were contemporaries, too, even if they didn't know each other, because they lived at the same time.

title: Liverpool, England
text:
Liverpool is found on the River Mersey in western England, near the Irish Sea. During the 1700s, the shipping port at Liverpool was very busy. Ships from Liverpool also carried goods all over the world. Ships from Liverpool even carried slaves from Africa to the West Indies and North America.

When factories first started using machines to create things that people used to make by hand, Liverpool was at the heart of this new way of doing things. People came from all over England to get jobs in the new factories. They also found jobs working in the shipyards, helping to send the products made here to places all over the world.

During the 1800s, business was booming in Liverpool, and the city grew quickly. When World War II started, however, many German airplanes bombed the docks at Liverpool, damaging or destroying them. Many of the docks were rebuilt, but because of changes in the way shipping is done, Liverpool never became the great shipping city that it once was. Many people have lost their jobs, and unemployment is a big problem here. The way business is done has changed and so has the city of Liverpool. By studying the history of Liverpool, we can see how things that happened in the past made the city what it is today.

title: Charles Lindbergh
text:
Born in Detroit, Michigan, in 1902, Charles Lindbergh was always interested in finding out how things worked. By the time he was 11, Charles' parents had put him in charge of both driving and fixing their car. Soon, Charles started dreaming of working with something even more exciting than cars - he wanted to work with airplanes. To become a pilot, Charles had to work and study hard. He wanted to be the best pilot there was, so he studied during every spare moment. He even brought his books into the bathroom with him! His hard work paid off, and he earned the highest grades in his class.

After becoming a pilot, Charles started flying an airmail route from St. Louis to Chicago. Before long, Charles heard about a contest offering a prize of $25,000 for the first nonstop flight from Paris to New York. He decided to enter the contest, and a group of St. Louis businessmen gave Charles the money he needed to have a special plane built. When the plane was finished, Charles called it the Spirit of St. Louis. Charles entered the contest, and in 1927, he became the first person to cross the Atlantic Ocean alone in an airplane. Millions of people got together to celebrate this event. Charles Lindbergh took to the skies and helped us see that dreams really can come true.

title: The Ballpoint Pen
text:
When the Pilgrims wrote about their lives in America, they didn't have pens like those that we use today. They probably used pens made from feathers dipped in ink.

Later, people used fountain pens. These pens were messy and ran out of ink often, and their scratchy points made holes in the paper. Many people tried to make a pen that had its own ink stored inside, but the ink in these pens either clogged or leaked out all over.

In 1938, Ladislo and Georg Biro, two brothers from Hungary, came up with an idea to make the ink in a ballpoint pen flow more smoothly. They created a special rough ball at the end of the pen that worked like a sponge, sucking the ink into the point when someone wrote with it.

Other companies, like Papermate and Bic, improved the ballpoint pen and sold it for a price that everyone could afford. Today, most of us write with ballpoint pens, which are cheap, clean and easy to carry.

title: Pocahontas Saves Jamestown
text:
Pocahontas was the favorite daughter of Powhatan. He was a powerful chief of the Virginia Confederacy of Tribes. Pocahontas American Indian name was Matoaka.

Captain John Smith was the leader of America's first English colony. He wrote in his journal that Pocahontas saved his life. He claims to have been captured by her father's warriors and was to be killed. Historians believe Smith exaggerated his adventures. He, like many other explorers of the time, promoted themselves and their adventures. We may never know the truth about what really happened.

Pocahontas converted to Christianity. She married John Rolfe, an English tobacco planter, who took her to England. "To convert" means "to join another religion." This marriage was the first alliance, or friendship, between the American Indians and the English settlers. Powhatan was happy about his daughter marrying an Englishman. The king of England breathed much easier knowing he had a powerful ally (friend) such as Powhatan.

Many English settlers moved to America. It was because this marriage helped the English and the American Indians get along better. Pocahontas later moved to England and had a son, who moved back to America to raise his family. Pocahontas died in England in 1617.

title: Milk Carton Log Cabin
text:
Build your own log cabin out of a milk carton!

Materials

Half-gallon waxed-paper milk or juice carton, emptied

Grease pencil

Scissors

Cardboard

Glue

Waxed-paper scraps

Pretzel sticks

Cheerios or pasta

Acrylic paint

Water

Water container

Paper towels

Ruler

Instructions

1. Measure three inches down the side of the carton. At three inches, draw a line around the entire carton with a grease pencil.

2. Cut along the line and separate the top from the bottom. Discard the bottom. You will use the top.

3. Draw the outline of the door and windows with a grease pencil.

4. Cut out the windows and door. If they are too small for scissors, ask your teacher to use an X-acto knife and help you. You can leave one side of the door attached and fold it out so that it opens and closes.

5. Glue a piece of waxed paper over the inside of each window.

6. Glue the cabin to a cardboard base that is slightly bigger than the cabin. Let the pieces dry before proceeding.

7. Glue pretzel sticks along the base of the carton walls and build up. If necessary, cut the pretzels to fit around the door and windows.

8. Glue a stack of Cheerios or pasta together as a chimney. Glue this on the roof of the cabin.

9. Cover the roof with pretzels or acrylic paint.

Note: Watercolor and tempera paint will not stay on the waxed carton.
