title: Regions of Missouri
text:
The United States is a large mass of land made up of many different types of land forms. New York and New Mexico are both part of the United States, but their geography doesn't have much in common. Because areas of our country are so different in terms of their temperatures, rainfall, soil types, landforms and wildlife, the United States is divided into regions, or areas that are similar to each other. These areas in each region are close to each other on the map and share many attributes in common. For example, the United States is divided into five regions. They are the Northeast, the Southeast, the Midwest, the Southwest, and the West. New York and New Mexico are both part of the United States, but we can also put each state into its own separate region, which will tell us more about what that state is actually like. New York is part of the Northeast Region, and New Mexico is part of the Southwest Region. The areas in each of these regions have things they share with each other, which make them the same in some way. The West Region has a warm, dry climate, while the Northeast Region is colder and more moist. Each piece of land in a region shares common elements such as climate and geography, which make it like other locations in the same region.

Missouri is also divided up into regions, or areas that have something in common as far as their land forms and geography are concerned. Missouri is divided into four regions. They are the Northern Plains, the Western Plains, the Ozark Highlands, and the Southeast Lowlands. Each of these regions has special features that make it unique. Each region is made up of different types of land that allow it to produce different products. In which region do you live? How many regions have you visited? What are the differences among the four regions?

In this issue, we will be learning about the four regions of Missouri and what makes them unique. Before we look at each region separately, let's decide why the regions are different from each other. Why is the land in the Northern Plains different from the land of the Southeast Lowlands? Why is the Western Plains Region smooth and flat, while the Ozark Highlands Region is covered with rugged hills, winding caves and beautiful forests?

Each region is different because of the forces of nature that were at work millions of years ago. Different forces gave each region the shape that we now see. Glaciers formed the gently rolling hills and smooth, flat plains of the Northern Plains and the Western Plains. Water carved out the magnificent caves and majestic hills of the Ozark Highlands. Water flooding the Southeast Lowlands over millions of years created the lush farmland that makes this region great for growing crops. Nature's finished product may be different from region to region, but each region has its own special claim to fame. Which is your favorite region? Keep reading for more information that will help you decide!

title: Regions of Missouri
text:
The Northern Plains Region

The land from the Missouri River north to the Iowa border is called the Northern Plains Region. This region of our state was formed by prehistoric glaciers. It is made up of gently rolling, rounded hills and shallow valleys called plains. Because the soil here is fertile, or good for growing crops, many farmers make this region their home. Among the many crops grown here are corn, wheat, soybeans, tobacco, fruits and vegetables.

Some of Missouri's larger cities are found in the Northern Plains Region, including St. Louis, Kansas City, St. Charles, Independence, Gladstone, Hannibal, Columbia and St. Joseph.

The Western Plains

The Western Plains Region is located to the south of the Missouri River along the border between Missouri and Kansas. This region is made up of flat, rolling prairie land, with only a few low hills and almost no trees. These prairies are perfect for growing grain, which is what the farmers of this region do, along with raising cattle.

Coal is the most important mineral found in the Western Plains Region, and coal mining is very successful here. Some of the important communities in this region are Blue Springs, Lee's Summit, Grandview, Raytown, Belton, Warrensburg and Sedalia.

The Ozark Highlands Region

This region is located in southern Missouri. It extends from the Missouri River south to the Arkansas border, but it does not include the Bootheel area of our state. The Ozark Highlands Region is the largest region in our state. The land in this region is rocky, and the soil is thin, so there isn't a lot of farming in the Ozark Highlands. Although the land may not be rich for farming, it is rich in minerals, or substances brought out of the earth by mining. Lead, zinc, iron, sand, clay, limestone and gravel are all important minerals taken from this region.

There are also forests covering much of this area of our state. Trees from the Ozark Highlands are used to make lumber, fence posts, furniture, gunstocks, and charcoal.

While there is some farming here, most farmers in this region raise cattle, chickens and hogs rather than grains or vegetables.

Many tourists (people who travel for fun) visit the Ozark Highlands every year because of its beautiful and rugged scenery. There are mountains, caves, forests and natural springs, which draw visitors from all over the world.

The largest cities in the Ozark Highland Region are Springfield, Joplin, Jefferson City, Carthage, Rolla, Arnold and Poplar Bluff.

The Southeast Lowlands Region

The Southeast Lowlands Region is located in Missouri's Bootheel. If you look at our state on a map, you will see that this region, in the bottom, southeast corner of the state, does indeed look like the heel of a boot. This area is lower than any of the surrounding countryside and the Southeast Lowlands Region is the smallest region in the state.

Since the land is very low and flat in this region, flood waters do not drain easily, and the region was once an enormous swamp. To drain the land, 1,500 miles of ditches and canals (man-made ditches or waterways) were built, and the land became dry enough to farm. This land is now unusually rich farmland that grows wonderful cotton, corn, wheat, soybeans and rice. Livestock (farm animals) is also raised in the Southeast Lowlands.

The largest cities in the Southeast Lowlands Region are Cape Girardeau, Sikeston, New Madrid and Kennett.

title: Taum Sauk State Park
text:
Are you interested in seeing some of the most spectacular sights in Missouri? How would you like to gaze off into the horizon from the top of our state's highest peak? Would you enjoy taking a look at Missouri's tallest waterfall? You can view all of these amazing natural beauties and more when you visit Taum Sauk State Park, located in Middlebrook, Missouri. Taum Sauk State Park is named after Missouri's tallest mountain, Taum Sauk Mountain, which rises 1,772 feet in the air. The park is part of the Ozark Highland Region of our state, Missouri's largest region.

When you come to Taum Sauk State Park, you can follow a short trail to the top of Taum Sauk Mountain, view the state's highest waterfall, 132-foot Mina Sauk Falls, and walk through the middle of Devil's Tollgate, a crazy, inverted crevice in the rock.

You can also camp out and enjoy the beauty of the night skies, as Taum Sauk State Park is far enough away from the big city that lights don't interfere with stargazing.

There are many miles of hiking trails, including a 10-mile section of the 500-mile Ozark Trail. There is even a three-mile loop trail in the park that lets you see the sights and end up back where you started.

title: Herdsmen
text: Mounted herdsmen, or drovers, take care of cattle and move them from place to place. They are more often called cowboys. Herdsmen still ride horses, but they use other technology too! Computer programs and GPS systems help owners and herdsmen keep track of the animals. Missouri is home to a number of cattle farms. The state’s many rolling, grassy hills are perfect for raising livestock. The next time you drive by a farm, look for a herdsmen. He might be on his smartphone!

title: Where do honeybees go in the winter?
text: The honeybee queen and some of her workers live through the winter inside their hive. In the fall, the workers collect sticky gum from trees. They use this and a wax that they secrete to seal cracks in their beehive to make it safe and warm. Then when winter comes, they stay inside the hive. When it grows cold, the bees crowd together to keep warm. They move their bodies and wings to make heat. They eat honey that they stored in honeycombs during the summer. Near winter's end, the queen bee begins laying eggs again. Soon the hive is busy with new worker bees making honey.

title: Honeybee
text:
The state insect of Missouri is the honeybee, whose scientific name is Apis mellifera. Honeybees are insects with a special appeal to humans, even though their stings aren't particularly pleasant. Honeybees are raised and kept by people so that they can harvest honey, a deliciously sweet substance made by the bees.

In the wild, honeybees make nests, or combs, out of wax formed inside their abdomens. They make hexagon-shaped cells out of this special wax in which to store their honey. In nature, most of these nests are made in caves or hollow trees, but beekeepers build nesting boxes, called hives, for their bees.

In a colony of honeybees, there are three types of bees, each with its own job: a queen produces eggs and keeps the hive populated; thousands of workers gather the nectar and make the honey; and a few hundred drones, or male bees, fertilize the eggs. Each type of bee works at doing its job so that the hive functions smoothly, and the honey is made. Honeybees make life in Missouri a little sweeter for all of us!

title: Did Medieval Knights Suffer Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder?
text:
Many movies show medieval knights as strong, fearless warriors who actually enjoyed fighting wars. But is that really true? A researcher from a Denmark university studied primary and secondary sources written by and about knights of the medieval era. He came to the conclusion that knights were no different than today’s soldier. They didn’t just go around mindlessly fighting battles; in fact they developed the code of chivalry to help them deal with the violence and horror. The code of chivalry said that knights must only fight for a good cause—to protect others, for example. They must never fight for their own glory.

The “Book of Chivalry” was written by a real knight more than 600 years ago. The author, Geoffroi de Charny, fought wars, not because he wanted to, but because it was his job. He saw terrible pain and suffering, was taken prisoner twice, and was chosen to carry the flag of the French king, one of the most dangerous responsibilities a knight could have. Researchers who have read his book believe that he showed signs of PTSD. PTSD is short for post-traumatic stress disorder. Symptoms may include a constant feeling of danger, flashbacks to awful events and frightening nightmares. Many soldiers who come back from war today suffer from PTSD too. For both knights of old and modern soldiers, the horrors of war leave an unforgettable impression on their lives!

title: The Gateway to the West!
text:
If you live in Missouri, you probably know that our state is famous for many things, but can you guess what aspect of our state has had more influence on more people than any other single thing? If you guessed our great rivers, you're right!

Missouri is home to the two longest rivers in the Unites States: the Missouri River and the Mississippi River. These two huge, rolling rivers have shaped our state and its history with greater power than any other single factor. One can't think of Missouri without thinking of her rivers.

Mark Twain, the author of many books dealing with life on and around the Mississippi River, even took his pen name, or the name he used on his books and stories, from terms used to describe the river. Mark Twain, whose real name was Samuel Clemens, loved the Mississippi River and worked here as a riverboat captain for many years. The river became very shallow in places, and a captain of the large riverboats had to be very careful when guiding his boat through these dangerous spots. It was important for the captain to know how deep the river was so he could avoid hitting bottom and either damaging his boat or becoming stuck in the mud. A crewman would measure the depth of the river, and when the water was no longer dangerously shallow, he would shout, "Mark twain!" meaning that the water was then at least 12 feet deep and safe for the boat to pass through. Samuel Clemens heard this phrase shouted so often that he decided it would make an interesting and unusual name to use in his writing. Some of Mark Twain's most famous works are "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer," "The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn" and "Life on the Mississippi."

Missouri's rivers not only influenced people like Mark Twain, but they also attracted explorers and settlers to our state in the first place. Missouri's two great rivers brought the earliest settlers here, as the rivers were our earliest highways. Before roads criss-crossed our country, the rivers were used as a fast and efficient way to get from one place to another.

The rivers were not only used to transport people, however. As goods were shipped along these waterways, towns and cities sprang up along the shores of both the Missouri and Mississippi Rivers. St. Louis, which stands just south of where the Missouri River and the Mississippi river join, became the jumping-off point for settlers moving West. Settlers stopped here to rest, buy supplies for the journey ahead and gather information about the route west. Missouri businesses that could provide goods and services for these early travelers grew rich, and Missouri settlements spread. Because of this, our state has become known as the "Gateway to the West." In 1964, the now-famous Gateway Arch was completed, representing the idea that Missouri is indeed the "Gateway to the West." The arch is 630 feet across and can be seen from as far as 30 miles away. Without the influence of both the Missouri and Mississippi rivers, Missouri would not have been destined for such an honor. The next time you see St. Louis's famous Gateway Arch, think about what the great rivers of Missouri had to do with making Missouri the "Gateway to the West."

title: Rivers of Missouri
text:
What do you think most people picture when they think of the state of Missouri? If you were to describe Missouri to a friend who lives in another state, what would you say? Can you imagine the state of Missouri without its rivers? When most people think of Missouri, one of the first things they think of is its beautiful, majestic rivers.

Missouri is home to parts of the two longest rivers in the United States. The Missouri River, the longest river in the country, forms part of the northwest border of our state. The Mississippi River, the largest river in terms of water volume (and second longest) in the United States, forms the entire eastern border of Missouri. These two mighty rivers have affected the way Missourians live since the region was first settled.

The Mississippi River

The Mississippi River also has many nicknames. Two of its most common nicknames are the “Father of Waters,” because of its enormous size, and also “Old Man River,” because of the river’s age and the respect people have for it.

The Mississippi is the second-longest river in the United States. It runs 2,348 miles from the Great Lakes in the north to as far south as the Gulf of Mexico. Tributaries of the Mississippi, or smaller rivers that flow into it, drain most of the land from the Rocky Mountains all the way to the Appalachian Mountains. The Mississippi is actually a huge river system that collects water from the land and empties it into the sea.

The Mississippi River is considered the largest river in water volume. Also, the Mississippi is the longest river flowing in a southern direction. Many people believe that the Mississippi is the longest river, but it is the second longest. The Missouri River is the longest river in length, based on recent studies from the United States Geological Survey. The Mississippi was longer than the Missouri at one time, but the Old Man River has become shorter over time. Some printed issues of Encyclopedia Britannica and the World Book still say that the Mississippi is longer. Because of this disagreement, many scholars simply refer to the two rivers combined as the Mississippi-Missouri River system, which is 3,710 miles long.

The Missouri River

The Missouri River is sometimes called the Big Muddy because of its brown, murky water. The American Indians who lived here more than 300 years ago first nicknamed the Missouri the Big Muddy, and because the name fits so well, we still use it today. The Big Muddy has its source, or beginning, far away from Missouri in the tops of the Rocky Mountains. From its beginning, the mighty Missouri winds its way some 2,540 miles, cutting across Missouri and finally joining the Mississippi near St. Louis at a point called the mouth of the Missouri. The mouth of a river is the place where it empties into a larger body of water.

Effects Rivers Have on Our Lives

How do these two great rivers affect life in Missouri? For many years, before the railroad began connecting the different regions of the United States, the rivers played a vital role in transporting goods and passengers from one place to another. These rivers were the country’s first highways. Although trains, planes and trucks are now used more often in carrying people and goods across the country, the rivers are still widely used for the transportation of many items, especially goods such as grain, coal, steel, petroleum and cement. These items are transported by river barge. A barge is a large, flat boat that is perfect for use on Missouri’s huge rivers.

Besides transportation, Missouri’s rivers also provide one of our most important resources—clean water for drinking, farming and manufacturing. Water-treatment plants have been built at many different locations along the rivers. These plants clean the water so it can be used for drinking, bathing and farming, as well as for businesses, which use water in making their products. Without these rivers, Missouri would be left without its major sources of clean water. The water from these rivers is also used to make power. Dams have been built across Missouri’s rivers at several spots. These dams hold back the water and help prevent flooding, but some of these dams also produce electricity. As the water rushes at high speeds through the dam, turbines in the dam create electricity. A turbine is a special machine that uses the force of the river to create electricity. This electricity is then used by businesses and homes throughout the state.

Missourians also use the Missouri, the Mississippi and other beautiful rivers for recreation. Fishing, swimming, boating and sailing are all popular activities that are made possible by our rivers. Our state’s rivers are probably the most-widely-recognized features of our landscape. They provide us with transportation, water, natural scenic beauty, power and recreation. The Big Muddy and the Father of Waters both help make Missouri the wonderful place we call home.

title: Hannibal
text:
One of Missouri's favorite tourist spots is the city of Hannibal. Hannibal is famous as the birthplace of author Mark Twain, who wrote many books and stories about life on and around the Mississippi River. Hannibal is also the birthplace of Margaret Tobin Brown, better known as "The Unsinkable Molly Brown" because she survived the sinking of the Titanic.

Hannibal is located in northeastern Missouri, bordering the Mississippi River. It is often listed among the top 10 places to visit in the United States because of its interesting museums, restored historical buildings, and fascinating antique and craft shops.

Some of the most interesting and popular places to see are the original boyhood home of Mark Twain; the Memorial Lighthouse, the farthest inland lighthouse in the world; and Mark Twain Cave, which Mark Twain used to explore as a child. He later wrote about this cave in "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer," one of his most famous novels.

Another fun and interesting spot to see is Lovers' Leap, a steep cliff that offers a beautiful view of Hannibal and the Mississippi River and which also has a romantic story to go with it. The spot was named for two young American Indian lovers who jumped from its heights when their parents refused to let them see each other.

title: Steamboat Invented
text:
John Fitch launched the first working steamboat on the Delaware River near Philadelphia. The 45-foot boat was driven by a steam engine that powered 12 paddles.

Robert Fulton created the first commercial steamboat that carried freight and passengers.

The success of his Clermont inspired shipbuilders worldwide, and the paddle wheel soon became a commonplace sight on the oceans and rivers of the world.

title: What is a river barge?
text:
A barge is a large, flat-bottomed boat used for transporting goods. Most barges are towed on the waterway, but there are some barges that are self-propelled, meaning they run on their own power.

Years ago, the barges carrying goods on the Mississippi River were towed by men, horses, or mules. Today, this towing is done by a steam or motor tugboat or by other self-propelled barges.

Barges have been around since time began. They were even used on the River Nile in ancient Egypt and in Europe for carrying royalty and other important people.

title: Bluebird
text:
The official state bird of Missouri is the bluebird, also known by its scientific name, Sialia sialis. The bluebird is about seven inches long, and its feathers are a bright, vivid blue. The breast of the bluebird is cinnamon red, and its under feathers are white. The coloring of the male bluebird is always brighter and more striking than that of the female.

The bluebird is one of the first birds to arrive in Missouri in the spring after spending the winter in the warmth of the south. It has a cheerful call and a warbling song. The bluebird eats insects, which makes it popular with humans, and it also enjoys wild berries and fruits.

The bluebird usually nests in orchards and in woodlands, as it prefers to build its nests in the hollows of old, dead trees.

The bluebird has been dying out in past years, as its nesting spots have become hard to find. Old, dead trees are often removed, leaving the birds with no place to build their nests. There has also been a great increase in the number of other birds, such as the English sparrow and the starling. These birds are very competitive and will fight and even kill bluebirds to take their nesting spots.

The last few years, many people have become interested in helping the bluebird by building nesting boxes. These nesting boxes provide the bluebird with a safe, comfortable place in which to lay and hatch its eggs. Because of the help of bird lovers in many states, the number of bluebirds is now increasing, and its beautiful song is being heard throughout Missouri.

title: Fifth Graders Talk to Congressmen on Skype
text:
Have you ever thought about different ways to power your parents’ cars? Fifth grade students at Columbus Elementary in Edwardsville, Ill., have been learning about other ways to power cars using alternative (substitute) fuels. In September 2011, Illinois Senator Bill Haine and Representative Dan Beiser visited the school to talk about the work being done to improve the environment and the use of “green” energy. Green energy is energy that produces less pollution. Fifth grade students from the entire school district “attended” the assembly. With the help of an internet video program called Skype, students from other schools were able to watch the assembly and ask the officials questions. After the assembly some students emailed questions to Sen. Haine and Rep. Beiser. Students were very excited to receive responses from the officials.

The teachers and students at Columbus Elementary are doing some amazing research when it comes to alternative energy. In fact, they are planning to run a diesel engine using vegetable oil instead of gas. Students are also learning how to reuse resources and are looking forward to turning used vegetable oil into hand soap. To learn more about alternative energy, visit

http://www.benefits-of-recycling.com/alternativeenergyforkids.html.

Visit www.studiesweekly.com/currentevents/ for more Connections and Current Events articles.

title: Weather Watch
text:
Since time began, people have tried to predict the weather by scanning the sky for colors and other clues. Test these bits of ancient meteorology to see if they are really true.

1. A rose-red sunset means fair skies are coming. A red sunrise means there will be a storm. (“Red sky at night, sailor’s delight; red sky at morning, sailors take warning.”)

2. A pale yellow sunset means rain is on the way.

3. An evening rainbow predicts fair weather.

4. A morning rainbow in the west means rain.

5. A pre-dawn copper-colored sky in the east means rain.

6. When the moon has a halo, there will be rain, especially if the halo is far from the moon.

title: Mound Builders of Missouri
text:
Some of Missouri's most interesting reminders of its early inhabitants are its historic mounds. The early American Indians who lived in and around Missouri built huge mounds of Earth as part of their culture. Many of these mounds are still around today and can be toured and visited by anyone interested in finding out more about Missouri's ancient settlers.

St. Louis was once the site of a huge settlement of early American Indians. These early people of Missouri settled on both sides of the Mississippi River, much as we have done today. We now call this large community Old Village, although we don't know what those who lived there long ago actually called it. There were once so many mounds remaining in this area that St. Louis was nicknamed the Mound City. Ancient mounds have been discovered in other areas as well. More than 1,800 mounds have been discovered in the Poplar Bluff region of Missouri. In Saline County, there is a large semi-circular mound from the Hopewell people called Old Fort. Missouri's largest mound can be found in the Bootheel region near Caruthersville. It is so large that it could hold an entire football field.

About 7,000 years ago, some of the earliest people of Missouri began to build homes and villages, farming for survival. Before this, most of the early people in our area were nomads, meaning that they drifted from place to place, trying to find food. Once these early American Indians began to settle in one place, they also began to build homes for shelter, and eventually they began to construct mounds.

We know these ancient mounds are here, but what were they actually used for? Why did the ancient American Indians build them? These mounds were first used as a place to bury their dead. Later, these mounds became places of religious worship. Temples were built on top of these sacred mounds, as well as the houses of the chiefs of the tribes. Some mounds were also built as a base for forts built on top of the mounds.

The Mound Builders, or the American Indians who built the mounds, were the first people in Missouri to organize a civilization, or an organized system of government, religion and education. These Mound Builders created large towns in which to live. Many of these towns had a central plaza, or what we might call a downtown area, with high mounds of earth in the center. These mounds would be flattened out on top, and then the important buildings of the town, such as the temples, forts or other public buildings, would be built on top of the mounds.

When the first explorers came from Europe to Missouri, the Mound Builders were already gone, but their mounds remained. At one time, there were more than 20 mounds in the area now called St. Louis, but over the years, many of the new settlers leveled off the mounds to make room for buildings. There is still a large and interesting group of mounds located across the Mississippi River a few miles west of Collinsville at a spot called the Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site. There are also exhibits that help to explain the mounds and the American Indians who built them.

By studying the Mound Builders and the mounds they have left behind here in Missouri, we can learn about the civilizations that existed here before history was written down. Although we will never know exactly what these early people were like or how they lived, the ancient mounds and other items they left behind give us many clues. Missouri's mounds are some of its most interesting reminders of the people who came before us.

title: The First People of Missouri
text:
Prehistoric American Indians

The first people to call Missouri home probably entered the Mississippi Valley thousands of years ago. We don't know exactly when they got here, who they were, where they were from, or what they called themselves because they didn't write their history down for us. Because they came here without a written history, we call them prehistoric American Indians, or Americans who were here before history was recorded.

While there may be a lot of things we don't know about Missouri's first people, there are some things we have discovered through studying things these first American Indians left behind. Archaeologists are scientists who dig up the remains of people and things that existed long ago and study them. They have found many clues that have helped them to piece together a brief history of our state's first inhabitants. These remains are called artifacts, and by studying them, archaeologists have learned a lot about the first people of Missouri.

Traveling from Asia to Missouri!

Some archaeologists believe the first people living in America came here from Asia more than 20,000 years ago. They believe these people traveled here by walking across a bridge of land that once connected Asia and North America. This strip of land is called the Bering Strait and is now covered by the Bering Sea. Scientists believe that these first American Indians were hunters and they crossed the strip of land from Asia to North America searching for more game to hunt. They probably never knew they had crossed into a new continent, but they continued to spread south throughout North America and South America.

Mammoths and Mastodons

The first American Indians found large beasts in the Missouri area and hunted them for food. Archaeologists have found the bones of two types of large beasts that are now extinct, or not living anymore, here in Missouri. The mastodon and the mammoth were huge animals that the early American Indians used for food. These animals were large and slow, so to hunt them, the early people of Missouri scared them and then chased them into large bogs, or muddy swamps. When the beasts got stuck in the mud, the American Indians could kill them with their spears. Archaeologists think this because they have found American Indian spear points near the bones of the ancient mastodons and mammoths, telling them that the animals were probably killed by the sharp spear points.

Gathering Food

Eventually, the American Indians killed all of the big game, and their lifestyle began to change. They had to learn to hunt and kill small animals, and they also began to gather wild plants, berries and nuts in order to survive. These American Indians often lived in caves. Archaeologists have found many early American Indian artifacts in these caves. They have found needles made of bone, which were probably used for making clothes, and also small nets and bags. Scientists think the nets were used for trapping animals for food and the bags were used for storing seeds and nuts. Graham Cave, located in Montgomery County, is a famous cave where some of these artifacts have been discovered.

The Hopewell Farmers

Later, the early American Indians began to settle in towns and villages and planted crops for food. The Hopewell people are a group of American Indians who had settlements in Missouri, Ohio, Illinois, Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi. They are called the Hopewells after the family who owned the farm on which many of their artifacts were found.

The Hopewells were Missouri's first real farmers. They were also the first to live in towns and villages over long periods of time. They are sometimes called Mound Builders, because they built huge mounds of earth in the center of their towns. They used these mounds to bury their dead, and they also built temples and public buildings on top of the mounds. The Hopewells are known for their clay dishes and pottery as well. They were some of the first early Americans to use clay pots to store food and water.

The Mississippian people, who moved into the Missouri area after the Hopewells left, were also Mound Builders. They lived along the Missouri and Mississippi rivers, which is why we call them the Mississippian people. They lived in well-planned towns and often surrounded these towns with fences. The Mississippi people built large settlements on both sides of the Mississippi River close to what is now St. Louis. The Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site still preserves mounds left from these settlements of the Mississippian people.

By the time the first French explorers arrived in Missouri, the early American Indians were gone. The only things left were their mounds and other artifacts. There are still many things we don't know about these early people of Missouri, but thanks to the things they left behind, there are many things we do know.

title: Graham Cave State Park
text:
Graham Cave State Park is located in Montgomery County, in the mid-eastern section of Missouri. This state park is the home of one of Missouri's most interesting and famous archaeological sites, Graham Cave.

Graham Cave was once used as a home for some of Missouri's earliest American Indians, more than 10,000 years ago. Archaeologists have found many American Indian artifacts here, including needles made of bone, small nets and handmade bags. These artifacts are important because they help us understand how the early people of Missouri lived.

Visiting Graham Cave is an interesting experience because you can imagine what it might have been like to live as the early people of our state lived. There is a small museum in the park with exhibits that tell about prehistoric life in Missouri. Plus there are several other exhibits along the trail leading to the cave and at the cave itself.

Occasionally, there are special events scheduled, during which a real archaeologist will be on hand to tell you more about the ancient American Indians who lived in the cave and to show you around. You may want to find out when these events are scheduled before traveling to the cave.

title: Making Moccasins
text: There were two kinds of moccasins: hard-soled and soft-soled. Though a few tribes wove them from corn husks and basswood fibers, almost all moccasins were made from soft, tanned skins, and many were decorated with beads and porcupine quills. Plains Indians, such as the Sioux, often made hard-soled moccasins to protect their feet from the sharp grass and hidden objects of the prairies. Woodland tribes most often used soft-soled moccasins. Our tribes here in Missouri probably wore soft-soled shoes in the forest regions of our state.

title: What do we call the earliest people of Missouri?
text: We call them "prehistoric" American Indians because they lived at a time before their people started writing down their history. "Pre" means "before," so "prehistoric" means "before history." It isn't that the early American Indians didn't have a history; of course they did! It is just that we don't know exactly what that history is because they didn't write it down for us. We study their artifacts and the things they left behind and write their history as well as we can with the facts we have.

title: Black Walnut
text:
What is Missouri's state nut tree? If you guessed the black walnut tree, you're right!

The black walnut, or Jugal nigra, is a tree that is used both for its fruits, or nuts, and its lumber. The black walnut is native to the north temperate zone of the United States, and it thrives here in Missouri.

Although its nuts are delicious, they are also hard to remove from the shell, so most people who want to harvest walnuts for eating plant the English walnut tree instead. The black walnut is grown more for its lumber than for its nuts.

The lumber of the black walnut is very hard and durable. It is used for furniture, wall paneling, gunstocks, musical instruments and cabinets. Since colonial times, the wood of the black walnut has been the most popular cabinet wood in the United States.

The black walnut is also a beautiful tree that grows tall and gives wonderful shade. You may have noticed the black walnut in many places around your own neighborhood.

title: Synonyms
text:
Synonyms are words that have the same or almost the same meanings.

Learning synonyms for common words is important. Synonyms build your vocabulary. They can make your writing more interesting (alluring, compelling, fascinating) to read.

Below, you will find a common (ordinary, average, passable) fairy tale. Work with a partner to find synonyms for as many words as possible. Rewrite the fairytale using your favorite synonyms.

Do you want to find synonyms on the computer? Use this website to see what you can find: http://thesaurus.reference.com

Goldilocks and the Three Bears

Once upon a time, there were three bears. They lived in the forest in a cute little cottage. There was a big papa bear, a middle-sized mama bear, and a little baby bear. One chilly morning, mama bear stirred up some porridge. It was too hot to eat, so they went for a walk in the forest.

While they were out, Goldilocks came right in. She saw the porridge on the table and, forgetting her manners, sat down to eat.

“Wow,” said Goldilocks, “this big bowl is really hot.” She tasted the porridge in the middle-sized bowl. It was cold.

“Oh my heart,” she said, “this bowl of porridge is too cold.” Then she spied a little bowl. She took a little bite.

“Yummy!” she squeaked. It was just right. With a big smile on her face, she ate all of the porridge. It was just perfect for a crisp fall morning.

title: Let's Write
text: Pretend that you belong to one of the mound-building tribes. Describe how to build a mound and what it will be used for. What is the mound made of? How big is it? What type of buildings will be built on top of the mound? Who is in charge of planning the mound? Who does the work to build it? Use your imagination and have fun!

title: Celebrate Missouri Day
text:
Happy Missouri Day! What? Never heard of it? Believe it or not, Missouri Day has been around a long time. Since 1915, the third Wednesday in October has been Missouri Day. It is a day to honor the people who have made our state a great place to live.

The idea for Missouri Day came from Mrs. Anna Brosius Korn, a Missouri schoolteacher. Mrs. Korn wanted Missouri Day to be October 1. State lawmakers wanted it to be the first Monday of October, so it would always fall on a school day when students could celebrate Missouri and Missourians in class. In 1969 the holiday was moved to the third Wednesday in October.

Why October? Former Secretary of State Robin Carnahan says October was chosen for two reasons. First, Mark Twain believed that Missouri is “at her best in October.” Second, Jefferson City became our state capital on October 1, 1826. How will your class celebrate Missouri Day this year?

title: What Did American Indians Give to Us?
text:
We have learned that Missouri’s first people were American Indians who hunted, farmed and settled here long before white people claimed the land as their own. Although it has been many years since the early American Indians roamed the land, Missouri still retains many reminders of their presence.

The names of many of our rivers, lakes and cities are American Indian names. The cities of Neosho, Chillicothe, Osceola and Sarcoxie all take their names from American Indian words. As for rivers, we have the Missouri, Mississippi, Nishnabotna and Meramec.

We use many American Indian words without even realizing it! Woodchuck, toboggan, pecan and skunk are all American Indian words that we use and know the meanings of.

Did you know that the name of our state, Missouri, is also an American Indian word? Missouri is an American Indian word that means, “the people who have big canoes.” This is what an Illinois tribe called the people who lived by the river. They’d need a big canoe to travel the Big Muddy! French explorers wrote Missouri on their maps. Eventually, the French began to call the large river that these American Indians lived near the Missouri River. A large part of the Louisiana Purchase was renamed Missouri Territory, and in 1821 we took it as our state name. Since the American Indians were probably the first people to live here, it is natural for us to call our state after them.

What other things do we have to remind us of the early American Indians of our state? Many of the foods we eat every day come from the American Indian culture. Most American Indian diets were based on the “Three Sisters,” or corn, beans and squash. Corn was eaten fresh, or dried and used to make tortillas, cornbread and cornmeal mush. Beans were eaten with most meals. Squash was made into soups and stews. Often all three “sisters” were combined to make a dish called succotash. American Indians also grew potatoes, peanuts, pumpkins, tomatoes, peppers and melons.

Hominy is another food that you may have eaten which was first eaten by Missouri’s early inhabitants. Hominy is made from hulled and dried kernels of corn, which are then boiled.

Today you can find American Indian influence in art and clothing. We have also borrowed ideas about government and ecology (the study of how things interact with their environment) from American Indians.

Even though the early American Indian tribes don’t live here as they once did, the influence of these people lives on in our state. Whenever we say “Missouri,” or wear a pair of moccasins, or eat a piece of corn bread, we can remember the people who first called Missouri home.

title: Using the Internet to Find Out About YOUR History!
text:
This year, you have been studying a lot about Missouri's history, but you may be just as interested in finding out about the history of someone equally important - you! Have you ever heard the word "genealogy?" Genealogy is the study of family histories, and there are more and more people becoming interested in this study all the time.

One of the biggest reasons why more people have become interested in finding out about their family histories is that doing the research has just become much easier. To find out about your great-great-grandmother, you used to have to go to a county courthouse and ask to see huge, old, dusty books full of birth, marriage and death records. Or you could have gone to the library and spent hour after hour looking at old microfilm of newspaper stories, searching for a name that matched the one you were looking for. Now, because of the Internet, you can do family research at home using your own computer.

Dawn Detring of Jackson found some information about the mother of one of her ancestors on the Internet that she had been unable to find anywhere else. After using the Internet for only one week, she found out that the reason she had been unable to find any information on this woman was that she was actually a Cherokee Indian. No one had ever told her that before. "That was the best-kept secret in my family," she said.

Even if you can't find the information you want on the Internet, you may be able to contact distant relatives of yours who can share the information they have already found with you, and you can share what you have with them. There can be a problem with getting incorrect information, but you can always check it with several different sources just to make sure.

If you're interested in finding out about your history, ask your parents to join you and sit down at the computer. You may be surprised at what you find!

title: The Tribes of Missouri
text:
The Missouri Tribe

When the French explorers first came to the Missouri area, they found two American Indian tribes, the Missouri and the Osage. The Missouri, which means "the people who have big canoes," had settled on the Missouri River in what is now Saline County.

The Missouri Tribe lived in much the same way that other American Indians did before the European settlers came to the area. In the winter, they tracked and hunted large game such as bison, elk and deer and even hunted for wild turkeys. In the spring, they planted corn, beans and squash. In the fall, they harvested their crops and also gathered berries, nuts and wild fruit.

The Missouri people wore breechcloths, blankets and buffalo robes. They also made and wore bracelets of bone, copper, beads and brass. They made household items such as pottery for cooking and storing food, and needles and scrapers of bone for sewing clothing and skinning animals. The Missouri people also made tools out of stone to use in building their homes.

The Missouri people lived in dwellings much like a wigwam, or a house made out of a framework of poles covered with mats made of reeds. These could be taken down and set up again, much like a tent, when the Missouri people moved from place to place during a hunt.

The Missouri people traveled on foot before the Europeans brought horses to this country. They used dogs to pull their travois, a type of sled or trailer used to carry their belongings when they traveled. Dogs were also used as watchdogs to signal the tribe if danger approached. Often, dogs would even end up being used for food.

The Missouri people began to decline soon after the French explorers arrived in Missouri. The Missouri Tribe was destroyed by two powerful enemies, the Sauk Indians and smallpox. Smallpox was a terrible disease brought here by the Europeans, and the Missouri people couldn't fight it. Eventually, what was left of the Missouri Tribe moved west and joined the Oto Tribe in Kansas. It is from this tribe that our state takes its name.

The Osage Tribe

The largest and most powerful American Indian tribe in Missouri at the time the French explorers arrived was the Osage Tribe. The Osage had villages along the Osage River in what we now call Vernon County and also along the Missouri River in today's Saline County.

The Osage people were large and broad shouldered. They have been described as resembling giants, as many of them were more than six feet tall, and some were as tall as seven feet! They were strong and healthy people, and it wasn't uncommon for the Osage men to run 60 miles in one day or shoot an arrow all the way through a full-grown buffalo. The Osage people often called themselves the "Little Ones," which seems funny to us, considering that they were among the largest American Indians ever known.

The Osage Tribe both hunted and farmed to survive. The entire tribe, except for the very old or the very sick, went on the hunts. The Osage went on a spring hunt, which began in March and lasted until May, then returned to their villages to plant corn, beans and pumpkins. They then went on another hunt in the summer and returned to their villages in the fall to harvest their crops and gather other foods for the winter. They gathered walnuts, hazelnuts, pecans, grapes, papaws, roots and acorns to eat when the weather got cold. Then, after the harvest was over, the Osage went on one more hunt in the fall. But they returned to their villages again once the coldest weather hit and stayed at home during the winter.

During the hunting trips, the men did the hunting, and the women were in charge of skinning, cleaning and preparing the animals killed by the men. They were also in charge of planting and caring for the crops, as well as for gathering the nuts and berries and preserving and cooking the food. This type of work was considered by the Osage Tribe to be women's work.

The Osage people lived in lodges called long houses. These long houses were about 100 feet long, and 10 to 15 people lived in each long house. These houses were dark and smoky inside and were covered on the outside by animal skins, bark and grass mats. The long houses were considered permanent dwellings, but when the Osage traveled on their hunts, they took wigwams with them, much like the houses of the Missouri Tribe.

The Osage people also had horses, which they had taken from other American Indians, who got them from the Spanish. They were expert riders and used the horses in their hunts. They loved to show off their daring riding skills.

The Osage Tribe was eventually forced off of its lands by European settlers. By around 1825, the Osage had given up most of the land they held in Missouri, finally moving to Kansas and eventually to the Indian Territory of Oklahoma. There were a few other wandering tribes in Missouri, such as the Shawnee, the Delaware, the Kickapoos, the Peorias, the Sauk, the Fox, the Kansas and the Ioway, but these tribes usually just passed through Missouri on hunting trips and didn't settle or build villages here. The Missouri and the Osage tribes are the two main American Indian groups who were here when the French explorers arrived.

title: Neosho
text:
Neosho is located in Newton County on the edge of the Missouri Ozarks. Neosho is known throughout the country as the Flower Box City. In 1955, the city received a grant from the government to try an experiment in making the city more beautiful. The city used money from the grant to install and plant flower boxes in front of businesses, churches, schools and homes. The project grew each year, and now nearly every building in the city boasts at least one flower box.

When a new building is planned, either a business or a home, the planners often add built-in flower boxes to the buildings. This unique project adds beauty and color to Neosho and gives it something to be proud of.

"Neosho" is an American Indian word that means "clear or abundant water." The first American Indians who lived in this area called it Neosho because of the nine natural springs of crystal-clear water that surround it, making the area green and beautiful.

Neosho is still beautiful. In early spring each year, Neosho celebrates its Annual Dogwood Tour. One weekend each spring is set aside for enjoying the outdoors when the dogwood and redbud trees are blooming at their peak. Maps of the city and the surrounding area are available in Neosho, and people from all over Missouri come to view the trees in bloom.

In the fall, the Annual Fall Festival is held, celebrating the beauty of this season with parades, craft exhibits, contests, food and entertainment. Neosho is a beautiful part of Missouri that you may enjoy visiting.

title: Building a Canoe
text: It would take 10 to 20 days for two men and four women to finish a new canoe. In assembling the necessary material, the women dug and prepared spruce and tamarack root for sewing seams and gum for caulking. Birch trees provided the large sheets of bark needed for the skin of the canoe. The inner frames, or ribs, were of molded wood planking, held in shape by rawhide thongs. The canoe was held together with glue and root-thread stitching. The interior of the canoe was sheathed with thin wood planking. These canoes were used for transportation along the rivers and for fishing.

title: Do we say “Native American” or “American Indian”?
text: Some individuals and some entire tribes of Native Americans prefer to be called American Indians. Some are offended by the name Indian because the name was a mistake that Christopher Columbus made when he sailed to America and thought he had reached India. It is considered correct to use the terms Native American, American Indian, Indian or indigenous people, according to the tribes’ websites. Everyone agrees that we are all proud to be called Americans!

title: Flowering Dogwood
text:
The flowering dogwood became Missouri's state tree in 1955. It is from the genus Cornus and is a small tree with a short trunk and pretty, spreading branches. Because it is such a small tree, it is often found growing under larger trees, enjoying their shade.

The flowering dogwood is most beautiful when it is in full bloom. The flowering dogwood blooms in early April, after the cherry blossoms are gone and just before the azalea bushes begin to flower. The blooms of the dogwood tree are white, pink or red.

Did you know that the beautiful blooms we see on the dogwood tree aren't actually flowers at all? The large blooms that we call the dogwood flowers are actually petal-like bracts, or colored leaves. These bracts surround the true flowers of the dogwood tree, which are small and yellowish-green.

The dogwood is native to the southern states, but it thrives in Missouri as well. Nothing signals that spring is on its way like the sight of the dogwood trees in full bloom.

title: Rumination and Contemplation: Bacon’s Rebellion
text:
rumination (n): a thought; a pondering contemplation (n): a deep thought; reflection

Were you ever in a situation where you reacted quickly without thinking the problem through? What happened? Let’s look at Bacon’s Rebellion in Jamestown, Virginia, in 1676. As you read, think about whether the leaders used rumination and contemplation during the events.

Most people in the Virginia colony were farmers who had to deal with high taxes, low tobacco prices and problems trading with Europe. Hailstorms, floods and hurricanes destroyed many crops, and some American Indian groups attacked plantations.

Governor William Berkeley ignored the farmers’ call for help, and a young Englishman stepped forward. Nathaniel Bacon asked for permission to lead the army to drive all Indians out of Virginia. Gov. Berkeley refused. He didn’t want to upset the friendly Indians who traded with them. Bacon took a group of volunteer soldiers anyway and led a raid. They attacked American Indians who had not even been part of the earlier attacks.

Gov. Berkeley declared Bacon a rebel guilty of treason, but Bacon gathered almost 500 soldiers and took over Jamestown. They controlled the town from July to September of 1676. When Gov. Berkeley and his army took back control, Bacon was furious. His troops burned Jamestown to the ground.

Suddenly, Bacon got very sick and died. Gov. Berkeley arrested and hanged many of Bacon’s men. However, King Charles II of England was not happy with Berkeley and chose a new governor.

Find examples when both leaders acted without rumination and contemplation. What might have been different if they had thought about the situation carefully? Imagine that you were Gov. Berkeley or Nathaniel Bacon. What would you have done differently?

title: Plenty of Prefixes
text:
A prefix is a group of letters added to the beginning of a word that changes its meaning.

You have learned many different strategies for learning vocabulary words. Learning what prefixes mean is another strategy to add to your bag of vocabulary tricks.

When you know what the parts of a word mean, you can put them all together, and then voila!—you know what the word means.

Below is a short list of prefixes and their meanings. Study them and then complete the exercise.

2. re (again, back)
3. in, im, ir, il (not)
4. dis (not, opposite )
5. en, em (cause to)
6. non (not)
7. in, im (in or into)
8. trans (across)

10. sub (under)
