title: Language Arts Connection
text: As you read this week’s magazine, circle or highlight five words that are new to you. Write the words on a piece of paper. Try to figure out the meaning of the words by reading the other words and sentences around them. Write what you think the words mean and compare your definition to a dictionary definition.

title: Let's Write
text: In a short paragraph or two, tell what you think it would have been like to be a member of one of the early American Indian tribes living in Missouri. Would you rather have been a member of the Missouri Tribe or the Osage Tribe? What types of activities would you have enjoyed? What things would you have disliked about life as an early American Indian? What foods would you have liked? What foods would you have disliked? How would you have protected yourself from your enemies?

title: Father Jacques Marquette
text:
One of the earliest French explorers of the Missouri area was Father Jacques Marquette. Father Marquette was a Catholic priest who explored the area with fellow explorer Louis Jolliet. These two Frenchmen were the first Europeans to explore the Mississippi River area.

Marquette was born on June 10, 1637, in Laon, Aisne, France. He began his training as a Jesuit priest when he was 17 years old, and before long, he knew exactly what he wanted to do with his life. He had heard about the excitement and adventure in faraway lands, and he wanted to see it for himself. Marquette wrote, "Would that I be ordered to set out for foreign lands. This has been the object of my thoughts since my earliest childhood." In 1666, Marquette got his wish when he was assigned to the Catholic missions in Canada.

While working as a missionary in Canada, Father Marquette met a French trader named Louis Jolliet. Jolliet wanted to explore the land to the south and find new American Indian tribes to trade with for furs. When Father Marquette heard about Jolliet's interest in exploring the area, he was excited about the possibility of going along. He hoped to convert new American Indian tribes to Catholicism. The two men spent a lot of time talking to the American Indians living in the Great Lakes area about the land located to the west and south. These American Indians told Marquette and Jolliet about a river they called the Mississippi, which in their language meant "The Father of the Waters." This river fascinated Marquette and Jolliet, and they decided to set off on a journey down this great and unexplored river.

The two men left from St. Ignace, on Green Bay, where Father Marquette had served as a missionary since 1670. They had with them a crew of five men, and they traveled in two birch-bark canoes. The date was May 17, 1673. They found the Mississippi River with help from their American Indian guides and began paddling down the huge and mysterious river.

As Marquette and Jolliet traveled down the river, they were careful to record everything they saw, from the giant catfish in the river to the wild turkeys and buffalo along the banks. They took notes describing each American Indian tribe they found and each twist and turn of the river they noticed. Near the spot where the Missouri and Mississippi Rivers join, the group met and visited with some American Indians from the Missouri Tribe. These Missouri people warned Marquette and Jolliet that the American Indian tribes farther down the river were dangerous and unfriendly. Jolliet and Marquette were also afraid to travel farther down the river because they knew they might accidentally enter land that had been claimed by Spain. The Frenchmen were afraid that the Spanish might capture or kill them. Marquette and Jolliet decided it would be better for them to turn back than to risk their lives.

By the time the Frenchmen turned back, they had already explored an area that no European had ever seen before. They had also traveled far enough to discover that the Mississippi River did not lead to the Pacific Ocean, but that it led to the Gulf of Mexico, something that no one had known for certain.

After they returned to Canada, Father Marquette drew a detailed map of the Mississippi River based on their journey and on the notes he had taken. This map showed an American Indian village near the area where the Missouri River joins the Mississippi. He called the spot "Ou- Missouri." This word on Marquette's map later became the name by which the state of Missouri was called.

Marquette later traveled south again and founded a Catholic mission among the Illinois Tribe. On his way back to Canada, he became ill and died at the age of 38.

title: French Explorers
text:
France in North America

After the discovery of the New World, or the Americas, Spain sent many explorers here searching for gold and other wealth. Spain found gold and silver in Mexico and parts of South America, and it became a wealthy nation. The French watched Spain getting rich from the gold and silver they found in the new land, and they, too, wanted some of the wealth. France sent explorers to North America, hoping they would discover gold as well.

The early French explorers arrived in Canada, but found no gold or silver. However, they did find something of great value there. Wealthy French men and women loved to wear fancy clothing and hats made from the furs of beaver, mink and otter. These furs and skins were widely available in North America. The American Indians of the area trapped and skinned these animals, so the French made friends with these American Indians and found ways to get them to trade the furs with them. The Frenchmen traded tools, cloth, beads and guns with the American Indians for these valuable furs. Then they sent the furs home to France for a good price. Eventually, the French wanted to explore the land to the south and west, hoping to find more furs and more American Indians willing to trade with them.

Louis Jolliet was one of these French fur traders who wanted to explore the land to the south, hoping to find more furs and more friendly American Indians. He also hoped to find a waterway that would lead to the Pacific Ocean. He joined with a Catholic missionary, Father Jacques Marquette, on a journey down the mighty Mississippi River, and the two became the first Europeans to explore the Mississippi. (See the Cover Story article.)

Robert de La Salle

After the famous expedition of Jolliet and Marquette, another French explorer decided to make the same trip. Robert de La Salle planned to explore the Mississippi River and build a series of forts and trading posts along its banks. He set out in January of 1682 to explore the river and the land around it, claiming everything he saw in the name of the King of France, King Louis XIV. La Salle's group was made up of 23 Frenchmen and 28 American Indians. He also had with him a Catholic priest, Father Zenobe Membre, and an Italian chief lieutenant named Henry Tonty. Father Membre represented the Catholic Church and its desire to convert the American Indians to Christianity. Henry Tonty, called "Iron Hand" because he had lost a hand and wore a metal one to replace it, kept a very detailed journal describing the land, river and the American Indians they met on their journey.

Instead of stopping where Jolliet and Marquette ended their journey, near present-day St. Louis, La Salle and his group continued down the river until they reached the Gulf of Mexico. He arrived at the Gulf of Mexico on April 9, 1682, and claimed the land from the Appalachian Mountains on the east to the Rocky Mountains on the west, and from Canada on the north to the Gulf of Mexico on the south, for France, calling it "Louisiana," in honor of King Louis XIV.

On his way back to Canada, La Salle built Fort St. Louis on the Illinois River. He then sailed back to France, hoping to get money and workers in order to built a fort at the mouth of the Mississippi River to protect this new land from the Spanish and the English. La Salle never reached his goal, as he was unable to find the mouth of the Mississippi after returning from France. Instead of landing near the mouth of the Mississippi River, as he had planned, he landed in Texas. La Salle's angry crew finally murdered him.

Besides the fur traders, another group also interested in the Missouri area was the Catholic Church. Although the French didn't immediately rush to settle in Missouri after La Salle's journey, his expedition did pave the way for many Catholic missionaries to begin preaching to the American Indians in this area. The Black Robes, as the American Indians called the French Catholic missionaries, traveled into country never before seen by Europeans. The American Indians called these missionaries Black Robes because of the black religious robes they wore. These priests established missions, built churches, and acted as go-betweens between the French government and the American Indians. They probably knew more about the land and its people than anyone else before the first settlers actually came to Missouri.

The French explorers who first came to the Missouri area came for two main reasons: to expand the fur trade and to convert the American Indians to Christianity. Both the French fur traders and the Catholic missionaries helped to explore and eventually settle the land we now call Missouri.

title: St. Louis
text:
St. Louis is one of Missouri's oldest and most-well-known cities. It is located in St. Louis County, in the middle of the state, bordering Illinois. St. Louis is named after a famous French king, King Louis IX. If you visit St. Louis today, you will find many exciting things to do. St. Louis's most famous landmark is probably the Gateway Arch, which marks St. Louis as the Gateway to the West. You can visit this arch and even go up inside for a breathtaking view of the city.

If you are interested in history, you can also visit the Museum of Westward Expansion at the Gateway Arch, or go to the Missouri History Museum in Forest Park. Forest Park was the spot where the 1904 World's Fair was held.

There are ancient American Indian ruins located at the Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site. If you are more interested in Missouri's wild inhabitants, the St. Louis Zoo might be on your list of places to visit.

St. Louis also has some amazing museums. City Museum has exhibits that include an art-glass studio, a giant fish tank, a walk-through whale, a real circus and secret caves. Visitors can even make their own pair of shoelaces as part of one of the exhibits. Other unusual museums include the International Bowling Museum and Hall of Fame as well as the A.K.C. Museum of the Dog. St. Louis also has many professional sports teams, including the St. Louis Blues hockey team, the St. Louis Cardinals baseball team and the St. Louis Rams football team.

title: Loyalty
text:
Are you a sports fan? Do you have a favorite team? You probably jump and scream with joy when they win a game! What about when they lose? Does it make you gloomy? Chances are that you still say they're the best team ever, and you go back cheering even louder for their next game. That's called loyalty, and loyalty is a character trait that is what good kids are all about! It's cool to be loyal to your favorite team or even your favorite TV show, but it's much more important to be loyal to your family and friends!

It's easy to love the people around you when everything's going great, but what about when they make mistakes? Do you stick by them through thick and thin? If you do, you can bet they're thankful! Your loyalty will help them tough out the rough times and celebrate the good times!

title: Why did La Salle’s crew murder him?
text: After sailing to France for money and supplies, La Salle returned to North America, only to become lost. He had lost three of his four ships on his return voyage, along with most of his supplies, making life miserable for the crew that remained. La Salle landed in Texas, mistaking it for the mouth of the Mississippi River. He established a colony there, thinking that he was in Missouri. He later traveled inland, looking for help, but his unhappy crew killed him in March of 1687. The rest of his colony died from disease, starvation and American Indian attacks.

title: Channel Catfish
text:
Missouri's state fish is the channel catfish, or Ictalurus punctatus. When Jolliet and Marquette traveled down the Mississippi, they saw these huge catfish and wrote about them in their journals.

The channel catfish has eight barbels, or whiskers, is olive-green to bluish in color, and has dark spots. It also has a deeply forked tail. It grows up to 24 inches long and normally weighs up to 20 pounds. Channel catfish can live as long as 11 years.

The channel catfish lives in deep streams, rivers and lakes in the eastern and central United States. It can also be found in lakes, reservoirs and ponds with a water temperature around 70 - 80 degrees Fahrenheit.

During the 1950s, the Mississippi River was a major producer of catfish for eating. During this period, commercial fishermen harvested nearly 270,000 pounds of channel catfish from the Mississippi River each year.

The largest channel catfish ever caught in Missouri weighed in at 34 pounds, 10 ounces.

title: Help a Rat and Learn to Run the Country This Year!
text:
Hey, kids! I’m Revere the Rat, but you can call me Rev. I’m your online Studies Weekly friend and I need your help. You can help me get great stuff by earning points while you learn. Just scan the code or go to www.studiesweekly.com and click on my picture.

Has your family ever bought something that came with an owner’s manual? Cars, TVs and other things have an owner’s manual, a book on how to use them. Your social studies class is the “owner’s manual” for the United States of America. You’ll learn about history, geography, government by the people, and much more, so you can do a good job of running our country someday.

In America rats can’t vote, so “you the people” govern (run) the country. Someday you will be in charge of this country, and you’ll choose leaders and representatives by voting. Then you can tell the representatives you help elect how you think the country should be run. In fact, Studies Weekly kids are so smart, that many of you will someday be mayors, senators, governors—maybe even the president!

For now you have two jobs: Learn about the country and how it works and earn points for me so I can get that great stuff I told you about. It’s easy. Just scan or click and you’re on your way!

title: Learn How to Research
text:
Where do I find Information?

There are two main sources you can use to find information. The first is print sources, like books and newspapers. The second is electronic sources, found on your computer and the Internet. The Internet has information from all over the world, including the latest research. The problem with the Internet is sometimes the information can be wrong. Anyone can write whatever they like and post it online. So when you use a computer, you have to be careful which sites you use. Some online sites like factmonster.com take you to a number of places that give you great information. Whenever you use print or electronic sources, you have to decide if what the article says is important to your report. If you are writing about bats in Ohio, an article about bats in South America wouldn’t be very useful to you.

What print information might help you?

A. Atlases are books of maps and information about places.

B. Encyclopedias have information on almost anything you are researching. They are always in alphabetical order.

C. Dictionaries are helpful to find what words mean or how to pronounce them. They are in alphabetical order too.

D. Newspapers give information on issues and what is currently going on.

E. Multimedia and electronic sources can link you to atlases, encyclopedias, dictionaries and even newspapers online. You can also find research and articles about your topic. It’s a great way of getting the most up-to-date information, but you have to make sure it is correct.

Reading and Interpreting Graphs and Tables

When you do research, you will often find graphs and tables with a lot of information. Tables, graphs and charts help people understand information and issues. Tables organize information in columns and rows. Charts use pictures, diagrams and graphs to organize information. You can use many different types of graphs to show the same kinds of information.

Pictographs use pictures to give you information. They need pictures and a title to represent the numbers of things you are talking about.

Fruit in Sarah’s Refrigerator

The bar graph and line graph below show the same information as the pictograph, just in a different type of graph. Using a graph in your report can help your reader understand your information.

title: Life in French Missouri
text:
The first settlers in Missouri came from France. They began settling in Missouri in the early 1700s, at the same time the English were settling along the Atlantic Coast. The French villages were different from the English colonies in many ways.

While the English built their shops and stores in one part of town and their homes in another part of town, the French mixed their homes, shops, stores and public buildings together. Many French merchants even had their shops and stores in their homes. The English built their houses and business close together, while the French villages were set up with lots of space in between each building. The homes in the French villages were built on large sections of land surrounded by their barns, stables and slave cabins. The French homes and outbuildings were also surrounded with fences to keep out wild animals and stray horses, cows and chickens. These fences were made of tall cedar posts.

The houses built by the French were also different from those built by the English. Both the French and the English used logs to build their houses, but the English built log cabins, laying the logs lengthwise on top of each other, while the French stood the logs up on their ends, like fence posts. They filled the cracks between the logs with mortar made of mud, twigs and animal hair. They also painted the walls with whitewash, something the English didn't usually do.

Most of the French houses had very tall, steep roofs. These roofs were covered with grass mats to keep out the rain and weather, so they had to be steep to allow the rain to run off quickly before it had a chance to leak into the rooms below. The grass mats were wonderful places for bugs and mice to build their homes, and sometimes bugs and mice would actually fall through the roof and into the rooms of the house. Most French women didn't like this, so eventually the grass mats were replaced with wooden shingles.

The French also built porches on three or four sides of their houses. These porches were called "galleries" and were an early form of air conditioning. The galleries protected the houses from the sun and heat and also let the breezes blow through easily. The galleries were also good protection from wind, snow and rain during bad weather. The French also set up their farms differently than did the English settlers. The English settlers owned their own farms on separate sections of land, but the French planted their crops in a large field owned by the entire village. Because the field was owned by everyone in the village, it was called the "common field." Each family received a long strip of land to farm in the common field, and everyone was responsible for keeping the fence around the field in good condition.

The French usually planted their crops in the spring and then left the crops pretty much to themselves until harvest time in the fall. They planted wheat, corn, oats, barley, cotton, flax, hemp, tobacco, pumpkins, watermelons and muskmelons. They also grew apples, peaches and grapes.

The French farmed, hunted, traded for furs with the American Indians and mined for lead. They enjoyed life and met together often to celebrate religious festivals, socialize and dance. The French brought their love of good food, celebrations and family with them from France and made their villages places of happiness and fun. Although the English and the French both settled in America during about the same time period, they each set up their villages according to what they were used to and what was familiar to them.

title: The First European Settlers in Missouri
text:
French Explorers

After the first explorers came to the Missouri area, more French people followed. Fur traders came to trade with the American Indians in the area, Catholic missionaries came to convert the American Indians to Christianity, and other Frenchmen came in search of precious metals, such as gold and silver. Eventually, the French gave up on their search for gold and silver, but were happy to discover large deposits of lead in the eastern Ozark Mountains.

The French began mining for lead, which was used to make bullets, at places like Mine La Motte and Old Mines in the Ozark Mountains. The French also discovered natural salt springs near Ste. Genevieve and came here to make salt. Salt was very important to the early settlers because of its many uses. Salt was used for seasoning food and also for preserving meats and tanning animal skins. Without salt, much of the food eaten by the early settlers would have spoiled.

These mining villages and salt-making areas were not actually settlements, as the French only spent part of the year in these areas, working the mines and making salt. The first real settlement in Missouri was located on the River Des Peres near what is now southern St. Louis. This settlement was started by French missionaries and was also used by fur traders. The French lived with the American Indians in this settlement until the American Indians decided to move back across the river into Illinois. When this happened, the French settlement disappeared.

Fort Orleans

By the early 1700s, the French had built another village on the Missouri River called Fort Orleans. Fort Orleans was a center of trade for the American Indians and the fur traders in the area, and the trading post was very busy. It was eventually closed, however, because it was too expensive to get supplies sent to this out-of-the-way spot. Supplies for Fort Orleans had to be brought all the way up the Missouri and Mississippi rivers from New Orleans, and getting them there cost too much money. By the time the French owners of the trading post paid for the supplies, they couldn't make a profit, so they decided to close the fort around 1729.

Missouri's Oldest Cities

While these first French settlements disappeared after only a few years, Ste. Genevieve, another early French settlement, still exists in Missouri today. Ste. Genevieve was first settled in 1750 by French farmers who had been living across the river in Illinois. The farmland across the river in Missouri was rich, and the settlement grew quickly.

The first settlers in Ste. Genevieve built their houses along the Mississippi River, and every time the river flooded, so did their houses. Because of this, the early settlers sometimes called Ste. Genevieve "Misere," which means "misery" in French. In 1785, the flooding was the worst it had ever been, and people traveling on the river could tie their boats to the chimneys of the houses. After this flood, most of the residents of Ste. Genevieve decided to move their homes to higher ground, away from the river. The city of Ste. Genevieve is still located on the Mississippi River, in Ste. Genevieve County. It is considered Missouri's oldest city.

Missouri's second oldest city is the city of St. Louis. St. Louis was settled in 1764 by a French merchant named Pierre Laclede. Laclede and a business partner planned to set up a trading post, and Laclede chose this spot on the Mississippi River to build their settlement.

Laclede sent his 14-year-old clerk, Auguste Chouteau, to the spot to clear the land and build the first buildings of the settlement. Chouteau brought 30 workers with him and supervised them in the building of the town of St. Louis. St. Louis later became a successful fur-trading center and still later, the gateway to the West. St. Louis is still one of America's oldest and most important cities.

title: Courage
text:
On Dec. 1, 1955, Rosa Parks had the courage to refuse to give up her seat to a white person on a crowded bus in Montgomery, Alabama. She was arrested and tried. The result of the trial triggered a boycott (all blacks refused to ride the bus), which was organized by Martin Luther King Jr. Because of the boycott, the laws were changed so whites and blacks were allowed to sit together beginning on the 21st of that same month.

The greatest kind of courage is to do what is right when others call you a coward or a chicken for doing it. Our friends and people our own age are called our "peers." Pressure from our peers is called peer pressure. Sometimes, our peers don't have to say anything or make fun of us to pressure us into doing wrong things. Some people are clever at using flattery or other manipulative ways of getting us to do what they want us to do. If we are aware of what they are trying to do, we can prepare and avoid dangerous situations. It takes courage to stand up to your peers, but having courage will give you other important character traits such as loyalty and integrity. Your parents, teachers, church leaders or good friends can help you prepare to deal with peer pressure and develop courage in hard situations.

title: Buffalo or Bison?
text:
Are the animals that once roamed the plains of the United States called buffalo or bison? The American buffalo is really not a true buffalo at all. It is actually related to the European bison and the Canadian woods bison, not the cape buffalo or the water buffalo of Africa and Asia.

The American buffalo is actually a bison and belongs to the Bovidae family of mammals, just like the common cow. Because the first explorers and settlers called them buffalo, we still call them that today, but they aren't actually buffalo at all. Oh, give me a home, where the bison roam!

title: Salt
text:
One of the important resources that first brought settlers to the Missouri area was its natural salt springs. Sodium chloride, or salt, as we commonly call it, is a chemical compound that is found in the natural saltwater springs of Missouri.

Salt is one of the Earth's most useful chemicals. Most of the salt that is mined or harvested in the world is used to make other chemicals. Salt is also used for human and animal nutrition. It is called an "essential nutrient," which means that it is a nutrient that our bodies must have to survive and one that our bodies can't make on their own.

Another important use for salt is to keep our roads and sidewalks clear in the winter. Salt is sprinkled on the roads when they are icy to help melt the ice and prevent cars and people from slipping and sliding.

Salt is also used to condition the water used in homes and businesses. The water supply in many areas of the world contains a lot of minerals that build up in the water. Adding salt to the water supply, through a water softener, helps to dissolve these minerals and prevent the problems they cause.

title: Making the World a Kinder Place
text:
We sometimes wonder why bad things happen to innocent people. Although we may never understand it, we can do our best to keep things like this from happening in the future. When we do this, we are doing our part to make the world a kinder place, without anger and violence.

One way to do this is by making a plan to replace bullying and violence with kindness. The Cool to Be Kind (C2BK) program was developed to help students create programs in their classes and schools that are based on pro-kindness – doing nice things for others. Students look for ways to “pay it forward” each day. Paying it forward means that when someone thanks you for doing something nice, you ask that person to pay it forward by doing something nice for someone else. By paying it forward, kindness continues to spread across the world and people start thinking kinder thoughts and ways that they can help other people. What are some ways you could practice paying it forward? How about doing yard work for an elderly neighbor for free? Or inviting a new student to eat lunch with you and your friends? What about giving up your seat on the bus to someone who looks tired, or helping someone pick up something they have dropped? Thinking kind thoughts and acting on them with acts of kindness is a simple change that you can do to change the world.

title: Ste. Genevieve
text:
Ste. Genevieve is Missouri’s oldest city. It is located on the Mississippi River in Ste. Genevieve County, about 50 miles south of St. Louis. Ste. Genevieve was settled around 1735 and has a very rich history. Each year, thousands of people come to Ste. Genevieve to visit its famous historic French district and enjoy the festivals that are planned throughout the year.

The Ste. Genevieve Museum has many interesting exhibits that teach about the early history of the area. The museum has prehistoric American Indian relics, old documents and items used by local citizens long ago.

There are also beautifully restored French homes, built as early as 1784, and tours are offered of both the outsides and insides of these historic buildings. The Bolduc House and the Felix Valle House are both fine examples of the types of houses that the early settlers once owned.

The citizens of Ste. Genevieve enjoy celebrating their French heritage with many festivals and events throughout the year. The King’s Ball has been held each February for nearly 300 years and is still held today. A Spring House Tour is open to the public each year, and La Fete Francaise, a festival with French food and entertainment, is also held in the spring. Bastille Day is celebrated in July, and Jour de Fete, one of the largest craft fairs in Missouri, happens every August. Fall Harvest is celebrated in October, and a Christmas Walk is held each December.

Ste. Genevieve is a beautiful city that preserves some of Missouri’s earliest history.

title: James Monroe
text:
James Monroe was one of our country's great statesmen. He served as president of the United States from 1817 to 1825 during what was later called the "Era of Good Feelings." It was called this because it was a time when the new country of America was beginning to feel good about itself and to have success in many areas. The political party that President Monroe was a member of, the Democratic-Republican Party, ruled almost without opposition. People were beginning to leave the colonies to settle the lands in the West, roads and canals were being built, and, most of all, people had begun to think of themselves not just as Missourians or Virginians, but as Americans. America as a nation was growing and becoming more powerful.

Before Monroe became president, he served his home state of Virginia as a congressional representative and later as governor. He also served his country as a US Senator. While serving in Congress, he became very interested in the lands west of the Mississippi River. During 1784, Monroe took a trip through the West. He went up the Hudson River, saw the Great Lakes, and returned down the Ohio River. After this visit, Monroe was more interested than ever in making these lands part of the United States.

Monroe is not only famous for serving his country here at home, but also for his work as a diplomatic minister (one who represents his or her nation to another country for the purpose of good relations) to France. Monroe had been serving as a United States Senator from Virginia when he was asked to go to France and try to improve relations between the United States and France. France was unhappy with the United States because it thought the United States was too friendly with Great Britain, France's greatest enemy.

Monroe went to France in 1794 to see what he could do. While he served as a minister to France, some people thought he showed too much love for France. He often gave speeches that were very much in favor of France and not in favor of Great Britain. Eventually, he was called back from France because the United States was afraid that the things Monroe was telling the French would upset the British. The United States was hoping to remain friendly with both France and Great Britain.

Although Monroe was called home from France because he seemed to be too friendly with the French, this good relationship would come in handy a few years later. In 1803, Monroe was sent back to France when the United States was ready to make what has been called the largest real estate deal in history, the Louisiana Purchase, which included our fair state. Monroe joined United States Diplomat Robert Livingston in France and helped to figure out the terms of the agreement. Monroe's good relationship with the French and his interest in expanding the United States westward helped to make the Louisiana Purchase a wonderful deal for America. By the time he died in 1831, Monroe had given more than 40 years to public service. He spent his life doing what he considered to be his duty in helping to make the United States a strong, honorable and lasting country.

title: Blowing in the Wind
text:
Missouri's population is always growing and our non renewable resources are always shrinking. We are beginning to look for new sources of electricity to power all our lights, televisions and computers.

Have you ever heard of a wind farm? Wind farmers don't actually grow wind, of course, but they do collect wind energy. Wind farms are large fields containing towering windmills whose propeller blades turn in the blowing wind. The turning blades power generators that change the motion into electricity.

The Wind Capital Group has built five wind farms in Northwest Missouri. In 2008, the Conception Wind Farm began producing energy for its community. This more than 7,000 acre farm is located in Nodaway County on the land that surrounds the Conception Abbey. The farm contains 24 turbines each standing 260 feet tall. Each turbine weighs almost 200 tons!

Wind power produces no pollution. It currently only makes up a small percent of Missouri's electricity, but wind power (and other clean, renewable resources) is becoming more important as our non renewable resources decline.

title: Missouri and the Louisiana Purchase
text:
French Gain the Louisiana Territory

By the late 1700s, Spain had taken control of the Missouri area, although the French settlers still lived there. In 1800, however, the Spanish made a deal with France to give control of the area back to France. France traded the region of Tuscany, in Europe, to Spain for the Louisiana region in North America. Spain was more interested in getting control of Tuscany, and France was very anxious to get back control of the Louisiana Territory to keep it out of the hands of Great Britain, its greatest enemy. Napoleon, the leader of France, was planning to make France a powerful nation by gaining control of some important lands.

When the United States heard about this new development, they were worried because when the French were in control of the port of New Orleans once before, they had closed it to the Americans. This made it impossible for them to float their goods down the Mississippi River and sell them in New Orleans. The western traders wanted the United States government to help them keep the port of New Orleans open for trade.

The United States Makes a Deal

President Thomas Jefferson decided to talk to the French and try to solve the problem. He asked Robert Livingston, the American minister to France, to talk to the French government about the Mississippi River. He also sent James Monroe, the former American minister to France, and told these two men to offer to buy New Orleans and western Florida from France as well.

When Livingston and Monroe visited with Napoleon about the problem, they were surprised to have Napoleon offer to sell the entire Louisiana Territory to the United States. Napoleon had lost interest in trying to hang on to land in America, and he was also in great need of money, as he was still trying to revive a war against Great Britain. He also wanted to make sure the Louisiana Territory never ended up under British control, the British were despised enemies of the French. Because he wanted to resolve the problem quickly, Napoleon offered to sell the entire Louisiana Territory, about 375 million acres, to the United States for the unbelievably low price of $15 million.

Livingston and Monroe were surprised, but they quickly worked out an agreement, and the treaty (an agreement between nations) for the Louisiana Purchase was signed on April 30, 1803. Neither of the American representatives had been told that they could spend that much money or buy that much land, but when the opportunity came, they couldn't refuse. President Jefferson later approved their actions, and most people in the United States were happy with the purchase of the new western lands.

This purchase doubled the size of the United States at the price of only a few cents per acre. The United States made a great bargain!

Missouri Territory Becomes Part of the U.S.

On Dec. 20, 1803, the French flag was lowered at New Orleans, and the American flag was raised. A few months later, another flag-raising ceremony was held, this time in St. Louis. On March 9, 1804, Captain Amos Stoddard accepted the transfer of Upper Louisiana from France to the United States. The American flag was raised for the first time over Missouri on this date.

Moses Austin, the colonizer of Texas, wrote in his journal around 1797, "It is Not possible a Country which has with in its self everything to make its settlers Rich and Happy can remain unnoticed [sic]" (Spelling and capitalization are as originally written.) The words of Austin proved to be true, as Americans began to flood this new area, in search of fertile soil, wide open spaces and the adventure of a new land.

title: Cape Girardeau
text:
Cape Girardeau is located in southeastern Missouri on the banks of the Mississippi River. Cape Girardeau was first settled around 1705 as a furtrading post by Sieur Jean B. Girardot. It joined the United States as part of the Louisiana Purchase in 1803.

Cape Rock Park has been established on the spot where the original trading post stood. A great rock once projected out into the Mississippi River at this spot, forming a natural cape, or point of land projecting out into the water. It is considered the only inland cape in the world. Most of the huge rock has since been blasted away to make room for the railroad, but the park still stands.

Cape Girardeau is nicknamed the "Rose City" because of the beautiful roses grown here. Capaha Rose Garden, located in Cape Girardeau, was started in 1953 as a test garden for new varieties of roses. It has since grown and developed into one of three Rose Display Testing Gardens in Missouri. It is a beautiful place to visit.

Missouri's first flag was designed and hand-stitched by one of Cape Girardeau's citizens, Marie Elizabeth Watkins Oliver, in 1913. The home where she made our first flag still stands near Southeast Missouri State University. There are also many Civil War monuments throughout Cape Girardeau. There are monuments to soldiers from both the North and the South. Although Cape Girardeau considered itself Confederate during the war, it was occupied by the Union forces throughout the war and chooses to remember both sides in its statues.

title: Conscience
text:
Did you ever stop to think about how lucky you are that your finger hurts when you hit it with a hammer? On the news recently was an 8-year-old boy in England who can't feel pain. For some reason, his nerves do not signal pain to his brain.

He doesn't know when he's hurting? He's lucky, you say? Well, that condition may just cost him his life. He was burned seriously not long ago by a red-hot oven door that he was leaning against and didn't realize was turned up high. He didn't realize that his skin was sizzling until he was snatched away. The doctors can't help him. All they can do is give him special protective clothing to help keep his wounds clean. The boy is still in danger of dying from his wounds.

Just as your nerve endings send signals to your brain when you're hurt, you have "nerve endings" called a conscience, which sends signals to your heart when you've done something wrong and you know it. Your conscience is one of your greatest gifts. Without it, you, like the boy and the oven door, wouldn't know enough to keep from getting burned - only in a far more serious way.

Let's cultivate our consciences and learn to listen to them. We have no better friend.

title: What’s our state flag look like?
text: Missouri's state flag, designed and sewn by Marie Elizabeth Watkins Oliver, has three horizontal stripes of red, white and blue. The red represents valor, or courage, the white represents purity, and the blue represents vigilance (alert watchfulness) and justice. In the center of the white stripe is the Missouri coat of arms, circled by a blue band containing 24 stars, because Missouri was the 24th state to join the Union. This flag was adopted as the official state flag of Missouri on March 22, 1913.

title: Roses
text:
The rose, or Rosa, is a familiar plant that is prized for its beautiful, sweetsmelling flowers. It is part of the same scientific family of plants as the raspberry, blackberry, dewberry, loganberry, almond, apricot, cherry, nectarine, peach and plum.

The rose plant is thorny, with stipules (small, paired leaves at the base of the larger leaves), and flowers made up of five sets of parts. The rose flower is one of the most beautiful and popular flowers of all time. The rose is a native of North America, which means it is found growing here naturally.

Missouri has a great climate for growing roses, as it is humid and neither too cold nor too hot. Missouri has three Rose Display Testing Gardens, where new varieties and types of roses are grown and displayed to those who come to visit. These gardens are located in Kansas City, St. Louis and Cape Girardeau.

Roses are used primarily for their beautiful flowers, but they are also used to make sweet perfumes and light-tasting jellies, as well as in hedges and landscaping.

title: Quadrorama
text:
Materials

Four 8-inch by 14-inch pieces of construction paper

Craft materials—construction paper, string, fabric scraps, cotton, markers and crayons

Scissors

Tape

Glue

Pencil

Ruler

Directions

Fold the top left corner of a piece of 8x14 construction paper diagonally so that the top edge of the paper is flush with the right edge of the paper.

Fold the top right-hand corner diagonally so that it touches the lower point of the previous fold.

Fold the panel at the bottom to make a horizontal crease along the edge. (Fold it to the back.)

Open the paper up and cut along the lower left-hand diagonal crease to the center of the paper.

Pull point A over to point B so that the piece you cut is flush with the lower right-hand diagonal crease. Glue the base into place. This is one triorama.

When four trioramas are finished, glue them together to form a pyramid. From underneath, tape the four lower panels so that they form four corners. This is now called a quadrorama.

Design the Inside

Color and cut out the pictures.

Glue the scenes inside each triorama.

Write a brief paragraph describing the scenes along the bottom flap. Make guiding lines by lightly drawing pencil lines after writing the paragraph.

You can decorate the scenes using any available craft materials to make the scene three-dimensional.

title: What are Idioms?
text:
Have you ever heard an adult say, “I’m sorry, but we’re up a creek on this one”? What did he mean? He was standing on dry ground when he said it! Well, you’ve just heard an idiom.

Idioms are Not Meant to Be Taken Literally

Idioms are sayings that mean something different from the literal meaning of their words. “Literal” means “following the exact wording.” But idioms are not literal, so the words do not mean exactly what they say. Listen carefully for clues to figure out an idiom.

The best way to learn what an idiom means is to learn it and use it in your own speech or writing. Ask someone what it means. Then use it in your own writing. Here are some idioms in sentences. See if you can figure out what they mean. Once you know what the idiom means, use it in your own sentence.

1. They were both so shy they had a hard time breaking the ice. Use “breaking the ice” in your own sentence.

2. When it comes to modesty in dress, I have to draw the line somewhere. Use “draw the line” in your own sentence.

3. By halftime, the game was in the bag. Use “in the bag” in your own sentence.

4. Chris and I are in the same boat because neither of us have extra cash to spend on the field trip. Use “in the same boat” in your own sentence.

5. Would someone lend me a hand with the dishes? Use “lend me a hand” in your own sentence.

title: Language Arts Connection
text: Use any color to highlight three relative adverbs (where, when, why) in this week’s magazine. Underline the clause that contains the relative adverb and circle the noun that the clause modifies.

title: Exploring a Strange Land!
text:
Welcome to another terrific issue of Missouri Studies Weekly! This week, our adventures take us back in time nearly 200 years to the land of the Rocky Mountains and beyond to the Pacific Ocean. We know all about this land today, but back in 1803 it seemed like a distant new world. No European Americans had ever been there. President Thomas Jefferson wondered if dinosaurs might still exist in the area. Exploring these lands seemed as unknown and scary to people then as sending a man to Mars may seem to us today. Come with us as we meet the two brave men chosen to lead the "Corps of Discovery," as they were called, into this strange and forbidding new land.

So who were Meriwether Lewis and William Clark? These were really great men - they were brave and smart and they loved adventure. They were friends of President Thomas Jefferson who were appointed to explore a huge chunk of land called the Louisiana Purchase (a large chunk of land that doubled the size of the United States). In 1803, this was the latest addition to America's backyard, but no one knew for sure what was there. Lewis and Clark were given the job to find out. They were to follow the Missouri River to its source and, from there, try to get to the Pacific Ocean. They accomplished their goal, but not without near starvation, one death, dangerous encounters all the way, and much sickness and hardship.

Sacajawea Joins the Expedition

The party of 33 departed on May 21, 1804, from St. Charles. By late fall, they reached Fort Mandan in what is now North Dakota, where they wintered. Their French guide had brought with him his wife, an American Indian woman named Sacajawea. She was a Shoshone and knew much about the country. She also helped negotiate with American Indians as an interpreter. Her first baby, Jean-Baptiste, was born at camp, and Clark nicknamed him Pompey. Before a difficult journey over the Bitterroot Mountains, the group stumbled onto Sacajawea's home tribe and family. There was much dancing, crying and embracing when she found her brother, friends and relatives, not seen since she was a little girl. The expedition traded with the Shoshone for horses so they could cross the Bitterroot Mountains.

title: Springfield
text:
Springfield is located in southwestern Missouri in Greene County. It is Missouri's third largest city and has become quite a tourist attraction in the last few years. It has gentle mountains, green forests, blue lakes and clear streams that make it a place people love to come and see.

Springfield has many exciting and interesting places to visit. One popular tourist site is Fantastic Caverns, a cave that allows visitors to ride rather than walk through on a 50-minute tour. Tourists ride through an ancient underground riverbed in train-like cars, viewing the cave formations from their seats as they ride by.

Another interesting place to see in the Springfield area is the Laura Ingalls Wilder Museum and Home. This is the home where the Little House books were written. The museum also has family pictures, Pa's fiddle, Laura's handwritten manuscripts for her books, and other interesting family items. If you have ever read any of the Little House books, you will enjoy your visit to this historic location.

If you like animals, Springfield has a place for you. Exotic Animal Paradise is a drive-through animal park where visitors can drive through more than 400 acres of land with wild animals and birds in their own natural habitats. There are more than 3,000 wild animals, including bears, lions, kangaroos and exotic birds, that can be seen from the comfort of your own car. The park is an amazing sight for anyone who enjoys animals.

Springfield has many other things to see and do. If you feel like seeing more of our beautiful state, be sure to put Springfield on your list!

title: Gunsmith
text: As pioneers moved west and explorers such as Lewis and Clark moved into unknown territory, the demand for rifles increased. The best known firearm manufactured at this time was the Kentucky rifle. The gunsmith made his own gun barrels by wrapping hot iron bands around a cylindrical rod then driving the rod back out of the formed barrel. In the late 19th century, mass production methods replaced traditional gunsmithing.

title: Can chirping crickets tell temperatures?
text: Yes! If you can count cricket chirps, you can tell the temperature. Count the number of cricket chirps from one cricket (or a group chirping in unison) for exactly 15 seconds, and then add 37. That will be the temperature in Fahrenheit. Celsius is a little harder. Count the chirps in 25 seconds, divide by three, add four, and that will be the temperature in Celsius.

title: The Beaver
text:
The beaver is the largest rodent in North America. A rodent is an animal like a rat or squirrel that has big, sharp teeth. Most adult beavers weigh around 40 to 50 pounds, but the largest ones weigh close to 100 pounds. The beaver has a big, flat tail that grows 12 to 18 inches long. The tail helps the beaver move and swim in water. A baby beaver is called a kit. A beaver family has three to four kits at a time. Beavers make dams in the water out of trees, plants and mud. A dam can measure up to 10 feet high and 100 feet wide! They are mainly nocturnal; this means they sleep during the day and are awake at night.

Some people think the beaver and beaver dams cause trouble. Did you know beavers also help nature? A beaver dam provides places for other animals and plants to live. Their dams also help clean water and stop trash from flowing downriver as the water drains through their dams.

Beavers are found all throughout Missouri in our state parks.

title: Celebrating a Hero’s Trip Around the Earth
text:
It was 1957 when the Soviet Union launched the first spacecraft into orbit. Americans were shocked! The space race had just begun and we were already behind! In 1961 President John F. Kennedy announced that the U.S. planned to land a man on the moon by the end of the decade. The Russians responded by first launching a dog into orbit, and later two men. The race was on!

On Feb. 20, 1962, a Marine Corps fighter pilot from Ohio stepped up to put his life on the line. John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth. The success of his Mercury mission was one of the first steps to landing a man on the moon in July 1969.

John Glenn served as the U.S. senator from Ohio for 24 years, but he longed to go back into space. In 1998 at the age of 77 he was able to see that dream come true. He traveled on the space shuttle Discovery and became the oldest person to ever go into space! On Feb. 20th, 2012, America celebrated the 50th anniversary of John Glenn’s first orbit. Mr. Glenn and the remaining members of the Mercury mission space team were given a hero’s welcome at Cape Canaveral in Florida. Because of Mr. Glenn’s service to our country as an astronaut and a senator, he has been called an American hero.

title: Critical Analysis: Henry Knox and the Cannons
text:
What does it take to be a good problem solver? Why is critical analysis, or careful judgment, so important? A bookseller from Boston named Henry Knox is an excellent example.

Knox was born in Boston in 1750. His father died when he was 12, so he left school to be a clerk in a bookstore. Later, Knox opened his own bookstore. He loved to read and learned a lot about military strategies and weapons from the books he read.

Knox sided with the American patriots and joined the Army in 1775. General George Washington soon noticed him because of his military knowledge.

The British forces were in Boston, and General Washington needed heavy artillery to force them out. Knox suggested bringing cannons from Fort Ticonderoga in northern New York down to Boston. This idea sounded impossible, but Washington trusted Knox’s judgment.

Using heavy sleds drawn by oxen, Knox and his men traveled 300 miles. They brought over 50 cannons across snow-covered mountains and frozen rivers. They placed them overnight on a hill overlooking the harbor. When British Gen. William Howe saw this, he withdrew his troops. He said, “The rebels have done more in one night than my whole army would have done in a month.”

Henry Knox used critical analysis again when he supervised Washington’s famous crossing of the icy Delaware River. Knox stood on the shore shouting directions while boats moved troops, horses and weapons across. Washington’s soldiers then won the Battle of Trenton. The next day they went back across the river with even more prisoners and supplies.

Washington promoted Henry Knox to brigadier general. When Washington became president, he made Knox the first secretary of war. Henry Knox used expert knowledge plus critical analysis to become a military mastermind. For what problem could you use your best judgment to solve?

title: How Do I Use a Dictionary?
text:
What does “native” mean? How do you pronounce “shaman”? To find the answers to these and many other questions, grab a dictionary. The dictionary just might be a student’s best friend. A dictionary lists and defines words.

Know Your ABCs

The words in a dictionary appear in alphabetical order. At the top of each page, two guidewords show the first and last words on that page. Guidewords help you find the word you need more quickly. For example, the word “tepee” might appear on a page with the guidewords “tension” and “territory” at the top of that page.

Is your word followed by numbers? That means it has more than one definition. Look up the word “native” and see all the definitions for it. Write some of them here:

After each word, you will find a letter that stands for a part of speech. For example, n. means “noun,” v. means “verb,” and adj. means “adjective.” Sometimes, one word can have two or more parts of speech. It depends on how it’s used in a sentence. Let’s show this with the word “hunt.” Look it up now in your dictionary.

title: An “Interest”ing Way to Make Money
text:
Why do people save money? Some people save up to buy something special; others save money for emergencies, like getting sick or needing a new roof after a storm. Many people save money for retirement, the time when they don’t have to work anymore. Those are all good reasons for saving money.

But there’s another reason to save money. Did you know there are ways to make your money grow faster by letting someone else use it for a while? That’s called investing. How does that work? Let’s take a look.

Imagine that you put $1 each week in a piggy bank or cookie jar. At the end of one year, you will have $52. Sounds pretty good, right? But if you put $1 each week in a savings account, the bank will pay you interest. Interest is the money you get for letting the bank use your money for a while. The bank invests your money in things like real estate (homes, farms and land) or the stock market, and your money makes more money. You get some, and the bank keeps some. So, at the end of one year, instead of having $52 you might have $53 or $54.

There are many ways to earn interest on your money. You don’t have to let the bank invest your money for you. You can invest in things like real estate or the stock market on your own. There are lots of other choices, too.

How do you know where to invest? You can do research to find out which investments are right for you. Or you can get some help from a financial planner, a person who gives people advice about how to invest money.

Are you getting “interested”? Then start saving!

title: Lewis and Clark Explore a Strange and Forbidding Land!
text:
Heading West

With the addition of the Louisiana Purchase land to the country, President Thomas Jefferson needed an expedition to explore and map the new land and to find a route to the Pacific ocean. Meriwether Lewis and William Clark were asked to lead this group, called the Corps of Discovery. Lewis and Clark began their expedition in May 1804. The Corps of Discovery started with three boats near St. Louis, Missouri, and headed west along the Missouri River.

York, an enslaved man owned by William Clark, also joined the expedition. He was allowed to hunt, which was very unusual since African Americans were not allowed to handle guns.

Winter Camp

When they were deciding on a location to spend the winter, both York and Sacagawea had a vote equal to that of a white man. The group built Fort Mandan in North Dakota and stayed there during the long, cold winter. While there, Lewis and Clark hired a man named Toussaint Charbonneau to be their guide and interpreter. He brought along his American Indian wife, Sacagawea, who also served as a translator. She was a Shoshone and knew much about the country. Her first baby, Jean-Baptiste, was born at camp. Clark nicknamed him Pompey. At risk to his own life, York saved Clark, Sacagawea and her son from a flash flood.

Dangers and Hardships

During their journey west, the group faced many dangers and hardships. They were often hungry, even though they had brought along food and supplies. They planned their meals around whatever meat, fish, berries or plants they could find while traveling. Sacagawea taught the men how to dig roots and find other foods.

Paddling their boats along the Missouri River was dangerous work. The boats would often tip over, soaking both the travelers and their supplies. There were times when supplies ran low and food was difficult to find. Sickness and injuries were common. Sacagawea showed the men how to make moccasins and leather clothes to keep them warm.

‘Ocean in View!’

Eventually, Sacagawea helped the men trade with a Shoshone tribe for horses. They used the horses to cross the Rocky Mountains. During a difficult journey over the Bitterroot Mountains, the group stumbled onto Sacagawea's home tribe and family. There was dancing, crying and hugging when she found her friends and relatives she had not seen since she was a little girl.

In November 1805, the Corps of Discovery finally reached the Pacific Ocean. Clark wrote in his journal, “Ocean in view! O! The joy!” When the Corps of Discovery returned from the expedition, all the members received double pay and 320 acres of land, except York. York was returned to slavery when the expedition returned.

title: The Star-Spangled Banner
text:
The words to our national anthem were written by Francis Scott Key during a battle of the War of 1812. The War of 1812 was fought between the Americans and the British and lasted about three years. Key was an attorney in Washington, D.C., during the time that the War of 1812 was being fought. He had spent some time serving in the Georgetown Light Field Artillery, part of the U.S. Army, during 1813 and 1814, but had gone back to his duties as a lawyer.

While in Washington, DC, Key found out that his friend, Dr. William Beanes, had been taken prisoner by the British army. As a lawyer, Key felt that he might be able to help get his friend released from prison. He went to Baltimore, Maryland, and asked Colonel John Skinner, the U.S. government officer in charge of exchanging prisoners of war, to come with him to try to free Dr. Beanes. Colonel Skinner agreed to go, and the two men sailed down the bay to the H.M.S. Tonnant, the ship where Dr. Beanes was being held prisoner.

The two men met with British officers, and at first, they were unable to convince the British to let Dr. Beanes go. Finally, some of the British soldiers came forward and told how the doctor had treated many injured British soldiers during the war. After hearing this, the British officers in charge finally decided to let the doctor go. They let Dr. Beanes, Colonel Skinner and Key return to their own ship, but sent a British warship to guard them until after the attack on Fort McHenry, an American fort at Baltimore, ended. The three Americans watched the battle between the British and the Americans from their ship and wondered what the outcome would be. The first day of the battle, it looked as if the British would win and the Americans would be defeated. The men kept a close watch to see whether the American flag flying over Fort McHenry would be replaced with the British flag.

The battle continued on into the night, and a fierce storm began. Rain, thunder and lightning, along with exploding shells, pelted the fort. When dawn finally broke, Key looked out to see if the fort had remained under American control. With gratitude and joy, he found that the "stars and stripes" still flew over Fort McHenry, and the battle had been won.

Key, who often wrote poems about important events in his life, wrote later, "Then, in that hour of deliverance, my heart spoke. Does not such a country, and such defenders of their country, deserve a song?" He sat down and wrote the words to "The Star-Spangled Banner," using the tune of a British song, "To Anacreon in Heaven." The poem detailed the events of the past day and night and told of his gratitude in finally seeing the flag of the United States of America still flying over Fort McHenry.

The song became popular because of its patriotic words and familiar tune. During the Civil War, the Union Army sang it often to raise their spirits and build patriotism. Later, during World War I, the U.S. Army sang "The Star-Spangled Banner" as its theme song. It wasn't until 1931, however, that "The Star-Spangled Banner" became the official national anthem of the United States of America. President Herbert Hoover decreed that Key's famous song should be the national anthem of our country nearly 117 years after it was first written.

title: War of 1812
text:
Westward Movement

After the Louisiana Purchase, Americans from the East began flocking to the new lands. The American Indians living in the area were pushed off of their lands, and many became upset with the new settlers. About this same time, the United States and Great Britain began to disagree over how shipping and trade were being handled in Europe. England and France were still at war, and France controlled most of Europe, while England controlled the oceans with its ships. American ships trading in the area were neutral, meaning that they were not involved in the war, and they didn't support one side or the other. Americans traded with both sides, which upset the British.

Blockades and Impressment

England set up a blockade of the European coast. A blockade is a closure of an area so that ships can't go into or out of that area. Later, the French set up a blockade of the British Isles. American ships couldn't trade in either area without risking being taken over by either the British or the French.

The British then began something called impressment. Impressment meant that when a British ship met up with an American ship, the British ship would capture it and take the American sailors prisoner, forcing them to serve the British military. Many of these British sailors had left British ships in order to make more money working on American ships.

After taking them prisoner, the British would then put these sailors to work on British ships once more. The problem was, American sailors would often be captured and "impressed" into service for the British fleets as well. This treatment of American sailors did not sit well with Americans, and their anger rose.

War is Declared

By 1807, President Thomas Jefferson saw that tempers were rising, but in an effort to avoid going to war, he persuaded Congress to pass an embargo against all foreign countries. An embargo is an act that makes it illegal to trade with certain countries. The United States chose not to buy goods from or sell goods to other nations. This embargo was supposed to punish Great Britain for its behavior toward America, but the British had most of the goods it needed already, and the embargo hurt America financially more than it did England.

Eventually, war could no longer be prevented, and on June 18, 1812, James Madison, now president of the United States, declared war on England.

Because of their frustration over the great numbers of white settlers coming into their lands, many American Indians chose to join the British during the War of 1812 and fight against the United States. The Missouri territory was immediately plagued by American Indian raids against the white settlers. Most settlements built wooden stockades around themselves, complete with strong log forts at each corner. The settlers complained to Washington about the attacks, but every available soldier was already busy fighting the British, so the territorial officials organized their own militia. They called themselves the "Minutemen of the Frontier." Each man brought with him his own horse, rifle and provisions. This group kept a constant eye out for American Indian attackers and patrolled the Missouri River to keep the settlements secure. After this, the American Indian attacks decreased, and the settlers felt more safe.

Battle of New Orleans

After fighting for a couple of years, both the British and the Americans began to realize that neither one of them were actually winning the war and that neither side was gaining much. Finally, after American victories at both Fort McHenry and Plattsburgh, the British statesmen agreed to end the war. The Russians had offered to help negotiate (settle an argument by talking about the problem) a peace treaty (formal agreement) between the two nations, and in 1814, the British and the Americans met in Ghent, Belgium, to end the war. America sent John Quincy Adams, Henry Clay and Albert Gallatin to these negotiations, and the Treaty of Ghent was finally signed on Dec. 24, 1814. The treaty said all fighting would cease, all conquered territories would be returned to their previous owners, and a boundary commission would be established to decide where any new boundaries would be.

One more battle took place just days after the treaty had been signed, as news of the end of the war hadn't yet reached the soldiers. Andrew Jackson defeated the British at New Orleans on Jan. 8, 1815, and even though the war had already officially ended, this victory gave Americans a new confidence and patriotism.

Although the end of the war didn't solve any of the shipping problems or the issue of impressment, it did make America more confident as a nation and helped develop a new belief in the strength of the new nation.

When the war ended, the British also left the American Indians on their own against the settlers in the new Missouri territory. Without the support of the British, the American Indians were forced to sign treaties with the United States government that moved them off their lands and opened up the area for more American settlements.

title: Columbia
text:
Columbia, Missouri, is located along Interstate 70 halfway between St. Louis and Kansas City. It is considered one of the nicest places in America to live and not just by the people who live there. Columbia has been rated by many popular magazines as one of America's top 10 places to live. It has also been called the fourth healthiest place in the nation to live and has been rated as one of the best places in America to retire. All things considered, Columbia is a very nice place to live. One thing that makes Columbia great is its low cost of living. The cost of living (how much it costs to buy the things needed to live) in Columbia is about 5-6 percent less than the national average. That means that it costs less to buy houses, food, clothing and other items in Columbia than it does in most other cities in the United States.

Columbia also has many interesting museums to visit. The Museum of Art and Archaeology has a collection of more than 13,000 art objects. It specializes in ancient art and even has a Cast Gallery that contains casts that were made from original Greek and Roman sculptures. The Museum of Anthropology and the Black Cultural Center also have many interesting and amazing exhibits. The Walters-Boone County Historical Society displays a history of Boone County, named after Daniel Boone, and shows how settlers expanded along the Boones Lick Trail.

The State Historical Society of Missouri is also located in Columbia, and it has many interesting documents, paintings and sculptures telling of Missouri's great history. Columbia also has wonderful parks and recreation areas such as Twin Lakes Recreation Area, Nifong Park, Finger Lakes State Park, Rock Bridge Memorial State Park, Gans Creek Wild Area and Three Creeks State Forest. With all it has to offer, Columbia is one of the cities that makes Missouri great.

title: Respect
text:
Part of being a happy and powerful person is showing proper respect. When we show respect to something or someone, we show honor.

Let's start with "things." What are some things that you respect? Do you show respect for the American flag? What about a loved one's grave? How about the laws of your country? Do you show respect for your body by not taking drugs or smoking? Think of three other things you can show respect for.

It's important to show common respect for all people. But people tend to honor or show the most respect to those who have done the most for them. This kind of respect comes from love and gratitude - just like your respect for a parent, grandparent or teacher who has always been kind and helpful.

How about people who have authority? Do you respect the principal of your school? What about a policeman? Do you respect your parents?

We also show respect to heroes. Did you hear about the firefighters who died rushing into the World Trade Center to save others? Do you show respect to true heroes such as those who serve in our armed forces?

title: What is a national anthem?
text: A national anthem is a song chosen to represent a country and the values it stands for. It often tells a story about an event in the country's history, reflects on the courage of those who helped to establish the country or praises those who have protected it in time of war. The national anthem of the United States is "The Star-Spangled Banner," written by Francis Scott Key during the War of 1812.

title: Mules
text:
Have you ever been told that you are "as stubborn as a mule?" Have you ever wondered if mules really are stubborn? The answer to that question is, yes, mules are stubborn and temperamental, but they are very useful and hard-working animals. For this reason, the mule was chosen as Missouri's official state animal in May of 1995. The mule is a cross between a mare, or female horse, and a jack, or a male donkey. It was first brought into the state of Missouri around 1820 and quickly became popular with farmers and settlers because of its sure-footed strength and endurance.

The mule has long ears, a tufted tail, slender legs, small hooves and a loud bray, much like a donkey, but it has the strength and size of a horse. It has long been used as a pack animal and was often used by armies to carry their supplies before trucks and jeeps were invented. For many years, Missouri was the No. 1 mule producer in the United States.

title: Joplin Works to Rebuild After a Deadly Tornado
text:
On May 22, 2011, a tornado hit the city of Joplin, Missouri. It wasn’t just any tornado. It was a monstrous EF-5, with winds over 200 miles an hour. This huge tornado was almost a mile wide and cut a path over 22 miles long. It crushed almost 1/3 of the city, killed 162 people and destroyed almost 8,000 buildings. It is considered one of the deadliest tornadoes in over 50 years.

Joplin is working hard to rebuild. Think about all of the parts that make a city work. In addition to houses and businesses, cities need electricity, sewers, roads, hospitals, parks and government buildings. In January 2012 federal and civic organizations in Joplin got together to give the “ok” to a plan called Joplin Area—Next Steps Plan. The plan outlined how to replace what was destroyed in the tornado. 4,000 building permits have been given to homeowners so they can begin construction on new homes. After the tornado hit, 530 businesses were either destroyed or badly damaged. The good news is that 420 of those businesses have reopened. Work has begun on a new hospital. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) is helping to clean up waste and keep the area safe for residents.

The people of Joplin will never forget that terrible day. Recovering from something this devastating is difficult, but Joplin is showing how it’s done!

Sailors from the USS Missouri helped with tornado clean-up efforts in Joplin

title: How Do I Use a Thesaurus?
text:
Do you use many of the same words over and over when writing? Are you getting bored with those same words? It’s time you learned to use a thesaurus!

Search for Synonyms

The word “thesaurus” almost looks like a name for a dinosaur, doesn’t it? It’s actually a book (it can be found online as well). This book or Web site provides synonyms (words similar in meaning) for common words. Using a thesaurus is a great way to broaden your vocabulary with more interesting words.

A thesaurus is usually alphabetical. Some are similar to dictionaries because they give you the part of speech, definition and sample sentences for words. Sometimes a thesaurus will give you directions to look up other entries. Here’s what you’ll find in a typical thesaurus.

Entry Word
The word you look up to find synonyms

Part-of-Speech Label
Tells you if the word is a noun, verb, adjective, etc.

Definition
Tells you what the entry word means

Example Sentence
Shows you how the entry word might be used in a sentence.

Synonyms
Words whose meanings are the same as or similar to the entry word

Antonyms
Words whose meanings are the opposite of the entry word

Try It!

Look up the word “grow” in a thesaurus. Write all the synonyms here.

title: Mary Easton Sibley
text:
Life in the Missouri Territory was exciting and often difficult. After the Louisiana Purchase was completed and the War of 1812 ended, more people than ever began to settle in the Missouri Territory. Those who came to the newly-opened territory (a part of the United States that is not yet a state) wanted to have the benefits of government, religion and schools, but so far, not much had been organized, especially in the way of schools to educate the children who grew up here.

When Mary Easton was only 13 years old, in around 1813, she and her family moved to the frontier town of St. Louis. Her father, Rufus Easton, became St. Louis's first postmaster. He was very interested in education and insisted that his daughter, Mary, go to school. The only problem was that there were no schools for girls in St. Louis at this time. In the early days of the Missouri Territory, most people believed it was more important for boys to receive an education than for girls. Girls were usually expected to take over the duties of running a home and caring for and raising children, so they were not given as many opportunities to go to school as were the boys.

Because there were no schools for girls in St. Louis at the time, Rufus Easton sent his daughter, Mary, away to boarding schools in Kentucky. A boarding school is a school where the students live and study away from home.

When Mary grew up, she married George C. Sibley, and they moved to Fort Osage in Jackson County. Fort Osage was located on the Missouri River many miles from any other settlements. Because she had been able to go to school and get an education, Mary tried to make life in this faraway settlement as refined and cultural as she could. She even brought a piano all the way from St. Louis so she could have music in her home and share that music with those who visited her. The piano had to be brought by keel boat, and the trip from St. Louis took about a month.

Later, in 1828, Mary and her husband moved to St. Charles. About this time, Mary decided it was time that the girls of Missouri had the chance to go to school. Although many boys were able to get an education, there were still very few schools that would accept girls. Mary knew that many parents wanted their girls to go to school, but that few of them wanted, or could afford, to send their girls away to boarding school as her parents had done for her. Mary came up with a solution. Mary Sibley began to hold classes for girls in her own home. Each year, the school grew, until finally Mary and her husband founded a college. They named the school Lindenwood and started their own college for women.

Lindenwood College is still located in St. Charles, Missouri, only it is now a coeducational college, meaning that both men and women can attend. Thanks to Mary Easton Sibley, girls as well as boys were able to get an education in the early Missouri Territory.

title: A Glimpse Into the Past on the Steamboat Arabia
text:
If you need to get somewhere today, all you have to do is get in a car, take a train, hop on a bus or climb aboard an airplane. Traveling from New York City to London, England, which is more than 3,000 miles, takes only a few hours in an airplane.

But if you wanted to travel great distances in the Missouri Territory hundreds of years ago, the fastest way was by steamboat on the Missouri River.

Have you ever wondered what life might have been like on a steamboat? The Steamboat Arabia Museum in Kansas City is home to the wreckage of the steamboat Arabia, which sank many years ago and was later discovered.

The museum has a massive collection of interesting objects found buried with the steamboat. Hundreds of items of clothing, like jackets, boots, trousers, dresses and hats from many years ago are on display - things travelers would have taken with them on their journey.

Since people often stayed many days on a steamboat, it was stocked with food. The museum has a huge collection of food found in the boat, including bottled pickles that are still green, coffee beans, ketchup, sardines, crates of wine and even blueberry and cherry pie fillings.

If you have ever wondered what people dressed like or ate during that time of steamboat travel, the Steamboat Arabia Museum is a great way to get a peek into life hundreds of years ago.

title: Missouri Territory
text:
Missouri Life on the Frontier

After the Louisiana Purchase became final, settlers began flocking to the Missouri area in great numbers.
