When the Americans took control of the land in 1804, there were 10,000 people living in the Missouri area. Most of these settlers lived in the area between St. Louis and New Madrid. Six years later, the population of the area had doubled to 20,000 people, and by 1812, there were enough people living in Missouri for it to become an official territory of the United States. By 1820, there were 67,000 settlers in the Missouri Territory. Most of the settlers who came to the Missouri Territory came because of the rich, fertile farmland available at very reasonable prices. Many of the settlers came from Tennessee, Kentucky, North Carolina and Virginia. These southern settlers also chose to settle in the Missouri Territory because slavery was allowed here, while it was not permitted in the territories north of the Ohio River.

What was life like in the Missouri Territory? Missouri was still a new and exciting place, where life was anything but stable and boring. Missouri was considered the western frontier of the United States. A frontier is the very edge of the settled area of a country. Because it was new and unsettled, Missouri had a reputation of being lawless and wild. Many people from the eastern United States were actually afraid to go to Missouri because of the stories they had heard about how dangerous it was to live there. One eastern newspaper warned people who may be considering moving to Missouri that it was full of "individuals quick to fight with dirks [knives] and pistols or to engage in personal encounters in which the eyes of opponents were gouged from their sockets and ears and noses bitten off" (William E. Parrish, Missouri: The Heart of the Nation, p. 45).

Religion on the Frontier

Although there were certainly some wild characters who lived in the new territory at this time, things weren't normally quite that exciting. While there were some wild and lawless people living in the Missouri Territory, there were also many who wanted to make sure religion played a part in the new area. The Catholic Church was the major religion in the Missouri area when the French were in control. After the French sold the land to the United States, the French no longer gave money to the Catholic Church in Missouri to help pay priests, build churches or take care of the needs of the people. For a time, the Catholic Church in Missouri was left without a leader, but in 1818, Bishop William L. DuBourg came to the new territory and helped give the church new leadership. Mother Philippine Duchesne came to the Missouri Territory as well, helping to establish a school for girls at St. Charles.

When more and more Americans began to come to Missouri, other religions also began to grow. Baptist, Methodist and Presbyterian were the major religions setting up congregations (groups of people who gather for religious worship) in the new Missouri Territory. The Baptists built churches, but also met in people's homes and outside during good weather. The Baptists didn't require that their preachers be formally educated, so many of their leaders were regular members of the community. They supported themselves by working just like their neighbors during the week and then preached to them on Sundays. The Methodists sent out their own preachers. These preachers rode great distances to visit with and preach to their members who lived many miles apart.

The Methodist preachers were called "circuit riders" because they rode many miles on a set route to reach their congregations. The first circuit rider to come to Missouri was John Travis, and he arrived in 1806. Travis and the other circuit riders like him were very brave and dedicated men, as they had to travel long distances in all kinds of rough weather to reach those who were depending on them. When they got to where they were going, the circuit riders stayed in the homes of their members or slept outside. They didn't make much money, but brought welcome news and spiritual messages to settlers who didn't often get to see anyone from the outside world. When there were enough members in an area, the circuit riders would set up a church.

The first known Methodist church was the McKendree Church, organized near Jackson in 1806. Missouri's first Presbyterian preachers came in about 1814. Samuel J. Mills and Daniel Smith brought messages from the Philadelphia Bible and Missionary Society, but didn't stay or set up any churches at this time. The first Presbyterian congregation in Missouri was established near Potosi in 1816. It was called the Concord Church. A year later, another congregation was started in St. Louis.

Missouri News

Other than schools and churches, the only other means of receiving information in the early Missouri Territory was from newspapers. The territory's first newspaper was the Missouri Gazette, which published its first issue on July 12, 1808, in St. Louis. Newspapers of the time published a lot of articles about government and politics. They also carried news about local citizens and stories that would be interesting to those living in the area. Books were still expensive, and the only book owned by most people at this time was the Bible. Many people of this period were still not able to read, but for those who were, newspapers were a welcome way to find out about what was happening around them. Life in the Missouri Territory was an adventure, but as more people settled here, things began to become more stable and civilized. With its new stability and its large number of settlers, by 1817, the Missouri Territory was looking toward becoming a state.

Missouri Timeline

1. Ste. Genevieve, 1750 - First permanent settlement in Missouri founded by Creole settlers from Kaskaskia, Ill.

2. St. Louis, 1764 - Founded by Pierre Laclede and Rene Auguste Chouteau.

3. Louisiana Purchase, 1803 - United States purchases the Louisiana Territory from France for 15 million dollars.

4. Lewis and Clark, 1804 - Expedition leaves St. Louis to go map out the western territories.

5. Missouri Territory Settlement, 1812 - Missouri Territory is organized by the United States Congress. Settlement by pioneers begins.

6. Steamboats Arrive, 1817 - The General Zebulon M. Pike arrives at St. Louis as the first steamboat to reach the city.

title: Boonville
text:
Boonville, Missouri, is named after Daniel Boone, who first came to Missouri in 1779. Boonville is located on Interstate 70 on the south side of the Missouri River about 100 miles east of Kansas City and 150 miles west of St. Louis. Boonville is the oldest town in central Missouri and is in the very center of the historic area of Missouri. This area was named for a famous salt lick that was discovered by Boone's sons, and the trail leading to and from the licks was later used as a trail for settlers traveling west.

Boonville is now a town of about 7,000 people, and it has several claims to fame. The first Missouri State Fair was held in Boonville in 1853. Boonville is also the place where one of the very last public hangings in Missouri took place in 1930. Boonville now has more than 450 buildings and sites listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and many of these can be visited today.

Some of the interesting events held each year in Boonville are the Old Time Fiddlers Contest and the Model Train Show. Both of these exciting events are held in March, and the Big Muddy Folk Festival is held each April. Heritage Days, held in June, celebrates Boonville's rich heritage with an antique show, parade, classic-car show and fireworks. The Prairie Home Fair, one of the oldest fairs in the country, is held in July, and the Missouri River Valley Steam Engine Association Show happens each September.

title: Printers
text: Printers were a very important part of frontier life. A printer not only printed a newspaper, but also acted as its publisher and editor. In addition to printing books and newspapers, the printer supplied his community with business papers, legal forms and handbills and frequently acted as postman. The apprentice seen on the right is inking type on a stone slab, preparatory to a press run. The master printer on the left is inspecting a proof sheet.

title: How did steamboats change Missouri?
text: On Aug. 2, 1817, the steamboat Zebulon M. Pike arrived at St. Louis. Two years later, the Independence was the first steamboat to travel up the Missouri River. Steamboats brought thousands of settlers to Missouri, and by 1860, the population had reached 1 million people. All of those people needed supplies, too. Steamboats carried sugar, cotton, grain, chickens and much more from New Orleans and other southern cities to Missouri. They carried furs from Missouri and the West to New Orleans. Without steamboats to carry people and goods, it would have been much harder for people and goods to get to Missouri.

title: Hawthorn
text: Missouri's state flower is the hawthorn. Its scientific name is Crataegus, and it is a member of the rose family. It is a common flower in Eastern North America, and it likes Missouri's temperate climate. The hawthorn plant has prickly thorns, clusters of beautiful white flowers in the spring, and colorful orange, red or yellow fruits in the fall. The fruits are called "haws" and look like tiny apples. Some people use the haws to make jellies. In England, the hawthorn is often used in hedges, and its flowers are used in May Day celebrations. The flower of the hawthorn has been used as a symbol of spring in English poetry for hundreds of years. Here in Missouri, the hawthorn is often grown as an ornamental shrub, as well as being used in hedges. The wood of the hawthorn plant is very hard and is often used to make small items like tool handles.

title: Fact vs. Opinion
text:
Right now you are reading a newspaper. A newspaper is a great place to find both facts and opinions.

Fact: A fact is a statement that can be proved. For instance, to say that most oranges are orange in color can be proven. All you have to do is look at an orange to tell what color it is.

Opinion: An opinion is a belief held by someone. It cannot be proven by fact. For instance, to say, “red apples are sweeter than green apples” is an opinion. It depends on who’s doing the tasting. Brian thinks red apples are sweeter. Brooke finds green apples the sweetest. They each have an opinion about the sweetness of apples.

Newspapers contain mostly facts on most of the pages. Certain pages are set aside for opinions. The editorial page contains letters to the editor, editorial cartoons and articles by the editors of that paper.

The purpose of the editorial page is to:

Make people think about events in the news

Try to get public officials to see your point of view

Give background and information about events in the news

Serve as a community “voice”

All your life you’ll be reading books and articles. You’ll also be doing a lot of writing for school and work. Get in the habit of asking yourself as you read or write, “Is this statement fact or opinion?” This habit will help you become a better thinker.

title: Fun Facts
text: According to Pennsylvania law, all drivers driving on a country road at night must stop every mile and send up a rocket signal, wait 10 minutes for the road to be cleared of all animals, and continue. (Source dumblaws.com)

title: Let's Write
text: Describe what you think life was like in the Missouri Territory. What do you think it would be like to ride a steamboat? How was news shared with citizens of the territory?

title: The Trailblazer’s Trailblazer
text:
Missouri was an exciting place to be in the early days of the westward movement. Most of the major trails leading to the West began in Missouri.

In towns like Franklin, Independence, Westport Landing and St. Joseph, there were always the hustle and bustle of pioneers buying goods and preparing to head west. All of this bustle and excitement caught the eye of a young Missourian named Christopher Houston "Kit" Carson. Carson, born on Christmas Eve 1809, spent most of his young life in Boone's Lick, Missouri. When he was only 9 years old, his father died, and he had to work in order to survive. He was apprenticed (legally bound to work for someone until you learn a skill) to a saddle-maker in Franklin when he was 14 years old, but he hated the job. He ran away to Independence with hopes of joining in the excitement of the western frontier.

When Carson got to Independence, he was thrilled to find traders and frontiersmen who told him exciting stories about Santa Fe. Santa Fe was a Spanish settlement located in what is now the state of New Mexico. Since Carson had run away from his job and had no education, he decided to join a wagon train and find out for himself what Santa Fe was like.

After going West, Kit Carson became a fur trapper. He used Taos, New Mexico, as a base camp for his fur-trapping expeditions and traveled from there all over the West. He learned all about the frontier regions from the Rocky Mountains to California.

Because he knew these regions so well, he became a guide and trailblazer for others who wanted to come here. Kit Carson was hired by the famous explorer John C. Fremont, who became known as the "Trailblazer," and helped guide him in his explorations through Oregon, California, the central Rocky Mountains and the Great Basin. Fremont wrote interesting articles and reports about his expeditions, and he often mentioned Kit Carson and his amazing skills as a frontiersman. Kit, therefore, became known as the "Trailblazer's Trailblazer."

These articles told stories about Carson's adventures, and when people read about them, Carson quickly became a national hero. One of Carson's interesting adventures involved a meeting with a couple of unfriendly bears. Two grizzly bears attacked Kit, and he was able to climb a tree to get away from them. He dropped his gun, however, and had to stay in the tree for several hours until the bears decided to leave so that he could climb down. Stories about Kit Carson grew and were exaggerated (stretched the truth) until many believed Carson could accomplish super-human tasks.

Because he spoke several different American Indian languages and knew and understood the American Indians in the area, he was also able to lead many wagon trains west, helping to keep them safe from American Indian attacks. He even served as an American Indian agent and as a guide for the U.S. Army. Later in his career, he joined the U.S. Army and eventually became a general. He served during the Civil War and also led a fight against the Navajos in the New Mexico area.

Kit Carson moved to Colorado after the Civil War ended. He planned to start a ranch in the area, but he died there in 1868. His body was later buried near his old home in Taos, New Mexico.

Kit Carson was a great western pioneer who became famous for his exciting adventures in the wild frontier. People still remember the famous trapper, explorer and trailblazer from Franklin, Missouri, who ran away to explore the West.

title: The 'Oregon Trail' Game Gets a Mobile Update
text:
The Oregon Trail played an important part in the settling of the western United States and now you can help settle the west too - on an iPhone.

The "Oregon Trail" game was one of the first computer games ever made, and it was popular. Kids all over the country loved to travel on a virtual Oregon Trail, hunting and protecting a virtual family as they headed west.

Now the popular game can be played on the touch screen of an iPhone.

In the newest version of the game, players choose a profession for their character. Players can choose to have one of three jobs: a banker, a carpenter or a farmer. Each of the jobs has a different skill that can be used during the game such as repairing wagons or making food last longer.

Players then choose a wagon and head west on the Oregon Trail, beginning in St. Louis. As they travel along the Oregon Trail, players must hunt for food. Players can hunt by tapping on the touch screen to "shoot" at animals like squirrels, rabbits and buffalo.

One of the main goals of the game is to make sure the player' virtual family arrives at its destination safely. But just like real life on the Oregon Trail, unexpected things can happen.

Members of the traveling party can become sick. Or players can lose wagons as they try to cross a river. Throughout the game, players learn what conditions might have been like on the real Oregon Trail.

title: Westward Movement
text:
Missouri marks the beginning of two of the most important and well-traveled trails that led to the newly opened West. In the early 1800s, there were no paved roads or multi-lane highways. There weren't even any well-worn trails leading to the West, where so many pioneers wanted to travel. Those who wanted to get to the new frontier out west often followed American Indian trails and hoped they could find routes to bring wagons later on.

Santa Fe Trail

By around 1821, William Becknell, from Franklin, Missouri, had established the Santa Fe Trail, leading from Franklin to Santa Fe. Santa Fe was a Spanish settlement 800 miles southwest of Missouri. It was a large settlement, but there were no other large settlements anywhere near Santa Fe, so the people who lived there weren't able to get many of the things they needed. Many people from Missouri saw that if they were able to bring goods the settlers in Santa Fe needed, they would be able to make money by selling these goods to them. William Becknell was one of the traders who saw the opportunity to make money by selling goods in Santa Fe. He made a trading trip to Santa Fe and soon became known as the "Father of the Santa Fe Trail."

Soon after Becknell's first trading trip to Santa Fe, other traders set out with their wagons loaded with goods to be traded. They brought cotton and woolen cloth, iron pots and pans, tools, knives, mirrors and other items to trade when they got to Santa Fe. When they arrived in the Spanish settlement, they traded their goods for things like furs, horses, burros, mules and silver. They were usually able to trade their goods for items worth much more back in Missouri and they made a good profit on their trades.

Santa Fe Trail Begins in Independence

Around 1830, the starting point of the Santa Fe Trail was moved to Independence because Independence was 100 miles closer to Santa Fe and a good place to start the journey. This trade route continued until 1843, when the Mexican authorities shut it down for a time because of problems with the United States government over Texas. Those who traveled this route learned a lot about how to bring wagons over long distances in unsettled country. Many of the skills these Santa Fe traders learned were later used by the pioneers who came west to Oregon and California.

Oregon Trail

The Oregon Trail also began at Independence, Missouri. By the early 1840s, people had heard about the wonderful land in the Oregon country and were anxious to go there to seek their fortunes. The Oregon Trail had been used by American Indians for years, but by 1843, large numbers of pioneers began using the trail to head west.

Six-Month Trip

The Oregon Trail was 2,000 miles long, and the trip from Missouri to the Oregon country took about six months to complete. The settlers would gather at Independence and buy everything they needed to make the trip. They traveled in large Conestoga wagons pulled by strong and hardy oxen.

Oxen were better suited for the trip, as they could pull the wagons over rough ground and keep up their strength eating the coarse grasses that horses didn't tolerate as well. They also chose strong leaders, set up rules for the road, loaded their wagons as lightly as possible and wore sturdy clothing and shoes.

Pioneers Leave in the Spring

The pioneers left Independence in the early spring of the year, hoping to get to the Oregon country before winter set in. It was important to get an early start to avoid getting caught in early snowstorms.

Along the trail, pioneers often tacked up messages on trees or posts and even wrote their messages on the skulls of dead buffalo or cattle. These messages told the pioneers who followed after where the best grass was, where to find water, and of any dangers that may lie ahead. This system of leaving messages was sometimes called the "roadside telegraph." With so many people traveling the Oregon Trail, it was important to let travelers coming in the future know what they could expect. More than 300,000 people took this trip during the years of "Oregon Fever," when people couldn't wait to go to the rich and exciting Oregon country.

title: Independence
text:
Independence marks the spot where both the Santa Fe and Oregon trails began. Independence is located in Jackson County in the western portion of Missouri, south of the Missouri River. The first settlement in the area was Fort Osage, built under the direction of William Clark in 1808.

The Independence of today is full of things to see. Historic Independence Square marks the spot where thousands of pioneers bought supplies for the journey west. There were once blacksmith shops, hotels and rows of businesses set up in the square to sell their goods to those heading west. The square is now lined with antique shops and historical markers, along with the 1859 jail and other buildings that can be toured.

The Truman Home and the Harry S Truman Library and Museum also attract many visitors to Independence. Harry S Truman is one of the most famous citizens to come from Independence. He was the 33rd president of the United States, and his home, along with many of his interesting personal items, are on display here for all to see.

There are many other historic sites to visit, such as the 1827 Log Courthouse, used by Harry Truman in the 1930s, the National Frontier Trails Center, the Pioneer Spring Cabin, the Missouri Mormon Walking Trail, the RLDS Temple and the Children's Peace Pavilion.

If you want to see some of Missouri's most interesting historic sites marking the beginning of the trails heading west, Independence is certainly the place to visit. You'll almost expect to see eager pioneers loading up their Conestoga wagons, ready to head out on their unforgettable journeys.

title: Self-Discipline
text: Self-discipline is probably one of the hardest character traits to achieve. Do you know what it means to have self-discipline? Well, since it has the word "self" in it, you know that it has to do with something you do yourself. No one can have self-discipline for you. Self-discipline is being able to control your thoughts and actions in a way that helps you be a better person. It means that you'll have the control to do your homework even when your friends come and ask you to play a great game of ball outside. It means you'll go to bed on time even though there's a movie on that you really wanted to watch. Or it's when you've had three chocolate frogs already, but there are still a couple left. You'll have the strength to say, "I've had enough tonight. I'll save those for later!" You need self-discipline in just about everything you do, including eating, sleeping, at school and at home - you name it! It's a great thing to have. By having it, you'll keep yourself healthy, strong and always doing what's best for you in the end. Self-discipline is just one of the many character traits that make people in our state what they are today - a great bunch of people!

title: What is a conestoga wagon?
text:
A Conestoga wagon is the type of wagon used by the pioneers to travel west. It was first built in the Conestoga region of Pennsylvania around 1725.

It had a wagon box that was curved, rising at both ends so that when it went up and down hills, the loads it carried wouldn't shift as easily, and the tailgate wouldn't have to bear as much strain. The Conestoga wagon could carry loads up to eight tons and was usually pulled by six horses or oxen. It had a white hood made of canvas to protect the wagon box from dust, sun and rain.

title: Hydrangea
text:
The hydrangea is a plant native to Missouri, meaning it is found growing naturally here. It is a member of the saxifrage family and is related to a large group of low rock plants including strawberry geraniums and other plants used as borders in flower gardens.

"Saxifrage" means "rock-breaker" in Latin. The plants in this group were called "rock-breakers" because their roots seem to have the ability to split rocks when they are growing and pushing down into the ground. Many years ago, doctors used to prescribe saxifrage for patients who had gall stones, as they thought that if they ate the plant, it might be able to break up the gall stones as well.

The hydrangea of Missouri is a beautiful plant with flattopped clusters of white, pink or blue flowers. The white and pink flowers grow naturally, but the blue flowers sometimes need to be helped along with the addition of alum or iron to the soil where they are grown.

Hydrangeas grow well in Missouri's climate, and the plants are often recommended to home gardeners by professional gardeners and nursery workers. Many home gardeners place nails around the roots of the hydrangea to help the plant grow beautiful blue clusters of flowers.

title: Clarity of Expression: Father Junípero Serra and the California Missions
text:
Do you like to give speeches? Can you convince others to see things your way? Then maybe you have a gift for expressing yourself clearly.

Father Junípero Serra was a Franciscan monk who some might call one of the “founding fathers” of California. He was born in Spain in 1713 and became a priest in his mid 20s. Many people noticed how well he spoke, or how clearly he expressed himself, during his powerful sermons, and he soon became a university professor.

Father Serra wanted to work as a Spanish missionary, so he first traveled to Mexico City in 1749. He started missionary work with the Sierra Gorda Indians. Soon he was made head of the Spanish missions in Baja (lower) California. Next, the Spanish governor asked him to start missions in Alta (upper) California. Father Serra personally built eight missions there and supervised the start of many more from San Diego to San Francisco.

Father Serra helped convert thousands of American Indians to Christianity. They lived and worked in the missions, but life was harsh. Many Indians died from overwork and diseases. But the missions kept going because of Father Serra’s preaching and care. His sermons were so dramatic that he would sometimes pound his chest with a stone or touch a lit torch to his chest.

Father Serra used his clarity of expression for what he thought was good. He argued with the Spanish army to get control of the missions. He even convinced Mexican officials to send more money and soldiers for his missions. Spanish colonists settled the area around the missions, which is all now the state of California.

Do you think you have a good ability to express yourself clearly as Father Serra did? What topic do you feel strongly about?

title: What are Homophones and Homographs?
text:
Homophones and homographs are the same but different! To find out the meaning of a word, carefully read the words and sentences surrounding it.

Homophones

Homophones are words that sound the same but have different spellings and different meanings. You can remember what a homophone is by remembering that a phone makes a sound, so a homophone sounds the same as another word.

It is important to know a homophone when you write it. If you need help with a homophone when you read or write, look it up in a dictionary. This will help you keep from making mistakes. For instance, would you write you have “bear hands” or “bare hands”?

Here are some common homophones:
Beat, beet
Earn, urn
Eye, I
Heal, heel, he’ll
Made, maid
Plain, plane
Rain, reign, rein
To, too, two

Homographs

These are words that are spelled the same but have different meanings. Sometimes they are pronounced differently even though they are spelled the same. You can remember what a homograph is by remembering that a graph is something you look at, so a homograph looks the same.

Here are some common homographs that are pronounced differently and have different meanings:

Bass: a low voice Bass: a fish
Content: things found inside Content: satisfied
Minute: 60 seconds Minute: tiny

Try It!

The next time you are not sure which homophone or homograph to use, be sure you know the meaning of the word you are trying to use. This will help you spell it correctly. A dictionary will help you a lot!

title: The Pony Express
text:
Missouri wasn't just the Gateway to the West for pioneers who wanted to travel to new frontiers. Missouri also marked the starting point of one of the most interesting and dangerous mail-delivery routes of all time.

The Pony Express route had its start at St. Joseph, Missouri, and the route continued on as far west as Sacramento, California. The Pony Express was a mail service that delivered the mail in the amazingly short time of only eight to 10 days. Before this, mail was sent to and from California on ships, wagon trains and stagecoaches. It usually took the mail at least 25 days, at very best, to make it by stagecoach and much longer by wagon train or ship. To be able to send and receive mail in only eight to 10 days seemed like a miracle to the people of the late 1800s.

The Pony Express was started by the stage-and-freight company of Russell, Majors and Waddell. The owners of the company came up with the idea of sending out riders to ride almost continuously, stopping every 15 miles for a fresh horse and every 50 miles or so to change riders. By riding with few stops, the mail could get through in record time.

The Pony Express riders had to be light, so they wouldn't slow their horses down. The rules stated that the riders could weigh no more than 125 pounds, so many of the riders were just young boys. A Pony Express rider had to be a good rider, and he had to be brave, as he often had to travel through unfriendly American Indian territory. He had to be more concerned about getting the mail through than about his own safety. An unwritten code of the Pony Express riders was to take care of the mail first, the horse second and himself third.

The Pony Express riders carried the mail in a "mochila," a Spanish word for knapsack. The mochila was a rectangle-shaped, leather, blanketlike bag designed to fit snugly over a saddle. The mochila had four pockets, or cantinas, in the four corners of the bag. The mail was wrapped in a protective covering and then placed in these four cantinas. These cantinas were each padlocked so the mail couldn't be stolen. Only the military and the station master in Salt Lake City had keys to the padlocks.

When the riders changed horses or exchanged riders, the mochila was simply lifted off of one horse and placed on the fresh horse. There were no straps to unbuckle or ropes to untie, because the rider sat on the mochila like a saddle blanket, and it was kept in place by his weight. The mochila, saddle and bridle together only weighed 13 pounds.

The Pony Express was a quick and exciting way to deliver the mail, but it didn't last long. The first rider set out from St. Joseph, Missouri, at 7:15 p.m. on April 3, 1860. Not long after this, the St. Louis, St. Joseph and Salt Lake telegraph line was completed. This made it possible to send messages across the continent in just a few minutes. The first telegram was sent to San Francisco on Oct. 24, 1861, and the Pony Express soon stopped making its runs.

The Pony Express may not have lasted long, but it still lives on in history. The picture of a young boy riding like the wind across the dangerous and barren West seems to capture the true spirit of those who had the courage to enter the new frontier.

title: Gateway Arch: Climb Inside an American Monument
text:
What is silver, made of metal, hollow, stands on two legs and is 630 feet tall? It's not a giant robot. It's the Gateway Arch in St. Louis!

The Gateway Arch is a huge monument built to represent Missouri's place in history as the Gateway to the West. The Arch is a main feature in the Jefferson National Expansion Memorial.

One of the most exciting things about the arch is that you can travel inside of it, all the way up to the very top. Visitors can climb aboard a tram that has been specially designed to travel inside the hollow part of the arch. Much like an elevator the tram has two doors that open to let passengers inside.

But once inside, the tram is shaped much differently. In order to be able to travel up the legs of the arch, the inside of the tram is shaped like an egg. Inside the egg there are five seats for passengers. Inside the arch, there are eight of these egg-shaped compartments. They form a train that travels most of the way up the arch.

At the top of the arch, the train stops, and visitors can exit the egg-shaped tramcar and climb into the observatory area. Inside the deck are 32 small windows that look out over the entire city.

But don't look out the window if you are afraid of heights: you're 630 feet in the air! Once you've seen enough, you can take the tram back down to bottom. It's quite a trip!

title: Gateway to the West
text:
With all of the pioneers who wanted to go west, Missouri soon became the "jumping-off place" (where pioneers began their journey) for those going west. Missouri was the place where most pioneers and traders began their journeys because it marked the spot where the two most important westward trails began. Both the Santa Fe and the Oregon trails had their beginnings in Missouri, and soon people began calling Missouri the "Gateway to the West."

Preparing for the Journey

Easterners who wanted to go West would first get on a steamboat and travel the Missouri River until they reached Franklin or Independence. Franklin was the most popular "jumping-off" spot until it was destroyed in a flood in 1928. After this, most people went to Independence to begin the journey west.

When the pioneers got to Missouri, they prepared for their journey by buying wagons and supplies that they would need for their trip. Independence was the main "jumping-off" city, but other cities such as Westport, St. Joseph, Omaha and Council Bluffs were very popular as well.

Supplies

So, what supplies did the early settlers need to take West? Lansford Hastings, an early immigrant, said each person traveling West should bring 200 pounds of flour, 150 pounds of bacon, 10 pounds of coffee, 20 pounds of sugar and 10 pounds of salt. A family of four should bring more than 1,000 pounds of food to carry them the 2,000 miles to the Oregon country. But often, the settlers would over-pack their wagons, not wanting to leave anything behind, and would have to lighten the load later on.

If the wagons were loaded too heavily, the horses or oxen would be unable to pull the load, and the extra baggage would have to be tossed out onto the prairie. The trail was usually littered with items that the pioneers had to throw away in order for their animals to be able to pull the wagons. Many times, people who lived in the jumping-off towns would ride along the trail with a wagon and collect items that the pioneers had thrown overboard-things like flour, bacon and even furniture!

Prices

Prices for the supplies needed for the journey west were fairly reasonable in places like Independence and St. Joseph, but the farther along the trail one traveled, the more outrageous they became. At the start of the trail, for example, flour cost about $4 per barrel, but farther along the trail, the price rose to $1 per pint. Bacon was something most setters had plenty of, so the price for bacon stayed low. In fact, bacon would often be one of the first things to be dumped if the wagons were too heavy. Items like coffee and liquor were worth much more, and the pioneers were often able to trade these for other items they needed farther along the trail.

Each spring, when the pioneers started arriving for their journey west, the jumping-off cities were crowded beyond their limits. By mid-April, the prairie (huge area of flat or rolling grassland) just outside Independence was covered with wagons, animals and people. There were more than three square miles packed with nothing but pioneers preparing to go West. The entire group bought supplies and then waited for just the right time to begin the journey.

Heading West

Heading west too early could be a disaster because the grass wouldn't be long enough for the animals to eat. If the pioneers waited too long to leave, however, they would still be on the trail when snow began to fall. Either way, the trip would be deadly for both people and animals, so the timing had to be just right. As soon as the grass was long enough to allow the animals to graze (feed on the plants growing on the land) freely, the wagon trains headed west.

The Missouri cities involved in helping to outfit the pioneers profited greatly from the great movement west. Missouri became famous as the "Gateway to the West," and many businesses established themselves here for good. Missouri played a great role in helping to send settlers to the west.

title: St. Joseph
text:
St. Joseph is located on the Missouri River along the western border of our state. St. Joseph is famous for being one of the "jumping-off" points for the trip west, as well as for being the home of the Pony Express. It was founded in 1826 by Joseph Robidoux and was incorporated as a city in 1843. The St. Joseph of today is a safe and pleasant city with many things to see. The Hotel Patee House, a grand hotel built in 1858, is a wonderful place to visit. It once served as a luxury hotel to many travelers who caught the train west after the railroad was completed. It is also the building where Russell, Majors and Waddell had their office when they started the Pony Express in 1860.

The St. Joseph Museum is also a great place to learn more about our state. Some of the most popular exhibits are "Indians of the Northwest Coast," "Wagons West" and "The Upland Forest." The Jesse James House is another site that draws visitors from across the state as well as across the nation. Bob Ford shot and killed Jesse James in this house in 1882. Ford was a member of the James gang who killed Jesse James to collect a $10,000 reward offered by Governor Tom Crittenden.

The Society of Memories Doll Museum, founded in 1968, is also an interesting place to see. The museum has a collection of beautiful, rare dolls that are on display for all to see.

St. Joseph was heavily damaged by the floods of 1993, and many businesses were forced to shut down. St. Joseph is now attracting new businesses and is still a wonderful place to visit to learn more about Missouri's great history.

title: Perseverance
text:
It could be said that perseverance is the father of all other character traits. If you fail at courage, but try again; if you forget to be just or fair, but try again; if you loose your temper, but keep trying to do better; if all other character traits are not complete in your character, but you never give up in your effort to improve them, THEN you have perseverance. You've probably heard the old saying... "If at first you don't succeed, try, try again." That's perseverance.

Sir Winston Churchill, the English leader who helped his country win the war against Nazi Germany, said it this way... "Never, never, never, never give in!" Here's a poem about a common boy who became a millionaire because he had the character trait of perseverance (author unknown).

Bill Brown made a million - Bill Brown! Think of that!
A boy, you remember, as poor as a rat;
He hoed for the neighbors, did jobs by the day,
But Bill made a million, or near it, they say.
You can't understand it? Well, neither could I,
And then I remembered, and now I know why:
The bell might be ringing, the dinner horn blow,
But Bill always hoed to the end of the row.

Bill worked for my father, you maybe recall;
He wasn't a wonder - not that, not at all;
He couldn't out-hoe me, or cover more ground,
Or hoe any cleaner, or beat me around.
In fact, I was better in one way that I know:
One toot from the kitchen, and home I would go;
But Bill always hoed to the end of the row.

We used to get hungry out there in the corn.
When you talk about music, what equals a horn?
A horn yellin' dinner, tomatoes and beans,
And pork and potatoes and gravy and greens?
I ain't blamin' no one for quittin' on time,
To stop with the whistle, that ain't a crime.
But as for the million - well, this much I know:
That Bill always hoed to the end of the row.

title: Why were oxen used to pull wagons?
text: Oxen were often used instead of horses for the trip across the plains for many reasons. Oxen (large, cow-like animals used to pull wagons) could be used for plowing, logging and hauling loads that were too heavy for a horse. Oxen also cost about one-sixth as much as horses; plus they ate much less and could survive on whatever feed was available along the trail. If an ox died, it was butchered and eaten, whereas a horse was not. The drawbacks of using oxen were that they were very slow and were also much less intelligent than horses.

title: The Bald Eagle
text:
The bald eagle, Haliaetus leucocephalus, is a member of the hawk family. The eagle is a very large bird with a wingspan of up to seven feet. They have long beaks, nearly as long as their heads, which they use to grasp and eat fish.

The eagle is a solitary bird, meaning that is likes to live alone. It mates for life and usually produces two eaglets, or baby eagles, at a time. Eaglets do not develop adult markings until they are 3 years old. They are protected by their parents until they reach this age. The eagle uses the same nest year after year, continuing to rebuild and repair its nest as needed.

Eagles are native to North America and live near water. Missouri has many bald eagles living near its rivers. Eagles eat mainly dead fish and rodents, often stealing their food from other birds.

The American bald eagle became the national emblem of the United States in 1782 and is protected by law. It is illegal to harm or even own a bald eagle in the United States. (A national emblem is something chosen by a country to represent its values.)

title: Weaving
text:
Materials

9-inch by 12-inch rectangle of thick cardboard

strips of cloth (quarter inch to half thick)

scissors

safety pin

Directions

Cut notches one-quarter inch apart into the nine-inch sides of the cardboard. Tie a strip of cloth to one corner of the cardboard, and then wrap it back and forth between the notches. Tie the other end of the strip at the corner of the rectangle diagonally across from the one you began with. You have now made your loom.

Attach another strip of cloth to the safety pin and close the pin. Begin weaving by threading the pin under the first strip at the top of your loom. Push the pin over the next strip, then under the one after it. Continue in this way, over and under, all the way across the loom.

When you reach the end of your loom, weave back the way you came, looping the cloth strips, as shown. This time, however, go under each strip you went over the first time, and go over each strip you went under.

Continue this for each row you want to weave, pulling the cloth strip over and under the loom. Make sure not to pull the strip too tight, or the edges of your final product will not be even.

Once you have woven a few rows, push the rows snugly together. If you come to the end of a strip of your weaving material and want to keep weaving, tie on a new strip with a strong double knot.

When you have finished weaving, be sure you are at the end of a row. Tie off each end of your cloth to the loom strip next to it, and lift both strip ends off the loom. To remove your work from the loom, bend down the tabs between the notches and slide the loom out. You can also break the loom by cutting it in half and removing the pieces.

title: How Do I Listen to an Oral Presentation?
text:
Listen closely to your classmates when they give presentations. Pay attention. You can learn a lot from them. Your teacher may tell you to take notes. You may also be asked to make written comments. Also, it’s just plain polite to be a good listener!

Be an active listener. Don’t daydream. Focus on the speaker’s main idea. Listen for the way he or she ties details to that main idea. Take notes, either in your mind or on paper.

Your teacher may help you to evaluate (to examine and judge carefully) your classmates’ presentations. Keep in mind that being honest can help your classmates learn how to give better presentations.

You may not agree with everything the speaker says, but you should listen to his or her ideas.

Don’t interrupt your classmates unless they ask for you to join in.

Think about the speaker’s conclusion. Is it logical?

Try It!

When your classmates give presentations, be a good listener. It will help them feel more comfortable. Make eye contact. Your evaluation will help them improve their future presentations. And you might learn something. Besides, you will want them to listen to you when it is your turn to give an oral presentation.

title: Missouri Compromises
text:
By 1817, the citizens of Missouri were ready to join the United States of America. They were eager to become a new state. Petitions (written papers asking for certain things) had been passed around the state, and citizens had signed these petitions asking that Missouri be allowed to join the Union. In 1818, the petitions were presented to Congress, and the debate (discussion or argument) over whether to allow Missouri to become a state began.

As soon as the discussion began, James Tallmadge Jr. - a congressman from New York City - proposed that if Missouri became a state, slavery (being owned by someone for whom you work) should gradually be made illegal there. No more slaves would be allowed to enter Missouri, and children of slaves already living in Missouri would be free. These children could be kept by their masters until they turned 25 years old, but then they would be allowed to go free.

John Scott, Missouri's territorial delegate to Congress, didn't agree with Tallmadge's proposal. He said when the Louisiana Purchase was signed, it said all of the citizens of Missouri could keep all of their property, including their slaves. Scott said Congress had no right to tell the citizens of Missouri they couldn't have slaves. Because neither side could agree, Missouri didn't become a state during this session of Congress.

When the citizens of Missouri found out about what had happened, most of them were angry that Congress was trying to tell them that they could no longer have slaves. They wanted to join the Union, but they wanted the right to keep their slaves as well.

One of the concerns of Congress was that if Missouri joined the Union as a slave state, it would upset the balance between slave and free states already in the Union. There were 11 free states and 11 slave states, so if Missouri joined as a slave state, the slave states would outnumber the free states, and those who favored slavery would be more powerful than those who didn't. It seemed impossible to reach a compromise (settling an argument with both sides giving up part of their demands) that would allow Missouri to join the Union.

In December 1819, Congress met again, and the same arguments over Missouri becoming a state started all over again. This time, however, there was someone who suggested a compromise that was acceptable to both sides. Speaker of the House Henry Clay, from Kentucky, came up with an idea that worked for both sides.

Clay suggested that, because Maine also wanted to join the Union and become a state, Missouri should be allowed to join as a slave state, and Maine should join as a free state, keeping the slave and free states balanced. He also suggested that slavery be prohibited in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase, including everything from Missouri's southern border north, except for Missouri, of course. This compromise was accepted, and Missouri was allowed to join the Union as a slave state. The compromise suggested by Henry Clay was called the Missouri Compromise, and it kept the United States from being split apart by slavery, at least for a time.

title: Missouri Compromise and Statehood
text:
Henry Clay Introduces the "Compromise"

After debate about whether Missouri should be a free or a slave state for more than two years, Rep. Henry Clay of Kentucky finally came up with an idea. Clay suggested that a compromise be reached. His plan stated that Missouri would be admitted to the Union as a slave state, and Maine, another district that also wanted to become a state, would be admitted as a free state. There would then be 12 slave states and 12 free states, so the balance would continue. The number of slave states would still be equal to the number of free states, so everyone would be happy. Clay's idea worked, and the Missouri Compromise, as his plan was called, helped Missouri to become the 24th state of the Union on Aug. 10, 1821.

The Missouri Compromise also drew some boundaries for where slavery could and could not be practiced in the United States. According to the Missouri Compromise, slavery was forbidden, or not allowed, north of an imaginary line drawn across Missouri's southern border. Missouri could practice slavery, but no other states to the north of this line could practice slavery within their boundaries. This compromise worked well for the time being, but it didn't solve the problem of slavery in the long run.

Missouri Becomes a State

The territory of Missouri was a wild, exciting, and rapidly-growing place. Soon the people who lived here wanted to join the Union as a state of the United States of America. Missouri was already a territory of the United States, but territories didn't have as much freedom to govern themselves, nor did they have much say in what happened in the national government. Missourians wanted to have the same rights that citizens of a state had, so they began pushing for statehood.

When Missouri first asked the United States to allow it to become a state, there were those who didn't want to allow it. Some important questions had to be decided before Missouri would be allowed to join the Union. The major issue keeping Missouri from becoming a state was slavery.

When Missouri first asked to become a state, there were already 11 free states and 11 slave states in the Union. Many Missourians wanted to join the Union as a slave state, because they were slaveholders (people who own slaves). If Missouri joined the Union as a slave state, it would upset the delicate balance of slave and free states. If it joined as a free state, it would still upset the balance of free states and slave states. Neither the Southern states, which favored slavery, nor the Northern states, which opposed slavery, wanted the other states to become more powerful than they were. Both sides wanted to keep things balanced so neither the slave states nor the free states would outnumber the other. This disagreement over slavery kept Missouri out of the Union for more than three years.

Missouri Has Its First Constitution

When Missouri knew for certain that it would soon become a state, it needed to write a state constitution to help plan how the government of the state would work. A constitution is an important document because it explains how the government protects the rights of the people living in that state. Missouri's first constitution was written by a group of people chosen by the voters of Missouri to complete this assignment.

The first constitution of Missouri had a bill of rights, just like the Constitution of the United States. The bill of rights protected things like freedom of religion, freedom of speech, freedom of the press and the right to have a jury trial. Missouri's constitution also said there would be a legislature, called the General Assembly, to make the laws of the state and there would be a governor to carry out the state's laws. It also said there would be courts and judges to help decide what the laws mean and to help settle disagreements. The first constitution also helped establish public schools and build roads throughout the state.

So far, the first constitution of Missouri sounds very much like the one we have today, but there were a few differences. The first constitution said only white men could vote. Women and blacks were not allowed to vote under Missouri's first constitution. This constitution also stated that slavery was allowed anywhere within the state's boundaries.

Missouri's first governor was Alexander McNair, and the first capital of our state was established in St. Charles. The leaders of the state wanted the capital of Missouri to be located in the middle of the state, so they began building a permanent capital there. They chose to call the new capital Jefferson City, after Thomas Jefferson, who was president of the United States when the Louisiana Purchase was signed. The permanent capital was finished in 1826, and the government moved to its new headquarters that same year.

title: Jefferson City
text:
Jefferson City, or the City of Jefferson, as it is officially called, was founded in 1821, the same year that Missouri became a state. It was named after the third president of the United States, Thomas Jefferson. Jefferson City is located in the center of the state along the Missouri River and is the capital of Missouri. Jefferson City was chosen to be the capital of the state because of its central location and because it was easy for people to travel to by using the Missouri River.

There are many interesting things to see in Jefferson City. The state capitol building is one of the most historic sites of the city. It is located high on a bluff above the city, so it can be seen from miles around. The current capitol building is the third one to be built here. The first two were destroyed by fire, and the current building was completed in 1918.

Some other interesting sites around Jefferson City include the Lake of the Ozarks, one of the largest man-made lakes in the United States, and Runge Nature Center, which features hands-on exhibits of the many wildlife habitats of Missouri. If you are interested in seeing some really different sites, visit Burger's Smokehouse to find out about making country-cured meats, or check out the Missouri Veterinary Medical Foundation Museum, where antique veterinary instruments and equipment, some used more than 100 years ago, are on display. Come to Jefferson City and see what our state's capital is really like.

title: Who was Henry Clay?
text: Henry Clay was the speaker of the House of Representatives at the time when Missouri was trying to become a state. He was a representative from the state of Kentucky and was known for being able to look for things that people could agree on and use to settle their differences. Clay was often called the Great Pacificator. A pacificator is one who pacifies, or calms, those around him. Clay was responsible for creating the Missouri Compromise, which allowed Missouri to join the Union as a slave state, while Maine joined as a free state.

title: Obedience
text:
You know what obedience means. It simply means obeying the rules or laws, and it's a very important character trait to have. Here's a basic example of when you should be obedient: "Look both ways before you cross the street." Everyone wants to avoid being run over by a car. That's a great benefit for keeping such a basic rule. Some rules are harder to keep than others, but most rules have a "built-in" benefit for obeying them.

Can you think of some other benefits of being obedient? What's the benefit of keeping the homework rule or of listening to your teachers? Great grades-and all the rewards that come with them!

Did you know that you can choose whether to obey the rules, but you cannot choose the consequences? That's right; if you keep a rule, whether you like it or not, you get to enjoy the benefits. Of course, that goes the other way, too. If you choose not to obey, then you must accept going without the benefits. Often, there's a penalty for not obeying the rules, like not being able to play with your friends because you didn't finish your chores. Can you think of other examples of benefits or penalties that come from obeying or disobeying rules?

title: Chigger
text:
Have you ever been bitten by a chigger? If you live in Missouri, especially in the southern part of our state, you are sure to have had this experience.

Chiggers are tiny, six-legged, reddish larvae of the harvest mite. They live throughout the world and are very common in the southern part of the United States. They are usually found in low, damp areas where there is a lot of plant growth. Chiggers like shrubs and small trees as well. They are even common in the lawns around our homes.

Chiggers are a nuisance to humans, as they attach themselves to our skin and bite us, causing itchy, red welts. The chigger sucks the cell tissue and fluid out of the host that it is attached to and injects its saliva into the bite. The saliva of the chigger is what causes the itchy reaction.

Chiggers may not be the most pleasant insects, but they are natives of Missouri and will probably stay here as long as we do.

title: Move Over, Brothers Grimm—New Fairy Tales Found
text:
There’s a magical world out there full of elves, evil queens and beautiful princesses! If you enjoy “Cinderella,” “Little Red Riding Hood” and “Rapunzel,” you have already discovered the work of the Brothers Grimm. These German fairy tales and legends were collected by the Grimm brothers and put into popular books about 200 years ago.

A new world of fairy-tale magic has just been revealed. Researchers found a collection of 500 stories gathered by Franz von Schonwerth, a German historian who did his work at the same time as the Grimm brothers. Because Schonwerth was a historian, he wrote the stories exactly as the German people told them to him. The Grimm brothers changed some of the stories to make them less frightening for children. The Grimm brothers admired Schonwerth’s work. Jacob Grimm said, “Nowhere in the whole of Germany is anyone collecting (fairy tales) so accurately, thoroughly and with such a sensitive ear.” Schonwerth’s collection was never as popular as the Grimm brothers’ books. His three volumes of stories collected dust for 150 years until they were rediscovered.

Schonwerth’s collection includes a story of a beautiful girl who gets away from a witch by turning herself into a pond and another tale about a turnip princess. As soon as the stories are translated into English, you will have a whole new collection of fairy tales to read!

title: Salem Poor, a Brave and Gallant Soldier
text:
Do you know people who you admire because of their ethics? What actions show that a person can be counted on to do the right thing? History has very few details about Salem Poor, an African American soldier who fought in the Revolutionary War. However, 14 officers from the Battle of Bunker Hill signed a document presented to the General Court of Massachusetts. It recommended that a soldier named Salem Poor be rewarded for his heroism. He is described as “a Brave & gallant Soldier.” That’s strong proof of Salem Poor’s ethics.

Salem Poor was born a slave in Massachusetts in the 1740s. He bought his freedom, married and had a son. When the war began, Poor left home to fight with the American colonists. Five times as many African Americans fought with the British because of promises of freedom. African Americans were not allowed to vote and faced many other types of discrimination.

For that reason, Salem Poor’s award is even more remarkable. The details of his actions are unknown. The document reads “…to Set forth Particulars of his Conduct would be Tedious.” But it does say “…under Our Own observation…we declare that…Salem Poor…behaved like an Experienced Officer, as Well as an Excellent Soldier.” From 14 officers present at the battle, that’s high praise indeed.

Some sources claim that Salem Poor shot and killed the British Lieutenant Colonel James Abercrombie at Bunker Hill. Other records show that he continued to fight in other battles. Like many African Americans of that time, exact details of both his birth and death remain a mystery. However, he was honored with a commemorative stamp in 1975.

title: Why Should I Follow Directions?
text:
Here’s a really good story about why it’s important to always follow directions. Once you read it, you’ll never have trouble following directions again!

One time a teacher handed out a test to her students. It was a long 10-page test. At the end of class, some students thought they did very well. They got most of the questions correct. But nobody passed! After the teacher had graded the tests, she pointed out the directions at the top: “Write your name on the top of page one and hand the test in. Do not complete any of the questions.” You can bet those students wished they had read the directions rather than do the whole 10-page test!

Reading directions carefully can mean the difference between an “A” and an “F” in school. It can mean the difference between a delicious pan of muffins and a mess of burnt, yucky dough.

1. Read the directions from beginning to end before you do anything else.

2. Make a list of any material you will need. Gather it up!

3. After you have everything you need, read the directions again carefully. Do you understand every step?

4. Do you still have questions? Ask your teacher, parent or a friend for input.

5. Follow the directions carefully, step by step.

If you follow all these steps, you will do all your assignments correctly. Or your muffins will be delicious!

title: Government Goods and Services
text:
Every day, we often use government goods and services without thinking about it. Some examples are the school you attend, if it is a public school, and the road that you took to school; they are provided for you by the government. People who work pay a part of their income to the federal government in the form of taxes. When you buy something, you pay a little more than the price tag says because you are also paying a small tax (sales tax) that will help the government provide goods and services to everyone.

Many of the goods and services provided by the government are known as public services. Businesses that are owned by people are considered private enterprises (businesses). An example of this would be going to the library in your community. It does not cost you any money to borrow books or other materials from your local library. The government provides this public service to the community through money collected from taxes. If you were to go to a bookstore, however, things would be a little different. The bookstore owner is in business to make money. That person probably wouldn’t allow you to borrow the book you wanted to read. Instead, you would buy it. The bookstore is not public, but is instead private enterprise. Other public services provided by the government include the police and fire departments, parks, the water department and public health department.

The fire department is a public service provided by the government.

title: Let's Write
text: You have been asked to help write Missouri’s first constitution. In a paragraph or two, write some of the things that you would want to have included in this constitution. What rights would you want to have? What things shouldn’t be allowed in our state?

title: Slavery in Missouri
text:
Home Life

Slaves had difficult lives. Not only were they not free to come, go and do as they pleased, but they also had to work long, hard hours. Slaves were usually awakened every morning at 4 a.m. and had half an hour to eat breakfast and get to the fields. By 4:30 a.m., a horn would sound, and the workday would begin.

Those who worked as house servants sometimes got to sleep a bit longer, but they also had to get up early, prepare breakfast and begin their chores. Usually, both field and house workers had jobs to do until sunset. There was a law that required slaves to be given Sundays off, and Missouri slaves often got Saturday afternoons off. William Wells Brown, a slave who was able to escape and write about his experiences, said once one of his masters became religious and required that all of his slaves go to church with him each Sunday. This took some of their free time away, because they had to do what their master said, not what they had planned to do.

The slaves usually lived in special huts or shanties behind the master's house. These shanties were made of the cheapest lumber that could be found and had only one or two rooms. Often, they had only dirt floors and a fireplace for cooking and heat. Some shanties didn't even have a fireplace, so the slaves who lived in these homes had to cook outside.

The food that the slaves had to eat was certainly nothing like what their masters enjoyed. They ate mainly things that could be raised on the farm itself, like hog jowls, bacon, turnip greens, potatoes, cabbage and beans. Once in a while, they might have molasses or coffee. Slaves usually hunted for wild game and fished to add to their diets. Slaves also made their own homemade bread.

One of the most difficult things about life as a slave was that, often, families were broken up when the master decided to sell one or more members of a family. Families were usually pulled apart, and few were allowed to spend their lives together.

Another horrible part of being a slave was the cruelty of many slave owners. Some masters were kinder than others, but many beat their slaves for any misbehavior, and often they were beaten just to keep them from becoming too independent. The life of a slave was very difficult in many ways.

Slavery in Missouri

The first black slaves were brought to Missouri by the French in 1720 to work in the lead mines. By the time Missouri was ready to become a state, slavery had become something that the residents of Missouri considered a necessity. From our point of view, we find that impossible to understand, but those living in Missouri at the time had grown up with the idea that slavery was necessary to run a farm and make a living, so it didn't seem strange or inhumane to them. Most of the slaves in Missouri lived along the Missouri River from Callaway County west to Clay County. These slaves worked mainly on the hemp or tobacco farms in the area, while some worked in their masters' homes, doing household chores. Most slaveholders in Missouri owned between 10 and 50 slaves rather than the hundreds owned by some of the large plantation owners in the southern states.

Should Slavery Be Allowed?

For the people of Missouri, slavery was seen as necessary and as a right that could not be taken away by the government. Even those who didn't have slaves of their own often believed it was the right of the slave owners to keep slaves. As more states joined the Union and people began to argue over whether these new states should or should not allow slavery, Missouri still tended to side with the slave states. The argument was far from over, however, and the nation was about to be torn apart by the issue of slavery.

title: Did most people in Missouri own slaves?
text:
No. Before the Civil War, most Missouri citizens of this period didn't own slaves, but many did, and a lot of those who didn't have slaves believed the slaveholders had the right to keep slaves if they chose to do so.

Missouri had the fewest slaves in any slave state except the state of Delaware.

In 1820, 15 percent of Missouri's population was made up of slaves. By 1860, slaves made up 9.7 percent of Missouri's total population.

title: Justice and Fairness
text: When you think of justice, do you think of our government, the Supreme Court, or a courtroom full of people? Well, justice and fairness certainly are important in those places, but justice is also an important character trait for everyday life. Can you think of a time when you thought you were not treated fairly? Maybe you were not recognized for something you worked hard at, or maybe someone accused you of doing something you didn't do. Wouldn't it be nice if everyone were treated fairly in this world? Well, you can start that right now. Do you treat your friends and family fairly? Do you ever cheat a little when you're playing cards or any other game? When you share something, do you always take the bigger half? What if a friend of yours was accused of stealing? Would you listen to both sides of the story, or just assume that he or she was guilty because someone else said so? Well, doing those things isn't very just. Being fair in everything we do in our lives will help us build character. Others will trust us and know that when they're dealing with us, they will be treated fairly.

title: Kansas City
text:
Kansas City is the largest city in Missouri. Its nickname is "The Heart of America" for a couple of reasons. First of all, Kansas City is located near the center of the 48 contiguous United States. That makes it the "heart" of America. Next, Kansas City is also the point where many forms of transportation (moving people and things from place to place) come together and the place where many people meet as they come and go. Many great and important railways, waterways and freeways meet in Kansas City, so it is the "heart" of American transportation as well.

Kansas City spans both sides of the Missouri River, so there are many bridges connecting the two parts of the city. Kansas City also has many parks and fountains that add beauty to the area.

The city can have very interesting weather. It is very hot and humid in summer, but the fall weather is mild and comfortable. Winter can bring blizzards and cold temperatures, and spring usually brings one or two tornadoes per year to the Kansas City area.

Kansas City is the center for many types of industry. It has huge grain terminals, which ship grain all over the world. Kansas City also has flour mills, livestock markets, steel plants, motor-vehicle assembly plants, oil refineries and printing and publishing companies.

Jazz music (American music with a strong rhythm and unstructured solos) has also had a home in Kansas City since the 1920s. Famous jazz musicians like Scott Joplin, Charlie Parker and Count Basie all came from Kansas City.

title: Hemp
text:
Hemp is an annual plant (plant whose life is completed in one year) that was once grown by farmers throughout Missouri. Hemp is planted each year and can grow anywhere between 36 inches and 15 feet tall, depending on the climate it is grown in.

Hemp is grown mainly for its strong, fibrous inner bark. The inner bark of the hemp plant is used to make ropes, sailcloth, packing cloth and other strong fabrics.

The seed of the hemp plant is used as birdseed. The seeds can also be crushed to produce oil of hemp, which is used to make soaps and oil paints.

title: A Slave No More!
text:
A letter written after the Civil War has shed light on the slave-master relationship. Jourdan Anderson was a slave who gained freedom when he and his family escaped to Ohio from Tennessee. In August 1865 his former owner, Colonel Anderson, wrote a letter asking Jourdan to come back to Tennessee to work on his farm.

The former slave’s reply gave a clear message about his feelings. He said he hoped that God had opened the colonel’s eyes to the wrongs done to slaves for generations. While he was glad his old master was alive, he was surprised that the Yankees hadn’t hung him yet. Jourdan wrote that there was one thing that might bring him back to Tennessee. He and his wife wanted to be paid for the 52 years of combined work that they provided as slaves (over $11,000). Without that, he said they had little faith in the colonel’s promises. He ended by asking the colonel to give his best regards to a man named George Carter. Mr. Carter had apparently taken a pistol away from the colonel when he tried to shoot Jourdan…twice.

Reading letters and newspapers from the past can help us understand the people who lived during that time. Jourdan and his family may have once been slaves, but their spirits were not broken.

title: Little Booklets
text:
1. Fold an 8.5”x11” piece of paper the “hot dog” way.

2. Open it up and fold it the “hamburger” way.

3. While still folded in the “hamburger” way, fold it the “hot dog” way again. Now unfold the “hot dog” way and cut halfway up the middle folded line, from the folded side.

4. Open it up. The cut will be in the middle. The dotted line is where it should be cut.

5. Open your paper, and fold it the “hot dog” way again.

6. Push the two ends so an open box forms in the middle. Fold pages.

7. Now illustrate your own story on the pages.

title: How Do I Read a Map?
text:
Maps can tell you a whole lot about the world. They show you which direction to travel and how to find an unknown place. But wouldn’t you like to know how high the mountains are around you? And just where are those lakes and railroads? If you want to know all that and more, maps are for YOU!

These map functions will help you read a map:

• Scale — On a map you’ll often see: 1 inch = 1 mile. That means one inch on the map represents one mile of the land around you. Easy, huh?

• Legend — What do those little pictures or symbols on a map mean? The legend is a box, usually in a corner of the map. It lists the symbols, then tells what they mean.

• Grid — Many maps are arranged on a grid. See the lines going up and down the sides of the map? There are more lines at the top and bottom. Those grid lines help you locate places on the map. Grids have letters along the sides and numbers across the top and bottom.

• Index — To use the grid to find a location, go to the map’s index. The index lists locations with a letter and a number for each location. Find the spot on the map where that letter and number cross. Now you know where to look for your location!

title: Let's Write
text: This week you have learned of the bravery of men, women and children in difficult situations and how they helped others. Imagine that you lived during the Civil War. How would you have helped others? Would you have volunteered at the hospital, prepared meals for other people, helped people gain their freedom like William Wells Brown? Write a story about your own bravery and how you helped others. Include details from what you have learned this week.

title: William Wells Brown
text:
William Brown is remembered today as one of America's great abolitionists. What's an abolitionist? An abolitionist was someone who was against slavery and wanted to abolish, or get rid of, it. Read about this great American who helped do away with or abolish slavery.

William Wells Brown was born in Kentucky to an enslaved mother. The moment he was born, he became enslaved, too. As an enslaved person, he provided medical assistance to others. William tried to escape to freedom several times during his life. Each time he was hunted down by slave catchers, people who found and caught runaway enslaved people. He would be whipped and jailed for running away. His mother no longer belonged to William's owner, but she still lived in St. Louis. He was worried about his mother and didn't want to leave her, so he stayed where he was.

Finally, William's owner sold him to a family who took him with them to Ohio on a trip. Ohio was a free state. He decided that it might be easier to try to escape there. He walked off the boat at Cincinnati, Ohio, and ran away to Canada in 1834. This time, he made it to freedom. A Quaker man helped him to escape. William took his family name, the first he had ever had.

William got a job on a steamer that ran on Lake Erie between the United States and Canada. He to help enslaved people escape to Canada. He wanted equal rights for African Americans. William was a conductor on the Underground Railroad.

He attended meetings of the Western New York Anti-Slavery Society. He let antislavery lecturers stay in his home. He often spoke at antislavery meetings. He worked with Frederick Douglass and Charles Lenox Remond in the antislavery movement. He became one of the movement’s best speakers. In 1847 he published his autobiography, Narrative of William Wells Brown, a Fugitive Slave.

William was able to travel to Europe. Because of the Fugitive Slave Law passed in 1850, it was dangerous for him to return to America. Friends in England purchased his freedom. When he did return, he became the African American to publish the novel Clotel. It is a story about President Thomas Jefferson and his relationship with one of his enslaved women, Sally Hemmings. He also wrote plays. He was one of the first American writers to talk about the importance of black people in history. He became a doctor and practiced medicine in the Boston area for the rest of his life.

William Brown died in 1884 in Chelsea, Massachusetts. He is remembered today as one of America's great abolitionists.

title: The Battle of Lexington
text:
After the Civil War began in 1861, Missouri became a battleground. When Missouri decided not to secede, or break away, from the Union, the Union sent troops to Missouri and set up military posts there. There were still many Missourians who fought for the Confederacy, and the battles that took place in Missouri were between the Union forces already in control of Missouri and the Confederate forces who wanted to take Missouri away from the North.

The Battle of Lexington took place in Lexington, Missouri, during the late summer of 1861. Union forces had set up a headquarters in the Masonic College in Lexington so they could control the Missouri River. General Sterling Price, a famous Missourian who chose to fight for the South, knew the Union forces were in Lexington, and he decided to try to get them out, and take over Lexington to get control of the river. General Price had just forced Union forces to retreat at Wilson's Creek, Missouri, so he marched his troops to Lexington to try his luck there.

Colonel James Mulligan was in charge of the Union forces at Lexington and had been busy preparing the town for possible battles. He had his Union troops dig trenches around the college and then surround these with mounds of dirt to make it difficult for invading troops to get to the Union headquarters. Colonel Mulligan heard that Price and his troops were on their way, but he believed that more Union troops were scheduled to arrive to add to his forces, so he felt confident that the Union would be able to defeat Price and his men. When Colonel Mulligan received a message from General Price demanding that he surrender to the Confederate army, he replied, "If you want us, you must take us." That is just what Price and his troops intended to do.

Price and his men arrived and began fighting on Sept. 12, 1861. The fighting continued for several days. General Price had a much larger army than did Colonel Mulligan, and soon, the Confederate forces were able to surround the Union forces and cut off both their water and their supplies. The Union forces found themselves surrounded, with no more Union troops in sight.

After several days, Colonel Mulligan and his men saw a strange sight. Lexington was built on a hill, and as the Union forces looked down, they saw bales of hemp moving slowly up the hillside. Hemp is a plant used in making cloth and rope. The Confederate army had soaked the large bales of hemp in the Missouri River, and they used them as shields as they moved up the hill.
