The heavy, watersoaked bales stopped any lead bullets fired from hitting the Confederate soldiers. When Price and his men reached the top of the hill, they captured Lexington, taking 3,500 prisoners, 3,000 rifles and 750 horses. The victory didn't last long, because Price and his men were forced to retreat on Sept. 30, 1861, because he didn't have enough men to defend Lexington if more Union troops arrived. This victory for the South, even though it didn't last long, helped give the Confederacy a feeling of success and let the Union forces know that this war would not be easily won.

title: Missouri Stays with the North!
text:
A civil war is a war fought between people of the same country. The Civil War was especially difficult for border states like Missouri, because people within these states didn't agree on which side should win the war.

Anti-Slavery Lincoln Becomes President

Although the Missouri Compromise calmed the slavery argument for a while, it didn't solve the problem. In 1860, a lawyer from Illinois named Abraham Lincoln was elected as president of the United States. President Lincoln did not believe that each state had the right to decide for itself whether or not to allow slavery. Lincoln didn't want slavery to be allowed in any of the new states that were being formed in the West. He believed slavery was wrong.

Most Southerners didn't agree with President Lincoln and thought they had the right to decide about slavery for themselves. They were also afraid that if slavery were to end, they would lose their way of life. Very few Southerners voted for Lincoln, but because there were more Northerners who opposed slavery than there were Southerners who were for it, these Northerners voted for Lincoln, and he won the election.

States' Rights

After Lincoln became president, many Southerners were afraid slavery would be outlawed in all the states of the Union. They were afraid the national government was getting too powerful and the states would no longer have any say about how they were governed. They were afraid they were losing their states' rights.

Eleven States Leave the Union

Because many Southerners were afraid of what would happen when Lincoln became president, many Southern states met together and began to talk about forming their own country. South Carolina was the first state to decide to leave, or secede from, the Union. Soon after South Carolina left the United States, other Southern states followed until 11 states had left the Union. The states that left the Union were Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, Florida, Tennessee, South Carolina, North Carolina and Virginia. These Southern states formed a new country called the Confederate States of America.

Missouri Decides to Stay with the North

As you can see from the above list, Missouri was not among the states to leave the Union. Missouri was a border state, which means that it bordered, or was right between, the Northern and the Southern states. Missouri was a slave state, and it had to choose whether to leave with the other Southern states or stay with the Union. Missouri finally decided not to secede, but to remain part of the United States of America.

The decision not to break away from the United States wasn't an easy one for the people of Missouri. Some Missourians wanted to join the other slave states and become part of the Confederacy, but after fighting among themselves, those who wanted to stay in the Union finally won. Union soldiers went to the capital in Jefferson City, and Governor Claiborne Fox Jackson, who supported the South, was forced to leave. Jackson was replaced by a new governor, Hamilton R. Gamble, who supported the Union, and Jackson became a leader in the fight against the North. Many other Missourians fought for the South as well.

The Civil War

Soon, America was involved in the Civil War. The Civil War was especially difficult for border states like Missouri, because people within these states didn't agree on which side should win the war. Often, neighbors and friends fought against each other, one for the North and another for the South.

Sometimes, even members of the same family would disagree about the slavery issue, and brother would fight against brother. The Civil War brought death and sadness to many Americans, especially to the citizens of Missouri.

More than 100,000 Missourians fought for the Union army during the Civil War. More than 8,000 of these were African Americans. Missourians who fought for the Confederate army numbered more than 30,000. The Union army wore blue uniforms, and the Confederate soldiers dressed in gray uniforms. Many times, Missourian fought against Missourian in the battles of the Civil War.

Freedom for the Slaves

After much fighting, death and destruction, President Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation in September 1862. (To emancipate means to free.) This was a document stating that as of Jan. 1, 1863, all slaves in the Confederacy would be free. It took nearly two more years for the slaves to gain their freedom, but finally, on Jan. 11, 1865, Missouri became the first Union state to free all of the slaves living within its borders.

The Civil War finally ended April 9, 1865. The Confederacy surrendered to the United States, and both sides agreed to stop fighting. More than 600,000 Americans died in the Civil War. With the end of the war came the end of slavery in America as well. But the United States faced the huge task of bringing the Union back together and rebuilding a strong and united nation.

title: Lexington
text: Lexington, Missouri, was founded in 1822 and soon became an important trading center for those traveling along the Santa Fe and Oregon trails. Lexington is located along the tops of the bluffs along the Missouri River in the western part of our state. The city has many important and interesting historical sites. Tourists can visit the Battle of Lexington State Historic Site, where a famous Civil War battle took place. Visitors can also tour Anderson House, a famous old mansion used as a hospital during the Civil War. This hospital passed between the North and the South several times, being used as a hospital for both Union and Confederate soldiers. Another place to visit is the Madonna of the Trail, a statue honoring the women who suffered so much coming West. This statue was donated to Lexington by the Daughters of the American Revolution. Visitors can also learn a lot about Lexington and about Missouri's history by visiting the Lexington Historical Museum. The Lafayette County Courthouse in Lexington is another famous historical site. This courthouse was hit by a cannonball during a Civil War battle, and a cannonball has been put on the front of the courthouse to remind people of this battle. Often, people will dress as Union and Confederate soldiers and reenact the Battle of Lexington near the courthouse.

title: What did Missouri women do to help during the Civil War?
text: Women in Missouri had to help during the war in many ways. Because their husbands, fathers and brothers were away fighting in battle, many women had to take care of their farms and businesses on their own. They also rolled bandages for those who were injured and fed and clothed wounded soldiers, nursing them back to health. Some even visited the battlefields to find the soldiers who had been wounded.

title: Peace Democrats
text:
From the first day of fighting, there were people in the North who were against the war. Most of them were members of the Democratic Party who didn't care if the Union split up. They wanted to compromise with the South and end the war. These people were called the "Peace Democrats." The Peace Democrats were always a problem for Lincoln. They attacked his war policy in the newspapers and called him a "tyrant" and a "joking fool." The Republicans, Lincoln's party, wanted to fight until the South gave up and came back into the Union (the states that did not secede from the United States.)

Most people hated the Peace Democrats. Northern men were going off to fight in the war, and these people were doing their best to help the South. It was believed that anyone who talked against the war was for the South. The Peace Democrats were dividing the North. People called them "Copperheads." A copperhead is a snake that hides in leaves that are the same color as the snake's skin, so they are very difficult to see. Their poisonous bites can be fatal.

title: The Prairie Chicken
text:
Prairie chickens, Tympanuchus cupido, are wild birds that live mainly in the grasslands and coastal prairies of North America. Prairie chickens are not really related to chickens, but are actually a type of grouse. They are about 16.5 inches long, weigh 1 to 2 pounds and have 28-inch wingspans.

Prairie chickens are noisy birds, and unlike chickens, they are strong flyers. Prairie chickens live in the grasslands of Missouri, but are in danger of becoming extinct because a lot of their habitat has disappeared. A habitat is the place where a plant or animal lives. Much of the prairie chickens' habitat has been used for farming, so many prairie chickens have died out.

Prairie chickens like to eat leaves, seeds, rose hips and many types of insects, such as grasshoppers. Predators (animals that kill other animals for food) of the prairie chicken include hawks, owls, skunks, coyotes, opossums, foxes, raccoons and snakes.

title: The Civil War Today!
text:
The Civil War began when Confederate troops attacked Union soldiers at Fort Sumter on April 12, 1861. The war lasted four years. The two sides fought over 50 major battles and hundreds of smaller clashes. The war ended after General Robert E. Lee surrendered to General Ulysses S. Grant on April 9, 1865.

2011 to 2015 marked the 150th anniversary of the Civil War. Many towns and communities took time to celebrate and remember this important part of our history. During those years, anyone who owned an iPad could “watch” the war happen using “The Civil War Today” app. The app showed users what had happened on that day 150 years ago. The app used pictures, maps and newspaper stories to show the events of the war one day at a time.

The anniversary has passed, but the app is still available. People with the app can look up any date during the war and read newspaper articles, letters soldiers wrote to their families and detailed descriptions of battles. If you or someone you know owns an iPad, ask for permission to look at “The Civil War Today” app. It can help you relive the drama of the Civil War with just the push of a button!

title: How Do I Read Charts?
text:
By learning to read charts, you can quickly compare information.

Charts are very organized because they are used to compare data. They would be harder to understand if it was all jumbled together. That’s why charts use lists or boxes placed into categories. They appear at the top and down the left-hand side of every chart. You can easily see what information is being compared. You can also spot the differences and similarities. Using charts can help you understand information faster.

Try It!

Study the chart below, then answer the questions that follow.

1. What categories are covered in this chart?

2. Which animals are all over Australia?

3. Which animals mainly eat plants?

4. Where does the Western Barred Bandicoot live?

5. Which animals live in Eastern Australia?

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you are a soldier in the Civil War. Write a letter home telling your family about your experiences as a soldier. For which side are you fighting? Where do you sleep? What do you miss most about your home? How do you feel about the war?

title: James Milton Turner
text:
James Milton Turner was born a slave in St. Louis County, Missouri. His parents were slaves, and his father was a very good veterinarian, or animal doctor. John Turner, James's father, took care of sick animals for many people who lived near him. The people who came to him for help with their animals paid John. His owner let John keep part of the money he earned. By saving this money, John was able to buy his freedom from his owner. He then saved enough money to buy freedom for the rest of his family, including James. James was 4 years old when his father bought him from his owner for $50.

When James Milton started to grow up, his parents wanted him to go to school and get an education, but this wasn't easy. It was illegal (against the law) for African American children living in Missouri to be taught to read and write. James Milton went to a school in St. Louis anyway, but after a while, Missouri leaders closed the school down. The man who had run the school in St. Louis started another school on a steamboat on the Mississippi River, and James Milton went to this school as well.

James Milton was able to attend Oberlin College in Ohio for a while. This college was different from most other colleges at this time because it allowed men and women to go to school together, and it also allowed African American students to go to school right along with the white students. This was very unusual during this time period.

James returned to St. Louis, and the Civil War broke out soon after. He became a servant to a Union officer and was wounded during the Battle of Shiloh. He limped the rest of his life because of the wound he suffered in the hip during this battle. He went back to St. Louis and spent the rest of the Civil War helping runaway slaves escape into Illinois.

After the Civil War, Turner became a great leader in the fight for equal rights and equal treatment for African Americans. He was the leader of the Missouri Equal Rights League, which was a group of people, both African American and white, who thought African Americans deserved to be treated just as well as whites. The league tried to make it legal for African Americans to vote, and it also tried to get good schools for African American children.

James Milton was very interested in making sure that African Americans had the opportunity to go to school. He knew how difficult it had been for him to get an education, and he didn't want other African American children to miss out on going to school. He raised money for the Lincoln Institute, a school in Jefferson City especially for African American students. This college is now known as Lincoln University, and it is open to all races of students. Turner also became a teacher himself. He was a teacher in Missouri's first public school for African Americans, located in Kansas City. He also ran the African American schools in the Boonville area and was even asked by the governor to help start public schools for African American children all over the state of Missouri.

One of Turner's greatest achievements was becoming one of America's first African American diplomats. He was chosen by President Ulysses S. Grant to represent the United States in Liberia, a country in Africa. Turner was one of Missouri's very first civil rights leaders. (Civil rights are the rights of those who are citizens of a particular state or country.)

title: Secrets in the Presidents Pocket
text:
"The moment of truth has come. Is there or is there not an inscription?" These were the words of watchmaker George Thomas as he carefully took the back off Abraham Lincoln's pocket watch at the National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C. Just like a scene out of one of the "National Treasure" movies, the crowd gasped when Thomas revealed that there was indeed a secret message engraved inside Lincoln's watch.

Watchmaker Jonathan Dillon was fixing the president's watch when he heard that the first shots of the Civil War had been fired. For nearly 150 years, rumors said that when Dillon learned that the war had begun, he engraved a message on the inside of the watch.

Doug Stiles, a great-great grandson of the watchmaker, heard the story when he was young and wanted to check it out. He passed along the rumors to the museum and the directors decided to open the watch to see what was inside. Sure enough, the rumors were true!

So, what did the secret message say? The first line says: "April 13, 1861. Fort Sumter was attacked by the rebels on the above date. J. Dillon." A second line reads: "April 13, 1861. Thank God we have a government. Jonathan Dillon."

These words may not seem very mysterious, but just knowing that the rumors are true is important to many people. What was Doug Stiles' reaction to knowing that his great-great grandfather left an inscription on the president's watch? "My gosh, that was Lincoln's watch," he said, "and my ancestor put graffiti on it!"

title: Recovery
text:
Rebuilding Missouri

After the Civil War ended on April 9, 1865, people hoped life would soon return to normal. There was a lot to do after the war in order to repair all of the damage that had been done. Many homes, farms, buildings, railroads and bridges had been destroyed during the war, both by Civil War battles fought in our state and by guerrilla raids on people and property. Guerrillas were men who didn't belong to either the Union or Confederate armies, but who hid in the bushes and attacked those they felt to be their enemies. Guerrilla warfare was very severe in Missouri, and it left a lot of damage behind after the war ended.

Reconstruction

When the war ended, Missourians began working hard to rebuild their state. This time period just after the war is called Reconstruction, which means "to build again." The people of Missouri worked hard to rebuild what they had once had before the war. Farmers replanted and soon were able to grow more crops than they had in the years before the war. Stores were repaired and were able to restock their shelves. Factories were rebuilt, and more jobs became available. New railroads were built to ship goods to other parts of the country. Missouri was once again on its way to becoming the Gateway to the West. Even more difficult to repair than the damage to homes and property was the damage to people's lives and feelings. Missourians who had fought for the Union believed they had been right all along, and the fact that the North had won the war proved them right. Those who had fought for the Confederacy thought they had been right and that it was terribly wrong that the South had lost the war. It was very difficult for neighbors who had been on opposite sides of the war to understand each other and to get over the bad feelings they felt toward each other.

Should the South Be Punished?

After the war ended, many northerners thought the South should be punished for seceding from the Union. Some of these people, called Radicals, thought those who had supported the Confederacy should not be allowed to vote or to run for political office. President Lincoln disagreed with the Radicals. He thought that the South had suffered enough and that it was time to stop being angry and to enjoy peace. He wanted the country to pull together again as a strong unit.

Lincoln Assassinated

President Lincoln was shot and killed just after the war ended. He and his wife had gone to see a play at Ford's Theatre in Washington, DC, and John Wilkes Booth shot and killed President Lincoln. Booth was an actor who was angry with President Lincoln because Booth had wanted the South to win the war.

Radicals Become Powerful

After President Lincoln's death, Vice President Andrew Johnson became the president. The Radicals didn't like him, and they pushed hard to have their own way when it came to the treatment of the South. The Radicals became more powerful and passed many laws to punish the South. Anyone who had supported the South during the war was not allowed to vote or to hold any public office.

In Missouri, the Radicals were in charge of the government. Not only couldn't those who had helped the South during the war vote or hold office in Missouri, but they weren't even allowed to work as lawyers, teachers or ministers in our state.

Slavery Abolished

Although the Radicals were very harsh in the way they treated those who supported the South, they also did some good things. They helped end slavery in Missouri, and they also worked hard to repair old schools and build new ones after the war. They opened schools for African American children and also helped to build new railroads in Missouri.

Unfair Laws Changed

It wasn't long before those who wanted to get over the pains of war and restore peace in Missouri were able to get rid of the unfair Radical laws. Voters in Missouri elected new leaders who wanted to forgive southern supporters and work at getting along. Soon all of the unfair laws were changed, and Missouri was on its way to becoming a unified and peaceful state once more.

title: Integrity
text:
What does it mean to have integrity? It means that you make your actions match what you say and believe. Integrity is one of the most important character traits a person can have. Here's an example.

A poor Mexican immigrant, Ascension Franco Gonzales, was walking in Los Angeles one evening in 2001 and came upon a bag of money, not just a couple of bucks, but $203,000! Gonzales thought about keeping the money, but knew it was wrong in his heart. After he heard on the news that the money was missing from an armored car, a truck that transports money from big banks, he knew what he had to do. He returned the money, even though he could have kept it. Though he did not ask for a reward, he received $25,000 for returning the money!

Gonzales showed integrity because he acted in the way that matched what he believed. He knew that keeping the money was wrong, so he gave it back. How can you show integrity in your life? You can clean up your room when you tell your mom you will. You can be honest with your friends and family. You can be kind to those around you because you know it is wrong to tease and gossip. You can make your actions match what your parents and teachers have taught you, and then you can say that you have integrity!

title: What did most African Americans want more than anything after the Civil War?
text: Education. Even though all African Americans were legally free citizens after the war, they still didn't have the same rights and freedoms that white people did. They wanted to be able to get good jobs, have nice homes and enjoy the same kind of life that white people did, but they knew that they would need educations in order to do these things. That is why African Americans tried to establish schools for themselves and their children as quickly as possible after the war.

title: Warrensburg
text:
Warrensburg was established in 1833 and is located about 50 miles east of Kansas City in Johnson County, Missouri. It was settled by a man named Martin Warren who built a cabin and blacksmith shop here in the early 1800s. Central Missouri State University is located in Warrensburg. It is the third largest university in Missouri with 12,000 students attending each year. Warrensburg is also the home of Whiteman Air Force Base. The base is famous for being the home of the B-2 bomber. You may know this plane better as the stealth bomber.

The railroad has always been important to the people of Warrensburg. The railroad came to Warrensburg during the Civil War and has been a part of the city ever since. It is the third largest stop in Missouri for the Amtrak train.

If you are ever in Warrensburg, you may want to visit Powell Gardens, a 835-acre botanical garden with hiking trails, displays of beautiful flowers and plants, and interesting nature lectures. Lions Lake and Truman Lake are also popular attractions in Warrensburg. Lions Lake is a wildlife refuge that provides a home for many migrating birds and other wildlife. Truman Lake is a 50,000-acre reservoir that offers water sports, camping and fishing.

title: Prairie Goldenrod
text:
Prairie goldenrod is a warm-season herb that lives in dry, open places on the slopes of valleys and on plains. It also grows on grassy roadsides, rocky slopes and along railroads, ditches and fences.

Prairie goldenrod is perennial, which means that it comes back every year without having to be replanted. Prairie goldenrod is a weedy plant that has clusters of pretty yellow flowers growing on tall, wand-like stems. They add beauty to prairies, hills and roadsides.

During the time of drought in the 1930s in the Midwest, prairie goldenrod took over and grew where the grass had died out from lack of water. A drought is a long period of time with little or no rain. After the drought ended, the patches of prairie goldenrod thinned out, and the grasses took over again. But you can still find prairie goldenrod if you watch for it.

title: Tops
text:
Poster board or file folder

Round lid or compass

Ruler

Scissors

Pencil

Colored markers

Masking tape

Nail or toothpick with pointed ends for spinning

Directions

1. On the poster board or file folder, draw several circles with a compass, or trace around a lid. Make small circles; tops more than three inches in diameter don’t spin well. Mark the center using a ruler.

2. Cut out your tops.

3. With a pencil and a ruler, divide each top into sections: halves, thirds, quarters and so on.

4. Use markers to draw designs. You may repeat the same design several times or alternate designs in sectioned parts.

5. Press the nail or toothpick through the center hole. Spin. If the spinner begins to slip, attach pieces of masking tape to keep it in place

Extra Activity: Use designs that match the theme of whatever you are learning in school, such as the pioneer era. You can also use designs that have to do with your hobby.

title: How Do I Use a Graph?
text:
Graphs show numbers, and then tell what those numbers mean.

Types of Graphs

Bar Graph — Bar graphs use bars of different lengths to give information. The bars can run from left to right across the graph, or from the bottom up. You can use a bar graph to show how the numbers compare.

Look at the bar graph about the U.S. population growth.

Line Graph — Line graphs show how information changes over time. One line shows units of time. Another line shows the information being measured. Inside the graph you’ll see points that meet. You can use a line graph to see if the information is going up or down.

This line graph shows the number of hurricanes since 1970. Have hurricanes increased or decreased?

Pictograph — Pictographs are like bar graphs, except they use pictures or symbols instead of bars.

This pictograph shows different countries and how much ice cream they eat.

Pie Graph — Pie graphs use a circle to show 100 percent of something. The circle is divided into sections, or slices of the pie. Each slice gives different information.

Of the population in 2003, what percentage lived in China?

title: Let's Write
text: You have just returned from fighting as a soldier in the Civil War. What do you notice about your home state of Missouri? What is different? What things have changed? What is the first thing that you would repair?

title: The Eads Bridge
text:
As a young boy living in St. Louis, James Eads had to quit school and sell apples in the street to help his struggling family. After he was hired as a clerk for a dry goods business, he educated himself from the owner's private library. His fascination with the mighty Mississippi began at age 18 when he became a purser's clerk on a Mississippi River steamboat. A budding entrepreneur, Eads soon went into business salvaging vessels wrecked by underwater snags in the muddy Mississippi. To do this, he invented a diving bell that allowed him to walk the shifting river bottom and guide the snagged boats to their targets. Within a few years, he had made himself rich and had acquired a formidable knowledge of hydraulics.

After the Civil War ended and life began to return to normal in Missouri, the railroad began to be the most important form of transportation. Missouri's rivers had once been the state's most important means of transportation, but now that railroads were becoming more popular, these same rivers sometimes got in the way. If a railroad line needed to cut across Missouri, it would surely have to cross a river to do it. To keep the railroad lines running across our state, engineers figured out how to build bridges across the rivers that got in the way. An engineer is someone who uses math and science to design and build things. Building bridges could get expensive, but most of these bridges didn't present too many difficulties to their builders. Engineers were even able to build a bridge across the Missouri River at Kansas City in 1869. When people thought of trying to build a bridge across the Mississippi River, however, they met up with more problems than they bargained for.

Most engineers who looked at the river thought it would be impossible to build a bridge across it. The river was very wide and deep at St. Louis, and the river bottom was sandy and unstable. If a bridge were built, it would also have to be at least 50 feet above the surface of the river so the smokestacks of the steamships would fit beneath the bridge. With all of these problems, most engineers thought building a bridge across the Mississippi couldn't be done. Then along came James B. Eads.

Eads was a famous engineer who had invented a diving bell and also designed and built ironclad ships for the Union during the Civil War. When Eads had been working on his diving bell, he had explored the bottom of the Mississippi, and he thought he could design and build the bridge that no one else thought possible.

After the Civil War, Eads was able to get Congress to say "yes" to his idea, and the St. Louis taxpayers agreed to give Eads $1 million to help with the project. Eads was on his way, and construction on the bridge began in 1867.

The bridge had three spans, or lengths of bridge between each support. Each span was more than 500 feet long, and the bridge had huge granite piers that were used for supports. These piers reached down below the depths of the river at least 90 feet and were cemented to bedrock. The bridge was different than any other bridge built before because it had longer arches, its supports went deeper into the water, and it used more steel than any bridge ever built.

The bridge was also unique because it had two levels. The top level was built as a road to carry carriages, wagons, etc., and the lower level held the railroad tracks to carry trains.

The Eads Bridge was completed in 1874 and was known as one of the man-made wonders of the world at that time. It allowed the railroad to continue on its way, bringing goods and people to St. Louis and beyond. The bridge still stands in St. Louis and is still a remarkable sight, especially when we realize how many years ago it was built.

title: Transportation
text:
Railroads and Automobiles Improve Transportation

Up until the time of the Civil War, Missouri's waterways had been the greatest means of transportation. Steamboats had been the most important providers of transportation for both goods and passengers. After the Civil War ended and the railroads were completed, things changed quickly.

Trains Move Goods Quickly

By 1904, nearly any part of Missouri could be reached by train. Goods that used to be shipped on the Mississippi or Missouri rivers could be shipped by train. Even as early as 1880, the railroads outdid steamboats in the amount of freight they hauled. For example, in 1880 railroads transported 464,291 bales of cotton to St. Louis, while steamboats transported only 32,279 bales of cotton that same year. The expansion of the railroads helped many of Missouri's cities to grow and develop, because access to the railroad allowed them to both send and receive goods.

The opening of new railroad lines helped the lumber industry grow by leaps and bounds. In the Ozarks, where wood was plentiful, the new railroad lines made it possible for the lumber cut there to be sent wherever it was needed. The need for lumber was greater than ever before, as the railroad used railroad ties made out of wood to build its railroad lines. As cities grew, they also needed more lumber to build buildings and houses. The lumber from the Ozarks was cut and milled in sawmills, then sent by train to places all over the country.

Another industry that was helped by the railroads was the mining industry. Lead, zinc and coal were mined in Missouri and then sent wherever they were wanted. More mining jobs were created as the demand for these ores increased.

Bridges were built to carry the trains over rivers in our state. The most difficult bridges to build were the Hannibal Bridge, which crossed the Missouri River at Kansas City, and the Eads Bridge, which crossed the Mississippi River at St. Louis. Both of these bridges were difficult and expensive to build, but after they were finished, goods could be brought into and taken out of these cities by railroad, improving businesses and the way of life for the people who lived there.

Automobiles Become Transportation for Everyone

Trains weren't the only type of transportation used by Missourians after the Civil War. Around 1890, Missourians first began to drive automobiles. These early automobiles were very different from the cars we drive today. They weren't fast, clean or even comfortable, yet many people were fascinated by this new invention.

Only the rich could afford to buy the first automobiles, so very few people actually owned them until much later. Many of Missouri's average citizens thought these new contraptions were dangerous and didn't like them. The cars were noisy and often frightened horses they met while on the road. People also thought these new automobiles went much too fast and that people would get hurt in these speeding machines. Laws were passed that set the speed limit at 9 miles per hour to protect the public safety. This seems very slow to us now, but to people who were used to riding in wagons and carriages, 9 miles per hour seemed like more than a safe and comfortable speed.

When more and more people started to drive cars, the roads in Missouri had to be changed so they could handle car traffic. Wagon roads were usually narrow dirt roads, but these didn't work well for cars. They were too narrow for cars to pass each other, and when it rained, the cars often got stuck in the muddy roads and had to be pulled out with teams of horses. Wider, paved roads were eventually built to make it easier for automobile travel. It is hard to imagine life without the automobile now that it has become the main source of transportation for nearly everyone in Missouri.

* To transport is to carry from one place to another.

title: Sedalia
text:
Sedalia, Missouri, is a city of about 25,000 people and is located in Pettis County. It is in nearly the very middle of our state and is known as a transportation center of the area. Major United States highways join at Sedalia, and it is also the home of a large airport. Amtrak passenger trains come to and go from here, as do piggyback freight trains. Sedalia is a place with a lot of coming and going!

Sedalia is also known as a successful farming community. Corn, wheat, oats and hay are all grown in Sedalia, and livestock is also raised here. Sedalia receives about 41 inches of rain per year and has fairly moderate temperatures. The soil is rich and fertile, and the land is well-suited for farming.

Industry also does well in Sedalia. Companies like Louis Rich, Levi, Rival, Kelsey Hays, Gardner-Denver and Pittsburgh-Corning all have plants in Sedalia. These companies provide jobs for workers in the area and ship their products throughout the country. Many people from Sedalia also work at Whiteman Air Force Base.

Lake of the Ozarks and Truman Lake are popular recreation spots for those who live in Sedalia. The area is also famous for its wonderful hunting spots, and people come for miles around to hunt deer, turkey, quail and dove. Sedalia also has an active kennel club that holds dog shows and competitions each year.

title: What is a diving bell?
text: A diving bell is an invention used to allow people to stay under water for long periods of time. It is a special chamber with an open bottom in which people can go underwater without using scuba-diving equipment. Water is kept out of the chamber by compressed air, which is fed into the diving bell by a hose. James Eads invented a special diving bell and used it to explore the bottom of the Mississippi River.

title: Quail
text:
Quail are small birds that live in many parts of the United States and North America. They are related to the partridge, pheasant and grouse and have mottled, or spotted, feathers.

The number of eggs produced at one time for hatching is called a clutch. Quail reproduce very successfully, usually laying 12-15 eggs per clutch.

Quail build their nests on the ground, protected by tall plants. The female is in charge of most of the incubation, or keeping the eggs warm, and she also takes care of the baby birds once they hatch.

Quail are very popular game birds, which means people like to hunt them. One reason they are so popular is that the meat of the quail is quite delicious, and many people enjoy its flavor.

Quail are easy to recognize because of the crests on top of their heads. The crest often flops down and looks like a "topknot" of hair. Quail eat insects and seeds and travel in flocks called coveys. Quail are native to Missouri and can be found throughout the state.

title: Pounded Plant Prints
text:
Materials

Several sheets of plain, ink-free newsprint

Just-picked leaves and flowers

100-percent cotton fabric

Washing soda

Hammer

Hard surface for hammering (such as a sidewalk or table)

Water

Soap

Paint brush

Bowl

Pan

Clothes line or dyer

Directions

1. Gather plants. Choose thin, flat leaves; juicy leaves do not work well. If you want to print flowers, choose small, bright flowers like pansies, violas and baby carnations. Remember, you never know how the dye is going to transfer to the fabric. The surprise is part of the fun.

2. Cover a hard surface with eight to 10 newsprint pages. Place a piece of fabric on the newsprint. We strongly recommend testing several plant parts on scrap pieces of fabric.

3. Place a leaf or flower on the fabric. Cover the plant with a double layer of newsprint.

4. Hammer the newsprint covering the plant. The tannin coloring in the plant will transfer to the fabric. Carefully lift your paper cover to see if your plant design is transferring to the cloth.

5. Dip cloth in a solution of 1/2 cup washing soda to 2 cups water. The green tannin of the leaves “fixes” successfully with the washing soda solution. After “fixing” the colors, wash your cotton in soapy water, rinse and dry. All flower petals “fix” differently. Many pinks and purples “fix” aqua and bright blue.

title: How Do I Read Tables?
text:
By learning to read tables, you can quickly compare information. Tables have text and numbers. When reading a table, carefully read the text.

Try It!

The table below shows baseball players and their career home runs. Study the table, then answer the questions that follow.

1. What does this table show?

2. Who hit the most home runs?

3. Who hit the least home runs?

4. Who had the same amount of home runs as another?

5. Who had 563 home runs?

6. Who had more home runs,Ted Williams or Mark McGwire?

7. How many home runs did Mike Schmidt hit?

title: Unions Improve Work Conditions
text:
Groups of workers decided to come together and organize themselves into labor unions. A labor union is a group of workers who join together to get better working conditions.

During the late 1800s, many new factories were built in Missouri's larger cities. Because these factories offered many new jobs, people began moving to the cities in search of employment. The factories offered a lot of new jobs, but many people were disappointed when they found that the jobs they offered weren't as nice as they had hoped.

Factories hired men, women and children and often made them work for long hours for low wages. Also, many of the conditions in the factories weren't pleasant or safe. Workers would often have to do jobs that were dangerous and use machines that could hurt them. Even children had to work under dangerous conditions and had to work all day.

Many people tried to improve the conditions in the factories, but when someone went to his employer and complained, he was usually fired and replaced with another worker who didn't complain.

Finally, groups of workers decided to come together and organize themselves into labor unions. A labor union is a group of workers who join together to get better working conditions. When the owners of the factories were approached by a labor union, it was much more difficult to just fire the workers and get new ones. The factories couldn't afford to fire all their workers, so they were forced to listen to their complaints.

If the owners of the factories wouldn't listen to the labor unions, the unions would sometimes go on strike. A strike occurs when workers refuse to work unless their bosses give them the things they are asking for. One group of girls who worked in a factory in St. Joseph wanted to be paid 60 cents for every 12 pieces of clothing they sewed. The factory owner only wanted to pay them 50 cents for every 12 pieces of clothing. When the factory owner refused to pay the girls what they thought the job was worth, the workers went on strike. After only a few hours of having the factory shut down, the factory owner agreed to pay the higher wages.

Workers also went on strike to get better working conditions and to be able to work fewer hours. But workers didn't always have to go on strike to get what they wanted. When all of the workers joined together and sent representatives to talk to the factory owners, they would often listen and work out a compromise that suited both sides. Many times, the labor unions were able to get the factory owners to give them what they wanted without having to go on strike.

Slowly, over time, Missouri's labor unions began to make a difference in the way workers were treated in the big cities. Working conditions became safer, hours were reduced, and wages increased. The government also passed a law limiting the number of hours that children could work in factories. Because the workers joined together and created labor unions, they were able to improve the way of life of all of the factory workers in the state of Missouri.

title: How Does Your Garden Grow?
text:
Have you been wondering what to do with last year's gym shoes - the ones with broken laces and holes in the soles? Turn them into planters! Just fill them with potting soil and put in seeds or a small plant from the local garden center. If your shoe doesn't already have a hole in the bottom, ask an adult to cut one. This will let the water drain. In a few weeks, you'll have a planter that everyone is sure to notice. Planters made from plastic pitchers, large bowls and wastebaskets can make your garden stand out. Or, stick with familiar containers like clay pots and hanging baskets.

First, you will need some basic items: seeds or seedlings, a container, potting soil and a trowel to scoop the soil. Be sure your plants get plenty of water, and don't forget to get your parents' permission before you begin!

What should you put in your garden? Marigolds, zinnias and geraniums are colorful choices for Missouri gardens. If you'd rather plant something you can eat, try lettuce and miniature (cherry) tomatoes. If you have room for a backyard garden, try planting sunflowers, pumpkins or watermelons. They're fun to grow, because they can get very big. In 1996, a New York couple grew a pumpkin that weighed 1,061 pounds!

title: Farming and Manufacturing
text:
Missouri: A Land of Farmers

Missouri has always been a land of farmers. The rich, fertile soil in our state has drawn many farmers to work the land. With the invention of new machines and gadgets to make the work of farming faster and easier, the farms in Missouri began to produce like never before. The farmer in the years before the Civil War had to do everything by hand or with the help of horses, mules or oxen. After the Civil War, many machines were invented to make farming easier. Though it was still pulled by a horse or mule, the sulky plow, which had wheels and a seat for the driver to sit on, made plowing the fields easier and more comfortable. Corn planters, threshing machines, hay bailers, corn shellers and hoisting forks all made the work of the farmer easier and faster. These machines also cost a lot of money, so the farmer had to spend more on supplies for his farm, but these new machines also helped him produce more crops, so he was able to make more money.

Science Helps Farmers

Another thing that helped the farmers of Missouri was the new interest that farmers were taking in science. The University of Missouri School of Agriculture was started in 1870 to do research on different kinds of seeds, fertilizers and ways of producing better crops. Missouri farmers started using new fertilizers and buying better kinds of seeds. Science helped to improve the crops in ways the farmers of just a few years before could never have imagined.

Missouri's Important Crops

The most important crops grown in Missouri during this time were corn, wheat, barley, tobacco, hay, fruit and vegetables. Apples and grapes became very important crops in the Ozarks, where a new variety of grapes was developed that was very hardy and was not prone to getting diseases. This variety of grape was later imported to France by French grape growers who were impressed with this new, disease-free plant.

Missouri also began producing livestock in record numbers. Farmers doubled the number of hogs they produced during this period, and they tripled the number of cattle produced. They also increased the number of horses and mules produced during this time. Farming and ranching were popular and successful careers in Missouri after the Civil War.

Manufacturing

Before the Civil War, most items that people needed to buy, such as shoes, tools or clothes, were made in small shops run by craftsmen who made those items. The craftsman often worked alone, or sometimes he would hire one or two people to help him. He usually used only small hand tools to make his product, and each item he made was unique and suited to the needs of his customers.

As more people moved to Missouri, the small shops couldn't keep up with the needs of these new residents. These small shops grew into larger shops and, eventually, into huge factories. Machines were invented that made it possible for products to be made more quickly and in greater quantities than ever before. The age of manufacturing had arrived.

Manufacturing is the making of large amounts of goods in factories. By the beginning of the 1900s, manufacturing was the state's second largest industry, second only to farming. Many people quit farming and moved to the cities to find jobs in the factories. The factories grew, and so did the cities.

St. Louis had more factories than any other city in Missouri. Products such as beer, chewing tobacco, medicines, machines, shoes, clothes, ironware and food were all manufactured in factories in St. Louis.

Kansas City was another of Missouri's cities that grew because of the growth of new factories. Kansas City's most important industry was its meat-packing plants. Ranchers from all over the West would send their cattle to Kansas City on railroad cars, and the meat packers there would kill the animals and prepare the meat. In those days, a lot of the meat was canned so it wouldn't spoil. The canned meat would then be shipped to cities in the East. Later on, refrigerated railroad cars were invented, and the meat packers were able to cut the meat and ship it fresh to cities throughout America. Kansas City also had many flour-milling plants. Again, grain could be brought to Kansas City in railroad cars, and then it would be milled into flour in the flour mills.

Other cities that grew because of the increase in manufacturing were St. Joseph, which had meat-packing plants, Springfield, where furniture, flour, lumber, cotton, wool and wagon factories were built, and Joplin, where the mining industry was important. Washington, Missouri, began manufacturing two of the most interesting and unusual items in our state. Factories were built there that made corncob pipes and zithers. Zithers are stringed instruments that people strum with their fingers. Washington is the only place in the world where corncob pipes are still manufactured.

title: Mexico, Missouri
text:
Mexico, Missouri, is located in the eastern section of our state. It was founded in 1836 by a group of immigrants from Kentucky, North Carolina, Virginia and Tennessee. Mexico became a thriving city in the early 1900s when a special type of clay was found here that was perfect for making firebrick. Firebrick is a special brick used to line furnaces, fire boxes, chimneys and fireplaces. The world's largest firebrick plant - A. P. Green Refractories Co. - was built here in 1910.

Mexico is also famous for its saddle horses. It was once the home of a world-famous saddle-horse breeding and training stable. There were also popular horse shows held here. Visitors still enjoy visiting the Saddle Horse Museum in Mexico.

Missouri Military Academy also makes its home in Mexico, Missouri. It was founded in 1889 and is known throughout the world as an outstanding military academy for boys in the fourth through 12th grades.

If you are interested in visiting Mexico, you may want to come during the first weekend in June. Each year during this weekend, the Miss Missouri Scholarship Pageant is held in Mexico. The winner of this pageant goes on to compete in the Miss America Pageant.

Mexico also has rich farmlands where farmers grow many crops. Some of the crops grown in this area are soybeans, milo, corn and wheat. Farmers in the area also raise livestock.

title: What’s a zither?
text:
A zither is a stringed instrument, similar to a guitar, but without any "neck" or "arms." The zither has only a body, or resonator, with the strings strung across this body. There are usually five metal melody strings across the body and 17 to 40 accompaniment strings, usually made of gut or nylon.

The player of the zither wears a plectrum, a piece of metal or bone, on his right thumb. He uses this to pluck out the melody and then uses his right-hand fingers to play the accompaniment and his lefthand fingers to stop the melody strings from vibrating. The world-famous zithermaker, Franz Schwanzer, lived and worked in Washington, Missouri, in the early 1900s.

title: American Saddle Horse
text:
Missouri has long been famous for its saddle horses. During the late 1800s, ranchers began raising and breeding saddle horses for sale and for show.

The American saddle horse is a breed of light horse. It is well known for its beauty as well as its easy gait and its strength and stamina. It is sometimes called the Kentucky saddler.

The American saddle horse was developed by breeding the thoroughbred and the Morgan horses together. It has an arched, swan-like neck and an uplifted tail, which makes it a very aristocratic and showy horse. It usually has a brown, black or chestnut-colored coat, and it often has a white face and white leg markings. It stands 15 to 16 hands tall (60 to 64 inches) and weighs around 1,000 pounds.

One of the things that makes the American saddle horse so popular is its unique ability to learn and do what a trainer demands. It trains and performs very well in shows. Mexico, Missouri, is still known for its saddle horses.

title: Haym Salomon, Financial Hero
text:
In 1975, the U.S. Postal Service issued a stamp [right] honoring Haym Salomon as a “Financial Hero of the American Revolution,” yet many Americans have never heard of him. Who was Haym Salomon?

Haym Salomon was a Jewish immigrant from Poland who came to New York City in 1772. He became a successful financial broker (someone who arranges business transactions). Salomon sided with the patriots and joined the Sons of Liberty. The British arrested him as a spy. In jail he became an interpreter for German soldiers but secretly encouraged many to desert (leave the army). He was supposed to be executed, but he escaped. He set up a new business in Philadelphia.

Salomon could see that the Continental Congress was struggling to get money to support the war. American soldiers did not have enough pay, food or supplies. Salomon began raising money. He helped Robert Morris, the Superintendent of Finance, get loans from France and other countries. He often made personal loans to the government and to American leaders like James Madison, Thomas Jefferson and James Monroe. When George Washington needed money for the Battle of Yorktown, he said, “Send for Haym Salomon.” Salomon’s clear thinking, generosity and dedication helped our country win its independence.

The Treaty of Paris in 1783 ended the war, but the new country still had money problems. Salomon continued to help America raise money. He was also a strong leader in Philadelphia’s Congregation Mikveh Israel. He worked to overturn a law that kept non-Christians from holding office.

Now that you have learned Haym Salomon’s story, why do you think history has often overlooked him? How has clarity of thought led to a positive result in your life?

title: Rubrics
text:
Rubrics tell you what is expected on an assignment. They can help you prepare for a project.

You have a big project coming up in your class on how to make chocolate chip cookies. You’re a little nervous because you haven’t made cookies before. Then, your teacher hands out a rubric. A rubric? What’s that? It’s a scoring guide that lets you know what you should do to get a good grade. A rubric looks like a chart and is divided into specific categories. Here are some ways to use a rubric.

1. Look at the categories. They will tell you what you need to focus on for the project. If you’re making chocolate chip cookies, the teacher may want you to focus on the color, taste, or the number of chocolate chips. The rubric should have these categories.

2. Look at what will give you a good grade. Once you know what to focus on, see what you need to do. This is often called the criteria. Do the cookies need to be a golden brown, or can they be a little crispy? Do your best to get that good grade.

3. If you have questions about the criteria, ask the teacher. Sometimes, it’s not clear what something means. For the cookies, what is a golden-brown color? Don’t be afraid to ask questions.

4. You can evaluate your project before handing it in. You can use the rubric to mark off what you’ve done right. Let’s say your cookies turn out to be chewy and golden brown. But they don’t have many chocolate chips. You can mark off the first two because you’ve done them right. Then you can work on the third.

It’s really simple to use a rubric. By using a rubric, you will know what to do to receive a high score. You can be prepared for any project!

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine that you are the head of a labor union for a shoe factory in St. Louis. Write a letter to the factory owner telling him or her your demands. What do you want to see changed? What do you and the other workers think is fair? What will happen if your demands are not met?

title: General John J. Pershing
text:
During World War I, Missouri contributed one of the most famous soldiers ever to serve in any war. General John J. Pershing, the commander of the United States Army in Europe during World War I, came from Missouri.

Pershing was born in Laclede, Missouri, in 1860. Laclede is located in Linn County, which is in the middle northern portion of our state. Pershing grew up on a farm and loved to ride horses.

After graduating from high school, John began teaching school. In those days, teachers were often hired to teach school, even if they had never been to college. John wanted to go to college, but his family didn't have enough money to send him. John found a way to get the education he wanted when he read about the United States Military Academy at West Point. He read that the school provided education for young men and that it trained them to become soldiers. He also read that the school didn't require its students to pay for the education they received there. In fact, West Point would pay students to attend! This sounded like the perfect place for John to get the education he wanted but couldn't afford, so he wrote a letter to the school, asking if he could attend.

The school wrote back, inviting John to become a student there.

John went to West Point, worked hard there and found that he liked being a soldier. He decided to make the Army his career. After his graduation from the military academy in 1886, Pershing became a cavalry officer. A cavalry officer is a soldier who fights on horseback. He fought in the Southwest and Northern Plains of the United States and also served in the Wounded Knee Campaign, which was a war fought against the American Indians. Pershing also spent some time leading African American soldiers and was very concerned about the way the African American soldiers were treated. He tried to help them to be treated fairly.

Because Pershing was a good soldier, he received many promotions (increases in responsibility or rank). Eventually, he became a general in the US Army. By the time World War I started in 1917, General Pershing was known as a skilled and experienced leader. The Secretary of War called General Pershing to Washington and asked him to lead all of the American troops in Europe. He became Commander of the American Expeditionary Forces in France and led the American forces in the greatest war the world had ever seen.

General Pershing was concerned that the American soldiers had not had much training. He worked hard to make sure that new soldiers were well-trained before they were sent into battle. He didn't want soldiers to die because they didn't know how to fight.

After World War I ended, Pershing was promoted to general of the armies of the United States. Only George Washington had ever received such a high military rank. He also became chief of staff of the Army and helped to improve officer training and to make sure that our country would be ready if war ever came again.

General Pershing died on July 15, 1948. He is one of Missouri's finest military heroes.

title: The Mighty Missouri
text:
Did you know there is a battleship named for our state? The U.S.S. Missouri is almost as long as three football fields and weighs 45,000 tons! The Mighty Mo, as it has been nicknamed, opened as a museum in 1999, at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. If you visit the Missouri, you can strap on a hard hat and a utility belt (complete with flashlight and bottled water) for the Explorer's Tour, where you will see the working areas of the ship. You can also climb four flights of stairs to the bridge or continue up another flight for an incredible view of Pearl Harbor and the Pacific Ocean. The U.S.S. Missouri has an interesting history. On Sept. 2, 1945, World War II officially ended when the Japanese signed surrender documents on the deck of the ship. The Mighty Mo also fought in the Korean War and Desert Storm.

In 1989, the ship made headlines for a different reason. Cher, the famous singer, recorded a music video on the forecastle (the front part of the ship). "If I Could Turn Back Time" was a huge hit and gave 200 sailors a chance to be on MTV.

If you visit Hawaii, don't miss seeing the Missouri and her sister ship, the U.S.S. Arizona, which actually lies at the bottom of the harbor where it sank on Dec. 7, 1941. The attack that sank the Arizona forced the United States to enter World War II. Now both ships-representing the beginning and the end of the war-call Pearl Harbor home.

title: World Wars and the Great Depression
text:
World War I

The beginning of the 20th century was an exciting time for our state and our nation. Farms and factories were growing, and new inventions were springing up everywhere. Life looked good to Missourians, but something happened then that affected the entire world.

In 1914, a war started in Europe that would change the lives of people in Missouri, half a world away. At first, this war was fought between Britain, Russia and some other smaller nations, who were called the Allied Powers, and Germany, Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria, and the Ottoman Empire, who were called the Central Powers. The United States tried to stay out of the war, but eventually, America joined the Allied Powers.

The German navy had come up with a new and dangerous weapon. When American ships sailed in the Atlantic Ocean, German U-boats, special boats that could travel under water, would sometimes sneak up on them and attack. Some Americans were even killed in Uboat attacks. U-boats are what we now call submarines. Because the Germans refused to stop attacking American ships with their new weapon, President Woodrow Wilson decided to declare war on Germany. The United States joined the Allied Powers and became part of what was then called the Great War. We now know this war as World War I.

Missourians helped to win the war in many ways. The United States sent troops to Europe to help fight the Central Powers, and more than 156,000 Missourians were part of these troops. Missourians at home helped by raising food to be sent to the Allied forces in Europe. They also made weapons, machinery, clothing, shoes, chemicals and other things needed to help fight the war. Because of the efforts of those in Europe and those at home, the Allied Powers won the war in 1918.

The Great Depression

After World War I ended, life was exciting and good here in Missouri. Most people had jobs and could afford to buy many of the new gadgets that were being invented. Many people bought their first automobiles in the 1920s, and people began to travel as never before. People filled their homes with refrigerators, toasters, irons, radios and other appliances and spent money on gas, oil and tires for their cars. Women were given the right to vote, and some began taking jobs outside the home. It was an exciting time to be alive! This period is known as the Roaring '20s.

Then things changed for all Americans with the stock market crash of 1929. Many people had hoped to make money in the stock market and had bought stock in a lot of companies. When the prices of the stock dropped, people lost money, and soon, businesses and banks throughout the country closed their doors. People lost their jobs and had no money to pay rent, buy food or provide for their families. Many people were forced to stand in soup lines, or long lines where they could receive free food. In St. Louis, one out of every 10 people had to stand in soup lines in order to be fed.

President Franklin D. Roosevelt came up with some new programs meant to help those who were out of work. He called his plan the New Deal, and it helped those who were unemployed by giving them jobs doing things the government needed done anyway. The New Deal gave people jobs repairing and building roads, building government buildings such as post offices, city halls, courthouses and schools and even planting trees and building dams. These jobs helped those who were out of work support their families and got them back on their feet.

World War II

In 1939, another great war began in Europe. This time, the Axis Powers, led by Germany, Italy and Japan, went to war against the Allies, led by Great Britain, France, China and the Soviet Union. Again, the United States was determined to stay out of the war, but something happened on Dec. 7, 1941, that left America no choice but to join the war.

On this date, Japanese airplanes dropped bombs on the US naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. Hundreds of Americans were killed, and many American ships were sunk. After the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, the United States declared war on Japan and the other Axis countries.

Missouri did its part in helping to win World War II, as this war was called. Nearly 450,000 men and women from Missouri served in World War II, but those who stayed at home helped with the war effort as well. Farmers had to produce extra food to feed those at home and those away fighting the war. Missouri's mines produced iron, lead and zinc. These minerals were then used to make weapons. Factories that had made cars started to make airplanes and tanks instead. Missouri factories also produced guns, bullets, chemicals, trucks, medical supplies, uniforms and shoes.

Missouri women who had once stayed at home had to enter the work force. With many of the men off fighting the war, thousands of women were forced to take over their jobs, doing work that they had never done before. Women worked in factories, making airplanes and tanks, and did other jobs that had been reserved for men only.

Finally, after four years of fighting, the Allies won the war. Japan was the last of the Axis Powers to give up the fight. They signed the final terms of surrender on board the battleship U.S.S. Missouri on Sept. 2, 1945. Missourians breathed a sigh of relief and looked forward to better times.

title: Fort Leonard Wood, Pulaski County
text:
Fort Leonard Wood was completed in 1941 and became one of the Army's largest training camps for soldiers during World War II. During the war, soldiers from all over the United States were sent to Fort Leonard Wood to receive military training before being sent into battle. Fort Leonard Wood is located in Pulaski County in the southern part of Missouri.

Fort Leonard Wood is still a large military training center. Each year, more than 25,000 soldiers receive training here. This military post is known as a maneuver support center, and it consists of three schools: military police school, chemical school and the Army's engineer school.

Fort Leonard Wood is like its own small city. It has everything the soldiers and their families could need such as a hospital, fitness center, child-development center, stores, schools and all kinds of entertainment spots. Fort Leonard Wood welcomes visitors and allows them to observe soldiers at work, learning how to do their jobs. If you choose to visit the base, stop by the information center, and you will receive directions to World War II museums and military-history displays. You are also welcome to attend graduation ceremonies for soldiers. These ceremonies are usually held on Thursday mornings. At the graduation ceremonies, you will catch a glimpse of military life, and you will also have a chance to hear the 399th Army Band perform.

title: What was the Spirit of St. Louis?
text: The Spirit of St. Louis was the airplane used by Charles A. Lindbergh to fly nonstop across the Atlantic Ocean from New York to Paris on May 20, 1927. He was the first person to fly across the Atlantic Ocean alone. Lindbergh made the flight in 33 hours and 30 minutes, and he took only five sandwiches and two canteens of water with him. The trip was more than 3,600 miles long. Lindbergh named his plane the Spirit of St. Louis because people from St. Louis had given him the money he needed to make the flight.

title: Zinc
text:
Zinc is a mineral that is found in large deposits in Missouri. Zinc is used to protect iron and steel from corrosion. Corrosion is a decaying or rusting of the metal. Zinc is used as a protective coating to help the metal resist chemicals that would break it down. Zinc was used in the past to "galvanize" or protect the bathtubs and water buckets used by our grandparents. It is now used to coat the steel used to make car bodies and fenders. Zinc is also used in making batteries and for making pennies. Most people think the penny is made of copper, but it is actually 98 percent zinc.

The United States is the leading producer of zinc in the world, and Missouri produces much of the zinc found in the United States.

title: Building on Base Words
text:
A base word is the basic word. As you create new words from a base word, they are all related.

Base words are used to make other words you use every day. Derivations are those words created by adding parts to the base word. Here’s an exercise to make you think. For each group of derivations, write the base word in the blank space. In the future, when you’re reading on your own, try to think what the base word is for many of the words you read.

happiness, happily, happier, happiest. Base word: ________________

drummer, drumming, eardrum. Base word: _____________________

stabbed, stabbing, stabber. Base word: _______________________

boring, bores, bored. Base word: ____________________________

boarding, boarder, boards. Base word: ________________________

believed, believing, believable, unbelievable. Base word: ___________

possibly, possibility, impossible. Base word: ____________________

omnibus, buses, bused, busing. Base word: _____________________

migrate, migration, immigration, migrating. Base word: ____________

title: Supply and Demand
text:
One Christmas, 10-year-old Tyler knew exactly what he wanted to find under his Christmas tree. He really wanted a special sports game for his gaming system. All of Tyler’s friends wanted the game too. As the holiday got closer, Tyler started to worry. Every store in town was out of the game. The demand for the game was high. A lot of people wanted this special game. However, the supply of the game was low. There were not enough games for everyone who wanted to buy it.

Supply is the amount of a product that a business has for sale. Demand is how much people want to buy it. Usually if the price of an item is very high, the demand will be low. This results in a high supply. If the item goes on sale then the demand may increase and the supply would then decrease.

The best thing is when the demand is equal to the supply. Everyone who wants the product can make the purchase and businesses make money. On Christmas morning, Tyler found the sports game under his tree. It seems the video game store got a new supply of the game the evening before the big day. The supply and demand were equal and everyone was happy.

title: Lucile H. Bluford
text:
After World War II ended, things improved for nearly all Missourians. Most people had good jobs and could afford to do things they had never been able to do before, such as own their own homes, go on vacations and buy cars. There were some groups of people, however, who weren't allowed to enjoy life as much as others. Blacks and other minorities still faced problems when it came to receiving fair treatment. Lucile H. Bluford was a black woman who knew all about what it meant to have the color of your skin decide what you could and could not do.

Lucile Bluford was a very intelligent woman who had attended the University of Kansas. She was an excellent student, and she worked hard in school. She graduated from the University of Kansas and wanted to continue her education by studying journalism at the University of Missouri. Journalism is the study of newspaper writing, and Lucile knew that the University of Missouri was famous for its school of journalism. When Lucile tried to apply to the school, she found out that she had a big problem. She was black, and the University of Missouri was closed to blacks. She was not allowed to be a student at the college.

Lucile believed it was wrong for her to be kept out of the University of Missouri just because she was black. She was a citizen of the United States of America, and she was also a good student. She knew that simply being black was not a good enough reason for her to be kept out of the school.

Lucile tried to fight the school. She went to court and asked the court to make the university change its mind, but the courts refused. This was in 1939, and most people weren't ready to accept that every person had certain civil rights that could not be taken away. Lucile was not allowed to attend the University of Missouri, but she took a big step toward helping others overcome discrimination when she tried to fight against the university's decision. In 1957, the governor of Missouri chose Lucile Bluford to help organize Missouri's Commission on Human Rights. This commission was set up to help make sure that all citizens of Missouri were treated fairly and that they had the same chances for jobs, education, etc. Later, she also became a leader in the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). Lucile Bluford became a newspaperwoman after all and was the editor of the Kansas City Call for many years. After years of work in the newspaper business, the University of Missouri, the same school that refused to let her attend because she was black, gave her an honorary doctorate degree. A doctorate degree is the highest degree that a university can give. She earned this honor by working hard trying to make sure that all people were treated fairly, no matter what color their skin was.

(Discrimination is unfairly favoring one type of person over another.)

title: Boom to Bust and Back Again
text:
You may have heard people compare the recent economic recession (2007 - 2009) to the Great Depression of the 1930s. But what some people call the "Great Recession" actually had more in common with a depression in the 1890s and something called "boom and bust."

In the early 1890s, the U.S. economy grew quickly ("boomed") but couldn't keep growing at that rate. When many companies and the housing market failed, there was an economic "bust." The railroad industry had been booming since the end of the Civil War, but in the 1890s more than 150 railroad companies closed. Other industries that depended on the railroads closed, and many people lost their jobs. Over 500 banks closed. Thousands of unemployed men marched to Washington, D.C., in 1894 to demand that the government take action to help families. Unemployment was over 10 percent for most of the 1890s. About one of every ten people had no job.

In the recent recession, the housing market slumped after several "boom" years. Some automakers went out of business and others filed for bankruptcy. The economy went "bust," just as it did in the 1890s. Hundreds of banks and thousands of businesses closed. The unemployment rate was about 8 percent - about one of every twelve people had no job. Make a chart or Venn diagram that compares these two events in history.

title: Civil Rights
text:
Time to Enjoy the Good Life

After World War II, the people of Missouri were ready to enjoy the good life. Many people had good jobs and could afford to buy houses, cars and products to make their lives easier. There was only one problem: not everyone in Missouri was enjoying prosperity. African Americans still did not enjoy the same privileges as did white people, and women also found that they were often treated unfairly, especially in the job market. Many Missourians were ready to fight for the rights of ALL of its citizens.

Although the Civil War had ended nearly 100 years before, black citizens in Missouri still didn't have the same rights as other citizens. They were allowed to vote, but they had to attend all-black schools and could not attend the schools of their choice. Missouri also had laws against black Missourians going to certain restaurants, hotels, theaters, parks and other public places. Missouri was still practicing segregation in many ways. Segregation means that blacks could not mix with whites in schools, churches or other public places. Blacks had to keep with other blacks and could not try to associate with whites in many public places.

Blacks in Missouri began fighting for their civil rights. Civil rights are the rights that all citizens of a country are entitled to. Many white Missourians also joined the civil rights movement and fought to see that all Missourians had equal rights.

Missouri Commission on Human Rights

In 1954, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that segregation was wrong and that it was against the law. Congress began passing laws to make certain that all Americans had the same rights.

To help make sure that Missouri treated its citizens fairly, the leaders of our state started the Missouri Commission on Human Rights. This organization's job was to make sure that people were treated fairly and that they had the same opportunities for jobs.

Conditions for blacks began to improve in Missouri, but there were still problems. In 1963, Ivory Perry started a protest (fight) against unfair treatment of blacks by the Jefferson Bank. Perry had learned that the bank refused to hire African Americans, so he organized a boycott of the bank by blacks and others who believed that this was wrong. A boycott is when people get together and refuse to buy from or deal with an organization unless it changes the way it does things. Perry also organized marches and demonstrations against the bank to let people know that it treated blacks unfairly. Perry's protests made a difference, as the Jefferson Bank hired its first African American teller in 1964.

Women Want Equal Rights

Many women also felt that they were being treated unfairly. After World War II, more and more Missouri women went to work, but they seldom received the same wages as did the men they worked with, even if they were working at the same job. Women were also unhappy that business, government and technological fields were almost always run by men. Women wanted to have more say in what happened in the world.

Women joined together to form organizations that would help them work for equal rights. Some of the organizations that Missouri women joined were the National Organization for Women (NOW), the League of Women Voters and the Business and Professional Women's Association. These groups worked to make sure that women were treated fairly in their jobs, that they received equal pay when they did jobs equal to those of men and that they were not discriminated against.

Women became leaders in every area of life, including education, business and government. Leonor Sullivan was the first Missouri woman to be elected to the U. S. House of Representatives. She served in Congress for 24 years. Other women have also held high positions in Missouri government.

Harriet Woods was elected as lieutenant governor, and Margaret Kelly was elected as state auditor. Life for women in Missouri has improved greatly.

Many Missourians have also fought against things that they found dangerous or unfair over the years. Protests have been held to oppose pollution of the air and water. There have also been protests against nuclear power and the treatment of the poor and homeless of our state. Because of the willingness of the people of Missouri to stand up for what they believe in, our state has continued to grow as a healthy, safe place to live.

title: Joplin
text:
Joplin is located in southwestern Missouri in the four corners region. The four corners region is the spot where four different states, Oklahoma, Kansas, Missouri and Arkansas, all come together.

Joplin began as a mining town and became a city in 1873. It is now the 10th-largest city in Missouri with a population of more than 46,000 people.

There are eight major lakes and many freshwater streams in the Joplin area. Many tourists come to fish, boat and swim in these beautiful waters every year.

Joplin has many interesting museums and theaters to visit. Joplin Little Theater is the oldest continuous community theater west of the Mississippi.
