There are always fun and exciting plays being performed here by people from the Joplin area. Each year, Joplin also presents the Missouri Southern International Piano Competition.

The George Washington Carver National Monument in Joplin is the birthplace of George Washington Carver, a famous scientist. He is well known for his research using the peanut and the soybean. When you visit his birthplace, you can go on a nature tour of the grounds and also visit an on-site museum telling all about Carver and his discoveries.

You could also visit the George A. Spiva Center of the Arts if you are ever in Joplin. This center has rotating exhibits, which means that the exhibits are always changing. There is a gallery that displays artwork from local artists, and the center also offers art classes for adults and children.

title: What's dust, and where does it come from?
text: Look around your classroom or at home for a flat surface that has not been touched for a week or two. It will be covered with a fine layer of dust. Believe it or not, most dust in a house or school is dead skin fragments from human bodies. (Yuck, that's YOU lying all over the place!) Other dust particles come from tobacco smoke, particles of pollen and plants, factory smoke and soil. In 1980, Mount St. Helens launched thousands of tons of dust into the air when it erupted. Dust can come from outer space, too. Could that thin layer of dust actually be millions of miniature UFOs all over the top of the piano? Who knows?

title: Raccoon
text:
The raccoon is a common animal in Missouri. It is a nocturnal animal, which means that it likes to sleep during the day and prowl during the night. The raccoon is sometimes called "coon" for short.

The raccoon has a heavy, rounded body and a pointed face. Its front paws look like hands, and the raccoon uses them very much like we use our hands. The raccoon is also covered with heavy gray, brown and black fur, and it has a large, bushy tail with black rings along it. The raccoon is usually 1 and 1/2 to 2 and 1/2 feet long, and its tail adds another 8 to 12 inches to its length. The raccoon is sometimes compared to a robber because it has a black "mask" of fur around its eye area. It can be found stealing corn and other vegetables from the gardens of local farmers.

Raccoons are good climbers, and they often build their nests in hollow trees. They live mostly in wooded areas and feed along lakes and streams. They eat all kinds of foods, including nuts, seeds, fruits, eggs, insects, frogs and crayfish. When the raccoon is near water, it likes to "wash" its food by dipping it in water before eating it.

title: Fact Cubes
text:
Materials

square boxes, milk cartons

solid-color butcher or wrapping paper

tape or glue

crayons or markers

pencils

Instructions

1. Make a cube from a square box of any kind. You can also make a cube by cutting two milk cartons in half and then inserting the open square end of one into the open square end of the other.

2. Cover both cubes with butcher or wrapping paper. If you use wrapping paper, make sure that it isn’t “coated,” or you won’t be able to draw or write on the paper without smearing the ink.

3. Write and illustrate facts about whatever subject that you choose. You could make a fact cube about your favorite animal or sport, or you could choose a subject in school to write about. For example, you could write what you have learned about the Earth from your science class, or you could copy one of your favorite poems you have learned in your English class.

4. Share your fact cube with family and friends and tell them about the facts you chose to write. Have fun!

Extra Activity: To improve your fact cube even more, you could have a parent help you type up the facts on your computer, print them out, and paste them on the fact cube. You could also look on the Internet or in magazines to find pictures to print/cut out and paste on your fact cube. Make sure you always have an adult with you when working on the Internet.

title: Using a Planner
text:
A planner can help you manage your time. It is a simple tool that will help you remember assignments.

Feeling stressed? Not sure if you’ll have time to do all of your homework? To keep up with your studies and have fun learning, you need to learn to manage your time. A planner is a perfect tool to do this.

A planner is like a calendar. It will have days, weeks and months in it. You can look ahead in a planner to see what’s due. You can also look at a day to see what you need to do. Planners help organize your time with just a little effort. Here are some ways to use a planner.

Write down assignments. Write down each assignment as you get it. You can include spelling lists, math homework and book titles. It’s your planner, so put down what you need to know. With each assignment, be sure to include the due date and other requirements. When you’re done with the assignment, check or cross it off.

Review your planner every day. To stay on top of things, review what you’ve written. You don’t want to forget an important assignment! Look ahead to see what assignments are coming up. You can even start early on some of them. It’s up to you to keep track of them.

Create a study schedule. Some people study well in the morning. Others do well in the afternoon or evening. When do you study best? Pick a schedule that works best for you. Block off some time in your planner. Then stick with it. Once you’re done studying, check it off. You may need to choose a quiet place that is free from distractions.

You can use your planner to schedule other things as well, like soccer matches or music recitals. Planners can help you remember anything.

title: Let's Write
text:
Imagine that you have applied for a job at a local candy store. When you don’t get the job, you ask why, and the owner tells you that only people with red hair can work in his store. Your hair is brown.

Write a paragraph or two telling what you would do to try to change things so that this store would hire qualified workers, no matter what the color of their hair.

title: Meet Alexander McNair - First Governor of Missouri
text:
Alexander McNair was born in Pennsylvania in 1775. He spent his first 30 years in the town of Derry before going away to school in Philadelphia. When his father died a year later, McNair returned home. To decide which of the McNair brothers would take control of their father's land, the young men chose to fight each other in a boxing match. The winner would take over all the family's land and property. McNair lost the fight and the family fortune, but he went on to do great things of his own.

McNair joined the Pennsylvania militia in fighting against the Whiskey Rebellion. He was soon chosen to lead the group. He said that the proudest moment of his life came when President George Washington visited his troops.

In 1800, McNair finished his service in the military and came to St. Louis, where he was chosen to help start the new police department. McNair served as the sheriff of St. Louis and as a colonel in the Missouri militia during the War of 1812. After the war, McNair became a U.S. marshal. He also worked for the federal register of lands, a job that made him wealthy.

McNair was one of the members of the Missouri Constitutional Convention in 1820. After the convention, he decided to run for governor. He ran against General William Clark, the famous explorer who mapped the Louisiana Purchase with Meriwether Lewis. Clark had served as the territorial governor of Missouri for seven years and was very popular, but McNair won the election with 72 percent of the voters choosing him over Clark.

As governor, McNair did not want to get rid of slavery in Missouri. He soon realized, however, that if Missouri wanted to become a state, some compromises had to be made. Governor McNair signed a Solemn Public Act promising the president of the United States that if Missouri was allowed to join the Union as a slave state, free blacks would still be allowed to live in Missouri without punishment. Missouri became a state in 1821.

McNair finished his term as governor in 1824 and took a job as a U.S. agent for the Osage Indians. He caught the flu and died in 1826 at the age of 51. He was buried at the Calvary Cemetery in St. Louis.

title: Our Three Government Branches
text:
The state of Missouri has a constitution that is patterned after the United States Constitution. A constitution is a plan for how the government should work. Our constitution tells about the three different branches of our government and explains how they work. It also tells about the rights of the citizens of the state of Missouri.

Our government is divided into three branches or parts. These three branches share the power of governing so that one person or one group of people won't become too powerful and force their will upon others.

Congress to Be Bicameral (Divided into Two Houses)

After much debate, the Connecticut compromise was proposed. Congress would be bicameral. That is, it would be divided into two houses. Any law made for the nation would have to pass through both houses. The first house, the Senate, would be composed of exactly two senators from each state regardless of the size of its population. In this way, each state would have equal representation. The second house, the House of Representatives, would have representation in proportion to the population of each state. In this way, the states with larger populations would have more representatives in Congress than states with small populations.

The Executive Branch

The governor is the head of the executive branch of government in our state. The governor's job is to carry out the laws of the state of Missouri. Our state's governor is elected by the people and serves for a term of four years. A term is the length of time that an elected official stays in office. The governor also gets to choose people who will help run the state, and he has veto power, which means that he can say "no" to any bill. A bill is a proposal for a law.

The Legislative Branch

The legislative branch makes the laws. The legislative branch is called the General Assembly, and it is made up of two parts - the Senate and the House of Representatives. There are 34 state senators and 163 representatives. State senators and representatives are elected by the people of Missouri. State senators serve four-year terms, and representatives serve two-year terms. These elected officials write bills and then vote on whether or not these bills should become laws.

The Judicial Branch

The job of the judicial branch of Missouri's state government is to interpret, or explain, the laws of our state. The judicial branch is made up of judges and courts.

The highest court in Missouri is called the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court consists of seven judges. These judges review the most important cases from the other courts in Missouri and decide if they have been handled correctly. They also review laws passed by the General Assembly to see if they are constitutional, or that they agree with our state's constitution. If the law doesn't agree with the constitution, then the Supreme Court rejects the law.

Missouri also has 45 circuit courts. These courts handle cases of crimes that are brought to court. They also handle disagreements over property and money.

Each of the three branches of government in our state keeps track of the other branches and makes sure that things are running as the constitution says they should. The executive branch keeps an eye on the legislative branch and the judicial branch, the legislative branch passes laws that keep the executive and the judicial branches in order, and the judicial branch makes sure that everything the executive and the legislative branches do is legal. This system is called the principle of checks and balances. Each branch of government checks on the other branches, and the power of government is balanced between each branch.

title: The Governor's Mansion
text:
The Missouri Governor's Mansion is located in Jefferson City, near the capitol. It is a beautiful Victorian mansion that serves as the home of the governor of Missouri during the time that he acts as governor. The mansion doesn't really belong to him, but to the state of Missouri.

The first governor to live in the mansion was Governor B. Gratz Brown and his family. They first moved into the mansion in 1872. The mansion is built in the Renaissance Revival style and has features such as 17-foot ceilings, hand-carved walnut stairways and a third-floor ballroom that is as wide as the entire house. The mansion has been restored to look much as it would have during Victorian times.

The governor's mansion is open to the public for tours and special events. If you visit the mansion in October, you will find that the mansion has been transformed into a spooky spot for Halloween. The governor and his wife host a Halloween SPOOKtacular every October and welcome children to the party. In December, the mansion is strung with twinkling Christmas lights, and the mansion is opened for the annual Christmas Candlelight Tours. At Easter, children are invited to the mansion for the annual Easter Egg Hunt, and there are other events throughout the year, such as the Children's Hour and the Walt Disney Children's Art Festival. If you go to Jefferson City, don't forget to stop at the governor's mansion.

title: How does the government get money to run our state?
text: The government gets its money from taxes. Without money, the government wouldn't be able to do much. You may have noticed that when you buy something at the store, there is a sales tax added on to the price of the items you buy. There is also an income tax charged on the money people earn. A property tax is charged on property, homes, cars, etc. When you hear people complaining about taxes, remember that the money collected in taxes is used to run our government.

title: Soybean
text:
The soybean first became important in Missouri during World War II. Farmers began growing soybeans as a substitute for other protein foods that were more expensive.

The soybean is native to the warm, tropical regions of the world and has been grown in Asia for at least 5,000 years. There are more than 2,500 varieties of soybeans being grown throughout the world. The soybean is easy to grow and harvest, and it produces large crops. It can be grown anywhere that corn can be grown, and it has become a very popular crop here in Missouri.

Soybeans can be used in dozens of ways. Soybeans are used to make soy sauces, soybean meal, vegetable oil, tofu (bean curd), miso (fermented soybean paste), soy milk and coffee substitutes. They are also used as a feed for animals and as a fertilizer. Soybean oil is used to make glycerin, paints, soaps, rubber substitutes, plastics, printer's ink and many other products.

title: Clarity of Expression: FDR and the Four Freedoms
text:
For most people around the world, the years of economic depression and war between 1929 and 1945 were dark and dangerous. Resources such as food, clothing and fuel were in short supply. Families were often torn apart as parents looked for work, served in the armed forces, or as children were sent to safe, sheltered areas. It was a time of stress and hardship, when people desperately looked to leaders for safety and hope. In the United States, that leader was Franklin D. Roosevelt, our 32nd president who served from 1933 to 1945.

During that time of chaos, on Jan. 6, 1941, President Roosevelt delivered to Congress a historic speech, which we now call the Four Freedoms Speech. After years of economic depression, his words were not angry. When world war was happening, his tone was not fierce or mean. But knowing that there were still darker days of war to come for many, he spoke with passion about peace, good fortune, safety, and about the freedoms that humans everywhere deserve. "In the future days," Roosevelt said, "we look forward to a world founded upon four essential human freedoms." Even today those four freedoms are essential (important). Can you list them? They are: the freedom of speech and expression, the freedom of worship for every person, the freedom from wants such as hunger and lack of shelter and the freedom from fear.

How are we doing? Have we achieved those freedoms for everyone? Everywhere?

To read or listen to the entire speech, with the permission of a parent or teacher go to: www.americanrhetoric.com. To see the paintings by Norman Rockwell inspired by the Four Freedoms: www.archives.gov

title: The Job of a Museum Director: ‘A Little Bit of Everything’
text:
The Campbell House Museum is a beautiful Civil War-era home in St. Louis, Missouri. The wealthy Campbell family lived there from 1854 to 1938. Studies Weekly asked Andrew Hahn, the director of the museum, about his job.

SW: How is a house museum different from other types of museums?

AH: A house museum is different because it gives you an opportunity to get the full experience of the past. If you go to an art museum, you can see paintings from the past that may tell a story about history or a particular event. But when you come to a house museum, you get the full picture of what it was like to live in the past. When people come here, they get to experience what it was like to be welcomed into the house or to work in the house. The house was so well preserved, and the Campbells’ collection is still here. This is their house and how they lived in it.

SW: What does a museum director do?

AH: I do a little bit of everything. We have to raise money so that we can keep the doors open and pay the utility bills. I write the checks for all the bills, and I organize our volunteers who do most of the work at the house. We do research, so I look into the Campbell story and read old documents and newspapers that tell stories about the past. I even take out the trash!

title: Getting Organized
text:
Is your backpack overflowing with papers? Is your desk stuffed to the brim? It’s time to get organized!

We all need to be a little organized in life. We need to know where to put our assignments and where to find our homework. But getting organized will take some effort. It will take some practice to come up with a system that works for you. Here are some ways to become more organized.

Avoid clutter. It’s very easy to collect clutter in your backpack and desk. Avoid doing this. It will be easier to find assignments. Have some folders where you can put school announcements or tests that have been graded. Throw anything away that has become outdated. Clean out your desk of all old assignments, broken pencils and dried-out markers.

Prepare your backpack the night before. By doing this, you’ll be ready to go. No more scrambling around in the morning. Put in your notebooks, textbooks and planner (if you have one).

Use one calendar. If you have a planner, you can use that. Write down when your assignments are due. Also, write down any other activities you have. Put down family activities, too! Write everything down so you can remember it.

Organize your notebooks. Color-code them if you need to. Choose one color for each subject. Now you can quickly spot the correct notebook. Also, write your name inside the notebook, in case it gets lost.

Choose a good study space. Make it clear to your family that this is where you’ll be studying. Have extra pens, pencils and paper in the area. It should have room for all of your books. It should also be away from distractions, like the television.

Now that you have some ideas for getting organized, try some of them out. You may be surprised at what a difference it makes in your study habits!

title: Let's Write
text: Write a letter to your state senator or representative telling him or her what you have learned about the government of the state of Missouri. Thank your senator or representative for the work he or she puts in representing the people of our state.

title: The Constitution Protects Our Rights
text:
Let's look at some human rights problems. After reading the following problems, you will see how the Constitution protects us and safeguards our freedoms. Inside Missouri Studies Weekly this week, see how the Constitution organizes our government so that we the people make our own laws. The Missouri State Constitution is patterned after the U.S. Constitution.

Is Drug Testing Fair?

Because of dangerous illegal drugs such as cocaine, crack, heroin and others, government officials are trying to have people tested for drugs. It is estimated that more than 26 million Americans are now using illegal drugs. The problem facing us is, "How can we stop this wave of drug abuse?"

Many think that the answer is to test people to find out if they are using drugs. The most common form of drug testing is through urinalysis. By analyzing a person's urine, an expert can determine if someone has used drugs even days before the test.

Drug Testing Now Being Used... Many of the nation's largest corporations are using some form of drug testing. The government wanted to test about 1 million federal employees in sensitive government jobs.

Will Schools Do Drug Testing? Many school districts and boards are doing some drug testing on students. They believe that it will cut down on student drug use, which is a great concern to parents and teachers. Is Drug Testing a Violation of Constitutional Rights? Many people think drug testing is in violation of the Fourth Amendment, which protects citizens' privacy by keeping the government from making unreasonable searches and seizures.

Recent polls by magazines and newspapers claim that more than 72 percent of Americans are willing to submit to drug testing at work. One school system in Texas wants all children to submit to a drug test. Most parents support the plan. How do you feel about it? (An amendment is a change to an existing law.)

Freedom of Speech in School?

Matt Fraser Suspended for Disruptive Speech

A high school senior from Washington state named Matt Fraser delivered a speech in a student assembly and used words that had double meanings, which caused the audience to hoot and holler. The principal and other administrators told Matt that his speech was indecent and had violated a school rule against disruptive behavior. As a result, he was suspended for three days from school.

Matt Goes to Court... Matt went to court and argued that the school had violated his right of free speech guaranteed under the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. The school administration argued that high school students do not have full rights of free speech. Schools have a right "to maintain and enforce minimum standards of decency" by not allowing indecent and disruptive behavior such as Matt's speech.

Judges Agree with Matt.... Judge Jack Turner from the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals heard all the arguments and judged in favor of Matt that the school had violated Matt's First Amendment rights. The school district appealed to a higher court at the state level, and again the state court agreed with Matt.

District Goes to U.S. Supreme Court... The nine justices of the U.S. Supreme Court do not hear just any case. They only have time to rule on important cases that involve the U.S. Constitution and the rights of citizens. Their decision is final. The school district appealed to the Supreme Court. Chief Justice Warren Burger wrote the following: "While the Constitution does give freedom of speech to adults, it does not automatically give this right to children in a public school. This is because schools are special places where indecent or offensive conduct would disrupt the learning process. Surely, it is appropriate for schools to prohibit the use of vulgar and offensive terms in speeches." By a 7-2 decision, the court overruled the two lower courts, saying Matt's right of free speech had not been violated.

Ruling Still Debated (Discussed)... Some say that the ruling puts student free speech in trouble and opens the way for school administration to clamp down on any expression by students, especially if they disagree with the official view.

The school board and others feel that this was an important victory for schools because the school should have the right to set standards for an orderly environment in which students can learn. How do you feel? Which side would you take? Why?

Are School Uniforms Good?

In three public schools in Baltimore, Maryland, all the children dress alike. They wear school uniforms. Public school children have always been free to dress as they wish. For private school children, however, this is not new. Private school students often wear special school clothes. The children are not forced to wear the uniform in Maryland. Almost all of them want to.

Committee of Parents Submits Plans for Uniforms... Recently, a committee of parents presented the plan to a principal of one of the schools. After meeting with the parents several times, about 97 percent of the parents supported the idea of the children wearing uniforms. The Baltimore school system approved the project, and a local designer designed and produced the uniforms for about $30.00 each.

Some Teachers Like Uniforms... Some teachers think that it would be good if children wore uniforms because their clothing is often distracting to their learning. Some children like to wear short dresses or cut-off pants or T-shirts with distracting slogans on them. Some children compete to be the best and frequently look down on others who can't buy expensive brand-name clothing.

Would Children Lose Their Identity? Many think that it would be like living in a dictator-type government school where children lose their identities and become like numbers. What do you think? Would uniforms improve your school?

title: Kirksville
text:
Kirksville is located in northeastern Missouri in Adair County. The name "Kirksville" literally means "village of the churches," as "kirk" means "church," and "ville" means "village." The city of Kirksville is sometimes called the village of churches, but it was actually named after Mr. Jesse Kirk, a member of a survey party that explored the area.

Kirksville is the home of Truman State University, which was founded in 1867. Missouri's General Assembly voted to make it the first Missouri-supported institution of higher education dedicated to training teachers to teach in public schools. It was first known as the First District Normal School and later as Northeast Missouri State. The name was later changed to honor Harry S. Truman, the only Missourian ever to serve as president of the United States.

Kirksville is also the home of the Kirksville College of Osteopathic Medicine. This college was founded by Andrew Taylor Still in 1892, and more than 500 medical students from around the country and the world attend each year.

Kirksville also has some interesting and educational museums. The E. M. Violette Museum in the Kirk Memorial Building displays American Indian artifacts, historical items from northeastern Missouri and household items from pioneer days. The Adair County Historical Society Museum houses displays of Adair County history and also a genealogical research library.

Kirksville is the county seat of Adair County and has a population of 17,000 people. The community focuses on business, medicine, education, agriculture and tourism. Make a visit to Kirksville and see what you can find out about the history of the area!

title: What requirements must you meet to vote in Missouri?
text:
To vote in Missouri, you must:

1. Be a citizen of the United States

2. Be a resident of Missouri

3. Be at least 18 years old

4. Not be on probation or parole for committing a felony crime

5. Not be convicted of a felony crime that takes away your right to vote

6. Not be declared incompetent by a court of law. “Incompetent” means that you are not mentally able to function in society.

7. Not be in prison

title: Sunflower
text:
The sunflower is a member of the aster family and is native to the United States. The common sunflower is an annual plant, which means that it only lasts one season and needs to be replanted each year. It grows wild here in Missouri, but it is also cultivated, or planted and grown by farmers. The sunflower is grown for its seeds, which can be used in many different ways. The seeds are used as a food for poultry and for humans, too. The oil from the sunflower seed is used for cooking and soap making. The sunflower oil cake is also fed to animals.

American Indians used the sunflower in many ways. They ate the seeds raw, ground them into meal for making bread and used the oil from the seeds on their hair. They made a yellow dye from the flowers and ate the roots of certain types of sunflowers. Sunflowers can still be found growing wild along the roadsides and in the fields of Missouri.

title: Constitutional Rights
text:
Our state constitution is patterned after our national constitution. There are two great ideas to look at. They are constitutional rights and constitutional lawmaking.

Constitutional Rights

Our State Bill of Rights

Worship in the church of your choice.

Say what you believe is right.

Print what you want to publish.

Own your own home.

Go to school.

Have guns within the law.

Vote when of age.

Have a trial by jury.

Don't have to testify against oneself

Our State Bill of Responsibilities

Obey the laws of the land.

Help correct things you disagree with.

Respect the rights of others.

Pay taxes.

Stay informed.

Defend your country.

Vote in elections.

Serve on a jury.

Help police and fire departments.

List Your Rights...

As an American citizen you have many rights.
List as many rights as you can that are guaranteed to U.S. citizens by the Constitution.

As a Missouri Citizen

List as many rights as you can that are guaranteed to every Missouri state citizen by the Constitution.

Constitutional Lawmaking

Our state constitution is a document of paper that states the basic laws, organization and character of our government. It describes a government that is divided into three parts or branches.

The Legislative Branch

This branch is called the state legislature and is made up of legislators. It makes up the laws or rules for us to follow. There are two parts to the legislature, the House of Representatives and the Senate. These representatives are chosen by the citizens of our state to represent them in making the laws. For example, the members of the Senate are elected to represent a district or area. They are the ones who turn bills into laws. (A bill is a piece of legislation before it becomes a law.)

The Executive Branch

This branch consists of the governor, attorney general and secretary of state. These people have the power to enforce the laws made by the legislature. The police and National Guard help them do this.

The Judicial Branch

These judges make up the Supreme Court of our state. They decide if the laws made by the legislature are constitutional. They also decide what punishment a person should receive for breaking the law.

title: Earth as an Apple
text:
Have an adult help you cut the apple with a knife.

Materials

Apple

Knife

Directions

1. Slice an apple into quarters. One-quarter of an apple represents the Earth’s land.

2. Slice one of the quarters into two. This 1/8 piece represents Earth’s land that is not swamps, deserts or polar regions.

3. Cut the 1/8 piece into four 1/32 pieces. One of these pieces represents land that can be farmed. The rest is buried under cities, is too wet or too cold or has poor soil.

4. Peel this 1/32 of the Earth’s surface carefully to represent the thin layer of topsoil that actually produces food.

Let this example remind us of how lucky we are to have the land we live on. Can you see how important it is to take good care of this valuable resource?

title: Keeping Deadlines
text:
Turning things in late only leads to stress. Who wants to be up late working on a big assignment the night before it is due? Take some time to stay ahead in your homework.

Every teacher will give you homework with a deadline. Sometimes, the homework is due the next day. When the project is big, it may be due in a few weeks. When that homework is given, it’s time to prepare yourself. You need to do a few things to turn that homework in on time. It’s all about keeping your deadlines.

Here are a few ways to stay ahead and keep on task.

1. Don’t procrastinate. Homework usually takes longer than you think it will. Start doing it as soon as possible. If you finish it early, you just have more time to make it better.

2. Break up big projects. Some projects may seem huge. Break them up into little pieces. Do you need to do some research for them? How about writing a report? Make a list of what you need to do. Try writing an outline for papers. Read a few chapters each day for a book report. Do something for the project every day before the deadline.

3. Keep a calendar with deadline dates. If you have a lot of homework, write down the deadlines on your calendar. Now you can see what’s due first. Find out which homework assignment will take the longest. Refer to the calendar often so you don’t forget.

title: Let's Write
text: What would you invent for the future? Would it help the world in communication? Maybe you’ll invent something that will make the world friendlier. Describe your invention and what it does. Include as many details as possible.

title: Joyce C. Hall, Founder of Hallmark Cards
text:
Joyce C. Hall was a man who never liked his first name because everyone thought it was a girl's name. Because of this, he went by his initials, J. C., when he got older. J. C. Hall was born in Nebraska to a very poor family. His father left the family when J. C. was still young, and he and his brothers had to go to work to help support their family. He was only 9 years old when he went to work selling perfume.

Later on, J. C.'s brothers bought a bookstore, and he worked for them whenever he could, after school and on Saturdays. The Hall brothers sold picture postcards (with pictures on the front and room to write on the back) in the bookstore, and the cards were very popular items. Because the family was poor and needed his help, J. C. dropped out of school to help run the business.

When J. C. was only 18 years old, he took the $3,500 that he had earned helping out in the bookstore and went to Kansas City to start his own business selling picture postcards. He had heard that Kansas City was a good place to start a business because it had hardworking people and because it had a lot of railroads to use for shipping goods. J. C. took a class at a business college to learn to type and began making and selling postcards, Valentines and Christmas cards.

J. C.'s brothers soon joined him in Kansas City, and the Hall Brothers Company was on its way. The Halls were some of the first in the card business to offer cards and envelopes sold together. This type of card replaced the postcard and elaborate Valentine cards that had been popular before. J. C. was also very concerned about the quality of his cards, and for many years, he insisted that he personally approve every drawing that appeared on the cards he sold. His concern for quality is the reason that he chose the slogan "When you care enough to send the very best" for his company. His cards were so well known for their beauty and quality that for many years, Hallmark Cards made all of the Christmas cards sent out by the presidents of the United States.

Hallmark Cards is now the world's largest greeting-card company with its headquarters located in the Crown Center in Kansas City, Missouri. Besides greeting cards, Hallmark also makes picture albums, ornaments, gift wrap, party supplies, art supplies and crayons. Hallmark Entertainment also produces television specials and videos.

Joyce Hall, the man who was embarrassed about his name and who had to drop out of school because he was so poor, later became one of the richest men in America. He built the most successful greeting-card company in the world and helped Kansas City grow. J. C.'s motto, "When you care enough to send the very best," is still one of the best-known slogans in the world. (A slogan is a motto or phrase used to help customers remember what a company stands for.)

title: Farming and Manufacturing Today
text:
Missouri is among the top states in the country for the production of hogs and turkeys. The farmers here also grow other livestock. It is also among the top five states in the country for its production of beef cattle.

Manufacturing

Missouri is a leader in manufacturing. There are many different types of factories in Missouri that make all kinds of products to be sent to people throughout the world. More than 500,000 people work in Missouri’s manufacturing industry.

Some of the products that Missouri manufactures are cars and trucks, space vehicles, chemicals, food products, and electronic equipment. Missouri has factories that make many different parts used in cars and trucks. We also have factories that assemble, or put together, these different parts to make complete cars and trucks. Missouri is also famous for its publishing industry, with more than 40,000 people working to publish books, newspapers and greeting cards in our state. Hallmark Cards, the world’s largest greeting card company, has its headquarters in Kansas City. Monsanto, a company that sells agricultural products, has its headquarters in St. Louis.

The Boeing department of Defense, Space and Security has headquarters in Missouri. Some other companies with large facilities in Missouri are Anheuser-Busch, a beer producer; Nestle Purina, a pet food manufacturer; and Panera Bread, a restaurant chain. There are also large meat-packing plants, insurance companies and electronics factories.

Farming

In the beginning, most of the people who lived in Missouri lived on farms. Around the end of the 1800s, when factories and industries began to grow, people started moving off the farms and into the big cities. Now, only two out of every 100 people in Missouri are farmers, but farming is still a very important business in our state. Missouri has more farms—more than 100,000—than any other state except Texas.

The Missouri farms of today grow more products than ever before. Most farms are larger than the small family farms of years ago, and the farmers use modern machines to get the work done. Most of Missouri’s farms are still family farms, which means that they are owned and run by the people who live on them. The average size of a Missouri farm is about 285 acres. An acre is about the size of a football field, so you can imagine about how large these farms are.

There are some farms in Missouri that are owned and run by companies. A large farm that is owned by a company instead of a family is called an agribusiness. These larger farms can save money on many things such as farm equipment and supplies because the company who owns them can afford to buy many items in larger quantities and get prices that the family farmer cannot. These large agribusinesses sometimes make it difficult for the family farmer to compete.

Agriculture is a large business in Missouri. Agriculture is the business of growing crops and raising animals. Corn is one of the top crops in Missouri, and the farmers in our state raise more than 200 million bushels of corn each year. Other important crops grown in Missouri are soybeans, wheat, rice, cotton and hay. Missouri farmers also raise livestock. They raise cattle, hogs and poultry. There are also farmers who have large dairy herds that produce milk and milk products. Other farmers in our state grow vegetables, fruit and berries. Missouri farmers ship their products all over the United States and throughout the world. Missouri is one of the nation’s leading farm states.

Missouri is a leading producer of butter and cheese. We also produce many other dairy products. Springfield has one of the country’s largest dairy processing plants.

Missouri is among the top five states in the country for its production of beef cattle, hogs and turkeys.

Missouri is one of the top 10 states in the country for the production of soybeans, corn, cotton, hay and watermelons.

Missouri dairy cows produce more than 150 million gallons of milk each year.

Missouri is one of the leading hat producers in the nation. Baseball caps and cowboy hats are two examples of the hats made here.

The Boeing Defense, Space and Security department supports, designs, produces and modifies military aircraft, satellite systems and more. Boeing is the largest aerospace company in the world.

Kansas City is the home of the world’s largest greeting-card company, Hallmark Cards. Our state produces more than 2.5 billion greeting cards per year.

Kansas City is the second most important grain-milling center in the United States.

Missouri manufactures beer, clothing, shoes, cement, food products, electrical equipment, books and medicine.

title: Sikeston, Missouri
text:
Sikeston is located in the southeastern corner of our state and it is part of both southern Scott County and northern New Madrid County. Sikeston is a great farming region. Wheat, corn, soybeans, cotton, milo, potatoes, watermelon, rice, sunflowers and peaches are all raised for sale in and around Sikeston.

In the winter months, Sikeston is home to some of the nation's largest farm auctions and equipment sales. Farmers come from miles around to bid on livestock and equipment to take home to improve their farms.

Sikeston also has many great outdoor spots. The General Watkins Conservation Area contains 1,037 acres of hardwood forests and offers something for everyone who likes to get back to nature. Fishing, camping, hunting, sightseeing and bird watching are all available in the area.

Sikeston is also the home of the New Madrid Historical Museum. Here you can view displays about various wars, ancient American Indian artifacts and other items of interest concerning the history of the area.

Historic Downtown Sikeston is also a great place to visit. Many old buildings have been restored, and the area helps you to imagine what life was like here long ago. The highlights of the area are the American Legion Park and the old Sikeston Train Depot. Each August, Sikeston holds its annual Jaycee Bootheel Rodeo with famous riders and rodeo stock from all over the United States. This event turns into a real celebration that people plan for all year. You may want to try it yourself.

title: How much milk does a dairy cow produce?
text:
An average milk cow produces nearly 200,000 glasses of milk in her lifetime. She weighs in at about 1,400 pounds and drinks between 25 and 50 gallons of water each day. That's nearly a bathtub full.

What happens to all of this milk?

About 40 percent of the milk produced in the United States is sold as drinking milk. Another 17 percent is made into butter. The rest is used to make cheese, ice cream, yogurt, sour cream and other dairy products.

title: Corn
text:
One of Missouri’s top crops is corn. Our state produces more than 150 million bushels of corn a year.

The name "corn" is given to the largest cereal crop of any region. In England, "corn" means wheat. In Scotland and Ireland, "corn" means oats. In the United States, "corn" means American Indian corn, or maize. Most of the corn grown in the United States is grown in the Corn Belt, which includes the states of Missouri, Indiana, Illinois, Ohio, Kansas, Iowa and Nebraska.

More than half of the corn grown in the Unites States each year is grown for animal feed. The rest of the corn is used as a vegetable for humans, either canned, frozen or fresh. It is also ground into cornmeal or corn flour and made into corn bread, tortillas and breakfast cereals. Corn is used for hominy, mush and grits. The corn kernel can also be pressed to get starch, sugar and oil.

title: What is Hydraulic Fracturing?
text:
People in the states of Colorado, Texas and Ohio have been feeling small earthquakes over the past few years. Some people are saying those quakes are the result of hydraulic fracturing.

Hydraulic fracturing is a way to get natural gas from underground rock formations up to the surface. We use natural gas for energy in homes and businesses. Water and chemicals are pumped underground through long, deep wells. The liquid causes fractures, or cracks, in the rock. Natural gas escapes through the cracks and gets piped up to the surface. Over 200,000 new wells have been drilled in the U.S. during the last 10 years.

The National Research Council released a report in 2012 that said hydraulic fracturing does not seem to be the culprit, but other human activity might be the problem. Some groups believe that it’s the wastewater (leftover water and chemicals), not the fracturing itself that is causing the earthquakes. The wastewater from the process is either treated at a facility or sent deep underground. When the liquid is injected back into the ground, it can make the tectonic plates slip and rub against each other, causing earthquakes.

The companies doing the drilling say that they are following safety regulations and protecting their workers, the residents and the environment. Companies have been injecting waste liquids into the ground since the 1930s, and only recently has there been an increase in earthquakes. We will certainly be hearing more about hydraulic fracturing in the years to come.

title: Native American Dream Catcher
text:
American Indians from the Northeast believe that good and bad dreams float around at night. They make a dream catcher to hang above the bed to entangle the bad dreams and allow the good dreams to float through the web, down the feather and onto the sleeping person.

Materials

Paper plate

Masking tape

Yarn

Feather

Scissors

Hole punch

Macaroni

Directions

1. Start with a nine-inch paper plate. Cut out the center of the plate to the outer ring.

2. Punch about 16 holes around the ring (using a paper punch).

3. Wrap masking tape around one end of a piece of yarn. Poke the yarn into the top hole and pull through, leaving about three inches at the end.

4. Begin creating a web by crisscrossing the yarn to fill up all the holes around the ring. Leave the center of the web open.

5. End by bringing the taped yarn end to the top hole and tying to the other end.

6. Cut a piece of yarn about eight inches long. Loop it through the bottom hole and even the ends. Pass macaroni beads up the yarn and slip a feather into the beads. Tie the ends of the yarn to the feather and knot the ends of the yarn. Hang over your bed. Sweet dreams!

title: Good Handwriting
text:
It takes some time to develop good handwriting, but it’s well worth the effort.

Have you ever gotten a test back and lost points because of messiness? Does your teacher have problems reading what you’ve written? Bad handwriting can lead to these situations. If no one can read your brilliant answer on the test, then it won’t help you get a good score. Most people think that bad handwriting means a lack in organizational skills. If it’s difficult to read, people won’t take the time to decipher the handwriting.

Developing good handwriting takes patience and diligence. It takes a lot of practice to get those perfect letters. Here are some tips to get you started.

It’s okay if you write slowly in the beginning. Focus on writing that can be read easily. Then move on to how fast you can write legibly.

Take some time each day to practice writing out letters. The more you practice, the better your handwriting will become.

Practice in one notebook so you can compare how well you are doing.

Choose a pen or pencil that you like and gives you the best grip. You may want to try out different pens or pencils to find the one just for you.

Good handwriting is a needed skill in this world. It’s needed when you take a test or write a paper in class. You’ll need it to write thank-you cards or to fill out invitations. And when you’re older, you’ll need it to fill out job applications. In the end, good handwriting will help people understand what you’ve written. And that’s the most important part.

title: Recreation in Missouri
text:
Branson is "The Country Music Capital of the Universe." Do you enjoy country music? Do you ever wish that you could see some real, live country music stars in person? If you like country music, you are lucky to live in the state that claims the city of Branson - the country music capital of the universe.

Branson is located in the Ozark country of southern Missouri. When it was first founded in 1903, no one thought of the town as a music center. Those who founded Branson pictured it as a thriving city that would send logs, lumber and manufactured goods by train to cities all over the United States. Within just a few years, however, the residents of Branson began to see that the town was better suited for a resort town, or a town that catered to tourists (people who travel for pleasure) and people looking for some recreation.

Because the town of Branson was located in such a beautiful spot with lakes and lush forests nearby, the town started making itself attractive to tourists who came to enjoy the scenery. Branson built an ice plant, a soft-drink bottling plant, a candy factory and an ice cream factory near the waterfront. Hobart McQuarter built Branson's first vacation cabins, called the Sammy Lane Resort, and the tourists began arriving.

Lake Taneycomo soon became a popular vacation spot, and Branson made sure that visitors had plenty to do while they were there. Branson offered boat races, street fairs, parades and community picnics to go along with the natural beauties of the lake and its surrounding hills. Table Rock Dam was built in 1959, creating another recreation area for tourists to enjoy. By 1960, the Branson area had become well known as a great vacation spot.

When a new highway was completed in the mid-1970s, making it easier than ever for tourists to get to Branson, there were only about five music shows here. The Baldknobbers, a musical comedy production, was Branson's first music show. The Baldknobbers, founded by Bill and Jim Mabe, along with their brothers Lyle and Bob, first entertained fishermen from Lake Taneycomo with their homemade musical instruments and their hilarious comedy routines.

In the 1980s, country music star Roy Clark discovered Branson and decided to bring a country music show of his own to the Missouri tourist town. Clark was unhappy because country music ticket prices were becoming so expensive that ordinary people couldn't afford to go to a show. He decided to build his own theater in Branson and charge reasonable prices so average people could come and enjoy live country music.

Soon after Roy Clark completed his theater, other country music stars began to build their own theaters in Branson. Stars such as Boxcar Willie, Glen Campbell, Mel Tillis, Jim Stafford, Mickey Gilley and Charley Pride all opened their own theaters, and by 1994, the town of Branson was home to about 50 music theaters. This is especially amazing when you realize that the population of Branson was only about 3,000 people. Other country music stars came to perform here as well, and Branson began attracting visitors from far and wide.

People now come from all over the world to enjoy some of the best country music anywhere in a setting where the stars really appreciate their fans. Branson is now one of the most popular recreation spots in Missouri and is known as "the country music capital of the universe."

title: Critical Analysis and Rumination: President Truman and The Atomic Bomb Decision
text:
rumination (noun): the act of giving serious thought and consideration to something

Adolf Hitler was defeated in May 1945 after years of war in Europe, and American troops would be coming home - wouldn't they? Victory in Europe meant that some U.S. soldiers would be returning home. Others would go to the Pacific to face Japanese armies. Scientists in the U.S. had made a weapon that could certainly end the war with Japan, but it was so powerful that tens of thousands of people would be killed, including civilians (citizens not in the military). President Harry Truman had a decision to make that would greatly affect the world. What would the commander in chief do?

In the years leading up to President Truman's decision, the Japanese had been a brutal enemy. They had killed thousands of Americans at sea and on Pacific islands, including the surprise attack on Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The president wondered how many more lives would be lost if we tried to end the war without the atomic bomb. What would happen if another country improved the weapon and used the bomb before we did? Would they use it on us?

President Truman tried several times without success to work out surrender with Japan. He then ordered atomic bombs to be dropped on the cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945. Within a week of the second attack, Japan did surrender, which put an end to World War II. Historians estimate that between 150,000 and 240,000 Japanese were killed from effects of the two bombings. They also estimate that thousands of American lives were saved. Do you think President Truman made the right decision?

title: Recreation in Missouri
text:
What do you do after a hard day at school? What do your parents do to relax after a long day at work? On the weekends, does your family do something special for fun? During the summer or on holidays, does your family go on vacation? The things we do to relax and refresh our minds and bodies are called recreation. Recreation is what we do when we play. Missouri is a great place to live if you like to play.

State Parks

Missouri has more than 75 state parks and historic sites (places where important events in our past took place). A state park is land set aside by the state government to be protected for all people to enjoy. Have you ever visited one of Missouri's state parks to enjoy nature? People from our state and from all over the world come to Missouri to explore caves, watch birds and wildlife and view the beautiful scenery.

Hunting and Fishing

Missourians and tourists from all over enjoy hunting and fishing in Missouri's hills, forests and lakes. The Missouri Department of Conservation lists more than 23 streams, 83 rivers and four trout parks where fishermen can fish for black bass, catfish, crappie, muskellunge, rainbow and brown trout, walleye and white bass. Hunters love to come to Missouri for many types of large and small game, but Missouri is especially famous for its white-tail deer and its wild turkeys. Nearly 3 million acres of state and federal lands are open to hunting in Missouri. (Game is wild animals hunted for food and sport.)

Historic Sites

Our state offers many interesting historical sites to visit. Many people who are interested in the history of our nation visit important frontier sites, such as the National Frontier Trails center in Independence. There is also the Patee House Museum, which houses the original Pony Express in St. Joseph. People come to St. Louis to see the famous Gateway Arch, celebrating Missouri's title as Gateway to the West.

People also love to visit Missouri's Civil War sites and museums, especially the spot where the Battle of Wilson's Creek took place and General Sweeny's Museum of Civil War History.

Museums

Missouri's museums are also popular recreation spots. Our state has many museums with displays about ancient American Indians, modern art, famous citizens of Missouri, science, history and just about anything else you might be interested in. Science City in Kansas City and the St. Louis Science Center in St. Louis are both popular science museums in our state. There is even an insect museum at the University of Missouri, called the Wilbur R. Enns Entomology Museum.

There are many art museums in Missouri, including the St. Louis Art Museum and the Museum of Art and Archaeology at the University of Missouri. Many people visit the Harry S. Truman Library and Museum each year, as well as the Molly Brown Museum in Hannibal. The "Unsinkable" Molly Brown was a passenger on the Titanic who survived the experience. Another popular museum is Ripley's Believe It or Not in Branson, where they have many strange and unusual displays, including a two-headed calf and the world's largest ball of twine.

Sports

Sports are an important form of recreation in Missouri. Whether you play sports, watch them, or do both, our state has plenty of activities to go around. Many people in Missouri enjoy playing all types of sports. We play basketball, baseball, soccer, football and hockey. We also enjoy rodeo and just about any other sport you can think of. Missouri has many professional sports teams that provide entertainment nearly year round. Missouri's professional baseball teams include the St. Louis Cardinals and the Kansas City Royals. We also have two professional football teams, the Kansas City Chiefs and the St. Louis Rams. The St. Louis Blues are Missouri's popular ice hockey team. Kansas City also sponsors the American Royal Rodeo each year.

Festivals, Theme Parks and Holiday Celebrations

Missourians also enjoy celebrating holidays and remembering their heritage with special celebrations. Hundreds of festivals are held throughout the year in nearly every town and city in Missouri.

Celebrations such as Tom Sawyer Days in Hannibal, Pony Express Days in St. Joseph, the Scott Joplin Ragtime Festival in Sedalia, Sheep Shearing Days in Sibley and Bastille Days in Ste. Genevieve are just a few examples of the festivals held throughout our state.

Many of you have probably enjoyed one of Missouri's exciting theme parks. Each year, thousands of people visit amusement parks such as the Worlds of Fun park in Kansas City, Six Flags over Mid-America in St. Louis and Silver Dollar City in Branson.

title: Lake of the Ozarks
text:
Lake of the Ozarks is one of Missouri's favorite vacation spots. It is located in central Missouri, about 180 miles from St. Louis, 170 miles from Kansas City and 90 miles from Springfield. Lake of the Ozarks was created when Bagnell Dam was built in 1932. The lake is more than 90 miles long and has 1,375 miles of shoreline. This is more shoreline than the entire state of California. There are thousands of coves along the shoreline where visitors enjoy the peaceful beauty of the lake. Boating, swimming, water sports and fishing are also part of the fun at Lake of the Ozarks.

There are many events scheduled throughout the year at Lake of the Ozarks. There is a St. Patrick's Day parade on the water, along with a St. Patrick's Day Festival. In May, the Magic Dragon Car Show is held here, and in the summer, the U.S.A. Power Boat Championship Races come to the lake. There are also an annual Mountain Man Festival, the Old Tyme Apple Festival, the Eldon Turkey Festival in November and the Lake Area Festival of Lights at Christmas.

From May to September each year, the highways leading to Lake of the Ozarks are crowded with cars, trucks, campers, boats and trailers on their way to some of the best recreation around. Many people come for the weekend and others for a week or more. Lake of the Ozarks is a great place to go to play.

title: Why is Missouri called the "Show Me" state?
text: Missouri is called the "Show Me" state because Missourians have always wanted to be given a logical explanation before they will accept an idea. In other words, Missourians don't believe everything they hear unless they see some proof that what they are hearing is true. In 1899, Missouri Representative Willard Duncan Vandiver said, "I'm from Missouri, and you've got to show me!" Missouri has taken this slogan as its own, and our state is now proudly known as the "Show Me" state.

title: Largemouth Bass
text:
The largemouth bass is a member of the sunfish family. It is also one of the black basses, which is a group that includes the largemouth, smallmouth and spotted basses.

The largemouth bass is easy to recognize. It has a dark horizontal stripe down its middle, a spiny dorsal fin, and a very large mouth that extends past its eye. The largemouth bass is between 10 and 20 inches long and weighs anywhere from five to eight pounds. Largemouth bass are the largest of the sunfish.

The largemouth bass is found throughout Missouri in slow-moving or standing water. It does not normally like to live in dirty or muddy water. It likes to hide in the water beneath trees, logs, weeds and stumps.

The largemouth bass spawns from mid-April to the end of May, and its eggs hatch in less than a week. The male largemouth bass watches the young until they are ready to venture out on their own.

The largemouth bass is a very popular game fish in Missouri. Most fishermen consider themselves lucky to catch a Missouri largemouth bass.

title: How Do I Take a Test?
text:
Do you get sweaty palms and butterflies in your stomach over the idea of taking a test? That happens to everyone at one time or another. Did you know test anxiety comes from a lack of self-confidence? How can you improve your self-confidence and improve your test-taking skills? The best way is to know the material very well. But here are some other important ideas that may help you:

Preview the test. What does it cover? How long is it?

Plan your time. Decide how much time you can spend on each section. Keep track of the time as you take the test.

Follow directions. Read all the directions and listen carefully to any directions read aloud.

Read the questions carefully. Look for keywords such as “when,” “where,” “why,” “different from,” “same as,” “before” and “after.”

Don’t get stuck on one question. If you can’t think of an answer, skip it and return to it later when you have finished the rest of the test.

Check your work. If you have time left after you finish the test, go back and double-check your work.

Use this list while taking this week’s Studies Weekly quiz. Practice good test-taking skills. You may want to use this list for the next few weeks until you have mastered the skills.

title: Let's Write
text: Imagine you are a travel agent in our state. Write about a place you would recommend that tourists see. Why do you think it’s a nice place to visit? What kinds of things will visitors learn at this place?

title: Famous People of Missouri
text:
Missouri has given the world many interesting and amazing people. From artists like Thomas Hart Benton, musicians such as Scott Joplin, entertainers like Ginger Rogers and athletes such as Casey Stengel, Missourians have made their mark in the world.

One of Missouri's most-well-known and respected citizens served as our country's 33rd president. Harry S. Truman, known as "the man from Missouri," brought honor to our great state as the most powerful man in the free world, the president of the United States.

Harry Truman was born in Lamar, Missouri, in 1884. His family moved to Independence when he was quite young, and Harry was raised there. As a child, Harry loved to read, and by the time he was 13 years old, he had read every book in the Independence library. His favorite kinds of books were biographies (written stories of people's lives). He loved to read about the lives of great men and women. He also loved to read books about history. When he became president later on in his life, he said that reading about history had helped him know how to lead our country.

When Harry grew up, he joined the Missouri National Guard. Soon after, the United States entered World War I, and Harry became an officer in the guard. He was a good leader, and his men liked him very much.

After the war, Harry opened a clothing store, but when the business failed, he decided to try to build a career in politics. He was elected to the Jackson County court and became popular as a hard worker and an honest man. Later on, Harry ran for the U. S. Senate and was elected as a senator representing his home state of Missouri.

Harry earned the reputation of being an honest politician and a good leader. (A reputation is what people think of a person; what he or she is known for.) Because of this, President Franklin D. Roosevelt asked him to run for vice president of the United States in 1944. Roosevelt and Truman were elected to the White House, and in 1945, when President Roosevelt died suddenly, Harry Truman became the 33rd president of the United States. Harry was not expecting this, and with the world at war (World War II), he said that he "felt like the moon, the stars, and all the planets had fallen on me."

Although he wasn't expecting to have to lead the United States out of war, Harry Truman was more than able to do so. He helped to start the United Nations and also started many new programs to help countries that had been devastated by the war. He also tried to improve life for all Americans.

After he had served his term as president, Harry Truman decided to come home to Missouri. He retired to Independence, the town where he grew up, and enjoyed his final years there. He died at the age of 88 on Dec. 26, 1972. Independence is now the site of the Harry S. Truman Library, a museum, and the old Truman home.

(Missourians celebrate Truman Day on May 8 (his birthday) each year.)

title: Famous Missourians
text:
There are many famous people from the state of Missouri. The following are just a few successful Missourians of whom you may have heard.

James Cash (J. C.) Penney (1875-1971)

Born in Caldwell County, Missouri, in 1875, James Cash Penney is the founder and owner of the J. C. Penney Company and was one of the most successful chain store operators in America. A chain store is a store that has more than one branch throughout an area.

Walter Cronkite (1916-2009)

Born in St. Joseph, he became one of America’s most famous journalists (writes down or reads the news). He is most recognized for his many years as the anchorman for “The CBS Evening News.”

Ginger Rogers (1911-1995)

Born in Independence, she was an Academy Award-winning dancer and actress. Her real name was Virginia McMath, and she began doing commercials when she was only 5 years old. You may have seen her dance in classic movies with her most famous partner, Fred Astaire.

Dick Van Dyke (1925-present)

He was born in 1925 in West Plains, Missouri. He has been in show business since the 1950s and was on the radio, on television and in the movies. You may have seen him in the children’s movie “Mary Poppins.” He also had a popular TV show named after him in the 1960s. Reruns of this show are still popular today. His most recent television series was “Diagnosis Murder.”

Harry S. Truman (1884-1972)

He was born in Lamar, but soon moved to Independence with his family. He fought as an officer in World War I and went on to become a Jackson County official, a U.S. senator, the vice president of the United States and finally, our 33rd president from 1945 to 1953.

George Washington Carver (1860-1943)

Born in Diamond Grove, Missouri, to slave parents, he later went on to become a famous scientist who did research into crop rotation methods for farmers. He developed more than 325 uses for peanuts, from printer’s ink to cooking oil.

Langston Hughes (1902-1967)

He was born in Joplin, Missouri. He was a famous poet and writer who wrote about what it was like to be a black person in America. His most famous works are “The Golden Piece” and “Harlem.”

Mark Twain (1835-1910)

His real name was Samuel Langhorn Clemens, and he was born in Florida, near Hannibal, Missouri. He took his pen name, Mark Twain, from his work as a riverboat pilot on the Mississippi River. He is a well-known author and humorist. His most famous works are “The Adventures of Tom Sawyer” and “The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn.” (A pen name is a name that a person uses when writing.)

Laura Ingalls Wilder (1867-1957)

She was actually born in Pepin, Wisconsin, but she moved to Mansfield, Missouri, in 1894. It was here at her home, called Rocky Ridge Farm, that she wrote the famous Little House books about her childhood. Her books were later made into a television series called “Little House on the Prairie.” Her books are more popular now than ever before.

Walt Disney (1901-1966)

Born in Chicago, Walt Disney grew up in Marceline and Kansas City, Missouri. He is most famous for creating Mickey Mouse and Donald Duck. He also created full-length cartoon movies, such as “Snow White,” and brought us Disneyland.

title: Mansfield
text:
Mansfield is located in south-central Missouri in Wright County. It is about 70 miles northeast of Branson and 50 miles east of Springfield.

Each year, thousands of visitors come to Mansfield to see Rocky Ridge Farm, the home of Laura Ingalls Wilder, her husband Almanzo, and their daughter Rose.

Mansfield, known as "The Land of the Apple," caught the eye of the Wilders as a comfortable and fertile spot to spend the rest of their lives, and that is exactly what they did. Rocky Ridge Farm eventually became a successful dairy and fruit farm of more than 200 acres.

It was at Rocky Ridge Farm that Laura Ingalls Wilder first began writing, and she spent many years writing the Little House books here at her home in Mansfield.

Visitors to Mansfield today can tour The Laura Ingalls Wilder Historic Home and Museum. Here you can see the rooms where Laura lived and wrote her famous books. You can also see items such as Pa's famous fiddle and Ma's treasured sewing machine.

If you are a true fan of Laura Ingalls Wilder, you may want to plan to visit Mansfield on the second Saturday in September, when the Laura Ingalls Wilder Festival is held.

There is food, entertainment, music and even the arrival of an authentic (genuine, real) wagon train to remind visitors of Laura's pioneer past. You can also plan to attend a musical pageant called "Little House Memories" while you are here. The festival also includes a craft show, pony rides, storytelling and a parade.

title: What's the correct pronunciation of Missouri?
text: Missourians have been arguing about how to pronounce the name of our state since the 1800s, and they will probably continue to argue about it for many years to come. The eastern half of our state tends to pronounce it "Missouree," and the western half tends to say "Missourah." The majority of Missourians younger than 45 years say "Missouree," but older Missourians still tend to disagree over how to pronounce the name of our state. Do YOU live in Missouree or Missourah?

title: Turkey
text:
The turkey is a large game and poultry bird that is related to the grouse and the pheasant. Some people believe the turkey got its name from the "turk turk" sound it makes when it is startled.

The wild turkey makes its home in Missouri, and it is a popular game bird here. Turkeys raised in captivity cannot fly, but wild turkeys can fly for short distances at speeds of up to 55 miles per hour.

Turkeys have a great sense of hearing, an excellent sense of taste, great vision and a terrible sense of smell. They also have a loud voice! A turkey's gobble can be heard up to a mile away. Turkeys eat insects, seeds, plants and fruit.

More than 45 million turkeys are cooked and eaten in the United States each year at Thanksgiving. The turkey industry makes about $4.7 billion per year raising and selling turkeys.

At one time, Benjamin Franklin suggested that the turkey, not the bald eagle, be considered the national symbol of our country. He said that although the turkey was "vain and silly," it was better than the "cowardly" bald eagle.

title: A Census Full of Treasure
text:
On April 2, 2012, the government released the 1940 census. A census is a count of all the people in the United States, and it is done every 10 years. It also gives other information about citizens’ jobs, income, birthplace and education level. The government only releases a census’ records to the public after 72 years have passed. The 1940 census was the first one done after the Great Depression and World War I. It shows how these events caused people to move around and where immigrants went. You can find interesting facts about family members and famous people. For example, the future President Ronald Reagan paid $135 in rent in 1940!

The 1940 census was the last time census takers went door-to-door to personally interview people and write down the information. For the 1950 census the government started using census questionnaires sent through the mail.

The release of the 1940 census data is different from past years. This information was made digital and released through the Internet. There are more than 3.8 million pages of data in this census. Genealogists, or people who study family backgrounds, use this information to trace family history. Researchers, like historians, often use the census as a primary source of information.

So, was this release a success? Well, so many people tried to get the information on its first day of release that the server crashed! If you would like to learn more about your family history you can go to the 1940 census site at: 1940census.archives.gov

title: Problem solving with charts.
text:
Using charts can be useful in helping you decide on how to solve a problem. Below is an example of using a chart to help solve the issue of children using the internet.

Identify Facts
(Make a list.)

Some parents do not let their kids use the Internet unsupervised while others do allow it. Some parents trust their kids to make the right decisions while online.
The kids who are allowed to use the Internet enjoy the freedom.
The kids who are not allowed to use the Internet do not like the extra rules.

Examine Both Sides
(Think of the good and bad points of each opinion.)

Pros of being allowed to use the Internet unsupervised:
Children can email classmates and discuss assignments.
They are free to express themselves without worrying about what their parents think.
The kids have a chance to prove they can be responsible and make good choices.
Cons on being allowed to use the Internet unsupervised:
The kids might find something inappropriate or talk to strangers online.
They won’t have anything to look forward to if they get a lot of freedom at a young age.
The parents won’t necessarily know what the children are doing on the computer.

Make a Decision Using Ethics and Values

Liberty is the freedom to follow your beliefs. It allows others to follow their own beliefs. Emily and Ashley were still great friends, and their parents were free to have their own opinions about how to raise their children.
Diversity means that we in America respect and appreciate everyone. We accept everyone’s different ideas, cultures and backgrounds. Both Ashley’s and Emily’s parents have different beliefs about parenting. They should still be respected for their different ideas.
Equality means that people have the right to be treated equally and fairly. However, that does not mean that every family follows the same rules. Ashley’s and Emily’s parents treated the girls fairly, but they did not have the same rules. Ashley and her brother did have the same rules and were treated equally.

Now use this example to fill out your chart.

title: Taking Notes in Class
text:
Learning how to take good notes in class is very important.

Taking notes in class can be difficult. Sometimes it’s hard to concentrate and you can miss some information. Or you can’t read what you wrote. Other times, you’re not sure what information to write down. It’s important to learn how to take good notes. Without notes, taking tests is much harder! Here are some ways to take good notes in class.

Be ready. You don’t always need to have a pen in hand, but have your notebook open to a clean page. And have a pen or pencil nearby. When the teacher enters the room, you’re ready to begin.

Put the date and topic on top of the page. Knowing when you took the notes will help you study for tests. You can quickly flip through the pages and find the topic.

Don’t waste time writing what you already know. Notes help you remember what you learned in class. If you’re sure you know something, then don’t write it down. Let’s say you know that George Washington was the first U.S. president. You don’t need to write it down. Instead, you can focus on his birth date, where he lived and what he did.

Make lists. Lists are easy to recognize and read. They organize the information. If you can make a list, you’ll likely remember the information later.

Remember, note taking will improve your learning. But your notes won’t make much sense if your eyes are always glued to the paper. Take some time to really listen to your teacher. Stop every now and then to listen and to watch your teacher. Write down the examples that are written on the board. By doing this, you’re sure to have success in class!

title: Let's Write
text: Write about a legendary person who you feel has made a big impact on your life or our state. The person may be real or make believe. Explain why this person is so important and the things he or she has accomplished. How has your life been helped by this person?

title: Mike Fink - American Folk Hero
text:
Mike Fink is one of the Mississippi Valley's famous American folk heroes. A folk hero is someone who may or may not be a real person. A folk hero is famous because he or she is able to do things that require super-human strength, intelligence or other remarkable abilities. Mike Fink was a real person who was born in the 1770s in Fort Pitt (now Pittsburgh), Pennsylvania. He was a larger-than-life keel-boat captain who piloted boats on the Mississippi and Ohio rivers. He was famous for his drinking, fighting, joking and shooting. Because he often had adventures and then bragged about them, adding a little to them each time, Mike Fink's abilities became exaggerated (stretched the truth), and he became a folk hero.

There are many stories told about the strength and abilities of Mr. Mike Fink. Here are two that you might enjoy.

Mike Fink and the American Indians

Mike Fink once happened to see a band of roving American Indians sneak into a cave. This cave was cool and protected, so a poor widow used it as a "refrigerator" to keep her food fresh. The widow used the cave as a storage place for her milk, cream, meat and cheese, so when Mike saw the American Indians slip into the cave, he knew that they were up to no good. They were planning to steal all of the food they could carry.

Mike watched the thieves until they were all safely inside. He then fastened the door shut on the outside, and the American Indians were trapped. Once Mike trapped them in a cave, he tricked them, chasing them away. Mike thought the trick worthy of a hearty laugh and figured that the American Indians would not be sneaking around the widow's cave again anytime soon.

Mike Fink Catches a Moose

It was late fall when Mike Fink and some of his friends went on a moose hunt. Moose hunting was often dangerous, as the huge animals were likely to charge a hunter if cornered and trample him to death. Mike set out far ahead of his hunting companions, and when darkness fell, Mike was nowhere to be found. Mike's fellow hunters lit signal fires, hoping to direct him back to camp, but still saw no sign of Mike.

Suddenly, the hunters heard the cry of a man, accompanied by the wild snorting of a moose. They quickly climbed to the top of a cliff and looked over the edge. There they saw below them Mike Fink clinging to the horns of an enormous moose that was swimming through the river toward a distant island.
