Mike held on with amazing strength, and once the animal reached the shore, the real battle began. The moose shook Mike from his horns and immediately tried to dash him to bits. Mike had his gun and his pistols, but they were wet and would not fire.

Mike quickly used the butt of his rifle to strike the moose, but on his second swing, the rifle shattered when it struck the moose's heavy antlers. The moose swung his gigantic head at Mike, but Mike ducked just in time and pulled out his long hunting knife. He plunged the knife into the moose's neck, and the battle was over. Mike Fink had done what no other man could do: wrestle and kill a moose without the use of a single bullet.

*A moose is a large, hoofed mammal of the deer family.

title: Momo, The Missouri Monster
text:
If you have ever been camping, you have probably listened to someone tell scary stories around the campfire after dark. Did you know that Missouri has its own spooky tale that might give you goose bumps? It's the legend of Momo, or the Missouri Monster. Those who claim to have seen Momo say that he has glowing, orange eyes, a pumpkin-shaped head, three-fingered hands and leaves three-toed footprints. Momo is also covered with hair, smells bad and is between six and nine feet tall. He has supposedly been spotted in the woods throughout Pike and St. Charles counties, but he has only been spotted at night. Most of the Momo sightings occurred during the 1970s, but there are still sightings today.

During the 1970s, the story of Momo became so popular that the town of Louisiana, Missouri, where the most famous sightings of Momo took place, started holding an annual festival called "Momo Days." A disc jockey at a Bowling Green radio station wrote and recorded a song about the beast called "Momo the Missouri Monster." The Six Flags amusement park just outside of St. Louis even named one of its rides after the monster.

Legends of similar creatures are told all over the world. You may have heard stories about Bigfoot from the Pacific Northwest or Sasquatch from Canada. If you have seen Rudolph, the Red-Nosed Reindeer, you have heard of the Abominable Snowman, or Yeti, as it is called in Tibet.

Many people believe that Momo is just a product of someone's overactive imagination, but others swear he is real. What do you think? Do you believe in Momo?

title: Legends and Superstitions
text:
Missouri has a rich history made up of interesting people and amazing events. Over the years, people have preserved this history by telling the stories of our past to each other and passing our heritage along. Some stories that we pass along are factual, which means that the people in the stories are real and the events are described just as they really happened. Other stories that have been passed along have been exaggerated, or added to, as each person has told the story. By the time a story has been passed along over many years, the final result might not be anything like a true, factual story. These types of stories are known as legends or folk tales.

Legends

Legends are popular stories handed down from earlier times. They are often about people who have actually lived and places that actually exist. The stories about these people and places have just been exaggerated, or added to, until they are nearly unbelievable. Other times, legends are told about people or places that may not exist at all.

Many tales are told about a real, live man who became a legend in the Mississippi River Valley and throughout the entire United States. Davy Crockett was born in eastern Tennessee in 1786. He spent much of his life exploring the wilderness to the West and even served in the U.S. House of Representatives. He became famous not only for the things he actually did, but also for the things that people SAID he did. In the following story, see if you can decide which things could have happened and which must only be a part of the legend of Davy Crockett.

Davy Crockett Teaches the Steamboat a Little Patriotism

One morning, Davy Crockett got up feeling very ornery and cantankerous. He decided to go over to the Mighty Mississippi to take a ride on one of the river's famous steamboats to cheer himself up. He brought his pet bear, Death Hug, along for the ride. Along the way, Davy and Death Hug met up with a well-known heroic sailor named Ben Hardin, and the three of them continued on to the Mississippi River. When they got to the gangplank to buy their tickets for the steamboat, the captain shook his head and said, "No bears allowed."

Well, this kind of attitude toward his best friend didn't set well with Davy, and he hollered in his loudest voice, "Maybe you ain't heard that this here is the United States of America, where every citizen, human or bear-like, has the right to ride in a steamboat!"

Davy Crockett's speech made no difference to the captain, and he refused to let the men board the ship with the bear along. Davy was so angry that he vowed to show the captain just what a couple of true American heroes and a bear could do.

Davy, Ben and Death Hug went into the forest nearby and cut down a tree. They made two 10-foot paddles, hollowed out the log like a canoe, and launched themselves into the Big Muddy.

The next thing the captain of the steamboat knew, along came the strangest water vessel he had ever seen. Davy and Ben were both paddling for all they were worth, puffing huge billows of smoke out of their lit pipes. The contraption passed the unpatriotic steamboat in a blur of smoke and motion, leaving the captain wondering what on Earth had happened. Davy Crockett crowed with joy, shouting, "Well, boys, I guess we taught that locomotive river town a little bit of patriotism. There's nothin' a steamboat can do that American brains and brawn-human or bear-like-can't do better."

(Patriotism is love of one's country.)

Superstitions

Superstitions are also part of our heritage in Missouri. In days gone by, many people used superstitions to explain things that they didn't understand. Superstitions cannot be proven true; in fact, most superstitions can be proven false, but people from the past often believed them anyway. Many people still believe certain superstitions to be true. How many superstitions have you heard of? Do you believe any of them?

title: New Madrid
text:
Have you ever wanted to visit an old Missouri river town? Would you like to see what things might have been like for the people who settled along the Mighty Mississippi more than 100 years ago? Visit New Madrid and step back in time to see what life might have been like on the river in days gone by.

New Madrid, Missouri, is located in the southeastern tip of our state, right in the bend of the Mississippi River. Trappers and businessmen settled in New Madrid to use the Mississippi River for their benefit.

Visitors to New Madrid today can stop at the Mississippi River Observation Deck to view eight miles of the greatest waterway in North America. The observation deck is built on a historic Civil War observation point.

You may also want to visit the Hunter-Dawson House while in New Madrid. This old mansion was built by William Washington Hunter in 1830 when he moved his business to New Madrid. A tour of the old building shows what life was like for the rich in the mid-1800s.

The New Madrid Historical Museum is also a place to get a feeling for life on the Mississippi River. The museum flies the five different flags that have flown over New Madrid throughout its history. The flags of Spain, France, the United States, the Missouri State Guard and the Confederacy all fly over the museum today to remind visitors that each of these flags once flew over New Madrid.

title: What is a “Ring-Tailed Roarer?”
text: A ring-tailed roarer was the frontier name for the folk heroes of the American West. Men like Davy Crockett, Daniel Boone and Mike Fink are some examples of ring-tailed roarers. They were said to be bigger, stronger and smarter than any other pioneer. They could "shoot straighter, fight harder and yell louder" than anyone else on the face of the Earth. Only America could give birth to a creature such as the ring-tailed roarer.

title: The White-Tailed Deer
text:
The white-tailed deer is one of Missouri's native mammals. Its scientific name is Odocoileus virginianus, and it is a member of the same family as the mule deer, the elk and the moose.

The white-tailed deer is about 3 to 3 and 1/2 feet tall at the shoulder. The male white-tailed deer, or buck, weighs up to 400 pounds, and the female, or doe, weighs up to 200 pounds. The buck has antlers, or branched horns, that he sheds once each year. This means that his antlers drop off and are re-grown later on.

White-tailed deer are usually shy and spend most of their days eating. They are herbivores, which means that they eat only plants. They especially enjoy eating grass, leaves, bark and acorns.

White-tailed deer babies, called fawns, are born each spring, usually in May or June. The deer often travel in herds, and the doe keeps her fawn with her while it is young.

title: Making Snowflakes
text:
Materials

Paper

Scissors

Pen or pencil to lightly sketch design on one side of snowflake

Directions

1. Fold the upper right corner down to meet the lower left corner.

2. Fold the upper left corner down to the right-hand edge of the paper.

3. Cut off the small area at the bottom and keep the folded triangle. (See illustration.)

4. Fold the right-hand corner of the triangle to cover the middle third of the triangle.

5. Fold the left-hand corner of the triangle to cover the same middle third of the triangle.

6. Cut off the two small triangles that form on the bottom. Keep the larger triangle for your snowflake. (See illustration.)

7. Sketch the design you’d like on one side of the snowflake. Use the below design as an idea, and then try some of your own. They’re fun.

8. Cut out the pattern you have just sketched.

9. Unfold the snowflake to see your pattern on all six sides.

Note: You may need to make a few trial snowflakes before you get it perfect. You do not want to completely separate the sides of your triangle, or your snowflake will fall apart.

title: Plagiarism
text:
Plagiarism is a long word and it’s hard to spell. But it’s very important you know and understand its meaning.

To plagiarize something is to steal another person’s writings, thoughts or inventions.

It means to take credit for that person’s ideas. This practice is dishonest, even if the writings have never been published. Another word for plagiarism is “copying.” In many schools, a student can be kicked out for plagiarizing. We should never steal another person’s ideas.

There are many ways to avoid plagiarism. Let’s look at some ideas you can use to become a writer who doesn’t plagiarize. By doing these things, you can always be confident in your work.

Paraphrase, or re-write in your own words. Read what several different writers say on the subject. Then write your version of what they’ve written.

Use quotations. It’s perfectly okay to state what another person has written on a subject. You just need to give credit to that person. Here’s an example: As Huckleberry Finn said to his buddy, Tom Sawyer, “. . . . .”

Your opinion. What you think about a subject is what really matters. Read about the subject first. Then put down on paper what you truly feel about it!

Your teachers really want you to succeed. If you worry your writing is not what you’d like it to be, ask your teacher for advice. You will never lose marks for asking a teacher questions.

title: Fun Facts
text: President Franklin Delano Roosevelt was related by either blood or marriage to 11 other U. S. Presidents. Those presidents were: John Adams, John Quincy Adams, Ulysses Grant, William Henry Harrison, Benjamin Harrison, James Madison, Theodore Roosevelt, William Taft, Zachary Taylor, Martin Van Buren and George Washington.

title: Welcome to North Dakota Studies Weekly!
text:
A new school year has begun, and you are about to set off on an exciting journey! Together, we’ll study where North Dakota fits in the region, nation, continent and the world. With Studies Weekly you will learn all about your state’s geography, try your hands at mapping and charting and get a feel for the land beneath your feet.

Once you learn about the land itself, you’ll focus on the people who first settled this place and called it home. Who were those people? Why did they come here, and how did they live? What did they do to turn North Dakota into the place we know and love today? By the end of the year, you will know the answers to these questions and many more.

You will also explore some other subjects that might hit a little closer to home. For example, how does your state get the things it needs? How does it make money? And, maybe even more importantly, how will YOU make (and spend) money?

Do you ever wonder how the government works or what it does to help you personally? We’ll answer those questions as well, along with others you haven’t even thought of yet!

How do you use North Dakota Studies Weekly?

Each magazine is divided into several sections that help make learning interesting and fun. The cover page will give you a headsup about what to expect from this week’s magazine, including clues about what you’ll find inside. You will also find a Connections article on the cover page of most issues. This story will be about something that connects us to the world. Often it will be about an important event or person in your community, state, nation or world. These articles will help us connect the past, present and future in interesting ways. Inside each issue of North Dakota Studies Weekly you’ll find the main lesson covering the topic of the week. Every week also includes several short articles that link to the lesson in some way, including articles about North Dakota wildlife, local citizens, amazing inventions and key character traits.

On the back of each issue, you’ll find all kinds of activities, including crossword puzzles, maps, charts, review questions, writing prompts and websites to visit. (Hang on to your weekly magazines to help with questions in review weeks!) There you have it, a summary of North Dakota Studies Weekly. Now that you know what it’s all about, let’s get started! Your journey through your state and its history is about to begin.

title: Are We Really in the Middle of It All?
text: In 1931, the United States Geological Survey determined that a spot near the city of Rugby, North Dakota, marked the official geographic center of North America. What does this mean? Well, the definition can get a little complicated, and people disagree on the exact location. To put it simply, Rugby marks the very middle of all of North America. When the people of Rugby realized they were in the middle of it all, so to speak, the town built a stone monument, printed postcards and invited tourists to visit. The stone monument marking the geographic center was later moved when the highway was widened, but no one seemed to mind. After all, what’s a few feet one way or another, as long as Rugby is still the center of the continent? If the 1931 definition of “geographic center” is used, the center of North America is really found about 16 miles to the southwest of Rugby, in the middle of a marsh. Since that isn’t the best place for tourists to take pictures, Rugby feels comfortable about keeping its claim to fame (even though the small town of Balta is a little closer to the spot). Have you ever wondered what it might be like to stand in the middle of the continent? Take a trip to Rugby and find out. Don’t forget your camera!

title: Where is North Dakota?
text:
This week, we’ll learn about North Dakota’s location in the United States. We’ll also learn more about maps, find out what they show and see what they can tell us about the great state of North Dakota!

All About Maps

Before we find out exactly where North Dakota is located, we need to learn a little about maps and what they can tell us. You probably already know that a map is a picture or drawing of a place that shows where things are. They usually have a title that tells what is shown on the map. Most maps also include symbols that help us understand and use the map. Symbols are not always easy to understand, so maps often include a box that shows the meaning of different symbols. This box is called a map legend, or key. A map legend might tell you that the capital city is marked with a star and that hospitals are each marked with a large blue H. A legend may show highways, airports, schools or national parks. Maps and their legends help us get a better idea of the shape, size and location of the areas that we will study. There are many different types of maps, but this week we will use both a physical map and a political map to learn more about North Dakota. Physical maps show the major landforms of an area. These may include lakes, rivers, deserts, mountains and forests. Political maps show the government boundaries of a city, state or nation. They may also show capital cities, roads and populations.

North Dakota — Physical Location and Features

North Dakota is in the middle of the North American continent. It is landlocked, meaning that it is not next to any oceans. Parts of eastern North Dakota are mostly flat, but there are areas with rolling hills. The western part of the state is marked by rocky hills and buttes (steep-sided hills with flat tops). Look at the physical map of North Dakota, and you will see that Lake Sakakawea is located in the central western half of our state. Lake Sakakawea is actually a reservoir (artificial lake) that formed when the Garrison Dam was built on the Missouri River. This physical map of North Dakota also shows Devils Lake, Long Lake, Lake Oahe, the Badlands and White Butte.

North Dakota — Political Location and Features

Look at the political map of North Dakota. What is different? Notice that North Dakota is located in the central northern (middle top) area of the United States. North Dakota forms part of the United States’ border with Canada. In fact, North Dakota’s northern neighbors are the Canadian provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Minnesota borders our state to the east, with South Dakota to the south and Montana to the west. The capital of North Dakota, Bismarck, is found just south of the center of the state. Bismarck is marked with a star on the map, as capital cities usually are. Notice that a compass rose can be found on both the physical and political maps. This addition can help you find different features on the maps by showing direction. Neither map tells everything there is to know about North Dakota, but both maps include features that make the state a great place to live!

title: The Compass Rose
text:
A very important part of every map is the compass rose. A compass rose is a drawing that often resembles a star, and it shows directions on a map. Compass roses are sometimes drawn to resemble a flower, which is where the name comes from. It first appeared on maps during the 14th century. A compass rose shows the cardinal directions. The cardinal directions are north, south, east and west. Compass roses may also show the intermediate directions. Intermediate directions fall between each cardinal direction, and they are northeast, northwest, southeast and southwest. Notice that both the physical and political maps of North Dakota found in this week’s lesson include a compass rose. Here’s your chance to find out how a compass rose can help you answer important questions when using a map. First, label the cardinal and intermediate directions on this compass rose. Then use the maps and compass rose to help you answer the following questions:

1. Which state is located directly west of North Dakota?

2. The province located to the northwest of Bismarck is ________.

3. To travel from Lake Sakakawea to Devils Lake, you would need to travel in which direction?

title: Bismarck
text:
Bismarck is one of the largest cities in North Dakota with a population of around 67,000 people. The city is located on the Missouri River in Burleigh County.

The first known people to live in the area were the Mandan Indians who settled there during the 16th century. By the early 1800s, the Mandan were almost completely wiped out. The smallpox virus, brought here by European settlers, killed almost all of them.

In 1872, the Northern Pacific Railway Company built a small town called Edwinton to serve as a stop for trains. The company soon renamed the town Bismarck in honor of Otto von Bismarck, the German Chancellor at the time. Northern Pacific hoped that Bismarck and other wealthy Germans would give money to the railroad. Chancellor Bismarck said “thank you,” but he didn’t donate any money. The name stuck anyway!

Bismarck became the capital of the Dakota Territory in 1883. When North Dakota became the 39th state in 1889, the city became a state capital. Bismarck’s first capitol building was completed in 1883. That building was destroyed by fire in 1930, and a new, modern-looking 19-story structure was built in 1934 to serve as the new capitol. The building is known as the “Skyscraper on the Prairie.” Other buildings have been added to the capitol’s grounds, but the original tower is still home to many government agencies, including the governor’s office. If you find yourself in Bismarck, you can take a tour of this grand old building, as well as the beautiful grounds that surround the area.

Another fun place to visit in Bismarck is the North Dakota Heritage Center. The Heritage Center is a museum full of dinosaur bones, artifacts from North Dakota’s first peoples and many other hands-on exhibits. The Dakota Zoo, the McDowell Dam Recreation Area and the hiking trails along the Missouri River are other Bismarck locations that will bring a smile to your face.

title: What Is a Map Scale?
text: A map scale is often part of the map legend. It helps us figure out distances. A map scale shows the relationship between real-life distances and the distances shown on the map. It makes it easy to figure out how far apart any two places are. For example, a map scale may show that one inch on the map is the same as 100 miles in actual distance. Measure the distance on a map with a ruler, and then multiply that number by the number of miles represented by one inch. You can find out how far it is to your next destination!

title: Bison or Buffalo?
text: You have probably heard the song “Home on the Range,” where the singer yearns for a home where the buffalo roam. Did you know that there were never any buffalo roaming the prairies of North Dakota—or any other Midwestern state? It may be hard to believe, but the animals that actually roamed the range are called bison, not buffalo! The animals look similar, but bison are found in North America. Buffalo are actually an entirely different species native to Asia and Africa. Buffalo and bison are about the same size, but buffalo have a shiny coat and long horns while bison have a shaggy coat and shorter horns. Even though the true name for the animals that once roamed the North Dakota plains is bison, most North Dakotans still refer to them as buffalo. After all, “bison” doesn’t sound as great in the song!

title: Out and About in North Dakota
text:
Let’s practice some map skills! Use the map on this page to answer the following questions:

1. If you were picnicking at Devils Lake, in which direction would you travel to reach Fargo?

2. About how many miles is it from Devils Lake to Fargo?

3. The Sheyenne National Grassland is located about how many miles from Little Missouri National Grassland?

4. The Little Missouri National Grassland is located to the ____________________________________________ of Devils Lake.

5. Which North Dakota lake is located south of both Lake Sakakawea and Devils Lake?

6. Which river empties into Lake Sakakawea?

title: Pack Your Bags!
text:
“Hey, everyone! My name is Jackson, and I’m a fourth grader, just like you. Social studies is my favorite subject in school because I love finding out how the past, present and future all connect. I especially love maps, geography and land formations, but I also like finding out how the government works and what it does with our money. I’ll be tagging along as you make your journey through North Dakota this year. Oh, and this is my friend Alana. She’ll be along for the ride as well!”

“Thanks, Jackson. I’m Alana and I love social studies, too. I like geography and maps, just like Jackson, but what I REALLY love is learning about the people and places that make things tick. I can’t wait to study the people who discovered, settled and shaped North Dakota into the amazing place it is today. This is going to be one exciting journey!”

“This week, we’ll begin with one of my favorite activities—a road trip!”

“That’s right, Jackson. We’ll head out for a journey across the United States to explore the country we call home. This is one huge piece of property, and you won’t believe how many types of geography join together to form one nation.”

“I can’t wait to start, Alana! You probably already know that the United States is found on the North American continent and that it extends from one ocean to the other. It also includes the states of Alaska and Hawaii. These states are separated from the rest of the nation physically, but they have some amazing physical features and landforms all their own.”

“We’ll pay a visit to each of the five U.S. regions to get a feel for what each one is like. We’ll climb mountains and hills, cross rivers and lakes, walk the Great Plains, observe geysers and volcanoes, peer down into canyons and gorges and even get acquainted with a hoodoo or two!”

“Hoodoo sounds a little spooky, Alana, but I’ve heard about those rock formations. Any way you look at it, this trip is shaping up to be one I’m sure we’ll never forget.”

“I’ve already started packing, Jackson. I’ve got my camera, toothbrush, hiking boots, swimsuit and plenty of sunscreen. Oh, and I have a brand new notebook with lots of room for recording our experiences.”

“Sounds good, Alana. My parents are letting me bring our tablet computer with all the latest maps and geography apps loaded and ready. Oh, and the most important thing? Plenty of snacks. Traveling makes me hungry!”

“Sounds like we’re ready. Here we go!”

title: Want a New Car? Just Hit ‘Print’!
text:
Your family is ready to buy a new car. Instead of shopping all over town for just the right one, imagine walking into the nearest car dealership, choosing the style, color and number of seats, and having your car printed out and ready to drive home a short time later. Wait a minute … printed out? Absolutely.

You may have heard of 3-D printers, which are special machines that can print 3-D plastic or metal shapes rather than flat pictures on paper. These amazing printers have been around since the 1980s, but in 2014 a 3-D-printed car was presented in Chicago. The car was produced at the International Manufacturing Technology Show using the same type of plastic pellets that are used to make Legos. It took 44 hours and $18,000 to print the 49 parts needed to assemble the 1,500-pound, battery-operated car.

Local Motors produced the car, called the Strati (Italian for “layers”), with the hope of selling the two-seater, 3-D-printed cars. The company’s goal is to build personalized, inexpensive cars for the public without wasting any materials. So when the time comes for you to buy a car, think about just hitting “Print”!

title: Exploring the United States
text:
Jackson and Alana are ready to help us explore part of the continent of North America, including our country’s boundaries and regions.

“Let’s look at the large chunk of land we call the United States. We’ll find out how the land is divided and what interesting physical features we can find here.”

“That’s a great idea, Jackson. We can use our map skills to help us along the way.”

“Of course! Alana, take a look at the map, and you’ll see that the United States extends from the Atlantic Ocean on the east all the way to the Pacific Ocean on the west — from ‘sea to shining sea’!”

“That’s true. The U.S. also borders Canada on the north and Mexico and the Gulf of Mexico on the south. The area we have just described is known as the Continental United States. Alaska and Hawaii are also part of the United States, but they are not directly connected to the rest of the country. The Pacific Ocean separates us from Hawaii, and the nation of Canada lies between Alaska and us.

“Yes, Alana, and you’ll also see on this map that the United States is divided into five separate regions. Regions are areas that share similar features, such as climate, geography and landforms.”

“The five regions of the United States are the Northeast, the Southeast, the Midwest, the Southwest and the West. Let’s take a quick tour of each region! As we visit each one, use the color code in the map legend to help locate the correct spot.”

Northeast Region

The Northeast Region includes the area where the Pilgrims first settled. The land here is mostly flat and rocky. Much of the soil is not good for farming. The winters are long and cold, and the summers are hot and humid. The region is home to many businesses and large cities, such as New York City.

If you visit the Northeast Region you can see Niagara Falls, a collection of three waterfalls located between Ontario, Canada, and the state of New York. Scientists estimate that about 45 million gallons of water pour over the falls every minute. Niagara Falls State Park is one of the oldest state parks in the country! Or, if you like long hikes, this region is also home to much of the Appalachian Trail. It’s a nearly 2,200-mile trail through the Appalachian Mountains and forests that stretches from Maine to Georgia, which is in the Southeast Region.

Southeast Region

If you head south from the Northeast Region, you’ll reach the Southeast Region. The climate here is cool and mild in the winter, but it is hot and humid in the summer. George Washington Carver lived in this region. He is the famous scientist and inventor who came up with many ways to use peanuts. You can still find acres of peanuts growing here, along with cotton, tobacco and citrus fruits. Look at the map, and you’ll see that the Florida Everglades are part of the Southeast Region. Everglades National Park covers more than 2,300 square miles. This is where alligators and crocodiles live together, side by side!

Midwest Region

The Midwest Region is mostly flat, and it has great farming soil. This area grows so much grain that it is sometimes called “America’s Breadbasket.” Here you’ll also find Mount Rushmore, one of our most famous national landmarks. Can you spell “Mississippi”? If so, you know how to spell the name of one of this region’s most famous rivers! The Great Lakes make up another major water source. The three largest Great Lakes are in the Midwest Region. The Badlands of North Dakota and South Dakota are also found here. The Lakota Indians called this area “mako sica” (land bad) because of its rough landscape.

Southwest Region

The Southwest Region is home to the enormous Grand Canyon. You will also find the Colorado River winding its way along the bottom of this famous formation. Petrified Forest National Park is found in northeastern Arizona. As you might guess from the name, this area is known for its large deposits of petrified wood, or fossilized plants that have turned to stone over time. The word “petrify” comes from the Greek word “petra,” meaning “rock” or “stone.” Some of the most colorful petrified wood in the world can be found here, but it’s against the law to remove samples from the park!

West Region

Have you ever heard of a hoodoo? Well, if you visit the West, you just might see one of these natural columns of rock, which have been carved by wind and water. (Bryce Canyon National Park in Utah is full of them.) The Rocky Mountains are also throughout this region, and Yellowstone National Park is located in Wyoming, Idaho and Montana. Yellowstone was America’s first national park, established in 1872. You may have heard of a famous geyser named Old Faithful — the hottest attraction in this park. Old Faithful is a natural hot spring that shoots water and steam into the air every 60 to 90 minutes.

title: Funding our National Parks
text: National parks let us enjoy the beauty of nature, but who pays for them? Most national parks charge visitors a small entrance fee. This money is used to help fund, or pay for, the care of the parks. However, it isn’t enough to cover all the parks’ expenses. Where do national parks get the rest of the money they need? Some money comes from federal (national) taxes. The rest of the money comes from citizens who donate money. When you visit a national park, you may see many roads, benches or lookout points named after generous people. Visit http://www.nationalparks.org/ to learn more about how you can help support national parks.

title: John Muir
text: Do you enjoy nature? John Muir did. He was born in Scotland in 1838, but he grew up in Wisconsin and traveled to California in 1868. Muir was surprised by the beauty of the California landscape. He was even more surprised that people were destroying so many of its natural wonders, especially the large sequoia and redwood trees! Muir began working to preserve California’s landscape for those who would come later. Muir convinced Congress to pass a bill that created Yosemite National Park in 1890. Muir also started the Sierra Club to help preserve the forests of the Sierra Nevada. The Sierra Club is now a national group that works to protect nature throughout the United States. We can thank John Muir for protecting America’s natural wonders for us to enjoy today.

title: What is ‘America’s Breadbasket’?
text: The Midwest Region of the United States is known for its rich, fertile farmland. The soil in these states is especially good for growing corn, wheat and oats. People sometimes call this area “America’s Breadbasket,” because we use the grains grown here to make the foods that keep us full and healthy. Foods such as bread, tortillas, hot and cold cereals, granola bars and pancakes are all made from grains grown in the Midwest. When we reach into our “breadbasket” to find healthy, filling foods, it is very likely they were made from grains grown here in America’s Breadbasket.

title: The Grand Canyon
text: A trip across the country would not be complete without a visit to the Grand Canyon. Listed as one of the Seven Natural Wonders of the World, the canyon truly is a grand site! It measures 277 miles long, 18 miles wide at its widest point and about one mile deep. That’s quite a gorge (narrow, deep valley)! Many geologists believe that the Colorado River slowly carved out the canyon over a 6-million-year period. For the most amazing view of the canyon, you might want to take a walk on the Grand Canyon Skywalk. This transparent (clear), horseshoe-shaped bridge lets you see all the way down to the canyon beneath your feet. Wow! Is your head spinning yet?

title: Mapping the United States: It’s All in Your Head!
text:
We’ve looked at maps and learned how to use them, but did you know that you also have maps in your mind? These maps are called mental maps. They are important because they help us visualize (picture) different locations and where they are in relation to each other. For example, you don’t carry a printed map of your room, school or street around with you each day, but you can probably sit down and draw maps of these places using the information stored in your brain. Close your eyes and picture your room. Where is your bed? Your closet? The door? You carry mental maps around in your head, and they help you to find your way around. Use mental map skills to draw major landforms on this map. Use the map in your head to mark the following locations on the map. You may first study the lesson map, but then complete the activity with no peeking!

1. Draw a blue line showing the Mississippi River.

2. Use a brown crayon to draw the Rocky Mountains.

3. Color the Northeast Region purple.

4. Color the Southeast Region blue.

5. Color the Midwest Region yellow.

6. Color the Southwest Region brown.

7. Color the West Region green.

8. Use a blue crayon to draw and label Niagara Falls.

9. Use an orange crayon to mark the Grand Canyon.

10. Use a brown crayon to mark the Badlands.

title: Do You Know Your Region?
text:
How much do you know about North Dakota? Do you know where the major cities are? How about our state’s lakes and rivers? Did you know that North Dakota is actually divided into three different regions? Hopefully, you already know some things about our state. This week, it’s time for a little detective work to find out exactly where you live.

Copy the following questions onto a separate sheet of paper. Then turn the page and use the Regions of North Dakota map, along with the descriptions of the regions, to pinpoint the area in which you live. Mark the spot on the map with a red X when you’re finished. (Ask a parent or teacher for permission to use the Internet if you need help answering some of the questions.)

1. Name the city or town where you live:

2. What is the weather like in the summer?

3. How much rain falls during an average year?

4. What is the weather like in the winter?

5. How much snow falls during an average winter?

6. Are there farms nearby?

7. If so, what types of crops are grown in or near your city? If not, what is produced in your city?

8. Are there any lakes or rivers nearby? If so,name them.

9. Are there any national or state parks in the area? If so, name them.

10. What types of wildlife live in the area?

After answering the questions from this page, don’t forget to use the map and lesson on Pages 2-3 to find your region. List it here and mark it on the map. I live in the ______________________ Region of North Dakota.

title: Cruising the Enchanted Highway
text: Gary Greff was born and raised in the small town of Regent, North Dakota, but he left town as an adult to become a teacher. Regent had always been small, but when Greff came back he found his hometown had nearly disappeared. In fact, its population had dropped to just over 200 people! Greff decided to give people a reason to visit Regent, and he decorated the 32-mile stretch of highway between the town and Interstate 94. He called it the Enchanted Highway. All along the highway, Greff designed and built huge sculptures using recycled metal scraps. Some of them are made from pipes, old oil tanks, oil drum lids and old farm machinery. The sculptures attract tourists from across the country and around the world. The Enchanted Highway includes one of the largest outdoor sculptures in the world—a flock of geese as wide as a football field and as tall as a 10-story building! Another sculpture is of a giant family so large that the father’s baseball cap is the size of a small car. There are also sculptures of deer, fishers and pheasants. Another sculpture shows President Theodore Roosevelt riding a bucking horse. The Enchanted Highway has defi nitely brought in new visitors and new businesses, including an RV park, gas station, gift shop and even a hotel. Greff hopes that these visitors will stay longer in Regent. Have you found yourself along the Enchanted Highway?

title: Regions of North Dakota
text:
Last week we learned that the United States is divided into five regions. Many states are also divided into regions. For example, North Dakota is divided into three different geographic regions. Look at the map on this page. You can see that our state’s regions are the Red River Valley, the Drift Prairie and the Missouri Plateau. Each region has certain geographic features that make it unique. Let’s explore each of these interesting areas of North Dakota.

Red River Valley

The Red River Valley lies along the banks of the Red River of the North (Red River), dividing North Dakota on the west from Minnesota on the east. The valley is flat and has some of the richest and most fertile soil in the world. That good soil is left over from glacial Lake Agassiz, which covered the area over 10,000 years ago. During the late 1800s, the area became famous for its booming wheat fields with huge farms. Some of these farms were 60,000 acres—that’s twice the size of Fargo! Today, most farms in the area are much smaller. In addition to growing wheat, farmers grow flax, potatoes and sugar beets. The climate of the Red River Valley is very harsh, with long, cold, windy winters and lots of snow. Fargo, a famous Red River Valley city, averages 43 nights per year with low temperatures at or below 0 degrees Fahrenheit (F). Fargo averages 50 inches of snow per year. That’s a lot of snow! In the summer, the highs can reach 90 degrees F or above, with frequent, severe thunderstorms.

Drift Prairie

To the west of the Red River Valley is the Drift Prairie. While the Red River Valley is nearly flat, the Drift Prairie is known for its rolling hills and many lakes. This region of North Dakota also has large areas of good soil where farmers grow oats, barley, soybeans and sunflowers. Other areas are used to raise cattle. The Turtle Mountains, Devils Lake and the city of Minot are found in this region. The region’s climate is not as harsh as Red River Valley’s. Minot has temperatures that dip below 0 degrees F about 39 nights of the year, and temperatures reach above 90 degrees F at least 16 days per year. This region gets less precipitation (rain, snow or sleet) than the Red River Valley, averaging only about 16 inches per year.

Missouri Plateau

To the west of the Drift Prairie, all the way to the border of Montana, is the region called the Missouri Plateau. A plateau is a flat, raised area of land. This region is home to the state capital of Bismarck and to the Badlands, an area of rough, dry land with little vegetation. The Badlands have many different formations, which were carved out of the land by wind and water over millions of years. Theodore Roosevelt National Park is found in this region, along with White Butte, North Dakota’s highest point (3,506 feet). This region has warm summers, with average temperatures in the 70s and 80s F, and it gets about 15 inches of precipitation per year. The temperatures during the winter months often fall into single digits, with frequent blizzard conditions. During the summer, thunderstorms are common. The area is also known for always being very windy.

title: The Badlands
text: The Badlands, located in southwest North Dakota, is a large, dry, rocky area filled with amazing rock formations, petrified forests and dinosaur fossils. Early settlers found it nearly impossible to cross this stretch of wilderness. Some of the people who tried called the area “The Land that God Forgot.” The Badlands rock formations were carved out by wind and water. The endless wind in the area picked up small bits of dirt and sand and blew them into rocks. Over time, this wore down the rock. The results are the special rock creations that the Badlands area is known for today. Scientists have also discovered fossils of alligators and of a crocodile-like reptile called a Champsosaurus. These fossils have led people to think that a swamp once covered the Badlands area thousands of years ago. The North Dakota Badlands is also home to Theodore Roosevelt National Park. Theodore Roosevelt, our 26th president, first came to the Badlands to hunt bison in 1883. He fell in love with the unique landscape. He then bought two cattle ranches, the Maltese Cross and the Elkhorn Ranch, and spent time there, hunting and enjoying nature. Roosevelt also wrote several books about his adventures in the Badlands. He said, “I never would have been President if it had not been for my experiences in North Dakota.” In 1947, President Truman formed the Theodore Roosevelt National Memorial Park. In 1978, more land was added, and the park became known as Theodore Roosevelt National Park. People who visit the Badlands will see many different animals, such as elk, deer, pronghorn, bighorn sheep and prairie dogs. The area also has turtles, snakes and golden eagles. If you visit the Badlands, you can hike, camp, view wildlife, take a scenic drive, tour the visitor centers, watch a ranger program, explore one of Theodore Roosevelt’s ranches, or just sit and enjoy the peaceful beauty of North Dakota. Whatever you do, you’ll be glad you came!

title: Our State Symbols
text:
Each state in the union has chosen official state symbols to represent its culture, history and geography. Here are four of North Dakota’s impressive state symbols.

State Flag

The official state flag of North Dakota is made up of a dark blue background with a bald eagle in the center. In its claws, the eagle holds an olive branch and a bundle of arrows, symbolizing peace and war. In the eagle’s mouth is a red ribbon with the Latin words, “E Pluribus Unum,” meaning “Out of Many, One.” This symbolizes the creation of one nation out of many states. The eagle also has a red, white and blue shield on its chest representing the United States. There are 13 stars above the eagle that represent the original 13 states. The name “North Dakota” appears on a scroll below the eagle.

The state flag was first adopted in 1911 and was a nearly exact replica (copy) of the flag the North Dakota Infantry carried in the Spanish-American War. In 2011, the governor signed a bill stating that all official copies of the North Dakota state flag must use the correct design and must include the approved colors listed by the state historical society.

State Flower: Wild Prairie Rose

The official name of our state flower is Rosa blanda, but it is better known as the wild prairie rose. This flower has bright green leaves and two-inch-wide flowers that come in shades of pale pink to deep rose. Each flower has five petals that surround bright yellow stamens. The wild prairie rose became the official state flower of North Dakota in 1907. Look for the wild prairie rose when you’re in the car on your next road trip. It’s all over our state!

State Bird: Western Meadowlark

The western meadowlark was chosen as the official state bird of North Dakota in 1947. This bird is about 8 to 11 inches long with a black-and-white striped head and long, pointed bill. Be on the lookout for its bright yellow cheeks and throat and a large black “V” on its chest.

The western meadowlark pecks beneath the soil for seeds, beetles, caterpillars and other insects. It weaves its nest on the ground out of dried grasses and plants. Meadowlarks lay an average of five eggs, twice per year, and the eggs take around two weeks to hatch. The western meadowlark is found in the grasslands of North Dakota and in most of the western United States.

State Tree: American Elm

In 1947, North Dakota chose the American elm as its official state tree. The American elm is a large, graceful tree that can grow over 100 feet tall. It was once one of the most popular trees planted in the U.S., but over the last few years, many of the nation’s elm trees have died from Dutch elm disease. The disease is spread by certain beetles and has killed millions of these lovely trees all across the country. Though more rare now, the American elm can still be found in North Dakota and other states.

title: The Constitution
text:
Did you know that you can see the original copy of the U.S. Constitution? It is in Washington D.C. in the National Archives Museum, where many tourists often visit. You probably know that a constitution is a written plan of government. It describes how our government works and explains what our leaders can and cannot do. A constitution creates the rules and laws that citizens must follow. Each state in our country also has its own constitution, and it is the same for North Dakota.

The introduction to North Dakota’s constitution says: “We, the people of North Dakota, grateful to Almighty God for the blessings of civil and religious liberty, do ordain and establish this constitution.” The introduction, which is also called a preamble, makes it clear that the people of North Dakota give the constitution its power!

Delegates (representatives) at the state Constitutional Convention wrote our constitution in August 1889. The people of North Dakota then had the chance to vote on the constitution and ratify, or approve, it by casting their votes. If the people did not agree with what the constitution said, they had the right to vote against it and ask that changes be made to the plan. The delegates had done a good job, though, and the people were happy with it. The North Dakota Constitution was ratified on Oct. 1, 1889, and it became official when North Dakota became a state on Nov. 2, 1889.

Besides setting out a basic plan for governing the state, the Constitution of North Dakota separates the government into three branches, or divisions. This helps to keep one person or group from becoming too powerful. It also states that the people have the right to choose their leaders by voting in elections. This week, we’ll learn more about our state’s constitution and how it gives North Dakota a plan to protect the rights of its citizens and keep our state running smoothly.

title: It’s Constitution Day! Let’s Celebrate!
text:
On September 17, 1787, the U.S. Constitution was finished. How are you celebrating Constitution Day this year? Did you know that Congress passed a law that schools across the country should celebrate this important day in history by learning more about our Constitution? It’s true. Some students celebrate by memorizing the Preamble and reciting it together on September 17. Others sing the national anthem or dress in red, white and blue. At some schools, students play games, act out plays or write reports that help them learn more about the Constitution.

Here are a few Constitution facts for you:

Benjamin Franklin, at 81, was the oldest delegate to attend the Constitutional Convention. He was very sick and had to be carried to the meetings in a special chair.

Jonathan Dayton was the youngest delegate at the age of 26.

The Constitution is made up of 4,543 words including the signatures.

The original Constitution is on display in the National Archives Building in Washington, D.C.

Now that you know a few interesting facts about the Constitution, it’s time to celebrate. What does your school do for Constitution Day?

title: Our Rights
text:
The State and U.S. Constitutions Protect Our Rights

A constitution has two purposes: to organize the government and to guarantee the rights of the people. The Bill of Rights of the United States Constitution outlines our rights as U.S. citizens. The First Amendment in the Bill of Rights lists five important rights that belong to every citizen of the United States. The first section of the North Dakota Constitution, after the preamble, is the Declaration of Rights. The Declaration of Rights in our state constitution also protects each of these rights. Let’s take a look at our five basic rights as U.S. citizens.

Freedom of Religion

The First Amendment tells us that Congress cannot pass any law that would stop people from worshipping the way they choose, or force them to worship in a certain way. Religious freedom is a very important part of the First Amendment. The governments of some nations demand that all citizens worship the same way. Both the U.S. Constitution and the North Dakota Constitution allow us to make that decision for ourselves.

Freedom of Speech

In a free society, it is important to be able to say what you think. You are not allowed to say things that will unfairly hurt someone, but all citizens have the right to speak their opinions. This means that sometimes, people may express opinions that we don’t like or agree with. As citizens, we know that they have the right to those opinions.

Freedom of the Press

In a free society, you also have the right to express your opinions in print, even if your opinion doesn’t agree with the government. When the government does things that people feel are wrong, newspapers can print stories about these actions and demand change. The government cannot punish the press in any way for demanding that change. Many countries do not allow freedom of the press because they don’t want people to limit the government’s power.

The Right to Assembly

In some countries, people are not allowed to gather together in groups to complain about the government. Governments in those countries know that this could limit their power. Both the U.S. and the North Dakota constitutions give citizens the right to gather together whenever they choose, because our government only works if it has the support of its citizens. This right does not allow citizens to gather together to plan illegal activities.

The Right to Ask the Government to Change

United States citizens have the right to ask the government to change how it does things. Citizens can also take the government to court if they think it has treated them badly. There are many governments where this is not allowed.

How are the U.S. and North Dakota Governments Set Up?

How do our U.S. and North Dakota constitutions set up the government? The North Dakota Constitution follows the pattern set by the U.S. Constitution by dividing the government into three separate branches. These branches have equal power and help balance each other out, making sure that no one branch becomes too powerful.

1. The legislative branch makes the laws of our country and our state.

2. The executive branch (president/ governor) enforces the laws.

3. The judicial branch interprets and applies the law.

Our state and national constitutions also tell us who can vote and how elections will happen. It’s important to vote in elections to choose our leaders and decide on issues. In a democracy, the people have the power!

title: Civic Participation
text:
Civic participation means being a part of what is happening in your community, state or nation. For our government to work, citizens need to get involved. This may mean running for office, signing a petition or making your opinion heard in some way.

U.S. citizens have many rights, but they come with responsibilities. A very important responsibility is voting in elections. Good voters use information wisely. This means finding information about the issues and candidates (those running for office). Then, citizens can be smart about who they vote for. How does a citizen of North Dakota go about voting? North Dakota is the only state that doesn’t require voters to register, but a voter must be:

a citizen of the United States

at least 18 years old on election day

a resident of North Dakota for at least 30 days before the election

Voters must also bring identification with them, such as a driver’s license, government ID card or student ID card from a college in North Dakota. Many schools hold mock (pretend) elections around the time real elections are taking place. During mock elections, students learn about the candidates and important issues being voted on in the elections. Then they cast their votes, just like in a real election. Their votes are counted to see how the election would turn out if students were the ones choosing. Does your school do mock elections? Ask your teacher to find out!

Civic participation also means working for the common good. This means doing things that help all the people in a community, not just yourself. Even something like picking up trash at a park in your town is working for the common good. What are some ways you can help your community?

title: Warren Christopher and the Rough Rider Award
text:
In 1961, North Dakota lawmakers created the Theodore Roosevelt Rough Rider Award. The award was named after Roosevelt’s famous First U.S. Volunteer Cavalry, the Rough Riders, that fought during the Spanish-American War. The award is given to people from North Dakota who have achieved great things.

In 1998, a man named Warren Christopher received this award. Christopher was born in Scranton, North Dakota, in 1925. He began his service to our country when he joined the Naval Reserve during World War II. After the war, he graduated from the University of Southern California and got a job as a lawyer in Los Angeles. Christopher was then chosen to serve as deputy secretary of state during Jimmy Carter’s presidency during the late 1970s. As deputy secretary of state, Christopher helped negotiate (work to reach an agreement) for the release of 52 American hostages held in Iran.

Warren Christopher did so well that in 1992, newly elected President Bill Clinton asked Christopher to become the 63rd secretary of state! The job meant advising the president on what was going on in other countries around the world. Christopher visited other leaders to work on treaties and agreements. In fact, he traveled over 780,000 miles during his time as secretary of state. That’s long enough to circle the Earth 31 times!

It’s easy to see why Warren Christopher was such a good choice for the Rough Rider award. All of his hard work helped the country and made North Dakota proud!

title: Why Do We Have Laws?
text: Countries have laws, or rules that must be followed, to help citizens live together peacefully and safely. It may sound fun to be able to do whatever you want, without worrying about rules. Imagine what would happen if there were no traffic laws. What if people drove through intersections without stopping to see if another car was coming? Think of how many accidents would happen! A law many people don’t like is one that says we have to pay taxes. However, taxes help pay for police officers and firefighters. What would your community be like if there was no money to pay for police officers? Laws help protect us from danger and make it easier for us to live together. What are some other important laws? Discuss some North Dakota laws with a partner.

title: Our Historical Documents
text:
A primary source is an eyewitness account of a historical event. Primary sources are firsthand reports, such as letters, diaries, photographs or newspaper articles, from people who experienced the event. Secondary sources are written about a historic event and may include pictures or quotes from primary sources. However, these authors weren’t actually there to see the event take place.

Some of our country’s most important primary sources are the Constitution, the Bill of Rights and the Declaration of Independence. Each of these valuable historic documents is displayed in the National Archives Museum in Washington, D.C. These primary sources are so valuable to our nation’s history that they are stored in special glass cases to keep them from being stolen or damaged.

title: First Amendment Rights
text:
The First Amendment in the Bill of Rights of the U.S. Constitution lists five important rights that belong to U.S. citizens. Read the examples given here and match each example to the right protected under the First Amendment. You may look back at the lesson if you need help.

title: Why Do We Have Government?
text:
“Good morning, friends! Jackson and I were just talking about government, and an interesting question came up. ‘Why do we have governments?’”

“It’s a great question, Alana, especially since we’ve been studying this topic in social studies. All of our Studies Weekly friends may have asked that question as well. Why DO we have governments?”

“There are many reasons, but the simple answer is to help the members of a community live together in safety, peace and order. Governments also help take care of our needs and protect our rights.”

“That’s true, Alana. There are several levels of government, and each has certain responsibilities to fulfill. The main levels of government that we deal with are local, state, tribal and national (federal) governments.”

“Each level of government has a special job to do. Local governments serve the people of a town or city. Local means ‘belonging to one community.’ Local governments help the people of their own cities and towns by making sure they have police officers, ambulances, garbage pickup, traffic lights and signs, libraries, sewer service and parks. Local governments collect taxes to pay for these important services.”

“State governments also work to make life better for the people living in each state. State governments collect taxes as well. States use tax money for roads, public buildings, a state police force, health care, schools and many other important services.”

“Don’t forget tribal governments, Jackson! American Indian tribes are considered sovereign nations. That means each tribal government is responsible for its people. Tribal governments make rules and laws for local American Indian tribes and help protect the rights of the tribe. Tribal leaders are often invited to join with nearby city leaders, as well as with state and national groups, to make sure that national, government and local laws are fair to their tribes.”

“That’s right, Alana. There’s one more type of government that also takes care of its citizens’ needs. The national government makes decisions and passes laws that help citizens of the entire country. It collects taxes to pay for things like military protection, interstate highways, national parks, welfare programs (programs that help people in need) and Social Security (money for retired people)."

“So, Jackson, the best answer to the question about why we have governments might be answered with a quote by Thomas Jefferson. He said, ‘The purpose of government is to enable the people of a nation to live in safety and happiness. Government exists for the interests of the governed, not for the governors.’”

title: Help a Rat and Learn to Run the Country This Year!
text:
Hey, kids! I’m Revere the Rat, but you can call me Rev. I’m your online Studies Weekly friend and I need your help. You can help me get great stuff by earning points while you learn. Just scan the code or go to www.studiesweekly.com and click on my picture. Has your family ever bought something that came with an owner’s manual? Cars, TVs and other things have an owner’s manual, a book on how to use them. Your social studies class is the “owner’s manual” for the United States of America. Then you can tell the representatives you help elect how you think the country should be run. In fact, Studies Weekly kids are so smart, that many of you will someday be mayors, senators, governors—maybe even the president!

For now you have two jobs: Learn about the country and how it works and earn points for me so I can get that great stuff I told you about. It’s easy. Just scan or click and you’re on your way!

title: Layers of Government
text:
“Jackson and Alana here. Don’t these parfaits look good enough to eat? These yummy desserts remind us of the levels, or layers, of government. Can you name them? If you said the levels of government are federal, state, local and tribal, then great job! Just like parfaits, the federal, state, local and tribal governments have layers, or different parts. These parts are usually called “branches,” and they make up each type of government. Sound familiar? The Constitution organized our national government into three branches: executive, legislative and judicial. Each branch has the ability to check up on the others, which keeps any one branch from becoming too powerful. Look at the parfaits and jukebox chart to see each branch of government and what positions are in each branch.”

The Executive Branch

The job of the executive branch is to carry out the law. The president of the United States is the head of the executive branch of our national government. The governor is the head of the executive branch in North Dakota. The mayor or city manager is the head of the executive branch in our cities and towns, and the tribal chairperson is the head of the executive branch of tribal governments.

The head of the executive branch of government is usually elected to serve for a four-year term. A term is the length of time that an elected official stays in office. The head of the executive branch also chooses people to help run the nation, state, city or tribe. This person has veto power, which means that he or she can say no to any bill. A bill is a plan for a law.

The Legislative Branch

The legislative branch makes the laws. In the national government and North Dakota’s state government, this branch is called the legislature. (The official name for North Dakota’s legislative branch is the Legislative Assembly.) In local and tribal governments, this branch is usually called a city council or tribal council. The national and state legislatures make laws to govern the people who live within their boundaries. The city and tribal councils make plans for the city and tribe. The people who serve on these councils try to make good decisions about issues that affect people living within the city, town or tribe.

The Judicial Branch

The job of the judicial branch is to interpret, or explain, the laws of the nation, state, city or tribe. The judicial branch is made up of judges and courts.

The highest court in our nation is the Supreme Court. It is made up of nine judges who review the most important cases from other courts in the nation. They decide if the cases have been handled correctly. The Supreme Court also reviews laws passed by the legislature to see if they are constitutional, or that they agree with the Constitution. If the law doesn’t agree with the Constitution, the Supreme Court rejects it.

North Dakota also has its own state supreme court to review cases and to make sure that laws passed in the North Dakota legislature agree with our state’s constitution. There are smaller courts throughout our state, cities and tribes that handle cases before the court. These courts also take care of disagreements over property and money.

Tribal Governments

The United States recognizes American Indian tribes as sovereign nations and allows them great freedom in governing themselves. They have the right to tax their own people, pass their own laws and set up their own courts. The United States Congress still has power to pass laws that affect American Indian tribes and their members, however.

There are five North Dakota Indian tribes that are recognized by the federal government. Each has its own tribal government. They are the Spirit Lake Tribe, the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe, the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians, the Sisseton Wahpeton Oyate and the Three Affiliated Tribes. These tribal governments each have their own constitutions and have created governments with three branches, just like our state and national governments. They elect a head of the executive branch (chairperson), along with a tribal council. They also have a tribal court system.

State Contributions to Federal Government

Each state has a say in what happens in the federal government. The people of each state elect representatives to serve in the U.S. House of Representatives. The population of each state determines how many representatives it sends to the House. States with larger populations have more representatives. Do you know how many representatives North Dakota has? Each state also elects two senators to serve in the Senate, the other legislative body. Senators and representatives are also called legislators, and these men and women work together to make laws that will benefit their states and the entire nation.

“Jackson, I bet that from now on, whenever I eat a parfait I’ll think about the layers of government.”

“Me too, Alana!”

title: Taxes
text:
You are standing in line at the grocery store. You have counted all of your change, and you have $1.03. It’s just enough to buy the biggest pack of bubble gum you’ve ever seen in your life. The bubble gum costs $1.00. You get to the front of the line, and the cashier rings it up. Your total comes to $1.06. What? That can’t be right. You are 3 cents short. How did that happen? Then you remember about sales tax. Lucky for you, you find an extra nickel in your pocket and pay for your gum. Taxes are sums of money the government collects from people and businesses. They use this money to provide services for the citizens. There are many different kinds of taxes, such as the sales tax you pay at the grocery store. Sales tax is a tax that is usually added to the price of your purchase for goods or a service. Taxes are also sometimes charged on things people already own, such as houses and cars.

There are three main types of taxes: progressive tax, regressive tax and proportional tax. A progressive tax can change. The tax depends on how much money a person makes. People who make more money pay more in taxes. People who make less money pay less in taxes. Regressive taxes are opposite of progressive taxes. This means that people with more income pay less in taxes and people with less income pay more in taxes. A proportional tax is the same tax for everyone. Which tax do you think is the most fair?

title: Young George Washington, Surveyor and Mapmaker
text:
Most people know about George Washington. He was born in Virginia. He was a general during the American Revolution and our first president. But his earliest jobs, surveyor and cartographer (mapmaker), taught him skills and values he would use for the rest of his life. Using reason and logic to solve problems helped Washington become one of our country’s most important leaders.

When Washington grew up, there were few roads or boundaries in much of the land. A surveyor’s job was to measure and map the land. He had to make exact measurements for boundaries and physical features. This was a very big responsibility. People needed accurate maps and surveys for traveling and buying land.

At age 17, Washington traveled across the Blue Ridge Mountains to map and survey part of the frontier. He was the surveyor for the whole county, and that was an important job. When he led the Continental Army, it was even more important to have reliable maps. He established the job of Geographer and Surveyor General and appointed a man named Robert Erskine to this position. He gave Washington some information that was very helpful in making reasonable and logical battle plans and decisions. You can use these same skills to make important decisions.

Be sure you have the facts and information you need instead of acting on opinions and emotions. In what areas of your life are reason and logic very important?

George Washington wrote these geometry problems when he was in school.
