title: Money Doesn’t Grow on Trees
text:
Have your parents ever told you that “money doesn’t grow on trees” after you asked them for some cash? Sadly, your parents are right. Unless you know someone who is willing to share his or her money with you for free, the only way to get money is to earn it.

What are some ways that kids your age can earn money? The best place to start is at home. Even if you already get an allowance, maybe you can offer to do some extra chores. Is your garage a mess? Offer to organize it (for a fair price, of course). Is the family car dirty? Offer to clean it inside and out. If there’s no more work to do at home, think about your neighborhood. Neighbors are usually willing to pay for lawn mowing, snow shoveling, leaf raking or window washing. Is anyone on your street about to go on vacation? Offer to look after their pets while they are away. Remember to ask for a fair price for your work!

Why do you want to earn extra money anyway? Is there anything you want to buy that your family doesn’t already give you? It’s likely that the adults in your life give you a home, food, clothing and even toys. But what about that special treat your parents just aren’t willing, or able, to get for you? You can buy them for yourself if you want, but it may take a little (or A LOT of) extra work for you to earn the money you need.

As you get older, earning money is different. Your parents may go to work every day to earn money for the family, but they probably aren’t organizing garages or walking neighbors’ pets. Adults usually get training to learn the skills needed for jobs to support their families. Adults may go to college for a degree, or they may go to a technical school to learn how to do a specific job. Some companies offer on-the-job training for people they hire. With knowledge, skills and training, adults can get well-paying jobs to buy all the things they need and many of the things they want.

Most of the money adults earn pays for necessities, or things they need to survive. Necessities include food, clothing, housing, electricity and transportation. If you’ve ever been to the dentist or doctor, those services cost money too. Your parents also pay taxes to keep the nation, state and city running! With all these places for money to go, wouldn’t it be nice if it really did grow on trees?

title: Paying It Forward
text:
Have you ever found money lying on the ground that didn’t belong to you? What did you do with it? Did you keep it? At first, Myles Eckert, an 8-year-old boy from Toledo, Ohio, thought about buying a new video game with the $20 he found in a local restaurant’s parking lot. But after entering the restaurant, Myles saw Lieutenant Colonel Frank Dailey, and instead he chose to pay it forward.

Seeing Lt. Col. Dailey reminded Myles of his father, an Army sergeant, who was killed in Iraq shortly after Myles was born. So, he decided to give the $20 he found to the soldier whom he had never met. Myles gave him the $20 bill with a note that said:

“Dear soldier-- My dad was a soldier. He’s in heaven now. I found this $20 in the parking lot when we got here. We like to pay it forward in my family. It’s your lucky day! Thank you for your service. Myles Eckert, a gold star kid.”

Lt. Col. Dailey, a member of the Air National Guard, said he was overwhelmed when Myles handed him the money and that he looks at the note every day. He also chose to pay forward that $20.

Since that day, Myles started a campaign to raise money for military families across the United States. The money raised benefits Snowball Express, an organization that brings children of fallen military heroes together for fun activities, like sporting events and amusement parks. What a wonderful campaign Myles!

title: How Much Money is in Your Pocket?
text:
If you spend time hanging out with your friends, you may notice that you don’t all have the same amount of money in your pockets. The same thing is true for your parents. People don’t all earn the same amount of money and have the same amount to spend. This week, we’ll read about personal income and why some people have more money to spend than others.

What is Personal Income?

Personal income is all the money someone earns from wages (money paid to people who work), tips and bonuses. Personal income is the money earned before any other expenses are taken out. Expenses include money for taxes and bills. Personal income is also called gross income.

Education Affects Personal Income

Just like you and your friends have different amounts of money to spend when you go to the movies, the amount of money adults have to spend is different from person to person. If everyone works hard and spends the same amount of time at their jobs each day, why don’t they have the same amount of money?

As you probably know, different jobs pay different amounts of money and require different training. Doctors usually earn a large salary, but they also have to spend 11 or more years in college, medical school and extra training. Becoming a lawyer means spending three years in law school after college. Teachers, accountants, engineers, architects, computer professionals and financial experts are all workers who finished college.

Other jobs require professional training that is different from college. Some of these include welders, bookkeepers, carpenters, auto mechanics, appliance repairers, heating and air conditioning technicians and administrative assistants (secretaries). You can learn a skill and receive a certificate to prove that you have been properly trained. It makes all the difference in getting a job with a good salary and benefits. Benefits are extra bonuses that many companies give to people who work for them.

Who Takes a Bite Out of Your Paycheck?

The amount of money you take home in your paycheck is less than the personal income you earned. That’s right—you don’t get to keep it all! Before you get the money you earned, the government takes some out for Social Security, Medicare and income taxes. Some companies offer health insurance to their workers, so part of each paycheck may also help pay for it. It isn’t surprising that after other groups have each finished taking a bite out of your paycheck, it won’t be as much as you hoped it would be. The money left over is called your net income.

The money taken out of your paycheck isn’t wasted, though. Tax money helps the government provide services and benefits for you, your friends and your family. Health insurance is also important because it helps pay for things like doctor visits, broken bones and trips to the hospital.

Usually, the more school and training you finish, the more money you will earn. This isn’t always the case, however. Many people simply choose jobs that they love, even if they pay less. Whatever job you choose to have, the money you make will pay for your needs and wants.

title: Changes in Personal Income
text:
Has it seemed busier at stores lately? Maybe you’ve noticed a few more new businesses around town. Over several years, North Dakota has led the nation in personal income growth. That’s quite an accomplishment! For example, in 2013, the national level of personal income growth actually fell, but in North Dakota it rose nearly 8 percent. That brought the average personal income level for North Dakotans to $57,084.

What caused this huge jump in personal income in our state? North Dakota is one of the top oil-producing states in the country. New technology, such as fracking (drilling for oil by shooting water into underground layers of shale rock), has made it easier and cheaper to make things from oil. Lots of workers have moved to North Dakota to take the high-paying jobs offered by the oil industry.

Manufacturing companies (companies that use machines to make products) have also added jobs in North Dakota over the last few years. The Bobcat Company makes construction equipment, and its main office is in North Dakota. Manufacturing companies of all kinds have benefitted from the oil industry in our state.

Agriculture (farming) is another big business in North Dakota. Our state is one of the nation’s leaders in producing honey, dry beans, spring wheat and canola. What else are we good at growing? Sunflowers, soybeans, sugar beets, flaxseed and potatoes are important North Dakota farm products as well.

Take a look at the graph to see how North Dakota’s personal income has changed in recent years. It’s a great time to live in North Dakota!

title: Sister Thomas Welder
text:
Sister Thomas Welder received the Theodore Roosevelt Rough Rider Award in 2004 for her work in education in North Dakota. Welder chose the name Sister Thomas as a young adult. Before that, she was known as Diane Welder.

Diane was born in Linton, North Dakota, in 1940. She and her family moved to Bismarck, and Diane attended Catholic schools. Diane had four aunts who became nuns, and she grew up wondering whether she would become a nun herself. Once she started classes at the College of St. Benedict in Minnesota, she realized that becoming a nun was the path she wanted to follow. Diane joined the community of the Benedictine Sisters of Annunciation Monastery near Bismarck. This was when she took her new name. Sister Thomas studied music in school and was named the president of Mary College in Bismarck in 1978. Sister Thomas Welder was the school’s president for more than 30 years. Under her leadership, the college became the University of Mary.

As university president, Sister Thomas Welder worked to improve the school so that more North Dakotans could receive a good college education. She helped the university spread classes into new towns and cities. As the university grew, it was able to reach more and more students.

Sister Thomas Welder believed that students should be taught to have strong moral values and that it’s important to give service to the community. Sister Thomas Welder retired from her duties as president of the university in 2009. Her name is now among other North Dakotans who have proudly served our state!

title: What is debt?
text:
When someone borrows money from a bank, that money must later be paid back with interest (a fee charged for borrowing money). Debt is money that one person owes to another. Individuals, businesses and even governments can have debt. The U.S. government is actually trillions of dollars in debt, and that number keeps rising. It’s a huge problem! Many people must go into debt to buy a house, buy a car or pay for college. If people aren’t careful with their money, they can also go into debt for everyday items like clothes, entertainment and even food.

One way to stay out of debt is to save up for large purchases and try not to spend more than you earn. To get rid of debt, begin paying it off a little at a time until the debt is gone.

title: Looking Back: Geography and Government
text:
“Well, Jackson, we’ve packed a lot of learning into the last few weeks, and I think we’ve had a lot of fun doing it!”

“No kidding, Alana! Now it’s time to see if we can remember everything we learned. Are you ready for a quick review?”

“I sure am!”

“Here are some highlights. …”

U.S. Regions

The United States stretches from the Atlantic Ocean on the east all the way to the Pacific Ocean on the west—from sea to shining sea. The country of Canada is on the north and Mexico is on the south. The area between Canada and Mexico is known as the Continental United States. Alaska and Hawaii are also part of the United States, but they aren’t directly connected to the rest of the country. Hawaii is located in the Pacific Ocean. Canada is between the Continental U.S. and Alaska.

The United States is divided into five separate regions. Regions are areas that have similar climates, geography and landforms. The five regions of the United States are the Northeast, the Southeast, the Midwest, the Southwest and the West.

North Dakota Regions

North Dakota is also divided into separate regions. What can you remember about the geographic features and climate of these regions?

Red River Valley

The Red River Valley is the land near the Red River. The valley’s rich soil helps farmers grow wheat, flax, potatoes and sugar beets. The harsh climate of the Red River Valley produces cold, windy winters and lots of snow. Thunderstorms are common during the warm summer months. The Red River also forms the border between North Dakota and Minnesota.

Drift Prairie

To the west of the Red River Valley is the Drift Prairie. You will find rolling hills and many lakes here. This region’s farmers raise barley, oats, soybeans, sunflowers and cattle. The Turtle Mountains, Devils Lake and the city of Minot are located in the Drift Prairie. The climate is a little milder than that of the Red River Valley, with less rain and snow.

Missouri Plateau

North Dakota’s western region is the Missouri Plateau. This region is home to the Badlands. The Badlands are filled with amazing rock formations. Wind and water slowly carved these formations out of the land over millions of years. The Badlands region has warm, dry summers and cold, windy winters.

Branches of Government

The government is divided into three groups called branches. No branch is too powerful, and all three work together to help run our country.

The Executive Branch

The job of the executive branch is to make sure everyone follows the laws. The head of an executive branch also chooses people to help run the nation, state, city or tribe. That person has veto power, which means that he or she can say no to any bill. A bill is a plan for a law.

The Legislative Branch

The legislative branch makes the laws. This branch includes senators, representatives, city councils and tribal councils.

The Judicial Branch

The judicial branch works to interpret the laws of the nation, state, city or tribe. The judicial branch is made up of judges and courts. Courts review laws to make sure they are constitutional. They also listen to criminal cases and make decisions about disagreements over property and money.

“Whew, Alana, that was one quick review, but I feel like we didn’t quite cover everything.”

“You’re right, Jackson. That’s why we’re going to use the rest of this week’s magazine to review our map skills, state symbols, personal rights and even a few money issues. Does that sound good?”

“Sounds GREAT!”

title: Reviewing our Map Skills
text:
“Let’s take a few minutes to review our map skills. After all, there’s nothing like a map to bring our studies of government, history and geography to life.”

“You’re so right, Jackson!”

Map Features

A map is a picture or drawing of a place that shows where things are. A map should always have a title and have symbols to help us understand the map. These symbols are not always easy to figure out, so most maps include a legend. A legend is a box that explains what the symbols on the map mean. Legends may show cities, highways, airports and other important places.

Most legends also include a scale. A map scale shows the relationship between real-life distances and the distances shown on the map. We can use a scale to figure out how far apart different places are on the map. For example, a map scale may show that one inch on the map is equal to 100 miles in actual distance.

Another important part of a map is the compass rose. It helps us locate different features on a map by showing directions. A compass rose shows cardinal directions and intermediate directions. The cardinal directions are north, south, east and west. Intermediate directions fall halfway between the cardinal directions, and they are northeast, northwest, southeast and southwest.

Physical and Political Maps

Physical maps show the major landforms of an area, including rivers, lakes, deserts, mountains and forests. Political maps show city, state and national boundaries. Political maps may also show major cities, roads and population.

North Dakota — Physical Location and Features

North Dakota is in the middle of the North American continent. Landforms that range from eastern rolling plains to western rocky hills and buttes (steep-sided hills with flat tops) fill up our state. Use the physical map on this page to find Lake Sakakawea, located in the central western half of our state. The Missouri River, held back by Garrison Dam, forms this lake. Keep looking, and you will find Devils Lake, Long Lake, the Badlands and White Butte. On this map, you can see the location of North Dakota, along with its major geographic features.

North Dakota — Political Location and Features

Look at the political map of North Dakota, and you will see our state in a different way. It is in the central northern area of the United States. North Dakota’s northern neighbors are the Canadian provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. On the east, we are bordered by Minnesota. South Dakota is on the south, and Montana is on the west. Our state capital, Bismarck, is marked with a star in the lower half of our state.

“OK, Jackson, now that we’ve brushed up on our map skills, it’s time to answer a few game show-style questions. I’ll tell you the answer, and YOU give me the question. Then we’ll see how much you REALLY know!”

title: North Dakota's First People
text:
Would you like to track and hunt a woolly mammoth or be the first person ever to set foot on a new land? If you had been a Paleo-Indian child, you might have had adventures just like these!

The Paleo-Indians were the first people known to have lived on the North American continent. Part of the land they settled would one day become North Dakota. The first known humans lived in Africa tens of thousands of years ago. They spread out across the Earth, hunting for food as they went. Some of these people eventually made their way to what is now Europe and Asia. By around 14,000 B.C., these hunters followed huge animals, such as woolly mammoths, caribou and bison. They ended up in Siberia, a region in present-day Russia.

North Dakota is a long way from Siberia! How did these hunters and their families find their way here? Many archaeologists and historians believe that these people came to North America by crossing an ancient land bridge, which once connected Asia and North America during the last ice age. This land bridge is known as Beringia, and it connected the two continents until about 10,000 years ago. Hunters traveled across this land bridge in search of food. They hunted their prey using spears with sharpened stone points, which they often threw using ancient spear-throwers called atlatls. Paleo-Indians first arrived in North Dakota as early as 9500 B.C. As centuries passed, the sea level rose and Beringia was covered by water.

The Paleo-Indians were nomads. Nomads are people who don’t settle in one spot and move from place to place in search of food. They most likely traveled in small groups. Paleo-Indians often hunted, but some of the animals they wanted were very large, so hunters had to work together. One of these large animals was the woolly mammoth. Fully grown mammoths were over 9 feet tall and had tusks that could grow up to 15 feet long! Hunters had to work together to bring down the animal, and it took several more people to cut off the meat and turn the hide into clothing and blankets.

At the time, this area was covered in glaciers. As these glaciers began to melt, new areas opened up for settling. At about the same time the glaciers began melting, many of the larger animals started to die off and become extinct. Fortunately, the land left behind after the glaciers melted was covered with rich, fertile soil that was perfect for farming.

title: Are Tar Pits Hiding Beneath U.S. Roads?
text:
If you live in Los Angeles, California, the answer may be yes. And those tar pits may contain the best-preserved fossils ever found! Near busy Wilshire Boulevard you can see the Le Brea Tar Pits. The area is still bubbling with the sticky tar that trapped animals up to 50,000 years ago. Scientists have found the bones of bears larger than any on Earth today, lions bigger than today’s African lions and camels larger than the elephants you can see at a zoo. Over one million bones have been found in the pits so far. (No dinosaur bones have been found because they were already extinct.) And in 2006, 16 new tar deposits were found where a parking garage was being built at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. Some scientists think they will find a million bones there too.

The tar pits show that many large animals went extinct at about the same time. Why? Many scientists say evidence points to the climate change that took place at the end of the ice age. The large animals couldn’t adjust fast enough to the warmer temperatures. At about that same time, man first migrated over the land bridge that used to exist between Asia and North America. Another theory is that man may have hunted many of these giants to extinction. What’s underneath that road you were on when you came to school today? Maybe more than you think!

title: Early American Indians
text:
Paleo-Indians

(9500 B.C.–5500 B.C.)

Evidence suggests that the Paleo-Indians first came to the North Dakota area as early as 9500 B.C. The word “paleo” means ancient or very old, and it definitely describes this group of early Americans! These people left no written record of how they lived, so archaeologists have made theories based on the few tools and other clues they have found. Paleo-Indians were nomadic, meaning they traveled from place to place, looking for food. They traveled in small bands of 20-50 people, working together to provide for the needs of the group.

Paleo-Indians built simple shelters using sticks, branches and animal skins. They also looked for natural shelters like caves. Paleo-Indians hunted large animals, such as mammoths, ground sloths, buffalo (bison), caribou and other animals to feed the group. Paleo-Indians may have killed larger animals by chasing them over cliffs or drop-offs. This made it easier for them to bring down animals that were too large to trap or kill with smaller weapons.

This group also made spears for hunting. The Paleo-Indians carved rocks into sharp, durable points and shaped them to fit into a groove they had cut into a wooden shaft. Later, they invented a spear-thrower called an atlatl. This was used to throw a spear farther and faster than just by hand. The atlatl made it easier to hunt and helped the Paleo-Indians keep their stomachs filled!

The Paleo-Indians also ate roots, plants, seeds and maybe even insects. They used animal skins for clothing and shelter. Where can you find a Paleo-Indian site in North Dakota? Check out Lake Ilo, which is now a National Wildlife Refuge.

Archaic Indians
(5500 B.C.–500 B.C.)

The Archaic Indians were the descendants of the Paleo-Indians. They also lived in small, nomadic groups, but they began to use different tools and had a different way of life. The Archaic Indians still traveled from place to place to look for food, but they also searched for the right kind of stone to make their spear points. They learned which stones worked best and where to find them. In North Dakota, the Knife River was a good source of flint. The Archaic Indians also relied on the atlatl more than the Paleo-Indians did. Archaeologists have found spear points and other artifacts from this period at a quarry in Richland County.

Over time, larger animals began to disappear. The Archaic Indians then used their hunting and gathering skills to hunt smaller animals, along with birds and fish. They traveled less and began living in even larger groups. There may not have been chiefs in these groups, but artifacts at burial sites show that some people were more important within the group than others. The Archaic people likely traded with other groups for the supplies they needed.

The Archaic Indians also learned how to make baskets, which they used to store the seeds, berries, nuts and fruit they had gathered for food. Toward the end of this period, some Archaic people made pots out of clay. They also made and used tools, such as grinding stones (used to turn seeds and nuts into powder), axes, fishnets, fishhooks and traps for snaring birds and other small animals.

Woodland Indians
(500 B.C.–A.D. 1000)

The Woodland people who lived in North Dakota had an even more advanced way of life than either the Paleo- or Archaic Indians. Some groups may have descended from Archaic people, but others may have migrated (moved from one part of the world to another) from other places. We do know that the Woodland Indians still traveled in search of food, but they also built permanent homes and returned to these settlements at the end of their hunting and gathering trips. They made their homes with wooden poles covered with bark, grass or animal skins. Woodland Indians also gathered plants, fruits and vegetables for food, and they grew crops near their settlements. They used these crops both for food and to trade with other groups.

The Woodland people also made large pots out of clay. They used the pots to cook and prepare food. Woodland Indians used the bow and arrow and became highly skilled hunters. They followed buffalo herds and hunted these large animals for food, as well as for their skins and bones. They used the skins and bones to make tools, clothing, blankets and shelters.

The Woodland Indians were very respectful of their dead. They buried the bodies in the ground and then built huge mounds of earth over the graves. If you visit North Dakota’s Pulver Mounds State Historic Site or the Standing Rock State Historic site, you can see some of these mounds for yourself!

The first people to live in our state used the natural resources around them to survive. Archaeologists are still learning about these early people. What other clues are buried in the ground? Maybe more artifacts will be discovered near you!

title: Louise Erdrich
text:
Louise Erdrich no longer lives in North Dakota, but she still thinks of Wahpeton and the Red River Valley as her home. Her father’s family was from Germany, and her mother was a member of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians. Erdrich is a member of that tribe as well. Both of her parents taught at a Bureau of Indian Affairs school in Wahpeton when she was a kid. Erdrich loved learning about both her German and American Indian background.

Erdrich studied writing at Dartmouth College and Johns Hopkins University. She finished her first book in 1984, and she has published novels, poetry and several children’s books. Some of her most popular children’s books are “The Birchbark House,” “Chickadee” and “The Game of Silence.” Her books are fiction, but many of her characters are based on people she knows from her family’s tribe.

Erdrich is the oldest of seven children, and her family has had a huge effect on her writing. She has always loved hearing stories about her ancestors and learning about the rich heritage she gets from both her parents. She has traced her family history back 200 years on both sides of her family and says she has just gotten started! Erdrich keeps a notebook that she fills with all of her writing ideas.

Louise Erdrich was honored with the Theodore Roosevelt Rough Rider Award in 2013. One reason she was chosen for the award was because she’s done such a good job showing North Dakota’s history in many of her stories. Keep an eye out for her books the next time you visit the library!

title: Menoken Indian Village
text:
Menoken Indian Village is a National Historic Landmark located in Burleigh County, North Dakota. The area is where around 30 houses were built sometime around A.D. 1200. These houses were home to the 200 community members who once lived there. The people built the village along the banks of Apple Creek, which had steep riverbanks that were difficult for any attackers to climb.

In 1938, two archaeologists began digging at the site. At first, they thought it had belonged to the Mandan Indians during the early 1700s. Since then, different archaeologists have proved that the village was actually much older than that. Indians of the late Woodland period likely settled it about 500 years earlier than the Mandan.

There is no evidence of any garden tools in this village, so archaeologists don’t believe that the villagers farmed any crops. This means that the people who lived there were hunters and gatherers. They probably gathered the wild fruits, plants and vegetables that grew in the area. These people also hunted buffalo and caught smaller animals, birds and fish.

The villagers built two types of homes in the area. They built surface houses on the ground out of wooden posts, branches and dirt. They also dug pit houses into the ground. These had sod stacked on the sides, and posts held up the ceiling. Which type of house would you have liked to live in?

Artifacts show that these Woodland Indians traded with other groups. Archaeologists found obsidian (a shiny, black rock that Indians often used to make knives and arrowheads) from the Yellowstone National Park area. They also used clay to make pots, and they gathered Knife River flint for making tools. Menoken Indian Village is important because it has helped us learn what life was like for the Woodland Indians who lived in North Dakota long ago.

title: A Different Life
text:
“So, Jackson, what did you think of our study of the early American Indians last week?”

“You KNOW I loved it, Alana! I really liked learning about the tools the Paleo-Indians used. Those atlatls sound really cool. What an exciting life!”

“It may have been exciting, but it was also tiring, dangerous and uncomfortable. Can you imagine what it was like to sleep in tents during the winter, chasing after mammoths and buffalo and hoping to find enough to eat? I think I’d trade some of that adventure for a little comfort and safety any day.”

“You may be right, Alana. Did you know that the American Indians who came after the earlier groups made a lot of progress toward getting more comfort and safety? This week, we’ll learn about the American Indians who lived in North Dakota after the Paleo-, Archaic and Woodland Indians disappeared. These groups developed into more advanced cultures with an easier way of life.”

“You’re right, and I am glad to hear it! We’ll study about the American Indians who lived in our area from about 1200 to 1600. These groups may have been the descendants of the people we studied last week, or they may have traveled here from other parts of North America. One thing is clear. As time passed, they learned better ways to take care of their needs. They planted crops, settled in long-term villages, traded with other groups of American Indians and built durable homes that were more comfortable.”

“Oh, those are called earth lodges, Alana! I’ve visited the Fort Berthold Indian Reservation, and I got to see them from the inside.”

“That’s great, Jackson! Some people don’t know that not all Plains Indians lived in tepees year-round. Many of these early North Dakota Indians were hunters and great farmers, so they ate better than the groups we studied last week.”

“I do like to eat good food. I think that hunting would be a lot of fun, but not on an empty stomach!”

“Are you ready to learn more about North Dakota’s early people?”

“You know it!”

title: 10-Year-Old Boy Discovers Ancient Hunting Point
text:
Noah Cordle was a fifth grader on vacation when he made a discovery he will never forget. His family was enjoying New Jersey’s Long Beach Island when Noah got his hands on a 14,000-year-old stone tool called a Clovis point.

Noah was boogie boarding when he felt something sharp brush against his leg. He reached down and picked up what he thought was a giant shark tooth. He showed it to his parents and had it checked out by the New Jersey State Museum. The museum workers told Noah that the 2 1/2-inch black object was really a hunting tool used by the Paleo-Indians. These early hunters shaped the stone into a sharp point, tied it to a spear and used it to hunt buffalo and other animals.

Noah and his family took the discovery to the National Museum of Natural History in Washington, D.C. While he was there, Noah gave the Clovis point to the museum. Clovis points aren’t very common, but they have been found at sites across the country. When Hurricane Sandy hit Long Beach Island in 2012, workers brought new sand in to rebuild the beach. All this mixing of the sand may have been what brought the long-buried Clovis point to the surface just in time for Noah to make his amazing discovery!

title: Daily Life of the Plains Village Indians
text:
What was life like for the people who lived in North Dakota between about 1200 and 1600? We know that their cultures were more advanced than the earlier prehistoric people we studied last week and that they had an easier way of life. Let’s do a little exploring to find out more…

This time is known as the Plains Village Period. During this period, groups changed where and when they built shelter. Some groups lived in more permanent settlements. These houses were made of wooden poles covered with branches, grasses and sod. Other groups may have lived in one village during the winter and switched to a different village in the summer. Winter villages were located in forests, which offered more warmth during cold weather. Summer villages were near the rivers. As more time passed, these people moved less and began to live in the same area year-round.

Farming was an important way of feeding the tribes. Archaeologists have found proof that groups grew corn along the James River as early as the mid 1200s. This may have been the very first corn grown in North Dakota! Each family probably had their own garden. People who farmed also needed a place to store the food they grew. One way they stored food was in a cache pit. This was a large hole dug in the ground of homes. These pits were big enough for a person to fit in! The hole was lined with hay, and then beans, corn and other food could be stored inside. Farming helped a lot, but these Indians also hunted and gathered food as well.

During the early part of this time period, some groups along the James River still built burial mounds. Ancestors of the Mandan people were among the earliest to settle here during the Plains Village Period. Let’s take a look at a few special places in North Dakota where you can find evidence of these cultures.

Huff Indian Village

Early Mandan people built a village by the Missouri River around 1450. It’s near the present-day town of Huff, North Dakota. Archaeologists began studying the area in the early 1900s, and the site is now a National Historic Landmark.

Archaeologists believe that the Mandan Indians only lived there for about 20 years. The village was once home to around 100 houses, which were built in rows near the river. A 2,000-foot-long ditch and a wall made of tree trunks also surrounded the village. Why? It was used to help defend the village against enemies.

The Mandan Indians who lived in this village were buffalo hunters. They needed the meat, hides and bones of these large animals to keep them fed, clothed and sheltered. Like earlier Plains Village Indians, the Mandan Indians were farmers who planted corn, beans and squash. Villagers traded with friendly people who passed by the village.

Double Ditch Indian Village

The Double Ditch Indian Village was home to the Mandan Indians for about 300 years, from around 1490 to 1785. The village was near the mouth of the Heart River, just north of where Bismarck is today. It is named for two large ditches that surround the village. The village grew until about 2,000 people lived there. There were nine villages in the area that were home to as many as 10,000 Mandan people.

The earliest people to live in Double Ditch built rectangular homes like the ones at Huff Indian Village. Later people built round earth lodges, or dome-shaped houses made of branches and mud. Much like the Mandan of Huff Indian Village, they were hunters and farmers who lived in family groups and traded with the travelers visiting the area. When the men went on hunting trips, they brought tepees, or small tents made of buffalo skins, for shelter. They used bows and arrows as weapons, both for hunting and to defend against enemies.

Double Ditch was abandoned after fur traders brought smallpox to the region. Smallpox is a very dangerous disease that causes a high fever and a rash that leaves large pimples, or pock marks, on the skin. It spreads quickly and is often fatal (deadly). The Mandan who survived decided to leave Double Ditch and look for other places to settle.

Chief Looking’s Village

If you visit Pioneer Park in Bismarck, you can walk around the site of Chief Looking’s Village. The Mandan lived on this spot from about 1500 to 1600. Over 40 houses were built there. Some were rectangular, and some were circular. Archaeologists aren’t sure why the Mandan changed their building styles, but they are working to find out. Artifacts found at the site include pieces of pottery and baskets, buffalo bones and stone tools.

More About the Mandan

Even after these villages were abandoned, the Mandan still made North Dakota their home. Some Mandan could speak many languages, which helped them become known for trading. Women took care of the crops, homes and families. Men hunted for food and protected the village. Clans, or family groups, were an important part of Mandan life. Today, the Mandan people are part of the Three Affiliated Tribes, along with the Hidatsa and Arikara people.

title: Sometimes, Archaeologists Change Their Minds
text:
You have read about archaeologists and some of their discoveries, but did you know that these scientists sometimes change their minds?

An archaeologist is someone who studies the past by studying artifacts, or things left behind by humans. They use these artifacts to help answer questions about out how people lived long ago.

Sometimes, archaeologists have to be willing to change their minds. When new clues are discovered, they sometimes need to come up with a different way of looking at what they found. This means that archaeologists may change their ideas about what life was like for American Indians hundreds of years ago.

For years, an old ruin in Colorado’s Mesa Verde National Park was believed to be an ancient reservoir (lake where water is stored). It is known as Mummy Lake, and archaeologists who have studied the area have changed their minds about it. Some now believe that this sunken area was used for religious ceremonies. Others believe that Mummy Lake was really just an ancient ball court. Only time will tell which theory archaeologists accept.

Another discovery has made archaeologists question the date when humans began leaving Africa. For many years, archaeologists believed that humans began migrating from Africa between 60,000 and 80,000 years ago. Then a collection of early stone tools was discovered in the United Arab Emirates. The tools are believed to be around 125,000 years old. This makes archaeologists think that people could have been in Western Asia thousands of years earlier than we thought. As more studies are finished, archaeologists may once again change their minds.

title: Early Mandan Creation Legend
text:
The Mandan Indians had many legends, or stories they passed down from one generation to the next. One legend is a creation story that the Mandan told to explain how people first came to the Earth. There are different versions of creation stories, even among the same tribe!

The Mandan were the first people to live in the world. Before this time, they lived in a dark place under the Earth, near a huge lake to the east. One day, the people discovered the roots of a large grapevine hanging down into their home. One brave young warrior decided to climb the vine to see what he could see. He climbed up and came out of a hole into the light of the Earth.

Up on the Earth, the young man could see endless prairies stretched out along the banks of a river. He saw juicy grapes growing on the vine, along with herds of buffalo roaming the plains. He used his bow and arrow to kill one of the buffalo and learned that it was good for food. He gathered some grapes and climbed back down the vine to his underground home.

The young man let his people taste the grapes and told them of the rich, beautiful land on the Earth above. The people held a council and decided that they would climb up the vine to live on the Earth. They began climbing the vine. A large woman started up, but she was too heavy for the fragile vine. The chiefs said, “Do not go,” but she kept climbing. The vine broke, and the rest of the people were trapped below the Earth. Those already on the Earth were very sorry, but no more people could climb up. The new Earth tribe was small, but it settled near the river and began making new homes on North Dakota’s rich, fertile plains.

title: Dosha, New Friend!
text:
“Hey, Alana! What’s new?”

“Jackson, you should ask ‘Who’s new?’ instead. This is Natalia, our new classmate.”

“Hi, Natalia. Welcome!”

“Dosha, Jackson. That means ‘hello’ in the Hidatsa language. Our teacher told me that we’re learning about American Indians this week. Some of my ancestors were Hidatsa, so I already know some things about them.”

“That’s cool, Natalia! American Indians in some old movies say ‘Hau.’ Alana, do you know if that’s a real greeting or just something made up?”

“Good question, Jackson! ‘Hau’ was used as a greeting by some Sioux tribes, and the people who make movies and cartoons decided to use it. Do you know any other ways to say ‘hello,’ Natalia?”

“I do! The men of the Cheyenne Indians would greet each other by saying ‘Haaahe!’”

“I love it! Alana, I’m guessing that we’ll be learning about the Hidatsa, Sioux and Cheyenne tribes this week.”

“You guessed it, Jackson! Those tribes all lived in North Dakota. We’re studying the years between about 1600 and 1738. Just like the other American Indian groups we’ve studied so far, they were alike in some ways and different in others. They farmed, built villages, hunted buffalo and made both friends and enemies with other tribes. Natalia, I bet you know what animal helped make life easier for these tribes.”

“Horses! When the tribes received horses, hunting for buffalo became easier. I’m excited to learn even more about these tribes!”

“Me too, Natalia. I can’t wait to find out more about these amazing people! Alana, I bet you have at least one more cool word to teach us.”

“I do, Jackson. It’s ‘Peveeseeva.’ That’s the Cheyenne word for ‘Good day!’ Natalia, I know you’ll love social studies class as much as we do.”

“Thanks, Alana. My first day here has been great!”

title: Many Different Tribes Throughout the United States
text:
This is Jackson, here to remind you that while we will only study three American Indian tribes this week, there are many more tribes out there! There are over 560 federally recognized American Indian and Alaska Native tribes in the United States.

What does it mean to be “federally recognized”? It means that the tribe’s leaders have an official relationship with the U.S. government. This gives the tribe special rights, duties and powers. It also means that the tribe may receive money and special government services, such as education, health care, food and housing.

Recognized tribes are spread out in 33 different states. Some tribes are very small, while others have thousands of members, and members speak around 200 different tribal languages. Five of these tribes live in North Dakota. They are the Three Affiliated Tribes (Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation), the Spirit Lake Tribe, the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe, the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians and the Sisseton Wahpeton Oyate of the Lake Traverse Reservation.

Want to learn more about these groups? Get permission to visit the following website and take a peek! (http://www.indians.org/tribal-directory.html)

title: Hidatsa, Sioux and Cheyenne Indians
text:
Hidatsa

Three separate groups made up the Hidatsa tribe. Two of the groups first farmed the land near Devils Lake, and around 1600 they moved west to the Missouri River. They joined a third group and built villages. You can visit the Knife River Indian Villages to see where the Hidatsa lived. They most likely learned to grow crops from their neighbors, the Mandan. They also built large, round houses out of wood and mud, similar to the houses used by the Mandan. Each house was used by several families and was built and cared for by the women of the tribe. A family’s best horses were also kept inside the house! The men used the village as a home base, but they often left to hunt or to fight with other tribes.

The Hidatsa were good at trading. They grew extra crops to trade with anyone who came their way. Their villages became a major trade center for the area.

As in many other tribes, Hidatsa women grew crops and took care of family members. The Hidatsa men were known as great warriors. These warriors worked hard to protect families and prove their bravery. Leaders of the Hidatsa were chosen based on their strength and skill in battle.

Religious ceremonies were very important to the Hidatsa people. They made medicine bundles that were passed down from parents to children. These bundles were filled with special objects that they believed were connected to the spiritual world.

Sioux

The Sioux are one of most well-known groups of American Indians, but did you know that there are many branches of the Sioux family? The name Sioux comes from one of their enemies. The Ojibwa tribe gave the group a nickname of “snakes” or “enemies.” The French version of the word became their name.

The Sioux people call themselves Dakota, Lakota or Nakota. Each of these names means “friends,” or “allies,” and each branch is made up of family bands. The branches speak languages that are very similar to one another.

The Sioux once farmed and hunted in regions to the east of North Dakota. They moved west into North Dakota to get away from other tribes. The Lakota moved west, across the Missouri River and to the plains. Many Sioux began to rely on the buffalo for food, and the Lakota branch began moving around to follow the herds. The Dakota lived in the eastern part of the state and in present-day Minnesota. They hunted, fished and grew crops. The Nakota were one of the last groups to arrive. They stayed near the Missouri River in central North Dakota. The Nakota hunted buffalo and grew crops.

When most people picture a Plains Indian, they are likely thinking about a Lakota Sioux. The Lakota rode on horses and followed buffalo herds. They took everything they had with them from place to place. They lived in tepees year-round. The women were in charge of setting up the tepees, taking them down and carrying them as the group moved. The women of the tribe also cared for the children, cooked meals and made clothing. The men of the tribe were hunters and warriors. They did all of the hunting and worked to protect the group.

The Sioux were known for being great warriors who were feared by other tribes, but their families were the center of their lives. They considered their children to be sacred gifts. The Sioux belief that all living things are connected is found among many different tribes.

Cheyenne

The Cheyenne tribe came from present-day Minnesota and settled along the Sheyenne River in eastern North Dakota. The river was named after the Cheyenne Indians, but notice the different spellings!

At first, the Cheyenne were farmers who settled in one spot, raising corn and beans and making beautiful pottery. They lived in houses made of wooden poles covered with mud and grass. Over time, they counted on hunting buffalo to make sure their families had food, clothing, tools and a place to live. The Cheyenne way of life changed, and they went on more and more hunting trips. They began making tepees out of long poles covered with buffalo hide. Tepees could be rolled up like tents and carried with them when they moved into new places. The Cheyenne began to slowly move west.

During the 1700s, the Cheyenne began using horses for hunting, transportation and carrying supplies. Riding a horse made it easier to hunt buffalo. The Cheyenne may have received their first horses from French traders, and soon the tribe came to depend on the large animals for their new nomadic way of life.

In the next lesson, we’ll explore how life in North Dakota began to change after 1738. What do you think happened?

title: Woodrow Wilson Keeble
text:
Did you know that the Medal of Honor is our nation’s highest military award? It is given to members of the military who are very brave. In March 2008, President George W. Bush awarded the medal to a man named Woodrow Wilson Keeble. Keeble was from North Dakota, and he was the first full-blooded Sioux to receive the Medal of Honor.

Keeble was born on a Sioux reservation in South Dakota in 1917. He then moved to Wahpeton, North Dakota, where he attended the Wahpeton Indian School along with his brothers and sisters. Keeble became a star baseball player. He hoped to be a major league pitcher, but his National Guard unit was called into action during World War II. So, what did this amazing North Dakota soldier do to earn the Medal of Honor?

Keeble served in both World War II and the Korean War. He was injured in battle multiple times, earning four Purple Hearts. Keeble also earned the Distinguished Service Cross, the Silver Star and the Bronze Star for his bravery. Another soldier from his unit said that the “safest place to be was right next to Woody.”

After the war, Keeble went back to North Dakota and taught at the Wahpeton Indian School. Keeble suffered many health problems after he finished his military service. He died in 1982 at the age of 65. He was not forgotten, however, as he was awarded both the Medal of Honor and the Theodore Roosevelt Rough Rider Award in 2008. Woody Keeble is one of many North Dakotans who served our state and country with honor.

title: What is counting coup?
text:
Counting coup means to hit or touch an enemy without wounding or killing him. In some tribes, counting coup was how American Indians became known for courage and skill. Counting coup earned them even more respect than just killing an enemy. It showed that they could get close enough to touch an enemy from another tribe without being injured or killed. Counting coup also showed an enemy that he was not worth the trouble to kill him.

Often, American Indians would keep track of their brave acts by putting notches in a coup stick, showing how many times the warrior had counted coup in battle. He could then show the “proof” to his fellow warriors and family members.

This picture shows a war bonnet with coup (pronounced “coo”) sticks on display in the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery. photo by Tim Evanson

title: Keeper of the Fire
text:
Keeper of the Fire was a game played by many different American Indian tribes. To play, all you need is a blindfold, a few sticks and a group of friends.

One person is chosen as the fire keeper. Another person acts as chief. The rest of the group will be wood gatherers. The chief blindfolds the fire keeper, who sits on the ground. The chief then places three sticks in front of the fire keeper and says, “Wood gatherers, we need wood!” and then silently points to a player in the group. The wood gatherer sneaks up as quietly as possible to steal a stick from the fire. If the fire keeper hears the wood gatherer and tags him or her, that person is out. If the wood gatherer is able to steal the stick, the wood gatherers get a point. When all the sticks are gone, a new fire keeper is chosen and the game continues.

title: The Race for Fur
text:
Life changed in North Dakota during the 18th century. American Indians had lived on the land for thousands of years. Their lives changed when large numbers of hunters from Europe arrived during the 1700s. What brought Europeans to North Dakota, and what kept them coming back? Fur.

Fur had become very popular in Europe, and some of the finest clothing used beaver fur. European gentlemen wanted a fancy hat made of beaver fur because they looked the best. They were also waterproof. This made them even more useful because many parts of Europe had a lot of rain. Many people wanted these hats, so lots of hunters came to North America to hunt and trade for beaver pelts. (A pelt is the skin of an animal with the hair or fur still on it.)

How were beaver pelts made into hats? First, hatmakers would pull the thick, coarse hairs from the pelt and shave off the soft wool. Then they brushed the wool with a special mixture that had mercury in it. This mixture made the wool easier to mold into a shape. Heat and pressure formed the wool into material called felt. Once the felt was ready, hatmakers (hatters) would form it into the shape they wanted and add a lining. The hat was ready to sell!

Beaver hats were so popular that by the late 1600s, beavers in Europe were in danger of becoming extinct. What would European hatmakers do without a steady supply of beaver pelts? That’s where North America came in.

When the first Europeans came to North Dakota, one of the things they looked for was a good fur supply. Pierre Gaultier de Varennes et de La Verendrye was a French-Canadian explorer and military officer who came to North Dakota in 1738. He was the first known white man to arrive in the area. One of the reasons for his trip was to find enough beavers to make the fur companies rich. La Verendrye was happy to find that North Dakota was home to lots of fur-bearing animals, including beaver.

For the next 100 years, North Dakota was an important part of the North American fur trade. Many American Indians began trapping beavers themselves to trade with white fur traders. Fur traders were happy to offer cloth, tools, beads, guns, knives and other goods in exchange for the valuable beaver pelts. Fur companies also competed against each other for the right to trap beaver, as well as trade with the American Indians. The race for fur was on.

title: Pocket Change … Can You Spare a Quarter?
text:
How would you like to carry a little piece of history around in your pocket? Thanks to the U.S. Mint’s 50 State Quarters Program, you can do just that! In 1999, the U.S. Mint began making special quarters. Each state got to choose its own design for the “tails” side of the quarter. George Washington stayed on the “heads” side. The mint released a new state quarter every 10 weeks, so it took 10 years before we got to see them all.

North Dakota’s state quarter was released in 2006. The quarter shows two buffalo grazing on the prairie and the Badlands in the background. The year North Dakota became a state, 1889, also appears on the quarter.

The North Dakota state quarter isn’t the first U.S. coin to use the buffalo in its design. The Buffalo Nickel, or Indian Head Nickel, was made from 1913-1938. It shows the head of an American Indian on one side and a buffalo on the other side. The Buffalo Nickel honors our country’s first people and the role that the buffalo played in their lives. Sadly, the design of the nickel hasn’t held up very well, and the dates have rubbed off quickly. Over 1 billion of these coins were made, so keep your eye out for the Buffalo Nickel!

title: Explorers and Traders
text:
During the 1700s and 1800s, eager Europeans and Americans came to North Dakota hoping to make a fortune. They weren’t looking for gold or silver. They wanted animal pelts. They planned to take as many pelts as possible from North Dakota’s fur-bearing animals. Fur trading was a great way to get rich in the New World. The fur trade did not last very long, but it had a big impact on this part of the country. Trappers and traders explored the land looking for animals to hunt. They shared what they saw with cartographers (people who make maps) and government leaders. You might say that the fur trade helped put North Dakota on the map!

Hudson’s Bay Company

The Hudson’s Bay Company formed in 1670. It was the largest and most powerful fur trading company in North America. The company controlled the fur trade all over Canada and North Dakota. The king of England gave the Hudson’s Bay Company control over the fur trade in all the land under his rule. This meant that it was the only company allowed to trade furs in the British Empire. The Hudson’s Bay Company built trading posts and made deals with many American Indian tribes. The company gave supplies to Indians who brought furs to their trading posts.

La Verendrye

Pierre Gaultier de Varennes et de La Verendrye came to North Dakota in 1738 with several goals in mind. He and his sons hoped to learn more about the Mandan Indians and find a river or sea that led to the Pacific Ocean. This would make it quick and easy to bring goods from North America to Asia. La Verendrye also hoped to find good fur-producing areas in the region. He wanted to take some business away from the Hudson’s Bay Company. Pierre and his sons never found the river or sea they hoped to find. They did meet the Mandan Indians who lived in villages by the Missouri River. They also discovered that the area was very rich in fur. La Verendrye’s sons kept exploring the region. During their trip back home, they buried a lead plate near present-day Pierre, South Dakota. Children playing in the area 170 years later noticed something sticking out of the ground. They dug it up, and historians realized that it was the plate from the La Verendrye exploration!

North West Company

In 1779, a group of businessmen in Montreal, Canada, started the North West Company. They hoped to challenge the Hudson’s Bay Company and get involved in the fur trading business. The North West Company began by setting up trading posts in Canada, but it later spread into the Pacific Northwest and North Dakota. As the company grew, it took business away from the Hudson’s Bay Company. Both companies tried to convince the American Indian tribes to only work with them. After years of fighting over the fur trade, the North West Company and the Hudson’s Bay Company joined forces in 1821. The new, larger company kept the Hudson’s Bay name and still does business today.

Fur certainly made people notice what North America had to offer. In the early 1800s, American leaders made a deal that would almost double the size of the United States. This led to an expedition that set out to explore the western lands. Stay tuned till next week …

title: Sharing Public Space: Vitus Bering and Russian Colonies in Alaska
text:
Imagine traveling 6,000 miles over land with supplies for an expedition, and THEN sailing through frigid seas to look for a new world. This was the job given to Vitus Bering, a Danish navigator who sailed for the Russian navy. Peter the Great, czar (ruler) of Russia, asked Bering to explore the eastern coast of Russia. He was wondering if land connected Asia and North America.

Bering’s first trip began in 1725. After spending three years getting his supplies to eastern Russia, Bering sailed along the coastline. He didn’t see any land to the east, and he didn’t realize he was sailing in the narrow passage between Russia and Alaska. This waterway is now called the Bering Strait.

Bering led another expedition in 1741. This time his ship landed on Kayak Island, off the coast of Alaska. They explored some of the Aleutian Islands and met the native people there, the Aleut. He was the first European to arrive in present-day Alaska.

Bering died before returning to Russia, but his voyages paved the way for Russian settlements in North America. Many fur traders came to the area. In 1799 the Russian government established a fur-trading operation in Alaska. Furs from foxes, sea otters and seals were very valuable.

Unfortunately, the Russians took advantage of the native people just as some Europeans had done in settling New England. The Russians took over their lands and forced them to hunt for furs. They also brought new diseases, which killed many natives.

Today, the Aleut people continue to live along the western coast of North America, and their population has grown. What might have been different if the Russians and the Aleut had shared public space fairly? Where in your community is there a debate over public land? How should such debates be handled?

title: Beaver
text:
During the 1700s, the price of a single beaver pelt rose from around 5 shillings to 16 shillings (units of British money). Beavers had about tripled in value to trappers and traders, and this has made them an important part of our state’s history.

The beaver is the largest rodent in North America. Beavers are semiaquatic, which means they spend some of their time in water and some on land. They have large, webbed back feet and a wide, flat tail that help them swim. They also close their ears and nose while swimming to help keep the water out.

Beaver fur is short and shiny. Its color ranges from light brown to almost black. Beavers also have long front teeth that never stop growing. Beavers chew on wood to wear their teeth down. If they don’t, their teeth can grow so large that they can’t eat! Aren’t you glad humans don’t have that problem?

Beavers live in ponds, rivers and lakes across North Dakota and North America. They build dams made of mud, rocks and branches that they gnawed off with their teeth. The dams create ponds, where the beavers build their lodges. Lodges are also made of mud and branches, and they have tunnels and rooms inside. Beavers stay dry and protected from predators inside their lodges.

During the 1700s and 1800s, trappers weren’t worried about killing too many beavers. In fact, they often tried to take as many as possible from some areas in order to keep other fur-trading companies from using that spot. What do you think happened as a result? Beavers became nearly extinct in North Dakota. Once beaver hats became less popular and the trappers went away, their numbers began to rise. Today, beavers are a common sight throughout the state.

title: What is bartering?
text:
Bartering is trading goods or services without using money. Trappers and fur traders bartered with the American Indians in North Dakota for beaver pelts. In exchange for the pelts, the American Indians could get knives, sugar, coffee, cooking pots, tools, guns, gun powder, beads and other items. Even without money, both sides got what they wanted by bartering.

It was important for fur traders to be fair with American Indians. If traders cheated them by taking too many furs, American Indians might stop dealing with those traders and take their pelts to other traders. Successful bartering had to be fair to both sides, or the deal was off.

title: Don’t Forget Your Blanket!
text:
In 1780, the Hudson’s Bay Company began offering special blankets at their trading posts. These blankets were made of wool and had “points,” or blue lines woven near the edge, showing the blanket’s size. Larger blankets had more blue lines than smaller ones. This way, a trader could know how big the blanket was without having to unfold it.

The first point blankets were usually white with two sets of stripes, mainly in this order: green, red, yellow and blue. These blankets were often called “chief’s blankets,” and they became very popular with the American Indians. The wool was warm and easier to sew through than animal pelts. Blankets were also made into coats called capotes. Point blankets are still popular today and are for sale by Hudson’s Bay Company (now called HBC).

title: Bartering
text:
Beaver pelts were once used like cash to barter for other goods. Use the chart on this page to answer the following questions.

Questions

1. How many beaver pelts would it take to get two shirts and one pair of pants?

2. What size blanket would you be able to get for six beaver pelts?

3. If you wanted to trade for a musket and a new pair of boots, how many beaver pelts would you need?

4. If you had two beaver pelts, would you be able to purchase hatchets and pelt scrapers OR a 3-gallon kettle?

5. How many beaver pelts would it take to get 10 pounds of sugar?

title: Corps of Discovery
text:
In 1803, Robert Livingston and James Monroe were visiting France. They were working as U.S. foreign ministers. President Thomas Jefferson hoped they could convince Napoleon Bonaparte, who was the leader of France, to sell the port of New Orleans. Owning the port would help American businesses grow. Napoleon was fighting wars in Europe and needed money, so he offered to sell not only New Orleans to the United States, but also the entire Louisiana Territory—all for the amazingly low price of $15 million. This almost doubled the size of the United States for about 4 cents per acre!

The American people were excited, but no one really knew what this new land was like. Thomas Jefferson planned an expedition to explore this large area so that Americans could begin settling the country’s newest frontier. (An expedition is a trip that is taken to achieve a certain goal.)

Jefferson chose Meriwether Lewis to lead the expedition. Lewis was Jefferson’s personal secretary and an Army captain. Lewis asked one of his friends to go with him. He was another Army captain named William Clark. The captains gathered a group of 31 people to join them. Together, the group was called the Corps of Discovery. Jefferson gave the group three main goals. The goals of the expedition were to:

•Find a water route to the Pacific Ocean.

•Build relationships with any American Indians they met along the way.

•Record important information about the area’s soil, water, plants, animals, weather and insects.

Jefferson wanted the group to map the area, but he also wanted to know all about the people, plants, animals and geography of the country’s new land. Lewis worked with several scientists before leaving on the journey so that he would be prepared to study and record his findings along the way. Clark, who was a great journal keeper, was also a good choice to help head up the expedition because of his attention to detail. Sometimes, Lewis and Clark copied from each other’s journals! They wanted to make sure that important information was not lost or forgotten. With these two men in charge, the Corps of Discovery was in good hands.

title: Join the Club—Explore the World
text:
Does exploring the North Pole, climbing Mount Everest or landing on the moon sound exciting to you? Members of the world famous Explorers Club have done all these things — and many more!

The Explorers Club was started in New York City in 1904 and has been around ever since. The club’s goal is to keep the spirit of exploration alive. It encourages its members to explore the land, sea, air and space and to teach others about science and the world around them. Many famous explorers have belonged to the Explorers Club, including Sir Edmund Hillary, the first person to climb to the top of Mount Everest; Robert Peary, the first person to explore the North Pole; Roald Amundsen, the first person to explore the South Pole; and Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, the first men to land on the moon.

Today, the club has more than 3,000 members in 60 countries around the world. Members of the club plan and carry out expeditions in interesting places around the globe. Each year, the Explorers Club gives special awards from the Youth Activity Fund to high school and college students who are interested in science and who have shown great talent in some way. These students sometimes get to go on special expeditions with members of the club.

If you are interested in finding out more about the Explorers Club, ask a parent or teacher to help you visit www.explorers.org.

title: Exploring the Louisiana Purchase
text:
Heading West

Lewis and Clark began the expedition in May 1804. The Corps of Discovery started with three boats near St. Louis, Missouri, and headed west along the Missouri River. They used a map drawn by David Thompson, an explorer and mapmaker who worked for the North West Company. Thompson had explored the Knife River region in 1797 and created the first accurate map of the area.

When the group reached what is now Washburn, North Dakota, they built Fort Mandan. The corps stayed here during the long, cold winter. While at Fort Mandan, Lewis and Clark hired a man named Toussaint Charbonneau to be their guide and interpreter. An interpreter is someone who translates from one language to another. Charbonneau brought along his American Indian wife, Sacagawea.

Sacagawea was able to translate the Shoshone language into Hidatsa. Charbonneau would then translate Hidatsa into French. Lewis and Clark didn’t speak French, but some of the members of the Corps of Discovery did. They translated for Lewis and Clark. Can you imagine a conversation with that many translations? Without Sacagawea, communication would have been impossible in many cases.

Dangers and Hardships

During their journey west, the group faced many dangers and hardships. They were often hungry, even though they had brought along food and supplies. They planned their meals around whatever meat, fish, berries or plants they could find while traveling. When game (wild animals, birds or fish hunted for food) was scarce (in short supply) or bad weather kept them from hunting, the group was very hungry.

Paddling their boats along the Missouri River was dangerous work. The boats would often tip over, soaking both the travelers and their supplies. There were times when supplies ran low and food was difficult to find. Sickness and injuries were common. The group also faced strong rainstorms, blistering heat, biting mosquitoes and bitter cold. Wild animals, especially grizzly bears, were also known to bother the group.

‘Ocean in View!’

Eventually, Sacagawea helped the men trade with a Shoshone tribe for horses. They used the horses to cross the Rocky Mountains. They crossed the Continental Divide at Lemhi Pass, then crossed the Bitterroot Mountains and continued on to the Columbia River. In November 1805, the Corps of Discovery finally reached the Pacific Ocean. After the long, difficult journey, they looked at the waves breaking on the rocky shoreline with wonder and awe. Clark wrote in his journal, “Ocean in view! O! The joy!”

The group then spent a difficult winter at Fort Clatsop on what is now the Oregon coast. They faced a cold, drizzly rain that continued for all but 12 days of that long winter. Finally, in the spring of 1806, the Corps of Discovery began the trip back to St. Louis.

A Successful Journey

Lewis and Clark arrived back in St. Louis in September 1806. They had achieved two out of the three goals that President Jefferson set for them. They did not find a direct water route to the Pacific Ocean. However, Lewis and Clark did create good feelings between the Americans and some of the American Indian tribes they met. Both men also wrote detailed notes about all of the new plants, animals and soils they found between St. Louis and the Oregon coast. They even brought some plant samples back to show Jefferson. Lewis and Clark’s journals and hand-drawn maps gave Jefferson just the information he wanted. The long, hard journey was a success, and it opened the way for settlers to come to America’s newest frontier.

title: Sacagawea
text:
Sacagawea was born around 1788 into a Shoshone tribe in present-day Idaho. When she was about 12 years old, the Hidatsa tribe kidnapped her and took her to their village on the Missouri River. The tribe raised her and later sold her to the French-Canadian fur trader Toussaint Charbonneau as one of his wives.

While Lewis and Clark were at Fort Mandan, North Dakota, they hired Charbonneau as an interpreter. Sacagawea’s knowledge of the Shoshone and Hidatsa languages made her skills as an interpreter just as valuable as her husband’s.

Not long after she joined the group, Sacagawea gave birth to a boy, Jean Baptiste Charbonneau. Sacagawea carried the baby on her back as they traveled. Clark became very fond of the young boy, and the group felt that both mother and baby brought them good luck. He called the boy “Pompy,” or “Pomp.” Many American Indian tribes welcomed the group because of Sacagawea and her baby.

Sacagawea helped Lewis and Clark make the trip a success. When a boat tipped over along the journey, she remained calm and saved valuable items from being destroyed. Sacagawea also used her communication skills to barter with a Shoshone Indian tribe for horses and supplies the group needed. The leader of the Shoshone tribe turned out to be Sacagawea’s brother—she hadn’t seen him since she had been kidnapped!

On the trip back home, Sacagawea helped guide the expedition along trails she remembered from her childhood. When the corps traveled through North Dakota again in 1806, Charbonneau and his family left the group. Unfortunately, we don’t know much about Sacagawea after this. She had one more child, a girl named Lisette, but Sacagawea probably died in 1812. William Clark eventually raised Pomp. Sacagawea’s contributions to this amazing expedition will never be forgotten.

title: The Metis—A Blending of Two Cultures
text:
The Metis people were the children of European fur traders and the American Indian women they married. Metis is the French word for “mixed.”

As fur traders moved into the Red River area in eastern North Dakota and southern Canada, many chose to marry American Indian women. The children of these marriages were raised in a blended culture. They learned the Catholic religion and European way of life from their fathers. They also learned tribal religious customs and American Indian traditions from their mothers. This meant that the Metis people understood both ways of life. Many of them grew up to become successful traders, interpreters and buffalo hunters.

Twice each year, the Metis people met at Pembina, North Dakota, to begin their traditional buffalo hunts. These hunts provided meat, hides and other important items for the group to use and trade.

The Metis people were known for their Red River carts. The two-wheeled carts were made of wood fastened together with rope, buffalo hide and buffalo sinew. A horse or ox would pull them. The carts were used to haul furs, tools, pemmican, point blankets and anything else they wanted to trade. The Metis people could remove the carts’ wheels and make them into rafts for floating down rivers or into sleds for hauling goods through the snow.

In 1821, there were around 500 Metis people living near Pembina. By 1870, that number had grown to more than 12,000. Today, people with Metis heritage can be found in North Dakota, Minnesota and Canada.

title: What is pemmican?
text:
Pemmican is an energy-packed food that the Metis first made using buffalo meat, berries and fat. Making pemmican was a way for them to use all the meat from a buffalo before it went bad. It was also easy to carry.

The Metis made pemmican by cutting buffalo meat into long strips and drying it on racks in the sun or over an open fire. Then they pounded the dried meat into a paste. They stuffed the paste into a bag made of buffalo hide and mixed it with dried berries and melted buffalo fat. They sewed the bag shut, and the pemmican would stay fresh for a year before spoiling! European fur trappers and traders learned to make pemmican from the Metis, and they rarely left home without taking some with them.

People still make pemmican today. See if you can find a recipe and try it for yourself!

title: Pembina
text:
Pembina is an American Indian word for cranberries. It is also a city a few miles south of the U.S.-Canadian border. Pembina was one of the first European settlements in North Dakota, and its first trading post was built in 1797. Irish and Scottish families arrived there in 1812 to build a more permanent settlement.

Over the years, companies like the North West Company and the Hudson’s Bay Company built trading posts at Pembina. Many Metis people also lived nearby and used it as a base for their trading. North Dakota’s first public school was built in Pembina in 1875. Today Pembina is a small city of about 600 people, and it is a popular place to cross the border between the U.S. and Canada. When you visit, be sure to go up in the observation tower at the Pembina State Museum!
