title: The Fur Trade Continues …
text:
“Hey, Jackson, I love your hat!”

“It’s a beaver hat, Alana. My dad and I were searching online, and we found this. Well, it isn’t really made of beaver fur, but it sure looks like it.”

“Very cool, and you should be happy to know that we aren’t done studying the fur trade. After Lewis and Clark finished their expedition in 1806, people became even more interested in moving out West.”

“That’s true. I know that several fur companies set up trading posts right here in North Dakota. In 1809, Manuel Lisa and his Missouri Fur Company built Fort Lisa on the Missouri River. That was just north of the Mandan and Hidatsa villages. In 1828, John Jacob Astor’s American Fur Company built Fort Union in western North Dakota. It became one of the most famous trading posts.”

“Yes, Jackson. Fort Union stayed in business for a long time. It was open from 1828 until 1867. We’ll learn more about Fort Union later on. The American Fur Company also built two more forts in North Dakota—Fort Clark in 1830 and Fort Berthold in 1845. All of these fur trading posts brought trappers and traders into parts of North Dakota that only American Indians had seen before.”

“The different fur companies and traders competed against each other. I bet these trappers shared many exciting stories about North Dakota with friends and family when they got back home!”

“People also got excited about coming to North Dakota because the area was no longer just ‘blank space’ on the map. Lewis and Clark drew in some of the landmarks in the area. Then a famous French mapmaker named Joseph N. Nicollet did his part to add even more detail to the basic maps that the Corps of Discovery drew. In 1838, the U.S. government asked Nicollet to explore the Mississippi River basin and make a detailed map of the area. Respected explorer John C. Fremont joined him. These men spent the next two years exploring the land that later became Minnesota, North Dakota and South Dakota.”

“I read about that, Alana. Experts at the time said it was the most accurate map of the area. Having such a good map made people even more willing to settle the wild frontier.”

title: Deer Ticks in the ‘Lyme’ Light
text:
Have you ever heard the phrase “be in the limelight”? It means to have people’s attention and interest. Well, you may be interested in a tiny creature that could ruin your time outdoors. Deer ticks carrying Lyme disease have been discovered in some eastern North Dakota counties. Deer ticks are small insects that can make people sick with Lyme disease, which causes aches, fever, nerve pain, arthritis and heart problems.

Ticks bury their heads into people’s skin. A tick needs to be on someone for around 24 hours for the disease to be spread. If you find a tick on you, use tweezers to gently grab the tick as close to the skin as possible, and carefully pull it out. Do your best to get the entire tick out of the skin at once. Then clean the bite with rubbing alcohol. Put the tick in a plastic bag, wrap it in tape or flush it down the toilet. Do not squeeze or smash it, or you might still catch the disease.

Wearing long sleeves, long pants and long socks is the best way to keep these hungry critters off your skin. Certain types of insect repellent can also work. Remember to check your skin for ticks after you return from any outdoor adventure. Being careful and keeping the danger of deer ticks in the “Lyme” light could keep you from getting sick!

title: Early Settlement of Dakota Territory
text:
Dakota Becomes a Territory!

The Louisiana Purchase meant that our state became part of America, but it didn’t have much of a government. In March 1861, President James Buchanan signed a law creating the Dakota Territory. The Dakota Territory was made up of what is now North and South Dakota, along with much of Montana and Wyoming. Abraham Lincoln became president, and he chose William Jayne to be the first governor of the territory. Gov. Jayne divided the territory into districts and set up elections. He was also in charge of American Indian relations, tax collections and the militia (army of citizens who volunteer in an emergency). Elections were held for the Territorial Legislature, the group of people in charge of making new laws.

Government records show that by 1860 about 2,400 people were living in the Dakota Territory who were not American Indians. More than half of these people lived in the Pembina area. Most of the others lived near Yankton, which was about 500 miles away. These people needed a government to keep order, make laws, build roads, start schools and help the new settlers have a safe, stable home.

The Homestead Act of 1862

After Dakota became a territory, Abraham Lincoln signed a law that made it possible for people with little money to own land. This law was the Homestead Act of 1862, and it said that anyone who was at least 21 years old and the head of a household could buy 160 acres of land in the new frontier. The cost was only $18, or about 11 cents an acre. Immigrants (people who move to a new country), single women and even former slaves could become homesteaders. To buy the land, people had to “prove up” within five years. This meant that the homesteader had to live on the plot for five years, “improve” it by adding a home, and grow crops.

At first, many of the settlers came from the Eastern states to claim land. Later, most of the settlers came all the way from Europe. No matter where they were from, the eager settlers were in for a lot of work.

Besides running a farm, settlers faced many obstacles that made homesteading difficult and sometimes even impossible. First, they had to break the hard prairie sod. Then they had to plant crops and care for them. At the end of the growing season, they needed to harvest and sell the crops at the market. The settlers also faced droughts, floods, hailstorms, blizzards, prairie fires and occasional fights with American Indians. Some years brought clouds of grasshoppers that swept across the plains and ate nearly everything in their path, including crops, clothing, leather boots and wooden furniture. Even with these challenges, if the homesteaders worked hard and had some luck, they made money.

The Homestead Act was in effect for 123 years, and more than 4 million people filed for homesteads all over the frontier. About 40 percent of these people were successful. People who “proved up” their land in five years received a patent, which was signed by the president of the United States. A patent is an official document that shows ownership. This piece of paper was the reward for much hard work and determination. These brave homesteaders, including those who did not succeed, helped settle the great state of North Dakota.

title: Rising Tensions
text:
As trappers, traders and settlers started making themselves at home in the Dakotas, tensions between the American Indians and the newest residents began bubbling up.

Arikara War of 1823

As Lewis and Clark prepared to leave Fort Mandan on their journey, they met some Arikara Indians. They learned that Arikara Chief Eagle Feather was interested in meeting President Jefferson. The captains made plans for the chief to visit Washington, D.C. Eagle Feather spent several months in the East, but nearly a year after leaving his village, he died and was buried in Virginia.

The Arikara were angry about the death of their chief and blamed the Americans for his death. In June 1823, the owner of the Rocky Mountain Fur Company, William Ashley, and his men were attacked as their boats neared an Arikara village on the Grand River. The Arikara killed about 15 of Ashley’s men and took the goods Ashley had planned to trade. U.S. soldiers were sent to deal with the Arikara during the next two months. They fought a few small battles, and then the Arikara slipped away quietly in the night, taking everything they had with them.

Dakota War of 1862

In August 1862, four young Dakota (also called Sioux) Indians killed five settlers in Minnesota. Some of their tribe members then decided to drive all the white settlers out of the area. They attacked nearby settlements, and many settlers were killed. The U.S. Army sent soldiers to fight back against the Dakota. Over the next few months, Americans and the Dakota Indians fought several bloody battles. By the time the Dakota surrendered, the U.S. had captured over 1,000 Indians. Many settlers and Dakota were killed during the conflict. In December 1862, the U.S. tried and executed 38 Dakota warriors.

The Arikara and Dakota wars marked the beginning of bad feelings and fighting between many American Indians and white settlers in the Dakota Territory for years to come.

title: Fort Union
text:
Fort Union was a fur-trading post in western North Dakota near the place where the Missouri and Yellowstone rivers meet. It was built in 1828 by John Jacob Astor’s American Fur Company and was a busy, exciting spot. The fort was the center of business and social interaction for the entire area. Thousands of furs were brought in each year, and thousands of dollars in goods were traded or sold. Around 200 people worked at Fort Union making these trades happen.

American Indians came to Fort Union to trade their furs for the goods they needed and wanted. The American Fur Company built this post because it wanted to make money by doing business with the many American Indian tribes in the area. Assiniboine, Dakota, Mandan and Hidatsa Indians all brought buffalo, beaver and other furs to trade at Fort Union. They exchanged these furs for clothes, guns and many other items.

Fort Union stayed open longer than any other fur-trading post in the western United States. It was in use from 1828 until it was bought by the U.S. Army and closed in 1867. The Army tore down the fort, but it has since been rebuilt on its original site near Williston. Visitors can go there to see what life was like during the glory days of the North American fur trade.

title: What was the ‘Yellowstone’?
text: John Jacob Astor wanted his American Fur Company to be the number one fur company in America. To get ahead of the others, he decided to try a new form of transportation. He had a special steamboat built just for navigating the Missouri River. The name of his steamboat was the Yellowstone. The large paddle-wheel steamboat had a cabin high above the deck so that the pilot could see rocks or rough waters up ahead. The steamboat also had a huge deck to hold all the furs and trade goods that would be hauled to and from Fort Union. When it arrived at Fort Union in 1832, it became the first steamboat to travel that far on the Missouri River. The Yellowstone was one of Astor’s biggest weapons in the fur trade, and it helped him become even more successful.

title: Smallpox—Anything BUT a Small Problem!
text:
Smallpox is caused by the variola virus and gets its name from the blisters, or pocks, that form on the skin. People with smallpox also have fevers and aches.

Most children in the U.S. received the vaccine for smallpox until the mid-1970s, when the World Health Organization said that smallpox had been wiped out. A vaccine is a small dose of a virus or germ that is given to a person to keep him or her from getting the real disease later on.

Smallpox killed many Dakota Indians in the 1780s and again in the late 1830s. The Mandan Indians were infected when white traders brought smallpox to Fort Clark. The Mandan had no natural immunity to the disease and had not received the smallpox vaccine. The disease killed about 90 percent of the Mandan Indians. This made American Indians even more distrustful of white settlers.

title: Homestead Hardships
text:
Life was hard for the settlers who came to the Dakota Territory hoping to “prove up” on the land and buy a homestead. You may have heard of Laura Ingalls Wilder, the author of the “Little House” books. She and her husband, Almanzo, tried their hand at homesteading in the Dakotas during the late 1800s. Read this short paragraph about their experiences written by their daughter, Rose Wilder Lane. Then answer the following questions.

“Conditions had changed when I was born; there was no more free land. Of course, there never had been free land. It was a saying in the Dakotas that the Government bet a quarter section against fifteen dollars and five years’ hard work that the land would starve a man out in less than five years. My father won the bet. It took seven successive years of complete crop failure, with work, weather and sickness that wrecked his health permanently, and interest rates of 36 per cent on money borrowed to buy food, to dislodge us from that land. I was then seven years old.”

(Rose Wilder Lane, from “American Life Histories: Manuscripts from the Federal Writers’ Project, 1936-1940,” Library of Congress)

1. What does Rose mean when she says that her father “won the bet”?

2. What were some of the challenges Rose’s family faced in trying to homestead land in the Dakotas?

3. Why did Rose’s family need to borrow money? How much interest was charged on the money they borrowed?

4. If Rose’s family had lived on the land for seven years and it only took five years to prove up on a homestead, why do you think they still chose to leave?

title: Looking Back: American Indians of North Dakota
text:
This week, we’ll review what we’ve learned about the earliest residents of North Dakota.

Paleo-Indians
(9500 B.C.–5500 B.C.)

The Paleo-Indians first came to the North Dakota area around 9500 B.C. They were nomadic, meaning they moved from place to place, looking for food. They followed large animals, such as mammoths and buffalo. They made spears to kill these animals for the meat to feed the group. The Paleo-Indians also ate roots, plants, seeds and insects. They used animal skins for clothing and shelter.

Archaic Indians
(5500 B.C.–500 B.C.)

The Archaic Indians were descendants of the Paleo-Indians, and they also lived in small, nomadic groups. They used different weapons and formed their own way of life. This group depended much more on the atlatl than the Paleo-Indians, and they made tools like axes and fishhooks. The Archaic people also learned to make baskets to store the seeds, berries, nuts and fruit that they gathered for food.

Woodland Indians
(500 B.C.–A.D. 1000)

The Woodland Indians were travelers, but they also built homes and returned to these settlements at the end of their hunting and gathering trips. Their homes were made of wooden poles covered with bark, grass or animal skins. The Woodland people made large clay pots and used the bow and arrow. They often followed buffalo herds and hunted them for food, tools, clothing, blankets and shelters. When people died, some Woodland groups built large mounds over the graves. Menoken Indian Village is a Woodland Indian site.

Plains Village Indians
(A.D. 1200–A.D. 1600)

Groups of the Plains Village Period settled in more permanent villages and planted crops. Those who lived along the James River grew corn during the mid 1200s. During this time, they stored extra food in cache pits in the ground. They hunted and gathered food as well. Early Mandan people lived at the Huff Indian Village from around A.D. 1450 to A.D. 1470. Here, a long ditch surrounded about 100 houses. Villagers hunted buffalo, planted crops and traded with other groups. Mandan Indians also lived in the Double Ditch Indian Village. The village was first built around A.D. 1490, and the families lived in rectangular houses. People who lived there later built round earth lodges, or dome-shaped houses made of branches and mud. They also used tepees when they went on hunting trips. People lived in Double Ditch until smallpox forced them to leave many years later.

Later Plains Tribes

Hidatsa

The Hidatsa first farmed the land near Devils Lake. Later on, they built villages along the Knife River. Hidatsa women grew the crops and took care of the homes. The men were known as great warriors, and leaders of the tribe were chosen for their skill in battle. Hidatsa villages became important trade centers.

Sioux

Branches of the Sioux tribe called themselves Dakota, Lakota or Nakota. Many Sioux relied on the buffalo for food. The Dakota and Nakota hunted buffalo and grew crops. The Lakota began following the herds. They lived a nomadic life and used horses to follow buffalo herds. They brought everything they had with them as they moved from place to place. They even brought their houses. The Sioux were great warriors who were feared by other American Indians, but they put their families at the center of their lives.

Cheyenne

The Cheyenne tribe settled along the Sheyenne River in eastern North Dakota. They began as farmers, but they started using horses around the mid-1700s to chase the buffalo herds. The Cheyenne once lived in houses made of wooden poles, mud and grass. When they began hunting buffalo, they used houses they could bring with them. They made tepees out of long poles covered with buffalo hide. The Cheyenne slowly moved west, along with the buffalo.

Life changed for the Indian tribes in the mid-1700s, when white traders and settlers began arriving in North Dakota.

title: The Fur Trade Takeover
text:
Hudson’s Bay Company

The Hudson’s Bay Company was the largest and most powerful fur trading company in North America. The company formed relationships with many American Indian tribes.

Fur Trading Posts:

•Turtle River Post – in the east, just south of the Forest River

•Fort Daer – in the far northeast corner

La Verendrye

Pierre Gaultier de Varennes et de La Verendrye first came to North Dakota in 1738. He is the first known white man to explore the area. La Verendrye and his sons hoped to learn more about the Mandan Indians and find a river or sea that led to the Pacific Ocean. This would make it easy to bring goods from North America to Asia. Verendrye also hoped to find places in the region that would provide a lot of fur, which would take business away from the Hudson’s Bay Company. La Verendrye never found the river he was searching for, but he and his sons did meet and study the Mandan Indians. They also discovered that the area was rich in fur.

North West Company

In 1779, the North West Company hoped to challenge Hudson’s Bay Company. The North West Company began by setting up trading posts in Canada, but it later spread into the Pacific Northwest and throughout North Dakota. The two companies joined forces in 1821 and used the Hudson’s Bay name.

Fur Trading Posts:

•Grand Forks – in the east, just north of the Goose River

•Pembina River House – in the northeast corner

•Park River Post – in the east, north of Park River

American Fur Company

John Jacob Astor founded the American Fur Company. He wanted to compete with the Hudson’s Bay Company and the North West Company. Fort Union became the longest-running fur post in the western United States. Astor had the steamboat Yellowstone built to travel to Fort Union to pick up furs.

Fur Trading Posts:

•Fort Berthold – on the Missouri River, east of where it meets the Little Missouri River

•Fort Clark – on the Missouri River, south of the Knife River

•Fort Union – in the west, near the place where the Missouri and Yellowstone rivers meet

•Sheyenne River Post – in the southeast on the Sheyenne River

•Kipp’s Post – in the west, near the place where the Missouri and White Earth rivers meet

Missouri Fur Company

Trader Manuel Lisa built posts throughout the northern Louisiana Purchase region. His post in North Dakota was built in 1809.

Fur Trading Post:

•Fort Lisa – on the Missouri River, north of the Knife River

Directions: Use what you read in this lesson to locate the fur-trading posts on the map. Label each post, and then color in the circle with the correct fur company color. Remember to use the legend!

title: Establishing a Territory
text:
Use what you learned from past weeks to help you fill in the blanks below.

Lewis and Clark Expedition

President Thomas _____________________ chose Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to lead the Corps of ____________________ on an expedition to explore the new Louisiana Purchase. The goals of the expedition were to:

The group began its journey in May 1804 near St. Louis, Missouri. They returned in September 1806. Lewis and Clark didn’t find a direct water route to the Pacific, but they did achieve the other two goals of the expedition. It also opened the way for settlers to come to America’s newest frontier.

North Dakota Becomes a Territory!

In March 1861, President Buchanan signed a law creating the Dakota Territory. Name the future states that were a part of this territory: ____________________________ ________________________ ____________________________ _________________________

The territorial governor was in charge of American Indian relations, tax collections and the militia (volunteer army of citizens). Who was the first territorial governor?
______________________________________________________

The Homestead Act of 1862

Shortly after the Dakota Territory was formed, President Lincoln signed a law that made it possible for people with little money to own land. This law was called the Homestead Act of 1862. It said that any adult who was at least 21 years old and was the head of a household could buy a 160-acre plot of land along the new frontier.

In order to “prove up” on the land, the homesteader had to:

• Live on the plot for ___________________________ years. • “Improve” it by adding a ____________________________.

• Grow __________________________________ on the land.

The Homestead Act was in effect for 123 years, and more than 4 million people filed for homesteads. Only about 40 percent of these people were successful. The increase of settlers led to conflicts with many American Indian tribes.

title: Changes Are Coming!
text:
“Jackson, is that another new hat you’re wearing?”

“Absolutely! I call this one my ‘All Aboard’ hat.”

“With a hat like that you must have been reading up on this week’s topic.”

“You mean the railroad coming to North Dakota? You’re right, Alana! I just love trains. That’s why I bought this great hat. My collection is getting pretty big, and each one has something to do with North Dakota’s history.”

“That’s pretty neat, Jackson, but if you really want to impress me, tell me something about the old railroads in North Dakota.”

“Sure! Did you know that when the Homestead Act of 1862 was first signed into law, it usually took settlers from the East months to travel to the

Dakota Territory to start settling their claims? And the trip wasn’t an easy one. They traveled over bumpy ground in wagons pulled by smelly oxen. When the railroad came to North Dakota, it gave settlers a new way to come to this area that was faster and more comfortable.”

“That’s right, Jackson. The first railroad reached the Dakota Territory in 1871. Not long after that, new towns started popping up. Fargo was one of the first towns built along the Red River. Bismarck followed soon after along the Missouri River. These towns had food, supplies, housing and other services that railroad workers and settlers needed.”

“I also learned that these early towns used to be rowdy places. The people who built the train tracks and the earliest homesteaders could get pretty wild!”

“Yes, when the railroad began making its way through North Dakota, it brought more than just new settlers and a faster way to travel. It also brought problems. Most of the American Indians who lived in the Dakota Territory did not like the idea of noisy, dirty trains chugging through their homeland.”

“I can understand that, Alana. Red Cloud, a Lakota Indian chief, said the men from the East came to rob the American Indians.”

“Not only that, Jackson, but the government also started taking away the land that the American Indians had been living on and using. It wasn’t long before the tribes were forced to move onto new land that our government had set aside for them. These areas were called reservations.”

“It looks like railroads brought both good and bad changes to North Dakota.”

title: The Disappearing Honeybee
text:
Just like the buffalo that once vanished from the Great Plains, another important creature is disappearing right before our eyes. That creature is the honeybee. During the 1940s, beekeepers in the United States cared for around 6 million honeybee colonies. There are only about 2.5 million today.

You may not think that losing bees is such a bad thing, especially if you are afraid of getting stung. However, if you like to eat you should know that honeybees are very important to many of the crops we use for food. Bees carry pollen from one plant to another, making it possible for the plant to make the food we eat. Fruit, nut and vegetable plants all need bees to bring them pollen. If that doesn’t happen, the plants can’t produce food. If they don’t make food, farmers have no crops to sell to the public. They lose money, and people will have less to eat.

What is causing the strange disappearance of the honeybee? Some scientists believe that insecticides are the main cause. Insecticides are chemicals used to kill harmful insects. Not too long ago, scientists from Harvard University found that certain insecticides might damage the honeybees’ nervous systems. This causes bees to leave their hives during the cold winter months, and they die. Scientists are still learning about why honeybees are dying. Until then, we can help by planting flowers that attract honeybees.

title: American Indians Uprooted
text:
“The life of white men is slavery. They are prisoners in towns or farms. The life my people want is a life of freedom. I have seen nothing that the white man has, houses or railways or clothing or food, that is as good as the right to move in the open country.” —Lakota Chief Sitting Bull

The American Indians were the first people to live in the wide-open spaces of North Dakota. They had great respect for the land and the way that nature provided for their needs. As trappers and traders trickled in, many North Dakota tribes learned to get along with them. They even started depending on traders to provide them with valuable supplies. Once the Homestead Act was signed, settlers began making their way to North Dakota and the Great Plains area, hoping to build a better life. The U.S. government saw the land as an important resource, especially when gold was discovered in the Black Hills and the soil in the area was found to be good for farming.

While the United States owned the land, American Indian tribes had been living there for thousands of years. Most tribes were not interested in giving up their homeland to homesteaders, gold miners or railroad owners. The government passed laws and signed treaties (official agreements) with tribes. These agreements were meant to force American Indians to live on reservations. The American Indian land “left over” could then be sold to settlers. Many promises that the government made were broken. White settlers were allowed on Indian lands, and supplies never reached the reservations. When Indian attacks did happen, rumors spread that all American Indians were dangerous.

As more railroads reached across the prairie, thousands of settlers moved into the area. During the time that the railroads were built, the buffalo herds that provided American Indians with food and shelter were being destroyed. Railroad workers often killed the buffalo for food, but hunters also shot the animals for fun and left the bodies to rot. By the late 1880s, the number of buffalo dropped from around 30 million to fewer than 1,000. Without the buffalo herds, the American Indians of the Great Plains came close to starvation. Some government and military leaders knew that without buffalo herds, American Indians would be forced to accept life on a reservation. These leaders encouraged settlers and railroad workers to kill as many buffalo as possible in order to make that happen.

Living on a reservation also meant that American Indians had to give up their nomadic way of life and find other ways to survive. Many tribes began to farm, but much of the land they were given by the government was not good for growing crops.

American Indians and the U.S. government fought many fierce battles over the tribes’ rights to stay on their homeland. In the end, the government won, and the American Indians were forced onto reservations. In North Dakota, the Spirit Lake Tribe and Lake Traverse reservations opened in 1867. Fort Berthold became a reservation in 1870, and the Turtle Mountain Indian Reservation opened in 1882. The Standing Rock Sioux Reservation was created from the larger Great Sioux Reservation in 1889. American Indians lost much of the land they called home, and they eventually lost much of their way of life.

title: The Railroad Changes Everything
text:
The railroad first reached North Dakota in 1871. This made it easier than ever for homesteaders to enter the territory. With the new railroad, the quiet, buffalo-covered plains were soon dotted with working farms and communities. By 1886, over 100,000 people had flocked to the Dakota Territory. For most communities, the town came first, and then the railroad followed.

The first railroad to enter North Dakota was the Northern Pacific Railway. The U.S. government gave the company 50 million acres of land throughout the northern states and territories. The government hoped the rail company would build railroad lines. The company built its first North Dakota line on some land between the Red River and Bismarck. It then traveled through the Badlands and eventually, all the way to the Pacific Ocean. The Northern Pacific also built several branch lines. Branch lines are shorter sets of tracks that connect the main line to smaller stations.

The Great Northern Railway, also known as the Manitoba Railroad, began laying track here in 1880. Eventually, the Great Northern Railway built two lines heading northwest from Wahpeton and west from Grand Forks. Branch lines headed north toward the Canadian border, making this railroad very popular in the northern part of the state. The Great Northern kept adding track until it also reached the West Coast.

Much of the land (especially in the east) was fairly flat, which made it easy to lay track. But railroad companies often had to build snow fences along the lines to protect the tracks from North Dakota’s harsh winters. What other challenges might be found in our geography? The railroad connected North Dakota farmers to Minneapolis, Minnesota. Large grain mills waited there to grind our wheat into flour. Without the railroads, the farmers would have had no fast, cheap way to get their grain to market. The railroads brought in settlers, connected cities and made it possible for farmers to succeed in the new Dakota Territory.

title: Elizabeth Bodine, A Helper to Many
text:
Elizabeth Bodine was a remarkable woman. She was born in Poland in 1898, but she later immigrated to the United States and settled in the Minot area. Bodine believed that going to school was one of the most important ways to prepare for a good life. We know this about her because she pushed all of her 18 children to continue their education after finishing high school.

Bodine had 10 sons and eight daughters. All 10 of her sons finished college, and six of her daughters attended college. Her other two daughters went to technical schools, where they learned business skills. At least one member of Bodine’s family attended Minot State University for 26 years in a row. She had a great influence over her family when it came to education!

Bodine was also very concerned about the needs and well-being of all people. During World War II, she shipped boxes of food and clothing to her family members living in Poland. During the Vietnam War, she collected clothing and sent it to relieve those suffering in Vietnam. She also spent much of her free time helping American Indians in the Belcourt area.

Bodine was chosen as the North Dakota Mother of the Year in 1968. She was also awarded the North Dakota Theodore Roosevelt Rough Rider Award in 1979.

title: How did railroads help bring us time zones?
text:
It may seem strange, but each town or city in the United States used to set its own time. This meant that the time could vary from town to town. If you asked what time it was, you could get different answers! That is, until the late 1800s …

Once the railroads spread all over the country, trying to figure out when trains would leave or arrive was very confusing. Can you imagine trying to set up train schedules when every station used a different time?

In 1883, the major U.S. railroad companies met and made a plan to solve this problem. They divided the country into time zones. Every town and city in each zone was lined up to have the same time. In 1918, Congress passed a law that made these time zones official. They were, from east to west in the Continental United States, the Eastern, Central, Mountain and Pacific time zones. We still use these time zones today.

title: Elk
text:
One of North Dakota’s most noble mammals is the elk. Elk are related to deer, but they are much bigger and more powerful. Elk stand four to five feet tall (not counting the antlers) and weigh between 500 and 700 pounds! The male elk uses antlers to fight off enemies or to compete with other males for the attention of the females. Elk have a reddish-brown coat with a lighter, creamy-colored belly and rump. Elk are also known as wapiti, a Shawnee Indian word meaning “white deer.” The elk’s coat is usually lighter in the spring.

In North Dakota, elk are found in the Killdeer Mountains and the Little Missouri National Grassland. They eat grass, flowers and small shrubs. An elk can eat as much as 20 pounds of vegetation in one day. Have you ever spotted an elk?

title: What time is it?
text:
This week, we learned that the Continental United States is divided into four time zones. You can use a time zone map as you travel across the United States. Each new time zone you enter either adds one hour to or subtracts one hour from the clock. If you travel east, you move your clock ahead one hour each time you enter a new time zone. If you travel west, you move your clock back one hour each time you enter a new time zone.

Using the time zone map, answer the following questions:

You live in Massachusetts, and your grandparents live in Colorado. If your grandparents ask you to call them when it’s 5:00 p.m. in Colorado, what time will it be for you?

North Dakota falls into which two time zones? Bismarck is located in which time zone?

How many hours difference is there between the time in California and Illinois? In which time zone is each state located?

The president lives in Washington, D.C., in the Eastern Time Zone. You want to watch a special live broadcast of a presidential speech that begins at 10:00 a.m. If you live in eastern North Dakota, what time will the speech be on at your house?

According to the map, which time zone do you live in?

text: This week, we learned that most of the American Indians living in North Dakota during the 1800s were removed from their homeland and forced to live on reservations. Describe how you think life changed for these people as a result. What parts of their lives would not work as well after moving to a reservation? How did the buffalo disappear and what impact did this have on the American Indians?

title: The Great Dakota Boom
text:
Between 1878 and 1890, North Dakota became a very popular place. There were so many people who wanted to move here that the population grew from around 16,000 to more than 191,000 in just over 10 years! These years are called the Great Dakota Boom. A boom is a time when the economy or population grows. What caused the Great Dakota Boom? Let’s find out!

The Homestead Act of 1862 made it possible for people without much money to settle on 160 acres of land and make it their own in five years. The promise of cheap land brought in people from the eastern states, as well as people from Europe. Many Europeans were excited to have a chance to own 160-acre farms, which were much larger than the smaller pieces of land they had in Europe. The greatest number of immigrants came from Scandinavia (Norway, Sweden and Denmark), Germany and Czechoslovakia.

The conditions in many of these European countries also made life in North Dakota look very inviting. In their home countries, many of the people were poor, hungry and unemployed. They also did not have freedom of speech or religion. The chance to own their very own land was a dream come true for many of these immigrants.

Once the railroad entered North Dakota, settlers rushed to hop aboard the trains and give homesteading a try. The Northern Pacific and Great Northern railways laid hundreds of miles of track, linking towns all across the area. Instead of having to travel across the prairie for weeks or months in a wagon, settlers could take a train ride and reach their new home in just a few days.

Finally, the great bonanza farms that rose in North Dakota during the late 1870s gave jobs to many farmers and settlers who wanted to work the land. Many of these people did not have the skills or the money to run the farms on their own. Bonanza farms were huge farms that were owned by rich businessmen who ran them like large companies. Many settlers came to North Dakota hoping to find a job working on one of these bonanza farms. (We’ll learn more about bonanza farms on the next page.)

Cheap farmland, better transportation and the good chance to find a job all brought new people into the Dakotas and helped bring about the Great
Dakota Boom of 1878-1890.

title: Agriculture a Way of Life for Fewer in the U.S.
text:
When the United States began, most of its people were farmers. In 1860, the population of the United States was about 31 million. Almost half of that population listed their occupation (job) as “farmer” that year. Today, less than two percent of people earn their family’s money by farming. There are about the same number of farms in the United States today as there were in 1860. This is very unusual because the total population has grown to well over 300 million people. Why do so few people choose agriculture as a way of life today? There are several important reasons.

Farming today involves a lot of work. With so many people to feed, farmers must operate their businesses with great care. Farmers say it takes a lot more than planting seeds to own a successful farm. The work is long and hard. Farmers must make many business decisions about the type of crops to plant, the machines to buy, how to pay taxes and how to meet payroll for the workers to run the farm. Crops often fail because of weather and other unpredictable situations. Farmers have to take many risks. Some seasons they make money and some seasons they don’t. Many people have tried to make a living by farming but later decided it isn’t the life they want. However, the nation has plenty of excellent farm products. The U.S. is lucky to have enough farmers to produce the goods our nation needs to survive.

title: Bonanza Farms: Changing Agriculture
text:
Birth of the Bonanza Farm

One of the biggest changes that came with the Great Dakota Boom was the rise of bonanza farms. The word “bonanza” comes from a Spanish word that means “good weather” or “calm sea.” Later, the word came to mean sudden wealth or good luck. Bonanza farms were huge—between 3,000 and 60,000 acres—and were usually owned by one or two businessmen. These owners hired managers to run their farms.

Railroads had something to do with the rise of bonanza farms. The Northern Pacific Railway went bankrupt in 1873. This was a problem for its investors, who were about to lose the money they had put in to help build the railroad. An investor is someone who helps pay for a new company to get started in return for some of the profits. The railroad offered investors their “extra” land at a low price. Those who took the deal built huge farms that they hoped would make them wealthy. Once others heard about the good first harvest, they made their way to the Dakota Territory to try their luck as well. Perhaps money could be made after all!

What Did They Grow? Wheat!

Most bonanza farm owners focused on growing wheat. By concentrating on wheat, bonanza farmers hoped to get the most out of their money. They only had to buy machinery and train workers to raise one crop. Large bonanza farms produced as many as 600,000 bushels of wheat each year. This wheat was taken to milling companies (companies that grind grain into flour) in Minneapolis, Minnesota. From there, it was sold and then ground into flour.

Farm Technology

It took lots of workers and the latest tools to keep bonanza farms up and running. One of these tools was the threshing machine. A Scottish engineer named Andrew Meikle invented it in the late 1780s. Threshing machines were used to separate the grain from the stalks of wheat. In 1831, Cyrus McCormick invented the mechanical reaper. The reaper was used to cut down the wheat during the harvest, and it made the job much faster and easier. John Deere invented the steel plow in 1837, and it quickly became one of the most important tools used on bonanza farms. The steel plow could cut through the tough North Dakota soil in record time. These machines were powered by steam engines or pulled by teams of horses.

Farm workers were needed to run these machines. One bonanza farm used as many as 200 plows, 200 mechanical reapers, 30 threshers and at least 400 teams of horses or mules. It took a lot of workers to keep all that going.

The invention of barbed wire in the 1870s also made it possible for bonanza farmers to fence off their land. There weren’t many trees around to cut down for wooden fences. These tools helped improve life for the workers and helped the owners make more money!

Goodbye to the Bonanza Farm

The time of the bonanza farm did not last very long. By the early 1920s, bonanza farms had almost all disappeared. Farm owners could no longer count on growing as much wheat as they had in the past. Many farmers had used up the nutrients in the soil by planting wheat in the same fields year after year. Wheat production around the world had also increased, bringing wheat prices down and taking away from their profits. Workers were harder to find, and taxes went up. Bonanza farm owners began selling off their land to smaller farmers. The era of the bonanza farm had ended, but not without showing the world that North Dakota was a great place to grow one of the world’s most important crops: wheat!

title: North Dakota Becomes a State!
text:
While there had been talk of North Dakota becoming a state for years, it was not until 1889 that the change finally took place. Why did it take so long? Not everyone who lived in northern Dakota wanted to make the switch from being a territory to a state. The railroad companies and bonanza farm owners had a lot of influence. Railroad companies often used their power to control the territorial government. They wouldn’t be able to do that once North Dakota became a state. Bonanza farm owners did not want to pay the higher taxes that would come with statehood.

The other residents of Dakota Territory, however, were tired of not choosing their territorial leaders. They wanted to have elections and enjoy the rights and privileges that belonged to citizens of a state.

Many members of the U.S. Congress were willing to let North Dakota and South Dakota become the newest states. However, the Republicans and Democrats did not agree about how to handle it. Who knew that there were so many things to worry about when trying to join the United States? Finally, Congress agreed to divide a large area of the West into four new states. Those states were North Dakota, South Dakota, Washington and Montana. President Benjamin Harrison signed the bill that added North Dakota and South Dakota to the United States on Nov. 2, 1889. He didn’t want to offend either of the very competitive states by choosing which one would be admitted first. Harrison signed the act and then shuffled the papers so that no one would know which state came first. When states are listed in order of statehood, North Dakota and South Dakota are in alphabetical order. North Dakota is the 39th state, and South Dakota is the 40th state. Changing from the Dakota Territory to North Dakota turned out to be a long, strange journey!

title: Bagg Bonanza Farm
text:
If you want to know what life was like on a real North Dakota bonanza farm, plan a visit to the Bagg Bonanza Farm. The farm is located near Mooreton, in Richland County. The farm had more than 7,000 acres that were used for animals, wheat and other crops. Today, the farm is a National Historic Landmark where visitors can take a step back in time.

J.F. Downing was a lawyer and businessman from Pennsylvania who originally established a large farm in the area. In 1886, Frederick Bagg came to work on the farm. He was Mr. Downing’s nephew. Bagg worked in the fields and did carpentry work around the farm for room and board (a place to sleep and all his meals) plus $20 per month. When the manager of the farm left in 1887, Bagg was offered the job. He worked hard, and the farm grew. When his uncle died in 1913, Bagg inherited one fourth of his uncle’s money and property. He used the money to start his own bonanza farm, which was about one mile down the road from Mr. Downing’s farm.

If you visit the Bagg Bonanza Farm, you can tour 20 restored buildings, including the beautiful 18-bedroom Main House and the huge dining room where farm workers ate each day. Imagine all of the effort it took to run such a huge farm! Bonanza farms like this one helped build our great state.

title: Why do some people want to take the ‘North’ out of North Dakota?
text:
There are some North Dakotans who want to “fix up” our state a little. They think that the name might be a little more attractive if only it weren’t so long. North Dakota is known across the nation as a cold, snowy place, not far from the even colder country of Canada. Some people are suggesting that we take off the word “North” and leave only “Dakota.” People who support this idea think it would make our state more attractive to visitors who think that anyplace with the word “North” in the title would be too cold for them.

Two proposals to drop the “North” from our name were brought before the state legislature, once in 1947 and again in 1989, but both were defeated. Do you think it’s time to try again? “Dakota” may sound warmer than North Dakota, but dropping a word probably won’t change the wind chill!

title: Richardson’s Ground Squirrel
text:
North Dakota is often called the Flickertail State because of all the Richardson’s ground squirrels, or flickertails, that live here. Flickertail is another name for the light-tan squirrels that make their homes in our pastures and grain fields. They have earned the nickname “flickertail” because of how they jerk their tails around whenever they dive into burrows.

Flickertail squirrels are about a foot long and weigh just over half a pound. They live in underground colonies just beneath the surface of the prairie. Farmers have found as many as 20 of these squirrels living on a single acre of ground. They prefer fields that have lots of grain, seeds or other plants for them to eat.

Flickertails gather food and carry it in their cheeks to eat later. These animals hibernate during the winter months, but you can see them become active again as soon as the warmer spring weather arrives.

title: The Same or Different?
text: North Dakota’s rich, fertile soil has been used to grow healthy crops for centuries. The soil and growing conditions may have remained about the same, but the way that farmers manage their farms has changed a lot over the years. Use the chart on this page to compare and contrast the way that early American Indians farmed the land with the way that owners ran their bonanza farms. These are some of the items you might want to compare and contrast: size of farms, types and number of crops grown, owners of the land, number of workers, purposes of the farms and ways that the crops were cared for. You may look back at past issues of North Dakota Studies Weekly for help, either online or printed issues.

title: Let's Write
text: Do you believe the word “North” should or should not be dropped from our state’s name? In a paragraph or two, explain your thinking. Be sure to support your opinion with reasons and give examples of how becoming Dakota instead of North Dakota might affect our state. Remember to use correct spelling, grammar and punctuation.

title: Think and Review
text:
What was the Great Dakota Boom? When did it happen? Explain the causes of this exciting event.

Think about what you know about the farms created by the Homestead Act. How were those farms different from the bonanza farms you read about this week?

Why did bonanza farms eventually disappear? Give several reasons.

Why didn’t some railroad and bonanza farm owners want North Dakota to become a state?

What is one of North Dakota’s nicknames? Where did this unusual nickname come from?

title: An Economic Turnaround
text:
“Jackson, I see you got back from vacation. How was your trip?”

“It was the best! I only wish it could have been longer. It seems like no matter how great vacations turn out to be, they are always too short.”

“That reminds me of North Dakota’s history, Jackson. Just like your vacation, the good times never seemed to last long enough. Last week, we learned about the Great Dakota Boom. The boom didn’t last forever, and North Dakota farmers were in for some hard times.” “You’re right, Alana. The first Dakota Boom didn’t last forever. But the hard years of struggling didn’t last forever either. The good times actually came back, and North Dakota enjoyed its Second Boom.”

“We learned that bonanza farmers made lots of money by growing wheat on huge farms. What happened?”

“In 1893, an economic depression hit the country. An economic depression is when a lot of banks, businesses and people all run low on money at the same time. Fewer railroads and buildings were built. Some farms ended up growing too much food! All that extra food made the price of wheat and other crops drop, which hurt farmers. Some bonanza farms were sold. People struggled to pay bills and taxes. The state government did not have enough money for the projects and programs that people needed.”

“That’s pretty amazing, Jackson. North Dakota faced some hard times, but around 1900, things started to turn around. Want to guess who helped make that happen? Immigrants! A lot of immigrants moved to the United States. That meant there were many new people to feed.”

“And that meant that farmers started growing crops to feed all the hungry people across the country. With the demand for farm products up, the prices for farm goods headed up too. Alana, did you know that during the 1890s, farmers were forced to sell their wheat for only 40 to 50 cents per bushel? By 1915, that price had gone up to as much as $1.25. That may not seem like much now, but at the time that was a big change!”

“By the early 1900s, North Dakota’s Second Boom was in full swing. The farmers who were able to hang on during the Depression of the 1890s were rewarded when good times came around again only a few years later. Maybe if you can be patient, good times will come back and you can go on another awesome vacation!”

“Well, history DOES tend to repeat itself. …”

title: Would you ride in a car without a driver?
text:
Think of how exciting it was for North Dakota’s early people to take their first train ride. After years of traveling on foot, on horseback or in wagons, riding a train must have seemed like a transportation miracle.

Are you ready to see your own transportation breakthrough? It might be here sooner than you think. People who work for Google have been working on a self-driving car. When you think about driving a car, one of the first things to come to mind is probably the steering wheel. You won’t see any of those in one of Google’s cars! They want to build a car that doesn’t need a person to drive. All you would need to do is push the start button, type in where you want to go and enjoy the ride!

So how does it work? The car uses a system called “LIDAR.” LIDAR stands for “Light Detection and Ranging” and uses lasers to “see” the road and anything else nearby. A computer uses that information to control the wheels and steer the car.

Test versions of the car have driven thousands of miles to make sure they are safe. Do you think that self-driving cars will be for sale by the time you’re ready to drive? The cars are big enough for two people. Talk with a partner about how you think self-driving cars might change how we get around.

title: The Golden Age of Agriculture
text:
After the hard times that hit North Dakota during the 1890s, farmers were happy when the economy finally started to get better. People from all over the country and the world wanted to buy land in North Dakota. It didn’t take long for the population to grow. By 1910, 71 percent of North Dakota’s residents came from other countries, or they had parents who came here from somewhere besides the United States. Immigrants from at least 16 different countries had made their homes in North Dakota by this time. That was a big deal for such a “young” state!

What brought people to our humble state? Opportunity. Good farmland was cheap to buy. Between 1900 and 1920, North Dakota’s population doubled, bringing the total number of people to 647,000. Even more immigrants settled in large cities like New York, Boston and
Chicago. With all these new people to feed, these cities needed dairy products and fresh fruits and vegetables more than ever. North Dakota farmers found that people wanted to buy all the food they could grow. Food prices began to skyrocket, and farmers were being paid top prices for their goods. There was also a lot of rain, which helped the land produce more crops than ever before. Many people saw this and decided to give North Dakota farming a try!

People weren’t the only ones coming to North Dakota. Cattle ranching also became big business. Since the number of buffalo had decreased because of over-hunting, there was more space to raise cattle and other livestock that could be sold for a huge profit. When the cattle industry started in 1870, there were 2,000 cattle in North Dakota. That number grew to over 1 million by 1920. Improvements in technology, such as the refrigerated railroad car, helped ranchers become even more successful. North Dakota beef and dairy products were kept fresh long enough to be shipped to and sold in markets all over the country.

A big reason for North Dakota’s boom was having better ways to travel from place to place. When the hard times of the 1890s were over, the railroads picked up the pace and started building more branch lines across the state. Immigrants and U.S. citizens hopped the trains and settled on North Dakota’s rich farmland again.

The new connecting railroad lines made it easier than ever for farmers to ship their grain and other products to larger cities. Towns along the railroad lines grew and became even more successful. Stores, churches and schools were built to serve the new residents. Between 1900 and 1910, the populations of both Bismarck and Fargo rose by almost 50 percent. New towns grew, too. Adams County, which is in the southern part of our state, was formed in 1907 and was soon home to over 5,000 people! All thanks to new railroad lines and better transportation. This included cars, which soon made their way to our cities, towns and farms. (We’ll read more about cars in the next article!)

The Golden Age of Agriculture brought North Dakota out of its economic depression and into the most successful and prosperous times it had ever seen. North Dakota was definitely the place to be!

title: The Automobile Comes to North Dakota
text:
The automobile first came to North Dakota in 1897. The next year, Norwegian immigrant Samuel Holland built a steam-powered automobile in Park River, ND. He later built one that used gasoline. It did not take long for people to see how much freedom these new vehicles could bring. Early automobiles were not cheap. Samuel Holland’s gasoline-powered automobile cost $700, which was a lot of money at the time. As time went on, car prices went down. More families decided to invest in this new form of transportation.

The first automobiles weren’t very reliable. They broke down a lot and some of the parts froze during the cold North Dakota winters. Rocky dirt roads led to a lot of flat tires. All this meant that car owners had to be good with tools if they wanted to keep going. Driving was definitely an adventure!

With the money coming in from successful farms and businesses, it’s no wonder that cars became more popular. People didn’t have to depend on slow horses or uncomfortable buggies if they had a powerful new car to drive. Railroads were limited to where they could take people, but cars allowed travel anywhere there was a road.

By 1911, there were nearly 10,000 automobiles in the state of North Dakota. The government started a tax on gas. It used the money from that tax to build roads. Drivers also had to follow the new laws of the road. In 1905, the speed limit in towns was eight miles per hour. The arrival of the car brought another new business to the state: car manufacturing. The Ford Motor Company built a car factory in Fargo in 1914. Ford was famous for its assembly line, a way to build cars quickly. You probably won’t be surprised to learn that the factory was built near railroad tracks! The new cars could be shipped all over the state and region.

Early cars may have had some problems, but they still made it much easier for people to get from place to place.

title: Herman Stern
text:
In 2014, Herman Stern became the 40th person from North Dakota to receive the Theodore Roosevelt Rough Rider Award. Stern was born in Germany, but he moved to Casselton when he was 16. It was in Casselton that Stern worked at the Straus Clothing store that his cousin had started. Stern worked hard, and in 1910 he was chosen as the manager of a new store in Valley City. That was where he spent the next 70 years serving the people of the community.

Stern was well known for working hard to help his friends and neighbors in Valley City. He helped bring the Boy Scouts of America to families in his community and other cities. He even helped raise money to build Camp Wilderness, a Boy Scout camp in Minnesota. Stern was also one of the founders of the North Dakota Winter Show, the oldest farming exhibition in the state.

Helping his community wasn’t the only good work Stern did. He also saved people from almost certain death. Stern helped many of his friends and relatives escape from Nazi-controlled Germany in the 1930s and 1940s. The people he helped were Jewish. Jewish people who lived in Germany faced persecution (unfair treatment because of race or religion) and even death. Stern helped bring as many as 200 men, women and children to safety in the United States. Sadly, two of his brothers were not able to escape, and they died in Germany.

Herman Stern died in 1980 at age 92. He was awarded the Rough Rider Award after his death. The Museum of Jewish Heritage in New York has also honored Stern. Herman Stern made a difference here in North Dakota and in Europe!

title: North Dakota’s State Fossil: Teredo-Bored Petrified Wood
text:
Did you know that we have a state fossil? The official state fossil of North Dakota is teredo-bored petrified wood. Teredos are actually tiny clams (also called shipworms). Around 60 million years ago, teredos bored, or drilled, small holes into pieces of wood. Minerals slowly filled in these holes, and each piece of wood became petrified, or turned into stone.

North Dakota chose teredo-bored petrified wood as the state fossil in 1967. We were one of the first states to pick an official state fossil. Once teredo-bored petrified wood became North Dakota’s state fossil, people began taking more of an interest in how minerals form. Have you ever found a piece of this special wood?

title: What is supply and demand?
text:
Supply and demand is an important idea for businesses. Supply is how much of a good or service that is offered for sale. Demand is how much of a good or service people are willing and able to buy. When demand for a good or service is high, the price goes up! When supply is up and demand is low, prices drop.

North Dakota’s Second Boom happened partly because farm products were in demand. More immigrants came to the United States in the late 1890s and early 1900s, so the demand for farm products to feed these people was high. North Dakota farmers responded by producing more meat, grain and dairy products, and they charged more for these products. Farmers were able to supply the products that were needed while raising prices to make a good living.

title: Buying an Automobile—Yes or No?
text: Early automobiles were new, interesting and exciting, but choosing whether or not to buy one was a big decision. Imagine that you are a successful, but not wealthy, farmer living in North Dakota around 1910. Use the chart on this page to help you list all the pros (reasons why buying a car is a good idea) and cons (reasons why buying a car is NOT a good idea) so that you can make a good decision. You may look back at the Trades and Technology article for help with your lists. Once you have filled out the chart, use the extra space to share your decision. Do you think buying an automobile is a good idea? Why or why not?

title: Let's Write
text: When large groups of immigrants moved to the United States during the late 1880s and early 1900s, why do you think so many of them chose to settle in North Dakota? In a paragraph or two, explain why many immigrants chose to come to our state rather than find jobs in large cities like New York, Boston and Chicago. Remember to use correct spelling, grammar and punctuation in your answer.

title: Think and Review
text:
What helped bring about the hard times of the 1890s?

Explain what is meant by North Dakota’s Second Boom. Analyze what caused this Second Boom.

How did improvements in transportation change the lives of North Dakotans?

Describe the concept of supply and demand. How does it apply to North Dakota’s Golden Age of Agriculture?

title: North Dakota’s Impact on a Future President
text:
“I would never have been President if it had not been for my experiences in North Dakota.” —Theodore Roosevelt

Even before he became the 26th president of the United States, Theodore Roosevelt was known for being a good soldier and a strong leader.

Roosevelt was born in 1858 and was often called Teddy as a young man. Teddy Roosevelt first came to North Dakota in September 1883 while it was still the Dakota Territory. He came because he wanted to hunt buffalo. The beauty of the Badlands and the challenging way of life excited Roosevelt. He decided to go into the cattle ranching business. He became an owner of the Maltese Cross Ranch before he went back to New York.

Then in February 1884, tragedy struck. Teddy’s wife and mother died on the same day. His wife died just after giving birth to their daughter, and his mother passed away from a disease called typhoid fever. Teddy’s sister agreed to take care of his daughter, and he decided to go back to the Dakota Territory. He hoped it would be a place where he would find comfort.

Teddy was 25 years old when he came back to the Badlands. He was a thin young man who wore glasses and suffered from asthma. Teddy spent much of the next three years in the Dakota Territory. He lived the life of a rancher. He spent part of that time serving as deputy sheriff of Billings County! He felt that hard work was the best medicine for his pain, and he sure worked hard. The quiet, harsh Badlands did make him stronger, and they calmed his spirit and healed his broken heart. Teddy often spent his evenings writing about hunting, ranching and his feelings about the freedom and beauty of the West. It was during these years that he realized how important it was to conserve, or protect, our nation’s natural resources.

The winter of 1886-1887 was very hard, and Teddy had to sell most of his cattle. After that, he did not visit the Dakota Territory as often. Teddy still wanted to protect the land, so he gathered some friends together. They worked to form a society (a group of people who work together) that agreed with him about how important it was to preserve nature.

The time Teddy Roosevelt spent in North Dakota changed him into a strong, confident man. He went on to become a big game hunter, military hero, powerful politician and president of the United States. North Dakota helped turn a sickly boy into a great man who became the leader of one of the most powerful countries in the world.

title: Exploring the Great Outdoors in North Dakota
text:
Teddy Roosevelt isn’t the only one who can have an amazing experience in North Dakota. You can too! Here are some fun ways you can enjoy the wonders of our state. …

The Knife River Indian Villages National Historic Site, the Lewis & Clark National Historic Trail and the Theodore Roosevelt National Park are just a few places that have “Junior Ranger” programs. Each program has different activities for you to try. Then, you can get a Junior Ranger certificate and a patch that you can put on a jacket or backpack.

If you can’t make it to a park, try the National Park Service’s WebRangers site: http://www.nps.gov/webrangers/. This site lets you design your own Ranger Station and earn rewards, all while learning about our awesome national parks! The Outdoor Learning Centers at Lake Metigoshe and Turtle River state parks offer some great programs as well.

Theodore Roosevelt had a special love for birds. The National Audubon Society works to protect our feathered friends. There are chapters, or groups, of the National Audubon Society in North Dakota. Members make observations, participate in bird counts and help bring attention to endangered species. For links to games, webcams and bird videos, visit http://www.audubonadventures.org/. Who knows? Maybe your North Dakota adventures will lead you to the White House, just like Teddy Roosevelt!

title: Theodore Roosevelt – The Conservationist President
text:
“There can be no greater issue than that of conservation in this country.” —Theodore Roosevelt

When he was young, Theodore Roosevelt wanted to be a naturalist. A naturalist is a scientist who studies nature and living things. He was not the only one in his family to love nature. Roosevelt’s father was one of the founders of the American Museum of Natural History in New York. Roosevelt loved learning about the natural world, but he also wanted to spend time hunting outdoors. On his trip to the Dakota Territory in 1883, he did indeed shoot a large buffalo. But the great buffalo herds of the past had disappeared.

Roosevelt quickly fell in love with the Dakota Territory and bought two cattle ranches in the Badlands. He also saw that the railroads that were bringing people to the Great Plains were also changing the natural beauty of the land. Animals were getting pushed aside, and natural habitats were being destroyed. Roosevelt knew that something had to be done to protect the nation’s land before more of it was lost. In January 1888, Roosevelt and a friend named George Bird Grinnell started a hunting and conservation club. They named it after two important frontiersmen, Daniel Boone and Davy Crockett. The Boone and Crockett Club is still around!

Preserving nature was very important to Theodore Roosevelt. He once said, “There can be nothing in the world more beautiful than the Yosemite, the groves of the giant sequoias and redwoods, the Canyon of the Colorado, the Canyon of the Yellowstone, the Three Tetons; and our people should see to it that they are preserved for their children and their children’s children forever, with their majestic beauty all unmarred.” Roosevelt wrote many books during his lifetime. Look up his book “Ranch Life and the Hunting Trail,” which is about his time in the Dakota Territory.

Roosevelt became president of the United States in 1901. As president, he worked to make laws that would protect our beautiful land. In 1906, he signed the Antiquities Act. This law protected landmarks and historic objects on land owned by the government. “Antiquities” means ancient artifacts or ruins that came from earlier groups of people. The act made it illegal to remove items from archaeological sites or destroy natural landmarks.

Roosevelt’s conservation record is pretty amazing! As president, he created four national game preserves, five national parks, 18 national monuments, 51 bird refuges and 150 national forests. Roosevelt helped protect more than 230 million acres of public land. Presidents still use the Antiquities Act to add parks and other sites to the long list of protected places in our country.

In 1947, Theodore Roosevelt National Memorial Park was first created in the Badlands of North Dakota to honor his work as a conservationist president. A conservationist is someone who works to protect and preserve wildlife and the environment. The park offers around 100 miles of beautiful trails that are just as much fun to enjoy on horseback as they are on foot. The park is home to about 200 types of birds, as well as many other amazing animals. The name of the park was changed in 1978 to the Theodore Roosevelt National Park.

You can see why North Dakota has a special love for Theodore Roosevelt. Some of the most beautiful parts of our state are protected because of his strong belief in the power of nature. If you could visit with President Roosevelt today, what would you tell him about North Dakota?

title: Rough Riders
text:
Have you ever wondered who the Rough Riders were? This group wore uniforms, but it wasn’t a football team or horseback riding club. It was the nickname for the First U.S. Volunteer Cavalry regiment that was formed during the Spanish-American War of 1898. A cavalry unit is a group of soldiers that ride horses into battle.

In 1898, Theodore Roosevelt was working as the assistant secretary of the Navy. He left that job to organize and lead a new, impressive military unit. Theodore Roosevelt loved horses and was excited to lead a group that used them. He gathered over 1,000 volunteer soldiers from across the country. He wanted to form a group that would never back down under pressure. The Rough Riders was a loud, strong, brave group of soldiers made up of cowboys, athletes and American Indians. The group was trained in Texas.

The first time the Rough Riders fought was during the battle for Cuba’s freedom from Spain. The Rough Riders played a big role in winning the battle on land. On July 1, 1898, the Rough Riders became known for charging Cuba’s San Juan Heights. The U.S. soldiers charged up Kettle Hill and then San Juan Hill. They defeated the Spanish and held their ground. Not long after this battle, the Spanish retreated and the war ended.

Theodore Roosevelt’s leadership of the Rough Riders made him famous with government leaders and the American public. That fame helped Roosevelt become president of the United States just a few years later.

You can see Theodore Roosevelt’s legacy all over North Dakota. There is a statue of Roosevelt (and his horse) from his days as a Rough Rider at Roosevelt Park in Minot. You’ve also read about North Dakotans who have made us proud. What’s the name of this award? The Theodore Roosevelt Rough Rider Award, of course!

title: The Story of the Teddy Bear
text:
The teddy bear has been a popular toy for more than 100 years. You may even have one yourself, but did you know that this cute stuffed animal was named after Teddy Roosevelt?

In 1902, the president went on a hunting trip near Onward Mississippi with Mississippi Governor Andrew Longino. Their guide on the trip was a former slave named Holt Collier.

The first day went by without any of them seeing a bear. On the second day, Collier tracked a 235-pound black bear. Collier wanted to save the bear for the president, but he also needed to protect his hunting dogs from being hurt. He hit the bear over the head with his rifle and tied it to a tree.

When Roosevelt made it to the bear, he refused to shoot it. He said that it wouldn’t be sportsmanlike. The story spread, and a cartoon drawing about Roosevelt and the bear made it into newspapers across the country. Two people who saw the story were Morris and Rose Michtom. They owned a candy store in New York. Rose made a stuffed bear out of velvet and put it in their store window. They called it “Teddy’s Bear.” Several customers wanted to buy the bear, so they wrote to the White House and asked for permission to name the bear after the president. Roosevelt said yes, and the rest is history!

It wasn’t long before the Michtoms gave up the candy business and became rich by making stuffed teddy bears full time. Now you know the real story behind the stuffed toys that are loved by adults and children all over the world.

title: True Dedication
text:
On Oct. 14, 1912, while on his way to give a speech, Theodore Roosevelt was shot in an assassination attempt. An assassination attempt is when someone tries to kill an important leader. The bullet entered the right upper pocket of Roosevelt’s overcoat. He had a case for his glasses and a folded copy of his 50-page speech in the pocket. The case and the speech slowed down the bullet, but it still entered his chest. Getting shot didn’t stop Roosevelt. He still insisted on delivering his speech.

He told the audience, “Friends, I shall ask you to be as quiet as possible. I don’t know whether you fully understand that I have just been shot—but it takes more than that to kill a Bull Moose.” Roosevelt spoke for 90 minutes. He didn’t go to the hospital until after the speech. Roosevelt was dedicated to doing his job, and not even a bullet could slow him down!

title: Famous Spectacles
text:
Theodore Roosevelt was a very smart child, but he had poor health and got sick easily. Teddy also had poor eyesight. He was nearsighted, which means he could see things that were up close but not far away. Nobody realized how bad Teddy’s sight was until he was given his first gun when he was 14. When he went to practice shooting with his friends, Teddy discovered that he couldn’t even see the targets his friends were shooting. He told his father, and Teddy soon had a pair of glasses. He said, “I had no idea how beautiful the world was until I got those spectacles.” “Spectacles” is another word for eyeglasses.

Teddy had always loved studying birds. Before he got glasses, he identified them by their songs. After getting glasses, a whole new world of bird-watching opened up for him. It remained one of Teddy Roosevelt’s favorite hobbies until he died in 1919.
