title: Culture is All Around
text:
“Nice hat, Jackson, but I’ve been wondering about it all afternoon. I can’t figure out what a blue knit beanie has to do with North Dakota history. Am I missing something?”

“No, Alana, this hat isn’t actually from my ‘Historical Hat Collection.’ I’m just wearing it because it’s a little chilly today. I guess you could also call it my thinking cap, because I’ve been wondering about something all afternoon, too.” “What’s on your mind?”

“I was wondering how people got to be so different from place to place. When I visited my cousins in Arizona, we ate a lot of Mexican food, but my cousins aren’t Hispanic. Then I told them about the lefse and lutefisk dinner that my town puts together every year, and they didn’t even know what those foods were! What makes people and places right here in the U.S. so different from each other?”

“I know what you mean, Jackson. I visited a friend in California last summer, and she had never heard of lefse or lutefisk either. She took me to her favorite restaurant for sushi. I’d never had it before! I think that different parts of the country enjoy different foods because of the influence of the people who settled in the area. And food isn’t the only thing that’s different. Different places also have their own language, music, customs, holidays, traditions and behaviors. Americans have a lot in common, but there are so many cultures represented throughout this country that we can seem pretty different from each other, too.”

“I guess you’re right, Alana. I hadn’t thought too much about there being different cultures in the U.S., but it really is true. Remember when our teacher said that culture is everything that makes up the way of life of the people living in a community? It makes sense that culture would be different from place to place. U.S. communities were settled by people from all over the world, so each community developed its own culture depending on the different beliefs, languages and traditions that each group brought to the area.”

“Now you’ve got it, Jackson. The reason your cousins in Arizona have never seen lefse or lutefisk is that Arizona wasn’t settled by Norwegians, like our community was. They are more familiar with prickly pear jelly and green corn tamales, because those foods come from the cultures of the people who settled in the area where they live.”

“I think it’s great that this country is made up of so many cultures. The things that make us different are often what make us interesting. After all, if everyone were the same, things would be way too boring!”

title: Kids Help Choose State Insect
text:
You may not think that you have any say in passing a law in our state, but you might be surprised. Did you know that a group of elementary school students helped pass a state law? Students from Kenmare Elementary School, their teacher Tamara McNeiley and state Representative Glen Froseth worked together to pass a law that named an official state insect.

Ms. McNeiley’s class was studying ladybugs when they found out that North Dakota was one of only eight states that didn’t have an official state insect. The more they learned about ladybugs, the more they felt that this helpful little critter would be the perfect insect to represent our state. After all, ladybugs eat the harmful insects that damage crops and flowers.

In 2009, Ms. McNeiley’s class got in touch with Representative Froseth, and he helped them write a bill to take before the State House of Representatives. In March 2011, Governor Jack Dalrymple invited four students from Ms. McNeiley’s class to come to the ceremony where he signed the bill into law. The Convergent Lady Beetle (the ladybug’s official name) became North Dakota’s state insect! The class became the youngest North Dakotans to help make a state law. They proved that you don’t have to be an adult to make a difference in the world.

title: Which Cultures Have Influenced North Dakota?
text:
The promise of cheap land during the late 1800s and early 1900s brought immigrants to North Dakota. These new arrivals often settled near others who came from their home countries. People tend to feel more comfortable living near those who speak the same language and share the same customs. The American Indian tribes were also living together in groups. However, they were forced to live together on reservations throughout the state. Let’s take a look at a few of the groups that have helped form North Dakota’s culture over the years.

American Indian

The American Indian tribes who first called North Dakota home have had a huge impact on our state. Part of our state name, “Dakota,” even comes from a Sioux word for “ally,” or “friend.” Powwows are celebrated across the state every year, usually during the spring or summer. Most of these celebrations welcome visitors. Powwows usually include singing, dancing, contests and good food. Speaking of food, American Indian dishes have found their way into the diets of many North Dakotans. Fry bread (a flat piece of dough deep fried in oil) is a very popular dish served with jam, honey or wojapi, a thick berry sauce. Fry bread can also be topped with beef, beans, lettuce and tomatoes to make a delicious taco. North Dakotans also have a strong appreciation for nature and for how beautiful our land really is. American Indians were one group that helped us learn to appreciate nature.

Scandinavian

The largest immigrant group to settle in North Dakota during its early years was from Scandinavia, particularly Norway. Most of these settlers made their homes in northwestern North Dakota and in the Red River Valley. During the early 1900s, around 20 percent of North Dakota’s population was originally from Norway. Today, Minot is home to a huge Scandinavian celebration called Norsk Hostfest. This is a celebration of all things Scandinavian and is held each fall. Visitors can watch performances and buy crafts, clothing and jewelry. People also enjoy delicious Scandinavian foods like aebelskivers (pancake balls), lutefisk (dried codfish), lefse (thin potato flatbread), krumkake (waffle cookies) and rommegrot (sour cream porridge). Norsk Hostfest is a great way to learn about some of our state’s early settlers.

Germans From Russia

During the 1800s, many German people moved to Russia. They were looking for a better life, but they didn’t always find it. By 1910, many of those German families were ready to try again, and they moved to North Dakota. This group settled mainly in the south central part of our state, where many lived in sod houses and had small farms. German immigrants often settled in groups who shared the same language, culture and religion. You can find some large, fancy Catholic churches in Linton and Strasburg in Emmons County. Lutherans settled in cities, such as Ashley and Zeeland, and built their own beautiful churches. North Dakotans still enjoy many German-Russian foods like knoephla (potato soup with dumplings), pfefferneusse (spice cookies), kuchen (coffee cake) and fleischkuekle (meat pie).

Other Groups

Many groups have found a home in North Dakota. British and Irish settlers found homes in the northeast part of the state near Pembina. More recent arrivals have had Asian, African and Hispanic, or Latino, origins. No matter where we came from, the people of our state have shared culture in many ways. Take a look around your neighborhood and see what (and who) you can find!

title: American Indian Recipes
text:
One of the best ways to see how different cultures work in our lives is to take a look at the foods we eat. As we learned in this week’s lesson, North Dakotans enjoy foods from many different cultures. Would you like to try to make some authentic American Indian foods? Take a look at these recipes. Follow these steps and you’ll enjoy some Ojibwa Indian fry bread and Dakota Indian berry wojapi in no time! It should be easy to find everything you need, and don’t forget to ask a parent or another adult for help!

Indian Fry Bread
Ingredients

4 cups flour

1 tablespoon baking powder

1 teaspoon salt

1 1/2 cups warm water

1 cup oil, shortening or lard for frying

Directions
Mix flour, baking powder and salt. Gradually add water a little at a time, just enough to make the dough stick together. Knead the dough until smooth. Form the dough into fist-sized balls. Cover the balls with a towel for 10 minutes and then pat them out into pancake-sized disks. Fry in hot cooking oil in a heavy skillet until brown on both sides. Drain on paper towels and serve with jam, honey, sugar or wojapi.

Wojapi
Ingredients

3/4 cup flour

1-3 tablespoons water

1 can (15 ounces) blueberries

3 cans water

1 cup sugar

Directions
Place flour in a small bowl. Stir the 1-3 tablespoons of water into the flour a little at a time until the mixture forms a smooth paste. (You may not need to use all the water.) Set aside. Combine blueberries and three cans of water in a medium saucepan. Add the sugar and mash into the blueberries with a fork. Heat mixture over medium heat until it boils, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon. Slowly add the flour paste to the blueberry mixture and stir until the mixture thickens into a smooth sauce. Serve warm or cold with fry bread.

title: Chester “Chet” Reiten
text:
Chester Reiten was a friendly, likeable man from North Dakota. He loved his home and his Norwegian and Scandinavian heritage. Born in Hastings in 1923, “Chet” Reiten served in the Navy during WWII. After the war, he finished college and began to work in television and radio. Reiten also started his own company that he named Reiten Broadcasting. He loved the broadcasting business and insisted on using the very latest technology at his radio and television stations.

Reiten also believed in giving back to the community. He decided to enter political life where he hoped to make a difference in the lives of his friends and neighbors. He was elected state senator for 16 years and mayor of Minot for 14 years. As mayor, Reiten worked to protect Minot from Souris River floods.

Reiten was proud of his heritage. In 1978, he started working with some of his friends to find a way to celebrate their Scandinavian background. Do you remember reading about North Dakota’s Norsk Hostfest? Well, Reiten was one of the people who started the festival! He was in charge of Hostfest for more than 30 years and helped it become a successful event. It has brought people together from all around the world! Norsk Hostfest became such a success that King Harald V, the ruler of Norway, presented Reiten the Medal of St. Olav. In 2002, Governor John Hoeven awarded the Theodore Roosevelt Rough Rider Award to Reiten.

Chet Reiten lived a long, productive life before he died in 2013 at the age of 89.

title: What is a powwow?
text:
A powwow is a traditional American Indian celebration that usually happens during spring or summer. Powwows have lots of singing and dancing! The singing and dancing tell stories. These stories remind people that family pride and traditions are important. Powwows are a time when men, women, children and even babies dress in traditional American Indian clothing. Drummers and dancers sometimes compete in contests.

If you go to the powwow, there are some important rules of etiquette you should follow. “Etiquette” means “good manners.” Some of these rules are:

Do not join the dance circle unless you are asked.

If someone does ask you to join the dance, do it! Saying no is rude.

Stand up during all the special songs.

Ask permission before taking pictures.

title: Scandinavian Heritage Park
text:
If you want to find out a little (or a LOT) more about North Dakota’s Scandinavian heritage, visit the Scandinavian Heritage Park in Minot. The park is a great place to learn about Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Finland and Iceland. Each of these countries has had an impact on the culture of our state.

Some interesting sites to see include a log house from Norway and a bright red, 30-foot-tall monument of a traditional Swedish Dala horse. There is also an authentic sauna (bath house) from Finland, a Danish windmill and a replica of a church that was built in Norway during the 13th century. Don’t forget to check out the replica of a stabbur, a wooden building used to store grain, meat and other items. Come for a visit. You won’t be disappointed!

title: Time for Timelines!
text:
We almost always describe historical events in chronological order. “Chronological” means in the order that they happened. When we put historical events in order, it joins them together like a chain. It is one way of thinking about the past with the present. A timeline is a useful way to show events in chronological order.

A timeline is a list of events in the order that they happened. It starts with the earliest event and ends with the last event included. So if you were to make a timeline of your day, it would start with the time you got up and end with the time you went to bed. You would list each important event that happened throughout your day, along with the time that it happened. A timeline about your morning might include when you woke up, took a shower, ate breakfast, rode to school and sat down at your desk. The timeline would continue throughout your day, with the earliest events listed on the left and the latest events on the right. If you wanted to make your timeline run up and down, the earliest events would be listed at the top, and the latest events would appear at the bottom.

How do you choose what to put on a timeline? First you will need to decide how much time you want to cover. A one-day timeline has room for lots of details about your day, but if you wanted to make a timeline of your life, you wouldn’t want to include everything you did each and every day. If you did, your timeline would be way too long! A timeline about your whole life only has room for your most important life events like when you were born, learned to walk, started school, lost your first tooth or won a contest. The longer the time period covered by a timeline, the less detailed it can be. This means you have to choose only those events that are the most important to your topic.

We usually study an important event all by itself, but timelines help us see how lots of important events connect with one another. This week, we’ll work with timelines for both North Dakota and the United States. We’ll see how important events in our state and our nation can both stand on their own, as well as connect. Let’s get started!

title: 1795 Time Capsule Found
text:
While repairing a water leak in the Massachusetts State House in Boston, workers discovered more than just a leaky pipe. They also found a time capsule that had been sealed up in the building’s cornerstone since 1795. The time capsule was actually a small metal box filled with items over 220 years old.

When workers carefully opened the box, they found five folded Boston newspapers, a seal from the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, a page from the early records of the Massachusetts Colony and 24 coins. There was also a copper medal that showed George Washington’s face and an engraved silver plate found at the bottom of the box that was probably made by Paul Revere. The newspapers looked almost new. Experts think that the copper coins included in the time capsule helped keep the papers fresh because copper fights the growth of fungus.

Three men first placed the time capsule into the cornerstone. They were: Paul Revere, the famous silversmith and Revolutionary War hero; Samuel Adams, the governor of Massachusetts at the time; and William Scollay, a Revolutionary War colonel. They placed the capsule on July 4, 1795.

People who visit the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston will be able to see the box and everything in it for a little while, but historians have decided they will return the box and bury it again in the cornerstone. How long to do you think it will be until someone finds it again?

title: Timelines: A Link to the Past
text:
North Dakota Timeline, 19th-21st Centuries

Look at the timeline of North Dakota. You should see some of the main events in our state’s history. Does this timeline show everything that has happened? Not at all! Too many events have happened in North Dakota and the United States to put all of them on one timeline. The person making the timeline has to choose what he or she thinks is important enough to include.

This timeline gives you an idea of North Dakota’s history, but there are many other details that could have been added. The growth of farms and the impact of American Indian tribes on our state aren’t part of this timeline, even though both are important parts of our history.

United States Timeline, 17th-21st Centuries

Who would you add to a timeline of birthdates of famous Americans? What would you choose for a timeline of important events in American music? How about important events in your own community? The history of the United States could fill up thousands of books. This timeline is a general outline of U.S. history. Why do you think the events that are shown were chosen for this timeline?

Look at both of the timelines on these pages. One timeline shows events that happened all over the United States, while the other only shows what happened in North Dakota. Take a close look at the North Dakota timeline. The events are missing!

Your assignment is to finish constructing the North Dakota timeline. Work with your teacher, parents or another adult to use the Internet or other resources to figure out what happened on those dates. Use what you learn to fill in the empty spaces on North Dakota’s timeline.

This isn’t the only timeline you will work on this week. As part of the activity on Page 4, you will have the chance to design your own community timeline.

title: Bury a Time Capsule
text:
The future is always full of new things, people and ideas. It’s also full of change! Everything from technology to the clothing styles of the day will probably be very different 50 or 60 years from now.

Wouldn’t it be great if 10 or 20 years from now you were able to look back and compare the past to the future? A time capsule will let you do just that! All you need to do is gather up some mementos. A memento is a reminder of a person, place or event. Some mementos from your life might be a list of your favorite books, a page from your journal, a copy of a newspaper or some school photos.

After you have gathered some of your favorite things, put them in a sturdy box that has a tight-fitting lid. Be sure to mark the date on the box. Now it’s time to find a good place to bury your time capsule. Look for a place that will stay safe for a long time. Don’t forget to ask permission first!

Finally, draw a map to where your time capsule can be found. You may want to let other people know about the time capsule in case your memory gets a little fuzzy. You should also decide how long you want to wait before opening your time capsule, and then plan a party to celebrate that special day. Choose a day you won’t forget like your 21st birthday, the day you graduate from college or the day you turn 40! Now all you have to do is wait!

title: Who uses timelines?
text: We often think about historians using timelines to show important events, but many other people use timelines in their work. Scientists often use timelines. For example, paleontologists use timelines to show when ancient animals lived. Biologists might show how a virus has changed over time. Astronomers might use a timeline to predict when a comet’s path will pass by Earth. But timelines aren’t just for scientists. Authors speaking to a group of readers can show when their books were published. Travel agents need to schedule customers’ vacations. Timelines can be useful to just about everyone!

title: Roger Maris
text:
Roger Maris grew up playing a lot of football and basketball. He was the star of both teams during his time at Shanley High School in Fargo. Roger chose to focus on baseball and played for the Cleveland Indians and the Kansas City Athletics before he was traded to the New York Yankees. Once he was with the Yankees, he became a very famous player.

Maris hit 39 home runs and had 112 RBIs (runs batted in) during his first season with the Yankees in 1960. He played so well that he was voted the Most Valuable Player that year, but he was just getting started! In 1961, Maris hit an amazing 61 home runs during the season. That number broke Babe Ruth’s record of 60 home runs that was set in 1927. Maris’ “61 in ‘61” record wasn’t beat until 1998. That’s 37 years!

Roger Maris was the fourth person to win the Rough Rider Award. The next time you visit Fargo, see if you can visit the Roger Maris Museum. He wanted to share his memories, so the museum is free for everyone!

title: Looking Back: Railroads and Changes for American Indians
text:
The Homestead Act of 1862 gave people a reason to settle in the Dakota Territory. At first, it often took months to make the trip. When the railroad came to North Dakota, it gave settlers a new way to come to this area that was faster and more comfortable.

The first railroad reached the Dakota Territory in 1871. The Northern Pacific Railway and the Great Northern Railway built miles of tracks. Before long, new towns began to pop up. Shorter branch lines connected stations in smaller towns to the main lines. These early towns sold the food, supplies, housing and other services that railroad workers and new settlers needed. Fargo (on the Red River) and Bismarck (on the Missouri River) were two of the first towns built.

When the railroad began making its way through North Dakota, it brought more than just new settlers and faster transportation. It also brought problems. While the U.S. owned the land where the railroads were built, Indian tribes had lived on that land for thousands of years. Most of the American Indians who lived in the Dakota Territory were not happy with the idea of noisy, dirty trains lumbering through their homeland. Not only did they dislike the trains, but they also did not like what the trains did to their way of life.

The U.S. government passed laws and signed treaties with tribes. A treaty is an official agreement. These treaties set aside areas of land called reservations where the Indian tribes were forced to live. As soon as American Indians had to leave their homeland, settlers started taking over the area.

As new railroad lines grew across the prairie, thousands of settlers moved into the area. Railroad workers often killed the buffalo for food, but hunters also shot the animals for sport and left the bodies to rot in the sun. By the late 1880s, the buffalo population dropped from around 30 million to fewer than 1,000. The buffalo herds had provided the Great Plains Indians with food, tools and shelter. Without those herds, many tribes faced starvation. Some government and Army leaders even told travelers, settlers and railroad workers to kill as many buffalo as possible. These leaders knew that without buffalo herds, the American Indians would be forced to accept life on reservations and find other ways to survive.

American Indians fought against the U.S. government over the right to stay on their land. After many battles, the American Indians lost and were forced to life on reservations. The reservations created during that time period are the Spirit Lake Tribe and Lake Traverse reservations, Fort Berthold, Turtle Mountain Indian Reservation and the Standing Rock Sioux Reservation. For people who loved their freedom, this was a terrible blow.

Living on reservations meant that the American Indians had to give up their nomadic way of life and make a living in other ways. Many tribes began to farm, but much of the land they were given by the government was not good for growing crops.

The trains that brought success to settlers also brought unhappy changes for many American Indians. Residents of the Dakota Territory looked to the future and worked to make their lives meaningful.

title: ‘Booms’ in North Dakota
text:

title: Influences From Near and Far
text:
Let’s review some of the groups and cultures that have influenced North Dakota over the years. Read each paragraph and write the name of the culture it describes.

Before moving to North Dakota, my ancestors moved to Russia and lived there for many years. When they came here, they looked for a town where people practiced the same religion as they did. My family helped build the church in town. On special occasions, we use recipes passed down from my grandparents. Some of our favorites are knoephla (potato soup with dumplings), pfefferneusse (spice cookies), kuchen (coffee cake) and fleischkuekle (meat pie).
Name of this culture: ______________________

My ancestors have lived here for thousands of years. Our state gets its name from our word for “ally,” or “friend.” When the settlers came to the Dakota Territory, my ancestors were moved to reservations. Even though this was difficult, my people continued to pass down our songs, dances and recipes. You can see some of our traditions at powwows, which are held across the state. When you visit, try the fry bread (a flat piece of dough deep fried in oil). It is often served with wojapi, a thick berry sauce.
Name of this culture: ______________________

My family comes from the largest group of immigrants to settle in North Dakota. My ancestors settled in the Red River Valley and farmed the land. Every year we go to Minot to celebrate our heritage. title: Theodore Roosevelt: Protector of Land and Wildlife
text:
Theodore Roosevelt first came to the Dakota Territory in 1883 with the goal of shooting a buffalo. On his trip, he discovered that the great buffalo herds of the past had been hunted to almost nothing. Roosevelt also was surprised at the huge impact the railroad had on the wildlife and the beauty of the land. He decided that our land needed to be protected before it was too late. He was afraid that the natural wonders of this great country could go away as quickly as the buffalo.

When he became president of the United States in 1901, Roosevelt began working to preserve our nation’s beautiful country. In 1906, he signed the Antiquities Act to protect public land. He also created four national game preserves, five national parks, 18 monuments, 51 bird refuges and 150 national forests. In total, Roosevelt protected more than 230 million acres of public land!

title: Living Comfortably—Wherever You Are!
text:
“Jackson! I didn’t know you were back! How was your trip?”

“It was a lot of fun, Alana. I realized that southern Arizona is a great place to visit, but I wouldn’t want to live there.”

“Why not? I thought you loved visiting your cousins out in the desert.”

“I do love going there to visit them, but the desert is a little too hot for me. The weather is really pretty nice this time of year. But while we were visiting there last August, it was still 92 degrees when I went to bed! My cousins don’t even go outside much during the day in summer. They stay indoors in the air conditioning until evening. One of my cousins plays baseball, and his games don’t even start until 7:00 or 8:00 at night. It’s just too hot to play before that.”

“It sounds like the environment in southern Arizona is a lot different from what we have here in North Dakota. When you stop to think about it, the environment affects the work we do, the houses we build, the foods we eat, the clothes we wear and the games we play. I bet your Arizona cousins can play tennis, soccer and basketball outdoors all year round. It’s too cold for any of that in the middle of a North Dakota winter! I’ll bet your cousins wear shorts most of the time, and I doubt they even own any winter coats.”

“That’s true, Alana. They came to visit us last winter, and the whole family had to buy coats just for the trip! Another thing I noticed during my visit was that their house doesn’t have a fireplace. Their air conditioner is much more important to them than their furnace. That’s opposite of how our homes are set up!”

“Right, Jackson. During a cold North Dakota winter, we drink a lot of hot cocoa and eat warm soups. I’m guessing that your cousins in Arizona drink a lot of cold lemonade, eat more sandwiches and salads and snack on popsicles and fruit smoothies.”

“You guessed it. There are a lot of people who work outdoors in both Arizona and North Dakota, but they have to dress very differently because of the extreme weather in both states. During a North Dakota winter, workers on oil rigs bundle up in insulated boots and high-tech outerwear. People who work outside in a scorching Arizona summer need to wear light-colored clothing and drink plenty of water.”

“The environment plays a role in almost every part of our lives. It’s neat to see how well people have learned to adapt to whatever Mother Nature dishes out!”

title: What would you do if you found a little extra money?
text:
What would you do if you found a bag of money in the middle of the road? Would you keep it or try to find the owner so you could return it?

Dan Kennedy was driving to his job in Utah when a truck in front of him hit a bump in the road. Out popped a large orange bag. Kennedy didn’t want the bag to cause an accident, so he stopped and moved it out of the road. That was when he discovered that the bag was full of money! The truck that had been ahead of him was transporting money between banks and other businesses. The bag that had fallen out held 75 pounds of cash.

Kennedy put the bag in his car, drove to the parking lot at his work and immediately called the police. Officers were shocked to see the huge bag of money and even more surprised that Kennedy hadn’t touched the cash. He never even thought about keeping the money for himself!

This type of honesty might seem strange, but Kennedy believes that most people would do the same thing. Other news stories show that he is probably right. Teachers in Texas and South Carolina recently returned lost bags of money to the right people. It’s nice to know that honesty isn’t so uncommon after all.

title: Interacting With Your Environment
text:
Whenever people move to a new place, they begin to interact with the environment in different ways. Let’s look at some of these ways....

Housing

All people need to have shelter, or a place to live. Early American Indians made shelters using animal skins, branches and mud. Later, North Dakota homesteaders built homes from thick layers of sod, or they lived in homes called dugouts. These were shelters carved into hillsides. Today, people use all sorts of building materials to build homes.

Dams

Water is one of our most important natural resources. People build dams along rivers to control water and use it to produce electricity for towns and cities.

Garrison Dam was built on the Missouri River in 1953. The dam produces electricity used in parts of North Dakota, Minnesota, Nebraska and Iowa. Besides producing electricity and controlling water, dams also affect the environment. When Garrison Dam was built, it caused parts of the Missouri River to flood. That water covered a lot of farmland that belonged to the Three Affiliated Tribes.

Industry

An industry is a group of businesses that produce goods or services. Farming and mining are important industries in North Dakota. In our state’s early days, farms were small, family-owned businesses. Later, North Dakota was home to huge bonanza farms that were run like large companies. Bonanza farms did not last, and smaller farms returned. Today, farms are increasing in size and are being run more like large businesses again.

Mining is another important industry in North Dakota. Companies mine coal, sand, gravel, natural gas and petroleum (used to make oil products like gasoline). Underground coal mines were once common in our state. These mines were harmful to the environment, and they closed by 1966.

Farming and mining can pollute our waterways when waste from these industries leaks into the ground or is washed into streams and rivers. Mining can also change the face of the land, causing flooding and erosion (slow breaking down) of the rocks and soil.

Irrigation Systems

Irrigation makes it possible for farmers to raise crops in dry areas. They use ditches and canals to bring water from the place it is found to the place where it is needed. For over 100 years, irrigation systems have given North Dakota’s farmers enough water to grow crops like corn, soybeans and potatoes.

Whenever water is moved from one place to another, the environment is changed. Too much irrigation can cause rivers to dry up. Irrigation can also affect how much salt gets mixed into the water and soil.

Transportation

Fur companies used steamboats to move goods and supplies up and down our rivers. Then, people saw the first railroad enter the Dakota Territory in 1871. This made it easier than ever for settlers to come to the Dakotas. The railroads also had a huge impact on the environment. Buffalo herds disappeared, and American Indians lost much of the land they used for hunting and farming.

During the early 1900s, automobiles became more popular. New roads were built all over the state. These roads made travel easier, but they changed the shape of the land.

Communication

Today’s communication systems need power lines, radio towers, satellite dishes, underground telephone lines and a large number of cell phone towers. These communication systems change the environment, but they also allow us to call, text, email and even watch movies on a hand-held device.

How have you observed people interacting with the environment? Talk to a partner and give another example from one of the categories above.

title: Natural Hazards of North Dakota
text:
Natural hazards are events caused by nature that can be harmful to people or the environment.

Blizzards

North Dakota is known for its blizzards. A blizzard is a harsh winter storm with strong winds and blowing snow.

1888: A terrible blizzard killed 112 people and nearly all of the cattle left out on the open range.

1966: Winds gusted up to 100 miles per hour and piled snow up to 30 feet high. Five North Dakotans died in the storm, along with thousands of farm animals.

Winter of 1996-1997: Eight blizzards caused 17 deaths and millions of dollars in damage. There were heavy floods when all the snow melted in spring.

Droughts

A drought is a long period of time with little or no rainfall. North Dakota usually gets around 18 inches of rain and snow each year. In 1936, the state received only 8.67 inches, making it one of the driest years on record.

Floods

1950: The Red River of the North flooded its banks, causing nearly $31 million in damage to homes and businesses. Seven people were injured and one person died.

2011: Melting snow and heavy rains caused the Missouri and Souris rivers to flood. Over 11,000 people had to leave their homes around Minot.

Tornadoes

A tornado is a destructive funnel of wind. North Dakota averages 32 tornadoes each year. One of the state’s most deadly tornadoes was in Cass County on June 20, 1957. It injured 103 people and caused 10 deaths.

Earthquakes

Earthquakes are rare in North Dakota. The first earthquake recorded by scientific equipment happened near Huff on July 8, 1968. The earthquake was small and didn’t cause any damage. Earthquakes centered in other states are sometimes felt in North Dakota.

Windstorms

1919: A severe windstorm hit Williams and Divide counties. It killed eight people, and 40 more were injured.

1930: Windstorms were common in North Dakota during the 1930s, blowing dust across the prairie. In 1930, a severe windstorm damaged 1,847 buildings.

Have natural disasters happened in your area? Do some research to find out!

title: Courageous: Hazel Miner
text:
The harsh North Dakota weather sometimes brings hard times to the people who live here. One of our great North Dakota heroes who lost her battle with the environment was Hazel Miner. Hazel was a 15-year-old girl who gave up her own life to save her siblings during a terrible blizzard.

On March 16, 1920, Hazel was at school with her 10-year-old brother, Emmet, and her 8-year-old sister, Myrdith. That day a blizzard hit. The children had traveled to school in a horse-drawn sleigh. Their father came to the school on horseback to lead his children home through the storm. The children loaded into the sleigh, but the sleigh horse took off into the storm before their father could climb back on his horse. Mr. Miner searched, but he couldn’t find them in the blowing snow.

The horse pulled the children deeper into the blizzard. The snow was so thick that the sleigh tipped over. Hazel laid two blankets down and had her siblings lie down on them. Then she held another blanket over them, trying to keep the wind and snow from covering them. To keep the blanket on the children in the whipping wind, Hazel lay down on top of the blanket herself. She kept telling her brother and sister to wiggle their feet so they wouldn’t freeze. She talked to them all night and kept kicking the snow off so it wouldn’t bury them. When a rescue party finally found them the next morning, they discovered that Emmet and Myrdith were fine, but Hazel had died from the cold. Her courageous efforts had kept her brother and sister alive. Hazel gave her life for them and became a true North Dakota hero.

title: What are Natural Resources?
text:
You have probably heard of natural resources, but do you know what they are? A natural resource is something found in nature that people can use. There are all kinds of natural resources in the world around us. These include soil, plants, coal, water, natural gas and even animals. We use natural resources to help us survive. Sometimes, we use natural resources just as they are. For example, we use water to drink and for cooking and cleaning. We also eat apples, berries, carrots and other fruits and vegetables right from the garden.

We use some natural resources to make other things that make our lives easier. We burn coal and natural gas to power and heat our homes, schools and businesses. We use trees to build furniture and houses and to make paper and books. We also use natural resources to make more items we use each day, such as cell phones, computers, clothing and even your toothbrush!

Natural resources can be either renewable or nonrenewable. Can you guess what the difference is between these two types? Renewable resources are those that can be renewed, or replaced. Trees are an example of a renewable resource because new trees can be planted to replace those that we cut down. Nonrenewable resources are resources that cannot be easily replaced. Oil and natural gas are two examples of nonrenewable resources. It took millions of years to form these resources. Once we use them all up, they are gone forever.

It is important to learn to conserve our natural resources so that there will be enough of them in the future. Conserve means to protect and use wisely. Conserving our natural resources also helps us protect the environment.

Take some time to complete the following activity. Decide which of the resources are renewable and which are nonrenewable. The first two have been done for you.

title: Using Resources Wisely
text:
Everyone knows natural resources are important, and most people agree that we need to conserve them (use them wisely so that they last longer). What can you do to help? Start with your classroom. Look around and see how much paper you waste. Make a list of ways you and your classmates could use less. Does your school recycle paper or just throw it away? If you don’t have a recycling program, maybe you and your friends could talk to the principal about starting one. Recycling paper saves trees, one of our most important natural resources.

Is there a river or stream in your community? How clean is it? Perhaps your class could take a field trip and clean up some of the trash. It’s a dirty job, but someone’s got to do it. Polluted water is dangerous for people and animals.

Oil is another natural resource we need to conserve. It’s a nonrenewable resource, because it takes millions of years to form. When we run out, we can’t grow or make more. Research some different kinds of energy—things like wind power, solar power and fuels made from plants. Write a letter to the mayor of your city and encourage him or her to find ways to use different energy sources in your community.

What are some other ways you can help conserve natural resources? Read books, talk to community leaders and look on the Web to get more ideas. Pick one and make it a class project. Your school and your community are counting on you!

title: North Dakota’s Resources
text:
Natural Resources

North Dakota is rich in many natural resources. Some people think that our state’s soil is our greatest natural resource. Soil allows our farmers to grow useful farm products like flax, oats, beans, wheat, barley, honey, soybeans, potatoes, sunflowers and sugar beets. We also use the land to raise hogs, beef cattle and dairy cows. These natural resources are renewable because they can be replaced.

Wind is also a renewable natural resource. Wind turbines take advantage of strong, steady winds to generate power for homes and businesses. More and more North Dakotans are looking to wind for their electrical needs.

Petroleum is another one of our most important natural resources. Since oil was discovered here in 1951, our state has experienced several oil booms. In the spring of 2014, our state broke records when it began producing over 1 million barrels of oil per day. Petroleum cannot be replaced and is a nonrenewable resource.

Natural gas and coal are also some of our nonrenewable resources. Natural gas is found in many of our western counties. Coal is mined and used in power plants to produce electricity. Wherever you look in North Dakota, you can find all kinds of natural resources.

Human Resources

To make the most of North Dakota’s natural resources, it takes another kind of resource. Human resources are the people who live and work in an area. In North Dakota, we think the human resources are the most important ones we have. Without them, the natural resources would not be used. The crops would die; the coal and oil would stay underground; and the livestock would wander around. It takes people to care for livestock, to plant and harvest crops, to build dams and wind turbines and to drill for petroleum. Mother Nature may provide natural resources, but it’s up to people to get them and use them wisely.

Capital Resources

Capital resources are the riches and wealth that people own. Capital can be cash, land, jewelry, factories or anything that is of value and could be sold. People use capital resources to buy things they need and to make improvements that will help them earn even more capital. If a state, a business or a person has more capital, he or she can do more with natural and human resources.

Using Our Resources

Ever since the first trappers started sending furs back to France and England, it’s been clear that North Dakota could provide many natural resources. Early settlers had to figure out the best way to use these natural resources. Once they did this, they had something to sell, whether it was beaver pelts, beef cattle or wheat. That meant capital resources, or money, in their pockets. This money went to pay for more land, better machines, bigger irrigation systems and more. The things bought with capital resources made it possible to use even more natural resources. So human resources turn North Dakota’s natural resources into capital resources. Then, human resources spend the capital resources so that they can use more natural resources. It’s enough to make you dizzy just thinking about it! But here in North Dakota, it’s been working for a long time.

title: Entrepreneurship
text:
An entrepreneur is a person who starts a new business to make money. It takes courage to start a new business and put your money on the line for an idea you believe in. Half of all new businesses fail within the first five years, so entrepreneurs really have to know their stuff. They have to come up with a great idea, use all their resources wisely and work very hard to be successful.

Starting a business is a risky thing. In our country we have more than 28 million businesses of all kinds. More than 99 percent of these businesses are small. A small business has fewer than 500 employees. In other words, if all the businesses in our country were represented by $1, the small businesses would take up more than 99 cents. The big businesses, like Coca-Cola and Nike, would be represented by less than one penny. One entrepreneur you may have heard of is Bill Gates, the founder of Microsoft. After dropping out of college, Bill and his partner, Paul Allen, built the world’s largest software business. Bill Gates has made billions of dollars from his work.

Another entrepreneur went from making tortillas to working as U.S. Treasurer. Romana Banuelos was born to a poor immigrant family. She worked hard to open her own tortilla factory and build a successful company. People in the government noticed how hard she worked and Banuelos was appointed Treasurer of the United States in 1971.

North Dakota has its share of entrepreneurs. Harold Schafer, from Stanton, started his own company in 1942. He named it the Gold Seal Company and became famous for household products, including Mr. Bubble. Hugo Magnuson opened his first grocery store in Grand Forks in 1939. The store was so popular that Magnuson went on to open a chain of grocery stores called Hugo’s throughout North Dakota and Minnesota.

A person must work hard and use skill and courage to become a great entrepreneur. Do you think you have what it takes to succeed?

title: Doug Burgum, Entrepreneur
text:
It takes bravery, knowledge and a lot of hard work to succeed as an entrepreneur. Doug Burgum is one North Dakotan who has proved that he has what it takes to make great things happen in the world of business.

Burgum was born in Arthur, North Dakota, and his ancestors were some of the earliest settlers of the town! He graduated from North Dakota State University (NDSU). In 1983, he started working for a very small North Dakota computer software company called Great Plains Software. He believed in the company and that the great people of North Dakota could make it succeed. Burgum’s confidence and skills helped him build Great Plains Software into a wildly successful company. It was so successful that it became part of the Microsoft Corporation in 2001.

Burgum worked for Microsoft for several years before he started a company called Kilbourne Group. His new company works to restore historic buildings in downtown Fargo. Their work convinced NDSU to build a downtown campus, which has helped bring people and businesses back to Fargo. Burgum’s ideas for schools, churches and skyscrapers should keep Fargo growing in the future.

Burgum also believes in helping other entrepreneurs make their dreams come true. He helped start a company called Arthur Ventures, which gives loans to small businesses to help them grow. He continues to give back to North Dakota by working to make our communities better. Doug Burgum received the Theodore Roosevelt Rough Rider Award in 2009.

Doug is the current governor of North Dakota and took office in December 2016. Although he did not have political experience, many North Dakota voters believed that if he is successful running businesses, he would be successful in running the state as well.

title: Wind Turbine
text:
Have you noticed some modern-looking windmills turning in the prairies? They may look like windmills, but they are really wind turbines! A wind turbine is a machine that uses wind to generate electricity.

Charles Brush invented one of the first wind turbines at his home in Cleveland, Ohio, in 1888. His turbine had 144 blades, weighed 80,000 pounds and was built on a 60-foot-tall tower. The wind turned the blades on the turbine, which generated electricity. Brush used that electricity to charge 12 large batteries in the basement of his mansion. The wind turbine generated enough electricity to power his house, and the system ran for 20 years.

Today, North Dakota has about 1,000 wind turbines that produce enough power to keep lights on all over our state.

title: Paddlefish
text:
If you have ever seen a North Dakota paddlefish, it’s probably a sight you won’t forget! Paddlefish are huge, shark-like fish that measure up to seven feet long and often weigh over 100 pounds. That’s one big fish! Paddlefish are named for their large snouts, which are paddle-shaped. These snouts take up about one-third of their total length. Paddlefish are greenish gray in color and live in the open waters of the Missouri and Mississippi river basins. In North Dakota, paddlefish can be found in Lake Sakakawea, Lake Oahe, the Yellowstone River and the Missouri River.

Paddlefish have very small teeth when they are young. As they get older, they eat their food by swimming with their mouths wide open, straining small fish, bugs and other animals from the water through parts of their gills. Many North Dakota fishers enjoy the challenge of catching one of these great fish.

title: Growth in North Dakota’s Economy
text:
When it comes to the economy, North Dakota’s has really boomed! What is our economy anyway? Economy is a word used to describe how our state makes, buys, sells and uses goods and services. North Dakota’s economy has thrived mainly because our major industries have been healthy. When our major industries do well, North Dakota’s economy thrives. Remember that an industry is a group of businesses that provides goods or services. Industries bring in money that can be used right here at home to make life better for everyone. North Dakota’s industries, and those who work in them, deserve most of the credit for our bright economy.

North Dakota has many industries that make things people want to buy. Agriculture, tourism, manufacturing, coal mining and the production of oil, natural gas and renewable energy are all industries that provide jobs and bring in lots of money for the people who live in our state. North Dakota has had plenty of high-paying jobs, good schools, family-friendly communities and lots of places to enjoy the outdoors. Taxes have been low, and since 2000, the average personal income of North Dakota’s citizens has doubled! Did you know that because of our good economy, North Dakota has had one of the lowest unemployment rates in the country? Many people think that the only jobs in North Dakota are in the oil industry. Oil companies do hire a lot of workers, but other industries have plenty of jobs as well. Good jobs are available in farming, health care, education and manufacturing.

This week, we’ll learn more about the industries that have helped North Dakota’s economy grow over the years. Having a good economy makes life more enjoyable for the people who live here. With a little luck and a lot of hard work, these industries can keep North Dakota booming for many years to come!

title: Friends, Football and French Fries at the Potato Bowl USA
text:
How much ketchup do you think it takes to go with over 5,000 pounds of french fries? The answer is about 120 gallons! It also takes 140 gallons of hot oil to fry up the crispy, golden snacks. Who would even think of eating this many french fries? More than 10,000 potato-crazed North Dakotans, that’s who!

In 1965, a football coach at the University of North Dakota (UND) began taking the players on a yearly trip to Hoople to eat potatoes and meet some of the local people. UND is located in Grand Forks, and Hoople is about 50 miles to the northwest. Both cities are famous for their potatoes. As time passed, the two cities started a tradition of playing a game of football during the visit. That game became known as the Potato Bowl USA. Potato Bowl USA is one way North Dakota honors its potato crop, and it builds school spirit.

A popular event during each year’s celebration is the French Fry Feed. The J.R. Simplot Company donates the potatoes and ketchup for the event. This company runs a factory that turns potatoes into french fries. In 2014, the French Fry Feed set a new world record when they served 5,130 pounds of fries! More than 10,000 people showed up to enjoy the free food. They proved that North Dakotans really do enjoy their potatoes!

title: North Dakota’s Industries
text:
North Dakota’s businesses bring in the money and jobs that keep our economy humming along. Let’s take a look at some of our most important and profitable industries.

Agriculture and Livestock

North Dakota’s rich soil makes farming one of our most important industries. Do you remember the three regions of North Dakota? Let’s look at important farm products of the Red River Valley, the Drift Prairie and the Missouri Plateau.

The Red River Valley is in the eastern part of the state and has some of the best soil in the country. Common crops in that area are soybeans, sugar beets and spring wheat. We grow much of the nation’s spring wheat and durum wheat. Durum wheat is used to make pasta. The next time you visit the Drift Prairie, look for oats, canola and bright yellow sunflowers bending in the wind. You’ll probably also hear lots of “moo” sounds from the cattle farms. North Dakota has more cows than people! The buzzing you’ll hear is from our busy bees. We produce more honey than any other state.

Land on the Missouri Plateau is more difficult to farm, but that doesn’t stop our farmers! Farms in that area grow barley, flaxseed, winter wheat and alfalfa hay. They also raise beef and dairy cattle.

Of course, there are all kinds of farms located across North Dakota. In fact, our 30,000 farms take up about 40 million acres of land. That means about 90 percent of our state is used for farming and ranching. As a result, agriculture and livestock make up a large part of our state’s employment and economy. North Dakota’s farm products are worth almost $6 billion.

Manufacturing

industry helps make all the things we use every day? The manufacturing industry takes resources and makes them into other useful items. Since North Dakota’s agriculture and livestock industries are so large, there are a lot of companies that make products using our crops. Businesses all over the state turn wheat into bread, milk into cheese and beef cattle into steaks and hamburgers.

North Dakota is also home to plants that manufacture farming and mining equipment that is sold around the world. Manufacturing plants are located across the state, especially in Bismarck, Fargo, Grand Forks and Minot.

Renewable Energy

Let’s keep our engines running! Biodiesel and ethanol are fuels made from renewable resources. Biodiesel is made from oils like soybean, canola or sunflower oil. Ethanol is made from corn. These fuels are cleaner and don’t create much pollution, but they only work in special engines. Our state has biodiesel and ethanol plants, and our farmers grow the canola and corn they need to make these fuels.

Besides fuel plants, North Dakota has about 1,000 wind turbines. These turbines produce power to keep the lights on all over our state. Our state gets almost 20 percent of its total energy from the wind, which is a resource that North Dakota has more than enough of. Wind farms are located across the state. Just look for the tall turbines.

Coal Mining

Just underneath our state’s rich soil lies a huge deposit of lignite coal. Miners dig up around 30 million tons of this coal each year. The coal industry is centered in western North Dakota, and companies use the coal found here to generate most of North Dakota’s electricity. We don’t keep all of the electricity for ourselves! We share with our neighboring states. People across the Midwest use electricity produced by North Dakota’s coal industry.

Oil and Natural Gas

North Dakota is one of the busiest oil-producing states in the U.S., and it’s one of our top industries. During good times, North Dakota’s oil companies produce over 1 million barrels of oil every day. Most of the oil in North Dakota is produced around Williston, in the northwest part of the state. The oil industry provides jobs for workers who want to make good money and who aren’t afraid of long hours and hard work. Over the years, oil production in North Dakota has increased greatly. In 2006, the oil wells filled about 40 million barrels. That total jumped to 312 million barrels by 2013. That’s an increase of more than 600 percent! The North Dakota oil boom has brought thousands of new workers, along with millions of dollars, into our state. Will the oil boom continue? Do some research on your own or with a partner to see how North Dakota’s oil industry is doing right now.

Along with producing oil, North Dakota also captures natural gas. Natural gas plants process the gas, and then it is transported to homes and businesses across the state and region. We use natural gas for heating, cooking and manufacturing.

Tourism

More than 24 million visitors flock to North Dakota each year to enjoy the great outdoors. They experience Theodore Roosevelt National Park, the National Buffalo Museum, Fort Abraham Lincoln State Park and the North Dakota Heritage Center and State Museum. Tourists bring in about $3.6 billion to North Dakota’s economy each year. Many different jobs are related to our state’s tourism industry, and we’ll discover even more about North Dakota tourism in a different issue.

There are many ways that our state can make money. Look around your city or town. Which industries are important in your area? Do you know anyone who works in one of these industries?

title: Ronald D. Offutt
text:
Ronald Offutt has been called many different names. He’s been called the Sultan of Spuds and the Lord of the Fries. With nicknames like that, it shouldn’t surprise you to learn that he’s had a lot to do with North Dakota’s potatoes!

Ronald Offutt founded the R.D. Offutt Company, and it’s one of the biggest potato growers in the country. Offutt’s company grows and sells potatoes to other businesses that make chips, french fries and hash browns, just to name a few. Lots of fast-food companies use R.D. Offutt Company as their main supplier of potatoes for their french fries.

Ronald Offutt wasn’t only interested in potatoes. He also started the RDO Equipment Company, which sells John Deere construction and farming equipment all over the country.

Offutt grew up on his family’s farm in Minnesota, but he chose to set up his business in North Dakota. His first John Deere store was in Casselton. Offutt’s family has been involved in the business, too. His children have run different parts of these successful companies.

Offutt believes in giving back to his community. The Offutt Family Foundation gives money to charities and offers scholarships to students. Ronald Offutt was given the Theodore Roosevelt Rough Rider Award in 2011. He is also a member of North Dakota’s Agricultural Hall of Fame.

title: What is North Dakota’s official state beverage?
text:
Milk! It is a great way to get protein, calcium and potassium. Milk is also used to make cheese, butter, yogurt and ice cream. North Dakota’s dairy herds produce about 40 million gallons of milk every year. That milk brings in around $65 million in sales for North Dakota. We aren’t the only state to choose milk as our official state beverage. Nebraska, South Dakota, Wisconsin and Minnesota have also picked milk as a state symbol.

Did you know that it takes 350 squirts of cow’s milk to make one gallon and that the average cow produces about six to eight gallons of milk per day? In order to produce this much milk, each cow needs to drink 30-50 gallons of water each day. That’s enough to fill a bathtub!

title: Sunflowers
text:
North Dakota sunflowers are brightly colored and cheery, and they are big moneymakers! Our state’s sunflower crop brings in about $250 million each year. North Dakota is usually one of the top producers of sunflowers in the United States.

The sunflower is native to North America. That means it was growing here before settlers arrived. American Indians ate sunflower seeds, and they ground them into flour for baking. When explorers found sunflowers and took them back to Europe, the flowers became popular in Russia. Russian immigrants brought them back to North America and grew fields full of the helpful flower. Today, there are two main types of sunflowers. One type has seeds that are great for eating. People and birds enjoy the seeds. The other type has seeds full of rich oil that is used in cooking and biodiesel fuel. North Dakota sunflowers aren’t just pretty; they’re also good for our economy!

title: North Dakota Road Trip!
text:
“Hey, Jackson, do you want to go to the park this weekend? Maybe we can get a group together and play soccer.”

“I don’t know, Alana. We do that all the time. I think I’m ready to try something different. Hey! I just had a great idea. You know what I’m really in the mood for? A road trip!”

“A road trip? Where would we go?”

“That’s the best part about my idea, Alana. There are hundreds of places right here in North Dakota where we could have a really great time.”

“Do you have a specific place in mind?”

“Well, I’ve heard that the Fargo Air Museum has some really cool exhibits. They have planes from World War II. I would love to go there.”

“That sounds fun, Jackson. So which hat would you bring on our road trip?”

“I’m not sure, Alana. Maybe I’ll have enough room to pack them all AND buy a new one! What do you want to do?”

“I think it would be awesome to go to the Medora Musical. We’d have to wait until school is out, though. The shows are all in the summer.”

“A visit to Medora could be fun. I also think it would be great to learn a little more about the people who first settled here. Maybe we could go to the Scandinavian Heritage Park in Minot. We could have a picnic there!”

“I figured you would get around to food sooner or later, Jackson. If you like sunflower seeds, we should go to Wahpeton. They have a huge sunflower seed factory there. I wonder if they give tours.”

“Sunflower seeds are great, and I would love to tour a sunflower seed factory. It might take more than just sunflower seeds to fill me up, though. I read somewhere that there’s a city in North Dakota that will give you all the french fries you can eat for free!”

“You’re thinking of Grand Forks, Jackson, but they only give out free fries during the annual French Fry Feed in September. So where exactly should we go on our road trip?”

“I say we ask our parents about starting it in Fargo and then hitting as many North Dakota cities as we can.”

“Sounds good to me. Let’s go!”

title: Would you want to visit a ghost town?
text:
If you have ever wanted to visit a real ghost town, then North Dakota is the place for you! A ghost town is a community that has been abandoned. Nobody lives there, but the stores, schools, houses and other buildings are still standing. North Dakota has dozens of ghost towns that are just waiting to be explored.

Why would people abandon their homes and communities? Well, there are lots of reasons. Harsh weather conditions, crop failure and loss of jobs are some reasons. People just get tired of struggling and decide to move on. They leave their old lives, along with their empty towns, behind. One interesting North Dakota ghost town you might want to visit is Arena. It is east of Wing in Burleigh County. The town was founded in 1906 and was once home to a post office, store, houses, a school and a church. In 1920, Arena had a population of 150, but 10 years later that number had shrunk to only 35. Today, the town has been completely abandoned, but visitors can still see the church and some of the houses.

title: Touring North Dakota—One City at a Time!
text:
North Dakota is full of historic, scenic, amazing cities. Let’s take a trip of our own to a few of our state’s one-of-a-kind, unforgettable locations.

Fargo

Fargo is in southeast North Dakota, along the Red River of the North near North Dakota’s border with Minnesota. It is the largest city in our state, with nearly 16 percent of North Dakota’s people. Fargo was founded in 1871 as a railroad town. It was named after William G. Fargo, who was a director of the Northern Pacific Railroad and a successful businessman.

Today, Fargo is a great place to enjoy lots of different family activities. Plan a visit to the Red River Zoo! The zoo has more than 300 animals, including several endangered species, so you’re sure to enjoy the trip. You will also want to make a stop at Bonanzaville, one of the largest historical attractions in the area. Bonanzaville is home to Pioneer Village, which has over 40 buildings dedicated to showing visitors what early North Dakota pioneer life looked like. Before you leave Fargo, plan on landing at the Fargo Air Museum to look at some of the great legends of the sky. The museum has planes like the P-51 Mustang, the L-39 Jet and the Huey helicopter.

Medora

Our next stop is Medora, a popular tourist attraction. Even though the city is small, it has a lot to offer. The North Dakota Cowboy Hall of fame is located here, as well as the trailhead of the Maah Daah Hey Trail. This trail runs for 96-miles and will take hikers through both the South and North Units of Theodore Roosevelt National Park.

It is easy to eat like a real cowboy in Medora. After a filling dinner at any of the city’s restaurants, you can head over to the Medora Musical. This outdoor, summer show honors North Dakota as it was when Theodore Roosevelt first visited in 1883.

Minot

We learned earlier this year that Minot is home to the Scandinavian Heritage Park and a festival called Norsk Hostfest. That’s not all that that Minot has to offer. This northern-central city has the honor of hosting the North Dakota State Fair each summer. If you enjoy learning about trains and railroads, you should visit the Old Soo Depot Transportation Museum or the Railroad Museum of Minot. There are also several national wildlife refuges nearby, so bring your binoculars!

Williston

When the oil boom hit North Dakota, it meant good times for Williston. The city grew quickly and saw its population grow by over 40 percent in just three years.

Williston is located in the northwestern part of our state. It is home to the Bakken formation, one of the richest oil deposits in the United States. The oil boom brought thousands of new workers and their families to the city. In fact, so many new people moved to the area that Williston has experienced a housing shortage. Since there were not enough houses and apartments to go around, the rent has been some of the most expensive in the United States. A small, one-bedroom apartment can cost over $1,500 a month!

To learn a little about the history of the area, drop in at the Fort Buford State Historic Site. This fort marks where Chief Sitting Bull surrendered to the U.S. government in 1881. Tourists can visit the cemetery and the original officers’ quarters, which is now a museum. You can also enjoy the outdoors in Lewis and Clark State Park near Lake Sakakawea.

Wahpeton

Let’s travel all the way to the southeastern corner of our state, where we’ll stop at the city of Wahpeton. This city was founded in 1869 and named after a local Dakota Indian tribe. It is home to the North Dakota State College of Science and is near the Bagg Bonanza Farm. Many successful businesses have offices and plants in Wahpeton. Wahpeton is a great place to pick up some tasty, homegrown sunflower seeds!

We’ll also want to spend some time at the corner of Dakota Avenue and 4th Street looking at the Wall. It’s an amazing “hidden picture” mural with 23 different objects for visitors to find.

Grand Forks

As one of the largest cities in North Dakota, Grand Forks is located in central eastern North Dakota. It’s along the Red River, right on the Minnesota border. The city is home to the University of North Dakota, as well as the North Dakota Museum of Art and an Air Force base. The city was founded in 1870 and was named Grand Forks because it is located at the fork of the Red River and the Red Lake River. Plan a visit for the Potato Bowl USA, held in September, to get your french-fry fix.

And we can’t forget about our capital city, Bismarck! We learned about Bismarck earlier this year, and we can see where it is on the map. If you live in one of the cities listed here, what information would you add about it? If your city wasn’t listed, work with a partner to write a paragraph about famous sites and special events that make your part of North Dakota special.

title: Stopping for Gas
text:
Before we head out on our road trip, we’ll need to stop for gas. Gas prices fluctuate, or change, from day to day, month to month and season to season. They almost always go up during the summer. Cities are required to sell a special blend of gas between April and September. The special gas causes less pollution, but it also costs more to make. Also, more people travel during the summer months. This means the demand for gas is higher, which causes gas prices to rise.

Before we head out on our road trip, let’s do some math to figure out how much it will cost to fill up the gas tank. Your family’s minivan has a tank that can hold 21 gallons of gas. The price of gas is $2.69 per gallon. How much will it cost to fill up the empty tank?

title: Keeping Our Cities Clean and Safe
text:
Being a good citizen means more than just covering your heart during the Pledge of Allegiance or voting once you turn 18. It also means keeping your city clean and safe and doing your part to make it a pleasant place to live. How can you do your part to be a good citizen?

Take a look at your local park. Is there trash on the ground? You and your friends could get together and help clean up the mess. All you need is a few adults to supervise, some gloves to protect your hands and a box of strong garbage bags! To keep things clean in the first place, always put garbage in trash cans and never throw anything into rivers, streams or lakes. It’s up to you to help keep your city clean, safe and beautiful.

title: Coyote
text:
Coyotes are members of the canine family, and they look a lot like large dogs. Coyotes can grow to be 4 1/2 feet long and weigh between 15 and 40 pounds. A coyote has bushy, gray fur and a long tail. Coyotes and wolves look similar, but coyotes have pointed ears and a longer snout.

Our entire state is a habitat for coyotes. They make their homes in grasslands and wooded areas. They even show up in our suburbs and larger cities from time to time.

Coyotes are omnivores. An omnivore is an animal that eats both plants and meat. Coyotes like to eat fruit, nuts, grass, mice, deer, rabbits and even larger animals like cows and other livestock. Listen for coyotes “talking” to each other at night.
