title: Come Visit North Dakota!
text:
“Alana, can I tell you how much I loved planning a road trip last week? I think it just might keep me going until school gets out for the summer.”

“I agree! Talking about the trip also reminded me of how important tourism is to our state. Did you know that tourism, or traveling for fun, is one of North Dakota’s largest industries? It brings nearly $4 billion into our state each year. That’s a nice chunk of change! If you’re looking forward to summer, you aren’t alone. That’s when tourist season really ‘heats up’!”

“I believe it, Alana. Some people think that North Dakota isn’t much more than farmland and snow. We do have those things, but we also have so much more! If you’re interested in history, North Dakota has plenty of attractions connected to our country’s past. You can walk in the footsteps of the great explorers Lewis and Clark at Fort Mandan. You can even take a ride in a stagecoach and see North Dakota the same way the early pioneers did.”

“That’s true, Jackson. If you’re interested in a little adventure, you can plan a trip to Theodore Roosevelt National Park where you can hike, canoe, mountain bike or ride on horseback. You might even want to bring your tent and spend some evenings counting the stars in our huge North Dakota skies.”

“Some city folks like to come to North Dakota to experience farm life for themselves. There are orchards, pumpkin patches and corn mazes that give everyone a chance to feel like a kid from the country. You can even visit a buffalo ranch or harvest fresh herbs, fruits and vegetables.”

“If you want to learn more about North Dakota’s American Indian culture and heritage, visit some burial mounds or the Knife River Indian Villages National Historic Site. You could even attend an American Indian powwow. I’d love to have more of that tasty fry bread!”

“That sounds like a great summer goal, Alana. There’s no way we could see all there is to see in North Dakota in one summer. If we plan our trips right, we could make it to all the great North Dakota tourist sites by the time we start college. Then we can start all over again!”

title: Writing Rock State Historic Site
text:
If you are interested in seeing how American Indians left their mark (literally) on North Dakota, plan a visit to the Writing Rock State Historic Site. You’ll find it in Williams County, north of Grenora.

Writing Rock is where you will see two large boulders that early American Indians covered with petroglyphs. A petroglyph is a picture carved into rock. The boulders have carvings of a creature called the thunderbird. This creature was part of the myths (stories) and art from many tribes of the Plains and Northwest regions. Pictures of thunderbirds were used as symbols of power. Some tribes believed that thunder and lightning came from these creatures. The earliest images of thunderbirds in North Dakota were carved around A.D. 1000.

The smaller of the two boulders was kept at the University of North Dakota for over 30 years so that experts could study its carvings. Today, both rocks are displayed together at the Writing Rock State Historic Site. Workers built a shelter over the two boulders, and iron bars keep people from getting too close. The site also has a park shelter, picnic tables and playground equipment, so bring a lunch and spend the day!

title: North Dakota Tourism
text:
North Dakota is full of historic, educational, breathtaking and just plain fun tourist attractions. This week, we’ll visit just a few of the sites that bring guests from all over the country to visit our humble home.

Jamestown: Where the Buffalo Roam

Imagine a buffalo that stands 26 feet tall, is 46 feet long and weighs 60 tons. This buffalo is really a cement statue named Dakota Thunder. A local businessman had the statue built in 1959. He wanted to give passing tourists a reason to stop in Jamestown. It worked!

Dakota Thunder is part of Frontier Village, a tourist stop that is full of historic buildings, stagecoach and pony rides and Wild West shoot-out shows. Jamestown is also where you can visit the National Buffalo Museum and see a herd of live buffalo. The herd has had three very special, rare white buffalo named White Cloud, Dakota Miracle and Dakota Legend. Many American Indians think that white buffalo are sacred animals. They are symbols of hope that there will be an end to suffering in the world.

Salem Sue and Tommy the Turtle

Dakota Thunder isn’t the only huge animal statue in North Dakota. New Salem has a 38-foot-tall cow named Salem Sue. It is the largest animal statue in North Dakota. Salem Sue was built in 1974 to honor the dairy industry in the area. Visitors love to stop and get their pictures taken with her.

Drive to Bottineau and you will see and a 30-foot turtle named Tommy. Tommy the Turtle is made of fiberglass and is riding a huge snowmobile. He was built in 1978. People driving through North Dakota know that when they see him, the Turtle Mountains are nearby!

Time for Some History

If you enjoy learning about history, be sure to visit Fort Abraham Lincoln State Park near Bismarck and Mandan. Visitors can see the fort where Lieutenant Colonel George Custer and his soldiers stayed before heading out to battle Lakota and Cheyenne Indians at Little Bighorn. Custer and his troops were defeated in what was one of the last major battles with American Indians. Many parts of the fort have been rebuilt, including the house where Custer lived. The site is also home to the On-A-Slant Indian Village. The village is a group of American Indian lodges that were also rebuilt. The village is a great place to learn about the lifestyle of the Mandan Indians, who lived in the area for centuries.

Let’s Get Wet!

North Dakota also has some great places to go if you like water activities like fishing, swimming, boating or water skiing. Lake Sakakawea is located about 75 miles north of Bismarck. It is a man-made lake that was created when Garrison Dam was built. It was named after the American Indian woman who traveled with Lewis and Clark on their journey through the West. Although many people call her Sacagawea, most North Dakota American Indians believe her name was really Sakakawea. If you don’t like water activities, Lake Sakakawea has hiking and biking trails and great bird-watching opportunities. People also visit during the winter for fantastic snowmobiling adventures.

Devils Lake is North Dakota’s largest natural body of water. It is located in northeastern North Dakota. The lake covers more than 200,000 acres and is great for fishing. Hunting is also a favorite pastime around Devils Lake with plenty of duck- and deer-hunting opportunities. Devils Lake is a great place for people who enjoy boating, hiking and camping. The lake is so big that it even has an island! Grahams Island is a great place to explore. You can also tour nearby Fort Totten State Historic Site, a former military post built in 1868.

International Peace Garden

The International Peace Garden is near Dunseith, on the border between the United States and Canada. The garden was created in 1932 to celebrate the peaceful relationship between the United States and Canada. The garden covers 2,300 acres and includes lakes, fountains, hiking trails and beautiful flower displays. All of the displays except for two are changed each year. The two that stay the same are grown to look like the American and Canadian flags. The Peace Chapel spans the border between the two countries, a symbol of the connection we share. The International Peace Garden has also been home to four concrete towers: two on the American side and two on the Canadian side. These towers have started to crumble and the decision was made to take them down. This was because falling concrete has become a danger to visitors. Park officials hope the towers will be replaced with another striking symbol of the two friendly countries.

Of course, there’s not enough space to write about all of the wonderful places in North Dakota. Did you know that you can be a tourist in your own state? Just do a little research, talk to your family and make a plan! North Dakota has a lot of choices. Pick a busy town with lots to do and see, or find a quiet place to relax for a day or two. Either way, you’re sure to have a good time.

title: Lawrence Welk: Wunnerful, Wunnerful!
text:
Lawrence Welk is one of North Dakota’s most famous people. If you haven’t heard of him yet, it’s about time you did! Welk’s family immigrated to Strasburg, North Dakota, in 1893. Lawrence was born in 1903, the sixth of eight children. Strasburg was full of German immigrants from Russia, and the Welk family only spoke German in their home.

Music was Welk’s first love. He learned to play the accordion at an early age. When he was a teenager, he asked his father to buy him a new accordion. He promised that he would work on the family farm until he was 21 years old to pay for it. Welk kept his word and worked, earning extra money by playing music for dances. He gave all the money to his family.

After a while, Welk started a band that played for dances. He also played on the radio in Yankton, South Dakota. He and his band did so well that they were invited to California to play on TV. By 1955, “The Lawrence Welk Show” was on national television. Welk’s show stayed popular until he retired in 1982. Reruns of his famous song and dance show still appear on public television today. Lawrence Welk died in 1992.

Welk spoke mostly German as a child, so he had a difficult time pronouncing the letter “D.” When he was pleased with the performance of his band, he would say that the song was “Wunnerful, wunnerful.” The phrase became well known. Lawrence Welk was the very first winner of the Theodore Roosevelt Rough Rider Award.

title: The Legend of Devils Lake
text:
The American Indian name for Devils Lake is “Miniwaukan,” which means “Spirit Water.” When the first explorers came to the area, they translated the name to “Bad Water.” As time passed, the lake became known as Devils Lake.

Legend says that a group of Sioux warriors had attacked the Chippewa in the area and had forced them north, toward present-day Canada. The Sioux planned to attack again to drive them even farther away. The Great Spirit Man appeared to them. He warned that if they attacked the Chippewa, a monster would come out of the lake and swallow them whole.

The Sioux warriors did not believe the warning and prepared for battle. Just as they were ready to attack, the lake began to boil and the ground shook. A hideous monster poked its head out of the water. It had a huge head, a short, chubby neck and short, squat legs. Its eyes burned with fire as the monster began to gobble up every Sioux in sight. A few were able to escape, but the rest were killed. The water became salty, like the ocean, and all the fish vanished without a trace.

A group of Sioux medicine men decided to explore the lake. They found a hole in the bottom where boiling water flowed into the lake. They discovered that this hole was a passage connected to an underground river running all the way to the Gulf of Mexico. The monster apparently came up from the hole and drew all the fish into the underground passageway. If you’ve ever visited Devils Lake, you know that the fish have returned. Whether the monster still haunts Devils Lake remains a mystery!

title: Discovering Black Gold
text:
North Dakota has experienced a huge oil BOOM! We’ve already learned that a boom is a time when the population or economy of a place grows. Since the oil boom started, our state has enjoyed a boost to our economy.

Why is oil so important to North Dakota? Well, petroleum is a fossil fuel also known as crude oil. Our culture depends on petroleum to help make everyday life possible. It is one of the world’s top sources of fuel, so there is always demand for petroleum. That’s what makes the oil and gas industry so important. Petroleum is very valuable because it is both useful and nonrenewable. We’ve also already learned that nonrenewable means not easily replaced. Oil may not be pretty, but it is always in demand, and there is only so much of it. This is why some people call oil black gold or say that it’s worth its weight in gold!

Petroleum takes millions of years to form. A long time ago, much of the Earth was covered by water. When plants and animals back then died, they sank to the bottom of swamps and oceans and were slowly covered by layers of rocks and sand. As years passed, pressure and heat turned these plants and animals into petroleum, natural gas and coal. Large amounts of these fossil fuels have collected together in the ground under North Dakota.

In order to get to these fossil fuels, oil companies use huge machines to drill into the ground and pump the crude oil to the surface. The petroleum must then be refined. Crude oil that is refined is cleaned of dirt and extra chemicals that have gotten mixed in. Refined oil can be used to make fuels and plastic items we use each day.

North Dakota’s oil boom started in 2006 when geologists discovered the Parshall Oil Field. Our economy has grown since then, and about 15 percent of our state’s workers work for the oil and gas industry. Experts think that most of the new oil wells in North Dakota will be able to pump oil for at least 30 more years. This means that North Dakota’s black gold could keep our state booming for many years to come!

title: High Gas Prices Could Tank Small Businesses
text:
There are many types of small businesses in the United States. Some are agricultural businesses. That means they are based on plants and animals. Some businesses manufacture goods in factories. Both types of businesses use transportation to ship goods from place to place. Whether goods are shipped by truck, train, ship or airplane, it takes fuel to get those goods where they need to go. When fuel prices go up, companies’ transportation costs go up.

Gasoline is a good example of how fuel costs affect businesses. The cost of gasoline goes up and down, but over time the price has mostly gone up. In March 1999, a gallon of gas cost only $1.05. How much is a gallon of gasoline where you live today? High gas prices are hard on everyone, especially some businesses.

Small businesses usually don’t make a lot of profit. When gasoline costs go up, some business owners are faced with difficult choices. They may have to close their businesses down. Or they may have to raise prices to make up for the cost of fuel. Then consumers may have to pay more for the goods they buy at the stores.

There are other ways for businesses to save money on transportation, too. Some pizza stores use bicycles instead of cars to deliver their pies. Other companies are using only small cars and trucks that don’t use as much gas.

No one knows what the price of gasoline will be in 10 years or even next year. What does your family do when the price of gas goes up? What do you do when it goes down?

title: The North Dakota Oil Boom
text:
The North Dakota oil boom began when geologist Michael S. Johnson and his team discovered an oil field. The field is near the town of Parshall in Mountrail County. The Parshall Oil Field is part of the larger Bakken Formation, one of the most active oil fields in the United States. The Parshall Oil Field covers almost 3 million acres and may hold 3 billion barrels of oil. Oil companies have already pumped millions of barrels of oil. The barrels of oil pumped and sold so far have had a huge impact on North Dakota’s economy.

So how much money does the oil and gas industry really bring into our state each year? One study says that the oil and gas industry contributes over $40 billion a year to the state’s economy. This industry also pays around $5 billion in salaries and wages to its workers each year. That’s a lot of cash! The oil and gas industry can take credit for much of our economy’s growth and our low unemployment rate.

The benefits of the oil boom go farther than our oil fields. North Dakota has enjoyed one of the fastest growing economies of any state in the country. Many states have a hard time finding enough money to run their states and often go into debt. North Dakota has had a budget surplus. This means that our state has had money left over after meeting all its needs. Our leaders have used the extra money to cut property taxes, improve our schools, build better roads and increase medical care. These improvements have made life better for all of us here in North Dakota!

A growing economy gives workers from other parts of the country a reason to move here. North Dakota has welcomed many new people. This means that many of our cities have grown, especially in western North Dakota near the oil fields. You may remember reading that the city of Williston has had a population explosion. In three years, the city grew over 40 percent. Experts believe that the city will keep growing. That’s a lot to deal with!

The oil boom has also brought a few challenges. Prices for houses and apartments have gone up, and housing shortages have become common in North Dakota. This means there haven’t been enough homes for everyone who wants to move here. These shortages have been worse in towns and cities that are closest to the boom. Prices for many other items have gone up as well. There has also been a shortage of doctors. Many communities have tried to bring in more doctors and nurses by building health care centers. With all those extra people, it also means more cars on the roads. Traffic has increased on many of North Dakota’s major highways, and the large number of big trucks and heavy machines on our roads can be dangerous for other travelers. Even though some problems have popped up, many people think the oil boom has helped our state more than it has harmed it. Here’s hoping that oil continues to fuel our state’s economy far into the future.

title: Michael S. Johnson
text:
Do you remember geologist Michael S. Johnson from this week’s lesson? He and his team discovered Parshall Oil Field, which kick-started North Dakota’s oil boom.

Johnson was born in Maryville, Missouri, in 1926. A few years later, his family moved to Tulsa, Oklahoma. At the time, Oklahoma was known as the oil capital of the nation, and Johnson became interested in learning about oil. Since then, he has never stopped studying, searching for and finding new sources of the rich, black liquid.

Johnson studied geology at Ohio State University. Geology is the study of the earth and the rocks that form it. He earned both a bachelor’s and a master’s degree. Johnson began working as a petroleum geologist. This is a person who predicts where oil is likely to be found. Oil companies hire petroleum geologists to help them find new oil supplies. The more oil a company can find, the more business they can do. Johnson worked for private oil companies until 1963. After that, he worked as an independent petroleum geologist. This means that he no longer worked for specific companies. He spent time studying maps of oil fields and looking closely at soil from promising sites. Johnson made maps that showed where he thought people could find oil. He sold these maps to companies who were willing to pay for the information.

Johnson helped discover more than 15 good oil fields throughout North Dakota and other states. The best find of his career came in 2006. His research led to the discovery of the Parshall Oil Field. The field is part of the Bakken Formation in northwestern North Dakota. Johnson’s discovery has had a huge impact on North Dakota’s oil and gas industry!

Johnson’s advice to students like you is to keep trying and never give up on your goals. Keep working hard and always believe that you will succeed, even if it seems impossible.

title: Oil Drilling Rig
text: If you are in the western part of our state, you may have noticed the huge structures in the oil fields. North Dakota oil is pumped out of the earth with oil drilling rigs. An oil drilling rig is a large machine that drills holes deep into the ground to bring oil or natural gas to the surface. The earliest oil drills made holes in the earth by hammering the bit (cutting part of a drill) into the ground. Workers then used a bailer device to lift the broken rock out of the hole. Later, spinning rotary drills were invented. These had two wheels and could drill thousands of feet into the ground to reach oil. In 1933, engineers invented a three-wheeled tricone bit. This bit is able to cut through even the hardest rocks and is used by many North Dakota oil drilling rigs today.

title: What is hydraulic fracturing?
text:
Hydraulic fracturing, or fracking, is a way to get oil or natural gas out of the ground. Workers shoot water deep into the ground, and the water cracks, or fractures, the rock. The water is mixed with chemicals and sand that help hold the cracks open. With the rocks fractured, oil or natural gas leaks out. Machines can then pump the oil out and capture the natural gas.

Oil companies first experimented with fracking during the 1940s. It worked so well that oil companies around the world have used the same method. Some people argue that we should not use fracking because it can cause water, air and noise pollution. Fracking has even been known to trigger earthquakes. Those who support fracking say it’s the only way to release the oil trapped inside of stubborn rock and unlock the ground’s rich supply of oil and natural gas.

This is a well head where fluids are injected into the ground.

title: Fisher
text:
The fisher is a member of the weasel family. It has a long body, a long, bushy tail, a pointed nose and short, rounded ears. Its fur is dark brown or black, with lighter-colored fur around its face. The fisher is three to four feet long and weighs up to 12 pounds.

They are called fishers, but these animals do not eat fish. Fishers are carnivores (meat eaters), but instead of fish, they eat squirrels, rabbits, mice and birds. Fishers are one of the few animals that eat porcupines. It’s a tricky task! Most fishers in North Dakota live along the wooded streams in the eastern part of our state. They are also good at climbing trees and will sometimes build their dens in hollow logs. They’re usually nocturnal, which means they are active at night and sleep during the day. Have you ever seen this unusual animal?

title: Looking Back: North Dakota Cities and Tourist Attractions
text:
You don’t have to go far from home to have a great vacation. North Dakota is full of historic, educational and fun tourist sites. There is enough to do and see that any trip here is sure to please all travelers.

Tourists bring about $3.6 billion to our state each year. That makes tourism one of North Dakota’s largest industries. Let’s take another look at a few of the places we have visited with Studies Weekly. …

Grand Forks

If you like potatoes, plan a visit to one of North Dakota’s largest cities, Grand Forks. It’s on the Red River. If you come in September, you can become a part of the French Fry Feed. You can load up on all the golden fries you can hold with all the ketchup you need, absolutely free! Once you are full, you can take a walk through the University of North Dakota and the North Dakota Museum of Art.

Jamestown

In Jamestown you can visit the 60-ton concrete buffalo named Dakota Thunder. The statue stands watch on the prairie. While there, you can also see the historic buildings at Frontier Village. Jamestown is where you will find three rare white buffalo named White Cloud, Dakota Miracle and Dakota Legend. White buffalo are sacred to the American Indians of the Plains tribes. They are symbols of hope that there will be an end to suffering in the world.

Salem Sue and Tommy the Turtle

After you’ve checked Dakota Thunder off your list, look for the other giant animal statues. Salem Sue is a huge cow in New Salem, and Tommy is a 30-foot turtle in Bottineau. Both statues are made of fiberglass. Sue stands in honor of the dairy industry in the area, and Tommy the Turtle is riding an enormous snowmobile. Tommy rides on the edge of the Turtle Mountains of North Dakota.

Medora

Medora is a small city with big adventures. This is where you can find the North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame, as well as the start of the Maah Daah Hey Trail. The town is also known for the Medora Musical. This is an outdoor show that honors North Dakota as it was when Theodore Roosevelt first came here in 1883. If you visit Medora in the summer, check out the show!

Fargo

Don’t miss out on our largest city! Fargo is built along the Red River in the southeastern part of our state. This railroad town has grown to include Bonanzaville, the Red River Zoo and the Fargo Air Museum.

International Peace Garden

Head up north to Dunseith, and you can visit two countries in one afternoon! The International Peace Garden was built to celebrate the friendship between the United States and Canada. You’ll find beautiful flower displays and a chapel that was built on the border between the two countries. Isn’t it nice to have such wonderful neighbors?

Let’s Get Wet!

North Dakota also has some great places to go if you like boating, fishing, swimming or any other water activities. Lake Sakakawea was created when Garrison Dam was built. The land surrounding Lake Sakakawea offers bird watching and trails for hiking or biking. If you visit in winter, those trails are great for snowmobiles!

Devils Lake is North Dakota’s largest natural body of water. It is located in northeastern North Dakota. The lake covers more than 200,000 acres and is a popular fishing spot. Visitors enjoy boating, hiking, camping and touring nearby Fort Totten State Historic Site.

title: Industry in North Dakota
text:
Let’s look at some of North Dakota’s very important industries that bring money and jobs to our state. Fill in the blanks at the end of each section. (Hint: Look at your Studies Weekly, Week 24 “Industry” issue for help.)

Agriculture and Livestock

North Dakota’s rich, fertile soil makes farming one of our most important industries. Many residents make their living from agriculture. There are more than 30,000 farms and ranches in North Dakota. Our state has about 40 million acres of land devoted to farming. This means that 90 percent of our state’s total land is used for agriculture and livestock. Agriculture brings in almost $6 billion to our state each year.

Much of our country’s spring wheat and durum wheat is grown in the Red River Valley. In the Drift Prairie region we grow oats, canola and sunflowers. Farms on the Missouri Plateau are where you’ll find barley, flaxseed and cattle. The land in this region is harder to farm.

Name three crops or animals (not already listed) that are grown or raised in North Dakota.

Manufacturing

The manufacturing industry uses resources to make other useful items. Food processing is one of North Dakota’s most important manufacturing areas. Our food processing plants produce bread, cheese and steaks, just to name a few.

North Dakota’s factories also make farming and mining equipment that is sold around the world. Factories are located across the state, especially in Bismarck, Fargo, Grand Forks and Minot.

Name two items (not already listed) that are manufactured in North Dakota.

Renewable Energy

Our state gets almost 20 percent of its total energy from the wind. North Dakota has about 1,000 wind turbines to generate power. Biodiesel and ethanol are also renewable resources, and we use them for fuel.

Name one of the ingredients in biodiesel or ethanol fuels.

Coal Mining

North Dakota has a huge deposit of lignite coal just underneath its soil. Our state mines about 30 million tons of coal each year. The coal industry is centered in western North Dakota.

Name the kind of power that is generated by burning coal.

Oil and Natural Gas

The oil and natural gas industry has had huge growth in recent years. During good times, over 1 million barrels of oil are produced in North Dakota every day! The oil boom has brought many new workers and much money to our state.

Name the area of North Dakota where much of the oil and natural gas is pumped. Is it northwest, southwest, northeast or southeast?

Tourism

More than 24 million visitors travel to North Dakota each year to enjoy the great outdoors. They visit popular sites like the Theodore Roosevelt National Park, the National Buffalo Museum, Fort Abraham Lincoln State Park and the North Dakota Heritage Center and State Museum. Tourists bring in about $3.6 billion to North Dakota each year.

Name three sites (not listed here or on the cover) that tourists come to visit.

title: North Dakota Oil
text:
The North Dakota oil boom began when geologist Michael S. Johnson discovered the Parshall Oil Field in 2006. The Parshall Oil Field may hold 3 billion barrels of petroleum, or crude oil. This discovery has had a huge impact on North Dakota’s economy!

Oil companies hire workers to get the oil out of the ground through hydraulic fracturing. Once it is out of the ground, it is refined and turned into gasoline and many other products. The oil and gas industry sends over $40 billion a year into our economy. The oil industry also pays around $5 billion in salaries and wages to its workers each year. Much of the growth in North Dakota’s economy and our low unemployment are thanks to the oil boom.

The oil boom has had an impact on nearly everyone in North Dakota. Our state has had one of the fastest growing economies in the country. A growing economy brings in workers from other parts of the country and the world. It means that our cities grow as well.

North Dakota has also had a budget surplus. This extra money has made it possible for our state to cut property taxes, improve our schools, build better roads and increase medical care.

Besides jobs, money and success, the oil boom has also brought a few challenges. Housing has become expensive and hard to find. Many other items have cost more as well. There is also a shortage of doctors and health care centers. Traffic has increased, and the large number of big trucks and heavy machines on our roads can make travel dangerous. Even with the problems that have come up along the way, many people feel the oil boom has helped our state more than it has harmed it.

A natural hazard is an event caused by nature that can be dangerous to people or the environment. Even though North Dakota is a nice place to live, our state is no stranger to natural disasters. North Dakota is famous for its blizzards, or harsh winter storms with strong winds and blowing snow. North Dakota has also experienced years of drought, or a long period of time with little or no rainfall. On the other hand, heavy rains sometimes hit our state. Tornadoes are also common here. An average of 32 tornadoes touch down each year. Severe windstorms have also happened from time to time. Earthquakes are rare in our state. The natural beauty of North Dakota is inviting, but we also have to be careful!

title: The Founding of Savannah
text:
While working for Parliament in England in 1729, James Oglethorpe was put in charge of investigating the conditions of prisons in England. Oglethorpe worked hard to improve conditions for prisoners. However, he was disturbed to find that many prisoners had been arrested for nothing more than owing debts.

Oglethorpe wanted to do more to help the large number of poor people in England. He eventually came up with the idea to create a colony that would be a fresh start for the poor in England. Oglethorpe worked with members of his committee, such as John, Lord Viscount Percival, to accomplish this. Percival and Oglethorpe wanted to provide opportunities to the poor and help them acquire marketable skills to become farmers, merchants, and skilled artisans.

In order to get permission and the means to establish a new colony, Oglethorpe had to persuade the king to grant him a charter. Oglethorpe and 20 others were named as trustees. The trustees were to be in charge of governing the new colony of Georgia.

The plan to take former prisoners to the colony quickly died out, but Oglethorpe preserved the idea of giving people a chance for a better life in the new colony. Rather than debtors and prisoners, the first group of 114 men, women, and children to set out for Georgia consisted of skilled workers, farmers, and merchants.

After landing in Port Royal, South Carolina, Oglethorpe was granted the help of William Bull of South Carolina. They were to find a suitable place south of South Carolina to establish the first city of the Georgia Colony. After exploring the area, Oglethorpe found a spot on the Savannah River where he wished to establish his colony.

After consulting with Bull, the first thing Oglethorpe did was go to a Yamacraw village near the site to talk with the chief and get permission to settle there. He made friends with Chief Tomochichi, and he promised to give gifts to the Yamacraw and be good neighbors to them. Tomochichi welcomed Oglethorpe and agreed to his proposition.

After surveying the area where he wished to establish his colony, Oglethorpe named the place "Savannah" after the Savannah River and brought the 114 colonists to the spot. Oglethorpe and Bull planned the layout of the city of Savannah together, and before long, the city plans became a reality. Oglethorpe strived to ensure that Savannah had an equal society. He wanted to erase divisions of class based on wealth and birth that were present back in England.

The new Georgia Colony was built on the motto Non Sibi Sed Aliis, which means "not for self, but for others." This slogan helped the colonists remember how Georgia would be different from the other 12 English colonies in North America. Georgia was the 13th colony for England in North America and the final one before the United States was created.

title: The Yamacraw
text:
The Yamacraw tribe broke off from the Creek and the Yamasee tribes to form their own group. There had been disagreement between the tribes about alliances that had been formed with European settlers. Those who did not agree with either alliance left and formed the Yamacraw.

The Yamacraw were a very young group, forming in about 1728. They had only been established as their own tribe for five years when James Oglethorpe arrived in 1733. The newly-formed Yamacraw were led by a mico, or chief, named Tomochichi. Tomochichi is believed to have originally come from the Creek tribe. He and his group of about 200 Yamacraw settled in bluffs along the Savannah River in what is now the state of Georgia.

Tomochichi chose this location because his ancestors were buried there and it was close to English settlers he and his people could trade with. They retained much of their old governmental and spiritual practices from their former tribes. They organized themselves based on their town and connections centered around familial clans. They also worshiped one god, believed in an afterlife, and believed that all things, both living and nonliving, had a spirit.

With Tomochichi’s guidance, the Yamacraw had peaceful relationships with English settlers. Already having some experience trading with white settlers, the Yamacraw had the skills and diplomacy to trade and negotiate successfully and peacefully with them.

title: Oglethorpe's Vision for Savannah
text:
James Oglethorpe wasn’t very active in the British Parliament when he was first elected in 1722. However, he became much more actively involved in politics when he was personally affected by a problem he saw in his community that he wanted to change.

James Oglethorpe's friend, Robert Castell, was imprisoned for debts he was unable to pay. Castell tried to pay off some of his debts while he was in prison by publishing and selling a folio called The Villas of the Ancients Illustrated with the help of some friends, but it wasn't enough. Castell was moved to a poorer part of the prison and given the bedding of a prisoner who had died of smallpox. Castell contracted smallpox from the bedding and died shortly thereafter. Oglethorpe was upset and angry about his friend's death. At first, he blamed Castell's creditors for his death, but after some investigation, Oglethorpe realized that the terrible conditions of the prison were the real reason for his friend's untimely end.

At this time, Oglethorpe was a member of Parliament. His first efforts focused on getting a bill passed that would help debtors pay off what they owed. He also encouraged the wealthy people of London to donate money to help pay off prisoners' debts and help improve their conditions. Oglethorpe then gathered evidence and information. He went into the prison where Castell died and took notes on the names of the debtors, how much they owed, and the conditions they were suffering in.

In 1729, Oglethorpe called for an investigation to be made into the conditions of prisons and jails in England. He was appointed the chairman of a committee to carry out these investigations.

Prisons in England, especially in London, were overcrowded and had poor conditions. Cells were crowded, cold, and often damp. What food was offered was of poor quality. In some prisons, a person had to pay for anything they hadn’t brought into the prison with them, such as blankets, food, and having their shackles removed. Adding insult to injury, prisoners had to pay for room and board. This only added to the debts they were in prison for. People couldn’t work to pay off their debts while they were in prison. As a result, their debts only got worse unless friends or family could find a way to pay off what they owed. Some people spent their entire lives in debtors' prisons without any hope of ever getting out.

Oglethorpe knew that the system for debtors' prisons needed to be fixed. He spoke up in Parliament and pushed for new laws to be passed that would improve prisoner’s lives and give them opportunities to pay off their debts. When a Dr. Thomas Bray left 5,000 pounds to Oglethorpe to use for good in the American colonies, he was inspired to find a more permanent solution to help out the poor and indebted people in England. He wanted to create a new colony where poor and indebted people could go to make a fresh start and have the chance for a new life. He met and discussed his idea with the Bray Associates, a group of administrators of Dr. Thomas Bray, in 1729.

A proposal for a new colony in the Americas was drawn up and submitted to Parliament. However, the prime minister was hesitant to grant a charter for a colony so far south. Spain had laid claim to Florida at that time, and he was worried that establishing a colony so close to Florida would provoke the Spanish settlers.

In order to persuade the prime minister and Parliament to grant Oglethorpe the charter, the wording of the proposal was slightly altered to say that, rather than debtors and prisoners, "the deserving poor" would be sent to live in the new colony. The deserving poor would be selected by Oglethorpe and his committee in order to ensure that the colony would succeed. It also proposed that the colony would benefit England by producing raw materials and providing a defensive barrier between Spanish-controlled Florida and the English colony of South Carolina.

In 1731, the British king granted the charter to Oglethorpe. The charter stipulated that the colonists would be granted the same rights as all Englishmen. It also stated that the government would be led by a board of trustees. The charter allowed for religious freedom in the colony, but forbade Roman Catholics and Jews from settling in the colony.

Oglethorpe and the Bray Associates, who became Georgia Trustees, busied themselves with preparations. They interviewed people living in poverty to find promising members to take with them to Georgia. None of the people were prisoners or in debt, as Oglethorpe had first intended. However, the people selected to go to Georgia were working people with skills that he believed would help the colony be successful. Many working people in England were very poor at that time. The offer to travel to a new land where they would have the chance to own land and rise above poverty sounded like a wonderful opportunity to them.

At last, in 1732, Oglethorpe and 114 colonists set sail on the ship Anne for their new colony, which Oglethorpe had named after the English king: Georgia.

title: Planning the City
text:
The city of Savannah was so well-planned that its layout has remained virtually unaltered, even today. The details about where the ideas came from for the design of Savannah are unknown. However, some scholars believe James Oglethorpe and William Bull based some of the city plans on the ideas and illustrations in Castell’s The Villas of the Ancients Illustrated.

Each settler received 50 acres of land outside the city and a place for a house within the city. The streets of the town were built on a grid system with houses and public buildings built around town squares. Originally, there were 24 town squares in the city of Savannah. Thanks to the careful planning and well-planned structure of Savannah, 22 of the original 24 squares still exist today. Closest to the water, the streets usually had cobblestone paving. The stones used to pave the streets came from ballast stones taken from the bellies of ships. Ballast stones were large rocks placed in the bottoms of ships to make sure they remained upright in the water. Today, these cobblestone streets can still be seen if you visit the old quarter of the city.

The Georgia Colony was meant to be a buffer between South Carolina and Florida. The city of Savannah was planned to be effective in defending against Spanish invasions and potential attacks from Native American groups in conflict with the settlers. While scouting out a place to build his city, Oglethorpe searched for a location as close to South Carolina and as far from Florida as possible. He was hoping to avoid any conflict with the Spanish. The place he selected rested on a bluff above the Savannah River, which gave it a natural defensive barrier against invasions and attacks. Its location near water also made Savannah an important port town, which later played several roles during the American Revolution and the Civil War.

Farther south than the other plantations and farms, Noble Jones, the colonist who had surveyed Savannah for Oglethorpe, built Wormsloe Plantation. His fortified plantation doubled as an outpost to guard against invasions. Fort Frederica was also constructed by Oglethorpe to serve as a defensive base on St. Simons Island. The fort provided a good lookout over the marshes and waterways that Savannah was settled on. Savannah is often considered America’s first planned city, and it stands today as a testament to how well-laid plans can stand the test of time.

Once the city was planned, the trustees set to work creating a local government and laws for the colony. The first act that Oglethorpe and the trustees passed required that any person trading with Native Americans west of Savannah River had to obtain a license from the Georgia trustees to do so. A second piece of legislation banned rum in the colony. The third act they passed outlawed legalized slavery in the colony.

title: The Growth of Savannah
text:
Thanks to careful planning and hard work, Savannah had a strong beginning and continued to thrive as it grew. Its population began with approximately 114 settlers who first came to Georgia to help James Oglethorpe establish the colony. Unlike members of earlier colonial settlements, such as Jamestown, Oglethorpe chose people from the working class who knew how to work hard and could handle the difficulties that came with building and establishing a new settlement.

Savannah started out very small, but thanks to Oglethorpe’s peaceful negotiations with the neighboring Yamacraw people, the settlement thrived and its population rapidly increased. More and more settlers came to Georgia Colony to join the Savannah settlers. Between 1734 and 1735, several immigrants from Germany, Moravia, and Scotland settled in Savannah. By 1740, just seven years after its establishment, Savannah had a population of about 600 people. The land Oglethorpe granted to settlers was fertile and good for farming. Cotton grew very well in Georgia’s climate, and it quickly became a profitable cash crop for the settlers to grow and sell.

One of the primary reasons for the rapid increase in population between the 1740s and 1760s was the legalization of slavery in the colony. Georgia Colony was founded with a ban on slavery. However, the ban was lifted and slavery in Georgia was legalized in 1751. As a result, settlers moved to Georgia from other British colonies to establish large plantations. They hoped to make a profit off of growing cash crops like cotton, rice, tobacco, and indigo. As the number of plantations increased, so did the enslaved population of the colony.

Look at the population table of Savannah. What changes do you notice? Before a formal census was created in 1790, the populations of cities and colonies weren't recorded very accurately. The numbers shown in the table are based on the estimates and counts of people who were alive in the 1700s.

title: The Rise of Cotton
text:
When the Georgia Colony was established, each colonist was given 50 acres to farm in the Savannah settlement. Laws prevented people from combining or expanding their lands. This was meant to keep people working their own lands and prevent enslaved labor. Fifty acres was a lot of land for one person to farm, even with the help of their family.

Cotton was the main crop grown in Savannah. The climate was ideal for growing this cash crop. Georgia’s summers are hot and humid, and it was hard work to grow and harvest cotton. Savannah colonists would have grown the inland variety of cotton, which is harder to harvest and separate seeds from. Some colonists were happy to have land to work on and earn a living. Others complained and felt that the work was too hard.

Colonists in Savannah were divided on the issue of whether or not to legalize slavery in Georgia. Many argued about the morality of enslaving people, while others argued that slavery was necessary to work plantations. Eventually, the demand to legalize slavery gained the majority of votes in the colony.

When enslavement was legalized, wealthy plantation owners came to Georgia and began buying up land from the original settlers to create plantations. Small farmers had no way to compete against the plantation system. Running a large plantation was expensive. Some small farmers chose to stay and continue working on their 50 acres. However, it didn’t take long for the plantation system to change the economy, landscape, government, society, and virtually everything that Georgia had originally been created for.

title: A Struggling Colony
text:
In 1751, when slavery was legalized in the Georgia Colony, plantation owners from other colonies began pouring into Georgia. They influenced the culture, economy, and government of the colony by establishing the plantation system in Georgia. The original settlers in Savannah, who had been making a living off of their farms, quickly lost majority control to these plantation owners and their economic and cultural beliefs.

By 1752, the original Georgia Trustees had resigned. They didn't want to be part of a colony where slavery was legal. Georgia then became a royal colony. This meant that it was ruled by the king of England through a governor, a council, and a House of Commons in the colony. The Church of England was established in the colony, and it took priority over other faiths. Catholicism was banned, and members of other faiths had to pay to support the English Church. Savannah was also made the capital of the royal colony.

In addition to these changes, the restrictions on land ownership were repealed. Thousands of people came flooding into Georgia with hopes for prosperity. Plantation owners converted marshes into profitable rice fields, while others began growing cotton. William Stephens, who led Georgia Colony until the new royal government was established, wrote that "people from all parts of his Majesty's dominions in America as well as from Germany and Great Britain are almost daily coming thither."

The plantation economy, which was based on the labor of enslaved people, grew rapidly in Georgia. Before long, it dominated Georgia’s economy and government. Plantation agriculture brought a lot of wealth to Georgia, but it also revived old social practices of class division based on wealth. Plantation owners were among the wealthiest in the colonies, and they lived lavish lifestyles. These wealthy few were called the "landed gentry."

The enslavement of African men, women, and children increased during this time in Georgia. Not only did plantation owners from other colonies bring the people they had enslaved into Georgia, but more people were enslaved and brought directly from Africa, through the Middle Passage, to Georgia. This increased the number of enslaved people in the colony. Within just 25 years of the legalization of slavery, beginning in 1751, Georgia’s enslaved population grew from less than 500 people to about 18,000. Estimates from the time show that one out of three people in Georgia was enslaved by the 1770s.

The plantation system transformed Georgia from a struggling colony to an established, economic powerhouse.

title: Essential Question
text: How is our life different from those who lived in the past? How is it the same?

title: Age of Encounters
text:
In the late 1400s, countries on Europe’s Atlantic coast were competing with each other for wealth and power. Portugal was the leader in exploration. In 1488, a ship from Portugal sailed to the southern tip of Africa. Then, in 1492, Spain paid for Christopher Columbus to sail west across the Atlantic Ocean. Columbus studied everything that was available. He believed he could reach India by sailing west. No one in Europe at the time knew there were continents between the Atlantic Ocean and India. When Columbus landed, he thought he had reached India. He called the people he met “Indians.”

Columbus brought evidence of his trip back to Europe. He shared his adventures and became famous in Europe. Once Columbus and his crew shared what they learned on the voyage, other explorers followed.

Portugal, England, and France sent explorers across the Atlantic. Many early explorers believed they had reached Asia. In 1503, an explorer named Amerigo Vespucci became convinced that the land they were exploring was really another continent. Amerigo Vespucci claimed it was a “new world.” People later called the land “America” in honor of this claim. “America” was a Latinized version of Amerigo’s name.

Explorers share information that helps others explore. Columbus opened a new door for exploration by sharing what he saw and learned. Many followed his example and shared their new knowledge.

Christopher Columbus

Spain paid Christopher Columbus to sail across the Atlantic Ocean in 1492. Columbus hoped to reach India by sailing west. Instead, his ships landed in the Caribbean. There, Columbus met the Taíno people. Columbus’s voyage increased Europe’s interest in exploration and led to many other voyages and colonies.

John Cabot

Learning from Columbus, John Cabot became interested in finding a shorter route across the Atlantic. England sponsored Cabot to sail through the North Atlantic in 1497. Cabot thought he had landed in Asia, but it was actually what is now Canada. His voyage proved that a northern route to the Americas could work. He met the Eastern Woodland Native Americans.

Pedro Álvares Cabral

In 1500, Portugal paid for Pedro Cabral to take 13 ships to India for trade. Cabral’s plan was to sail around Africa, but on the way, his ships sailed far into the Atlantic. This misdirection caused Cabral to land on the coast of South America. There, he met the Tupiniquim people.

Jacques Cartier

France hoped to find a northwest passage to reach the Pacific Ocean through North America. In 1534, France paid for Jacques Cartier to search for such a route. Cartier sailed up rivers in what is now Canada. He didn’t find a route to the Pacific, but he did meet the Mi’kmaq people and the powerful Iroquois Confederacy. Cartier’s trips started French trade in North America.

Adriaen Block

Like the Spanish, English, and French, the Dutch government hoped to find riches and trade routes in North America. In 1613, Dutch explorer Adriaen Block arrived in present-day New York on a small ship called the Tyger. He anchored at what is now Manhattan, New York. With the help of the Lenape tribe, he and his men built homes and settled in the area for the winter. Block and his crew were the first European settlers in New York. In 1614, they traveled up the Hudson River and established a trading post near present-day Albany, New York.

title: Tools of Exploration
text:
Hundreds of years ago, explorers traveled the oceans. How did they know where they were? Advances in technology, mathematics, and measurement in the 1400s made long-distance navigation possible. One good example of the methods they used comes from Columbus, who was one of the first navigators to keep detailed accounts of his voyage.

Some tools that Columbus used helped with celestial navigation, or using the sun, moon, and stars to find location. Sailors used an instrument called an astrolabe that they would point to the sky. Light from the sun during the day and the North Star at night shone through it. Sailors then read a dial to determine their latitude. Another tool explorers used was the quadrant. A quadrant was used to determine altitude, the height of a fixed point above sea level.

These tools led to advances in map-making, or cartography. The original purpose of maps wasn’t to be accurate in size or proportion. Instead, they showed who had control of the land. Once maps showed more exact distances and details, they were easier to follow. The invention of printing also made maps easier to obtain.

Even the new ships Columbus sailed on aided in exploration. The caravel, a ship with broad bows and beams, was smaller, lighter, and easier to navigate than older boats. Their lighter weight and smaller design also made them faster. Most ships only had one kind of sail, but caravels were equipped to use both. With both square and triangular sails, caravels could sail into the wind. It also allowed them to sail both along shorelines and in open water. Though they were small, they had thick planking and could carry a lot of goods or people.

title: Mapping It Out
text:
This is a map created in 1507 by Martin Waldseemüller at the beginning of the Age of Exploration. This was considered the most accurate map at the time. Compare this map to a current map of the world. List three things Waldseemüller was fairly accurate about.

From what you can remember, list three things that are not accurate on the 1507 map.

title: Trade, Taxes, and Scarcity
text:
Trade is one way people meet their wants and needs. Trade with others creates a trade network. In Europe, there was a trade network between Europe and the Indies. The “Indies” was the name given to islands in the Caribbean and Southeast Asia by Europeans during the 1400s. The trade network covered a route known as the Silk Road. This trade route was used for centuries.

Caravans were groups of traders that traveled together. Caravans brought spices, tea, silk, and other goods from the Indies to sell to the people of Europe. The caravans traveled through many countries to reach Europe. Each country traded with the caravans. Goods that come into a country for sale are called imports. Goods made in a country and sent to another country for sale are called exports.

Spices were not a natural resource in Europe. The supply of spices imported to Europe depended on the caravans on the Silk Road. In the 1490s, the supply of spices and other goods from Asia was stopped. The Ottoman Empire controlled a large section of the Silk Road. The Ottomans put high taxes on the goods coming into their country. This made the goods very expensive. Many traders could not afford to pay the taxes to the Ottomans. Therefore, the goods did not move on to Europe.

When the demand for a good such as spices is high but the supply is low, there is scarcity. The monarchs of Spain, Ferdinand and Isabella, wanted spices and goods from Asia to be in the markets in Spain. They were not able to export any Spanish goods or import goods from the Indies. The Ottomans were blocking the land route. Another route to the Indies was needed. If Ferdinand and Isabella could meet the high demand for Asian goods, they could sell for a great profit. Spain could become very wealthy.

This is the reason Columbus came to Spain. He had the idea of sailing west across the Atlantic Ocean to reach the Indies. The new technology for navigation on the seas made this a reasonable plan. Ferdinand and Isabella became the patrons of Columbus. They took a financial risk on Columbus, hoping he would reach the Indies and return with spices. Columbus returned to Spain with a cargo of goods far greater than spices. The risk Ferdinand and Isabella took paid off greatly. The trade that began in 1492 between Spain and the Americas is called the Columbian Exchange. This exchange would have an impact on both worlds.

title: Tribes of the Southwest
text:
The landscape of the Southwest varies between deserts, valleys, plateaus, and coastal areas. Tribes such as the Apache, Pueblo, Navajo, and Hopi lived in this area. These tribes found different ways to use the resources of their environment. People on the coast fished for food. People who lived in the plateau areas were skilled in using acorns for food. They hunted for antelope, rabbits, and deer.

Many tribes in this region lived in homes built of dried clay called adobe. Adobe is a mixture of straw, water, and clay baked into hard bricks. Some tribes built adobe homes into the rock cliffs in the area. Other tribes built hogans made of wood and packed dirt. Like other tribes across the continent, these tribes utilized the resources around them to build their homes.

The tribes of the Southwest also farmed the land. Water can be a scarce resource in the Southwest. Southwest tribes were very resourceful and found ways to irrigate farmland. They gathered water from rivers and underground water sources to grow crops. They grew many crops, like corn, pumpkins, beans, squash, melons, and other types of fruit. After contact with the Europeans, some tribes raised cattle, sheep, and horses. One example of a tribe that raised livestock is the Hopi of Arizona.

title: Declaration of Independence
text:
The Declaration of Independence is one of the most important documents in American history. It helped create the foundations of the United States as an independent nation.

Many American colonists felt that King George III and his government were unfair and did not respect their rights and freedoms. In the summer of 1776, the Second Continental Congress met in Philadelphia to discuss these concerns. After many attempts to compromise with the king, the Congress voted for independence. They created a document explaining their reasons for independence. They also provided evidence of the king’s mistakes and what they intended to do about their concerns. The Continental Congress argued that the king had denied them of their inalienable rights. These are the rights to “life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.” These rights cannot be taken away.

The colonists provided a list of twenty-seven grievances, or complaints, to support this claim. The colonists explained that if the king did not respect their freedoms, they would break all political ties. They would become an independent sovereign nation. The ideas and beliefs in the Declaration of Independence laid the foundation for other important documents in our nation’s history.

title: The Constitution of the United States of America
text:
In the summer of 1787, the Founding Fathers met to create a new government for our young nation. After months of conflicting views and heated debates, they finally compromised.

The Founders of the Constitution were delegates appointed by state legislatures to represent each state's welfare. The Founders' purpose was to revise the Articles of Confederation. The Articles of Confederation was our nation's first constitution. It was written in 1777, after the Revolutionary War with Great Britain. The Constitution was the result of our Founders' hard work and dedication.

The U.S. Constitution is the supreme law of our country and the blueprint for our government. Its purpose is to describe the duties of the government and the rights of the people being governed. The Constitution establishes our government with specific principles, or basic truths, in mind. It defines the basic responsibilities of the federal, or national, government. The Constitution organizes the three branches of government. It also guarantees our individual rights, which cannot be denied or taken away by the government.

The Constitution establishes the principle of popular sovereignty. Popular sovereignty means that people should be in charge of creating the government. It means that the government must listen to the will of the people, or what the majority of the people want. The Constitution is informed by the unique foundation of protecting individual rights and giving power to the people.

Our country has been governed by the Constitution for over 200 years. It's the world's oldest written constitution still in effect.

title: Many Nations
text:
Before European contact, North America was and has always been home to hundreds of Native American tribes. A tribe is a name for a group of families and communities that have a common language, religion, and government. Languages, beliefs, and governments could have had differences within the same region.

Each tribe has its own myths on creation. For example, the Natchez believe they came from the sun. The Cherokee believe water is spiritually important. Historically, these Indigenous people also spoke many different languages, not just one. Some believe there might have been as many as 250 languages in North America at the time of contact. When one group of people met another, they might have used hand gestures to communicate.

Traditionally, each individual tribe used its region’s resources to meet its wants and needs. Some tribes planted crops. Some followed migratory animals that they hunted for food and supplies. Native peoples fished, gathered berries, hunted, and made good use of the resources around them.

Although many of the same resources were used within the same region, no two tribes looked exactly the same. Some tribes used trees and woven grasses to make long, rectangular dwellings. Others within the same region made dome-shaped houses out of the same materials.

Each tribe put its distinct mark on the appearances of their families and communities. Some tribes would wear their hair long and make their clothing out of animal skins. Other tribes made their clothing from plant fibers. Visually, each tribe’s appearance made them distinct and recognizable to both friend and foe, even within the same region. Today, traditional dress and accessories still reflect these differences.

The natural resources of a region have influenced the economic and cultural customs of each tribe. Animals of each region are used in tribal stories and beliefs. For example, alligators are prominent in the Everglades of the Southeast region. However, other areas of the Southeast region do not have alligators at all. The Calusa tribe reveres the alligator in the Southeast, but the Cherokee, who do not live near alligators, revere the owl. This reverence is based on the environment and the available resources of each region.

As you learn about Native American tribes this week, you may find that there are many commonalities between them. As you study, remember each tribe is unique and extraordinary. Further analysis will help you to learn about the distinct culture and individuality of each tribe.

title: Governments of the Native Americans
text:
Native Americans had organized communities. Women played many different roles within the tribes. Some tribes had women in their government as leaders and advisors. In other tribes, women supported family and community survival.

Long ago, some native peoples lived in small, independent groups. Other tribes formed large confederacies. The smallest native political unit was the individual. They had complete freedom to make their own decisions. Next was the band or village. A band was a group of people of the same tribe who were closely connected, often by family ties. They might fish, hunt, and grow food together. There were leaders for different duties. Bands had one chief for war and a leader during peacetime.

Clans were larger groups of distant relatives. The clan elders were chosen to make decisions for the group. Clans were often shared by many tribes. Bands or clans joined together to form tribes.

A tribe was a group of people connected by a common language, belief, land, and culture. Tribes didn’t always have just one specific leader. They worked together to make major decisions, like going to war, choosing who to trade with, or choosing how to use natural resources.

A chiefdom was a group of tribes under one leader, or chief. For the Haudenosaunee, or the Iroquois, a woman might not be the chief of her tribe, but women helped make decisions on who their chief should be. The chief’s authority often stayed in the same family. The Iroquois believed authority was passed down through the matriarchal line. That means the power was passed through the mother's line. Cultures like the Navajo also passed authority down through the mother’s side. Other cultures were patriarchal, or passed authority down through the father’s side of the family.

For most tribes, if a chief wasn’t doing well for their people, that chief would be removed. With some groups, women made the decision to change the chief.

Some tribes joined together to form confederacies. Hundreds of years ago, the Mohawk, Onondaga, Cayuga, Oneida, and Seneca fought. To end the wars, an Iroquois woman named Jikonhsaseh, Chief Hiawatha, and the prophet the Great Peacemaker convinced the tribes to unite.

The Iroquois created a constitution called the Great Law of Peace. This agreement included a balance of power between bigger and smaller groups, a two-branch legislature, procedures for passing laws, and more.

As the Cherokee were being pushed west, groups of Cherokee women asked the leaders of their tribes to not give the land away.

No matter the structure, the purpose of having a government was the same—to provide safety and security for those in the community. How each group’s government achieved this varied. Some restricted freedoms and liberties, while others ensured them to provide safety and security. Both Native American men and women worked together to provide safety and security for their people.

A government also provides justice and maintains order within the community and helps the members of the community meet their wants and needs. Every community, past and present, has a form of government. The amount of authority given to government leaders varies based on the community. Each tribe chose leaders in different ways. Leadership varied between men and women in the government. Leadership authority was based on age, wisdom, leadership skills, or heredity. Each tribe chose the best leader to ensure the safety of the community.

Authority was distributed across the community, and leaders had authority over smaller numbers of people. A chief had authority over more people than a band leader. In a confederacy, the leaders had authority over a great number of people from many communities or nations. Women worked right alongside the men. The goal was to provide safety, justice, and welfare for the people.

title: Record Keeping in North America
text: Many Native American tribes didn't have a written alphabet or use a written system of language. However, this doesn't mean that they did not keep records of important events and experiences. An example of Native American records is called petroglyphs. A petroglyph is a picture carved into rock. Petroglyphs represent important cultural beliefs, tribal stories, and significant events. Tribes living in the United States today consider petroglyphs sacred. They often gather around petroglyphs for celebrations and ceremonies.

title: Respect for the Land
text:
Native American tribes have a deep respect and connection to nature. They feel connected to the land. It played a vital role in their sacred beliefs and everyday life. They cared for the land and used resources wisely. They believed that if they took care of the Earth, the Earth would take care of them. Many tribes use the same name to describe the Earth: Mother Earth.

Native Americans did not believe in individual land ownership. The land was used by tribes and belonged to the tribe. Products from the land were communal and shared among the bands that lived there. Because tribes relied so much on the land for their resources, they needed lots of land to get those resources. Tribes would cover millions of acres to get food, fuel, water, and other resources. A certain area may be used for several years. Then, the tribe would leave so the area could replenish itself. Eventually, the tribe would come back to that area when it was ready.

title: Native American Trade Routes
text:
For thousands of years, Native Americans operated huge trade networks to get what they needed from other people in the Americas. For example, people in what is now North Dakota quarried a hard stone called flint near Knife River. The stone was so valuable in ancient times that 4,000 years ago, it was being traded far from the quarry. Copper and obsidian have also been discovered far from their natural locations. This proves a trade system existed.

Another example of trade comes from the Hohokam tribe in what is now Arizona. The Hohokam traded bison hides for seashells. Neither resource comes from Arizona! The hides came from tribes on the Plains. Plains tribes often traded bison robes, dried meat, and tallow with other tribes for corn and squash. The shells came from the Mojave tribe in California. By trading with both groups, the Hohokam became middlemen within a larger trade route. Middlemen took goods from one group to another during trade.

Trade was an essential part of the government. Agreements had to be made in order to trade safely. But not all trade was peaceful. Sometimes tribes would go to war to control trade routes and resources. Eventually, peace would be made with chiefs making agreements for their bands.

Rivers and Trails

Rivers were extremely important when native people needed to travel. Many traveled by canoe on major rivers like the Mississippi, Ohio, Columbia, and Missouri. Some canoes could haul thousands of pounds of goods for trade. Rivers were the “highways” for tribes. If rivers were the highways, paths were like the smaller “roads” we use today. Paths crossed all over North America.

Native peoples made and named other paths. One well-known route stretched from the forests by Lake Erie to the South Carolina coast. This trail, called the Trading Path, appeared on maps in the 1700s. Parts are still marked today.

Trails often followed the “military crest” of the ridge. Trails ran alongside, but not on the ridge tops. This way, a person could travel along the trail without being seen by those on the other side of the ridge. Many Native Americans disciplined themselves to walk heel-to-toe in a single file. This left the smallest marks on the ground and allowed them to travel without being seen.

Trading Sites

Trade was very important to tribes. They exchanged food, goods, and information. Some locations were more permanent trading locations, while others moved where the people went.

One example of a permanent trading station is the straits of Mackinac. The straits of Mackinac is where Lakes Michigan and Huron meet. This area in the Great Lakes attracted tribes from all over the eastern woodlands to trade. The Odawa and Chippewa had villages at Mackinac and conducted the trade.

Most of the trade happened when native people went to other villages or designated areas for trade. These areas were often convenient locations along travel routes. One such site, the Dakota Rendezvous site, was held along the James River.

title: Trade, Barter, and Money
text:
How people use resources to meet their wants and needs is the basis for economics. There are goods and services needed or wanted in a community. Meeting the wants and needs of the community is considered a trade network.

The Native Americans had resources they used to meet their wants and needs. We see this in how the homes and shelters of the tribes varied depending on what natural resources were around them in the environment. Tribes on the coast did not have the same resources as the people of the Great Plains. The same is true about their daily lives and their art. To meet their wants and needs, people would trade.

One tribe might have a good year farming and raising maize. Another tribe’s crops might be destroyed in a weather disaster. The extra maize of the first tribe would be needed in the second tribe. To acquire the maize, the second tribe would offer the first tribe another resource they had plenty of, such as furs or carved utensils.

Sometimes, a tribe would send representatives out to communicate and make connections with other tribes. Sometimes, the traders were welcomed with music and celebration. A market would be opened for goods to be shown and opportunities for families to make a trade on their own. This is called bartering. Each trader had to negotiate for a satisfactory trade. The trade would depend on how much one of the traders wanted or needed the goods or service. If every family had sufficient furs for the winter, they wouldn’t look to trade for furs. However, if there was a scarcity of items, trade values would go up in those goods, and more goods would be required to make a satisfactory deal.

Tribes in the local region would offer common items for trade. What was common in one geographic region could be highly valued in different geographic regions. Coastal tribes found dentalium seashells common. However, inland tribes who had never been to the ocean found seashells a high-value trade item.

Bartering still occurs today. Any time you trade a good like an apple for another good, such as a string cheese, that is bartering.

title: Customs and Traditions of Native Americans
text:
The tribes of North America have many different cultures and traditions. Each tribal group has its own beliefs, rituals, and traditions. Many traditions are connected with the land the tribes call home. This connection to their homeland is similar for many tribes. Native American tribes are different in many ways, but they also share many similar customs and traditions. Tribes have marriage ceremonies, funerals, and rites of passage for youth. Tribal culture includes language, storytelling and the arts, celebrations, food, and clothing.

Language

Before the arrival of Europeans in North America, there were approximately 500 different Native American languages spoken by millions of indigenous people. The languages of various tribes were diverse. Some languages were spoken within a very small area, while others were spoken by large numbers of people across the continent. Many Native American languages are still spoken today. However, many languages have also become extinct after the European colonization of North America. Today, many tribes are trying to bring back their original languages.

Storytelling and the Arts

The arts and storytelling are a large part of Native American culture. Native peoples living in North America did not use an alphabet to communicate, but they did have symbols that were part of stories. These symbols were placed on important, ceremonial items or painted on rocks. They mainly used the spoken word to communicate and to preserve their history and traditions. Often, their speeches took the form of stories. Many stories explained their beliefs and the creation of the world. Some stories represented actual events that happened in the tribe’s past. Some represented relationships between families and their ancestors. Other stories are more like religious stories for the tribes. These stories have lessons on how to be a good person and treat everything with respect. Elders often taught these stories to children. Animals, birds, and the environment were often part of these important stories, creating a special bond to the land.

Throughout North America, native peoples made beautiful pieces of art from natural materials around them. They used shells, porcupine quills, or feathers for decoration. Jade, turquoise, and other stones were used to create their art. They crafted jewelry and other items from silver, turquoise, and gold. Some cultures were known for creating elaborate sculptures out of stone, wood, and other materials. Many tribes wove baskets and made pottery. But not all the things made by native peoples were simply art. Many items were used in ceremonies and considered very sacred. These sacred items are only used for special occasions, like a funeral. Early Native American art continues to influence artists, and many tribes continue to create art in the same way as their ancestors.

Ceremonies and Celebrations

Native American tribes had their own individual ceremonies and celebrations, but many tribes celebrated for common reasons. Ceremonies and celebrations were often held to honor their ancestors and celebrate the natural elements around them. Many holidays honor the sun, rain, and harvest.

Dancing, singing, and praying are very important in Native American ceremonies. Many ceremonies are performed to help people who are sick. Some ceremonies are to celebrate when a child becomes an adult. When warriors came back from battle, special ceremonies were performed to help them not be angry. There were celebrations for a good harvest, giving thanks for the food. When a young hunter killed their first deer or bison, a special feast would be held to honor the animal and the new hunter for the community.

Food

Native Americans across North America relied on the land for food. Tribes hunted, gathered, and farmed for food. Many of the foods Native Americans ate were based on the seasons. Seasonal crops and hunting patterns played a huge role in community activities. Members of each tribe worked together to provide food for the community. Many of the foods that we enjoy today can be traced back to the crops grown by Native Americans. These include corn, potatoes, tomatoes, peanuts, wild rice, squash, and beans.

Clothing

Before European exploration, Native American tribes used natural resources from the land to create clothing. Native American clothing represented the natural environment in which they lived. Clothing was practical and reflected the climate where they lived. Native Americans used animal products, such as fur, feathers, bones, teeth, and claws to make clothing and jewelry. They also used plants like tree bark and various grasses to make woven fabrics. Native Americans wore different forms of clothing for different purposes.
