Many tribes wore decorative headdresses, masks, and clothing for ceremonies and celebrations.

title: Important Documents
text:
The government of the United States is based on specific values. The values of our nation are defined in legal, political, and historical documents. Documents written during our nation’s history are visible outcomes of rules and laws. They protect the rights of citizens. We find these documents on local, state, and national levels.

On a national level, important documents include the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution of the United States, and the Bill of Rights. Laws, treaties, and trade agreements are also considered important national documents. These documents outline our rights and responsibilities as citizens. On a state level, important documents include the state constitution, state laws and codes, voter registration, and documents that protect animals and land.

title: What Are Physical Features?
text:
Physical features are the natural parts of the Earth’s surface. They tell us what a place looks like. Landforms and bodies of water are physical features.

Landforms are natural features on Earth’s surface. Landforms include continents, mountains, forests, deserts, and plains. Some other landforms include volcanoes, wetlands, and islands.

Bodies of water are areas of water on Earth’s surface. Some important bodies of water are oceans, rivers, and lakes.

A physical map often shows major landforms and bodies of water.

title: Landforms
text:
Mountains are landforms. They rise above the surrounding land. Usually, a mountain will rise at least 1,000 feet above sea level.

Hills are also areas that rise above the surrounding land. Their tops are usually rounded. They are similar to mountains but not as tall.

Plains are large areas of land that do not have many trees. They are usually grassy and flat. This is why some plains are also called grasslands. Plains can be found in various climates. They cover more than one-third of the land on Earth.

Islands are areas of land surrounded by water. They are not connected to a continent.

Forests are areas with many trees. They can be hot or cold. The trees in forests produce oxygen that people and animals breathe.

Deserts are places where rainfall is usually less than 25 inches per year. The plants found in a desert are mostly shrubs and short trees.

Wetlands are areas of land that are often covered by water. There are wetlands in almost every climate.

title: Essential Question
text: How can I describe places?

title: Bodies of Water
text:
Oceans are the largest bodies of water. They cover about 71 percent of the Earth.

Rivers are flowing bodies of water. This means the water in them moves. Rivers usually run from mountains toward the ocean.

Lakes are large areas filled with water. They are surrounded by land. Unlike rivers, the water in lakes tends to remain still or move very slowly.

title: Natural Landmarks
text:
Natural landmarks are well-known, or famous, physical features that mark a certain place. There are famous natural landmarks all over North America.

Look at the map and identify some important natural landmarks of North America. Mark the landmarks you have heard of or seen with a circle. Mark the ones you’d like to know more about with a star.

title: Monopolies
text:
Monopolies became a big economic issue during the early 20th century. A monopoly is when only one business or company offers a good or service. For example, if there is only one company that provides internet service, everyone who wants to use the internet has to purchase the service from that company. That gives the company a monopoly of the internet provider market. With a monopoly, consumers do not have a choice of which product or service they will buy. This has many benefits for the company with a monopoly. That company can charge consumers whatever price they want for their product. They can raise prices whenever they want. If a consumer wants or needs that product, they have to pay whatever the company is charging.

With monopolies, there is no competition between producers to sell products. The monopoly company doesn’t have an incentive to produce high quality products because consumers have to buy whatever the company produces. The company also doesn’t have a reason to create new and improved products because there is no one they have to outsell in the market.

However, some people, like monopoly holders, would argue that there were key advantages to having monopolies. When a company gets very large, it has access to many resources and markets. This allows the company to produce more goods and sell them for lower prices. When a company controls a market and brings in high profits, it can use that money to invest in research and development of new and improved products. Both of these aspects of a monopoly can benefit consumers of the company’s products.

When more than one company is in the same kind of business, producing the same kinds of products, it creates competition. Each company needs to attract consumers to buy its products instead of another company’s products. This competition to bring in buyers has several advantages. First, consumers are usually living on budgets. So, they look for the lowest price for a good product. With competition, companies will often try to give consumers lower prices than other companies.

Consumers also want the best quality products for their money. Even if a company has the lowest prices, if their products are poor quality, no one will buy them. In a competitive market, consumers have a choice. They don’t have to buy whatever is out there. This encourages companies to improve the quality of their products to appeal to more consumers.

During the Second Industrial Revolution, the difference between monopolies and business competition became especially important. At this time, a number of monopolies were built by men like Andrew Carnegie and John D. Rockefeller. These monopolies resulted in poor working conditions for employees who had nowhere else to go for work. Owners of the companies became very rich while their workers struggled. Small businesses could not compete with the monopolies, so they failed. Often, the monopolies even controlled access to raw materials, so small businesses couldn’t even create products to sell.

Total control of an industry also resulted in corruption. Owners who wanted to stay in control of the market would sometimes do anything to hang on to their monopolies. This included bribing government officials and threatening anyone they saw as a danger to their control with violence.

The federal government realized something had to be done to control monopolies. In 1880, Congress passed the Sherman Antitrust Act. This act said that no business could monopolize trade or join with other businesses to restrict trade. When multiple businesses act together to restrict trade, that is called a “trust.”

Later, in 1914, the Federal Trade Commission Act established a government commission. The commission's purpose was to monitor business and prevent unfair and anticompetitive business practices. Through the years, these acts have continued to keep healthy competition working in the American economy.

title: Explorers Set Their Sights on Florida
text:
During the 1500s, explorers sailed to Florida to obtain valuable natural resources, colonize the area, and spread Christianity to the Indigenous peoples of the region. The first Spanish explorer reached Florida by accident. This accidental landing led to years of exploration and the eventual colonization of the area. Each explorer obtained and shared knowledge of the land that we now call Florida.

Juan Ponce de León

The first European explorer to reach Florida was Juan Ponce de León. Ponce de León was a Spanish conquistador. Conquistador means one who conquers. This title was given to Spanish soldiers who explored, conquered, and settled lands around the world. Before exploring Florida, Ponce de León sailed with Columbus on his second voyage to the Americas. He was also the first European explorer to explore Puerto Rico, which he claimed for Spain.

In 1513, Ponce de León set out on another expedition through the Bahamas. He hoped to find the fabled Fountain of Youth, as well as rich natural resources and new lands to colonize. In March 1513, Ponce de León and his crew landed on the east coast of Florida. Initially, he thought that he had discovered a new island in the Bahamas. In reality, he landed near present-day St. Augustine. He named the area “La Florida,” in honor of the Spanish celebration “Feast of the Flowers” and because the area was covered in flowers. He returned to Florida in 1521 with the hopes of creating the first European settlement in the area. The settlement quickly failed due to hostilities between the settlers and the Calusa tribe.

Juan Garrido

Juan Garrido was an African explorer who joined Ponce de León on his expeditions of the Americas. Garrido was born in western Africa around 1487. As a young man, he was enslaved by Portuguese traders and taken to Portugal. Eventually, Garrido was granted his freedom, and he sailed to the Americas in the hopes of becoming a conquistador.

In 1513, Garrido joined Ponce de León on his first expedition to Florida. He was also a member of the 1521 expedition to Florida. Following Ponce de León’s death, Garrido joined Hernán Cortés on his conquest of Mexico. He continued to explore other areas of the Americas, including present-day Baja California. Garrido was the first recorded African explorer to reach Florida.

Pánfilo de Narváez

Following the expeditions of Ponce de León, the Spanish government hoped to create a successful settlement in Florida. The Spanish chose Pánfilo de Narváez to complete this mission. Narváez was a Spanish soldier who served under famous conquistadors on their expeditions of the Americas. In 1527, Narváez set sail from Spain with 300 hundred soldiers and 40 horses.

Narváez and his men landed near present-day Tampa on April 14, 1528. Narváez ordered several members of the expedition to remain on the ships while the bulk of his forces traveled inland. The ships would carry the expedition's supplies and meet Narváez and the rest of the expedition farther up the coast. Unfortunately, the ships traveled farther north than Narváez intended. The sailors searched for Narváez and his men, but after a year of searching, the ships set sail for Cuba and eventually returned to Spain.

Narváez continued to search for his ships and traveled as far north as present-day Tallahassee. The Native American tribes they encountered along their route refused to help them. Narváez decided to sail to Mexico to obtain new supplies and more soldiers. The remaining members of the expedition built five barges from pine and palmetto trees and used their shirts to make sails.

In September 1528, Narváez and his men left Florida with the hopes of reaching Spanish settlements in Mexico. Shortly after setting sail, the expedition encountered a terrible storm. Three of the barges were destroyed, including the one carrying Narváez. He did not survive, but this was not the end of the expedition he started.

Alvár Núñez Cabeza de Vaca

Historians have been able to learn about Pánfilo de Narváez’s failed expedition because of the writings of another member of the expedition: Alvár Núñez Cabeza de Vaca. Cabeza de Vaca’s writings are among the first to detail information about the Native American tribes of Florida and the southeast region of what is now the United States.

Cabeza de Vaca sailed to Florida with Narváez. He survived the trek along Florida’s coast and the shipwreck of September 1528. Cabeza de Vaca and a small group of survivors made it to shore, near present-day Houston, Texas. He was taken prisoner by people of the Karankawa tribe. He served as a healer for the tribe for many years before he was set free.

After he was set free, Cabeza de Vaca and three other members of the expedition walked from Texas to Mexico City. He returned to Spain in 1537 and wrote about his experiences in Florida and the American south. Cabeza de Vaca’s book, The Journey of Alvar Nuñez Cabeza de Vaca and His Companions from Florida to the Pacific 1528-1536, is the first book written solely about North America by a European author.

Esteban de Dorantes

Esteban de Dorantes was another member of Narváez’s failed expedition to Florida who survived the terrible ordeal. Dorantes was an enslaved African who accompanied his enslaver, Captain Andrés Dorantes, on the expedition. Esteban was one of the four survivors of the expedition. He survived imprisonment by various Native American tribes and the perilous overland journey from Texas to Mexico City.

Following this ordeal, Dorantes was once again enslaved by Spanish merchants. He accompanied Spanish explorer and priest Marcos de Niza in his search for the fabled Seven Cities of Gold, also known as Cíbola. He served as a guide and interpreter for the expedition. Dorantes became the first explorer to make contact with the Zuni tribe in present-day New Mexico. While searching for Cíbola, Dorantes’s companions claimed he was killed by Native Americans. There is no physical or written evidence to prove that Dorantes was killed by Native Americans in New Mexico. Some historians believe that he used this attack as an opportunity to escape slavery. Others believe he could not have survived this attack. Nevertheless, Dorantes was a courageous and persistent explorer who shared his knowledge of Florida with others.

Hernando de Soto

Despite Pánfilo de Narváez's failure to settle Florida, the Spanish government still hoped to find vast amounts of gold and silver in Florida. In 1536, King Charles V of Spain appointed Hernando de Soto as the governor of Cuba and ordered him to lead an expedition through Florida. De Soto set sail from Cuba and landed near present-day Tampa on May 25, 1539.

De Soto and his army marched north from Tampa. The expedition encountered a Spanish soldier named Juan Ortiz, who was a survivor of Narváez's expedition. Ortiz lived with Native American tribes of the area for 11 years before he joined De Soto as a translator and guide. De Soto and his army explored areas that were previously unexplored by other European and African explorers. He explored much of the peninsula of Florida and traveled north into the panhandle before traveling farther north into present-day Georgia. De Soto and his army also explored present-day South Carolina, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Alabama before crossing the Mississippi River. In 1542, De Soto fell ill and died. Members of his expedition marched south and eventually reached Spanish settlements in Mexico and shared their experiences with other explorers.

Don Tristán de Luna y Arellano

The failed expeditions of Pánfilo de Narváez and Hernando de Soto did not deter the Spanish government from wanting to colonize Florida. They still hoped to find valuable resources, convert the Indigenous population to Christianity, and be the first European nation to colonize North America.

In 1559, King Phillip II of Spain chose the conquistador Don Tristán de Luna y Arellano to colonize Florida and create trade routes throughout the southeast. De Luna landed at present-day Pensacola Bay with 1,500 settlers on Aug. 15, 1559. He decided to keep the bulk of the settlement's supplies on the ships until a town and proper storehouses were constructed. This proved to be a huge mistake. On Sept. 19, 1559, a hurricane destroyed three of De Luna’s ships and most of the colony’s supplies. One ship survived and returned to Mexico to obtain more supplies.

De Luna made the decision to send a group north into Alabama and Georgia to search for Native Americans who would be willing to give them much-needed supplies. This expedition was a failure, and resupply ships did not reach the colony. In 1561, De Luna and the remaining settlers abandoned the settlement at Pensacola.

title: Encounters
text:
When European and African explorers arrived in the Americas, thousands of Native Americans lived in Florida. It is estimated that about 350,000 Native Americans lived in Florida before European exploration. Historians widely believe that most explorers who led expeditions to Florida encountered one or more Native American tribes during their journeys.

Historical accounts show that most of the encounters between the explorers who came to Florida and the Native Americans of the region were hostile. Spanish explorers hoped to take control of all land, resources, and peoples of Florida, but the native tribes were unwilling to give up their resources, cultures, and traditions.

Several explorers violated the orders from the Spanish government to treat the Native Americans of Florida well and encourage them to convert to Christianity through peaceful means, including Juan Ponce de León and Hernando de Soto. The Spanish also stole from numerous tribes and took important members of the tribes as prisoners in order to obtain resources they wanted. In return, many tribes in Florida refused to meet with the Spanish and often attacked Spanish expeditions.

The story of first encounters between Europeans and native peoples is a difficult story to tell. For Europeans, their nations expanded, and they acquired many resources. For the native peoples, new people came to take their lands and resources, resulting in many conflicts and wars. Today, Native Americans make up only one percent of the population in the United States.

title: The American Indians in the War
text:
The American Indian nations were not bystanders in the Civil War. They knew that they could not remain neutral. There was division between tribes over which side to support. American Indians hoped each government would look at them as friends and allies. Each tribe sent men to enlist in both the Confederate and Union armies. These regiments were involved in major battles of the war. There were also regiments that stayed home within their assigned reservations.

Falleaf, a member of the Delaware tribe, recruited American Indians to start Company D of the 2nd Kansas Indian Home Guard. The regiment members were Delaware, Kickapoo, Osage, Shawnee, Seneca, Cherokee, Seminole, Creek, Choctaw, and Chickasaw. This regiment reported that no members were killed or wounded in action during the Civil War.

Approximately 20,000 natives served in the Union and Confederate armies during the Civil War. The hope was that whichever side was victorious, the government would treat the American Indians as valued allies in the future. However, the government continued to remove native people from their lands after the war.

title: The First People of the Americas
text:
Before European exploration and colonization, thousands of Native Americans lived in the Americas and the Caribbean Islands. However, their ancestors were not originally from these regions. Historians, scientists, and archaeologists have developed many theories to explain how Native Americans first arrived in the Western Hemisphere.

For many years, researchers believed that the ancient ancestors of Native Americans came to America from Siberia, a region in northern Asia. They concluded that these people arrived about 12,000 years ago by hiking across a narrow strip of land that once bridged Asia and Alaska. This land bridge is known as the Bering Strait. From there, they settled in other areas of North America. Eventually, they migrated to Central and South America and the Caribbean Islands.

In recent years, archaeologists in North and South America have discovered ancient tools, weapons, campsites, and skeletons that are even older than artifacts from the land-bridge travelers. The bones, in particular, were very different from those linked to the people who crossed the land bridge. This new research suggests that a large group of migrants crossed the Bering Strait as early as 30,000 years ago. This larger group split into smaller tribes about 15,000 years ago. Some traveled south through the Americas.

Other researchers have proposed that the first people in the Americas traveled here by boat from southern Asia, Australia, India, Japan, or even Europe, arriving long before the land-bridge travelers. These people may have later died out. However, they also could have joined the Siberian tribes who migrated from Asia to Alaska via the Bering Strait. Combined, these groups could represent the Native Americans’ earliest ancestors.

Despite differing theories, experts refer to these people as Paleo-Indians. The Paleo-Indians were nomadic, meaning they traveled from place to place looking for food. They hunted large animals, such as mammoths, ground sloths, bison, caribou, and others. They traveled in small bands of 20 to 50 people. They worked together to provide for the needs of the group. They built shelters using sticks, branches, and animal skins. They also looked for natural shelters like caves.

This group also made spears for hunting. The Paleo-Indians carved rocks into sharp, durable points and shaped them to fit into a groove they had cut into a wooden shaft. Later, they invented a spear-thrower called an atlatl. This was used to throw spears farther and faster than they could be thrown by hand. The atlatl made it easier to hunt and helped the Paleo-Indians keep their stomachs filled. The Paleo-Indians also ate roots, plants, seeds, and possibly even insects. They used animal skins for clothing and shelter.

The climate thousands of years ago was very strange. The ice age was ending, and that caused some pretty crazy weather. Plants and trees that many animals depended on died out over time. This changing environment may have caused many animals to become extinct. It is thought that 30 kinds of "mega-mammals" may have become extinct during this time. This includes mammoths, mastodons, and giant bison. Of course, there are lots of ideas about the disappearance of these animals. Some scientists think it is possible that the Paleo-Indians hunted these animals to extinction. However, the newest evidence suggests that a comet exploded over Canada and changed the weather very, very fast. This event could have easily caused animals to die off.

The Paleo-Indian culture gradually became more advanced over generations. With advancements in their culture, their children's children became separate groups of Native Americans. Some of these Paleo-Indian groups settled in Florida. Over time, they developed different languages, customs, traditions, and arts. The Americas were eventually inhabited by many tribes with different traditions. Time passed, and generations changed, but the Paleo-Indians' descendants are still here. In fact, every Native American tribe in North America has its roots in the Paleo-Indian culture.

Although they left no written records, researchers have learned much about these ancient peoples. Archaeologists specifically have discovered many examples of stone tools and weapons they used. By studying these artifacts, we can catch glimpses into the lives of Paleo-Indians thousands of years ago.

title: The Apalachee
text:
The Apalachee tribe was one of the five ancient Native American tribes that lived in Florida before European exploration and colonization. The Apalachee lived in northwest Florida. Their largest tribal settlements were located near present-day Tallahassee. Historians and archaeologists estimate that about 50,000-60,000 Apalachee lived in the Florida panhandle before European contact.

The Apalachee were hunters, gathers, and farmers. Male members of the tribe were responsible for hunting. They hunted deer, bears, and small mammals. They also fished in the rivers and lakes of the panhandle. Women were responsible for gathering wild plants, nuts, and berries. All members of the tribe, including children, tended to and harvested crops for the tribe. The Apalachee traditionally grew corn, beans, and squash.

Resources from the environment were used to make clothing, tools, and homes. Men traditionally wore clothing made of deer skins, while women wore clothing made of Spanish moss. The Apalachee constructed huts using palm trees and palm fronds.

The Apalachee lived in small villages throughout northwest Florida. Each village had their own chief. Tribal chiefs were in charge of the social, cultural, and political practices of the tribe. Village chiefs worked together to meet the needs of the larger tribe, especially in times of war. The Apalachee were considered fierce warriors by neighboring tribes in the area.

Apalachee culture centered around religious ceremonies and exercises. Members of the tribe built ceremonial mounds in the center of the village. The chief's home was often constructed on the top of the mound. These ceremonial mounds were used as a meeting place for the tribe. The primary ceremonial mound for the whole tribe was located in present-day Lake Jackson. The most important tribal meetings and ceremonies took place there.

One of the most important cultural traditions of the Apalachee was a ceremonial game dedicated to gods of rain and thunder. Villages would challenge each other to a match. The game was similar to basketball. The objective was to knock over a stuffed eagle on the top of a goal post with a small, clay ball covered in buckskin. Each team was tasked with protecting their goal post. This game was traditionally played in the spring and summer to ask the gods to provide rain for the tribe’s crops.

title: The Calusa
text:
The Calusa tribe lived in southwest Florida, primarily along the Gulf of America. The word “Calusa” means “fierce people.” Members of the Calusa tribe were fierce warriors. They controlled much of the territory in south Florida and often attacked neighboring tribes to gain control of land and resources.

The Calusa used resources from their environment to survive. The Calusa did not engage in farming. They hunted, gathered, and fished for the majority of their food. The Calusa built several types of boats, including large seagoing vessels, canoes, and platform barges, which were used to fish offshore and along the rivers in south Florida. Boats were constructed from cypress trees. Men and boys constructed fishing nets from palm leaves to catch fish. Women and children were primarily responsible for catching shellfish, such as oysters, crabs, clams, conchs, and lobsters, and gathering wild berries, nuts, and roots.

Calusa homes were constructed on stilts to prevent flooding from coastal and inland waters. They did not have walls. They constructed roofs from palm leaves, which were supported by wooden poles. The Calusa also constructed canals to travel across the state more easily. Tools were made from shells and fish bones. Men made fish hooks and arrowheads from fish bones. Shells were used to make spears, tools, jewelry, and special decorations for religious ceremonies.

The Calusa were a very powerful tribe with a sophisticated government. The tribe was ruled by a chief, who was often referred to as a king by explorers who encountered the tribe in the early 1500s. The Calusa chief was in charge of all political and spiritual decisions for the tribe. Villages that were conquered by the Calusa were required to send gifts and tributes to the Calusa chief in exchange for peace.

Like the Apalachee, the Calusa tribe constructed large earthen mounds. The Calusa originally used these mounds as trash heaps, where they threw away shells, bones, broken pottery, and other items. Over time, the mounds were used to mark the boundaries between territories as well as memorials to deceased members of the tribe. By studying these mounds, archaeologists have been able to learn about the culture, traditions, and lives of the ancient Calusa who lived in this area.

title: The Tequesta
text:
The Tequesta tribe lived in southeast Florida near present-day Biscayne Bay, the city of Miami, and the Florida Keys. The Tequesta were a much smaller tribe than the other ancient Native American tribes of Florida. The majority of the tribe lived in small villages constructed along the Miami River. Smaller communities that belonged to the tribe lived on various islands of the Florida Keys.

The Tequesta hunted, fished, and gathered food. The men were responsible for hunting and catching large fish and aquatic mammals, including sailfish, sharks, porpoises, and manatees. The manatee was an important animal to the Tequesta. It was only eaten by the tribal chief and other important members of the tribe. The men were also expert hunters. They hunted alligators, bears, deer, wild boars, and small mammals in and around the Everglades.

Women and children gathered plant roots, palmetto berries, coco plums, sea grapes, and palm nuts. They also collected turtle eggs and shellfish, including clams, oysters, and conches, to feed the members of the tribe. Flour was produced from ground plant roots. This flour was used to make bread.

The Tequesta made tools from shells and shark teeth. They constructed canoes out of small trees and used shark teeth to carve the wood. Tequesta homes were similar to the homes of the Calusa. They were open structures with thatched roofs made of palm leaves. Clothing was made from palm or palmetto leaves and Spanish moss. The Tequesta did not wear clothing made from animal skins because of the high temperatures year-round in south Florida.

The tribe was controlled by a primary chief. The chief lived in the largest of the Tequesta villages near the mouth of the Miami River. Various Tequesta chiefs were related to the chiefs of the Calusa tribe. This meant that the Tequesta were loyal to the Calusa and often paid them tribute in exchange for peace. The village of the Tequesta chief was the center for tribal gatherings, religious ceremonies, and trade.

title: The Timucua
text:
The Timucua lived in villages throughout northeast and central Florida, from present-day Tallahassee to Orlando. Historians believe that the Timucua were the first Native American tribe of Florida to encounter European explorers who traveled to Florida. Early Spanish explorers described the Timucua as giants covered head to toe in tattoos.

Like other tribes in Florida, the Timucua were hunters and gatherers and fished for food. The men were responsible for hunting and fishing. Timucua men were skilled hunters. They hunted large animals with spears, bows and arrows, and clubs, including deer, wild turkey, bears, and alligators.

Seafood was the primary source of food for the Timucua. Men built canoes to travel along inland waterways to catch fish. They also constructed fish traps called “weirs” to collect shellfish and freshwater fish. A weir was a wooden fence that was constructed across a river or stream. Fish and other sea animals would swim or be washed over the fence at high tide. As the tide went out, animals would become trapped behind the weir. The Timucua were also farmers. They grew cucumbers, peas, melons, pumpkins, gourds, corn, and beans.

Women were responsible for cooking and gathering nuts, berries, moss, and plant roots for food. They also created clay pots for cooking and storing food. They were responsible for cleaning, preparing, and creating clothing from animal hides. Clothing was also made from Spanish moss. Members of the tribe often wore jewelry made from shells, fish bones, and small pebbles.

Timucua homes were different from the homes of the Calusa and Tequesta. There were two types of homes constructed in Timucua villages. Longhouses were constructed from poles carved from palmetto trees. Bark was used to cover the walls, and roofs were made from palm leaves. Longhouses were used for tribal meetings and meals. Smaller homes, where members of the tribe lived, were round with palm-thatched roofs. Tools and weapons were often made from animal bones.

The Timucua had an organized government headed by a chief. The tribal chief was responsible for all political decisions. The position of chief was passed down through the female line of a family. Unlike other tribes, women were permitted to serve as chiefs among the Timucua. Ceremonies were held throughout the year to celebrate planting, the harvest, and to honor leaders of the tribe. Ceremonies were conducted by a shaman. A shaman is a religious or spiritual leader of a tribe. The Timucua believed that shamans were healers, doctors, and prophets who told the future. They were also believed to control the weather and perform blessings.

title: The Tocobaga
text:
The Tocobaga lived near the Tampa Bay area. Their territory extended from present-day Tarpon Springs to Sarasota. The larger tribe was made up of smaller tribal groups, including the Ucita, Pohoy, and Mococo. Historians and archaeologists believe that the primary settlement of the tribe was also called Tocobaga and was located near present-day Safety Harbor.

Like other tribes that lived along the coast, the Tocobaga relied heavily on fish and seafood as their main source of food. They also hunted small mammals, including squirrels, rabbits, deer, and armadillos, and they gathered berries, nuts, and wild fruit. Another important staple of the Tocobaga diet was corn. Archaeologists have found enough evidence to support the idea that the Tocobaga did not grow corn themselves and most likely engaged in trade with tribes that lived in the northern parts of Florida.

The Tocobaga constructed homes similar to those of the Calusa and Tequesta. Tocobaga homes were open with poles that supported roofs made of palm leaves. Villages also included a central meeting area and a temple mound. The temple mound was often the home of the chief and his family. Other important buildings were constructed on the temple mound.

The Tocobaga made various tools using resources found in their environment. One of the most important tools they used was called an adz. An adz was used for digging and was made from a tree branch with a pointed stone or shell attached to the end. They used a similar tool to dig for clams in sandy areas along the coast. The Tocobaga also used an atlatl for hunting. Atlatls were often used to hunt larger animals, including deer.

Like the other ancient Native American tribes of Florida, the Tocobaga tribe was ruled by a chief. Early Spanish explorers in the area described Tocobaga society in detail. There were four separate groups within the tribe’s society. These included the chief, headmen, warriors, and ordinary people. Headmen, warriors, and ordinary people all had to answer to the chief, who made all of the decisions for the tribe.

title: Comparing Native American Tribes
text: Choose two of the tribes discussed in this week’s publication. Compare and contrast government, economy, homes, use of natural resources, and cultural customs and traditions of the tribes you choose.

title: An Industrial Revolution
text:
The United States territory and businesses expanded during the late 19th century. From this period into the early 20th century, industrialization also changed in the United States. The growing economy created a demand for more raw materials and efficient transportation. Factories needed supplies to produce goods and transportation to ship them to customers. Businessmen known as the “captains of industry” contributed to the industrialization of the United States. They manufactured steel, produced oil, and reorganized financial institutions. Their big businesses continued to help the economy grow.

Advances in steel production during the Second Industrial Revolution made steel cheaper. The process also produced more steel in less time. Steel production became a big business, and other industries were affected. Railroads could expand using lower cost steel. More industrial machines for factories could be purchased because costs were lower.

The expanding availability of electricity was also changing the lives of Americans. Many inventions used this power to make life easier. For example, in 1876, a man named Alexander Graham Bell found a way to use electricity to transmit sound from one place to another through wire. He had invented the telephone. Thomas Edison, another inventor, experimented with electricity until he perfected a light bulb that could be safely used in the home. At the end of the 19th century, electric streetcars began to replace horse-drawn carriages. In 1901, the first radio waves were successfully transmitted across the Atlantic Ocean.

More factories were being built that produced goods using an assembly line system. Before the assembly line, a product had to be made by hand. One worker, or a group of workers, would create the entire product by hand, one at a time. In an assembly line, the product being created moved along a moving belt or track. Each worker along the line had one task that they did over and over as the product came to them. For example, if a car was being built, the basic frame would begin moving on the assembly line. Each worker along the line would add their part to the car. By the end of the line, the car would be complete. Using the assembly line process, many cars could be created in a shorter period of time.

Industrialization also changed the South. Henry Grady, editor of The Atlanta Constitution, wanted to see the South become economically strong without relying on cotton or tobacco. He led the cause of industrialization in the South. The idea caught on. Northern investors helped build plants to process agricultural goods (cotton, tobacco, etc.) and textile mills to weave cotton fabric. Mining efforts produced iron ore and coal in such large quantities that steel-making in the South could be cheaper than in the North. The South's rail lines were changed to match the North's so trains could move freely. Lastly, the South's great forests of southern yellow pine came into high demand.

This growth was not all good. Some of the industrial giants made deals with suppliers and transportation companies. These deals gave the larger companies exclusive access to resources and other benefits. This hurt smaller competing companies that needed the same resources to stay in business. These giant corporations became monopolies. They controlled the supply and trade in specific products. Becoming a monopoly allowed a company to control prices and availability of a product. It also led to corruption. The companies often made illegal payments to government and business officials in order to grow their businesses and get rid of competition. When these actions were publicly revealed, the federal government created laws to end monopolies.

title: The Sherman Antitrust Act
text:
In the early 1900s, the railroad industry was growing fast. Corrupt politicians started helping certain railroads grow very quickly. These politicians would even take bribes from railroad companies. Railroad companies were also known to have a bit of control over both political parties. It wasn't long before corporations wanted some of that power.

The Standard Oil Company was run by John D. Rockefeller. He set up the first trust in the nation in 1882. He persuaded the stockholders, people who invest in a company, to combine their stock and give control to nine trustees. Soon, other companies followed suit. Trusts kept growing as industrialization spread.

Trusts operated similarly to legal monopolies. They would combine multiple firms into one. This eliminated the competition and controlled the market. Trusts also made it hard for unions, or groups of workers who wanted a better workplace, to organize. Trusts controlled both political parties. Without union efforts, working conditions became even worse and child labor increased. A state inspector reported, "The average age at which these children went to work was nine years. All of them worked 10 hours a day, and many of them 13 or more."

The Sherman Antitrust Act was named after Senator John Sherman. The Act made it illegal for companies to work together to destroy competition. It also became illegal to prevent free trade among the states or with foreign countries, or to keep prices high or unfair.

For over 100 years, antitrust laws like the Sherman Antitrust Act have protected consumers and helped keep prices down through fair competition among companies.

title: Andrew Carnegie
text:
Andrew Carnegie was born on Nov. 25, 1835, into a poor family in Scotland. When he was 13, his family moved to Pennsylvania. They hoped to find better economic opportunities in America. He found a job as a bobbin boy at a cotton factory, where he earned $1.20 per week. Over the years, he had other jobs. He became a messenger in a telegraph office. Later, he was hired as a secretary and telegraph operator for the superintendent of the Pennsylvania Railroad’s Pittsburgh division. By the age of 24, he succeeded his boss.

Eventually, Carnegie left his job as superintendent. However, he continued to invest in railroads and other industries. Carnegie built the country's largest steel mill near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. His plant could make steel cheaper, stronger, and more quickly than all his competitors' plants could. He sold thousands of tons and made millions of dollars. Carnegie bought everything he needed to make steel: mining companies, rail lines, ships, and pig-iron plants. His steel went to build ships, buildings, bridges, machines, trains, rails, and other projects.

To build his empire, he beat out his competitors until he stood as the king of steel in America. However, as a philanthropist, he turned around and gave away at least $350 million to colleges, universities, medical research facilities, libraries, hospitals, museums, theaters, child-welfare centers, and scientific research centers. He also donated millions to support international peace projects.

title: John D. Rockefeller
text:
Born on July 8, 1839, in Richford, New York, John D. Rockefeller was the son of a traveling salesman. As a child he was enterprising and business oriented from raising turkeys to doing odd jobs for neighbors.

When a teenager, his family moved near Cleveland, Ohio. There, at the age of 16, he found a job as an office clerk at a business that bought, sold, and shipped commodities like grain and coal. By 1859, he and a partner established a business. Oil drilling was a success in Pennsylvania. This inspired Rockefeller and partners to invest in a Cleveland oil refinery. Two years later, he bought out his fellow investors and took full ownership of the refinery. From there, he found new partners and expanded his business interests.

The result of Rockefeller’s efforts was the Standard Oil Company, built in 1870. As he grew in wealth and power in the oil industry, he aggressively eliminated his competition. He began to control everything from the oil refineries to the railroads that shipped the oil. In this way, he developed a monopoly in the oil industry, owning nearly every oil company in America. The Sherman Antitrust Act, established by the Supreme Court, eventually broke up his trust as an example to other monopolies. When Rockefeller retired, he became a philanthropist, someone who gives money to charity. He established the Rockefeller Sanitary Commission in 1909, which successfully cured hookworm disease in the southern United States. He also founded the University of Chicago.

title: Henry Ford
text:
Henry Ford was born on July 30, 1863, and grew up on a farm in Dearborn, Michigan. At the age of 16, he left home to study machines in Detroit, Michigan. When he returned home, he continued work on the farm and in factories. He also operated and serviced steam engines. In 1891, he took a job as an engineer at the Edison Illuminating Company in Detroit.

In his free time, Ford worked on a gasoline-powered automobile. He called the resulting invention the “Quadricycle.” It was the very first of its kind. His invention drew a lot of attention from investors, who helped support him as he built more vehicles. Some of them formed the Detroit Automobile Company, where Ford worked until 1902. The following year, he created his own company, the Ford Motor Company.

In 1913, Ford developed a new system of making cars in his factory. He began using a moving assembly line, where each worker had one job to do in the car's assembly. Using this idea, factories made cars more quickly than if they were assembled one car at a time. Ford believed that this mass production would make his company very successful.

Ford also had new and interesting ideas on how to treat workers in his car factory. He offered them up to $5 a day to work for him. At the time, this was a very large wage to be paid for a day's work. Ford wanted to be sure his own employees could afford to buy one of the cars they were helping to produce.

Today, Henry Ford's ideas about assembly lines and mass production of goods are still used at factories around the world.

title: Reconstruction of Government, Economics, and Society
text:
The new president, Andrew Johnson, was facing a dilemma. Following Abraham Lincoln as president was intimidating. The Civil War was over. The government had to reunite as one nation. What would the southern states have to do to return to Congress?

The destruction of the land and people in the southern states was extensive. How could the government help ease the impact of the destruction?

There were newly emancipated African Americans who deserved a place in society. How could the government support and assist in giving African Americans a life of equality beyond enslavement?

There were also former soldiers and leaders of the Confederacy who had been defeated. Should they be punished or pardoned?

As president, Johnson’s actions would lead the nation in the reconstruction of the South and building the future.

The constitutions of each southern state that had seceded had to be rewritten to take out slavery. The revised constitutions had to recognize the newly emancipated citizens who were eligible to vote. African Americans were now to be included in each state’s government. However, no state constitutional convention was required to include African Americans in the process of writing a new state constitution.

Prior to the Civil War, the southern states had an economy based on agriculture. An agriculture economy is based on the planting, harvesting, and selling of harvested crops. After the war, there were miles of plantation land that had been ruined. The plantation owners had no money to buy seeds for planting. The greatest reality the South struggled with was the absence of forced labor. Enslaved people had planted and cared for the crops without pay. That form of exploitation was no more.

Another critical factor in the rebuilding of the nation after the war was managing the tensions among social beliefs. War and laws cannot change a person's beliefs. It was up to each individual to change their beliefs. The beliefs held by the southern people were what caused them to secede. They believed that African Americans were meant to be enslaved. They believed African Americans were not equal to any of the enslavers or other people of the community. Sadly, that belief was still held by many people in 1865, both in the north and south.

African Americans in the south embraced their new circumstances. Many African Americans came forward to be leaders. The majority of the emancipated people had been denied an education. They could not read or write. This made building a new life as a citizen extremely difficult. They also had few to no tools or possessions. Everything belonged to the plantation owners. Their status had changed, but the living conditions for many African Americans were very much the same.

The former Confederate leaders were required to sign an oath of allegiance to the United States. Only President Jefferson Davis was held in prison. No charges of treason were brought against any Confederate soldiers or sailors. This decision was to help the country heal and not punish those who had participated in the war.

President Johnson pardoned the high-ranking Confederate officers who personally wrote letters asking for a pardon. Johnson came up with a plan to let the South rebuild itself. The southern governments would determine voting rights and laws for the state. The presidential plan was not supportive in enforcing equality for African Americans.

Congress had many views on accepting the rebellious states back into the government. In late 1866, the majority of members in Congress were from the Republican party. One group became known as the “Radical Republicans” for their aggressive reforms for the South. The passing of the Reconstruction Act of 1867 enforced participation by African Americans in the southern government. This act also divided the regions of the South into five military districts. The military would be a physical presence in southern communities for the next 12 years.

title: Resistance in the Old Confederacy
text:
Most white people in the former Confederate States had become comfortable with slavery. It gave them power over a whole group of people. They made money from it and they benefited from free labor. They wanted African Americans to remain enslaved. They were unwilling to accept that African Americans were equal to them. Most white southerners were embittered by their defeat in the Civil War and did all they could to resist the authority of Washington, D.C. They did everything they could to keep things as they were before the war.

The states held conventions to write new constitutions, but didn’t invite any African Americans. As a result, many states created laws that limited the freedoms of African Americans. These laws became known as the “Black Codes.”

The laws varied from state to state. The law codes were passed by former enslavers to control African American families. The laws made it a crime to be unemployed. If an African American man did not have a job, he could be fined a large amount of money. This made African Americans sign job contracts for very low wages. The codes also controlled the type of jobs that could be offered to African Americans. African Americans were denied access to the courts and participation in juries. Violence against African Americans mostly went unpunished.

In 1871, Congress passed a series of enforcement acts for the reconstruction of the South. The acts were designed to stop violence and protect the civil rights of African Americans.

title: Abraham Lincoln and John Wilkes Booth
text:
The news of the Confederate surrender at Appomattox Court House on Sunday, April 9, 1865, created jubilation in the country. Washington, D.C., celebrated for days. The joyous people wanted to hear a victory speech from their president. On Tuesday evening, April 11, Abraham Lincoln addressed the crowd. He talked about the future. He said that the coming years should not be used to punish the southern states. He talked of a new nation that would have equality for all. Lincoln then asked a band to play the song “Dixie.” The crowd listened quietly, then went home.

John Wilkes Booth was in the crowd that night. He was angry about the surrender of the Confederacy. He was not willing to change the way he thought. He believed African Americans should remain enslaved. He did not believe in the things Lincoln talked about for the future of the country. He did not want African Americans to be equal in the law. He did not want African American men to be able to vote. In Booth's mind, the way to stop equality of African Americans was to stop Lincoln.

Abraham Lincoln was the happiest he had been in years the week of April 9. The Union had been saved, and slavery was gone. The public continued their celebrations throughout the rest of the week. The crowds cheered and wanted to see more of their president. Mrs. Lincoln made plans to go to Ford's Theater on Friday, April 14. A popular comedy play entitled “Our American Cousin” was playing. John Wilkes Booth also made plans to be at the theater.

The audience at the theater cheered and applauded the Lincolns when they arrived. The president’s guard left his post to get a drink. It was then that Booth made his way to Lincoln’s seat. Booth shot Lincoln, then escaped by leaping onto the stage in the middle of the play. Everyone in the audience saw him and knew who he was. He escaped out the back and rode into the night. Booth thought of himself as a hero, not a murderer.

Abraham Lincoln died the next morning, April 15, 1865. The happiest week in his life was, sadly, the last week in his life.

title: Physical Features
text: Physical features tell us what a place looks like. They are part of the natural environment. Continents and oceans are the largest physical features on Earth. A continent is a landform. An ocean is a body of water.

title: Essential Question
text: How can maps help us describe places?

title: Landforms
text:
Landforms are features on Earth’s surface. They include mountains, valleys, plains, and islands.

Mountains are landforms. They rise above the surrounding land. A mountain usually rises at least 1,000 feet above sea level.

Hills are also areas that rise above the surrounding land. Their tops are usually rounded. They are similar to mountains, but not as high.

Valleys are low areas between hills or mountains. Mountains and hills can prevent rain from falling in valleys.

Plains are large areas of flat land. They grow a lot of grass. Plains are found on all continents. They cover a large portion of the land on Earth.

Islands are areas of land surrounded by water. They are not connected to a continent.

title: Bodies of Water
text:
Bodies of water are large areas of water. Some important bodies of water are oceans, rivers, and lakes.

Oceans are the largest bodies of water. They cover about 71 percent of the Earth. Imagine the world as a huge pizza. If you divide it into four equal parts, the oceans would take almost three!

Rivers are flowing bodies of water. This means the water in them moves. Rivers usually run from mountains toward the ocean.

Lakes are large areas filled with water. They are surrounded by land. Unlike rivers, the water in lakes tends to remain still or move very slowly.

title: Climate
text: Climate is a physical feature of a place. Sometimes we want to study the weather of a place. We want to know if it is warm or cold. We may want to know if it is sunny or rainy. The weather can change in just a few hours. The climate of a place takes years to change. Climate is the weather pattern of an area. Climate includes the temperature and how windy it is. Rain and snow are also part of the climate. Climate helps people make decisions about food, clothing, and shelter.

title: Work
text:
Work is important. Work is when we do something that produces a good or provides a service. Work can be a physical or mental activity. A person might choose to work as a baker or a firefighter. They could also work as a writer or an accountant. The work we do is called our job.

When people work, they earn money. The money they earn is called income. People use income to buy things they need and want. Money can buy goods or services.

title: Essential Question
text: What should I do with my money?

title: Spending
text: Spending your money carefully is not easy. There are many choices to make. The goods and services we need and want do not always cost the same amount of money. People must choose where to spend their money. They also must choose how much they are willing to pay. For example, not all shoes cost the same amount. Responsible people make good decisions about spending their money.

title: Saving
text: Saving is keeping some of your money for the future. When you save money, you must decide where to keep it safe. Many people save money in a bank or credit union. This works well to save up for something expensive. For example, your family may be saving for a vacation, house, or car. Sometimes we only need to save for a short amount of time. You can save money at home in a piggy bank, wallet, or safe. This works to save for less expensive things, like a new toy or shirt.

title: Donating
text: Donating is giving part of what you have to others. Donations can be money, resources, or time. Many people donate resources such as food and clothing. People donate extra food to a food bank for those who need it. Others donate money to people and organizations that solve community problems. You can also donate your time by serving others. When you volunteer to clean a park, you are donating time.

title: Banks, Credit Unions, and Credit Cards
text:
Banks and credit unions help you save money. You can set up a bank account or a savings account to put your money in. Banks can also help you invest your money, or set up a loan. The bank's job is to keep your money safe until you are ready to use it.

Many banks and other companies give people credit cards. Credit cards are small pieces of plastic. They let you buy something now and pay for it later. You will usually have to pay interest to use a credit card. Interest is extra money we pay back over time in order to use money now. People who have credit cards agree to pay back the money they use.

title: Creating a Budget
text: We can set goals for spending, saving, donating, or investing our money. When we plan how we spend and earn money, we call that a budget. Setting goals and creating a budget helps people pay for things they need and want. Budgets change as wants and needs change. Earning, saving, and spending are parts of a budget. It is important that when people are creating a budget they set short-term and long-term goals. This helps people make decisions between wants and needs.

title: Days
text: There are 24 hours in one day. The new day starts at midnight. Each day has a number or date. What date is circled on the calendar?

title: How Do People Get Food?
text: Today, people get most of their food from grocery stores. With ships, airplanes, and refrigerated trucks, food can travel around the world. This makes food supply more interdependent. Interdependent means people depend on each other for what they need. Farmers do not grow many different foods. They can grow just one kind of food. They go to a grocery store to get other things they need. Our grocery stores have food from all over the world. We can buy apples from Washington. We can buy bananas from Ecuador. Corn from Ohio gets transported to other parts of the United States. It also gets transported around the world.

title: Week 25 Guiding Question
text: How do people get food today?

title: Production: How Do They Produce Corn?
text:
Ohio is a great place for farming. It has some of the most fertile soil in the nation. Over half of the land in Ohio is farmland. Ohio is the nation’s seventh-largest producer of corn.

Ohio farmers plant corn in the spring. They wait for the soil to be warm. The corn kernels (or seeds) need warm soil to grow. Today, farmers use technology to help them. Computers and even satellite images can show them just where to plant the kernels. Each kernel needs to have space. It needs to get nutrients, water, and sun.

Over the summer, the corn plant grows. Its leaves take in heat and sunlight. Its roots soak up water and nutrients. Each plant will grow two ears of corn. Hundreds of silks attach to each ear. The silks get pollinated. Once pollinated, each silk forms a new kernel. These kernels grow on a cob until ripe.

title: Processing: How Do They Harvest Corn?
text:
Field corn gets harvested when the kernels and the whole plant dry out. Sweet corn is different. The ears and plants are still green at harvest time. The kernels are still soft. Farmers know to harvest sweet corn when the silk on the end of the ears turns brown.

Sweet corn can be harvested by hand or by machine. As the ears are picked, workers sort them by hand. They pack the ears into crates that each weigh about 42 pounds. Each crate holds about five dozen ears of corn.

As soon as an ear of corn is picked, the sugar in the kernels begins to change. It starts to become starch. Starchy corn is less sweet. Cooling slows the process of sugar becoming starch. It is usually hot when farmers harvest sweet corn in late summer. It is important to cool the ears within hours of the harvest. Farmers run cold water through crates of packed ears to cool them down.

title: Distribution: How Does Corn Get To Market?
text:
The clock starts ticking on fresh sweet corn as soon as the harvest begins. Farmers store the crates of cooled ears in sheds. There are many types of sweet corn. Farmers can store the different types for 5-8 days. The sooner they ship the corn, the better.

Fresh sweet corn ships in refrigerated trucks or rail cars. Temperatures for shipping are kept around freezing. The corn must stay cold. This is so the sugars inside the kernels stay fresh and sweet.

Once the corn reaches stores, employees set the corn out. Stores buy sweet corn by the crate. They sell the corn by the ear, though. Customers buy only as many ears of corn as they need. They can cook it right away, store the ears in the fridge, or freeze them.

title: From Farm to Table
text: Explain the process of getting sweet corn from the farm to your table. Draw pictures to show each step.

title: Responsible Citizens in History
text: Responsible citizens make their communities better. They help their communities. There are many responsible citizens in history.

title: Essential Question
text: Who are some responsible citizens in history?

title: Fred Korematsu
text: Fred Korematsu grew up in California. He wanted to be treated with respect. Some people treated him differently because he was Japanese American. He worked hard for everyone to be treated with respect.

title: Rosa Parks
text: Rosa Parks showed courage. One day, she rode the bus. She was told to move to the back of the bus because she was Black. She did not. She did what she believed was right.

title: Roberto Clemente
text: Roberto Clemente was a famous baseball player. He was a responsible citizen. He helped people in need. He gave people money and food. He taught children how to play baseball.

title: Susan B. Anthony
text: Susan B. Anthony believed everyone should be treated fairly. There was a time when women could not vote. Susan helped change that. Now women can vote.

title: Daniel Webster
text: Daniel Webster was a senator. He wanted everyone to have the same rights and be free. He worked for this to happen. He showed determination.

title: Abraham Lincoln
text: Abraham Lincoln was honest with people. Some people called him “Honest Abe.” He was the 16th president of the United States.

title: Who Were the First Inhabitants of the Americas?
text:
People lived in the Americas long before Europeans arrived. These people lived in groups called tribes or nations. Each tribe or nation had its own culture. Some of these tribes still live in the Americas today.

A tribe is a community that is related through family ties and culture. Different Native American tribes lived in different regions of the Americas. The natural resources around them affected their ways of life. They used these natural resources to build their homes. They also used these natural resources to make clothes and create art. The food they ate and the things they believed were also affected by their environment. All the things that mark a vibrant society in any time period were present in the indigenous tribes of North America.

title: Essential Question
text: Who were the first inhabitants of North America?

title: The Northeast
text:
Many Native American tribes lived in the Northeast. They grew corn, beans, and squash. The tribes used all the natural resources around them to meet their basic needs. They used birch bark to cover their homes. They hunted animals for food. Animal hides, or skins, were used to make clothes, containers, and bags. Everything was used. Nothing was wasted.

Northeast tribes lived in wigwams in the winter. In summer, they lived in longhouses. Both dwellings were built around wooden frames. The wigwams were smaller. They could be built once a year. Longhouses were bigger. They could house many families.

Art was part of the culture of the tribes. They built canoes and made tools. They used the tools for work and as weapons. Some tribes made face masks. One type of mask was woven with corn husks. Another type was carved out of wood. They also used deerskin to make clothes, shoes, and bags.

title: The Southeast
text:
The Native Americans who lived in the Southeast were mostly farmers. They used the resources around where they lived. They had good soil for growing crops. Some of their main crops were corn, beans, and squash. They hunted and fished as well.

Many early tribes in the region built large mounds. These mounds were used for important ceremonies. This area is a mixture of forests and grasslands, so homes ranged from grass huts to wooden houses.

Some of the tribes used music and dance for recreation and healing. They were sculptors and basket weavers. They made glazed pottery as well.

title: The Midwest
text:
The Native American tribes that lived in the plains region had a large space for hunting. They often moved with the animals they hunted. Their main source of meat and materials was bison. The people used every part of the bison to meet their needs. Bison skin was used for tepees, clothing, containers, and blankets. Bison dung was used as fuel for fires. These tribes lived in tepees when they hunted. This is because tepees could be packed up and moved easily. Usually, they lived in wigwams in winter and in longhouses in summer.

The tribes had artistic skills that they still practice today. They also made clothes and shoes that had beautiful beadwork. Beading was common to most of the tribes in the Midwest.

title: Colonial Life - A Hard Life
text:
Can you imagine living without televisions, cars, grocery stores and computers? The early colonists who settled in North Carolina had a very different life from the one we live today.

When the colonists wanted to get from one place to another, they could travel on foot or on horseback. They also had wagons that could be pulled by horses or oxen.

To communicate with friends or family, they had to visit or write a letter. The mail was slow. The first regular mail route to the Carolina territory was from Boston to Charleston, South Carolina. It began about 1738.

Colonists did not have grocery stores or fast food restaurants. Instead, they hunted and fished. They grew their own vegetables and fruit.

Colonial families were usually larger than most families of today. Everyone had a job to do so that the family would survive. Children often helped feed the animals, clean the house, work in the fields and prepare meals.

What did the colonists do for fun? Many of them sang and some played instruments. Storytelling was also a popular pastime. Kids played with homemade toys and enjoyed playing games. Some families owned a few books. The colonists who lived in Bath were lucky, because North Carolina's first public library was there. It was founded in 1700 with books sent from England by Reverend Thomas Bray.

The colonists faced many dangers. Doctors did not have the same medicines that we have today, and colonists often died of diseases. Diseases killed many North Carolina American Indians because they had never been exposed to those illnesses before the colonists came. Therefore, they had no immunity to the diseases.

Some of the American Indians who lived in the Carolina territory were not happy. They didn't like that the colonists were building homes and farms on their hunting grounds. Some colonists cheated the American Indians when they traded with them. Others kidnapped American Indians and sold them as slaves. Some American Indians defended themselves and their families. They knew they were being treated unfairly.

Want to know more about life as a Carolina colonist? Check out this week's lesson.

title: The Columbian Exchange
text:
The Columbian Exchange was the exchanging of plants, animals, ideas, and technology between Europe, Africa, and the Americas. European powers, such as Spain, Portugal, England, France, Denmark, Russia, and the Netherlands, collected raw materials from the Americas. Then, the materials were sent to Europe to be processed into goods. These were then exchanged for other products from around the world.

Food and Livestock

Europeans came to America searching for gold. One of the things they unexpectedly found as they interacted with the indigenous people was new crops. Corn was a very useful crop for early settlers. It was easy to grow, animals could eat it, and it grew where wheat and rice could not. Native Americans taught Europeans about corn's many benefits. Potatoes were another important crop introduced to Europeans by Native Americans.

In exchange for corn and potatoes, Europeans brought wheat, rye, barley, and oats to the indigenous peoples of the Americas. These grains helped add many new foods to the diet of Native Americans. Today, America is so successful at growing and producing grains that people have nicknamed the United States the "breadbasket of the world.”

Explorers also brought animals with them to the Americas. The Spanish brought pigs, sheep, cows, and chickens to the Americas. Over time, hogs and cattle replaced bison and deer at mealtimes. This helped keep settlers alive.

Plants

Sugarcane was one of the important plants that settlers brought to the Americas through the Columbian Exchange. It thrived in many areas of the Americas and was sent back to Europe through trade. Europe also introduced oranges to North America.

Explorers brought many plants from the Americas to Europe through their travels. Tobacco was an important plant discovered by the early settlers. It was popular in Native American ceremonies.

Technology

Europeans came to the Americas with horses and tools used in their daily life. These were new to the Native Americans. When the Europeans returned home, they left many things in the Americas. This made more room in their ships for the goods they had taken.

Native Americans began to use the tools and animals that were left behind. Cattle were used to move heavy things or plow fields. The Native Americans made a special connection with horses. They learned to use them to make life easier. Horses made hunting and traveling easier for Native Americans. Horses were also traded for things to meet Native Americans' wants and needs.

Europeans also left behind important tools that changed the way native peoples lived. Before European exploration, Native Americans used resources found in their environment to create tools. Europeans brought metal tools with them that were unknown to Native Americans. This included cooking utensils, pots, pans, axes, and knives. The most life-changing tools that Europeans brought to the Americas were guns. Guns had a large impact on the way Native Americans hunted and defended themselves.

title: Effects of European Exploration
text:
Goods weren't the only things introduced to Europe and the Americas during the Columbian Exchange.

Beliefs

Before European exploration of the Americas, Native Americans had very different beliefs from Europeans. Many Europeans wanted Native Americans to convert to Christianity. Some Native Americans chose to convert, while others did not. These differences in beliefs often led to conflicts between Native American tribes and European settlers.

Slavery

As European colonization of the Americas began to spread, the demand for labor increased. European enslavers and traders from Portugal, France, England, and the Netherlands bought enslaved people from Africa. Enslavers, traders, and merchants packed their ships with enslaved people and made the dangerous journey across the Atlantic Ocean to sell them in the Americas.

Wealthy businessmen took advantage of the slave trade to increase their wealth. Cash crops like sugarcane, tobacco, and cotton all required a great amount of work to grow. Enslaved people were bought by plantation owners, or owners of large farms, as soon as they were brought to the Americas. Enslaved people had no freedom and were considered property.

Disease

Europeans unknowingly brought many diseases with them to the Americas. These diseases included smallpox, measles, and influenza. These diseases were very contagious and often deadly. Native Americans had no immunity to these diseases. They spread very quickly and easily in Native American communities. Millions of Native Americans died from these diseases. These diseases had a devastating impact on Native American tribes.

title: How Are Goods Produced from Corn?
text:
People have grown corn in North America for thousands of years. It is a very useful crop. Only one percent of the corn grown in the U.S. is for people to eat. The other 99 percent gets used for other things. Corn is used to meet many different types of needs.

There are two basic types of corn. Corn grown for people to eat is called sweet corn. The corn grown to be used for making other products is called field corn.

Sometimes we use corn whole, just as it is. We eat sweet corn right off the cob. Corn can be frozen or canned for later use. We use whole kernels of field corn to feed animals.

Most field corn gets processed, or changed to make it more usable. Then the processed corn becomes an ingredient used in making other products. It can be turned into ethanol fuel. It can be turned into a starch or a syrup. Cornstarch and corn syrup are added to many products. There are about 4,000 products in your grocery store with corn listed as an ingredient!

title: The Corn Connection
text: Corn is an important part of many foods, even when it is not listed as an ingredient. In a way, milk and eggs come from corn. So do bacon and hamburgers. This is because a lot of the corn grown in the U.S. is used to feed animals. The country’s cows, chickens, and pigs eat tons of whole-kernel corn. Remember the importance of corn the next time you pour a glass of milk or bite into a hamburger!

title: Cornstarch
text:
Dry corn kernels are a type of grain. Like other grains, dry corn can be ground into flour. Corn flour gets used to make food. Cornbread and corn tortillas have corn flour in them.

To make cornstarch, the starchy center of the kernel gets ground up. The ground-up kernels create cornstarch. Cornstarch is much finer than corn flour.

Cornstarch has many uses. It gets used in recipes. It can be added to liquids to make them thicker. Cornstarch is also used to make corn syrup. Corn syrup sweetens food like sugar does. Your favorite candy probably has corn syrup as an ingredient.

Cornstarch has many uses outside of cooking. Cornstarch gets added to baby powder and deodorant. It also helps keep things from sticking. A thin coat of cornstarch on the inside of latex gloves helps doctors take them on and off. Cornstarch also lines plastic molds for tires. This prevents the rubber from sticking. Cornstarch is a very useful product.

title: Ethanol
text:
Corn ethanol is made when water is added to corn flour and the mixture is heated. The starch in the corn gets broken down into sugars. Those sugars go through another process. The result is a form of alcohol called ethanol.

Ethanol is a common ingredient in many personal care products. It helps hairspray stick to hair. It is also in hand sanitizer. This is because it kills bacteria and many viruses. Ethanol is also used in many cleaning products for the same reason. It is in some types of paint because it helps the paint dry smoother and faster.

The biggest use for ethanol is as fuel. Ethanol is added to gasoline to help the gas burn efficiently in the engine. This means we can use less gasoline. Almost half of the corn grown in Ohio is used to make ethanol. There are seven ethanol plants in Ohio.

title: POPCORN!
text:
Planting

Farmers plant the type of corn that is good for popcorn.

Harvesting

The corn is picked by large tractors, and the kernels are removed from the husks. The husks can be fed to farm animals.

Storage

The corn kernels are stored in large silos. Farmers can store the kernels for up to five years. The temperature is monitored so that the kernels keep their moisture for popping.

Testing

Popcorn is test-popped in the factory to be sure that the kernels are ready.

Sorting

The corn is cleaned and sorted by the size of the kernels.

Packaging

After the kernels are sorted, they are put into large bags for shipping to the businesses that ordered them.

Shipping

The corn is shipped to its destination in large trucks. Some of these destinations are places that repackage the popcorn into smaller bags to sell in stores.

Selling

Workers pop the popcorn kernels in theaters for us to enjoy with movies. Popcorn is also sold in stores to enjoy at home.
