title: Border Disputes Between Spain and the United States
text:
Following the American Revolution, Spain regained control of Florida for its role in supporting the American colonists during the war. Despite their alliance in the war, peace between the two nations was short-lived. When the war ended, the United States agreed to cede Florida to Spain, but the two countries could not agree on where the northern boundary of West Florida should be. In 1795, the United States and Spain signed Pinckney’s Treaty, which created the new boundary between Florida and the United States.

This was not the end of the disputes over Florida’s borders, however. In 1803, France sold the Louisiana territory to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase. At the time, Florida extended all the way to the Mississippi River. The United States felt that the territory of West Florida was actually part of the Louisiana territory, but the Spanish disagreed. Many settlers living in West Florida had migrated to the territory from the United States. They did not want to live under Spanish rule.

In September 1810, a small group of colonists rebelled against the Spanish crown and formed the Republic of West Florida. The revolutionaries signed their own declaration of independence and created a constitution. This rebellion lasted only 74 days before the United States intervened and took possession of West Florida. It would be years before the United States would legally regain the territory from Spain.

title: The British Invasion
text:
The late 1700s and the early 1800s were a period of great conflict between the major powers of Europe and the Americas. The relationship between Great Britain and the United States was hostile. The United States’ relationship with France, its former ally in the American Revolution, was strained. This stemmed from the constant conflict between Great Britain and France.

The United States wished to remain neutral during the war between Great Britain and France. Both countries wanted the support of the U.S. government. In order to maintain neutrality, Congress passed the Embargo Act in 1807, but it was repealed in 1808. President James Madison had to come up with a new plan to protect American ships, sailors, and goods from the British and French navies. Congress attempted to peacefully settle its issues with Great Britain. Peaceful negotiations failed. In 1810, Madison forbade trade with Great Britain altogether.

On June 1, 1812, President James Madison asked Congress to officially declare war on Great Britain, which it did 17 days later. This became known as the War of 1812. The United States wasn’t prepared to fight another war. Congress had to quickly expand the army and navy to protect the country from a British invasion. The United States, Great Britain, and their Native American allies fought many land and sea battles throughout the United States.

In August 1814, British forces occupied Pensacola to gain control of the port and oppose American settlers in Georgia and the Louisiana Territory. The British were helped by Native Americans who had been pushed off their land by American settlers and formerly enslaved people who had escaped from American plantations. On Nov. 6, 1814, U.S. General Andrew Jackson marched into Pensacola with 4,000 soldiers and drove the British out. Jackson captured the city, placing Florida under the control of the United States.

title: The Newest Territory
text:
The United States was victorious over the British and their allies in the War of 1812, including Spain. The U.S. victory opened the door for negotiations to transfer ownership of Florida to the United States. In 1815, Spanish politician and diplomat Don Luis de Onís was sent to Washington, D.C., to negotiate the transfer of Florida with the U.S. government. Both parties could not agree on the terms of the transfer, and the negotiations broke down. The matter was not discussed again until 1818.

In 1818, General Andrew Jackson once again captured the city of Pensacola from the Spanish as well as forts in St. Marks while fighting Native American forces in the area. President James Monroe and Secretary of State John Quincy Adams used this event to begin negotiations for Florida again. Onís and Adams met to discuss the terms of surrender.

The Adams-Onís treaty was drafted and signed in 1819. This treaty created peace between Spain and the United States. It required Spain to cede all land holdings east of the Mississippi River to the United States, including East and West Florida. It also created the boundary between the United States and all remaining Spanish colonies in North America. The treaty was approved by Spain in 1820 and by the United States in 1821. Andrew Jackson was appointed the temporary territorial governor of Florida.

In July 1821, Florida was officially ceded to the United States and officially became an organized territory on March 30, 1822. Lawyer and politician William P. Duval was appointed as the first territorial governor of Florida. Within a period of fewer than 50 years, Florida had been under the control of three powerful nations. Florida’s admittance to the United States as a territory encouraged American settlers to migrate to the new territory. Florida’s population grew steadily in the years that followed, and life in the territory changed in many ways. These changes had both positive and negative effects on the people, culture, geography, and economy of Florida.

title: Florida's Response to the War
text:
Even before South Carolina seceded from the Union, small militias of volunteers began to organize in Florida. These volunteer units later joined with Confederate forces. About 16,000 Floridians fought in the war. Some supported the Union and were opposed to secession. Of the 16,000 who fought, about 2,000 were fighting for the Union.

There were other small militia groups during the war. These groups were made up mostly of farmers and cattle hands. They were known as the “Cow Cavalry.” These groups formed to protect parts of Florida farther inland. They protected cattle ranches and roads. They also helped to defend salt work plants along the coast. During the Civil War, salt was vital. Before refrigerators, salt was used to keep meat from spoiling. Floridians boiled sea water or evaporated it naturally to collect salt.

With most of the men participating in the war, women, children, and people who were enslaved had to keep farms running. They worked to feed themselves and provide Confederate troops with supplies. Florida’s cattle herds and farms provided a supply of meat, vegetables, fruits, and salt, particularly toward the end of the war.

As the war started to end, many deserters and those wanting to avoid the draft fled to Florida. They hoped to escape the war. More and more Floridians strongly opposed the war the longer it dragged on.

title: Major Battles in Florida
text:
Although it wasn’t at the heart of the fighting during the Civil War, Florida saw its share of battles.

October 1861: Battle of Santa Rosa Island

In October 1861, Union soldiers were stationed at Fort Pickens on Santa Rosa Island, just off the coast of Pensacola. The Union attacked and sank a Confederate ship, the Judah, while it was being repaired in the Pensacola shipyard. In response, Confederate Brigadier General Richard Anderson and 1,000 of his men crossed from the mainland to Santa Rosa Island. They hoped to take the Union troops by surprise. They were successful, but the Union troops were victorious in the battle. The Confederates were driven from the island.

June 1862: Tampa Incident

On June 30, 1862, a small battle broke out in Tampa Bay. A Union boat landed in Tampa Bay. Soldiers disembarked and went into the town. They demanded that the Confederates surrender. When the small Confederate militia guarding the town refused, the Union boat began to fire on the town. When the firing ceased, the Union general aboard the ship informed the Confederates that the boat would fire again at six p.m. They had until then to evacuate the townspeople.

Again, the small Confederate militia, called the Osceola Rangers, refused to surrender to the Union. The Union soldiers began firing on the Confederates. They continued to fight until the afternoon of the next day. Finally, the Union troops stopped firing, and their boat withdrew.

October 1863: Battle of Fort Brooke

On the night of Oct. 16, 1863, two Union gunboats created a diversion by firing 126 shells on Confederate-held Fort Brooke. While the Confederate forces were busy dealing with the bombardment, Acting Master T.R. Harris led 130 Union troops 14 miles from Ballast Point to Hillsborough River.

To prevent the Federals from capturing it, Confederates destroyed their own steamer, A.B Noyes. The Federals captured two other ships, called the Scottish Chief and the Kate Dale. The Union force then headed back to its own ship. They turned their attention to Confederate-owned saltworks on the coast. However, Confederate forces led by Captain John Wescott of the 2nd Florida Battalion cut them off and prevented the raids.

Blockade of Ports

Early in the war, the Union navy began blockading major Florida ports and military forts. These blockades included St. Augustine, Jacksonville, Key West, Pensacola, Fort Pickens, and Fort Zachary Taylor. This was done to keep goods and weapons from going in or out of Florida. Confederate forces were prevented from getting supplies. Blockading was difficult to do, because Florida is a peninsula with thousands of miles of coastlines. Sometimes, smaller ships were able to slip through and deliver supplies to the Confederate forces.

As the Union navy gained more ships, they were able to more effectively prevent Confederate ships from getting through the blockades. Some of Florida’s larger rivers were also patrolled by the Union for boats transporting goods for the Confederacy.

February 1864: Battle of Olustee

The Battle of Olustee was the largest battle to happen in Florida during the Civil War. The battle started out as a small skirmish, but it quickly turned into a full-blown battle. Union troops encountered Confederate soldiers and began to fire on them. The Confederates retreated for a few miles until they regrouped with reinforcements.

The Confederate troops turned to face the Union soldiers. Union troops advanced on the Confederates amidst gunfire. The Confederate soldiers were ready to fight and well organized. The Union troops, however, descended into confusion and chaos when a series of conflicting orders were given from their commanding officers. The Confederates pressed their advantage in the confusion and gained the upper hand.

The entire battle lasted about three and a half hours. After taking heavy casualties, the Union was forced to retreat. In a letter to his father, Union soldier Oliver Wilcox Norton wrote of the battle:

First, I think no battle was ever more wretchedly fought. I was going to say planned, but there was no plan. No new regiment ever went into their first fight in more unfavorable circumstances. Second, no braver men ever faced an enemy … You may judge of the severity of the fight by this: Of fifty-five men in Company K who went into the fight but two came out untouched ... Of twenty-two officers engaged but two were untouched. I got a ball in my hat … Another took off the corner of my haversack.

March 1865: Battle of Natural Bridge

The Battle of Natural Bridge took place on March 6, 1865, near the town of St. Marks. The Union force intended to take St. Marks and then Tallahassee from the rebels. One Confederate soldier wrote of the experience:

We left Tallahassee for St. Marks on foot; quick time. We expected to meet Yanks any minute. However, we did not meet them until we got near St. Marks, at a place called Natural Bridge … We met them and gave them such a hot reception that we soon had them rattled …

-Sylvanus M. Hankins

Many people who were close to the action in and around St. Marks were not soldiers. The fighting was so close that people could hear and see the battle as it played out.

Our evergreen hills have resounded again to the roar of cannon, which came suddenly in the night … A courier from St. Marks brought news that the enemy were landing in great numbers at the Light-house on the Bay. The cavalry were there, and kept them back until artillery and infantry could support them. Every old man and young boy that could handle a gun went forth, and companies from adjoining counties were soon in the field. The cadets of the college (boys of twelve), shouldered their muskets like veterans, and followed with the confidence of inexperience …

The enemy [Union], two thousand five hundred strong … under Gen. Newton, arrived at the bridge of Newport, on the St. Marks River. Not being able to cross under the fire of our men, they moved up to the "Natural Bridge," where the actual fight took place. Gen. Sam Jones, the commander of our force of six hundred, is said to have conducted the engagement with great coolness and tact, often turning the fire of the artillery himself where he saw it would be most effective … It was a gallant defense on the part of our people, and if it accounted for any result in the main, it would be great, for it prevented the Federals from securing Middle Florida and lower Georgia, which are the granaries of the South …

-Ruth, a Florida resident (Recorded in the book Florida Breezes)

title: African American Regiments in the Civil War
text:
Many people escaped slavery by making their way to the northern states. Once there, many of them wanted to fight for the Union and end slavery. So many wanted to join the army that the planning, training, and amount of paperwork quickly overwhelmed government officials. As a result, the Bureau of Colored Troops was created. The Bureau helped build and manage regiments of volunteer Black soldiers. Several Black regiments were created as a result. Among these regiments were the 8th U.S. Colored Infantry, the 35th U.S. Colored Infantry, and others.

After the Emancipation Proclamation was released in 1863, an abolitionist named John A. Andrew, the governor of Massachusetts, organized one of the first Black regiments in the U.S. Army: the 54th Massachusetts Infantry. The 55th Massachusetts Infantry had to be created as well to accommodate the huge number of formerly enslaved men who signed up to fight. White officers with anti-slavery views were recruited to lead these regiments.

At first, the men of the 54th did manual labor to help with the war effort. However, they soon had their first combat experience. The 54th was one of the first regiments of free Black men to face combat in the Civil War.

Their first major battle took place at the attack on Battery Wagner. The 54th pushed through enemy lines, taking heavy casualties. Union regiments behind them attempted to take Battery Wagner. Unfortunately, the Confederate forces overwhelmed the Union troops. They were forced to retreat. Renowned for their bravery, the number of free Black recruits was increased by the U.S. Army. Between 1863 and 1865, nearly 200,000 fought for the Union.

title: First Florida Cavalry
text:
Not everyone in the South agreed with seceding from the Union. Some southerners took up arms and joined Union forces to fight against the Confederacy. This was not an easy decision to make. Dissenters were in the minority. Despite this, many brave individuals chose to stand up and fight for what they believed in.

One group that did was the First Florida Cavalry. This group formed in Pensacola, Florida. These men helped the Union take control of the area. Over 650 southerners enlisted in the First Florida Cavalry. Throughout the war, they fought in many raids and battles throughout western Florida and southern Alabama. Due to a shortage of horses, parts of the First Florida Cavalry were forced to become an unmounted unit. They did their fighting and marching on foot. The First Florida Cavalry wasn’t the only Union regiment fighting in the South. However, it was able to provide much-needed support to other Union regiments in order to achieve victory in battles and skirmishes.

title: The Cow Cavalry
text:
Not everyone who fought in the Civil War was a professional, trained soldier. Much like the Minutemen of the Revolutionary War, everyday people armed themselves with whatever skills they had to offer to help with the war effort.

One of the most important and difficult tasks in maintaining an army is keeping it supplied. During the Civil War, Florida became one of the main suppliers of beef to Confederate soldiers. However, battles and troop movements made getting beef to the soldiers increasingly difficult. Union troops and army deserters frequently raided Florida cattle herds. The raids decreased the availability of beef supplies.

Some Confederate soldiers were sent to help defend the cattle herds. Even being guarded wasn't enough, though. Finally, Confederate Captain James McKay wrote to Confederate Secretary of War James A. Seddon with a request. He wanted to create a special unit that would be in charge of gathering and protecting southern cattle herds. Several similar requests had already been made. Finally, it was agreed that a special unit would be created to protect and drive the cattle. This would ensure that a steady supply of beef could be delivered to Confederate troops.

The battalion was officially called the First Battalion, Florida Special Cavalry. However, It quickly became known as the "Cow Cavalry" because of the work its members did. Not all who were recruited to the Cow Cavalry were soldiers. After a call for volunteers, many cattle hands and ranchers volunteered to join the ranks. Although not soldiers, their skills were invaluable in driving and caring for the cattle.

title: How Volcanoes Erupt
text:
Volcanoes

Volcanoes are openings in the Earth’s surface. They are vents in the crust of the Earth. When a volcano vents, we say it is erupting. A volcano erupting can be like an explosion.

When volcanoes erupt, earth materials shoot out. These materials include lava, rock fragments, and hot gases. These materials come from deep inside the Earth. When volcanoes erupt, they change the Earth around them.

Volcanoes can be active, dormant, or extinct. An active volcano is a volcano that has recently erupted. A dormant volcano is a volcano that hasn't erupted in a long time. It is a type of active volcano. Dormant volcanoes can still erupt in the future under the right conditions. An extinct volcano is a volcano that hasn’t erupted for at least 10,000 years.

title: Weathering and Erosion
text: The Earth's surface is always changing. Some of these changes take a long time. There are two ways the Earth changes very slowly. They are weathering and erosion. Weathering occurs when earth materials are broken down into pieces. Weathering changes a rock but does not move it. Erosion occurs when the broken materials are carried away. These pieces get carried away by water, wind, or ice.

title: Canada’s Physical and Human Features
text:
Canada has many physical features. Each feature is important. Often, they provide necessities like food, water, transportation, and trade. Some of these physical features include the St. Lawrence River and the Hudson Bay. They also include the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, the Great Lakes, and the Rocky Mountains.

The border between Canada and the United States is very long. In fact, it is the longest border between two countries in the world. Canada is divided into sections. They are called provinces. Canada has 10 provinces and three territories. Territories are sections of the country with fewer people. People have built many bridges over Canada’s waterways. One famous bridge is the Capilano Suspension Bridge. It hangs over the Capilano River. This bridge was first built in 1889. It is 450 feet long.

title: Essential Question
text: How can I describe Canada?

title: Canada’s Climates
text:
The climate in Canada gets colder as you go north. Northern Canada is extremely cold. Very few people live in the north. In fact, 90 percent of Canadians live within 100 miles of the border with the United States. Canada covers a large part of the North American continent. The climates differ, or vary, from one area to the next.

Polar

The northern part of Canada is polar. This means it has very cold temperatures and little rainfall.

Continental

The middle areas of Canada are mostly continental. This means they have short summers and long, cold winters with lots of rainfall.

Temperate

Along the coastlines, the climate is temperate. While the summers are pleasant, these regions can be very cold throughout the winter.

Dry

Small parts of Canada have a dry climate. The winters here are cold, and the summers are warm and dry. There is very little rainfall, though it's not considered a "desert."

title: Canada’s Biomes
text: There are a wide variety of plants and animals in Canada's biomes. There are different types of forests in the forest biome of Canada. Squirrels, moose, and wolves live in these forests. There are also many pine trees in the forests. In the mountain biome, there are grizzly bears and cougars. Trout, pike, and bass are some of the types of fish that live in Canada’s freshwater biome. The tundra biome is home to polar bears, snowy owls, and arctic hares. Very few plants live in the tundra because it is cold and dry. One plant that can survive in the tundra is moss.

title: Canada’s Natural Resources
text: Canada is a land rich in natural resources. The vast forests in the country provide many natural resources. The trees in the forests provide raw materials for lumber and pulp for paper. The lumber industry provides jobs for 10 percent of Canada’s population. Alberta and the eastern coast are known for their oil and natural gas. Minerals are exported from Canada to other places. These minerals are nickel, silver, and gold.

title: Canada's Landmarks
text:
The Rocky Mountains form a beautiful mountain range. They are in the western part of North America, through the United States and Canada. They are often called the Rockies for short. The Rockies also have many streams and rivers. These help provide water and food to animals like beavers, moose, and deer. The Rockies are home to four national parks. Many campers and tourists visit these national parks each year. The Rockies are one of Canada’s natural landmarks.

Stanley Park is in British Columbia, Canada. It was created in the year 1888. It is the third-largest urban park in North America. About eight million people visit the park each year. One man-made landmark of the park is its many totem poles. Totem poles are symbols of the Pacific Northwest Native Americans. Each tribe had its own designs and styles. Historians think the Haida, Tlingit, and Tsimshian tribes were the first to make totem poles. Families used them to help tell important stories. Totems also honored the special relationship families had with different animals. Stanley Park and its totem poles are part of Canada’s important man-made landmarks.

title: Canada: Mixed Cultures
text:
Native Americans have lived in Canada for thousands of years. The First Nations are the people of Native tribes who lived in Canada before Europeans. Over 600 different cultural groups make up the First Nations. Bannock is a type of bread that came from the First Nations people. Pemmican is another First Nations food. It is made by mixing dried meat with fat, berries, and, sometimes, nuts. Both of these foods are still eaten in Canada today. There are also over 30 different Native American languages spoken by the First Nations peoples. In Nunavut, Inuktitut and Inuinnaqtun are official languages alongside English and French.

It has only been in the past 500 years that immigrants from all over the world made Canada their home. In 1534, explorer Jacques Cartier claimed northern North America for France. French settlers followed. They called the land they settled on New France. Later, England took over New France and renamed it Canada. But French settlers and culture remained. Today, almost one-fourth of Canadians are of French ancestry. French is the official language in Quebec. There, people eat traditional French-Canadian foods. One type of food is a meat pie called tourtière. Another is called poutine. It is made with French fries and gravy.

Today, Canadians can trace their roots to almost every continent of the world. Canada has a variety of customs, religions, and languages.

title: The Seminole Tribe
text:
Florida has been home to hundreds of Native American tribes for thousands of years. One of these tribes was the Seminole Tribe. The Seminole were not one of the five ancient tribes of Florida, which included the Apalachee, Calusa, Tequesta, Timucua, and Tocobaga. The Seminole are the descendants of some of the ancient tribes of Florida, as well as the Creek, Choctaw, Muscogee, Miccosukee, Yuchis, Yamasses, and other tribes from different areas of North America.

Within a few years of Spanish exploration and colonization of Florida, thousands of Native Americans died from European diseases. Some tribes completely disappeared due to disease. Others banded together to form new tribes. As more Europeans settled in North America, Native American tribes were driven out of their ancestral homelands. Several bands of the Creek and Choctaw tribes, who historically lived in Alabama and Georgia, migrated to Florida and joined the Indigenous peoples of the area in the early 1700s.

The tribes of Florida, Alabama, and Georgia were similar to one another, but they were not the same. They spoke different languages and had their own traditions, cultures, and governments. Despite their differences, these various tribes came together to create new settlements and protect their way of life. They came together and formed a new tribe called the Seminoles. During the British period of Florida history, which lasted from 1763 to 1783, all Florida Native Americans were called “Seminoles.” This comes from the Spanish word “cimarrón,” meaning wild or runaway.

During the 1700s, the Seminole settled primarily in the panhandle and central Florida. They built large settlements around the state. The largest towns were located near present-day Micanopy, Brooksville, and Palatka, Florida. They established trading posts and traded animal hides and furs to white settlers in the area in exchange for guns, tools, cloth, and food. The Seminole also practiced agriculture. They grew corn, beans, potatoes, squash, melons, and oranges. They also raised cattle. They also gathered wild plants and fished in Florida’s abundant waterways.

Clothing was made from animal furs and skins, but the Seminole also traded with the Spanish and English for cloth to make clothing. The Seminole constructed a type of log home with roofs made from palmetto and palm leaves called a chickee. Some chickees were two stories tall, with a living area on the ground floor and sleeping quarters on the second floor.

The Seminole relied on the members of the tribe who could negotiate with Spanish and British merchants. These members of the tribe became the ruling class among the Seminole people. There was not a single chief that spoke for the whole tribe.

The population of the Seminole was relatively small compared to neighboring tribes in Florida, Georgia, and Alabama. The tribe included about 1,200 members by the late 1700s. The Seminole embraced Native Americans from many tribes searching for a new home. They also welcomed people who had escaped enslavement into their tribe. This caused tension between the Seminole and white settlers in neighboring areas.

The tensions continued to grow as more and more settlers came to Florida and took Seminole land for themselves. This would lead to a nearly 100-year struggle between the Seminole Tribe and other groups coming into Florida.

title: The First and Second Seminole Wars
text:
The Creek War: The Prequel to the Seminole Wars

Tensions between settlers and Native American tribes in Florida, Georgia, and Alabama led to armed conflict in the early 1800s. During this time, the tribes of the Creek Nation were at war with one another. This happened during the War of 1812. To gain supplies and support, some Creek tribes allied with the United States and fought alongside American forces, while others allied with the British.

The first battle of the Creek War occurred near present-day Baldwin County, Alabama. Red Stick warriors attacked settlers at Fort Mims. This attack was in response to American attacks on tribal villages. General Andrew Jackson was ordered to put down the rebellion. The Creek War ended following Jackson’s defeat of Creek forces at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend in 1814. The Creek Nation was forced to give 21 million acres of their land to the United States as a result of the war.

Many members of the Creek Nation migrated to Florida hoping to obtain help from the Spanish. This help would be short-lived as the United States sought to gain control of Florida and its people.

The First Seminole War

Tensions were at an all-time high between the United States and the majority of Native American tribes in the southeast in the early 1800s. As conflicts arose, more and more people poured into Florida looking for safety, including formerly enslaved people from plantations in Alabama and Georgia. The Seminole Tribe welcomed these people into their tribe. This caused even more tension between the Seminole and the United States. Enslavers were angry that the Seminole allowed formerly enslaved people to join their tribe. They expected the Seminole to return enslaved people back to them, but the Seminole refused. Settlers also wanted to take control of Seminole land for themselves. In 1817, American military forces attacked a Seminole village in southwest Georgia. In response, the Seminole attacked a military ship sailing on the Apalachicola River in Florida. The United States then declared war on the Seminole Tribe.

General Andrew Jackson was ordered to invade Florida and drive the Seminole out of north Florida. Jackson destroyed and captured several Seminole villages throughout East Florida. Hundreds of Seminole people retreated farther south into central Florida to get away from Jackson and his men. Jackson’s actions ended the First Seminole War in 1818.

Despite completing his mission, Jackson turned his attention to invading West Florida, where he captured the city of Pensacola. He did not have Congress’s permission to invade West Florida. Jackson felt he had to invade West Florida to prevent the Spanish from giving supplies to the Seminole and escaped formerly enslaved people.

Jackson’s actions caused many issues between the United States and Spain. After years of debating back and forth with one another, the United States and Spain signed the Adams-Onís Treaty, which ceded Florida to the United States. The Seminole Tribe was not present at the negotiations, which caused even more tension between the United States and the tribe.

The Second Seminole War

Florida officially became a territory of the United States in 1821. Almost immediately, U.S. officials and the new territorial governor of Florida encouraged the Seminole to leave the territory and move to “Indian Territory,” located in present-day Oklahoma. The Seminole refused to move. As more people settled in the Florida panhandle, they pushed the Seminole off their lands. This led to fighting between the settlers and the Seminole. In 1823, Governor William P. Duval signed the Treaty of Moultrie Creek with the Seminole Tribe. The treaty created a reservation for the tribe near present-day Ocala.

A reservation back then was a designated area away from land that American settlers wanted to claim. On the reservation, the Seminole were allowed to govern themselves and practice their culture. The Treaty of Moultrie Creek also prevented the Seminole from allowing escaped formerly enslaved people to join the tribe. The lands on the reservation that the tribe received were different from their ancestral homeland. They could not grow many of the crops they once grew, and the environment was very different from what they were used to.

In 1830, President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act. This act required any Native Americans living east of the Mississippi River to leave their land. Native Americans were forced to move to lands in Oklahoma Territory. Despite the passage of this act, the Seminole refused to leave Florida.

In 1832, U.S. government officials and delegates representing the Seminole Tribe met to discuss a new treaty called the Treaty of Payne’s Landing. The purpose of the Treaty was to convince the remaining Seminole in Florida to move west to “Indian Territory” in Oklahoma. The Seminole delegates signed the treaty, but they did not fully understand its requirements. They disagreed with the terms of the treaty and refused to follow it. Many members of the Seminole Tribe refused to leave their current reservation that had been created by the Treaty of Moultrie. However, the U.S. government was determined to have them move to Indian Territory. This disagreement was the cause of the Second Seminole War.

The first battle of the war occurred in December 1835. Seminole warriors attacked U.S. soldiers near present-day Bushnell, Florida. By January 1836, Seminole warriors destroyed almost all of the sugar plantations in Florida and freed hundreds of enslaved people. The U.S. government sent thousands of soldiers to Florida to put down the Seminole rebellion.

During this time, several Seminole members emerged to lead the tribe, including Osceola and Micanopy. They led their people in open resistance against the United States and fought for the right to live in their ancestral homelands. As more U.S. soldiers poured into Florida, the Seminole retreated farther south into the swamps and wilderness of South Florida. In 1837, Osceola was taken prisoner. He remained a prisoner until his death in 1838.

Following the death of Osceola, Seminole resistance started to decline. Hundreds of Seminole were captured and sent to reservations in the Oklahoma Territory, but many still resisted capture and forced removal.

The Second Seminole War finally came to an end on Aug. 14, 1842. The United States reached an agreement with the Seminole that remained in Florida after years of war. This agreement stated that the remaining Seminole could stay in Florida, but they were forced to move to a small area in the southwest part of the territory. The close of the Second Seminole War did not end the hostilities between the Seminole, white settlers, and U.S. government.

title: “Black Seminoles”
text:
The Seminole Tribe was one of the most diverse Native American tribes in North America. For many years, the Seminole welcomed formerly enslaved people, most of whom escaped enslavement, into their tribe. Other African members of the tribe were purchased by the Seminole but were treated as equal members of the tribe. They developed their own unique cultural customs, which were a combination of Native American, African, and American traditions. They also established their own towns and villages. These people became known as the “Black Seminoles.” They were also called Seminole Maroons, Seminole Freedmen, and Estelusti (meaning “black” in the Muskogee language) by the Seminole and other settlers in Florida.

By 1820, about 400 Black Seminoles lived in Florida. The Black Seminoles played an important role in Seminole society. Many of these people were experienced in agriculture. They helped the Seminole plant and harvest various crops. They also served as interpreters and helped members of the tribe understand American trade and cultural customs. Others served as warriors and war leaders of the tribe.

One of the most prominent leaders of the Black Seminoles was John Horse. Horse was born enslaved. He was of Spanish, African, and Native American descent. He emerged as a leader of the Seminole Tribe during the Second Seminole War. He was quickly appointed to the position of war chief of the tribe. Horse was captured in November 1837 and was sent to Indian Territory at the end of the war. He did not stay in Indian Territory for long and eventually settled in Mexico, where he created a new life for himself and many of his people.

title: Micanopy
text:
Micanopy was a revered leader and warrior among the Seminole people. He played a large role in the Second Seminole War. He was born near St. Augustine during the late 1700s. He was a member of the Alachua band of the Seminole. He inherited the role of chief from his uncle in 1819, following the First Seminole War.

Micanopy was present at the negotiations for the Treaty of Payne’s Landing. He refused to sign the treaty and move his people to Indian Territory in Oklahoma. He supported the resistance efforts of Osceola and other tribal leaders against the U.S. government. He played a crucial role in the first battle of the Second Seminole War.

Micanopy continued to resist the forced removal of the Seminole from Florida until June 1837. With more well-supplied U.S. troops coming to Florida, he realized the Seminole could not hold off the U.S. Army forever. He surrendered to American soldiers at Fort Dade, but he was quickly captured by Seminole leader Osceola. Osceola knew that if Micanopy surrendered, many other Seminole warriors would follow his example. Unfortunately, Osceola’s plan did not last long. Both men were captured by American soldiers and sent to Fort Moultrie in South Carolina.

Following his imprisonment, Micanopy agreed to leave Florida and settle in Indian Territory. He remained there until his death in 1849.

title: Osceola
text:
One of the most well-known and successful leaders of the Seminole Tribe was Osceola. Osceola was born Billy Powell in Alabama around 1804. He was a member of the Creek Tribe. He moved with his mother to West Florida following the Creek Wars. After moving to Florida, Osceola and his mother joined the Seminole Tribe. He was given the Native American name “Osceola” by his new tribe.

Osceola spoke out against the Indian Removal Act of 1830 and other treaties that would have forced the Seminole to leave Florida. He emerged as a leader during the Second Seminole War. Osceola and his men defeated American soldiers at the Battle of Withlacoochee in December 1835. Osceola continued to attack and ambush American troops until he was captured by trickery in October 1837. The U.S. Army offered a flag of truce, meaning a ceasefire or break in fighting. When Osceola met to talk about the truce, he was arrested. He was transported to and imprisoned at Fort Moultrie. Within three months of his arrest, Osceola died of malaria.

Despite his capture and death, Osceola remained a symbol of Seminole resistance in the years to come.

title: The Third Seminole War
text:
By the end of the Second Seminole War, about 500 Seminole remained in Florida. They were pushed out of their ancestral homeland and the reservation created in the Treaty of Moultrie Creek and forced to settle in southwest Florida. This area of Florida was very different from the area that the Seminole originally inhabited. This part of Florida is dominated by the Everglades. The Everglades provided protection from invading forces, but it was not an easy place to live. The soil is sandy and very wet, making it difficult to farm. There are also many animal species that are dangerous to humans. Despite these challenges, the Seminole refused to leave Florida.

The threat of Seminole attacks and rebellion kept many settlers from coming to Florida. In 1855, the U.S. government attempted to remove the tribe from Florida once and for all. The new chief of the tribe, Chief Billy Bowlegs, refused to leave. War erupted in Florida again between the United States and the Seminole Tribe. Seminole warriors raided frontier settlements and then quickly retreated to the Everglades. This tactic was very successful at first.

As troops were pulled from Florida to fight in other areas of the country, the bulk of the fighting was left to the volunteers and local militia units in Florida. These volunteer troops knew the area better and could easily locate Seminole towns and villages. Members of the tribe were captured and sent west to Oklahoma. Seminole leaders, who were forced to migrate to Indian Territory during the Second Seminole War, were brought back to Florida to convince the remaining members of the tribe to leave.

In 1858, tribal leaders convinced Billy Bowlegs to migrate to one of the reservations in Indian Territory. A small group went with him, but 300 Seminole remained in Florida by the end of the Third Seminole War. Today, the Seminole are often referred to as the “unconquered people” because they refused to leave their home and resisted forced removal. Approximately 3,000 members of the tribe live in Florida today on six different Seminole reservations. They engage in many economic activities, including tourism, agriculture, and cattle ranching. Members of the tribe work hard to preserve their tribal customs and traditions. They share these customs and traditions with one another and other people in the state.

title: Maps of Seminole Lands
text: The following map shows the land where the Seminole people and their ancestors lived before European settlers arrived in the Americas. Over time, the Seminole were forced to give up parts of their lands to the British colonies. When the United States was established, the new government continued to take more land from the Seminole. Eventually, much of the Seminole’s ancestral homeland was overrun by white settlers coming into Florida.

title: Scientific Diver: Kara Norman
text:
Kara Norman grew up in the Florida Keys. She has been diving for five years, the most recent of which have been dedicated to scientific diving. As a 15-year-old scientist, Norman dives to collect data and information that help her discover more about the ocean. This includes what problems the ocean is facing and what she can do to fix those problems. In order to become a scientific diver, she had to study many different things. These topics ranged from marine organisms and environments to the physics behind diving. Each dive brings an exciting new challenge. She has surveyed marine life, restored coral reefs, and cleaned up marine debris. She, like her fellow scientific divers, is always learning and experiencing whatever she can!

Studies Weekly: Why did you decide to become a scientific diver?

Kara Norman: Becoming a scientific diver meant that I would get to be involved in more experiences and opportunities to boost my resume and also fulfill what I love to do: help the ocean! I knew that my hard work and extensive learning would be worth the recognition, and the doors opened when I became a sci-diver.

SW: What’s the best part about your job?

KN: The best part of being a scientific diver is the work that I get to do. I use my after-school time, weekend[s], and breaks to dive and make an impact on the world. The more I learn, the larger and more impactful the projects get. I especially love meeting new people who have the same passions and interests as me.

SW: Tell me about how you safety check your equipment and air tank before a dive.

KN: Before every dive, it is crucial that I complete a safety check on my gear. Once I have everything set up, I check all of the air hoses by doing a test to see if they perform their function correctly. I go from head to toe, making sure I have everything I need for the dive and that everything is in working order. After I check my own gear out, my buddy and I follow a checklist called the GUEEDGE. GUEEDGE stands for Goal, Unified team, Environment, Exposure, Decompression obligations, Gas, and Equipment. Instead of just relying on memory, each buddy team in the group uses this written checklist to go over the details of the dive and check out each other’s gear. By having a second pair of eyes on my gear, I can be sure that anything I missed is taken care of for my safety. Additionally, it provides the opportunity for me to familiarize myself with my buddy’s gear.

title: Scientific Diver: Christopher Peters
text:
Christopher Peters began his scientific diving career in 2009. At Florida State University (FSU), he helped two scientists with their research on reef fish ecology. He graduated two years later and moved to Hawaii. In Hawaii, he worked in education and marine conservation for The Nature Conservancy. In 2017, he moved back home to Tallahassee, Florida, and started working at FSU. Today, he leads the FSU Academic Diving Program. This program helps students develop research skills while exploring different underwater environments.

Studies Weekly: Why did you decide to become a scientific diver?

Christopher Peters: When I was in college, my advisor was working on goliath grouper aggregations in South Florida. It sounded so exciting! I knew it was something I wanted to see for myself.

SW: What’s the best part about your job?

CP: I love the sense of discovery and exploration that comes with scientific diving. But my FAVORITE part about my job is that I get to work with a lot of really smart people doing a variety of research, from underwater archaeology to marine biology. They are each passionate about their work. And I get to help them work toward their goals.

SW: Tell me about how you safety check your equipment and air tank before a dive.

CP: All of our equipment must follow manufacturer specifications for service, and all of our compressed gas cylinders have to meet federal regulations to ensure safety. Everything has to be just so. Organization and preparation are the keys to a successful dive mission.

title: Scientific Diver: Ryan Yuen
text:
Ryan Yuen has been scuba diving for 12 years. Determined to become a scientific diver, he received his certification at 21. From there, he started working as a diving instructor, an assistant dive safety officer, and an aquarist. An aquarist is a person who manages the care of an aquarium. Today, he splits his time between caring for marine animals, educating, and diving. His main scientific diving project involves monitoring populations of invasive lionfish. Lionfish were accidentally introduced to the South Carolina coast. They have no natural predators in this area. So, they are able to eat other animals without being eaten themselves. This upsets the balance of the local marine ecosystem. Luckily, scientific divers like Yuen can remove lionfish from the reef if their numbers grow too large. Yuen’s team hopes to address the lionfish problem by setting up a sustainable lionfish fishery.

Studies Weekly: Why did you decide to become a scientific diver?

RY: I very much enjoyed studying animal behavior in the ocean. There is much hidden underwater that we don’t ever get to see, even when on a boat or fishing from a pier. Diving underwater is also very similar to flying in a dream. You can twist, roll, and flip like a bird through the sky. Or relax and hover above the ocean ground, watching fish below, above, and in front of you.

There are parts of the ocean that look like deserts, with sandy floors; there are mountains with tall rock structures and walls going deeper than [it] is safe [for people] to go; and [there are] forests of kelp towering from the floor all the way to the surface. As a diver, you get to fly underwater, exploring all those areas from top to bottom, and see all the animals and plants that make that area home.

SW: What’s the best part about your job?

RY: It’s a tie between education and the field diving. Field diving is an exciting adventure. Divers usually try to anticipate what sorts of things they’ll encounter, but sometimes you’ll still be surprised by a shy shark, a large ocean sunfish, or a smack of jellyfish.

Being able to share these experiences by showing and educating the public at an aquarium is just as exciting. I help to allow anyone a small window to experience the sorts of things I do in the ocean.

SW: Tell me about how you safety check your equipment and air tank before a dive.

RY: If you compare it to a car, which has a fuel gauge and a nice engine roar, or even sometimes a nice electric hum, we too have an air gauge and expect a nice breathing sound.

Scuba gear always has a scuba tank, two breathing hoses, a buoyancy vest, and an air gauge.

To safety check our gear, we turn the tank on, check on our gauge that we have enough air, smell-check that our air isn’t old, test a breathe from both hoses, and test that we can add and remove air from our buoyancy vest. We also listen carefully while doing this. We shouldn’t hear any air hissing or humming unless we’re breathing or using the buoyancy vest.

The buoyancy vest helps us to hover anywhere in the water without kicking, just like some fish can hover without swishing their fins. Fish do this naturally with their swim bladder.

title: Foreign Alliances
text:
The Continental Congress and the leaders of the American military knew that in order to defeat the British, they would need assistance from foreign allies. The first alliance the Congress hoped to create was with France. The French had long been enemies of Great Britain and were a powerful and well-supplied military force in Europe. In 1776, Benjamin Franklin was appointed by the Continental Congress to serve as an ambassador between the American and French governments.

Franklin was very popular in France and influenced French diplomats and aristocrats to support the American fight for independence. Franklin’s efforts in France proved to be successful. On Feb. 6, 1778, Franklin and representatives from the French government signed two treaties, one that allied the French with the Americans and the other that promoted trade between the two countries. These treaties changed the tide of war between the United States and Great Britain. About 12,000 French soldiers and 32,000 French sailors fought with the American military between 1778 and 1781.

Franklin was not the only American diplomat who worked tirelessly to secure foreign assistance for the new American nation. John Adams, who served as a member of the Continental Congress and helped draft the Declaration of Independence, was sent to the Netherlands to secure an alliance and funding from the Dutch government. Adams was successful and secured a large loan, which was used to stabilize the new American government.

France and the Netherlands were important allies for the new United States, but they were not the countries that formed vital alliances with the American colonists. In June 1779, Spain declared war on Great Britain and joined the fight for American independence. Spain hoped to regain control of the colonies it lost during the French and Indian War. The Spanish supplied the colonists with much-needed weapons, ammunition, clothing, and funds to buy necessary supplies. Spanish troops also fought alongside Patriot forces in Florida, Georgia, and the Carolinas.

Foreign alliances during the American Revolution ultimately helped the United States succeed in winning the war and gaining independence.

title: Bernardo de Gálvez
text:
Like the Marquis de Lafayette, Bernardo de Gálvez was inspired by the Patriot resistance to British authority in the colonies. By the age of 16, De Gálvez was an active member of the Spanish military and participated in his first battle when the Spanish invaded Portugal during the Seven Years' War (the European theater of the French and Indian War).

In 1777, De Gálvez became the governor of the Louisiana Territory. He quickly became a supporter of the Patriot cause and began to smuggle supplies to American forces. He entered military service once again when Spain declared war on Great Britain. De Gálvez was instrumental in capturing the city of Pensacola, the capital of West Florida, in 1781. This prevented the British Army and Navy from surrounding American military forces in the southern colonies and sending more troops into the other southern colonies. His efforts proved invaluable and were a contributing factor in ending the war.

title: Casimir Pulaski
text:
Another foreign soldier that had a profound impact on the American Revolution was Casimir Pulaski. Pulaski was an aristocrat from Poland. At this time in history, Polish politics were heavily influenced by the Russian monarchy. In the late 1700s, Pulaski fought against Russian control of Poland. This rebellion failed and he fled to France, where he met Benjamin Franklin, who was serving as the American ambassador to the French government.

While in France, Franklin convinced Pulaski to join the Patriot cause. In 1777, Pulaski sailed to Boston and traveled to meet George Washington, hoping to receive a military commission. He proved himself a capable soldier at the Battle of Brandywine in Pennsylvania and was given the rank of brigadier general by the Continental Congress. Washington sent Pulaski to South Carolina with a small cavalry force to assist Continental troops in the southern colonies.

In the fall of 1779, Pulaski traveled to Savannah and assisted colonial forces during the siege of the city. On the last day of the siege, he was struck down by British gunfire and died from his injuries. Pulaski is remembered as an influential figure in the fight for Polish and American independence.

title: The Economy of New Jersey
text:
Many factors contribute to a successful economy. A place’s geography, climate, and available natural resources all play a role. The availability of technology and transportation are important, as well. Of course, without people to create and consume the products, an economy would not work at all.

Historically, the economy of New Jersey was based on agriculture and manufacturing. Today, New Jersey’s economy uses a wide range of resources to run a diverse group of businesses. Some of the most important industries in New Jersey’s economy are transportation, medical research, and production of medicines. Tourism is an important economic industry, as well. Even as it grows, New Jersey’s economy still includes its traditional industries: agriculture and manufacturing.

title: Resources in New Jersey
text: Resources are materials that people use. There are all kinds of resources, including natural resources, human resources, and capital resources. New Jersey’s natural resources are varied. They include water, forests, and minerals. One of the most important natural resources in New Jersey’s economy is water, because oceans, lakes, and rivers are vital to the transportation and tourism industries. The people who live in New Jersey are the state’s human resources. They are indispensable to the state’s economy. They work in all economic sectors as researchers, laborers, farmers, and much more. The capital resources of New Jersey include a robust transportation infrastructure, a manufacturing center in the north, universities, and a thriving hospitality network.

title: Transportation
text:
The Atlantic Ocean borders New Jersey’s eastern edge. The major metropolitan area of Philadelphia is on its southern border. To the north is New York City. Because New Jersey sits between these two important cities, it is an important travel corridor on the East Coast. A travel corridor is a route people and vehicles travel to get from one place to another. Early in New Jersey’s history, people tried to develop this important travel corridor. First came roads, stagecoach services, and plank roads. Next, people organized steamboat ferries and railroads. Bridges and tunnels came last, but all of these innovations helped improve the transportation on the East Coast. In the 1950s, the New Jersey Turnpike and the Garden State Parkway were completed. These routes increased people’s ability to travel in and across the state.

In early 1921, New Jersey and New York formed an agency called the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey. The Port Authority, as it is often called, funds and builds transportation projects. These projects make travel and transportation between New Jersey and New York more efficient. The Port Authority also manages the Port Newark–Elizabeth Marine Terminal. This port is the largest container ship port for the New York Metropolitan area. It is also one of the largest ports in the U.S. All of these transportation resources and services make New Jersey an important crossroads for the eastern U.S.

title: Medical Research and Manufacturing
text:
Universities and research institutions are some of New Jersey’s most important capital resources. New Jersey has many well-known universities. The city of Princeton, New Jersey, is home to a university as well as the Institute of Advanced Study. The Institute is where Albert Einstein studied and worked during the last years of his life. The Institute is just one of the major institutions in New Jersey that has trained the researchers and students who have developed innovations that have helped improve the state’s economy.

One of these businesses that researchers support through their work is the pharmaceutical industry. The pharmaceutical industry is responsible for making medicine, vaccines, medical supplies, and much more. The New Jersey pharmaceutical industry has many international companies that help people all around the world. These institutions also conduct medical research to find solutions to all kinds of problems, ranging from knee pain to cancer.

title: Agriculture and Manufacturing
text:
The Industrial Revolution reached the United States in the late 1700s. Because New Jersey is near the port cities of New York City and Philadelphia, industrialization reached the state quickly. New Jersey’s early factories produced textiles and trains, as well as clay and steel products. These manufacturing industries grew as transportation pathways improved. Manufacturing prospered in New Jersey until the Great Depression, which began in 1929. The Depression ended as World War II’s production needs increased. New Jersey’s factories produced electronic and chemical products for the war. Today, factories, transportation, and the strategic location of New Jersey make manufacturing very successful in the state. Chemical, pharmaceutical, and food production are key manufacturing industries.

Agriculture has always played a role in New Jersey’s economy. However, as manufacturing centers grew, the availability of agricultural land decreased. The majority of modern New Jersey is now urban and industrial. Despite the reduction in agricultural land, farming still plays a large role in New Jersey’s economy. According to the New Jersey Agricultural Department, farming is a top industry. It made more than one billion dollars in 2021. New Jersey farmers grow all kinds of crops by using traditional farming techniques and greenhouses. Greenhouses help New Jersey’s farmers grow crops in the cold winter months. Among the most profitable crops in New Jersey are sod, berries, and vegetables. New Jersey’s farmers are among the top 10 producers of blueberries, cranberries, and peaches. They are also among the top 10 producers of tomatoes, bell peppers, and eggplant.

title: Tourism
text:
Tourism is an important part of the economy of New Jersey. Tourism is when people travel for fun. People travel to New Jersey from all over. New Jersey has six tourism regions, which are different from the geological regions. Each region has a unique offering for tourists. The Skylands Region is heavily wooded. People come to the area to hike the Appalachian Trail, fish, or attend the New Jersey State Fair in Sussex. The Delaware River Region’s most important physical characteristic is the Delaware River. The River is a great place for water activities like canoeing and boating. The Delaware River is also the home of the USS New Jersey, a decorated naval ship that tourists can visit.

The Southern Shore Region sits along the Atlantic Coast. It is also a very popular tourist destination because of its festive beach towns such as Cape May and Wildwood. These destinations are particularly popular in the summer when New Jersey is warm and humid. Another popular vacation destination is the Greater Atlantic City Region. Tourists visit Atlantic City for its boardwalk, spas, and casinos. People come to visit this area of New Jersey from all over the East Coast. The Shore Region, similar to the Southern Shore Region, hosts a variety of beach towns. These towns are popular summertime destinations. Towns in the Shore Region have lighthouses, roadside fruit and vegetable stands, amusement parks, and sandcastle building contests.

The last tourism region of New Jersey is the Gateway Region. This region is the southern portion of the New York Metropolitan area. From this region, tourists can easily access Manhattan, Liberty, and Ellis Islands. It also claims the title for having the most diners in the world.

title: Valley Forge, Morristown, and Hard Winters
text:
In the winter of 1777-1778, General Washington camped with the 12,000 men of the Continental Army at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania. The winter weather was unpredictable with rain, snow, sleet, cold, and freezing temperatures. Most had no shoes, and their clothes were old and torn. There was not enough food to feed the men. They were sick and hungry. Many soldiers deserted. Many more stayed and endured the trials in support of their leader and the war they were fighting.

The British Army occupied nearby Philadelphia that winter. They quartered their men in public housing and private homes at the expense of the citizens.

Washington spent much of his time writing to Congress demanding more supplies for his men. If they lost the army, the nation and independence would also be lost. Washington said of these loyal troops"

To see the men without clothes ... without blankets to lie upon, without shoes ... without a house or hut to cover them until those could be built, and submitting without a murmur, is a proof of patience and obedience which ... can scarcely be paralleled.

The men spent their days training to be soldiers. Baron Friedrich von Steuben, a military officer from the European country of Prussia (today’s Germany and Poland), provided training. Von Steuben was a seasoned soldier and military commander. He joined the Prussian Army when he was 17 years old and was an active member of the Prussian military for many years before offering his military expertise to the American colonists. As the drillmaster of Valley Forge, he taught them military skills. They learned to follow orders from an officer. They learned how to move together quickly as a fighting unit.

There would be more winters ahead for the Continental Army. In 1780, while camped at Morristown, New Jersey, the weather was far more severe. The rivers were frozen 18 feet deep. Major General John Kalb wrote in his diary on Feb. 12, 1780: “Those who have only been at Valley Forge or Middlebrook during the last two winters, but have not tasted the cruelty of this one [1780] know not what it is to suffer.”

Historians tend to focus on Valley Forge more than Morristown. The reason for this is not because of the severity and suffering. It is because the men who survived Valley Forge became a well-disciplined army. It was an army ready to fight the professional British Army and win.

title: The Northeast Region
text:
We organize the Earth into regions to help us learn about our world. A region is an area with characteristics that make it different from the land around it. Some regions are organized based on physical characteristics. These include landforms, bodies of water, climate, biomes, or natural resources. Other regions are organized by their human characteristics, like population, culture, or language.

New Jersey is part of the Northeast region of the United States. The Northeast region has 11 states. Washington D.C., the capital of the United States, is also a part of the region. Other major cities include New York City, New York; Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; Boston, Massachusetts; Baltimore, Maryland; and Newark, New Jersey. Of all the regions in the United States, the Northeast has the largest population.

Nine states in the region, including New Jersey, have coastline on the Atlantic Ocean. A coastline, sometimes called shoreline, is where the land meets the water. Some areas of the region also have coastline on two of the Great Lakes: Lake Erie and Lake Ontario. Many rivers flow through the region as well.

Water isn’t the only important geographical feature of the Northeast. The Appalachian Mountains cover large parts of the region. The area is also filled with diverse forests. The mountains and forests make good homes for white-tailed deer, black bears, foxes, hawks, woodpeckers, and many more types of wildlife.

The Northeast is also marked by human characteristics. These characteristics are the result of people’s ideas, choices, and actions as they interact with the physical environment. Human characteristics include where people live, the kinds of houses they build, the work they do, and the activities they do for fun. Human characteristics are often determined by physical characteristics of a region.

The first inhabitants of what is now the Northeast Region arrived thousands of years ago. They created the first human characteristics of the Northeast. They cut trees to build shelter, planted crops, and created rock carvings that can still be seen today. Many different tribes settled in the area over time, including the Iroquois, Mohican, and Huron tribes. Several of the regional tribes were Algonquin. This meant they spoke dialects of the Algonquin language and shared many of the same customs. The Lenni Lenape is an Algonquin tribe that historically lived in what is now New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delaware.

title: New Jersey’s Regions
text:
New Jersey is divided into four regions: Ridge and Valley, Highlands, Piedmont, and Coastal Plain. Each region has characteristics that set it apart from the surrounding area. The geography of these regions has also influenced the human characteristics of each place.

People interact with each other and with the world differently depending on the physical characteristics around them. For example, groups may choose to settle in areas with rich soil, where they can grow food. Cities may grow where there is access to waterways that make trade and travel easier. Landforms such as lakes and beaches attract tourists from other regions. The physical characteristics of New Jersey and the human characteristics have combined and changed over the centuries. Together, they form a truly unique state.

title: Ridge and Valley
text:
The northwest part of New Jersey is called the Ridge and Valley region. A ridge is a raised piece of land that is long and narrow, like a chain of mountains. In the Ridge and Valley region, the ridge is formed by the Kittatinny Mountain Range. The region also includes the Kittatinny Valley. Early Indigenous tribes settled in the valley thousands of years ago were drawn to this area by its freshwater streams and dense forests filled with wildlife. When European settlers arrived in the 1740s, they cut down trees for timber and used the land for agriculture. The region has many dairy farms and other forms of agriculture.

An important geographic feature of the Ridge and Valley region is the Delaware Water Gap. Millions of years ago, the Delaware river began to slowly cut a path through the Appalachian Mountains. The gap widened over time as wind, rain, and ice wore the rock down. Today, the gap is a popular spot for visitors. The Delaware Water Gap also helps mark the border between New Jersey and Pennsylvania.

title: Highlands
text:
The Highlands region is sometimes also called the New England Upland. It is part of a geographical feature that stretches into New York and Pennsylvania. It is similar to the Ridge and Valley in many ways. For example, both regions have valleys and raised ridges of rock. However, the ridges in the Highlands have flat tops. Also similar to the Ridge and Valley region, the Highlands has acres of forest and many farms. However, there is something important that sets the Highlands apart: water. The Highlands region is known for its many freshwater lakes.

Early European settlers were slow to settle the most northern parts of the Highlands. The region was rocky and often icy. Today, however, many people visit the region to fish and enjoy the outdoors. It is also a popular spot for vacation homes. The region isn’t just beautiful, though. It’s also important to the health of New Jersey. The Highlands supply fresh drinking water to more than half the state’s population.

title: Piedmont
text:
The Piedmont region covers only one-fifth of the state. Although it is small, the region contains almost all of New Jersey’s largest cities. In fact, New Jersey’s first European settlement, Bergen, is located in this region. It was founded in 1660 as a Dutch trading post.

Trade is an important part of the history of New Jersey, especially in the Piedmont region. In the 1600s, a group of Dutch merchants wanted to control trade in New York and New Jersey. They wanted to use the region’s ports on the Atlantic Ocean to trade goods. They also wanted to use the rivers in the area. Five of New Jersey’s major rivers cross through the Piedmont region. The Hudson, Passaic, Remapo, and Raritan rivers made it easy for traders and merchants to transport goods like furs and gold.

The same features that brought traders and merchants to New Jersey nearly 400 years ago are still important today. The Piedmont region is home to companies that create medicine, technology, toys, and much more. The region’s ports and rivers are still important for moving goods in and out of the state.

On the southern edge of the Piedmont region, dividing it from the Coastal Plain, is a fall line. A fall line is the border between a high-elevation region and a low-elevation region. When a river crosses the fall line, the water tumbles down and creates a waterfall.

title: Coastal Plain
text:
The Coastal Plain region covers the largest part of New Jersey, from the fall line to the southern tip of the state. The northwest and western part of the Coastal Plain has rich soil that is perfect for growing crops. Indigenous groups made this region their home for thousands of years before Europeans arrived. Eventually, settlers from Denmark, Sweden, and Finland began arriving in the region and building their own farms.

The southern and eastern parts of the Coastal Plain are very different from the land close to the Piedmont region. In these areas, the ground is sandy, salty, and not useful for growing agricultural crops. Early European settlers called this area the Pine Barrens. If something is barren, it means nothing will grow there. This sandy land isn’t a desert, though. Although agricultural crops do not grow well, the region is filled with large pine forests. New Jersey’s Pinelands is the largest example of this rare ecosystem in the United States.

Closer to the Atlantic coast, there are fewer pine trees and more sandy beaches. Visitors from nearby areas fill the beaches every summer. There are many resort areas near the New Jersey coastline. Resort areas focus on attracting tourists with restaurants, gift shops, entertainment, and hotels. Atlantic City and Ocean City are two popular resort areas in the Coastal Plain region.
