If an African American man did not have a job, he could be fined a large amount of money or imprisoned. These laws also prevented African Americans from serving on a jury. The 15th Amendment guaranteed the right to vote for African American men. The state and local governments attached qualification rules and fees at polling places that made voting more difficult for specific groups of people. Public buildings had separate entrances and facilities for use by African Americans and white Americans. The separation of people based on skin color included all schools, churches, and government buildings. The policy of “separate but equal” was supported by the Supreme Court until 1954.

title: Florida Constitution of 1885
text:
Reconstruction in the South officially ended in 1877. Federal troops were sent home, and new government officials were voted into office. Many southern states, including Florida, created new constitutions in order to change the laws they put in place during Reconstruction. On June 9, 1885, delegates met in Tallahassee to create a new state constitution to replace the Florida Constitution of 1868.

From June to August 1885, 63 delegates worked together to write a new state constitution. Voters approved the new constitution in November 1886. The new constitution had positive and negative impacts on Floridians. One of the positive changes supported by the 1885 constitution was the way in which government officials were chosen. All government offices were changed to elected positions, meaning it was up to the people to choose their leaders.

The Constitution of 1885 also negatively impacted many people in Florida. The new constitution created poll taxes. A poll tax required people to pay money to vote. Since Black Americans were struggling to make a living, they often did not have money to pay the poll tax. Because of this, Black Americans found it very hard to vote. The constitution also made it illegal for Black children and white children to attend the same schools. Marriage between white people and Black people was also made illegal. These laws remained in place until a new constitution was created and adopted in 1968.

title: Benjamin Franklin: Inventor
text:
Benjamin Franklin was known as the most innovative person of his time. He was always full of new ideas. He began inventing new innovations when he was a boy. Franklin wanted to be a faster swimmer, so he made two oval planks of wood with holes drilled into them. He held the planks as he swam, and while they helped him move faster, Franklin said “they fatigued the wrists.” This invention did not catch on with a wide audience, but many of his other inventions did. He invented many things, including:

a glass jar that he collected electricity in

the lightning rod

the rocking chair

the American penny

a lending library

the first fire department

a chair that changed into a footstool

a claw that allowed him to reach books on upper shelves

Have you heard of the Franklin stove? It’s a stove that Benjamin Franklin invented. In the 1700s, people heated their homes with a fireplace. Franklin came up with an idea of putting the fire into an enclosed cast-iron box, then adding a door and a way for smoke to be funneled out of the house. This allowed heat to fill the room and not go up the chimney.

On one occasion, Benjamin Franklin heard a wine glass player at a concert. This gave him an idea. He fashioned varying sizes of wine glasses on a rod that could be rotated by a foot pedal. The glasses spun in place. By adding a bit of water to the spinning glasses and resting their fingers on the rims, people could make different sounds from the instrument, which he called the glass armonica. The famous composer Mozart even wrote a piece of music for the glass armonica.

As he aged, Franklin’s sight grew worse. He could neither see long distances nor up close very well. He had to use two pairs of glasses. To overcome this problem, he invented bifocals. Bifocals have lenses made of two parts that help a person see both near and over far distances. Now Franklin could see far away and close up while wearing the same pair of glasses.

Some of Benjamin Franklin’s inventions are still being used today, hundreds of years later.

title: Lord Baltimore
text:
Cecil Calvert, Second Lord Baltimore, was an influential figure in colonial America. Calvert’s father, George Calvert, was good friends with King James of England. Because of this friendship, George Calvert became the First Lord of Baltimore. George’s goal was to establish a new colony in North America. He established the colony of Maryland, where he hoped Catholics could live in peace. Before he could realize this dream, George Calvert died.

Upon his father’s death, Cecil Calvert became the Second Lord Baltimore. He continued with the colonization of Maryland that his father began. He decided that someone from the Calvert family needed to go to Maryland to establish the colony. Although he had lived in America early on with his father and mother, Cecil Calvert never laid eyes on Maryland Colony himself. He sent his younger brother, Leonard, to America with hundreds of colonists.

The Second Lord Baltimore might not have traveled to America, but he did send instructions on how things should be done there. Leonard Calvert was told to set up laws to govern Maryland Colony. In England, Catholics were persecuted and treated unfairly. One important law for the Maryland colony allowed people to worship the way they wanted. When civil war broke out in England, Leonard Calvert had to go back to England. He later returned to Maryland in 1644, where he regained control of Maryland and retained that control until his death in 1661.

In 1661, Lord Baltimore made his son, Charles, the governor of Maryland. Charles Calvert became the third Lord Baltimore in 1675 when Cecil Calvert died. The Calvert family and their efforts in Maryland Colony helped to establish freedom of religion and tolerance for others in the Americas.

title: Martha Washington
text:
Martha Washington was America’s first First Lady. She was married to George Washington, the very first president of the United States. Before the United States became an independent country, a war was fought for freedom from Great Britain. During the American Revolution, George Washington led the Continental Army.

During the war, George and Martha were often separated, but Martha wanted to be near her husband when she could. Though the war went on for eight years, Martha traveled to be with George every winter. Martha stayed at the army camps with George. She gathered with other women who were there with their husbands. She was a hostess, making sure those who visited were cared for. She made sure they had tea and maybe an evening meal. She also organized social gatherings.

At the end of the American Revolution, the couple moved back to their home at Mount Vernon. Martha was happy to be home. However, the new country needed a leader. Martha hoped it wouldn’t be George, but he was voted to be the first president of the United States. While there wasn’t a term called “First Lady” yet, Martha had to figure out how to fulfill her role. Since she was the first-ever in this position, others who followed would look to see what she did.

Martha had her work cut out for her. She ran the household where the president of the United States lived, and. everyone wanted to meet with the president. Martha Washington hosted social gatherings with important people. Some events included members of Congress, people from other countries, and even those who were considered “common.” This meant they didn’t have any social status or a great deal of wealth.

While being in this position wasn’t what she wanted, Martha believed that her own happiness was up to her. She said, “I have learned that the greater part of our misery or unhappiness is determined not by our circumstances but by our own disposition.” Martha supported her husband for another eight years during his presidency.

title: Mary Ludwig Hays
text:
Women played an important role during the American Revolution. If a man went off to war, his wife had to take over all the duties on the farm or run the family business. Some women were spies. Some women warned of advancing enemy movements. There were also women who fought on the battlefield. They dressed as men and fought with the other troops. Some followed their husbands onto the battlefield. There they tended to the wounded, brought pitchers of water to the soldiers, and made meals.

Mary Ludwig Hays followed her husband, William, onto the battlefield. Hays helped the soldiers by bringing them pitchers of water to drink. She washed and mended their clothes and cooked for them. On June 28, 1778, Hays’s role changed.

The day was hot and humid. Some historians believe as many soldiers died from heat exhaustion that day as were killed by the enemy. All day long, Hays brought water pitchers to those who fought in the hot sun. A common nickname for women named Martha or Mary was “Molly,” so the common cry of “Molly! Pitcher!” would have been heard on the battlefield from soldiers in need of water. Hays and other women carried water and cared for the wounded. Then, the unthinkable happened. Hays’s husband died during the battle.

Mary Hays made a decision then. She took her husband’s place at the cannon and fired on the British soldiers. While many women brought water to soldiers and many were nicknamed Molly Pitcher, this Molly Pitcher was almost struck by a cannonball. Joseph Plumb Martin later wrote about Hays. He said she worked after her husband was carried from the field. At one point, an enemy cannonball struck the bottom of her dress, tearing away part of her skirts but not injuring her. In spite of this, she continued to fight.

This account, as well as many more, shows that a free country meant as much to the women in the colonies as it did to the men.

title: Mercy Otis Warren
text:
In the 1700s, women were expected to take care of their families and tend to the household chores. This means they learned to cook, sew, clean, and care for a family. Not many girls were sent to school or learned the same subjects as boys. Mercy Otis Warren came from a family that allowed her to learn more than housework. She studied with her brothers, who did get an education. Her learning benefited her so well that she became an influential writer.

Warren’s family members were involved in politics. She heard talk of what was going on in the colonies. Her father held several jobs, including being a politician. The Otis family supported the idea of a free America. They thought the colonies shouldn’t be under British rule anymore.

In 1754, Mercy Otis married James Warren. He later served in the Massachusetts state legislature. This brought politics right into her home. Warren decided to hold meetings in her home and invited her husband’s colleagues. These meetings were held to discuss what was happening politically in the country, even though politics were considered a man’s job.

Warren began to write stories and plays that expressed her opinions. Her plays criticized the British government. John and Abigail Adams and others encouraged Warren to keep writing. She wrote poems, pamphlets, and short writings that talked about how badly colonists were being treated by the British government. Her plays cast the British as villains.

Those who supported a revolution for freedom agreed with Warren’s political writings. After years of working, Warren completed her longest work about the American Revolution. It was published in 1805 and was called A History of the Rise, Progress, and Termination of the American Revolution.

Warren was one of the first women published in both fiction and nonfiction. Even though education, writing, and politics were considered things only men did, Mercy Otis Warren was successful in all three.

title: George Whitefield
text:
George Whitefield was born on Dec. 16, 1714, in Gloucester, England. In 1736, Whitefield became a deacon in the Anglican Church. He preached in England, saving money so he could meet John Wesley, a religious reformer, who had moved to America. He journeyed to Georgia to meet Wesley, and they became friends. However, Wesley and Whitefield eventually had a disagreement about religion and did not stay friends.

Once in Georgia, Whitefield didn’t stay long. He quickly returned to England. He wanted to raise money so he could set up an orphanage near Savannah, Georgia. He traveled between America and England seven times. That was almost 23,000 miles at sea!

Whitefield was a preacher, but he taught in a different way than many preachers of the time. When churches in England wouldn’t allow him to teach their members, Whitefield went outside. This was called open-air preaching. People listened to Whitefield because he was such a good public speaker. He taught people to depend on God. He said, “What! Get to heaven on your own strength? Why, you might as well try to climb to the moon on a rope of sand!”

Back in America, Whitefield taught Presbyterian congregations. He kept preaching outside. He preached where other ministers would not. Whitefield taught Native Americans, people who had little money, and people who were enslaved. He preached more than 15,000 sermons and was considered the most popular preacher of the Great Awakening. The Great Awakening lasted about a decade and helped turn many people to religion.

title: Volunteering
text:
Citizens who want to give something back to the community can volunteer, or donate their time to help others. Many people volunteer because they want to help others in need. There are many ways you can volunteer in your community.

People can volunteer for drives. Different types of drives collect things for people in need. Some volunteers help with community clean ups. Other volunteers serve in community fire departments and neighborhood watch programs. The list of volunteer jobs is very long. If you want to give back to your community, find out about where you could volunteer. Someone will really appreciate your help!

title: Essential Question
text: How can I be a participating citizen?

title: Drives
text: Drives are events that collect things for people in need. There are book, food, and blood drives. You can participate in a book drive by donating some of your books. You can participate in a food drive by donating cans or boxes of food. When you become an adult, you can participate in a blood drive. This means giving some of your blood to help people who are hurt or sick. If you don’t have items to donate to a drive, you can still donate your time to help collect things for the drive.

title: Neighborhood Programs
text:
It is the job of the police to enforce laws in the city. But community members can help too. People can form neighborhood watch groups in their area. People in these groups watch their neighborhood for problems. They tell police about bad things that happen. They get training from the police. The training helps them learn how to help keep their community safe.

Other community programs plant community gardens. These are gardens that a whole community shares. People in the community volunteer their time to help take care of the garden. The food that comes from the garden helps feed the people in the community. Do you have a community garden near you?

title: Draining the Everglades
text:
The Everglades is a wide and very shallow wetlands region that covers most of the southern tip of the Florida peninsula. It covers over 5,000 square miles of Florida in roughly half a foot of water. Grasses and bits of land stick out of the water, providing a rich ecosystem for plants and animals.

At the turn of the 20th century, the Everglades presented a new opportunity for economic growth in southern Florida. As a swamp submerged in shallow water, it provided little in the way of economic possibilities. However, the climate was good for growing certain crops. In fact, Hawaii was the only other area in the United States that had a similar tropical climate at that time. If people could drain the Everglades and expose the rich soil underneath, they could grow crops there that no one else in the continental United States could, especially sugarcane.

In 1905, the Florida State Legislature created a board to oversee the draining of the Everglades. Their main idea was to dig out a series of canals to collect water. Levees and pumping stations moved water away from low-lying areas to expose more land. They even tried planting water-needy trees to soak up water.

As the water drained or was pumped into the canals, land in other parts of the Everglades became exposed. This land could be used for farming the many crops that could survive and thrive in the warm, wet climate of southern Florida. Crops grown in the “reclaimed” land included sugarcane and various vegetables, like tomatoes, potatoes, and peppers. The canals would also provide water transportation across the shallow Everglades.

Populated areas in southern Florida also took advantage of the new land available for development. Cities like Fort Lauderdale and Miami were geographically limited by the size and scope of the Everglades. Drainage projects made more of the land available to these cities and allowed them to undergo large population booms in the 20th century. The growth and size of these cities today are directly related to the draining of the Everglades.

Lake Okeechobee is on the northern border of the Everglades. The wetlands around the lake were targeted for draining as well. These lands, in addition to providing more area to grow crops, also saw the establishment of large cattle ranches.

The drainage of the Everglades and the reclamation of lands in southern Florida provided a great economic boost to Florida. It was not always healthy for the ecosystem in southern Florida. Changing the depth and flow of water in the Everglades impacted the animals and plants that called this special area home. Floods became more frequent, as storms often caused the water to flow back into areas it had been removed from.

Animals drowned and crops were wiped out during large storms and hurricanes. The people living in these reclaimed areas also dealt with the flooding brought on by large storms or even really rainy periods, like Florida often gets. The threat became so significant to the continued existence of the Everglades that the National Park Service at this time began the discussions that would eventually make the Everglades a national park.

title: Lighting Up the Coast
text:
Florida had a growing population and a quickly developing economy as the 1800s turned to the 1900s. As activity increased in Florida, traffic on the waters in and around the state increased as well. Ships carried people and goods into and out of Florida. But the coast of Florida provided a challenge. The sandy beaches extend out just below the ocean waters. The shallow water presented a danger to ships: they could get stuck on the sandy shoals.

The U.S. Lighthouse Service began building lighthouses in Florida as soon as it became a territory. They put a light at the top of an old Spanish watchtower in St. Augustine. Despite this early lighthouse, it took some time before there were enough lighthouses in Florida to support the growing ocean traffic. Into the 1900s, lighthouses continued to be built along the coast and among the reefs of southern Florida.

In the late 1800s, tall brick lighthouses began dotting the coast at places like St. Augustine and Pensacola. These lighthouses, often over 150 feet tall, could be seen for many miles. Shorter iron lighthouses were placed near dangerous shoals and reefs, like American Shoal Light and Pacific Reef Light in the Florida Keys. While these lighthouses had a shorter visible range, they were just as crucial in protecting ships from wrecking on submerged shoals and reefs. Lighthouses helped ships arrive safely at their destinations in Florida with their passengers and cargo.

The lighthouses of Florida did more than just warn sailors of hazards. They also served as a way for sailors to figure out where they were. Each lighthouse had a unique paint job called a “daymark” that sailors could use to identify which lighthouse they were near. Each lighthouse also flashed its light in a unique pattern to help with identification. Before things like GPS, which tell you exactly where you are on the Earth, lighthouses were a reliable way for ships to confirm their location out at sea.

Even with lighthouses, sailors made mistakes or had their ships forced aground by bad weather. Although Florida’s population was growing, much of the coastline was still unpopulated. Shipwreck victims who made it ashore were not guaranteed to be in an inhabited area. Instead, they were often able to find shelter at one of several Houses of Refuge and Life Saving Stations established along the Atlantic Coast of Florida. The U.S. government set up these stations to provide assistance to sailors and passengers of ships that ran aground or wrecked. The men who lived at these stations with their families were responsible for assisting with the rescue of shipwreck victims.

Lighthouses were operated by lighthouse keepers. These were usually men (but also, sometimes, women) who were responsible for keeping the oil lantern at the top of the lighthouse burning during the night. These keepers and their families lived at the lighthouses, usually in a separate keepers’ house. Although it was the job of the keepers to maintain the light, everyone in the family pitched in because the light could not be allowed to go out during the night.

title: Thomas Edison
text:
From the late 1800s and into the 1900s, Florida became a popular vacation destination, especially for people looking to escape the cold winters of the northern United States. Travel to Florida was not cheap, so not everyone could afford the trip. Those who could found Florida to be a state that was still developing. One visitor was the inventor Thomas Edison. Famous for inventing and popularizing the first marketable electric light bulb, among over 1,000 other inventions, Edison first visited Florida in 1885. After arriving in St. Augustine, he ventured to the small town of Fort Myers.

In a town where the cattle outnumbered the people, Edison saw possibilities. By the turn of the century, he was spending almost every summer in Fort Myers. He initially promised to electrify the entire town, but work at his lab in Menlo Park, New York, kept him from following through on this promise. His home was the first to be electrified in the small Florida town. He constructed one of the first home pools in the country. It is believed that he used a type of cement he invented in the pool’s construction.

His work in his laboratory in Fort Myers brought curiosity and interest to the area. In his Florida lab, he worked on using plant fibers as light bulb filaments and finding a new source of rubber. Edison’s fondness for Florida and Fort Myers even attracted one of his famous friends to the area as well. Automotive giant Henry Ford built a home in Fort Myers as well, after accepting an invitation from Edison to visit in 1914. The town of Fort Myers honored Thomas Edison by building the Edison Bridge in 1931.

title: James Weldon Johnson
text:
James Weldon Johnson was born in Jacksonville, Florida, in 1871. After graduating from college in Atlanta, Georgia, he studied law while teaching in his hometown. In 1898, he passed the Florida Bar Exam and earned the right to practice law in the state.

Although he was driven by a desire to excel in academics, Johnson also pursued poetry and art with equal passion. He wrote the song “Lift Every Voice and Sing” with his brother, John Rosamond Johnson. The song "Lift Every Voice and Sing" has been referred to as the "Black National Anthem."

President Theodore Roosevelt appointed Johnson as consul to Venezuela before he served in Nicaragua in the same position. He continued to write during his years there. After returning to the United States, he joined the NAACP and became an important figure in the Civil Rights Movement. He eventually served as leader of the NAACP for 10 years. Following his years there, he taught and continued to write until his death in 1938.

title: Julia Tuttle
text:
Miami is unique in American history as the only major U.S. city whose founding is primarily attributed to a woman. Julia Tuttle owned much of the land upon which the modern city of Miami was built. By 1891, she had purchased Fort Dallas, the old fort that had been built there during the Seminole Wars. She began the first businesses in Miami, and her efforts brought attention and other business to the area.

Tuttle recognized the potential of the area to support a grand city. The orange groves around her home were not damaged during the hard freezes of the late 1800s. She used this fact to advertise the area to Henry Flagler. She wanted him to extend his railroads and hotels down the Atlantic coast of Florida to Miami. In the end, she was able to successfully convince him that building a railroad and hotel in Miami was a good idea. She donated land to Flagler that would begin the development of the Miami we know today.

title: Alfred du Pont
text:
By the 20th century, the du Pont family was a wealthy and influential force in American society. Alfred I. du Pont was an heir to the du Pont family gunpowder business. After many years of both success and failure with the family business, Alfred made his home in Florida. He wanted to bring success to the booming state and the growing economy there.

Du Pont’s various business ventures in Florida helped encourage growth in the state. He purchased land in the panhandle and supported the construction of roads throughout the state with his Gulf Coast Highways Association. He took advantage of the vast pine forests of Florida by building a paper mill at Port St. Joe.

He used his wealth to support Floridians as well. During the Great Depression, he hired unemployed men to clean up the public parks and streets of Jacksonville, Florida. When he died, his will called for the creation of the Nemours Foundation, a children’s hospital that continues to operate today.

title: Mary McLeod Bethune
text:
Mary McLeod Bethune was a civil rights and education leader in Florida during the early 1900s. Born in 1875 to a mother and father who were formerly enslaved, she dedicated her life to education in Florida. After securing an education in the post-Civil War South, she moved with her husband to Florida.

In 1904, she began a boarding school for young African American girls in Daytona, Florida. Her school quickly grew to educate hundreds of students. It eventually merged with an all-male school to become Bethune-Cookman College, today known as Bethune-Cookman University.

Given her status as an educational leader, Bethune served in various positions where she was able to advocate for the advancement of women in Florida and throughout the country. She organized efforts to register women to vote and served in various positions under multiple U.S. presidents.

title: Florida's Population Continues to Grow
text:
Florida was home to one of the fastest-growing populations in the country during the 20th century. In many decades of the early 1900s, the population grew between 25 and 50 percent. There were many causes for this population growth. Land was still readily available. Industries were growing and providing new economic opportunities. The Florida climate was much milder compared to the northern states.

Population growth in Florida was pushed by immigration to the state. In the early 1900s, most people moving to Florida came from nearby states like Georgia and South Carolina. As the decades progressed, more people moved from states farther away, like New York, Pennsylvania, and Ohio. By 1950, people born in these three states were the fourth-, fifth-, and sixth-biggest sources of migrants to Florida. Florida’s climate was appealing to northerners who were tired of cold and snowy winters.

Florida also saw more immigrants from outside the United States during the first half of the 20th century. Given its location, Florida is close to many islands in the Caribbean Sea. People from islands like Cuba and those in the West Indies began moving to Florida for the economic opportunities provided by the many industries that were growing in the state. Immigration from outside the United States and migration to Florida from inside the United States changed Florida’s population. By 1930, people born in Florida were outnumbered by people who had moved to Florida.

Where people lived in Florida changed during this time as well. Most Floridians lived in northern Florida at the beginning of the century. The development of southern Florida and the extension of railroads attracted more people to places like Miami, Fort Lauderdale, and Tampa. These areas of Florida were also closer to the Caribbean islands that immigrants were coming from. These people arrived and began making lives for themselves in the growing and developing cities of southern Florida.

title: Spotlights
text:
There are many organizations that serve Florida. Here are a few you can learn about:

Volunteer Firefighters

Fire departments can have full time firefighters. These people make a living fighting fires. Fire departments can also have volunteer firefighters. These people don’t work as firefighters full time. They have other jobs, but are trained to help put out fires and respond to disasters. Our country and communities are full of people who are trained and ready to jump in and help. They also help people before fires start by teaching their communities about fire prevention.

Keep Florida Beautiful

Keep Florida Beautiful is an organization that protects Florida’s environment. It is one of Florida’s largest volunteer based organizations. Volunteers for Keep Florida Beautiful help with many different projects. They help with cleaning up beaches and animal habitats. Volunteers also go to schools and teach kids about respecting the environment. Keep Florida Beautiful has a youth council. Kids on the council volunteer to help make their communities better.

Mound House

There is a place called Mound House in Fort Myers, Florida. This is a special place. Some of the first Native Americans made villages there. They were called the Calusa. They are known as the “Shell Indians” because they used shells for many things. They created mounds with these shells. There is now a museum built on top of one of the mounds. This museum teaches about how the Calusa lived. Some volunteers give tours and presentations. Other volunteers help take care of artifacts found at the site.

Habitat for Humanity

Habitat for Humanity is a program that builds homes and helps improve communities for low-income families. Habitat for Humanity does not give away homes for free. It helps people in need afford homes. It can do this with the help of donations and volunteers. Many people, clubs and businesses volunteer to help Habitat for Humanity. Families who buy the homes also help build them. Habitat for Humanity is trying to help fix the problems of poverty and homelessness.

title: New Technology Improves American Lives
text:
One major factor influencing the growth of Florida was the invention and innovation of new technologies. New transportation methods helped move people and goods faster. Improved entertainment created new industries. And a new way of cooling air made the hot Florida humidity more bearable for the many people moving into the state.

In the early 1900s, airplane technology developed quickly. Florida’s climate provided excellent conditions for flight. The first powered flight in Florida occurred in 1910, and by 1912, there was a flight school in Miami Beach. By the 1920s, passenger airline service was available between the major cities of Florida, and before long, this extended to national and international flights. People and goods could move into and out of Florida more easily as air traffic improved. The U.S. Navy used the state to establish several airfields to support their growing aviation efforts at this time. They established their first air station and flight school at Pensacola, Florida.

Cars became much more common during this time and provided more people with the freedom to explore and settle the growing state. The first automobiles arrived in Florida around 1900. The growth of cars and the expansion of Florida’s road system spurred the tourism industry in Florida. Cars provided more independence than trains, which had been the most popular way to travel to and around Florida. More freedom for tourists and residents meant that they could visit more places.

Thomas Edison began a movie-making company and produced the first production filmed in Florida. Soon, Florida was standing in for locations around the world on film. Any director wanting to film in the Caribbean or the far-off islands of the Pacific could simply use Florida’s dense tropical forests and beaches to mimic those places. Famous films like Creature from the Black Lagoon were filmed in Florida. Many credit Florida’s film industry with popularizing Florida’s sunlit beaches and partially contributing to the growing population of the state.

People moving to Florida may have loved the beaches, but Florida’s warm, humid climate could be downright miserable, especially for those used to the cooler northern weather. Doctor John Gorrie, working in Apalachicola, Florida, invented an ice-making machine that laid the groundwork for the first air conditioner. By the middle of the 1900s, the air conditioner became a household item, with most buildings in Florida providing shelter from the hottest and most humid summer days.

title: Identify Participating Citizens
text: Identify a person or organization that demonstrates volunteerism or other civic virtues. Write a paragraph to explain your choice. Create an award for them in the box.

title: Patriotic Celebrations
text: American citizens celebrate our country's history. We celebrate historic events that shape our nation. We celebrate heroic people that protect our freedoms. Americans celebrate and honor what it means to be an American in many ways.

title: Essential Question
text: Why do we celebrate patriotic holidays?

title: Independence Day
text: The Fourth of July is also called Independence Day. The Declaration of Independence was voted on and accepted on July 4, 1776. This is the day we celebrate the United States becoming a country. We honor the people who worked for freedom. Many people celebrate this holiday. People watch parades and spend time with family and friends. People also watch fireworks.

title: Martin Luther King Jr. Day
text:
Martin Luther King Jr. is an important part of American history. He believed in equal rights for all people. He taught people that everyone should be treated equally. He used words to solve problems. He was born on January 15, 1929.

On the third Monday in January, we honor and remember his work.

title: Memorial Day
text: Memorial Day is a national holiday. We celebrate Memorial Day on the last Monday of May. We honor the men and women who died while serving the country.

title: Constitution Day
text: On September 17, we celebrate the Constitution of the United States. The Constitution is the law of our land. We celebrate this document. This document reminds us that we are all people of the United States.

title: Veterans Day
text: A veteran is any person who has served in the military. November 11 is the day we honor veterans. We remember their sacrifice and service for the country. We can show our respect by flying the American flag.

title: Celebrate Freedom Week
text: During Celebrate Freedom Week, we learn about how our country was made. We learn about our country’s important documents. We celebrate our Founding Fathers. We celebrate the work they did for our country.

title: My Holiday Tradition
text: Choose your favorite patriotic holiday. Fill in the boxes with your answers about your family traditions for that holiday.

title: Florida's Tourism Industry Grows
text:
Florida experienced many changes during the late 1800s and the early 1900s. In the late 1800s, Florida experienced a period of rapid economic growth. The state’s timber, citrus, cattle, mining, shrimping, sponge diving, and wrecking industries grew rapidly. The rapid growth of these industries encouraged successful entrepreneurs, such as Henry Plant and Henry Flagler, to expand their businesses into Florida.

Plant and Flager knew that there was a lot of money to be made in Florida. They expanded their railroad empires into Florida. They bought thousands of acres of land and built luxury hotels for rich Americans to visit. Many famous Americans began to spend the winter months in Florida. Harriet Beecher Stowe, Thomas Edison, Andrew Carnegie, Henry Ford, and U.S. presidents Warren G. Harding, Grover Cleveland, and Teddy Roosevelt all came to Florida for luxury vacations. Thousands of people also came to Florida during this time to recover from illnesses. They believed Florida’s warm climate could help them overcome long periods of sickness.

The construction of reliable roadways also made overland travel much easier. In 1911, the first major highway in the state was completed, connecting Jacksonville to Miami. By the early 1920s, large stretches of highways connected most of the major cities in the state. These new highways allowed tourists to travel to Florida in their automobiles. These visitors became known as “tin-can tourists.” They traveled, slept, and ate in their cars, often eating foods from tin cans. This did not stop them from coming to Florida to enjoy the natural beauty of the state, however. This system of transportation connected Florida with the rest of the country. The construction of railroads into Florida and across the state, as well as new forms of travel, such as the automobile, caused Florida’s tourism industry to grow quickly.

Florida entrepreneurs hoped to take advantage of the growing number of tourists traveling to the state. They set up roadside attractions, created amusement parks, and built more affordable hotels and motels to accommodate all tourists. One of the first roadside attractions in the state was the Ostrich Farm in Jacksonville. Tourists could watch ostrich races, ride in carriages pulled by the ostriches, and even ride the enormous birds themselves. Jacksonville was also the home of the Dixieland Amusement Park. Visitors to the park enjoyed rides, concerts, animal exhibits, and areas to swim.

Cities like Jacksonville, Pensacola, St. Augustine, Tampa, St. Petersburg, and Miami began to build affordable hotels to accommodate the thousands of tourists who visited the cities each year. Entrepreneurs also hoped to draw tourists to Florida to take in the natural beauty of the state. Tours and wildlife shows began in South Florida, and the Everglades became a prime destination to experience “wild” Florida. People also flocked to Florida’s many beaches to swim, fish, sunbathe, and enjoy the sea air.

Florida’s tourism industry continued to grow after World War I. Thousands of “tin-can tourists” continued to pour into Florida. To accommodate these tourists, people began to set up shops, gas stations, restaurants, and travel camps along Florida’s new highways. By 1925, about 210 travel camps dotted the state. Many Floridians left their jobs to work in Florida’s booming tourism industry. Within 20 years, Florida became one of the most popular vacation destinations in the United States.

title: The Florida Land Boom of the 1920s
text:
In the first decades of the 1900s, thousands of visitors came to Florida to enjoy the natural and human-made wonders of the state. Many of these tourists decided to make Florida their permanent home. At this time, land was cheaper in Florida compared to many other areas of the country. Thousands of people bought property, packed up their belongings, and headed to Florida to start a new life. Other people came to Florida to buy land and sell it for more money to these new settlers. These entrepreneurs were known as land speculators.

Some of these land speculators were known as “binder boys.” They were hired by wealthy investors to sell the property they owned. These salespeople would accept a small down payment on the property known as a “binder.” The rest of the money had to be paid within 30 days of the purchase. Many people who bought property in Florida during this time hoped to sell it for a profit, even before the rest of the money they owed was due. This system worked for many people who were hoping to get rich quickly.

During this time, the state government passed laws to encourage more people to come to Florida. The legislature passed laws that got rid of state income and inheritance taxes. An inheritance tax is a tax that is paid on property or money that someone inherits. The legislature hoped that people would use the extra money they now had to buy land and property.

Florida entrepreneurs used this opportunity to start new businesses and new towns across the state. Davis Island, a resort community near Tampa, was established by Dave Davis in the early 1920s. Carl Fisher began to develop and build resorts along Miami Beach. He encouraged visitors to come to his resorts through his creative advertising. He even used a baby elephant to advertise his new resorts! Barron Collier, a native of Tennessee, bought thousands of acres in Southern Florida. He built hotels, banks, and transportation lines and started newspapers and telephone companies throughout South Florida. Within 10 years, Collier owned more land than anyone else in the state.

During the early 1920s, Florida was one of the fastest-growing states in the country. In 1920, the population of Florida was 968,470. By 1930, the population grew to 1,468,211. Florida’s land boom also boosted the economy of the state, but this boom was about to bust.

title: The Land Bust of the 1920s
text:
As quickly as the land boom occurred, the land bust came even faster. Many factors led to the land bust that happened in Florida during the mid-1920s. Companies could not keep up with the demand for workers and supplies. The railroad also had a difficult time shipping supplies to Florida and around the state. As a result, many railroad companies were forced to close. Without these supplies, people could not build homes or businesses. This made the land useless, and speculators struggled to sell it for the high prices they hoped to get.

Newspapers around the country reported about the issues in Florida. Many people who had wanted to buy land in Florida changed their minds. The U.S. government also accused land speculators of raising prices based on the amount they were hoping to get. This was not what was supposed to happen. The government told speculators that they had to base their prices on the value of the land, not the amount they hoped to make.

A series of natural disasters also caused land prices to drop in Florida during this time. The winter of 1925 had been very cold. Many people came to Florida during the winter to escape the cold in other areas of the country. The unusually cold winter kept tourists from coming to Florida. This winter also destroyed thousands of acres of crops. This caused a shortage of citrus fruits and vegetables in the state.

In September 1926, a large hurricane struck South Florida. It made landfall near Miami. Most of the city was flooded by the surge of water brought on by the hurricane. It caused millions of dollars worth of damage to the city and the surrounding areas. Many people were unable to rebuild their homes and decided to leave Florida. Land prices continued to fall and would not rise again until the late 1930s. The land boom of the early 1920s officially came to an end.

title: The White House
text: The White House is located in Washington, D.C. It is a symbol of the United States. It represents freedom and democracy. This is because it is where the President of the United States lives. It was first called the Executive Mansion. Then, President Theodore Roosevelt named it the White House.

title: The Declaration of Independence
text: The Declaration of Independence is a document that represents the United States. Our country was founded using this document. It explains the rights of people. It says people have the right to "life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness." These rights are very important. The writers of the Declaration believed governments should protect these rights. The Declaration of Independence declared that Great Britain was violating those rights. It officially broke our ties with Great Britain. This began the creation of our nation.

title: Essential Question
text: What are symbols that represent the United States?

title: Women’s Suffrage Movement
text:
For much of America’s history, women did not have the same rights as men. They could not vote, own their own property, or be in charge of their own money. Men, particularly white men who owned property, were the ones who had these rights. However, things started to slowly change after the Civil War and during the Industrial Revolution. As more and more factories and industries opened in cities, they needed workers to make the products and run the machinery.

Families began moving away from their rural farmlands and into the cities to find work and make more money. This opened more opportunities for women to find work outside of the home and caused a shift in their beliefs. If they held jobs like men, then why didn’t they have the same rights as men? All of these inequalities led to a powerful and important movement in the mid-1800s called the Women’s Suffrage Movement.

The Women’s Suffrage Movement in Florida

The Women’s Suffrage Movement in Florida was led by Ella C. Chamberlain. Chamberlain established the Florida Woman Suffrage Association in 1893. The state’s suffrage movement grew slowly, but suffrage groups began to form all over the state. By 1913, most major cities, including Jacksonville, Orlando, Tallahassee, and Pensacola, had their own suffrage organizations. In 1915, Zena B. Dreier became the first woman in Florida, and the South, to vote in a local election.

The 19th Amendment

WWI brought women out of the home and into the job market. In 1918, President Woodrow Wilson said, "We have made partners of the women in this war. Shall we admit them only to a partnership of suffering and sacrifice and toil and not to a partnership of right?"

In 1919, Congress passed the 19th Amendment to the Constitution, giving women the right to vote. In August 1920, enough states had ratified the amendment that it became a law. Women could now vote with men in every election. For women who wanted to make their voices heard, this decade was off to a great start!

title: The U.S. Capitol
text: The U.S. Capitol is the meeting place of the U.S. Congress. Elected representatives do the work of the people there every day. The large white dome in the center of the building makes it easy to recognize. The Capitol has many paintings, statues, and artwork to represent the history of the nation.

title: The Supreme Court Building
text: The Supreme Court building is where the Supreme Court justices work. The building has symbolic statues. Each of the statues outside the building has a name. There is a statue called Contemplation of Justice. There is a statue called Guardian of Law. There is a statue called Majesty of the Law. By knowing the names of the statues, we can begin to understand what they stand for. We can see that justice and law are the foundations of our courts. The statues are symbols that represent these important things.

title: World War I
text:
Europe in 1914

During the late 1800s and early 1900s, many European nations were competing against each other for business and trade opportunities. Germany felt that it was being blocked from trade and blamed England for its troubles. Many nations started to form alliances to protect themselves.

Germany formed the Triple Alliance with Austria-Hungary and Italy. To oppose the Triple Alliance, England, France, and Russia formed the Triple Entente. The two alliances protected their own interests. They also threatened that if one member nation was attacked, the others would join the fight. As the countries began to strengthen their borders with troops and supplies, tensions grew.

On June 28, 1914, the heir to Austria’s throne, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, and his wife were assassinated by a young member of a Serbian terrorist group called the Black Hand. The Austrian government blamed the Serbian government for the attack. A month later, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. This triggered the alliances into action to protect each other.

Russia mobilized against Austria. Germany declared war on Russia. When Germany marched through Belgium, England declared war on Germany. Once the war began, the Triple Entente became the Allies, and the Triple Alliance became the Central Powers. By Christmas in 1914, England, France, and the other Allies were bitterly fighting the Central Powers of Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, and the Ottoman Empire. America was not yet in the war, but that was about to change. The sinking of the British passenger ship the Lusitania by a German U-boat and other acts of terror brought the war to America in 1917.

The United States Declares War

President Wilson protested the sinking of the Lusitania but was treated coldly by the German government. Then, an intercepted telegram sent by Arthur Zimmermann, the German secretary of state for foreign affairs, set off a firestorm of concern in America. Zimmermann offered to help Mexico regain Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona from the United States. In exchange, Zimmerman wanted Mexico to allow Germany to set up submarine bases on the Mexican coast.

Mexico's president, Carranza, was angry with the United States. He was willing to provide submarine bases for Germany. These actions made Americans very angry with Germany. This led to the United States entering the war. President Wilson approached Congress and said that our country should fight Germany "to make the world safe for democracy." On April 6, 1917, the United States declared war on Germany. Congress then passed the draft law. Two million men were sent overseas to serve in the Navy and the American Expeditionary Force (AEF).

With the entrance of the United States, World War I became a total war. This means the war impacted every area of society. About 42,000 Floridians joined the fight and served in the U.S. Army, Navy, Marine Corps, and Coast Guard. The country’s first naval air station was established in Pensacola, Florida. Over 6,000 pilots and personnel were trained at Naval Air Station Pensacola for the war. Women also played a vital part in the war. About 200 women from Florida served as secretaries and nurses in the army and navy, including the famous author Marjorie Stoneman Douglas.

Several military camps, forts, and training facilities were established in Florida because of its mild climate and proximity to the Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of America. Pensacola, Jacksonville, Miami, Tampa, and Key West all became important centers for military training during World War I. The largest of these military bases was Camp Joseph E. Johnson in Jacksonville. During the war, over 27,000 soldiers received training at Camp Joseph E. Johnson. These soldiers were eventually sent to fight in Europe.

The United States Breaks Through German Lines

In 1918, the Germans launched five massive offensives (attacks) against Allied troops. They tore a huge hole in Allied lines and tried to reach the English Channel and Paris. American troops helped stall both drives. For about two months after this, the Allied nations began a counterattack all along the Western Front. The fighting was bitter. U.S. casualties (people who were wounded and killed) grew quickly to 100,000. Finally, the Americans broke through the German lines and began advancing on them.

All across the Western Front, Allied troops pushed back the Germans and their supporting troops. It was too much for the Central Powers. Bulgaria petitioned for peace on Sept. 29, 1918. On Oct. 30, 1918, the Ottoman Empire signed an armistice. Austria-Hungary surrendered to Italy on Nov. 3, 1918. The Allied troops finally pushed Germany into surrendering and demanded that the German Kaiser step down before a peace treaty could be signed.

The End of the War

At 11 a.m. on Nov. 11, 1918, the war ended. Troops couldn't believe that it was over. The Treaty of Versailles, drafted by England and France, laid out conditions that had to be agreed on before there would be peace. Germany had to agree to give up its colonies around the world, surrender most of its fleet and all of its artillery and heavy military equipment, and pay for the damages they caused during the war.

title: The Statue of Liberty
text: The Statue of Liberty is a symbol of freedom. It reminds us of our American beliefs. The Statue of Liberty was given to the United States by France. It represents hope for people who are seeking a better life in America.

title: The Liberty Bell
text:
The first name of the Liberty Bell was the State House Bell. The first time it was rung, it cracked. The broken bell was melted down and remade again. This happened two more times. The third time it cracked was when they rang the bell for George Washington’s birthday.

The Liberty Bell is a symbol. It represents American independence and freedom. It first rang in the tower of Independence Hall. The words “Proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof” are written on the bell.

title: The Bald Eagle
text: The bald eagle is the United States national bird. Our Founding Fathers chose the bald eagle. The bald eagle is a symbol. It represents dignity and strength.

title: America's Postwar Prosperity
text:
With the end of World War I, the United States entered the 1920s. This was an exciting, energetic period in American history. It was an age of prosperity and wealth for the nation. From 1921 to 1929, the average income per person rose from $522 to $716 a year. Americans had more money to spend and more time for entertainment.

Henry Ford’s assembly line process in factories created affordable cars. This made car ownership possible for many people. Other factories adopted this method of production. Consumers bought new products, including radios, beauty products, frozen foods, watches, clothing, and more. Homemakers were also enjoying new labor-saving devices like electric irons, toasters, washing machines, and refrigerators.

During the 1920s, Americans consumed products in mass amounts. New technologies made previously expensive items available to the middle class. Even those who did not see a rise in their incomes could join the buying spree by purchasing goods with credit. Of course, the credit wasn’t free money. It was a type of loan with interest that had to be calculated into the repayment plan.

Consumers could also make use of another new financing option: installment buying. A family could buy its first radio and pay for it over time in small monthly payments rather than all at once. Installment loans included interest, too. However, the introduction of credit and installment buying came at a cost. Overbuying without having enough money sometimes led people into debt. This would become a huge issue for many people in the years to come.

title: The Constitution of the United States of America
text:
The Constitution consists of the preamble, seven articles, and 27 amendments. The preamble explains the purpose of the document. The seven articles lay out the three branches of government and the rules for each branch. The 27 amendments guarantee the rights of the people. The amendments have been added as the nation has grown. The amendments give clarity and specific rules to the government.

Article 1: The Legislative Branch

“All legislative Powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress of the United States, which shall consist of a Senate and House of Representatives.”

Section 1 grants Congress the power to make laws in two organized parts: the Senate and the House of Representatives.

Section 2: The House of Representatives is defined. The election of members is every two years. Each member must be at least 25 years old and a citizen of the United States for at least seven years.

The number of representatives will be determined by the population “... of free persons, including those bound to Service for a term of years [indentured] and excluding Indians not taxed, three fifths of other persons.” The country will be counted every 10 years in a census. If there is a vacancy from any state, the executive branch will call for an election. The House of Representatives will have the sole power of impeachment (to challenge and investigate a member of government).

Section 3: The Senate is defined. Each state will have two elected senators to Congress for a six-year term. Each senator must be at least 30 years old and a citizen of the United States for at least nine years. The vice president of the executive branch will be president of the Senate. The vice president may only vote to break a tie. The Senate will also elect a president to serve in the absence of the vice president. The Senate will have the sole power to try all impeachments. Impeachment will not extend to more than a removal from office in the government.

Section 4: Congress will meet at least once every year on the first Monday in December.

The remaining six sections define the rules and responsibilities of each group in the system of checks and balances. They help to keep power distributed across the branches of government. There are clear directions on what Congress is forbidden to do. Only Congress can raise and spend money. Congress is responsible for the Army, Navy, Marines, Air Force, and Coast Guard. The representatives of the people are in charge of the military. The final section closes with powers forbidden to the states.

Article 2: The Executive Branch

“The executive Power shall be vested in a President of the United States of America. He shall hold his Office during the Term of four Years, and, together with the Vice President, chosen for the same Term.”

Section 1: A person who is a natural-born citizen, at least 35 years old, and a resident of the United States for 14 years can work for the executive office. Once elected, the president shall take the following oath or affirmation: "I do solemnly swear (or affirm) that I will faithfully execute the Office of President of the United States, and will to the best of my Ability, preserve, protect and defend the Constitution of the United States."

Section 2: Sets up the president as the commander-in-chief of the armed forces. It further defines the powers within the office for hiring people for government posts with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Section 3: The president is required to give information on the state of the Union to Congress.

Section 4: "The President, Vice President, and all civil Officers of the United States shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of, Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors."

Article 3: The Judiciary

“The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.”

As established under Article 2, the president will nominate a judge for the judicial branch. The nominee must then be confirmed through the Senate.

Section 2: The office of the judiciary will extend to all cases of law arising under the Constitution. It also covers the laws of the United States and all controversies between the state, citizens and states, and citizens and citizens.

Section 3: Treason against the United States is defined. Treason is giving aid and comfort to enemies or waging war against the United States.

title: Relations of the States to Each Other
text:
Article 4 establishes relations between the states. It also defines the state's relations with the federal government.

“The Citizens of each State shall be entitled to all Privileges and Immunities of Citizens in the several States.”

Section 1: All legal documents in one state must be accepted by the other states.

Section 2: Criminals must be returned to their state of citizenship by state law enforcement agencies. Any person held to service or labor who escapes to another state will be delivered to the person who claims their labor.

Section 3: Admission of new states to the Union is held in Congress. Congress can change any state boundaries when deemed necessary. State constitutions are to be a representative democracy like the federal government. The states will be protected by the national government against invasion or violence within the state.

title: Amending the Constitution
text:
“The Congress, whenever two thirds of both Houses shall deem it necessary, shall propose Amendments to this Constitution.”

Article 5: Unique to the United States government, this article defines the process for changing the Constitution. Other governments have to create an entirely new government or Constitution. This was usually done through much conflict.

Any amendments to the Constitution must have the people involved in writing, reviewing, and ratification. Since 1789, 33 amendments have been introduced over the years, but only 27 have been ratified.

One amendment that failed to be ratified was the “Titles of nobility.” This amendment would have taken U.S. citizenship from any American who accepted a title of nobility from a foreign country.

The last amendment that was introduced was in 1985. The District of Columbia would have been treated as a state. The ratification period ended without the required votes for passage.

title: The Supreme Law of the Land
text:
Article 6: This article provided for the peaceful transfer of power from the Articles of Confederation to the new federal government.

The new government honored all debts and contracts made by the Confederation Congress. This also established the Constitution as the “Supreme Law of the Land.” No state law could go against the Constitution. This article established the strong federal government wanted by the Federalists. There were still many parts of the country that supported states' rights. All disagreements went to the Supreme Court to be resolved.

“The Senators and Representatives ... and the Members of the several State Legislatures, and all executive and judicial Officers, both of the United States and of the several States, shall be bound by Oath or Affirmation, to support this Constitution; but no religious Test shall ever be required as a Qualification to any Office or public Trust under the United States.”

title: Ratification Process
text:
The final article of the Constitution defines the process for ratification.

Nine of the 13 states had to vote to approve the Constitution to create the new government. Each state held conventions where each part of the document was discussed. The Federalists and Anti-federalists practiced civil discourse. Civil discourse is when each side tries to persuade people to their views and beliefs in a respectful and open manner. There was concern about the absence of a bill of rights to protect individual rights. Compromises and promises were made to get the Constitution ratified by nine states.

The states and the dates of ratification are listed here, in order of ratification:

Delaware: Dec. 7, 1787

Pennsylvania: Dec. 12, 1787

New Jersey: Dec. 18, 1787

Georgia: Jan. 2, 1788

Connecticut: Jan. 9, 1788

Massachusetts: Feb. 6, 1788

Maryland: April 28, 1788

South Carolina: May 23, 1788

New Hampshire: June 21, 1788

title: The First European Settlers
text:
About 500 years ago, a ship sailed into what is now called Sandy Hook Bay. The ship carried an Italian explorer named Giovanni da Verrazzano. Members of the Lenni Lenape tribe rowed out in canoes to meet the boat. This meeting, which took place in 1524, was the first recorded encounter between the Lenape and Europeans. It was also the first known time a European laid eyes on New Jersey. Although da Verrazzano mapped the coast of New Jersey, he did not explore past the shore.

Dutch Settlement

In 1609, an explorer named Henry Hudson reached the coast of Newfoundland in Canada. He was working for the Dutch East India Company. The word “Dutch” describes people who live in the Netherlands. The Dutch wanted Hudson to find a way to Asia. When Hudson reached Canada, he sailed his ship south along the northeastern coast of the United States. In time, he reached the mouth of what is now called the Hudson River. He traveled up the river until it became too shallow. Then, he turned around and returned to the Netherlands to report what he had found.

At the time, France was building colonies in North America to get fur and tobacco to send back to Europe. The Dutch wanted to do the same. They claimed the land and started a colony called New Netherland. The colony included areas of New Jersey, New York, Delaware, and Connecticut. The Dutch sent traders to begin trading with the local Indigenous tribes. In New Jersey, this included the Lenni Lenape people.

Over the next decades, more Dutch settlers arrived, ready to build communities. The first permanent European settlement in New Jersey was built by the Dutch in 1660. It was called Bergen and is now part of Jersey City.

Swedish Settlement

The Dutch weren’t the only people interested in the land we now call New Jersey. Sweden created its only colony in North America along the lower part of the Delaware River. The colony began in 1638, after a Swedish ship led by Peter Minuit landed near Wilmington, Delaware.

Years before, Peter Minuit had been the director of the New Netherland colony. However, he had been fired. After he was fired, Minuit went to the Swedish government and suggested they build a colony in North America. The Swedes wanted to participate in the fur trade, too, so they agreed and sent Minuit back to North America.

The place where the Swedish ship landed had already been claimed by the Dutch. However, Minuit knew that the Dutch didn’t have strong settlements nearby. The Swedes established a colony that included pieces of Delaware, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and southwestern New Jersey. They called their colony New Sweden. Hundreds of people from the Swedish empire settled in the area.

Dutch and Swedish settlers fought for control of land and trade in New Jersey. Then, in 1655, a Dutch army marched into New Sweden and claimed the land as part of New Netherland.

title: The Effect of Colonization
text:
In 1623, the Dutch government asked the Dutch West India Company to make New Netherland an official settlement. At the time, the land only had a few trading posts. The government wanted more Dutch people to settle there and claim the land.

The area the Dutch wanted to settle was already occupied by Indigenous tribes, including the Mohican, Mohawk, and Lenape peoples. The Dutch West India Company made a rule that settlers had to buy the land they wanted to settle. The Dutch believed this gave them official ownership of the land. When Peter Minuit started the New Sweden colony, he also believed that purchasing the land gave settlers the right to own it. However, the Indigenous people who lived in the region didn’t think land could be owned. Land ownership was a European idea. Many of the tribes migrated to different areas depending on the season. According to their traditions, they didn’t own the land they lived on, just like they didn’t own the air they breathed.

Europeans bought land from the local tribes with items like cloth, cookware, and tools. To the European settlers, this meant the Indigenous people would leave the land because it no longer belonged to them. However, Indigenous people may not have understood what the settlers expected. This misunderstanding led to many conflicts, some of which were violent. Hundreds of years later, people still question whether these trades were fair.

Dutch colonists also brought enslaved Africans to New Netherland in the early 1600s. Enslavement of Africans and Black people continued in New Jersey until slavery was abolished in 1865.

title: A Changing Colony
text:
In 1664, a fleet of English ships sailed into New York Harbor and took control over New Netherland. The king of England, Charles II, gave the land between New England and what is now Maryland to his brother James, the Duke of York. James gave the land between the Hudson River and the Delaware River to his friends Sir George Carteret and Lord Berkeley. They called the land the Province of New Jersey. A province is a part of a country with its own government.

People from New York and New England began traveling down to New Jersey. They settled along the rivers of the Piedmont region and built farms. Other settlers came from Europe to settle in New Jersey.

In 1673, Lord Berkeley sold his land in western New Jersey to English Quakers. Quakers are members of a religious group that began in England in the 1650s. They faced religious discrimination and persecution because of their beliefs. They wanted to come to a place where they could worship freely. The Quakers who purchased the land immigrated to New Jersey and settled near the Delaware River.

After Lord Berkeley sold his portion of land, New Jersey split into two provinces: East Jersey and West Jersey. One of the first governors of East Jersey, Robert Barclay, was Scottish. He encouraged people to immigrate from Scotland to East Jersey, where land was inexpensive. Because of this, East Jersey had many Scottish immigrants. Perth Amboy, which was named after a city in Scotland, became the capital of East Jersey. Burlington, where many English Quakers lived, became the capital of West Jersey. Leaders couldn’t agree where the exact border was between the two provinces, which led to conflicts and frustration. The two provinces were united again in 1702 under Governor Edward Hyde.

New Jersey went through some more changes over the next few decades. Although the province had its own governor after 1702, it was put under the rule of New York’s governor in 1708. In 1738, New Jersey had its own separate governor again. After the American Revolution, ownership of New Jersey passed to the United States of America. New Jersey officially became a state in 1787, when leaders approved the United States Constitution. It was the third state to join the United States.

title: The Bill of Rights
text:
When New Jersey became an English colony, Sir George Carteret and Lord Berkeley gave the European settlers political and religious freedom. Many other colonies had dominant religions. For example, most of the settlers in New England were Puritans. In Pennsylvania, many were Quakers. In Virginia, most colonists were Protestants. However, New Jersey did not have an established religion. As a result, it quickly became much more religiously diverse than other colonies. The people of New Jersey also had diverse heritage, because waves of immigrants came from different countries and regions of North America.

Because freedom was so important to the European settlers, it’s no surprise that New Jersey was the first state to sign the Bill of Rights in 1791. The Bill of Rights is a set of 10 amendments to the United States Constitution. It guarantees important rights such as freedom of religion and the right to free speech.

title: Governor William Livingston
text:
Over time, the British colonies in North America became unhappy with British rule. They felt like the British government wasn’t listening to their needs. The colonies were eager for independence. New Jersey elected five representatives to participate in the First Continental Congress in 1774. The Continental Congress governed the colonies during the American Revolution. During the first meeting of the Congress in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, leaders discussed how the colonies would rebel against the British government. The Continental Congress included many important founders of the United States, including George Washington. One of New Jersey’s representatives was named William Livingston.

William Livingston was born in 1723 in Albany, New York. When he was around 14 years old, he started college at Yale University. When he was 18, he began studying law. While he worked as a lawyer in New York, Livingston became involved in politics. He founded a weekly publication called the Independent Reflector where he shared his political opinions. He also served on the New York General Assembly, or legislature, from 1768 to 1769.

In 1772, Livingston moved to New Jersey. He built a house in Union, New Jersey, for his large family. They called the house Liberty Hall. Then, in 1774, Livingston was elected to join the Continental Congress.

Not everyone in New Jersey wanted to rebel against the British. In fact, the governor of New Jersey, William Franklin, was loyal to the king. He had been chosen by the king to serve as governor. But most of New Jersey wanted change. Franklin was arrested in January 1776 for opposing the revolution.

Later that year, on July 2, 1776, political leaders signed the New Jersey Constitution. Two days later, the colonies declared their independence from Britain. According to the New Jersey Constitution, New Jersey voters could elect government officials. They chose William Livingston as New Jersey’s first elected governor. The Revolutionary War was still raging, and British troops tried to kidnap or hurt Livingston many times. However, he and his family survived the danger.

The Revolutionary War ended in 1783, but there was still work to be done. In 1787, Livingston joined the United States Constitutional Convention. He helped create the nation’s constitution and was one of 39 people who signed the document.

Livingston served as Governor of New Jersey from 1776 until his death in 1790.

title: Continuing Immigration
text:
After the American Revolution, New Jersey continued to grow. People began building cloth mills and other factories along the rivers in the Piedmont region. Farmers planted crops in regions of rich, fertile soil. Immigrants were drawn by the opportunities for work and land ownership. Many new arrivals came from Germany and the northern part of Ireland. Immigrants also continued coming down to New Jersey from New England and New York.

By the early 1800s, New Jersey’s growth slowed. Most of the farmland was already claimed, so many immigrants—and even some New Jersey natives—began moving west into Pennsylvania and Ohio. Then, things in the United States began to change.

In the mid-1800s, new technology changed the way people made things. Instead of making objects by hand, people could produce more objects in less time in a factory. Factories were built throughout the Northeast Region. New York and New Jersey were especially popular because they had access to rivers and ports that made it easy to ship goods and materials.

More factories meant more jobs, and immigrants began pouring into New Jersey again. Many of the immigrants during this period were from Ireland. In the early and mid-1800s, Ireland faced famine. A famine is when people cannot get enough food for months or even years. Many Irish people left Europe hoping for a better life in the United States.

One of the causes of the Irish famine was a mold that made potatoes inedible. The disease was called the potato blight. Most Irish farmers worked on land that belonged to English lords. They grew all kinds of crops, like wheat, barley, and vegetables. However, those crops belonged to the English lords. The farmers grew potatoes for themselves. When the potato blight came, the farmers could no longer feed themselves or their families.

In the late 1800s, immigrants began coming from countries like Italy, Hungary, Poland, and Greece. Many of these immigrants faced poverty, discrimination, and violence in their home countries. Unfortunately, life was often difficult in the United States, too. Although there were many jobs available, immigrants were often discriminated against.

In 1892, Ellis Island opened at the mouth of the Hudson River, between New York and New Jersey. Ellis Island was where many immigrants first arrived in the United States. There, immigrants went through long inspections to determine whether they could enter the country. After they were allowed to come into the country, many stayed in New York and New Jersey, where they got jobs working at factories. These waves of immigration made New Jersey one of the most diverse states in the nation. Today, it continues to be one of the most diverse states in the country.

title: The Wizard of Menlo Park
text:
Technology fascinated Thomas Edison from an early age. He began conducting science experiments when he was only 12, living in Michigan. He patented his first invention, an electric vote counter, when he was 22 years old. A patent is an official document that gives an inventor the right to be the only person to make their invention. That first patent was only the beginning of Edison’s inventions.

In 1871, Edison built a laboratory in an empty factory building in Newark, New Jersey. He hired assistants to help him work on new inventions and improve existing technology. Soon, Edison decided he needed more space for equipment. He purchased land in Menlo Park, New Jersey, and built a much larger laboratory. It was the first lab of its kind. Edison designed the lab to include everything he and his assistants would need. There was a main facility for building and conducting experiments. There were also buildings for a carpenter, blacksmith, glassmaker, and more. Today, many research and development laboratories still use the all-in-one design Edison created at Menlo Park.

One of Edison’s first inventions at Menlo Park was the phonograph in 1877. The phonograph was the first machine to record sound. The voice recording Edison made was the poem “Mary Had a Little Lamb.” People began calling Edison “The Wizard of Menlo Park” because of his incredible inventions.

In 1878, Edison turned his attention to electric lights. The first incandescent light bulb had already been invented by a British scientist in 1840, but it was too expensive for regular use. Incandescent light bulbs work by heating a wire until it produces light. Edison created many, many light bulbs that didn’t work. Many of the materials that could produce light burned too quickly. But Edison didn’t give up. Neither did his assistants at Menlo Park. After a lot of hard work, Edison and his assistants invented the first long-lasting electric light bulb. On New Year’s Eve of 1879, Christie Street in Menlo Park became one of the first streets in the world to be lit by electric lights. In 1883, Roselle, New Jersey became the first town to be lit by electric light using overhead wires.

In 1887, Edison moved his laboratory to West Orange, New Jersey. There, he continued to patent new inventions. One important invention was the motion picture camera, which Edison called the Kinetograph. Edison came up with the design for the camera, then gave the design to an assistant named William Dickson. Dickson conducted research and completed the invention. The Kinetograph was first shown to the public in 1891.
