Thomas Edison made New Jersey home to some of the most important inventions in modern history. He patented more than 1,000 inventions in his lifetime. Many were created by his hardworking assistants. Without the inventions created at Edison’s laboratories, the world would not be the same.

title: Grover Cleveland
text:
New Jersey was home to both the 22nd president and the 24th president of the United States. In fact, the same person served as both presidents! As of 2022, Grover Cleveland is the only U.S. president to serve a nonconsecutive term. Nonconsecutive means the two terms were not in sequence, or back-to-back.

Grover Cleveland was born in 1837 in Caldwell, New Jersey. Not long after he was born, Cleveland moved with his family to New York. In 1859, he became a lawyer in Buffalo, New York. He used the money he earned to support his mother and sisters.

When Cleveland was 33 years old, he was elected to his first political position. He became the Sheriff of Erie County, New York. As the sheriff, Cleveland was responsible for enforcing laws. After his two-year term as sheriff, he returned to work as a lawyer.

In 1881, Cleveland ran for Mayor of Buffalo and won. This began a quick rise through political offices. He became the mayor in January 1882, and started running for governor of New York later that year. He won that election, as well, and began serving as governor of New York in 1883. The next year, in 1884, he began his campaign to become the 22nd President of the United States. He won the vote in 20 states, including the state where he was born: New Jersey. Grover Cleveland won the election and began serving as president in 1885. In only four years, he went from being a mayor to leading the United States.

Grover Cleveland is the only president to have his wedding in the White House. He was unmarried when he entered the office, but met a woman named Frances Folsom later that year. The two married in 1886 in the Blue Room at the White House.

In 1888, Cleveland ran for president again. The election was very close, but Cleveland lost to Benjamin Harrison. He ran against Harrison again in 1892 and won, making history as the 24th president.

After his second presidency, Grover Cleveland retired to Princeton, New Jersey. He died in 1907 and was buried in Princeton.

title: Count Basie
text:
The Harlem Renaissance was a period of social and artistic expression that began in Black communities during the 1920s. The movement shone a light on African Americans and their history, heritage, and talents. Although the renaissance was centered in the Harlem neighborhood of New York City, its influence spread around the world.

One of the most popular developments during the Harlem Renaissance was jazz. Jazz is a style of music that originated in New Orleans in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is a mix of African American musical traditions. One important jazz artist was William “Count” Basie.

Count Basie was born in Red Bank, New Jersey in 1904. Both of his parents played instruments, and his mother gave him his first piano lessons. Basie began playing the piano at local shows and dances, as well as events at the Jersey Shore. However, he wanted to travel outside of his home state. Around 1920, he followed the pull toward Harlem.

In Harlem, Basie met up with a friend who introduced him to other musicians. Basie toured the country with other musical acts, including the famous trumpeter Louis Armstrong. Basie joined a few jazz bands, and by 1935 he was the leader of his own band called Barons of Rhythm.

At the time, there were two popular bandleaders named Earl Hines and Duke Ellington. “Earl” and “Duke” are both royal titles. An announcer joked that Basie, who went by Bill, should change his name to a royal title, too. The announcer introduced him as "Count" Basie. The nickname stuck for the rest of his life.

In 1937, Basie changed the name of his band to the Count Basie Orchestra. Through the years, the orchestra had many members, but it was always led by Basie on the piano. Other members of the orchestra played the trumpet, saxophone, trombone, drums, bass, and more. Basie and his orchestra played with many famous singers and recorded many albums. Count Basie died in 1984, but his legacy lives on. The Count Basie Orchestra continues to perform today.

title: John T. Dorrance
text:
Some things are such a normal part of life, we might not think about what life was like without them. One of those things is canned soup. Cans of soup can sit on a shelf for months, or even years before they’re opened and used. Before a determined chemist discovered a new way to make soup, those familiar cans didn’t exist.

John T. Dorrance was related to the president of a company located in Camden, New Jersey. This company preserved fruits and vegetables. Canned produce lasts much longer than fresh produce. Dorrance wanted to add soup to the other products the company sold. Shoppers could already buy ready-to-eat soup in jars, but the jars were heavy and expensive, and the soup spoiled quickly. People could also buy bouillon cubes, which were cubes of dried, concentrated soup, but they didn’t have much flavor. Dorrance wanted to find a way to put soup into smaller packaging that was more affordable. He also wanted to make the soup something people would actually want to eat.

Dorrance was a chemist. This meant he studied the composition of things. He knew that soup was mostly water, and that water was heavy. He used his knowledge to reduce the water content of soup without losing flavor. One of his first flavors used local New Jersey beefsteak tomatoes. He sold his soups door-to-door. Soon, the popularity of his condensed soups spread across the country. Store shelves and cupboards were never the same again.

title: Alice Stokes Paul
text:
Alice Stokes Paul was born in Mount Laurel, New Jersey in 1885, the same year Grover Cleveland became president of the United States. However, Paul’s mother, Tacie Paul, had not voted for Cleveland. In fact, Tacie Paul had never voted for a president at all. Neither had her mother or her grandmother. Women were not allowed to vote in federal elections when Alice Stokes Paul was born. She devoted her life to fighting for women’s rights, including the right to vote.

Alice Paul’s mother, Tacie, was a suffragette. Suffragettes were women who worked for women's right to vote. This belief was known as suffrage. When Paul was young, her mother brought her to meetings of the National American Woman Suffrage Association (NAWSA). There, she learned about the fight for the right to vote.

Paul gained a remarkable education. She earned a Master of Arts degree from the University of Pennsylvania. Then she moved to England to continue studying. She also became involved in women’s suffrage in the United Kingdom. She was arrested for her participation in suffrage demonstrations and even served time in jail.

In 1910, Paul returned to the University of Pennsylvania, where she earned her PhD. She rejoined NAWSA, determined to fight for an amendment to the United States Constitution that allowed women the right to vote. However, NAWSA wanted to focus on winning the right to vote in individual states first. Paul created her own group, the National Woman’s Party (NWP). In January 1917, the NWP held the first political protest at the White House. The protest lasted for more than two years. Women dressed in white stood silently outside the White House six days a week. They held signs and banners, demanding the right to vote. These women were called the Silent Sentinels. Around 2,000 women participated between January 1917 and June 1919. Although the protest was peaceful and legal, many of the women faced threats and violence. Nearly 500 were arrested. Many, including Alice Paul, went to jail for a time.

Finally, the suffragettes’ message got through. In 1920, the 19th Amendment passed, allowing women to vote in federal elections. Paul celebrated, but knew her work wasn’t over. She continued to fight for women’s rights for the rest of her life. Today, grateful voters still leave notes on her grave in Moorestown, New Jersey.

title: Dorothea Lange
text:
In 1929, the United States economy crumbled. During the 1920s, people had purchased shares of stock, which is partial ownership of a company. Stock prices rose, and people borrowed money so they could buy more stock. Then, the prices of stocks fell. People lost the money they’d spent on stocks. They couldn’t pay banks back for their loans. Banks ran out of money. Businesses closed. People lost their homes, farms, and jobs. This period was called the Great Depression. During the Great Depression, reports and news articles were filled with facts and numbers. People wrote about the lack of jobs and the difficulties people faced. The accounts were important. But sometimes, photographs tell a story that can go deeper than words.

Dorothea Lange was born in Hoboken, New Jersey in 1895. When she was 12, she moved with her mother and her brother to New York City. After high school, Lange attended Columbia University, where she studied photography.

In 1918, Lange moved to San Francisco, where she married a painter. She supported her family, including two children, by taking portraits of wealthy residents of San Francisco. Then, the Great Depression came. As the world changed, so did Lange’s photography.

People from the southern and midwestern U.S. began migrating west into California. Lange started traveling through California, photographing the people coming into the state.

Lange’s second husband studied the economy. Together, they traveled through the country, taking photographs and writing about what they found. They worked for the Farm Security Administration. This was a government agency that worked to help poor farmers. They also worked for the Resettlement Administration. This was an agency that helped struggling families move to new communities. During her work, Lange took some of the most important pictures of the Great Depression. Her photographs brought attention to the difficulties people were facing. Her photographs brought human faces to issues such as homelessness and starvation.

Years later, during World War II, Lange continued her work. She photographed the Japanese Americans forced into internment camps in California. For the rest of her life, Lange continued documenting the lives of people who might have otherwise been forgotten.

title: Buzz Aldrin
text:
Edwin Aldrin Jr. was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey in 1930. When he was young, his sister mispronounced the word “brother” as “buzzer” when she talked about him. The nickname "Buzz" stuck.

Aldrin’s trip to the moon began in school. After he graduated from high school, he attended West Point, a training academy for the Army. He studied mechanical engineering, which is the study of how things are made and how machines work. After he graduated in 1951, he joined the United States Air Force. He learned to fly fighter planes, which he flew in combat missions during the Korean War.

In 1959, while still in the Air Force, Aldrin enrolled in the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). He studied astronautics, which is the study of traveling into space. Two years after Aldrin began his studies, the first human entered space. Yuri Gagarin, from the Soviet Union, orbited the Earth in 1961. The next year, in 1962, John Glenn became the first astronaut from the United States to orbit the Earth. Aldrin wanted to join these space explorers. He graduated with a doctorate degree in 1963. Later that year, he was selected to join the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) as an astronaut.

On November 11, 1966, Buzz Aldrin and Jim Lovell broke through the Earth’s atmosphere inside the Gemini 12 spacecraft. While the craft orbited the Earth, Aldrin stepped out the door and completed the first successful spacewalk. After Aldrin and Lovell returned to Earth, Aldrin continued his training.

Then, on July 16, 1969, Buzz Aldrin, Neil Armstrong, and Michael Collins climbed into the Apollo 11 spacecraft and launched into the sky. Four days later, Aldrin piloted the Lunar Module Eagle onto the surface of the moon. Armstrong, who was also in the Eagle, took the first step on the moon. Armstrong’s first words on the moon were, “One small step for man. One giant leap for mankind.” Nineteen minutes later, Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon. His first words were, “Beautiful view.”

Aldrin has never returned to the moon, but he has continued to speak about the importance of space exploration.

text:

title: Holidays Help Us Remember
text:
How can someone learn about a country’s history? One way is to learn about its patriotic celebrations. We honor people and events in United States history through celebrations and holidays. We also build monuments and memorials to recognize their contributions.

National monuments and memorials are symbols of our nation. They were built to remind us of important events and people in our history. Monuments and memorials teach us why these people are important to America. Knowing the history of our country helps to unite us as citizens.

title: Essential Question
text: What do we celebrate on patriotic holidays?

title: Martin Luther King Jr. Day
text: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. is an important part of American history. He believed in equal rights for all people. He taught that everyone should be treated equally. His words guided people to solve problems peacefully. On the third Monday in January, we honor and remember his work. It’s called Martin Luther King Jr. Day. The Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial is in Washington, D.C. It is a symbol of King’s ideals and sacrifice.

title: Memorial Day and Veterans Day
text: We honor those who have served in the armed forces on Veterans Day. We honor military members who died serving our country on Memorial Day. These veterans are examples of courage and sacrifice. We can go to Arlington Cemetery and the Vietnam Veterans Memorial to honor those who served our country. Other memorials include the World War II Memorial and the Iwo Jima Monument. The Korean War Memorial, and the Pearl Harbor Memorial are also memorials.

title: Independence Day
text: The Fourth of July is also called Independence Day. The Declaration of Independence was voted on and accepted on July 4, 1776. This is the day we celebrate the United States becoming a country. We honor the people who worked for freedom. Many people celebrate this holiday. People watch parades and spend time with family and friends. People also watch fireworks.

title: Constitution Day
text: On Sept. 17, 1787, the U.S. Constitution was finished. Today, many people celebrate Constitution Day on September 17. Some people celebrate by memorizing the Preamble of the Constitution and reciting it together. Others sing the national anthem or dress in red, white, and blue. At some schools, students play games, act out plays, or write reports that help them learn more about the Constitution.

title: Celebrate Freedom Week
text:
During Celebrate Freedom Week we celebrate freedom. We also learn about how our country was created. This holiday reminds us to think about the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. Celebrate Freedom Week helps us recognize the contributions and sacrifices made by our veterans and Founders. It also reminds us of our freedoms and rights as guaranteed in the Constitution.

Mark the things you would like to do to celebrate your American freedom and add some ideas of your own!

Visit or talk to a soldier

Study the Declaration of Independence

Recite part of the Constitution

Sing or listen to a patriotic song

Look at primary source pictures of our freedom documents

Learn about a Founding Father

Draw a picture or make a poster about celebrating freedom

Wear red, white, and blue clothing

title: Patriot Day
text: We honor Patriot Day. It is on September 11. We remember the attacks that occurred on Sept. 11, 2001. We honor the people who were affected. We remember the heroes. It is a day to reflect on our freedom.

title: American Founders Month
text: We celebrate American Founders’ Month. We learn about the difficulties of creating a new nation. We learn about the founders of the United States. We study the history of the United States and its leaders. We study the important documents of the United States.

title: Medal of Honor Day
text: In March, we celebrate Medal of Honor Day. This day honors people in the military who received the Medal of Honor. The Medal of Honor is the highest military award for valor in the United States. Valor means courage and bravery. The award was created in 1861.

title: Physical and Human Features of the Caribbean
text:
The Caribbean is south and east of the continental United States. This region has 26 island nations. There are lakes and rivers on many of these islands. There are also mountains, volcanoes, coral reefs, and rainforests in the Caribbean. The climate is tropical and mild. Tourists come to visit the region year-round to see the beautiful physical features there.

The population of the Caribbean varies greatly depending on the place. It ranges from over 10 million people in Cuba to under 5,000 people in Montserrat. Most of the countries in the Caribbean manufacture and process oil and agricultural goods for other countries. Many of the people living on the islands work in the tourism industry.

title: Essential Question
text: How can I describe the Caribbean?

title: Climate of the Caribbean
text:
The Caribbean has a mostly tropical climate. Tropical climates are warm, wet, and humid. The average temperature stays almost the same all year. In most places in the Caribbean, there is a dry season and a wet season. The dry months are usually from February to May, and June to November is the wet season. Hurricanes can happen during the wet season.

The temperatures vary in the Caribbean islands. However, the average high temperature is about 82°F (28°C). Generally the best time to visit the Caribbean is during its driest months.

There are many islands in the Caribbean. The amount of rain that falls depends on the physical environment of the specific island. The islands of Aruba, Bonaire, and Curaçao get the least amount of rain. In fact, their climate can be very dry. These islands are also much less likely to experience hurricanes.

title: Biomes of the Caribbean
text:
The Caribbean has freshwater, forest, and mountain biomes. Most of the plants growing there are tropical. There are rainforests with many plants and animals here. Parrots and monkeys live in the rainforests. Palm trees grow on the sandy beaches.

The ocean has many animals that live in salt water, such as sea turtles and rays. Many sea animals make their homes in and around coral reefs. A great variety of plants, animals, and insects form the wildlife of the Caribbean. The Caribbean is an example of a diverse biome.

title: Natural Resources of the Caribbean
text: The location and climate of the Caribbean make it rich in natural resources. The soil and temperature on many Caribbean islands make them great places to grow bananas, sugar cane, and coffee. Because the islands are located in the ocean, fish are a plentiful resource as well. The islands are also places where sailing ships get supplies of fresh water and food. There are natural oil deposits in the earth that are mined and then used.

title: Landmarks of the Caribbean
text:
One very famous place in the Caribbean is called the Caguana Ceremonial Site. It is located in Puerto Rico. This is where the Taíno Native American people built ancient structures out of stone. Many of these stones have beautiful carvings called petroglyphs. The site was used for different things. It was used for ceremonies, religion, and ball games. The ball games had ceremonial significance and influenced important decisions for the Taíno. The site is around 800 years old. The site has a museum with Taíno artifacts. It also has a garden featuring the plants the Taíno used for food. The site is one of the Caribbean’s ancient man-made landmarks.

Did you know that the Caribbean is home to the only tropical rainforest in the U.S. forest system? It is called the El Yunque National Forest. It gets its name from the Taíno god Yukiyú. This forest is located in Puerto Rico. It is rich in plants and animals. There are 23 plants and animals there that are not found anywhere else in the world. Eight large rivers flow through this rainforest. About 600,000 people visit this rainforest every year. Rainforests are one of the Caribbean's natural landmarks.

title: The Caribbean: Mixed Cultures
text:
Most people living in the Caribbean have mixed ancestry coming from different places. The Caribbean was and is home to many Native American people. The Arawak and Caribs are a few of these groups. Africans were enslaved and brought to the Caribbean to work shortly after Columbus arrived. Europeans immigrated to the Caribbean to take advantage of the natural resources there. Native peoples of the Caribbean, enslaved Africans, and European immigrants all influenced the culture of the Caribbean. Most people living there today are descended from one or a mix of these groups. This mix of cultures has influenced language and religion.

Language

European languages like Spanish, French, and English are usually the official languages of the Caribbean Islands. People also speak native languages and Creoles, which are mixes of multiple languages.

Religion

The Spanish, Portuguese, and other Europeans brought Christianity to the Caribbean. Santeria and Rasta are two religions that came to the Caribbean from Africa. Hinduism was brought to the Caribbean from Asia. There are many different religions being practiced in the Caribbean today.

title: What Is Extinction?
text:
Why are dinosaurs no longer found on Earth? The most common cause for an animal’s disappearance from Earth is a change to the place they live. Animals cannot survive sudden changes to their habitat.

Scientists have evidence that, long ago, an asteroid hit the Earth. An asteroid is a small, rocky object that orbits the sun. The impact of the asteroid caused a large amount of dust to leave the surface of the Earth and enter the atmosphere. This reduced the amount of sunlight that could reach the Earth’s surface. Plants could not grow well. Without plants, herbivores, or plant-eating dinosaurs, didn't have food. They died. With herbivore dinosaurs gone, the carnivores, or meat-eating dinosaurs, didn’t have anything to eat. So they died too.

Scientists learned the story of the dinosaurs through fossil evidence. Fossils are the remains of plants and animals that lived a long time ago. Fossil records tell scientists what organisms looked like, and the type of environment they lived in. Using tooth fossils, scientists know that T. rex was a carnivore, and the triceratops was an herbivore. Scientists are still finding fossils today. They use fossils to explain what happened on the Earth a long time ago.

title: Audio Support: Reader’s Theater: Oh, Deer! The Case of Matter in Ecosystems
text:
Reader’s Theater:

Oh, Deer! The Case of Matter in Ecosystems

Cast

Scientist #1

Scientist #2

Scientist #3

Nonliving Matter

Plants

Mountain Lion

Rotter

Sun/Caterpillar/Deer #2

Optional Reader of Stage Directions

The scene opens on three Scientists investigating a forest, one finishing up a conversation on the phone.

Scientist #1: Roger that. (Hangs up the phone.) Yeah, we’ve got a report about a missing deer nearby.

Scientist #3: Well, we know matter like a deer can’t just disappear. It has to be somewhere.

Scientist #1: Boss wants us to investigate. Let’s touch base with each component of the ecosystem. Maybe we’ll get some clues there.

Scientist #2: Would you just look at this ecosystem? It’s filled to the brim with organisms. Where do we even start?

Scientist #3: Well, let’s start off with the stuff that isn’t alive. (Walks to Nonliving Matter.)

Nonliving Matter: Hi. Thank you so much for coming.

Scientist #3: State your name for the record, please.

Nonliving Matter: I’m the nonliving things in an ecosystem: water, gases in the air, and even nutrients in the soil that help plants grow.

Scientist #1: We received word that there was a deer in this ecosystem, but it hasn’t been seen in a while. Would you happen to know anything about that?

Nonliving Matter: I’m happy to help! In the ecosystem, my air, water, and nutrients are absorbed by plants. It’s possible the deer could have drunk my water from the stream or breathed my air. But my major contribution to moving matter is my relationship with my plant buddies. I’m sorry I can’t be more helpful.

Exits.

Scientist #2: Well, what’s the connection from nonliving matter to our deer?

Scientist #3: Don’t deer eat plants?

Scientist #1: That’s right! Deer are herbivores, a.k.a. plant-eaters. Let’s talk to Plants next.

Plants and Caterpillar enter. Scientists walk up to Plants.

Scientist #3: Excuse me? Are you matter in the form of plants?

Plants: That’s me: green, leafy, and loving it.

Scientist #2: Have you happened to run across a deer lately? Tall, furry herbivore?

Plants: Who’d you hear that from? Was it Nonliving Matter? Man, that guy gets under my skin. Oh, yeah, I know that deer. Took a chunk from my stem once.

Scientist #1: You’ve had a rough go. I’m sorry. You probably get eaten by all sorts of things.

Plants: Yeah, all herbivores. You’ve got your plant-eating animals and insects. But I don’t mind. It’s all part of an ecosystem. I’m just lucky I can use nonliving matter to make my own food, all with the energetic help of my buddy, Sun. (Looks at Sun.)

Sun: ‘Sup.

Plants: Last time I saw that deer, it had finished its snack and gone deeper into the forest. Then I hung out with my buddy, another herbivore. He’s a caterpillar.

Caterpillar: (Smiles, but doesn’t know what to say.) I like leaves.

Plants: You won’t get too much information out of Caterpillar. He’s kinda going through some changes right now. Anyway, hope that helps!

Plants and Caterpillar exit.

Scientist #1: So our deer had a little snack on a plant, which had already absorbed nonliving matter. We don’t have any clues after that! The trail is dead.

Scientist #3: Wait a minute. Look at these animal tracks.

Scientist #2: That’s it! If the deer is a herbivore and eats plants, then maybe something else ate the deer.

Scientist #1: Hey! Mountain Lion, can you come over here please?

Mountain Lion enters with her cubs.

Mountain Lion: Yes, can I help you?

Scientist #3: We’re looking for a missing deer. Seen anything?

Mountain Lion: (Becomes visibly nervous.) Listen, last time I checked, mountain lions eat deer! This is a healthy ecosystem. Meeting my needs isn’t a crime; it’s what keeps this place in balance. There are plenty of deer, and I have kids to feed, sir.

Scientist #3: Listen, ma’am. No one is in trouble here.

Scientist #1: Right. We just need some information. You’re a meat-eater, correct?

Mountain Lion: That’s right. I’m a carnivore. I also happen to be at the top of my food chain. Nothing else in my ecosystem eats me. There aren’t many of us to go around. We eat just enough to keep the deer and the carnivore populations stable. That will keep all the food chains in this ecosystem balanced.

Scientist #2: Right. A food chain, what we scientists call the chain that links a string of interactions in an ecosystem, specifically the consumption of living and nonliving things. So Plants absorbed nonliving matter and used the sun to change it into food, the deer ate Plants, and you ...

Mountain Lion: I ATE IT, OKAY? AND IT WAS SWEET AND MEATY AND DELICIOUS.

Scientist #3: Mystery solved, then!

Mountain Lion: Wait just a minute. I didn’t eat everything from the deer.

Scientist #1: What do you mean?

Mountain Lion: I am a carnivore, a meat-eater. But I left the big bones and the other parts animals can’t digest right there. (Points.)

Scientist #3: So where did the leftovers go?

Scientist #2: Look!

In front of the Scientists and Mountain Lion, Deer #2 strolls in. Upon seeing Mountain Lion, Deer #2 screams and runs away.

Mountain Lion: That’s funny. He looks exactly like the deer I ate. Could have sworn … then who did I eat?

Scientist #1: You mean, you don’t know which deer you ate?

Mountain Lion: Like you expect me to keep track?

Scientist #2: Well, did you eat this deer or not?

Mountain Lion: I’m honestly very upset by all this questioning. I have no idea. I can neither confirm nor deny my actions in the forest regarding the deer population, okay?

Scientist #3: We are back to square one! Do we know anything new?

Rotter enters.

Rotter: Beg your pardon. I think I might be able to help.

Scientist #3: (Turns to Rotter, with a surprised look.) Who are you?

Rotter: I’m the one who keeps this place clean! None of these other organisms care to clean up after themselves. Just leaving their dinners left and right. Dead leaves muckin’ up the forest floor. Can’t plants and animals just die in a neat little pile?!

Scientist #1: So you cleaned up the eaten deer?

Rotter: In a way. I break down plant and animal remains through rot, mold, or even eating the dead stuff. Eventually, it’s all broken back down into nonliving matter.

Scientist #2: How?

Rotter: That’s what makes me special. I’m the mushrooms, the worms, even the bacteria moving all the dead things right back into the ecosystem. I rot it all away. The water in living things returns to the soil. I turn other matter into nutrients for the soil, and I even put gases from rotting matter back into the air.

Scientist #1: Wait, so the deer is right back to where we started. Who knows if it was already absorbed again by Plants?

Scientist #3: Everyone, stop! Caterpillar. Have you eaten since we talked?

Caterpillar: (Swallows mouthful of food.) Maybe.

Scientist #2: Has anyone else eaten or absorbed anything since we talked to them?

Everyone guiltily raises their hand.

Scientist #1: So whatever happened to the deer, I guess it’s not really missing anymore. It’s here, and there, and everywhere. (Points to all of the components.) All matter is constantly changing and moving, cycling through its ecosystem.

title: Events That Represent the U.S.
text:
What are two events that represent the United States?

The Constitutional Convention (May 1787–September 1787)

The Constitution of the United States was written over a long period of time at an event called a convention. A convention is a series of meetings. The Constitutional Convention was held in Philadelphia, from May through September of 1787. Fifty-five representatives from 12 of the new 13 states were there. George Washington was also there. Later, he would become our first president. The members of the Constitutional Convention wrote most of the laws that we still follow in our country today.

The Signing of the U.S. Constitution (September 17, 1787)

At the end of the Constitutional Convention, the United States Constitution was finished. Thirty-nine out of the 55 representatives signed the Constitution. This ratified, or put into effect, the new Constitution.

These events represent the United States because they created the foundation for the laws and government of our country.

title: Essential Question
text: What are symbols that represent the United States?

title: Mount Rushmore
text: Mount Rushmore is a sculpture in South Dakota. It represents four important presidents. George Washington and Thomas Jefferson were Founding Fathers. Abraham Lincoln helped free people who were enslaved. Theodore Roosevelt developed the National Parks Service. We honor their service to our country through this sculpture.

title: Uncle Sam
text: Uncle Sam isn’t a real person, but a symbol of the United States. Uncle Sam is a cartoon figure whose name first showed up on containers of supplies during the War of 1812. Soldiers joked that the initials “U.S.” on the containers stood for “Uncle Sam.” In 1832, the first pictures of Uncle Sam began appearing in newspapers. Uncle Sam had a long, white beard and wore a tall, star-spangled hat. He also wore a suit covered in red, white, and blue stripes. The red, white, and blue colors of the poster remind people of the American flag. Later, Uncle Sam appeared on posters asking Americans to stick together during times of war and to fight for liberty and justice. The United States Congress made Uncle Sam an official national symbol in 1961.

title: The Washington Monument
text: Many people think that George Washington represents the United States because he was our first president and a great leader. He is often called the "Father of his country." The Washington Monument was built in honor of George Washington. The monument is located at the center of the nation’s capital, Washington, D.C.

title: The American Flag
text: One of the patriotic symbols of the country is the flag. The stripes represent the 13 original colonies that became the new United States. The stars represent each state of the union. The red, white, and blue colors have meaning, too. Red symbolizes valor, or courage, and being willing to sacrifice for the country. White symbolizes innocence and purity in holding to the ideals of the country. Blue represents vigilance, perseverance and justice for all.

title: The Statue of Liberty
text: The United States and France have a special relationship. France helped the colonies in the War for Independence from Great Britain. The people of France wanted to give America a gift to honor freedom and democracy. The gift was the Statue of Liberty. The statue was placed in the harbor of New York City. The statue is of a woman holding a torch for all to see the light of freedom. The statue is a symbol of freedom, a sign of hope for people seeking a better life in America.

title: The Great Seal of the United States
text: The Great Seal of the United States was designed and approved in 1782. It is a symbol of freedom. It represents the United States as an independent country. It shows our beliefs and values. The bald eagle holds a saying that means "out of many, one" to remind us that we are a unity of states. In one claw is an olive branch to represent peace. In the other claw, there are arrows to represent defending our country. There is a shield with 13 stripes for the original 13 colonies. Above the eagle is a cloud with 13 stars.

title: Governments and Community Values
text:
The purpose of government is to create systems and laws that manage the rights and liberties of individuals. Governmental systems include courts systems, elections, police departments and more. Laws are the formal rules of a society that all citizens must follow. The government enforces the consequences for breaking laws.

The systems and laws that governments create reflect the values and customs of the society the government represents. Imagine you live in a community where people own lots of pets. What if your local government outlawed owning a pet? Would you be upset? Would someone you know be upset? Do you think that this law would reflect your community’s values?

When the United States government was formed, the founders wanted to make a government that reflected their own values and the values of their communities. Many different communities and people lived in the Americas and the colonies. Each had their own beliefs and values. Some of these groups were Native Americans, Africans, and Europeans. The United States government was shaped by these groups and their values.

Compelling Question: How did early structures impact the development of the U.S. government and its institutions?

title: Historical Sources
text:
Supporting Question: What kinds of sources could help answer the compelling question?

When compelling questions are about historical topics, researchers and historians use primary and secondary sources to find out about the event or time period. Primary sources are created by people who saw or experienced the event or time period. They include historical and legal documents. They also include books, newspaper articles, letters, diaries, and census data. Visual sources like photographs, maps, and drawings are also primary sources. Artifacts, or human-made objects, are primary sources. They can be ordinary things that people used in the past like tools, pottery, clothing, or jewelry. Oral histories can also be primary sources. An oral history is usually an interview with someone who experienced an event in the past. The interview is recorded on audio or video. People usually record oral histories after a significant amount of time has passed since the time period or event.

Secondary sources are made by people who didn’t see or experience the event. These are usually created by people who have studied primary sources and then provide their interpretation of the source. Secondary sources are biographies, magazine articles, and documentaries. For example, if you write a journal entry about your vacation, it is a primary source because you were there and experienced the vacation. If someone interviews you and writes about your vacation, their story is a secondary source.

title: Belief Systems
text:
Supporting Question: What types of beliefs can be found in the U.S. governmental system?

European

Members of the Society of Friends, commonly called Quakers, came from Europe and settled in Pennsylvania and western New Jersey. Quakers believed that they did not need creeds or clergy to lead them correctly. They believed in following the “Inner Light.” They also believed in religious tolerance and pacifism, meaning they didn’t believe in using violence to solve problems.

Puritans began a religious movement in England to get rid of the last influences of Roman Catholicism on the Anglican Church. Eventually, many Puritans believed they should leave the Anglican Church altogether. Puritans believed that covenant relationships with God, preaching, and having the Holy Spirit were very important. Many Puritans settled in Massachusetts.

Roman Catholics settled in Maryland after the 1649 Act of Toleration was passed. This stated that anyone who believed in the Trinity could live in Maryland. The Trinity is the Christian concept of deity as Heavenly Father, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit.

Native American

The Lenni Lenape believed in a Creator, a being who controlled the natural world. They also believed that there were spirits, called manitou, that had control over some natural elements. It was important to respect the Creator and manitou. They had dances and celebrations throughout the year that recognized the Creator and manitou.

Members of the Iroquois Confederacy, like the Lenape, believed in a Creator and manitou. They also believed that evil spirits caused sickness. Healers set bones and made medicine from the plants and resources around them. They also prayed and performed spells, dances, and ceremonies to heal the sick.

African

Many African beliefs are referred to as spiritualism. In his autobiography, Olaudah Equiano describes his tribe’s belief in a Creator and the belief that dead ancestors protected their living kin.

In West Africa, many people were Muslim. Muslims are followers of Islam. They believe in a God, called Allah in Arabic. They also believe that Muhammad was Allah’s final prophet.

Many Africans who had been forcibly brought to the Americas as enslaved people kept their traditional beliefs. Some, however, blended these beliefs with Christian theologies. Some religions in the Caribbean and southern North America are a blend of traditional African beliefs and Roman Catholicism.

Primary Source

Native American groups use oral history to preserve stories about the past and about beliefs. The stories are passed on from one generation to the next. Many cultures, particularly those without a written language, have preserved their history through oral retellings. The Cherokee tribe had an oral history culture until 1821, when Sequoyah, a Cherokee, invented the Cherokee alphabet with the help of his daughter.

This is a transcription of an oral telling of a Cherokee origin story. The origin story is on display at the Cherokee National History Museum. It features animation by Cherokee artist Roy Boney and narration by Cherokee storyteller Anna Sixkiller.

One Cherokee creation story recounts a long time ago ...
When the people lived on an island south of what is now the United States.

Their island became tormented by earthquakes that led to a volcanic eruption.
Around fourteen groups departed in canoes to find a new home.

The people set forth across a vast expanse of water, traveling for weeks.
Not every canoe survived this dangerous journey.
Only seven canoe groups remained when they reached the shores of an unfamiliar land.

These groups would become the Seven Clans.
Wolf, Blue, Long Hair, Paint, Bird, Deer, and Wild Potato.

The seven groups traveled north to the land of the Iroquois in the northeastern part of present-day United States.

There, the Cherokees lived among the Iroquois for a brief time until they began their journey heading south and east where they settled living in towns and communities, becoming Cherokee Nation.

title: Family Structures
text:
Supporting Questions: Does family structure influence value systems? Does family structure influence government systems?

European:

European families were arranged in nuclear family units, which consisted of parents and their children. Fathers were in charge of the family. They directed the religious, economic, and social lives of all family members. The settlers who came from Europe to the Americas structured their families the same way. This type of structure is usually called a patriarchal structure.

Native American:

Native American families were structured differently in every tribe. Some were patriarchal, while others were not. Many tribes arranged themselves into family clans. The Lenape had three clans: the Turtle, the Wolf, and the Turkey clans. The Cherokee had seven clans.

Iroquois, Lenape, and Cherokee tribes were all arranged matrilineally. This means that kinship, or family relationships, are traced through the mother’s genealogy. Also, most children lived with their mother and their mother’s family.

African:

African families were structured differently according to their tribal customs. These customs varied widely. Some were arranged into family clans, and some had matrilineal relationships. Others had nuclear families.

Once Africans were enslaved by Europeans and American colonists, they did not have much control over their families. Family members were often sold to different enslavers, and families were forced to live apart.

Primary Source:

Olaudah Equiano was taken from his home by African slave traders. He was traded again and again until he reached the coast of Africa. Then he was sold to European enslavers. He was enslaved by a ship captain. Eventually, he saved enough money to be able to buy his freedom. He wrote an autobiography describing his life before and after his enslavement. He wrote it as an abolitionist tool to help convince Europeans to end the practice of enslavement. In his record, he describes the family structures among his tribe. Most men practiced polygyny, meaning they had more than one wife. Equiano describes a family structure that was patriarchal:

The head of the family usually eats alone; his wives and slaves have also their separate tables.

Each master of a family has a large square piece of ground, surrounded with a moat or fence, or enclosed with a wall made of red earth tempered; which, when dry, is as hard as brick. Within this are his houses to accommodate his family and slaves; which, if numerous, frequently present the appearance of a village. In the middle stands the principal building, appropriated to the sole use of the master, and consisting of two apartments; in one of which he sits in the day with his family, the other is left apart for the reception of his friends. He has besides these a distinct apartment in which he sleeps, together with his male children. On each side are the apartments of his wives, who have also their separate day and night houses. The habitations of the slaves and their families are distributed throughout the rest of the enclosure.

title: Government Structures
text:
Supporting Question: Are there any principles from government systems that existed before the U.S. government that can be found in the Constitution or other government institutions?

European:

The House of Burgesses was the first form of elected government in the British colonies. It was formed in the Virginia Colony. The Governor of Jamestown created the House of Burgesses in 1619. Two House members were elected from each of Virginia’s 11 settlements.

Another type of government in the British colonies was called a proprietary colony. In a proprietary colony, the king chose a man or a group of men to rule over a section of land. They called these men the Lords Proprietors. They had the right to rule everyone living in the land. Their power was given to them in an official document called a charter.

Native American:

Some Native American groups banded together in alliances called confederacies. The Iroquois Confederacy, or the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, began as a group of five bands. Eventually there were six bands in the confederacy. Each band had a separate government. However, their governments and societies had similar characteristics. They also supported each other in times of war.

The Cherokee had a Council of Women that was separate from the tribal council. The Council of Women was very active in making decisions about war and peace as well as land use and food production.

Some tribes, like the Lenape, were overseen by a chief or sachem. This individual was male, but inherited their power through their mother’s family. When a chief died, his sister’s son would be the next chief.

African:

Throughout African history, many different types of governments existed. In western Africa, there were very large empires that existed until about the 1400s. One of the largest was the Mali Empire. It was ruled over by a king called a sundiata.

By the time Europeans came in contact with Africa, most governments were smaller kingdoms or tribal governments. Most were controlled by men.

Primary Source:

The Mayflower Compact was a document drafted by the Puritans who settled Plymouth. There were some disputes between the passengers of the Mayflower. They decided that they should create a binding agreement before they left the ship and began to settle in the land. They wrote the Mayflower Compact and most of the men on the ship signed it. The Compact outlined principles like self-government and consent of the governed, meaning the people agreed to be led by the same rules. The compact also unified the new colonists.

In the name of God, Amen. We whose names are underwritten, the loyal subjects of our dread sovereign lord King James, by the grace of God, of Great Britain, France, and Ireland King, Defender of the Faith, etc.

Having undertaken, for the glory of God, and advancement of the Christian faith, and honor of our king and country, a voyage to plant the first colony in the northern parts of Virginia, do by these presents solemnly and mutually in the presence of God and one of another, covenant, and combine ourselves together into a civil body politic, for our better ordering and preservation, and furtherance of the ends aforesaid; and by virtue hereof to enact, constitute, and frame such just and equal laws, ordinances, acts, constitutions, offices from time to time, as shall be thought most meet and convenient for the general good of the colony: unto which we promise all due submission and obedience. In witness whereof we have hereunder subscribed our names; Cape Cod, the 11th of November, in the year of the reign of our sovereign lord King James, of England, France and Ireland eighteenth and of Scotland fifty-fourth, Anno Domini 1620.

title: Historians and Perspectives
text:
Supporting Question: What have historians interpreted from the past that helps us understand how different values influenced the creation of the United States government?

Everyone brings a unique perspective to a situation or event. Experiences or events may be interpreted differently by people with different cultural or individual perspectives. It is important to look at multiple perspectives to have a deeper understanding of the past. This helps us create a more accurate analysis of the people and events in history. Here are two historical analyses of the past:

In 2007, historian Jack P. Greene wrote that historians need to look at more than the colonial or local perspectives when studying U.S. history. He argued that historians need to look at European events to understand the history of the British colonies.

Many historians in the 1900s argued that the American Revolution and the creation of the U.S. government was driven by economic desires. They interpreted that the U.S. government wasn’t only shaped by family, existing government structures, or beliefs. These historians interpreted that most of the founders were motivated by economic forces.
