title: The New Deal
text:
In 1933, the United States was in the middle of a great economic depression. Businesses had closed. Many people had lost their jobs. Banks failed. The banks that didn’t fail needed farmers and homeowners to repay their loans. People who were unable to repay their debts had their farms and homes taken away. Most people had very little hope that things would get better. In that same year, Franklin Delano Roosevelt was sworn in as the new President of the United States.

President Roosevelt’s greatest challenge was finding a way to bring the country out of the Great Depression. Roosevelt and his advisors created a new plan to bring prosperity back to America called the New Deal. The New Deal created many new government agencies that would help the unemployed, the poor, farmers, and the elderly. The plan also created jobs and changed America’s economic policies.

The WPA, or Works Progress Administration, provided jobs for the unemployed in every economic sector, including social services, public health, conservation, education, fine arts, and scholarly research. For example, the WPA helped to restore water lines, improve parks, laid miles of new roads, produced articles of clothing, and even served school lunches.

The Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) had total authority to conserve and develop the waterways of the Tennessee River and its tributaries. The TVA completed projects in Kentucky, Tennessee, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, North Carolina, and Virginia.

The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) was a New Deal program. It provided jobs for millions of single young men between the ages of 18 and 25. They worked mostly in the countryside. They planted trees, fought forest fires, and maintained forest roads and trails.

The Social Security Act (SSA) was another part of Roosevelt’s New Deal legislation. Under the SSA, the government taxed workers’ salaries. This money was given to older citizens when they reached a certain age, usually 65. The Social Security Act is still in use today.

People all over the nation started feeling hopeful. They had confidence that President Roosevelt was leading the country in the right direction.

title: Culture Changes for African Americans
text:
The 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments to the United States Constitution were ratified during and directly after the American Civil War. These amendments gave all citizens of the United States, regardless of race, the right to freedom from slavery and equal treatment under the law. For all males, the amendments guaranteed the right to vote. For a short period called Reconstruction, it appeared that the lives of formerly enslaved African Americans might really improve.

However, prejudice and racism in America, particularly in the South, had not gone away. Resentment grew as African Americans began to exercise their rights. States and local governments began to pass a series of statutes. These statutes legalized racial segregation, marginalized African Americans, and denied them any hope of equality. These statutes were called Jim Crow laws. They were named after a derogatory nickname for African Americans that was used by some white people.

Jim Crow laws placed restrictions on who could vote. Some states required voters to own property or pay a fee to vote. Others required people to take literacy tests before they could register to vote. These laws were designed to prevent African Americans from voting. However, they also prevented anyone who was poor or who couldn’t read and write from exercising their right to vote.

A wide range of laws separated African Americans from white Americans. African Americans were required to sit in the balconies of movie theaters and drink from separate water fountains. They were required to stay in separate waiting areas for services and sit in the back of buses. A separate but unequal school system was also established.

Other restrictions under the Jim Crow laws included:

Segregation of hospitals, community swimming pools, jails, parks, and other public areas

Separate cemeteries for African Americans

No mixed race dating or marriage

At this time in America, African Americans had nowhere to turn to fight this discrimination. Nearly all of the police, judges, and government officials were white. Any attempts to stand up to these restrictions resulted in arrest, fines, jail sentences, and even violence and death.

title: The Civilian Conservation Corps
text:
When Franklin D. Roosevelt was elected president, he started something called the New Deal. This was a plan to provide jobs for people all over the United States. These jobs helped people survive through this difficult time.

The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) was a New Deal program. It provided jobs for millions of single young men between the ages of 18 and 25. The CCC worked to help conserve, or save, the nation's natural resources. People worked to create state parks. During the CCC's nine years of existence, they built nature trails, lookout towers, and planted trees for new forests. The Corps developed over 700 state parks and provided most of the work for the Great Smoky Mountain National Park. These projects included building log cabins, picnic shelters, and lodges.

Other people found work building things that people needed. They built highways, bridges, public housing, libraries, and airports. The Works Progress Administration sponsored a Writer's Project to give jobs to talented writers. These people interviewed different people to find out about their lives. Then, the writers published these interviews. Many of the writers interviewed formerly enslaved people. Because of the Writer's Project, we can read about the lives of enslaved people during and after the Civil War.

The programs of the New Deal helped to improve the nation and provided jobs for many of its citizens. However, many citizens still struggled. It was not until a war in the 1940s that hard times changed in the United States.

title: Discrimination in America in the 1930s
text:
The 15th Amendment was ratified in 1870. This addition to the U.S. Constitution gave formerly enslaved men the right to vote. “The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States, or by any State, on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” By the end of the century, many states had created laws to get around the amendment. The new laws were discriminating on factors such as intelligence, having money or living in certain areas. States implemented segregation laws which kept black and white people “separate but equal.” This type of law was called “Jim Crow.” Jim Crow was a fictitious character that portrayed African Americans in a belittling manner.

Such laws were created to keep white people separate from anyone else. The laws identified people who were Black, Chinese, or Japanese. The laws identified who could vote, what entrances could be used to public buildings, and who could apply for jobs. By the time World War II started in 1941, four generations of Americans had lived with segregation and discrimination.

Some of the laws were:

“Marriages are void (not legal) when one party is a white person and the other is possessed of one-eighth or more [Black], Japanese, or Chinese blood.” Nebraska, 1911.

“It shall be unlawful for a [Black] and white person to play together or in company with each other in any game of cards or dice, dominoes or checkers." Birmingham, Alabama, 1930.

"Separate free schools shall be established for the education of children of African descent, and it shall be unlawful for any colored child to attend any white school, or any white child to attend a [Black] school." Missouri, 1929.

“There shall be maintained by the governing authorities of every hospital maintained by the state for treatment of white and colored patients separate entrances for white and [Black] patients and visitors, and such entrances shall be used by the race only for which they are prepared.” Mississippi.

“No persons, firms, or corporations, who or which furnish meals to passengers at station restaurants or station eating houses, in times limited by common carriers of said passengers, shall furnish said meals to white and [Black] passengers in the same room, or at the same table, or at the same counter.”

Public places were kept separate. Doors, sidewalks, drinking fountains and restrooms were segregated by race. African Americans were primary in leading the protest against Jim Crow laws, though not all of these laws were in the South or were specific to African Americans. There were racial laws in other states, such as a law in California that made it illegal for people of Chinese ancestry to vote. Another California law made it illegal to sell alcohol to American Indians.

As America was involved in World War II, there were places in America where people were segregated and not legally allowed to live, eat, or attend work. The families of men in the military fighting in the European and Pacific theaters for liberty were not experiencing liberty at home.

title: Economic Impact of War
text:
During the Great Depression, the nation's economy suffered. President Franklin Delano Roosevelt created a plan called the New Deal. It was intended to reduce the negative effects of the Great Depression. The New Deal included many new government programs to help people and states recover from the economic downturn. Many states were already starting to recover when World War II started.

World War II was beneficial to the economies of farming states. The war increased the demand for cotton to make military uniforms. As a result, textile mills and other industries grew. They needed to hire more workers to increase production. The government also needed food that grew in many farming states to feed the military. However, farms became shorthanded when farm workers left to join the war.

To deal with the shortage of workers, many farmers changed the crops they grew. They began to grow crops like soybeans that could be harvested by machines instead of by hand. Farmers employed more women and children in the fields. In many states, more jobs became available to increase war production to support soldiers. By 1943, about 350,000 people had employment because of the war. Employed citizens had more money to spend to support their families.

During the war, military bases expanded and new ones opened. These military bases boosted local economies and aided the war effort. More military bases meant more trained soldiers for the war. The bases also meant more jobs for citizens. This created stable incomes for many civilian and military employees. With more money available, the demand for goods and services increased.

One of the most important military bases was the Charleston Navy Yard. The Yard was responsible for building medium-sized and small vessels. It was also one of the places where other vessels came for repairs. In 1941, the Charleston Navy Yard employed around 6,000 people to meet these needs. Two years later, the Yard employed close to 28,000 people.

Fort Jackson was one of the busiest military bases. It has been around since before World War II and is still in use today. In the 1940s, Fort Jackson employed 7,000 to 8,000 people. Today, 12,000 military families call Fort Jackson home. It employs about 3,500 civilians. In 1941, Fort Jackson was the sixth largest military base in the United States. Now, it is the largest training center for soldiers in the United States. Almost half of all new soldiers train at Fort Jackson.

Another military base is Marine Corps Recruitment Depot (MCRD) at Parris Island. During World War II, around 200,000 army recruits trained there. Today, it is the main MCRD in the United States. About 19,000 new recruits train there each year. Their mission statement is, “We make Marines.”

Camp Croft employed 12,000 people during World War II. Around 900 German POWs (prisoners of war) were housed at Camp Croft. However, in 1947, the camp became unnecessary and shut down. Today, it is a state park.

All of this activity during World War II helped the economy recover from the devastation of the Great Depression. Many of the changes in agriculture, industry, and the military paved the way for new developments after the war.

title: Segregation in the United States
text:
Television programs from the decades following World War II depict white families enjoying perfect, stable lives. Nuclear families (families with a mother and a father in the home) were shown as the norm. Everyone lived in well-kept suburban homes with a shiny new car in the driveway. Mothers stayed home to take care of their houses and children. The fathers grabbed their briefcases and went to work. Kids played Little League baseball and learned to play the piano. Families traveled the new interstate highways on vacations to beaches, national parks, and theme parks. Most children in the suburbs graduated from high school and college, and then went on to enjoy married life and a stable career in the suburbs. Some people in the U.S. lived like this. Yet, for many living in rural areas and cities, this ideal was out of reach.

In southern states and many northern industrial cities, African Americans and other minority groups had very different lives. At this time, about two-thirds of African American citizens in the U.S. still lived in the South. Racism and discrimination kept many from opportunities in education, employment, and housing. Many middle-class families left the cities for new suburbs. Industries and jobs followed them. This left once thriving industrial cities without enough tax money to maintain public property or services like schools. Parks, streets, and public buildings became run-down. Jobs were hard to find, so poverty spread.

Schools in the South were segregated, which meant that attendance was based on the color of the child’s skin. Schools are paid from local taxes. An employed population increased the amount of taxes collected. Unemployed population had lower taxes collected. Schools gave older and used supplies to the schools with high poverty. Wages for staff were determined by the color of a person’s skin.

African Americans could only drink from designated fountains or use specific restrooms. They were not allowed to use the same public spaces as white people because of the color of their skin. They were required to sit at the back of trains and buses, even if there were empty seats in the front. Many restaurants would not serve African Americans. Movie theaters had separate entrances that led to separate seating areas.

A difficult and sad part of our history is the persecution of people in the United States. As African Americans began to organize and stand up for their rights, white people in power retaliated, often using violence. The Ku Klux Klan was a secret society formed after the Civil War. Its aim was to keep African Americans from making progress in society. This group persecuted African Americans who tried to assert their rights. Intimidation and fear were used to keep the idea of segregation alive.

African Americans and many other citizens of the United States knew that this treatment of other human beings was unjust and inexcusable. They joined efforts to protect the rights of African Americans. They filed lawsuits in courts concerning violations of civil rights. Gradually, the U.S. government began to make decisions and enact legislation to help create equality in housing, education, and employment. However, progress was slow, hindered by opposition.

title: Brown v. Board of Education
text:
Lawsuits challenging segregation were made in multiple states. A suit was filed called Briggs v. Elliott. It was filed by 20 African American parents in Clarendon County, South Carolina. The NAACP’s legal advisor, Thurgood Marshall, was assigned the case. The suit began as a request for a school bus to transport African American students. The lawsuit expanded to include correcting other inequities and to end segregation. It was the first case in the 20th century to challenge the constitutionality of segregation in public schools. The U.S. District Court was given evidence of the inequities. Nothing was equal, but it was all separate. The judges ruled that the school board had to begin equalization. Segregation was still in place.

In 1951, Oliver Brown filed a lawsuit against the Topeka Board of Education. His daughter had not been allowed to attend an all-white school close to their house. Thurgood Marshall was one of the key lawyers in the case. Marshall argued that segregation was illegal. He insisted segregated schools could never be equal. The loss in the lower court helped the case to move to the Supreme Court. The justices debated their decision. Finally, on May 17, 1954, Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote, “In the field of public education the doctrine of ‘separate but equal’ has no place.” He also stated that the African American children were being deprived of the equal protection guaranteed by the 14th Amendment. The decision of the court ordered schools across the United States to integrate.

This decision set the standard for later events of the Civil Rights Movement. The process was not easy and did not happen quickly. In many places, integration was strongly opposed. Nine years later, many places had not complied with the court's decision. In 1963, the governor of Alabama, George Wallace, gave a speech declaring, "I say segregation now, segregation tomorrow, segregation forever."

The president used the powers of the executive branch to enforce the integration decision. National Guard units were called in to assure the safety of students.

title: The United States in the 1980s
text:
The 1970s was a time of political and economic upheaval in the United States. The Vietnam War ended in 1973. Many Americans opposed the war and became increasingly distrustful of the United States government. The Cold War continued to rage on. The Soviet Union continued to expand its empire and install communist governments in conquered areas. In 1974, Richard Nixon resigned as President of the United States following a campaign scandal. This scandal weakened the national government and intensified the feelings of distrust that many Americans felt towards the United States government.

The energy crisis of the 1970s caused great distress throughout the country. The shortage of oil during this time was a result of the oil embargo of the Middle East. The United States produced a lot of petroleum products, but just enough to supply the entire country's needs. Millions of barrels of oil were bought from nations in the Middle East, a region in Asia. These countries controlled more than half of all of the world's petroleum.

Many Middle Eastern nations were angry at the United States because of its support of the country of Israel. They immediately stopped all shipments of petroleum to the United States and other western nations. Because of the low supply and high demand for petroleum products, the cost of gasoline and heating oil skyrocketed.

Drivers all across the United States had to wait for hours to purchase small amounts of gasoline for their cars. Sometimes the gasoline ran out. Oil used to heat buildings was also in short supply. During the cold winter months, many schools and businesses were forced to cut hours or close altogether. Americans had to find ways to quickly adapt to the serious situation.

The crisis forced Americans to rethink the ways they used fuel. People drove less and shared rides with one another. The highway speed limits were reduced to help save gasoline. At home, people burned wood and lowered their thermostats. Some people even began to try to find other energy sources. Solar energy collectors used energy from sunlight to heat homes and businesses.

Unlike the 1970s, the 1980s was a time of political and economic stability in the United States. In 1980, Americans elected a new president who was charismatic and bold in asserting the United States' role in world politics and economy. Ronald Reagan served as the president of the United States from 1981 to 1989.

At the start of his presidency, he faced a strong, capable Soviet Union. The two nations were still deeply locked in the Cold War conflict. To defeat the Soviet Union, Reagan believed that the United States needed to match their foe’s military might. The economic philosophy he came up with to make this possible was called Reaganomics. His goal was to increase employment, stimulate growth, and strengthen the national defense. He did this by cutting taxes and increasing the amount of government spending on the U.S. military. Reagan also supplied naval escorts for oil transportation in the Middle East, which led to more stable energy sources for the U.S.

Reagan was reelected in 1984. His speeches against communism and the Soviet Union marked a strong and new approach in the Cold War.

In his 1985 State of the Union Address, Reagan discussed the new approach the United States would take to combat communism. He stated, “We must not break faith with those who are risking their lives–on every continent from Afghanistan to Nicaragua – to defy Soviet-supported aggression and secure rights which have been ours from birth." This became known as the Reagan Doctrine. The Reagan Doctrine supported anti-Communist insurgencies around the world.

Reagan gave what may have been his most famous speech at the Berlin Wall in 1987. Talking directly to Mikhail Gorbachev, the General Secretary of the Soviet Union, he said, “Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!”

title: What is Civil Disobedience: Rosa Parks and the Greensboro Sit-In
text:
A department store seamstress in Montgomery, Alabama, named Rosa Parks headed home after a day of work one December day in 1955. The African American woman climbed aboard a city bus. Mrs. Parks took an appropriate seat and settled in for the ride home. Public bus drivers were authorized to enforce segregation laws on the bus. A public bus had clearly marked seating for white people and African American passengers. As passengers continued to board, the designated section for whites filled to capacity. The bus driver, James Blake, believing he was authorized to do so, instructed Mrs. Parks and three other African American passengers to give their seats to white passengers. Parks refused and was arrested for refusing the orders of the bus driver. Parks went peacefully with the arresting officers without any resistance. This was an act of civil disobedience.

Civil disobedience is the active refusal of a citizen to obey certain laws, demands, orders or commands of a legal authority. The citizen will accept the consequences of the arrest. Civil disobedience is used to call attention to a law that many feel is unjust.

In reaction to Rosa Parks's arrest, African Americans in Montgomery boycotted the city bus system. Led by a minister named Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., people refused to ride the bus for over a year. Through it all, Rosa Parks remained a leader in the civil rights struggle. She continued working for equal rights for all people for over 40 years. Rosa Parks is remembered today as the "mother of the civil rights movement."

Inspired by Rosa Parks’s simple act of rebellion against segregation, more civil rights leaders emerged to take up the fight for equality. Segregation was not going to be accepted. Civil rights leaders decided that something had to be done about the unfair treatment of different racial groups. They came up with a plan to have "sit-ins" at public places. This was nonviolent and a peaceful means of protesting.

Five years after Parks refused to give up her seat, four African American college students decided to get something to eat. They left their college, North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University, and headed to a lunch counter at a local store in the town of Greensboro, North Carolina. No one paid attention to the young men as they entered the store. It was open to customers of all races. The lunch counter in the store, however, was for white customers only. The four students sat down at the lunch counter and asked the server to take their order. The other customers were shocked. The server reminded them that the lunch counter was segregated, so African Americans were not allowed to eat there. The students were asked to leave, but they silently remained where they were.

When the store closed for the evening, the Greensboro students left peacefully. The following day, the group of four students brought more people to sit at the lunch counter. The sit-in lasted for many days. Both African Americans and white people participated. Many people supported the sit-in, while others believed the students were trying to cause trouble. Some people even taunted and harassed them. In other cities across the South, thousands of people held the same types of demonstrations.

The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) was an organization to help people learn peaceful ways to protest. In order to keep all of their protests nonviolent, the SNCC created a set of rules for those who wanted to participate. They were instructed to follow these instructions exactly:

Do Not:

Strike back nor curse if abused.

Laugh out.

Hold conversations with the floor walker [store supervisor].

Leave your seat until your leader has given you permission to do so.

Block entrances to stores outside nor the aisles inside.

Do:

Show yourself friendly and courteous at all times.

Sit straight; always face the counter.

Report all serious incidents to your leader.

Refer information seekers to your leader in a polite manner.

Remember the teachings of Jesus Christ, Mahatma Gandhi and Martin Luther King. Love and nonviolence is the way.

These examples illustrate the force for change that can come from standing up (or sitting in) against injustice, and are examples of civil disobedience.

title: September 11, 2001: The Day the World Stopped
text:
The morning of Sept. 11, 2001, began like any other day in the United States. People made their way to work. Students boarded buses or walked to their schools. Thousands of people arrived at airports to board planes. They were going on business trips, vacations, or family visits.

Among those ordinary passengers were 19 members of the terrorist organization Al-Qaeda. They had declared war against the United States and they were about to carry out their largest attack ever. Their leader, Osama bin Laden, created a plan for them to fly hijacked airplanes into important buildings in the United States.

The 19 terrorists boarded four planes leaving major airports in cities like Boston, Washington, D.C., and Newark, New Jersey. Once in the air, the hijackers took over the airplanes. Passengers in those planes were familiar with how hijackings usually occurred. The terrorists would demand money or the release of other terrorists in prison. The passengers thought they would be safe by following instructions.

Instead of making demands, the Al-Qaeda terrorists turned the airplanes back toward New York City and Washington, D.C. They intentionally flew two of the airplanes into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York City. They crashed the third airplane into the military complex known as the Pentagon in Washington, D.C.

Flight 93, the fourth airplane hijacked that day, was delayed on take off and running behind the other three. The passengers on Flight 93 found out that the terrorists were crashing into buildings instead of making demands. They decided to launch a counterattack on the hijackers. The passengers and crew of the plane caused the airplane to crash in an empty field in Pennsylvania, rather than into another building. There is no way to know how many lives were saved by the passengers and crew of Flight 93.

The reaction to the terrorist attacks was immediate. Within seconds of the first airplane hitting the North Tower of the World Trade Center, first responders rushed to the scene. Firefighters, paramedics, and police officers converged on the burning building. Even after the second airplane hit the South Tower, first responders continued to make their way to the World Trade Center and enter the buildings.

They helped as many people as possible to evacuate the buildings and surrounding area. Many first responders were still in the buildings helping the victims when the towers collapsed from the attacks.

The government grounded all flights in the United States. Every airplane in the air was ordered to land wherever they could. Passengers ended up stranded at whichever airport they landed. No one knew if there were more hijackers, so air travel stopped in the entire country. Important government buildings were evacuated in case they were targets, too.

The news about the attacks was shared on television. There were very few internet news sites and no social media like we know it today. Instead, people focused on the videos and pictures on their TVs. Television stations cut into their regular programming to cover the news. People in the United States and around the world stopped everything to watch their televisions. All day, and for days after, the world watched together as more information about these attacks came out.

Every passenger on the four flights lost their lives that day. Many people in the buildings died from the impact of the airplanes, and many died when the towers fell. Nearly 3,000 people from over 80 countries were killed in the attacks that day. Many more people were injured. The terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2001 were the single largest loss of life resulting from a foreign attack on the United States soil ever.

On Sept. 12, 2001, cleanup began. The World Trade Center site became known as Ground Zero. It took rescue workers and volunteers nine months to remove the rubble and debris from Ground Zero.

title: The G.I. Bill
text:
As the U.S. entered WWII, government leaders made a plan to care for returning soldiers. President Franklin Delano Roosevelt passed the Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944. However, most people called this act the G.I. Bill. After the war, veterans found themselves in new and different lives. The G.I. Bill made low interest loans available, which returning soldiers could use to buy a home or car, or pay for college. There were also funds to cover tuition and expenses for college or trade schools. With this plan in place, veterans were able to ease back into civilian life without worrying about finding a job immediately. They were able to make the transition from soldier to civilian more smoothly by taking classes and preparing themselves to work at stable, higher-paying jobs.

When government officials first began writing the G.I. Bill, they didn't expect that nearly 8 million members of the military would take advantage of the education benefits. Veterans studied hard and earned their degrees. They contributed to their local economies by buying goods and services from nearby businesses. They secured higher-paying jobs and paid taxes. Some opened their own businesses and hired others to work for them. They bought new cars and built houses filled with the newest inventions of the 1950s and 1960s.

Soon, the nation's economy was growing dramatically. Houses, highways and technology were creating an industry that needed more workers. The G.I. Bill helped many veterans gain financial stability.

However, African American veterans were not given the same opportunity in the G.I. Bill that their white comrades were. Banks, new housing, and new jobs were not centered in African American communities. The benefits were available in the legislation, but were not available in real life.

title: What Is History?
text: History is what happened in the past. It tells us about people, events, and places.

title: Essential Question
text: How can I find answers to questions about history?

title: Asking Questions About History
text: You can ask questions about history. You can ask about people and places. You can ask about events in the past. You can ask why an event happened.

title: Finding Answers About History
text: You can find answers to your questions. You can look at primary sources. You can use media centers and books. You can look at other sources.

title: Primary Sources
text: Primary sources are made by people who are at an event. They saw or heard what happened. Primary Sources teach us about people and events.

title: Types of Primary Sources
text: Primary sources can be pictures or letters. They can be videos or recordings of events.

title: Historical Facts
text: Facts are things that are true. Historical facts are things that really happened in history.

title: Historical Fiction
text: Fiction is something that is not true. Historical fiction is a story that takes place in the past. The story may have people and places from history, but it is not true.

title: Essential Question
text: How do people meet their needs?

title: Meeting Our Needs
text: People meet their needs in different ways. Some people make their own goods. Some work for money to buy goods. Others trade to get what they need and want.

title: Making Choices
text: Sometimes we have to choose between needs and wants. We see how much money we have. We choose what we want or need most.

title: Essential Question
text: What affects the economic choices that people make?

title: Budgets
text: A budget is a plan for how to spend and save your money. It helps you to keep track of your money.

title: I Learned I Am ...
text: This year, I learned I am many things. I am a friend. I am a learner. I am part of history.

title: Essential Question
text: What have you learned this year?

title: A Member of a Community
text: I learned I am a member of a community. I learned about rules and laws. I learned about why it is important to follow rules and laws.

title: A Responsible Citizen
text: I learned I am a citizen. I have rights and responsibilities. I can be a responsible citizen in my communities.

title: A Geographer
text: I learned about geography. I have map skills. I can tell the location and features of a place. I learned about state and community geography.

title: Themes of Geography
text:
Maps help us explore the world. When we study geography, we are asking questions about various people and places around the world. Questions about geography fit into several main themes.

Location: Where is something located?

Place: What is it like there?

Human-Environment Interaction: What is the relationship between people and the environment?

Movement: How and why are places connected with one another?

Region: How and why is one area similar to or different from another area?

We call these themes of geography.

title: Tough Times for Floridians
text:
The 1920s began with a boom in Florida. In the first decades of the 1900s, thousands of visitors came to Florida to enjoy the natural and man-made wonders of the state. Many of these tourists decided to make Florida their permanent home. Land speculators came to Florida with the hopes of selling land for high prices. Florida entrepreneurs took advantage of the land boom. Dave Davis, Carl Fisher, Barron Collier, and other prominent entrepreneurs built resort communities throughout central and southern Florida, which drew thousands of visitors and new residents to the state. The population of the state grew quickly and Florida’s future seemed secure. Unfortunately, this was not the case.

Many factors led to the land bust of the mid-1920s. Companies could not keep up with the demand for workers and supplies. The railroad also had a difficult time shipping supplies to Florida and around the state. Newspapers around the country reported about the issues in Florida. Many people who had wanted to buy land in Florida changed their minds. The federal government forced speculators to set their prices based on the value of the land, not what they hoped to earn.

A series of natural disasters also caused land prices to drop in Florida during this time. The winter of 1925 was very cold, which destroyed thousands of acres of crops. This caused a shortage of citrus fruits and vegetables in the state. In September 1926, a large hurricane struck South Florida. It made landfall near Miami, causing millions of dollars worth of damage to the city and the surrounding areas. Many people were unable to rebuild their homes and decided to leave Florida.

Things continued to get worse for Floridians following the land bust of the mid-1920s. In September 1928, a catastrophic hurricane, called the Okeechobee Hurricane, hit the Atlantic Coast of Florida. The hurricane made landfall near Lake Okeechobee. The hurricane caused massive flooding near the lake, destroying several towns. Thousands of people were left homeless. Some chose to stay, while others migrated to other areas of the country.

Floridians also faced another threat much smaller than a hurricane during the spring and summer of 1929. Citrus groves became infested with Mediterranean fruit flies. These fruit flies are not native to Florida or North America. They are considered an invasive species. Invasive species are organisms that have been brought to a place where they are not meant to live. Invasive species have a negative impact on the environment. Sometimes, they come from the ocean in ships or in a ship's cargo. They may also be accidentally released into the environment.

The Mediterranean fruit fly destroyed thousands of acres of citrus groves in central Florida. Over 900 farms were impacted by the infestation of the fruit flies. Citrus production decreased quickly. The federal government also prevented Florida farmers from sending their crops to other states. They wanted to prevent the spread of the fruit flies to other areas of the country. Florida’s economy suffered greatly and it would take many years for it to fully recover.

title: The Tamiami Trail
text:
The 1920s were a time of great change in Florida. Many of these changes negatively impacted the state, but some of the changes were positive. One positive change was the building of the Tamiami Trail. Travel across South Florida was difficult during this time. Many tourists and even residents were unwilling to travel through the swamps and wetlands of the Everglades Region. They would travel around it, which added hours to their journey.

For many years, land developers in South Florida hoped to connect Naples and Miami by building a highway. Their dreams were realized in 1916 when construction on the Tamiami Trail began. It was completed in 1928. The Tamiami Trail made travel through the Everglades much easier. The Tamiami Trail connected the east and west coasts of Florida. It is still used by travelers today.

title: Labor Day Hurricane of 1935
text:
As Floridians began to recover from the economic depression of the 1920s, they faced another major setback in 1935. A massive hurricane made landfall in the Florida Keys on Sept. 2, 1935. This hurricane has become known as the Labor Day Hurricane because it occurred over Labor Day weekend. Hurricanes are a common occurrence in Florida. Even during this time, Floridians were used to hurricanes hitting Florida. However, the Labor Day Hurricane of 1935 was different.

Wind gusts reached over 200 miles per hour. These heavy winds caused massive flooding in the Florida Keys. Waves reached over 20 feet high before crashing onto the shore. Islamorada, a small island community in the Florida Keys, was completely destroyed, and many other towns in the Florida Keys suffered massive damage. The Labor Day Hurricane also destroyed the Overseas Railroad constructed by Henry Flagler over 20 years earlier. The Labor Day Hurricane of 1935 still holds the record as the strongest hurricane to make landfall in the United States in recorded memory.

title: Great Depression-Era Projects in Florida
text:
Florida’s economy began to recover from the Great Depression during the late 1930s. Banks began to reopen and entrepreneurs started to look for new business opportunities in the state. Alfred Du Pont purchased thousands of acres of forestland and started Florida’s first paper mill. The citrus industry finally recovered from several years of bad harvest, frosts, hurricanes, and other natural disasters. Airlines began scheduling flights to and from Florida. This new form of transportation brought more tourists to Florida. After many years, the economy of Florida was booming once again.

Roosevelt's New Deal programs improved life for many Americans. Over 40,000 Floridians participated in projects led by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC). One of the major projects led by the CCC in Florida was planting over 13 million trees across the state.

Thanks to the New Deal, many projects were completed in Florida during the Great Depression.

Citrus Bowl Stadium (1936-Present)

The Citrus Bowl Stadium, now known as Camping World Stadium, was built by the CCC in Orlando. At the time it was built, it could accommodate 8,900 people. The stadium housed sporting events and continues to do so today.

Coral Gables Museum (1939-Present)

Construction of the Coral Gables Museum began in 1939. The Works Progress Administration (WPA) was responsible for the construction of the museum. The museum includes many exhibits on the history of the city of Coral Gables. In recent years, the museum has been renovated and expanded to include more exhibit space and the city’s official visitor center.

Jacksonville Beach Seawall (1938-Present)

The Jacksonville Beach Seawall was built by the WPA in 1938 to protect the beachfront communities from rising water levels.

Overseas Highway (1935-Present)

Much of Henry Flagler’s Over-Sea Railroad was damaged during the Labor Day Hurricane of 1935. The Florida East Coast Railroad did not have the money to rebuild it, so lawmakers hoped to turn the railroad into a highway for automobile traffic. The Overseas Highway opened on July 2, 1938, and continues to be used by visitors to the Florida Keys to this day.

Pensacola International Airport (1933-Present)

Construction of Pensacola’s first airport began in 1933 by city officials. In 1935, the WPA took over the project and completed construction in 1937. That year, the first passenger flight began to arrive and depart from the airport. Today, over 100,000 passengers travel through the airport each month.

title: Zora Neale Hurston
text:
One famous Floridian who rose to fame during the Great Depression was African American author Zora Neale Hurston. Hurston was born in Alabama in 1891 but moved with her family to Eatonville, Florida, at a very early age. While growing up in Eatonville, Hurston was surrounded by colorful stories and folklore. These stories shaped her work later in her life. In 1917, Hurston moved to Baltimore, Maryland, to complete high school and begin her college education.

Hurston’s love for writing and theater grew while attending college. She studied folklore and earned a degree in anthropology. Anthropology is the study of culture, communities, and how they develop. She used this knowledge to study African and Caribbean cultures and their folklore. She traveled throughout the American South and the Caribbean for inspiration and recorded the stories of the people she met.

Hurston began her writing career by publishing short stories and articles in journals and magazines. She also worked with other prominent writers of the time, including Langston Hughes, to create plays. Many of her early works and plays were based on her life in Eatonville and the stories she recorded throughout her travels. In the early 1930s, Hurston returned to Florida to pursue her dream of writing and producing plays. She wrote and produced two plays, which were performed at Rollins College in Winter Park, Florida.

Hurston continued to write and publish short stories during the Great Depression. In 1935, she wrote her first book called Mules and Men. Mules and Men centered on the stories, folklore, sermons, and songs she heard as a child in Eatonville. Her first book was a success, but it was her second book that became her most famous work. Hurston published Their Eyes Were Watching God in 1937, which was based on her life and experiences.

After publishing several books, Hurston continued writing and researching African and Caribbean culture and folklore. She worked as a writer for the Federal Writers Project, a program sponsored by the WPA. She traveled around Florida and conducted interviews with formerly enslaved people. She recorded their stories and wrote about her experiences. She remained in Florida until her death in 1960. Zora Neale Hurston's writings still continue to give readers a glimpse into the lives of Floridians during this time.

title: The Intolerable Acts
text:
In response to the damage of the tea cargo in Boston, Parliament created the Coercive Acts. These were designed by King George III to punish Massachusetts for the tea party and their continued resistance to his actions and his government.

The following was directed at Massachusetts:

Boston Port Act (June 1, 1774): closed off the port of Boston, eliminating commerce and trade in the city

Administration of Justice Act (May 20, 1774): granted a change of location to Great Britain or a British Colony in the event of a jury trial

Massachusetts Government Act (May 20, 1774): repealed the colony’s charter and created an unprecedented amount of royal control

Quartering Act (June 2, 1774): allowed new royal governor General Thomas Gage to house British soldiers in private homes, inns, and other buildings without permission from colonists

Quebec Act (June 22, 1774): designated the western region north of the Ohio River as part of Quebec and made Roman Catholicism the established religion of Quebec; this upset colonial Protestants.

Each colonial legislature called for a meeting of representatives. This was called the First Continental Congress. Representatives gathered in Carpenters Hall in Philadelphia on Sept. 5, 1774. Twelve of the 13 colonies sent delegates.

The first order of business was to write a petition to King George to remove the recent Acts applied to Massachusetts. Each colony had protested the Tea Act in some manner, but Massachusetts was receiving the punishment. The delegates at the congress knew the king could do the same to each of their colonies at any time.

The delegates continued to prepare. They agreed that if the offending Acts of Parliament were not repealed, the colonies would boycott British goods. The congress also recommended that each colony continue to defy Parliament and the king. They also recommended that each colony prepare a militia of Patriots and to begin gathering supplies for them.

The delegates of the congress sent their petition to King George through Benjamin Franklin, who was in London as an agent for the Pennsylvania colony.

At the end of the congressional session in October 1774, the members agreed to meet in a second continental congress the following May, in 1775.

title: Ordinary People and the Fight for Rights
text:
Many ordinary people assisted in the struggle for African American civil rights. They did not become famous for their efforts outside of their own towns and neighborhoods, but their efforts made a difference.

Septima Poinsette Clark was the daughter of a formerly enslaved person. When she grew up, she decided to become a schoolteacher. At the time, African Americans were not allowed to teach school in her town. In an attempt to change this law, Clark joined the NAACP. With the NAACP’s help, she managed to make this goal a reality in 1919. After 40 years of teaching, her contract was not renewed by the city of Charleston. The state government made it illegal for public employees to join civil rights groups. She lost her job. However, she increased her efforts with the NAACP and the civil rights movement. Her next move was to accept a job at the Highlander Folk School in Monteagle, Tennessee.

In the 1950s and 1960s, the Highlander Folk School supported the civil rights movement. There, Clark became the director of the Citizenship School Program. Citizenship schools were designed by civil rights leaders to teach African American adults how to read and write so that they could pass literacy tests and register to vote. Under her leadership, more than 800 citizenship schools were established. For all of her hard work, Clark was given the Living Legacy Award by President Jimmy Carter in 1979. This award honors African Americans for their extraordinary efforts to improve the lives of U.S. citizens.

Modjeska Monteith Simkins was another leader in the Civil Rights Movement. She was born in Columbia, South Carolina, in 1899 and grew up on a farm. When she got out of school, she became a public school teacher at Booker T. Washington High School in 1921. She had to resign when she got married in 1929 because where she lived married women were not allowed to teach.

Simkins began working in public health in 1931. She became the only full-time statewide African American public health worker. She worked in that position for nearly 11 years. She was fired in 1942 because she had become increasingly involved with the NAACP. She worked with this organization to push her state closer to racial equality, particularly in the area of education. Simkins passed away in 1992. At her funeral, she was remembered as someone who “challenged Black citizens to stand up and demand their rightful place in the state and the nation.”

title: Landforms
text:
Landforms are natural features on the Earth's surface. They form in many different ways. There are many types of landforms. Each has its own name.

Mountains and hills are raised areas of land. Valleys are large dips in the land. They are usually “V”- or “U”-shaped. Canyons are like valleys but deeper. Canyons are narrow and have steep sides. Deserts and beaches are also landforms. Deserts and beaches can have sand dunes. These are mounds of sand shaped by the wind. Plains are large, flat stretches of land. A plain raised higher than the land around it is a plateau.

Maps and globes can show us where landforms are located. We have many large landforms in the United States. The Appalachian Mountains are in the East. The Rocky Mountains are in the West. The Mojave Desert is in the Southwest.

title: Models
text:
A model is a representation of something. Models can show large or small things. They can show things from long ago or how things are now. Models can help us remember things that happen. They can help us understand something. A model can even help us explain something. A map can be a model. A picture can be a model. Some toys are models of real things. All these models can help us learn about real things.

You can make a model. You can draw a model. You can draw objects and ideas. You can draw what you see. You can draw things that happen. You can also build a model out of many different types of materials. When creating a model, it is important to include clear labels. Labels help people understand what the model is trying to show.

Models help scientists explain the world. Look around your classroom. Do you see any models?

Is it possible to have a perfect model? Are there some things that models fail to show well compared to the real thing?

title: Segregation in the United States
text:
The decades following World War II were a period of expansion and growth in the United States. Many Americans lived in well-kept suburban homes with at least one shiny new car in the driveway. Families traveled the new interstate highways on vacations to beaches, national parks, and theme parks. Most children in the suburbs graduated from high school and went on to college. Many people were able to take advantage of this new American dream, but there was still a large part of the population that struggled to achieve these goals.

This new way of life was not experienced by all Americans. Following the Civil War, many state and local governments restricted the rights of different racial and ethnic groups, including African Americans, Native Americans, Latin Americans, and other racial and ethnic groups. Laws and policies were put in place that created segregation. Segregation is the forced separation of different groups of people in a country, state, or community based on race, age, gender, religion, abilities, or beliefs. These policies also prevented various groups from using their civil, political, and economic rights. Segregation kept many people from opportunities in education, employment, housing, and other areas of life.

In 1896, the Supreme Court ruled in a case called Plessy v. Ferguson that segregation was constitutional, or not illegal. The ruling allowed segregation if people of different racial groups were given “separate but equal” accommodations. As a result, segregation became more common. Many facilities and areas of life were not equal. When it came to education, there was rarely any equality.

For example, Black children were not allowed to attend the same schools as white children in many areas of the country. Public schools and their funding, or the money provided for supplies and teachers' salaries, were controlled by elected government leaders who were not African American. Schools for Black children did not receive as much funding as schools for white children. As a result, these schools could not provide their teachers and students with adequate or enough materials. Schools for Black students were often housed in older buildings that were not safe. African American teachers were also paid less than white teachers.

African Americans and other minority groups were not allowed to sit in the same area of a bus or train as white people. They were required to sit at the back of trains and buses, even if there were empty seats in the front. Many restaurants would not serve African Americans. Movie theaters had separate entrances that led to separate seating areas. African Americans and other racial groups were not allowed to use the same public spaces as white people. They could only drink from designated fountains or use specific restrooms. Many Americans faced difficulties with voting, getting jobs, and gaining an education because of the practice of segregation and laws that were passed to enforce this practice.

Many Americans believed that this treatment was unjust and did not follow the principles outlined in our country’s founding documents. They joined together to protect the rights of everyone. Many people filed lawsuits in courts concerning violations of civil rights. Gradually, based on court rulings, the U.S. government began to make decisions and enact legislation to help create equality in housing, education, and employment. However, progress was slow and was often hindered by public and political opposition.

title: The Civil Rights Movement
text:
The American Civil Rights Movement was a response to laws that limited the rights of many American citizens based on their race. These laws were put in place soon after the Civil War ended. More were added as the decades went on.

Brown v. Board of Education

In 1951, Oliver Brown filed a lawsuit against the Topeka Board of Education. Brown's daughter, Linda, was not allowed to attend the school closest to the family home because it was a school for white children and the Brown family was African American. Thurgood Marshall was one of the key lawyers in the case. Marshall argued in court that “separate but equal” was illegal. He insisted that segregated schools could never be equal. The Brown family lost their case at the state level. The loss in the lower court helped the case move to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Marshall presented the case to the U.S. Supreme Court in the spring of 1954. The justices debated their decision. On May 17, 1954, Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote, “In the field of public education the doctrine of ‘separate but equal’ has no place.” He also stated that segregation violated the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment. The decision of the court ordered schools across the United States to integrate. This decision set the standard for later events of the Civil Rights Movement. The process was not easy and did not happen quickly. In many places, integration was strongly opposed by community members and their leaders.

Montgomery Bus Boycott

The Civil Rights Movement gained momentum in 1955. In December 1955, an African American department store seamstress in Montgomery, Alabama, named Rosa Parks headed home after a day of work. Parks boarded a city bus and took a seat. Public bus drivers were authorized to enforce segregation laws on the bus. A public bus had clearly marked seating for white people and African American passengers. As passengers continued to board, the designated section for whites filled to capacity. The bus driver instructed Parks and three other African American passengers to give their seats to white passengers. Parks refused and was arrested for refusing the orders of the bus driver. Parks went peacefully with the arresting officers without any resistance.

In response to Rosa Parks's arrest, African Americans in Montgomery boycotted the city bus system. Led by Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., many African Americans refused to ride the bus for 381 days. The boycott ended when the Supreme Court ruled segregation on buses was illegal. Dr. King and other leaders of the movement continued their efforts. They held peaceful protests and marches, gave speeches, and wrote articles. They worked on changing laws to ensure that all Americans’ civil rights would be protected.

Little Rock Nine

In 1954, the Supreme Court made its decision in a case called Brown v. Board of Education. The Supreme Court stated that segregation was unconstitutional. One of the first places where people complied with the ruling was at Little Rock Central High School in Arkansas. Nine African American students who attended a segregated school were chosen to go to the school in 1957. Many people in Little Rock did not like the idea of integration. Crowds of white people tried to stop the students from getting to their classes. The governor sent the Arkansas National Guard to prevent the students from going inside the school. The group of students became known as the Little Rock Nine.

President Eisenhower intervened with the authority of the executive branch of the national government. The students were able to go to class, but people continued to bully and threaten the students every day. This did not stop the Little Rock Nine, and they continued to attend the school. The courage shown by these nine students strengthened the Civil Rights Movement and helped ensure that all Americans had access to a quality education.

Tallahassee Bus Boycott

On May 26, 1956, two African American college students, Wilhelmina Jakes and Carrie Patterson, boarded a city bus in Tallahassee, Florida. They sat in seats that were normally reserved for white passengers. The bus driver told them to move, but they refused. The driver called the police and the two women were arrested. The next day, students from the Florida Agricultural and Mechanical University (FAMU) agreed that they would stop using buses in Tallahassee.

For the next seven months, people all over Tallahassee boycotted the city’s bus system. They worked together to carpool or walk wherever they needed to go. Police arrested carpool drivers for illegally transporting people. Some of these drivers were forced to pay fines. The boycott made it difficult for bus companies to make money. They realized that they had to change their rules to stay in business. By the summer of 1957, Tallahassee’s buses were integrated. The boycott was a success and also proved that peaceful protests could work.

Tallahassee Inter-Civic Council

To support the Tallahassee bus boycott, Reverend C.K. Steele and other members of the African American community organized the Inter-Civic Council (ICC). Steele stated, "I would rather walk in dignity than ride in humiliation." The ICC, which was run by Steele, organized carpools to help those who were boycotting the city’s buses. They wrote letters to representatives in the state government to urge them to desegregate the buses in the city. Following the bus boycott, the ICC continued to support civil rights efforts throughout Florida.

Sit-Ins

Sit-ins were a form of peaceful protest during the Civil Rights Movement. The purpose of the sit-in was to have people occupy a public place. This would restrict access and movement of other customers or patrons. Sit-ins were a way to draw attention to inequalities and injustices of a business or public policy. People all over the country conducted sit-ins to protest segregation. Many sit-ins took place across Florida during the 1950s and 1960s.

The first sit-in in Florida occurred in Tallahassee on Feb. 13, 1960. African American students and members of local civil rights organizations staged a sit-in at the Woolworth's store in downtown Tallahassee. They sat at the lunch counter, which was designated for white customers, to protest segregation. A few weeks later, on March 5, 1960, civil rights leaders staged sit-ins at two restaurants in Orlando. In August 1960, members of the Jacksonville Youth Council participated in several sit-ins at restaurants in downtown Jacksonville.

Because of the actions of civil rights activists and the peaceful sit-ins, many restaurants and stores across Florida began to change their policies of segregation.

title: Harry and Harriette Moore
text:
Harry and Harriette Moore were two of Florida’s earliest civil rights leaders who spoke out against segregation and discrimination in the state. Harry Moore met Harriette Vyda Simms while he was teaching elementary school in Brevard County. They married and furthered their education at Bethune Cookman College. In 1934, the Moores organized a chapter of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, a national civil rights organization, in Brevard County.

The Moores and their colleagues worked tirelessly to end segregation and discrimination in Florida. They fought against segregation in schools, registered thousands of Americans being discriminated against to vote, and worked to gain equal pay for teachers of all backgrounds. Because of their efforts, membership in the Florida branch of the NAACP grew to over 10,000 members. In 1951, Harry and Harriette Moore were assassinated in their home by Ku Klux Klan members. The legacy of the Moores still lives on. Today, several landmarks in Brevard County bear their name and their efforts inspired many other civil rights leaders across the country.

title: Virgil Darnell Hawkins
text:
Virgil Darnell Hawkins was one of the first people in Florida to advocate for equal education for all students. Hawkins was born and raised in Florida. As an African American man, he dealt with segregation on a daily basis. He wanted to change the laws in Florida and hoped to become a lawyer. In 1949, Hawkins applied to the University of Florida to study law. Although he met all of the academic requirements to attend, the university refused his admission because he was African American. Hawkins refused to take no for an answer, and he took the matter to court.

For the next nine years, he fought in the courts for the right to attend the University of Florida. Hawkins argued that the university was not upholding the 14th Amendment to the Constitution. The case was eventually sent to the U.S. Supreme Court. The Supreme Court agreed with Hawkins, but people still found ways to stop him from attending law school at the University of Florida. Hawkins refused to give up. In 1965, Hawkins finally earned his law degree from the New England School of Law in Boston.

Following his graduation, Hawkins petitioned the Florida Supreme Court to become a lawyer. In 1976, after 28 years of fighting, Hawkins was given permission to practice law in Florida. He opened up his own law office in Leesburg, Florida. He helped hundreds of clients who were too poor to afford legal services and continued to support civil rights legislation until his death in 1988. Because of his and others' efforts, the University of Florida was desegregated in 1958. Virgil Darnell Hawkins exemplified perseverance and resilience throughout his life.

title: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.
text:
Martin Luther King Jr. was one of the most important African American leaders of the Civil Rights Movement. King was born in Alabama on Jan. 15, 1929. King graduated from high school at the age of 15. He earned numerous college degrees, including a Ph.D. from Boston University. In 1954, he became a pastor in Montgomery, Alabama. There, he began organizing and working with other civil rights leaders to end segregation and ensure equality for all Americans. King soon became recognized nationally as a leader of the movement. He continued his efforts, wrote numerous articles, and led peaceful protests and marches. King gave countless speeches in support of civil rights, including his famous “I Have a Dream” speech during the historic March on Washington in 1963.

In the spring of 1964, King and members of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC) visited St. Augustine, Florida. Their goal was to end segregation in the city before it celebrated its 400th anniversary. King stated that “We are determined this city will not celebrate its quadricentennial as a segregated city.” They organized demonstrations, sit-ins, and peaceful marches throughout the city.

King and other civil rights organizers were arrested in St. Augustine for requesting to be seated at a segregated restaurant. This did not deter King and other civil rights leaders from their peaceful fight for equal rights. On Oct. 14, 1964, King was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. On April 4, 1968, he was in Memphis, Tennessee, preparing to lead another protest when he was assassinated. Although Dr. King died, the Civil Rights Movement continued and grew. Dr. King has been memorialized in a monument in Washington, D.C. There is also a national holiday in January to honor his legacy.

title: Civil Rights Legislation
text:
Public Protests against segregation and violence in the Civil Rights Movement increased after the ruling to desegregate schools in 1954. Gradually, the federal government saw the need to create laws on a federal level to guarantee civil rights to all Americans.

Civil Rights Act of 1957

The first of the acts passed in the U.S. Congress was the Civil Rights Act of 1957. It was the first civil rights act passed by Congress since 1875. The act created the Civil Rights Division in the U.S. Justice Department. It gave federal officials the power to prosecute any individual or group who tried to take away another citizen’s right to vote.

Civil Rights Act of 1960

The Civil Rights Act of 1960 was passed to strengthen the 1957 act. The new act provided the opportunity for federal inspection of local voter registration rolls. It also authorized courts to appoint people to help all Americans to register and vote.

Civil Rights Act of 1964

The most significant civil rights legislation of this time was the Civil Rights Act of 1964. This act outlawed discrimination on the basis of race, color, sex, or national origin. The law required equal access to public places and jobs. It reinforced the desegregation of schools and the right to vote for all Americans. This act has been used many times in defense of the civil rights of many citizens in America.

Voting Rights Act of 1965

President Lyndon Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act of 1965 into law. This act banned unfair requirements that prevented citizens from voting. It also provided federal supervision of the voter registration processes. This was important in areas where different racial and ethnic groups had a low rate of registration. As a result of this law, the percentage of these groups who were registered to vote grew from around 10 percent to nearly 65 percent in less than 10 years.

Civil Rights Act of 1968

In 1968, Congress passed a new Civil Rights Act, which was also called the Open Housing Law. This law made it illegal for anyone to be denied the right to buy or rent a home based on race, gender, or ethnicity. As a result, all Americans could choose to live wherever they wanted. Slowly, neighborhoods across Florida and throughout the United States began to integrate. However, some cities and officials did not always follow the law. It took many years and multiple lawsuits for things to improve.
