title: Treaty of Paris, 1783
text:
The last major battle of the American Revolution was fought in 1781. The Americans and French forced British Army General Cornwallis to surrender at Yorktown. After years of fighting, the British decided that the war was too expensive to continue. Although the battles were over, British forces remained in the U.S. They were still stationed around Charleston, South Carolina. The powerful main army was still in New York. While neither side took any decisive action, it took another two years for all the issues to be resolved.

At last, both sides agreed to meet and discuss terms for a treaty to end the war. The king sent representatives from Great Britain. The United States was represented by Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, and John Jay. They met in Paris, France, near the end of 1782. They spent 10 months working out the details of the Treaty of Paris. The treaty set out conditions that each side agreed to follow:

Britain would recognize the United States of America as an independent nation.

Britain ceded (gave up) its territory east of the Mississippi River. This doubled the size of the new country.

Florida would be ceded to Spain.

The United States was granted fishing rights off of the British-Canadian coast. This was a very valuable fishing region.

The Mississippi River was opened to navigation, or travel, by both U.S. and British citizens.

Issues of American debt owed to British creditors were resolved.

Many colonists had remained loyal to the king during the war. The treaty guaranteed that they would be treated fairly. The property that had been taken from them during the war would be restored to them.

Great Britain knew the value of continued trade with the new United States, so they were very agreeable in the process of creating the treaty. The Treaty of Paris was signed on Sept. 3, 1783. The British signed a separate peace treaty with France and Spain, officially ending the Revolutionary War.

title: Washington Resigns His Commission
text:
Only once before in history had a victorious general stepped away and resigned his commission. Cincinnatus, an ancient Roman patriot, quietly returned to his farm after his victories in war. This was more than 2,000 years before the American Revolution. It was extremely rare for a military leader to walk away from such power and authority. Most would have remained in their position and used their power in the military to rule. However, George Washington knew that he and his army fought for freedom from this kind of military rule. He knew that for the Revolution to be complete, he had to step away from power. On Dec. 23, 1783, he reported to the Continental Congress:

Having now finished the work assigned me, I retire from the great theatre of Action; and bidding an Affectional farewell to the August body under whose orders I have so long acted, I here offer my Commission, and take my leave of all the employments of public life.

Washington’s action impressed even his enemies. King George III was reported to have said that Washington’s resignation would “place him in a light the most distinguished of any man living.” The king went so far as to say that he “thought him [Washington] the greatest character of the age.”

There is a painting titled General George Washington Resigning His Commission by John Trumbull. It is on display in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol. This painting depicts the scene on Dec. 23, 1783, in the Maryland State House in Annapolis. There, George Washington resigned his commission as commander-in-chief of the Continental Army. This voluntary action was significant for establishing civilian authority over the military. This was a fundamental principle of American democracy. The artist, John Trumbull, considered Washington's resignation to be “one of the highest moral lessons ever given to the world.”

title: The End of the War
text:
There were many factors that ultimately led to the end of the American Revolution. The United States formed several key alliances with several powerful European nations. The rising cost of the war heavily impacted the British government. This led to a major decline in the British war effort in North America.

In May 1781, Cornwallis led 7,000 British troops out of North Carolina and retreated to Yorktown, Virginia. Yorktown was on the coast and could be attacked by French ships. The British set up their defenses and waited for reinforcements. French ships moved toward Yorktown through the Chesapeake Bay, blocking British supply lines.

George Washington sent 4,500 troops, led by Marquis de Lafayette, to Yorktown. They would prevent the British Army from leaving. Washington sent other troops to join the French fleet in the Chesapeake Bay. Washington arrived in Yorktown on Sept. 28, 1781, and besieged the city for 11 days. Unable to defend the city, Cornwallis surrendered on Oct. 19, 1781.

Cornwallis’s surrender and the American victory at Yorktown did not bring an end to the fighting in North America, however. The fight to control the continent continued between American and British forces and their allies through the end of 1782.

Jan. 2: British forces defeat American militiamen near Charleston, South Carolina.

Jan. 19 to Feb. 13: French forces capture British-held St. Kitts in the Caribbean Sea.

March 8 and 9: American militiamen attack a group of Native Americans they believed were allies of the British near Gnadenhutten in present-day Ohio.

April 8: Battle of Delaware Bay. American naval vessels are attacked by three British ships but fought back, resulting in an American victory.

May 8: American and Spanish forces capture Nassau, Bahamas, a strategic port and major center of trade, from the British.

July 11: The remaining British soldiers and Loyalists evacuate Savannah, Georgia.

July 13: British forces and members of the Seneca tribe attack Hannahstown, Pennsylvania. The townspeople retreat to the fort, but the attacking force burns homes, farms, and other buildings in the town. Michael Huffnagle, a member of the town, records the event in a letter to American General William Irvine, stating that, “Such wanton destruction I have never beheld, burning and destroying as they went. The People of this Place behaved brave; retired to the Fort, left all of their prey to the Enemy, and with twenty men only and nine guns in good order, we stood the attack ‘til dark.”

Aug. 19: Battle of Blue Licks. British rangers and their Native American allies ambush members of the Kentucky militia, killing 64 Americans. Frontiersman and explorer Daniel Boone is present at the battle. He records the event in a letter to the governor of Virginia:

We discovered the enemy lying in wait for us. On this discovery we formed our columns into one single line, and marched up in their front within about forty yards before there was a gun fired … The inhabitants of this county are very much alarmed at the thoughts of the Indians bringing another campaign into our country this Fall. If this should be the case, it will break up these settlements. I hope therefore your Excellency will take the matter into your consideration, and send us some relief as quick as possible…

Aug. 27: The Battle of Combahee River. British sailors and soldiers sail up the Combahee River in South Carolina to capture supplies from American farmers in the area. The Americans drive the British out of the area but suffer heavy losses. Colonel John Laurens, one of the heroes of Yorktown, is one of the many American soldiers killed during this conflict.

Nov. 10: Battle of Piqua. American General George Rogers Clark raids villages of the Shawnee, allies of the British, near Chillicothe, in present-day Ohio. Clark also destroys the British trading post, Loramie's Store.

Dec. 14: The remaining British soldiers and Loyalists evacuate Charleston, South Carolina.

title: Fate of the Loyalists
text:
Not all American colonists supported the cause for independence. Historians estimate that about 500,000, or 20 percent of all colonists remained loyal to the British government. Loyalists faced a very different fate than the colonists who supported independence. Between 60,000 and 80,000 Loyalists left the American colonies during or after the American Revolution. They primarily settled in Great Britain, Canada, the Caribbean, and even Spanish Florida.

Many Loyalists stayed and faced significant hardships. Thousands of Loyalists who remained in the new United States had their property vandalized or destroyed. Those who lost their property during the war often did not regain it after the war. Some Loyalists were able to recover their property but were forced to pay additional taxes to reclaim it. Others faced public humiliation, ridicule, and violence.

Life for most Loyalists was very difficult following the war. Many Loyalists recorded their experiences in letters and other publications during and after the war. Judge Samuel Curwen, who was born in Massachusetts, spent nine years in exile for remaining loyal to the British government. During his exile, he wrote in a letter to a friend:

I abandoned my dwelling, friends, and means of life, which you know I possessed in no small degree and might have retained on the comparative trifling condition of insults, reproaches, and perhaps a dress of tar and feathers; an alternative I now see much to be preferred to the distresses of mind I am daily suffering.

In 1786, merchant James Clarke, who went into exile following the war, wrote, "My Attachment to our native Country is so fervent and sincere that I could freely give up my Life, and Ten Thousand more if I possess them, could I restore dear Rhode Island to its former happy, happy Situation."

title: Families Torn Apart
text:
The American Revolution had a profound impact on Patriots, Loyalists, and thousands of other colonists in the new American nation. Families were often at odds with one another and had differing opinions over American independence. Many families were torn apart because of these differing opinions.

Benjamin Franklin and his son William were an example of how differing opinions tore families apart during the American Revolution. Benjamin Franklin was an early supporter of American independence. He was a member of the Continental Congress and helped draft the Declaration of Independence. He also served as an ambassador to France and played a vital role in forming an alliance with the French government. Franklin was a Patriot, but his son had a very different opinion.

In 1762, King George III appointed William Franklin, Benjamin Franklin’s son, the Royal Governor of New Jersey. He worked closely with the British Parliament and was a loyal supporter of the king. When tensions began to rise between the colonists and the British government, William opposed the actions of the colonists. Benjamin Franklin was convinced that he could change his son’s mind, but William refused to abandon his allegiance to Great Britain. The relationship between Benjamin and William Franklin never recovered. William left the colonies in 1777, and the two only exchanged a few letters following the Revolution before they cut all ties with one another.

The Franklins were not the only family torn apart by the American Revolution. The Flucker family of Massachusetts was also a casualty of divided loyalties. The Fluckers were a wealthy and well-known family from Massachusetts. Thomas Flucker served as the Secretary of Massachusetts and worked closely with British colonial leaders. In 1774, Lucy Flucker, the daughter of Thomas and his wife Hannah, disobeyed her family’s wishes and married Henry Knox, a book shop owner from Boston.

The Fluckers remained loyal to the British government, while Henry and Lucy Knox joined the Patriot cause. Henry Knox joined the Continental Army and quickly rose through the ranks. He was promoted to the rank of brigadier general by 1777. The Flucker family left Boston and settled in England in 1775. The relationship between Lucy Knox and her family remained strained, and they never fully reconciled, even after the war ended.

title: Dissent Among the Colonies
text:
Following the American Revolution, the colonies disagreed on how best to move forward as a nation. There were many issues that needed to be addressed by the new country. What shape would the new government take? What powers would it have, and which powers would the states keep? What kind of economic policies would the country pursue and put in place?

The main problem was that any attempt to entrust a central government with power meant that individual states would have to give up power. This is something they did not want to do. Larger colonies like Virginia and New York would lose the ability to govern themselves and give up some of their independence to a new U.S. government. Taxes imposed on the new states by the government caused disagreements and rebellion in certain states as they opposed what they saw as government overreach.

Individual colonies borrowed money during the war, and each one owed a different amount to various countries following the war. Northern colonies supported Alexander Hamilton’s idea to have the new national government take on all debts taken out by the colonies during the war. Southern colonies, which generally owed less money following the war, did not want the central government to have to pay back money their colonies did not borrow. Ultimately, the U.S. government took on all colonial debts, which gave the newly formed states a clean economic slate.

title: Shays's Rebellion
text:
Though the end of the American Revolution meant that the United States would be a country free from British rule, that did not mean that the new nation was free from problems. Waging a war was very expensive, and the new American government faced many economic challenges.

One of these challenges was how to pay veterans who fought either in the Continental Army or one of the state militias. These veterans received very little to no pay for their service, and many had to go into debt to provide for their families. When it came time to pay those debts, they were unable to do so. In spite of this, the state government demanded payment, even though they were not paying the veterans their pensions.

One person facing this struggle was Daniel Shays, a former captain in the Continental Army. Shays was a farmer, and when he and other veterans began losing their land to debt collectors, tensions boiled over. In August 1786, the Massachusetts state government refused to help Shays or any other war veterans. Between August and December 1786, Shays and his followers, called “Regulators,” led many protests against debt collectors taking veterans’ lands.

On Jan. 25, 1787, Shays and 1,500 Regulators approached the federal armory in Springfield, Massachusetts. Their intent was to take control of the building to force the government to listen to their concerns. There were 1,200 Massachusetts militiamen guarding the armory. Confrontation between the two groups increased from shouting to the firing of weapons. Four of the Regulators were killed and 20 more were wounded.

This event contributed to the current government realizing that the Articles of Confederation did not protect the liberties of the people. A delegation of representatives from each state convened in Philadelphia to discuss changes in the current government. The Philadelphia Convention of 1787 was created for the United States government to be stronger and better able to address the economic and political needs of the people.

title: Elbridge Gerry
text:
Elbridge Gerry came from a large Massachusetts family of 11 children. He grew up watching his father serve as an important leader in the community. As a young man, Gerry attended Harvard University. The more he learned, the more he felt that the colonists were justified in resisting unfair rules placed upon them by the British government. Gerry served in several local government positions after graduating. He was chosen to serve as a delegate of Massachusetts at the 1787 Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

As an Anti-Federalist, Gerry was concerned about the proposed document of the Constitution. He saw several issues that he believed would make the federal government too powerful. He refused to sign the document unless several amendments were added. These amendments, known as the Bill of Rights, were added in 1791.

After the Constitution was ratified, Gerry was elected to serve in the House of Representatives in the new Congress. He later went on to serve as vice president to James Madison from 1812 until his death in 1814.

title: George Washington
text:
George Washington is often called the Father of Our Country. He was an active member of his community and nation. He served as the leader of the Continental Army during the American Revolution. He inspired the colonial soldiers to be brave and have faith in themselves. Washington led the new United States to victory over Great Britain. People trusted him and believed in him as a leader. He believed that governments should listen to the opinions of the people. Washington served bravely in the war with the other Patriots. Following the Revolutionary War, he left the army and returned to his farm in Virginia to live as a normal citizen.

In 1787, Washington was elected as chairman of the Constitutional Convention. He believed that the new nation could not and would not survive without a strong central government, national freedoms, and the protection of individual liberties. He worked with the other members of the convention to create a document that reflected their ideas for a new government. He believed so strongly in the principles and values outlined in the new Constitution that he was willing to sign it.

In 1789, George Washington became the first president of the United States. Washington tried to get the country's finances in order with the help of Alexander Hamilton, the new secretary of the treasury. He appointed Henry Knox his secretary of war. Knox advised the president on military matters and on relations with American Indians. He worked to create strong alliances with foreign nations. During his first term, Washington toured the United States and learned that most Americans supported their new government leaders. He hoped that the new United States would expand its territory west of the Mississippi River during his presidency.

He served two terms as president and refused to run for a third because he believed that one man should not hold that much power for that long. He set the standards for those that followed in his footsteps. Today, you can find his portrait on the dollar bill and quarter.

title: Conflict and Compromise at the Convention
text:
One of the greatest challenges faced at the Constitutional Convention of 1787 was dividing the power between state and federal government. Some delegates wanted a strong central government that had more power over the people and states. They were called Federalists. Other delegates favored a weaker federal government that gave more power to the states and the people. They were called Anti-Federalists. Both sides wrote essays that argued their points. These became known as the Federalist Papers and Anti-Federalist Papers. During the convention, several plans were presented to help balance the power of the new government.

The Virginia Plan

James Madison, a delegate from Virginia, presented the Virginia Plan. This plan gave Congress more power over the states and also provided for an executive branch of national government. This branch would carry out the laws passed by Congress. The plan also included a judicial branch to interpret, or explain, the laws. However, negotiations began to get sticky when the smaller states learned that states with larger populations would have more representatives in Congress than the smaller states.

The New Jersey Plan

William Paterson, a delegate from New Jersey, proposed a different plan. The New Jersey Plan said that each state, no matter its size, would have the same number of representatives in Congress. The large states didn’t agree with this idea. They felt that because they had more people, they should also have more say in running the nation.

The Great Compromise

Roger Sherman of Connecticut came up with an idea that bridged ideas from both plans. He proposed that Congress be made up of two parts, called houses. In the Senate, each state would have two senators, giving both large states and small states equal power. In the House of Representatives, the number of representatives would be determined by population. The larger the state, the more representatives it would have. Both sides agreed to the Great Compromise.

Slavery

The economy of the South relied on enslaved people to keep farms and plantations running. Many delegates of the North wanted to outlaw the slave trade, but delegates of the South disagreed. A compromise was finally reached. The slave trade would be allowed to go on for another 20 years and then be outlawed in 1808.

The North and South also disagreed over how to count the enslaved people when figuring out the population of each state. Population determined how many representatives each state had in Congress and affected collecting taxes. Finally, the Three-Fifths Compromise was agreed upon. Three out of every five, or three-fifths, of the enslaved people would be counted in the population. This ensured that state populations wouldn’t be too high in slave states. From their perspective, the issue of slavery was considered solved, at least for the time being.

Status of Native American Nations

During the Articles of Confederation, each state interacted with the Native American nations. Some states treated the Native Americans fairly. Other states did not. James Madison proposed that Congress be given the power to manage all interactions with the Native Americans, whether they lived within the boundaries of a state or not. This gave consistency in actions for all Native American nations through the federal government. The final wording of the Constitution said that Congress had power “to regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes.”

Individual Rights

Some delegates wanted to add a bill of rights to the Constitution to protect important individual rights. Others felt that since most states had their own bills of rights, this was unnecessary. Thirty-nine of the 55 delegates signed their names to the Constitution without a formal bill of rights on Sept. 17, 1787. Failing to add a bill of rights would prove to be a mistake that had to be corrected in the near future.

title: Week 27 Essential Question
text: How did the Constitutional Convention attempt to balance the interests of all of the states?

title: Week 28 Essential Question
text: How did the United States change in the first decades following the founding of the country?

title: The Northwest Ordinance, 1787
text:
When the new United States government signed the Treaty of Paris with Great Britain in 1783, they gained more than just the land within the 13 American Colonies. They also received a large area of land west of the colonies that came to be known as the Northwest Territory. The question of what was to happen with this unorganized territory was one of the first major issues faced by the new country. The answers to this question would impact all future U.S. land claims and territories.

Each new state wanted to gain as much land as they could for themselves, and Virginia was moving aggressively to claim as much of the Northwest Territory as they could. Small eastern states like Connecticut and Rhode Island had no realistic claim to the territory because they were separated from it by other states.

Because of this, they opposed the enlargement of states like Virginia. Giving those states more land would make them more powerful in the new national government. As a democracy, the states with more land and more people would have a larger say in how the country was run.

To further complicate issues of land in the West, soldiers from the Continental Army were given pieces of land for their service during the Revolutionary War. Those former soldiers and other settlers moving west began claiming land for themselves. Some argued that they had bought the land from Native Americans, while others simply chose an empty piece of land upon which to build their homestead. This led to arguments and disputes over land ownership.

To solve these problems, Congress passed the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. The Ordinance laid out the process by which the Northwest Territory, and future territories, would be admitted as a state to the country. It also ensured that each new state would be equal to all other states, which is not something that was guaranteed before the ordinance was passed.

Each territory would have a governor and other government officials appointed by the U.S. Congress. Once 5,000 free men were living in a territory, it would need to have an elected legislative body. Finally, once the population reached 60,000 people and a state constitution had been drafted, the territory could apply for statehood. The ordinance also outlawed slavery in any newly created territory, which would have major consequences as there was increased conflict over the issue of slavery between the states into the 1800s.

However, the specific question of what to do with the Northwest Territory remained. Using the guidance of the Northwest Ordinance of 1787, Congress eventually annexed Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota into the United States from the land that originally made up the Northwest Territory.

title: The Louisiana Purchase
text:
Thomas Jefferson faced many challenges during his time as president. He made positive improvements to the United States. His greatest achievement was the Louisiana Purchase. On April 30, 1803, President Jefferson and his ambassador in France purchased the Louisiana Territory from France for $15 million. This territory was 828,000 square miles of land west of the Mississippi River. As a result, the United States gained control of the Mississippi River and important trading posts along its banks.

Jefferson knew that acquiring the Louisiana Territory was the key to westward expansion. Most Americans knew nothing of the land west of the Mississippi River. Jefferson wanted to know more about this vast area of land. He wanted to establish trade with the Native American tribes of the territory. He also wanted to find a water route from the Mississippi River to the Pacific Ocean. With Congress's approval, he created a Corps of Discovery to achieve his goals. However, who would lead this monumental expedition into the unknown?

title: The Corps of Discovery
text:
Thomas Jefferson chose Meriwether Lewis to lead the Corps of Discovery. Lewis was a former soldier who served as Jefferson’s personal secretary. In the summer of 1803, Lewis was tasked with recruiting members and gathering supplies for the long and arduous expedition. To prepare, Jefferson sent Lewis to Philadelphia to study medicine, botany, zoology, and navigation from experts in each field. While there, Lewis also purchased supplies. He commissioned the building of several vessels for transportation and secured weapons for hunting and defense, too.

Lewis chose Captain William Clark to help him lead the expedition. Clark was an experienced soldier. He recruited and trained the men who would serve as members of the expedition. Clark also served as the company’s principal cartographer.

On May 21, 1804, the Corps of Discovery began their expedition. They traveled west from St. Louis, Missouri. Lewis and Clark kept detailed journals throughout the expedition. They cataloged hundreds of plants, wrote detailed descriptions of countless animals, and created new maps of the territory. They even sent plant and animal specimens back to President Jefferson in Washington, D.C.

Along their journey, the Corps of Discovery negotiated peace treaties with many Native American tribes. They exchanged gifts and set up trade agreements in the hopes of creating lasting friendships with the tribal leaders of the territory. Many tribes agreed to peaceful trade with the United States. However, other tribes didn't welcome the Corps and had no desire to negotiate terms of peace.

In November 1804, the Corps arrived in the Dakota Territory and built their winter quarters. They resided at Fort Mandan until April 1805. Before continuing their journey, they met a few friendly people. They were a French-Canadian fur trader named Toussaint Charbonneau, his Shoshone wife, Sacagawea, and their infant son, Jean Baptiste. Charbonneau and Sacagawea joined the Corps of Discovery as guides and interpreters with their young son.

The expedition continued overland through the rough terrain of the Rocky Mountains. Sacagawea guided the explorers through Native American territory. She had knowledge of the land, plants, animals, and the native peoples of the West. This knowledge helped the explorers survive the difficult journey to the Pacific. Eighteen months after leaving St. Louis, the Corps of Discovery reached the Pacific Ocean in present-day Oregon.

On March 23, 1806, the members of the expedition began their journey back home. It took six months to reach St. Louis, Missouri. They didn't find a direct water route to the Pacific Ocean as they had hoped for. However, the Corps of Discovery strengthened the relationship between the United States and many of the Native American tribes they encountered. They also identified, cataloged, and collected plant and animal specimens that were unknown to most Americans at the time. Their expedition marked the beginning of America’s settlement of the frontier.

title: Needs
text: A need is what you must have to live. There are many things we need.

title: Shelter

title: Jean Baptiste Point DuSable
text:
One of the earliest-known colonists to settle in the Northwest Territory was a man named Jean Baptiste Point DuSable. There are very few sources that survive today that record DuSable’s early life. Most historians believe that DuSable was born in Haiti around 1745. His father was a French sailor and his mother was an enslaved African woman. He landed in New Orleans, Louisiana, sometime in the early 1770s. He traveled to the Louisiana Territory to start his own trading company.

From New Orleans, DuSable sailed up the Mississippi River. He formed good relationships with the Native American tribes that lived in the Great Lakes region. These relationships and his entrepreneurial spirit led to his success in the fur trading industry. He became a chief negotiator between the Indigenous people of the area and European settlers.

In 1778, DuSable settled along the Chicago River near Lake Michigan. He built an outpost, which included his home and a dairy, smokehouse, poultry house, bakehouse, stable, barn, and workshop. He traded the goods he made for other items and sold them to explorers and fur traders who passed through the area. DuSable’s outpost was the first European settlement in what is now the city of Chicago. He remained in the area for many years before selling his property and retiring to Missouri in 1800. Today, DuSable’s story is not as well-known as other explorers, but his story serves as an important reminder of the rich Native American and African history of the region.

title: Week 29 Essential Question
text: Why is the War of 1812 considered the second war for American independence?

title: A New Nation on the Brink of War
text:
During the early 1800s, the United States was a new country, forging its own path in the world. The people of the United States had just fought and won their independence from Great Britain. The former colonies were working hard to create a government and economy that could survive and thrive. However, the new government faced many challenges at home and abroad.

At home, relations between the Native American tribes of the Northwest Territory and the United States, including its settlers, were turning violent. This territory included present-day Ohio, Michigan, Indiana, Illinois, and Wisconsin. The tribes of this area were competing with settlers for valuable natural resources. These resources included land to grow food and hunt. Some tribes had been forced off their lands to the east and had to settle in Ohio.

The violence turned into an open war in 1790 in the Northwest Territory. The Odawa, Shawnee, Ojibway, Potawatomi, Delaware, Miami, and other tribes banded together to fight against the United States taking over their lands. This was called the Northwest War or Little Turtle’s War. Little Turtle was a Miami war chief. The United States suffered two great defeats in this war in 1790 and 1791.

The war finally ended with the Greenville Treaty of 1795. Boundaries between tribes and settlers were established with this treaty. However, within a few years, American settlers did not honor the treaty, and they moved onto tribal lands. This led to more conflict between Indigenous peoples and white settlers.

After the American Revolution, Great Britain still maintained a powerful empire, despite losing the war with the United States. Tensions were at an all-time high between Great Britain and France at this time. In 1803, the United States purchased the Louisiana Territory from France for $15 million. This expanded the United States by 828,000 square miles. As a result, the United States gained control of the Mississippi River and important trading posts along its banks. Following the Louisiana Purchase, France declared war on Great Britain.

The United States wished to remain neutral during the war between Great Britain and France. Both countries wanted the support of the U.S. government. In order to maintain neutrality, Congress passed the Embargo Act in 1807. An embargo is an order to stop ships from delivering goods. The law stated that goods couldn't be shipped to any foreign port. The United States hoped that both France and Great Britain would be devastated without American supplies. Unfortunately, the Embargo Act backfired. Great Britain and France survived without U.S. goods and were able to buy needed supplies and goods from other countries. The U.S. economy, on the other hand, suffered greatly due to the act. By keeping our supply of goods from meeting the demand in European markets, our industries were hurt and the economy declined because fewer people were buying U.S. goods.

President Thomas Jefferson repealed the Embargo Act before leaving office in March 1809. With conflict and uncertainty all around, the United States had a lot of work to do before it would become the country we live in today.

title: Alliances with Native Americans
text:
As war broke out between Great Britain and the United States during the War of 1812, Native American tribes were under threat. They were in danger of losing their land to American settlers. Settlers were spreading out across the country. Many Native Americans felt that their only hope of survival might be to join forces with the British. Defeating the settlers could stop their expansion and allow the Native American tribes to keep their lands.

The Native American alliance with the British began during the French and Indian War in the mid-1700s. The British used the tribes to protect their colonies in Canada. As the War of 1812 began, the British hoped to use their alliances for the same purpose. In addition to the chance to retain their lands, the Native Americans received goods and weapons as part of the alliance.

In response to American attacks, Shawnee leader Tecumseh created a unified confederation of tribes to oppose the Americans. Instead of facing Canadian settlers and the few soldiers the British had in Canada, American troops faced the combined strength of Tecumseh’s confederation. This confederation included members of several tribes, including the Shawnee, Kickapoo, and others. The confederation was successful against the Americans for a time. However, Tecumseh was killed in battle in Ontario, Canada. After his death, the confederation fell apart and ended its alliance with the British.

Not all Native American tribes allied with the British. Some tribes maintained friendly relationships with American settlers. When war broke out between tribes, some found support in alliances with American forces. The Creek tribes had the support of American troops under General Andrew Jackson in the Creek War. The Treaty of Fort Jackson ended that conflict. Unfortunately for the Native Americans, the treaty gave millions of acres of Native American land to the United States.

title: The Treaty of Ghent
text:
In 1814, leaders from Great Britain and the United States met in Ghent, Belgium. Their goal was to find a peaceful end to the War of 1812. The war had seen brutal fighting across the country and the burning of the U.S. Capitol building by British forces. Both sides had tired of conflict and decided that an end to the war would be beneficial to everyone.

The Treaty of Ghent began with the declaration of a “firm and universal peace” between the two countries. This ended several decades of conflict between the two countries. The United States had gained its independence and successfully survived a second war with Great Britain. Despite these early struggles, the Treaty of Ghent created peace between these two countries that lasts to this day.

The United States was not the only North American country affected by the Treaty of Ghent. The treaty also set the border between the United States and Canada. Much of the actual fighting between Great Britain and the United States occurred in and along the border of Canada. The Treaty of Ghent established a long and lasting peace between the United States and Canada. These two countries maintain that border today.

Many Native tribes fought in the war. However, they were not included in the peace talks that led to the Treaty of Ghent. Their British allies abandoned them following the war. With no support, they were left to resist American expansion alone. At the same time, the war convinced Congress to make the U.S. Army into a permanent, professional fighting force.

If the American Revolution created the United States, the Treaty of Ghent secured its position as a permanent country. In the years to come, the United States would claim even more Native People territory during the period after the War of 1812 and the Treaty of Ghent.

title: The Missouri Compromise
text:
In 1816, James Monroe of Virginia became the fifth president of the United States. His presidency was known as the “Era of Good Feelings.” This was due to the calm and prosperous atmosphere in the United States. Many Americans turned their attention to the West. They wanted to create a better life for themselves and their families in the western territories.

In 1819, the United States created the Arkansas Territory from the southern portion of the Missouri Territory. The nation also acquired the territory of Florida from Spain. At this time, many U.S. territories wished to become states in the Union. One territory that wished to become a state was Missouri. However, Missouri statehood raised many questions for the United States government.

By 1817, the citizens of Missouri were ready for their territory to become a state. Petitions were created and signed in support of Missouri’s entrance into the Union. In 1818, the petitions were presented to Congress, and the debate over Missouri statehood began. Congress was concerned about Missouri’s entrance into the Union as a slave state. “Slave states” were states that allowed slavery within their borders. If Missouri was admitted as a slave state, it would upset the balance between slave states and free states already in the Union. It seemed impossible to reach a compromise that would allow Missouri to join the Union.

James Tallmadge Jr., a congressman from New York, had an idea. He proposed that if Missouri became a state, slavery should gradually be made illegal there. Enslaved people would no longer be allowed to be brought into Missouri. Additionally, the children of enslaved parents already living in Missouri would be free. These children could be kept by enslavers until they turned 25 years old. Then, they would be granted their freedom.

John Scott, Missouri's territorial delegate to Congress, disagreed with Tallmadge's proposal. Scott said Congress had no right to tell the citizens of Missouri they couldn't enslave people. A compromise wasn't reached. As a result, Missouri didn't become a state during this session of Congress.

In December 1819, Congress met again, and the same arguments for and against Missouri statehood arose. This time, however, someone suggested a compromise that was acceptable to both sides. The Speaker of the House, Henry Clay from Kentucky, came up with an idea that worked for both sides.

At this time, the territory of Maine also wanted to become a state. Clay proposed that Maine could join the Union as a free state, while Missouri could enter as a slave state. He also suggested that slavery be prohibited in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase territory. The terms of the Missouri Compromise would have lasting effects on the United States. It would eventually lead to civil war.

title: The Cherokee Nation
text:
In the 1820s, the Cherokee Nation was a vibrant society in Georgia, Alabama, eastern Tennessee, and North and South Carolina. The Cherokee Nation had a written language. There was a newspaper that published in both Cherokee and English. They had a constitutional government. There were communities of merchants, churches, and plantations.

Between 1791 and 1818, many treaties were signed that reduced the Cherokee land. The treaties gave land to white people for American settlement. In 1819, the Cherokee Nation declared they would no longer trade any of their lands. The American settlers refused to accept this. The settlers continued to move into Cherokee land. They refused to obey Cherokee law.

In 1828, the state of Georgia passed legislation stating that all laws of the Cherokee Nation were nullified (canceled) after June 1, 1830.

Then, an event occurred that would change everything in the Cherokee Nation. Gold was found on their land in northern Georgia in 1829. There was no stopping American settlers from invading the nation and taking over the land after that.

The Cherokee Nation went through the American judicial system to stop the Georgia legislation and the takeover of their land. President Andrew Jackson supported Georgia. He acted to nullify all treaties with Native Americans that had been made in the past. Jackson then started talking about removing the Cherokee from their land.

In 1830, the United States Congress passed the Indian Removal Act. President Andrew Jackson was authorized to negotiate the removal of the Native American tribes in the eastern United States.

In 1831, Chief John Ross of the Cherokee Nation went to the U.S. courts to stop the negotiations. The Supreme Court, under Chief Justice John Marshall, ruled that the Cherokee had to follow U.S. law.

Plans moved forward to negotiate removing the Cherokee Nation from Georgia.

In 1832, another case involving the Cherokee was brought to the Supreme Court. The court had the same justices as in 1831. In this case, they decided that the Cherokee were a sovereign nation and that the federal law did not apply. The Cherokee could legally stay on their land.

President Andrew Jackson refused to honor the Supreme Court’s decision. A small group of Cherokee negotiated with the federal representatives. The Treaty of Echota was made in 1835. No official member of the Cherokee Nation was present at negotiations or signed the treaty. The eastern lands of the Cherokee Nation were sold for $4.5 million. In return for the money, the Cherokee people had to move beyond the Mississippi River, 1,200 miles away.

The U.S. Senate ratified the treaty knowing that no official representative of the Cherokee Nation had signed it. A petition from the Cherokee with over 15,000 signatures was presented asking Congress to nullify the treaty. The petition was ignored. By 1837, the Cherokee and their neighbors, the Creek, Choctaw, Seminole, and Chickasaw, had been forcibly removed from their homelands.

title: The Trail of Tears
text:
One of the largest displacements of native people in U.S. history happened from 1837 to 1839. This event, known as the Indian Removal Act, forced the removal of 100,000 Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole, and Cherokee living in the Southeast. The march of these Native American people, forced by the U.S. military, became known as “The Trail of Tears.”

The people of these tribes, including the young and the old, were forced from their land and their homes. The majority had few resources to move their belongings. Few wagons were made available for their use. Sixteen thousand Cherokee carried what they could and began to walk to Oklahoma.

They walked over 1,200 miles in all conditions of weather. They walked over mountains, valleys, rivers, and places where there were no roads. Food and shelter were not always available. Water for drinking and cleaning was not always available. People became sick, injured, starved, and weak. There was misery, suffering, and death.

When the survivors arrived in Oklahoma, it took time for them to regain their strength. They had to learn how to survive in a new environment. Over time, the Cherokee Nation began to rebuild its government, culture, and way of life. A constitution was written and ratified. Three branches of government were established. The newspapers began printing, and the education of children started again.

The tribes continued to work with each other. In 1851, the Cherokee Nation established higher education for young men and women. The Cherokee Female Seminary was the first college for female students west of the Mississippi River. The Cherokee continued to have businesses, churches, and communities in the new land. The Cherokee Nation and its people worked to preserve their cultural traditions through their art, language, and the preservation of their history.

title: The Cherokee Nation in the 21st Century
text:
Today, the Cherokee Nation is the largest tribal nation in the country and one of the largest employers in northeast Oklahoma. Although ancient, Cherokee culture is not frozen in time. It is still evolving and being practiced today. The traditional culture has been passed down through many generations. However, many modern aspects and practices have also become part of Cherokee culture today. The Cherokee language is one of the only Native American languages that has a written language. Many active efforts are being made today to preserve the spoken Cherokee language, including online classes, translation offices, and language technology.

The Cherokee Nation has several community resources and programs for members of the tribe who live both inside and outside of the traditional service area of the tribe. Much of the spiritual and ceremonial practices are kept private out of respect for the Cherokee people, but other parts of the culture can be shared with and celebrated by anyone. The Cherokee National Holiday, for example, commemorates, or honors, the signing of the Cherokee Constitution of 1839. Thousands of people come together for an intertribal powwow. People demonstrate traditional arts and crafts. They have a competitive stickball game. There is also a parade and a cook-off with native dishes like fry bread.

The Cherokee constitution is another modern but important part of the Cherokee Nation. The preamble of the constitution shares that they want to protect their relationship with the United States. Why do you think it is important to protect this relationship? They also want to save their sovereignty, or the right to rule themselves. The Cherokee Nation has three branches of government, just like the United States. The executive branch includes the principal chief. The nation has a supreme court and district courts. This makes up their judicial branch. The legislative branch consists of the tribal council. The tribal council is made up of 17 members who are elected to serve for a four-year term.

text: Local officials across the country are wondering how to reduce the local litter of single-use plastic grocery bags. In 2011, San Jose, California local officials created an ordinance or local law to tackle the issue. The ordinance banned the use of single-use plastic bags from pharmacies, grocery stores, and other retailers. They also included a possible fine for violations of the law up to $1000. Using a budget helps you think about what you want to do with your money. It also helps keep you from spending more than you have. A budget helps you plan for the future. By sticking to a budget, you will make more responsible money choices.

You are going to make a practice budget for a month that shows income and spending. Use the steps below to help you complete your budget.

Your income is $3,000 a month.

The money you have left after meeting your needs can be spent on Wants, Savings, or Donations.

Think about Savings and Donations first. What will you save for future needs or emergencies? How much money do you want to give? Subtract your Savings and Donations from your budget.

Look at the list of Wants and think about what you really want vs what can wait until next month. Write your choices in the correct box and subtract the amount from your budget.

title: Budgeting Time
text: When we are in third grade, we may not have money. However, we can have a budget for our time. We need to spend our time wisely. We save time when we don’t spend it on things that are not useful. If we spend too much time playing, we may not have enough time for school work. If we do our chores on time, we save enough time to play. There are five hours between 1:00 p.m. and 6:00 p.m. If we have five things to do within that time, we can budget one hour for each of them. If we finish all the chores in three hours, we would save two hours. We can use those two hours to do something fun.

title: How to Make a Budget
text:
Some people make budgets for a whole year. Others prefer to budget month to month.

Most people look at the amount of money that they receive from their job. They then set aside, or allocate, money to the important items that they have to pay for each month. This includes things like housing, food, utilities, and transportation.

After you set aside money for your needs, it is wise to plan (or make goals) for the things that you want. These could be things like a vacation, a new car or computer, or even a special hobby like water skiing. You decide how much money you want to save each month toward these goals.

title: A Tour of Alabama Regions
text:
Alabama has two areas of land: the Appalachian area and the Coastal Plain. These two areas are separated by the fall line. The fall line is where erosion-resistant rock gives way to softer rock. Rivers that flow to the sea reach the fall line, forming waterfalls and rapids. The fall line stretches from the Appalachian area in the north to the Coastal Plain in the south.

The Appalachian Area

On the very north of the Appalachian area, you can find the region called the Highland Rim. This area is made up of valleys, surrounded by rolling hills. The area has fertile soil that is good for growing plants. The Highland Rim region is not only in Alabama but also stretches north through Tennessee and Kentucky.

Just south of the Highland Rim region is the Cumberland Plateau. This region is very large and is filled with mountains. In the Cumberland Plateau region, the mountains can be anywhere from 400 feet to more than 1,000 feet above sea level. The major rivers are the Black Warrior and Tennessee Rivers. Both tourists and local residents often fish in these rivers.

The Ridge and Valley Region is a thin region south of the Cumberland Plateau. The Ridge and Valley Region is full of mountains and valleys. This region has Red Mountain, Oak Mountain, Shades Mountain, Lookout Mountain, and Blount Mountain. Some are 500 feet above sea level. Some mountains are more than 1,200 feet above sea level.

Besides mountains, the Ridge and Valley Region is where the Coosa River and the Cahaba River run. These rivers are the main waterways of the region.

The region farthest south in the Appalachian area is the Piedmont Region. Mount Cheaha is in the Piedmont Region. It is the highest point in the state. From the top of the mountain, you can look down and see the Talladega National Forest. You may also see the long paths of the Coosa River and the Tallapoosa River far below you.

The Coastal Plain

The main difference between the Coastal Plain area and the Appalachian area is its elevation, or the height above sea level. The Coastal Plain’s elevation starts higher up in the mountains. However, it gradually slopes lower and lower until reaching sea level. The very south of Alabama has a border on either Florida or the Gulf of Mexico.

The major rivers of the Coastal Plain are the Tombigbee River, the Black Warrior River, the Alabama River, and the Chattahoochee River.

The Coastal Plain is divided into three regions. The Upper Coastal Plain Region begins at the fall line, in the very northwest tip of the state, and flows southward, diagonally across the state. Because of where this line is, the elevation is not all the same in the Upper Coastal Plain.

The land in this region is good for growing crops. You can find farms with cotton, corn, oats, and hay.

The Black Belt Region cuts across the state, just like a belt. The Black Belt Region has very rich, dark soil that is ideal for growing crops.

Agriculture is a very important part of the economy of the Black Belt Region. Soybeans, cattle, corn, other crops, and livestock come from the region.

Another important part of the region is the city of Montgomery, which is the state capital.

The Lower Coastal Plain Region includes the part of Alabama that lies south and east of the Black Belt Region. The region has excellent soil for growing corn, cotton, peanuts, potatoes, and soybeans. The elevation ranges from sea level to 500 feet above sea level. The region also has a border on the Gulf of Mexico. This provides access both for fishing and trading goods with other parts of the country and around the world.

title: Amazing Alabama Cities
text:
Alabama is home to beautiful landscapes and a rich culture. Those two parts of the state come together in the cities of Alabama.

Montgomery is the capital city of Alabama. The state capitol, governor’s office, state senate, and House of Representatives are located there. This beautiful city includes many historic antebellum homes, built before the Civil War. The city is filled with history, so it’s no surprise that the Archives and History Building and the Rosa Parks Museum are in Montgomery.

The city of Huntsville is world-famous for space and rocket research. It is the center of economic activity for northern Alabama. The space program began in the U.S. Space and Rocket Center and the Redstone Arsenal. There are also historic sites, like the Early Works Children’s Museum and the Alabama Constitution Village.

Birmingham is in the foothills of the Appalachian Mountains. It was named for Birmingham, England, a great iron and steel manufacturing city. The Birmingham in Alabama used to be a center for steel manufacturing. It is now a major medical and business center. It also has fun places to visit. The Birmingham Zoo, the Botanical Gardens, the Alabama Sports Hall of Fame, and the Birmingham Civil Rights Museum are just a few.

Mobile is located at the mouth of Mobile Bay, 30 miles from the Gulf of Mexico. It is an important seaport city. Many goods are imported and exported from this port. There are history connections at the Phoenix Fire Museum, Bellingrath Gardens, and the World War II battleship, the USS Alabama, anchored in Mobile Bay.

title: Lexile Test 1 Article
text:
Migration, or movement from one place to another, to Alabama was increased by cotton crops. Alabama had the perfect conditions and climate to grow cotton. However, in 1910, a small insect also migrated to Alabama, and the cotton crops were never the same again. Thousands of lives across over a hundred years of history have been impacted by one insect, namely the boll weevil.

A boll weevil is a type of beetle that eats cotton plants. As the plant grows, seeds and the cotton around them, begins to grow in buds. These buds swell into bolls of ripe cotton. Boll weevils eat the buds and bolls of cotton, which destroys the plants.

Boll weevils spread very quickly. By 1916, cotton production was much, much smaller than it had been. This was a serious problem for farmers who needed to make a living. They began to research ways to control the boll weevils. They also researched new crops and Alabamian farmers began to grow peanuts, soybeans, and other crops. Farmers found that they could make a good living again as they learned to control the boll weevil pests.

The problem with boll weevils was not completely gone until 1995, but today, boll weevils do not harm cotton crops. And cotton continues to be an important crop in Alabama.

title: Alabama Climate
text:
Alabama is in a subtropical climate zone. That means that the state has short, mild winters and long summers. Alabama also gets a lot of precipitation, or water that falls to the ground as rain, snow, or ice. The state averages between 50 and 60 inches of rain every year. That’s about an inch each week. With Alabama’s warm temperatures, most of the precipitation comes in the form of rain.

While Alabama usually has more mild weather, the state can be hit by tropical storms and hurricanes. In 2005, Hurricane Katrina had a dramatic impact on Alabama. In 2021, tropical storm Claudette also caused problems by spawning tornadoes. However, these kinds of storms are not common.

Alabama has a very long growing season because of the rain, long summers, and warm temperatures. Depending on where you are in the state, the growing season can be between seven and 10 months of the year.

title: Treaty of Paris, 1783
text:
Fighting in the Revolutionary War ended in 1781. The Americans and French forced British Army General Cornwallis to surrender at Yorktown. After years of fighting, the British decided that the war was too expensive to continue. Although the battles were over, British forces remained in the U.S. They were still stationed around Charleston, South Carolina. The powerful main army was still in New York. While neither side took any decisive action, it took another two years for all the issues to be resolved.

At last, both sides agreed to meet and discuss terms for a treaty to end the war. The king sent representatives from Great Britain. The United States was represented by Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, and John Jay. They met in Paris, France, near the end of 1782. They spent 10 months working out the details of the Treaty of Paris. The treaty set out conditions that each side agreed to follow:

Britain would recognize the United States of America as an independent nation.

Britain ceded (gave up) its territory east of the Mississippi River. This doubled the size of the new country.

Florida would be ceded to Spain.

The United States was granted fishing rights off of the British-Canadian coast. This was a very valuable fishing region.

The Mississippi River was opened to navigation, or travel, by both U.S. and British citizens.

Issues of American debt owed to British creditors were resolved.

Many colonists had remained loyal to the king during the war. The treaty guaranteed that they would be treated fairly. The property that had been taken from them during the war would be restored to them.

Great Britain knew the value of continued trade with the new United States, so they were very agreeable in the process of creating the treaty. The Treaty of Paris was signed on Sept. 3, 1783. The British signed a separate peace treaty with France and Spain, officially ending the Revolutionary War.

title: Malcolm X
text:
Malcolm Little joined a religious group called the Nation of Islam (NOI) while he was in prison as a young man. When he was released, Little decided to change his name. He believed that enslavers had forced the last name “Little” onto his ancestors. Malcolm replaced his last name with the letter “X,” which represented his unknown past. From then on, he was known as Malcolm X. Malcolm X later became a minister in the NOI. The NOI preached about evils of the white community and believed that African Americans were a superior race. Malcolm spoke about equal rights for African Americans, but he believed in segregation. He also felt that African Americans needed to practice self-defense, including the use of violence, if necessary. Malcolm X became a powerful leader in the Civil Rights Movement, but he also made many enemies. Three of these enemies assassinated him on Feb. 21, 1965.

Malcolm X came from a family that experienced much persecution due to race. He was determined to make his life and the lives of other African Americans different. His road to change was not an easy one. In 1931, when Malcolm was just a child, his father died in what was officially an accident but what Malcolm believed to be racist violence. Several years later when his mother was committed to a mental institution, he and his siblings were separated and raised in foster homes.

As he began to look at his options in life, his teacher tried to discourage his plans to become a lawyer. She told him that becoming a lawyer was unrealistic for an African American. Malcolm did not listen to her. Instead, he was inspired by his older half-sister, Ella, who was proud of her skin color.

Malcolm had a rough time as a young adult and ended up being sent to jail. While there, he read and studied a great deal. One of the things he studied was religion.

When he left jail, he became a leader and human rights activist. His ideas for change differed from the majority of civil rights activists. Yet he continued and inspired thousands of people until his assassination in 1965.

title: The Founding of Plymouth
text:
In 1564, King Henry VIII of England defied the pope, the head of the Catholic Church, and broke away to create his own church, the Church of England. Citizens of England were then required to attend the Church of England. It was against the law to worship in any other way.

Some people did not support the new religion. One group of people believed that the king’s church was still too much like the Catholic Church. They wanted to break away from it completely so they could worship in their own way. They became known as the Separatists.

The Separatists were very unpopular with the king. They were harassed and persecuted in England. This conflict created great political, economic, social, and religious strain on the Separatists. Wanting to worship freely, they turned their eyes to America.

The king only granted charters to colonies for business reasons. The Separatists approached the London Company to seek wealthy investors to sponsor their trip and their charter. The company sold shares in this new colony proposal for 12 pounds and 10 shillings (about $250 in today’s currency).

After many negotiations, the king granted a charter to the London Company for a colony to be established in northern Virginia, near present-day New York City.

The charter promised:

Twenty percent of all gold and silver went to King James.

All colonists had the rights of Englishmen.

No law made could be contrary to the king’s law.

The colonists could only trade with England.

The colonists were exempt from taxation.

The charter did not establish any religion for the colony. This gave the Separatists freedom to worship in their own way.

The London Company agreed to provide ships and supplies for the journey. In exchange, the colonists committed to work for the company for seven years. After that time, the colonists and the London Company investors would divide the profits. The colony would no longer owe anything to the company.

The colony had to have at least 100 residents. The Separatists were only half of that number. They invited others outside of their religion to join them. The Separatists called this group of people “Strangers” because they were not familiar with the Separatist’s beliefs. Their differences in beliefs created conflict between the two groups.

The 102 people set sail on a ship called the Mayflower in September 1620. Forty-six were Separatists, 30 were non-Separatists (Strangers), 36 were crew members, and 21 were servants to various passengers. Two dogs, a female mastiff and a small springer spaniel, were aboard the Mayflower, according to Edward Winslow in his book Mourt’s Relation. Other animals aboard the ship were pigs, goats, and chickens. The passengers of the Mayflower, both Separatist and non-separatist, are commonly referred to today as "Pilgrims."

The Mayflower encountered terrible weather. Storms drove the ship off of its course. When the ship reached land on Nov. 11, 1620, it was much farther north than the land granted to the people in the charter. This area of New England was known for the great fishing, mild summers, and long, hard winters of snow, cold temperatures, and wind. The Mayflower could stay there. However, doing so would make the charter invalid. The passengers were now in a new land. The mission would remain the same, but there was no legal claim to be there. This new settlement became known as Plymouth Colony.

title: Responsibilities and Duties of Citizens
text:
The United States government was created for the people and relies on them to succeed. Citizens can make a difference in their communities. Responsible citizens vote, obey laws, and pay taxes. Active citizens participate in their community, state, and national governments. Civic participation also means working for the common good. This means working for things that help everyone in a community, and not just yourself.

Responsible citizens also respect and protect the rights of others. Good citizens contribute to their community's economic development. They respectfully hold leaders to their word. Good citizens stay informed about issues, share their opinion, and get involved in creating solutions. Citizens can also contact leaders at the local, state, and federal levels by writing letters, making phone calls, and sending emails to express their concerns and opinions. This allows them to have a voice in decisions that improve their community.

text:
Do the following and describe the patterns in motion. You will need a meter stick, some string, and a two-inch washer.

Patterns

You just built a pendulum. Using your own words, describe a pendulum.

__________________________________________________________________________________

A pendulum is an object suspended from a fixed point so that it swings freely back and forth. The long piece of the pendulum that swings back and forth is called the “arm.” The weight or object at the end of the pendulum’s arm is called a “bob.”

A pendulum swings along a curved path. The length of time it takes for a pendulum to swing along its path is called “the period.” A pendulum’s motion follows a pattern. Because of this pattern, a pendulum can help keep time. This is why pendulums are often used in clocks. Their motion can keep the gears inside the clocks moving.

A pendulum can also help keep time for music. A metronome is a tool that makes a steady beat. This helps people while they play music. The original metronomes are upside down pendulums. The arm of the pendulum swings at a steady rhythm. Moving the bob lower or higher on the arm makes the beat faster or slower.

Pendulums can also have great force. A wrecking ball is a type of pendulum. A crane operator carefully guides the heavy steel ball into position. Crane operators know the pattern of the curved path this pendulum will take. They can pull the ball back and release it to target only the area to demolish.

title: Alabama Rivers and Waterways
text:
Alabama is covered by a network of rivers, tributaries, lakes, and more. There are thousands of miles of rivers in Alabama that flow either all of the year or part of the year. This network is divided into three main sections: the Tennessee River Drainage, the Mobile River Basin, and Coastal Drainages. These waterways are important for providing drinking water and for travel. They serve as a resource for farming, electricity, and industry. They’re also a place to have fun. Because all communities need a water source, many cities in Alabama are located near water.

The Chattahoochee River runs along the border of Alabama and Georgia. The river begins in the Blue Ridge Mountains of Georgia. From there, it flows down between Georgia and Alabama. As it flows through the panhandle of Florida, it joins another river and finally ends in the Gulf of Mexico.

The Alabama River is in the south-central part of the state. This river is not very wide in some places but very wide in others. The river is also famous for being the location of the Edmund Pettus Bridge, near Selma. The Edmund Pettus Bridge was the site of civil rights marches in 1965.

The Tallapoosa River enters the state on the eastern side. It joins up with the Alabama River in the middle of the state. The Tallapoosa River is a tributary of the Alabama River, meaning that it flows into the Alabama River. The Tallapoosa River begins in the Appalachian Mountains of Georgia, just like the Chattahoochee River.

The Black Warrior River is in the central part of the state, north of the Alabama River. The river is slightly northwest of Birmingham. During Alabama’s Antebellum period, the Black Warrior, Alabama, and Tombigbee Rivers were major waterways for transportation. Steamboats traveled up and down these rivers to trade. During this time, the city of Mobile became a key city for trade because it had access to the river system and the ocean.

The Tombigbee River is on the western side of the state. It comes into Alabama from Mississippi and joins with the Alabama River. Together, they form the Mobile River, which flows into the ocean. That means that the Tombigbee and Alabama Rivers are tributaries to the Mobile River. The Tombigbee River once was the eastern boundary of where the Choctaw lived. Tombigbee means “box-maker” in the Choctaw language.

Alabama Aquifers

Have you ever used a sponge to clean up a puddle of spilled water? It’s amazing just how much one little sponge can hold. Just like a sponge, there are some places in Alabama that act like sponges. Huge layers of crumbled rock lie right beneath the Earth’s surface. Stored within these layers of rock are millions and millions of gallons of fresh water.

Crumbled rock layers that are filled with water are called aquifers. The underground water stored there is called groundwater. Sometimes, the groundwater leaks up through springs into wells or rivers. There are 19 large aquifers in Alabama. Right below your feet might be millions of gallons of water. That water might someday find its way to a river or lake and eventually to the ocean.
