title: How Do Alabamians Use Water?
text:
Alabama naturally has a lot of water. Thousands of miles of rivers run through the state. There are more than 100 lakes in the state. Groundwater in Alabama, or the water held in the aquifers under the ground, includes millions of gallons of water. However, Alabama’s population has grown so much that water that once seemed endless must now be carefully managed.

Government Services

One of the services of the state government in Alabama includes the Alabama Department of Economic and Community Affairs (ADECA). One of the things that ADECA does is plan for water usage throughout the state.

They also take care of communication and plan with neighboring states for water management and rights. ADECA collects data about how much water is available and how much water is used across the state.

There are 67 counties in Alabama. Data is collected to show how much water is used by each county. Additionally, data shows how much water is used for different purposes. For example, the public supply of water was by far the largest use of water. The data shows that only a very small amount of water was used for livestock and mining.

Water Management

Because the state collects data, officials are able to make decisions. Other groups, like the Alabama Rivers Alliance, make plans for building safe dams to store water and to use it to create electricity. Alabama has a lot of electricity that comes from water pouring over dams. So if something happened to the water, there would be less electricity.

Different groups in the state work to keep the water of Alabama clean. Another problem that Alabama manages is to keep many species of plants and animals safe. If the water in an area changes, then it can disrupt the ecosystem, or the living things and resources, in that area. Some types of plants and creatures in Alabama have gone extinct as the amount of available water (or how clean the water is) has changed. Groups like the Alabama Rivers Alliance try to take care of the water and ecosystem of the state.

Each Community Member Can Help

ADECA has recommendations for what you can do to help conserve, or save, water. One idea is to plant a lawn that only needs watering about once a week. Watering a lawn one time can take as much water as a family uses inside a house in a whole week. By putting a car on the lawn before washing it, the lawn also gets watered while the car gets clean. Using special car soaps can be safer for the car and the lawn. They also recommend taking shorter showers and only using a dishwasher or a washing machine when it is full.

By paying attention, everyone can do a little that adds up to a lot of water.

title: Important Figures in the Civil Rights Movement
text:
Fred L. Shuttlesworth

Civil rights leader Fred L. Shuttlesworth was another member of the SCLC and a minister from Birmingham, Alabama. He was part of the Birmingham Campaign. This project’s goal was to end discrimination in restaurants, stores, and public places throughout the city.

Hugo Black

Born in 1886 in Harlan, Hugo Black started out attending Birmingham Medical College because his mother wanted him to become a doctor. However, after one year, he decided that he didn’t like medicine, so he enrolled in the University of Alabama Law School. He graduated when he was only 20 years old.

Black represented the state of Alabama in the U.S. Senate from 1926 to 1937 and served on the Supreme Court of the United States from 1937 to 1971. He is considered one of the most influential Supreme Court justices in the 20th century.

George Wallace

George Wallace ran for the office of governor of Alabama in 1962. He asked people to "Stand Up for Alabama" and won the support of many Alabamians because he was strongly in favor of segregation. After being elected, he said, "I draw a line in the sand ... and I say, segregation now, segregation tomorrow, segregation forever." In 1963, Governor Wallace stood in the doorway of a University of Alabama building to protest the federal court ruling that allowed African American students to attend the school. Wallace served four terms as Alabama's governor. Later in life, he admitted that he had been wrong about segregation and apologized to African American civil rights leaders.

John Lewis

John Lewis was born in Alabama on Feb. 21, 1940. His parents were sharecroppers. He attended segregated schools. Listening to Martin Luther King Jr. on the radio inspired Lewis to join the Civil Rights Movement. John Lewis was a young African American working for civil rights with Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and his fellow advocates. Lewis participated in many peaceful protests including sit-ins, boycotts, and marches. Lewis was a speaker on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial in the March on Washington in August 1963. In 1965, Lewis led hundreds across the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama, in a demonstration for voting rights. The attack on those marchers hastened the passage of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Lewis entered local politics in 1981. In 1987, Lewis was sent to Congress by the people of Georgia. He served in Congress until his death in 2020.

title: Alabama Becomes a State
text:
In 1814, the Creek War ended with the signing of the Fort Jackson Treaty. The treaty gave the United States control of 21 million acres of land in central and south Alabama Territory that formerly belonged to the Creek.

At the same time, a person could make a lot of money by growing cotton. Cotton prices had shot up. More and more factories needed cotton to make textiles. However, cotton quickly depletes the soil in which it grows. Much of the cultivated land in southern states couldn’t grow as much as it used to.

Alabama’s soil had not yet been depleted. In fact, a region called the Black Belt had especially fertile soil, perfect for growing cotton. The sudden availability of this land started what became known as “Alabama Fever.” Everyone wanted to get their piece of Alabama.

The population grew very quickly. In 1810, 10,000 people lived in the Alabama Territory. By 1820, the population had exploded to 127,000. However, one-third of this new population was made up of enslaved people brought in to work the plantations.

The Northwest Ordinance said that there needed to be 5,000 men in an area to make it a territory and 60,000 to make it a state. By 1819, Alabama Territory had the population it needed, and its leaders asked the U.S. Congress to make it a state. Congress approved their request, and Alabama became the 22nd state to enter the Union.

title: The Cold War and the Space Race
text:
Following World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union began competing for power and influence on the world stage. The former allies found that their ambitions directly opposed one another. Each country wanted to spread their economic systems and forms of government to other countries. The United States supported democracy and capitalism, while the Soviet Union opposed those ideologies with communism. As the years progressed, the two countries found themselves facing off in many conflicts around the world.

Despite the intense competition between the United States and the Soviet Union, the two countries never actually fought one another. Their conflict became known as the Cold War. As opposed to a “hot” war, this war was “cold” because there was no fighting between soldiers of the two countries. Instead, they found other ways to challenge and compete with each other.

In some cases, the two sides got involved in the wars of other countries. Each joined the side that matched their ideologies. In the countries of Korea and Vietnam, civil wars broke out between people who wanted to make those countries democratic and others who wanted the countries to be communist. The United States provided support and soldiers to pro-democratic forces. The Soviet Union gave supplies and equipment to the pro-communist forces.

Tensions between the two countries during these conflicts remained high. Even though they never actually fought each other, the threat was always there. Because of this, the two countries got caught up in an arms race. Each one tried to build more and better weapons and equipment than the other side. Neither wanted to let the other country gain a military advantage over them. Because of the distance between the two countries, they focused much of their efforts on developing bigger and better missiles that could deliver nuclear warheads across that distance.

The improvements in rocket technology led to the next phase of the Cold War. These new rockets made it possible to send things and people into space. The United States and the Soviet Union engaged in a new competition, known as the “Space Race.” Each wanted to be the first to send a satellite, an animal, and then a person into space for increasing amounts of time.

The Soviet Union placed Sputnik, the first satellite, into orbit around the Earth on Oct. 4, 1957. Additional Sputnik missions sent dogs to space. The Soviet Union furthered their lead in the Space Race by sending in the Luna 3 spacecraft around the moon in 1959. It took the first pictures of the far side of the moon. In a major milestone of the Space Race, the Soviet Union put Yuri Gagarin in orbit once around the Earth on April 12, 1961. The Soviet Union was putting the effort of their entire country behind winning the Space Race, and they were well on their way with Gagarin’s feat.

As the Soviet Union continued to achieve space “firsts,” the United States focused on putting a person on the moon. John Glenn became the first American in orbit in February 1962. The Gemini missions increased the duration of space flight. The United States poured great effort and resources into making up the gap between their capabilities and those of the Soviet Union.

Despite the head start and “firsts” of the Soviet Union, they could not develop a rocket strong enough to reach the moon. The progress of the United States space program continued with the creation of the Saturn V rocket, which was powerful enough to reach the moon. On July 21, 1969, U.S. astronaut Neil Armstrong set foot on the moon as part of the Apollo 11 mission. The two countries continued to improve their capabilities in space, but putting a man on the moon is often considered the moment when the United States “won” the Space Race.

title: Florida Reaches for the Stars
text:
For the United States to compete in and win the Space Race, they needed somewhere to develop and test their rockets and other equipment. Rocket testing was dangerous, so the right location needed to have certain characteristics. It needed to be far away from populated areas. People did not want a failed rocket test near a big city. A temperate climate that would stay warm throughout the year was a requirement as well. Those involved could not afford to waste any time with cold and windy weather that could delay rocket launches.

The east coast of Florida met each of these conditions. It also had one more advantage. The Earth spins from west to east, and the land at the Equator moves faster than near the poles. Rockets launching from the east coast of Florida could launch over the Atlantic Ocean and use the natural movement of the Earth in that direction to boost their momentum. Rocket failures over the ocean would not threaten any humans below. The U.S. government chose an isolated location south of Jacksonville, Cape Canaveral, for their base of operations in Florida.

1947: The Department of Defense acquired 15,000 acres of land at Cape Canaveral to establish a missile testing site.

July 24, 1950: A small rocket was launched from Cape Canaveral, marking the true beginning of the space program.

July 29, 1958: Congress created the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) to “provide for research into problems of flight within and outside the Earth's atmosphere, and for other purposes.”

August 21, 1958: Congress passed the National Defense Education Act. This act provided funding for continued education, particularly in the areas of science, mathematics, and foreign languages.

May 5, 1961: Alan Shepard became the first American in space. Shepard’s capsule launched from Cape Canaveral.

May 25, 1961: President John F. Kennedy announced the United States would put a man on the moon by the end of the decade.

1962: NASA established a launch center at Cape Canaveral with the mission to send American astronauts to the moon.

February 20, 1962: John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth. Glenn's mission launched from Cape Canaveral.

1963: NASA acquired almost 90,000 acres on Merritt Island near Cape Canaveral. They constructed a large complex of buildings for the American space industry.

Between 1964 and 1972, the United States sent dozens of rockets to explore the moon. They had no idea what they would find. Was the moon’s surface solid, or would spacecraft sink into dust? NASA scientists knew the only way to know for sure was to send a manned spacecraft to the moon.

title: One Small Step for Man...
text:
The ultimate goal of the Apollo program was to send people to the moon, allow them to survive their time on the moon, and then return to Earth safely. Each mission in the Apollo program was designed to take the next step in accomplishing this goal. Missions launched from Cape Canaveral involved testing the Saturn V rocket, the lunar module, and various other technological components of the moon mission.

These missions also served as test runs for the various maneuvers that the spacecraft and astronauts would have to perform during their trip to the moon and back. Orbiting Earth and the moon, as well as reentering the Earth’s atmosphere, had to be performed precisely and accurately.

On July 16, 1969 three astronauts sat in the command module known as Columbia, ready to begin the Apollo 11 mission. Commander Neil Armstrong, Command Module Pilot Michael Collins, and Lunar Module Pilot Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin were launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida, at 9:32 a.m., local time. The technology and maneuvers had been tested. It was time to land on the moon.

Three days later, they arrived in orbit around the moon. On July 20, Armstrong and Aldrin descended to the moon in the lunar module known as the Eagle. In a little over 12 minutes, the Eagle had landed on the moon, and Neil Armstrong became the first man to step foot on the lunar surface. Armstrong and Aldrin spent about two and a half hours collecting rock samples and performing other scientific and ceremonial functions. When they returned to Columbia in orbit, they left behind an American flag. The three astronauts safely reentered Earth's atmosphere and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean near Hawaii.

title: The Space Shuttle Program
text:
From 1981 to 2011, Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral was the home to the Space Transportation System, more commonly known as the Space Shuttle Program. The space shuttle was a completely new way of sending people into space. The early space programs relied on single-use spacecraft. The newer space shuttle was designed to be reused.

The rocket boosters that propelled a shuttle into orbit were dropped into the Atlantic Ocean. There, they could be recovered and used in the next shuttle launch. The shuttle had wings similar to an airplane. This would allow it to glide back to Earth after reentering the atmosphere. From there, it could land on a long runway, just like an airplane.

Six space shuttles were built for the program. They were named after famous ships that had been involved in science and exploration. The first shuttle, Enterprise, never flew in space but was used to test the capabilities of the shuttle design. The other five shuttles orbited the Earth over 20,000 times during a collective flight time of just over 1,334 days.

The shuttle launches at Cape Canaveral became spectator events. People came to see the space shuttles blast off on their missions to conduct scientific missions or help construct the International Space Station. The rockets were so powerful that viewing locations were several miles away from the launch pad. In spite of this, people could hear and feel the power of the rockets as they propelled astronauts into space.

title: The Space Coast
text:
Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral became so well-known as the home of the space program that the whole area became known as the Space Coast. The region attracts visitors who want to explore the history of the area, learn more about the space program, and enjoy the beaches of central Florida.

Many of the cities in this area were founded in the late 1800s. The region became more popular when Henry Flagler extended his railroad south from St. Augustine along the coast. Space Coast visitors explore these historic areas and the many museums there as well. The beaches along the coast provide an alternative to the busier South Florida beaches of Miami.

Kennedy Space Center attracts many tourists who are interested in experiencing rocket launches and learning more about the U.S. space program. There are also many museums in the area that are focused on the military history of the area. The impact of all these visitors to the Space Coast is a huge boost for the region’s economy. Tourists stay in local hotels, visit museums and attractions, eat at restaurants, and buy things at the various shops and stores in the area. This economic activity supports those businesses and brings money to the Space Coast.

title: Kennedy Space Center
text:
Today, Kennedy Space Center serves two main purposes. It is still a major spaceport offering launch capabilities to government organizations and private entities. It is also home to a visitor center that educates visitors about the history, current endeavors, and future possibilities of space travel.

Kennedy Space Center is the main launch site for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). Partnerships between NASA and almost 100 private companies have kept the rocket pads busy. Visitors and residents of the area can still see (and hear and feel) the familiar sight of a rocket launching over the Atlantic Ocean.

Launching rockets is dangerous, so Kennedy Space Center is also a research and development facility. Each rocket undergoes extensive testing to ensure it will operate correctly and safely. Rocket construction occurs in the Vehicle Assembly Building. It is one of the largest buildings in the world by area. It had to be that big in order to construct the Saturn V rockets that took the first people to the moon.

Launching rockets is not the only work being done at Kennedy Space Center. New efforts are being made to make it possible to live on the moon. Research is being done to create the technology and techniques needed to inhabit the lunar surface. The work and money being poured into the research at Kennedy Space Center has the potential to improve the lives of people both on Earth and off of it.

In addition to the important work at Kennedy Space Center, it hosts a large visitor center. Exhibits and experiences there include explanations of the science and history of space exploration. Visitors can get an up-close view of the gigantic rockets and other craft involved in the early years of space travel. Immersive, interactive exhibits give visitors a hands-on opportunity to see what space exploration really involves.

title: Cape Canaveral Today
text:
Cape Canaveral is a part of the Atlantic coast of Florida. It is a low-lying strip of land that runs alongside Merritt Island, which sits between the Cape and mainland Florida. Like much of coastal Florida, Cape Canaveral is very low and flat with sandy soil. The presence of Kennedy Space Center has kept commercial and residential development away from the Cape and the immediate area. Native plants of the area include smaller brush and small trees. The eastern coast of Florida is endangered by hurricanes, which occasionally cause problems for the work being done at Kennedy Space Center.

The economy of the Cape Canaveral area is centered around the space exploration industry. Federal organizations like NASA and private space companies invest incredible amounts of money in the area on supplies, construction, and wages for their workers. Those workers and scientists live in the area around Kennedy Space Center, supporting other businesses, including healthcare and education.

Port Canaveral is also an important part of the Cape Canaveral economy. Its location on the Atlantic coast provides an excellent location for goods and people to enter and exit the state by water. The port contributes almost $4 billion to the state’s economy. Materials shipped through the port arrive for use at Kennedy Space Center and other places throughout the state. Two-thirds of all activity at Port Canaveral are related to passenger cruises. Cruise ships carry passengers to destinations around the Caribbean and Mexico. Those same passengers stay at hotels and eat at restaurants in the area, putting more money into the Cape Canaveral economy.

The culture of Cape Canaveral reflects the wider Florida culture. Passenger cruise ships and miles of beaches provide hours of leisure activity in the bright Florida sun. Tourists travel from inside and outside of the state and country to enjoy the climate and geography of the area. It is also close to Orlando, which boasts some of the most popular amusement parks in the world.

title: Moving the Capital, Again and Again!
text:
As territories become states, they go through a lot of changes. One of them is figuring out where to put the capital. Alabama changed its capital city five times.

When Alabama became a territory, its first capital was St. Stephens. St. Stephens had only 40 houses at the time. The first session of the Alabama Territorial assembly met in a hotel. In 1819, the capital was moved to Huntsville for Alabama’s constitutional convention. The delegates drafted Alabama’s constitution in a cabinet shop.

At the constitutional convention, Cahaba was named as the next capital, but only temporarily. A capitol building was built there, and the population grew quickly. In 1835, Tuscaloosa was chosen as the next state capital because of Cahaba’s frequent flooding. Cahaba declined quickly and became a ghost town by 1900.

Tuscaloosa served as the capital for 20 years. During that time, the population of Alabama shifted to the east, and people wanted easier access to the capital. So, Montgomery was chosen as the next capital. Montgomery is still Alabama’s capital today.

title: Alabama's Early Leaders
text:
John Williams Walker

Born in Vermont, John Williams Walker made a real splash in Alabama when he and some friends bought half of the newly created Madison County. With all that land, he became very involved in politics. He was a representative in the first and second territorial legislatures. Then he was elected president of Alabama’s constitutional convention. He topped it all off by being voted almost unanimously as Alabama’s first U.S. senator. However, he served for only three years before he resigned because of illness. He died a few months later. He is buried in Walker County, which was named after him.

William Wyatt Bibb

William Wyatt Bibb started his life in Georgia. He trained as a doctor but went into politics at age 21, when he was elected to Georgia’s state senate. Then he was elected to represent Georgia in Congress four years later. However, after backing an unpopular bill that doubled congressional pay, he moved to Alabama Territory. President James Madison appointed him to be the territorial governor. In 1819, he was elected as Alabama state’s first governor. He pushed hard for Cahaba to become the new state’s capital. However, in 1820, he fell from a horse during a thunderstorm. He died a few months later from his injuries. He was 39 years old.

Thomas Bibb

Thomas Bibb was William Bibb’s younger brother. They grew up together in Georgia. Thomas became president of the Alabama senate when William was governor. Alabama law at the time said that if a governor became incapacitated or was killed, the president of the senate would step into the position. So, when William was thrown from his horse and became incapacitated, Thomas took over his duties. Thomas maintained the state government and wrote plans for creating a state bank. When re-election time came up a year later, he refused to run. Later, he represented Limestone County in the legislature and directed the Huntsville branch of the state bank.

Israel Pickens

Like the Bibb brothers before him, Israel Pickens was a transplant to Alabama. He started his career in North Carolina, where he was elected to the state senate and then to the U.S. House of Representatives. Then he caught “Alabama fever” and moved to St. Stephens. He bought land for plantations and became president of a bank. When Thomas Bibb didn’t run for re-election to the governorship, Pickens ran and won. He picked up where Thomas Bibb left off and used his financial knowledge to create the Bank of Alabama, a state bank. The bank’s profits funded Alabama’s state government for many years.

William Rufus King

A long road led William Rufus King to Alabama. Like Pickens, King started his political career in North Carolina. There, he was elected three times to the U.S. House of Representatives. But then he was appointed to the staff of the U.S. minister to Russia and spent a year in Europe. When he returned, he moved to Alabama, where he helped write Alabama’s state constitution and was elected to the U.S. Senate. Later he became U.S. minister to France and then vice president of the United States. However, he became very ill during the presidential campaign and died soon after being sworn into office.

title: Reconstructing Alabama
text:
After the Civil War ended in 1865, Alabama and the other southern states worked to recover from the destruction of the war. This period of time was called Reconstruction. During this time, people in Alabama struggled to give formerly enslaved people rights they had never had before. At the same time, they supported plantation owners who were adjusting to life without free labor.

During Reconstruction, education and property ownership got better. But political power went back and forth between Republicans and Democrats for the next decade. Republicans wanted laws to help formerly enslaved people. Democrats wanted laws that helped white people. The conflict between the two groups was intense.

Transitioning to Freedom

When the 13th Amendment was passed, the enslaved people in Alabama became free. African Americans embraced their new freedom. However, building new lives as citizens was extremely difficult. Most of the emancipated, or freed, people had not been allowed to have any formal education. They could not read or write. They also had few tools or possessions. Everything belonged to the plantation owners. The status of the freed people had changed, but their living conditions had not.

In 1865, Congress passed an act that “established a Bureau for the Relief of Freedmen and Refugees.” The purpose of this office was to help African Americans transition to a life of freedom.

The Freedmen’s Bureau operated for five years in Alabama. During that time, it established schools, provided teachers, and built hospitals. The bureau gave clothing, food, and tools to those in need. It also helped find and reunite family members who had been sold to other enslavers. In addition, the agency assisted African American veterans in obtaining their pensions and benefits.

In many ways, the work of the Freedmen’s Bureau was successful. By 1867, nearly 10,000 African American students were enrolled in schools, and more than 17,000 people received medical support and assistance. But the state struggled with violence and political unrest. The bureau was eventually forced to stop operating.

A Decade of Conflict

The Reconstruction period was marked by conflict. One of the greatest challenges was creating a state government that was united rather than divided. Andrew Johnson, who was president of the United States, appointed new governors for each state that had seceded from the Union during the Civil War. He appointed Lewis Eliphalet Parsons to serve as the provisional governor of Alabama until the people elected a new governor.

Governor Parsons called a constitutional convention to meet on September 12, 1865. At that gathering, the government leaders repealed the ordinance of secession. They renounced the state's war debts. They abolished slavery. They scheduled elections to choose state officials and representatives to Congress.

Robert M. Patton was elected the governor in November 1865 and was sworn in as the new governor in December. That marked the beginning of an extremely difficult time for Alabama. For the next 10 years, political power moved back and forth between former Confederates, who were generally Democrats, and Unionists, who were mostly Republicans.

Throughout the remainder of the Reconstruction period, Alabama experienced intense racial conflict and even violence as the state tried to deal with important issues, such as civil rights, the economy, public education, and property ownership. Because the constitution that was adopted in 1865 didn’t guarantee legal equality for African Americans, Congress didn’t officially recognize the state. So, Alabama delegates had to gather again to pass a second constitution. This was called Congressional Reconstruction.

Alabama was the first state to experience Congressional Reconstruction. The 1867 gathering included about 100 delegates. The group included 18 African Americans, who had been elected as delegates.

The new constitution was ratified, or accepted, by voters across the state in early 1868. It was the first constitution in state history to be voted on by the people. It guaranteed the rights of all citizens. It created a free public school system for all Alabama residents. On July 13, 1868, Alabama was officially readmitted into the Union.

title: Economic Challenges and Changes
text:
The Civil War caused severe economic challenges for Alabama. Before the war, the state’s economy was based on agriculture, primarily cotton. After the war, many enslaved people who had worked on cotton plantations became sharecroppers. Sharecroppers lived on land owned by someone else and grew crops, keeping some of the crops they grew for themselves and giving some of the crops to the landowner in exchange for seeds, tools, living quarters, and food.

The state continued to grow mostly cotton. In fact, Alabama became known as the Cotton State. The state also grew corn. Corn was used to feed livestock and the people who worked the land. For several years following the Civil War, cotton prices were low and crops were poor, so the economy remained weak. Many people suffered, especially freed African Americans and rural farmers. State officials tried to provide food for the poor and prevent the state from going bankrupt by renegotiating existing state debt. However, violence and political fighting increased as the state tried to recover from the Civil War. It was difficult to make much economic progress because the government was so unstable.

Railroads were important in the state’s efforts to strengthen the economy. Railroads transported cotton to the north. In addition, areas of the state began mining iron ore and coal. Railroads were essential in transporting those natural resources to areas where they could be sold. The state began shifting from an agrarian society, or one focused on agriculture, to an industrial society.

Alabama’s economy recovered very slowly from the destruction of the Civil War. The state continues to grow cotton today. It’s still one of the top cotton-producing states in the nation. But Alabama also began developing its other natural resources. A few decades after the war ended, the state had become one of the most highly industrialized states in the South.

title: The 1875 Constitutional Convention of Alabama
text:
In 1875, a new constitution was written and passed. That constitution addressed public education and tried to solve some of the problems of Reconstruction.

After a decade of political fighting, Alabama Democrats regained control in 1874. Voters elected George Smith Houston as governor. The two branches of the government, the Senate and the House, also had a Democratic majority. The Democrats now had the power to call for a new constitutional convention.

On September 6, 1875, a group of delegates gathered to create a new constitution. More than half of the delegates were lawyers. Eighty delegates were white Democrats, a group that had been largely left out when the 1865 constitution had been written. Many of them had fought for the Confederate Army, and for several years after the war, they couldn’t hold office or even vote. Twelve were Republicans, including several African Americans. Seven were political independents.

The delegates wanted to create a document that would reduce the size of the state government. They wanted to decrease taxes. They wanted to cut funding for programs supported by the state, including education. They also wanted to restrict the political power and civil rights of African Americans. In many ways, they wanted to return to life the way it had been before the Civil War, except for the existence of slavery, which was now illegal.

The men who wrote the constitution were careful about the words they used. They did not want to anger the federal government. When it was complete, the new 1875 Constitution contained 17 articles. The constitution lowered taxes, which supported the state’s agricultural and industrial efforts. It also reduced the salaries of people who worked for the government. It limited taxation powers for local governments.

In addition, the new constitution retained public education for formerly enslaved people but established segregated schools. The constitution also preserved voting rights for different economic levels and races. The constitution did change the wording from the previous constitution. The previous wording had been taken from the Declaration of Independence: “All men are created equal.” The new constitution said: "All men are equally free and independent." The difference was small, but they felt it was important to make.

The constitution also outlined some basic rights that included most of the same rights mentioned in the U.S. Constitution's Bill of Rights. Those rights included:

freedom of religion

freedom of speech

freedom from unreasonable search and seizure

the right to a trial by jury

the right to legal counsel

the right of assembly

the right to bear arms.

The document also outlawed slavery and included suffrage, or the right to vote, for all men. However, to vote, individuals had to pay a poll tax, which many poorer people, especially formerly enslaved people, could not afford.

title: Immigration in Alabama
text:
Despite the challenges and hardships that Texans faced as a result of the Civil War, people continued to move to Texas. They came in search of economic opportunities and religious freedom. Many immigrants who settled in Texas left their homelands to escape war, disease, and famine. Thousands of European immigrants settled in Texas following the Civil War.

In 1871, the Texas legislature created the Texas Bureau of Immigration. The purpose of this organization was to promote immigration and protect the rights of immigrants. Members of the Texas Bureau of Immigration published guidebooks that described the environment, economy, government, and people of Texas. Immigration agents traveled throughout the United States and Europe to encourage immigrants to move to Texas. Their efforts paid off. Thousands of immigrants settled in Texas during the late 1800s.

Most immigrants who came to Texas during the late 1800s immigrated from countries in northern and eastern Europe. Between 1865 and 1890, about 40,000 German immigrants settled in the established towns and rural areas of the German Belt. Some German settlers moved farther west and created new communities. Swedish immigration began before the Civil War but increased dramatically during the 1870s and 1880s. Most of the Swedish immigrants who settled in Texas established farms and communities in northwest Texas.

Hundreds of Polish immigrants settled in Texas after the Civil War. Many of them settled near large farms in South and Central Texas and became farm laborers. Some Polish immigrants eventually became sharecroppers. Jewish immigrants came to Texas in search of religious freedom. Jewish communities across Europe were discriminated against and faced constant persecution from other religions. In Texas, Jewish immigrants were free to practice their religion and establish their own communities, schools, businesses, and synagogues throughout the state.

Other groups of immigrants came from southern Europe and Asia. Italian immigrants sought economic independence and a better life for their families. Thousands of Italian immigrants came to the United States. Most Italian immigrants settled in larger cities on the east coast of the United States. However, some made the arduous journey to Texas to farm and open businesses of their own.

Chinese immigrants settled in Texas beginning in the 1870s. Many immigrants from China came to Texas to help build railroads throughout the state. Most of the immigrants who came to work on the railroad left Texas after completing their work, but a small portion stayed. Small Chinese communities formed around the state.

Immigrants from around the world continued to settle in Texas into the 20th century. They brought with them their culture, traditions, and beliefs. As more people came to Texas, they shared their cultural traditions and created unique communities that encompass the traditions of many cultures.

title: Phenomenon

text:

title: The Chemistry Behind Ice Cream
text:
Instructions:

Fill in the table with all of the ingredients’ weights from Activity 2.

Add up the weights of the ingredients to get the total, or sum.

Graph the sum on the bar graph.

Empty all of the ingredients into one bag and mix. Weigh the bag and any additional bags or containers that held the ingredients.

Graph the weight of the mixture on the bar graph.

Read the article “Career Spotlight: Ice Cream Chemist” with your group.

Career Spotlight: Ice Cream Chemist

There are many different types of scientists out there, but they all have something in common: they are curious about the world around them. When a scientist’s curiosity focuses on matter and how substances interact, combine, and change, they are called a chemist.

Dr. Maya Warren first discovered that she loved chemistry while making slime during her childhood. As a chemistry major in college, she decided that she wanted to use her scientific knowledge to investigate how different flavors of food are made. Her interest applied to all foods, but one food in particular intrigued her the most: ice cream!

After graduation, Warren was hired by an ice cream company to make new flavors. That makes her an ice cream scientist! But to her, it isn’t just a job. It’s a lifestyle in which she incorporates her passion: food chemistry!

Warren spends most of her time traveling the world and helping countries set up dairies to produce the cream and milk necessary to make ice cream for residents. She also explores local cultural foods and creates ice cream flavors based on the regions she visits.

Chemistry is involved in more than just the flavor-making for ice cream. Warren also has to understand how different ice cream ingredients will interact. She knows that the ice cream, including its flavor and texture, will only be perfect if she measures and balances the ingredients correctly. So, planning new, exciting flavors of ice cream always comes with experimentation. Warren adjusts the combinations and amounts of ingredients to come up with the best product in the end. Her favorite creation she has made so far was a honey cornbread and blackberry jam ice cream.

One ingredient in ice cream that many people don’t think about is air. A thick, heavy ice cream has less air in it, while a lighter kind of ice cream, like soft serve, has more air. Warren considers ice cream to be a very complex food because it is solid (sugar and ice), liquid (milk and cream), and gas (air), all wrapped up in one package.

Does the thought of experimenting with matter excite you? Maybe chemistry is the right path for you, like it was for Warren! If you were an ice cream chemist and could create any flavor of ice cream, what would you choose?

Reflect and Connect:

How has your understanding of the weight of matter changed from this activity? What new evidence do you have? What do we still not know?

title: Sundae Story
text:
You are going to be the main character in the interactive story “Sundae Cup 500.” Use your data from previous activities to fill in the blanks.

As your teacher reads, follow along and circle sections of dialogue in the story.

Sundae Cup 500

BEEP, BEEP, BEEEEEEEP! The alarm goes off, waking ________ (your name) up for the day. But not just any day … it’s race day! ________ (your name) has been racing every week and they haven’t won yet. Racing season may be coming to an end, but they won’t give up now!

The first step to prepare for the race is to make the ice cream. The race officials are very picky about their ice cream weight criteria. ________ (your name) gathers all of the ingredients and weighs each one separately. They measure out ¼ cup of cream, which weighs ______ (Activity 2); ¼ cup of milk, which weighs ______ (Activity 2); one tablespoon of sugar, which weighs ______ (Activity 2); and ¼ teaspoon of vanilla, which weighs ______ (Activity 2). When they add all of those weights together, it equals ________ (Activity 4).

________ (your name) mixes all of the ingredients together. Looking inside the bowl, they panic for a moment. “Where did the sugar go?” But then they remember that sugar dissolves in most liquids. It may look like the sugar has disappeared, but its weight should still show up in the total weight of the mixture. Moment of truth: the mixture weighs … ______ (Activity 4). “Perfect!” says ________ (your name). They know that the sum of all of the ingredients’ weights must match the total weight of the mixture, or else they will be disqualified.

The next step is to get the ice cream from a liquid state to a solid state. After a few hours, ________ (your name) removes the ice cream from the freezer, and it’s rock-solid. “Now for the real test. Will it weigh the same as it did when it was liquid?” ______ (your name) weighs the frozen ice cream and it’s ________ (Activity 5). Woohoo! It matches again; the weight stayed the same. They are now qualified to race!

Over the speakers, ________ (your name) hears, “Ladies and gentlemen, start your engines! … On your mark … get set … GO!” They start off with a great lead, moving smoothly around the track. ________ (your name) enters the pit stop for the first ice cream topping to add to their sundae. It’s 20 grams of strawberry syrup. Then it’s back to the track for lap two. Lap two is a breeze; there are no other opponents in sight. They’re really feeling confident now! They pull in for the second topping: sprinkles, at 6 grams. Off to lap three!

Before you know it, ________ (your name) is back for another topping. The third topping, whipped cream, is added, with a weight of 3 grams. On lap four, their vehicle is really starting to heat up. This worries ________ (your name) because the ice cream is melting. Luckily, the law of conservation of matter has their back. When matter changes state, its weight isn’t affected; it is the same amount of matter, whether solid, liquid, or even gas. “What a relief!”

________ (your name) pulls in for the fourth and final topping, the cherry on top, which weighs 11 grams. All four toppings come to a total of 40 grams. The pit crew quickly adds up the weight of the ice cream and the weight of the toppings. The total is ________, exactly as it should be. Now they just have to finish the race without the weight of the ice cream changing.

FINAL LAP! __________ (your name) starts to get a little nervous because the toppings are starting to mix with the ice cream. They radio their pit crew and say, “Oh, no! I’m afraid the weight will decrease if the sundae gets all mixed up!”

Complete the story with your final weigh-in. Include at least one piece of dialogue in your ending.
