title: The Dawn of the 20th Century
text:
With the dawn of a new century on the horizon, many Alabamians felt that the future was bright. There were many new jobs available in the steel mills, cotton mills, and mines. Cities and towns were getting larger. New stores were opening. Railroads linked Alabamians to the rest of the country. Storekeepers could buy goods from as far away as New York.

Farmers were still having a hard time paying their bills and providing for their families. Crop prices were low. Factory workers also had a hard time supporting their families. Wages were low. Farmers and factory workers got together and started a new political party. They called it the Populist (People’s) Party.

The Populist Party wanted a fairer system of taxation. They wanted to raise taxes for rich people. They wanted lower railroad rates on farm products. They asked for government-funded warehouses to store their crops. Doing so meant farmers could wait until prices were higher instead of having to sell at harvest time. Populists wanted the government to put more money into circulation. They thought that would improve the economy and help them pay their debts. They asked for a lower tariff, or tax, on imports. They demanded that all voters in the state, not just state elected officials, be allowed to vote for U.S. Senators.

The head of this new party was Reuben Kolb. Kolb ran for governor of Alabama three times but never won. He and his party claimed he had received more votes than his opponent. They believed that the Democrats had not counted the votes fairly. Politicians often used tricks to stay in power. They threatened to fire African Americans as sharecroppers or household workers if they voted. African Americans were challenged at the voting polls by being asked confusing questions. Sometimes, politicians even marked the ballots for those African Americans who were unable to read or write.

The Populists never won a seat in the state government. However, Democrats later used the Populists’ ideas. They voted to put more money into circulation and to adopt a fairer income tax system. They also voted to lower railroad rates and allow all citizens to vote for U.S. senators. So, the Populists’ hard work and defeats paid off.

Once in a while, people change the world around them without even realizing it. Sometimes those changes affect the course of history.

title: Jim Crow Laws
text:
The name "Jim Crow'' started as a disrespectful term for African Americans. After a time, it became the name for laws that segregated and discriminated against African Americans between the 1870s and the 1960s. Several events marked the “Jim Crow Era.”

End of Slavery: The 13th Amendment to the US Constitution in 1865 officially abolished slavery in the U.S.

Reconstruction: From 1865 to 1877, the federal government oversaw the reconstruction of the government in Southern states. Many states created new state constitutions that contained laws that discriminated against African Americans.

Plessy v. Ferguson: In 1896, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that segregation of African Americans and white people was legal. It was legal as long as what was available to each group was equal. Oftentimes, what was available to African Americans was not equal to what was available to white people.

National Negro Conference: In 1909, the National Negro Conference met in New York City and founded the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP).

World War I: Between 1917 and 1919, more than 350,000 African American soldiers served in segregated units. Three African American regiments received the Croix de Guerre medal for valor.

Congress of Racial Equality: In 1942, the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) was founded. It was inspired by Mahatma Gandhi's use of nonviolence to protest unjust laws in India.

Tuskegee Airmen: A group of African American pilots and airmen from Tuskegee, Alabama, fought in World War II (1941–1945). They endured segregation and discrimination in the U.S. military.

Brown v. Board of Education: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled to end segregation in schools in 1954.

Civil Rights Acts of the 1960s: “Jim Crow” laws were dismantled when Congress passed a series of Civil Rights Acts in the 1960s.

title: Agricultural Innovations
text:
George Washington Carver was a famous African American scientist. In 1896, he began working at the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama. It was one of the first African American colleges in the United States. While Carver worked there, he helped farmers with the boll weevil infestation that was devastating cotton crops. Carver found many new and innovative uses for peanuts. He also introduced new agricultural innovations, such as crop rotation and soil testing. Crop rotation is when farmers plant different crops in their fields at different times of the year. Crop rotation keeps the soil healthy.

Cotton plants were almost wiped out by the boll weevil. Carver encouraged Alabama farmers to diversify their crops. To diversify means to expand the number of types of something. Farmers started planting different crops that would be resistant to the boll weevil. Peanuts and sweet potatoes were plants that could grow well in Alabama’s environment. They could be sold for a large profit. Farmers also began raising hogs to eat the leftover crops. Hogs were also very profitable. Without the boll weevil, farming in Alabama would not be as diverse as it is now. The citizens of Enterprise in Coffee County even constructed a statue to honor the boll weevils. Those insects changed Alabama agriculture forever!

title: Men and Women Who Shaped a New Century
text:
Helen Keller (1880–1968)

Helen Keller was born in Tuscumbia. When she was nine months old, she got an illness that left her unable to hear or see. She lived a dark, silent, lonely life. Her parents searched for ways to communicate with her and to improve her life. They wrote to a school for students who were blind, asking for help. The school sent Anne Sullivan to teach Keller. Sullivan was eventually able to teach Keller to communicate with others by using sign language. Keller also learned to read Braille, a system of printing and writing for blind people, using raised letters. Years later, she became the first person who was deaf and blind to graduate from college.

Because of her successes, many more books were published in Braille. More teachers were trained to work with students who were deaf and blind. Keller traveled throughout the world, visiting schools for people who were deaf and blind and sharing her inspirational life story. Her autobiography has been translated into 50 languages and continues to inspire others, especially people with disabilities.

Maria Fearing (1838–1937)

Maria Fearing grew up enslaved on a plantation near Gainesville. After receiving her freedom, she traveled to Talladega to attend a school for African Americans. As an enslaved person, she had not been allowed to learn how to read or write. She was placed in first grade, even though she was 33 years old. When she finished school, she became a teacher.

While she was teaching, she heard a missionary speak about his work in Africa and about the need for more workers. Fearing volunteered to travel to Africa that very day. In less than a year, she started a school for homeless girls. Some of the girls had been kidnapped by warriors from other tribes. Fearing taught them how to read, write, cook, sew, and do housework. Often, she read Bible stories aloud to them. After 25 years in Africa, poor health forced her to return to the United States. She settled in Selma, where she lived until her death in 1937.

William Pettiford (1847–1914)

William Pettiford was a pastor of Birmingham’s 16th Street Baptist Church. He encouraged his congregation of African Americans to work hard, save money, and start businesses. When he became the president of the Penny Loan and Savings in the late 1890s, Pettiford helped them to do just that. He became a leader in the economic life of Birmingham’s African Americans. He provided loans for building homes and creating small businesses. Through newspaper articles, pamphlets, and lectures, he educated community members in finance and investments. His goal was to teach ordinary people how to “sacrifice today to build for tomorrow.”

W. C. Handy (1873–1958)

Born in Florence, William C. Handy loved music from the time he was a little boy. He and his friends even made their own instruments. When William grew up, he decided that he wanted to write and play the music of African Americans. He moved to New York City, where he started his own company publishing the slow, sad songs of his people. These songs were known as the blues. Since he was the first one to write them down, he became known as the Father of the Blues. He became blind later in life and started the W. C. Handy Foundation for the Blind, to which he gave much time and money until his death. The log cabin in which Handy was born is now a museum.

Robert Van de Graaff (1901–1967)

Robert Van de Graaff was born in Tuscaloosa in 1901. He attended public schools and graduated from the University of Alabama with a mechanical engineering degree. After studying in France and England, he returned to the United States and developed an amazing machine. The Van de Graaff Generator is a machine that produces high voltage electricity. The results look almost like bolts of lightning. You may have seen one of these generators in pictures or at a science museum. It’s the one that makes your hair stand on end when you touch it. Scientists use them to conduct research in physics and electricity.

Richmond Pearson Hobson (1870–1937)

Born in Greensboro, Richmond Pearson Hobson graduated from the United States Naval Academy in 1889. He is remembered for volunteering for a very dangerous military mission during the Spanish-American War. He and seven other men planned to sink a ship at the entrance to a bay where Spanish ships were waiting to attack. The men were able to blow up the ship and escape on a raft. The Spanish, however, managed to get out and fight the American forces. The Americans won the war. Hobson was later awarded the Medal of Honor for his bravery. Later, voters in Alabama elected him to the U.S. House of Representatives.

title: Immigration Over Time
text:
Immigrants have come to America for hundreds of years. People move from one place to another for many reasons. Geographers call these reasons push-pull factors. Push-pull factors help us understand why people move. Things may be pulling people to a new place. Pull factors include better jobs, more freedom, or different resources.

The push factors in Europe made thousands of people leave their homes. They came by ship to New York. In the 1840s, Ireland had a shortage of food. This pushed many people to move to America. In the 1870s, there was war in Europe. War can cause people to leave their homes for safety. A poor economy can cause many people to lose their jobs. Many people from Europe came to America because they could get jobs there, in new factories and steel mills.

title: Essential Question
text: Why do people come to America?

title: The Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island
text:
Ellis Island is in the Hudson River. It is between New York and New Jersey. The Statue of Liberty is on Liberty Island. The two small islands are close to each other. People have to travel there by boat.

Though Ellis Island is small, it played a large part in the history of the United States. Between 1892 and 1954, ships carrying immigrants from Europe stopped at Ellis Island. It is where immigrants would register with the United States government. More than 12 million immigrants came through Ellis Island. It represents the dreams of millions for a better life.

The Statue of Liberty was a gift from France. The statue was made in France and completed in July 1884. Then it was disassembled, packed in large crates, and shipped to New York. It arrived in June 1885. The pedestal, or base, of the statue was made and paid for by Americans. It was completed in April 1886. The Statue of Liberty was finally dedicated on October 28, 1886.

The Statue of Liberty is now a beloved landmark for Americans. It has also become one of the most recognizable landmarks in the world. It is a symbol of freedom, inspiration, and hope.

title: Ellis Island Museum
text: Ellis Island is now a museum. Visitors to the museum can learn about peoples' journeys to the United States. The museum was opened in 1976. Visitors can see the Main Arrivals Hall and the Registry Room, where people waited to go through the immigration process. There are lots of photos and artifacts, too. Many of the artifacts were donated by the families of people who came to the United States through Ellis Island.

title: Why Do People Come to the United States Today?
text:
People around the world still come to live in the United States today. They don’t enter through Ellis Island anymore. The types of push and pull factors that affect people have not changed. Immigrants to the United States might have experienced war, hunger, or natural disasters. But there are also many people who come for jobs and political or religious freedom.

Becoming an immigrant takes courage and strength. The process to come can be long and cost money. Many people want to come to the U.S. because it is still a symbol of freedom and a better life.

title: Comparing North American Cultures
text:
We can compare cultures by looking at the elements of culture. The environment and natural resources shape culture. History also affects culture. The North American continent has many different cultures. The Native people of the land have their own culture. People have come from other parts of the world. In Canada, the Caribbean, Mexico, and the United States, Indigenous traditions have mixed with different cultures.

One way to compare cultures is by asking questions. For example, what kinds of houses do the people build? What languages do they speak? What festivals do they have? What is the most common food that the people eat? Answers to these questions tell us a lot about a culture and its people. This allows us to compare the similarities and differences.

title: Essential Question
text: How do I compare the culture of different places?

title: Housing in the Southeast
text:
The environment affects the ways people build their homes and the materials they use. In the Southeast Region of the United States, the weather is often hot. As a result, many homes have wide windows to let in the air. They also have elevated verandas, where people can sit and enjoy the breeze.

In marshy areas or areas close to the sea, flooding can occur. So some people build their homes on stilts or with a washout floor. In case of flooding, the water would flow under or through the lower level of their homes. The main rooms they live in would not be flooded.

Some areas in the Southeast Region have a lot of red clay. Red clay is great for making bricks. There are many brick houses in such areas.

Places near the beach also use seashells to decorate floors and their yards. Seashells may also be used to decorate pavements and walls.

title: Alabama's Contributions to World War I
text:
Many important military bases and training facilities in Alabama can trace their origins back to before World War I. These important military facilities were instrumental in Alabama’s war effort, and many remained as an important part of the U.S. Armed Forces.

Fort McClellan

Fort McClellan was established in 1917 outside of Anniston, Alabama, and was an important U.S. Army Base until 1999. Now, it is used by the Alabama National Guard as a training site. Part of the base has been converted into the Mountain Longleaf National Wildlife Refuge.

Camp Sheridan

Camp Sheridan was an important Army Base in World War I. It was where the 167th Rainbow Regiment was located. After the war, Montgomery residential neighborhoods, the Montgomery Zoo, and local businesses incorporated Camp Sheridan back into the city.

Forts Morgan and Gaines

These forts are located across from each other on the Mobile Channel and date back to the Civil War. Both forts played an important part in WWI when they defended the Alabama coastline. Both are now historical sites where tourists can go and revisit the past.

Marion Military Institute (MMI)

This is the oldest military junior college in the country, dating back to 1887. It is located in Marion, Alabama. During WWI, MMI started the Reserve Officers Training Corps (ROTC) program and established the Early Commissioning Program, through which cadets could be commissioned as officers after only two years of college. Because of this, many MMI students (called cadets) served in World War I.

title: Housing in Canada
text:
Canada has a varied climate and biomes. The north is very cold. This influences the resources and the homes that are built. For example, in the past, some Native tribes in Canada used to build their winter homes with snow. These homes were called igloos. Igloos were built in places where there was a lot of snow and hardly any trees.

There is a lot of variety in Canadian housing today. It is important for Canadian homes to be able to handle the cold and snow. The roofs are often steep. This allows snow to slide off the roofs more easily. Smaller, cottage-style homes are also common, especially further north. A smaller space is easier to keep warm in the cold. Often, traditional homes in Canada will have some type of cover over the front door to shield it from rain and snow. There are a lot of forests in Canada, so many homes are built and decorated with wood.

title: Housing in Mexico
text:
Most countries have many different styles of homes. Mexico is no different.

One style of home in Mexico is the hacienda. Haciendas are often built with stone and concrete. Haciendas have high ceilings, wide windows, and rounded archways. They also have open-air courtyards in the center. The courtyard in the center is often planted with trees and other flowers and greenery. These plants help cool the area and make the courtyard a lovely place. All these features help keep the house cool.

Another style of housing in Mexico is the adobe home. Adobe homes are built with brick, mud, and wood. These homes also have thick walls. These prevent the rooms from getting too hot or too cold. Flat roofs are also common in adobe homes. Adobe homes come from the ideas of the Native tribes of Mexico.

Tile is a very important building material. Red clay tile roofs are common. They are strong and last a very long time. Tile is also common on the floors and as decoration. It is easy to clean and lasts a long time.

Stucco is another material that is often used in Mexico. It is very easy to use and shape. Some areas have very colorful stucco walls.

title: Housing in the Caribbean
text:
There are many types of homes in the Caribbean. Many are colorful. They range from small huts to large mansions. Before European settlers arrived, the Native tribes of the region used timber to build their homes. They used palm fronds or grass for roofing. These made the rooms cool.

The architectural styles of homes in the region were then influenced by the different European settlers that came to each island.

There are some features that tend to be common in many areas of the region. Often the features are based on staying cool. For example, many larger houses in the Caribbean have high windows and ceilings. These features let the breeze in and keep the heat out. Some houses have a courtyard with a colonnade. Others have porches or verandas. These features allow people to sit or move about in the shade.

A lot of people live in the Caribbean. Many islands have steep mountainous land. Many places have houses and apartments built close together on the sides of mountains.

title: What Is Money?
text:
Before people used money, they bartered for the goods or services they wanted. Bartering is trading goods and services. If you were a farmer and raised chickens, you might trade a chicken or two for sugar, bread, or a cooking pot. You might also give someone food for working on your farm.

Eventually communities began to exchange goods and services with other mediums. This meant they used valuable items like shells, salt, or pieces of precious metal in exchange for goods or services. Eventually, gold and silver became the most acceptable mediums of exchange. They were rare, and this made them valuable. Since mediums of exchange must be easy to carry, precious metals began to be made into coins. Gold, silver, bronze, copper, and iron were made into coins.

The word “money” began to be used to describe all mediums of exchange. It comes from the word “minted,” which is the way coins were made.

title: Essential Question
text: What are the characteristics of money?

title: Port of Mobile
text:
World War I was one of the first times in American history when war was waged simultaneously on the sea, land, and air and when everyone in society played an important part in the war effort. This is also known as “total war.” With part of World War I being fought on the sea, it was important to be able to build ships and make sure that they were prepared for war. States along the United States coasts were all expected to contribute to this effort. In Alabama, the Port of Mobile became an important resource to support the war.

In 1917, the U.S. government awarded a shipbuilding contract to the Alabama Drydock and Shipbuilding Company. To prepare for this, the Port of Mobile was rebuilt to include heavy drydock equipment. A drydock is an area of a port where the water can be drained out so ships can be built, inspected, and repaired. Because it was very difficult to install the drydock equipment necessary, only one ship, the freighter Banago, was built during the war. Between 1918 and 1921, however, more than 50 ships were built in the Port of Mobile.

The Port of Mobile is also the only deep-water channel in Alabama, which means that the waterway is deep enough for large, ocean-going cargo and warships to pass through. This was extremely valuable to the war effort, as ships could easily sail through the Port of Mobile to be restocked and repaired when needed. The Port of Mobile is still important in Alabama and the United States today.

title: The SS Selma
text:
Can you make a ship out of concrete? That’s exactly what the SS Selma is! Named after the city of Selma, Alabama, the SS Selma was an oil tanker built in 1919 in the Port of Mobile. The Selma weighed a massive 7,500 tons. That is over 16 million pounds! The Selma was one of 24 concrete vessels approved by President Woodrow Wilson. Why would the president want ships made from concrete? Because of the need for steel to make other resources for the war, steel to build ships was in short supply. Using concrete that was reinforced, or made stronger, by putting some steel in it could ensure that the ship was sturdy. Using less steel meant that more could be used in other parts of the war effort.

The SS Selma was officially launched on June 28, 1919. That was the same day that the Germans signed the treaty that ended World War I. Because of this, the Selma never served in the war. Instead, the ship was placed into service as an oil tanker in the Gulf of Mexico. The Selma hit a jetty, or pier, in Tampico, Mexico, on May 31, 1920. This ripped a 60-foot hole in the ship’s hull. The Selma was taken to Galveston, Texas, for repairs, but it could not be fixed. The SS Selma was intentionally sunk in Galveston Bay, where you can still see the remains today.

title: Characteristics of Money
text:
There are some qualities that money must have to be a good medium of exchange.

It must be portable. That means it is easy to travel with it.

It must be durable. This means it is strong and will last a long time.

Money has to be divisible. This means it can be divided to pay for things that cost different amounts.

Money needs to be recognizable. This means everyone must recognize it as money.

Money must also be acceptable. This means that it must be accepted by everyone. You must be able to use it to pay the government and others.

Today, the money people use comes in two main forms. These are paper and coins. However, digital money is also widely acceptable. Paper and coins are also called cash.

Digital money is not physical money. It is money that can be transferred online. It allows people to pay for goods and services with a card. A debit or credit card represents a lot of paper and coins.

title: Hattie Wilkins
text:
Born in 1875 in Selma, Alabama, Hattie attended Normal College in Nashville, Tennessee. She worked as a teacher until she married Joseph Wilkins in 1898. Hattie and Joseph had four children and were active in their community of Selma.

Hattie was a strong supporter of women’s suffrage, or the right to vote, and helped start the Selma Suffrage Association in 1910. She was also a member of the Alabama Equal Suffrage Association, which fought to secure the right to vote for women in Alabama. She worked for 10 years until the 19th Amendment was added to the U.S. Constitution in 1920. After that, Hattie Wilkins remained active in politics. She wanted to improve healthcare and education for Alabamians.

In 1922, Wilkins and five other women ran for seats in the Alabama State Legislature. Wilkins was the only woman to win, making her the first woman in Alabama history to be elected to the state legislature. A state legislature is a group of people who represent the residents of a state. The members are called legislators because part of their duty is to write and propose laws and policies for their state. As a state legislator, Wilkins oversaw the Committee on Public Health and presented bills relating to healthcare, education, children, and the specific concerns of the residents she represented. She served one term in the Alabama House of Representatives. She was respected by her fellow legislators because she was so dedicated to helping all Alabamians.

title: Money in the United States
text:
When the United States was founded, there were 13 states. Each state had its own currency. The federal government decided that one currency should be made for the whole country. In 1787, the first U.S. coin was minted. In 1792, Congress decided that our currency would officially be called “dollars” instead of “pounds.”

The government kept minting coins using gold and silver. The coins came in denominations like $10, $5, and $2.50. Today’s coins are made of a mixture of metals.

In 1861, the government began printing paper money. It was nicknamed “greenbacks” because the back of the money was green.

Before 1913, some banks and companies used to print their own paper money. These were called notes. People exchanged these at banks for gold or silver coins. In 1913, the federal government decided that only the government could print money. From 1913 on, everyone used the same coins and bills as a medium of exchange.

title: Alabama National Guard
text:
The National Guard is a unique part of the U.S. military that serves both the local community and the nation. A state’s Guard responds to emergencies that happen in the state (like natural disasters, such as flooding or weather events). Because they are a part of the U.S. military, National Guard units can also be sent on overseas combat missions, support rescue efforts in other states, and more.

Alabama’s National Guard was established in 1807, but the Militia Act of 1903 organized different state guard units into the National Guard we know today. One of Alabama’s National Guard units made up part of the Rainbow Division, which is credited for helping the Allies win World War I.

Before the U.S. military entered World War I, Alabama’s National Guard units served in a military effort in Mexico against Francisco "Pancho" Villa's rebellion from October 1916 to April 1917. When they first returned to Alabama, the units protected public utilities and infrastructure (roads and buildings) in the state. Then, in August 1917, they were mustered, or called, into federal service. Just four months after their service in Mexico, the Alabama National Guard was trained and sent to Europe to support the effort in World War I.

Alabama’s National Guard soldiers were respected and had a reputation for bravery. In fact, General Edward Plummer, who helped lead the Alabama National Guard units of the Rainbow Division, is quoted as saying, "In time of war, send me all the Alabamians you can get!"

title: Changing Technology and Changing Warfare
text:
Technology influences how wars are fought. World War I saw many advancements and innovations. New weapons, communication systems, and medical procedures reshaped warfare in the new century.

Advancements in Weapons

The development of airplanes was a huge advancement in World War I and changed warfare forever. The ability to produce heavy steel in large amounts led to factories making weapons like tanks and machine guns. Transport vehicles like jeeps and trucks could move soldiers to battlefields more quickly.

Advancements in Communications

Field radios and telephones developed during this time made it possible for troops in the trenches and on the front lines to quickly receive orders from their commanders from over long distances. Before, field orders had to be written down. Then soldiers literally ran to deliver them to the front lines. Another advancement was a special camera, called a reconnaissance camera, that was fitted onto airplanes so they could take pictures of enemy troops and defenses.

Advancements in Medicine and Science

One advancement in battlefield medicine was the use of a splint to make sure broken bones didn’t move. While this may not sound like an important advancement, it saved many lives! When World War I began, 80 percent of soldiers with a broken thigh bone died from their injury. By 1916, when the splint was in full use, 80 percent of soldiers suffering that injury survived.

title: Money in Mexico
text:
Mexico’s money is the peso. One peso can be divided into 100 centavos. The symbol for the peso is the “$” sign. Centavos are shown using the “¢” symbol.

Paper pesos are in denominations of $20, $50, $100, $200, $500, and $1,000. There are also coins worth 1, 2, 5, 10, and 20 pesos. There are also 20 and 50 centavos coins. The one-, two-, and five-peso coins each have a gold-colored center with a silver border. The size of each coin depends on how much the coin is worth. The bigger the coin, the more it is worth. Mexican money has important people, places, and events pictured on it. Every coin has Mexico’s coat of arms on it. It is the image of an eagle sitting on a cactus and holding a snake.

Around 2005, printers added raised bumps to the peso bills so that people who can’t see can still identify the value of each bill.

title: Supplies for the Soldiers
text:
Did you know that soldiers in World War I were called, “Doughboys”? No one knows exactly how they got that name, but according to one explanation, the term dates back to the Mexican War of 1846-48, when American soldiers marched over dusty terrain, giving them the appearance of being covered in flour, or dough. Whatever the real story is, all soldiers needed to have the supplies necessary to survive in the field. The graphic below shows some of the items that soldiers in World War I carried with them into battle.

The haversack was the pack that soldiers used to carry all their supplies. This held their tools, canteen for water, their mess kit (they used that to eat), and other supplies they needed to survive on the battlefield.

Soldiers wore a campaign hat while on duty. Soldiers also wore the smaller Overseas Cap in France and, of course, a steel helmet when in battle. The O.D., or olive drab uniform, was made of either cotton or wool, depending on the season. This color helped camouflage the soldier in the trenches.

The Springfield M1903 was the standard-issue rifle for all American soldiers. Their ammunition and other supplies for their weapon were kept in their rifle belt, or "roundabout." Soldiers carried all these supplies with them into battle!

Two of the most important parts of a soldier’s uniform might not be the things you first think of. Puttees, or leggings, supported soldiers as they marched, and protected them from dangers like snakebites. Trench Boots were sturdy and made of thick leather to help protect soldiers’ feet from the harsh conditions on the battlefield.

title: Money in Canada
text: The official currency of Canada is the Canadian dollar. There are 100 cents in a dollar. The Canadian bills are in $5, $10, $20, $50, and $100 denominations. Canadian bills are brightly colored, which makes it easy to tell them apart. That makes them difficult to counterfeit as well. Canadian coins come in 1-, 5-, 10-, 25-, and 50-cent denominations. There are also one- and two-dollar coins. The one-dollar coin is nicknamed the loonie, and the two-dollar coin is the toonie. They have replaced the one- and two-dollar bills.

title: Money in the Caribbean
text:
The Caribbean has many countries and territories. Each country has its own currency. A territory usually uses the currency of the nation that controls it. As a result, the region has many different currencies. For example, the Cayman Islands has its own dollar. However, eight countries use one currency known as the East Caribbean dollar. Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands both use the United States dollar because they are territories of the United States. Here are some Caribbean nations that have their own official currencies.

Cuba

The official currency is the Cuban peso. Cuban pesos feature Cuba’s national heroes, important buildings, and important places. At the top of the bill, it says in Spanish “Central Bank of Cuba.”

The Bahamas

The Bahamas’ unit of currency is the Bahamian dollar (B$). It is based on the U.S. dollar. The Bahamian currency features important island symbols, like a starfish. It also features national heroes and important places. The phrase “Central Bank of The Bahamas” and the Bahamian coat of arms are printed on all the notes.

Jamaica

The Jamaican currency unit is the Jamaican dollar (J$). The Jamaican coat of arms appears on all Jamaican money. You can find it on the front of notes and on the back of coins. All the monies also have the face of a national hero on them.

Haiti

Haiti’s currency is the gourde, and one gourde (G) is equal to 100 centimes. Important historic figures of the Haitian Republic appear on all coins and bills.

Dominican Republic

The Dominican Republic’s unit of currency is the peso. The peso is made up of 100 centavos, and its symbol is the “$” sign. Important people and buildings are featured on the paper money.

title: Florida Tourism After World War II
text:
Tourism became a major part of Florida’s economy during the late 1800s. Land developers and entrepreneurs flocked to Florida to build resort communities and luxurious hotels for tourists. The construction of reliable roadways and the invention of the automobile made overland travel much easier. Florida became more accessible to average Americans searching for a sunny vacation destination.

Florida entrepreneurs opened amusement parks, roadside attractions, and affordable hotels to accommodate the growing number of tourists. The tourism industry grew rapidly following World War I. In just a few years, Florida became one of the most popular tourist destinations in the United States.

Florida’s tourism industry was hit hard by the Great Depression. Despite the challenges of the Great Depression, Floridians continued to promote Florida as the country’s best tourist destination. Florida entrepreneurs created new ways to draw people to the state. In 1938, W. Douglas Burden, Cornelius Vanderbilt “Sonny” Whitney, and Ilya Tolstoy opened Marineland, the world’s first oceanarium, in St. Augustine. Visitors were dazzled by dolphin shows and programs that taught them about marine life. The tourism industry began to recover during the late 1930s. However, the United States' entrance into World War II caused tourism in the state to decline again. Hotels were occupied by military personnel training at bases across Florida. Some hotels were even converted into hospitals and classrooms for training soldiers.

World War II ended in 1945. Floridians hoped that tourists would return to Florida after four years of war. Their hopes were realized. In 1945, about 2.5 million tourists visited Florida. By 1950, that number doubled to five million. The tourism industry experienced another boom, similar to the boom of the early 1900s. Soldiers and sailors who were stationed in Florida during the war returned to Florida with their families after the war. More people began to see the value of buying land and building homes, hotels, and businesses in Florida.

In 1947, Newton Perry opened Weeki Wachee Springs State Park in Spring Hill, Florida. Perry knew the natural beauty of the spring would draw tourists to the area, but he wanted to do more. He created a theater and hired people to perform as mermaids for onlookers. By the late 1950s, Weeki Wachee Springs was one of the most popular tourist stops in the United States.

During the 1950s, Florida’s tourism promoters used new and innovative ways to reach tourists throughout the United States. Television commercials promoted hotels, theme parks, and the natural beauty of Florida. Airlines began to expand their business to Florida. Air conditioning became more affordable and made hotels more appealing to tourists who were not used to the Florida heat.

Florida also became a destination for the film industry during this time. Many movies featured the state’s beautiful beaches and clear waters. Moviegoers became fascinated with Florida’s natural beauty and flocked to the state’s many beaches. Coastal towns, including Miami, Daytona, Clearwater, and Panama City, grew rapidly. Films also piqued tourists' interests in the tropical environment of Florida. They toured the Everglades hoping to see exotic animals, and visited the state’s many zoological parks to view thousands of animals on display.

By 1970, Florida’s tourism industry had completely changed the state. Many tourists who visited Florida began to make the state their permanent home. Within 20 years, the population of the state grew from 2,735,413 in 1950 to 6,789,443 in 1970. In the next few decades, Florida’s tourism industry experienced even more massive growth thanks to the imagination of Walt Disney.

title: Disney Comes to Florida
text:
The city of Orlando was founded in 1856. Within 20 years, Orlando grew from a small settlement to the center of Florida’s citrus industry. It continued to grow and became a popular destination for tourists during the early 1900s. Thousands of military service members came to Orlando during World War II. Many of these soldiers and sailors moved to Orlando with their families following the war. The city grew quickly, and the population reached almost 100,000 by 1970. Even though the town grew quickly, Orlando still felt like a small town to many. It was a quiet place where residents and visitors enjoyed the natural wonders of the state. The city grew from a quiet town to a bustling city in 1971 with the opening of Walt Disney World® Resort.

Walt Disney World® Resort was the vision of a man named Walt Disney. After opening Disneyland® in California in 1955, Disney began to look for a location to build his second amusement park. Disney knew that he wanted to build it on the east coast of the United States. He also wanted to purchase as much land as possible for a low price. After years of research, Disney selected Orlando as the location for his new park. Orlando was the ideal location. The city already had a large tourism industry. Land in and around the city was readily available and inexpensive. New highways made travel to the city easier.

In 1965, Disney purchased 27,258 acres of land south of Orlando and began construction on the Walt Disney World® Resort. It took six years to complete the amusement park in the resort. On Oct. 1, 1971, Walt Disney World®’s first park, Magic Kingdom®, opened. During its first year in operation, more than 10 million tourists visited the park. Orlando’s tourism industry boomed during that first year. Entrepreneurs scrambled to build hotels, restaurants, and stores to accommodate the growing numbers of tourists. More and more people began to visit Orlando over other resort communities and cities in Florida.

Disney World® continued to expand, and new parks were constructed. In 1982, Epcot®, which stands for Experimental Planned Community of Tomorrow, opened. Epcot® included futuristic rides, exhibits, and a world showcase, featuring food, arts, and traditions from 11 different countries. In 1989, Disney World® added its third park, called Disney-MGM Studios®. The park was renamed Hollywood Studios® in 2008 but continues to feature rides, restaurants, and shops dedicated to the film industry. Disney World®’s fourth park, Animal Kingdom®, opened in 1998. This park is a mix of an amusement park and a zoo, featuring thousands of species of animals.

Today, Walt Disney World® Resort includes four major theme parks, two water parks, 31 hotels, and over 200 restaurants. On average, about 58 million people visit Disney World® each year. Walt Disney’s vision and imagination have made Orlando one of the most popular tourist destinations in the world.

title: Theme Parks in Florida
text:
When Walt Disney opened the Magic Kingdom® in Orlando in 1971, it represented a new era in Florida tourism. People flocked to the area to enjoy the park, which opened the area up to new opportunities. Other entrepreneurs saw a chance to take part in the new business of theme parks. Millions of visitors were enough to support more than just Disney attractions.

Attractions that were already established in Central Florida benefitted from the increase in tourism brought by Disney World®. Busch Gardens started as a wildlife attraction in Tampa in 1959. In 1970, just before the opening of Magic Kingdom®, admission to Busch Gardens was free. By the end of the decade, the rise in tourism allowed Busch Gardens to increase its admissions to almost $8 per person. Looking to attract visitors and compete with the larger parks, Busch Gardens opened its first roller coaster in 1976.

SeaWorld was another theme park that started with a focus on animals. The original SeaWorld opened in San Diego, California. The opening of Disney World® in the ‘70s made central Florida a prime location for another SeaWorld, which opened in 1973. Tourists were already arriving in the area for Disney World®, and SeaWorld wanted to join in the economic opportunity. As the years passed, SeaWorld added more and bigger rides to compete directly with Disney and increase its attendance.

The park that most closely rivals the modern Disney World® in size and scope is also a relative newcomer on the attractions scene in Florida. Universal Studios opened its Florida park in 1990. Perhaps most well-known in Florida for its theme park, Universal Studios is an actual movie studio. Its theme park features rides and attractions that connect visitors to the studio’s movies. The success in Florida allowed Universal Studios to add a second park, called Islands of Adventure.

Of the 12 most-attended theme parks in the United States, eight of them are located in central Florida. The opening of Magic Kingdom® and the additions of other Disney parks, like Epcot® and Animal Kingdom®, spurred the growth of the theme park economy in central Florida. Other parks, hotels, restaurants, and other attractions benefit from the tourism that the Magic Kingdom® started.

title: Walt Disney
text:
Walt Disney was born in Illinois in 1901. As a young man, he drew a lot and attended the Kansas City Art Institute. He learned how to animate and created his first animated series. In 1923, Disney moved to Hollywood, California, with just his suitcase in his hand and $20 in his pocket. Walt joined his brother, Roy, who already lived in California, and the two started Disney Brothers Cartoon Studio in their uncle’s garage.

After a few small successes, Disney started his own company. In 1932, Disney released the first color cartoon ever, Flowers and Trees. It won the studio’s first Academy Award. It was during these early years that Walt Disney created the most famous cartoon character in the world, Mickey Mouse. Disney Studios later made the classic cartoon movies Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, Pinocchio, Fantasia, Dumbo, and Bambi. Walt Disney also completed his life-long dream of creating a clean, magical amusement park when Disneyland® opened in 1955.

Disney’s creativity and imagination didn’t stop with the opening of Disneyland®. During the 1950s and 1960s, Disney continued to create and produce monumental films, including Sleeping Beauty, Swiss Family Robinson, The Sword in the Stone, Mary Poppins, One Hundred and One Dalmatians, and The Jungle Book. With the success of Disneyland®, Disney set his sights on creating a larger amusement park on the East Coast of the United States. Under Disney’s direction, the Walt Disney Company purchased 27,258 acres of land near Orlando, Florida, to build a second amusement park.

Construction of Walt Disney World® Resort began in 1965, but Disney would never see his dream of a new park realized. Walt Disney died on Dec. 15, 1966. His work and vision live on in his movies and amusement parks.

title: Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings
text:
Like Walt Disney, Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings boosted tourism in Florida, but in a different way. Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings was born in Washington, D.C., on Aug. 8, 1896. She began writing short stories at a young age. When she was 11 years old, Rawlings won a $2 prize for a story she wrote, which was published in The Washington Post. She attended the University of Wisconsin, where she studied writing and drama. Rawlings used her education to further her writing career.

In 1919, she married Charles Rawlings, whom she met at the University of Wisconsin. After graduating from college, Rawlings and her husband moved around the country, looking for work. She wrote for several newspapers, including the Louisville Courier-Journal and the Rochester Evening Journal. In 1928, Rawlings and her husband decided to move to Florida. They purchased a large farm in Cross Creek, a small community 20 miles southeast of Gainesville.

Rawlings’s new home inspired her writings. She wrote about the environment and the people around her. In 1938, she published her most famous novel, The Yearling. The Yearling chronicles the lives of the people in her small community and the natural wonders of the state. The book won the Pulitzer Prize, one of the most important awards for literature. It was also translated into 13 languages and made into a movie. The Yearling brought attention to the natural beauty and quaint towns of Florida and encouraged thousands of tourists to visit the state.

Rawlings continued to write and publish books about Florida, including The Golden Apples, Cross Creek, and Cross Creek Cookery. Many of her books were later turned into movies that were filmed in Florida. Rawlings died in 1953, but she continues to have a profound impact on the state. Today, visitors can experience Rawlings’s life in Cross Creek at the Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings Historic State Park.

title: Sports, Cultural, and Historic Attractions
text:
Florida is home to many cultural and historic attractions that provide entertainment and education to millions of residents and tourists alike. The state’s large population and major cities also support many teams in the major sports leagues.

St. Augustine Lighthouse

The St. Augustine Lighthouse is a working aid to navigation. It also houses a museum dedicated to the maritime history of the town and the state. Tourists and residents can learn about the shipping and shrimping industries in Florida and enjoy a climb to the top of the lighthouse. The museum also shares the history of the area during World War II. An active maritime archaeology program is also recovering shipwreck artifacts around the lighthouse.

Ringling Circus Museum

The Ringling Circus Museum opened in Sarasota, Florida, in 1948 to document the operation of what was a hugely popular form of entertainment at the time. Visitors can see the many wardrobes, equipment, props, and tents the circus performers used to put on their shows. Like other museums, the Ringling Circus Museum is focused on preserving history as it shares its stories with visitors.

Bok Tower Gardens

Created by Dutch immigrant Edward W. Bok, the Bok Tower Gardens opened in 1929. During visits to the state, Bok was inspired by the natural beauty of Florida. His vision was to create a bird sanctuary with striking vegetation for visitors to enjoy. He worked with the famous landscape architect Frederick Law Olmstead Jr. to make his vision a reality. The gardens get their name from Bok Tower, a 205-foot-tall bell tower constructed from Georgia marble and coquina stone from St. Augustine.

Ernest Hemingway’s Home

The home of famous writer Ernest Hemingway is now an attraction and museum in Key West. Hemingway arrived on the island in 1928. Hemingway and his wife acquired the home, which dates back to the 1800s. Visitors to the home can see the many additions and alterations completed by the couple. The most famous curiosity at the home today is the presence of dozens of six-toed cats, which are descendants of a six-toed cat named Snow White, given to Hemingway by a ship’s captain.

The Dalí Museum

The Dalí Museum serves as the center of the collection and preservation of the art of Salvador Dalí. The museum protects the works for future generations. It also displays his art to visitors from around the world. Located in St. Petersburg, the Dalí Museum maintains not only works of art but also historical documents and other materials related to the life and work of the famous artist.

Sports

With a rapidly growing population, sports teams from each of the major American sports have been established in the state. Major League Baseball established the Tampa Bay Rays and the Miami Marlins in the 1990s to take advantage of the increased demand for professional baseball in Florida. The National Football League has three teams in the state: the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, the Miami Dolphins, and the Jacksonville Jaguars. The National Basketball Association has the Orlando Magic and the Miami Heat.

Other sports are becoming more popular in the state as well. The National Hockey League supports the Tampa Bay Lightning and the Florida Panthers. Major League Soccer has added franchises in Orlando and Miami as well. Sports are a major part of Florida’s economy.
