title: Three Branches of Government
text:
To keep any one person or group from having too much power, the Constitution divides the government into three branches. We call this a system of checks and balances. Each branch was designed to address specific issues and concerns. Each branch has its own structure, processes, and leaders. These leaders use different processes as checks to protect individual liberties. Individual liberties are rights that the government cannot take away. For example, the president may veto legislation passed by Congress. A veto can stop a bill from becoming a law, but Congress can override the veto with a two-thirds majority vote. Congress also has checks on the president. For example, the Senate must confirm executive appointments. The courts can check Congress by declaring laws unconstitutional. This basic structure of the national government is also used to guide the development of state and local governments.

The three branches of government are the executive, legislative, and judicial branches. The executive branch of government enforces our country’s laws. It is also in charge of the military. The head of the executive branch is the President of the United States. The president is chosen by voters. The president and vice president are elected together for four years. They may serve two terms, for a total of eight years. The president chooses members of the cabinet to advise him or her. Cabinet members are often experts in their fields. They help run the executive branch by leading departments. For example, the Department of Defense is in charge of the military. At the state level, the executive branch includes the governor, departments, and agencies that enforce state laws.

The legislative branch makes the laws and sets taxes. Congress is the legislative branch of our government. It is divided into two parts: the Senate and the House of Representatives. Two senators are elected from each state. A state’s number of representatives depends on how many people live there. Larger states send more representatives. Smaller states send fewer. Today, there are 100 senators in the Senate and 435 representatives in the House. All of them were elected by the people of their states.

The judicial branch interprets the laws, or decides what they mean. It also determines whether the laws follow the Constitution. The judicial branch is headed by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court is made up of judges called justices. They are chosen by the president and voted on by senators. State supreme courts are similar to the U.S. Supreme Court. They decide whether laws go against their state’s constitution. The judicial branch also includes other federal courts and local courts. Local courts decide whether someone is guilty of a crime. The judicial system’s role is to make sure the law is followed and all citizens’ rights are protected.

title: Political Parties of Alabama During Reconstruction
text:
Up until the Civil War, Alabama had one main political party, the Democratic Party. There was also a political party called the Whig Party, but it didn’t have much power in the state.

That didn’t mean politics were quiet. The Democrats from different areas of Alabama had different ideas about how the state should be run. The one thing they were united on was their opposition to the Republican Party. The Republican Party was a new party that was against slavery. It had almost no power in Alabama before and during the Civil War.

But after the Civil War ended in 1865, things changed. By 1867, more African Americans were registered to vote in Alabama than whites. African American voters overwhelmingly favored Republican candidates. African American men were also allowed to hold political office. So in October 1867, 96 of the 100 delegates to Alabama’s constitutional convention were Republicans. Eighteen of those Republicans were African Americans.

When Alabama was readmitted to the United States, Republicans dominated Alabama’s politics for the next three elections. Three African American men were elected to represent Alabama in the U.S. Congress. They were Benjamin Sterling Turner, James T. Rapier, and Jeremiah Haralson.

The Republican Party also dominated the state legislature. African Americans accounted for 27 members of the state’s House and Senate.

However, Republican domination didn’t last long. By 1874, Democrats had regained the majority of seats in the legislature. In 1875, the Democrats wrote a new constitution for Alabama. They passed it easily since 80 members of the convention were Democrats and only 12 were Republicans.

title: African American Political Leaders During Reconstruction
text:
Benjamin Sterling Turner

Benjamin Sterling Turner was born enslaved in 1825. Turner learned to read and write. When he was 20 years old, while still enslaved, he was made manager of a hotel and earned wages from his enslaver. Soon he had purchased some of his own property, but lost it during the CIvil War.

After the Civil War, Turner started the first school for African Americans in Selma, Alabama. Because of his efforts to start a school, Turner received recognition and rose politically. Turner ran for office in 1870 and took his seat in 1871. He was Alabama’s first elected African American representative. He worked for equal political rights for all races and classes. He sponsored a bill to build a federal building and a church in Selma. After serving his term, Turner returned to his businesses and served on the Selma City Council.

James T. Rapier

Born free in Alabama in 1837, James T. Rapier attended a secret school for African American children. In 1856 Rapier attended schools in Scotland and Canada where he studied law and became a lawyer. He dedicated his life to promoting civil rights.

When Rapier returned to the United States after the Civil War, he bought farmland in Tennessee and hired African Americans to work the land. Returning to Alabama, Rapier started working in politics. He continued promoting equality and civil rights. He led an African American labor union and later became Alabama’s second African American representative in the U.S. Congress. He supported the Civil Rights Bill of 1875. Rapier also owned and operated Alabama’s first African American newspaper.

Jeremiah Haralson

Jeremiah Haralson was born enslaved in Georgia in 1846 and was moved to Alabama in 1859. After emancipation, he taught himself to read and write. Later, he worked as a farmer, minister, and civic leader.

Haralson started his political career as a Democrat. This was unusual because Alabama Democrats generally supported enslavement. After making an unsuccessful run for Congress as a Democrat, Haralson changed parties.

As a Republican, Haralson won the election for Congress. He was the third African American from Alabama to be elected to the U.S. Congress. Haralson had his own ideas, and his relationship with other Republicans was strained. At the next election, Haralson was not reelected.

title: Working to Be United
text:
The Civil War had lasted four long years. Neither side had planned for the war to last as long as it did. When the fighting was finally over, it was time to return to a stable life, but that wouldn’t be easy.

Formerly enslaved people were experiencing newfound freedom. Many of them married, searched for family members, and made plans for the future. Some of the freed people wanted to farm the land they already knew well. Others wanted to head north and start new lives. However, for many, the economic realities of owning no land and having little or no education was a daunting prospect.

Southerners looked at their homes, land, and communities with despair. Beautiful plantation mansions were destroyed. Soldiers had burned many to the ground. Fields where farmers grew crops were now overgrown with weeds. Industrial machines lay destroyed. Nearly every village was devastated from the effects of a long, brutal war. Confederate soldiers returned home to find their families and communities shattered. White Southerners were tired, frustrated, and angry at the whole situation.

Northerners were relieved the fighting had ended. During the Civil War, troops turned many of their cities into defense zones. They were filled with soldiers and medical corps that were taking care of the injured. While the Civil War affected the North, life for northern states had fewer long-term changes.

A President’s Death

During the Civil War, the nation had looked to President Lincoln as their leader. People hoped he would be able to guide the country through Reconstruction as well. However, one devastating event destroyed the nation’s hope. It happened the evening of April 14, 1865.

President Lincoln and his wife were attending a play at Ford’s Theater in Washington, D.C. During the play, a well-known actor and Confederate supporter, John Wilkes Booth, crept up behind the president and shot him. Soldiers carried Lincoln across the street to a boarding house, where doctors tried to save the president’s life. A crowd gathered to hear if the doctors could save him.

President Abraham Lincoln died early in the morning on April 15. Federal troops later caught and executed President Lincoln’s assassin, or killer. Several other people had helped plan the murder as a way to punish Union leaders for damage done to the South. Authorities later executed them for their part in the assassination of President Lincoln.

A New President

Vice President Andrew Johnson was immediately sworn in as the new U.S. president after Lincoln’s death. He announced that he would continue with Lincoln’s plan for Reconstruction. At first, Northerners were pleased with President Johnson’s performance. However, they soon realized that Johnson did not think the formerly enslaved people should have equal rights. Many people became worried and angry. One group in Congress spoke up. The Radical Republicans believed African Americans should have the right to vote and own land.

The 13th Amendment

President Johnson’s plan for new state governments to reenter the Union was simple. States had to declare secession illegal and pass the 13th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. This amendment abolished slavery forever in the United States. Abolished means that it was not allowed. Many of the Southern states did not want to say that secession was wrong. For a long time, Mississippi refused to ratify the 13th Amendment. People in both regions of the country were not getting along with each other the way they had hoped.

Black Codes

Southern governments began passing laws called Black Codes that would return the freed African Americans to slavery. Under the laws, African Americans and people of color were not allowed to vote or hold political office. If they wanted to travel, they needed permission from a white employer. Freed people were not even allowed to choose their own careers. If they wanted to work at any job besides farming, they needed permission to do so from a white judge. In addition to these laws, many African Americans were the victims of violence. Many people worried that another Civil War was on the way.

The 14th and 15th Amendments

President Johnson and Congress could not agree on how best to carry out the Reconstruction process. Congress was especially upset that Johnson did not support the Civil Rights Act, which ensured basic human rights for freed people and protected them from unfair treatment. The Radical Republicans led the push to amend the Constitution. In July 1868, the 14th Amendment was ratified. Now African Americans would have their civil rights protected.

By mid-1870, Congress had also realized that the freed enslaved people had little chance at living truly free lives unless they had the right to vote. The 15th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution was ratified in 1870. It guaranteed that all men would have the right to vote, regardless of race. Women did not receive the right to vote until 1920.

Life in the New South

In the South, life was still far from settled, even though the states were making changes. Free African Americans and formerly enslaved people became members of national and state governments. New state governments established public schools for both African American and white children. Freed people learned to read and write. Agriculture and industry grew again. Southerners slowly made progress rebuilding their communities.

Eventually, Ulysses S. Grant replaced President Johnson. Rutherford B. Hayes then followed Grant. All these men worked hard to bring the U.S. back together again. It was many years before all people in the U.S. would truly have their civil rights protected as promised in the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments. Even today, the U.S. continues to work to provide freedom and equality to all citizens.

title: Sharecropping in the South
text: Eventually, Southern farmland was returned to the wealthy landowners and planters who had owned the land before the war started. Formerly enslaved people and poor white people wanted the chance to own their own farms. However, they found it difficult to raise enough money to buy land. They were forced to become sharecroppers. They rented land on which to grow crops. As payment for rent, they would give part of the crop to the landowner. Sharecropping was difficult work. Crops often failed in periods of poor weather or drought. Many sharecroppers found they could not pay their land rents and went into debt. Most Southern sharecroppers never had the chance to call any piece of land their own.

title: Hiram Revels: First African American Senator
text:
At the end of the Civil War, African Americans from the Southern states began to be elected to local governments. By 1870, several African American men had won positions in the federal government. An especially important day in U.S. history was February 25, 1870. On that day, 42-year-old Hiram R. Revels of Mississippi became the first African American to serve in the U.S. Senate.

Revels was a teacher and a minister. During the Civil War, he had gathered troops of African American soldiers. He also established schools for formerly enslaved people in North Carolina. When he moved to Mississippi, he was elected to the state Senate. He was a strong leader, admired by his co-workers. When Mississippi was ready to re-enter the U.S. during Reconstruction, Revels took one of Mississippi’s Senate seats.

Revels only served one year in the Senate, but he spent his life working for the equal treatment of African Americans.

title: Carpetbaggers and Scalawags
text:
During the period known as Reconstruction, the South needed to be rebuilt. New industries and businesses were needed. Workers were building factories that produced farm equipment and machinery. Mineral mines were being opened. People were replanting cotton and tobacco farms and operating them as big businesses. Many Northerners moved to the South to take part in these opportunities.

However, most Southerners did not like the “Yankee invaders.” They called Northerners “carpetbaggers” because Northerners often arrived in the South carrying their belongings in cloth luggage bags. Southerners felt that these Northerners were business people trying to make money off the South’s difficult situation. They felt the carpetbaggers cared more about making money for themselves than improving the lives of Southerners. In fact, most carpetbaggers weren’t rich businesspeople out to make money off the people of the South. Most were former soldiers looking for opportunities that were not available in the North. Some of the anger the Southerners felt came from the carpetbaggers openly supporting the rights of formerly enslaved people.

“Scalawags” were Southerners who worked with carpetbaggers or supported the freed people. Many of these people were white Southerners who joined the Republican Party after the Civil War. Southerners considered the scalawags traitors to the South. Many of the so-called scalawags held government positions during Reconstruction. They worked to make sure that state governments considered the equality of all citizens in the South when developing plans for the states.

With so many different people coming into contact, it was not surprising that there would be different opinions and misunderstandings. All of the changes happening brought different values and ways of seeing the world into the same time and place. It was a challenge for people to understand each other.

title: Cultural Contributions
text:
There are many ways to contribute to our community, state, and nation. Writers inform and entertain us. Musicians and artists create beauty and enjoyment. Scientists work to improve our lives and discover new things. Educators teach us and help us improve. Adventurers explore new places. Business people create companies and products people need and want. Politicians make a difference by leading us. Journalists tell us what is happening around the world. Many people have contributed to our state and national heritage.

A culture is the way a group of people live, speak, and act. Cultures express a group's heritage. These expressions come through art, stories, music, clothing, food, religion, and language. People bring their culture with them when they move from one place to another. Elements of different cultures often combine to create new traditions.

American societies today are multicultural, which means they are influenced by many cultures. This week, you are going to research some of the ethnic groups that have contributed to the United States.

title: Essential Question
text: How have different groups contributed to the United States?

title: Plants
text:
Native Americans grew many plants that we use regularly in the United States today. One of the most important plants Native Americans grew is corn. The United States produces 15 billion bushels of corn a year. It is the most widely produced crop in the country.

Often, tribes also grew beans and squash along with corn. Native Americans grew many other plants depending on where they lived. Other crops included pumpkins, peppers, tomatoes, and potatoes. These plants are eaten every day in the United States.

Native Americans in Mexico and central America also grew cacao, coffee, sunflowers, avocados, peanuts, quinoa, and cotton. Many of these foods are grown and eaten in the southern areas of the United States. Cotton is now a major crop in the United States.

European settlers brought apple, peach, and watermelon seeds with them. They also brought sugarcane, olives, citrus, and even bananas with them. Now there are many varieties of these fruits, and they provide food and jobs for people all over the U.S.

title: Food
text:
The food that we eat comes from the plants that we grow. Each different culture prepares similar foods in different ways. For example, tomatoes are often used in sauces. Spaghetti Bolognese sauce comes from Italy, and salsa roja is a Mexican type of sauce. Both use tomatoes. Noodles and bread are similar. Basic ingredients, like flour, salt, water, and eggs, can be made into many different products.

The United States is a multicultural society today. Common foods we eat in the United States have been influenced by many different cultures. Look at the images of foods that we eat in the United States. What culture influenced them?

title: Music
text:
Because the United States is multicultural, its music has roots in cultures from around the world. Each style has evolved and often influenced other styles.

Native Americans frequently use vocals, drums, percussion, and flutes in their music. People can experience their music at powwow performances.

The music genres of gospel, blues, jazz, R&B, soul, funk, and Zydeco all have roots in African American culture.

Bluegrass and country music come from the Appalachian region. It has been influenced by English and Celtic (Scottish and Irish) ballads. The fiddle and the guitar are the main instruments used.

Polkas and waltzes were popular with eastern European immigrants. The style and beat were combined with instruments like fiddles, guitars, and accordions. Western swing bands were influenced by these elements.

New York salsa is a style of music that developed from influences of different Caribbean islands.

title: Celebrations
text:
There are a lot of celebrations that people in the United States enjoy. These celebrations come from different cultures.

Day of the Dead: Mexico

Chinese New Year: China

Cinco de Mayo: Mexico

St Patrick’s Day: Ireland

Kwanzaa: African America

Mardi gras: Europe

Shakespeare festivals: England

Powwows: Native American tribes

title: Language
text:
People in the United States speak many different languages. The influence of these languages can be seen in place names all around the country. There are also many words from these different languages that we now use in American English. We have included some of them here.

Native American Languages’ Influence on American English

Early settlers and trappers began interacting with Native American tribes, they began using many of their words to describe plants, animals, and places that they had never seen before. Many of the words and place names we use today come from tribal languages that have been used for hundreds of years. Some of these words are:

caribou

woodchuck

toboggan

pecan

skunk

moccasin

African Influence on American English

Enslaved people who were brought to the United States had their own native languages. As they learned the English language, they also dropped some of their own words into it. Words like “okra,” “bongo,” and “zombie” are all from African languages. Some of the words we still use in modern English include:

jenga

yarn

zebra

cola

Hispanic Influence on American English

Parts of the United States used to belong to Spain. Many people have immigrated to the U.S. from Spanish-speaking countries. Many Spanish words have become part of American English over the years. Here are just a few:

armadillo

mesa

adobe

plaza

cafeteria

rodeo

canyon

tobacco

jerky

tornado

llama

Asian Influence on American English

Many of the words we use each day are actually borrowed from Asian words. Take a look at the list to see the Asian roots of many familiar English words.

bangle (Hindi): bracelet

jungle (Hindi): forest

typhoon (Chinese): great wind

tycoon (Japanese): great prince

ketchup (Chinese): fish sauce

shampoo (Hindi): to knead or massage

tattoo (Polynesian): to make marks on the skin

ukulele (Hawaiian): jumping flea

honcho (Japanese): group leader

title: The Boll Weevil and Alabama Agriculture
text:
Migration is the movement from one place to another. In Alabama, migration was increased by cotton crops. Alabama had the perfect conditions and climate to grow cotton. However, in 1910, a small insect also migrated to Alabama. Cotton crops were never the same again. For over 100 years, farms in Alabama were affected. This insect is the boll weevil.

A boll weevil is a type of beetle that eats cotton plants. As the plant grows, seeds and the cotton begin to grow in buds. These buds swell into bolls of ripe cotton. Boll weevils eat the buds and bolls of cotton.

Boll weevils spread very quickly. By 1916, cotton production had declined. This was a serious problem for farmers who needed to make a living. They began to research ways to control the boll weevils. They also researched new crops. Alabamian farmers began to grow peanuts, soybeans, and other crops. Farmers found that they could make a good living again as they learned to control the boll weevil pests.

The problem with boll weevils was not completely gone until 1995. Today, boll weevils are not a problem. Cotton continues to be an important crop in Alabama.

title: The United States Speeds into a New Century
text:
It was the turn of the century. The 1800s were ending, and people looked forward to a new century as the 1900s began. America was becoming a world leader in industry. The nation grew stronger as more cities began to use technology to manufacture more goods. Manufacture means to use machinery to make a lot of something quickly.

By 1910, the United States led the world in the production of iron, steel, and oil. Miners also mined coal and gold in large amounts. The nation’s agricultural, or farming, economy was also doing well. The transcontinental railroad system made shipping goods across the country easy. Goods and products were also being shipped to other countries all over the world. Americans were working harder than ever to earn their living.

As the 1900s began, not everything was perfect. People in rural areas, or places in the countryside, were still struggling. It was hard to make money in the country. Stores didn’t have very many different things to buy.

Life could be hard in cities too. There were so many people that it was hard to have enough space. People had a hard time getting clean water and other resources.

However, most Americans were making larger incomes and spending more money than in previous decades. The increase in industry meant there were many more goods for people to buy. People shopped in new department stores and ordered goods from mail-order companies. In cities, people could even order goods using the telephone.

Electricity was also reaching more and more people. People used electric lights in more and more of their homes and businesses. Communities built hospitals, public schools, and churches. They also built colleges, libraries, and theaters. These additions helped people have healthier lives with more opportunities.

Immigrants, or people who move to a new country, continued to arrive from all over the world. These people wanted to have a better life in the United States. Millions of Europeans crowded cities on the East Coast. Other immigrants settled in the Midwest. Many immigrants could make more money in the U.S. than they could in their homelands. Communities adopted many parts of the cultures that immigrants brought with them.

Many Americans felt cheerful as the new century began. The Civil War and Reconstruction were difficult times. It looked like the future would be better. With new opportunities, new technology, and new cultures, the turn of the century was a time of change.

title: Turn of the Century Life
text:
The turn of the century brought many new and exciting changes to the country. Many of these changes happened because of the fast growth of industry and cities. Even though the wheels of change were turning quickly, some Americans held on to ideas from the previous century. Therefore, change in other areas didn’t happen as quickly.

Technology in Cities

By 1900, four out of every 10 Americans lived in cities. In 1900, New York City had over three million residents. The cities of Chicago and Philadelphia had over one million residents each. Cities had to make advances to keep up with the challenges of an expanding population. Cities were quickly running out of space to expand outward. In 1900, cities began to build upward. Builders began constructing very tall buildings, called skyscrapers, to solve the problem of space in cities. Cities also found ways to connect neighborhoods together. Networks of electric trolley cars and subway trains made transporting people easier. More and more people were also brought together by telephones and radios.

Improving Public Education

After the Civil War, the United States made some effort to require children to attend school. Between 1865 and 1895, many states passed laws requiring children between the ages of eight and 14 to attend school for three to four months each year. The schools cost nothing to attend. However, these early schools were not successful. Some of the teachers weren’t qualified, and it was difficult to get good books and materials. As the country entered the 20th century, more and more people realized how important an education was to the future success of the country. By 1918, all American children were required to attend school at least through the elementary years. New schools were built, and high schools began to offer classes in different subjects, such as math, science, government, and social studies.

At that time, education was segregated, or kept separate. White children and African American children were not allowed to attend the same schools. Most African American children weren’t allowed to attend high school or college. Some of these students were able to continue their education at schools started by African Americans. One such man was Booker T. Washington. After being freed from slavery, Washington became a teacher. He started Tuskegee University in Alabama, which is still open today.

Segregation and Discrimination

The end of the Civil War did not end unfair treatment of African Americans. Discrimination, or unfair treatment, was common. In schools, theaters, restaurants, and other public places, segregation was normal. African Americans were set apart from whites. They did not sit together on buses and trains. Most public places had separate restrooms and water fountains for each group. Many Southern states continued to pass Black Codes. These laws made it difficult for African Americans to vote, own property, or work at certain jobs. The legal system and police supported these unfair laws. Decades would pass before all of the unfair laws were repealed, or canceled.

The Vote for Women

In the early 1900s, Women did not have the same rights as men. Many believed that women should only care for their families and homes. Many believed women should not take part in politics or speak out in public. The public considered married women to be under the “control” of their husbands. Women weren’t allowed to own property, sign contracts, attend college, or work at high-paying professional jobs.

There were also many people who did not think women were being treated fairly. The 14th and 15th Amendments to the U.S. Constitution guaranteed citizenship and the right to vote for all American men. Women did not have the right to vote.

Even before the Civil War, women wanted the chance to vote. They wanted the same opportunities as men. They wanted to go to college, own land, and choose their own careers. By the 20th century, women were fighting for suffrage, or the right to vote. Women began forming political groups. The National Women’s Party was led by a young woman named Alice Paul. They often marched in front of the White House, demanding to vote. The suffragettes, as these women were known, were sometimes faced with both verbal and physical violence. Paul was once sent to prison for seven months.

After many years of marching and fighting, the 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution was ratified. The amendment gave women the right to vote.

title: Susan B. Anthony: Women’s Rights Leader
text:
Many important women worked to improve the quality of life for women in the beginning of the 20th century. One such woman was Susan B. Anthony. Anthony had worked as a school teacher before beginning her work for social reform, or change. She supported the anti-slavery and women’s rights movements. Anthony proved that women could be leaders in society.

She wanted women to have the same rights as men, including the right to vote. After the Civil War, Anthony and her fellow women’s rights workers wanted both formerly enslaved people and women to have the right to vote. They were disappointed when the 14th and 15th Amendments to the Constitution did not talk about women at all.

They didn’t give up, though. Anthony traveled all over the nation to convince people to support her cause. She was once arrested and fined $100 for voting illegally in a presidential election. Women did not gain the right to vote during Anthony’s lifetime. The right came 14 years after her death. Anthony did, however, influence many other Americans to speak out for social reform. Thanks to Susan B. Anthony, women today don’t have to think twice about voting on election day.

title: The Progressive Era
text: Business and industry grew fast in the first 20 years of the 20th century in the United States. Before the turn of the century, the government tried hard not to get involved in private businesses. However, by 1900, many people felt businesses were getting too big and too greedy. They wanted the government to help control large businesses and industries. These people called themselves Progressives. They asked the government to pass laws that would make sure businesses could compete with each other. The government passed laws that prevented one large company from controlling a single industry. Many agencies were created to make sure businesses made and traded goods according to the laws. During this time, the 16th Amendment to the Constitution was ratified. This amendment allowed the government to collect income taxes from citizens.

title: Henry Ford and Mass Production
text: In 1913, car designer and manufacturer Henry Ford developed a new system for making cars in his factory. He began using a moving assembly line, where each worker had one job to do in the car’s assembly. Using this idea, factories could manufacture, or use machinery, to make cars faster than if they were assembled one car at a time. Ford believed that manufacturing cars would make his company very successful. Ford also had new ideas on how to treat workers in his car factory. He offered them up to $5 a day to work for him. At the time, this was a very large wage. Ford wanted to be sure his employees could buy one of the cars they were helping to produce. Today, many of Henry Ford’s ideas about assembly lines are still used at factories around the world.

title: Alabama and World War I
text:
Alabama played an important part in America's war effort in World War I. It provided 5,000 National Guardsmen and 7,000 other volunteers. It also contributed approximately 74,000 white and Black drafted soldiers, called "selectmen," to the Army. Soldiers from Alabama fought bravely in many battles. Their bravery was rewarded with military honors.

Corporal Homer Givens was one of these honored soldiers. Corporal Givens and his fellow soldiers were attacked while on a mission in 1917. According to historical records, “Following a bloody two-hour battle on November 1, 1917, Corporal Givens stood alone after his comrades had fallen. He then managed to kill three enemy soldiers before being severely wounded by twenty-three pieces of shrapnel.” Homer was only 19 years old when he received the title of “America’s first World War I hero.” Besides earning the Purple Heart medal for being injured in battle, Corporal Givens was also awarded the French Cross of War (Croix de Guerre), one of France’s highest military honors.

The soldiers who went away to war were not the only ones who deserve honor and recognition. Many Alabamians pitched in to help the war effort. They supported the war effort by joining voluntary organizations such as the Red Cross, the Women's Committee of the Council of National Defense, the War Camp Community Service, the YMCA, and the YWCA. The Four-Minute Men and Women were groups of speakers who promoted the war effort. Some women formed service groups near Camps Sheridan and McClellan, assisting soldiers' families, providing transportation to and from camps, and hosting social gatherings to keep soldiers well cared for. Local community groups, professors from the Alabama State “Normal School for Negroes,” and women's clubs in Montgomery and Tuscaloosa organized canning factories to preserve Victory Garden produce and keep food affordable in their cities.

title: Alabama's 167th Regiment of the Rainbow Division
text:
Did you know that soldiers from Alabama played an important role in winning World War I? Soldiers from the Alabama National Guard were part of a larger group of soldiers called the Rainbow Division. The Rainbow Division often gets credit for helping to turn the tide in the war.

Major Douglas MacArthur, who would later become an important general in World War II, picked the best National Guard units from coast to coast and put the four best regiments from across the country together to form the Rainbow Division. It was called the Rainbow Division because it stretched “like a rainbow from one end of America to the other.” Alabama’s 167th Alabama Regiment was selected to be a part of the Rainbow Division because it had the reputation of being one of the bravest and best regiments in the country.

On August 28, 1917, a force of 3,677 soldiers left Montgomery on eight trains for Camp Mills, New Jersey to join its new division. After meeting up with the other regiments of the Rainbow Division, they made their way to the battlefields of Europe.

The Rainbow Division fought in many battles in France and Germany. The most famous was the Battle of Croix Rouge Farm on July 26, 1918. For four and a half hours, the Rainbow Division fought in hand-to-hand combat against German soldiers, who ultimately were forced to retreat. In the end,168 Alabamians and 283 Germans were killed. The Battle of Croix Rouge Farm was the second-deadliest battle in history involving Alabamians.

The 167th Infantry Regiment returned to Alabama after four years but lost 616 soldiers on Europe's battlefields. Many Allied forces considered the time when the Rainbow Division entered World War I to be a turning point in the war. Without the bravery and leadership of Alabama’s 167th Infantry Regiment, the outcome of World War I might have been very different.

title: The Great Migration
text:
Between 1915 and 1940, approximately 1.7 million Black people moved from where they had lived in the South to states in the North and West, like Illinois and California. This period of time came to be known as the “Great Migration.” The Great Migration was triggered by both natural and political events.

Natural Disasters

Many Alabamians faced difficult times as farmers in the early 1900s. Massive flooding in 1909 and a boll weevil infestation that began in 1910 caused jobs in agriculture to start disappearing. With so many crops being destroyed, Alabama’s economy soon fell into a depression.

Political Factors

Politically, Black people in Alabama and throughout the South faced segregation, discrimination, and acts of violence. Many families looked to the North, where there appeared to be more opportunities. These opportunities became more appealing when the need for workers in factories in the North grew in World War I. Because the United States was limiting the number of Europeans who could enter the county, Northern factory owners recruited people from the South to work. Many Black Alabamians took this opportunity to move to the Northern or Western states in search of a better life.

The effects of the Great Migration can still be seen today. By 1980, more than one-third of all Black people who had been born in Alabama lived in a Northern or Western state.

title: Industrialization in Alabama
text:
Before the Civil War began in 1861, most free citizens of Alabama made their living by farming cotton. After the Civil War, there was not as much demand (desire to purchase) for cotton. African Americans and poor white farmers were affected by the decreased market prices and limited opportunity for credit. Mobile struggled during this time as well.

But Jefferson County had large deposits of coal, iron, ore, and limestone all close together. So, investors started mining operations in the area. With the mines came work. And with the work came workers and their families.

In 1872, railroad lines connected Mobile, Montgomery, Birmingham, and Nashville. Alabama no longer had to ship raw materials north like other areas did. It could produce iron ore within the state. Eventually, many people began working in mines instead of farming. Alabama soon became a leading provider of iron products.

This time period marked the movement in Alabama from farming toward industrial development. Mills for flour, grist, and wool started to grow, and the demand for laborers increased. This period of industrial and manufacturing expansion is called the New South era.

However, most Alabama citizens were still living on farms and working the land. They were usually tenant farmers or sharecroppers. Tenant farming was when people rented farmland to work instead of owning it. Sharecropping was when landlords received a share of the crop from the farmers who rented from them. These systems usually led to farmers trying to produce the largest crops possible, but they often didn’t make enough to pursue other opportunities. Tenant farmers and sharecroppers often lived close to poverty.

By 1900, Birmingham had become a capital for commerce. Its population rose to roughly 40,000. Railroad lines were built to transport iron, coal, and limestone products to and from Birmingham. Seeing Birmingham’s success, investors started towns near areas predicted to have iron and coal reserves. Several towns were successful, but some were not and ended up bankrupt.

Huntsville, Montgomery, and Gadsden, Alabama, grew because of successful textile mills and manufacturing. The new excitement of industrial labor brought challenges and growth to Alabama. Industrialization brought reform for workers. Many people formed and joined labor unions. These unions helped improve wages, increase the availability of jobs, and reduce child labor.

These changes brought great success and prosperity to Alabama for a time. In the 1920s, farming and industrialization reached economic highs. But production was so successful that soon there was an overproduction (producing more than needed) of goods. Across the country, this overproduction led to an economic crash called the Great Depression. In Alabama, the effects of the Great Depression were devastating. President Franklin D. Roosevelt called the city of Birmingham “the worst-hit town in the country.”

title: Mining Towns in Alabama
text:
As the coal and iron industry developed, mining towns became very popular in Alabama. Mining towns started as small, camp-like communities but soon grew into thriving towns. They built meeting houses, libraries, and community centers.

Seeing these benefits, many people decided to leave sharecropping and tenant farming and move to mining towns. Mining towns were a big improvement over sharecropping and tenant farming. Still, there were challenges, like keeping things clean, keeping town citizens healthy, and helping immigrants adjust to living in a new country. As the mines grew, mine owners expanded the towns and created opportunities for more businesses to start.

title: The Changing Technology of Mining
text:
In the 1870s, many iron makers changed their fuel from coal to coke, a type of coal. Coke was easier to make and cost less. With this change, investors surged into the Alabama coal and iron fields. Several mining companies found success. The Eureka Mining and Transportation Company was located in Oxmoor. Sloss Furnace Company was in Birmingham, built in the early

1800s. Woodward Iron Company operated until 1973. Birmingham became a popular production site for pig iron, a type of crude iron. Something else that helped mining progress was the blast furnace. A blast furnace is a type of furnace used for smelting to create pig iron.

A miner might have been known to carry a pick, shovel, ax, and a kerosene lamp in the 19th century. In the early 1900s, mining technology advanced. Miners started to carry carbide lamps instead of kerosene. Mines started to use rail cars to help with moving large loads of materials and tools.

title: Goods and Services in Mining Towns
text: As more people moved to mining towns, they needed more goods and services. Goods are items that can be sold. Services are tasks performed for some benefit. Investors in mining towns saw a demand for more products. To make those products, producers needed to mine for raw materials. The demand for goods increased. Investors spent a lot of money to mine enough materials to meet those demands. As more people came to the mining towns, there was a demand for more goods and services. Communities worked together to build churches, schools, shops, and medical facilities. Although more goods and services were available, miners did not make a very high wage. Many needed to look for work outside the town as well. Despite the low wages, life in mining towns was an improvement from previous circumstances for migrant workers.

title: Coal Dust
text: Miners faced many challenges to their health and well-being. It was especially difficult for migrant mine workers and those who economically struggled. Miners who had a lower economic status lived closer to the mines. Those who had more wealth lived farther from the mines. The location of homes also contributed to the health of the town members. Working conditions in the mines included long shifts and cramped conditions. There were other hazards to the miners’ physical health. Kerosene lamps had open flames and posed fire risks. Collapsing mines posed risks for workers getting stuck or crushed. Mine workers spend many hours in the mines, breathing in the dust in the air. Breathing in the dust could cause “black lung disease.” Many miners spent long hours in the mines and suffered health challenges as a result. These safety challenges led to improvements in working conditions over time. On April 8, 1911, the Banner Coal Mine had an explosion. It resulted in the greatest loss of life to date in an Alabama mine. The explosion killed over 100 people. This situation brought about change and legislation that improved mine safety in future years.

title: Waterways and Transportation
text:
Changes in transportation in Alabama are a big factor in how the state developed. Waterways, railroads, and modern roads are all ways to move around. Airlines and aerospace industries have also helped with transportation, even to the moon. These exciting modes of transportation have all benefited Alabama.

Horses were an important part of transportation in the early history of Alabama. Horses were used to transport goods and for travel. They provided work on farmlands. Horse shows and competitions have created a demand for goods and services. The equipment and care for horses contribute to the state’s economy.

The Alabama Scenic River Trail was created in 2006. The waterways that make up the trail show travelers many beautiful types of scenery. Along the way, travelers can enjoy mountains, forests, farms, cities, animal life, and topography. Many people enjoy canoeing and kayaking the waterways. Waterways are a great place for recreation and transportation.

Railroads solved many transportation problems in Alabama. Railroads provided opportunities for work and the expansion of business. Many towns were built in Alabama because of the railroads.

Aerospace, biotechnology, and automotive industries also contribute to the economy of Alabama. Alabama is a national leader for research and development in the aerospace industry. Alabama is also a leader of the manufacturing in the aerospace industry. The wages in these industries are high and boost the economy.

title: A Nation Divided
text:
The United States was a divided nation. Legalized slavery had split the country. During the 1800s, compromises were made to keep slavery legal and deter conflict. In 1820, the 22 states of the country were evenly divided between prohibiting or permitting slavery.

The Maine and Missouri territories wanted to become states. To admit both as non-slavery states would upset the balance in the U.S. Senate.

The South wanted to keep the balance. The Missouri Compromise admitted the Missouri territory as a “slave state,” meaning it permitted slavery. The Maine territory was admitted as a “free state,” meaning slavery was illegal. The compromise included banning slavery in the remainder of the Louisiana Territory.

Admitting states to the Union always created conflict. New states threatened the balance of “free” and “slave” states. California was admitted as a free state. The territory of New Mexico (including present-day Arizona and part of Nevada) legalized slavery. The Compromise of 1850 made the buying and selling of people illegal within Washington, D.C.

The final part of the legislation was the Fugitive Slave Act. It required all people escaping slavery to be captured by law enforcement and returned to their enslavers. Officials and citizens of free states were required to cooperate.

The territories of Kansas and Nebraska were officially preparing to become states. Congress passed the Kansas-Nebraska Act. This act let the population of the territory vote to decide if they would legalize enslavement. This act repealed, or canceled, the Missouri Compromise of 1850. There would no longer be a balance between anti-slavery states and pro-slavery states.

In 1860, Abraham Lincoln of Illinois was elected president of the United States. Lincoln and the newly-formed Republican Party believed in expansion and growth without legalized slavery. The Southern states did not approve of Lincoln as president. Nine Southern states, including Alabama, did not include his name on the ballot. The state governments of these nine states threatened that if Lincoln was elected president, they would leave the Union.

Within days of Lincoln’s election, the two senators from South Carolina resigned. On Dec. 20, 1860, the South Carolina state legislature met. They voted 169 to 0 for “the union now subsisting between South Carolina and other States, under the name of ‘The United States of America,’ is hereby dissolved.”

South Carolina’s action of leaving the Union of the United States is called secession. On Jan. 11, 1861, Alabama seceded too and joined the newly formed Confederate States of America. The secession of Alabama and 10 other Southern states would lead to the Civil War.

title: Draw a Picture
text: Draw a community where you learn.

title: Emancipation Proclamation
text:
The Civil War had been going for over a year and a half. Battles had been won and lost on both sides. No one was sure how the war was going to end. Abraham Lincoln was worried because the South had won many battles. He wrote the Emancipation Proclamation, which said that depending on the outcome of the war, enslaved people would be freed. The Emancipation Proclamation included many important ideas. However, it was the 13th Amendment to the Constitution that granted freedom to enslaved people.

Some of the ideas in the Emancipation Proclamation talked about freedoms to work and serve the country. Those freedoms were not given to anyone enslaved at that time.

[...] And I hereby enjoin upon the people so declared to be free to abstain from all violence [...] and I recommend to them that, in all cases when allowed, they labor faithfully for reasonable wages. And I further declare and make known, that such persons of suitable condition, will be received into the armed service of the United States to garrison forts, positions, stations, and other places, and to man vessels of all sorts in said service.

title: The Gettysburg Address
text:
The Gettysburg Address was a speech given by Abraham Lincoln. It was only 272 words long. The speech only took about two minutes for him to give. The speech was given to honor all those who had died fighting in the war. It is considered to be one of the most powerful speeches in America’s history.

This is a part of the speech:

We have come to dedicate a portion of that field, as a final resting place for those who here gave their lives that this nation might live. It is altogether fitting and proper that we should do this.

But, in a larger sense, we can not dedicate — we can not consecrate — we can not hallow — this ground.

The brave men, living and dead, who struggled here, have consecrated it, far above our poor power to add or detract. The world will little note, nor long remember, what we say here, but it can never forget what they did here.

title: Alabama's Response to the War
text:
A Big Decision

A civil war means that citizens within a country are fighting against each other. The war in the United States in the 1860s was a civil war.

One of the causes of the war was about what rights the states had. The Southern states did not want Abraham Lincoln as president. They wanted to be able to make their own choices without influence from Northern states. One choice the Southern states wanted to make was about the legalization of slavery. The question was whether states could decide on their own whether slavery was legal.

Some Americans quickly decided whether to join the Confederate States of America or stay in the Union. Others weighed the decision and had great difficulty making a choice.

Alabama Secedes

Alabama seceded from the Union on Jan. 11, 1861. They left the Union in response to the election of Abraham Lincoln. Alabama’s second constitution was drafted in 1861 as well. This document kept a structure of three branches of government. It also protected enslavement practices. The constitution was not ratified, or approved, by the people. Instead, it was ratified by a committee. Eventually, it was replaced with a different constitution.

When Alabama seceded, many celebrations occurred with cannon fire, shouting, cheers, and more. The newspapers of Alabama were an important communication tool for people in the state. Before the state seceded, some of the newspapers wrote that leaving the Union was a bad idea. After secession, most papers either supported Alabama’s secession or quit publishing.

Goods and Services in War Time

Soon after the Civil War began, the Union Army took over the telegraph. Communication between Confederate states and the Northern states stopped. The Union Army also set up blockades, which meant that Union ships wouldn’t let any trade ships come or go. The Union wanted to keep supplies from coming into Alabama and exports from leaving. Alabama relied on selling cotton and other crops to make money. They relied on trade at the Port of Mobile to be able to buy other goods that they needed.

At first, blockade runners could get past the Union ships to take goods out of Alabama for sale in other places. They brought goods that Alabama needed into the state. But by the last two years of the war, the Union had so many ships that blockade running did not work very well.

Alabama Soldiers

Almost all of the free men from Alabama fought in the Civil War. Some were not able to fight. A small number supported the Union. Most free men enlisted and fought for the Confederacy.

Enslaved Workforce

Thousands of men who would have worked on plantations were forced to help with the Civil War effort. They took care of supplies, transportation, and cooking, and helped in the hospitals. Having enslaved people taking care of these needs meant more white soldiers could fight in the war. These enslaved men were not paid. Thousands of them took their chance to escape and join the Union Army.

Alabama Women in the Civil War

Before the blockades, many goods were available to families in Alabama. However, after the blockades, many goods that people depended on were hard or impossible to get. Some goods, like coffee and a variety of foods, were not needs but were wants that people were not happy to be without. Confederate women worked hard to make things that they could not buy. They fixed things to make them last longer. They found creative ways to make do and make what money they had last.

title: No Jobs, No Money, No Food
text:
Life in Alabama improved after World War I. Most people had jobs and could afford to buy some modern inventions, like vacuums. The 1920s marked a time period of great economic improvements across the country. The flourishing economy made it seem easy to purchase many items beyond what people needed for basic survival. Many people bought their first automobiles in the 1920s, and people began to travel more frequently. Individuals also began to invest in the stock market and buy goods and services on credit.

After 1926, the economic climb in Alabama slowed. Overproduction began to become prominent, and agriculture declined. A slow economic recession began to affect industries. Workers were let go. As people lost their jobs, they could not afford to make payments on credit. Many lost their homes and farms. In Alabama, the steady decline of agriculture created a depressed economy that worsened because of the national crash. When an individual cannot work, they cannot earn money. Without money, they cannot buy the food and necessities they need. During this time, when people did not have jobs, money, or food, many became discouraged.

In 1929, the stock market in the United States crashed. Across the nation, people who had invested in the market began to panic and withdraw their money from the stock market. Many farmers, investors, and individuals in Alabama had overextended their credit. When the market crashed, they were left with debt and little employment opportunity. Soon, many businesses and banks throughout the country closed their doors. People lost their jobs, their businesses, their farms, their homes, and their savings. Many had no money to pay rent, buy food, or provide for their families. Without jobs and wages, people had no other option than to stand in long lines, where they could receive free food. This period of time in the U.S. is known as the Great Depression. In Alabama, the depressed economy lasted from the early 1920s through the 1940s, much longer than the nation as a whole.

Many farming communities suffered during the Great Depression. They were already struggling before the market crash. The dismal days of the depression left many families starving and bankrupt. A farmer’s diet consisted of less meat and more starches, like beans and corn. Growing children would be seen wearing fertilizer or burlap feed sacks as clothing. Many activities were also limited, like going to school, church, or other social gatherings.

In response to the economic downturn, President Franklin D. Roosevelt came up with some new programs meant to help those who were out of work. He called his plan the New Deal. It helped those who were unemployed by giving them jobs doing things that the government needed done.

title: Agricultural Decline
text:
Agriculture means growing crops, farming, and raising livestock. Strong agricultural locations have long growing seasons. The climate in Alabama makes it easy to grow plants. Alabama’s growing season is about 300 days long. Farmers in Alabama grow many crops, including peanuts, corn, soybeans, and cotton. Agriculture has been a common practice for many years in Alabama.

Indigenous peoples farmed Alabama lands for thousands of years. When Indigenous peoples were forced to cede their land, settlers moved to Alabama to buy land for low prices and sell high-priced cotton crops. Prior to the Civil War, much of the agricultural revenue (income or money earned) in Alabama was based on the cotton economy. The demand for cotton created a demand for labor. The two primary labor systems used for cotton farming were slavery and sharecropping. Cotton farming was extremely successful prior to the Civil War. The cotton gin was invented and introduced in Alabama. The cotton gin made it much faster to sell cotton.

In 1861, the Civil War changed agricultural trends in Alabama. The war took farmers from the plow field to the battlefield. Fields fell into disrepair. As soldiers returned to farming, they had little money and few resources (money, materials, and supplies) to invest in new agricultural advancements. Some farmers were sharecropping (sharing profits of farming), or tenant farming (renting farmland). They were not as prosperous as others during the economic upturn of the 1920s. Many people did not have the means to meet their basic needs. Basic needs are things people need to survive, like food, water, and shelter. Farmers insisted that cotton crops would yield the greatest return on their investment. They thought they did not need to rotate crops. However, doing so exhausted the land and decreased crop yields. So many people lost money farming that the agricultural system declined.

Mark the chart to show how many days in the year are considered part of the growing season.

title: Cotton Prices
text: Cotton was one of the greatest sources of economic strength in Alabama. In 1820, Alabama supplied almost four percent of the nation's cotton. In 1830, Alabama was exporting millions of dollars of cotton. Over the next 20 years, the value of cotton changed drastically. Before the Civil War, cotton was a large cash crop for Alabama. It made up about 60 percent of all United States exports. After the Civil War, labor from enslaved people decreased, and production of cotton decreased. Agricultural pests, called boll weevil, also halted production and decreased supply. A shortage (not having enough) in a good or service increases the price. Surplus of a product means there is too much of it and causes the price to fall. Challenges to growing cotton created shortages of cotton and drove the price up. Shortages in 1860 drove the price of cotton up from 10 cents per pound to $1.89 per pound in 1864.

title: From Landowners to Tenants
text:
Alabama economics changed drastically during the Great Depression. The state’s debt increased, industries declined, and unemployment increased. The people in migrant economic situations were not affluent, like those experiencing the highs of the Roaring ‘20s. The economic downturn leading to and throughout the Great Depression was much harsher for this group. Farmers and small towns depending on farming were hit hard. Alabama was one of the hardest-hit states in the nation.

Many farmers had overextended their credit. They had invested in the hope of a high future yield. When the stock market crashed, their credit overextension forced them to give land back to the banks or sell it to the government for low prices. Many farmers had to rent their land back from the government to survive. Poverty (not having enough money to pay for basic necessities) was widespread, especially among low-wage workers. The economic devastation created an awakening to the economic inequalities associated with the social, racial, and industrial culture in Alabama.

title: Early European Explorers
text:
Some eastern parts of the American continents, including parts of Alabama, were first mapped out by explorers from Spain.

Juan Ponce de León

One explorer was Juan Ponce de León. He was governor of Hispaniola, an island in the West Indies. In 1506, he was given three ships and went in search of more land for Spain. He arrived in Puerto Rico and started a settlement there. However, he continued to explore.

In the spring of 1513, he found what he thought was a large island. He called it “La Florida,” which means “full of flowers.” He explored the coast of what we now call the Florida peninsula. He claimed it for Spain. Its boundaries went all the way to Alabama.

In 1521, Ponce de León returned to La Florida to establish another Spanish settlement. However, the Native Americans who already lived there attacked his group. He was shot with a poisoned arrow. He died soon afterward.

Hernando de Soto

Hernando de Soto took Ponce de León’s explorations further. De Soto was the governor of Cuba. The Spanish king told de Soto to conquer Florida for Spain. De Soto sailed for Florida along with 600 soldiers.

After landing on the west coast of Florida, de Soto and his soldiers marched northeast through Georgia. From there, they continued through South Carolina and North Carolina. Then, they explored parts of Tennessee, Alabama, and Mississippi. They fought with Native Americans along their route. De Soto and his men were among the first Europeans to see the Mississippi River.

In 1542, de Soto caught a fever and died later that year. However, the explorers continued, going through parts of Arkansas, Louisiana, and Texas. Eventually, they turned back and sailed down the Mississippi River, returning to the ocean.

Vasco Núñez de Balboa

In 1500, Vasco Núñez de Balboa set off for adventure along the east coast of Panama and Colombia. He made a fortune and settled down to raise pigs. But his farm failed, and he stowed away on a ship to escape his creditors.

He was caught by this ship’s captain. However, he soon became a popular member of the crew. They established a new settlement and made Balboa the mayor and then the governor.

Balboa spent his power and wealth on exploration, conquest, and gold-hunting. In 1513, there was news of a city so rich its people ate off gold plates. The story sent Balboa toward the Isthmus of Panama. The isthmus is a narrow strip of land between Central and South America. From the top of a mountain, Balboa and his soldiers were some of the first Europeans to see the Pacific Ocean. When they reached the coast, Balboa walked into the water and claimed everything the ocean touched for Spain.

title: The New Deal in Alabama
text: The Great Depression created a lot of poverty. The government stepped in to help address poverty. Before that, states attempted to solve the problems on their own. However, government funds were limited. State leaders did their best to address the needs of the citizens within state borders. Many programs for relief did little to help. Job referral service attempts failed when there was not enough work for applicants. Many citizens relied on church groups to assist with food and clothing needs. Alabama citizens began to see relief when the New Deal arrived in 1933. It would take a long time for true relief to come. The economy wouldn’t really begin to recover until after World War II.

title: Industry in Alabama
text: Industry in Alabama changed drastically during the Great Depression. Industry is the economic activity involving raw materials and manufacturing goods. The Civil War, the Great Depression, the New Deal, and World War II all impacted industry in Alabama. The Civil War took farmers away from the fields and put them to work on the battlefield. The outcome of the Civil War led to decreased enslaved labor and increased numbers of unskilled wage workers. The Great Depression caused hardship for farmers and those in the mining industry. The New Deal allowed people to receive federal aid (money from the government). People then returned to farming. The effects of the boll weevil and failure to rotate crops brought migration from farm to factory again. However, the challenges to the economy, farming, and individuals brought innovation and new industry to Alabama. Farmers embraced new technologies in farming equipment and methods. New businesses emerged. Government programs assisted individuals and encouraged signing up for new government programs.

title: Cherokee
text:
The Cherokee are a group of Native Americans. During the Age of Exploration, they lived in what we now know as Georgia, North and South Carolina, and Tennessee. Their land was controlled by the entire tribe of Cherokee people. However, each group lived separately. These groups survived on their own, coming together in times of war or to council together.

Men and women were equally important in Cherokee society. Each played a role that kept them alive.

Men hunted for big and small game. Food and clothing came from turkey, deer, elk, and bear, as well as rabbits and squirrels. The men hunted with bows and arrows and knives. Arrowheads and knives were made of stone.

Men were also warriors. They protected their families and the tribe.

Women gathered plants and nuts to eat. They grew maize, beans, and squash. They made clothing from the skins of animals and blankets to keep their families warm. Women also raised the children.

Cherokee homes were situated near a council building. It was big enough to hold all the members of the community. Tribal events were held here, as well as religious ceremonies.

Homes were usually big because the mother’s family all lived together. The mother’s parents, children, and unmarried brothers and sisters were in one home. When a man married a woman, he moved in with her family.

title: The Chickasaw
text:
The Chickasaw first lived in what is now known as Alabama, Mississippi, Kentucky, and Tennessee. In times of war, this group of people lived close together. When there was peace, the Chickasaw spread out. They lived in small villages.

A village was set up so homes formed a circle around the main meeting place. This council house was in the center of the village. Homes and structures were built with wood frames. A mixture of mud and straw covered the frame like plaster might.

Women cared for the children. Women gathered nuts and berries for food and grew corn, beans, and squash. They made the family’s clothing from animal skins.

Men hunted. Like many other Native Americans, they used all parts of the animals they hunted. Nothing went to waste. Animals were sacred and respected. Only what was needed was killed for food and clothing.

The men fought when it was necessary. The Chickasaw played stickball to help them be better warriors. They also played for fun. Many villages had their own playing fields.

The Chickasaw lived with rules and religion. They believed in a supreme being called Abaꞌ Binniꞌli. The name means “Sitting Above” or “Dwelling Above.” Abaꞌ Binniꞌliꞌ made all the animals. He created warmth and life. He lived above the clouds in the sky.

title: The Choctaw
text:
The Choctaw lived in what is now known as western Alabama and Mississippi. They were skilled farmers, warriors, and sportsmen.

The Nanih Waiya Mound, or Mother Mound, was sacred to the Choctaw. Mother Mound was considered the birthplace of the Choctaw. Houses were built on or near Nanih Waiya. Homes were frames of wood covered in mud. A roof was constructed from reeds or grass.

The women of the Choctaw tribe grew corn, beans, and squash. They tended the crops, cared for their children, and made clothes for the family. Men hunted both large and small game. They fished, too.

If it was necessary for the Choctaw to go to war, the tribe would do a war dance. Women joined the men in this dance. It prepared the men for battle. Rather than fight, though, tribes sometimes settled arguments by playing stickball.

Stickball was played on a large field. There were goals at each end. The field might be as long as a modern-day football field. It might also be miles long, running between two villages. The game helped settle arguments between tribe members. It also helped settle disputes over hunting grounds. A game between two tribes might have more than a thousand players. Stickball was also played for fun.

title: A Brief History of the Poarch Band of Creek Indians
text:
The Muscogee, or Creek, Indians descend from the peoples of the Mississippian period (c. 800-1500 C.E.). In the 16th century, the arrival of Spanish colonizers brought epidemics, violence, and unrest to the southeastern United States, resulting in a reorganization of the Indigenous peoples.

Did you know that the English settlers gave the Muscogee people the nickname “Creek Indians”? They named them this because all of their etvlwv (ee-dull-wuh), or tribal towns, were situated by creeks, rivers, and streams. These etvlwv shared language, customs, and lifestyles and became a confederation covering most of present-day Alabama and Georgia that lasted until the early 19th century. The Poarch Band of Creek Indians are direct descendants of the original Muscogee Nation.

Creek Indians were well-established farmers who produced corn, beans, and squash, among many other cultivated crops. They also used what nature provided them, like berries, fruit, and nuts. Hunting and fishing was also a large part of culture. They regularly hunted deer, bear, turkey, rabbit, and squirrel to feed their people.

In 1830, President Andrew Jackson and the United States Congress passed the Indian Removal Act, which called for thousands of American Indians of various tribes to be forcibly removed from their ancestral homelands to Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma). The forced journey to Oklahoma is commonly referred to as the Trail of Tears. For various reasons, several pockets of Creek Indians from different tribal towns were able to remain in Alabama.

On Aug. 11, 1984, the U.S. formally acknowledged that the Poarch Creek Indians officially exist as an “Indian tribe.” A segment of the original reservation land granted by U.S. government land grants became the center of tribal operations. It is the only land within the original domain of the Creek Confederacy to still be occupied by Creek people to this day.

title: The Creek War
text:
Tension

Times were changing in the early 1800s. The United States was a brand-new nation. However, British influence was still strong, as proved by the War of 1812. These two factors influenced the groups of people native to the South in several ways.

One important way was tension about who would get the land. More settlers were coming in. Land looked free and open to the settlers. The land was taken for farms. However, the land was not considered free for the taking by the tribes who hunted and fished there.

Economics were changing too. People wanted goods that had been imported from Europe. That included indigenous people as well as white settlers. Some Creek wanted access to cloth and other goods. These items had to be purchased from either the white settlers or the British. The Creek also began farming animals like the white settlers and British did.

Other bands did not like taking on European ways. They thought that farming and raising, or domesticating, animals was not natural. They did not want their people to change to this different way of living. They wanted to fight the settlers and drive them away.

Early Conflict

One early battle, on July 27, 1813, was called the Battle of Burnt Corn Creek. The battle involved a group of militia, or men who were not professional soldiers. They were civilians fighting as soldiers for the time. They came across a band of Creek and surprised them with an attack. Men were killed on both sides, though eventually the militia ran away.

The Red Stick Band of Creeks wanted to retaliate, or fight back.

On Aug. 30, 1813, about 700 Red Stick warriors attacked the poorly defended Fort Mims. They killed about 250 people. It was the first of several attacks. The Creek War had begun. They were called Red Stick after the Fort Mims massacre because they had war clubs that they painted red when they fought. In other words, they raised the “red stick” of war.

Conflict Grows

The different groups of Creeks gathered together to prepare for more conflicts. They built barriers to protect them from soldiers. These barriers became the sites of fighting. John Cocke, Andrew Jackson, and John Coffee all led soldiers to attack.

Fighting lasted for months. By January 1814, only Andrew Jackson’s soldiers kept fighting for the settlers. Jackson had enlisted more men so that he had over 1,000 soldiers. When the 39th U.S. Infantry Regiment with 600 men joined him, they decided to attack the largest remaining Red Stick settlement.

The battle of Horseshoe Bend took place on Mar. 27, 1814. Jackson’s army, supported by Cherokee and Creek supporters, defeated the Red Sticks. Even after the battle, many of the Red Stick warriors’ families died of starvation or exposure to the weather. Many surrendered. Others fled as refugees to Florida and joined the Seminole.

Outcomes of the Creek War

Andrew Jackson insisted on a treaty that gave large amounts of Muscogee Creek land to white settlers. While few Creek agreed with the treaty, they could not fight it. On Aug. 9, 1814, Creek leaders signed the treaty.

title: Resources of Alabama
text:
Resources are things that people find, make, or use in their environment. They can come from plants and animals. They can be things that are on the surface of or under the Earth, like minerals or water. People are also a resource to help each other survive and build a community. Alabama is an especially rich state with forests, mountains, and other natural resources in the north and good farmland in the south. The network of rivers and lakes hold resources such as water and fish. They also provide a way to transport people and goods around the state and to the Port of Mobile. From here, Alabama sends goods out through the Gulf of Mexico to trade with other states and countries.

Forests are a source of natural resources in more than one way. They provide wood for making other goods. They are a home for an ecosystem of different plants and animals. Forests are also good for Alabama’s economy. The beautiful forests and mountains of Alabama allow people to spend time in nature. Alabama is special because a lot of forest land is owned by individual families. The families of Alabama help care for our natural resources.

Below ground, Alabama has an unusual combination of metals and minerals. Iron ore, limestone, and coal are resources that are all found in Alabama. These three resources are used in making steel. That is why Alabama produces so much steel.

Steel isn’t the only technology in Alabama. Alabama produces over one million cars a year. Many people in Alabama have jobs with car companies. Alabama is also part of the space program. A combination of Alabama’s natural and human resources help solve problems on Earth and in space. Human resources are people who can get work done and solve problems.

Human resources and natural resources also come together on Alabama’s farms. The state was first known for its cotton crops. The Black Belt region of Alabama was an ideal place to grow cotton. While cotton is still an important resource, farmers also grow corn, soybeans, peanuts, and other crops. They raise farm animals, like cows, chickens, and hogs. The soil, climate, and ecosystem provide a good environment for human resources. The people who work on the farms raise food to eat and to sell or trade, all of which supports Alabama’s economy.

Even though Alabama has so many different resources, trade is still important. Not everything needed can be raised or made inside the state, so buying and selling goods and services around the state, the nation, and the world is what Alabama’s economy is all about.

title: Treaties, Negotiation, and War
text:
A treaty is a formal document that creates an agreement between two nations. Representatives of the government are authorized to create a treaty on behalf of their nations. The goal of a treaty is to end conflict and prevent further conflict. The discussion to get nations to agree on the terms of a treaty is called a negotiation. Conflict can occur when people or groups of people disagree. Usually conflict can be solved by following conflict resolution steps.

State the problem.

Identify the cause of the problem.

Suggest solutions for the problem.

Attempt to solve the problem.

Reach out to experts to brainstorm possible solutions.

When conflict between large groups of people, like countries and nations, cannot be resolved, they may resort to war. War is a state of armed conflict between groups of people, states, or nations. Conflict over critical issues can make it difficult to identify a solution. Critical issues may include areas like power, resources, beliefs, or basic human rights. Conflicts in situations like these may result in war if no solutions seem possible. However, sometimes these types of conflict can be resolved through the use of treaties.
