title: Analyze the Impact
text: Use the timeline and the maps to analyze the impact of the Trail of Tears on Alabama’s Indigenous people.

title: Social, Political, and Economic Consequences
text:
Because of the rich agricultural lands in what is present-day Alabama, Georgia, Mississippi, and Tennessee, U.S. settlers wanted this land for farming. Settlers pressured American Indian nations to cede, or give up control, of their land. Alabama became a state in 1819 and in the 1820s, populations of settlers increased. The federal government began offering western territory in exchange for American Indian homelands. Increasing numbers of settlers and increasing demand for land led to conflict between settlers and Indigenous people.

When President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act in 1830, it required many changes for the territories involved. At the time, settlers had the idea that their right to the land was stronger than the right of the Indigenous people. This disagreement led to conflict and hostilities. American settlers wanted the freedom to discover and use gold and other valuable resources. Americans felt the need to take the lands and expand their territories. American Indian people felt the need to protect their territories from expansion and maintain it for their use. Expansion helped settlers use the land for farming, resources and to search for gold. Leaving the land cost the American Indians much.

title: The Indian Removal Act
text:
Conflict, war, and negotiations all leave an impact on the people involved. Between 1837 and 1839, military troops forced more than 200,000 American Indians from their land in the Southeast. Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole, and Cherokee were affected. This painful historical event in U.S. history is known as the Indian Removal Act. The forced march, known as the “Trail of Tears,” left a great impact on the territory, lives, and rights of the Indigenous people involved.

Tribe members, including the young and old, were forced to give up their lands and move. Many had few personal resources. They suffered greatly as they carried their belongings and walked to their westward destination. During their travels, they had few resources. They had limited water and food. They suffered exposure to all types of weather. Many became sick, injured, weak, and starved. More than 1,000 Cherokee died during the trip west. All were affected physically, socially, and emotionally by the forced relocation. After tribes were moved, the forts and camps in Alabama were abandoned and the property was sold at public auction.

Today, the National Park Service educates visitors about the Trail of Tears National Historic Trail. Many people visit the sites along the trail to learn about the people who traveled the trails. On September 28, 2013, the Etowah Historical Society’s Heritage Museum in Gadsden, Alabama, dedicated an exhibit to recognize the event. The exhibit includes a memorial, artwork, photographs, and information about the Cherokee history and removal process.

title: Consequences of Conflict
text:
Conflict tends to have consequences for all involved. When groups of people demonstrate respect for and kindness to one another, the likelihood of resolution with minimal consequences increases.

The consequences of the War of 1812 and the Trail of Tears are much larger and long lasting than the consequences of small conflicts. The lives of those affected were changed forever. The survivors of the Indian Removal Act had to start new lives in Oklahoma and Kansas. The tribes were given small parcels of lands called allotments. They had to farm and build their homes on these allotments. It proved difficult to produce food. The tribes were not familiar with farming in the new environments. Many times, the removed tribes had to rely on the government for food. The tribes helped each other out as best they could. However, many of the tribes were from very different parts of the country and spoke different languages. Although the impact of the Trail of Tears was devastating, the Cherokee people displayed resilience. Today, the members of the independent tribe recognize the adversity they endured, and do their best to invest in a future filled with hope and opportunity.

title: 31st Dixie Division
text:
The 31st Dixie Division was created when Alabama’s National Guard unit was called into service for World War I in 1917. Over 3,600 soldiers from this unit became part of the famous Rainbow Regiment, and the remaining 1,300 soldiers became the 31st Infantry Division. The 31st was made up of soldiers from all over Alabama, as well as Georgia and Florida. Because they were all from Southern states, the 31st was known as the "Dixie Division,” with the motto "It shall be done." The 31st Division’s insignia is back-to-back red double Ds on a white field circled in red. Between World War I and World War II, the 31st remained a National Guard unit, helping in times of unrest in the United States.

Because of war in Europe and unrest in Asia, President Franklin D. Roosevelt ordered the 31st into active service on November 25, 1940. The Division was stationed in Birmingham until their base at Camp Blanding in Florida was completed. As the division began its training, recruits from other parts of the United States joined the division, but the nickname “Dixie Division” remained. From January 1941 until March 1944, the 31st trained and prepared for war. The unit was on the move a lot and completed training in many states, including Florida, North Carolina, Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, West Virginia, and Virginia. But training in the Deep South's summer heat and humidity proved very good for the Division, as it helped prepare soldiers for battle in the harsh weather of the South Pacific.

World War II was the most active period for the 31st. Soldiers first trained and then were sent to battle in what is known as the Pacific Theater. First the Division was deployed to the islands of Morotai and Sansapor, where it remained and trained until April 1945. The 31st was then sent to Mindanao Island in the Philippines. There, the 31st encountered fierce resistance and heavier fighting than it had experienced before. The division's brave actions in the Battle of Mindanao helped liberate, or free, the Philippines from Japanese control, which helped lead to the end of the war. The soldiers of the 31st Division were recognized for their bravery in battle, with soldiers earning some of the military’s highest honors, including the Silver Star, the Medal of Honor, and the Distinguished Service Cross.

The 31st Division returned to the United States to Camp Stoneman, California, and was deactivated in December 1945, returning to National Guard status.

title: Alabama Resources for the War Effort
text:
Besides supplying soldiers to battlefields in Europe and the Pacific, Alabama contributed to the war effort in many ways. On the home front (back home in Alabama), Alabamians contributed by holding scrap drives, where residents collected metal and rubber needed to build weapons and other machines important to the war effort. They also sent care packages to soldiers on the battlefields of Europe and the Pacific. People in home front communities did all they could to contribute to the war effort.

The war also benefited Alabama’s agriculture industry. Cotton prices, which fell throughout the Great Depression, rose as textile mills won contracts to produce military uniforms, bedding, tents, and sandbags. Alabama's forest-products industry also contributed to the war effort. Because of increased demand for Alabama’s lumber and paper products, the production of Alabama’s forest products ranked third in the nation.

One of the most important contributions that Alabama made to the war effort was in the production of aluminum. Aluminum was the most important resource in the manufacturing of military aircraft. At the time, there were only five plants in the United States that played a part in the manufacture of aluminum, and two of these plants were in Alabama. A plant at Listerhill and a plant at the docks in Mobile were extremely important to the aluminum industry. By 1943, the plant in Mobile was producing 34 percent of all aluminum made in America. Aluminum companies operated a fleet of 29 ships that hauled bauxite (a mineral used in making aluminum) from South America to the Mobile plant. Alabama’s aluminum plants were so important to the war effort that the plant in Mobile was among the targets of German spies arrested in the summer of 1942.

title: The Civilian Pilot Training Program
text:
In 1939, when World War II began in Europe, the U.S. Army had only 4,502 pilots. While the number of new Army pilots grew each year as war seemed more likely, many more were needed, and the Army by itself could not train the huge numbers of pilots needed when the U.S. entered the war. To help expand the number of trained pilots, the U.S. government created the Civilian Pilot Training Program, or CPTP. The CPTP operated at over 1,000 American colleges and 1,400 flight schools. Through the CPTP, civilians (people who were not in the military) were given basic flight training in the classroom. Individuals who completed this training would then conduct in the air flight training at flight schools or in the military. The CPTP trained 435,165 pilots from 1939 to 1944.

One of the most famous Civilian Pilot Training Programs was established at The Tuskegee Institute in Tuskegee, Alabama. Tuskegee was one of six Historically Black Colleges that participated in the CPTP. Tuskegee began its first class in late 1939, with 20 students: 18 men and two women. With their classroom training complete, students had to travel 40 miles (each way!) to Montgomery to complete their flight training. Nineteen of the first 20 students completed this training and became the first group of licensed pilots to graduate from the Tuskegee program. Between 1941 and 1946, over 1,000 pilots were trained through the Tuskegee CPTP. Many of these pilots became part of the world-famous Tuskegee Airmen. Overall, The Tuskegee Airmen destroyed 251 enemy airplanes and were awarded a total of 150 Distinguished Flying Crosses for their service.

title: The Women of World War II
text:
Women in the Workforce

Women took on many roles during WWII. While the men were fighting overseas, many women had to fill vacant positions in the workforce. Many job opportunities opened up for women that had previously been reserved for men. They began working as drivers, firefighters, and police officers. Some women took on work that was very physically demanding, such as building ships in shipyards or working in welding shops and factories. The need for agricultural workers drastically increased during the war. Cotton and citrus fruit farming spiked. Women poured into the agriculture industry to keep up food production. At one point, they made up roughly one-fourth of the farmworkers in America.

Women in the Military

Women also took jobs on military bases. They joined programs like Women’s Auxiliary Air Corps (WAAC) and the Navy-based Women Accepted for Volunteer Emergency Service (WAVES). There, they served as drivers, mechanics, phone operators, and postal clerks. They also performed clerical and communications work and more.

Women’s Army Corps

In 1943, the WAAC received full military status and became the Women’s Army Corps (WAC). This means that women who served in the WAC were the first women other than military nurses to serve in the United States Army. The WAC supported the war effort in World War II and later the Korean and Vietnam wars. The WAC was discontinued in 1978, but the women who served were always considered full members of the U.S. Army.

Women’s Army Nurse Corps

More than 59,000 American nurses served in the Army Nurse Corps during World War II. These nurses worked closer to the front lines than they ever had before. Nurses in the Army Nurse Corps often cared for injured soldiers while they were under fire themselves. They were dedicated to supporting the war effort and through their care, more than 96 percent of soldiers who were wounded in the field and cared for by a field nurse survived their injuries.

title: Alabama's Workforce During WWII
text: When the United States entered World War II after the attacks on Pearl Harbor, many men from Alabama signed up to protect the United States and the world from the Axis Powers of Germany, Italy, and Japan. Over the course of the war, about 300,000 people from Alabama served in the military. Women served an important role in World War II as well. Women volunteered to serve in the Women’s Army Corps (WAC), Women’s branch of the U.S. Naval Reserve (WAVES), as well as in the Army Nurse Corps. However, it wasn’t just in the army or through nursing that women played an important role in the war effort. When men left to serve in the military, the jobs previously held by men now were open to women. Women left working in the home or as school teachers to now hold jobs that had not been available to them before the war, such as working in the shipping yards in Mobile Bay, Alabama or the arsenal located in Huntsville. Not only women helped in the workforce at home. Many African American men signed up for military service, while others remained and also were able to take jobs that were previously not available to them, such as welders at the dry shipping docks. Having capable workers at home allowed Alabama's economy to grow. Towns such as Mobile, Montgomery, and Huntsville where there was plenty of work and good wages for workers also grew. Industry and the economy in Alabama were able to grow during World War II due to this important workforce at home!

title: Rationing During WWII
text: Once the United States entered World War II, it was important to gather materials to create all of the necessary items that soldiers would need to fight in the war. Because the country was coming out of the Great Depression and manufacturing was just starting up again, there was a need to be resourceful and creative when it came to getting what the soldiers needed. Alabamians rose to the challenge of being resourceful and creative by holding drives to collect scrap metal or rubber, as well as making bandages and knitting sweaters for the Red Cross to send to soldiers in need around the world. Alabama led the entire nation in raising money by buying war bonds to support the troops. Another way to make sure that soldiers were able to get the supplies that they needed was through rationing. Rationing is a system of setting limits on purchasing in-demand goods. Everyone in the country was issued points, even babies! They could then turn in these points along with money to buy certain items such as tires, gasoline, shoes, sugar, and bacon. Many people in Alabama and throughout the country planted gardens, which became known as “Victory Gardens,” in order to grow their own vegetables and free up large manufacturers to send canned food to the troops. While rationing during World War II was hard for a lot of people, Alabamians knew that they could play an important part in the war effort and make sure soldiers had what they needed through rationing.

title: Winnie the Welder and Zaddie Johnson
text:
Alabama Dry Dock and Shipbuilding Company (ADDSCO) played a vital role in Mobile’s economy and shifted production during WWII to wartime production. As demand for ships increased, ADDSCO became Mobile’s largest employer of wartime workers. About 2,000 women went to work in shipyards and worked in industrial positions across the nation.

In Alabama, women took jobs as welders during the war efforts. Welding was hard and dangerous work. Women workers needed to learn how to climb platforms safely, pull heavy electrical cables as they worked to weld, or join pieces of metal together with high heat. “Winnie the Welder” became a WWII icon, a symbol of the women welders across the nation. Zaddie Johnson was a wartime welder who took on more responsibilities and worked hard in the war effort as a welder. Zaddie became a leader of an all-female welding crew in Mobile, Alabama. Zaddie and her crew were instrumental in creating battle-ready ships. In fact, they created one ship every day!

It wasn’t just welding that women were doing. At the height of the war production, women made up about 25% of the labor force in Alabama industries. Women working outside of the home also earned more money to support their families while men were off at war. African American women made up a significant number of female workers at Huntsville Arsenal helping to create weapons and other materials to send across seas to the war. Women contributed great efforts, hard work, and innovation to the wartime efforts during WWII.

title: Educational Improvements In Alabama
text:
Wartime industry didn’t just have an effect on businesses and women entering the workforce in the welding and arsenal industries. With more work and funding from military contracts and more workers in Alabama during World War II, there was also an increase in people paying taxes. This increase in state taxes allowed Alabama to make many improvements in education. While many male teachers left the classroom to fight in the war or work in wartime industries, more women became school teachers to fill the need. Having more tax money also allowed Alabama to pay teachers to work with their students longer throughout the year, and by 1943, the school year had increased to eight months a year in Alabama. This longer school year allowed more time for students and teachers to work together on their subjects. Increased money from taxes also helped students in other ways.

The Alabama State Department of Education administered the National School Lunch Program to improve student nutrition during WWII. Also, with so many new workers supporting the war effort, school buses were used to transport wartime workers to their jobs! However, not every student in Alabama benefitted from these educational improvements. During this time in many states in the United States, schools were segregated by race. Because of segregation and the laws that enforced it, many non-white segregated schools did not receive the same funding that other schools did. Schools were like this until 1954 when the U.S. Supreme Court case of Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka ruled that schools in the United States could not be segregated by race. While great improvements in education were beginning at this time, there were still many obstacles to overcome.

title: Montgomery's Soldier's Center
text:
There were many forts and training facilities located in Alabama during World War I and II for soldiers to learn how to serve in the military. When soldiers weren’t training and preparing for war, they were allowed to go to serviceman centers. These were centers where soldiers could hear live music, dance, and have some fun before leaving for war. The very first civilian-run Soldier's Center was established in Montgomery, Alabama, during WWII. A civilian is a person who is not in the armed forces or police force.

Montgomery’s Soldier’s Center eventually became one of the Army-Navy USO Clubs. The United Service Organization (USO) played an important role in WWII. With locations near military training centers, these centers often provided entertainment to troops stationed across the world, helping keep the soldiers' morale and spirits up while fighting in a very difficult war. USO clubs were a place for soldiers to gather. Often they could get free coffee and donuts, as well as cookies and sandwiches. Stationery to write letters to family and friends back home was also available. Often local women from Montgomery would volunteer at the Montgomery Army-Navy USO center as “hostesses” to help mend soldiers' uniforms, talk to soldiers about their lives and families back home, and even dance with soldiers during the evening live-music dances. The USO Clubs were a very important part of the home effort in the war, not only providing food and entertainment to soldiers but also helping them make the transition from training to going into battle.

title: Redstone Arsenal, Fort Rucker, Fort McClellan, and Craig Air Force Base
text:
Alabama played a very important role in the United States participation in World War II. Alabama’s location, ports, and wartime industries made it an ideal location to also train and prepare soldiers to fight in World War II.

Redstone Arsenal:

Located in Huntsville, Redstone Arsenal was a very important ordnance plant during World War II for the United State military. An ordnance plant was a factory where weapons for World War II were manufactured, tested, stored, and eventually shipped out to military locations. Redstone Arsenal employed many women from the local area, including many African American women, many of whom were able to enter the workforce for the first time. The workers at the Redstone Arsenal attended school at night to learn how to meet the demands of their new jobs. Free classes from the University of Alabama and Auburn University included basic accounting, structural design, mechanical and electrical maintenance, industrial management, chemistry, and engineering drawing, as well as chemical laboratory techniques. These classes trained women workers for new careers while they also served their country working at Redstone Arsenal.

Fort Rucker:

Fort Rucker is the largest military base in Alabama. Located in Coffee and Dale counties, this military base stretches over 64,000 acres! Built during World War II, this military base trained thousands of soldiers to fight in the war. There were specialty trainings that occurred here as well, for driving tanks and the Women’s Army Corps (WAC). Today, Fort Rucker is home to the U.S. Army Aviation Center of Excellence. Due to the large airspace available, all Army Aviation training has been at Fort Rucker since 1973, as well as training of U.S. Air Force, helicopter pilots, and aircrew. Also, Fort Rucker is the home to the U.S. Army Aviation Technical Test Center (ATTC), which conducts developmental aircraft testing for Army Aviation.

Fort McClellan:

Located in Anniston, Alabama, Fort McClellan played an important role in WWI. During WWII, Fort McClellan was expanded to include an artillery range for National Guard training. Artillery refers to large weapons such as cannons or rockets, often too heavy for a person to carry. Fort Mclellan was also home to the segregated African American divisions, who trained for battle in WWII. In one year (1942-43), over 6,500 African American troops were trained and prepared at Fort McClellan. Fort McClellan also trained two divisions of the Women's Army Corps, one white and one African American. The Fort also housed approximately 3,000 German and Italian prisoners of war between 1943-46. These prisoners were returned to their home countries following the end of the war.

Craig Air Force Base:

Located outside of Selma, Craig Airforce Base was an important training facility for the U.S. Air Force Undergraduate Pilot Training program. Between 1941-45, over 9,000 American and British pilots graduated from the training program at Craig Airforce Base! During World War II, on this large training facility, there were two 8,000-foot runways for pilots to use in their training, as well as maintenance hangers and parking ramps. Today, this former base is used as a civilian airport and is known as Craig Field Airport and Industrial Complex.

title: The Invasion of the Bay of Pigs
text:
Three days in April 1961 have become memorable in history as an invasion that didn’t work out. This attempted invasion happened in the Bay of Pigs. The bay is located in Cuba, a small island country in the West Indies. Cuba is about 90 miles from the United States, just south of the tip of Florida.

Cuba had experienced a lot of change in its government. Between 1902 and 1959, it had several different governments and military occupations. After the Cuban Revolution in 1959, Fidel Castro and his supporters took over the country.

The United States had been involved in events in Cuba for over 100 years. Cuba is very close to the United States. The U.S. did not like Fidel Castro’s new government. Castro quickly took over America-owned properties and executed, or killed, his political enemies. He also started working with countries that had communist governments instead of governments based on democracy. Castro worked with China and North Korea and made an alliance with Russia.

The U.S. government was worried that the Republic of Cuba would become a communist country. They did not want to have a communist country so close to the United States. President Dwight D. Eisenhower authorized the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) to secretly support efforts to overthrow Castro. Invading the Bay of Pigs was one of those efforts.

Some Cubans wanted to fight against Castro. The United States trained these soldiers in secret. There were 1,400 secretly trained Cuban soldiers who landed on a beach in the Bay of Pigs. They landed on the evening of April 17. Unfortunately, they were quickly outnumbered by Castro’s troops. After only three days, the fighting was over. Castro had won.

The Bay of Pigs is of particular interest to Alabama. Although most of the invasion involved Cuban exiles, members of the Alabama Air National Guard secretly took part. Most of these men volunteered to help train the Cubans for the invasion. Eight of them, four pilots and four enlisted crew members, actually flew four bombers during the invasion. Four of them, Riley Shamburger, Wade Gray, Pete Ray, and Leo F. Baker, were killed.

Cuban Missile Crisis
October 14: A U.S. spy plane captures photographs of Soviet forces installing missile sites on the island of Cuba.

October 16-21: U.S. President John F. Kennedy meets with advisors to assess the situation in Cuba.

October 22: In a televised speech, Kennedy discusses the threat of attack from Cuba and announces the blockade of the island.

October 23: Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev writes to Kennedy, refusing to remove the missiles. Kennedy responds by blaming the current crisis on the Soviet Union.

October 24: Khrushchev writes to Kennedy again, stating that Kennedy is openly threatening the Soviet Union.

October 25: Soviet ships carrying missiles and weapons to Cuba return to Europe. Kennedy lifts the blockade to allow the oil tanker Bucharest to deliver its cargo to the island and prevent further hostilities.

October 26: Cuban leader Fidel Castro urges Khrushchev to launch a nuclear strike against the United States, but Khrushchev refuses. Instead, he sends a letter to President Kennedy to solve the problem diplomatically.

October 27: U.S. plane piloted by Major Rudolf Anderson is shot down over Cuba. Many government officials encourage Kennedy to declare war.

October 28: Kennedy and Khrushchev reach an understanding. Khrushchev agrees to remove all missiles from Cuba. Kennedy agrees not to attack Cuba after the Soviets withdraw and to remove American missiles from Turkey.

title: What Does a New Country Look Like?
text:
In the early 1990s, Iraqi President Saddam Hussein was trying to rebuild Iraq after the Iran-Iraq War. Iraq had helped protect neighboring countries. Hussein asked that the money Iraq owed to those countries be forgiven. When this request was denied, Hussein attacked Kuwait so that Iraq could take over their oil fields.

The United States had been working with Iraq to end conflicts and avoid war. President George H. W. Bush learned of the attack. He decided the United States needed to intervene. The United Nations and the U.S. invaded Iraq from the air and land. During the attacks, many of Iraq’s major structures were destroyed. The destruction included oil refineries and power and hydroelectric stations. So began the Gulf War, named for the Persian Gulf.

The attacks themselves lasted about a month. They took an enormous toll on the land and people. Lawlessness was abundant. Violence and looting impacted the economy. Iraq’s economic recovery slowed. The U.S. used ground forces to stop groups of people from fighting. The U.S. worked with the United Nations to provide relief aid, such as medicine, food, and water. The World Bank loaned money to help rebuild Iraq. It took eight years for change to take place after the Gulf War.

The U.S. invaded Iraq again in 2003. In 2005, Iraq became a federal parliamentary republic. It was led by 19 governorates. These governorates, or provinces, had power at both the national and subnational levels. Iraq established three branches of government to divide power. The legislative branch is the Council of Representatives, elected by the people. The Council oversees presidential elections. It also approves other governmental appointments. The executive branch is composed of the president and a council of ministers. They oversee the general operation of the country. The judicial branch serves as the final court of appeal.

Rebuilding Iraq is a continuing process.

title: WWII Heroes
text:
Commander Howard Gilmore, who was born in Selma, won the Medal of Honor for saving his submarine and its crew when it was attacked by the Japanese. He knew that the only way to save everyone was to order the submarine to submerge. He had been wounded and couldn't move. He knew that he would die if they submerged, but he gave the order anyway.

First Lieutenant William Lawley, Jr., has a bridge near Wetumpka named after him for his bravery. Badly wounded, he somehow managed to land his damaged airplane and save his crew.

Staff Sergeant Henry "Red" Erwin of Bessemer was on a bombing raid over Tokyo when a phosphorous bomb inside the airplane accidentally went off. He grabbed the bomb and threw it from the plane. Because of his bravery, the pilot was able to regain control of the plane, and all aboard were saved. Erwin had to go through many operations and skin grafts to heal the serious burns he received because of his selfless actions.

The five Crommelin brothers from Wetumpka all graduated from the United States Naval Academy and served their country in the Pacific. Two of the brothers, Richard and Charles, were killed in plane crashes. The other three - John, Quentin, and Henry - continued to fight overseas after their brothers' deaths.

Tuskeegee Airmen

The Tuskeegee Airmen were a group of African American pilots who flew for the U.S. Army Air Force during World War II. They were part of the 332nd Fighter Group and were trained at Tuskeegee Institute, the school founded by Booker T. Washington. They flew more than 1,600 missions over Europe and earned more than 800 awards for their bravery. These men were part of the only fighter group who never lost a pilot to the enemy. They were later represented in the G.I. Joe line of action figures. In 1995, a movie called The Tuskeegee Airmen told the story of their accomplishments and their bravery. The airfield where these men trained is now known as the Tuskeegee National Historic Site.

title: Remembering Veterans
text:
War can destroy governments, lands, buildings, and lives. Many people are willing to make sacrifices. They are fighting to protect something very important to them. Remembering these brave people is one way we honor them and show gratitude for what they did.

We can remember veterans in many ways. In the United States, we build museums and memorials, dedicate cemeteries, and observe federal holidays.

Alabama has several military museums. One museum is the U.S. Veterans Memorial Museum in Huntsville. It is known for its collection of more than 30 rare, fully restored military vehicles from World War I through the Vietnam War. Another museum is the Alabama Veterans Museum and Archives in Athens. Visitors can see artifacts from the Revolutionary War up to today. The world’s largest museum display of helicopters is at the United States Army Aviation Museum in Fort Rucker. At the U.S.S. Alabama Battleship Memorial Park in Mobile, people can tour a real battleship. They can also explore the oldest submarine on public display.

Other states have museums too. In fact, there are hundreds of military and war museums in the United States and around the world. There are also hundreds of veterans cemeteries, monuments, and memorial sites honoring members of the military.

The U.S. remembers all those who have served in the military on Veterans Day. Originally called Armistice Day, the first Veterans Day was on Nov. 11, 1919. It was the first anniversary of the end of World War I. In 1938, Congress made that day a national holiday. Later, the name of the holiday was changed to Veterans Day.

The U.S. also celebrates Memorial Day. It is a day that honors people who have died while serving in the U.S. military. It started soon after the Civil War and became a federal holiday in 1971. This special day used to be on May 30, but now it is observed on the last Monday of May.

Honoring veterans is important. When we honor these brave people, we show them how grateful we are. We also remember how important it is to live in a land that has many freedoms.

title: Florida the Beautiful and Bountiful
text:
Why do people live and work in Florida? Florida is filled with an abundance of natural and man-made resources. For this reason, many businesses have chosen Florida as their base of operations. The fertile soil, large forests, and rich deposits of minerals make Florida a leading producer of agricultural products, lumber, and mineral resources.

Florida has other successful industries. These include tourism, life sciences, aerospace and defense, manufacturing, shipping, and information technology. Tourism is one of the top industries in the state. Each year, millions of people visit Florida to enjoy thousands of tourist attractions. Many companies in Florida produce technology that is used by people around the world. These products include computers, software, and other electronic devices that help people communicate and do business with one another.

These industries contribute billions of dollars to the state’s economy each year. All of these economic activities have made Florida's economy the fourth-largest economy in the United States and the 15th-largest economy in the world.

title: Mining
text:
Mining has been an important part of Florida’s economy for many years. Mining is the process of locating and extracting natural metals or minerals from under the Earth’s surface. Florida mines are among the top producers of attapulgite, peat, limestone, and phosphate. Attapulgite is a type of clay used as a thickening agent in many products, such as paint and clay. Peat is a soil-like mineral formed from decomposing plants. It is found in many places in Florida because of the climate and natural environment. Peat mined in Florida is often used as an alternative to firewood.

Limestone is primarily found in the peninsula of Florida. Limestone has been mined in Florida since the 1600s. Today, limestone is used in building materials, including cement, chalk, crushed stone, and building stones. Phosphate is another important mineral mined in Florida. Phosphate is a natural mineral used in fertilizers, animal feed, industrial products, and food preservatives. Currently, there are 27 active phosphate mines in the state.

Florida is also the only state where staurolite is mined. Staurolite is a type of mineral that looks like a crystal and is often found in other rocks. Unlike other minerals mined in Florida, staurolite has very few uses. Geologists use it to study the age of surrounding rocks. Because it resembles a crystal, staurolite is also collected and sold as a souvenir or used to make jewelry. Florida’s mining industry generates over $2 billion and employs more than 22,000 people.

title: Aerospace and Defense
text:
The aerospace industry is the business of designing, building, and selling items that have to do with flying, including spacecraft, missiles, aircraft, and other equipment. This industry is a leading contributor to Florida’s economy. Many of the largest aerospace manufacturers in the country have operation centers in Florida. These include Lockheed Martin, Boeing, SpaceX, and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). These companies provide jobs for more than 150,000 Floridians.

Florida has always been an integral part of space exploration. In October 1958, the United States formed NASA to research and create ways to explore space. U.S. President John F. Kennedy also pledged that the United States would land a man on the moon and return him safely home. To achieve this goal, the federal government built a research and launch facility at Cape Canaveral, Florida. Since 1950, over 3,000 missiles and rockets have been launched at Kennedy Space Center to further space exploration and research.

Florida is also important to the United States military. There are 21 military bases across the state. These bases and offices provide jobs to over 61,000 active service members and 24,000 civilians. Florida is home to the nation’s first naval air station, located in Pensacola. The military uses the deepwater harbors in Florida for naval bases. The strong military presence and Florida’s favorable weather conditions also allow the government to build and test many military weapons, such as missiles and bombers.

title: Life Sciences
text:
Life science is a growing sector of Florida’s economy. This field includes finding new ways to prevent and treat diseases, as well as designing and manufacturing medical equipment and devices. Life science companies continue to experiment, learn, and grow while helping people in many ways.

The state’s life science sector is a leader in medical research and development. Research and development is the process companies use to gain new knowledge to make or improve goods and services. The purpose of research and development is to expand human understanding in a way that benefits people and the economy. More than 1,500 life science companies employ over 29,000 people throughout the state. Florida’s life science industry is the second-largest producer of medical equipment and pharmaceuticals in the United States. It is also home to the fifth-largest medical research and development industry in the country.

Many major medical companies have facilities in Florida, including Mayo Clinic, Johnson & Johnson, and Bausch + Lomb. Scientists and doctors at Mayo Clinic in Jacksonville are researching and developing new ways to treat cancer, brain conditions, and other diseases. Many Florida universities have advanced research and development facilities. Scientists at the University of Central Florida’s Burnett School of Biomedical Sciences are currently conducting research to cure and prevent different types of heart disease. Research and products developed in Florida’s life science sector help millions of people each year.

title: Manufacturing
text:
Manufacturing is the business of using raw materials to make products or goods to sell. There are many types of manufacturing companies. Some examples of manufactured products are cars, computers, toys, and tools. Some manufacturing products are made from natural resources. Others are made from man-made resources. People often work in factories to manufacture goods. They work together to make products for consumers to purchase. Workers depend on each other, and they need to do their jobs well so the product is made correctly.

Florida is home to more than 20,000 manufacturing companies, employing more than 371,000 workers. It ranks among the nation’s top 10 states for manufacturing. Florida’s factories are among the leading producers of aerospace and aviation equipment, hospitality products, ships, tools, and chemicals. Florida’s manufacturing industry contributes about $58 billion to the state’s economy each year.

title: Information Technology
text:
Another important section of Florida’s economy is information technology. Information technology is the study and development of computer systems to store, retrieve, and send information. Florida has the third-largest information technology sector in the United States, with more than 33,000 companies. These companies provide over 300,000 jobs to Floridians.

One of the oldest information technology companies in Florida is the International Business Machines Corporation (IBM). IBM opened a manufacturing facility in Boca Raton in 1967. In 1981, researchers and engineers developed the company’s first personal computer in the Boca Raton facility. IBM’s success encouraged other information technology companies to expand their facilities to Florida. Leading information technology companies, including Microsoft, Citrix, Motorola, and Electronic Arts, each have large facilities in Florida. Researchers and engineers work in these facilities to improve the way people communicate.

title: Agriculture
text:
Agriculture is the business of growing crops and raising livestock. Agriculture impacts the goods and services in the state, the country, and the world. Growing and harvesting plants and products is a part of agriculture. Examples of products that are grown are fruits, vegetables, plants, flowers, grains, and cotton.

Raising animals or livestock is also another part of agriculture. Examples of these types of agricultural activities include ranching, dairy farming, and beekeeping. Agriculture is affected by the environment and the location. The crops and animals used for agriculture depend on temperature, rainfall, and soil. For example, climates that have ample amounts of sunshine and rain are ideal for growing wheat and corn.

Agriculture is one of the largest industries in Florida. Growing and selling crops contributes over $3 billion to the state’s economy. Thousands of Floridians work in the agriculture industry across the state. Family-owned and operated farms and large food manufacturers produce a variety of agricultural products that are shipped all over the world. About 80 percent of all citrus fruits, including oranges, grapefruit, lemons, and limes, grown in the United States are grown in Florida. Other important crops grown in Florida include watermelons, tomatoes, soybeans, corn, peanuts, hay, tobacco, cotton, and sugarcane.

Many Florida farmers have continued the tradition of raising cattle. The state is home to over a million head of cattle. Florida is also the home of the largest single herd of cattle in the United States. The cattle industry of Florida contributes about $900 million to the state’s economy each year. Florida farmers also raise chickens, hogs, and goats. Florida is unique because it also raises and catches ornamental fish, alligators, and different types of shellfish. Florida’s aquaculture products contribute over $16 million to the state’s economy each year.

title: Tourism
text:
Tourism is the business of encouraging people to travel for fun. Tourism is an economic activity. Florida's natural resources and wonders provide more than just products for consumers to use. They help create opportunities for tourism. Nature lovers travel throughout the state to visit Florida’s natural wonders. The warm beaches are among the top destinations for tourists in Florida. The state’s extensive waterways and beaches provide tourists with many opportunities for fishing, boating, kayaking, and water sports. Thousands of people also visit the Everglades each year to experience “wild” Florida.

People also come to Florida to visit the state's many museums and lighthouses and to attend sporting events. Florida’s amusement parks attract more tourists to the state than any other attraction. It is home to five of the top 10 most-visited amusement parks in the world. Walt Disney World Resort®, Universal Studios, and SeaWorld are among the top-visited parks in the state. In 2021, over 120 million tourists visited Florida. Tourism contributes about $100 billion to the state’s economy each year and employs over 1.5 million Floridians.

title: Shipping
text:
Florida’s manufacturing industry relies heavily on the shipping industry. Shipping has always been an integral part of Florida’s economy because of its proximity to the ocean, inland waterways, and thousands of miles of rail lines and state highways. Ground shipping and transportation also have a large impact on the state’s economy. Over 2,700 miles of railroad lines cross the state. The railroad is used to transport goods to ports and distribution centers throughout Florida. Trucking companies use 267,793 miles of Florida roadways to move goods in and out of the state for consumers to enjoy.

Maritime shipping also plays an important role in Florida’s economy. Florida is home to 15 deepwater seaports. Port Tampa Bay is the largest of Florida’s seaports. This port specializes in importing and exporting cargo. About 33 million tons of cargo move through Port Tampa Bay each year. Other major cargo ports in the state are located in Jacksonville, Miami, Palm Beach, Pensacola, and St. Petersburg. Florida’s maritime shipping industry contributes over $14 billion to the state’s economy each year and employs more than 65,000 Floridians.
