title: Climate Change
text:
Climate change is one of the consequences of humans depending on and modifying the environment. To understand these consequences, we need to understand what climate is. Climate is the average weather conditions over an extended period of time. So, climate change is a long-term change in average weather conditions that is caused by human activities.

The most common cause of climate change is burning fossil fuels. We burn fossil fuels to heat homes and help businesses run. Fossil fuels release carbon dioxide and methane into the air. These are types of greenhouse gases. Greenhouse gases get trapped in our atmosphere and make our Earth hotter.

Even small changes in climate can affect our environment. Earth’s average temperature has risen 1 degree Celsius in the past 50 years. The ocean’s temperature has also warmed .33 degrees Celsius since 1969. These may seem like small changes, but they affect plants and animals. When temperatures change, some plants might stop growing. Animals might lose their food source. Growing seasons may get longer. As weather changes, some places might flood while others become dry.

title: Jefferson Becomes President
text:
The election of Thomas Jefferson in 1800 was the first peaceful transfer of power for the United States. There were many disagreements over the presidency between the two major political parties, the Federalists and the Democratic Republicans, or Anti-Federalists. After many weeks, both sides came to a compromise and Jefferson was elected president. Jefferson was a firm believer in the tenets of the Constitution. He wished to strengthen these principles through his presidency. His first goal as president was to create peaceful cooperation between the Federalists and the Democratic Republicans. This was not an easy task. In many ways, it wasn't successful because both groups had opposing beliefs and ideas.

Jefferson also had to attend to U.S. foreign policy issues. Foreign policy is how one country interacts with other countries. During his second term, Washington signed a Proclamation of Neutrality that prevented the United States from entering foreign conflicts. Jefferson agreed that the United States should remain neutral and not enter foreign wars. France and Great Britain were at war with one another. The United States refused to enter the conflict.

Jefferson and his cabinet hoped to maintain a friendship with both countries. This angered Great Britain. The British Navy blockaded European ports. This affected American trade immensely. The British also seized American goods and forced American sailors to work on British vessels. In response, Jefferson asked Congress to expand the U.S. Navy and restrict the import of goods from Great Britain.

Jefferson served a second term as president from 1804 to 1808. Hostilities between France and Great Britain continued, as did their issues with U.S. neutrality. Both countries attacked American ships and seized their cargo. Jefferson encouraged Congress to act. In 1807, the government passed the Embargo Act. An embargo is an order to stop ships from delivering goods. The law stated that goods couldn't be shipped to any foreign port.

The United States hoped that both France and Great Britain would be devastated without American supplies. Unfortunately, the Embargo Act backfired. Great Britain and France survived without U.S. goods. The U.S. economy, on the other hand, suffered greatly due to the act, angering American citizens. President Jefferson repealed the Embargo Act before leaving office in March of 1809.

title: People Who Represent the United States
text: People who represent the United States are men, women, and children who love our country. They are responsible citizens. They work to build a better country. Some of these people were the first leaders of the United States. Others believed in freedom, equality, and justice for all. They all believed in American principles.

title: How Have Immigrants Influenced Our Culture?
text: The culture of a place is influenced by the people who live there. Many people coming from many different areas will bring great diversity to a culture. When people move, they bring many things with them. They bring their possessions, like furniture and clothing. They also bring their recipes for food. They bring their decorations, traditions, and celebrations. When people move to an area, everyone gives and receives ideas, music, language, and art from each other.

title: Essential Question
text: How have immigrants influenced our lives?

title: Food
text:
There are many types of bread in the United States. Pita, challah, and naan are all types of bread. They were brought to the United States by immigrants. These breads have become part of the culture here.

Pizza, salsa, and sausages can all be found in the United States. These are all foods that came from immigrants. They brought their recipes to share in their new home.

We also use seasonings and flavorings from many parts of the world. Immigrants brought these to the United States as well.

title: Celebrations
text: Every culture in the world celebrates special events. Immigrants have brought some of these celebrations to the United States. Special birthdays are celebrated in different ways. It could be a bar mitzvah or quinceañera. Some cultures celebrate a lunar new year. Others celebrate Diwali, and Día de los Muertos. These celebrations are now part of life in the United States. Sometimes people copy some events from another culture’s celebrations to enrich their own festivals.

title: Music
text: People enjoy different types of music in the United States. Instruments from different cultures blend in harmony. Jazz music combines African and Caribbean music with European instruments. Bluegrass is borrowed from English and Celtic styles. Salsa combines Spanish and African styles. Music in the United States has grown from cultures of many nations.

title: Contributing to the Community
text: There are many ways to contribute to our communities. Our towns, states, and nation can do better with our help. We can contribute by working to make a difference. We can participate actively in government or protect the environment. We can also volunteer in organizations that work for the common good. Let’s look at some examples of diverse individuals and groups who have contributed to civic life.

title: Essential Question
text: Who are examples of responsible citizens?

title: The WASP
text: During World War II, many American men left their homes and went to war. This left many jobs open that needed to be filled. The United States military decided to train women to fill these jobs. They wanted women to fly military planes. These women were known as the Women Air Service Pilots, or WASPs. They flew new military aircraft to places where they were needed. They also delivered supplies to many places. It was a dangerous job, but the WASPs were willing to help their community and country.

title: Martin Luther King Jr.
text:
Martin Luther King Jr. worked hard to help others. He became famous for speaking out against racism and discrimination.

King organized peaceful rallies and marches. He gave speeches about peace and fairness. He also met with leaders like President Lyndon B. Johnson to come up with ideas to end discrimination. King was at the March on Washington, D.C., on Aug. 28, 1963. He gave a moving speech about equality and peace. That speech is now remembered as the “I Have a Dream'' speech. Later, in 1964, President Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act. This made it illegal to discriminate against people because of their skin color.

King was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964 for his non-violent efforts for civil rights. It is a very important international honor. There is also a monument in Washington, D.C., in King’s honor.

title: Mary Jane McLeod Bethune
text:
Mary Jane McLeod Bethune was an educator. She was also an advocate for equal rights. She was born in 1875. Her parents were formerly enslaved people. Bethune wanted to become a church missionary. However, she was not allowed to because she was African American. She became a teacher instead.

Bethune wanted to make sure that all African American children could get an education. She started her own school in 1904. It was a school for African American girls. This school later joined another one and became Bethune-Cookman College. Thousands of African American students attended Bethune-Cookman College.

In 1920, Bethune led campaigns to help African American women register to vote. She worked with local, state, and national leaders to end discrimination in education. President Franklin D. Roosevelt named Bethune the Director of [African American] Affairs of the National Youth Administration. This made her the highest-ranking African American woman in government at the time. Bethune made a difference in the United States.

title: Rachel Carson
text:
Rachel Carson was a scientist. Her work helped the environment and saved many lives. She was born in Pennsylvania in 1907. Carson was a marine biologist. This means that she studied living things in the ocean. She was a writer as well.

Carson wrote many books. One of the things she wrote about was how pesticides harm people and the environment. Pesticides are chemicals that kill insects which attack crops. This book became so famous that Carson was invited to speak in Congress. Many people asked the government to do something. In the end, the government asked people to stop using dangerous chemicals in pesticides. The whole world benefited from Rachel Carson’s books.

title: Fred Korematsu
text:
In 1941, the nation of Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. After the attack, Japanese Americans suffered from discrimination by the U.S. government. Anyone of Japanese descent was moved to an internment camp, even if they were not part of the Pearl Harbor attack.

Fred Korematsu was one of the Japanese Americans who faced this discrimination. He refused to go to the camps at first. While still in an internment camp, Korematsu's lawyers took his case to the Supreme Court in 1944. The Supreme Court decided that imprisoning Japanese Americans was legal. After World War II ended, Japanese Americans were released from the internment camps. Korematsu continued to speak out against discrimination. In 1988, the U.S. government apologized for putting Japanese Americans into internment camps. As part of the apology, the government paid a lot of money to the survivors of those internment camps.

Korematsu continued to speak out against discrimination for the rest of his life. In 1998, he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom for fighting against discrimination and injustice. California passed the Fred Korematsu Day bill in 2010. This bill designated Jan. 30 as a day to remember Korematsu’s sacrifice and dedication to equal rights.

title: Archie Carr Jr.
text:
Archie Carr was a scientist who taught many people about protecting the environment. Carr was born in Mobile, Alabama. The Carr family loved nature. Their love of nature encouraged Carr to study and research as much as he could about the environment and wildlife.

Carr studied zoology at the University of Florida. Zoology is the science of studying animals. Through his studies, Carr became very interested in sea turtles. He worked for many years to protect sea turtles in Florida. He wrote many books and articles to share his knowledge with others. He helped others understand how people’s actions impact the lives of animals. Archie Carr used his knowledge to make a difference in his community and the world.

title: Junior League Organizations of Florida
text:
Junior Leagues started in New York in 1901. Mary Harriman was 19 years old when she started the first one. Her idea was to train women to volunteer in their communities. There were many immigrants coming to America in those days. Harriman and her friends wanted to help those immigrants to live comfortably in the United States. Many states started their own Junior Leagues as well.

Many cities in Florida have their own Junior Leagues. They train young women to serve their communities. They raise funds to help them train the young volunteers and make their communities better. Junior league organizations also help women develop leadership skills.

title: Essential Question
text: Who are people that represent the United States?

title: Rosa Parks
text: In the 1950s and 1960s, African Americans were still fighting for equality. African Americans had to follow strict rules. These rules told them where they could eat, go to school, and even sit. African Americans could only sit in certain parts of buses. They had to give up their seats to any white person who asked. In 1955, Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a bus. She believed it wasn't fair for her to stand so that a white person could sit. Because of this, Rosa Parks was arrested. She was willing to give up her freedom. This was to gain equal rights for all African Americans. Others followed her example. They organized a boycott against the buses. This meant that African Americans refused to ride the buses until the rules were changed. The boycott lasted 381 days. Then the Supreme Court changed the law. They ruled that the segregation of buses was unfair. Rosa Parks' act of bravery inspired people. It helped get unfair laws changed. Later Rosa wrote a book about her life to tell people her story.

title: Thomas Jefferson
text: Thomas Jefferson was the third president of the United States. He was also one of our country's founders. He was born in Virginia in 1743. He was a talented and intelligent man. He studied many things. These were things like art, music, history, and law. He loved education and learning. Many ideals of American government were influenced by Jefferson. Jefferson was also a very skilled writer. He was the main author of the Declaration of Independence. He believed that all people are born with certain rights. He believed that these rights should never be taken away. He believed in “life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.” These ideas influenced the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution.

title: George Washington
text: George Washington is often called the Father of Our Country. He was an active member of his community and nation. He was a leader in the army. He inspired other soldiers. People trusted him and believed in him as a leader. He believed that governments should listen to their citizens. In 1787, he was elected chairman of the Constitutional Convention. He worked with the other members of the Convention. Together, they created a document that reflected their ideas for a new government. This document was the Constitution of the United States. In 1789, George Washington became the first president of the United States. Washington tried to get the country's finances in order. Washington worked to create strong alliances with foreign nations. Washington served two terms as president. He refused to run for a third term. This was because he believed that one man should not hold that much power for too long. He set the standards for those who followed in his footsteps. Today, you can find Washington's portrait on the dollar bill and the quarter. He is a symbol of our country.

title: Abigail Adams
text:
Abigail Adams was the wife of America's second president, John Adams. Abigail Adams was a good citizen. She stayed informed about political issues of her time. She spoke out for what she believed. Her husband, the president, was working on forming a new government. She gave him this advice:

“… Remember the ladies, and be more generous … to them than your ancestors.”

All her life, she worked for women's rights. She wanted women to be able to own property. She wanted women to be allowed to go to school. Unlike most women of her time, Abigail lived a life of public service. She helped to shape the United States.

title: Harriet Tubman
text:
Harriet Tubman was born on March 6, 1822, in Maryland. She was born while her parents were still enslaved. Since her parents were enslaved, she was considered the property of their enslaver.

On September 17, 1849, Tubman escaped from bondage. However, she did not forget other people who were still enslaved. She returned many times to free other enslaved people. This was very dangerous. She used a network of people known as the Underground Railroad. Tubman fought hard to help end slavery. She also fought for women’s right to vote.

title: Navajo Code Talkers
text:
During World War II, secret American codes were being broken. Codes were used to send messages during battles. When the codes were broken, battles were lost.

A man named Philip Johnston had an idea to fix this. He thought the Navajo language could be used to create new military codes. The Navajo language is very complex. Very few non-Navajo people knew how to speak it at the time. The U.S. military liked this idea. Navajo soldiers were trained as Code Talkers. They created a code using their language. The code was unbreakable. This code guided and protected American troops. The Navajo Code Talkers contributed much to this country and helped win the war.

title: César Chávez
text: César Chávez was the son of Mexican immigrants. He and his family were migrant workers. These are people who move from place to place to work. Chávez saw that migrant workers were not treated well. He believed that migrant workers should have the same rights as others. When Chávez grew up, he helped migrant workers get better pay and homes. He founded the United Farm Workers of America. This was a union of workers who made sure they got fair pay and good working conditions. The union still exists today. It still works to make sure that farm workers are treated fairly. César Chávez worked for equality for thousands of migrant workers throughout the United States.

title: The Florida Constitution
text: Florida has a Constitution. The Florida Constitution tells how to organize the state's government. It protects the rights of citizens of Florida. This document represents Florida. Florida’s current constitution was written in 1968. This constitution has an introduction, called a preamble. The preamble helps citizens know why it was written. The rest of the constitution is divided into 12 sections, called articles. The first article contains a Declaration of Rights. This part of the constitution tells us about all of the rights of every Florida citizen. The other articles explain how the Florida government should work.

title: Essential Question
text: What symbols, documents, and events represent Florida?

title: The State Capitol Building
text: The capitol building is a symbol of our state. The first Florida capitol buildings were three log cabins. In 1826, a stone building was built. In 1845 a brick capitol building was built. The new state government moved into this building. In 1891, this building needed to be repaired. In 1902, a dome was added to the building. In 1977, other buildings were added to the capitol complex. The original capitol building was restored and is still there today. This building is a symbol of our great state.

title: The Everglades National Park
text: Everglades National Park is another symbol of Florida. It is one of our top places visited by tourists. Some people call it the “River of Grass.” This is because of the slow-moving water that flows through marshy grassland. In some places, the grass is very high and thick. This can make it hard to see that a river flows through it. Everglades National Park is full of all kinds of plants and animals. It’s a beautiful place that is worth visiting.

title: The State Seal of Florida
text: Most states have a seal. A seal has phrases and pictures. They describe the state. Florida’s seal was first created in 1868. It was changed in 1985 to fix mistakes. Our seal has a picture of a sunset over a boat. It also has a Seminole woman and a tall sabal palm tree on it. Why do you think each part was included?

title: The Florida Panther
text: In 1982, Florida students chose our state animal. They picked the Florida panther. The Florida panther is important. It helps keep the plants and animals balanced. The Florida panther used to live in a few states. Now it only lives in Florida. It is an endangered species. This means that it needs to be protected. It has been protected from being hunted since 1958.

title: The Orange Blossom
text: Our state flower is the orange blossom. It became our state flower in 1909. It is a fragrant flower. This means it has a nice, strong scent. Millions of orange blossoms bloom in Florida every year. When people smell orange blossoms, they often think of Florida.

title: The Sabal Palm
text: State animals, plants, songs, and places all have something in common. They all say something special about the state. It is the same with the state tree. In 1953, the sabal palm became our state tree. It was picked because it is part of Florida’s history. Native Americans used the tree. Settlers used the tree, too. It has been used for food, medicine, and landscaping. It can grow in almost any soil and grows all over Florida.

title: The State Anthem
text:
Our state anthem is "Florida, Where the Sawgrass Meets the Sky." It became our state anthem in 2008. It was written by a music teacher from Pompano Beach named Jan Hinton. The anthem describes things that are common in Florida. One of those is a plant called sawgrass. It is found in Florida's everglades and marshes. Sawgrass can grow to be over nine feet tall.

"Florida, where the sawgrass meets the sky,
Florida, where our hearts will ever lie,
Sitting proud in the ocean like a sentinel true,
Always shielding your own, yet giving welcome.Florida, land of flowers, land of light.
Florida, where our dreams can all take flight.
Whether youth's vibrant morning or the twilight of years,
There are treasures for all who venture here in Florida.

Mockingbirds cry and 'gators lie out in the sun,
Bridges span southward to the Keys and rockets skyward run,
The orange blossoms' sweet perfume and fireworks fill the air,
And cultures rich our native people share.

Florida, where the sawgrass meets the sky,
Florida, where our hearts will ever lie,
Sitting proud in the ocean like a sentinel true,
Always shielding your own, yet giving welcome.

Florida, land of flowers, land of light.
Florida, where our dreams can all take flight.
Whether youth's vibrant morning or the twilight of years,
There are treasures for all who venture here in Florida, Florida."

title: How Did Florida Become a State?
text: The first people in Florida were Native Americans. These included the Apalachee, Calusa, Mayaimi, and Tocobaga. Spanish, French, and British explorers and settlers then came to the area. Later, In 1821, Florida became a territory of the United States. The population of Florida kept growing, and it became the 27th state of the United States. This happened on March 3, 1845. This was the beginning of Florida state as we know it now.

title: Essential Question
text: What are symbols that represent Florida?

title: The Florida Constitution
text:
Just like the U.S. Constitution, state constitutions guarantee and protect citizens' basic rights. State constitutions list the rules for state government. They also explain how a state can make laws. State constitutions describe how the state government divides and shares power with counties and cities. Florida has a state constitution. It has a similar structure to the United States Constitution. It has changed over time to reflect the unique needs of the people of Florida. The first state constitution was written in 1838, before Florida became a state.

Florida’s current constitution was written in 1968. This document represents Florida. This constitution is set up with an introduction, called a preamble. The preamble helps citizens know why the constitution was written. The rest of the constitution is divided into 12 sections, called articles. The first article contains a Declaration of Rights. This part of the constitution tells us about all of the rights of every Florida citizen. The other articles explain how the Florida government should work.

title: Immigration
text:
People moving from place to place in the world is called migration. The motivations for people migrating are called “push-pull factors.” A push factor could be considered forceful, or negative. Usually, a push factor is when a person’s way of life is in danger. The danger could be because of war, persecution, famine, or any other factor that endangers the welfare of a person or a family.

A pull factor could be considered an attraction or draw to a place. Usually, a pull factor is when a person wants something more in their life. Leaving a location would then be considered a positive. A pull factor could be the availability of land, new jobs, better climate, fewer natural disasters, and other things.

Push-pull factors work together. We consider them when we study movement. Historians look at push-pull factors to analyze the past.

From 1800 to 1850, many things were happening around the world. Countries in Europe were experiencing continual wars. People living in the path of armies had push factors to emigrate to America. The pull factor was not living in a war zone.

In Great Britain, people were being pushed off their rented land. Often, landlords found they could make more money by using the land for animals. In some cases, the landlord paid for the tenants to emigrate. Some tenants emigrated to Australia. Some emigrated to America.

In Ireland, there was a famine when the potato crops failed. Millions of Irish people were pushed by starvation to emigrate to all parts of the world. The pull factor in America was more resources than they had in Ireland.

The American slave trade was illegal after 1808. In Africa, many people were still captured and forced (push factor) into enslavement and brought to America illegally and against their will.

All those people coming to America gave Henry Clay’s American System the labor it needed. America’s canals, railroads, and roads west were built by the work of many newcomers.

title: The Great Seal of Florida
text: Most states have a symbol, or seal, that has phrases and pictures that describe the state. Florida has one, too! Florida’s first seal was first created in 1868. It was changed in 1985. Our seal has a picture of a sunset over a boat. It also has a woman and a tall sabal palm tree on it. The revised seal corrected errors that were on the old one. The woman on the seal is now a Seminole Native American rather than a Western Plains Native American. The steamboat is more accurate. Look at each part of our seal. Why do you think each part was included?

title: The State Shell
text: In 1969, the Florida legislature named the horse conch as our state shell. The horse conch is a sea snail that can grow up to two feet long. It is native to the marine waters around Florida. People find horse conch shells all along our Florida coastlines. Horse conchs are quite heavy for their size. Adult horse conchs can be orange, cream, or brown.

title: The Florida Panther
text:
In 1982, Florida students chose our state animal. They picked the Florida panther. The Florida panther is an important animal. It helps keep the plants and animals balanced. The Florida panther used to live in a few states. Now it only lives in Florida. It is an endangered species. This means that it needs to be protected. It has been protected from being hunted since 1958.

The Florida panther is cream-colored on its back and gray on its belly. The tip of its tail, back of its ears, and sides of its nose are dark brown or black.

title: The Mockingbird
text: Did you know Florida has the same state bird as four other states? Our popular state bird is the mockingbird. It has amazing vocal abilities. It can make the sounds of other birds. It can even sound like a machine. It also fiercely defends its family nest. It also helps people by eating bugs and seeds that grow into weeds. It became our state bird in 1927.

title: The Moonstone
text: The moonstone is our state gem. But moonstone doesn’t come from the moon. It doesn’t come from Florida either. So why is moonstone our state gem? In 1969, American astronauts landed on the moon. They left Earth from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Florida lawmakers chose moonstone to mark this special event.

title: Choose a Problem
text:
Read each problem. Choose the problem you want to solve.

Jackson loves to ride his bike, but the rainy spring days have ruined his helmet and always leave his body wet and cold.

Natalia’s tree house falls over whenever it is windy.

Claire’s dog often comes into her bedroom and steals her stuffed animals.

title: Ideate: Research
text:
Engineers, Plants, and Animals

Engineers study plants and animals. They use what they learn to solve problems. Engineers can mimic plant and animal structures in their designs. Think about the problem you want to solve. What plant or animal structures can you mimic?

title: Animal Structures for Survival
text: All animals have parts, called structures. Their structures help them grow and survive.

title: Plant Structures for Survival
text: Plants also have structures that help them grow and survive. Most plants have the same structures. Most plants have roots, stems, and leaves. Some plants have flowers or fruit with seeds.

title: Animals Receive Information
text: Animals receive information the same way you do, through their five senses! Their structures help them see, hear, feel, smell, and taste. Some animals have a few other senses too. Octopuses can sense light and color. Snakes can sense temperature.

title: Animals Respond to Information
text: After animals use their senses, they respond to the information. When animals sense danger, they respond in different ways. They keep themselves safe and alive.

title: Waves of Immigrants Come to Florida
text:
Many factors have had an impact on the geography, government, and culture of Florida throughout its history. Many immigrants came to Florida during the Age of Exploration. They created settlements and communities that came together to form a colony. The colony of Florida was fought over by the major powers of Europe for hundreds of years. As power changed hands, new immigrants settled in the established communities of the colony and formed new towns and cities.

Florida’s annexation by the United States and eventual statehood encouraged more people to move to the state. During the 1800s, many immigrants wanted to become Americans. They came from all around the world. Some factors that pushed people from their homes were starvation, unemployment, and fear. In Europe and Asia, there was disease, war, and a lack of freedom in many countries. Millions crossed the oceans and settled in cities throughout Florida. They risked their lives and everything they owned to create a better life in Florida.

Immigrating to a new country was not an easy task. Immigrants often faced many challenges in their new homes. They had to find a way to support themselves and their families. They had to find shelter. Often, they had to learn a new language and customs. Immigrants also had to adapt to a new climate and environment. Many immigrants faced discrimination from other groups in Florida. They were often forced to shop in separate businesses, eat in separate restaurants, and attend separate schools.

As more and more immigrants settled in Florida, the culture of the state changed. When people immigrate to a new country, they bring their traditions, language, and cultural customs with them. Large groups of immigrants created their own communities within larger cities. They formed their own social organizations and opened businesses. They also taught people from other cultures about their traditions and customs. Because of these factors, Florida has one of the most diverse populations in the United States. Take a look in your own community today, and you might be surprised by just how much history and culture is right in your own backyard!

title: Cuban Immigrants Flock to Florida
text:
Many factors led to large-scale Cuban immigration to Florida from the 1950s to the present. By 1950, Florida already had a large Cuban population. Historians estimate that between 50,000 and 100,000 Cubans immigrated to Florida each year during the first decades of the 1900s. They left Cuba because of economic and political unrest. Many came to Florida to work in the cigar industry. They created new communities and towns, primarily in southern Florida.

Another large wave of Cuban immigrants came to Florida as a result of the Cuban Revolution. In 1959, revolutionaries led by Fidel Castro took control of the Cuban government. Many people did not agree with the ideas and beliefs of Castro and his government. As a result, thousands of Cubans decided to leave their homeland.

The majority of Cubans who left Cuba immigrated to the United States. In 1961, Congress passed the Cuban Refugee Assistance Program to provide healthcare, educational services, and employment assistance to Cuban refugees coming to the United States. This act encouraged even more Cubans to immigrate to the United States. Many of the Cuban refugees who came to the United States during this time settled in Florida. By 1970, the Cuban-born population of Florida totaled 206,347.

Cuban refugees continued to immigrate to Florida after the Cuban Revolution and continue to do so today to escape political and economic instability in Cuba. By 2017, the Cuban-born population of Florida totaled 997,342. Today, Florida has the largest population of Cuban immigrants and people of Cuban descent in the United States.

Cuban immigrants have had a profound impact on the culture of the state, particularly in South Florida. Miami has the largest Cuban population of any city in the United States. Cuban immigrants have influenced the culture of the city in many ways. There are hundreds of Cuban restaurants and Cuban-owned businesses in the city. A small section of the city is known as “Little Havana.” Thousands of tourists visit the area to take in the sights and sounds of the Cuban neighborhood. Spanish is widely spoken throughout the city.

Many Cuban immigrants and people of Cuban descent have played a huge role in the economy, government, and culture of Florida. Musician Gloria Estefan moved from Cuba to Miami when she was a young girl. She helped to bring Latin American music to mainstream America and spread awareness of the contributions of Cubans in the United States. Melquiades R. Martinez, a Cuban immigrant who settled in Miami in 1962, became the first Cuban American to serve in the U.S. Senate.

Another Cuban immigrant who settled in Miami, Myriam Marquez, serves as the executive editor of El Miami Herald, one of the most popular Spanish newspapers in the United States. Casimiro Hernandez Sr. immigrated to Florida from Cuba in 1905. He settled in Ybor City and opened a small cafe, which eventually blossomed into a large restaurant. Hernandez's restaurant, Columbia Restaurant, is now the oldest restaurant in Florida and provides diners with an authentic Cuban experience.

title: Plants Respond to Information
text: Plants also respond to information. They keep themselves safe and alive, too.

title: Latin American Immigrants
text:
Latin American immigrants have played a crucial role in the history, culture, and economy of Florida since the Age of Exploration. Small groups of Latin American immigrants came to Florida during the periods of Spanish rule. Latin American immigrants continued to settle in Florida following its annexation to the United States and throughout the 1900s. Today, the majority of Latin American immigrants who settle in Florida come from Haiti, Columbia, Mexico, Puerto Rico, and the Dominican Republic.

Many push-pull factors have encouraged Latin American immigrants to settle in Florida. Florida’s proximity to Latin America, its economic prosperity, and its large number of Spanish-speaking individuals and communities make it an ideal location for settlement.

Additionally, many push factors encourage immigration from Latin America to the United States. In 2017, Puerto Rico was struck by a massive hurricane. Hurricane Maria caused billions of dollars of damage. Millions of people lost their homes and all of their belongings. Some of these people chose to move to Florida. Most Puerto Ricans who moved to Florida following Hurricane Maria settled in south and central Florida.

During the 1980s, thousands of Haitian immigrants came to Florida to escape economic depression in Haiti. At the same time, many Haitian immigrants who had originally moved to the northeastern United States relocated to Florida because of its favorable climate and large Latin American communities, where they could share their cultural customs and traditions. Most Haitian immigrants settled in south Florida. Miami has the largest Haitian population in the state. Like the Cuban immigrants who came before them, Haitian immigrants formed their own community in the city of Miami, called “Little Haiti.”

Like other immigrant groups, Latin American immigrants often formed their communities within larger cities, such as Miami, Tampa, and Orlando, to preserve their traditions and protect themselves from discrimination. Latin American immigrants have played and continue to play a large role in the culture, economy, and government of Florida.

*Note: This table shows data for the five largest Latin American immigrant groups that live in Florida.

title: Reflect and Connect
text:
Describe the problem you chose.

Plants and animals I can mimic to solve the problem:

title: Asian and Pacific Island Immigrants
text:
Asian and Pacific Island immigrants have contributed to the state in many ways. Economic and political instability in many Asian countries encouraged immigrants to move to the United States during the late 1800s. Following the American Civil War, a small number of Chinese immigrants came to Florida to work on large farms and in construction. In the late 1800s, a number of Chinese immigrants settled in Jacksonville. The population of Chinese Americans grew steadily. The first Chinese grocery store and restaurant opened in Jacksonville in 1889. By 1917, Jacksonville newspapers reported 25 Chinese laundry shops in the city and published reports of Chinese New Year celebrations.

By 1900, some Chinese immigrants began to settle in Southeast Florida. Hundreds of Chinese and other Asian immigrants began to settle in the area during the land boom of the 1920s. They went to great efforts to maintain their culture and traditions. They opened Chinese-language schools to teach their children the language of their ancestors. They also started their own newspapers that were written and printed in Chinese.

Among the most famous Chinese immigrants to settle in Florida was Lue Gim Gong. He moved to Deland, Florida, in 1886. Upon his arrival, he began experimenting with citrus fruit and eventually developed a type of orange that was more resistant to the cold. Gong’s work revolutionized the citrus industry in Florida.

Other groups of Asian and Pacific Island immigrants began to settle in Florida during the early 1900s. Japanese entrepreneur Kamosu Jo Sakai settled in Jacksonville in 1903. He established the Yamato farming colony and encouraged other Japanese farmers to settle in the area. A small number of Filipino immigrants made their home in Florida by 1920. By 1980, Filipino immigrants and their descendants made up the largest group of Asian Americans living in Florida. Within 20 years, this changed. By 2000, Asian Indians made up the largest group of Asian Americans living in Florida. Thousands of Vietnamese refugees settled in Florida during the 1970s to escape the Vietnam War. They established their own communities in many of the state’s major cities.

In 2017, the total population of Asians and Pacific Islanders in Florida totaled 730,615. Today, there are thousands of Chinese, Japanese, Vietnamese, Korean, and Indian businesses, places of worship, cultural centers, and neighborhoods across Florida. Orlando is home to a large Chinese neighborhood called Chinatown, which is filled with Chinese restaurants, shops, and architecture. Asian Americans and Asian immigrants continue to play an integral role in the economy, culture, government, and history of Florida.

title: European Immigrants
text:
From the Age of Exploration in the early 1500s, Europeans began settling in Florida and bringing their culture and customs with them. In the 1800s, thousands of Europeans began to immigrate to the United States. Several European countries, such as Germany, France, Portugal, Russia, Spain, and others, were experiencing revolutions and wars. Others, such as Ireland, Scotland, Denmark, the Netherlands, and others, suffered from famine and crop failure. These push factors forced millions to leave their native countries to find better prospects in the United States.

By 1865, Florida was in the process of rebuilding after the American Civil War. Floridians had to think of a way to rebuild their economy. Some believed that increasing the population would be the best way to do this. A call went out for settlers and workers to move to Florida. Pamphlets, essays, and advertisements were published to entice immigrants to make their home in Florida. Professionals were even hired to travel to foreign countries to persuade people to immigrate to Florida. Many immigrants experienced prejudice and discrimination when they came to the United States. One Florida promotional magazine, The Semi-Tropical Florida, stated that people of all backgrounds were welcome and wanted in Florida and that "we have no prejudices to overcome."

Italian farmers were especially desired because they were believed to possess the skills necessary for working on citrus farms and in vineyards. They were also more accustomed to warmer climates. As the years progressed, Florida's efforts proved to be successful in drawing immigrants to the state. By 1910, about 22,315 Germans, English people, and Italians lived in Florida, as well as a number of Finns, Russians, and Greeks. These groups made up the largest numbers of European immigrants in the state.

The 20th century also brought about much change for the population of Florida. Refugees fleeing war zones and persecution in Europe during World War I and World War II brought many new people to Florida. After the wars, many of those immigrants wanted to stay and make America their permanent home. As the years progressed, immigration laws changed in the U.S. to help reunite families who had become separated. More Europeans continued to immigrate to America to join their families and find better opportunities.

Today, eight percent of all European immigrants in the U.S. have made their home in Florida. European culture and influence can be seen everywhere in Florida. Spanish influence can be seen in the architecture of St. Augustine and Pensacola, while Florida’s sponging industry exists thanks to Greek divers who immigrated to Florida over 100 years ago.

German culture can be experienced in South Florida each year at Oktoberfest in October and at a Christkindlmarkt in December. French influence can be found at art galleries, in fashion magazines, and in French restaurants. There are even more pieces of European culture to be found in Florida, and the number of Europeans moving to the Sunshine State continues to grow each year.

title: African Immigrants
text:
In the United States today, about three percent of African immigrants live in Florida. This may seem like a small percentage when, according to the state census, 16.9 percent of Florida’s population is African American. The reason Florida has a higher African American population than other states is because the first Africans to come to Florida did not come voluntarily. These first people were not immigrants. African men, women, and children were captured in Africa during the transatlantic slave trade and brought to the Americas against their will to be sold into slavery. These people never made it back to their homes in Africa. They lived, worked, and eventually died in the Americas. They married and had families. The descendants of these people account for the higher population of African Americans in Florida and other southern states today.

Today, slavery is abolished in the United States. Africans now immigrate voluntarily to America to pursue new opportunities. Florida has a diverse and rich mix of cultures, from the first Africans who preserved their culture while enslaved to those who immigrate to the U.S. today, bringing their cultures with them.

Pieces of African culture can be seen all over Florida today. The picturesque Victorian neighborhood of Lincolnville in St. Augustine is one example. Lincolnville was founded in 1866 by formerly enslaved Africans. Many of the houses there reflect the Victorian architecture of the time when they were built.

Art and history combine to tell a story in Perry Harvey Sr. Park in Tampa. Here, statues, tile art, and wall murals paint a vivid and informative scene of African history in Florida. Tampa is also home to the 10-day Tampa Black Heritage Festival every January. For 10 days, people celebrate African American art, food, music, and culture. Music, in particular, has deep roots in African culture. Enslaved African people sang songs they remembered from their homelands. Today, music continues to be an important part of African culture and heritage for descendants and immigrants alike. Each year, Tampa hosts the Tampa Bay Gospel Awards, where people gather to support and recognize Black musicians, singers, dancers, and more.

In Jacksonville’s LaVilla neighborhood, you can find any number of concerts and plays at the Ritz Theatre and Museum. LaVilla was sometimes called the “Harlem of the South.” In the museum, you can find the story of the African American national hymn, “Lift Ev’ry Voice and Sing,” written by James Weldon Johnson and John Rosamond Johnson. Orlando is home to the African American Museum of the Arts, where African American artwork and African artifacts can be viewed and even purchased. There are countless other places to see and experience African culture and history, both traditional and modern, in Florida today.

title: Natural Resources of Alabama in the 19th Century
text:
In the 19th century, nothing influenced Alabama more than agriculture. Rich, fertile soils and a complex river system run throughout the state. Due to those features, cotton, timber, iron, and rivers have helped make Alabama an agriculturally unique place to live.

Cotton

In 1804, Eli Whitney introduced an invention called the cotton gin. Cotton was one of the largest crops found in Alabama. The cotton gin sped up the process of removing seeds from raw cotton. This quicker process sped up production so more cotton could be processed.

In 1839, more than half of all United States cotton came just from Alabama. The Black Belt Region is known for its black-colored fertile soil and temperate climate. This is where most cotton in Alabama was grown.

Timber

Alabama is naturally dense with beautiful forests. When cotton production began to decrease after the Civil War, the state turned to timber as its leading industry. The plantation-based economy fell in the south after the Civil War. This led to much of the plantation land returning over time to lavish forests. These areas are sometimes referred to as “second forests." With the growth of railroads in the south after the Civil War, the timber industry grew rapidly, especially in Northern Alabama. More timber could now be exported around the country quicker than before.

Iron

During the Civil War, the Confederate States had an increased need for iron. Iron was needed for rifles, trains, and cannons. After the Civil War, railroads continued to expand. The shipping industry also began to grow in places like Mobile, Alabama. The largest iron deposits were found around Birmingham, Alabama. This mineral known as hematite is known as “Red Iron Ore.” It is also the state mineral of Alabama! Around Birmingham, newspapers even used the phrase “Birmingham Iron Age” due to the rapid growth in both the industry and population.

Rivers

Rivers are an important source of water for people and crops like cotton. They also played a vital role in the movement of goods and resources around the entire state of Alabama. Rivers like the Tallapoosa, Alabama, and Coosa Rivers helped to move cotton and timber to places like the Port of Mobile.

The geography of rivers even impacted the development of railroads, iron smelting plants, textile mills, and sawmills.

title: Human Environments: Housing
text:
Housing

The need for housing in 19th century Alabama was greatly influenced by the growing population of settlers to the region. Tribal nations like the Chocktaw, Cherokee, and Creek already inhabited the territory. Conflicts arose when settlers moved in and competed for land and resources. Housing boomed as the population increased. Settlers used materials that varied by region and built what are now known as folk buildings.

Folk Buildings

Folk buildings are the oldest types of structures still standing in Alabama. What makes these buildings unique are the materials, shapes, and sizes of the buildings. No two folk buildings are the same. They reflect the cultural traditions of the owners and builders. Each building tells a story. The unique characteristics help tell about individual owners and the time when these buildings were occupied and how they were used. The few remaining folk houses standing today may be recognized by a low roof, rock chimneys, and exposed timbers. Based on the map, where did most people build folk homes?

Materials

Materials used to build folk buildings varied by region. One common feature was the need for a heat source. In the 19th century, homes were still heated with a fireplace. Folk building fireplaces and chimneys were made with bricks, shaped rocks, or fieldstones. Mud was mixed with grass or sticks were used when quality rock was not available. As the timber industry grew, many folk homes were built in log style.

title: Human Interaction: Roads
text:
Roads

The earliest roads in Alabama were more like trails. They were used mainly for trading, communication, and the movement of the military. These roads followed rivers and mountains. Roads helped shape Alabama’s growth. In the 19th century, better roads became necessary. People wanted to travel quickly through the rapidly growing United States. This growth led to more settlers moving into the territory. It also led to the growth of cities like Mobile and Montgomery.

Old Federal Road (1805-1840)

After the Louisiana Purchase, a road needed to be built to connect the Port of Mobile with the state of Georgia. This road, later called the “Old Federal Road,” ran through tribal territories. The road sparked land conflicts, particularly between white settlers and the Creek. Because the road flooded regularly, it was difficult to travel. The road declined with more people turning to railroads for their transportation needs during the 19th century.

Plank Roads (1848-1857)

An estimated 150 miles of plank roads were built in Alabama in the middle of the 19th century. Plank roads were designed to help with muddy conditions and rough travel. These roads seemed ideal due to the vast timber available in Alabama. However, they were expensive to build. They also required a lot of maintenance. The first plank road in Alabama was called the Central Plank Road. It began at Montgomery, crossed the Tallapoosa River, and ran all the way to Talladega.

title: Human Environments: Place Names
text:
Place Names

Places get their names for a variety of reasons. Some are from interesting stories. Some come from historical events. Names can also come from geographic or environmental features or the area or region. The name Alabama came from a tribe of the Creek Confederacy originally called the Alabamas or Alibamons.

In North Alabama, the region calls itself the Alabama Mountain Lakes Association (AMLA). This is due to the many lakes and mountains that are part of the geographic area. The Black Belt Region of Alabama is named for its dark, rich soils. This region in the central part of the state is where the cotton industry grew. The coastal region has been referred to as the Wiregrass Region for the long-stemmed grass that is native to the area. It stretches along the coastal plain from southern Georgia and northern Florida into nine counties of southeastern Alabama.

The Muscle Shoals Region is also known as a National Heritage area. The region is located in the northwest corner of Alabama. Muscle Shoals is an important center of music production and musical history. The origin of its name is uncertain. Many believe the name came from local tribes who had difficulty navigating the strong current of the river.

Regardless of the region, Alabama’s place names are unique and represent the local culture and geography. What else do you know about your region?

title: Movement of Settlers in Alabama in the 19th Century
text:
Throughout the 19th century, settlers from the United States came to Alabama for a variety of reasons. Here is a timeline of Alabama’s population growth in the 19th century.

Louisiana Purchase from France doubles size of United States

1803

1805

1819

1820

Rural population: n/a

1830

President Andrew Jackson's Indian Removal Bill approved by Congress, forcing tribes to give up their remaining lands east of the Mississippi in exchange for western lands.

1833

Daniel Pratt established the Cotton Gin factory north of Montgomery. Prattville became a manufacturing center in the South by 1839.

1835
